# OF PLATO

*is called a **praise** <note>original: "encomium"</note>. Then the sixth, since it proves one to be base and evil, can be called **Vituperation** <note>original: "Vituperatio"</note>.*
*Rightly speaking he divides into four parts. First, one must observe **what** ought to be said; second, **how much** should be said; third, **to whom**; fourth, **when** it should be spoken. Therefore, one ought to say those things which will be useful to both the speaker and the listener. The things that are appropriate to say are those that are neither too many nor fewer than is sufficient. As for those to whom one ought to speak: if indeed one must speak to elders who have done wrong, let us speak words suitable to that age; but if words must be made to younger people, let us use greater authority in our speaking. Regarding when one should speak: let it be said neither earlier nor later than reason demands. Otherwise, he who acts differently will certainly not escape fault. **Beneficence** <note>the act of doing good or charity</note> is divided fourfold. For a benefit may be provided either by **money**, or by **bodies**, or by **disciplines**, or by **words**. A benefit consists of money when someone helps the needy with funds so that they may be freed from poverty. It consists of bodies when men cherish one another and defend them from the injury and insolence of those who would strike them. Furthermore, those who instruct in the disciplines, or assist by the art of medicine, or teach something good, use that third kind of beneficence. But when someone has entered into a legal judgment and spoken on behalf of a friend, and assisted him by the power of his oratory, he has fulfilled the duty of beneficence with words. Likewise, he makes the **end of things** <note>the purpose or completion of an action</note> fourfold. For things receive an end either according to **laws**, as when a decree is confirmed and fulfilled by law; or an end comes to things according to **nature**, for both the day and the year and the seasons of the year pass away by natural law. Or an end is imposed on a thing according to **art** <note>skill or craft</note>; for an architect completes a building by art, and a shipbuilder likewise finishes a ship. Or an end happens by **chance**, as when something occurs differently than we thought and beyond our expectation. Therefore, the end of things is either legal, or natural, or consists in art, or in chance. **Power** <note>or potential/capacity</note> he likewise divides into four species: one is that by which we can think in the mind and form opinions; the second is that by which we are strong in body, such as to travel, to receive, to give, and other things of that kind; the third is that by which we are called powerful either by an abundance of money or a multitude of soldiers (from which a king is also said to have much power); the fourth distribution of power is that by which we can both do and suffer well and ill. For we have the capacity to be weakened, to be instructed, to grow healthy, and all things of this sort. Thus, the first species of power consists in the **mind**, the second in the **body**, the third in **armies and money**, the fourth in **doing and suffering**. **Humanity** <note>or kindness/philanthropy</note> he introduces as threefold. One kind occurs in **address**, as when someone by chance humanely greets whoever he meets, and extending his right hand, receives him courteously. Another species is when someone mercifully spends effort to **help** those who are afflicted. A third kind is that by which men celebrate **banquets** among themselves. Therefore, humanity consists either in the duty of greeting, or in help and aid, or in feasting and frequent gathering. **Happiness** <note>original: "Felicitatem", Greek: "eudaimonia"</note> he defines as divided into five parts. Its first part is **good counsel**; the second is to be vigorous in the **senses** and in the good health of the body; the third is to be **fortunate** in the conduct of affairs; the fourth is to excel in **glory and authority** among men; the fifth is to abound in **money** and other things for all the uses of life. **Good counsel** <note>wise decision-making</note> results from education and from the skill and experience of many things.* <meta>catchword: Of the senses</meta>

<column-break/>

**noble and good** <note>original: "καλὸν κἀγαθόν"</note>; and such a kind is called a **praise** <note>original: "ἐγκώμιον"</note>. Another kind is when one declares someone to be base; and such a kind is called **blame** <note>original: "ψόγος"</note>. Therefore, of rhetoric, one part is praise, another blame, another persuasion, another dissuasion, another accusation, and another defense. **Speaking rightly** is divided into four: one, what one must say; one, how much one must say; third, to whom one must say it; and fourth, when it is necessary to speak. The things one must say are those which are going to benefit the speaker and the listener; "how much" is neither more nor less than what is sufficient. As for "to whom one must speak," if one is speaking to elders who are at fault, one must speak with words fitting for elders; if to younger people, one must speak words fitting for the young. As for "when one must speak," it should be neither too early nor too late; otherwise, one will fail and speak poorly. **Beneficence** is divided into four: either by **wealth**, or by **bodies**, or by **knowledge**, or by **words**. By wealth, when someone assists another in need with money; these are the impoverished. By bodies, they do good to one another when they come to the aid of those being struck. Those who **educate**, and **heal**, and **teach** something good, these do good through knowledge. When someone enters into a court of law as a helper for another, and speaks a formal speech on his behalf, he does good through words. Therefore, of beneficence, one is through wealth, another through bodies, another through knowledge, and the fourth through words. The **end of things** is divided into four kinds: one, things reach an end according to **law**, when a decree is made and the law completes it. Things reach an end according to **nature** in the case of the day, the year, and the seasons. Things reach an end according to **art**, such as architecture (for someone completes a house) and shipbuilding (for ships). An end happens to things according to **chance** when it turns out otherwise, and not as one expects. Therefore, the end of things is either according to law, nature, art, or chance. **Power** is divided into four kinds: one, that which we can calculate and suppose in our **intellect**; another in the **body**, such as to travel, to give, to receive, and such things; third, through a great multitude of **soldiers and wealth**, whence a king is called "having the power of many." The fourth division of power is **to suffer**, and **to do** well or ill; for example, we have the power to be ill, to be educated, to become healthy, and all such things. Thus, of power, one is in the intellect, another in the body, another in the camp and wealth, and another in doing and suffering. There are three kinds of **humanity** <note>original: "φιλανθρωπίας" (philanthropy)</note>: one occurring through **address**, such as when people address everyone they meet and, joining right hands, greet them; another kind is when one is **helpful** to everyone who is unfortunate; another kind of humanity is that in which some are **fond of dining** together. Therefore, of humanity, one is through address, another through doing good, and another through hosting and fond social gathering. **Happiness** <note>original: "εὐδαιμονία"</note> is divided into five parts: one part of it is **good counsel**; another is **sensitivity and health** of the body; third, **good fortune** in one’s actions; fourth, **good reputation** among men; fifth, **abundance of money** and things useful for life. Good counsel comes from education and from becoming experienced in many things; sensitivity comes from the...

<meta>This page continues the definitions of philosophical and civic concepts attributed to Plato. It specifically transitions from discussing types of beneficence to defining the components of a happy life, the classification of various arts, the nature of "the good," and the structures of legal order and lawlessness. The text is presented in parallel Greek and Latin columns, both of which are translated here into English.</meta>

# L I F E .

<column-break/>

...of the members of the body. For example, if someone sees with their eyes, hears with their ears, and perceives with their nose and mouth the things they ought to perceive; such a condition is called **good perception** <note>original: "εὐαισθησία"</note>. **Good fortune** <note>original: "εὐτυχία"</note> is when someone achieves what they aimed for, acting correctly as a serious and virtuous man should. **Good reputation** <note>original: "εὐδοξία"</note> is when one is well-spoken of by others. **Prosperity** <note>original: "εὐπορία"</note> is when someone is so situated regarding the necessities of life that they are able to benefit their friends and perform public services both generously and easily. He who possesses all these things is perfectly happy. The components of **happiness** <note>original: "εὐδαιμονία"</note> are: good counsel, good perception, bodily health, good fortune, good reputation, and prosperity.

The **arts** are divided into three kinds: the first, the second, and the third. The first consists of mining and wood-cutting, for these are preparatory arts. The second consists of blacksmithing and carpentry, for these are transformative arts; for from iron the blacksmith makes tools or weapons, and from wood the carpenter makes flutes and lyres. The third consists of the usage of these things, such as horsemanship, which uses bridles; the art of war, which uses weapons; and music, which uses flutes and the lyre. Thus, there are three types of art: one that prepares, a second that creates, and a third that utilizes.

The **good** is divided into four kinds: one which we say is the possession of virtue in an individual; another which is virtue itself and <margin>to be justly punished; and such evils are the opposites of evils.</margin> **justice**; a third kind includes things like suitable food, exercise, and medicines; a fourth kind we say are things like flute-playing, acting, and the like. Therefore, there are four kinds of the good: possessing virtue; virtue itself; beneficial food and exercise; and finally, we say flute-playing, acting, and poetry are good.

Of the things that exist, some are **evil**, some are **good**, and some are **neutral**. Among these, we call "evil" those things that are always capable of doing harm, such as intemperance, folly, and injustice, and other such things; their opposites are "good." Those things which sometimes benefit and sometimes harm—such as walking, sitting, and eating—or those things which are entirely unable to either benefit or harm, are neither good nor evil. Therefore, of existing things, some are good, some are evil, and some are neither.

**Good order** <note>original: "εὐνομία"</note> is divided into three parts: first, if the laws are excellent, we call it good order; second, if the citizens abide by the established laws, we also call this good order; third, if even without formal laws, the people live by good customs and practices, we call this good order. Thus, one part of good order is in excellent laws, another is in abiding by existing laws, and the third is in the practice of good customs.

**Lawlessness** <note>original: "ἀνομία"</note> is likewise divided into three: one is if the laws are wretched, both for foreigners and citizens; another is if people do not obey the laws that exist; a third is if there is no law at all. Thus, one part of lawlessness is the laws being wretched; another is the failure to obey them; and the third is the absence of law.

**Opposites** are divided into three types. For instance, we say good things are the opposites of evil things, such as justice being the opposite of injustice, or wisdom the opposite of folly, and so on. But there are also evils that are the opposites of other evils, such as wastefulness being the opposite of stinginess <note>original: "ἀνελευθερία," meaning a lack of liberal spirit or meanness with money</note>, or being unjustly punished being the opposite of <insert>being justly punished; and such evils are the opposites of evils.</insert> Furthermore, there are neutrals that are the opposites of neutrals, such as being poor and being wealthy—for each of these is in itself neither good nor evil, yet they are opposites. Likewise, heavy is the opposite of light, fast the opposite of slow, and black the opposite of white; thus neutrals are the opposites of neutrals. Therefore, of opposites, some are good things opposed to evils, some are evils opposed to evils, and some are neutrals opposed to neutrals.

There are three classes of good things: some are **possessions**, some are **participations**, and some are **existences** <note>referring to things that simply are, or qualities inherent in existence</note>. Possessions are those things that one can have, such as justice or health. Participations are those things which one cannot "have" as a physical possession but can share in, such as...

<column-break/>

...integrity happens as a result of the body's members, as when someone sees with eyes, hears with ears, and is healthy in the senses of the nose and mouth where necessary. The third is when one performs what they intend to do in the manner that befits a wise and vigorous man. The fourth is the celebrity of glory that flows from a reputation for goodness. The last is an abundance of things, when one has such a supply of money for the uses of life that they can assist friends with favors and benefits and supply all necessities largely and liberally. Furthermore, whoever has all these things, we consider them to be perfectly happy and blessed.

He divides the **arts** into three parts. The first consists in the handling of iron, metals, and the cutting of timber, because these things are, as it were, preparatory. The second is that which makes something out of these; for from iron the smith fashions weapons, and from wood the carpenter makes flutes and lyres. The third is in the use of those things; for the equestrian uses bridles, the soldier uses weapons, and the musician uses flutes and the lyre.

The **good** is divided into four kinds. First, we call that man "good" who possesses virtue. Second, we call virtue itself and justice "good." Third, food, convenient exercise, and medicines. Fourth and finally, we call "good" the sound of flutes, acting, and other things of this sort.

Of the things that are, some we call evil, some good, and others neutral. Of these, the **evils** are those which can always do harm, such as intemperance, madness, injustice, and the like. **Good** things are those which are contrary to these. **Medium** <note>neutral</note> things are those which support neither part, such as these: walking, sitting, and the taking of food, which are entirely unable to either benefit or hinder; these therefore are neither good nor evil.

The best moderation of laws is divided into three. First, if the laws are distinguished and serious. Second, if the citizens observe those laws that were so passed with all zeal. Third, if the Republic is well-administered according to the customs and pursuits of each person, even if laws have been set aside. Therefore, the first part of this moderation is that the laws be the best; the second, that one remains within them; the third, that one lives by distinguished customs and pursuits.

**Injustice** <note>here meaning lawlessness or lack of order</note>, the contrary to this laudable moderation of laws, is likewise split into three. The first of these is if the laws passed are harmful to foreigners and citizens. The second is if the existing laws are not obeyed in the least. Third, if there is no good law at all.

**Contraries** are divided into three ways, just as we say good things are contrary to evil things—as justice to injustice, wisdom to foolishness, and other such things. However, evils are also contrary to evils, such as prodigality <note>wastefulness</note> to illiberalness <note>stinginess</note>, and unjust punishment to unjust impunity, and other evils of that kind are contrary to evils. Furthermore, neutrals are contrary to neutrals, such as being poor and being wealthy; for neither is per se good or evil, yet they are contraries. Truly, light things are contrary to heavier ones, fast to slow, and black to white, as neutrals are contrary to neutrals. Therefore, of contraries, some are good things contrary to evils, and some are called neutrals contrary to neutrals.

There are three kinds of good things: some of these are **had**, others are **shared** <note>participated in</note>, others **exist**. The first are those which can be held, such as justice and health. The second are those which cannot be held as possessions, yet a part of them...

<meta>This page continues the classification of philosophical concepts. The previous page ended mid-sentence discussing the types of arts. # LIFE OF PLATO

<column-break/>

...we are able to be **participants** <note>original: "ticipes," likely "participes"</note>, just as it is not possible to possess the Good itself, yet it is not impossible to enjoy participation in it. Those things which are **inherent** <note>original: "subsistẽtia," referring to things that simply exist in a subject</note>, however, do not admit participation, nor is it possible to "possess" them, but they simply must *be*; such as being upright, being just, and being good. These things one can neither possess nor participate in, but it is enough that they *are*, such as being upright and being just.

**Counsel** <note>deliberation or advice</note> is likewise tripartite: one part is taken from the past, another from the future, and another from the present time. The **past time** supplies examples, as we observe what and why every nation has suffered, so that we might be cautious; or what it has done prudently, so that we might imitate it—such as what the **Lacedaemonians** <note>Spartans</note> suffered while they were overconfident. The **present**, however, warns us to consider the matter itself which is at hand, such as weak walls, fearful men, the high price of grain, and other things of this sort. The **future** urges us to look ahead, so that nothing is done rashly, and that regard be had for a good reputation; for instance, that embassies should not be violated by suspicion, lest Greece lose her glory of integrity.

**Voice** is divided into two parts: for one is **animate** <note>living</note>, the other **inanimate**. Animate voice belongs to living creatures; inanimate voice belongs to sounds and clatter. Furthermore, animate voice is divided in two: for one is **literate** <note>articulate/speech</note>, the other **illiterate**. Literate voice belongs to humans, illiterate to animals.

Of those things which exist, some we call **divisible**, others **indivisible**. Of the divisible, some are of **similar parts** <note>homogeneous</note>, others of **dissimilar parts** <note>heterogeneous</note>. **Indivisible** things are those which do not admit division and are simple, not composed of anything; such as a **monad** <note>a mathematical unit</note>, a point, and a sound. **Divisible** things are those composed of something, such as syllables, harmonies, living beings, water, and gold. **Similar parts** are those composed of like elements, where the whole differs from the part only in quantity—such as water and gold and others of this sort. We call those **dissimilar parts** which consist of unlike things, such as a house and other things of this kind.

Of those things which exist, some are said to be **absolute** <note>original: "per se"</note>, others **relative** <note>original: "ad aliquid"</note>. We call **absolute** those which need no interpretation to be understood; of this sort are man, horses, and the rest of the animals; none of these need an interpretation. Those are called **relative** which require a certain interpretation, such as that which is "greater" than something, "faster" than something, or "better," and other things of this sort. For the greater is greater than the smaller, and the faster is faster than something else, and so on in this manner.

In this way he also divided the primary things according to **Aristotle**. There was also another **Plato**, a philosopher from **Rhodes** and a disciple of **Panaetius**, as **Seleucus the Grammarian** says in the first book of *On Philosophy*; and another who was a **Peripatetic** and disciple of Aristotle; and another who was a disciple of **Praxiphanes**; and also another who was a poet of **Old Comedy**.

<column-break/>

...it is not possible to possess the **Good** <note>original: "ἀγαθὸν"</note>, but it is possible to participate in it. **Inherent** things <note>original: "ὑπαρκτὰ"</note> are those which one can neither participate in nor possess, but they must simply be present: for example, to be serious and to be just is a good; and these one can neither possess nor participate in, but they must be present—to be serious and to be just. Therefore, of goods, some are **possessable**, some **participable**, and some **inherent**.

**Counsel** <note>original: "συμβουλία"</note> is divided into three. For one part of it is taken from **past times**, one from the **future**, and one from the **present**. Those from the past are examples, such as: "What did the Lacedaemonians suffer by being too trusting?" Those from the present are, for example, to point out weak walls, cowardly men, or a shortage of grain. Those from the future are, for example, to take care not to wrong embassies through suspicion, so that Greece is not covered in shame. Therefore, of counsel, one part is from the past, one from the present, and one from the future.

**Voice** <note>original: "φωνὴ"</note> is divided into two. One part of it is **animate** <note>endowed with soul</note>, and one is **inanimate**. Animate is the voice of living creatures; inanimate is sounds and echoes. Of animate voice, one kind is **literate** <note>capable of being written</note>, and the other is **illiterate**. Literate is that of humans; illiterate is that of animals. Therefore, of voice, one is animate, the other inanimate.

Of things that exist, some are **divisible** <note>original: "μεριστὰ"</note>, others **indivisible** <note>original: "ἀμέριστα"</note>. Of the divisible, some are **homogeneous** <note>of similar parts</note>, others **heterogeneous** <note>of dissimilar parts</note>. **Indivisible** things are all those that have no division, nor are they composed of anything, such as the **monad**, the **point**, and the **tone**. **Divisible** things are all those composed of something, such as syllables, harmonies, animals, water, and gold. **Homogeneous** things are those composed of similar parts, where the whole differs from the part in nothing except quantity; such as water and gold and everything of that sort. **Heterogeneous** things are those composed of dissimilar parts, such as a house and such things. Therefore, of things that exist, some are divisible and some are indivisible; and of the divisible, some are homogeneous and some are heterogeneous.

Of things that exist, some are **absolute** <note>original: "καθ' ἑαυτὰ," in themselves</note>, and some are said to be **relative** <note>original: "πρός τι," toward something</note>. Those called **absolute** are those which in their explanation need nothing else; these would be such as man, horse, and the other animals. For none of these proceeds through an external explanation. Of those called **relative** are those which need some further explanation, such as that which is "greater" than something, "faster" than something, "more beautiful," and such things. For the greater is greater than the lesser, and the faster is faster than something. Therefore, of things that exist, some are said to be absolute, and some relative.

In this way he divided the primary things, according to **Aristotle**. There was also another **Plato**, a philosopher of **Rhodes**, a pupil of **Panaetius**, as **Seleucus the Grammarian** says in the first book *On Philosophy*. And another, a **Peripatetic**, a pupil of Aristotle. And another, a pupil of **Praxiphanes**. And the poet of the **Old Comedy**.

## FROM THE MANY WORKS ON PLATO
### Epigrams <note>original: "Epigrammata"; short, clever poems often intended for inscriptions</note>.

Aristotle established this altar for Plato;
A man whom it is not lawful for the wicked even to praise. <note>original: "Βωμὸν Ἀριστοτέλης ἱδρύσατο τόνδε Πλάτωνος..." This famous couplet emphasizes that Plato was so virtuous that the "bad" are not even worthy of speaking his name.</note>

->ON THE SAME MAN.<-

God-like Plato once stood here, he who first in Athens
Showed the holy paths of virtues ordained by the gods.

->ON THE SAME MAN.<-

Phoebus <note>A name for Apollo, the god of prophecy, music, and healing</note> fathered Asclepius <note>The god of medicine</note> and Plato for mortals:
The one to save the body, the other to save the soul.
And having celebrated a wedding, he went to the city which he once
Built for himself, and settled upon the floor of Zeus <note>This imagery suggests Plato’s soul returning to the "Republic" or the ideal divine realm he described in his writings</note>.

->ON THE SAME MAN.<-

This earth holds the body of Plato in her bosom;
But his soul holds a rank among the god-like blessed.

->ON THE SAME MAN.<-

Not the most excellent mouth of the Attic <note>The region of Athens, known for the purest Greek speech</note> tongue, nor any city
Of all the Greeks has hidden a voice greater than yours;
Being the first to stretch your eye toward God and toward heaven,
Divine Plato, you looked upon the character and the life of man;
Mixing the Samian <note>Refers to Pythagoras of Samos, whose mathematical and mystical ideas influenced Plato</note> wisdom in the Socratic bowl,
You created the most beautiful sign of a noble distinction <note>original: "διχοστασίης," referring to the creative tension or reconciliation between different schools of thought</note>.

->Some New Epigrams.<-

## ON JOINING PLATO AND
### Aristotle together.

The fiery sun, spinning upon its axis,
Darkened the stars and the holy circles of the moon;
Just as you, divine Plato, a second sun for life,
Obscure all the spokesmen of wisdom;
But you also love the resourceful Aristotle,
Having adorned him abundantly with the law of temperance <note>original: "σαοφροσύνης," often translated as "soundness of mind" or "self-control"</note>.

->I. S. <note>Likely the initials of Isaac Casaubon, a renowned Renaissance classical scholar</note><-

---

## AGAINST THE PLATONISTS AND
### Aristotelians.

Some say they belong to Aristotle, others to Plato.
Nothing is more ridiculous than this discord.
Was not one the teacher, and the other the student?
Did the one not learn the truth, and the other teach it?
How then, for the sake of truth, can there be friendship among men?
Let your sorrowful strife then cease.

->Theodorus Gaza <note>A 15th-century Greek scholar and translator who was a leader in the revival of learning in Italy</note><-

# PLATO'S HIPPARCHUS,
# OR, THE LOVER OF PROFIT.

## ETHICAL.

# PLATO'S HIPPARCHUS,
# OR, ON THE DESIRE FOR PROFIT.

## PERTAINING TO MORALS.

### Marsilio Ficino, translator.

->**SUMMARY OF THE DIALOGUE.** Socrates brings Hipparchus—who holds a poor opinion regarding the desire for profit and defines it incorrectly—to the point where he no longer censures it entirely, but concedes that there is a certain kind of profit-seeking appropriate to a good man. Plato’s purpose in this dialogue is to teach that the love of profit or utility is naturally implanted in all human beings, and therefore not all profit is to be condemned universally and simply; rather, one must carefully define what that profit actually is.<-

---

->**THE CHARACTERS OF THE DIALOGUE,**<-
->**CHARACTERS OF THE DIALOGUE HIPPARCHUS,**<-

->**OF HIPPARCHUS,**<-

->**SOCRATES, HIPPARCHUS.**<-
->**SOCRATES, HIPPARCHUS.**<-

<margin>A</margin> SOCRATES: What is the love of profit? What exactly is it, and who are the lovers of profit? HIPPARCHUS: It seems to me they are those who think they should profit from things of no value. SOCRATES: Do you think they know they are of no value, or are they ignorant? For if they are ignorant, you are calling the lovers of profit fools. HIPPARCHUS: I do not call them fools, but rather rogues and villains, and those overcome by profit; they know that the things from which they dare to profit are worthless, yet they dare to be greedy out of shamelessness.

<margin>B</margin> SOCRATES: Do you then describe the lover of profit as someone like a farmer who, while planting and knowing the plant is worthless, expects to profit from it once it is grown? Is that the kind of person you mean? HIPPARCHUS: A lover of profit, Socrates, thinks he must profit from everything. SOCRATES: Do not speak so recklessly, as if you have been wronged by someone, but pay attention and answer me as if I were asking from the beginning again. Do you not agree that the lover of profit is knowledgeable about the value of that from which he expects to profit? HIPPARCHUS: I do. SOCRATES: Who then is knowledgeable about the value of plants? In what soil and at what season it is worth planting them? Let us also throw in some of those clever phrases <note>original: "σοφῶν ῥημάτων"; Socrates is playfully mimicking the sophisticated rhetoric of contemporary lawyers</note> with which the skillful lawyers adorn their speeches. HIPPARCHUS: I think it is the farmer.

<margin>C</margin> SOCRATES: By "worthy of profit," do you mean anything other than thinking one ought to profit? HIPPARCHUS: That is what I mean. SOCRATES: Then do not try to deceive me, a man who is already old, while you are so young, by answering as you just did things you do not even believe yourself. But tell me truly: do you believe any man skilled in farming, who knows he is planting a plant that is worth nothing, expects to profit from it? HIPPARCHUS: By Jove <note>original: "Μὰ Δί’" (By Zeus). The Latin uses "per Iouem"</note>, certainly not. SOCRATES: What then? Do you think a horseman, knowing he provides fodder of no value to his horse, is ignorant that he is ruining the horse? HIPPARCHUS: Not I. SOCRATES: Therefore he does not expect to profit from this worthless fodder. HIPPARCHUS: No. SOCRATES: What then? Do you think a pilot, having equipped his ship with rudders and sails of no value, is ignorant that he will suffer loss, and be in danger of perishing himself, and losing the ship and everything he carries? HIPPARCHUS: Not I.

<margin>D</margin> SOCRATES: Therefore he does not think he will profit from worthless equipment. HIPPARCHUS: Indeed not. SOCRATES: But would a general, knowing that his army has worthless weapons, think to profit from them, or expect to profit? HIPPARCHUS: By no means. SOCRATES: But would a flute-player, having worthless flutes, or a lyre-player with a lyre, or an archer with a bow, or any other craftsman or wise man in short, having worthless tools or other useless equipment, think to profit from them?

<column-break/>

<margin>Who are the lovers of profit, according to Hipparchus's opinion.</margin>
<margin>A rebuke of that opinion.</margin>
<margin>A</margin> SOCRATES: What is the love of profit? And who are the lovers of profit? HIPPARCHUS: It seems to me they are those who think they should profit from things that are worthy of no esteem. SOCRATES: Do they seem to you to know that they are of no value, or to be ignorant? If they do not know, you call the lovers of profit madmen. HIPPARCHUS: I do not call them madmen, but rather clever and wicked, and conquered by profit; they are aware that the things from which they seek profit are of no value, and yet they seek profit through shamelessness. SOCRATES: Do you call someone of this sort a lover of profit? For instance, if a farmer, while planting and knowing

<margin>B</margin> that the plant is of no value, nevertheless thinks it is a worthy thing from which to profit—do you call such a man a lover of profit? HIPPARCHUS: From everywhere, Socrates, the lover of profit thinks it must be sought. SOCRATES: Do not pour out words so rashly, as if angry at someone because of an injury received, but rather answer me attentively, as if I were asking again from the beginning. Do you agree that the lover of profit knows the value of that from which he thinks he should profit? HIPPARCHUS: I agree. SOCRATES: Who is it that knows concerning the value of plants, in which region and at what time it is worthy to plant, so that we too may bring into the discussion some of the wise words with which those elegant lawyers abound? HIPPARCHUS: The farmer, I believe.

<margin>He notes the Greek phrasing as being affected.</margin>
<margin>C</margin> SOCRATES: Do you call "worthy of profit" anything other than thinking one should profit? HIPPARCHUS: That very thing. SOCRATES: Do not attempt to deceive me, a man now old, you being so young, by answering—as you just did—things which you yourself least believe. But answer as truly as possible. Would you judge a true farmer to be one who, knowing a plant is unworthy of planting, thinks to profit from it? HIPPARCHUS: No, by Jove. SOCRATES: Furthermore, if a horseman knows the fodder he gives his horse is of no value, do you think he is ignorant that the horse will be ruined? HIPPARCHUS: Not at all. SOCRATES: He does not, therefore, think there is profit from such faulty fodder. HIPPARCHUS: Not in the least. SOCRATES: And the pilot who has equipped his ship with a rudder and sails of no value, do you think he is ignorant that he will be affected by loss, and will come into danger, so that both the ship

<margin>D</margin> and whatever is in the ship may be lost? HIPPARCHUS: He is certainly not ignorant. SOCRATES: He does not therefore think he will profit from instruments of no value. HIPPARCHUS: Not at all. SOCRATES: Likewise, seeing a leader of war relying on an army with worthless weapons, would he hope or think it worthy to seek profit from these? HIPPARCHUS: Not at all. SOCRATES: In the same way, if a flute-player has a flute, a lyre-player a lyre, an archer a bow, and to embrace it briefly, any craftsman or expert in any matter should have instruments and other equipment of no value, would he think to profit from these...

<summary>This page introduces Plato's Hipparchus, where Socrates begins to dismantle the definition of greed by arguing that no expert intentionally uses worthless tools to achieve a successful or profitable outcome.</summary>

# OF PLATO

...did he profit? HIPPARCHUS: No, it appears. SOCRATES: Who then
<margin>A</margin> do you call lovers of profit? For surely not those we mentioned before, who think they ought to profit from things of no value. Yet in this way, wonderful man, as you wish it, no human would be a lover of profit. HIPPARCHUS: But I... SOCRATES: ...say those are lovers of profit who, because of insatiable greed, thirst for even the smallest and cheapest things of no value in a marvelous way, and even in these they seek profit. SOCRATES: But they do not, O best of men, know that those things are of no value. For we have already driven ourselves to this point, to confess it is impossible. HIPPARCHUS: So it seems to me. SOCRATES: If they do not
<margin>B</margin> know it, they are ignorant then; do they nonetheless think that things of no value are worth much? HIPPARCHUS: Certainly. SOCRATES: Is profit said to be the opposite of loss? HIPPARCHUS: It is. SOCRATES: Is it good for anyone to suffer a loss? HIPPARCHUS: For no one. SOCRATES: Is it an evil then? HIPPARCHUS: Entirely. SOCRATES: Are men then harmed by loss? HIPPARCHUS: They are harmed. SOCRATES: Is loss then an evil? HIPPARCHUS: An evil. SOCRATES: Is profit the opposite of loss? HIPPARCHUS: The opposite. SOCRATES: Is profit then a good? HIPPARCHUS: Certainly. SOCRATES: Do you then call those who love what is good "lovers of profit"? HIPPARCHUS: It seems so. SOCRATES: You do not, O
<margin>C</margin> friend, call the insane "lovers of profit." But do you yourself love what is good, or do you not love it? HIPPARCHUS: I certainly love it. SOCRATES: Is there any good thing that you do not desire, but rather an evil thing? HIPPARCHUS: Not by Jove <note>original: "per Iouem." A common oath to the king of the gods.</note>. SOCRATES: But you desire all good things equally. HIPPARCHUS: All of them. SOCRATES: Ask me as well, whether I too—I will confess that I certainly love good things: but besides me and you, do not all other mortals also seem to you to love good things and hate evil ones? HIPPARCHUS: It seems so. SOCRATES: And did we not confess that profit is a good? HIPPARCHUS: Indeed. SOCRATES: All people then appear to be lovers of profit in this way: but according to what we said before, no one would be a lover of profit. Which of these accounts should we follow, lest we err? HIPPARCHUS: If someone, O Socrates, were to correctly
<margin>D</margin> define a lover of profit, I think he would consider him a lover of profit who is devoted to these things and thinks he should seek profit from things from which good men would never choose to profit. SOCRATES: But do you not see, O sweetest one, what we agreed upon a little while ago, namely that to profit is to be benefited? HIPPARCHUS: What then? SOCRATES: Because we also agreed on this: that all people always want what is good. HIPPARCHUS: We confessed it. SOCRATES: And do not good men also seek all profit, if indeed all profit is good? HIPPARCHUS: But not those profits by which they might be harmed. SOCRATES: Do you call being harmed "suffering a loss," or something else? HIPPARCHUS:
<margin>E</margin> Nothing other than being affected by loss. SOCRATES: Do men suffer loss by profit, or rather by loss? HIPPARCHUS: By both. For by loss, and by base profit, they are affected by loss. SOCRATES: Does it seem to you that anything useful and good can be base? HIPPARCHUS: Not at all. SOCRATES: Did we not grant a little while ago that profit is the opposite of loss, which is an evil? HIPPARCHUS: I admit it. SOCRATES: And since it is the opposite of an evil, is it a good? HIPPARCHUS: We confessed it. SOCRATES: You see then how you try to deceive me, by industry bringing forth the opposite of those things which we confessed above. HIPPARCHUS: Not by Jove, O Socrates: but on the contrary, you deceive me, and I know not how, by your arguing, you turn everything upside down. SOCRATES: Good words, I pray <note>original: "Bona verba." A polite way of saying "Hush" or "Speak nobly."</note>. For I would not be doing rightly unless I obeyed a good and wise man. HIPPARCHUS: To whom? Or what is this finally? SOCRATES: To my
<margin>F</margin> fellow citizen and yours, Hipparchus, the son of Peisistratus of the Philaidae, the eldest and wisest of the sons of Peisistratus, who, while he exhibited many other famous examples of wisdom, also first brought the books of Homer into this region, and compelled the rhapsodes <note>original: "recitatores." Professional performers of epic poetry.</note> to recite them at the Panathenaea <note>A great Athenian festival.</note> in turns and in order, which they observe even to these times. And he summoned Anacreon of Teos <note>A famous lyric poet known for drinking songs and love poetry.</note> to this city, having sent a ship of fifty oars. He also always had Simonides of Ceos with him, having induced him with great stipends and gifts. All these things he did, wanting to lead his citizens to education, so that he might rule over them as they lived as well as possible, thinking it was not at all right to envy anyone's wisdom, since he himself was honorable and good. When therefore the citizens were abundantly
<margin>G</margin> learned, and admired his wisdom, he turned his mind to educating the farmers and foreigners. Therefore he erected columns <note>original: "columnas." Specifically, the Hermae—square pillars topped with the head of the god Hermes.</note> at every three-way intersection of the city and in every tribe: and from that wisdom, which he had partly learned and partly discovered himself, drawing out what he judged better, he enclosed it in elegies, and inscribed it as precepts of wisdom: first so that the citizens would no longer wonder at those famous sayings, "Know thyself," "Nothing too much," and others of this kind, inscribed at Delphi: but rather they would take up the precepts of Hipparchus as superior. Then, passing by this way and that and tasting his wisdom by reading, they would proceed from the fields and forests to learn the rest of the institutions of doctrine. There were, moreover, two epigrams:
<margin>H</margin> one on the left side of each column, in which Hermes warned the reader (for so it was inscribed) that he stood in the middle of the city and the people; the other on the right, inscribed thus: "This is a monument of Hipparchus." Soon a precept was added, "Go forth, taking care for what is just." And as in other columns there were other...

<column-break/>

So it appears. SOCRATES: Who then
<margin>A</margin> do you say are the lovers of profit? For surely they are not those we have gone through, who, knowing things are worth nothing, think they should profit from them; but in this way, O marvelous man, as you say, no human being is a lover of profit. HIPPARCHUS: But I, O Socrates, wish to say that lovers of profit are those who, at every turn, through insatiable greed, long exceedingly for even very small and little-worth things that are worth nothing, and they love profit. SOCRATES: Surely not, O best of men, knowing that they are worth nothing. For this we have already refuted for ourselves in our speech, showing that it is
<margin>B</margin> impossible. HIPPARCHUS: So it seems to me. SOCRATES: Therefore if they do not know it, it is clear they are ignorant; but they think that things worth nothing are worth much. HIPPARCHUS: So it appears. SOCRATES: Is it anything else then, that those who love profit love the profit? HIPPARCHUS: Yes. SOCRATES: And do you say that profit is the opposite of loss? HIPPARCHUS: I do. SOCRATES: Is it then so good a thing for anyone to suffer loss? HIPPARCHUS: For no one. SOCRATES: But is it an evil? HIPPARCHUS: Yes. SOCRATES: Are men then harmed by loss? HIPPARCHUS: They are harmed. SOCRATES: Is loss then an evil? HIPPARCHUS: Yes. SOCRATES: And is profit the opposite of loss? HIPPARCHUS: Opposite. SOCRATES: Is profit then a
good? HIPPARCHUS: Yes. SOCRATES: Those then who love the good,
<margin>Γ</margin> do you call them lovers of profit? HIPPARCHUS: It seems so. SOCRATES: You do not, O companion, say that lovers of profit are insane. But do you yourself love whatever might be good, or do you not love it? HIPPARCHUS: I do. SOCRATES: And is there any good that you do not love, but rather an evil? HIPPARCHUS: By Zeus, not I <note>original: "Μὰ Δί’." A typical Greek oath.</note>. SOCRATES: But you probably love all good things. HIPPARCHUS: Yes. SOCRATES: Ask me also if I do not as well. For I too will agree with you that I love good things; but besides me and you, do not all other men seem to you to love good things and hate evil things? HIPPARCHUS: So it appears to me. SOCRATES: And did we agree that profit is a good? HIPPARCHUS: Yes. SOCRATES: All, in turn, appear to be lovers of profit in this way; but in the way we spoke of before, no one was a lover of profit. Which of these accounts then should one use, so that
<margin>Δ</margin> one might not be deceived? HIPPARCHUS: If someone, O Socrates, I think, should correctly take the lover of profit—and it is correct to lead this man as a lover of profit—it is he who is eager for those things and thinks to profit from them, from which the upright do not dare to profit. SOCRATES: But do you see, O sweetest one, we just now agreed that to profit is to be benefited. HIPPARCHUS: What then of this? SOCRATES: That we also agreed with him on this, that all people always want good things. HIPPARCHUS: Yes. SOCRATES: Therefore all good men also want to have profits, if indeed they are good things. HIPPARCHUS: But not those profits, Socrates, from which they are likely to be harmed. SOCRATES: And by being harmed do you mean suffering a loss,
<margin>Ε</margin> or something else? HIPPARCHUS: No; I mean suffering a loss. SOCRATES: Do men suffer loss by profit or by loss? HIPPARCHUS: By both. For they suffer loss by loss, and by wicked profit. SOCRATES: Does it seem to you that anything wicked is also good? Or that the wicked exists as good? HIPPARCHUS: Not to me. SOCRATES: Therefore did we not agree a little while ago that profit is the opposite of loss, which is an evil? HIPPARCHUS: I say so. SOCRATES: And that the opposite of evil is good? HIPPARCHUS: We agreed. SOCRATES: Do you see then, you are attempting to deceive me, purposefully saying things opposite to what we just agreed. HIPPARCHUS: No, by Zeus, Socrates; but on the contrary you are deceiving me, and I do not know how you turn everything up and down in your speeches. SOCRATES: Speak well <note>original: "Εὐφήμει." A religious or polite command to avoid ill-omened speech.</note>. For I would not be doing well if I did not obey a man who is both good and
<margin>Ϛ</margin> wise. HIPPARCHUS: Who is this? and especially? SOCRATES: My citizen and yours, the son of Peisistratus of the Philaidae, Hipparchus, who was the eldest and wisest of Peisistratus's children, who displayed many other beautiful works of wisdom, and first brought the epics of Homer into this land and forced the rhapsodes at the Panathenaea to go through them in order by taking them up where the last left off, just as they still do now. And having sent a fifty-oared ship for Anacreon of Teos, he brought him into the city. And he always had Simonides of Ceos with him, persuading him with great wages and gifts. He did these things wishing to educate the citizens so that he might rule over them as they were the best possible; not thinking he should envy anyone for wisdom, since he was beautiful and good. And when his citizens in the city
<margin>Ζ</margin> were educated and admired him for his wisdom, planning to educate those in the fields, he set up Hermae <note>The statues of Hermes mentioned in the Latin column.</note> for them along the roads in the middle between the city and each of the districts. And then, from his own wisdom, both what he learned and what he found out himself, having selected what he thought was wisest, he put these things into elegiac verse, and he inscribed them as his own poems and inscriptions of wisdom. He did this so that, first, his citizens would not admire those wise inscriptions at Delphi, "Know thyself" and "Nothing too much" and other such things, but would rather think the sayings of Hipparchus were wise. Then, as they passed up and down and read them, and took a taste of his wisdom, they would come from the fields to be educated in the remaining things. There were two epigrams: on those to the
<margin>Η</margin> left of each Hermes, the stone-carver had Hermes saying that he stood in the middle of the city and the district; and on those to the right,
-> This is the monument of Hipparchus: walk on, thinking just thoughts, <-
he says. And there are many other of his poems on other Hermae and...

<summary>Socrates argues that because all people desire the good, and profit is a type of good, everyone is naturally a "lover of profit." He then shifts to a historical defense of the tyrant Hipparchus, depicting him as a wise educator who used public monuments to spread morality.</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Hipparchus, profit, greed, Peisistratus, Homer, Anacreon, Simonides, Hermae, ethics, Athenian history, education</keywords>

--- Page 35 ---
<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and a companion (named Hipparchus in this text) concerning the nature of "profit" or "gain." Socrates has just argued that since profit is the opposite of loss, and loss is an evil, then profit must be a good. Here, Socrates digresses into a historical account of the Athenian ruler Hipparchus to illustrate the importance of honesty between friends.</meta>

### HIPPARCHUS

<margin>A</margin> ...excellent poems were inscribed; there was one indeed on the Steirian Road, in which he says:
->This is the monument of Hipparchus: Do not deceive a friend.<-
I, therefore, would certainly not dare to deceive you, who are my friend, nor would I dare to mistrust that great man. After he died, the <margin>B</margin> Athenians were ruled by the tyranny of his brother Hippias for three years, and you would hear from all the elders that only during those three years was there a "tyranny" in Athens; for the rest of the time, the Athenians lived very much as if they were under the reign of Cronus <note>original: "Κρόνου," the father of Zeus; his reign was considered a Golden Age of peace and plenty</note>. It is said by the more refined people that his death occurred not for the reason the common folk believe—the dishonor of his sister regarding the basket-bearing <note>The Canephoria was a prestigious religious role where young women carried baskets in processions; to be rejected from this role was a public insult</note> (for that would be a silly reason)—but because Harmodius had become the favorite of Aristogiton and had been educated by him. Aristogiton took great pride in educating the man and considered Hipparchus a rival. At that time, it happened that Harmodius himself was in love with one of the noble and beautiful youths of the day (they still tell his name, though I do not remember it). This youth initially admired Harmodius and Aristogiton as wise men, but later, after associating with Hipparchus, he began to look down on them. They, being deeply pained by this loss of honor, then killed Hipparchus. <margin>C</margin> **HIPPARCHUS:** You seem, then, O Socrates, to either not consider me a friend, or if you do, you do not believe Hipparchus. For I cannot be persuaded that you are not somehow deceiving me in these arguments. **SOCRATES:** Well then, just as if we were playing checkers, I am willing to let you "take back" <note>An ancient Greek term for retracting a move in a board game</note> whatever you wish of what has been said, so that you do not think you are being deceived. Which point should I retract? That all men desire good things? **HIPP:** Not that. **SOCR:]** Or that suffering a loss and the loss itself is an evil? **HIPP:** Not that either. **SOCR:** Or that profit and profiting are the opposites of loss and suffering a loss? **HIPP:** Not that. **SOCR:** Or that since it is the opposite of an evil, profiting is a good? **HIPP:** <margin>D</margin> Do not retract all of that for me. **SOCR:** It seems to you then, as it appears, that some profit is a good, and some is an evil. **HIPP:** To me, yes. **SOCR:** I will retract this for you then. Let it be that one kind of profit is good, and another kind of profit is evil. But is the good profit any more "profit" than the evil one? Or are they both? **HIPP:** How are you asking me? **SOCR:** I will explain. Is there such a thing as both good and bad food? **HIPP:** Yes. **SOCR:** Is one of them more "food" than the other? Or are they both equally food? And in this respect, do they differ at all from one another, insofar as they are food? Except that one of them is good, and the other is bad? **HIPP:** Yes. **SOCR:** And isn't it the same with drink and all other things that belong to the same category? If some are good and some are bad, they do not differ in the respect that they are the same thing? <margin>E</margin> Just as one man, I suppose, is virtuous and another is wicked. **HIPP:** Yes. **SOCR:** But I think neither of them is more or less a "human" than the other—neither the virtuous than the wicked, nor the wicked than the virtuous. **HIPP:** You speak the truth. **SOCR:** Therefore, should we not think the same way about profit? That both the virtuous and the wicked acquisition are equally "profit"? **HIPP:** Necessarily. **SOCR:** Then he who has a virtuous profit gains no more than he who has a wicked one. Neither appears to be "more" of a profit, as we have agreed. **HIPP:** Yes. **SOCR:** For neither of them possesses "more" or "less" of that quality. **HIPP:** Certainly not. **SOCR:** How could anyone do or suffer anything more or less in such a matter, where neither of these qualities is present? **HIPP:** It is impossible. **SOCR:** Since, therefore, both are equally profits and profitable, we must now consider this: why do you call them both "profit"? What is the common element you see in both? Just as if you asked me why I call both good food and bad food "food," I would tell you: because both are dry nourishment for the body. This is what it is to be food, and you would agree with me, wouldn't you? **HIPP:** I would. **SOCR:** And about drink, the same way of answering would apply: that it is the moist nourishment for the body, whether it be good or bad; that is what the name "drink" signifies. And so it is with other things. Try then to imitate me in answering this way. You say both "good profit" and "bad profit" are profit. What is the common element <margin>G</margin> in them that makes them both profit? If you cannot answer yourself, then consider what I say: Do you call profit every possession that one acquires by spending nothing, or by spending less than what one receives? **HIPP:** To me, that seems to be what profit is called. **SOCR:** Do you mean it in cases like this? If a man at a feast, without spending anything but being fed, acquires a disease? **HIPP:** By Zeus, I do not! **SOCR:** But if he acquired health from a feast, would he have acquired a profit or a loss? **HIPP:** A profit. **SOCR:** Therefore, profit is not just acquiring any possession whatsoever. **HIPP:** Certainly not. **SOCR:** Is it that if one acquires an evil, it is not a profit, but it is only a profit if it is a good? **HIPP:** It appears so, if it is a good. **SOCR:** And if it is an evil, will he not acquire a loss? **HIPP:** To me, it seems so. **SOCR:** Do you see then how you have run back to the same point? Profit appears to be a good, and loss appears to be an evil.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...splendid poems were inscribed, and many other things; on the Steirian road there was such a one: "This is the monument of Hipparchus; do not deceive a friend." For which reason I would never dare to deceive you, being my friend, nor would I resist that great man. After his life ended, the Athenians were pressed by the tyranny under his brother Hippias for three years. You yourself have heard from all the elders that only this three-year period of tyranny flourished in this city. <margin>B</margin> In other times, the Athenians lived almost in the same way as when Saturn <note>The Roman equivalent of Cronus</note> was reigning. It is passed down by more refined men that the cause of his death was not what is commonly said—namely, the contempt shown to the sister of the Basket-bearer—for to believe that is absurd. But when Harmodius was loved and taught by Aristogiton, something great remained for him from this education: for he suspected that Hipparchus would be an adversary. Meanwhile, it happened that Harmodius loved a certain noble youth whose name I do not quite remember. At first, he admired Harmodius and Aristogiton as wise men, but after becoming familiar with Hipparchus, he began to despise them. Hence, they, being indignant, slew Hipparchus. <margin>C</margin> **HIPP:** You seem then, O Socrates, either not to think me a friend, or if you do think me a friend, to believe Hipparchus not at all. For I cannot be persuaded that I am not being deceived by your delaying. **SOCR:** And yet I am willing, as if we were playing such a game, to retract whatever you please, lest you think yourself deceived. Do you wish that which we said—that all men desire good things—to be changed? **HIPP:** I do not. **SOCR:** What about this: that we granted loss, and being affected by loss, to be an evil? **HIPP:** I do not want that changed either. **SOCR:** But what about this: that profit and profiting are contrary to both loss and that which is suffering loss? **HIPP:** Nor that indeed. **SOCR:** But perhaps this: that profiting, as it is the contrary of an evil, is a good? **HIPP:** Retract nothing. **SOCR:** It seems to you then, as it appears, <margin>D</margin> that some profit is a good, and some truly an evil? **HIPP:** Indeed to me. **SOCR:** I retract this for you then. For one profit is good, another evil; yet nothing is "more" a profit than the other, is it not so? **HIPP:** Why do you ask? **SOCR:** I will say: food is both good and bad. **HIPP:** It is. **SOCR:** Is one any more "food" than the other, or is each equally food, and does one differ from the other not in being food, but in that one is good and the other bad? **HIPP:** It is as you say. **SOCR:** And is it not the same for drink and all other things of the same form, that they are partly good and partly bad, and they do not differ among themselves in that in which they are the same, just as among men, one is good and another bad? **HIPP:** So it is. **SOCR:** Furthermore, neither of them, as I think, <margin>E</margin> is more or less a human than the other—neither the good than the bad, nor the bad than the good. **HIPP:** You speak the truth. **SOCR:** Shall we not judge similarly of profit? That profit is equally profit, whether it be good or bad? **HIPP:** It is necessary. **SOCR:** He gains no more, then, who attains a good profit than he who attains a bad one: nor does either of these appear to be "more" of a profit, as is now agreed. **HIPP:** Certainly. **SOCR:** And to neither is it present more or less? **HIPP:** To neither. **SOCR:** In such a thing, to which neither of these applies, can anyone do or even suffer anything more or less? **HIPP:** It is impossible. **SOCR:** After both are equally profits, this remains to be considered next: why do you call both "profit"? What same thing <margin>F</margin> do you see in both? Just as if you were to ask me why I call food, whether good or bad, by the name "food," I would surely answer that because both are the dry nourishment of the body, therefore I name both "food"—which you would also grant us, would you not? **HIPP:** I admit it. **SOCR:** And concerning drink, the same reason for answering would exist: that the moist nourishment of the body, whether it be good or bad, we call "drink," and in other things in the same way. Strive then to imitate me in answering thus. A good profit and likewise a bad profit—you call both "profit." What <margin>G</margin> do you see that is the same in good and bad profit, by reason of which you call both "profit"? But if you do not have an answer, then listen to me speaking. Do you call "profit" every possession which someone has acquired, either spending nothing at all or spending very little, while receiving more? **HIPP:** I seem to myself to call that profit. **SOCR:** Do you mean it in this way: if someone, spending nothing, has feasted abundantly, and from the feast has acquired a disease? **HIPP:** No, by Jove. **SOCR:** But having attained good health from a feast, would he have secured a profit or a loss? **HIPP:** A profit. **SOCR:** It is not, therefore, profit to acquire just anything. **HIPP:** Certainly not. **SOCR:** Is it not so, that he does not profit who <margin>H</margin> attains just whatever, whether good or bad? **HIPP:** It appears so. **SOCR:** Nor does he incur a loss who incurs whatever, whether good or bad? **HIPP:** So it seems to me. **SOCR:** Do you see then that you have revolved back to the same point? For profit appears to be a good, and loss truly an evil.

<summary>Socrates and his companion discuss the nature of profit, using a historical digression about the Athenian ruler Hipparchus to emphasize honesty. They conclude that profit, regardless of its source, must be an acquisition of something good, while loss is the acquisition of something evil.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the dialogue "Hipparchus" (concerning the nature of profit) and begins a new dialogue titled "The Lovers" (also known as "On Philosophy"). In the previous page of the Hipparchus, Socrates and his companion were discussing the moral character of the ruler Hipparchus and the definition of a "lover of profit."</meta>

# OF PLATO

<margin>A</margin>HIPPARCHUS: I am at a loss for what to say.
SOCRATES: And you are rightly at a loss. But answer me this further: if someone spends less and receives more, would you say he has made a profit?
HIPPARCHUS: I would say so, provided he does not profit from something evil; but if, for instance, by spending a small amount of gold or silver, he receives more back.
SOCRATES: Indeed, I will ask this in addition: if someone spends half a pound of gold and receives double that in silver, is that a profit or a loss?
HIPPARCHUS: A loss, certainly, Socrates! For he only receives double, instead of twelve times the value <note>original: "duodecuplo" / "δωδεκαστασίου." In ancient Athens, the value of gold was traditionally twelve times that of silver.</note>.
SOCRATES: But he still received "more." Is double not "more" than half?
HIPPARCHUS: Silver does not possess the same dignity and price as gold.
SOCRATES: Therefore, it seems we must add "value" to this idea of profit—specifically, its estimation and price. Now you say that silver, even when there is more of it, should not be valued as highly as gold; <margin>B</margin> and gold, even though there is less of it, is more precious and worthy.
HIPPARCHUS: Exactly; for that is how the matter stands.
SOCRATES: Thus, it is the value and dignity itself that constitutes profit, whether the thing be small or large. That which lacks value, then, lacks profit?
HIPPARCHUS: Certainly.
SOCRATES: And when you speak of what is precious and worthy, do you mean anything other than that which is "worthy of being acquired"?
HIPPARCHUS: I mean worthy of being acquired.
SOCRATES: And is that which is worthy of being sought useful or useless?
HIPPARCHUS: Useful.
SOCRATES: And is the useful not good?
HIPPARCHUS: It is.
SOCRATES: O bravest of men, have we not now concluded for the third or fourth time that profit is a good?
HIPPARCHUS: So it seems.
SOCRATES: Do you remember how this conversation began?
HIPPARCHUS: I believe so.
SOCRATES: Well, if you don't remember, I will remind you. It began when you denied that good men would accept just any profit, but only the good ones, never the bad.
HIPPARCHUS: Indeed.
<margin>C</margin>SOCRATES: And did not our reasoning force us to admit that all profits—whether large or small—are good?
HIPPARCHUS: It did indeed force me, Socrates, more than it actually persuaded me.
SOCRATES: Perhaps it will persuade you later. But for now, whether persuaded or however else you feel, do you agree with us that all profits, both large and small, are good?
HIPPARCHUS: I agree.
SOCRATES: And you admit that all good men want all good things?
HIPPARCHUS: I admit it.
SOCRATES: But you said that bad men also desire all profits, both small and large.
HIPPARCHUS: I did.
SOCRATES: Therefore, according to your own argument, would not all men—the good and the bad alike—be "lovers of profit" <term>lucricupidi / φιλοκερδεῖς (philokerdeis): literally those who are greedy for gain</term>?
HIPPARCHUS: It appears so.
SOCRATES: Then no one can rightly reproach another for being a lover of profit, since he himself is a lover of profit as well.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>HIPPARCHUS: I for my part am at a loss for what to say.
SOCRATES: It is not without reason that you are at a loss. But answer me this as well: if someone, having spent less, acquires more, do you say that is profit?
HIPPARCHUS: I do not mean if it is an evil thing; but if, having spent a smaller amount of gold or silver, he takes back more.
SOCRATES: And I shall ask this as well. Come now, if someone spends half a weight of gold and receives double that in silver, has he received a profit or a loss?
HIPPARCHUS: A loss surely, Socrates. For his gold stands at twelve times the value of the silver.
SOCRATES: Yet he has received more. Or is double not more than half?
HIPPARCHUS: Not in value, at least not silver compared to gold.
SOCRATES: It seems, then, that value must be present for there to be profit. Now you say that silver, though being more, is not worthy; but gold, though being less, you say is worthy.
HIPPARCHUS: Very much so. For it is thus.
<margin>B</margin>SOCRATES: Therefore, the worthy is profitable, whether it be small or large; but the unworthy is profitless.
HIPPARCHUS: Yes.
SOCRATES: And by "worthy," do you mean worthy of anything other than being possessed?
HIPPARCHUS: Yes, of being possessed.
SOCRATES: And by that which is worthy of being possessed, do you mean the useful or the useless?
HIPPARCHUS: The useful, surely.
SOCRATES: And is the useful not good?
HIPPARCHUS: Yes.
SOCRATES: Therefore, O most courageous of all, has it not come back to us for the fourth time, by agreement, that the profitable is good?
HIPPARCHUS: It seems so.
SOCRATES: Do you remember where this argument of ours came from?
HIPPARCHUS: I think so.
SOCRATES: If not, I will remind you. You disputed with me, saying that good men do not wish to gain all profits, but only some, and not the wicked ones.
HIPPARCHUS: Yes.
SOCRATES: Then did the argument not force us to agree that all profits, both small and large, are good?
HIPPARCHUS: It did force me, Socrates, more than it persuaded me.
<margin>C</margin>SOCRATES: But perhaps after this it might even persuade you. For now, whether you are persuaded or however you are disposed, you at least agree with us that all profits are good, both small and large?
HIPPARCHUS: I do agree.
SOCRATES: And you agree that good men want all good things, every one of them?
HIPPARCHUS: I agree.
SOCRATES: But indeed, you said that the wicked love both small and large profits.
HIPPARCHUS: I said so.
SOCRATES: Therefore, according to your argument, all men would be lovers of profit, both the good and the wicked.
HIPPARCHUS: So it appears.
SOCRATES: Therefore, it is not right to reproach anyone for being a lover of profit. For it happens that the one who reproaches is also such a person himself.

# THE LOVERS, OR ON PHILOSOPHY.
# ΕΡΑΣΤΑΙ, Η ΠΕΡΙ ΦΙΛΟΣΟΦΙΑΣ.

-> SUMMARY OF THE DIALOGUE. *What a philosopher is and what his duty consists of is taught here. The duty of a philosopher is to know divine things and to govern human affairs: the former comprises contemplative philosophy, the latter active philosophy. Wisdom <note>Latin: "sapientia"</note> leads to the contemplative, while prudence and justice lead to the active. First, however, two opinions of others are refuted. The first is of those who say the philosopher’s duty is to learn as many things as possible; the second is that of Hipparchus the sophist, who wants philosophy to be a mastery of all the arts.* <-

---

<columns>2</columns>

-> SOCRATES. <-

<margin>D</margin>I entered the school of Dionysius the Grammarian <note>A teacher of "letters" or basic literacy and literature</note> and I saw there certain youths who seemed to be of noble character and born of famous parents, and with them were their admirers. There happened to be two young men arguing with each other; exactly what the argument was about, I did not quite catch. However, they appeared to be disputing about Anaxagoras or Oenopides <note>Anaxagoras was a famous philosopher who studied the cosmos; Oenopides of Chios was a mathematician and astronomer</note>; at any rate, they appeared to be drawing circles and were depicting certain inclinations of the sphere <note>the tilt of the earth's axis or the zodiac</note>, leaning on their elbows and very intent. I then nudged the admirer of one of them, next to whom I was sitting, and asked him what the two youths were so serious about. I said, "Is it some great and beautiful thing upon which they have placed such study?" But he replied, <margin>E</margin> "What 'great and beautiful' thing? They are just babbling about celestial matters and playing the fool with their 'philosophizing'." I was surprised by his answer and said, "O young man, does it seem shameful to you to practice philosophy? Why do you speak so bitterly?" But the other man—for he happened to be sitting nearby, a rival for the youth's affections—having heard me questioning and the other answering, said, "It is no use to you, Socrates, to ask this man if he thinks philosophy is shameful or not. Don't you see that he has spent his whole life in a state of bloating, stuffing himself, and sleeping? Do you really believe he would give you any answer other than that philosophy is shameful?" Now this man <margin>F</margin> was one of those lovers devoted to music <note>In this context, "music" refers to all intellectual and cultural arts</note>, while the other, whom he was mocking, was devoted to gymnastics <note>Physical training and athletics</note>. It seemed to me that I should let the first man go, as he did not even pretend to be experienced in words but rather in deeds. Instead, I decided I should question the one who wanted to appear wiser, so that if I could, I might gain some benefit from him. I said, therefore, that I had proposed the question for everyone: "If you think you can answer this better than he, I ask you..."

<column-break/>

-> SOCRATES. <-

<margin>D</margin>I went into the school of Dionysius the teacher of letters, and I saw there the most respectable-looking of the youths and those of well-known fathers, and their lovers. There happened to be two striplings arguing; about what, I did not clearly hear. They seemed, however, to be arguing about Anaxagoras or Oenopides. At any rate, they were seen drawing circles, and they were imitating certain inclinations with their hands, leaning over and being very earnest. And I—for I was sitting by the lover of one of them—nudged him with my elbow and asked what the two striplings were so earnest about; and I said, "Is it perhaps some great and beautiful thing about which they have made such a fuss?" But he <margin>E</margin> said, "What 'great and beautiful' thing? These guys are just babbling about the things in the sky, talking nonsense as they philosophize." And I, wondering at his answer, said, "Young man, does it seem shameful to you to philosophize? Or why do you speak so harshly?" And the other (for he happened to be sitting near them, being a rival lover), hearing me asking and the other answering, said, "It is not to your advantage, Socrates, to ask this man if he thinks philosophy is shameful. Or do you not know him, that he has spent his whole life being past his prime, stuffing himself, and sleeping? So what else do you think he will answer you, except that philosophy is shameful?" Now <margin>F</margin> this one of the two lovers had spent his time on music; but the other, whom he was insulting, on gymnastics. And it seemed to me that I ought to let the other one go, the one being questioned, because he himself did not claim to be experienced in words, but in deeds; but I should question the one who made himself out to be wiser, so that if I were able, I might be benefited by him. I said then that the question had been put forward in common: "If you think you would answer better than this man, I ask you..."
