--- Page 37 ---
<meta>This page continues the transition from the previous dialogue, "Hipparchus," into a new dialogue titled "The Lovers" (also known as the *Erastai* or *Amatores*). This work, often attributed to Plato, explores the definition of philosophy through a conversation between Socrates and two rival suitors—one who prides himself on intellectual "polymathy" (learning many things) and another who focuses on physical training.</meta>

# THE LOVERS

->[Signature: A iii]<-
<meta>catchword: maximè</meta>

<margin>A</margin> I asked the same thing as before: whether he thought that to practice philosophy was a noble thing, or not. While we were saying these things, the two youths overheard us and stood still; ceasing their own quarrel, they became our audience. I do not know what the lovers felt, but I myself was struck with awe—for I am always struck by those who are young and beautiful. It seemed to me that the other youth was in no less a state of anxiety than I; nevertheless, he answered me quite ambitiously. "If ever, Socrates," he said, "I thought practicing philosophy was a shameful thing, I would not consider myself a human being, nor anyone else so disposed." He said this as a riddle aimed at his rival, speaking in a loud voice so that his favorite might hear him. "So," I said, "it seems to you that practicing philosophy is noble?" "Most certainly," he replied.

<margin>B</margin> "What then?" I asked. "Does it seem possible to you to know whether a thing is shameful or noble if one does not know from the start what that thing is?" He said it was not. "Do you know then," I asked, "what it is to practice philosophy?" "Certainly," he said. "What is it then?" I asked. "What else," he replied, "than that which follows Solon's saying? For Solon said somewhere: *I grow old ever learning many things.* <note>original Greek: "Γηράσκω δ᾽ αἰεὶ πολλὰ διδασκόμενος." Solon was one of the Seven Sages of Greece; this quote suggests that wisdom comes from a lifetime of accumulating diverse knowledge.</note> And it seems to me that he who intends to be a philosopher must always be learning something in this way, whether he be young or old, so that he may learn as many things as possible in his life." At first, it seemed to me he had said something significant, but then, reflecting on it, I asked him if he considered philosophy to be the same as 'much-learning' <note>term: <term>Polymathy</term> (from the Greek *polymathia*), meaning the knowledge of many different subjects.</note>. And he said, "Entirely so." <margin>C</margin> "And do you think philosophy is only noble, or also good?" I asked. "Also good," he said, "very much so." "Do you see this quality as unique to philosophy, or does it seem to you to be the same in other things? For instance, do you think the 'love of exercise' <note>term: <term>Gymnastics</term> (Greek: *philogymnasia*), which in ancient Greece referred to the whole system of physical education and athletics.</note> is not only noble, but also good? Or not?" He replied quite ironically to the argument he had just made: "I say this so that you might never say, Socrates, that I do not confess it to be both noble and good. Do you not also consider 'much-labor' in the gymnasiums to be the love of exercise?" And he said, "Certainly; just as in practicing philosophy, I consider 'much-learning' to be philosophy." And I said, <margin>D</margin> "Do those who love exercise desire anything else than that which will make their bodies be in good condition?" "That is it," he said. "Do 'many labors' then," I asked, "make the body be in good condition?" "How," he said, "could a body be in good condition from only a few labors?"

<margin>E</margin> At this point, I thought I should rouse the 'lover of exercise' <note>The second youth, who favored physical training over intellectual study.</note> so that he might help me with his experience in gymnastics. So I asked him, "Why are you silent, my good man, while he says these things? Do you also think that men have good bodies from many labors, or from moderate ones?" "I, Socrates," he said, "thought it was a well-known saying even now, that moderate labors <note>original: "μέτριοι πόνοι" / "moderati labores." The concept of the 'mean' or moderation is a central theme in Greek ethics.</note> produce a good condition of the body." "How so?" I asked. "Do you not see a man who is sleepless, without food, with a neck unbowed <note>original: "ἄσφαγόν τινα αὐχένον" / "ceruicéque molli." The Greek suggests a neck that hasn't been sacrificed or broken, implying a rigid, wasted, or strained appearance from over-study.</note>, and thin—just like you people?" And when he said this, the youths laughed, and the other one blushed. Then I said, "What then? Do you now agree that it is neither many nor few labors that make men's bodies in good condition, but the moderate ones? Or will you fight us both on this point?" He replied, "Against him, I would gladly compete, and I know I would be able to defend my position, even if it were weaker than it is. But with you, I have no need to contend against my own opinion. I confess that it is not many, but moderate exercises that provide a good habit of body to <margin>F</margin> men." "And what about food?" I asked. "Moderate or much?" He agreed on moderate food as well. Furthermore, I compelled him to admit that in all other things concerning the body, the moderate is most beneficial, and neither the 'many' nor the 'few.' And he agreed with me on the moderate. "And what of the things concerning the soul?" I asked. "Are the moderate things beneficial, or the immoderate?" "The moderate," he said. "And are not the subjects of study among the things applied to the soul?" He agreed. "Therefore, of these studies, the moderate ones bring utility, but not the 'many'?" He consented.

<margin>G</margin> "Whom then should we rightly ask which labors and foods are moderate for the body?" We three agreed it would be a physician or a gymnastic trainer. "And whom should we ask about the sowing of seeds, as to what amount is moderate?" We agreed on the farmer. "But concerning the planting and sowing of studies in the soul, whom should we rightly ask how many and what kind are moderate?" At this point, we were all full of confusion. And I, joking with them, said, "Do you wish, since we are in confusion, that we ask these youths? Or perhaps we are ashamed, just as Homer says the suitors were, not deigning that there should be anyone else who could string the bow?" <note>A reference to the *Odyssey*, where the suitors of Penelope are unable to string the great bow of Odysseus, a task requiring specific strength and skill rather than just 'much' effort.</note> Since they seemed discouraged by the argument, I tried to investigate another way, and said, <margin>H</margin> "What sort of studies should we guess those are which the philosopher must learn, since he should follow neither 'all' nor 'many'?" The 'wiser' one replied and said that these studies are the most beautiful and most fitting for the soul, from which one might attain the greatest glory in philosophy; and one would attain the greatest glory if he appeared to be skilled in all arts—or if not all, then at least as many as possible, and especially the most noteworthy.

<column-break/>

[This column contains the Latin translation of the preceding Greek text. To maintain the reader's experience of the bilingual layout, the English translation continues below, reflecting the Latin phrasing where it varies slightly.]

...I ask whether it seems that practicing philosophy is noble, or otherwise?
<margin>A</margin> While we were saying these things, the youths approached, and having set aside the contention that was between them, they prepared themselves in silence to hear the things we were discussing. What happened to the lovers, I do not know; I certainly was amazed. For I am always amazed by what is new and beautiful. It seemed to me that the one was no less eager to compete, but indeed he answered me, and quite ambitiously at that. "If ever, O Socrates, I should think practicing philosophy to be base, I would not think myself a man, nor anyone else so affected." Hinting at his rival, he said these things in such a voice that his friends could overhear. Here I said, "Does practicing philosophy then seem noble to you?" "Very much so," he said. <margin>B</margin> "What then," I said, "does it seem possible to you that anyone should know if something is base or noble, unless he first knows what the thing itself is?" "No." "Do you know then," I said, "that practicing philosophy is something?" "I do know." "What is it?" "What else than according to Solon? For Solon said somewhere: *Learning many things continually, old age comes.* And it seems to me that he who would be a philosopher ought always to learn something in this way, whether he be young or old, so that he may learn as many things as possible in life." And at first he seemed to me to have said something. Then, reflecting with myself, I asked whether philosophy seemed to him the same as learning many things. And he said, "Altogether." "Do you think," I asked, "that philosophy is something noble alone, or also good?" "Also good," he said. <margin>C</margin> "Do you make that proper to philosophy alone, or do you attribute it to others in the same way: as for example, the study of gymnastics—is it not only noble, but also good?" Then that one, playing, brought forth two points. "Against this man," he said, "I say it is neither; but against you, O Socrates, I confess it is both noble and good together." "Therefore, in the gymnasiums, do you also think that much labor is the study of gymnastics?" "Very much so," he said, "just as in practicing philosophy, I think learning many things is philosophy." But I said, <margin>D</margin> "Do you believe those studious of gymnastics desire anything else than that their bodies be in good condition?" "That very thing," he said. "Do many labors produce a good condition of the body?" "By what means," he said, "could a robust body be made from few labors?"

Here it seemed to me that the gymnast should be provoked, who might bring me help on account of his skill in gymnastics. Him <margin>E</margin> therefore I questioned: "Why, best of men, are you silent while he speaks? Does it also seem to you that men acquire strength from many labors rather than from moderate ones?" "Indeed, O Socrates, I seem to see that which is commonly said, namely that the body is in good condition from moderate things." "From where do you see this?" I asked. "Do they not rather produce a man who is sleepless and nauseated, with a soft neck and thinned by cares?" And when he had nodded to these things, the youths were delighted and laughed. But the other one blushed. Then I said, "What about you then? Do you concede that neither small nor great labors produce a good habit of body, but moderate ones? Or do you resist us two, who are of the same opinion?" "Gladly indeed," he said, "I would resist him, and I would be strong enough to defend what I proposed against him, even if I had a less valid cause. For he is of no worth. But with you, it is not fitting to contend too insolently: I confess therefore, that not many, but tempered exercises provide a good habit of body to <margin>F</margin> men." "And food," I said, "much or moderate?" "And for you," he said <note>meaning: "I agree with you."</note>. Moreover, I compelled him to concede all other things which concern the body, that the moderate indeed benefit most, but the few or the excessive benefit nothing. And he confessed that moderate things help. "But what things regard the soul," I said, "when moderate things are applied, do they conduct more [to good] or the immoderate?" "The moderate." "Are not disciplines <note>term: <term>Disciplines</term> (Latin: *disciplinae*), here used to mean subjects of study or branches of knowledge.</note> among those things which are applied to and confer upon the soul?" He agreed. "Therefore, do those disciplines which are tempered, and not those which are many, bring utility?" He confessed. <margin>G</margin> "Whom then is it rightly fitting to ask what kind of labors and foods are accommodated to bodies?" "In this I think we three agree, namely a physician or a trainer should be asked." "But whom concerning the scattering of seeds, as to how much is commodious?" "It is agreeable to ask a farmer." "But indeed, concerning the sowing and planting of disciplines in the soul, whom should we rightly question, as to what kind and how many suffice?" Here, when we were full of ambiguity, I said jokingly, "Do you wish, since we are ambiguous in this, that we ask these youths? Or perhaps we blush, just as Homer introduces the suitors, when they were unwilling that anyone else besides themselves should intend the bow?" <margin>H</margin> But when they seemed to bear it heavily, I began to investigate by another way: "What kind of things," I said, "shall we conjecture those must be which it behooves a philosopher to learn, since he ought to follow neither all nor many?" Answering then, that wiser one said, "They are the most beautiful, and the disciplines most congruous to the soul are those from which he may follow the greatest glory in philosophy; but to attain the greatest glory, if he be skilled in all arts; or if less than all, at least of most, and especially those..."

<summary>In this opening of "The Lovers," Socrates challenges a youth's definition of philosophy as "polymathy" (learning many things), using the analogy of physical exercise to argue that moderation, rather than sheer quantity, is what leads to excellence in both body and soul.</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Solon, philosophy, gymnastics, moderation, polymathy, soul, body, Homer, pedagogy</keywords>

# P L A T O ’ S

<margin>A</margin> "These things are worthy of esteem," he said, "learning those things above all others which befit free-born men—those things involving the exercise of the intellect, rather than the labor of the hands." "Then," I said, "do you mean it in the same way it happens in the crafts? For in building, you might buy a lead workman for five or six minae <note>original: "minis". A mina was a significant unit of currency, roughly 100 drachmae; five minae was the price of a skilled slave.</note> at most, but an architect <term>architectum (Greek: ἀρχιτέκτονα)</term> <note>In antiquity, an architect was a "master-builder" who directed others rather than performing manual labor.</note> you could not buy for even ten thousand drachmae. Indeed, throughout all of Greece, such men are quite rare. Is this the sort of thing you mean?" Having heard me, he agreed that this was exactly what he meant. I then asked him whether it was possible for the same person to learn just two such arts in this way, let alone many great ones. And he replied:

<margin>B</margin> "Do not think, Socrates, that I am saying a philosopher must pursue every single art to the highest degree, as the craftsmen do. Rather, as befits an educated and free man, he should be able to follow along with what is produced by every craftsman better than anyone else present, and to contribute his own opinion, so that he always appears to be the most elegant and wisest of all in whatever is being said or done regarding the arts." And I—for I was still uncertain as to where his argument was heading—said: "Do I understand what sort of man you say the philosopher is? For you seem to describe someone like the pentathletes <note>original: "pentathli". Athletes who competed in five different events: running, jumping, discus, javelin, and wrestling.</note> in a competition compared to runners or javelin-throwers. For those pentathletes are inferior

<margin>C</margin> to the specialists in their particular contests and hold the second place compared to them, but they are the first and victors among the other, ordinary athletes. Perhaps you are saying that the study of philosophy produces this effect in those who pursue it: they are surpassed in understanding of a specific art by those who are supreme in that craft, holding second place, but they surpass all others. Thus, the philosopher exists as a kind of 'second-best' man in every faculty. This seems to be the kind of person you are describing." "You have understood my point well, Socrates," he said, "by comparing the philosopher to the pentathlete. For he is truly the kind of person who does not wish to be a slave to any one business, nor to labor over any one thing to the point of absolute precision—

<margin>D</margin> lest, through the exact diligence given to one thing, he be surpassed in all others as the craftsmen are. Instead, he touches upon all things in a moderate and balanced way." After this answer, desiring to know more clearly what he meant, I said: "Do you think good men are useful or useless?" "Useful, Socrates," he replied. "If the good are useful, then are not the bad useless?" He agreed. "What then? Do you think philosophers are useful or useless men?" At this, he asserted that philosophers were the most useful of all. "Come then, let us see if what you say is true: how are these 'second-best' men useful to us? For it is clear

<margin>E</margin> that the philosopher is inferior to every specialized craftsman." He nodded. "Tell me then," I said, "if you or one of your dearest friends fell ill, would you bring this 'second-best' philosopher into your house to care for your health, or a doctor?" "Both," he said. "Do not say 'both' to me," I replied, "but which one rather, and first?" "No one would doubt," he said, "that the doctor is to be preferred both more and earlier." "What about in a ship tossed by waves? Would you entrust yourself and your property to the pilot or to the philosopher?" "To the pilot," he said. "And so in all other matters, as long as a craftsman is present, will there be no place for the philosopher?" "It appears so," he said. "The philosopher, then, is useless whenever craftsmen are available. Yet we agreed that good men are useful and bad men are useless." He was forced to admit it. "What then should I ask

<margin>F</margin> you next? Or is it perhaps a bit rude to inquire further?" "Ask whatever you like," he said. "I seek nothing else," I said, "except to review what has already been stated. It stands like this: we agreed that philosophy is a noble thing, and that there are philosophers, and that they are good, and that the good are useful, while the bad are useless. Then we agreed that as long as craftsmen are present, philosophers are useless, and that craftsmen are always present. Was this not granted?" "It was," he said. "We must admit then, it seems, according to your argument—if indeed practicing philosophy is to be knowledgeable in the arts in the way you described—that such men are bad and useless as long as arts exist among men. But surely, my friend, it is not so. Practicing philosophy is not being busily occupied with the arts, nor stooping over many businesses, nor learning many things, but something else entirely.

<margin>G</margin> Indeed, I thought this was a disgrace, and that those who occupy themselves with the manual arts were called 'mechanical' <note>original Latin: "mechanicos"; Greek: "βαναύσους" (banausos). This term carried a strong social stigma, referring to labor that supposedly degraded the soul and body.</note>. We shall understand more clearly if I am telling the truth or not if you answer this: Who knows how to rightly break horses? Is it those who make them better, or others?" "Those who make them better." "What about dogs? Do not those who know how to make them better also know how to rightly discipline them?" "Entirely so." "Therefore, the same art both makes them better and disciplines them rightly?" "The same." "What then? Does the art that makes them better and disciplines them also distinguish the good from the bad, or is it another?" "The same," he said. "Will you then," I asked, "agree to the same regarding men? That the art which makes men best is the same

<margin>H</margin> that also rightly restrains them and distinguishes who are good and who are bad?" "Certainly," he said. "And does that which knows how to distinguish one, also know how to distinguish many? And that which knows many, also know one?" "Yes." "And is it the same for horses and all other things?" "I agree," he said. "What—"

<meta>This page concludes the dialogue "The Lovers" (Amatores), where Socrates successfully argues that philosophy is not a broad, shallow knowledge of many crafts (polymathy), but rather the master science of justice and self-knowledge. # T H E L O V E R S

<margin>A</margin> "Is it not the judicial art that correctly punishes those who act lawlessly and break the laws in our cities?" "Indeed," he said. "And do you call justice anything other than this art?" "No, nothing else." "Is it not also true that the same art by which men punish correctly is the same one by which they recognize the good and the wicked?" "It is the same." "And whoever can recognize one person can surely recognize many?" "He can." "And he who is ignorant of the many must also be ignorant of the one?" "He agreed." "If, then, a horse <note>original: "equus". Socrates uses analogies of animals to show that knowledge of a species' nature is required for self-knowledge.</note> were ignorant of which horses were good or bad, would he not also be ignorant of what sort of creature he himself is?" "He conceded he would." "And if an ox did not know which oxen were good or bad, would it not also be ignorant of its own nature?" "Yes," he said. "And would it be the same for a dog?" "He confessed it would." "But what of a man? 

<margin>B</margin> If a man is ignorant of which men are good or bad, is he not also ignorant of himself—whether he is good or bad—since he himself is a man?" "He nodded in agreement." "And is being ignorant of oneself the same as being wise, or is it a lack of wisdom?" "It is a lack of wisdom." "Therefore, to know oneself is to be wise <term>prudentia (Greek: σωφροσύνη)</term> <note>While often translated as 'temperance' or 'moderation,' in this context it refers to the 'self-mastery' that comes from knowing one's own nature.</note>." "I agree," he said. "This, it seems, is what the inscription at Delphi <note>The famous maxim "Gnothi Seauton" or "Know Thyself."</note> commands: to practice wisdom and justice." "It appears so." "And by this same art, we also know how to govern others correctly?" "He nodded." "So, the art by which we govern correctly is justice, but the art by which we discern ourselves and others is wisdom?" "It seems so," he said. "Therefore, justice and wisdom are the same thing?" "It appears so." "And cities are best governed when those who do wrong are punished." "That is true." "So this is also the political science." 

<margin>C</margin> "He agreed." "What then? When one man correctly governs a city, is he not called a tyrant or a king?" "I agree." "And does he not govern by the royal or tyrannical art?" "Certainly." "Are these arts then the same as those we mentioned before?" "They appear to be." "And when one man correctly manages a household, what is he called? Is he not a householder <term>oeconomus</term> or a master?" "Yes." "Does he govern his household well by means of justice, or by some other art?" "By justice." "It seems then that the king, the tyrant, the politician, the householder, the master, the wise man, and the just man are all one and the same. And there is but one single art: the royal, the tyrannical, the political, the master’s art, the art of household management, justice, and wisdom." "It appears so." "Is it then shameful for a philosopher 

<margin>D</margin> to be unable to follow along or contribute anything when a doctor speaks about the sick, or any other craftsman speaks?" "And when a judge, or a king, or any of those we just listed speaks, is it not even more shameful for him not to be able to follow or contribute to the conversation?" "How could it not be shameful, Socrates," he asked, "to have nothing to contribute to matters of such great importance?" "Should we say then," I asked, "that in these matters too the philosopher is like a pentathlete <note>original: "pentathlum". An athlete who competes in five events; usually good at all, but best at none.</note>—always taking second place and being useless as long as a specialist is present? Or should he first and foremost not entrust his own house to another, nor take second place in that, but rather be the one who punishes and judges correctly if his home is to be well-managed?" "He agreed with me." "Then, whether his friends entrust him with an arbitration, or the city commands him to judge or decide a matter, would it not be shameful, my friend, to appear in second or third place rather than acting as the leader?" "So it seems to me," he said. "It is far from the truth, then, my good man, that philosophy is merely the learning of many things or the meddling in various crafts." When I said this, the "wise" man, overcome with shame by the argument, remained silent. But the unlearned man affirmed that it was so, and all the others praised what had been said.

### T H E A G E S  O R  O N  W I S D O M ,  Midwifery.

> **SUMMARY OF THE DIALOGUE.** *A man named Demodocus, being urged by his son Theages to hand him over to some teacher to learn wisdom, approaches Socrates. Socrates counsels them, bringing the son into the conversation. Socrates begins by stating that nothing is more important than the correct education of the youth, who are the "seedbed" of the republic. He defines wisdom as a noble science—the primary and chief of all sciences—concerned with maintaining human society through reason and just governance, thereby avoiding the lack of self-control which is a plague to mankind. He concludes that while practical wisdom is learned through the company of wise men, the true power to achieve it depends on God, who alone makes such human association fruitful.*

->THEAGES.<-

->THEAGES.<-

<margin>E</margin> **DEMODOCUS:** I had need, Socrates, to speak with you privately about certain matters, if you have the leisure—and even if you have some business, provided it is not too great, I would ask you to find the time for my sake. **SOCRATES:** I happen to be at leisure in any case, and especially for your sake. If there is anything you wish to say, you may. <margin>F</margin> **DEMOD.:** Shall we then step aside here into the Portico of Zeus the Liberator? **SOCR.:** If it pleases you. **DEMOD.:** Let us go then, Socrates. All plants seem to follow the same nature, whether they spring from the earth or are animals—including man himself. For those of us who till the soil, it is easiest to prepare everything before we plant and even to do the planting itself. But once that which we have planted begins to live, after that...

# PLATO

...it is said, it lives: then its care is varied and difficult: and so it seems among men. From my own circumstances, I infer the rest. Indeed, the planting—or perhaps I should say the procreation—of this son of mine was the easiest of all things; however, his education has been difficult and always full of fear, for I have always felt a great dread on his account. Many other things could be said about this, but specifically the desire that now possesses him troubles me greatly. It is not an ignoble desire, yet it is of such a kind that it can be deceptive. For he desires, Socrates, as he himself says, to become wise. <margin>A</margin> And as it seems to me, some of his peers from the same district come into the city and repeat certain discourses to him, which have stirred him up. He has begun to emulate them and has long been a burden to me, wanting me to take care of him and pay money to some <term>sophist</term> <note>Sophists were professional teachers in ancient Greece who traveled from city to city, charging fees to teach rhetoric and "wisdom."</note> who might make him wise. <margin>B</margin> For my part, I care little for the money, but I believe that because of this pursuit, he will incur no small danger. Up until now, I have resisted him by offering consolation; but when I can no longer do so, I thought it worthwhile to comply with him, so that he does not frequently associate with others without me and become corrupted. Now, however, we are setting out for this very purpose: to commend him to one of those who are considered sophists. You, therefore, have met us most opportunely, for I greatly desired you as a counselor in this matter. Thus, if you have anything you can advise me regarding what you have heard, it is both permitted and beneficial.
<margin>C</margin> **SOC.** Moreover, Demodocus, there is a common saying that "counsel is a sacred thing" <note>original: "consilium res sacra est". This reflects the high value Socrates placed on honest advice in education.</note>. And if ever there was one, this is foremost among the things you ask. For there is nothing more divine about which one might consult than the education of oneself and one's family. First, then, let us agree on what we think this thing is that we are consulting about, lest—as often happens—I think it is one thing and you think it is another, and we then find ourselves far apart; we would look ridiculous, both I who give the advice and you who ask for it, having agreed on nothing. **DEMOD.** You seem to speak rightly to me, Socrates. Therefore, I think we should do as you say. **SOC.** Rightly, I say, yet not altogether rightly: <margin>D</margin> for I will change that slightly. I suspect that perhaps this young man desires something other than what we supposed; for if he wants something else, we would be acting quite absurdly by consulting about something different. It seems most right to me, then, starting from here, that we ask him what it is he specifically intends. **DEMOD.** That seems best, as you say. **SOC.** Tell me then, what is the boy's fair name? By what name shall we call him? **DEMOD.** Theages, Socrates. **SOC.** You have given your son a beautiful and divine name <note>original: "Theages". The name roughly translates to "God-led" or "Divine-born," which Socrates finds auspicious for a dialogue on wisdom.</note>, Demodocus. But tell me, Theages, do you desire to be wise? And do you think it worthy for this father of yours to find a man who, through his company, can make you wise? <margin>E</margin> **THE.** I do. **SOC.** And do you call those who possess knowledge "wise," whatever it is they may know, or not? **THE.** Those with knowledge, certainly. **SOC.** What then? Did your father not teach you what the sons of noblemen are taught here? Specifically: letters <note>reading and writing</note>, playing the lyre, wrestling, and other contests? **THE.** He did. **SOC.** Do you think you still lack some knowledge about which it would be proper for your father to take care for your sake? **THE.** I do. **SOC.** What then is it? Tell us, so that we may gratify you. **THE.** This man also knows, Socrates, since I have told him very often, but he purposely says these things with you now as if he did not know what I desire. For in this way, and in many other things, he fights with me and does not want to hand me over to anyone. **SOC.** But what you have said so far against him lacks witnesses; now, however, take me as your witness and recount it again in my presence. What is this wisdom that you seek? Come, if you desired that by which men govern ships, and I asked you, "Theages, lacking what wisdom are you angry with your father because he does not hand you over to those by whom you can be made wise?", what would you answer? Would it not be the art of navigation <note>original: "gubernatoriam"</note>? **THE.** Certainly. **SOC.** And if you desired to become learned in that by which chariots are driven, and were angry with your father, and I asked what it was, would you not answer "charioteering" <note>original: "aurigariam"</note>? **THE.** Indeed. **SOC.** But does this which you now desire have a name, or not? **THE.** I believe it does. **SOC.** Do you then know it, but are ignorant of its name? Or do you know the name as well? **THE.** I know the name too. **SOC.** Tell us then, what is it? **THE.** What other name could one say fits this, Socrates, than "wisdom"? **SOC.** Is not charioteering also a wisdom? Or does it seem like ignorance to you? **THE.** By no means. **SOC.** Is it not a wisdom? **THE.** A wisdom. <margin>H</margin> **SOC.** For what do we use it? Is it not that by which we know how to rule teams of horses? **THE.** Truly. **SOC.** And navigation, is that not also a wisdom? **THE.** So it seems to me. **SOC.** Is it not that by which we govern ships? **THE.** That indeed. **SOC.** And what is that wisdom which you now desire? What do we know how to govern once we have attained it? **THE.** It seems to me it is that by which we know how to rule men. **SOC.** Do you mean those who are sick? **THE.** Not at all. **SOC.** For that is medicine, is it not? **THE.** It is. **SOC.** But is it that by which we know how to lead those who sing in choirs? **THE.** By no means. **SOC.** For that is music. **THE.** Yes. **SOC.**

<column-break/>

...care for this [living thing] becomes great, hard, and difficult. And so it seems to be regarding men. From my own evidence, I make inferences about other things as well. For the planting of this son of mine—or the begetting of children, if one should call it that—was the easiest of all things; but his upbringing is difficult and always full of fear, as I am always afraid for him. Many other things could be said, but the current desire that is present in him terrifies me. It is not an ignoble desire, but it is a dangerous one. For he desires, Socrates, as he says, <margin>A</margin> to become wise. I believe that some of his peers and fellow-townsmen, coming down into the city and remembering certain speeches, have stirred him up; he has emulated them, and for a long time now has been causing me <margin>B</margin> trouble, demanding that I take care of him and pay money to one of the sophists who will make him wise. I care less about the money, but I believe he is going into no small danger where he is rushing. For a time I held him back by comforting him; but since I am no longer able, I believe it is best to obey him, lest he be corrupted by associating with someone frequently without me. Now, therefore, I have come for this very reason: to introduce him to one of those who seem to be sophists. You have appeared to us most fortunately, for you are the one I would most wish to consult with when about to act in such matters. If you have any advice to give from <margin>C</margin> what you have heard, it is both possible and necessary. **SOC.** Indeed, Demodocus, counsel is said to be a sacred thing <note>original: "συμβουλὴ ἱερὸν χρῆμα εἶναι"</note>; if any other thing is sacred, this would be it, about which you now seek counsel. For there is nothing more divine about which a man could deliberate than the education of himself and his household. First, then, let you and I agree on what we think this thing is that we are deliberating about, lest I take it to be one thing and you another, and then later in our conversation we realize we are being ridiculous, I who advise and you who are advised, having no common understanding. **DEMO.** You seem to me to speak correctly, Socrates, and so we must do. **SOC.** I do speak correctly, <margin>D</margin> but not entirely. For I will change my mind a little. I am thinking that perhaps this lad does not desire what we think he desires, but something else; then we would be even more absurd, deliberating about something else. It seems most correct to me to start from this point: by inquiring what it is he desires. **DEMO.** It is likely, then, that it is best as you say. **SOC.** Tell me then, what is the youth’s fine name? What shall we call him? **DEMO.** Theages is his name, Socrates. **SOC.** You have given your son a fine and holy name, Demodocus. Tell me then, Theages, do you say you desire to become wise, and do you <margin>E</margin> expect this father of yours to find the company of some man who will make you wise? **THE.** Yes. **SOC.** And do you call those who have knowledge "wise," in whatever they have knowledge of, or those who do not? **THE.** Those with knowledge, I say. **SOC.** What then? Did your father not teach you and educate you in what others here are educated, the sons of fine and good fathers? Such as letters, and lyre-playing, and wrestling, and the other contests? **THE.** He did. **SOC.** Do you still think you lack some knowledge which it is proper for your father to look after for you? **THE.** I do. **SOC.** What is it? Tell us also, so that we may favor you. **THE.** He knows it too, Socrates, since I have told him many times. But he says these things to you on purpose, as if he did not know what I desire. For he fights against me on these and other points and is unwilling to introduce me to anyone. **SOC.** But the things you said before to your father were said without a witness; now make me a witness, and declare before me what this wisdom is that you desire. For come: if you desired that by which men navigate ships, and I asked you, "Theages, lacking what wisdom do you blame your father because he is unwilling to introduce you to those from whom you might become wise?", what would you answer me? That it was what? Is it not navigation? **THE.** Yes. **SOC.** And if you desired the wisdom by which men drive chariots, and then blamed your father, and I in turn asked what this wisdom was, what would you answer it was? Is it not charioteering? **THE.** Yes. **SOC.** And this which you now happen to desire, is it nameless, or does it have a name? **THE.** I believe it has one. **SOC.** Do you know it, though you do not know the name? Or the name as well? **THE.** The name as well. **SOC.** What is it then? Tell me. **THE.** What other name, Socrates, would anyone say it has, but "wisdom"? **SOC.** Is not charioteering also a wisdom? Or does it seem to you to be ignorance? **THE.** Not to me. **SOC.** But wisdom? **THE.** Yes. **SOC.** For what do we use it? Is it not that by which we know how <margin>H</margin> to rule teams of horses? **THE.** Yes. **SOC.** And is not navigation also a wisdom? **THE.** So it seems to me. **SOC.** Is it not this by which we know how to rule ships? **THE.** This indeed. **SOC.** And this wisdom which you desire, what is it? That by which we know how to rule what? **THE.** It seems to me, that of men. **SOC.** Is it that of the sick? **THE.** Certainly not. **SOC.** For that is medicine, is it not? **THE.** Yes. **SOC.** But that by which we know how to rule those who sing in choirs? **THE.** No. **SOC.** This is music.

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and the young Theages, who is accompanied by his father, Demodocus. In the previous section, Demodocus expressed concern that his son has been "corrupted" by a desire for wisdom and wants to find a teacher. Socrates now begins his characteristic "cross-examination" to determine exactly what kind of wisdom Theages is seeking.</meta>

# THEAGES

<margin>A</margin> **SOCRATES:** But is it the wisdom by which we know how to lead those who are competing?
**THEAGES:** Not at all.
**SOCRATES:** For that is the art of gymnastics.
**THEAGES:** It is.
**SOCRATES:** Then try to describe the wisdom by what the people are doing, just as I did with the previous examples.
**THEAGES:** It seems to me, at least, to be the wisdom used for those who are in the city.
**SOCRATES:** Are there not also sick people in the city?
**THEAGES:** Yes.
**SOCRATES:** I do not mean just those, but all who are involved in the city.
**SOCRATES:** I think I understand the art you mean. You do not seem to mean the one by which we know how to lead reapers, or vintagers, or those who plant, or sow, or thresh; for that is agriculture, the art that governs these things. Is it not?
**THEAGES:** Yes.
**SOCRATES:** <margin>B</margin> Nor again is it the art of leading those who saw, or drill, or polish, or work at the lathe; for that belongs to the carpenters.
**THEAGES:** Certainly.
**SOCRATES:** But perhaps you mean the wisdom by which we rule over all of them—farmers, carpenters, all craftsmen, and all private citizens, both women and men. Perhaps this is the wisdom you mean.
**THEAGES:** That is exactly what I have been wanting to say for a long time, Socrates.
**SOCRATES:** Can you say, then, whether Aegisthus <note>The lover of Clytemnestra who usurped the throne of Agamemnon in the myths of the Trojan War.</note>, who killed Agamemnon at Argos, ruled over those you describe—the craftsmen, private citizens, and all the men and women—or some others?
**THEAGES:** No, it was those.
**SOCRATES:** What about Peleus, the son of Aeacus, in Phthia? Did he not rule over these same people?
**THEAGES:** <margin>C</margin> Yes.
**SOCRATES:** And have you heard that Periander <note>One of the "Seven Sages" of Greece, though he ruled Corinth as a dictator.</note>, the son of Cypselus, became a ruler in Corinth?
**THEAGES:** I have.
**SOCRATES:** And did he not rule over these same people in his city?
**THEAGES:** Certainly.
**SOCRATES:** What about Archelaus, the son of Perdiccas, who recently took power in Macedonia? Do you not think he rules over these same people?
**THEAGES:** I do.
**SOCRATES:** And Hippias, the son of Pisistratus, who once ruled in this city—whom do you think he led? Was it not these same people?
**THEAGES:** How could it be otherwise?
**SOCRATES:** Can you tell me, then, what title we give to Bacis, and the Sibyl <note>Famous legendary prophets or oracles.</note>, and our own countryman Amphilytus?
**THEAGES:** What else, Socrates, except "prophets"?
**SOCRATES:** You are right. In the same way, try to answer me: <margin>D</margin> what title do we give to Hippias and Periander because of their rule?
**THEAGES:** I suppose we call them "tyrants." <note>In Ancient Greece, a 'tyrant' was simply an absolute ruler who took power unconstitutionally, not necessarily a cruel one.</note> What else?
**SOCRATES:** Therefore, whoever desires to rule over all the people in the city desires this same rule—tyranny—and wishes to be a tyrant?
**THEAGES:** It appears so.
**SOCRATES:** And you say this is what you desire?
**THEAGES:** It seems so, from what I have said.
**SOCRATES:** You rogue! So you desire to be a tyrant over us, and for a long time you have been blaming your father for not sending you to some "teacher of tyranny"! And you, Demodocus, are you not ashamed? You have known for a long time what he craves, and though you have the means to send him, where he might have become a master of the wisdom he seeks, you are jealous of him and refuse to send him? But look now: since he has accused you in my presence, <margin>E</margin> let us consult together—you and I—as to where we might send him, and through whose company he might become a wise tyrant.
**DEMODOCUS:** By Zeus, Socrates, let us indeed consult! For it seems to me that this requires no small amount of counsel.
**SOCRATES:** Wait, my good man; let us first question him thoroughly.
**DEMODOCUS:** Question him then.
**SOCRATES:** What if we were to cite Euripides to him, Theages? For Euripides says somewhere: *"Tyrants are wise by the company of the wise."* <note>original: "Σοφοὶ τύραννοι τῶν σοφῶν συνουσίᾳ"</note> If someone were to ask Euripides: "O Euripides, in what matter do you say tyrants are wise by the company of the wise?" Just as if he had said, "Farmers are wise by the company of the wise," and we asked him "wise in what?" he would surely answer that it was in matters of agriculture?
**THEAGES:** <margin>F</margin> No, nothing else but that.
**SOCRATES:** And what if he had said, "Cooks are wise by the company of the wise," and we asked him "wise in what?" what else would he answer but "in the art of cooking"?
**THEAGES:** That very thing.
**SOCRATES:** And what if he said, "Wrestlers are wise by the company of the wise," and we asked "wise in what?" would he not say "in the art of wrestling"?
**THEAGES:** Yes.
**SOCRATES:** But since he said, "Tyrants are wise by the company of the wise," if we were to ask him, "O Euripides, what is this wisdom you speak of?" what would you say he would answer? What kind of things would these be?
**THEAGES:** By Zeus, I do not know.
**SOCRATES:** Do you want me to tell you?
**THEAGES:** If you wish.
**SOCRATES:** It is that which Anacreon said Callicrete knew. Or do you not <margin>G</margin> know the song?
**THEAGES:** I do.
**SOCRATES:** What then? Do you desire the company of some man who happens to share the same skill as Callicrete, the daughter of Cyane, and who knows "tyrannical arts"—as the poet said of her—so that you may become a tyrant over us and the city?
**THEAGES:** You have been mocking me and playing with me for a long time, Socrates.
**SOCRATES:** Why? Do you not say that you desire this wisdom by which you would rule all the citizens? And in doing this, would you be anything other than a tyrant?
**THEAGES:** I would pray, I think, to become a tyrant—ideally over all men, but if not, over as many as possible. And I think you would too, and so would all other men. Perhaps I would even pray to become a god! But that was not what I said I desired.
**SOCRATES:** <margin>H</margin> But what is it then that you desire? Do you not say you desire to rule the citizens?
**THEAGES:** Not by force, certainly, nor as tyrants do; but with their consent, just as other reputable and good men have done in the city.
**SOCRATES:** Do you mean men like Themistocles, Pericles, and Cimon <note>Famous Athenian statesmen and generals known for their leadership during the Golden Age.</note>, and all those who have been skilled in political affairs?
**THEAGES:** By Zeus, those are the ones I mean.
**SOCRATES:** What then? If you happened to desire to become wise in horsemanship, to whom would you go to become skilled? Would it be to any others than the horsemen?
**THEAGES:** By Zeus, not to any others.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> But is it by the wisdom for those who contend that one rules? **THEAGES:** By no means. **SOCRATES:** For that is the gymnastic art. **THEAGES:** It is. **SOCRATES:** But try to express it by what the people are doing, just as I did with the previous points. **THEAGES:** It clearly seems to me to be that by which one rules those who are in the city. **SOCRATES:** Are there not also sick people in the city? **THEAGES:** There are indeed, but I do not speak only of those, but of all who dwell in the city. **SOCRATES:** I understand which art you mean. You seem not to mean that by which we know how to lead reapers, or vintagers, or planters, or sowers, or threshers; for the art through which we command those is agriculture. **THEAGES:** It is. **SOCRATES:** Nor again is it the art for those who cut, or bore, or polish, or work with a lathe: for these belong to the craftsmen. <margin>B</margin> **THEAGES:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** But perhaps you mean the wisdom by which we command all of these—farmers, craftsmen, all artisans, and all private citizens, both women and men. That is the wisdom you speak of. **THEAGES:** That is the very one, Socrates, I have long wanted to say. **SOCRATES:** Can you say whether Aegisthus, who killed Agamemnon at Argos, commanded all these whom you mentioned—craftsmen, private citizens, and all men and women—or some others? **THEAGES:** Not others, but all of these. **SOCRATES:** What of Peleus, the son of Aeacus, in Phthia? Did he not rule over the same? **THEAGES:** <margin>C</margin> The same. **SOCRATES:** And have you not heard that Periander, the son of Cypselus, ruled among the Corinthians? **THEAGES:** Indeed. **SOCRATES:** Did he not rule over the same in his own city? **THEAGES:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** What of Archelaus, the son of Perdiccas, recently ruling in Macedonia? Do you think he ruled over the same? **THEAGES:** Indeed. **SOCRATES:** And Hippias, the son of Pisistratus, ruling in this city—whom do you think he presided over? Was it not the same? **THEAGES:** Why not? **SOCRATES:** But Bacis, and the Sibyl, and our own Amphilytus—by what name would they seem to be called by you? **THEAGES:** By no other than the name of prophets. **SOCRATES:** You speak rightly. In the same way, try to find <margin>D</margin> by what title you would name Hippias and Periander on account of that same leadership. **THEAGES:** What else could I call them but tyrants? **SOCRATES:** Therefore, whoever desires to rule over all his fellow citizens in the manner of those men, seeks a tyranny and strives to be a tyrant? **THEAGES:** So it seems. **SOCRATES:** And is this what you desire? **THEAGES:** It seems so from what I have said. **SOCRATES:** You wicked boy! Do you desire to rule over us in the manner of a tyrant? And for a long time now you have been angry with your father because he does not send you to some teacher of tyranny? And are you not ashamed, Demodocus? You who have long known what he craves, and since you have the means to send him, could have made him a master of that wisdom he seeks—do you envy him and refuse to send him? But now you see. Since he <margin>E</margin> has accused you in my presence, let us consult together, you and I: is there somewhere we might send him, so that by someone's company he might be made a wise tyrant? **DEMODOCUS:** By Jove, Socrates, let us consult. For it seems to me there is need of counsel, and of the greatest kind. **SOCRATES:** Allow it, good man; let us first question him. **DEMODOCUS:** Question him. **SOCRATES:** What if we use Euripides for something, Theages? For he says: *"Tyrants are wise by the company of the wise."* If someone were to ask Euripides: "O Euripides, in what matter do you say tyrants are wise by the company of the wise?" Just as if he had said, "Farmers are wise by the company of the wise," and we asked him, "In what <margin>F</margin> matter of the wise?" what do you think he would say? Anything other than in rural matters? **THEAGES:** Nothing else. **SOCRATES:** In the same way, if he had said, "Cooks are wise by the company of the wise," and we asked him "In what matter of the wise?" what else would he answer but "in the art of cooking"? **THEAGES:** That very thing. **SOCRATES:** What if he had said, "Athletes are wise by the company of the wise," and we asked him "In what matter of the wise?" would he not answer "in competing"? **THEAGES:** Indeed. **SOCRATES:** And because he said, "Tyrants are wise by the company of the wise," if we were to ask him, "In what matter, O Euripides, of the wise?" what do you think he would answer? **THEAGES:** By Jove, I do not know. **SOCRATES:** Do you want me to tell you? <margin>G</margin> **THEAGES:** As you please. **SOCRATES:** These are the things which he says Anacreon knew, and Callicrete too. Have you heard the song? **THEAGES:** I have. **SOCRATES:** What then? Do you desire the company of such a man who holds that art which Callicrete, the daughter of Cyane, held, and who knows the tyrannical things which the poet says Callicrete knew, so that you may exercise tyranny over us and the city? **THEAGES:** For a long time you have been biting me, Socrates, and mocking me. **SOCRATES:** Why? Do you not say you desire this wisdom by which you may command everyone? But in doing this, would you be anything other than a tyrant? **THEAGES:** I would desire, I think, to obtain the tyranny either of all men or of as many as possible—which I am persuaded is true of you and all others—or even to be a god. However, I was not saying that I sought this. **SOCRATES:** What then is this that you desire? Is it not to lead the citizens? <margin>H</margin> **THEAGES:** Not by force, indeed, nor like tyrants; but with their consent, just as other well-mannered and good men in the city have done. **SOCRATES:** You mean then as Themistocles was, and Pericles, and Cimon, and whoever else flourished in the administration of the republic? **THEAGES:** By Jove, I mean those men. **SOCRATES:** But what if you were eager to be a noble horseman and wise in that art? To whom else would you go but to horsemen? **THEAGES:** To no others. **SOCRATES:**

<summary>Socrates examines Theages' ambition to be "wise," leading him to admit he wants to rule the city. Through a series of analogies, Socrates clarifies that Theages does not want to be a violent tyrant, but rather a statesman who rules with the consent of the people.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue of the Theages. Having established that Theages desires "wisdom" to rule the city, Socrates is now testing whether such wisdom can be learned from the current politicians of Athens, or if it requires a different kind of teacher.</meta>

# OF PLATO

Indeed, go to those very men who excel in the equestrian art, and who use many horses, both their own and those of others. **THEAGES.** Of course. **SOCRATES.** And in the same way, if you desired to obtain the art of javelin throwing wisely, you would go to those who are the best at throwing javelins, and who use many spears, both those belonging to others and their own. **THEAGES.** So it seems to me. **SOCRATES.** Come then, since you wish to be educated in civil matters so that you may become wise in them, do you think you should go to any others than these statesmen? These are the men who are most powerful in civil discipline and who deal both with our own fatherland and with other cities, and for that reason, they are involved with both Greeks and barbarians. Or do you think that by associating with some others, you will become wise in those things in which they themselves are experts, and not in these men themselves? **THEAGES.** I have heard, Socrates, certain speeches—which they say are yours—claiming that the children of statesmen are no better than the children of cobblers. <note>original: "cerdonum." Socrates famously argued that if virtue or political skill could be taught, the great Athenian leaders would have successfully taught it to their sons, which they often failed to do.</note> And in my opinion, you speak the truth. I would therefore be foolish—one of their number—if I persuaded myself that any of those men would hand down his wisdom to me, when they have not helped their own sons in the least. I cannot believe they could be of use to me or to any other mortal in this matter. **SOCRATES.** What would you do then, best of men, if you had a son who presented you with this kind of trouble? Suppose he showed a desire to become an excellent painter and was angry with you because you would not spend any money on him for that purpose; yet when he saw the masters of painting themselves, he refused to learn anything from them. Or if he wanted to become a flute-player or a lyre-player but rejected the teachers. Would you have any idea what to do with him, or where you would eventually send him, if he was unwilling to learn from those experts? **THEAGES.** I certainly would not. **SOCRATES.** Then are you not doing these same things? Do you wonder why your father is angry and hesitates about what to do with you or where to send you? We were ready to recommend you to any of the most excellent Athenians in the administration of the republic whom you wished, who would have associated with you without a fee. In this way, you would have both saved your money and gained a greater reputation from such an association than from any of the others. **THEAGES.** What then, Socrates? Are you not one of these good and honorable men? If you will take me, I am satisfied and seek no other. **SOCRATES.** Why do you say this? **DEMODOCUS.** He does not speak badly, Socrates, nor could anything be more pleasant or useful to me, I think, than if your company pleased him and if you were willing to associate with him. Truly, I am hindered by shame from saying how vehemently I desire it. Therefore, I would ask both of you: you, that you be willing to take him, and you, my son, that you seek no other than Socrates. I beg you both to free me from these greatest cares, full of dread, for now I fear greatly that he may seek the company of someone else by whom he might then be ruined. **THEAGES.** Fear for me no longer, father, if you can persuade him to take me on. **DEMODOCUS.** You speak rightly. And to you, Socrates, all my speech shall henceforth be turned. To put it briefly, I most willingly hand over myself and all my most dear possessions—whatever you may need—if you will take this Theages and do him good to the best of your ability. **SOCRATES.** Truly, Demodocus, I do not wonder at this zeal of yours, if indeed you believe that he can be helped most by me. For I do not see where there is a need for greater diligence—if one has any sense—than in making one’s son as good as possible. But from where did this idea come to you, that I could make your son a better citizen than you yourself could? And how did he persuade you that he could be helped more by me than by you? For I wonder at this greatly: first, you are older than I; next, you have held many of the greatest offices among the Athenians; and no one is more honored by your fellow people of Anagyrasij <note>A local district or "deme" of ancient Attica.</note> and the rest of the citizens. Neither of you sees any of these things in me. But if young Theages here despises the company of statesmen and seeks others who profess to instruct youth, there is Prodicus of Ceos, and Gorgias of Leontini, and Polus of Agrigentum, and many others. These men are so wise that when they enter cities, they attract the most noble and wealthy young men. Although these youths could associate with any of the best citizens for free, they leave those associations behind and are persuaded to join the others, offering a fee—and a huge one at that—and feeling the greatest gratitude besides. It would have been fitting for you and your son to choose one of these; choosing me was not appropriate. For I know none of those blessed and beautiful disciplines, though (to be brief) I wish I did know them. Truly, I have always claimed to know nothing, except for a certain small discipline of love <note>original: "amandi disciplinam" / Greek "erotics." Socrates often ironically claimed that the only thing he understood was the nature of desire and how to lead others toward the Good.</note>, in which I seem to be more excellent than the common lot, and superior to men both of the past and the present. **THEAGES.** Do you see, father, that Socrates does not seem very willing to accept my companionship? As far as I am concerned, I was ready, if only he had been willing; but he says all these things in jest against us. For I know some of my peers, and some a bit older, who before they associated with him were of no value; but after they enjoyed his company, in a short time they turned out to be the best of all, whereas before they were the lowest. **SOCRATES.** Do you know what sort of thing this is, O Demodocus?

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> **SOCRATES:** But again, go to those who are skilled in these matters, who possess horses and use them constantly, both their own and those of others. **THEAGES:** Obviously. **SOCRATES:** What then? If you wished to become wise in javelin throwing, would you not go to the javelin throwers to become wise—those who have spears and use many of them, both others' and their own, every time? **THEAGES:** So it seems to me. **SOCRATES:** Tell me then: since you now wish to become wise in political matters, do you think you will become wise by going to any others? Or rather to these politicians, who are themselves active in political works and use them every time in their own city and many others, associating with both Greek cities and barbarians? Or do you think that by associating with some others, you will become wise in these things that they are, <margin>B</margin> but not among these men themselves? **THEAGES:** I have heard, Socrates, the speeches they say are yours: that the sons of political men are no better than those of the leather-cutters <note>original: "skytotomon" (shoemakers/cobblers).</note>. And you seem to me to speak most truly, as far as I am able to perceive. I would therefore be senseless if I thought any of these men would hand over his own wisdom to me, yet would not benefit his own son at all, if he were indeed able to benefit any other human being in these matters. **SOCRATES:** What then, best of men, would you do with yourself, if you had a son who caused such trouble? Suppose he said he desired to become a good painter, and he blamed you, his father, because you were not willing to spend money on him for these very things; yet he held the craftsmen of this very thing—the painters—in contempt <margin>C</margin> and did not want to learn from them. Or if he wanted to be a flute-player, but rejected flute-players; or a lyre-player, but rejected lyre-players. Would you have any idea what to do with him, or where you would send him, since he was unwilling to learn from these people? **THEAGES:** By Zeus, I certainly would not. **SOCRATES:** Now then, since you are doing these very things to your father, do you wonder and blame him if he is at a loss as to what to do with you and where he should send you? For as for the good and honorable <note>original: "kalōn kagathōn." This term implies the ideal of a perfect gentleman, possessing both beauty and virtue.</note> Athenians in political matters, we will introduce you to whichever one you wish, who will let you associate with them for free; and at the same time, you will not spend money, and you will gain much more of a good reputation among the multitude of men than by associating with anyone else. **THEAGES:** What then, Socrates? Are you not also one of the good and honorable men? For if you <margin>D</margin> are willing to associate with me, that is enough, and I seek no one else. **SOCRATES:** Why do you say this, Theages? **DEMODOCUS:** Socrates, he does not speak badly, and at the same time you would do me a favor. For there is nothing I would consider a greater godsend than if he were pleased with your company and you were willing to associate with him. I am even a bit ashamed to say how much I want it. But I beg both of you: you, to be willing to associate with him, and you, my son, to seek no one else to partner with than Socrates. And free me from many fearful worries; for now I am quite afraid of this boy, lest he meet someone else who might corrupt him. **THEAGES:** No longer now, father, be afraid on my account, if you are able to persuade this man to accept <margin>E</margin> my company. **DEMODOCUS:** You speak very well. Socrates, the speech after this must be directed to you. For I am ready (to speak briefly) to provide myself and my possessions as intimately as possible, for whatever is needed, if you will welcome this Theages and do him good, as far as you are able. **SOCRATES:** Demodocus, I do not wonder that you are earnest, if indeed you think that he would be most benefited by me. For I do not know anything about which a man of sense would be more earnest than about his own son—how he might become the best possible. But from where the idea came to you that I would be more able to benefit your son toward becoming good in politics than you yourself, and why it appears that I would benefit him more than you, this I wonder at greatly. For you are first <margin>F</margin> older than I; then, you have already held many of the greatest offices for the Athenians, and you are honored by the people of the Anagyrasij deme by far the most, and by the rest of the city no less than anyone. Neither of you sees any of these things in me. But if Theages here despises the company of political men and seeks some others who profess to educate young people, there is Prodicus of Ceos, and Gorgias of Leontini, and Polus of Agrigentum, and many others. They are so wise that when they go into cities, they persuade the most noble and wealthiest of the youth—who could associate for free with any citizen they liked—they persuade these boys to leave those associations and join them instead, paying a <margin>G</margin> very large fee in money, and feeling gratitude besides. It would be reasonable for your son or even yourself to choose one of these. But it is not reasonable to choose me; for I know none of these blessed and beautiful lessons. I wish I did; but I always say that I happen to know (so to speak) nothing, except for one small lesson: that of erotics <note>The study of desire/love.</note>. However, in this lesson, I claim to be more formidable than anyone else, both of the men of old and those of today. **THEAGES:** Do you see, father, that Socrates does not seem to want to spend time with me? For my part, I am ready, if he is willing. But he says these things in jest to us; for I <margin>H</margin> know some of my peers, and some a little older, who before associating with him were worth nothing, but since they have been with him, in a very short time they appear better than all those to whom they were formerly inferior. **SOCRATES:** Do you know what sort of thing this is, O son of Demodocus?

<summary>In this passage, Theages and his father Demodocus attempt to convince Socrates to become Theages' teacher. Socrates modestly demurs, claiming he knows nothing except "erotics" and suggesting the boy seek out the famous paid Sophists instead.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue of the *Theages*. Previously, Socrates and Theages were discussing whether political wisdom can be taught by current statesmen. Theages expressed doubt because these men often fail to teach their own sons. Now, Socrates explains the mysterious "divine sign" that governs his choice of students and his interactions with others.</meta>

### THEAGES.

<margin>A</margin>**THEAGES.** Yes, by Zeus, I certainly do; for if you are willing, I shall be able to become the same sort of man that they are. **SOCRATES.** No, my good man; you have not noticed what this thing actually is. But I will tell you. By a divine decree, a certain spiritual presence <term>daimonion</term> <note>original: "δαιμόνιον" (daimonion). Socrates famously claimed to be guided by a private "divine sign" or "voice" that warned him against certain actions.</note> has followed me, beginning from my childhood. This is a voice which, whenever it occurs, always signals to me a redirection from what I am about to do, but it never pushes me forward. And if one of my friends consults with me, and the voice occurs, it redirects him in the same way and does not allow him to act. I will provide you with witnesses of these things. For you know this Charmides, the son of Glaucon, who became so handsome. He once happened to consult with me when he was intending to train for the race <note>The "stadion" was a prestigious short-distance sprint at ancient Greek games.</note> at Nemea. Immediately, as he began to say that he intended to train, the voice occurred. I tried to prevent him, <margin>B</margin> and I said, "While you were speaking, the voice of the spirit came to me; do not train." He said, "Perhaps it is signaling to you that I will not win; but even if I am not going to win, I will at least benefit during this time by exercising." Having said this, he went to train. It is worth asking him, therefore, what happened to him as a result of that training. Or, if you wish, ask Clitomachus, the brother of Timarchus, what Timarchus said to him when he was going straight to his death <note>Timarchus was involved in a political assassination plot; Socrates here claims to have foreseen its fatal end.</note> after ignoring the spirit—both he and Euathlus the runner, who received Timarchus when he was a fugitive. For he will tell you that Timarchus said these very things to him. **THEAGES.** What things? **SOCRATES.** "O Clitomachus," he said, "I am going to my death <margin>C</margin> now, because I was not willing to obey Socrates." Now, why Timarchus said this, I will explain. When Timarchus and Philemon, the son of Philemonides, rose from the banquet to kill Nicias, the son of Herosamander—only the two of them knew of the plot—Timarchus, as he stood up, said to me: "What do you say, Socrates? You stay here and drink, but I must get up and go somewhere; I will return a little later, if I am able." And the voice came to me, and I said to him: "By no means should you get up. For the accustomed sign of the spirit has come to me." So he stayed. But after a short interval, he again started to go, and said, "I am going now, Socrates." Again the voice came; so again I forced him to stay. The third time, wishing <margin>D</margin> to escape my notice, he stood up and said nothing more to me; he slipped away when I had my attention turned elsewhere. And thus he went off and did the deed that was the cause of his death. This is why he said to his brother what I just told you: that he was going to his death because he had distrusted me. Furthermore, you will hear from many people in Sicily <note>Refers to the disastrous Athenian expedition to Sicily (415–413 BC), which Socrates allegedly predicted would end in ruin.</note> what I said regarding the destruction of the army. While past events can be heard from those who know them, you can test the sign right now to see if it speaks truly. For when Sannio "the Fair" set out on the expedition, the sign came to me. He has now gone with Thrasyllus to serve in the campaign against Ephesus and Ionia. <margin>E</margin> I believe he will either be killed, or something very close to it; and I fear greatly for the rest of that enterprise. I have told you all this because the power of this spirit also completely controls the associations of those who spend time with me. It opposes many, and it is not possible for those people to benefit by spending time with me; therefore, it is not possible for me to associate with them. To many others, it does not prevent me from being with them, but they gain no benefit from our association. But those whom the power of the spirit assists in their association are those whom you have noticed yourself. For they make progress immediately and rapidly. And of those who make progress, some have a benefit that is firm and lasting. Many others, <margin>F</margin> as long as they are with me, make wonderful progress; but when they depart from me, they again differ not at all from anyone else. This once happened to Aristides, the son of Lysimachus <note>Aristides the Just was a famous Athenian statesman; here his grandson is the student.</note>. For while spending time with me, he had made very great progress in a short time. Then a military expedition occurred, and he sailed away. When he returned, he found Thucydides, the son of Melesias, spending time with me. This Thucydides had been at odds with me in some arguments the day before. When Aristides saw me, after he had greeted me and discussed other matters, he said, "Socrates, I hear that Thucydides is putting on airs with you and is angry, as if he were someone of importance." "That is so," I said. "What then?" he asked. "Does he not know what a mere slave <note>original: "ἀνδράποδον" (andrappodon). A harsh term for someone without intellectual or moral freedom.</note> he was before he associated with you?" "It seems not," I replied. <margin>G</margin> "But truly," he said, "I myself have become ridiculous, Socrates." "In what way especially?" I asked. "Because," he said, "before I sailed away, I was able to dispute with any man and appear inferior to none in argument, so that I even sought out the company of the most refined men. But now, on the contrary, I flee if I perceive anyone who is educated; I am so ashamed of my own worthlessness." "Did this power leave you suddenly," I asked, "or little by little?" son: <margin>A</margin>**THEAGES.** I know, by Jove: for if you will it, I shall become such as those men were. **SOCRATES.** Not so, O best of men, but this has escaped you, what it really is: however, I will tell you. There is present with me, by a certain divine fate, a certain spirit <note>original: "dæmonium." In Latin, this refers to the Socratic spiritual sign.</note> that has followed me from early childhood. This is a certain voice which, when it happens, always suggests a dissuasion from the thing I am about to do, but it never provokes <note>original: "prouocat." Here meaning to incite or urge forward.</note> me. If any of my friends communicates something to me, and the voice comes, it dissuades them and does not allow them to act. Of which matter I will give you witnesses. You know Charmides, the good man, the son of Glaucon; he once communicated with me when he was about to exercise in the stadium at Nemea. And immediately, as he began to say <margin>B</margin> that he was going to exercise, the voice was present. I prohibited him, declaring how, while he was speaking, the voice of the spirit had stood forth, warning him not to exercise. He, however, said, "Perhaps it signifies to you that I will not emerge as the victor, but even if I do not gain the victory, yet by exercising during this time, I will profit somewhat." And having spoken thus, he went away into the contest. It is worthwhile, therefore, to hear from him what happened to him from that contest. Now if you wish, ask also Clitomachus, the brother of Timarchus, what Timarchus said to him when he was about to die; for he and a certain runner named Euathlus, who received him while he was fleeing, will report to you what he said then. **THEAGES.** What was it? **SOCRATES.** "O Clitomachus," he said, "I come <margin>C</margin> soon to die, because I was unwilling to obey Socrates." Why Timarchus said this, I will explain. For when Timarchus and Philemon, the son of Philemonides, had risen from the banquet to kill Nicias, the son of Hiroscamandrus—for they alone were conscious of the ambush—this Timarchus said, "What do you say, O Socrates? You indeed are drinking, but I must go elsewhere; I will return a little later, if there is an opportunity." Then the voice was present with me. Therefore I said, "Do not get up, for the sign accustomed to me from the spirit has been made." He rested. Then, having delayed a little while, he burned again with the desire of going, saying, "I am going now, Socrates." And because I heard the voice again, I restrained him once more, until he, for the third time, <margin>D</margin> desiring to escape my notice, got up, saying nothing to me, but watching for when I had turned my mind elsewhere. And thus having set out, he perpetrated those things which were the cause of his death. These same things he said to his brother, just as I am now telling you: namely, that he came to his death because he had been unwilling to believe me. You will hear besides from many who are in Sicily what I predicted concerning the slaughter of the army. And past things can indeed be heard from those who knew them. But to experience the sign of the spirit, if it should perchance say anything, is possible even now. For Samionus, the son of Calus, has gone out on an expedition. The sign was present to me; he sets out now with Thrasyllus to fight against Ephesus and Ionia. I however <margin>E</margin> think that he will either be killed, or run into something of this sort, and I fear vehemently for the rest of the business. All these things I tell you for this reason: because all power for establishing friendships with those who are with me lies with the spirit. For it opposes many, nor is it permitted to bring help to those who converse with me against the spirit's will; wherefore it is impossible for me to live with them. To many others, it does not prohibit me from clinging, but they are helped not at all by our familiarity. Those, however, whom the power of the spirit favors in that very friendship, they are the ones about whom you noticed that they profit in a short time. But of those, some have this benefit firm and durable; many others, <margin>F</margin> as long as they are with me, are wonderfully powerful, but when they have departed, they again differ not at all from the rest. This once happened to Aristides, the son of Lysimachus, who was the son of Aristides. For staying with me, he profited much in a short time; afterwards, however, he set out for military service. Returning then, he found Thucydides, the son of Melesias, acting as my student. This Thucydides, the day before, had objected to me in a dispute about I know not what matter. When Aristides had greeted me and talked further, he said, "O Socrates, I hear Thucydides boasting and even contending in certain matters, as if he were something." "It is," I said, "as you say." "Does he not remember," he asked, "before he clung to you, what sort of <margin>G</margin> slave he was?" "It does not seem so, by the gods," I said. "But I," he said, "am ridiculous." "In what way most of all?" I asked. "Because before I went away from here, I dared to dispute with anyone, nor did I seem inferior to anyone in debating, so much so that I boldly entered the gatherings of prominent men. Now, on the contrary, I flee from anyone I have understood to be learned, I am led so much by shame on account of my ignorance." "Did that power leave you then," I asked, "immediately, or little by little?" "Little by little," he said. "When it came upon you, did it happen because of something you were learning from me, or otherwise?" "I will say, O Socrates, a thing indeed incredible by the gods, yet true. I never <margin>H</margin> learned anything from you, as you yourself know; yet I profited whenever I was with you, even if I was only in the same house, though not in the same part of the house, yet more often when I was in the same part. and it seemed to me I profited much more when, being in the same part, I watched you saying something, than when I was turned away elsewhere. But I profited far more when I sat near you—

<summary>Socrates explains his "daimonion" (divine sign), a voice that warns him against certain actions and dictates which students he can successfully teach. He recounts several historical anecdotes where ignoring the sign led to failure or death, and explains that some students improve simply through his physical presence rather than formal instruction.</summary>
