# MENO, OR,
# ON VIRTUE.

->Exploratory, or instituted for the sake of testing.<-

*SUMMARY OF THE DIALOGUE. This work discusses what Virtue is and how it comes to be present in us. Virtue is defined as a disposition or habit of the soul by which its natural power performs its work as excellently as possible; it performs this when it is directed toward its proper end. There are several species of virtues, corresponding to the diversity of the soul's powers and actions: namely, wisdom, which pertains to the mind; knowledge and prudence, which pertain to reason; right opinion or sagacity, which pertain to the imagination <note>original: "phantasiam". In Renaissance philosophy, this refers to the faculty that processes sensory images.</note>; justice and liberality, which pertain to the will; fortitude and its attendants, which pertain to the spirited power <term>vis irascibilis</term> <note>The "irascible" power is the part of the soul associated with courage, anger, and the drive to overcome obstacles.</note>; and continence and temperance, which pertain to the desiring power <term>vis concupiscibilis</term> <note>The "concupiscible" power is the part of the soul associated with basic desires and appetites.</note>. All these virtues are possessed in various ways, but in such a manner that none succeeds unless the efficacy of the divine power is added, by which men are surely equipped with virtue.*

->MENO, SOCRATES, MENO’S SLAVE BOY, ANYTUS.<-

<margin>Aristotle approves of Gorgias’s method of enumerating virtues, which is related in this dialogue, in Politics, Book 1, chapter 7.</margin>
<margin>C</margin>**MENO:** Can you tell me, Socrates, whether virtue can be taught, or if it is not teachable but rather acquired by practice? Or is it neither by teaching nor by practice, but comes to men by nature or in some other way? **SOCRATES:** O Meno, in former times the Thessalians were famous among the Greeks and admired for their horsemanship and their wealth. But now, it seems to me, they are also famous for wisdom—not least the fellow citizens of your friend Aristippus in Larissa. The cause of this for you was Gorgias; for when he arrived in your city, he won over the leaders <margin>D</margin> of the Aleuadae <note>The Aleuadae were a powerful noble family in Thessaly who claimed descent from Heracles.</note> (of whom your admirer Aristippus is one) and the other Thessalians as lovers of his wisdom. Indeed, he has accustomed you to this habit of answering fearlessly and with a high mind if anyone asks a question, as is fitting for those who know; just as he himself offered to be questioned by any of the Greeks who wished, and there was no one he did not answer. But here, my dear Meno, the opposite has happened. It is as if a drought of wisdom has occurred, and wisdom seems to have departed from these places to yours. If you should ask any of the people here such a question, there is no one who would not laugh and say: "O guest, you likely think me some blessed person, to know whether virtue is acquired by teaching or in some other way. But I am so far from knowing this that I plainly do not even understand what virtue itself is." And I myself, Meno, am in the same state. I share this poverty of mind with my fellow citizens, and I often reproach myself <margin>E</margin> because I am utterly ignorant about virtue. But when I do not know what a thing is, how could I know what its qualities are? Or does it seem possible to you that someone who does not know at all who Meno is, could know whether he is handsome, rich, or noble, or the opposite of these? **MENO:** Not to me, certainly. But do you really, Socrates, not know what virtue is? Shall we report this about you back home? **SOCRATES:** Not only that, my friend, but also that I have never yet met anyone else who knew, as I believe. **MENO:** What? Did you not meet Gorgias when he was here? **SOCRATES:** I did. **MENO:** Did he not seem to you to know? **SOCRATES:** My memory is not very good, Meno, so I cannot say at present how he seemed to me then. But perhaps he does know, and you remember what he taught; remind me, then, of how he spoke. Or if you prefer, explain it yourself, for you surely agree with him. **MENO:** I do indeed. <margin>F</margin> **SOCRATES:** Let us leave him aside then, since he is not here. But you yourself, Meno, by the gods, I beseech you: what do you say virtue is? Tell me, and do not be begrudging, so that I may be proven to have told a most fortunate lie by saying I never met anyone who knew, if you and Gorgias should appear to know it. **MENO:** But Socrates, it is not at all difficult to say. First, if you wish to know the virtue of a man, it is easy: it is to be capable of managing the affairs of the city, and in so doing, to benefit one's friends and harm one's enemies, while taking care that he himself suffers no such thing. If a woman is strong, will she be strong by the same form and the same strength? By "the same," I mean that strength does not differ, as strength, <margin>D</margin> whether it is in a man or in a woman. Or does it seem to you to differ in any way? **MENO:** Not to me. **SOCRATES:** And will virtue differ in any way as virtue, whether it is in a child, or in an old man, or in a woman, or in a man? **MENO:** Somehow, O Socrates, this no longer seems to me to be like those other examples. **SOCRATES:** Why? If indeed you are seeking one thing that applies to all. **SOCRATES:** Indeed I am seeking that. But is this also the virtue of a child, O Meno? And of a slave—to be able to rule over the master? And does it seem to you that one who rules would still be a slave? **MENO:** It does not seem so to me at all, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** For it is not likely, my excellent friend. Consider this also: you say "to be able to rule." Shall we not add to that "justly, and not unjustly"? **MENO:** I think so; for justice, Socrates, is virtue. **SOCRATES:** Is it virtue, O Meno, or a certain virtue? <note>Socrates is distinguishing between "Virtue" as a whole and "a virtue" as one specific example.</note> **MENO:** What do you mean by this? **SOCRATES:** As with anything else. <margin>G</margin> For example, if you like, concerning roundness, I would say that it is a certain shape, and not simply "shape." And I would say this because there are other shapes as well. **MENO:** You speak correctly. For I also say that not only is there justice, but there are also other virtues. **SOCRATES:** Tell me what these are. Just as I could tell you other shapes if you asked; so you tell me other virtues. **MENO:** Courage, then, seems to me to be a virtue, and temperance, and wisdom, and magnificence, and very many others. **SOCRATES:** Again, O Meno, we have suffered the same thing. We have found many virtues again while seeking one, though in a different way than before; but the one virtue, which is through all of these, we are unable to find. **MENO:** <margin>H</margin> For I am not yet able, O Socrates, as you seek, to grasp one virtue for all, as in the other examples. **SOCRATES:** Naturally. But I will be eager, if I am able, to bring us forward. For you understand, I suppose, that it is this way with everything. If someone asked you what I was just saying—"What is shape, Meno?"—and you told him it was roundness, and if he asked you as I did, "Is roundness shape, or a certain shape?" you would surely say that it is a certain shape? **MENO:** Certainly.

We have found many virtues again while seeking one, but in another way; but the one which is diffused through all, we are unable to find. **MENO:** <margin>H</margin> I am not yet able, O Socrates, to attain that which you seek—one virtue in all—as in the other cases. **SOCRATES:** Not without reason; but I will strive, if only I am able, to lead us through. <summary>Socrates challenges Meno’s definition of virtue as a list of different traits for different people, using the "swarm of bees" analogy to argue that all virtues must share a single, essential form. They conclude that if all people (men, women, children) are to be "good," they must all possess the same core qualities of justice and temperance.</summary>

<margin>A</margin> **SOCRATES:** Is it not because there are also other figures? **MENO:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** And if he should ask what those others are, would you answer him immediately? **MENO:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** Furthermore, if he should ask in a similar way what color is, and you said it was "whiteness," and the questioner then followed up by asking whether whiteness is *color* or *a* color, would you say it is "a color" because other colors are also found? **MENO:** Most certainly. **SOCRATES:** And if he ordered you to name the other colors, would you tell him of many others which are no less colors than whiteness is? **MENO:** I would. **SOCRATES:** What if he proceeded with the argument as I am doing now, and said: "We are always falling back into 'the many'; do not do this, but since you call these 'many' by one single name, and you say that every one of them is a 'figure'—even though they are contrary to one another—what is this thing that contains the round no less than the straight, which you call 'figure'? If you were to answer someone asking about figure or color in this way—"I simply do not understand what you want, man, nor do I know what you are saying"—he would perhaps be astonished and say: "Do you not understand that I am seeking the same thing in all of these?" Or would you have nothing to say, Meno, if someone asked: "What is the same in the round and the straight, and in the others which you call 'figures,' being the same in all of them?" Let "figure" be for us that which, alone of all things, always follows color. Is this enough for you, or do you perhaps require something else? For I would be satisfied if you would later show me virtue in the same way. **MENO:** But that is a silly <note>original: "absurdum" (Latin) / "εὔηθες" (Greek) - Socrates' definition is technically correct but "simple" or "naive" because it relies on another undefined term.</note> sort of thing, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Why so? **MENO:** Because, according to your argument, figure is that which always follows color. But if someone were to say he did not know what color was, and was in the same doubt as he was about figure, what would you answer him? **SOCRATES:** I would answer the truth. For if the questioner were one of those "wise" men—those contentious and litigious debaters—I would say to him: "I have spoken; if I have not spoken correctly, it is your business to take up the argument and refute my words." But if, like us now, they were friends and wished to discuss together, it is surely proper to answer in a gentler and more dialectical <note>original: "dialectice" - referring to a cooperative search for truth rather than a competitive debate.</note> manner. It is perhaps more "dialectical" not only to offer the truth, but to prove it through those reasons which the questioner himself admits he knows. I will try to use this method with you now. Tell me, do you call an "end" a certain "boundary" or "extremity"? For I am using all these as the same thing, though perhaps Prodicus <note>Prodicus was a Sophist famous for his precise distinctions between synonyms.</note> would treat them as different. I understand nothing different <margin>E</margin> by those words. **MENO:** I do indeed, and I think I understand what you say. **SOCRATES:** And do you call something a "plane," and another thing a "solid," such as those things treated in Geometry? **MENO:** I do. **SOCRATES:** Now then, from these you may perceive what I call "figure." For in every figure I assert this: figure is that in which a solid terminates. And to put it briefly, I call figure the "limit of a solid." **MENO:** <margin>F</margin> And what do you call "color," Socrates? **SOCRATES:** You are being troublesome, Meno; you impose the burden of answering upon an old man, yet you yourself are unwilling to remember and tell me what Gorgias <note>Gorgias was a famous Sophist and Meno's teacher.</note> said virtue was. **MENO:** But after you have declared this to me, Socrates, I will tell you that. **SOCRATES:** Even someone with his eyes covered, hearing you speak, would know that you are handsome and not without lovers. **MENO:** <margin>G</margin> Why so? **SOCRATES:** Because you do nothing but command in your speech, which is what pampered people do—those who act like tyrants as long as they are in their prime. At the same time, perhaps you have judged me to be a slave to the beautiful; I will therefore gratify you and answer. **MENO:** Gratify me, I beg you. **SOCRATES:** Do you wish me to answer you according to Gorgias? Would you follow that best? **MENO:** I would indeed. **SOCRATES:** Do you not say, according to Empedocles <note>Empedocles was a philosopher who taught that perception happens through physical "effluences" entering "pores" in the sense organs.</note>, that certain "effluences" flow from things? **MENO:** Most certainly. **SOCRATES:** And there are "pores," that is, passages <margin>H</margin> into which and through which these effluences flow? **MENO:** Precisely. **SOCRATES:** And that of these effluences, some fit into certain pores, while others are too small or too large? **MENO:** That is so. **SOCRATES:** And do you call "vision" something? **MENO:** I do. **SOCRATES:** From these then, as Pindar says, "understand what I mean." Color is an effluence of figures, commensurate with sight and perceptible. **MENO:** You seem to me, Socrates, to have given an excellent answer. **SOCRATES:** Perhaps because it was answered in a way you are accustomed to hear, and at the same time you notice

And if the questioner were one of the "wise" and eristic <note>original: "eristikōn" - those who debate for the sake of winning rather than finding truth.</note> and competitive men, I would say to him: "My part has been spoken. -># PLATO'S [MENO]#<-

<column-break/>

...so that you would not tear virtue apart any further, nor break it into pieces, and I had given you examples of how to respond. Yet, neglecting this, you say that virtue is being able to obtain good things with justice, and you have confessed that justice is but a part of virtue. *MENO.* That is so. *SOCRATES.* Does it not then follow from what you have already granted, that to act with a part of virtue—whatever is done—is virtue itself? For you admit that justice and each of these things are parts of virtue. *MENO.* What of it? *SOCRATES.* Because when I asked you to show me virtue as a whole, what it is in itself, you did not explain it at all. Instead, you said that every action, provided it is done with a part of virtue, is virtue—as if you had already said what virtue is as a whole, and as if I could then understand it even if it were divided into parts by you. Therefore, the same question arises for you again, O Meno: what is virtue, if indeed every action done with a part of virtue is itself virtue? For that is what is said when every action is defined as virtue if it is accompanied by the justice of virtue. Do you not see that the same question is needed once more? Do you think anyone can know a part of virtue who does not know the nature of the whole? *MENO.* It does not seem so. *SOCRATES.* If you remember what I answered you earlier regarding "figure," we rejected that kind of response which relies on things that still need further proof and are not yet agreed upon. *MENO.* And we were right to reject it. *SOCRATES.* Do not then, my excellent man, when the question is "what is virtue as a whole and in general," expect to make it clear to those who ask by answering with its parts; nor by answering anything else in the same way. Rather, the same question will be needed again: what is this "virtue" to which these parts you speak of belong? Or do I seem to be saying nothing to you? *MENO.* To me, you seem to speak rightly. *SOCRATES.* Answer then again from the beginning: what do both you and your friend assert virtue to be? *MENO.* I had heard, Socrates, even before I spoke with you, that your habit is nothing other than to doubt and to cast the sting of doubt into others. And now, as it seems to me, you are disturbing me with charms, and spells, and incantations, so that I am full of uncertainty. Indeed, you seem to me entirely—if it is permitted to bite back a little in jest—to be most like, both in form and in all other ways, to that very broad sea-fish called the Torpedo <note>original: "Torpedo" (the electric ray). This fish numbs its prey with an electric shock.</note>; for it makes anyone who approaches and touches it go numb. You too now seem to have done something like that to me, to make me numb. For in truth, I find both my soul and my <margin>body, in the Greek.</margin> mouth to be numb, and I hesitate, nor do I find what I should answer you, though I have already disputed about virtue ten thousand times to many people, and quite well too, as it seemed to me. But at present, I am not able to say in any way what virtue itself is. Therefore, I think you have consulted your own safety by never traveling abroad. For if, as a stranger in another city, you did such things, acting as a sorcerer and a magician, you might perhaps be led away to punishment. *SOCRATES.* You are clever, Meno, and you almost deceived me. *MENO.* How so, Socrates? *SOCRATES.* I see now for what reason you portrayed me with this image. *MENO.* What do you think was the reason? *SOCRATES.* So that I might portray you in return. For handsome men, when they are depicted, are usually delighted, because it is to their advantage; for the images of the handsome are also handsome. But I shall not depict your person in return. Indeed, if that numb-fish is itself numb while making others numb, then I am very much like it; but otherwise, not at all. For I do not make others waver while being clear-headed myself; rather, being more in doubt than anyone else, I make others doubt as well. And so at present, what virtue is, I certainly do not know; you, however, perhaps knew before you met me, but now you have become like one who does not know. Nevertheless, I wish to discuss the matter with you and investigate together what virtue might be. *MENO.* But by what path will you investigate this, Socrates, which you do not know at all what it is? For what sort of thing among the things you do not know will you set before yourself to seek? Or even if you should happen upon it, by what sign will you recognize that this is the thing you did not know? *SOCRATES.* I understand what you want to say, Meno. But do you see what a contentious argument you have brought into our midst: namely, that a man can seek neither what he knows nor what he does not know. For if he knows it, there is no need for inquiry. But neither will he investigate what he does not know, for he does not even know what he should seek. *MENO.* Do you not think this reasoning is soundly introduced, Socrates? *SOCRATES.* Not at all. *MENO.* Can you say why it does not please you? *SOCRATES.* I can. For I have heard it from men and women who are skilled in divine matters. *MENO.* What is their story? *SOCRATES.* A true one, as it seems to me, and a noble one. *MENO.* What is it, I ask? And who are those who testify to it? *SOCRATES.* Those who say it are holy men and holy women who have made it their care to be able to give an account of the things they profess. Furthermore, Pindar <note>A famous Greek lyric poet known for his odes.</note> and others among the poets who are divine hand down such things; pay attention, I pray, to whether they seem true to you. For they say that the soul of man is immortal, and that it sometimes departs—which they call dying—and then returns again, but never perishes. For which reason they advise that one should lead the holiest possible life. For those who have paid to Proserpina <note>The Roman name for Persephone, queen of the underworld.</note> the penalty for ancient grief, she returns their souls to the sun above in the ninth year; from these arise illustrious kings, mighty in strength and greatest in wisdom. For the rest of time, they are called holy heroes among men.

<column-break/>

**A** ...not to break or fragment virtue, provided that one answers in the way that is necessary. You have neglected all this, and you tell me that virtue is being able to provide good things with justice; and this you say is a part of virtue. **MEN.** I do. **SOCR.** It follows then, from what you agree, that to do whatever one does with a part of virtue, this is virtue. For you say justice is a part of virtue, and so is each of these. **MEN.** What then do I mean by this? **SOCR.** That when I asked you to speak of virtue as a whole, you are far from doing so, yet you say that every action is virtue, provided it is done with a part of virtue. It is as if you had said what **B** virtue is in its entirety, and as if I would already know it even if you fragment it into parts. It is necessary for you then, as it seems to me, to face the same question again from the beginning, my friend Meno: what is virtue, if every action done with a part of virtue is to be virtue? For this is what is said when someone says every action with justice is virtue. Or do you not think the same question is needed again? Do you think anyone knows what a part of virtue is, without knowing virtue itself? **MEN.** It does not seem so to me. **SOCR.** For if you remember when I **C** answered you just now about "figure," we rejected such a hypothesis, which attempts to answer through things still being sought and not yet agreed upon. **MEN.** And we were right to reject it, Socrates. **SOC.** Do not then, my best of men, while virtue as a whole is still being sought, think that by answering through its parts you will make it clear to anyone; nor by saying anything else in this same manner; but the same question will be needed again: what is this "virtue" you are speaking of when you say what you say? Or do I seem to be saying nothing? **MEN.** You seem to me to speak rightly. **SOCR.** Answer then again from the beginning, what do you and your companion say virtue is? **MEN.** O Socrates, I heard even before I met you that you do nothing else but doubt yourself and make others doubt; and now, so it seems to me, you bewitch me and drug me, and simply cast a spell over me, so that I am filled with doubt. **D** And you seem to me entirely (if I may joke a bit) to be most like, in appearance and otherwise, to that flat sea-torpedo fish; for it makes anyone who approaches and touches it go numb. And you seem to me now to have done something of the sort to me, to make me numb. For truly, I am numb in both soul and mouth, and I do not know what to answer you. And yet ten thousand times I have spoken many words about virtue to many people, and very well, as I thought; but now I cannot even say what it is at all. And you seem to me to be well-advised not to sail away from here or go abroad. For if a stranger did such things in another city, you might be led away as a sorcerer. **SOCR.** **E** You are a rogue, Meno, and you almost deceived me. **MEN.** Why especially, Socrates? **SOCR.** I know why you compared me. **MEN.** Why do you think? **SOCR.** So that I might compare you in return. For I know this about all beautiful things, that they rejoice in being compared. For it is profitable for them; for beautiful, I think, are the images of the beautiful. But I will not compare you in return. As for me, if the torpedo is itself numb and thus makes others numb, then I am like it; if not, then not. For I do not, being clear myself, make others doubt; but being more in doubt than anyone else, I thus make others doubt as well. And now about virtue, what it is, I do not know; but you perhaps knew before you touched me, though now you are like one who does not know. Nevertheless, I am willing to consider and investigate with you what it might be. **MEN.** And in what way will you seek, **F** Socrates, for this which you do not know at all what it is? For what sort of thing among the things you do not know will you set as your goal for seeking? Or even if you should happen upon it most definitely, how will you know that this is the thing which you did not know? **SOC.** I understand the sort of thing you wish to say, Meno. Do you see what a contentious argument you are bringing down? That it is not possible for a man to seek either what he knows or what he does not know. For he would not seek what he knows (for he knows it, and there is no need for seeking for such a man) nor what he does not know. For he does not even know what he will seek. **MEN.** Does not this argument seem to you to be well-said, Socrates? **SOC.** Not to me. **MEN.** Can you say how? **SOC.** I can. For I have heard from men and women wise in divine matters. **MEN.** What story do they tell? **SOCR.** A true one, in my opinion, and beautiful. **MEN.** **G** What is it? And who are those who say it? **SOCR.** Those who say it are among the priests and priestesses who have made it their concern to be able to give an account of the things they handle. Pindar also says it, and many other of the poets who are divine. What they say is this; but consider if they seem to you to speak the truth. For they say that the soul of man is immortal; and at one time it ends (which they call dying) and at another time it is born again; but it is never destroyed. It is necessary then, because of this, to live one's life as holily as possible. For those from whom Persephone <note>original: Φερσεφόνα (Phersephona)</note> receives compensation for ancient grief, to the sun above in the ninth year she returns their soul again. From these arise illustrious kings and men mighty in strength and greatest in wisdom; for the remaining time they are called holy heroes by men.

<summary>Meno compares Socrates to a "torpedo fish" for his ability to numb his interlocutors into doubt, leading to the famous "Meno's Paradox" about the impossibility of seeking knowledge. Socrates counters this with a religious myth about the immortality of the soul and reincarnation, suggesting that learning is actually a process of remembering (recollection).</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Meno, Virtue, Torpedo Fish, Numbness, Meno's Paradox, Inquiry, Immortality of the Soul, Pindar, Persephone, Reincarnation, Recollection</keywords>

--- Page 49 ---
<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion where Meno raised a "debater's puzzle": how can one search for what they do not know at all? Socrates responds here by introducing the famous theory of "recollection" (anamnesis), suggesting that the soul already possesses all knowledge from previous lives.</meta>

-># M E N O #<-

<margin>A</margin> Since the soul is immortal and has been born many times, and has seen all things both here on earth and in the underworld, there is nothing it has not learned. Thus, it is no wonder that the soul is able to recollect <note>original: "anamnesis," the idea that learning is actually "remembering" truths the soul knew before birth</note> what it previously knew about virtue and other matters. For as all nature is akin and the soul has learned all things, there is nothing to prevent a person, upon recalling just one thing—which people call "learning"—from discovering everything else, provided they are brave and do not tire of the search. Truly, seeking and learning are entirely a matter of recollection. Therefore, we should not be persuaded by that contentious argument <note>Referring to the "eristic" paradox that inquiry is impossible</note>; for that would make us idle, and it is 
<margin>B</margin> pleasant for soft people to hear. This other view, however, makes people energetic and inquisitive. Trusting this to be true, I am willing to search with you for what virtue is. *MENO.* Yes, Socrates. But do you mean this simply, that we do not "learn," but that what we call "learning" is actually recollection? Can you teach me that this is so? *SOCRATES.* As I said just a moment ago, Meno, you are a clever rogue. Now you ask if I can "teach" you, when I have just said there is no such thing as teaching, only recollection—clearly so that I might immediately be caught contradicting myself! *MENO.* No, by Zeus, Socrates, I did not say that with such an intention, but rather out of habit. But if you are able to demonstrate to me in some way that things are as you say, then demonstrate it. *SOCRATES.* It is 
<margin>C</margin> not easy, but for your sake I am willing to try. Call over one of your many attendants here, whichever one you like, so that I may demonstrate this to you through him. *MENO.* Certainly. You there, come here. *SOCRATES.* Is he Greek, and does he speak Greek? *MENO.* Very much so; he was born in my household. *SOCRATES.* Now pay close attention to whether he appears to be recollecting or learning from me. *MENO.* I will pay attention. *SOCRATES.* Tell me, boy, do you know that a "square" area is a figure like this? <note>Socrates likely draws a square in the sand here</note> *BOY.* I do. *SOCRATES.* Does a square area have all these four lines equal? *BOY.* Certainly. *SOCRATES.* And does it not also have these lines through the middle equal? *BOY.* Yes. *SOCRATES.* 
<margin>D</margin> Could such an area be larger or smaller? *BOY.* Certainly. *SOCRATES.* If, then, this side were two feet long and this side two feet, how many feet would the whole area be? Look at it this way: if it were two feet long here, but only one foot there, would the area be anything other than two feet once? *BOY.* Yes, once. *SOCRATES.* But since it is also two feet on this side, is it not "twice two" feet? *BOY.* It is. *SOCRATES.* So it becomes twice two feet? *BOY.* Yes. *SOCRATES.* And how many are twice two feet? Calculate and tell me. *BOY.* Four, Socrates. *SOCRATES.* Now, could there be another area double the size of this one, but of the same shape, having all its lines equal just like this one? *BOY.* Yes. *SOCRATES.* How many feet will that area be? *BOY.* Eight. *SOCRATES.* Come then, try to tell me 
<margin>E</margin> how long each line <note>the "side" of the square</note> of that new area will be. For the side of this one is two feet; what will be the side of that double area? *BOY.* It is obvious, Socrates, that it will be double. *SOCRATES.* Do you see, Meno, that I am teaching him nothing, but only asking him questions? And now he thinks he knows what sort of line produces an eight-foot area. Does it not seem so to you? *MENO.* It does. *SOCRATES.* And does he actually know? *MENO.* Certainly not. *SOCRATES.* But he thinks it comes from a double line? *MENO.* Yes. *SOCRATES.* Watch him recollecting in order, as one must recollect. Now tell me, boy, do you say that the double area comes from the double line? I mean a figure like this, not long in one way and short in another, but equal on all sides like this one, 
<margin>F</margin> only double the size—that is, eight feet. See if you still think it will come from the double line. *BOY.* I do. *SOCRATES.* Does this line not become double if we add another of the same length here? *BOY.* Certainly. *SOCRATES.* And from this line, you say, the eight-foot area will be formed if four such lines are joined? *BOY.* Yes. *SOCRATES.* Let us then describe four equal lines from it. Is this anything other than what you say is the eight-foot area? *BOY.* Certainly. *SOCRATES.* And are there not within it these four areas, each of which is equal to the four-foot area? *BOY.* Yes. *SOCRATES.* How large is it then? Is it not four times as large? *BOY.* Of course. *SOCRATES.* Is something that is four times as large the same as "double"? *BOY.* 
<margin>G</margin> No, by Zeus! *SOCRATES.* Then how many times larger is it? *BOY.* Four times. *SOCRATES.* So, boy, from a double line, we do not get a double area, but a quadruple one. *BOY.* You are right. *SOCRATES.* For four times four is sixteen, is it not? *BOY.* Yes. *SOCRATES.* Then from what line do we get an eight-foot area? Does this line not give a quadruple area? *BOY.* I agree. *SOCRATES.* And a four-foot area comes from a line half that length? *BOY.* Yes. *SOCRATES.* Very well. Is the eight-foot area not double this one, but half of that one? *BOY.* Yes. *SOCRATES.* Will it not then be formed by a line longer than this two-foot one, but shorter than that four-foot one? *BOY.* It seems so to me. *SOCRATES.* Good; answer according to what you think. Tell me: was this line not two feet, and that one four? *BOY.* Yes. *SOCRATES.* Therefore, the line for the eight-foot area must be longer than two feet but shorter than four feet. *BOY.* It must. *SOCRATES.* Try then to say 
<margin>H</margin> how long you think it is. *BOY.* Three feet. *SOCRATES.* If it is three feet, then we shall take half of this line and add it on, and it will be three feet? For two...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Since therefore the soul is immortal, and has returned to this life many times, and has very often seen both the things in this life and the things in the other life, and has perceived all things, nothing remains but that it has learned them. For this reason, it is no wonder if it can remember those things which pertain to virtue and other matters, since it once knew them. Since all nature is related and in harmony with itself, and the soul has learned all things, nothing prevents a person who remembers one certain thing—which they call "learning"—from recovering all the rest, if they are so constant that they are by no means fatigued by searching. Searching, therefore, and learning, is recollection.
<margin>B</margin> Wherefore, one should by no means believe that contentious argument, for it would somehow make us lazy. It is also wonderfully pleasing to softer men. Our reasoning, however, makes people skillful investigators of things; and since I trust it to be true, I desire to search out with you what virtue is. *MENO.* Truly, O Socrates, but do you not assert this absolutely, that we do not learn? And that what we call learning is recollection? Can you teach me that this is so? *SOCRATES.* I said before, O Meno, that you were clever, and now you ask whether I can teach you, when I previously asserted that there is no teaching, but only recollection, so that I might immediately be seen to contradict myself.
<margin>C</margin> *MENO.* By Jove, O Socrates, I did not intend that, but rather spoke that way out of some habit. But if you can show me in any way that it is so, please show me. *SOCRATES.* It is by no means easy, yet for your sake I will try. But summon here to me one of the many who follow you, whomever you wish, so that we may test this demonstration on him. *MENO.* Gladly. Hey you, come here. *SOCRATES.* Is he Greek? And does he speak Greek? *MENO.* He is both Greek and was born and raised in my house. *SOCRATES.* Attend then to whether I bring things back to his memory or teach him. *MENO.* I will certainly attend. *SOCRATES.* Tell me now, boy, do you recognize this kind of quadrangular space?
<margin>D</margin> *BOY.* Indeed. *SOCRATES.* Does a quadrangle <note>a square</note> have all these four lines equal? *BOY.* It does. *SOCRATES.* And does it not also have those lines which are drawn through the middle equal? *BOY.* Just so. *SOCRATES.* Can it not be both larger and smaller? *BOY.* It can. *SOCRATES.* If therefore this side were of two feet, and that one also of two, how many feet would the whole itself be? Consider it thus: if this side were of two feet, but that one of one, would this space be anything more than once two feet? *BOY.* Once. *SOCRATES.* But since the other side is also of two feet, does it result in anything other than twice two feet? *BOY.* That very thing. *SOCRATES.* It results, therefore, in twice two feet. *BOY.* So it is. *SOCRATES.* How many are twice two feet? Calculate. *BOY.* Four. *SOCRATES.* Can there not be another space double this one, similarly having all equal lines just as you see 
<margin>E</margin> this one has? *BOY.* Entirely. *SOCRATES.* Of how many feet will it be? *BOY.* Eight. *SOCRATES.* Come now, try to tell me what each of its lines is like: since the line of this one is of two feet, what is the line of that double area? *BOY.* It is clear, O Socrates, that it is double. *SOCRATES.* You see, O Meno, that I am teaching him nothing of these things, but rather questioning him on each point. And now he thinks he knows what sort of line it is from which an eight-foot space is made. Does it not seem so to you? *MENO.* To me indeed. *SOCRATES.* Does he know then? *MENO.* By no means. *SOCRATES.* But he thinks it is from the double line. *MENO.* So it is. *SOCRATES.* Watch him next as he recollects in order as he ought. Now tell me, I pray, do you confess that a double space is born from a double line? I mean such a thing as this, which is not long in this part and short in that, but equal everywhere just like this one:
<margin>F</margin> but double that one, eight feet. But look to see if it still seems to you to be made from a double line. *BOY.* To me, clearly. *SOCRATES.* Would this not be the double of this one, if we add another equal to it here? *BOY.* Entirely. *SOCRATES.* You say that from this line there will be an eight-foot space, if four equal to this were produced? *BOY.* I say so. *SOCRATES.* Let us therefore draw four equal lines from it again; will anything else arise than what you call an eight-foot space? *BOY.* This very thing. *SOCRATES.* Are there not in it these four, each of which is equal to that four-foot one? *BOY.* Certainly. *SOCRATES.* How much does it become then? Is it not four times as much? *BOY.* Why not? *SOCRATES.* Is that which is four times as much the double? *BOY.*
<margin>G</margin> Not by Jove! *SOCRATES.* But quadruple? *BOY.* Quadruple. *SOCRATES.* From a double line, therefore, O Boy, not a double but a quadruple space is produced. *BOY.* You speak the truth. *SOCRATES.* For four times four completes sixteen? *BOY.* So it is. *SOCRATES.* But an eight-foot space is from what line? Does this line not give a quadruple space? *BOY.* I confess it. *SOCRATES.* And this fourth part from this half line? *BOY.* So it is. *SOCRATES.* Come then, is eight feet not double this one, but half of that one? *BOY.* Yes. *SOCRATES.* Will it not then be from a line longer than this much, and shorter than that much? *BOY.* So it seems to me indeed. *SOCRATES.* You speak rightly then, for you should answer what seems so to you; and tell me, was this one
<margin>H</margin> of two feet, and that of four? *BOY.* So it was. *SOCRATES.* Therefore it is necessary that the line of the eight-foot space be longer than the line of the two-foot space, but shorter than the line of the four-foot space. *BOY.* It must be. *SOCRATES.* Strive to tell us what sort of line you say it is. *BOY.* Three-foot. *SOCRATES.* If it is three feet, shall we not take half of this and it will be three feet? For two...

<summary>Socrates argues that all learning is actually the soul's recollection of knowledge from previous lives and begins a geometric demonstration with a slave boy to prove that "teaching" is merely asking questions to trigger this memory.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Meno. Socrates is in the middle of a practical demonstration with Meno’s slave boy to prove that "learning" is actually the soul recollecting knowledge from a previous existence. In the preceding lines, the boy has just realized that doubling the sides of a square actually quadruples its area, leaving him confused about how to create a square of exactly eight square feet.</meta>

-># OF PLATO #<-

<margin>A</margin> SOCRATES: ...one side, and this is one. And in the same way here, these two, and this one. And let this be the space you speak of. BOY: Yes. SOCRATES: If this side is three feet and that side is three feet, is not the whole space three times three feet? BOY: It appears so. SOCRATES: And three times three, how many feet are they? BOY: Nine. SOCRATES: But how many feet was the double space supposed to be? BOY: Eight. SOCRATES: So, the eight-foot space does not come from the three-foot line. BOY: Certainly not. SOCRATES: From what line, then? Try to tell us clearly; and if you do not want to count it, at least point to it. BOY: By Jove, Socrates, I truly do not know. SOCRATES: Do you see again, Meno, where he has now progressed in <margin>B</margin> recollecting? At the beginning of the discussion, he did not know which line produced the eight-foot space, just as he does not know now. But back then, he thought he knew it and answered boldly as if he were knowledgeable, not believing himself to be at a loss. But now he realizes he is at a loss, and just as he does not know, he no longer thinks he knows. MENO: You speak the truth. SOCRATES: Is he not now in a better position regarding the thing he did not know? MENO: I think this is also true. SOCRATES: By causing him to doubt, and making him "numb" <note>original: "stupidum" / "νάρκη" (narkē). Socrates compares himself to a stingray or torpedo fish that numbs its prey; here, the numbness is the productive confusion of realizing one's own ignorance.</note> like that fish, have we done him any harm? MENO: It does not seem so to me. SOCRATES: Indeed, it seems we have done something useful for finding the truth. For now, being conscious of his ignorance, he would gladly <margin>C</margin> and willingly search; but then, he thought he could speak well—often and before many people—about the double space, claiming it must have a line double in length. MENO: So it seems. SOCRATES: Do you think he would have ever tried to find or learn what he thought he knew (though he was ignorant), before he fell into this doubt and discovered his own ignorance, and began to long for knowledge? MENO: Not at all, Socrates. SOCRATES: Then the "numbness" was beneficial to him. MENO: It seems so. SOCRATES: Now watch how, starting from this doubt, he will discover the truth by searching with me, while I <margin>D</margin> teach him nothing, but only ask questions. Watch closely to see if I am teaching or demonstrating anything to him, rather than drawing out his own opinions. Now you, tell me: is this our four-foot space? Do you understand? BOY: I do. SOCRATES: And can we add to it another equal to it? BOY: We can. SOCRATES: And a third equal to each of these? BOY: Yes. SOCRATES: And can we not fill in the one in the corner? BOY: Certainly. SOCRATES: Do these four equal spaces not result? BOY: Yes. SOCRATES: How many times larger, then, is this whole space than the first one? BOY: Four times. SOCRATES: But we needed to get a double space; do you remember? BOY: Very much so. SOCRATES: Does not this line, drawn from corner to corner, cut each of these spaces in two? BOY: Yes. SOCRATES: And so there are four equal lines enclosing this space? BOY: There are. SOCRATES: Now consider: how large is this space? BOY: I do not understand. SOCRATES: Since there are four squares, did not each line cut off half of each square on the inside? BOY: Yes. SOCRATES: And how many such halves are in this central space? BOY: <margin>E</margin> Four. SOCRATES: And how many in the first square? BOY: Two. SOCRATES: And what is the relation of four to two? BOY: It is double. SOCRATES: So how many feet does this central space become? BOY: Eight. SOCRATES: From which line specifically? BOY: From this one. SOCRATES: From the one that stretches from corner to corner of the four-foot square? BOY: Yes. SOCRATES: This line is what the experts <note>original: "sophistæ." Socrates uses this term for "wise men" or learned scholars.</note> call the "diagonal" <note>original: "diametrum" / "διάμετρος." In geometry, the diagonal of a square.</note>; and if its name is the diagonal, it is from the diagonal, as you say, O boy of Meno, that the double space is born. BOY: Exactly, Socrates. <margin>F</margin> SOCRATES: What do you think, Meno? Did he ever answer with any opinion that was not his own? MENO: No, always from his own. SOCRATES: And yet he did not know, as we admitted a moment ago. MENO: You speak the truth. SOCRATES: So these opinions were already in him. MENO: They were. SOCRATES: Therefore, in a man who does not know, there are true opinions about the things he does not know. MENO: It appears so. SOCRATES: And now these opinions have been stirred up in him as if in a dream. If someone were to ask him these same things many times and in many ways, you know that in the end, he will <margin>G</margin> know them as accurately as anyone. MENO: So it seems. SOCRATES: And will he not know them without being taught, but only questioned, recovering the knowledge from within himself? MENO: Yes. SOCRATES: And to recover knowledge within oneself, is that not what we call "recollecting"? MENO: Certainly. SOCRATES: Now, the knowledge he has either he received at some time, or he always had it. MENO: True. SOCRATES: If he always had it, he was always knowledgeable. But if he received it at some time, it was certainly not in this life. For no one has taught him geometry—especially since he would do the same with all geometry and every other branch of learning. Is there anyone who taught him all this? You should know, since he was born and raised in your own house. <margin>H</margin> MENO: But I know for certain that no one ever taught him. SOCRATES: And yet he has these opinions? MENO: That appears necessary, Socrates. SOCRATES: But if he did not acquire them in this present life, it is clear that he had them and had learned them at some other time. MENO: It appears so. SOCRATES: And was that not the time when he was not yet a human being? MENO: That very time. SOCRATES: Therefore, if during the time when he is a human and the time when he is not, there are true opinions in him which, when awakened by questioning, become knowledge, has his soul not then learned these things for all time?

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...knows; and this one is one. And from here likewise: two, these; and this one is one. And there is created this space which you speak of. BOY: Yes. SOCRATES: Therefore, if it is three on this side and three on that, the whole space becomes three times three feet. BOY: It appears so. SOCRATES: And how many feet are three times three? BOY: Nine. SOCRATES: And how many feet was the double supposed to be? BOY: Eight. SOCRATES: So the eight-foot space does not yet come from the three-foot line. BOY: Certainly not. SOCRATES: But from what sort of line? Try to tell us exactly; and if you do not wish to count, then show us from what sort. BOY: But by Zeus, Socrates, I for one do not know. SOCRATES: Do you perceive again, Meno, where he is now walking <margin>B</margin> in the process of recollecting? At first, he did not know what the line of the eight-foot space was, just as he does not yet know now. But then he thought he knew it, and he answered boldly, as if he knew, and did not think he was at a loss. But now he thinks he is already at a loss, and just as he does not know, he does not think he knows. MENO: You speak the truth. SOCRATES: Is he not then better off regarding the matter he did not know? MENO: This also seems so to me. SOCRATES: By making him be at a loss and "numbing" him like the stingray, have we done him any harm? MENO: Not in my view. SOCRATES: We have at least done something useful (it seems) toward finding how the matter stands. For now he would gladly search, as if he knew; but then he would have easily thought he was speaking well, both to many people and many times, about the double space, saying it must have a line double in length. MENO: <margin>C</margin> It seems so. SOCRATES: Do you think he would have previously attempted to search or learn this which he thought he knew but did not, until he fell into a state of loss, believing he did not know, and longed for the knowing? MENO: It does not seem so to me, Socrates. SOCRATES: Then he was benefited by being "numbed." MENO: It seems so to me. SOCRATES: Look now, out of this state of loss, what he will also find by searching with me; I am doing nothing but questioning him, and not teaching. Watch if you ever find me teaching or explaining to him, instead of asking for his own opinions. For tell me, you: do we not have this four-foot space? Do you understand? BOY: I do. SOCRATES: And can we add to it this other equal one? BOY: Yes. SOCRATES: <margin>D</margin> And a third here, equal to each of these? BOY: Yes. SOCRATES: Can we not then fill in this one in the corner? BOY: Quite so. SOCRATES: But would these not then become four equal spaces? BOY: Yes. SOCRATES: What then? How many times the size of this one is the whole space? BOY: Four times. SOCRATES: But we needed it to become double for us, or do you not remember? BOY: Quite so. SOCRATES: Is there not this line from corner to corner, cutting each of these spaces in two? BOY: Yes. SOCRATES: And do these four lines not become equal, enclosing this space? BOY: They do. SOCRATES: Look now, how large is this space? BOY: I do not understand. SOCRATES: Since there are these four, did that line not cut off half of each on the inside? Or not? BOY: Yes. SOCRATES: How many such parts are in this? BOY: Four. SOCRATES: <margin>E</margin> and how many in that one? BOY: Two. SOCRATES: And what are four compared to two? BOY: Double. SOCRATES: So how many feet does this become? BOY: Eight feet. SOCRATES: From what line? BOY: From this one. SOCRATES: From the one stretching from corner to corner of the four-foot square? BOY: Yes. SOCRATES: The scholars call this the "diagonal"; so if its name is the diagonal, then from the diagonal, as you say, O boy of Meno, the double space would be produced. BOY: Entirely so, Socrates. SOCRATES: What do you think, Meno? Is there any opinion he gave that was not his own? MENO: No, only his own. SOCRATES: And yet he did not know, as we said a little while ago. MENO: <margin>F</margin> You speak the truth. SOCRATES: Were these opinions in him? Or not? MENO: Yes. SOCRATES: So in one who does not know about things he may not know, there are true opinions about these things he does not know. MENO: It appears so. SOCRATES: And now these opinions have just been stirred up in him like a dream. But if someone asks him these same things many times and in many ways, you know that finally he will understand them no less accurately than anyone. MENO: It seems so. SOCRATES: Therefore, with no one teaching him but only questioning, he will understand, having recovered the knowledge himself from within himself? MENO: Yes. SOCRATES: And to recover knowledge himself in himself, is that not to recollect? MENO: Quite so. SOCRATES: <margin>G</margin> Does he not then either have the knowledge he now has from some time he received it, or he always had it? MENO: Yes. SOCRATES: If he always had it, he was always knowledgeable; but if he received it at some time, he would not have received it in this present life. Or has someone taught him geometry? For he will do these same things regarding all geometry and all other subjects of learning. Is there then anyone who has taught him everything? You are certainly the one to know, especially since he was born and raised in your house. MENO: But I know that no one ever taught him. SOCRATES: Does he have these opinions, or not? MENO: It appears necessary, Socrates. SOCRATES: And if he did not receive them in this life, yet knew them then, it is clear that in some other time he had them and had learned them. MENO: <margin>H</margin> It appears so. SOCRATES: And is this not the time when he was not a human being? MENO: Yes. SOCRATES: If then, both during the time he is a human and the time he is not, true opinions are in him, which when awakened by questioning become knowledge, has his soul not been in a state of having learned for all time?

<summary>Socrates completes a geometric proof with a slave boy to demonstrate that the boy possesses innate knowledge of the diagonal, leading to the conclusion that the soul is immortal and "learning" is actually the recollection of pre-existing truths.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Meno. Socrates now uses this conclusion to encourage Meno to continue their search for the definition of virtue.</meta>

# MENO.

...his soul exists; for it is clear that for all time he either is or is not a man.
<margin>A</margin> **MENO:** So it appears. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, if the truth of the things that are is always in our soul, would the soul not be immortal? So that you should take courage and attempt to search for and recollect what you happen not to know now (that is, what you do not remember). **MENO:** You seem to me to speak well, Socrates, though I do not know how. **SOCRATES:** I think so too, Meno. And while I would not strongly defend the rest of the argument, I would contend to the end, if I were able, in both word and deed, that by believing we must search for what one does not know, we would be better, braver, and less idle than if we believed that what we do not know is neither possible to find nor necessary to seek.
<margin>B</margin> **MENO:** In this too, Socrates, you seem to me to speak well. **SOCRATES:** Since, then, we are in agreement that one must search for what one does not know, do you wish for us to attempt to search together for what virtue is? **MENO:** By all means. However, Socrates, I would most gladly consider and hear the answer to what I first asked: whether one should approach virtue as something taught, or as something innate by nature, or as coming to men in some other way. **SOCRATES:** If I were the master, Meno, not only of myself but also of you, we would not have considered whether virtue is taught or not taught until we had first searched for what it is. But since you do not even attempt to master yourself, so that you may remain free, yet you attempt to master me and indeed do master me, I will yield to you. For what else can I do? It seems, then, that we must consider what sort of thing it is, when we do not yet know what it is. If nothing else, then, at least slacken your rule over me a little, and allow us to consider *from a hypothesis* <note>original: "ἐξ ὑποθέσεως" (ex hypotheseos). Socrates proposes a method used by geometricians: assuming a premise is true to see what logically follows, even if the primary definition is still unknown.</note> whether it is taught or whatever else. I mean "from a hypothesis" in the way that geometricians often consider a problem when someone asks them, for example, about an area—whether it is possible for this specific area to be inscribed as a triangle in this circle. One might say: "I do not yet know if it is such a thing, but I think I have a certain hypothesis useful for the matter, as follows: If the area is such that when one applies it to the given line <margin>D</margin> of the circle, it falls short by an area similar to the one applied, then one thing seems to follow; but something else follows if these things are impossible." Having made this hypothesis, then, I am willing to tell you what happens regarding its inscription in the circle, whether it is impossible or not. In this same way, let us speak about virtue: since we know neither what it is nor what sort of thing it is, let us consider whether it is taught or not taught by using a hypothesis, saying this: "If virtue is the sort of thing among those belonging to the soul, would it be taught or not taught?" First, if it is something other than knowledge, is it taught or not? Or (as we were just saying) is it recollected? Let it make no difference to us which name we use. But is it taught? Or is it clear to everyone that a human is taught nothing other than knowledge?
<margin>E</margin> **MENO:** It seems so to me. **SOCRATES:** But if virtue is a kind of knowledge, it is clear it would be taught. **MENO:** How could it be otherwise? **SOCRATES:** We have quickly settled this point: if it is of this sort, it is taught; if not of this sort, it is not. **MENO:** Exactly. **SOCRATES:** Next, it seems, we must consider whether virtue is knowledge or something other than knowledge. **MENO:** I agree that this should be considered next. **SOCRATES:** What then? Do we not say that virtue is itself something good? And does this hypothesis remain firm for us: that it is a good? **MENO:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, if there is any other good that is <margin>F</margin> separate from knowledge, then virtue might not be a kind of knowledge. But if there is no good that knowledge does not encompass, then if we suspected it to be knowledge, we would be suspecting rightly? **MENO:** That is true. **SOCRATES:** And further, is it by virtue that we are good? **MENO:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** And if good, we are useful; for all good things are useful. Are they not? **MENO:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** So virtue is also something useful. **MENO:** That follows necessarily from what we have agreed. **SOCRATES:** Let us then consider, taking each one up individually, what sorts of things benefit us. Health, we say, and strength, and beauty, and wealth; these and things like them we call useful. Do we not? **MENO:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** But we also say these same things sometimes cause harm. Or do you <margin>G</margin> say otherwise? **MENO:** No, I agree. **SOCRATES:** Consider then, what guides each of these things when it benefits us, and what guides it when it harms us. Is it not that when right use leads, it benefits, but when it does not, it harms? **MENO:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** Furthermore, let us consider the qualities of the soul. Do you call anything temperance, and justice, and courage, and quickness of learning, and memory, and magnificence, and all such things? **MENO:** I do. **SOCRATES:** Consider then, which of these seem to you not to be knowledge, but something other than knowledge. Do they not sometimes harm and sometimes benefit? For example, courage, if courage is not wisdom <note>original: "φρόνησις" (phronesis), often translated as practical wisdom or prudence.</note> but a kind of boldness. When a man is bold without sense, is he not harmed, but when he is bold with sense, is he benefited? **MENO:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** And is it not the same with temperance and quickness of learning? Things learned and prepared <margin>H</margin> with sense are useful, but without sense, they are harmful? **MENO:** Most certainly. **SOCRATES:** In short, then, all the undertakings and endurances of the soul, when guided by wisdom, end in happiness, but when guided by folly, they end in the opposite? **MENO:** So it seems. **SOCRATES:** If, therefore, virtue is one of the things in the soul, and it must necessarily be useful, then it must be wisdom, since all things concerning the soul, by themselves, are neither...

<column-break/>

...the mind of man will know. For throughout all time, he either is or is not <margin>A</margin> a man. *MENO:* It seems so. *SOCRATES:* Isn't it then, if the truth of all things is always in the mind, that it has existed immortally? For which reason one ought to give effort with boldness and great confidence to inquire into and remember what you do not know at present—that is, what you do not remember. *MENO:* You seem to me to speak well, Socrates, I know not how. *SOCRATES:* To me as well, O Meno. And I do not contend very much for the other points; but that those who think they must inquire into what they do not know are better, more resolute, and less lazy in searching than those who think that what they do not know cannot even be sought—this I will contend for in words and, if I am able, in deed. *MENO:* This <margin>B</margin> also you seem to say rightly, O Socrates. *SOCRATES:* Do you wish then, since we have confessed that it is permitted to search for the unknown, that we investigate together what virtue is? *MENO:* Most certainly; yet it would be more pleasing to me to consider and hear first what I asked at the beginning of the dispute: how one must apply oneself to virtue, whether as that which is perceived through teaching, or that which is in us by nature, or that which is prepared for men by some other means. *SOCRATES:* But if I, O Meno, were to command you as I command myself, we would not have searched whether virtue is taught or not before we had investigated what it is itself. But since you do not even strive to master yourself so that <margin>C</margin> you may live as a free man, and yet you wish to master me, and do indeed master me, I shall agree with you. For what else could I do? It seems, then, that we must consider what sort of thing it is, whose nature we do not yet know. However, turn aside a little from your purpose, and allow us to consider from a hypothesis whether virtue is possessed through teaching or by some other means. I speak of "from an admission" in this way, just as geometricians often discuss things after someone has asked them: as if concerning an area, whether this triangular area can be expanded in this circle. If someone should say he does not yet know if it is of this kind, I think such an admission is useful: "If indeed this area is such that <margin>D</margin> when you extend it along its given line, it falls short by an area as large as the one extended, I think one thing will follow; and another thing if it cannot undergo such things." From this admission, therefore, I have decided to dispute concerning those things that happen regarding its expansion in the circle, whether it can be done or not. So let us also do regarding virtue; since we know neither what nor of what sort it is, let us seek whether it can be taught in this manner, using this admission. If virtue is something of those things that concern the mind, can it be taught, or not? Firstly, if it is something other than knowledge, can it be taught or not? Or rather, as we just said, can it be recalled to memory? Let it matter nothing to us by which name we use, but can it be taught? <margin>E</margin> Or is it manifest to all that a man is taught nothing except knowledge? *MENO:* It certainly seems so to me. *SOCRATES:* But if virtue is a certain knowledge, it is perceived through teaching. *MENO:* Why not? *SOCRATES:* We have therefore quickly dispatched this: for if it is of such a kind, it is taught; if not of such a kind, by no means. *MENO:* Exactly. *SOCRATES:* After this, I think it must be investigated whether virtue is knowledge, or something else. *MENO:* It seems to me that the same must be sought. *SOCRATES:* Do we say virtue is anything other than a good? And this position remains stable for us: namely, that virtue is a good. *MENO:* Strongly so. *SOCRATES:* If indeed there is some good separate from knowledge, <margin>F</margin> perhaps virtue will be no knowledge; but if there is no good that is not encompassed by knowledge, then in suspecting that virtue is knowledge, we will surely suspect rightly. *MENO:* These things are true. *SOCRATES:* Furthermore, are we good by virtue? *MENO:* We are. *SOCRATES:* And if good, useful: for all good things are useful. *MENO:* It is so. *SOCRATES:* Therefore, virtue is also something useful. *MENO:* From those things we have confessed, it necessarily follows. *SOCRATES:* Let us consider again in individual cases what sorts of things profit us: are health, and strength, and beauty, and riches, and other such things said to be beneficial? *MENO:* Yes. *SOCRATES:* We admit these same things sometimes cause harm. Or do you feel otherwise? <margin>G</margin> *MENO:* I certainly feel so. *SOCRATES:* See then, what guide makes these things harmful or profitable; is it not that when right use is present, they help, but on the contrary, they harm? *MENO:* Precisely. *SOCRATES:* Furthermore, let us consider the things that concern the mind. Do you call anything temperance, and justice, and fortitude, and docility, and memory, magnificence, and all other such things? *MENO:* I do. *SOCRATES:* Observe, I pray, which of these by no means seem to be knowledge, but something other than knowledge; do they not sometimes help, sometimes hurt? As for example, fortitude <note>original: "fortitudo" / "ἀνδρεία" (andreia). While often translated as "courage," the Latin "fortitudo" emphasizes strength of mind.</note> when removed from prudence? Is fortitude anything other than a certain boldness? And when anyone is bold with reason, he is helped; when without reason, he is harmed? <margin>H</margin> *MENO:* It is so. *SOCRATES:* Temperance also and docility in the same way, when perceived and established with reason, are an advantage, but on the contrary, a detriment? *MENO:* Most certainly. *SOCRATES:* To say it briefly, then, all the impulses of the soul, and all its turnings, under the guidance of prudence, tend toward happiness, but under imprudence, toward the contrary. *MENO:* It seems so. *SOCRATES:* Therefore, if virtue is something of those things that consist in the soul and is necessarily useful, it must be this prudence:

<sig>B iiij</sig> <note>This is a printer's signature mark, used by bookbinders to assemble the pages in the correct order.</note>

<summary>Socrates argues that searching for knowledge is a moral duty that makes people better. He proposes investigating whether virtue can be taught by using the "hypothesis" that virtue is a form of knowledge (wisdom), as only things guided by wisdom are truly beneficial to the soul.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Meno. Previously, they agreed that if virtue is a kind of knowledge, it must be teachable. Socrates is now leading Meno through an inquiry into whether virtue is indeed a form of wisdom or practical knowledge.</meta>

# PLATO'S

<page-num>20</page-num>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>Since all things concerning the soul are, in and of themselves, neither advantageous nor disadvantageous, but when wisdom or folly is added, they become either useful or harmful. By this reasoning, since virtue is the most beneficial of all things, it is clear that it must be a kind of wisdom <note>original Latin: "prudentiam"; Greek: "phronesis," meaning practical wisdom or intelligence</note>. <term>MENO.</term> It certainly seems so to me. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Furthermore, regarding the other things we were just mentioning—wealth and the like—which are sometimes useful and sometimes harmful: just as wisdom, presiding over the other powers and duties of the soul, makes them useful, while folly makes them the opposite, so too does the soul make these external things good by using and leading them rightly, but evil when using them wrongly? <term>MENO.</term> Exactly. <term>SOCRATES.</term> And the wise soul leads rightly, while the foolish soul leads astray. <term>MENO.</term> That is true. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Therefore, it must be stated generally that all other human affairs depend on the soul, but the things of the soul itself depend on wisdom, if they are to be good. By this logic, wisdom would be the beneficial thing itself—and we have already said that virtue is beneficial. <term>MENO.</term> Entirely so. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Therefore, wisdom is virtue, either as a whole or as some part of it. <term>MENO.</term> All these things seem to me to be well said. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Now, if this is how it stands, would men not be good by nature? <term>MENO.</term> It does not seem so to me. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Besides, this would happen: if men became good by nature, we would surely have experts among us who could recognize which of our youth were good by nature. Once they were identified for us, we would take them and keep them in a citadel, guarding them much more carefully than gold, so that no one could corrupt them; then, once they reached adulthood, they would be useful citizens for the State. <term>MENO.</term> That seems likely, Socrates. <term>SOCRATES.</term> But since they are not good by nature, could it perhaps be through instruction? <term>MENO.</term> That appears necessary. And according to our premise, it follows that if virtue is knowledge, it must be something that can be learned. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Perhaps, by Hercules! Yet I fear we may have admitted that too hastily. <term>MENO.</term> Just a moment ago it seemed to be a correct statement. <term>SOCRATES.</term> But it ought to seem correct not only in the past, but also in the present and the future, if there is to be anything sound in it. <term>MENO.</term> What is it, then, that you see which displeases you, and makes you doubt that virtue is knowledge? <term>SOCRATES.</term> I will tell you, Meno. I do not retract the idea that virtue can be taught, provided it is knowledge; that was well said. But see if I am not right to doubt that it *is* knowledge. Tell me this: if anything can be taught—and I speak not only of virtue, but of any subject—is it not necessary that there be both teachers and students of it? <term>MENO.</term> It seems so to me. <term>SOCRATES.</term> On the contrary, then, if there were a subject for which there are neither teachers nor students, would we not reasonably guess that it cannot be taught? <term>MENO.</term> That is so. But do you really think there are no teachers of virtue? <term>SOCRATES.</term> I have often searched to see if there were any masters of this, and with all my effort I have never found any, even though I have searched alongside many others, specifically those I thought were most experienced in the matter. And now, Meno, Anytus <note>Anytus was a prominent Athenian politician who later became one of the primary accusers in the trial of Socrates</note> has opportunely sat down beside us; let us make him a partner in our discussion. And it is right to take him as a companion. For he is the son of Anthemion, a man both wealthy and wise, who became wealthy not by chance or by gifts—like Ismenias the Theban <note>Ismenias was said to have received a large sum of Persian gold</note> who recently came into the money of Polycrates—but increased his fortune through his own wisdom and vigilance. Furthermore, he is not a proud citizen, nor puffed up or difficult, but has proven to be a modest, upright, and easy-going man. Moreover, he has raised and educated this son well, as the whole Athenian people testify, having elected him to the highest offices. It is right to investigate with such men whether there are any teachers of virtue, and who they might be. Come then, Anytus, search with me and your guest Meno here: who might be the instructors in this matter? Consider it this way: if we wanted Meno here to become an excellent doctor, to which teachers would we send him? Would it not be to the doctors? <term>ANYTUS.</term> Certainly. <term>SOCRATES.</term> And if we desired him to become an excellent shoemaker, would we not send him to the shoemakers? <term>ANYTUS.</term> Yes. <term>SOCRATES.</term> And in other matters likewise? <term>ANYTUS.</term> Entirely. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Tell me then again about the doctors: we said we would be right to send him to the doctors if we wanted him to be a doctor; when we say this, do we mean that we would be wise to send him to those who profess that art and who openly take a fee for it from their students, showing themselves to be those who can teach anyone willing to learn? Is this not the reason we would send him, if we were acting prudently? <term>ANYTUS.</term> It is. <term>SOCRATES.</term> And the same judgment applies to flute-playing and all other things. For it would be a great folly, while we desired someone to become a flute-player, to refuse to send him to those who promise to teach the skill and receive payment for it, and instead to trouble others who neither profess to be teachers nor have any student in that art which we wish the person we are sending to be instructed in. Does that not seem very absurd to you? <term>ANYTUS.</term> By Zeus, it is not only absurd, but a kind of ignorance. <term>SOCRATES.</term> You speak well. Now, therefore, you may deliberate together with me about your guest Meno here: for he, Anytus, has long been telling me that he desires that wisdom and virtue by which men...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>...whether they are beneficial or harmful. But when wisdom or folly is present, they become harmful or beneficial. According to this reasoning, since virtue is beneficial, it must be some kind of wisdom. <term>MENO.</term> So it seems to me. <term>SOCRATES.</term> And indeed, the other things we were just mentioning—wealth and the like—which are at times good and at times harmful: just as wisdom, leading the rest of the soul, made the things of the soul beneficial, but folly made them harmful, so too for these things, the soul, by using and leading them rightly, makes them beneficial, but wrongly, harmful? <term>MENO.</term> Certainly. <term>SOCRATES.</term> And does the wise soul lead rightly, while the foolish soul leads in error? <term>MENO.</term> That is right. <term>SOCRATES.</term> So then, one may say this regarding all things: for a man, <margin>B</margin> all other things depend on the soul, and the things of the soul itself depend on wisdom, if they are to be good. And by this argument, wisdom would be the beneficial. And we say that virtue is beneficial? <term>MENO.</term> Certainly. <term>SOCRATES.</term> We say, then, that wisdom is virtue, either as a whole or some part of it. <term>MENO.</term> What you say, Socrates, seems to me to be well spoken. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Therefore, if these things are so, the good would not be so by nature? <term>MENO.</term> I do not think so. <term>SOCRATES.</term> For then, I suppose, this would also follow: if the good were born so by nature, we would likely have those who could recognize the good natures among the young; we would take them, after they had been identified, and guard them in the Acropolis, sealing them up much more than gold, so that no one could corrupt <margin>C</margin> them; and when they reached the proper age, they would become useful to the cities. <term>MENO.</term> It seems likely, Socrates. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Since, then, the good do not become good by nature, is it through learning? <term>MENO.</term> This now seems to me to be necessary; and it is clear, Socrates, according to the hypothesis, that if virtue is knowledge, it is teachable. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Perhaps, by Zeus; but what if we did not agree to this correctly? <term>MENO.</term> And yet it seemed just now to be well said. <term>SOCRATES.</term> But it must seem to be well said not only just now, but also now and in the future, if it is to be at all healthy. <term>MENO.</term> What then? Looking at what do you find it difficult, and doubt that virtue is knowledge? <term>SOCRATES.</term> I will tell you, Meno. That it is teachable, <margin>D</margin> if indeed it is knowledge, I do not retract as being poorly said. But see if I seem to you to reasonably doubt that it *is* knowledge. For tell me this: if any matter whatsoever is teachable, and not just virtue, is it not necessary that there be both teachers and students of it? <term>MENO.</term> It seems so to me. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Conversely, then, where there are neither teachers nor students, would we not be right in guessing it is not teachable? <term>MENO.</term> That is so. But do you think there are no teachers of virtue? <term>SOCRATES.</term> Often, at least, though I seek if there are any teachers of it, doing everything I can, I am unable to find them. And yet I seek with many, and especially with those whom I think are most experienced in the matter. And indeed now, Meno, at a good moment, Anytus here has sat down by us, to whom we may give a share in the search. And it would be reasonable to give him a share. For Anytus here is, first of all, the son of a wealthy and wise father, Anthemion; who became wealthy not by chance, nor because someone gave it to him (like Ismenias the Theban, who recently received the wealth of Polycrates), but having acquired it by his own wisdom and diligence. Then, also, in other respects, he seems to be a citizen who is not arrogant, nor puffed up and offensive, but a well-ordered and well-mannered man; then, he raised and educated this son well, as it seems to the majority of Athenians. They certainly elect him to the greatest offices. It is just, then, to seek with such men for teachers of virtue, whether there are any or not, and who they are. You then, Anytus, join the search with me and your guest Meno here, concerning this matter: who might be the teachers? Look at it this way: if we wanted Meno here to become a good doctor, to what teachers would we send him? Would it not be to the doctors? <term>ANYTUS.</term> Certainly. <term>SOCRATES.</term> What if we wanted him to become a good shoemaker, would it not be to the shoemakers? <term>ANYTUS.</term> Yes. <term>SOCRATES.</term> And other things in the same way? <term>ANYTUS.</term> Certainly. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Now tell me again about these same things. We say that in sending him to the doctors, we would be sending him well, wanting him to become a doctor; when we say this, do we say it because we would be acting sanely in sending him to those who claim the art rather than <margin>G</margin> those who do not? And to those who charge a fee, having declared themselves teachers for anyone who wants to come and learn? Is it not by looking to these things that we would be right to send him? <term>ANYTUS.</term> Yes. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Then is it not the same regarding flute-playing and the others? It is great folly, if we want to make someone a flute-player, to be unwilling to send him to those who promise to teach the art and who charge a fee, but instead to cause trouble for others by seeking to learn from those who neither pretend to be teachers nor have any student of that subject which we expect the person we send to learn from them. Does it not seem to you to be a great irrationality? <margin>H</margin> <term>ANYTUS.</term> Yes, by Zeus, to me at least, and ignorance besides. <term>SOCRATES.</term> You speak well. Now then, it is possible for you to deliberate in common with me about this guest Meno; for he, Anytus, has long been saying to me that he desires this wisdom and virtue by which...

<summary>Socrates and Meno conclude that virtue must be a form of wisdom, as it is only beneficial when guided by the mind. However, Socrates begins to doubt if virtue is actually "knowledge" because he cannot find any recognized teachers of it, and he invites Anytus to help identify where a student might go to learn virtue.</summary>
