<margin>A</margin>...to manage both their households and their cities well, to care for their parents, and to know how to receive and send away both citizens and strangers in a manner worthy of a good man. Consider, then, to whom we might rightly send him to learn this virtue. Is it not clear, according to our previous argument, that we should send him to those who profess to be teachers of virtue, and who have presented themselves as available to any of the Greeks who wish to learn, having fixed and collected a fee for this? **ANYTUS:** And who are these you speak of, Socrates? **SOCRATES:** Surely you also know that these are the men whom people call <term>Sophists</term> <note>Professional teachers in ancient Greece who traveled from city to city teaching various subjects, including rhetoric and politics, for a fee.</note>. **ANYTUS:** By Hercules, Socrates, speak words of good omen! May no one among my kinsmen, or relatives, or friends, whether citizen or stranger, be seized by such madness as to be <margin>B</margin> ruined by going to them. For these men are a manifest plague and corruption to those who associate with them. **SOCRATES:** What are you saying, Anytus? Are these the only men among those who claim to know how to do some good who differ so much from the others that they not only do not improve what is handed over to them, as others do, but on the contrary, actually corrupt it? And for this, they openly demand payment? I do not know how to believe you. For I know of one man, Protagoras, who earned more wealth from this wisdom than <term>Phidias</term> <note>The most famous sculptor of the age, responsible for the statue of Athena in the Parthenon.</note>, who produced such conspicuously beautiful works, and ten other sculptors combined. Yet you tell a wonder, for if those who repair old <margin>C</margin> shoes and mend clothes could not hide for thirty days that they were returning the garments and shoes in worse condition than they received them—and if they did such things, they would quickly die of hunger—yet it seems Protagoras escaped the notice of all Greece for more than forty years while he corrupted his associates and sent them away in worse condition than he received them. For I believe he died at nearly seventy years of age, having spent forty years in his craft. And in all that time, even to this very day, he has never ceased to be held in high repute. And not only Protagoras, but many others as well, some born before him and others still living now. Shall we then <margin>D</margin> say, according to your word, that they knowingly deceived and harmed the young, or that they were unaware even of themselves? Shall we deem them so mad, when some say they are the wisest of men? **ANYTUS:** They are far from being mad, Socrates; rather, much more mad are the young men who give them money, and even more so their relatives who entrust the young to them. But most of all are the cities that allow them to enter and do not drive them out, whether a stranger or a citizen attempts such a thing. **SOCRATES:** Has any of the Sophists wronged you, Anytus, or why are you so harsh toward them? **ANYTUS:** By Zeus, I have never associated with any of them, nor would I allow any of my people to do so. **SOCRATES:** Then you are altogether without experience <margin>E</margin> of these men. **ANYTUS:** And may I remain so. **SOCRATES:** How then, my dear sir, can you know about this matter—whether it has anything good in it or anything foul—if you are altogether without experience of it? **ANYTUS:** Easily. I know what sort they are, whether I have experience of them or not. **SOCRATES:** Perhaps you are a prophet, Anytus, for I would wonder how else you could know about them based on what you yourself say. But we were not asking who they are that Meno might go to and become wicked—let those, if you wish, be the Sophists. But come, tell us, and do a favor for this friend of your father's, by telling him to whom in so great a city he should go to become worthy of <margin>F</margin> notice in the virtue I was just describing. **ANYTUS:** Why did you not tell him yourself? **SOCRATES:** I did mention those whom I thought were teachers of these things, but you happen to be saying that I am talking nonsense, as you claim. **ANYTUS:** And you are right to say so. **SOCRATES:** But now it is your turn; tell him to which of the Athenians he should go. Give the name of anyone you wish. **ANYTUS:** Why is there a need to hear the name of one man? For whichever of the <term>noble and good</term> <note>original Greek: "kalōn kagathōn"; a phrase describing the traditional Athenian ideal of a gentleman, possessing both beauty and moral goodness.</note> Athenians he happens upon, there is no one who will not make him better than the Sophists would, provided he is willing to listen. **SOCRATES:** But did these "noble and good" men become so by chance, learning from no one, yet nevertheless being able to teach others these things which they themselves never learned? **ANYTUS:** I expect that they learned from those who were "noble and good" before them. Or do you not <margin>G</margin> think there have been many good men in this city? **SOCRATES:** To me, Anytus, there seem to be men here who are good at political affairs, and there have been no fewer in the past than there are now. But have they also been good teachers of their own virtue? For this is what our discussion happens to be about: not whether there are or have been good men here, but whether virtue can be taught. In considering this, we are asking whether the good men of both now and the past knew how to hand down to another that virtue by which they themselves were good, or whether this is not something to be handed over or received by one person from another. This is what Meno and I have been seeking for a long time. Consider it this way, <margin>H</margin> from your own argument: would you say that <term>Themistocles</term> <note>The famous Athenian general and statesman who led the Greeks to victory against the Persians at Salamis.</note> was a good man? **ANYTUS:** I would, most certainly of all. **SOCRATES:** And therefore a good teacher, if ever anyone was a teacher of his own virtue, would you not say he was one? **ANYTUS:** I suppose so, provided he wished to be. **SOCRATES:** But do you think...

<margin>A</margin>...to be used, by which states and houses are rightly governed, children are best educated, and citizens and guests are both received and sent away skillfully, as is worthy of a good man. For they record that he departed from life having been born nearly seventy years; and forty years were spent in this art. And through all that time up into this day, he has stood out as famous. Nor was it Protagoras only, but many others also, partly <margin>D</margin> before him, and partly even now living their lives. And even worse than these are those who, if the care of someone belongs to them, commit them to those men. Finally, the most insane of all are the cities which receive them and do not expel them, whether a stranger or a citizen attempts such a thing. **SOCRATES:** Has any of the Sophists, Anytus, ever affected you with an injury? Or why are you so angry with them? **ANYTUS:** I have never had any <margin>E</margin> association with any of them, nor would I permit any of my people to use them. **SOCRATES:** You have never, therefore, experienced their ways. **ANYTUS:** And would that I may never experience them. **SOCRATES:** By what reason, O divine man, will you distinguish whether it be good or evil, of which you have made no trial? **ANYTUS:** I clearly know what sort they are, whether I have experienced them or not. **SOCRATES:** Perhaps you are a prophet, Anytus. But bring help to your father's friend: and show him to which of those who inhabit so large a city he might cling to acquire that virtue which we described. <margin>F</margin> **ANYTUS:** Why do you not indicate it yourself? **SOCRATES:** But those whom I had thought were teachers of these things, I have already brought into the midst: but according to your opinion, I have profited nothing at all. **ANYTUS:** Perhaps you speak the truth. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, you also now fulfill your part of this duty. Show to which of the Athenians he shall go. Bring forward the name of whomever you wish. **ANYTUS:** What is the need to hear the name of one man? Whomever of the Athenians he happens upon from the good and famous men, he will turn out better from that man's company, if only he obeys, than from the association of the Sophists. **SOCRATES:** But were those excellent and good men made such from themselves with no one instructing them, and are they able to teach others, <margin>G</margin> though they themselves learned from no one? **ANYTUS:** I think they perceived it from earlier men who were excellent and good. Do you not think many distinguished and excellent men have existed in this city? **SOCRATES:** To me indeed, Anytus, it seems there are men here skilled in civil administration, and that no fewer were here in the past. But were they fit teachers of that virtue? For this is what is now being discussed: not whether there are or were good men here, but whether virtue can be taught: and because of this, whether good men, whether those of old or those who live now, knew how to hand down to another that virtue with which each was endowed: or perhaps, virtue can neither be handed to another nor received. That, I say, is what I <margin>H</margin> and Meno have long been inquiring into. Consider the matter thus from your own speech. Do you confess Themistocles to have been a good man? **ANYTUS:** Most of all. **SOCRATES:** And that Themistocles stood out as a good teacher of his own virtue, if anyone at all was a master of virtue? **ANYTUS:** I suppose so, provided he wished it. **SOCRATES:** Do you think...

Was he himself unwilling for others to become good? Do you think he especially begrudged his own son, and intentionally did not share the virtue he had acquired? Have you not heard that Themistocles <note>A famous Athenian general and statesman, hero of the Battle of Salamis.</note> made his son Cleophantus a vigorous horseman, so that he could stand upright on a horse, and throw a javelin while standing upright on horseback, and perform many other wonderful feats in which his father had him diligently trained? He made him wise in everything that requires a teacher. Have you heard this from your elders? **ANYTUS:** I have. **SOCRATES:** No one, therefore, could blame the son's nature for being bad. **ANYTUS:** I think not. **SOCRATES:** But what of this: have you heard from anyone, old or young, that Cleophantus, the son of Themistocles, turned out to be a good and wise man in the same things his father was? **ANYTUS:** Never. **SOCRATES:** Do we think Themistocles wanted to imbue his son with foreign arts, but cared nothing for making him any better than his neighbors in his own fatherly virtue—if, indeed, virtue could be taught at all? **ANYTUS:** By Jove, perhaps not. **SOCRATES:** Such, then, was this teacher of virtue, whom you yourself assert was one of the best men of old. Let us now consider another, Aristides, the son of Lysimachus <note>Aristides "the Just," an Athenian statesman known for his integrity.</note>. Do you not also think he was a good man? **ANYTUS:** Most certainly. **SOCRATES:** And did he not also wish his son Lysimachus to turn out the best educated of all Athenians in everything taught by masters? Yet did he make him any better than anyone else? For you have spoken with him and know what sort of man he is. Furthermore, if you wish, consider Pericles, that greatly wise man: he educated two sons, as you well know, Paralus and Xanthippus. **ANYTUS:** I know them. **SOCRATES:** These, as you know, he instructed better than other Athenians in horsemanship, music, and athletics. In short, he did not want them to be inferior to others in anything that can be learned by art. But did he desire them to turn out to be good men? I believe he did, but that virtue could not be taught. And lest you think only a few ignoble Athenians failed in this, look at Thucydides <note>Not the historian, but Thucydides the son of Melesias, a political rival of Pericles.</note>: he raised two sons, Melesias and Stephanus, whom he taught diligently in other things, and especially in wrestling, so that they easily surpassed the rest of the Athenians; he entrusted one to Xanthias and the other to Euodorus. These were thought to excel all others in wrestling in those times. Do you not remember? **ANYTUS:** I have heard of it. **SOCRATES:** Is it not clear that while he was willing to spend a great sum for his sons to learn these things, he would not have refused to teach them virtue—which he could have passed on without cost—if only it could be taught? Or was Thucydides perhaps an ignoble man, who did not have many friends among the citizens and allies? On the contrary, he came from a great family and held the highest authority both among his fellow citizens and all other Greeks. Therefore, if goodness could be acquired through teaching, he would have found someone, either a citizen or a foreigner, to make his sons good, if he himself lacked the leisure due to the affairs of the Republic. But see, friend Anytus, lest perhaps virtue cannot be taught. **ANYTUS:** O Socrates, you seem to me to speak ill of men more freely than is proper. Therefore I advise you, if you are willing to obey me, to take care of yourself: for perhaps in another city it is an easy thing to do men either an injury or a benefit, but in this one it is far too serious and dangerous. I think this does not escape you. **SOCRATES:** O Meno, Anytus here seems to be angry with me, and I do not wonder at it. First, because he thinks I am slandering these men; second, because he considers himself to be one of them. But if he ever learns what it truly means to disparage men, he will cease to be angry; for now, he is ignorant of it. But you, tell me, are there noble and good men among your people? **MENO:** Certainly there are. **SOCRATES:** Are they willing to offer themselves as teachers to the youth, and do they profess or admit that virtue can be taught? **MENO:** No, by Jove, Socrates; but sometimes you will hear them say it can be taught, and at other times that it cannot. **SOCRATES:** Should we say they are teachers of this matter, when they cannot even agree on it themselves? **MENO:** It does not seem so to me, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** What then? Do you think these <term>Sophists</term> <note>professional traveling teachers</note>, since they alone proclaim it, are the teachers of virtue? **MENO:** In this, Socrates, I greatly admire and love Gorgias, because you never hear him promising this. Indeed, he laughs at the others whenever he hears them promising it; he thinks one should only promise to make men eloquent. **SOCRATES:** So you do not think the Sophists are teachers of this matter. **MENO:** I do not know what to say, Socrates. For the same thing has happened to me as to many others: sometimes I think they can, and sometimes I deny it. **SOCRATES:** And it is not only you and the other citizens who sometimes believe virtue is taught and sometimes deny it; even the poet Theognis says the very same things. **MENO:** In which poems? **SOCRATES:** In the elegies, in this manner: <margin>The precepts of Theognis are worthy of being known.</margin> "Drink and eat with these, sit with them, and please those who have great power; for from the good you will learn good things. But if you cling to the wicked, you will undoubtedly lose even the mind you have." Do you see that in these lines he speaks as if virtue can be learned? **MENO:** It appears so.

<column-break/>

...unwilling for others to become noble and good, especially his own son? Or do you think he envied him, and intentionally did not hand down the virtue in which he himself was good? Or have you not heard that Themistocles taught his son Cleophantus to be a good horseman? At any rate, he remained standing upright on his horse, and threw his javelin while standing upright; and he performed many other marvelous deeds which his father had him taught, making him wise in all things that belong to good teachers. Have you not heard these things from the elders? **ANYTUS:** I have heard them. **SOCRATES:** No one, then, would ever have blamed his son’s nature as being bad. **ANYTUS:** Perhaps not. **SOCRATES:** But what about this? Have you ever heard from anyone, young or old, that Cleophantus the son of Themistocles became a good and wise man in the same way his father was? **ANYTUS:** Certainly not. **SOCRATES:** Do we suppose he wished to educate his own son in those other things, but in the wisdom he himself possessed, he made him no better than his neighbors—even though virtue would be teachable if it were possible? **ANYTUS:** Perhaps not, by Zeus. **SOCRATES:** This man, then, was such a teacher of virtue to you, whom you also admit was among the best of former times. But let us look at another, Aristides the son of Lysimachus. Do you not admit he became a good man? **ANYTUS:** I do, entirely. **SOCRATES:** Did he not also educate his son Lysimachus most beautifully among the Athenians in everything that belongs to teachers? But has he made him a better man than anyone else? For you have associated with him, and you see what he is like. And if you wish, consider Pericles, such a magnificently wise man; you know he raised two sons, Paralus and Xanthippus. **ANYTUS:** I do. **SOCRATES:** These, as you also know, he taught to be horsemen inferior to no Athenian; and in music and athletics and other things that belong to art, they were inferior to none. But did he not wish to make them good men? I think he did, but perhaps it is not teachable. And so you do not think it was only a few, or the most base Athenians, who were unable to do this, consider that Thucydides also raised two sons, Melesias and Stephanus; he educated them well in other things, and they wrestled best among the Athenians. For he gave one to Xanthias and the other to Euodorus; and these were thought to be the best at wrestling at that time. Do you not remember? **ANYTUS:** I do, by hearsay. **SOCRATES:** Is it not clear that he would never have taught his children these things which required spending money, while failing to teach them to be good men—which required no spending—if it were teachable? But perhaps Thucydides was a base man, and did not have many friends among the Athenians and the allies? He was of a great house, and had great power in the city and among the other Greeks, so that if this were teachable, he would have found someone who would make his sons good, either one of the locals or a stranger, if he himself lacked leisure because of his care for the city. But, friend Anytus, perhaps virtue is not teachable. **ANYTUS:** Socrates, you seem to me to speak ill of people too easily. I would advise you, if you are willing to listen to me, to take care. For perhaps even in another city it is easy to do people harm or good, but in this one it is very much so. I think you know this yourself. **SOCRATES:** Meno, Anytus seems to me to be angry, and I am not at all surprised. For he thinks, first, that I am slandering these men, and then he believes himself to be one of them. But if he ever realizes what it is to speak ill, he will cease being angry; for now he does not know. But you tell me, are there not noble and good men among you? **MENO:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** What then? Are they willing to offer themselves as teachers to the young, and to admit both that they are teachers and that virtue is teachable? **MENO:** No, by Zeus, Socrates; but sometimes you would hear them say it is teachable, and sometimes that it is not. **SOCRATES:** Shall we say then that they are teachers of this thing, when they cannot even agree on this very point? **MENO:** It does not seem so to me, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** What then? Do these Sophists of yours, who alone proclaim it, seem to be teachers of virtue? **MENO:** I admire this most in Gorgias, Socrates: that you would never hear him promising this. On the contrary, he laughs at the others when he hears them promising it. He thinks one should make men clever at speaking. **SOCRATES:** So you do not think the Sophists are teachers? **MENO:** I cannot say, Socrates. For I have suffered the same thing as the many: sometimes they seem so to me, and sometimes they do not. **SOCRATES:** Do you know that not only you and the other politicians think it is sometimes teachable and sometimes not, but you know that the poet Theognis says this too? **MENO:** In what verses? **SOCRATES:** In the elegies, where he says: "And drink and eat with those, and sit with those, and please those whose power is great. You know that in these lines he speaks as if virtue is teachable? **MENO:** It appears so. **SOCRATES:** But in other lines, changing a little, he says: "If a mind could be made (he says) and implanted in a man," he says something like "many and great would be the rewards for those able to do this," and "never would a bad son be born from a good father, if he followed <note>The text cuts off here, continuing on the next page.</note>

**MENO:** It appears so. **SOCRATES:** Elsewhere, changing it a little, he says this: "If a sound mind could be handed over to a man, surely those who could achieve this would carry away many great rewards; nor would a bad son ever come from a good father."

<margin>A</margin> ...imbued with wise tales <note>Socrates is quoting the poet Theognis here.</note>; but by teaching you will never make a bad man good." Do you perceive that he is contradicting himself again on these very points?
**MENO:** It appears so. **SOCRATES:** Can you then name any other matter where those who claim to be teachers are not only not recognized as teachers of others, but are admitted to not even understand the subject themselves, and are even considered wicked in the very thing they profess to teach? Or where those who are themselves admitted to be "noble and good" <note>original: "καλοὶ κἀγαθοὶ" (kaloi kagathoi) — a standard Greek phrase for the aristocratic ideal of a gentleman.</note> say at one time that the thing can be taught, and at another time that it cannot? Would you say that people who are so confused about a subject are its proper teachers?
**MENO:** By Zeus, I certainly would not. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, if neither the Sophists <note>Professional teachers in ancient Greece who charged fees to teach excellence and rhetoric.</note> nor the men who are themselves "noble and good" are teachers of this matter, it is clear that no 
<margin>B</margin> others are. **MENO:** I think not. **SOCRATES:** And if there are no teachers, there are no students either? **MENO:** It seems to be as you say. **SOCRATES:** But have we not agreed that a thing for which there are neither teachers nor students is not something that can be taught? **MENO:** We have agreed. **SOCRATES:** And so, no teachers of virtue are to be found anywhere. **MENO:** That is true. **SOCRATES:** And if there are no teachers, there are no students. **MENO:** So it appears. **SOCRATES:** Virtue, then, cannot be taught.
**MENO:** It seems not, if we have investigated correctly. I am now wondering, Socrates, whether there are any good men at all, or what the manner of the birth of good men might be. **SOCRATES:** We are in danger, Meno—both you and I—of being rather poor specimens, and it seems Gorgias has not 
<margin>C</margin> sufficiently educated you, nor Prodicus <note>A Sophist known for his focus on the precise meaning of words; Socrates occasionally called himself Prodicus's pupil.</note> me. Above all, then, we must turn our minds to ourselves and seek someone who will, by some means or another, make us better. I say this looking back at our recent inquiry, noting how we ridiculously failed to see that it is not only under the guidance of knowledge <note>original: "ἐπιστήμη" (episteme) — formal, certain knowledge.</note> that human affairs are conducted correctly and well; and if this point escapes us, it may also escape us how it is that good men are produced. **MENO:** What do you mean by this, Socrates? **SOCRATES:** This: that good men must be useful, we were correct to agree on that, as it could not be otherwise. Is that not so? **MENO:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** And that they will be useful if they 
<margin>D</margin> guide our affairs correctly—we surely agreed well on that too? **MENO:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** But that it is impossible to guide correctly unless one is "prudent" <note>original: "φρόνιμος" (phronimos) — possessing practical wisdom or foresight.</note>—that is what we seem to have agreed upon incorrectly. **MENO:** What do you mean by "correctly"? **SOCRATES:** I will tell you. If someone who knew the road to Larissa <note>A city in Thessaly, Meno’s home region.</note>, or anywhere else you like, were to walk it and lead others, would he not lead them correctly and well? **MENO:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** But what if someone had a *correct opinion* about which road it was, but had never traveled it and did not "know" it in that sense—would he not also lead them correctly? **MENO:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** And as long as he has a correct opinion about the things that the other man has certain knowledge of, he will be no worse a leader—thinking the truth but not actually "knowing" it—than the man who knows it. **MENO:** Not at all. **SOCRATES:** True opinion, then, is no worse a guide than 
<margin>E</margin> knowledge when it comes to the correctness of an action. This is what we passed over earlier in our investigation of virtue: we said that knowledge alone leads to correct action, but in fact, true opinion does the same. **MENO:** So it seems. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, correct opinion is no less useful than knowledge. **MENO:** Except for this, Socrates: that the man with knowledge would always be successful, whereas the man with correct opinion would sometimes succeed and sometimes not. **SOCRATES:** How so? Would the man who always has a correct opinion not always be successful, so long as his opinion is correct? **MENO:** That seems necessary to me. So I wonder, Socrates, since this is the case, why knowledge is 
<margin>F</margin> considered so much more honorable than correct opinion, and why they are two different things. **SOCRATES:** Do you know why you wonder? Or shall I tell you? **MENO:** Tell me, by all means. **SOCRATES:** It is because you have not paid attention to the statues of Daedalus <note>A mythical inventor said to have created statues so lifelike they would run away if not tied down.</note>—though perhaps there are none in your country. **MENO:** Why do you say this? **SOCRATES:** Because those statues, if they are not tied down, run away and escape; but if they are tied down, they stay put. **MENO:** What of it? **SOCRATES:** To possess one of his works that is loose is not worth much—it is like a runaway slave, it does not stay. But tied down, it is worth a great deal, for they are very beautiful works. What is the point of this comparison? It refers to true opinions. For true opinions, as long as they stay, are a fine thing and perform all sorts of good; but they do not care to 
<margin>G</margin> stay for long. They run away from the human soul, so they are not worth much until one ties them down by "calculating the cause" <note>original: "αἰτίας λογισμῷ" — working out the underlying reason or logic.</note>. And this, my friend Meno, is "recollection" <note>original: "ἀνάμνησις" (anamnesis) — the Platonic theory that learning is actually the soul remembering truths it knew before birth.</note>, as we agreed in our previous discussion. Once they are tied down, they first become knowledge, and then they become stable. That is why knowledge is more honorable than correct opinion; knowledge differs from correct opinion by this bond. **MENO:** By Zeus, Socrates, it seems like something of that sort! **SOCRATES:** And yet I too speak not as one who knows, but by conjecture. But that correct opinion and knowledge are two different things, I do not think I am merely 
<margin>H</margin> conjecturing. If there is anything I would claim to know—and there are few things—I would put this down as one of them. **MENO:** And you speak correctly, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** And what of this? Is it not also correct that true opinion, when it guides an action, performs no worse than knowledge? **MENO:** I think you are right about this too. **SOCRATES:** Correct opinion, then, is no worse than knowledge 
<margin>I</margin> and no less useful in our actions; nor is the man who has correct opinion inferior to the one who has knowledge. **MENO:** That is so.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...imbued with prudent warnings: but in truth, by teaching you will never make a good man out of a bad one. Do you see how he establishes these contradictions regarding the same things? <margin>ME. It seems so.</margin> <margin>SOCRATES:</margin> Can you therefore point out any matter to me, whatever it may be, whose self-professed teachers are not admitted to be teachers of others, nor to possess that matter themselves, but who confess themselves to be worthless and of no account in the very thing they profess? Or if they do claim to be excellent, they affirm at one time that the matter can be 
perceived, and at another time deny it? Would you correctly call those who are so wavering in a matter "teachers" of that thing?
<margin>MENO:</margin> Not at all. <margin>socRATES:</margin> Therefore, if neither the sophists nor the good and famous men are teachers of this matter, much less will others be.
<margin>B</margin> <margin>MENO:</margin> Certainly. <margin>socRATES:</margin> If there are no instructors, there are no disciples either. <margin>MENO:</margin> It seems to me as you say. <margin>socRATES:</margin> Have we not confessed that that for which there are neither masters nor disciples can by no means be taught? <margin>MENO:</margin> We have confessed it. <margin>socRATES:</margin> And are no instructors of virtue found anywhere? <margin>MENO:</margin> Nowhere. <margin>socRATES:</margin> If no instructors, then no disciples either. <margin>MENO:</margin> So it appears. <margin>socRATES:</margin> Virtue, therefore, cannot be taught. <margin>MENO:</margin> So it seems, if indeed we have judged correctly. For which reason I greatly wonder, O Socrates, whether any good men are to be found among humans, and I am in doubt as to the method by which they become good. <margin>socRATES:</margin> It seems, O Meno, that both I and you are poor specimens. It 
<margin>C</margin> seems Gorgias has not sufficiently educated you, nor <margin>Prodicus me.</margin> <margin>Prodicus was a teacher of Socrates</margin>
Therefore, above all, we must recall our own minds and seek someone who might make us better in this one way. I say these things looking back at our previous inquiry. Has this not been ridiculously overlooked by us: that it is not only with science <note>original: "scientia" — used here to translate "episteme" or certain knowledge.</note> as our leader that the affairs of men proceed rightly? Unless this is conceded—namely, that there is something else besides that knowledge—there would perhaps be no explanation for how good men are made. <margin>MENO:</margin> In what way do you say this, O Socrates? <margin>socRATES:</margin> In this way: we have rightly confessed that it is necessary for good men to be useful, since it could never be 
otherwise, could it? <margin>MENO:</margin> So it is. <margin>socrATES:</margin> And that they will be useful if they are in charge of conducting affairs rightly—is this also well 
<margin>D</margin> agreed between us? <margin>MENO: Well agreed.</margin> <margin>socrATES:</margin> But that no one can be rightly in charge unless he is prudent <note>original: "prudens"</note>—it is clear that this was not quite rightly asserted by both of us. <margin>MENO:</margin> How do you say "rightly"? <margin>socRATES:</margin> I will tell you. He who knows the way to Larissa, or anywhere else, and either goes there himself or leads others—will he not lead them rightly and well? <margin>MENO:</margin> Entirely. <margin>socRATES:</margin> But what if someone has a right opinion as to which way leads to Larissa, yet has never set out nor known it—would he not also lead rightly? <margin>MENO:</margin> Greatly so. <margin>socrATES:</margin> And as long as he has a right opinion about those same things of which the other has knowledge, will he be a leader any worse—believing the truth, though knowing it not at all—than he who knows those things thoroughly? <margin>MENO:</margin> Not at 
<margin>E</margin> all. <margin>socrATES:</margin> True opinion, therefore, is no less powerful for acting rightly than prudence. And that is what we overlooked in the earlier consideration of virtue, while we were asserting that prudence alone was the leader of right action; for this other thing was true opinion. <margin>MENO:</margin> It seems so. <margin>socRATES:</margin> Therefore, <margin>does right opinion contribute any less than knowledge?</margin> <margin>Right opinion and knowledge.</margin>
<margin>MENO:</margin> It contributes less in this way, O Socrates: that whoever has knowledge always attains his goal, but he who has right opinion sometimes succeeds and sometimes is mistaken. <margin>socRATES:</margin> What are you saying? He who proceeds with right opinion—is he not always successful in his desire as long as he opines rightly? <margin>MENO:</margin> It appears necessary. For which reason I wonder 
<margin>F</margin> why, since this is so, knowledge is nevertheless held to be so much more excellent than right opinion; and I am in doubt as to why each of them is something different. <margin>socRATES:</margin> Do you know why you wonder? Or do you want me to tell you? <margin>MENO:</margin> Tell me by all means. <margin>socRATES:</margin> Because you have never considered the statues of Daedalus; perhaps they do not exist among you.
<margin>MENO:</margin> To what end do you say this? <margin>socRATES:</margin> Because these, unless they are tied, depart and run away; but tied, they remain. <margin>MENO:</margin> What then? <margin>socRATES:</margin> Among his works, that which is loose is not of much value, like a runaway man—for it does not stay. But tied, it is worthy of admiration, for they are most beautiful works. For what purpose do I say this? For the sake of true opinions. Indeed, as long as these remain stable, 
<margin>G</margin> they are beautiful works and accomplish all good things. However, they are unwilling to stay for long, but run away quickly from the mind of a man; wherefore they are not of much value until one ties them with reasoning from their causes. This, indeed, friend Meno, <margin>is recollection,</margin> <margin>Right opinion is recollection.</margin> as was agreed between us above. But after they are tied, they first become knowledge, and then they become permanent; and for that reason, knowledge is more excellent than right opinion, and differs from it by a certain bond. <margin>MENO:</margin> By Jove, O Socrates, a fitting comparison. <margin>socRATES:</margin> Furthermore, I myself speak not as one knowing, but as one conjecturing. But that true opinion is something other than knowledge, I do not seem to myself to be entirely 
<margin>H</margin> conjecturing. But if there is anything else I would confess to knowing—which are surely few things—this is one I would number among those I know. <margin>MENO:</margin> You speak well, O Socrates. <margin>socrATES:</margin> What then? Is this not also right: that true opinion leading any work achieves it 
<margin>I</margin> no worse than knowledge? <margin>MENO:</margin> This also is true. <margin>socRATES:</margin> Therefore, true opinion is nothing worse than knowledge,

<summary>Socrates and Meno conclude that virtue is not teachable because it has no recognized teachers. Socrates then introduces the famous distinction between "true opinion" and "knowledge," using the analogy of Daedalus's moving statues to explain how knowledge is "tied down" by understanding the underlying cause.</summary>

and it is no less useful for actions, so that a man who possesses true opinion is no less useful than one endowed with knowledge. <term>MENO.</term> That is so. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Furthermore, we agreed that a good man must be useful. <term>MENO.</term> We did. <term>SOCRATES.</term> If, therefore, men are not good and useful to their cities through knowledge alone—if indeed such men could be found—but also through right opinion; and since neither of these belongs to men by nature, neither knowledge nor true opinion, nor are they acquired as extras <note>original: "adventitia"; Greek: "ἐπίκτητα" (epikteta) — meaning things added later rather than being innate.</note>: does it seem to you that either of them is there by nature? <term>MENO.</term> Not at all. <term>SOCRATES.</term> And since they are not there by nature, then good men are not good by nature either? <term>MENO.</term> Certainly not. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Since it is not by nature, we were then considering whether it comes through teaching? <term>MENO.</term> Yes. <term>SOCRATES.</term> And it seemed it could be taught if virtue were a form of prudence <note>original: "prudentia"; Greek: "φρόνησις" (phronesis) — practical wisdom or intelligence.</note>? <term>MENO.</term> It did. <term>SOCRATES.</term> And if it were teachable, it would be prudence? <term>MENO.</term> Exactly. <term>SOCRATES.</term> And if there were teachers, it could be taught; but if not, then it could not? <term>MENO.</term> That is right. <term>SOCRATES.</term> And we have agreed that there are no teachers of it. <term>MENO.</term> We have. <term>SOCRATES.</term> We concluded, then, that it is neither taught nor is it prudence? <term>MENO.</term> We did. <term>SOCRATES.</term> However, we also granted that it is a good thing. <term>MENO.</term> We did. <term>SOCRATES.</term> And that which leads rightly is both good and useful. <term>MENO.</term> Most certainly.

<margin>Two things lead rightly: true opinion and knowledge.</margin>
<term>SOCRATES.</term> Finally, then, these two things alone lead rightly: true opinion and knowledge. A man who possesses these can be a leader to others. For things that happen by chance are not directed by human leadership; but in those matters where a man acts as a leader toward what is right, these are the two: true opinion and knowledge. <term>MENO.</term> I agree. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Therefore, since virtue cannot be grasped through teaching, it is by no means knowledge. <term>MENO.</term> It does not appear so. <term>SOCRATES.</term> So, of these two good and useful things, one is ruled out—namely knowledge—and it does not hold the leadership in civic action. <term>MENO.</term> I think not. <term>SOCRATES.</term> It is not, then, by any wisdom, nor by being wise, that such men govern the republic—men like Themistocles <note>A famous Athenian statesman and general.</note> and those whom Anytus mentioned a moment ago. This is why they cannot make others like themselves, because they are not what they are through knowledge. <term>MENO.</term> It seems to be as you say, Socrates. <term>SOCRATES.</term> If not by knowledge, it remains that these statesmen govern their cities by using right opinion, being no different in their relation to prudence than soothsayers and those seized by divine frenzy. For these men utter many true things, yet they understand nothing of what they say. <term>MENO.</term> So it seems. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Is it not right then, Meno, to call such men "divine," who, though they have no understanding, nevertheless achieve many great things in what they do and say? <term>MENO.</term> Certainly. <term>SOCRATES.</term> We should rightly call "divine" those we just mentioned—the soothsayers, the prophets, and all the poets. And we should say that the statesmen, no less than the others, are divine, being inspired by the divine breath <note>original: "divino afflatos numine" — divinely inspired or "enthused."</note> and possessed by God, whenever they successfully direct the republic by saying many great things while understanding nothing of it. <term>MENO.</term> Very much so. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Even women, Meno, call good men "divine." and the Spartans, whenever they wish to praise a good man, say, "This is a divine man." <term>MENO.</term> And they seem to speak correctly, Socrates, although perhaps Anytus here is annoyed with you for saying such things.

<margin>From where virtue comes.</margin>
<term>SOCRATES.</term> I do not mind that at all. With him, Meno, we shall talk another time. But if in all this discussion we have investigated and spoken correctly, virtue will come to us neither by nature nor by teaching; rather, it comes by a divine lot <note>original: "divina sorte" — a gift from the gods.</note> without the use of the mind to those who receive it—unless there should be someone among the statesmen who is capable of making another into a statesman. If such a man existed, he would be among the living what Homer says Tiresias <note>The blind prophet of Thebes.</note> is among the dead, saying: <margin>Odyssey, Book 10</margin> "Among those in the underworld, he alone has his wits; the rest flit about as shadows." In the same way, such a man would be like a solid reality among shadows when it comes to virtue. <term>MENO.</term> You seem to speak excellently, Socrates. <term>SOCRATES.</term> From this reasoning, then, Meno, it appears that virtue comes by a divine lot to those who have it. But we shall only grasp the clear truth of this when, before asking *how* virtue comes to men, we first attempt to investigate *what* virtue is in and of itself. But now it is time for me to go elsewhere. You, for your part, must persuade your host Anytus of these things you are convinced of, so that he may be gentler. For if you persuade him, you will also benefit the Athenians.

**A** ...no less useful for actions; nor is the man who has right opinion less so than he who has knowledge. MEN. If that is so. SOC. And surely we agreed that a good man is useful to us? MEN. Yes. # THE FIRST ALCIBIADES,
## OR, ON THE NATURE
## of man.
### Obstetric.

---

->SUMMARY OF THE DIALOGUE.<-

In the person of Alcibiades, the philosopher proposes the vices of human nature and their remedies. Those vices are negligence, ignorance, and arrogance. The remedies, however, are care for ourselves and serious self-knowledge. Care for ourselves consists in applying the greatest diligence to cultivating ourselves (that is, our soul, which we ought to consider our true self), and not in spending useless effort on things outside ourselves—which is a backward sort of diligence, concerning the body...

<meta>Catchword: namely</meta>

<summary>Socrates concludes that virtue is neither innate nor teachable but a gift of "divine lot," likening inspired statesmen to prophets. The text then transitions to the First Alcibiades, focusing on self-knowledge and the soul.</summary>
<keywords>virtue, true opinion, knowledge, divine inspiration, Meno, Socrates, Anytus, Tiresias, Homer, Alcibiades, self-knowledge, Athenian statesmen</keywords>

--- Page 57 ---
<meta>This page transitions from the concluding thoughts of the previous dialogue (Meno) into the opening of the First Alcibiades. The introductory Latin text provides a moral framework for the dialogue to follow, emphasizing self-knowledge and the distinction between the soul and the body.</meta>

# ALCIBIADES I.

...namely, also those things which pertain to the care of the body, which are indeed not ourselves: since the body is the instrument of the soul; that is, not the man himself, but that which the man uses: however, those things which pertain to the body, such as strength and riches, etc., are clearly outside the man. Truly, the serious knowledge of ourselves looks toward this: that we might be ashamed of our arrogance, since we are nothing if we know ourselves well; then, that we may depend upon the one God, who is the true and solid foundation of our happiness, and who accordingly makes those remedies effective in men. Piety, therefore, is especially commended, so that it may exist as the head of an honorable and blessed life, whether in private persons or in the state.

---

->SOCRATES, ALCIBIADES.<-

<margin>A</margin> <image-desc>Large decorative drop cap Ω with floral motifs.</image-desc> O son of Clinias, I think you wonder that I, having been your first lover, remain the only one who does not leave now that the others have stopped; and that while others troubled you with their talk, I have not even spoken to you for so many years. The cause of this was not human, but a certain divine hindrance <note>original: "δαιμόνιον ἐναντίωμα" (daimonion enantioma) — Socrates famously referred to a 'daimon' or divine sign, an inner voice that warned him against taking certain actions.</note>, the power of which you will learn later. But now, since it no longer opposes me, I have come to you. And I am hopeful that it will not oppose me in the future. Throughout almost all this time, I have been observing how you conducted yourself toward your lovers. Though they were many and high-minded, there was not one who was not driven away, surpassed by your pride. <margin>B</margin> I wish to explain the reason why you looked down on them. You say you stand in need of no man for anything. For the things belonging to you are great, starting from the body and ending with the soul. You think first that you are the most handsome and greatest; (and indeed it is plain to see that you are not lying;) then, that you are of the most vigorous family in your city, which is the greatest of the Greek cities; and there your father's friends and kinsmen are most numerous and excellent, who could serve you if needed. Your mother’s side is no less so. <margin>C</margin> But greater than all these is the power you think you have through Pericles, son of Xanthippus, whom your father left as guardian for you and your brother; who is able to do whatever he wishes not only in this city, but in all of Greece, and among many great nations of the barbarians. I would add also that you are among the wealthy; but you seem to me to take the least pride in this. Because of all these things, you have triumphed over your lovers in your boasting, and they, being your inferiors, were overcome. And this has not escaped you. Wherefore I know well that you wonder what I intend by not abandoning my love, and what hope I hold while others have ceased.

<margin>D</margin> ALCIB. And perhaps, Socrates, you do not know that you have barely anticipated me. For I had it in mind to approach you first and ask these very things: what is it you want, and looking to what hope do you trouble me, being most diligently present wherever I am? For I truly wonder what your business is, and I would gladly learn.

SOCR. You shall hear me then (as is likely) eagerly, if indeed, as you say, you desire to know what I am thinking. I will speak to one who will listen and remain.

AL. By all means, speak.

SOCR. See then. It would not be surprising if, just as I have barely begun, I should also barely finish.

AL. My good man, speak. I will listen.

SOCR. Then I must speak. It is difficult indeed to offer love to a man who does not yield to lovers; nevertheless, I must dare to express my thought. <margin>E</margin> For I, Alcibiades, if I saw you content with the things I just recounted, and thinking you ought to spend your life in them, I would have long ago abandoned my love, as I have convinced myself. But now I will declare other thoughts of yours about yourself; by which you will know that I have continued to pay close attention to you. For you seem to me, if some god should say to you, "Alcibiades, do you wish to live possessing only what you now have, or to die immediately if you are not permitted to acquire greater things?" you would, I think, choose to die. But now I will tell you on what hope you live. <margin>F</margin> You believe that as soon as you come before the assembly of the Athenian people (which I think will happen in a few days), you will demonstrate to the Athenians that you are worthy of being honored more than Pericles, or any other who has ever lived. And having shown this, you will have the greatest power in the city. And if you are greatest here, you will be so among the others; and not only among the Greeks, but also among the barbarians who inhabit the same continent as us. And if that same god should tell you that you must rule here in Europe, but that you would not be allowed to cross into Asia or touch the affairs there, you would not, I think, be willing to live on those terms alone; unless you fill all mankind, so to speak, with your name and your power. <margin>G</margin> And I think you consider no one worthy of mention except Cyrus and Xerxes. That you hold this hope, I know well, and I am not guessing. Perhaps then you might say, knowing I speak the truth: "What then, Socrates, is this to the matter you said you would tell me, why you do not leave me?" I will tell you, dear son of Clinias and Dinomache. It is impossible for you to bring these thoughts to an end without me; so much power I think I have over your affairs and over you. For this reason, I think the god has long not permitted me to speak with you, for which I waited until it should be allowed. For now it is allowed; it no longer opposes me.

<column-break/>

->S O C R A T E S, A L C I B I A D E S.<-

<margin>A</margin> <image-desc>Large decorative drop cap F with floral motifs.</image-desc> SON of Clinias, I think you wonder that, although I was the very first of all to begin to love you, and while the others have turned away, I alone persevere in this goodwill; and while your other friends were constantly troublesome to you with their frequent company, I have not even addressed you for so many years. The cause of this matter was not anything human, but a certain opposing power of a spirit <note>original: "vis dæmonij" — Latin for 'daimonic force'.</note>, the power of which you will hear in what follows. But now, since it no longer opposes me, I have come here. I hope, however, <margin>B</margin> that it will not oppose us in the future. Throughout almost all this time, I was considering how you behaved toward your friends. Although they were many and proud, there was none among them whom you did not send away, surpassed by your own pride. I will explain the reason why you looked down on them. For you say that you lack nothing from other men, since the things that are in you are so excellent that you need no one's help for the goods of either body or soul. You think yourself to excel most of all in your tall and handsome physical stature. And indeed it is clear to anyone that you are not lying in the least. Furthermore, you proclaim yourself born of a most vigorous family <margin>C</margin> in this greatest of Greek cities: on your father's side, you have very many and excellent friends and kinsmen who can provide you with everything when needed. Your mother’s side is neither inferior to these, nor fewer in number. But much greater authority than all these for conducting your affairs is brought to you by Pericles, son of Xanthippus, whom your father left as a guardian for you and your brother; he who is able to do whatever he wants not only in this city, but in all Greece, and even among many and great nations of the barbarians. I would also add the very great riches of your family, were I not aware that you boast of these least of all; because of all these things, uplifted by pride, you have subdued all your friends. And they, being inferior, have yielded to you. Truly, these things have not escaped you. Therefore, I know well that you wonder with what intention I have persevered in my goodwill toward you, and what hope I have conceived of you, that I alone of all have remained while the others fled. <margin>D</margin> ALCIB. But perhaps you do not know, O Socrates, that you have now anticipated me by a little. For it had come into my mind that I should approach you first and ask these same things of you. What do you want? With what hope, finally, are you troublesome to me, you who are always most carefully present wherever I am? Indeed, I wonder what your counsel is, and I would gladly hear it. SOCR. You shall hear this from me then, as is fitting, as soon as possible, if as you say you desire to know and hear what I am thinking. For I shall relate it as if to one who is waiting and <margin>E</margin> listening. ALCIB. And most certainly, speak now. SOCRAT. Look then; for it ought not to seem strange if, just as I have barely begun, I should barely finish. ALCIB. Come, speak now, for I will listen. SOCRAT. I must indeed speak. It is difficult, truly, to enter into an association with one who dismisses none of his friends <note>Note: The Latin translator here seems to interpret "yielding to lovers" as "dismissing friends."</note>. Nevertheless, I must be bold and express my opinion. Indeed, O Alcibiades, if I had known you were content with those things which we recounted above, and were passing your life in them, I would have long ago (so I am convinced) laid aside my goodwill toward you. But now I will indicate to you two other thoughts about yourself, so that you may understand that since <margin>F</margin> I first applied my mind to you, I have never ceased. It seems to me, truly, if some god said, "O Alcibiades, do you wish to live possessing only those things you now have? Or to die immediately unless it be permitted to attain more excellent things?" you would seem to choose death instead. But truly, I will reveal with what hope you now spend your life; for you think that if you soon ascend to the assembly of the Athenian people—which you think will happen in a few days—you will demonstrate to the Athenians that you are worthy of greater honor than either Pericles is, or anyone else has been among those who flourished in previous ages. And if you show this, you will attain the greatest authority among your citizens. And yet, if you are most powerful in this city, you will be the most famous of all Greeks, and also of the barbarians, whoever inhabit the same region as the <margin>G</margin> Greeks. And if the same God granted you the empire of Europe, but forbade you to cross into Asia and there strive for empire, you would not yet, it seems to me, choose to spend your life with these things alone, unless you spread your name and power, so to speak, through all races of men. And I <margin>A note on the speaker.</margin> think you consider no one worthy of memory except Cyrus and Xerxes. That you are nourished by such a hope, I do not guess, but know for certain. You will say perhaps, being conscious that I have spoken the truth: "What are these things, O Socrates, to the reason you wished to assign, for which you have not yet deserted me?" I will tell you, O friend, son of Clinias and Dinomache: you are in no way able to lead these thoughts of yours to their desired end without me; to such an extent do I trust in my power over you and your affairs. Therefore, I believe the God himself formerly did not permit me to converse with you; and I waited...

...until he should permit. For just as you hope to show your city that you are worthy of every honor among them, and that once these things are demonstrated, nothing remains so great that you could not immediately accomplish it: so too I trust that I can do the most for you, once I have shown that I am more worthy than all others. Neither your guardian, nor your kinsman, nor any other person except me alone, with God’s favor, will deliver to you that power which you desire. Therefore, as long as you were younger and had not yet come into such great hope, in my opinion, God prohibited me from disputing with you, so that I would not contend in vain. These
**E** are the things you have knowledge of—unless perhaps you have learned something without my knowing. Surely not when it is about buildings? **ALCIBIADES:** Certainly not. **SOCRATES:** For a builder will advise better than you. **ALCIBIADES:** True. **SOCRATES:** Nor yet when they debate about prophecy. **ALCIBIADES:** Not at all. **SOCRATES:** For a prophet <note>original: "fatidicus" / "μάντις" — a seer or diviner.</note> knows these things better than you. **ALCIBIADES:** Better.
**F** Whether he be small or great, handsome or ugly, noble or ignoble. **ALCIBIADES:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** For I think it belongs to the one who knows, not the one who is rich, to give counsel on each thing. **ALCIBIADES:** Why not? **SOCRATES:** And therefore, whether the one who advises be rich or poor, it will make no difference to the Athenians when they deliberate on how the citizens may be healthy; rather, they will seek only that the counselor be a physician. **ALCIBIADES:** And rightly so. **SOCRATES:** When, then, and in what deliberation will you be a suitable counselor? **ALCIBIADES:** When they deliberate about their own affairs. **SOCRATES:** When they inquire about naval matters, what kind of ships they ought to build? **ALCIBIADES:** No, O Socrates. **SOCRATES:** For I suppose you do not know how to build ships. Is this the
**G** cause, or is it something else? **ALCIBIADES:** Nothing else. **SOCRATES:** But truly, about which of their affairs were you speaking? **ALCIBIADES:** When about war, O Socrates, or peace, or any other business of the city. **SOCRATES:** Do you mean when they dispute with whom peace should be made, and against whom war should be waged, and in what manner? **ALCIBIADES:** Exactly. **SOCRATES:** And is it necessary to declare these things to those with whom it is worthwhile? **ALCIBIADES:** To these very ones. **SOCRATES:** And only then when it is better? **ALCIBIADES:** Entirely. **SOCRATES:** And for as long as it is preferable? **ALCIBIADES:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** If, therefore, the Athenians were inquiring against whom they should wrestle, or engage in hand-to-hand combat <note>original: "summis digitis" / "ἀκροχειρίζεσθαι" — literally 'wrestling with fingertips,' a specific light style of sparring.</note> while the rest of the body remains untouched, and how they should compete, would you advise better than the master of the gym? **ALCIBIADES:** The master of the gym would advise better. **SOCRATES:** Can you say what he is looking toward when he advises
**H** <margin>In every pursuit, the "better" is that which is right in all respects.</margin> with whom they should wrestle in the gym, or not, and when, and in what manner? <meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and the young Alcibiades. Having established that Socrates is the only one who can help Alcibiades achieve his political ambitions, Socrates now begins a dialectical examination to see if Alcibiades actually possesses the knowledge required to lead.</meta>

# ALCIBIADES I.

<margin>A</margin>SOCRATES: Therefore, at that time when it is better? ALCIBIADES: Yes. SOCRATES: And where is this "better"? ALCIBIADES: I say it is there. SOCRATES: What then? Since you have already named "better" in both cases, what do you call the "better" in playing the cithara correctly, or in playing the flute? Just as I call the "better" in wrestling "gymnastic," what do you call that other one? ALCIBIADES: I do not perceive your meaning. SOCRATES: But try to imitate me. For I gave an answer that was right in every respect. Surely that which is done according to an art <term>art</term><note>original Greek: "techne". This refers to a systematic skill or craft that can be taught.</note> is right; is it not? ALCIBIADES: Yes. SOCRATES: And is this not an art, the gymnastic art? ALCIBIADES: How could it not be? SOCRATES: And I said that the "better" in wrestling is the gymnastic. ALCIBIADES: You did say that. SOCRATES: And was it not well said? ALCIBIADES: It seems so to me.

<margin>B</margin>SOCRATES: Come then, you too (for it is fitting for you to discourse well): tell me first, what is the art to which correct singing, playing, and dancing belong? What is this whole art called? Can you not say yet? ALCIBIADES: Not yet. SOCRATES: But try this way: who are the goddesses of this art? ALCIBIADES: Do you mean the Muses, O Socrates? SOCRATES: I do. See now what name the art takes from them? ALCIBIADES: It seems to me you mean Music. SOCRATES: I do indeed. What, then, is that which is done correctly according to this art? Just as in that other art I told you what was done correctly according to the art was "gymnastic," what do you say here? How is it done? ALCIBIADES: "Musically," it seems to me.

<margin>C</margin>SOCRATES: You say well. Come now, what do you call the "better" in waging war and the "better" in keeping peace? What do you name this "better"? Just as in each of the previous cases you named the superior thing—in one that it was "more musical," and in the other that it was "more gymnastic"—try now to say what the "better" is in these matters. ALCIBIADES: But I do not have any answer at all.

SOCRATES: But surely it is a shameful thing, if you were speaking and giving advice about food—saying that this is better than that, both now and in such an amount—and someone then asked you, "What do you call 'better,' O Alcibiades?" and you were able to say it is "healthier" (even though you do not pretend to be a doctor); yet in the matter where you *do* pretend to be knowledgeable, and stand up to give advice as one who knows, you are unable to say what the "better" is when asked. Is this not shameful? Or does it not appear shameful? ALCIBIADES: Very much so.

<margin>D</margin>SOCRATES: Consider then, and try to tell me: toward what does the "better" tend in maintaining peace and in waging war against those whom one must? ALCIBIADES: Though I consider it, I cannot think of it. SOCRATES: Do you not even know what we accuse each other of when we go to war? What do we name that which leads us to fight? ALCIBIADES: I do: we say we have been deceived in some way, or forced, or robbed. SOCRATES: Stay a moment: how do we suffer each of these things? Try to say what the difference is between this way and that way. ALCIBIADES: If by "this way," O Socrates, you mean "justly or unjustly"? SOCRATES: That is exactly it. ALCIBIADES: But that makes all the difference in the world.

<margin>E</margin>SOCRATES: What then? Which side will you advise the Athenians to fight? Those who act unjustly, or those who act justly? ALCIBIADES: That is a terrible thing you ask. For even if someone were thinking that one should fight against those who act justly, he would never admit it. SOCRATES: Because it is not lawful, it seems. ALCIBIADES: Not at all; nor does it seem to be honorable. SOCRATES: Therefore, you will make your arguments based on the "just." ALCIBIADES: Necessarily. SOCRATES: Is the "better" in waging war or not, and against whom one must or not, and when one must or not, anything other than that which is "more just"? Or is it not? ALCIBIADES: It appears so.

<margin>F</margin>SOCRATES: How is this, my dear Alcibiades? Have you forgotten that you do not know this? Or did it escape my notice that you were learning and attending a teacher who taught you to distinguish the more just from the more unjust? And who is this person? Tell me as well, so that you may introduce me to him as a student. ALCIBIADES: You are mocking me, Socrates. SOCRATES: No, by the god of friendship, whom I would least of all swear falsely by. But if you have a teacher, tell me who it is. ALCIBIADES: What if I don't have one? Do you think I could not know about the just and unjust in some other way? SOCRATES: Yes, if you had found it. ALCIBIADES: But do you think I could not have found it? SOCRATES: Certainly you could, if you had searched for it. ALCIBIADES: And you think I did not search? SOCRATES: I would, if you had thought you did not know. ALCIBIADES: And was there never a time when I did not think so?

<margin>G</margin>SOCRATES: You say well. Can you then tell us that time when you did not think you knew the just and the unjust? Come, were you searching and thinking you did not know last year? Or not? Answer the truth, so that our dialogue does not become useless. ALCIBIADES: I thought I knew. SOCRATES: And in the third year, and the fourth, and the fifth—was it not the same? ALCIBIADES: It was. SOCRATES: But surely before that you were a child, were you not? ALCIBIADES: Yes. SOCRATES: Then I know well that you thought you knew even then. ALCIBIADES: How do you know that? SOCRATES: I often heard you as a child at your teachers' houses and elsewhere, when you were playing with dice or some other game; you did not speak as if you were in doubt about the just and unjust, but you spoke very loudly and boldly about whichever of the boys happened to be there—that he was "wicked and unjust" and that he "acts unjustly." Is this not the truth? ALCIBIADES: But what was I supposed to do, O Socrates, when someone was treating me unjustly? SOCRATES: But if you happened to be ignorant at the time whether you were being treated unjustly or not, would you then say what you must do? ALCIBIADES: By Zeus, I was not ignorant; I clearly understood that I was being treated unjustly. SOCRATES:

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>SOCRATES: And by how much is it "better"? ALCIBIADES: I confess. SOCRATES: What then? After you have said something is "better" in both cases—both in the singing of the cithara and in the wrestling-school—what do you call "better" in a sound that is correctly tuned for a song? For I, in the wrestling-school, call it "gymnastic." What about you? ALCIBIADES: I do not understand. SOCRATES: But try to imitate me. I would call "better" that which is right in all respects. And what is done according to an art <term>art</term><note>Latin: "ars". Like the Greek "techne", it refers to specialized knowledge or skill.</note> is right, isn't it? ALCIBIADES: It is. SOCRATES: Isn't it the gymnastic art? ALCIBIADES: Why not? SOCRATES: That which I called "better" in the wrestling-school, I called "gymnastic." ALCIBIADES: You did indeed. SOCRATES: And was it not right? ALCIBIADES: It seems so to me.

<margin>B</margin>SOCRATES: Come then, you too (for it is fitting for you to discourse correctly): Tell me first, what is the art to which correct singing, playing, and dancing belong? What is this whole art called? Can you not express it yet? ALCIBIADES: Not yet. SOCRATES: But strive to exert yourself: who are the goddesses of this art? ALCIBIADES: Do you mean the Muses, O Socrates? SOCRATES: Indeed. See now what name the art takes from them. ALCIBIADES: You seem to be saying "Music." SOCRATES: I am indeed. What, then, is that which is done correctly according to this art? Just as just now in that other art I called that which was done correctly according to the art "gymnastic." What do you call "better" here, and how is it done? ALCIBIADES: It seems to me "musical," and "musically."

<margin>C</margin>SOCRATES: You say well. Come now, what do you call "better" in war and "better" in peace? Just as you showed above what was better in each case: in this one what is more "musical," and in that one what is more "gymnastic." Try similarly to pronounce what is "better" in these things. ALCIBIADES: I do not have anything to say. SOCRATES: But it would be a shameful thing, if someone brought you food and said this was better than that, and when and how much—and if someone then asked, "What do you call 'better' itself, O Alcibiades?"—that you would have nothing to answer (namely, that it is "healthier"), even though you do not claim to be a doctor. Yet in that which you boast of being skilled, and for which you stand up to give advice as if you were educated, you are at a loss when asked what is "better."

<margin>D</margin>Is this not, I say, shameful? ALCIBIADES: Most shameful. SOCRATES: Consider then and try to show us: toward what does "better" tend in peace—with whom it ought to be established—and in war—against whom it is necessary? ALCIBIADES: Even though I search, I cannot find it. SOCRATES: Have you noticed, when we wage war, what it is that we accuse each other of when we set out for war, and what we call that for the sake of which the war is undertaken? ALCIBIADES: I have indeed noticed that we are provoked to arms when we are either deceived, or forced, or despoiled of something. SOCRATES: Come, tell me: how does it differ to suffer these things in this way or that way?

<margin>E</margin>ALCIBIADES: When you say "this way or that way," do you mean the same as if you said "justly or unjustly"? SOCRATES: Exactly that. ALCIBIADES: Truly, that makes all the difference in the world. SOCRATES: Against whom will you urge the Athenians to go to war? Against those who do wrong <note>original: "iniuriosos"</note> or those who are just? ALCIBIADES: That is a hard question you ask. For even if someone thought war should be waged against those who cultivate justice, he would not admit it to you. SOCRATES: For that is not lawful, as it seems. ALCIBIADES: Not at all; nor does it appear honorable. Socrates: Therefore, you will make your speeches concerning the "just." ALCIBIADES: Necessarily. SOCRATES: Is there anything else, then, as I was just asking—in waging war or not, and with whom one ought or not, and when one ought or not—is there anything "better" than that which is "more just"?

<margin>F</margin>ALCIBIADES: This seems "better." SOCRATES: Is it possible then, O friend Alcibiades, that it has escaped you that you are ignorant of this? Or have you gone to a teacher without my knowledge, from whom you learned to judge what is more just and what is more unjust? Come, show him to me, so that you may make me his disciple and guest. ALCIBIADES: You are mocking me, O Socrates. SOCRATES: No, by the god of friendship, whom I would least of all deceive with an oath. But if you have one, tell me who he is. ALCIBIADES: What if I don't have one? Do you think I cannot distinguish just and unjust things in some other way?

<margin>He discerns who finds. He finds who seeks. He seeks who thinks he is ignorant.</margin>
<margin>G</margin>SOCRATES: Indeed, if you have found it. ALCIBIADES: Do you not think I have found it? SOCRATES: Most certainly, provided you have searched for it. ALCIBIADES: Then you don't believe I searched? SOCRATES: I would believe it, provided you thought you were ignorant. ALCIBIADES: Was there ever a time when I did not think so? SOCRATES: You speak well; but can you assign to us that time when you did not believe you had knowledge of just and unjust things? Come, did you seek to know these things last year or not? And did you think you knew them or not? Answer truthfully, lest our discussion be in vain. ALCIBIADES: I thought I knew. SOCRATES: And in the third year before that, and the fourth, and the fifth—was it not the same way? ALCIBIADES: The same.

<margin>H</margin>SOCRATES: But before these times you were a boy, weren't you? ALCIBIADES: I was. SOCRATES: I know for certain that you thought you knew then. ALCIBIADES: How do you know? SOCRATES: I often heard you as a boy, when you were with your teachers and elsewhere, in the throwing of dice and other boyish pursuits, not doubting in the least about just and unjust things; but speaking boldly about whichever boy the conversation turned to—that he was "bad and unjust," and that he "acted unjustly." Do I speak the truth? ALCIBIADES:

---

What was I supposed to do, when someone treated me with injustice? SOCRATES: But if you were ignorant, whether an injustice was being done or not, would you then ask what you ought to do? ALCIBIADES: By Jove, I was not ignorant; I clearly understood that an injustice was being done to me.

<summary>Socrates uses the analogies of music and gymnastics to show that the "better" path in politics is Justice. He then exposes Alcibiades' lack of true education by demonstrating that the young man cannot identify when or how he actually learned what justice is.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialectic between Socrates and the young, ambitious Alcibiades. Socrates is testing whether Alcibiades actually possesses the knowledge of "justice" required for political leadership, or if he merely assumes he knows what he cannot explain.</meta>
