<margin>A</margin> SOCRATES: Therefore, you thought even while you were a boy that you could distinguish between what is just and what is unjust. ALCIBIADES: Indeed, I did know. SOCRATES: At what time did you discover this? For it certainly was not during that time when you believed you already knew it. ALCIBIADES: Not at all. SOCRATES: When, then, did you think you were ignorant of these things? Consider it; you will not find such a time. ALCIBIADES: By Jupiter <note>original Latin: "Per Iouem". Alcibiades is swearing by the king of the gods, known as Zeus in Greek.</note>, O Socrates, I have no answer to give. SOCRATES: So you do not know these things through your own discovery? ALCIBIADES: It does not appear so. SOCRATES: But a moment ago you said you had not received them through instruction either. If you have neither discovered nor learned them, how and from where do you hold this knowledge? ALCIBIADES: Perhaps I did not answer correctly when I asserted that I knew through my own discovery. SOCRATES: How then does the matter stand? ALCIBIADES: I learned them myself, I suppose, just as others do. SOCRATES: Re-
<margin>B</margin> turning to the same point: tell me, from whom did you learn? ALCIBIADES: From the common people <term>common people</term><note>original Latin: "vulgus"; original Greek: "hoi polloi". Socrates is often skeptical of the masses as a source of philosophical truth.</note>. SOCRATES: You do not retreat to very reliable teachers when you refer yourself to the common people. ALCIBIADES: Are they not sufficient for teaching even these things? SOCRATES: They are not even sufficient for teaching that which pertains—or does not pertain—to a board game <term>board game</term><note>original Latin: "talarem ludum"; Greek: "petteia". This refers to games like checkers or backgammon, considered trivial skills.</note>, although these are of less value than justice. Do you not also think so? ALCIBIADES: I think so. SOCRATES: Therefore, can they teach greater things if they cannot teach the trivial? ALCIBIADES: I certainly think they can. Indeed, they can teach many things better than a board game. SOCRATES: What sort of things? ALCIBIADES: Such as how to speak Greek. For I learned it from them, and I
<margin>C</margin> had no other teacher besides those whom you said were not sufficiently reliable masters. SOCRATES: O noble youth, the common people are indeed suitable teachers for this matter, and they are rightly praised for this instruction. ALCIBIADES: Why? SOCRATES: Because they possess what good teachers ought to have. ALCIBIADES: What is that? SOCRATES: Do you not know that it is necessary for those who are going to teach anything to first understand it themselves? Is it not? ALCIBIADES: Why not? SOCRATES: And when they understand, do they not agree with themselves and not disagree? ALCIBIADES: Yes. SOCRATES: But if they disagree on something, shall we say they know it? ALCIBIADES: Not at all. SOCRATES: How then could they be good teachers of those things? ALCIBIADES: In no way. SOCRATES: Does the multitude seem to you to disagree when-
<margin>D</margin> ever it is asked what is stone and what is wood? ALCIBIADES: No, all confess the same thing and are moved toward the same point when they want to take up wood or stone; and in the same way in all such things? For I understand that by "knowing Greek," you meant this, did you not? ALCIBIADES: I did indeed. SOCRATES: And for that reason, do they not agree in these things, as we said, both privately and publicly, and do not cities disagree with each other, one calling this thing one way and another calling it something else? ALCIBIADES: They do not disagree. SOCRATES: They would, therefore, be suitable teachers of these things. ALCIBIADES: Certainly. SOCRATES: And so, if we wished to turn out someone learned in these things, we would rightly send him to the instruction of the multitude. ALCIBIADES: Entirely so. SOCRATES: But if
<margin>E</margin> we wished to know not only which are men and which are horses, but also which of them are best at running and which are not, would the common people be able to teach this? ALCIBIADES: Not at all. SOCRATES: This should be sufficient evidence for you that the common people do not know, nor are they fit teachers of these things, since they by no means agree among themselves about them. ALCIBIADES: It seems so. SOCRATES: If I desired to know not only who are men, but who are healthy and who are sick, would the multitude teach me? ALCIBIADES: No. SOCRATES: You will easily notice that the multitude cannot teach these things if you consider their discordant opinions. ALCIBIADES: Truly. SOCRATES: But concerning just
<margin>F</margin> men and things, does the multitude agree with itself? ALCIBIADES: Not at all, by Jupiter, O Socrates. SOCRATES: But they disagree greatly in these? ALCIBIADES: Most greatly. SOCRATES: I think you have never seen nor heard of men disagreeing among themselves so much about the healthy and the sick that they waged war because of it and killed one another. ALCIBIADES: Never. SOCRATES: But regarding the just and the unjust, how bitterly they disagree! And if you have not seen it yourself, I think you have encountered it from many others, and even from Homer; for you have heard the *Odyssey* and the *Iliad*. ALCIBIADES: Entirely so, O Socrates. SOCRATES: Are not all these poems about the distinction between the just and the unjust? ALCIBIADES: They are. SOCRATES: And the battles and deaths between the Achaeans and the Trojans were surely on account of this same disagreement, and in the
<margin>G</margin> same way between the suitors of Penelope and Ulysses <note>Odysseus</note>. ALCIBIADES: You speak the truth. SOCRATES: And I think that among the Athenians, Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note>, and Boeotians—who perished first at Tanagra and then at Coroneia <note>Historical battles of the 5th century BCE; Alcibiades' father died at Coroneia in 447 BCE.</note>, where your father Clinias also met his end—that most bitter fight arose from no other matter than the difference between the just and the unjust. ALCIBIADES: You speak the truth. SOCRATES: Shall we then say they knew those things about which they fought so sharply that, in disputing over the just and the unjust, they suffered the ultimate extremities? ALCIBIADES: It does not seem so. SOCRATES: Therefore, you refer yourself to those teachers whom you yourself admit are ignorant? ALCIBIADES: I seem to. SOCRATES: How then is it consistent for you to know just and unjust things, about which you wander so much, neither appearing to have learned from anyone, nor to have found out for yourself? ALCIBIADES: From what you say, it is not consistent. SOCRATES: Do
<margin>H</margin> you see again, Alcibiades, that you have not said this correctly? ALCIBIADES: What? SOCRATES: That you said I was saying these things. ALCIBIADES: What? Do you not say that I am ignorant of the just and the unjust? SOCRATES: Not at all. ALCIBIADES: Is it I, then?
What sort? SOCRATES: That which you say I am saying. ALCIBIADES: What then? Do you not say it? SOCRATES: Certainly not. ALCIBIADES: But I do?

<margin>A</margin> You thought, then, that you knew even as a child (as it seems) the things that are just and the things that are unjust. **ALCIBIADES:** I certainly thought I knew them. **SOCRATES:** At what time did you find out? For it surely was not when you thought you already knew. **ALCIBIADES:** Certainly not. **SOCRATES:** When then did you think you were ignorant? Look: for you will not find this time. **ALCIBIADES:** By Zeus, O Socrates, I am not able to say. **SOCRATES:** So it is not by finding them out that I know these things. **ALCIBIADES:** It does not at all appear so. **SOCRATES:** But just now you said that you did not know by learning either. If you neither found out nor learned, how do I know, and from where? **ALCIBIADES:** But perhaps I did not answer you correctly in saying that I found them out for myself. **SOCRATES:** How then was it? **ALCIBIADES:** I learned,
<margin>B</margin> (I suppose) I also, just like the others. **SOCRATES:** We have come back to the same argument. From whom? Tell me as well. **ALCIBIADES:** From the many. **SOCRATES:** You do not flee to serious teachers when you refer to the many. **ALCIBIADES:** Why? Are they not sufficient to teach these things? **SOCRATES:** Not even the game of pebbles and what is not. And yet I think these are more trivial than just things. Or do you not think so? **ALCIBIADES:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** Then they are not able to teach the more trivial things, but can teach the more serious? **ALCIBIADES:** I think so, at least. But they are able to teach many things more serious than playing at pebbles. **SOCRATES:** What sort of things? **ALCIBIADES:** For example, even to
<margin>C</margin> speak Greek I learned from them; and I would not be able to name a teacher of my own, but I refer to the same people who you say are not serious teachers. **SOCRATES:** But O noble one, the many are good teachers of this, and they would rightly be praised for their teaching. **ALCIBIADES:** Why so? **SOCRATES:** Because they have concerning these things what good teachers ought to have. **ALCIBIADES:** What are you saying this is? **SOCRATES:** Do you not know that those who are going to teach anything whatsoever must first know it themselves? Or not? **ALCIBIADES:** For how could they not? **SOCRATES:** And must not those who know agree with one another and not differ? **ALCIBIADES:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** In those things where they differ, will you say they know them? **ALCIBIADES:** Certainly not. **SOCRATES:** Of these things, then, how-
<margin>D</margin> ever could they be teachers? **ALCIBIADES:** In no way. **SOCRATES:** What then? Do the many seem to you to differ about what sort of thing is a stone or wood? And do they not all agree on the same things and reach for the same things when they want to take a stone or wood? And likewise in all other such things? For I almost understand that you are saying this about "speaking Greek." Or not? **ALCIBIADES:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** And so in these things (as we said) they agree with one another and with themselves privately, and publicly the cities do not dispute with one another, some saying these things and others saying those? **ALCIBIADES:** No indeed. **SOCRATES:** Likely then they would be good teachers of these things. **ALCIBIADES:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, if
<margin>E</margin> we wanted to make someone know about them, we would rightly send him to the instruction of the many? **ALCIBIADES:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** But what if we wanted to know not only what sort of things are men, or what sort are horses, but also which of them are runners and which are not, would the many still be sufficient to teach this? **ALCIBIADES:** Certainly not. **SOCRATES:** And is it a sufficient proof to you that they do not know, nor are they master teachers of these things, since they do not agree with themselves about them? **ALCIBIADES:** To me, yes. **SOCRATES:** And what if we wanted to know not only what sort are men, but what sort are healthy or sickly, would the many be sufficient teachers for us? **ALCIBIADES:** Certainly not. **SOCRATES:** And would the wretchedness of the teachers be a proof to you, if you saw them differing? **ALCIBIADES:** To me, yes. **SOCRATES:** And what now? Concerning just
<margin>F</margin> men and things, do the many seem to you to agree with themselves and one another? **ALCIBIADES:** Least of all, by Zeus, O Socrates. **SOCRATES:** What then? Do they differ most of all about them? **ALCIBIADES:** By far. **SOCRATES:** I do not think you have ever seen or heard of men differing so strongly about healthy things and not, so as to fight and kill one another because of them. **ALCIBIADES:** Certainly not. **SOCRATES:** But about just and unjust things, I know that even if you have not seen it, you have at least heard from many others and from Homer. For you have listened to the *Odyssey* and the *Iliad*. **ALCIBIADES:** Surely, O Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Are not these poems about the difference of just and unjust things? **ALCIBIADES:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** And the battles
<margin>G</margin> and the deaths on account of this difference happened to the Achaeans and the other Trojans, and to the suitors of Penelope, and to Odysseus. **ALCIBIADES:** You speak the truth. **SOCRATES:** And I think that for those who died at Tanagra of the Athenians, Lacedaemonians, and Boeotians, and those later at Coroneia (among whom your father Clinias died), the death and the battles were made concerning nothing else than the difference of the just and the unjust? Or not? **ALCIBIADES:** You speak the truth. **SOCRATES:** Shall we then say these people know something, who differ so strongly that, in disputing with one another, they do the ultimate things to themselves? **ALCIBIADES:** It does not appear so. **SOCRATES:** Therefore you refer-
<margin>H</margin> ence such teachers whom you yourself admit do not know? **ALCIBIADES:** I seem to. **SOCRATES:** How then is it likely that you know the just and the unjust things, about which you wander so much, and you do not appear to have learned from anyone, nor found out yourself? **ALCIBIADES:** From what you say, it seems so. **SOCRATES:** Do you see again how you did not say this well, O Alcibiades? **ALCIBIADES:** What sort of thing? **SOCRATES:** That you say I am saying these things. **ALCIBIADES:** What? Do you not say them? **SOCRATES:** Not I. **ALCIBIADES:** But I do?

<summary>Socrates argues that the "common people" are inadequate teachers of justice because, unlike their agreement on language or basic objects, they disagree so violently on morality that it leads to war and death. He concludes that Alcibiades cannot have learned justice from the masses, leaving his supposed knowledge of the subject in doubt.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the conversation where Socrates is dismantling Alcibiades's claim to political wisdom. Socrates has just forced Alcibiades to admit he doesn't know the source of his own ideas about justice. Now, Socrates moves to prove that Alcibiades is actually the one asserting his own ignorance, using a clever logical trap.</meta>

->ALCIBIADES I.<-
->Signature: C iij <note>This "signature" is a printer's mark used to help the bookbinder assemble the pages in the correct order.</note><-

<margin>a</margin> **SOCRATES**: Yes. **ALCIBIADES**: How so? **SOCRATES**: You will understand it this way. If I ask you whether one or two is the greater number, you will say two is more? **ALCIBIADES**: I will. **SOCRATES**: By how much? **ALCIBIADES**: By one. **SOCRATES**: Which of us, then, is the one saying that two is more than one by one? **ALCIBIADES**: I am. **SOCRATES**: So, I was the one asking, and you were the one answering? **ALCIBIADES**: Yes. **SOCRATES**: In this matter, then, who appears to be the speaker—I, who am asking, or you, who are answering? **ALCIBIADES**: I am. **SOCRATES**: And what if I were to ask what letters make up the name "Socrates," and you told me—which of us would be the speaker? **ALCIBIADES**: I would. **SOCRATES**: Come then, tell me in a word: whenever there is a question and an answer, who is the speaker: the one asking, or the one answering? **ALCIBIADES**: The one answering, it seems to me, Socrates. **SOCRATES**: And throughout this whole time, was I not the one asking? **ALCIBIADES**: Yes. **SOCRATES**: And you were the one answering? **ALCIBIADES**: Quite so. **SOCRATES**: What follows then? Which of us has said the things that were spoken? **ALCIBIADES**: It appears from our agreement, Socrates, that I did.

<margin>b</margin> **SOCRATES**: Was it not said that just things are not unjust? Did the handsome Alcibiades, son of Cleinias, say then that it was possible—as he intended—to go into the assembly and advise the Athenians about things he does not know? Was that not it? **ALCIBIADES**: So it appears. **SOCRATES**: Then the saying of Euripides <note>original Greek: "τὸ δὲ Εὐριπίδου" (to de Euripidou). Socrates refers to a line from the play *Hippolytus*: "You hear it from yourself, not from me."</note> applies here, Alcibiades: you seem to have heard these things from yourself, not from me. I am not the one saying this, but you are; you accuse me in vain. **ALCIBIADES**: And yet, you are indeed the one speaking. **SOCRATES**: But it is a mad undertaking, my good man, to try to teach what you do not know, having neglected to learn it.

<margin>c</margin> **ALCIBIADES**: I think, Socrates, that the Athenians and other Greeks rarely deliberate on what is more just or more unjust. For they believe such things are obvious; so, setting those aside, they inquire into what will be advantageous <term>advantageous</term><note>original Greek: "συνοίσει" (synoisei). This refers to political expediency or what is "useful" for the state, which Alcibiades tries to separate from moral "justice."</note> for them to do. For I do not think that just things and advantageous things are the same; many have profited by committing great injustices, while others, I think, have gained nothing by acting justly. **SOCRATES**: What then? If the just and the advantageous happen to be entirely different things, surely you don't think you know what is advantageous to men, or why? **ALCIBIADES**: Why not, Socrates? Unless you are going to ask me again from whom I learned it or how I found it for myself.

<margin>d</margin> **SOCRATES**: What a thing you are doing! If you say something incorrectly, and it can be proven by the same logic as before, you think you need to hear something new and different proofs—as if the previous ones were like worn-out clothes that you wouldn't wear again unless someone brought you something pure and spotless. I will let your rhetorical flourishes go, but I will ask nonetheless: where did you learn what is advantageous, and who was your teacher? I ask all the previous questions in a single inquiry. But it is clear you will arrive at the same result, and you will not be able to show that you know what is advantageous by discovery or by learning. But since you are so pampered <note>original Greek: "τρυφᾷς" (tryphas). Suggests a fastidious or spoiled nature.</note> that you don't care to taste the same argument again, I will let this pass—whether you know or not what is advantageous to the Athenians.

<margin>e</margin> **SOCRATES**: But why haven't you demonstrated whether the just and the advantageous are the same or different? If you like, question me as I did you, or if you prefer, explain it in a speech. **ALCIBIADES**: I don't know, Socrates, if I would be able to explain it to you. **SOCRATES**: But, my good man, imagine that I am the assembly and the people; even there, you will have to persuade each person individually, will you not? **ALCIBIADES**: Yes. **SOCRATES**: Is it not the mark of the same person to be able to persuade one person alone and many together about what he knows? Just as a teacher of letters <term>grammaticus</term><note>A teacher of literacy and literature.</note> persuades one person about letters as well as many. **ALCIBIADES**: Yes.

<margin>f</margin> **SOCRATES**: And is it not the arithmetician who knows how to persuade one and many? **ALCIBIADES**: Quite so. **SOCRATES**: And so, you are also able to persuade one person of the same things you can persuade many? **ALCIBIADES**: It is likely. **SOCRATES**: And these are clearly the things you know? **ALCIBIADES**: Yes. **SOCRATES**: The only difference between the orator speaking before the people and the one in a conversation like this is that the former persuades a crowd, while the latter persuades one at a time? **ALCIBIADES**: It seems so. **SOCRATES**: Come then, since it appears that the same person can persuade many and one, practice on me and try to demonstrate that the just is sometimes not advantageous. **ALCIBIADES**: You are being insolent <note>original Greek: "Ὑβριστὴς" (Hybristes). Alcibiades feels mocked by Socrates's relentless logic.</note>, Socrates. **SOCRATES**: Now, through "insolence," I am going to persuade you of the opposite of what you refuse to tell me. **ALCIBIADES**: Speak then.

<margin>g</margin> **SOCRATES**: Only answer my questions. **ALCIBIADES**: No, you speak yourself. **SOCRATES**: Why? Do you not wish most of all to be persuaded? **ALCIBIADES**: By all means. **SOCRATES**: If you yourself say that these things are so, will you not be most fully persuaded? **ALCIBIADES**: I think so. **SOCRATES**: Then answer; and unless you hear from your own mouth that the just is advantageous, do not believe anyone else who says it. **ALCIBIADES**: I will not; I must answer, for I don't think I will be harmed. **SOCRATES**: You are a prophet! Tell me: do you say some just things are advantageous and others are not? **ALCIBIADES**: Yes. **SOCRATES**: What then? Are some beautiful <term>beautiful</term><note>original Greek: "καλά" (kala). This term implies both physical beauty and moral nobility/virtue.</note> and others not? **ALCIBIADES**: How can you ask that? **SOCRATES**: Has it ever seemed to you that someone did something shameful <note>original Greek: "αἰσχρὰ" (aischra). The opposite of 'kala'; something morally or physically ugly.</note> but just? **ALCIBIADES**: Never to me. **SOCRATES**: Then all just things are also beautiful? **ALCIBIADES**: Yes. **SOCRATES**: And what about beautiful things? Are they all good, or some good and some bad? **ALCIBIADES**: I think, Socrates, that some beautiful things are bad. **SOCRATES**: And are some shameful things good? **ALCIBIADES**: Yes.

<margin>h</margin> **SOCRATES**: Do you mean things like this?

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> **SOCRATES**: You, I say. **ALCIBIADES**: In what way? **SOCRATES**: You will understand it this way: if I ask you whether one or two is more, will you answer two? **ALCIBIADES**: Two. **SOCRATES**: By how much? **ALCIBIADES**: By one. **SOCRATES**: Which of us, then, is the one who says two is one more than one? **ALCIBIADES**: I am. **SOCRATES**: I was asking, and you were answering? **ALCIBIADES**: Yes. **SOCRATES**: Of these things, then, which of us seems to be speaking: I, the one asking, or you, the one answering? **ALCIBIADES**: I am. **SOCRATES**: What if I were to ask how many letters are in "Socrates," and you answered—which of us would be the speaker? **ALCIBIADES**: I would. **SOCRATES**: Come, say in a word: whenever there is a question and an answer, who is the speaker: the one asking or the one answering? **ALCIBIADES**: The one answering, it seems to me, O Socrates. **SOCRATES**: And you were the one answering? **ALCIBIADES**: I was.

<margin>B</margin> **SOCRATES**: Of the things spoken so far, then, which of us said them? **ALCIBIADES**: From what has been granted, I seem to have said them. **SOCRATES**: Was it not said that Alcibiades—the handsome son of Cleinias—ignorant of what is just and unjust, yet thought he knew, and was about to go before the Athenian assembly to advise them on things he does not know? Are these things true? **ALCIBIADES**: They are. **SOCRATES**: That saying of Euripides now occurs to us, O Alcibiades: you seem to have heard these things from yourself, not from me. Neither I, but you, said these things; you accuse me in vain. **ALCIBIADES**: And indeed, you speak well. **SOCRATES**: For you have decided, O excellent man, to attempt a mad thing: to teach those things which you neither know nor care to learn.

<margin>C</margin> **ALCIBIADES**: I think, O Socrates, that the Athenians and other Greeks rarely ask which things are more just or more unjust. For they think such things are obvious. Therefore, setting these aside, they inquire into what is advantageous <term>advantageous</term><note>original Latin: "vtilia". This is the equivalent of the Greek "sympheronta," referring to what is useful or profitable.</note> for those acting. Nor do I think the same things are both just and useful; indeed, injustice has profited many who act unjustly, while on the contrary, justice has not helped others who act justly. **SOCRATES**: What then? If the just and the useful are entirely different, do you again think you know what is useful to men, and for what reason? **ALCIBIADES**: And what prevents it, Socrates? Unless you again inquire from whom I learned it, or how I found it myself.

<margin>D</margin> **SOCRATES**: See what you are doing. Although you speak incorrectly, and though it can be shown by the same reasoning as the things before, you nevertheless think you must hear some new things, and new demonstrations must be brought into the open—as if the previous ones were like the worn-out gear and costumes <note>original Latin: "apparatuum atque vestium". Socrates compares arguments to stage props or costumes that get old and lose their appeal.</note> used on the stage, which you would no longer wear unless someone brought something pure and immaculate. But I will let the introductions of your speech go; I will nonetheless ask from where you learned these things to be useful, and who was the teacher, and I will ask all the rest in a single question. Nevertheless, you will, I think, be rolled back to the same point, and you will not be able to show whether you knew these things by learning or by discovery. But since you are so delicate that you do not seem to taste the same argument gladly: I let this pass—whether you know or not what is useful or useless for the Athenians.

<margin>E</margin> **SOCRATES**: Why do you not demonstrate whether the same things are just and useful, or different? Demonstrate it either by questioning me, as I did you, or if it pleases you, by using a continuous speech. **ALCIBIADES**: I do not know, O Socrates, whether I am able to dispute against you or not. **SOCRATES**: But O good man, imagine me at this moment to be the assembly or the people: would you not have to persuade each one of them? **ALCIBIADES**: I would. **SOCRATES**: Is it not the mark of the same man to be able to demonstrate something to one person alone and to many together—at least among the things he knows? Just as the grammarian instructs one person and many alike in letters. **ALCIBIADES**: It is.

<margin>F</margin> **SOCRATES**: And in numbers, in the same way, who can show it to one and many? **ALCIBIADES**: Certainly. **SOCRATES**: This is the arithmetician. **ALCIBIADES**: It is. **SOCRATES**: And you, therefore, can persuade one person of the same things you can persuade many. **ALCIBIADES**: That is consistent. **SOCRATES**: These are, clearly, the things you know. **ALCIBIADES**: Indeed. **SOCRATES**: The only difference is that the orator who speaks before the people persuades all at once, while the one in this kind of meeting persuades each individually. **ALCIBIADES**: It seems so. **SOCRATES**: Come then, since it appears to be the mark of the same man to show things to many and to one, practice now before me and strive to show me that what is just is sometimes not profitable. **ALCIBIADES**: You are being insolent, O Socrates.

<margin>G</margin> **SOCRATES**: Now by "insolence" I am going to demonstrate to you the opposite of what you do not want to tell me. **ALCIBIADES**: Speak. **SOCRATES**: Only answer the one questioning. **ALCIBIADES**: Not at all; you speak yourself. **SOCRATES**: Do you not wish to be persuaded as much as possible? **ALCIBIADES**: Certainly. **SOCRATES**: If you say these things are so, will you not be most persuaded? **ALCIBIADES**: It seems so to me. **SOCRATES**: Answer then; for unless you hear from yourself that all just things are useful, do not believe another saying it. **ALCIBIADES**: I will not believe it; but I must now answer, for I think there is no danger in it.

<margin>H</margin> **SOCRATES**: You are a prophet indeed; tell the truth. Do you assert that some just things are beneficial and others not at all? **ALCIBIADES**: I do. **SOCRATES**: And what of these—are some beautiful <term>beautiful</term><note>original Latin: "pulchra". Used here in the philosophical sense of 'noble' or 'virtuous'.</note> and some the opposite? **ALCIBIADES**: Why do you ask this? **SOCRATES**: Whether anyone has ever seemed to you to do things that were shameful <note>original Latin: "turpia". Things that are morally ugly or disgraceful.</note> but nevertheless just? **ALCIBIADES**: Never to me. **SOCRATES**: Therefore, all just things are also beautiful? **ALCIBIADES**: So it is. **SOCRATES**: Again, are all beautiful things good, or are they partly good and partly bad? **ALCIBIADES**: I think indeed, Socrates, some beautiful things are bad. **SOCRATES**: And some shameful things are good? **ALCIBIADES**: Certainly. **SOCRATES**: Is this what you mean...

<vocab>Plato, Alcibiades, Socrates, dialexeis, iustitia, utilitas, pulchrum, bonum, rhetorica, arithmetica</vocab>

<summary>In this passage, Socrates employs his famous method of questioning to prove that Alcibiades is the source of his own admissions, specifically that he lacks knowledge of justice despite his political ambitions. The dialogue shifts from a debate on justice to whether "just" actions are always "advantageous," "beautiful," and "good."</summary>
<keywords>Socratic method, justice, expediency, political ambition, Alcibiades, self-refutation, Euripides, moral philosophy</keywords>

--- Page 62 ---
<meta>This page continues the dialogue from the previous page where Socrates established that the person answering the questions is the one actually making the claims. Here, Socrates leads Alcibiades to examine the relationship between "the beautiful" (moral nobility) and "the good," eventually forcing him to confront his own internal contradictions and ignorance regarding justice.</meta>

->**OF PLATO**<-

Just as if some, while wishing to bring help to a friend or relative in battle, died of their wounds; while those who did not bring help, although they ought to have, departed unharmed?
**ALCIBIADES**: Exactly so. **SOCRATES**: Do you not call help of this kind "beautiful" <note>The Latin *pulchrum* and Greek *καλόν* can mean "beautiful," "noble," or "fine." In this ethical context, it refers to actions that are morally admirable.</note> where one tries to save those they ought to? And that is courage? **ALCIBIADES**: Certainly. **SOCRATES**: But you call it "bad" because of the deaths and wounds, do you not? **ALCIBIADES**: I do. **SOCRATES**: Is courage one thing, and death another? **ALCIBIADES**: Yes, they are different. **SOCRATES**: Therefore, it is not according to the same respect that it is both "beautiful" and "bad" to bring help to friends.
**ALCIBIADES**: It does not seem so. **SOCRATES**: Consider then whether, by the same reasoning that it is "beautiful," it is also "good," as in these cases. For you

<margin>
Insofar as something is good, it is beautiful; insofar as it is bad, it is base.
</margin>

perhaps grant that it is beautiful to bring help. But is courage itself a good or an evil? Consider it truly: which would you choose to have, good things or bad things? **ALCIBIADES**: Good things. **SOCRATES**: And would you not desire the greatest goods the most? **ALCIBIADES**: Most of all. **SOCRATES**: And would you least of all wish to be deprived of them? **ALCIBIADES**: Why not? **SOCRATES**: What do you say of courage? At what price would you trade it? **ALCIBIADES**: I would not even wish to live if I were a coward <note>original: *timidus*; Greek: *δειλὸς*. Literally "fearful" or "lacking courage."</note>. **SOCRATES**: Does cowardice seem to be the extreme evil to you? **ALCIBIADES**: It does to me. **SOCRATES**: Equal to dying, it appears? **ALCIBIADES**: Equal. **SOCRATES**: Are life and courage the opposites of death and cowardice? **ALCIBIADES**: They are. **SOCRATES**: And you would most desire the former to be present in you, and the latter least? **ALCIBIADES**: Certainly. **SOCRATES**: Is it not because you think the former are the best, and the latter the worst? **ALCIBIADES**: Precisely. **SOCRATES**: Therefore, you called bringing help to friends in battle "beautiful" according to the action of the good—that is, courage. **ALCIBIADES**: So it seems. **SOCRATES**: But according to the action of the evil—that is, death—you called it "bad." **ALCIBIADES**: So it seems to me. **SOCRATES**: Is it not fitting to name each action in this way? For if you call it "bad" insofar as it produces an evil, should you not, conversely, call it "good" insofar as it brings a good? **ALCIBIADES**: It seems so. **SOCRATES**: And is it not also "beautiful" insofar as it is "good," and "base" <note>original: *turpe*; Greek: *αἰσχρόν*. Often translated as "shameful" or "ugly," the opposite of "beautiful/noble."</note> insofar as it is "bad"? **ALCIBIADES**: Most certainly. **SOCRATES**: When, therefore, you say that bringing help to friends in war is beautiful but bad, it is the same as if you said it is good, yet bad. **ALCIBIADES**: You seem to me to speak the truth, O Socrates. **SOCRATES**: Nothing, therefore, is bad insofar as it is Beautiful, nor is anything good insofar as it is Base. **ALCIBIADES**: It does not seem so. **SOCRATES**: Furthermore, consider it in this way: does not whoever acts beautifully, also act well? **ALCIBIADES**: Indeed. **SOCRATES**: And are those who act well not happy?

<margin>
They are happy on account of the possession of goods.
</margin>

**ALCIBIADES**: Why not? **SOCRATES**: And are they not happy because of the possession of good things? **ALCIBIADES**: Most of all. **SOCRATES**: And they acquire these things because they act beautifully and well? **ALCIBIADES**: Certainly. **SOCRATES**: Therefore, acting well is a good. **ALCIBIADES**: Why not? **SOCRATES**: And is not a beautiful action a good one? **ALCIBIADES**: Certainly. **SOCRATES**: The same thing, therefore, appears to us again: the beautiful and the good. **ALCIBIADES**: It appears so. **SOCRATES**: Whatever, therefore, we find to be beautiful, we shall also find to be good by this same reasoning. **ALCIBIADES**: It must be so. **SOCRATES**: Now, do good things benefit us or not? **ALCIBIADES**: They benefit us. **SOCRATES**: Do you remember what we agreed upon earlier regarding just things? **ALCIBIADES**: I believe we said that those who act justly must necessarily do beautiful things. **SOCRATES**: And those who do beautiful things, do they not also do good things? **ALCIBIADES**: Yes. **SOCRATES**: And do good things profit? **ALCIBIADES**: Thoroughly. **SOCRATES**: Therefore, O Alcibiades, just things are useful. **ALCIBIADES**: So it seems.
**SOCRATES**: And were you not the one who said these things, while I was the one asking? **ALCIBIADES**: It appears so. **SOCRATES**: If someone, then, should stand up to advise the Athenians or the Peparethians <note>Peparethos was an island in the Aegean Sea, used here as a humorous contrast to the great city of Athens.</note>, thinking he could distinguish between just and unjust things, and said he knew that just things are sometimes bad—would you not laugh at him, since you yourself assert that the same things are both just and useful? **ALCIBIADES**: By the gods, Socrates, I do not know what I am saying! I seem to be in a truly absurd state. For sometimes one thing seems true to me when you question me, and now another. **SOCRATES**: Do you not know, my friend, what this condition is? **ALCIBIADES**: I do not. **SOCRATES**: If someone asked you whether you had two or three eyes, or two or four hands, or something else of that sort, do you think you would answer one thing now and another then, or always the same thing? **ALCIBIADES**: Although I am now worried about myself, I think I would answer the same thing. **SOCRATES**: Is the cause of this not that you know the truth?

<margin>
Ignorance is the cause of giving varied and inconsistent answers.
</margin>

**ALCIBIADES**: I suppose so. **SOCRATES**: Regarding those things, then, about which you unwillingly give contradictory answers, it is clear that you are ignorant of them. **ALCIBIADES**: That is likely. **SOCRATES**: Do you not confess that you have erred in your answers regarding just and unjust, beautiful and base, good and bad, useful and useless? Is it not then manifest that you have erred because you are ignorant of them? **ALCIBIADES**: It seems so. **SOCRATES**: Is it not the case that if someone is ignorant, his mind must necessarily waver regarding that subject? **ALCIBIADES**: Why not? **SOCRATES**: Do you know how to climb up into heaven? **ALCIBIADES**: Not at all, by Jupiter! **SOCRATES**: Does your opinion waver regarding these things? **ALCIBIADES**: Certainly not. **SOCRATES**: Do you know the cause of this, or do you want me to tell you? **ALCIBIADES**: Tell me. **SOCRATES**: It is because, while you do not know, you do not *think* you know. **ALCIBIADES**: How is that, my friend? Say it again. **SOCRATES**: Think with me. In those things you do not know, but realize that you do not know, do you fail in them? For instance, regarding the preparation of side-dishes, you surely know that you do not know? **ALCIBIADES**: Entirely. **SOCRATES**: Do you have an opinion on how they should be prepared and thus make mistakes? Or do you rather leave it to the one who knows? **ALCIBIADES**: In that way. **SOCRATES**: What if you were sailing? Would you have an opinion on whether the tiller should be turned inward or outward, and err in your ignorance? Or would you rather be quiet and leave it to the pilot? **ALCIBIADES**: To the pilot.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> For example, many who have brought help in war to a companion or a kinsman have received wounds and died; while those who did not bring help, when they should have, came away healthy. **ALCIBIADES**: Quite so. **SOCRATES**: Therefore, you call such help "beautiful" (noble) on account of the attempt to save those whom one ought; and this is courage, or is it not? **ALCIBIADES**: Yes. **SOCRATES**: But "bad," however, on account of the deaths and the wounds. Is it not so? **ALCIBIADES**: Yes. **SOCRATES**: Is courage, then, not one thing, and death another? **ALCIBIADES**: Certainly. **SOCRATES**: It is not, therefore, in the same respect that it is both beautiful and bad to help one's friends? **ALCIBIADES**: It does not appear so. **SOCRATES**: See then if, as it is beautiful, it is also good, just as in this case. For you agreed that the help was beautiful
<margin>B</margin> on account of courage. Consider this very thing—courage—as to whether it is a good or an evil. Look at it this way: which would you choose to have: good things or bad things? **SOCRATES**: Would you not choose the greatest? **ALCIBIADES**: Especially so. **SOCRATES**: And would you least of all choose to be deprived of them? **ALCIBIADES**: How could I not? **SOCRATES**: What then do you say about courage? At what price would you choose to be deprived of it? **ALCIBIADES**: I would not even choose to live if I were a coward. **SOCRATES**: Cowardice, then, seems to you to be an extreme evil. **ALCIBIADES**: To me, yes. **SOCRATES**: On a par with dying, as it seems. **ALCIBIADES**: I say so. **SOCRATES**: Are death and cowardice not most opposite to life and courage? **ALCIBIADES**: Yes. **SOCRATES**: And you would wish the former most for yourself, and the latter least?
<margin>C</margin> **ALCIBIADES**: Yes. **SOCRATES**: Do you then consider the former the best, and the latter the worst? **ALCIBIADES**: Quite so. **SOCRATES**: Helping friends in war, therefore, insofar as it is beautiful, you have called it beautiful according to the action of a good thing—namely, courage. **ALCIBIADES**: I appear to have. **SOCRATES**: But according to the action of an evil thing—namely, death—you called it bad. **ALCIBIADES**: Yes. **SOCRATES**: Is it not just, then, to address each of these actions in this way: if it works an evil, you call it bad; but if it works a good, it must be called good? **ALCIBIADES**: It seems so to me. **SOCRATES**: And is it not also, insofar as it is good, beautiful; and insofar as it is bad, base? **ALCIBIADES**: Yes. **SOCRATES**: In saying, then, that helping friends in war is beautiful but bad, you are saying nothing else than that, insofar as it is
<margin>D</margin> good, it is good, but it is also bad. **ALCIBIADES**: You seem to me to speak the truth, Socrates. **SOCRATES**: Nothing, then, insofar as it is beautiful, is bad; nor insofar as it is base, is it good. **SOCRATES**: It does not appear so. **ALCIBIADES**: Consider it still further in this way: whoever acts beautifully, does he not also act well? **ALCIBIADES**: Yes. **SOCRATES**: And those who act well, are they not happy? **ALCIBIADES**: How could they not be? **SOCRATES**: And are they not happy because of the possession of good things? **ALCIBIADES**: Especially so. **SOCRATES**: And do they possess these things by acting well and beautifully? **ALCIBIADES**: Yes. **SOCRATES**: Acting well, then, is a good? **ALCIBIADES**: How could it not be? **SOCRATES**: And is "faring well" <note>original: *εὐπραγία*; can mean "acting well" or "success/faring well."</note> a beautiful thing? **ALCIBIADES**: Yes. **SOCRATES**: The beautiful and the good, therefore, have appeared to us again as the same thing.
<margin>E</margin> **ALCIBIADES**: It appears so. **SOCRATES**: Whatever, then, we find to be beautiful, we shall find to be good, at least from this argument. **ALCIBIADES**: Necessarily. **SOCRATES**: What then? Do good things benefit us, or not? **ALCIBIADES**: They benefit us. **SOCRATES**: Do you remember what we agreed regarding just things? **ALCIBIADES**: I think we said those who do just things must necessarily do beautiful things. **SOCRATES**: And are beautiful things not also good? **ALCIBIADES**: Yes. **SOCRATES**: And good things benefit us? **ALCIBIADES**: Yes. **SOCRATES**: Therefore, O Alcibiades, just things are beneficial. **ALCIBIADES**: It seems so. **SOCRATES**: What then? Are you not the one saying these things, and I the one asking? **ALCIBIADES**: I appear to be, as it seems. **SOCRATES**: If then someone stands up to advise either the Athenians or the Peparethians, thinking he knows what is just and what is unjust, and says he knows that just things are sometimes bad, would you do anything other than laugh at him? Since you yourself happen to be saying that
<margin>F</margin> the same things are both just and beneficial. **ALCIBIADES**: But by the gods, Socrates, I do not know what I am saying! I truly seem to be in a strange state. For at one moment things seem one way to me while you are questioning, and at another moment they seem another. **SOCRATES**: Are you then ignorant, my friend, of what this condition is? **ALCIBIADES**: Entirely. **SOCRATES**: Do you think that if I asked you while you were ignorant if you had two eyes or three, or two hands or four, or any such thing, you would answer one way at one time and another way at another? Or would you always say the same? **ALCIBIADES**: I am already afraid for myself, but I think I would say the same. **SOCRATES**: Is the cause not that you know? **ALCIBIADES**: I think so. **SOCRATES**: Therefore, concerning things about which you give contradictory answers against your will, it is clear that you do not know them. **ALCIBIADES**: That is likely. **SOCRATES**: And concerning things just and unjust, beautiful and base, bad and good, and beneficial and not, in answering you say you waver. Is it not then clear that you waver because of not knowing
<margin>G</margin> about them? **ALCIBIADES**: To me, yes. **SOCRATES**: Is it not so? Whenever someone does not know something, is it not necessary that his soul wavers regarding those things? **ALCIBIADES**: How could it not be? **SOCRATES**: What then? Do you know in what way you might ascend into heaven? **ALCIBIADES**: By Jupiter, not I! **SOCRATES**: Does your opinion waver regarding these things? **ALCIBIADES**: Not at all. **SOCRATES**: Do you know the cause? Or shall I tell you? **ALCIBIADES**: Tell me. **SOCRATES**: It is because, my friend, you do not think you know it when you do not. **ALCIBIADES**: How are you saying this again? **SOCRATES**: Look at it together with me. In things you do not know, but realize that you do not know, do you waver? Such as regarding the seasoning of a dish—you know, surely, that you do not know? **ALCIBIADES**: Quite so.
<margin>H</margin> **SOCRATES**: Do you then yourself have an opinion on how it is necessary to season it, and so waver, or do you leave it to the one who knows? **ALCIBIADES**: I do so. **SOCRATES**: What if you were sailing in a ship? Would you have an opinion on whether the tiller should be brought in or out, and since you do not know, would you waver? Or would you leave it to the pilot and keep quiet? **ALCIBIADES**: To the pilot.

<summary>Socrates argues that "the beautiful" (moral nobility) is fundamentally identical to "the good" and the "useful." He demonstrates to Alcibiades that self-contradiction is a certain sign of ignorance—specifically, the dangerous ignorance of thinking one knows what they do not.</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Alcibiades, Socratic method, courage, the Good, the Beautiful, moral nobility, ignorance, ethics, justice</keywords>

--- Page 63 ---
<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Alcibiades. On the previous page, Socrates argued that one cannot be both "beautiful" (noble) and "bad" in the same respect, forcing Alcibiades to reconsider his definitions of justice and advantage. This page moves into the famous Socratic exploration of "double ignorance"—the state of not knowing, yet thinking that one knows.</meta>

# ALCIBIADES I.

**SOCRATES**: So then, you do not wander in error regarding things you do not know—provided you know that you do not know them?
**ALCIBIADES**: It seems not.
**SOCRATES**: Do you realize, then, that errors in action are caused by this specific kind of ignorance: the kind where a person who does not know something thinks that they do?
**ALCIBIADES**: How do you mean?
**SOCRATES**: We only attempt to act, I suppose, when we think we know what we are doing?
**ALCIBIADES**: Yes.
**SOCRATES**: But when people do not think they know, they surely hand the matter over to others?
**ALCIBIADES**: Of course.
**SOCRATES**: And so, such people live without making mistakes in those matters, precisely because they do not know and instead entrust the task to others?
**ALCIBIADES**: Indeed.
**SOCRATES**: Who, then, are those who make mistakes? Surely not those who know.
**ALCIBIADES**: Certainly not.
**SOCRATES**: And since it is neither those who know, nor those among the ignorant who *realize* they do not know, who else is left but those who do not know, yet think they do?
**ALCIBIADES**: None but them.
**SOCRATES**: This, then, is the ignorance that causes evils, and is the most blameworthy form of stupidity.
**ALCIBIADES**: Yes.
**SOCRATES**: And when it concerns the greatest matters, is it not then most harmful and most shameful?
**ALCIBIADES**: By far.
**SOCRATES**: Well then, can you name anything greater than matters of justice, beauty, goodness, and advantage?
**ALCIBIADES**: No, I cannot.
**SOCRATES**: And is it not regarding these very things that you admit you are wandering in error?
**ALCIBIADES**: It is.
**SOCRATES**: If you are wandering, is it not clear from what we said before that you are not only ignorant of the greatest things, but that while not knowing them, you think you do?
**ALCIBIADES**: I fear so.
**SOCRATES**: Oh, Alcibiades! What a condition you are in! I hesitate to name it, but since we are alone, it must be said. You are wedded to the most shameful stupidity, my dear friend—as the argument accuses you, and as you accuse yourself. This is why you are leaping into politics before you have been educated. And you are not the only one in this condition; most of those who handle the city’s affairs are the same, except for a few, and perhaps your guardian, Pericles.
**ALCIBIADES**: It is said, Socrates, that Pericles did not become wise by chance, but by associating with many wise men, such as Pythoclides <note>A famous musician and intellectual who was said to be a secret sophist teaching politics.</note> and Anaxagoras <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher who was a close friend and advisor to Pericles.</note>. Even now, at his great age, he associates with Damon <note>A music theorist and political advisor to Pericles.</note> for this very reason.
**SOCRATES**: Well, did you ever see a man wise in anything who was unable to make another man wise in the same thing? For instance, the man who taught you your letters was himself wise in them, and he made you wise, and anyone else he wished to?
**ALCIBIADES**: Yes.
**SOCRATES**: And you, having learned from him, will be able to teach another?
**ALCIBIADES**: Yes.
**SOCRATES**: And the same applies to the music teacher and the gym master?
**ALCIBIADES**: Quite so.
**SOCRATES**: For this is surely a fine proof that people know a thing—when they are able to produce another who knows it.
**ALCIBIADES**: I agree.
**SOCRATES**: Well then, can you tell me whom Pericles made wise? Shall we start with his sons?
**ALCIBIADES**: But what if the two sons of Pericles were simpletons, Socrates?
**SOCRATES**: Well, what about your brother, Clinias?
**ALCIBIADES**: Why mention Clinias? The man is a madman!
**SOCRATES**: Since Clinias is mad and Pericles’ sons were simpletons, what reason shall we give for him allowing you to be in this state?
**ALCIBIADES**: I suppose I am to blame for not paying attention.
**SOCRATES**: But tell me of any other Athenian or foreigner, slave or free, who is reputed to have become wiser through association with Pericles? Just as I can tell you that Pythodorus, son of Isolochus, and Callias, son of Calliades, became wise and distinguished by paying Zeno <note>Zeno of Elea, famous for his logical paradoxes.</note> one hundred minae <note>A significant sum of money, equivalent to several years' wages for a laborer.</note>.
**ALCIBIADES**: By Zeus, I cannot think of one.
**SOCRATES**: Very well. What do you intend to do about yourself? Will you leave yourself as you are, or take some care?
**ALCIBIADES**: We must deliberate together, Socrates. Though I see what you mean and I agree. It seems to me that those who run the city are uneducated, with a few exceptions.
**SOCRATES**: And what of that?
**ALCIBIADES**: If they were educated, anyone attempting to compete with them would need to learn and practice, as if preparing for an athletic contest. But since they have entered politics as amateurs, why should I bother with practice and study? I am certain that my natural gifts will give me a great advantage over them.
**SOCRATES**: Oh, my friend! What a thing to say! How unworthy of your noble character and your other advantages.
**ALCIBIADES**: Why exactly do you say that, Socrates?
**SOCRATES**: Because I am distressed both for you and for my love for you.
**ALCIBIADES**: Why?
**SOCRATES**: Because you think your contest is against the men here in this city.
**ALCIBIADES**: Against whom else would it be?
**SOCRATES**: Is that a proper question for a man who considers himself high-minded?
**ALCIBIADES**: What do you mean? Is my contest not against these men?
**SOCRATES**: If you intended to pilot a warship about to go into battle, would it satisfy you to be a better pilot than your fellow sailors? Or would you realize that you must possess that skill, yet keep your eyes on your true rivals—the enemy—rather than your own crew? You ought to excel your crew to such an extent that they do not compete with you, but rather, out of respect, follow you against the enemy—if you truly intend to perform a noble deed worthy of yourself and the city.
**ALCIBIADES**: That is indeed what I intend.
**SOCRATES**: Is it fitting then for you to be satisfied with being better than your own soldiers, rather than looking toward the leaders of your rivals to see when you might become better than them, by watching and practicing against them?
**ALCIBIADES**: And who are these rivals you speak of, Socrates?
**SOCRATES**: Do you not know that our city is constantly at war with the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans.</note> and the Great King <note>The King of the Persian Empire.</note>?
**ALCIBIADES**: True...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> **SOCRATES**: Therefore, you do not err in the things you do not know, if you recognize that you do not know them. **ALCIBIADES**: It does not seem so. **SOCRATES**: Do you see that errors in actions arise from this ignorance: that he who does not know thinks he knows? **ALCIBIADES**: In what way do you say this? **SOCRATES**: We set out to act when we think we know what we are doing. **ALCIBIADES**: It is so. **SOCRATES**: On the contrary, those who are conscious of their ignorance entrust themselves to others. **ALCIBIADES**: Why wouldn't they? **SOCRATES**: Therefore, among those who are ignorant, only these pass through life without fault, because they trust themselves to the care of others. **ALCIBIADES**: Truly. **SOCRATES**: Who then are those who sin? For surely it is not those who know. **ALCIBIADES**: Certainly not. **SOCRATES**: <margin>B</margin> Since neither those who know, nor those among the ignorant who are conscious of their ignorance err, who else remains but those who, while they do not know, think they know? **ALCIBIADES**: They alone. **SOCRATES**: This ignorance, therefore, is the cause of evils, and is a lack of learning to be blamed. **ALCIBIADES**: Indeed. **SOCRATES**: And when it concerns the greatest things, it is then most foul and most shameful. **ALCIBIADES**: Most of all. **SOCRATES**: Do you have anything greater than the just, the good, and the useful? **ALCIBIADES**: Not at all. **SOCRATES**: Do you not assert that you have erred regarding these things? **ALCIBIADES**: I do. **SOCRATES**: But if you err, is it not clear from the above that you are not only ignorant in the greatest matters, but also that while you are ignorant, you think you know? **ALCIBIADES**: I seem to be. **SOCRATES**: Amazing, O Alcibiades, by what disease you are oppressed; I shudder to even name it. What then <margin>F</margin> do you think of yourself? Whether to <unclear>remain as you are now</unclear>, or rather to attempt something? **ALCIBIADES**: There is need of common counsel, O Socrates. For I understand your words and I agree with them. For those who administer the Republic, except for a very few, seem to me also to be unlearned. **SOCRATES**: What then? **ALCIBIADES**: If they were skilled, it would be necessary for him who is about to contend with them to go only after he had learned the same art and exercised himself; then at last, as if going to the athletes. But now, since even those unskilled men have approached the republic, why is there need for me to exercise? Why for the study of discipline? For I know that by the gifts of nature I shall far surpass these men. **SOCRATES**: Amazing! What have you said, best of men? How <margin>G</margin> unworthy of your nature and those other gifts of yours. **ALCIBIADES**: To what purpose is this, O Socrates? **SOCRATES**: It grieves me, both on your account and because of our mutual goodwill. **ALCIBIADES**: What is it? **SOCRATES**: That you should think your contest will be against the men who are here. **ALCIBIADES**: Against whom then? **SOCRATES**: Is it fitting that a man who makes so much of himself should ask that? **ALCIBIADES**: What are you saying? Is not my contest against these men? **SOCRATES**: If you decided to pilot a fighting trireme, would you think it enough for you to surpass your <unclear>fellow sailors</unclear> in piloting? Or, while you understand it must be so, do you look rather toward strenuous adversaries, and not, as you do now, toward your own defenders, <margin>H</margin> whom it is necessary for you to excel so much that you do not think of fighting against *them*, but rather you think little of them, and use them as servants against the enemy—if indeed you wish to perform some truly excellent deed worthy of yourself and your republic? **ALCIBIADES**: Indeed, I do think of that. **SOCRATES**: Is it fitting then that you should think it enough if you are the most excellent of your own soldiers, and not rather look to the leaders of the enemy, by what means you might rather excel them, always intent upon them and fortifying yourself against them? **ALCIBIADES**: Whom do you mean, O Socrates? **SOCRATES**: Do you not know that our city carries on war everywhere with the Lacedaemonians <margin>I</margin> and the great King of the Persians? **ALCIBIADES**: [It is] true...

<summary>Socrates humbles Alcibiades by defining the worst form of ignorance as thinking one knows what they do not, and points out that Athenian politicians (including Pericles) have failed to prove their wisdom by being unable to teach it to others. He concludes by warning Alcibiades that his real competition is not the local Athenian politicians, but the powerful leaders of Sparta and Persia.</summary>

### ALCIBIADES I.

<margin>A</margin> If you look at self-control <term>sophrosyne: a core Greek virtue implying self-control, moderation, and a healthy mind</term>, you would be ashamed of how much you fall short. If you would instead turn your eyes to the self-control and orderliness of the Spartans—their ease, gentleness, magnanimity, discipline, courage, endurance, love of labor, and their spirit of competition and honor—you would consider yourself a mere child in all such things. If you also look at wealth, and think that this makes you someone of importance, let us not leave this unmentioned either, so you may realize where you stand. If you wish to see the wealth of the Spartans, you will find that our riches here fall far short of theirs. As for the land they possess, both their own and that of Messene, no one here could challenge them in quantity or quality, nor in the number of slaves—especially the Helots <note>The Helots were a subjugated population in Sparta who worked the land</note>—nor in horses, nor in all the other livestock that graze in Messene. But I set all these things aside. As for gold and silver, there is more held privately in Sparta than in all the rest of Greece. For many 
<margin>B</margin> generations now, money has been flowing into Sparta from all the Greeks, and often from the barbarians as well, but it never flows out. Truly, as in the fable of Aesop—where the fox speaks to the lion—the tracks of the money entering Sparta are clearly turned toward it, but one can nowhere see tracks of it leaving. Thus, you should know well that in gold and silver, those there are the wealthiest of the Greeks, and among them, the king is the wealthiest of all. For the kings receive the greatest and most frequent revenues from such things. Furthermore, the royal tax which the Spartans pay to their kings is not small. While the Spartan wealth is great compared to other Greeks, it is nothing compared to the Persians and their King. I once heard from a reliable man among those 
<margin>C</margin> who had gone up to the King <note>Referring to the King of Persia</note>, who said that he traveled through a very vast and good land, which the locals called "The Queen's Girdle." He said there was another called "The Veil," and many other beautiful and good places set apart for the Queen’s adornment, each location taking its name from a specific piece of her jewelry. So I think if someone told the King's mother, Amastris—the wife of Xerxes—that the son of Dinomache 
<margin>D</margin> intended to attack her son, she would marvel. Dinomache’s finery is perhaps worth fifty minae <note>An ancient unit of currency; fifty minae was a significant but not royal sum</note> at most, while her son's land at Erchia is not even three hundred plethra <note>Approximately 70 acres</note>. I think she would say that this man attempts such a thing relying on nothing other than diligence and wisdom, for these alone are worth mentioning among the Greeks. <margin>E</margin> he refuses and says he is sufficient as he is—I think she would be amazed and ask: "On what then does the youth rely?" If we were to say "on beauty, stature, birth, wealth, and his natural soul," she would think us mad, Alcibiades, seeing that they possess all such things in far greater measure. I think even Lampido—the daughter of Leotychides, wife of Archidamus, and mother of Agis, all of whom were kings—would marvel, looking at her own resources, if you intended to contend with her son while being so poorly trained. Does it not seem shameful if the wives of our enemies have a better idea of what we ought to be like to attack them than we have of ourselves? But, my blessed friend, obey me and the

ALCIBIADES: You are joking, O Socrates. SOCRATES: Perhaps, yet I speak the truth that we both stand in need of care—indeed all men do, but we two especially. ALCIBIADES: That I stand in need, you are by no means mistaken. SOCRATES: Nor indeed that I do myself. ALCIBIADES: What then is to be done? SOCRATES: We must not hesitate, nor must we indulge in softness, O friend. ALCIBIADES: It is not becoming, O Socrates. SOCRATES: Certainly not; but we must consider in common. But tell me, do we wish to be the best? ALCIBIADES: Certainly. SOCRATES: In what faculty? ALCIBIADES: That, obviously, of good men. SOCRATES: Good in what matter? ALCIBIADES: In conducting affairs. ### OF PLATO

**A** SOCRATES: In what things? In horsemanship? ALCIBIADES: No. SOCRATES: For we would go to the horsemen for that. ALCIBIADES: Indeed. SOCRATES: Did you mean in the steering of a ship? ALCIBIADES: Not at all. SOCRATES: For we would go to the sailors for that. ALCIBIADES: We would. SOCRATES: In what business then, and by the duty of which men? ALCIBIADES: In those things which the noble and good men of the Athenians perform. SOCRATES: Do you call the noble and good "prudent," or "imprudent"?
<margin>In that which anyone is prudent, in the same he is good.</margin>
ALCIBIADES: Prudent. SOCRATES: In whatever a person is prudent, is he good in that same thing? ALCIBIADES: Certainly. SOCRATES: And the imprudent is bad? ALCIBIADES: Bad.

**B** SOCRATES: Is a shoemaker prudent in the work of shoes? ALCIBIADES: Entirely. SOCRATES: Is he then good at this? ALCIBIADES: Good. SOCRATES: What about making clothes? Is this cobbler <note>original: "cerdo" — a term for a low-level craftsman or laborer</note> not imprudent in that? ALCIBIADES: Yes. SOCRATES: Bad at this then? ALCIBIADES: Yes. SOCRATES: Therefore, by this reasoning, the same man will be both good and bad. ALCIBIADES: So it seems. SOCRATES: Would you say good men are also bad? ALCIBIADES: Not at all. SOCRATES: Then whom do you call good? ALCIBIADES: Those who are able to lead in the city. SOCRATES: Not horses, surely? ALCIBIADES: No, certainly. SOCRATES: But men? ALCIBIADES: Men. SOCRATES: Sick men? ALCIBIADES: No. SOCRATES: Or perhaps sailors? ALCIBIADES: I do not mean them. SOCRATES: Harvesters? ALCIBIADES: Nor them. SOCRATES: Men doing nothing, or doing something? ALCIBIADES: Doing something.

**C** SOCRATES: Doing what, then? Declare it to me. ALCIBIADES: I mean those managing commerce and using mutual services, just as we live our lives in cities. SOCRATES: Do you say they rule over men who make use of men? ALCIBIADES: I do. SOCRATES: Like pilots who use rowers? ALCIBIADES: No. SOCRATES: For that is the virtue of the pilot’s skill. ALCIBIADES: It is. SOCRATES: Perhaps you meant ruling over flute-players, who lead singers and use dancers? ALCIBIADES: Nor them. SOCRATES: For that belongs to the skill of the choir-master. ALCIBIADES: Entirely.

**D** SOCRATES: What then do you call being able to rule over men who use men? ALCIBIADES: Ruling over men who communicate <note>original: "communicantibus" — sharing in common life or business</note> with each other in the administration of the Republic and in commerce. SOCRATES: What art is this? Just as if I asked you again, what faculty makes us know how to rule those communicating in sailing? ALCIBIADES: Pilotry. SOCRATES: And for those communicating in song, as was said before, what science teaches how to rule? ALCIBIADES: What you just said: the discipline of the choir. SOCRATES: In the Republic, for those communicating, what do you call that science? ALCIBIADES: Good counsel <term>euboulia: soundness of judgment or good policy</term>, O Socrates. SOCRATES: Does the art of pilots seem to you to lack counsel? ALCIBIADES: Least of all. SOCRATES: It itself is also good counsel. ALCIBIADES: So it seems to me. SOCRATES: Toward the safety of those sailing. ALCIBIADES: You speak rightly. SOCRATES: But what you call "good counsel," toward what does it look? ALCIBIADES: Toward the better management and safety of the city.

**E** SOCRATES: By what thing being present or absent is it better disposed and preserved? As if you asked me what being present or absent makes bodies well: I would answer health being present and disease being removed. Do you think the same? ALCIBIADES: The same. SOCRATES: If you asked the same about eyes, I would answer by the same reason: blindness being driven away, and sight being present. And ears are cured when deafness is fled and hearing is present. ALCIBIADES: Correct. SOCRATES: But the city—by what being removed or applied does it become better and better established? ALCIBIADES: It seems to me, O Socrates, when there is friendship <term>amicitia/philia: social bonding and political cooperation</term> among citizens, and hatreds and seditions are absent. SOCRATES: Do you call friendship "concord" or "discord"? ALCIBIADES: Concord <term>homonoia: literally "sameness of mind"</term>. SOCRATES: Through what art do cities have concord regarding numbers? ALCIBIADES: Through arithmetic.

**F** SOCRATES: Private individuals also, through the same? ALCIBIADES: Surely. SOCRATES: And each man with himself? ALCIBIADES: Certainly. SOCRATES: Through what art does each agree with himself about whether a span or a cubit is larger? Is it not through the skill of measuring? ALCIBIADES: Why not? SOCRATES: Both privately and publicly? ALCIBIADES: Indeed. SOCRATES: And regarding weights in the same way? ALCIBIADES: I agree. SOCRATES: Then this concord you spoke of, what is it? About what? What art provides it? For that concord is of such a kind that it exists in the state and in every private person toward himself and toward others. ALCIBIADES: It is likely. SOCRATES: What then is it? Do not be reluctant to answer; speak promptly. ALCIBIADES: I suppose it is friendship and concord, like that by which a father and mother love their son, and a brother his brother, and a wife her husband. SOCRATES: Do you think, O Alcibiades, that a husband agrees with his wife about wool-working, an unskilled man with a skilled woman? ALCIBIADES: Not at all.

**G** SOCRATES: Nor should he: for this is a woman's discipline. ALCIBIADES: Indeed. SOCRATES: What then? Will a woman agree with a man about military work, since she has not learned it? SOCRATES: There are then certain disciplines for women and others for men, according to this opinion of yours. ALCIBIADES: Why not?
