<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Alcibiades. Having previously discussed what makes a citizen "good," Socrates now steers the conversation toward the nature of friendship and agreement in the city, eventually leading to the famous philosophical inquiry into "Self-Knowledge" and the "Care of the Self."</meta>

# ALCIBIADES I.

...friendship being absent? Which, as we agreed, when present, allows cities to be well-governed, but otherwise not? ALCIBIADES: But it seems to me that friendship arises among them at that time, when each person performs their own business. SOCRATES: Not just now, at least. But how do you mean it now? Does friendship arise when agreement <note>original: "ὁμονοίας" (homonoia) — literally 'same-mindedness' or concord</note> arises? Or is it possible for agreement to exist about those things which some people know, but others do not? ALCIBIADES: Impossible. SOCRATES: And do they act justly or unjustly when each person performs their own business? ALCIBIADES: Justly, of course. SOCRATES: Therefore, when the citizens in the city act justly, would friendship arise among them? ALCIBIADES: Again, Socrates, it seems to me that it must be so. SOCRATES: What then do you mean by this friendship or agreement, about which we must be both wise and well-advised in order to be good men? For I am not able to learn what it is, nor in whom it resides. For sometimes it appears to be present in the same things, and sometimes not, according to your words. ALCIBIADES: But by the gods, Socrates, I do not even know what I am saying myself. I am in danger of having been for a long time in a most shameful state without realizing it. SOCRATES: But you must take heart. For if you had realized you were in this state at fifty years old, it would be difficult for you to take care of yourself. But now you are at the very age when one ought to learn these things. ALCIBIADES: What then should the one who realizes this do, Socrates? SOCRATES: Answer the questions asked, Alcibiades. And if you do this, if God wills (if any trust is to be placed in my own prophecy), both you and I shall be in a better state. ALCIBIADES: It shall be so, at least as far as my answering is concerned. SOCRATES: Come then, what is it to "take care of oneself"? <note>Socrates begins the famous inquiry into 'epimeleia heautou' or the care of the self.</note> (so that we do not often unknowingly fail to take care of ourselves, while thinking we are doing so) and when does a man actually do this? Is it when he takes care of the things that belong to him, that he then also takes care of himself? ALCIBIADES: It seems so to me, at least. SOCRATES: What then? When does a man take care of his feet? Is it when he takes care of the things that belong to the feet? ALCIBIADES: I do not understand. SOCRATES: Is there something you call a "belonging" of the hand, such as a ring? Does it seem to belong to anything other than the finger? ALCIBIADES: Certainly not. SOCRATES: And the shoe to the foot? ALCIBIADES: Yes. SOCRATES: Then when we take care of shoes, do we take care of the feet? ALCIBIADES: I do not quite understand, Socrates. SOCRATES: What about this, Alcibiades: do you call something the "right care" of any matter? ALCIBIADES: I do. SOCRATES: Is it not when someone makes a thing better that you call it "right care"? ALCIBIADES: Yes. SOCRATES: What art then makes shoes better? ALCIBIADES: The craft of cobbling. <note>original: "Σκυτική" (skutikē) — the art of working with leather/shoes.</note> SOCRATES: By cobbling, then, we take care of shoes. ALCIBIADES: Yes. SOCRATES: And do we also take care of the feet by cobbling? Or is it by that art by which we make the feet better? ALCIBIADES: By that art. SOCRATES: And do we not make the feet better by the same art as the rest of the body? ALCIBIADES: It seems so to me. SOCRATES: And is this not gymnastics? <note>original: "γυμναστική" — refers to general physical training and health.</note> ALCIBIADES: Most certainly. SOCRATES: So by gymnastics we take care of the foot, but by cobbling, we take care of the things belonging to the foot. ALCIBIADES: Exactly. SOCRATES: And by gymnastics, the hands; but by the art of ring-engraving, the things belonging to the hand. ALCIBIADES: Yes. SOCRATES: And by gymnastics, the body; but by weaving and other arts, the things belonging to the body. ALCIBIADES: Entirely so. SOCRATES: Therefore, the art by which we take care of the thing itself is different from the art by which we take care of its belongings. ALCIBIADES: So it appears. SOCRATES: Therefore, when you take care of your belongings, you are not taking care of yourself. ALCIBIADES: Not at all. SOCRATES: For it is not the same art, it seems, that would take care of both the self and the things belonging to the self. ALCIBIADES: It does not appear so. SOCRATES: Come then, by what art might we take care of ourselves? ALCIBIADES: I cannot say. SOCRATES: But this much at least has been agreed: it is not the art by which we would make any of our belongings better, but that by which we make ourselves better. ALCIBIADES: You speak the truth. SOCRATES: Would we ever know what art makes a shoe better, if we did not know what a shoe is? ALCIBIADES: Impossible. SOCRATES: Nor could we know what art makes rings better, if we were ignorant of the ring. ALCIBIADES: True. SOCRATES: What then? Could we ever know what art makes the self better, if we were ignorant of what we ourselves actually are? ALCIBIADES: Impossible. SOCRATES: Now, is it an easy thing to "know oneself," and was he some simpleton who inscribed this on the temple at Pytho? <note>Referring to the Delphic Oracle's famous motto 'Gnothi Seauton' (Know Thyself).</note> Or is it something difficult, and not for everyone? ALCIBIADES: To me, Socrates, it has often seemed to be for everyone, but often also to be very difficult. SOCRATES: But Alcibiades, whether it is easy or not, this is how it stands for us: if we know it, we might perhaps know the care of ourselves, but if we are ignorant of it, we never could. ALCIBIADES: That is so. SOCRATES: Come then, in what way might "the self itself" be found? For in this way we might perhaps find what we ourselves are; but while we are still in ignorance of this, it is surely impossible. ALCIBIADES: You speak rightly. SOCRATES: Attend then, by Zeus! With whom are you now conversing? Is it with anyone other than me? ALCIBIADES: No. SOCRATES: And am I not conversing with you? ALCIBIADES: Yes. SOCRATES: Then it is Socrates who is conversing. ALCIBIADES: Certainly. SOCRATES: And Alcibiades who is listening. ALCIBIADES: Yes. SOCRATES: Does Socrates not converse by means of speech? ALCIBIADES: Of course. SOCRATES: And you call conversing and using speech the same thing, I suppose? ALCIBIADES: Certainly. SOCRATES: But the one who uses a thing, and the thing he uses, are they not different? ALCIBIADES: How do you mean? SOCRATES: Just as a cobbler cuts with a cutting-tool and a blade and other instruments. ALCIBIADES: Yes. SOCRATES: Therefore, the one who cuts and uses the tools is one thing, and the tools which the cutter uses are another. ALCIBIADES: How could it be otherwise? SOCRATES: In the same way, does the harper play the harp, and is the harper himself something different from the harp? ALCIBIADES: Yes. SOCRATES: This is what I was asking just now: whether the user and that which he uses always seem to be different. ALCIBIADES: They do. SOCRATES: What then shall we say of the cobbler?

<column-break/>

**A** ...you say, friendship being taken away? Which, as we confessed while it was present, cities are well-ordered, but otherwise the contrary. ALCIBIADES: Yet it seems to me that friendship consists among men for this reason: that each person performs his own duty. SOCRATES: But you were saying something else a little while ago; now, however, how is it that you again say friendship is made when agreement is applied? Or can agreement exist concerning those things in which some are skilled and others are unskilled? ALCIBIADES: It cannot happen. SOCRATES: Do they act justly or unjustly when individuals perform those things that pertain to themselves? ALCIBIADES: Justly, certainly. SOCRATES: Therefore, when citizens act justly, there is no friendship in the city? <note>original: "amicitia" — Latin for friendship.</note> ALCIBIADES: It seems **B** necessary likewise, O Socrates. SOCRATES: What then do you call friendship or agreement, concerning which it behooves us to be wise and counselors, so that we may be good men? For I cannot perceive what it is, or in what things it exists; since from your speech it seems sometimes to be in the same things, and sometimes to be absent from them. ALCIBIADES: By the gods, O Socrates, I do not even understand what I am saying: and I seem to have long deceived myself, while I am in a most base condition. SOCRATES: It is proper to be confident. For if you had noticed this only now at fifty years of age, it would indeed be arduous to care for yourself; but now you are at that age in which it is proper for you to notice it. ALCIBIADES: What then must the one who notices this do? SOCRATES: Answer those things which I shall ask **C** you, Alcibiades. If you do this, and God wills, if any faith at all is to be given to my prophecies, both you and I shall be in a better state. ALCIBIADES: So it shall be, as far as my answering is concerned. 
<margin>What it is to care for oneself.</margin>
SOCRATES: Come, what is it to care for oneself, lest we often deceive ourselves, not caring for our own selves when we think we are caring for them well? And when does a man do this? Does he not have a care for himself as often as he has a care for his own things? ALCIBIADES: It seems so to me. SOCRATES: What? Does someone care for his feet when he cares for those things which belong to the feet? ALCIBIADES: I do not understand. SOCRATES: Do you say there is something belonging to the hand itself, just as a ring is? Do you think the ring belongs to any other member than the finger? ALCIBIADES: Not at all. SOCRATES: And a shoe to the foot in the same **D** way? ALCIBIADES: So it is. SOCRATES: When we manage the care of shoes, is there also a care of the feet? ALCIBIADES: I do not understand much. SOCRATES: What then, O Alcibiades, do you call something the right care of anything? ALCIBIADES: I do. SOCRATES: Or do you not say it is rightly cared for when something becomes better? ALCIBIADES: I say so. SOCRATES: What art makes shoes better? ALCIBIADES: Cobbling. <note>original: "Cerdonica" — the craft of the 'cerdo' or manual laborer.</note> SOCRATES: By cobbling, therefore, we have the care of shoes? ALCIBIADES: By this very one. SOCRATES: And also the feet by cobbling? Or rather by that art by which we make the feet better? ALCIBIADES: By that one. SOCRATES: And are the feet not made better by that which also makes the rest of the body better? ALCIBIADES: It seems so. SOCRATES: Is this not gymnastics? ALCIBIADES: Greatly so. SOCRATES: Therefore, by gymnastics we care for the feet, but by cobbling **E** those things which belong to the feet. ALCIBIADES: Exactly. SOCRATES: And by gymnastics also the hands, but by the art of rings those things which belong to the hands. ALCIBIADES: So it is. SOCRATES: And by gymnastics the body, but by weaving and other faculties those things which belong to the body. ALCIBIADES: Altogether. SOCRATES: Therefore, by one art we care for each thing itself, and by another those things which belong to it. ALCIBIADES: It seems so. SOCRATES: Therefore, when one cares for his own things, he does not then care for himself. ALCIBIADES: In no way. SOCRATES: For it is not the same art, as it seems, which cares for us and which cares for our things. ALCIBIADES: It does not appear to be. SOCRATES: Come then, by what art can we care for ourselves? ALCIBIADES: I have nothing to say. SOCRATES: But this much however is agreed between us: that we do not care for ourselves by that art which makes something of ours better, but by that which **F** corrects us to a better state. ALCIBIADES: You tell true things. SOCRATES: Is it ever possible to know what art makes a shoe better, unless we know the shoe itself? ALCIBIADES: It cannot be done. SOCRATES: Nor even that which makes a ring better, being ignorant of the ring. ALCIBIADES: True. SOCRATES: Shall we ever know by what art we might become better, as long as we are ignorant of ourselves? ALCIBIADES: Never. SOCRATES: Is it an easy thing to know oneself, and was he ridiculous who inscribed that on the temple of Apollo, or rather an arduous thing, and not for just any man? ALCIBIADES: To me indeed, O Socrates, it has sometimes seemed easy and for anyone, but sometimes the most difficult of all. SOCRATES: But whether this be easy or difficult, it surely stands thus for us: that **G** understanding this, we may also understand by what reason we are to be cared for; but being ignorant, the contrary. ALCIBIADES: It is as you say. SOCRATES: Come, how shall we find that thing itself? For thus perhaps we might find what we ourselves are. But being ignorant of this, never. ALCIBIADES: You speak rightly. SOCRATES: Attend then, by God, does anyone else dispute with me than you? ALCIBIADES: With you. SOCRATES: And do I not with you? ALCIBIADES: And you with me. SOCRATES: Therefore it is Socrates who disputes. ALCIBIADES: It is. SOCRATES: And Alcibiades who hears. ALCIBIADES: So it is. SOCRATES: Does Socrates not dispute by means of reason? ALCIBIADES: Why not? SOCRATES: And to dispute and to use **H** reason, do you now call that the same thing? ALCIBIADES: The same. SOCRATES: But the one using and that which we use, are they not different? ALCIBIADES: How do you say? SOCRATES: Just as a cobbler cuts with a circular and semi-circular tool, and with other instruments. ALCIBIADES: And as you say. SOCRATES: 
<margin>That the thing which uses is different from that which is used.</margin>
Is it not one thing which divides, and another by which anything is divided? ALCIBIADES: Why not? SOCRATES: Likewise, the harper is one thing, and that by which he strikes the harp is another? ALCIBIADES: Another. SOCRATES: This is what I was asking a little while ago, whether the user and that which he uses always seem to be different. ALCIBIADES: It seems so. SOCRATES: Do we say the cobbler cuts with instruments only, or with that which he uses?

<summary>Socrates guides Alcibiades to realize that caring for one's possessions (like shoes or rings) is distinct from caring for one's body, and further, that caring for the body is distinct from caring for the 'self.' They conclude that one cannot improve oneself without first achieving the self-knowledge famously commanded by the Delphic Oracle.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the pivotal dialogue between Socrates and Alcibiades, moving from a general discussion of justice and politics to a profound philosophical inquiry into the nature of the "Self." Socrates lead Alcibiades to distinguish between the person (the soul) and the instruments the person uses (the body and its possessions).</meta>

# OF PLATO

<margin>Man is something other than his body.</margin>
SOCRATES: Or even with his hands? ALCIBIADES: With his hands too. SOCRATES: He uses these then? ALCIBIADES: He uses them. SOCRATES: Does he not also use his eyes when cutting leather? ALCIBIADES: Entirely. SOCRATES: And we have agreed that the one who uses a thing is something different from the things he uses. <note>original: "Utentem verò aliud quiddam ab iis quibus utitur" / "Τὸν δὲ χρώμενον, καὶ οἷς χρῆται, ἕτερα"</note> ALCIBIADES: We have agreed. SOCRATES: Therefore, the shoemaker and the harper are something other than the eyes and hands they work with. ALCIBIADES: That appears to be so. SOCRATES: Does a man not use his whole body? ALCIBIADES: Completely. SOCRATES: And the user is distinct from what is used? ALCIBIADES: It is so. SOCRATES: A man, therefore, is something other than his own body. ALCIBIADES: It seems so. SOCRATES: What then is a man? ALCIBIADES: I do not know. SOCRATES: You know at least that he is the thing that uses the body. ALCIBIADES: I know. SOCRATES: Is there anything that uses the body other than the soul? ALCIBIADES: Nothing else. SOCRATES: And does it not rule over it? ALCIBIADES: It rules. SOCRATES: Moreover, I think no one would judge otherwise. ALCIBIADES: About what? SOCRATES: That man must be one of three things. ALCIBIADES: Which ones? SOCRATES: Either the soul, or the body, or the whole composed of both. ALCIBIADES: Why not? SOCRATES: But we have agreed that the thing which rules the body is the "man." ALCIBIADES: We have agreed. SOCRATES: What then is man? Does the body rule itself? ALCIBIADES: In no way. SOCRATES: For we said it was the thing being ruled. ALCIBIADES: Certainly. SOCRATES: Therefore, this body is not what we are looking for. ALCIBIADES: It does not seem so. SOCRATES: But perhaps the two together rule the body, and that is what "man" is. ALCIBIADES: Perhaps. SOCRATES: No, least of all; for if one of them is not the ruler, there is no way that the combination of both could be the ruler. ALCIBIADES: You speak rightly. SOCRATES: Since, then, neither the body nor the combination of the two is the "man," it remains, I think, either that man is nothing at all, or if he is something, he is nothing other than the soul. ALCIBIADES: Precisely. SOCRATES:
<margin>Man is nothing other than the soul.</margin>
Must it be shown to you even more clearly that the soul is the man? ALCIBIADES: No, by Jove; this seems sufficient to me. SOCRATES: And if it has not been discussed with perfect precision, yet for the present it is sufficiently introduced. For we shall understand it perfectly then, when we have found that which we just now passed over, because it required a more extensive investigation. ALCIBIADES: What was that? SOCRATES: It was said a little while ago that we should first consider the "Self" itself <note>original: "ipsùm idem" / "αὐτὸ τὸ αὐτό" — Socrates is making a distinction between "the self" and "particular things belonging to the self."</note>; but now, instead of the "Self" itself, we have considered what each individual thing is. And perhaps that will suffice. For we could say there is nothing more essential in ourselves than the soul. ALCIBIADES: Certainly not. SOCRATES: Should we not think then, that you and I are conversing with one another by using speech, soul to soul? ALCIBIADES: Very much so. SOCRATES: This, therefore, was what we were saying a little while ago: that Socrates disputes with Alcibiades by using speech, directing words not to your outward person <note>original: "personam" / "πρόσωπον" — literally 'mask' or 'face'</note>, as it appears, but to Alcibiades himself: and this is the soul. ALCIBIADES: It certainly seems so to me. SOCRATES: He who commands us "Know Thyself," therefore, commands us to know the soul. ALCIBIADES: It seems so. SOCRATES: Whoever, therefore, knows only his body, knows the things that are his, but not himself. ALCIBIADES: So it is. SOCRATES: And therefore no doctor, insofar as he is a doctor, knows himself, nor does any trainer, insofar as he is a trainer. ALCIBIADES: It does not seem so. SOCRATES: Much less do farmers and other craftsmen know themselves; for they do not know themselves, nor even their own things, but things even more remote from themselves through their arts: for they are intent on those things by which the body is cared for. ALCIBIADES: You speak the truth. SOCRATES: Therefore, if <term>prudence</term> <note>original: "prudentia" / "σωφροσύνη" (sophrosyne) — often translated as temperance or self-mastery, here linked to self-knowledge</note> is to know oneself, none of these men is prudent according to his art. ALCIBIADES: It does not seem so. SOCRATES: For this reason, these mechanical arts seem to be vulgar, and not the studies of a good man. ALCIBIADES: Entirely so. SOCRATES: Is it not true again, that whoever takes care of the body takes care of his own things, but not himself? ALCIBIADES: It appears so. SOCRATES: But he who cares for money cares neither for himself nor for his own things, but for things even further removed from his own. ALCIBIADES: It seems so. SOCRATES: Therefore the money-maker does not busy himself with his own affairs. ALCIBIADES: Correct. SOCRATES: And whoever ever loved the body of Alcibiades, did not love Alcibiades himself, but something that belongs to Alcibiades. ALCIBIADES: You speak the truth. SOCRATES: But he who loves you, loves your soul. ALCIBIADES: It seems to follow necessarily from your reasoning. SOCRATES: Does not the lover of your body, as soon as its bloom fades, go away and desert you? ALCIBIADES: It appears so. SOCRATES: But he who loves your soul never departs, so long as you advance toward better fruit. ALCIBIADES: That is consistent. SOCRATES: For this reason, I am the one who does not desert you, but I persevere in friendship, while others depart as your body ages. ALCIBIADES: Oh, how well you do, my Socrates; I beseech you, do not desert me in the future. SOCRATES: Then strive to become as beautiful as possible. ALCIBIADES: I will try. SOCRATES: This is how it stands with you: there never was, nor is, I think, any lover of Alcibiades the son of Clinias except one: and he is the lovely Socrates, son of Sophroniscus and Phaenarete. ALCIBIADES: You speak the truth. SOCRATES: Did you not say that I had slightly anticipated you when I came to greet you? For you had decided that you would be the first to meet me, to ask why I alone have not left you. ALCIBIADES: That was how it was. SOCRATES: This is undoubtedly the cause: because I alone was a lover of *you*, while the others were lovers of *yours*. Your belongings are fading with time, but you are now just beginning to bloom. And henceforth, unless you are corrupted by the Athenian people <note>Socrates warns that the flattery of the masses (the Demos) is the greatest threat to a promising young man's soul.</note> and become more base, I will never desert you. For I fear this greatly, lest becoming a lover of the people, you should be corrupted by us. For this has happened already to many and even noble men among the Athenians. For the people of the great-hearted Erechtheus <note>Erechtheus: A legendary king of Athens; Socrates uses his name to refer to the Athenian populace with a touch of irony.</note> are fair-faced; but one must see them stripped naked. Therefore, use the caution I tell you. ALCIBIADES: What caution? SOCRATES: Strip them first—

<meta>This page continues the pivotal dialogue between Socrates and Alcibiades. Having previously established that the "Self" is the soul and not the body, Socrates now moves to explain how one can actually "know" this soul, using the famous analogy of the eye reflecting in a mirror or another eye.</meta>

# ALCIBIADES I. 37
<note>The header in this 16th-century edition labels this as "Alcibiades II," but the text is actually the "First Alcibiades."</note>

...you will know, and learn what you must learn before entering into the affairs of the city, but not before; so that you may go equipped with protective medicines <note>original: "alexipharmaka" — charms or antidotes to ward off evil or corruption</note> and suffer no harm. ALCIBIADES: You seem to speak well, Socrates; but try to explain in what way we should take care of ourselves. SOCRATES: Has this not been sufficiently settled for us in what was said before? For what we are has been fairly well agreed upon; but we were afraid that, having been mistaken, we might unknowingly be taking care of something else instead of ourselves. ALCIBIADES: That is true. SOCRATES: And after this, that the soul is what must be cared for, and into this we must look. ALCIBIADES: Clearly. SOCRATES: But the care of bodies and possessions should be handed over to others. ALCIBIADES: Why not? SOCRATES: In what way, then, could we know the soul most clearly? For knowing this, it seems, we shall also know ourselves. By the gods, do we not now recognize that the Delphic inscription we mentioned is well-spoken? ALCIBIADES: Which one? What do you have in mind, Socrates? SOCRATES: I will tell you what I suspect this inscription says and advises us. For there is perhaps no other example of it except in the case of sight. ALCIBIADES: How do you mean? SOCRATES: Consider this yourself: if the inscription advised our eye, as if it were a person, "See yourself," how would we understand its advice? Would it not be to look at that thing in which the eye, by looking, would see itself? ALCIBIADES: Clearly. SOCRATES: Let us consider, then, what object exists that we can look into and see both it and ourselves at the same time. ALCIBIADES: It is clear, Socrates, that we would look into mirrors and things of that sort. SOCRATES: You speak rightly. But is there not also something of this kind in the eye with which we see? ALCIBIADES: Certainly. SOCRATES: Have you noticed, then, that when one looks into an eye, the face of the person looking appears in the vision of the person opposite him, as if in a mirror? This is what we call the "pupil" <note>original: "kore" — in Greek, this word means both "pupil of the eye" and "little girl/maiden," referring to the tiny reflected image one sees in another's eye.</note>, being an image of the one looking. ALCIBIADES: You speak the truth. SOCRATES: An eye, therefore, contemplating an eye, and looking into that part which is the best part of it and by which it sees, would thus see itself. ALCIBIADES: So it appears. SOCRATES: But if it looks at any other part of the man, or at anything else except that which this part happens to resemble, it will not see itself. ALCIBIADES: You speak the truth. SOCRATES: Therefore, if an eye is to see itself, it must look into an eye, and into that place of the eye in which the virtue <term>virtue: "arete" — the specific excellence or "best state" of a thing</term> of the eye resides; and this is sight. ALCIBIADES: Quite so. SOCRATES: Therefore, my dear Alcibiades, if the soul too is to know itself, must it look into a soul, and especially into that place of the soul in which the virtue of the soul—wisdom—resides, and into anything else that this happens to resemble? ALCIBIADES: It seems so to me, Socrates. SOCRATES: Can we say that there is anything in the soul more divine than that which concerns knowing and thinking? ALCIBIADES: We cannot. SOCRATES: This part of it, then, resembles the divine; and anyone looking into this, and knowing all that is divine—God and wisdom—would thus also know himself most of all. ALCIBIADES: It appears so. SOCRATES: And we agree that knowing oneself is temperance <term>temperance: "sophrosyne" — a core Greek virtue meaning sound-mindedness, self-control, or prudence</term>. ALCIBIADES: Entirely. SOCRATES: If we do not know ourselves and are not temperate, could we know our own affairs, whether they are good or bad? ALCIBIADES: How could that be, Socrates? SOCRATES: For it perhaps appears impossible that someone who does not know Alcibiades could know that the things belonging to Alcibiades really belong to him. ALCIBIADES: By Zeus, that is impossible. SOCRATES: Nor then can we know our own things as our own, if we do not know ourselves? ALCIBIADES: How could we? SOCRATES: And if we do not know our own things, we cannot know the things that belong to our things. ALCIBIADES: It does not seem so. SOCRATES: Therefore, we were not entirely correct in agreeing before that there are some who do not know themselves but do recognize their own affairs, or even the things belonging to their affairs. For it seems to be the work of one and the same skill to recognize all these: oneself, one's own, and the things belonging to one's own. ALCIBIADES: It's likely. SOCRATES: And whoever is ignorant of his own things would also be ignorant of the things of others. ALCIBIADES: Why not? SOCRATES: And if he is ignorant of the things of others, he will also be ignorant of the things of the city. ALCIBIADES: Necessarily. SOCRATES: Such a man, then, could never become a statesman. ALCIBIADES: Certainly not. SOCRATES: Nor indeed a manager of a household. ALCIBIADES: Certainly not. SOCRATES: Nor will he know what he is doing. ALCIBIADES: He will not. SOCRATES: And will not the one who does not know fall into error? ALCIBIADES: Entirely. SOCRATES: And in erring, will he not fare badly, both privately and publicly? ALCIBIADES: How could he not? SOCRATES: And faring badly, is he not miserable? ALCIBIADES: Very much so. SOCRATES: And what of those for whom he acts? ALCIBIADES: They too. SOCRATES: It is not possible, then, for anyone to be happy unless he is temperate and good. ALCIBIADES: It is not possible. SOCRATES: Therefore, those among men who are bad are miserable. ALCIBIADES: Very much so. SOCRATES: Therefore, it is not the one who has become rich who is delivered from misery, but the one who has become temperate. ALCIBIADES: It appears so. SOCRATES: Therefore, cities do not need walls, nor triremes <note>Ancient Greek warships</note>, nor shipyards, O Alcibiades, if they are to be happy; nor do they need numbers or size, without virtue. ALCIBIADES: Truly not. SOCRATES: If, then, you intend to manage the affairs of the city rightly and nobly, you must impart virtue to the citizens. ALCIBIADES: How could I not? SOCRATES: But can anyone give to others what he does not have himself? ALCIBIADES: How could he? SOCRATES: Therefore, you yourself must first acquire virtue, as must anyone else who intends to rule and take care not only of himself and his own, but of the city and its affairs. ALCIBIADES: You speak the truth. SOCRATES: Therefore, you must not provide yourself or the city with power or authority to do whatever you wish, but rather with justice and temperance. ALCIBIADES: It appears so. SOCRATES: For by acting justly and temperately, both you and the city will act in a way pleasing to God. ALCIBIADES: It is likely.

<column-break/>

<sig>A</sig> O blessed one, and learn whatever things are to be known before you handle civil matters or approach the republic, carrying with you an antidote <note>original: "alexipharmacum"</note>, lest you suffer any adversity. ALCIBIADES: You seem to speak well to me, Socrates, but now try to explain to us by what reasoning we may care for ourselves. SOCRATES: Has this not been sufficiently defined by us in the preceding parts? For we have defined what we are by common consent. For we feared lest, being deceived in this, we might perhaps fail ourselves, having a care for something else, not for ourselves. ALCIBIADES: It is as you say. SOCRATES: Then it was granted that care must be had for the soul, and one must always look back toward it. ALCIBIADES: It is manifest. SOCRATES: But the care of bodies and money is to be left to others. ALCIBIADES: Why not? SOCRATES: In what way then might we know these things clearly, <sig>B</sig> since once this is understood, we also understand ourselves? Or perhaps, by the gods, have we not yet understood that Delphic inscription giving right warning, <margin>Explanation of the Delphic inscription, Know thyself.</margin> of which we made mention above? ALCIBIADES: Of what kind? What indeed are you thinking, when you speak thus, O Socrates? SOCRATES: I will tell you what I suspect this inscription counsels us. Indeed, its example is not to be found everywhere, but seems to be found in sight alone. ALCIBIADES: How do you say that? SOCRATES: Consider you also if he had counseled our eye just as he would a man, "See yourself," how might we think he had admonished it: was it not that the eye should look into that through the intuition of which it would see itself? ALCIBIADES: It is established. SOCRATES: Let us consider therefore into what thing looking most of all, <sig>C</sig> we might see it and ourselves at the same time. ALCIBIADES: Without doubt, Socrates, into mirrors and other things of this sort. SOCRATES: You speak rightly: but in the eye with which we see, is there not in it something of this kind? ALCIBIADES: Greatly. SOCRATES: Have you not noticed that the face of a man looking into an eye is reflected in the sight of the one opposite, as if in a mirror, which we call the pupil, existing as the image of the one looking in? ALCIBIADES: I have noticed. SOCRATES: The eye therefore only then discerns itself when it looks into an eye, and besides intends toward that which is the best of the eye, and by which the eye itself sees. ALCIBIADES: It appears so. SOCRATES: But if it looks back at some other member of the man, or at any other thing whatever, except that to which this is similar, it will by no means perceive <sig>D</sig> itself. ALCIBIADES: True. SOCRATES: The eye therefore, when it is to see itself, must look back into an eye, and into that place of the eye in which the virtue of the eye is. That however is the sight and the sharpness of the pupil. ALCIBIADES: So it is. SOCRATES: By the same reasoning also the soul, O friend Alcibiades, if it wishes to know itself, let it look into a soul, and especially into that place of the soul in which the virtue of the soul is, wisdom, and into another thing to which this is similar. ALCIBIADES: So it seems to me, O Socrates. SOCRATES: Can we find anything in the soul more divine than that around which intelligence and wisdom are occupied? ALCIBIADES: By no means. SOCRATES: That part of the soul, therefore, is like the divine, into which indeed if anyone looks, and discerns all that is divine, namely God and wisdom, <sig>E</sig> so also he will recognize himself. ALCIBIADES: It appears so. SOCRATES: But to know oneself, we grant to be prudence. ALCIBIADES: Entirely. SOCRATES: But if we neither knew ourselves, nor were prudent, could we know our own things, whether they be bad or good? ALCIBIADES: How could it be done, O Socrates? SOCRATES: It seems perhaps impossible to you that anyone who does not know Alcibiades, could nevertheless know that the things which are Alcibiades' belong to Alcibiades? ALCIBIADES: Impossible, by Jove. SOCRATES: Nor our things that they are ours, unless first ourselves? ALCIBIADES: In no way. SOCRATES: If we are ignorant of our own things, neither do we understand those things which belong to our things? ALCIBIADES: Not, as it seems. SOCRATES: We did not therefore entirely agree, when we asserted above that there were some who, being ignorant of themselves, nevertheless distinguished their own affairs. And yet not even those things which are of their own things. For to distinguish all these seems to be the duty of one and the same art: namely, to know itself, and what are its own, <sig>F</sig> and what are of its own things. ALCIBIADES: It seems so. SOCRATES: But he who is ignorant of his own, is likewise ignorant of the things of others. ALCIBIADES: Why so? SOCRATES: Will he not therefore, if he is ignorant of the things of others, also be ignorant of the things which are the republic's? ALCIBIADES: It is necessary. SOCRATES: Never therefore is a man of this sort a statesman. ALCIBIADES: Certainly not. SOCRATES: Nor even a manager of a household. ALCIBIADES: Nor this. SOCRATES: Nor will he understand what he does? ALCIBIADES: Not at all. SOCRATES: But being ignorant, will he not err? ALCIBIADES: Very much. SOCRATES: He who errs, will he not act badly, both privately and publicly? ALCIBIADES: Why not? SOCRATES: Acting badly, will he not be miserable? ALCIBIADES: And very much indeed. SOCRATES: And also those with whom he does these things? ALCIBIADES: These also. SOCRATES: No one therefore can be happy, unless he be wise and <sig>G</sig> good. ALCIBIADES: No one. SOCRATES: It follows that bad men are miserable. <margin>No one is happy except the wise. The bad are miserable.</margin> ALCIBIADES: Especially. SOCRATES: Not therefore he who is rich, but he who is prudent, avoids misery. ALCIBIADES: It seems so. SOCRATES: Wherefore neither with walls, nor with ships, triremes, and shipyards, O Alcibiades, nor with a multitude, nor with amplitude, does a city have need for happiness without virtue. ALCIBIADES: Not indeed. SOCRATES: If you are to govern the city rightly and excellently, the citizens must be imbued with virtue. ALCIBIADES: Why not? SOCRATES: Can anyone give to others what he himself does not have? ALCIBIADES: How could he? SOCRATES: Therefore he himself ought first to be adorned with virtue, whoever is to rule not only for himself and his own, but also for the republic and those things which look toward it? ALCIBIADES: You say true things. SOCRATES: Neither therefore is sovereignty, nor the license of doing whatever you please, to be prepared for you or for the republic, but rather justice and prudence are to be acquired. ALCIBIADES: It appears so. SOCRATES: For acting justly and prudently, both you and your republic together will do a work pleasing to God. ALCIBIADES: It is fitting.

<summary>Socrates uses the analogy of an eye reflecting in a pupil to demonstrate that the soul can only know itself by looking into the "divine" part of another soul—the seat of wisdom. He concludes that private and political success depends entirely on personal virtue (justice and temperance) rather than power or wealth.</summary>

# OF PLATO

<margin>A</margin>SOCRATES: And so, just as we said before, you will act by looking into the divine splendor. ALCIBIADES: It seems so. SOCRATES: Furthermore, by looking there, you will clearly discern yourselves and your own good. ALCIBIADES: Certainly. SOCRATES: Will you not then act rightly and well? ALCIBIADES: We shall. SOCRATES: Indeed, I am ready to guarantee that if you live in this way, you will be happy. ALCIBIADES: You are certainly a reliable guarantor. SOCRATES: On the contrary, if you live unjustly, looking into darkness devoid of divinity, you will—as is inevitable—perform works similar to those dark things, being utterly ignorant of yourselves. ALCIBIADES: It seems so. SOCRATES: For if a man, my friend Alcibiades, has the power to do whatever he pleases, but is captive in his mind, what do you think will happen to him? Whether he is a private citizen <margin>B</margin> or the state itself? Just as if a sick man had the free license to take no account of a doctor, but to exercise a kind of tyranny so that no one could deter him—what do you think would happen to him? Is it not likely that his body would be destroyed? ALCIBIADES: You speak the truth. SOCRATES: And what if on a ship someone had total license to do whatever he saw fit, yet lacked the mind and skill of navigation—do you see what would happen to him and his shipmates? ALCIBIADES: I believe he would destroy both himself and his companions. SOCRATES: Does it not follow, then, for every state and every office and power where virtue is absent, that it fares ill? ALCIBIADES: Necessarily. SOCRATES: Therefore, best Alcibiades, it is not tyranny that must be prepared for ourselves or for the state, but virtue, if we wish to be happy. ALCIBIADES: You say true. SOCRATES: Moreover, before virtue is present, it is better for a man—and not just a boy—to be ruled by one who is better, <margin>C</margin> than to rule. ALCIBIADES: That is apparent. SOCRATES: And is not that which is better also more beautiful? ALCIBIADES: It is. SOCRATES: And what is more beautiful is more fitting? ALCIBIADES: Why not? SOCRATES: It is fitting, therefore, for the wicked man to serve, for that is better. ALCIBIADES: It is fitting. SOCRATES: Vice, then, is a slavish thing. ALCIBIADES: It appears so. SOCRATES: But virtue is noble <note>original: "liberalis" — befitting a free person</note>. ALCIBIADES: So it is. SOCRATES: Should not slavery be fled, my friend? ALCIBIADES: Most especially, Socrates. SOCRATES: Do you perceive your own condition now? Are you in a state of freedom, or the opposite? ALCIBIADES: I feel this most strongly, I think. SOCRATES: Do you know how you might escape that which now occupies you? For I would not like <margin>D</margin> to name it in a man of such distinction. ALCIBIADES: I do indeed know. SOCRATES: How then? ALCIBIADES: If you yourself should wish it, Socrates. SOCRATES: You do not speak rightly, Alcibiades. ALCIBIADES: Then how should I say it? SOCRATES: "If God wills it." ALCIBIADES: I say it then; and I add this besides: there is a danger that we might trade roles, I taking yours and you taking mine. For it cannot be otherwise than that I shall follow you from this day forward, and you shall be led by me. SOCRATES: O noble youth, my love for you is then no different from a stork: if, after it has hatched a winged love in you as in a nest, it is in turn nourished by that love. ALCIBIADES: Indeed, that is how it stands; and from this moment I shall begin to meditate on justice. SOCRATES: Oh, how I wish you would persevere! But I fear, distrusting your nature and seeing the power of this city, lest it overcome both me and you.

<column-break/>

SOCRATES: And as we were saying just before, you will act by looking toward the divine and the radiant. ALCIBIADES: It appears so. SOCRATES: But surely, by looking at these things, you will behold and know both yourselves and your own goods. ALCIBIADES: Yes. SOCRATES: Will you not then act rightly and well? ALCIBIADES: Yes. SOCRATES: And if you act in this way, I am willing to guarantee that you will truly be happy. ALCIBIADES: You are a safe guarantor. SOCRATES: But if you act unjustly, looking toward the godless and the dark, you will, in all likelihood, do things similar to those, being ignorant of yourselves. ALCIBIADES: It seems so. SOCRATES: For to whom, dear Alcibiades, there is power to do what he wants, but he has no sense—what is likely to happen, whether to a private individual or a city? For example, if a sick man has the power to do what he wants, but does not have a medical mind, and acts like a tyrant so that no one can rebuke him, what will be the result? Will not his body likely be destroyed? ALCIBIADES: You speak the truth. SOCRATES: And what about in a ship, if someone had the power to do what he pleased, but was deprived of the mind and the skill of a pilot—do you see what would happen to him and his fellow sailors? ALCIBIADES: I do; they would all perish. SOCRATES: In the same way then, in a city and in all offices and powers that lack virtue, it follows that they fare badly. ALCIBIADES: Necessarily. SOCRATES: It is not tyranny then, my excellent Alcibiades, that you should provide for yourself or the city if you intend to be happy, but virtue. ALCIBIADES: You speak the truth. SOCRATES: And before one has virtue, it is better to be ruled by one who is better than to rule, for a man as well as a child. ALCIBIADES: It appears so. SOCRATES: And is not the better also more beautiful? ALCIBIADES: Yes. SOCRATES: and the more beautiful more fitting? ALCIBIADES: How could it not be? SOCRATES: It is fitting then for the bad man to be a slave, for it is better. ALCIBIADES: Yes. SOCRATES: Vice then is a slavish thing. ALCIBIADES: It appears so. SOCRATES: And virtue is befitting of a free man. ALCIBIADES: Yes. SOCRATES: Must we not then flee slavishness, my friend? ALCIBIADES: It seems to me I should be very much ashamed. SOCRATES: Do you know then how you will escape this state you are in now? Let us not name it when speaking of a beautiful man. ALCIBIADES: I do. SOCRATES: How? ALCIBIADES: If you wish it, Socrates. SOCRATES: You do not speak well, Alcibiades. ALCIBIADES: But how should I speak? SOCRATES: That if God wills it. ALCIBIADES: I say it then. And in addition, remember my saying this: we shall likely exchange our roles, Socrates—I taking yours, and you mine. For there is no way I shall not be your attendant <note>original: "paidagogeso" — literally, to be a pedagogue or guide</note> from this day on, and you will be guided by me. SOCRATES: O noble one! My love then will be no different from a stork's, if after nesting a winged love in you, it is cared for by that love in return. ALCIBIADES: It is so; and I will begin from here to care for justice. SOCRATES: I could wish that you would continue; but I shudder, not because I distrust your nature, but seeing the strength of the city, I fear it may master both me and you.

# ALCIBIADES
## THE SECOND, OR,
### On Prayer.

> *SUMMARY OF THE DIALOGUE. As Alcibiades is setting out to perform a sacrifice and appears deep in thought—though unable to explain the cause of his reflections—Socrates warns him how difficult and dangerous it is to pray to God. He explains that men often believe they are asking for good things from God when they are actually asking for evils, because they are ignorant of what is truly necessary and useful to know. He offers certain remedies for this ignorance, not to teach what a "perfect" prayer is (for he admits he does not know), but so that men might pray to God with less absurdity and less danger.*

->SOCRATES, ALCIBIADES.<-

<margin>E</margin>SOCRATES: Are you going to God to offer a prayer, Alcibiades? ALCIBIADES: Most certainly, Socrates. SOCRATES: You seem to show a certain gloominess and keep your eyes fixed on the ground, as if you are thinking about something. ALCIBIADES: And what would I be thinking about, Socrates? SOCRATES: Something of the greatest importance, it seems to me. For tell me, I beseech you by Jove, do you not think that the gods sometimes grant part of what we pray for, whether privately or publicly, and sometimes deny it—granting to some and not at all to others? ALCIBIADES: Entirely so. SOCRATES: Does it not seem to you, then, that one needs great foresight <note>original: "providentia" / "prometheias" — forethought or precaution</note> lest he unknowingly pray for great evils while believing he is asking for good? And the gods might be in such a state or disposition that they grant what the person happens to ask for. Just as they say Oedipus <margin>F</margin> once prayed to God that his sons should divide their father's kingdom with the sword. When he could have asked for a turning away of his present evils, he called down other curses instead. Thus those things came to pass, and many other grave consequences followed, which there is no need to recount one by one. ALCIBIADES: But you have brought up a madman as an example! For what man of sound mind, do you think, would dare to ask for such things? SOCRATES: Does being mad seem to you to be the opposite of being prudent?

### ALCIBIADES II.

<margin>A</margin>ALCIBIADES: Certainly. SOCRATES: Do not some men seem to you to be wise, and others unwise? ALCIBIADES: Most certainly. SOCRATES: Come then, let us consider who these people are. For it is agreed that there are some who are wise and others who are unwise, and some who are mad. ALCIBIADES: That is agreed. SOCRATES: Furthermore, are there some who are healthy? ALCIBIADES: There are. SOCRATES: And are there others who are sick? ALCIBIADES: Quite so. SOCRATES: Therefore, they are not the same people. ALCIBIADES: Certainly not. SOCRATES: And are there any others who suffer from neither of these states? ALCIBIADES: Not at all. SOCRATES: For it is necessary that a man is either sick or not sick. ALCIBIADES: So it seems to me. SOCRATES: What then? Is it not the case that every man is either wise or foolish? ALCIBIADES: Certainly. SOCRATES: What do you mean? <margin>Plato denies there is a middle state between the healthy and the sick.</margin> SOCRATES: Does it seem possible to you to be neither wise nor foolish? Or is there some middle ground between these, such that a man is neither wise <margin>B</margin> nor foolish? ALCIBIADES: Not at all. SOCRATES: It is necessary then to be one or the other. ALCIBIADES: So it seems to me. SOCRATES: Do you remember agreeing that madness is the opposite of wisdom? <margin>Between the wise and the unwise.</margin> ALCIBIADES: I do. SOCRATES: And that there is no middle ground between the two, so that being unwise is a form of madness? ALCIBIADES: I have agreed to that. SOCRATES: And yet, can two things be contrary to the same thing if they are not the same themselves? ALCIBIADES: By no means. SOCRATES: Then it must be that folly and madness are the same thing? <margin>One thing cannot have two contraries: but if they are contraries, they are two.</margin> ALCIBIADES: So it appears. SOCRATES: For instance, if there are some among those of your own age who happen to be foolish, as is likely, or among your elders—for by the gods, do you not think there are few wise men in this city, but many foolish ones, whom you call mad? ALCIBIADES: I do. SOCRATES: Do you think then that we would be safe living among so many madmen, and that we would not have been long ago assaulted and struck, and suffered what madmen usually do? But see, my friend, if the matter might be otherwise. ALCIBIADES: How so, Socrates? It seems it is not as I thought. SOCRATES: It does not seem so to me either. But perhaps we should look at it this way. <margin>D</margin> ALCIBIADES: In what way do you mean? SOCRATES: I will tell you. We recognize that some people are sick, do we not? ALCIBIADES: Certainly. SOCRATES: Now, do you think it necessary for every sick person to have <term>podagra</term> <note>original: "ποδαγρᾷν" (podagran); a painful form of inflammatory arthritis, usually gout.</note>, or a fever, or <term>lippitudo</term> <note>original: "ὀφθαλμιᾷν" (ophthalmian); an inflammation of the eyes or bleary-eyedness.</note>? Or does it seem to you that even if one suffers from none of these, they might still be sick with something else? For there are many and diverse kinds of disease, not just these. ALCIBIADES: So it seems to me. SOCRATES: Does every eye-inflammation seem to you to be a disease? ALCIBIADES: Yes. SOCRATES: And is every disease an eye-inflammation? ALCIBIADES: Not to me; however, I am at a loss as to what you mean. SOCRATES: But if you give me your attention, we shall perhaps reach an agreement. ALCIBIADES: I am attending, Socrates, to the best of my ability. SOCRATES: Did we not agree that every eye-inflammation is a disease, but not every disease is an eye-inflammation? ALCIBIADES: We agreed. SOCRATES: And it seems to me we were right to agree. <margin>E</margin> For everyone with a fever is sick, but not everyone who is sick has a fever, nor gout, nor eye-inflammation, I think. But all such things are commonly called disease; yet those we call doctors say that their treatments differ. For they are not all the same, nor are they treated the same way, but each according to its own nature—yet they are all diseases. Just as we assume there are certain craftsmen, do we not? ALCIBIADES: Certainly. SOCRATES: And there are shoemakers, and carpenters, and sculptors, and many others whom we mention individually? They possess specific parts of craftsmanship. And all these are craftsmen, but they are not all carpenters, nor shoemakers, nor sculptors—though as a whole they are all craftsmen. ALCIBIADES: That is so. SOCRATES: In the same way, people are divided <margin>F</margin> by their lack of wisdom. <margin>Many kinds of imprudence.</margin> Those who have the greatest share of it we call "mad," while those with a slightly lesser share we call "simple" or "thunderstruck." Those who wish to use more honorable names call some "high-minded" and others "mindless," or "innocent," "inexperienced," or "silly." You will find many other such names. But all these are forms of folly. They differ, however, just as one art appeared to us to differ from another, and one disease from another. Or how does it seem to you? ALCIBIADES: Just so. SOCRATES: Then let us return to where we started, since at the beginning of the discussion our purpose was <margin>G</margin> to determine who are the wise and who are the unwise. <margin>Who are the wise.</margin> We agreed that such people exist, did we not? ALCIBIADES: We did. SOCRATES: Do you consider those to be wise who know what ought to be done and said? ALCIBIADES: I do. SOCRATES: And the unwise are those who know neither of these? ALCIBIADES: Those very ones. SOCRATES: And will not those who know neither of these things be unaware of themselves, both in what they say and what they do when it is not appropriate? ALCIBIADES: It appears so. SOCRATES: It was of such men, Alcibiades, that I was saying Oedipus was one. You will find many even in our own times who are not driven by anger, as he was, nor who think they are praying for evils for themselves, but rather for goods. For he, <margin>Concerning the quality of a request.</margin> while he did not desire it, did not think so. But there are some who suffer the <margin>H</margin> opposite of these. I think that if the god to whom you are going to pray were to appear before your eyes, and before you offered any prayer, he were to ask you if it would satisfy you to become the tyrant of the city of Athens; and if you thought this a cheap and small thing, he added all the Greeks; and if he saw you still not satisfied unless he added all of Europe—and not only added it, but also granted that on one and the same day everyone should know that Alcibiades, son of Cleinias, was the master,

SOCRATES: Come then, let us consider who those people are. For it is already agreed <margin>Plato denies there is a middle ground between healthy and sick.</margin> that some are unwise, others wise, and some insane. ALCIBIADES: It is agreed. SOCRATES: Moreover, there are some who are in good health. ALCIBIADES: There are. SOCRATES: And others who are sick. ALCIBIADES: Entirely so. SOCRATES: Therefore, they are not the same. ALCIBIADES: Certainly not. SOCRATES: Are there some who suffer from neither? ALCIBIADES: Not at all. SOCRATES: For it is necessary for a man either to be sick or not to be sick. ALCIBIADES: It seems so. SOCRATES: Do you <margin>Between the prudent and the imprudent.</margin> <margin>B</margin> judge the same regarding prudence and imprudence? ALCIBIADES: How do you mean? SOCRATES: Do you think a man must be either prudent or imprudent, or that there is a third thing besides these, like a middle ground, by which he is neither prudent nor imprudent? ALCIBIADES: Nothing of the sort. SOCRATES: It is necessary then to suffer one or the other. ALCIBIADES: It appears so. SOCRATES: Do you remember having granted that insanity is the contrary of prudence? ALCIBIADES: Indeed. SOCRATES: And that there is no third thing in the middle that makes a man neither prudent nor imprudent? ALCIBIADES: I did agree to that. SOCRATES: <margin>Two contraries cannot belong to one thing: but if they are contraries, they are two.</margin> Furthermore, how can two things be contrary to the same thing? ALCIBIADES: In no way. SOCRATES: Imprudence and insanity, therefore, seem to be the same thing. ALCIBIADES: They seem so. SOCRATES: If, therefore, we call all imprudent people insane, we shall speak rightly. SOCRATES: Do you think we could live safely among these insane people, without being struck or beaten by them, or suffering whatever madmen are accustomed to do, if they had not long ago been punished? But see, my friend, lest the matter be otherwise. ALCIBIADES: In what way is it otherwise, Socrates? For it appears it is not as I thought. SOCRATES: Not certainly, as it seems to me; but perhaps it must be thought of in this way. ALCIBIADES: In what way? SOCRATES: I will tell you. We posit that some people are sick, do we not? ALCIBIADES: Entirely so. SOCRATES: Now, do you think it is necessary that every sick person is tormented only by <term>podagra</term> <note>gout</note>, or by <margin>D</margin> fevers, or by <term>lippitudo</term> <note>eye inflammation</note>? Or if he suffers none of these, can he still be afflicted by other diseases, since there are many species of diseases besides these? ALCIBIADES: So it seems to me. SOCRATES: Does every eye-inflammation seem to you to be a disease? ALCIBIADES: To me, certainly. SOCRATES: And is every disease also an eye-inflammation? ALCIBIADES: Not to me, though I do not know what to say. SOCRATES: If you apply your mind to what I say, and we investigate both together, we shall obtain nearly what we want. ALCIBIADES: I am applying it as much as I can. SOCRATES: Does it not stand between us that every eye-inflammation is a disease, but not every disease is an eye-inflammation? ALCIBIADES: It is agreed. SOCRATES: And we seem to have agreed rightly. For all those with fevers are sick, but not all who are sick also have fevers, or are afflicted with gout or eye-inflammation. ALCIBIADES: Exactly. SOCRATES: And shoemakers, and carpenters, and sculptors, and many others whom there is no need to list individually, who have distinct parts of craftsmanship: and all are indeed craftsmen, yet not all are carpenters, nor tanners, nor sculptors, but all are generally craftsmen. ALCIBIADES: So it is. SOCRATES: In the same way, many people share <margin>F</margin> imprudence among themselves; and those who obtain the greater part of imprudence are called insane and mad. But those who have a somewhat smaller part are called dull and "thunderstruck." Those who wish <margin>Several kinds of imprudence.</margin> to signify the same things with more honorable names call some "magnanimous," and others "inept." Some call them "not bad," "innocent," "inexperienced," and "stupid"; you will also find many other names by which all imprudence is signified. But they differ, as it appeared in the previous examples that art differs from art, and disease from disease. What do you think? ALCIBIADES: That very thing. SOCRATES: But to return to where we digressed: it was proposed at the beginning of the discussion <margin>G</margin> to judge who were prudent and who were imprudent. <margin>Who are the prudent.</margin> We agreed that such people exist, did we not? ALCIBIADES: We agreed. SOCRATES: Do you think those are prudent who know what things are to be done and said? ALCIBIADES: Indeed. SOCRATES: And the imprudent are those who see neither? ALCIBIADES: Those very ones. SOCRATES: Is it not so that those who are ignorant of both these things are hidden from themselves, both acting and speaking what they ought not? ALCIBIADES: It appears so. SOCRATES: Among these men, Alcibiades, you were saying that Oedipus was one. You will also find in our times many who are not moved by anger, like him, nor who think they are wishing for evil things for themselves, but rather good things. For he, since <margin>Dealing with the quality of the petition.</margin> he did not wish it, so also he did not think it. But there are some who suffer the <margin>H</margin> opposite of these. I truly think that if perhaps that God whom you are approaching to pray to, showing himself to your eyes, were to ask you—before you prayed for anything—whether it would be enough for you to gain lordship over the Athenians; and if you judged this something vile and small, he were to add all the Greeks; and if he saw you not even satisfied with those, unless he also added all of Europe, nor only added it, but also that you should desire that on one and same day everyone should know that Alcibiades, son of Cleinias, was the master,

<summary>Socrates leads Alcibiades to conclude that folly (imprudence) is a form of madness, comparable to how various specific ailments are all classified as diseases. He illustrates that many people unknowingly pray for things that would actually harm them, using the ambition for political power as a potential trap.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the Second Alcibiades, a dialogue attributed to Plato. Socrates is currently arguing that humans often pray for things that are actually harmful to them because they lack the wisdom to discern true "good." -># OF PLATO<-

...and so if he were to grant you all these things, I think you would depart from him with great joy, as if you had successfully obtained the greatest goods. <margin>Alcibiades</margin> I believe so, O Socrates, as would anyone else who attained such a lot. SOCRATES: But would you exchange your life for the region and rule of all Greeks, and even of the barbarians? <margin>Alcibiades</margin> Not in my opinion, since I would not be able to use it. SOCRATES: What if you were to use it, but badly and to your own harm? Would you accept it then? <margin>That it is not safe to accept things blindly.</margin> <margin>Alcibiades</margin> Certainly not. SOCRATES: You see, then, that it is not safe to blindly accept what is offered, nor to wish for it, if one is to suffer disadvantages because of it or even lose one's life straight away. We could cite many who, having sought a tyranny <note>A "tyranny" in this context refers to absolute power or kingship, often seized by force rather than inherited.</note> and having struggled with burning zeal to possess it—as if they were about to obtain some great good—perished because they were ensnared by the plots surrounding that power. I think you have also heard of things that happened just yesterday or the day before, <margin>B</margin> <margin>He refers to Crateuas.</margin> when someone killed Archelaus, the tyrant of the Macedonians and a lover of pleasures, because he thirsted for those same pleasures no less than the tyrant did, believing he would soon be a tyrant and a happy man himself. But when he had possessed the tyranny for only three or four days, he was in turn oppressed by the plots of others and perished. And to recall things we did not just hear about, but witnessed ourselves, you see among our own citizens those who sought the command of the army and obtained it. Some are even now <margin>C</margin> wandering as exiles, while others have been condemned to death. Even those who perhaps seemed to have acted vigorously through extreme dangers and fears—not only in the army itself but also after they returned to their own homes—were oppressed by the plots of sycophants <note>In ancient Athens, "sycophants" were professional informers or legal extortionists who brought malicious lawsuits against prominent citizens.</note> and slanderers no less than by their enemies, so that many of them finally wished they had lived as private citizens rather than in command. If dangers and labors of this kind brought us some utility, then this pursuit would have some reason. Furthermore, you will find in the same way some men who long for sons in their prayers; but when they have obtained sons, they fall into the greatest calamities and <margin>D</margin> sorrows. For many, when their children persevere in wickedness throughout their whole lives, finish their own lives in grief. Those who obtain honorable sons but lose them through some adverse accident are no less wretched than the former, so that they utterly wish they had never fathered children. And although these and many other such things are manifest, one would rarely find a person who would either abstain from what is given or, if he were about to obtain it by praying, would omit the vow. Very many would not depart from the pursuit of tyranny, or from a command once gained, or from countless other things which, when possessed, hurt rather than help; instead, they would rather pray for those things to be granted <margin>E</margin> if they are absent. Sometimes, after a short time, they condemn their past vows, returning to their opposites. Therefore, I truly fear that men blindly accuse the gods, as if evils were brought by them; but they themselves, through a certain perversity or foolishness, produce for themselves sorrows sharper than death. Wherefore that poet <margin>The poet's upright request.</margin> seems wise to me, who, having experienced foolish friends and seeing them both acting and praying for things that were not at all conducive to them (though they seemed useful to them), <margin>Odyssey, book 2</margin> spoke thus on behalf of them all:
> King Jupiter, grant us the best things both when we pray for them and when we do not. But command that evil things be absent even for those who ask for them. <note>original: "Iuppiter rex, optima quidem nobis & vouentibus, & non vouentibus tribue. Mala autem poſcentibus quoque abeße iube."</note>

The poet seems to me to speak rightly and cautiously. But if you have anything in your mind to bring against these points, do not be silent. <margin>Alcibiades</margin> It is difficult, <margin>F</margin> O Socrates, to contradict things that have been well said. I am thinking, however, of how many evils ignorance is the cause for men; since because of it we are unaware when we do something badly, and what is worst, because of it we sometimes pray for the very worst things for ourselves, which no one would think he was doing. Rather, anyone would think he was able to seek for himself not the worst, but the best; for to seek the worst would truly be like a curse, not a prayer. SOCRATES: But perhaps, O best of men, someone wiser than you and me might say that we do not speak quite correctly when <margin>G</margin> we thus blindly blame ignorance, unless we add what kind of ignorance it is and of what things. For to some people, affected in a certain way, <margin>On the goodness and badness of ignorance.</margin> ignorance is perhaps a good, just as it is an evil to others. <margin>Alcibiades</margin> What are you saying? Is there anything that it is ever better to be ignorant of than to know? SOCRATES: It certainly seems so to me; does it not to you? <margin>Alcibiades</margin> Not by Jupiter. SOCRATES: Truly, I will not judge that you would ever wish to have done to your mother what they say Orestes and Alcmaeon and others of that sort committed. <margin>Alcibiades</margin> Speak words of good omen, <note>A traditional Greek expression meaning "Don't say something so unlucky or terrible."</note> by Jupiter, O Socrates! SOCRATES: It is not proper, O Alcibiades, for the one who says you would not wish <margin>H</margin> to have done these things to be told to speak words of good omen, but rather for someone who said the opposite. Since a deed so horrendous seems to you such that it ought not even be easily spoken, do you think Orestes—if he had been prudent and had known what was good for him—would have dared to commit such a crime? <margin>Alcibiades</margin> Certainly not. SOCRATES: Nor any other, I suppose. <margin>Which ignorance is bad.</margin> <margin>Alcibiades</margin> Not one. SOCRATES: Therefore, it seems that ignorance of the best, and not knowing what is best, is an evil. <margin>Alcibiades</margin> It certainly seems so to me. SOCRATES: And for him, and for all others as well? <margin>Alcibiades</margin> I admit it. SOCRATES:

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Alcibiades, the son of Cleinias, is a tyrant; I think you would go away overjoyed, as having obtained a very great good. ALCIBIADES: I think so, Socrates, and so would anyone else, if such things happened to him. SOCRATES: But would you not want the land and the tyranny of the Greeks and barbarians to be yours at the cost of your own soul? ALCIBIADES: I think not. For how could I, if I were not going to make any use of them? SOCRATES: What if you were going to use them badly and harmfully? Not even then? ALCIBIADES: Certainly not. SOCRATES: You see then that it is not safe for you to receive things thus offered at random, nor to pray for them to happen, if one is going to be harmed by them, or even be released from this life. And we could <margin>B</margin> name many who, having desired tyranny and having striven for it to be theirs, as if they were doing something good, were deprived of their life by plots because of that tyranny. I think you are not unheard of what happened yesterday and the day before, when the beloved of Archelaus, the tyrant of the Macedonians—being a lover of the tyranny no less than that man was of his beloved—killed his lover, so as to be a tyrant and a happy man. But having held the tyranny for three or four days, he himself was in turn plotted against by others and died. And you see also among our citizens (for these things we have not heard from others, but know ourselves by being present) those who, having desired the command of the army and having obtained it, some are even <margin>C</margin> now exiles from this city, and others have ended their lives. And those who seemed to have fared best among them, having gone through many dangers and fears—not only during that command but after they returned to their own place—ended their lives being besieged by sycophants with a siege no less than that by their enemies; so that some of them prayed to have been without command rather than to have commanded. If these dangers and labors led to some benefit, there would be some reason for it; but now it is quite the opposite. And you will find the same thing concerning children: some who have prayed for offspring to be born to them, and when they were born, they were established in the greatest misfortunes and pains. For some, whose children were wicked throughout, <margin>D</margin> spent their whole lives grieving. Others, whose children were good but met with misfortunes so as to be deprived of them, were established in no less misfortunes than the former; they would have preferred the children to have never been born. But nevertheless, though these and many other things like them are so very manifest, it is rare to find anyone who would either abstain from things given, or who, being about to obtain them through prayer, would stop praying. Most people would not abstain from tyranny if offered, nor from command, nor many other things which, being present, harm rather than benefit; but they would even pray for them to happen, if they were not present. But after a little while, they sing a different tune, praying against what they first prayed for. <margin>E</margin> I then am at a loss whether in truth men blame the gods in vain, saying that evils come from them; while they themselves, whether one should call it through their own recklessness or foolishness, have pains beyond their fate. It seems then, O Alcibiades, that that poet was a wise man, who, as it seems to me, having some foolish friends and seeing them both doing and praying for things that were not better for them, though it seemed so to them, made a prayer on behalf of them all in common. He says something like this: "King Jupiter, the good things [he says] give to us both when we pray and when we do not pray; but the dangerous things, even if we pray for them, command to be kept away." To me, then, the poet seems to speak well and safely. But you, if you have anything in mind against <margin>F</margin> these things, do not be silent. ALCIBIADES: It is difficult, Socrates, to speak against things well said. I am thinking, however, of how many evils ignorance is the cause for men; since, as it seems, we are unaware of ourselves through it, both in acting and, most extreme of all, in praying for the worst things for ourselves. Which no one would think; but then everyone would think himself sufficient to pray for the best for himself, but not the worst. For this would truly be like a curse rather than a prayer. SOCRATES: But perhaps, O best of men, a man who happens to be wiser than you or I might say that we are not speaking correctly, thus blindly blaming ignorance; unless we should <margin>G</margin> add what kind of ignorance it is, and that there are some for whom it is even a good, just as it is an evil for those others. ALCIBIADES: How do you mean? For is there any matter that it is better for anyone to be ignorant of than to know? SOCRATES: So it seems to me; does it not to you? ALCIBIADES: No, by Jupiter. SOCRATES: But I will not judge of you that you would wish to have done to your own mother what they say Orestes and Alcmaeon did, and if indeed any others among you have done these same things. ALCIBIADES: Speak words of good omen, by Jupiter, O Socrates! SOCRATES: It is not the one who says, O Alcibiades, that you would wish these things done to you, whom you should tell to speak words of good omen, but rather if someone were to say the opposite; since the thing seems so very terrible to you that it should not even be spoken of. <margin>H</margin> Do you think Orestes, if he had been prudent and had known what was best for him to do, would have dared to do any of these things? ALCIBIADES: Certainly not. SOCRATES: Nor any other, I think. ALCIBIADES: Certainly not. SOCRATES: Therefore, it is an evil (as it seems) to be ignorant of the best things, and to be ignorant of what is best. ALCIBIADES: It seems so to me. SOCRATES: Therefore, both for that man and for all others? ALCIBIADES: I say so.

<summary>Socrates argues that power, wealth, and children are not inherently good if the possessor lacks the wisdom to use them well, citing the tragic fate of the Macedonian tyrant Archelaus. The dialogue concludes that ignorance of "the best" is the root of human misery and misguided prayers.</summary>
