<meta>This page continues the Second Alcibiades, a dialogue frequently attributed to Plato. Socrates is further developing his argument that "knowledge" without the "knowledge of the best" (moral wisdom) is not only useless but potentially dangerous.</meta>

### ALCIBIADES II.

**SOCRATES:** Come then, let us also consider this: if it should suddenly come into your mind—thinking it were for the better—to take a dagger in hand and go to the doors of **Pericles** <note>Pericles was a prominent Athenian statesman and the actual guardian of the young Alcibiades; here, Socrates uses him as a hypothetical target of a misguided assassination.</note>, your own guardian and friend, and ask the servants if he is within, intending to kill him and no one else; and they should say he is inside. Now, I do not say you would actually wish to do such a thing. But if, I suppose, it should seem to you—and nothing prevents a man who is ignorant of the "best" <term>the "best" (Greek: to beltiston): refers to the ultimate moral good or the most beneficial course of action</term> from occasionally having an opinion that makes him think even the worst thing is actually the best—does this seem possible to you? **ALCIBIADES:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** If, then, you went inside and saw him, but failed to recognize him and thought he was someone else, would you still venture to kill him? **ALCIBIADES:** No, by Zeus, I think not. **SOCRATES:** For you did not intend to kill just anyone you met, but that specific man whom you wished to kill, is that not so? **ALCIBIADES:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** And even if you tried many times, if you always failed to recognize Pericles when you were about to do the deed, you would never actually attack him. **ALCIBIADES:** Not at all. **SOCRATES:** What then? Do you think **Orestes** <note>In Greek tragedy, Orestes killed his mother, Clytemnestra, to avenge his father. Socrates argues that if Orestes hadn't recognized her, he wouldn't have committed the crime.</note> would have ever attacked his mother if he had similarly failed to recognize her? **ALCIBIADES:** I do not think so. **SOCRATES:** For he did not intend to kill just any woman he met, nor any mother, but specifically his own. **ALCIBIADES:** That is true. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, to be ignorant of such things is better for those in such a state of mind and holding such opinions. **ALCIBIADES:** So it seems. **SOCRATES:** Do you see then that there are cases where ignorance is a good thing for certain people in certain conditions, and not an evil, as it recently seemed to you? **ALCIBIADES:** It appears so. **SOCRATES:** Furthermore, if you wish to consider what follows, it might perhaps seem even more strange to you. **ALCIBIADES:** What is that, Socrates? **SOCRATES:** That, to put it simply, it is likely that the possession of various sciences <note>original: "epistemē" (knowledge/science)</note>, if one lacks the science of the "best," will rarely benefit the possessor, but will mostly harm him. Look at it this way: does it not seem necessary to you that when we are about to either do or say something, we must first either think we know, or truly know, that which we are so ready to say or do? **ALCIBIADES:** I think so. **SOCRATES:** Now, take the orators for instance. Either because they know how to give counsel, or because they think they know, they advise us on every occasion: some about war and peace, others about building walls or constructing harbors. In a word, whatever the city does toward another city, or within itself, all happens because of the advice of the orators. **ALCIBIADES:** You speak the truth. **SOCRATES:** Observe then what follows, if you can. Do you call some people wise <note>original: "phronimos" (prudent/wise)</note> and others unwise? **ALCIBIADES:** I do. **SOCRATES:** And the many are unwise, while the few are wise? **ALCIBIADES:** Precisely. **SOCRATES:** And do you call them both by looking at something specific? **ALCIBIADES:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** Now, do you call a man wise if he knows how to give advice without knowing whether it is better to do so, and when it is better? **ALCIBIADES:** Not at all. **SOCRATES:** Nor, I think, a man who knows the art of war, without knowing when it is better to wage it, and for how long. Is that right? **ALCIBIADES:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** Nor if someone knows how to kill another, or to seize property, or to make someone an exile from his country, without knowing when it is better and whom it is better to treat so. **ALCIBIADES:** Certainly not. **SOCRATES:** He, then, who knows something of this kind, provided he also possesses the science of the "best"—and this is the same, I suppose, as the science of the "useful"—is that not so? **ALCIBIADES:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** We shall call him wise and a sufficient counselor both for himself and for the city; but the man who does not, we call the opposite. Or how does it seem to you? **ALCIBIADES:** It seems so to me. **SOCRATES:** What if someone knows how to ride or use a bow? Or again, how to wrestle or box? Or any other such competition or anything else we know through art <term>art (Greek: technē): technical skill or craft</term>? What do you call the man who knows what is better according to that specific art? Do you not call the one who knows how to ride a "horseman"? **ALCIBIADES:** I do. **SOCRATES:** And the one who knows boxing a "boxer," and the flute-player a "flutist," and so on for the others, I suppose, or is it different? **ALCIBIADES:** No, it is thus. **SOCRATES:** Does it then seem necessary to you that a man who is knowledgeable in one of these things is also a wise man? Or shall we say he falls far short of it? **ALCIBIADES:** Far short indeed, by Zeus! **SOCRATES:** What sort of state, then, do you think it would be if it were made up of good archers and flutists, as well as athletes and various craftsmen, mixed with those we just mentioned who know the art of war itself and the act of killing itself, and also political men puffed up with political pride—but all of them lacked the science of the "best," which knows when it is better to use each of these skills, and against whom? **ALCIBIADES:** A wretched state, I should say, O Socrates. **SOCRATES:** You would say so, I think, whenever you saw each of them being ambitious and "devoting the greatest part of the state's affairs to that portion in which he happens to be most powerful" <note>This is a likely reference to a lost poetic fragment or a common proverb about specialization without moral direction.</note>—meaning that which is "best" according to his specific art—while failing in what is best for the city and for himself, because, I suppose, he has trusted in opinion without intellect. Since they are all in this condition, would we not be right to say that such a state is full of great turmoil and lawlessness? **ALCIBIADES:** Right, by Zeus. **SOCRATES:** Did it not seem necessary to us that we must first either think we know, or truly know, that which we are ready to do or say? **ALCIBIADES:** It did. **SOCRATES:** And if a man does what he knows, or thinks he knows, and is accompanied by the knowledge of what is useful and profitable, we and the city and he himself will be well off? **ALCIBIADES:** How could it be otherwise? **SOCRATES:** But if he does the opposite, I think, it is good neither for the city nor for himself? **ALCIBIADES:** Not at all.

<column-break/>

Let us consider besides this: if it should come into your mind that it would be better to kill your tutor and friend **Pericles**, and taking a sword you should hasten to his doors and ask if he were within, wishing to kill only him and no one else, and the servants should answer that he was inside. I do not say you would attempt any such thing, but whether it seems to you—and nothing prevents it—that for one who is <margin>Certain paradoxes.</margin> ignorant of what is best, there can sometimes be an opinion that leads you to judge that what is worst is sometimes the best. Does it not seem so to you? **ALCIBIADES:** Entirely so. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, if you entered the house and saw him, yet did not recognize him but thought he was someone <margin>B</margin> else, would you kill him? **ALCIBIADES:** Not by Jove, as it seems to me. **SOCRATES:** For you would not kill the one who happened to be there, but the one you had determined to kill, would you not? **ALCIBIADES:** Truly. **SOCRATES:** And if you frequently attempted the deed, but always failed to recognize it was Pericles, would you ever rush upon him? **ALCIBIADES:** Never. **SOCRATES:** Do you think **Orestes** would have ever laid hands on his mother if he had not recognized her? **ALCIBIADES:** I do not think so. **SOCRATES:** For he did not intend to kill whatever woman he met, nor any mother, but specifically his own. **ALCIBIADES:** These things are true. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, for <margin>C</margin> men thus affected, and involved in such opinions, it is better to be ignorant of such things. **ALCIBIADES:** It seems so. **SOCRATES:** You see now that for men disposed in a certain way, ignorance is a certain good, and not, as it seemed to you, an evil. **ALCIBIADES:** It is apparent. **SOCRATES:** Furthermore, if you wish to discuss what is next brought forward, though it be strange to say, it will perhaps seem <margin>Certain paradoxes.</margin> probable to you. **ALCIBIADES:** What is that, Socrates? **SOCRATES:** It seems that the possession of all other sciences, unless one has obtained the science of the best, rarely profits, and for the most part harms him who is endowed with such sciences. Consider it thus: does it not seem necessary to you that when we are <margin>The possession of sciences is harmful without the knowledge of the best.</margin> <margin>D</margin> about to do or say something, we ought first either to think we know, or truly know, that which we are ready to do and say? **ALCIBIADES:** It plainly seems so to me. **SOCRATES:** Do not the orators, as soon as they either know how to advise, or at least think they know, advise us everywhere—some concerning war and peace, others concerning the building of walls or the preparing and fortifying of harbors—and to put it briefly, whatever the state itself does against another state, or within itself, is it not accomplished by the advice of orators? **ALCIBIADES:** You tell the truth. **SOCRATES:** See also what follows, if it can be. Do you call some "prudent" and others "imprudent"? <margin>E</margin> **ALCIBIADES:** I do. **SOCRATES:** And many are imprudent, but few are prudent? **ALCIBIADES:** Truly. **SOCRATES:** Do you not name them both by looking toward something? **ALCIBIADES:** Yes indeed. **SOCRATES:** Will you call him who knows how to advise así, unless he knows how to teach whether it is better, and what is better, "prudent"? **ALCIBIADES:** By no means. **SOCRATES:** Nor, I think, should he know anything of fighting, yet be ignorant of when and how much is better. **ALCIBIADES:** It is so. **SOCRATES:** Nor if anyone knows how to kill someone, and to despoil them of money, and to make them an exile from their fatherland, unless he knows when and whom it is better. **ALCIBIADES:** Not at all. **SOCRATES:** Whoever therefore knows any of these things, provided the science of the best is also present—which indeed is the same as the science of the useful—this man perhaps we shall call prudent. **ALCIBIADES:** This very one. **SOCRATES:** And we shall say that the prudent man himself is a <margin>F</margin> sufficient counselor to himself and to his country; but the imprudent man, on the contrary. What does it seem to you? **ALCIBIADES:** The same. **SOCRATES:** But what if someone knows how to ride, or to shoot arrows, or to exercise in the wrestling ground, or in boxing, or some other contest, or anything else of those things which we know through art? By what name do you call him who understands what is better in the art? Is it not "horseman" according to the equestrian art, "boxer" according to boxing, "flutist" according to flute-playing, and in others in the same way, or otherwise? **ALCIBIADES:** Thus certainly. **SOCRATES:** Does it seem to you that he who understands any of these things should be called a "wise man" <margin>Who should be called prudent.</margin> or is he still far off? **ALCIBIADES:** Far off, by Jove! **SOCRATES:** What <margin>G</margin> then will you think of that state which consists of skilled archers and flutists and athletes and other craftsmen, and if over these whom we have mentioned there are admitted those skilled in the military art, and those ready for killing, and those also puffed up because of the administration of civil affairs—but the science of the best is lacking, and there is no one who knows when and for whom it is better to use each of these? **ALCIBIADES:** An ignoble state, O Socrates. **SOCRATES:** You would say this most especially, I think, if you saw each of them being ambitious and occupying for himself the most parts of the republic in this, so that he might continually surpass himself and have the most power—I say the most in that art of ruling—but in that which is best for himself and the republic, he is frequently hallucinating, because he has believed in opinion without mind. Since these things are so, would we not rightly call this republic full of the greatest tumult and iniquity? **ALCIBIADES:** Rightly, by Jove. **SOCRATES:** Did it not seem necessary to us, that first indeed we must think we know, or truly know, this which we are ready to do or say? **ALCIBIADES:** It did seem so. **SOCRATES:** Is it not so that if someone does what he knows, or thinks he knows, and adds the science of the best, it follows that he acts usefully, both for himself and for the republic? **ALCIBIADES:** Why not? **SOCRATES:** But on the contrary, neither for the republic nor for himself? **ALCIBIADES:** It is so.

He concludes that a state filled with technical experts but lacking moral wisdom is destined for chaos and lawlessness.</summary>

# PLATO

**SOCRATES:** What then? Does it still seem so to you now, or otherwise? **ALCIBIADES:** Not otherwise. **SOCRATES:** Did you say that you call the many unwise, and the few wise? **ALCIBIADES:** I did indeed. **SOCRATES:** Shall we say again that the many miss what is best, since for the most part they have trusted in opinion without intellect <term>intellect (Latin: *mens*; Greek: *nous*): the faculty of the mind that perceives truth directly, as opposed to mere opinion</term>? **ALCIBIADES:** We certainly said that. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, it is beneficial for the many neither to know anything, nor to think they know; for they will be more eager to do those things which they either know or think they know. In acting, however, they will more often harm themselves than benefit. **ALCIBIADES:** You speak most truly. **SOCRATES:** When I said, therefore, that all other sciences <note>original: *scientias*; here meaning technical skills or branches of knowledge</note>, if the science of the best be absent, more often harm than help the one who possesses them, did I seem to you then to speak correctly? **ALCIBIADES:** If not then, at least now, O Socrates. **SOCRATES:** It is necessary, therefore, for both a city and a soul that is to live correctly to embrace this science—just as a sick man needs a physician, and he who wishes to sail without danger needs a pilot. For the more the soul attempts to gain riches, or bodily strength, or any such thing without this science, the greater the errors that must necessarily be committed from them. But he who is adorned with many and various arts and sciences, yet is devoid of this specific science, being led by each of the others, will he not deservedly be tossed by a great storm? Truly, as one wandering on the deep sea without a pilot, he is destined to perish in a short time. To him, surely, that song of the poet seems to apply, in which, censuring a certain man, <margin>Homer in the Margites.</margin> he says: "He knew many things indeed: but he knew them all badly." **ALCIBIADES:** But how does that saying of the poet apply? To me, it seems to have nothing to do with our proposal. **SOCRATES:** On the contrary, it fits perfectly; but here, as almost all other poets do, he speaks through enigmas <term>enigmas (Greek: *ainigmata*): riddles or obscure allegories that require interpretation</term>. For the nature of poetry itself is entirely full of enigmas, <margin>Poetry is full of enigmas.</margin> and not just anyone can discern them. Added to this nature is the fact that if it resides in an envious man, who is unwilling to reveal his thoughts to other men, it is a wonder how difficult it is to know what the poet intended. For you must not think that Homer, that most divine and wise poet, was ignorant that it is impossible to "know badly"; for it is he who says that **Margites** <note>The *Margites* was a famous comic poem in antiquity, now lost, which was traditionally attributed to Homer. It told the story of a man who was foolish despite knowing many facts.</note> knew many things, but knew them all "badly." But he hides his meaning in an enigma, I think, putting "badly" for "a bad thing," and "to know" for "knowing": from which a certain composition outside the meter of the poem is made. What he really means is this: "He knew many things indeed, but it was a bad thing for him to know all these things." It is clear, then, that if it was a bad thing for him to know many things, he himself was also "bad," if any faith is to be placed in our previous arguments. **ALCIBIADES:** It certainly seems so to me, O Socrates. For what words would I ever believe, if I do not believe these? **SOCRATES:** And you are right to think so. But come, by **Zeus**, do you see how great and of what kind the ambiguity is in this? You seem to have been involved in it yourself; for being tossed up and down, you never stand still, but what you once asserted, you now condemn. If by chance the God to whom you are going to pray should present Himself to your eyes before you make your vow, and should ask you if it is enough for you to have any of those things mentioned at the beginning, or if He should grant you the license to ask for whatever you please, what do you think would be timely for you: to accept what the God offers, or to ask for yourself? **ALCIBIADES:** By the gods, O Socrates, I do not know what to answer. It seems to me a kind of madness to pray to God rashly, and it must be carefully considered lest one deceive himself, seeking evils while thinking he prays for good things, and then a little later, as you were saying, change himself to contrary vows. **SOCRATES:** Is not the poet more prudent than we, the one whom we mentioned at the beginning of the discussion, who prayed that even evils be kept away from those who pray for them? **ALCIBIADES:** It seems so to me. **SOCRATES:** The **Lacedaemonians** <note>The Lacedaemonians are the Spartans, known for their laconic (brief) speech and austere lifestyle.</note> also, O Alcibiades, whether imitating this poet or noticing it for themselves, keep the same vow both privately and publicly, praying the gods to grant them noble things along with good things; no one would hear them pray for more than that. And yet, up to these times, they are no less happy than other men. If, however, anything has ever succeeded less prosperously for them, it is not their prayer that is the cause, since it is in the power of the gods, I think, to grant what we pray for, or the opposite. I wish, moreover, to relate to you another thing which I once heard from certain elders. For they said it always happened to our city that whenever the **Athenians** waged war with the Lacedaemonians, our people were unfortunate both on land and at sea, and never returned as victors. Therefore, the Athenians, being indignant since they had no art by which to avoid such great calamity, decreed to consult **Ammon** <note>Ammon was an Egyptian deity with a famous oracle in the Libyan desert, often identified by the Greeks with Zeus.</note>, asking for what reason the gods granted victory to the Lacedaemonians rather than to the Athenians—since they themselves offered sacrifices both more numerous and more beautiful than the rest of the Greeks, adorning the temples with images and gifts as no others did, and celebrated the most expensive and elegant processions every year, and in all expenses regarding divine matters, stood out as more magnificent than all the Greeks, while

<column-break/>

**SOCRATES:** What then? Does it seem the same to you now, or otherwise? **ALCIBIADES:** Not otherwise. **SOCRATES:** Did you say that you call the many foolish, and the few, wise? **ALCIBIADES:** I did. **SOCRATES:** Shall we say again that the many have missed what is best, since for the most part (I think) they have trusted in opinion without mind? **ALCIBIADES:** We do say that. **SOCRATES:** It is profitable, therefore, for the many neither to know anything, nor to think they know; since they will be more eager to do those things which they know, or think they know; but in doing them, will they not harm themselves more than they are helped? **ALCIBIADES:** You speak most truly. **SOCRATES:** You see then, when I said that the possession of other sciences, if one possesses them without the science of the best, is likely to help the owner only rarely, but to harm him in most cases. Did we not seem to be speaking correctly? **ALCIBIADES:** And if I did not think so then, I do now, O Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Therefore the city or soul that intends to live correctly must cling strictly to this science, just as a sick man clings to a doctor, or someone who intends to sail safely clings to a pilot. For when the science of the soul is not present, but instead there is the pursuit of wealth, or strength of body, or any other such thing, the greater the errors from them must necessarily be, as it seems. And it happens that he who has acquired so-called "much-learning" and "much-skill," but is orphaned of this science, being led by each of the others—will he not truly and justly experience a great storm? Since, I think, he continues without a pilot on the open sea, running through life for a time that is not long. So it seems to me that the saying of the poet applies here, which he says in accusing someone: "He knew many works, but," he says, "he knew all these things badly." **ALCIBIADES:** And how does the poet's saying apply, O Socrates? To me, it seems he spoke nothing to the purpose. **SOCRATES:** And yet it is very much to the purpose; but he speaks in riddles, my good friend, both he and almost all other poets. For all poetry is by nature riddling, and it is not for any chance person to recognize it. And in addition to being such by nature, whenever it takes hold of an envious man who does not wish to show us his wisdom, but to hide it as much as possible, the thing appears exceedingly difficult to know, whatever each of them might mean. For surely you do not think that **Homer**, the wisest and most divine poet, was ignorant that it was not possible to "know badly." For it is he who says that the one speaking of Margites says that he "knew many things, but knew them all badly." But he speaks in a riddle, I think, putting "badly" instead of "a bad thing," and "he knew" instead of "to know." It becomes, then, when put together, outside the meter, but it is what he means: that "he knew many works, but it was a bad thing for him to know all these." It is clear, then, that if it was a bad thing for him to know many things, he happened to be a base person—if indeed I am to be persuaded by the previously mentioned arguments. **ALCIBIADES:** It seems so to me, O Socrates. I would hardly be persuaded by other arguments if not by these. **SOCRATES:** And you are right to think so. But come, by Zeus. For you see how great and of what kind this perplexity <term>perplexity (Greek: *aporia*): a state of being at a loss or a philosophical dead-end</term> is; and you seem to me to have shared in it. For changing back and forth, you do not stop anywhere, but whatever seems most certain to you, you seem to have slipped out of it again. And there it seems to be just as it was then. If, therefore, the God to whom you happen to be going should appear to you now and ask you, before you make any prayer, if it would suffice you to have any of those things that were spoken of to you in the beginning, or if He should permit you yourself to pray, what do you think? Would you take what is given by Him, or pray for something yourself to happen, and so obtain moderate things? **ALCIBIADES:** But by the gods, O Socrates, I do not know what I could say to you, O Socrates. But it seems to me to be a frantic thing, and truly a matter of much caution, lest one should forget himself and pray for evils while thinking they are goods; then, after waiting a little (as you were saying), he would sing a recantation, praying against what he had first prayed for. **SOCRATES:** Did not the poet, whom I mentioned at the beginning of the argument, see something more than we, when he commanded us to pray for the gods to ward off terrible things even from those who pray for them? **ALCIBIADES:** It seems so to me. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, O Alcibiades, the Lacedaemonians, having either emulated this poet or having looked into it themselves in this way, always offer a simple prayer both privately and publicly, commanding the gods to give them "noble things in addition to good things." No one would hear any of them praying for more. Therefore, for the remaining time, they are men no less fortunate than others. And if it has happened to them not to be unfortunate in all things, it was not because of their prayer; but it is in the power of the gods, I think, to give whatever one happens to pray for, and also the opposites of these. And I want to tell you another thing, which I once heard from some elders: how, when there was a dispute between the Athenians and the Lacedaemonians, it always happened to our city that, whenever a battle occurred by land or by sea, we were unfortunate and never able to prevail. The Athenians, therefore, being annoyed at the matter and being at a loss as to what device they should find for the turning away of the present evils, deliberated and decided that it was best to send to Ammon and ask him, they say, to find out for what reason the gods give victory to the Lacedaemonians rather than to themselves: "we who (they said) perform the most and most beautiful sacrifices of the Greeks, and have adorned their temples with offerings as no others have, and gave the most expensive and most solemn processions to the gods every year, and paid as much money as all the other Greeks together." But for the Lacedaemonians (they said), they never cared for any...

<summary>Socrates explains that specialized knowledge is dangerous without the "science of the best" and uses Homer's Margites to show how poets hide truths in riddles. He contrasts the Athenians' expensive, failing religious rituals with the Spartans' simple, wise prayers for "noble and good things."</summary>

### ALCIBIADES II.

<margin>A</margin> ...the Spartans have no such care for these things; they are so negligent toward the gods that they sacrifice mutilated animals, and in all other ceremonies they are far more frugal than the Athenians, even though their wealth is not surpassed by ours. After the messengers had said these things, and asked in what way they might find a release from their present calamities, the prophet replied with nothing else (for the god, clearly, would not permit it), but calling the Athenian legate, he spoke in this manner: "Thus says Ammon: he says he prefers the **pious prayer** <note>original Greek: *euphemia*; Latin: *acclamationem*. In this context, it refers to the simple, traditional prayer used by the Spartans</note> of the Lacedæmonians more than all the combined rituals of the Greeks." Having said this much, he spoke no further. It seems to me that by "pious prayer," the god means nothing other than their actual prayer. For in truth, it differs greatly from others. For while the other Greeks—some bringing bulls with gilded horns, <margin>B</margin> others decorating temples with magnificent offerings—ask the gods for whatever occurs to them, whether it be good or bad. Therefore, when the gods hear them uttering such ill-omened things, they do not accept these costly processions and sacrifices. But it seems to me that great caution and reflection are needed as to what should be said and what should not. You will find similar things said in **Homer**. For he says that the Trojans, when they were building their camp, offered to the immortals perfect sacrifices of a hundred bulls; and the winds carried the sweet smell from the plain
---
up to heaven. But the blessed gods did not <margin>C</margin> <margin>Iliad 8</margin> partake of it, nor did they wish to. For sacred Ilion was deeply hated by them, as was Priam, and the people of Priam of the good ashen spear. Thus, it profited them nothing to sacrifice and offer gifts in vain, since they were hated by the gods. For I believe the nature of the gods is not such that they are won over by gifts, like a **corrupt moneylender** <term>moneylender: the original Latin *foenerator* implies someone who takes interest; Socrates is suggesting the gods cannot be "bought" or "bribed" with interest-bearing gifts</term>. Indeed, we speak foolishly if we think we are more acceptable to the god than the Lacedæmonians because of our gifts. For it would be a terrible thing if the gods looked to our gifts and sacrifices rather than to the soul, to see if a person happens to be holy and just. I believe they pay much more <margin>Justice and prudence are honored among gods and men</margin> attention to the soul than to these costly processions and sacrifices, <margin>D</margin> which nothing prevents a man—or a city—from performing every year, even if they have committed many sins against gods and men. But the gods, being incorruptible by gifts, despise all these things, as the god and his prophet have said. It is likely, then, that both among gods and among men of sound mind, **justice** and **prudence** are honored above all else. And those who are prudent and just are <margin>Who are the prudent and just</margin> none other than those who know what they ought to do and say toward both gods and men. I would like to hear from you, then, what your own thoughts are on these matters.

**ALCIBIADES:** To me, O Socrates, it seems no different than it does to you and to the god; for it would not be fitting for me to cast a vote against the god.

**SOCRATES:** Do you remember, then, saying that you were in great doubt, lest you should <margin>E</margin> unknowingly pray for evils while thinking they were goods?

**ALCIBIADES:** I do.

**SOCRATES:** Do you see, then, that it is not safe for you to go to pray to the god, lest he hear you uttering such things and reject your sacrifice? You might even chance upon some other misfortune. It seems best to me, therefore, to keep quiet. For I do not think you would wish to use the prayer of the Lacedæmonians because of your **magnanimity** <margin>Magnanimity is a most honorable name for folly</margin> <note>Socrates is being ironic here; "magnanimity" or "greatness of soul" is used as a polite euphemism for the pride or lack of sense that prevents Alcibiades from being humble</note>. It is necessary, therefore, to wait until one learns how he ought to behave toward gods and men.

**ALCIBIADES:** When will that time come, O Socrates, and who is the teacher? For I would most gladly see who this man is.

**SOCRATES:** It is he who cares for you. But it seems to me that, just as Homer says **Athena** removed the <margin>F</margin> **mist** from the eyes of **Diomedes**, "so that he might well discern both god and man," so too must the mist first be removed from your soul which now happens to be over it; then, after that, the means should be applied by which you will discern both good and evil. For now, it does not seem to me that you are able.

**ALCIBIADES:** Let him remove the mist, whether he wishes to or something else. For I am prepared to skip nothing that is commanded by him, whoever that man may be, provided I am to become better.

**SOCRATES:** Indeed, he has a wonderful eagerness for your benefit.

**ALCIBIADES:** It seems best to me, then, to postpone the sacrifice until that time.

**SOCRATES:** <margin>G</margin> And you are right to think so. For it is safer than to run such a great risk.

**ALCIBIADES:** So be it, Socrates. However, since you seem to have advised me well, I will place this **garland** upon you; and we shall give to the gods both garlands and all other customary things when I see that day has arrived. And it will arrive soon, if the gods are willing.

**SOCRATES:** I accept this, and I would gladly see myself receiving anything else given by you. Just as **Creon** in **Euripides**, seeing **Tiresias** wearing garlands and hearing that he had received them from the soldiers as the first-fruits of his skill, said: "I take as an omen your victorious <margin>H</margin> crowns." For we are in a storm, as you know; and so I take this honor from you as an omen. For I seem to myself to be tossed in no less a storm than Creon, and I would wish to come off victorious over all your other lovers.

<meta>This page transitions from the end of the "Second Alcibiades," where Socrates discussed the nature of prayer and sacrifice, to the beginning of the "Minos." # MINOS, OR ON THE LAW.
# MINOS, OR, ON LAW.

->SUMMARY OF THE DIALOGUE. A brief discussion on what law is, its origin, its use, and its purpose: so that this dialogue appears to have been established by Plato as a sort of introduction to his books on the Republic. It is inscribed with the name of Minos so that the august memory of that most venerable legislator might be invoked; although the philosopher does not bring him in here as a speaker, but rather a certain namesake <note>The dialogue is technically between Socrates and an anonymous "Companion," though some traditions identify the interlocutor as Minos himself.</note>: yet by the use of the name alone, he wished to provide authority for the first principles of this most sacred doctrine.<-

->SOCRATES, MINOS.<-

<margin>
When we are asked a general question, it is incorrect to respond regarding only a specific part or instance.
</margin>

What exactly is law, in our view? MINOS. About which law are you asking? SOCRATES. Is there anything by which one law differs from another, insofar as it is a law? Pay close attention to what I am asking. I am asking in the same way as if I were to say, "What is gold?" and if you were to ask in return what kind of gold I was asking about, I would judge your inquiry to be incorrect. For gold does not differ from gold insofar as it is gold, nor does a stone differ from a stone insofar as it is a stone. In the same way, one law does not differ from another, but they are all the same thing. For each of them is a law in the same way, not one more and another less. Therefore, I am asking about this very thing in its entirety: what is law, in a general sense? If you have the answer ready, please explain.

<margin>
A definition derived by analogy.
</margin>

MINOS. And what else would law be, Socrates, other than things traditionally accepted and approved <note>original: "lege recepta & approbata"; Greek: "ta nomizomena." This refers to customs or established practices.</note>? SOCRATES. Does speech seem to you to be the things that are spoken, or sight the things that are seen, or hearing the things that are heard? Or is speech one thing and the words spoken another; sight one thing and the things seen another; and hearing one thing and the things heard another? And likewise, is law one thing, and the things traditionally accepted another? Does it seem so to you, or otherwise? MINOS. It seems so now. SOCRATES. Therefore, law is not simply "things traditionally accepted." MINOS. It does not seem so. SOCRATES. What then might law be? Let us consider it in this way. If someone were to ask us about what we just said: "Since you say that things seen are perceived by sight, what is sight by which they are perceived?" we would answer that it is the sense which, through the eyes, reveals colors to us. And if asked about hearing, we would say it is the sense which, through the ears, receives sound. In the same way, if he asks: "Since things accepted are established by law, what is the law by which they are accepted? Is it a kind of sense, or a revelation, just as things learned are grasped by the revelation of knowledge, and things found are shown by discovery—just as healthy and harmful things are shown by medicine, while the things the gods intend, as the prophets say, are known through the faculty of divination?"

<margin>
What prophecy is.
</margin>

For prophecy is the discovery of such things, is it not? MINOS. Entirely so. SOCRATES. Which of these do we most strongly presume law to be? Is it those institutes and decrees? MINOS. It seems so to me. For what else would anyone say law is? From this it appears that the whole thing you were asking about—the law of the city—is an established decree. SOCRATES. You call the opinion of the city "law"? MINOS. Indeed. SOCRATES. And perhaps you speak correctly; but perhaps we will understand it better in this way. Do you call some people wise? MINOS. I do. SOCRATES. And are not the wise wise by wisdom? MINOS. Yes. SOCRATES. And are the just just by justice? MINOS. Entirely. SOCRATES. Therefore, the law-abiding are law-abiding by law? MINOS. Certainly. SOCRATES. And the lawless are lawless by lawlessness? MINOS. Indeed. SOCRATES. And the law-abiding are just? MINOS. Yes. SOCRATES. And the lawless are unjust? MINOS. Unjust. SOCRATES. Is not law and justice something most beautiful? MINOS. It is so. SOCRATES. And is not injustice and lawlessness most foul? MINOS. Most foul. SOCRATES. And the former preserves cities and all other things, while the latter ruins and destroys them? MINOS. Yes. SOCRATES. Therefore, one must think of law as something beautiful, and seek it as something good. MINOS. Why not? SOCRATES. And did we not say that law is a decree of the city? MINOS. We did. SOCRATES. And are there not some good decrees, and some bad ones? MINOS. There certainly are. SOCRATES. But law was not something bad. MINOS. Certainly not. SOCRATES. Therefore, it is not correct to assert so simply that law is the decree of the city. MINOS. It does not seem so to me at all. SOCRATES. For it is not fitting for an unjust constitution to be law. MINOS. No.

<margin>
Another false definition of law, and its refutation.
</margin>

<margin>
Law is a certain opinion.
</margin>

SOCRATES. Nevertheless, law seems to me also to be a kind of opinion; and since it is not a wicked opinion, is it not clear that, if it is an opinion, it must be a worthy opinion? MINOS. It is established. SOCRATES. And a worthy opinion—is it not a true opinion? MINOS. It is. SOCRATES. And true opinion is the discovery of reality <note>original: "veritatis inuentio"; Greek: "tou ontos exeuresis," literally "the discovery of that which is."</note>. MINOS. Certainly. SOCRATES. Law, therefore, is the discovery of reality. MINOS. If law is the discovery of reality, how is it, Socrates, that we do not always use the same laws regarding the same things, if reality has been discovered? SOCRATES. Law nonetheless wishes to be the discovery of reality. But if men do not use the same laws, as it seems, it is because they are not always able to find that reality which the law seeks. But come, let us see if it might become clearer to us from this point, whether we always live by the same laws or different ones at different times, and whether all men use the same ones or some use one kind and others another. MINOS. Truly, Socrates, that is not difficult to know: that neither do the same people always use the same laws, nor do different people always use the same ones. For instance, it is not a law for us to sacrifice human victims; rather, it is an unholy act.

<margin>
Among the Carthaginians, it is legal to sacrifice sons.
</margin>

But among the Carthaginians, that is considered a holy and legal practice, so much so that some of them sacrifice their sons to Saturn <note>Greek text: "Krono" (Cronus).</note>, as you perhaps have heard. And not only barbarians...

<column-break/>

->SOCRATES, MINOS.<-

What is <term>Law</term> <note>original: *Nomos*</note> to us? MINOS. Of what kind of law are you asking? SOCRATES. What? Is there anything in which law differs from law in this very respect, in being law? Consider what I happen to be asking you. For I ask just as if I had asked what is gold; if you had asked me in the same way what kind of gold I meant, I think you would not have asked correctly. For surely gold does not differ from gold, nor stone from stone, at least in being stone and in being gold. In this way, neither does law differ at all from law, but all are the same. For each of them is a law equally; not one more so and another less. This is the very thing I ask: what is law as a whole, if it is easy for you to say? MINOS. What else could law be, Socrates, but the things traditionally practiced? SOCRATES. Does speech also seem to you to be the things spoken, or sight the things seen, or hearing the things heard? Or is speech one thing and the things spoken another? And sight one thing and the things seen another? And hearing one thing and the things heard another? And so is law one thing, and the things traditionally practiced another? Is it this way, or how does it seem to you? MINOS. It appeared differently to me just now. SOCRATES. Therefore, law is not the things traditionally practiced. MINOS. It does not seem so to me. SOCRATES. What then might law be? Let us examine it thus. If someone asked us what we were just saying: "Since you say that things seen are seen by sight, by what thing, being sight, are they seen?" we would answer him that it is by this sense which through the eyes shows us colors. And if he asked again, "By what thing, being hearing, are things heard?" we would answer him that it is by the sense through the ears that shows us sounds. Thus then, if he should ask us, "Since traditionally practiced things are practiced by law, by what thing, being law, are they practiced? Is it by some sensation or revelation? Just as things learned are learned by knowledge revealing them, or by some discovery? Just as things found are found: for instance, healthy and diseased things by medicine; and what the gods think, as the prophets say, by prophecy. For surely prophecy is for us the art of the discovery of things. Is it not?" MINOS. Certainly. SOCRATES. Which of these then should we suppose law to be most of all? MINOS. These dogmas and decrees, it seems to me. For what else could one say law is? So it turns out that the thing you ask about—this whole thing called law—is the opinion of the city. SOCRATES. You call law, it seems, political opinion. MINOS. I do. SOCRATES. And perhaps you speak well; but perhaps we will know better this way. Do you call some people wise? MINOS. I do. SOCRATES. Are not the wise wise by wisdom? MINOS. Yes. SOCRATES. And what of the just? Are they just by justice? MINOS. Certainly. SOCRATES. Therefore, are the law-abiding law-abiding by law? MINOS. Yes. SOCRATES. And the lawless lawless by lawlessness? MINOS. Yes. SOCRATES. And the law-abiding are just? MINOS. Yes. SOCRATES. And the lawless are unjust? MINOS. Unjust. SOCRATES. Is not both justice and law a most beautiful thing? MINOS. It is. SOCRATES. And injustice and lawlessness most foul? MINOS. Yes. SOCRATES. And the one saves cities and all other things, while the other destroys and overturns them? MINOS. Yes. SOCRATES. So one must think of law as being something beautiful, and seek it as a good. MINOS. How could one not? SOCRATES. And did we not say that law is the decree of the city? MINOS. We said so. SOCRATES. What then? Are there not some good decrees, and some wicked? MINOS. There are. SOCRATES. And yet law was not wicked. MINOS. No. SOCRATES. Therefore, it is not correct to answer so simply that law is the decree of the city. MINOS. It does not seem so to me. SOCRATES. Then a wicked decree would not fit being a law. MINOS. Certainly not. SOCRATES. But indeed, law appears to me also to be a certain opinion; and since it is not the wicked opinion, is it not already clear that it is the worthy one, if indeed opinion is law? MINOS. Yes. SOCRATES. And what is a worthy opinion? Is it not the true one? MINOS. Yes. SOCRATES. Is not true opinion the discovery of reality? MINOS. It is. SOCRATES. Law, then, is the discovery of reality. MINOS. How then, Socrates, if law is the discovery of reality, do we not always use the same laws concerning the same things, if reality has been discovered by us? SOCRATES. Law wishes to be the discovery of reality no less; but if men do not always use the same laws, as it seems, they are not always able to find out that which law wishes: reality. Come then, let us see if it might become clear to us from here whether we always use the same laws, or different ones at different times; and if everyone uses the same, or different people use different ones. MINOS. But this, Socrates, is not hard to know: that neither do the same people always use the same laws, nor do different people always use the same. For instance, with us it is not the law to sacrifice humans, but it is unholy; yet the Carthaginians sacrifice them, as it is holy and legal for them; and some of them sacrifice to Cronus, as perhaps you have heard. And not only barbarians...

<summary>Socrates and an anonymous companion (referred to as Minos) attempt to define the essence of law, moving from the idea that law is merely "custom" or "city decrees" to the philosophical conclusion that true law is the "discovery of reality." They address the paradox of why laws vary across cultures, such as the Carthaginian practice of human sacrifice, if law is meant to be a universal truth.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from the previous page, shifting from the abstract definition of law to the observation that human customs and legal practices appear to vary wildly across different cultures and eras, which the companion uses to challenge Socrates’ search for a single, universal definition of Law.</meta>

# MINOS.

But people follow different laws than we do, and even those who live in Lycia—these successors of Athamas—what kind of sacrifices do they offer, even though they are Greeks? You have also heard what kind of laws we ourselves used to follow regarding funeral rites <note>original: "circa inferias"</note>, slaughtering victims before the corpse was carried out, and summoning professional mourners <note>original: "praeficas". These were women hired to weep and sing dirges at funerals.</note>. <margin>Ancient ceremonies regarding the dead.</margin> And those even older than these people used to bury the dead right inside the house; yet we do none of these things today. One could mention countless examples of this kind. For there is a very wide field for demonstrating that neither do we always live by the same laws as ourselves, nor do different peoples live by the same laws as one another.

SOCRATES: It is no wonder, my excellent friend, if you are speaking correctly and this has escaped my notice. But as long as you state what you think in a long speech by yourself, and then I do the same in turn, we shall never, I think, reach an agreement. But if a common inquiry is proposed, perhaps we might agree. So, if you wish, examine this together with me by questioning me; or if you prefer to answer, then answer.

MINOS: I am certainly willing, Socrates, to answer whatever you like.

SOCRATES: Come then, do you think that just things are unjust, and unjust things just? Or rather that just things are just, and unjust things are indeed unjust?

MINOS: For my part, I think just things are just, and unjust things are unjust.

SOCRATES: And is it not thought so everywhere, just as it is here?

MINOS: Yes.

SOCRATES: And among the Persians too?

MINOS: Among the Persians too.

SOCRATES: And always, I suppose?

MINOS: Always.

SOCRATES: Are those things that weigh more considered heavier here, and those that weigh less, lighter? Or is it the opposite?

MINOS: No, rather those that weigh more are heavier, and those that weigh less are lighter.

SOCRATES: Is this also the case in Lycia and in Carthage?

MINOS: Yes.

SOCRATES: Beautiful things, it seems, are thought beautiful everywhere, and shameful things, shameful; but beautiful things are not thought shameful, nor shameful things beautiful.

MINOS: That is so.

SOCRATES: Then, to speak generally, things that *are* real are thought to exist, and things that are *not* real are not thought to exist, both among us and among all other people?

MINOS: So it seems to me.

SOCRATES: Therefore, whoever misses what is real, misses what is legal <note>The Greek "nomimon" and Latin "legitimum" refer to that which is in accordance with law or custom.</note>.

MINOS: According to your reasoning, Socrates, these same legal things appear to be the same always, both among us and among everyone else. But when I notice that we never stop changing our laws up and down every day, I cannot be convinced by you.

SOCRATES: Perhaps you do not perceive that while these things are shifted around, they remain the same. But look at it this way with me: have you ever come across a book about the healing of the sick?

MINOS: I have.

SOCRATES: Do you know to what art that book belongs?

MINOS: I know it belongs to medicine.

SOCRATES: Do you call those who are experts in these matters "doctors"?

MINOS: I do.

SOCRATES: Do those who know these things hold the same views about the same subjects, or do different people hold different views?

MINOS: They seem to hold the same views.

SOCRATES: Do Greeks alone agree with Greeks, or do the Barbarians <note>In this context, "Barbarians" refers to any non-Greek speakers, such as Persians or Egyptians.</note> also agree with themselves and with the Greeks about the things they know?

MINOS: It is absolutely necessary that those who know—both Greeks and Barbarians—agree with one another.

SOCRATES: You have answered well. And is this not always the case?

MINOS: Yes, always.

SOCRATES: And do not doctors write about health the very things they believe to be true?

MINOS: Certainly.

SOCRATES: Therefore, these writings of the medical art are medical laws.

MINOS: They are indeed.

SOCRATES: And are the writings on geometry the laws of the geometricians?

MINOS: Yes, certainly. <margin>All instructions of the arts are laws.</margin>

SOCRATES: Whose, then, are the writings and regulations regarding the cultivation of gardens?

MINOS: The gardeners'.

SOCRATES: These, then, are the gardening laws.

MINOS: Yes.

SOCRATES: Belonging to those who know how to manage a garden?

MINOS: Of course.

SOCRATES: And the gardeners are the ones who know.

MINOS: Indeed.

SOCRATES: And whose are the writings and regulations regarding the seasoning of food?

MINOS: The cooks'.

SOCRATES: These, then, are the laws of cooks.

MINOS: They are.

SOCRATES: Belonging, it seems, to those who know how to manage the preparation of food.

MINOS: Undoubtedly.

SOCRATES: And the cooks, they say, are the ones who know.

MINOS: They know.

SOCRATES: Very well. Now then, whose are the writings and regulations regarding the governance of a city? Are they not the work of those who are skilled in administering the state?

MINOS: It seems so.

SOCRATES: Does anyone else know this besides the statesmen and the royal men?

MINOS: Only them.

SOCRATES: These, therefore, are the political writings, which people call the decrees of kings and of good men.

MINOS: You speak the truth.

SOCRATES: Those who know do not establish different rules about the same things at different times.

MINOS: Certainly not.

SOCRATES: Therefore, the regulations do not change from one to another.

MINOS: Not at all.

SOCRATES: If we see some people disagreeing or changing them, shall we say they know, or are they ignorant?

MINOS: They are ignorant.

SOCRATES: And whatever is correct in each case, shall we call that the "legal" rule for each: for instance, that which is according to the reasoning of the doctor, or the cook, or the gardener?

MINOS: Without a doubt.

SOCRATES: But on the other hand, whatever is not correct, we shall no longer call "legal."

MINOS: No longer.

SOCRATES: So it becomes lawless.

MINOS: It must.

SOCRATES: Therefore, in the regulations concerning just and unjust things, and generally concerning the order of the city and the manner of governance, <margin>What a royal law is.</margin> whatever is correct is the "royal law"; but what is not correct is not a royal law, because it lacks knowledge, and it is seen to be lawless.

MINOS: That is so.

SOCRATES: We were right, then, to agree <margin>Law is the discovery of truth.</margin> that law is the discovery of truth.

MINOS: It appears so.

SOCRATES: Let us also consider this further: who is the expert who knows how to distribute the appropriate seeds to each kind of soil?

MINOS: The farmer.

SOCRATES: And does he distribute the seeds worthy of each soil?

<summary>Socrates argues that while human customs change, the "Law" itself must be rooted in universal truth and expert knowledge, just as medicine and gardening have fixed principles that experts agree upon. He concludes that true law is the "discovery of reality," and any incorrect decree is not a law at all, but lawlessness.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue where Socrates and his companion (labeled here as Minos) shift from discussing the general nature of law to identifying who the most ancient and divine lawmakers were. Socrates is steering the conversation toward the legendary King Minos of Crete to challenge the companion’s negative perception of him.</meta>

# PLATO

**A** MINOS: Certainly. SOCRATES: The farmer, then, is a good lawmaker in those matters, and his laws and distributions regarding them are correct. MI: True. SOCR.: Who is the good establisher of laws regarding the rhythms of music, and who distributes what is fitting according to merit, and whose laws are correct? MI: The flute-players and the lyre-players do these things. SOCR.: He who is most law-abiding in these matters, therefore, is the most skilled flute-player. MIN.: So it is. SOCR.: Who can best adapt nourishment to human bodies? Is it not he who knows how to apply what is suitable to each? MIN.: He himself. SOCR.: His partitions and instructions are the best; and whoever is most law-abiding regarding these things is the best creator of laws. MIN.: Exactly. SOCR.: And who is that? MI: The physical trainer <note>original: "Paedotriba", a teacher of gymnastics and physical excellence.</note>. SOCR.: He knows best how to shepherd the flock of the human body. MIN.: Certainly.

**B** SOCR.: But for him who knows how to shepherd a flock of cattle, what is his name? MIN.: A shepherd. SOCR.: Therefore, the shepherd’s laws are best for the sheep. MI: Best indeed. SOCR.: And the cowherd’s for the oxen. MIN.: Yes. SOCR.: But whose laws <margin>The King’s laws are best for the souls of men.</margin> are best for the souls of men? Are they not the King’s? MIN.: The King’s. SOCR.: You speak well. But can you say which of the men of old <margin>Marsyas was the first to impose laws on the playing of flutes.</margin> was the best creator of laws concerning the blowing of flutes? Perhaps you do not remember; do you wish me to remind you? MIN.: Very much so. SOCR.: It was Marsyas, and the one he loved most, Olympus the Phrygian. MI: You speak the truth.

**C** SOCR.: Indeed, the flute-melodies of these men are most divine, and they alone stir the listeners; they especially reveal those who are in need of the gods, and they alone have endured to this day as being divine. MI: These things are true. SOCR.: But who among the ancient <margin>Who were the first creators of laws among the Greeks.</margin> kings is said to have been the best creator of laws, whose institutions still remain as if divine? MIN.: I do not remember at all. SOCR.: Do you not know which of the Greek nations use the most ancient laws? MIN.: Perhaps you mean the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans.</note> and Lycurgus, the law-giver of the Lacedaemonians. SOCR.: But these institutions have perhaps not yet completed three hundred years, or only a little more. But do you know where the best of those laws came from? MI: They say from Crete.

**D** SOCR.: These people, then, of all the Greeks, live by the most ancient laws. MIN.: True. SOCR.: Do you know who were <margin>Regarding Rhadamanthus and Minos.</margin> the most excellent kings among them? Minos, of course, and Rhadamanthus, the sons of Jupiter <note>original: "Iouis" (Zeus).</note> and Europa, to whom these laws belong. MIN.: They say, Socrates, that Rhadamanthus was a just man, but that Minos was savage, harsh, and unjust. SOCR.: You are repeating, my good friend, an Attic and tragic myth <note>Socrates suggests the negative view of Minos comes from Athenian playwrights who resented him as a historical enemy.</note>. MIN.: Is this not what is said about Minos? SOCR.: Yet Homer and Hesiod do not testify to such things, although they are far more trustworthy witnesses than all the tragic poets, on whose testimony you speak. MIN.: And what do they say about Minos? SOCR.: I will tell you, lest you, like many others, speak impiously. For nothing is more impious than this.

**E** For first, we must take care lest we ever sin against God, either in word or <margin>Care must be taken both in praising and in accusing.</margin> deed; and second, lest we sin against divine men. Indeed, it is fitting to take great care whenever you are about to praise or blame any man, lest you err. For the sake of this, we must primarily strive to distinguish good and bad men. For God is exceedingly indignant whenever someone disapproves of one who is like Himself, or approves of one who is unlike Himself. But the good man is <margin>The good man is like God.</margin> like God. You should not think that stones and wood, birds and serpents are sacred, but men are not. On the contrary, <margin>A good man is the most sacred thing.</margin> the most sacred of all things is a good man, and the most profane is a bad man.

**F** And now I shall relate how Homer and Hesiod extol Minos himself, for this reason: so that you, being a man born of man, may no longer speak wrongly against a hero who is the son of Jupiter. For when Homer mentions Crete <margin>Crete of the ninety cities.</margin>, saying that it was very populous and had ninety cities in it, he says, "Among these is Knossos, a great city, where Minos reigned, for nine years the companion of great Jupiter." This praise of Minos in Homer's words is so explicit that he never extolled any of the heroes with equal praise.

**G** For <margin>Jupiter the teacher <note>original: "sophista". In this context, it refers to a master of wisdom or a teacher rather than a deceiver.</note>.</margin> that Jupiter is a teacher, and that this art is most noble, he reveals very clearly in many other places and especially here. For he says that Minos conversed with Jupiter for nine years, and was accustomed to go to him for the sake of instruction, as if Jupiter were a teacher. That Homer attributed such a great gift—that is, to have been educated by Jupiter—to no other hero, must be considered a wondrous praise. Furthermore, in the *Odyssey*, where he describes the funeral rites, he introduced Minos judging the souls of the dead, holding a golden scepter. But he does not introduce Rhadamanthus judging here or elsewhere, nor conversing with Jupiter. Therefore, I assert that Minos was honored by Homer above all others. For even though he is a son of Jupiter, the fact that he was educated by him alone carries great praise. Indeed, that verse signifies this: "Minos reigned for nine years, accustomed to converse with great Jupiter." That is, Minos met with Jupiter for nine years in conversation. For <gloss>talks</gloss> <note>original Greek: "ὀαροι"</note> are conversations, and a <gloss>companion</gloss> <note>original Greek: "ὀαριστής"</note> is one who meets in conversation. Thus, every nine years Minos went to the cave of Jupiter to be educated. From there he both learned and then taught others what he had received from Jupiter in those nine years. Yet there are some who explain <gloss>companion</gloss> <note>original Greek: "ὀαριστὴν"</note> otherwise, as a drinking companion, a reveller, or a playmate of Jupiter.

**H** But we can gather that those people do not explain it correctly from this fact: that no one, whether Greek or Barbarian, abstains from symposia—that is, drinking parties—and

<column-break/>

**A** MIN.: Yes. SOCR.: The farmer, then, is a good shepherd of these; and his laws and distributions for these are correct. MIN.: Yes. SOCR.: And who is a good shepherd for striking the rhythms of songs, and for distributing what is worthy? And what laws are correct? MI: Those of the flute-players and the lyre-players. SOCR.: He who is most law-abiding in these things, therefore, is the most skilled flute-player. MI: Yes. SOCR.: Who is best at distributing nourishment to the bodies of men, so they are healthier according to their merit? MI: Yes. SOCR.: His distributions and laws are therefore best; and whoever is most law-abiding in these matters is the best shepherd. MIN.: Certainly. SOCR.: Who is he? MI: The physical trainer. SOCR.: Is he the best at shepherding the bodies of the human flocks? MI: Yes.

**B** SOCR.: And who is the best at shepherding the flocks of the soul? What is his name? MI: A shepherd. SOCR.: The laws of the shepherd are best for the sheep. MIN.: Yes. SOCR.: And those of the cowherd for the cattle. MI: Yes. SOCR.: And whose laws are best for the souls of men? Are they not those of the king? MI: I say so. SOCR.: You speak well then. Can you say, therefore, which of the ancients became a good lawmaker in the laws of flute-playing? Perhaps you do not have it in mind; but do you wish for me to remind you? MI: Certainly. SOCR.: Is it not said to be Marsyas, and his beloved, Olympus the Phrygian? MI: You speak the truth.

**C** SOCR.: The flute-melodies of these men are indeed most divine, and they alone move and reveal those who are in need of the gods; and even now they alone remain, as being divine. MI: That is so. SOCR.: And who of the ancient kings is said to have been a good lawmaker, whose legal customs remain even now as being divine? MI: I do not have it in mind. SOCR.: Do you not know which of the Greeks use the most ancient laws? MI: Perhaps you mean the Lacedaemonians, and Lycurgus the lawmaker? SOCR.: But these things are perhaps not even three hundred years old, or only a little more than that. But do you know where the best of these legal customs come from? MI: They say from Crete.

**D** SOCR.: Do they not then use the most ancient laws of the Greeks? MI: Yes. SOCR.: Do you know then which of these were good kings? Minos and Rhadamanthus, the sons of Zeus and Europa, to whom these laws belong. MI: They say, Socrates, that Rhadamanthus was a just man; but Minos was someone savage, harsh, and unjust. SOCR.: You are telling, my friend, an Attic and tragic myth. MI: But is this not what is said about Minos? SOCR.: Not by Homer and Hesiod, at any rate; and yet they are more persuasive than all the tragic poets together, whom you listen to when you say these things. MI: But what then do they say about Minos? SOCR.: I will tell you; so that you, like the many, do not act impiously. For there is nothing more impious than this, nor is there anything one should more

**E** carefully guard against, than sinning against the gods both in word and deed; and secondly, against divine men. But one must always take very great forethought, whenever you are about to blame or praise a man, that you do not speak incorrectly. For this reason, one must learn to distinguish good and bad men. For God is indignant when someone blames his like, or praises one who is the opposite. And this is the good man. For do not think that stones are sacred, and wood, and birds, and snakes; but men are not. Rather, the most sacred of all is the good man; and the most defiled is the wicked one.

**F** So now, regarding Minos, both Homer and Hesiod praise him. For this reason I will speak, so that you, being a man, do not sin in speech against a hero, the son of Zeus. For Homer, speaking about Crete, says that there are many people in it, and ninety cities: "Among them (he says) is Knossos, a great city, where Minos reigned for nine years, the companion of great Zeus." This is Homer's praise for Minos, spoken briefly, such as Homer did for not even one of the heroes. For that Zeus is a teacher <note>original: "sophistēs"</note>, and that this art is all-beautiful, he shows in many other places, but also here. For he says that Minos associated with Zeus in the ninth year in words; and went to be educated as if by Zeus being a teacher.

**G** That Homer does not assign this privilege to any other of the heroes, to be educated by Zeus, but only to him—this is a wondrous praise. And in the *Odyssey* in the Book of the Dead, he made Minos judging, having a golden scepter. He did not make Rhadamanthus judging there, nor associating with Zeus anywhere. For these reasons I say that Minos is praised by Homer most of all. For being the son of Zeus, and being educated only by Zeus, has no excess of praise. For this the verse signifies: "He reigned for nine years, the companion of great Zeus," that Minos was an associate of Zeus. For "oaroi" are words; and "oaristēs" is an associate in words. Minos therefore went every ninth year into the cave of Zeus, partly to learn, and partly to show what he had learned from Zeus in the previous nine-year period.

**H** And there are some who understand "oaristēs" to be a drinking companion and a playmate of Zeus. But one might use this as a proof that those who understand it this way do not speak well. For though there are many people, both Greeks and barbarians, there are none who abstain from drinking-

<summary>Socrates defends the character of King Minos of Crete, arguing that he was a divine lawmaker educated directly by Zeus, contrary to the negative "tragic myths" presented by Athenian playwrights. He emphasizes the importance of correctly identifying and honoring good men as they are the most sacred of beings.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue of the Minos, where Socrates is rehabilitating the reputation of the legendary King Minos of Crete as a divine lawmaker, contrasting the Cretan and Spartan customs with those of other Greeks.</meta>

# ALCIBIADES II <note>Note: Though the header reads "Alcibiades II," the text on this page is actually the conclusion of the "Minos" and the beginning of the "Euthyphro."</note>

**A** From such games <note>Referring to the drinking parties mentioned previously.</note> they abstain, except for the Cretans and the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans.</note>, who learned from the Cretans. In Crete, moreover, among the other laws of Minos himself, this one stands out: *Do not drink with one another to the point of intoxication.* It is clear that he commanded his citizens to observe what he himself judged to be honorable; for Minos was not like a base man who would do one thing himself while commanding others to do another. Rather, that gathering was, as I said, a conversation for the sake of education through words. For this reason, he established such laws for his citizens, through the observation of which Crete has been happy through all time, as has Lacedaemon <note>Sparta</note>, from the moment it began to use these laws as if they were divine. Now, Rhadamanthus was indeed a good man, for he was instructed by Minos. 

<margin>Rhadamanthus was a skilled judge, not a lawmaker.</margin>

**B** However, he did not learn the entire royal art of education, but only how to serve the king in the courts of justice; hence he was called a "good judge." Minos used him specifically as a guardian of the laws throughout the city, but for the rest of Crete, he used Talos. For Talos would travel through all the villages three times a year to observe their laws, carrying the laws inscribed on bronze tablets; hence he was called "The Bronze One" <note>original Greek: "chalkous." In mythology, Talos was often depicted as a giant bronze automaton.</note>. Hesiod also spoke of things brotherly to these regarding Minos. For when he mentioned that name, he said: "He who surpassed mortal kings, and ruled over many neighboring peoples, holding the scepter of Zeus, by which he also ruled the cities." And he further says that the scepter of Zeus is nothing other than the education of Zeus, by which he guided all of Crete. 

**C** MINOS: Why then, Socrates, has this rumor spread among men that Minos was an uneducated and harsh man? SOCRATES: For the same reason that you, O best of men, and every other man who cares for a good reputation, must—if you are wise—be carefully on guard never to make an enemy of any poetic man. For poets have the greatest power over reputation, in whichever direction they choose to act upon men, whether by praising or by slandering. This is exactly where Minos went wrong: he waged war against this city <note>Athens</note>, which is filled not only with much other wisdom, but especially with poets of every kind, and particularly those of tragedy. For tragedy is very ancient here; it did not begin, as most people think, with Thespis or Phrynichus. 

<margin>Tragedy is a very ancient invention of Athens.</margin>

**D** But if you wish to investigate, you will find that tragedy is a much more ancient invention of this city. Of all poetry, tragedy is the most popular and the most soul-stirring; in it, we have attacked Minos, taking our revenge because he forced us to pay those famous tributes <note>A reference to the myth of the Minotaur, where Athens had to send youths to Crete as a blood-tax.</note>. In this, therefore, Minos erred by making us his enemies. From this, as you ask, it happened that he became ill-reputed. However, that he was a good man and a lawful one—as we said before, a "good shepherd"—is most strongly proven by the fact that his laws remain unchanged, as they were discovered through the true understanding of how to govern a city. 

**E** MINOS: You seem to me, Socrates, to have found a plausible explanation. SOCRATES: Therefore, if I speak the truth, do the ancient Cretans, the citizens of Minos and Rhadamanthus, seem to you to use the most ancient laws? MINOS: They certainly do. SOCRATES: These men, then, were the most excellent of all the ancient lawmakers, shepherds and herdsmen of men; just as Homer said that a good leader of an army is a "shepherd of the people." MINOS: Entirely so. SOCRATES: Come then, by Zeus the Friend, if someone were to ask us what a good lawmaker and shepherd of the body applies to the body to make it better, we would surely answer correctly and briefly: food and labor—by the one increasing it, and by the other exercising and strengthening the body. MINOS: Quite right. 

**F** SOCRATES: If he should then ask us: "What is it that the good lawmaker and shepherd of men applies to the soul to make it better?" What could we answer that would not make us ashamed of ourselves and our age? MINOS: I can no longer say. SOCRATES: But truly, it is a great shame for the soul of each of us to appear ignorant of those things within itself where good and evil reside, while appearing to have examined the things of the body and of others.

<column-break/>

### EUTHYPHRO, OR, ON
->HOLINESS.<-
->A Probing Dialogue.<-

**SUMMARY OF THE DIALOGUE.** A dispute concerning Holiness or Religion is established here, not so much to teach what the true kind is, but rather to refute the false. For Socrates brings forward and refutes the false opinions of men on this matter, even though he himself was being accused of violating religion. Meanwhile, he shows that religion itself is the true and solid foundation of both the entire life and human society. He demonstrates that the religion of the Pagans—that is, their opinions concerning divine worship—is not true and genuine religion, but a ridiculous impiety entirely foreign to the nature of God. Therefore, this is a refutation of false religion against all superstitious people, coming from the mouth of an Ethnic <note>A non-Christian or "Pagan" philosopher</note> man, who nevertheless himself did not know the true religion.

<vocab>Minos, Rhadamanthus, Talos, Socrates, Hesiod, Cretans, Lacedaemonians, Tragedy, Thespis, Phrynichus, Euthyphro, Holiness, Religion</vocab>

<summary>Socrates concludes the Minos by arguing that the king's poor reputation in Athens was due to the power of Athenian poets and tragic playwrights, rather than his laws, which were divine and enduring. The page then transitions into the Euthyphro, introducing a dialogue focused on defining true holiness against common superstitions.</summary>
