<meta>This page marks the transition from the end of the "Minos" (a dialogue about law) to the beginning of the "Euthyphro," one of Plato's most famous dialogues. The previous page concluded the discussion of King Minos of Crete as a divine lawmaker. This page introduces Socrates on the steps of the courthouse, facing the charges that will eventually lead to his execution.</meta>

# PLATO’S EUTHYPHRO: SOCRATES AND EUTHYPHRO

**A**
<margin>A</margin> What new thing has happened, Socrates, that you have left your accustomed haunts in the Lyceum <note>The Lyceum was a public gymnasium and grove where Socrates frequently engaged in philosophical discussion.</note> and are now spending your time here at the King’s Porch? <note>The *Stoa Basileios*, the office of the King Archon, who oversaw religious matters and legal indictments in Athens.</note> Surely you do not also have a lawsuit before the King, as I do? **SOCR.** The Athenians, Euthyphro, do not call this a civil suit, but a criminal indictment. <note>original Latin: *accusationem*; Greek: *graphe*. Socrates distinguishes between a private dispute (*dike*) and a public crime against the state.</note> **EUT.** What are you saying? Has someone brought an indictment against you? For I would never imagine that you would bring one against another. **SOC.** Certainly not. **EUT.** But has another brought one against you? **SOCR.** Precisely. **EUT.** Who is he? **SOCR.** I hardly know the man myself, Euthyphro. He appears to be young and unknown; but I believe they call him Meletus, of the Pitthean deme <note>A "deme" was a local subdivision or suburb of Athens.</note>—if <margin>B</margin> you happen to know a Meletus from Pittheus with straight, lanky hair, a hooked and prominent nose, and a thin beard. **EUT.** I do not recall him, Socrates. But what is the charge he has brought against you? **SOC.** What charge? One that seems to me no mean thing, and not the work of a base or humble mind. For it is no small matter for a young man to have gained knowledge of such a great thing. For he, as he says, understands how the youth are corrupted, and who it is that corrupts them. He seems to be a wise man, and having observed my ignorance—seeing how I lead his peers astray—he has run to the city as if to his mother <margin>C</margin> to accuse me. Indeed, he seems to me the only one who knows how to begin his political career correctly. For it is right to care for the young first, so that they might become as excellent as possible, just as a good farmer ought to care for the tender plants first, and then look after the others. And so Meletus, perhaps, is first weeding us out—those who, as he says, corrupt the sprouts of the youth. After this, it is clear that by caring for the elders, he will become the cause of many and great blessings for the city, as is likely to happen to one who has made such a beginning. **EUT.** I would hope so, Socrates, but I fear the opposite may happen. For <margin>D</margin> he seems to me to be attacking the city at its very heart <note>original Latin: *ab ipsa Vesta* (from Vesta herself); Greek: *aph' estias* (from the hearth). This refers to the sacred central fire of the city.</note> by attempting to do you wrong. Tell me, what does he say you are doing that infects the youth? **SOCR.** Absurd things to hear, my wonderful friend! For he says that I am a maker of gods; and on the grounds that I invent new gods and do not believe in the ancient ones, he has summoned me to court for these very reasons. **EUT.** I understand now, Socrates; it is because you say the "divine sign" <note>The *daimonion*, a private "inner voice" Socrates claimed warned him against certain actions.</note> is always with you. He has therefore written this indictment against you as one who is an innovator in divine matters, and he comes to the court to slander you, knowing that such things are easily misrepresented to the crowd. Even me, when I speak about divine matters in the assembly and predict the future, they laugh at as if I were a madman—though <margin>E</margin> I have never predicted anything that was not true. But they envy all of us who are like this. We must not worry about them, however, but go and face them. **SOCR.** My dear Euthyphro, being laughed at is perhaps of no importance. The Athenians, it seems to me, do not care much if they think someone is clever, provided he does not try to teach his wisdom to others. But if they think he is making others like himself, they become angry, whether out of envy, as you say, or for some other reason. **EUT.** As for that—how they are disposed toward me—I have <margin>F</margin> no great desire to find out. **SOC.** Perhaps it is because you seem to show yourself only rarely and are unwilling to spread your wisdom. But I fear that because of my love for humanity, I appear to them to pour out whatever I have too lavishly to every man—not only without payment, but even being willing to pay someone to listen to me. If, therefore, as I was saying, they were only going to laugh at me, as you say they do at you, it would not be at all unpleasant to pass the time in court with joking and laughter. But if they take the matter seriously, the outcome is uncertain, except to you prophets. **EUT.** Perhaps it will come to nothing, Socrates; you will likely fight your case with all your might, as I think <margin>G</margin> I shall fight mine. **SOC.** Do you also have a case? Are you the defendant, or the prosecutor? **EUT.** I am the prosecutor. **SOC.** Against whom? **EUT.** One whom I seem mad to pursue. **SOC.** Why? Is he perhaps someone with wings that you are "pursuing"? **EUT.** He is far from flying, for he is a very old man. **SOC.** Who is he? **EUT.** My father. **SOC.** Your own father, my good man? **EUT.** Precisely. **SOC.** What is the crime? What is the case? **EUT.** Homicide, Socrates. **SOC.** By Hercules! Surely, Euthyphro, the common people are ignorant of how this <margin>H</margin> could be right. For I do not think it is the work of just anyone to do this correctly, but of someone far advanced in wisdom. **EUT.** Far advanced indeed, by Jove! **S.** Was it one of your kinsmen who was killed by your father? Surely it must be? For you would not be prosecuting your father for homicide on behalf of a stranger. **EV.** It is ridiculous, Socrates, that you think it makes any difference whether the dead man was a stranger or a kinsman; one should only observe whether the killer acted justly or not. If he acted justly, let him be; but if not, one must prosecute him, especially if the killer lives under the same roof and eats at the same table. For the pollution is equal if you associate with such a man knowing of his crime, and do not purify both yourself and him by bringing him to justice. Now, the man who died was a laborer of mine; when we were farming in Naxos, he served us for wages. While stirred up by wine and anger against one of our household servants, he slaughtered him.

<margin>A</margin> What new thing has happened, Socrates, that you have left your accustomed haunts in the Lyceum and are now spending your time here at the King’s Porch? Surely you do not also have a lawsuit before the King, as I do. **SOCR.** The Athenians, Euthyphro, do not call this a civil suit, but a criminal indictment. **EU.** What are you saying? Has someone brought an indictment against you? For I would never imagine that you would bring one against another. **SO.** Certainly not. **EU.** But has another brought one against you? **SO.** Precisely. **EU.** Who is he? **SO.** I hardly know the man myself, Euthyphro. He appears to be young and unknown; but I believe they call him Meletus, of the Pitthean <margin>B</margin> deme—if you happen to know a Meletus from Pittheus with straight hair, a thin beard, and a hooked nose. **EU.** I do not recall him, Socrates. For he says that I am a maker of gods; and on the grounds that I invent new gods and do not believe in the ancient ones, he has summoned me to court for these very reasons. **EU.** I understand, Socrates; it is because you say the "divine sign" is with you. He has therefore written this indictment against you as one who is an innovator in divine matters, and he comes to the court to slander you, knowing that such things are easily misrepresented to the crowd. The Athenians, it seems to me, do not care much if they think someone is clever, provided he does not try to teach his wisdom to others. But if they think he is making others like himself, they become angry, whether out of envy, as you say, or for some other reason. **EU.** As for that—how they are disposed toward me—I have no great desire to find out. **SOCR.** Perhaps it is because you seem to show yourself only rarely and are unwilling to teach your wisdom. But I fear that because of my love for humanity, I appear to them to pour out whatever I have too lavishly to every <margin>F</margin> man—not only without payment, but even being willing to pay someone to listen to me. If, therefore, as I was saying, they were only going to laugh at me, as you say they do at you, it would not be at all unpleasant to pass the time in court with joking and laughter. But if they take the matter seriously, the outcome is uncertain, except to you prophets. **EU.** Perhaps it will come to nothing, Socrates; you will likely fight your case according to your mind, as I think I shall fight mine. **SO.** Do you also have a case? Are you the defendant, or the prosecutor? **EU.** I am the prosecutor. **SO.** Against whom? **EU.** One whom I seem mad to pursue. **SO.** Why? Is he perhaps someone with wings that you are pursuing? **EU.** He is far from <margin>G</margin> flying, for he is a very old man. **SO.** Who is he? **EU.** My father. **SO.** Your own father, my good man? **EU.** Precisely. **SO.** What is the crime? What is the case? **EU.** Homicide, Socrates. **SO.** By Hercules! Surely, Euthyphro, the common people are ignorant of how this could be right. For I do not think it is the work of just anyone to do this correctly, but of someone far advanced in wisdom. **EU.** Far advanced indeed, by Jove! **SO.** Was it one of your kinsmen who was killed by your father? Surely it must be? For you would not be prosecuting your father for homicide on behalf of a stranger. **EU.** It is ridiculous, Socrates, that you think it makes any difference whether the dead man was a stranger or a kinsman; one should only observe whether the killer acted justly or not. If he acted <margin>H</margin> justly, let him be; but if not, one must prosecute him, especially if the killer lives under the same roof and eats at the same table. For the pollution is equal if you associate with such a man knowing of his crime, and do not purify both yourself and him by bringing him to justice. Now, the man who died was a dependent of mine; when we were farming in Naxos, he served us for wages. While drunk and angry at one of our household servants, he slaughtered him.

<summary>This page begins the "Euthyphro," where Socrates meets a religious expert named Euthyphro at the court of the King Archon. Socrates explains the charges against him for impiety, while Euthyphro reveals he is prosecuting his own father for the death of a laborer, leading to a discussion on justice and religious duty.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Euthyphro outside the courtroom. Euthyphro has just explained that he is prosecuting his own father for the death of a laborer, a move that has shocked his family. Socrates, facing his own trial for "impiety," begins to question Euthyphro's absolute certainty about what is holy and what is not.</meta>

->### EUTHYPHRO.<-

<margin>A</margin> ...he died. <note>The text begins mid-sentence, describing the death of a laborer.</note> My father bound his feet and hands, threw him into a ditch, and sent a man here to inquire of the legal interpreter <note>original Greek: *exegetou*; an official responsible for interpreting religious law and ritual purification.</note> what ought to be done. In the meantime, he neglected and disregarded the captive as a murderer and a person of no consequence, even if he were to die—which is exactly what happened. For he perished from hunger, cold, and his bonds before the messenger returned from the interpreter. This is why my father and other relatives are indignant: because I am pursuing a murder charge against my father on behalf of a murderer. They claim he did not even kill him, and even if he had, since the deceased was a murderer, one should not concern oneself with such a person. They say it is impious <note>original Greek: *anosion*</note> for a son to prosecute his father for murder—knowing poorly, Socrates, how the divine stands regarding piety <note>original Greek: *hosios*</note> and impiety.

<margin>B</margin> **SOCRATES.** But by Zeus, Euthyphro, do you believe you understand divine things so accurately, and things both pious and impious, that when these events occurred as you describe, you are not afraid that by bringing your father to trial you might be committing an impious act yourself? **EUTHYPHRO.** I would be of no use, Socrates, nor would Euthyphro differ at all from the common run of men, if I did not have accurate knowledge of all such things.

<margin>C</margin> **SOCRATES.** Then, my admirable Euthyphro, it is best for me to become your student. Before the indictment by Meletus <note>Meletus was the primary accuser of Socrates.</note> proceeds, I should challenge him on these very points. I should say that in the past I have always placed a high value on knowing divine matters; and now, since he claims I have done wrong by acting on impulse and innovating regarding the gods, I have become your student. I would say: "Meletus, if you agree that Euthyphro is wise in such matters and holds the correct beliefs, then consider me to be correct as well and do not bring me to trial. But if you do not, then bring a suit against this teacher of mine before you sue me, on the grounds that he is corrupting the elderly—both me, by his teaching, and his own father, by his admonishment and punishment." And if he is not persuaded by me, and does not drop the suit or indict you instead of me, I would have to say these same things in court that I have proposed to him.

<margin>D</margin> **EUTHYPHRO.** Yes, by Zeus, Socrates! If he should attempt to indict me, I think I would find where he is weak, and he would be discussed in court long before I would. **SOCRATES.** And I, my dear friend, knowing this, desire to be your student. I know that while this Meletus does not even seem to notice you, he has seen through me so sharply and easily that he has indicted me for impiety. <note>original Greek: *asebeias*</note> So now, by Zeus, tell me what you just claimed to know so clearly: What sort of thing do you say piety and impiety are, both concerning murder and all other matters? Is not the pious <note>original Greek: *to hosion*</note> always the same as itself in every action? And is not the impious the opposite of all that is pious, yet similar to itself, having a single "form" <note>original Greek: *idean*; the fundamental essence or pattern that makes a thing what it is.</note> regarding its impiety, whatever that impious thing may be?

<margin>E</margin> **EUTHYPHRO.** Certainly, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** Tell me then, what do you say the pious and the impious are? **EUTHYPHRO.** I say that the pious is exactly what I am doing now: prosecuting the wrongdoer who commits murder or robs temples or commits any other such sin, whether he happens to be your father or mother or anyone else. Not to prosecute is impious. Behold, Socrates, I will give you a great proof of the law (which I have already told others) that these things are rightly done and that one must not yield to the impious person, no matter who he may be. For men believe that Zeus is the best and most just of the gods, yet they admit he bound his own father <note>Euthyphro refers to the myth where Zeus imprisoned his father Cronus for swallowing his children.</note> because he swallowed his sons unjustly; and that Cronus, in turn, castrated his own father <note>Uranus</note> for similar reasons. Yet they are angry with me because I prosecute my father for his wrongdoing. Thus, they contradict themselves when they speak about the gods and about me.

<margin>F</margin> **SOCRATES.** Is this the reason, Euthyphro, that I am a defendant—because when someone says such things about the gods, I find them difficult to accept? For this reason, it seems, someone will say I am in error. Now, if these things also seem true to you, who know so much about such matters, then it seems I must also concede. For what can I say, when I admit myself that I know nothing about these things? But tell me, in the name of friendship, do you truly believe these things happened this way? **EUTHYPHRO.** Yes, Socrates, and things even more wonderful than these, which the masses do not know.

<margin>G</margin> **SOCRATES.** So you believe there is actually war among the gods, and terrible enmities and battles, and many other such things as are told by the poets? Are we to believe these things are true, Euthyphro, even as our holy places are adorned with them, and at the Great Panathenaea <note>A major festival in Athens honoring Athena; a ceremonial robe (peplos) decorated with mythological scenes was carried to the Acropolis.</note> the robe full of such embroideries is carried up to the citadel? **EUTHYPHRO.** Not only those, Socrates; but as I said before, I will relate many other things to you about divine matters if you wish, which I am sure will amaze you. **SOCRATES.** I would not be surprised. But you can relate those to me another time at your leisure. For now, try to answer more clearly what I asked you before. For you did not teach me sufficiently, my friend, when I asked what the pious is; instead, you told me that this thing is pious which you are doing now, prosecuting your father for murder. **EUTHYPHRO.** And I spoke the truth, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** Perhaps. But, Euthyphro, you say many other things are also pious. **EUTHYPHRO.** And so they are. **SOCRATES.** Remember then, I did not ask you to teach me one or two of the many pious things, but that "form" itself by which all pious things are pious. For you said that by one single form the impious are impious and the pious are pious. Or do you not remember? **EUTHYPHRO.** I do. **SOCRATES.** Then teach me this very form, what it is, so that I may look upon it and use it as a model <note>original Greek: *paradeigmati*</note>; so that whatever action is of this sort, whether performed by you or anyone else, I may call it pious, and what is not of this sort, I may say it is not.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...strangled. <note>The Latin text here picks up the end of the previous page's thought.</note> Wherefore the father, having bound his hands and feet, cast him into a pit, and sent a man here to ask the interpreter of the law what should be done. Meanwhile, he neglected the bound man as a murderer, as if it mattered nothing at all if he should happen to die—which did occur. For before the messenger could return from the interpreter, he perished from hunger, cold, and the bonds. For this reason, the father and other relatives are aggrieved that, on account of a murderer's death, I should pursue a charge of killing against my father, who, as they say, did not kill him; or even if he had, that one should not care about the death of a murderer. For they say it is impious for a son to bring a day of judgment against his father,

<margin>B</margin> poorly judging, O Socrates, how the divine power stands regarding the holy and the profane. **SOCRATES.** Then, by Jove <note>original Latin: *Iouem* (Jupiter/Zeus)</note>, O Euthyphro, do you presume to know divine, holy, and profane things so sincerely as they are, that with these things having been done as you say, you do not fear lest, in accusing your father of a killing, you might be attempting something profane? **EUTHYPHRO.** My study would be of no use to me, O Socrates, nor would Euthyphro excel so many mortals in any way, unless I clearly discerned such things. **SOCRATES.**

<margin>C</margin> O admirable Euthyphro, nothing is better than that I should become your disciple, and in the dispute I have with Meletus, I should primarily object this: that previously I have indeed made the knowledge of divine things of the greatest importance; but now, after he said that I, by my own vain opinion and error, have fashioned new gods, I have become your disciple. Therefore, O Meletus, I shall say, if you think Euthyphro thinks rightly in these things, think the same of me, and do not condemn me. If not, summon that teacher to judgment before me, as he is corrupting old men—namely me and his father—me by teaching, and him by correcting and punishing. But if he does not obey me, nor drop the judgment, nor accuse you instead of me, will you say those same things in judgment that I objected? **EUTHYPHRO.** Yes, by Jove, O Socrates! For if he

<margin>D</margin> should attempt to accuse me, I would find, as I think, where he is weak and infirm, and the dispute in judgment would be about him long before it would be about me. **SOCRATES.** And yet I, O sweet friend, considering these things, would wish to be your disciple, since I know that perhaps someone else, and this Meletus, seems not even to have seen you, yet he has perceived me so sharply and easily that he has accused me here of impiety. Now, therefore, by Jove, tell me what you asserted you were plainly able to do: what you wish the pious and the impious to be, both in killing and in all other things. Is it not the same in individual actions, the holy itself being consistent with itself, and every profane thing again being the contrary to the holy, yet consistent with itself, and having one single "idea" <note>original Latin: *ideam*</note> according to which it is profane, whatever is destined to be profane? **EUTHYPHRO.** Entirely,

<margin>E</margin> O Socrates. **SOCRATES.** Tell me then, what do you call holy, and what profane? **EUTHYPHRO.** I call holy that which I am doing now: to bring to judgment him who acts unjustly, whether regarding killings, or sacrileges, or anything else of this kind, whether it be father or mother or anyone else who has sinned. But not to pursue him is profane. Indeed, look, I pray, O Socrates, what a strong conjecture of the law I bring to you, as I have told others as well, saying that then at last is it rightly done when we spare no one at all who has sinned, whoever he may be.

<margin>F</margin> For these men believe Jove himself to be the best and most just of all the gods, yet they confess he bound his own father because he had devoured his children without right. They also assert that he castrated his father on account of such things. But they are angry with me because I pursue a parent liable for injustice. And so these men think contrary things regarding the gods as well as regarding me. **SOCRATES.** And yet for this reason, O Euthyphro, I am accused, and I do not have enough of an answer. For as often as someone says such things about the gods, I bear it with difficulty; for which reason, as it seems, they say I sin. But now, if this seems so to you, an expert in these matters, it is necessary that we also agree. For what else could we say? Seeing that we profess to understand nothing about them. But by friendly Jove, tell me whether you yourself believe those things truly happened so. **EUTHYPHRO.** And even more wonderful things, O Socrates, which are hidden from the many. **SOCRATES.**

<margin>G</margin> Do you therefore think that war is waged among the gods in turn, and grave enmities and battles and many other things, which are recorded by poets and skilled writers? Whence also our other sacred things are full of such variety, and in the great Panathenaea the robe full of such varieties is carried into the citadel. Shall we confess these things to be true, O Euthyphro? **EUTHYPHRO.** Not these alone, O Socrates, but what I said a little before, I will set forth many other things about divine matters, if you wish, which when you hear them, I know well you will be stunned. **SOCRATES.** I would by no means wonder at it. But you shall relate those things hereafter with greater leisure; for the present, strive to explain more plainly what I just asked. For you did not sufficiently teach me at the beginning, friend, when I asked what the holy was; but you said that it was holy which you were doing now, while you accuse your father as a defendant of killing. **EUTHYPHRO.** And I said true things, O Socrates. **SOCRATES.** Perhaps. But are there not many other things, O Euthyphro, that you call holy? **EUTHYPHRO.** There are others. **SOCRATES.** Remember therefore that I did not exhort you to teach me one or two from the many holy things, but that very "species" <note>original Latin: *specie*</note> by which all holy things are holy. For you said that by one idea all holy things are holy, and again by one that those which are profane are profane. Or do you not remember? **EUTHYPHRO.** Indeed. **SOCRATES.** Show me therefore what that very idea is, so that to it...

...looking at it, and using it as a sort of model, I may say that whatever you or anyone else does of such a kind is holy; but what is not such, I may deny. **EUTHYPHRO.** If that is how you want it, Socrates, I will say it so.
<margin>The second definition of the holy is given.</margin>
**SOCRATES.** Indeed, I do want it. **EUTHYPHRO.** That which is beloved by the gods is holy <note>original Latin: *sanctum*</note>; but what is not beloved is profane <note>original Latin: *prophanum*</note>. **SOCRATES.** Most beautifully, Euthyphro! You have now answered exactly as I wished you to answer. Whether you have answered truly, I do not yet know, but you will clearly demonstrate to us that these things are true. **EUTHYPHRO.** Entirely so.

**A** **SOCRATES.** Come then, let us consider what we are saying. A deed beloved by God is holy, and a man beloved by God is holy; but a deed hateful to God is profane, and a man hateful to God is profane. The holy and the profane are not the same, but are entirely opposite, are they not? **EUTHYPHRO.** It is so. **SOCRATES.** And do these things seem well said? **EUTHYPHRO.** I think so, for they have been said. **SOCRATES.** And has it not also been said that the gods disagree and fight with one another, and that there are enmities among them? Has this also been said? **EUTHYPHRO.** It has indeed. **SOCRATES.** But my excellent friend, what kind of disagreement produces enmity and anger?
<margin>Disagreement about a matter causes anger and enmity.</margin>
Let us consider it this way: if you and I were to disagree about a number—debating which of two was greater—would a disagreement of this kind make us enemies and stir up anger? Or would we rather turn to the method of counting and quickly cease from this disagreement? **EUTHYPHRO.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** And if we disagreed about the larger and the smaller, would we not resort to measurement and immediately settle the controversy? **EUTHYPHRO.** That is true. **SOCRATES.** And if we turn to weighing and balancing, would we not resolve a controversy about the heavier and the lighter? **EUTHYPHRO.** Why not? **SOCRATES.** What then are the things about which we disagree and cannot easily judge, so that we become enemies and grow angry? Perhaps you do not have it ready at hand. But I will say it, and you consider:
<margin>Justice and injustice, the beautiful and the ugly, good and evil are the things that those who cannot judge become angry about.</margin>
are they not justice and injustice, the beautiful and the ugly, and good and evil? Are these not the things about which we disagree, and when we cannot arrive at a sufficient judgment of them, we become enemies—whenever we do become so—both you and I, and all mankind? **EUTHYPHRO.** This is indeed the disagreement, Socrates, and it concerns these very things. **SOCRATES.** And the gods, Euthyphro, if they disagree about anything, surely they would disagree about these things. **EUTHYPHRO.** It is entirely necessary. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, noble Euthyphro, according to your argument, different gods think different things are beautiful and ugly, good and evil. For they would never fight with one another unless they disagreed about these things, would they? **EUTHYPHRO.** You speak rightly. **SOCRATES.** Then the things each god thinks are beautiful, good, and just, these they love; and the opposites of these they utterly hate? **EUTHYPHRO.** Entirely. **SOCRATES.** But the same things, as you say, some gods consider just and others consider unjust; and in disputing these things, they strive and fight with one another. Is it not so? **EUTHYPHRO.** It is. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, it seems the same things are loved by the gods and held in hatred; and these same things are both dear to the gods and hateful to them. **EUTHYPHRO.** So it seems. **SOCRATES.** By this reasoning, Euthyphro, the same things will be both holy and profane. **EUTHYPHRO.** It appears so. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, admirable man, you have not answered the question I asked. For I did not want to know what happens to be both holy and profane at the same time; yet what is dear to a god seems also to be hateful to a god. Wherefore, Euthyphro, it would be no wonder if, in what you are now doing—punishing your father—you were doing something that would be pleasing to Zeus but hateful to Cronus and Uranus, and pleasing to Hephaestus but annoying to Hera; and if any other of the gods disagrees with another about it, the same would happen regarding them. **EUTHYPHRO.** But I think, Socrates, that in this no god differs from another: that he who has unjustly killed anyone ought to pay the penalty. **SOCRATES.** But Euthyphro, have you ever heard any man doubting this: that a man who kills someone unjustly, or does anything else unjustly, ought to pay the penalty? **EUTHYPHRO.** They never stop disputing these things, both elsewhere and in the courts. For those who have done wrong try every word and action to escape the penalty. **SOCRATES.** Do they confess to acting unjustly, and at the same time say they ought not to pay the penalty? **EUTHYPHRO.** Not at all. **SOCRATES.** Then they do not say and do everything; for they do not dare to say or dispute this: that if they have acted unjustly, they should not be punished. Instead, I think, they claim they have not acted unjustly. Is it not so? **EUTHYPHRO.** You speak the truth. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, they do not dispute whether the unjust person should be punished; but rather they dispute about this: who acted unjustly, by doing what, and when. **EUTHYPHRO.** You tell the truth. **SOCRATES.** Do not these same things happen to the gods, if they disagree about the just and the unjust, as your argument testifies? And some say they act unjustly toward one another, while others deny it? Since, admirable friend, no one among either gods or men dares to say this: that the unjust person should not pay the penalty. **EUTHYPHRO.** Yes, you speak the truth in this, Socrates, at least in the main point. **SOCRATES.** But I think, Euthyphro, that those who dispute—whether men or gods, if indeed gods dispute—dispute about each particular deed that has been done. They disagree about some action, some saying it was done justly, and others unjustly. Is it not so? **EUTHYPHRO.** Entirely. **SOCRATES.** Come then, dear Euthyphro, teach me also so that I may become wiser: what is your proof that all the gods consider that man to have been unjustly killed, who, while serving for hire, became a murderer, and being bound by the master of the dead man, perished in his bonds before he who had bound him...

**A** Therefore, teach me this very form <note>original Greek: *idean*</note>, whatever it may be, so that looking toward it and using it as a model, I may say that whatever is of such a kind, among the things that you or anyone else may do, is holy <note>original Greek: *hosion*</note>; and whatever is not of such a kind, I may say is not.
**EUTHYPHRO.** Well, if that is how you wish it, Socrates, I will also tell you in that way. **SOCRATES.** But indeed, I do wish it. **EUTHYPHRO.** It is this: what is dear to the gods is holy, and what is not dear is unholy <note>original Greek: *anosion*</note>. **SOCRATES.** Most excellently, Euthyphro! You have now answered just as I was seeking for you to answer. However, whether it is true, I do not yet know. But you will clearly show me that what you say is true. **EUTHYPHRO.** Certainly.
**B** **SOCRATES.** Come then, let us examine what we are saying. The god-beloved <note>original Greek: *theophiles*</note> thing and the god-beloved man are holy; but the god-hated thing and the god-hated man are unholy. And they are not the same, but the holy is the direct opposite of the unholy. Is it not so? **EUTHYPHRO.** It is indeed. **SOCRATES.** And it seems to have been well said. **EUTHYPHRO.** I think so, Socrates. Or would we, having come to a calculation about such things,
**C** be quickly rid of the difference? **EUTHYPHRO.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** And also, if we differed about the greater and the smaller, would we not, by coming to a measurement, quickly stop the difference? **EUTHYPHRO.** That is so. **SOCRATES.** And by coming to a weighing, as I think, we would be distinguished regarding the heavier and the lighter. **EUTHYPHRO.** How could it be otherwise? **SOCRATES.** But about what subject would we differ and be unable to reach a judgment, so that we would be enemies to one another and be angry? <summary>Socrates challenges Euthyphro's second definition of piety—that which is dear to the gods—by pointing out that if the gods disagree about justice, then the same act could be both holy and unholy. They transition into discussing whether disagreement lies in the principle of punishment or the specific facts of a case.</summary>

->EUTHYPHRO<-

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...from the legal authority on what should be done? <note>Euthyphro is prosecuting his own father for the death of a laborer, and Socrates is questioning whether this action is truly "holy."</note> And for this reason, is it right for a son to bring his father into a capital trial? Come, I beg you, try to demonstrate something clearly to me: that all the gods, without exception, consider this specific action to be right. If you can show this to me sufficiently, I will never stop praising your wisdom. **EUTHYPHRO.** But perhaps this is no small task, Socrates; though I could certainly show it to you quite clearly. **SOCRATES.** I understand; I seem to you to be slower at learning than the judges, since you will clearly demonstrate to them that these actions are unjust and that all the gods hate such things. **EUTHYPHRO.** Quite clearly indeed, Socrates, provided they listen to me speaking. <margin>B</margin> **SOCRATES.** But they will listen, if you seem to speak well. However, while you were speaking, a thought occurred to me, and I am observing myself: "Even if Euthyphro should teach me most perfectly that all the gods consider this death to be unjust, what more have I learned from Euthyphro about what is holy and what is profane?" For this deed would, it seems, be hated by the gods; yet it appeared just a moment ago that the holy and the unholy were not defined by this <note>original Greek: *theomises* (god-hated) and *theophiles* (god-loved)</note>, for what appeared hateful to some gods also appeared loved by others. Therefore, I will let you off on this point, Euthyphro: if you wish, let all the gods consider it unjust, and let them all hate it. But shall we now correct our definition in this way: that whatever all the gods hate is profane, and <margin>C</margin> conversely, whatever all the gods love is holy? But whatever some might love and others hate would be neither, or both at once. Is this how you want us to define the holy and the profane now? **EUTHYPHRO.** What is stopping us, Socrates? **SOCRATES.** Nothing on my part, Euthyphro, but you look to your own side; consider whether, by making this assumption, you can easily teach me what you promised. **EUTHYPHRO.** Indeed, I would say that the holy is that which all the gods love, <margin>Third definition.</margin> and the opposite, which all the gods hate, is the profane. **SOCRATES.** Then let us examine this again, Euthyphro, to see if it is well said, or should we let it go? Should we just accept it from ourselves and others, so that if someone merely asserts something, we admit it? Or must we examine what the speaker is saying? **EUTHYPHRO.** It must be examined; however, I believe this is now well said. **SOCRATES.** Perhaps, my good man, we shall understand it better. For consider this: Is the holy loved by the gods because it is holy? <margin>D</margin> Or is it holy because it is loved by the gods? <note>This is the famous "Euthyphro Dilemma": does God love what is good because it is inherently good, or is it only good because God decided to love it?</note> **EUTHYPHRO.** I do not know what you mean, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** I will try to explain more clearly. We speak of a thing being carried and a thing that carries; a thing being led and a thing that leads; a thing being seen and a thing that sees. You understand that all these are different from one another, and in what way they differ? **EUTHYPHRO.** I think I understand. **SOCRATES.** Is there not also something called "being loved," and something else that is "the lover"? **EUTHYPHRO.** Of course. **SOCRATES.** Tell me then: is the thing being carried "carried" because it is being moved, or for some other reason? **EUTHYPHRO.** No, for that very reason. **SOCRATES.** And the thing being led because it is led? And the thing being seen because it is seen? **EUTHYPHRO.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, it is not because it is a "seen thing" that it is seen, but on the contrary, because it is seen, it is a "seen thing." <margin>E</margin> Nor is it because it is a "led thing" that it is led, but because it is led, it is "led." Nor is it because it is a "carried thing" that it is carried, but because it is carried, it is "carried." Is it now clear, Euthyphro, what I want to say? I mean this: if something becomes a certain way or suffers something, it is not because it is a "finished thing" that it becomes; rather, because it becomes, it is "finished." Nor because it is a "passive thing" does it suffer, but because it suffers, it is "passive." Do you agree to this? **EUTHYPHRO.** I do. **SOCRATES.** Then is the "loved thing" either something that is becoming or something suffering an action from someone? **EUTHYPHRO.** Entirely so. **SOCRATES.** This, then, is the same as the previous examples: it is not because it is a "loved thing" that it is loved by those who love it, but because it is loved, it is a "loved thing." **EUTHYPHRO.** Necessarily. **SOCRATES.** What then do we say about the holy, Euthyphro? Is it not loved by all the gods, according to your statement? **EUTHYPHRO.** Yes. **SOCRATES.** Is it because it is holy, <margin>F</margin> or for some other reason? **EUTHYPHRO.** For that very reason. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, because it is holy, it is loved; but it is not holy because it is loved? **EUTHYPHRO.** So it seems. **SOCRATES.** Yet, because it is loved by the gods, it is a "loved thing" and "dear to the gods." **EUTHYPHRO.** Of course. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, "dear to the gods" is not the same as "the holy," Euthyphro, nor is "the holy" the same as "dear to the gods," as you claim, but they are different things. **EUTHYPHRO.** How so, Socrates? **SOCRATES.** Because we agree that the holy is loved for this reason—because it is holy—but it is not holy because it is loved. Isn't that right? **EUTHYPHRO.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** But the "god-loved," by the very fact that it is loved by the gods, is "god-loved"; it is not loved because it is "god-loved." **EUTHYPHRO.** You speak the truth. **SOCRATES.** But if, my friend Euthyphro, "god-loved" and "the holy" were the same thing, then if the holy were loved because it is holy, the "god-loved" would also be loved because it is "god-loved." <margin>G</margin> Or, if the "god-loved" were "god-loved" because it was loved by the gods, then the holy would also be holy because it was loved. But now you see that they are opposite, being entirely different from one another. For one <note>the god-loved</note> is of a nature to be loved because it is loved; the other <note>the holy</note> is loved because it is of a nature to be loved. And you seem to me, Euthyphro, when asked what the holy is, to be unwilling to show me its essence <note>original Latin: *essentiam*; Greek: *ousian*</note>, but instead you mention a certain attribute <note>original Latin: *passionem*; Greek: *pathos*</note> of it—namely, that this "holy" happens to be loved by all the gods. But what it actually *is*, you have not yet said. So if you please, do not hide it from me, but say again from the beginning: what is the holy, whether it is loved by the gods or whatever else it may experience? For we will not disagree about that. Tell me readily, what is the holy and what is the profane? **EUTHYPHRO.** But Socrates, I do not know how to express what I am thinking. For whatever we propose always wanders around on us and refuses to stay where we set it. **SOCRATES.** Your words, Euthyphro, seem to be the works of our ancestor, Daedalus <note>Socrates jokingly claimed descent from Daedalus, the mythical craftsman whose statues were so lifelike they would walk away if not tied down.</note>. If I were the one saying these things and setting them down, you might perhaps mock me, saying that because of my kinship to him, my arguments run away and won't stay put. But since these assumptions are yours, we need another joke; for they do not stay still for you, as you yourself can see.

<summary>Socrates challenges Euthyphro’s third definition of holiness—that it is what all gods love—by introducing the famous dilemma: is something holy because the gods love it, or do they love it because it is inherently holy? <meta>Continuity: On the previous page, Socrates and Euthyphro were attempting to find a universal definition of holiness. Euthyphro's previous attempt—that holiness is what all the gods love—ran into the problem that even if they all agree on what is "holy," we still don't know the *nature* of holiness itself. Socrates now begins to push Euthyphro to define holiness as a specific category of justice.</meta>

# PLATO

If I had said those things and put them forward myself, perhaps you would have mocked me (hurling a joke at me) because the creations of my speech flee away—as if they were relatives of that man <note>Socrates refers to his mythical ancestor Dædalus, the legendary inventor whose statues were said to be so lifelike they would walk away if not tied down.</note>—and they refuse to remain where one has placed them. But now, since these are your own premises, we need a different kind of joke; for they do not wish to stay put for you, as you yourself can see. <margin>The works of Dædalus.</margin> **EUTHYPHRO.** On the contrary, Socrates, it seems to me that what you have said can be marked with that same joke and mockery. I am not the cause of them wandering about and not staying in the same place; rather, you seem to me to be Dædalus himself. For as far as I am concerned, they would have stayed exactly as they were. **SOCRATES.** Then I seem, my friend, to have become more skilled in this art than that man, in that he only made his own works unstable, while I—it appears—do so for others' works as well as my own. And the most elegant part of my "art" is that I am wise against my own will. For I would prefer my arguments to remain and stand firm, rather than to possess the wisdom of Dædalus and the riches of Tantalus <note>Tantalus was a king in Greek myth famous for his immense wealth, though he is now better known for his eternal punishment.</note> combined. But enough of this. Since you seem to me to be acting daintily and shirking the labor, I myself will strive to help you show how you might instruct me about holiness, so that you do not give up in the middle of our talk. See if you think it is necessary that everything holy be just. **EUTHYPHRO.** I do think so. **SOCRATES.** Is everything just also holy? Or is everything holy indeed just, but not everything just is holy—rather, one part of justice is holy, while another part is something else? **EUTHYPHRO.** I do not quite follow your words, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** And yet you are younger than I am by no less than you are wiser! But as I said, you are "dainty" because of your wealth of wisdom. Come, blessed man, rouse your strength and exert yourself. It is not at all difficult to grasp what I am saying. I am stating the opposite of what the Poet said when he wrote:

> Why should I fear to write, when I write of highest Jove?
> For fear brings shame as its companion always. <note>original Latin: *Scribere cur metuam...* Socrates is quoting a verse often attributed to Stasinus of Cyprus, though here he uses it to make a logical point about the relationship between two concepts.</note>

<margin>This is criticized: "where there is fear, there is also shame."</margin> I disagree with this Poet. Shall I tell you where I disagree? **EUTHYPHRO.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** It does not seem to me that wherever there is fear, there is also shame. For many people seem to me to fear poverty and disease and other such things; they feel fear, yet they feel no shame at all regarding the things they fear. Does it not seem the same to you? **EUTHYPHRO.** It does. **SOCRATES.** But wherever there is shame, there is also fear. Is there anyone who feels shame and blushes, who does not also dread and fear the reputation of being wicked? **EUTHYPHRO.** He certainly dreads it. **SOCRATES.** Therefore it is not correctly said: "wherever there is fear, there is shame." Rather, where there is shame, there is fear; yet it is not true that wherever there is fear, there is always shame. For fear, I believe, is broader than shame, since shame is a part of fear—just as "odd" is a part of "number." Thus, it is not the case that wherever there is a number, there is an odd number; but where there is an odd number, there is also a number. Do you follow me now? **EUTHYPHRO.** Very much so. **SOCRATES.** This, then, is what I was asking earlier: whether where there is justice, there is also holiness; or rather, where there is holiness, there is justice, but where there is justice, there is not always holiness. For holiness is a part of justice. Shall we say it is so, or do you think otherwise? **EUTHYPHRO.** No, let us say it is so. It seems to me you are speaking correctly. **SOCRATES.** Now look at what follows: if holiness is a part of justice, we must, it seems, discover what *kind* of part of justice holiness is. If you were asking me now about one of the things we just mentioned—for example, what kind of part of a number is the "even," and what kind of number it happens to be—I would reply that it is the number which has two equal sides, not unequal ones. <note>original: *non laterum... inæqualium, sed æqualium duorum*. This refers to even numbers being "equilateral" or divisible into two equal parts.</note> Don't you agree? **EUTHYPHRO.** I certainly do. **SOCRATES.** Try then to teach me in the same way what part of justice holiness is, so that we may immediately tell Meletus <note>The man who brought the legal charges against Socrates.</note> to stop doing us an injustice and accusing us of impiety, since we have now sufficiently learned from you what things are pious and holy, and what are not. <margin>The definition of the holy begins to appear.</margin> **EUTHYPHRO.** I believe, Socrates, that the part of justice that is holy and pious is the one concerned with the <term>care of the gods</term> <note>original Greek: *therapeia*. This can mean service, tending, or medical care.</note>. The other part of justice, which concerns the care of men, remains the other portion. **SOCRATES.** You seem to me to speak excellently, Euthyphro, but I still require one small thing: I do not yet understand what you call "care." Surely you do not mean that this care for the gods is the same as the care we have for other things? For instance, we say: Not everyone knows how to care for horses, but only the horseman. Is that not so? **EUTHYPHRO.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** For the skill of horsemanship is the care of horses. **EUTHYPHRO.** Yes. **SOCRATES.** And the hunter's skill is the care of dogs, and the herdsman's is the care of oxen. **EUTHYPHRO.** Entirely. **SOCRATES.** And holiness and piety is the care of the gods: is this what you are asserting, Euthyphro? **EUTHYPHRO.** I am. <margin>All care tends toward this: to bring good and utility to that which is cared for.</margin> **SOCRATES.** Does not all care intend the same thing: that it should bring some good and benefit to that which is being cared for? Just as you see that horses, when cared for by the horseman's skill, are benefited and become better. Do they not seem so to you? **EUTHYPHRO.** They do indeed. **SOCRATES.** And dogs by the hunter's skill, and oxen by the herdsman's, and all other things similarly. Or do you think care tends toward the damage of that which is cared for? **EUTHYPHRO.** By Jove, no. **SOCRATES.** But toward its benefit? **EUTHYPHRO.** Why not? **SOCRATES.** Then holiness, since it is the care of the gods, must benefit the gods? And make them better? Would you ever concede this: that when you perform a holy act, you are making one of the gods better? **EUTHYPHRO.** Never, by Jove! **SOCRATES.** Nor do I think that is what you meant, Euthyphro; far be such a suspicion from me. That is why I asked what kind of "care of the gods" you meant, not believing you meant this kind. **EUTHYPHRO.** And you were right, Socrates; for I do not mean that kind of care. **SOCRATES.** Very well; but then what kind of care for the gods will holiness be? **EUTHYPHRO.** The kind of care that <term>servants</term> <note>original Greek: *douloi*</note> give to their masters. **SOCRATES.** I understand: it would be a kind of service to the gods, it seems. **EUTHYPHRO.** Precisely. **SOCRATES.** Can you say, then, to what result the "service to physicians" tends? Do you not think it is toward health? **EUTHYPHRO.** I do. **SOCRATES.** What about...

**SOCRATES.** [A] If I were the one saying these things and setting them down, you would perhaps mock me, saying that because of my kinship with that man [Dædalus], my works in these arguments run away and refuse to stay where someone puts them. But now—for these are your hypotheses—some other joke is needed. For they do not want to stay put for you, as it seems even to you. **EUTHYPHRO.** To me, Socrates, it seems that these things said require nearly the same joke. For this "wandering about" and not staying in the same place—I am not the one who puts it there. You seem to me to be the Dædalus. As far as I'm concerned, they would have stayed [B] exactly like this. **SOCRATES.** Then I am in danger, my friend, of being even more skilled in my art than that man, to the extent that he only made his own works not stay put, while I, it seems, do so for my own and for those of others. And indeed, this is the most clever part of my art: that I am wise against my will. For I would wish my arguments to stay and be fixed immovably, more than to have the wealth of Tantalus added to the wisdom of Dædalus. But enough of this. Since you seem to me to be acting daintily, I will myself help you show how you might teach me about the holy, and do not get tired beforehand. See if it does not seem necessary to you that all that is holy is just. [C] **EUTHYPHRO.** To me, at least. **SOCRATES.** Is it then also the case that all that is just is holy? Or is all that is holy indeed just, but the just is not all holy, but some of it is holy and some of it is something else? **EUTHYPHRO.** I do not follow, Socrates, what is being said. **SOCRATES.** And yet you are younger than I am, no less than you are wiser; but as I say, you are dainty because of your wealth of wisdom. But, O blessed one, exert yourself. For it is not even hard to understand what I am saying. [D] I am saying the opposite of what the poet wrote, the one who wrote: "Zeus, who did this and planted all these things, you are unwilling to name; for where there is fear, there is also shame." Now I differ from this poet. Shall I tell you how? **EUTHYPHRO.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** It does not seem to me that "where there is fear, there is also shame." For many people seem to me—fearing diseases and poverty and many other such things—to fear them, but to feel no shame at the things they fear. Doesn't it seem so to you? **EUTHYPHRO.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** But where there is shame, there is also fear; for is there anyone who, feeling shame at a thing and being disgraced, [E] does not also fear and dread the reputation of wickedness? **EUTHYPHRO.** He does dread it. **SOCRATES.** Then it is not correct to say: "where there is fear, there is also shame"; but where there is shame, there is also fear. However, it is not the case that wherever there is fear, there is everywhere shame. For I think fear is more extensive than shame. For shame is a part of fear, just as "odd" is a part of "number." Thus, it is not the case that where there is number, there is also the odd; but where there is the odd, there is also number. Surely you follow now? **EUTHYPHRO.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** Then it was something like this I was asking before: Is it that where there is justice, there is also holiness? Or is it that where there is holiness, there is also justice, but where there is justice, it is not everywhere holy? [F] For the holy is a part of the just. Shall we say it this way, or does it seem otherwise to you? **EUTHYPHRO.** No, but this way. For you seem to me to be speaking correctly. **SOCRATES.** Now look at what follows this. If the holy is a part of the just, we must, it seems, find out what kind of part of the just the holy would be. Now if you were asking me one of the things just now—for instance, what kind of part of number is the "even," and what this number happens to be—I would have said it is that which is not "scalene" but "isosceles" <note>In ancient Greek mathematics, even numbers were called "isosceles" because they could be split into two equal parts.</note>. Or does it not seem so to you? **EUTHYPHRO.** To me, yes. **SOCRATES.** Try then yourself to teach me in this way what kind of part of the just is holy; so that we may tell Meletus no longer to wrong us, nor to indict us for impiety, as we have already learned sufficiently from you the things that are pious and holy, and those that are not. [G] **EUTHYPHRO.** This then is what seems to me, Socrates: that the part of the just that is pious and holy is that which concerns the <term>service</term> <note>original Greek: *therapeia*</note> of the gods; and that which concerns the service of men is the remaining part of the just. **SOCRATES.** And you seem to me, Euthyphro, to speak beautifully. But I am still in need of one small thing: for I do not yet understand this "service" you name. For you surely do not mean that it is the same kind of service as for other things—as we say: We say, for instance, not everyone knows how to serve horses, but the horseman. Isn't that so? **EUTHYPHRO.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** For horsemanship is the service of horses? **EUTHYPHRO.** Yes. **SOCRATES.** And not everyone knows how to serve dogs, but the hunter. **EUTHYPHRO.** Just so. **SOCRATES.** For hunting is the service of dogs? [H] **EUTHYPHRO.** Yes. **SOCRATES.** And herdsman's skill is that of oxen? **EUTHYPHRO.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** And holiness and piety is that of the gods, Euthyphro? Is that what you mean? **EUTHYPHRO.** I do. **SOCRATES.** Does not all service achieve the same thing? For instance: it is for some good and benefit of the one served. Just as you see that horses served by horsemanship are benefited and become better. Or do they not seem so to you? **EUTHYPHRO.** To me, yes. **SOCRATES.** And the dogs by hunting, and the oxen by the herdsman's skill, and all other things likewise. Or do you think service is for the harm of the thing served? **EUTHYPHRO.** By Zeus, not I! **SOCRATES.** But for benefit? **EUTHYPHRO.** How could it not be? **SOCRATES.** Is holiness then, being the service of gods, a benefit to the gods, and does it make the gods better? And would you agree to this: that whenever you do something holy, you are making one of the gods better? **EUTHYPHRO.** By Zeus, not I! **SOCRATES.** Nor do I, Euthyphro, think you say this—far from it. But for this reason I was asking, thinking you did not mean this. **EUTHYPHRO.** And correctly so, Socrates; for I do not mean such a thing. **SOCRATES.** Very well. But then what kind of service to the gods would holiness be? **EUTHYPHRO.** The kind, Socrates, which slaves give to their masters. **SOCRATES.** I understand. It would be a kind of <term>assistant's work</term> for the gods, it seems. **EUTHYPHRO.** Precisely so. **SOCRATES.** Can you then say, what kind of work the assistant's work for doctors happens to produce? Do you not think it is for health? **EUTHYPHRO.** I do. **SOCRATES.** What about...

# EUTHYPHRO.

...to health, do you think? **EUTHYPHRO.** I do. **SOCRATES.** What then? To what kind of result does the service of shipbuilding provide its assistance? **EUTHYPHRO.** Clearly, Socrates, it is for a ship. **SOCRATES.** And the service of house-building, I suppose, is for a house? **EUTHYPHRO.** Yes. **SOCRATES.** Tell me then, my good man: to what kind of result would the service to the gods provide its assistance? For it is clear that you know, since you claim to have the finest knowledge of divine matters among all men. **EUTHYPHRO.** And I am telling the truth, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** Tell me then, by Zeus, what is that wonderful work which the gods accomplish by using us as their servants? **EUTHYPHRO.** They accomplish many fine things, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** So do generals, my friend; but nonetheless, you could easily state the "chief point" <note>original Greek: "κεφάλαιον" (kephalaion) – meaning the head, summit, or summary of a matter.</note> of their work, which is victory in war. Or not? **EUTHYPHRO.** Of course. **SOCRATES.** And farmers, I think, also accomplish many fine things; yet the chief point of their work is the production of food from the earth. **EUTHYPHRO.** Quite so. **SOCRATES.** What then? Of the many fine things the gods accomplish, what is the chief point of their work? **EUTHYPHRO.** I told you a little while ago, Socrates, that it is a rather long task to learn exactly how all these things stand. But I will tell you simply this: if a man knows how to say and do things that are pleasing to the gods by praying and sacrificing, those things are holy; and such practices preserve both private houses and the common interests of cities. The opposites of these pleasing things are impious, and they overturn and destroy everything. **SOCRATES.** You could have told me the "chief point" of what I asked much more briefly, Euthyphro, if you had wanted to. But it is clear that you are not eager to teach me. Even now, when you were right at the point of answering, you turned away; if you had answered, I might have already learned the nature of holiness from you. But now (for the questioner must follow wherever the one being questioned leads), what do you say holiness and the holy are? Is it not a certain science <note>In this context, "science" refers to "techne" or "episteme"—a systematic knowledge or skill.</note> of sacrificing and praying? **EUTHYPHRO.** I agree. **SOCRATES.** And is not sacrificing a way of giving gifts to the gods, and praying a way of asking from the gods? **EUTHYPHRO.** Very much so, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** According to this argument, holiness would then be a science of asking from and giving to the gods. **EUTHYPHRO.** You have understood what I said perfectly, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** That is because I am a lover of your wisdom, my friend, and I apply my mind to it so that nothing you say shall fall to the ground. But tell me, what is this "service" to the gods? You say it is asking from them and giving to them? **EUTHYPHRO.** I do. **SOCRATES.** Then would not the right way of asking be to ask them for the things we need from them? **EUTHYPHRO.** What else? **SOCRATES.** And the right way of giving would be to give back to them the things they happen to need from us? For it would not be a very skillful way of giving gifts to offer someone things they do not need. **EUTHYPHRO.** You speak the truth, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** Then holiness, Euthyphro, must be a kind of "trading skill" <note>original Greek: "ἐμπορική τις τέχνη" (emporikē tis technē) – literally a merchant's craft or commerce.</note> between gods and men. **EUTHYPHRO.** Call it trading, if you prefer to name it so. **SOCRATES.** It is not "preferable" to me unless it happens to be true. Tell me then: what benefit do the gods get from the gifts they receive from us? For what they give is clear to everyone, since we have nothing good that they have not provided. But what benefit do they get from what they receive from us? Or do we have such an advantage in this "trade" that we receive all good things from them, while they receive nothing from us? **EUTHYPHRO.** But Socrates, do you really think the gods are benefited by what they receive from us? **SOCRATES.** But then what could these gifts of ours to the gods possibly be, Euthyphro? **EUTHYPHRO.** What else do you think they are but honor, marks of respect, and as I just said, gratitude? **SOCRATES.** Then holiness, Euthyphro, is something that is "pleasing" to the gods, but not beneficial or "dear" to them? **EUTHYPHRO.** I think it is, above all things, "dear" to them. **SOCRATES.** So it seems that holiness is, once again, "that which is dear to the gods." **EUTHYPHRO.** Most certainly. **SOCRATES.** And when you say this, are you surprised that your arguments do not stay put, but walk away? Will you accuse me of being the Daedalus who makes them walk, when you yourself are far more skillful than Daedalus in making them go around in a circle? Or do you not see that our argument has come back around to the same place? For you surely remember that earlier, the "holy" and the "dear to the gods" appeared to us not to be the same, but different from one another. Or do you not remember? **EUTHYPHRO.** I do. **SOCRATES.** Now, then, do you not realize that you are saying that what is "dear to the gods" is "holy"? And is this not the same as being "dear to the gods"? Or is it not? **EUTHYPHRO.** It certainly is. **SOCRATES.** Then either we were wrong to agree before, or if we were right then, we are making an incorrect claim now. **EUTHYPHRO.** So it seems. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, we must examine from the beginning what the holy is; for I will not willingly give up until I learn it. Do not look down on me, but apply your mind in every way and tell me the truth now more than ever. For you know it, if any man does; and I must not let you go—like Proteus <note>A sea god in myth who could change his shape; one had to hold onto him tightly to force him to tell the truth.</note>—until you speak. For if you did not know clearly what is holy and unholy, you would never have attempted to prosecute your elderly father for murder on behalf of a laborer; you would have feared the gods (lest you act wrongly) and been ashamed before men. But now I am sure that you think you clearly know what is holy and what is not. So speak, best of men, Euthyphro, and do not hide what you think it is. **EUTHYPHRO.** Some other time then, Socrates. For now I am in a hurry to get somewhere, and it is time for me to go. **SOCRATES.** What are you doing, my friend! You are leaving, casting me down from the great hope I had: that by learning from you what is holy and what is not, I might be rid of Meletus's indictment <note>Socrates refers to the upcoming trial that will lead to his death.</note> by showing him that...

<column-break/>

...to health? **EUTHYPHRO.** To this very thing. **SOCRATES.** But the "service" of those who build ships—what result does it serve? **EUTHYPHRO.** Surely, Socrates, it is for the construction of a ship. **SOCRATES.** And that of house-builders, is it not for the construction of a house? **EUTHYPHRO.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** Tell me then, excellent man: this service-like care for the gods, toward the completion of what work does it obey the gods? For it is plain that you know, since you claimed to know divine things beyond all other men. **EUTHYPHRO.** And I speak the truth, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** Tell me then, by Jove <note>original Latin: "per Iouem" (by Jove/Jupiter) – translating the Greek "πρὸς Διὸς" (by Zeus).</note>, what is this marvelous work which the gods perform through our service? **EUTHYPHRO.** Many and beautiful things indeed, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** Generals of armies also produce many and beautiful things, my friend; <margin>The chief work of generals.</margin> nevertheless, you could easily say their chief work is to be victorious in battle, could you not? **EUTHYPHRO.** Why not? **SOCRATES.** Farmers, too, I think, produce many and beautiful things; yet the sum of them is to gather food from the earth. **EUTHYPHRO.** Exactly. **SOCRATES.** But of the many and beautiful deeds that the gods perform, <margin>The chief work of farmers.</margin> what is the sum of them? **EUTHYPHRO.** I told you a little while ago, Socrates, that it is a task of great labor to perfectly grasp all these things. But I tell you simply this: if anyone knows how to say and do things pleasing to the gods, by vowing and sacrificing, these things are holy. These duties preserve both one's own home and the city. But the opposites of those things which are pleasing to the gods are impious; they subvert and destroy everything. **SOCRATES.** You could have explained the sum of what I was asking in far fewer words, Euthyphro, if you had wished. But it appears by fate how little you are ready or willing to teach me. Indeed, just when you were at the point of doing so, you turned back; if you had answered, I might have long ago learned the nature of holiness from you. But now (since the questioner must follow the one being questioned wherever he leads), what do you say holiness and sanctity are? <margin>Another definition of the holy. What it is to vow; what it is to sacrifice.</margin> Is it not a certain science of vowing and sacrificing? **EUTHYPHRO.** Indeed. **SOCRATES.** Is not sacrificing the offering of gifts to the gods, and vowing the asking of things from the gods? **EUTHYPHRO.** Most certainly, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, holiness would be the science of giving to the gods and asking from them. **EUTHYPHRO.** You have understood what I said very well, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** I am greedy for your wisdom, my friend, and I apply my mind to it; I will not let anything fall in vain. But tell me, I pray, what is this "service" toward the gods? Do you say it is to ask something of them and give to them? **EUTHYPHRO.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** To ask rightly of them—is that not to ask for the things we need? **EUTHYPHRO.** What else? **SOCRATES.** And to give rightly—is that not to offer them those things which they require? For it would not be a skillful act to bestow on someone things they do not need. **EUTHYPHRO.** You tell the truth, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, holiness would be a certain mutual "commerce" <note>original Latin: "mercatura" (merchandise/trade).</note> between gods and men. **EUTHYPHRO.** Commerce, if you like to call it that. **SOCRATES.** Nothing pleases me unless it is true. Tell me then: what is the utility of our gifts to the gods? For what they give, no one is ignorant of. We have no good thing that they do not provide. But what do they gain from what they receive from us? Are we so much better than them in this "trade" that while we receive all good things from them, they receive nothing good from us? **EUTHYPHRO.** Do you really think, Socrates, that the gods are helped in any part by what they receive from us? **SOCRATES.** But what then are these gifts of ours offered to the gods? **EUTHYPHRO.** What else do you think but honor, veneration, and as I just said, gratitude? **SOCRATES.** Therefore, Euthyphro, holiness is something "pleasing" to the gods, but not "useful" or "dear" to them? **EUTHYPHRO.** I believe it is, most of all, "dear" to them. **SOCRATES.** So holiness is, once again, as it seems, that which is dear to the gods? **EUTHYPHRO.** Most certainly. **SOCRATES.** Is it any wonder then, when you say these things, that your arguments do not stay put at all, but seem to wobble? And you blame me as if I were Daedalus, for making them move? Yet you yourself are far more of an artisan than Daedalus, for you make your words revolve in a circle. Do you not see that our discourse has flowed back to the same point? Do you not remember that earlier, the "holy" and the "loved by God" appeared not as the same thing, but as different? Or do you not remember? **EUTHYPHRO.** I remember. **SOCRATES.** But now you do not notice that you are calling the "dear to God" "holy"? And is this not the same as the "loved by God"? Is it not? **EUTHYPHRO.** Entirely. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, either we did not grant it correctly then, or if we did, we are judging incorrectly now. **EUTHYPHRO.** It seems so. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, we must examine from the beginning again what holiness is. For I will not refuse to stand and learn with a willing mind. Do not despise me, but applying your mind fully, express the truth now. For you know it if any man does. You must not be let go, just like Proteus, until you have spoken. For unless you clearly knew the holy and the profane, you would never have decided to pursue an old man and your own father for the death of a laborer; you would have feared the gods, lest you should attempt it wrongly, and you would have respected the opinions of men. But now I know that you believe you clearly know the holy and the profane. Tell us then, best Euthyphro, and do not hide what you think it is. **EUTHYPHRO.** Another time, Socrates; for now I am hurrying elsewhere, and it is the hour for me to go. **SOCRATES.** What are you doing, friend? You have cast me down from a great hope; for I hoped that by learning from you what is holy...

<summary>In this final section of the dialogue, Euthyphro defines holiness as the "science of prayer and sacrifice," which Socrates characterises as a form of "commerce" between gods and men. Realizing their argument has circled back to a definition already proven faulty, Euthyphro makes a hasty exit, leaving Socrates's quest for a definition unfulfilled.</summary>

### PARMENIDES, OR, PARMENIDES,
### ON THE IDEAS, OR, ON THE IDEAS.
->That is, on the forms or species of things.<-

**SUMMARY OF THE DIALOGUE.** The philosopher's <note>Referring to Plato.</note> aim is to explain the opinion of the most celebrated Pythagorean philosopher, Parmenides, regarding the <term>Ideas</term> <note>Also called "Forms"; the perfect, eternal patterns of which physical things are only shadows.</note>. First, therefore, Zeno of Elea, a disciple of Parmenides, proves that the "One" exists among sensible things <note>Things perceived by the senses.</note>, showing that if these things were many, and in no way participating in the nature of the One, many errors would follow. Next, Socrates—not indeed opposing Zeno, but lifting him higher—leads the way to the consideration of the One and the unities that exist in <term>intelligible</term> things <note>Things understood by the mind rather than the senses.</note>, lest he linger only on this "one" which exists in sensible things. From this, they arrive at investigating the Ideas, in which the unities of things consist. Finally, Parmenides himself, now an elder, in no way contradicting Socrates but completing his unfinished contemplation, explains the entire theory of the Ideas. Here he introduces four questions concerning the Ideas: First, whether they exist; second, of what things they are (and of what they are least of all); third, what kind they are and what power they have; fourth, how they are participated in by those things which are below them. From here he ascends to the One which exists above the Intelligibles and the Ideas, and brings forward nine suppositions about it—five if the One exists, four if the One does not exist—seeking what follows in either case. Parmenides intends to assert generally that the One is the principle of all things, and that if it is granted, all things are granted, but if it is removed, all things are destroyed. Furthermore, it should be noted that in this dialogue, when "the One" is mentioned, in the Pythagorean manner any substance entirely free from matter may be signified, such as God, Mind, or the Soul. But when "the other" and "others" are mentioned, one may understand both matter and those things which come to be within matter. Moreover, this discourse is <term>autoproswpos</term> <note>original: "αὐτοπρόσωπος" – meaning a direct narrative delivered by a character.</note>: Socrates is not the speaker but a listener, and events that happened long ago are recounted, so that Plato seems to have wanted to demonstrate another’s opinion rather than his own, although he did not entirely disagree with Parmenides. Parmenides was a <term>contemporary</term> <note>original: "σύγχρονος" (synchronos).</note> of Socrates, for he says he saw him as an old man when he himself was still a youth.
