<margin>Occasion of the dialogue.</margin>
<margin>A</margin> When we had set out from our home in Clazomenae to Athens, we came upon Adeimantus and Glaucon near the forum. Taking me by the hand, Adeimantus said, "Greetings, Cephalus! If there is anything you need here that is within our power, speak." "Indeed," I replied, "I am here for that very purpose, as I shall need your help." "Tell me," he said, "what it is you need." Then I said, "What was the name of your <margin>C</margin> half-brother? I do not remember it. He was only a boy when I first came here from Clazomenae, and much time has passed since then. I believe his father's name was Pyrilampes." "Exactly," he said, "and his own name is Antiphon. But why do you ask?" "These citizens of mine," I said, "are ardent lovers of wisdom. They have heard that Antiphon was once very familiar with Pythodorus, the associate of Zeno, and that having frequently heard them from Pythodorus, he retains in his memory the arguments which Socrates, Zeno, and Parmenides once discussed." "What you say is true," he replied. "Those are the arguments we desire to hear." "That is not difficult," he said, "for when he was <margin>C</margin> a young man, he practiced them very diligently. Though now, like his grandfather and namesake, he spends most of his time with horses. But if we must, let us go to him; he has just now left for home, and he lives nearby in Melita." When this <margin>D</margin> was said, we went there and found Antiphon at home, handing over a certain bridle to a smith to be repaired. After he had finished with him, and his brothers had explained the reason for our coming, he recognized me from my previous visit and greeted me. When we begged him to recount that discussion, he was at first reluctant (for he said it was no small <margin>E</margin> task), but later he set it forth. Antiphon said, then, that Pythodorus related that Zeno and Parmenides once came to the celebration of the Great Panathenaea <note>A major religious festival in Athens.</note>. Parmenides was already quite an old man, very grey, but of a noble appearance, being about sixty-five years of age. Zeno was then nearly forty, tall and handsome to look at; it was said he had been Parmenides's favorite. They were staying with Pythodorus outside the walls, in the <term>Ceramicus</term> <note>The potters' quarter of Athens.</note>. Socrates and many others with him arrived there, desiring to hear Zeno's writings, for they had then been brought by them for the first time. Socrates was at that time a very <margin>F</margin> young man, and Zeno himself was reading to them. Parmenides happened to be out of the house. Pythodorus said that very little was left to be read when he himself entered the house along with Parmenides and Aristotle (the one who became one of the Thirty <note>Refers to the "Thirty Tyrants" who ruled Athens briefly.</note>). Thus they heard the few things that remained to be read. But he had heard everything from Zeno before.

**SOCRATES**, when he had heard these things, asked him to read again the first hypothesis of the first discourse. When it was read, he said: "How do you mean this, O Zeno? If the things that exist are many, must they then be both like and unlike? For that is impossible. For neither can the unlike be like, nor the like unlike. Is this not what you say?" "Certainly," Zeno replied. "Then if it is impossible for the unlike to be like and the like...

<column-break/>

...when we arrived at Athens from our home in Clazomenae, we happened upon Adeimantus and Glaucon in the marketplace. Adeimantus took my hand and said, "Welcome, Cephalus! If you need anything here that we can provide, let us know." "Well indeed," I said, "I am here for this very thing, to make a request of you." "Tell me your request," he said. And I said, "What was your <margin>C</margin> half-brother's name? For I do not remember; he was a child, I suppose, when I previously visited here from Clazomenae. Much time has passed since then. His father's name was Pyrilampes." "Quite so," he said, "and his name is Antiphon. But why do you ask?" "These men here," I said, "are my fellow citizens, very much philosophers, and they have heard that Antiphon frequently met with a certain Pythodorus, a companion of Zeno; and that having often heard from Pythodorus the discourses which Socrates, Zeno, and Parmenides once held, he remembers them." "You speak the truth," he said. "We request, then, to hear these." "It is not difficult," he said, "for as a <margin>D</margin> youth he practiced them very well. Though now, following his grandfather and namesake, he spends most of his time with horses. But if necessary, let us go to him. He just went home from here; he lives nearby in Melita." Having said this, we walked; and we found Antiphon at home, giving a bit to a blacksmith to prepare. When he was free of that, his brothers told him why we were there, and he recognized me from my previous visit and embraced me. When we asked him to go through the discourses, at first he hesitated (for he said it was a great work), but then he narrated it. Antiphon said that Pythodorus said that <margin>E</margin> Zeno and Parmenides once came to the Great Panathenaea. Parmenides was already very much an old man, quite grey, but handsome and good in appearance, about sixty-five years old. Zeno was then nearly forty, tall and graceful to see; and it was said he had been Parmenides's beloved. He said they were staying with Pythodorus, outside the wall, in the Ceramicus; and Socrates arrived there, and many others with him, desiring to hear Zeno's writings. For they had then been brought by them for the first time. Socrates was then very young. So Zeno himself was reading to them; Parmenides happened to be <margin>F</margin> outside, and there was a very short part of the discourses still left to be read when Pythodorus said he himself entered from outside, and Parmenides with him, and Aristotle (the one who became one of the Thirty); and they heard a few small things still of the writings—not that he heard them then for the first time, but he had heard them before from Zeno.

**SOCRATES** then, having heard, asked him to read again the first hypothesis of the first discourse; and it having been read, he said, "How do you mean this, O Zeno? If beings are many, that they must then be both like and unlike? But this is impossible. For neither can unlike things be like, nor like things, unlike. Do you not say so?" "So it is," said Zeno. "Therefore, if it is impossible for unlike things to be like, and like things...

<summary>This page concludes the Euthyphro and begins the Parmenides, introducing the setting of the latter dialogue where a young Socrates meets the elder philosophers Parmenides and Zeno to discuss the nature of the "One" and the "Many."</summary>

<meta>Continuity: This page continues the introductory dialogue of Plato's *Parmenides*. Socrates has just finished listening to Zeno read his book and is now questioning the fundamental premise of Zeno's arguments against the existence of "the Many."</meta>

# PARMENIDES.

<margin>A</margin> ...that things which are unlike cannot be like, nor can things that are like be unlike? And if that is impossible, is it not also impossible for there to be "many" things? For if there were many, they would be subject to these impossible conditions. Is this the point of your arguments—to contend, against everything usually said, that "the Many" do not exist? And do you consider each of your arguments to be a proof of this, so that you believe you have provided as many proofs as you have written arguments to show that the Many do not exist? Is this what you mean, or do I misunderstand? "No," said Zeno, "you have perfectly understood the whole purpose of my writing." "I see, Parmenides," said Socrates, "that our friend Zeno here wishes to be allied with you not only in his friendship but also in his compositions. For he has written the same thing as you in a different way, and by changing it he tries to deceive us into thinking he is saying something new.
<margin>B</margin> For you, in your poems, say that the All is One, and you provide excellent and beautiful proofs for this. He, on the other hand, says there are not 'many,' and he too offers very many and very great proofs. So, while one says 'One' and the other says 'not Many,' and each speaks in such a way that they seem to have said nothing the same—even though you are saying almost the same things—your words seem to be spoken far above the heads of the rest of us." "Yes, Socrates," said Zeno. "But you have not perceived the whole truth of my writing, even though you track and follow the arguments as well as <note>original: "αἱ Λάκαιναι σκύλακες"</note> Lakonian hounds <note>A famous breed of hunting dog in antiquity, prized for their keen sense of smell and ability to stay on a scent trail.</note>. First of all, you fail to notice that
<margin>C</margin> my writing does not boast of having been composed with the intention you describe—trying to hide its purpose from men as if it had achieved some great feat. Rather, what you mentioned was a side effect. In truth, these writings are a kind of defense for Parmenides' argument against those who attempt to mock him, claiming that if the One exists, many ridiculous consequences and self-contradictions follow for the argument. Therefore, this writing speaks against those who assert the existence of the Many; it pays them back in their own coin and then some, intending to show that their own hypothesis—that 'the Many exist'—would suffer even more ridiculous consequences than the hypothesis of the 'One,' if someone were to examine it sufficiently.
<margin>D</margin> It was because of such a spirit of controversy that I wrote it when I was a young man, and then someone stole the manuscript. Thus, I did not even have the chance to deliberate whether it should be brought to light or not. So, you are unaware of this, Socrates: you think it was written not from the controversy of a young man, but from the ambition of an elder. Yet, as I said, your guess was not a bad one." "I accept that," said Socrates, "and I believe it is as you say. But tell me this: do you not believe there is a <term>Form</term> <note>original: "εἶδός" / "speciem"; in Platonic philosophy, a Form is the perfect, eternal, and unchanging essence or blueprint of a thing.</note> of Likeness existing by itself, and another Form contrary to it, which is Unlikeness? And that you and I, and all the other things we call 'many,' <term>participate</term> <note>original: "μεταλαμβάνειν" / "participemus"; the philosophical concept of how physical, changing things "share in" or take their qualities from the eternal Forms.</note> in these two? And that those things which participate in Likeness
<margin>E</margin> become 'like' in that respect and to the extent that they participate? And those that participate in Unlikeness become 'unlike'? And those participating in both become both? If all things participate in both of these contraries, and by sharing in both are both like and unlike themselves, what is the wonder in that? For if someone showed that Likeness itself became unlike, or Unlikeness became like, that would be a marvel, I think. But if he shows that things which participate in both are affected by both, it seems to me, Zeno, not at all strange. Nor is it strange if someone shows that all things are 'one' by participating in the One, and that these same things are also 'many' by participating in Plurality. But if he should demonstrate that the One itself is many, or that the Many are one, that is what I shall truly wonder at. And concerning all
<margin>F</margin> the other things likewise: if he should show the <term>genera</term> <note>Classes or categories of things.</note> and Forms themselves undergoing these contrary affections in themselves, that would be worthy of wonder. But if someone demonstrates that I am both 'one' and 'many,' what is the wonder? When he wants to show that I am 'many,' he will say that my right side is one thing and my left another, or my front and back, or upper and lower—for I think I participate in plurality. But when he wants to show I am 'one,' he will say that of the seven of us present, I am one man, participating also in the One. So he shows both to be true. Therefore, if anyone attempts to show that such things—
<margin>G</margin> like stones and wood and the like—are both many and one, we shall say he is demonstrating that a thing is many and one, not that the One is many or the Many one. He says nothing wonderful, but only what we would all admit. But if someone should first divide and separate the Forms themselves by themselves—such as Likeness and Unlikeness, Plurality and the One, Rest and Motion, and all such things—as I was just saying, and then show that these are able to be mixed and separated among themselves, I would be wonderfully amazed, Zeno. I think these matters have been handled very bravely in your book, but I would be much more amazed, as I say, if someone could show this same difficulty being woven into the Forms themselves in every way—just as you traced it in visible things, so also to show it in things grasped by reason."
<margin>H</margin> While Socrates was saying these things, Pythodorus said he thought Parmenides and Zeno were annoyed at each point. However, they were actually paying very close attention to him, frequently looking at each other and smiling, as if they were admiring Socrates. Indeed, when he finished speaking, Parmenides said: "O Socrates, how worthy you are of admiration for your impulse toward arguments! Tell me, then, have you yourself made this distinction you speak of, between...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...or that it is impossible for like things to be unlike, and thus also impossible for there to be "many"? For if there were many, an impossible thing would happen to them. Is this what your discourses intend? And do they intend nothing else but to assert through all points that there are not many things? And do you think that every single one of your reasons is a proof of this, and do you believe you have brought forth as many proofs as you have brought reasons, to show that there are not many? Is this what you say? Or do I myself not perceive it rightly? "On the contrary," Zeno responded, "you have understood extremely well what these writings mean." "I understand," said Socrates, "O Parmenides, that this Zeno here wishes to agree with you not only in friendship, but also in those things which he has composed. For he has written, in a way, the same thing as you; but by
<margin>B</margin> a certain variation he tries to deceive us, as if he were saying something other than what you say. For you, in your poems, contend that this whole which exists is One, and you exhibit most beautiful arguments for this. He, however, denies that there are many, providing very many and powerful proofs himself. While, therefore, one says 'One' and the other says 'not Many,' and both speak in such a manner that they do not seem to be inferring the same thing—even though they say nearly the same—those things seem to us to be spoken above our level." "It is so, O Socrates," said Zeno. "However, you do not entirely grasp the matter, although like Lakonian hounds you follow and track the sayings well. For first, this escapes you: that these writings do not exalt themselves for the reason that you think—as if it were a great achievement of ours
<margin>C</margin> that others could not follow. But what you think was intended, resulted instead as a defense. For these are truly written in support of Parmenides, against those who strive to pluck at him, saying that if indeed all is 'one,' many ridiculous things follow from this opinion, and even things thoroughly repugnant to itself. This writing, therefore, attacks those who wish there to be many things, and in turn objects to even more things, so that it may be clear that much more absurd things follow from their opinion—namely, that there are many—than from the opinion of Parmenides that there is One, if anyone should examine it diligently. On account of this contention, therefore, I composed the book in my very youth; but
<margin>D</margin> someone stealing it published it before I could deliberate whether it should be brought into the light or not. This, therefore, escapes you, O Socrates: that you think it was written not from youthful contention, but from elderly ambition. Nevertheless, as I said, you have guessed not ineptly." "I accept it," said Socrates, "and I think it is as you say. But answer me this: do you think there is a certain Form <note>original: "speciem"</note> of Likeness existing by itself? And another Form of Unlikeness contrary to this? In which two both I and you participate, and other things which we certainly call 'many'? And that whatever things participate in
<margin>E</margin> Likeness become like to the extent that they participate? And those in Unlikeness, unlike? And those in both, both? But if all things participate in both contraries existing, in that they participate in both, they are like and unlike among themselves; what is the wonder? For if someone were to say that Likeness itself was unlike, or Unlikeness itself like, he would be saying something monstrous, as I judge. But if someone should assert that things participating in both suffer both, it would seem to me, O Zeno, to be nothing to wonder at. Nor indeed would I wonder at it if someone said all things were 'one' because they participate in the One, and these same things again were 'many' because they also participate in plurality. But if he should show that which is the One itself to be many,
<margin>F</margin> and the many themselves to be one, I shall then wonder exceedingly. And concerning all other things in the same way. For if he should say the genera themselves and Forms receive those contraries in themselves, it will surely be worthy of admiration. Indeed, if someone demonstrates that I am 'one' and 'many,' it is nothing strange. If indeed, wishing to assert that I am many, he says that my right side is one thing, my left another, my front another, my back another, and finally my upper and lower parts similarly; for I myself am a participant in plurality, as I think. But wishing to show me as 'one,' he says that of us who are seven, I am one man,
<margin>G</margin> a participant in the 'one'; similarly, there is nothing to wonder at. Therefore, both are affirmed truly. If, then, anyone should attempt such things—to demonstrate the same things as one and many, namely stones and wood and other such things—we shall admit he has shown the thing itself to be one and many, but not the One to be many, nor the many to be one; nor has he said anything wonderful, but what we all confess. But if someone, from those things I said a little while ago, should first distinguish the Forms themselves separately according to themselves—such as Likeness, Unlikeness, Plurality, the One, Rest, Motion, and others of this kind—then should assert that these can be mixed and separated in themselves, I would indeed be astounded, O Zeno. And if I think those things you have written have been treated as becomes a brave man, yet I would wonder and rejoice much more if someone could
<margin>H</margin> explain more clearly this same question deeply entangled in the Forms themselves, just as it has been set forth in the things that are seen, so also in those which are grasped by reason." While Socrates was saying these things, Pythodorus said he thought Parmenides and Zeno were indignant at Socrates in each point; but they listened with a certain greatest attention, and frequently looking at one another, they smiled as if admiring Socrates. Whence, when Socrates had made an end of speaking, Parmenides said: "O Socrates, how worthy you are of admiration on account of that impulse for disputing. But I pray you tell me, have you yourself thus distinguished separately, as you say..."

E iiij <note>A printer's signature mark, used to keep the pages in order during binding.</note>

<summary>Socrates challenges Zeno to move beyond physical paradoxes—like a single person having many parts—and instead prove that abstract Forms like Unity and Plurality can themselves be contradictory. Zeno and Parmenides are impressed by the young Socrates' philosophical ambition and the clarity of his distinction between the sensible and intelligible worlds.</summary>

# OF PLATO

<margin>A</margin> "Have you yourself distinguished these <term>Forms</term> <note>original: "species" (Latin) / "εἴδη" (Greek). In Plato's thought, these are the perfect, eternal blueprints of things that exist in a higher reality.</note> as you say, and likewise separated the things that participate in them? And does it seem to you that there is such a thing as 'Likeness' itself, separate from the likeness we possess? And similarly a 'One' itself, and a 'Many' itself, and all those things you just heard from Zeno?" "It certainly seems so to me," Socrates replied. "And what about these?" asked Parmenides. "Is there a Form of Justice itself, and of the Beautiful, and of the Good, and of all such things?" "Yes," he said. "And is there a Form of Man, separate from us and all others like us—a Form of Man itself, or of Fire, or even of Water?"

<margin>B</margin> "Often, Parmenides," said Socrates, "I have been in doubt about these—whether one should speak of them in the same way as the others, or differently." "And do you also doubt, Socrates, whether things that might seem ridiculous—such as hair, mud, and filth, or any other very base and worthless thing—should have a separate Form assigned to each of them, existing as something distinct from the things we handle, or not?" "Not at all," said Socrates. "Rather, these things are just as we see them. To think there is a Form for them would perhaps be too absurd. Yet sometimes the thought has troubled me whether there might be something identical in all things; but when I stop there for a moment, I turn away,

<margin>C</margin> fearing that I might fall into an abyss of nonsense and perish. So, returning to those things which we previously said have Forms, I occupy myself with them." "You are still young, Socrates," said Parmenides, "and Philosophy has not yet fully embraced you. But it will embrace you, in my opinion, when you no longer neglect any of these things; for now, because of your age, you still look to the opinions of men. Tell me this, then: does it seem to you, as you say, that certain Forms exist, and that the things participating in them are named after them? For instance, those participating in Likeness become 'like,' those in Magnitude become 'great,' and those in Beauty and Justice become 'beautiful' and 'just'?" "Very much so,"

<margin>D</margin> said Socrates. "Then does each participant partake in the whole Form, or only a part of it? Or can there be some other way of participating?" "How could there be?" Socrates said. "Does it seem to you, then, that the whole Form, being one, is in each of the many participants? Or how is it?" "What prevents it from being one?" Socrates asked. "If it is one and the same in many separate things, it will be a whole one in many places at once, and thus it would be separate from itself." "Not at all," said Socrates. "Just as a single day is present everywhere at once and yet is not separated from itself, so nothing prevents each Form from being one and the same in all things at once without being separated from itself." "You gracefully show, Socrates, how one and the same thing is in many places at once, as if

<margin>E</margin> you were to cover many men with a sail and say that one whole thing is over many. Isn't that what you mean?" "Perhaps." "Then would the whole sail be over each man, or would a different part be over each?" "A part." "Therefore, Socrates," he said, "the Forms themselves would be divisible, and the things participating in them would partake only in a part; the whole would no longer be in each thing, but only a part of it." "So it appears." "Are you willing, then, to say that our one Form is truly divided, and yet remains one?" "In no way," he replied. "Consider this: if you divide 'Magnitude' itself, and each of many large things is large by a part of Magnitude that is smaller than Magnitude itself, does that not seem irrational?" "Entirely." "What then? If something has a small part of 'Equality,' will it, by possessing something smaller than Equality itself, be equal to anything?"

<margin>F</margin> "Impossible." "But if one of us has a part of the 'Small,' the Small itself will be larger than that part, since it is a part of it; and thus the Small itself will be 'large.' And that to which the removed part is added will be smaller, not larger, than it was before." "That cannot happen," he said. "In what way, then, Socrates," he asked, "will other things participate in your Forms, if they can participate neither in the whole nor in the parts?" "By Zeus, this does not seem at all easy to determine." "And what do you say to this?" "To what?" "I think you believe each Form is one for this reason: when many things seem 'large' to you, perhaps one single <term>Idea</term> <note>original: "idea" (Latin/Greek); often used interchangeably with "Form."</note> seems to be the same over all of them as you look at them, and so you think 'the Large' is one." "That is true," he said. "But what if you consider 'the Large' itself and the other large things

<margin>G</margin> in your soul in the same way? Will not another 'Large' appear again, by which all these must appear large?" "It seems so." "Therefore, another Form of Magnitude will appear, distinct from Magnitude itself and the things participating in it; and over all these, yet another, by which they are all large; and so each Form will no longer be one, but infinite in number." "But perhaps, Parmenides," Socrates said, "each of these Forms is a <term>notion</term> <note>original: "notio" (Latin) / "νόημα" (Greek); a "thought" or "concept" in the mind.</note>, and cannot exist anywhere but in our souls. In this way, each would be one, and the problems you just mentioned would not occur." "What then?" he asked. "Is each notion a 'one,' but a notion of nothing?" "That is impossible," he said. "But it is a notion of something?" "Yes." "Of something that exists, or does not exist?" "Of something that exists." "Is it not

<margin>H</margin> a notion of some one thing, which that notion recognizes as being the same over all instances—a single Idea?" "Certainly." "Then will this thing which is understood to be one, always being the same over all, not be a Form?" "That also seems necessary." "What then?" asked Parmenides. "If you say that other things participate in Forms, must you not also think that each thing is made of notions, and that all things 'think'? Or that they are notions, yet do not think?" "But..."

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> "Do you say," asked Parmenides, "that these Forms exist by themselves, and that the things which partake in them are separate? And does it seem to you that Likeness itself is something separate, of which we have a share, and similarly for the 'Many,' and all the things you heard from Zeno?" "It does," said Socrates. "And would you say the same of such things as a Form of Justice itself, and of the Beautiful, and the Good, and all such things?" "Yes," he said. "And is there a Form of Man, separate from us and all who are like us—a Form of Man itself, or of Fire, or even of Water?" "I have often been in doubt, Parmenides," he said, "about whether one should say the same of these as of the former, or something else." "And what about these, Socrates, which might seem even ridiculous—such as hair, or mud, or dirt, or any other very cheap and worthless thing? Do you doubt whether one should say there is a separate Form of each of these, being something other than the things we handle, or not?" "Not at all," said Socrates. "Rather, these things are exactly as we see them. To think there is a Form for them would be too strange. Yet sometimes the thought has troubled me whether there might be one same thing in all of them; but when I stand there, I flee,

<margin>B</margin> fearing I might fall into some bottomless pit of nonsense and be destroyed. So, returning to those things which we were just saying have Forms, I spend my time occupied with them." "You are still young, Socrates," said Parmenides, "and philosophy has not yet taken hold of you as it will, in my opinion, when you will not despise any of these things. But now, because of your age, you still look to the opinions of men. Tell me this: does it seem to you, as you say, that there are Forms, and that these other things, by partaking in them, get their names from them? For example, by partaking in Likeness they become like; in Magnitude, large; in Beauty and Justice, beautiful and just?" "Certainly," said Socrates. "Then does each partaker partake of the whole Form, or only a part? Or could there be some other way of partaking?" "How could there be?" he said. "Does it seem to you, then, that the whole Form is in each of the many things, while remaining one?" "What prevents it from being one, Parmenides?" said Socrates. "Because, being one and the same in many separate things, it will be a whole that is one in many places at once, and so it would be separate from itself." "It would not," he said. "For example, if a day is one and the same, it is in many places at once, and is no more separate from itself; so each of the Forms could be one and the same in all things at once." "Very pleasantly, Socrates," he said, "you make one and the same thing be in many places at once; as if, covering

<margin>E</margin> many men with a sail, you said there was one whole thing over many. Is that not the sort of thing you mean?" "Perhaps," he said. "Then would the sail be a whole over each man, or would a part of it be over one and another part over another?" "A part." "Then the Forms themselves, Socrates, are divisible," he said, "and the things partaking in them would partake of a part, and the whole would no longer be in each, but a part of each would be in them." "It appears so." "Are you then willing to say, Socrates, that our one Form is truly divided, and will it still be one?" "Not at all," he said. "For look," he said, "if you divide Magnitude itself, and each of the many large things is large by a part of Magnitude that is smaller than Magnitude itself, will that not seem irrational?" "Completely," he said. "What then? Will that which has a small part of 'the Equal' possess something by which, being smaller than the Equal itself, it will be equal to something?" "Impossible." "And if one of us has a part of 'the Small,' the Small itself will be larger than that part, since it is a part of it; and so the Small itself will be larger. And that to which the removed part is added will be smaller, not larger, than it was before." "That could not happen," he said. "In what way, then, Socrates," he asked, "will things partake of the Forms for you, if they can partake neither in the whole nor in the parts?" "By Zeus," he said, "it does not seem easy to me to define this at all." "And what about this? How do you feel about this next point?" "What is it?" "I think you believe each Form is one for this reason: when many things seem large to you, there seems perhaps to be one same idea over all of them when you look at them. Hence you think 'the Large' is one." "You speak the truth," he said. "But what about the Large itself and the other large things—if you look at them all in the same way with your soul, will not another 'Large' appear again, by which all these must appear large?" "It seems so." "Then another Form of Magnitude will appear, besides Magnitude itself and the participants; and over all these again another, by which all these will be large. And so each of your Forms will no longer be one, but infinite in number." "But, Parmenides," said Socrates, "might not each of these Forms be a thought, and not exist anywhere else but in souls? For in this way each would be one, and would no longer suffer the problems just mentioned." "What then?" he asked. "Is each of the thoughts a 'one,' but a thought of nothing?" "That is impossible," he said. "But of something?" "Yes." "Of something that is, or is not?" "Of something that is." "Is it not of some one thing, which that thought perceives as being over all, being a single idea?" "Yes." "Then will not this thing which is thought to be one, being always the same over all, be a Form?" "That seems necessary again." "What then?" said Parmenides. "Does it not follow that if you say other things partake of Forms, you must think either that everything is composed of thoughts and all things think, or that they are thoughts but do not think?"

<summary>Parmenides challenges young Socrates' theory of Forms, specifically questioning how physical objects can "participate" in an abstract Idea without dividing it. The dialogue introduces the famous "Third Man" argument, suggesting that if we need a Form to explain a group of things, we might need infinite layers of Forms to explain the relationship between the first Form and the objects.</summary>

# P A R M E N I D E S.

<margin>A</margin> "But this, too," he said, "does not stand to reason. Rather, Parmenides, it seems to me most likely that it is this way: these <term>Forms</term> <note>original: "εἴδη" (Greek) / "species" (Latin). These are the perfect, eternal archetypes of all things.</note> stand in nature like patterns; and other things resemble them and are likenesses of them. This 'participation' of other things in the Forms is nothing else than being made in their image." "If then," he said, "anything resembles the Form, is it possible for that Form not to be like <margin>B</margin> that which has been made in its image, insofar as the image was made to resemble it? Or is there any way for the like to be unlike that which is like it?" "There is not." "And is there not a great necessity that the like and that which it resembles must participate in one and the same Form?" "There is." "And that in which the like things participate so as to be like—will that not be the Form itself?" "Absolutely." "It is not possible, then, for anything to be like the Form, nor the Form like anything else. Otherwise, alongside the Form, another Form will always appear; and if that one is like something, yet another will appear; and there will never be an end to this constant production of new Forms, if the Form becomes like that which participates in it." "What you say is very true." "Therefore, it is not through likeness that other things participate in the Forms; we must seek some other way by which they participate." "So it seems." "Do you see then, Socrates," he said, "how great the <term>aporia</term> <note>original: "ἀπορία" (Greek) / "ambiguitas" (Latin). A state of philosophical deadlock or puzzle where no clear way forward exists.</note> is, if one defines Forms as being entities existing by themselves?" "Very much so." "Know well then," he said, "that you have not yet, so to speak, even grasped how great the difficulty is if you posit <margin>C</margin> each Form as something distinct and unified for every thing that exists." "How so?" he asked. "There are many other reasons," he said, "but this is the greatest: if someone were to contend that the Forms—being such as we say they must be—cannot even be known, no one could prove to the speaker that he is wrong, unless the one disputing it happened to be a man of great experience and natural ability, and was willing to follow a very long and complicated demonstration. Otherwise, the person who insists they are unknowable would remain unpersuaded." "Why so, Parmenides?" Socrates asked. "Because, Socrates, I think that you, or anyone else who posits that there is some <margin>D</margin> essence of each thing that exists 'in itself,' would agree first of all that none of these essences exist within us." "For how could it then exist 'in itself'?" said Socrates. "You are right," he said. "Therefore, those <term>Ideas</term> <note>original: "ἰδεῶν" (Greek) / "ideis" (Latin).</note> which are what they are in relation to one another have their essence in relation to themselves, and not in relation to the things in our world—whether you call them likenesses or however you define them—by participating in which we are named. Conversely, these things in our world, which share the same names as the Forms, exist in relation to themselves and not to the Forms; they belong to their own sphere, not to that of the Forms." "What do you mean?" Socrates asked. "For example," said Parmenides, "if one of us is a master or a slave of someone, he is not the slave of <margin>E</margin> 'Mastery itself' (the Form), nor is the master the master of 'Slaviness itself' (the Form). Rather, being a human, he is a master or slave of another human. But 'Mastery itself' is what it is in relation to 'Slaviness itself'; and likewise, 'Slaviness itself' is slaviness in relation to 'Mastery itself.' The things in us do not have their power over the things there, nor do the things there have power over us. As I said, the Forms are of themselves and relate to themselves, and the things in our realm likewise relate to themselves. Do you understand what I am saying?" "I understand perfectly," Socrates said. "And so," he said, "would not <term>Knowledge itself</term> <note>original: "ἐπιστήμη" (Greek) / "scientia" (Latin).</note>—that which is the essence of Knowledge—be the knowledge of that which is Truth itself?" "Certainly." "And furthermore, each specific branch of knowledge would be the knowledge of some specific thing that truly exists, would it not?" "Yes." "But the knowledge we possess would be the knowledge of the truth in our own realm? and likewise, each branch of knowledge in our world <margin>F</margin> would turn out to be the knowledge of some particular thing that exists in our world?" "Necessarily." "But as for the Forms themselves, as you admit, we do not possess them, nor can they be in our realm." "Certainly not." "And are the various genera of things known by the Form of Knowledge itself?" "Yes." "Which we do not possess." "No, we do not." "Therefore, none of the Forms are known by us, since we do not participate in Knowledge itself." "It does not seem so." "Then the <margin>Beautiful itself</margin> <note>original: "αὐτὸ τὸ καλὸν" (Greek) / "ipsum pulchrum" (Latin).</note> and the <margin>Good itself</margin> <note>original: "τὸ ἀγαθὸν" (Greek) / "ipsum bonum" (Latin).</note> are unknown to us, as are all the things we suppose to be Ideas existing in themselves." "It appears so." "Now consider something even more formidable than this." "What is that?" "You would say, I presume, that if there is such a thing as a genus of Knowledge itself, it is much more accurate than the knowledge in our world—and the same for Beauty and all the others?" "Yes." "Therefore, if anything else participates in Knowledge itself, would you not say that <margin>G</margin> God, more than anyone else, possesses this most accurate knowledge?" "Necessarily." "Then will God, possessing Knowledge itself, be able to know the things in our world?" "Why not?" "Because," said Parmenides, "we have agreed, Socrates, that those Forms do not have their power in relation to the things in our world, nor do the things in our world relate to the Forms. Each realm relates only to itself." "We did agree on that." "Therefore, if this most accurate Mastery and this most accurate Knowledge belong to God, his Mastery could never rule over us, nor could his Knowledge ever know us or anything else in our world. Just as we do not rule the gods with our earthly authority, nor do we know anything of the divine with our knowledge, so they, by the same logic, <margin>H</margin> are not our masters, nor do they know human affairs, being gods." "But surely," Socrates said, "it would be a most wondrous argument if one were to deprive God of knowledge." "These difficulties, Socrates," said Parmenides, "and many others besides, necessarily follow for the Forms, if these Ideas of things exist and if one defines each Form as something existing by itself. The result is that the hearer is perplexed and argues..."

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> "That," he said, "stands to reason. But it seems to me most likely that it is this way: these species <note>translated from Latin: "species" (Forms)</note> stand in nature like patterns, while other things are made similar to them and are their likenesses; and the participation of these things in the species is nothing other than being made similar to them. If, therefore, as you say, anything is similar to the species, is it possible for the species itself not to be similar to that which was made similar to it, insofar as it was made similar? Or can it be thought that the similar is not similar to the similar?" "Certainly not." "And must not the similar necessarily participate in the same species as that which it resembles?" "It must." "And that in which similar things participate to become similar, <margin>B</margin> will that not be the species itself?" "Altogether." "Therefore, nothing can be similar to the species, nor the species to another. For besides the species itself, another species would always emerge; and if that were similar to anything, yet another again. This progression will never cease, and a new species will always occur if the species becomes similar to the participant." "You speak very truly." "Therefore, it is not through similarity that other things participate in the species, but some other way of participating must be sought." "It appears so." "Do you see, O Socrates, how great an ambiguity follows if one distinguishes the species, which are species, as existing according to themselves?" "Very much so," he said. "Know further that you do not yet, so to speak, comprehend how <margin>C</margin> great the difficulty is if you place each species of things apart from others." "How so?" he asked. "There are many other points, but this is the greatest: because if someone were to contend that they ought not to be known, since they are such as we say species ought to be, no one could truly refute the one who says this, unless he were skilled in many things and possessed of genius—the one who contends this—and were prepared, moreover, to follow a demonstrator and one introducing many things through a long circuitous route. For he who contends they are unknown cannot be persuaded." "Why, O Parmenides?" said Socrates. "Because, O Socrates, I think both you and anyone else who posits a certain <margin>D</margin> essence existing by itself, would not grant that it exists in us. For in what way," said Socrates, "would it exist according to itself?" "You speak rightly. Therefore, do not all the ideas that relate to each other have their essence in relation to themselves, and not to the things that are around us—whether they be likenesses or however one might name them—by participating in which we are named for each thing? But the things around us, which share names with them, are themselves similarly in relation to themselves and not to the species; and they are of themselves, not of those species which are again named similarly." "How do you mean?" said Socrates. "As if one of us were the master or servant of someone, he does not exist as the servant of the 'Master' itself <margin>E</margin> which is the Form; nor is he who is called master the master of the 'Servant' itself which is the Form; but both of these exist as human beings. But Mastery itself is what it is of Servitude itself; and Servitude again in the same way is the servitude of Mastery itself. Neither the things that are in us refer to those, nor do the things that are there refer to us; but, as I said, they are of themselves and relate to themselves, and the things here relate similarly to themselves. Do you understand what I say?" "I understand entirely." "And is not Knowledge itself, which is Knowledge, the knowledge of that which is Truth itself?" "Entirely so." "And would not any of the sciences, which is what it is, be the science of some existing thing?" "Certainly." "But our science—will it not be the science of the truth that is around us? And again, will not each of our sciences be the science of each of those things <margin>F</margin> that are around us?" "It must be so." "Yet you admit that we neither have the species themselves, nor can they be around us?" "Certainly not." "Are not individual genera known by the species of Science?" "Certainly." "Which species we do not have." "Not at all." "Therefore, no species is known by us, since we are not participants in Science itself." "It does not appear so." "Thus the Beautiful itself and the Good itself are unknown to us, and finally all things which we suppose to be ideas." "So it seems." "Consider this also, which is even more serious." "What is that?" "Would you not confess that if there is some genus of Science itself, it would be much more excellent than this science of ours, and likewise Beauty itself and the rest?" "Yes." "Therefore, if anything <margin>G</margin> else is a participant in Science itself, you would say no one but God has the supreme knowledge?" "Necessarily." "But can God, having embraced Science itself, discern our affairs by it?" "Why not?" "Because," said Parmenides, "we have confessed, O Socrates, that those species do not have power over our things, nor our things over those above, but each refers to itself." "We agreed plainly." "Therefore, if the supreme Mastery itself and the supreme Science itself are with God, neither will their mastery ever rule us, nor will that science know us or any other of our things; but just as we do not rule the gods with our authority, nor do we perceive anything divine with our science, so they, by the same logic, will neither <margin>H</margin> be our masters, nor will they, being gods, notice human affairs." "But will this speech not seem very wonderful," he said, "if one deprives God of knowledge?" "These things, O Socrates," said Parmenides, "and many others besides these, must necessarily happen to the species, if indeed these are the ideas of things, and each of these is something distinct by itself. Whence anyone who hears vacillates..."

<margin>The Beautiful itself and the Good itself are unknown to us.</margin>

<summary>Parmenides presents the "Third Man" argument, suggesting that if Forms resemble physical things, an infinite chain of Forms is required. He also argues that if Forms are separate from the human world, they are unknowable to us, and conversely, human affairs are unknowable to God.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: On the previous page, Parmenides concluded his "Third Man" argument, demonstrating the logical difficulties in Socrates's early theory of "Forms" or "Ideas." He now moves to explain why, despite these difficulties, the theory is necessary for the very possibility of thought and speech.</meta>

# PLATONIS
<note>original: "Platonis" (Latin). The Works of Plato.</note>

He hears these things and doubts whether perhaps <term>Ideas</term> <note>original: "ideae" (Latin) / "εἴδη" (Greek). The perfect, eternal archetypes or blueprints of things in the world.</note> are nothing at all; or, if they do exist, he suspects they must be entirely unknown to human nature. In saying this, while he may seem to have a point, the matter—as was shown just before—appears strange and difficult to believe. It belongs to a man of very great natural talent to be able to perceive what the <term>Genus</term> <note>original: "genus" (Latin) / "γένος" (Greek). A class or kind of being.</note> of each thing is by itself, and what the essence of each thing is according to itself. Furthermore, it is the task of an even more wonderful man to be able to teach these things to others once he has discovered them, having sufficiently distinguished all things. "I agree with you, Parmenides," said Socrates, "for what you say resonates wonderfully with my own mind." "Nevertheless," said Parmenides, "if someone, moved by the aforementioned reasons, does away with the <term>Forms</term> of existing things and does not distinguish a specific Form for each individual thing, he will find nowhere to turn his intellect, since he has not allowed the <term>Idea</term> of each existing thing to remain always the same; and in this way, he will utterly subvert the faculty of <term>discourse</term> <note>original: "differendi" (Latin) / "διαλέγεσθαι" (Greek). The art of philosophical debate or dialectic.</note>. You, too, seem to me to have perceived such a reason especially." "What you say is true," he replied. "What then will you do about philosophy? Where will you turn if these things are unknown?" "I do not seem to discern that at the present time." "Before you have exercised yourself, O Socrates," he said, "you are attempting to define what the beautiful, the just, the good, and each of the other Forms are. I noticed this lately when I heard you here disputing with this <term>Aristotle</term> <note>A different Aristotle than the famous philosopher; this was a young man who later became one of the Thirty Tyrants in Athens.</note>. Believe me, that impulse of yours which carries you toward rational arguments is beautiful and divine. But gather yourself, and exercise yourself more diligently in that faculty which seems useless to many and is called <term>idle chatter</term> <note>original: "garrulitas" (Latin) / "ἀδολεσχία" (Greek). A derogatory term used by critics of philosophers to describe their long, abstract debates.</note> while you are still young; otherwise, the truth will escape you." "What then is the method of this exercise, Parmenides?" "The one," he said, "which you heard from Zeno. But I also admired that remark of yours to him, when you said that one should not stop the thought on those things which are perceived by the eyes and their errors, but should ascend to those things which one might chiefly comprehend by reason and believe to truly exist." "Because it seems to me," Socrates said, "that in this way it is not difficult to explain things like likeness and unlikeness, and other things that belong to existing things." "And you have spoken well," he said. "But besides this, one must also observe this: that you should not only suppose 'if something is' and then consider what follows from that supposition, but you should also suppose 'if it is not,' if you wish to be properly exercised." "How do you mean that?" "For example," he said, "if you wish to exercise concerning that supposition which Zeno introduced: 'if many things exist,' what will happen to the many themselves in relation to themselves and to the One, and to the One in relation to itself and to the many? And again, if many things 'do not exist,' one must again consider what happens to the One and to the many, both in relation to themselves and to each other. And again, if you suppose that 'likeness exists' or 'does not exist,' what follows from each supposition, both for the things supposed and for all other things, in relation to themselves and to each other. The same logic applies to unlikeness, motion, rest, generation, corruption, being, and non-being. To embrace it in one word: concerning whatever is supposed to either be or not be, or to undergo any other condition, one must consider the consequences in relation to itself and to each of the others you choose—to several, and to the whole similarly. And then consider the others in turn, in relation to themselves and to whatever else you choose, whether you have posed the thing as existing or as not existing—if you are to perfectly inspect the truth after being absolutely exercised." "The task you describe is a difficult one," he said, "and I do not entirely understand you. Why don't you yourself take up a hypothesis and run through it in that manner, so that I may understand more clearly?" "O Socrates, you impose a great burden on an old man." Then Socrates said, "Why don't you yourself, O Zeno, run through this matter?" To which Zeno, smiling, replied, "Let us, O Socrates, ask Parmenides himself, for what he says is no light matter. Do you not see how great a task you are demanding? If there were more of us, it would not be proper to ask this. For it is unseemly to treat such things in the presence of many, especially for an old man. For many are ignorant that without this wandering and discourse through all things, it is impossible for the mind to encounter and possess the truth. Therefore, O Parmenides, I join Socrates in his prayer, so that I too may hear these things after so much time has passed." When Zeno had said this, Antiphon said that Pythodorus related that he himself, and Aristotle, and all the rest entreated Parmenides to demonstrate what he had said and not to do otherwise. Then at last Parmenides said, "I must comply, 

<margin>The Ibycean horse.</margin>
even though I feel I am falling into the same situation as the <term>horse of Ibycus</term> <note>Ibycus (6th century BC) was a poet who compared himself to an old, prize-winning racehorse who trembles as he is forced to return to the chariot races in his old age.</note>. To him, an athlete and an elder about to undergo a chariot contest and fearing the outcome because of his experience, Ibycus compared himself, saying: 'Unwillingly, I too, now an old man, am forced to return to love.' For the same reason, I seem to myself to be trembling greatly when I think how I, at my age, can swim through such a deep sea of discourse. Nevertheless, I must be compliant, since Zeno himself asks; for we are of the same company. Where then shall we begin? What shall we first suppose? Or, since we have decided to play this <term>laborious game</term> <note>original: "negotiosum ludum" (Latin) / "πραγματειώδη παιδιάν" (Greek). A famous Platonic oxymoron describing the serious work of philosophy as a kind of play.</note>, shall I start from myself and my own position—about the One itself—asking whether it is 'One' or 'not One,' and what follows?" "By all means," said Zeno. "Who then will answer me? The youngest? For he will give the least trouble, and what he thinks...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...that either these things do not exist, or if they do exist, it is a great necessity that they are unknown to human nature. And the person saying these things seems to have a point, and as we were just saying, it is wonderfully difficult to be persuaded otherwise. It requires a man of very good natural parts to be able to learn that there is a certain <term>Kind</term> <note>original: "γένος" (Greek). A class or category.</note> for each thing, and an essence itself according to itself; and it requires a still more wonderful man to be the one who will find this out and be able to teach another to distinguish all these things sufficiently. "I agree with you, Parmenides," said Socrates, "for you speak entirely according to my mind." "But yet," said Parmenides, "if someone, O Socrates, does not allow that there are <term>Forms</term> <note>original: "εἴδη" (Greek).</note> of things that exist, looking at all these difficulties and others like them, and does not define a Form for each individual thing, he will have nowhere to turn his thought, not allowing that the <term>Idea</term> of each existing thing is always the same; and in this way he <margin>B</margin> will utterly destroy the power of <term>discourse</term> <note>original: "διαλέγεσθαι" (Greek). The practice of dialectic or logical conversation.</note>. You seem to me to have been especially aware of this." "You speak the truth," he said. "What then will you do about philosophy? Where will you turn while these things are unknown?" "I do not think I see clearly, at least for the present." "For," he said, "before you are exercised, O Socrates, you are attempting to define something beautiful, and just, and good, and each one of the Forms. For I noticed it the other day as well, hearing you here as you were conversing with this Aristotle. Truly, the impulse you have toward arguments is beautiful and divine, you may be sure; but draw yourself back and exercise yourself more through what is thought to be useless and is called <term>idle chatter</term> <note>original: "ἀδολεσχίας" (Greek).</note> by the many, while <margin>C</margin> you are still young; otherwise, the truth will escape you." "What then, Parmenides," he said, "is the manner of this exercise?" "This one," he said, "which you heard from Zeno. Except for this, I also admired you for what you said to him: that you did not allow the wandering of thought to look at the visible things or be about them, but about those things which one might especially grasp by reason and might lead one to think they are Forms." "For it seems to me," he said, "that in this way it is not at all difficult to show that things are both like and unlike, and undergo anything else that happens to existing things." "And well said," he said. "But it is necessary to do this one thing more in addition to that: not only to suppose 'if each thing exists' and look at the consequences of that hypothesis, but also to suppose 'if this same thing does not exist,' if you wish to be better exercised." "How do you mean?" he said. "For example," <margin>D</margin> he said, "if you wish to suppose concerning this hypothesis that Zeno hypothesized, 'if many things exist,' what must follow both for the many things themselves in relation to themselves and to the One, and for the One in relation to itself and to the many; and again, 'if many things do not exist,' to look again at what will follow both for the One and for the many, both in relation to themselves and to each other. And again, if you suppose 'if likeness exists,' or 'if it does not exist,' what will follow on either hypothesis for the things themselves hypothesized and for the others, both in relation to themselves and to each other. And concerning unlikeness the same logic holds, and concerning motion, and rest, and generation and corruption, and concerning being itself and non-being. And in one word, concerning whatever you might ever suppose as existing or as not existing, or undergoing any other condition, you must look at the consequences in relation to the thing itself and to each one of the others—whichever you might choose—and <margin>E</margin> to more and to all of them likewise; and the others again in relation to themselves and to whatever else you might ever choose, whether you suppose that which you hypothesized as existing or as not existing—if you intend, after being perfectly exercised, to see the truth in a sovereign way." "You describe a massive undertaking, Parmenides," he said, "and I do not quite understand. Why don't you yourself go through a hypothesis for me, so that I may learn better?" "You assign a lot of work, O Socrates," he said, "to one of my age." "But you, Zeno," said Socrates, "why don't you go through it for us?" And he said that Zeno, laughing, said, "Let us ask Parmenides himself, O Socrates. For it is no small thing he speaks of. Or do you not see how great a task you are assigning? If we were more people, it would not be worthy to ask. For it is unseemly <margin>F</margin> to speak of such things before many, especially for one of such an age. For the many are ignorant that without this wandering and traversal through all things, it is impossible to have a mind that has encountered the truth. I therefore, O Parmenides, join with Socrates, so that I myself may hear it after such a long time." When Zeno had said this, Antiphon said that Pythodorus said that he himself and Aristotle and the others begged Parmenides to demonstrate what he was saying and not to do otherwise. Parmenides then said, "It is necessary to comply. And yet, I feel I have suffered the same thing as the horse of Ibycus. To that horse, who was an athlete and rather old, about to compete in a chariot race, <margin>G</margin> and who was trembling at what was to come because of his experience, Ibycus compared himself, saying that he himself, being so old, was being forced unwillingly to go into love. And I, when I remember, seem to be very much afraid how a man of my age is to swim through such a great and vast multitude of words. Nevertheless, I must be gracious, since Zeno also asks. For we are of the same group. Where then shall we start? And what shall we hypothesize first? Or do you wish, since it seems we are to play a <term>laborious game</term> <note>original: "πραγματειώδη παιδιάν" (Greek).</note>, that I start from myself and my own hypothesis, hypothesizing about the One itself—whether it is One or not One—what must follow?" "By all means," said Zeno. "Who then," he said, "will answer me? Shall it be the youngest? For he would <margin>H</margin> be the least meddlesome, and would most likely answer what he thinks; and at the same time, I..."

<summary>Parmenides explains that despite the logical flaws in the Theory of Forms, they are necessary for meaningful thought and speech. He agrees to lead a complex logical exercise (the "laborious game") to train the young Socrates, using his own hypothesis about "the One."</summary>

<meta>Continuity: On the previous page, Parmenides concluded his critique of the young Socrates’s theory of Ideas. He suggested that despite the logical difficulties, one must maintain the existence of absolute Forms to avoid destroying the possibility of philosophical thought. Now, at the request of the company, Parmenides agrees to demonstrate his rigorous method of "dialectical exercise" using his own famous "One" as the subject. He chooses the youngest person present—Aristotle—to be his respondent.</meta>

# PARMENIDES

...that hypothesis would be a rest <note>original: "ἀνάπαυλα" (Greek). A pause or respite from the labor of the argument.</note> for me. "I am ready for you, Parmenides," said Aristotle. "For you mean me when you say 'the youngest.' So ask your questions, and I will answer." Very well then, he said. If the **One** <term>One</term> <note>original: "τὸ ἕν" (Greek) / "vnum" (Latin). The ultimate principle of unity or being in Parmenides's philosophy.</note> exists, can it be anything other than not being many? "How could it be?" Then it must have neither a part nor be a whole. "Why is that?" A part, surely, is a part of a whole. "Yes." And what about a whole? Is it not a whole from which no part is missing? "Certainly." In both cases, then, the One would be composed of parts, whether it is a whole or has parts. "Necessarily." And in either case, the One would thus be many, and not one. "True." Yet it must be not many, but one. "It must." Therefore, if the One is to be truly one, it will neither be a whole nor have parts. "Indeed not."

Now, if it has no parts, it has no beginning, no end, and no middle; for such things would already be parts of it. "Correct." Furthermore, a beginning and an end constitute the limit <note>original: "πέρας" (Greek). A boundary or defining edge.</note> of each thing. "Of course." The One is therefore **infinite** <note>original: "ἄπειρον" (Greek). Literally 'without limit' or 'unbounded.'</note>, if it has neither beginning nor end. "Infinite." And it is also without shape; for it partakes of neither the round nor the straight. "How so?" The round is surely that whose extremities are everywhere equidistant from the center. "Yes." And the straight is that whose middle is directly in front of both extremities. "Exactly." Thus, the One would have parts and be many if it partook of either a straight or a circular shape. "Entirely so." Therefore, it is neither straight nor circular, since it has no parts. "Correct."

Furthermore, being such as this, it could be nowhere. For it could be neither in another nor in itself. "How?" If it were in another, it would be contained in a circle by that in which it exists, and would be touched by it in many places. But it is impossible for that which is one, partless, and does not partake of a circle to be touched in many places all around. "Impossible." On the other hand, if it were in itself, it would be its own container; for it could not be in itself unless it also contained itself. "Impossible indeed." For then the container would be one thing and the contained another; for the same thing as a whole cannot both act and be acted upon in the same way at once. Thus, the One would no longer be one, but two. "It would not." Therefore, the One is not anywhere, being neither in itself nor in another. "It is not."

Consider now whether, being in this state, it is possible for it to stand still or be in motion. "Why should it not?" Because if it moved, it would either be carried along or undergo alteration; for these are the only types of motion. "Yes." But if the One were altered from itself, it would surely be impossible for it to still be one. "Impossible." Therefore, it does not move by way of alteration. "It seems not." But does it move by being carried along? "Perhaps." Now, if the One were carried along, it would either revolve in a circle in the same place or change from one place to another. "Necessarily." But that which revolves in a circle must stand upon a center, and the other parts that revolve around the center must be different from the center itself. But for that which has neither center nor parts, what possible way is there for it to be carried in a circle around a center? "None at all." But what if it changes place, appearing now here and now there, and moves in that way? "If it moves at all." Did we not say it was impossible for it to be in anything? "Yes." Is its "becoming" in something even more impossible? "I do not understand how." If something is in the process of "becoming" <note>original: "γίγνεται" (Greek). Refers to the state of coming-to-be or entering into a condition.</note> in something, is it not necessary that it is not yet in it while it is still becoming, nor yet entirely outside of it if it is already becoming? "Necessarily." Now, if anything experiences this, it can only be something that has parts; for part of it would already be inside, while another part would be outside. But that which has no parts cannot possibly be entirely inside or entirely outside of something at the same time. "True." And if it has no parts and is not a whole, is it not even more impossible for it to become anywhere? Since it can neither become there by parts nor as a whole? "So it appears." Therefore, it does not change its location by going anywhere or becoming present in anything, nor is it moved by revolving in the same place, nor by alteration. "It does not seem so."

According to every type of motion, then, the One is **immobile**. "Immobile." Furthermore, we say it is impossible for it to be in anything that is the same. "We do." Therefore, it is never in the "same" <note>original: "τῷ αὐτῷ" (Greek). Refers to self-sameness or a fixed location.</note>. "Why?" Because it would then be in that thing which is "the same." "Exactly." But we saw it was impossible for it to be either in itself or in another. "Indeed." Therefore, the One is never in the same state or place. "It seems not." But that which is never in the same state or place never enjoys rest or stands still. "It cannot." The One, then, it seems, neither stands still nor moves. "So it appears."

Furthermore, it will not be the same as another or itself, nor again different from itself or another. "How so?" If it were different from itself, it would be different from the one, and would not be one. "True." And if it were the same as another, it would be that other, and would not be itself; so in this way also it would not be what it is—namely, one—but something other than one. "Exactly." Therefore, it will not be the same as another or different from itself. "No." Nor will it be different from another, so long as it is one. For it does not belong to the "one" to be different from something, but only to "the different." "Correct." By virtue of being one, then, it will not be different. "Certainly not." But if it is not different by virtue of being one, it will not be different by virtue of itself; and if not by itself, not it itself. And since it is in no way different, it will be different from nothing. "Correct."

Nor will it be the same as itself. "Why not?" Is the nature of the One the same as the nature of the "Same"? <note>original: "τοῦ ταὐτοῦ" (Greek). The concept of identity or sameness.</note> "Why not?" Because when a thing becomes the same as something, it does not thereby become one. "How so?" That which becomes the same as "the many" must necessarily become many and not one. "True." But if the One and the Same did not differ, whenever something became the same, it would always become one; and whenever it became one, it would be the same. "Certainly." Therefore, if the One is to be the same as itself, it will not be one with itself; and thus, being one, it will not be one. But this is surely impossible. "It is therefore impossible for the One to be either different from another or the same as itself." "Impossible." Thus the One would be neither different nor the same, either in relation to itself or to another. "It would not."

<column-break/>

<margin>The first supposition: if the One exists, how the division should be understood. For the word "Is" is added for the sake of the argument.</margin>
<margin>Reasons by which it is denied that identity is in itself.</margin>
<margin>Locomotion and alteration are the only forms of motion.</margin>
<margin>That which moves in a circle must stay at a center.</margin>
<margin>To be acted upon through parts.</margin>
<margin>The nature of the "one" is different from that of the "same."</margin>

<summary>In this opening movement of the "First Hypothesis," Parmenides uses a series of negative deductions to show that if the "One" is absolutely one, it can have no parts, no limits, no shape, no location, no motion, and no identity with itself or others. This demonstrates the paradoxical nature of absolute unity, which seems to exclude all qualities that would allow it to exist in the world.</summary>
<keywords>The One, unity, parts and wholes, infinity, shape, motion, alteration, locomotion, identity, difference, Aristotle (respondent)</keywords>
