<meta>Continuity: On the previous page, Parmenides established that the "One" cannot have parts or be a whole, and thus has no beginning, middle, or end, making it infinite and formless. He now moves into more abstract relations: whether the One can be "the same" or "different," "like" or "unlike," or exist within the framework of "time."</meta>

# PLATO

nature, which is the nature of the same thing. Why? Because when something is the same as another, it does not yet become one. Why is that? Because if it were the same as many things, it would necessarily become many, not one. True. But if "the one itself" and "the same itself" did not differ at all, whenever something became the same, it would always become one; and whenever it became one, it would always be the same. Most certainly. Therefore, if the one itself were the same as itself, it would not exist for itself as one; and thus, being one, it would not be one. That is impossible. It is therefore impossible for the one itself to be either different from another or the same as itself. Impossible. By this reasoning, the one can be neither the same nor different, whether in relation to itself or to another. Certainly not. But neither can it be like or unlike anything, either itself or another. Why? Because that which is "like" is that which has something "the same" happen to it. Indeed. However, it appeared from what was said before that "the same" is distinct in nature from "the one." It certainly appeared so. Nevertheless, if the one receives anything beyond being one, it undergoes becoming more than one. But that is impossible. So it is. For this reason, the one never allows itself to be "the same," either to itself or to another. It does not seem so. Therefore, it cannot be like itself or another. So it appears. Nor does it endure being "different" any more than that; for here it would happen to be more than one. More indeed. Because that which is "different" from itself or from another is also made "unlike" either to itself or to some other; just as that which receives being "the same" becomes "like." Correct. Hence, since the one in no way admits "different," it will never become "unlike" either itself or another. Never indeed. Therefore, the one is never either like or unlike itself or another. It seems not. Furthermore, being of this kind, it is neither equal nor unequal to anything, either itself or another. 
<margin>What equality is.</margin>
How so? That which is equal is of the same measures as that to which it is called equal. That is so. That which is greater or smaller has more measures than the smaller things it is compared to, and fewer than the larger ones. Certainly. And to those with which it is incommensurable, it will be of smaller measures in some cases and larger in others. Why not? Is it not impossible that what in no way participates in "the same" should have the same measures or anything else "the same"? Impossible. Therefore, it will be equal neither to itself nor to another, since it does not use the same measures. Not at all, it appears. Furthermore, if it were measured by more or fewer measures, it would consist of as many parts as measures; and again it would no longer be one, but rather as many as there are measures in it. Correct. But if it were of one measure, it would become equal to the measure itself. However, it appeared impossible for the one itself to be equal to anything. It certainly appeared so. Therefore, because it participates neither in one measure nor in many, nor even in a few, nor in any way in "the same," it will never, it seems, be equal to itself or to another; nor furthermore will it be greater or smaller than itself or another. It is exactly so. Or perhaps the one appears to be older, or younger, or even of the same age as something? What prevents it? Truly. For if it shares the same age with itself or with another, it will participate in equality and similarity of time. Yet it has been shown that no equality or similarity can belong to the one itself. It has indeed been shown. Did we not also say that it possesses neither inequality nor dissimilarity? Most definitely. In what way, then, can that which is of this sort be older or younger than anything, or equal in age to any? In no way. Therefore, the one itself will not be younger, nor older, nor of equal age either to itself or to another? It does not appear so. Likewise, the one itself, being such as it is, will never be in any time at all. For it is necessary that whatever is in time always becomes older than itself. It is necessary. That which is older is always older than something younger. Why not? Therefore, that which is becoming older than itself is also at the same time becoming younger than itself, if indeed it is to have something it becomes older than. How do you mean? In this way: one thing does not need to become different from another when it already is different; rather, to that which already is, it "is" already; to that which has been, it "has been"; to that which will be, it "will be." But for that which is "becoming," the difference has not yet "been," nor "will be," nor "is"; but it "becomes," and not otherwise. It must be so. But indeed "older" is something opposite to "younger," and to nothing else at all. It is. Therefore, that which becomes older than itself must also necessarily become younger than itself at the same time. It seems so. Furthermore, it does not become for a longer time than itself, nor a shorter one; but it becomes, and is, and was, and will be for an equal time with itself. These things are also necessary. It seems necessary, then, that whatever is in time and participates in such a thing, must share the same age with itself, and at the same time become both older and younger than itself. It appears so. But none of these attributes <note>original: "passionibus" (Latin) / "παθημάτων" (Greek). In a philosophical sense, these are properties or "undergoings" of a subject.</note> happen to the one itself. None. Therefore, it does not participate in any time, nor is it in any time. Truly not, as the argument dictates.
<margin>The words Is, Was, etc. signify time.</margin>
What then? Do not "it was," "it has been," and "it was becoming" seem to signify participation in time that is past? Indeed they do. And will not "it will be," "it will become," and "it will have been made" designate the future for us? The future. And "is" and "becomes" are marks of the present time. Entirely so. If then the one in no way participates in time, it neither was ever, nor was becoming, nor was it; nor has it now become, nor is it becoming, nor is it; nor will it afterwards become, nor will it be...
<meta>Catchword: born (fragment of "become")</meta>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...becomes [the same] as something, it becomes one. But how else? Becoming the same as the many, it must necessarily become many, and not one. True. But if "the one" and "the same" do not differ at all, whenever something becomes the same, it would always become one; and whenever it becomes one, it becomes the same. Quite so. If then the one shall be the same as itself, it will not be one with itself; and thus being one, it will not be one. But indeed this is impossible. It is therefore impossible for the one either to be different, or to be the same as itself. Impossible. Thus the one could be neither different nor the same, either to itself or to another. Indeed not. Nor will it be like anything, nor unlike, either to itself or to another. Why so? Because that which has experienced "the same" is "like." Yes. But "the same" appeared to be separate in nature from "the one." It did indeed. But if the one experienced anything <margin>B</margin> apart from being one, it would experience being more than one; and this is impossible. Yes. In no way then will the one have experienced "the same," either with another or with itself. It does not appear so. Therefore it is not possible for it to be like either another or itself. It does not seem so. Nor can it experience being "different"; for thus it would experience being more than one. For more indeed. That which experiences being "different" from itself or another would be unlike itself or another; if indeed that which experiences "the same" is "like." Correct. But the one, as it seems, in no way experiencing "different," is in no way unlike either itself or another. Indeed not. Therefore the one would be neither like nor unlike either another or itself. It does not appear so. And being <margin>C</margin> such a thing, it will be neither equal nor unequal, either to itself or to another. How so? If it were equal, it would be of the same measures as that to which it is equal. Yes. But being greater or smaller, to those things with which it is commensurable, it will have more measures than the smaller, and fewer than the larger. Yes. To those with which it is not commensurable, it will be of smaller measures than some, and larger than others. How could it be otherwise? Is it not impossible for that which does not participate in "the same" to be of the same measures, or of any other thing that is "the same"? Impossible. It would not be equal, then, to itself or another, if it is not of the same measures. It certainly appears so. But indeed, if it were of more or fewer measures, it would have as many parts as it has measures; and thus it would no longer be one, but as many as the measures. Correct. And if it were of one measure, it would become equal to the measure; but this appeared impossible, that it should be equal to anything. It did indeed. Therefore, participating neither in one measure nor many nor few, nor participating at all in <margin>D</margin> "the same," it will never, as it seems, be equal to itself or to another; nor again greater nor smaller, either than itself or another. Entirely so. What then? Does it seem possible for the one to be older, or younger, or to have the same age? Why not? Because if it has the same age, either with itself or another, it will participate in equality and likeness of time; which we said did not belong to the one—neither likeness nor equality. We did say that. And furthermore, we also said that it does not participate in unlikeness and inequality. <margin>E</margin> Quite so. How then will it be possible for it to be older or younger than anything, or to have the same age as something, being such as it is? In no way. The one therefore would be neither younger nor older, nor have the same age as itself or another. It does not appear so. Could the one then be in time at all, if it were such as this? Or is it not necessary, if anything is in time, that it always becomes older than itself? Necessary. And is not the older always older than a younger? Of course. Therefore, that which is becoming older than itself is becoming younger than itself at the same time; if indeed it is to have that which it becomes older than. How do you mean? Like this: nothing needs to become "different" from another when it is already "different"; <margin>F</margin> but to that which already is, it "is" already [different]; to that which has been, it "has been"; to that which will be, it "will be." But for that which is "becoming," the "different" has not yet "been," nor "will be," nor "is" yet; rather it "becomes," and not otherwise. It must be so. But "older" is a difference from "younger," and from nothing else. It is. Therefore that which becomes older than itself must necessarily also become younger than itself at the same time. It seems so. But indeed, it does not become for a more or less time than itself; but it becomes, and is, and has been, and will be for an equal time with itself. This is also necessarily so. It is necessary then, as it seems, that whatever things are in time and participate in it, each of them must have the same age as itself, and become at once both older and younger <margin>G</margin> than itself. It's likely. But none of these attributes belong to the one. They do not. Therefore it does not participate in time, nor is it in any time. Not indeed, as the argument says. What then? Do not "it was," "it has become," and "it was becoming" seem to signify a participation in time that once was? Very much so. And what of "it will be," "it will become," and "it will have become"—do they not signify what is to come, the future? Yes. And "it is" and "it becomes" <margin>H</margin>—do they not signify the present now? Entirely so. If then the one participates in no way in any time, it never became, nor was becoming, nor ever was; nor has it now become, nor is it becoming, nor is it; nor will it become hereafter, nor will it be.

<summary>This page presents a rigorous dialectical argument concluding that "the One" cannot have relations of identity, similarity, or equality, nor can it exist within time or age, as these would imply it is "many" or "becoming."</summary>
<keywords>The One, sameness, difference, likeness, unlikeness, equality, inequality, time, age, Parmenides, Plato, metaphysics</keywords>

--- Page 93 ---
<meta>Continuity: On the previous page, Parmenides concluded that if the "One" has no parts and no form, it cannot exist in time or space. He now moves to the logical conclusion of this "First Hypothesis": that such a "One" would be completely unknowable and, effectively, non-existent. He then proposes a "Second Hypothesis"—starting from the premise that the One *does* exist—which leads to the discovery of multiplicity and number.</meta>

# PARMENIDES.

<margin>A</margin> It is disputed; it is not. Most true. Is there any way for anything to participate in **essence** <note>original: "ousia" — often translated as "being" or "substance"</note> other than according to one of these? There is not. In no way, then, does the One participate in essence. It does not seem so. In no way, therefore, is the One. It does not appear so. It is not even so as to be "one," for it would then already be a "being" and a participant in essence. But as it seems, the One is neither one nor is it at all, if this argument is to be trusted. It is in danger of being so. And that which "is not"—could anything belong to this non-being, or come from it? And how? It has no name, then, nor any definition, nor any knowledge, nor perception, nor opinion. It does not appear so. It is not named, then, nor spoken of, nor thought of, nor known; nor does any of the things that exist perceive it. It does not seem so. Is it possible, then, that these things are so concerning the One? It does not seem so to me, at least. Do you wish, then, that we should return to the hypothesis from the <margin>B</margin> beginning, to see if anything different appears to us as we examine it? I certainly do wish it. If the One is, we say, what must its consequences be? Is that not so? Yes.
Observe then from the beginning. If the One is, is it possible for it to *be*, but not to participate in essence? It is not possible. Therefore, essence would belong to the One, though essence is not the same thing as the One. For if they were the same, that essence would not be "of the One," nor would the One participate in it; rather, saying "the One is" would be the same as saying "the One, one." But now our hypothesis is not "if the One is one, what follows," but "if the One is." Is it not so? Certainly. Does "is" not signify something different from "One"? <margin>C</margin> Necessarily. Does the One, then, participate in essence whenever one says "the One is"? Does the phrase "the One is" imply a union? Certainly. Let us say again: if the One is, what will follow? Consider then: is it not necessary that this hypothesis signifies the One is of such a kind as to have parts? How? In this way: if "is" is said of the One-that-is, and "one" is said of the Being-that-is-one—and yet essence and the One are not the same thing—must not the whole, being this very "One-Being," have as its parts "the One" and "Being"? Necessarily. Shall we say that each of these parts is a part only? Or must we say that a part is a part of a whole? <margin>D</margin> Of a whole. That which is One, then, is a whole and has parts. Entirely so. What then? Do these two parts of the One-Being—namely, "the One" and "Being"—ever leave each other? Does the One lack the part of Being, or Being lack the part of the One? It could not be. Again, then, each of the parts contains both the One and Being, and the smallest part is thus formed from at least two parts. And by the same logic, this continues forever: whatever part appears, it always contains these two parts. For the One always contains Being, and Being always contains the One. <margin>E</margin> So it is necessary that it always becomes two, and is never just one. Absolutely. In this way, then, would not the One-Being be an infinite multitude? So it seems. Come, follow this further. How? We say the One participates in essence, because of which it exists? <margin>E</margin> Yes. And for this reason, the One-Being appeared to be many. So it is. But what of the "One itself," which we say participates in essence—if we take it in thought alone, by itself, without that which we say it participates in, will it appear to be only one, or also many? One alone, I think. Let us look at something else. Essence must be one thing, and the One must be another, if the One is not essence, but participates in essence as a One. <margin>F</margin> Necessarily. If essence is one thing and the One another, the One is not different from essence because it is "One," nor is essence different from the One because it is "Essence"; rather, they are different from each other by "Difference" and "Otherness." Certainly. Therefore, "Difference" is not the same as the One or Essence. How could it be? What then? If we choose from among them—whether you want to choose Essence and Difference, or Essence and the One, or the One and Difference—in each choice, are we not choosing a pair which can rightly be called "both"? How? Like this: is it possible to say "Essence"? It is. And again to say "One"? That too. Has not each of them been spoken? Yes. And when I say "Essence and One," do I not say "both"? Certainly. And if I say "Essence and Difference" or "Difference and One," in each case am I not saying "both"? Yes. And those things which are rightly called "both," can they be "both" without being "two"? They cannot. And where there are two, is there any way for each of them not to be "one"? None at all. Since these things occur in pairs, each of them must be one. It appears so. And if each of them is one, and any one of them is added to any pair, do they not all become three? Yes. And three is an odd number, while two is even? How could they not be? <margin>G</margin> And where there are two, is it not necessary that "twice" exists? And where there are three, "thrice"? If the number two has the property of being twice one, and three has the property of being thrice one. Necessarily. And if there are two and there is "twice," must there not be "twice two"? And if there are three and "thrice," must there not be "thrice three"? How not? And if there are three and "twice," or two and "thrice," must there not be "twice three" and "thrice two"? Entirely necessary. There will then be even-times-even, and odd-times-odd, and even-times-odd, and odd-times-even. Certainly.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...nor will it happen, nor will it be. These things are most true. Can anything participate in **essence** <note>original: "essentia"</note> in any way other than according to one of these? Not otherwise. In no way, therefore, is the "One itself." <margin>In the word "Is," there is time & essence.</margin> It does not seem so at all. It is not, therefore, in such a way that it is "one." For it would then be "being" and a participant in essence; but, as it seems, the One itself is neither one, nor does it exist, if this reasoning is to be believed. It appears so. But for that which "is not," is there anything that belongs to it or is of it? But how? Therefore, it has no name, no discourse, no certain knowledge, no sense, no opinion. It does not seem so. Wherefore it is neither named, nor spoken of, nor thought of in opinion, nor known, nor is it perceived by any of those things that exist. <margin>B</margin> It certainly does not seem so. Is it possible for these things to be so concerning the One? Not as it seems to me. Do you wish, then, that we return to the principle of its <margin>Second hypothesis concerning the one, if it is.</margin> position, considering if perhaps as we return, things might appear differently to us? I certainly wish it. Did we not admit that if the One is, we must see what its consequences are? Indeed. Meditate again from the beginning: if the One is, is it possible for it to be, yet in no way participate in essence? Impossible. But the essence of the One will not be the same as the One itself. Otherwise, if it were the same, it would not be "its essence," nor would the One participate in it; but as often as "One is" was uttered, it would signify the same thing as if <margin>C</margin> we were saying "One." But now our position is not of this kind—namely, if "one," what will happen—but "if one is," is it not so? It is exactly so. Is it not said as if the word "is" signifies one thing, and the word "one" signifies another? Necessary. When we say "One is" as a shorthand, does that speech signify anything other than that one essence is communicated? Entirely. Again, then, let us say: if the One is, what may happen? Come, observe this. Is it not necessary for this hypothesis to predicate the One itself as if it has parts? In what way? In this way: if "to be" is said of the "existing One," and the "One" itself is said of the "one being," and essence and the One are the same, the one we have supposed <margin>An vnum & ens sit idem.</margin> <note>Translation of margin: "Whether the One and Being are the same."</note> being the same, is it not necessary that the whole "One-Being" itself exists, and its parts are both "One" and "Being"? Necessary. But do we call each of these parts merely a "part"? Or <margin>D</margin> is it necessary to predicate "part" of a whole? Of a whole. The One, therefore, is a whole and has a part. Completely. What then? Do these parts of the One-Being—namely, "One" and "Being"—so desert each other that "One" is lacking to "Being" itself, and "Being" is lacking to "One" itself? Certainly not. Therefore, each part embraces both One and Being at the same time: so much so that any part is constituted of at least two small parts. And according to the same reasoning, whatever small part is encountered, both are always enclosed in it. For the One always embraces Being, and Being always embraces the One in mutual <margin>E</margin> bonds. Whence, so that two emerge everywhere in any small part, it is necessary that "one" never exists [alone]. Entirely. Does not the "One-Being" by this reasoning become an infinite multitude? It <margin>That the one regarding essence is also many.</margin> seems so. Come, I pray, and continue this. In that we say the One participates in essence insofar as it *is*? We have said it. And for this reason, the One-Being appeared to be many? So it is. What if we think of the "One itself," which we said participates in essence, according to itself alone in the intelligence, apart from that which we said it participates in? Will it appear as one alone? Or will this itself be many? One alone, I think. Let us consider <margin>F</margin> now another thing. It is necessary for essence to be one thing, and the One itself to be another; if indeed the One is not essence, but participates in essence as a "one." It is necessary. But if essence is one thing and the One another, the One itself is not different from essence because it is "One," nor is essence different from the One because it is "Essence"; but by that which is itself "difference," and itself "otherness," they are different from each other. Entirely. For which reason "difference" is identical neither to the One nor to essence. True. What then? If we choose from these, whether you wish Essence and Difference, or Essence and the One, or the One and Difference—do we not in any assumption elicit things which can rightly be called "both"? How? In this way, I say: is it permitted to say "Essence"? It is. And again to say "One"? That too. Has not each of those been spoken? Each has been spoken. Whenever I say "Essence and One," <margin>G</margin> do I not say "both"? You do. And if "Essence and Difference," or "Difference and One," do I not in each of these say "both"? Entirely. But those things which are rightly called "both," can they be "both" yet not be "two"? By no means. But those which are "two," can they be thought of in such a way that each of them is not "one"? Not at all. Since, therefore, these things are "two" together, for that reason each one exists as "one." It seems so. If each of them is "one," and each one is connected to the other in a certain mutual marriage, do not three result in total? Greatly. But are not three "odd," and two "even"? Why not? And since there are two, is it not necessary that "twice" is present; and when there are three, "thrice"? Since in two, "one" is present twice, and in three, "one" is present thrice. Necessary. Finally, with two existing twice, it is necessary that there are "twice two"; and with three existing thrice, is it not necessary again that there are "thrice three"? Why not? What then: with three existing twice, and two existing thrice, is it not necessary that there be "twice three" and "thrice two"? It is entirely necessary. There will therefore be even-times-even, and odd-times-odd, as well as odd-times-even, and even-times-odd. Certainly.

<sig>F</sig>
<meta>catchword: Necessary</meta>

<summary>This page marks the transition between Parmenides' First Hypothesis (the One that does not exist) and the Second (the One that exists). It demonstrates that if the One exists, it must have "Being" as a part, leading to an infinite fractal of parts and the derivation of all numbers through addition and multiplication.</summary>

This leads to the realization that the One must participate in essence (existence), creating a duality between "One" and "Being."</meta>

# PLATO

**A** If these things are so, do you think any number is left out that does not necessarily belong there? None. Therefore, if the One is, there must also be number. Without doubt. Also, if there is number, there are many things, and an infinite multitude of beings; or is number not infinite in multitude while also participating in essence <note>original: "essentia" in Latin, "ousia" in Greek; refers to the fundamental substance or "being" of a thing</note>? Very much so. But if the whole number participates in essence, every tiny part of number will also participate in essence. Absolutely. Therefore, through all things which are many, essence is distributed, and it is absent from none of those things that are, whether it be the smallest or the largest. To doubt this is absurd; for how could essence be absent from any of the things that exist? In no way. It is divided, therefore, as much as possible, into the smallest and largest and into all things that are in any way, distributed most of all, and there are infinite parts of essence. So it is. Therefore, its parts are very many. Very many indeed.

**B** What then: is there any of these which is a part of essence, yet not itself a "one" thing? How could that happen? But since, I believe, it exists, it must always, as long as it exists, be some one thing; to be nothing is impossible. Without doubt. Therefore, not only is the One present in the whole of essence, but also in each of its individual parts, leaving no part behind, whether it be larger or smaller, or however it may be. So it is. Since it is the One, is it everywhere whole at the same time? Consider that carefully.

**C** I am considering it, and I see that this is impossible. It is therefore divided, if it is not whole. For it cannot be present to all the parts of essence at once unless it is divided. So it is. Furthermore, that which is divisible must necessarily be as many as there are parts. Necessarily. For this reason, we were not speaking correctly just now when we said essence was distributed into "very many" parts: for it is not divided into more than the One itself, but into an equal number. For neither does being <note>original: "ens"</note> lack the One, nor the One lack being, but these two are thoroughly equal throughout all things.

<margin>The One is both one and many, a whole and parts, etc. Every whole has a beginning, middle, and end.</margin>
**D** Exactly so, it appears. Therefore, the One itself, distributed by essence, is an infinite multitude. It is clear. So, not only is "one being" many, but the One itself, distributed by essence, must be many. It must indeed. Furthermore, from the fact that all parts are parts of a whole, the One will be limited according to the whole. Are not all the parts contained by the whole? They are contained. But that which contains is a boundary <note>original: "terminus" in Latin, "peras" in Greek</note>. It is. Therefore, "one being" is in a way one and many, whole and parts, and both finite and infinite in multitude. It appears so. Since it is limited, does it not also have extremes? It is necessary. Moreover, if it is a whole, will it have a beginning, a middle, and an end? Can any whole be found without these three? And if any of these were absent from that which is one, would it still be a whole? Not at all. Therefore, the One has a beginning, a middle, and an end. It has. The middle, moreover, is at an equal distance from the extremes on every side; for otherwise it would not be the middle. Certainly not.

**E** Furthermore, since the One is such, it participates in some shape <note>original: "figura"</note>, whether straight or round, or some other composed of both. It participates, without doubt. And if it is of this kind, it will be in itself and in another. In what way? Every part is in the whole, and none at all is outside the whole. Let it be so. Are the individual parts enclosed under the whole? Yes. But the One exists as all its parts, neither more nor less than the whole. So it is.

<margin>How it is understood to be contained by the One and itself.</margin>
**F** Is not the whole also one? Why not? If all parts are enclosed by the whole, and all things are the One and the whole itself, and each part is contained under the whole, then the One will be contained by the One, and thus the One itself will already be in itself. It seems so. Nevertheless, the whole is not in the parts, neither in all of them nor in any one. For if it were in all, it would necessarily be in one; and if it is not in some one part, it cannot be in all of them. But if this "one" consists of all parts, and the whole is in it, but not in one [part], how can it any longer be "one" in all of them? In no way. But it is no more in some of the parts. For if the whole were in some, the greater would be in the smaller. But that is impossible.

<margin>That which is nowhere, is nothing at all.</margin>
**G** Impossible. Since, therefore, the whole is neither in several, nor in one, nor even in all parts, is it not necessary for it either to be in some other thing, or to exist nowhere? Necessary. If it were nowhere, would it not be nothing at all? And yet, since it is a whole, and is not in itself, does it not remain for it to consist in another? Entirely. Insofar as the One is a whole, it is in another; but insofar as all things are its parts, and it is all those parts, it is in itself. And therefore it is necessary for the One to be both in itself and also in another. Without doubt.

<margin>How and why it stands and moves.</margin>
**H** And since such is the nature of the One, does it not necessarily follow that it stands and also moves? Why so? It stands, indeed, if it consists in itself. For being in the One, and not departing from it, it is in the same place in itself. It is indeed. But that which is always in the same place must always be at rest. It must. But on the contrary, that which is always in another must necessarily never be in the same place; if it is never in the same place, it can never be at rest; and that which does not stand still must move. So it is. It is necessary, therefore, that the One, since it is always in itself and in another, must also always stand and move. It seems so. Moreover, it must be the same as itself, and different from itself, and similarly the same and different in relation to other things, if indeed the things said above apply to it. In what way? For everything stands in relation to everything else in this way: it is either the same as it, or different; if it is neither the same nor other, it will be a part of that to which it is related, or as a part...

<column-break/>

<summary>This page contains a central section of Plato’s Parmenides, where the character Parmenides argues that if the "One" exists, it must be infinitely divisible and present in all parts of existence. He concludes that the One must simultaneously possess contradictory qualities: being both limited and infinite, whole and part, at rest and in motion.</summary>
<keywords>Plato, Parmenides, One and Many, Essence, Infinity, Paradox of Motion, Whole and Part, Dialectic</keywords>

<meta>Continuity: On the previous page, the dialogue examined how "the One" is distributed throughout essence, concluding that "the One" must be present in every part of being, no matter how small. This page continues the logical deduction of the properties of "the One" relative to itself and to "the others."</meta>

# PARMENIDES.

<margin>A</margin>...would be a whole. It appears so. Is the One, then, a part of itself? By no means. Therefore, it would not be a whole of itself, as if it were a part of itself. For that is not possible. But is the One something other than the One? No, indeed. So it will not be other than itself. Certainly not. If, then, it is neither other, nor a whole, nor has parts of itself in relation to itself, must it not already be the same as itself? It must. What then? If that which is elsewhere than itself exists in the same place where it is, must it not be other than itself, if indeed it exists elsewhere? It seems so to me. And yet we said the One is thus: both in itself and in another at the same time. For so it appeared. It follows, then, as it seems, that the One is other than itself. It seems so. What then? If something is other than something, will it not be other than an <margin>B</margin> "other"? Necessarily. Are not all things that are not "one," other than the One? And the One other than the "not-ones"? How could it be otherwise? Thus, the One is other than all the others. Other. Consider this also: are not "the Same" and "the Other" opposites of one another? Why not? Will "the Same" ever be in "the Other," or "the Other" in "the Same"? Never. If, then, "the Other" is never in "the Same," there is nothing among beings in which "the Other" exists for any length of time. For if it were in something for any time, during that time "the Other" would be in "the Same." Is that not so? It is. Since it is never in "the Same," "the Other" is never in any of the things that exist. <margin>C</margin> True. Therefore, "the Other" is neither in the "not-ones" nor in the One. No indeed. It follows then that the One is not other than the "not-ones," nor are the "not-ones" other than the One, by virtue of "the Other." Indeed not. Nor will they be other than one another, if they do not participate in "the Other." How could they? But if they are other neither by themselves nor by "the Other," will they not entirely escape being other than one another? They will. Furthermore, the "not-ones" do not participate in the One; for then they would not be "not-one," but would in some way be "one." True. For this reason, the "not-ones" are not even a <margin>D</margin> number; for if they had any number, they would not be entirely devoid of the One. Certainly not. What then? Are the "not-ones" parts of the One? Or would the "not-ones" then participate in the One? They would. If, therefore, this is altogether "one," and those are "not-one," the One will not be a part of the "not-ones," nor a whole with them as its parts; nor again will the "not-ones" be parts of the One, nor wholes of which the One is a part. No, indeed. But we said that things which are neither wholes, nor parts, nor other than one another, must be the same as one another. We did. Shall we then say that the One, being in this state relative to the "not-ones," is the same as them? Let us say so. <margin>E</margin> Therefore, the One, as it seems, is both other than the others and itself, and again the same as itself and them. So the argument persuades us. Is it then also both similar and dissimilar to itself and to the others? Perhaps. Since it has appeared to be other than the others, the others must also be other than it. Why not? Is it not other than the others in the same degree as they are other than it, neither more nor less? Why not? If neither more nor less, then similarly. Similarly. Furthermore, if it happens to the One to be other than the others, in the same way as the others are from it, it follows that the same condition belongs to both the One and the others. How do you mean? <margin>F</margin> Like this: Does not every name have a meaning <note>original: "significatum" in Latin; refers to the specific thing or essence a word points to</note>? It does. And do you speak the same name once or many times? I do. Whether you utter it once, do you name that of which it is the name: and if you speak it many times, do you not name the same thing? Or whether you utter the same name once or repeatedly, is it not necessary that you always mean the same thing? Always the same. Is not "the Other" also a name used for a certain specific thing? It is. Whenever you utter it, whether once or many times, you refer to nothing else, and name nothing else, than that of which it is the name. Necessarily. <margin>G</margin> When, therefore, we say that the One is other than the others, and the others other than the One, by saying the name "other" twice, we are not using it to signify anything else than that nature of which it is the name. Entirely so. If then the One is other than the others, and the others are other than the One, the One possesses the very same quality of "otherness" that is in the others; and whatever possesses the same quality is similar, is it not? Yes. Insofar as the One has the property of being other than the others, it is similar to all of them; for every thing is other than every other thing. It seems so. But is not "similar" the opposite of "dissimilar"? It is. And is not "the Other" the opposite of "the Same"? That also. And yet it was shown that the One is both the same as and other than the others. It was. To be the same as the others is a contrary state to being other than the others. Entirely. But insofar as it was other, it appeared similar. Yes. Therefore, insofar as it is the same, it will be dissimilar, according to the state contrary to that which produced similarity. For "the Other" produced similarity? Yes. Therefore "the Same" will produce dissimilarity; or it will not be the opposite of "the Other." It seems so. Therefore, the One will be both similar and dissimilar to the others: insofar as it is other, it is similar; insofar as it is the same, it is dissimilar. It has, as it seems, this reasoning as well. And it has this one too. Which? That insofar as it has the same property, it does not have a different property; and not having a different property, it is not dissimilar; and if not dissimilar, it is similar. But insofar as it has another property, it has a different one; and being different, it is dissimilar. You speak truly. Therefore, the One, because it is the same as the others...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...would be a whole. It is clear. Is not the One itself a part of itself? By no means. Therefore, it will not be a whole in relation to itself, as if it were a part of itself. For that is not possible. Is the One perhaps other than the One? Not at all. Therefore, it is not other than itself. Certainly not. If it is neither other, nor a whole, nor a part in relation to itself, what else now remains but that it be the same as itself? That very thing. But what? That which is elsewhere than its very self existing in the same way in itself, is it not forced to become other than itself, if indeed it exists elsewhere than its very self? It seems so to me. It appeared clearly that the One is of this kind, namely being in itself and being in another. It appeared indeed. From this, therefore, it is established that the One is other than itself. It seems so. <margin>B</margin> If indeed something is other than something, is it not other than an other? Necessarily. Whatever things are not "one," are they not other than the One, and the One other than those which are not "one"? Why not? Therefore, the One will appear other than all the others. Other. Consider besides whether "the Other" itself and "the Same" itself are opposites to each other. Why not? Will "the Same" ever want to consist in "the Other," or "the Other" in "the Same"? Never. Therefore, if "the Other" is never in "the Same," there is nothing among those things which are, in which "the Other" exists for any time. For if it were in something for any time, during that time "the Other" would be in "the Same." Is it not so? Certainly. Since indeed it never consists in "the Same," "the Other" will surely never be in any <margin>C</margin> of those things that are. You say true things. Therefore, neither in those things which are not "one," nor in the One will "the Other" be. Not indeed. It follows that the One cannot be other than those things which are not "one," nor those which are not "one" other than the One, through "the Other" itself. It follows clearly. Because unless they participate in "the Other" itself, they will not be able to be other in relation to each other. For in what way? But if they are other neither by themselves nor by "the Other" itself, they can in no way be other than each other. In no way. Furthermore, those things which are not "one" do not participate in the One; for they would not be "not-one," but in some way "one." True. For this reason, those which are not "one" are not even <margin>D</margin> a number. Otherwise, they would not be entirely devoid of the One if they should have any number. Not certainly. But are those which are not "one" parts of the One? Or would those which are not "one" perhaps participate in the One in this way? They would participate. If therefore this is altogether "one," and those are "not-one," the One will not be a part of those which are "not-one," nor a whole in relation to them as if they were parts; nor again will those which are "not-one" be particles of the One, nor even wholes as if the One existed as a part. Not indeed. But we have asserted that those things which are neither wholes nor parts, nor other than each other, must be the same as each other. We have asserted it. Do we then admit the One, since it behaves in this way toward those which are not "one," is the same as them? We admit it. <margin>E</margin> Therefore the One, as it seems, is something other than the others and from itself, and again the same as itself and them. So the logic persuades. Is it also similar and dissimilar to itself and the others? Perhaps. After it appeared to be other than the others, the others will also be other than it. What forbids it? Is it not so other than the others as the others are from it, neither anything more nor less? Why not? If neither more nor less, it remains that it is similarly. Similarly. Furthermore, if it happens to the One that it be other than the others in the same way as the others are from it, from this it follows that the same certain condition belongs both to the One and to the others. <margin>F</margin> In what way do you say this? Thus. Does not every name have its own signified meaning? It has. But do you pronounce the same name either many times or once? I do. Whether when you bring it forth once, do you call upon that of which it is the name; but when many times, not that? Or rather, whether you pronounce the same name once or again and again, is it necessary that you always imply the same thing? Always the same. Is not "the Other" itself a name established to signify something proper? It is. Therefore, as often as you bring forth this name, whether once or many times, you do not refer it to another, nor do you name anything else than that of which this is the name. Necessarily. When therefore we say the One is other than the others, and those are other than the One, <margin>G</margin> pronouncing this name "other" twice, we are never led to signify anything else than the nature of which it is the proper name. Entirely so. If therefore the One is other than those, and the others are other than the One, it experiences that same "otherness" which is in the others; according to that, not according to something else, the One is other than the others. But whatever experiences the same thing is similar, is it not? Yes indeed. But according to what the One has, namely that it be other than the others, according to this same thing anything is similar to anything; for anything is other than anything else. It seems so. Is "similar" the opposite to "dissimilar"? It is indeed. And is not "the Other" itself [the opposite] to "the Same" itself? Also that. But this also appeared, that the One itself becomes both the same as and other than the others. It appeared clearly. But it is a contrary experience to be the same as the others and to be other than the others. Entirely. Yet where it was other, it appeared similar. And this. Therefore, where it is the same, it will be dissimilar according to the experience contrary to the experience that made it similar. For "the Other" made it similar? Yes. Therefore "the Same" will make it dissimilar; otherwise, it will not be the opposite of "the Other" itself. It seems so. Therefore, the One will be similar and dissimilar to the others: where it is other, similar; where it is the same, dissimilar. It has, as it seems, such a reasoning. And indeed it has this one. Which? That those which have experienced the same thing are not experiencing something different; if it has not experienced something different, it is not dissimilar; and if not dissimilar, it remains that it is similar. But if it has taken up something else and different; if different, it also becomes dissimilar. You say truly. Therefore, the One, both because it is the same as the others...

<summary>Parmenides argues that the "One" is paradoxically both the same as and different from itself and other things. By analyzing how names like "the Same" and "the Other" function, he concludes that the One must also possess both similarity and dissimilarity to all things.</summary>

# OF PLATO

<margin>A</margin> And because it is "other," in both of these ways and in each of them, it will be both similar and dissimilar to the others. Most certainly. And will it not be the same way toward itself? Since it appeared both "other" than itself and "the same" as itself, in both ways and in each, will it not appear both similar and dissimilar? It must be so. Consider further, I pray, in what way the One stands in relation to touching, or not touching, itself and the others. I am considering it. For it was agreed that the One exists as a whole within itself. Quite right. And is the One not also in the others? It is. Insofar as it is in the others, it would touch the others; but insofar as it is in itself, it is prevented from touching the others, but it touches itself, since it exists <margin>B</margin> within itself. So it appears. In this way, then, the One touches both itself and the others. It touches them. But what about this? Must not everything that is going to touch something lie next to that which it is going to touch, occupying that place which follows the place of the first thing? This is necessary. Therefore, if the One is to touch itself, it must be placed immediately next to itself, occupying the place adjacent to the one in which it is. It must indeed. Now, if the One were two, it could do this and exist in two places at once; but as long as it is one, it will not be able to? It is as you say. Therefore, the same necessity that makes the One not two, also makes it <margin>C</margin> not touch itself. The same. But neither will it touch the others. Why is that? Because we say that whatever is going to touch something must be separate and placed next to that which is to be touched, with no third thing in between them. True. Therefore, at least two things must be present if there is to be a "touching." There must. But if a third term is added in between the two limits, there will be three things in sequence, but only two points of contact. Exactly. And so, whenever one thing is added, one contact is also added. From this, it follows that the number of contacts is one less than the number of things: for the amount by which the first two things <margin>D</margin> exceeded the contact (so that the things were more numerous than the contacts), by that same amount the total number will always exceed the total contacts. For in the future, one thing is added to the number and, at the same time, one contact is added to the contacts. Correct. Therefore, however many things there are, the contacts are always fewer by exactly one. You speak the truth. So if there were only the One, and not two, there would be no contact at all. How so? We said that "the others" are different from the One, and are not the One, nor do they participate in it, as long as they are "others." We did. From this it follows that the number "one" is not in the others, since the One is not present in them at all. Indeed, how could it be? Therefore the others are not one, nor two, nor designated by any other number. Certainly not. Thus, only the One itself is one, and "two" does not exist. It seems not. And if there is no "two," <margin>E</margin> there is also no contact. None. Therefore, the One does not touch the others, nor do they touch the One, since no contact exists. Not at all. For all these reasons, the One touches itself and the others, and likewise does not touch them. So it seems. Is it also both equal and unequal, both to itself and to the others? In what way? If the One were greater or smaller than the others, or the others greater or smaller than it, would they not be greater or smaller than each other simply by their own essences, the One being the One and the others being "other" than the One? But if, besides these characteristics, both had "equality" <term>equality: the Greek 'isotes' implies balance or being of the same measure</term>, they would be equal to each other. If one side had "magnitude" <term>magnitude: the quality of greatness or large size</term> and the other "smallness," or if the One had magnitude and the others smallness, then whichever form magnitude <margin>F</margin> was present in would be the greater, and whichever smallness was in would be the lesser. Necessarily. Are there not two such forms as Magnitude and Smallness? For if they did not exist, they could never be opposites of one another nor exist within things. It is as you say. Therefore, if smallness comes to be in the One, it must reside either in the whole of the One or in some part of it. Necessarily. If it resides in the whole, it will either be spread equally throughout the entire One, or it will encompass it from the outside. Clearly. Smallness spread equally through the One would be equal to it; but if it encompasses it, it would be greater. Why not? But can smallness be equal to anything, or larger? Can it perform the functions of magnitude and equality rather than its own? It cannot, <margin>G</margin> surely. Therefore, smallness cannot be in the whole of the One. It remains, perhaps, that it is in a part. It remains. Yet not in the whole part either; for it would do the same to the part that it did to the whole: it would be either equal to or greater than whatever part it happened to be in. That follows necessarily. Therefore, smallness will never be in any existing thing, since it is in neither a part nor a whole. From this it follows that nothing will ever be "small" except Smallness itself. It seems so. But "magnitude" (greatness) will not be in it either. For then something else, other than Greatness itself, would be greater—namely, that in which the Greatness resides. And yet, there is <margin>H</margin> nothing small for Greatness to exceed, if indeed something is to be "great." For how can you find anything small if Smallness does not reside anywhere? You speak the truth. Furthermore, Greatness itself will be greater than nothing but Smallness, and Smallness itself will be smaller than nothing but Greatness. Nothing. Therefore, the others are neither greater than the One, nor smaller, since they lack both greatness and smallness. Nor will these two have any power over the One itself to exceed it or be exceeded by it, but...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> And since it is "other" <note>original: ἕτερον</note>, in both ways and in each, it would be both similar and dissimilar to the others. Certainly. And will it not be the same for itself, since it appeared both other than itself and the same as itself? In both ways and in each, would it not appear similar and dissimilar? It must. Now consider how the One stands regarding touching <note>original: ἅπτεσθαι</note> itself and the others, and not touching. I am looking. For the One appeared as a whole existing in itself. Correct. And is the One not also in the others? Yes. Insofar as it <margin>B</margin> is in the others, it would touch the others; but insofar as it is in itself, it would be prevented from touching the others, yet it would touch itself, being in itself. So it appears. Thus the One would touch itself and the others. It would. But what about this? Must not everything that is going to touch something lie next to that which it is going to touch, occupying that seat which is after the seat where the thing it touches is placed? Necessarily. And the One, then, if it is to touch itself, must lie in sequence immediately after itself, occupying the region adjacent to that in which it is. It must indeed. Would not the One do this if it were two, and be in two places at once? But as long as it is one, it will not be willing? Surely not. The same necessity, then, applies to the One: to be neither two nor <margin>C</margin> to touch itself. The same. But neither will it touch the others. Why? Because we say that what is going to touch, being separate, must be next to that which it is to touch, and there must be no third thing between them. True. Two things at minimum are required if there is to be contact. There must. But if a third thing is added in sequence to the two limits, they themselves will be three, but the contacts will be two. Yes. And so, always, as one thing is added, one contact is added; and it happens that the contacts are one fewer than the quantity of the numbers. For by the same amount that the first two exceeded the contact (in being more numerous as a number than the contacts), by that same amount every subsequent number <margin>D</margin> exceeds all the contacts. For thereafter, one is added to the number and one contact is added to the contacts at the same time. Correct. Therefore, however many things there are, the contacts are always fewer by one. True. But if there is only one, and no duality exists, there could be no contact. How could there be? We say that "the others" are not one, and do not participate in it, since they are "others." We do. There is, therefore, no number in the others, since "one" is not in them. How could there be? Neither, then, are the others "one," nor "two," nor do they have the name of any other number. No. Therefore the One alone is one, and duality would not exist. It appears not. There is no contact, then, if two do not exist. There is not. Neither then does the One touch the others, nor the others touch the One, since contact does not exist. Certainly not. Thus, according to all these things, the One both touches the others and itself, and <margin>E</margin> does not touch them. It seems so. Is it not also equal and unequal to itself and to the others? How? If the One were greater or smaller than the others, or the others greater or smaller than the One, would they not be so by being "the One" and "the others"—others than the One—and not by their own essences being "greater" or "smaller"? But if, in addition to being such things, each also had equality, they would be equal to each other. But if some had magnitude and others smallness, or if the One had magnitude and the others smallness, whichever form magnitude was added to would be greater, and whichever smallness was added to would be smaller? Necessarily. Are there not these two forms, Magnitude and Smallness? For they would not, if they did not exist, be opposites of each other and come to be in existing things. How could they? If smallness, then, comes to be in the One, it would be in <margin>F</margin> either the whole or a part of it. Necessarily. But what if it were in the whole? Would it not either be stretched equally throughout the One, or encompass it? Clearly. If smallness were equal to the One, would it not be equal to it? And if it encompassed it, would it not be greater? How not? Is it possible for smallness to be equal to or greater than something? And to perform the functions of magnitude and equality, rather than its own? Impossible. Smallness, then, would not be in the whole of the One; but if at all, it would be in a part. Yes. But not in every part either. For if it were, it would do the same things it did toward the whole: it would be equal to or greater than the part in which it resided. Necessarily. Therefore, smallness will never be in <margin>G</margin> any existing thing, being found in neither part nor whole. Nor will anything be small except Smallness itself. It seems not. Neither then will Magnitude be in it. For something else would be greater besides Greatness itself—namely, that in which the Greatness resided. And this, even though there were no smallness for it to exceed, which it must exceed if it is "great." But this is impossible, since smallness is nowhere. True. But Greatness itself is greater than nothing but Smallness itself, and Smallness is smaller than nothing but Greatness itself. No. Therefore, the others are not greater than the One, nor smaller, having neither magnitude nor smallness. Nor do these two possess toward the others the power of exceeding or being exceeded, but... <margin>H</margin>

<summary>This page explores the logical paradoxes of "the One" regarding its physical and mathematical properties, specifically touching, number, and size. It concludes that if the One is truly singular, it cannot touch itself or others, and that concepts like "greatness" and "smallness" cannot exist within it without leading to contradictions.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the logical exploration of "the One" from the previous section. Having discussed contact and position, Parmenides now leads young Aristoteles through a series of paradoxes regarding size (magnitude), number, and finally, the nature of time and existence.</meta>

# PARMENIDES.

<margin>A</margin> ...between one another. Nor, again, could the One be greater or less than these two or any others, since it possesses neither magnitude nor smallness. So it appears. Therefore, if the One is neither greater nor less than the others, is it not necessary that it neither exceeds them nor is exceeded by them? It is necessary. And is it not a great necessity that that which neither exceeds nor is exceeded be on an equal footing? And being on an equal footing, would it not be equal? How could it be otherwise? And furthermore, the One would stand in this same relation to itself: having neither magnitude nor smallness within itself, it would neither be exceeded by itself nor exceed itself; but being on an equal footing, it would be equal to itself. Certainly. The One, then, would be equal both to itself and to the others.

<margin>B</margin> It so appears. And yet, if it is within itself, it would also be around itself on the outside; and as the container, it would be greater than itself, but as the contained, it would be smaller. Thus the One would be both greater and smaller than itself. It would indeed. And is this not also necessary: that nothing exists outside of the One and the others? How could it be otherwise? But surely that which exists must always be somewhere. Yes. And does not that which is in something exist as a smaller thing within a greater? For one thing cannot otherwise be in another. It cannot. Since, then, there is nothing else apart from the others and the One, and they must be in something, is it not necessary that they be in each other—the others in the One, and the One in the others—or else be nowhere at all? It so appears. Because the One is in the others, the others would be greater than the One, since they contain it; but the One would be

<margin>C</margin> smaller than the others, being contained. But because the others are in the One, the One, by the same logic, would be greater than the others, and the others smaller than the One. So it seems. The One, therefore, is equal to, greater than, and smaller than both itself and the others. It appears so. And further, if it is greater, smaller, and equal, it must be of equal, more, and fewer measures than itself and the others; and if it has measures, it also has parts. How could it be otherwise? Being of equal, more, and fewer measures, it will also be fewer and more in number than itself and the others, as well as equal to itself and the others, based on the same principles. How? If it is greater than something, it must have more measures than that thing; and however many measures it has, it has that many parts. And the same applies to being smaller or equal. Just so.

<margin>D</margin> Being greater, smaller, and equal to itself, will it not have equal, more, and fewer measures than itself? and if measures, then also parts? How could it be otherwise? Having parts equal to itself, it would be equal to itself in multitude; having more, it would be more in number; and having fewer, it would be less in number than itself. It appears so. And will the One not stand in the same relation to the others? Insofar as it appears greater than them, must it not also be more in number? Insofar as it is smaller, must it be fewer? And insofar as it is equal in magnitude, must it be equal in multitude to the others? It is necessary. Thus, it seems, the One will be equal, more, and fewer in number, both in relation to itself and to the others. It will be so. Does the One then also participate in time? And

<margin>E</margin> is it, and does it become, both younger and older than itself and the others, and yet neither younger nor older than itself or the others, despite participating in time? How? "To be" <note>Greek: εἶναι (einai)</note> must surely belong to it, if indeed the One is. Yes. But is "to be" anything else than the participation in essence <note>Greek: οὐσία (ousia)</note> along with the present time? Just as "was" is the participation in essence along with the past, and "will be" is the participation in essence along with the future? It is indeed. Therefore, it participates in time, if it participates in being. Certainly. And is time not always moving forward? Yes. Therefore, it is always becoming older than itself, if it moves forward according to time. It must be so. Do we not remember that "the older" becomes older than something that is becoming younger? <margin>F</margin> We remember. Therefore, since the One is becoming older than itself, it must be becoming older than a self that is becoming younger? It must be so. In this way, it becomes both younger and older than itself. Yes. But is it not older than itself when, in its "becoming," it reaches the "now" <note>Greek: νῦν (nyn); the instantaneous moment</note> which is between the "was" and the "will be"? For it will surely not skip over the "now" as it moves from the "once" to the "after." It will not. Does it not then stop "becoming" older when it encounters the "now," and is no longer becoming, but is then already older? For while it is moving, it could never be caught by the "now." For that which moves is in such a state that it touches both the "now" and

<margin>G</margin> the "after," letting go of the "now" and seizing the "after," becoming between the two, the "after" and the "now." True. But if it is necessary that everything which "becomes" cannot pass by the "now," then whenever it is at this point, it always stops "becoming" and is then whatever it happened to be "becoming." It appears so. And so the One, when in the process of becoming older it encounters the "now," stops becoming and is then older. Quite so. And is it not older than that which it was becoming older than? And was it not becoming older than itself? Yes. And is "the older" older than a "younger"? It is. Therefore, the One is younger than itself at the moment when, in becoming older, it encounters the "now." It must be so. But the "now" is always present to the One throughout all its "being"; for it is always "now" whenever it is. How could it be otherwise? Always, then, the One is and

<margin>H</margin> becomes both older and younger than itself. So it seems. But is it, or does it become, for a longer time than itself, or for an equal time? For an equal time. But that which is or becomes for an equal time has the same age. How could it be otherwise? And that which has the same age is neither older nor younger. By no means.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...between themselves they will effect this. Nor yet will the One itself be greater or less than these two, or any others whatsoever, since it is devoid of both magnitude and smallness. So at least it appears. And therefore, since the One is neither greater nor less than the others, it will neither surpass the others nor be surpassed by the others. Without a doubt. Does it not follow by necessity that what neither surpasses nor is surpassed must stand on equal footing? And if on equal footing, that it be equal? Indeed. But in this way, the One itself relates to itself: being devoid, namely, of both magnitude and smallness, so that it neither exceeds itself nor is exceeded by itself, but standing on equal footing, it is always equal to itself. Most certainly.

<margin>B</margin> Therefore the One is equal to itself and to others. It seems so. Nevertheless, since the One is in itself, it goes around itself from the outside, and thus embracing itself, it stands out as more than itself; and since it is also contained, it is narrower, whereby it happens that the One is both greater and also smaller than itself. It happens indeed. Is this also not necessary: that nothing, namely, is found besides the One and the others? Necessary. Likewise, whatever is, must it not always be somewhere? It must. Furthermore, that which is in something, is it not always smaller in a greater? For one thing is not in another in any other way. It is as you say. Since truly nothing exists besides the One and the others, and it is necessary that those things be in something, is it not necessary that these exist in each other in turn:

<margin>C</margin> namely, the others in the One, and the One in the others, or else exist nowhere at all? It is established. Because, therefore, the One is in the others, for that reason the others are greater than the One, inasmuch as they contain the One; the One, however, is smaller than the others because it is contained. But because the others are in the One, the One is greater than the others for the same reason, while they are smaller. It seems so. The One, therefore, is equal, greater, and smaller than itself and the others. It appears so. Yet if it is greater and smaller and equal, it will be of equal measures, and of more and fewer, in relation to itself and to others; and if of measures, also of parts. What prevents it? Having, therefore, the same measures, and more, and fewer,

<margin>D</margin> in number also it will be more and less both in relation to itself and to the rest, and also equal to itself and others for the same reasons. In what way? Those things than which it is greater, it has more measures than they; and as many measures as it has, so many parts also. And in the same way with those things than which it is smaller, and similarly with those than which it is equal. So it is. Is it not so that since it is greater and smaller than itself, and equal, it participates in equal measures, and more, and fewer, in relation to itself; and since it participates in measures, also in parts? Why not? And having parts equal to itself, in multitude it will also be equal to itself; with more parts, it will be more; and finally, with fewer parts, it will be less in number than itself? It

<margin>E</margin> seems so. Will the One not relate to others in a similar way? Because it appears greater than them, it is necessary that it be more in number than they; because truly it is smaller in magnitude, it is also fewer in number; because finally it is equal in magnitude, it must also be equal in number. It happens by necessity. By this logic again, the One will be equal, more, and fewer according to number in relation to itself and others. It will be indeed. Does the One not also participate in time, and is it and does it become younger and older than itself and at the same time others? And again, on the contrary, is it neither younger nor older than itself or others while

<margin>F</margin> <margin>What the word "to be" means.</margin> it participates in time? But how can that happen? To be <note>Latin: Esse</note> surely belongs to it, if indeed it is the One. It belongs. But this very "to be," what else is it than the participation of essence <note>Latin: essentiae</note> with the present time, just as "was" was the communication of essence itself with the past, and "will be" will be the communication of essence with the future? That very thing. Therefore, if it participates in being itself, it must also be a participant in time. Certainly. And is it not of flowing time? Surely. Always, therefore, it becomes younger than itself, if indeed it runs according to time. Necessary. Do we remember that "the older" always becomes older than that which becomes younger? We remember. Therefore, since the One becomes older than itself, while it becomes younger than itself, does it become both older and younger? It is

<margin>G</margin> necessary. It becomes, therefore, by this mode, younger than itself and older. It becomes. But is it not older then, when it reaches the present time, which is the middle of its "was" and "will be"? For in running from the preceding to the following, it does not overstep the present itself. Not certainly. Does it not then cease becoming older when it first touches the present, and is not then becoming, but is now already older? For in proceeding, it is by no means gripped by the present itself. For that which proceeds is so held that it touches both—namely, the present and the future—leaving the present, seizing the future, falling as a middle between both the present and the future. True. But if it is necessary that whatever becomes cannot at all transcend the present, as soon as it has reached that, it ceases

<margin>H</margin> becoming, and is then already that which it was becoming. It appears so. The One, therefore, when having been made older it reaches the present, stops becoming, and is now older. Altogether. Is it not older than that by which it was becoming older? But it was becoming older than itself. So it is. But is the older older than the younger? It is. The One is therefore younger than itself then, when having been made older, it reaches the present. Necessary. Moreover, the present itself is always at hand for the One through its universal being; for it is always present as long as it is. Why not? Always, therefore, the One is and becomes younger than itself. It seems so. But is it or does it become for a shorter time than itself, or rather an equal time? Equal. But that which is or becomes for an equal time lives the same age. What prevents it? But that which fulfills the same age is neither older nor younger. By no means.
