<meta>This page continues the investigation into the properties of "the One" (Latin: *vnum*; Greek: *τὸ ἓν*). Following the discussion of magnitude and equality on the previous page, Parmenides now turns to the temporal relationship between the One and the "others," exploring whether the One is older or younger than itself and the rest of existence.</meta>

# OF PLATO

->**PARMENIDES**<-

A **Therefore**, since the One both is and becomes for a time equal to itself, it is neither older nor younger than itself, nor does it become so. It does not seem so to me. But how does it relate to other things? I do not know what to say. Yet you can say this: that the others, being different from the One—if indeed they are "others" and not "another"—are more than one. For if they were "another," they would be one; but since they are "others," they are more than one and possess a multitude. They certainly do. And a multitude possesses a greater number than the One. Surely. What then? Of things which pertain to number, which shall we say are produced or have been produced first? Those that are more, or those that are fewer? Those that are fewer.

<margin>Which are fewer? Those that are the first one and the one.</margin>
B **Therefore**, that which is fewest comes first. And that is the One, is it not? Indeed. The One, then, was produced first among all things that possess number; and all other things have number, since they are others and not just another. They do indeed. But that which was produced first came into being earlier, and the others later; and those produced later are younger than that which was produced earlier. Thus, in this way, the others are younger than the One, and the One is older than them. Certainly. But what of this? Can the One be produced contrary to its own nature, or is that impossible? Impossible. Yet the One appeared to have parts; and if it has parts, it also has a beginning, a middle, and an end. Clearly.

<margin>In the beginning of all things, the principle is made.</margin>
C **Does not** the beginning <note>original: *principium*; Greek: *ἀρχὴ*</note> come into being first of all—both of the One itself and of each of the others—and after the beginning, all the rest until the end? Why not? Do we not admit that all these other things are parts of the whole and of the One, and that the One itself was produced as a whole and a one at the same time as the end? We do admit it. The end, I think, is produced last, and at that same moment the One is naturally completed. Therefore, if the One must not be produced contrary to its own nature, it is produced at the same time as the end, and by nature is the last of all to be completed. It appears so. Thus the One is younger than the others, and the others are older than the One. So it appears to me again.

D **What then?** Must not the beginning, or any other part of the One or of anything else, if it is a part and not "parts," be "one," precisely because it is a part? It is necessary. It follows from this that the One is produced at the same time as the first part produced, and at the same time as the second, and is never absent from any of the others as they are produced, until, passing through all to the very last, it becomes a whole One—excluded from nothing in the process of generation, neither from the first, nor the middle, nor the last, nor any other. True.

E **The One**, therefore, is of the same age as all the others. Consequently, if the One is not born contrary to its own nature, it is produced neither earlier nor later than the others, but at the same time. And according to this reasoning, the One is neither older nor younger than the others, nor they than it; but according to the previous reasoning, the One is both older and younger than all others, and they likewise to it. It is entirely so. This, then, is how it stands and how it has been produced. But what do you think of this: that the One becomes older and younger than the others, and the others than the One, and also that it becomes neither younger nor older? Does it stand in the same relation regarding "becoming" as we said regarding its "being," or otherwise?

F **I do not know** what to say. But I will say this much: if one thing is older than another, it can never "become" older still than it was originally by any greater interval of age; nor can that which is younger "become" younger in the future. For equal things added to unequals—whether to time or anything else—always cause them to differ by the same interval as they did before. Nothing prevents it. Therefore, that which *is* cannot "become" older or younger than the One, since the same distance of age always remains; it is and was older or younger, but it is by no means "becoming" so. It is as you say. Thus the One never becomes younger or older than the others. Never. But look and see if they become younger and older in another way. In what way? In this way. Did we not agree that the One is older than the others, and the others than the One?

G **What then?** Since the One is older than the others, it has existed for a longer time than they. Certainly. Consider again: if we add an equal time to a longer and a shorter time, will the longer differ from the shorter by an equal fraction, or a smaller one? A smaller one. Therefore, the One, not having been allotted the same duration of age as the others, will always differ from them in age by a smaller proportion than before. Will it not? Certainly. And does not that which exceeds something in age by a smaller proportion than before "become" younger than before, relative to those things than which it was older? Younger, without a doubt. And if that becomes younger, will not the others, in comparison to the One, be older than before?

H **Exactly.** Therefore, that which was produced younger "becomes" older in relation to that which was produced earlier and was older; yet it is never actually older, but is always "becoming" older than it, for the one increases toward the younger, the other toward the older. Conversely, that which is older "becomes" younger than the younger in the same way. For as they move in opposite directions, they become the opposite of each other: the younger becoming older than the older, and the older becoming younger than the younger. But they are never able to have "become" so.

<column-break/>

A **The One**, therefore, being and becoming for a time equal to itself, is neither younger nor older than itself, nor does it become so. It does not seem so to me. But what of the others? I cannot say. Yet you can say this: that the others, being different from the One—if they are indeed different and not another—are more than the One. For if they were one, they would be the One; but being different, they are more than one and must possess a multitude. They would indeed. And being a multitude, they would participate in a greater number than the One? How could they not? What then? Shall we say that in number, the more are produced and have been produced earlier than the fewer? The fewer. Therefore, the fewest is first. And that is the One. Is it not? Yes. The One, then, has been produced first of all those things that have number. And all other things have number, if they are indeed others and not another

B **thing.** They have it. And having been produced first, I think, it was produced earlier; and the others, later. And things produced later are younger than that produced earlier. And so the others would be younger than the One, and the One older than the others. They would be. What of this? Could the One have been produced contrary to its own nature? Or is that impossible? Impossible. But I said the One has parts; and if it has parts, it has a beginning, an end, and a middle. Yes. Does not the beginning come into being first of all, both of the One itself and of each of the others? And after the beginning, all the others until the end? Why not? And we shall say that all these other things are parts of the end and of the One; but the One itself

C **is** produced as a one and a whole at the same time as the end. We shall say so. The end, I think, is produced last; and at this same time, the One is naturally produced. So that if it is necessary for the One not to be produced contrary to its own nature, having been produced at the same time as the end, it would naturally be produced last of the others. It appears so. The One, then, is younger than the others, and the others are older than the One. So it appears to me again. What then? Is it not necessary that the beginning, or any other part of the One or of anything else, if it is a part and not parts, be one, being a part? Necessary. Therefore the One would come into being at the same time as the first part produced, and at the same time as the second; and it is never left behind by any of the

D **others** being produced, whatever is added to whatever, until passing through to the last, it becomes a whole one; not being left behind in its generation by the middle, nor the last, nor the first, nor any other. True. Therefore the One has the same age as all the others. So that if the One itself is not naturally produced contrary to its nature, it would have been produced neither earlier nor later than the others, but at the same time. And according to this argument, the One would be neither older nor younger than the others, nor the others than the One; but according to the previous argument, it is both older and younger, and the others likewise to it. Certainly. Let it be, then, that it is thus and has been so produced. But what again of its "becoming" older and younger than the

E **others**, and the others than the One, or becoming neither younger nor older? Does "becoming" stand differently for you than "being"? I cannot say. But I can say this much: that if one thing is older than another, it could not become still older than it was originally by any greater difference in age; nor could the younger become still younger. For equal things added to unequals, whether in years or anything else, always make them differ by as much as they differed at first. How could it be otherwise? Therefore, that which is cannot ever become older or younger than the One, if it always differs by an equal age; but it is and

F **has been** older, and the other younger; but it does not "become" so. True. And the One, being, never becomes older or younger than the other things that are. It does not. See if it becomes older and younger in this way. In what way? In that the One, we said, was older than the others, and the others than the One. What then? When the One is older than the others, it has been produced for a longer time than the others. Yes. Consider again: if we add equal time to a longer and a shorter time, will the longer differ from the shorter by the same proportion, or a smaller one? A smaller one. Therefore, the difference in age that the One first had toward the others will not remain the same afterward, but receiving equal time with the others, it will always differ in age

G **less** than before. Or not? Yes. And does not that which differs less in age toward something than it did before become younger than it was previously, relative to those things toward which it was older? Younger? And if that is younger, are not those others in turn older than before relative to the One? Certainly. That which has been produced younger, therefore, becomes older toward that which was produced earlier and is older. But it is never actually older; rather, it is always becoming older than it. For the one increases toward the younger, the other toward the older. And the older in turn becomes younger than the younger in the same way. For moving toward the opposite, they become the opposite of each other: the younger becoming older than the older, and the older younger than the younger. But they could not have "become" so.

H **If they had become**, they would no longer be "becoming," but would already "be." But as it is, they are becoming older and younger than each other. The One becomes younger than the others because it appeared to be older and produced earlier; and the others become older than the One...

<summary>This page explores a temporal paradox: if the "One" is the first principle of number, it must be older than all other things; however, as a "whole" that is only completed by its final part, it must also be younger than its parts. The dialogue further argues that while the absolute difference in age remains constant, the relative proportion of their ages changes as time passes, leading to a state of constant "becoming" older and younger.</summary>
<keywords>Plato, Parmenides, The One, Multitude, Chronology, Age, Paradox of Time, Dialectics, Becoming vs Being, Principle and End</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the logical deduction regarding the "One." Having previously discussed whether the One is older or younger than itself, Parmenides now extends this inquiry to the relationship between the One and "the others" (the rest of the universe), eventually transitioning into the famous "Third Supposition" concerning the nature of change and the "instant."</meta>

# PARMENIDES

...because they were created later. And according to the same reasoning, the other things relate to the One in the same way, since they appeared to have been created both older and younger than it. So it seems, at least. Is it not true that in one sense, neither becomes older or younger than the other—because they must always differ by an equal number—and so the One would not become older or younger than the others, nor the others than the One? But in another sense, because the prior things must always differ from the posterior by a different part <note>The argument hinges on the ratio of age; as time passes, the proportional difference in age changes, even if the numerical difference remains the same.</note>, is it not necessary that the others and the One become both older and younger than one other? Certainly. According to all these points, then, the One is and becomes both older and younger than itself and the others; and yet it neither is nor becomes older or younger than itself or the others.

Entirely so. But since the One participates in time, and in the process of becoming older and younger, is it not also necessary that it participates in the "past," the "after," and the "now," if indeed it participates in time? It is necessary. Therefore, the One was, and is, and shall be; and it was becoming, and is becoming, and will become. Of course. And there would be something belonging to it and of it, both in the past, the present, and the future. Certainly. And thus there would be knowledge, and opinion, and perception of it, since even now we are engaging in all these activities concerning it. You speak rightly. It also has a name and a definition, and it is named and spoken of; and whatever such things pertain to other objects, they also pertain to the One.

This is exactly how it stands. Now let us speak of the third point. If the One is as we have described it—being both one and many, and neither one nor many, and participating in time—is it not necessary that, because it "is," it participates in essence <term>essence: Greek 'ousia', referring to the fundamental being or existence of a thing</term> at some time? And because it "is not," it must also not participate in essence at some time? It is necessary. When it participates, is it possible for it not to participate at that same time? Or when it does not participate, to participate? It is impossible. It participates, therefore, at one time, and does not participate at another. For only in this way can it both participate and not participate in the same thing. Correct. And is there not also a time when it acquires existence, and a time when it departs from it? How else could it sometimes possess the same thing and sometimes not, unless it at some point receives it and at another lets it go? In no other way. Now, do you not call "becoming" the act of receiving essence? I do. And is not "perishing" the act of departing from essence? Certainly.

The One, then, as it seems, by taking on and letting go of essence, is born and perishes. It is necessary. And since it is both one and many, being born and perishing, when it becomes one, does its being many not perish? And when it becomes many, does its being one not perish? Certainly. And in becoming one and many, must it not be separated and combined? Entirely so. And when it becomes unlike and like, must it not be assimilated and "dissimilated" <note>original: "ἀνομοιοῦσθαι" / "dissimilari" - to become unlike</note>? Yes. And when it becomes greater, smaller, or equal, must it not increase, decrease, or be equalized? Just so. But when, being in motion, it comes to a stop, or when, being at rest, it changes to being in motion, it must surely be that this transition happens in no time at all. How so? For it to be at rest first and later in motion, or in motion first and later at rest, it cannot suffer these changes without a transition. It cannot. But there is no time in which a thing can be neither in motion nor at rest. There is none. Yet it surely does not change without changing.

That is unlikely. When, then, does it change? For it does not change while it is at rest, nor while it is in motion, nor while it is in time. It does not. Does this strange thing then exist—that in which the One is at the moment it changes? What sort of thing? The sudden <note>original: "ἐξαίφνης" / "momentarium" - the instant or the sudden moment</note>. For the "sudden" seems to signify something of this sort: a transition from one state to either of two others. For it does not change from rest while it is still resting, nor does it change from motion while it is still moving. Rather, this "sudden" nature is something strange that lies between motion and rest, being in no time at all. Into this and out of this, that which is in motion changes into rest, and that which is at rest changes into motion.

<column-break/>

**A** It seems so. And the One, if indeed it stands still and moves, must change to each state. For only in this way could it do both. But in changing, it changes suddenly; and when it changes, it would be in no time, and it would neither move then, nor would it stand still. No. Does it not also stand in this same relation to other changes? When it changes from being into perishing, or from non-being into becoming, it is then between certain motions and states of rest; and it neither "is" then, nor "is not"; it neither becomes, nor perishes?

**B** It seems so. By the same logic, when it goes from one to many, and from many to one, it is neither one nor many, neither separated nor combined. And in going from like to unlike, or unlike to like, it is neither like nor unlike, neither being assimilated nor dissimilated. And in going from small to large, or to equal, or to the opposite, it would be neither small, nor large, nor equal, nor increasing, nor decreasing, nor being equalized.

**C** It seems so. All these things the One would experience, if it exists. How could it be otherwise? But should we not also consider what "the others" must experience, if the One exists? We should. Let us say then, if the One is, what must the things other than the One experience? Let us speak. Since they are "others" than the One, they are not the One, are they? For then they would not be "others" than the One. Correct. Yet the others are not entirely deprived of the One, but they participate in the One in a certain way. By what...

<margin>Third supposition: that is, if the One is considered under the aspect of Being.</margin>

<margin>The "moment" or "instant" is discovered.</margin>

<margin>The moment is the midpoint between motion and rest.</margin>

<margin>Fourth supposition.</margin>

<summary>Parmenides explores the paradoxical nature of the "One" in time, concluding that change occurs in a timeless "instant" (the sudden) where the object is neither moving nor at rest, neither existing nor non-existing. He then moves to investigate how "the others" (the rest of reality) relate to the One.</summary>

--- Page 100 ---
<meta>This page continues the logical exploration of the "One" in Plato's Parmenides. Following the discussion on time and existence, the text now examines the "Others"—everything that is not the "One"—to see how they relate to unity and plurality. It specifically looks at how "the others" can have parts and yet be a whole.</meta>

# OF PLATO

<margin>A part is not of many, but of a whole.</margin>
**A** By what reason? Because things other than the One, by the fact that they consist of parts, are different from the One; for if they did not have parts, they would be completely One. Right. And we have asserted that parts are parts of that which is a whole. We have indeed. But the whole itself must be a "one" made of many, of which the parts are parts; for each of the parts is not a part of many, but of a whole. <note>The argument here is that a "part" implies a single unified entity (the whole) to which it belongs. You cannot be a part of a "many" unless that many is gathered into a single "one."</note>

But how is that? If something were a part of many, among which it itself was included, it would in a way be a part of itself—which is impossible—and a part of each of the others, if indeed it is a part of all. For if it is not a part of one, it will be a part of all the others except that one; and thus it would not correctly be a part of each. But if it is not a part of each, it will be a part of none of the many. And if it belongs to none, it is impossible for it to be anything belonging to all those things of which it is neither a part nor anything else.

**B** That is certainly evident. Therefore, a part—whatever part it may be—is not a part of the many, nor of all, but of a single **Idea** <note>original: "ideæ" / "ἰδέας". In Platonic thought, this refers to the perfect, abstract form that gives a thing its identity.</note> and a single thing that we call a "whole," which has become a single perfect entity out of all its components. It is a part of this, I say, whatever part it may be. Entirely so. If, then, other things have parts, they participate in the "whole" and the "one." Most certainly. Whence it is necessary that those other things be different from the One, while the One remains a perfect whole containing parts. Necessary. Furthermore, the same reasoning applies to each individual part. For it, too, must participate in the "one."

**C** For if each of them is a part, this very word "each" signifies a "one" in a certain way; it signifies something distinct from the others and existing by itself, if indeed they are "each." Right. But it will participate in the One if it is something other than the One; otherwise, it would not participate, but would be the One itself. But truly, nothing can be "one" except the One itself. Nothing. Yet both the whole and the part must participate in the One. For the One itself will be a whole of which the parts are individual parts; and each of the parts will be a part of the whole, whatever part of the whole it may be. So it is. Is it not therefore true that since they are different from the One, all things that participate in the One do so? Why not?

**D** But things other than the One are, in a sense, "many." For if they were neither the One, nor more than the One, they would be absolutely nothing. Nothing indeed. Since, however, they are more than one, being participants in a single part and a single whole, is it not necessary that these things participating in the One be infinite in multitude? <note>Parmenides is arguing that without the "limit" provided by the One, the "nature of the other" is a boundless, blurry plurality.</note> In what way? In this way: they are something other than the One, and they do not participate in the One at the very moment they begin to participate in it. Certainly. Are they not then multitudes in which the One is not present? Multitudes, certainly. But if we should wish to take the smallest possible portion from them by the mind alone, is it not necessary that the portion extracted—since it lacks the One—be a multitude and not a one? It is necessary.

**E** Does it not seem to you that by always considering the "other" nature of the **form** <note>original: "speciei" / "εἴδους". Here referring to the essence of "Otherness" or "Difference."</note> according to itself, however much of it you look at, it will always appear infinite in multitude? Very much so. Nevertheless, after each individual part has been produced, the parts now have a limit <note>original: "terminum" / "πέρας". The boundary or "limit" that defines a thing's shape or identity.</note> in relation to each other and to the whole, and the whole in relation to the parts. Quite so. And so it happens to the others besides the One that, from the One itself and from themselves now communicating within the One, something else arises within them: which provided a limit to each other, while their own nature according to itself is infinity. It is manifest. In this way, then, the things other than the One—both as wholes and as parts—are both infinite and participants in a certain limit. Precisely.

**F** Are they not, then, both similar and dissimilar to each other and to themselves? Why? Insofar as they are infinite according to their own nature, they all experience the same thing in a certain way. They do. Likewise, insofar as they all participate in a limit, they all experience the same thing in this regard as well. Why not? Yet, insofar as it happens to them to be both finite and infinite at the same time—which are contrary states—they are as dissimilar as can possibly be. To be sure. Therefore, according to either of these reasons, they will be similar to themselves and each other; but according to both together, they will be entirely contrary and dissimilar. It is established. Thus, the others will be the same as themselves and each other, and both similar and dissimilar. They will. And again, they will be the same and different, in motion and at rest, and receiving all other contrary qualities—all other things which happen to those things that are other than the One, we shall easily find, once these points are established for us.

<margin>Fifth supposition.</margin>
**G** You speak rightly. What then? Shall we not pass over these things as if they were clear, and look again: if the One exists, do the others—which are not the One—stand only in this way, or in some other? By all means. Let us see from the beginning, if the One is, what must happen to the others. Let us see. Must the One not be separate from the others, and the others separate from the One? Why so? Because there is nothing else besides these which is either the One or the others, for all things are included when the One and the others are mentioned. All things. Therefore, nothing remains besides these in which both the One and the others might reside as if in the same seat. Nothing at all. Never, then, will the One and the others be in the same thing. Never. Are they then separate? Separate. We have said, moreover, that the One truly itself has no parts. How could it? Neither, then, will the One as a whole be in the others, nor will its parts be in them, if indeed it is separate from the others and is not composed of parts. That is so. In no way, then, will the others participate in the One, since they receive neither the whole of it nor a part of it. In no way, it seems. And for that reason, the others are in no way "one," nor do they have any "one" within themselves. Not at all. Whence the others are not even "many." For if they were many, each of them would be a "one" as a part of the whole.

<column-break/>

**A** ...participates in some way. In what way? Because the others are surely parts of the One, being "the others"; for if they did not have parts, they would be completely One. Right. And parts (we say) belong to that which is a whole. We do say so. But surely the whole must be a "one" made of many, of which the parts will be parts. For each of the parts must not be a part of many, but of a whole. How is this? If something were a part of many, in which it itself was present, it would surely be a part of itself (which is impossible) and of each of the others, if indeed of all. For not being a part of one, it will be a part of the others besides that one; and thus it will be a part of each, not being a part of that specific one, and it will be a part of none of the many; and being a part of none, it is impossible for it to be any of all those things of which it is neither a part nor anything else.

**B** It certainly appears so. Therefore, the "many" is not a part, nor is it a part of all the parts, but of some single **Form** <note>original: "ἰδέας". This Greek term is the root for "Idea" and refers to the intelligible structure of a thing.</note>, and of some "one" which we call a whole, having become a single perfect thing out of all; it would be a part of this. Entirely so. If then the others have parts, they would participate in both the whole and the "one." Quite so. It is necessary then for the others to be a single perfect whole having parts. Necessary. And indeed, the same logic applies to the part. For it too must participate in the "one." For if each of them is a part, the "each" surely signifies something defined and separate from the others, existing by itself, if it is to be "each." Right. And it participates in the "one," obviously being something other than one. For it would not participate, but would be that which it was. But now, to be one for anything except the One itself is surely impossible, except as participating in the One itself. Impossible.

**C** But it is necessary for both the whole and the part to participate in the One. For the One will be a whole, of which the parts are parts; and again each will be a single part of the whole, of whatever it is a part. So it is. Therefore, those things that are other than the One, do the participants participate in it? How not? And the things other than the One would surely be "many." For if the others were neither one, nor more than one, they would be nothing. They would not. But since the parts of the One and the participants of the One as a whole are more than one, is it not necessary that those very things which take part in the One be infinite in multitude?

**D** How? Let us see it this way. Clearly, they take part in it not being "one," nor participating in the One at the moment they take part in it. Clearly. Are they not then "multitudes" in which the One is not present? Multitudes indeed. What then? If we should wish to take away from such a thing in thought the smallest possible amount, is it not necessary that the part taken away—if it does not participate in the One—be a multitude and not one? Necessary. Therefore, by always looking at the "other nature" of the form itself by itself, however much of it we always see, it will be infinite in multitude? Entirely so. And indeed, as soon as each individual part is created, it already has a **limit** <note>original: "πέρας". The principle of boundary that brings order to chaos.</note> toward others and toward the whole, and the whole toward the parts. Exactly so.

**E** It happens then to the others of the One that, from the One and from themselves having shared together (as it seems), something different arises in them, which indeed provided a limit toward each other; but their own nature by itself provides infinity. It appears so. Thus the others of the One, both as wholes and according to parts, are both infinite and participate in limit. Quite so. Are they not then both similar and dissimilar to each other and to themselves? In what way? Insofar as they would all be infinite according to their own nature, they would have experienced the same thing in this way. Quite so. And indeed, insofar as they all participate in limit, in this way too they would have experienced something that is the same. How not? But insofar as they have experienced being both limited and infinite—which are contrary states to each other—they have experienced these states. Yes.

**F** And contrary things are, as much as possible, most dissimilar. What else? According to each individual state, they would be similar to themselves and to each other; but according to both, they are in both ways most contrary and most dissimilar. It is likely. Thus the others would be both the same as themselves and each other, and similar and dissimilar. Thus. And they would be both the same and different from each other, both moving and standing still, and would have experienced all the contrary states, which we shall find the others of the One have experienced without difficulty, since these things have already appeared. You speak rightly. If then we now leave these things as manifest, should we look again: if the One exists, do the others of the One not also have it this way, or only this way? Entirely so. Let us say then from the beginning: if the One exists, what must the others of the One experience? Let us say. Is the One separate from the others, and the others separate from the One? Why? Because surely there is no other thing besides them, which is either the One or the others. For all things have been said when the One and the others are spoken. All things indeed. There is then no other thing besides these, in which the One and the others might be. There is not. Never then are the One and the others in the same thing.

**G** It does not seem so. Are they then separate? Yes. Nor do we say the truly One has parts. How could it? Neither then would the One be in the others as a whole, nor its parts, if it is separate and has no parts. How indeed? In no way then would the others participate in the One, participating neither in a part of it nor in the whole. It does not seem so. In no way then are the others "one," nor do they have any "one" in themselves. They do not. Neither then are the others "many." For each of them would be a "one" part of the whole, if they were many.

<summary>This page explores the logical relationship between "the One" and "the others," arguing that for things to have parts or be a whole, they must participate in unity. It concludes that without the "limit" of the One, the natural state of the world is an infinite, incomprehensible multitude.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the rigorous dialectical exercise in Plato's *Parmenides*. The previous discussion established that "parts" only make sense in relation to a "whole" that is "one." Here, the dialogue concludes the consequences of the "One" existing for "the others" and then transitions to a new, famous hypothesis: what follows if the "One" does not exist?</meta>

# PARMENIDES

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> But now, the other forms are neither one, nor many, nor a whole, nor parts, since they in no way participate in the One. Correct. Therefore, the others are not two, nor three, nor are they the same, since they are entirely deprived of the One. So it is. Thus, the others are neither similar nor dissimilar to the One; for if they were similar or dissimilar, or if they possessed similarity and dissimilarity within themselves, the other forms would surely contain two contrary forms within themselves. It seems so. But is it possible for things to participate in two things when they participate in nothing at all? <note>Parmenides is pointing out a logical trap: if "the others" don't participate in the "One," they cannot even participate in a pair of opposites, because a "pair" (two) requires the concept of "one" to be counted.</note> Im-
<margin>B</margin> -possible. Therefore, the others are neither similar, nor dissimilar, nor both. For if they were similar or dissimilar, they would participate in one of the two forms; and if both, they would participate in two contrary forms. But this was shown to be impossible. True. Therefore, they are neither the same, nor different, nor moving, nor at rest; nor becoming, nor perishing; nor greater, nor smaller; nor equal; nor have they suffered any other such thing. For if the others were to suffer any of these, they would participate in one, and two, and three, and odd, and even—in which it appeared impossible for them to participate, if they are truly deprived of the One in every way. Most true. Thus, if the One exists, the One is all things, and it is not even one, both in relation to itself and to the others likewise. Entirely so. Well then. If the
<margin>C</margin> One does not exist, should we not consider what must follow after this? We must indeed. What would this hypothesis be: "if the One is not"? Does it differ at all from this: "if the not-one is not"? It certainly differs. Does it only differ, or is saying "if the not-one is not" the complete opposite of saying "if the One is not"? The complete opposite. What if someone were to say, "if greatness is not," or "smallness is not," or any other such thing; does he not show in each case that he is speaking of something different when he says "what is not"? Certainly. Does he not then now declare that he means something different from the others when he says "if the One is not"? And do we know what he is saying? We know. First, he speaks of something known; next, of something different from the others, when he says "the One," whether he adds "to be" or "not to be" to it. For it is known nonetheless what is said "not to be," and that it is different
<margin>D</margin> from the others. Is it not so? Necessarily. Thus we must say from the beginning: if the One is not, what must it be? First, this must belong to it, as it seems: there must be a certain knowledge of it, or else nothing that is said would be known when one says "if the One is not." True. And must not the others be different from it, or could it not even be said to be different from the others? Certainly. Therefore, diversity also belongs to it; for he does not speak of the diversity of the others when he says the One is different from the others, but of the diversity of that thing itself. It appears so. And indeed, "of that," and "of some," and "of this," and "to this," and "of these," and all such things belong to the "non-existent One." For the "One" would not be spoken of, nor would the things "of the One" be different, nor would there be anything "for it," nor would anything be said "of it," if it did not participate in "something" or in
<margin>E</margin> these others. Right. To be "the One" is impossible if it does not exist; but nothing prevents it from participating in many things—indeed, it is necessary, if that "One" and not another is what is non-existent. However, if neither "the One" nor "that" is not, but the discourse is about something else, nothing should be uttered at all. But if that "One" and not another is hypothesized not to be, it must participate in "that" and in "of some" and many other things. Most certainly. Therefore, it also has dissimilarity to the others. For the others, being different from the One, would be of another kind. Yes. And are things of another kind different? How could they not be? And are different things dissimilar? Dissimilar indeed. Therefore, if they are dissimilar to the One, it is clear that they would be dissimilar by means of dissimilarity. Clear. Thus there would also be a dissimilarity in the One, in relation to which the others are dissimilar to it. It seems so. And if it
<margin>F</margin> has dissimilarity to the others, must it not necessarily have similarity to itself? How? If there is a dissimilarity of the One to the One <note>original: "ἑνὸς ἀνομοιότης ἔστι τῷ ἑνὶ". This logical pivot suggests that if we define the One as being dissimilar to others, it must have a consistent "likeness" to itself to maintain that definition.</note>, then the discourse would not be about such a thing as the One; nor would the hypothesis be about the One, but about something other than the One. Quite so. But that must not be. Indeed not. There must, therefore, be some similarity of it to itself. There must. Furthermore, it is not equal to the others. For if it were equal, it would already be, and it would also be similar to them according to equality. But both of these are impossible if the One is not. Impossible. Since it is not equal to the others, is it not necessary that the others also be not equal to it? Necessary. And are things that are not equal, unequal? Yes. And are unequal things unequal to something that is unequal? How could they not be? So the One also participates in inequality, in relation to which the others are unequal to it. It participates indeed. But truly, magnitude and smallness belong to inequality. They do. There is, therefore, both magnitude and smallness in such a
<margin>G</margin> One? It seems likely. Magnitude and smallness are always standing apart from each other. Certainly. Therefore, there is always something between them. There is. Can you name anything else between them except equality? No, only that. To whatever, then, there is magnitude and smallness, there is also equality, being between these two. It appears so. To the One which is not, as it seems, equality, magnitude, and smallness would belong. It seems so. And indeed, it must participate in being in some way. How so? It must be as we say it is. For if it were not so, we would not speak truly—

<margin>A</margin> But now, they are not one, nor many, nor a whole, nor parts—these other things—since they participate in nothing of the One. Correct. Wherefore they are neither two nor three, nor does the "one" exist within them, since they are entirely deprived of the One. So it is. Therefore, they are neither similar, nor dissimilar, nor are the others the same as the One, nor does similarity or dissimilarity exist within them. For if they were similar and dissimilar themselves, by the fact that they had similarity and dissimilarity within themselves, they would contain two contrary species within themselves, both the "others" themselves and the "one." It appears so. And it cannot happen that those things which participate in nothing, participate in two. Certainly not. Therefore they are neither
<margin>B</margin> similar, nor dissimilar, nor both—whatever things are other than the One; for if they were similar or dissimilar, they would participate in some one or other species; and if both, in two certain contrary species. But these things were shown to be impossible. You speak truly. Therefore, they will not be the same, nor different, nor moved, nor at rest, nor rising, nor perishing, nor greater, nor smaller, nor equal, nor finally will anything else of this kind happen to them. For if they received any such thing, they would participate in one and two and three, and in even and odd: which we saw to be impossible, since they are destitute of the One in all things. These things are most true. For these reasons, then, if the One is, the One is all things, and it is nothing, and toward itself and toward others, the matter stands entirely in this way. But truly,
<margin>C</margin> <margin>The sixth supposition. A negative from an infinite subject is the contrary of a negative from a finite subject.</margin> if the One should not be, must it not be considered thereafter what would happen? It must be considered. What is this supposition: "if the One is not"? Does it differ in any way from this: "If the not-one is not"? It surely differs. Does it only differ, or is this—"If the not-one is not"—entirely contrary to that—"If the One is not"? Entirely contrary. What then? If someone said, "if magnitude is not," or "smallness is not," or anything else of this kind, does he not intimate in each case that he is speaking of something else as the "non-being" itself? Entirely. Does he not therefore now declare that he speaks of something else besides the others as the "non-being" itself, when he says, "if the One is not"? And do we understand what he says? We understand. First, he expresses something else that can be known; then, something other than
<margin>D</margin> the "others," when he says "the One," whether adding "to be" to it or "not to be." Nonetheless, it is known what is said "not to be," and that it is a certain thing differing from the others. Or not? Necessarily. In this way, therefore, it must be said from the beginning: if the One is not, what must it be. First, therefore, this must happen to it, as it seems: namely, that there is some knowledge of it, or else we would understand nothing of what we say when we utter "if the One is not." You speak truly. And are not the "others" different than it, or else it would not be predicated as different than the "others"? Most especially. Therefore, diversity also belongs to it besides knowledge; for he does not speak of the diversity of
<margin>E</margin> others when he calls the One "different" than the others, but of its own diversity. It appears so. Moreover, the "non-being" itself is said to be a participant of "that very thing," and of "something," and of "this," and "to this," and "of these," and of all things of this kind. For neither would "the One" be spoken of, nor "others" than the One, nor would anything be "to it," nor anything "of it"; nor would it be called "something," unless it were a participant of "some" or of "certain" things of this kind. Right. Nevertheless, for the One "to be" is impossible unless it exists; but nothing prohibits it from participating in many things. But if neither the One itself nor "that" will be, but the discourse is held concerning another, nothing ought to be pronounced. But if that "One" alone and no other is presupposed not to be,
<margin>F</margin> it must be said to be a participant both of that very thing and of many others. And most especially indeed. Wherefore, it has dissimilarity toward the others; for since the others are "different" than the One, they must be "extraneous." They must. And are not extraneous things "alien"? Why not? And are not alien things "dissimilar"? Clearly dissimilar. And yet, if they are dissimilar to the One, they will be dissimilar to a dissimilar thing. Clearly. Therefore, dissimilarity will also be present in the One, according to which the others are dissimilar to it. It seems so. And if it possesses dissimilarity toward the others, will not similarity toward itself be appropriate? In what way? If dissimilarity to the One were in the One, the discourse would certainly not be held concerning such a thing as the One, nor would the supposition be concerning the One, but concerning some other thing. Entirely. But that is not fitting. Certainly not. For this reason, it is necessary for similarity
<margin>G</margin> toward itself to be present in the One. It is necessary. Likewise, it is not equal to the others. But since it is not equal to the rest, is it not also necessary that the others be in no way equal to it? Necessary. But those things which are not equal are unequal. Unequal. And are unequal things unequal to some unequal thing? Certainly. Whence the One also appears as a participant in inequality, according to which the others are unequal to it. A participant indeed. But magnitude and smallness pertain to inequality. Therefore, magnitude and smallness also belong to such a One. It seems so. Magnitude again and smallness are always distant from each other. To whatever, therefore, magnitude and smallness happen, equality also happens, occupying the middle of these. It is established. To the One, therefore, while it is not, equality, magnitude, and smallness seem to happen. They seem so. Moreover, it must also participate in essence in a certain way. But how? It must possess itself in the way we have said; for unless it were so, it would not be true—

<meta>This page continues the logical investigation of the "One." Having previously discussed the consequences if the One exists, the dialogue now shifts to the hypothesis: "If the One does not exist." Specifically, it examines whether a "non-existent One" can still have properties or participate in "being" in a paradoxical sense.</meta>

# OF PLATO

<margin>
If a thing exists, and the speech about it is true, and if the reasoning derived from the thing is true, then the thing itself is true.
</margin>
...would we say, while we confess the One is not? But if these things are true, it is manifest that we are speaking of things that *are*. Is it not so? It is so. Since we have said that we speak the truth, it is necessary that we profess to assert things that exist. Necessary. Therefore, the One is, as it seems, a non-existent thing. <note>original: "non ens"</note> For if it were not "non-existent," but were to relinquish something of its "being" toward "not being," it would immediately become an "existent." <note>original: "ens"</note> Entirely so.

It is necessary, therefore, that the non-existent have the "being of non-being" as its bond, if it is to be non-existent; just as, conversely, the existent has as a bond of its being the "not being of non-being," so that it may again be perfectly. For in this way, the existent will most truly be, and the non-existent will most truly not be: if the existent participates in the essence of being an existent, but not in the essence of being a non-existent, if it is to be entirely; while the non-existent does not participate in the essence of not-being a non-existent, but in the essence of being a non-existent, if indeed it is to appear fully as non-existent. These things are most true.

Therefore, since the One participates in not-being, and non-being participates in being, is it not also necessary for the One, since it is not, to participate in being in order to truly not be? It is necessary. Essence, therefore, appears to be present in the One if it is not. It appears so.

And yet "non-essence" is also present, if indeed it is not at all. Why not? For can something that is said to be in a certain state not be in that state, when it has not yet been changed from that habit? It cannot. Whatever, therefore, is in this state and not in this state, suffers a certain change. It suffers it. And shall we say that change is "motion," or something else? Motion. <note>The Greek term used is <term>κίνησις</term> (kinesis), which refers to any type of change or movement.</note> And did the One not appear as both being and non-being? It appeared so. Therefore, it appears to be both in this state and not in this state. It seems so. Therefore, the non-existent One appears to move, since it receives a change from being into non-being. It is clear.

Yet truly, if it is nowhere in the nature of things, since it is not, it surely cannot migrate from one place to another. For how could it? Therefore, it does not move by way of transition. Not at all. Nor can it revolve in the same place. For the "same" is nowhere touched by it, because the "same" is an existent, and it is impossible for the non-existent to be among any of the things that exist. Certainly impossible. Therefore, the One, when it is not, could never revolve in that in which it is not at all. Never. Nor is the One altered from itself, neither as an existent nor as a non-existent; for the discourse would no longer be about the One if it were altered from itself, but about something else besides the One. Correct. If it is neither altered, nor revolves in the same place, nor proceeds forward, in what way will it move? In no way. But that which cannot be moved must necessarily be at rest, and that which rests stands still. Necessary. Therefore, the One, if it is not, both stands still and moves. It seems so.

Furthermore, if it moves, it is undoubtedly necessary for it to be altered; for insofar as something is moved, to that extent it is no longer in the same state as before, but in another. Clearly. Therefore, while the One moves, it is also altered. Truly. Yet, if it is moved in no way, it is altered in no way. Not at all. For which reason, the One which is not, insofar as it moves, is without doubt altered; but insofar as it does not move, it is not altered. Not at all. And therefore, if the One is not, it is altered, and also not altered. It is established. But must not that which is altered become different than before, and cast off its former state? And must not that which is not altered neither become nor perish? It follows necessarily.

<margin>
The opinion of the hypothesis.
</margin>
Hence, the One which is not, because it is altered, is both "becoming" and "perishing"; but because it is not altered, it neither "becomes" nor "perishes." And so it both "becomes" and "perishes" equally, and again neither "becomes" nor "perishes." So it is. Now let us return again to the beginning, to see clearly whether these things appear hereafter as they have until now, or otherwise. This is worthwhile. Have we not already discussed what happens regarding the One if it is not at all? We have.

<margin>
Non-being.
</margin>
But whenever we utter "non-being," it signifies nothing else to us than the absence of essence <note>original: <term>οὐσία</term> (ousia)</note> from that which we pronounce not to be. Nothing else. When we say something "is not," do we mean that in some way it is, and in some way it is not? Or do we mean that it is in no way at all, and since it is not, it is in no part capable of essence? It signifies that absolutely. Therefore, the non-existent can neither "be" itself, nor in any other way touch essence. Not at all.

<margin>
Non-being simply cannot be, nor touch essence.
</margin>
And are "becoming" and "perishing" anything other than one receiving essence and the other losing it? Nothing else. Therefore, that which can have no part of this can never either receive it or lose it. Never. Therefore, since the One is in no way, it is not fitting for it to obtain, or cast away, or in any other way take hold of essence. It is fitting. Therefore, it is not capable of essence on its part. It does not seem so. Nor, again, is it altered in any way. For it would already be both becoming and perishing if it could suffer this. True. If it is not altered at all, is it not also necessary that it is in no way moved? Necessary. Nor shall we assert that what is in no way can stand anywhere; for that which stands must always be in some "same" place. Why not? Thus, clearly, we shall confess that the non-existent never stands nor moves. Never. Furthermore, nothing of the things that exist is present to it. For it would then participate in essence, as if it were a participant of some existing thing. It is manifest. Therefore, neither greatness, nor smallness, nor equality belongs to it. Certainly not. Nor will similarity or diversity be present to it, either toward others or toward itself. It in no way seems so. What then? Can other things be in any way present to it, if nothing at all can be in it? It is not possible. Therefore, other things are not similar to it, nor dissimilar, nor the same,

<column-break/>

<note>The following Greek text is the original version of the Latin text translated above. It follows the same logical progression: A) The non-existent One must have some form of "being" to be talked about; B) and C) Arguments regarding its motion and change; D) Paradoxes of becoming and perishing; E) and F) The definition of absolute non-being; G) The conclusion that absolute non-being can have no qualities.</note>

A Or should we say, in saying that the One is not? But if it is true, it is clear that we are saying it is a thing that exists. Is it not so? So it is. Since we say we speak the truth, it is necessary for us to say we speak of things that are. Necessary. It seems, then, that the One is non-being. For if it will not be non-being, but will let go of some of being toward not-being, it will immediately be being. Entirely so. It must, then, have the being of not-being as a bond for not-being, if it is to not be; just as being must have the not-being of not-being, so that it may completely be. For thus being would most completely be, and non-being would not be, if being participates in the essence of being being, and non-being in the essence of being not-being (if it is to completely not be). But non-being, not participating again in the essence of not-being, but in the essence of being not-being, if non-being is also to completely be. Most true.

B Therefore, since both being partakes in not-being and non-being partakes in being, the One also, since it is not, must partake in being in order not to be? Necessary. And essence indeed appears to belong to the One, if it is not. It appears so. And non-essence then, if it is not. How could it not? Is it possible then, for that which is in a certain state, not to be in that state, without changing from that state? It is not possible. Everything of this sort, then, signifies change, whatever is both in this state and not in this state. How could it not? And is change motion? Or what shall we say? Motion. Did the One not appear as both being and not being? Yes. It appears then to be in this state and not in this state. It seems so. And the non-existent One has appeared to be moving, since it also has change from being to not-being.

C It is likely. But surely, if it is nowhere among things that are, as it is, if indeed it is not, it could not move from anywhere to anywhere. How could it? It would not move by changing place then. It would not. Nor would it turn in the same place. For the "same" is nowhere touched. For the "same" is being. And non-being is impossible to be among beings. For it is impossible. The non-existent One, then, could not turn in that in which it is not. It could not. Nor does the One somehow alter from itself, neither being nor non-being. For the discourse would not be about the One, if it were altered from itself, but about something else. Right.

D And if it is neither altered, nor turns in the same place, nor changes place, could it still move in any way? How indeed? But that which is unmoved must necessarily be at rest, and that which is at rest, stand still. Necessary. The One, then, as it seems, as you said, both moves and stands still. And very much so, if it moves, there is a great necessity for it to be altered. For whatever is moved, insofar as it is moved, no longer holds itself as it did, but differently. So it is. Moving indeed, the One is also altered. Yes. And surely, being in no way moved, it would in no way be altered. It would not. Insofar as the non-existent One moves, then, it is altered; but insofar as it does not move, it is not altered. It would not. The non-existent One, then, is both altered and not altered. It appears so. And must not that which is altered become different than before, and perish from its former state? And that which is not altered, neither become nor perish? Necessary. And the One, then, being non-existent, when it is altered, becomes and perishes; but when it is not altered, it neither becomes nor perishes. and thus the One, being non-existent, both becomes and perishes, and neither becomes nor perishes.

E Is it not so? Let us go back again to the beginning, to see if the same things will appear to us as now, or others. We must. Did we not say, if it is not, what must happen concerning it? Yes. When we say "it is not," does it signify anything other than the absence of essence from that which we say is not? Nothing else. When we say something is not, do we say it "is not" in some way? Or do we say this "is not" simply signifies that it is in no way anywhere, and in no way partakes of essence, that which is non-existent? Most simply indeed.

F Therefore non-being can neither be, nor in any other way partake of essence. It cannot. And is becoming and perishing anything other than partaking in essence, or losing essence? Nothing else. To that which has no part of this, it could neither take it nor lose it. How could it? To the One, then, since it is in no way, it neither has, nor can it be rid of, nor partake of essence in any way. Likely. The non-existent One, then, neither perishes nor becomes, since it in no way partakes of essence. It does not appear so. Nor then is it altered in any way. For already it would become and perish by suffering this. True.

G And if it is not altered, is it not necessary that it also not be moved? Necessary. Nor shall we say that what is nowhere stands. For that which stands must always be in some same thing. How could it not? Thus again we should say that non-being neither stands nor moves. No indeed. But surely nothing of beings belongs to it. For already, partaking of this being, it would partake of essence. Clear. Therefore neither magnitude, nor smallness, nor equality belongs to it. It does not. Nor indeed similarity, and difference, either toward itself or toward others would belong to it. It does not appear so. What then? Can other things be in any way part of it, if nothing is to be part of it? It is not possible. Therefore neither similar, nor dissimilar, nor the same...

<summary>This page explores the ontological status of "non-being." It argues that for the "One" to be non-existent, it must paradoxically possess the "being of non-being," yet concludes that absolute non-existence precludes any properties like motion, change, or similarity.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the dialogue's exploration of the "One." Having previously examined what follows if the One exists and if the One does not exist, Parmenides now moves toward the final, paradoxical conclusion of the entire logical exercise.</meta>

# PARMENIDES

<margin>A</margin> ...nor are the others "other" than them. Certainly not. What then? Does that which belongs to it, or to those, or of such a kind, or this, or of this, or of another, or to others, or at some time, or thereafter, or now, or knowledge, or opinion, or sensation, or a definition, or a name, or anything else that exists, have any place regarding that which is not? <note>original: "τὸ μὴ ὂν" (to mē on). This refers to the concept of absolute non-existence.</note> It does not. Thus, the One, being non-existent, does not possess any state in any way. It seems, then, it does not have any state anywhere. Let us then state, if the One is not, what must happen to the "others." <note>The "others" refers to everything else in the universe that is not the "One."</note> Let us speak of it. Surely there must be "others"; for if there were no others, we would not be speaking about "the others." True. And if the speech is about the others, the others are different. Or do you not call "other" and "different" the same thing? I do. And we say, I suppose, that the different is different from something different, and the "other" is "other" than something "other"? Yes. And so for the others, if they are to be "others," there must be something they will be "other" than. There must be. But they will not be other than the One, since it does not exist. They will not. They are, therefore, other than one another. For if they are not other than the One, the only remaining option is to be other than each other, or else they are "other" than nothing. Correct. They are "other" than each other according to multitudes; for they cannot be "other" according to the One, since the One is nowhere. Instead, they must be multitudes.
<margin>B</margin> For how else could they be? And if the One is nowhere, these multitudes must be infinite in number. Even if one takes what seems to be the smallest part, just like a dream in sleep, it suddenly appears to be many instead of the one it seemed to be; and instead of being the smallest, it appears vast compared to the fragments into which it is subdivided. Most true. From such masses, <note>Greek: "ὄγκων" (onkon), meaning bulk or volume without defined structure.</note> the others would be other than one another, if the others exist while the One does not. Entirely so.
<margin>C</margin> Therefore, there will be many masses, each appearing to be one, though not actually being one, if the One is not? Quite so. And there will seem to be a certain number of them, if each appears to be one despite being many. Certainly. And even and odd numbers will seem to exist among them, though not truly, if the One is not. Indeed. And further, we say they will seem to have a "smallest" part. But this part appears as many and great compared to each of the many fragments, as if they were tiny. How could it be otherwise? And each mass will be thought equal to many small ones; for it would not seem to pass from a greater to a smaller size before appearing to reach a middle point, which would be an illusion of equality. It is likely.
<margin>D</margin> Will it not also have a limit in relation to another mass, while having no beginning, middle, or end in relation to itself? How so? Because whenever someone grasps a part of these in their mind as being a beginning, another beginning always appears before it; and after the end, another end always remains; and in the middle, there are always other "middles" more internal than the middle, yet smaller, because each of them cannot be grasped as a "one," since the One does not exist. Most true. Everything that is grasped by the mind must, I think, be broken into fragments; for whatever is grasped would be a mass without a "one." <note>Without the concept of a "One" or a single unit, any object can be infinitely divided, never reaching a basic building block.</note> Certainly.
<margin>E</margin> Must not such a thing appear to be "one" to someone looking from a distance and dimly? But to one who considers it closely and with a sharp mind, must not each thing appear infinite in multitude, since it is deprived of the One, which does not exist? Most necessarily. Thus, each of the "others" must appear both infinite and limited, and both one and many, if the One is not but the others are. It must. And will they not also seem to be both similar and dissimilar? In what way? Like shadow-paintings, <note>Greek: "ἐσκιαγραφημένα" (eskiagraphēmena). This refers to a type of perspective painting intended to be viewed from a distance, which loses its form when viewed up close.</note> to one standing far off, they all appear as one, seeming to be in the same state and similar. Quite so.
<margin>F</margin> But to one standing near, they appear many and different, and by the illusion of difference, they appear of different kinds and dissimilar to themselves. Just so. Thus, the masses themselves must appear both similar and dissimilar to themselves and to each other. Entirely so. And also the same and different from each other, both touching and separate from themselves, and moving with all kinds of motion, and standing still in every way; and becoming and perishing, and neither of these, and all such things, which would be easy for us to go through, if many exist while the One is not. Most true indeed.
<margin>G</margin> Returning once more to the beginning, let us say: if the One is not, but the others are, what must be the case? Let us say it. First, the others will not be the One. For how could they? Nor will they be many; for if they were many, the One would be in them. If none of them is one, they are all nothing, so they could not even be many. True. If the One is not present in the others, the others are neither many nor one. They are not. Nor do they even *appear* to be one or many. Why? Because the others have no communion in any way with any of the things that are not; nor does anything that is not belong to any of the others. For the non-existent has no parts. True. Therefore, there is no opinion of that which is not among the others, nor any illusion; nor is the non-existent ever imagined in any way by the others. Certainly not. If, therefore, the One is not, none of the others is imagined to be one or many. For it is impossible to imagine "many" without "one." It is impossible. If the One is not, then, the others neither are, nor are they imagined to be, one or many. It does not seem so. Neither then are they similar or dissimilar. No. Nor the same nor different; nor touching nor separate; nor any of the other things we previously went through as appearing; of these, nothing exists and nothing appears.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...they are not others. Indeed not. But truly, will that which belongs to it, or that which is for it, or anything of a certain kind, or this, or of this, or of another, or for another, or at some time, or thereafter, or now, or science, or opinion, or sense, or speech, or a name, or any other thing among those that are, exist regarding that which is least of all? <note>The Latin "minimè est" translates the Greek "not being."</note> Not at all. By these reasons, therefore, if the One is not, it does not exist in any way or anywhere. It certainly does not seem to exist in any way or anywhere.
<margin>The Eighth Hypothesis.</margin> <note>These "Hypotheses" are the structural divisions of the dialogue's logic.</note> Must we discuss again what must happen to the things other than the One, if the One is not? We must.
<margin>B</margin> First, then, those "others" must be something. For unless they were something, there would be no discussion about the others themselves. This is so. And if there is speech about others, they are surely different. Or do you not call "other" and "different" the same thing? I do. Do we not say that the "different" is different from something else, and the "other" is other than another? Certainly. Therefore, for the others, if they are to be others, there will be something from which they will be other. Necessary. What then will that be most of all? They will not be "other" than the One, since it is not. Certainly not. Therefore, they are "other" than each other; for this alone remains: that they are other than nothing else. Right. Therefore, each is "other" than each other according to multitudes. For they cannot be "other" according to the "one," since the One does not exist. But each mass <note>Latin: "aceruus," meaning a heap or pile.</note> of them, as it seems, exists as an infinite multitude. And if someone takes what appears to be the minimum, just as
<margin>C</margin> in a dream, suddenly instead of that which had seemed to be "one," a multitude occurs; and instead of that which had appeared smallest, it will now appear very great if you compare it to those things into which it has been dissected. Most correctly. Such masses, I say, will be diverse from one another besides the One, if the others exist while the One does not exist. Most certainly. But will there not be many masses, of which any one will seem at first glance to be one, yet none will be one, since the One itself is not? Certainly. A certain number of them will also seem to exist, if indeed each seems to be one, even though they are many. Very much so. Furthermore, even and odd will falsely seem to exist, with the One being entirely absent?
<margin>D</margin> Falsely. Moreover, that which at first will seem small among them, as was said, immediately appears very great and very numerous compared to the individual small parts, which are also many. What prevents it? Furthermore, each mass will seem to be equal to many small masses. For it would not clearly seem to have passed from greater to smaller, unless it first seemed to reach a middle point; this, however, will be a certain phantom <note>Latin: "phantasma."</note> of equality. It is likely. Does it not have a boundary in relation to another mass, while having neither beginning, nor middle, nor end in relation to itself? For what reason? Because always when someone looks upon any of these with the intellect, another beginning always occurs before the beginning; and after the end, another end always follows.
<margin>E</margin> Also in the middle, there are always other things more interior than the middle, and always smaller, because one cannot grasp any "one" thing in these, since the One is not. You speak most truly. Finally, I think it is necessary that whatever the intellect grasps is torn apart and dispersed; for a mass is always grasped as being devoid of the One. Without a doubt. Does not such a thing appear to be "one" to someone looking from afar and dimly? Necessary. But to someone perceiving it closely and sharply, each thing is infinite in multitude, if indeed it is abandoned by the non-existent One. This is necessary above all else. In this manner, then, any other things must appear both infinite and having a limit, and one and many, if it is not the One, but others besides the One that exist. It must be so. Will they not also seem similar and
<margin>F</margin> dissimilar? But how? For when, as if in a shadow-painting, they all appear as "one" to someone looking from a distance, they will seem to share in something of the same and to be similar. Entirely. But to one approaching closer, they appear many and different, and by the very phantom of diversity, they appear different from themselves and dissimilar. So it happens. It is necessary that the masses themselves appear both similar and dissimilar, both to themselves and to each other. And most especially so. Will they not also appear both the same and different from each other, both touching themselves and separate from themselves, moved by all motions and standing still everywhere, being born and perishing, and neither, and all such things, which it would be easy for us to run through, if many things exist while the One does not? You tell the truest things.
<margin>The Ninth Hypothesis.</margin> Returning now again to the beginning, let us declare: if the One is not, what will happen to the things other than the One? Let us declare it. In the first place, then, the "others" will not be the One. For how could they be? Nor will they be many. For in those things which are many, the One is also present. For if none of them is one, all are nothing, wherefore they are not even many. You speak truly. Since, therefore, the One is not present in the others, they are neither many nor one. Not clearly. Nor do they even appear to be one or many. Why?

---

Because the "others" have no commerce at all with those things which are not, nor does anything from those things which are least of all belong to anything among the others; for no part is present in those things which are not. True. Therefore, neither an opinion of that which is least of all, nor a phantom, exists in the rest, nor in any way is that which is not conceived by the others in opinion. Certainly not. Wherefore, if the One is not, nothing of the others is conceived in opinion, either to be one or to be many. For without the "one," it is entirely impossible to imagine "many." Too impossible. Therefore, if the One is not, the others neither are, nor are they even thought in opinion to be one or many. They do not seem so. Whence they are neither similar nor dissimilar. No. Nor are they the same, or different, nor touching, nor separated, nor any of the remaining things we related in the previous sections as those which seemed to belong to the others; neither are they the others, nor does it seem that they are the others.

<summary>This page concludes the Parmenides by demonstrating the ultimate paradox: if the "One" (unity) is rejected, then the "Many" (the rest of the universe) can neither exist nor even be perceived or thought of, resulting in total nothingness.</summary>

The Philebus is one of Plato's later dialogues, focusing on the nature of the "Good" and whether pleasure or wisdom is the key to a happy life. This edition includes a summary of the dialogue's philosophy before the text begins.</meta>

PLATONIS

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
...if the one is not. True. In short, if we should say that if the one is not, nothing is, would we speak correctly? Most certainly. Let this then be said by us, and this further: that, as it seems, whether the one is or is not, both it and the others, in relation to themselves and to each other, all things in every way both are and are not, and both appear and do not appear. These things are most true. <note>original: "Verissima quidem hæc sunt." This marks the final sentence of the Parmenides dialogue, concluding its long series of paradoxes about unity and being.</note>
