# PHILEBUS, OR, ON THE SUPREME GOOD.

->SUMMARY OF THE DIALOGUE.<-

In this discussion, the Philosopher treats the supreme good of man in such a way that, having proposed two things—namely, Pleasure and Wisdom—in which men variously place their happiness, he teaches that the supreme good consists in neither of these, by itself and separately, but that a certain third thing is needed. By participation in this third thing, those other two may be useful for human happiness, insofar as they are joined with it. That third thing, truly and supremely good, is God: whom Plato designates by these names, calling him <term>the Good itself, and Intellect, and the Cause</term> <note>original: "αὐτοαγαθὸν καὶ νοῦν, αἰτίαν τε"</note>, etc. Therefore, he says that from the fellowship of this supreme and absolute good, all things, whatever they may be that are good, are called good. He derives five degrees of this participation; however, among those good things that fall within human life, he attributes the greatest part of happiness to Wisdom and intelligence; the second part to Pleasure; and he teaches that the Good is constituted by the mixture of these two. Therefore, the simple aim and thesis of the discussion is: Concerning human happiness, which is indeed defined thus: Happiness is in no way present in human affairs by itself and separately, but only insofar as they communicate with a certain third thing, that is, the supreme good, namely God; and thus human happiness consists in the mixture of Pleasure and Wisdom, insofar as those two communicate with that supreme good. The introduction to the dialogue is as follows: When Socrates and Philebus had exchanged many arguments back and forth concerning the supreme good, and Philebus was already exhausted by the arguing, he congratulated Protarchus on his recent arrival and requested that he take up his role in the debate. Protarchus, being a young man, immediately agreed. Turning to him, Socrates begins the dialogue and warns Protarchus to consider carefully what a task he is undertaking, and not to rush headlong into the argument.

---

->SOCRATES, PROTARCHUS, PHILEBUS.<-

<margin>B</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'V' showing a landscape with a figure and architectural elements.</image-desc>
**L**ook, O Protarchus, at what argument you are now about to receive from Philebus, and against which of us you will instead have to fight, if any part of it does not please you. Do you wish for us to summarize both positions? *PROT.* I certainly do. *SOC.* Philebus says that for all living things, the good is joy, pleasure, delight, and everything else of this kind. Our argument against him, however, is that these are not the good, but rather to be wise, to understand, to remember, and things related to these—such as right opinion and true reasoning—are better and more powerful than pleasure for all who are capable of sharing in them; and that the attainment of these is the most useful of all things, both for those now living and for those to come. Was this not the position of each of us, Philebus? *PHIL.* Most certainly, Socrates.
<margin>C</margin>
*SOC.* Do you then take up, Protarchus, this argument that is now offered to you? *PROT.* I must take it up, since our beautiful Philebus has grown weary. *SOCR.* We must indeed define with all zeal what is involved in these matters. *PROT.* We must indeed. *SOCRAT.* Come then, let us agree on this in addition. *PROT.* On what? *SOC.* That each of us will attempt to demonstrate a certain state and disposition of the soul which is able to provide a happy life for all men. Is that not so? *PROT.* Certainly. *SOCRA.* And you will demonstrate the state and disposition of rejoicing, while we will demonstrate that of being wise. *PROT.* So it is. *SOC.* But if some other state should appear that is better than both of these, and if it should be more closely related to pleasure, and provide a firmer foundation for life, would we not both be defeated, while pleasure would triumph over wisdom? *PR.* Truly. *SOC.* But if it should be nearer to wisdom, then wisdom will overcome pleasure, and pleasure will succumb. Do you grant these things, or how shall we proceed? *PRO.* They seem to me things that must be granted. *SOC.* But what does Philebus think? What do you say? *PHIL.* To me, pleasure seems to be superior, and it always will. You must see to it yourself, Protarchus. *PRO.* Since you have already handed over the duty of the argument to us, Philebus, you no longer have the power to agree or disagree with Socrates. *PHIL.* You speak the truth. But I wash my hands of it, and I now call the goddess herself to witness. <note>Philebus refers to Aphrodite, who represents Pleasure here.</note> *PROT.* And we also will be witnesses that you said what you said. But let us next, O Socrates, attempt to finish the matter, whether Philebus is willing or however you wish.
<margin>E</margin>
*SOCR.* Let us attempt it, beginning from the goddess herself, whom this man says is called Venus <note>original: "Venerem" (Latin) / "Ἀφροδίτην" (Greek)</note>, but whose truest name, he says, is Pleasure. *PROT.* Quite right. *SOCRAT.* My reverence toward the names of the gods is always great; it is not merely human, but surpasses the greatest fear. And now I call her Venus, just as it is pleasing to her; but I know that pleasure is a varied thing. But making our beginning from her, as I said, we must investigate what nature she has. We hear her spoken of as one thing, yet she takes on many forms, and in some way they are unlike one another. For look: we say a profligate man takes pleasure; but we also say a temperate man takes pleasure in his very temperance; a foolish man is full of foolish opinions and vain hope; but a wise man takes pleasure in his wisdom. If anyone should say these pleasures are similar to one another, he would rightly be seen as a fool.
<margin>F</margin>
*PROTARCH.* These, Socrates, are from op-

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
...these things, if the one is not. True. Therefore, if we should say in short, if the one is not, nothing is, would we speak correctly? Altogether so. Let this then be said, and also that, as it seems, whether the one is or is not, both itself and the others, both in relation to themselves and to each other, all things in every way both are and are not, and both appear and do not appear. Most true.

# PHILEBUS, OR, CONCERNING PLEASURE.

---

->SOCRATES, PROTARCHUS, PHILEBUS.<-

<margin>B</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'Ω' with floral and architectural designs.</image-desc>
**I**t is time, Protarchus, to see what argument you are about to receive from Philebus, and against what position of ours you are to contend, if what is said is not to your mind. Do you wish for us to summarize each? *PROT.* By all means. *SOC.* Philebus says that the good for all animals is to rejoice, and pleasure, and delight, and whatever is in harmony with these. But our contention is that it is not these, but to be wise, and to understand, and to remember, and things related to these—right opinion and true reasonings—which are better and more desirable than pleasure for all who are able to participate in them. And for those able to participate, it is the most beneficial of all things, for all who are and shall be. Do we not each speak in this way, Philebus? *PHIL.* Most certainly of all, Socrates.
<margin>C</margin>
*SOC.* Do you then accept this argument now offered, Protarchus? *PROT.* I must accept it. For our beautiful Philebus has given up. *SOC.* We must then determine the truth about these things in every way. *PROT.* We must indeed. *SOC.* Come then, let us agree on this in addition. *PROT.* On what sort of thing? *SOC.* That each of us will now attempt to show a certain habit and disposition of the soul, which is able to provide a happy life for all men. Is it not so? *PROT.* It is so. *SOC.* Therefore, you on the side of rejoicing, and we on the side of being wise. *PROT.* That is it. *SOC.* But what if another state should appear better than these? If it should appear more closely related to pleasure, would we both be defeated by the life that holds these things firmly, but the life of pleasure would prevail over the life of wisdom?
<margin>D</margin>
*PROT.* Yes. *SOC.* But if it is closer to wisdom, then wisdom wins over pleasure, and pleasure is defeated? Do you say these things are so agreed? Or how? *PROT.* It seems so to me, at least. *SOC.* But what about Philebus? What do you say? *PHIL.* To me, pleasure seems to win entirely, and always will. But you, Protarchus, will know for yourself. *PROT.* Having handed the argument over to us, Philebus, you would no longer be the master of the agreement with Socrates, or its opposite. *PHIL.* You speak the truth. But I discharge my conscience, and I call the goddess herself to witness. *PROT.* And we would be fellow-witnesses for you of these very things, that you said what you are saying. But let us, Socrates, try to finish the following things in order, even with Philebus willing, or however he may wish.
<margin>E</margin>
*SOC.* We must try, beginning from the goddess herself, whom this man says is called Aphrodite, but her truest name is Pleasure. *PROT.* Most correctly. *SOC.* My fear, O Protarchus, always regarding the names of the gods, is not according to man, but beyond the greatest fear. And now I address Aphrodite in whatever way is pleasing to her; but I know that pleasure is a complex thing; and, as I said, we must begin from her and consider and examine what nature she has. For to hear the name, it is simply one thing, but surely she has taken on all kinds of forms, and in some way they are unlike each other. For look: we say the profligate man takes pleasure; but the temperate man also takes pleasure in his very temperance; and the foolish man, full of foolish opinions and hopes, takes pleasure; but the wise man also takes pleasure in his very wisdom. And how could anyone, saying each of these pleasures is like the other, not rightly appear foolish?
<margin>F</margin>
*PROTARCH.* For they are from opposites, O Socrates—

<meta>The previous page concluded the *Parmenides* with a series of logical paradoxes regarding "The One" and transitioned into the opening summary of the *Philebus*. This page begins the dialogue itself, where Socrates and Protarchus debate whether pleasure or wisdom is the "Good."</meta>

# PHILEBUS.

<margin>A</margin> even if they arise from opposite things, they themselves are not contrary to one another. For how could pleasure not be the most similar thing of all to pleasure—this very thing to itself?
SOCRATES: Indeed, my dear friend <note>original: "ὦ δαιμόνιε," a respectful but sometimes ironic address</note>, color does not differ from color in the respect that it is a color, yet we all know that black is not only different from white but is its absolute opposite. So too, shape is the same as shape in its general kind; yet its parts <note>specific types of shapes</note> are often either entirely opposite to each other or possess infinite variety. We shall find many other things like this. Therefore, do not trust this argument which makes all opposites into one. I fear we may find some pleasures that are actually contrary to one another.
<margin>B</margin> PROTARCHUS: Perhaps; but how will this harm our argument?
SOCRATES: Because we will say that you are calling things that are unlike by a different name. For you say that all pleasant things are good. Now, no argument disputes that pleasant things are indeed pleasant; but while many of them are bad and others are good (as we maintain), you nevertheless call them all "good," even though you would admit they are unlike if pressed in argument. What common element, then, exists in both bad and good pleasures that leads you to call them all "good"?
<margin>C</margin> PROTARCHUS: What do you mean, Socrates? Do you think anyone who has established that Pleasure is "The Good" would concede to you, or even tolerate you saying, that some pleasures are good while others are bad?
SOCRATES: But you will at least admit they are unlike one another, and some are even opposites.
<margin>D</margin> PROTARCHUS: Not insofar as they are pleasures.
<margin>E</margin> SOCRATES: We are drifting back to the same argument, Protarchus. We shall end up saying that no pleasure differs from another, but all are alike. The examples we just used would have no effect on us, and we would speak and act just like the most foolish and immature of debaters.
PROTARCHUS: In what way?
SOCRATES: If I were to imitate you and defend myself by daring to say that the most unlike thing is actually the most like the most unlike, I would be saying the same things you are. We would appear more immature than is proper, and our argument would collapse and vanish. Let us take it back to the start; perhaps by returning to the points of similarity, we might reach an agreement.
PROTARCHUS: Tell me how.
SOCRATES: Let me be questioned by you in turn, Protarchus.
PROTARCHUS: Regarding what?
SOCRATES: Consider Wisdom, Knowledge, and Intellect, and all those things I originally proposed as "good" when I was asked what the Good is. Will they not suffer the same fate as your argument?
PROTARCHUS: How so?
SOCRATES: The various sciences <note>original: "ἐπιστῆμαι," referring to branches of knowledge or crafts</note> as a whole will appear to be many, and some of them unlike one another. If some even turn out to be opposites, would I be worthy of this discussion if, out of fear, I claimed no science was unlike another? Our argument would then vanish like a fairy tale, and we would be saved only by our own irrationality. But this must not happen, except perhaps for the sake of consistency. I am satisfied that both our arguments should stand on equal footing: that there are many unlike pleasures, and many different sciences. Let us not hide the difference between my "Good" and yours, Protarchus, but bring it into the open and dare to see if examination reveals whether we should call Pleasure "the Good," or Wisdom, or some third thing. For we are surely not competing just so that my side or yours wins; we must both fight as allies for whatever is most true.
PROTARCHUS: Indeed we must.
SOCRATES: Let us then establish this principle even more firmly by mutual agreement.
PROTARCHUS: Which one?
SOCRATES: The one that gives all men trouble—sometimes willingly, sometimes unwillingly.
PROTARCHUS: Speak more clearly.
SOCRATES: I mean the problem that just cropped up, which is marvelous by nature. For saying that "the many are one" and "the one is many" is a marvelous thing to say, and it is easy for a person to dispute with whoever proposes either side.
PROTARCHUS: Do you mean when someone says that I, Protarchus, who am by nature one person, am also many—claiming that I am both tall and short, heavy and light, and countless other things?
SOCRATES: You, Protarchus, have mentioned the common and popular "wonders" regarding <term>the One and the Many</term> <note>A fundamental Greek philosophical problem: how can a single concept (the One) apply to many different physical things (the Many)?</note>. It is now generally agreed, so to speak, that one should not even touch such things, as they are considered childish and easy, and a great hindrance to serious discussion. Nor should we care about cases where someone divides a person's limbs and parts by logic and, having forced the agreement that all these parts are that single "one," mocks the result as a monstrous conclusion that "the one is many and infinite" and "the many are only one."
PROTARCHUS: Then what other wonders do you mean, Socrates, which are not yet common knowledge regarding this same subject?
SOCRATES: I mean, my boy, when a person proposes a "One" that is not among the things that are born and perish <note>i.e., not physical objects like people or oxen</note>. For in the case of those physical "ones," as we just said, it is agreed we should not waste time on them. But when one tries to establish a single "Man," a single "Ox," a single "Beauty," or a single "Good," it is about these <term>monads</term> <note>original: "ἑνάδων," units or abstract Ideas</note> and such units that great effort and intense disagreement arise during division.
PROTARCHUS: In what way?
SOCRATES: First...

<column-break/>

even if they proceed from contrary things, they are not themselves contrary. For how could pleasure not be most similar to pleasure of all things, since it is the same as itself?
<margin>A</margin> SOCRATES: Truly, O blessed one, color does not differ from color in the fact that each is a color; but we all know that black is not only different from white but is also most contrary to it. Furthermore, shape is the same as shape in its general kind; however, the parts of that kind either differ immensely from each other or are even contrary, and we shall find many other such things. For this reason, do not believe this reasoning which makes all most contrary things one. For I fear we may find some pleasures to be contrary to each other.
<margin>B</margin> PROTARCHUS: Perhaps, but how will this harm our reasoning?
SOCRATES: It will harm it in this way: that you call these things, though they are dissimilar, by another name (so to speak). For you say all sweet things are good. Now, no reason prevents sweet things from being sweet. But since many of them are bad, and many also (as we say) are good, you nevertheless call them all good, even though you would be forced to confess they are dissimilar if someone compelled you. What then is found in all pleasures, both bad and good, that is the same or common, on account of which you call them all good?
<margin>C</margin> PROTARCHUS: What are you saying, O Socrates? Do you think anyone, having asserted that pleasure is the good, would then grant you or tolerate you saying that some are good and some are bad?
SOCRATES: Nevertheless, you will confess that many are dissimilar, and most are even contrary to each other.
<margin>D</margin> PROTARCHUS: Not at all, insofar as they are pleasures.
<margin>E</margin> SOCRATES: We fall back into the same point, O Protarchus, and we shall say that pleasure does not differ from pleasure, but all are alike. The examples brought forward a little while ago will move us not at all, and we shall struggle like those who are inept and unskilled in disputations.
PROTARCHUS: Why do you say that?
SOCRATES: Because if I, imitating you, were not afraid to say that the most dissimilar of all things is most similar to its most dissimilar, I could say the same things you do. Thus we shall appear more unlearned than is fitting, and our speech will fail us and be finished. Let us therefore begin it again; for perhaps by progressing further, we shall concede to the same opinion.
PROTARCHUS: Tell me how.
SOCRATES: Suppose I am questioned by you in turn, Protarchus.
PROTARCHUS: What then?
SOCRATES: Wisdom, knowledge, mind, and whatever things I, at the beginning, when asked what the good itself is, called "good"—will they not suffer the same fate as your argument?
PROTARCHUS: By what reasoning?
SOCRATES: For all the sciences will seem many, and some of them dissimilar to each other; but if some are even contrary, would I be worthy of the present discussion if, fearing this truth, I said no science was dissimilar to another science? Thus at last our speech would vanish like a fable, and we would be held back by a certain lack of reason. But it is not at all fitting for it to happen thus; rather, the way of safety must be held. It pleases me equally, therefore, in both your speech and mine: that there are clearly many and dissimilar pleasures, and moreover many and different sciences. Therefore, O Protarchus, not hiding the difference between my good and yours, but rather bringing it into the light, let us endure it if some who examine us inquire whether it is right to call pleasure, or wisdom, or some third thing besides these, the "good." For now we ought by no means to contend for this—that the things I propose or the things you propose should win—but let us favor that which is most true.
PROTARCHUS: So it must be.
SOCRATES: Let us establish this even more by mutual confession.
PROTARCHUS: What thing?
SOCRATES: That which is troublesome to all men, both to those willing and even sometimes to those unwilling.
PROTARCHUS: Speak more plainly.
SOCRATES: I mean the discourse that just now occurred, which is marvelous by nature. That "the many are one" and "the one is many" is marvelous to say. In which it is easy, whichever part you defend, to raise a doubt.
PROTARCHUS: Do you say this: when someone asserts that I, Protarchus, for example, being one by nature, am again many; and again those who posit me as both contrary to myself—heavy, light, large, small—likewise posit the same and single man, and many things of <margin>G</margin> this kind?
SOCRATES: You indeed, O Protarchus, bring up things concerning the One and the Many that have ceased to seem marvelous, and which, so to speak, everyone agrees should not be attempted, as they are childish things and easy to know, and most likely to hinder discourse if someone admits them. Nor should they be considered marvelous if someone, dividing the limbs and parts of someone by reason, and having confessed all those to be that one thing, then refutes and mocks him, as if he were forced to confess monsters—namely, that the one is many and infinite, and the many are one.
PROTARCHUS: But what other things do you mean, O Socrates, which have not yet been conceded or made public regarding this same discourse?
SOCRATES: Whenever someone, O boy, posits the One <margin>H</margin> as nothing from those things which are born and die, as we said a little while ago; then it is agreed that such a "one" ought by no means to be refuted. But when one tries to affirm one man, one ox, one beauty, and one good, now truly in these and such unities, anxious study and even ambiguous division occurs.
PROTARCHUS: In what way?
SOCRATES: First indeed...

<summary>Socrates and Protarchus begin a dialogue on whether pleasure or wisdom is the ultimate "Good," leading into the complex philosophical problem of the "One and the Many." Socrates distinguishes between trivial paradoxes of physical objects and the serious challenge of defining abstract "monads" or Forms like Beauty or Goodness.</summary>

<meta>The previous page introduced the debate between Socrates and Protarchus (representing Philebus's view) regarding whether Pleasure or Wisdom is the highest Good. Socrates began questioning the nature of pleasure and its diversity, leading to a broader philosophical problem regarding how "one" thing can also be "many." This page dives into the logical heart of that problem: the theory of Monads or Forms.</meta>

->PLATONIS<-

<margin>A</margin>
...whether it must be admitted that certain units <term>monads; the Platonic Forms or Ideas</term> of this kind truly exist. Next, how each of them must be thought of as being always one and the same, admitting neither of generation nor destruction, but remaining most firmly in its own unity. Finally, whether among things that are generated and infinite, each of these units must be placed either as dispersed and having become many from one, or as a whole separate from itself—which would seem the most impossible of all—that one and the same thing should become simultaneously in the one and the many. These are the issues, Protarchus, concerning the One and the Many, and if they are poorly agreed upon, they are the cause of all difficulty and failure; but if well examined, they lead to ease of understanding. **PROT.** It is necessary for us, Socrates, to discuss this first in the present circumstances. **SOC.** So I should judge, at least.

<margin>B</margin>
<margin>Do not stir a well-settled evil. <note>original Latin: "Malum bene sopitum ne moue"; similar to the English idiom "let sleeping dogs lie."</note></margin>
**PROT.** You may consider that all of us here agree with you on these points. But perhaps it is best now not to stir Philebus by asking questions, like a "sleeping evil" (as the saying goes) that is well-settled. **SOC.** Very well. But where shall we best begin, since the battle in these doubts is so great and varied? From here? **PROT.** From where? **SOC.** We say that the One and the Many, having become the same through reasoning, wander everywhere in every speech, both long ago and now. This will never cease to be, nor did it just begin now; rather, as it seems to me, Protarchus, this is an immortal and never-aging quality of reasoning itself within us. When a young person first tastes this <note>original: "γευσάμενος," meaning to have a first experience of a philosophical concept</note>, he congratulates himself as if he had found a treasure of wisdom, and full of pleasure he exults and runs wild. He gladly attempts every kind of argument, sometimes turning it to one side and mixing it into one, then again unfolding it and distributing it into many. In this, he first and foremost casts himself into doubt and difficulty; then he does the same to anyone near him, whether younger, older, or of his own age, sparing neither father nor mother nor any of his listeners—and hardly even sparing other living creatures, let alone humans, since he would not even spare the barbarians <note>original: "βαρβάρων," meaning non-Greek speakers</note> if only he could find an interpreter from somewhere.

<margin>C</margin>
**PROT.** Do you not see, Socrates, that all of us standing here are young? And do you not fear that we might join Philebus in attacking you if you insult us? Nevertheless—for we understand what you are saying—if there is any way or any device by which this confusion can be kindly removed from our discussion, and a more convenient path to the argument can be found, you yourself should consider it, and we will follow you as best we can; for the present discussion is no small matter, Socrates.

<margin>D</margin>
**SOC.** Certainly not, boys—for that is what Philebus called you. Yet there is no more beautiful path, nor can there be, than the one I have always loved. But it has often fled from me, leaving me deserted and helpless. **PROT.** Which path is that? Just tell us. **SOC.** It is one that is not so difficult to point out, but very difficult to follow. For whatever things have been discovered through art <note>original: "per artem," referring to technical or scientific knowledge</note> have come to light for mankind by this path. Pay attention, I pray, to what I am saying.

<margin>E</margin>
**PROT.** Just tell us. **SOC.** It is a gift of the gods to men, as it appears to me, which descended through some Prometheus <note>The Titan who stole fire and gave it to humans; here used as a metaphor for the light of reason</note> along with a most brilliant fire.

<margin>F</margin>
<margin>The ancients were better than us and closer to the gods.</margin>
<margin>At this point, one might ask, since it is posited that science is a virtue and virtue consists in a mean, whether science is also in a certain mean—that is, between the one and the infinite. <note>A scholastic marginal note attempting to link Plato's "limit" to Aristotle's "golden mean."</note></margin>
For the ancients, who were better than us and lived closer to the gods, passed down this oracle to us: that while all things which are always said to exist consist of the One and the Many, they have within them an innate Limit and Infinity. It is necessary for us, since things are thus ordered, to always search by positing one idea <term>Form; a universal concept</term> in every single thing according to its kind, for we shall find it inherent there. If we grasp it, we must then look for two (if there are two) after the one, or if not, for three or some other number; and then divide each of those units in the same way, until someone perceives that the original "One" is not only one, many, and infinite, but also exactly *how many* it is. But we should not apply the idea of the infinite to the multitude until one has perceived the entire number falling between the infinite and the one; only then should one let each "one" of all the things pass away into the infinite. The gods, then, as we said, granted us the ability to investigate, learn, and teach one another in this way. But the wise men who exist now among humans introduce the One and the Many however it happens—faster or slower than they should—and after the One they immediately jump to the infinite, while the intermediate numbers escape them. This is what distinguishes the method of <term>dialectic; the logical search for truth through division</term> from that of <term>eristic; arguing merely for the sake of winning</term> in our discussions with one another. **PROT.** I seem to partly understand what you have just said, Socrates, but I desire to hear other parts more clearly.

<margin>G</margin>
<margin>By this reasoning, Aristotle reduced the eleven [or ten] genera. <note>original: "undecim decem genera coegit." This likely refers to Aristotle's Categories.</note></margin>
**SOC.** This is clearly seen in the letters of the alphabet, Protarchus, as we have said. Therefore, take this lesson from those things you have already learned. **PROT.** In what way? **SOC.** The voice that breaks from our mouth is one, yet it is also infinite in number—the voice of all together and of each one. **PROT.** Certainly. **SOC.** But we are not made learned by either of these: not because we know its infinity, nor because we know its unity; but because we grasp how many and of what kind they are. This is what makes each of us a grammarian. **PROT.** You speak most truly. **SOC.** The same thing also makes a man a musician. **PROT.** By what reasoning? **SOC.** In a certain way, the sound in that art is also one. **PROT.** Of course. **SOC.** And two things must be posited: the low and the high, and a third, the middle tone. Is it not so? **PROT.** It is. **SOC.** But you would not yet be learned in music if you knew only these; and if you were ignorant of the rest, you would be (so to speak) of no value in music. **PROT.** Of no value. **SOC.** But after...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
...whether it is necessary to assume that such units exist, truly being. Then how, again, each of these—being always the same, and admitting neither generation nor destruction—nevertheless remains most firmly this one. After this, in the things that are becoming and are infinite, whether it is to be placed as dispersed and having become many, or as a whole separate from itself—which would seem the most impossible of all—that the same and one should become simultaneously in one and in many. These are the issues concerning such "one and many." But not those other matters, Protarchus, which are the cause of all difficulty when not well agreed upon, and of ease when they are. **PROT.** Therefore it is necessary for us, Socrates, to work through this first at the present time. **SOC.** So I think, indeed.

<margin>B</margin>
**PROT.** Assume then that we, as children, agree with you on such things. But perhaps it is best for now not to move Philebus, who is asking questions, as he is "well-placed" <note>original: "εὖ κείμενον," referring to the proverb of not disturbing something that is settled</note>. **SOC.** So be it. From where then shall one begin again this battle of the disputed points, which is great and of all kinds? Shall it be from here? **PROT.** How? **SOC.** We say, I suppose, that the same "one and many" produced by reasoning run about everywhere in every single thing said, both of old and now. And this will never cease, nor did it begin now. Rather, such a thing is (as it seems to me) an immortal and ageless condition of the arguments themselves within us. He who first tastes of it among the young is delighted, as if having found a treasure of wisdom; in his pleasure he is inspired and moves every argument gladly, at one time rolling it to one side and mixing it into one, and at another time unrolling it again and dividing it, casting himself first and foremost into difficulty, and always doing the same to those next to him, whether younger or older or his own age; sparing neither father nor mother, nor any other of his listeners—and almost even other living creatures, not only humans. Since he would spare none of the barbarians, if only he could have an interpreter from somewhere.

<margin>C</margin>
**PROT.** Socrates, do you not see our number, that we are all young? And are you not afraid that we might attack you along with Philebus if you insult us? Nevertheless—for we understand what you are saying—if there is any way and device for such confusion to leave our argument in a kindly way, and to find a more beautiful path than this to the argument, you be eager for this, and we will follow along to the best of our ability. For the present argument is not small, Socrates.

<margin>D</margin>
**SOC.** Not at all, boys. For as Philebus called you, indeed there is no more beautiful path, nor could there be, of which I have always been a lover, though many times it has already escaped me and left me deserted and helpless. **PROT.** Which is this? Let it only be told. **SOC.** One which is not very difficult to point out, but very difficult to use. For all things ever discovered that belong to art have become manifest through this. Consider what I am saying.

<margin>E</margin>
**PROT.** Only speak. **SOC.** It is a gift of the gods to humans, as it appears to me, thrown down from the gods from somewhere through a certain Prometheus along with a most bright fire. And the ancients, being better than us and living closer to the gods, passed down this tradition: that things said to exist always are composed of One and Many, and have Limit and Infinity innate within them. We must, therefore, since things are thus ordered, always posit one idea concerning everything and seek it. For we shall find it within. If we grasp it, after the one we look for two, if somehow they exist, and if not, three or some other number; and each of those "ones" again in the same way. Until one sees not only that the original "one" is one and many and infinite, but also exactly *how many*. But one should not bring the idea of the infinite to the multitude until one has seen its entire number—the number between the infinite and the one; then at last, having let each one of the whole pass into the infinite, one may let it go. The gods, as I said, handed down to us this way to investigate, learn, and teach one another. But the wise men of today make "one" and "many" however it happens, and more quickly or slowly than they should; after the one they immediately make it infinite; but the intermediates escape them. It is by these that the difference between the dialectical and the eristic way of making arguments with one another is defined.

<margin>F</margin>
**PROT.** Some things, Socrates, I seem to understand; but other things I still need to hear more clearly. **SOC.** What I am saying, Protarchus, is clear in the letters of the alphabet; take the example from these in which you have been educated. **PROT.** How? **SOC.** Voice is, I suppose, one thing that goes through the mouth, and again it is infinite in multitude, both for everyone and for each. **PROT.** Indeed. **SOC.** And we are not yet wise by either of these—neither because we know its infinity, nor its unity; but *how many* they are and of what kind, this is what makes each of us a grammarian.

<margin>G</margin>
**PROT.** Most true. **SOC.** And indeed, what makes one a musician is the same thing. **PROT.** How? **SOC.** Voice is surely one in that art as well. **PROT.** How could it not be? **SOC.** And let us posit two things, the low and the high, and a third, the "equal-toned" <note>unison or middle pitch</note>. Is it so? **PROT.** Thus. **SOC.** But you would not yet be wise in music knowing only these; if you did not know these, so to speak, you would be of no value in these matters. **PROT.** Truly not. **SOC.** But...

<summary>Socrates introduces the "Promethean" method of dialectic, explaining that to truly understand anything, one must identify the specific finite number of categories (the "limit") between the overarching "One" and the "Infinite" variety of particulars. He uses the examples of grammar (letters) and music (intervals) to illustrate how expertise requires knowing the specific "how many" rather than just the one or the infinite.</summary>

# PHILEBUS #

->**SOCRATES**<-

My friend, once you have grasped how many intervals there are in the voice <note>original Greek: "φωνῆς" (phōnēs); referring to the human voice or sound in general</note> regarding high pitch and low pitch, and of what kind they are, as well as the limits of these intervals and how many systems <note>musical scales or structures</note> have been formed from them—which those who came before us, having observed them, passed down to us their followers to call them "harmonies." In the movements of the body, they also found other such properties, which they say must be measured by numbers and called "rhythms" and "measures." At the same time, they realized that this is the way one ought to consider every "one" and "many." For when you grasp these things in this way, you have become wise; and whenever you grasp any other thing among the things that exist by looking at it in this manner, you have become sensible regarding that thing. However, the infinite <note>unstructured plurality</note> of individuals and the infinite variety within them makes your thinking infinite <note>aimless or wandering</note> each time; it leaves you without an account or a number, since you have never looked toward any specific number in anything.

**PROTARCHUS:** It seems to me, Philebus, that Socrates has spoken most excellently just now.

**PHILEBUS:** I agree with that myself. But why exactly has this argument been spoken to us now? What is its purpose?

**SOCRATES:** Indeed, Protarchus, Philebus has asked a correct question.

**PROTARCHUS:** Entirely so. Please, answer him.

**SOCRATES:** I will do so, after I have discussed these same things a little further. Just as if one were to take some "one," as we said, they should not look immediately to the nature of the infinite, but toward some number; so also the reverse: when someone is forced to take the infinite first, they must not look immediately to the "one," but rather toward some number that holds a certain plurality, and finally conclude from all these into the one. Let us take up this point again in the case of letters.

**PROTARCHUS:** How so?

**SOCRATES:** When some god or divine man—as the story goes in Egypt, saying his name was Theuth—observed that sound was infinite, he was the first to notice that the vowels in that infinity were not one, but many. Again, he noticed other sounds that did not have a full voice but partook of some noise, and that there was a certain number of these as well. Thirdly, he distinguished a class of letters which we now call "mutes." After this, he divided the voiceless and the mutes down to each individual unit, and the vowels and the intermediates in the same way, until he grasped their number. He then gave the name "element" <note>original: "στοιχεῖον" (stoicheion); a letter or fundamental component</note> to each one and to the whole group. Seeing that none of us could learn any one of them by itself without all of them, he considered this bond as being one, making all these things one in a way, and he announced that there was a single art belonging to them, which he called "grammar."

**PHILEBUS:** I have understood these things more clearly than the previous ones, Protarchus, by comparing them to each other. But I still find the same thing missing in the argument as I did a moment ago.

**SOCRATES:** Do you mean, Philebus, the question of "what does this have to do with the matter at hand?"

**PHILEBUS:** Yes. That is what Protarchus and I have been seeking for a long time.

**SOCRATES:** Have you really been seeking it for a long time, though you have just now reached it?

**PHILEBUS:** How so?

**SOCRATES:** Was not our argument from the beginning about wisdom and pleasure, and which of the two is to be chosen?

**PHILEBUS:** Of course.

**SOCRATES:** And we say that each of them is "one."

**PHILEBUS:** Certainly.

**SOCRATES:** This then is exactly what the previous argument requires of us: how each of them is both one and many; and how they are not immediately infinite, but each possesses a certain number before they become infinite.

**PROTARCHUS:** Socrates has led us around in a circle in some way, Philebus, and thrown us into no small question. Consider which of us shall answer what is now being asked. Perhaps it is ridiculous for me, having completely taken over the succession of the argument, to command you to do this again because I cannot answer the present question. But I think it would be much more ridiculous if neither of us could do it. Consider what we shall do. For Socrates seems to be asking us now for the "forms" <note>types or species</note> of pleasure—whether they exist or not, how many they are, and of what kind. And the same for wisdom as well.

**SOCRATES:** You speak most truly, son of Callias. For unless we can do this regarding every "one," "similar," "same," and "contrary"—as the preceding discourse showed—none of us will ever be worth anything in any matter.

**PROTARCHUS:** It seems to be almost that way, Socrates. It is a fine thing for a wise man to know everything; but the "second-best voyage" <note>a Greek idiom for the next best course of action when the ideal fails</note> seems to be for him not to be ignorant of himself. I will tell you why I say this now. You, Socrates, have offered us this whole conversation, and offered yourself, to determine what is the best of human possessions. For when Philebus said it was pleasure, delight, joy, and all such things, you argued against them, saying it was not these, but those things which we often remind ourselves of—rightly so, so that both may be tested in the memory. You say, as it seems (and I think you are right to add this), that the good is something better than pleasure: namely mind, science, intelligence, art, and everything related to these, which we ought to acquire instead of the former. These two positions having been stated and disputed, we playfully threatened you that we would not let you go home until a sufficient end to these arguments was defined. You agreed and gave yourself to us for this purpose. We say now, as children do, that what is rightly given cannot be taken back. Stop, then, this manner of meeting us in the present discussion.

**SOCRATES:** What manner?

**PROTARCHUS:** Throwing us into difficulty <note>original Latin: "In aporiam"; a state of philosophical puzzlement or a dead end</note> and always asking questions for which no easy exit of an answer is available at the moment. Let us not think that our current confusion is the final end; rather, we must act toward the whole matter, as this thing applies to everything equally. If none of us can explain it in another way, you must speak. For you did indeed promise.

**PHILEBUS:** And as for me, if I were able, I would not be asking questions when I am the one being questioned; but now I am at a loss, and the rest lies with you.

<column-break/>

A **O** friend, when you have accepted how many intervals of the voice there are in number, regarding the low and the high, and of what kind they are, as well as the limits of the intervals, and however many compositions arise from these. These things our ancestors, observing them, handed down to us as their followers, so that we might call them "harmonies" of this kind. Furthermore, in the movements and gestures of the body, they showed that other such things exist, which, when measured by numbers, they ordered to be called "rhythms" and "measures." They commanded us to think, moreover, that we ought to consider in the same way every thing that is "one" and "many." For when you accept these things thus, you then turn out to be wise. When, however,
<margin>Wisdom exists regarding the finite, that is, the middle ground.</margin>
B you comprehend any other thing in this way, you will again be made wise regarding that thing. But the infinite multitude of individuals and within individuals
<margin>There is no reasoning concerning the infinite.</margin>
renders you wandering, uncertain, and deprived of reason and number, inasmuch as you are looking toward no limit in anything. **PROTARCHUS.** Socrates seems to me to have spoken these things excellently, O Philebus. **PHILEBUS.** To me as well, but what does this speech have to do with the matter: what does it intend? **SOCRATES.** That is a correct question, Protarchus, which Philebus has asked. **PROT.** Entirely. Answer him then. **SOCRATES.** I shall do what you wish, when I have also disputed a little more about these same things. For just as if someone accepts any "one" thing, as we said, he must not immediately descend into the nature of the infinite,
C but into some number; so conversely, if someone is forced to take the infinite first, he must by no means intend for the "one" immediately, but for some number that has a certain multitude, and finally end from all things into the "one." What we have just said may be inferred again in the case of letters. **PROT.** In what way? **SOCRATES.** After he contemplated the infinite voice—whether it was some God or a divine man, such as a certain Theuth is said to have been among the Egyptians—who first considered the vowel letters in that infinity
<margin>Theuth.</margin>
of the voice, which are not one but many, and again others which were not voiced but partook of some sound, and he similarly defined a certain number of these. Then he distinguished a third
D species of letters, those which we now call mutes. Finally, he discriminated those void of sound and the mutes down to individual units, as well as the vowels and the intermediates in the same way, until, the number of them being found in the individual species and in the universal, he called them "elements." And when he saw that none of us would perceive any of these things separately unless he perceived them all, he meditated upon this as a kind of bond, existing as one thing and bringing back the dispersed things into one, and he noticed that there was one art of grammar among these, and called it by that name. **PHILEBUS.** These things, Protarchus, I have comprehended more clearly than the former ones, having compared them with each other. Yet I still find the same thing missing, both now and earlier, in this disputation. **SOCRATES.** Do you ask, Philebus, what these things contribute to our discourse? **PHILEBUS.** That is indeed what I and Protarchus together have been asking for some time. **SOCRATES.** Have you not reached this, and yet you have been asking for it a long time, as you say? **PHILEBUS.** In what way? **SOCRATES.** Was not our discussion from the very beginning about wisdom and pleasure, as to which of them is to be understood [as the good]? **PROT.** Indeed. **SOCRATES.** And yet we said that each of these is "one." **PROT.** We certainly said so. **SOCRATES.** The prior discourse requires this very thing: in what way
E each of these is "one" and "many," or by what means it did not immediately receive an infinite number, but a certain number for each, before it is extended into the infinite. **PROT.** Socrates has led us around, I know not how, Philebus, into a question that is not light. Therefore come, consider which of us may respond to the present interrogation. Yet perhaps it is ridiculous that I,
F the successor of the whole disputation, should again command this very thing of you, because I am unable to answer it now. But it would be much more ridiculous if neither of us were able. Meditate, therefore, on what we should do. For Socrates seems to want to demand from us the species of pleasure—whether they exist or not, and how many furthermore, and of what kind they are—and to inquire similarly about wisdom. **SOCRATES.** You speak the truth, O son of Callias. For unless we are able to observe that [principle] regarding any one thing, whether similar, the same, or contrary, as the preceding speech showed, none of us will ever be useful for anything. **PROT.** It seems to be almost so, Socrates. And it is indeed a
G magnificent thing for a prudent man to know all things. But a "second-best voyage," and what seems next to that, is for him not to be hidden from himself. But for what purpose I have said these things now, I shall declare. You yourself, Socrates, emerged as the author of this disputation, and offered yourself for investigating what is best among human things. For when Philebus asserted that pleasure, delight, joy, and others of this kind were best for men, you immediately contradicted him, saying it was not those, but rather those things which we frequently bring back to our memory of our own accord, acting rightly so that both, being brought back to memory, may be discussed. You say, as it seems (which I think is rightly added), that the good is
H more excellent than pleasure: namely mind, science, intelligence, and other such things, and that we ought to grasp these rather than those. Since both of these have been called into doubt, we have threatened you as if in jest that we would not let you go home until a suitable end was imposed on this controversy. You indeed conceded and exposed yourself to executing that. We therefore say what children are accustomed to: it is not permitted to take away what has been rightly given. Cease therefore that manner of disputing...

<summary>Socrates explains the dialectical method of moving from the "One" to the "Infinite" by finding the specific "number" of categories in between, using the invention of the alphabet by the Egyptian god Theuth as a primary example. Protarchus and Philebus urge Socrates to apply this rigorous method to their debate on whether Pleasure or Wisdom is the ultimate Good.</summary>

### PLATO'S PHILEBUS.

<margin>A</margin>
...at this moment. SOCRATES: Whom do you mean? PROTARCHUS: You, who throw in the difficulties of doubt, and ask questions which none of us at present is able to answer properly. For we must not think the discussion has reached its end when you have merely rendered us all perplexed. If we are unable to do this, then you must act; for you promised to do so. Consider this yourself then: whether the types of pleasure and wisdom are to be distinguished, or rather set aside, or if you are able and willing to reveal in some other way how these matters now in dispute between us might be clarified. SOCRATES: I have nothing further to fear, then, since you have spoken this way. For when one says "if you are willing," all fear is driven away from any matter; additionally, it seems to me that some god has provided us with a certain memory.

<margin>B</margin>
<margin>Neither pleasure nor wisdom is the highest good, but a third thing.</margin>

SOCRATES: I heard certain discourses once, whether dreaming or awake <note>Socrates often attributes his insights to divine "dreams" or inspiration.</note>, and now I am thinking about pleasure and wisdom: that neither of these is the Good, but some third thing, which is different from both and better than both. And if this should now become clearly apparent to us, pleasure will be far from victory; for it would certainly no longer be the same as the Good itself. Is that so, or otherwise? PROTARCHUS: Certainly so. SOCRATES: We will therefore, in my opinion, no longer need to divide the types of pleasure, which will become clearer in what follows.

<margin>C</margin>
<margin>The condition and lot of the Good is threefold.</margin>
PROTARCHUS: You speak excellently; please continue. SOCRATES: Let us first agree on a few small points. PROTARCHUS: Which ones? SOCRATES: Whether the condition of the Good itself is necessarily perfect or imperfect. PROTARCHUS: Of all things, Socrates, it is the most perfect. SOCRATES: What then? Is the Good itself sufficient <note>Original: *sufficiens*. In Greek philosophy, "sufficiency" (autarkeia) means needing nothing else to be happy.</note>? PROTARCHUS: Why shouldn't it be? Indeed, it must differ from all other things in this very respect and surpass them all.

<margin>D</margin>
SOCRATES: This also is most necessary to assert about it, I think: that every knowing being hunts for it and desires to grasp it, wishing to possess it within itself and other things pertaining to it, and cares for nothing else except what is perfected together with good things. PROTARCHUS: This cannot be argued against. SOCRATES: Let us then consider and judge by looking at the life of pleasure and the life of wisdom separately. PROTARCHUS: How do you mean? SOCRATES: Let there be no wisdom in the life of pleasure, and no pleasure in the life of wisdom. For if indeed either of these is the Good, it ought to need nothing more; but if either appears lacking, it is truly no longer our Good. PROTARCHUS: Certainly not. SOCRATES: Shall we make the trial upon you? PROTARCHUS: By all means. SOCRATES: Answer then. PROTARCHUS: Speak. SOCRATES: Would you choose, Protarchus, to live your whole life enjoying the greatest pleasures? PROTARCHUS: Why wouldn't I? SOCRATES: Would you think you needed anything else besides that, if you enjoyed the perfect possession of them? PROTARCHUS: Not at all.

<margin>E</margin>
SOCRATES: Consider then, would you not need wisdom itself, and intelligence, and proper reasoning, and other things related to these—and even sight? PROTARCHUS: Why? I would have everything, presumably, if I enjoyed pleasure. SOCRATES: And living thus, would you abound in the highest pleasures throughout your entire life? PROTARCHUS: Assuredly. SOCRATES: But if you entirely lacked mind, memory, knowledge, and true opinion, you would first of all necessarily be ignorant of this very thing: whether you were rejoicing or not, since you would be void of all wisdom. PROTARCHUS: Necessarily.

<margin>F</margin>
SOCRATES: And since you would be deprived of memory, you would surely not remember that you had ever been delighted, nor would any memory remain of a pleasure happening in the moment; and lacking true opinion, while you were rejoicing, you would not even think that you were rejoicing. Deprived of reason, you would not be able to calculate that you would obtain any pleasure in the future. You would lead the life not of a human, but of a certain "sea-lung" <note>original: *pulmonis*. This refers to a jellyfish or a similar mindless marine creature.</note>, that is, a sea sponge, or those marine animals that have shells. Is this true? Or is it possible to think otherwise of these things? PROTARCHUS: And how could it be otherwise? SOCRATES: Is such a life to be sought by us? PROTARCHUS: This discourse, Socrates, has rendered me speechless.

<margin>G</margin>
SOCRATES: Let us not grow weary here, I pray, but let us now consider further by bringing the other life—the life of the mind—into our midst. PROTARCHUS: What kind of life do you mean? SOCRATES: Whether any of us would choose to live so as to possess wisdom, mind, knowledge, and full memory of all things, but enjoy no pleasure at all, nor on the other hand be affected by pain, but live entirely without any such feeling? PROTARCHUS: Neither of these lives, Socrates, seems to me or to anyone else, I believe, to be choice-worthy. SOCRATES: What then, Protarchus, of a life mixed from both, made common by the joining of the two into one? PROTARCHUS: You mean a life of pleasure, and wisdom, and mind?

<margin>H</margin>
<margin>Which of the three lives is best.</margin>
SOCRATES: That is the very one I mean. PROTARCHUS: Everyone would certainly choose this one rather than either of the former two; and not just one person, while another does not, but everyone will equally seek it. SOCRATES: Do we see, then, what follows from the present discussion? PROTARCHUS: Certainly: three lives have been proposed, and of the two, neither is sufficient or choice-worthy for humans or other living creatures. SOCRATES: Is it not then clear concerning these that neither of them possesses the Good itself? For if it did, it would be sufficient and perfect, and choice-worthy for all plants and animals that could live thus forever. And if any of us chooses otherwise, he chooses against the nature of what is truly to be desired, not willingly, but out of ignorance or some unhappy necessity. PROTARCHUS: It seems these things are so. SOCRATES: That we must not think Philebus's goddess <note>A reference to Aphrodite, representing Pleasure.</note> is the same as the Good itself, is now sufficiently...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
...things being said now. SOCRATES: What do you mean? PROTARCHUS: That you throw us into aporia <note>original: *ἀπορίαν*. A state of philosophical puzzlement or a "dead end."</note>, and ask things that we would not be able to give a sufficient answer to at the present time. For let us not think the current discussion has reached its goal, except for the confusion of all of us; but if we are unable to do this, you must do it. For you promised. Deliberate then, placing these things before yourself, whether you must divide the forms of pleasure and knowledge, or let them be, if you are somehow able and willing in another way to show how the matters now disputed among us stand. SOCRATES: There is no need for me to fear anything terrible hereafter, since you have said this. For the word "if you are willing," once spoken, dissolves all fear about each thing; and besides these things, it seems to me that some god has given us a certain memory. PROTARCHUS: How so?

<margin>B</margin>
And of what things? SOCRATES: Having once heard some discourses long ago in a dream, or even while awake, I now consider concerning pleasure and wisdom that neither of them is the Good, but some third other thing, different from these and better than both. And yet if this should appear clearly to us now, pleasure is released from victory. For the Good would no longer be the same as it. Or how? PROTARCHUS: Just so. SOCRATES: And we shall no longer require any of the forms of pleasure for the division, in my opinion. As the argument proceeds, it will show this more clearly. PROTARCHUS: You have spoken most beautifully; so then, finish it. SOCRATES: Let us then agree on some small things beforehand. PROTARCHUS: What sort of things? SOCRATES: Whether it is necessary for the lot of the Good 

<margin>C</margin>
to be perfect or not perfect? PROTARCHUS: Surely the most perfect of all things, Socrates. SOCRATES: What then? Is the Good sufficient? PROTARCHUS: How could it not be? And in this, it differs from all other existing things. SOCRATES: And I think, as I think, it is most necessary to say of it that everything that knows it hunts for it and desires to catch it and to possess it around itself, and cares for nothing of other things except those which are completed together with good things. PROTARCHUS: It is not possible to speak against these things. SOCRATES: Let us then look at and judge the life of pleasure and the life of wisdom, seeing them separately. PROTARCHUS: How did you say? SOCRATES: Let wisdom not be present in the life of pleasure, nor pleasure in the life of wisdom.

<margin>D</margin>
For if indeed either of them is the Good, it must no longer have need of anything. But if either should appear to be in need, it is surely not yet the truly Good for us. PROTARCHUS: For how could it be? SOCRATES: Shall we then try to test these things in you? PROTARCHUS: By all means. SOCRATES: Answer then. PROTARCHUS: Speak. SOCRATES: Would you, Protarchus, accept to live your whole life enjoying the greatest pleasures? PROTARCHUS: Why not? SOCRATES: Would you then think you still had need of anything if you had this completely? PROTARCHUS: Not at all. SOCRATES: Look now: would you not need to think, to perceive, to calculate what is necessary, and all things that are sisters to these? PROTARCHUS: And why? SOCRATES: And furthermore, not possessing memory, you would necessarily not even remember that you once rejoiced, and of the pleasure falling upon you in the immediate moment, not even any memory at all would be left behind. And not possessing true opinion, you would not think you were rejoicing when you were rejoicing; and being deprived of calculation, you would not be able to calculate that you will rejoice in the time to come. You would live not the life of a human, but of some lung-fish, or of those living things in the sea with shell-covered bodies.

<margin>F</margin>
Are these things so? Or can we think of them in some other way than this? PROTARCHUS: And how? SOCRATES: Is such a life then choice-worthy for us? PROTARCHUS: This argument, Socrates, has thrown me into total speechlessness for now. SOCRATES: Let us not be softened yet, but taking up in turn the life of the mind, let us see it. PROTARCHUS: What sort of life do you mean? SOCRATES: If any of us would accept to live, possessing wisdom and mind and knowledge and all memory of all things, but participating in pleasure neither great nor small, nor again in pain, but being altogether unaffected by all such things. PROTARCHUS: Neither life, Socrates, is choice-worthy to me at least. Nor would it ever,

<margin>G</margin>

SOCRATES: Exactly; that is the kind I mean. PROTARCHUS: Surely everyone will choose this one before either of those two, and besides this, not just one person while another does not. SOCRATES: Do we understand then what is happening to us in the preceding arguments? PROTARCHUS: Very much so. That three lives were proposed, and of the two, neither is sufficient nor choice-worthy, neither for men nor for any animals. SOCRATES: Is it not then already clear concerning these that neither of them held the Good? For it would be sufficient, and perfect, and choice-worthy for all plants and animals that were able to live thus always through life. And if any of us chose

<margin>H</margin>
the other of them, he would take it against the nature of the choice-worthy, unwillingly from ignorance or some unhappy necessity. PROTARCHUS: These things seem to be so. SOCRATES: That we should not think Philebus's goddess is the same as the Good, is now sufficiently...

<summary>Socrates conducts a thought experiment to show that neither a life of pure pleasure (without intellect) nor a life of pure intellect (without feeling) is the ultimate Good. He concludes that the "Mixed Life," combining both, is the only one sufficient and choice-worthy for humans.</summary>

### PHILEBUS.

**A** ...it seems to me has been said. PHILEBUS: But neither is your "Mind," Socrates, the same as the Good itself; it will surely be subject to the same criticisms. SOCRATES: Perhaps mine would be, Philebus. However, I do not think the true and divine Mind <note>original: "θεῖον οἶμαι νοῦν"</note> is like that, but rather exists in a different state. Now, I do not contest the claim of Mind for the first prize in the "combined life," but we must look and see what we shall do regarding the second prize. For each of us might claim to be the cause of this "combined life"—one of us saying it is Mind, the other saying it is Pleasure. And so, while the Good itself would be neither of these two, someone might suppose that one of them is the *cause* of the Good. On this point, I would fight even harder against Philebus: that in this "mixed life," whatever it is that makes a life desirable and good, it is Mind that is more akin <note>In Greek philosophy, "kinship" refers to things sharing the same fundamental nature.</note> and more similar to it than Pleasure. And by this reasoning, Pleasure could never truly be said to share in the first prize, nor even the second. Indeed, if my mind is to be trusted at all right now, Pleasure is even further away from the third prize.

**B** PROTARCHUS: Truly, Socrates, it seems to me that Pleasure has now been knocked down, as if struck by your arguments; she lies there, defeated in the struggle for the first prize. As for Mind, it seems we must say it was wise of it not to claim the first prize for itself, for it would have suffered the same fate. But if Pleasure were to be deprived of the second prize, she would suffer a total loss of honor in the eyes of her lovers; for she would no longer appear as beautiful to them as she did before.

**C** SOCRATES: What then? Is it not better to let her go now, rather than to cause her pain by bringing her to the most exacting of tests and exposing her? PROTARCHUS: You speak nonsense, Socrates. SOCRATES: Is it because I spoke of the impossible—that Pleasure could feel "pain"? PROTARCHUS: Not only that, but because you seem unaware that none of us will let you go until you have reached the very end of these arguments. SOCRATES: Goodness, Protarchus! Then we have a long discussion ahead of us, and it is certainly not an easy one right now. For it seems that one who is approaching the "second prize" on behalf of Mind needs a different sort of "machine"—that is, we need different weapons <note>original: "βέλη" (arrows or missiles), used metaphorically for logical arguments.</note> than the previous arguments, though some may be the same. Must we do this? PROTARCHUS: How could we not?

**D** SOCRATES: Let us then attempt to define its beginning with care. PROTARCHUS: What sort of beginning do you mean? SOCRATES: Let us divide all things that now exist in the universe into two parts—or rather, if you prefer, into three. PROTARCHUS: On what basis would you do so? SOCRATES: Let us take some concepts from our recent discussion. PROTARCHUS: Which ones? SOCRATES: We said, I believe, that God has revealed two elements of existence: the "Infinite" and the "Limit." PROTARCHUS: Certainly. SOCRATES: Let us set these two down as the first two types; the third is a single thing formed by the mixture of these both. But I seem to be quite a ridiculous fellow, attempting to divide and count things by their "kinds" <note>term: <term>Kind</term> (Greek: *eidos*). Here refers to a fundamental category or "Form" in Plato's philosophy.</note>.

**E** PROTARCHUS: What are you saying, my good man? SOCRATES: It appears I need a fourth kind as well. PROTARCHUS: Tell me what it is. SOCRATES: Look for the *Cause* of the mixture of these things with one another, and set that down for me as a fourth besides those three. PROTARCHUS: And will you perhaps need a fifth, capable of making a further division? SOCRATES: Perhaps; but I do not think so for the present. However, if there is a need, you will surely forgive me as I pursue a fifth "life." PROTARCHUS: Of course. SOCRATES: First, then, having distinguished three of the four, and seeing that two of these are fragmented and split into many parts, let us try to gather each of them back into a unity so that we can understand how each was both "one" and "many." PROTARCHUS: If you would speak more clearly about them, I might be able to follow.

**F** SOCRATES: I mean the two I just proposed: the "Limit" and the "Infinite." I will try to show that the "Infinite" is, in a sense, many. As for the "Limit," let it wait for us. PROTARCHUS: It waits. SOCRATES: Indeed. For what I am asking you to consider is difficult and controversial, but consider it nonetheless. First, look at "hotter" and "colder" and see if you could ever conceive of a limit to them, or if the "More and Less" <note>original: "μᾶλλον τε καὶ ἧττον"</note> dwelling within their very nature do not prevent them from ever reaching an end as long as they reside there. For if an end were reached, they themselves would cease to be. PROTARCHUS: That is very true. SOCRATES: And we always say that "more" and "less" are present in the hotter and the colder. PROTARCHUS: Quite so. SOCRATES: Our argument therefore always shows that these things have no end; and being without end, they are surely altogether "Infinite." PROTARCHUS: Very much so, Socrates.

**G** SOCRATES: Well done, friend Protarchus! You have caught the point and reminded me that the word "vehemently" <note>original: "σφόδρα"</note>, which you just uttered, and the word "mildly" have the same power as "more" and "less." For wherever they are present, they do not allow a thing to be of a fixed quantity <note>original: "ποσὸν"</note>; rather, by always introducing a "stronger" against a "milder" (and vice versa) into every action, they produce a "more and less" while making any fixed quantity vanish. For as was just said: if they did not make quantity vanish, but instead allowed quantity and "the moderate" to take their place in the seat of the "more and less," then the "more and less" would flee from their own territory. Hotter and colder would no longer exist if they received a fixed quantity.

**H** For "hotter" is always moving and never stays still, and the "colder" likewise. But quantity stands still and stops all progress. Therefore, by this reasoning, the hotter and its opposite must be "Infinite." PROTARCHUS: So it appears, Socrates. But as you said, these things are not easy to grasp. Perhaps if they were repeated again and again, they would eventually show the questioner and the answerer to be in sufficient agreement. SOCRATES: You speak well, and we must try to do so with all our strength. But first, look and see...

<column-break/>

**A** ...it seems to me has been said. PHILEBUS: But neither even is your mind the good itself, O Socrates; for it is subject to the same reproaches. SOCRATES: Perhaps, my Philebus, yet I do not think the true and divine Mind is so, but rather that it is otherwise. Indeed, that Mind should hold the first place in that common life, I for one do not contend. Regarding the second place, however, we must see what we shall do. For perhaps one of us might bring forward Mind as the cause of the common life, and the other Pleasure; and thus the Good itself would be neither of them. But perhaps someone will judge one or the other of these to be the cause.

**B** Therefore, I would fight all the more against Philebus, because in this mixed life, whatever it is that—having been taken up by life—renders it desirable and good, the Mind itself is more akin and similar to it than is Pleasure. And by this reasoning, Pleasure will truly hold neither the first nor even the second part; and it will be further away from the third, perhaps, if any faith is now to be placed by us in my mind. PROTARCHUS: And yet, O Socrates, Pleasure now seems prostrate, as if struck down by your arguments; for even as she fought for victory, she lies defeated. Regarding Mind, however, it seems it must be said that it would not wisely claim victory for itself. For it would suffer the same fate.

**C** Pleasure, however, having perhaps been deprived of the second place, will now be altogether despised by those lovers; for she will no longer appear equally beautiful. SOCRATES: What then? Is it not better to let her go, and not afflict her with pain through exquisite examination and refutation? PROTARCHUS: You say nothing, O Socrates. SOCRATES: Is it because I brought forth something impossible—that Pleasure could be afflicted with pain? PROTARCHUS: Not for this reason alone, but also because you are unaware that none of us will permit you to go before you have arrived at the end of these matters by reason. SOCRATES: Oh, Protarchus! What a long discourse there is to be! Or rather, it is almost easy now. For it seems there is a need for certain other instruments, as if such were required besides the superior reasons,

**D** if anyone intends to approach to secure the second prize for Mind. Perhaps we even have these. Therefore, is it necessary? PROTARCHUS: Why not? SOCRATES: Let us then, setting down the beginning of this matter, occupy ourselves cautiously and distinctly. PROTARCHUS: What kind of beginning do you mean? SOCRATES: Let us distinguish all things that are now in the universe in two ways. Indeed, if you wish, in three ways. PROTARCHUS: In what manner? SOCRATES: Let us take some of those things which have now been said by us. PROTARCHUS: Which ones? SOCRATES: We were saying that God showed one of the things that exist to be "Infinite," and the other to be "Limit." PROTARCHUS: Entirely so. SOCRATES: Let us therefore set down these two species: and a third, one mixed from both of them. Yet I seem quite ridiculous while I contend to divide and enumerate those things by their species. PROTARCHUS: What are you saying, O good

**E** man? SOCRATES: It is clear that a fourth kind is still needed. PROTARCHUS: Which one? SOCRATES: Consider the cause of the mutual mixture of these things, and set that down as a fourth besides those three. PROTARCHUS: Will you not also need a fifth in addition, some discerning thing? SOCRATES: Perhaps; not however at present, as I think. But if there is a need, you will forgive me for pursuing a fifth "life." PROTARCHUS: What stands in the way? SOCRATES: In the beginning, therefore, dividing three of these four, and seeing each of the two split and torn into many parts, then soon joining each back together into one, let us strive to perceive how far each of these is either "One" or "Many." PROTARCHUS: If you say these things more clearly to me, perhaps I will follow. SOCRATES: I speak indeed of the two which were proposed:

<margin>That the infinite is many.</margin>

**F** I mean the "Finite" <note>Here the Latin uses 'finitum' for the Greek 'peras' (Limit).</note> and the "Infinite." That the Infinite is in some way "many," I shall endeavor to show; but let the Finite be deferred for later. PROTARCHUS: Let it be deferred. SOCRATES: Attend then: for that which I command you to consider is arduous and greatly controversial.

<margin>The "More" and "Less" effect a limit, and quantity.</margin>

But nevertheless, take notice. First, consider regarding the "hotter" and "colder," whether you find any limit in them; or rather, whether the "More and Less," while they are in those kinds, reject an end; for if an end were applied, they themselves would also be ended. PROTARCHUS: You speak the truest things. SOCRATES: But we always confess that "More and Less" are in the hotter and colder themselves. PROTARCHUS: Very much so. SOCRATES: Therefore this reasoning always shows us that an end is absent from these; and since they are without end, let them be altogether "Infinite." PROTARCHUS: Entirely so, O Socrates.

**G** Well done, friend Protarchus; you have understood, and you have noticed now that this very thing, "vehemently" and just now pronounced, and also that which is said "mildly," have the same power as "more" or "less." For wherever they are present, they do not permit each thing to be a fixed quantity; but always by bringing in a more "vehement" than a "milder," and conversely a "milder" than a "vehement" in all actions, they produce "plus and minus"; but they always destroy "quantity." For what was just said: not destroying quantity, but leaving it and "measure" in the seat of the "more" and "less," and "vehemently" and "mildly," these things would disappear from their own region in which they were. For "hotter" and "colder" no longer exist

**H** if they receive a fixed quantity. For it will flee away, nor will the "hotter" and "colder" itself stay longer; but quantity stands, and ceases to progress. Wherefore, by this reasoning, it is now established that hotter and colder are "Infinite." PROTARCHUS: So it appears, O Socrates; nevertheless, as you said yourself, these things can hardly be perceived. But perhaps, repeated again and again, they will declare the questioner and respondent alike to be in agreement. SOCRATES: You speak well, and so we must act according to our strength. But look first whether...

<summary>Socrates introduces a four-fold metaphysical classification—the Infinite, the Limit, the Mixture, and the Cause—to analyze the nature of the Good. He demonstrates that things like heat and cold are "Infinite" because they always admit of degree (more or less) and lack a fixed quantity.</summary>
