# OF PLATO

<margin>Sign of the infinite nature.</margin>
**SOCRATES:** Let us set this as the sign of the infinite nature <note>original: "infinitæ naturæ"; in Greek "ἀπείρου φύσεως". This refers to things that have no inherent limit or "stop" point.</note>, so that we do not drag out the discussion by running through every individual example. **PROTARCHUS:** What sign do you mean? **SOCRATES:** Whatever appears to us to become "more or less," or admits of "strongly" and "mildly," or "too much," and all such things,
<margin>Those in the genus of the infinite.</margin>
must all be placed into the single genus of the infinite. This is just as we said before: we must collect all things that are divided and dispersed into one group, and mark them according to a single power, as if they were one nature. Do you remember? **PROTARCHUS:** I remember. **SOCRATES:** But those things that do not admit of these "more or less" qualities, but instead receive their opposites—
<margin>Those in the genus of the finite.</margin>
first the "equal" itself and "equality," then after the equal, the "double," and every proportion that number has to number, or measure has to measure—if we referred all these to the genus of the finite <note>original: "finiti"; in Greek "πέρας". This refers to things defined by exact limits, ratios, or math.</note>, would we be doing the right thing? What do you say to this? **PROTARCHUS:** Most excellently, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Well then. What idea shall we say the third genus has, which is a mixture of both of these? **PROTARCHUS:** I think you will be the one to tell me that. **SOCRATES:** Rather, a God will, if only some God graciously hears my prayers. **PROTARCHUS:** Pray then, and observe. **SOCRATES:** I am observing. And it seems to me, Protarchus, that some god has now breathed upon us in a friendly way. **PROTARCHUS:** How do you mean? What evidence are you using? **SOCRATES:** I will tell you plainly; stand by with attentive ears. **PROTARCHUS:** Speak then. **SOCRATES:** Were we not just now speaking of "hotter" and "colder"? **PROTARCHUS:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** Add to these "drier" and "moister," "more" and "less," "faster" and "slower," "larger" and "smaller," and finally everything we previously reduced to that one nature which accepts "more or less." **PROTARCHUS:** Do you mean the nature of the infinite? **SOCRATES:** Yes. And after this, mix into that nature the offspring of the "Limit" <note>original: "termini"; in Greek "πέρατος".</note>. **PROTARCHUS:** Which offspring? **SOCRATES:** That which we ought to have collected into one, just as we collected the genus of the infinite, but we have not yet done so. But perhaps it will achieve the same thing now: for when these two are brought together, that third genus will immediately be revealed. **PROTARCHUS:** Which one do you mean, and how? **SOCRATES:** The offspring of the "equal" and the "double," and whatever prevents opposites from being at odds and hostile to one another; by introducing proportion and harmony, it creates number. **PROTARCHUS:** I understand. You seem to be saying that if these are mixed, certain "generations" <note>original: "generationes"; in Greek "γενέσεις". This refers to things coming into being or being produced.</note> will result from each of them. **SOCRATES:** And I seem to be right. **PROTARCHUS:** It is said so. **SOCRATES:**
<margin>The correct communion of these, that is of the equal or the double, or the others. Disease exists when heat, cold, moist, and dry cease [to be balanced].</margin>
In cases of disease, did not the correct communion of these things generate the nature of health? **PROTARCHUS:** Entirely so. **SOCRATES:** And in the high and low [notes], the fast and slow, though they are infinite, did this mixture not bring about a "Limit" and produce the perfection of all music? **PROTARCHUS:** Most excellently. **SOCRATES:** Furthermore, when applied to freezing cold and stifling heat, it took away the "too much" and the infinite, and produced what is measured and proportional. **PROTARCHUS:** Why not? **SOCRATES:** From these mixtures the seasons of the year and all beautiful things have flowed to us, when the infinites and the finites are joined together. **PROTARCHUS:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** And I omit countless other things—such as beauty and strength along with health. In souls, too, there are many other very beautiful things. For this goddess <note>This "goddess" likely refers to the divine principle of Order or Measure.</note>, my dear Philebus, observing that insolence and all wickedness had no limit <note>original: "termino"; in Greek "πέρας".</note> in their pleasures and fulfillments, established Law and Order, which contain the Limit. You say she harms and destroys, but I on the contrary say she saves. And you, Protarchus, what do you think? **PROTARCHUS:** These things are entirely in accordance with my own opinion. **SOCRATES:** Have I not now presented these three kinds, if you understand? **PROTARCHUS:** I think I understand. You seem to be asserting that one is the infinite. The second is the limit in existing things. But as for that third one, I do not quite grasp what you wish to say. **SOCRATES:** The multitude of its generation, O wondrous man, has stunned you. And yet, the infinite also contained many types; nevertheless, because they were all marked by the "more or less," they appeared as one. **PROTARCHUS:** You speak the truth. **SOCRATES:** Furthermore, the Limit neither contained many types, nor were we bothered as if it were not one by nature. **PROTARCHUS:** How could it be otherwise? **SOCRATES:** In no way. But know that by the "third" I mean this: everything that is born from these—namely, a "coming-into-being" into essence <note>original: "generationem in eſſentiā"; in Greek "γένεσιν εἰς οὐσίαν". This means things moving from mere change into stable, defined existence.</note>—from the measures established together with the Limit. **PROTARCHUS:** I have understood. **SOCRATES:** But besides these three, what the fourth genus might be, remains to be discussed. This is a common investigation. For see if it does not seem necessary to you that everything which is generated, is generated through some cause? **PROTARCHUS:** To me, plainly. For how could it happen without one? **SOCRATES:** And the nature of the "Maker" <note>original: "efficientis"; in Greek "ποιοῦντος".</note> differs from the "Cause" in name only; the Maker and the Cause may rightly be called one. **PROTARCHUS:** Rightly. **SOCRATES:** Furthermore, that which is "made" and that which is "generated" will differ only in name. **PROTARCHUS:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** The nature of the Maker always precedes and leads, while that which is made and generated by it follows after. **PROTARCHUS:** Exactly. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, the cause is not the same thing, but something different from that which serves the cause for generation. **PROTARCHUS:** What prevents it? **SOCRATES:** Did not the things generated, and the things from which they are generated, provide us with three kinds? **PROTARCHUS:** Very much so. **SOCRATES:** Shall we not then call the "Maker" of all these things the fourth kind, and call it the Cause <note>original: "cauſαm"; in Greek "αἰτίαν".</note>, as it has been demonstrated to be something other than the previous three? **PROTARCHUS:** We shall, without a doubt. **SOCRATES:** Now that the four have been distinguished, it is proper to list them one by one in order, so that we may better remember each one.

<column-break/>

...to do thus. Now the ends of the nature of the infinite have been defined, if we accept this sign, so that we do not lengthen the discourse by going through everything. **PROTARCHUS:** What kind do you mean? **SOCRATES:** Whatever appears to us as becoming "more or less," admitting the "strongly" and "mildly," and the "too much," and all such things, all these we must place into the genus of the infinite <note>original: "ἀπείρου γένος"</note> as into one category. And according to the previous argument we mentioned, all those things that are torn apart and dispersed must be gathered together and marked as one nature according to one power, if you remember. **PROTARCHUS:** I remember. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, those things that do not admit of these, but admit all their opposites—first the equal and equality, and after the equal, the double, and whatever is number to number or measure to measure—if we account all these together into the Limit <note>original: "πέρας"</note>, would we seem to be doing well? Or how do you say? **PROTARCHUS:** Most beautifully, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Well. And the third, the mixture from both of these, what idea shall we say it has? **PROTARCHUS:** You will tell me, I think. **SOCRATES:** A God, if indeed some one of the gods hears my prayers. **PROTARCHUS:** Pray then and look. **SOCRATES:** I am looking. and it seems to me, Protarchus, that some [god] has now become a friend to us. **PROTARCHUS:** How do you say? By what evidence do you judge? **SOCRATES:** I will tell you clearly. But follow along with me in the argument. **PROTARCHUS:** Only speak. **SOCRATES:** Did we not just now speak of some "hotter" and "colder"? **PROTARCHUS:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** Then should we not also add "drier" and "moister," and "more" and "less," and "faster" and "slower," and "larger" and "smaller," and as many things as we previously placed into the one nature that admits of "more or less"? **PROTARCHUS:** Do you mean the nature of the infinite? **SOCRATES:** Yes. And mix into it thereafter the whole offspring of the Limit. **PROTARCHUS:** What kind? **SOCRATES:** That which we ought to have gathered into one, just as we gathered the infinite into one, so too we should have gathered the "limit-form," but we did not. But perhaps it will do the same thing now. When both of these are gathered together, that [third] one also becomes manifest. **PROTARCHUS:** Where and how do you mean? **SOCRATES:** The kind of the "equal" and the "double," and whatever stops opposites from being differently disposed towards each other, and by putting in the proportional and the harmonious, produces number. **PROTARCHUS:** I understand. For you seem to me to be saying that by mixing these, certain "becomings" <note>original: "γενέσεις"</note> occur in each case. **SOCRATES:** For I do seem to speak rightly. **PROTARCHUS:** Speak then. **SOCRATES:** Is it not so that in diseases, the right communion of these generated the nature of health? **PROTARCHUS:** Entirely so. **SOCRATES:** And in the high and low, the fast and slow, being infinite, did not these same things appearing together produce a "Limit," and constitute the whole of music most perfectly? **PROTARCHUS:** Most certainly. **SOCRATES:** And indeed, occurring in frosts and heatwaves, it took away the "too much" and the infinite, and produced the measured and the proportional. **PROTARCHUS:** What then? **SOCRATES:** Therefore, from these the seasons and all beautiful things have come to be for us, the infinites and those having a limit having been mixed together. **PROTARCHUS:** How could it be otherwise? **SOCRATES:** And I leave out ten thousand other things; such as beauty and strength along with health, and in souls again very many other and most beautiful things. For the goddess, seeing I suppose the insolence and all the wickedness of all things, there being no limit in them of pleasures and fulfillments, established Law and Order as things having a limit. You said she was harming them with pains, but I on the contrary say it was to save them. But to you, Protarchus, how does it appear? **PROTARCHUS:** Very much so, Socrates, to me as well. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, I have spoken of these three, if you understand. **PROTARCHUS:** But I think I understand. For one, you seem to me to say, is the infinite; the second is the limit among existing things. But the third I do not quite grasp what you wish to say. **SOCRATES:** For the multitude, O wondrous man, of the generation of the third has stunned you. And yet, the infinite also provided many kinds; but nevertheless, having been sealed with the kind of the "more and its opposite," they appeared as one. **PROTARCHUS:** True. **SOCRATES:** And indeed the Limit neither had many kinds, nor were we troubled as if it were not one by nature. **PROTARCHUS:** For how could we be? **SOCRATES:** In no way. But they say I am speaking of the third, setting as one all the offspring of these, a "becoming into essence" <note>original: "γένεσιν εἰς οὐσίαν"</note> from the measures produced with the limit. **PROTARCHUS:** I learned it. **SOCRATES:** But then we said a fourth kind must be considered. And the consideration is common. For see if it seems necessary to you that all things that come to be, come to be through some cause. **PROTARCHUS:** To me, certainly. For how could it come to be without this? **SOCRATES:** Therefore the nature of the "Maker" <note>original: "ποιοῦντος"</note> differs in nothing, except in name, from the cause; the "Maker" and the "Cause" would rightly be called one. **PROTARCHUS:** Rightly. **SOCRATES:** And indeed, that which is "made" and that which "comes to be" differ in nothing but name, just as before? **PROTARCHUS:** Thus it is. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, does the Maker always lead by nature, while that which is made follows, coming to be from the former? **PROTARCHUS:** Quite so. **SOCRATES:** Then the cause is something else, and not the same as that which serves the cause for generation. **PROTARCHUS:** Why not? **SOCRATES:** Therefore, the things that come to be, and the things from which they come to be, provided us with all three kinds. **PROTARCHUS:** Very much so. **SOCRATES:** And let us call that which crafts all these things the fourth, the Cause, as it has been shown to be sufficiently different from those. **PROTARCHUS:** Let us call it so. **SOCRATES:** It is right then, since the four have been defined, to list them in order for the sake of remembering each one. **PROTARCHUS:** What then? **SOCRATES:** First then I say the infinite; second, the limit.

<summary>In this passage, Socrates establishes a metaphysical framework of four "kinds": the Infinite (variables of degree), the Limit (mathematical ratio), the Mixture (ordered reality like health and music), and the Cause (the creative agent). He argues that beauty, health, and cosmic order arise when the Limit is applied to the Infinite.</summary>

# PHILEBUS. 72

<margin>A</margin>
...the limit <note>original: "πέρας" / "terminum"</note>. Then, from these two, a third: the essence that is mixed and generated from them. And for the fourth, I name the cause of this mixture and generation. Tell me, would I be making any mistake here? **PROTARCHUS:** Not at all. **SOCRATES:** Come then, what is our next argument? What was our primary goal in coming to this point? <margin>B</margin>

For that third genus is not merely a mixture of any two things, but of all things that are infinite <note>original: "ἀπείρων" / "infinitis"</note> when they are bound together by the limit. For the danger seems to me no small thing whether we succeed or fail in answering the current question correctly. **PHILEBUS:** You are exalting your own God, Socrates! **SOCRATES:** And you, my friend, are exalting your own Goddess <note>Philebus champions Aphrodite (Pleasure), while Socrates champions the Mind.</note>. to become our "interpreter" <note>original: "ὑποφήτην" / "propheta"; a spokesman or one who declares the divine will.</note> yourself, so that we do not make a mistake or say something out of tune during this competition. **SOCRATES:** I must obey you, Protarchus, for you ask nothing difficult. For all the wise agree—exalting themselves in truth—that Mind <note>original: "νοῦς" / "intellectus"</note> is the king of us, and of heaven and earth. and perhaps they speak well. If you wish, let us perform a more thorough examination of these genera. **PROTARCHUS:** Speak as you wish, Socrates; do not worry about being long-winded, for you will not annoy us.

<margin>E</margin>
**SOCRATES:** You speak well. Let us begin then by asking this. **PROTARCHUS:** What? **SOCRATES:** Should we say, Protarchus, that all things—this whole universe we call the "all"—is governed by a power that is irrational, random, and accidental? Or, on the contrary, as our ancestors said, is it ordered and governed by Mind and a certain wonderful Wisdom? **PROTARCHUS:** There is no comparison, my wonderful Socrates! For what you just said—about randomness—seems profane to me. To say that Mind orders all these things is the only view worthy of the sight of the world, the sun, the moon, the stars, and the whole celestial revolution. I would never speak or think otherwise of them.

<margin>F</margin>
**SOCRATES:** Do you wish, then, that we should agree with those of old and confess that this is so? And should we not only think it right to repeat the words of others without risk, but also share the danger and the reproach if some clever man should claim that these things are not so, but are moved without order? **PROTARCHUS:** How could I not wish that? **SOCRATES:** Come then, look at the argument that follows this regarding the Mind. **PROTARCHUS:** Just say it. **SOCRATES:** In the nature of the bodies of all living creatures, we see fire, water, breath, and earth present in their composition—just as sailors say they see land in a storm. **PROTARCHUS:** Quite so. Indeed, we are truly "tossed by a storm" of confusion in our current discussion.

<margin>G</margin>
**SOCRATES:** Consider this regarding each of those elements in us. **PROTARCHUS:** What? **SOCRATES:** That each of these in us is small and poor, and nowhere is it found in a pure state, nor does it possess a power worthy of its nature. Take one example and understand it for all: there is fire in us, and there is also fire in the universe. **PROTARCHUS:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** Now, is the fire in us not small, weak, and poor? But the fire in the universe is marvelous in its quantity, its beauty, and in every power that belongs to fire. **PROTARCHUS:** What you say is very true. **SOCRATES:** What then? Is the fire of the universe nourished and generated by our fire? Does the universal fire take its start from ours? Or is it the opposite—that my fire, and yours, and that of all living creatures, derives all its qualities from that universal fire? **PROTARCHUS:** This question does not even deserve an answer.

<margin>H</margin>
**SOCRATES:** Correct. You would say the same, I believe, about the earth in living creatures here and the earth in the universe, and indeed about all the other elements I asked about a moment ago. <summary>Socrates and Protarchus use the four-genus metaphysical framework to classify pleasure as "infinite/unlimited" and the mixed life as a "mixture." They begin to argue that the individual mind is derived from a universal, divine Mind that governs the cosmos, just as the small amount of fire in a human body is derived from the vast fire of the universe.</summary>

# OF PLATO

<columns>

**SOCRATES:** Perhaps no one would deny it, but let us move to what follows. For when we look at all these things we have just mentioned combined into one, we call it a "body" <note>original: "corpus" / "σῶμα" (sôma)</note>. **PROTARCHUS:** Why not? **SOCRATES:** Take the same view regarding this which we call the "world" <note>original: "mundus" / "κόσμον" (kosmos)</note>. For by the same reasoning, it is a body, being composed of the same elements. <margin>A</margin> **PROTARCHUS:** You speak most correctly. **SOCRATES:** Does our body get its nourishment and everything we mentioned earlier entirely from this [world] body, or does the world's body get its nourishment from ours? **PROTARCHUS:** This second option, Socrates, is not even worth an answer. **SOCRATES:** But is the other worth it, or not? **PROTARCHUS:** Tell me, which one? **SOCRATES:** Shall we admit that our body has a soul? <margin>B</margin> **PROTARCHUS:** It is agreed. **SOCRATES:** Where then, my friend Protarchus, did it receive it, unless the body of the universe—which contains the same things as ours and even more excellent things—also has a soul? **PROTARCHUS:** It is agreed. It could come from nowhere else. **SOCRATES:** For we must not think, Protarchus, that those four—the limit, the infinite, the mixture, and the fourth genus of the cause—exist in all things, providing soul and body to us, providing medicine when the body fails, and establishing and restoring other things in other places, being called the sum of all wisdom; yet while these same things are in the whole heaven and its larger parts, which are purer and more excellent, that the nature <margin>C</margin> of the most beautiful and precious things is not to be found in them? **PROTARCHUS:** That would truly make no sense. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, following that reasoning further, we would do better to say, as we have often said, that a great "infinite" exists in this universe, and a sufficient "limit," and a noble "cause" is always present, ordering and disposing the hours, months, and years, which is rightly called "Mind" and "Wisdom." **PROTARCHUS:** Rightly so. **SOCRATES:** But Wisdom and Mind never exist without a Soul. **PROTARCHUS:** Certainly never. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, you will confess that in the nature of Zeus <note>The Greek "Διὸς" refers to the king of the gods, here representing the cosmic order.</note> himself there is a royal soul and a royal mind <margin>D</margin> because of the power of the Cause, and in other gods there are other beautiful things, according to how it pleases each to be named. **PROTARCHUS:** Most certainly. **SOCRATES:** Do not think, Protarchus, that we have introduced this discourse in vain; for it supports the opinion of those who long ago showed that Mind presides over all things. **PROTARCHUS:** Truly. **SOCRATES:** And it provides an answer to my inquiry: that Mind is a certain progeny of that Cause which is called the cause of all things, and which is one of the four we categorized. Now you have our exposition. **PROTARCHUS:** I have it, and quite sufficiently. Although when you answered the same thing before, I did not understand. **SOCRATES:** A relaxation <margin>A joke is often a relaxation of study.</margin> of serious study, Protarchus, is often a joke. **PROTARCHUS:** You speak excellently. <margin>E</margin> **SOCRATES:** Now then, my friend, it has been shown well enough to which genus Mind belongs and what power it has. **PROTARCHUS:** Entirely so. **SOCRATES:** Furthermore, the genus of pleasure was already made clear long ago. **PROTARCHUS:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** Let us now remember these points about both: that Mind was recognized as related to the Cause and of the same genus as it; but pleasure is itself "infinite," belonging to the genus that contains neither beginning, middle, nor end within itself by its own nature, nor ever will. **PROTARCHUS:** How could we not remember? **SOCRATES:** It is necessary then to observe hereafter in which of these each consists, and by what affection they arise whenever they do. Just as we first investigated the genus of pleasure, so we shall now inquire into these things first. However, we cannot sufficiently examine pleasure apart from pain. **PROTARCHUS:** If we must walk this path, <margin>F</margin> then let us walk it. **SOCRATES:** Does the same thing seem true to you as to me regarding their governance? **PROTARCHUS:** What is that? **SOCRATES:** Pain and pleasure seem to exist naturally within the common and same genus. **PROTARCHUS:** This "common genus," friend Socrates, bring it back to our memory: which of those things distinguished above do you mean? **SOCRATES:** I will do so as best I can, wonderful man. **PROTARCHUS:** You say well. **SOCRATES:** By "common," let us understand that which we numbered as the third among the four things. **PROTARCHUS:** Do you mean the one you placed after the infinite and the finite, in which you located health and, I believe, harmony? **SOCRATES:** You speak correctly, but now pay the closest <margin>G</margin> attention. **PROTARCHUS:** Speak then. **SOCRATES:** I say that when harmony <note>term: "harmonia" (Greek: "ἁρμονία"); the proper balance or fitting-together of elements in a living being.</note> is dissolved in living beings, the dissolution of nature and the generation of pains happen at that same time. **PROTARCHUS:** That is very likely. **SOCRATES:** Again, when harmony is tempered and restored to its own nature, we must say that pleasure is produced, if we must conclude such great matters in a few words. **PROTARCHUS:** I believe you speak rightly, Socrates, but we should try to express these same things even more clearly. **SOCRATES:** Are not common and well-known things easiest to understand? **PROTARCHUS:** What things? **SOCRATES:** Hunger is surely a dissolution and a distress. **PROTARCHUS:** It is. **SOCRATES:** But eating is a replenishment and a pleasure. **PROTARCHUS:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** Thirst again is a corruption, a dissolution, and a pain. But the power of moisture refilling what has been dried out is pleasure. Furthermore, a separation and dissolution contrary to nature caused by a certain heat is distress. But restoration and cooling according to nature is <margin>H</margin> pleasure. **PROTARCHUS:** Entirely so. **SOCRATES:** Also, the freezing of a living thing's moisture contrary to its nature by cold is pain. But when things return to the same state and are dispersed, that journey back to nature is pleasure. Consider in short whether this discourse seems acceptable to you: whenever the animate species <note>original: "animata species" / "ζώου"</note> composed of the infinite and the limit according to nature is corrupted...

<column-break/>

**SOCRATES:** Hardly anything at all, but now follow the next point. All <margin>A</margin> these things we have just mentioned—did we not name them "body" when we saw them as combined into one? **PROTARCHUS:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** Apply the same thinking to what we call the "world" <note>original: "κόσμον" (kosmos)</note>. For it would likely be a body, being composed of the same elements. **PROTARCHUS:** You speak most correctly. **SOCRATES:** Does our body get its nourishment entirely from this [world] body, or does the world's body get its nourishment from ours, and has it received and held all those things we just mentioned? **PROTARCHUS:** This too, Socrates, is another question not worth asking. **SOCRATES:** Why? How will you say this next one is more worthy? **PROTARCHUS:** Tell me, what kind is it? **SOCRATES:** Shall we not say that our body has a soul? **PROTARCHUS:** Clearly we will <margin>B</margin> say so. **SOCRATES:** From where, friend Protarchus, did it receive it, unless the body of the universe happened to be ensouled, having the same things as this body, and even more beautiful things? **PROTARCHUS:** Clearly from nowhere else, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** For we surely do not think, Protarchus, that those four—the limit, the infinite, the mixture, and the genus of the cause—while this fourth one is present in all things, providing soul and producing a proper body in our case, and providing medicine for a failing body, and in other cases composing and correcting other things, being called every kind of wisdom—yet while these same things are in the whole heaven and in its great parts, and in addition are beautiful and pure, that in these <margin>C</margin> the nature of the most beautiful and precious things has not been devised? **PROTARCHUS:** But this would in no way make sense. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, if not that, we would follow the other argument and say better that there is, as we have often said, much "infinite" in the universe and sufficient "limit." And over them is a cause of no small account, ordering and coordinating the years, seasons, and months, which would most rightly be called "Wisdom" and "Mind." **PROTARCHUS:** Most rightly indeed. **SOCRATES:** But Wisdom and Mind could never come to be without a Soul. **PROTARCHUS:** No indeed. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, in the nature of Zeus you will say a royal soul and a royal mind are present through the power of the Cause; and in other things, other beautiful qualities, according to what is dear to each to be called. **PROTARCHUS:** Very much so. **SOCRATES:** Do not think, Protarchus, that we have spoken this argument in <margin>D</margin> vain. But it is an ally to those who declared long ago that Mind always rules the universe. **PROTARCHUS:** It is indeed. **SOCRATES:** And it has provided an answer to my search, that Mind is of that genus which was called the Cause of the four, which was this one thing for us. For you now have our answer quite completely. **PROTARCHUS:** I have it, and quite sufficiently. And yet you answered me without my noticing. **SOCRATES:** For play, Protarchus, is sometimes a relaxation from serious study. **PROTARCHUS:** You have spoken well. **SOCRATES:** Now then, friend, to which <margin>E</margin> genus Mind belongs and what power it possesses has been shown fairly well by us. **PROTARCHUS:** Entirely so. **SOCRATES:** And indeed, the genus of pleasure appeared in the same way long ago. **PROTARCHUS:** Quite so. **SOCRATES:** Let us also remember these things about both: that Mind was akin to the Cause and of nearly that genus. But pleasure is itself "infinite," and of the genus that has neither beginning, middle, nor end from itself or within itself, nor ever will have. **PROTARCHUS:** We shall remember; how could we not? **SOCRATES:** It was then necessary to see after this in what each of them exists, and through what affection they come to be when they come to be—pleasure first. Just as we examined its genus before, so also these things first. We will likely not be able to examine pleasure without pain in whatever we may pursue; but if we must travel this way, let us travel this way. Does it appear to you as it does to me concerning nature itself? **PROTARCHUS:** What kind of thing? **SOCRATES:** It seems to me that pain and pleasure come to be together in the common genus <margin>F</margin> according to nature. **PROTARCHUS:** Remind us, friend Socrates, what you wish to show by "common" among the things previously mentioned. **SOCRATES:** This shall be done to the best of my power, wonderful man. **PROTARCHUS:** You say well. **SOCRATES:** By "common," then, let us understand that which we said was the fourth <note>Socrates here refers back to the "mixture," which was the third or fourth depending on how they are listed.</note> of the four; which you said was the limit and... in which health and, I think, harmony were placed. **PROTARCHUS:** You speak most excellently. **SOCRATES:** Now pay the closest attention. **PROTARCHUS:** Only speak. **SOCRATES:** I say, then, that when harmony is dissolved for us in living beings, a dissolution of nature and the generation of pains occur at that time. **PROTARCHUS:** What you say is very likely. **SOCRATES:** But again, when harmony is tuned and returns to its own nature, it must be said that pleasure is produced; if such great matters must be spoken <margin>G</margin> thus in a few words. **PROTARCHUS:** I think you speak correctly, Socrates; but let us try to say these same things even more clearly. **SOCRATES:** Is it not easiest to see things that are public and manifest? **PROTARCHUS:** What kind? **SOCRATES:** Is not hunger a dissolution and a pain? **PROTARCHUS:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** And eating, becoming a replenishment again, is pleasure. **PROTARCHUS:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** And thirst again is a destruction, a pain, and a dissolution; but the power of the liquid refilling what was dried out is pleasure. Again, the melting and dissolution—the suffering from heat contrary to nature—is pain; but <margin>H</margin> restoration and cooling according to nature is pleasure. **PROTARCHUS:** Entirely so. **SOCRATES:** And the freezing of the living thing's moisture contrary to nature by cold is pain; but when they return to the same state and are thawed, the path according to nature is pleasure. In a single word, consider if the argument seems moderate to you, which says that the species composed from the infinite and the limit according to nature...

</columns>

<summary>Socrates argues that since human bodies have souls, the universe must also possess a cosmic Soul and Mind (Nous) derived from the "Cause." He then defines pain as the dissolution of natural harmony and pleasure as its restoration, using hunger and thirst as primary examples.</summary>

<keywords>Cosmic Soul, Mind, Nous, Zeus, Cause, Pleasure, Pain, Harmony, Dissolution, Restoration, Philebus, Socrates</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Protarchus from the previous page, where they discussed the role of the Mind in the universe. Now, Socrates moves to a more psychological and ethical level, analyzing the specific nature of pleasure and pain, and how they relate to the body and the soul.</meta>

### PHILEBUS.

<columns>

**A** ...a living form brought into being (as I was saying before); whenever this is destroyed, the destruction is **pain** <note>original: "λύπην" / "dolor"</note>, but the path back toward its own essence, this return of all things, is **pleasure**. **PROTARCHUS:** Let it be so; for it seems to me to have a certain clear outline. **SOCRATES:** Let us then establish this as one species of pain and pleasure within these two states of experience. **PROT.** Let it be established. **SOCR.** Now, establish a second kind: the expectation within the soul itself regarding these experiences. One part is the hope before pleasant things, which is pleasant and encouraging; the other is the expectation before painful things, which is fearful and distressing. **PROT.** This is indeed another kind of pleasure and pain, belonging to the soul itself apart from the body, arising through expectation. **SOCR.** You have understood correctly. For in **B** these, I believe—at least in my opinion—when each occurs in its pure and unmixed form, as it seems, without the mixture of pain and pleasure, it will become clear regarding the nature of pleasures whether the entire genus is to be welcomed, or whether this is something we must grant to one of the previously mentioned classes (like heat and cold and all such things), that they are sometimes to be welcomed and sometimes not; for while they are not inherently "good," they sometimes take on the nature of the good. **PROT.** You are most correct that we must hunt down the subject of our pursuit in this way. **SOCR.** First, then, let us consider this: if it is truly as we said, that destruction is pain and restoration is pleasure, let us consider what state must exist **C** in living beings when they are in neither a state of destruction nor restoration. Focus your mind intently and tell me: is it not an absolute necessity that every living being at such a time feels neither pain nor pleasure, whether great or small? **PROT.** It is a necessity. **SOCR.** Therefore, we have a third disposition or state, besides those of the one who rejoices and the one who suffers. **PROT.** Indeed. **SOCR.** Come then, let us be eager to remember this. For it matters quite a bit for our judgment of pleasure whether we remember this state or not. Let us, if you wish, briefly conclude something about it. **PROT.** Tell me what. **SOCR.** You know that for a man who has chosen the life of wisdom <note>original: "φρονεῖν" / "contemplationis"</note>, nothing prevents him from living in this manner. **PROT.** You mean the life of neither rejoicing nor grieving? **SOCR.** Yes, for it was said earlier in our comparison of lives that the one who chooses the life of thought and wisdom need not rejoice either much or little. **PROT.** It was indeed said so. **SOCR.** Such a state would then belong to him; and perhaps it is not at all strange if **D** this is the most divine of all lives. **PROT.** It is certainly not likely that the gods feel joy, nor the opposite. **SOCR.** It is not likely at all; for either would be unbecoming to them. But let us investigate this later, if it is relevant to the discussion; and we shall credit it to the Mind's account for the second prize, if we cannot award it the first. **PROT.** You speak most correctly. **SOCR.** And yet, that other kind of pleasure, which we said belongs to the soul itself, is entirely created through **memory** <note>original: "μνήμη" / "memoria"</note>. **PROT.** How so? **SOCR.** It seems we must first grasp what memory is; and perhaps even before memory, we must grasp **sensation** <note>original: "αἴσθησιν" / "sensus"</note>, if these matters are to become clear to us in the proper way. **PROT.** What do you mean? **SOCR.** Suppose that among the various experiences of our body, some are extinguished in the body before they reach the soul, leaving the soul **E** unaffected; but others pass through both, causing a kind of disturbance or "shaking" that is both unique to each and common to both. **PROT.** Let that be established. **SOCR.** If we say that the soul "forgets" those which do not pass through both, but does not "forget" those that pass through both, would we be speaking correctly? **PROT.** Certainly. **SOCR.** Now, do not assume I am speaking of the actual birth of "forgetfulness" <note>original: "λήθης" / "obliuio"</note> here. For forgetfulness is the exit of memory, but in the case we are describing, memory has not yet come into being. It is absurd to say there is a "loss" of something that does not yet exist and has not yet happened. Is it not? **PROT.** Indeed. **SOCR.** Then simply change the names. **PROT.** How? **SOCR.** Instead of saying the soul "forgets" when it remains unaffected by the disturbances of the body, call that state **insensibility** <note>original: "ἀναισθησίαν" / "insensibilitatem"</note>, which you are now calling forgetfulness. **PROT.** I understand. **SOCR.** But when the soul and body are affected together in a single experience and are moved together, if you call that movement **sensation**, you would not be speaking out of turn. **PROT.** That is very true. **SOCR.** So we now understand what we mean by sensation. **PROT.** Certainly. **SOCR.** If one were to call memory the **preservation of sensation** <note>original: "σωτηρίαν αἰσθήσεως" / "sensùs conseruationem"</note>, he would, in my opinion, be speaking correctly. **PROT.** Correct indeed. **SOCR.** But do we not say that **recollection** <note>original: "ἀνάμνησιν" / "reminiscentiam"</note> is different from memory? **PROT.** Perhaps. **SOCR.** Is it not in this way? **PROT.** In what way? **SOCR.** When the soul, by itself and without the body, recovers as much as possible an experience it once had in common with the body, then we say it "recollects." Is that not so? **PROT.** Very much so. **SOCR.** Furthermore, when the soul has lost the memory of a sensation or a piece of knowledge and then brings it back again **G** by itself within itself, we call all these instances "recollections" and "memories." **PROT.** You speak correctly. **SOCR.** Now, the reason all this has been said is this. **PROT.** What is it? **SOCR.** So that we might understand the pleasure of the soul apart from the body as clearly and distinctly as possible, and at the same time understand **desire** <note>original: "ἐπιθυμίαν" / "concupiscentiam"</note>. For both of these seem to be made manifest through these things. **PROT.** Let us then discuss what comes next, Socrates. **SOCR.** Much remains to be considered regarding the origin of pleasure...

<column-break/>

**A** As we stated in previous sections, when such a generated form is corrupted, that corruption is **pain**. But when these things flow back into their own essence, we call that return **pleasure**. **PROTARCHUS:** So be it. For this seems to me quite probable. **SOCRATES:** Let us therefore place this one species of pleasure and pain in each of these experiences. **PROT.** Let it be placed. **SOCR.** Next, consider the expectation of these experiences in the soul. I mean the expectation that precedes pleasures—hoping, rejoicing, and feeling secure; and that which precedes painful things—fearful and sorrowful. **PROT.** There is therefore this **B** other species of pleasure and pain, separate from the body, proceeding from the expectation of the soul alone. **SOCR.** You have understood rightly. In these, as I see it, when both exist in a pure state and are not mixed—pleasure and pain, that is—we shall clearly discern whether the whole genus of pleasure is to be loved, or if this should rather be attributed to one of the things previously mentioned. For pleasure and pain, like heat and cold and other such things, may sometimes be loved and at other times not; as they are not inherently good, but when they occasionally take on a certain character, they follow the nature of the good. **PROT.** You say rightly that one who investigates such things must proceed in this way. **SOCR.** First, then, let us look at this: if it is true what was said, that pain follows their destruction and pleasure follows their preservation, then when they are **C** neither perishing nor being preserved, what specific state should we then attribute to individual animals? Answer me with an attentive mind: does it seem necessary to you that any animal at that very time would in no way either rejoice or be distressed? **PROT.** Certainly necessary. **SOCR.** There is therefore this third state, besides the condition of the grieving and the rejoicing. **PROT.** There is indeed. **SOCR.** Try to remember this: for in order to judge pleasure, it matters a great deal whether we remember it or not; let us, however, briefly touch upon it if you wish. **PROT.** Tell me then, what is it? **SOCR.** Nothing prevents the man who chooses the life of contemplation from living in such a way. **PROT.** You mean separate from joy and distress? **SOCR.** For it was said in the **D** comparison of each life, that the man devoted to contemplation does not in any part either rejoice or suffer. **PROT.** It was altogether said so. **SOCR.** <margin>The contemplative life is most divine.</margin> Does this not suit him? And perhaps it would be no wonder if this life is the most divine of all others. **PROT.** <margin>The Gods feel neither joy nor sorrow.</margin> Is it absurd for the Gods to rejoice or, conversely, to be sad? **SOCR.** Entirely absurd. For both are unbecoming [of them]. But let us investigate this next, to see if it contributes anything to this discussion; and let us adapt the mind to the second prize of victory, even if we are not permitted the first. **PROT.** You speak correctly. **SOCR.** And yet, another species of pleasures, which we assigned as proper to the soul, consists entirely of memory. **PROT.** In what way? **SOCR.** It seems we must first grasp what memory is; **E** and perhaps even what the sensation of memory is, if we wish these things to be more clearly elucidated. **PROT.** In what way do you mean? **SOCR.** Suppose that of all bodily experiences, some are extinguished in the body before they flow into the soul, leaving it free from experience; others are spread through both and bring about a certain "shaking" or disturbance, both proper to each and common to both equally. **PROT.** Let them be so placed. **SOCR.** And if we say that experiences not propagated through both remain hidden from the soul, while those flowing through both become known to the soul, shall we be speaking correctly? **PROT.** Certainly. **SOCR.** Therefore, do not in any way suppose that this "remaining hidden" is the generation of forgetfulness. For **F** forgetfulness is the exit of memory. But in those things just mentioned, memory did not yet exist. It is absurd that there should be any "loss" of that which neither is nor was. **PROT.** Absurd. **SOCR.** Therefore, only change the names. **PROT.** How? **SOCR.** For that which we said was hidden from the soul, when it exists without the disturbance of bodily tumult—which you now seem to call forgetfulness—name it instead **insensibility**, or the absence of sensation. **PROT.** I have it. **SOCR.** However, if you call the movement made in the common experience of body and soul "sensation," you will name it not inappropriately. **PROT.** You speak the truth. **SOCR.** Do we not now perceive what we wish to be called sensation? **PROT.** We do. **SOCR.** <margin>Memory.</margin> Furthermore, in my opinion, one will correctly call the preservation of sensation "memory." **G** **PROT.** Correct indeed. **SOCR.** And do we admit that recollection differs from memory, or not? **PROT.** Perhaps. **SOCR.** Is it not chiefly in this? **PROT.** In what? **SOCR.** Whenever the soul recovers within itself, without the body, those things it once experienced with the body, then we say it "remembers," do we not? **PROT.** Very much so. **SOCR.** Moreover, when having suffered the loss of memory, whether of a sensation or a lesson, it again recalls it within itself, it is thought to "recollect." And all these we call memories and recollections. **PROT.** You speak well. **SOCR.** <margin>Suffering belongs to the body, but not desire.</margin> Now, the reason all these things have been said is this. **PROT.** What is that? **SOCR.** So that we may grasp the pleasure of the soul without the body as greatly and clearly as possible, and along with it, desire; for through both of these, those things seem to be declared. **PROT.** Let us now proceed to the rest, Socrates. **SOCR.** It seems many things must be considered regarding the origin of pleasure...

</columns>

<summary>In this passage, Socrates and Protarchus define pleasure as a restoration to a natural state and pain as its destruction. They distinguish between bodily sensations and the soul's mental states, such as expectation, memory (the preservation of sensation), and recollection (the soul's independent recovery of past knowledge).</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Protarchus, Philebus, pleasure, pain, memory, recollection, sensation, contemplative life, divine nature, psychology of the soul</keywords>
