<meta>This page continues the dialogue from the previous section where Socrates and Protarchus defined pleasure as a return to a natural state and pain as its disruption. Here, they transition into a psychological analysis of desire (concupiscentia) and the role of memory in physical needs.</meta>

# PLATO'S

<columns>

<insert>A</insert> ...and investigating its entire form. And now, first of all, we must see what **desire** <note>original: "concupiscentia" / "ἐπιθυμία" (epithymia). In this context, it refers to an appetite or drive toward something.</note> is, and where it is born. **PROTARCHUS:** Let us look into it now, I pray; for we shall lose nothing. **SOCRATES:** On the contrary, Protarchus, by finding what we are now seeking, we shall lose something: namely, our doubt concerning these matters. **PROT.** How well you have turned that back on me! But let us now explain what follows. **SOCR.** Did we not say that hunger and thirst, and many such things, are certain kinds of desire? **PROT.** Most certainly. **SOCR.** Looking toward what common feature do we call such diverse things by a single name? **PROT.** By Jove, it is not easy to say, Socrates; yet it must be said. **SOCR.** Let us begin again from those same things. **PROT.** Which things? **SOCR.** Do we <margin>To thirst is not a function of the body, but of having been dried out.</margin> <insert>B</insert> say that someone is thirsty? **PROT.** We do. **SOCR.** And is this to be "empty"? **PROT.** Why not? **SOCR.** And is thirst a desire? **PROT.** It is. **SOCR.** For a drink? **PROT.** For a drink. **SOCR.** Or rather, is it a desire for **repletion**? <note>Filling up or being satisfied after a lack.</note> **PROT.** Certainly for this. **SOCR.** Therefore, he who is empty and exhausted seeks the opposite of what he is suffering. For since he is empty, he desires to be filled. **PROT.** That is manifest. **SOCR.** What then? Can he who is empty for the first time ever grasp repletion—either by sense or by some memory—if he has never experienced it in the present or in any past time? **PROT.** In no way. **SOCR.** But we confess that he who desires, desires something. **PROT.** Why not? **SOCR.** Therefore, he does not desire what he is currently suffering. For he is thirsty, and thirst is an emptiness, yet he <insert>C</insert> affects a repletion. **PROT.** Yes. **SOCR.** Something, therefore, of that which desires will grasp repletion. **PROT.** It must. **SOCR.** The body certainly cannot, for it is exhausted. **PROT.** Certainly. **SOCR.** It remains, then, that the soul achieves repletion through **memory**. **PROT.** That is clear. **SOCR.** For by what else would it achieve it? **PROT.** By almost nothing else. **SOCR.** Do we notice what is being established for us by these arguments? **PROT.** What is that? **SOCR.** This logic dictates that desire is not of the body. **PROT.** In what way? **SOCR.** Because in every living creature, desire shows an effort contrary to the sufferings of the body. **PROT.** Entirely so. <insert>D</insert> **SOCR.** Moreover, an impulse toward the opposite of what is being suffered implies a memory contrary to those sufferings. **PROT.** Absolutely. **SOCR.** Therefore, the argument showing that memory leads toward the things desired attributes all impulse, desire, and the governing principle of every living thing to the **soul**. **PROT.** Most correctly. **SOCR.** This logic, therefore, in no way admits that our body thirsts or hungers, or suffers anything of that sort. **PROT.** You speak the truth. **SOCR.** Furthermore, we shall consider this: that this argument seems to want to demonstrate a certain kind of life in these things. **PROT.** In what things? And what life are you speaking of? **SOCR.** In filling and emptying, I mean, and in all things that pertain to the safety or destruction of living beings. If any of us, being in either state, is affected by pain, and then rejoices according to the changes. **PROT.** So it is. **SOCR.** <insert>E</insert> What about when someone remains in the middle of these? **PROTARCHUS:** How in the middle? **SOCR.** Because of his suffering he is sad, but meanwhile he remembers past pleasures; the sadness ceases somewhat, yet he is not yet filled. What should be said then? Is he not in the middle of these sufferings? **PROT.** He must be. **SOCR.** Is he then altogether grieving, or on the contrary, rejoicing? **PROT.** Not rejoicing, by Jove, but rather affected by a **double sadness**: according to the body in its suffering, and according to the soul in the heat of expectation. **SOCR.** In what way, Protarchus, did you say the pain was double? Is it not that <insert>F</insert> an empty man sometimes hopes for a certain repletion, and at other times, on the contrary, despairs? **PROT.** Most certainly. **SOCR.** And while he hopes to attain it, does he not seem to rejoice by that very recollection? Yet at the same time, being empty, is he not tortured at that moment? **PROT.** It is necessary. **SOCR.** Then at that time, both man and other animals rejoice and grieve simultaneously. **PROT.** It appears so. **SOCR.** But when someone who is empty altogether despairs of repletion, does not a double passion then arise concerning pains, which you, having looked upon it a moment ago, thought was simply double? **PROT.** These things are true. **SOCR.** Let us use this consideration of such passions for <insert>G</insert> this purpose. **PROT.** To what purpose do you say? **SOCR.** Whether we ought to call these pleasures and distresses "true," or some true and others false? **PROT.** How, Socrates, can pleasures or distresses be false? **SOCR.** How also, Protarchus, can fears be false, or expectations be true or not true? Or opinions be true or false? **PROT.** I would admit that opinions are so; but these others, not at all. **SOCR.** What do you say? We seem to be starting a discussion that is not at all brief. **PROT.** You tell the truth. **SOCR.** But if it is consistent with what went before, O son of that famous man, it must be considered. **PROT.** Perhaps so. **SOCR.** Therefore, everything superfluous, and whatever is said beyond what is proper, must be omitted. **PROT.** Correct. <insert>H</insert> **SOCR.** Tell me then; a constant wonder always holds me regarding these questions we have just introduced. **PROT.** How do you mean? **SOCR.** Are there not some from the number of pleasures that are false, and others true? **PROT.** How could they be? **SOCR.** Neither in a dream, then, nor while awake (as you say), nor in madness, nor in any insanity, could anyone be said to think they rejoice when they do not, or think they grieve when they do not? **PROTARCHUS:** We all suspect, Socrates, that all these things are as you say. **SOCR.** But is it correct? Or perhaps we should consider whether these things are said correctly or not? **PROT.** It must be considered, in my opinion. **SOCR.** Let us distinguish more clearly, therefore, what was just...

<column-break/>

...investigating its entire form, it is necessary, as it seems, for the speaker to consider it. And now once again, it appears another point must be grasped: what desire is and where it occurs. **P.** Let us consider it then; for we shall lose nothing. **S.** We shall lose this, Protarchus: by letting go of what we are now seeking, namely the doubt concerning these very things. **P.** You have defended your position rightly; let us try to say what follows. **S.** Did we not just now say that hungering and thirsting, and many other such things, were certain desires? **P.** Very much so. **SOC.** Looking toward what same thing, then, do we call these things, which differ so much, by one name? **P.** By Zeus, it is perhaps not easy to say, Socrates; but nonetheless, it must be said. **SOC.** Let us take it up again from the same point. **P.** From where? **SOC.** Do we not say on each occasion that something "thirsts"? **P.** How could we not? **S.** And is this to be emptied? **P.** Of course. **S.** Is thirst then a desire? **P.** Yes. **SOC.** For drink? **P.** For drink. **SOC.** Or for repletion? **P.** I think for repletion. **S.** Therefore, the one among us who is being emptied (as it seems) desires the opposite of what he suffers. For being emptied, he longs to be filled. **P.** Most clearly. **S.** What then? Can he who is being emptied for the first time grasp—either by perception or by memory—that which he is neither suffering in the present time, nor has ever suffered in time past? **P.** How could he? **S.** But indeed, we say that he who desires, desires something? **P.** For how could he not? **S.** Therefore, he does not desire that which he suffers. For he thirsts, and this is an emptying; but he desires repletion. **P.** Yes. **S.** Therefore, something of the one who thirsts would grasp repletion. **P.** It is necessary. **S.** It is impossible for the body, then; for it is being emptied somewhere. **P.** Yes. **S.** It remains, then, for the soul to grasp repletion through memory. **P.** Evidently. **S.** For by what else could it grasp it? **P.** By almost nothing. **S.** Do we understand then what happens to us from these arguments? **P.** What sort of thing? **S.** This argument says that desire of the body does not happen to us. **P.** How? **S.** Because it reveals that the attempt of every living thing is always contrary to its physical sufferings. **P.** Very much so. **S.** And the impulse leading toward the opposite of the sufferings surely shows that there is memory of the things contrary to the sufferings. **P.** Quite so. **S.** By showing that memory leads toward the things desired, the argument has revealed that every impulse and desire, and the governing principle of the entire living being, belongs to the soul. **P.** Most correctly. **S.** Therefore, the argument in no way allows that our body thirsts, or hungers, or suffers any such things. **P.** Most true. **S.** Furthermore, let us also consider this again in relation to these same things. For the argument seems to me to want to show a certain form of life in these very matters. **P.** In what sort of thing, and about what sort of life are you speaking? **S.** In being filled and being emptied, and in all things that are concerned with the preservation and the destruction of living things; and if any of us, being in either of these states, feels pain, but then rejoices during the changes. **P.** These things are so. **S.** What when one is in the middle of these? **P.** How in the middle? **S.** On account of the suffering he feels pain, but he remembers the pleasant things that happened; he would cease from the pain, yet he is not yet filled. What do we say then? Shall we not say he is in the middle of the sufferings? **P.** We certainly say so. **S.** Whether as one grieving entirely, or rejoicing? **P.** By Zeus, rather as one grieving with a certain double grief: according to the body in its suffering, and according to the soul, with a certain longing of expectation. **S.** How, Protarchus, did you say the grief was double? Is it not that sometimes one of us, being emptied, is in a clear hope of being filled, but at other times, on the contrary, is hopeless of it? **P.** Very much so. **S.** Does it not seem to you that while he hopes to be filled, he rejoices by remembering? Yet at the same time, being emptied in these times, he feels pain? **P.** Necessarily. **S.** At that time, then, a man and other living things both grieve and rejoice at the same time. **P.** It seems so. **S.** But what when one is hopeless, being emptied, of attaining repletion? Does there not then occur a double state regarding the pains, which you, just now seeing it, thought was simply double? **P.** Most true, Socrates. **S.** Let us use this investigation of these sufferings in this way. **P.** In what way? **S.** Shall we say these pains and pleasures are true or false? Or that some are true, and others not? **P.** How, Socrates, could there be false pleasures or pains? **S.** And how, Protarchus, could there be true or false fears, or true expectations or not? Or true or false opinions? **P.** Opinions I might somehow grant, but these others I would not. **S.** How do you mean? We are in danger of stirring up a discussion that is not at all small. **P.** You speak the truth. **S.** But if it is appropriate to what has gone before, O son of that man, this must be considered. **P.** Perhaps so. **S.** One must then say "farewell" to other long arguments, or to anything said besides what is appropriate. **P.** Correct. **S.** Tell me then; for a certain thought always holds me to the end regarding these same puzzles we are now disputing. **P.** How do you mean? **S.** Are there not false, and also true, pleasures? **P.** For how could there be? **S.** Neither in a dream, nor awake (as you say), nor in madness, nor in any delusions, is there anyone who ever thinks he rejoices, but rejoices in no way; nor again thinks he feels pain, but feels no pain. **P.** We have all, Socrates, assumed that all these things are so. **S.** Is it then correct? Or should it be considered whether these things are said correctly or not? **P.** It must be considered, as I would say. **S.** Let us then distinguish more clearly...

</columns>

<summary>In this passage from Plato's Philebus, Socrates argues that desire is a function of the soul rather than the body, because the body only experiences its current state (emptiness), while the soul uses memory to aim for the opposite state (repletion). They also begin to explore the concept of "false pleasures" and the simultaneous experience of joy and pain through hope and memory.</summary>

<keywords>Plato, Philebus, Socrates, Protarchus, desire, epithymia, soul vs body, memory, repletion, emptiness, double sadness, true and false pleasures, psychological philosophy</keywords>

--- Page 115 ---
<meta>This page continues the dialogue from the previous section where Socrates and Protarchus were discussing the relationship between desire and the state of the body. Here, the focus shifts to the psychological nature of pleasure and whether it, like opinion, can be "false" or "mistaken."</meta>

# PHILEBUS.

<columns>

<margin>A</margin> **SOCRATES:** ...concerning what was just being said about pleasure and opinion. Now, is there not a process in us of **holding an opinion**? <note>original: "τὸ δοξάζειν" (to doxazein). This refers to the act of forming a belief or judgment.</note> **PROTARCHUS:** Yes. **SOCR.** And of **feeling pleasure**? **PROT.** Yes. **SOCR.** Furthermore, that which is the object of the opinion is something, is it not? **PROT.** How could it not be? **SOCR.** And that which the person feeling pleasure is pleased by is also something? **PROT.** Absolutely. **SOCR.** Now, whether one opines correctly or incorrectly, does he ever lose the reality of the act of opining? **PROT.** How could he? **SOCR.** Likewise, if someone feels pleasure, whether he is pleased correctly or incorrectly, it is clear he will never lose the reality of the act of feeling pleasure. **PROT.** Yes, that is also the case. **SOCR.** In what way, then, does **opinion** <note>original: "δόξα" (doxa)</note> usually become both false and true for us, while **pleasure** <note>original: "ἡδονῆς" (hedones)</note> is only true—even though both the act of opining and the act of rejoicing are equally real? <margin>B</margin> **PROT.** That must be considered. **SOCR.** Is it because truth and falsehood are added to opinion, making it not just an opinion, but an opinion of a certain quality in each case? Is that what you say we must consider? **PROT.** Yes. **SOCR.** Moreover, we must agree whether some things have qualities, while pleasure and pain are simply what they are, and do not become "of a certain quality." **PROT.** That is clear. **SOCR.** But it is not hard to see that they do indeed have qualities. For we said long ago that both pains and pleasures become great or small, or intense. **PROT.** Certainly. <margin>C</margin> **SOCR.** And if **wickedness** <note>original: "πονηρία" (poneria) — moral badness or defect.</note> is added to them, Protarchus, shall we say the opinion is then bad, and the pleasure is also bad? **PROT.** Why, of course, Socrates. **SOCR.** What if **correctness**, or its opposite, is added to them? Shall we not call the opinion "correct" if it possesses correctness, and the pleasure "correct" likewise? **PROT.** Necessarily. **SOCR.** And if the thing being opined is mistaken, must we not admit that the opinion, being mistaken, is not correct or opining rightly? **PROT.** How could it be? **SOCR.** Well then, if we see a pain or a pleasure being "mistaken" about the object of its pain or pleasure, shall we call it "correct" or "good" or any other noble name? **PROT.** It is impossible, if the pleasure is mistaken. <margin>D</margin> **SOCR.** Indeed, it seems that pleasure often arises in us not with a correct opinion, but with a false one. **PROT.** Of course. And in such a case, Socrates, we call the opinion false; but the pleasure itself, no one would ever call it "false." **SOCR.** You are defending the cause of pleasure very zealously right now, Protarchus! **PROT.** Not at all; I am only saying what I hear. **SOCR.** Is there no difference for us, my friend, between a pleasure that follows correct opinion and knowledge, and one that often arises in each of us following falsehood and ignorance? **PROT.** It is likely there is a great difference. **SOCR.** Let us proceed to observe this difference between them. **PROT.** Lead on wherever you think best. **SOCR.** I lead this way, then. **PROT.** In what way? <margin>E</margin> **SOCR.** Opinion, we say, can be false and can be true. **PROT.** It can. **SOCR.** And as we were just saying, pleasure and pain often follow these—I mean, true and false opinion. **PROT.** Quite so. **SOCR.** Does not opinion, and the attempt to form a judgment, arise for us from **memory** and **sensation** <note>original: "μνήμης τε καὶ αἰσθήσεως" (mnemes te kai aistheseos)</note> in every case? **PROT.** Very much so. **SOCR.** Must we suppose our situation regarding these things is like this? **PROT.** How? **SOCR.** Would you say it often happens that someone, seeing things from a distance and not very clearly, wishes to judge what he sees? **PROT.** I would say so. **SOCR.** And after this, might he not ask himself a question like this? **PROT.** What? **SOCR.** "What is that which appears to be standing there by the rock under a tree?" Do you think someone might say these words to himself when he catches sight of such things appearing to him? **PROT.** To be sure. **SOCR.** And after this, such a person might answer himself, saying "It is a man," and in so saying, he might happen to be right. **PROT.** Certainly. <margin>F</margin> **SOCR.** Or, having been misled, he might call what he sees a "statue," the work of some shepherds. **PROT.** Most likely. **SOCR.** And if someone is present with him, he might speak out loud what he had said to himself, repeating those same things to the bystander; and so what we previously called "opinion" has now become a "statement" <note>original: "λόγος" (logos) — a spoken account or word.</note>? **PROT.** What else? **SOCR.** But if he is alone and thinks this same thing to himself, he continues on his way with the thought in his mind, sometimes for quite a long time. **PROT.** Certainly. **SOCR.** What then? Do you feel about this as I do? **PROT.** About what? <margin>G</margin> **SOCR.** It seems to me that our **soul** <note>original: "ψυχὴ" (psyche)</note> at such a time is like a **book**. **PROT.** How? **SOCR.** It seems to me that memory, coinciding with sensations, and the feelings associated with them, almost "write" words in our souls. And when this experience writes the truth, true opinion and true statements arise in us; but when this **scribe** <note>original: "γραμματεὺς" (grammateus)</note> within us writes falsely, the result is the opposite of the truth. **PROT.** I entirely agree, and I accept what has been said in this way. **SOCR.** Accept also another **craftsman** <note>original: "δημιουργὸν" (demiourgon)</note> who exists in our souls at that time. **PROT.** Who is he? **SOCR.** A **painter** <note>original: "ζωγράφον" (zographon) — literally a "life-drawer."</note>, who, after the scribe, paints images of these spoken things in the soul. **PROT.** How and when do we say he does this? <margin>H</margin> **SOCR.** When someone, having drawn away from sight or any other sensation the things then opined and spoken, "sees" in himself somehow the images of those things. Does this not happen in us? **PROT.** It certainly does. **SOCR.** Therefore, the images of true opinions and statements are true, and those of false ones are false. **PROT.** Absolutely. **SOCR.** If we have spoken correctly so far, let us also consider this further point.

<column-break/>

...has been said concerning pleasure and opinion. Is there something among men called "opining"? **PROT.** There is. **SOCR.** And "rejoicing"? **PROT.** And "rejoicing." **SOCR.** And is that which we opine something? **PROT.** Why not? **SOCR.** And this by which we are pleased? **PROT.** That also. **SOCR.** He who opines, whether he opines rightly or not, does not lose that which is truly "to opine." **PROT.** For in what way could he? **SOCR.** One who rejoices also, whether he rejoices rightly or not, does not lose that which is truly "to rejoice." **PROT.** Indeed, these things are so. **SOCR.** In what way then does opinion become true and false, while pleasure is only true, when both opining truly and rejoicing truly have been accepted similarly? **PROT.** This must be considered. **SOCR.** Is it not because truth and falsehood are instilled into opinion: and not only because of these is it made an opinion, but each becomes a certain quality of opinion? Is this what you say must be considered? **PROT.** Yes. **SOCR.** Furthermore, it must be investigated whether pleasure and pain remain only what they are, or whether they are ever made into certain qualities. **PROT.** It is clear. **SOCR.** Truly, it is in no way difficult to see that they do become certain qualities. For a long time now we have conceded that pleasures and troubles become great and small, vehement and mild. **PROT.** We conceded it. **SOCR.** But if **depravity** <note>original: "prauitas"</note> is added to any of these, we shall confess that just as a bad opinion is created, so is a bad pleasure. **PROT.** What prevents it? **SOCR.** What if rectitude, or the contrary of rectitude, is applied to any of these? Shall we call it a "right" opinion when it has undergone rectitude, and similarly a "right" pleasure? **PROT.** It follows necessarily. **SOCR.** And if that which is grasped by opinion is deceptive, shall we not call the opinion "false" rather than "right"? **PROT.** Indeed. **SOCR.** Likewise, if we perceive pleasure or pain to wander away from that in which we rejoice or are distressed, shall we call it a "right" or "good" pleasure, or honor it with some noble name? **PROT.** That cannot be done, if the pleasure itself is at fault. **SOCR.** Nevertheless, frequently for us pleasure arises not from the truth, but from a falsehood. **PROT.** Without a doubt. Yet, Socrates, we call an opinion of that sort false; but as for the pleasure itself, no one would ever name it "false." **SOCR.** You defend the logic of pleasure too promptly in the present, O Protarchus. **PROT.** Not at all, but I speak what I hear. **SOCR.** Does it make no difference to us, my friend, whether a pleasure proceeds from right opinion and knowledge, or from that which follows false opinion and ignorance? **PROT.** It is consistent that they differ by no small interval. **SOCR.** But let us come to examine this very distance. **PROT.** Lead on as you please. **SOCR.** Look, I lead you this way. **PROT.** In what way? **SOCR.** Opinion, we say, is partly true, and partly false. **PROT.** So be it. **SOCR.** Often (as we were just saying) pleasure and pain follow these—true and false opinion, I mean. **PROT.** They follow. **SOCR.** Does not opinion beget itself in us from **sense** and **memory**, along with the very ability to opine? <margin>Opinion arises here from sensation and memory.</margin> **PROT.** Chiefly. **SOCR.** Is it not to be thought that we are thus disposed concerning these things? **PROT.** How? **SOCR.** That you might admit a man sometimes seeing something confusedly from a distance, desires to discern more clearly those things which he sees? **PROT.** I certainly admit it. **SOCR.** He will therefore question himself in some such way. **PROT.** In what way do you mean? **SOCR.** "What is that which appears from afar next to the rock under the tree?" Does he not seem to you to bring these things forth to himself, while he looks at such things as have at some time appeared? **PROT.** Why not? **SOCR.** Then, as if answering himself, he says "it is a man," as if he has now attained the truth. **PROT.** Truly. **SOCR.** Again, perhaps having moved forward, he asserts it is some **statue** <note>original: "simulacrum"</note> fashioned by shepherds. **PROT.** Very much so. **SOCR.** Here, if someone were present, he might pour out into his voice the same things he was turning over in his mind, and say them to the one present, and then a **speech** <note>original: "sermo"</note> would be made, which before we were calling "opinion." **PROT.** Manifestly. **SOCR.** But if he is alone, he proceeds reflecting on this same thing within himself, and sometimes keeping it within himself for a long time. **PROT.** Exactly. **SOCR.** What then? Do you feel the same here as I do? **PROT.** What is that? **SOCR.** It seems to me then that the soul of a man is very similar to a **book**. <margin>The soul is similar to a book and a blank slate.</margin> **PROT.** For what reason? **SOCR.** Memory, falling into the same place as the senses, along with those things which are around these experiences, seems to me in a way to "inscribe" certain words in the soul. And when they write true things, we call such an experience true, and true orations proceed from us because of this. But when this scribe of ours writes false things, the opposite of the truth results. **PROT.** It seems entirely so to me, and I gladly accept what has been said. **SOCR.** Accept another **worker** <note>original: "opificem"</note> of those things which then happen in our souls. **PROT.** Whom? **SOCR.** The **Painter**, who after the scribe himself, paints images of the spoken things in the soul. **PROT.** How and when is he to be said to do this? **SOCR.** When someone, drawing out the things said and perceived by opinion from the feeling or some other sense, beholds in himself in some way the images of the things said and perceived by opinion. Is this not done in us? **PROT.** Powerfully so. **SOCR.** And are not the images of true opinions and speeches true, but the false ones images of the false? **PROT.** Entirely. **SOCR.** If we have said these things rightly, let us look further into this...

</columns>

<summary>In this passage, Socrates uses the metaphors of an internal "scribe" and "painter" to explain how the soul processes sensations into opinions and mental images. He argues that just as opinions can be false, pleasures can also be "false" or "bad" if they are based on these internal misrepresentations.</summary>

<keywords>Plato, Philebus, Socrates, Protarchus, pleasure, false pleasure, opinion, soul as a book, internal scribe, internal painter, memory, sensation, Greek philosophy, Latin translation</keywords>

--- Page 116 ---
<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Protarchus regarding the "writer" and "painter" within the human soul. Previously, Socrates argued that our memories and perceptions act like a scribe recording thoughts and an artist illustrating them. Here, they apply this imagery to hopes and the distinction between true and false pleasures.</meta>

# OF PLATO

<columns>

<margin>A</margin>
...let us consider this further. **PROTARCHUS:** What is it? **SOCRATES:** Is it necessary that this happens to us only concerning the present and the past, or can it also concern the future? **PROTARCHUS:** By the same logic, it concerns all times. **SOCR.** Were not the pleasures and distresses belonging to the soul itself said earlier to precede the pleasures and pains of the body? And does it not happen that we feel "pre-joy" <note>original: "prægaudere" (Latin) / "προχαίρειν" (Greek). This refers to the anticipation of a future pleasure.</note> and "pre-pain" <note>original: "prædolere" (Latin) / "προλυπεῖσθαι" (Greek)</note> regarding what is to come? **PROT.** You speak the truth. **SOCR.** Do the "writings" and "paintings" which we imagined were being imprinted in us a moment ago look only to the past and present, and not at all to the future? **PROT.** They look to all times. **SOCR.** Do you agree, then, that all these things are certain expectations <term>spes/elpis: in this context, it refers to any expectation of the future, whether positive or negative</term> belonging to a future time, and that we are nourished by constant hope throughout our entire lives? **PROT.** Entirely so.

<margin>
Pleasure and sadness, which are proper to the soul, precede the pleasures and pains of the body.
</margin>

<margin>B</margin>
**SOCR.** Come, answer me this in addition to those things. **PROT.** What do you ask? **SOCR.** A man who is just, pious, and good—is he not a friend to God? **PROT.** Of course. **SOCR.** And is the unjust and wicked man not the opposite? **PROT.** He is. **SOCR.** Yet, as we were saying, every person is led by many hopes. **PROT.** Certainly. **SOCR.** There are "discourses" <note>original: "sermones/logoi." Socrates is personifying internal thoughts as speech.</note> within each of us, which we have called hopes? **PROT.** There are. **SOCR.** And indeed, there are "painted images" as well. For anyone may imagine themselves possessing a massive heap of gold and enjoying various delights with every possible sweetness. **PROT.** Nothing prevents it.

<margin>C</margin>
**SOCR.** Must we not say that these internal "writings" often turn out to be true for good men, because they are friends to God, but frequently the opposite for the wicked? **PROT.** We must certainly say so. **SOCR.** And yet, the wicked also have pleasures present in their minds, though they are fabricated and, in the end, false. **PROT.** Why would they not? **SOCR.** Therefore, wicked men mostly delight in false pleasures, while good men are nourished by true ones. **PROT.** You say what is necessary. **SOCR.** According to this reasoning, then, there are certain false pleasures in the souls of men, which are mere imitations of the true ones—though they are quite ridiculous—and pains in the same way. **PROT.** They certainly exist.

<margin>
It is concluded that true and false pleasures and pains exist.
</margin>

<margin>D</margin>
**SOCR.** Was it not possible for someone who is holding an opinion at all to hold an opinion about things that never were, are not, and will never be? **PROT.** It was. **SOCR.** And these were the things that made the opinion "false," and the person to be "opining falsely." Was it not? **PROT.** It was. **SOCR.** Must we not then attribute to pleasures and pains a certain state that corresponds to those opinions? **PROT.** In what way? **SOCR.** That it is possible for someone to truly rejoice, even if they are doing so randomly or for no reason, yet the things they are rejoicing over neither exist, nor have existed; and most often, they rejoice over things that will never happen. **PROT.** This too, Socrates, is necessary. **SOCR.** And the same reasoning would apply to fears and desires and all such things: that all of them can often be false. **PROT.** Exactly so.

<margin>E</margin>
**SOCR.** Do we call opinions "good" or "bad" for any reason other than that they are true or false? **PROT.** For that reason alone. **SOCR.** And do we think pleasures are "bad" for any other reason than that they are false? **PROT.** Quite the contrary, Socrates, you have put it the wrong way. For one should hardly assert that pleasures and distresses are bad solely because they are false; they often stumble into the greatest and most varied wickednesses besides. **SOCR.** We will discuss bad pleasures that are such because of their wickedness a little later, if you like. But as for false ones, we must say that many of them exist and arise in us frequently in another way: for this may perhaps help us in our judgment. **PROT.** Why not—provided they actually exist. **SOCR.** But in my opinion, Protarchus, they do. And as long as this doctrine remains with us, it is impossible for it to remain unchallenged. **PROT.** Well said.

<margin>F</margin>
**SOCR.** Let us approach this argument again, in the manner of athletes <note>original: "athletarum more." Socrates is suggesting they "re-wrestle" or "round two" of the debate.</note>. **PROT.** Let us. **SOCR.** We said earlier, if we remember correctly, that while the so-called "desires" were within us, the body was occupied by passions <note>original: "passio/pathos" meaning an experience or a suffering, not necessarily romantic passion.</note> separate from the soul. **PROT.** We remember, and this was undoubtedly said. **SOCR.** Did the soul not desire a state contrary to that of the body? And was it not the body that was the container of pain and pleasure arising from the experience? **PROT.** It was. **SOCR.** Gather, then, what follows from this. **PROT.** Speak on.

<margin>G</margin>
**SOCR.** Whenever these things coincide, pleasures and pains meet together, and one senses things that are opposites—which indeed has just become clear. **PROT.** It appears so. **SOCR.** Has this not also been agreed upon and established as confessed by us earlier? **PROT.** What? **SOCR.** That both pleasure and pain admit of a "more or less," and belong to the class of the infinite? <note>original: "genus infiniti" (the Unlimited). In this dialogue, Socrates categorizes everything into the Limited and the Unlimited.</note> **PROT.** It is certainly agreed. **SOCR.** There is, therefore, a certain way to judge these correctly. **PROT.** Where, and how?

<margin>H</margin>
**SOCR.** Is our purpose in this judgment not to distinguish, here and there, which of these is greater and which is smaller, which is more intense and which is more violent—comparing pleasure to pain, pain to pain, and pleasure again to pleasure? **PROT.** These are indeed the things we seek, and that is the goal of our judgment. **SOCR.** What then? In the case of sight, does looking at magnitudes from a distance or up close not destroy the truth and compel us to hold false opinions? And does the same not happen in the case of pains and pleasures? **PROT.** Much more so, Socrates.

<note>original Greek: "falsely making one think, but in pains and pleasures is this same thing not happening?"</note>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
**PROTARCHUS:** What kind of thing? **SOCRATES:** If it is necessary that we experience these things even when they have not happened, and never will happen... **PROT.** In the same way regarding all time. **SOCR.** Now, were not the pleasures and pains of the soul said previously to occur before the pleasures and pains of the body, so that we happen to "pre-joy" and "pre-pain" concerning the future time? **PROT.** Most true. **SOCR.** Therefore, do the writings and paintings, which we established a little earlier as being produced within us, concern the past and present time, but not the future? **PROT.** Very much so. **SOCR.** Do you say "very much so" because all these things are hopes belonging to the time that follows? And are we not filled with hopes throughout our whole life? **PROT.** Absolutely.

<margin>B</margin>
**SOCR.** Come now, answer this in addition to what has been said. **PROT.** What? **SOCR.** Is a man who is just, pious, and good in every way not dear to God? **PROT.** How could he not be? **SOCR.** And what of the unjust and entirely bad man? Is he not the opposite? **PROT.** How not? **SOCR.** Every man is full of many hopes, as we were saying just now. **PROT.** Certainly. **SOCR.** Are there "discourses" in each of us, which we call hopes? **PROT.** Yes. **SOCR.** And indeed, there are painted "phantasms." A person often sees himself getting an abundance of gold, and many pleasures along with it; and indeed, he sees himself "painted" within himself as rejoicing greatly. **PROT.** Why not?

<margin>C</margin>
**SOCR.** Of these, should we say that for good men, the "paintings" are usually true because they are dear to God, while for the bad, the opposite is usually true? **PROT.** Should we not? **PROT.** We must certainly say so. **SOCR.** Then the wicked also have pleasures "painted" within them no less, but these are surely false. **PROT.** Indeed. **SOCR.** Therefore, the wicked mostly rejoice in false pleasures, and the good among men in true ones. **PROT.** You say what is most necessary. **SOCR.** There are then, according to the present discussion, false pleasures in the souls of men, imitating the true ones in a rather ridiculous way; and pains likewise. **PROT.** There are.

<margin>D</margin>
**SOCR.** Now, it was possible for one who holds an opinion to do so about things that do not exist, and never have existed, and will never exist. **PROT.** Quite so. **SOCR.** And it was these things, I believe, that produced false opinion and opining falsely at that time. Was it not? **PROT.** Yes. **SOCR.** What then? Must we not grant to pains and pleasures the corresponding state in those circumstances? **PROT.** How? **SOCR.** That it is possible for a person to truly rejoice in any way whatsoever or even randomly, yet not over things that are, nor over things that have been, and often—perhaps most often—over things that are never going to happen. **PROT.** These things too, Socrates, are necessarily so. **SOCR.** Then the same logic would apply to fears and angers and all such things, that all such things are also sometimes false. **PROT.** Entirely so.

<margin>E</margin>
**SOCR.** What then? Can we speak of opinions being "wicked" and "good" in any way other than by their becoming false? **PROT.** In no other way. **SOCR.** Neither do we perceive pleasures, I believe, as being "wicked" in any other way except by being false. **PROT.** You have said quite the opposite, Socrates. For one would hardly consider pains and pleasures very wicked because of falsehood, but rather because they coincide with some other great and frequent wickedness. **SOCR.** We will speak of wicked pleasures, and those that are such because of wickedness, a little later if it still seems right. But now we must speak of the "false" ones that exist and arise in us in another way, many of them and many times; for we may use this to help with our judgments. **PROT.** Why not, if they indeed exist? **SOCR.** But, Protarchus, in my view, they do. And as long as this opinion stands among us, it is impossible for it to go unrefuted. **PROT.** Good.

<margin>F</margin>
**SOCR.** Let us stand around <note>original: "Περιστώμεθα." A metaphor for athletes surrounding an opponent or moving into position for a match.</note> this argument once more, like athletes. **PROT.** Let us go. **SOCR.** But surely we said (if we remember) a little while ago, that as long as the so-called "desires" are within us, the body and the soul are divided in their experiences. **PROT.** We remember, and that was said.

<margin>G</margin>
**SOCR.** Was not the soul the thing that desired states opposite to the body, while the body was the thing providing the pain or the pleasure through some experience? **PROT.** It was indeed. **SOCR.** Reason then on what happens in these cases. **PROT.** Tell me. **SOCR.** It happens, whenever these are present, that pains and pleasures are placed side by side; and the perceptions of these opposites are produced simultaneously, as has just been shown. **PROT.** It appears so. **SOCR.** And has this not been stated and agreed upon by us previously? **PROT.** What? **SOCR.** That both of these, pain and pleasure, admit of the "more and less," and that they belong to the class of the infinite? **PROT.** Certainly.

<margin>H</margin>
**SOCR.** What means is there, then, for these to be judged correctly? **PROT.** In what way and how? **SOCR.** If our intention in the judgment of these things is to discern in such cases which is greater and which is smaller compared to one another, and which is more intense—pain against pleasure, pain against pain, or pleasure against pleasure. **PROT.** These are indeed the things, and this is the purpose of the judgment. **SOCR.** What then? In sight, seeing magnitudes from far away and near at hand obscures the truth and makes one hold false opinions. Does this same thing not happen in the case of pains and pleasures? **PROT.** Much more so, Socrates...

</columns>

<summary>In this passage from Plato's Philebus, Socrates argues that pleasures and pains can be "false" just like opinions, often occurring through the anticipation of future events. He uses the metaphor of an internal painter to show how good men imagine true things while wicked men imagine false ones, and notes that the "distance" of an event affects our judgment of how much pleasure or pain it contains.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Protarchus from the previous discussion on the "painter" and "writer" in the soul. Having established that our expectations of the future can be true or false, they now examine whether the feelings of pleasure and pain themselves can be "false" through comparison or misidentification.</meta>

# PHILEBUS

<columns>

->**SOCRATES:**<- Distress, then, is the opposite of rejoicing. **PROTARCHUS:** What do you mean by that? **SOCRATES:** Earlier, we said that opinions, by becoming false or true, fill pleasures and pains with their own condition. <note>original: "παθήματι" / "passione". In this context, it refers to the "affection" or "impression" that an opinion leaves on the soul.</note> **PROTARCHUS:** Most true. **SOCRATES:** But now, look at these from another perspective. When pleasures are viewed from a distance or up close, or when they are placed side-by-side with pains, the pleasures appear greater and more intense because of the presence of the painful, and the pains likewise appear the opposite because of the pleasures. **PROTARCHUS:** Such things must necessarily happen for those reasons. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, since both appear larger or smaller than they actually are, if you cut away that part which merely *appears* to be so but is not real, you will not say that what you see is a correct appearance, nor will you dare to say that the portion of pleasure or pain resulting from such an appearance is right or true. **PROTARCHUS:** Certainly not. **SOCRATES:** Next, then, let us see if we might encounter pleasures and pains in living creatures that are even more false than these. **PROTARCHUS:** What kind do you mean, and how? **SOCRATES:** It has been said many times that when the nature of a being is corrupted by mixing or separating, by filling or emptying, or by any growth or decay, then distresses, aches, pains, and everything called by such names occur. **PROTARCHUS:** Yes, that has been said many times. **SOCRATES:** But when a being is restored to its own nature, we have accepted among ourselves that this restoration is pleasure. **PROTARCHUS:** Correct. **SOCRATES:** But what happens when neither of these things is occurring in our body? **PROTARCHUS:** When could that ever happen, Socrates? **SOCRATES:** That question you just asked, Protarchus, is not relevant to the argument. **PROTARCHUS:** Why so? **SOCRATES:** Because it does not stop me from asking my question again. **PROTARCHUS:** Which was? **SOCRATES:** If such a state were to occur, Protarchus—as they say it does—what must necessarily follow for us? **PROTARCHUS:** You mean if the body is not moved in either direction? **SOCRATES:** Exactly. **PROTARCHUS:** It is clear, Socrates, that in such a state, neither pleasure nor pain would ever arise. **SOCRATES:** You have spoken well. But I suppose you think that one of these must always happen to us, as the "wise men" say; for they claim all things are always flowing "upwards and downwards." <note>original: "ἄνω τε καὶ κάτω ῥεῖ" / "sursum deorsumve semper fluunt". This is a reference to the philosophy of Heraclitus, who famously argued that the universe is in a constant state of flux.</note> **PROTARCHUS:** They do say that, and it seems they speak with some weight. **SOCRATES:** How could they be light-minded, being such as they are? But I want to avoid the argument that is bearing down on us; I think I will flee from it, and you should flee with me. **PROTARCHUS:** Tell me how. **SOCRATES:** Let us grant them their view for now. But you, answer me: does a living creature always perceive everything it undergoes? Do we notice ourselves growing, or undergoing any such change? Or is it quite the opposite—that almost all such things escape our notice? **PROTARCHUS:** Completely the opposite. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, we were not correct just now when we said that changes moving "up and down" produce pains and pleasures. **PROTARCHUS:** What then? **SOCRATES:** This would be a better and more unassailable way to put it. **PROTARCHUS:** How? **SOCRATES:** That great changes cause pains and pleasures in us, but moderate or small changes cause neither of them at all. **PROTARCHUS:** That is more correct than the other way, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** If this is so, then the life we mentioned just now returns. **PROTARCHUS:** Which life? **SOCRATES:** The one we said was without distress and without joy. **PROTARCHUS:** Most true. **SOCRATES:** Based on this, let us establish three lives for us: one pleasant, one painful, and one that is neither. How would you speak of them? **PROTARCHUS:** I would say exactly that: there are three lives.

<column-break/>

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, the state of not feeling pain would never be the same as the state of rejoicing. **PROTARCHUS:** How could it be? **SOCRATES:** Whenever you hear someone say that the sweetest of all things is to live one's whole life without pain, what do you think they mean? **PROTARCHUS:** They seem to me to be saying that not feeling pain is a pleasure. **SOCRATES:** Imagine any three things you like—to use fine names, let us call one Gold, another Silver, and a third which is neither. **PROTARCHUS:** It is set. **SOCRATES:** Could the one that is neither ever become one of the others—either Gold or Silver? **PROTARCHUS:** How could it? **SOCRATES:** Therefore, the middle life—called neither pleasant nor painful—would never be correctly thought of or spoken of as pleasant or painful, if one follows correct reasoning. **PROTARCHUS:** No, indeed. **SOCRATES:** And yet, my friend, we perceive people who speak and think this way. **PROTARCHUS:** Very much so. **SOCRATES:** Do they think they are then "rejoicing" when they are not in pain? **PROTARCHUS:** So they say, at least. **SOCRATES:** They believe, then, that they are rejoicing at that time; otherwise, they would not say so. **PROTARCHUS:** It seems likely. **SOCRATES:** But they hold a false opinion about rejoicing, if indeed "not-paining" and "rejoicing" have distinct natures. **PROTARCHUS:** And they certainly are distinct. **SOCRATES:** Should we, then, choose to believe there are three states (as we just did), or only two: pain as an evil for humans, and the escape from pain as being "the good," which is then called "pleasure"? **PROTARCHUS:** Why are we asking ourselves this now, Socrates? I do not understand. **SOCRATES:** Truly, Protarchus, you do not understand who the "enemies" of Philebus are. <note>Philebus is the character in this dialogue who argues that pleasure is the highest good. His "enemies" are the ascetic philosophers who doubt the reality of pleasure.</note> **PROTARCHUS:** Whom do you mean? **SOCRATES:** Those who are said to be very skilled in the study of nature, who deny that pleasures exist at all. **PROTARCHUS:** What then? **SOCRATES:** They call all these things "escapes from pain"—the very things that Philebus's followers now name "pleasures." **PROTARCHUS:** Do you advise that we believe them, Socrates, or how should we proceed?

<margin>

<summary>Socrates and Protarchus discuss the "neutral life" that is neither pleasant nor painful, concluding that many people mistakenly identify the mere absence of pain as true pleasure. Socrates introduces a group of natural philosophers who argue that all pleasures are merely "escapes from pain" and do not truly exist as a positive state.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Protarchus. Having previously discussed how opinions can make pleasures and pains "false," Socrates now introduces a group of "churlish" thinkers who reject pleasure entirely as a deceptive snare. They use this rigorous perspective to examine whether the most intense pleasures are found in a healthy state or a diseased one.</meta>

# PLATO

<columns>

### Column 1

**SOCRATES:** Not at all; rather, let us treat them as if they were certain prophets <note>original: "vatibus"</note> who prophesy ->A<- not by any technical skill, but by a certain churlishness of a nature that is not ignoble. These people have come to hate the very power of pleasure and believe that there is nothing healthy in it; indeed, they call its very enticements a kind of wicked entrapment rather than true pleasure. You may use their insights for our purpose, considering their other points of churlishness as well. After this, I shall present the pleasures that I consider to be true, so that by considering the power of pleasure from both of these arguments, we may finally apply them to our judgment. **PROTARCHUS:** You speak rightly.

<margin>What things ought to be distinguished when considering a form.</margin>

**SOCRATES:** Let us follow these men, then, as if they were our defenders, ->B<- along the track of their harshness. I suspect they would say something like this, beginning from a point far back: if we wished to know the nature of any "form" or kind—for instance, the nature of "hardness"—would we understand it better by looking at the hardest things, or at things that are only slightly hard? You, Protarchus, must answer these churlish men just as you would answer me. **PROTARCHUS:** Certainly; and I tell them that we must look to the greatest magnitudes. **SOCRATES:** Then, if we wish to know what kind of nature the genus of pleasure has, we must not look at minor pleasures or those far removed from the peak, but rather at those which are called the highest and most vehement. **PROTARCHUS:** Anyone would agree with you on that point now. ->C<- **SOCRATES:** Now, are not the most prominent and greatest pleasures, as we have often said, those which exist around the body? **PROTARCHUS:** Why not? **SOCRATES:** And are they found to be more vehement in those who are sick, or in those who are in good health? Let us be careful, I pray, lest we stumble by answering too hastily. **PROTARCHUS:** In what way? **SOCRATES:** For perhaps we might say they are in the healthy. **PROTARCHUS:** That seems likely. **SOCRATES:** But do not those pleasures greatly exceed others where the greatest desires are present? **PROTARCHUS:** That is true. **SOCRATES:** Do not people suffering from fevers and similar diseases thirst more violently, feel colder, and suffer ->D<- all such bodily conditions much more intensely than others? Because of this, they experience a greater lack, and when they fill that lack, they feel the most vehement delight. Or shall we deny that this is true? **PROTARCHUS:** It appears entirely true, as you have said. **SOCRATES:** What then? Would we not seem to be thinking correctly if we asserted that if one wishes to see the greatest pleasures, one must look not to health, but to disease? And do not think I am asking whether the sick experience *more* delights than the healthy; rather, consider that I am asking about where the *magnitude* and *vehemence* of pleasure are most often found. For we said we must scrutinize what its nature consists of, and what those people mean who assert that pleasure does not exist at all. **PROTARCHUS:** I almost follow what you are saying. **SOCRATES:** Perhaps, Protarchus, you will show it no less clearly yourself. Answer me: do you see greater pleasures—I do not say *more* in number, but more vehement and greater in force—in a life of lechery and wantonness, or in a temperate life? Speak, I pray, and pay close attention. **PROTARCHUS:** I perceive what you mean, and I see a very great difference. For the temperate are always held back by the proverb that instructs "nothing in excess," <note>original: "nihil nimis" / "mēden agan"</note> and they obey it. But as for the intemperate and wanton, the heat of pleasure occupies them even to the point of madness, compelling them to cry out with immoderate shouts. **SOCRATES:** Well said. And if this is true, it is clear ->E<- that vehement pleasures and vehement pains consist in a certain depravity of both soul and body, rather than in virtue. **PROTARCHUS:** That is certainly clear. **SOCRATES:** Should we not select some of these many instances and investigate by what reason they ought to be called the "greatest"? **PROTARCHUS:** It is necessary. **SOCRATES:** Observe, then, the pleasures of such ->F<- diseases, and see what nature they have. **PROTARCHUS:** Which ones? **SOCRATES:** The pleasures of the unseemly, which those whom we called "difficult and churlish" utterly abhor. **PROTARCHUS:** Which ones, I say? **SOCRATES:** For instance, the relief of the itch <note>original: "scabiei"</note> which is achieved by scratching, and other such things that require no other medicine. For this condition—by the immortal gods!—shall we call it a pleasure or a pain? **PROTARCHUS:** It seems to be a certain mixed evil, O Socrates. **SOCRATES:** I did not produce this example for the sake of Philebus; but unless these pleasures and those that follow them are ->G<- inspected, Protarchus, we can hardly ever judge the question we are now seeking. **PROTARCHUS:** Then we must proceed to the relatives of these. **SOCRATES:** Do you mean those which share in a "mixture"? **PROTARCHUS:** Precisely those. **SOCRATES:** There are mixtures, then, of the body itself <margin>Mixtures of pleasure and pain in the body.</margin> within the body, and of the soul in the soul. And the soul and body sometimes name their mixture of pains "pleasure," and sometimes "pain." **PROTARCHUS:** In what way? **SOCRATES:** As, for example, when someone is in a state of restoration or corruption and suffers opposites at the same time: being cold he often grows warm, and being warm he sometimes grows cold, seeking, I think, to attain the one and cast off the other; and as it is said, "bitter mixed with sweet," combined with the difficulty of rejection, it causes distress after a fierce encounter. **PROTARCHUS:** What you say is very true. **SOCRATES:** Are not some of these mixtures composed ->H<- of an equal part of both pleasure and pain, and others of one part exceeding the other? **PROTARCHUS:** Nothing prevents it. **SOCRATES:** He says, therefore, that among those which contain more pain than delight are those which follow the itch and titillations, when the heat within seethes and swells, and one cannot reach it by scratching or rubbing; but what concerns...

<column-break/>

### Column 2

**SOCRATES:** No; but as if to certain prophets who speak beforehand, prophesying A not by art, but by a certain difficulty of a nature that is not ignoble; they have hated the power of pleasure and have judged nothing in it to be healthy. Thus, even this very quality of hers—her attractiveness—they say is a piece of sorcery and not pleasure. You should use these men in this way, having looked also at their other points of difficulty. After these, I shall speak of those which seem to me to be true pleasures, so that by examining the power of pleasure from both accounts, we may reach our judgment. **PROTARCHUS:** You speak rightly. **SOCRATES:** Let us then follow these men as allies, B along the track of their difficulty. For I think they would say something like this, starting from somewhere further up: if we wished to see the nature of any form whatsoever—such as that of the "hard"—would we understand it better by looking at the hardest things, or by looking at those things that possess only a tiny degree of hardness? You must, O Protarchus, answer these difficult men just as you answer me. **PROTARCHUS:** By all means; and I tell them that one must look toward the greatest magnitudes. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, if we also wished to see the nature of the genus of pleasure, we must not look toward the smallest pleasures, but toward those called the highest and most vehement. **PROTARCHUS:** Everyone would grant you that now. **SOCRATES:** Are not, then, the most available C and greatest pleasures (as we have often said) those concerning the body? **PROTARCHUS:** How could they not be? **SOCRATES:** Are they greater, and do they occur more, in those who are suffering in sickness or in those who are healthy? Let us be careful not to stumble by answering rashly. **PROTARCHUS:** How so? **SOCRATES:** Perhaps we might say they are in the healthy. **PROTARCHUS:** It is likely. **SOCRATES:** But what of those pleasures which exceed others—do they not occur where the greatest desires precede them? **PROTARCHUS:** This is true. **SOCRATES:** Do not those who are feverish, or held by such diseases, suffer more from thirst and cold, and everything they are accustomed to suffer through the body? Do they not feel a greater D lack, and when they are replenished, do they not have greater pleasures? Or shall we say this is not true? **PROTARCHUS:** It certainly appears to be exactly as you said. **SOCRATES:** What then? Would we not appear to be speaking rightly if we said that if someone wished to see the greatest pleasures, they should look not toward health, but toward those going into sickness? And see that you do not think I am asking whether those who are very sick rejoice *more* than the healthy; but realize I am seeking the *magnitude* of pleasure, and where the "vehement" in such cases occurs from time to time. For we say we must examine the nature of pleasure, and what those people mean who say it does not exist at all. **PROTARCHUS:** I am following your argument fairly well. **SOCRATES:** Soon, Protarchus, you will show it no less. For answer: in lechery <note>original: "hybris"</note> do you see greater pleasures—I do not say more—but pleasures made E more fierce by vehemence and intensity, or in a temperate life? Speak now, applying your mind. **PROTARCHUS:** I see what you mean, and I see a great difference. For the proverb always restrains the temperate, every time exhorting "Nothing in excess," <note>original: "Mēden agan"</note> which they obey. But for the foolish or the lecherous, the vehement pleasure that holds them even unto madness makes them cry out. **SOCRATES:** Excellent. And if this is so, it is clear that in the vice of the soul and the body, but not in virtue, the greatest pleasures and the greatest pains occur. **PROTARCHUS:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, taking some of these, we must consider what kind of delight they have, that we call them the greatest. **PROTARCHUS:** It is necessary. **SOCRATES:** Consider now the pleasures of such diseases, and what manner they have. **PROTARCHUS:** Which ones? **SOCRATES:** Those of the needy, which those we called "difficult" hate entirely. **PROTARCHUS:** Which ones? **SOCRATES:** For example, the treatments of the itch <note>original: "psōras"</note> by scratching, and all such things F that require no other medicine. For this affection of ours—by the gods!—what should we say it is: pleasure or pain? **PROTARCHUS:** It seems, Socrates, to be a certain mixed evil. **SOCRATES:** We should not give up the argument for Philebus's sake. But without examining the pleasures of the whole world, Protarchus, and the desires for them that do not turn out correctly, we could hardly ever distinguish the thing we are now seeking. **PROTARCHUS:** Then we must go toward their relatives. **SOCRATES:** You mean those that share in a mixture? **PROTARCHUS:** Exactly. **SOCRATES:** There are mixtures, G some in the body itself, within the bodies themselves; and others of the soul itself within the soul. And we shall find pains of the soul and body mixed with pleasures; sometimes the combination is called pleasure, sometimes pain. **PROTARCHUS:** How so? **SOCRATES:** Whenever, in a state of restoration or destruction, one suffers opposite affections at once: being cold, one is warmed, or being warmed, one is cooled; seeking (I suppose) to have the one and be rid of the other. This "bitter mixed with sweet," as it is called, being present with the difficulty of escape, causes irritation and later a wild internal struggle. **PROTARCHUS:** What has just been said is very true. **SOCRATES:** Are not such mixtures composed either of equal parts of pain and pleasure, or of one exceeding the other? **PROTARCHUS:** How could they not be? **SOCRATES:** Speak then: when the pains are more than the H pleasures—those mentioned just now, called the pleasures of the itch and the titillations—whenever the boiling or the inflammation is within, and one does not reach it by rubbing or movement, then...

<summary>Socrates and Protarchus explore the nature of pleasure by looking at its most extreme forms, concluding that the most intense pleasures are often found in states of disease or lack (like thirst in a fever) and are frequently mixed with pain, such as the relief found in scratching an itch.</summary>

--- Page 119 ---
<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Protarchus in Plato's Philebus. They have been discussing "mixed" pleasures—those where pain and pleasure are intertwined. On the previous page, they focused on bodily sensations. Here, they move toward internal mental states, such as anger and envy, and begin an analysis of "the ridiculous" and the Delphic command to "know thyself."</meta>

# PHILEBUS

->H ij<-

### Column 1

**SOCRATES:** ...when it is being filled from the beginning, then flowing into the fire itself, and changing back again into ashes, they sometimes produce inconceivable pleasures. But at other times, when the internal heat is mixed with external pains, they provide a mixture of pleasures and pains, depending on which way the balance tips. This happens because the mixture is violently dispersed or the scattered elements are confounded, creating pain and pleasure at once. 
**PROTARCHUS:** Most true. 
**SOCRATES:** Therefore, whenever a greater amount of pleasure is mixed with such things, the hidden portion of pain tickles and causes a gentle annoyance, while the much larger portion of pleasure, being poured out, intensifies and sometimes causes one to leap. It produces all sorts of colors, all sorts of postures, and all sorts of breaths, crying out in total amazement and shouts alongside a kind of madness. 
**PROTARCHUS:** Very much so. 
**SOCRATES:** And it makes a man say of himself—and others say of him, too—that in being delighted by these pleasures, he is "dying" <note>This refers to the common ancient metaphor of intense pleasure or orgasm as a "little death."</note> of joy. He pursues these pleasures all the more the more he happens to be intemperate and foolish. He calls these the greatest pleasures and considers the man who lives most fully in them to be the happiest of all. 
**PROTARCHUS:** Socrates, you have perfectly described the opinions held by most people. 
**SOCRATES:** We have spoken, Protarchus, of the pleasures found in common experiences of the body, where internal and external sensations are mixed. But as for those in the soul, where the soul contributes the opposite of what the body feels—pleasure against pain, and pain against pleasure, so that both come into a single mixture—we touched on these before. We said that when the soul is "emptied" of something, it desires to be filled; it rejoices in hope but suffers in its emptiness. We did not emphasize it then, but we say now that when the soul is at odds with the body, in all these countless cases, a single mixture of pain and pleasure occurs. 
**PROTARCHUS:** You seem to be quite right. 
**SOCRATES:** There is still one more type of mixture of pain and pleasure left for us to examine. 
**PROTARCHUS:** Which one do you mean? 
**SOCRATES:** The one we said the soul itself often takes on within itself. 
**PROTARCHUS:** How do we describe this one? 
**SOCRATES:** Anger, fear, longing, lamentation, love, jealousy, envy, and all such things—do you not categorize these as certain "pains" of the soul itself? 
**PROTARCHUS:** I do. 
**SOCRATES:** Shall we not find them to be full of inconceivable pleasures? Or do we need to be reminded of the words of Homer: "Anger, which makes even a wise man grow harsh," and is "much sweeter than dripping honey"? <note>original Greek: "ὅς τ' ἐφέηκε πολύφρονά περ, χαλεπῆναι... ὅς τε πολὺ γλυκίων μέλιτος καταλειβομθύοιο" — quoting the Iliad, 18.108-110.</note> And do we not remember that in our lamentations and longings, there are pleasures mixed within the pains? 
**PROTARCHUS:** No, we do not need reminding; these things happen in exactly that way and no other. 
**SOCRATES:** And do you remember how those watching tragedies often weep even while they are enjoying them? 
**PROTARCHUS:** Of course. 
**SOCRATES:** And regarding the state of our soul in comedies, do you realize that even in those there is a mixture of pain and pleasure? 
**PROTARCHUS:** I do not quite understand that. 
**SOCRATES:** Indeed, Protarchus, it is not at all easy to understand such an affection in that context every time. 
**PROTARCHUS:** It certainly is not, at least to me. 
**SOCRATES:** Let us take it up all the more because it is obscure, so that one might more easily understand the mixture of pain and pleasure in other things. 
**PROTARCHUS:** Please explain. 
**SOCRATES:** Regarding the name "envy," which we just mentioned: would you call it a kind of pain of the soul, or what? 
**PROTARCHUS:** I would call it that. 
**SOCRATES:** Yet, the envious man will clearly be seen to rejoice at the misfortunes of his neighbors. 
**PROTARCHUS:** Very much so. 
**SOCRATES:** Now, ignorance is a misfortune, as is the habit we call "stupidity." 
**PROTARCHUS:** Certainly. 
**SOCRATES:** From this, then, see what the nature of "the ridiculous" is. 
**PROTARCHUS:** Just tell me. 
**SOCRATES:** In short, it is a kind of vice, specifically a habit called by that name. It is a part of vice in general that is the opposite of what the inscription at Delphi says. 
**PROTARCHUS:** You mean "Know thyself," Socrates? <note>original: "Γνῶθι σαυτόν"</note> 
**SOCRATES:** I do. And the opposite of that, in the language of the inscription, would clearly be to not know oneself at all. 
**PROTARCHUS:** Certainly. 
**SOCRATES:** Protarchus, try to divide this into three parts. 
**PROTARCHUS:** In what way? I fear I am not able. 
**SOCRATES:** Are you saying I must make this division now? 
**PROTARCHUS:** I am; I even beg you to do so. 
**SOCRATES:** Must not everyone who is ignorant of themselves suffer from this in one of three ways? 
**PROTARCHUS:** How? 
**SOCRATES:** First, regarding wealth: they think they are richer than they actually are. 
**PROTARCHUS:** Many people are indeed afflicted by that. 
**SOCRATES:** But even more think they are taller and more beautiful, and imagine they excel in all physical qualities beyond the truth of their existence. 
**PROTARCHUS:** Quite so. 
**SOCRATES:** But by far the most, I think, are mistaken regarding the third type—the virtues of the soul—imagining they are better than they are when they are not. 
**PROTARCHUS:** Very much so. 
**SOCRATES:** And of all the virtues, is it not wisdom that the majority of people claim for themselves, being full of contention and a false opinion of their own knowledge? 
**PROTARCHUS:** Of course. 
**SOCRATES:** If someone called all such states "evil," they would be speaking correctly. 
**PROTARCHUS:** Very much so. 
**SOCRATES:** This, then, Protarchus, must be divided once more, if we are to see the childish nature of envy, which is a strange mixture of pleasure and pain. 
**PROTARCHUS:** How do we divide it in two? 
**SOCRATES:** All those who foolishly hold this false opinion of themselves—just as is the case for all men...

<column-break/>

### Column 2

**SOCRATES:** ...it only spreads. Then, bringing those things into the fire, and turned this way and that by a lack of counsel, they often produce inestimable pleasures. At other times, on the contrary, with external troubles mixed with internal pleasures, they show which way the decline occurs, because they violently spread the mixed elements or confound the scattered ones, and at the same time move pains toward pleasures. 
**PROTARCHUS:** You tell the truth. 
**SOCRATES:** Is it not also true that when a fuller pleasure is mixed according to all these things, then the mixed portion of pain tickles and produces a certain light indignation? And again, the more abundant part of pleasure, being infused, provokes and sometimes compels one to leap forward, and 
<margin>Mixtures of pleasure and pain of the soul within the soul.</margin> 
produces multi-colored appearances, all kinds of figures, and all types of spirits with every kind of excitement, and shouts with madness? 
**PROTARCHUS:** Very much so. 
**SOCRATES:** It forces a man, my friend, to shout about himself, or another to shout about him, that overwhelmed by these pleasures he almost dies. And the more intemperate and unwise someone is, the more he pursues such pleasures. He proclaims these to be the highest delights, and he counts as most blessed the one who spends his whole life in these luxuries. 
**PROTARCHUS:** You have gathered all the things that have come into the common opinion of many, O Socrates. 
**SOCRATES:** It has been said, Protarchus, of the pleasures that are mixed internally or externally in the common passions of the body. 
<margin>Pleasures of the soul within the soul.</margin> 
But concerning those which are mixed in the soul, certain contrary things are cast toward the body—namely, pleasure with pain, and pain with pleasure, running together into one mixture. We ran through these earlier: that when one is emptied, he desires fulfillment; and hoping, he rejoices, but being empty, he is distressed. We did not confirm those with testimonies then, but now we say that when the soul is at odds with the body in all these things (the multitude of which is not easily grasped), a single mixture of pain and pleasure emerges. 
**PROTARCHUS:** You seem to speak all too correctly. 
**SOCRATES:** There remains one more meeting of pain and pleasure. 
**PROTARCHUS:** Which one? 
**SOCRATES:** That which we said the soul often receives within itself. 
**PROTARCHUS:** In what way do we assert this? 
**SOCRATES:** Anger, fear, desire, lamentation, love, emulation, envy, and the rest of this kind—do you not set all these down as certain pains of the soul itself? 
**PROTARCHUS:** Indeed. 
**SOCRATES:** Can we not find such pains to be full of certain wonderful pleasures? Or perhaps we should bring back to memory that line: "Which caused even a very wise man to rage with bitterness," and "Much sweeter than honey poured out," and the pleasures mixed in lamentations and the longings of sadness. 
**PROTARCHUS:** Not at all [we don't need reminding], for these things happen in this way and no other. 
**SOCRATES:** Moreover, do you remember those who attend tragic spectacles, how they often mourn while they are delighted? 
**PROTARCHUS:** I remember. 
**SOCRATES:** And in comedies, have you felt the affection of our mind decline toward delight and sorrow at the same time? 
**PROTARCHUS:** I have not sufficiently noticed. 
**SOCRATES:** For it is not easy, O Protarchus, to grasp such an affection everywhere. 
**PROTARCHUS:** Certainly not, as it seems to me. 
**SOCRATES:** Let us therefore take it up all the more as it is more obscure, so that in other things one might more easily perceive the meeting of pleasure and sadness. 
<margin>The name of Envy.</margin> 
**PROTARCHUS:** Tell me. 
**SOCRATES:** The name of Envy, introduced a little while ago—do you think it signifies a certain pain, or not? 
**PROTARCHUS:** I think so. 
**SOCRATES:** Yet the envious person is found to rejoice at the misfortunes of his neighbors. 
**PROTARCHUS:** Vehemently. 
**SOCRATES:** Ignorance is indeed an evil, and as we are now speaking, it is a kind of stupidity. 
<margin>Names for Ignorance.</margin> 
**PROTARCHUS:** Why not? 
**SOCRATES:** From these, see what nature that "ridiculous" thing has. 
**PROTARCHUS:** Just tell me. 
**SOCRATES:** It is, in short, a certain depravity of a habit, called by a specific name; it is a certain kind of universal wickedness, having the exact opposite quality of what the Delphic precepts teach. 
**PROTARCHUS:** You mean this precept, O Socrates: "Know thyself"? 
**SOCRATES:** I do. It would be the opposite to this if it were perhaps commanded: "In no way know yourself." 
**PROTARCHUS:** It would be. 
**SOCRATES:** O Protarchus, try now to distribute that into three parts. 
**PROTARCHUS:** I cannot say how. 
**SOCRATES:** You say, then, that I must divide it now? 
**PROTARCHUS:** And I beseech you indeed, which is more. 
**SOCRATES:** Must not everyone who is ignorant of themselves necessarily suffer this according to three things? 
**PROTARCHUS:** How? 
**SOCRATES:** First, in terms of money: someone sometimes thinks himself wealthier than he is. 
**PROTARCHUS:** Many are indeed so deceived. 
**SOCRATES:** Even more who think themselves greater and more handsome, and whatever pertains to the body, beyond what they truly are. 
**PROTARCHUS:** More indeed. 
**SOCRATES:** But by far the most, as far as the third species is concerned, think they have greater gifts of the mind than they actually have. 
**PROTARCHUS:** And most especially so. 
**SOCRATES:** As for the virtues of the mind, does not the common crowd, claiming wisdom for itself, become full of contentions and a false opinion of that very wisdom? 
**PROTARCHUS:** Why not? 
**SOCRATES:** If anyone, therefore, calls that affliction an "evil," they will call it so all too correctly. 
**PROTARCHUS:** Most certainly. 
**SOCRATES:** This, then, Protarchus, must be divided in two again, if we wish to know the strange mixture of pleasure and modesty <note>The Latin text here uses "modestiae" (modesty/moderation) where the Greek suggests "pain." The translator may be interpreting the restraint of envy.</note> by recognizing ridiculous envy. 
**PROTARCHUS:** How should it be divided in two? 
**SOCRATES:** Thus: whoever foolishly presumes this false opinion of themselves, as it happens to them and all other mortals...

<summary>This page explores the concept of "mixed" pleasures and pains within the soul, using examples like the "sweetness" of anger in Homeric poetry and the simultaneous joy and sorrow experienced in tragedy and comedy. Socrates defines "the ridiculous" as a form of self-ignorance, specifically regarding one's wealth, physical appearance, or wisdom, which serves as the foundation for his analysis of envy.</summary>
