# OF PLATO

<margin>The ignorance of the powerful is a most foul thing.</margin>
**A** It is necessary that some of them possess strength and power in what they profess, while others do not. **PROTARCHUS.** That is necessary. **SOCRATES.** Use this logic, then, to distinguish them: those among them who are weak and unable to take revenge when they are mocked are rightly called "ridiculous." But those who are able to take revenge are rightly called formidable, powerful, and hostile. For ignorance in powerful and strong men is a hostile and most foul thing; it is harmful to everyone near them, as are all its likenesses. But when ignorance resides in the weak <note>Original text uses a tilde/flourish over the e</note>, it takes on the nature of the ridiculous. **PROTARCHUS.** You speak correctly. However, the mixture of pleasure and pain in these cases is not yet clear to me. **SOCRATES.** First, consider the power of envy.

<margin>The power of envy.</margin>
**B** **SOCRATES.** Is it not an unjust sorrow and an unjust joy? **PROTARCHUS.** It must be so. **SOCRATES.** To rejoice in the misfortunes of enemies is neither unjust nor envious. **PROTARCHUS.** No, it is not. **SOCRATES.** But to rejoice in the misfortunes of friends, rather than being saddened, is that not unjust? **PROTARCHUS.** It is. **SOCRATES.** We have said that ignorance is an evil for everyone. **PROTARCHUS.** Correct. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, when our friends imagine they possess wisdom, or beauty, or the other three types we mentioned earlier, do we not admit that this state of mind—when it is harmless to others—is ridiculous in our friends? **PROTARCHUS.** We certainly admit it. **SOCRATES.** And do we not agree that this is an evil, since it is a form of ignorance? **PROTARCHUS.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** Do we feel pleasure or pain when we laugh at this? **PROTARCHUS.** Clearly, we feel pleasure. **SOCRATES.** But did we not say that pleasure felt at the misfortunes of friends proceeds from envy? **PROTARCHUS.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, our reasoning concludes that when we smile at the ridiculous aspects of our friends, we mix pleasure with pain, for we are adding joy to our envy. Indeed, it was established long ago that envy is a certain sorrow of the soul, while laughter is a pleasure, and it is clear that both occur at the same time in these moments.

**C** **PROTARCHUS.** You speak the truth. **SOCRATES.** This reasoning tells us that not only in mournings and tragedies, nor only in plays, but in the entire tragedy and comedy of life, pains are mixed with pleasures—and in a thousand other things as well. **PROTARCHUS.** It is impossible not to concede this to you, Socrates, even if one were strongly inclined to take the opposite side. **SOCRATES.** We proposed anger, longing, mourning, fear, love, emulation, envy, and the like, in which we said we would find those things we have often repeated: that they are mixed. Is that not so? **PROTARCHUS.** It is. **SOCRATES.** Do we see that regarding mourning, anger, and envy, everything has now been settled for us? **PROTARCHUS.** How could we not see it? **SOCRATES.** Many things, then, still remain. **PROTARCHUS.** Yes, quite many.

**D** **SOCRATES.** For what reason do you think I have shown you this mixed emotion in comedies? Was it not for the sake of proof? Because in cases of love, fear, and the like, the mixture itself can be more easily demonstrated. Since you understand these things from your own experience, let me go, and do not force me to descend into each of those cases one by one in order, lengthening the dispute. Simply accept this: the soul without the body, the body without the soul, and the union of both together in all disturbances of the mind, possess a confluence of pleasure and pain. Tell me now, will you let me go, or will you keep me until midnight? I think that if I say just a few more things, you will release me; for I promise to speak to you about all these things tomorrow. At present, I wish to proceed toward the judgment that Philebus <note>Philebus is the character who initially argued that pleasure is the "highest good," a claim Socrates is currently dismantling.</note> established.

**E** **PROTARCHUS.** You speak excellently, Socrates; therefore, relate what remains in whatever way pleases you. **SOCRATES.** By nature, then, after discussing mixed pleasures, we must by necessity come in turn to the pure and unmixed ones. **PROTARCHUS.** Very right.

<margin>On pure pleasures.</margin>
**F** **SOCRATES.** I will try, in my turn, to describe them. For I do not at all agree with those who say that all pleasures are merely the cessation of pains. But, as I said, I use them as witnesses to show that many things seem to be pleasures when they are not, and that other pleasures appear great and numerous but are actually mixed with sorrow and are merely reliefs from great pains, relating to defects of both body and soul.

<margin>Which are true pleasures.</margin>
**G** **PROTARCHUS.** Which pleasures then, Socrates, should one rightly consider to be true? **SOCRATES.** Those relating to beautiful colors and shapes, and most smells and sounds; furthermore, those things in which the lack is neither felt nor painful, but the fulfillment is both perceptible and sweet, and free from sorrow. **PROTARCHUS.** In what way, Socrates, do we say these things? **SOCRATES.** What I am saying is not immediately obvious, yet I must try to explain. For I am not trying to speak of the "beauty of shapes" as most people might understand it—such as the beauty of animals or certain paintings.

**H** Rather, I mean (as the argument says) something straight and circular, and from these, the things made with lathes, both flat and solid, and those constructed with rules and squares—if you follow me. For I say these are not beautiful in relation to something else, like other things, but are always beautiful by their very nature, possessing their own pleasures that are in no way similar to the delights of mere stimulation. In the same way, I say that colors are beautiful and pleasant. Do we understand this, or what? **PROTARCHUS.** I am trying, Socrates; but you too must strive to explain it even more clearly. **SOCRATES.** I say further

<column-break/>

**A** and the most necessary consequence of this is that among private citizens, some possess power and ability in their skills, while others possess the opposite. **PROTARCHUS.** Necessarily. **SOCRATES.** Distinguish them in this way: those among them who are such that they are weak and unable to take revenge when laughed at, you would speak truly if you called them "ridiculous." But those who are able to take revenge must be called fearsome and hateful. For this is the most correct description given by true reason: ignorance in the strong is hostile and shameful—for it is harmful both to the person themselves and to those near them—while the weak form of ignorance has been allotted the nature of the "ridiculous." **PROTARCHUS.** You speak most correctly. But the mixture of pleasure and pain in these things is not yet visible to me. **SOCRATES.** First, then, grasp the power of envy. **PROTARCHUS.** Only speak it. **SOCRATES.** Is there not a certain unjust pain and pleasure? **PROTARCHUS.** That is certainly necessary. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, is it not the case that rejoicing at the evils of enemies is neither unjust nor envious? **PROTARCHUS.** How could it be? **SOCRATES.** But when we see the evils of friends, is it not unjust to fail to be pained, and instead to rejoice? **PROTARCHUS.** How could it not be? **SOCRATES.** And did we not say that ignorance is an evil to all? **PROTARCHUS.** Correct. **SOCRATES.** What then? When we see the false conceit of wisdom, or the false conceit of beauty, and the other things we just went through—saying they occur in three forms—do we not say that these states of our friends are ridiculous when they are weak, and hateful when they are strong? As I said just now, is it not ridiculous when someone has this habit in a way that is harmless to others?

**B** **PROTARCHUS.** Very much so. **SOCRATES.** And do we not agree that it is an evil, being ignorance? **PROTARCHUS.** Strongly so. **SOCRATES.** Do we rejoice or feel pain when we laugh at it? **PROTARCHUS.** Clearly, we rejoice. **SOCRATES.** And did we not say that it is envy that produces this joy in the evils of friends? **PROTARCHUS.** Necessarily. **SOCRATES.** Our argument then says that when we laugh at what is ridiculous in our friends, we are mixing pleasure with envy, mixing joy with pain. For envy was agreed long ago to be a pain of our soul, while laughing is a pleasure; and these two things happen together at those times. **PROTARCHUS.** True.

**C** **SOCRATES.** Remember also that our argument showed how in mournings and tragedies—not only in plays, but in the entire tragedy and comedy of life—pains are mixed together with pleasures, and in countless other instances as well. **PROTARCHUS.** It is impossible not to agree with these things, Socrates, even if someone were to be very contentious in the opposite direction. **SOCRATES.** We mentioned anger, longing, mourning, fear, love, zeal, and envy; were we lying when we said we would find the things we have now often mentioned mixed within them? Or what? **PROTARCHUS.** Yes, they are mixed.

**D** **SOCRATES.** Do we understand, then, that regarding mourning and envy and anger, we have now completed all the points we set out? **PROTARCHUS.** How could we not understand? **SOCRATES.** Therefore, many things still remain. **PROTARCHUS.** Very many indeed.

**E** **SOCRATES.** Now, why do you suppose I chose to show you the mixture in comedy? Was it not for the sake of conviction? Because in fears and loves and the others, it is easy for anyone to see the same mixture. Having grasped this for yourself, you can release me from having to go through those other things and lengthen the discussion. Simply accept this: the body without the soul, the soul without the body, and both together in their shared experiences are full of pleasures mixed with pains. Now tell me, do you release me, or will you make me stay until midnight? By saying a few more things, I think I will obtain my release from you. For I am willing to give you an account of all these things tomorrow, but for now, I wish to set out toward what remains: the judgment that Philebus enjoined. **PROTARCHUS.** You have spoken well, Socrates; go through the remaining things in whatever way is dear to you. **SOCRATES.** Naturally, then, having dealt with mixed pleasures, we should move in turn to unmixed <term>unmixed: also called 'pure' pleasures, these are not dependent on the relief of a prior pain</term> pleasures.

**F** **PROTARCHUS.** You speak most excellently. **SOCRATES.** I shall try, by shifting the topic, to indicate them to you. For I am not at all persuaded by those who claim that all pleasures are merely the cessation of pains. Instead, as I said, I use them as witnesses to the fact that some things seem to be pleasures but are not at all; others appear great and numerous but are actually entangled with pains and are merely reliefs from the greatest agonies, concerning the distresses of both body and soul.

**G** **PROTARCHUS.** But what pleasures, Socrates, would one rightly suppose to be true? **SOCRATES.** Those concerning what are called beautiful colors and shapes, and most smells, and those of sounds; and all those things where the lack is imperceptible and painless, while the fulfillments are perceptible, pleasant, and pure of pains. **PROTARCHUS.** How exactly, Socrates, are we saying this? **SOCRATES.** What I am saying is not immediately clear, but I must try to make it so. I am trying now to speak of the beauty of shapes—not what the many might suppose, such as of living creatures or certain paintings;

**H** but (as the argument says) I mean the straight and the round, and from these, the things made by lathes, both flat and solid, and those made with rulers and squares—if you understand me. For I say these are not beautiful relative to something else, as other things are, but are always beautiful according to their own nature, and possess certain inherent pleasures that are not at all like the pleasures of stimulation. And colors, having the same characteristic, are beautiful and have their own pleasures. <summary>Socrates explains how complex emotions like envy are mixtures of pleasure and pain, using the "comedy of life" as an example. He then shifts the dialogue toward "pure" pleasures, which he defines as the aesthetic appreciation of geometric forms, colors, and sounds that are beautiful in themselves.</summary>

# PHILEBUS

...and those sounds which are clear and sweet, and which form a single, purely harmonious melody, are not beautiful for any other purpose, but are beautiful in their own nature and offer an innate pleasure. **PROTARCHUS.** This is also true. **SOCRATES.** Furthermore, the class of pleasures involving <margin>The class of pleasures from smells is more common, but less divine.</margin> smells is of a less divine nature. However, because they do not necessarily involve a mixture of pain, and wherever they happen to occur, I consider them to be of the same nature as the previous ones. Thus, we have gathered two species of pleasures, if you follow me. **PROTARCHUS.** I follow. **SOCRATES.** Now let us <margin>The twofold pleasures of the sciences.</margin> add the pleasures of the disciplines <note>In this context, "disciplines" refers to branches of knowledge or sciences, such as mathematics or logic.</note>; if it seems to us that learning involves no hunger <note>Socrates uses "hunger" as a metaphor for a painful lack or craving.</note> in its beginning, and that no pains are introduced at the start due to a craving for knowledge. **PROTARCHUS.** So it seems to me. **SOCRATES.** But what if someone, having been filled with knowledge, later loses it through forgetfulness? Do you not see some sadness following that? **PROTARCHUS.** Not by the nature of the thing itself, but through a certain reflection on the experience, when someone is saddened by the loss because of a specific need. **SOCRATES.** Yet, my dear friend, we are currently discussing the natural experiences themselves, not the calculations of opinion. **PROTARCHUS.** Then what you say is true: forgetting a piece of knowledge often occurs without sadness. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, we must admit that the pleasures of learning are free from pain, and belong not to the many, but to a very few men. **PROTARCHUS.** We must certainly admit that. **SOCRATES.** Now that we have separated the pure pleasures from those that might correctly be called impure, we must attribute immoderation to the intense pleasures, and moderation to the gentler ones. Those which admit of being "more" or "less," or "great" or "small," or occurring "rarely" or "frequently," we should assign to the class of the "infinite," which runs through both the soul and the body. But those that do not admit such variations should be assigned to the class of the "measured." **PROTARCHUS.** You speak most rightly, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** Beyond this, we must determine something else regarding them. **PROTARCHUS.** What is that? **SOCRATES.** Whether we should say that "purity" and "sincerity" contribute more to truth, or rather that which is "intense," "much," "great," and "sufficient"? **PROTARCHUS.** What are you aiming at with these questions, Socrates? **SOCRATES.** I wish to omit nothing in this examination of pleasure and knowledge. If there is a pure part and an impure part of each, then when both are brought to judgment in their pure state, they will provide a clear and easy verdict for me, for you, and for all these others. **PROTARCHUS.** Very clever. **SOCRATES.** Come then, let us think about the pure classes in this way, bringing one of them forward first for examination. **PROTARCHUS.** Which one shall we choose? **SOCRATES.** Let us consider the class of "white," if you will. **PROTARCHUS.** By all means. **SOCRATES.** How should we define the purity of white? Is it that which is greatest in size and quantity? Or is it that which is most sincere, in that no other color is mixed within it? **PROTARCHUS.** Clearly, it is that which is most sincere. **SOCRATES.** Right. Shall we not affirm, Protarchus, that this is the truest and most beautiful of all whites, rather than that which is greatest in quantity? **PROTARCHUS.** Most correctly. **SOCRATES.** If, therefore, we say that a small amount of pure white is whiter, more beautiful, and "truer" than a large amount of mixed white, we shall be entirely correct. **PROTARCHUS.** Entirely so. **SOCRATES.** What then? Shall we need many such examples to judge pleasure? Or is it sufficient to see from this that any pleasure, no matter how small or slight, is sweeter, truer, and more beautiful than a large one, provided it is free from pain? **PROTARCHUS.** That is quite certain, and the example is sufficient. **SOCRATES.** And what of this? Have we not heard <margin>Pleasure is always a "becoming," but never a "being."</margin> it said of pleasure that it is always a "becoming" <note>original: *generatio* / *genesis*</note>, and that "being" <note>original: *essentia* / *ousia*</note> never exists for it at all? For certain elegant men attempt to teach us this doctrine, and we should be grateful to them. **PROTARCHUS.** What do you mean? **SOCRATES.** I will explain it to you by questioning, my friend Protarchus. **PROTARCHUS.** Speak, and ask away. **SOCRATES.** There are two things: one is "something in itself," and the other is "always desiring something else." **PROTARCHUS.** How do you mean? **SOCRATES.** One is by its nature most venerable, while the other is deficient. **PROTARCHUS.** Express this more clearly. **SOCRATES.** We have often seen beautiful and good youths, as well as brave men who are their lovers. **PROTARCHUS.** We have. **SOCRATES.** In the same way that these two exist, seek two other things through everything we say: the one exists for the sake of another, and the third is the goal. **PROTARCHUS.** Tell me even more clearly, Socrates, what you mean. **SOCRATES.** It is nothing complicated, Protarchus; we are just playing with words. I mean that among the things that exist, one is always "for the sake of something," while the other is "that for the sake of which" the thing is made. **PROTARCHUS.** I have barely grasped it after so much repetition. **SOCRATES.** Perhaps as the discussion proceeds, my boy, we will understand it more clearly. **PROTARCHUS.** Why not? **SOCRATES.** Let us take these other two things. **PROTARCHUS.** Which ones? **SOCRATES.** One is the "becoming" of all things, and the other is "being." **PROTARCHUS.** I accept these two from you: being and becoming. **SOCRATES.** Correct. Now, which of these is for the sake of the other? Shall we say becoming is for the sake of being, or being for the sake of becoming? **PROTARCHUS.** Are you asking whether that which is called "being" is for the sake of "becoming"? **SOCRATES.** It seems I am. **PROTARCHUS.** By the gods, what are you asking me? **SOCRATES.** I am asking something like this, Protarchus: do you say that ship-building exists for the sake of the ship, or the ship for the sake of ship-building?

<summary>Socrates distinguishes between "pure" pleasures (like knowledge and simple beauty) and "mixed" pleasures. He introduces the metaphysical argument that pleasure is a process of "becoming" (genesis) rather than a final "being" (ousia), using the analogy of ship-building to explain teleology.</summary>

<meta>On the previous page, Socrates and Protarchus were discussing "pure" pleasures—those belonging to beauty, sounds, and the sciences—which do not require a preceding pain or lack. They are now moving into a deeper metaphysical argument about whether pleasure is an "end" or merely a "process" toward an end.</meta>

# OF PLATO

**SOCRATES.** Or on the contrary, is the building of a ship for the sake of the ship? And of all such things, I say the same, O Protarchus. **PROTARCHUS.** Why do you not, O Socrates, answer this for yourself? **SOCRATES.** Nothing prevents it. However, you should speak along with me. **PROTARCHUS.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** I say that for the sake of "becoming" <note>original: "generationis" (genesis). In Platonic philosophy, this refers to the process of coming-into-being, as opposed to "essence" or "being," which is the stable result.</note>, medicines and all tools and all matter are applied to all things; but each specific process of "becoming" happens for the sake of a specific "essence" <note>original: "essentia" (ousia). This refers to the true, stable reality or the finished "being" of a thing.</note>, and universal "becoming" happens for the sake of universal "essence." **PROTARCHUS.** Quite clearly indeed. **SOCRATES.** <margin>That pleasure is not the good.</margin> Therefore, if pleasure is a form of "becoming," must it not necessarily happen for the sake of some "essence"? **PROTARCHUS.** Why not? **SOCRATES.** <margin>That for which a thing happens is the good.</margin> Now, that for whose sake something else is always being made is placed in the rank of the "good"; but that which is made for the sake of another must be placed in a different rank, O best of men. **PROTARCHUS.** That is entirely necessary. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, if pleasure is a "becoming," we shall rightly refer it to a rank other than that of the "good." **PROTARCHUS.** Quite rightly. **SOCRATES.** Then, as I said at the beginning of this discussion, should we not be grateful to the person who pointed out that regarding pleasure, there is only "becoming," and that no "essence" of it exists at all? For it is clear that those who claim pleasure is the good are mocked by this argument. **PROTARCHUS.** Greatly so. **SOCRATES.** Indeed, this same argument will mock those who are too devoted to processes of "becoming." **PROTARCHUS.** In what way, and of whom do you speak? **SOCRATES.** Of those who, while they quench their hunger and thirst, or anything else that "becoming" cures and settles, take delight in the "becoming" itself, as if it were pleasure. They even say they would not choose to live if they did not thirst and hunger, and suffer the other things that follow such states. **PROTARCHUS.** They certainly seem to be that way. **SOCRATES.** However, we all agree that the opposite of "becoming" is "being destroyed." **PROTARCHUS.** Necessarily. **SOCRATES.** Thus, whoever chooses these things chooses "destruction" and "becoming," rather than that third life, which we proposed as being void of both joy and sadness, but possessing the purest possible degree of intelligence. **PROTARCHUS.** It would be far from reason, Socrates, for anyone to assert that pleasure is our "good." **SOCRATES.** Far indeed, since we can also show this by another reasoning. **PROTARCHUS.** Which one? **SOCRATES.** Why would it not be absurd if nothing were good or beautiful in bodies or in anything else except the soul, and even in the soul, to call only pleasure the "good"? While courage, temperance, intelligence, and all the other goods the soul has obtained were not called good? And besides, to be forced to say that a man who feels no joy but feels pain is "evil" while he suffers, even if he is the best of all men; and on the other hand, to say that he who is charmed by pleasures is more excellent in virtue the more he rejoices? **PROTARCHUS.** All these things, Socrates, are as absurd as can be said. **SOCRATES.** Let us not, however, spend our entire discussion on pleasure, lest we seem to neglect Mind and Science. <margin>Purity of the sciences.</margin> Come now, let us shake out any "shabbiness" <note>The text uses "sordidum" (dirty/shabby) to refer to knowledge that is imprecise or purely practical rather than theoretical and pure.</note> that might be attached to these, until we penetrate their purest nature and, by inspecting it, we can use the truest parts of both these sciences and pleasure for our judgment. **PROTARCHUS.** Skillfully put. **SOCRATES.** Does not one kind of science present itself to us concerning learning, and another concerning education or nutrition? **PROTARCHUS.** It is so. **SOCRATES.** In the manual arts, first let us see if one part of their knowledge is more [precise] and another less, and if we ought to consider one part the purest and the other most impure. **PROTARCHUS.** We surely should. **SOCRATES.** <margin>The most powerful in the arts.</margin> We must therefore distinguish the leading parts from each of them. **PROTARCHUS.** Which ones, and in what way? **SOCRATES.** For example, if someone were to separate from all arts the skill of counting, measuring, and weighing, what remained in each would be a paltry thing. **PROTARCHUS.** Paltry indeed. **SOCRATES.** What would be left would be to follow through by a kind of imagination, sensory experience, and practice, using the powers of "guesswork," which most people call "arts"—having gained their strength through care and labor. <margin>Music is common and without measure.</margin> **PROTARCHUS.** What you say is quite necessary. **SOCRATES.** Is not music full of these? First, it tunes harmony not by measure, but rather by the "guesswork" of practice; then, all its ability to strike notes seeks the measure of each string by the guesswork of its movement. Thus, it has a great deal of obscurity mixed in, and very little stability. **PROTARCHUS.** Most true. **SOCRATES.** <margin>The weakness of medicine.</margin> Furthermore, we shall find that medicine, agriculture, <margin>The nobility of architecture.</margin> piloting, and military strategy are established in a similar way. **PROTARCHUS.** Very much so. **SOCRATES.** But architecture <note>original: "Architecturam." In this context, it refers to carpentry or construction, which Plato views as more precise than music because it uses physical tools for measurement.</note>, I believe, uses many measures and instruments which, being frequently employed, make it both very clear and more scientific than the other crafts. **PROTARCHUS.** In what way? **SOCRATES.** In the construction of ships and houses, and in many other things related to the working of wood, it uses the straightedge and the lathe, the compass, the chalk line, the plumb line, and an instrument suited for leveling wood. **PROTARCHUS.** You speak very rightly, O Socrates. <margin>Arts in a double order.</margin> **SOCRATES.** Let us therefore place the so-called arts in two orders: those that follow music in their works, participating in less precision; and those that follow architecture, participating in somewhat more. **PROTARCHUS.** Let us so place them. **SOCRATES.** And the most precise of all these are those which we called "first" a moment ago. **PROTARCHUS.** You seem to mean the skill of counting and those you joined with it above. **SOCRATES.** Precisely. But, O Protarchus, must we not say that these again are twofold, or should we say otherwise? **PROTARCHUS.** Which do you mean? **SOCRATES.** <margin>Arithmetic is twofold.</margin> Arithmetic, first: should we not say there is one of the common people, and another of the philosophers? **PROTARCHUS.** By what reasoning could anyone divide arithmetic to make it one and then another?

<column-break/>

**SOCRATES.** Does [the shipwright's art] or shipbuilding as a whole, and all such things—I say these very things, O Protarchus. **PROTARCHUS.** Why then do you not answer these things yourself, Socrates? **SOCRATES.** There is no reason why not. But you, however, share in the argument. **PROTARCHUS.** By all means. **SOCRATES.** I say then, for the sake of "becoming," medicines and all tools and all matter are set before all things; and each "becoming" happens for the sake of some other particular "essence," each from its own source; and universal "becoming" happens for the sake of universal "essence." **PROTARCHUS.** Most clearly indeed. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, if pleasure is "becoming," it must necessarily happen for the sake of some "essence." **PROTARCHUS.** How could it be otherwise? **SOCRATES.** Moreover, that for the sake of which that which is "becoming" always happens, is in the rank of the "good"; but that which happens for the sake of something else must be placed, O best of men, in another rank. **PROTARCHUS.** Most necessary. **SOCRATES.** Then if pleasure is "becoming," shall we be placing it correctly by putting it in a rank other than that of the "good"? **PROTARCHUS.** Most correctly indeed. **SOCRATES.** Therefore (as I said at the beginning of this argument), we must be grateful to the person who revealed regarding pleasure that it is "becoming," but that no "essence" of it exists at all. For it is clear that this person laughs at those who claim pleasure is the good. **PROTARCHUS.** Very much so. **SOCRATES.** And indeed, he will also laugh from time to time at those who find fulfillment in processes of "becoming." **PROTARCHUS.** How so, and of whom do you speak? **SOCRATES.** Of all those who, when they cure hunger or thirst or any of those things which "becoming" cures, are glad because of the "becoming," since it is pleasure. And they say they would not accept living without thirsting and hungering, and without suffering the other things that one might call the passions that follow such states. **PROTARCHUS.** They certainly seem to be so. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, we would all say that "being destroyed" is the opposite of "becoming." **PROTARCHUS.** Necessary. **SOCRATES.** So, one who chooses this would be choosing "destruction" and "becoming," but not that "third life," the one in which there is neither rejoicing nor grieving, but thinking as purely as possible. **PROTARCHUS.** Much absurdity, it seems, O Socrates, results if someone proposes pleasure to us as the "good." **SOCRATES.** Much indeed, since we may also speak of it in this way. **PROTARCHUS.** In what way? **SOCRATES.** How is it not absurd that there is nothing good or beautiful, neither in bodies nor in many other things, except in the soul, and there, only pleasure? And that courage, or temperance, or mind, or any of the other things that the soul has received as "goods," are nothing of the sort? And in addition to these, that a man who does not rejoice, but feels pain, is forced to say he is "evil" then when he suffers, even if he were the best of all; and that the one who rejoices, on the other hand, the more he rejoices at the time he rejoices, the more he differs in respect to virtue? **PROTARCHUS.** All these things, Socrates, are as absurd as possible. **SOCRATES.** Let us not, then, attempt to make a total examination of pleasure, while appearing to be very sparing in our examination of mind and science. But like noble men, if there is anything "rotten" in them, let us strike it all around, until we see what is by nature the purest of them, and then use the truest parts of these and of pleasure for our judgment. **PROTARCHUS.** Correct. **SOCRATES.** I suppose then, that one part of the science concerning learning is "productive" <note>original: "demiurgikon" (craft-like/creative).</note>, and the other is concerned with education or nourishment? Or how is it? **PROTARCHUS.** Thus it is. **SOCRATES.** In the manual arts, let us first consider whether one part of them is more closely related to science, and the other less. And we must consider some as most pure, and others as most impure. **PROTARCHUS.** One must indeed. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, should we take the leading arts and distinguish each separately? **PROTARCHUS.** Which ones and how? **SOCRATES.** For instance, if one were to separate arithmetic from all arts, and measuring, and weighing, so to speak, what is left of each would be "paltry." **PROTARCHUS.** Paltry indeed. **SOCRATES.** What would remain after that would be "guesswork," and the training of the senses by experience and a certain routine, using the powers of "conjecture," which many call "arts," having perfected their strength by practice and toil. **PROTARCHUS.** You say what is most necessary. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, music is full of this, first in fitting harmony together not by measure but by the "conjecture" of practice; and all of flute-playing, seeking the measure of each string as it is moved by "conjecture." So that it has much "unclear" mixed in, and little that is "stable." **PROTARCHUS.** Most true. **SOCRATES.** And indeed, we shall find medicine, agriculture, piloting, and military strategy being in the same condition. **PROTARCHUS.** Quite so. **SOCRATES.** But the art of building, I think, uses the most measures and instruments, which provide it with great accuracy, making it more "technical" <note>original: "technikoteran" (more skilled/artistic/scientific).</note> than many sciences. **PROTARCHUS.** In what way? **SOCRATES.** Both in shipbuilding and house-building, and in many other branches of wood-working. For it uses, I believe, the ruler, the lathe, the compass, the chalk line, and a certain elegant leveling-tool. **PROTARCHUS.** You speak very correctly indeed, O Socrates. **SOCRATES.** Let us then divide the so-called arts into two: those following music, participating in less accuracy in their works, and those following building, which have more. **PROTARCHUS.** Let it be so. **SOCRATES.** And of these, the most accurate are the arts we mentioned first. **PROTARCHUS.** You seem to me to be speaking of arithmetic and the arts you joined with it just now. **SOCRATES.** Certainly. But O Protarchus, must we not say that these are again twofold? **PROTARCHUS.** How? What do you mean? **SOCRATES.** Arithmetic first. Must we not say that one kind belongs to the many (the common people), and another to those who philosophize? **PROTARCHUS.** By what distinction would one propose that there is one arithmetic and then another?

<summary>Socrates argues that pleasure is a process of "becoming" and therefore cannot be the ultimate "good," which must be a stable "essence." He further distinguishes between arts based on precision (like carpentry) and those based on guesswork (like music or medicine).</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Protarchus, Plato, Philebus, pleasure vs. good, becoming vs. being, precision in arts, arithmetic, architecture, music as guesswork</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Protarchus from the Philebus. On the previous page, they established that pleasure belongs to the realm of "becoming" (generation) rather than "being" (essence), and therefore cannot be the ultimate Good. Now, Socrates turns to the various sciences and arts to determine which among them possesses the highest degree of truth and purity.</meta>

# PHILEBUS

### PAGE 91

**SOCRATES.** There is no small dispute here, O Protarchus. For some count unequal units <note>original: "monadas" (units). In basic math, one might count "two armies," but in philosophical math, every "one" must be identical to every other "one."</note> in their numbers—for instance, two armies, or two oxen, or two of the smallest things, or even two of the very largest. But the others would never follow them unless one posits that among all the countless units, no single one differs at all from any other. **PROTARCHUS.** You speak very well; there is indeed a great difference between those who deal with numbers in this way, so it is reasonable to say there are two kinds of arithmetic. **SOCRATES.** And what of calculation and measurement as used in building or trade, compared to the geometry and calculations practiced in philosophy? Should we say each of these is one, or should we posist two? **PROTARCHUS.** Following the previous example, I would cast my vote that each of these is two. **SOCRATES.** Correct. But do you realize why we have brought these examples into our midst? **PROTARCHUS.** Perhaps, but I would like you to explain the current question yourself. **SOCRATES.** It seems to me that this argument, no less than when we began it, is seeking an equivalent for the pleasures. It investigates whether one science is purer than another science, just as one pleasure was purer than another. **PROTARCHUS.** It is quite clear that this is the reason he <note>Socrates refers to the "argument" as if it were a person.</note> attempted this. **SOCRATES.** What then? Did he not find in what came before that one art was clearer than another, and one less clear than another? **PROTARCHUS.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** And in these cases, did he not speak of them under a single name, creating the impression that they were one, but now asks again as if they were two—whether the clarity and purity of these things belongs more to the practitioners of philosophy or to those who are not philosophers? **PROTARCHUS.** It seems to me he is asking exactly that. **SOCRATES.** What answer, then, O Protarchus, shall we give him? **PROTARCHUS.** O Socrates, we have reached a wonderful difference in the degree of clarity among the sciences. **SOCRATES.** Then we shall answer more easily. **PROTARCHUS.** Of course. **SOCRATES.** And let it be said that these arts differ greatly from others; but among these themselves, the arts that occupy those who are truly philosophers are infinitely superior in precision and truth regarding measures and numbers. **PROTARCHUS.** Let it be as you say; believing you, we shall boldly answer those who are clever at dragging out an argument. **PROTARCHUS.** Answer what? **SOCRATES.** That there are two arithmetics and two arts of measuring, and many other such arts following them that have this double nature, sharing a single name. **PROTARCHUS.** Let us give this answer, O Socrates, with good luck, to those you call "clever." **SOCRATES.** Do we say, then, that these are the most precise sciences? **PROTARCHUS.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** But, Protarchus, the power of dialectic <note>original: "dialegesthai" (the power of discourse or logical debate). For Plato, this is the highest form of reasoning.</note> would disown us if we judged any other science to be superior to it. **PROTARCHUS.** Which one must we call by that name now? **SOCRATES.** Clearly the one that knows all that has just been mentioned. For I think that everyone who possesses even a small amount of intellect believes that the knowledge which deals with "being," with what is truly real, and with what is by nature always the same, is by far the truest knowledge. But you, Protarchus—how would you decide? **PROTARCHUS.** I used to hear Gorgias <note>Gorgias of Leontini was a famous Sophist and teacher of rhetoric who claimed that the art of persuasion was the most powerful tool in the world.</note> say many times that the art of persuasion is far superior to all other arts. For it makes all things its slaves, not by force but by their own will, and is by far the best of all arts. Now, I would not want to oppose either you or him. **SOCRATES.** It seems to me you wanted to say "arms" <note>Socrates jokes that Protarchus has dropped his "arms" (his defense of Gorgias) out of modesty or shame.</note>, but you have let them fall. **PROTARCHUS.** Let these things be as you see fit. **SOCRATES.** Am I the cause of your misunderstanding? **PROTARCHUS.** In what way? **SOCRATES.** My friend Protarchus, I was not yet asking which art or science is superior to all others by being the greatest, best, or most useful to us. Rather, I am asking which one looks toward what is clear, precise, and most true, even if it is small and offers little utility. This is what we are seeking now. But look: you will not offend Gorgias if you grant that his art is superior in its use for human needs, while the study I just mentioned is like what I said about the color white: even if it were small, if it were pure, it would excel a great amount of impure white by its very truth. And now, having thought deeply and discussed it sufficiently, without looking at the utility or reputation of the sciences, but rather at whether there is a power in our soul that by nature loves the truth and does everything for its sake—let us say, having searched this out, whether we should say we possess this power, or must we seek something else more sovereign than this? **PROTARCHUS.** I am considering it, and I think it is difficult to concede that any other science or art holds onto the truth more than this one. **SOCRATES.** Did you say what you just said because you realized that most arts, and those who labor at them, first of all use opinions and diligently seek things related to opinions? And even if someone thinks they are investigating nature, you know they spend their whole lives investigating this world—how it was made, how it is acted upon, and how it acts. Is this what we would say? **PROTARCHUS.** It is. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, such a person has not taken up labor concerning the things that *always are*, but rather concerning the things that are *becoming*, will become, and have become. **PROTARCHUS.** Most true. **SOCRATES.** And which of these things can we say has any clarity or truth...

<column-break/>

**SOCRATES.** There is no small discrepancy, O Protarchus. For those others count the unequal units of those things which exist according to number, such as two armies, two oxen, two of the smallest things, or even two of the very largest: but these people would never follow them, unless one posits that no unit of the parts differs from another unit. **PROTARCHUS.** You speak most excellently, while you introduce a great diversity among those who deal with number, so much so that it is fitting to divide them into two. **SOCRATES.** What of the faculty of counting and measuring according to architecture or trade, and also that <margin>Geometry is twofold.</margin> geometry and diligent reasoning according to philosophy—are they one certain art, or rather two? **PROTARCHUS.** Following my previous answer, in my opinion, I would posist that they are two. **SOCRATES.** Rightly so, but do you understand for what reason we have brought these into our midst? **PROTARCHUS.** Perhaps, yet I would wish for you to explain what has now been asked. **SOCRATES.** Our discussion, which for a long time has sought a certain proportion corresponding to the pleasures by an equal conversion of division, seems to me now to have achieved what it sought no less than at the beginning, while it investigates whether there is some science <margin>Arts differ.</margin> purer than another science, just as pleasure is to pleasure. **PROTARCHUS.** It is clear that these things were treated for that sake. **SOCRATES.** What then, was it not found in the previous parts that one art exists within another, and one is clearer, and another more obscure? **PROTARCHUS.** Greatly so. **SOCRATES.** But in these matters, does not reason, producing a certain art as if it were equivocal and hinting at it as if it were one, inquire again as if they were two, whether the clarity and purity of them exists in those who practice philosophy or those who do not? **PROTARCHUS.** And indeed, it seems to me to inquire into that very thing. **SOCRATES.** What sort of answer, O Protarchus, shall we give here? **PROTARCHUS.** O Socrates, we have descended into a marvelous declaration of the difference between the sciences. **SOCRATES.** Is the answer not easy? **PROTARCHUS.** Why not: let us therefore assert that these arts differ from the others by a long interval. Furthermore, that the study of those who are truly philosophers differs from them in a wonderful way in sincerity and truth regarding measures and numbers. **SOCRATES.** Let those things be according to your opinion, then, and we, believing you, may boldly answer the troublesome debaters. **PROTARCHUS.** Answer what? **SOCRATES.** That there are two arithmetics and two arts of measuring, and many other faculties that are companions to these, having a doubling of this kind, and sharing in one name. **PROTARCHUS.** Let us give this answer, with favorable fortune, to those you called troublesome, O Socrates. **SOCRATES.** Do we assert that these sciences are the most sincere and supreme? **PROTARCHUS.** Entirely so. **SOCRATES.** Nevertheless, O Protarchus, the <margin>Logic (Dialectic) is preferred to all arts.</margin> faculty of discourse itself would not suffer us to act if we preferred any other to it. **PROTARCHUS.** What, again, is it proper to call this one? **SOCRATES.** That which knows all the skill just now introduced. For since this is concerned <margin>Gorgias preferred the art of speaking to all arts.</margin> with that which *is*, and *truly is*, and *always is* in the same manner, I think all who have even a small amount of sound mind will immediately concede that this is by far the truest knowledge of all. But you, O Protarchus, what do you think? **PROTARCHUS.** I often heard Gorgias when he said that the faculty of persuading excels all arts: because it is clear that it subjects all things to itself not by force, but by their own will, and is by far the best of all arts. But now I would wish to oppose neither you nor him. **SOCRATES.** You seem to me to have wanted to say "arms," but led by shame, you have omitted them. **PROTARCHUS.** Let these things be as you please. **SOCRATES.** Am I the cause that you have understood less well? **PROTARCHUS.** How? **SOCRATES.** I did not ask you, O friend Protarchus, which art or science <margin>A determination of two arts, one of which seems to excel the others.</margin> excels all others in being the greatest, most powerful, and most useful of all: but which one contemplates the clear, the sincere, and the most true, however small it may be and however little useful: this is surely what we are seeking now. But look: you will not offend Gorgias at all if you grant the praise of utility and excellence to his art; but to that faculty which I myself just described, you grant the excellence of truth: just as I said above concerning white, which though small, if it were pure, would excel much that is impure according to the excess of truth. And now indeed, having applied intense meditation, and having completed a sufficiently suitable discussion, let us not look at either the commendations or the advantages of any of the disciplines: but if there is any soul by nature loving of truth, and for the sake of that performs all things, let us say that we have searched this out with purity of mind and wisdom, considering whether it is seen to be acquired mostly from the science of discourse (dialectic), or rather from some other art more excellent than this. **PROTARCHUS.** I am considering it, and I concede that it would be difficult to find another art or science that claims truth for itself more than this one. **SOCRATES.** Did you say what you are saying now because you were thinking of something like this? That many arts, and whoever labors around them, first use opinions, and investigate those things which consist of opinions; or even if anyone thinks they are investigating nature, they spend their whole life scrutinizing the things concerning the world, how it was made, how it is acted upon, and how it acts. Do we admit these things, or not? **PROTARCHUS.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** Nor does such a person labor concerning those things which...

# PLATO'S PHILEBUS

### PAGE 92

<column-break/>

Regarding things that have happened in the past, or will happen in the future, or are happening now in the same way, shall we say that anything is clear with the most exact truth? **PROTARCHUS.** We cannot. **SOCRATES.** Indeed, in those things which possess no stability at all, in what way could we attain anything stable? **PROTARCHUS.** By no reasoning, I think. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, neither mind [mens] nor any science concerning those things possesses the supreme truth. **PROTARCHUS.** That is consistent. **SOCRATES.** Let us then bid farewell to you and me, and Gorgias and Philebus <note>Gorgias was a famous rhetorician; Philebus is the character who argues that pleasure is the highest good. Socrates is suggesting they set aside personal opinions to focus on the logical path of the argument itself.</note>, and instead bring this forward in our reasoning. **PROTARCHUS.** What is that? **SOCRATES.** That the faculty within us which contains firmness, purity, truth, and sincerity is that which is concerned with things that are always the same and most simple <note>In Platonic thought, "simple" things are not "easy," but rather "undivided" or "pure" essences that do not change.</note>, or that which is in the second place closest to them. All other things must be called secondary and posterior. **PROTARCHUS.** Very true. **SOCRATES.** And those names which are the most beautiful of all, should they not be assigned to the most beautiful things? **PROTARCHUS.** It is only fair. **SOCRATES.** "Mind" and "wisdom" are the most precious names of all. **PROTARCHUS.** They are. **SOCRATES.** These, therefore, are correctly applied to the understandings of that which truly is, perfected and assigned by the most exact reason. **PROTARCHUS.** Entirely so. **SOCRATES.** And the very names I brought into judgment above were none other than these. **PROTARCHUS.** None other. **SOCRATES.** Furthermore, if someone were to say that the mixture of pleasure and wisdom is set before us as if we were craftsmen, so that we might seek from what and in what it is composed, he would guess correctly, I think. **PROTARCHUS.** Most certainly. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, we must next attempt to mix them. **PROTARCHUS.** We must plainly attempt it. **SOCRATES.** Would it not be better to say this first and recall it to memory? **PROTARCHUS.** What? **SOCRATES.** That which we mentioned before: that 
<margin>Proverb.</margin>
famous proverb which says that beautiful things should be repeated twice and even thrice. <note>original: "bis et ter repetenda." This is a common Greek proverb suggesting that important or excellent points are worth hearing many times.</note> **PROTARCHUS.** Why not? **SOCRATES.** Come then, by Jove! For I believe the previous things were stated in this way. **PROTARCHUS.** How? **SOCRATES.** Philebus says that pleasure is the right goal for all animals, and that everyone ought to aim for it, and that this "Good" itself exists for all; moreover, that these two names, "Good" and "Pleasant," apply to the same nature. Socrates, however, says first that this is not the case at all: just as there are two names, "Good" and "Pleasant," so there are two different natures. Furthermore, he says that wisdom participates in the "Good" to a greater degree than pleasure does. Is this not, O Protarchus, what was being said? **PROTARCHUS.** Very much so. **SOCRATES.** And must this not also be confessed now as it was then? **PROTARCHUS.** What thing? **SOCRATES.** That the nature of the Good
<margin>How the nature of the Good differs from others.</margin>
itself differs from other things especially in this way. **PROTARCHUS.** In what way? **SOCRATES.** To whichever living being this is present—always, entirely, and everywhere—that being requires nothing else and possesses perfect sufficiency. Is it so? **PROTARCHUS.** Entirely so. **SOCRATES.** Did we not try by reason itself to separate one from the other, pleasure from wisdom and wisdom from pleasure, so that neither participates in even the smallest part of the other, to see how each would appear in a life? **PROTARCHUS.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** Did either of them then seem to be sufficient? **PROTARCHUS.** To whom could it seem so? **SOCRATES.** But if someone perhaps passed over it then, let him now, taking it up again, affirm it more correctly: when he places memory, science, wisdom, and true opinion within the same idea, let him consider whether anyone, without these, would want himself or another to either be anything or become anything—much less choose pleasure, whether the most abundant or the most intense, without them. For if he is deprived of these, he will neither think he is truly enjoying himself, nor will he know in what condition he is affected, nor will he retain any memory of the feeling over time. You might say the same of wisdom. Would anyone prefer to attain wisdom far from even the slightest pleasure, rather than with some pleasures? Or all pleasures without wisdom rather than with some wisdom? **PROTARCHUS.** No one, O Socrates. There is no need to ask this so often. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, neither of these is perfect, nor to be sought by all, nor entirely "the Good." **PROTARCHUS.** Neither. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, we must grasp either the Good itself clearly, or some form of it, so that, as we said, we may see to whom the second prize should be given. **PROTARCHUS.** You speak very skillfully. **SOCRATES.** Have we not entered upon a certain path toward the Good itself? **PROTARCHUS.** In what way? **SOCRATES.** If someone seeking a certain man first knew the house where he lived, he would surely have a great aid in finding him. **PROTARCHUS.** Why not? **SOCRATES.** So the present and previous reasoning has warned us not to search for the Good itself in the simple life, but in the mixed. **PROTARCHUS.** Entirely. **SOCRATES.** And there is a surer hope that we will find what we seek in that which is beautifully mixed than in that which is not. **PROTARCHUS.** Surer indeed. **SOCRATES.** Let us mix then, O Protarchus, first vowing to the gods—whether Dionysus, or 
<margin>The mixing is dedicated to Dionysus and Vulcan.</margin>
Vulcan, or some other god who has been allotted the office of mixing. <note>Dionysus is the god of wine (pleasure), and Vulcan (Hephaestus) is the god of the forge and craftsmanship (representing the structure of wisdom). Socrates is using the metaphor of mixing wine and water to represent blending pleasure and wisdom.</note> **PROTARCHUS.** It must be done just so. **SOCRATES.** Now, as if we were wine-pourers, certain springs stand by us. One might compare the spring of pleasure to honey; but the spring of wisdom is sober and devoid of wine, like a sharp and very healthy water. Let us strive to blend these liquids as beautifully as possible into one. **PROTARCHUS.** We must strive indeed. **SOCRATES.** Tell me first: if we mix all pleasure with all wisdom, would we have joined them beautifully? **PROTARCHUS.** Perhaps. **SOCRATES.** But it is by no means safe. However, in what way we might mix more securely...

If someone were to speak of the mixing of wisdom and pleasure with one another, as if we were craftsmen from whose materials something must be forged, he would be making a good comparison. PR. Very much so. SOC. Must we not attempt C to mix them after this? PR. Why not? SOC. Would it not be more correct to first remind ourselves of these things? PR. Which things? SOC. Those we mentioned before. The proverb seems to be right: that which is good should be repeated twice and even thrice in the argument. PR. Why not? SOC. Come then, by Zeus. For I think the things said then were spoken somewhat like this. PR. How? SOC. Philebus says that pleasure has been made the right goal for all living things, and all must aim for it; and that this very thing is the Good for all, and the two names, "Good" and "Pleasure," are correctly applied to one and the same nature. Socrates, however, says first that it is not one, but two, just as the names are; that the "Good" and "Pleasant" have different natures from one another. D And that wisdom participates more in the portion of the Good than pleasure does. Is this not what was said then and now, O Protarchus? PR. Very much so. SOC. And would this not also be agreed upon by us both then and now? PR. What? SOC. That the nature of the Good differs from other things in this way especially. PR. In what? SOC. That in whichever living thing it is present, always, through to the end, and in every way, that thing never has need of anything else, but possesses the most perfect sufficiency. Is it not so? PR. It is so. SOC. That was it. SOC. Did either of them E then seem sufficient to us? PR. How could they? SOC. If we passed over anything then, take it up again now and speak more correctly: setting memory, wisdom, science, and true opinion in the same category, consider if anyone would accept having anything or becoming anything without these—not to mention pleasure, whether the greatest or most intense—if he neither truly opined that he was rejoicing, nor knew at all what he was experiencing, nor had any memory of the experience for any length of time. Say these same things about wisdom: if anyone would choose to have wisdom devoid of all pleasure, even the briefest, rather than with some pleasures, or all pleasures without wisdom rather than with some wisdom. PROT. It is not possible, O Socrates. There is no need to ask these things many times. F SOCRATES. Therefore, neither of these would be the perfect, universally desirable, and altogether Good thing. PROT. How could it be? SOCRATES. Therefore, we must grasp the Good either clearly or in some outline, so that, as we said, we might have something to which we give the second prize. PROT. You speak most correctly. SOCRATES. Have we not taken a certain path toward the Good? PRO. Certainly. SOCRATES. Just as if someone seeking a man were to first learn where he lives, he would surely have a great help toward finding the one he seeks. PR. How could he not? SOCRATES. And now a certain argument has indicated to us, as at the beginning, not to seek the Good in the unmixed life, but in the G mixed one. PR. Certainly. SOCRATES. Is there more hope that what we seek will be more apparent in that which is well mixed than in that which is not? PR. Much more. SOCRATES. Let us pray to the gods, O Protarchus, while mixing—whether it be Dionysus, or Hephaestus, or whoever of the gods has received this honor of blending. PR. Entirely so. SOCRATES. And truly, just as if we were wine-pourers, springs stand by us: one of pleasure might be compared to honey, and that of wisdom to a sober and wineless spring, a harsh but healthy water. These we must try to mix as beautifully as possible. PROT. How could we not? SOCRATES. Come then, first: if we mix all pleasure with all wisdom, would we most likely succeed? PROTARCHUS. Perhaps. H SOCRATES. But it is not safe. By what way we might mix them more without danger, I have an opinion...

<summary>Socrates and Protarchus conclude that neither pure pleasure nor pure wisdom is the "Greatest Good" because neither is self-sufficient. They agree to seek the Good in a "mixture" of the two, using the metaphor of mixing honey-like pleasure with sober, watery wisdom.</summary>

# PHILEBUS

### PAGE 93

<margin>A</margin> ...I am confident that I have now made it clear. **PROTARCHUS.** Tell me how. **SOCRATES.** Did it not appear in what we said before that one pleasure differs from another, and one science <note>original: *scientia* (Latin) / *ἐπιστήμη* (Greek). In this context, it refers to any organized body of knowledge or skill.</note> is more exact than another? **PROTARCHUS.** It certainly did. **SOCRATES.** And that one science differs from another in that one looks toward things that come into being and perish, while the other looks toward things that neither come to be nor pass away, but are always the same and unchanging. Looking toward truth itself, we judged this latter science to be truer than the former. **PROTARCHUS.** That is quite right. **SOCRATES.** If, then, we first take the truest portions of each and mix them together, would the mixture of these be sufficient to provide us with the most desirable life? Or do we still need something else, perhaps even things that are not of this "pure" kind? **PROTARCHUS.** It seems to me we should proceed in that way.

<margin>B</margin> **SOCRATES.** Let us imagine a man who is wise and knows what justice itself is, and who possesses the reasoning to understand it, and similarly has knowledge of all other things that exist. **PROTARCHUS.** Let us assume that. **SOCRATES.** Now, will this man be sufficiently endowed with science if he holds the reasoning of the "divine circle" and "divine sphere" themselves, but is entirely ignorant of this human sphere and these human circles of ours, even when he uses scales and circles in architecture and other similar works? **PROTARCHUS.** Our knowledge would be ridiculous, Socrates, if it were concerned only with divine things. **SOCRATES.** What do you say? Must we also bring in and mix together the impure and unstable art of the false scale and the false circle? <note>Socrates is asking if "practical" knowledge—which is technically "impure" because it deals with imperfect physical objects—is necessary for life.</note>

<margin>C</margin> **PROTARCHUS.** This is necessary, if any of us is even going to find the way home! **SOCRATES.** And what about music, which we said a little while ago was full of guesswork and imitation, and therefore lacked purity? **PROTARCHUS.** That also seems necessary to me, if our life is to be a life at all. **SOCRATES.** Do you wish then, like a gatekeeper pushed and crowded by a mob, that I should throw open the doors and let all the sciences flow in and mingle together—the pure with the less pure? <margin>No one is harmed by other sciences if they possess the primary ones.</margin> **PROTARCHUS.** I do not know, Socrates, how any man could be harmed by other sciences if he already possesses the primary ones. **SOCRATES.** Then I shall let them all flow into the "Homeric mixing bowl" <note>original: *misgankeia* (Greek). This refers to a meeting of mountain streams in a valley; Socrates uses it as a metaphor for the confluence of different kinds of knowledge.</note>, a very poetic meeting place. **PROTARCHUS.** Let them flow.

<margin>D</margin> **SOCRATES.** Now we must return to the fountain of pleasures. For when we thought of mixing them, the "true" parts of them did not appear to us first; rather, because of our love for all knowledge, we allowed all sciences to rush in together before we considered pleasures. **PROTARCHUS.** You speak very truly. **SOCRATES.** It is time, then, to consult about the pleasures as well: whether they should all be let in together, or whether we should admit only the primary and true ones first. **PROTARCHUS.** It is much safer to admit the primary and true ones first. **SOCRATES.** Let these be admitted then. But what next? If there are some that are "necessary," should they also be mixed in, just as we did with the sciences?

<margin>E</margin> **PROTARCHUS.** Why not? Certainly the necessary ones. **SOCRATES.** And if, just as it was agreed that knowing all arts throughout life is harmless and useful, we now say the same of pleasures—if indeed it is profitable and harmless for all of us to enjoy all pleasures throughout our lives—then they should all be mixed in. **PROTARCHUS.** How then shall we speak of these very things? And how shall we act? **SOCRATES.** It is not for us, Protarchus, to ask this, but for the pleasures and the sciences themselves, as they inquire about one another.

<margin>F</margin> **PROTARCHUS.** What do you mean? **SOCRATES.** "O friends (whether it is right to call you pleasures, or by some other name), would you choose to live with all wisdom <note>original: *φρόνησις* (phronesis) / *sapientia* (Latin). This refers to practical wisdom or prudence.</note>, or to be apart from wisdom?" I think they would necessarily reply as follows. **PROTARCHUS.** What would they say? **SOCRATES.** That, as was said before, it is neither possible nor profitable for any class of things to be pure and solitary by itself. They would say: "We think it best for all classes to live together with us, especially the knowledge of all things and, specifically, the perfect knowledge of each of our own powers." **PROTARCHUS.** "And you have answered well," we shall say to them. **SOCRATES.** Rightly so. Next, we must ask Mind <note>original: *νοῦς* (nous) / *mens* (Latin).</note> and Wisdom: "Do you have any need for pleasures in your mixture?" To this, Mind and Wisdom would surely answer: "What kind of pleasures?" **PROTARCHUS.** That is likely. **SOCRATES.** And our question to them would be this: "Besides those true pleasures, do you also need the greatest and most intense pleasures to live with you?"

<margin>G</margin> "And how could we, Socrates?" they would perhaps say. "For they provide us with a thousand obstacles, disturbing the souls in which we dwell with their mad delights. They prevent us from even coming into existence, and as for our children—those things we produce—they utterly destroy them through neglect and by causing forgetfulness. But as for the other pleasures, which you called true and pure, consider them almost part of our own family. And besides those, include the pleasures that come with health and temperance, and indeed all those that follow in the train of Virtue as if she were a goddess. But for the pleasures that always follow after folly and other wickedness, it would be quite irrational for anyone to mix them with Mind if he wishes to see the most beautiful and stable mixture and temperament, or to learn what is naturally good in man and in the universe, and to divine what its true Form <note>original: *idea* (Greek). In Platonic philosophy, the "Idea" or "Form" is the perfect, eternal blueprint of a thing.</note> might be." Shall we not say that Mind has answered wisely and like itself in this, speaking on behalf of memory and right opinion? **PROTARCHUS.** Entirely so. **SOCRATES.** And yet this also is necessary, and could never happen otherwise.

<margin>H</margin> <margin>Which pleasures belong to wisdom, and which are foreign to it.</margin>

<summary>Socrates and Protarchus conclude that a good life requires a mixture of both divine and practical knowledge. They also determine, through a personified dialogue, that Wisdom only harmonizes with true and virtuous pleasures, while rejecting intense, "mad" pleasures as disruptive and destructive.</summary>

---

->**SUMMARY OF THE DIALOGUE**<-
> *Socrates, taking an opportunity from a speech Hippias had given regarding beautiful duties, asks him what is "Beauty itself," by which all other things are made beautiful. First, Hippias answers that a beautiful young woman is Beauty itself. When Socrates refutes this, the Sophist <note>A Sophist was a professional teacher in Ancient Greece who traveled to different cities charging fees for instruction in rhetoric and virtue.</note> flees to the idea of gold, asserting that all things are made beautiful by gold and thus gold is Beauty itself. Socrates refutes this as well, along with a third opinion of the same Sophist, who thinks beauty consists of being healthy in body, wealthy and honored, dying old, and being buried by one's children. Having refuted these, Socrates, now tending toward higher things, introduces not what sense-perception offers to opinion, but what reason offers to opinion—not so much to teach what beauty is, but to show what it is not, and to expose the vain and deceptive doctrine of the Sophists in the person of Hippias. From this dispute, let it be observed what is the true and convenient way of acting against the Sophists: one should not labor so much in refuting their trifles as in pointing them out, for once pointed out, they fall and vanish of their own accord.*

And they pass down other such stories about the other wise men of those times. Therefore, you seem to have brought forth an excellent proof that our wise men excel those of former times; and many agree on this: that the wise man must first of all be wise for himself. The definition of this is, essentially, that he
<margin>E</margin>
acquires the most silver. But enough of these things. Tell me this: since you have visited many cities, where did you earn the most? Was it in Lacedaemon <note>The ancient name for the city-state of Sparta.</note>, where you have gone most frequently? **HIPPIAS.** No, by Jove, O Socrates. **SOCRATES.** What do you say? Was it the least? **HIPPIAS.** On the contrary, nothing at all, ever. **SOCRATES.** What you say is a marvelous wonder, O Hippias! Tell me, is your wisdom not able to make those who spend time with you and learn from you better in virtue? **HIPPIAS.** Most certainly it can. **SOCRATES.** Were you able to make the sons of the citizens of Inycus better, but the sons of the Spartans not at all? **HIPPIAS.** Far from it. **SOCRATES.** Or do the Sicilians desire to become better, while the Lacedaemonians neglect it?
**HIPPIAS.** On the contrary, the Lacedaemonians also strive for it. **SOCRATES.** 
<margin>F</margin>
Was it for lack of money that they lacked your company? **HIPPIAS.** Not at all, for they are wealthy enough. **SOCRATES.** Since, therefore, they strove for wisdom and had the resources, and you were able to bring them great benefits, why did you not return from there most wealthy? Do the Lacedaemonians themselves perhaps educate their sons better than you do? Shall we say that, and do you agree? **HIPPIAS.** In no way. **SOCRATES.** Were you unable to persuade the young men in Lacedaemon that by sticking with you they would progress more in virtue than if they lived with their own people? Or could you not induce the parents to entrust their sons to you rather than to their own care, if indeed they cared for their sons? For surely they did not envy their sons so much that they did not want them to turn out best. **HIPPIAS.** I do not think they were envious. **SOCRATES.** 
<margin>G</margin>
Is Lacedaemon not established with good laws? **HIPPIAS.** With good ones indeed. **SOCRATES.** In cities established with good laws, virtue is honored above all things. **HIPPIAS.** Most certainly. **SOCRATES.** And you know how to pass this virtue to others better than all other men. **HIPPIAS.** Precisely, O Socrates. **SOCRATES.** Would not he who can excellently teach the art of horsemanship be honored more in Thessaly than in the rest of Greece, and earn the most money there, and anywhere else where this art is prized? **HIPPIAS.** That is likely. **SOCRATES.** Then should not he who is able to instruct youth in the most noble precepts of virtue be greatly honored in Lacedaemon,
<margin>H</margin>
and there accumulate an abundance of money, and similarly in any city of the Greeks where virtue is highly esteemed? But perhaps you think we ought to believe these things happened more in Sicily and Inycus, Hippias. If you command it, we must believe it. **HIPPIAS.** It is not the ancestral custom, O Socrates, for the Lacedaemonians to change their laws, nor to educate their sons contrary to what is usual. **SOCRATES.** What do you say? Is it not ancestral for the Lacedaemonians to act rightly, but rather to go astray? **HIPPIAS.** I would not assert that.

<column-break/>

**HIPPIAS.** It would be most troublesome, O Socrates, as you say. For I am not accustomed to praise the ancients and those before us more than those now living; being on guard against the envy of the living and fearing the wrath of the dead. **SOCRATES.** You seem to me, O Hippias, to speak and think well, and I can bear witness that you speak the truth. For indeed your art has increased toward the ability to manage public affairs along with private ones. For that famous Gorgias of Leontini, the Sophist, came here, serving as an ambassador from home on behalf of the public, as he was the most capable of the Leontines in handling common affairs. In the assembly,
<margin>B</margin>
he was judged to have spoken best, and by making demonstrations in private and associating with the young, he earned and received much money from this city. And if you wish, our companion Prodicus often came here on public business at other times, but most recently he came publicly from Ceos and spoke in the council and was very well received, and by making private demonstrations and associating with the youth, he received an amazing amount of money. But of those ancients, no one ever thought it right to demand a money fee, nor to give demonstrations of their own wisdom among all kinds of men. So simple-minded were they, and it escaped them that money was worth so much. But each of these moderns has earned more money from wisdom than any other craftsman from any art whatsoever; and even before them, Protagoras did this. **HIPPIAS.** For you know nothing,
<margin>C</margin>
O Socrates, of the beauties in this. For if you knew how much money I have earned, you would wonder. I leave aside the rest, but once having gone to Sicily, while Protagoras was staying there and being well-regarded, and though he was older and I much younger, in a very short time I collected more than one hundred and fifty minae; and from one very small place, Inycus, more than twenty minae. And when I went home, I gave these to my father, so that he and the other citizens were amazed and struck with awe. And I think I have earned more money than any other two Sophists you might choose put together. **SOCRATES.** You speak of fine things, Hippias, 
<margin>D</margin>
and a great proof of your own wisdom, and of how much men today differ from the ancients. For according to your account, great ignorance is told of those earlier men like Anaxagoras. For they say the opposite happened to Anaxagoras than to you. For although much money was left to him, he neglected it and lost it all; so foolishly did he play the philosopher. And they tell other such stories of the ancients elsewhere. This, therefore, you seem to show as a fine proof of the wisdom of men now compared to those before; and many agree that the wise man must be wise for himself above all. The limit of this, it seems, is whoever earns the most money. And let these things 
<margin>E</margin>
be sufficient. But tell me this: from which of the cities you visited did you earn the most money? Or is it clear that it was from Lacedaemon, where you have gone most often? **HIPPIAS.** Not by Zeus, O Socrates. **SOCRATES.** How do you say? Was it the least? **HIPPIAS.** Nothing at all, ever. **SOCRATES.** You tell a marvel and a wonder, O Hippias. And tell me: is your wisdom not such as to make those associating with it and learning from it better in virtue? **HIPPIAS.** Very much so, O Socrates. **SOCRATES.** But were you able to make the sons of the Inycans better, but you were powerless with the sons of the Spartans? **HIPPIAS.** Far from it. **SOCRATES.** Then is it because the Sicilians desire to become better, while the Lacedaemonians 
<margin>F</margin>
do not? **HIPPIAS.** Certainly, O Socrates, the Lacedaemonians do too. **SOCRATES.** Then did they flee your company for lack of money? **HIPPIAS.** Not at all, since they have enough. **SOCRATES.** Then what could it be, that when they desired it and had money, and you were able to benefit them in the greatest things, they did not send you away full of silver? But could it be that the Lacedaemonians could educate their own children better than you? Or shall we say this is so, and do you agree? **HIPPIAS.** Not in any way. **SOCRATES.** Was it then that you were not able to persuade the young men in Lacedaemon that by associating with you they would improve more in virtue, or were you unable to persuade their fathers that they should hand them over to you rather than taking care of them themselves, if indeed they 
<margin>G</margin>
cared for them? For surely they did not envy their own children becoming the best. **HIPPIAS.** I do not think they envied them. **SOCRATES.** But surely Lacedaemon is well-governed. **HIPPIAS.** How could it not be? **SOCRATES.** And in well-governed cities, virtue is most honored. **HIPPIAS.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** And you know how to hand this down to another best of all men. **HIPPIAS.** By far, O Socrates. **SOCRATES.** Then would not he who knows best how to hand down horsemanship be most honored in Thessaly in Greece and receive the most money? And elsewhere where this is taken seriously? **HIPPIAS.** It is likely. **SOCRATES.** And would not he who is able to hand down the most valuable lessons for virtue be most honored in Lacedaemon, 
<margin>H</margin>
and earn the most money, if he wished? And in any other city of the Greeks that is well-governed? But do you think, my friend, that we should believe these things rather of Sicily and Inycus? If you command it, Hippias, it must be believed. **HIPPIAS.** For it is not the ancestral custom, O Socrates, for Lacedaemonians to move the laws, nor to educate their sons contrary to what is customary. **SOCRATES.** How do you say? Is it not ancestral for Lacedaemonians to act rightly, but rather to err? **HIPPIAS.** I would not say so, O Socrates. **SOCRATES.**

<summary>This page contains the opening of the Hippias Major, where Socrates uses heavy irony to contrast the great wealth of modern Sophists like Hippias with the poverty of ancient philosophers like Anaxagoras. The discussion focuses on why Hippias, despite his alleged wisdom, was unable to earn any money in the well-governed city of Sparta.</summary>
