<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and the Sophist Hippias. Following the discussion on the wealth acquired by modern teachers, Socrates now probes Hippias on why he earns so little in Sparta (Lacedaemon), despite his fame, leading to a discussion on the nature of law and the definition of 'The Beautiful.'</meta>

# HIPPIAS MAJOR

<margin>A</margin> **SOCRATES.** Would they not be acting rightly, then, if they educated the youth to be better rather than worse?
**HIPPIAS.** Rightly, indeed. But is it not against their laws to allow a foreign education? For you should know well, that if anyone else had ever received money there for the sake of education, I would have received by far the most. They certainly delight in hearing me and they praise me; but, as I say, it is not the <term>law</term><note>The Greek "nomos" (νόμος) refers to both written laws and established social customs or traditions.</note>.
**SOCRATES.** Do you say, Hippias, that law is a harm to a city, or a benefit?
**HIPPIAS.** It is established, I believe, for the sake of benefit; yet sometimes it also causes harm, if the law is poorly established.
**SOCRATES.** What then? Do not those who establish the law establish it as the greatest good for the city? And is it not impossible, without this, to live in a well-ordered city?
**HIPPIAS.** You speak the truth.
<margin>B</margin> **SOCRATES.** Therefore, whenever those who attempt to establish laws miss the "good," they have also missed what is lawful and the law itself; or how do you say it?
**HIPPIAS.** In strict reasoning, O Socrates, it is so; however, men are not accustomed to naming it in this way.
**SOCRATES.** Which men, Hippias? Those who know, or those who do not know?
**HIPPIAS.** The many.
**SOCRATES.** Are these "many" those who know the truth?
**HIPPIAS.** Certainly not.
**SOCRATES.** But surely those who do know consider that which is more beneficial to be more "lawful" in truth for all men, rather than that which is useless. Or do you not agree?
**HIPPIAS.** I agree that it is so in truth.
**SOCRATES.** Is it not then exactly as those who know believe it to be?
**HIPPIAS.** Entirely so.
**SOCRATES.** Now, for the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans.</note>, as you say, it is more beneficial to be educated by your instruction, though it is foreign, rather than by their local one.
**HIPPIAS.** And I speak the truth.
**SOCRATES.** And do you also say, Hippias, that whatever is more beneficial is also more lawful?
**HIPPIAS.** I did say so.
<margin>C</margin> **SOCRATES.** According to your reasoning, then, it is more lawful for the sons of the Lacedaemonians to be educated by Hippias, and less lawful to be educated by their fathers, if indeed they will truly be more benefited by you.
**HIPPIAS.** But they certainly would be benefited, Socrates.
**SOCRATES.** Therefore, the Lacedaemonians act against the law by not giving you gold and entrusting their own sons to you.
**HIPPIAS.** I agree with this; for you seem to be speaking the argument on my behalf, and it would not be right for me to oppose it.
**SOCRATES.** We find, then, my friend, that the Spartans are law-breakers, and in the most important matters too, though they seem to be the most law-abiding of men. But by the gods, Hippias, for what kinds of things do they praise you and delight in hearing? Is it not clearly those things which you know best—the stars and the celestial phenomena?
<margin>D</margin> **HIPPIAS.** Not in the least; they cannot even tolerate those things.
**SOCRATES.** But do they delight in hearing about geometry?
**HIPPIAS.** Not at all; since many of them, to put it simply, do not even know how to count.
**SOCRATES.** Then they are far from tolerating you giving a demonstration on arithmetic.
**HIPPIAS.** Far indeed, by Zeus!
**SOCRATES.** Well then, is it those things which you know how to distinguish more accurately than any other man: the properties of letters, syllables, harmonies, and rhythms?
**HIPPIAS.** What harmonies or letters are you asking about, my good man?
<margin>E</margin> **SOCRATES.** But what then are the things they listen to with pleasure and for which they praise you? Tell me yourself, since I cannot find them.
**HIPPIAS.** They listen most with pleasure, Socrates, to the genealogies of heroes and men, and to stories of settlements—how cities were founded in ancient times—and, in short, to all <term>ancient history</term><note>original: "archaeologia" (ἀρχαιολογία). Here meaning "old stories" or "tales of the past" rather than the modern scientific discipline.</note>. So much so that I have been forced to learn by heart and practice all such things for their sake.
**SOCRATES.** By Zeus, Hippias, you are lucky that the Lacedaemonians do not delight in someone reciting our list of magistrates from the time of Solon; otherwise, you would have had a struggle learning them all.
**HIPPIAS.** Why a struggle, Socrates? I can repeat fifty names after hearing them only once.
**SOCRATES.** True; I forgot that you possess a <term>mnemonic art</term><note>Hippias was famous for his memory systems.</note>.
<margin>F</margin> So I realize that the Lacedaemonians naturally delight in you because you know so many things; they use you just as children use old women to tell stories for their pleasure.
**HIPPIAS.** And by Zeus, Socrates, I recently won great favor there by discoursing on the noble pursuits a young man should follow. I have a very beautiful speech composed about them, well-arranged in its wording. The premise and beginning of the speech is something like this: After Troy was taken, the story goes that Neoptolemus asked Nestor what kind of fine pursuits a young man might follow to become most famous. After this, Nestor speaks and suggests to him many most excellent and beautiful customs.
<margin>G</margin> This speech I delivered there, and I am going to deliver it here as well, on the day after tomorrow, in the school of Phidostratus, along with many other things worth hearing; for Eudicus, the son of Apemantus, requested it of me. See to it that you are present yourself, and bring others who are capable of judging what is said.
**SOCRATES.** That shall be done, God willing, Hippias. But for now, answer me a brief question about it. You have reminded me at just the right moment. For recently, my excellent friend, someone threw me into a state of confusion during a conversation; as I was blaming some things as <term>ugly</term><note>original: "aischra" (αἰσχρά) - can mean physically ugly, shameful, or morally base.</note> and praising others as <term>beautiful</term><note>original: "kala" (καλά) - encompasses physical beauty, nobility, and moral excellence.</note>, he questioned me quite insultingly: "How do you know, Socrates, what is beautiful and what is ugly?
<margin>H</margin> <margin>Here one may see the art of examination.</margin> Come now, could you say what <term>The Beautiful</term> is?" And I, because of my worthlessness, was confused and could not answer him properly. Leaving the gathering, I was angry with myself and reproached myself, vowing that as soon as I met one of you wise men, I would listen, learn, and practice, so that I could return to my questioner and fight the argument again. Now, as I said, you have come at the right moment. Teach me sufficiently what The Beautiful itself is, and try to speak to me as accurately as possible.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> **SOCRATES.** Would they not act rightly if they educated the youth better, and not for the worse? **HIPPIAS.** Rightly, but their law does not admit foreign disciplines. Otherwise, if anyone else had ever profited there by teaching, know that I would have profited the most. They rejoice when they hear me and they praise me; but as I was saying, their law forbids foreign things. **SOCRATES.** Do you call the law, O Hippias, the ruin of a city or its salvation? **HIPPIAS.** In my opinion, law is established for the sake of utility, though it sometimes hinders if it is badly established. **SOCRATES.** Do not the lawmakers establish the law as a certain maximum good for the city, and if the law is removed, can we not no longer live lawfully in the city? **HIPPIAS.** You speak the truth. **SOCRATES.** <margin>B</margin> Therefore, as often as those who strive to pass laws wander away from the good, they depart from what is lawful and the law. What do you say to this? **HIPPIAS.** By an exact reasoning, O Socrates, that is how it stands; yet men are not accustomed to naming it so. **SOCRATES.** Which ones, O Hippias, those who know or those who are ignorant? **HIPPIAS.** The common people. **SOCRATES.** Are the common people those who recognize the truth? **HIPPIAS.** Not at all. **SOCRATES.** But truly those who know, they judge that which is more useful to be more lawful than that which is useless, indeed for all men. Do you not confess this? **HIPPIAS.** I confess indeed that it is so in truth. **SOCRATES.** Is it not so, as those who know think? **HIPPIAS.** Entirely. **SOCRATES.** But it is better, as you say, for the Lacedaemonians to be imbued with your discipline, although foreign, rather than their own. <margin>C</margin> **HIPPIAS.** And I speak the truth. **SOCRATES.** Furthermore, whatever things are more useful are more lawful. Is this what you say, O Hippias? **HIPPIAS.** I have said it indeed. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, according to your reasoning, it is more according to the law that the sons of the Lacedaemonians be taught by Hippias rather than by their parents, since you truly benefit them more than they do. **HIPPIAS.** I would benefit them without a doubt, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** The Lacedaemonians therefore act against the law when they do not hand over their sons to be educated by you, even when offered a reward of gold. **HIPPIAS.** I agree indeed; for you seem to speak for me, wherefore it is not fitting to oppose you. **SOCRATES.** We have found the Laconians <note>Spartans.</note> to be destitute of good laws, <margin>D</margin> and indeed in the greatest matters, though they seem to use the best laws. But when do they especially praise you, Hippias, and in what things heard do they especially delight? Is it when you tell those things which you yourself know excellently: the stars and celestial motions? **HIPPIAS.** In no way do they tolerate these. **SOCRATES.** Does a discourse on geometry delight them? **HIPPIAS.** Least of all; for very many of them, so to speak, do not even know how to count. **SOCRATES.** It is far off then that they would listen to calculations willingly. **HIPPIAS.** Far off indeed, by Jove! **SOCRATES.** What about those things which you understand most sharply of all men: the distinctions of letters and syllables, and the natures of rhythms and harmonies? **HIPPIAS.** What <margin>E</margin> harmonies and letters, O good man? **SOCRATES.** But what then are those things which they, hearing, rejoice in and praise you for? You at least should tell me, since I am unable to find them. **HIPPIAS.** The lineage of heroes and men, and dwellings—how cities were once built—and in summary, they listen attentively to every history of antiquity. Wherefore, for their sake, I was compelled to learn and meditate on all things of this kind. **SOCRATES.** How well it has gone for you, O Hippias, that the Lacedaemonians are annoyed if anyone were to recount our leaders starting from Solon. Otherwise, you would have had to be exhausted by learning their names. **HIPPIAS.** Why exhausted, Socrates? <margin>F</margin> Hearing fifty names once, I can repeat them from memory. **SOCRATES.** Is that so? But I had not noticed that you were so powerful in memory. Wherefore I now understand that you are deservedly delighted in by the Lacedaemonians as one skilled in many things, and they use you just as boys use old women for the sweetness of storytelling. **HIPPIAS.** By Jove, Socrates, I was recently an object of admiration there, discussing fine studies in which it befits a youth to be occupied. For there exists a certain brilliant oration composed by me about these things, which is powerful in its particular elegance of words; the form and beginning of the oration is of this sort: "Troy having been captured," says the oration, "Neoptolemus questioned Nestor as to what were the most beautiful things which a youth, pursuing them, might become an illustrious man." To whom Nestor, responding, recounts many and <margin>G</margin> beautiful precepts. This oration I indeed showed there, and here also on the third day from now, in the school of Phidostratus, I am about to show it and many other things worthy of being heard. For Eudicus, the son of Apemantus, asked me. Therefore, see to it that you also are present, and bring others with you, whoever knows how to judge such speech. **SOCRATES.** It shall be so, if God wills, Hippias. But for the present, answer a certain brief thing about this very matter, for you have warned me opportunely. For recently, O best of men, when in a certain conversation I praised some things as beautiful and vituperated others as base, someone brought this doubt into the open, very contumeliously asking me thus: "From whence, Socrates, do you know what is beautiful or <margin>H</margin> <margin>Here one may see the testing art.</margin> base? Can you define what the beautiful is?" But I, on account of my ignorance, hesitated, nor did I have what I might respond appropriately; and departing from the gathering of men, I was angry with myself and vehemently accused my own rudeness. And I threatened that when I first should have one of you who profess wisdom in my way, I would strive to hear and learn it...

<vocab>Hippias Major, Socrates, Lacedaemonians, the beautiful, the noble, the base, law, lawful, Neoptolemus, Nestor, Phidostratus, Eudicus son of Apemantus</vocab>

<summary>Socrates and Hippias discuss why the law-abiding Spartans do not hire Hippias despite his wisdom, concluding that if his teaching is beneficial, the law should theoretically permit it. Hippias explains he pleases the Spartans by reciting ancient histories and genealogies, leading Socrates to ask Hippias to define the essence of "The Beautiful."</summary>

--- Page 130 ---
<meta>This page marks the transition into the core philosophical inquiry of the *Hippias Major*. After discussing the customs of the Spartans, Socrates shifts the focus to the nature of "Beauty" (the Beautiful itself). He introduces a fictional, aggressive challenger—who is actually a reflection of his own critical mind—to force Hippias into providing a rigorous definition. The dialogue moves from abstract agreement that "Beauty" exists to Hippias’s first attempt at a definition: a beautiful young woman.</meta>

# PLATO'S [HIPPIAS MAJOR]

...and carefully premeditated, to return to the man who had questioned me, so that I might do battle over the same matter again. For this reason, you have come most opportunely now, as I was saying. Teach me, I beseech you, what "the Beautiful itself" <term>the Beautiful itself</term><note>Socrates is looking for the "Form" or "Essence" of Beauty (the quality that makes all beautiful things beautiful), rather than just an example of a beautiful thing.</note> is. Try, I say, to reveal the whole matter to me with the greatest care in your answer, lest I be argued against once more and become a laughingstock. For you surely know it clearly, and it must be a small thing among the many disciplines you have mastered. **HIPPIAS.** A small thing indeed, by Jove, Socrates, and of no value, so to speak. **SOCRATES.** I shall learn it easily then, and no one will refute me further. **HIPPIAS.** No one, certainly. For otherwise my study would be worthless and amateurish. **SOCRATES.** By Hera, you speak well, Hippias, if we are to overcome that man. But perhaps I am a hindrance to you, imitating that man if I hold onto his ways of objecting. If it is no trouble, I will set myself against you, so that I may learn more vehemently and firmly. **HIPPIAS.** Object as you please; for, as I was just saying, it is not a difficult question, and I could teach you to answer far more difficult things, so that no man could refute you. **SOCRATES.** O, how well you speak! But since you command it, I shall take on his persona and attempt to question you. If you had shown him your speech about beautiful practices, as soon as you had finished speaking, he would ask about nothing else

<margin>An extraction [of the truth], so that he confesses it is a real thing.</margin>
before asking about the Beautiful. For this is his custom, and he would ask in this manner: "O guest from Elis, are not the just made just by justice?" Answer, I pray, Hippias, as if he were asking. **HIPPIAS.** By justice, certainly. **SOCRATES.** And is this justice itself not a "thing"? **HIPPIAS.** Entirely so. **SOCRATES.** And are the wise not wise by wisdom, and similarly all good things by "the Good"? **HIPPIAS.**

<margin>The respondent agrees; the question is what it is.</margin>
What prevents it? **SOCRATES.** Indeed, wisdom and the good must be something in themselves. For if they did not exist, other things would never become such through them. **HIPPIAS.** So it is. **SOCRATES.** And are not all beautiful things beautiful by the Beautiful itself? **HIPPIAS.** By the Beautiful, certainly. **SOCRATES.** Is this "Beautiful" then a real thing? **HIPPIAS.** It is, without a doubt; but to what end do you ask? **SOCRATES.** He will immediately ask: "Tell me, stranger, what is this 'Beautiful itself'?" **HIPPIAS.** Does the one asking this seek to hear anything other than "what is beautiful"? **SOCRATES.** It does not seem so to me; he wants to know what "the Beautiful itself" is. **HIPPIAS.** And how does that differ from the other? **SOCRATES.** Does it seem like nothing to you? **HIPPIAS.** Nothing certainly, for there is no difference. **SOCRATES.** Yet it is clear you know better. Consider, however: he does not ask what thing is beautiful, but what "the Beautiful itself" is. **HIPPIAS.** I understand now, O good man, and I will answer what the Beautiful itself is, so that he may never

<margin>The first definition of the beautiful.</margin>
refute me. If I must tell the truth, know, Socrates, that a beautiful maiden is the Beautiful itself. **SOCRATES.** Splendidly, by the dog <note>original: "per canem" / "νὴ τὸν κύνα". This was Socrates's favorite eccentric oath.</note>, O Hippias, and quite elegantly have you answered. If I answer this, then, will I have answered the question correctly, and will I not be refuted? **HIPPIAS.** How could he seize upon you, if you answer what is apparent to everyone, and for which every single person listening will testify on your behalf? **SOCRATES.** Let it be so. But I am reflecting on what you say, Hippias. For that man will question me thus: "Come, answer me, O

<margin>Refutation of the definition.</margin>
Socrates, are all these things which are called beautiful, beautiful because of the Beautiful itself?" And I shall answer: "If a maiden is beautiful, she is the Beautiful itself through which these things become beautiful." **HIPPIAS.** Do you think he will dare to rebuke you further, as if what you say is not beautiful? Or if perhaps he should dare, will he not be laughed at by everyone? **SOCRATES.** I know for certain that he will dare, O wonderful man; but whether his daring will turn out to be ridiculous, the matter itself will show. I wish to tell you what he will bring up next. **HIPPIAS.** Tell me now. **SOCRATES.** "How charming you are, Socrates," he will say. "A beautiful mare, is she not beautiful? One which even a God praised in an oracle." What shall we say to this, Hippias? Shall we not confess that a beautiful mare is beautiful? For how could we deny that what is beautiful is beautiful? **HIPPIAS.** You speak the truth, Socrates; for the God spoke rightly. For very beautiful mares are bred among us. **SOCRATES.** After this he will add, "Is not a beautiful lyre beautiful?" **HIPPIAS.** Yes. **SOCRATES.** He will ask again (for I am certain of this, guessing from his character): "O best of men, what of a beautiful pot? Is it not beautiful?" **HIPPIAS.** O Socrates, who is so rude as to mix such vulgar names into a serious matter? **SOCRATES.** Such a man he is, Hippias: not elegant or refined, but a common fellow, caring for nothing but the truth. Nevertheless, he must be answered, and I will speak for him. If a pot has been shaped by a good potter, smooth and round and well-fired—like some of those beautiful two-handled pots that hold six measures—if he asks about such a pot, we must answer that it is beautiful. For how can we assert that what is beautiful is not beautiful? **HIPPIAS.** By no means, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** "Is not even a beautiful pot," he will ask, "a beautiful thing?" Answer him. **HIPPIAS.** I think it is so, Socrates; even this vessel is beautiful when it is crafted with skill. <summary>In this passage, Socrates challenges Hippias to define the essence of beauty, leading Hippias to propose that a "beautiful maiden" is the Beautiful itself. Socrates counters this by showing that beauty is relative, using examples of horses, lyres, and even common pots to show that an object's beauty depends on what it is compared to.</summary>

### HIPPIAS MAJOR

<margin>A</margin>...will she not suffer the same fate as the pot when compared to a maiden? Will not the most beautiful of maidens appear ugly? Does not Heraclitus <note>Heraclitus of Ephesus (c. 535 – c. 475 BC) was a pre-Socratic philosopher. Then he will say: "Being asked for the Beautiful, do you respond with something that happens to be no more beautiful than it is ugly, as you yourself admit?" I shall say, "So it seems." The man is most ignorant and knows nothing of fine possessions. For if you answer him that this thing he asks about—the Beautiful—is nothing other than gold, <margin>The second definition is false</margin> he will be at a loss and will not attempt to refute you. For we all know <margin>Refutation</margin> that wherever this is added, even if it seemed ugly before, it will appear beautiful when adorned with gold. **SOCRATES.** You do not know the man, Hippias, how troublesome he is and how he does not easily accept what is said. **HIPPIAS.** What of it, Socrates? He must accept what is said correctly; <margin>D</margin> if he rejects it, he will be a laughingstock to everyone. **SOCRATES.** Yet he will not only refuse to accept this answer, my best friend, but he will mock me bitterly and say: "You puffed-up man, do you think Phidias <note>Phidias was the most famous sculptor of the 5th century BC, known for the colossal statues of Zeus at Olympia and Athena in the Parthenon.</note> was a bad craftsman?" Is <margin>The third definition is false</margin> a beautiful stone also beautiful, Hippias?" Shall we say so? **HIPPIAS.** We shall say so, at least <margin>E</margin> whenever it is appropriate. **SOCRATES.** "But when it is not appropriate, is it ugly?" ...in that response, where I say that the beautiful is gold, it will appear that gold is no more <margin>Fourth definition: false.</margin> beautiful than fig-wood. Thus, this definition suffers the same fate as the maiden and the pot; even more ridiculously, it is beautiful for some and not for others. <summary>In this segment of the dialogue, Hippias attempts to define "the Beautiful" as a life of worldly success and traditional burial rites, which Socrates refutes by demonstrating that such a definition cannot apply to immortal gods or heroes with divine parents. The argument shifts toward considering beauty as "the appropriate" (to prepon).</summary>

### HIPPIAS MAJOR.

<margin>A</margin>
To those in whom it is not present, they are not; and all other things to which this is present, it is by this very thing that they are becoming. Consider then if this nature of the becoming <note>original: "τὸ πρέπον" (to prepon) / "decorum." This refers to what is appropriate, fitting, or suitable for a specific purpose.</note> happens to be the beautiful. Now, I am accustomed to agreeing to such things whenever they arise, for I do not know what else to say. But does it seem to you that the becoming is the beautiful? **HIPPIAS.** Entirely so, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** Let us be careful lest we are somehow deceived. **HIPPIAS.** Indeed, we must be careful. **SOCRATES.** Look then: do we call the becoming that which, when it is present, makes each thing *appear* beautiful, or that which makes it *be* so, or neither of these? **HIPPIAS.** It seems so to me. **SOCRATES.** Which one? That which makes things appear beautiful? For instance, when someone puts on clothes or shoes that fit well, even if he is ridiculous, he appears more beautiful. If, then, the becoming makes a thing appear more beautiful than it actually is, the becoming would be a kind of deception regarding the beautiful, and would not be what we are seeking, Hippias. For we are surely
<margin>B</margin>
seeking that by which all beautiful things are beautiful—just as all great things are great by that which exceeds. For by this all things are great, and even if they do not appear so, they must necessarily be great if they possess it. So we are asking what the beautiful is, by which all things are beautiful, whether they appear so or not. For it cannot be the becoming; for that makes things appear more beautiful than they are, according to your argument, and does not allow them to appear as they truly are. But that which makes them <gloss>be</gloss> beautiful (as I just said), whether they appear so or not, is what we must try to define. For this is what we are seeking, if indeed we are seeking the beautiful. **HIPPIAS.** But Socrates, the becoming
<margin>C</margin>
makes things both *be* and *appear* beautiful when it is present. **SOCRATES.** Then it is impossible for things that are truly beautiful not to appear beautiful, if that which makes them appear so is present? **HIPPIAS.** Impossible. **SOCRATES.** Shall we then agree on this, Hippias: that all truly beautiful laws and customs are thought to be beautiful and appear so to everyone at all times? Or, on the contrary, are they not ignored, and is there not more strife and contention over them than anything else, both privately among individuals and publicly among cities? **HIPPIAS.** Rather the latter, Socrates; they are ignored. **SOCRATES.** They would not be, if the *appearance* were present to them. And it would be present if the becoming were the beautiful and made things not only *be* beautiful, but also *appear* so. Thus,
<margin>D</margin>
if the becoming is that which makes things *be* beautiful, it would be the beautiful we are seeking, but it would not be that which makes them *appear* so. If, on the other hand, the becoming is that which makes things *appear* beautiful, it would not be the beautiful we are seeking, for that makes them *be* so. For the same thing cannot make things both appear and be, not only in the case of the beautiful, but in any other case. Let us choose, then, whether we think the becoming is that which makes things appear beautiful or that which makes them be so. **HIPPIAS.** That which makes them appear, Socrates, is my opinion. **SOCRATES.** Oh, no! Then the knowledge of what the beautiful is has slipped away and escaped us, Hippias, since the becoming has turned out to be something other than the beautiful. **HIPPIAS.** By Zeus, Socrates, this is very strange indeed to me. **SOCRATES.** But my friend, let us not let go of it yet, for I still have some hope that
<margin>E</margin>
the beautiful will reveal itself. **HIPPIAS.** Most certainly, Socrates; for it is not difficult to find. I know well that if I were to go away into solitude for a little while and consider it by myself, I could tell it to you with more accuracy than accuracy itself. **SOCRATES.** Ah, Hippias, do not speak so grandly! You see how much trouble it has already caused us; let us not make it angry so that it runs away even further. But I say nothing; for I believe you will easily find it when you are alone. But by the gods, find it while I am present! And if you wish, let us search for it together as we have been. If we find it, it will be best; if not, I shall be content, I suppose, with my lot, and you can go and find it easily later. But if we find it now, I will certainly not bother you by asking what
<margin>F</margin>
you discovered by yourself. Now, look at this and see if it seems to you to be the beautiful: I say it is... but wait, look closely and pay full attention so I don't talk nonsense. Let us say that whatever is **useful** is beautiful. I say this considering the following: we say eyes are beautiful, not those that appear to be of a certain kind but are unable to see, but those that are both capable and useful for seeing. Isn't that so? **HIPPIAS.** Yes. **SOCRATES.** And so we say the whole body is beautiful, one for running, another for wrestling; and likewise all animals—a beautiful horse, or cock, or quail—and all utensils, and vehicles both on land and at sea, ships and triremes; and all instruments both in music
<margin>G</margin>
and in the other arts; and, if you like, customs and laws. We call nearly all of these beautiful by looking at the same idea: how each of them is naturally made, or fashioned, or situated. That which is useful, in the way it is useful, for the purpose it is useful, and when it is useful, we call beautiful; but that which is useless in every way, we call ugly. Does it not seem so to you as well, Hippias? **HIPPIAS.** It does to me. **SOCRATES.** Then we were right just now in saying that the useful, more than anything else, happens to be the beautiful. **HIPPIAS.** Perfectly right, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** And is not that which is capable of producing something useful, insofar as it is capable, also useful? But that which is incapable, is it not useless? **HIPPIAS.** Entirely.
<margin>H</margin>
**SOCRATES.** Power, then, is beautiful, and lack of power <note>original: "ἀδυναμία" (adynamia). This can mean weakness, inability, or powerlessness.</note> is ugly. **HIPPIAS.** Most certainly. Other things, Socrates, testify for us that this is so, but especially political matters. For in the affairs of one's own city and state, to be powerful is the most beautiful of all things, while to be powerless is the most ugly. **SOCRATES.** Well said! Then, by the gods, Hippias, is it because of this that wisdom...

<column-break/>

<margin>Fifth definition of the beautiful. Refutation.</margin>
On the contrary, to those it is not present in, they are not; and all other things to which the becoming <note>original: "decens" / "decorum." Ficino's Latin translation uses "decorum" for the Greek "to prepon."</note> is present, which is natural to them, become beautiful. See then whether this very thing is the beautiful; I have usually conceded such points. For I find nothing to object to. But does the decorous seem to you to be the beautiful itself? **HIPPIAS.** Entirely, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** Let us beware lest we are deceived in some way. **HIPPIAS.** Certainly we must beware. **SOCRATES.** See then: do we call that "decorum" which, by its arrival, makes individual things appear beautiful to which it is present, or which makes them *be* so, or neither of these? **HIPPIAS.** It seems so to me. **SOCRATES.** Which one? That which makes them appear beautiful, just as if someone who is deformed, being adorned with decorous clothing and shoes, appears more beautiful? Is it not true that if the decorous makes those things in which it is present appear more beautiful than they are, the decorous would be a kind of deception regarding the beautiful? And it would not be this that we are seeking, Hippias? For we sought that by which all beautiful things are beautiful, just as all great things are great by excess. For all these things are great, and even if they are not seen to be, they nevertheless exceed, and must be great. Thus we also sought the beautiful, by which all things are beautiful, whether they appear so or not, asking what it might be. It is certainly not the decorous; for it makes things appear more beautiful than they are, as you yourself said, and does not allow them to appear as they truly are. But that which makes them *be* beautiful, as I was saying a little while ago, whether they appear so or not, what is it? This is certainly what is being asked, if the beautiful is what is being sought. **HIPPIAS.** But the decorous, Socrates, makes things both *be* and *appear* beautiful when it is present. **SOCRATES.** Therefore it is impossible for those things which are truly beautiful not to appear beautiful, while that which makes them appear is present. **HIPPIAS.** Impossible. **SOCRATES.** Shall we confess this, Hippias? That all things truly beautifully instituted and all pursuits are also thought to be beautiful by men? Or, on the contrary, are they unknown, so much so that men fight most bitterly over them both privately and publicly? **HIPPIAS.** I think they are rather unknown, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** Yet they would not be unknown if they appeared as beautiful as they are; and they would appear so if the decorous were the beautiful, and forced them not only to be, but also to appear beautiful. Therefore, if the decorous is what makes things be beautiful, it is indeed what we seek as the beautiful, but it is not that which forces them to appear so; but if the decorous makes them only appear so, it is by no means the beautiful itself that we seek. For it compels them to *be*. But the same thing cannot make things both appear and be beautiful at the same time, nor can it do so for anything else. Let us choose now, whether we think the decorous is that which makes things appear beautiful, or that which makes them be so. **HIPPIAS.** That which makes them appear, Socrates, I think. **SOCRATES.** Oh! How far, Hippias, the knowledge of the beautiful itself has fled from us, since the decorous has appeared to be something other than the beautiful itself. **HIPPIAS.** By Jove <note>original: "Per Iovem." Translated from "νὴ μὰ Δία" (By Zeus).</note>, Socrates, to me this seems excessively absurd. **SOCRATES.** But, my friend, let us not yet dismiss it; for I have not cast away all hope of finding what the beautiful is. **HIPPIAS.** One must certainly hope, Socrates, for it is not difficult to find; I am convinced that if I were to go away for a short while and consider it by myself, I could explain it to you more accurately than accuracy itself. **SOCRATES.** Alas, do not say it with such a loud voice, Hippias, lest it take offense and flee further from us. Do you not see how much it has fatigued us so far? But I say nothing. For when you are alone, you will find it easily and safely. But come, by the gods, find it while I am present; and if you wish, as before, so hereafter search for it together with me. If we find it, it will be well. If not, I shall be content with my lot; but you, after you have gone, will find it easily. If we find it now, however, I will no longer be a nuisance to you, asking what you have thought out for yourself. For the present, consider whether this seems to you to be the beautiful. Pay attention, I pray, diligently, lest I rave. This is certainly beautiful: that which is **useful**. Indeed, I make this conjecture mostly from this: that the eyes are beautiful,
<margin>The useful is proposed as the genus of the beautiful.</margin>
not those which are powerless of seeing, but those which are fit and useful for seeing. **HIPPIAS.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** And the whole body we call beautiful in the same way, one for running, another for wrestling. Likewise all animals, such as a beautiful horse, a cock, and a quail, and all vessels, and vehicles both land-based and maritime, ships and triremes, also all instruments pertaining to music as well as to other arts; also, if you wish, pursuits and laws—we call each of these beautiful for the same reason: looking
namely at what condition each was born, or made, or placed so as to be useful, and in what way useful, and for what useful, and when useful, we say it is beautiful; but that which is useless according to these things, we call ugly. Does not the same seem so to you as well, Hippias? **HIPPIAS.** It does to me. **SOCRATES.** Correctly, therefore, have we now said, that above all other things, that which is useful is the beautiful. **HIPPIAS.** Very correctly, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** Is it not true that what is able to produce something is useful for that which can be produced? And what cannot is useless? **HIPPIAS.** Entirely. **SOCRATES.** Power, therefore, is beautiful, and lack of power is ugly. **HIPPIAS.** Most especially; for all other things testify to us that this is so, and civil matters especially. Since in one's own city and republic, to be powerful is the most beautiful of all things, while to be powerless is the most base. **SOCRATES.** You speak excellently. But is it not for this very reason that wisdom...

<vocab>Hippias Major, Socrates, Hippias, beautiful, decorous, useful, τὸ πρέπον (the becoming/appropriate), τὸ καλόν (the beautiful), τὸ χρήσιμον (the useful), wisdom, power</vocab>

<summary>In this passage, Socrates and Hippias debate whether "the appropriate" (the becoming) defines beauty, concluding that if it only makes things *look* beautiful without making them *be* beautiful, it is merely a deception. They then pivot to a new definition: that the beautiful is "the useful" and that power is inherently beautiful while weakness is ugly.</summary>

### PLATO

<margin>A</margin> ...the most beautiful of all, while ignorance, on the contrary, is the most shameful? **HIPPIAS.** Indeed, what else do you think, Socrates? **SOCRATES.** Wait a moment, my dear friend. I am suspicious and fearful about what we are now saying. **HIPPIAS.** What do you fear, Socrates? For your argument has just now proceeded most excellently. **SOCRATES.** I would wish it so. But consider this with me: would anyone ever perform a thing that he neither knows how to do nor is able to do? **HIPPIAS.** By no means. For how could he act in a way that he is unable? **SOCRATES.** Those who fail, and do evil deeds, and act poorly against their own will—if they were not able to do these things, would they have done them? **HIPPIAS.** Not at all. **SOCRATES.** But surely those who are able, act by their power <note>original: "potentia" / "δύναμις" (dynamis)</note>, for it is not by lack of power that they act. **HIPPIAS.** Certainly not. **SOCRATES.**
<margin>B</margin> And are all people able to do the things they actually do? **HIPPIAS.** Without a doubt. **SOCRATES.** But all men, starting from childhood and throughout their whole lives, do many more evil things than good ones, and they do not err on purpose. **HIPPIAS.** You speak the truth. **SOCRATES.** What then? This power, and these useful things that lead to the execution of evil—shall we call these "beautiful," or are they far from it? **HIPPIAS.** Far from it, it seems to me, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, the "powerful" and the "useful" do not, as it seems, constitute the beautiful itself. **HIPPIAS.** Unless, Socrates, it is powerful for good, or is useful for such a purpose. **SOCRATES.** That idea, then—that the powerful and useful is simply the beautiful—is rejected. But was this perhaps what our minds were aiming at, Hippias: that the powerful and the useful for *achieving good* is the beautiful? **HIPPIAS.** So it seems to me. **SOCRATES.** And this is the "beneficial" <note>original: "conducibile" / "ὠφέλιμον" (ophelimon)</note>,
<margin>C</margin> is it not? **HIPPIAS.** Very much so. **SOCRATES.** Thus beautiful bodies, beautiful legal institutions, wisdom, and the other things we mentioned a moment ago are all beautiful because they are beneficial. **HIPPIAS.** That is clear. **SOCRATES.** The beneficial itself, then, seems to us to be the beautiful. **HIPPIAS.** Most of all, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** And yet, the beneficial is that which produces good. **HIPPIAS.** It is. **SOCRATES.** And that which produces is nothing other than the cause, is it not? **HIPPIAS.** It is so. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, the beautiful is the cause of the good. **HIPPIAS.** It certainly is. **SOCRATES.** But the cause is one thing, and that which is caused is another. For a cause cannot be the cause of itself. You can see it best this way: did we not agree that the cause is a producer? **HIPPIAS.** Clearly. **SOCRATES.**
<margin>D</margin> And from the producer, the "produced" is made, not the producer itself. **HIPPIAS.** That is true. **SOCRATES.** The producer is one thing, the produced another. **HIPPIAS.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, the cause is not the cause of the cause, but of that which is produced by it. **HIPPIAS.** It is so. **SOCRATES.** So, if the beautiful is the cause of the good, the good is made by the beautiful. And for this reason, it seems, we desire prudence and all other beautiful things: because their work and their offspring—the good—is desirable. Thus, from what we have found, the beautiful seems to stand in the place of a father to the good. **HIPPIAS.** Entirely so. You speak excellently. **SOCRATES.** But is this also excellent: that the father is not the son, nor the son the father? **HIPPIAS.** That is also excellent. **SOCRATES.**
<margin>E</margin> Neither then is the cause the effect, nor the effect the cause. **HIPPIAS.** You speak the truth. **SOCRATES.** By Jove, my good man! Then neither is the beautiful good, nor is the good beautiful. Does that seem possible to you from what has been said? **HIPPIAS.** Not to me, by Jove. **SOCRATES.** Does it please us to assert that the beautiful is not good, and the good is not beautiful? **HIPPIAS.** No, by Jove, it does not please me at all. **SOCRATES.** And by Jove, Hippias, it pleases me least of all the things we have said. **HIPPIAS.** So it seems. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, that definition which seemed so noble—that the beautiful is the beneficial, the useful, and the powerful to produce some good—is no longer valid. Rather, if possible, it is to be judged more absurd than our earlier attempts where we called a young girl or the other things mentioned "the beautiful itself." **HIPPIAS.** So it appears. **SOCRATES.**
<margin>F</margin> Indeed, Hippias, I do not know where to turn; I am stuck and in doubt. Do you perhaps have something? **HIPPIAS.** Not at the moment, but as I said before, I am certain I will find something if I reflect on it. **SOCRATES.** But I think that in my burning desire for learning, I shall not be able to wait for your delay. Look, another idea has just come to mind. Consider this: should we call "beautiful" that which delights us—I do not mean every pleasure, but that which comes through sight and hearing? For how can we resist this, when beautiful people, all ornaments, paintings, and sculptures delight us when we look at them? Beautiful songs and voices, all music, speeches, and storytelling affect us similarly. If we were to answer that persistent man <note>Socrates refers to his own critical "inner voice" as if it were a separate, harsh interrogator.</note> that the beautiful is that which delights through sight and hearing, would we not check his boldness? What do you think? **HIPPIAS.** Now, Socrates, it seems to me that "what the beautiful is" has been well said. **SOCRATES.** But what of it? Shall we say that beautiful practices and laws are beautiful because they are pleasant to sight and hearing, or do they belong to some other kind? **HIPPIAS.** These perhaps, Socrates, might escape the man's notice. **SOCRATES.** By the dog <note>A characteristic oath of Socrates.</note>, Hippias, not the one I would most of all feel ashamed before, whenever I were to talk nonsense and claim to be saying something when I am saying nothing. **HIPPIAS.**
<margin>G</margin> Of whom do you speak? **SOCRATES.** Socrates, the son of Sophroniscus, who would no more allow me to judge these things easily without investigation than he would allow me to think I know what I do not know. **HIPPIAS.** But indeed, to me too...

<column-break/>

...the most beautiful of all. And is ignorance the most shameful of all? **HIPPIAS.** What else do you think, Socrates? **SOCRATES.** Hold on then, my friend; for I am afraid of what we might be saying again. **HIPPIAS.** Why are you afraid again, Socrates? Since your argument has now proceeded most beautifully. **SOCRATES.** I would wish so. But look into this with me: could anyone do something that he neither understands how to do nor is at all able to do? **HIPPIAS.** Not at all. For how could he do what he is unable to do? **SOCRATES.** Then those who err, and work and do evil deeds against their will—is it not true that if they were not able to do these things, they would never do them? **HIPPIAS.** That is clear. **SOCRATES.** But surely those who are able, are able by power. For it is not by lack of power. **HIPPIAS.** Certainly not. **SOCRATES.** And are all who do what they do able to do it? **HIPPIAS.** Yes. **SOCRATES.** And all men do many more evil things than good, starting from their childhood; and they err against their will. **HIPPIAS.** It is so. **SOCRATES.** What then? This power, and these useful things—those that are useful for working some evil—shall we say these are beautiful? Or is that far from the truth? **HIPPIAS.** Far from it, it seems to me, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** Then the able and the useful, Hippias, are not for us, as it seems, the beautiful. **HIPPIAS.** Unless, Socrates, they are able to do good, and are useful for such things. **SOCRATES.** That other idea is gone then—that being simply able and useful is beautiful. But was this what our soul wanted to say, Hippias: that the useful and the able for *producing something good* is the beautiful? **HIPPIAS.** It seems so to me. **SOCRATES.** But surely this is the beneficial, is it not? **HIPPIAS.** Entirely so. **SOCRATES.** Thus beautiful bodies, beautiful laws, wisdom, and all the things we just spoke of, are all beautiful because they are beneficial. **HIPPIAS.** Clearly. **SOCRATES.** The beneficial, then, seems to be the beautiful to us, Hippias. **HIPPIAS.** By all means, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** But the beneficial is that which produces good. **HIPPIAS.** It is. **SOCRATES.** And the producer is nothing other than the cause. Isn't that right? **HIPPIAS.** Thus. **SOCRATES.** Of the good, then, the beautiful is the cause. **HIPPIAS.** It is. **SOCRATES.** But the cause, Hippias, and that of which the cause is a cause, are different. For the cause would not be the cause of the cause. Look at it this way: did the cause not appear to be a producer? **HIPPIAS.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** Is it not true that by the producer, the thing "becoming" is produced, which is something other than the producer? **HIPPIAS.** It is so. **SOCRATES.** Then the thing becoming is one thing, and the producer is another. **HIPPIAS.** Yes. **SOCRATES.** The cause, then, is not the cause of the cause, but of that which becomes by it. **HIPPIAS.** Entirely. **SOCRATES.** If then the beautiful is the cause of the good, the good would be produced by the beautiful. And because of this, it seems, we are serious about and drawn toward all beautiful things: because their work and offspring, the good, is worth being serious about. It is likely, from what we find, that the beautiful is in the form of a father to the good. **HIPPIAS.** Entirely so. You speak well, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** Then do I also speak well in saying that neither is the father the son, nor the son the father? **HIPPIAS.** Well indeed. **SOCRATES.** Nor is the cause the thing becoming, nor is the thing becoming, in turn, the cause. **HIPPIAS.** You speak the truth. **SOCRATES.** By Zeus, my best of men! Then neither is the beautiful good, nor is the good beautiful. Or does it seem possible to you from what has been said? **HIPPIAS.** No, by Zeus, it does not appear so to me. **SOCRATES.** Does it please us then, and would we wish to say that the beautiful is not good, and the good is not beautiful? **HIPPIAS.** No, by Zeus, it does not please me at all. **SOCRATES.** Indeed, by Zeus, Hippias, it pleases me least of all the arguments we have spoken. **HIPPIAS.** For so it seems. **SOCRATES.** It is likely then, as it appeared just now, that the argument—that the beneficial and the useful and the able to produce something good is beautiful—is not the most beautiful argument after all. Instead, it is as possible as can be that it has appeared to be one of those more ridiculous ones, like those earlier ones where we said a young girl was the beautiful, or each of the things spoken of before. **HIPPIAS.** It seems so. **SOCRATES.** And for my part, Hippias, I do not know where to turn, but I am at a loss. Do you have anything to say? **HIPPIAS.** Not at the present; but as I just said, after looking into it, I know well that I shall find it. **SOCRATES.** But I think that because of my desire for knowing, I am not able to wait for you while you delay. For I even think I have just now found something. For see if we were to say that what makes us rejoice—not all pleasures, but what is through hearing and sight—this we call beautiful. How then would we struggle? For beautiful men, Hippias, and all embroideries, and paintings, and sculptures, delight us when we see them, if they are beautiful; and beautiful sounds, and all music, and speeches, and storytelling produce this same thing. So if we were to answer that bold man: "O noble one, the beautiful is that which is pleasant through hearing and sight," do you think we would stop his boldness? **HIPPIAS.** To me now, Socrates, it seems that "what the beautiful is" has been well said. **SOCRATES.** What then? Shall we say that beautiful practices and laws, Hippias, are beautiful by being pleasant through hearing or sight, or that they have some other form? **HIPPIAS.** These things, Socrates, might perhaps go unnoticed by the man. **SOCRATES.** By the dog, Hippias; not by the one I would most be ashamed of if I were talking nonsense and pretending to say something when saying nothing. **HIPPIAS.** Who is this? **SOCRATES.** Socrates, the son of Sophroniscus; who would no more allow me to say these things easily as if they were unsearched, than he would allow me to speak as if knowing what I do not know. **HIPPIAS.** But indeed, to me...

<summary>Socrates and Hippias reject the definition of "the beautiful" as that which is useful or powerful for good, because this logic implies that beauty and goodness are separate causes and effects. They then propose a new hypothesis: that beauty is defined by the pleasure derived specifically from the senses of sight and hearing.</summary>
<keywords>Plato, Socrates, Hippias Major, the beautiful, the good, causality, utility, sensory pleasure, sight and hearing</keywords>

# HIPPIAS MAJOR

<page-num>103</page-num>
<header>HIPPIAS MAJOR.</header>
<sig>I iiij</sig>

<margin>A</margin> ...after you spoke yourself, it seems that something else regarding the laws is coming to light. **SOCRATES.** Be quiet for a moment, Hippias. For I seem to have fallen back into the same ambiguity regarding the beautiful in which we were just a little while ago, even though we thought we held something certain. **HIPPIAS.** Why do you say that, Socrates? **SOCRATES.** I will tell you what occurs to me, if indeed I am saying anything at all. For these matters concerning customs and laws might perhaps not be outside the senses of seeing and hearing. Furthermore, let us maintain this argument—which asserts that what is pleasing to these senses is "beautiful"—and let us not bring the laws into the discussion yet. But if someone were to ask us—either the man I keep mentioning <note>Socrates often uses an "anonymous critic" (who is likely his own conscience or inner logic) to challenge his arguments</note> or anyone else—in this manner: "Why, Hippias and Socrates, <margin>B</margin> do you judge only that which is perceived by these two senses to be beautiful? Why do you not say that the things which bathe the other senses in sweetness—food, drink, sexual acts, and all other such things—are beautiful? Or do you perhaps claim that these are not sweet, and that you do not place any pleasure in the senses except in hearing and seeing?" What, I ask you Hippias, shall we reply? **HIPPIAS.** We shall certainly agree, Socrates, that great pleasures exist in the other senses as well. **SOCRATES.** "But," he will say, "since these are pleasures no less than those others, why do you deprive them of the title 'beautiful'?" We shall reply that <margin>C</margin> there is no one who would not laugh at us if we said that eating is not "sweet" but "beautiful," or that a pleasant smell is not "sweet" but "beautiful." Regarding sexual acts <note>original: "Veneris motus" - the movements of Venus</note>, everyone would contend as much as we do that it is a most sweet thing, but if someone performs it, he must do so in a way that he removes it from the sight of men, as if it were a most shameful thing to be seen. When we have said these things, Hippias, he will perhaps answer: "I have understood for a long while that shame prevents you from calling these types of pleasures beautiful, because they do not seem so to men. But I was not asking what *seems* beautiful to the common crowd, but what is beautiful in itself." We shall then say, I think, what we proposed as our definition: that the beautiful is that part of the pleasant which delights through the eyes and ears. But you, Hippias, <margin>D</margin> can you use this same argument, or shall we say something else? **HIPPIAS.** We shall say nothing else besides this, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** "You speak excellently," he will interject. "If, therefore, only that which comes as a delight through sight and hearing is beautiful, then that which delights through another sense is clearly not beautiful." Shall we confess this? **HIPPIAS.** We shall. **SOCRATES.** "But," he will ask again, "is that which is pleasant through sight also pleasant through both sight and hearing? And is that which is pleasant through hearing also pleasant through both hearing and sight?" To this we shall answer: "In no way can that which exists through one be said to exist through both," for that seems to be what you are asking. But we said that either of these two pleasures is beautiful in itself, and also both of them together. Must we not respond in this way? **HIPPIAS.** Exactly so. **SOCRATES.** "Does one pleasure differ from another pleasure," he will ask, "precisely in this: that it is a pleasure? I do not ask whether one pleasure is greater or smaller, or more or less intense, but whether, among many pleasures, one differs from another specifically in the fact that one is a pleasure and the other is not." We shall say that it does not seem so to us. **HIPPIAS.** It clearly does not. **SOCRATES.** "Then," he will continue, "it is not because they are pleasures that you have selected these specific pleasures from among all others. Rather, you must have seen something in both of them—namely, that they have a certain nature differing from the others—and looking toward this quality, you assert that they are beautiful. For the pleasure of sight is not beautiful simply because it occurs through sight. If that were the cause of its beauty, then the pleasure of hearing would in no way be beautiful, since it is certainly not produced through sight." Shall we confess that he speaks the truth? **HIPPIAS.** We shall indeed. **SOCRATES.** "Nor, again, is the pleasure of hearing beautiful because it occurs through hearing; otherwise, the pleasure perceived through sight would not be beautiful, since it is not the same as that produced through hearing." Shall we admit, Hippias, that the man who says these things speaks the truth? **HIPPIAS.** Truth indeed. **SOCRATES.** "And yet," he will say, "both are beautiful, as you say." Do we say this? **HIPPIAS.** We certainly do. **SOCRATES.** They must have, then, something in common and identical which makes them beautiful, <margin>G</margin> which is present in both of them collectively and in each one individually. Otherwise, they would not both be beautiful, nor would each one be. Come now, answer me as if you were answering him. **HIPPIAS.** I answer that it seems to me as you say. **SOCRATES.** If these pleasures both experienced something that neither of them experienced individually, they could never be beautiful by means of that experience. **HIPPIAS.** How can that be, Socrates? How can it be that both suffer a condition which neither of them suffers? **SOCRATES.** It does not seem possible to you? **HIPPIAS.** I would have to be entirely ignorant of the nature of things and of this kind of speech to think so. **SOCRATES.** You speak pleasantly, Hippias. But perhaps there is a danger that I seem to myself to see something

<column-break/>

that is exactly as you say is impossible. And yet I see nothing. **HIPPIAS.** There is no danger, Socrates; rather, you are seeing it quite clearly. **SOCRATES.** In truth, many things of this sort hover before my mind, in which I do not place my trust, since they are not approved by you—a man who has amassed more money through the study of wisdom than any other mortal of our time. I, however, my friend, as one who has never earned anything, think that perhaps you are mocking me and deceiving me on purpose, so many things do they seem to be. **HIPPIAS.** No one will know better than you, Socrates, whether I am mocking or not, if you begin to set forth these things that occur to you; for nothing...

<summary>Socrates and Hippias propose a new definition: beauty is pleasure derived from sight and hearing. They then encounter a logical problem: if both are beautiful, there must be a shared quality they both possess that makes them so, even if they are distinctly different senses.</summary>

<keywords>The Greater Hippias, Plato, Socrates, aesthetics, definition of beauty, sight and hearing, sensory pleasure, logical contradiction, shared properties</keywords>

# PLATO

<page-num>104</page-num>
<header>THE DIALOGUES OF PLATO</header>

<margin>A</margin> ...you will seem to be saying nothing, since you will never find a case where a property is shared by both of us together, but not by each of us individually, nor something that each of us possesses that both do not. **SOCRATES.** What are you saying, Hippias? Perhaps you are saying something that I don't quite grasp. But listen to me more carefully, and I will explain more clearly what I mean. For it seems to me that it is possible for both of us to experience something that I am not experiencing, nor am I such a thing, nor are you; and likewise, there are other things that both of us experience, but neither one of us is that thing. **HIPPIAS.** You seem to be bringing forth monsters <note>original: "monstra" / "τέρατα". In Greek philosophy, a 'monster' often refers to a logical absurdity that defies the natural order.</note> again, Socrates, and your answers are certainly more bizarre than they were a moment ago. Consider this: if we were both just, would not each of us be just as well? <margin>B</margin> Or if each were unjust, would not both be? Or if both were healthy, would not each be? And if each of us suffers in some way, or is wounded, or struck, or has experienced anything else whatsoever, would we not both be affected by that same thing? Furthermore, if we were both made of gold, or silver, or ivory, or if you like, noble, or wise, or honored, or old, or young, or anything else common to humans: would it not be absolutely necessary for each of us to be that thing? **SOCRATES.** Certainly. **HIPPIAS.** But you, Socrates, do not consider the whole of things, nor do those with whom you are accustomed to dispute. You strike at the surface, taking beauty and each of the existing things in your discussions and cutting them into pieces. Because of this, great <margin>C</margin> and continuous bodies of reality <note>original: "essentiam" / "οὐσίας". Here, Hippias is arguing that nature is "continuous" and that properties cannot be split between a group and its members.</note> escape you. And now you have missed the truth to such an extent that you think there is some condition or essence that applies to both things together, but not to each individually—or conversely, something that applies to each but not to both. You are all so irrational, careless, simple-minded, and foolish. **SOCRATES.** Such is our lot, Hippias—not as a man might wish, as the common <margin>Proverb.</margin> proverb goes, but as it is possible to be. <note>original: "οἷα οὐκ οἷα βούλεταί τις... ἀλλ' οἷα δύναται". A Greek proverb meaning "A man lives as he can, not as he wants."</note> But you always help us by offering correction. Indeed, even now, before you corrected us, I will show you even more clearly how foolishly we were affected, by telling you what we were thinking about these things. Or should I not speak? **HIPPIAS.** Speak to one who already knows, Socrates; for I know the condition of everyone involved in these debates. However, if you wish, go ahead and tell me. **SOCRATES.** I do wish it. In truth, <margin>D</margin> my excellent friend, we were so ignorant before you said these things to us that we held the opinion concerning you and me that each of us is "one," but that we were not both together that which each of us is individually. For we are not one, but two. We were that foolish. But now we have been taught by you that if we are both "two," then each of us must also be "two"; and if each is "one," then both must be "one." For it is impossible, according to the continuous logic of reality as Hippias explains it, for it to be otherwise. Whatever the pair is, the individual is; and whatever the individual is, the pair is. So now, persuaded by you, I sit here. But first, Hippias, remind me: are we both "one"—you and I together—or are you "two" and I "two"? **HIPPIAS.** What are you saying, Socrates? **SOCRATES.** Exactly what I said. For I am afraid to speak openly before you, because you get angry with me whenever you think you are saying something right. But tell me: is not each of us one, and does each of us not experience being "one"? <margin>E</margin> **HIPPIAS.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** If each is "one," then each is also "odd." Or do you not consider "one" to be an odd number? **HIPPIAS.** I do. **SOCRATES.** Well then, since we are "two" together, are we also "odd"? **HIPPIAS.** Not at all, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** But we are both "even," are we not? **HIPPIAS.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** Does it follow that because we are both even, each of us is also even? **HIPPIAS.** Of course not. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, it is not absolutely necessary, as you just said, that whatever is true of both must be true of each, and whatever is true of each must be true of both. **HIPPIAS.** Not in these types of cases, but in the ones I mentioned before. **SOCRATES.** That is enough for me, <margin>F</margin> Hippias. For it is sufficient that some things seem to be one way and other things another. I said—if you remember where this conversation began—that the pleasures of sight and hearing were "beautiful" not because of something that each of them has but the pair does not, nor because of something the pair has but each does not, but because of what they both have as a pair and as individuals. This is why you conceded that both together and each individually are beautiful. I concluded that if they are indeed beautiful, they are so through that very essence which follows them both. And now, the pleasures are no less beautiful; <margin>G</margin> the pleasures that come through sight and hearing, both together and each individually, are beautiful. Does it not follow for both and for each? **HIPPIAS.** Entirely. **SOCRATES.** Is it because each is a pleasure that they are both beautiful? Or by that logic, would all other pleasures be no less beautiful? For we agreed they were no less pleasures, if you remember. **HIPPIAS.** I remember. **SOCRATES.** But it was said they were beautiful because they occur through sight and hearing. **HIPPIAS.** That was indeed said. **SOCRATES.** See if I speak the truth. For as I remember, we said that "the beautiful" is that which is pleasant—not all pleasant things, but specifically what comes through sight and hearing. **HIPPIAS.** That is true. **SOCRATES.** Does not this property follow <margin>H</margin> both of them together, but not each individually? For surely each of them is not through "both" senses (as we said before), but both are through both, while each is not. Is that so? **HIPPIAS.** It is. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, each of them is not beautiful by that property which does not follow each of them; for the property of being "both" does not follow the "individual." Consequently, we may call both of them beautiful according to our hypothesis, but we cannot call each of them so. Or what do we say? Is this not necessary?

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...since you are saying nothing. For you will never find that what I have not experienced, nor you either, is experienced by both of us together. **SOC.** How do you mean, Hippias? Perhaps you are saying something, but I do not understand. Listen more clearly to what I want to say. For it seems to me that it is possible for both of us to have experienced something that I have not experienced myself, nor am I that, nor are you; and again, other things that we have both experienced, but neither of us is that thing. **HIP.** You seem to be answering with monsters again, Socrates, even greater ones than you answered with a moment ago. For look: if we are both just, would not each of <margin>B</margin> us be so? Or if each is unjust, would not both be? Or if healthy, not each? Or if anyone of us is weary, or wounded, or struck, or has experienced anything whatever, would not both of us have experienced that very same thing? Furthermore, if we were golden or silver or ivory, or if you will, noble or wise or honored, or old or young, or anything else you like of human things, being both, would not each of us be so? Indeed, by all means, there is a great necessity that each of us be this. **SOC.** Entirely so, I suppose. **HIP.** But you, Socrates, do not look at the whole of affairs, nor do those with whom you are accustomed to converse; but you strike at it, taking the beautiful apart, and cutting each of the existing things to pieces in your arguments. Because of this, such great <margin>C</margin> and continuous bodies of reality escape you. And now you have missed it to such an extent that you think there is some property or essence which exists regarding both of these together, but not regarding each; or again regarding each, but not regarding both. You are in such an irrational, unreflective, simple, and mindless state. **SOC.** Such are our affairs, Hippias, not as one wishes (as men say in the proverb each time) but as one is able. But you help us by always admonishing us. Since even now, before being admonished by you, we were in such a simple state—I will show you even more, by telling you what we were thinking about them. Or should I not tell? **HIP.** You will be telling one who knows, Socrates; for I know how each of those involved in arguments is disposed. Nevertheless, if it is more pleasant for you, speak. **SOC.** Indeed, it is more pleasant. For we, my best friend, were so foolish before you said these things to us, that we held the opinion about me and you that <margin>D</margin> each of us was "one." But that which each of us was, it turns out we were not both. For we are not "one," but "two." Such simple ideas we had! But now we have been re-taught by you that if we are both "two," it is necessary that each of us be "two"; and if each is "one," it is necessary that both be "one." For it is not possible, according to the continuous account of reality as Hippias says, to have it otherwise. But whatever both are, that is each; and whatever each is, that is both. Being persuaded by you, I sit here. However, before that, Hippias, remind me: are we one—both you and I—or are you two, and I also two? **HIP.** What are you saying, Socrates? **SOC.** These very things I am saying. For I am afraid to speak clearly to you, because you are harsh with me whenever you think you have a point. Nevertheless, tell me: is not each of us one, and is not each of us in this state of being "one"? **HIP.** Quite so. **SOC.** Therefore, if indeed one, each of us is also odd. <margin>E</margin> Or do you not think "one" is odd? **HIP.** I do. **SOC.** And are we both, being "two," also odd? **HIP.** That could not be, Socrates. **SOC.** But both are even? Is it not so? **HIP.** Quite so. **SOC.** Then is it because we are both even, that for this reason each of us is also even? **HIP.** Certainly not. **SOC.** Then it is not an absolute necessity (as you were just saying) that whatever both are, each is; and whatever each is, both are. **HIP.** Not such things as these, but such as I was saying before. **SOC.** That is enough, Hippias. For even this is welcome, since it appears some things are this way, and others are not. For I was saying (if you <margin>F</margin> remember from where the argument was spoken) that pleasure through sight and hearing would be "beautiful" in this way: because they possess something that each does not possess individually, nor both together, or both together but each does not; but by that which both and each possess. Because of this, both of them together are beautiful, and each of them. For this reason, by the essence that follows both, I thought that if both are beautiful, they must be beautiful by that; but by that which leaves out one or the other, they are not. And I still think so. But tell me, as if from the beginning: if the pleasure through sight and the pleasure through hearing are both beautiful and each is, does not that which makes them beautiful follow both of them together and each of them? **HIP.** Quite so. **SOC.** Is it then because each is a pleasure, <margin>G</margin> and both are, that for this reason they are beautiful? Or for this reason would all other pleasures be no less beautiful? For they appeared to be no less pleasures, if you remember. **HIP.** I remember. **SOC.** But because they are through sight and hearing, for this reason it was said they were beautiful. **HIP.** It was so said. **SOC.** Look then if I speak the truth. For it was said (as my memory has it) that the "beautiful" is the pleasant—not all of it, but whatever is through sight or hearing. **HIP.** True. **SOC.** Does not this property follow both of them together, but not each individually? For surely each of them (as you were saying in your list of experiences) is not through both; but both are through both, and each is not. Is this so? **HIP.** It is. **SOC.** Then it is not by this property that each of them is beautiful, which does not follow each. For the property of being <margin>H</margin> "both" does not follow "each." So that it is possible to say both are beautiful according to the hypothesis, but not each. Or how do we say? By necessity.

<summary>Socrates uses mathematical logic to dismantle Hippias's claim that a property of a pair must belong to its individuals, demonstrating that a pair (two) can be even while its members (ones) are odd. They apply this to the definition of beauty as pleasure through sight and hearing, noting this property belongs to the senses combined but not to either sense in isolation.</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Hippias, logic of properties, collective vs individual, even and odd numbers, definition of beauty, sight and hearing, philosophy of aesthetics</keywords>
