# HIPPIAS MAJOR

<page-num>105</page-num>
<header>HIPPIAS MAJOR.</header>

**HIPPIAS.** It appears so. **SOCRATES.** Shall we say then, that both are beautiful, but each one by itself is not? **HIPPIAS.** What is to stop us? **SOCRATES.** This is what seems to stop me, my friend: there were certain attributes, as we saw, that apply to individuals in such a way that if they apply to both, they apply to each; and if they apply to each, they apply to both—all those qualities you listed. Is that not so? **HIPPIAS.** Yes. **SOCRATES.** But the ones I listed were not like that; among them were the concepts of "each" and "both." Is that right? **HIPPIAS.** It is. **SOCRATES.** To which group, Hippias, does "the beautiful" seem to belong? Is it like the things you mentioned? If I am strong and you are strong, are we both strong? If I am just and you are just, are we both? And if we are both, is each of us also? So, too, if I am beautiful and you are beautiful, are we both? And if we are both, is each of us beautiful? Or is there nothing to prevent it being like the case where we are both an even number <note>The Greek text uses the example of "even" (artia). If two people are individually "one" (an odd number), together they are "two" (an even number). Thus, the pair has a property that the individuals do not.</note>, but perhaps each of us is odd, or perhaps even? Or as when each of two magnitudes is inexpressible <note>original: "arrhēta" / "irrational." In Greek mathematics, these are numbers or ratios that cannot be expressed as a simple fraction, like the square root of two.</note>, but their sum is expressible <note>original: "rhēta" / "rational."</note>, or perhaps inexpressible? And a thousand other such things which I said appeared to me. In which group do you place "the beautiful"? Does it appear to you as it does to me? For it seems to me a great absurdity for us both to be beautiful, yet for each of us not to be; or for each to be beautiful, but both not to be—or anything else of that sort. Do you choose as I do, or the other way? **HIPPIAS.** I choose that way, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** You do well, Hippias, so that we may be spared further inquiry. For if the beautiful is in this group, then the "pleasure through sight and hearing" can no longer be "the beautiful." For the combination "sight and hearing" makes things beautiful, but each one alone does not. But this was impossible, as you and I agree. **HIPPIAS.** We do agree. **SOCRATES.** It is impossible, then, for the pleasure through sight and hearing to be "the beautiful," since when it becomes beautiful, it presents a logical impossibility. **HIPPIAS.** That is true. **SOCRATES.** "Tell us again from the beginning," that man <note>Socrates refers to his unnamed, harsh critic—often interpreted as his own conscience or logical mind—who cross-examines him.</note> will say, "since you missed the mark: what do you say this 'beautiful' is, which exists in both these pleasures, such that you honored them above the others and called them beautiful?" It seems necessary to me, Hippias, to say that these are the most harmless of pleasures and the best, both together and each individually. Or do you have something else to say that distinguishes them from others? **HIPPIAS.** Not at all; they really are the best. **SOCRATES.** "This, then," he will say, "is what you call the beautiful: beneficial pleasure?" "It seems so," I shall answer. And you? **HIPPIAS.** I also. **SOCRATES.** "And the beneficial," he will say, "is that which produces the good. But the producer and the product appeared just now to be different. And so your argument has come back to the same place as before. For the good would not be the beautiful, nor would the beautiful be the good, if each of them is something else." Above all, Hippias, we shall agree to this if we are sane; for it is not right to disagree with one who speaks correctly. **HIPPIAS.** But Socrates, what do you think all this amounts to? They are but the shavings and clippings of arguments, as I said before, divided into tiny pieces. But this is what is beautiful and worth much: to be able to present a speech well and beautifully in a court of law, or in the Council, or before any other authority to whom the speech is addressed; to persuade them, and to depart carrying away not the smallest but the greatest of prizes—the safety of oneself, one's property, and one's friends. One ought to cling to these things, bidding farewell to these petty nitpickings, lest you seem to be a fool, meddling as you are now with trifles and nonsense. **SOCRATES.** My dear Hippias, you are blessed because you know what a man should practice, and you have practiced it sufficiently, as you say. But I, it seems, am held by some demonic fortune; I wander and am always in doubt. And when I show my doubt to you wise men, I am barked at by you in speech whenever I show it. For you say to me what you are saying now: that I busy myself with silly, small, and worthless matters. But when, persuaded by you, I say what you say—that it is by far the best thing to be able to produce a speech well and beautifully and to succeed in court or any other gathering—I hear nothing but insults from certain other people here, and especially from that man who is always cross-examining me. He happens to be a very close relative of mine and lives in the same house. So when I go home and he hears me saying these things, he asks if I am not ashamed to dare to discuss beautiful practices when I have been so clearly proven ignorant about the beautiful, that I don't even know what the thing itself is! "And yet," he says, "how will you know whose speech is beautifully composed, or whose is not, or any other beautiful action, when you are ignorant of the beautiful? And since you are in such a state, do you think it is better for you to live than to be dead?" It has happened to me, as I say, to be insulted and reproached by you, and insulted by him. But perhaps it is necessary to endure all this. For it is not strange if I were to be benefited by it. I think, Hippias, that I have been benefited by the conversation of both of you. For I think I now know what the proverb means when it says, "Beautiful things are difficult."

<column-break/>

**HIPPIAS.** It seems so. **SOCRATES.** Should we say both indeed are beautiful, but each one by no means? **HIPPIAS.** What prevents it? **SOCRATES.** This, my friend, seems to stand in my way: that some things are judged to be present in others in such a way that if they are present in both, they are present in each; and conversely, if in each, then in both. Are these all the things you described? **HIPPIAS.** They certainly were. **SOCRATES.** But the ones I reported are not so; in whose number were the words "both" and "each." Is it not so? **HIPPIAS.** It is. **SOCRATES.** Which of these, O Hippias, from those you set forth yourself, does the beautiful seem to be? Just as if I were strong and you were, then both are strong. Likewise if I am just and you are, then both are; and conversely, if both are, then each is. Or does nothing prevent it happening as it does in the case of even and odd numbers: where both are sometimes even, but each is odd; and sometimes both are even, and each is also? Or sometimes they are such that they cannot be expressed, yet both can be; and sometimes they cannot be. And many other things of this kind which I said occurred to me—in which number do you place the beautiful? Does it appear to you as it does to me? For it seems to me too absurd that we should both be beautiful, yet not each of us. Or conversely, each beautiful, but not both, or any other such thing. Do you choose as I do? Or rather in that other way? **HIPPIAS.** In this way, certainly.

**SOCRATES.** You do rightly, Hippias, so that we may free ourselves from a longer inquiry. For if the beautiful is among these, that which delights through sight and hearing will no longer be beautiful. For it makes both beautiful, but each one not at all. But this is impossible, as we have agreed. **HIPPIAS.** We certainly agreed. **SOCRATES.** It is impossible, therefore, for that which is pleasant to sight and hearing to be beautiful; for if that were beautiful, something impossible would follow. **HIPPIAS.** These things are true. **SOCRATES.** Here that contentious fellow will say: "Explain again from the beginning, since this has deceived you: what do you say this 'beautiful' is, which is in both pleasures, on account of which you called these beautiful, honoring them above the rest?" It seems necessary to me, O Hippias, that we answer that they are more harmless than other pleasures, and the best, both together and each individually. Or do you have something else by which they differ from the others? **HIPPIAS.** Nothing; for in truth they are the best.

<margin>Another false definition of the beautiful.</margin>
**SOCRATES.** Then he will say: "So you say the beautiful is beneficial pleasure?" We shall answer that it seems so. And you? **HIPPIAS.** I also. **SOCRATES.** He will say to this: "Is not the beneficial that which produces the good?"

<margin>Refutation.</margin>
"But the producer and the produced have just now been established as different." Whence we slide back to the same point. For neither would the good be the beautiful, nor the beautiful the good, if indeed each of them were something else. That it is so, O Hippias, if we are wise, we shall answer him at once. For it is a sin not to agree with one who speaks correctly.

<margin>Another false definition of the beautiful.</margin>
**HIPPIAS.** What else do you think all these things are, Socrates, than certain contractions and clippings of speech, as I said before, resolved into the smallest bits? But that which is beautiful and worth much is for a man to be able, having delivered an excellent speech in a court, or a council, or before any other power to which words are addressed, to persuade the listeners and carry off not some small prizes, but the greatest: the safety of himself, his property, and his friends. It is fitting to embrace these things, leaving aside these tiny little questions, lest you seem to be out of your mind while you handle such delusions and trifles, as you are doing now.

**SOCRATES.** O my friend Hippias, you indeed are blessed, who know what things a man ought to study, and have yourself studied them abundantly, as you assert. But a certain strange fortune detains me: for I am always wandering and in need. Whenever I show my lack to you wise men, I am reproached by you in words. For you immediately object, as you have just now, that I handle stupid, meager things, of no value. Finally, when persuaded by you, I offer the same things you do—that it is by far the best to be able to deliver a speech elegantly and ornately composed in court or any other assembly—then some of our people here, and that man who always refutes me, heavily rebuke me. That man is my closest relative and lives with me. Therefore, when I first enter my home and he hears me saying such things, he asks why I do not blush to dispute about beautiful institutions of life, when I have been so clearly refuted regarding the beautiful, because I am ignorant of what the beautiful itself is. For he says, "By what reason will you understand which speech is beautifully composed and which is not, or any other action whatsoever, whether it be beautiful or shameful, while you are ignorant of what the beautiful itself is? And when you are in such a state, do you think it is better for you to live than to die?" So it has happened to me, as I was saying, to be poorly received in words by both you and him, and to hear ill things. But perhaps it is worth the effort to endure all these; for it is not absurd, provided I have gained something. For I have profited so much from the company of both of you, Hippias, that

<margin>Proverb.</margin>
I think I now understand that proverb which says that "beautiful things are difficult."

<summary>In this concluding section of the Hippias Major, Socrates and Hippias fail to define "the beautiful," leading Hippias to dismiss the entire philosophical inquiry as useless pedantry compared to the practical power of rhetoric. Socrates concludes with the famous proverb "beautiful things are difficult," highlighting the elusive nature of defining absolute values.</summary>

# OF PLATO
## LYSIS, OR,
### ON FRIENDSHIP.
#### The Obstetric Method. <note>original: "Obstetricius" / "Μαιευτικός". This refers to Socratic "Maieutics," the philosopher's method of acting as a "midwife" to help others give birth to their own ideas through questioning.</note>

->SUMMARY OF THE DIALOGUE. The aim of this discussion is Friendship, which is certainly of the greatest importance in human society. It truly and wisely distinguishes false friendship—such as that foul and impure lust for boys—from true and genuine friendship. True friendship embraces a firm agreement of minds and pursuits, and a shared community of all things, free and exempt from all envy. Its efficient cause is God; its assisting cause is a similarity and kinship of character. This friendship does not belong to the wicked, but only to the good. Nevertheless, God, through mutual necessity, holds men together by a certain mutual bond, so that they are compelled to cultivate mutual society whether they wish to or not. It most greatly contributes to the constancy and firmness of friendship that friends cultivate one another and deserve well of each other through mutual services. The use of friendship is the greatest and most excellent in human life, so that it would be a supreme crime to have no regard for it. This distinction, therefore, is handed down between true and false friendship: the definition of true friendship, with its causes noted, and finally its use.<-

->SOCRATES, HIPPOTHALES, CTESIPPUS, MENEXENUS, LYSIS.<-

**I** was going from the Academy <note>A gymnasium and school outside the city walls of Athens, later famous as the site of Plato's school.</note> straight to the Lyceum along the outer road, right under the wall. When I had come to the gate where the fountain of Panops is, I happened upon Hippothales, the son of Hieronymus, and Ctesippus of Paeania, and many other youths standing together with them. Why don't you come straight to us? It would be worth your while." I asked, "To where do you mean? And who are 'you'?" "Here," he said, showing me an enclosure opposite the wall and an open door. "There we spend our time," he said, "we ourselves and many other handsome young men." "What is this place, then? And what is your occupation?" "It is a wrestling school <note>original: "palaestra". A site for physical training and, in Athens, a popular spot for social and philosophical debate.</note> recently built," he said. "Our occupation is mostly in discussions, which we would gladly share with you." "You do well," I said. "But who is the teacher there?" <margin>Miccus, a companion of Socrates.</margin> "Your companion and admirer, Miccus," he said. "By Zeus," I said, "he is no mean man, but a quite capable sophist." <note>original: "sophista". While later a pejorative, here it suggests a professional teacher of wisdom or rhetoric.</note> "Do you wish to follow me inside," he said, "so that you may see those who are there?" "I would first gladly hear what I am entering for, and who is the 'beautiful one' there?" "One seems so to one of us, O Socrates, and another to another." "But who seems so to you, O Hippothales? Then Ctesippus said, "How charming you are, Hippothales, that you blush and hesitate to tell Socrates the name. Indeed, if he has been drinking a little, it is easy for us, even when waking from sleep, to imagine we hear the name of Lysis. "The eldest son of Democrates of Aexone," he said. "Well then," I said, "O Hippothales, you have found a noble and vigorous love in every respect. "Do you think anything he says is worth weighing, Socrates?" "Do you mean to deny," I said, "that you are in love with the one he mentions?" "Not I," he said, "but I say I do not compose or write about my darling." To this Ctesippus said, "He is not of sound mind, but is babbling and insane." Then I said, "O Hippothales, I do not care to hear verses, nor even a song, if you have composed any for the youth. But I desire to understand your mindset toward boys in love." Then he said, "Ctesippus here will tell you; for he knows and remembers it. Indeed, as he says, he is worn out from hearing it from me every day." "By the gods," said Ctesippus, "certainly! # PLATO'S [LYSIS]

A Or as you wish: Answer me this. If you desired to be carried along in one of your father's chariots, taking the reins yourself when he competes, would he allow it? Not at all. Whom, then, would he allow? There is a certain charioteer hired by my father for wages. What do you say? Your parents trust a mercenary more than you with the free management of the horses? And they even pay out money for this work besides. But what then? Will they allow you to drive the mule-team and strike them with the whip? Why would they allow me? Is no one allowed to beat them? Certainly, the muleteer. A slave or a free man? A slave. It seems, then, they value a slave more than you, B their son, and they trust their property to him rather than to you; they permit him to do as he likes, but they forbid you. Furthermore, answer me this. Do they permit you to rule yourself, or not? Not in any way. Who rules you? The pedagogue <note>The "pedagogue" (paidagogos) was not a teacher, but a trusted slave whose job was to escort the boy and oversee his conduct.</note>. Is he a slave? Our slave. It is a heavy thing indeed for a free man to be subject to a slave. But in doing what does this pedagogue command you? While he leads me to my teachers. And these teachers also command you? Entirely. Therefore, your father has voluntarily set many masters and rulers over you. But when you return home to your mother, does she let you do whatever you please so that you may be happy—perhaps with the wool-work, or with the C loom when she weaves? Does she let you touch the shuttle or the comb, or the other instruments of wool-working? Then he, laughing, said: By Jupiter <note>original: "per Iouem" (by Jove/Zeus)</note>, O Socrates, she would not only forbid it, but she would strike me if I dared to touch them. By God! Have you done some injury to your father or mother? None at all. For what reason, then, do they refuse to let you be happy and dispose of things as you see fit, and instead educate you daily so that you are always serving someone, and—to put it briefly—you do nothing according to your own will? Thus it happens that such great wealth seems to profit you nothing, D since anyone else manages it more than you do; and what is more, not even your own body, so noble as it is, belongs to you, since another feeds and cares for it. You, Lysis, have no command, and you are not the master of any of your own desires. Not yet, Socrates, because of my age. See to it, son of Democrates, that age is not the real hindrance. For I think both your father and mother grant you some things and do not wait for a later age—for instance, whenever they want something read or written for them. For I think they entrust these tasks to you before any of the other servants. Most certainly. In these matters, you are allowed to keep whatever order of letters you wish, whether writing or reading. And when you take up the lyre, I suppose your parents do not prevent you from tightening or loosening any of the strings, and you may pluck them and strike them with the plectrum <note>A small tool, like a modern guitar pick, used to play the lyre.</note>. Certainly. What is the cause, Lysis, that they allow these things but forbid the ones mentioned before? Because I know these things, but those I do not. Look, E excellent Lysis, your father does not wait for age to grant you license, but as soon as he perceives you have become more prudent <term>prudentiorem|The Latin "prudens" implies both practical wisdom and technical skill.</term> than himself, he will immediately entrust both his affairs and himself freely to you. I expect so. What about your neighbor? Will he not act toward you by the same rule as your parents? Do you think a neighbor will entrust to you the management of his house if he understands you to be more skilled in household affairs than himself, or will he manage it himself? I think he will entrust it to me. Do you doubt that the Athenians will also entrust the state to you when they perceive that you are sufficiently wise? I do not doubt it. What about the Great King <note>The King of Persia, the standard example of ultimate power in Greek thought.</note>? Would he rather allow his eldest son, to whom the kingdom of F Asia shall belong, to throw whatever he wants into the broth of the boiling meat, or would he rather allow us, if we went to him and made it clear that we were more skilled in preparing food than his son? Us, clearly. And he would allow his son to throw in nothing at all, but us, even if we wanted to throw in handfuls of salt, he would certainly permit it. Why not? And if his son had a disease of the eyes, would he allow him to touch his own eyes, if he did not think him a physician, or would he forbid it? He would surely forbid it. But if he thought us to be physicians, he would not hinder us even if we wanted to open the eyelids and sprinkle in ashes, thinking we were of sound mind. You speak the truth. Furthermore, he would entrust everything else to us rather than to himself or his son, in whatever matters he thought us wiser than them. G It must be so, Socrates. This is how it stands, friend Lysis: <margin>How much trust and dignity prudence brings.</margin> in every matter in which we are prudent, everyone will yield to us—both Greeks and Barbarians, both men and women—and in these matters we shall act according to our own judgment, and no one will willingly stand in our way. Not only shall we be free in these things, but we shall be leaders of others. And since we bring benefit to these things, they will be ours. But in those matters of which we are ignorant, no one will permit us to act as we please, but all will resist us as much as they can—not only strangers, but even parents, and what is closer to us, even we ourselves will not serve ourselves, but others. Since these things provide no benefit to us, they will be foreign to us. Do you agree? I do agree. Shall we then be friends to any man, or will anyone love us in those matters in which we are H useless? Never. Therefore, neither your father, nor anyone else—

A Or as you wish; tell me this, Lysis: if you desire very much <unclear>μάλιστα</unclear> to ride in your father’s chariot, taking the reins when he competes in a race, would he let you, or would he prevent you? By Zeus, he would not let me, he said. But who then? There is a certain charioteer who receives pay from my father. How do you mean? They entrust a hired man more than you to do what he wants with the horses, and they pay him money besides? Well, why not? he said. But I suppose they entrust you to drive the mule-team; and if you wanted to take the whip and strike them, would he let you? Why would he let me? he asked. What? I said. Is no one allowed to strike them? Certainly, he said, the muleteer. Is he a slave or a free man? A slave, he said. And so it seems they think more of a slave than of you, B the son, and they entrust their property to him more than to you, and they let him do what he wants, but they prevent you. And tell me this further: do they let you rule yourself, or do they not even entrust you with this? How could they entrust me? he said. But does someone rule you? This pedagogue here, he said. Surely not a slave? But why not? Ours, anyway, he said. It is a terrible thing, I said, for a free man to be ruled by a slave. And in doing what does this pedagogue rule you? By leading me, I suppose, to my teacher. And surely these teachers also rule you? Completely, I suppose. So your father voluntarily sets many masters and rulers over you. But then, when you go home to your mother, does she let you do whatever you want, so that you might be happy in her sight—either with the wool or the loom when she weaves? For she surely does not prevent you from C touching the shuttle or the comb, or any other of the tools for working wool. And he, laughing, said: By Zeus, Socrates, she not only prevents me, but I would even be beaten if I touched them. Heracles! I said. Have you done some wrong to your father or your mother? By Zeus, not I, he said. But for what reason then do they so terribly prevent you from being happy and doing what you want? Why do they keep you all day long always serving someone, and in a word, doing almost nothing of what you desire? So it seems that you D get no benefit from such great wealth—but everyone rules it more than you do—nor from your body, being so noble; but someone else shepherds and cares for it. And you, Lysis, rule nothing, nor do you do anything you desire. For I am not yet of age, Socrates, he said. May that not be the thing that prevents you, son of Democrates. For even this much, I think, both your father and mother entrust to you; and they do not wait until you are of age. For whenever they want something to be read or written for them, they turn to you first (I think) of those in the house for this. Is that so? Certainly, he said. Is it not permitted to you then to write whatever letter you want first, and whatever second; E and it is the same with reading. And whenever (I think) you take up the lyre, neither your father nor your mother prevents you from tightening or loosening whichever of the strings you want, or plucking it, or striking it with the plectrum. Or do they prevent you? Surely not. What then is the cause, Lysis, that they do not prevent you in these things, but they do in those we were just speaking of? Because, I think, he said, I understand these things, but I do not understand those. Well then, I said, my best friend. So your father does not wait for your age to entrust everything; but on whatever day he thinks you are wiser than himself, on that day he will entrust both himself and his affairs to you. I think so, he said. Well then, I said. What about the neighbor? F Does not the same rule apply to him as to your father? Do you think he will entrust his house to you to manage when he thinks you have better sense regarding household management than himself, or will he oversee it himself? He will entrust it to me, I think. And what of the Athenians? Do you think they will not entrust their affairs to you when they perceive that you have sufficient sense? I think so. By Zeus, I said, what about the Great King? To his eldest son, who is to have the rule of Asia, would he rather entrust the throwing of whatever he wants into the meat broth for us, or to us, if we <unclear>esteemed</unclear> showed him that we had better sense than his son concerning the preparation of food? G To us, clearly, he said. And he would not let his son throw in even a little; but for us, even if we wanted to throw in salt by the handful, he would let us. How could he not? What if his son had a disease of the eye? Would he let him touch his own eyes, not thinking him a physician, or would he prevent him? He would prevent him. But if he supposed us to be medical men, even if we wanted to open the eyes and sprinkle in ashes, I think he would not prevent us, thinking that we have the right sense. You speak the truth. Therefore, would he not entrust everything else to us rather than to himself or his son, concerning whatever things we seemed to him to be wiser in than they are? It must be so, Socrates, he said. So it is, I said, dear Lysis. In those things in which we become H wise, everyone will entrust them to us—both Greeks and barbarians, both men and women. And we shall do in these things whatever we want, and no one will willingly hinder us; but we ourselves shall be free in them, and rulers of others. And these things will be ours, for we shall derive benefit from them. But in those things where we do not gain understanding, no one will entrust us to do

-> what seems best to us, but everyone will hinder us as much as they can, not only strangers, but also father and mother, and if there is anything more intimate than these. And we ourselves shall be subject to others in these things, and they will be foreign to us, for we shall gain no benefit from them. Do you agree it is so? I agree. Will we then be friends to anyone, or will anyone love us in those things in which we are useless? Surely not, he said. Now then, neither your father nor anyone else... <-

Why don't you ask, then? he said. 

I will ask, I said. Tell me, Menexenus, what I shall ask you. For I have happened, since I was a child, to desire a certain possession, <margin>E</margin> just as one man desires one thing and another another. For one man desires to possess horses, another dogs, another gold, and another honors. I, however, am indifferent toward these things, but toward the possession of friends I am quite passionate. I would rather have a good friend than the best quail or cock in the world; yes, by Zeus, I would rather have one than a horse or a dog. I believe, by the <term>Dog</term> <note>Socrates' famous idiosyncratic oath "by the dog" (of Egypt).</note>, I would choose to acquire a companion much sooner than the gold of Darius, or even Darius himself. Such a "lover of companions" I am. 

Seeing you two then, you and Lysis, I am struck with wonder and I call you happy, because being so young you have been able to acquire this possession so quickly and easily; for you have acquired him as such a friend, so quickly and so deeply, and he has acquired you. But I am so far from this possession <margin>F</margin> that I do not even know the manner in which one person becomes a friend to another. This is exactly what I want to ask you, since you are experienced. 

Tell me: when one person loves another, which of the two becomes the friend? The one who loves (the lover), or the one who is loved (the beloved)? Or is there no difference? There seems to me to be no difference, he said. How do you mean? I asked. Do both, then, become friends of each other if only one loves the other? I think so, he said. What then? Is it not possible for one who loves not to be loved in return by the one he loves? It is possible. And is it possible for the lover even to be hated? As lovers <margin>G</margin> sometimes seem to suffer at the hands of their beloveds. For though they love as much as possible, they think they are not loved in return, or are even hated. Does this not seem true to you? Very true, he said. Therefore, in such a case, I said, one loves and the other is loved? Yes. Which of them, then, is the friend of the other? Is it the lover of the beloved, whether he is loved in return or even hated? Or is it the beloved of the lover? Or is neither of them a friend to the other in such a case, unless both love each other? It seems to be the latter. 

<margin>H</margin>
Then it seems to us now differently than it did before. For then we thought that if one loves, both are friends; but now, it seems that unless both love each other, neither is a friend. It appears so, he said. Therefore, nothing is a "friend" to the lover if it does not love him back. It seems not. Neither then are they "lovers of horses" if the horses do not love them back, nor "lovers of quails," nor "lovers of dogs," nor "lovers of wine," nor "lovers of exercise," nor "lovers of wisdom" <note>original: "philosophoi" — philosophers</note>, unless wisdom loves them back. Or does each person love these things, even though they are not "friends" <note>Socrates is playing on the Greek word "philos" which can mean both "friend" and "dear/beloved."</note>? 

The poet was then speaking falsely when he said: 
"Happy is the man who has dear children, and single-hooved horses, 
And hunting dogs, and a friend in a foreign land." 
It does not seem so to me, he said. But do you think he speaks the truth? Yes. The beloved, then, is a friend to the lover, it seems, Menexenus, whether it loves or even hates. Just as newborn children, who do not yet love, or even hate when they are punished by their mother or their father; nevertheless, even while hating them at that time, they are more than anything...

<margin>In those things where we are wise, we boast and are proud.</margin> 
Is it possible for someone to be proud and boast in those things in which he does not yet have any wisdom? How can that be? If you are in need of a teacher, you are not yet wise? Not yet, certainly. Therefore you are not proudly wise, if you know nothing. Not by Jove, as it seems to me. When I had heard these things, I turned my eyes toward Hippothales, and I was not far from making an offense: for it came <margin>B</margin> into my mind to say: O Hippothales, in this way one must dispute with youths, by correcting them and casting them down, not by flattering them, as you yourself do, and corrupting them. 

But when I saw him anxious and troubled by the things said before, I remembered that he wanted to remain hidden from Lysis's presence. I recovered myself and held my tongue. Meanwhile Menexenus returned and sat down next to Lysis, where he had risen. Give effort, therefore, that you may diligently remember, so that you may report each thing to him clearly. <margin>C</margin> But if anything perhaps escapes you, you shall ask me again when you first meet me. But tell him at least something new, so that I may hear, until it is the hour for returning home. I replied that they must be imparted. This boy here does not quite perceive some of the things we are discussing, and thinks that Menexenus understands; wherefore he bids me to inquire of him. There has been innate in me from an early age a certain desire for one possession, just as in others. For behold, one desires horses, another dogs, another gold, another honors; I indeed value these things little, nor do these things move me much. But I burn with the desire for acquiring friends. Therefore I would rather have a good friend than a most precious quail, or a cock, and by Jove rather than a horse and a dog; furthermore, as I think, rather, by the Dog, than to obtain the gold of Darius, or to capture Darius himself, I would choose a best friend. 

You see how greedy I am for friendship. When therefore I observe you and Lysis, I am truly amazed, and I judge you happy, because at such a tender age it has been established that you have obtained such a great gift shortly and easily; and you have reconciled this one to yourself so easily with such great benevolence, and <margin>F</margin> he in turn has embraced you with love. But such a gift is so far from me that I do not even understand in what way one becomes a friend to another. 

But I desire to ask these things of you, as of one who is skilled. Wherefore answer me, I pray: when someone loves another, which one is made the friend of the other? The lover of the beloved, or the beloved of the lover? Or does it make no difference? It seems to me to make no difference, he said. What do you say? I asked. Do both become friends in turn, if only one loves the other? So it seems to me. What further? Can there not be found a certain lover whose friend does not respond in turn in friendship? It can. And does it not often happen that a friend is held in hatred? This sometimes happens <margin>G</margin> to lovers toward their beloveds. For though they love as ardently as possible sometimes, they are not at all loved in return, but rather are sometimes even held in hatred. Do I not seem to you to say true things? Most true. 

In these cases, does not this one indeed love, while that one is loved? Certainly. Which therefore is the friend of the other? The lover of the beloved, whether he is loved back or held in hatred? Or the beloved of the lover? Or is neither the friend of the other then, when they do not both love in turn? It seems to be thus. Otherwise, therefore, we judge now than we did above. For then it seemed that if only one loves, both are made friends; <margin>Unless both love, neither is a friend.</margin> on the contrary, unless both love each other, it must be said that neither is a friend. It appears so. 

Therefore nothing is a friend to him who loves that by which he is not loved in return. It seems not. Therefore they are not friends of horses, whom the horses do not love in return, nor friends of quails, nor of dogs, nor of wine, nor of exercise, nor of wisdom, unless wisdom loves them in turn: though individuals love these things. Yet these things are not "friends." Wherefore that Poet is a liar who says: "Happy is he who has sweet boys, who has a wealth of horses, and who has a pack of dogs and a guest from a foreign land." Not at all does it seem so to me. Does he seem to you to say the truth? Truth. The beloved therefore is a friend to the lover, as it appears, O Menexenus, whether he loves or hates: just as tender boys partly do not yet love, and partly hate, when by their parents...

<summary>Socrates shifts his dialogue from Lysis to Menexenus, exploring the paradoxes of friendship. He questions whether love must be reciprocal for a "friendship" to exist, challenging the common definitions of being a "lover" of things or people.</summary>

# PLATO'S LYSIS
## Page 110

...are beaten, yet at the very time they are being intensely hated <note>original: "odio habeant" — Socrates is using a paradoxical example of parents punishing children to show that being loved is not the same as being a friend</note>, they are dearest of all to their parents. I certainly think so, he said. Therefore, according to this reasoning, it is not the lover who is the friend, but the one who is loved. So it seems. And the one who is hated is the enemy, not the one who hates. It appears so. Thus, many are loved by their enemies and hated by their friends; they are friends to their enemies and enemies to their friends—if it is the beloved, rather than the lover, who is the friend. But what an absurdity this is, my sweet friend! Indeed, it is impossible for a friend to be an enemy, or an enemy to be a friend. You seem to speak the truth, Socrates. And if this is in no way possible, it remains that the lover is the friend of the beloved. It appears so. Likewise, that which hates is the enemy of that which is hated. Necessarily.

We must now grant the same points we did before: that often something is a friend to a non-friend, and often even to an enemy, whenever someone loves one who does not love back or who even dislikes them. Sometimes an enemy will be the friend of a non-enemy, or even of a friend, when someone hates one who does not hate back, or hates one who loves them. So it seems.

What then shall we say, if neither the lovers are friends, nor the beloved, nor those who both love and are loved? Shall we say there are some others besides these who become friends to one another? By Jove, Socrates, I do not find an answer. See, Menexenus, if perhaps we have not searched correctly in our previous points. Then Lysis said: It seems so to me, Socrates—and having spoken, he blushed. For it seemed to me that the words had escaped him against his will, because he was paying such close attention. It was clear while he was listening that he felt the argument was not holding up. Therefore, wishing to let Menexenus rest, and being very delighted with the boy’s <term>philosophy</term> <note>original: "philosophia" — here meaning Lysis’s natural love of wisdom and inquiry</note>, I addressed Lysis: O Lysis, you seem to me to speak the truth, for if we had considered correctly, we would not have wandered so far. Let us not proceed further by this path. For this inquiry seems to me like a rough and difficult road.

<margin>Friends are made by the guidance of God.</margin>
<margin>Homer, Odyssey book 17.</margin>
<margin>Like is friend to like.</margin>
But the journey we have now entered upon should be completed with the help of the poets. For they are, as it were, our fathers and guides in wisdom. They certainly speak well when they advise us who friends are; moreover, they claim that men become friends through the guidance of a reconciling God. For they say: "God always leads like to like, and makes them known to one another." <note>A reference to Homer’s Odyssey 17.218: "God always brings like to like."</note> Have you not perhaps come across these verses? I have. Perhaps also in the writings of the wisest men, in which they affirm the same thing: that like is necessarily always a friend to like. And this is the opinion of those who have treated nature and the universe. You speak truly. Do they speak well? Perhaps. And this is perhaps true in part, and perhaps even as a whole, but we do not yet understand it. For it seems to me that the wicked man, the closer he comes to another wicked man and the more frequently he associates with him, the more he becomes an enemy. For he does him injury; and it cannot be that the one who inflicts and the one who receives an injury are friends. Is it not so? Entirely so.

By this reasoning, half of that saying would be false, if indeed the wicked are "like" one another. Certainly. But they seem to me to say that the good are like one another and are friends; while the wicked, as is often said of them, are never even like themselves, but are entirely fickle and unstable. He who disagrees with himself can in no way agree with another, nor be a friend to anyone. Do you not think the same? Indeed. This then, in my opinion, is what they mean, my friend, when they say like is friend to like: that only the good is a friend to the good, while the bad man is never truly a friend to either the good or the bad.

<margin>A certain definition of friends.</margin>
<margin>Refutation.</margin>
Do you agree? I assent. We have now found who friends are. For reason dictates that those who are good are friends. It is settled. I think the same. But there is something that troubles me. And please see what I suspect. In what way is like useful to like insofar as it is like? Let us consider it this way. What benefit or harm can any "like" thing bring to another "like" thing that it could not bring to itself? Or what could it experience from another that it could not experience from itself? Since these things are such that they do not help each other, how can they be desired by each other? In no way. And what is not desired, how can it be a friend? It cannot. Or perhaps like is not a friend to like insofar as it is like; but the good man is a friend to the good man insofar as he is good, not insofar as he is like? Perhaps. But what? Is not the good man, insofar as he is good, sufficient unto himself? Yes. And he who is sufficient unto himself, in that which he suffices for himself, needs nothing at all. How could he? He who needs nothing, desires nothing.

Truly nothing. If he does not desire, he does not love. No. And he who does not love is not a friend. It does not seem so. How then will the good be friends to the good, who neither long for each other when absent (since each is separately sufficient for himself) nor have any need of each other’s help when present? By what means can such men value each other highly? By none. And they will never be friends if they do not value each other. Never. Consider now, Lysis, where we have fallen, and if we have been altogether deceived.

<margin>The opinion of Hesiod, that not likes, but unlikes seem to be friends.</margin>
In what way? I heard once from someone—I remember it still—that like is the enemy of like, and the good are most hostile to the good. He used the testimony of <term>Hesiod</term> <note>A famous Greek poet (c. 700 BC)</note>, who said that "potter is jealous of potter, singer of singer, and beggar of beggar." <note>From Hesiod’s "Works and Days," suggesting that people in the same profession or state of being are rivals, not friends.</note> And he thought this was necessarily true in all other things.

<column-break/>

**A** ...dearest to their parents. It seems so to me, he said. Therefore the lover is not the friend, according to this argument, but the one who is loved. It seems so. And the one who is hated is then the enemy, but not the one who hates. It appears so. Many, then, are loved by their enemies, and hated by their friends; and they are friends to their enemies, but enemies to their friends—if the one who loves is not the friend, but the one who is loved. Yet it is a great absurdity, my dear companion, or rather I think it is impossible, for a person to be an enemy to a friend and a friend to an enemy. You seem to speak the truth, Socrates. Therefore, if this is impossible, the one who loves would be the friend of the one loved. It appears so. And the one who hates, in turn, the enemy of the one hated. Necessarily.

**B** Thus it happens to us as it did before; from which we must admit what we did earlier: that often a friend is a friend to a non-friend, and often even to an enemy; whenever one who is not loved loves, or even one who is hated loves. Often an enemy is an enemy to a non-enemy, or to a friend, when one who is hated loves, or one who loves is hated. It is likely, he said. What then shall we do, if neither those who love are friends, nor those who are loved, nor those who both love and are loved? And besides these, shall we say there are some others who become friends to one another? By Zeus, Socrates, he said, I am not at all sure. Perhaps then, Lysis and Menexenus, we have been searching altogether incorrectly? It seems so to me, Socrates, said Lysis. And as he spoke, he blushed.

**C** For it seemed to me that the words escaped him against his will, because he was attending so closely to what was being said; it was clear even while he was listening that he was not comfortable with the argument. I, therefore, wanting to give Menexenus a rest, and being pleased by the other’s <note>original: "philosphia" — Lysis's philosophical nature</note> love of wisdom, took up the discourse again and addressed Lysis: O Lysis, you seem to me to speak the truth, that if we were looking correctly, we would never have wandered so. But let us go no further this way. For the inquiry seems to me like a difficult path; but where I have turned, it seems I must go, looking at the works of the poets; for they are to us as fathers of wisdom and guides. They speak, I suppose, not poorly when they declare who friends happen to be; but they say that God himself makes them friends, leading them to one another.

**D** They say it somewhat like this, as I believe: "God always leads like to like, and makes them known." Have you not encountered these verses? I have, he said. Have you not also encountered the writings of the wisest men, saying these same things, that like is necessarily always a friend to like? These are surely those who discourse and write about nature and the whole. You speak the truth, he said. Do they speak well then? I said. Perhaps, he said. Perhaps, I said, half of it; and perhaps even all of it. But we do not understand. For it seems to us that the wicked man, the closer he comes to another wicked man and the more he associates with him, becomes all the more an enemy. For he does wrong. And those who do wrong and those who are wronged cannot, I suppose, be friends. Is it not so? Yes.

**E** Thus, he said. In this way, then, the saying would be half true, if indeed the wicked are like one another. You speak the truth. But they seem to me to mean that the good are both like one another and are friends; while the bad (as is also said of them) are never like even themselves, but are impulsive and unstable. That which is unlike itself and different would hardly be like or a friend to another. Or does it not seem so to you? It does, he said. This then is what they hint at, I think, my friend, those who say like is friend to like: that only the good man is a friend to the good man, but the bad man never enters into true friendship with either the good or the bad. Do you agree? He nodded. We have then already found who friends are. For

**F** our argument signifies to us that they are whoever are good. It certainly seems so, he said. And to me, I said. Yet I am troubled by something in it. Come then, by Zeus, let us see what I suspect. Is the like, insofar as he is like, of any use to his like? Or rather this: where can like have any benefit or do any harm to like that it could not do to itself? Or what could it suffer that it would not suffer from itself? How could such things be loved by one another, having no help for each other? Is there any way? There is not. And that which is not loved, how could it be a friend? In no way. But then, is like not a friend to like, but the good a friend to the good, insofar as he is good, not insofar as he is like? Perhaps. What then? Is not the good man, insofar

**G** as he is good, in that respect sufficient for himself? Yes. And he who is sufficient has no need of anything according to his sufficiency. How could he not? And he who does not need anything would not love anything. Certainly not. And he who does not love would not be a friend. Surely not. How then will the good be friends to us, if they do not long for each other when absent (for they are sufficient for themselves even when apart) and have no need of each other when present? By what device could such people value each other highly? None, he said. And they would not be friends, who do not value each other. True. See then, Lysis, how we are being led astray. Are we perhaps being deceived in the whole matter? How so? he said. I once heard someone saying—and I just now remember—that like is most hostile to like, and the good to the good. And he brought forward Hesiod as a witness, saying: "Potter is angry with potter, and singer with singer, and beggar with beggar." And all other things, he said, must necessarily be so...

<summary>Socrates debates Lysis and Menexenus on whether friendship is based on similarity, eventually questioning if "the good" can even be friends if they are self-sufficient and do not need one another.</summary>

### III

The most similar things are filled with envy, rivalry, and hostility toward one another; but the most dissimilar are filled with friendship. For the poor man is forced to be a friend to the rich, and the weak to the strong for the sake of help, and the sick to the physician; and indeed everyone who is ignorant must desire and love the one who knows. He <note>Socrates refers to a poet or philosopher like Hesiod or Heraclitus who proposed that strife and opposition drive the world.</note> added further, speaking more grandly, that it was far from the case that like is friend to like; on the contrary, the most opposite is most friendly to the most opposite. For each thing desires its opposite, not its like: the dry desires the wet, the cold the hot, the bitter the sweet, the sharp the dull, the empty desires filling, and the full desires emptiness; and other things in the same way. For the opposite provides nourishment to its opposite, whereas like cannot enjoy anything from like. Indeed, my companion, he who taught such things seemed to be an eloquent and elegant man. For he spoke well. But how does it seem to us? "Quite well," said Menexenus, "as it appears at first glance." Shall we then say that the opposite is the greatest friend to its opposite? "Certainly." Let it be so, Menexenus. But I ask, is this not strange and foreign? Immediately those "all-wise" men, who excel in the eloquence of refuting <note>Socrates refers to the "Eristics," philosophers who enjoyed winning arguments through logic puzzles rather than seeking truth.</note>, will rise up against us and ask: "Is not the most contrary of all things hate and friendship?" What will you answer them? Must we not be forced to admit they speak the truth? "We must." Will they then say the enemy is a friend to the friend? Or the friend a friend to the enemy? "Neither." Can the just be a friend to the unjust, or the temperate to the intemperate? Or the good to the bad?

C It does not seem so to me. And yet, if a thing is a friend to something according to its opposite nature, these things must be friends. "Necessarily." Therefore, neither is like friend to like, nor opposite friend to opposite? "It seems not." Come, let us notice this too, lest it deceive us further: that in truth none of these things we mentioned is the "friend," but that which is neither good nor bad becomes a friend of the good. "What do you mean?" I myself am unsure, by Jove! For I waver because of the ambiguity of the discourse. And it seems, as the old proverb has it, that "the beautiful is the friend." <margin>Proverb: The beautiful is the friend.</margin> <margin>Properties of the beautiful.</margin> 
D It appears to be something soft, smooth, and sleek, and therefore it perhaps easily slips into us, creeps in and penetrates us as something slippery and smooth. For I say that the good itself is the beautiful. Do you not think so? "I do." Indeed, I am divining <note>Socrates often uses "divining" or "prophesying" when he is making an intuitive leap in logic that he cannot yet fully prove.</note> this for you: that the friend of the good and the beautiful is that which is neither good nor bad. Listen to why I prophesy this. It seems to me that there are three classes: one good, another bad, and the last, which is neither good nor bad. What do you think? "I agree." And neither is good friend to good, nor bad to bad, nor good to bad, as the previous reasoning showed. <margin>Three classes: good, bad, and neutral.</margin> <margin>Another definition of friends.</margin> 
E It remains that if anything is a friend to something, it is that which is neither good nor bad that is a friend either to the good, or to something like itself. For nothing is a friend to the bad. "Certainly." Nor yet is like to like, as we showed a little while ago. "Indeed." Therefore, that which is neither good nor bad will not be a friend to that which is exactly like itself. "It seems not." Only that which is neither good nor bad, then, can become a friend to the good alone. "That seems to follow necessarily." Now, boys, has this been correctly explained by us? If we consider a healthy body, it has no need of the art of medicine, nor of help at all, for it is sufficient as it is. Hence, no one who is healthy is a friend to the physician because of their health. "No one." But the sick person, I think, is a friend because of the illness. "How could it be otherwise?" Illness is indeed an 

F evil, while the skill of medicine is a certain good and useful thing. "So it is." The body, insofar as it is a body, is neither good nor bad. "True." Thus the body is forced, on account of illness, to seek and love medicine. "It appears so." It follows that what is neither good nor bad becomes a friend of the good on account of the presence of an evil. "It seems so." It is clear, however, that this happens before it is made fundamentally bad by the presence of that evil. For an object that has actually become bad would not seek the good, nor be its friend. For we showed it is impossible for the bad to be a friend to the good. "Impossible, without a doubt." Notice, I pray, what I am saying. For I claim some things become 

G such as that which is present to them, while others do not. As if someone wished to dye something with a color, the dye would be present in some way to the thing colored. "Certainly." Would the colored thing then be the same as the color itself? "I do not understand," he said. Perhaps you will understand it this way: if someone were to smear your blond hair with white lead, would the hairs become white, or would they only appear so? "They would appear so." Yet whiteness would be present to them. "It would." But they would be no more truly white yet; and even with the whiteness present, they are neither white nor black. "You speak the truth." But when, my friend, old age brings this color upon them, then they become truly such as that which is present—white by the presence of whiteness. "How could it be otherwise?" This is what I was asking: if a thing has something present to it, does the thing itself immediately become like that which is present? Or does it only become so if it is present in a certain way, and otherwise not? "The latter," he said.

H By the same reasoning, that which is neither good nor bad, when evil is present to it, is not yet bad. However, there are times when it has already become so. "Certainly." When it is not yet bad even though evil is present, this presence makes it desire the good; but the presence which makes it actually bad strips it of both the desire and the friendship of the good. For it is no longer neutral, but bad. And a bad thing cannot be a friend to the good, nor the good to the bad. "Certainly not." For this reason, we might say that those who...

<summary>Socrates explores whether friendship arises from opposites (like dry desiring wet) or from a "neutral" state (neither good nor bad) seeking the good to remedy a present evil, such as a body seeking medicine to cure a disease.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates, Lysis, and Menexenus. those who are already wise no longer need to practice philosophy <note>The word "philosophize" literally means "to love wisdom." Socrates argues that gods or perfectly wise men do not "love" wisdom because they already possess it.</note>, whether they are gods or men; nor do those who are so corrupted by ignorance that they have become wicked, for no one who is evil and thoroughly ignorant seeks wisdom. There remain, therefore, those who possess this evil—namely, ignorance—but are not yet entirely unrefined or ignorant; rather, they acknowledge their own ignorance, and because of this awareness, they practice philosophy—that is, they love wisdom—being as yet neither good nor evil. For the evil do not practice philosophy, nor do the good. For we saw above that neither is an opposite a friend to an opposite, nor like to like. Do you remember? "We certainly remember," they said. Entirely so, O Lysis and Menexenus; we have discovered what is a friend and what is not. For we concluded above, regarding both the soul and the body: that which is neither good nor evil becomes a friend to the good because of the presence of evil itself. They agreed to all these things. And I was greatly delighted, like a hunter who had successfully caught the prey I was tracking. Then, I know not how, a certain strange and absurd suspicion arose in me, as if the things we had agreed upon were less than true. And immediately troubled, I said: "Alas, Lysis and Menexenus, we seem to have been enriched only by a dream." "Why is that?" Menexenus replied. I fear lest we have fallen into false arguments about friendship, as if we were dealing with proud and vain men. "By what reasoning?" "By this: Is a friend a friend to someone, or not?" "Necessarily so." "Is he a friend for no reason and for the sake of nothing, or for the sake of someone and because of something?" "Certainly for someone's sake, and because of something." "Is that thing for whose sake a friend is a friend, itself a friend? Or perhaps it is neither friend nor enemy?" "I do not quite understand," he said. That which is neutral, because of the perception of evil, becomes a friend to the good for the sake of the good.

If it is a friend, it is a friend for the sake of something. "It is." For the sake of a friend, surely, if our previous agreements hold. "And a friend." Will that, in turn, be a friend for the sake of another friend? "Certainly." It is necessary, then, that by this progress we arrive at a certain principle <note>original: "principium" / "ἀρχή" (arche). Socrates is looking for the "First Friend," the ultimate source of value that makes all other things worth loving.</note> which is no longer referred back to another friend, but to that which is the **first friend**, for whose sake all other things which are called friends are so named. "It is necessary." This is what I was saying must be considered: lest all those other things, which we said were friends for the sake of that one, deceive us like mere shadows of it, while that first thing is the truly real friend. Let us consider it in this way. Whatever someone values highly—as a father does his son—he prefers above all other things. And such a man, because he values his son so highly, also values several other things for his sake. For example, if he perceives that his son has drunk hemlock, he will value wine very highly, if he hopes that by this he might cure the poison. "Most certainly." And does he not also value the jar in which the wine is kept? "Greatly." Does he then value the earthenware cup, or three measures of wine, more than his son? Or is it rather the opposite? So that all this devotion does not look to those things which are prepared for the sake of another, but tends toward that for whose sake the other things are sought. Nor is it true what we often say, that we value gold and silver highly. For all our intention and estimation belongs to that alone for which these things are prepared. Shall we say it is so? "Most certainly." The same logic applies to a friend. For whatever things we said were friends to us for the sake of some friend, we named with an improper term; but it appears that the truly real friend is that toward which all these so-called friendships tend. <margin>
A friend is not a friend for the sake of any other friend.
</margin>

Wherefore, the real friend is a friend for the sake of no other friend. "True." This, therefore, is rejected: that a friend is a friend because of some other friend. But is not the "good" a friend? Does it stand thus: if out of the three things we mentioned—good, evil, and neutral—two were taken and the evil went away and touched nothing, neither body nor soul nor any of the things which we said are in themselves neither good nor evil, would the good then be entirely useless to us? For if nothing further harmed us, we would have no need of any benefit from the good.

<column-break/>

**A** ...who are already wise no longer seek wisdom, whether they are gods or men. Nor, on the other hand, do those seek wisdom who have such ignorance that they are made evil. For no one who is evil and ignorant seeks wisdom. There remain those who have this evil, ignorance, but are not yet made senseless or ignorant by it; they still think they do not know what they do not know. Therefore, those seek wisdom who are not yet either good or evil. But as many as are evil do not seek wisdom, nor do the good. For neither the opposite of the opposite, nor the like of the like, appeared as a friend to us in our earlier discourse. Or do you not remember? "Certainly," they said. "Then, O Lysis and Menexenus," I said, "have we found above all else what a friend is and what is not? For we say that **B** in the soul and in the body and everywhere, that which is neither evil nor good, through the presence of evil, is a friend of the good." They altogether agreed and conceded that this was how it stood. And I myself was very glad, like a hunter, happily grasping what I was hunting for. But then, I know not from where, a most strange suspicion came to me, that the things we had agreed upon were not true. "I fear," I said, "that like boastful men, we have encountered some such false arguments regarding the friend." "How so?" he said. "**C** Let us look at it this way," I said. "Whatever is a friend, is it a friend to someone, or not?" "Necessarily," he said. "Is it for the sake of nothing and because of nothing? Or for the sake of something and because of something?" "For the sake of something and because of something." "Is that thing a friend, for whose sake the friend is a friend to the friend? Or is it neither friend nor enemy?" "I don't quite follow," he said. "Naturally," I said, "but perhaps you will follow this way, and I think I will know better what I am saying. The sick man, we just said, is a friend to the physician. Is it not so?" "Yes." "Therefore, because of disease and for the sake of health, he is a friend to the physician?" "Yes." "And disease is an evil?" "How could it not be?" "But what is health?" I said. "**D** A good, or an evil, or neither?" "A good," he said. "We were saying, then, as it seems, that the body—being neither good nor evil—because of disease (which is the evil) is a friend of medicine. And medicine is a good; and medicine has sought friendship for the sake of health; and health is a good, is it not?" "Yes." "Is health a friend or not a friend?" "A friend." "And disease an enemy?" "Certainly." "That which is neither evil nor good, then, because of the evil and the enemy, is a friend of the good, for the sake of the good and the friend." "It appears so." "For the sake of the friend, then, the friend is a friend, because of the enemy." "It seems so." But nevertheless let us look at this, lest the present argument deceive us. **E** Medicine, we say, is a friend for the sake of health?" "Yes." "Is not health also a friend?" "Certainly." "If then it is a friend, it is for the sake of something?" "Yes." "A friend of something? If it follows our previous agreement." "Certainly." "Then that thing will also be a friend, for the sake of a friend?" "Yes." "Is it not then necessary that we grow weary of going on like this, and arrive at some principle which will no longer refer to another friend, but will reach that which is the **First Friend**, for whose sake we say all other things are friends?" "Necessarily." "This then is what I mean: lest all those other things, which we say are friends for the sake of that one, deceive us as if they were certain images <note>original: "εἴδωλα" (eidola). For let us consider it thus: whenever someone values something highly (as sometimes a father values a son), he prefers him above all his possessions. If then he considers his son as everything to him, would he also value anything else highly? "And also the vessel in which the wine is contained?" "Certainly." "Does he then value the earthenware cup more than his son? Or three measures of wine more than his son? It is not what we often say, that we value gold and silver highly; **G** but rather, the truth is not at all like that. But that which we value above all is that thing, whatever it may appear to be, for whose sake both gold and all other preparations are prepared. Shall we say so?" "Certainly." "Is not the same argument true of the friend? For as many things as we say are friends to us, for the sake of some other friend, we seem to be calling them so by another name. But the true friend is likely that very thing in which all these so-called friendships end." "It is likely to be so," he said. "Then the true friend is not a friend for the sake of some other friend?" "True." "Let this then be dismissed: that a friend is a friend for the sake of a friend. But is the good a friend?" "It seems so to me." "Then is the good loved because of the evil? **H** And does it stand thus: if out of the three things we just mentioned—good, evil, and neither good nor evil—two were left, and evil were to go out of the way and touch nothing, neither body nor soul, nor those things which we say we love for themselves; if evil were never to exist, would the good then be of no use to us? Would it have become useless? For if nothing were to harm us any longer, we would have no need of any benefit."

<summary>Socrates deconstructs the definition of friendship, proposing that while we value many things for the sake of others (like medicine for health), there must be a "First Friend" or ultimate good that is loved for its own sake. He suggests that we only pursue the "good" as a remedy for the presence of "evil."</summary>

<margin>A</margin>And thus it would then become clear that we loved and cherished the good because of the evil, as if the good were a medicine for evil, and evil were a disease. But where there is no disease, there is no need for medicine. Is it then the nature of the good to be loved by us—who are in the middle between the good and the evil—only because of the evil? Does the good itself, for its own sake, offer us no use?
"It seems so," he said.
Therefore, that "friend" <note>original: *philon*</note> to which all those other things led—those things we said were "dear" only for the sake of another dear thing—is nothing like them. For those were called "dear" for the sake of a friend; but that which is truly a friend appears to be exactly the opposite. It appeared to be a friend to us only for the sake of an enemy. But if the enemy <note>Here, "the enemy" refers to "evil" or "harm."</note> were gone, it seems it would no longer be a

It seems so.
Does then, as we were just saying, desire
<margin>D</margin><margin>Whether desire is the cause of friendship.</margin>cause friendship? And is that which desires, a friend to the desired thing at the time when it desires? But what we said above about being a friend, was it some nonsense, like a long poem composed?
Perhaps.
Indeed, what it hungers for, it hungers for that which it lacks.
That very thing.
Therefore, that which is in need is a friend to that which it lacks.
So I think.
Anything lacks that of which it is deprived.
What prevents it?
Of that which is proper and akin, therefore, as it seems, love, friendship, and appetite exist, O Menexenus and Lysis.
We grant it.
Wherefore, if you are friends to each other, you are by nature in some way related.
And most especially so.
And whoever else desires
<margin>E</margin>another, O boys, or loves, he desires and prizes and loves for this reason: because he is related to him either according to the soul, or the habit of the soul, or manners, or appearance: otherwise he would never prize him.
Menexenus plainly agreed. Lysis, however, was silent.
But I said: what is proper by nature, it is necessary that we love.
It seems so.
Therefore it is necessary that a legitimate and non-pretending lover be loved in turn by his beloved.
To this Lysis and Menexenus finally nodded, with difficulty. Hippothales, however, exulting with joy, was of varying countenance and color.
But wishing to discuss the discourse more diligently, I added these things. If "proper" and "similar" differ, we have already said, O Lysis and Menexenus, what a
<margin>F</margin>friend is: but if the similar and the proper are the same, it is not easy to reject the former discourse—that the similar is not useless to the similar according to its similarity: but the useless, in no way a friend. Do you wish then, after we have become as if drunk by the discussion, that we confess the proper to be one thing, and the similar another?
We certainly wish it.
Shall we then place the good as proper to everyone, and the evil as alien? Or evil proper to evil, good to good, and finally neither to neither?
Each of these seems to us to be proper to each.
Again, O boys, we have now fallen into those discourses about friendship which we refuted from the beginning. For the unjust will be no less a friend to the unjust, and the bad to the bad, than the
<margin>G</margin>good to the good.
So it seems.
What further, if we say the good and the proper are the same, is not the good only a friend to the good?
Altogether.
But we thought that this, too, had been refuted by you long ago. Do you remember?
Very well.
What discourse shall we use next? To no purpose, evidently.
It is worthwhile, therefore, like wise men in the courts, to resume by enumerating all that has been said. For if neither the lovers, nor the loved, nor the similar, nor the dissimilar, nor the good, nor the proper, nor however many others we have numbered—the multitude of which I do not remember—if, I say, none of these is a friend, I have nothing further to bring forward.
When I had said these things, I noticed one of the elders moving, but immediately like certain demons the tutors, both of Lysis and Menexenus, together with their brothers, ordered them to return home. For evening had come. First, therefore, we and the others standing around repelled the tutors.

The conversation ends abruptly when the boys' tutors arrive to take them home.</summary>

# PLATO

<margin>A</margin>But when they <note>Referring to the boys' tutors or "pedagogues" mentioned in the preceding text.</note> took no notice of us, and began shouting in their foreign-sounding way, taking it poorly, they nevertheless called for the boys. Overcome by their boldness, we broke up the gathering. For it seemed to us that, because they had succumbed to the feast <note>The Hermaea, a festival of Hermes popular among schoolboys.</note>, they had nothing further to bring to the discussion. Afterward, as they were leaving, I turned to Menexenus and Lysis and briefly said: "For the present, we seem to have turned out quite ridiculous and foolish—I, an old man, as well as you boys. For as these people leave, they will mock us, saying that we think we are each other's friends (for I count myself among you), yet we have not yet been able to discover what a friend actually is."

<column-break/>

But when they took no notice of us, but in their somewhat barbaric speech began to grow angry and were no less insistent, it seemed to us they had drunk a bit too much at the festival of Hermes and were difficult to reason with. So, yielding to them, we broke up the gathering. However, as they were going away, I said: "Truly, O Lysis and Menexenus, we have made ourselves laughingstocks—I, an old man, and you two. For these people will say as they go that we think we are dearly friends to one another (for I place myself among you), but we have not yet been able to find out what 'the friend' is."
