# THEAETETUS, OR ON KNOWLEDGE.
## THEAITĒTOS, Ē, PERI EPISTĒMĒS.

->A Probing Dialogue.<-
->Peirastikos.<- <note>Greek term for a "testing" or "exploratory" dialogue, rather than one that presents a final doctrine.</note>

**SUMMARY OF THE DIALOGUE.** *Plato’s intention in this discussion is partly to prove the emptiness of sophistic doctrine—which nevertheless was spreading far and wide and had gained great authority—and partly to teach what true knowledge <note>Latin: *scientia*; Greek: *epistēmē*</note> is. With this goal, he recounts various opinions on knowledge and refutes them. Next, for this reason, he treats the state and condition of the philosopher, comparing him with political men and vividly illustrating the character of both. Furthermore, from the overall method of the discussion, he teaches what sort of reason the philosopher ought to employ to rightly acquire knowledge: namely, that he should not rashly assent to all things, but should prudently explore and examine them until he has attained a solid and true understanding of them through skillful study and effort. Moreover, the sequence and arrangement of this dialogue are as follows: After the prefaces—one showing the reason for the writing, the other the occasion for the discussion—Socrates, in order to draw Theaetetus, a youth of fortunate disposition, into conversation, testifies about his "midwifery" faculty <note>The "Socratic method" or maieutics, where he helps others give birth to their own ideas.</note> and teaches at length what it is. Then, the path for discussion being laid and the thread of speech conveniently drawn out, it is asked what Knowledge is: four definitions of which are both proposed and refuted. The first definition is that all individual sciences are knowledge. The second, that Knowledge is sense-perception. The third, that it is true opinion. The fourth, that it is true opinion with an account <note>Greek: *meta logou*.</note>. Socrates rejects and refutes all of these. This is the general description of the arrangement, from which it follows that the definition of knowledge remains pending; let no one think a certain dogma concerning Knowledge is handed down here. For this discussion is not dogmatic, but "peirastic," that is, designed for refuting the errors of the sophists.*

**EUCLIDES, TERPSIO, SOCRATES, THEODORUS, THEAETETUS.**
**ΕΥΚΛΕΙΔΗΣ, ΤΕΡΨΙΩΝ, ΣΩΚΡΑΤΗΣ, ΘΕΟΔΩΡΟΣ, ΘΕΑΙΤΗΤΟΣ.**

<margin>B</margin>**EUCLIDES:** JUST now, O Terpsio, or have you come from the country long ago? **TERPSIO:** Quite some time ago. Indeed, I looked for you in the marketplace, and I wondered that I could not find you. **EVC.** I was not in the city. **TER.** But where then? **EVC.** As I was going down to the harbor, I met Theaetetus being carried to Athens from the camp at Corinth. **TER.** <margin>C</margin> Alive or dead? **EVC.** Scarcely alive; for he is suffering from certain wounds, and what is worse, he has been seized by the lingering disease that broke out in the army. **TER.** Surely not dysentery? **EVC.** That very one. **TER.** O, what a man you describe as being in such danger. **EVC.** A truly noble and excellent man, O Terpsio; for just a little while ago I heard some people praising him wonderfully for his conduct in battle. **TER.** And that should not seem strange; rather, it would be far more amazing if it were otherwise. But why did he not stop here in Megara? **EVC.** He was hurrying home. I indeed both advised and entreated him, but he would not. And so, having escorted him part way and returning again, I remembered Socrates and wondered how divinely he spoke on other occasions, and especially how he prophesied about this man. For a few days before he died, meeting Theaetetus while he was still a mere youth, he conversed with him and both approved of and admired his natural talent. <margin>D</margin> Afterward, when I went to Athens, Socrates related to me the details of that discussion—which were most worthy of being heard—and added besides that he would certainly be an outstanding man if he reached adulthood. And he seems to have predicted all too truly. **TER.** Certainly; but what were the speeches? Can you relate them? **EVC.** Not by words, by Jove, as if from memory, but by writing. For having returned home, I immediately sketched them out in my notebooks; afterward, remembering them at my leisure, I wrote them out more fully, and as often as I went to Athens, if anything had slipped my mind, I would ask Socrates and, coming back here, I would correct it. Thus it happened that almost the entire discussion has been written down. **TER.** You speak the truth. For I heard this from you before, and desiring to know those things, I have often come here to ask you. What then hinders us now from running through it? Truly, I have need of rest, for <margin>E</margin> coming from the field, I am exhausted. **EVC.** I also escorted Theaetetus as far as Erineum; therefore, I would very gladly rest. Let us go then. For while we rest, a boy shall read it to us. **TER.** Excellent. **EVC.** Here, O Terpsio, is the book, not composed as if Socrates were relating it to me—as he actually did—but as if he were disputing in person with those with whom he said he had discussed. He said these were the geometer Theodorus and Theaetetus. <margin>F</margin> Lest, therefore, it should be troublesome in the writing if "I said" and "he said" <margin>Why speaking characters are introduced in dialogues. Cicero imitated this passage in his book *On Old Age*.</margin> were too often interposed when he agreed or denied, I have avoided these and introduced Socrates himself disputing together with them. **TER.** Cleverly done, Euclides. **EVC.** Here, boy, take the book and read. **SOCRATES:** If the people in Cyrene <note>A Greek colony in modern-day Libya, famous for its mathematicians.</note> were more of a concern to me, O Theodorus, I would inquire of you most especially about their affairs, whether any of the youths there are ardently applying themselves to geometry or any other study of philosophy. But now I love our own people more than them, and I desire rather to know which of our youths seem likely to turn out to be worthy men. These things I always explore for myself as much as I can, and I ask others whom I see the youths are willing to associate with. Now, not a few follow you, and rightly so; for you are worthy of a following for many reasons, but especially for your geometry. If, therefore, you have met anyone worthy of mention, I would gladly hear of it.

<column-break/>

**EUCLIDES, TERPSIO, SOCRATES, THEODORUS, THEAETETUS.**

**EUCLIDES:** Just now, O Terpsio, or have you come from the country long ago? **TER.** A fair while ago. And I was searching for you in the marketplace, and I wondered that I was not able to find you. **EVC.** For I was not in town. **TER.** Where then? **EVC.** Going down to the harbor, I met Theaetetus being carried to Athens from the camp at Corinth. **TER.** Living, or having died? **EVC.** Living, but only just. For he is in a bad way from some wounds; but more than that, the disease that broke out in the army has taken hold of him. **TER.** Not dysentery? **EVC.** Yes. **TER.** What a man you say is in danger. **EVC.** A beautiful and good man, Terpsio; for even now I heard some people greatly praising him concerning the battle. **TER.** And it is nothing strange; but it would be much more wonderful if he were not such a man. But why did he not stop here in Megara? **EVC.** He was pressing homeward. Since I indeed begged and advised him, but he was not willing. And so, having escorted him and coming back again, I remembered and wondered at Socrates, how prophetically he spoke of other things and especially of this man. For it seems to me that a little before his death he met him as a youth, and having been with him and talked with him, he was altogether amazed at his nature. And when I came to Athens, he related to me the words he spoke with him, and they were very worthy of being heard; and he said that it was a great necessity that this man should become famous, if he should reach his prime. And he spoke truly, as it seems. **TER.** But what were the words? Could you relate them? **EVC.** No, by Zeus, not so as to say them from my mouth; but I wrote down notes then as soon as I got home; later, at my leisure, remembering them, I wrote them out, and as often as I went to Athens, I would ask Socrates what I did not remember, and coming back here I would correct it. So that almost the whole speech has been written by me. **TER.** True. I heard it from you before, and indeed I have always been intending to ask you to show it, though I have delayed until now. But what hinders us from going through it now? And anyway, I need to rest, as I have come from the country. **EVC.** But I myself also went as far as Erineum with Theaetetus; so that I would gladly rest. But let us go, and while we are resting the boy shall read to us. **TER.** You speak rightly. **EVC.** This, Terpsio, is the book. And I wrote the speech in this way: not as Socrates relating it to me as he related it, but as talking with those he said he talked with. He said he spoke with the geometer Theodorus and with Theaetetus. So that in the writing the narrative descriptions between the speeches about himself—whenever Socrates spoke, such as "And I said" or "And I told him"—or again about the one answering, that "He agreed" or "He did not acknowledge"—should not cause trouble; for the sake of these things, I wrote it as if he were talking with them himself, leaving out such things. **TER.** And it is not at all out of character, Euclides. **EVC.** But, boy, take the book and read. **SOCRATES:** If I cared more for those in Cyrene, O Theodorus, I would ask you about things there and the people from there, if any of the young men there are taking care for geometry or any other philosophy; but now I love these here less than those, and I more desire to know which of our young men are likely to become respectable. These things I myself look for as much as I am able, and I ask others with whom I see the young men are willing to associate. And not a few come near to you, and justly; for you are worthy of it for other things, and for the sake of geometry. If then you have met anyone worthy of mention, I would gladly learn of it.

<insert>A</insert> I have heard. THEODORUS: And truly, Socrates, it is very worth my telling and you hearing what kind of lad among your citizens I have encountered. If he were handsome, I would be quite afraid to speak, lest someone think I was in love with him. But as it is—and do not be offended with me—he is not handsome, but actually resembles you in the snubness of his nose and the protrusion of his eyes, though he has these features less extremely than you do. I speak without fear. For you should know well that of all those I have ever met (and I have associated with many), I have never yet perceived anyone so wonderfully gifted by nature. For while he is a quick learner—a difficult thing for anyone else—he is also remarkably gentle, and on top of that, as brave as anyone I know. I would not have thought such a combination could exist, nor do I see it <insert>B</insert> happening often. Usually, those who are sharp like him, quick-witted, and have good memories, are also mostly prone to anger and are carried away like ships without ballast <note>original: "anermatista ploia"</note>; they grow up more frantic than brave. Those who are more steady, on the other hand, meet their studies in a sluggish way, filled with forgetfulness. But he approaches his studies and investigations so smoothly, without stumbling, and effectively, with such great gentleness—like a stream of oil flowing silently—that it is a marvel that one so young could accomplish these things so well. SOCRATES: And is he also an astronomer, a calculator, a musician, and skilled in all branches of education? THEAETETUS: He seems so to me. SOCRATES: If then he says we are alike in some part of our bodies, whether praising or blaming us, it is not very worthwhile to pay him attention. THEAETETUS: Perhaps not. SOCRATES: But what if he should praise <insert>E</insert> the soul for its virtue and wisdom? THEAETETUS: That is good to hear, Socrates; but see that he was not speaking in jest. SOCRATES: That is not Theodorus’s way. Do not withdraw from what has been agreed upon by pretending he was joking, lest he be forced to testify. For certainly no one will cross-examine him; but stay boldy by the agreement. THEAETETUS: Well, it must be done, if you <insert>F</insert> think so. SOCRATES: Tell me then: you learn some geometry from Theodorus? THEAETETUS: I do. SOCRATES: And also things concerning astronomy, harmonies, and calculations? THEAETETUS: I certainly strive to. SOCRATES: And so do I, my boy, from him and from others whom I think understand anything of these matters. But nevertheless, while I am moderately well-off in other things, I am puzzled by one small thing which must be considered with you and these others. Tell me: is not learning to become wiser in that which one learns? THEAETETUS: How could it be otherwise? SOCRATES: And by wisdom, I think, the wise are wise. THEAETETUS: Yes. SOCRATES: Now, does this differ at all from knowledge? THEAETETUS: Which thing? SOCRATES: Wisdom. Or are men not wise in the <insert>G</insert> very things in which they are knowledgeable? THEAETETUS: Of course they are. SOCRATES: Then wisdom and knowledge are the same thing? THEAETETUS: Yes. SOCRATES: This is the very thing that puzzles me, and I cannot sufficiently grasp by myself what knowledge actually is. Can we then say what it is? What do you say? Who among us will speak first? He who misses the mark, and whoever misses every time, shall sit as the "ass," as the children say when they play ball; but he who survives without missing shall be our "King" and shall command whatever answer he wishes. Surely, Theodorus, I am not being rude through my love of talk <note>original: "philologia"</note>, being eager to make you discuss and become friends and companions with one another? The steady ones, however, when they apply themselves to disciplines, are often slow, sluggish, and forgetful. For in truth, youth profits in all things; and as you have begun, do not let Theaetetus go, but question him. **SOCRATES.** You hear this, O Theaetetus, what Theodorus says: whom you, as I think, will gladly obey. For it is not right that in such matters a youth should obey a wise man less. Therefore, answer nobly: what do you think knowledge is? **THEAETETUS.** I must obey, O Socrates, since you both command it; for if I should err in anything, you will correct me. **SOCRATES.** We shall do so, without doubt, if in any way we are <margin>The first definition of knowledge.</margin> able. **THEAETETUS.** It seems to me that the things one can learn from Theodorus B are knowledge: geometry, and the rest which you enumerated before; furthermore, the crafts of cobblers and other artisans—each and all of these are nothing other than knowledge. **SOCRATES.** Generously and magnificently, O friend, when asked for one thing, you have given many and various things instead of a simple one. **THEAETETUS.** For what reason do you say that, O Socrates? **SOCRATES.** Perhaps I say nothing, but I will show you what I think. Whenever you say "cobbling," do you mean anything other than the knowledge of making shoes? **THEAETETUS.** Nothing else. **SOCRATES.** What then, when you say "carpentry," that is, the builder's craft? Is it anything other than the knowledge of wooden works? **THEAETETUS.** Certainly not. **SOCRATES.** In both cases, then, do you not C declare that of which each is the knowledge? **THEAETETUS.** Exactly. **SOCRATES.** But our question was not this—of what things there is knowledge, nor how many they are; for we were not seeking to count them, but to know what knowledge itself is. Or do I say nothing? **THEAETETUS.** No, you speak correctly. **SOCRATES.** Consider also this: if someone asked us about some of these common and cheap things, such as clay <note>original: "lutum"</note>, "what is it?" and we answered him: "the clay of the potters, the clay of the doll-makers, and the clay of the brick-makers," would we not appear ridiculous? **THEAETETUS.** Perhaps. **SOCRATES.** First, indeed, because we think that he who asks can understand from our answer <margin>To be ignorant of the simple is to be ignorant of the specific.</margin> if we say "clay," and only add "of the doll-makers" or of whatever D other artisans; or do you think anyone understands the name of any thing, who does not know what that thing itself is? **THEAETETUS.** Not at all. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, he does not understand the knowledge of shoes who does not know what knowledge is. **THEAETETUS.** Certainly not. **SOCRATES.** He also does not understand cobbling who is ignorant of what knowledge is, nor any other craft. **THEAETETUS.** It is so. **SOCRATES.** Thus it is a ridiculous answer, if someone, when asked what knowledge is, answers with the name of some craft. For he answers that it is the knowledge *of something*, when he was not asked that. **THEAETETUS.** It seems so. **SOCRATES.** Furthermore, when it is possible to answer simply and briefly, he wanders E through an immense circuit. Just as in the question about clay, something light and simple can be returned: that earth mixed with moisture is clay. But whose clay it is should be left aside. **THEAETETUS.** It seems easy now, O Socrates. For you seem to ask for what recently came to the mind of me and this "Socrates" <note>Referring to "Young Socrates," another student present</note> who shares your name, while we were discussing. **SOCRATES.** What was that, O Theaetetus? **THEAETETUS.** Theodorus here was writing about the powers <term>potestates/dynameis: in this context, the side lengths of squares whose areas are not perfect squares (irrational roots)</term> of three-foot and five-foot magnitudes, showing that in length they are not commensurable with the one-foot magnitude. And proceeding in this way, selecting each one up to the magnitude of seventeen feet, he finally stopped there. Thus a similar thing came to our mind: since the powers appeared infinite in number, we should try to comprehend them in one term by which we might describe them all. **SOCRATES.** And did you find such a thing? **THEAETETUS.** It seems so to me; you also consider it. **SOCRATES.** Speak. F **THEAETETUS.** We divided all numbers into two parts. One which can be produced by multiplying equal by equal, which we compared to the square figure, calling it square and equilateral. **SOCRATES.** Excellent. **THEAETETUS.** And the number which is between these, such as three and five, and every number which cannot be produced by equal multiplied by equal, but is produced either by a larger number taken fewer times or a smaller number taken more often, and always has a greater and a smaller side containing it—this we compared to an oblong figure <note>original: "altera parte longiori"</note>, and called it an oblong number. **SOCRATES.** Excellent, what then? **THEAETETUS.** All the lines which square the equilateral and plane number, G we defined as "lengths"; those however which square the oblong number, we called "powers," as they are in no way commensurable in length with the former, but only in the planes <note>areas</note> they are able to form: and concerning solids, something else of this kind. **SOCRATES.** Best of all men, O boys! So it seems Theodorus will by no means be guilty of false testimony. **THEAETETUS.** Truly, O Socrates, what you ask about knowledge, I cannot answer as I did about length and power, although you seem to me to seek something of this kind. So it happens that Theodorus appears false in turn. **SOCRATES.** What then? if he had praised you for speed in running, adding that he had seen no one among the youths more ready in the race: and then in running you were defeated by an adult and a very fast man, would you think he had praised you any less truly? **THEAETETUS.** Not at all. **SOCRATES.** But do you think knowledge, as I was saying a little while ago, is something light to find, or rather one of the weightiest and highest things? **THEAETETUS.** By Jove, I think it is something of the highest. **SOCRATES.** Trust in your own strength, and do not think little of Theodorus's testimony. Strive with all zeal to attain the definition of what knowledge is, as with other things. **THEAETETUS.** For the sake of striving, O Socrates, we shall do this. **SOCRATES.** Come then...

<column-break/>

...not. Those to whom this would be pleasing, and much more than the former. For in A truth youth has progress in everything. But as you have begun, do not let go of Theaetetus, but question him. **SOCRATES.** Do you hear, Theaetetus, what Theodorus says? Whom to disobey (as I think) you would not wish, nor is it right in such matters to disobey a wise man when he commands a younger one. But well and nakedly say what knowledge seems to you to be. **THEAETETUS.** Well, it is necessary, Socrates, since you two command it. For if I should fail in anything, you will set it right. **SOCRATES.** Certainly, if indeed we are able. **THEAETETUS.** It seems then to me that both the things one might learn from Theodorus are knowledge—geometry and those things you just ran through—and B again cobbling and the crafts of the other artisans; all and each of these are nothing else than knowledge. **SOCRATES.** Nobly and generously, my friend, when asked for one thing you give many, and various things instead of the simple. **THEAETETUS.** How and what do you mean by this, Socrates? **SOCRATES.** Perhaps nothing; however, I will explain what I think. When you say "shoemaking," do you mean anything other than the knowledge <note>original: "episteme"</note> of the production of shoes? **THEAETETUS.** Nothing. **SOCRATES.** And what when you say "carpentry"? Is it anything other than the knowledge of the production of wooden vessels? **THEAETETUS.** Not even this. **SOCRATES.** Therefore in both you define that of which each is the knowledge. **THEAETETUS.** Yes. **SOCRATES.** But the thing asked, Theaetetus, was not this: of C what is knowledge, nor how many they are. For we did not ask wishing to count them, but to know knowledge itself, whatever it is. Or do I say nothing? **THEAETETUS.** Most correctly indeed. **SOCRATES.** Consider then also this. If someone asked us of some common and ready-to-hand things, such as clay, what it is? If we answered him: "the clay of the potters, and the clay of the doll-makers, and the clay of the brick-makers," would we not be ridiculous? **THEAETETUS.** Perhaps. **SOCRATES.** First indeed, for thinking the questioner could understand from our answer when we say "clay," adding "of the doll-makers," or of whatever other artisans. Or does anyone think they understand the name of a thing who does not know what D it is? **THEAETETUS.** Not at all. **SOCRATES.** Then he does not understand the knowledge of shoes who does not know knowledge. **THEAETETUS.** No indeed. **SOCRATES.** Then he does not understand cobbling who is ignorant of knowledge, nor any other craft. **THEAETETUS.** It is so. **SOCRATES.** Ridiculous then is the answer to the one who asked what knowledge is, when one answers with the name of some craft. For he answers that it is the knowledge *of something*, not having been asked this. **THEAETETUS.** It seems so. **SOCRATES.** Then, when it is possible to answer commonly and briefly, he goes around an endless road. As in the question of clay, it is common and simple to say that earth mixed with moisture would be clay. But whose it is, let be. **THEAETETUS.** It is easy, Socrates, now it seems so. But you E happen to ask what recently occurred to us as we were talking, both me and this namesake of yours, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** What sort of thing, Theaetetus? **THEAETETUS.** Concerning powers <note>original: "dynameon"</note> Theodorus here was writing for us, about the three-foot and five-foot, showing that in length they are not commensurable with the one-foot; and thus taking each one by one, up to the seventeen-foot. But at this one he somehow stopped. So something like this occurred to us, since the powers appeared infinite in number, to try to collect them into one, by which we would address all these powers. **SOCRATES.** And did you find some such thing? **THEAETETUS.** I think so. You also look. **SOCRATES.** Say it. **THEAETETUS.** We divided all number in two. That which is F able to be produced by equal times equal, likening its shape to the square, we called "square" and "equilateral." **SOCRATES.** And well done. **THEAETETUS.** Then the number between this, of which are three and five, and every one that is unable to be equal times equal, but is either more times fewer or fewer times more, and a greater and a smaller side always contains it, likening this to the oblong shape, we called "oblong number." **SOCRATES.** Excellent. But what after this? **THEAETETUS.** As many lines as square the equilateral and plane number, we defined as "length"; but as many as square the oblong, we called "powers"; as being in length not commensurable with those, but in the planes which they are able to form. And about G solids, another such thing. **SOCRATES.** Best of men, boys! So it seems to me Theodorus will not be liable to charges of false witness. **THEAETETUS.** And yet, Socrates, what you ask about knowledge, I would not be able to answer as I did about length and power. Although you seem to me to seek something like that. So that again Theodorus appears false. **SOCRATES.** What? If praising you for running, he said he had met no youth so runner-like, then running, you were defeated by one in his prime and very fast, do you think he would have praised you any less truly? **THEAETETUS.** Not I. **SOCRATES.** But do you think knowledge (as I was just saying) is a small thing to find out, and not one of those things that are altogether at the top? **THEAETETUS.** By Zeus, I think it is very much of the highest. **SOCRATES.** Have courage then about yourself, and believe what Theodorus said, and be eager in every way concerning other things and knowledge to grasp the account of what it happens to be. **THEAETETUS.** For the sake of eagerness, Socrates, it will be clear. **SOCRATES.** Go on then; for you just led the way well.

<summary>In this passage, Socrates challenges Theaetetus to define knowledge, rejecting a list of examples in favor of a singular essence. Theaetetus illustrates his understanding by describing how he and his friend mathematically categorized different types of numbers and square roots into single definitions.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue where Socrates presses Theaetetus for a single definition of "knowledge" rather than a list of examples. Socrates now begins his famous explanation of his "maieutic" or midwifery method of teaching.</meta>

### THEAETETUS

# THEAETETUS

<margin>A</margin> Take heart, for you have just explained it beautifully. Try to imitate your answer regarding the mathematical powers; just as you grouped those many examples into one single form, try also to describe the many types of knowledge with a single definition. **THEAETETUS.** Rest assured, Socrates, I have often attempted to consider this when I heard the questions you were asking. But I cannot persuade myself that I have any adequate answer, nor have I heard anyone else speak in the way you require. Yet, for all that, I cannot stop worrying about it. **SOCRATES.** You are in labor, my dear Theaetetus, because you are not empty, but pregnant <note>Socrates uses the metaphor of pregnancy (ἐγκύμων/gravidus) to describe the state of having a difficult idea that is ready to be expressed.</note>. **THEAETETUS.** I do not know, Socrates; I am only telling you what I am experiencing. **SOCRATES.** O you ridiculous man, have you not heard that I am the son of a midwife—a very noble and formidable one named Phaenarete? **THEAETETUS.** I have heard that much. **SOCRATES.** And have you also heard that I practice the same <margin>B</margin> art? **THEAETETUS.** Not at all. **SOCRATES.** Know that it is so, but do not betray me to others. For I have kept it secret, my friend, that I possess this art. People, because they do not know this, do not say this about me; instead, they say that I am a most eccentric man <note>The Greek "atopōtatos" implies someone who is "out of place" or profoundly strange.</note> who leads men into a state of doubt. Have you heard that too? **THEAETETUS.** I certainly have. **SOCRATES.** Shall I tell you the reason for this? **THEAETETUS.** Please do. **SOCRATES.** Consider the whole business of midwives, and you will easily understand what I mean. You know that none of them attend to other women in childbirth as long as they themselves are still conceiving and bearing children; they only do so when they are <margin>C</margin> no longer able to bear. **THEAETETUS.** Quite true. **SOCRATES.** They say the cause of this is the goddess Diana <note>Original Greek: "Artemis." The Latin column uses "Diana," the Roman equivalent of the Greek goddess of the hunt and childbirth.</note>, who, though she is childless, has taken childbirth under her protection. She did not allow sterile women to be midwives, because human nature is too weak to master an art regarding things of which it has no experience. Instead, she assigned the task to those who can no longer conceive due to their age, honoring them for their likeness to herself. **THEAETETUS.** That makes sense. **SOCRATES.** Is it not also likely and even necessary that those who are pregnant—and those who are not—are better recognized by midwives than by anyone else? **THEAETETUS.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** Furthermore, by using medicines and incantations, midwives are able to stir up the labor <margin>D</margin> pains or make them milder if they wish. They can help those who have difficulty giving birth and, if it seems best to induce a miscarriage while the fetus is young, they do so. **THEAETETUS.** That is true. **SOCRATES.** Have you also noticed this about them: that they are the most clever matchmakers <note>Greek: "promnestriai"; Latin: "pronubae." Women who arranged marriages based on who would produce the best children.</note>, being entirely wise in knowing which woman should be joined to which man to produce the best children? **THEAETETUS.** I did not know that. **SOCRATES.** You should know that they pride themselves on this more than on the cutting of the umbilical cord. Think about it: do you think the care and harvesting of the fruits of the earth belongs to one art, and the knowledge of which plant should be put in which soil belongs to another? **THEAETETUS.** No, to the same art. **SOCRATES.** And in the case of women, my friend, do you think one art is for the sowing and another <margin>E</margin> for the harvest? **THEAETETUS.** That is not likely. **SOCRATES.** Certainly not. But because of the unjust and unskillful joining of man and woman, which is called "pandering," respectable midwives avoid matchmaking. They fear that through this praise-worthy study they might be accused of being procurers; yet, it belongs truly only to genuine midwives to arrange marriages correctly. **THEAETETUS.** So it seems. **SOCRATES.** Such then is the office of midwives, but my own drama is slightly different. For it does not happen to women that they sometimes give birth to phantoms <note>Greek: "eidola"; Latin: "simulacra." Here meaning false ideas or empty images of truth.</note> and sometimes to real things. This is not easy to distinguish. If it were, it would be the <margin>F</margin> greatest and most beautiful task for midwives to judge what is true and what is not. Don't you think? **THEAETETUS.** I do. **SOCRATES.** My own art of midwifery possesses all the same qualities as theirs. But it differs in that I attend to men, not women, and I watch over the births of their souls, not their bodies. The greatest thing in our art is this: to be able to test in every way whether the young man’s mind is bringing forth a phantom and a lie, or something fertile and true. For I myself suffer the same thing as the midwives: I am barren <margin>G</margin> of wisdom. And what many have reproached me for—that I always ask others but never answer anything myself because I have no wisdom to give—is a true reproach. The cause of this is that God compels me to act as a midwife, but has forbidden me to give birth. Therefore, I am not at all wise myself, nor have I any discovery that is the offspring of my own soul. But those who associate with me, though they may seem very ignorant at first, eventually make wonderful progress if God favors them—both in their own eyes and in the eyes of others. This much is certain: they never learn anything from me, but rather they find many beautiful things within themselves. Of this midwifery, both God and I are the cause. <margin>H</margin> This is clear from what follows: many who did not know this and took the credit for themselves, while looking down on me, either left me sooner than they should have or were persuaded to do so by others. Once they left, they miscarried the rest of their ideas due to bad company, and they lost the ideas I had delivered by nurturing them poorly—valuing phantoms and lies more than the truth. In the end, they seemed ignorant both to themselves and to others. One of these was Aristides, the son of Lysimachus, and many others. When they come back to me, begging for my company again and doing remarkable things to get it, the divine sign <note>The "daimonion" (δαιμόνιον) was an internal voice or spirit that Socrates claimed warned him against certain actions.</note> that comes to me forbids me from associating with some of them...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Be of good heart, for you have just set it forth excellently. Try, by imitating that response concerning the powers, just as you included those many things in one category, to likewise embrace many sciences in one definition. **THEAETETUS.** Know, O Socrates, that I have tried this many times while I heard these questions of yours being circulated. But I can neither persuade myself that I am fit for these things, nor do I hear anyone else disputing as you prescribe; yet, I cannot desist from the inquiry. **SOCRATES.** You are in pain, O friend Theaetetus, because you are not empty, but pregnant. **THEAETETUS.** I do not know, O Socrates, but I am telling you what has happened to me. **SOCRATES.** O ridiculous man, have you not heard that I am the son of a midwife, very noble and stern, named Phaenarete? **THEAETETUS.** I have indeed heard it. **SOCRATES.** Have you also heard that I am engaged in the same art? <margin>B</margin> **THEAETETUS.** Not at all. **SOCRATES.** Know that it is so, but do not betray me before others. For it has been hidden from everyone until now that I am endowed with this art; and they, being ignorant, do not say this about me, but rather that I am most absurd and lead men <margin>Midwives.</margin> into ambiguity—have you heard this? **THEAETETUS.** Exactly that. **SOCRATES.** Do you wish for me to assign a cause <margin>Diana forbade sterile women from becoming midwives.</margin> for this? **THEAETETUS.** Why would I not? **SOCRATES.** Think of what midwives are like, and you will easily perceive what I want. For you know that none of them help those in labor as long as she herself conceives and bears, but only <margin>C</margin> when they themselves are already unfit for offspring. **THEAETETUS.** Precisely. **SOCRATES.** They say the cause of this is Diana, who, since she is sterile, took up the protection of births; she forbade sterile women from becoming midwives, because human nature is too weak for the arts of those things which it has never experienced. However, to those who can no longer conceive because of age, she commanded this, honoring her own likeness. **THEAETETUS.** That is indeed likely. **SOCRATES.** Is it not also probable and necessary that those who are pregnant, and those who are not, are more sharply noticed by midwives than by others? **THEAETETUS.** Entirely. **SOCRATES.** Furthermore, with medicines and incantations, midwives are able to stir up or soften <margin>D</margin> the distress of birth, and to help those giving birth with difficulty, and to bring out the offspring, or if it seems untimely, to dull and push it back. **THEAETETUS.** You tell the truth. **SOCRATES.** Have you also heard this about them, that they are most fit as matchmakers in arranging marriages? For they best understand who should be joined to whom for the procreation of noble offspring. **THEAETETUS.** I did not know that well enough. **SOCRATES.** Indeed, you should know they glory in this no less than in the cutting of the umbilical cord itself. For what, do you think it belongs to another art, or the same one, to care for and collect the fruits of the earth, and again to distinguish which plant or which seed should be cast into which soil? **THEAETETUS.** The same. **SOCRATES.** In the case of women, then, O friend, do you think this is of one faculty and that of another? **THEAETETUS.** Surely it is not <margin>E</margin> fitting. **SOCRATES.** Certainly not; but because of the unjust and absurd joining of male and female, which is named "pandering," <margin>Why midwives are unwilling to be matchmakers.</margin> chaste midwives flee the duty of conciliating marriage; they fear lest for their laudable zeal they be marked with the brand of pandering, since it belongs only to legitimate midwives to correctly join males and females. **THEAETETUS.** It is established. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, that is the duty of midwives; my work is in some way lighter. For it does not happen to women that they sometimes give birth to phantoms, and sometimes to true things. This indeed is not easy to discern; but if it were <margin>F</margin> joined to their office, the greatest and most distinguished task of midwives would <margin>Socrates's art of midwifery.</margin> be to discern the true from the false. But what do you feel? **THEAETETUS.** The same, surely. **SOCRATES.** To my art indeed is present whatever pertains to their midwife-like diligence. But it excels in this: that it helps males, not females, in labor, and that it watches over the offspring of souls, not of bodies. Moreover, it is most especially in my art to be able to diligently examine whether the thought of the youth brings forth <margin>Why Socrates always asks and never answers.</margin> a phantom and a falsehood, or something native and true. Furthermore, what happens to midwives happens also to me. I am sterile, and empty of wisdom; and what many have cast against me— <margin>G</margin> that I question each person but answer none, because I have nothing that I can wisely answer—is an accusation they cast too truly. This is surely the cause: God compels me to help those in labor, but has prohibited me from generating. Wherefore, I am not myself wise in any matter at all, nor does any invention of my mind exist that was born of me. But those who associate with me appear at first to be unlearned, but then by my association, those whom God himself favors profit in a wonderful way, as they seem both to themselves and to others. Yet this is established: that they never learn anything from me; rather, they themselves, possessing many excellent things within themselves, find them. Of the duty of midwifery, surely, God and I are the cause, which <margin>H</margin> can be guessed most of all from this: for many in the past, being ignorant of this and considering themselves the cause, despised me—perhaps persuaded by others—wherefore they departed from me sooner than was fitting. These, having departed, because of wicked association, miscarried the rest; and moreover, those things which I had already pulled out from the guts of their souls by my midwife’s help, by poorly nourishing them, they utterly lost, since they preferred falsehoods and phantoms too much over the truth. At last, they seemed unlearned to themselves and to others. Among their number was Aristides, the son of Lysimachus, and very many others. When they return to me, needing my association again and seeking it wonderfully, my divine sign immediately prohibits me from associating with some of them...

<summary>Socrates introduces the "Maieutic" method, comparing his role as a philosopher to that of a midwife like his mother. He explains that he does not teach wisdom but helps others deliver the truths already pregnant within their own souls.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Socrates’s explanation of his "intellectual midwifery." He has just told Theaetetus that he (Socrates) is the son of a midwife and practices the same art on the souls of men. He now explains the difficult process of "delivering" an idea and begins the formal examination of Theaetetus's first definition of knowledge.</meta>

->P L A T O’ S<-

...to others he allows it, those who once again make great progress. For my associates suffer this same thing as women in labor. They are tormented and filled with difficulties day and night, much more than those women are. My art is able to both stir up and soothe this pain. And so it is with them. But sometimes, O Theaetetus, when I notice those who do not seem to me to be "pregnant," seeing that they have no need of my work, I gladly match them in marriage to others; and, if I may speak with God's help, I have a sharp foresight as to whose company will benefit them most. Many of these I have handed over to Prodicus <note>Prodicus of Ceos was a contemporary Sophist known for his lectures on linguistics and ethics.</note>, and many to other wise and divine men. I have recounted all these things at length, my dear boy, for this reason: I suspected that you were in pain, being pregnant with some inner concept, just as you yourself believe. Therefore, commit yourself to me as to the son of a midwife, one who is himself an expert in the midwifery of the soul; and when I ask you questions, strive to answer to the best of your ability. And if, while I am examining what you say, I should decide it is a mere phantom <note>original: "simulachrum" / "εἴδωλον" (eidōlon). This refers to a "wind-egg" or a false, hollow idea that lacks substance.</note> rather than the truth, and I refute it and cast it aside, I pray you do not be angry with me, as women experiencing their first birth are prone to be toward their midwives. For many before now, O wonderful youth, have been so affected toward me that they were ready to attack me with their teeth when I took away some nonsense of theirs. They did not think I did this out of benevolence, for they were unaware that no God is ill-willed toward men, nor do I do any such thing out of ill-will. To me, it seems utterly forbidden to accept what is false or to suppress what is true. Therefore, Theaetetus, try again from the beginning to explain what knowledge is, as well as you can. Never say that you cannot; for if God wills it and gives you courage, you will be able.

<margin>Second definition: knowledge is perception.</margin>
**THEAETETUS.** Since you command it so, Socrates, it would be shameful if someone did not put forward his opinion. It seems to me that he who knows something perceives that which he knows; and as it now appears, knowledge is nothing other than perception <note>original: "sensus" / "αἴσθησις" (aisthesis). This is the first of three major definitions of knowledge explored in this dialogue.</note>. **SOCRATES.** How nobly you have answered, my boy! For this is how one who wishes to define anything ought to speak. But let us consider this together, whether this "offspring" is solid or a mere empty wind-egg. You say knowledge is perception? **THEAETETUS.** I do. **SOCRATES.** You seem to have brought forth a definition of knowledge that is by no means contemptible, but it is the same one that Protagoras put forward, though in a different way. For he says that "Man is the measure of all things; of those that are, that they are, and of those that are not, that they are not." Have you ever read it? **THEAETETUS.** I have indeed, many times. **SOCRATES.** Does he not say something like this: "As each thing appears to me, so it is to me; and as it appears to you, so it is to you"? And we are both men. **THEAETETUS.** That is certainly what he says. **SOCRATES.** Yet it is probable that a wise man is not talking nonsense. Let us follow him. Does it not often happen that when the same wind is blowing, one of us feels cold and the other does not? And one feels it slightly, the other intensely? **THEAETETUS.** Without a doubt. **SOCRATES.** Shall we then say the wind itself is in itself cold or not cold? Or shall we believe Protagoras, that to the one who feels cold it is cold, and to the one who does not, it is not? **THEAETETUS.** It seems so. **SOCRATES.** And does it not "appear" so to each of them? **THEAETETUS.** Yes. **SOCRATES.** But to "appear" is to perceive? **THEAETETUS.** It is. **SOCRATES.** Appearance and perception are therefore the same in matters of heat and all such things. For as each person perceives things, such they seem to be for each person. **THEAETETUS.** So it seems. **SOCRATES.** Perception, then, is always of that which exists, and it is never false, since it is knowledge. **THEAETETUS.** That appears to be the case. **SOCRATES.** By the Graces! Was Protagoras not an exceptionally wise man? He hinted at this to us, the common rabble, but he explained the truth in secret to his disciples. **THEAETETUS.** In what way do you say that, Socrates? **SOCRATES.** I will tell you—and it is no small theory—that nothing is ever one thing by itself, nor can you rightly call anything by any name or quality. For if you call it "great," it will also appear "small"; if "heavy," then "light." And so it is with everything, as if nothing were "one," or "something," or "of a certain kind." Instead, from transit, motion, and mutual mixture, all things arise which we say "are," though we name them incorrectly. For nothing ever *is*, but everything is always *becoming* <note>This introduces the Heraclitean doctrine of Flux, which Socrates will link to Protagoras's relativism.</note>.

<margin>All the wise, except Parmenides, said that all things are always being transformed.</margin>
And in this, all the wise men in order, except Parmenides <note>Parmenides was the famous dissenter who argued that Being is one, changeless, and eternal, and that motion is an illusion.</note>, have agreed: Protagoras, Heraclitus, Empedocles, and the greatest of the poets in both kinds of poetry—Epicharmus in comedy, and Homer in tragedy. For when Homer called Oceanus the origin of the gods and Tethys their mother, he proclaimed that all things are born from flux and motion. Does he not seem to be saying this? **THEAETETUS.** To me, he does. **SOCRATES.** Who then would dare to fight against such an army, with Homer as its leader, without being considered ridiculous? **THEAETETUS.** It is a hard task, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** Hard indeed, Theaetetus. Especially since these points can serve as evidence for the argument: that motion creates what "is" or what "becomes," while rest causes non-existence and destruction.

<margin>The origin of fire.</margin>
For fire and heat, which beget and govern other things, are themselves produced by transit and friction; and this is motion. Is this not the origin of fire? **THEAETETUS.** It certainly is. **SOCRATES.** Furthermore, the race of living animals is born from the same things. **THEAETETUS.** Why not? **SOCRATES.** And what about the condition of bodies? Is it not destroyed by rest and idleness, but preserved for the most part by exercise and motion? **THEAETETUS.** Yes.

<margin>Exercises benefit the body and the soul.</margin>
**SOCRATES.** And the condition of the soul, through learning and meditation—which are motions—acquires knowledge, is preserved, and is made better. But through rest—that is, through neglect and laziness—it learns nothing at all, and if it has learned anything, it forgets it.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...to spend time with, but to some he permits it, and again they make progress. Those who associate with me suffer this same thing as women in labor; for they suffer birth-pangs and are filled with difficulties nights and days much more than those women. My art is able to stir up and to stop this labor. And these men are thus. But sometimes, Theaetetus, those who do not seem to me to be pregnant, knowing that they have no need of me, I very kindly act as a matchmaker for them and (to speak with God's help) I guess quite well in whose company they might benefit. Many of them I gave to Dictyna, and many to other wise <margin>B</margin> and divine men. I have drawn this out for you, my best of men, for this reason: suspecting that you, as you yourself think, are in labor, being pregnant with something inside. Therefore, come to me as to the son of a midwife, and one who is himself a midwife; and whatever I ask, be eager to answer as best you are able. And if, while examining something of what you say, I consider it a phantom and not true, then I take it away and throw it aside, do not be angry, like women having their first-born children. For many already, O wonderful man, have been so disposed toward me as to be literally ready to bite me, whenever I take away some nonsense from them, and they do not think I do this out of goodwill; being far from knowing that no god is ill-disposed toward men, nor do I do any such thing out of ill-will; but for me <margin>C</margin> to concede a lie and to suppress the truth is in no way permitted. Again then from the beginning, Theaetetus, whatever knowledge is, try to say; but that you are not able, never say. For if God wills it and you act like a man, you will be able. **THEAETETUS.** Indeed, Socrates, with you encouraging me so, it would be shameful not to be eager in every way to say what one has. It seems then to me that he who knows something perceives this which he knows, and, as it now appears, knowledge is nothing else than perception. **SOCRATES.** Well and nobly said, my boy; for one must speak out in this way when making a definition. But come now, let us look at it together, whether it happens to be fertile or a wind-egg. Perception, you say, <margin>D</margin> is knowledge? **THEAETETUS.** Yes. **SOCRATES.** You have likely spoken no mean theory about knowledge, but the one which Protagoras also said. But he has said these same things in another way. For he says somewhere that "man is the measure of all things, of those that are, that they are; and of those that are not, that they are not." For you have read it somewhere? **THEAETETUS.** I have read it and many times. **SOCRATES.** Does he not say it in this way, that as each thing appears to me, such it is for me; and as it appears to you, such it is in turn for you, and you and I are men? **THEAETETUS.** For he does say it so. **SOCRATES.** It is likely, however, that a wise man is not talking nonsense. Let us follow him then. Is it not sometimes when the same wind is blowing, one of us shivers and the other does not? And one slightly, the other intensely? **THEAETETUS.** Very much so. **SOCRATES.** Whether then shall we say the wind itself by itself is cold or not <margin>E</margin> cold? Or shall we be persuaded by Protagoras, that to the one shivering it is cold, and to the one who is not, it is not? **THEAETETUS.** It seems so. **SOCRATES.** Does it not also appear so to each? **THEAETETUS.** Yes. **SOCRATES.** And "appears" is "perceives"? **THEAETETUS.** It is. **SOCRATES.** Appearance then and perception are the same, in heat and all such things. For such as each perceives things, such they are likely to be for each. **THEAETETUS.** It seems so. **SOCRATES.** Perception then is always of that which is, and is unerring, as being knowledge. **THEAETETUS.** It appears so. **SOCRATES.** By the Graces then, was Protagoras some all-wise person, and did he hint this to us, the great rabble, but to his disciples in secret tell the <margin>F</margin> truth? **THEAETETUS.** How then, Socrates, do you say this? **SOCRATES.** I will tell you, and it is no mean theory; that nothing is one itself by itself, nor could you correctly call anything any sort of thing, but if you address it as great, it will also appear small; and if heavy, light. And all things in this way, as nothing being one, nor any, nor any sort. But from transit and motion and mixture with one another, all things become which we say "are," not correctly addressing them; for nothing ever is, but always becomes. And about this all the wise in order, except Parmenides, let them agree: Protagoras and Heraclitus and Empedocles; and of the poets the tops of each kind of poetry; of comedy, <margin>G</margin> Epicharmus; of tragedy, Homer, saying, "Oceanus the origin of the gods and mother Tethys." All things are the offspring of flux and motion. Or does he not seem to say this? **THEAETETUS.** To me he does. **SOCRATES.** Who then could still against such an army and general Homer be able to dispute, without becoming a laughingstock? **THEAETETUS.** It is not easy, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** For it is not, Theaetetus. Since even these are sufficient signs for the argument: that what seems to be and to become, motion provides; but not being and perishing, rest. For heat and fire, which indeed also begets and governs the other things, itself becomes from transit and friction. And this is motion. Or are these not the origins of fire? **THEAETETUS.** These indeed. **SOCRATES.** And moreover, the <margin>H</margin> race of animals grows from the same things. **THEAETETUS.** How could it not? **SOCRATES.** What then? Is the condition of bodies not destroyed by rest and idleness, but by exercises and motions for the most part saved? **THEAETETUS.** Yes. **SOCRATES.** And the condition in the soul, is it not by learning and study, which are motions, that it both acquires lessons and is saved and becomes better; but by rest, which is lack of study and ignorance, it neither learns anything, and what it has learned, it forgets?

<summary>Socrates explains his "midwifery" method of examining ideas and leads Theaetetus to define knowledge as perception. He then connects this definition to Protagoras's relativism and the Heraclitean doctrine that all reality is in constant motion or flux.</summary>
