<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Theaetetus. Socrates is exploring the Heraclitean idea that "all is motion" and how this relates to Protagoras's claim that "man is the measure of all things." He is currently testing the idea that nothing has a fixed identity but is always "becoming" through interaction.</meta>

->T H E A E T E T U S<-

<margin>A</margin> ...forgets what he learns? THEAET. Very much so. SOC. Therefore, the good, whether in the soul or in the body, is motion; while rest is the opposite? THEAET. So it seems. SOC. Furthermore, I tell you of those states called calms and quietudes, and other such things: that stillness rots and destroys, while the other—motion—preserves. And to these points, I add the "finishing touch" <note>original: "κολοφῶνα" (kolophōna). A "Colophon" was a final stroke or crowning argument.</note> by bringing in the "golden chain," which Homer means is nothing else than the sun. He shows that as long as the celestial circuit and the sun continue to move, all things among both gods and men exist and are preserved; but if this motion were to stand still as if bound, everything would be destroyed and turned (as the saying goes) "upside down." <margin>Homer's Golden Chain, Iliad book 8.</margin>
<margin>B</margin> THEAET. It seems to me, Socrates, that Homer means exactly what you say. SOC. Then consider it this way, my excellent friend: first, regarding the eyes, that which you call "white color" is not some thing that exists outside your eyes, nor is it inside your eyes. Do not assign it any fixed place. For if it were in a fixed place, it would already be in a stable order and remain there, rather than being in a state of "becoming" <note>Socrates is arguing that color is not a "thing" but a temporary event that happens when your sight meets an object.</note>. THEAET. But how can this be? SOC. Let us follow our previous argument: nothing is a single thing existing by itself. Thus, black and white and every other color will appear to us as something generated by the meeting of the eyes with the appropriate motion. And that which we call a "color" will be neither the eye that sees nor the object that is seen, but something intermediate that is unique to each observer. Or would you insist that every color appears to a dog, or any other animal, exactly as it appears to you? THEAET. By Zeus, I would not! SOC. And what about another man? Does anything appear to him exactly as it does to you? Do you hold to this firmly, or are you rather convinced that things do not even appear the same to *you* yourself, because you are never in exactly the same state? THEAET. I think the latter is more likely. SOC. Therefore, if the object we measure or touch were inherently "large" or "white" or "hot," it would never become something else when it met someone else, provided it underwent no change itself. On the other hand, if the person measuring or touching it were inherently any of these things, then when something else approached him or he experienced a change, he would not become something else if he himself suffered no change. But as it stands, my friend, we are easily forced to say strange and even ridiculous things, as Protagoras and anyone who attempts to say the same things as he does would admit.
<margin>D</margin> THEAET. How so? What kind of things do you mean? SOC. Take a small example, and you will understand everything I want to say. If you have six dice, and you put four next to them, we say the six are "more" than the four—one and a half times as many. But if you put twelve next to them, we say the six are "fewer"—half as many. It would be intolerable to say otherwise. Would you tolerate it? THEAET. Not at all. SOC. What then? If Protagoras, or someone else, asked you: "Theaetetus, is it possible for anything to become greater or 'more' in any other way than by being increased?" what would you answer? THEAET. If I answer what I think regarding this present question, Socrates, I would say it is not possible. But if I look back to our previous discussion, I might say it is possible, to avoid contradicting myself. SOC. Well said, by Hera! My friend, you speak divinely. But if you answer that it *is* possible, something like the line from Euripides will happen: "The tongue will be unrefuted, but the mind will not be unrefuted." <note>A reference to Hippolytus: "My tongue swore, but my mind remains unsworn." Socrates means Theaetetus might say one thing while his reason tells him another.</note> THEAET. True. SOC. Now, if you and I were clever and wise men, having already examined all the corners of our minds, we would spend the rest of our time testing one another out of sheer abundance. We would come together in a Sophistic <note>The Sophists were professional teachers known for clever, often deceptive, debating techniques. Socrates is being playful here.</note> battle, clashing argument against argument. But since we are just ordinary people, we want first to look at our thoughts in themselves to see what they really are—whether they agree with each other or not at all. THEAET. I would certainly like that. SOC. And so would I. Since this is the case, and since we have plenty of leisure, let us look at this again quietly, not being irritable, but truly examining ourselves to see what these "phantoms" <margin>Phantoms</margin> inside us are. In considering them, we will say first (I think) that nothing can ever become greater or smaller in size or number as long as it remains equal to itself. Is that not so? THEAET. Exactly. SOC. Second, that to which nothing is added and from which nothing is taken is never increased or decreased, but always remains equal. THEAET. Very much so. SOC. And third, that which was not before, but is later, cannot exist without having "become" or been "made." THEAET. So it seems. SOC. These three admissions, I think, fight against each other in our souls when we talk about the dice, or when we say that I—a man of my age, neither growing nor shrinking—am in one year taller than you (who are young) and later I am shorter, even though my size was not taken away, but yours merely increased. For I am later what I was not before, without ever having "become" so. Without "becoming," it is impossible to "be." Since I lost nothing of my mass, I could never have "become" smaller. And there are ten thousand times ten thousand other such examples, if we accept these. Tell me, Theaetetus, for you seem to be not unacquainted with such things. THEAET. By the gods, Socrates, I wonder greatly what these things are, and sometimes when I look at them, I truly get dizzy. SOC. My friend, it seems Theodorus did not guess poorly about your nature. For this feeling—**wonder**—is very much that of a philosopher. <margin>The beginning of philosophy.</margin> There is no other beginning of philosophy than this. And whoever said that Iris <note>Iris is the rainbow and the messenger of the gods.</note> is the daughter of Thaumas <note>Thaumas means "Wonder."</note> did not explain her genealogy badly. But do you now perceive why these things are as they are according to the theories of Protagoras, or not yet? THEAET. Not yet, I think.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...forgets. THEAET. And very much so. SOC. Therefore, motion is good both in the soul and in the body, but rest is the opposite. THEAET. It seems so. SOC. Furthermore, regarding those things called "serenity" and "tranquility," I bring this forward: that rest rots and destroys, while other things [motion] preserve. Therefore, I shall finally drive home the "Colophon," bringing in the Golden Chain itself. Which Homer understands as nothing other than the sun: because as long as the sun's circuit persists, <margin>Homer's Golden Chain, Iliad book 8.</margin> all things of both gods and men exist and are preserved. But if this were to stand still as if bound, all things would immediately be dissolved, and it would happen as they say: everything "up-side down."
<margin>B</margin> THEAET. To me also, O Socrates, it seems he feels the same as you say. SOC. Think then thus, O best of men, first regarding the eyes: that the color we call white is not itself anything outside your eyes, nor in your eyes, nor should you attribute a certain place to it. For then it would be in an order and remain there, and would no longer be in a state of generation. THEAET. But how? SOC. Let us follow the previous discourse, positing nothing as being one thing according to itself; and so black and white and any other color appears to us as generated from the meeting of the eyes and the appropriate motion. And each thing that we call by the name of color will be neither the eye pressing nor the object pressed, but a certain intermediate state proper to each. Or would you assert that as each color appears to you, it appears the same to dogs and every other animal? THEAET. Not by Jove. SOC. What about another man and you? Does each thing seem to appear similarly? Or rather, does it not even seem the same to you yourself, because you are never similar to yourself? THEAET. I think this rather than that. SOC. If, therefore, that which we measure or which we touch were "large" or "white" or "hot," it would never, in meeting anything else, become something else itself—as if it were not changed. But if the measured thing which we touch were white or hot, even if nothing else happens or is suffered, it will also be changed while suffering nothing itself. For at present, my friend, we are easily forced to say certain wonderful and laughable things, as Protagoras himself and whoever else is of the same opinion confesses.
<margin>D</margin> THEAET. In what way? And what kind of things do you say? SOC. Take a brief example, and you will understand what I want. Six dice: if you put four next to them, we say they are "more" than four and exceed them by half, whence it is called a "sesquialter" proportion. But if you put twelve, they are "fewer" and a half [part]; nor can it be said otherwise. Or can you? THEAET. Truly, in no way. SOC. What then? If Protagoras, or anyone else, asked you: "Is it possible, O Theaetetus, for anything to become greater or 'more' in any other way than by being increased?" what would you respond? THEAET. If I bring forth what seems to me, O Socrates, to this question, I will assert it is not possible. But if I look back to the previous position, lest I perhaps contradict myself, I will say it is possible. SOC. Well and divinely, by Juno, O friend. Therefore, as it seems, if you answer that it is so, that saying of Euripides will happen: "The tongue remains unrefuted, but the mind is refuted." THEAET. Certainly so. SOC. If, therefore, you and I were eloquent and wise, after we had shaken out all the corners of the mind, soon, as if from an abundance of strength, each testing his own powers and clashing in this arena in the manner of Sophists, we would engage in a conflict of speeches. Now, however, as if unlearned, we want first to contemplate these things according to themselves—of what kind are those things we think, and whether they agree among ourselves or not. THEAET. I would very much want that. SOC. And I no less. But since we are thus disposed, let us calmly and as people of leisure examine them again, not following one after another, but truly shaking ourselves out [to see] what these visions and "phantoms" in us are. <margin>Phantoms.</margin> Having first considered these, we shall say, as I think: nothing ever becomes greater or smaller, either in mass or in number, as long as it remains equal to itself, is it not so? THEAET. Entirely so. SOC. Next, that to which nothing is added and from which nothing is subtracted never grows nor decreases, but always stands equal. THEAET. Very much so. SOC. Third, <margin>G</margin> we shall say that what was not before, and is afterwards, cannot be unless it is "made" or has "become." THEAET. So indeed it seems. SOC. These three concessions certainly fight among themselves in our minds when we speak of those dice, or when we admit that I, an old man, while I remain as large as I am, having been neither increased nor diminished in any part, am in the same year larger than you—a youth—and afterwards smaller, although my mass has not been taken away, but yours alone increased. Thus I am afterwards what I was not before, yet having become nothing. For without "becoming," to have been "made" is impossible. Losing nothing of mass, I was never "made" smaller. and infinite other things of this kind happen in many cases, if we admit these. Tell me, O Theaetetus, for you seem to me not unskilled in these matters. THEAET. By the gods, O Socrates, I wonder greatly what those things are; and sometimes, looking at them intensely, I am overwhelmed by darkness. SOC. Theodorus, O friend, seems not to have guessed poorly regarding your talent. For this happens especially to philosophers: to wonder. For there is no other <margin>Principle of philosophy.</margin> principle of philosophy than this. and he who handed down that Iris is the daughter of Thaumas—that is, of wonder—did not absurdly explain her origin. But do you perceive for what reason such things are from which we asserted Protagoras speaks, or not? THEAET. [Not yet.]

<summary>Socrates explains that perception is a product of motion and interaction, leading to paradoxes about size and change. He concludes that "wonder" is the essential starting point for all philosophical inquiry.</summary>
<keywords>motion vs rest, Homer's Golden Chain, relativity of color, Protagoras, paradox of the dice, becoming vs being, wonder as the beginning of philosophy, Iris and Thaumas</keywords>

--- Page 152 ---
<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and the young mathematician Theaetetus. Socrates is introducing the "Secret Doctrine" of thinkers like Protagoras and Heraclitus—the idea that nothing "is" in a fixed state, but everything is always "becoming" through motion and interaction. This transition moves from a critique of crude materialists to a sophisticated theory of sense perception.</meta>

->PLATO'S<-

<column-break/>

<margin>The opinion of those who say nothing is invisible.</margin>
**A** ...not yet, I think. **SOCRATES.** Will you be grateful to me then, if I reveal to you the hidden truth of the thinking of a man—or rather, of very famous men? **THEAETETUS.** How could I not be? Indeed, I would be very grateful. **SOCRATES.** Look around then, and take great care that none of the uninitiated <note>original: "prophanus" / "ἀμυήτων". Socrates refers to those not initiated into the "mysteries" of philosophy.</note> are listening. These are the people who think nothing else exists except what they can grip with their hands. Actions, processes of becoming, and whatever is invisible, they do not include in the number of things that truly exist. **THEAETETUS.** You describe very stubborn and defiant men, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** They are indeed, my boy, quite far removed from the Muses. But there are others, more refined, whose mysteries I am about to tell you. **B** <margin>The opinion of those who say the universe is motion, and nothing exists besides motion.</margin> The starting principle upon which everything we have just said depends is this: that the universe is motion, and there is nothing besides motion. Now, there are two types of motion: each is infinite in number, but one has the power of acting, and the other the power of being acted upon. From the union and mutual friction of these two, offspring are produced that are infinite in number but twin in nature: namely, the perceived object and the perception, which always coincides and is born along with the perceived object. These are the names of the perceptions: sight, hearing, smell, taste, and the touch of cold and heat. These are followed by pleasures, pains, desires, and fears, and countless other unnamed ones, though many have been named. **C** Furthermore, the category of the perceived object is related to each sense. To every kind of vision, there are every kind of colors; to the ears, likewise, voices; and for the other senses, other related objects of perception are present. So then, Theaetetus, does this discourse relate to what we said before? **THEAETETUS.** Not quite, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** See then if it can be brought to a conclusion this way. For it means this: all these things, as we said, are in motion, and there is a speed or slowness in their movements. As far as the slow motion goes, it keeps its movement in the same place and toward what is near, and thus it generates. But the things generated in this way are faster. For they are carried along, and their motion consists in being carried. **D** Therefore, when the eye and something else commensurate with it come near and generate whiteness and the sensation related to it—which would never have come into being if either of them had come toward something else—then, in that moment while the vision is carried from the eyes and the whiteness from the thing that produces the color, the eye is filled with vision and sees; it has become not "vision" itself, but a seeing eye. That which produced the color is then filled with whiteness; it has become not "whiteness" itself, but a white thing—whether it be wood or stone or whatever else happens to be colored with such a color. The same judgment must be made for all other things, such as hot and hard and everything else. **E** None of these things is anything in itself, as we were discussing before, but all things come to be in all their variety through mutual interaction because of motion. For one cannot firmly think of either the "actor" or the "acted upon" as being a single thing in itself, as they say. For the "actor" is nothing until it meets the "acted upon," nor is the "acted upon" anything until it meets the "actor." For that which meets one thing and has the power of acting, when it falls upon something else, is revealed as being acted upon. From all this follows what we said from the beginning: that nothing is one thing by itself, but is always "becoming" in relation to something else. The word "to be" <note>original: "esse" / "εἶναι". Socrates argues we should stop saying things "are" and start saying they "become."</note> should be removed from everywhere, even though we have often been forced by habit and ignorance to use it. However, as the speech of the wise dictates, one must not allow the use of "something," or "of someone," or "mine," or "this," or "that," or any other name that signifies stable existence. **F** Instead, one should speak according to nature: that things are being moved, are becoming, are being destroyed, and are being changed. For if anyone tries to make a thing stand still in speech, he will be easily refuted. We must speak this way both about parts and about many things collected together—a collection to which people give the names "man," "stone," "animal," or "species." Does this seem pleasant to you, Theaetetus? Will you taste these ideas to see if they please you? **THEAETETUS.** I do not know, Socrates; and concerning you, I am unsure whether you bring these things up because they are your own thoughts, or whether you are testing me. **SOCRATES.** **G** Do you not remember, my friend, that I know none of these things, nor do I claim any of them as my own? For I am barren of such things. But I act as a midwife to you, and for this reason, I chant incantations and offer you the sayings of the wise to taste until I can bring your own judgment out into the light. When it has finally been brought out, then I will examine it to see if it is a "wind-egg" <note>An unfertilized or empty egg; a metaphor for a false or hollow idea.</note> and barren, or if it is fruitful and solid. Therefore, boldly and steadily, answer well and manfully what you think about the things I ask. **THEAETETUS.** Ask then. **SOCRATES.** Tell me again if it pleases you that nothing "is," but that the good and the beautiful and all those things we just listed are always "becoming." **THEAETETUS.** While I hear you explaining it, it seems wonderfully probable and must be accepted. **SOCRATES.** Then let us not overlook what remains. <margin>Concerning dreams and diseases against Protagoras.</margin> For it remains for me to speak of dreams and diseases, especially madness, and of those things that are wrongly seen or heard or perceived in any other way. For you know that in all these cases, the argument we just gave seems to be undeniably refuted, since the senses in these states are utterly deceived. Far from it being the case that what appears to each person "is," on the contrary, nothing of what appears actually exists. **THEAETETUS.** What you say is very true, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** Where then, my boy, will that man take refuge who affirmed that perception is knowledge, and that what appears to each person is to that same person...

<column-break/>

**A** ...not yet. **THEAET.** It does not yet seem so to me. **SOC.** You will be grateful to me, then, if I search out with you the hidden truth of the thought of a man—or rather, of famous men? **THEAET.** How could I not be? Indeed, quite a lot. **SOC.** Look around then and watch out that none of the uninitiated listen. These are the ones who think nothing else exists except what they can grasp firmly with their two hands; but actions and processes of becoming and all that is invisible they do not accept as having a part in being. **THEAET.** Truly, Socrates, you speak of hard and resistant men. **SOC.** For they are, my boy, quite unrefined. But there are others, much more clever, whose mysteries I am about to tell you. The principle from which everything we have just said depends is this: that the whole was motion, and **B** there is nothing else besides this. Of motion there are two kinds: each infinite in number, but one has the power of acting, the other of being acted upon. From the interaction and friction of these against one another, offspring are produced, infinite in number but twin: the one, the perceived object, the other, perception, which always happens and is born along with the perceived object. Now, the perceptions have for us such names as: sights, hearings, smells, and coldings and burnings, and indeed pleasures and pains, and desires and fears as they are called; and others, those without names are endless, but those with names are very many. **C** Again, the category of perceived objects is kin to each of these: to sights of all kinds, colors of all kinds; to hearings likewise, sounds; and for the other senses, the other perceived objects are born as relatives. Now, what does this story want for us, Theaetetus, in relation to our earlier points? Do you perceive it? **THEAET.** Not entirely, Socrates. **SOC.** But watch if it can somehow be completed. For it wants to say that all these things, as we say, are in motion; and speed and slowness are in their motion. Now, as much as is slow, it has its motion in the same place and toward things nearby, and thus it generates; but the things thus generated are slower. But as much as is fast, it has its motion toward things further away, and thus it moves; but the things thus generated are faster. For they are carried, and their motion is by nature in transit. **D** When, therefore, an eye and something else of the things commensurate with it come near and generate whiteness and the sensation naturally joined with it—which would never have happened if either of them had gone toward something else—then, in the space between as they are carried (vision toward the eyes, and whiteness toward the thing that helps produce the color), the eye becomes full of vision and then sees, and has become not "vision" but a seeing eye; while that which helped generate the color is filled with whiteness and has become not "whiteness" again, but white—whether it be wood or stone or whatever happened to be colored with such a color. And the other **E** things likewise—hard and hot and all—must be understood in the same way: that nothing is any one thing itself by itself (which we were also saying then), but in their interaction with one another, all things become all sorts of things from motion. Since even the "acting" thing and the "acted upon" thing, if considered as one, cannot be firmly thought of, as they say. For the acting thing is nothing until it has come together with the acted upon, nor is the acted upon anything until it has come together with the acting. And that which, coming together with one thing, is "acting," if it falls upon another, is revealed as "acted upon." So that from all these things, as we said from the beginning, nothing is one thing itself by itself, but is always "becoming" for someone, and "being" must be removed from everywhere. Not that we have not been forced many times, even just now, by habit and lack of knowledge to use it. But one should not, as the speech of the wise says, allow "something," or "of someone," or "mine," or "this," or "that," **F** or any other name that brings things to a standstill; but one should speak according to nature of things becoming and being produced, and being destroyed and being altered. Since if anyone makes a thing stand still in speech, he who does so is easily refuted. And one must speak this way both concerning the parts and concerning many things collected together. To which collection they give the names "man" and "stone" and each animal and species. Do these things, Theaetetus, seem pleasant to you, and would you taste them as being to your liking? **THEAET.** I do not know, Socrates. For I cannot even understand you, whether you say these things as your own beliefs or whether you are testing me. **SOC.** Do you not remember, friend, that I neither know nor make any such thing my own, but I am barren of them? But I am acting as your midwife, and for this reason I chant incantations and set before you each of the **G** wise things to taste, until I can help bring your own doctrine out into the light. And when it has been brought out, then I will examine whether it will appear to be a wind-egg or a fruitful one. But be bold and endure, and answer well and manfully whatever appears to you concerning the things I ask. **THEAET.** Ask then. **SOC.** Say then again if it pleases you that nothing "is," but the good and the beautiful are always "becoming," and all the things I just went through. **THEAET.** To me at least, since I hear you going through it this way, it seems wonderfully to have reason, and must be accepted as you have described it. **SOC.** Let us not, therefore, leave out what is missing from it. And what remains is concerning dreams and diseases, and other things including madness; and all those things said to be mis-hearings or mis-seeings or other mis-perceptions. For I know surely that in all these things the argument we just went through seems admittedly to be refuted; as false perceptions happen to us in them above all else; and it is far from the case that the things appearing to each person "are" these things, but on the contrary, nothing of what appears "is." **THEAET.** You speak very truly, Socrates. **SOC.** What argument then, my boy, remains for the one who...
<note>catchword: τῶ αὐτὴ (to the same [person])</note>

<summary>Socrates explains the "Secret Doctrine" of universal flux, where perception is an event born from the interaction of motion, and introduces his role as an intellectual midwife (maieutics). He then challenges this theory of relative truth by bringing up the problem of dreams and madness.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue where Socrates explains the relativistic theory of perception (attributed to Protagoras). On the previous page, Socrates argued that nothing "is" in isolation, but everything "becomes" through the interaction of an active force and a passive receiver. Here, he addresses the classic skeptical challenge: how can we trust our senses if dreams and madness feel just as real as waking life?</meta>

->THEAETETUS<-

...of perceptions, and that which appears to each person *is* for that person to whom it appears. <note>Socrates is summarizing the Protagorean view: "Man is the measure of all things."</note>
<margin>A</margin> **THEAETETUS.** I am hesitant, Socrates, to tell you that I don't know what to say, because you just rebuked me for saying that. But in truth, I could not dispute that those who are mad or dreaming hold false opinions; for some of them think they are gods, while others imagine they have wings and are flying in their sleep.
**SOCRATES.** Do you not then consider the following sort of dispute about them, especially regarding being asleep versus being awake?
**THEAETETUS.** What sort?
**SOCRATES.** A question which I think you have often heard people ask: what evidence could one provide, if someone asked right now, at this very moment, whether we are sleeping and all that we think is a dream, 
<margin>B</margin> or whether we are awake and conversing with each other in reality? <note>original: "ὕπαρ" / "hypar", referring to a waking state as opposed to a dream.</note>
**THEAETETUS.** Indeed, Socrates, it is difficult to see what evidence one should use as proof. For all the same features follow each state like a mirror image. The very things we have just discussed, nothing prevents us from thinking we are discussing these in our sleep as well; and when in a dream we seem to be telling our dreams, the similarity between the two experiences is extraordinary.
**SOCRATES.** You see then that it is not difficult to raise a dispute, since it is even disputed whether we are awake or in a dream. And since the time we spend sleeping is equal to the time we are awake, in each state our soul contends that the opinions present at the time are altogether true. So for half the time we 
<margin>C</margin> say these things are real, and for the other half we say those are; and we are equally confident in both.
**THEAETETUS.** Absolutely.
**SOCRATES.** Is not the same logic applied to diseases and madness, except for the difference in time? <note>Meaning, madness or sickness doesn't always last exactly half of one's life like sleep does.</note>
**THEAETETUS.** Correct.
**SOCRATES.** What then? Shall the truth be defined by the length or brevity of time?
**THEAETETUS.** That would be ridiculous in many ways.
**SOCRATES.** But do you have any other clear way to show which of these opinions is true?
**THEAETETUS.** I do not think I do.
**SOCRATES.** Listen then to me, and hear what those would say who define "truth" as whatever appears to the perceiver. They would ask, I imagine, "Theaetetus, can something that is altogether different from something else ever have the 
<margin>D</margin> same power as that other thing? And let us not suppose that the thing we are asking about is the same in one way and different in another, but that it is entirely different."
**THEAETETUS.** It is impossible for it to have anything the same, either in its power or in any other way, when it is completely different.
**SOCRATES.** Must we not also admit that such a thing is necessarily unlike the other?
**THEAETETUS.** It seems so to me.
**SOCRATES.** If, therefore, it happens that something becomes like or unlike something else—whether to itself or to another—shall we say that when it becomes like, it becomes the "same," and when it becomes unlike, it becomes "different"?
**THEAETETUS.** Necessarily.
**SOCRATES.** Did we not say before that the factors that act are many and infinite, and likewise the factors that are acted upon?
**THEAETETUS.** Yes.
**SOCRATES.** And further, that one thing mixing with one object, and then with another, will not produce the same results, but different ones?
**THEAETETUS.** Quite so.
**SOCRATES.** Let us speak then of me and you, or any other example. Shall we say "Socrates healthy" and "Socrates ill" are like or unlike each other? 
<margin>E</margin> **THEAETETUS.** When you say the "ailing Socrates," are you comparing that whole state to the whole state of the "healthy Socrates"?
**SOCRATES.** You have understood perfectly. That is exactly what I mean.
**THEAETETUS.** They are surely unlike and different.
**SOCRATES.** And therefore, being unlike, he is a different person?
**THEAETETUS.** Necessarily.
**SOCRATES.** And you would say the same for Socrates sleeping, or for any of the states we just described?
**THEAETETUS.** I would.
**SOCRATES.** Then each of those things which are naturally inclined to act upon me—when they find Socrates healthy, they will treat me as one person, but when they find me ill, they treat me as another?
**THEAETETUS.** How could they not?
**SOCRATES.** And so, will not I, the "patient" <note>In this philosophical context, the "patient" is the one receiving a sensation.</note>, and the "agent" <note>The object causing the sensation.</note> produce different results in each case?
**THEAETETUS.** Of course.
**SOCRATES.** When I drink wine while healthy, does it appear pleasant and sweet to me?
<margin>F</margin> **THEAETETUS.** Yes.
**SOCRATES.** For, as we agreed, the agent and the patient produced sweetness and perception, both moving together. The perception, being on the side of the patient, made the tongue a perceiving thing; while the sweetness, being on the side of the wine and moving around it, made the wine both *be* and *appear* sweet to the healthy tongue.
**THEAETETUS.** Certainly, that was our previous agreement.
**SOCRATES.** But when the wine finds me ill, first of all, does it not in truth find a different person? For it approaches one who is now unlike.
**THEAETETUS.** Yes.
**SOCRATES.** Then a different set of results is produced by the "Socrates-of-this-state" and the drinking of the wine: on the side of the tongue, a perception of bitterness; and on the side of the wine, a bitterness that is produced and moves. The wine is made not "bitterness" itself, but "bitter," and I am made not "perception," but "perceiving."
**THEAETETUS.** Exactly so.
**SOCRATES.** Therefore, I shall never become anything else while perceiving in this way; for there is a different perception for a different object, which makes the perceiver different and changed. Nor can that 
<margin>G</margin> object, if it acts on someone else, ever produce the same result or become the same thing. For by producing a different result from a different person, it will itself become different.
**THEAETETUS.** That is true.
**SOCRATES.** Nor indeed shall I become "such a way" for myself, nor will the object become "such a way" for itself.
**THEAETETUS.** Certainly not.
**SOCRATES.** It is necessary that I become a perceiver *of something* when I perceive; for it is impossible to be perceiving and yet perceive nothing. And it is necessary for the object to become something *for someone* when it becomes sweet or bitter or anything of that sort; for it is impossible for something to be sweet, yet sweet to no one.
**THEAETETUS.** Entirely so.
**SOCRATES.** It follows then, I think, that whether we "are" or "become," we do so in relation to one another, since necessity binds our 
<margin>H</margin> essence together, but binds it to nothing else—not even to our own selves. We are left bound to one another. So, whether one uses the word "to be" or "to become," he must say it is "for someone," or "of someone," or "in relation to something." But to say that anything *is* or *becomes* just by itself, he must neither say this himself nor accept it from anyone else, as the argument we have traced out indicates.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...to say that things are as they have seemed? **THEAETETUS.** I am ashamed to speak further, Socrates. For I have nothing to bring forward. What I had previously established, you have completely overturned by showing its dangers. Truly, I could never deny that those who are mad or dreaming imagine things that are quite false, since some of them think they are gods, and others believe themselves to be flying like birds. **SOCRATES.** Do you not then also consider this controversy about them, specifically regarding dreams and reality? **THEAETETUS.** 
<margin>Ambiguity regarding dreams and true things.</margin> What is it? **SOCRATES.** That which I think you have often heard asked, by what specific conjecture could it be shown whether we are 
<margin>B</margin> all sleeping now and dreaming every single thing we think, or whether we are awake and truly conversing with one another. **THEAETETUS.** Indeed, it is a doubt, O Socrates, by what conjecture one might be able to discern it. For everything follows from one to the other in a reciprocal way. For nothing prevents us from seeming to talk to one another while dreaming, as we were just doing. And when in sleep we think we are recounting dreams, these are wondrously similar to those of waking life. **SOCRATES.** You see now how easily we come into controversy: since it can even be doubted whether the things we see are dreams or true things. Moreover, since the time given to sleep is equal to the time given to waking, in both states our soul strives to assert the present 
<margin>C</margin> opinions as true. For this reason, we shall call these things true for an equal time, and those for an equal time, and we will maintain both. **THEAETETUS.** Entirely. **SOCRATES.** The same logic also applies to diseases and fits of madness, except that the time is unequal. **THEAETETUS.** Quite right. **SOCRATES.** Is truth then determined by the length or shortness of time? **THEAETETUS.** But that would be most ridiculous. **SOCRATES.** Can you show by any other argument which of these opinions are true? **THEAETETUS.** Not, it seems to me. **SOCRATES.** Listen to me then, to what those would perhaps respond who wish that things which appear are always true for the one to whom they appear. For they would ask you, I think, "O Theaetetus, can that which is entirely 'other' ever have the same 
<margin>D</margin> power as 'another'? And let us not understand it as being the same in part and other in part, but entirely other?" **THEAETETUS.** It is impossible, therefore, for this thing to have anything the same as that, either in power or in any way, when it is entirely other. **SOCRATES.** Must we not also necessarily admit that it is 'unlike'? **THEAETETUS.** So it seems to me. **SOCRATES.** If therefore something becomes like or unlike anything, either to itself or to another, we shall confess that insofar as it becomes like, it is the same; and insofar as it becomes unlike, it becomes 'other'. **THEAETETUS.** It necessarily follows. **SOCRATES.** Did we not grant above that the agents are many and innumerable, and similarly the patients? **THEAETETUS.** We granted it. **SOCRATES.** Furthermore, that which is different from 
<margin>E</margin> another, when mixed with one thing or another, will not generate the same things but different ones. **THEAETETUS.** Exactly so. **SOCRATES.** Let us say then of me and of others according to the same logic—namely, a healthy Socrates and a sick Socrates—shall we say this one is like that one, or unlike? **THEAETETUS.** Are you asking about the sick Socrates as a whole, compared to that whole healthy Socrates? **SOCRATES.** You have understood perfectly; that is what I was saying. **THEAETETUS.** Clearly unlike and other. **SOCRATES.** And is he 'other' in the sense that he is 'unlike'? **THEAETETUS.** It must be so. **SOCRATES.** And will you say the same of the sleeping and the waking man, and all those things we recounted above? **THEAETETUS.** I will indeed. **SOCRATES.** Any of those things which by nature can produce an effect, when it 
<margin>F</margin> encounters a healthy Socrates, it will use me as one person; but when it encounters a weak one, it will use me as another? **THEAETETUS.** Why not? **SOCRATES.** And we shall generate different things in each case—I, the patient, and that other thing, the agent? **THEAETETUS.** Nothing prevents it. **SOCRATES.** Whenever I, being healthy, drink wine, it seems pleasant and sweet to me. **THEAETETUS.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** Further, from those things which were granted—the agent and the patient—they have produced sweetness and sensation, and both were set in motion: the sensation, arising from the patient, made the tongue feel; and the sweetness, arising from the wine and moving around it, made the wine both *be* and *appear* sweet to the healthy tongue. **THEAETETUS.** Our previous agreements were exactly so. **SOCRATES.** But when it finds me sick, first of all, does it not truly find a different person? For it comes to one who is unlike. **THEAETETUS.** It is so. **SOCRATES.** Then the Socrates affected in this way and the wine-
<margin>G</margin> drink generate other things: on the tongue, a sensation of bitter taste; and in the wine, a bitterness that is made and set in motion. And the wine becomes not "bitterness," but "bitter," and I become not "sensation," but "perceiving." For one sensation belongs to one person, and another to another, and it makes the perceiver different and other. Nor will that agent, in making me such a thing, ever produce the same thing when it meets another person. For by generating something different from another person, it will become different and other itself. **THEAETETUS.** These things are true. **SOCRATES.** Neither shall I become such a way to myself, nor will that object become such a way to itself. **THEAETETUS.** Certainly not. **SOCRATES.** But it is necessary that I become [a perceiver] of something, whenever I become perceiving. For it is impossible to be perceiving and yet perceive nothing. And it is also 
<margin>H</margin> necessary for that object to become something to someone, whenever it is rendered sweet or bitter or anything of this sort. For sweetness cannot be sweet to no one. **THEAETETUS.** It is so, entirely. **SOCRATES.** It remains, therefore, I think, that whether we "are" or "become," we do so in relation to one another; since 

---

necessity itself binds our essence together. But it binds it to none of the others, nor to ourselves; it follows therefore that we are bound to one another. For this reason, whether someone says a thing "is" or "becomes," it must be understood as being or becoming *for someone*, or *of someone*, or *in relation to something*. But he must not himself claim that anything *is* or *becomes* in and of itself, nor allow another to assert it, as the logic we have discussed advises.

L <note>Signature mark for the printer/bookbinder.</note>

<summary>Socrates argues that because our physiological state (health, sleep, or madness) changes our perceptions, "truth" is relative to the observer's current condition. He uses the example of wine tasting sweet to a healthy person but bitter to a sick one to prove that objects only have qualities (like sweetness) in relation to a perceiver.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from page 121, where Socrates and Theaetetus are examining the definition of knowledge as "perception." Socrates has just finished explaining the relativistic implications of Protagoras's famous claim that "Man is the measure of all things."</meta>

# PLATO

**THEAETETUS.** It is exactly as you say, Socrates.
**SOCRATES.** Therefore, since that which acts upon me is for me and no one else, do I not also perceive it myself, and no one else?
**THEAETETUS.** Why not?
**SOCRATES.** My perception, then, is true for me; for it is always part of my own being. According to Protagoras, I am the judge both of the things that are, as they are to me, and of the things that are not, as they are not to me.
**THEAETETUS.** So it seems.
**SOCRATES.** How then, since I am unerring and my mind does not stumble concerning the things that are or are becoming, could I fail to be a "knower" of the very things I perceive?
**THEAETETUS.** You could not.
**SOCRATES.** It was an excellent thing, then, for you to say that knowledge is nothing other than perception. These ideas all converge into the same point: according to Homer and Heraclitus and that whole tribe, all things flow like a river; according to Protagoras, the wisest of men, man is the measure of all things; and finally, according to Theaetetus—given these premises—knowledge is perception. Shall we say then, Theaetetus, that this opinion is like your newborn child, recently fathered by you, but brought into the light by me through a kind of midwifery? <note>Socrates famously compared his method of questioning to midwifery (maieutics), helping others "give birth" to their own ideas.</note> What do you say?
**THEAETETUS.** It must be so, Socrates.
**SOCRATES.** Well, it seems we have finally given birth to this, whatever it may turn out to be. But after the birth, as is the custom, we must perform the "running-around" <margin>See Suidas <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia.</note> under the word *amphidromia*.</margin> <note>The *Amphidromia* was a Greek ritual where a newborn was carried around the family hearth to be named and accepted into the family.</note> of our argument, examining it from all sides to see if it escapes us—lest it be something not worth raising, but merely a wind-egg and a falsehood. Or do you think your child must be reared at all costs and never discarded? Will you bear it patiently if you see your firstborn proven a fraud and taken away?
**THEODORE.** Theaetetus will bear it patiently, Socrates, for he is not at all ill-tempered. But tell me, by the gods, is the matter not as we've said?
**SOCRATES.** You are quite fond of argument, Theodore, and a good man to boot, to think that I am a sort of sack <margin>Socrates explains what it means to know.</margin> of speeches, from which I can suddenly pull out an argument to show that these things are not so. You do not perceive what is happening: that no argument ever flows from me, but always from the one who is disputing with me. I myself know nothing except for one small thing: how to take an argument from another wise man and receive it fairly. And now I will try to do that with this young man, rather than speaking for myself.
**THEODORE.** You speak better than I do, Socrates. Please, proceed.
**SOCRATES.** Do you know, Theodore, what surprises me about your friend Protagoras’s words?
**THEODORE.** What is it?
**SOCRATES.** Most of what he said pleased me well enough—that what seems to each person *is* for that person. But I was amazed at the beginning of his discourse. Why did he not say at the start of his *Truth* <note>Protagoras's famous lost book was titled "Truth."</note> that a pig, or a dog-faced baboon, <note>original: "cynocephalum" / "κυνοκέφαλος", an Egyptian baboon or dog-headed creature.</note> or some other even more bizarre creature that possesses perception, is the measure of all things? That would have been a magnificent and utterly contemptuous opening, showing us that while we admire him as if he were a god for his wisdom, he is actually no wiser than a tadpole, <note>original: "rana Gyrina" / "βατράχου γυρίνου".</note> let alone any other man. How else should we put it, Theodore? If for each person that which he perceives is true, and no one can judge another's experience better than himself, nor has anyone more authority to examine whether another’s opinion is right or wrong—but as we have said many times, each person will hold only his own opinions, and these are all correct and true—then why, my friend, was Protagoras so wise that he was thought worthy to be a teacher of others for a large fee? And why are we more ignorant, needing to go to him as pupils, if each of us is the measure of his own wisdom? How can we say that Protagoras wasn't just playing to the crowd? I will say nothing of my own "art of midwifery," which would be a joke, as would the entire practice of dialectic. For the effort of examining and trying to refute one another’s fancies and opinions—when everyone's are correct—is nothing but a great and long-winded piece of folly, if the *Truth* of Protagoras is actually true and not just speaking in jest from the inner sanctuary <note>original: "adyto" / "ἀδύτου", the most sacred, restricted part of a temple.</note> of his book.
**THEODORE.** Socrates, he is my friend, as you just said. Therefore, I would not allow Protagoras to be refuted by my own concessions, nor would I want to oppose you against my better judgment. Take up the argument again with Theaetetus; he seemed to be following you quite diligently just now.
**SOCRATES.** Theodore, if you went to the wrestling schools of Sparta and saw others stripping naked to exercise, would you not think it fair to show your own form alongside theirs?
**THEODORE.** Why do you ask? If they would allow me—as I hope you will allow me now—I would rather be a spectator and not be dragged into the gymnasium, for my skin is already toughened by age; they would do better to wrestle with someone younger and more flexible.
**SOCRATES.** Well, if that is what pleases you, Theodore, it does not bother me, as the old proverb goes. <margin>Proverb: "If it pleases you, it is no trouble to me."</margin> Let us then go back to the wise Theaetetus. Tell me, Theaetetus, first regarding what we just discussed: are you not amazed if you suddenly appear to be no less wise than any man or even any god? Or do you think Protagoras’s "measure" applies any less to the gods than to men?
**THEAETETUS.** By Zeus, no, I do not. I am indeed greatly surprised by what you ask. When we were explaining how what seems to each person is true for that person, it seemed to be a very fine argument; but now, suddenly, the opposite opinion has taken hold of me.
**SOCRATES.** You are still young, my dear boy, and therefore you are easily swayed by public speaking. For Protagoras, or someone speaking for him, would say: "O noble boys and old men, you are sitting together and haranguing the crowd, bringing the gods into the middle of it—gods about whom I refuse to speak or write as to whether they exist or not..."

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from page 122. Socrates is pushing Theaetetus and the geometer Theodorus to examine the logical consequences of the theory that "knowledge is perception." If every individual’s perception is their only truth, Socrates argues, then any creature’s perception is as valid as a philosopher's.</meta>

# THEAETETUS

<margin>A</margin> ...to all people, whether things are or are not; and you say those things that the many accept when they hear them. But you offer no proof or necessity whatsoever; instead, you rely only on what is likely. Yet if Theodorus, or any other geometer, chose to use "likelihood" while doing geometry, he would be worth absolutely nothing. Consider then, both you and Theodorus, whether you will accept arguments spoken about such great matters based only on persuasive talk and probabilities. **THEODORUS:** But that would not be right, Socrates; neither you nor we would say it is. **SOCRATES:** Then it seems we must look at it in another way, as your argument and that of Theodorus suggest. **THEODORUS:** Indeed, in another way entirely.

<margin>B</margin> **SOCRATES:** Let us look at it this way: is knowledge and perception the same thing, or something different? For this is surely the point toward which our whole discussion has been tending, and for the sake of this we have stirred up all these many strange ideas. Is that not so? **THEODORUS:** Entirely so. **SOCRATES:** Shall we agree then, that whatever we perceive by seeing or hearing, we also simultaneously "know" all those things? For example, before we have learned the language of foreigners <note>original: "barbarians," a term the Greeks used for anyone who did not speak Greek.</note>, shall we say that we do not hear them when they speak? Or do we both hear and know what they are saying? Again, if we do not know our letters, and we look at them, shall we insist that we do not see them, or that if we do see them, we must also know them? **THEODORUS:** We shall say, Socrates, that we know exactly that part of them which we see and hear. We see and know the shape and color of the letters, and we hear and know the high and low pitches of the voice; but as for what the grammarians and interpreters teach about them, we neither perceive those things by seeing and hearing, nor do we know them. **SOCRATES:** Excellently put, Theaetetus! It is not worth arguing with you on these points, so that you may grow in your understanding. But look now at this other problem approaching, and consider how we might push it aside. **THEODORUS:** What sort of problem is it? **SOCRATES:** It is this: if someone were to ask whether it is possible for a person who has once come to know something, and still has a memory of that thing and preserves it, to not know that very thing which he remembers at the moment he remembers it? I am being long-winded, it seems, when I only mean to ask: can someone who has learned something, and remembers it, not know it? **THEODORUS:** How could that be, Socrates? <margin>D</margin> What you are saying would be a monstrosity! **SOCRATES:** Am I talking nonsense then? Look at it this way. Do you not say that "seeing" is "perceiving," and that "sight" is "perception"? **THEODORUS:** I do. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, he who sees something has become a "knower" of that which he sees, according to our recent argument? **THEODORUS:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** Well then, do you not say there is such a thing as memory? **THEODORUS:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** Memory of nothing, or of something? **THEODORUS:** Of something, surely. **SOCRATES:** Is it not of the things he learned and perceived? **THEODORUS:** Of such things, yes. **SOCRATES:** Well, what a man has seen, does he not sometimes remember it? **THEODORUS:** He remembers. **SOCRATES:** Even when he closes his eyes? Or does he forget the thing by doing this? **THEODORUS:** It would be a terrible thing to say that, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** And yet it must be said, if we are to save our previous argument; if not, the argument is gone. **THEODORUS:** By Zeus, I suspect as much, though I do not quite understand. Tell me how. **SOCRATES:** In this way: the one who <margin>E</margin> sees, we say, has become a "knower" of that which he sees; for sight, perception, and knowledge have been agreed to be the same. **THEODORUS:** Quite so. **SOCRATES:** But the one who sees, and has become a knower of what he saw, if he closes his eyes, he remembers, but he does not see it. Is that not right? **THEODORUS:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** But "not seeing" is "not knowing," if indeed "seeing" is "knowing." **THEODORUS:** True. **SOCRATES:** It follows then, that a person who has come to know something, and still remembers it, does not know it—because he does not see it. And we said this would be a "monstrosity" if it were to happen. **THEODORUS:** You speak the absolute truth. **SOCRATES:** Thus, an impossible conclusion seems to follow if one says that knowledge and perception are the same. **THEODORUS:** So it appears. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, we must say they are different. **THEODORUS:** It seems so. **SOCRATES:** What then could knowledge be? It seems we must speak from the beginning again. And yet, Theaetetus, what are we about to do? **THEODORUS:** About what? **SOCRATES:** We seem to me like an ignoble rooster <note>Socrates compares their premature confidence to a rooster that crows before it has actually won the fight.</note> who jumps away from the argument and starts crowing before he has won. <margin>F</margin> **THEODORUS:** How so? **SOCRATES:** We seem to have reached a conclusion based only on the common agreement of words, and having gained the advantage by such linguistic tricks, we are satisfied. And though we claim not to be mere debaters but seekers of wisdom <note>original: *philosophoi* vs *rabulas* (in Latin) or *agonitai* (in Greek), meaning "philosophers" vs "competitive debaters/wranglers."</note>, we are unknowingly doing exactly what those clever men do. **THEODORUS:** I do not yet understand what you mean. **SOCRATES:** Well, I will try to explain what I have in mind. We asked whether a man who has learned and remembers something can "not know" it. And by showing that the man who saw and then closed his eyes remembers but does not see, we proved that he does not know—even while remembering. <margin>G</margin> But this is impossible. And so, the "fable" of Protagoras has perished, and your fable—that knowledge and perception are the same—has perished with it. **THEODORUS:** So it seems. **SOCRATES:** I do not think it would be so, my friend, if the "father" of the first fable <note>Socrates refers to Protagoras as the father of the theory.</note> were still alive; he would have defended it vigorously. But now it is an orphan, and we are insulting it. Even the guardians Protagoras left behind are unwilling to help—one of whom is Theodorus here. So, for the sake of justice, we ourselves will have to try to help him. **THEODORUS:** Not I, Socrates! Rather Callias, son of Hipponicus, is the guardian of his affairs. We turned away from those abstract words to geometry too soon. But we will be grateful to you if you help him. **SOCRATES:** Well said, Theodorus. Look then at how I shall help him. <margin>H</margin> For a person might agree to even stranger things than these if he does not pay close attention to the words we are so accustomed to using for affirming and denying. I will tell you how...

<column-break/>

...I judge: and these things he says, which many listeners would admit (which would be a grave matter, unless any man far surpassed any brute in wisdom); but you bring no demonstration or necessity, but use only a likely reason. Which, if Theodorus or any other geometer wished to use in geometric disputes, he would be valued at nothing at all. Consider therefore, both you and Theodorus, whether you wish to receive speeches about such great matters confirmed only by probable reasoning. **THEAETETUS:** Both you, O Socrates, and we would receive them unjustly. **SOCRATES:** But now another matter, just as it was agreed between you and Theodorus, must be considered. **THEAETETUS:** Another, certainly. **SOCRATES:** Let us think then, whether knowledge and sense are the same, or something else. For toward this all the previous speech was tending, and for the sake of this we touched upon so many and wonderful things. Is it not so? **THEAETETUS:** It is entirely so. **SOCRATES:** Shall we confess that whatever we feel by seeing or hearing, we also know all those same things at the same time? As for example, the voice of foreigners <note>original: *barbarorum*</note> before we have learned it, shall we say we do not hear it when they speak; or do we hear and know it at the same time? And being entirely ignorant of letters, when we look at a string of them, shall we deny that we see them? Or shall we assert that we also know them, if only we have seen them? **THEAETETUS:** That very thing, O Socrates, which we discern and hear in these cases, we shall affirm that we know: of the letters, we shall say we likewise look upon and know the shape and color; of the voices, we shall say we hear and likewise know the sharp and heavy pitch. But what grammarians and interpreters pass down concerning these things, we neither feel by seeing and hearing, nor do we know. **SOCRATES:** Excellent, O Theaetetus, nor should you be resisted in these things, so that you may profit more therefrom; but look at another thing which happens regarding these matters, and consider by what reasoning it can be repelled and avoided. **THEAETETUS:** What is that? **SOCRATES:** This surely: if anyone should ask, whether it could happen that what someone once knew, and still holds in memory fixed and preserved, he should nevertheless not know that same thing. I am drawing out the speech into a long one, desiring to ask whether someone who retains in memory what he learned does not know it. **THEAETETUS:** How could this happen, O Socrates? It would be a monstrosity <note>original: *monstrum*</note> that you speak of. **SOCRATES:** Am I then raving? Pay attention, I pray. To see—do you not call this "to feel," and vision "sense"? **THEAETETUS:** I do. **SOCRATES:** He who sees something, does he not know the same thing that he sees, as the present speech proposes? **THEAETETUS:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** Do you call memory something? **THEAETETUS:** I do indeed. **SOCRATES:** Of something, or of nothing? **THEAETETUS:** Of something, certainly. **SOCRATES:** Is it not of those things which he learned and felt? **THEAETETUS:** Of these, surely. **SOCRATES:** What one has seen, does he sometimes remember? **THEAETETUS:** He remembers. **SOCRATES:** What then when he closes his eyes? Does he immediately forget when he does this? **THEAETETUS:** It would be absurd to say this, O Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Yet whoever wishes to preserve the previous speech is forced to confess it; otherwise, not at all. **THEAETETUS:** I also suspect as much, by Jove <note>original: *per Iouem*</note>, though I do not yet sufficiently understand. Tell me, I pray, in what way? **SOCRATES:** This way surely: he who sees, knows the same thing that he sees, as we have confessed; for we agreed that vision, sense, and knowledge are the same thing. **THEAETETUS:** We agreed. **SOCRATES:** But he who saw, and therefore knows, remembers what he saw even with closed eyes, and does not then see anything. **THEAETETUS:** So it happens. **SOCRATES:** But not to see is not to know, if indeed to see was to know. **THEAETETUS:** TRUE. **SOCRATES:** It happens therefore that what one once knew, even while he remembers it, he does not know it, if he does not see it. Which, if it were to happen, we predicted would be a kind of monstrosity. **THEAETETUS:** You speak the truth. **SOCRATES:** Something impossible, therefore, seems to follow, if anyone posits that knowledge and sense are the same. **THEAETETUS:** So it appears. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, it must be confessed that each is different. **THEODORUS:** It seems so. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, what knowledge is must be sought again from the beginning. But what are we doing, O Theaetetus? **THEAETETUS:** About what do you ask? **SOCRATES:** We seem to ourselves like a cowardly cock, jumping away from the dispute immediately to crow before we have conquered. **THEAETETUS:** How so? **SOCRATES:** We seem to have reached a contradictory agreement against the concessions of names, and having dealt with such a thing, to search out words and stop in them; and while we profess ourselves to be not brawlers <note>original: *rabulas*</note> but philosophers, we do nothing else meanwhile but act like those fierce men in secret. **THEAETETUS:** I do not yet understand what you wish. **SOCRATES:** Indeed, I will endeavor to explain what I feel in these matters. We asked whether anyone who has learned and remembers something can not know it; and having shown that he who saw, even with closed eyes, remembers and yet does not see, we demonstrated him to be both unknowing and remembering at the same time, which is quite impossible. And thus the fable of Protagoras has entirely vanished, and yours as well, which sang that sense and knowledge are the same. **THEAETETUS:** It is certain. **SOCRATES:** By no means so, as I think, friend, if the father of the other fable were surviving, but he would defend it most vehemently. Now, however, we pursue and despoil the orphan herself, nor do the tutors whom Protagoras left behind—among whose number is this Theodorus—wish to help. But we, for the sake of justice, will undertake to support her. **THEAETETUS:** Not I indeed, O Socrates, but rather Callias son of Hipponicus is the guardian of Protagoras's affairs. We indeed have suddenly deflected from bare speeches to geometry. We shall be grateful to you, however, if you bring help to him. **SOCRATES:** You speak skillfully, O Theodorus. Pay attention, therefore, to the way in which I shall help. If one does not observe the force of words, by which we are mostly accustomed to affirm and deny anything, he will be forced to confess even more absurd things than the previous ones. I will tell you how...

<summary>Socrates logicially deconstructs the definition of "knowledge as perception" by showing that if seeing is knowing, then a person who remembers something with their eyes closed would technically not know it, which is an absurd conclusion. Socrates also notes that they are acting like competitive debaters rather than true philosophers by relying on linguistic traps rather than deep truth.</summary>
<keywords>epistemology, memory vs perception, Protagoras, the closed eye paradox, Socratic method, philosophy vs sophistry, Theaetetus</keywords>

--- Page 156 ---
<meta>This page continues the investigation into the definition of knowledge. Having explored the idea that "knowledge is perception," Socrates now introduces a logical trap involving physical sight to challenge the young Theaetetus. He then shifts into a famous defense of Protagoras’s "Man is the Measure" doctrine, arguing that while every person's perception is "true" for them, some perceptions are "better" or "healthier" than others—a key distinction for the role of the Sophist and the physician.</meta>

# PLATO'S

<column-break/>

...or for Theaetetus? **THEAETETUS:** For both of us in common. But let the younger one answer; for if he slips up, he will feel less shame. **SOCRATES:** I speak then of the most difficult question. It is, I believe, something like this: is it possible for the same person who knows something, to not know that which he knows? **THEAETETUS:** Heavens! What then shall we answer, Theaetetus? **THEAETETUS:** I, for one, think it is impossible. **SOCRATES:** Not at all, if you insist that "to see" is "to know." For how will you deal with an <margin>A Proverb.</margin> inescapable question—caught, as the saying goes, in a well—when an intrepid man asks you, while covering one of your eyes with his hand, whether you see the cloak with the eye that is covered? **THEODORUS:** I would say not with that one, but certainly with the other. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, you both see and do not see the same thing at the same time? **THEAETETUS:** In a way, yes. **SOCRATES:** "I am not asking about the 'how,'" he will say, "nor about simplicity, but whether <margin>B</margin> what you know, you also do not know." Now it appears you see what you do not see; and you have already agreed that seeing is knowing, and not seeing is not knowing. Calculate, then, what happens to your argument from these points. **THEAETETUS:** Indeed, I calculate that the opposite of my premises has occurred. **SOCRATES:** And perhaps, my wonderful boy, you would have suffered more such things if someone had asked you whether it is possible to know both sharply and dully, or to know from up close but not from a distance, or to know the same thing both intensely and faintly—and a thousand other such things. A <term>peltast</term> <note>original: "peltastikos," a light-armed soldier; here used to describe a debater who uses quick, stinging arguments for pay.</note>, a mercenary in words, lying in wait and having set his trap, would have attacked you once you claimed that knowledge and perception are the same. He would have charged into your senses of hearing and <margin>C</margin> smelling, and other such senses, and would have refuted you by holding you fast until, admiring his much-beloved wisdom, you were entangled by him. Then, having overpowered and bound you, he would have released you only for as much money as you and he agreed upon. What argument then (you might ask), would Protagoras himself offer in defense of his works? Shall we try to say something else? **THEAETETUS:** By all means. **SOCRATES:** He will say all these things that we have said in his defense, and he will, I think, come to close quarters with us, looking down on us and saying: "This good Socrates, when a child he questioned became frightened at the thought of whether it is possible for the same person to remember the same thing and simultaneously not know it—and because the child in his fear denied it, being unable to see ahead—Socrates made me look ridiculous in his discussions. But the truth, <margin>D</margin> you most lazy Socrates, is this: whenever you examine any of my doctrines through questioning, if the person questioned answers as I would answer and is tripped up, then I am refuted; but if he answers differently, then only the one questioned is refuted. For example, do you think anyone will grant you that a memory remains in someone of what they suffered, being the same kind of experience as when they were suffering it, when they are no longer suffering? Far from it. Or again, will they shrink from admitting that it is possible to know and not know the same thing? Or if they fear that, will they grant that a person who is becoming unlike his former self is the same person as he was before he became unlike? Or rather, that he is 'someone,' but not 'these' people, and that these versions of him become infinite in number if the process of becoming unlike continues? This is just to <margin>E</margin> avoid your hunting for words against one another. But, you blessed man," he will say, "attack what I actually say in a more noble way, if you can, and prove that our perceptions do not occur uniquely to each of us; or that, even if they are unique, it does not follow that what 'appears' to someone 'becomes' only for that person. When you talk of pigs and <term>dog-headed apes</term> <note>original: "cynocephalos," refers to a species of baboon or a mythical creature; Socrates previously joked that Protagoras might as well have said a pig is the measure of all things.</note>, you are not only acting like a beast yourself, but you persuade your listeners to do the same to my writings, which is not right. For I claim the truth is exactly as I have written: that each of us is the measure <margin>F</margin> of both what is and what is not. However, one person differs immensely from another in this very thing: that for one person, some things are and appear, while for another, different things do. I am far from saying that wisdom and the wise man do not exist; rather, I call a man wise who, by changing the condition of someone for whom things appear and are 'bad,' makes them appear and be 'good.' Do not pursue my argument merely by its words, but learn more clearly what I mean. For instance, remember what was said before: to a sick man, the food he eats appears to be and is bitter; but to a healthy man, it is and appears the opposite. Now, one should not make one of these men 'wiser' than the other (for that is not possible), nor should it be asserted that the sick man is ignorant because he has such opinions, or that the healthy man is wise because his are different. Instead, one must change the state <margin>G</margin> to the other, for the one state is better. So it is also in education: one must change a person from one state to a better state. But whereas the physician changes things with drugs, the Sophist does so with words. For no one ever made someone who has false opinions later have true ones; it is not possible to have an opinion of things that are not, nor of anything other than what one experiences, and these experiences are always true. But I believe that when a person with a wretched soul has opinions akin to it, a good soul can make him have different, better opinions—which some people, out of inexperience, call 'true' appearances. I, however, call some better than others, but not truer. And the wise, my dear Socrates, I am far from calling frogs; rather, in regard to bodies I call them physicians, and in regard to plants, farmers. For I say that these men, when a plant is sickly, instill in it good, healthy, and 'true' perceptions instead of wretched ones. And the wise and <margin>H</margin> good orators make the 'good' things seem just to the cities instead of the 'wretched' ones. For whatever seems just and honorable to each city, is so for that city as long as it holds that opinion. But the wise man, in place of the wretched things that exist for them, makes good things both seem and be true for them."

<meta>catchword: for them</meta>

<column-break/>

**A** or for Theaetetus? **THEAETETUS:** For both of us in common. But let the younger one answer; for if he slips up, he will be less ashamed. **SOCRATES:** I speak of the most fearsome question. It is, I believe, something of this sort: Is it possible for the same person, knowing something, to not know this which he knows? **THEAETETUS:** Heavens! What then shall we answer, O Theaetetus? **THEAETETUS:** I, for one, think it is impossible. **SOCRATES:** Not if you define seeing and knowing as the same thing. For what will you do with an inescapable question—trapped as they say in a well—when an intrepid man asks you, while covering one of your eyes with his hand, whether you see the cloak with the covered eye? **THEAETETUS:** I would say not with that one, but certainly with the other. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, you both see and do not see the same thing at the same time? **THEAETETUS:** In a way, yes. **SOCRATES:** "I am not asking that," he says, "nor about the 'how,' but whether **B** what you know, you also do not know. For currently, what you do not see, you appear to see; and you have already agreed that seeing is knowing, and not seeing is not knowing. Calculate then, from these points, what happens to you." **THEAETETUS:** Indeed, I calculate that the opposite of my premises has occurred. **SOCRATES:** And perhaps, my wonderful boy, you would have suffered more such things if someone had asked you whether it is possible to know both sharply and dully, or to know from up close but not from a distance, or to know the same thing both intensely and faintly—and a thousand other such things. A peltast, a mercenary in words, lying in wait, having set his trap once you claimed that knowledge and perception are the same, would have attacked you once you claimed that knowledge and perception are the same, charging into your hearing, **C** smelling, and other such senses, and would have refuted you by holding you fast until, admiring his much-beloved wisdom, you were entangled by him. Having overpowered and bound you, he would then have released you for as much money as you and he agreed upon. What argument then (you might say) will Protagoras offer for his own works? Shall we try to say something else? **THEAETETUS:** By all means. **SOCRATES:** He will say all these things that we have said in his defense, and he will, I think, come to close quarters with us, looking down on us and saying: "This good Socrates, when a child he questioned became frightened at the thought of whether it is possible for the same person to remember the same thing and simultaneously not know it—and because the child in his fear denied it, being unable to see ahead—Socrates made me look ridiculous in his discussions.
