<meta>This page continues the "Defense of Protagoras" initiated on the previous page. Socrates is speaking as if he were Protagoras, defending the "Man is the Measure" doctrine while simultaneously urging his companions to engage in a more rigorous, "adult" critique of the theory rather than merely tripping up the young student Theaetetus.</meta>

# THEAETETUS

...makes things appear and be good. <margin>A</margin> By the same logic, a sophist <note>A professional teacher of virtue and rhetoric in ancient Greece.</note> who is able to educate his pupils in this way is wise and deserves a high fee from those he has taught. And thus some are wiser than others, yet no one holds false opinions. And you, whether you like it or not, must accept being a "measure." For this argument is preserved in these principles.

If you have a counter-argument from the beginning, oppose it with a speech of your own; but if you prefer questions, do it through questions. For this is not to be avoided, but especially pursued by a man of sense. However, do it like this: do not be unjust in your questioning. It is a great absurdity for one who claims to care for virtue to do nothing but act unjustly in arguments. <margin>B</margin> Being "unjust" in such matters occurs when someone fails to distinguish between "competing" <note>original Greek: *agonizomenos*, referring to a contest for victory</note> and "conversing." In the first, one plays and trips up the opponent as much as possible; but in conversation, one is serious and corrects the partner, pointing out only those errors they fell into themselves or from previous associations. 

If you act this way, those who associate with you will blame themselves for their own confusion and impasse, not you. They will pursue you and love you, while hating themselves; <margin>C</margin> they will flee from themselves into philosophy, so that by becoming different people, they may be rid of who they were before. But if you do the opposite, as many do, the opposite result will follow: instead of philosophers, you will turn your companions into haters of the subject when they grow older. 

If you follow me (as was said before), not in a hostile or combative way, but with a gracious and gentle mind, you will truly examine what we mean when we say that all things are in motion, and that whatever seems true to each person is indeed true for them, both privately and for the city. From these points you will investigate whether knowledge and perception are the same or different—not, as you did just now, from the <margin>D</margin> habitual use of words and names which most people drag about however they please, causing all sorts of difficulties. 

This, Theodorus, is the assistance I have offered to your friend <note>Protagoras</note> to the best of my ability—small help from my small resources. If he were alive himself, he would have defended his cause more magnificently.

<term>THEODORUS.</term> You are joking, Socrates, for you have defended the man quite vigorously.

<term>SOCRATES.</term> You speak well, my friend. But tell me: did you notice Protagoras saying just now, and rebuking us, that we were addressing our words to a mere child, and using a child's fear to fight against his ideas? Calling it a mere "pleasantry," he solemnly invoked the "measure of all things" and urged us to be serious about his argument?

<term>THEODORUS.</term> Of course I noticed, Socrates.

<term>SOCRATES.</term> What then? Do you bid us obey him?

<term>THEODORUS.</term> Most certainly.

<term>SOCRATES.</term> <margin>E</margin> Do you see that everyone here except you is a child? If we are to obey the man, you and I must question and answer each other seriously about his theory, so he cannot complain that we examined it while playing with boys.

<term>THEODORUS.</term> But would not Theaetetus follow an investigation better than many with large beards?

<term>SOCRATES.</term> Not better than you, Theodorus. Do not think that I must defend your deceased friend by every means, while you do nothing. Come, best of men, follow me a little until we see whether you ought to be the "measure" regarding geometric diagrams, or if everyone is equally as capable as you in astronomy and the other fields where you are said to excel.

<term>THEODORUS.</term> It is not easy, Socrates, for one <margin>F</margin> sitting beside you not to give an account. I was talking nonsense just now when I said you would allow me not to "strip" <note>The Greek *apodyesthai* refers to stripping naked for wrestling or gymnastics; Socrates uses it as a metaphor for intellectual cross-examination.</note> or be compelled like the Spartans. You seem to lean more toward the ways of Sciron <note>A mythical bandit who forced travelers to wash his feet before kicking them off a cliff.</note>. The Spartans tell one to either leave or strip, but you seem to act more like Antaeus <note>A giant wrestler who forced all passersby to wrestle him to the death.</note>; for you do not let whoever approaches go until you have forced them to strip and wrestle in words.

<term>SOCRATES.</term> You have hit upon a very good comparison for my "disease," Theodorus. Yet I am stronger than they. For countless Herculesses and Theseuses, mighty in speech, have encountered me and given me a good drubbing; but I do not <margin>G</margin> desist for all that, so terrible is the love for this kind of exercise that has entered me. So do not begrudge me the chance to test yourself against me, and thus benefit both of us.

<term>THEODORUS.</term> I no longer object; lead where you will. I must endure the fate you spin for me and be cross-examined. However, I cannot offer myself to you beyond what you have proposed.

<term>SOCRATES.</term> That will be enough. But watch carefully that we don't accidentally slip into a childish style of speaking, lest someone mock us for it again.

<term>THEODORUS.</term> I will try as hard as I can.

<term>SOCRATES.</term> Let us then take up the point we touched on earlier, and see if we were right or wrong to be annoyed when we criticized the idea that every person is self-sufficient in wisdom. Protagoras granted us that <margin>H</margin> some people differ from others in respect to better or worse, and these he called "wise." Did he not?

<term>THEODORUS.</term> He did.

<term>SOCRATES.</term> If he were here himself and had confessed this, rather than us making the concession on his behalf, we would not need to confirm it again. But now someone might claim we lack the authority to make such an agreement for him. Therefore, it is better to reach an agreement through his own words as much as possible. For it makes a great difference whether this is so or otherwise.

<term>THEODORUS.</term> True.

# OF PLATO

<margin>A</margin> ...you speak. Socrates: Therefore, let us take the agreement not from the words of others, but from Protagoras's own speech, as briefly as possible. THEODORUS: How? SOCRATES: In this way. He said that what seems to each person, is indeed what it seems to that person. THEODORUS: He certainly said that. SOCRATES: Do we not also, O Protagoras, speak of the opinions of a man—indeed, of all men—and assert that there is no one who does not think himself wiser than others in some respects, yet others wiser than himself in other respects? For in the greatest dangers, whenever men are tossed about in military camps, or by disease, or at sea, do they not look to those who excel in each matter as if they were gods, and expect them to be their saviors, though they excel the rest in nothing other than knowledge? And in all human affairs, do they not seek teachers and leaders for themselves and for other living creatures and for their works, believing them to be sufficient both for teaching and for commanding? In all these instances, what else shall we say, except that men themselves believe that <term>wisdom and ignorance</term><note>Latin: *sapientiam & ignorantiam*. Socrates is distinguishing between having actual knowledge and being unlearned.</note> exist among them? THEODORUS: Nothing else. SOCRATES: And do they not consider wisdom to be true thought, and ignorance to be false opinion? THEODORUS: How could they not?
<margin>B</margin> SOCRATES: Where, O Protagoras, shall we turn the argument? Shall we say that men always have true opinions? Or that sometimes they are true, and sometimes false? From either side it follows that they do not always think the truth, but rather both. For consider, Theodorus, whether any of Protagoras's followers, or perhaps you yourself, would wish to contend that no one thinks anyone else is either unskilled or holds a false opinion. THEODORUS: That is unbelievable, O Socrates. SOCRATES: And yet that speech which proclaims "man is the measure of all things" falls into this very necessity. THEODORUS: In what way? SOCRATES: When you determine something within yourself and then declare your opinion to me, let it be true for you according to his speech; but for us, can we not become judges of your judgment, or do we always judge that you think the truth? Is it not rather that countless men fight against you every day, holding opposite opinions and thinking that you judge and think wrongly? THEODORUS: By Jove, O Socrates, there are very many indeed who—as Homer says—give me a great deal of trouble among men.
<margin>C</margin> SOCRATES: What then? Do you want us to say that you then think the truth for yourself, but what is false for those others? THEODORUS: From what has been said, that seems to follow necessarily. SOCRATES: And what of Protagoras himself? Is it not necessary? For if neither he himself thought that man was the measure, nor did the many (as indeed they do not), then it would follow that this "Truth" which he wrote belongs to no one. But if he himself believed it, yet the multitude does not agree, know first that by as much as those to whom it does not seem so outnumber those to whom it does, by so much more is it "not" rather than "is." THEODORUS: It must be so, if it is to "be" or "not be" according to each individual opinion. SOCRATES: Furthermore, this has a most elegant result: He acknowledges that the opinion of those who disagree with his own opinion—those who believe he is lying—is somehow true, since he admits that everyone thinks what is true. THEODORUS: Without a doubt. SOCRATES: Does he not then admit that his own opinion is false, if he admits that the judgment of those who believe his opinion is false is itself true? THEODORUS: Necessarily. SOCRATES: But the others do not at all concede that they themselves are lying. THEODORUS: Certainly not. SOCRATES: And he, in turn, admits that this opinion of theirs is also true, based on what he has written. THEODORUS: It is clear. SOCRATES: From all this, it will be disputed by everyone, starting with Protagoras—or rather, it will be conceded by him most of all. For when he concedes that the one who contradicts him thinks the truth, then Protagoras himself will surely admit that neither a dog nor any random man is the measure, not even of a single thing which he has not learned. Is it not so? THEODORUS: It is certainly so. SOCRATES: Since it is doubted by everyone, Protagoras's "Truth" will be true to no one—not to anyone else, nor even to himself. THEODORUS: Socrates, we are attacking my friend too harshly. SOCRATES: But truly, my friend, it is unclear whether we are also overshooting the mark. For it is likely that he, being older, was also wiser than us. If he were suddenly to pop up from the ground right here as far as his neck, he would catch me talking much nonsense (as is probable) and you for agreeing with me; then he would duck back down and run away. However, it is necessary for us to use ourselves as we are, and always to speak what seems to us. And now, indeed, let us say that anyone would concede this: that one person exists who is wiser or more skilled than another. THEODORUS: So it seems to me. SOCRATES: Shall we say that the argument stands most firmly on what we ourselves conceded when supporting Protagoras? Namely, that many things are as they seem to each person—such as hot, dry, sweet, and all things of this kind? But if he will confess that in certain things one man differs from another, it would be in matters of health and disease; he would surely assert that not every little woman, child, or beast is capable of curing itself through its own knowledge of what is healthy. In this, if anywhere, they differ most. THEODORUS: That seems right to me as well. SOCRATES: Furthermore, in political matters, concerning what is honorable and base, just and unjust, holy and impious—whatever each city thinks and establishes as law for itself, these things are truly so for each city. And in these things, no private citizen is wiser than another, nor one city wiser than another. But in the matter of establishing what is useful or useless for the republic, here, if anywhere, he will admit that one counselor differs from another, and one city's opinion differs from another's in finding the truth. He would never dare to admit that whatever a city establishes, thinking it useful to itself, will always turn out to be beneficial. But as I say, in matters of the just and unjust, and the holy and profane, they wish to insist that none of these has a substance by its own nature...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...true. SOCRATES: Let us then not take the agreement through others, but from his own argument as briefly as possible. THEODORUS: How? SOCRATES: Thus: What seems to each, is that so to the one it seems to? THEODORUS: He says so. SOCRATES: Then, O Protagoras, we also speak of the opinions of a man, or rather of all men, and we say there is no one who does not consider himself wiser than others in some things, and others wiser than himself in others. And in the greatest dangers, when they are in campaigns, or diseases, or storms at sea, they look to the leaders in each case as gods, expecting them to be saviors, differing in nothing else than in <term>knowing</term><note>Greek: *τῷ εἰδέναι* (tō eidenai). This refers to specialized knowledge or expertise.</note>. And everywhere in human affairs, people seek <margin>B</margin> teachers and leaders for themselves and for other animals and for their labors, thinking themselves capable of teaching and capable of leading. And in all these things, what else shall we say but that men themselves believe that wisdom and lack of learning exist among them? THEODORUS: Nothing else. SOCRATES: Therefore, they consider wisdom to be true thought, and lack of learning to be false opinion? THEODORUS: Of course. SOCRATES: What then, O Protagoras, shall we do with the argument? Shall we say that men always have true opinions, or sometimes true and sometimes false? For from both it follows that they do not always have true opinions, but both. For consider, O Theodorus, if anyone from Protagoras's circle, or you yourself, would fight to the death to claim that no one considers anyone else <margin>C</margin> unlearned or to have false opinions. THEODORUS: That is unbelievable, Socrates. SOCRATES: And yet the argument which says man is the measure of all things arrives at this necessity. THEODORUS: How so? SOCRATES: When you, having judged something in yourself, declare an opinion to me about something, let this be true for you according to his argument; but for us others, is it not possible to become judges of your judgment? Or do we always judge that you think the truth? Or do ten thousand others at any time fight against you, holding opposite opinions, believing that you judge and think falsely? THEODORUS: By Zeus, Socrates, very many indeed (<margin>D</margin> as Homer says) are those who give me all the trouble in the world. SOCRATES: What then? Do you want us to say that you then think the truth for yourself, but the ten thousand think what is false? THEODORUS: It seems to be a necessity from the argument. SOCRATES: And what of Protagoras himself? Is it not a necessity? If he himself did not think man was the measure, nor did the many (as indeed they do not), then this Truth which he wrote would be for no one. But if he thought so, but the multitude did not agree, you know that the more those to whom it does not seem so outnumber those to whom it does, by so much more it is "not" than "is." THEODORUS: It is a necessity, if indeed it shall be or not be according to each opinion. SOCRATES: Then this is the most clever part. He, concerning his own opinion, concedes that the opinion of those who think differently—by which they believe he is lying—is somehow true, since he agrees that everyone thinks what is. THEODORUS: <margin>E</margin> Entirely so. SOCRATES: Would he not then concede that his own opinion is false, if he agrees that the opinion of those who think he is lying is true? THEODORUS: Necessarily. SOCRATES: But the others do not concede that they are lying? THEODORUS: No, they do not. SOCRATES: And he, in turn, agrees that this opinion is also true, from what he has written. THEODORUS: So it appears. SOCRATES: Therefore, it will be disputed by all, starting from Protagoras—or rather, it will be agreed by him; when he concedes to the one saying the opposite that he thinks the truth, then Protagoras himself will concede that neither a dog nor just any man is the measure, not even about one thing which he has not learned. Is it not so? THEODORUS: It is so. SOCRATES: Therefore, since it is disputed by all, Protagoras's "Truth" would be true to no one—neither to anyone else, nor to himself. THEODORUS: <margin>F</margin> Socrates, we are running down my friend too much. SOCRATES: But, O friend, it is unclear if we are also running past the truth. It is likely that he, being older, is wiser than us; and if he should suddenly pop up from here as far as his neck, he would catch me talking much nonsense (as is likely) and you for agreeing, and then he would sink down and be gone, running off. But it is necessary for us (I think) to use ourselves as we are, and to always say what seems so. And now, shall we say that anyone would agree with this: that one person is wiser than another, and also more unlearned? THEODORUS: To me at least, it seems so. SOCRATES: And would the argument stand most firmly in the way we outlined when helping Protagoras: that most things are as they <margin>G</margin> seem to each—hot, dry, sweet, all things of that type? But if it is conceded that one person differs from another in some things, it would be concerning the healthy and the diseased—he would want to say that not every woman and child or beast is capable of healing itself, knowing what is healthy for it; but here, if anywhere, one differs from another. THEODORUS: To me at least, it seems so. SOCRATES: And also concerning politics: the beautiful and the base, the just and the unjust, the holy and the impious—whatever each city, having thought it so, establishes as law for itself, these things are in truth for each city. And in these things, no one is wiser, neither a private citizen than another, nor one city than another. But in establishing what is advantageous or not advantageous to itself, <margin>H</margin> here, if anywhere, he will again agree that counselor differs from counselor, and the opinion of one city from another in respect to truth; and he would not at all dare to say that whatever a city establishes, thinking it advantageous to itself, will most certainly be advantageous. But there, as I say, in the just and unjust, the holy and the unholy, they wish to insist that none of them has any existence by nature...

L iiii <note>This is a "signature" mark used by printers to help assemble the book's pages in the correct order.</note>

<summary>Socrates argues that Protagoras's "Man is the Measure" theory is self-refuting because, if all opinions are true, then the opinion that Protagoras is wrong must also be true. He concludes that while sensory perceptions might be relative, expertise in fields like medicine or politics requires objective wisdom.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and the mathematician Theodorus. Having just discussed Protagoras’s theory that truth is relative to the observer, Socrates begins a famous "digression" where he contrasts the lifestyle and mindset of the philosopher with that of the legal and political "man of the world."</meta>

# THEAETETUS
L iiij

...to have some [truth] of his own, but that what seems to a community is true for it at the time it seems so, and for as long as it seems so. And those who do not entirely follow the doctrine of Protagoras practice philosophy in some such way. But for us, O Theodorus, a greater discussion is emerging from a lesser one, and it occupies us. THEODORUS: We are surely at leisure, O Socrates. SOCRATES: It seems so. And often at other times, O blessed man, I have noticed—but especially now—how reasonable it is that those who have spent much time in philosophy appear as ridiculous speakers when they go into the law courts. THEODORUS: In what way do you mean this? SOCRATES: Those who have been tossed about in the courts and such places from their youth seem, when compared to those raised in philosophy and similar pursuits, like servants compared to freemen. THEODORUS: In what way? SOCRATES: In this: that for the latter, as you said, <margin>On the leisure of philosophers and their manner of disputing.</margin> leisure is always available, and they carry on their discussions in peace and at their own pace. Just as we are now taking up a third discussion after the previous one, so do they, if a new subject pleases them more than the one at hand—as is happening to us now. They do not care whether they speak at length or briefly, provided they attain the truth. But the others are always hurried in their speaking by the shortage of time. For the <term>flowing water</term><note>Latin: *aqua defluens*; Greek: *hydor reon*. This refers to the *clepsydra* or water-clock used in Athenian courts to strictly limit the time a speaker had to present his case.</note> urges them on, and they are not permitted to speak on whatever they desire. Instead, the opposing party stands over them with necessity, reading out the <term>indictment</term><note>Latin: *libelli formulam*; Greek: *antomosia*. The formal sworn statement or written charges that restricted the scope of the legal argument.</note>, <margin>That the orator can never speak freely, but must always fear the judge.</margin> outside of which nothing may be said. Their speeches are always about a fellow-slave, addressed to a master who sits in judgment and holds the verdict in his hand. The contests are never for nothing, but always for a specific point, often a race for life itself. And so, for all these reasons, they become intense and sharp, knowing how to flatter the master with words and win favor with deeds—yet they are small and crooked in their souls. For their growth, uprightness, and freedom have been stripped away by their servitude since youth, forcing them to perform crooked and perverse deeds by casting great dangers and fears upon their still-tender souls. Since they cannot endure these things with justice and truth, they turn immediately to lies and mutual injuries, bending and breaking in many ways. Thus, they pass from youth into manhood with nothing healthy in their minds, becoming clever and wise, as they believe. And these men are such as they are, O Theodorus. But as for those of our "chorus," do you wish for us to describe them, or shall we leave them aside and return to our argument? We should not, as we were just saying, abuse our freedom and our habit of wandering from one topic to another. THEODORUS: By no means, Socrates; let us describe them. For you said it very well: we who move in such a chorus are not the servants of our arguments, but the arguments are our servants, and each of them waits to be finished whenever it seems right to us. For no judge, nor any spectator—as is the case for the poets—presides over us to censor or command us. SOCRATES: Let us speak then, since it pleases you, about the leaders of the chorus. For why should one speak of those who spend their time poorly in philosophy? These leaders, from their youth onward, first of all do not know the way to the marketplace, nor where the court is, or the council-chamber, or any other public assembly of the city. They neither see nor hear the laws or decrees, whether spoken or written. The strivings of political factions for office, the meetings, the dinners, and the revels with flute-girls—these things do not even occur to them in their dreams. Whether someone in the city has been born of high or low birth, or what disgrace has come to someone from their ancestors, whether male or female, is more hidden from the philosopher than—as the <margin>Proverb.</margin> saying goes—the "measures of the sea." And he does not even know that he does not know these things. For he does not abstain from them for the sake of reputation, but in reality only his body dwells and resides in the city, while his mind, considering all these things small and of no value, "flies everywhere," as Pindar says, measuring what is beneath the earth and upon its surface, and observing the stars above the heavens, searching out the entire nature of every thing in the universe, but never lowering itself to what is close at hand. THEODORUS: In what way do you say this, Socrates? <margin>The fall of Thales.</margin> SOCRATES: Just as the story goes, Theodorus, that while <term>Thales</term><note>Thales of Miletus (c. 624–546 BC) is often called the first philosopher. He was famous for his study of astronomy.</note> was gazing upward at the stars and fell into a well, a clever and pretty Thracian servant-girl is said to have mocked him, saying that he was eager to know the things in the heavens but failed to notice what was before him and at his feet. This same mockery applies to all who spend their lives in philosophy. For in truth, such a man is unaware of his neighbor—not only of what he does, but almost whether he is a man or some other creature. But what a human being actually is, and what is fitting for such a nature to do or to suffer, differing from all others—this he seeks and labors to investigate. Do you understand, Theodorus, or not? THEODORUS: I do, and what you say is true. SOCRATES: For indeed, my friend, as I was saying at the beginning, when such a man is forced to discuss things at his feet and before his eyes—whether in private with an individual or publicly in court—he causes laughter not only to Thracian girls but to the rest of the crowd, falling into wells and every kind of difficulty through his lack of experience. His awkwardness is terrible, making him look like a fool. For when he is in a situation where he must insult someone, he has nothing personal to cast as a reproach, as he knows no evil of anyone, having never studied such things. Therefore, being at a loss, he appears ridiculous.

# PLATO
Book 4

<margin>
The philosopher is inept at legal disputes.
</margin>
A In praising and extolling men, since the philosopher simulates or dissimulates nothing, but laughs openly, he is thought to be delirious. For when he hears a tyrant or a king being praised, he imagines he is hearing the praises of some swineherd, or a shepherd of sheep, or a cattle-driver, because he yields an abundance of milk <note>original: *quòd abundè mulgeat*. Socrates is using a metaphor: kings "milk" their subjects for wealth just as shepherds milk their flocks</note>. He considers there to be only this difference: that kings and tyrants tend to and "milk" a more hostile and treacherous animal than sheep. Such men must become no less rustic and uneducated through their lack of leisure than shepherds are, though they are enclosed within city walls as if in a sheepfold on a mountain. When he hears ten thousand acres of land, or even more, being proclaimed as if the owner possessed something magnificent, he thinks he is hearing of something tiny, since he is accustomed to looking at the entire orb of the earth. Furthermore, whenever someone recounts their noble lineage—how they can enumerate seven wealthy ancestors—he considers such praise to be the mark of a dull mind that thinks of nothing great due to ignorance. It is as if such a person cannot look toward the nature of the whole world and see that countless ancestors and great-grandfathers have preceded every one of us, among whom were innumerable rich and poor, kings and slaves, Barbarians and Greeks. Even when someone counts twenty-five generations of ancestors and traces their origin back to Hercules, the son of Amphitryon, the matter seems unworthy of mention to the philosopher. He laughs at those who cannot calculate that even the twenty-fifth person back from Hercules was simply whatever fortune made them—even if they were the fiftieth from Hercules—and who cannot cast away the vanity of an insane mind. In all these things, the philosopher is held by the common crowd to be ridiculous, partly because he appears proud and contemptuous, and partly because he is ignorant of what is right before his eyes and is full of doubt. **THEODORUS.** You have described the situation exactly as it happens, O Socrates. **SOCRATES.** But when the philosopher, O friend, draws someone toward the heights, and that person is prepared to leave this place—dismissing the lawsuits in which it is asked "How have I wronged you?" or "How have you wronged me?"—he ascends to the contemplation of justice and injustice themselves, D what each is, and how they differ from one another and from all other things. Or, having dismissed the controversy of whether a king who possesses much gold is happy, he turns to the contemplation of kingship itself, and of human happiness and misery in general—what their nature is for each person, and by what means it is fitting for human nature to attain the one and flee the other. When, I say, it is necessary to give an account of all these things, that small-souled, sharp-witted lawyer in turn pays the penalty to the philosopher. For he suffers from dizziness from looking down from such a high vantage point with blurred eyes, as he is unaccustomed to looking from above. He is distressed, he stammers, and he utters <term>barbarisms</term><note>Latin: *barbarica*; Greek: *βαρβαρίζων*. This implies the lawyer is so out of his element in abstract thought that he loses his command of sophisticated language.</note>. Therefore, he does not move the Thracian servant-girls or the uneducated to laughter (for they do not perceive it), but rather all those who have been educated in freedom and far from a life of servitude. This, O Theodorus, is the condition of each. The first is the man educated in liberty and leisure, whom you call a philosopher. Although he should not truly be blamed, he appears foolish and inept whenever he undertakes servile duties, as he knows neither how to tie up a bundle of bedding, nor how to season a dish, nor how to craft the flattering words of an adulator. The second is the condition of the man who can perform these tasks quickly and efficiently, but does not know how to wear the clothing of a free man with proper grace. Furthermore, he is utterly ignorant of how to sing the true life of the gods and of blessed men with a fitting harmony of speech. **THEAETETUS.** <note>The OCR text labels this speaker as "THEA." (Theaetetus) in Latin but "THE." (Theodorus) in Greek. Based on the context of the dialogue, Socrates is speaking to Theodorus.</note> If you could persuade all men of what 

<column-break/>

A [The philosopher] appears [ridiculous]. In praises and the boastings of others, he is seen to be nonsensical, laughing not in pretense but in reality. When a tyrant or king is eulogized, he thinks he hears one of the herdsmen—such as a swineherd or shepherd or some cattleman—being congratulated for a great milking. He considers that they shepherd and milk a more difficult and treacherous animal than those others do. Such a man must necessarily become no less rustic and uneducated through lack of leisure than the herdsmen, though he is hedged in by a wall in the mountains. When he hears of ten thousand <term>plethra</term><note>A Greek unit of area, roughly 100 feet or a quarter-acre.</note> of land or even more being possessed by someone, it seems to him that he is hearing of a very small amount, as he is accustomed to looking at the whole earth. And when B they sing of lineages—how someone is noble because they can show seven wealthy grandfathers—he considers the praise to belong to those who see things in a dull and narrow way. Because of their lack of education, they are unable to look always at the whole, nor to calculate that every person has had countless myriads of grandfathers and ancestors, among whom there have been—many times over for anyone—myriads of rich and poor, kings and slaves, Barbarians and Greeks. But when people pride themselves on a catalog of twenty-five ancestors and trace them back to Hercules, the son of Amphitryon, the smallness of their logic appears absurd to him. He laughs because they cannot calculate that the twenty-fifth ancestor up from C Amphitryon was simply what fortune happened to make him, as was the fiftieth from him, and they cannot rid their foolish souls of vanity. In all these things, such a man is laughed at by the many, appearing—as it seems—to be arrogant, ignorant of what is at his feet, and at a loss in every situation. **THEODORUS.** You speak of exactly what happens, O Socrates. **SOCRATES.** But whenever he himself, O friend, drags someone upward, and someone is willing to go with him out of the question "How do I wrong you, or you me?" into a search for justice and injustice themselves—what each of them is and how they differ from everything else or from each other—or from the question "Is a king happy because he possesses much gold?" into an inquiry concerning kingship and D human happiness and misery in general—what kind of things they are and in what way it is fitting for human nature to acquire the one and flee the other—when that man with the small, sharp, legalistic soul must in turn give an account of all these things, he pays the opposite penalty. Hanging dizzy from a height and looking into the air from above out of unaccustomedness, he is distressed, at a loss, and stammers. He does not provide laughter for Thracian girls or any other uneducated person (for they do not notice), but to all those who have been brought up in the opposite way of slaves. This is the character of each, O Theodorus: the one, brought up in true freedom and leisure, whom you call a philosopher. It is not held against him to seem simple-minded E and to be nothing when he falls into servile tasks—such as not knowing how to pack a bundle of bedding, nor how to sweeten a sauce, nor how to give a flattering speech. The other is the man who is able to serve in all such things sharply and quickly, but does not know how to cast his cloak over his right shoulder like a free man, nor having grasped the harmony of words, how to rightly hymn the true life of gods and happy men. **THEODORUS.** If, O Socrates, you could persuade all men of what you say as you have persuaded me, there would be more peace and fewer evils among men. **SOCRATES.** But it is not possible for evils to be destroyed, O Theodorus (for it is necessary that there always be something opposite to the good), nor for them to have a place among the gods; but of necessity they haunt mortal nature and this F region here. Therefore, one must try to flee from here to there as quickly as possible. And flight consists in becoming like God as much as is possible. To become like God is to become just and holy, together with wisdom. But indeed, O best of men, it is not at all easy to persuade people that it is not for the reasons the many say that one should flee wickedness and pursue virtue—that is, so that one may not seem bad and may appear good. For these things seem to me to be what is called "old wives' tales," as it appears to me. But let us state the truth in this way: **GOD** is in no way and in no manner unjust, but is as just as possible. And there is nothing more like Him than whichever of us becomes as just as possible. Regarding this is the true cleverness of a man, and his worthlessness and unmanliness. For the G knowledge of this is true wisdom and virtue; but ignorance of it is manifest unlearnedness and wickedness. Other seeming "clevernesses" and "wisdoms," when they occur in political power, are vulgar; in the arts, they are menial. For the man who does wrong and says or does unholy things, it is by far the best not to grant that he is "clever" through his villainy. For such men exult in the reproach, and they think they hear that they are not "nonsense" or "useless burdens on the earth," but men such as they ought to be to survive in a city. Therefore, the truth must be told: that they are all the more what they do not think they are, precisely because they do not think it. For they are ignorant of the penalty of injustice, of which they should be least ignorant. For it is not what they think—blows and deaths (which those who do no wrong sometimes suffer)—but a penalty that is impossible to escape. **THEODORUS.** Which one do you mean? **SOCRATES.** Since there are two patterns, O friend, set up in the order of things...

<summary>In this famous passage from the Theaetetus, Socrates contrasts the philosopher's focus on universal truths with the lawyer's narrow focus on earthly gain, concluding that human virtue consists in "becoming like God" through justice and wisdom.</summary>
<keywords>Plato, Socrates, Theaetetus, Theodorus, philosophy, justice, virtue, evil, becoming like God, homoiosis theo, genealogy, legal vs philosophical mind</keywords>
