<meta>This page continues the "digression" within Plato’s *Theaetetus*. On the previous page, Socrates described the philosopher's detachment from worldly status. Here, he concludes that detachment by contrasting the divine and the godless, before returning to the main debate: Protagoras's claim that "Man is the measure of all things."</meta>

# PLATO
### Theaetetus

<margin>The divine</margin>
<margin>A</margin> The divine nature is most blessed, whereas the godless is most miserable. Because they do not see that this is the case, those occupied by extreme stupidity and the height of folly fail to notice that through their unjust actions they are becoming like the latter and unlike the former. They pay the penalty for this by living a life that corresponds to the likeness they have taken on. Truly, if we tell them that unless they rid themselves of this "cleverness," that pure place of the good will not receive them after they die, and that here on earth they will always lead a life similar to their own nature—the wicked consorting with the wicked—these men, who think themselves formidable and unscrupulous, will think they are hearing the ramblings of fools.

THEODORUS: Quite so, Socrates.
SOCRATES: I know it well, my friend. One thing, however, happens to them: whenever they are required to give and receive an account of the things they criticize in private, and they are willing to endure a long discussion like men rather than fleeing like cowards, then—how strange, my dear friend—they end up dissatisfied with their own arguments. Their famous rhetoric somehow withers away, until they seem no different from children. 

<margin>B</margin> But since these matters are merely a side issue <note>original: *πάρεργα*. Socrates refers to the "digression" on the life of the philosopher which began earlier</note>, let us set them aside. If we do not, a growing flood of them will bury our original argument. Let us return to where we were before, if you agree.

THEODORUS: For my part, Socrates, I do not find listening to such things unpleasant; at my age, it is easier to follow. But if you prefer, let us return to the main point.

SOCRATES: We were at the point in the argument where we discussed those who claim that "essence" is in constant motion, and that whatever seems true to each person is actually true for the person to whom it seems so. 

<margin>C</margin> In other matters, they are willing to stand firm—not least regarding justice—asserting that whatever a city decrees as "just" really is just for that city as long as the law stands. But regarding the *good*, no one is so bold as to fight for the claim that whatever a city thinks is "advantageous" or "useful" for itself actually *is* useful for as long as it is decreed—unless one is just talking about the mere name "useful." But that would be a mockery of our point, wouldn't it?

THEODORUS: Certainly.

SOCRATES: Let him not speak of the name, but of the reality being named. For surely, whatever name a city gives to "utility," it aims for it when making laws. All its laws, as far as it is able and as far as it knows, are established to be as useful as possible to itself. Does it have any other goal in mind when it legislates?

<margin>D</margin> THEODORUS: Not at all.

SOCRATES: Does every city always succeed, or do they often miss the mark?

THEODORUS: I believe they often miss the mark.

SOCRATES: This will be even more obvious to everyone if we ask about the whole class of things to which "the useful" belongs. This class includes the future. When we make laws, we make them with the expectation that they will be useful in the time to come. We would rightly call this "the future."

THEODORUS: Quite so.

SOCRATES: Come then, let us ask Protagoras, or someone who follows his teaching: "You say, Protagoras, that 'Man is the measure of all things'—of white things, heavy things, light things, and everything of that sort. For since man has the criterion within himself, what he experiences he believes to be the truth for him." Isn't that right?

<margin>E</margin> THEODORUS: It is.

SOCRATES: Shall we also say, Protagoras, that he has the criterion of the future within himself? And whatever he thinks will happen, does it actually happen for the one who thought it? For example: heat. When an ordinary person thinks they are going to catch a fever and that this particular heat is coming, but a doctor thinks the opposite, according to whose opinion shall we say the future will turn out? Or will it be according to both? To the doctor, will the man be neither hot nor feverish, but to himself, will he be both?

THEODORUS: That would be ridiculous.

<margin>F</margin> SOCRATES: And I imagine that regarding the future sweetness or bitterness of wine, the opinion of the farmer, not the musician, is the authority.

THEODORUS: Certainly.

SOCRATES: Nor would a gymnastics teacher have a better opinion than a musician about what will sound harmonious or discordant, even if the gymnast later has to judge the harmony of the music.

THEODORUS: By no means.

SOCRATES: And when a feast is being prepared, the judgment of the guest who is not a cook is less valid than that of the cook regarding the future pleasure of the meal. We are not arguing about the pleasure someone *is* currently feeling or *has* felt in the past, but about what will seem and be pleasant to each person in the future. Is each person the best judge for themselves? Or would you, Protagoras, be able to predict better than any layman what would be persuasive to us in a court of law?

<margin>G</margin> THEODORUS: In this very thing, Socrates, he claimed to surpass everyone.

SOCRATES: By Zeus, my friend! No one would have paid him so much money to talk with him if he hadn't persuaded his followers that neither a prophet nor anyone else can judge better than one's own self what is going to be and seem to be in the future.

THEODORUS: Very true.

SOCRATES: Then legislation and utility are also concerned with the future? And wouldn't everyone agree that a city, when making laws, must often miss the mark of what is most useful?

THEODORUS: Very much so.

SOCRATES: It is fair for us to say to your teacher that he must admit that one man is wiser than another, and that such a man is "the measure." But as for me, who is ignorant, there is no necessity at all that I should become a measure, as the argument on his behalf just now tried to force me to be, whether I liked it or not.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> The divine is indeed most blessed, whereas that which is devoid of God is most wretched. People do not see that this is the truth of the matter, being seized by extreme stupidity and the furthest reach of madness. Unknowingly, they are made similar to the latter by their unjust actions, and conversely, dissimilar to the former. They pay the penalty for this transgression while they lead a life suited to that which they have become. But if we should say that unless they cease from their wickedness, that place free of evil will not receive them when they have finished their life, and that they will always dwell here in the likeness of their own life, evil men living among the evil—then these clever and malicious men will answer that they are hearing mere delusions.

<margin>B</margin> THEODORUS: And most emphatically, Socrates. 
SOCRATES: I know it well, my friend. One thing at least happens to them: if ever they are willing to give an account in private, and bring into the open the reasons for the things they disparage, and if they are willing to endure the delay of a manly dispute rather than fleeing like cowards, then finally—what is an amazing absurdity, my blessed friend—they will even disapprove of their own words, and their rhetoric utterly vanishes, so that they seem to differ in no way from children. But let us now put an end to these things, since they are outside our main purpose. Otherwise, the material flowing in from all sides will overwhelm the discourse we originally began. Let us return, therefore, to the earlier points, if it seems good to you.

THEODORUS: To me, Socrates, those things were no less pleasant to hear. For at my age, I follow them easily. 

<margin>C</margin> Nevertheless, if it pleases you, let us return to where we left off. 
SOCRATES: We had arrived at the point in the dispute where we were saying that those who place all essence in motion, and say that what seems to each person *is* for that same person, would assert this most vehemently in all other matters, and not least regarding matters of justice. They say that whatever a city establishes for itself as appearing just, these things are just for it as long as the decrees remain. But indeed, no one would be so bold as to contend the same regarding the "good" and the "useful"—namely, that whatever things a city establishes as appearing useful to itself, these are consequently useful to it for as long as they were so established—unless perhaps one were to speak only of the name. 

<margin>D</margin> But this would be a mockery of what we intend, would it not?
THEODORUS: Without a doubt. 
SOCRATES: Let him not speak of the name, but look at the thing named. Whatever a city calls "utility," it looks to that when establishing laws; and it establishes each law to be as useful as possible to itself, as far as it thinks and is able. Does it intend anything else in passing laws?
THEODORUS: Nothing else. 
SOCRATES: Is it always successful in its wish? Or does opinion often deceive it?
THEODORUS: I think it is often deceived. 
SOCRATES: Furthermore, everyone will agree more with these same points if one asks about every "form" <note>original: *specie*. Here referring to the Greek *eidos* or category of things</note> in which the useful consists. It exists in some way regarding the future. 

<margin>E</margin> For as often as we establish laws, we establish them as being profitable for the future, which we would more rightly call "the future." 
THEODORUS: Entirely so. 
SOCRATES: Come then, let us ask either Protagoras or any other of his followers: "You say, O Protagoras, that man is the measure of all things: of white, heavy, and light things, and of every such thing. For since he contains the judicial power <note>original: *iudiciariam vim*. The capacity to judge or perceive</note> of those things in himself, and judges them as he experiences them, he judges things that are true for him and that exist. Is it not so?"
THEODORUS: Plainly so. 
SOCRATES: Shall we also say of the future, O Protagoras, that man has the power of judgment in himself? And such as he thinks things will be for him, so they turn out for the one so thinking? 

<margin>F</margin> When someone unskilled in medicine thinks they are going to fall into a fever, and thus will become hot, but a doctor disagrees, having a contrary opinion: whose opinion do we think will be true regarding the future? Both? Will it be for the doctor neither hot nor feverish, but for the man himself both?
THEODORUS: That would be ridiculous. 
SOCRATES: Even regarding wine that is to be sweet or dry, the opinion of the farmer, not the musician, prevails. 
THEODORUS: Why not? 
SOCRATES: Nor, regarding what will be harmonious or discordant, does the gymnast have a better opinion than the musician, which will afterwards seem harmonious to the gymnast himself. 
THEODORUS: In no way. 

<margin>G</margin> SOCRATES: When a table is prepared and the feast is to be served, and something must be predicted about their future sweetness, is not the cook’s opinion more powerful than that of any other unskilled person? We do not fight about what *is* or *was* pleasant to someone, but rather about that which in the future must be and seem so: whether each person is a suitable judge for himself, or whether you, Protagoras, would better foresee what will be persuasive to each of us in a trial than any unlearned person?
THEODORUS: In this very thing especially, O Socrates, Protagoras professed to excel all others. 
SOCRATES: O wretched man! By Jupiter, no one would have sought him out with offered money unless he had persuaded his associates that he alone could predict what will be probable and what will seem to be in the future better than a prophet or anyone else. 

<margin>H</margin> THEODORUS: You speak the absolute truth. 
SOCRATES: Do not the making of laws and utility also look to the future? And would not anyone without controversy admit that the constitution of a republic often wanders away from what is useful?
THEODORUS: Greatly. 
SOCRATES: Enough has been said now against your teacher, who is forced to admit that one person is wiser than another, and that such a person is a measure. But as for me, since I am devoid of knowledge, the argument does not compel me to become a measure in any way, even though his discourse recently urged that, whether I wanted to or not, I should be such a thing.

<summary>In this passage, Socrates concludes his digression on the philosopher's life and returns to refuting Protagoras. He argues that while perception might be subjective in the moment, wisdom and expertise are necessary for judging the future, particularly regarding a law's utility.</summary>
<keywords>Theaetetus, Socrates, Theodorus, Protagoras, Plato, epistemology, measure, man, justice, law, legislation, future utility</keywords>

--- Page 162 ---
<meta>This page marks the transition from the famous "digression" back to the core investigation of the *Theaetetus*. Having finished discussing the character of the philosopher, Socrates and Theodorus now return to Protagoras’s claim that "Man is the measure of all things" and its connection to Heraclitus’s theory that everything is in a state of constant change.</meta>

# PLATO
### Theaetetus

<margin>A</margin> **THEAETETUS.** From that point, O Socrates, his argument <note>Protagoras’s claim that "Man is the measure of all things," meaning truth is relative to the observer.</note> seems most thoroughly refuted, and also from this: that it makes the opinions of others valid, yet these others clearly reject his own arguments, deeming them false. 
**SOCRATES.** Furthermore, O Theodorus, one may discover in many ways that not every opinion of every person is true. However, regarding the immediate experience <note>original: *passio* / *πάθος*. Here meaning the raw data of the senses.</note> from which sensations and the opinions based on sensations arise, it is more difficult to prove that these are not true. But perhaps I am saying nothing of substance. For if they are indeed indomitable, they are certain; and those who assert that they are clear and are "knowledge" might perhaps not be wandering from the truth. Therefore, our friend Theaetetus here was not far off the mark when he said that sensation and knowledge are the same thing. Because of this, we must approach more closely, just as the argument of Protagoras commanded, and examine this "agitated essence" <note>The idea that reality is a constant stream of change.</note> by striking it, to see if it gives off a solid or a cracked sound. A struggle over this matter has arisen that is no small thing, nor among a few people.

<margin>B</margin> **SOCRATES.** It is certainly far from being a trivial contention, as it has spread far and wide through Ionia; indeed, the followers of Heraclitus support this argument with the greatest zeal. 
**THEODORUS.** Therefore, O friend Socrates, we must inspect these things from their first principles, just as they themselves propose. 

<margin>The manner of the Heracliteans in disputing.</margin> **SOCRATES.** Entirely so. For regarding these Heracliteans—or, as you say, "Homerics" <note>Socrates jokingly links Heraclitus to the poet Homer, implying that the idea of a world in flux is an old, poetic tradition.</note>—and those even more ancient than the Ephesians, who wish to seem especially skilled: one can no more talk to them than to people driven by a gadfly <note>meaning they are in a state of wild, erratic frenzy.</note>. For their writings are carried along by a sheer impulse. Any delay or waiting in a discussion, any questioning, or any quietness between answering and asking is less present in them than nothing at all. Indeed, even less than nothing; so little rest is there in the minds of those men. If you ask one of them anything, they shoot off enigmatic little phrases like arrows drawn from a hidden quiver. And if you seek a reason for what was said, they strike you with another, but with the name changed. You will never finish anything with any of them, nor will they with each other. They take the most careful care of one thing: to allow nothing to be stable, either in speech or in their own souls, thinking (it seems to me) that stability itself is "the enemy," and they hunt it down with all their might and drive it out from everywhere.

<margin>C</margin> **SOCRATES.** Perhaps, O Theodorus, you have seen these men in battle, but never in peace, for they are not your friends. But I suppose they say such things to their disciples in their leisure time—those whom they wish to make like themselves. 
**THEODORUS.** What disciples, my good man? For among such people, one does not become the student of another; they simply spring up spontaneously, wherever each happens to be seized by their divine frenzy. And one thinks the other knows nothing. From these people, as I was just saying, you will never get an account, whether they are willing or unwilling. We must take up the matter ourselves and consider it like a formal proposition.

<margin>D</margin> **SOCRATES.** You speak wisely. Indeed, we have received this doctrine from the ancients, who hid it from the common people with poetry: that the origin of all other things is Oceanus and Tethys <note>The ancient gods of the sea, representing the source of life as a flowing river.</note>, and that all things are in flux and nothing stands still. From the more recent thinkers, however, who are so much wiser, they demonstrate the matter so clearly that even cobblers could learn their wisdom by listening, and might stop foolishly thinking that some things stand still while others move. Having learned that "all things move," they honor these authors as their teachers. I almost forgot, Theodorus, that others have shown the opposite: namely, that "The All" is a single, unmoving thing. This is what the followers of Melissus and Parmenides <note>Eleatic philosophers who argued that change is an illusion and reality is a single, unchanging One.</note> assert against all the others—that all things are one, and this "one" stands within itself, having no place at all in which it might move. What shall we do with all these people, my friend? For progressing bit by bit, we have secretly fallen into the middle of both sides. If we do not somehow escape and defend ourselves, we shall pay the penalty like those in the wrestling schools who play "at the line" when they are caught by both sides and dragged in opposite directions.

<margin>E</margin> Therefore, it seems we should first deal with those whom we first set out toward: the "Flow-ers." And if they seem to say something probable, we will pull ourselves over to their side, trying to escape the others. But if those who posit a stable universe seem to speak more truly, we will flee to them from the ones who move even the immovable. If it appears that neither side says anything reasonable, we shall become ridiculous, thinking that we, mere common little men, know something great when we have done nothing but reject those ancient and wise men. See then, O Theodorus, whether it is better or not to undergo such a great danger. 
**THEODORUS.** It is in no way to be permitted, Socrates, that we should fail to discuss what truth or falsehood each of these men possesses.

<margin>F</margin> **SOCRATES.** We must discuss it then, since you desire it so much. It seems to me that the beginning of this inquiry should be taken from motion: what sort of motion do they mean when they say that "all things move"? What I mean is this: do they propose one species of motion, or (as it seems to me) two? I do not wish this to seem so to me alone, but to you as well, so that we may both suffer whatever must be suffered together. Tell me, then: do you call it "moving" when something changes

<margin>G</margin> from one place to another, or turns in the same spot? 
**THEODORUS.** I do. 
**SOCRATES.** Let this, then, be one species. But when something stays in the same place but grows old, or becomes black from white, or hard from soft, or some other...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> **THEAETETUS. THEODORUS.** It seems to me, O Socrates, that his argument is most caught out by that point, and especially in this: that it makes the opinions of others authoritative, but these were shown to think his arguments are by no means true.
**SOCRATES.** In many other ways, O Theodorus, it might be caught out that not every opinion of every person is true. But as for the immediate experience <note>original: *πάθος* / *pathos*.</note> from which sensations and the opinions according to them arise, it is harder to catch them as not being true. But perhaps I say nothing. For if they happen to be unassailable, they are indeed certain. And those who say they are manifest and are "knowledges" <note>original: *ἐπιστήμας* / *epistēmas*.</note> might perhaps be speaking the truth. And Theaetetus here has not spoken off the mark in setting sensation and knowledge as the same. We must therefore go closer, as the argument of Protagoras commanded; we must examine this "flowing essence" by striking it, to see if it sounds healthy or hollow. A battle of no small kind has arisen over it, and among many people.

<margin>B</margin> **THEODORUS.** It is far from being small; indeed, it is spreading throughout Ionia at a great rate. For the companions of Heraclitus provide for this argument with great vigor.
**SOCRATES.** Because of this, dear Theodorus, we must rather examine it from the beginning, just as they themselves lay it down.
**THEODORUS.** Entirely so. For regarding these Heracliteans, or as you say, "Homerics," and those even older, among the Ephesians themselves who pretend to be experts, one can no more discourse with them than with people driven by a gadfly. For they are simply carried along by their writings. To stay still upon an argument or a question, and to answer or ask quietly in turn, is less in them than nothing. Or rather, it exceeds "less than nothing," so much is there a lack of even a small amount of stillness in these men. But if you ask someone anything, they pull enigmatic little phrases out as if from a quiver and shoot them at you. And if you seek to get an account of this—what he has said—you will be struck by another newly renamed term. You will never reach a conclusion with any of them. Nor indeed do they reach one with each other; but they take very good care to let nothing be stable, neither in speech nor in their own souls. They think, as it seems to me, that the stable is itself a "stationary thing" <note>The Greek term *stasimon* implies both stability and a dead stop.</note>. They fight against this entirely, and as much as they can, they cast it out from everywhere.

<margin>C</margin> **SOCRATES.** Perhaps, Theodorus, you have seen these men fighting, but have not been with them when they are at peace, for they are not your companions. But I think they tell such things to their students at leisure, those whom they want to make like themselves.
**THEODORUS.** What students, you divine man? Among such people, one does not become the student of another, but they grow up spontaneously, from wherever each of them happens to be "inspired," and one thinks the other knows nothing. From these people, therefore (as I was just saying), you would never get an account, either willing or unwilling. We must take the matter from them and look into it as if it were a formal problem.

<margin>D</margin> **SOCRATES.** And you speak reasonably. As for the problem, we have received it as something else from the ancients (who hid it from the many by means of poetry): that the generation of all other things, Oceanus and Tethys, are actually streams, and nothing stands still. From the moderns, however, as being wiser, they demonstrate it openly, so that even the cobblers might learn by hearing their wisdom, and might stop their silly notion that some things stand still and others move; by learning that "all things move," they honor them. But I almost forgot, Theodorus, that others have declared the opposite of these: such as "immovable is the name for the All," and other things that the followers of Melissus and Parmenides maintain in opposition to all these, asserting that all things are One, and that this "One" stands in itself, having no place in which it might move. How shall we deal with all these people, my friend? For advancing little by little, we have failed to notice that we have fallen into the middle of both. And if we do not somehow defend ourselves and escape, we shall pay the penalty, like those who play the "line game" <note>original: *διὰ γραμμῆς* / *dia grammēs*. A game where two teams try to pull a player across a center line.</note> in the wrestling schools when they are caught by both sides and dragged in opposite directions.

<margin>E</margin> It seems to me, therefore, that we must first consider the one group, toward whom we first set out: the "Flow-ers." And if they seem to say anything reasonable, we will join them in pulling ourselves along, trying to escape the other group. But if the "Partisans of the Whole" <note>Those who believe the universe is a stable, unchanging whole.</note> seem to speak more truly, we will flee to them from those who move even the immovable. But if both appear to say nothing moderate, we shall be ridiculous, thinking that we, being of little account, have something to say, while having rejected ancient and all-wise men. Look then, Theodorus, whether it is profitable to enter into such a great danger.
**THEODORUS.** It is not at all to be tolerated, Socrates, not to examine what each group of men says.

<margin>F</margin> **SOCRATES.** It must be examined, then, since you are so eager. It seems to me that the start of the examination should be about motion: what sort of thing are they saying when they say that "all things move"? I want to say something like this: do they say there is one kind of motion, or (as it seems to me) two? Let it not only seem so to me, but you take part as well, so that we may suffer whatever happens in common. Tell me: do you call it "moving" when something changes place from place, or also when it turns in the same spot?
**THEODORUS.** I do.
**SOCRATES.** Let this, then, be one kind. But when it stays in the same place, but grows old, or becomes black from white, or hard from soft, or some other...

<margin>G</margin> **THEODORUS.** It seems so to me.
**SOCRATES.** It is necessary, then. These are the two kinds of motion I name: alteration, and the other, locomotion <note>original: *ἀλλοίωσιν* (*alloiosin* - change of quality) and *φοράν* (*phoran* - change of place/carrying).</note>.

<summary>Socrates and Theodorus transition from their philosophical digression to a formal investigation of the Heraclitean theory that "everything is in flux." They categorize motion into two distinct types—locomotion and alteration—to prepare for a rigorous critique of the idea that reality is never stable.</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Theodorus, Heraclitus, Protagoras, Parmenides, Melissus, flux, motion, alteration, locomotion, Ephesian philosophers, Oceanus, Tethys</keywords>

--- Page 163 ---
<meta>On the previous page, Socrates and Theodorus began their critique of the "Flux" philosophers (the followers of Heraclitus), who argue that everything in the universe is in a constant state of change. Having just finished a long "digression" on the nature of the philosopher, they now return to the core question: whether knowledge is the same thing as sense perception.</meta>

# THEAETETUS

<margin>A</margin> ...alteration <note>original: ἀλλοίωσιν / alloiosin</note> when it is changed from one thing into another. Should we not say this is a second form of motion? **THEODORUS.** It seems so to me. **SOCRATES.** It is necessary, then. I say there are these two forms of motion: one is alteration, and the other is local motion <note>original: περιφοράν / periphoran, literally "carrying around" or "revolving"</note>. **THEO.** You are speaking correctly. **SOCRATES.** Having divided it this way, let us now speak to those who claim that "all things are in motion" and ask: Do you say everything moves in both ways—both being moved in space and being altered—or that some things move in both ways and others in only one? **THEO.** By Zeus, I cannot say; but I think they would say it moves in both ways. **SOCRATES.** If they did not, my friend, things would appear to them to be both moving and standing still; and it would be no more correct to say that "all things move" than to say "all things stand still." **THEO.** You speak very truly. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, since they must be in motion, and nothing can be without motion, all things must always move with every kind of motion. <margin>B</margin> **THEO.** That is necessary. **SOCRATES.** Now consider this point of theirs: regarding the generation of heat, or whiteness, or whatever it may be—did we not say they described it like this: that each of these properties moves along with the act of sensing, occurring between the "agent" <note>the object acting upon the senses</note> and the "patient" <note>the person sensing the object</note>? And that the "patient" becomes a percipient, but not yet a "perception"; while the "agent" becomes a certain "quality," but not yet "quality" itself? Perhaps the word "quality" <note>original: ποιότης / poiotēs. Socrates is credited with coining this term here, and he worries it sounds strange to his audience.</note> seems like an odd name, and you don't understand it as a general term. So, listen to it in parts. For the "agent" is neither heat nor whiteness, but becomes "hot" or "white," and so on with the rest. You likely remember that we said earlier <margin>C</margin> that nothing exists as one thing in and of itself—neither the agent nor the patient—but from the two meeting together, they give birth to both the sensations and the objects of sensation, making the objects be of a certain quality and the other be a perceiver. **THEO.** I remember, of course. **SOCRATES.** Let us leave the rest of their theory aside and keep only to the point we are discussing. We ask: Do all things move and flow, as you say? **THEO.** Yes. **SOCRATES.** And do they move with both kinds of motion we distinguished—moving in space and also altering? **THEO.** How could they not, if they are to be in perfect motion? **SOCRATES.** Now, if they were only moving in space and not altering, we might be able to say what these flowing things are like. Is that not so? **THEO.** It is. **SOCRATES.** <margin>D</margin> But since even this does not remain stable—that the "flowing white" stays white—but instead it changes, so that there is a flux of the whiteness itself, shifting into another color so it cannot be caught staying the same—is it then ever possible to name a color so as to address it correctly? **THEO.** And how could one do that, Socrates? Or name anything else of that sort, if it always slips away while one is speaking, because it is in flux? **SOCRATES.** And what shall we say of any sensation, such as that of seeing or hearing? Does it ever remain stable in the act of seeing or hearing? **THEO.** It certainly cannot, if all things are in motion. **SOCRATES.** Then we must not call something "seeing" any more than "not-seeing," nor any other sensation more than "not-sensation," since all things are moving in every way. **THEO.** <margin>E</margin> Indeed not. **SOCRATES.** And yet, we said that "knowledge is sensation," as I and Theaetetus agreed. **THEAETETUS.** That was said. **SOCRATES.** It turns out, then, that when we were asked what knowledge is, we gave an answer that describes "not-knowledge" just as much as "knowledge." **THEO.** So it seems. **SOCRATES.** This would be a fine "correction" of our answer! We were eager to prove that all things move just so that our answer would appear correct. But it appears, instead, that if all things are in motion, every answer to any question is equally correct: one can say things are "thus" and "not thus"—or, if you prefer, "become" <note>original: γίγνεσθαι / gignesthai</note> thus, so as not to make them stand still in our speech. **THEO.** You are right. **SOCRATES.** Except, Theodorus, that I said "thus" and "not thus." One shouldn't even use the word "thus," for that which is "thus" would no longer be in motion; nor can one say "not thus." <margin>F</margin> Indeed, those who hold this theory must find another language, for they currently have no words for their own hypothesis—unless perhaps the phrase "not even in any way" <note>original: οὐδ’ ὅπως / oud' hopōs</note>. This might suit them best, being an indefinite expression. **THEO.** That would be the most appropriate dialect for them. **SOCRATES.** So, Theodorus, we are finally rid of your friend <note>Protagoras</note>, and we do not yet concede to him that "every man is the measure of all things," unless he is a man of understanding. Nor will we concede that knowledge is sensation, at least not according to the theory that "all things move"—unless our friend Theaetetus here has something else to say. **THEO.** You have spoken excellently, Socrates. For now that these matters are concluded, I too am supposed to be released from answering you, according to our agreement, since the discussion of Protagoras's theory has reached its end. **THEAETETUS.** <margin>G</margin> Not until you and Socrates have discussed those who hold the opposite view, Theodorus—those who claim that the All stands still—just as you proposed a moment ago. **THEO.** Theaetetus, you are young, yet you teach your elders to be unjust by breaking their agreements! But prepare yourself to give an account to Socrates for the remainder of the talk. **THEAETETUS.** If he wishes it; though I would have most gladly heard about what I just mentioned. **THEO.** You are "inviting cavalry into the open plain" <note>A Greek proverb meaning to challenge someone in their area of greatest strength.</note> when you invite Socrates to speak. Ask him, then, and you shall hear. **SOCRATES.** But I think, Theodorus, that I shall not obey Theaetetus in what he asks. **THEO.** Why will you not obey? **SOCRATES.** I feel a sense of shame when it comes to examining Melissus and the others who say the All is "One and motionless," lest we do it in a crude way; but I feel even more shame before Parmenides, who is himself "One." <margin>H</margin> Parmenides seems to me, to use the words of Homer, to be "revered" and yet "terrible" <note>original: αἰδοῖός τε μοὶ ἅμα δεινός τε / aidoios te moi hama deinos te. A quote from the *Iliad* (3.172) used by Socrates to express profound respect mixed with awe.</note>. I met him when I was very young and he was very old, and he appeared to me to possess a depth that was altogether noble. I fear, then, that we may not understand his words, and even less the thought behind them. But my greatest fear is that the primary question we started with—"what is knowledge?"—will be lost under the flood of these other arguments if we follow them. Especially since the argument we are now waking up is of an impossible magnitude. If one looks at it as a side issue, it would be treated unworthily; but if one treats it worthily, it will grow so long it will destroy our search for knowledge. We must do neither. Instead, we must try to use my "midwifery" <note>Socrates's method of helping others give birth to their own ideas.</note> to help Theaetetus give birth to the ideas he is pregnant with concerning knowledge. **THEO.** Very well, let us do that, if it seems best to you.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> When something is changed by a certain alteration, shall we not rightly call this the second species of motion? **THEODORUS.** Rightly. **SOCRATES.** From these points, it is necessary that two species of motion exist: namely, alteration and local motion <note>original: motum localem</note>. **THEO.** Excellent. **SOCRATES.** With this distinction established, let us now proceed to those who want all things to be moved, and let us ask them in this manner: Do you admit that anything whatever is moved in both ways—being altered as well as being carried along? Or is one thing moved in both ways, and another in only one? **THEO.** For my part, I do not have an answer to give, but I think they would say it moves in both ways. **SOCRATES.** Otherwise, O friend, things would seem to them to be both agitated and standing still at the same time, and it would be no more permitted to assert that "all things move" than to say that "all things stand still." <margin>B</margin> **THEO.** You speak the truth. **SOCRATES.** Since it is necessary that they be moved, and that the absence of motion does not belong to them, then all things are always moved by every kind of motion. **THEO.** It follows necessarily. **SOCRATES.** Now consider this based on their words: the generation of heat, or whiteness, or of anything else. Did we not say they believe each of these is carried along together with the sense between the "agent" <note>original: agens</note> and the "patient" <note>original: patiens</note>? And that the "patient" is the sensible object, not the sensation, while the "agent" is something effective, yet not a "quality"? Perhaps "quality" <note>original: qualitas</note> seems like a foreign name to you, and you do not perceive it when spoken of in general; so hear it in its parts. For the "agent" is neither heat nor whiteness, but rather "the hot" and "the white," <margin>C</margin> and other things in the same way. You remember we said above that nothing is one thing according to itself, nor furthermore is there an agent or a patient, but from both meeting together in turn, the senses and sensible things emanate—partly becoming certain qualities, and partly perceiving. **THEO.** I remember, and why should we not say so? **SOCRATES.** Let us therefore pass over the other points, whether they say them this way or otherwise. But let us inquire more diligently into that one thing for the sake of which we are disputing. All things move and flow, as you say. Do they not? **THEO.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** And do they not move with both those motions we distinguished—carried along and altered at the same time? <margin>D</margin> **THEO.** Why not, if it is necessary for them to be moved perfectly? **SOCRATES.** If therefore they were only carried along, but were not altered, we would be able to say what sort of things these flowing, carried-along things are. Or how shall we say it? **THEO.** In this way. **SOCRATES.** But since not even that remains stable—that is, that the "white" which flows continues to flow as white—but it is changed so that there is a flux of this very whiteness, and a transition into another color, so that it cannot be caught remaining in any way—can we ever pronounce any one color so that we name it correctly? **THEO.** And by what means, O Socrates, can that happen in this or in any other case, if indeed while we are speaking it immediately escapes, seeing that it always flows? **SOCRATES.** What further should be said about any sense, such as seeing or hearing? Does it ever <margin>E</margin> remain stable in vision or hearing? **THEO.** Not at all, if indeed all things are moved. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, we should not say we "see" any more than we "do not see," nor should we say we use any other sense more than we "do not use" it, since all things are being utterly transformed. **THEO.** Certainly not. **SOCRATES.** Nevertheless, sensation itself is knowledge, as I and Theaetetus said. **THEO.** It was indeed said. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, we were not answering what knowledge is any more than what "non-knowledge" is when we were asked. **THEO.** So you certainly seem to be. **SOCRATES.** And so we would conveniently amend that answer if we contended to demonstrate that all things move, <margin>F</margin> so that the answer would appear correct. But this, as it seems, has appeared: that if all things move, any answer whatever, about whatever one might answer, is equally "correct"—stating both that it is so, and that it is not so. Or if you prefer, one should say it "becomes" so, so that we do not stop them in their speech. **THEO.** You speak correctly. **SOCRATES.** Except in this, O Theodorus: that I said "so" and "not so." But one ought not to say even this "so." For it would no longer be moved "so," nor again "not so." For this is not motion, but some other name must be imposed by those who discuss such things; since now they have no words for their own hypothesis, unless perhaps <margin>G</margin> they might be seen to have this expression, namely "not in any way whatever," which indeed fits them best when uttered indefinitely. **THEO.** This expression is very convenient for them. **SOCRATES.** Now, O Theodorus, we are finished with your friend; nor have we yet conceded to him that any man whatever is the measure of all things, unless he exists as a wise man. Furthermore, we will by no means concede that sensation is knowledge according to that reasoning which proclaims that all things move, unless perhaps Theaetetus here says it in some other way. **THEO.** You have spoken best, O Socrates. For these things being finished, it is right that I too should be released from these matters, as was agreed between us. Now that the discussion against Protagoras has received its end, do not stop, I pray, Theodorus, before you and Socrates run through <margin>H</margin> those others who wanted all things to stand still, just as you proposed a little while ago. **THEO.** Since you are a youth, O Theaetetus, you teach your seniors to do an injury, while you exhort them to transgress their pacts. But gird yourself so that you may give an account of the remaining things to Socrates, if he wishes. **THEO.** I would, however, most willingly hear those things of which I speak. **THEO.** You challenge horsemen into the field when you summon Socrates to dispute. Ask, then, and you shall hear. **SOCRATES.** I seem indeed, O Theodorus, in those things which Theaetetus commands, to be by no means about to obey him. **THEO.** What prevents you from obeying? **SOCRATES.** Even if I fear that we may seem burdensome by shaking Melissus and the others who say the universe is "one and standing still," I fear it less than I fear the "one" Parmenides. But Parmenides, to use Homeric words, is to me "revered and sharp..."

<margin>Nothing is one thing in and of itself.</margin>

<summary>Socrates and Theodorus conclude their critique of the Heraclitean theory of total flux, arguing that if everything is constantly changing in both position and quality, language itself fails and knowledge cannot be identified with sensation. Socrates then expresses his profound hesitation to critique Parmenides and the Eleatic school, who believe the universe is entirely motionless, because of his deep respect for Parmenides's philosophical depth.</summary>

<keywords>Plato, Theaetetus, Socrates, Theodorus, Protagoras, Parmenides, Melissus, motion, kinesis, alteration, local motion, sense perception, knowledge, episteme, total flux, Heraclitus</keywords>

--- Page 164 ---
<meta>Socrates has just finished dismissing the "ever-shifting" philosophy of Heraclitus. He now turns to the opposite extreme—the "Stillness" of Parmenides—but hesitates to critique such a profound thinker. Instead, he returns to his primary task: testing the young Theaetetus’s definition of knowledge as "perception."</meta>

# PLATO

<margin>In this passage, Plato seems to agree with Parmenides.</margin>

**A** ...it seems. I once met that man <note>Socrates refers to the philosopher Parmenides of Elea, whom he met in his youth.</note> when I was very young and he was quite old, and he appeared to me to possess a depth of wisdom that was altogether noble. I fear, therefore, that we may not understand his words or his voice, and even more, that we may miss the meaning hidden beneath his words. But most of all, I fear that the very purpose for which this discussion began—inquiring into what knowledge is—might be left unexamined because of these distracting arguments that come rushing in if one follows them. Especially since the question we have just raised <note>The nature of motion and the "all is flux" theory.</note> is so vast; if treated as a mere side-note or digression, it would be treated unworthily, and if handled thoroughly, it would block our search for the nature of knowledge itself. We should do neither. Rather, we should try to bring Theaetetus’s "conception" regarding knowledge into the light through the art of midwifery and examine it carefully. **THEAETETUS.** If that is how it seems to you, that is how we must act.

**B** **SOCRATES.** Consider this then, Theaetetus, regarding what was said before. You answered that knowledge is perception, did you not? **THEAETETUS.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** If someone were to ask you: "With what does a person see white and black, and with what does he hear high and low sounds?" I suppose you would answer, "With the eyes and the ears." **THEAETETUS.** Indeed I would. **SOCRATES.** To use names and words loosely, rather than with exact curiosity, is often the mark of a noble mind, while the opposite is a sign of a small mind. However, sometimes it is necessary to be precise, as we are compelled to be now. Look closely at your answer and tell me: which is more correct—to say that the eyes are that **with which** we see, or **through which** we see?

**C** And likewise, do we hear **with** the ears or **through** them? **THEAETETUS.** It seems to me, Socrates, that it is better to say "through which" we perceive each thing, rather than "with which."

<margin>He alludes to the Trojan Horse.</margin>

**SOCRATES.** It would be a strange thing indeed, my boy, if many different senses sat within us as if inside a wooden horse <note>The Trojan Horse, used here as a metaphor for the body containing separate, uncoordinated senses.</note>, and all these did not tend toward a single idea—whether we call it the soul or something else—through which we perceive all the objects of the senses, using the sense organs as instruments.

**D** **THEAETETUS.** This way seems more likely to me than the other. **SOCRATES.** I am examining this with you so carefully because I want to see whether it is by some single and the same part of ourselves that we reach out through the eyes to perceive white and black, and through other organs to perceive other things. When asked, you would refer all these to the body. Perhaps it is better for you to answer this yourself rather than me wearing myself out speaking for you. Tell me: the things through which you perceive heat, hardness, lightness, and sweetness—do you not assign these to the organs of the body, or to something else? **THEAETETUS.** To nothing else. **SOCRATES.** And will you agree that what you perceive through one power, you cannot perceive through another? For example, what you perceive through hearing, you cannot perceive through sight, and vice versa? **THEAETETUS.** How could I not agree?

**E** **SOCRATES.** If, then, you think something about both of these together, you cannot be perceiving that "common" quality through one organ or the other. **THEAETETUS.** Certainly not. **SOCRATES.** Now, regarding sound and color, you first think this about both: that they both exist. **THEAETETUS.** I do. **SOCRATES.** And also that each is different from the other, but the same as itself? **THEAETETUS.** Yes. **SOCRATES.** And that both together are two, but each is one? **THEAETETUS.** That too. **SOCRATES.** And you are also able to judge whether they are similar or dissimilar to each other? **THEAETETUS.** Perhaps. **SOCRATES.** Through what, then, do you think all these things about them? For it is not possible to grasp what is common to both through either hearing or sight. Here is further proof: if it were possible to judge whether both were salty or not, you would surely be able to say what instrument you would use to judge it; and that instrument is clearly neither sight nor hearing, but something else. **THEAETETUS.** Of course, it would be the power of the tongue. **SOCRATES.** Well said. But what is the power that reveals to you that which is common to all things—that which you call "being" and "non-being," and those other qualities we were just asking about? What organs will you assign to all these, through which the perceiving part of us senses them?

**F** **THEAETETUS.** You mean "essence" <note>original: οὐσίαν / ousian, also translated as "being" or "existence"</note> and "non-existence," and likeness and unlikeness, and the same and the different, as well as unity and number. It is clear you are asking through which of the body's instruments the soul perceives things like "even" and "odd," and what follows from them. **SOCRATES.** You follow me excellently, Theaetetus; these are exactly the things I am asking about. **THEAETETUS.** By Zeus, Socrates, I have no answer to give, except that it seems to me there is no special organ for these things as there is for the others. Rather, the soul itself, through itself, seems to examine the common properties of all things.

**G** **SOCRATES.** You are beautiful, Theaetetus, and not "ugly" as Theodorus said! For he who speaks beautifully is beautiful and good. Besides being beautiful, you have done me a great favor by releasing me from a very long argument, since it seems to you that the soul examines some things through itself and other things through the powers of the body. This was my own opinion, and I wanted it to be yours as well. **THEAETETUS.** It certainly seems so to me. **SOCRATES.** In which group do you place "essence" <note>being or existence</note>? For this, above all, accompanies everything. **THEAETETUS.** I place it among those things that the soul itself reaches for on its own. **SOCRATES.** And do you also include the similar and the dissimilar, and the same and the different? **THEAETETUS.** Yes. **SOCRATES.** What about the beautiful and the ugly, and the good and the evil? **THEAETETUS.** 

**H** Of these too, it seems to me the soul considers the essence above all in their relationship to one another, reflecting within itself on the past and the present in relation to the future. **SOCRATES.** Wait—will it not perceive the hardness of a hard thing through touch, and the softness of a soft thing in the same way?

<meta>Catchword: THEAETETUS</meta>

<column-break/>

**A.** ...met with the man, when I was very young and he was very old; and he seemed to me to have a depth that was altogether noble. I fear, then, that we may neither understand what he said, nor be even further from understanding what he had in mind when he said it. And the greatest danger is that the very thing for the sake of which our argument was started—the nature of knowledge—may go unexamined because of the arguments that come rushing in to join the feast, if one listens to them. Especially since the one we are now stirring up is of an impossible size. If one treats it as a side-issue, it would be treated unworthily; but if it is stretched out sufficiently, it will make the question of knowledge disappear. We must do neither. Instead, we must try to use the art of midwifery to deliver Theaetetus of what he is pregnant with concerning knowledge. **THEAETETUS.** Well, we must do so, if it seems best. **SOCRATES.** Then consider this much more, Theaetetus, about what has been said.

**B.** For you answered that perception is knowledge. Did you not? **THEAETETUS.** Yes. **SOCRATES.** Now if someone were to ask you this: "With what does a man see white and black, and with what does he hear high and low sounds?" you would say, I think, "with the eyes and ears." **THEAETETUS.** I would. **SOCRATES.** Now, the easy-going use of names and phrases, without being overly precise in examination, is for the most part not ignoble; in fact, the opposite is rather unfree. But sometimes it is necessary, as it is now necessary to take hold of the answer you gave, in that it is not correct. For look, which answer is more correct: that "eyes" are that **with which** we see, or **through which** we see? And "ears" that **with which** we hear, or **through which** we hear? **THEAETETUS.** "Through which" we perceive each thing

**C.** seems to me, Socrates, better than "with which." **SOCRATES.** Yes, for it would be a strange thing, surely, if many senses were sitting inside us, as if in wooden horses, and did not all tend toward some one nature—whether we should call it soul or whatever—with which, through these as instruments, we perceive all that is perceptible. **THEAETETUS.** Yes, that seems more likely to me than the other way. **SOCRATES.** Now, why am I being so precise with you? It is to see if, with some one and the same part of ourselves, we reach through the eyes to white and black things, and through the others to other things again. And you will be able, when asked, to refer all such things to the body. But perhaps it is better that you say them by answering, rather than me being a busybody on your behalf.

**D.** Tell me: the hot and the dry, and the light and the sweet—do you not set each of the things through which you perceive them in the body? Or in something else? **THEAETETUS.** In nothing else. **SOCRATES.** And would you be willing to agree that it is impossible to perceive through one power what you perceive through another? For instance, what you perceive through hearing, you cannot perceive through sight, or what you perceive through sight, through hearing? **THEAETETUS.** Of course I am willing. **SOCRATES.** If, then, you think something about both of them, you could not be perceiving it about both through one of the organs, nor again through the other. **THEAETETUS.** No, indeed. **SOCRATES.** Now, regarding sound and color, first of all, do you think this about both of them: that they both are? **THEAETETUS.** I do. **SOCRATES.** And that each is different from the other, and the same

**E.** as itself? **THEAETETUS.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** And that both are two, and each is one? **THEAETETUS.** That too. **SOCRATES.** And are you able to examine whether they are unlike each other or like? **THEAETETUS.** Perhaps. **SOCRATES.** Through what do you think all these things about them? For it is not possible to grasp what is common to them through either hearing or sight. And here is further proof of what we are saying: if it were possible to examine whether both are salty or not, you know you would be able to say what you would examine them with—and this appears to be neither sight nor hearing, but something else. **THEAETETUS.** Why, of course; it is the power that acts through the tongue. **SOCRATES.** You say it well. But through what does the power that makes clear to you that which is common to all things, and to these as well—that to which you give the name "it is" and "it is not," and the other things we were just asking about—

**F.** what organs will you assign to all these, through which the perceiving part of us perceives each of them? **THEAETETUS.** You mean being and not-being, and likeness and unlikeness, and the same and the different, and further, unity and the rest of number applied to them. And it is clear you are also asking about even and odd, and all the other things that follow these—through what part of the body do we perceive them with the soul? **SOCRATES.** You follow me excellently, Theaetetus; these are the very things I am asking. **THEAETETUS.** But by Zeus, Socrates, I at least could not say—except that it seems to me there is no such special organ for these things at all, as there is for the others. Instead, it seems to me that the soul itself, through itself, examines the common properties

**G.** in all things. **SOCRATES.** For you are beautiful, Theaetetus, and not, as Theodorus said, ugly. For he who speaks beautifully is beautiful and good. And besides being beautiful, you have done me a favor by releasing me from a very long argument, if it seems to you that the soul examines some things itself through itself, and other things through the powers of the body. For this was what I myself thought, but I wanted it to seem so to you too. **THEAETETUS.** Well, it certainly does seem so. **SOCRATES.** In which group then do you place being? For this, most of all, accompanies everything. **THEAETETUS.** I place it among the things that the soul itself reaches for by itself. **SOCRATES.** And also the like and the unlike, and the same and the different? **THEAETETUS.** Yes. **SOCRATES.** And what about the beautiful and the ugly, and the good and the

**H.** bad? **THEAETETUS.** Of these too, it seems to me the soul especially examines their being in relation to one another, calculating in itself the past and the present in relation to the future. **SOCRATES.** Hold on—will it not perceive the hardness of the hard through touch, and the softness of the soft in the same way?

<meta>Catchword: THEAETETUS</meta>

<summary>In this passage, Socrates and Theaetetus distinguish between physical sensations (like sight and hearing) and the higher mental concepts (like being, likeness, and number) that the soul perceives on its own. They conclude that while sense organs are "channels" for data, it is the soul itself that synthesizes this data to grasp universal truths.</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Theaetetus, Parmenides, soul, perception, sense organs, being, essence, common properties, midwifery, Trojan Horse metaphor</keywords>
