<meta>The dialogue continues from the previous page, where Socrates and Theaetetus were investigating whether perception is the same thing as knowledge. Socrates has just demonstrated that various senses (sight, hearing) are distinct, yet there must be a central power—the soul—that compares their data.</meta>

# ->THEAETETUS<-

<margin>A</margin>**THEAETETUS.** Yes. **SOCRATES.** Now, regarding their essence <note>original: "ousia" — being or reality</note>, what they both are, their opposition to one another, and the essence of that opposition—the soul itself attempts to judge these for us by revisiting them and comparing them with one another. **THEAETETUS.** Quite so. **SOCRATES.** Is it not true, then, that while humans and animals are naturally able to perceive certain things from the moment of birth—specifically, those impressions <note>original: "pathemata" — sensations or affections</note> that reach the soul through the body—the reasoning <note>original: "analogismata" — calculations or reflections</note> about these things, regarding their essence and their benefit, comes only with difficulty, over time, and through much trouble and education, for those to whom it comes at all? **THEAETETUS.** Most certainly. **SOCRATES.** Is it possible, then, to attain truth if one cannot even attain essence? **THEAETETUS.** Impossible. **SOCRATES.** And if someone fails to attain the truth of a thing, will he ever have knowledge of it? **THEAETETUS.** How could he, Socrates?

<margin>B</margin>**SOCRATES.** In those impressions, then, there is no knowledge, but rather in the reasoning about them; for it seems possible to touch upon essence and truth in the latter, but impossible in the former. **THEAETETUS.** So it appears. **SOCRATES.** Do you then call that and this by the same name, when they possess such great differences? **THEAETETUS.** Certainly it would not be right. **SOCRATES.** What name then do you give to the first—to seeing, hearing, smelling, feeling cold, and feeling heat? **THEAETETUS.** I call it "perceiving" <note>original: "aisthanesthai" — sensing or perception</note>; what else could it be? **SOCRATES.** You call the whole of it, then, "perception"? **THEAETETUS.** Necessarily.

<margin>C</margin>**SOCRATES.** And this, we say, has no share in attaining truth, since it has no share in essence. **THEAETETUS.** Indeed it does not. **SOCRATES.** Nor, therefore, in knowledge. **THEAETETUS.** No. **SOCRATES.** Then perception and knowledge, Theaetetus, can never be the same thing. **THEAETETUS.** It appears they are not, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** And now it has become very clear that knowledge is something other than perception. But we did not start this conversation just to find out what knowledge is *not*, but to find out what it *is*. Nevertheless, we have progressed far enough not to look for it in perception at all, but in that name—whatever it may be—which the soul has when it occupies itself, by itself, with the things that are. **THEAETETUS.** But that, I believe, Socrates, is called "forming an opinion" <note>original: "doxazein" — thinking, judging, or holding a belief</note>.

<margin>D</margin>**SOCRATES.** You believe correctly, my friend. Now look again from the beginning, erasing all that went before, to see if you can perceive anything more clearly, now that you have progressed to this point. Tell me again: what is knowledge? **THEAETETUS.** To say it is "every opinion," Socrates, is impossible, since there is also false opinion. But it is likely that *true* opinion is knowledge. Let that be my answer. If, as we proceed, this does not seem to be the case, we will try to say something else. **SOCRATES.** This is the way you ought to speak, Theaetetus—with enthusiasm—rather than being hesitant to answer as you were at first. For if we do this, one of two things will happen: either we shall find what we are looking for, or we shall be less likely to think we know what we do not know at all. And truly, such a reward would not be contemptible. So, what do you say now? Since there are two kinds of opinion—one true and the other false—do you define knowledge as true opinion? **THEAETETUS.** I do. That is how it seems to me for now.

<margin>E</margin>**SOCRATES.** Is it worth our while, then, to take up the subject of opinion again? **THEAETETUS.** What do you mean? **SOCRATES.** Something about it troubles me now, as it often has at other times, so that I have been in great difficulty both with myself and with others, being unable to say what this experience in us is, or how it arises. **THEAETETUS.** What experience? **SOCRATES.** That a person can "form a false opinion." I am considering even now, still doubting, whether we should let it go or examine it in a different way than we did a little while ago. **THEAETETUS.** Why not do it, Socrates, if it seems even slightly necessary? For you and Theodorus were just saying quite rightly regarding leisure that nothing is urgent in such matters.

<margin>F</margin>**SOCRATES.** You have reminded me well. Perhaps it is not out of place to go back and follow the trail again. For it is better to complete a small task well than a large one insufficiently. **THEAETETUS.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** How then shall we proceed? What is it we are saying? Do we claim that there is a false opinion in every case? And that one of us thinks falsely while another thinks truly, as if this were the natural state of things? **THEAETETUS.** Yes, we do say that. **SOCRATES.** Is it not true for us, regarding all things and each thing individually, that we either know it or do not know it? For I will leave aside "learning" and "forgetting" for the moment, as they are intermediate states and contribute nothing to our current argument. **THEAETETUS.** Indeed, Socrates, there is nothing else left regarding each thing except knowing it or not knowing it.

<margin>G</margin>**SOCRATES.** Is it then necessary that a person who forms an opinion must be thinking of something he either knows or does not know? **THEAETETUS.** Necessary. **SOCRATES.** And surely it is impossible for one who knows a thing not to know that same thing, or for one who does not know it to know it? **THEAETETUS.** How could it be otherwise? **SOCRATES.** Does the person who forms false opinions, then, think that the things he knows are not those things, but some other things he knows? And knowing both, does he then ignore both? **THEAETETUS.** That is impossible, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** Or does he suppose that things he does not know are other things he does not know? Is it possible for someone who knows neither Theaetetus nor Socrates to take it into his mind that Socrates is Theaetetus or Theaetetus is Socrates? **THEAETETUS.** How could he?

<margin>H</margin>**SOCRATES.** But surely a person does not think that the things he knows are the things he does not know; nor, conversely, that the things he does not know are the things he knows. **THEAETETUS.** That would be a monstrosity. **SOCRATES.** How then could anyone still form a false opinion? For it is seemingly impossible to form an opinion outside of these cases, since we either know all things or do not know them. Within these bounds, there seems to be no place where false opinion can exist. **THEAETETUS.** Most true. **SOCRATES.** Perhaps, then, we should not look for what we seek by going the way of "knowing and not knowing," but by the way of "being and not being"?

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>SOCRATES. But essence, and what things are, and their mutual contrariety, and the essence of that very contrariety, the soul itself, revolving them within and comparing them with each other, strives to discern. THEAETETUS. Entirely so. SOCRATES. Is there not a certain natural faculty present in men and beasts from birth, by which they perceive the impressions flowing through the body into the soul? But reasoning and the comparison of these in respect to essence and utility—does this not finally arrive, with difficulty, after a long passage of time and through much study and discipline, to those whom it reaches? THEAETETUS. Just so. SOCRATES. Can we perceive truth in that which we do not perceive essence? THEAETETUS. Not at all. SOCRATES. But if someone lacks the truth of a thing, can he have any knowledge of it? THEAETETUS. And in what way could that happen?

<margin>B</margin>SOCRATES. In the impressions, therefore, knowledge is by no means present; yet in the reasoning which is occupied with them, it seems to be present. For here we can touch upon essence and truth, but there, by no means. THEAETETUS. That is clear. SOCRATES. Do you then call that and this the same, when they differ by such a great gap? THEAETETUS. It would certainly not be fitting. <margin>Missing in the Greek.</margin> SOCRATES. What name do you attribute to that: namely, to seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, being warmed, and being cooled? <margin>Sense does not perceive essence.</margin> Do you call it "perceiving"? THEAETETUS. That very thing. For what else? SOCRATES. You call this whole thing, then, "sense" <note>original: "sensum" — perception/sensation</note>? THEAETETUS. Necessarily. SOCRATES. We denied that the perception of truth belongs to this, since it does not perceive essence. THEAETETUS. So it is. SOCRATES. It will not, therefore, be possessed of knowledge. THEAETETUS. No.

<margin>C</margin>SOCRATES. From these things it follows, O Theaetetus, that knowledge and sense shall never be the same. THEAETETUS. Never at all. SOCRATES. In these matters it has become clearly evident that sense is one thing, and knowledge is another. But we did not begin to discuss this for the sake of finding what knowledge is not, but rather what it is. We have, however, proceeded so far in disputing that we have judged that knowledge is by no means to be sought in sense, but rather in that name which the soul then obtains when it, according to itself, is occupied and acts regarding those things which are. THEAETETUS. But this, O Socrates, as I myself think, is called "opining" <note>original: "opinari" — to think or form an opinion</note>. SOCRATES. You think correctly, my friend. And now look again from the beginning, all previous things having been deleted from your mind, to see if you might perceive anything more, now that you have been carried this far. Explain again what knowledge might be. THEAETETUS.

<margin>D</margin>To say that any opinion whatever is knowledge, O Socrates, is impossible, since there is also a certain false opinion. <margin>When it is an opinion.</margin> It appears, however, that true opinion is knowledge, and let that be my answer for now: but if it shall seem otherwise as we continue to dispute, we shall endeavor to bring forward something else. SOCRATES. Well done, Theaetetus. It is fitting to dispute with such a ready mind, and not to hesitate as you began to do. For if we do so, one of two things will happen: either we shall find what we desire, or certainly we shall think that we know less of that which we are ignorant of: and that will be no mediocre gain. And now, what do you say? Since there are two species of opinion, one true and the other false, do you define true opinion as knowledge? THEAETETUS. I do define it so. For this seems right to me at present. <margin>Second definition of knowledge.</margin>

<margin>E</margin>SOCRATES. Should we then treat opinion once again from the beginning? THEAETETUS. What do you mean? SOCRATES. It troubles me now and often at other times, so that I am in much ambiguity regarding myself and others, not being able to explain what this affection in us is, or in what way it comes. THEAETETUS. What is this? SOCRATES. Namely, that someone opines falsely, about which I am even now in doubt—whether we should omit it, or consider it differently than we did above. THEAETETUS. Why not, O Socrates, if you think it fitting in any way? For you and Theodorus said excellently in the previous parts regarding leisure, that nothing is urgent in such matters.

<margin>F</margin>SOCRATES. You have reminded me opportunely. For perhaps it will not be out of place to run through it again like a trail: for it is better to determine a little well, than much insufficiently. THEAETETUS. It is better indeed. <margin>It is better to determine a little well, than much insufficiently.</margin> SOCRATES. How then, and what do we say? Do we say that opinion is often false, and that some of us opine falsely, and others truly, as if these things were so by nature? THEAETETUS. We say so without a doubt. SOCRATES. Does this not apply to us concerning all things, as well as single things? Namely, to know or to be ignorant: for learning and forgetting, as being in the middle of these, I pass over for the present, since they contribute nothing to our proposal. THEAETETUS. Nothing else at all, O Socrates, remains besides knowing or being ignorant regarding each thing. <margin>Knowing and being ignorant, concerning all things and individuals. The second mode of thinking.</margin>

<margin>G</margin>SOCRATES. Is it not therefore necessary for one who opines to opine about those things of which he knows something, or does not know? THEAETETUS. Necessary. SOCRATES. Moreover, is it impossible for one who knows to be ignorant of the same thing, or for one who is ignorant to know? THEAETETUS. Why not? SOCRATES. Does he who opines falsely about things he knows, think those things are not those things, but certain other things which he also knows: and knowing both, is he again ignorant of both? THEAETETUS. But this cannot happen, O Socrates. SOCRATES. Or perhaps does he think those things which he does not know are certain other things which he does not know: and can he who knows neither Theaetetus nor Socrates ever think that Socrates is Theaetetus, or conversely that Theaetetus is Socrates? THEAETETUS. Never.

<margin>H</margin>SOCRATES. Nor yet does he think those things which he knows are the things which he does not know: nor again those things which he does not know are the things which he knows. THEAETETUS. For it would be a monster. SOCRATES. In what way then will someone opine falsely? Indeed, besides these it is not permitted to opine, since we either know or are ignorant of all things: but in these it seems that no one can opine falsely in any way. THEAETETUS. You speak the truth. SOCRATES. Perhaps, then, what we seek should not be considered by proceeding according to "knowing and not knowing," but according to "being and not being"?

<summary>In this passage, Socrates and Theaetetus conclude that knowledge cannot be perception, leading Theaetetus to propose a second definition: knowledge is true opinion. They then begin an investigation into how false opinion is possible, struggling with the logical difficulty of mistaking one thing for another when we either know or do not know them.</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Theaetetus, knowledge, perception, true opinion, false opinion, essence, reasoning, soul, epistemology</keywords>

--- Page 166 ---
<meta>The dialogue continues from the previous page, where Socrates and Theaetetus concluded that knowledge is not found in the raw impressions of the senses, but in the reasoning (analogismata) that the soul performs upon them. They are now transitioning to investigate the nature of "false opinion"—how it is possible for the mind to be mistaken.</meta>

# ->PLATO'S<-
### ->THEAETETUS<-

<columns>
<margin>Whether anyone might think that which is not.</margin>
A **THEAETETUS.** How do you mean? **SOCRATES.** Perhaps it is not so simple: for someone who thinks of things that are nowhere, in whatever matter, cannot but think falsely, in whatever way he may think. **THEAETETUS.** That too is likely, O Socrates. **SOCRATES.** How then, Theaetetus, shall we respond if someone asks us (and this is possible for anyone to ask): "Who among men could think that which is not <note>Socrates is exploring the paradox that if you are thinking, you must be thinking of *something*. If "what is not" is nothing, then thinking "what is not" would be thinking nothing—which is effectively not thinking at all.</note>, whether concerning one of the things that exist, or the thing itself in its own right?" To this we shall surely answer: "When someone, in thinking, does not think the truth." Or what shall we say? **THEAETETUS.** Just so. **SOCRATES.** Does such a thing happen elsewhere? **THEAETETUS.** In what way? **SOCRATES.** Can someone see something, yet see nothing? **THEAETETUS.** And how could that be? **SOCRATES.** But surely if he sees one thing, B he sees one of the things that exist. Or do you think "one" can be among the things that are not? **THEAETETUS.** Not at all. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, he who sees one thing, sees something that exists. **THEAETETUS.** It appears so. **SOCRATES.** And he who hears something, hears one thing, and hears an existing thing. **THEAETETUS.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** Likewise, he who touches something, touches one thing, and an existing thing besides, if indeed it is one. **THEAETETUS.** That also. **SOCRATES.** And he who thinks, does he not think one thing? **THEAETETUS.** It is necessary. **SOCRATES.** And he who thinks one thing, does he not think an existing thing? **THEAETETUS.** I agree. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, he who thinks what does not exist, thinks nothing. **THEAETETUS.** So it seems. **SOCRATES.** But he who, as it seems, thinks nothing, does not think at all. **THEAETETUS.** It is clear. **SOCRATES.** It is impossible, therefore, to think that which is not, whether about things that exist or about the thing itself in its own right. **THEAETETUS.** It seems impossible. **SOCRATES.** Thinking falsely is therefore something other than thinking that which 
<margin>The third mode</margin>
is not. **THEAETETUS.** Something else indeed. **SOCRATES.** Neither in this way, C nor in the way we considered a little while ago, is false opinion present in us. **THEAETETUS.** Certainly not. **SOCRATES.** But perhaps we call it by this name in this manner: **THEAETETUS.** In what manner? **SOCRATES.** We say that false opinion is a kind of "other-opinion" <term>Allodoxia: The Greek term for mistaking one thing for another.</term>, when someone says that one of the things that exist is another of the things that exist, as the soul's thought has interchanged them. In this way, he always thinks of something that exists, but one thing in place of another; and since he misses the mark of what he was considering, he may rightly be said to think falsely. **THEAETETUS.** Now you seem to me to have spoken most correctly. For whenever someone thinks the ugly instead of the beautiful, or D conversely the beautiful instead of the ugly, he may be judged to think falsely, and not without reason. **SOCRATES.** You clearly look down on me, O Theaetetus, and do not fear me? **THEAETETUS.** Why so? **SOCRATES.** Because I do not think it seems to you that I have truly grasped what is false, having been asked whether the swift can become slow, or the light heavy, or any other contrary become its own contrary, not according to its own nature, but according to the nature of its opposite. Therefore, lest you be emboldened in vain or rashly, I let that pass; and it pleases you, as you say, that thinking falsely is the same as thinking one thing for another. **THEAETETUS.** To me it does. **SOCRATES.** It is possible then, as you E think, to place in thought one thing as another, and not as itself. **THEAETETUS.** It is possible. **SOCRATES.** When the thought does this, then, is it not necessary for it to think of both, or one of them? **THEAETETUS.** Entirely necessary. **SOCRATES.** Either together, or in turn? **THEAETETUS.** That as well.
<margin>What it is to think.</margin>
**SOCRATES.** And do you call "thinking" the same thing that I do? **THEAETETUS.** What do you call it? **SOCRATES.** The discourse which the soul itself carries out with itself concerning the things it considers. I am explaining this to you as one who is not at all an expert. For this is how it appears to me: the thinking soul F does nothing else than carry on a dialogue with itself, asking and answering, affirming and denying. but when it 
<margin>What it is to form an opinion.</margin>
has defined something, and asserts it—whether noticing it slowly or more sharply—and no longer wavers, we call this its opinion. Wherefore I call "to think" to speak, and "opinion" a discourse, not to another, nor with the voice, but in silence and to oneself. But what do you feel? **THEAETETUS.** The same. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, when someone thinks one thing is another, then, as it seems, he says to himself that the one is the other. **THEAETETUS.** Why not? **SOCRATES.** Recall, I pray, if you have ever said to yourself that the G beautiful is entirely ugly, or the unjust is just; or indeed, to put it briefly, whether you have ever tried to persuade yourself that one thing is most certainly another, or quite the contrary: have you ever dared, even in your dreams, to say to yourself that odd numbers are entirely even, or any other thing of this sort? **THEAETETUS.** Never, certainly. **SOCRATES.** Do you think anyone else, whether sane or insane, would dare in speaking to himself to earnestly persuade himself that an ox is necessarily a horse, or that two is one? **THEAETETUS.** By Jove, not at all. **SOCRATES.** If speaking to oneself is thinking, no one while thinking and speaking of both, and grasping both in his soul, would ever say or think that the one is the other. Let us dismiss, if you please, this word "other." But this is what I mean: no one thinks the ugly is beautiful, or anything else of that kind. H **THEAETETUS.** I dismiss it indeed, O Socrates, and what you say pleases me greatly. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, it is impossible that he who thinks of both should think that the one is the other. **THEAETETUS.** It is clear. **SOCRATES.** But neither will he who thinks of one alone, and not at all of the other, ever think that the one is the other. **THEAETETUS.** You speak the truth; for he would be compelled to grasp that which he does not think. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, neither he who thinks of both, nor he who thinks of one, can think of things as "other." Wherefore, he who defines false opinion as "other-thinking" achieves nothing. For in this way, as in the previous ways, it is clear that false opinion is not in us. **THEAETETUS.** So it seems. **SOCRATES.** Nevertheless, O Theaetetus, if this does not appear to be the case, we shall be forced to admit many absurd things. **THEAETETUS.** What sort of things? **SOCRATES.** I shall not tell you until I have in every way...

<column-break/>

A **THEAETETUS.** How do you say? **SOCRATES.** Perhaps it is not simple: that he who believes that which is in no way existent, in whatever other way his thoughts may be, does not believe falsely. **THEAETETUS.** That is likely, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** How then shall we answer, Theaetetus, if someone examines us (as is possible for anyone to do): "Can any man believe that which is not, whether concerning the things that are, or the thing itself by itself?" And we, it seems, shall say to this: "Whenever he who believes does not believe the truth." Or how shall we say it? **THEAETETUS.** In this way. **SOCRATES.** Is this sort of thing found elsewhere? **THEAETETUS.** What sort? **SOCRATES.** If someone sees something, yet sees nothing. **THEAETETUS.** And how? **SOCRATES.** But surely if he sees one thing, B he sees something of the things that are. Or do you think "the one" is ever among the non-existent? **THEAETETUS.** Not I. **SOCRATES.** He who sees one thing, then, sees something that is. **THEAETETUS.** So it appears. **SOCRATES.** And he who hears something, hears one thing, and hears a thing that is. **THEAETETUS.** Yes. **SOCRATES.** And he who touches something, touches some one thing, and a thing that is, if it is one? **THEAETETUS.** That too. **SOCRATES.** And he who believes, does he not believe one thing? **THEAETETUS.** Necessity. **SOCRATES.** And he who believes one thing, does he not believe a thing that is? **THEAETETUS.** I grant it. **SOCRATES.** He who believes that which is not, then, believes nothing. **THEAETETUS.** It does not appear so. **SOCRATES.** But surely he who believes nothing, does not believe at all. **THEAETETUS.** It is clear, as it seems. **SOCRATES.** It is not possible then to believe that which is not, either about things that are, or the thing by itself. **THEAETETUS.** It does not appear so. **SOCRATES.** Believing falsely is therefore something other than believing that which is not. **THEAETETUS.** It seems to be something else. **SOCRATES.** Neither in C this way, nor as we were considering a little while ago, is there false belief in us. **THEAETETUS.** For it is not. **SOCRATES.** But do we address this thing as happening in this way? **THEAETETUS.** In what way? **SOCRATES.** We say false belief is a certain "other-believing" <note>original: "allodoxia"</note>, when someone exchanges in his mind one of the things that are for another of the things that are, and says it is that. For in this way he always believes in a thing that is, but one instead of another; and missing what he was looking for, he might justly be called one who believes falsely. **THEAETETUS.** Now you seem to me to have spoken most correctly. For when someone believes the ugly instead of the beautiful, or the beautiful instead of the ugly, then he truly believes falsely. **SOCRATES.** It is clear, O Theaetetus, that you look down on me and do not fear me. **THEAETETUS.** Why especially? **SOCRATES.** I do not D think you believe there is any hope of me laying hold of the "false," if I were to say that "swiftly" is "slowly" or "light" is "heavy," or any other contrary becomes contrary to itself, not according to its own nature, but according to the nature of the contrary. However, so that you do not take heart in vain, I let this go. But does it please you, as you say, that to believe falsely is to believe "otherly"? **THEAETETUS.** It does. **SOCRATES.** Is it possible then, in your opinion, to set in the mind one thing as another, and not as that which it is? **THEAETETUS.** It is. **SOCRATES.** Whenever the mind does this, then, is it not necessary that it thinks of both or one of the two? **THEAETETUS.** It is necessary. Either together, or in E turn. **THEAETETUS.** Excellent. **SOCRATES.** And do you call "thinking" <note>original: "dianoeisthai"</note> the same thing as I do? **THEAETETUS.** What do you call it? **SOCRATES.** A discourse <note>original: "logos"</note> which the soul itself carries out with itself about whatever it considers. I reveal this to you as a kind of form. For it appears to me that the thinking soul does nothing else but converse, asking itself questions and answering, affirming and denying. And when it has defined something, whether it has reached it slowly or more sharply, and it now says the same thing and does not doubt, we set this down as its opinion. So I call "to believe" to speak, and "opinion" a spoken discourse; not indeed to another, nor with the voice, but in silence to oneself. And what do you say? **THEAETETUS.** I also. **SOCRATES.** Whenever someone believes one thing is another, he says to himself, it seems, that the one is the other. **THEAETETUS.** Why not? **SOCRATES.** Remember if you F have ever said to yourself that the beautiful is certainly ugly, or the unjust is just, or (the sum of all things) consider if you have ever attempted to persuade yourself that one thing is absolutely another, or quite the contrary; not even in sleep have you ever dared to say to yourself that odd numbers are absolutely even, or anything else of the sort. **THEAETETUS.** You speak the truth. **SOCRATES.** Do you think anyone else, sane or mad, would dare to say earnestly to himself, persuading himself, that a horse is necessarily an ox, or that two is one? **THEAETETUS.** By Jove, not I. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, if speaking to G oneself is believing, no one speaking and believing both, and touching both with his soul, would say and believe that the one is the other. We must also let go of the phrase "of the other," for I say it in this way: no one believes that the ugly is beautiful, or any other such things. **THEAETETUS.** Socrates, I let it go, and you seem to me to speak well. **SOCRATES.** To one believing both, then, it is impossible to believe that the one is the other. **THEAETETUS.** So it seems. **SOCRATES.** But surely one believing only the one, and the other not at all, will never believe that the one is the other. **THEAETETUS.** You speak the truth. **SOCRATES.** For he would be forced to touch also that which he does not believe. **THEAETETUS.** Yes. **SOCRATES.** Neither to one believing both, nor to one believing one, is "other-believing" possible. So if anyone defines false opinion as "other-believing" H, he would say nothing. For in this way, nor according to the previous ways, does it appear that false opinion exists in us. **THEAETETUS.** It does not seem so. **SOCRATES.** But surely, O Theaetetus, if this does not appear to be so, we shall be forced to admit many strange things. **THEAETETUS.** What things? **SOCRATES.** I shall not tell you until I have in every way...
</columns>

<summary>Socrates and Theaetetus investigate "false opinion," concluding that it cannot be "thinking what is not" (since that is thinking nothing) nor "allodoxia" (mistaking one thing for another), as no one consciously tells themselves that one thing is its opposite. This page also provides a famous definition of thought as the soul's silent internal dialogue.</summary>

<keywords>Socrates, Theaetetus, false opinion, allodoxia, nature of thought, internal dialogue, dianoia, doxa, epistemology, contradiction, logic</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from the previous section, where Socrates and Theaetetus are investigating the nature of "false opinion" (making a mistake). They have just transitioned from a failed definition to a new inquiry into how the mind can mistake one thing for another.</meta>

# ->THEAETETUS<-

<columns>
<margin>A</margin> ...I will try to consider the goal. For I would be ashamed on our behalf, regarding the things we are proposing, if we were forced to admit what I am saying. But if we find the way and become free, then we shall speak of others as experiencing these things, while we stand safely outside of the ridiculous. But if we are completely at a loss, being humbled, I think, we shall submit ourselves to the argument—like sea-sick passengers <note>The original Greek uses "nautiōntes," referring to the dizziness and helplessness of sea-sickness.</note>—to be trodden upon and used however it pleases. Listen, then, to how I still find a path for our inquiry. **THEAETETUS.** Just speak. **SOCRATES.** I say we were not right when we agreed that it is impossible for a person to think that things he knows are things he does not know, and thus be deceived; rather, in a certain way, it is possible. **THEAETETUS.** Do you mean what I also suspected at the time when we said such a thing? It was something like this: that sometimes I, knowing Socrates, but seeing another person from a distance whom I do not know, <margin>B</margin> might think he is the Socrates whom I know. For in such a case, it happens as you say. **SOCRATES.** Did we not move away from that idea because it made us, in our knowing, both know and not know the things we know? **THEAETETUS.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** Let us not set it down that way, then, but like this; and perhaps in this way it will be granted to us, or perhaps it will be resisted. For we are in such a position that it is necessary to turn every argument over and test it. See if I am making sense: Is it possible for someone who did not know something before to learn it later? **THEAETETUS.** It certainly is. **SOCRATES.** And then another thing after that, and another? **THEAETETUS.** Why not? **SOCRATES.** Suppose then, for the sake of argument, that there is in our souls a waxen block for taking impressions <note>original: "kerinon ekmageion." This is the famous "Wax Tablet" analogy for memory.</note>—larger in one person, smaller in another; of purer wax in one, and in another, more filled with dirt and harder; and in some, too soft, <margin>C</margin> while in others, it is of a middling sort. **THEAETETUS.** I suppose so. **SOCRATES.** Let us say then that this is a gift of Memory, the mother of the Muses <note>Socrates refers to Mnemosyne, the goddess of memory.</note>. And whenever we wish to remember anything we have seen or heard or thought of ourselves, we hold this wax under our perceptions and thoughts and imprint them upon it, just as we take the marks of signet rings. Whatever is imprinted, we remember and know as long as the image remains; but when it is blotted out or cannot be imprinted, we forget and do not know. **THEAETETUS.** Let it be so. **SOCRATES.** Now, consider a man who knows these things, but is looking at or hearing something else, and see whether he might think falsely in the following way. **THEAETETUS.** In what sort of way? <margin>D</margin> **SOCRATES.** By thinking that the things he knows are sometimes the things he knows, and sometimes things he does not know. For we did not agree well in our previous discussion when we said this was impossible. **THEAETETUS.** How do you say it now? **SOCRATES.** We must speak about them by distinguishing them from the beginning: That which someone knows, having a memory of it in his soul, but does not currently perceive, he cannot think to be something else that he knows (and of which he has an imprint, but does not perceive). Nor can he think that what he knows is what he does *not* know (and of which he has no seal). Nor can he think that what he does not know is something else he does not know. <margin>E</margin> [Socrates continues listing permutations of knowing and perceiving...] All these cases make it impossible for anyone to hold a false opinion. It remains, then, if anywhere, that such a thing occurs in the following cases. **THEAETETUS.** In which ones? Perhaps I will learn better from them, for now I do not follow. **SOCRATES.** In those things which someone knows, thinking they are other things which he knows and perceives; or things he does not know, but perceives; or things he knows and perceives, which he in turn perceives. **THEAETETUS.** Now I am left far more behind than I was before. **SOCRATES.** Listen again. I, knowing Theodorus and remembering in myself what he is like, and likewise Theaetetus, sometimes I see them, sometimes I do not; sometimes I touch them, sometimes not; I hear them or perceive them with some other sense. At other times, I have no perception of you at all, but I remember you nonetheless and know you in myself. **THEAETETUS.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** Understand this first among the things I wish to show: that it is possible for one not to perceive what he knows, and also possible to perceive it. **THEAETETUS.** True. **SOCRATES.** And is it not also true that regarding what he does not know, he often does not even perceive it, but often he perceives it only? **THEAETETUS.** That is also true. **SOCRATES.** See if you follow better now. Socrates recognizes Theodorus and Theaetetus, but sees neither, nor is any other perception of them present to him; he could never then think in himself that Theaetetus is Theodorus. Am I saying anything sensible or nothing at all? **THEAETETUS.** Yes, you are speaking the truth. **SOCRATES.** This, then, was the first of those cases I was mentioning. **THEAETETUS.** It was. **SOCRATES.** The second, then: that knowing one of you but not the other, and perceiving neither, I could never think the one I know is the one I do not know. **THEAETETUS.** Correct. **SOCRATES.** And third: knowing neither and perceiving neither, I could not think that one I do not know is some other person I do not know. And imagine you have heard all the previous cases again in order, in which I would never hold a false opinion about you and Theodorus...

This was indeed the first of those things I was saying. **THEAETETUS.** It was.
...I know, but am ignorant of the other, and perceive neither, never...
...Correct. **SOCRATES.** This third thing, truly, while I know neither, and neither...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...I will strive to consider: for I would be ashamed of us in those things which we doubt, if we were compelled to confess what I say. But if we find it and escape free, then at last we will speak of others to whom such things happen, as if we ourselves were entirely foreign to such a ridiculous error. But if we fail altogether, being made humble, like those who are tossing and suffering nausea, we will permit ourselves to the discourse so that it may either trample us or lead us wherever it wishes. Therefore, if I find any exit to this question, hear it now. **THEAETETUS.** Just speak. **SOCRATES.** I will not confess that we agreed correctly when we conceded that a person cannot think that which he knows is that which he does not know, and thus lie. Rather, <margin>B</margin> it can happen in a certain way. **THEAETETUS.** Are you saying what I also suspected then, when we said it was such a thing? That sometimes I, knowing Socrates, and seeing another unknown to me from a distance, might think that known Socrates is the one I see? For it happens in this way which you say. **SOCRATES.** Have we not already been driven away from that, because it caused us, who know, to not know while we are knowing? **THEAETETUS.** Entirely. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, let us not put it that way any longer, but in this manner, and perhaps someone will agree with us, or perhaps someone will oppose us. But let us attend to that in which it is necessary to examine that speech which turns all things upside down. See therefore if I say anything: Can one who was previously ignorant of something later learn it? **THEAETETUS.** <margin>C</margin> He certainly can. **SOCRATES.** And then one thing after another? **THEAETETUS.** What stands in the way? **SOCRATES.** Suppose, for the sake of example, there is a single waxen image in our souls—larger in this one, smaller in that one; and in this one of purer wax, but in another of filthier or harder wax; in some softer, and in some even tempered. **THEAETETUS.** I suppose it. **SOCRATES.** <margin>Memory, the Mother of the Muses.</margin> Let us say then that this is a gift of Memory, the mother of the Muses. And in this, whatever we wish to remember of those things which we either see, or hear, or think of ourselves, we press it in through the senses and intellects, marking it just as we express signs with rings. And whatever has been signed, we remember and know as long as the figure <margin>D</margin> remains; but when it is erased, or cannot be inscribed, we forget and do not know. **THEAETETUS.** Let it be so. **SOCRATES.** He who knows those things, but considers anything of those he sees or hears, see whether he thinks falsely in this way. **THEAETETUS.** In what way? **SOCRATES.** Thinking that the things he knows are, now indeed what he knows, but now what he does not know. These things, certainly, we did not correctly concede above when we confessed they were impossible. **THEAETETUS.** But how do you say it now? **SOCRATES.** Let us speak of them by distinguishing from the beginning in this way: that this which someone knows, and keeps a monument of it in his soul, but does not perceive, he cannot think to be some other of those things; which he also knows, and keeps an image of it, but does not perceive... <margin>E</margin> [Socrates continues the permutations...] or that he knows it, and thinks it is what he does not know, or of which he keeps no image; or that he does not know, and thinks it is that which he does not know; or that he does not know, and thinks it is that which he knows... And much less can he think that what he knows and perceives, and of which he keeps the image according to the sense, is some other thing which he also knows and perceives and keeps the image in the same way; or that what he knows and perceives and retains, he correctly thinks it is what he knows. Or that what he knows and perceives and similarly retains, is that which he perceives; or that what he neither knows nor perceives is that which he neither knows nor perceives... All these things are such that no one can think falsely in them by any reason. It remains, therefore, that in some such cases—if such a thing happens anywhere—it occurs. **THEAETETUS.** In which ones? Let us see, I pray, if I may understand better from them. For at present I do not follow: how in the things someone knows, he might think them to be some other things which he both knows and perceives, or which he does not know but yet perceives, or which he knows and perceives, to be those which he both knows and perceives. Therefore, I now fail far more than above. **SOCRATES.** Come, hear it again this way. Indeed, I, knowing Theodorus and holding his image in memory, and Theaetetus similarly, sometimes I see them, sometimes I do not see them; and I touch them sometimes, at other times not at all; in the same way I both hear and perceive them by other senses. Often I perceive them by no sense, but within myself I know and remember them nonetheless. **THEAETETUS.** Entirely. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, notice this first from those things which I am about to set forth: that one can indeed not perceive what he knows, and can also perceive it. **THEAETETUS.** So it is. **SOCRATES.** And is it not also that what he does not know, he often neither perceives, and often only perceives? **THEAETETUS.** This is also true. **SOCRATES.** See if you now follow this more at present. Socrates, while he recognizes Theodorus and Theaetetus, but sees neither, nor perceives them by any other sense, never thinks to himself that Theaetetus is Theodorus. What say you to this? **THEAETETUS.** They are true. **SOCRATES.** This was the second thing: that while I recognize one of you and am ignorant of the other, and perceive neither, I never think that he whom I know is he whom I am ignorant of. **THEAETETUS.** Correct. **SOCRATES.** And this third thing: while I know neither and perceive neither, I think he whom I do not know is he whom I do not know. And so consider the above-mentioned things repeated in order, in which I never about you and Theodorus...

<sig>M ij</sig>
</columns>

<summary>In this excerpt from Plato's Theaetetus, Socrates introduces the "Wax Tablet" analogy to explain how memory functions and how false opinions (errors) arise. He argues that mistakes occur not in simple knowing or simple perceiving, but in the incorrect "mismatching" of a current perception with a stored memory seal.</summary>
<keywords>Plato, Theaetetus, Socrates, epistemology, wax tablet analogy, memory, Mnemosyne, false opinion, perception, soul, knowledge</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue where Socrates and Theaetetus are exploring how "false opinion" (error) occurs. They have just introduced the "wax tablet" metaphor for the mind, where perceptions are stamped into our memory like a seal in wax.</meta>

# ->OF PLATO<-

<columns>

**A**
...I shall hold false opinions, neither knowing nor being ignorant of both, nor knowing one while being ignorant of the other; and the same logic applies to the senses, if you follow me. **THEAETETUS.** I certainly follow. **SOCRATES.** It remains, then, that we hold false opinions in this way: when I know both you and Theodorus, and I possess in that waxen mental image the seal-impressions <note>original: "signacula," referring to the mark made by a signet ring</note> of both of you from a long time past, but I do not see you both clearly. I try to assign the proper mark of each to its own proper vision, fitting it into its own trace so that recognition may occur. But I miss the mark, and like those who put their shoes on the wrong feet, I switch them; I transfer the vision of each to the "mental image" belonging to the other. This is similar to what happens in mirrors when the reflection is reversed, and the sight shifts the right side to the left. It is then that this "other-judging" occurs, and false opinion is born. **THEAETETUS.** Exactly so, Socrates; that description of how opinion is affected is wonderfully illustrated. **SOCRATES.** Furthermore, it happens when knowing both, I perceive one through the senses but not the other, and my knowledge of that other is not based on current sensation—a point I made earlier, though you did not understand me then. **THEAETETUS.** Certainly not. **SOCRATES.** This is what I was saying: someone who recognizes and perceives a person, and has knowledge of them through the senses, will never think that person is someone else whom they also recognize and perceive. Was that it? **THEAETETUS.** Yes. **SOCRATES.** But we somehow bypassed the point we are making now: that false opinion occurs when someone, knowing and seeing both (or perceiving them by some other sense), and holding the seal-impressions of both, fails to match each one to its own proper sensation. Like a clumsy archer, he misses the mark and errs—which is precisely why it is called a "lie" or a mistake. **THEAETETUS.** And rightly so.

**B**
<margin>In whom there is no false opinion, and in whom it seems to be.</margin>
**SOCRATES.** And when the sensation matches the seal-impression of one, but not the other—when the mind applies the sensation of the absent person to the one who is present—the thought is entirely deceived. To put it briefly: regarding things a person has never known or sensed, it is not possible (it seems) to be deceived or to have a false opinion, if our current argument is sound. However, it is in the things we both know and sense that our opinion turns and twists, becoming true or false. When it collects and shapes the proper images through direct and straight effort, the opinion is true. When it does so transversely and obliquely, it is false. **THEAETETUS.** Socrates, are these points not excellently stated? **SOCRATES.** When you hear what follows, you will assert it even more strongly. For to hold true opinions is beautiful, but to lie is shameful. **THEAETETUS.** How could it be otherwise?

**C**
<margin>The heart of the soul.</margin>
<margin>Those who are mindful and sharp.</margin>
**SOCRATES.** They say these things arise primarily from this: when the waxen image in someone’s soul is deep, abundant, smooth, and well-kneaded, the things that flow in through the senses are engraved into this—which Homer called the "heart of the soul" <note>Homer used the word "kēar" for heart; Socrates puns on this, suggesting it sounds like "kēros," the Greek word for wax</note>—and because the wax is pure, these seal-impressions become clear, deep, and long-lasting. People formed this way are first of all quick to learn and sharp, then also possess good memories; finally, they do not confuse the images of their senses, but truly form opinions. Because their impressions are clear and have plenty of room, they quickly distribute each to its own proper image. Such things are called "realities," and such men are said to be wise. Does it not seem so to you? **THEAETETUS.** Wonderfully so.

**D**
<margin>Those who are forgetful.</margin>
**SOCRATES.** But when someone's "heart" is "shaggy" <note>Socrates refers to a line from the Iliad where Homer describes a brave/dense heart as "shaggy"</note> (as the all-wise poet praised), or when it is muddy and not made of pure wax, or too soft or too hard, then it does not function correctly. For very soft wax makes people quick to perceive but also prone to forgetting.

**E**
<margin>Those who are quick and those who are slow to perceive.</margin>
Hard wax, on the contrary, makes them remember for a long time, but they are clumsy and slow to learn. Those who have a dense, rough, stony, or earthy heart mixed with filth possess obscure mental images. Those with hard wax also have obscure images, for there is no depth to them.

**F**
Furthermore, those with softer wax also have obscure images, for because the impressions are confused, they easily vanish. If, in addition to all this, the impressions are crowded on top of one another due to lack of space—if the "little soul" <note>original: "animula" / "psycharion," a diminutive implying a cramped or narrow mind</note> is small—the images will be even more obscure. All such men, as we have described them, are rendered prone to false opinion.

**G**
<margin>Those prone to false opinion.</margin>
For when they see, hear, or think of anything, because they cannot quickly assign each thing to its proper place, they are slow and they "prevaricate" <note>in the sense of "straddling" or missing the truth</note>. They see, hear, and think of most things perversely and wrongly, often taking one thing for another; and these are the ones called deceived, liars, and ignorant.

**H**
<margin>Those who are ignorant.</margin>
**THEAETETUS.** You speak most correctly of all, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** Must we admit then that false opinions exist in men? **THEAETETUS.** Definitely. **SOCRATES.** And true ones as well? **THEAETETUS.** And true ones. **SOCRATES.** So we should think it is now sufficiently agreed that these two types of opinion exist? **THEAETETUS.** Most certainly. **SOCRATES.** Truly, Theaetetus, a talkative man seems to be a very troublesome and annoying creature. **THEAETETUS.** Why do you say that? **SOCRATES.** Because I am frustrated with my own dullness and, to tell the truth, my own "garrulity" <note>original Greek: "adoleschia," meaning idle chatter or babbling</note>. For what else could one call a person who, because of a slow wit, drags arguments up and down, unable to be persuaded, and like a blunt tool, is incapable of finishing any debate or escaping doubts? **THEAETETUS.** But why are you frustrated? **SOCRATES.** I am not only uneasy, but I also fear what I shall answer if someone asks: "Socrates, have you then discovered that false opinion exists neither in the senses among themselves, nor in thoughts, but in the meeting of sense and thought?" And I shall say, I suppose—boasting as if I had found something remarkable—

<meta>The text ends mid-sentence with the catchword "quasi" (as if), indicating the dialogue continues on the next page.</meta>

<column-break/>

**A**
...I will judge falsely, neither knowing nor being ignorant of both, nor knowing one and not the other. And regarding the senses, the same applies, if you follow. **THEAETETUS.** I follow. **SOCRATES.** What remains, then, is to judge falsely in this: when knowing you and Theodorus, and having in that waxen tablet—as if from rings—the marks of you both, I see you both from a distance and not clearly enough. I strive to assign the proper mark of each to the proper sight, fitting it into its own footprint so that recognition may happen. Then, failing in this, and like those who put their shoes on the wrong feet, switching them, I apply the sight of each to the "other-mark" <note>the impression belonging to the other person</note>. Or it is like the experiences of sight in mirrors, where the image flows from right to left—I suffer the same thing. It is then that "other-judging" and false opinion occur. **THEAETETUS.** It seems, Socrates, that you are describing the experience of opinion wonderfully. **SOCRATES.** Furthermore, it is when, knowing both, I also perceive one but not the other; my knowledge of the other is not according to sensation—which is what I was saying before, and you did not understand me then. **THEAETETUS.** No, I did not. **SOCRATES.** I was saying this: that one who knows the other and perceives him, and has knowledge according to the sensation of him, will never think he is someone else whom he also knows and perceives, and of whom he likewise has knowledge according to sensation.

**B**
**THEAETETUS.** Yes. **SOCRATES.** But what was left out, as we said, is the way we now say false opinion arises: knowing both and seeing both (or having some other sensation of both), one does not have the marks according to their own sensation. Like a poor archer, he misses the target and errs, which is why it was called "falsehood." **THEAETETUS.** Naturally.

**C**
**SOCRATES.** And so when sensation is present for one mark but not for the other, and the mind fits the sensation of the absent one to the present one, in every such way the thought is deceived. In a word, regarding things one never knew or sensed, there is (it seems) neither erring nor false opinion, if what we are saying is healthy. But regarding things we both know and sense, it is in these that opinion turns and revolves, becoming false and true. When it brings together the proper impressions and types directly and straight, it is true; but when it does so sideways and crookedly, it is false. **THEAETETUS.** Is this not well-said, Socrates? **SOCRATES.** When you have heard these things, you will say so even more. For to judge truly is beautiful, but to be deceived is shameful. **THEAETETUS.** How could it not be?

**D**
**SOCRATES.** They say, then, that these things arise from this. When the wax in someone’s soul is deep, abundant, smooth, and moderately worked, the things entering through the senses are stamped into this "heart" <note>Greek: "kēar"</note> of the soul (which Homer mentioned, hinting at the likeness to "wax" <note>Greek: "kēros"</note>). Then the marks that occur are pure and have sufficient depth, and they become long-lasting. Such people are, first, quick to learn, and second, they have good memories; then they do not swap the marks of their senses, but judge truly. For being clear and in a wide space, they quickly distribute them to their own "molds" <note>original: "ekmageia," the impressions in the wax</note>, which are called "things that are." And these people are called wise. Or does it not seem so to you? **THEAETETUS.** Most exceedingly so.

**E**
**SOCRATES.** But when someone's "heart" is "shaggy" (which the all-wise poet praised), or when it is like dung and not made of pure wax, or very moist or hard—in those where it is moist, they are quick to learn but forgetful; where it is hard, the opposite. Those who have a shaggy and rough heart, something stony or full of earth or mixed dung, have obscure "molds."

**F**
Those with hard wax also have obscure ones, for there is no depth in them. Those with moist wax also have obscure ones, for because they are confused, they quickly become faint. And if, in addition to all these, they are fallen upon one another due to narrowness—if someone's "little soul" is small—they are even more obscure than the others. All these people, then, become prone to judging falsely. For when they see or hear or think of something, they are unable to quickly assign each thing to its own, they are slow, and they "judge wrongly" <note>Greek: "allotrionomousi," literally "distributing to the wrong place"</note>. They see and hear and think of most things incorrectly, and these are called deceived about things that are, and ignorant. **THEAETETUS.** You speak most rightly of all men, Socrates.

**G**
**SOCRATES.** Shall we say then that false opinions exist in us? **THEAETETUS.** Let us say so. Very much so. **SOCRATES.** And true ones too? **THEAETETUS.** And true ones. **SOCRATES.** Do we think it is now sufficiently agreed that both these opinions most certainly exist? **THEAETETUS.** Exceedingly so. **SOCRATES.** A terrible thing, Theaetetus, it truly risks being, and an unpleasant one—a man who is a "babbler." **THEAETETUS.** Why? To what purpose do you say this? **SOCRATES.** Out of frustration at my own dullness, and truly, my "babbling." For what other name could one give it when someone drags arguments up and down out of sluggishness, and because of an inability to be persuaded, is hard to get away from every argument? **THEAETETUS.** But why are you frustrated?

**H**
**SOCRATES.** I am not only frustrated, but I also fear what I shall answer if someone asks me: "Socrates, have you found that false opinion exists neither in the senses among themselves, nor in the thoughts, but in the junction of sensation with thought?" And I shall say, I think, boasting as if I had found some...

</columns>

<summary>In this passage from Plato's *Theaetetus*, Socrates uses the famous "wax tablet" metaphor to explain how false opinions arise from the mismatch between current sensory perceptions and stored mental impressions. He categorizes different types of minds (slow, forgetful, or wise) based on the quality—purity, depth, and consistency—of their internal "wax."</summary>

<keywords>Socrates, Theaetetus, wax tablet metaphor, false opinion, memory, sensory perception, Homeric pun, kēar, kēros, epistemology</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from the previous page, shifting from the "Wax Tablet" metaphor to a more complex exploration of how we can possess knowledge without currently using it. Socrates and Theaetetus are investigating how a person who "knows" a number can still make a mistake in calculation.</meta>

# THEAETETUS

<columns>

<margin>A</margin> ...found it. **THEAETETUS.** It seems to me, Socrates, that what has been shown is not at all shameful <note>original: "καλόν" / "turpe" - Socrates is playfully asking if their previous failed definitions are "ugly" or "shameful" in a logical sense</note>. **SOCRATES.** Won't that man <note>referring to a hypothetical critic</note> say then: "Is it possible that a man whom we only think of, but do not see, we might ever imagine to be a horse—a horse which we currently neither see nor touch, but only think of, and perceive nothing else about it?" I suppose I should admit that I would say that. **THEAETETUS.** And rightly so. **SOCRATES.** Then he will ask: "Regarding the number eleven, which one only thinks about, would he ever, according to this logic, think it is twelve, which he also only <margin>B</margin> thinks about?" Come now, you answer him. **THEAETETUS.** I will answer that if someone were seeing or touching eleven things, they might think they were twelve; however, as for the numbers he holds only in his thought, he would never judge them in such a way. **SOCRATES.** What then? Do you think anyone has ever considered within himself "five and seven"—I do not mean five men and seven men, or anything else of that sort, but the abstract "five" and "seven" themselves, which we said are like impressions stored in the waxen block <note>term: "ἐκμαγείῳ" (ekmageio) - a mold or waxen surface used to take an impression, here a metaphor for memory</note>, and wondered if it were possible to have a false opinion about them? Has anyone ever examined these very numbers, asking themselves what their sum is, and one person said eleven while another said twelve? Or does everyone say and believe they are twelve? **THEAETETUS.** No, by Zeus! <margin>C</margin> Many say they are eleven. And if someone considers a larger number, he is even more likely to stumble. For I suppose you are speaking about all numbers. **SOCRATES.** You are right to think so. Consider then whether anything else is happening there than thinking that the "twelve" itself, which is in the waxen block, is actually "eleven." **THEAETETUS.** So it seems. **SOCRATES.** Does this not bring us back to our first arguments? For the one who suffers this mistake thinks that one thing he knows is actually another thing he knows. We said this was impossible, and by this very fact we are forced to conclude that false opinion does not exist, so that the same man is not forced to both know and not know the same thing at the same time. **THEAETETUS.** Most true. <margin>D</margin> **SOCRATES.** Therefore, we must show that holding a false opinion is something other than the misaligned shift of thought to sensation. For if it were that, we would never be deceived within our abstract thoughts themselves. But now, either there is no such thing as false opinion, or it is possible for someone not to know what they actually know. Which of these do you choose? **THEAETETUS.** You offer a difficult choice, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** But the argument seems likely to refuse both. Yet we must dare everything—what if we tried to be "shameless"? **THEAETETUS.** In what way? **SOCRATES.** By venturing to say what it is "to know" <note>original: "ἐπίστασθαι" - to have scientific or certain knowledge</note>. **THEAETETUS.** Why is that shameless? **SOCRATES.** You seem not to realize that our whole <margin>E</margin> discussion from the beginning has been a search for the nature of knowledge, as if we did not already know what it is. **THEAETETUS.** I realize that. **SOCRATES.** Then does it not seem impudent for people who do not know what knowledge is to declare what "knowing" is like? But the truth is, Theaetetus, we have long been infected by a lack of purity in our discourse. We have said "we recognize" and "we do not recognize," and "we know" and "we do not know" ten thousand times, as if we understood one another, while all the while we are still ignorant of what knowledge is. If you like, even now in this moment, we are using the terms "to be ignorant" and "to understand," as if it were proper to use them while we are still deprived of knowledge. **THEAETETUS.** But how will you argue, Socrates, if you abstain from these words? **SOCRATES.** Not at all, being the man I am. However, if I were a professional debater <note>term: "ἀντιλογικὸς" (antilogikos) - a person skilled in contradiction or eristic debate</note>, such a man would tell us to abstain from these words and would severely rebuke me for what I am saying. But since we are only ordinary men, do you <margin>F</margin> want me to venture to say what "knowing" is like? For it seems to me it might be worth the effort. **THEAETETUS.** Venture it, then, by Zeus! You will be granted much indulgence even if you do not abstain from those terms. **SOCRATES.** Have you heard what they currently say "to know" is? **THEAETETUS.** Perhaps, but I don't remember it at the moment. **SOCRATES.** They say it is "the having of knowledge." **THEAETETUS.** True. **SOCRATES.** Let us then make a small change and say it is "the possessing of knowledge." **THEAETETUS.** How would you say this differs from the other? **SOCRATES.** Perhaps not at all; but listen to how it seems to me, and then examine it with me. **THEAETETUS.** I will, if I am able. **SOCRATES.** To me, "possessing" does not seem to be the same thing as "having." For instance, if someone bought a cloak <margin>G</margin> and, being its master, did not wear it, we would not say he "has" it, but we would say he "possesses" it. **THEAETETUS.** And rightly so. **SOCRATES.** See then if it is possible to "possess" knowledge without "having" it—just as if someone had hunted wild birds, like doves or something else, and having built an aviary <note>term: "περιστερεῶνα" (peristereōna) - a dovecote or pigeon-house</note> at home, he kept them there. In a way, we could say he "has" them always, because he possesses them. Is that not so? **THEAETETUS.** Yes. **SOCRATES.** But in another sense, he "has" none of them, though he has acquired a power over them, since he has brought them under his hand in his own enclosure. He can catch them and "have" them whenever he wants, hunting whichever one he wishes and letting it go again; and he is free to do this as often as he likes. **THEAETETUS.** That is so. **SOCRATES.** Once again, then—just as earlier we fashioned a sort of "waxen" thing in our souls, I know not what kind of fiction—let us now make in each soul a sort of aviary of all kinds of birds: some in flocks apart from the others, some in small groups, and some solitary, flying among all the others wherever they happen to go. **THEAETETUS.** Let it be fashioned; but what follows? **SOCRATES.** In childhood, one might say this vessel is empty; but instead of birds, let us imagine pieces of knowledge. Whichever piece of knowledge a man has acquired and shut up in his enclosure, we should say he has learned or discovered the thing of which this was the knowledge; and this constitutes "knowing." **THEAETETUS.** Granted. **SOCRATES.** Now, consider again: when he wishes to hunt any of these pieces of knowledge, and having caught it, to hold it...

<column-break/>

found. <margin>A</margin> **THEAETETUS.** To me indeed it seems, O Socrates, by no means shameful what has now been shown. **SOCRATES.** Will he not therefore, as that man might ask, say that if we only think of a man, and do not see him at all, we would never think he is a horse, whom we neither see nor touch in the present, but only think of, and perceive nothing else about him? These things indeed, as I think, I will admit that I assert. **THEAETETUS.** And deservedly. **SOCRATES.** Then he says: "Eleven, which one only thinks of, according to this reasoning, he will never think to be twelve, which he also only <margin>B</margin> thinks of." What do you answer to these things? **THEAETETUS.** I answer: if someone is perhaps seeing or touching eleven things, he might think they are twelve; but those things which he has in thought, he would never judge similarly. **SOCRATES.** What further, he asks, do you think—would someone think to himself "five and seven"—not five men, I say, and seven men, nor any other such thing, but the "five" and "seven" themselves, which we said were the monuments in the image there, and that no one can have a false opinion in them? These, I say, if any so consider with themselves, searching for how many they are, will not some of them judge them to be eleven, and some twelve? Or will all say and think that they are twelve? **THEAETETUS.** Not by Jove, <margin>C</margin> but many indeed say eleven; and if one asks about a larger number, he is more mistaken. For I think you are speaking more about every number. **SOCRATES.** You judge rightly. Observe therefore, whether this also happens: that is, that someone thinks the "twelve" themselves which are in the image are "eleven." **THEAETETUS.** It seems so. **SOCRATES.** Does this not revolve back to the former points? For he who suffers this regarding what he knows, thinks it is some other thing which he similarly knows, which we previously rejected as impossible. And from this very thing we are forced to confess that false opinion is not that, lest one and the same person be forced to know and not know the same things at the same time. **THEAETETUS.** You speak true things. **SOCRATES.** From these things it is now <margin>D</margin> clear that false opinion must be defined otherwise than as the exchange of thought for sensation. For if it were so, we would never be deceived in the thoughts themselves. But now, either there is no false opinion, or if there is any, it is possible that what one knows, he might be ignorant of at the same time. Which do you prefer to choose? **THEAETETUS.** You have proposed an ambiguous choice, O Socrates. **SOCRATES.** Reason seems to forbid admitting both. Nevertheless, all things must be dared. What if we dared to set aside shame? **THEAETETUS.** In what way? **SOCRATES.** By daring to pronounce what "to know" itself is. **THEAETETUS.** Why is this impudent? **SOCRATES.** You seem not to have noticed enough that our whole speech from the beginning has been an investigation of science <note>note: Here "science" is used in the older sense of "knowledge" (scientia)</note>, as if we are ignorant of what it is. **THEAETETUS.** I hold your point. **SOCRATES.** Is it not the sign of an impudent <margin>E</margin> mind, that those ignorant of science should show what "to know" is? But, O Theaetetus, for a long time we have wandered far from the purity of disputation; for we have said these things a thousand times: "we recognize," "we do not recognize," "we know," "we do not know," as if we understood each other while we are meanwhile ignorant of knowledge. Therefore even now, if it pleases you, let us use those words—"to be ignorant" and "to understand"—as it is convenient to use them, if indeed we are experts of science. **THEAETETUS.** But in what way, if these are taken away, O Socrates, would you be able to dispute? **SOCRATES.** In no way, while I remain as I am; I could, however, in some way, if I were a contentious man. And even now if such a man were present, he would profess to abstain from these words, and would vehemently deter us from these things which I myself narrate. But because we are simple and <margin>F</margin> lazy, do you wish that I dare to bring forth what "to know" itself is like? For it seems to me to be worth the effort. **THEAETETUS.** Dare, by Jove. For we will give you pardon for using these. **SOCRATES.** Have you heard what they say "to know" is at this time? **THEAETETUS.** Perhaps, but I do not remember at present. **SOCRATES.** They say it is "to have knowledge." **THEAETETUS.** So it is. **SOCRATES.** We, however, changing it a little, <margin>It is one thing to have knowledge, another to use and possess it.</margin> let us say it is "to possess knowledge." You will ask, perhaps, in what way this differs from the other. In nothing, perhaps; but what seems so to me, after you have heard it, examine it with me. **THEAETETUS.** Provided I am able. **SOCRATES.** Indeed, "to possess" does not seem the same as "to have"; as if <margin>G</margin> someone, having bought a garment, keeping it and being able to use it at his will, does not wear it; we would by no means confess him to "have" it, but rather to "possess" it. **THEAETETUS.** And rightly indeed. **SOCRATES.** See moreover whether it can happen that one who similarly possesses knowledge, does not have it: just as if someone hunted wild birds, whether doves or any other, and nourishes them in an aviary constructed at home; in a certain way he will always be said to "have" them, because he possesses them. **THEAETETUS.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** But in a certain way he does "not have" them, but he has the power, and since he has enclosed them in the dove-cote, he can take them as often as he wishes, and "have" any one at his whim and dismiss it again; and it is permitted to him to do this as often as he pleases. **THEAETETUS.** It is so. **SOCRATES.** Again, just as we previously devised some waxen fiction in our minds, so now let us fabricate in any soul a certain aviary of every kind of birds: of which some wander in flocks separate from others, some in small numbers, and some alone everywhere, wherever it happens, they fly. **THEAETETUS.** Let it be done; what then after? **SOCRATES.** Let us say this cage is empty in children; but in the place of birds, let us understand sciences: and whoever has obtained a science and has shut it in this circuit, let us say he has found and learned the thing itself of which there is science, and this itself is "to know." **THEAETETUS.** Be it so. **SOCRATES.** Then again, whichever science he wishes to catch, and having caught it, to have it...
