<vocab>Plato, Socrates, Theaetetus, epistemology, science, knowledge, avian analogy, mental wax, birdcage analogy, possessing vs having knowledge</vocab>

<summary>Socrates and Theaetetus transition from the "Wax Tablet" model of memory to the "Aviary" metaphor to explain how one can possess knowledge (like birds in a cage) without currently "having" or using it. This is intended to solve the problem of how a person can make an error in calculation regarding things they technically already know.</summary>

<keywords>epistemology, mental models, calculation error, abstract numbers, memory vs. possession, aviary metaphor, Plato's Theaetetus</keywords>

--- Page 170 ---
<meta>This page continues the "Aviary" metaphor introduced previously. Socrates and Theaetetus are attempting to distinguish between "possessing" knowledge (having it stored in the mind's aviary) and "having" knowledge (actually holding the bird/thought in one's hand of consciousness). This distinction is intended to explain how a person who knows a fact can still make a mistake.</meta>

# PLATO'S THEAETETUS

<columns>

...and to release them again: all these things, I say, consider by what names they should be expressed. Should they be the same names as before, when they were merely possessed after being acquired, or should we use others? From this, perhaps, you will understand me more clearly. Do you call Arithmetic an art? **THEAETETUS.** I do. **SOCRATES.** Suppose this to be the hunt <note>original: "aucupium" - literally fowling or bird-catching</note> for the knowledge of every even and odd number. **THEAETETUS.** I suppose it. **SOCRATES.** By this art, the arithmetician himself holds the knowledge of numbers as if they were certain possessions <note>original: "mancipia" - a term for property or slaves over which one has legal control</note> subjected to him, and he hands them over to others. **THEAETETUS.** Exactly. **SOCRATES.** And he who hands them over, we say "teaches"; he who receives them, "learns"; and he who holds them by virtue of possessing them in the cage <margin>B</margin> itself, we say "knows." **THEAETETUS.** Precisely. **SOCRATES.** Now, pay close attention to what follows. A perfect arithmetician, does he not know all numbers? For the knowledge of all numbers is present in his mind. **THEAETETUS.** Nothing prevents it. **SOCRATES.** Does he not sometimes count, either internally with himself or externally, things that consist of numbers? **THEAETETUS.** Why not? **SOCRATES.** But we shall posit that "counting" is nothing other than considering how great each number is. **THEAETETUS.** Nothing else, certainly. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, he who we admitted knows every number appears to consider what he knows as if he were ignorant of it. Do you hear these ambiguities? **THEAETETUS.** Indeed. **SOCRATES.** Since we have compared it to the possession and hunting of doves, <margin>C</margin> we shall say there is a double hunt: one before acquisition for the sake of possessing; the other after one has acquired and possessed them, for the sake of catching and holding in the hand those very things one has long possessed. And so, the things for which he was already endowed with knowledge by learning long ago, and which he knew before, he can "learn" again by taking up the knowledge of each and holding it—in his thought, that is; for while he possessed it before, he did not have it in his hand. **THEAETETUS.** You speak the truth. **SOCRATES.** That is why I asked a little while ago how we should use names when speaking of these things—for instance, when an arithmetician is about to count, or a grammarian is about to read. For then, though he knows, he attempts to "learn" from himself again what he already knows. **THEAETETUS.** But this is absurd, <margin>D</margin> Socrates. **SOCRATES.** Or perhaps should we say that he counts or reads what he *does not* know, even though we have already granted him the understanding of all letters or numbers? **THEAETETUS.** This too is absurd. **SOCRATES.** Do you want us to say, then, that we do not care how anyone uses the names "knowing" and "learning"? But since we have determined that possessing knowledge is one thing, and "having" what one possesses is another, we say it is impossible for someone not to possess what they possess. Therefore, it never happens that someone does not know what they know. However, a false opinion can be accepted concerning that very thing. For it can happen that we take the knowledge of one thing for the knowledge of another; as when one of us, hunting for one of the internal knowledges, mistakenly catches another that flies in front of it. Just as when someone thinks eleven is twelve, taking the knowledge of eleven instead of the knowledge of twelve (since both stay within), as if taking a wood-pigeon <note>original: "palumbem" / "φάτταν" (phattan)</note> instead of a dove <note>original: "columba" / "περιστερᾶς" (peristeras)</note>. **THEAETETUS.** That seems likely. **SOCRATES.** But when he catches the one he is aiming for, then he is said to be free from falsehood and to judge things as they are. In this way, both true and false opinion exist, and nothing that troubled us before will be an obstacle. Perhaps <margin>E</margin> you agree with me, or what will you do? **THEAETETUS.** I agree. **SOCRATES.** Now we have escaped that dilemma where people were forced to say they "do not know what they know." For it does not happen that we do not possess what we possess, whether we are mistaken or judge truly. Yet another, more serious matter seems to appear to me. **THEAETETUS.** What is that? **SOCRATES.** If the exchange of knowledges becomes a false opinion. **THEAETETUS.** How so? **SOCRATES.** First, is it not very absurd that he who has knowledge of a thing should be ignorant of that very thing—not through ignorance, but by that very knowledge itself? Then, that he should think this thing is another, and that another is this? <margin>F</margin> How irrational is it that, when knowledge is present, the soul should know nothing and be ignorant of everything? Indeed, according to this reasoning, nothing prevents present ignorance from making us know something, or blindness from making us see—if knowledge can make someone ignorant. **THEAETETUS.** Perhaps, Socrates, we did not introduce the birds well when we put only knowledges in the soul; we should have also introduced "ignorances" <note>original: "inscitias" / "ἀνεπιστημοσύνας" - specific pieces of non-knowledge or errors personified as birds</note> flying about together with the knowledges in the soul. Then the hunter, sometimes catching a knowledge and often an ignorance about the same thing, would judge truly when he hits upon a knowledge, and falsely when he hits upon an ignorance. **SOCRATES.** It is difficult not to praise you, Theaetetus; yet consider again what you have said. Let it be as you say. He who hits upon an ignorance will judge falsely, as you say; right? **THEAETETUS.** Certainly. <margin>G</margin> **SOCRATES.** But he will not think that he is judging falsely. **THEAETETUS.** Certainly not. **SOCRATES.** But rather truly, and he will be affected as if he knows those things in which he errs. **THEAETETUS.** Why not? **SOCRATES.** And therefore he will think he has caught a knowledge in his hunt, not an ignorance. **THEAETETUS.** It is clear. **SOCRATES.** Now, after a long circuit, we have fallen back into our first difficulty. For that mocking critic <note>Socrates refers to a personified logic or a hypothetical debater</note> will laugh and say: "Tell me, my good men, does someone who knows both—the knowledge and the ignorance which he knows—think that one which he knows is another which he also knows? Or knowing neither, does he judge one which he does not know to be another which he does not know? Or knowing one but not the other, does he think the one he knows is the one he does not know, or the one he does not know is the one he knows? Or will you tell me again that there are knowledges <margin>H</margin> of knowledges and of ignorances, which their owner, enclosing them in some other ridiculous cages or waxen models,

<column-break/>

...to hold, and to release again; consider what names are needed, whether the same <margin>formerly: "ones which they were," or "others"</margin> <margin>A</margin> as they were, or some others. You will learn from this: I will speak more clearly. Do you say Arithmetic is an art? THEAETETUS. Yes. SOCRATES. Suppose this then to be a hunt for the knowledge of everything even and odd. THEAETETUS. I suppose it. SOCRATES. By this art, I think, he himself has the knowledges of numbers under his hand, and he who hands them over delivers them to another. THEAETETUS. Yes. SOCRATES. And we call the one who hands them over "to teach," and the one who takes them "to learn"; and the one who, by possessing them, turns them over <margin>B</margin> in that same way, "to know." THEAETETUS. Quite so. SOCRATES. Now, have you ever noticed from this that a man who is a perfect arithmetician knows all numbers? For the knowledges of all of them are within his soul. THEAETETUS. Why not? SOCRATES. Would such a man ever count anything, either himself with himself internally, or any of the external things that have number? THEAETETUS. Yes, how could he not? SOCRATES. But we shall posit that "to count" is nothing other than to consider how great a certain number happens to be. THEAETETUS. Yes, thus. SOCRATES. Therefore, he who knows, in considering it, appears now as if not knowing—he whom we agreed knows every number. For you surely hear of such disputes. THEAETETUS. Yes, I do. SOCRATES. Therefore, we, likening it to the possession and hunting of doves, <margin>C</margin> will say that the hunt is double: one, before possessing, for the sake of possessing; the other, for the one who possesses, to take and have in the hands what he possessed long ago. And thus, even those things of which he had knowledges long ago by learning, he can again "learn" these same things, taking up the knowledge of each and holding it, which he possessed long ago but did not have ready in his thought. THEAETETUS. True. SOCRATES. This is what I was asking just now: how should we use names to speak of them, when the arithmetician goes to count, or the grammarian to read? As if knowing, then, in such a case, he comes again to "learn" from himself what he knows. THEAETETUS. But that is absurd, Socrates. SOCRATES. <margin>D</margin> But will it not appear absurd that he, given that we granted he knows all letters and all numbers, should then read or count them? THEAETETUS. That too is irrational. SOCRATES. Do you wish then that we say we care nothing for names, however anyone chooses to drag around "knowing" and "learning"? But since we defined one thing as "possessing" knowledge and another as "having" it—we say it is impossible for someone not to possess what he possesses. So it never <margin>E</margin> happens that what one knows, one does not know; however, it is possible to sometimes take up a false opinion about it. For it is possible not to have the knowledge of *this* thing, but another instead of it, when hunting for some knowledge from those flying about, and instead of one, he catches another by mistake; as when he thinks eleven is twelve, taking the knowledge of eleven instead of the knowledge of twelve—taking, as it were, a wood-pigeon in himself instead of a dove. THEAETETUS. That makes sense. SOCRATES. But when he catches what he attempts to take, then he is not deceived and judges the things that are. And in this way there is both true and false opinion; and none of the things we were troubled by before will be an obstacle. Perhaps then you will agree with me; or what will you do? THEAETETUS. Yes, thus. SOCRATES. And indeed we are rid of the problem of "not knowing what one knows." For it no longer happens that we do not possess what we have acquired, whether we are deceived about something or not. However, another more terrible condition seems to appear to me. THEAETETUS. What kind? SOCRATES. If the exchange of knowledge will ever become a false opinion. THEAETETUS. How so? SOCRATES. First, that one who has knowledge should be ignorant of this very thing—not through lack of knowledge, but by his own knowledge. Then, to judge this to be another, and another to be this— <margin>F</margin> how is that not great irrationality, that when knowledge is present, the soul should know nothing, but be ignorant of everything? For by such a logic, nothing prevents ignorance, when present, from making one know something, and blindness from making one see—if indeed knowledge will ever make someone be ignorant. THEAETETUS. Perhaps, Socrates, we did not set the birds well, saying they were only knowledges. We should have also had "ignorances" flying together with them in the soul; and the hunter, sometimes taking a knowledge, and sometimes an ignorance instead of the other, would judge falsely with the ignorance, but truly with the knowledge. <margin>G</margin> SOCRATES. It is not easy, Theaetetus, not to praise you. But what you said, consider again. For let it be as you say. He who takes the ignorance, you say, will judge falsely. Is that so? THEAETETUS. Yes. SOCRATES. He surely will not think he is judging falsely. THEAETETUS. How could he? SOCRATES. But rather truly, and he will be disposed as if knowing those things about which he has been deceived. THEAETETUS. Of course. SOCRATES. He will think he has hunted and caught a knowledge, not an ignorance. THEAETETUS. Clearly. SOCRATES. Therefore, having gone around a long way, we are back again at the first difficulty. For that cross-examiner will laugh and say: "Which of these, O best of men, knowing both knowledge and ignorance, does he think that the one he knows is another which he also knows? Or knowing neither, does he judge one which he does not know to be another which he does not know? Or knowing one, <margin>H</margin> and not knowing the other, does he think the one he does not know is the one he knows, or vice versa? Or will you tell me again that of the knowledges and ignorances there are yet again other knowledges, which the owner possesses, enclosing them in some other ridiculous aviaries or waxen models...

</columns>

<summary>This page explores the "Aviary" metaphor for the mind, distinguishing between the possession of knowledge (storing birds in a cage) and the actual use of it (holding a bird in the hand). Socrates and Theaetetus struggle to explain how a person can "know" something yet still make a mistake, eventually suggesting that "ignorances" might also be birds trapped in the same cage.</summary>

<keywords>Plato, Socrates, Theaetetus, Aviary Metaphor, Epistemology, Arithmetic, False Opinion, Knowledge vs Possession, Ignorance, Wood-pigeon and Dove analogy</keywords>

--- Page 171 ---
<meta>This page follows the discussion of the "Aviary" metaphor, where Socrates and Theaetetus attempted to define knowledge as the possession of information. Having found that model insufficient because it allows for the "possession" of ignorance, they now move toward a new definition: "True Opinion."</meta>

# THEAETETUS

<columns>

<margin>A</margin> ...as long as he possesses it, he knows it, even if he does not have it ready <note>original: "procheirous" — literally "at hand" or "handy"</note> in his soul. In this way, he will be forced to circle back to the same problem a thousand times, making no progress. What shall we say to this, Theaetetus? **THEAETETUS.** By Zeus, Socrates, I do not know what to say. **SOCRATES.** Does not our argument rightly rebuke us, child? It shows that we were wrong to seek "false opinion" before "knowledge," leaving the latter unexamined. It is impossible to understand what a false belief is until one has sufficiently grasped what knowledge itself is. **THEAETETUS.** At the moment, Socrates, I must agree with you. **SOCRATES.** Then what shall we say knowledge is, starting again from the beginning? We aren't giving up, are we? **THEAETETUS.** Not at all, unless you give up.

<margin>B</margin> **SOCRATES.** Tell me then: what definition could we give that would least contradict ourselves? **THEAETETUS.** The one we tried before, Socrates. I see no other way. **SOCRATES.** Which one was that? **THEAETETUS.** That **true opinion is knowledge**. <note>Theaetetus suggests that if you believe something and it happens to be true, you "know" it.</note> Surely, holding a true opinion is free from error, and all the results it produces are fine and good. **SOCRATES.** The man leading the way across a river, Theaetetus, said "the water itself will show its depth." If we go forward and search, perhaps the very thing we seek will appear as an obstacle; but if we stand still, nothing will be clear. **THEAETETUS.** You are right. Let us go forward and look. **SOCRATES.** This search will not take long. There is an entire profession that proves knowledge is not simply true opinion. **THEAETETUS.** How so? What profession is that? **SOCRATES.** The profession of those greatest in wisdom, whom men call orators and

<margin>C</margin> lawyers. These men, you see, do not use their art to *teach*, but to *persuade*, making people believe whatever they wish. Or do you think there are any teachers so powerful that, in the short time allowed by the water-clock <note>original: "hydōr smikron" — referring to the *clepsydra* or water-clock used to limit the time of legal speeches in Athenian courts</note>, they can sufficiently teach the truth of a robbery or a violent act to people who were not there to see it? **THEAETETUS.** I do not think so at all; they only persuade them. **SOCRATES.** And by "persuading," don't you mean making them hold an opinion? **THEAETETUS.** Of course. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, when judges are justly persuaded about things that only an eyewitness can know, they are judging by hearsay. Even if they reach a true opinion and judge

<margin>D</margin> rightly, they have done so without knowledge, having been correctly persuaded. **THEAETETUS.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** But, my friend, if true opinion and knowledge were the same thing, a perfect judge would never hold a correct opinion without knowledge. As it is, they seem to be two different things. **THEAETETUS.** Now I remember something I heard someone say, Socrates—I had forgotten it, but it comes back to me now. He said that **true opinion combined with a rational account** <note>original: "logos" — can mean word, reason, explanation, or definition</note> **is knowledge**, but that opinion without such an account is outside of knowledge. Things for which there is no account are "unknowable"—that is the word he used—while things that have an account are "knowable." **SOCRATES.** You put it well. But how did he distinguish between these knowable and unknowable things? Tell me, to see if you and I have heard the same thing. **THEAETETUS.** I am not sure I can remember the details, but I think I could follow if someone else explained it.

<margin>E</margin> **SOCRATES.** Listen then to "a dream for a dream." <note>A playful way of saying Socrates will trade his own theory for the one Theaetetus just mentioned.</note> I, too, seem to have heard from certain people that the primary "elements" —the building blocks from which we and all other things are composed—have no rational account. Each element can only be named by itself; you cannot say anything more about it, neither that it "is" nor that it "is not." For if you did, you would be adding "existence" or "non-existence" to it, which you must not do if you are speaking only of the element itself. You should not even add terms like "itself," "that," "each," "alone," or "this." These terms wander around and are applied to everything, being different from the things to which they are added. If it were possible for an element to be explained, it would have to be spoken of

<margin>F</margin> on its own, without any other terms. But in fact, it is impossible to give an account of any of the primary elements; they can only be named, for they have nothing but a name. However, when we come to the things composed of these elements—the "syllables" <note>Socrates uses the metaphor of letters (elements) and syllables (complexes).</note>—just as the elements themselves are woven together, so their names are woven together to become a rational account. For a "weaving together of names" is the very essence of an account. Thus, the elements are unaccountable and unknown, though they can be perceived by the senses; but the "syllables" are known and can be spoken of and grasped by true opinion. So, when someone gets hold of the true opinion of something without the account, his soul is right about the truth, but he does not *know* it. For a man who cannot give and receive an account <note>original: "logon" — here meaning a logical explanation</note> of a thing is ignorant of it. But if he adds the account, he is capable of all these things and is perfectly possessed of knowledge. Is this the "dream" you heard, or was it different? **THEAETETUS.** It was exactly like that.

<margin>G</margin> **SOCRATES.** Does it please you then, and do you take it as a rule, that "true opinion with a rational account is knowledge"? **THEAETETUS.** Entirely. **SOCRATES.** Is it possible, Theaetetus, that today we have captured the very thing that many wise men sought for ages and grew old before finding? **THEAETETUS.** It seems to me, Socrates, that what has just been said is well said. **SOCRATES.** And it is likely so. For what knowledge could there be without a rational account and correct opinion? Yet one thing in this theory bothers me. **THEAETETUS.** What is that? **SOCRATES.** Something that seemed rather clever: the idea that the elements are "unknown," but the class of syllables is "known." **THEAETETUS.** Is that not correct? **SOCRATES.** We must look into it...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...insofar as he possesses it, he knows, even if he does not have it at hand.
And so you will be forced to revolve around the same point infinitely,
without making progress. What shall we answer to these things, O Theaetetus?
**THEAETETUS.** By Jove, O Socrates, I do not know what should be answered. **SOCRATES.**
Does not the argument, O boy, rightly both rebuke and admonish us, that
we did not rightly investigate false opinion before knowledge, and
left knowledge unexamined? For it is impossible to know
those things before knowledge has been sufficiently defined. **THEAETETUS.**
It is necessary, O Socrates, to assert what you say in the present case. **SOCRATES.**
What then shall we say again from the beginning about knowledge? For
we are not yet tired of speaking. **THEAETETUS.** Not at all, provided
<margin>B</margin> you yourself do not refuse. **SOCRATES.** Come, say, by defining it in what way
will we least oppose ourselves? **THEAETETUS.** Just as we
contended above. For I have nothing else. **SOCRATES.** How so, above?
**THEAETETUS.** I wanted true opinion to be knowledge. For to have
a true opinion is far from error; and those things which proceed from true opinion
are all decorous and good. **SOCRATES.** He who, O Theaetetus,
in crossing a river goes before those following, when they ask
how deep the water is, says "it will show itself." Which if we, having entered,
search thoroughly, perhaps the very obstacle which is sought
will demonstrate itself; to us remaining still, nothing will be open. **THEAETETUS.**
You speak well. Let us go now to seek. **SOCRATES.** Is this not a matter of a brief
<margin>C</margin> investigation? For the whole art is a proof to us
that it is by no means knowledge. **THEAETETUS.** By what reasoning? And what is this faculty?
**SOCRATES.** That of those who are wise above others, whom they call orators and
lawyers. For these indeed persuade by their art, they do not teach.
For they lead the auditors to think what they themselves desire. Or
do you think some are so powerful in teaching that when
no witnesses were present for certain robberies and other injuries, yet
they can teach the truth of the crimes committed with a little water? <note>original: "ad aquam paucam" — refers to the short time allowed by the water-clock in court.</note> **THEAETETUS.**
In no way do I think they teach, but they persuade. **SOCRATES.** But to
persuade, do you not assert the same thing as to induce an opinion?
**THEAETETUS.** Exactly the same. **SOCRATES.** Is it not so that when judges are justly
<margin>D</margin> persuaded in those things which only he who saw knows, and otherwise
not at all, then judging those very things from hearsay, and
having obtained a true opinion without knowledge, they judge rightly those things
in which they were persuaded, if only they judge well? **THEAETETUS.** Entirely. **SOCRATES.** Yet if
it were the same, O friend—true opinion, judgment, and knowledge—never
would that highest judge judge rightly without knowledge. Now,
however, each seems to be something different. **THEAETETUS.** That
which I once heard from someone, O Socrates, about knowledge, I had
forgotten, but now I remember. He said, moreover, that true opinion
with a rational account <note>original: "cum ratione"</note> is knowledge, and without an account it is devoid of knowledge; and those
things which lack an account cannot be known; but those which have an account
<margin>E</margin> can be known. **SOCRATES.** How excellently you speak. But these very things which can
be known and which cannot, say how he distinguished them, so that we may see
whether you and I have received them similarly. **THEAETETUS.** Whether I shall find it
I do not know; but perhaps with another explaining it, I might follow. **SOCRATES.**
Hear then a dream for a dream. I also seem to have received from
certain people that the primary elements themselves, from which
men and other things are composed, do not admit of a rational account. For
each of them can only be named according to itself,
but it is by no means possible to call it anything else, neither that it is, nor that it
is not. For already "existence" or "non-existence" would happen to be applied
to it. But it is necessary to add nothing, if one would say only that thing
<margin>F</margin> itself. For they will not allow "itself," nor "that," nor "each,"
nor "alone," nor "this," nor other such things to be
applied. For they say these things, circulating around, are applied to all things, and
are certain other things besides that to which they are added. But it is necessary,
if only it were possible for the thing itself to be spoken of and to admit its own
rational account, that it be spoken of apart from all others. Now, however,
none of the primary things can be brought forth in speech. For nothing else
is present to it but a name, and it has only a name. But those things
which are composed from them, just as they are joined together, so also
their names joined together become a rational account. For the joining together of
names is the substance of a rational account. <margin>The substance of discourse.</margin>
Wherefore the elements are
without an account or reason, and are unknown, but are to be perceived by the
<margin>G</margin> senses; but syllables can both be known and spoken, and
grasped by true opinion. When therefore someone obtains a true opinion
about something without a rational account, they say his mind senses
truly about it, but knows it by no means. For he
who cannot give and receive an account is ignorant.
But when he attains the account, he is able to know all these things,
and to obtain perfect knowledge. Did you find it thus, or have you
heard otherwise? **THEAETETUS.** Thus entirely. **SOCRATES.** Does it then please you: and in this way
do you assert that true opinion along with a rational account is knowledge? **THEAETETUS.** And
most especially indeed. **SOCRATES.** Is it thus, Theaetetus, that we today have
<margin>H</margin> grasped that which many wise men of old, searching,
grew old before they found? **THEAETETUS.** To me indeed, O
Socrates, what was just said seems well said. **SOCRATES.** And deservedly so, for what knowledge
without discourse and right opinion can there ever be?
One thing among the things said, however, displeases me. **THEAETETUS.** What is that? **SOCRATES.**
That which seemed to be said most magnificently:
that the elements are unknown, but the class of syllables is known. **THEAETETUS.** Is it not right? **SOCRATES.** It must be considered indeed...

</columns>

<summary>Socrates and Theaetetus reject the idea that knowledge is merely "true opinion" by pointing out that lawyers can persuade a jury of the truth without the jury having actual knowledge. They then explore a new definition: knowledge is true opinion supported by a "rational account" (logos), using a metaphor of unknowable letters (elements) and knowable syllables (complexes).</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Theaetetus, true opinion, logos, rational account, elements and syllables, persuasion vs. teaching, judicial knowledge, definitions of knowledge</keywords>

# PLATO

<columns>

<margin>On the elements of letters and syllables.</margin>
**A** For we have, as it were, the very examples of speech as hostages, which he used when he said all these things. **THEAETETUS.** Which ones? **SOCRATES.** The elements of letters and syllables. Or do you think the person who said what we are now recounting was looking at something else? **THEAETETUS.** No, certainly at those things. **SOCRATES.** Let us then examine them by reviewing them. Or rather, let us examine ourselves: is this how we learned our letters? Tell me first: do syllables have a "reason" <note>original: "rationem" (Latin) / "logon" (Greek) — in this context, it means a rational definition or explanation</note> or definition, while the elements have none at all? **THEAETETUS.** Perhaps. **SOCRATES.** It seems entirely so to me as well. If someone were to ask about the first syllable of "Socrates"—tell me, Theaetetus, what is "SO"? How would you best answer? **THEAETETUS.** That it is "S" and "O." **SOCRATES.** You have, then, this "reason" or definition of the syllable.
**B** **THEAETETUS.** Indeed. **SOCRATES.** Come now, tell me the definition of the "S" itself. **THEAETETUS.** But how can anyone state the elements of an element? For indeed, Socrates, the "S" is merely a sound among the "mute" letters, like a hissing of the tongue. <note>The Greeks categorized letters like 'S' as 'semivowels' or 'mutes' because they lacked a full vowel tone.</note> Of the letter "B," however, there is neither voice nor sound—and the same is true for most of the elements. Therefore, it is quite right to say they lack a "reason," since even the seven clearest ones <note>The seven vowels of the Greek alphabet.</note> have only a voice, but no "reason" or definition whatsoever. **SOCRATES.** We have therefore correctly asserted this point, my friend, regarding knowledge. **THEAETETUS.** So it seems. **SOCRATES.** But what about when we said that the element is unknown, but the syllable is known? Did we define that correctly? **THEAETETUS.** It is probable. **SOCRATES.** Now, do we say that the syllable is both elements, 
**C** or if there are more than two, all of them? Or is it rather a single "idea" <note>original: "ideam" — a unified form or essence</note> produced from their composition? **THEAETETUS.** It seems to me it is "all of them." **SOCRATES.** Look then at these two, "S" and "O." If both are the first syllable of my name, does he who knows the syllable know both letters? **THEAETETUS.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, he knows the "S" and the "O." **THEAETETUS.** Plainly. **SOCRATES.** What then? If he is ignorant of each, and knowing neither, will he know both together? **THEAETETUS.** That would be absurd and beyond reason. **SOCRATES.** Yet, if it is necessary to know each one in order to know both, it follows that he who is ever to know a syllable must first know the elements. 
**D** And so, our beautiful argument will slip away and escape us. **THEAETETUS.** And quite suddenly, too. **SOCRATES.** For we are not guarding it well. Perhaps we should have posited that the syllable is not the elements themselves, but a single "form" <note>original: "speciem"</note> constituted from them, which possesses its own unified "idea" and differs from the elements. **THEAETETUS.** Exactly; and perhaps it is better this way than the other. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, we must consider this diligently, for it is not right to lazily betray such a great and noble argument. **THEAETETUS.** Certainly not. **SOCRATES.** Let it be, then, as we were just saying: the syllable is a single "idea" made from individual fitting elements, whether in letters or in all other things. **THEAETETUS.** Quite so. **SOCRATES.** Now, should it not have no parts? 
**E** **THEAETETUS.** Why so? **SOCRATES.** Because where there are parts, the "whole" must necessarily be all the parts. Or do you call the "whole" a single form made from parts that is different from all the parts? **THEAETETUS.** I do. **SOCRATES.** Do you call "the all" <margin>Whether "the all" and "the whole" are the same.</margin> and "the whole" the same, or is each one different? **THEAETETUS.** Although I have no certain answer, because you bid me respond promptly, I will take the risk and say they are different. **SOCRATES.** Your promptness, Theaetetus, is correct; but we must consider if your answer is correct. **THEAETETUS.** Indeed. **SOCRATES.** Do not "the whole" and "the all" differ according to this argument? **THEAETETUS.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** Furthermore, is there any difference between "all the parts" and <margin>Whether "all the parts" and "the all" are the same.</margin> "the all"? For instance, when we say one, two, three, four, five, six; or twice three, or thrice two, or four and two, or three, two and one—in all these, do we say the same thing or something else? **THEAETETUS.** Exactly the same. **SOCRATES.** Is it anything other than "six"? **THEAETETUS.** Nothing else. **SOCRATES.** In each way of speaking, did we not find "all six"? **THEAETETUS.** Yes. **SOCRATES.** And again, do we not say one certain thing when we say "all of them"? **THEAETETUS.** Necessarily. **SOCRATES.** Is it anything other than "six"? **THEAETETUS.** Nothing else. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, in things consisting of number, we say that "the all" and "all the parts" are the same. **THEAETETUS.** So it appears. **SOCRATES.** Let us speak of them in this way: the number of an acre and the acre itself are the same, are they not? **THEAETETUS.** The same. **SOCRATES.** And the number of a furlong and the furlong itself similarly? **THEAETETUS.** Yes, that too. **SOCRATES.** And so it is with an army. **THEAETETUS.** Truly. **SOCRATES.** But is the number of each thing anything other than its parts? **THEAETETUS.** Not at all. **SOCRATES.** Whatever has parts, therefore, consists of parts. **THEAETETUS.** It appears so. **SOCRATES.** But it has been conceded that "all the parts" are "the all," since every number is "the all." **THEAETETUS.** It is so. **SOCRATES.** Thus, "the whole" does not consist of parts; for if it did, it would be "the all," since it would be "all the parts." **THEAETETUS.** It does not seem so. **SOCRATES.** Again, is a "part" a part of anything other than a "whole"? **THEAETETUS.** Yes, of "the all." **SOCRATES.** You fight manfully, Theaetetus. But is not "the all" that from which nothing is missing? **THEAETETUS.** Necessarily. **SOCRATES.** And is not a "whole" also that same thing from which nothing is absent? But that from which something is missing is neither a "whole" nor "the all." **THEAETETUS.** It seems to me now that "the whole" and "the all" do not differ at all. **SOCRATES.** Did we not say that where there are parts, "the whole" and "the all" will be all the parts? **THEAETETUS.** Plainly. **SOCRATES.** To return to what we attempted just before: if the syllable is not the elements, is it not necessary that it does not have the elements as its parts? For if it were the same as them, it would be as knowable as they are? **THEAETETUS.** Truly so. **SOCRATES.** To prevent this...

<column-break/>

**A** For just like hostages of discourse, we have these examples which he used to say all these things. **THEAETETUS.** Which ones? **SOCRATES.** The elements and syllables of letters. Or do you think the person who said what we are saying was looking elsewhere? **THEAETETUS.** No, but at these very things. **SOCRATES.** Let us then examine them by taking them up, or rather, let us examine ourselves: did we learn our letters in this way or not? Tell me first: do syllables have a reason <note>original: "logon"</note>, while elements are without reason <note>original: "aloga" — literally "without logos," meaning both without speech and without a rational account</note>? **THEAETETUS.** Perhaps. **SOCRATES.** It certainly seems so to me too. For if someone asked about the first syllable of "Socrates," saying, "Theaetetus, tell me what is SO," what would you answer? **THEAETETUS.** That it is Sigma and Omega. **SOCRATES.** You have, then, this "reason" of the syllable. **THEAETETUS.** I do. **SOCRATES.** Come then, tell me in the same way the "reason" of the 
**B** Sigma. **THEAETETUS.** And how can one tell the elements of an element? For indeed, Socrates, the Sigma is one of the "voiceless" letters, merely a certain noise, like the tongue hissing. As for Beta, it has neither voice nor noise, nor do most of the elements. So it is very well said that they are "without reason," since even the seven most distinct ones have only a voice, but no "reason" whatsoever. **SOCRATES.** This point, then, my friend, we have correctly established regarding knowledge. **THEAETETUS.** So it appears. **SOCRATES.** But what about this: have we correctly shown that the element is not known, but the syllable is? **THEAETETUS.** It is likely. **SOCRATES.** Come now, do we say the syllable is both elements, and if there are more 
**C** than two, all of them? Or is it a single "idea" produced when they are put together? **THEAETETUS.** It seems to me it is "all of them." **SOCRATES.** Look then at these two, Sigma and Omega. Do both make up the first syllable of my name? He who knows the syllable, does he know both? **THEAETETUS.** Of course. **SOCRATES.** Then he knows the Sigma and the Omega. **THEAETETUS.** Yes. **SOCRATES.** But what if he is ignorant of each one? Knowing neither, can he know both? **THEAETETUS.** That would be strange and irrational, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** Yet if it is necessary to know each if one is to know both, it is absolutely necessary for one who is ever to know the 
**D** syllable to first know the elements. And thus our fine argument will run away and vanish. **THEAETETUS.** And very suddenly too. **SOCRATES.** For we are not guarding it well. Perhaps we should have posited the syllable not as the elements, but as a single form arising from them, having its own "idea" distinct from the elements. **THEAETETUS.** Certainly; and perhaps it is more likely this way than that. **SOCRATES.** It must be considered, and we must not manfully surrender such a great and venerable argument. **THEAETETUS.** Certainly not. **SOCRATES.** Let it be then, as we now say: the syllable is a single idea arising from each of the fitting elements, similarly in letters and in all other things. **THEAETETUS.** Entirely so. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, it must not 
**E** have parts? **THEAETETUS.** Why? **SOCRATES.** Because where there are parts, the whole must be "all the parts." Or is the "whole" also something arising from the parts, a single form different from "all the parts"? **THEAETETUS.** I think so. **SOCRATES.** Now, as for "the all" and "the whole," do you call them the same thing, or is each different? **THEAETETUS.** I have nothing clear to say; but since you tell me to answer promptly, I will risk saying they are different. **SOCRATES.** Your promptness, Theaetetus, is right; we must see if your answer is too. **THEAETETUS.** We must indeed. **SOCRATES.** Then "the whole" would differ from "the all," according to the present argument. **THEAETETUS.** Yes. **SOCRATES.** But what about this? Is there any difference between "all things" and "the all"? For instance, when we say one, two, three, four, five, six; and if we say twice three, or thrice two, or four and two, or three and two and one, or five and one—do we say the same or something else in all these? **THEAETETUS.** The same.
**F** **SOCRATES.** Is it anything other than "six"? **THEAETETUS.** Nothing. **SOCRATES.** Then in every expression we have said "all six." **THEAETETUS.** Yes. **SOCRATES.** And do we say nothing further when we say "all things"? **THEAETETUS.** Necessarily. **SOCRATES.** Is it anything other than "six"? **THEAETETUS.** Nothing. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, in things that are of number, we use "the all" and "all the parts" to mean the same thing. **THEAETETUS.** It appears so. **SOCRATES.** Let us speak of them thus: the number of a "plethron" <note>An ancient Greek unit of area, roughly 100 feet.</note> and the plethron itself are the same, are they not? **THEAETETUS.** Yes. **SOCRATES.** And the number of a stadium likewise? **THEAETETUS.** Yes. **SOCRATES.** And indeed the number of an army and the army itself, and all such things similarly? For the whole number is the whole reality of each of them. **THEAETETUS.** 
**G** Yes. **SOCRATES.** But is the number of each anything other than the parts? **THEAETETUS.** Nothing. **SOCRATES.** Then whatever has parts would be made of parts. **THEAETETUS.** It appears so. **SOCRATES.** But it is agreed that "all the parts" is "the all," if indeed the "whole number" is "the all." **THEAETETUS.** So it is. **SOCRATES.** The "whole," then, is not from parts. For it would be "the all," being "all the parts." **THEAETETUS.** It does not seem so. **SOCRATES.** But is a "part" a part of anything else besides the "whole"? **THEAETETUS.** Of "the all," certainly. **SOCRATES.** You fight manfully, Theaetetus. But is not "the all" that from which nothing is missing? **THEAETETUS.** Necessarily. **SOCRATES.** And will not the "whole" be this same thing, that from which nothing is lacking anywhere? And that from which something is removed is neither "whole" nor "all," as both would have become the same thing from the same cause. **THEAETETUS.** It seems to me now that "all" and "whole" do not differ at all. **SOCRATES.** Did we not say that where there are parts, the "whole" and "all" will be "all the parts"? **THEAETETUS.** 
**H** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** Again then (as I was just attempting), if the syllable is not the elements, is it not necessary that it does not have the elements as its parts? For if it were the same as them, would it not be as knowable as they are? **THEAETETUS.** So it is. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, so that...

<summary>Socrates and Theaetetus debate the nature of syllables and elements, questioning whether a whole is simply the sum of its parts or a unified idea. They conclude that in terms of knowledge, if you cannot define the basic elements (letters), it is logically difficult to claim you truly "know" the syllable composed of them.</summary>
<keywords>Plato, Theaetetus, Socrates, elements, syllables, whole vs all, epistemology, Greek mathematics, philosophy of language</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Theaetetus. Having previously discussed whether syllables are simply the sum of their letters (elements) or a new unified whole, they now investigate whether the "elements" are inherently unknowable while the "syllables" they form are knowable.</meta>

### THEAETETUS

**SOCRATES.** ...would it be something else than what we proposed? **THEAETETUS.** Something else. **SOCRATES.** Now, if the elements are not parts of a syllable, can you name anything else that are parts of a syllable, yet are not its elements? **THEAETETUS.** Not at all, Socrates; if I were to admit it had parts, it would be quite ridiculous to skip over the elements and go looking for something else. **SOCRATES.** Then, according to our current reasoning, Theaetetus, a syllable must be a single, indivisible idea. <note>The word "idea" here refers to a unified form or essence that cannot be broken down.</note> **THEAETETUS.** So it seems. **SOCRATES.** Do you remember then, my friend, that a little while ago we accepted the claim that there is no "reasoned explanation" <note>original: "logos" (Greek) / "ratio" (Latin)</note> for the primary elements from which everything else is composed? This was because each thing, in and of itself, would be uncompounded. We said that one couldn't even correctly say that it "is," as that would be adding something else to it, as if they were separate and foreign things—and 

<margin>B</margin>
this very cause makes it both irrational and unknowable? **THEAETETUS.** I remember. **SOCRATES.** Is there, then, any other cause for it being unknowable other than its being uniform and indivisible? For I certainly see no other. **THEAETETUS.** There doesn't seem to be one. **SOCRATES.** Does the syllable not fall into the same category as that element, if it has no parts and is a single idea? **THEAETETUS.** Entirely so. **SOCRATES.** Unless, perhaps, the syllable is many elements—a sort of "whole"—and these elements are its parts? In that case, both syllables and elements would be equally knowable and expressible, since we found that all the parts are the same thing as the whole. **THEAETETUS.** Quite so.

<margin>C</margin>
**SOCRATES.** But if it is one and indivisible, then a syllable—just like an element—is without reason and unknown. For the same cause will make them both so. **THEAETETUS.** I cannot say otherwise. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, let us not accept it if someone says that a syllable can be known and expressed, but an element cannot. **THEAETETUS.** Certainly not, if we are to trust this reasoning. **SOCRATES.** What if someone said the opposite? Would you not rather accept that, based on your own experience when you first learned your letters? **THEAETETUS.** In what way?

<margin>D</margin>
<margin>The class of elements contains a clearer understanding than that of syllables.</margin>
**SOCRATES.** In that you spent your time doing nothing other than trying to distinguish the elements by sight and by ear—each one by itself—so that their position, whether spoken or written, would not confuse you. **THEAETETUS.** That is very true. **SOCRATES.** And in the school of the lyre-player, was "perfect learning" anything other than being able to follow each individual note and know which string it belonged to? These are the things that everyone would agree are the "elements" of music. **THEAETETUS.** Nothing else. **SOCRATES.** If, then, we are experienced in elements and syllables, and if we should judge other things by these examples, we shall say that the class of elements provides a much clearer and more fundamental knowledge than the syllable for the sake of mastering any subject. And if someone says the syllable is knowable but the element is by nature unknown, we shall think he is joking—whether he means to or not. **THEAETETUS.** Most definitely.

<margin>E</margin>
**SOCRATES.** Still, other proofs of this very point might appear, it seems to me. But let us not forget the question before us: what is meant by the claim that "true opinion combined with a rational explanation" <note>original: "logos"</note> constitutes the most perfect knowledge? **THEAETETUS.** Indeed, we must look into it. **SOCRATES.** Come then, what does he want this "rational explanation" to signify for us? It seems to me he might mean one of three things. **THEAETETUS.** Which ones?

<margin>F</margin>
<margin>For the Greeks, "logos" signifies reason, speech, and definition; hence the Greek term had to be used here.</margin>
**SOCRATES.** The first would be making one's own thought manifest through the voice with verbs and nouns—as if mirroring one's opinion in the stream of sound coming through the mouth, like an image in a mirror or in water. Does it not seem to you that "speech" is something like that? **THEAETETUS.** It does. We say that one who does this is "speaking." **SOCRATES.** But then anyone can do this—some faster, some slower—showing what they think about each thing, provided they are not born deaf or mute. And so, all who hold a correct opinion would appear to have it "with a rational explanation," <note>original: "meta logou"</note> and correct opinion would never exist apart from knowledge. **THEAETETUS.** True. **SOCRATES.** Let us not, therefore, lightly condemn the man who defined knowledge as we are now considering it, as if he said nothing. For perhaps that is not what he meant. Perhaps he meant that when asked what a thing is, one is able to give the answer to the questioner through its elements. **THEAETETUS.** What do you mean by that, Socrates? **SOCRATES.** Just as Hesiod says of a wagon: "a wagon consists of a hundred timbers." <note>Hesiod was an early Greek poet; here Socrates uses a wagon as an analogy for complex objects made of parts.</note> I could not name them all, and I don't think you could either. We would be satisfied if, when asked what a wagon is, we could say "wheels, axle, body, rails, and yoke." **THEAETETUS.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** But he might think we were as ridiculous as if we were asked your name and answered syllable by syllable. We would be thinking and speaking correctly, but we would be mistaken to think we were "grammarians" or that we were giving a grammatical "explanation" <note>original: "logos"</note> of the name Theaetetus. He might say it is impossible to speak with scientific knowledge until one can describe each thing through its elements along with true opinion, as was said before. **THEAETETUS.** It was indeed said.

<margin>G</margin>
**SOCRATES.** So it is with the wagon: we might have a correct opinion, but the man who can go through its essence by those hundred parts has added a "rational explanation" to his true opinion. Instead of a mere believer, he has become a craftsman and a scientist regarding the essence of the wagon, having traversed the whole through its elements. **THEAETETUS.** Does that seem right to you, Socrates? **SOCRATES.** If it seems so to you, my friend, and if you accept that a discourse through the elements of a thing is its "rational explanation," whereas a discourse by syllables or larger units is "irrational"—then tell me, so that we may examine it more closely. **THEAETETUS.**

<column-break/>

[This section repeats the logic of the Greek text above in Latin translation, focusing on the same dialogue points regarding parts, elements, and the definition of 'logos'.]

...nothing else than what we proposed. **THEAETETUS.** Something else. **SOCRATES.** But what if the elements are not parts of a syllable? Can you point to any other things which are parts of a syllable, but not its elements? **THEAETETUS.** I would never call things parts if they were not elements. It is ridiculous to omit the elements and seek other things. **SOCRATES.** Entirely so, according to this reasoning, O Theaetetus: a syllable seems to be a single, indivisible idea. **THEAETETUS.** It certainly seems so. **SOCRATES.** Do you remember, friend, that we previously admitted that there was no "reason" <note>original: "ratio"</note> for the primary things from which others are composed, because each thing exists simply as itself, and one cannot even properly say "it is" of it, nor "this," nor "that," as if these were external and foreign things, and 

<margin>B</margin>
we said this very cause prevents it from being described or known? **THEAETETUS.** I remember. **SOCRATES.** Is there any other cause besides this which makes a thing uniform and indivisible? For I see no other. **THEAETETUS.** There seems to be none. **SOCRATES.** Does not the syllable fall into the same case, since it is a single form <note>original: "species"</note> and has no parts, but is a single idea? **THEAETETUS.** Very much so. **SOCRATES.**

<margin>C</margin>
If, then, a syllable is many elements and a kind of "whole," and these are its parts, then the syllables and elements can be known and described in the same way, since he confesses that all the parts are the same as the whole. **THEAETETUS.** Especially so. **SOCRATES.** But if it is something one and simple, the syllable is just as devoid of definition and knowledge as the element. For the same cause will produce such results. **THEAETETUS.** I cannot say otherwise. **SOCRATES.** Let us therefore not accept the speech of one who says that a syllable can be spoken of and known, but the elements by no means. **THEAETETUS.** Not indeed if we believe this reasoning. **SOCRATES.** What if someone said the opposite? Would you not rather concede that, from those things of which you were conscious in the first rudiments of letters? **THEAETETUS.** Which things are those? **SOCRATES.**

<margin>D</margin>
<margin>The class of elements contains a clearer understanding than that of syllables.</margin>
That you studied nothing else than to distinguish the elements with your eyes and ears, and to note each one according to itself, lest their position—either when they were spoken or written—should disturb you. **THEAETETUS.** You tell the truth. **SOCRATES.** Indeed, what else is learning the art of the lyre-player than to distinguish each tone of every string? For anyone would call these the "elements" of music. **THEAETETUS.** Nothing else. **SOCRATES.** When, therefore, we are skilled in elements and syllables, and we wish to make a conjecture from these to other things, we shall surely assert that the class of elements contains a clearer and more primary understanding than the syllable for the sake of absolutely perceiving individual disciplines. And if anyone calls a syllable known, but says the element is unknown by nature, we shall think he is playing with us, whether he wants to or not. **THEAETETUS.** And very much so. **SOCRATES.** Moreover, there may be other proofs of this same 

<margin>E</margin>
thing, as it seems to me. But let us not forget the proposal because of these: namely, what should be judged of this saying, that "rational explanation <note>original: "ratio"</note> joined with true opinion is perfect knowledge." **THEAETETUS.** We must investigate entirely. **SOCRATES.** Come now, what 

<margin>F</margin>
<margin>For the Greeks, "logos" signifies reason, speech, and definition; hence the Greek term had to be used here.</margin>
does "logos" <note>Greek term used in the Latin text</note> signify for us here? For it seems to me to signify one of three things. **THEAETETUS.** From which ones? **SOCRATES.** I think the first is to express one's thought with the voice through verbs and nouns, showing one's own opinion in the voice just as in a mirror or in water. Does not such a thing seem to you to be "speech" <note>original: "oratio"</note>? **THEAETETUS.** To me, it does. **SOCRATES.** We say that the one who does this "speaks." Can't everyone do this? Namely, to show more quickly or more slowly what they think about individual things—unless perhaps they are naturally mute or deaf. And thus, whoever holds a right opinion seems to hold it "with a rational explanation." <note>original: "meta logou"</note> And right opinion will never be without knowledge. **THEAETETUS.** These things are true. **SOCRATES.** Let us not, therefore, easily condemn the one who affirmed knowledge as we have just said, as if he were saying nothing. For perhaps he did not mean that, but that when asked "what is each thing?", one can answer the questioner through the elements. **THEAETETUS.** What kind of thing is that, Socrates? **SOCRATES.** Just as Hesiod says of a wagon: "A wagon is a hundred timbers." Which I could hardly say, and nor could you, as I think. But it will be enough for us if, to someone asking "what is a wagon?", we can answer: "wheels, axle, planks, hoops, yoke." **THEAETETUS.** Entirely so. **SOCRATES.** But he would perhaps think that we, as if asked about your name and responding by the syllable, were to be laughed at; rightly opining and saying what we say, but thinking we were grammarians, and that we possessed and spoke the "rational explanation" <note>original: "rationem"</note> of the name Theaetetus in a grammatical way. But this is not to speak according to knowledge until someone determines each thing through the elements along with true opinion, as was said above. **THEAETETUS.** It was said without a doubt.

<margin>G</margin>
**SOCRATES.** So surely also regarding the wagon, we have a right opinion. But the one who can run through those hundred parts, grasping the essence of the wagon itself, has also apprehended the "rational explanation" together with true opinion; and in place of a mere believer, he has emerged as a craftsman and one possessed of knowledge regarding the essence of the wagon, determining the whole through the elements. **THEAETETUS.** Does it not seem well to you, Socrates? **SOCRATES.** If it seems so to you, O friend, and you approve that this discourse through the elements regarding each thing is "rational explanation," but that which is through syllables or something greater is "devoid of reason," I want you to tell me, so that we may consider it more diligently. **THEAETETUS.**

# OF PLATO

**THEAETETUS.** I agree, and most strongly. **SOCRATES.** Now, do you think that anyone is a "knower" of anything when it seems to him that the same thing belongs now to one thing and now to another? Or when he holds an opinion that the same thing is now this, and now that? **THEAETETUS.** No, by Jove, I do not. **SOCRATES.** Have you forgotten what happened to you and others at the beginning, when you were learning your letters? **THEAETETUS.** Do you mean when we thought now one letter and now another belonged to the same syllable? Or when we placed the same letter sometimes in its proper syllable and sometimes in another? **SOCRATES.** That is exactly what I mean. **THEAETETUS.** By Jove, I have not forgotten, nor do I think those who are in such a state possess knowledge. **SOCRATES.** What then? If at such a time someone, while writing "Theaetetus," thinks he ought to write and actually does write "Th" <note>original Greek: "τ η" (Tau-Eta)</note> and "e" <note>original: "ε" (Epsilon)</note>; and again, wanting to write "Theodorus," thinks he ought to write and does write "Th" and "e," shall we say he knows the first syllable of your names? **THEAETETUS.** We just now agreed that someone in that condition does not yet know. **SOCRATES.** And is there anything to prevent the same person from being in that state regarding the second, third, and fourth syllables? **THEAETETUS.** Nothing at all. **SOCRATES.** Then will he, possessing the sequence of the elements, <term>elementum</term> <note>Socrates uses "elements" to refer to the basic building blocks, like letters in a word or fundamental principles in a theory.</note> write "Theaetetus" with a correct opinion when he writes them in their proper order? **THEAETETUS.** Clearly he will. **SOCRATES.** Is he not still without knowledge, though he holds a correct opinion, as we said? **THEAETETUS.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** And yet he possesses "reason" along with his correct opinion? For he wrote while following the path of the elements, and we agreed that this constitutes "reasoned explanation." **THEAETETUS.** True. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, my friend, there is such a thing as correct opinion with reason, which it is not yet right to call knowledge. **THEAETETUS.** So it seems. **SOCRATES.** We have, it seems, gained a "dream-wealth," <note>A Greek idiom for an illusory gain that vanishes upon waking.</note> while we trusted that we had the truest definition of knowledge. **THEAETETUS.** But perhaps we should not condemn it yet; for perhaps someone would not define "reason" <note>original: "λόγον" (logos)</note> in that way, but would choose the remaining one of the three species, one of which we said would be chosen by the person defining knowledge as correct opinion with reason. **SOCRATES.** You have reminded me well. For one species still remains: the first was as it were an image of thought in the voice; the second, which we just discussed, was the path to the whole through the elements. **THEAETETUS.** And what do you say the third is? **SOCRATES.** That which most people would say: being able to state some mark by which the thing in question differs from all others. **THEAETETUS.** Can you give me an example of such a definition? **SOCRATES.** As an example, if you like, you will accept, I think, that the Sun is that which excels in brightness all things that revolve in the heavens around the earth. **THEAETETUS.** Entirely so. **SOCRATES.** Now take the reason why this was said. It is what we were just mentioning: that if you grasp the difference of each thing by which it is distinguished from others, you will have grasped its definition, <term>definitio</term>, as some say. But as long as you touch upon something common, your "reason" will be about those things to which that community belongs. **THEAETETUS.** I understand, and I think it is right to call such a thing "reason." **SOCRATES.** But he who, along with correct opinion, grasps the difference by which one thing is separated from any other, will then become a "knower" of that which he previously only held an opinion of. **THEAETETUS.** That is consistent. **SOCRATES.** Now, Theaetetus, since I have come closer to this statement, as if to a shadow-painting, <note>A "skiagraphia" or shadow-painting was a type of ancient perspective painting that looked coherent from a distance but blurred or messy up close.</note> I perceive that I understand nothing of it at all. While I was looking at it from a distance, it seemed to me to say something. **THEAETETUS.** Why so? **SOCRATES.** I will tell you if I can. If I have a correct opinion about you, and I also grasp your definition, I know you; otherwise, I only have an opinion. **THEAETETUS.** That is so. **SOCRATES.** And "reason" was the interpretation of your difference. **THEAETETUS.** It was. **SOCRATES.** When, therefore, I was only opining, did I grasp with my thought any of those things by which you are distinguished from others? **THEAETETUS.** It seems not. **SOCRATES.** I was therefore attending to certain common things, which you possess no more than anyone else. **THEAETETUS.** That necessarily follows. **SOCRATES.** Come then, by Jove, how was I then opining about you rather than anyone else? Suppose me thinking that Theaetetus is he who is a man, and has a nose, and a mouth, and eyes, and so on for the rest of the limbs. Does this thought make me think of Theaetetus any more than of Theodorus, or, as the saying goes, the "last of the Mysians"? <note>A proverb for the most insignificant or generic person imaginable.</note> **THEAETETUS.** How could it? **SOCRATES.** But if I think of one not only having a nose and eyes, but also a snub nose and prominent eyes, will I opine about you any more than about myself, or anyone else who is like that? **THEAETETUS.** Not at all. **SOCRATES.** Indeed, I do not think I shall have an opinion of Theaetetus in my mind until this "snubness" has impressed upon me a unique memorial of itself, different from all other "snubnesses" I have seen—and likewise for the other things from which you are composed. This mark, if I meet you tomorrow, will remind me and make me have a correct opinion about you. **THEAETETUS.** You speak most truly. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, correct opinion about each thing also concerns its unique difference. **THEAETETUS.** So it appears. **SOCRATES.** What then will it be to "add reason" to correct opinion? For if it means to opine further how a thing differs from others, the instruction becomes quite ridiculous. **THEAETETUS.** How? **SOCRATES.** It commands us to "take up a correct opinion" of how things differ from others, for those very things of which we already "hold a correct opinion" of how they differ from others. And so your speech will be like the turning of a whip-top or a pestle, or any such thing. It says nothing to the purpose of this instruction. It might more rightly be called the instruction of a blind man. For to command us to take up what we already have, in order to learn...

**THEAETETUS.** But I agree entirely. **SOCRATES.** Is it your view, then, that a person knows anything whatever when the same thing seems to him at one time to belong to the same object and at another time to a different one? Or when he holds an opinion that the same thing is now one thing and now another? **THEAETETUS.** By Zeus, not I. **SOCRATES.** Then do you not remember your own and others' behavior in the learning of letters at the beginning? **THEAETETUS.** Do you mean when we thought at one time one letter and at another time another belonged to the same syllable, and when we put the same letter sometimes in its proper syllable and sometimes in another? **SOCRATES.** That is what I mean. **THEAETETUS.** By Zeus, I do not forget, nor do I yet think that those in that state have knowledge. **SOCRATES.** What then? When at such a time someone, while writing "Theaetetus," thinks he ought to write "Th" <note>original: "τ η"</note> and actually writes it, and again, when attempting to write "Theodorus," thinks he ought to write "Th" and writes it, shall we say that he knows the first syllable of our names? **THEAETETUS.** But we just now agreed that a person in that state does not yet know. **SOCRATES.** And is there anything to prevent the same person from being in that state regarding the second and third and fourth syllables? **THEAETETUS.** Nothing at all. **SOCRATES.** Then will he, having the sequence of elements in mind, write "Theaetetus" with correct opinion when he writes them in order? **THEAETETUS.** Clearly so. **SOCRATES.** And is he not still without knowledge, though opining correctly, as we say? **THEAETETUS.** Yes. **SOCRATES.** Even though he has "reason" with his correct opinion. For he wrote while following the way of the elements, which we agreed was "reason." **THEAETETUS.** True. **SOCRATES.** There is, then, my friend, a correct opinion with reason which should not yet be called knowledge. **THEAETETUS.** It seems so. **SOCRATES.** It seems we have become wealthy in a dream, thinking we had the truest account of knowledge. **THEAETETUS.** Or let us not accuse it yet. For perhaps someone will not define "reason" in this way, but as the remaining one of the three species, one of which we said he would choose who defined knowledge as correct opinion with reason. **SOCRATES.** You have rightly reminded me. For there is still one left. The first was an image of thought in speech; the second, just mentioned, was the path through the element to the whole. **THEAETETUS.** And what do you say the third is? **SOCRATES.** That which most people would say: being able to tell some sign by which the thing asked about differs from all others. **THEAETETUS.** What "reasoned explanation" <note>original: "λόγον" (logos)</note> can you give me of such a thing? **SOCRATES.** For example, if you like, I think you can accept that the Sun is the brightest of the things that move through the heavens around the earth. **THEAETETUS.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** Now grasp why this was said. It is what we were just saying: that if you grasp the difference of each thing by which it differs from others, you have grasped the "reason," as some say; but as long as you touch upon something common, your account will be about those things to which that commonness belongs. **THEAETETUS.** I understand; and it seems to me well to call such a thing "reason." **SOCRATES.** And whoever, along with correct opinion about any of the things that are, also grasps its difference from others, will have become a "knower" of that of which he was previously a "believer." **THEAETETUS.** We certainly say so. **SOCRATES.** Now indeed, Theaetetus, since I have come close to the statement as if to a shadow-painting, I do not understand even a little; though while I stood far off, it seemed to me to say something. **THEAETETUS.** How is that? **SOCRATES.** I will tell you if I can. If I have a correct opinion about you, if I also grasp your "reason," I know you; but if not, I only have an opinion. **THEAETETUS.** Yes. **SOCRATES.** And "reason" was the interpretation of your difference. **THEAETETUS.** So it was. **SOCRATES.** When, therefore, I was only opining, was it not the case that I grasped with my mind none of the things by which you differ from others? **THEAETETUS.** It seems not. **SOCRATES.** I was therefore thinking of some of the common things, which you possess no more than anyone else. **THEAETETUS.** Necessarily. **SOCRATES.** Come then, by Zeus. How in such a case did I ever opine about you more than anyone else? For suppose me thinking that "Theaetetus is he who is a man, and has a nose and eyes and a mouth," and so for each of the limbs. Can this thought make me think of Theaetetus more than of Theodorus, or, as the saying goes, "the last of the Mysians"? **THEAETETUS.** Why should it? **SOCRATES.** But if I do not only think of the one having a nose and eyes, but also the one who is snub-nosed and has prominent eyes, shall I opine about you any more than about myself or as many as are like that? **THEAETETUS.** Not at all. **SOCRATES.** But I think I shall not have an opinion of Theaetetus in me until this snubness has deposited in me a distinct memorial, different from the other snubnesses I have seen, and the other things likewise of which you consist; which, if I meet you tomorrow, will remind me and make me have a correct opinion about you. **THEAETETUS.** Most true. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, correct opinion of each thing would also be about its difference. **THEAETETUS.** So it appears. **SOCRATES.** What then would "adding reason" to correct opinion still mean? For if it means to opine in addition how a thing differs from others, the command becomes quite ridiculous. **THEAETETUS.** How? **SOCRATES.** Of those things of which we have a correct opinion of how they differ from others, it commands us to "add a correct opinion" of how they differ from others. And so the turning of a "scytale" <note>A staff used for secret messages; here it refers to a circular or repetitive process.</note> or a pestle, or whatever it is called, would be nothing compared to this command. It might more justly be called the "exhortation of a blind man." For to command us to add what we already have, so that we may learn...

They conclude that if knowledge is "true opinion plus the distinguishing mark," the definition is circular, as one must already hold that mark in mind to have a true opinion of the specific thing.</summary>

# ION, OR, CONCERNING THE ILIAD
## OR, CONCERNING THE POETIC CHA-
->racter; or, Concerning the interpretation of poets.<-

->Pertaining to speech or reason.<-

> **SUMMARY OF THE DIALOGUE.** The philosopher teaches here that neither Poetry itself, nor the power and faculty of interpreting it, consists in the principles and industry of a particular art; rather, it is a certain impulse or divine madness <note>Latin: "divinum furorem," a central concept in Plato’s aesthetics where artists are seen as possessed by a higher power.</note> by which both poets and their interpreters are carried away, so that they might fashion images of things and imitate their nature, and, stirred by a certain divine force, bring the customs of human life onto the stage, as it were. The goal of this discussion, therefore, is to show the origin and nature of poetry. Plato establishes God—that is, the Muse—as the primary cause, by whose power even unskilled men may sometimes pour forth good verses.

SOCRATES, ION.
<image-desc>An ornamental drop cap 'I' showing a seated or standing figure in classical attire, likely representing a teacher or a philosopher.</image-desc>
<margin>D</margin> **I** bid Ion greetings. From where have you now come to visit us? Have you come from home, from Ephesus? ION: Not at all, Socrates, but from Epidaurus, from the festivals of Asclepius <note>Asclepius was the god of healing; festivals in his honor included athletic and musical competitions.</note>. SOCRATES: Did the Epidaurians also establish a contest for rhapsodes <term>rhapsodos</term> <note>A professional performer who recited epic poetry, especially Homer, from memory.</note> in honor of the god? ION: Certainly, and in every other kind of music too. SOCRATES: What then? Did you compete for us there? And how did you fare in the contest? ION: We carried away the first of the prizes, Socrates.
SOCRATES: Well said! Come then, let us also see that we win at the Panathenaea <note>The Great Panathenaea was the most important festival in Athens, featuring prestigious musical and athletic competitions.</note>. ION: These things shall be, if God wills. SOCRATES: Indeed, Ion, I have often envied you rhapsodes for your art; for it is fitting for your art that you adorn your body and appear as beautiful as possible; <margin>E</margin> and at the same time, it is necessary to be constantly occupied with many good poets, and especially with Homer, the best and most divine of all poets, and to learn his thought thoroughly, not merely his verses. For one could never become a rhapsode unless he understands the things spoken by the poet. For the rhapsode must become an interpreter of the poet’s mind to the listeners. To do this well, while not knowing what the poet says, is impossible. All these things are truly worthy of envy. ION: You speak the truth, Socrates. This has indeed provided me with the greatest labor in my art; and I believe I speak more beautifully about Homer than anyone else—more than Metrodorus of Lampsacus, or Stesimbrotus of Thasos, or Glaucon <note>These were famous ancient scholars and commentators on Homer.</note>, or any <margin>F</margin> other who has ever lived could speak so many and so beautiful thoughts concerning Homer as I can. SOCRATES: You speak well, Ion; for it is clear you will not grudge me a demonstration. ION: Indeed, Socrates, it is worth hearing how well I have adorned Homer. I think I am worthy to be crowned with a golden crown by the followers of Homer. SOCRATES: I shall certainly find leisure to listen to you sometime; but for now, answer me this one thing: are you skilled only concerning Homer, or also concerning Hesiod and Archilochus? ION: Not at all; only concerning Homer. For that seems sufficient to me. SOCRATES: Are there any matters about which Homer and Hesiod <margin>G</margin> say the same things? ION: I believe there are many. SOCRATES: Would you then explain better the things Homer says, or the things Hesiod says? ION: Equally well, Socrates, regarding those things in which they say the same. SOCRATES: What about those things where they do not say the same?

In this dialogue, Socrates examines Ion, a celebrated "rhapsode" (a professional reciter of epic poetry), to determine whether his skill comes from technical mastery or divine inspiration.
