A Since both Homer and Hesiod speak about the art of prophecy. ION: They certainly do. SOCRATES: And in those matters where these poets agree and where they disagree when they speak of prophecy, would you or some skilled prophet explain it better? ION: A prophet would. SOCRATES: But if you were a prophet, could you not explain those points where they agree, as well as those where they differ? ION: Clearly. SOCRATES: Why is it then that concerning Homer you are powerful and eloquent, but concerning Hesiod and other poets, not at all? Does Homer deal with different subjects than those which the other 
B poets treat? <margin>What things are explained in all of Homer’s poetry.</margin> Has he not related many things pertaining to war, and the social dealings of good and bad men toward one another, of private citizens and craftsmen? And does he not sing of how the gods interact with each other and with men, and of the movements of the heavens, and of those things in the underworld, and the genealogies of gods and heroes? Does not all of Homer's poetry concern these things? ION: You speak the truth, Socrates. SOCRATES: And do the other poets not sing of these same things? ION: Certainly the same, Socrates, but not in the same way as Homer. SOCRATES: Is it perhaps worse? ION: Much worse. SOCRATES: Therefore Homer is better? ION: Better, certainly. SOCRATES: Oh Ion, you charming fellow, when many people speak about numbers and one of them speaks correctly, cannot someone recognize the one who speaks well in that matter? ION: He can. SOCRATES: Is it that same person who recognizes the one who speaks poorly, or is it someone else? ION: It is the same person. SOCRATES: Is this not the person who possesses the 
C art of arithmetic? <note>Socrates uses arithmetic as his first example of a technical "art" (techne), where one set of rules applies to all instances.</note> ION: Indeed. SOCRATES: When many speak about which foods are healthy, and someone speaks correctly on the matter, will one person notice the one who speaks well, and another person notice the one who speaks poorly? Or will it be one and the same person? ION: The same, without a doubt. SOCRATES: Who is this? What is his name? ION: A doctor. SOCRATES: Shall we say then, in summary, that when many speak about the same subject, one and the same person will distinguish both the one who speaks poorly and the one who speaks well? And unless he recognizes the one who is in error on the subject, he will never recognize the one who thinks correctly? ION: Indeed. SOCRATES: Is not 
D the same man skilled in both? ION: Entirely. SOCRATES: Do you assert that Homer and the other poets, among whom are Hesiod and Archilochus, relate the same things, though not in the same way—but that Homer is better, and the others worse? ION: I do, and it is the truth. SOCRATES: If you recognize the one who speaks well, you must also understand that those who speak poorly are in error. ION: That follows. SOCRATES: If then we were to say, my dear friend, that Ion is equally skilled and eloquent regarding Homer and the other poets, we would not be wrong; for he himself admits that the same judge is capable of evaluating everyone who deals with the same subject, and that almost all poets depict the same things. ION: Why is it then, Socrates, that when someone discusses another poet, 
E I pay no attention and can say nothing worth mentioning, but I yawn immediately and grow numb? Yet as soon as someone mentions Homer, I am immediately awakened and attentive, and whatever I plan to say flows forth. SOCRATES: It is not at all difficult, my friend, to guess the cause of this. For it is clear that you are unable to speak skillfully about Homer by any art <note>original: "arte" (Latin) / "techne" (Greek). This refers to a systematic body of knowledge that can be taught.</note> or knowledge. For if it were by art, you would be able to speak similarly about all the other poets, for poetry is a whole, is it not? ION: It is indeed. SOCRATES: When someone has mastered any other art in its entirety, is not the method of judgment the same for all things that fall under that art? For there is the same way of considering all arts. Do you want me to explain why I say this? ION: 
F I do, by Jove, Socrates. For whenever I hear you wise men, I am immediately filled with a wonderful joy. SOCRATES: I wish you were telling the truth, Ion. But you rhapsodes and actors are the wise ones, along with those whose poems you sing. I, however, speak nothing but the truth, as becomes a common man. <note>original: "idiotam hominem." In this context, it refers to a layman or a private citizen without specialized technical training, rather than its modern derogatory meaning.</note> For look at how trivial and easy to recognize is the thing I was asking about; so that anyone might perceive what I was saying—that the consideration is the same for all other things if one has mastered an art in its entirety. For example, is not the art of painting a whole? ION: It is. SOCRATES: And are there not many painters, 
G some good and some bad, both now and in the past? ION: Certainly. SOCRATES: Have you ever seen anyone who could sufficiently demonstrate what was painted well and what was not by Polygnotus <note>A famous Greek painter from the 5th century BCE known for his character-driven murals.</note> the son of Aglaophon, but who could not do the same for other painters? And if someone showed him the work of other painters, he would fall asleep and have no ability to say or contribute anything; but when he had to judge Polygnotus, or any one painter you like, he would wake up, pay attention, and have plenty to say? ION: No, by Jove. SOCRATES: What about in sculpture? Have you seen anyone who can explain the successes of Daedalus <note>The mythical architect and sculptor, often cited by Socrates as the archetype of early craftsmanship.</note> the son of Metion, or Epeius the son of Panopeus, or Theodorus of Samos, or any other individual sculptor, but who becomes numb and speechless regarding the works of other sculptors? ION: By Jove, I have never found such a man. SOCRATES: And indeed, I think, neither in flute-playing, nor in playing the cithara, nor in singing to the cithara, nor in rhapsody, have you ever seen a man who is skilled at explaining the works of Olympus, or Thamyras, or Orpheus, or Phemius the rhapsode of Ithaca, but who is at a loss regarding Ion of Ephesus, and cannot perceive or compare what he does well in rhapsodizing...

<summary>Socrates begins his interrogation of Ion, arguing that if Ion's skill in interpreting Homer were a technical "art" (techne), he would be able to judge all poets equally, just as a doctor judges all talk of health. Ion admits he only feels inspired by Homer, leading Socrates to suggest that Ion’s talent is not based on systematic knowledge.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and the rhapsode Ion. Socrates is developing his famous theory of poetic inspiration, arguing that the power of poetry is not a technical skill (techne) but a divine "charge" passed from the gods through the poet to the performer.</meta>

# ION
**N**
<meta>Catchword: which (Latin: que)</meta>

## Left Column

...does not rhapsodize and what...

<margin>A</margin> **ION:** I have nothing to say against you on this point, Socrates. But this I know within myself: that I speak about Homer more beautifully than any other man, and I am never at a loss for words, and everyone else says that I speak well. But regarding other poets, I do not. See then, what this might be. **SOCRATES:** I do see it, Ion, and I am coming to reveal to you what I think it is. For this is not a technical skill <note>original: "techne"</note> that you possess for speaking well about Homer—as I was just saying—but a divine power that moves you, just like in the stone which Euripides named the Magnet, but which most people call the Heraclean stone. For this stone not only attracts iron rings themselves, but it also imparts a power to the rings so that they, in turn, can do the same as the stone and attract other rings. Sometimes a very long chain of iron rings hangs from one another; but for all of them, the power is suspended from that one stone. <margin>B</margin> In this same way, the Muse herself makes some men inspired, and through these inspired men, a chain of others is suspended who catch the enthusiasm. For all the good epic poets compose all those beautiful poems not by art, but because they are inspired and possessed <note>original: "katechomenoi", meaning held or gripped by a spirit</note>. So too it is with the good lyric poets. Just as the Corybantes <term>Corybantes: priests of the goddess Cybele who performed ecstatic, frenzied dances</term> dance when they are not in their right minds, so the lyric poets compose these beautiful melodies when they are not in their right minds. But when they embark upon harmony and rhythm, they fall into a Bacchic frenzy and are possessed—just like the Bacchantes <term>Bacchantes: female followers of Dionysus who, in a state of religious ecstasy, were said to possess supernatural powers</term> who draw honey and milk from the rivers when they are possessed, but cannot do so when they are in their right minds. <margin>C</margin> And the soul of the lyric poets works in this same way, as they themselves say. For the poets tell us, I believe, that they bring us their melodies from certain honey-flowing springs in the gardens and glades of the Muses, gathering them like bees, and flying just like them. And they speak the truth. For a poet is a light thing, winged and holy, and he is not able to compose until he becomes inspired and out of his senses, and his mind is no longer in him. As long as a man possesses his own intellect, he is powerless to compose poetry or to utter oracles. <margin>D</margin> Since, therefore, they do not compose by art—though they say many beautiful things about their subjects, as you do about Homer—but by a divine lot, each is only able to compose well that to which the Muse has impelled him: one dithyrambs, another hymns of praise, another dance-songs, another epics, and another iambics. In all other styles, each of them is poor. For they do not speak these things by art, but by divine power; for if they knew how to speak well about one subject by art, they would be able to do so for all others. For this reason, God takes away their mind and uses them as his ministers, as he does with oracle-singers and divine prophets, so that we who hear them may know that it is not they who say these things—being of such great value while their minds are absent—but that it is God himself who speaks, and through them he utters his voice to us. <margin>E</margin> The greatest evidence for this argument is Tynnichus the Chalcidian, who never composed any other poem that anyone would think worth remembering, except for the Paean <note>A song of praise or triumph, usually dedicated to Apollo</note> which everyone sings—nearly the most beautiful of all melodies—which he himself calls an "invention of the Muses." In this, it seems to me, God has most clearly shown us, so that we might not doubt, that these beautiful poems are not human nor the work of men, but are divine and the work of gods. The poets are nothing but interpreters of the gods, possessed by whatever spirit may possess them. To demonstrate this, God deliberately sang the most beautiful melody through the most mediocre poet. Do I not seem to speak the truth, Ion? **ION:** Yes, by Zeus, you certainly do. For you touch my soul with your words, Socrates, and it seems to me that the good poets interpret these things to us from the gods by a divine lot. <margin>F</margin> **SOCRATES:** And do not you rhapsodes, in turn, interpret the works of the poets? **ION:** That is also true. **SOCRATES:** So you are the interpreters of interpreters? **ION:** Absolutely. **SOCRATES:** Stay now, Ion, and tell me this—and do not hide what I ask of you. When you perform the epics well and most astonish the spectators—whether you are singing of Odysseus leaping onto the threshold, revealing himself to the suitors and pouring out his arrows before his feet, or of Achilles rushing at Hector, or one of the pitiable tales about Andromache, or Hecuba, or Priam—are you in your right mind then, or are you carried out of yourself? Does your soul, in its inspiration, think it is present at the events you describe, whether they are in Ithaca or in Troy, or wherever the epics take place? <margin>G</margin> **ION:** How vivid an evidence you have produced for me, Socrates! I will not hide it from you. For whenever I speak of something pitiable, my eyes fill with tears; and when I speak of something terrifying or dreadful, my hair stands on end from fear and my heart leaps. **SOCRATES:** What then, Ion? Shall we say that a man is in his right mind when, standing amidst twenty thousand friendly people, adorned in colorful clothing and golden crowns, he weeps at sacrifices and festivals although he has lost none of these things? Or that he is terrified when no one is stripping him or doing him wrong? **ION:** No, by Zeus, Socrates, to tell the truth, he is not. <margin>H</margin> **SOCRATES:** And do you know that you produce these same effects in most of the spectators? **ION:** I know it very well indeed. For I look down at them from the stage as they weep and look on with dread, and are filled with amazement at what is being told. For I must pay very close attention to them; since if I make them weep, I myself shall laugh when I receive their money, but if they are laughing, I myself shall weep because I am losing money.

<column-break/>

## Right Column

...and which responds in turn. **ION:** I have nothing with which to contradict you in this, but nevertheless I am conscious within myself that I relate the most beautiful things about Homer compared to all other men, and that I do not lack a store of eloquence. Everyone else praises me in this matter, but in other matters, they do not at all. See then, what this might be. **SOCRATES:** I see it, Ion, and I will begin to open to you what it seems to me to be. That you speak well of Homer is not an art that is present in you, as I was just saying, but it is a divine power that moves you, just like in the stone which Euripides named the Magnet, though some call it the Heraclean stone. This stone not only attracts iron rings, but it also pours its power into the rings themselves, so that they can perform this same feat and, just like the stone, attract other rings. Thus, a long chain of iron and rings often hangs together, and for all of them, the power of attraction is drawn from that stone. <margin>He seems to act in this way to show that even Homer himself did not write by art, but relied on a certain divine power of genius.</margin> Thus the Muse herself excites the poets with a divine instinct, and the excited poets seize others with a frenzy. Therefore, from all of these, the chain itself is woven. Thus all the good epic poets compose all those famous poems not by art, but captured by a divine breath; and the good lyric poets do similarly. Just as the Corybantes do not dance with a sane mind, so the excellent lyric poets do not fashion these songs with a sane mind; but when they rise into harmony and rhythm, they are seized and become like Bacchants. Just as the female Bacchants, when their minds are not sane, draw honey and milk from the rivers, but cannot draw them when their minds are sane, so too the soul of the lyric poets performs that which they themselves describe. For the poets tell us that, drawing from the fountains from which honey gushes, and plucking songs from the gardens and hills of the Muses, they bring them to us just as bees bring honey from flowers, and they say they fly like bees. In this, they speak the truth: for a poet is a light, volatile, and sacred thing, and he cannot sing until he is full of the god, and placed outside of himself, and alienated from his own mind. For as long as anyone remains in control of his mind, he can neither fashion songs nor give oracles. Therefore, it is not by some art that they sing these famous things which you relate about Homer, but by a divine lot each can correctly perform that to which the Muse has incited him. This one sings Dithyrambs, that one praises someone, this one sings Hyporchemata <note>Choral songs accompanied by dance</note> and dances, another epic poems, another likewise iambics. But in other matters, each of them is unskilled and inept. For they do not say these things by art, but by divine power. For if they knew how to speak correctly about any one of these through art, they would be able to do the same for all others. For this cause, God, stealing away their minds, uses them as ministers and messengers of oracles and as divine prophets, so that we who hear may perceive that it is not they who relate such worthy things, since they are least in control of their own minds, but that God speaks these things, and through them shouts these things to us. To this matter, Tynnichus the Chalcidian can be a most evident proof; he had previously composed no poem worthy of memory, but he says he found the hymn to Apollo which everyone sings—almost the most beautiful of all songs—by the inspiration of the Muses. In this, God seems most greatly to have shown us that we should not argue, but that these famous poems are divine and the works of gods rather than human and the works of men. The poets are nothing else <margin>Poets are the interpreters of the gods.</margin> than interpreters of the gods while they are seized by frenzy, by whatever deity someone may be seized. Indeed, God, wishing to show this, sang the most beautiful melody through the most inept poet. Do I not seem to relate the truth to you? **ION:** To me certainly, by Jove. And you soothe and affect my mind, Socrates, with these speeches. And by a certain divine lot from the gods, the distinguished poets seem to interpret these things to us. **SOCRATES:** Do you rhapsodes not, in turn, interpret the writings of the poets? **ION:** You speak the truth. **SOCRATES:** Are you not the interpreters of interpreters? **ION:** We are. **SOCRATES:** Note what I want, and answer me this, Ion: and do not hide from me that which I shall ask you. When you relate songs aptly and render the spectators struck with stupor—whether when you sing of Ulysses leaping onto the threshold <margin>Odyssey, Book 22</margin> and showing himself openly to the suitors and pouring his arrows before his feet, or Achilles making an attack upon Hector, <margin>Iliad, Book 22</margin> or while you bring forth something pitiable and plaintive concerning Andromache, or Hecuba, or Priam—are you then in control of your mind? Or are you alienated from your mind? And does your inspired soul think it is present in those deeds which you relate, whether they were done in Ithaca or at Troy, or wherever else the songs may carry you? **ION:** You have brought me a clear proof, Socrates, and I will recount it to you without hiding it. For as often as I say anything pitiable, my eyes are filled with tears. When I say something terrible or vehement, my hair stands up on end because of the terror, and my heart leaps. **SOCRATES:** Shall we then assert that that man is in control of his mind who, in sacrifices and celebrations, adorned in a beautiful garment and golden crowns, weeps when he has lost none of these things? Or that he is too fearful, who is standing among twenty thousand men who are his friends, with no one stripping him or affecting him with injury? **ION:** Not by Jove, Socrates, if we wish to confess the truth. **SOCRATES:** Do you not affect the multitude of spectators with these same things? **ION:** Certainly, very much so: and I always look down from the very platform at them weeping and looking grim, and struck senseless by these things which are being told. And it is necessary for me to apply my mind to them very much. For if I strike out tears, I myself, receiving money, shall laugh.

# PLATO’S [ION]

...but if I move them to laughter, I myself, losing my money, will weep. **SOCRATES:** Do you see, then, that the spectator is the last of those rings which, as I was saying, receive their power from one another by the Heraclean stone? You, the rhapsode and actor, are the middle ring; the first is the poet himself. But it is the god who, through all these, draws the souls of men wherever he wishes, suspending the power of one from another. From this, as if from that stone, a long chain hangs, in which those who dance in the chorus, and the teachers and sub-teachers, are joined side-by-side; they are suspended from the rings that hang from the Muse. One poet is suspended from one Muse, another from another. We call this being "possessed" <note>original: "mente capi" / "katechetai"</note>, which is very nearly the same thing, for he is "held." From these first rings—the poets—others are in turn suspended and inspired; some by Orpheus, others by Musaeus. But the majority are possessed and held by Homer. You, Ion, are one of these; you are possessed by Homer. When anyone sings the works of another poet, you fall asleep and have nothing to say; but when anyone chants a melody of this poet, you are immediately awake, your soul leaps, and you have plenty to say. For you do not speak what you say about Homer by art or science <term>science: here meaning "episteme," or systematic knowledge</term>, but by a certain divine fate and possession. Just as the Corybantes <term>Corybantes: priests who performed ecstatic, frenzied dances</term> are only sharply sensitive to that melody which belongs to the god by whom they are possessed, and have an abundance of words and gestures for that specific tune while ignoring all others; so you, Ion, when someone mentions Homer, you are eloquent, but regarding others you are at a loss. Therefore, the reason for what you asked—why you are fluent regarding Homer but fail regarding others—is this: you are a heavy praiser of Homer not by art, but by divine fate. **ION:** You speak well, Socrates; yet I would be surprised if you could speak so persuasively as to convince me that I am "possessed" and "mad" when I celebrate Homer with praise. I do not think I would seem mad to you if you were to hear me speaking on Homer. **SOCRATES:** Indeed I wish to hear you, but not until you answer me this: of the things Homer speaks of, which does he speak of well? For surely he does not speak well of everything. **ION:** Rest assured, Socrates, there is nothing he does not speak well of. **SOCRATES:** But surely you do not handle well those things which you yourself do not know, even if Homer writes of them. **ION:** And what are those things which Homer relates, but which I do not know? **SOCRATES:** Does not Homer frequently and extensively explain many things regarding the arts? For example, regarding the craft of charioteering. If I can remember the lines, I will recite them to you. **ION:** But I will recite them; for I remember. **SOCRATES:** Tell me then what Nestor mandates to his son Antilochus, when he warns him to turn the horses cautiously at the horse-race held in honor of Patroclus. **ION:** 

<margin>Iliad, Book 23</margin>
> *Lean yourself in the well-polished chariot*
> *slightly to the left; then urge on the right-hand horse*
> *with a shout and a blow, and give him rein with your hands.*
> *But let the left horse hug the turning-post,*
> *so that the hub of the well-made wheel seems to touch*
> *the very edge; but avoid hitting the stone.*

**SOCRATES:** These are enough, Ion. Whether Homer speaks rightly or wrongly in these verses, who would perceive it better: a doctor or a charioteer? **ION:** A charioteer, without a doubt. **SOCRATES:** Is this judgment made by art, or by something else? **ION:** By no other way than by art. **SOCRATES:** Has not a capacity for judging a certain work been assigned to each art by the god? For we will not perceive through the medical art those things which we know through the art of navigation. **ION:** Certainly not. **SOCRATES:** Nor will we observe through architecture the things we perceive through medicine. **ION:** No, indeed. **SOCRATES:** Is it not likewise in all arts, that what we understand by one specific art, we will by no means understand by another? But answer me this first: do you assert that one art is different from another? **ION:** I do. **SOCRATES:** Do you distinguish arts by the same conjecture as I do? For when the knowledge is of one set of things, and another knowledge is of another set, I call this one art and that another. And you? **ION:** I also. **SOCRATES:** For if there were a knowledge of the same things, why would we call this one art and that another? Especially since the same things would be known by both. Just as I perceive that there are these five fingers, and you, like me, notice the same thing. Therefore, if I asked you whether we know these same things by the same art of arithmetic, or by another, you would surely answer by the same. **ION:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** Now tell me what I was asking just now: does it seem to you that it must be said of all arts, that by the same art the same things must be known, but by another art not the same, but different things—since the art itself is different? **ION:** It seems so to me, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** If someone has not acquired a certain art, he will by no means be able to judge well the things said or done in that art. **ION:** You speak the truth. **SOCRATES:** Those verses which you recited, whether they are sung well or poorly by Homer—who would perceive this better, you or a charioteer? **ION:** A charioteer. **SOCRATES:** For you are a rhapsode, not a charioteer. **ION:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** And the rhapsodic faculty is different from the charioteering faculty. **ION:** Obviously. **SOCRATES:** If it is different, it is also a knowledge of different things. **ION:** Of different things, indeed. **SOCRATES:** What then, when Homer mentions this: Hecamede, the mistress of Nestor, offers a medicinal potion to the wounded Machaon, into which she pours Pramnian wine, and on top of it she grates goat's cheese with a bronze grater, and mixes meal with the cheese, and serves an onion with it as a relish. Whether these things are said correctly or otherwise by Homer, who—

# ION

### A
...is it the business of the medical art or the rhapsodic art to judge correctly? **ION:** The medical art. **SOCRATES:** And what about when Homer says:
<margin>Iliad, Book 24</margin>
> She plunged into the depths of the sea like a leaden weight,
> Which, set upon the horn of a field-dwelling ox,
> Goes down to bring certain death to the ravenous fish.
<note>original: "Ἡ δὲ μολυβδαίνῃ ἰκέλη..." / "In mare se mersit..." Socrates quotes a passage describing a fishing line weighted with lead and protected by a piece of horn.</note>

Is it the art of fishing or the art of recitation that can better judge whether these things are well-said or not? **ION:** It is clear, Socrates, that it is the art of fishing. **SOCRATES:** Now consider, if you were to ask me: "Socrates, since you are finding in Homer the things that belong to each of these arts to judge, come now and find for me the things that belong to the seer and the art of prophecy <term>prophecy: the art of "manteia," or divining the future and the will of the gods</term>, and what sorts of things he ought to be able to distinguish as either well or poorly written." 

### B
Observe how easily and truly I can answer you. He speaks of this in many places in the *Odyssey*, such as the words spoken to the suitors by Theoclymenus, the seer of the line of Melampus:
<margin>Odyssey, Book 20</margin>
> Wretched men, what evil is this you suffer? Your heads,
> your faces, and your limbs below are shrouded in night;
> Wailing blazes out, and your cheeks are wet with tears;
> The porch is full of ghosts, and the courtyard too,
> Hurrying into the darkness of the underworld; the sun
> has perished from the sky, and a foul mist spreads over all.

### C
And he speaks of it in many places in the *Iliad* as well, such as during the battle at the wall. For there he says:
<margin>Iliad, Book 12</margin>
> A bird came upon them as they were eager to cross,
> A high-flying eagle, skirting the host on the left,
> Carrying in its talons a monstrous, blood-red snake,
> Still alive and gasping; it had not yet forgotten the fight.
> For it bit the eagle on the breast, near the neck,
> Reaching back. The eagle, stung with pain, dropped it to the ground,
> And it fell into the midst of the throng;
> Then the bird, with a cry, flew away on the gusts of the wind.

I would say that these things and those like them are for the seer to examine and judge. **ION:** You speak the truth, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** And you too, 

### D
Ion, speak the truth. Come then, just as I have selected for you from both the *Odyssey* and the *Iliad* the parts that belong to the seer, the doctor, and the fisherman, you likewise select for me—since you are more experienced in the works of Homer than I am—what belongs to the rhapsode and the rhapsodic art, which the rhapsode ought to consider and judge better than other men. **ION:** I say, Socrates, that it is everything. **SOCRATES:** You did not say "everything" before, Ion. Or are you so forgetful? Truly, it does not befit a rhapsode to be a forgetful man. **ION:** What is it that I am forgetting? **SOCRATES:** Do you not remember that you said the rhapsodic art was different from the art of the charioteer? **ION:** I remember. 

### E
**SOCRATES:** And since it is different, did you not admit it would know different things? **ION:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** Then the rhapsodic art will not know everything, according to your own reasoning, nor will the rhapsode. **ION:** Except, perhaps, for such things as these, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** By "such things," you mean almost everything except the topics of the other arts. But what exactly will it know, since it does not know everything? **ION:** It will know, I think, what is fitting for a man to say, and what for a woman; what for a slave, and what for a free man; what for a subject, and what for a ruler. **SOCRATES:** Do you mean that the rhapsode will know better than the pilot what is fitting for a ruler of a ship to say when it is tossed by a storm at sea? **ION:** No, the pilot will know that better. **SOCRATES:** And will the rhapsode know better than the doctor what is fitting for a ruler to say to a sick person? **ION:** Not that either. **SOCRATES:** 

### F
But you mean what is fitting for a slave? **ION:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** For instance, what a slave who is a cowherd should say to calm his enraged cattle—will the rhapsode know this, rather than the cowherd? **ION:** Certainly not. **SOCRATES:** Or what is fitting for a woman who works in wool to say about the spinning of wool? **ION:** No. **SOCRATES:** But he will know what is fitting for a man who is a general to say when he is exhorting his soldiers? **ION:** Yes, such things as those the rhapsode will know. **SOCRATES:** What? Is the rhapsodic art the same as the art of generalship? **ION:** I would certainly know what a general ought to say. **SOCRATES:** Perhaps that is because you are also skilled in generalship, Ion. For if you happened to be both a horseman and a lyre-player, you would know how to tell good riders from bad. But if I asked you: "By which art, Ion, do you know the good riders? By the art of the horseman or the lyre-player?" What would you answer me? **ION:** By the art of the horseman. **SOCRATES:** 

### G
And if you distinguished those who play the lyre well, you would admit you did so by the art of the lyre-player, not the art of the horseman? **ION:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** Since you understand the business of the military, do you understand it by the art of generalship or by the art of being a good rhapsode? **ION:** It seems to me there is no difference at all. **SOCRATES:** How can you say there is no difference? Do you mean that the rhapsodic art and the art of generalship are one and the same? **ION:** They seem so to me. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, whoever is a good rhapsode is also, as it happens, a good general? **ION:** Precisely, Socrates. 

### H
**SOCRATES:** And is it also true that whoever happens to be a good general is also a good rhapsode? **ION:** No, I don't think that follows. **SOCRATES:** But you do think that whoever is a good rhapsode is also a good general? **ION:** Most certainly. **SOCRATES:** And you are the best rhapsode among the Greeks? **ION:** By far, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Then are you also the best general, Ion? **ION:** You can be sure of it, Socrates; and I learned that, too, from the poems of Homer.

<meta>This page concludes the "Ion," a dialogue exploring whether poetic skill is a matter of art (technē) or divine inspiration. It then begins the "Sophist," a deeper investigation into the nature of Being, Non-being, and the definition of a philosopher versus a deceptive teacher.</meta>

**ION:** Quite so, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Are you then, Ion, the best general among the Greeks? **ION:** Be assured, Socrates; I learned that as well from the writings of Homer. **SOCRATES:** Why then, by the gods, Ion, since you are the best of the Greeks in both—as a general and as a rhapsode <note>A rhapsode was a professional performer of epic poetry</note>—do you go about the Greek world reciting poems but never leading an army? Does it seem to you that the Greeks have a great need for a rhapsode crowned with a golden wreath, but no need at all for a general? **ION:** My city, Socrates, is ruled and governed by you Athenians, and thus has no need of a general. Your own city and Sparta would never choose me as a general, for you believe yourselves to be sufficient for the task. **SOCRATES:** My dear Ion, do you not know Apollodorus of Cyzicus? **ION:** Which one? **SOCRATES:** The one whom the Athenians have often chosen as their general, even though he is a foreigner; <sig>B</sig> and Phanosthenes of Andros, and Heraclides of Clazomenae. This city grants commands and other powers to these men, even though they are foreigners, because they have shown themselves to be men of excellence. Will the city then not choose Ion of Ephesus as a general and honor him, if he appears worthy of the title? What then? Are you Ephesians not Athenians by ancient origin, and is Ephesus inferior to any city? But you, Ion, if you speak the truth—that you are able to praise Homer through art and knowledge—then you are treating me unjustly. After professing to know many beautiful things about Homer and promising to demonstrate them to me, you now deceive me and are far from showing them. Indeed, you are unwilling even to state what those things are in which you are skilled, despite my long-persisting requests. Instead, like Proteus <sig>C</sig> <note>A sea god capable of changing his shape to avoid being caught</note>, you change into all sorts of forms, turning up and down and every which way, until finally you escaped me by turning into a general, so that you would not have to demonstrate how great your skill in Homeric wisdom truly is. If you are a man of art (as I just said) and you deceive me by promising a demonstration you do not give, you are certainly unjust. But if you possess no art, and are instead possessed by a divine fate through Homer—knowing nothing, yet saying many beautiful things about the poet, just as I have judged of you—then you do no injustice. Choose then, whether you wish to be thought of by us as an unjust man or as a divine one. **ION:** There is a great difference, Socrates, and it is much more beautiful to be judged divine. **SOCRATES:** This more beautiful title, then, is what we grant to you, Ion: that you are a divine rather than a professional <note>original: "artificiosum / τεχνικὸν" implying a master of a technical craft or art</note> praiser of Homer.

# THE SOPHIST, OR, ON BEING.
->Pertaining to logic or discourse.<-

> SUMMARY OF THE DIALOGUE. Plato's purpose in this dialogue is to teach the definition of the Sophist, specifically in a way that shows the difference between him and the philosopher. The thesis, therefore, is: "What is a Sophist?"—as the final clause of the disputation states in express words. To demonstrate this primary end, a most extensive and serious discussion is added "On Being," or "On That Which Is." Thus, the title of the dialogue is twofold: one shows the scope of the entire dispute (the Sophist), while the other indicates that additional topic joined to illustrate the chief and primary question. These are treated in the same order in which they are proposed. For at the beginning of the discussion, since the Sophist is defined as an imaginary craftsman who deals in the inventions of false things—that is, he teaches things that are not as though they were true, and in that way entangles and involves men's minds in false opinions—the very serious question arises: how can it be that the Sophist teaches things that are not? Therefore, Plato here explains more fully what <term>Being: τὸ ὂν (to on), the state of existing or true reality</term> is; since (from the doctrine of opposites) being must be understood by him who wishes to correctly understand what non-being is. Thus far, Plato treats of Being so that the definition of the Sophist may be perfected.

->THEAETETUS.<-

<sig>D</sig> **THEODORUS:** We have come, Socrates, just as we agreed yesterday, and we bring this stranger with us. He is an Eleatic by nation <note>From Elea, a Greek colony in Italy famous for the philosophy of Parmenides</note>, a companion of the followers of Parmenides and Zeno, and a man who is very much a philosopher. **SOCRATES:** Perhaps, Theodorus, while you think you are bringing a stranger, you are actually bringing some god. For Homer says that the gods—and especially the God of Strangers—dwell among men <sig>E</sig> who participate in just shame, to observe the insolence and lawfulness of mankind. Perhaps even here one of the higher powers has followed you to observe and correct us who are poor in the ways of argument—a kind of god of refutation. **THEODORUS:** That is not the manner of this stranger, Socrates. He is more moderate than those who are devoted to contentiousness. To me, he seems not to be a god at all, though he is certainly divine, for I call all philosophers <sig>F</sig> divine. **SOCRATES:** And rightly so, my friend. However, the race of philosophers is not much easier to discern, so to speak, than the race of gods. For all those who are not faking it but are truly philosophers appear in many forms because of the ignorance of others as they wander through cities, looking down from above at the life of those below. To some, they are thought to be of no value, while by others they are held in the highest honor. Sometimes they appear as statesmen, sometimes as sophists, and sometimes they give the impression to some that they are altogether insane. I would like to ask this stranger, then, if it would be pleasing to him, what his associates in Elea think about these matters and what they call them. **THEODORUS:** Which matters? **SOCRATES:** The Sophist, the Statesman, and the Philosopher. **THEODORUS:** What specifically, and what sort of difficulty about them, do you wish to investigate and ask? **SOCRATES:** This:

<column-break/>

**ION:** Quite so, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Are you then, Ion, the best general of the Greeks? **ION:** Be assured of it, Socrates, and I learned this from the works of Homer. **SOCRATES:** Why then, by the gods, Ion, since you are the best of the Greeks as both a general and a rhapsode, do you go about the Greeks as a rhapsode but not as a general? Or does it seem to you that the Greeks have a great need for a rhapsode crowned with a golden wreath, but no need for a general? **ION:** Our city, Socrates, is ruled and led by you [Athenians], and needs no general; but your city and that of the Spartans would not choose me as a general, for you think yourselves sufficient. **SOCRATES:** Excellent Ion, do you not know Apollodorus of Cyzicus? **ION:** Which man is that? **SOCRATES:** The one whom the Athenians have often chosen as their general despite him being a foreigner; and Phanosthenes the Andrian, and Heraclides the Clazomenian, whom this city—though they are foreigners—brought into the generalship and other offices because they showed themselves worthy of mention. Will it not then choose Ion of Ephesus as a general and honor him, if he seems worthy of mention? What then? Are you Ephesians not Athenians of old, and is Ephesus inferior to any city? But if you, Ion, are telling the truth—that you are able to praise Homer by art and knowledge—you are doing wrong; for after promising me that you know many beautiful things about Homer and saying you would demonstrate them, you deceive me. You are far from demonstrating them, since you are not even willing to say what these things are in which you are skilled, despite my long pleading. Like Proteus, you become all kinds of things, twisting up and down, until finally escaping me, you appeared as a general, so that you might not demonstrate how skilled you are in the wisdom concerning Homer. If, then, being a man of art (which is what I just said), you deceive me after promising to demonstrate your skill in Homer, you are unjust. But if you are not a man of art, but are possessed by a divine fate from Homer, knowing nothing but saying many beautiful things about the poet, as I said of you, you do no wrong. Choose then whether you wish to be considered by us an unjust man or a divine one. **ION:** There is a great difference, Socrates. For it is much more beautiful to be considered divine. **SOCRATES:** This more beautiful thing, then, belongs to you from us, Ion: to be a divine and not a professional <note>original: "technikon / τεχνικὸν"</note> praiser of Homer.

->THEODORUS, SOCRATES, STRANGER<-
->ELEATIC, THEAETETUS.<-

**THEODORUS:** According to our agreement yesterday, Socrates, we have come ourselves in good order, and we bring this certain stranger, an Eleatic by birth, a companion of those around Parmenides and Zeno, a man who is very much a philosopher. **SOCRATES:** Have you not, Theodorus, without knowing it, brought not a stranger but a god, according to the word of Homer? He says that other gods—and not least the God of Strangers—become companions to men who participate in just shame, to look upon both the insolence and the good order of men. So perhaps one of the higher powers follows you to look upon and refute us who are poor in speech, being a kind of refuting god. **THEODORUS:** That is not the stranger's way, Socrates; he is more moderate than those who are zealous about disputes. To me, he does not seem to be a god at all, but he is divine; for I call all philosophers by such a name. **SOCRATES:** And beautifully so, my friend. Yet this race [of philosophers] is likely not much easier to discern, so to speak, than that of the gods. For these men, appearing in all sorts of ways because of the ignorance of others, visit cities—those who are not faking it but are truly philosophers—looking down from above at the life of those below. To some, they seem to be worth nothing, but to others, they are worth everything. Sometimes they appear as statesmen, sometimes as sophists, and sometimes they might give the impression to some that they are altogether insane. I would gladly learn from him, then, if it is pleasing to him, what those in that place thought and what they named them. **THEODORUS:** What things do you mean? **SOCRATES:** The Sophist, the Statesman, the Philosopher. **THEODORUS:** What specifically do you doubt about them, that you ask after having searched? **SOCRATES:** This:

# THE SOPHIST

<column-break/>

Whether they considered all these to be one, or two, or—dividing the classes into three as there are three names—whether they assigned one name to each class <note>The Stranger asks if "Sophist," "Statesman," and "Philosopher" are different names for the same thing, or represent distinct roles.</note>.
**THEODORUS:** I do not think they would mind going through them. Or how else should we say it, Stranger?
**STRANGER:** Precisely so, Theodorus. I do not mind, nor is it difficult to say they thought there were three. But to distinguish each one clearly, and to define what each actually is, is no small or easy task.
**THEODORUS:** Indeed, by chance, **Socrates**, you have hit upon the very questions we were asking him before we arrived here. He told us then, as he says now, that he had heard enough on the subject and had not forgotten it.
**SOCRATES:** Do not then, Stranger, refuse our first request. But tell us this first: do you usually prefer to explain what you wish to teach in a long speech by yourself, or through the method of questioning, as **Parmenides** <note>original: "Παρμενίδῃ" - Parmenides was a towering figure in Greek philosophy who argued that reality is a single, unchanging "Being."</note> once used? I myself, when I was young, heard him debating in that way when he was quite old, delivering most beautiful arguments.
**STRANGER:** If the person one is talking to is cooperative and gentle, it is easier to discourse with another; if not, it is easier by oneself.
**SOCRATES:** You may choose any of those present you wish; they will all follow you gently. I suggest you choose a young person—either this **Theaetetus** or any of the others who seems right to you.
**STRANGER:** O Socrates, a certain shame possesses me, now that I am meeting you for the first time, not to exchange word for word in a brief manner, but to stretch out a long and tedious speech by myself—or even toward another—as if I were making a formal display. For the matter just raised is not as simple as one might expect from the question, but requires a very long discussion. On the other hand, to refuse you and these others a favor (especially since you have spoken so kindly) seems to me a bit rude and unrefined. For I certainly accept **Theaetetus** as my partner in this discussion, both because I have talked with him before and because you now recommend him.
**THEAETETUS:** Then do as you say, Stranger; if you do this, as Socrates said, you will have done a favor to us all.
**STRANGER:** It seems nothing more needs to be said on this, Theaetetus. From here on, the discussion is with you. If you grow weary of the length of the task, do not blame me, but these companions of yours who are the cause of it.
**THEAETETUS:** I do not think I shall tire now. But if such a thing should happen, we will call upon this **Socrates** here—the namesake of Socrates, who is my own age and my partner in the gymnasium—with whom I am accustomed to working through many difficult tasks.
**STRANGER:** Well said. You shall deliberate on that yourself as the talk proceeds. But now you must consider with me, beginning first (as it seems to me) by searching for the **Sophist**, and making clear in speech what he is. For now, you and I have only the name in common; as for the reality of the work we call by that name, we might each have our own private idea of it. One must always, concerning everything, come to an agreement through reasoned argument about the thing itself, rather than just the name alone without a definition. The class we now intend to seek—the **Sophist**—is not the easiest of all things to catch. And as everyone has long agreed, if one wishes to labor well on great matters, one must practice them in small and easier things before attempting the greatest. Now then, Theaetetus, since we think the "Sophist" is a difficult and hard-to-hunt breed, I advise that we first practice the method on something easier—unless you have another way to suggest?
**THEAETETUS:** I have none.
**STRANGER:** Do you wish, then, that we pursue some trivial thing and try to use it as an example for the greater subject?
**THEAETETUS:** Yes.
**STRANGER:** What then can we propose that is well-known and small, yet has a logic no less significant than the larger things? For example, an **angler** <note>A fisherman who uses a hook and line.</note>. Is that not known to everyone, and not worthy of any great seriousness?
**THEAETETUS:** That is so.
**STRANGER:** Yet I hope it possesses a method and a logic that is suited to what we want.
**THEAETETUS:** That would be excellent.
**STRANGER:** Come then, let us begin here. Tell me, shall we consider him a man of art, or someone without art but possessing some other power?
**THEAETETUS:** Certainly not one without art.
**STRANGER:** But of all arts, there are roughly two types.
**THEAETETUS:** How so?
**STRANGER:** Agriculture, and all care for any mortal body, and also the care for things that are put together and shaped—which we call "vessels"—and the art of imitation; all these would most justly be called by a single name.
**THEAETETUS:** How? And by what name?
**STRANGER:** Whenever someone brings into existence something that did not exist before, we say that the one who brings it into being "produces" <term>poiein</term> <note>The root of our word "poetry," but here meaning any kind of making or production.</note>, and that which is brought into being is "produced."
**THEAETETUS:** Correct.
**STRANGER:** And all the things we just listed have this power.
**THEAETETUS:** They do indeed.
**STRANGER:** Let us then summarize them and call them the **Productive Art**.
**THEAETETUS:** So be it.
**STRANGER:** Next, consider the whole class of learning, and knowledge, and the arts of business, combat, and hunting. Since none of these creates anything, but instead takes possession of things that already exist or have come into being—subduing some with words or deeds, and preventing others from being subdued—it would be most fitting to call all these parts together an **Acquisitive Art**.
**THEAETETUS:** Yes, that would be fitting.
**STRANGER:** Since all arts are either acquisitive or productive, in which class, Theaetetus, shall we place the art of angling?

<column-break/>

Whether they intended all these to be one, or two. Or if, as there are three names, they distinguished three classes, assigning single names to single classes.
**THEODORUS:** They will not do so reluctantly, as I believe, but will explain these to us. Or how shall we say it, o **Stranger**?
<margin>B</margin>
**STRANGER:** Thus, o Theodorus. For I shall not be reluctant, nor is it difficult to say that they thought there were three. But to distinguish them one by one, and to define what each one is, is neither a small work, nor an easy one.
**THEODORUS:** By chance, o Socrates, you have fallen upon the same question which we were asking him before we came here; and he answered us then just as he does to you now, saying that he had indeed heard it and remembered it.
**SOCRATES:** In that which we first asked, therefore, you ought to grant us the favor, o Stranger. But declare this to us first: whether you are accustomed to explain by yourself in a continuous speech that which you wish to teach, or rather by questioning, in the manner **Parmenides** used to use? <margin>Parmenides used to debate by questioning.</margin> For I, as a youth, heard him once disputing in this way when he was quite an old man, and bringing forth most beautiful reasonings.
**STRANGER:** If someone responds in a friendly and calm manner, it is easier to discourse with another by questioning; but if on the contrary, one disputes more easily by oneself.
**SOCRATES:** You may therefore choose whomever you wish from these. For all will obey most willingly. I indeed advise you to choose some youth, either this **Theaetetus**, or another, whoever seems more fit to you.
**STRANGER:** It would shame me, o Socrates, since I am now speaking with you for the first time, not to return word for word, but to begin a prolix discourse, whether alone by myself or with another responding, for the sake of a demonstration. For that which was just sought, no one should trust can be explained lightly. For it requires a long discussion. On the other hand, if I do not comply with you and these others—especially when you have asked so modestly—it seems to me it would be something boorish and foreign to the gentleness of a guest. Especially since I shall have this **Theaetetus** as a companion in the discussion, from those things which both I was saying and you just commanded.
**THEAETETUS:** Certainly so, o Stranger; as Socrates said, you will gratify all.
**STRANGER:** Nothing further seems needed to be said against this,
<margin>D</margin>
o Theaetetus. Henceforth I must deal with you: but if by chance the length of the speech happens to be distasteful to you, and you are burdened by the labor, I pray you, do not accuse me, but these your friends who are the cause.
**THEAETETUS:** I think nothing will be troublesome; for if by chance I happen to become weary, we shall employ this **Socrates**, similar in name to Socrates, my companion in exercise and my equal, with whom I am accustomed to performing many laborious tasks.
**STRANGER:** You speak well, and concerning these things you shall deliberate with yourself as the speech proceeds. But in common with me, you must now consider, and begin—as it seems to me—first from the **Sophist** himself, seeking and explaining by my speech what he is. For at present, you and I have only this name in common; but the thing itself which is designated by the name, perhaps each of us thinks of differently. It is better in each case to perceive the thing itself <margin>To know a thing with reasons excels just knowing the name. A proverb concerning the knowing of great things.</margin> with its definitions than the name alone without a definition. This genus of the **Sophist** which we are now investigating can by no means be easily defined as to what a sophist is. It is an old and common opinion of all, that if anyone wishes to correctly transact those things which are great, he ought to consider them in certain small and easier things first, before the greatest. Indeed, having judged that the genus of the Sophist can only be comprehended with difficulty, I advise you, o Theaetetus, that we first premeditate on its progress in something else easier. Unless you perhaps can show a more convenient way.
**THEAETETUS:** I have no <margin>A transition must be made to easier things, so that what is sought may be known.</margin> more convenient way.
**STRANGER:** Do you wish us to bring some small and vile thing into the middle, as an example for the greater thing itself?
**THEAETETUS:** I do.
**STRANGER:** Should we not propose something known and small, which nevertheless contributes to the understanding of greater things? Such as the man who is a **fisherman** (an angler). Is he not known to all, and least of all worthy of great study and meditation?
**THEAETETUS:** Certainly.
**STRANGER:** Yet it seems to have a way and a logic suited to that which we are treating.
**THEAETETUS:** In that case, the matter would be excellent.
**STRANGER:** Come, let us begin from here. Tell me <margin>The division of all the arts.</margin> whether we should place him as one possessing an art, or as one unskilled in art, but participating in some other power.
<margin>G</margin>
**THEAETETUS:** By no means as one unskilled in art.
**STRANGER:** There are roughly two species of almost all arts.
**THEAETETUS:** How?
**STRANGER:** Agriculture, and the care of any mortal body, and the faculty of all things which concern any composite or fashioned thing—which are commonly called "household goods"—and that which imitates these; I say the entire faculty of this kind ought to be called by one certain common name.
**THEAETETUS:** In what way? and by what name?
**STRANGER:** Whenever someone brings into being that which was not before, we say that what he does is "to make"; and that which is done, "to be made."
**THEAETETUS:** Correct.
**STRANGER:** All the things which we recounted a little while ago have power toward this.
**THEAETETUS:** They certainly do.
**STRANGER:** Let us therefore summarize them and name them the **Productive faculty**.
**THEAETETUS:** Let it be so.
**STRANGER:** But instruction, and every species of knowledge, and the skill of gain, of contest, and of hunting, ought to be called, in summary, the **Art of Acquiring**; for none of these makes anything, but instead acquires things which are or were, partly capturing them by speeches and actions, and partly yielding to those who capture.
**THEAETETUS:** It is fitting.
**STRANGER:** Since all arts are occupied either in acquiring or in producing, in which genus [shall we place] the skill of fishing...

<summary>In this opening of the "Sophist," the Eleatic Stranger and Theaetetus begin their philosophical investigation by establishing a method of "division," choosing the simple example of an angler (fisherman) to practice defining a craft before attempting to define the complex nature of a Sophist.</summary>

<meta>The previous page introduced the dialogue between Socrates, Theodorus, and a Stranger from Elea. They have agreed to investigate the definitions of the Sophist, the Statesman, and the Philosopher. The Stranger has suggested using the "Method of Division"—a logical tool that splits broad categories into smaller ones—to pin down exactly what a Sophist is.</meta>

# PLATO

<margin>A</margin> **STRANGER:** Shall we place it <note>The art of the Sophist.</note> there?
**THEAETETUS:** In acquisition, clearly.
**STRANGER:** And are there not two species of acquisition? One is a mutual exchange between willing parties, through gifts, purchases, or wages. The other is a taking of possession, accomplished through either deeds or words.
**THEAETETUS:** From what has been said, it is clear that this is so.
**STRANGER:** Now, taking must be divided into two parts.
**THEAETETUS:** By what logic?
**STRANGER:** One part is open and takes by fighting; the other is hidden and takes by hunting.
**THEAETETUS:** That is so.
**STRANGER:** It is also fitting to divide hunting in two.
**THEAETETUS:** How so?
**STRANGER:** For it hunts either a thing without a soul, or living creatures.
**THEAETETUS:** Why not? <margin>B</margin> Since both of these exist.
**STRANGER:** They certainly do. We should set aside the hunting of inanimate things, which has no specific name—as well as certain parts of the art of swimming and other such minor things—and let them go. But the capture of living creatures we shall call animal hunting.
**THEAETETUS:** So let it be.
**STRANGER:** Two species of this kind of hunting may rightly be counted. One is the hunting of land animals, distinguished by various species and names. The other is the hunting of agile creatures that swim.
**THEAETETUS:** Entirely so.
**STRANGER:** Of those agile creatures, some wander through the air with wings, and some through the water.
**THEAETETUS:** Certainly.
**STRANGER:** The hunting of winged creatures is called fowling.
**THEAETETUS:** Without a doubt.
**STRANGER:** And the hunting of water creatures is generally called fishing.
**THEAETETUS:** Entirely so.
**STRANGER:** Now, shall we not divide fishing into two major parts?
**THEAETETUS:** What are they?
**STRANGER:** We fish either by means of enclosures or by striking.
**THEAETETUS:** In what way do you distinguish the two?
**STRANGER:** Whatever binds for the sake of restraint, by surrounding something, is called an enclosure.
**THEAETETUS:** Quite right.
**STRANGER:** Will you call wicker-baskets, nets, snares, drag-nets, and other such things anything other than enclosures?
**THEAETETUS:** Not at all. <margin>C</margin>
**STRANGER:** This, then—and any other similar way of hunting that is performed by restraint—is a certain species of fishing.
**THEAETETUS:** It is.
**STRANGER:** There exists another species that captures by hooks and spears. This we should generally call striking-fishing, unless perhaps you can suggest something better.
**THEAETETUS:** Let us not worry about the name; this is sufficient. <margin>D</margin>
**STRANGER:** Some perform this at night by the light of a fire, which is why it is called fire-fishing.
**THEAETETUS:** Exactly.
**STRANGER:** Others do it by day, using tridents with hooks at the end of a rod. From this, all such fishing is called hooked and curved fishing.
**THEAETETUS:** That is clear.
**STRANGER:** He who strikes while fishing with a barbed instrument, and thrusts the spear from an upper part to a lower part, is said to use trident and spear-fishing.
**THEAETETUS:** So they say.
**STRANGER:** Only one species remains.
**THEAETETUS:** Which one?
**STRANGER:** A kind of striking made with a hook, unlike the previous one; it does not strike just any part of the fish, but only in the head <margin>E</margin> and mouth. It pulls upward from a lower part toward a higher part with rods and reeds. What shall we say is the most fitting name for this, Theaetetus?
**THEAETETUS:** It seems that the very thing we proposed to seek out has now been accomplished. <note>They have successfully defined the "angler" or hook-fisherman.</note>
**STRANGER:** Now, therefore, you and I have not only agreed upon the name for fishing by common consensus, but we have also sufficiently grasped the logic of the work itself. Half of the entire art was in division, dealing with acquisition; half of this was taking; half of this was hunting; hunting of animals; hunting of swimming animals; generally called fishing; a type of striking and hitting; fishing that is done with a hook; and finally, that striking which is done from the <margin>F</margin> lower part toward the upper part by pulling back—which, taking its name from that action, is called pulling and hook-fishing <note>original: "hamatoria" - angling.</note>.
**THEAETETUS:** This has been shown abundantly.
**STRANGER:** Yet, following this example, we determined to find what a Sophist is.
**THEAETETUS:** Exactly.
**STRANGER:** And this was asked first: whether we should consider the man who fishes with a hook to be completely unskilled, or a participant in some art.
**THEAETETUS:** That is so.
**STRANGER:** And now, shall we call the Sophist unskilled or skilled?
**THEAETETUS:** In no way unskilled. I understand that he who is called by such a name must not be ignorant, but instructed in a certain art.
**STRANGER:** In what art, then?
**THEAETETUS:** What art indeed?
**STRANGER:** By the gods, do we not recognize the kinship of one with the other?
**THEAETETUS:** Of which ones?
**STRANGER:** Of the angler and the Sophist. <margin>G</margin>
**THEAETETUS:** In what way?
**STRANGER:** They both seem to me to be hunters.
**THEAETETUS:** What prey does the latter follow? For we have already spoken of the other.
**STRANGER:** We divided all prey into two parts: swimming and land-walking.
**THEAETETUS:** Indeed. <margin>H</margin> And we came to this: we set aside the hunting of land animals, saying it was manifold.
**THEAETETUS:** Without a doubt. So far, the angler and the Sophist both proceed from the art of hunting.
**THEAETETUS:** They seem to.
**STRANGER:** From the hunting of animals, one descends into the sea, rivers, and lakes to hunt the animals within them.
**THEAETETUS:** Why not?
**STRANGER:** But the other goes toward the land and other rivers—as if into certain meadows rich with wealth and youth—to capture the animals there.
**THEAETETUS:** In what way?
**STRANGER:** There are two main parts of land-hunting.
**THEAETETUS:** What are they?
**STRANGER:** One is the hunting of tame creatures, the other of wild ones.
**THEAETETUS:** Is there such a thing as hunting tame creatures?
**STRANGER:** Consider what I say as you please: either man is a domestic animal,

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> **STRANGER:** Theaetetus, let us be persuaded.
**THEAETETUS:** In acquisition, it is clear.
**STRANGER:** Are there not then two kinds of acquisition? One is a change between willing parties, through gifts, purchases, and wages; the other is a total mastery through either deeds or words—this would be the art of taking.
**THEAETETUS:** So it appears from what we have said.
**STRANGER:** What then? Should taking not be cut in two?
**THEAETETUS:** How?
**STRANGER:** By setting one part as entirely competitive and open; and all the hidden part of it as hunting.
**THEAETETUS:** Yes.
**STRANGER:** It would be illogical not to cut hunting in two.
**THEAETETUS:** Say how.
**STRANGER:** By dividing it into the hunting of the soulless and the hunting of the living.
**THEAETETUS:** Why not? If indeed both exist.
**STRANGER:** How could they not? <margin>B</margin> We must let the hunting of the soulless go, as it is nameless—except for certain parts of the art of diving and other such brief things—and let them be. But the hunting of living animals we shall set apart as animal-hunting.
**THEAETETUS:** Let it be.
**STRANGER:** May animal-hunting not be said to have a double form in justice? One of the land-walking race, divided by many forms and names, called land-hunting; the other of the swimming animal, entirely water-hunting?
**THEAETETUS:** Entirely so.
**STRANGER:** Of the swimming, we see one tribe is winged, the other aquatic.
**THEAETETUS:** How could it be otherwise?
**STRANGER:** And the hunting of the winged animals is surely called fowling.
**THEAETETUS:** It is indeed.
**STRANGER:** And of the aquatic, almost the whole is called fishing.
**THEAETETUS:** Yes.
**STRANGER:** What then? Should we not divide this very hunting into two greatest parts?
**THEAETETUS:** By what means?
**STRANGER:** According to whether one performs the hunt with enclosures or by a strike.
**THEAETETUS:** How do you mean? And how do you distinguish each?
**STRANGER:** Because everything that hems something in for the sake of stopping it is likely to be called an enclosure.
**THEAETETUS:** Entirely so. <margin>C</margin>
**STRANGER:** Must we call wicker-traps, nets, snares, and weels <note>original: "πόρκους" - a type of wicker fish trap.</note> anything other than enclosures?
**THEAETETUS:** Nothing else.
**STRANGER:** This part of the hunt, then, we shall call enclosure-hunting or something similar.
**THEAETETUS:** Yes.
**STRANGER:** But that which happens by a strike with hooks and tridents, being different from that, we must now call by the single name of striking-hunt. Or how, O Theaetetus, could one say it better?
**THEAETETUS:** Let us not care about the name. For this is sufficient. <margin>D</margin>
**STRANGER:** Of the striking-hunt, that which is nocturnal—happening, I believe, by the light of a fire—is called fire-fishing.
**THEAETETUS:** Entirely so.
**STRANGER:** But that which is by day, since they have hooks at the ends of rods and tridents, is entirely hooked-fishing.
**THEAETETUS:** So it is called.
**STRANGER:** Of hooked-fishing, which is part of the striking-hunt, that which happens from above downward because of the tridents—how is it mostly called? I believe it is trident-fishing.
**THEAETETUS:** Yes, so some say.
**STRANGER:** The remaining kind is only one form, so to speak.
**THEAETETUS:** What kind is that? <margin>E</margin>
**STRANGER:** The strike opposite to that one, happening with a hook, and not striking any part of the body of the fish as tridents do, but around the head and the mouth of whatever is hunted each time; pulling it from below in the opposite direction upward with rods and reeds. By what name, Theaetetus, must we say this is called?
**THEAETETUS:** I think that what we just set out to find has now been completed.
**STRANGER:** Now, therefore, regarding fishing—with all of us in agreement—we have grasped not only the name, but also the logic of the work itself. Of the whole art, half was acquisition; of acquisition, taking; of taking, hunting; of hunting, animal-hunting; of animal-hunting, water-hunting; of water-hunting, the lower part of the whole division, fishing; of fishing, striking; of striking, hook-hunting. And of this, the part concerning the strike from below upward with a pull—named from the action itself—is now called angling <note>original: "ἀσπαλιευτική" - the Greek term for hook-fishing.</note>.
**THEAETETUS:** All this has been sufficiently shown. <margin>F</margin>
**STRANGER:** Come then, according to this example, let us attempt to find what the Sophist is.
**THEAETETUS:** By all means.
**STRANGER:** Indeed, that was our first question: whether the angler should be placed as a private person or as having some art.
**THEAETETUS:** Yes.
**STRANGER:** And now, shall we place him as a private person, Theaetetus, or truly as a Sophist?
**THEAETETUS:** In no way a private person. For I understand what you mean: that he who has this name must be such a person.
**STRANGER:** But we must place him as having some art, as it seems.
**THEAETETUS:** What then could this art be?
**STRANGER:** By the gods, have we ignored that the man is a kinsman?
**THEAETETUS:** Who to whom? <margin>G</margin>
**STRANGER:** The angler to the Sophist.
**THEAETETUS:** How?
**STRANGER:** Both appear to me to be hunters.
**THEAETETUS:** What is the hunt of the Sophist? For we have spoken of the other.
**STRANGER:** We just now divided all hunting into two parts: the swimming part and the land-walking part.
**THEAETETUS:** Yes.
**STRANGER:** And we divided the swimming part, which is aquatic; but we left the land-walking part undivided, saying it was manifold.
**THEAETETUS:** Entirely so.
**STRANGER:** Up to this point, then, the Sophist and the angler proceed together from the art of acquisition.
**THEAETETUS:** Yes, so they seem.
**STRANGER:** But they turn away from each other at animal-hunting. One goes to the sea and rivers and lakes to hunt the animals in them.
**THEAETETUS:** Why not? <margin>H</margin>
**STRANGER:** But the other goes toward the land, and toward other certain "rivers" of wealth and youth—like abundant meadows—to master the nurslings in them.
**THEAETETUS:** How do you mean?
**STRANGER:** Of land-hunting, there are two greatest parts.
**THEAETETUS:** What is each?
**STRANGER:** One is of tame animals; the other of wild ones.
**THEAETETUS:** Is there any hunting of tame animals?
**STRANGER:** If indeed man is a tame animal.

<summary>In this opening exercise of logical division, the Stranger and Theaetetus define the "Angler" as a hunter of aquatic animals who strikes from below. They then use this definition as a template to categorize the Sophist as a "hunter" of wealthy young men.</summary>

# THE SOPHIST

-> A <- **STRANGER:** Now, assume that you are pleased to call man a "tame" animal. Or do you prefer to say there is no such thing as a tame animal, or that man is a wild one? Or will you say that man is indeed tame, but that there is no such thing as a "hunt" for men? Tell me which of these options you prefer.
**THEAETETUS:** I believe, Stranger, that we are indeed a tame animal, and I agree that there is a "hunt" for men.
**STRANGER:** Then let us say that the hunting of tame animals is also twofold.
**THEAETETUS:** On what basis?
**STRANGER:** We define one kind as piracy, kidnapping, and tyranny—in short, the entire art of war—which we categorize as hunting by violence.
**THEAETETUS:** Excellent.
**STRANGER:** But the other kind—legal defense, public speaking, and social conversation—we may group together as a single art of "persuasion."
**THEAETETUS:** Correct.
**STRANGER:** Now, let us say there are two types of this art of persuasion.
**THEAETETUS:** What are they?
-> B <- **STRANGER:** One takes place in public, the other in private.
**THEAETETUS:** Each of these is indeed a distinct type.
**STRANGER:** And of this private hunting, one type involves a "wage," while the other involves "gift-giving."
**THEAETETUS:** I do not follow.
**STRANGER:** It seems you have never paid attention to the "hunting" performed by lovers.
**THEAETETUS:** In what regard?
**STRANGER:** In that they actually give gifts to those they wish to catch!
**THEAETETUS:** You speak the absolute truth.
**STRANGER:** Let this, then, be called the "amatory" <note>The art of the lover.</note> species of hunting.

**THEAETETUS:** Of course.
**STRANGER:** What should we call it? Try to say.

This is what the word "Sophistry" must mean.

**THEAETETUS:** In what way?

**THEAETETUS:** There were.
**STRANGER:** Now, let us say there are two types of exchange: one is "giving," and the other is "trading."
**THEAETETUS:** So let it be said.
**STRANGER:** And we shall say that trading is divided in two.
**THEAETETUS:** How?

**THEAETETUS:** Certainly.

**THEAETETUS:** What do you mean by that?
**STRANGER:** Perhaps we do not recognize the trade in things for the soul; we certainly recognize the other kind.
**THEAETETUS:** Indeed.
**STRANGER:** I am speaking of music in all its forms, which is bought in one city and sold in another; and painting, and stage-magic, and many other things for the soul—some brought and sold for entertainment, others for serious study. The one who brings and sells these is no less a "merchant" than the one who sells food and drink.
**THEAETETUS:** You speak the absolute truth.
**STRANGER:** Then will you not also give the same name to the one who buys up knowledge <note>original Greek: "μαθήματα" (mathemata) — lessons or branches of learning.</note> and moves from city to city, exchanging it for money?
**THEAETETUS:** Most certainly.
**STRANGER:** One part of this "merchantry of the soul" might be called the "art of display." The other part, though it may seem a bit ridiculous, must still be called by a name related to selling, since it is a sale of knowledge.
**THEAETETUS:** Entirely so.
**STRANGER:** In this
-> G <- "sale of knowledge," we must distinguish between the sale of other arts and the sale of the knowledge of virtue.
**THEAETETUS:** Of course.
**STRANGER:** The sale of other skills could be called "art-selling." But you must think of a name for the sale of virtue.
**THEAETETUS:** What other name could one use without making a mistake, except the one we are currently hunting—the **Sophist**? <margin>The second definition of the sophist.</margin>

**THEAETETUS:** Very much so.
**STRANGER:** Third, I think you would also call a man a Sophist if he settled down in a city and, instead of traveling, partly bought and partly manufactured his own lessons on these same subjects, and sold them to make a living.
**THEAETETUS:** Why not?

**STRANGER:** We establish, then, that the hunting of domestic creatures is also twofold.
**THEAETETUS:** By what reasoning?
**STRANGER:** Predatory hunting—which reduces people to slavery, tyranny, and military captivity—all these we collectively call "violent hunting."
**THEAETETUS:** Optimally said.

**THEAETETUS:** Correct.

**THEAETETUS:** To which, then?
**STRANGER:** Within the art of acquisition, two species were reported: hunting and commerce.
**THEAETETUS:** Certainly.
**STRANGER:** There are two species of commerce: one consists in giving, the other in buying and selling.
**THEAETETUS:** That is indeed how it is.
**STRANGER:** Again, we divide the part pertaining to buying and selling into two.
**THEAETETUS:** In what way?
**STRANGER:** Because he who makes his own works for sale is called a "producer-seller"; he who sells the work of others is an "exchanger."
**THEAETETUS:** Entirely.
**STRANGER:** This exchange is either conducted between citizens of the same city, which we call "retailing."
**THEAETETUS:** So it is.

-> E <- of the body, the other to the education <note>original Latin: "disciplinam" — learning or discipline.</note> of the soul, and exchanges knowledge for money.
**THEAETETUS:** How do you say this?
**STRANGER:** Perhaps we are ignorant of what pertains to the soul. For we recognize what pertains to the body.
**THEAETETUS:** Truly.
**STRANGER:** Indeed, a man who buys music in one place by learning it and sells it elsewhere by teaching it—and similarly with literacy,
-> F <- and stage-craft, and other disciplines of the soul, whether serious or for play—we call him a "merchant" no less than the one selling food for the body.
**THEAETETUS:** You speak the truth.
**STRANGER:** Will you not similarly call him a merchant who, having bought knowledge for money, travels through various cities to exchange it?
**THEAETETUS:** Certainly.
**STRANGER:** One part of this kind of merchantry is most deservedly called "demonstrative," and the other part is "ridiculous"; nevertheless, since it is a sale of knowledge, it must be called by a name similar to selling.
**THEAETETUS:** Entirely.
**STRANGER:** But he who sells other skills should be called by one name, and he who sells the precepts of virtue by another.
**THEAETETUS:** Nothing prevents it.
**STRANGER:** It is proper to call the one who sells other skills an "art-seller."

**THEAETETUS:** Very much so.
**STRANGER:** Third, I think you will likewise call him a Sophist who, staying in the same city, partly buys and partly invents his own lessons on these same things, intended for sale to earn a living.

**STRANGER:**

**STRANGER:** Would not everyone recognize that there are two species of purification? **THEAETETUS:** Perhaps, if someone thought about it for a while, but for the moment I do not know. **STRANGER:** Nevertheless, it is fitting to embrace many species of bodily purifications under a single name. **THEAETETUS:** Which ones do you mean, and by what name? **STRANGER:** There is the purification of the living body acting from within through gymnastics and medicine, and that which cleanses from without via baths—which is trivial to mention—likewise the cleaning of inanimate bodies by the work of laundrymen, which through wiping and rubbing provides color; all these things that take care of the body's adornment have various and humble names. **THEAETETUS:** Indeed. **STRANGER:** Entirely so, O Theaetetus. But the method of reasoning cares no more for one than for another; it does not care if a purification performed with sponges and ointments cleanses less, or if a medicine purifies and helps more. For in order to achieve an understanding of all arts, by investigating what is related and what is not, it honors all arts equally; it does not judge one more ridiculous than another based on their similarities. Indeed, it does not think it any more honorable to demonstrate the art of hunting through military discipline than through the most humble task of catching lice <note>original: "phtheiristike," literally the art of catching lice.</note>.
