**A** ...habit, you always bring up, as one might say, a "sophistic" one. **THEAETETUS:** It is necessary to follow where the argument leads. **STRANGER:** Let us look further to see if the object we are now pursuing resembles something else. **THEAETETUS:** Like what? **STRANGER:** A certain part of the "art of acquisition" was, for us, "competitive." **THEAETETUS:** Indeed it was. **STRANGER:** It is not out of character, then, to divide it in two. **THEAETETUS:** Tell me in what way. **STRANGER:** By making one part of it "contesting" and the other "fighting." **THEAETETUS:** It is so. **STRANGER:** Regarding the fighting part, that which happens between body and body is reasonably and appropriately called something like "violent." **THEAETETUS:** Yes. **STRANGER:** But for the fight of words against words, what else could you call it, Theaetetus, but "disputatious"? **THEAETETUS:** Nothing else. 

**B** **STRANGER:** Now, within the realm of disputes, we must posit two kinds. **THEAETETUS:** How? **STRANGER:** Insofar as it occurs in public through long opposing speeches concerning justice and injustice, it is "judicial." **THEAETETUS:** Yes. **STRANGER:** But that which occurs in private, chopped up into questions and answers—are we not accustomed to calling this anything other than "antilogic" <note>original: "antilogikon," the art of contradiction.</note>? **THEAETETUS:** Nothing else. **STRANGER:** Of the antilogic kind, that part which disputes about business contracts, doing so randomly and without art, must be placed in its own category, since reason distinguishes it as something different; but it received no name from those before us, nor is it worthy of receiving one from us now. **THEAETETUS:** True. 

**C** **STRANGER:** For it is divided into too many small and varied parts. **THEAETETUS:** But the "artful" kind, which disputes about justice itself and injustice, and about other things in general—are we not accustomed to calling that "eristic"? **THEAETETUS:** How could we not? **STRANGER:** Of the eristic kind, one happens to be "money-making," and the other "soul-leading" <note>original: "psychagogikon," often meaning charming or persuasive.</note>. **THEAETETUS:** Absolutely. **STRANGER:** Let us try to say what name we should call each of them. **THEAETETUS:** We should. **STRANGER:** I think that the one which, out of pleasure in such pastimes, becomes neglectful of its own household affairs, and whose style of speaking is not heard with pleasure by the many who listen, would in my opinion be called nothing other than "loquacity" <note>original: "adoleschikon," meaning idle talk or chattering.</note>. **THEAETETUS:** It is indeed called something like that. 

**D** **STRANGER:** Now, you try to name the one of these who makes money from private quarrels. **THEAETETUS:** Who else could one name without error, but that marvelous one who has come to us again for the fourth time—the "Sophist" whom we are pursuing? **STRANGER:** The Sophist, then, is nothing other (as the argument now reminds us) than the money-making branch of the eristic art, which is part of the antilogic art, the disputatious art, the fighting art, the competitive art, and the art of acquisition. **THEAETETUS:** Entirely so. 

**E** **STRANGER:** Do you see, then, how truly it is said that this beast is "variegated," and (as the saying goes) not to be caught with one hand? **THEAETETUS:** Then we must use both. **STRANGER:** We must, and we must do so as much as we are able, following this track of his. And tell me: do we use certain "domestic" names? **THEAETETUS:** Many. But what sort of the many are you asking about? **STRANGER:** Such things as when we speak of "sifting," "straining," "winnowing," and "discerning." **THEAETETUS:** Of course. **STRANGER:** And besides these, "carding," "drawing down thread," "beating the web," and we know thousands of other such things existing in the arts. Right? **THEAETETUS:** What is it about them that you wish to show by putting forward these examples to ask about everything? **STRANGER:** All the things mentioned are surely called "discretive." **THEAETETUS:** Yes. **STRANGER:** According to my reasoning, then, since there is one art in all of these, let us grant it one name. **THEAETETUS:** What shall we call it? **STRANGER:** The "Discretive" art. **THEAETETUS:** Let it be so. **STRANGER:** Look then to see if we can somehow see two species of this. 

**F** **THEAETETUS:** You are demanding a very quick inspection. **STRANGER:** And yet, in the aforementioned "discernments," one was the separating of the worse from the better, the other of like from like. **THEAETETUS:** It seems roughly as you have now said. **STRANGER:** For one of these I have no common name; but for the discernment that leaves behind the better and throws away the worse, I do have one. **THEAETETUS:** Say what it is. **STRANGER:** Every such discernment (as I understand it) is called by everyone a "purification." **THEAETETUS:** It is indeed so called. **STRANGER:** And would not everyone see that the "purifying" kind is twofold? **THEAETETUS:** Yes, perhaps with leisure; but I do not see it now. 

**G** **STRANGER:** Yet it is proper to encompass many kinds of purifications concerning bodies under one name. **THEAETETUS:** What kinds, and by what name? **STRANGER:** Those of living things, such as are rightly purified within bodies through gymnastics and medicine, and those concerning the outside—which are trivial to mention, such as the bath-house provides; and of inanimate bodies, of which the fuller's art and the whole of "adornment" provide care in small ways, having many names that seem ridiculous. **THEAETETUS:** Quite so. 

**H** **STRANGER:** Entirely so, Theaetetus. But for the method of definitions, it happens to care no less nor any more for "sponging" or "drinking medicine," whether the one helps us by purifying in small ways and the other in great ways. For the sake of acquiring intelligence, this method tries to understand what is related and what is not in all arts, and it holds all arts in equal honor; it does not consider some more ridiculous than others based on their similarity. It does not think the hunter's art as shown through "generalship" is any more "stately" than that shown through "lice-hunting," but only more "pompous" for the most part. And so now, regarding what you asked, what name...

# THE SOPHIST.

Come then, let us again give a name to all the powers together that have been allotted the task of purifying bodies, whether animate or inanimate; it will make no difference to the art what name is most decorous to be spoken. For the art of logic has no concern for the distinction between the purification of the soul and other things, provided it joins together everything that purifies anything else. But let it now attempt to set apart the purification of the mind from all others, if indeed we understand what it is we wish to learn. **THEAETETUS:** I have indeed learned and I grant that there are two species of purification, and that the kind concerning the soul is one, distinct from those that concern the body. <insert>B</insert> **STRANGER:** Most excellent. And listen to me in what follows, trying to cut what has been said in two again. **THEAETETUS:** Wherever you lead, I will try to cut along with you. **STRANGER:** Shall we say that wickedness in the soul is something different from virtue? **THEAETETUS:** How could it be otherwise? **STRANGER:** And indeed, we said purification was the leaving of one thing while casting out whatever is base. **THEAETETUS:** We did say that. **STRANGER:** Therefore, in the case of the soul, whenever we find a removal of vice, we shall be speaking harmoniously if we call it a purification. **THEAETETUS:** Very much so. **STRANGER:** We must speak of two species of vice regarding the soul. **THEAETETUS:** What kind? **STRANGER:** One is like a disease in the body, the other is like a deformity occurring. **THEAETETUS:** I do not follow. **STRANGER:** Perhaps you have not considered that disease and discord <note>original: "stasis," meaning internal strife or civil war.</note> are the same thing. **THEAETETUS:** Again, I do not know how I should answer this. **STRANGER:** Do you think discord is anything other than the disagreement of things naturally related, arising from some corruption? **THEAETETUS:** Nothing else. **STRANGER:** And is deformity anything other than the presence of the class of disproportion, which is everywhere unsightly? **THEAETETUS:** It is <insert>C</insert> nothing else. **STRANGER:** What then? Do we not see in the soul of those in a base condition that opinions disagree with desires, anger with pleasures, and reason with pains, and all these things with one another? **THEAETETUS:** Very much so. **STRANGER:** Yet they are all necessarily of a related nature. **THEAETETUS:** How could they not be? **STRANGER:** Therefore, we shall be speaking correctly if we call wickedness a discord and a disease of the soul. **THEAETETUS:** Most correctly indeed. **STRANGER:** What then? When things that possess motion and set for themselves a certain target, attempting to reach it, are carried wide of it and fail at every impulse, shall we say they suffer this because of a mutual proportion toward one another, or on the contrary, because of disproportion? **THEAETETUS:** <insert>D</insert> Clearly because of disproportion. **STRANGER:** But indeed, we know that every soul is ignorant of anything only against its will. **THEAETETUS:** Quite so. **STRANGER:** Now, being ignorant is nothing other than a wandering of the mind when the soul is impelled toward truth but is carried wide of understanding. **THEAETETUS:** Entirely so. **STRANGER:** Therefore, we must consider a thoughtless soul to be deformed and disproportionate. **THEAETETUS:** So it seems. **STRANGER:** There are, then, these two kinds of evils in it, as it appears. One is called "wickedness" by the many, and it is most clearly its disease. **THEAETETUS:** Yes. **STRANGER:** The other they call "ignorance," but they are unwilling to admit that it is a vice when it occurs only in the soul. **THEAETETUS:** It must be entirely granted—though I was just doubting as you spoke—that there are two kinds of vice in the soul. And <insert>E</insert> cowardice, intemperance, and injustice should all be considered a disease in us; but the condition of great and many-sided ignorance must be set down as a deformity. **STRANGER:** Now, regarding the body, were there not two arts found for these two afflictions? **THEAETETUS:** Which two? **STRANGER:** For deformity, there is gymnastics; for disease, the skill of medicine. **THEAETETUS:** So it appears. **STRANGER:** And is it not true that for insolence, injustice, and cowardice, the art of chastisement <note>original: "kolastike," the art of correction or punishment.</note> is naturally the most appropriate of all arts, according to justice? **THEAETETUS:** That is likely, so to speak, according to human opinion. **STRANGER:** And what of all ignorance? Could anyone correctly name any remedy other than instruction? **THEAETETUS:** None. **STRANGER:** Come then. Should we say there is only one kind of instruction, or more? Look and see that there are two primary kinds. **THEAETETUS:** I am looking. <insert>F</insert> **STRANGER:** I think we might see it in this way. **THEAETETUS:** In what way? **STRANGER:** By seeing if ignorance has a cut through its middle. For if it is double, it is clear that it also forces the art of instruction to have two parts, one for each of its own parts. **THEAETETUS:** What then? Is the thing we are seeking now clear to you? **STRANGER:** I think I see one great and difficult type of ignorance, set apart as a distinct species, which outweighs all its other parts. **THEAETETUS:** What is it? **STRANGER:** Thinking that one knows something when one does not. Through this, it is likely that all the errors we make in our thinking occur for everyone. **THEAETETUS:** True. **STRANGER:** And indeed, I think to this part of ignorance alone the name "lack of learning" <note>original: "amatheia," often translated as stupidity or gross ignorance.</note> is given. **THEAETETUS:** Certainly. **STRANGER:** What then must we call the part of the art of <insert>G</insert> instruction that rids us of this? **THEAETETUS:** I believe, Stranger, that the other part is called "handicraft instruction," but here among us, this part is called "education." **STRANGER:** And so it is called, Theaetetus, among almost all the Greeks. But we must still consider whether this is now an indivisible whole, or whether it has some division worthy of a name. **THEAETETUS:** We must indeed consider it. **STRANGER:** It seems to me that this too is still split in some way. **THEAETETUS:** By what division? **STRANGER:** Of the instruction that takes place in discourse, one path seems to be rougher, and the other part of it smoother. **THEAETETUS:** What do we call each of these? **STRANGER:** One is the ancient, ancestral way, which people used to use especially toward their sons, and many still use now whenever <insert>H</insert> they do something wrong—sometimes being harsh with them, and at other times more softly admonishing them. One might most correctly call this whole method "admonition" <note>original: "nouthetike," literally "putting in mind" or warning.</note>. **THEAETETUS:** That is so. **STRANGER:** But on the other hand, as some have themselves concluded upon reflection...

<column-break/>

...a more suitable name might be found, provided it is distinct from the purification of the soul, including all those things that purify the body. Furthermore, the Stranger now intends to separate the purification of the mind from all others, if we look toward where he is heading. **THEAETETUS:** I have indeed observed this, and I admit there are two species of purification, and the purification of the soul is different from the purification of the body. **STRANGER:** You speak excellently; and follow me in this as well: try to divide what I am about to say in two again. **THEAETETUS:** However you lead, I will endeavor to share the division with you. **STRANGER:** Do we say that wickedness in the soul is something other than virtue? **THEAETETUS:** Certainly something other. **STRANGER:** Indeed, we said that purification is nothing other than casting out what is wicked and preserving what remains. **THEAETETUS:** We said so without a doubt. **STRANGER:** If, therefore, we find any removal of wickedness regarding the soul, we ought deservedly to call it purification. **THEAETETUS:** Most certainly. **STRANGER:** Two species of wickedness are established in the soul. **THEAETETUS:** Which ones? **STRANGER:** One is like a bodily disease, the other like a deformity. **THEAETETUS:** I do not understand. **STRANGER:** Perhaps you do not call disease and "sedition" <note>original: "seditionem," translating the Greek *stasis*.</note> the same thing. **THEAETETUS:** I do not know what I should answer to this. **STRANGER:** Do you think sedition is anything other than the corruption of a natural relationship, arising from a certain discord? **THEAETETUS:** Nothing else. **STRANGER:** And what is deformity, if not the ugliness resulting from a dissonance of those things that are naturally related? **THEAETETUS:** That is it exactly. **STRANGER:** Furthermore, do we not see in those whose minds are depraved that opinions differ from desires, anger from pleasures, and reason from pains? **THEAETETUS:** Most certainly. **STRANGER:** Yet, all these things are necessarily related. **THEAETETUS:** It is evident. **STRANGER:** It is therefore fitting to call wickedness a sedition and a disease of the soul. **THEAETETUS:** Correct. **STRANGER:** If we see anything that, having a certain goal proposed, deviates and wanders in its individual movements while striving to reach it, shall we say it errs because of some mutual harmony and fitting agreement, or because of contrary causes? **THEAETETUS:** It is clear that it is because of dissonance and intemperance. **STRANGER:** And yet we know that no soul is <margin>What ignorance is and what an ignorant soul is like.</margin> willingly ignorant of anything. **THEAETETUS:** Clearly. **STRANGER:** Ignorance is indeed a certain dementia of the soul, which wanders from its own intelligence while striving toward the truth. **THEAETETUS:** Entirely. **STRANGER:** It is therefore fitting to call an ignorant soul unharmonious and deformed. **THEAETETUS:** It seems so. **STRANGER:** There are therefore these two types of evils in the soul. One is commonly called "improbity," which is undoubtedly a disease of the soul. **THEAETETUS:** So it is. **STRANGER:** The other they call "ignorance," yet they are unwilling to confess that this is a wickedness of the soul. **THEAETETUS:** It must be entirely conceded—as I was just now doubting while you spoke—that two types of wickedness exist in the soul. And <insert>E</insert> we should consider cowardice, intemperance, and injustice, and all other such things, as a disease; but the vast and varied ignorance, we must consider a deformity. **STRANGER:** Regarding the body, were there not also two arts discovered for these two evils? **THEAETETUS:** Which ones? **STRANGER:** Against deformity, gymnastics; against disease, the skill of medicine. **THEAETETUS:** It appears so. **STRANGER:** And against petulance, injustice, and cowardice, is not the most fitting of all arts the chastisement and judicial censure of punishment? **THEAETETUS:** This is indeed consistent with what human opinion holds. **STRANGER:** But against universal ignorance, what other remedy is found besides instruction? **THEAETETUS:** None. **STRANGER:** But should we say that instruction is only one and simple, or that there are many kinds? Observe that there are two primary kinds. **THEAETETUS:** I do observe it. **STRANGER:** And we seem likely to find the way very quickly. **THEAETETUS:** By what way? **STRANGER:** If we consider that ignorance is twofold, then this double nature requires a double method of teaching, so that each of these may be applied to each of those. **THEAETETUS:** Is what we are seeking now clear to you? **STRANGER:** I see a certain great and burdensome part of ignorance, outweighing all its other parts. **THEAETETUS:** Which one? **STRANGER:** This: when someone thinks they know those things which they do not know. From this, surely, all those opinions that deceive us proceed. **THEAETETUS:** So it is. **STRANGER:** And I think the name "lack of skill" <note>original: "inscitiæ," lack of knowledge or ignorance.</note> fits this part of ignorance alone. **THEAETETUS:** Entirely. **STRANGER:** What then do you think we should call the part of instruction by which we are freed from this ignorance? **THEAETETUS:** I believe, O Stranger, that the other part is named the instruction of the arts, but this part here is called "discipline." **STRANGER:** It is called so by almost all the Greeks. But we must further consider whether this whole thing is indivisible, or whether it has some division worthy of a name. **THEAETETUS:** It must certainly be considered. **STRANGER:** It seems to me that this too admits of division. **THEAETETUS:** By what reasoning? **STRANGER:** Of that faculty which teaches by speech, one part seems to be harsher, and the other milder. **THEAETETUS:** What do we call each of these? **STRANGER:** One is the old and ancestral way, which they used to use especially against their sons—and many still use it now—whenever they do wrong; partly rebuking them severely, and partly admonishing them more gently. We can call this whole thing "admonition." **THEAETETUS:** It is so. **STRANGER:** But some, on the other hand, have granted to themselves by reasoning...

# PLATO'S [SOPHIST]

<gloss>A</gloss> [They believe] that all ignorance is involuntary, and that no one who thinks himself wise will ever desire to learn those things in which he believes himself to be an expert. Thus, they feel that the "admonitory" <note>original: "nouthetikòn," referring to the traditional method of giving advice or scolding</note> form of education achieves very little despite great effort. **THEAETETUS:** They are right to think so. **STRANGER:** Therefore, they set out to cast out this opinion in another way. **THEAETETUS:** In what way? **STRANGER:** They cross-examine a man on those subjects where he thinks he is speaking the truth while saying nothing of value. Then, they easily challenge the opinions of those who wander in error; collecting these opinions in discourse, they place them side-by-side. By doing this, they show that these opinions are contrary to themselves, at the same time, regarding the same things, and in the same respects.

<gloss>B</gloss> When those being examined see this, they grow angry with themselves and become gentle toward others. In this way, they are liberated from great and stubborn prejudices. This liberation is, of all such releases, the most pleasant to hear and the most stable for the sufferer. Indeed, my dear boy, those who perform this "purging" <note>original: "purgare" / "kathairontes"</note> believe, just as doctors believe the body cannot benefit from food until internal obstacles are removed, that the soul likewise will not profit from the teachings offered to it until someone, by refuting the student and bringing him to a state of shame, removes the opinions that stand in the way of learning. Thus, they make him "pure" <note>original: "purus" / "katharon"</note>, believing he knows only what he actually knows, and nothing more. **THEAETETUS:** This is the best and most temperate of all mental states.

<gloss>C</gloss> **STRANGER:** For these reasons, Theaetetus, we must say that refutation <note>original: "redargutionem" / "elenchon"</note> is the greatest and most sovereign of purifications. He who has not been refuted—even if he were the Great King of the Persians—must be considered "unpurified" in the most important matters. He remains uneducated and scarred in those very areas where he who is to be truly happy ought to be most pure and beautiful. **THEAETETUS:** That is absolutely true. **STRANGER:** But whom shall we say uses this art? I fear to call them "Sophists." **THEAETETUS:** Why so? **STRANGER:** Lest we grant them a higher honor than they deserve.

<gloss>D</gloss> **THEAETETUS:** And yet, what has just been described seems very much like a Sophist. 
<margin>A similarity to be avoided.</margin> 
**STRANGER:** Well, a wolf also greatly resembles a dog—the wildest of animals resembling the most tame. He who wishes to remain safe from deception must always be on guard regarding similarities, for this "species" <note>referring to the Sophist</note> is most slippery. But let it be so; for we are not debating over small definitions when they are so carefully guarded. **THEAETETUS:** That is reasonable. **STRANGER:** Let it be decided, then: within the "art of separation," there is "purification"; within purification, let the part that cleanses the soul be set apart. Within this is the "faculty of teaching"; and within teaching is "education." Finally, within education is that "refutation" which deals with the "vain conceit of wisdom." As our current discourse shows, this is nothing other than the "Sophistry of the noble sort."

<gloss>E</gloss> **THEAETETUS:** Let it be called that. However, I am now at a loss, because so many different forms have appeared to us, as to what one should truly affirm the Sophist to be. **STRANGER:** You are right to be at a loss. But we must believe that the Sophist himself is now in even greater doubt as to how he might escape our argument. For as the proverb says: "It is not easy to escape every trap." 
<margin>A proverb.</margin> 
Now, therefore, we must press him most of all. **THEAETETUS:** You speak well. **STRANGER:** First, let us pause for a moment as if to catch our breath, and while resting, let us reason together. Come, let us recount how many different forms the Sophist has already taken. In our first investigation, he appeared as a paid hunter of the young and the wealthy. **THEAETETUS:** Yes. **STRANGER:** In the second, he was a merchant of knowledge for the soul.

<gloss>F</gloss> <margin>Six forms and definitions of the Sophist.</margin> **THEAETETUS:** Indeed. **STRANGER:** In the third, he appeared as a retailer of these same things. **THEAETETUS:** Entirely so. **STRANGER:** Fourth, he was a seller of his own intellectual discoveries. **THEAETETUS:** You have remembered well. **STRANGER:** And I will try to remember the fifth. He was an athlete of words, distinguished by the "art of eristic" <note>original: "eristicam," the art of arguing for the sake of winning rather than truth</note> or contention. **THEAETETUS:** He certainly was. **STRANGER:** The sixth form was ambiguous, yet we granted it for the moment: he appeared as a "purifier" of the soul, rooting out opinions that impede learning. **THEAETETUS:** Exactly so. **STRANGER:** Now, do you notice that whenever someone appears to be an expert in many things, but is called by the name of a single art, there is something "unhealthy" about this appearance? Is it not clear that the person who views him this way is unable to see the one point of that art toward which all these different branches of knowledge look? That is why he calls the man by many names instead of one. **THEAETETUS:** That seems to be the very nature of the case.

For one of them seemed to me to describe him most especially. **THEAETETUS:** Which one? **STRANGER:** We said he was a "contradictor" <note>original: "contradicorem" / "antilogikon," a disputer</note>. **THEAETETUS:** We did. **STRANGER:** And does he not also teach others to do the same? **THEAETETUS:** Certainly. **STRANGER:** Let us see, then, in what subjects these Sophists claim to make others into "contradictors."

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from page 154, shifting from the discussion of "purification" of the soul to a specific examination of the Sophist’s primary tool: the art of contradiction. # SOPHIST

[They are] able to make others like themselves. **THEAETETUS:** Absolutely. **STRANGER:** And what about laws and all political matters? Do they not profess to make men capable of disputing these as well? **THEAETETUS:** Indeed, no one would ever converse with them, so to speak, if they did not promise this. **STRANGER:** Furthermore, regarding the specific arguments to be used against practitioners of every single art, books have been published and are available to anyone who wishes to learn them. **THEAETETUS:** You seem to be referring to what Protagoras wrote about wrestling and the other arts. <note>Protagoras (c. 490–420 BCE) was one of the most famous Sophists; he famously claimed that "man is the measure of all things."</note> **STRANGER:** Yes, and those of many others, my dear boy. But in short, does the art of contradiction <note>original: "antilogikēs technēs," the skill of arguing against any position</note> not seem to be a power sufficient for disputing about all things? **THEAETETUS:** It certainly seems to leave nothing out. <margin>B</margin> **STRANGER:** By the gods, my boy, look at this point with me: perhaps you young people see this more sharply, while we elders are more dull-sighted. **THEAETETUS:** What is it? What are you referring to? **STRANGER:** Whether it is even possible for any human being to know all things. **THEAETETUS:** If that were so, Stranger, our race would be truly blessed! **STRANGER:** How then could someone who lacks knowledge say anything sound in an argument against someone who possesses knowledge? **THEAETETUS:** He couldn't. **STRANGER:** Then what is the "miracle" of the Sophist’s power? **THEAETETUS:** Regarding what? **STRANGER:** How they are able to create the opinion in young people that they are the wisest of all men in every subject? For it is clear that if they did not contradict correctly, or if they did not appear to do so to the youth, or if—even appearing to do so—they were not thought to be wiser because of their disputing, then (as you said) hardly anyone would be willing to give them money to become their student. <margin>C</margin> **THEAETETUS:** Hardly anyone indeed. **STRANGER:** But now, people are willing. **THEAETETUS:** Very much so. **STRANGER:** Because they are thought, I imagine, to have knowledge themselves of the very things they contradict. **THEAETETUS:** How could it be otherwise? **STRANGER:** And they do this regarding all things? **THEAETETUS:** Yes. **STRANGER:** Therefore, they appear all-wise to their students. **THEAETETUS:** Of course. **STRANGER:** Though they are not; for that was shown to be impossible. **THEAETETUS:** It is indeed impossible. **STRANGER:** The Sophist has thus been revealed to us as possessing a kind of belief-based knowledge <note>original: "doxastikē... epistēmē"</note> about all things, but not the truth. **THEAETETUS:** <margin>D</margin> Entirely so. What has just been said seems to be the most accurate description of them. **STRANGER:** Let us then take a clearer example of these things. **THEAETETUS:** What sort of example? **STRANGER:** This one; try to pay close attention and answer well. **THEAETETUS:** What is it? **STRANGER:** Suppose someone claimed—not to speak or contradict—but to produce and create all things by a single art. **THEAETETUS:** What do you mean by "all things"? **STRANGER:** You missed the very beginning of my statement; you don't seem to understand what "all things" signifies. **THEAETETUS:** I do not. **STRANGER:** I mean you and me, and all other animals and trees. **THEAETETUS:** What are you saying? **STRANGER:** If someone promised to make you and me and all other living things. <margin>E</margin> **THEAETETUS:** What kind of "making" do you mean? You certainly don't mean a farmer, for you spoke of him as a maker of animals. **STRANGER:** I do—and of the sea, the earth, the sky, the gods, and everything else besides. And furthermore, having made each of them quickly, he sells them for a very small price. **THEAETETUS:** You must be talking about some kind of joke. **STRANGER:** Well, is it not a joke when someone says he knows everything and can teach it to another for a small fee in a short time? **THEAETETUS:** It certainly is. **STRANGER:** And do you know any form of play more artistic or more delightful than the imitative art? <note>original: "mimētikon"</note> **THEAETETUS:** Not at all; you have named a vast category that encompasses all things in one, and it is perhaps the most varied of all. **STRANGER:** Therefore, we know that he who professes to be able to make all things by a single art, <margin>F</margin> will be able—by producing imitations and namesake-images of real things through the art of painting—to deceive the mindless among young children, showing them his drawings from a distance and making them believe he is capable of performing in reality whatever he chooses to do. **THEAETETUS:** Of course. **STRANGER:** And what about speeches? Do we not expect there to be another art that can bewitch the young through their ears with words? By displaying spoken images <note>original: "eidōla legomena"</note> of all things, they make it seem that the truth is being spoken, and that the speaker is the wisest of all men in every matter. **THEAETETUS:** Why should there not be such an art? **STRANGER:** Is it not necessary, Theaetetus, that many of those listeners, after enough time has passed <margin>G</margin> and they have reached a certain age, will encounter realities up close and be forced by their experiences to lay hold of things as they truly are? Then they will change the opinions they held before, so that what seemed great will appear small, and what seemed easy will appear difficult; all the phantoms <note>original: "phantasmata"</note> created in words will be overturned by the facts of actual practice. **THEAETETUS:** So it seems to me, as far as I can judge at my age. I think I am still among those who are far away from the truth. **STRANGER:** Therefore, we who are here will try—and are trying now—to bring you as close as possible to the truth without those painful experiences. But tell me this about the Sophist: Is it clear to you now that he is one of these "enchanters," being an imitator of real things? Or are we still doubting whether he might actually possess true knowledge of all the things he seems able to contradict? **THEAETETUS:** How could he, Stranger? It is almost clear now...

<column-break/>

[The Sophist is] able to make others like themselves. **THEAETETUS:** Entirely so. **STRANGER:** But what about regarding laws and the republic? Do they not profess to make men contentious in these matters as well? **THEAETETUS:** No one, so to speak, would argue with them unless they promised this. **STRANGER:** For those things that ought to be brought against the professors of individual arts out of a zeal for contention, writings are spread everywhere if anyone wishes to learn them. **THEAETETUS:** You seem to be speaking of what Protagoras wrote about wrestling and <margin>The art of contradiction can bring all things into controversy.</margin> the other arts. **STRANGER:** And about many other things, oh blessed one. But the art of contradiction itself—is it not, in short, a faculty that can bring all things into controversy? **THEAETETUS:** It seems to omit almost nothing. **STRANGER:** But by the gods, oh boy, do you think this can be done? For perhaps you young people see this more sharply, while we old men see more dully. **THEAETETUS:** What is that, and to what end do you say this especially? For I do not understand what <margin>No one can know all things.</margin> you are asking now. **STRANGER:** I was asking whether any man is able to know all things. **THEAETETUS:** Truly, Guest, our race would be blessed! **STRANGER:** In what way can one who is ignorant, by contradicting one who is intelligent, bring forward anything valid? **THEAETETUS:** In no way. **STRANGER:** What then would seem wonderful in that faculty of the Sophists? **THEAETETUS:** Concerning what specifically? **STRANGER:** By what means they could finally persuade the young that they alone of all people are the wisest in every single thing? For it is established that unless they contradicted correctly, or unless they seemed to contradict correctly to them, and when they so appeared, unless they were thought to be wiser by their opposing, they would be idle, and no one (as you were saying) would desire to be taught by them for money. **THEAETETUS:** No one at all. **STRANGER:** But now they do desire it. **THEAETETUS:** And vehemently. **STRANGER:** They are thought, I believe, to know those things in which they act as adversaries best of all. **THEAETETUS:** Why not? **STRANGER:** But they fight against all things, do they not? **THEAETETUS:** Without a doubt. **STRANGER:** Therefore, they seem to their disciples to be wise in all things. **THEAETETUS:** Why shouldn't they? **STRANGER:** And yet they are not. For it is established that this is impossible. **THEAETETUS:** Impossible indeed. **STRANGER:** Therefore, the Sophist has appeared to us to hold an opinion-based science regarding all things, rather than true knowledge. **THEAETETUS:** Utterly. And what you just said seems to be spoken very correctly. **STRANGER:** Let us therefore set forth some more transparent example of these things. **THEAETETUS:** Of what kind? **STRANGER:** This one, but attend diligently and respond aptly. **THEAETETUS:** What kind, I say? **STRANGER:** It is just as if someone were to claim, not that he speaks or contradicts, but that he performs and effects all things so that they are known by a single art. **THEAETETUS:** How were you saying "all things"? **STRANGER:** You are immediately ignorant of the beginning of this speech. For what this word, "all," signifies, you do not (it seems) understand. **THEAETETUS:** Certainly not. **STRANGER:** I say therefore that in the number of all things are you and I, and other animals and trees as well. **THEAETETUS:** How so? **STRANGER:** If someone should promise that he will make me and you and all other living things. **THEAETETUS:** What way of making do you mean? For you are not speaking of some farmer; for you said he was a "maker of animals." **STRANGER:** I do say so, and furthermore of the earth, and the sea, and heaven, and the gods, and all other things: and when he has fashioned each thing in a short time, he sells each one for a small price. **THEAETETUS:** You are telling a kind of joke. **STRANGER:** Indeed: and should he not also be said to be joking, who proclaims that he knows all things, and professes to teach another all things for a small fee and in a short time? **THEAETETUS:** Entirely. **STRANGER:** Do you have any species of joking more artful or more pleasant <margin>He makes all things imitative.</margin> than imitation? **THEAETETUS:** None. Indeed, you have named a broad species, comprehending all things in one and being manifold. **STRANGER:** Do we not understand that he who professes to be able to make all things by one art—by the art of painting, which fashions <margin>In speeches there is an art similar to painters.</margin> images of things of the same name—can deceive even foolish children, while he offers the paintings to be looked at from afar, as if he could effect whatever he wished? **THEAETETUS:** What forbids it? **STRANGER:** And do we not think there is another such art concerning speeches, which can deceive adolescents who are still far from the truth of things, like seducers using certain charms, by drumming into their ears certain life-like images in place of true things, so that they seem to speak the truth and to be the wisest of all men in all things? **THEAETETUS:** Nothing forbids there being another art of this kind. **STRANGER:** It is necessary, oh Theaetetus, that many of those who have heard these things, when they have grown up and considered the things themselves up close, and are forced to handle things clearly with true minds, should cast away their former opinions and change them so that what was great seems small, what was easy seems difficult, and the individual phantoms conceived in speeches are forced to be turned into their opposites by the progress of actions. **THEAETETUS:** So it seems to me, as far as the judgment of this age of mine goes. For I think I am still among the number of those who are far from the truth. **STRANGER:** But indeed we who are present will endeavor to bring you help. And now let us try to apply understanding as closely as possible without [painful] teachings. <margin>Seventh definition of the sophist.</margin> Tell me first about the sophist. Is it agreed between us that he is a certain charlatan, and an imitator of true things? Or do we still suspect that he might perhaps have a true knowledge of those things about which he seems to be able to contradict others? **THEAETETUS:** Who could suspect further...

<summary>In this passage, the Stranger defines the Sophist as an "imitator" who uses the art of contradiction to appear all-knowing to the youth, comparing his verbal trickery to a painter who deceives children from a distance. The dialogue concludes that the Sophist possesses only an "opinion-based" knowledge rather than true understanding, leading to his seventh definition as a charlatan and maker of images.</summary>

<keywords>Sophist, Plato, Theaetetus, art of contradiction, antilogic, imitation, mimesis, Protagoras, phantasm, deception, image-making</keywords>

# PLATO'S SOPHIST

<margin>A</margin>
[...of] that number who are powerful in a single discipline. **STRANGER:** He must therefore be called a sort of conjuror <note>original: "praestigiator," a juggler or someone who performs sleight of hand</note> and an imitator. **THEAETETUS:** Undoubtedly. **STRANGER:** Next, we must be careful not to let this prey escape, for we have nearly caught the Sophist as if entangled in a kind of dragnet <note>original: "verriculo," a sweep-net or dragnet used for fishing</note> of reasoning. Therefore, at least this much he will not escape. **THEAETETUS:** What is that? **STRANGER:** That he is clearly one of those who deceive by impostures and conjuring tricks. **THEAETETUS:** That seems so to me as well. **STRANGER:** It seems best, then, to divide the image-making art <note>original: "artem imaginariam," the craft of producing representations</note>—that is, the maker of likenesses—as quickly as possible. And once we have entered into it, if the Sophist still awaits us, we should seize him according to the command given by the royal discourse <note>original: "regio sermone," likely referring to the logical method directed by the leading speaker</note> and show our prey by handing him over. But if he should hide himself by slipping into the subdivisions of the art of imitation, we must pursue him and divide the part where he hides himself, opening it up until he is entirely apprehended. For neither he nor any other kind of person will escape the one who can investigate everything point by point through this method. **THEAETETUS:** You advise well, and so it must be done.

<margin>B</margin>
**STRANGER:** According to the previous method of dividing, I now seem to see two species of imitation. But as for the specific Form <note>original: "ideam," the essential archetype or category</note> we are seeking, I do not yet think I can recognize in which of the two species it should be placed. **THEAETETUS:** Really? First, distinguish and declare these two species to us. **STRANGER:** I see one as the art of likeness-making <note>original: "assimilandi artem," or in Greek "eikastikēn"</note> in which the work consists of producing an imitating image according to the proportions of the model in terms of length, width, and depth, and also by adding the appropriate colors. **THEAETETUS:** But what? Do not all who imitate something do this to the best of their ability? **STRANGER:** By no means—especially those who either mold or paint some large-scale work. For if they gave the true proportions of beautiful things to their statues, the upper parts would appear smaller than they should, and the lower parts would appear larger, because the former are seen by us from a distance and the latter from close at hand. **THEAETETUS:** Entirely so. **STRANGER:** Therefore, artists, leaving truth behind, do not provide the statues with the proportions that are truly beautiful, but rather those that *appear* beautiful. **THEAETETUS:** Precisely.

<margin>C</margin>
<margin>See Vitruvius on the proportion of columns.</margin> <note>Vitruvius was a Roman architect who discussed how columns must be adjusted to look straight to the human eye, even if the math says they are curved.</note>
**STRANGER:** Is it not right, then, that the other species, since it is an image, should be called the art of appearance? <note>original: "imaginatricem"</note> **THEAETETUS:** Certainly. **STRANGER:** We shall call the first part of the imitative art "likeness-making," as we said above. **THEAETETUS:** Exactly so. **STRANGER:** And what about that which appears similar to the beautiful, but is not actually beautiful, and if one could look closely, is not even similar to what it seems to resemble? What name shall we give it? Shall we not call it a "phantasm" <note>original: "phantasma," an illusion or mere appearance</note> because it appears to be something but is not actually like it? **THEAETETUS:** Indeed. **STRANGER:** And is this not a very large part of painting and the entire genus of imitation? **THEAETETUS:** To be sure.

<column-break/>

<margin>D</margin>
<margin>See Quintilian, Book 12, Chapter 10.</margin> <note>Quintilian was a Roman rhetorician who discussed the history of art and how perception affects judgment.</note>
**STRANGER:** We think that the art by which a phantasm is fashioned, and not a true image, should rightly be called "fantastic." <note>original: "phantasticam," the art of creating illusions</note> **THEAETETUS:** That is appropriate. **STRANGER:** I was placing these two species under the faculty of image-making: one that produces likenesses, and the other that produces phantasms. **THEAETETUS:** Correct. **STRANGER:** But as for what I was doubting—in which of these species the Sophist should be placed—I still do not see clearly. Truly, this man is marvelous and difficult to recognize, since even now he has very skillfully shifted his ground and retreated into the hiding places of an obscure species. **THEAETETUS:** It seems so. **STRANGER:** Do you agree with me now because you understand this, or has the momentum of the argument led you by habit to confess it so suddenly? **THEAETETUS:** Why do you ask this? **STRANGER:** We have indeed fallen into a difficult and blessed consideration. For both in the past and the present, what is being said is extremely doubtful: that something "appears" and "seems" to be, but is not at all; and that someone says certain things, which are yet not true. For in this way, the speaker must either lie or judge that things really are so; and for someone to say this without being caught in a manifest contradiction, O Theaetetus, is plainly difficult. **THEAETETUS:** Why?

<margin>E</margin>
<margin>F</margin>
<margin>The opinion of Parmenides regarding that which is not.</margin> <note>Parmenides of Elea (c. 515 BCE) was a foundational philosopher who argued that "Being" is the only reality and "Non-being" (nothingness) is impossible to think or speak about.</note>
**STRANGER:** Because such a way of speaking admits that "that which is not" exists. <note>original: "id quod non est, esse," the core paradox of falsehood</note> For otherwise, falsehood could not come to be. But the Great Parmenides, my boy, from the very beginning and throughout our childhood, always detested this idea. For he jokes everywhere in his poems: "Never," he says, "shall this be proved, that things that are not, are. But keep your mind away from this path of inquiry." From him, therefore, this testimony is provided, and if this argument is discussed moderately, it will reveal the matter. Come, let us first look at this, if you please. **THEAETETUS:** It makes no difference to me; you proceed where you think best, and lead me. **STRANGER:** That is how it must be done. Now answer me: do we dare to pronounce "that which in no way is"? <note>original: "Non ens," non-being</note> **THEAETETUS:** Why not? **STRANGER:** If we were to ask or answer these things not for the sake of contention or a joke, but if one of the listeners were seriously required to declare to us where this name "Non-being" should be referred, where do we think he would turn, or what would he show to the questioner? **THEAETETUS:** You ask a difficult thing, and for me, it is—so to speak—entirely unknown. **STRANGER:** At least this is clear: that the name "Non-being" must not be attributed to any of the things that exist. **THEAETETUS:** How could it be? **STRANGER:** And since it cannot be referred to "being," as it were, it also cannot be referred to "something." **THEAETETUS:** In what way? **STRANGER:** It is also clear to us that we use this word "something" <note>original: "aliquid"</note> everywhere in relation to some being, and it is impossible...

<margin>G</margin>

<summary>The Stranger and Theaetetus divide the art of image-making into "likeness-making" (accurate representation) and "appearance-making" (illusory phantasms), identifying the Sophist with the latter. This leads to a profound philosophical crisis regarding the nature of falsehood and the challenge of speaking about "non-being," famously forbidden by Parmenides.</summary>
<keywords>Sophist, imitation, likeness-making, phantasm, appearance, non-being, Parmenides, Plato, illusion, proportions</keywords>

--- Page 189 ---
<meta>This page continues the dialogue from the previous discussion on the nature of the Sophist. The Stranger and Theaetetus are now grappling with the logical impossibility of "non-being"—the idea of that which does not exist. This is a crucial turning point where they realize that to define the Sophist as a "deceiver," they must first explain how it is possible for a "falsehood" (a non-being) to exist or be spoken of at all.</meta>

# S O P H I S T A.
# THE SOPHIST.

...to speak of it as if it were naked and stripped of all things, is impossible, is it not? THEAETETUS: Impossible.
<margin>A</margin> STRANGER: Looking at it this way, would you agree that it is necessary for someone who says "something" to be saying at least "one thing"? THEAETETUS: Quite so. STRANGER: For you will say that "something" <note>original: "τὶ" / "aliquid"</note> is a sign of one thing? THEAETETUS: Yes. STRANGER: And to say "nothing" is not to speak of "something" at all, but to not speak at all. THEAETETUS: It is most necessary that one is not even speaking. STRANGER: Must we not also concede this: that such a person is not saying "something," but rather saying nothing? Indeed, we must say that he who attempts to utter "non-being" <note>original: "μὴ ὂν" / "non ens"</note> is not even speaking at all. THEAETETUS: That would certainly be the end of the argument's difficulty. STRANGER: Do not say anything so great yet. For, my dear friend, there is still—and indeed this is the greatest and first of those difficulties—something that concerns its very beginning. THEAETETUS: How so? Speak, and do not hesitate.
<margin>B</margin> STRANGER: To that which *is*, I suppose you say some other thing from among those that *are* can be added. THEAETETUS: Of course. STRANGER: But will we say it is possible for something that *is* to be added to that which *is not*? THEAETETUS: How could it? STRANGER: Now, we place the whole class of numbers among the things that *are*. THEAETETUS: Certainly, if anything else is to be placed among things that exist. STRANGER: Therefore, let us not attempt to apply either the multitude of number or "the one" to non-being. THEAETETUS: We would not be attempting it correctly, it seems, as the argument shows. STRANGER: How then could anyone utter with the mouth, or even grasp at all with the mind, the things that are not, or non-being, apart from number? THEAETETUS: Tell me how.
<margin>C</margin> STRANGER: When we say "non-beings," are we not attempting to add a plurality of number? THEAETETUS: Certainly. STRANGER: And when we say "non-being," do we not add "the one"? THEAETETUS: Most clearly. STRANGER: And yet we say it is neither just nor right to attempt to attach "being" to "non-being." THEAETETUS: You speak very truly. STRANGER: Do you perceive then that it is impossible to correctly utter, or to speak, or even to think of non-being itself according to itself, but it is unthinkable, ineffable, unpronounceable, and irrational? THEAETETUS: Entirely so.
<margin>D</margin> STRANGER: Was I lying just now when I said I would bring up the greatest difficulty concerning it? THEAETETUS: What then? Can we mention another even greater than this? STRANGER: What, my wonderful young man? Do you not see from these very things said, that non-being throws the one who refutes it into such difficulty that whenever he attempts to refute it, he is forced to contradict himself? THEAETETUS: How do you mean? Speak even more clearly. STRANGER: There is no need to look for clarity in me. For I, having supposed that non-being should participate in neither the one nor the many, just now and even at this moment spoke of it as one thing; for I say "non-being." Do you understand? THEAETETUS: Yes. STRANGER: And even a little while ago, I said it was unpronounceable, ineffable, and irrational. Do you agree? THEAETETUS: I agree, of course.
<margin>E</margin> STRANGER: Therefore, while attempting to attach "to be" to it, I was saying things contrary to what I said before. THEAETETUS: It seems so. STRANGER: And what of this? Did I not attach this term to it as if speaking of one thing? THEAETETUS: Yes. STRANGER: And even when calling it irrational, ineffable, and unpronounceable, I was making my speech as if it were a single thing. THEAETETUS: How could you not? STRANGER: But we say that if one is to speak correctly, one must define it neither as one nor as many, nor even call it "it" at all. For even by that naming, one would be addressing it as the form of "one." THEAETETUS: Absolutely.
<margin>F</margin> STRANGER: As for me, then, anyone could find that I was defeated long ago, and even now, in the refutation of non-being. Therefore, let us not look to my speaking for the correct way to speak about non-being, but come now, let us look at it in you. THEAETETUS: How do you mean? STRANGER: Come, since you are young, try with all your might and as nobly as you can to utter something about non-being according to the correct reasoning, without applying existence, or the one, or the multitude of number to it. THEAETETUS: I would have a great and absurd eagerness for the attempt if, seeing you suffer such things, I were to attempt it myself. STRANGER: Well, if it seems best, let us leave you and me aside; and until we can find someone who can do this, let us say that the Sophist has hidden himself in a most troublesome and difficult place. THEAETETUS: It certainly seems so.
<margin>G</margin> STRANGER: Therefore, if we say he possesses some sort of art of creating appearances <note>original: "phantasticam," relating to the production of phantasms or likenesses</note>, he will easily take hold of our words from this use of language and turn the argument against us, whenever we call him a maker of images <note>original: "εἰδωλοποιὸν" / "idolo-factor"</note>. He will ask what we mean by an "image" at all. We must consider, Theaetetus, what answer one should give the young man to this question. THEAETETUS: It is clear that we will mention the images in water and mirrors, and also those in paintings and sculptures, and all other such things. STRANGER: It is clear, Theaetetus, that you have not seen a Sophist. THEAETETUS: Why is that? STRANGER: He will seem to you to be closing his eyes, or to have no eyes at all. THEAETETUS: How? STRANGER: When you give him this answer, if you speak of mirrors or sculptures, he will laugh at your words as if you were speaking to someone who can see; he will pretend to know neither mirrors nor water, nor sight at all, but will ask you only from the standpoint of reason. THEAETETUS: What sort of thing? STRANGER: That which is common to all these many things you mentioned, which you saw fit to call by one name, "image," as if it were one thing. Speak <margin>H</margin> then and defend yourself, not giving way to the man. THEAETETUS: What else, Stranger, could we say an image is, except that which is made to be like the true thing, being another such thing? STRANGER: Do you mean another such "true" thing?

<column-break/>

...himself to pronounce it as something alone and, as it were, stripped of all those things which are separate. THEAETETUS: Truly impossible. STRANGER: Do you then, considering it thus, admit that it is necessary for him who says something to say *one* thing? THEAETETUS: Yes. STRANGER: Furthermore, you will say that "something" is a sign of one, <margin>Something is a sign of one.</margin> and "some things" of two or many? THEAETETUS: I will say so clearly. STRANGER: But for him who says "not something," is it not necessary that he says not even one thing—that is, he says nothing? THEAETETUS: It is entirely necessary. STRANGER: Nor is it to be granted that such a man says *something*, but not *one* thing—that is, he says nothing. And yet, he who attempts to utter non-being should not even be said to speak. THEAETETUS: The discourse would then have an end of doubting. STRANGER: You should not say this is a great thing yet. <margin>The greatest and first doubt concerning non-being.</margin> For there still remains, O blessed one, the greatest and first of doubts concerning these things, which happens concerning its very principle. THEAETETUS: Declare in what way you say this, and do not be reluctant. STRANGER: Surely to that which *is*, some other thing of those which *are* can happen. THEAETETUS: Nothing prevents it. STRANGER: But to that which *is not*, shall we say that any of those things which *are* can ever be present? THEAETETUS: By no means. STRANGER: Do we place the whole genus of numbers in the order of those things which *are*? THEAETETUS: Certainly, if indeed anything else is to be placed therein. STRANGER: Therefore, let us apply neither the multitude of numbers, nor "the one," to non-being. THEAETETUS: We would not apply them correctly, as reason shows us. STRANGER: How then could anyone either utter with the mouth, or grasp with the thought, those things which are not, or non-being, apart from number? THEAETETUS: Tell me how? STRANGER: Whenever we say "non-beings," do we not attempt to apply a multitude of number? THEAETETUS: Indeed. STRANGER: And whenever we say "non-being," we apply "the one." THEAETETUS: That is manifest. STRANGER: Yet we have said it is neither just nor right for anyone to dare to join *being* to *non-being*. THEAETETUS: You speak the truth. STRANGER: Do you perceive, then, that non-being can neither be uttered, nor correctly spoken, nor thought of by itself, <margin>Non-being is unthinkable and ineffable.</margin> but it exists as unthinkable, ineffable, unpronounceable, and irrational? THEAETETUS: Totally. STRANGER: Did I not lie a little while ago when I said I would bring in the greatest doubt concerning it? THEAETETUS: Can we bring in another greater than that? STRANGER: What indeed, O wonderful youth? Do you not see from these things which have been said, that non-being pours such darkness over him who refutes it, that as soon as he attempts a refutation, he is forced to contradict himself? THEAETETUS: Speak more clearly. STRANGER: There is no need to consider anything more clearly in my opinion. For although I had supposed that non-being was a participant of neither one nor many, yet both a little while ago and even now I uttered it as "the one" while I was pronouncing this very "non-being"—do you perceive? THEAETETUS: I perceive. STRANGER: Moreover, a little above I said it was inexplicable, ineffable, and irrational. Do you hold that? THEAETETUS: I hold it, why not? STRANGER: Was I not, while attempting to apply "to be" to it, uttering things contrary to the former? THEAETETUS: You seem so. STRANGER: Did I not attribute this to it as if I were speaking of one thing? THEAETETUS: Without a doubt. STRANGER: Furthermore, while I called it irrational, inexplicable, and ineffable, I was pronouncing it singularly, as if it were one thing; I was making my words about this. THEAETETUS: Why not? STRANGER: We said surely, if indeed anyone wished to speak correctly, he ought to determine it neither as one nor as many, nor to call it "it" at all. For in a certain species, it would be placed by a naming of this kind. THEAETETUS: Exactly. STRANGER: What then would someone say of me? <margin>† In Greek thus: for "the one" would now be named even according to this very appellation.</margin> For he will find that both before and now I have succumbed in this battle against non-being. Therefore, as I said, there is no reason why you should expect anything firm or correct from me speaking about non-being. But let us now see about you, if you please. THEAETETUS: What do you say? STRANGER: Come, try well and generously (for you are a youth), and with every effort of the mind to utter something correct about non-being, applying to it neither essence, nor the one, nor a multitude of number. THEAETETUS: How rash I would be if I were to attempt the same battle in which you succumbed. STRANGER: Therefore, if you wish, let us pass over you and me, and until we fall upon someone who can perform this, let us say in the meantime that the Sophist has hidden himself most craftily in obscure retreats. THEAETETUS: And most especially indeed. STRANGER: Nevertheless, if we say the Sophist is powerful in some "phantastic" art: he will easily, having found an occasion against us from that use of speaking, turn the discourse to the contrary. For while we call him the author of images, he will ask what we especially mean by an "image." It must be considered, Theaetetus, what we should respond to the Sophist questioning thus. THEAETETUS: We will clearly say that images are those which are offered in waters and mirrors, also those painted and expressed in types, and others of this kind. STRANGER: You seem, Theaetetus, never to have seen a Sophist. THEAETETUS: Why? STRANGER: He will seem to you to hallucinate, or to lack eyes entirely. THEAETETUS: For what reason? STRANGER: He will laugh at you who respond by means of figures and mirrors, just as if you, seeing, were speaking with one who sees: and he will pretend to know neither waters, nor mirrors, nor any of those things which are seen, nor even sight itself, but he will ask you from the words alone what is common to all these things you mentioned, and which is as if one in a certain way, when you call it something else— <margin>h. <summary>In this passage from Plato's Sophist, the Stranger and Theaetetus explore the logical paradox of "non-being," concluding that it is impossible to speak or think of that which does not exist without inadvertently treating it as a "being" or a "unity." They define the Sophist as a master of creating "images" (likenesses that are not the truth) and prepare to defend this definition against a hypothetical skeptical challenge.</summary>
<keywords>Non-being, Sophistry, Aporia, Image-making, Paradox of Language, Logic, Plato, Theaetetus, Ineffability, Being vs. Non-being</keywords>

...whether you mean the truth, or something else entirely? STRANGER: Not the truth at all, but a likeness. <margin>A</margin> STRANGER: And do you call the truth that which <term>truly is</term> <note>original: "verè ens" / "ὄντως ὂν"</note>? THEAETETUS: Exactly. STRANGER: And is that which is not true the opposite of the truth? THEAETETUS: What prevents it? STRANGER: If, therefore, you deny that what you call a "likeness" is the truth, you also deny that it truly exists; yet it does exist. THEAETETUS: In what way? STRANGER: You admit it exists, but not that it "truly" exists. THEAETETUS: Certainly not a "true being," but a "true image." STRANGER: Therefore, that which we call a "true image" is not <term>truly being</term>, and yet it is "truly" that which is "not truly being." THEAETETUS: It seems that "non-being" is entwined with "being" in a wondrous way. STRANGER: Why should it not seem wondrous? Do you see how cleverly this <note>Plato uses the metaphor of the many-headed Hydra to describe the Sophist's evasiveness.</note> multi-headed Sophist has once again, by turning and twisting, forced us against our will to admit that "non-being" exists in some way? THEAETETUS: I see it clearly. <margin>B</margin> STRANGER: By what reasoning, then, shall we define his art so that we remain consistent? THEAETETUS: Why do you speak with such great fear? STRANGER: Because we are asserting that the Sophist is a deceiver concerning "phantasms" <note>Appearances that are not merely copies, but distorted images intended to look like the truth from a certain perspective.</note>, and we call this art of deceiving "shrewdness." Shall we say that our soul is stirred by his tricks to hold false opinions, or shall we say something else? THEAETETUS: This very thing. For what else could we say? STRANGER: A "false opinion" is to have an opinion of things that are contrary to those that *are*. STRANGER: Do you say, then, that a false opinion is an opinion of things that <term>are not</term>? THEAETETUS: STRANGER: Does it think that things which *are not* do not exist? Or that things which in no way exist, do somehow exist? THEAETETUS: H. If someone is ever to be mistaken in their opinion in any way, it is necessary that they judge that things which *are not*, do somehow exist. STRANGER: Will he not also think that things which entirely *are*, in no way exist? THEAETETUS: H. That too. STRANGER: And is this similarly false? THEAETETUS: It is. STRANGER: Furthermore, <margin>C</margin> will not a "lying speech" be judged by the same reasoning, namely, one that pronounces that things which *are not* exist, and conversely, that things which *are* do not exist? THEAETETUS: In no other way can a lie be made. STRANGER: Almost never. Yet the Sophist will not admit these things. For how could a man in his right mind admit what was granted above, when it was already agreed that "non-being" can neither be spoken of, nor uttered, nor described, nor even thought? Do we understand what you are saying, Theaetetus? <margin>D</margin> THEAETETUS: Why should we not understand? For he will object to us that our own speech contradicts itself, since we have dared to say that "non-being" is involved in opinion and speech. From this, he will say we are often forced to attach "being" to "non-being," which we previously agreed was entirely impossible. STRANGER: You have recalled this correctly. But we must now deliberate on what we ought to do regarding the Sophist. For if we attempt to define him by placing him in the art of jugglers and liars, many objections and doubts will arise. STRANGER: So far we have pursued only a small fraction of them, though they are, so to speak, innumerable. THEAETETUS: If these things are so, it is impossible to catch the Sophist. <margin>E</margin> STRANGER: What then? Shall we desist from the investigation because of our "softness"? THEAETETUS: I think we should in no way desist, if we are able to catch this man from any side. STRANGER: You will give me your pardon then, and as you were just saying, you will be content if we make even the slightest progress in such a difficult quest. THEAETETUS: I will give it, and gladly. STRANGER: I ask this of you most of all. THEAETETUS: What is it? STRANGER: That you do not think of me as becoming a <term>parricide</term> <note>original: "patricidam" / "πατραλοίαν". The Stranger fears that by challenging the core doctrine of Parmenides, he is "killing" his philosophical father.</note>. THEAETETUS: Why is that? STRANGER: Because it will be necessary for us, in our defense, to examine the speech of our Father Parmenides, and to force "non-being" to exist in some way, and conversely, to force "being" to not exist in some way. THEAETETUS: It seems this must indeed be contended in these speeches. <margin>F</margin> STRANGER: How could it not? For as the saying goes, even a blind man can see it. Unless these things are refuted and granted, no one will be able to speak of false speeches, or opinion, or likenesses, or images, or imitations, or phantasms—nor of the arts concerned with these things—without making the listeners laugh, while he himself is forced to utter contradictions. THEAETETUS: You speak the truth. STRANGER: Because of this, we must dare to press against the paternal speech, or dismiss the matter entirely if we are held back by any laziness or shame. THEAETETUS: But nothing shall prevent us from doing so. STRANGER: Furthermore, I ask a third small thing of you. THEAETETUS: Please, say it. STRANGER: I said a little while ago that I am always—and especially now—utterly exhausted <margin>G</margin> by the refutation of such things. THEAETETUS: You did say that. STRANGER: I fear that because of what I have said, I may seem "mad" to you, suddenly turning myself upside down and inside out. For it is for your sake that we will attempt the refutation of that speech, if perhaps we are able to refute it. THEAETETUS: For this reason, then, prepare yourself for the fight with a brave heart. For in my judgment, you will not be said to have done anything wrong if you take up this refutation. STRANGER: From where, then, shall we most conveniently begin this discussion full of peril? I think, my boy, we must necessarily travel by this path. THEAETETUS: Which one? STRANGER: That we first discuss those things which seem easier, lest, deterred by the difficulty of the subject, we immediately desist from our undertaking; rather, let us proceed by consensus, as if we could judge these things lightly and well. THEAETETUS: Express what you mean more clearly. STRANGER: Parmenides seems to have proceeded with an easy discussion, as has anyone else who ever dared to determine how many and of what kind <term>beings</term> <note>original: "entia" / "ὄντα"</note> there are. THEAETETUS: In what way? STRANGER: Each one seems to have told us a fable, as if we were children. One says that there are three things that exist, and that some of them sometimes fight with each other, while at other times they are reconciled and enter into marriage, giving birth and offspring...

...or in what way did you say such a thing? THEAETETUS: Not at all a true thing, but a likeness. STRANGER: Are you then calling the true thing "that which truly is"? THEAETETUS: Yes. STRANGER: So that which we call an image is "truly being" while not "truly" being? THEAETETUS: It seems that "non-being" has been woven into a certain entanglement with "being," and it is very strange. STRANGER: How can it not be strange? STRANGER: What then? By what art shall we define him, so that we can be in agreement with ourselves? THEAETETUS: Why and with what fear do you speak this way? STRANGER: When we say he deceives with phantasms, and that his art is one of deception, shall we then say that our soul holds false opinions by his art? Or what shall we say? THEAETETUS: That. STRANGER: You say then that false opinion holds opinions of things that *are not*. THEAETETUS: Necessarily. STRANGER: Does it hold the opinion that the things that *are not* do not exist, or how? STRANGER: And a speech (I think) will be considered false in the same way, saying that things which *are* are not, and things which *are not* are. THEAETETUS: How else could it become such a thing? He will say we are saying the opposite of what we just said, having dared to say that falsehood exists in both opinions and speeches; for he will say we are often forced to attach "non-being" to "being," though we just now agreed this was most impossible. STRANGER: You have remembered correctly. But now is the time to deliberate what must be done about the Sophist. For the objections or difficulties, which one might see when placing him in the art of falsehood-makers and sorcerers, are easy to find and many. THEAETETUS: Very much so. STRANGER: We have gone through only a small part of them, they being (so to speak) infinite. THEAETETUS: It seems impossible to catch the Sophist if these things are so. STRANGER: What then? STRANGER: Will you then have forgiveness, and as you just said, be satisfied if we can pull away even a little from such a strong argument? THEAETETUS: How could I not? STRANGER: I beg this of you even more. THEAETETUS: What is it? STRANGER: Do not suppose that I am becoming a "parricide" of any kind. THEAETETUS: Why so? STRANGER: It is necessary for us, in our defense, to put the speech of Father Parmenides to the test, and to force both "non-being" to exist in some way, and "being," in turn, to not exist in some way. THEAETETUS: It appears such a battle must be fought in our speeches. STRANGER: How could it not appear so? As the saying goes, even to a blind man. THEAETETUS: Most true. STRANGER: Because of this, one must dare to set upon the paternal speech; or it must be let go entirely, if some hesitation prevents one from doing this. THEAETETUS: But let nothing prevent us from this in any way. STRANGER: I will then ask one small favor of you. THEAETETUS: Just say it. STRANGER: I said just now that I have always been exhausted regarding the refutation of these things, and I am so now. THEAETETUS: You said so. STRANGER: I fear what I have said, lest I seem mad to you, turning myself up and down, this way and that. THEAETETUS: Since I will in no way think you are doing anything wrong if you go toward this refutation and proof, go forth boldly for my sake. STRANGER: Come then, what beginning should one make of such a perilous speech? I think, O boy, the road we must necessarily turn to is this. THEAETETUS: Which one? STRANGER: To first examine the things that now seem clear, lest we be disturbed by them and easily agree with each other as if we held them accurately. THEAETETUS: Say more clearly what you mean. STRANGER: Parmenides seems to have discussed things with us easily, as has everyone who ever set out to distinguish how many and of what sort beings are. THEAETETUS: How? STRANGER: Each one seems to me to tell a fable to us as if we were children. One says that beings are three; that sometimes they are at war with one another, and at other times they become friends, marrying and giving birth...
