<margin>Concerning beings.</margin>
<margin>Concerning the opposition within beings</margin>
<margin>A</margin> ...and having said that they provide two different forms of nourishment for both—the moist and the dry, or the hot and the cold—they then join them together and give them away in marriage. The <term>Eleatic tribe</term> <note>The Eleatic school was a group of philosophers in ancient Italy, most famously Parmenides and Zeno, who argued that reality is a single, unchanging "One."</note> among us, starting from Xenophanes and even earlier, proceeds with their myths on the assumption that what are called "all things" are actually one. But certain <term>Ionian and Sicilian Muses</term> <note>The "Ionian Muses" refers to Heraclitus, and the "Sicilian Muses" to Empedocles. Plato uses this poetic language to describe their philosophical systems.</note> later realized it was safer to weave both views together and to say that Being is both many and one, held together by both strife and friendship. <margin>The Eleatic tribe. The Ionian and Sicilian Muses.</margin> <margin>B</margin> For the "tenser" Muses <note>Referring to Heraclitus's philosophy of constant change and tension.</note> say that what is pulled apart is always being drawn together; but the "softer" Muses <note>Referring to Empedocles, who suggested a cycle of alternating states.</note> relaxed the requirement that this must always be so, saying that the whole is alternately one and friendly through the power of Aphrodite, and then many and at war with itself due to a kind of strife. Whether any of them spoke the truth or not in these matters, it is difficult and improper to find fault with men so famous and ancient. However, one may declare this much without giving offense.

THEAETETUS: What is that?

STRANGER: That they looked down on us, the common people, far too much and were quite negligent. For without caring whether we follow them as they speak or are left behind, each of them carries out their own business to the end.

THEAETETUS: How do you mean?

STRANGER: When one of them speaks and says that there "is," or "has been," or "is becoming" many things or one, or hot and cold mixed together, assuming <margin>C</margin> separations and combinations elsewhere—by the gods, Theaetetus, do you ever understand what they are saying? For my part, when I was younger, I thought I precisely understood whenever someone spoke of this "non-being" which now perplexes us; but now you see what a state of difficulty we are in regarding it.

THEAETETUS: I see.

STRANGER: Perhaps, then, our souls have been affected in the same way regarding "Being" as well; we claim to be at ease when we speak of it, while we find ourselves in a poor state regarding the other <note>i.e., Non-Being</note>, though we are actually in a similar condition regarding both.

THEAETETUS: Perhaps.

STRANGER: And let what we have said stand as our position regarding all those other thinkers.

THEAETETUS: Certainly.

STRANGER: We should consider the many later, if we wish; <margin>Inquiry concerning being</margin> <margin>D</margin> but now we must first consider the greatest and the primary leader.

THEAETETUS: Which one do you mean? Or is it clear you are saying we must first investigate "Being," and what those who speak of it think they are revealing?

STRANGER: You have followed me closely, Theaetetus. For I say we should use this method as if we were questioning them in their presence: "Come now, all you who say that hot and cold, or any two such things, are the 'all,' what is this you are pronouncing regarding both when you say that both and each 'are'? How should we understand this 'to be' of yours? Is it a third thing alongside those two, and should we then posit that the 'all' is three things according to you, and no longer two? For surely you do not call one of the two 'being' and then say that both are 'being' in the same way. For then both would be nearly one, and not two."

THEAETETUS: You speak the truth.

STRANGER: "But then do you wish to call both of them 'being'?"

THEAETETUS: Perhaps.

STRANGER: "But, friends," we shall say, "even in this way you would very clearly be saying that the two things are one."

THEAETETUS: You have spoken most correctly. <margin>Concerning the One</margin> <margin>E</margin>

STRANGER: "Since we are in difficulty, you should clarify for us what you mean when you say 'being.' For it is clear that you have known this for a long time, while we formerly thought we knew but now are stuck. Teach us this first, so that we do not imagine we are learning what you say when the opposite is actually happening." If we speak this way and make these demands of them and of all others who say the "all" is more than one, shall we be doing anything wrong?

THEAETETUS: Not at all.

STRANGER: What then? Should we not also inquire as best we can from those who say the "all" is one, what they mean by "being"?

THEAETETUS: Of course.

STRANGER: Then let them answer this: "Do you say that there is only one thing?" "We do," they will say, will they not?

THEAETETUS: Yes.

STRANGER: "What then? Do you call something 'being'?"

THEAETETUS: Yes.

STRANGER: "Is it the same thing as 'the one'? Are you using two names for the same thing? Or how do you mean it?"

THEAETETUS: What would their answer be to this, Stranger?

STRANGER: It is clear, Theaetetus, that it is not the easiest thing in the world for one who has laid down this hypothesis to answer the present question, or any other for that matter.

THEAETETUS: Why?

STRANGER: To admit that there are two names while maintaining there is nothing but "the one" is surely ridiculous.

THEAETETUS: How could it not be?

STRANGER: And it is entirely absurd to accept the statement that a name "is," if it has no account to give.

THEAETETUS: In what way?

STRANGER: If he posits that the name is different from the thing, he is surely speaking of two things.

THEAETETUS: Yes.

STRANGER: And yet if he posits the name as being the same as the thing, he will be forced to say it is the name of nothing; or if he says it is the name of something, it will turn out that the name is only a name of a name, and of nothing else.

THEAETETUS: That is so. <margin>Concerning the Whole</margin> <margin>G</margin>

STRANGER: And "the one" will be only the "one of the one," and it will also be the "one of the name."

THEAETETUS: It must be.

STRANGER: What then? Will they say that "the whole" is different from "the one being," or the same?

THEAETETUS: How could they not say it is the same—as they actually do?

STRANGER: If, therefore, it is a whole, as Parmenides also says: 
> Like the mass of a well-rounded sphere, 
> equally balanced from the center in every direction; for it must be 
> neither larger nor more fixed in any part, 
then "being," having such a nature, must have a center and extremes. And having these, it is absolutely necessary that it has parts. Or what do you say?

THEAETETUS: Just so.

STRANGER: Yet there is nothing to prevent that which is divided from having the *attribute* of unity in all its parts, and in this way the "all being" and the "whole" can be "one."

THEAETETUS: Why not?

STRANGER: But is it not impossible for that which is affected in this way to be "the one itself"?

THEAETETUS: Why?

STRANGER: Surely "the one," correctly defined, must be spoken of as entirely without parts.

THEAETETUS: It must indeed.

STRANGER: But such a thing,

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...they provide nourishment for the shining ones. The other, however, posited two—the moist and the dry, or the hot and the cold—and joined them together, and sent them forth. The Eleatic doctrine among us, originating from Xenophanes and even from those before him, posits all things as one, and discusses them in a legendary manner. But the Ionian and certain Sicilian muses later than these thought it safer to involve both of these with one another, so that being is both many and one, and is held by discord and concord. <margin>B</margin> For what is at variance always comes together, as the more vehement muses sing. But the more relaxed muses always loosen and suspend these things. And this universe is alternately one and friendly to itself on account of Venus <note>original: "Venerem" / Aphrodite</note>, and then many and distrustful of itself through discord. It is hard to pass judgment against men so famous and ancient, whether they spoke true or false things. This much only we can assert without ill-will.

THEAETETUS: What?

STRANGER: That they have too much contempt for us, the many. For each carries out his own work, with no care for us, whether we follow them in their arguments or not.

THEAETETUS: In what way? he asks.

STRANGER: Whenever one of them says that what "is," or "was," or "becomes," is many <margin>C</margin> or one, or two, and that the hot is mixed with the cold, introducing certain separations and concretions, what, by the gods, Theaetetus, do you suppose is meant by these things? I indeed, when I was younger, if ever that very "non-being" about which we now hesitate were brought forward, I was confident that I understood it exactly. Now you see where we have been brought by doubting this.

THEAETETUS: I see indeed.

STRANGER: But perhaps our mind suffers no less concerning "being." For we used to affirm that we understood this whenever it was brought forward, but the other not at all, whereas I think we understand both in a similar way.

THEAETETUS: Perhaps.

STRANGER: Let the same be said of the other things we narrated above.

THEAETETUS: Indeed.

STRANGER: We shall consider the many later, if it seems right; but concerning the greatest and the principal <margin>D</margin> and the first, we must think now.

THEAETETUS: WHAT do you say? Do you think we should first inquire about being, what they most want to signify who announce it?

STRANGER: You have understood clearly, Theaetetus. I say indeed that we ought to dispute as if they were present, and so to question them: "O you, whoever asserted that hot and cold, or any two such things, are all things, what do you want this to be in both, whenever you say both and each are? What should we understand by this very 'to be' when you utter it? Is it a third something besides those two? If it is so, then three kinds seem now to be posited according to you, not just two. But if you call one of the two 'being' itself, you will not be saying both are in a similar way. For both would be one, not two."

THEAETETUS: You speak the truth.

STRANGER: "Do you wish to call both 'being'?"

THEAETETUS: Perhaps.

STRANGER: "But, O friends," we shall say, "in this way also you would be affirming these two things to be one."

THEAETETUS: You infer correctly. <margin>E</margin>

STRANGER: "Since therefore we have failed in this, at least declare the matter to us finally: what do you want to signify by this name 'being' when you pronounce it? For it is established that you have known the matter for a long time, but we hitherto thought we knew, and now we hesitate. Therefore teach us this first, lest while we think we are learning what you hand down, an opinion should deceive us." If we demand these things from them, as well as from others who posit more than one as the "all" itself, shall we err?

THEAETETUS: Least of all.

STRANGER: What about those who hand down that the "all" is one—should we not inquire as best we can what they call being itself?

THEAETETUS: Why not?

STRANGER: Let them answer these things: "Do you say that there is only one?" "We will say so," they will answer, will they not?

THEAETETUS: Yes.

STRANGER: "Do you call something 'being'?"

THEAETETUS: Certainly.

STRANGER: "Is it the same as 'the one,' using two names for the same thing? Or something else?"

THEAETETUS: How will they answer these things, Stranger?

STRANGER: It is clear, O Theaetetus, that he who has made this assumption will not easily answer these and other objections of this kind.

THEAETETUS: For what reason?

STRANGER: To confess two names, when only one is posited, is absurd.

THEAETETUS: Why not?

STRANGER: Furthermore, it is altogether absurd to accept if anyone should say there is a name, of which there is no account.

THEAETETUS: In what way?

STRANGER: He who posits a name different from the thing, introduces two certain things.

THEAETETUS: It is clear.

STRANGER: Moreover, if he grants the name is the same as the one thing, he will be compelled either to say it is the name of nothing, or if it is the name of something, to confess it is a name of a name, but of nothing else.

THEAETETUS: So it is.

STRANGER: And the one is the one of the one alone; and this name itself is the one being of the name.

THEAETETUS: It is necessary. <margin>G</margin>

STRANGER: What further? Will they say the whole is different from the one being, or the same?

THEAETETUS: Why should they not say so? For they do say it.

STRANGER: If therefore it is a whole, as Parmenides says:
> equal in mass to a sphere well-rounded on all sides, from the center to the circumference entirely equally distant, for nothing is either greater or more powerful than it,
it is necessary because of such a circumference that being itself has a middle and extremes, and therefore also consists of parts.

THEAETETUS: So it must be.

STRANGER: And yet nothing prevents that which is divided into all parts from admitting the *passion* <note>In this philosophical context, "passion" refers to an attribute or a state of being acted upon, rather than an emotion.</note> of the one, and in this way both the "all being" and the "whole" exist as one.

THEAETETUS: Nothing at all.

STRANGER: But is it not impossible for that which suffers these things to be "the one itself"?

THEAETETUS: Why?

STRANGER: Because that which according to true reason is indivisible must be posited as truly and entirely one.

THEAETETUS: It must indeed.

STRANGER: But that which is such, as if from many...

<summary>The Stranger reviews the theories of previous philosophers (Eleatics, Ionians, and Sicilians) on "Being," pointing out that they never clearly explained what they meant by "Being" or "The One," leading to logical contradictions regarding names and parts.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of "Being." The Stranger and Theaetetus are currently examining the theories of Parmenides and others who argued that "All is One." They are now testing whether "Being" can be synonymous with "the Whole" without creating logical contradictions regarding parts and unity.</meta>

...if it is constructed from parts, it will by no means be consistent with universal reason.
**THEAETETUS.** I understand. **STRANGER.** But will the "Whole" itself, by receiving the quality of the "One," thus be both "One" and a "Whole"? Or should we not say at all that "the One" exists as a "Whole"? **THEAETETUS.** You have proposed a difficult choice. **STRANGER.** You speak the truth; for since Being admits to being "One" in a way, it will appear as not identical to "the One," and thus all things will be more than one? **THEAETETUS.** Certainly. **STRANGER.** And yet, if Being is not a "Whole" because it has received that quality from the One, but the "Whole" itself exists, then Being turns out to be in need of itself. **THEAETETUS.** Very much so. **STRANGER.** Indeed, according to this argument, since it is deprived of itself, Being itself will not be Being.

B **THEAETETUS.** That follows. **STRANGER.** And so, once again, all things will be more than one, since Being and the "Whole" have each taken on their own nature apart from the other. **THEAETETUS.** Indeed. **STRANGER.** And if the "Whole" does not exist at all, these same things happen to Being: and besides the fact that it happens not to be, it happens that Being could never have even come into existence. **THEAETETUS.** Why so? **STRANGER.** Whatever has come to be, has always come to be as a whole.
<margin>Whatever has come to be, has always come to be as a whole.</margin>
Therefore, he who does not place "the One" or "the Whole" in the rank of things that are, should not speak of either essence <note>original: "essentiam" / "οὐσίαν". In this context, it refers to "Being" or the fundamental nature of a thing.</note> or generation as existing. **THEAETETUS.** It certainly seems to be so. **STRANGER.** Furthermore, that which is not a "Whole" cannot be a quantity of any kind. For however much a quantity is, it must necessarily be that much of a whole. **THEAETETUS.** Exactly.

C **STRANGER.** Countless other doubts, besides these, arise against Being for anyone who says Being is either only one or only two. **THEAETETUS.** The things we have just shown testify to this. For one doubt after another, each more serious, always arises against these statements. **STRANGER.** We have not yet recounted the arguments of those who distinguish precisely between Being and Non-Being. Nevertheless, let these suffice. Let us now bring forward those who speak differently, so that we may clearly understand from all of them that it is no easier to define what Being is than what Non-Being is. **THEAETETUS.** Certainly, we should approach these men as well. **STRANGER.** There seems to be among them a sort of <term>Battle of the Giants</term> <note>original: "gigantomachia". A reference to the mythological war between the Olympian Gods and the Giants. Plato uses it here to describe the fierce intellectual struggle between materialists and idealists.</note> because of the controversy in which they contend with one another about essence. **THEAETETUS.** In what way? **STRANGER.** Some of them drag everything down from heaven and the invisible region to the earth with their very hands, seizing rocks and oaks.
<margin>The position of those who say that only what is touched exists.</margin>
D For since they touch all such things, they affirm that only that exists which can be perceived and touched in some way, and they define "body" and "essence" as the same thing. But whatever is said to exist without a body, they despise, refusing to hear anything else. **THEAETETUS.** I know the men you speak of. I have met many such people. **STRANGER.** Their adversaries, however, fight very cautiously and piously from above, from an invisible seat, on behalf of an invisible essence, contending that certain intelligible and <term>incorporeal</term> <note>Bodiless or spiritual; existing without physical matter.</note> forms <note>original: "species" / "εἴδη". Often called "Platonic Forms" or "Ideas," these are the perfect, unchanging archetypes of things.</note> constitute true essence. But the bodies of the others, and that which they call "truth," they break into small pieces in their arguments, calling it a "generation" <note>Process of becoming or changing, rather than permanent Being.</note> that flows instead of essence.
<margin>The position of those who say that only what is understood exists.</margin>
E Whence a huge and inextricable battle between both sides has always existed concerning these things. **THEAETETUS.** You speak the truth. **STRANGER.** Let us now demand from both groups, one by one, an account of the "essence" they propose. **THEAETETUS.** How shall we demand it? **STRANGER.** From those who place essence in the Forms, it will be easier, for they are gentler; but from those who violently drag everything toward bodies, it will be harder, and perhaps almost impossible. But it seems we must deal with them in this way. **THEAETETUS.** In what way? **STRANGER.** It would be best to make them better in reality, if it were possible. But if that cannot be done, we must take care to make them better at least in speech, by assuming they would answer more modestly and correctly than they do now. For what is conceded by better men carries more weight than what is conceded by worse men. But we do not care about that; we are seeking the truth.

F **THEAETETUS.** Quite right. **STRANGER.** Command those who have been "made better" to answer you immediately, and interpret what they say. **THEAETETUS.** So be it. **STRANGER.** Do they say that what they call a "mortal animal" is something that exists? **THEAETETUS.** Why wouldn't they? **STRANGER.** And do they not call this an "animated body"? <note>A body with a soul (anima).</note> **THEAETETUS.** Certainly. **STRANGER.** By saying this, do they mean that the soul is something that exists? **THEAETETUS.** Yes. **STRANGER.** And do they think one soul is just and another unjust, one wise and another foolish? **THEAETETUS.** Of course. **STRANGER.** And is it not by the possession and presence of justice and other such qualities that such a soul becomes just, and by the presence of opposites, it becomes the opposite? **THEAETETUS.** They admit this too. **STRANGER.** But will they grant that something which can be present to or absent from a thing is itself "something"? **THEAETETUS.** They certainly grant it. **STRANGER.** Since, therefore, justice and wisdom and every virtue exist, as well as the opposite of each virtue, and also the soul in which these occur, do they believe that each of these can be seen and touched, or not? **THEAETETUS.** Almost none of these can be seen.

G **STRANGER.** Do they think any of these has a body? **THEAETETUS.** They do not give a simple answer to this; they think the soul itself possesses some kind of body, but as for wisdom and the other things you asked about, they do not yet dare to say either that they are nothing at all or that they are all bodies. **STRANGER.** Clearly, Theaetetus, these men have now turned out better. For if they were truly <term>Earth-born</term> <note>original: "indigenæ" / "αὐτόχθονες". Referring to the materialists as if they were the mythological men born directly from the soil, who recognize only physical reality.</note> and from Sparta, they would not be afraid to assert either of these; rather, they would contend that whatever cannot be squeezed in a fist is absolutely nothing. **THEAETETUS.** You have described their feelings almost exactly. **STRANGER.** Let us ask them again. For if they concede that even some small thing is incorporeal, it is enough. For we want them to explain what is common to both these incorporeal things and those that have bodies, which they look at when they say both exist... **THEAETETUS.** They might perhaps be at a loss for an answer...

<column-break/>

...being made of many parts, it will not be in harmony with the whole. **THEAETETUS.** I understand. **STRANGER.** Now, whether the "Whole" has been affected by the "One" so as to be both "One" and a "Whole," or should we not say at all that Being is a "Whole"? **THEAETETUS.** You have stated a difficult choice of alternatives. **STRANGER.** You say what is true. For if Being has been affected so as to be "One" in some way, it will not be the same as the "One," and so all things will be more than one. **THEAETETUS.** Yes. **STRANGER.** And yet, if Being is not a "Whole" by having been affected by that quality, but the "Whole" itself exists, it follows that Being is deficient in itself. **THEAETETUS.** Entirely so. **STRANGER.** And so Being, falling short of itself in this argument, will be Non-Being. **THEAETETUS.** Thus it is. **STRANGER.** And so all things become more than one, with Being and the "Whole" each having taken a nature of their own. **THEAETETUS.** Yes. **STRANGER.** But if the "Whole" does not exist at all, these same things apply to Being, and besides not being, it would never even come into being. **THEAETETUS.** Why? **STRANGER.** That which comes into being has always come into being as a whole. So one should not speak of essence or generation as being real, if one does not place "the One" or "the Whole" among the things that are. **THEAETETUS.** It certainly seems these things are so. **STRANGER.** And further, that which is not a whole must not be a quantity at all; for whatever its quantity may be, it must necessarily be that much of a whole. **THEAETETUS.** Precisely. **STRANGER.** And so a thousand other infinite difficulties will appear to anyone who says that Being is either two things or only one. **THEAETETUS.** The points now coming to light show this. For one thing falls out from another, bringing a greater and more difficult wandering than what was said before. **STRANGER.** Those who speak with precision about Being and Non-Being we have perhaps not fully discussed; nevertheless, let this be enough. Now we must look at those who speak differently, so that we may know from all of them that Being is no less difficult to define than Non-Being. **THEAETETUS.** So we must proceed to the rest of them. **STRANGER.** And indeed, there seems to be a kind of "Battle of the Giants" among them because of their dispute with each other about essence. **THEAETETUS.** How? **STRANGER.** Some drag all things down from heaven and the invisible to the earth, literally grasping rocks and oaks in their hands. For by laying hold of all such things, they insist that only that exists which provides impact and touch, defining "body" and "essence" as the same. And if anyone says that something without a body exists, they despise him utterly and refuse to listen to anything else. **THEAETETUS.** You have described formidable men; I have already met many of them. **STRANGER.** Therefore, those who dispute with them defend themselves very cautiously from above, from some invisible place, insisting that certain intelligible and incorporeal forms are the true essence. But the bodies of the others, and what they call "truth," they break into small pieces in their arguments, calling them a "generation" in flux instead of essence. In the middle of this, Theaetetus, a vast battle between both sides is always going on. **THEAETETUS.** True. **STRANGER.** Let us, then, take an account from both these groups concerning the essence they propose. **THEAETETUS.** How then shall we take it? **STRANGER.** From those who place it in Forms, it is easier (for they are more civilized), but from those who violently drag everything into body, it is harder—perhaps almost impossible. But this is how I think we should act. **THEAETETUS.** How? **STRANGER.** Ideally, if it were possible, we should make them better in their actions; but if this is not allowed, let us make them better in our argument, by assuming they would be more willing to answer lawfully than they are now. For what is agreed upon by better men is more reliable than what is agreed by worse men. We do not care for these things, however, but we seek the truth. **THEAETETUS.** Most right. **STRANGER.** Bid those who have become better to answer you, and interpret what is said by them. **THEAETETUS.** It shall be so. **STRANGER.** Let them say if they affirm there is such a thing as a "mortal animal." **THEAETETUS.** Of course. **STRANGER.** And they will agree this is an "en-souled body"? **THEAETETUS.** Certainly. **STRANGER.** Placing the soul among things that exist? **THEAETETUS.** Yes. **STRANGER.** What then? Do they not say that one soul is just and another unjust? One wise and another foolish? **THEAETETUS.** Certainly. **STRANGER.** But doesn't each of them become so by the possession and presence of justice, and the opposite by the opposite? **THEAETETUS.** Yes, they agree to this too. **STRANGER.** But they will surely say that what is able to be present or absent is "something." **THEAETETUS.** They say so indeed. **STRANGER.** Since, then, justice and wisdom and other virtues exist, and their opposites, and indeed the soul in which these arise—do they say any of them is visible and tangible, or are they all invisible? **THEAETETUS.** Practically none of these is visible. **STRANGER.** What then? Do they say that such things have a body? **THEAETETUS.** To this they no longer all answer the same way. The soul itself seems to them to possess a body, but as for wisdom and each of the other things you asked, they are ashamed to dare either to deny they are among existing things or to insist they are all bodies. **STRANGER.** For clearly, Theaetetus, the men have become better. Since those of them who were truly "sown men" and "earth-born" would be humbled; they would insist that anything they cannot squeeze with their hands is nothing at all. **THEAETETUS.** You say almost exactly what they think. **STRANGER.** Let us ask them again. For if they are willing to admit that even a small part of existing things is incorporeal, that is enough. For what is natural to both these and those things together... looking at which they say both exist... as I myself was saying. **THEAETETUS.** Perhaps they would be at a loss again...

<summary>This page describes the "Battle of the Giants" in Greek philosophy—the conflict between materialists, who believe only physical bodies exist, and idealists, who believe in invisible, incorporeal forms. The Stranger attempts to find a middle ground by forcing the materialists to admit that invisible qualities like "wisdom" and "justice" must exist.</summary>

<meta>The dialogue continues from the previous discussion regarding the nature of Being. Having examined those who believe all is "One" or "Many," the Stranger now attempts to find a common definition of "Being" that both materialists (the "Earth-born") and idealists (the "Friends of Forms") might accept. On the previous page, they discussed how Being cannot be purely a "Whole" or purely "One" without contradiction.</meta>

...if they have experienced something of this sort.

**STRANGER.** See whether they would be willing to accept and agree to a proposal from us of the following kind. **THEAETETUS.** What sort of proposal? **STRANGER.** I say that anything which possesses any sort of power <note>original: "δύναμιν" / "potentiam". Plato introduces a famous "functional" definition of Being here: to be is to have the capacity to affect or be affected.</note>, whether to act upon another thing of any nature, or to be acted upon even in the slightest degree by the most trivial thing, even if only once—everything of this sort truly "is." For I set down a definition to define those things which "are," that Being is nothing else but power. **THEAETETUS.** Well, since they themselves have nothing better to say at present, they accept this. **STRANGER.** Very well. Perhaps later on something else might appear to both us and to them. For now, let this remain agreed upon between us and them. **THEAETETUS.** It remains so.
<margin>B</margin>
**STRANGER.** Let us now go to the others, the "Friends of Forms" <note>A term likely referring to earlier Platonists or followers of Italian philosophy who believed true reality consists of unchanging, non-material Ideas.</note>. You must interpret their views for us. **THEAETETUS.** It shall be done. **STRANGER.** Do you not say that "Being" <note>original: "οὐσίαν" / "essentiam"</note> is one thing, and "Becoming" <note>original: "γένεσιν" / "generationem"</note> is another, keeping them separate? **THEAETETUS.** Yes. **STRANGER.** And you say that with the body, through sensation, we communicate with "Becoming," but with the soul, through reasoning, we communicate with "True Being"—which you say always remains the same and in the same state, whereas "Becoming" varies from one time to another. **THEAETETUS.** We do indeed say that.
<margin>C</margin>
**STRANGER.** But this "communicating," O best of men, what do you say it is in both cases? Is it not what we just said? **THEAETETUS.** What was that? **STRANGER.** An experience or an action <note>original: "πάθημα ἢ ποίημα". These terms refer to "passion" (being acted upon) and "action" (doing something).</note> arising from some power based on things coming together with one another. Perhaps, Theaetetus, you do not hear their answer to this, but I do, perhaps, because of my long habit with them. **THEAETETUS.** What then do they say? **STRANGER.** That "Becoming" participates in the power of being acted upon and acting, but they say the power of neither of these fits with "Being." **THEAETETUS.** Is there not some sense in what they say? **STRANGER.** To which we must reply that we need to learn more clearly from them whether they agree that the soul knows, and that Being is known. **THEAETETUS.** They certainly say that. **STRANGER.** What then? Do you call "knowing" or "being known" an action, or a passion, or both? Or is one a passion and the other an action? Or does neither participate in either of these at all? **THEAETETUS.** Clearly they would say neither participates in either; otherwise, they would be saying the opposite of what they granted before. **STRANGER.** I understand.
<margin>D</margin>
**STRANGER.** For if knowing is to act upon something, it necessarily follows that the thing being known is acted upon. Thus "Being" <note>original: "οὐσίαν"</note>, being known by the act of knowledge, would, insofar as it is known, be moved because of being acted upon—which we say could not happen to that which is at rest. **THEAETETUS.** Correct.
<margin>E</margin>
**STRANGER.** But for Zeus' sake! Are we to be easily persuaded that movement, life, soul, and wisdom are not present in that which perfectly "is"? Can we imagine it neither lives nor thinks, but stays standing, motionless, a solemn and holy thing without mind? **THEAETETUS.** That would be a terrifying thing to admit, Stranger. **STRANGER.** But shall we say it has mind, but not life? **THEAETETUS.** How could we? **STRANGER.** But if we say both are in it, must we not also say it possesses them in a soul? **THEAETETUS.** How else could it have them? **STRANGER.** But then, if it has mind, life, and soul, can it possibly stand completely motionless while being alive? **THEAETETUS.** All these things seem to me to be entirely irrational.
<margin>F</margin>
**STRANGER.** Therefore, both that which is moved and movement itself must be admitted as things that "are." **THEAETETUS.** Of course. **STRANGER.** It follows then, Theaetetus, that if things are motionless, mind cannot exist anywhere, about anything, in any way. **THEAETETUS.** Precisely. **STRANGER.** And yet, if we grant that all things are in motion and flux, we shall also remove "mind" from the category of things that "are" by that very argument. **THEAETETUS.** How so? **STRANGER.** Does it seem to you that "sameness" and "being in the same state" and "acting toward the same thing" could ever exist without rest? **THEAETETUS.** In no way. **STRANGER.** Do you see mind existing or having ever come to be anywhere without these? **THEAETETUS.** Not at all. **STRANGER.** Indeed, one must fight with every argument against anyone who, by doing away with knowledge, wisdom, or mind, makes a strong assertion about anything whatsoever. **THEAETETUS.** Very much so.
<margin>G</margin>
**STRANGER.** It seems then that the philosopher, who honors these things above all, must for these reasons refuse to accept that "the All" is at rest, whether from those who speak of one form or many; nor should he listen to those who move Being in every way. Instead, like a child's prayer for "both together," he should say that "Being" and "the All" consist of both: whatever is unmoved and whatever is moved. **THEAETETUS.** Most true. **STRANGER.** What then? Do we not seem now to have fairly encompassed "Being" in our argument? **THEAETETUS.** Certainly. **STRANGER.** But oh, Theaetetus, how little we knew! Now we are about to see the difficulty of this investigation. **THEAETETUS.** Why so? What do you mean by this? **STRANGER.** My dear friend, do you not realize that we are now in the greatest ignorance about "Being," yet we think we are saying something meaningful? **THEAETETUS.** I don't quite see how we have fallen into this state without noticing. **STRANGER.** Look more closely, whether by agreeing to these things we might not be rightly asked the same questions we ourselves asked those who said the "All" was "Hot and Cold." **THEAETETUS.** Remind me what those were. **STRANGER.** Certainly; and I will try to do this by questioning you, just as I questioned them then, so that we may make some progress together. **THEAETETUS.** Rightly said.

<column-break/>

...if some such thing should happen to them. **STRANGER.** See whether they would be willing to admit that Being is such a thing as we propose. **THEAETETUS.** Declare what it is. **STRANGER.** I say that whatever has obtained any power whatsoever, either for acting upon another, or

suffering <note>original: "patiendum". In this context, to "suffer" means to be the object of an action, rather than to feel pain.</note> from another, however small and from the most trivial source, and even if only once—anything of that sort truly exists. And by this statement I define Being as nothing other than "power" <note>original: "potentiam"</note>. **THEAETETUS.** Since they have nothing better than this to say at present, they accept it. **STRANGER.** Good; perhaps later it will seem otherwise to us and to them. <margin>The soul knows, essence is known.</margin>
**STRANGER.** To this they say that "Becoming" participates in the power of acting and suffering, but no such power is suited to "Essence." **THEAETETUS.** Is there not something in what they say? **STRANGER.** To this we must object with what we desire to hear more clearly from them: whether they assent that the soul knows, and essence is known. **THEAETETUS.** They certainly affirm it. **STRANGER.** Do you call knowing or being known an "action," or a "passion," or both? Or do you want one to be a suffering and the other an acting, or neither of these to participate in the other at all? It is clear they would say "neither in the other." Otherwise, they would now be admitting the opposites of what they had conceded before. **THEAETETUS.** I understand. **STRANGER.** If indeed knowing were to act upon something, it would follow that what is known must "suffer" or be acted upon. And therefore, by this logic, "Essence" would happen to be acted upon by the act of cognition while it is being known: and insofar as it is known, it is acted upon; and insofar as it is acted upon, it is also moved. Which we say cannot happen regarding a stable thing. **THEAETETUS.** But what; tell me by Jove, can it truly be 
<margin>All things are moved.</margin>
<margin>From that which truly is, life, soul, and motion cannot be absent.</margin>
thought that motion, life, soul, and wisdom are entirely absent from that which is totally and truly Being? Does it neither live, nor think, nor possess a venerable and holy mind, but instead stands motionless? **THEAETETUS.** It would be too absurd, Stranger, if that were conceded. **STRANGER.** Shall we say it has mind, but not life? **THEAETETUS.** How so? **STRANGER.** Or shall we say both are in it, yet not contained by it in a soul? **THEAETETUS.** But in what other way would it contain them? **STRANGER.** Must it be said to have mind, life, and soul? Yet while being entirely animate, does it stand motionless? **THEAETETUS.** All these things seem to me to lack reason. **STRANGER.** Therefore it must be confessed that what is moved and motion itself are present as things that exist. **THEAETETUS.** What prevents it? **STRANGER.** From this, O Theaetetus, it follows that "mind" is present to none of the immobile things, nowhere, and in no way. **THEAETETUS.** It follows plainly. **STRANGER.** Nevertheless, if we agree that all things are driven and moved, by this speech we shall take "sameness" itself out of the genus of existing things. **THEAETETUS.** In what way? **STRANGER.** Does it seem to you that what is called "according to the same things, in the same way, and regarding the same thing" can ever exist without a state of rest? **THEAETETUS.** By no means. **STRANGER.** Do you see mind anywhere, either having been or being, without these? **THEAETETUS.** Not at all. **STRANGER.** One must fight with every effort of reason against him who, having removed science, prudence, and mind, asserts anything else. **THEAETETUS.** And vehemently so. **STRANGER.** It is necessary for him who philosophizes, and who honors these things above all, for that reason neither to admit the speech of those who, introducing one or many species of things, say the "Whole" stands alone; nor should he listen to those who affirm that Being is moved only. Rather, according to the opinion of children, having encompassed all things as many as either stand or move, he should call both together "Being" and "the All." **THEAETETUS.** You speak the truth. **STRANGER.** Do we not seem now to have properly encompassed Being in our speech? **THEAETETUS.** Entirely. **STRANGER.** Oh my, Theaetetus, in what great ambiguity are we now turned? For nothing else now seems to be known to me except 
<margin>Second definition of being.</margin>
the difficulty of the consideration. **THEAETETUS.** Why this? **STRANGER.** Do you not see, O blessed one, that while we were utterly ignorant...

---

<meta>Catchword: ramus, (we were ignorant)</meta>

...of it, we nevertheless thought we were saying something about it?
**STRANGER.** Observe more diligently, I pray, whether in the present case we, having granted these things, might not be interrogated just as we interrogated those who wanted "the All" to be "the Hot and the Cold."

<column-break/>

**THEAETETUS.** I also think so, but where we have deceived ourselves, I do not plainly understand.
**THEAETETUS.** In what way? Remind me if it pleases you. **STRANGER.** It pleases me indeed, and I shall endeavor to do it, seeking from you now in the same way as from them, so that we may make some progress. **THEAETETUS.** Excellent.

o iij

<summary>In this pivotal passage of the Sophist, the Stranger defines "Being" as the power to act or be acted upon and argues that "True Being" cannot be static; it must encompass life, soul, mind, and therefore both movement and rest.</summary>

<meta>Continuity note: On the previous page, the Stranger and Theaetetus arrived at a functional definition of "Being" as "power" or the capacity to act or be acted upon. They are now testing this definition against the concepts of Motion and Rest to see if Being can truly encompass both.</meta>

# OF PLATO

<margin>A</margin>
<margin>Third definition of being.</margin>
**STRANGER.** Do you not call motion and rest <note>original: "κίνησιν καὶ στάσιν" / "motum & statum"</note> the greatest of opposites? **THEAETETUS.** Why not? **STRANGER.** Yet you say that they both equally "are," and that both together and each individually exist? **THEAETETUS.** I certainly do. **STRANGER.** When you concede that both and each "are," do you then mean that they are "moving"? **THEAETETUS.** In no way. **STRANGER.** Or do you perhaps mean that they "stand still," when you say both and each "are"? **THEAETETUS.** Not that either. **STRANGER.** Therefore, you think of Being itself as some third thing, as if motion and rest were contained under it; you encompass both, and looking toward their shared participation in essence, you thus say they both "are." **THEAETETUS.** We truly seem to be divining that Being is some third thing when we say that motion and rest exist. **STRANGER.** For this reason, Being itself is not both motion and rest together, but something else besides them.

<margin>B</margin>
**THEAETETUS.** So it appears. **STRANGER.** Being, then, by its own nature, neither stands still nor moves. **THEAETETUS.** That is almost what we must say. **STRANGER.** Where then should the mind turn if it wishes to have any firm and clear understanding of Being? **THEAETETUS.** I do not know. **STRANGER.** I think it is nowhere easy. For if a thing does not move, how can it not stand still? Or that which in no way stands still, how can it not move? Yet Being has appeared to us to be outside both of these; is that possible? **THEAETETUS.** It is the most impossible thing of all.

<margin>C</margin>
**STRANGER.** We ought to remember this for the present. **THEAETETUS.** What is that? **STRANGER.** That when we were asked what the name of "Non-Being" <note>original: "μὴ ὄντος" / "non entis"</note> should be applied to, we were caught in utter perplexity. Do you remember? **THEAETETUS.** How could I not? **STRANGER.** Are we then now in any less perplexity regarding Being? **THEAETETUS.** To me, Stranger, if it can be said, we seem to be in even greater difficulty now. **STRANGER.** Let this then be set down as our impasse <note>original: "ἀπορίαν" / "ambiguum"</note>. Since both Being and Non-Being have shared equally in our confusion, there is hope that if one of them appears more clearly or more obscurely, the other will appear in the same way. And if we can see neither, we shall push through the argument as decently as we can, dealing with both at once. **THEAETETUS.** Well said.

<margin>D</margin>
**STRANGER.** Let us explain clearly in what way we call this same thing by many names. Give an example of this. **STRANGER.** Calling a single man by many names, we attribute to him colors, shapes, sizes, virtues, and vices; in all these and many other things, we say he is not only a "man," but also "good" and many other things. Whatever single thing we posit, we then call it many things by many names. **THEAETETUS.** You speak the truth.

<margin>E</margin>
**STRANGER.** From this, I believe, we have provided a feast for the young and for those old men who are late-learners <note>original: "ὀψιμαθέσι" / "tardo ingenio senibus". This refers to people who come to philosophy late in life and get stuck on simple logical puzzles.</note>. For it is easy for anyone to immediately object that it is impossible for the many to be one, and the one to be many. They take delight in not allowing a man to be called "good," but they want "good" to be called "good," and "man" to be called "man." You have often, I think, Theaetetus, run into people who study such quibbles—mostly older men who admire these things because of their poverty of wisdom, and who boast as if they had discovered something magnificent. **THEAETETUS.** Very much so.

<margin>F</margin>
**STRANGER.** In order then that our argument may encompass all who have ever spoken anything regarding essence, let the questions we shall now pose be understood as directed both toward these men and toward the others we discussed before. **THEAETETUS.** What sort of questions? **STRANGER.** Whether we shall neither join essence with motion and rest, nor anything else with anything else, but rather treat them as if things cannot communicate with each other, and separate them entirely in our speech? Or shall we force everything together, as if everything could be mixed? Or is it possible for some things, but not for others? Which of these, Theaetetus, do we think they would choose? **THEAETETUS.** I do not know how to answer for them. Why don't you investigate what follows from each choice by answering yourself? **STRANGER.** Good advice. Let us suppose, if you will, that they say nothing has the power to communicate with anything in any way. Would not motion and rest then have no share in essence? **THEAETETUS.** Certainly not. **STRANGER.** Then will either of them exist, since neither shares in essence? **THEAETETUS.** It will not. **STRANGER.** By this admission, it seems everything is immediately overturned—the doctrines of those who say all things move, those who say all things stand still as "One," and those who believe things "are" according to Forms <note>original: "κατ’ εἴδη" / "secundum species"</note> that always remain the same. For they all add "Being" to their theories, some saying things truly move, others saying things truly stand still. **THEAETETUS.** Quite so.

<margin>G</margin>
**STRANGER.** Furthermore, those who sometimes combine all things and sometimes divide them—whether they divide into "One" and from "One" into "Infinite," or into limited elements and then compose from them—whether they say this happens in turn or always—all of them would be saying nothing true if there is no mixture of things. **THEAETETUS.** Correct. **STRANGER.** Moreover, we would be conducting our own discourse most absurdly if we permitted nothing to be called by the name of another through the sharing of properties. **THEAETETUS.** How so? **STRANGER.** They are forced to use the word "Being" regarding everything, as well as "apart," "from others," "by itself," and countless other terms. Since they cannot refrain from including these in their speech, they do not need others to refute them, but as the saying goes, they have an enemy and adversary at home 
<margin>Proverb.</margin>
muttering within them, walking about like that strange Eurycles <note>A famous Athenian ventriloquist who was believed to have a prophetic spirit speaking from his belly. Here, it refers to a person whose own words contradict their theories.</note>, always carrying him around. **THEAETETUS.** What you say is very true and—

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
**STRANGER.** Very well then. Do you not say that motion and rest are most opposite to one another? **THEAETETUS.** How could I not? **STRANGER.** And yet you say that both of them, and each of them, equally "are"? **THEAETETUS.** I do indeed. **STRANGER.** And when you say they both and each exist, do you mean they are moving? **THEAETETUS.** Not at all. **STRANGER.** But do you mean they are standing still when you say both of them are? **THEAETETUS.** And how could I? **STRANGER.** Do you then place Being in the soul as a third thing alongside these, as if motion and rest were grasped and contained by it? Seeing their communion with essence, is that why you say they both "are"? **THEAETETUS.** We seem truly to be divining Being as a third, different thing whenever we say that motion and rest exist. **STRANGER.** Therefore, Being is not both motion and rest together, but something else besides them.

<margin>B</margin>
**THEAETETUS.** It seems so. **STRANGER.** According to its own nature, then, Being neither stands still nor moves. **THEAETETUS.** Almost. **STRANGER.** Where then must one turn the mind who wishes to establish for himself any clear certainty about Being? **THEAETETUS.** Where indeed? **STRANGER.** I think it is no longer easy to turn anywhere. For if something does not move, how is it not standing still? Or that which in no way stands still, how is it not moving? Yet Being has now appeared to us apart from both of these; is this possible? **THEAETETUS.** It is the most impossible of all things. **STRANGER.** It is right then to be reminded of this in these circumstances. **THEAETETUS.** Reminded of what? **STRANGER.** That when we were asked where the name of "Non-Being" should be applied, we were 

<margin>C</margin>
completely stuck in perplexity. Do you remember? **THEAETETUS.** How could I not? **STRANGER.** Are we then now in any less perplexity regarding Being? **THEAETETUS.** To me, Stranger, if it is possible to say so, we appear to be in more. **STRANGER.** Let this then be laid down as our perplexity. But since Being and Non-Being have shared equally in the difficulty, there is now hope that if one of them—whether the more obscure or the more clear—should come to light, the other will also come to light in the same way. And if we are unable to see either, we shall at least try to push our argument through as respectably as possible, dealing with both together. **THEAETETUS.** Good.

<margin>D</margin>
**STRANGER.** Let us say, then, in what way we call this same thing by many names on each occasion. **THEAETETUS.** Give me an example; what do you mean? **STRANGER.** We speak of a man, surely, and give him many additional names, mentioning his different colors, shapes, sizes, and his vices and virtues. In all these and a thousand other ways, we say he is not only a man but also "good," and an infinite number of other things. And in the same way, assuming each other thing is "one," we then speak of it as "many" and by many names. **THEAETETUS.** You speak the truth.

<margin>E</margin>
**STRANGER.** This, I believe, is how we have provided a feast for the young and for those old men who are late-learners. For it is easy for any man to grasp immediately that it is impossible for the many to be one and the one to be many. And they certainly delight in it, not allowing one to call a man "good," but rather the good is "good" and the man is "man." For I think you have often, Theaetetus, met people who take such things seriously—sometimes older men who, because of their poverty in acquiring wisdom, marvel at such things, and even think they have found something of supreme wisdom. **THEAETETUS.** Entirely so. **STRANGER.** So that our argument may be addressed to all who have ever discussed anything about essence, let what we are now about to say in the form of questions be addressed to these men and to all the others with whom we have previously conversed. **THEAETETUS.** What sort of things? **STRANGER.** Should we neither attach essence to motion and rest, nor anything else to anything else, but treat them as being unmixed and impossible to partake in one another, and so place them in our arguments? Or shall we bring all things together into the same, as if they were able to communicate with one another? Or some things and not others? Which of these, Theaetetus, should we say they would choose? 

<margin>F</margin>
**THEAETETUS.** I have nothing to answer on their behalf; why don't you carry out what follows from each of these choices in your own answers? **STRANGER.** You speak well. Let us suppose them to say first, if you will, that nothing has any power of communion with anything else for any purpose. Will motion and rest then have no share in essence? **THEAETETUS.** No, they will not. **STRANGER.** What then? Will either of them exist if it does not share in essence? **THEAETETUS.** It will not exist. **STRANGER.** Quickly, it seems, all theories have been overturned—both those of the people who move the universe, those who make it stand still as "One," and those who say that things which "are" consist of Forms that are always the same. For all these people attach "Being" to their theories, some saying things "truly move," others that they "truly stand still." **THEAETETUS.** Exactly so.

<margin>G</margin>
**STRANGER.** And furthermore, those who sometimes combine all things and sometimes divide them—whether they speak of an infinite number of things coming from "One" and into "One," or of elements that have a limit and are combined from these—likewise, whether they say this happens in turn or always; in all these cases they would be saying nothing if there is no mixture. **THEAETETUS.** Correct. **STRANGER.** Moreover, those who allow no thing to be called by another's name through the sharing of a property would have carried out their argument most ridiculously of all. **THEAETETUS.** How? **STRANGER.** They are forced to use the word "Being" about everything, and "apart," and "from others," and "by itself," and a thousand other terms. Being unable to refrain from these or to keep them out of their speech, they do not need others to refute them, but—as the saying goes—they have an enemy at home always ready to contradict them, and they go about always carrying that absurd Eurycles inside them like a living thing. **THEAETETUS.** What you say is very similar and—

<summary>In this passage, Plato explores the "Third Definition of Being," arguing that Being must be a distinct category that allows for the communion of opposites like Motion and Rest. He refutes "late-learners" who deny that one thing can have multiple attributes, showing that if things could not "blend" or communicate, all philosophical systems would collapse.</summary>

<keywords>Plato, Being, Motion, Rest, Communion of Forms, Aporia, Eurycles the Ventriloquist, Late-learners, Ontology, Sophist</keywords>

<meta>Continuity note: On the previous page, the Stranger and Theaetetus concluded that Being is a distinct third concept from Motion and Rest. They are now moving to investigate the "communion of kinds"—how different concepts can or cannot combine with one another.</meta>

### THE SOPHIST

<margin>A</margin>
**STRANGER.** What if we say that everything has the power of mutual communion with one another? This is something I myself can refute.
**THEAETETUS.** In what way?
**STRANGER.** Because motion itself would altogether stand still, and rest, in turn, would move, if they were to mingle with one another. But by the highest necessity, it is impossible for motion to stand still and for rest to move.
**THEAETETUS.** How could it be otherwise?
**STRANGER.** Then only the third option remains.
**THEAETETUS.** Yes.
**STRANGER.** Indeed, one of these is necessary: either everything blends, or nothing does, or some things are willing to mix and others are not.
**THEAETETUS.** Certainly.
**STRANGER.** And we found that the first two are impossible.
**THEAETETUS.** Yes.
<margin>B</margin>
**STRANGER.** Therefore, anyone who wishes to answer correctly will posit the remaining of the three.
**THEAETETUS.** Quite so.
**STRANGER.** Now, since some are willing to do this and others are not, they are in much the same condition as letters. For some letters do not fit with one another, while others do fit.
**THEAETETUS.** Of course.
**STRANGER.** The vowels, differently from the others, run through them all like a bond <note>original: "δεσμός" (desmos)</note>, so that without one of them, it is impossible for the other letters to fit one to another.
**THEAETETUS.** Very much so.
**STRANGER.** Does everyone know which kinds can associate with which? Or is an art needed for the one who intends to do this sufficiently?
**THEAETETUS.** An art is needed.
**STRANGER.** Which one?
**THEAETETUS.** The art of grammar.
<margin>C</margin>
**STRANGER.** And is it not the same regarding high and low sounds? The one who has the art to know which are blended and which are not is a musician; the one who does not understand is unmusical?
**THEAETETUS.** It is so.
**STRANGER.** and we shall find similar things in the other arts and lack of arts.
**THEAETETUS.** Of course.
**STRANGER.** Then, since we have agreed that the kinds <term>kinds: also known as "forms" or "genera"—the fundamental categories of reality</term> relate to one another in the same way regarding mixing, is it not necessary to proceed through arguments with a certain science if one is to correctly show which kinds harmonize with which, and which do not admit one another? And also, whether there are certain kinds that run through all of them, holding them together so that they are able to blend? And again, in divisions, whether there are others that run through the wholes and are the causes of the division?
<margin>D</margin>
**THEAETETUS.** How could there not be a need for science, and perhaps nearly the greatest of them all?
**STRANGER.** What then, Theaetetus, shall we call this one? Or, by Zeus, have we stumbled unknowingly into the science of free men, and do we risk, while seeking the Sophist, having found the Philosopher first?
**THEAETETUS.** What do you mean?
**STRANGER.** Dividing by kinds, and neither thinking the same form <note>original: "εἶδος" (eidos)</note> to be another, nor another to be the same—shall we not say that this belongs to the science of dialectic <term>dialectic: the highest form of philosophical reasoning and logic</term>?
**THEAETETUS.** Yes, we shall.
**STRANGER.** Therefore, the one who is able to do this perceives clearly one idea extended everywhere through many, where each one lies apart, and many ideas different from one another encompassed from without by one, and again one idea connected in one through many wholes, and many ideas entirely set apart.
<margin>E</margin>
This is to know how to distinguish by kind how individual things can commune and how they cannot.
**THEAETETUS.** Entirely so.
**STRANGER.** But surely, you will not grant the practice of dialectic to anyone else, I imagine, except to the one who philosophizes purely and justly.
**THEAETETUS.** How could it be given to anyone else?
**STRANGER.** We shall find the philosopher in such a place as this, both now and later, if we look for him, though he too is difficult to see clearly; however, the difficulty in seeing the Sophist is of one kind, and that of the philosopher is of another.
**THEAETETUS.** How so?
**STRANGER.** The Sophist runs away into the darkness of "non-being," making contact with it by habit, and because of the darkness of the place, he is hard to perceive. Is it not so?
**THEAETETUS.** It seems so.
**STRANGER.** But the philosopher, always adhering to the idea of "being" through reasoning, is not at all easy to see because of the brightness of the region.
<margin>F</margin>
For the eyes of the souls of the many <margin>The eyes of common souls cannot endure the rays of divinity.</margin> are unable to endure looking toward the divine.
**THEAETETUS.** This is likely to be no less true than the other.
**STRANGER.** Then we shall perhaps look into this more clearly soon, if we still wish to; but we must not let the Sophist go until we have sufficiently observed him.
**THEAETETUS.** You have spoken well.
**STRANGER.** Since, then, it has been agreed that some of the kinds are willing to commune with one another and some are not, and some with a few, others with many, and some even through all, so that nothing prevents them from having communed with all—let us follow the argument next, looking at it in this way: not concerning all the forms, so that we are not confused by the multitude, but selecting some of the greatest <margin>G</margin> among those that are spoken of. Let us see what each of them is, and then what power of communion they have with one another. Thus, even if we cannot grasp "being" and "non-being" with complete clarity, we shall at least not lack a proper account of them, as far as the manner of our current inquiry allows. If we can somehow say that "non-being" really is "non-being," let us hope to escape unscathed.
**THEAETETUS.** It is necessary to do so.
**STRANGER.** The greatest of the kinds which we just went through are being itself, and rest, and motion.
**THEAETETUS.** Very much so.
**STRANGER.** And we say that two of these are unmixed with each other.
**THEAETETUS.** Certainly.
**STRANGER.** But being is mixed with both, for both, in some way, "are."
**THEAETETUS.** Of course.
**STRANGER.** These then become three.
**THEAETETUS.** Indeed.
**STRANGER.** Therefore, each of them is "other" than the remaining two, but the "same" as itself.
<margin>H</margin>
**THEAETETUS.** It is so.
**STRANGER.** But what do we mean now when we say "the same" and "the other"? Are they two kinds, different from the three mentioned, yet necessarily always joined with them? And should we consider five kinds instead of three? Or are "the same" and "the other" actually one of those...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
...similar. **STRANGER.** But what if we say that all things have the power of mutual communion? Surely even I can refute this. **THEAETETUS.** By what reasoning? **STRANGER.** Because motion itself would entirely rest, and rest would be moved, if they were mixed in turn. But this is impossible by a certain supreme necessity, that motion stands or rest moves. **THEAETETUS.** Why not. **STRANGER.** Thus only the third remains. **THEAETETUS.** Indeed. **STRANGER.** For one of these is necessary: either all things mix, or none, or some mix and others do not. **THEAETETUS.** Altogether necessary. **STRANGER.** Two of these cannot be found to be true. **THEAETETUS.** Certainly not. <margin>B</margin> **STRANGER.** It follows that whoever wishes to answer correctly must posit the remaining one of the three. **THEAETETUS.** Very much so. **STRANGER.** Since some things want to come together and others do not, it is much the same with things as it is with letters. For some letters are coupled with one another, and some are not. **THEAETETUS.** It is evident. **STRANGER.** The series of vowel letters is stretched through all the others like a bond, without which no other letters can be bound together. **THEAETETUS.** And very much so indeed. **STRANGER.** Does everyone understand which letters agree with which? Or is there a need for art so that it may be done correctly? **THEAETETUS.** For art. **STRANGER.** Which? **THEAETETUS.** Grammar. <margin>C</margin> **STRANGER.** Is it not the same regarding the sounds of low and high? For he who distinguishes consonant or dissonant voices by art is a musician; he who is ignorant is devoid of music. **THEAETETUS.** It is so. **STRANGER.** And in other arts and the defects of arts, we shall find other such things. **THEAETETUS.** That is manifest. **STRANGER.** Since we have said that the kinds of things have mutual communion in the same way, must not a certain science conduct the discourse, whoever is to correctly show which kinds agree with which, or are dissonant? Moreover, to know through all things if they agree, so that they can be mixed, and again in divisions, if through all things the other is the cause of the division? **THEAETETUS.** There is certainly a need for science, and almost the greatest of all. <margin>D</margin> **STRANGER.** What then shall we call this, Theaetetus? Have we, by Jove, inadvertently fallen into the science of free men? And while we were seeking the Sophist, we seem to have found the philosopher first. **THEAETETUS.** How so? **STRANGER.** To divide by kinds, and neither to think the same species to be another, nor again to think another is the same, shall we not say this is the duty of dialectic? **THEAETETUS.** We shall certainly say so. **STRANGER.** Whoever can do this sharply perceives one idea extended everywhere through many, with each positioned separately, and many which are diverse among themselves encompassed from without under one, and again one idea through all those many, joined in one, and many separately and entirely distinct. <margin>E</margin> This, however, is to know how to discern by kind how individual things can communicate in turn, and how they cannot. **THEAETETUS.** Entirely. **STRANGER.** But you will give the work of dialectic to no other, I think, than to the one who philosophizes purely and legitimately. **THEAETETUS.** How could it be given to another? **STRANGER.** We shall find the philosopher in such a place both now and in the future, if we look, although he too cannot be easily seen. But the philosopher escapes the gaze of the eyes for one reason, the Sophist for another. <margin>How the philosopher and the sophist remain hidden.</margin> **THEAETETUS.** How? **STRANGER.** I place the Sophist as one who flees into the darkness of "non-being," and by long habit is poured over by those shadows; therefore, he is discerned with the greatest difficulty. **THEAETETUS.** So it is. **STRANGER.** But the philosopher, always clinging to the reasoning of the idea of "being" itself, is not easily seen because of the splendor of that region. <margin>F</margin> <margin>The eyes of common souls cannot endure the rays of divinity.</margin> For the eyes of common souls cannot endure the rays of divinity. **THEAETETUS.** It is agreeable that those things are so no less than the others. **STRANGER.** We shall treat this more clearly elsewhere, if it be our will. But the Sophist must not be dismissed before he has been sufficiently recognized by us. **THEAETETUS.** Excellent. **STRANGER.** Since, therefore, it is agreed between us that some of the kinds meet in turn and some altogether disagree, and some with few, others with many, and some even through all things with all things, let us next follow the reasoning of this discourse, considering it in this way. Not about all species, I say, lest we be confounded by the multitude, but choosing some of those which are called the greatest, <margin>G</margin> first indeed what kind each one is, then what power of mutual communion they have, so that "being" and "non-being," if we cannot grasp them with a completely clear notion, at least we may not lack a suitable way of disputing about them, as far as the condition of this investigation allows. So that if we say "non-being" is, as if by imagining it, and in truth it is non-being, we may perhaps escape innocent. **THEAETETUS.** It is indeed fitting. **STRANGER.** The greatest kinds of all, which we were just mentioning, are being itself, and rest, and motion. **THEAETETUS.** Greatly so. **STRANGER.** It must be said that these two cannot be mixed with each other. **THEAETETUS.** Certainly. <margin>H</margin> **STRANGER. BEING**, however, is mixed with both, for both in a certain way "are." **THEAETETUS.** Nothing prevents it. **STRANGER.** It follows that these are three. **THEAETETUS.** It follows. **STRANGER.** And is not any of these "other" than the remaining two, but the "same" as itself? **THEAETETUS.** It is. **STRANGER.** Why then have we now said "the same" and "the other"? Are they two kinds other than the three above, yet necessarily always annexed to them? And so should we think of five kinds? Or are "the same" and "the other" one of those...

<summary>This page defines the science of Dialectic as the ability to correctly divide reality into its fundamental kinds (genera) and identifies the "Greatest Kinds": Being, Rest, Motion, Same, and Different. It also contrasts the Philosopher, who is hidden by the blinding light of truth, with the Sophist, who hides in the darkness of non-existence.</summary>

...did we state something, which nevertheless escaped us? **THEAETETUS.** Perhaps.

**THEAETETUS.** Rightly indeed. **STRANGER.** Moreover, if in any way motion itself admitted "rest," it would not be absurd to call it "stable motion." **THEAETETUS.** Correct, provided we have granted that some of the kinds are willing to communicate with one another, and others are not.

<summary>This page features a pivotal dialogue where the Stranger and Theaetetus identify the "Five Greatest Kinds" of reality: Being, Motion, Rest, The Same, and The Other. Crucially, they define "non-being" not as the opposite of existence, but as "Otherness," allowing things to both "be" themselves and "not be" other things simultaneously.</summary>

# SOPHISTA.

...we shall assert that "Not" and "Neither" signify something from among the number of "others" when they precede names—or rather, whenever they precede the very things about which the names following the negation are pronounced. **THEAETETUS.** That is entirely so. **STRANGER.** Let us consider this further, if it seems right to you. **THEAETETUS.** What is that? **STRANGER.** The nature of <term>The Other</term> <note>original: "alterum", meaning difference or the quality of being distinct</note> <margin>A meditation on the nature of "the Other."</margin> seems to be partitioned in the same way that <term>Knowledge</term> <note>original: "scientia" / "episteme"</note> is. **THEAETETUS.** In what way? **STRANGER.** Knowledge is one, yet each part of it that resides in a particular subject and is marked off on its own has received its own special name; because of this, there are said to be many arts and sciences. **THEAETETUS.** Certainly. **STRANGER.** Don't the parts of the nature of "The Other"—which is also one—suffer the same fate? **THEAETETUS.** Perhaps. But let us say in what way. **STRANGER.** Is there a part of "The Other" that is set in opposition to the <term>Beautiful</term>? **THEAETETUS.** There is. **STRANGER.** Shall we say this part is nameless, or does it have a name? **THEAETETUS.** It has a name. For that which we call "not beautiful" in each case is nothing other than what is different from the nature of the beautiful. **STRANGER.** Come then, tell me this. **THEAETETUS.** What? **STRANGER.** When something is marked off as a part of the things that exist, and is in turn set against something else that exists, does it not follow that this is what "the not-beautiful" is? **THEAETETUS.** It does. **STRANGER.** It follows, then, that "the not-beautiful" is indeed a certain reality, since it exists as that to which it is opposed. **THEAETETUS.** Very true. **STRANGER.** What then? Must we conclude that the "beautiful" belongs to the number of existing things more so than the "not-beautiful"? **THEAETETUS.** Not at all. <margin>Proof that non-being exists.</margin> **STRANGER.** Similarly, then, "the not-great" must be said to exist just as much as "the great" itself. **THEAETETUS.** Similarly. **STRANGER.** And should we not also place "the not-just" on the same level as "the just," so that one is no more a "being" than the other? **THEAETETUS.** Without a doubt. **STRANGER.** And the same reasoning will apply to other things, since the nature of "The Other" has appeared to be among the kinds of existing things. And if that nature exists, its parts must necessarily exist no less. **THEAETETUS.** What could prevent it? **STRANGER.** The very opposition between a part of the nature of "The Other" and a part of "Being" is—if it is permitted to say so—no less an <term>essence</term> <note>original: "essentia", a fundamental reality</note> than Being itself; it does not signify its contrary, but only something different from it. **THEAETETUS.** Most clearly. **STRANGER.** What, then, shall we call it? **THEAETETUS.** It is clear that this is <term>Non-being</term> <note>original: "non ens", not-being</note>, the very thing we were seeking for the sake of the Sophist. **STRANGER.** Does it, as you said, possess essence no less than anything else? <margin>That non-being firmly possesses its own nature.</margin> And must we now boldly say that non-being firmly has its own nature—just as the great was great, and the beautiful was beautiful, and the not-great and not-beautiful existed? In the same way, non-being was and is non-being, one form numbered among the many other beings. Do we have any further doubt about this, Theaetetus? **THEAETETUS.** Not at all. **STRANGER.** Do you realize how far we have strayed from the mind of <term>Parmenides</term> <note>The pre-Socratic philosopher who famously argued that one cannot think or speak of what is not.</note>? **THEAETETUS.** Why so? **STRANGER.** We have crossed his boundaries, investigating further than he commanded. **THEAETETUS.** In what way? <margin>The verses of Parmenides.</margin> **STRANGER.** Because he says, <margin>In the Greek, Theaetetus speaks; the Stranger responds, which I have omitted here, following Ficino, as it was not pleasing. <note>The translator is referring to Marsilio Ficino’s famous 15th-century Latin translation of Plato.</note></margin>
> "Never, and in no way, are there non-beings; but you, in your search, restrain your mind from this path."
Those are his words. But we have not only shown that non-beings exist, but we have demonstrated what the specific *form* of non-being is. For in showing that the nature of "The Other" exists, divided and scattered throughout all existing things in relation to one another, we then asserted that the part of it opposed to the "being" of each thing is, in truth, that very thing: <term>Non-being</term>. **THEAETETUS.** Truly, Stranger, we seem to have spoken most accurately. **STRANGER.** Let no one say, then, that we dare to claim non-being exists because we have shown it to be the *contrary* of being. For we have long since said "goodbye" to the question of whether a contrary of being exists, and whether it has a rational explanation or is altogether irrational. <margin>He who does not believe this position must disprove it; he who cannot disprove it must believe it.</margin> As for what we have now said non-being is—either someone must refute us by proving we speak incorrectly, or as long as they cannot refute us, they must believe as we say: that the <term>Kinds</term> <note>original: "genera", the great categories of reality</note> are mixed with one another, and that Being and "The Other" penetrate through each other and through all things. "The Other" participates in Being, and thus *is* because of this participation, yet it is not the very thing in which it participates, but something else. Because it is something else than Being itself, it necessarily follows that it is "not-being." Likewise, Being, because it participates in "The Other," is something different from the other kinds; and being different from all of them, it is not each one of them individually, nor is it all the others together, but only itself. Therefore, without a doubt, Being *is not* in myriad ways; and all other things, both collectively and individually, in many ways *are*, and in many ways *are not*. **THEAETETUS.** What you say is true. **STRANGER.** If anyone lacks faith in these contradictory-seeming mixtures, he must think of something better than what has been said here. Or, if someone thinks they have found a difficult trick and enjoys dragging the argument now this way and now that, let him know he has devised nothing worthy of much study, as our current discourse testifies. For this is neither an extraordinary thing nor difficult to find; rather, the following is both difficult and noble. **THEAETETUS.** What is that? **STRANGER.** That which was said before: that leaving aside these trivialities as possible, one should be able to follow and refute each point of a speaker. When someone says that "the other" is in some way "the same," or "the same" is "other," one must prove in what specific sense and according to what specific relation they have undergone this. But to simply show that "the same" is somehow "other," or "the other" is "the same," or "the great" is "small," or "the like" is "unlike," and to delight...

These are his words. We, however, have not only shown non-beings to exist, but we have demonstrated what is the species of non-being.
