For we have long since said farewell to him who asks whether what is contrary to something truly exists or not, and subsists by some reason, or lacks reason. But what we have now said to be non-being, either he who believes less ought to refute, or if he is not able to refute it, <margin>He who does not believe the position ought to refute it: he who is not able to refute it, ought to believe it.</margin> he ought to believe it so far as he cannot contradict it: namely, that the genera are mixed in turn, and being and the other, by penetrating through themselves in turn and through all other things, mutually take hold of themselves, while the other participates in being. For it is because of participation of this kind, yet it is not that very thing in which it participates, but something else. Since truly it is other than being itself, it follows necessarily, that it is said to be non-being. Being also from this, that it is a participant of the Other itself, is to be called something else from the other genera. And since it is other than all the rest, it exists neither as one thing from them, nor all the others, but only that which it is; wherefore being without doubt is not very many things among very many. And others also similarly, as much universal as singular, are in many ways, and in many ways are not. **THEAETETUS.** You tell true things. **STRANGER.** If anyone does not grant faith to these contrary confusions, he ought to think so that he may bring in better things than these. Or if anyone, as if he had found something arduous, rejoices drawing the discourses now here, now there, let him know that he has devised things hardly worthy of much study, just as these discourses testify. For this is neither something extraordinary, nor difficult in finding, but that is arduous and excellent. **THEAETETUS.** What? **STRANGER.** What was also said above, that these things having been omitted as light, you might be able to refute those things which are plainly the same in each thing: whether what is other, is the same, or what is same, is other, and you will convince both to be in the same reason. For that which is the same, is other, or what is other, is also the same in some way, and what is great, is small, and what is like, becomes also unlike, to show:

<summary>In this passage from Plato's Sophist, the Stranger and Theaetetus define "Non-Being" not as the opposite of existence, but as "The Other" or Difference. They argue that "Not-Being" exists as a legitimate category because it simply describes things that are different from a given subject, much like "not beautiful" is a real quality distinct from "beautiful."</summary>
<keywords>Non-Being, Being, The Other, Difference, Parmenides, Theaetetus, Dialectic, Plato, Kinds, Participation</keywords>

...and to connect opposites in this fashion is not a true refutation, but one that barely touches upon the matter, being crude and newly born. **THEAETETUS.** Entirely so. **STRANGER.** For to attempt to sever everything from everything else, my best young man, is not only unharmonious but belongs to a man completely devoid of the Muses and philosophy. **THEAETETUS.** Why is that? **STRANGER.** The total separation of each thing from all others is the most complete destruction of all discourse. For it is through the mutual weaving together of species <note>original: "specierum copulam"; Greek: "eidōn symplokēn". This is the famous Platonic concept that meaning arises only when different "Forms" or "Kinds" are joined together.</note> that discourse is established for us. **THEAETETUS.** That is true. **STRANGER.** Observe then how opportunely we have now fought against those who would separate them, and forced them to permit one thing to be mixed with another. **THEAETETUS.** To what end especially? **STRANGER.** To the end that discourse might be one of the kinds of things that exist; for if we were deprived of this, we would be deprived of the greatest part of philosophy. Furthermore, we must at present define by common consent what discourse is. If it were entirely taken away from our midst, we would be unable to speak of anything at all. And it would be taken away if we conceded that there is no mixing of things. **THEAETETUS.** That is certainly right. But I do not understand why discourse must be defined now. **STRANGER.** But perhaps you will perceive it in this way. **THEAETETUS.** In what way? **STRANGER.** Non-being <note>original: "non ens"; Greek: "to mē on"</note> has appeared to us as one certain kind among the rest, diffused through all things that exist. **THEAETETUS.** It has. **STRANGER.** We must therefore consider next whether it mixes with opinion and discourse. **THEAETETUS.** Why? **STRANGER.** Because if it does not mix with them in any way, then it is necessary that all things are true. But if it does mix, then false opinion and false discourse arise. <margin>Falsehood arises from non-being, from falsehood arises deception, etc.</margin> For to say or to opine things that are not—this is precisely what constitutes falsehood, occurring in discourse and thought. **THEAETETUS.** So it is. **STRANGER.** And where there is falsehood, deception follows. **THEAETETUS.** Immediately. **STRANGER.** Once deception has arisen, all things must be filled with images, likenesses, and appearances <note>original: "phantasia"; referring to the mental images or "fantasies" that mislead us when they don't match reality.</note>. **THEAETETUS.** Nothing stands against that. **STRANGER.** But we said the Sophist had fled to this very place, while he denied that falsehood exists at all, because no one can think or pronounce non-being, since non-being participates in essence in no way. **THEAETETUS.** So it was said. **STRANGER.** But now this "non-being" has appeared to us as a participant in being; therefore, he will perhaps no longer fight on that ground. But he might say that some species participate in non-being, while others do not, and that discourse and opinion are among those that do not participate. And therefore he will contend that the appearance-making faculty <margin>The imaginative faculty is the mistress of likenesses.</margin>—the mistress of likenesses in which we placed him—does not exist at all, since opinion and discourse have no communion with non-being. He will say there is no falsehood at all since no such communion is found. For this reason, we must first investigate what discourse, opinion, and appearance are, so that once these are clarified, we may behold their communion with non-being. Having seen that, we may show that falsehood exists; and having shown that, we may bind the Sophist within it, if indeed he is guilty, or else set him free and seek him in some other kind. **THEAETETUS.** It truly seems, Stranger, as we said of the Sophist from the beginning, that this genus is indeed difficult to catch. For he seems to be hedged about with many obstacles, and no one can reach him unless they first remove the barrier he has thrown up. Even now, we have barely escaped that objection by which he argued that non-being does not exist. Immediately another obstacle is thrown up. Thus it is necessary to show that both discourse and opinion can be false, and perhaps after this another, and another after that, and it seems no limit will ever be found. **STRANGER.** He who is able to make even a little progress forward, Theaetetus, ought to keep his courage. For how should one who falters in these things ever dare to try others? <margin>A proverb.</margin> For he who accomplishes nothing in these, or is pushed backward, will never—as the proverb goes—capture the city. But now, my good friend, since that which you spoke of has been traversed by us, and the greatest bulwark has been taken, the remaining tasks are smaller and easier. **THEAETETUS.** You speak excellently. **STRANGER.** Let us then first take up discourse and opinion, as was said, so that we may show more clearly whether non-being touches them, or whether both are entirely true and neither is ever false. **THEAETETUS.** Very well. **STRANGER.** Come then, just as we spoke concerning species and letters, let us again consider in the same way regarding names. For it seems that what we are now seeking behaves in this manner. **THEAETETUS.** What specifically do you want to be understood about names? **STRANGER.** Whether they all fit together, or none, or whether some harmonize and others do not. **THEAETETUS.** It is clear that some fit and some do not. **STRANGER.** Perhaps you mean something like this: those which, spoken in sequence, express something, fit together; but those that continue <margin>Which voices are congruent, and which are not.</margin> without signifying anything do not fit. **THEAETETUS.** How? What did you mean? **STRANGER.** Exactly what I thought you understood and admitted. For there are two kinds of declarations made by the voice concerning essence. **THEAETETUS.** In what way? **STRANGER.** One kind consists of names, the other of verbs. **THEAETETUS.** Describe each. **STRANGER.** The declaration <margin>Verb. Noun.</margin> that signifies actions, we call a verb. **THEAETETUS.** Truly. **STRANGER.** But the vocal sign imposed upon those who perform the actions, we call a name <note>original: "nomen"; in this context, it refers to nouns or subjects of a sentence.</note>. **THEAETETUS.** Exactly. **STRANGER.** Discourse is never formed from names alone uttered in sequence, nor again from verbs pronounced without names. **THEAETETUS.** I have not learned this. **STRANGER.** It is clear that you were looking elsewhere when you agreed a moment ago. For this is exactly what I wanted to say: that if these things are merely pronounced in such a continuous way,

**A** All these things are always being carried about in discussions, and such a refutation is a true one, appearing clearly as one that touches upon something real. **THEAETETUS.** Entirely so. **STRANGER.** For, my good man, to attempt to separate everything from everything else is not only unharmonious, but belongs to someone entirely unrefined and unphilosophical. **THEAETETUS.** Why? **STRANGER.** The most complete vanishing of all discourse is the dissolving of each thing from all others. For discourse has come to be for us through the interweaving of the Forms with one another. **THEAETETUS.** True. **STRANGER.** Consider then how timely it was that we just now fought against such people and compelled them to allow one thing to be mixed with another. **THEAETETUS.** To what end? **STRANGER.** To the end that discourse might be one of the kinds of things that exist for us. If we were robbed of its very existence, we would no longer be able to say anything. And we would be robbed of it if we conceded that there is no mixture of anything with anything. **THEAETETUS.** This is correct. But if it does mix, then false opinion and discourse arise. For to opine or speak of things that are not—this is where falsehood arises in thought and speech. **THEAETETUS.** So it is. **STRANGER.** And where there is falsehood, there is deception. **THEAETETUS.** Yes. **STRANGER.** And indeed, if deception exists, all things must already be full of idols, images, and appearances. **THEAETETUS.** How could they not be? **STRANGER.** But we said the Sophist had fled to this place and had altogether denied that falsehood exists at all. So perhaps he will not fight on this point. But he might quickly say that some Forms participate in non-being and some do not, and that discourse and opinion are among those that do not. For he would say falsehood does not exist at all if this communion is not established. Because of this, we must first search out what discourse, opinion, and appearance are; so that when they are revealed, we may also see their communion with non-being. For I wanted to say this very thing: that these things, if spoken continuously in this way...

<summary>The Stranger and Theaetetus establish that discourse (speech) is only possible because different "Forms" or concepts can be woven together. They argue that because "Non-being" is a real category that mixes with speech and opinion, falsehood and deception are philosophically possible, effectively cornering the Sophist who claims falsehood cannot exist.</summary>

learns," do you say that this is the smallest and first of sentences? **THEAETETUS.** I do. **STRANGER.** For it now points to things that are, or are becoming, or have happened, or will be. <summary>This page defines a "sentence" (logos) as a combination of a noun and a verb, and explains that truth or falsehood arises from whether this combination describes things as they are or as they are not. It also establishes that thought is merely silent speech within the soul, while opinion and imagination are its conclusions and sensory mixtures.</summary>

...image, nor can an apparition exist at all, because in no way, anywhere, would falsehood ever exist. <term>THEAETETUS.</term> What you say is true. <term>STRANGER.</term> But now, since false speech has appeared, and false opinion has appeared as well, it is possible for there to be certain imitations of true things, and for an art of deception to arise from this state of affairs. <term>THEAETETUS.</term> Certainly possible. <term>STRANGER.</term> Furthermore, did we not agree in our earlier discussion that the Sophist is involved in these things? <term>THEAETETUS.</term> We did. <term>STRANGER.</term> Let us then try again, dividing the proposed class in two, always proceeding toward the right-hand part of the division; and let us keep hold of the Sophist's associations<margin>B</margin> until, having stripped away all his common traits and left only his own unique nature, we may behold him ourselves and point him out to those whose nature is most suited to this kind of method. <term>THEAETETUS.</term> Rightly said. <term>STRANGER.</term> Did we not begin by dividing art into the "productive" <note>original: "ποιητικήν" (poiētikēn), the art of making or creating.</note> and the "acquisitive"? <term>THEAETETUS.</term> Certainly. <term>STRANGER.</term> And under the acquisitive art, we envisioned the Sophist in hunting, combat, commerce, and other such forms. <term>THEAETETUS.</term> That is exactly what happened. <term>STRANGER.</term> But now, since the art of imitation has encompassed him, it is clear that we must first divide the productive art itself in two. Or shall we follow the doctrine and common speech of the many? <term>THEAETETUS.</term> Which one? <term>STRANGER.</term> Those who say that nature generates these things from some spontaneous cause, and without a creating mind; or rather with reason and divine knowledge, which originates from God himself? <term>THEAETETUS.</term> Perhaps because of my age, I often shift between both opinions. But now, looking at you and seeing that you believe these things are produced by God, I hold that same opinion myself. <term>STRANGER.</term> Very well, <term>THEAETETUS.</term> If we thought you were someone who would think otherwise in the future, we would now try to make you agree by means of reason combined with necessary persuasion. But since I know your nature is such that, even without our demonstration, you will move toward that which you now say you are drawn to, I will let it go. For such a dispute would be a waste of time. I will then posit that the things said to be made by nature are produced by divine art; but the things composed out of these by men are produced by human art. And by this reasoning, there are two kinds of productive faculty: the human and the divine. <term>THEAETETUS.</term> Excellent. <term>STRANGER.</term> Since there are two arts, divide each of them in two again. <term>THEAETETUS.</term> How? <term>STRANGER.</term> Just as the whole productive art was previously divided "by width," let it now be divided "by length," and thus four parts are created: two human ones regarding us, and two divine ones regarding the gods. <term>THEAETETUS.</term> Indeed. <term>STRANGER.</term> From these, divided again in another way, one part of each division is productive [of the things themselves], and the remaining parts are called "image-making." Whence the productive faculty is again divided in two. <term>THEAETETUS.</term> Say again how each is divided. <term>STRANGER.</term> We ourselves and the other animals, and the elements from which natural things are made—fire, water, and their brothers—we know that all these are individuals produced and worked by God, do we not? <term>THEAETETUS.</term> Of course. <term>STRANGER.</term> Following these are the images of each, produced by a certain divine craftsmanship. <term>THEAETETUS.</term> Of what kind? <term>STRANGER.</term> The appearances <note>original: "φαντάσματα" (phantasmata).</note> that occur in sleep, and those things called "natural appearances" seen by day without art: a shadow, when darkness is mixed with fire; or a double image, when the light of the eye and external light meet as one on bright and smooth surfaces <margin>E</margin>—providing a sensation contrary to ordinary sight and creating a "form" <note>This refers to reflections in mirrors or water.</note>. <term>THEAETETUS.</term> These then are two works of divine production: the thing itself, and the image that follows each thing. <term>STRANGER.</term> And what of our own art? Shall we not say that by the art of architecture we build a house itself, but by the art of painting we produce another thing, like a man-made dream for those who are awake? <term>THEAETETUS.</term> No doubt. <term>STRANGER.</term> And so in other things as well, by dividing in two, we find twin works of our productive action: making the thing itself by a primary faculty, and the image by an imitative one. <term>THEAETETUS.</term> Now I understand better, and I <margin>F</margin> posit two kinds of productive faculty: first, the division into divine and human; and second, the division into the production of things themselves and the production of images. <term>STRANGER.</term> <margin>G</margin> Let us remember, I pray, that we said there must be two kinds of image-making: "likeness-making" <note>original: "εἰκαστικόν" (eikastikon), which produces an accurate likeness.</note> and "appearance-making" <note>original: "φανταστικόν" (phantastikon), which produces an appearance that seems like the truth but is distorted by perspective.</note>, if indeed falsehood were truly to be a false thing and one of the things that exist. <term>THEAETETUS.</term> It was certainly said. <term>STRANGER.</term> Did it not stand firm, and shall we not now assign two species to it without controversy? <term>THEAETETUS.</term> Certainly. <term>STRANGER.</term> Let us then divide the appearance-making art again in two. <term>THEAETETUS.</term> In what way? <term>STRANGER.</term> One kind is made through instruments; the other is where the person making the appearance offers himself as the instrument. <term>THEAETETUS.</term> What do you mean by that? <term>STRANGER.</term> Whenever someone, I suppose, using your shape for his own body, or his voice...

<column-break/>

...apparition would be nothing at all, for the reason that nowhere, ever, and in no way is there such a thing as falsehood. <term>THEAETETUS.</term> You speak the truth. <term>STRANGER.</term> But now, since speech has appeared, and false opinion has appeared in turn, it is certainly possible for there to be imitations of things that are, and for a certain deceptive art to arise from this disposition. <term>THEAETETUS.</term> It is possible. <term>STRANGER.</term> And indeed, that the Sophist was among these—was this not something agreed upon by us in what preceded? <term>THEAETETUS.</term> Yes. <term>STRANGER.</term> Let us then try again, splitting the proposed class in two, to travel always along the right-hand part of the cut, clinging to the Sophist’s fellowship, until, having stripped away all his commonalities and leaving his own unique nature, we may demonstrate him especially to ourselves, and then also to those who are by nature closest to such a method. <term>THEAETETUS.</term> Correct. <term>STRANGER.</term> Did we not start then by dividing art into the productive and the acquisitive? <term>THEAETETUS.</term> Yes. <term>STRANGER.</term> And he appeared to us within the acquisitive art in hunting and in competition, and in commerce, and in all such forms. <term>THEAETETUS.</term> Quite so. <term>STRANGER.</term> But now, since the imitative art has encompassed him, it is clear that the productive art itself must first be divided in two. For imitation is surely a kind of production; of images, however, we say, but not of each thing itself. Or shall we use the doctrine and speech of the many? <term>THEAETETUS.</term> Of what kind? <term>STRANGER.</term> That nature generates them from some spontaneous cause, and produces them without thought; or with reason and divine knowledge coming from God? <term>THEAETETUS.</term> I, perhaps because of my age, often change my mind between both. But now, looking at you, and assuming that you think they come into being according to God, I have come to believe this way myself. <term>STRANGER.</term> Well said, O Theaetetus. And if we thought you were one of those who would think otherwise in the time to come, we would now try by argument with the necessity of persuasion to make you agree. But since I know your nature, and that even without arguments from us it tends toward that which you now say you are drawn to, I will let it go. For the time would be wasted. But I will posit that the things said to be by nature are made by a certain divine art, and the things composed out of these by men are made by a human art; and according to this word, there are two kinds of production: one human and one divine. <term>THEAETETUS.</term> Correct. <term>STRANGER.</term> Now cut each of the two in two. <term>THEAETETUS.</term> How? <term>STRANGER.</term> As before you had to cut the whole of production "by width," now cut it "by length." <term>THEAETETUS.</term> Let it be cut. <term>STRANGER.</term> Thus all its parts become four: two on our side, the human; and two on the side of the gods, the divine. <term>THEAETETUS.</term> Yes. <term>STRANGER.</term> And again, of those divided the other way, one part from each portion is productive [of the thing itself], and the remaining parts could almost best be called "image-making." And according to these, production is again divided in two. <term>THEAETETUS.</term> Tell me of each again. <term>STRANGER.</term> We and the other animals, and those things from which natural things are made—fire and water and their brothers—we know that all these individuals are worked as the offspring of God. Or how? <term>THEAETETUS.</term> Thus. <term>STRANGER.</term> And images of each of these follow, but not the things themselves, these also having come into being by a supernatural device. <term>THEAETETUS.</term> Which ones? <term>STRANGER.</term> Those in sleep, and those called natural appearances by day; a shadow, when darkness arises in fire; and a double image, when the light belonging to the eye and external light meet as one on bright and smooth surfaces, and providing a sensation contrary to the usual sight of before, produce a form. <term>THEAETETUS.</term> For indeed these are two works of divine production: the thing itself and the image that follows each. <term>STRANGER.</term> And what of it? Shall we not say that our own art makes a house itself by the art of building, and another thing by the art of painting, as if a human dream produced for those who are awake? <term>THEAETETUS.</term> Entirely so. <term>STRANGER.</term> And so also the other things in two: the double works of our own productive action, one being the thing itself, which we say is by the art of "self-working" <note>original: "αὐτουργικῇ" (autourgikē), referring to the production of the actual object.</note>, and the image, which is by "image-making." <term>THEAETETUS.</term> Now I have learned better; and I set down two kinds of production in two ways: divine and human according to one cut; and according to the other, the making of the things themselves and the offspring of certain likenesses. <term>STRANGER.</term> Let us then remember of the image-making art, that one kind was to be likeness-making and the other appearance-making; if indeed falsehood, being truly false, was to be. Shall we now number these two as forms under it without dispute? <term>THEAETETUS.</term> Yes. <term>STRANGER.</term> Let us then define appearance-making again in two. <term>THEAETETUS.</term> How? <term>STRANGER.</term> One kind being produced through instruments, and the other where the producer of the appearance provides himself as the instrument. <term>THEAETETUS.</term> How do you mean? <term>STRANGER.</term> When, I think, someone uses your shape...

<meta>catchword: himself</meta>

<summary>In this passage from Plato's Sophist, the Stranger and Theaetetus categorize the art of production into divine and human branches, further distinguishing between the creation of real objects and the creation of images (such as reflections, shadows, or paintings). This classification is used to locate the Sophist within the realm of human "appearance-making" or deceptive imitation.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the dialogue of the "Sophist" with a final definition of the title character as a deceptive "image-maker" of wisdom. It then transitions into a new dialogue, the "Politicus" (or "Statesman"), where Socrates, Theodorus, and the Stranger begin a search for the true nature of a ruler.</meta>

# THE STATESMAN.

<margin>A</margin> ...making oneself appear like someone else, using one's own body or voice—this part of the appearance-making art <note>The "phantastic" or appearance-making art creates likenesses that look "right" from a certain perspective but aren't true to the original's proportions.</note> is specifically called imitation. **THEAETETUS.** Indeed. **STRANGER.** Let us then designate this as the imitative part and set it aside; as for the rest, let us be soft and leave it for someone else to gather into a single unit and give it a fitting name. **THEAETETUS.** Let this be our division, and let the rest be dismissed. **STRANGER.** And yet, Theaetetus, there is still a double nature here worth considering; look and see. **THEAETETUS.** Tell me. **STRANGER.** Of those who imitate, some do so knowing what they are imitating, while others do so without knowing. And yet, what greater division can we propose than that of ignorance and knowledge? **THEAETETUS.** None. **STRANGER.** Was not the imitation we just mentioned performed by those who know? For a man who knows your shape could imitate it. <margin>B</margin> **THEAETETUS.** How could he not? **STRANGER.** But what about the "shape" of justice and of virtue as a whole? Do not many people, though ignorant of it but having a certain opinion of it, strive with all their might to make that which seems to be within them appear to exist, imitating it as much as possible in both deeds and words? **THEAETETUS.** Very many indeed. **STRANGER.** And do they all fail in their attempt to seem just when they are not just at all? Or is it quite the opposite? **THEAETETUS.** Quite the opposite. **STRANGER.** Then I think we must call this imitator different from the other: the one who is ignorant is distinct from the one who knows. **THEAETETUS.** Yes. **STRANGER.** Where, then, shall one find a suitable name for each? Or is it clearly difficult, because an ancient cause <note>The Stranger suggests that earlier thinkers were lazy or "without mind" regarding the systematic division of types, leading to a lack of specific vocabulary today.</note> for the division of genera into species was overlooked by our predecessors, so that no one even attempted to divide them? Consequently, there is a lack of necessary names. Nevertheless, <margin>C</margin> even if it seems a bit bold to say, for the sake of distinction let us call imitation accompanied by opinion "opinion-imitation" <note>original: "δόξομιμητικήν" (doxomimetic)</note>; and that accompanied by science, a "scientific" or "inquiry-based" imitation. **THEAETETUS.** So be it. **STRANGER.** We must use the first of these, then. For the Sophist was not among those who know, but rather among those who imitate. **THEAETETUS.** Very much so. **STRANGER.** Let us then examine this "opinion-imitator" like a piece of iron, to see if he is sound, or if he has some double-fold within himself. **THEAETETUS.** Let us examine him. **STRANGER.** He certainly has a very deep one. For one type of them is simple-minded, thinking he knows that which he only has an opinion of; but the other type, because of his tossing about in arguments, has much suspicion and fear that he is ignorant of those things which he has posed as knowing before others. **THEAETETUS.** Certainly, both types you mention exist. **STRANGER.** Shall we then call one the "simple imitator" and the other the "ironic imitator"? <margin>D</margin> **THEAETETUS.** That seems likely. **STRANGER.** And shall we say this genus is one, or two? **THEAETETUS.** You see it. **STRANGER.** I am looking, and I think I see two types: one who is able to practice irony in public with long speeches before the crowds, and another who does so in private with short arguments, forcing his conversation partner to contradict himself. **THEAETETUS.** You speak most correctly. **STRANGER.** Whom, then, shall we declare the one who makes the longer speeches to be? A statesman, or a demagogue <note>original: "δημολογικόν" (demological), literally a "people-speaker."</note>? **THEAETETUS.** A demagogue. **STRANGER.** And what shall we call the other? Wise, or a sophist? **THEAETETUS.** It is impossible to call him wise, since we established that he is ignorant; but being an imitator of the wise man, he will clearly take a name derived from him. Indeed, I have now nearly learned that <margin>E</margin> we must truly call this man that absolute and "really real" Sophist. **STRANGER.** Shall we then bind up his name as we did before, weaving it together from the end back to the beginning? **THEAETETUS.** By all means. **STRANGER.** The art of contradiction-making, which is part of the ironic sort, of the opinion-based imitative art, within the "phantastic" genus, derived from the image-making art—a human, not divine, production, defined in speech as the wonder-working portion of the work. Whoever says the "really real" Sophist is of this generation and blood will, it seems, speak the absolute truth. **THEAETETUS.** Most certainly.

<column-break/>

...makes it seem like a similar voice, that imitation is called "phantastic." <margin>A</margin> **THEAETETUS.** Certainly. **STRANGER.** Calling this the imitative part, let us so distribute it, and let us pass over all the rest as if we were now desirous of rest, and grant to another to collect it into one and give it a suitable surname. **THEAETETUS.** Let it be distributed as you wish, and let this be dismissed. **STRANGER.** This further double nature, O Theaetetus, must be considered. But for what reason, take note. **THEAETETUS.** Speak. **STRANGER.** Of those who imitate, some do so knowing what they imitate, while others do so in ignorance. Shall we place any greater discrepancy or division than that between ignorance and knowledge? **THEAETETUS.** None. **STRANGER.** Was not that which we <margin>B</margin> just spoke of the imitation of those who know? For he who knows you imitates your figure. **THEAETETUS.** That very one. **STRANGER.** But what must be said of the figure of justice and of universal virtue? Do not many, while they are ignorant, but think they know it, strive both in words and deeds to make it appear to be in them, imitating that which seems so to them? **THEAETETUS.** And very many indeed. **STRANGER.** Does their hope fail them so that, just as they are not just, so they do not even seem so? Or the contrary? **THEAETETUS.** The contrary. **STRANGER.** We shall say this imitator is different from that former one: the ignorant from the knowing? **THEAETETUS.** We shall clearly say so. **STRANGER.** From where, then, shall a proper name for each be derived? Is it perhaps difficult? Because some ancient cause of the division of genera into <margin>C</margin> species was unknown to our predecessors, so that no one struggled to divide them, and therefore they must be in want of names? And even if it might seem a bit bold to say, yet for the sake of declaration and distinction, let us call that imitation which is the companion of opinion "opinable imitation"; but that which is of science, we may call a certain "historical" or "scientific" imitation. **THEAETETUS.** Let it be. **STRANGER.** We must use only one of these names. For the sophist, though in the genus of imitators, we did not place in the genus of the knowing. **THEAETETUS.** So it is. **STRANGER.** Let us therefore examine this imitator of opinion like iron, whether he be solid and simple, or on the contrary has something twin and double <margin>D</margin> in himself. **THEAETETUS.** Let us examine him. **STRANGER.** Certainly he is very manifold. For one sophist is foolish and inept, thinking he knows what he only has an opinion of. But the form of the other, because of a varied revolution in speeches, certainly has much suspicion and fear, lest he be ignorant of those things which he pretends to know before others. **THEAETETUS.** He is altogether of both kinds, as you have narrated. **STRANGER.** Shall we not then place one as the simple and the other as the ironic imitator? **THEAETETUS.** It is agreeable. **STRANGER.** Of this again, do we say the genus is one or two? **THEAETETUS.** You see to it. **STRANGER.** I am thinking indeed, and two offer themselves to me as I think. One indeed uses irony publicly with a long oration before the people; the other privately <margin>E</margin> with certain minute little traps, forcing him who disputes with him to contradict himself in his speeches. **THEAETETUS.** You speak very rightly. **STRANGER.** How shall we name the former one: a statesman, or a demagogue? **THEAETETUS.** A demagogue. **STRANGER.** And the other: a "Sophon," that is, a wise man, or a Sophist? **THEAETETUS.** It is not permitted to call him a wise man, since we have placed him as ignorant; but because he imitates the wise man, <margin>Why he is called a Sophist.</margin> he shall obtain a certain name similar to his. And finally I understand that this very man ought to be called, altogether and in reality, a Sophist. **STRANGER.** Shall we not, as above, now bind his name together, <margin>The final definition of the sophist.</margin> embracing all from the end back to the beginning? **THEAETETUS.** By all means. **STRANGER.** He will finally define the Sophist truly, who shall assert his generation and stock to be this: the Sophist, I say, is he who in speeches forces the disputant to contradict himself; who is also part of the ironic sort coming from the opinion-imitator; likewise of the phantastic genus, flowing from the imaginary faculty; a progeny determined not by divine but by human production, and from the number of those who by words, as if by certain marvels, wonderfully deceive their hearers. **THEAETETUS.** It must be said exactly so.

### THE STATESMAN, OR, ON
### KINGSHIP.
->Logical.<-

### THE STATESMAN, OR
### CONCERNING THE KINGDOM,
->Pertaining to speech or reason.<-

---

*SUMMARY OF THE DIALOGUE.* The thesis of this dialogue is that the definition, as well as the true causes and origin of Politics, and finally its mode and best form, should be declared. The Philosopher investigates the definition in various ways, which he finally collects as follows: It is surely the science or discipline instituted for this purpose, that it may rule the assembly and multitude of men, who among the other living creatures are the most <term>ἀγελαῖοι</term> <note>original: "agelaioi," meaning "gregarious" or "living in herds."</note>. He says the guardian of this science is the King, whom he calls, with Homer, the "shepherd of the peoples"—the one, surely, who is suited by nature for commanding and for wisely accommodating laws. He records the true origin and cause of this civil discipline: namely, that God, who watches over men with His singular providence, granted them these helps and protections against those difficulties by which this life is beset. Therefore, repeating the matter from a bit deeper back, he says that man was created by God from the earth, and at first in a most happy and truly golden condition, which however fell from the best state into a worse one; and consequently the human race, when it fell into these straits, had need of helps to repel those <term>ἀναμφίσια</term> <note>original: "anamphisia," referring to controversial or inextricable troubles.</note> inconveniences in which its mind is involved and with which its whole life is filled. These things having been explained, he prescribes the mode and reason of commanding, and teaches that the command of the King or Statesman is not infinite, so that he may do whatever he pleases according to his whim; but it is necessary that he command piously, justly, and wisely, according to the prescription of the laws: not that he should act by the highest and most rigorous law, and accommodate all laws to all people in the same way, but that, having taken account of things, persons, places, and times, he should moderate the intent and end of the laws.

# PLATO’S
## THE STATESMAN

<columns>

**SOCRATES.** From Theodorus, we shall say we have heard from a man most skilled in both reasoning <note>original: "logismous," referring to calculations or mathematical reasoning</note> and geometry. **THEODORUS.** Why is that, Socrates? **SOCRATES.** Because you have placed each of these men at the same value, yet they actually differ in honor by a greater distance than can be explained by your mathematical proportion. **THEODORUS.** By our god Ammon, Socrates, you speak well and justly! You have quite accurately reminded me of my error in calculation. I will come after you for this later. But you, Stranger, do not be reluctant to favor us; proceed to describe either the statesman or the philosopher, whichever you prefer first. **STRANGER.**
**B** It must be done as you bid, Theodorus, since we have once begun; we must not stop until we reach the goal. But what should we do regarding Theaetetus? **THEODORUS.** In what regard? **STRANGER.** Shall we let him rest now and take this Socrates <note>This refers to a different student named Socrates, often called "Young Socrates" to distinguish him from the philosopher.</note> in his place as a partner in our exercises and studies? What do you advise? **THEODORUS.** Take him as you suggested. Since they are both young, they will bear every labor more easily by taking turns. **SOCRATES.** And yet, Stranger, they both seem to be related to me in a way. You all judge Theaetetus to be like me in the features of his face; as for this Socrates, 
**C** since he shares my name, that naming provides a certain mutual kinship between us. It is fitting that we who are kin should eagerly examine the matter through discussion. I met with Theaetetus yesterday in debate, and today I have heard him responding to our guest. But neither has happened yet with Young Socrates. He must also be examined. Let him respond to me at another time, but to you now. **STRANGER.** So we shall do. Do you hear Socrates? **YOUNG SOCRATES.** I hear. **STRANGER.** Do you agree with him? **YOUNG SOCRATES.** I agree. **STRANGER.** As far as you are concerned, then, nothing prevents us from discussing it. And it is even less fitting for me to be an obstacle to this debate. Rather, after the Sophist, it seems 
**D** necessary that we investigate the statesman. Answer me, then: should he be placed among the number of those who are called "knowers" <note>original: "scientes" / "epistemonon"</note>? **YOUNG SOCRATES.** He should. **STRANGER.** Therefore, we must divide the sciences, just as we did when seeking the Sophist. **YOUNG SOCRATES.** Perhaps. **STRANGER.** However, the method of dividing does not seem the same to me, Socrates. **YOUNG SOCRATES.** How so? **STRANGER.** It is another way. **YOUNG SOCRATES.** So it seems. **STRANGER.** Where then shall we find the path of political science? We must find it, and having separated it from all others, impress upon it a single idea, and likewise mark the other deviations with another single form. We must persuade ourselves that all sciences are contained within two forms. **YOUNG SOCRATES.** This is now your task, Stranger, not mine. **STRANGER.** Yet it is yours too, once it has been made clear. **YOUNG SOCRATES.** You speak wisely. **STRANGER.** 
<margin>Mathematics are free from action, possessing knowledge alone.</margin>
**E** Arithmetic, furthermore, and some others very like it, are free from action; they offer only knowledge <note>original: "gnostike," the root of "gnostic," meaning theoretical or intellectual knowledge.</note>. **YOUNG SOCRATES.** That is certainly true. **STRANGER.** But those things pertaining to architecture and manual service possess a science that is innate to actions; they complete physical objects produced by them which did not exist before. **YOUNG SOCRATES.** That is clear. **STRANGER.** Divide all sciences in this way: calling
<margin>Two species of science.</margin>
one "acting" <note>original: "praktike," the root of "practical."</note> and the other "knowing." **YOUNG SOCRATES.** Let there be two species of science, since science as a whole is one. **STRANGER.** Whether 
<margin>The same: statesman, king, master, householder.</margin>
**F** statesman, king, master, and householder <note>original: "paterfamilias" / "oikonomon"</note>—do we want these to be the same? Or shall we say there are as many arts as there are names? Rather, follow me this way. **YOUNG SOCRATES.** Which way? **STRANGER.** This way: if some private citizen is capable of advising a public physician, is it not necessary that he be called by the name of the same art as the one he advises? **YOUNG SOCRATES.** Certainly. **STRANGER.** What then? If a private citizen can advise and instruct the king of a city, shall he not be said to possess the science which the one who rules ought to have? **YOUNG SOCRATES.** He shall. **STRANGER.** But the science of a true king is the royal discipline. **YOUNG SOCRATES.** It is. **STRANGER.** Whoever possesses it, whether he holds a public office or lives as a private citizen, will rightly be called "royal" according to this skill. **YOUNG SOCRATES.** Rightly so. **STRANGER.** Moreover, the householder and the master are the same. **YOUNG SOCRATES.** The same. **STRANGER.** Does it matter whether 
**G** a city is large or a house is small for the purpose of ruling? **YOUNG SOCRATES.** Not at all. **STRANGER.** Therefore, as we were just inquiring, the science of all these is one: whether one calls it royal, political, or household management, let us consider it to make no difference. **SOCRATES.** None. **STRANGER.** This at least is least doubtful: that every king can do very little with his hands or the rest of his body for the safety of his kingdom, but can do very much through intelligence and strength of mind. **SOCRATES.** It is established. **STRANGER.** Do you wish then that we say the king is closer to theoretical science <note>original: "speculatrice" / "gnostike"</note> than to the active or manual arts? **SOCRATES.** I certainly do. **STRANGER.** Therefore, the political science and the statesman, the royal science and the king—we shall combine all these as one and the same thing. **SOCRATES.** Plainly. **STRANGER.** And we shall proceed in order to the next steps, especially 
**H** if we distinguish the parts of theoretical science. **SOCRATES.** Entirely. **STRANGER.** Pay attention, I pray: do we see any division within it? **SOCRATES.** Tell me, of what kind? **STRANGER.** Of this kind. There is an art of calculation. **SOCRATES.** There is. **STRANGER.** That, I believe, is among the number of those that consist in contemplation. **SOCRATES.** It is so. **STRANGER.** It is certainly of that number. **STRANGER.** The art of calculation surely recognizes the difference between numbers. We attribute no other task to it than to discern and judge what is known. **SOCRATES.** What then?

<column-break/>

**A** We shall say we have heard well regarding calculations and geometry from one who is most excellent in them. **THEODORUS.** How so, Socrates? **SOCRATES.** By placing each of the men at an equal value, though they are further apart in honor than <gloss>according to</gloss> any proportion of your art. **THEODORUS.** By our god Ammon, Socrates, you have rebuked my error in calculation very well, justly, and quite memorably. I shall get back at you for these things in turn. But you, Stranger, do not grow weary of doing us a favor; rather, proceed and 
**B** go through either the statesman or the philosopher first, whichever you choose. **STRANGER.** This must be done, Theodorus, since we have once undertaken it; and we must not stop until we reach their end. But what should I do regarding Theaetetus here? **THEODORUS.** About what? **STRANGER.** Should we let him rest and take this Socrates in his place as a fellow-exerciser? Or how do you advise? **THEODORUS.** As you said. **YOUNG SOCRATES.** I will take his place. For being young, he will bear any labor more easily if he has a rest. **SOCRATES.** And indeed, Stranger, both of them seem to have some kinship with me. For you say one appears like me in the nature of his face; for the other, our sharing a name provides a certain intimacy. We must 
**C** always eagerly recognize our kin through discussion. I myself joined in discussion with Theaetetus yesterday, and now I have heard him answering; but with Socrates, neither has happened. He must be examined as well. Let him answer me later, but you now. **STRANGER.** It shall be so, Socrates. Do you hear Socrates? **YOUNG SOCRATES.** Yes. **STRANGER.** Do you agree with what he says? **YOUNG SOCRATES.** Entirely. **STRANGER.** Your side seems to offer no hindrance; but perhaps I must consider the matter with you even more. After the sophist, it is necessary (as it seems to me) to search for the statesman now. Tell me, then: must we place him among those who possess knowledge, or how? **YOUNG SOCRATES.** Just so. **STRANGER.** We must then divide the sciences, as when we were considering the former man. **YOUNG SOCRATES.** 
**D** Perhaps. **STRANGER.** Yet it does not seem to me, Socrates, to be the same cut. **YOUNG SOCRATES.** Why not? **STRANGER.** By another way. **YOUNG SOCRATES.** It seems so. **STRANGER.** By what path then might one find political science? For we must find it, and having set it apart from the others, seal it with one idea, and marking the other branches with one other form, make our soul think of all sciences as being of two forms. **YOUNG SOCRATES.** This is now your task, I think, Stranger, and not mine. **STRANGER.** It must also be yours, Socrates, once it becomes clear to us. **YOUNG SOCRATES.** 
**E** You have spoken well. **STRANGER.** Is it not then that arithmetic and certain other arts akin to it are stripped of action, and provide only the knowing? **YOUNG SOCRATES.** It is so. **STRANGER.** But those involving carpentry and all manual labor possess science as if it were innate in the actions themselves, and they help complete the bodies produced by them which were not there before. **YOUNG SOCRATES.** Certainly. **STRANGER.** In this way, then, divide all sciences, calling one "practical" and the other only "cognitive." **YOUNG SOCRATES.** Let these be your two forms of the one whole science. **STRANGER.** Shall we then place the statesman, the king, the master, and further the householder, as one, addressing all these as the same? Or should we 
**F** say there are as many arts as there were names spoken? Rather, follow me here. **YOUNG SOCRATES.** Where? **STRANGER.** This way. If anyone in a private capacity is capable of advising one of the public physicians, though he is a private citizen himself, is it not necessary that he be addressed by the same name of the art as the one he advises? **YOUNG SOCRATES.** Yes. **STRANGER.** What then? One who is clever at advising a man who is king of a country, though being a private citizen himself, shall we not say he has the science which the ruler himself ought to possess? **YOUNG SOCRATES.** We shall. **STRANGER.** But the science of a true king is the royal science. **YOUNG SOCRATES.** Yes. **STRANGER.** And the one who possesses this, whether he happens to be a ruler or happens to be a private citizen, will surely be rightly addressed as "royal" according to the art itself? **YOUNG SOCRATES.** It is at least just. **STRANGER.** And indeed, the householder and the master are the same. **YOUNG SOCRATES.** Certainly. **STRANGER.** And what about the size of a great house or the bulk of a small city—will they differ at all in regard to ruling? **YOUNG SOCRATES.** Not at all. **STRANGER.** Is it not clear then, as we were just laboring to show, that 
**G** there is one science regarding all these? Whether one calls it royal, political, or household management, let us not quarrel with him. **SOCRATES.** Why should we? **STRANGER.** But this much is clear: that for a king, any power of the hand or the whole body is small in holding his rule compared to the intelligence and strength of the soul. **SOCRATES.** Clear. **STRANGER.** Shall we say then that the king is more closely related to cognitive science than to manual or generally practical science? **SOCRATES.** Certainly. **STRANGER.** Therefore, we shall put together political science and the statesman, or royal science and the king, all into the same thing. **SOCRATES.** Clear. **STRANGER.** Should we not then proceed in order, since we have defined this as cognitive science? **SOCRATES.** Very much so. **STRANGER.** Pay attention now, to see if we can perceive a 
**H** division within it. **SOCRATES.** Tell me what kind. **STRANGER.** Such as this. We had an art of calculation. **SOCRATES.** Yes. **STRANGER.** It belongs entirely, I believe, to the cognitive arts. **SOCRATES.** How could it not? **STRANGER.** Since calculation knows the difference in numbers, does it provide any further work than to judge what has been known? **SOCRATES.** Certainly.

</columns>

<summary>In this opening of the "Statesman," Socrates and the Stranger decide to examine the nature of a ruler, enlisting "Young Socrates" as the interlocutor. They begin by classifying knowledge into two categories: cognitive (theoretical) and practical (manual), concluding that the art of ruling is a single cognitive science regardless of whether it is applied to a household or a city.</summary>

# THE STATESMAN. 171

<columns>

<margin>A</margin>STRANGER. For indeed, no architect uses the service of his own hands, but rather presides over those who do. SOCRATES. That is so. STRANGER. He provides a kind of judgment, not manual ministry. SOCRATES. That is also true. STRANGER. He may rightly be called a sharer in the science of knowing <term>gnostike: theoretical or knowledge-based science</term>. SOCRATES. Most certainly. STRANGER. This, I think, belongs to the judge <note>In this context, the "judge" refers to the one who analyzes and makes decisions based on knowledge.</note>: not merely to reach a conclusion and then depart—as the calculator does when he finishes a sum—but to stay at the task and assign each worker their appropriate duty until they have completed what was commanded. SOCRATES. Quite right.

<margin>B</margin>STRANGER. Are not all these theoretical sciences, along with those that follow the art of calculation? Yet do not these two classes—the judging and the commanding—differ from one another? SOCRATES. They appear to. STRANGER. Therefore, if we divide the whole of contemplation into two, assigning one part to judgment and the other to command, we might perhaps believe we have divided correctly. SOCRATES. Correct, in my opinion. STRANGER. Those who handle something together are satisfied with one another whenever they can reach an agreement. SOCRATES. Why not? STRANGER. As long as we are in agreement on this, we may let the opinions of others pass by. SOCRATES. Entirely.

<margin>C</margin>STRANGER. Come then, in which of these arts should we place the royal man? In the judicial, as a kind of spectator? Or rather in the commanding art, as a master? SOCRATES. In the latter, surely. STRANGER. We must see further if the commanding art admits any distinction. It seems to me thus: as a retailer <note>original: "caupo," a shopkeeper or middleman</note> differs from one who sells his own work, so a king differs from a herald. SOCRATES. In what way? STRANGER. Retailers take up the works of others that were previously sold and sell them again. SOCRATES. True. STRANGER. In the same way, the class of heralds receives the command of another and commands others in turn. SOCRATES. So it is. STRANGER. Shall we then mix the royal faculty with the arts of the interpreter, the instructor, the prophet, the herald, and many other related arts that all issue commands? Or would you prefer—as I suggested just now—that we devise a name by comparison, since the class of those who issue their own orders <term>autepitaktike: the "self-commanding" art</term> almost lacks a name? Let us divide them this way: we shall place the royal class among those who issue their own commands, while ignoring the others and letting someone else give them whatever name they please. For our discussion was started for the sake of the ruler, not the subordinate. SOCRATES. Indeed.

<margin>D</margin>STRANGER. Since this is now sufficiently distinguished from those other things, and brought back from what is foreign to its own place, it must be divided again, if we can find any further partition within it. SOCRATES. Certainly. STRANGER. It seems one can be found. Follow me in the division. SOCRATES. Where shall I follow?

<margin>E</margin>STRANGER. Whoever presides by commanding does so so that something may be produced. SOCRATES. Without a doubt. STRANGER. Indeed, it is not very difficult to divide all produced things into two. SOCRATES. In what way? STRANGER. Some are living beings, and some are inanimate. SOCRATES. That is clear. STRANGER. If we wish to divide the commanding part of the theoretical faculty into these members, let us cut it. SOCRATES. Into what? STRANGER. Let one part be placed over the production of inanimate things, and the other over the production of living beings. And so the whole will be cut into two. SOCRATES. Truly. STRANGER. Let us leave one part and take up the other, dividing that whole again into two. SOCRATES. Which of those do you think should be taken up? STRANGER. The one that commands regarding living beings. For the royal majesty does not preside over inanimate things like architecture does, but more nobly over living creatures; its power is concerned with them. SOCRATES. Excellent.

<margin>F</margin>STRANGER. Concerning the production and nourishment of animals, a double care is found: the care of a single animal, or the care of the whole herd. SOCRATES. Right. STRANGER. The statesman, however, does not care for a single individual—like a groom who tends one horse—but rather takes the place of one who feeds horses or cattle in herds. SOCRATES. What has just been said appears true. STRANGER. Of the nourishment of animals, shall we call the part that feeds them in groups "herd-nourishment" or "collective nourishment"? SOCRATES. Whichever term happens to come up.

<margin>G</margin><margin>Avoid wordy curiosity <note>original: "Euitanda curiositas verbosum," a warning against being too literal or obsessive about terminology</note></margin>STRANGER. You have answered excellently, Socrates. If you avoid being too fussy about words, you will turn out much wiser in your old age. For now, we must do as you suggest. But do you see how one might show that "herd-nourishment" is twofold, so that what we are seeking—which is now in a double form—might then be sought in one of the halves? SOCRATES. I will certainly try; and it already seems to me that one is the guardianship of humans, and the other is the guardianship of beasts. STRANGER. You have divided with great spirit and courage. However, we must take care as much as possible that this does not happen to us hereafter. SOCRATES. What do you warn us to avoid? STRANGER. That we do not cut off one tiny part against many large ones, nor take a part that lacks a distinct species; rather, the part should also be a species. It is most beautiful to immediately set apart what is sought from the rest, if done correctly—just as you, a moment ago, hurried to divide, seeing the argument turning toward humans. But, my friend, it is not safe to proceed to the very end and too thinly. It is better to go through the middle; in this way, one finds ideas more easily. This makes all the difference in our investigations. SOCRATES. What do you mean by this, Stranger? STRANGER. I must try to speak even more clearly...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>For no architect uses the ministry of his hands, but presides over those who do. SOCRATES. That is so. STRANGER. While he applies judgment, not ministry. SOCRATES. That too is true. STRANGER. Therefore, he is rightly said to be a sharer in the science of observation. SOCRATES. And most especially so. STRANGER. This, I believe, pertains to the judge: not to reach the end and then depart, like that calculator, but to apply himself and command suitable work to each worker, until they have finished what was ordered. SOCRATES. Well said.

<margin>B</margin>STRANGER. Are not all these observational sciences, and as many as follow the science of calculation? But do these two classes differ between themselves in judgment and command? SOCRATES. They appear so. STRANGER. Wherefore, if we distribute all contemplation into two, and assign one part to judgment and the other to command, we shall perhaps think we have distributed correctly. SOCRATES. Correct indeed, in my opinion. STRANGER. Those who treat something in common think themselves satisfied with one another if they can confer. SOCRATES. Why not? STRANGER. As long as we are in agreement on this, the opinions of others must be omitted. SOCRATES. Entirely.

<margin>C</margin>STRANGER. Say then, in which of these arts is it fitting to place the royal man? Perhaps in the judicial, as a kind of spectator? Or rather in the commanding art as a master? SOCRATES. In this very one rather. STRANGER. It must be seen further if the commanding art admits any distinction. And it seems so to me. By what a retailer differs from him who sells his own work, by that a king differs from a herald. SOCRATES. In what way? STRANGER. Retailers, receiving the works of others already sold, sell them again themselves. SOCRATES. True. STRANGER. Not otherwise the heraldic class, having a sententia <note>a command or thought</note> of another entrusted to it, entrusts it to others. SOCRATES. It is so. STRANGER. Or shall we mix the royal faculty with the interpretative, the prescriptive, with prophecy and heraldry, and very many other arts of the same kind, which all command? Or do you wish rather, according to the previous comparison, that we also devise a name through some comparison, since the class of those who command their own things is almost without a name? And let us so divide these, that we place the royal class in the number of those who command their own things, omitting all others, on whom anyone else may impose a name as he pleases: for our discourse was instituted for the sake of the Prince, not the subject. SOCRATES. Surely.

<margin>D</margin>STRANGER. After this has been sufficiently distinguished from those things, and reduced from the foreign to its own, it is to be divided again, if we find any partition in it that admits us. SOCRATES. Greatly. STRANGER. And yet it seems it can be found. Follow me therefore by dividing. SOCRATES. What shall I follow?

<margin>E</margin>STRANGER. Whoever presides by commanding, they command for the sake of something being done. SOCRATES. Without a doubt. STRANGER. For indeed, to divide all things generated into two is not very difficult. SOCRATES. By what reason? STRANGER. Partly they are animate, partly inanimate. SOCRATES. It is agreed. STRANGER. If we want to make the commanding part of the observational faculty into these members, let us cut it. SOCRATES. Into what? STRANGER. Let a part of it be placed in the generation of inanimate things, and a part in the generation of animate things. And so the whole will be cut into two. SOCRATES. In truth. STRANGER. Let us send away one part, taking the other, and divide that whole again into two. SOCRATES. Which of those do you think should be resumed? STRANGER. That which commands concerning animals. For the royal majesty does not preside over things not animate like architecture, but more nobly over animate things, and its power is occupied about those. SOCRATES. Most well.

<margin>F</margin>STRANGER. Around the generation and nutrition of animals, a double care is found. This one of a certain single animal. That one of the whole herd. SOCRATES. Right. STRANGER. But the civil [man] does not carry on care privately and for a single one, like he who drives an ox, or the servant who saddles a horse, but takes the place of him who feeds horses or oxen. SOCRATES. What has now been said seems to be true. STRANGER. Whether from the nutrition of animals do we call that which feeds them in herds "herd nutrition" or "common nutrition"? SOCRATES. It happens that both are used in speaking.

<margin>G</margin><margin>Avoid wordy curiosity</margin>STRANGER. Excellently, Socrates, you have answered: and if you will avoid curiosity of words, you will turn out much wiser in old age. Therefore at present, as you order, it must be done. But do you see in what way someone showing the nutrition of the herd to be twin, might cause that which is investigated in both for what is now proposed, to be searched for thereafter in the other? SOCRATES. I will strive indeed, and now it seems to me, one is the common guardianship of men, the other of brutes. STRANGER. Promptly and bravely you have distinguished. Yet it is to be guarded against with all our might, lest hereafter that happens to us. SOCRATES. What do you warn is to be guarded against? STRANGER. Lest we separate one tiny little part against ample and very many parts, nor take that without a species, but let that part have a species at the same time. For it is most beautiful to immediately discern what is sought from others, if only it be done rightly, just as you a little before, judging concerning dividing, hastened to divide, seeing the discourse declining toward men in the other member. But it is not safe enough, friend, to follow all things to the extreme and too thinly. It is better to progress through the middle; for thus we find ideas more easily and better. This refers to the whole towards those things which are searched for. SOCRATES. In what way do you say this, Stranger? STRANGER. It must be attempted because of the kindness of your nature...

</columns>

<summary>The Stranger and Young Socrates distinguish the King's art as a "self-commanding" theoretical science that rules over the collective care of living beings. The Stranger warns against the logical error of dividing a small group (like humans) away from a vast group (like animals) without following natural species or "ideas."</summary>

# OF PLATO

<columns>

<margin>A</margin>
...so that it may be explained more clearly. For the present, it is impossible to declare the proposal so perfectly that nothing is lacking; however, for the sake of clarity, we should trace it back a little further. SOCRATES THE YOUNGER. What fault then do you find in this division of ours? STRANGER. Something like this: it is as if someone, intending to cut the human race in two, were to divide it the way most people here do. These people separate the race of the Greeks as one group from all others. All other humans—who are innumerable and possess no shared language or communion among themselves—they label with the name "barbarian" <note>original Latin: "barbarico nomine"; Greek: "βάρβαρον". The Greeks categorized the world into themselves and everyone else ("Barbaroi"), which Plato here criticizes as a logical error.</note>. Because of this single name, they mistakenly think it constitutes a single, universal genus. It would be similar if someone, wanting to divide numbers in two, took ten thousand aside from all the rest as one species, and then gave a single name to all the remaining numbers, considering them a single genus.

<margin>B</margin>
A more correct division, following the species and dividing into two members, would be if one divided numbers into even and odd, or the human race into male and female. One should only separate the Lydians, Phrygians, or any others from the whole when one lacks the power to find a genus that is also a natural part of the thing being divided. SOCRATES. You speak skillfully, Stranger. But show me how I might more clearly understand that a "part" and a "species" <term>species: often translated as "form" or "kind" (eidos in Greek)</term> are not the same thing, but different.

<margin>C</margin>
STRANGER. O Socrates, best of men, you ask no small thing. We have already wandered further from our original purpose than we ought. Yet you bid us wander even further! For now, as is proper, let the discourse return to where it departed. We shall pursue those other matters at our leisure another time, following their tracks. Nevertheless, be very careful, Socrates, lest you think you have heard something definitively settled by me regarding this. SOCRATES THE YOUNGER. Regarding what? STRANGER. That a "part" and a "species" differ from one another.

<margin>What the difference is between a part and a species</margin>
SOCRATES. Why so? STRANGER. Whatever is a species of something, that same thing must also be a part of the genus of which it is said to be a species. However, it is not necessary for a part to be a species, or a part of a species. Always assert, O Socrates, that I say it is this way rather than that. SOCRATES THE YOUNGER. It shall be as you command. STRANGER. Now tell me what follows. SOCRATES THE YOUNGER. What is it?

<margin>D</margin>
STRANGER. This, I say, from which we wandered. I think we have strayed this far for this reason: when you were asked into what members the nursing of a herd should be divided, you responded very promptly that there were two kinds of animals—one being humans, and the other being a single group of all "beasts" together. SOCRATES. That is true. STRANGER. At that time, it seemed to me that by cutting off one part, you thought you should place all the remaining animals into one genus because you could call them all by one common name: "beasts." SOCRATES. That is what happened. STRANGER. This, O bravest Socrates, seems just as if some other animal, like a crane <note>The "Crane Analogy" is a famous Platonic argument against human-centrism, suggesting that to a crane, humans would be just another type of "beast."</note>—or some other creature endowed with intelligence—were to act as you did. It might call "cranes" a single rational genus distinct from other animals, and then, grouping all other things (including humans) together, it might call that other genus "beasts." Let us therefore strive to avoid all errors of this kind. SOCRATES. By what path?

<margin>E</margin>
STRANGER. By not dividing the universal genus of animals all at once, lest we fall into these errors. SOCRATES. Indeed, we must not. STRANGER. And yet, we failed in that way above. SOCRATES. How so? STRANGER. That part of the science of knowledge which involves commanding was found to belong to the genus that cares for animals—specifically, gregarious animals <term>gregabilia: animals that live in herds or flocks</term>. Was it not? SOCRATES THE YOUNGER. Certainly. STRANGER. Therefore, even then, the whole genus of animals should have been distinguished into the tame and the wild. For those whose nature is such that they can be tamed are called domestic, while others are called wild. SOCRATES THE YOUNGER. Excellent. STRANGER. And the science we seek is found among the domestic ones, and it should be sought regarding the sociable genus of animals. SOCRATES. Indeed. STRANGER. Therefore, let us not divide by looking at everything at once, as we did then, nor should we hurry too much in our partitioning, hoping to grasp the science of the city all in an instant.

<margin>Proverb.</margin>
For too much haste has caused that old proverb to happen to us. SOCRATES. Which one? STRANGER. That by hurrying too much in our division, we finish more slowly. SOCRATES. And it has happened rightly, Stranger. STRANGER. So much for these things. Let us attempt again from the beginning to divide the common nursing of animals. For perhaps the discourse itself, led step by step to its end, will more clearly demonstrate what you so earnestly desire. Answer this. SOCRATES. To what shall I answer?

<margin>F</margin>
<margin>Fishes being tamed around the Nile.</margin>
STRANGER. Perhaps you have heard this from many, for I do not think you have been present among those who tame fishes in the Nile or in the royal lakes. But perhaps you have seen it yourself at some springs. SOCRATES. I have seen it myself, and I have heard the other from many. STRANGER. Moreover, you have heard and believe—even if you have never traveled through the plains of Thessaly—that certain people breed flocks of geese and cranes. SOCRATES. Without a doubt. STRANGER. I asked you these things because the care of animals in herds seems to be divided: some are aquatic, others are terrestrial. SOCRATES. It is so. STRANGER. Do you agree that the care of the herd should be distinguished into two parts, so that it feeds partly moist and partly dry animals? SOCRATES. I certainly agree. STRANGER. No one will ask which of these the "royal concern" looks toward, for it is doubtful to no one. SOCRATES. To no one. STRANGER. For everyone would distinguish the nursing of land-dwelling animals especially. SOCRATES. Into which members? STRANGER. Into the care of the winged and the walking.

<column-break/>

...to speak, through the ignorance of your nature, O Socrates. While we are prepared to show it now without deficiency, it is impossible; yet we must try to make it more manifest for the sake of clarity. SOCRATES. What sort of thing do you mean when you say we were not dividing correctly just now? STRANGER. Something like this: as if someone, attempting to divide the human race in two, divided it as many here do, taking the Greek race as one, separated from all others; but to all the other races, which are infinite and unmixed and discordant with each other, they give the name "Barbarian," and because of this one name, they expect it to be one single genus. Or as if someone thought to divide numbers into two species by cutting off ten thousand from all the rest, separating it as one species, and then giving one name to all the rest, claiming that because of that name, it becomes a single genus different from the other. It would be better and more according to species and divided in two if someone cut numbers into even and odd, or the human race into male and female; and only separated Lydians or Phrygians or any others against the whole when one found it impossible to find a genus that was also a part of each thing divided. SOCRATES THE YOUNGER. Most correctly. But indeed, Stranger, how could one more clearly know that a genus and a part are not the same, but different from each other? STRANGER. O best of men, you ask no small task, Socrates. We have even now wandered further than necessary from the proposed discourse, and you command us to wander still more. For now, as is likely, let us return again; we shall pursue these things another time at leisure, tracking them down. But do not think that you have heard this from me as something entirely and clearly defined. SOCRATES THE YOUNGER. What sort of thing? STRANGER. That a species and a part are different from each other. SOCRATES. How so? STRANGER. That when something is a species of something, it is also necessarily a part of that genus of which it is called a species; but there is no necessity for a part to be a species. Always say that I speak in this way rather than that, Socrates. SOCRATES. It shall be so. STRANGER. Tell me then what follows. SOCRATES. What? STRANGER. That point from which our wandering led us here. For I think it was mostly when you were asked how the feeding of herds should be divided, and you said very eagerly that there are two kinds of animals: one human, and another one for all other beasts together. SOCRATES. True. STRANGER. And to me then you seemed, by taking away a part, to think that the remainder was one genus of all things because you could name them all by the same name, calling them "beasts." SOCRATES. That was also so. STRANGER. But indeed, O bravest of all men, perhaps if there is some other prudent animal, as the crane seems to be, or some other such thing which perhaps gives names in the same way you do, it would set "cranes" as one genus for itself against other animals, magnifying itself; and grouping all others together with humans into the same category, it would perhaps call them nothing else but "beasts." Let us therefore try to be careful of all such things. SOCRATES. How? STRANGER. By not dividing the whole genus of animals all at once, so that we suffer less from this. SOCRATES. Indeed, there is no need. STRANGER. For we also erred in this way then. SOCRATES. Why so? STRANGER. That part of the commanding science of knowledge, as it relates to the feeding of animals, was of the kind that herds animals. Was it not? SOCRATES. Yes. STRANGER. It had already been divided then into the tame and the wild. For those having a nature to be tamed are called mild, and those not having it, wild. SOCRATES. Well said. STRANGER. And the science we seek is again among the mild ones; it is to be sought among those that are fed in herds. SOCRATES. Yes. STRANGER. Let us not divide as we did then, looking at everything at once, nor let us hurry, so that we might quickly reach the science of the city. For it has made us suffer that which is said in the proverb. SOCRATES. Which one? STRANGER. By not dividing calmly, we finished more slowly. SOCRATES. And it has done so well, Stranger. STRANGER. Let us try these things again from the beginning, to divide the common nursing of animals. For perhaps the discourse itself, proceeding through the steps you desire, will show it more beautifully to you. And tell me. SOCRATES. What thing? STRANGER. This which you have probably heard from many. For you have not yourself seen the taming of fishes in the Nile, and those in the royal lakes. But you might have seen them in springs. SOCRATES. I have seen these very things, and I have heard of the others from many. STRANGER. And indeed of the breeding of geese and cranes, even if you have not wandered about the Thessalian plains, you have heard and already believe. SOCRATES. Why not? STRANGER. For the sake of this: because of the feeding of herds, there is the aquatic and the terrestrial. SOCRATES. There is indeed. STRANGER. Does it also seem to me that we should divide the science of common nursing in this way, assigning each part of it to each of these? One, the nursing of those in the water, the other, the nursing of those on dry land? SOCRATES. To me, yes. STRANGER. And indeed, we shall not seek which of the arts the royal one belongs to in this way. It is clear to everyone. SOCRATES. How could it not be? STRANGER. Everyone would divide the dry-land-nursing part of the herd-feeding kind. SOCRATES. How? STRANGER. By distinguishing the winged and the walking.

</columns>

<summary>This page contains a critical discussion on the logical method of division, where the Stranger corrects Socrates' habit of grouping all non-humans as "beasts" and all non-Greeks as "Barbarians." He uses the famous "Crane Analogy" to show that such divisions are human-centric rather than natural, leading into a more systematic division of animal husbandry into aquatic and terrestrial types.</summary>
