# THE STATESMAN.

<columns>

<margin>A</margin>
YOUNG SOCRATES. That is most true.
STRANGER. What then? Should we look for the statesman's art among the walking animals? Or do you think even the most foolish person—to put it bluntly—would have this opinion?
SOCRATES. I certainly do.
STRANGER. And for the art of herding walking animals, we ought to reveal its divisions into two parts, just as we did with even numbers.
SOCRATES. That is clear.
STRANGER. And yet, regarding the part toward which our argument was hastening, two paths now seem to be stretched out before us. One is a shorter path, which reaches a small part by separating it from a large one. The other, as we said before, follows the principle that one should cut through the middle as much as possible, though it is a much longer line. We may, therefore, proceed by whichever of these we wish.
SOCRATES. Is it impossible to go by both?
STRANGER. Not at the same time, O wonderful youth! But clearly it is possible to do so in turn.

<margin>B</margin>
SOCRATES. Then I choose to go by both, one after the other.
STRANGER. That is easy, since what remains is short. At the beginning or the middle of our journey, such a request would have been difficult for us; but now, since we have decided this way, let us take the longer path first. For since we are young <note>The Stranger is addressing Young Socrates, who is a student here</note>, we shall travel the long road more easily. Observe this distinction.
SOCRATES. Speak on.
STRANGER. For us, the genus of walking, tame, and herded animals has already been divided by nature into two parts.
SOCRATES. How so?
STRANGER. Into those with horns and those without horns.
SOCRATES. So it appears.
STRANGER. Now, dividing the art of herding walking animals, assign the description of each part to its respective group. For if you try to give them specific names, you will complicate the matter more than necessary.

<margin>C</margin>
SOCRATES. How then should we speak of them?
STRANGER. In this way: let the science of herding walking animals be divided into two, with one part assigned to the horned portion of the flock, and the other to the hornless.
SOCRATES. Let it be spoken of in that way, for it has been sufficiently demonstrated.
STRANGER. And indeed, it is clear to us that our King shepherds a certain hornless flock.
SOCRATES. How could it not be clear?

<margin>D</margin>
STRANGER. Let us then try to break this down further and assign to him what belongs to him.
SOCRATES. By all means.
STRANGER. Do you wish to divide this flock by the difference of solid hoofs versus cloven hoofs, or rather by their mode of breeding—whether it is mixed or simple? For you surely understand this.
SOCRATES. Understand what?
STRANGER. That the race of horses and donkeys is naturally inclined to breed with one another.
SOCRATES. Yes.
STRANGER. But the rest of the tame and social animals breed only within their own kind, without such mixing.
SOCRATES. Certainly.
STRANGER. What then? Does the statesman appear to have care for a nature that allows promiscuous breeding, or one that is simple?
SOCRATES. Clearly it is for the unmixed and simple kind.

<margin>E</margin>
STRANGER. This nature of living things, just as we have done before, we must now cut into two members.
SOCRATES. We must indeed.
STRANGER. And yet, almost this entire genus of tame and herded animals has already been divided, except for two types. For it is not fitting to number the race of dogs among the herded cattle.
SOCRATES. No, certainly not. But how shall we divide these two?
STRANGER. In the way that is fitting for you and Theaetetus <note>Theaetetus was a famous mathematician and a character in this dialogue's companion piece</note> to distribute them, since you are both students of geometry: by the diameter, and then again by the diameter of the diameter.
SOCRATES. How do you mean?
STRANGER. Has the condition of the human race not been naturally established for movement in such a way that it is like a diameter whose power is two-footed?
SOCRATES. Not otherwise.
STRANGER. And the condition of the remaining genus is again, according to its power, the diameter of our power, since it is constituted with twice two feet.
SOCRATES. Nothing prevents it being so. And I almost understand what you wish to show.
STRANGER. Do we see, O Socrates, something else worthy of a laugh that has happened to us in the previous division?
SOCRATES. What is that?

<margin>F</margin>
STRANGER. Our human race is mixed together and running alongside the most noble and easiest of all genera.
SOCRATES. I see it, and indeed it is clear how absurd it is.
STRANGER. Is it not fitting that the slowest things arrive last?
SOCRATES. That is reasonable.
STRANGER. But we did not notice that the King appears even more ridiculous, running along with the flock of men and performing his race with the animal that is best trained of all for an easy life. <note>original Greek: "ἀχειρῆ βίον"; Latin: "vitę facilitatem". This is a joke comparing humans to pigs in the way they are herded.</note>

<margin>G</margin>
SOCRATES. Entirely so.
STRANGER. Now it is clearly evident, O Socrates, what was said during our inquiry into the Sophist.
SOCRATES. What was that?
STRANGER. That in this methodical way of disputing, the argument cares no more for what is elegant than what is inelegant, nor does it value a shorter path more than a longer one, but only accomplishes what is most true.
SOCRATES. So it seems.
STRANGER. After this, do not get ahead of me by asking for a shorter way to define the King; I shall proceed to it on my own.
SOCRATES. By all means.
STRANGER. I say then that we ought to have divided the walking animal into two-footed and four-footed; and since man was then left alone with the winged creatures, we should have divided the two-footed genus again into the "naked" or "featherless" and the "winged." Once this distinction was made, and the art of nourishing and preserving humans was shown, we could then place the statesman and royal man over it like a charioteer, giving him the reins and the rudders of the city, as this science belongs to him.

<margin>H</margin>
SOCRATES. You have paid this argument back to me most excellently, as if it were a debt, with the digression added on as a sort of interest to fulfill it.
STRANGER. Come then, let us collect our discourse from the beginning to the end regarding the name of the statesman's art.
SOCRATES. Certainly.
STRANGER. Of that science which is concerned with contemplation, one part was the skill of commanding; under this was the faculty that commands by its own authority. A significant member of this was the nurturing of living things; and within that, the herding of flocks...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
SOCRATES. Thus stands the truth.
STRANGER. That the civil faculty deals only with those things that walk, even the most foolish person, so to speak, would notice.
SOCRATES. Without controversy.
STRANGER. Furthermore, we must divide the nourishment of the walking genus into two parts, like an even number.
SOCRATES. It is evident.
STRANGER. Moreover, to that place where our discourse tends, it seems that twin paths can lead us. One indeed by a short track, while it separates a narrow portion from a wide one. But the other by a longer circuit, while it preserves that precept mentioned before, that division should be made through the middle; it is permitted to enter whichever we wish.
SOCRATES. Is it not permitted to proceed through both?
STRANGER. Not simultaneously, O marvelous youth, but it is permitted separately.
SOCRATES. I would desire both separately, then.
STRANGER. That is easy indeed, since what remains is small. Truly, in the beginning or middle of the journey, this precept would have been hard for us. But now, since it seems so, let us enter the longer way first. For since we have not long ago set out on the matter, we shall complete a long journey more lightly. See this distinction thus.
SOCRATES. Only tell me.

<margin>B</margin>
STRANGER. By which the genus of walking, tame, and herding things is divided into two parts according to nature.
SOCRATES. Why?
STRANGER. Armed with horns, and lacking horns.
SOCRATES. It appears so.
STRANGER. Dividing the care of walking things, describe the condition of each part in speech. For if you wish to name them, you will complicate the matter too much.
SOCRATES. How then do you think it should be said?
STRANGER. Thus: since the care of walking things is divided in two, this one is in the horned part of the flock, and that in the non-horned.
SOCRATES. Let those things be said so, for they are sufficiently shown.
STRANGER. It is certain, therefore, that the king is the shepherd of a certain flock lacking horns.
SOCRATES. It is certainly certain.

<margin>C</margin>
STRANGER. Tearing this apart, therefore, let us try to exhibit what is done by him.
SOCRATES. Altogether.
STRANGER. Which do you prefer: to divide it by the difference of solid-hoofed and cloven-hoofed animals, or rather by this proper generation and that common one? For you understand.
SOCRATES. What?

<margin>D</margin>
STRANGER. That the genus of horses and donkeys generates promiscuously among themselves.
SOCRATES. To be sure.
STRANGER. But the remaining animals of a domestic and social genus, without foreign mixing, procreate only from their own species.
SOCRATES. Clear to anyone.
STRANGER. Does the <margin>Promiscuous and simple generation.</margin> civil discipline, therefore, care for animals of promiscuous generation or simple?
SOCRATES. Of unmixed and simple, without a doubt.

<margin>E</margin>
STRANGER. This nature of living things, just as we have preserved in the matters above until now, we must cut through twin members.
SOCRATES. It teaches so.
STRANGER. Indeed, we have already discerned this whole genus of domestic and herded animal, which they call tame, with two genera excepted. Furthermore, it is not fitting to number the genus of dogs among herded cattle.
SOCRATES. Certainly not. But by what means shall we divide these two?
STRANGER. This, I say, by which it is fitting to distribute you and Theaetetus, since you have been engaged in geometry: namely, by the diameter, and again by the diameter of the diameter.
SOCRATES. Why do you say that?
STRANGER. Has the condition of the human genus not been instituted by nature for progress in a way other than as a diameter with the power of two feet?
SOCRATES. Not otherwise.
STRANGER. Truly, the condition of the remaining genus is again, according to power, the diameter of our power, since it is constituted with these two feet <note>The Latin here implies "twice two" or four feet</note>.
SOCRATES. Nothing prevents it from being so. And I almost understand what you wish to show now.
STRANGER. Do we perceive anything else worthy of laughter, O Socrates, that has happened to us in the superior division?
SOCRATES. What indeed?

<margin>F</margin>
STRANGER. The genus of men mixed together, and running along with the most noble and easiest genus of all.
SOCRATES. I perceive it, and clearly indeed, how absurd it is.
STRANGER. Is it not fitting that those which are slowest arrive last?
SOCRATES. It is agreeable.
STRANGER. But we did not at all notice that the king appears more ridiculous, running about together with the flock of men, and performing a race with that animal best exercised of all for the ease of life?

<margin>G</margin>
SOCRATES. Entirely so.
STRANGER. Now that which was said in the inquiry of the sophist is clearly open, O Socrates.
SOCRATES. What is that?
STRANGER. That in this sort of methodical reasoning of disputation, it cares no more for the beautiful than the unbeautiful, nor does it make more of a shorter way than a longer one, but only transacts what is most true.
SOCRATES. It seems so.
STRANGER. After this, do not anticipate me, asking about the shorter way to establish the definition of the king; I enter it voluntarily.
SOCRATES. Altogether.
STRANGER. I say therefore it was necessary above to distribute the walking animal into two-footed and four-footed; and since man then remained only with the flying things, again to divide that two-footed genus into the naked/featherless and the winged; this distinction being performed, and the art that is the nurse and preserver of men being shown, to set the civil and royal man over it like a charioteer, and to give him the reins and rudders of the city, as if this science were his own.

<margin>H</margin>
SOCRATES. Most excellently have you indeed paid this speech to me as if a debt, with the digression itself added in place of interest and fully completed.
STRANGER. Come then, let us collect from the beginning to the end the sermon about the name of the civil art.
SOCRATES. Thoroughly.
STRANGER. Of that science, therefore, which is engaged in contemplating, one part is the skill of commanding; subject to this is that faculty which commands by its own will; to this, a member not at all small is the nourishing of animals; to this also, the herding of the flock...

<sig>P iij</sig>

</columns>

<summary>This page details the "diaeresis" or logical division used to define the Statesman, moving from walking animals to herded animals, specifically those that are hornless and breed only within their own species. It concludes by defining the Statesman's subject as the "featherless biped" (man) and the Statesman himself as the "charioteer" of the city.</summary>
<keywords>Statesman, Socrates, Eleatic Stranger, Dialectic, Division, geometry, diameter, animal-rearing, horned animals, two-footed animals</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from the previous page, where the Stranger and Young Socrates categorized the statesman's art as the herding of "hornless" and "bipedal" animals (humans). They are now beginning to question if this definition is too broad, leading into the famous "Myth of the Reversal of the Cosmos."</meta>

# PLATO

<columns>

Finally, for these walking animals there is nourishment, and then again that species which feeds animals lacking horns. It is necessary that this part embrace at least a threefold division if one wishes to encompass it under a single name, calling it the science of herding the unmixed race. The portion of this which feeds only humans from the bipedal flock is the very thing we are seeking: the imperial faculty, which we name equally as the royal and the civil art. **SOC.** Entirely so. **HOS.** Do you think, O Socrates, that we have acted rightly, just as you have already said? **SOC.** Regarding what? **HOS.** Has the definition we proposed been sufficiently completed? Or is this the very thing most overlooked in our inquiry: that we have described it in a certain way, yet have not yet thoroughly defined it? **s.** In what way do you say this? **h.** I will try to explain more clearly what I perceive. **so.** Speak now. **h o s.** Since it was established that there are many faculties of herders, that one specific type—the guardianship of a single flock—seemed to be the civil discipline itself. **s o.** Indeed. **h o s.** We showed that this is the communal nutrition not of horses, nor of other beasts, but of humans alone. **s o c.** That also. **h o s.** Therefore, let us look at the specific difference between all other herders and kings. **s o c.** In what way? **h o s.** If someone holding the name of another art should claim for himself the communal nutrition of the human flock, what should be said? **s.** In what sense do you ask? **h.** If, I say, merchants, farmers, and cooks—and in addition, physical trainers and doctors—should rise up against the herders whom we called "politicians," and assert that they themselves are the true herders of men? For they provide the means of life not only to the common people, but even to kings and magistrates. **s.** Would they not be speaking the truth? **h.** Perhaps. And let us consider this. For we know that no one contends with a cowherd over such things; he is, without controversy, the herder of the herd. He himself is the doctor, he is the matchmaker, and he alone is the expert in the obstetric art regarding the births and offspring of the newborns. Furthermore, no one delights, draws, and soothes the herd with jokes and music better than he, so far as their nature is capable of it, practicing music for his flock either with instruments or with his voice alone. And the same reasoning applies to other herders. Is it not so? **s.** Very much so. **h.** How then does our discourse concerning the king seem right and sound, when we position him as that herder and nourisher of the human flock, setting him apart from all others, while many others contend for this very title? **s.** Not at all. **h.** Did we not rightly doubt a little while ago, when we suspected that we might only be introducing a certain "figure" of a king, but had not yet perfectly defined the statesman himself? Not until we have grasped those who entangle themselves with him and profess to be herders no less than he; and, separating the king from them, show him alone in his purity. **s.** Quite right. **h o s.** This, therefore, must be done by us, O Socrates, unless we wish to carry away infamy at the end of our discourse. **s.** And that is by no means expedient. **h o s.** We must proceed again from another principle, along a different path. **s.** Which one? **h o s.** We must interject a certain playfulness here, and employ a large portion of a long fable <note>The "Myth of the Statesman" or the "Myth of the Reversal," used to explain the cosmic order.</note>, and then execute what remains as we did before, by always subdividing part from part, and thus lead the inquiry to the summit of what is sought. Is this not necessary? **s.** It is indeed necessary. **h.** Now then, listen to my little story with attentive ears, just as children do; for you are not far removed from your childhood years. **s.** Tell it, I pray. **h o s.** There was then, and there will still be, a memory of many ancient things; and among the rest, a memorable prodigy which is told concerning the contention of Atreus and Thyestes <note>Atreus and Thyestes were brothers competing for the throne of Mycenae; the sun reversed its course as a divine sign of Atreus's right to rule.</note>. For you have surely heard and remember what they say happened then. **s.** Do you mean the omen of the golden lamb? **h o s.** Not at all, but rather the change in the rising and setting of the sun and the other stars. For from where they now rise, they then used to set, and conversely they rose from the opposite side. At that time, God, providing a testimony for Atreus, changed the heaven into this current form. **s.** That is indeed told. **h.** Furthermore, we have heard from many about the reign of Saturn <note>Saturn is the Roman name for the Greek god Cronus; his reign was considered a "Golden Age."</note>. **s.** From many indeed. **h.** And what of this? Did not those ancient men <margin>The Fable of the Earth-born men.</margin> spring from the earth, and were not born from one another? **s.** This too is commemorated among ancient matters. **h o s.** All these things proceed from the same phenomenon <note>original: *malo* (evil/misfortune), though the Greek *pathos* suggests an event or experience</note>, along with many other things far more wonderful than these. But through the length of time, some have faded away, and others are told in a scattered, disorderly way. Yet no one has told of that event which is the cause of all these. But now it must be told, for it will contribute to the demonstration of the king. **s.** You speak excellently. Tell it then, and omit nothing. **h o s.** Listen then. This universe is sometimes guided, moved, and rotated by God himself; but at other times he lets it go, when the circuits of the world have filled the measure of time appropriate to it. Then the world, by its own accord and by a free motion, is turned back in the opposite direction. For it is a living thing, and has obtained wisdom from him who constructed it from the beginning. <margin>Why the rotation is innate to the heavens.</margin> And this reverse rotation is necessarily innate to it for this reason. **s.** For what reason, do you say? **h o s.** To be always the same, and to stay in the same state <margin>The condition of divine things.</margin> and in the same way, belongs only to the most divine of all things. But the nature of the body is not capable of this order. Moreover, all that which we call the heaven and the world has received many and blessed gifts from its progenitor,

<column-break/>

...herding. And of herding, again, the walking-pasture division. And of the walking-pasture division, the art was most particularly cut away that nourishes the hornless nature. If one wished to encompass this part—for instance, the deer and the sheep—under one name, it would be necessary to weave them together, calling it the non-mixed science of herding. And the segment under this, which is the herding of the bipedal flock—the "human-herding"—is the only thing now left. This is the very thing we sought, called at once the royal and the political art. **SOC.** Entirely so. **XEN.** <note>The "Stranger" is titled *Xenos* in Greek.</note> Is it truly so for us, O Socrates, just as you have now said? Is it so, and has it been performed by us? **SOC.** What do you mean? **XEN.** Has the proposal been stated entirely or sufficiently? Or does the inquiry fail in this very point: that the account has been stated in a way, but has not yet been completely and perfectly worked out? **SOC.** How do you mean? **XEN.** I will try to make what I am thinking even more clear now. **SOC.** You may speak. **XEN.** Now, many herding arts appeared to us just now, and the political art was one of them, a care for one certain kind of flock. **SOC.** Yes. **XEN.** But our account distinguished this not as the nourishment of horses or other beasts, but as the communal-nourishing science of humans. **SOC.** Thus it was. **XEN.** Let us then observe the difference between all herders and our kings. **SOC.** Of what kind? **XEN.** If any of the others, having the name of another art, says and claims to be a communal foster-parent of the flock. **SOC.** How do you mean? **XEN.** As if merchants, and farmers, and grain-providers, and besides these, physical trainers and the race of doctors—you know that all these would utterly dispute with the herders of humans (whom we called politicians) in their argument, claiming that they themselves take care of human nourishment, not only of the flocked humans, but even of the rulers themselves. **SOC.** Would they not be speaking rightly? **XEN.** Perhaps. And this we should examine. But this we know: that no one will dispute any of these things with a cowherd. Rather, the cow-feeder is himself the nourisher of the flock, himself the doctor, himself as it were the matchmaker, and he alone is the expert in the midwife's art concerning the births and deliveries of the offspring. Furthermore, in play and music, as far as the creatures themselves naturally partake in them, no one else is better at charming and soothing them, whether with instruments or with the mouth alone, practicing the music of his own flock best. And indeed, the same manner applies to other herders. Is it not so? **SOC.** Most rightly. **XEN.** How then could our account concerning the king appear right and unblemished, when we set him down as the herder and nourisher of the human flock, selecting him alone, while ten thousand others dispute him? **SOC.** Not at all. **XEN.** Were we not rightly afraid a moment ago, suspecting that we might be describing some "royal shape," yet had not yet worked out the "statesman" for us with precision, until we have stripped away and separated him from those who crowd around him and claim to share his herding, and thus show him alone in his purity? **SOC.** Most rightly indeed. **XEN.** This, then, O Socrates, we must do, if we are not to bring shame upon the argument at the end. **SOC.** Indeed, this must by no means be done. **XEN.** Again, therefore, we must travel a certain other path from a different beginning. **SOC.** What kind? **XEN.** Mixing in, as it were, a bit of play. For we must use a substantial part of a great myth, and for the rest, as in the previous parts, by always taking away part from part, arrive at the height of what is sought. Should we not? **SOC.** Yes, indeed. **XEN.** But give your mind quite closely to my myth, just like children. You have certainly not escaped the years of childhood by much. **SOC.** You may speak. **XEN.** There were then, and there still are, many other things among the ancient tales, and specifically the marvel told concerning the strife of Atreus and Thyestes. For surely you have heard and remember what they say happened then. **SOC.** You mean perhaps the sign concerning the golden lamb. **XEN.** Not at all; but rather the change in the setting and rising of the sun and the other stars; how then they used to set in the place where they now rise, and they rose from the opposite side. Then indeed, God, having borne witness for Atreus, changed it to the current form. **SOC.** For that is indeed told. **XEN.** And furthermore, we have heard from many concerning the kingship under Cronus. **SOC.** From very many, indeed. **XEN.** And what of this? That those of former times were produced "earth-born," and were not born from one another? **SOC.** This too is one of the things told of old. **XEN.** All these things, then, come from the same event, and in addition to these, ten thousand others even more wondrous than these. But through the abundance of time, some of them have been extinguished, and others are told separately and scattered from one another. But that event which is the cause of all these, no one has told. But now it must be told. For it will be fitting for the demonstration of the king. **SOC.** You have spoken most beautifully; tell it, and omit nothing. **XEN.** Listen then. This whole universe God himself sometimes guides as it proceeds and circles it together; but at other times he lets it go, when its periods have already received the measure of the time fitting to it. And it, of its own accord, is revolved back to the contrary direction, being a living thing and having obtained intelligence from the one who fitted it together in the beginning. And this backward motion has become innate to it by necessity. **SOC.** Because of what reason? **XEN.** To be always in the same state and in the same way, and to be the same, belongs only to the most divine of all things; but the nature of body is not of this rank. But that which we have named "heaven" and "cosmos" has partaken of many and blessed things from its generator...

</columns>

<summary>The Stranger and Socrates refine the definition of a Statesman as a "herder of humans" but realize that many others (doctors, farmers) also claim this role. To distinguish the true King, the Stranger begins a cosmological myth about how the universe periodically reverses its rotation, moving from a Golden Age under God's direct care to an age of self-governance.</summary>

**STRANGER** But it is also impossible for it to have no share in a body. For this reason, it is impossible for it to remain entirely free from change throughout all time. Yet, according to its power, it moves as much as possible in the same place, in the same way, and with a single motion. Therefore, it has received a circular revolution—the smallest possible deviation from its own internal motion. But to turn oneself forever is possible for almost nothing except the Leader of all things that move. And it is not permitted for Him to move the world now one way, and then again in the opposite way. From all this, one must say that the world neither turns itself forever, nor is it always turned as a whole by God in two distinct and opposite rotations. Nor, again, do two gods with opposing minds turn it. Rather, as was just said—and this is the only remaining possibility—at one time it is guided by a different divine cause, gaining life again and receiving a restored immortality from its Creator; but at another time, when it is released, it proceeds by itself. Having been let go at the proper moment, it travels back through many tens of thousands of revolutions, because it is of the greatest size and perfectly balanced, stepping upon the smallest pivot <note>original: "ἐπὶ σμικροτάτου βαίνον ποδὸς" - literally 'walking on the smallest foot', a poetic Greek metaphor for the world's axis.</note>.

**SOCRATES** Indeed, everything you have gone through seems very likely to have been said.

**STRANGER** Let us then consider the event that follows from what has just been said, which we claimed was the cause of all those wonders. It is this very thing.

**SOCRATES** What thing?

**STRANGER** That the motion of the whole world is sometimes carried in the direction it now circles, and sometimes in the opposite direction.

**SOCRATES** How so?

**STRANGER** This change must be considered the greatest and most complete reversal <term>reversal: "τροπή" (tropē), meaning a turning or pivot point, as in the solstice.</term> of all the turnings that occur in the heavens.

**SOCRATES** So it seems.

**STRANGER** Therefore, we must believe that the greatest changes also occur at that time for those of us who live within it.

**SOCRATES** That is also likely.

**STRANGER** And do we not know that the nature of living creatures finds it hard to endure great, many, and manifold changes?

**SOCRATES** Of course.

**STRANGER** Thus, the greatest destructions necessarily occur then, both among other animals and especially the human race, of which only a small part remains. Many other wondrous and strange things happen to these survivors, but the greatest is this, which follows immediately upon the reversal of the universe, when the turn opposite to the current birth cycle occurs.

**SOCRATES** What is that?

**STRANGER** The age which each animal then had was first halted in all of them, and everything mortal ceased to be seen moving toward an older appearance. Instead, changing back to the opposite, they grew younger and more delicate. The white hairs of the elderly turned black; the cheeks of those with beards became smooth again, restoring each to the past bloom of youth. The bodies of young men became smooth and smaller every day and night, returning again to the nature of a newborn child, becoming like it in both soul and body. From there, they wasted away entirely and finally disappeared. Moreover, the bodies of those who died by violence in that time suffered these same effects rapidly, and in a few days they vanished, having decayed without a trace.

**SOCRATES** But what was the generation of animals then, O Stranger? And in what way were they born from one another?

**STRANGER** It is clear, Socrates, that in that nature there was no such thing as being born from one another. But the race that is sometimes called "earth-born" <note>original: "γηγενὲς" (gēgenēs) - referring to the myth of people springing fully formed from the soil.</note> was the one that at that time was returning back out of the earth. This was remembered by our first ancestors, who lived in the time immediately following the end of the previous revolution and were born at the beginning of this second one. They were the heralds to us of these stories, which are now wrongly disbelieved by many. For one must consider what follows: logically, since the old return to the nature of children, it follows that those who are dead and lying in the earth are reconstituted there and return to life, following the reversal of generation as it circles back in the opposite direction. By this logic, they are necessarily born as "earth-born," and this is the origin of their name and story—excepting those whom God translated to another fate.

**SOCRATES** This certainly follows from what went before. But the life which you say existed under the power of Saturn <note>original: "Κρόνου" (Cronus) - the Greek name for the Titan who ruled during the Golden Age.</note>, was it in those previous turnings or in these? For it is clear that the change of the stars and the sun occurs in both types of reversals.

**STRANGER** You have followed the argument well. As for your question about everything growing spontaneously for humans, that does not belong at all to the present rotation, but rather to the previous one. For then, God himself first presided over the entire revolution as its caretaker, just as now the parts of the world are distributed in various places under the rule of many gods. Furthermore, divine spirits <term>spirits: "δαίμονες" (daimones), intermediary beings between gods and humans.</term> like divine shepherds had divided the animals by species and flocks, each being sufficient in all things for the flock he tended. Therefore, there was nothing wild, no eating of one another, and no war or strife at all. There are ten thousand other things to tell that follow from such an arrangement. However, what is said about the "spontaneous life" of those men was spoken because of this: God himself tended them and was their protector. Just as humans now, being a more divine animal, tend other lesser races, so it was then. While He was shepherd, there were no states, nor any ownership of...

<column-break/>

<margin>He who partakes in a body is not free from change.</margin>
...however, partaking in a body, it cannot be entirely free from any change whatsoever: yet as far as it can, it moves in the same way, according to the same things, and with one motion: for which reason it has obtained a circuit in which the smallest change of its own agitation occurs. But to turn itself always is possible for almost nothing, except that which provides the course for all things that are moved. To move it now one way, then another, and again in a contrary manner, is forbidden. From all these things it must be said that the world neither turns itself always, nor is it always reflected by God himself in a double and contrary circuit, nor again do two gods turn it with contrary opinions. Only what we recently said remains: that at one time it is led by a certain other divine power, receiving life again from the outside, and taking up an immortality prepared by its maker; but at another time, when it is released, it runs by itself. At that time, power having been granted, it performs many thousands of retrograde revolutions, because it is both very great and thoroughly balanced on all sides, and is revolved on a certain smallest pivot. **SOCRATES** All those things which you have commemorated seem very likely. **STRANGER** From these things which have been said, let us now consider that evil which we said was the cause of all wonders. For it is something of this kind. **SOCRATES** Of what kind? **STRANGER** That the motion of the whole world is revolved now as it is, then in the opposite way. **SOCRATES** In what way? **STRANGER** One must think this change to be the greatest and most extreme of all celestial alternations. **SOCRATES** It seems so. **STRANGER** Therefore, it is consistent that then the greatest changes occur concerning us who inhabit the interior of the world. **SOCRATES** That also is likely. **STRANGER** Nor indeed are we unaware how painfully and with what difficulty the nature of living things tolerates great, many, and all-encompassing changes. **SOCRATES** It is established. **STRANGER** Therefore, many animals necessarily perish then, and few humans survive; these truly are affected then by many new and wondrous passions. But that which is the greatest of all happens, and follows continually upon that revolution by which the heaven is reflected in a way contrary to how it is now. **SOCRATES** What is it? **STRANGER** In the beginning, in whatever age any animal was established, it ceases to progress in that same age, nor does anything of mortals become older, but it passes into a contrary figure, and puts on a younger and softer habit; the white hairs of the elders grow black: and those whose cheeks were bearded before, now with the beard laid aside, are restored to their former appearance. The bodies of those reaching puberty also become soft as their hair is shed, and gradually through individual days and nights, decreasing, they return to the nature of a child, and in these both the souls and the bodies take on the habit of boys, at last wasting away they fail and perish. Moreover, the corpses of those who fell suddenly by the change of the celestial turning suffer the same things, and in a similar manner, they rot secretly and in a short time. **SOCRATES** What was the generation of animals then, O stranger? Or in what way were they generated from one another? **STRANGER** O Socrates, in those times this race propagated nothing from itself. But what is said, that at some time a race was born from the earth, this was that time when they were turned back from the earth again. Our first ancestors handed these things down to us, who were born immediately after the first revolution: they were surely the witnesses and heralds of these speeches, to whom very little faith is now given by the common people, although it is very appropriate to have it. What follows from here, I think, should be noticed. For this which is said, that old men return into the nature of boys, is consistent with this: that from the dead, but buried in the earth, those then restored again, and reviving, follow that rotation of the heaven, or of the age, with generation revolved into the contrary; and that the earth-born were necessarily brought forth by this reason, and are so called by name and speech, as many as God did not transfer and adorn into another lot. **SOCRATES** This certainly follows from the previous things. But the life, which you say was under the reign of Saturn, did it exist under those conversions of heaven, or under these? For it is certain that the change of the sun and the remaining stars happens in both volutions. **STRANGER** You have followed the speech excellently. But what you were asking, that all things are born spontaneously for men, least of all belongs to the present conversion, but rather belonged to the former one. For then surely God stood forth as the first prince and caretaker of the whole circuit, just as now through various regions of the world its individual parts are distributed by presiding gods. <margin>The life of men under Saturn.</margin> The kinds of animals were also distributed in flocks, which certain spirits [daemons] as divine shepherds obtained by lot; since each was sufficient for performing his own duty, they were set over individuals, just as he willed, whom he himself was over. For which reason nothing was wild, and all rapacity and gluttony was far away; war and sedition were altogether absent: and besides, the other things which followed the condition of those times are innumerable. But what is said concerning the ease of food and the freedom of life, is said because God fed them, himself their shepherd and guardian: just as men now, whose nature is more divine, are shepherds of brutes. Therefore, with God guarding them, there were no political states, nor...

<margin>The erratic administration of the world.</margin> There were no marriages of men and women for the procreation of children. For all rose back to life from the earth, having no memory of their past lives. All such things <note>referring to families and private property</note> were absent. Instead, the trees and the fertile soil provided them with fruits, apples, and grain in abundance, spontaneously and without the labor of farming. Moreover, they lived mostly naked and unencumbered, dwelling under the open sky. For the climate was harmless to them, and soft beds were prepared everywhere by the many grasses sprouting from the earth. You hear, O Socrates, the life of men living under Saturn <note>original: "Saturno" / Greek: "Κρόνου" (Kronos)</note>; but this present life, which they say belongs to Jove <note>original: "Iouis" / Greek: "Διὸς" (Zeus)</note>, you have experienced yourself. As to which of these is the happier, are you willing and able to judge?

**SOCRATES** Not at all.

**STRANGER** Would you like me, then, to judge it for you in some way?

**SOCRATES** Most certainly.

->B<-

**STRANGER** If the fosterlings of Saturn, possessing so much leisure and the freedom to converse not only with men but even with beasts, used all these advantages for **philosophy**, living together with beasts and one another, and inquiring from every nature whether any part had some private power of perception different from others to help in the gathering of wisdom—if they did this, it is easily judged that they surpassed us in living happily by a vast distance. But if, being filled with food and drink, they only shared with one another and with the beasts such fables as are now told about them, then this too, in my opinion, would be quite easily judged. But let us set these things aside until some suitable messenger appears to tell us whether those men actually devoted themselves to science and conversation. However, the reason why we entered upon this myth must now be told, so that we may join what follows with what went before. 

When the time of all those things was fulfilled, and it was necessary for a change in the cycle to occur—the entire terrestrial race having been exhausted, since every soul had completed its allotted number of births and had cast as many seeds into the earth as were commanded for each—then the Governor of the universe, as if letting go of the handles of the rudders, returned to his own watchtower. The world was then revolved again by **Fate** and its own **innate desire**. Moreover, all the gods who acted as colleagues of the supreme deity, being assigned to particular regions and noticing what had happened, abandoned their care of the parts of the world. Then the world, turning back with an impulse contrary to its beginning and its end, and shaking its interior with a great earthquake, again destroyed many animals of every kind. 

But as the fixed cycles of time passed, the shaking and confusion ceased, and the world, resting from its turbulent crashing, ran in its accustomed course. Having been restored to due order, it took up the administration and authority over itself and all things within it, remembering and imitating the guidance of its author and father as much as it could. At the beginning, it executed this more perfectly, but later it degenerated further from that imitation. The cause of this defect is its <term>bodily nature</term> <note>Plato argues that matter is inherently chaotic and only temporary order can be imposed upon it.</note>, which was the companion of its ancient state. For it was full of great disorder before it was adorned with its present beauty. From its builder, it possesses all good things; but from its prior deformity, it retains and inflicts upon living things all the hardships and injustices that arise within the heavens and the world itself. 

While it nourishes its animals together with its Governor, it produces small evils and great goods; but when it is separated from Him, it conducts everything beautifully during the time immediately following the departure. As time proceeds, however, forgetfulness takes hold of it, and the vice of its former deformity begins to dominate more strongly. Finally, as a long period of time elapses, it fades away; producing only meager goods and mixing into them a great deal of the nature of evils, it runs the risk of dissolving itself and everything within it. For this reason, God—who was once the author of this order—seeing the world placed in such great danger, takes pity on it. Lest it be tossed about by such turbulent confusion and sink into the <term>infinite region of dissimilarity</term> <note>original: "locum dissimilitudinis" / Greek: "ἀνομοιότητος... τόπον" - a state of total chaos.</note>, He stands at the rudders again. Straightening all that had become diseased and dissolved in the world's own previous motion, He adorns and corrects it, rendering it immortal and free from old age.

<margin>After Saturn.</margin> This, then, is the end of the entire account. This is sufficient to demonstrate the nature of the King, provided that what was said above is kept in mind. For when the world was turned back again toward its present path of generation, the process of aging stopped and returned to a state contrary to what it was then. Animals that were close to death because of their frailty grew larger; those who had recently risen gray-haired from the earth died and returned to the earth again. All other things were likewise transformed, following the condition of the whole world. Indeed, the imitation of conception, birth, and nourishment necessarily followed the whole. For it was no longer possible for an animal to be born in the earth through the assistance of other causes. But just as it was ordained that the world should be master of its own motion, so by a similar guidance it was ordained that the parts of the world should, as far as possible, generate, be born, and nourish themselves. 

Now we have come to the point toward which our whole discourse has looked. For concerning the other animals, many great things could be told—from what they were transformed and for what causes. # THE STATESMAN

### 177

<column-break/>

...deprived of the care of the guardian <note>Greek: δαίμονος (daimon). In this context, a divine spirit or lesser god assigned to watch over humanity.</note> who possessed and tended us, and as many beasts as were savage by nature became wild again, while men, becoming weak and unguarded, were torn to pieces by them. Furthermore, in those first times, they were without means and without crafts, for their spontaneous food had failed them, and they did not yet know how to provide for themselves because no necessity had previously compelled them. From all these things, they were in great difficulty. This is why those gifts of the gods, mentioned of old, were given to us along with the necessary instruction and training: fire from Prometheus, arts from Hephaestus and his fellow-craftsman <note>Referring to Athena, the goddess of wisdom and craft.</note>, and seeds and plants from others. Everything that has equipped human life has come from these; for since the care of the gods (as was just said) had failed men, they had to have the management and care of themselves, just as the whole world does. In imitating and following the world through all time, we now live and are born in this way, and at other times in that. And so, let the myth have its end. But we shall make use of it to see how much we erred when we defined the King and the Statesman in our previous discourse.

**SOCRATES:** In what way, and how great an error do you say it was?

**STRANGER:** In one way it was smaller, but in another, it was very grand—much greater and more significant than before.

**SOCRATES:** How?

**STRANGER:** Because when we were asked for the King and Statesman of the current cycle and generation, we instead spoke of the shepherd of the human flock from the opposite period, and what is more, a god instead of a mortal. In this, we went very far astray. But in showing him to be the ruler of the whole city, without specifying the manner of his rule, we spoke the truth, though it was not stated fully or clearly. Therefore, we erred less in this regard than in the other.

**SOCRATES:** True.

**STRANGER:** We must, then, as it seems, define the manner of the government of the city, and only then expect to have a complete account of the Statesman.

**SOCRATES:** Well said.

**STRANGER:** This is why we introduced the myth: to show that regarding the "tending of the flock," not only do all others challenge the one we are seeking, but we might also see more clearly the one who alone deserves that title—the one who, after the pattern of shepherds and cowherds, has the care of nourishing human life.

**SOCRATES:** Correct.

**STRANGER:** I think, Socrates, that the figure of the divine shepherd is too great for a king. The statesmen who exist here and now are much more like their subjects in their natures, having shared in a similar education and upbringing.

**SOCRATES:** Absolutely.

**STRANGER:** Nevertheless, he must be investigated no less, whether he is of one nature or the other.

**SOCRATES:** Certainly.

**STRANGER:** Let us then return to this: we defined the "self-commanding" art <note>The art of giving orders on one's own authority.</note> as being over living creatures, not privately but as a collective care, and we immediately called it the "tending of the flock." Do you remember?

**SOCRATES:** Yes.

**STRANGER:** Now, this is where we erred. For we never fully grasped or named the Statesman; he escaped us in our naming.

**SOCRATES:** How?

**STRANGER:** To "nourish" <note>Greek: τρέφειν (trephein). This implies providing food and physical sustenance.</note> each flock is something shared by all other shepherds, but it does not apply to the Statesman, yet we gave him that name when we should have used a name common to all.

**SOCRATES:** You speak the truth, if such a name exists.

**STRANGER:** Why should "caring" <note>Greek: θεραπεύειν (therapeuein). This implies broader attendance or tending.</note> not be common to all, without specifying "nourishing" or any other specific task? We could have used a term like "flock-tending," or "management," or "care" as a name that covers everyone, including the Statesman along with the others, since the argument indicated this was necessary.

**SOCRATES:** Correct. But how would the division have been made after that?

**STRANGER:** In the same way as before, when we divided the tending of the flock into walking and winged, and hornless and unmixed; by these same divisions we could have divided "care of the flock," and our discourse would have embraced both the present reign and the reign of Kronos.

**SOCRATES:** It appears so. But I ask what comes next.

**STRANGER:** Clearly, if the name "care of the flock" had been used, no one would have argued that there is no care at all. It was justly argued then that there is no art among us worthy of the title of "nourisher," and if there were, many others would have a prior and better claim to it than any king.

**SOCRATES:** Correct.

**STRANGER:** But no other art would claim to be the care of the whole human community more than the royal art, or to be the art of ruling over all men.

**SOCRATES:** You are right.

**STRANGER:** After this, Socrates, do we realize that we made a great error right at the very end?

**SOCRATES:** What was it?

**STRANGER:** This: even if we were convinced that there is an art of nourishing the two-legged flock, we should not have immediately called it the royal and political art, as if it were finished.

**SOCRATES:** Why not?

**STRANGER:** First, as we said, we must change the name to something closer to "care" than to "nourishing." Then we must divide this care, for it may yet have significant divisions.

**SOCRATES:** What kind?

**STRANGER:** That by which we separated the divine Shepherd...

<column-break/>

...destitute of the providence of their own spirit [daemon], and many animals, which had been savage by their nature, became wild again. Being themselves unarmed, weak, and left without guardianship, they were everywhere torn apart by them. Added to this was the sluggishness and lack of skill of former times; for they had lived without the need for labor or care. <margin>Necessity created the industry of preparing food.</margin> The earth no longer supplied food of its own accord, but the industry of preparing it was not yet discovered, because no necessity had previously forced them. For these reasons, their affairs were reduced to the greatest danger and penury. Therefore, those gifts <margin>Fire given by Prometheus, arts by Vulcan.</margin> which are recorded as being granted to men by the gods of old were bestowed with a certain necessary discipline and instruction. From Prometheus indeed, fire; from Vulcan [Hephaestus] and his companion, the arts; seeds also and plants from others. In short, all the aids of human life were then provided by the work of the gods, when the providence of the gods had deserted men, and it was necessary for them now to have the care of their own propagation and nourishment, just like the whole world, which we imitate and follow through all time, being born and living now in one way, then in another. But let the fable now have an end. Truly, it will lead us to discern how much we erred above in the definition of the king and the citizen.

**SOCRATES:** In what way?

**STRANGER:** Because while a king and a civic man were being sought from the present cycle and generation, we brought in a shepherd from the opposite revolution, and we mentioned a God instead of a mortal shepherd of the human flock; thus we wandered too far. In showing him as the prince of the entire city, but not declaring in what manner he was prince, we spoke the truth indeed, but we did not describe it completely or clearly. Therefore, we seem to have failed less in this than in that.

**SOCRATES:** You speak the truth.

**STRANGER:** We ought to think, therefore, that we have only then sufficiently explained the civic man when we have distinguished the mode of governing the city to a sufficient degree.

**SOCRATES:** Excellently.

**STRANGER:** It was for this reason that we undertook that fable: not only so that those who claim for themselves that common nutrition against the king of the human flock might be shown, but so that we might more clearly behold him whom alone it is fitting to call so, when, like a shepherd of oxen or sheep, he manages the care of feeding the human race.

**SOCRATES:** Rightly.

**STRANGER:** I believe, O Socrates, that the figure of that divine shepherd is greater than what fits a king. These civic men are more like their subjects, whether we look at their nature, their education, or their discipline.

**SOCRATES:** Entirely so.

**STRANGER:** Nor truly must it be examined whether they were more or less, or whether they were born thus or otherwise.

**SOCRATES:** Why not indeed.

**STRANGER:** So then let us take it up again. The art which commands by its own authority, and provides not privately but publicly for animals, we immediately called above the "nourishing of the flock." Do you remember?

**SOCRATES:** I remember.

**STRANGER:** In this, however, there was an error. For we have neither yet comprehended the civic man, nor have we named him; his name still escapes us.

**SOCRATES:** In what way?

**STRANGER:** To feed the individuals of the flock belongs to all other shepherds. But we did not give a fitting name to the civic man, when it was proper that something common to all be applied.

**SOCRATES:** You tell the truth, if only it were allowed.

**STRANGER:** Nay, indeed it was allowed to attribute "care" [curatio] commonly, without the distinction of nourishing or any other task: and to bring in some other common appellation, calling it either the "leading of the flock," or "care," or "diligence," and thus embrace the civic man together with the others, after reason had dictated that it ought to be so.

**SOCRATES:** Best. But in what way was it to be distinguished afterward?

**STRANGER:** Just as we divided the "nourishing of the flock" according to the species of walking and flying creatures, and those unmixed and lacking horns, so it was also possible to part "the leading of the flock" according to those same things, and thus both the reign of Saturn [Kronos] and the present would have been encompassed in the discourse.

**SOCRATES:** It seems so. But what then?

**STRANGER:** If the name had been so imposed on that faculty, so that we called "the leading of the flock" that which we called "the nourishing of the flock," it is certain that no one would have contended against us, as if all care did not exist: just as it might not absurdly be contended that there is no art in us worthy of the name of "nourisher," and if there were any, that name would fit many others before and more than it fits the king.

**SOCRATES:** Rightly.

**STRANGER:** But no other art contends about this, as if there were a greater or milder care of the entire human community than the royal art.

**SOCRATES:** You speak rightly.

**STRANGER:** After these things, do we notice, Socrates, how heavily we failed near the end?

**SOCRATES:** Where do you say the fault is?

**STRANGER:** In this, I say: that if we thought some art was the nourisher of the two-legged flock, we ought not therefore immediately to have called it royal and civic as if it were absolute.

**SOCRATES:** Why not?

**STRANGER:** First indeed, it was necessary, as I was saying, to accommodate the name more to "care" than to "nourishing": afterward to divide that care. For it admits of no small divisions besides. <margin>An error occurring to one who defines by division.</margin>

**SOCRATES:** Which?

**STRANGER:** Into the divine shepherd...

<summary>This page concludes Plato's myth of the cosmic reversal and begins the philosophical correction of the definition of a "Statesman." The Stranger explains that they erred by defining the king as a "nourisher" (like a divine shepherd) rather than a human "caretaker" of the community.</summary>

The art of definition through example, which is a type of collection and a method praised by Aristotle.

The generation of an example (paradigm).

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from page 179, where the Stranger and Young Socrates are using the craft of weaving as a model to understand the art of statesmanship. Having established weaving as a type of protective craft, they are now refining the definition by distinguishing the primary craft from auxiliary tools and related processes like cleaning and spinning.</meta>

### 180 PLATO’S

<column-break/>

### A
Shall we say that the art of weaving is the greatest and most beautiful of all the faculties that deal with woolen garments? Or would that be a true statement, yet neither clear nor complete, until we have separated all those other arts from it? **SOCRATES:** Yes, certainly. **STRANGER:** Should we not then proceed step by step, so that our discourse follows a logical order? **SOCRATES:** Nothing prevents it. **STRANGER:** First, then, let us consider two types of arts involved in everything that is produced. **SOCRATES:** Which ones? **STRANGER:** One is the contributory cause <note>original: "causa adiuvans" / "συναίτιον" (sunaiton)</note>, and the other is the cause itself. **SOCRATES:** In what way? **STRANGER:** Those arts which do not manufacture the object itself, but provide the tools for the manufacturers—without which the intended work could never be completed—we call "contributory causes." Those that actually produce the object itself, we call "causes." **SOCRATES:** 

### B
That seems reasonable. **STRANGER:** Next, let us call all the arts that produce the spindle, the shuttle, the comb <note>A tool used to push the weft threads together during weaving.</note>, and other instruments used in making clothing, "contributory causes." But those arts which care for and produce the garments themselves, we shall call "causes." **SOCRATES:** Correct. **STRANGER:** Now, among these primary causes, we should take the part that washes, mends, and performs other such care—since there is much diligence required in decoration—and group them together under the name of the "fuller’s art" <note>The process of cleaning, thickening, and finishing cloth.</note>. **SOCRATES:** Very good. **STRANGER:** Furthermore, there is the part that cards, separates, and spins, and all 

### C
those tasks involved in the making of clothes; these are all encompassed by one art commonly called <term>wool-working</term> <note>original: "lanificium" / "ταλασιουργική" (talasiourgike)</note>. **SOCRATES:** Why not? **STRANGER:** Now, there are two divisions of wool-working, and both are simultaneously parts of two other arts. **SOCRATES:** How so? **STRANGER:** The faculty that cards, and that which uses the comb, and generally whatever separates things that are joined together—all of this, to put it in one word, is called a part of wool-working. Of this, there are two great divisions: the "separating" art <note>original: "discretoria" / "διακριτική" (diakritike)</note> and the "combining" art <note>original: "concretoria" / "συγκριτική" (sunkritike)</note>. **SOCRATES:** That is exactly right. **STRANGER:** Within the separating branch are carding and the other tasks we just mentioned. For that which divides the wool and the threads, whether by comb or by hand, has received all the various names we just 

### D
recalled. **SOCRATES:** Quite so. **STRANGER:** Now, let us take the part that is both "combining" and part of wool-working; let us pass over the "separating" parts we found there, and divide all wool-working into two parts: the combining and the separating. **SOCRATES:** Let us divide them. **STRANGER:** It is necessary, Socrates, to further divide the "combining" part and "wool-working" together, if we truly wish to grasp the art of weaving we have proposed. **SOCRATES:** We must indeed. **STRANGER:** We must without doubt. Therefore, let us say that one part of it involves twisting and turning, 

### E
while the other involves intertwining. **SOCRATES:** Do I understand this? You seem to me to place the work of the <term>warp</term> <note>The set of longitudinal threads held in tension on a loom. Original: "stamen" / "στήμων" (stemon)</note> in the twisting. **STRANGER:** Not only that, but the <term>weft</term> <note>The crosswise threads woven through the warp. Original: "subtegmen" / "κρόκη" (kroke)</note> as well. Can we find any production of these without twisting? **SOCRATES:** By no means. **STRANGER:** Define each of these; for perhaps such a description will be timely. **SOCRATES:** In what way? **STRANGER:** Observe: when the work of the carder is drawn out into length and breadth, we call it a "sliver" <note>A continuous strand of loose wool. Latin: "deductionem"; Greek: "κάταγμα".</note>. **SOCRATES:** Certainly. **STRANGER:** When this is twisted by the spindle and becomes a solid thread, they call the thread the "warp"; and the art 

### F
which directs and draws this out, they call the "art of the warp." **SOCRATES:** Correct. **STRANGER:** But those threads which receive a softer twist, and attain a softness moderated by the pull of the spindle for the sake of being intertwined, we call those "wefts," and the art itself we call "the art of the weft." **SOCRATES:** Excellent. **STRANGER:** And so, that part of the weaver's art which we set out to find is now clear to everyone. For when that part of the combining faculty in wool-working produces a web by the straight-forward intertwining of the weft and the warp, we call the whole finished product a "woolen garment," and the art that produces it, we call "weaving." **SOCRATES:** Very correctly. **STRANGER:** But why did we not immediately 

### G
answer that the art of weaving is that which intertwines the weft and the warp, instead of wandering around in a long, vain circle of definitions? **SOCRATES:** To me, Stranger, nothing that has been said seems to have been said in vain. **STRANGER:** That is no surprise. But perhaps it will seem so, my dear friend, if you fall into this "disease" <note>The "disease" of being overly long-winded or pedantic.</note> frequently in the future. Listen to a principle that should always be brought forward concerning all such matters. **SOCRATES:** Tell me then. **STRANGER:** Let us first look at the nature of excess and defect, so that we may reasonably praise what is moderate and blame, in each case, whatever does not observe the proper measure of speech, whether we speak more lengthily or more briefly than is fitting in such disputes. **SOCRATES:** We must certainly do so. **STRANGER:** It is right that we should give an account of these things. **SOCRATES:** Of what things? **STRANGER:** Of length and brevity, and of all excess and defect. For the <term>faculty of measurement</term> <note>original: "dimetiendi facultas" / "μετρητική" (metretike)</note> pertains to all of them. **SOCRATES:** Indeed. **STRANGER:** Let us therefore distinguish it into two parts. For this is useful for our current goal. <margin>The "greater" is spoken of in two ways: in respect to the lesser, and in respect to the moderate.</margin> **SOCRATES:** Tell me how it should be divided. **STRANGER:** Like this. One part is according to the mutual relationship of greatness and smallness; the other is according to the necessary essence of generation <note>That is, measurement relative to a standard of "due measure" or the "ideal mean."</note>. **SOCRATES:** How do you mean? **STRANGER:** Does it not seem natural to you that what is "greater" should be called "greater" than nothing other than the "lesser"? And the "lesser" should be called "lesser" only in relation to the "greater"? **SOCRATES:** To me, yes. **STRANGER:** But what of that which exceeds the moderate?

<margin>By what good men differ from the bad.</margin>
**STRANGER:** And that which exceeds or falls short, whether in speech or in action, shall we not say that this is truly the point where good men differ from the bad? **SOCRATES:** It appears so. **STRANGER:** Therefore, we must posit two forms of existence and two ways of judging the great and the small. It should not be as we said just now, that they are only relative to one another; rather, as has just been stated, we should say that one kind is relative to each other, while the other is relative to the due measure <note>original: "τὸ μέτριον" (to metrion) / "mediocritatem". This refers to the "mean" or the ideal standard between extremes.</note>. Do we wish to understand the reason for this? **SOCRATES:** Why wouldn't we? **STRANGER:** If someone allows the nature of the greater to be compared to nothing other than the smaller, it will never be compared to the due measure. Is that not so? **SOCRATES:** Exactly. **STRANGER:** Shall we not then, by this reasoning, destroy the arts themselves and all their works? Indeed, we would even make the art of statesmanship, which we are now seeking, and the previously mentioned art of weaving disappear. For all such arts avoid that which is greater or less than the due measure, not as if it were non-existent, but as something difficult to avoid in practice. It is by preserving the due measure in this way that they produce all things good and beautiful. **SOCRATES:** Certainly. **STRANGER:** And if we make the art of statesmanship disappear, will not our subsequent search for the kingly science be left without a path? **SOCRATES:** Very much so. **STRANGER:** Therefore, just as in our discussion of the Sophist <note>A reference to Plato's dialogue *The Sophist*, where the characters had to prove that "non-being" exists in some sense to define falsehood.</note> we forced the conclusion that "non-being" exists—since our argument escaped us at that point—must we now also force the conclusion that the "more" and the "less" are measurable not only relative to each other, but also relative to the production of the due measure? For it is surely impossible for either a statesman or anyone else to possess practical knowledge of action beyond dispute unless this is agreed upon. **SOCRATES:** Then we must certainly do the same now. **STRANGER:** This task, Socrates, is even greater than that previous one, even though we remember how lengthy that one was. Yet, it is quite right to suppose something like this about them. **SOCRATES:** What sort of thing? **STRANGER:** That we will one day need what has just been said for a precise demonstration of the Truth itself. But for our present purpose, it seems to me that this argument assists us magnificently in showing that all arts alike should be thought to measure the greater and the lesser not only in relation to one another, but also in relation to the production of the due measure. For if this exists, then those arts exist; and if those arts exist, this also exists. If either of these is taken away, neither will ever exist. **SOCRATES:** This is correct. But what comes next? **STRANGER:** Clearly, we should divide the art of measurement <note>original: "μετρητικὴν" (metretikēn) / "artem dimetiendi"</note> into two, as was said, cutting it in two. In one part, we place all the arts which measure number, length, depth, width, and speed against their opposites. The other part contains all those arts that look toward the due measure, the appropriate <note>original: "τὸ πρέπον" (to prepon) / "moderatúmque"</note>, the opportune moment <note>original: "τὸν καιρὸν" (ton kairon) / "opportunum"</note>, the necessary, and all those things that have found their home in the middle, away from the extremes. **SOCRATES:** Both of the portions you describe are large, and they differ greatly from one another. **STRANGER:** Indeed, Socrates, what many clever men sometimes say—thinking they are speaking some great wisdom—is that the art of measurement is concerned with everything that comes into being; and this is exactly what we have just said. 
<margin>Whatever belongs to craftsmanship is a participant in measurement.</margin>
For in a certain way, all things that belong to a craft partake in measurement. However, because people are not accustomed to investigating by dividing according to specific kinds <note>original: "εἴδη" (eidē) / "genera"</note>, they immediately lump together these things that are so different, judging them to be similar. They also do the opposite: they fail to distinguish things that are different by their parts. 
<margin>How far one must divide.</margin>
One ought not to stop when they perceive a commonality among many things until they see all the differences within it that constitute distinct kinds. Conversely, when various dissimilarities are seen in a multitude, one should not be able to turn away in frustration until they have gathered all the related traits within a single similarity and enclosed them in the essence of one genus. Regarding these matters, then, and regarding excess and deficiency, let this suffice. Let it merely be remembered that two kinds of measurement have been found, and let us keep in mind what they are. **SOCRATES:** We shall remember. **STRANGER:** After this discussion, let us take up another concerning both the object of our search and the entire conduct of such philosophical discourses. **SOCRATES:** What is that? **STRANGER:** If someone were to ask us about the practice of children learning their letters: when a student is asked what letters make up a certain name, do we say the inquiry is conducted for the sake of that one name alone, or rather so that they might become more skilled in grammar regarding all names? **SOCRATES:** Clearly, so they become better at all of them. **STRANGER:** What then of our inquiry into the statesman? Is it proposed more for the sake of the statesman himself, or rather so that we might become better dialecticians <note>original: "διαλεκτικώτεροι" (dialektikōteroi) / "acutiores" (sharper). Dialectic is the Socratic method of logical division and synthesis.</note> regarding all things? **SOCRATES:** This too is clear: it is for the sake of all things. **STRANGER:** Surely no one of sound mind would want to hunt down the definition of the art of weaving for its own sake. But I think most people fail to notice that for some things, there are easily understood sensory likenesses <note>original: "αἰσθηταί τινες ὁμοιότητες" / "sensibiles nonnullas imagines"</note> which are not difficult to show when someone wants to point them out to a person asking for an explanation, doing so easily without a long argument. 
<margin>Here the saying is not true, that nothing is in the intellect which was not first in the senses.</margin>
But for the greatest and most precious of things, there is no image <note>original: "εἴδωλον" (eidōlon)</note> clearly fashioned for human perception which, if shown, would satisfy the soul of the inquirer by fitting it to one of the senses. Therefore, we must practice being able to give a rational account of each thing...

->### THE STATESMAN<-

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> **STRANGER:** I almost understand. But for the whole class of things that provide the materials for these—from which and in which the arts we just mentioned create their works—this varied form, which is the offspring of many other arts, should we not place it as a sixth class?
**SOCRATES:** What kind do you mean?
**STRANGER:** Gold and silver, and all things that are mined; or whatever the art of wood-cutting and general pruning provides for carpentry and weaving; and the art that strips the bark of plants or the skins of living animals <note>Greek: *ἔμψυχον δέρματα* (living skins); Latin: *animalium pelles* (animal hides).</note> for the shoemaker’s craft; and all other such arts that work with cork, papyrus, and bindings, providing the means to create composite forms from non-composite types. Let us call this whole group the "primary possession" of humans <note>Greek: *πρωτογενὲς κτῆμα*; Latin: *primogenitâ possessionem*—referring to raw materials that haven't been shaped into tools yet.</note>, which is simple and by no means the work of the kingly science.

<margin>B</margin> **SOCRATES:** Well said.
**STRANGER:** Seventh, we must speak of the possession of nourishment, and whatever things, when mixed with the body, have the power to heal its parts by their own parts. We should call this whole group our "nourisher," unless we have something better to call it. For we shall more rightly assign the whole of agriculture, hunting, gymnastics, medicine, and cooking to this class rather than to the political art.
**SOCRATES:** How could it be otherwise?
**STRANGER:** Almost all possessions, then, except for domestic animals, I believe have been found to fall within these seven classes. Consider them: there was the "primary form" <note>Raw materials.</note>, then the "instrument," the "vessel," the "vehicle," the "defense" <note>Or "protection," such as clothing or walls.</note>, the "plaything," and "nourishment." We may have passed over some small thing that we forgot, but it can be fitted into one of these—for instance, the idea of coins, seals, and every kind of stamp.

<margin>C</margin> For these things do not have a great genus in common with the others; but some will harmonize with "ornament" and others with "instruments," though they may be pulled in by force, they will nevertheless fit in somehow. As for the possession of domestic animals—excluding slaves—the art of herding, which was already divided, will be seen to include them all.
**SOCRATES:** Certainly.
**STRANGER:** Now there remains the class of slaves and all servants, among whom I suspect we shall find those who dispute the very fabric of the kingly art, just as the spinners and carders disputed with the weaver earlier. All the others we called "co-workers" <note>Greek: *συνεργοὶ*; Latin: *adiuuantes*—those who assist the main task but don't define it.</note>, and they have been separated from the kingly and political action along with the works we just mentioned.
**SOCRATES:** So it seems.

<margin>D</margin> **STRANGER:** Come then, let us look at those who remain, approaching them more closely so we may know them more surely.
**SOCRATES:** We must do so.
**STRANGER:** We shall find that the greatest servants, as seen from here, have an occupation and a condition quite the opposite of what we expected.
**SOCRATES:** Who are they?
**STRANGER:** Those who are bought, and in this way acquired as property; whom we can undoubtedly call slaves, and who lay no claim to the kingly art.
**SOCRATES:** Of course not.

<margin>E</margin> **STRANGER:** And what of the free men who willingly devote themselves to the service of those we just mentioned? I mean those who transport the products of agriculture and other arts between people, equalizing them—whether in the marketplaces

<margin>F</margin> or by traveling from city to city by sea and land, exchanging money for goods or money for money—those whom we call money-changers, merchants, ship-owners, and petty traders. Will they claim any part of the political science?
**SOCRATES:** Perhaps they might claim the art of commerce.
**STRANGER:** But surely we shall never find those whom we see as hired laborers and serfs, who offer themselves to everyone for service, laying claim to the kingly art.
**SOCRATES:** How could they?
**STRANGER:** What then of those who perform various administrative services for us?
**SOCRATES:** What services do you mean, and who are they?
**STRANGER:** I mean the class of heralds, and those who become skilled in writing and serve in public offices, and many other clever workers

<margin>G</margin> who labor in various duties around the government. What shall we say of them?
**STRANGER:** As you just said: they are servants, but not themselves the rulers in the cities.
**STRANGER:** But I do not think I was dreaming when I said that somewhere in this direction we would find those who most strongly dispute the claim to the political art. And yet it might seem very strange to look for them in some servant-like portion.
**SOCRATES:** Very much so.
**STRANGER:** Let us bring our scrutiny even closer. There are some who have not yet been examined: those who deal with divination <note>Greek: *μαντικὴν*; Latin: *vaticinium*.</note>, which is a part of some servant-like science. For they are considered interpreters of the gods to men.
**SOCRATES:** Yes.
**STRANGER:** And there is also the class of priests, who, as custom holds, are skilled in giving gifts from us to the gods through sacrifices,

<margin>H</margin> and in asking for the possession of good things for us from them through prayers. Both of these are parts of a servant’s art.
**SOCRATES:** So it appears.
**STRANGER:** Now I think we have finally touched upon a kind of footprint of the thing we are pursuing. For the status of priests and diviners is filled with a great deal of pride and receives a solemn reputation because of the greatness of their undertakings. So much so that in Egypt, it is not even permitted for a king to rule without the priestly office; and even if someone from another class should happen to force his way to the throne, it is necessary for him to be initiated into this class later. Furthermore, among the Greeks, you would find that in many places the highest offices are commanded to perform the greatest of such sacrifices. This is nowhere more evident than among you <note>Addressing Young Socrates regarding the customs of Athens.</note>. For they say that the "King" chosen by lot <note>The *Archon Basileus* of Athens, a magistrate who held traditional religious duties.</note> is tasked with the most solemn and ancestral of the ancient sacrifices.

<margin>H</margin> <margin>That it befits kings to have the greatest priesthood.</margin>
Indeed, if someone from another class usurps the kingdom by force, he must eventually become a priest. Moreover, this is established in the highest magistracies of many Greek states. For among you, it is said that once the [king] is created... <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence at the catchword "regi".</note>
