<summary>The Stranger continues the systematic division of arts and possessions, identifying seven basic classes of objects before turning to the various human servants in a city. He concludes by noting that while laborers and merchants are clearly subordinates, diviners and priests hold a more complex, prestigious status that is often intertwined with kingship, especially in Egypt and Athens.</summary>

...be assigned. **SOCRATES:** Exactly so. **STRANGER:** Therefore, we must consider those who have perhaps been created as kings, priests, and their ministers, as well as a certain other very large crowd that has come to light now that the previous groups have been set aside. **SOCRATES:** Who do you mean? **STRANGER:** I mean some very strange creatures. **SOCRATES:** Why? **STRANGER:** For as I reflect, a multiform genus <note>original: "multiforme horum genus"; Greek: "Παμφυλον τι ζωος" (a diverse, all-tribed creature)</note> of them appears to me. Many men become like lions, centaurs, and others of this kind; many also like satyrs and weak, shape-shifting beasts. They quickly transform their forms and powers into one another. Indeed, Socrates, I think I have only now noticed such men. **SOCRATES:** Tell me, I pray. You seem to see something wonderful now. **STRANGER:** Indeed. For ignorance causes us to always find something wonderful. And the same has just happened to me. Suddenly, I found myself in doubt as I gazed upon the chorus of civil affairs. **SOCRATES:** Which one? **STRANGER:** The greatest illusionist <note>Latin: *prestigiatorem*; Greek: *γοητα* (goēta)—referring to a sorcerer, charlatan, or master of tricks.</note> of all the sophists, and the most skilled of all in this art, whom we must distinguish from truly royal and civil men, even though it is difficult, if we wish to see clearly what we are seeking. **SOCRATES:** This must by no means be skipped. **STRANGER:** Certainly not, I think. Tell me. **SOCRATES:** What? **STRANGER:** Is not monarchy—that is, the rule of one—one of the forms of civil government? **SOCRATES:** It is. **STRANGER:** After this, we can place the power of the few. **SOCRATES:** Certainly. **STRANGER:** And the third is the government of the multitude, which they call popular <note>The Greek term is *Demokratia* (democracy).</note>. **SOCRATES:** Precisely. **STRANGER:** Do these three not somehow become five, since they produce two other names from themselves? **SOCRATES:** Which ones? **STRANGER:** Those who consider whether the rule is over the unwilling or the willing, or by law or by whim, or whether the rulers are poor or elevated to power by wealth; they divide the rule of one and the rule of the few into two species. The rule of one they call by two names: Tyranny and Kingship. **SOCRATES:** Indeed. **STRANGER:** The government which is in the hands of the few they divide into the power of the few <note>Oligarchy</note> and the power of the best men <note>Aristocracy</note>. **SOCRATES:** Entirely so. **STRANGER:** But no one is ever accustomed to change the name of the popular government <note>Democracy</note>, whether the people rule over the rich by force or willingly, or whether they rule by law or by whim. **SOCRATES:** That is true. **STRANGER:** Do we then think that any of these civil governments is correct when defined by these limits: by the one, the few, or the many; by poverty or wealth; by violence or willingness; by written laws or by whim? **SOCRATES:** What prevents it? **STRANGER:** Consider more carefully, and follow me this way. **SOCRATES:** Which way? **STRANGER:** Shall we stand by what was said in the beginning, or not? **SOCRATES:** By what? **STRANGER:** We said that the royal dignity is one of the sciences. **SOCRATES:** We did. **STRANGER:** And we did not place it in just any kind of science. From many others, we chose that discerning kind which both judges and commands. **SOCRATES:** Certainly. **STRANGER:** Then, dividing the commanding art—partly over inanimate things and partly over animate things—and following that same order, we progressed until we kept the name of "science"; but we have not yet been able to declare exactly which science it is. **SOCRATES:** You speak correctly. **STRANGER:** Therefore, do we not see that their description should be made not according to violence or willingness, nor according to the few or many, nor through poverty or wealth, but through a certain science, if we are to follow what was said before? **SOCRATES:** That must be the case. **STRANGER:** Necessarily, then, we must now consider which of these possesses the science of the commanding faculty <note>The "imperial faculty" or *regia peritia*—the specific knowledge required to rule.</note>, which is perhaps the greatest and most difficult of all to acquire. For it is necessary to inspect it, so that we may see who must be separated from the wise king—those who claim civil skill for themselves and persuade many, though they are very far from it. **SOCRATES:** This must be done exactly as the earlier reasoning advised. **STRANGER:** Does it seem to you that a multitude in a city could possess this science? **SOCRATES:** How could they? **STRANGER:** In a city of a thousand men, is it possible for a hundred, or fifty, to acquire it sufficiently? **SOCRATES:** This would be the easiest of all arts! We know that in a thousand men, one would never find that many who surpass the rest of the Greeks at the game of dice <note>Latin: *talorum ludo*; Greek: *πεττευταὶ* (petteutai)—a game of skill and strategy similar to draughts or backgammon, used here to show how rare true expertise is.</note>, let alone kings. And yet, according to our earlier reasoning, we must call anyone who is instructed in the royal skill a king, whether he rules or lives as a private citizen. **STRANGER:** You have advised me well. I think, however, according to this discourse, the right government—if it is ever right—must be sought among one, or two, or a very few. **SOCRATES:** Why not? **STRANGER:** It is necessary to consider those men to be civil and royal who rule by a certain art, regardless of whether they rule over willing or unwilling subjects, according to written rules or without written institutions and laws, or whether they themselves are poor or rich.

<margin>Concerning the nature of right government.</margin> For we nonetheless call physicians thus, whether they cure us against our will or with our consent, by cutting, burning, or bringing some other painful thing, or whether they cure by written rules or by experience, being poor themselves or rich; provided they use a certain art in curing our bodies, whether by purging, or thinning, or filling and increasing them. We name them physicians equally, as long as those who care for the body look toward its good, making it better from a worse state...

<column-break/>

...assigned. **SOCRATES:** Exactly so. **STRANGER:** Therefore, for these, how should we consider the kings chosen by lot and the priests, of whom this is fitting, and another very great crowd that has just become visible to us, now that the previous groups have been separated? **SOCRATES:** Who do you say they are? **STRANGER:** Truly, some very strange ones. **SOCRATES:** Why so? **STRANGER:** They seem to be a diverse creature <note>original: "Παμφυλον τι ζωος" (a creature of all kinds/tribes).</note> as I look at them just now. For many resemble lions and centaurs, and others such as these; and very many resemble satyrs and weak, versatile beasts. They quickly change their appearances and their power into one another. And yet, Socrates, I think I have only now perceived these men. **SOCRATES:** Speak on. **STRANGER:** You seem to see something strange. **SOCRATES:** Yes. **STRANGER:** For strangeness happens to everyone out of ignorance. And indeed, this has just happened to me suddenly. I was in doubt, looking at the one who always handles the affairs of cities. **SOCRATES:** What kind? **STRANGER:** The greatest sorcerer <note>Greek: *γοητα* (goēta)—a charlatan or illusionist.</note> of all the sophists, and the most experienced in this art; he must be separated from those who are truly political and royal, even though it is very difficult to remove him, if we are to see clearly what is sought. **SOCRATES:** Truly, this must not be let go. **STRANGER:** Not at all, at least according to my view. And tell me this. **SOCRATES:** What is it? **STRANGER:** Is not monarchy one of the political rules for us? **SOCRATES:** Yes. **STRANGER:** And one might call monarchy, I think, the dominion of the few. **SOCRATES:** How could they not? **STRANGER:** And the third form of constitution—is it not the rule of the multitude, called by the name "democracy"? **SOCRATES:** Exactly so. **STRANGER:** Since there are three, do they not somehow become five, by producing two other names for themselves? **SOCRATES:** Which ones? **STRANGER:** Looking now toward violence and willingness, and poverty and wealth, and law and lawlessness occurring in them, let us divide each of the two into two parts. Monarchy they address as providing two forms with two names: one, tyranny; the other, kingship. **SOCRATES:** Certainly. **STRANGER:** And the city ruled by the few at any time, they call aristocracy and oligarchy. **SOCRATES:** Exactly so. **STRANGER:** Of democracy, however, whether the multitude rules over those who have property by force or willingly, and whether they guard the laws strictly or not, no one is ever accustomed to change its name. **SOCRATES:** True. **STRANGER:** What then? Do we think any of these constitutions is correct when defined by these limits: by one, few, or many; by wealth or poverty; by force or willingness; and by occurring with written codes or without laws? **SOCRATES:** Why should anything prevent it? **STRANGER:** Look more clearly, following this way. **SOCRATES:** Which way? **STRANGER:** Shall we abide by what was said at the beginning, or shall we disagree? **SOCRATES:** To what kind of thing do you refer? **STRANGER:** We said that royal rule was one of the sciences. **SOCRATES:** Yes. **STRANGER:** And not all of them, but surely we chose a certain discerning and commanding kind from the others. **SOCRATES:** Yes. **STRANGER:** And of the commanding kind, one was over inanimate works, the other over living things. And moving in this way, we have always come forward, not wandering from "science," but we are not yet able to distinguish sufficiently what kind it is. **SOCRATES:** You speak correctly. **STRANGER:** Therefore, we perceive this: that the definition must not be based on few or many, nor on willingness or unwillingness, nor on poverty or wealth; but it must be a certain science, if we are to follow the things said before. **SOCRATES:** Indeed, it is impossible not to do this. **STRANGER:** By necessity, then, we must now consider in which of these a science happens to arise concerning the rule over men, which is perhaps the most difficult and greatest to acquire. For it must be seen, so that we may observe who must be removed from the wise king—those who pretend to be political and persuade many, but are not so at all. **SOCRATES:** For this must indeed be done, as the argument has already told us. **STRANGER:** Does it seem possible for a multitude in a city to be able to acquire this science? **SOCRATES:** How could they? **STRANGER:** But is it possible in a city of a thousand men for a hundred or even fifty to acquire it sufficiently? **STRANGER:** It would then be the easiest of all the arts. For we know that among a thousand men, that many top-tier dice players <note>Greek: *πεττευταὶ* (petteutai)—draughts players.</note> compared to those in the rest of Greece could never be found, let alone kings. For the one who has the royal science, whether he rules or not, must be addressed as royal according to the previous argument. **STRANGER:** You have remembered well. Following this, I think, we must seek the right rule in one, or two, or altogether a few, whenever it becomes right. **SOCRATES:** Why not? **STRANGER:** And these men, whether they rule over willing or unwilling subjects, whether according to written codes or without written codes, and whether they are rich or poor, must be considered as rulers according to whatever art they possess. Just as we have recognized physicians, whether they heal us with or without our consent, by cutting, burning, or applying some other pain; and whether according to written rules or without written rules; and whether they are poor or rich; in every way we call them physicians, as long as they preside with art, purging, or otherwise thinning, or even increasing us—provided it is only for the good of the bodies, making them better...

<vocab>Socrates, Plato, Politicus (The Statesman), Monarchy, Democracy, Aristocracy, Oligarchy, Tyranny, Sophist, Science (Knowledge), Royal skill (Kingship), Government</vocab>

<summary>In this passage from Plato's Statesman, the Stranger argues that the only true criterion for a "correct" government is the possession of scientific knowledge or skill, rather than the number of rulers, wealth, or the consent of the governed. He uses the analogy of a physician to show that a ruler's legitimacy comes from their expertise in improving the state, much as a doctor's legitimacy comes from the art of healing.</summary>
<keywords>Plato, Politicus, statesmanship, types of government, political science, sophistry, physician analogy, expert rule, rare knowledge</keywords>

->### THE STATESMAN<-

...restoring them to a better condition <note>original: "HABITUDINE"; Greek: "ποιοῦντες ἐπὶ χείρονα" (making from worse to better)</note>, those who provide care preserve each of the things they treat. In this way alone, I think, and in no other, shall we say that the correct definition of medicine or any other form of rule is found. **SOCRATES:** That is exactly how we must think of it. **STRANGER:** It is necessary then, it seems, to consider that state to be most of all—and the only—correct government, in which those who hold office truly know how to govern, and do not merely appear to. Whether they rule according to laws or without laws, over willing or unwilling subjects, and whether they are poor or rich: none of these things should be factored at all into the standard of correctness. **SOCRATES:** Excellent. **STRANGER:** Furthermore, it does not matter 
<margin>B</margin>
whether they purge the city for the sake of the common good—either by executions or banishments—or if they reduce the population by sending out colonies like swarms of bees <note>This "bee swarm" metaphor was a common Greek way of describing the founding of new cities/colonies</note>, or if they increase it by bringing in people from elsewhere to be citizens. So long as they act with science <note>term: "scientia" / "ἐπιστήμη" (epistēmē) — here meaning systematic, expert knowledge or "political science"</note> and justice to make the city better instead of worse to the best of their ability, and preserve it, then we must say that the definition of a correct government consists in this alone. All other forms we speak of are not to be called legitimate or truly existing, but rather imitations of this one. Those we call "well-ordered" have imitated it for the better, while others have imitated it for the worse. 
<margin>C</margin>
**SOCRATES:** Everything else, Stranger, seems to have been said fairly; but the idea that it is possible to have a correct government without laws is a harder thing to hear. **STRANGER:** You have anticipated me by just a little with your question, Socrates. I was about to ask whether you accept all this, or if any of what was said is troubling to you. Now it is clear that we must discuss the correctness of those who rule without laws. **SOCRATES:** Of course. **STRANGER:** It is clear in a way that the making of laws <note>term: "νομοθετική" (nomothetikē) — legislation</note> belongs to the royal dignity. But the best thing is not for laws to have power, but for a wise and royal man to have it. 
<margin>The making of laws belongs to the king.</margin>
<margin>D</margin>
Do you understand the reason for this? **SOCRATES:** Please explain. **STRANGER:** Because law could never accurately embrace what is best and most just for everyone at once, and so prescribe what is most beneficial. For the differences between people, the variety of human actions, and the fact that human affairs are never, so to speak, at rest, prevent any art <note>term: "τέχνην" (technēn) — a craft or specialized skill</note> from declaring anything simple and universal that applies to all things for all time. Do we agree on this? **SOCRATES:** Certainly. **STRANGER:** But we see the law striving toward this very goal, like a stubborn and ignorant man who permits nothing to be done contrary to his own order—not even if someone asks a question, or if some new thing happens to be better for someone than the rule he originally prescribed. **SOCRATES:** True. For the law treats us exactly as you have described. **STRANGER:** And it is impossible for a simple, fixed order to be well-suited to things that are never simple and are always changing. 
<margin>E</margin>
**SOCRATES:** So it seems. **STRANGER:** Since, then, the law is not the most correct thing, we must find the reason why it is necessary to establish laws at all. 
<margin>Why the establishment of laws is necessary.</margin>
**SOCRATES:** Indeed. **STRANGER:** Are there not among us, as in other cities, group exercises for men, whether for racing or some other contest? **SOCRATES:** Yes, very many. **STRANGER:** Come then, let us recall the instructions of those who preside over such gymnasiums with their art. **SOCRATES:** Such as what? **STRANGER:** They think it is impossible 
<margin>F</margin>
to prescribe what is appropriate for each individual separately and specifically. Therefore, they think they must set an order that is more general, which they believe will benefit the greatest number of bodies. **SOCRATES:** Excellent. **STRANGER:** For this reason, they give equal labors to the whole group today, driving them on together and stopping them together, whether in the race, wrestling, or any other bodily labors. **SOCRATES:** That is true. **STRANGER:** We should think of the lawgiver in the same way, who presides over his "herds" to give them justice and rules for their mutual dealings. When he provides for the whole group, he cannot accurately provide what is fitting for each individual. **SOCRATES:** That is likely. **STRANGER:** Rather, I think, he will establish laws for the majority, based on what is generally useful, and he will introduce such laws both in writing and in unwritten ancestral customs. **SOCRATES:** Correct. **STRANGER:** Quite correct. For how could anyone, Socrates, ever be capable of sitting beside each individual through their whole life and accurately prescribing what is fitting? Indeed, I think if someone truly possessed 
<margin>G</margin>
the royal science, he would hardly ever impose such impediments as laws upon himself. **SOCRATES:** That certainly seems to be the case from what has been said. **STRANGER:** Or rather, my friend, from what is about to be said. **SOCRATES:** What is that? **STRANGER:** This: Suppose a doctor or a trainer, when about to go on a long journey, thinks he will be away from his patients for a long time. Thinking that those being trained or those who are sick will not remember his instructions, he will want to write down reminders for them, will he not? **SOCRATES:** He will. **STRANGER:** What if he returns sooner than he expected? Would he not dare to prescribe other things to them besides what he had previously written, if better things could be applied to the sick 

<column-break/>

due to the winds, or something else happening unexpectedly by the will of God <note>original: "ex Διὸς" / "from Zeus"</note> contrary to what is usual? Would he, I say, persist in his original plan, and allow no one to transgress the first instructions, nor himself command anything else, nor the patient dare to do anything other than what was customary...

<summary>In this passage, Plato argues that the only true government is one led by a ruler with genuine knowledge, rather than one strictly bound by law. He compares law to a "stubborn man" who cannot account for the complexity of human life, explaining that laws are only general shortcuts for when an expert ruler cannot be present for every individual.</summary>

...to be observed, as if they are the properties of the medical art and most healthful, while those done otherwise are against the art and harmful? For they say that if someone finds certain laws better than the previous ones, and persuades the citizens of them, he ought to establish those laws; but if he does not persuade them, he ought not. **SOCRATES:** Is that not correct? **GUEST:** Perhaps. But if someone, not through persuasion but by force, introduces what is better, what will be the most fitting name for that violence? Answer. Would it not be anything else rather than a "violation of the art," which is to say, the infliction of disease? And should we not say that anything else happened to the compelled person rather than a violation of the art or a disease? **SOCRATES:** You speak the truth. **GUEST:** But what was the offense against the civil art? Is it not what is called shameful, evil, and unjust? **SOCRATES:** Exactly that. **GUEST:** Come now, when some are compelled to act contrary to ancestral laws and customs to do things that are more just, better, and more honorable, will not any man be the most ridiculous of all who blames that force and says that those who were compelled suffered shameful, evil, and unjust things from their caretakers? **SOCRATES:** You speak the absolute truth. **GUEST:** If the one who compels is rich, is the compulsion just; but if he is poor, is it unjust? Or rather, whether he persuades or does not persuade, whether he be poor or rich, and whether it be according to the written rules or contrary to them, provided he carries out what is useful, 
<margin>The duty of kings.</margin>
should it not be said that this is the true definition of correct civil governance? By this logic, a wise and good man will always govern by looking to the safety of his subjects, just as a pilot <note>term: "gubernator" / "κυβερνήτης" (kybernētēs) — the origin of the word "governor," referring to the steersman of a ship</note> looks to the safety of the sailors and the ship. For just as the pilot preserves the sailors not by written rules, but by providing his art as a kind of law, so too is the administration of civil affairs correct among those who can rule in this way, applying the power of art as something superior to the laws. In short, whatever prudent princes do, they never err, as long as they preserve this one great thing: that by applying what is most just with mind and art to the citizens, they are able to protect them and, as far as possible, make them better instead of worse. **SOCRATES:** One cannot argue against what has just been said. **GUEST:** Nor against those points in addition. **SOCRATES:** Which ones 
<margin>That the multitude cannot rule.</margin>
did you mean? **GUEST:** That no multitude can ever excel in that discipline by which a city is ruled according to the mind. But that one correct administration of the city must be sought either in 
<margin>Perfect rule is with one or very few.</margin>
one man or certainly in very few. Other forms of government must be considered as mere imitations, as was said a little while ago; some imitating it for the better, others for the worse. **SOCRATES:** How did you mean that? For I did not sufficiently understand what you said earlier about imitating. **GUEST:** It would not be bad if someone, having introduced this discourse, stopped before showing the error that is now committed regarding this. **SOCRATES:** What error do you mean? **GUEST:** It is necessary now to seek such a thing which, although neither common nor easy to know, we shall nevertheless strive to grasp. Since this whole thing we have mentioned is the correct civil government, is it not necessary that the others, using its institutions, be preserved by doing what we were just praising, even though it is not the most correct? **SOCRATES:** What is that? **GUEST:** That no one dare to commit anything contrary to the laws, and whoever dares, let him be punished by death and afflicted with all the furthest punishments. This is the second-most correct and honorable path; for the first place must be given to what was just said. But let us declare in what way that which we just called "second" comes about. Do you wish to? **SOCRATES:** Very much so. **GUEST:** Let us return again to the images to which it is always necessary to compare royal princes. **SOCRATES:** What images do you mean? **GUEST:** I mean the noble pilot of a ship, 
<margin>Iliad, Book 11</margin>
and the physician who, as that man said, is "worth many others." <note>A reference to Homer’s Iliad (11.514), where the physician Machaon is praised.</note> Let us now consider an image by 
<margin>Whether unchangeable laws should be enacted.</margin>
imagining something. **SOCRATES:** Of what kind? **GUEST:** Something like this: suppose we all imagine that we suffer the most terrible things from them. For instance, suppose they save whichever of us they want to save, but on the contrary, they destroy those they want to destroy by cutting, burning, and demanding a kind of tribute from this practice of theirs as a fee; and though they compel us to spend much when we are sick, they themselves spend nothing for the patient, but they and their families use the remaining things themselves; finally, having accepted money either from...

<column-break/>

...do what is written? Should we say that in the art of medicine, these things are healthful, and that things done otherwise are diseased and unskillful? Or would such an occurrence, where it concerns true science and art, be entirely the greatest cause for laughter for that legislation? **SOCRATES:** Entirely so. **GUEST:** And for the one who has written down what is just and unjust, honorable and shameful, good and bad, or established unwritten laws for the herds of men—however they are governed in each city according to the law of the writers—if the man who wrote the art, or someone else like him, should arrive, should it not be permitted for him to prescribe other things contrary to these? Or would this prohibition appear no less truly ridiculous than the former? **SOCRATES:** How could it not? **GUEST:** Do you know, then, the argument said by the many regarding such a thing? **SOCRATES:** I do not at this moment. **GUEST:** But indeed, my friend, for they say that if someone knows laws better than those of the predecessors, he must legislate for his city by persuading the persuaded; otherwise, he must not. **SOCRATES:** What then? Is that not correct? **GUEST:** Perhaps. But if someone, not by persuading but by force, effects what is better, tell me what the name of that force shall be. Not yet, however; let us look at the previous example. **SOCRATES:** Which do you mean? **GUEST:** If someone, not by persuading the patient but correctly possessing the art, compels a child, or some man, or even a woman to do what is better contrary to the written rules, what shall be the name of this violence? Shall it be anything rather than the "error against the art" called unhealthiness? And would it be most correct to say that the person forced suffered violence because he was treated well, except that he suffered "unhealthful and unskillful" things from the physicians who forced him? **SOCRATES:** You speak most truly. **GUEST:** But what is the thing called an "offense against the political art" for us, if it is not the shameful, the evil, and the unjust? **SOCRATES:** Entirely so. **GUEST:** For those, then, who are forced contrary to the written and ancestral rules to do other things that are more just, better, and more honorable than the previous ones—come, tell me of the blame for such force—if he is not to be completely ridiculous, must he not say anything rather than that those forced by the ones forcing them have suffered shameful, unjust, and evil things? **SOCRATES:** You speak most truly. **GUEST:** But if the one who uses force is rich, are the forced acts just, but if he is poor, are they unjust? Or if someone, whether by persuading or not persuading, whether rich or poor, whether according to written rules or contrary to written rules, does what is advantageous, must this be the standard—the most true standard of the correct administration of a city—by which the wise and good man will administer the affairs of those he rules? Just as the pilot, always watching over the advantage of the ship and the sailors, not by setting down written rules but by providing his art as the law, saves his fellow sailors; so in this same way, from those capable of ruling thus, a correct government might arise, providing the strength of the art as something superior to the laws. And for those who act as prudent rulers, there is no error, so long as they guard one great thing: always distributing what is most just with mind and art to those in the city, they are able to save them and, as far as possible, render them better from worse. **SOCRATES:** It is not possible to speak against what has now been said. **GUEST:** And indeed, one must not speak against those points either. **SOCRATES:** Which ones did you say? **GUEST:** That no multitude, nor any whatsoever, having received such science, would be able to administer a city with mind; but it is in something small and few and the "One" that we must seek that one correct government. Other governments must be set down as imitations, just as was said a little while ago; some imitating this one for the better, others for the more shameful. **SOCRATES:** How and why did you say this? For I did not understand just now about the imitations. **GUEST:** Indeed, it is not a trivial thing if someone, having set such a discourse in motion, should drop it and not go through it to show the error currently occurring about it. **SOCRATES:** What kind of error? **GUEST:** One must seek such things as are not at all common, nor easy to see; nevertheless, let us try to grasp it. For come, if this government we have described is the only correct one, do you know that the others must be preserved by using its writings, doing what is now praised, even though it is not the most correct? **SOCRATES:** What is that? **GUEST:** That no one dare to do anything contrary to the laws; and let the one who dares be punished with death and all the furthest penalties. And this is most correct and most honorable as a "second" choice, after someone has put aside the first thing that was just said. Let us explain the way in which this has happened, which we called "second." Shall we? **SOCRATES:** By all means. **GUEST:** Let us return again to the images to which it is necessary to always liken the royal rulers. **SOCRATES:** Which images? **GUEST:** The noble pilot, and the physician who is "worth many others." For let us look at a certain form we have fashioned among these very things. **SOCRATES:** What kind? **GUEST:** Such as if we all thought about them, that we suffer the most terrible things from them. For whichever of us either of these wish to save, they save; but whom they wish to treat badly, they treat badly, cutting and burning them, and imposing taxes to be brought to them daily, like tribute. Of these, they spend only a little on the patient, while they and their servants use the rest...

<summary>The Guest argues that a ruler with true "science" or expertise is like a doctor or ship's pilot: they should govern by their skill (art) rather than by rigid written laws. If true expert rule is impossible, the "second-best" option is strict adherence to established laws with severe penalties for those who break them.</summary>

# THE STATESMAN <note>original: "POLITICVS"</note>

...from relatives or from some enemies of the sick person, receiving money as a reward, they kill them. Navigators too are said to commit many other such deeds, such as those who often leave men alone in retreats by design when they set sail, or when they have caused some damage on the open sea, they cast them into the water and do harm in many other ways. Let us then persuade ourselves, being provoked by these reasons, to deliberate about them: in what way might we take away authority from these arts, so that they no longer rule freely over either slaves or free men. And for this purpose, having formed a gathering, we should convene either the whole people or only the wealthy, where even the advice of unlearned men and other craftsmen regarding navigation and diseases may be heard: on what way the doctors should use their medicines and medical instruments for the sick; and likewise for the ships themselves and their nautical instruments for the use of the ships, whether for avoiding the dangers of storms and waves, or for escaping the snares of pirates, and even if it should be necessary to fight at sea with long ships against similar ones, what method is best to use. Let us imagine, I say, that whatever seems best to this crowd concerning these things—whether advised by doctors and pilots or by unlearned men—should be inscribed on certain public tablets and columns, and some unwritten ancestral customs and rituals be established concerning these things, so that for all time to come, navigation and the treatment of the sick must be performed according to this standard. **SOCRATES:** You have imagined things that are truly absurd. **GUEST:** Furthermore, every year magistrates should be appointed from the wealthy, or chosen by lot from the whole people, who shall govern ships and heal the sick according to those written institutions. **SOCRATES:** These things seem even harsher than what came before. **GUEST:** Look further at what follows from this. When each annual magistrate's time has expired, it will be necessary to set up a court of men, either from the selected wealthy or chosen by lot from the whole people, to stand those who served as magistrates before them and demand an account. Any person who wishes may bring a lawsuit against them, charging that they governed the ships or treated the sick in a way other than what the laws command and ancestral custom teaches. And those found to have acted otherwise shall, by a passed sentence, be afflicted by the judges with a penalty or some other disadvantage. **SOCRATES:** Would not anyone who willingly took up a magistracy among such people deserve to suffer any penalty or loss? **GUEST:** It will be necessary, moreover, to pass a law for all these things: if anyone is found investigating a new method of navigation beyond the written constitutions, or the true way of maintaining health and the medical truth according to the laws, and philosophizes and teaches about these things from his own talent—first, he should not be named a pilot or a doctor, but some meddlesome, babbling sophist <note>original: "sophistam"; Greek: "σοφιστήν" — here used in a derogatory sense for someone who uses clever but false arguments</note>. Then he may be dragged into court by anyone who is permitted, as one who corrupts the youth and persuades others to take up navigation and medicine not according to the laws, but to rule ships and the sick by their own authority. And if he is found to have persuaded either young or old against the laws and writings, he shall be afflicted with the extreme penalties. For nothing ought to be wiser than the laws. For no one can be ignorant of the nature of medicine and health, or the best way of governing and navigation, if they are willing to learn the written laws and ancestral customs. If these things happened regarding the sciences we have mentioned, and many others, so that things were done according to prescriptions rather than according to art <note>original: "artem"; Greek: "τέχνην" (technē) — meaning craft, skill, or systematic knowledge</note>, what shall we say, O Socrates? For example, if the same were established for military matters, and every kind of hunting, for painting and all imitation, for architecture and the making of all tools and furniture, for agriculture and the care of plants, the keeping of horses and all herds, for prophecy and the various duties of servants, for the game of dice, for pure arithmetic, or geometry, or the study of speed and slowness. **SOCRATES:** It is certain that if things were so, all arts would be utterly overturned, and would never again be reborn because of this very law which forbids the investigation of new things. Thus life, which is difficult now, would then become altogether intolerable. **GUEST:** <margin>If anyone were placed above the laws, what evil would follow.</margin> What of this? If we forced each of these things to be done according to the written laws, and placed a man in charge of the laws—either designated by the consent of the people or created by lot—who then, despising the laws for the sake of profit or personal pleasure, attempted to do other things beyond what is established, being himself unskilled, would this not be an even worse evil than the first? **SOCRATES:** Most certainly. **GUEST:** For he who, being unskilled, dares to act against those laws—which were established through long experience by those who, consulting with the people, persuaded them to accept them—commits a crime far worse than the previous error. He confuses and perverts the duties of life much more than the written laws. **SOCRATES:** Greatly so. **GUEST:** Therefore, when laws have been established, the "second voyage" <note>original: "nauigatio"; Greek: "δεύτερος πλοῦς" (deuteros plous) — a Greek proverb meaning the "next best way" when the ideal method, like sailing with the wind, fails and one must resort to oars</note> is this: that no one, whether an individual or a crowd, should ever be permitted to do anything at all contrary to them. **SOCRATES:** Correctly said. **GUEST:** Would these things not be imitations of the truth, which are [written] by those who know? <margin>Laws are imitations of the truth.</margin>

<column-break/>

<summary>Plato presents a thought experiment where doctors and pilots are legally forbidden from using their expertise if it contradicts rigid written laws. This illustrates that while laws are "imitations" of true wisdom, they become destructive when they prevent the exercise of actual knowledge and innovation.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: On the preceding page, the Guest and Socrates discussed the absurdity of forcing experts, like doctors or ship pilots, to follow rigid written rules created by an unlearned crowd. They concluded that true governance must be based on "science" or "art" (knowledge), not just written law. This page continues that discussion, exploring how existing governments are merely imitative of the one true, scientific form of rule.</meta>

# PLATO <note>original: "PLATONIS"</note>

established for the people to the best of their ability? <term>SOCRATES.</term> Nothing prevents it.
->A<-
<term>GUEST.</term> And yet, if we remember, we said earlier that a truly statesmanlike and skilled man would often, by his <term>art</term> <note>original: "ex arte"; referring to the "royal science" of ruling</note>, do many things beyond the institutions he had previously written down, whenever he thought he had found something better than what he left behind for those who are absent. <term>SOCRATES.</term> We certainly said that. <term>GUEST.</term> Is it not true that if individuals, or the people themselves for whom laws were prescribed, attempt something different as being better than what was handed down in those laws, they are doing—to the best of their power—the same thing that the true statesman does? <term>SOCRATES.</term> Very much so. <term>GUEST.</term> If, therefore, unlearned men were to do this, they would be striving to imitate the truth, but they would imitate it perversely. However, if those with skill and knowledge were to contend for the same, this would no longer be a mere imitation, but that very thing which is most true. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Entirely so. <term>GUEST.</term> Indeed, it was agreed between us earlier that no "art" or science belongs to the many <note>Plato argues that high-level expertise, like statesmanship, cannot be grasped by a large crowd, only by a few individuals</note>. <term>SOCRATES.</term> It was certainly agreed. <term>GUEST.</term> Therefore, if the "royal art" is a certain faculty of knowledge, the crowd of the wealthy and the whole populace will never obtain this science of statesmanship. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Never. <term>GUEST.</term> It is necessary, then, that if such republics are ever to imitate—to the best of their ability—that true government of the one man who commands by "art," they must never do anything contrary to the written laws and ancestral customs. <term>SOCRATES.</term> You have spoken excellently. <term>GUEST.</term> When the wealthy imitate <margin>How one becomes a king by governing.</margin> that same government, we call such a state an <term>aristocracy</term> <note>literally "the rule of the best"</note>; but when they hold the laws in no regard, we call it an <term>oligarchy</term> <note>the rule of the few, usually for their own benefit</note>. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Perhaps so. <term>GUEST.</term> Furthermore, whenever one man rules according to the laws, imitating the one who has knowledge, we call him a "king," not distinguishing by name the one who rules alone by science from the one who rules alone by opinion according to the laws. <term>SOCRATES.</term> So it seems. <term>GUEST.</term> Therefore, if one man possessed of true science rules, does he not have the same name—that is, "king"—and is called by no other title? For out of the five names of civil governments we have recounted, this was the only one. <term>SOCRATES.</term> It seems so. <term>GUEST.</term> What follows: whenever someone rules neither according to law nor custom, pretending that he knows better and that things should be done more rightly than the written laws—while in truth it is a certain lust and ignorance that leads him to such an imitation—must not such a man be called a **tyrant**? <term>SOCRATES.</term> Most certainly.
->D<-
<term>GUEST.</term> In this way, there arose the "king," as we said, and the tyrant, the power of the few, the government of the best, and also the administration of the people. This happened because men found it difficult to bear the command of a single person and distrusted that any man could ever be found worthy of such great power—one who would be both able and willing to rule with virtue and science, and to distribute justice and holiness to each person correctly. They feared that a single man, having gained license, would instead harm, oppress, and kill whomever he pleased according to his own whim. Yet, if such a man as we have described were to be found among us, his administration would surely be loved, for it alone of all is the most correct and leads to living well and happily. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Truly. <term>GUEST.</term> But now, since no such king is born in our cities—one who, like the <term>king bee</term> <note>original: "rex apum"; the Greeks believed the leader of a beehive was a king, not a queen</note> in a swarm, is immediately from the start superior to the others in both body and mind—it is necessary, it seems, to gather together, form a council, and write down institutions, following in the footsteps of that most true republic. <term>SOCRATES.</term> So it appears. <term>GUEST.</term> And do we wonder, Socrates, that in such governments the evils we see happen do occur, and will occur, given that they are built on a foundation that relies not on science, but only on certain written institutions and customs in conducting affairs? If any other art or craft were to use such a foundation, it is certain everything would be utterly overturned. Or perhaps it should seem more wonderful how naturally robust a city is: for although some <margin>The city is naturally robust.</margin> cities have been thus affected for a long time, they nevertheless remain and do not collapse. Yet many, like sinking ships, have perished, are perishing, and will perish because of the wickedness of their "pilots" and "sailors" <note>Metaphors for rulers and citizens</note>, who are held by an extreme ignorance in the greatest matters. For while they are entirely ignorant of civil affairs, they nevertheless seem to themselves to be most wise in them. <term>SOCRATES.</term> You speak the truth. <term>GUEST.</term> Since, therefore, all these republics are not "correct" and are difficult to live in, we must see which is the lightest and which is the most burdensome of all. Even if this seems to pertain less to our current topic, perhaps in general we do everything for the sake of such a goal. <term>SOCRATES.</term> That is exactly what we must do.
->G<-
<term>GUEST.</term> Of the three forms, they say one and the same is both the easiest and the most difficult. <term>SOCRATES.</term> How do you mean? <term>GUEST.</term> Only that there are three civil governments: that of the one, of the few, and of the many, as we discussed in our confused discourse at the beginning. <term>SOCRATES.</term> There were indeed. <term>GUEST.</term> By dividing each of these into two, let us make six, and set aside the "correct" government itself as a seventh from the others. <term>SOCRATES.</term> In what <margin>The seven forms of government and a fine comparison between them.</margin> way? <term>GUEST.</term> We distribute the rule of one into "kingdom" and "tyranny." The dominion of the few we divide into one form that is to be praised—"aristocracy"—and another that is to be blamed—"oligarchy." As for the administration of the many, we previously called it simply "democracy"; but now we must also say that this is twofold. <term>SOCRATES.</term> By what reasoning shall we divide it? <term>GUEST.</term> By no other than the others, even if its name is not doubled. For this is common to this as to the others: whether one rules according to the laws or...

<column-break/>

...the things written well to the best of their power by those who know. <term>SOCRATES.</term> How could it be otherwise?
<term>GUEST.</term> And indeed, we said that the one who knows, the true statesman (if we remember), will do many things by his art in his own practice, paying no mind to the written words, whenever something seems better to him than what was written by him and sent to those not present. <term>SOCRATES.</term> For we did say that. <term>GUEST.</term> Therefore, if any man whatsoever, or any multitude, for whom laws happen to be established, attempts to do anything contrary to these as being better, are they not doing the same thing that the true statesman does? <term>SOCRATES.</term> Entirely so. <term>GUEST.</term> If, then, they do such a thing while being without knowledge, they would be attempting to imitate the truth, yet they would be imitating it altogether badly; but if they were skilled, this is no longer an imitation, but that very most true thing. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Absolutely. <term>GUEST.</term> And indeed, it was previously agreed by us that no multitude is capable of receiving this art. <term>SOCRATES.</term> It was indeed. <term>GUEST.</term> Therefore, if there is a certain "royal art," the crowd of the wealthy and the whole people could never receive this political science. <term>SOCRATES.</term> How could they? <term>GUEST.</term> It is necessary then, as it seems, that such states, if they intend to imitate to the best of their power that true government of the one who rules with art, must never, once laws are established for them, do anything contrary to the written words and ancestral customs. <term>SOCRATES.</term> You have spoken most beautifully. <term>GUEST.</term> Whenever the wealthy imitate this, then we call such a state an aristocracy; but whenever they do not care for the laws, it is an oligarchy. <term>SOCRATES.</term> It likely is. <term>GUEST.</term> And again, whenever one man rules according to the laws, imitating the man of science, we call him a king, not distinguishing by name the one who rules according to the laws with science or with opinion. <term>SOCRATES.</term> We likely do not. <term>GUEST.</term> Therefore, even if one man who truly has science rules, he will certainly be called by the same name, "king," and nothing else. Because of this, the five names of the governments now spoken of have become only one. <term>SOCRATES.</term> So it seems. <term>GUEST.</term> What then when one ruler acts neither according to laws nor customs, but pretends—just like the man of science—that surely this thing must be done as being better than what is written, yet it is a certain desire and ignorance that leads him to this imitation? Must we not then call each such person a tyrant? <term>SOCRATES.</term> What else? <term>GUEST.</term> Thus, we say, have come into being the tyrant and the king, and oligarchy, and aristocracy, and democracy; because men were displeased with that one monarch, and did not believe that anyone worthy of such a rule would ever be born—someone who would be both willing and able to rule with virtue and science, and to distribute justice and holiness correctly to all—but rather that he would harm and kill and mistreat whichever of us he wished. For if such a man were to arise as we describe, he would be loved and would dwell among us, governing a state alone, happily, correctly, and accurately. <term>SOCRATES.</term> How could it not be so? <term>GUEST.</term> But now, since as we say, such a king is not born in our cities like the one born in beehives—distinct from the start in both body and soul—it is necessary, it seems, for us to come together and write down laws, following the traces of the most true government. <term>SOCRATES.</term> It likely is. <term>GUEST.</term> Do we wonder then, Socrates, at all the things that happen and will happen in such states, given that such a foundation is laid for them—conducting their affairs according to written words and customs and not with science? For everyone can see that if any other pursuit were to use such a method, it would destroy everything there. Or should we wonder more at how strong a thing a city is by nature? For cities suffer such things for an endless time, yet some of them remain stable and are not overturned; though many sometimes, like sinking ships, perish and have perished and will perish, through the worthlessness of their pilots and sailors, who have taken on the greatest ignorance about the greatest things—those who, knowing nothing about political matters, think they have most clearly grasped this science in every way. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Most true. <term>GUEST.</term> Which then of these incorrect states is the least difficult to live in, since all are difficult, and which is the most burdensome? We must observe this, even if it is a secondary matter compared to our present goal; yet perhaps, on the whole, we do everything for the sake of such things. <term>SOCRATES.</term> We must. <term>GUEST.</term> Say then that the same form, being threefold, becomes exceptionally difficult and easy at the same time. <term>SOCRATES.</term> How do you mean? <term>GUEST.</term> I mean only that monarchy, the rule of the few, and the rule of many are the three forms spoken of by us at the start of the discourse we have now undertaken. <term>SOCRATES.</term> They were indeed. <term>GUEST.</term> Dividing these each in two, let us make six, setting the correct one apart from these as a seventh. <term>SOCRATES.</term> How so? <term>GUEST.</term> From monarchy, we have the kingly and the tyrannical; from the rule of the not-many, the well-named aristocracy and oligarchy. From the rule of the many, we then set it down as simple democracy, but now we must set this down as twofold. <term>SOCRATES.</term> How so? And by what shall we divide it? <term>GUEST.</term> It differs in no way from the others, even if its name is already double; but to rule according to the laws or against the laws divides this and all the others. <term>SOCRATES.</term> It indeed seems so.

<summary>This page analyzes why humans rely on written laws despite their inherent limitations, concluding that laws are a necessary "imitation" of the ideal ruler (the "king bee") who does not naturally exist among humans. It introduces a seven-fold classification of governments based on whether they follow laws or the whims of their rulers.</summary>

# THE STATESMAN <note>original: "POLITICVS"</note>

...and it belongs to this art and the others to lead out <note>The text discusses the power of various arts to influence the state.</note>. **SOCRATES.** It certainly does. **GUEST.** Therefore, when one seeks the right forms of government, the distinction between voluntary and involuntary rule is not the primary concern, as we demonstrated before. But since we have set aside the ideal form, and the others are deemed necessary, we must now divide each of these existing forms in two, according to whether they are law-abiding or lawless. **SOCRATES.** That seems to follow from what has just been said. **GUEST.** Monarchy, therefore, when bound by good written rules—which we call laws—is the best of all the six. But when it is lawless, it is harsh and the most burdensome to live under. **SOCRATES.** It likely is. **GUEST.** As for the rule of the few <note>Aristocracy or Oligarchy</note>—just as the "few" is a middle point between one and many—we should consider it a middle state in both directions. But as for the rule of the multitude <note>Democracy</note>, it is weak in all respects and capable of nothing great, whether for good or for evil, when compared to the others. This is because authority in a democracy is distributed in small portions among many people. Therefore, of all the law-abiding constitutions, this is the worst; but of all the lawless ones, it is the best. If all are unrestrained, life is best in a democracy; but if all are orderly, it is the least desirable place to live. However, the first form <note>Lawful Monarchy</note> is by far the first and best—excepting only the seventh. For that one must be set apart from all other constitutions, like a god among men. **GUEST.** That appears to be the case; it happens exactly as you say. **GUEST.** Must we not, then, remove the participants in all these constitutions—except for the one based on science—as not being true statesmen, but rather partisans? We must see them as presiding over the greatest of phantoms, being themselves like phantoms; they are the greatest mimics and sorcerers, and they become the greatest sophists of all sophists. **SOCRATES.** This term "sophist" seems to have quite rightly circled back to those we call "statesmen." **GUEST.** Indeed. This group appeared to us like a drama, as we just said—a band of Centaurs and Satyrs <note>Hybrid creatures representing the confusion and "monstrous" nature of politicians who lack true knowledge</note> who must be separated from the statesman's art. Now, with much difficulty, they have been set apart. **SOCRATES.** So it seems. **GUEST.** But there remains another group even more difficult to distinguish, because it is more closely related to the royal class and harder to recognize. We seem to have suffered something like those who refine gold. **SOCRATES.** How so? **GUEST.** Those craftsmen first separate the earth, stones, and many other things. After these are removed, there remain the substances kindred to gold and precious—copper, silver, and sometimes adamant <note>Likely referring to a hard metal or diamond-like impurity</note>—which can only be separated by fire. These are only removed with difficulty through the trial of the furnace, leaving us to see what is called "unmixed gold," alone by itself. **SOCRATES.** Yes, that is how it is said to happen. **GUEST.** By the same logic, it seems we have now separated the things that are different, alien, and unfriendly to the science of statesmanship, but there remain those that are precious and kindred to it. Among these are the art of the general, the judge, and that part of rhetoric which shares in the royal power by persuading people of what is just, thus helping to steer the affairs of the city. If one can somehow easily set these aside, he will reveal that person we are seeking—the statesman—naked and alone by himself. **SOCRATES.** Clearly, we must try to do this. **GUEST.** For the sake of the trial, he will be made manifest; we must attempt to show him through the lens of <term>music</term> <note>original: "mousike"; here referring to the broad education in the arts and sciences</note>. Tell me. **SOCRATES.** Tell you what? **GUEST.** We have a certain learning of music, and generally of the sciences involving handiwork? **SOCRATES.** We do. **GUEST.** What then? Of these things, whether we ought to learn them or not—shall we say that this is also a science regarding those very subjects? Or how shall we put it? **SOCRATES.** We shall say it is so. **GUEST.** And shall we not admit that this science is different from the others? **SOCRATES.** Yes. **GUEST.** Should none of them rule over the others? Or should the others rule over this one? Or should this science rule over all the others? **SOCRATES.** This science should rule over those, in deciding whether one should learn them or not. **GUEST.** You are declaring, then, that the science which decides whether to learn or teach should rule over the thing being learned. **SOCRATES.** Very much so. **GUEST.** And the science that decides whether we should persuade or not should rule over the science of persuasion itself. **SOCRATES.** How could it be otherwise? **GUEST.** Well then. To what science shall we attribute the power of persuading the multitude and the crowd through storytelling <note>original: "mythologia"</note> rather than through formal teaching? **SOCRATES.** It is clear, I think, that this must be given to rhetoric. **GUEST.** But to which science shall we assign the decision of whether to act toward certain people through persuasion, or through some form of force, or to take no action at all? **SOCRATES.** To the science that rules over the arts of persuasion and speech. **GUEST.** And this would be no other, I think, than the power of the statesman. **SOCRATES.** You have spoken most excellently. And so rhetoric seems to have been quickly separated from statesmanship, as a different species, though one that serves it. **SOCRATES.** Yes. **GUEST.** But what should we think about the following power? **SOCRATES.** Which one? **GUEST.** That which concerns how to wage war against those whom we have chosen to fight. Shall we say this is an art or not? **SOCRATES.** How could we think of generalship and the whole practice of war as anything but an art? **GUEST.** But the power that decides whether we should wage war or depart in friendship—should we assume this science is different from generalship, or the same? **SOCRATES.** Following our previous logic, it must be different. **GUEST.** Then we shall declare that this science rules over generalship, if we are to follow our earlier conclusions. **SOCRATES.** I agree. **GUEST.** What then...

<column-break/>

**A** ...is left for us to consider? **SOCRATES.** It is so. **GUEST.** At that time, surely, for those seeking the correct government, this partition contributed nothing, as we showed above. But after we segregated that ideal form and considered the others as necessary, then the custody or transgression of the laws divides each of them in two. **SOCRATES.** From the speech just made, it seems so. **GUEST.** Therefore, the rule of one person joined with good constitutions—which we have called laws—is the best of all those six. But the form without laws is hard and most burdensome for the subjects. **SOCRATES.** It appears so. **GUEST.** The government in which not many command <note>Oligarchy/Aristocracy</note> must be judged as the middle, just as "few" occupies a **B** middle ground between one and many. Furthermore, we must consider the administration by the many to be weak in all things, as one which, compared to the others, can effect nothing magnificent, whether good or evil, because the magistracies have been reduced to small parts and divided among many. Therefore, of all law-abiding republics, this is the worst; of all the lawless ones, it is the best. And if all are intemperate, it is better to live in a popular state <note>Democracy</note>; but if all are temperate, one should live in that state least of all. In the first form <note>Monarchy</note>, however, it is most excellent and best to lead one's life—except for the seventh. For that one teaches us to separate it from all other governments, no differently than a God from men. **SOCRATES.** These things seem to **C** happen and occur in this way, and we must act as you say. **GUEST.** Is it not right, then, to segregate the administrators of all these Republics—except for that one which belongs to the wise man—as men who are not truly civil, but rather seditious, presiding over vast phantoms? Indeed, they are phantoms themselves, the greatest mimics, the greatest jugglers, and the sophists of sophists. **SOCRATES.** This name seems rightly to apply to those who are called "civil" <note>i.e., the "statesmen" of ordinary cities</note>. **GUEST.** Now at last we have finally separated from the civil art that chorus of Centaurs and Satyrs which we said above we were seeing, and which we judged should be separated from the civil art. **SOCRATES.** So it seems. **GUEST.** Furthermore, a **D** harder task remains, which is more difficult to discern from the king because it is more closely joined by nature—just as happens to those who dig for gold. **SOCRATES.** In what way? **GUEST.** First, the craftsmen separate earth, stones, and many other things from it; but after these, there remain certain things more akin to gold and more precious, mixed with it, which are to be separated from gold by fire alone: copper, silver, and sometimes adamant. These are finally explored through the test of fire, allowing us to see gold that is pure and bright. **SOCRATES.** So it is said of them. **GUEST.** By the same reason, we now seem to have separated from the science of statesmanship those things that are vehemently **E** alien and quite distant; but we have left those things that are proximate and honorable. Among their number is the command of the army, <margin>The majesty of the oratorical faculty.</margin> the judicial office, and the oratorical dignity which communicates with the royal authority while it persuades of what is just, and while it governs public affairs. If someone can easily segregate these, he will show us that statesman we seek, now naked and alone. **SOCRATES.** There is no doubt we must strive for this with all zeal. **GUEST.** For the sake of experience, he will be revealed; but we must try to make him manifest through music. And tell me— **SOCRATES.** What do you want me to say? **GUEST.** Is there for us any discipline of music and **F** generally of the arts which are carried out by the service of the hands? **SOCRATES.** There is. **GUEST.** What then? Shall we say there is some science here which teaches which of the arts are to be learned, and which are not? **SOCRATES.** We shall plainly say there is. **GUEST.** Shall we not confess this to be different from the others? **SOCRATES.** Indeed, this also. **GUEST.** Then shall we say that none of them rule over the others, or that one rules another, or that this science stands before all the others as a leader? **SOCRATES.** That one which judges which of the arts are to be learned and which are not. **GUEST.** Do you assert then that it commands the teacher and the learner? **SOCRATES.** Entirely. **GUEST.** And should the art that judges whether one must persuade or not command the art **G** that is able to persuade? **SOCRATES.** Why not? **GUEST.** To which science shall we primarily attribute that persuasion which is made to the crowd through a kind of storytelling and exhortation rather than doctrine? **SOCRATES.** It is established that it must be attributed to the orator. **GUEST.** Of which art do we say it is the office to judge whether to use force or persuasion, and in what things, and against whom it is fitting to use them? **SOCRATES.** That faculty of the statesman which possesses the skill of persuading and speaking. <margin>How oratory is distinguished from statesmanship.</margin> **GUEST.** Very well. Thus, oratory is immediately seen to be distinct from the statesman's faculty, like another species subject to the statesman. **SOCRATES.** Certainly. **GUEST.** What more must be thought concerning this faculty? **SOCRATES.** Which one? **GUEST.** That by which we fight against those to whom we have declared war. Shall we say this is a matter of art, or void of art? **H** **SOCRATES.** Who would say that all those things which belong to the commander's and the military discipline lack art? **GUEST.** But that faculty which can prudently deliberate by consulting as to those with whom war is to be waged, or peace entered—shall we think it is different from the former, or the same? <margin>The science of military affairs is subordinate to statesmanship.</margin> **SOCRATES.** Different, if indeed we stand by our previous points. **GUEST.** If we follow the reasoning of the previous points, shall we not declare that this science which consults about war rules over the one that conducts war? **SOCRATES.** Precisely. **GUEST.** Which then...

<summary>In this passage, Plato's Guest and Socrates categorize the six common forms of government (monarchy, aristocracy, democracy, and their lawless counterparts) and argue that the true "Royal Science" of statesmanship is the master art that dictates when to use subordinate arts like rhetoric, generalship, and the law.</summary>

# PLATO'S <note>original: "PLATONIS"</note>

...shall we say that any power truly besides that royal discipline of civil affairs <note>Statesmanship</note> presides over the most potent art of all military matters?
**SOCRATES.** None other at all. **GUEST.** Therefore, the science of those who lead armies—since it obeys and serves another—we shall by no means consider to be the civil faculty itself. **SOCRATES.** It certainly does not seem so. **GUEST.** Come now, let us consider the duty of judges who judge individual cases justly. **SOCRATES.** Let us consider it. **GUEST.** Does it extend any further than this: that concerning all kinds of contracts, it considers what is just and what is not? And looking toward the standard of the laws which the king himself established, does it not judge each case, always applying its own virtue? Through this virtue, neither by bribes, nor threats, nor pity, nor hatred, nor love, does it dissolve mutual accusations by transgressing the laws. **SOCRATES.** 
<margin>The judiciary is the king's handmaiden.</margin>
The office of the judge is certainly nothing other than what has just been said by you. **GUEST.** It is agreed, then, that the power of judges is not that royal majesty itself, but a guardian of the laws and a servant of the king. **SOCRATES.** It appears so. **GUEST.** Anyone who considers all the arts we have mentioned must think that none of them is the civil discipline <note>the science of politics</note> we seek. For the duty of royal majesty is not to act itself, but to command those who are able to act, and to recognize the authority and power of those things that are greatest in the city; it knows what is proper and what is opportune, and what is the opposite. The other faculties, however, are to carry out the orders and perform the mandates. **SOCRATES.** Excellent. **GUEST.** For this reason, those arts we just described, since they are masters neither of themselves nor of one another, but each is intent on its own specific works, they have also deservedly obtained their own names for their own duties. **SOCRATES.** It appears so. **GUEST.** But
<margin>What civil science is.</margin>
that which presides over all these, and has care of the laws and all things in the city, and weaves everything together—rightly comprehending its power under a common title—we call "civil science" <note>Statesmanship</note>. **SOCRATES.** Entirely so. **GUEST.** Should we not now proceed through this, according to the example of the weaver's art, since all the types of things in the city have been made clear to us? **SOCRATES.** Most certainly. **GUEST.** Next, it seems, we must declare what the royal arrangement <note>original: "concinnatio regia"</note> is, in what manner it entwines and weaves, and what kind of texture it produces for us.
<margin>The nature of the king's weaving.</margin>
**SOCRATES.** So it is. **GUEST.** The matter is indeed difficult to demonstrate; but since it seems necessary, it must be declared according to our strength. **SOCRATES.** It must be declared entirely. **GUEST.** For that a part of virtue differs from a species of virtue can easily be proven to the opinion of many, even against contentious men. **SOCRATES.** I do not understand. **GUEST.** Perhaps you will understand it this way. I think you consider **Fortitude** <note>original: "Fortitudinem" / Ancient Greek: "andreia" - often meaning courage or manliness</note> to be some part of virtue. **SOCRATES.** Deeply so. **GUEST.** And that **Temperance** <note>original: "Temperantiam" / Ancient Greek: "sophrosyne" - meaning moderation, self-restraint, or sound-mindedness</note> is different from fortitude, but is nevertheless a part of the same thing that fortitude is. **SOCRATES.** Yes. **GUEST.** We must dare to state something wonderful about these. **SOCRATES.** What is that? **GUEST.** That these two are, in a certain way, in many things, greatly opposed to each other. **SOCRATES.** How can you say that? **GUEST.** This is unheard of, since all parts of virtue are said to be bound by a mutual friendship. **SOCRATES.** Certainly. **GUEST.** Let us therefore consider carefully whether this is so simple, or if they have a very great difference in their related types. **SOCRATES.** Indeed, but tell me where we should look. **GUEST.** In all the things we call "beautiful" <note>original: "pulchra" / Ancient Greek: "kala" - also meaning noble or excellent</note>, we refer them to two contrary species. **SOCRATES.** Speak more clearly. **GUEST.** Speed—whether of bodies, or of minds, or of voices—or these things themselves, or even of the images which either music or painting expresses by imitation: have you ever praised any of these yourself, or heard another praise them? **SOCRATES.** Why shouldn't I? **GUEST.** Do you remember in what way they are praised in each of these? **SOCRATES.** Not at all. **GUEST.** I wish I could explain these things in words just as they seem to me. **SOCRATES.** What prevents it? **GUEST.** This seems easy to you, as I see. Therefore let us consider it in the sub-contrary types. This happens whenever we admire the speed, vehemence, or sharpness of many things, whether in thought, body, or voice; we are accustomed to use the single name of "fortitude" <note>courage</note> in our praise. **SOCRATES.** In what way? **GUEST.** We say it is sharp and brave, fast and brave, vehement and brave; and we are accustomed to praise these natures with the common name of fortitude. **SOCRATES.** Indeed. **GUEST.** And do we not often praise something when it is done slowly and gently in many actions? **SOCRATES.** Very much so. **GUEST.** And do we not speak here in a way contrary to the praises used there? **SOCRATES.** How so? **GUEST.** We often say these things are "quiet" and "temperate"; we love these in thought, and in actions we call them "deliberate" and "soft," and in voices "smooth" and "deep," and we call all rhythmic and musical movement—and all music that uses an opportune slowness—by the name of moderation, not fortitude. **SOCRATES.** You speak the truth. **GUEST.** But whenever these things do not maintain their opportuneness <note>original: "opportunitatem" / Greek: "kairos"</note>, we conversely criticize them with changed names. **SOCRATES.** How? **GUEST.** When they become sharper and faster and harsher or harder than the opportunity requires, we call them "insolent," "wanton," and "furious." But when they become deeper and slower and softer, we call them "timid" and "inept," and...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...and whenever we attempt to show that it [Statesmanship] is the mistress of such a terrible and great art as the whole of military science, should we not again call it "royal"?
**SOCRATES.** None other. **GUEST.** Therefore, we shall not classify the science of generals as "political," for it is a subordinate art. **SOCRATES.** That is not likely. **GUEST.** 
<margin>B</margin> Come then, let us now examine the power of judges as they judge. **SOCRATES.** By all means. **GUEST.** Does it have any power beyond judging what is just or unjust concerning contracts, having received the established laws from the law-giving king? It provides its own specific virtue: that it is not defeated by gifts, nor by fears, nor by pity, nor by any other enmity or friendship, and so is willing to settle the complaints of people against each other without violating the order of the lawgiver. **SOCRATES.** No; its work is almost exactly as much as you have said of this power. **GUEST.** And so we have discovered that the strength of judges is not "royal," but a guardian of the laws and a servant of that royal power. **SOCRATES.** It seems so. **GUEST.** This must be understood by looking at all the aforementioned sciences: that none of them appeared to be "political." For that which is truly "royal" ought not to act itself, but to rule over those who are able to act, recognizing the beginning 
<margin>C</margin> and the impulse of the greatest things in the cities, concerning both what is timely and what is untimely; while the others do what is commanded. **SOCRATES.** Correct. **GUEST.** Because of this, the arts we just went through rule neither each other nor themselves, but each performing its own specific action, it has rightly taken its own name according to the character of those actions. **SOCRATES.** It seems so. **GUEST.** But the art that rules over all of these, and takes care of the laws and all things throughout the city, and weaves everything together most correctly—if we encompass its power with a common title, we would most justly, it seems, address it as "political." **SOCRATES.** Entirely so. **GUEST.** 
<margin>D</margin> Should we then wish to go through it now according to the example of the weaver's art, since all the classes of things in the city have become clear to us? **SOCRATES.** Very much so. **GUEST.** We must say, it seems, what the royal "interweaving" is, in what way it interweaves, and what kind of fabric it gives back to us. **SOCRATES.** Clearly. **GUEST.** It has become necessary, as it seems, to demonstrate a more difficult thing. **SOCRATES.** It must certainly be said. **GUEST.** For to the disputatious and those who argue with words, it is very easy to attack the opinions of the many by saying that a part of virtue is somehow different in kind from virtue. **SOCRATES.** I did not understand. **GUEST.** Let's try again this way. I think you 
<margin>E</margin> believe courage is a part of virtue for us? **SOCRATES.** Certainly. **GUEST.** And indeed temperance <note>moderation</note> is different from courage, yet it is also one part of that of which the other is also a part. **SOCRATES.** Yes. **GUEST.** Concerning these, one must dare to reveal a somewhat startling argument. **SOCRATES.** What kind? **GUEST.** That in some way they have a great mutual enmity and a contrary faction against each other in many existing things. **SOCRATES.** How do you mean? **GUEST.** In a way not at all customary. For all parts of virtue are usually said to be friendly to one another. **SOCRATES.** Let us look then, paying very close attention, whether this is so simple, or if there is a difference between them most of all in their related types. **GUEST.** Yes, you should say where we must look. **GUEST.** One must search among all the things we call "beautiful" <note>noble/excellent</note>, but which we place into two contrary classes. **SOCRATES.** Speak more clearly. **GUEST.** Sharpness and speed—whether in bodies, or in souls, or in the movement of the voice—whether in these themselves or in their images, as much as music 
<margin>F</margin> and painting provide imitations: have you ever been a praiser of any of these, or present when someone else was praising them? **SOCRATES.** Of course. **GUEST.** And do you remember the way they do it in each of these cases? **SOCRATES.** Not at all. **GUEST.** I wonder if I could demonstrate it to you through words, just as I am thinking of it? **SOCRATES.** Why not? **GUEST.** You seem to think such a thing is easy; let us then look at it in those types that are opposite to each other. For indeed, in many actions, and frequently on each occasion, when we admire the speed and intensity and sharpness of thought and body, and also of voice, we speak of it in praise, using the one term of "courage." 
<margin>G</margin> **SOCRATES.** How? **GUEST.** First, I suppose, we say "sharp and courageous," and "quick and courageous," and "intense" likewise; and by applying the common name which I say belongs to all these natures, we praise them. **SOCRATES.** Yes. **GUEST.** And what of the type of quiet behavior? Have we not often praised this in many of our actions? **SOCRATES.** Very much so. **GUEST.** Do we not then say the opposite of what we said about those others? **SOCRATES.** How? **GUEST.** As we always say, for instance, "quiet" and "temperate," when admiring things done by the mind, and again actions that are "slow" and "gentle," and concerning voices those that are "smooth" and "deep," and all rhythmic motion and the whole of music that employs an opportune slowness; we apply to all of them not the name of courage, but the name of "decorum" <note>orderliness/moderation</note>. **SOCRATES.** Most true. **GUEST.** And yet, whenever both of these occur for us at an inopportune time, we change our minds and criticize each of them, assigning them contrary names. **SOCRATES.** How? **GUEST.** When things become sharper 
than the right moment <note>original: "καιροῦ" / kairos</note> and faster and appear harder, we call them "outrageous" and "manic"; but those that are deeper and slower and

<summary>In this passage, Plato defines the "Royal Science" (Statesmanship) as a master art that does not perform manual or subordinate tasks itself, but rather commands and "weaves" together all other civic functions like the military and the judiciary. The dialogue then explores a central paradox of virtue: that courage (associated with speed and intensity) and moderation (associated with slowness and calm) are often in conflict, despite both being essential parts of a virtuous state.</summary>
