# THE STATESMAN <note>original: "POLITICVS"</note>

A ...softer, cowardly, and sluggish; and we find that these qualities, belonging to the **temperate nature**, and **courage**, which belongs to its opposite, are like hostile forms allotted to opposing factions. We find that they do not mix with one another in the actions concerning these things; furthermore, if we investigate closely, we shall see that those who possess these qualities in their souls are at odds with one another. **SOCRATES.** Where do you mean? **GUEST.** In all those things we just mentioned, as is likely, and in many others. For I believe that because each group praises certain things as their own due to a natural affinity, and rejects the things of the different group as foreign and strange, they fall into great enmity with one another on many accounts. **SOCRATES.** They seem to. **GUEST.** Now, this difference between these types is a kind of game <note>or "child's play"</note> when it involves small things, but in 
B the greatest matters, it becomes the most hateful of all diseases to happen to cities. **SOCRATES.** In what kind of matters do you mean? **GUEST.** In the entire arrangement of how one chooses to live. For those who are exceptionally well-ordered <note>the temperate</note> are always ready to live a quiet life, managing their own affairs by themselves; they deal with everyone at home in this way, and likewise toward foreign cities they are ready to maintain peace in whatever way they can. Because of this love of peace, which is more poorly timed than it ought to be, when they do what they want, they unwittingly become un-warlike themselves and render the youth the same way, leaving them at the mercy of whoever attacks them. From these actions, within a few years, they 
C and their children and the entire city often unwittingly become slaves instead of free men. **SOCRATES.** You have described a hard and terrible suffering. **GUEST.** But what about those who lean more toward courage? Do they not always strain their cities toward some war because of an excessive desire for such a life? By entering into enmity with many powerful nations, they either utterly destroy their own homelands or place them in slavery and subjection to their enemies. **SOCRATES.** This also happens. **GUEST.** How then can we deny that in these matters both classes always have great and the ultimate enmity and discord toward one another? **SOCRATES.** We cannot deny it. **GUEST.** Have we not then found what we were looking for at the beginning: that significant parts of virtue <note>courage and temperance</note> 
D naturally differ from one another, and they cause those who possess them to do the same? **SOCRATES.** It appears so. **GUEST.** Let us then take up this point again. **SOCRATES.** Which point? **GUEST.** Whether any of the "synthetic" sciences <note>sciences that put things together, like weaving or building</note> willingly constructs any of its works, even the most trivial, out of a mix of bad and good materials. Or does every science everywhere reject the bad as much as possible, while taking up the suitable and the good? From these—both the similar and the dissimilar—it brings everything together into one, creating a single power and form. **SOCRATES.** Certainly. **GUEST.** Therefore, the truly natural science of politics will never willingly 
E constitute a city out of good and bad men. But it is clear that it will first test them in education. After the test, it will hand them over to those who are able to teach and serve this very purpose, while it itself commands and presides. Just as the art of weaving presides over the carders and those who prepare the other things for its texture, following along and commanding them, showing each one how to complete the tasks it deems suitable for its own weaving. **SOCRATES.** Exactly. **GUEST.** In the same way, the royal majesty seems to me to preside over all those who educate and nurture according to the laws. It keeps the power of supervision for itself and will not permit any training unless it produces 
F a character that fits its own blend. It commands them to teach only these things. Those who are unable to share in a courageous and temperate character and whatever other traits lead toward virtue, but are pushed toward godlessness, insolence, and injustice by the force of a bad nature, it casts out through death, exile, and the punishment of the greatest dishonors. **SOCRATES.** So it is said, at least. **GUEST.** But those who wallow in ignorance and great baseness, it subjects to the class of slaves. **SOCRATES.** Most rightly. **GUEST.** As for the rest, whose natures are capable of reaching a noble state through education and can submit to being blended together by art, the Statesman takes those that tend more toward courage—regarding their solid character as being like the 
G **warp** <note>the strong, vertical threads in a loom</note>—and those that tend toward moderation—which are like the **woof** <note>the softer, horizontal threads, here called "saffron-colored"</note>—and though they tend in opposite directions, he tries to bind and weave them together in such a way. **SOCRATES.** In what way? **GUEST.** First, according to their affinity, he binds the eternal part of their soul with a **divine bond**; and after the divine, he binds the animal part of the soul with **human bonds**. **SOCRATES.** How do you mean this? **GUEST.** Whenever a true and firm opinion concerning the beautiful, the just, the good, and their opposites is produced in souls, I say that this is a divine thing appearing in a god-like race. **SOCRATES.** 
H That is fitting. **GUEST.** Do we not know that it is proper only for a statesman and a good lawmaker to be able, by the "royal music" <note>the art of leadership</note>, to instill this very thing in those who have rightly participated in education, whom we just mentioned? **SOCRATES.** That is likely. **GUEST.** But whoever is unable to do such a thing, Socrates, let us never address him by the names we are now seeking <note>i.e., King or Statesman</note>. **SOCRATES.** Most rightly. **GUEST.** What then? When a courageous soul takes hold of this kind of truth, does it not become civilized, and would it not then be most willing to share in justice? But if it does not participate...

<column-break/>

A ...slothful; and nearly both these and the nature of temperance and fortitude we shall find to be contrary, like hostile forms, and stirring up discord among themselves. Never in the actions concerning these things are they mixed, nor do those in whose minds these qualities exist agree among themselves, but rather they disagree, if only we investigate diligently. **SOCRATES.** Where do you say? **GUEST.** In all those things I have recounted, and indeed it is consistent in many others: for since both, according to the affinity of their own nature, praise some things as their own and proper, and reject others as foreign and external, it happens that they vehemently oppose one another in many things. **SOCRATES.** They seem to. **GUEST.** This dispute of such types is a kind of sport to some, but in 
B the greatest matters it becomes the most serious disease of all for cities. **SOCRATES.** In what kind of things do you mean? **GUEST.** In every constitution of living, as is consistent. For those who excel others in modesty study a life of tranquility, always doing their own business privately, eager for peace and harmony both toward foreigners and toward fellow citizens. And by an excess of this love, it happens that while they attend to their 
<margin>What evils arise from a lack of balance <note>original Latin: "intemperantia" used here to mean a lack of proportion</note>.</margin>
private works, they themselves are secretly rendered unwarlike and weakened, and they soften and effeminate the younger ones by their example. Whence they are exposed to any who envy them, and 
C shortly they themselves, their children, and the whole fatherland succumb, having gradually lost their liberty. **SOCRATES.** You have described a very hard and heavy disease. **GUEST.** But those who decline more toward fortitude and too much affect a warlike life, these often incite and exhort their fatherland to war, whence they render many and powerful nations hostile to their city. For which reason they either utterly overturn their states or imprudently reduce them to the slavery of enemies. **SOCRATES.** So it also happens. **GUEST.** Therefore, who would deny that in these things both are very much opposed to one another? **SOCRATES.** No one, certainly. **GUEST.** Have we not now found what we were seeking from the beginning? Namely, that 
D certain significant parts of virtue are naturally at war with themselves, and make those who have them disagree greatly among themselves? **SOCRATES.** It appears so. **GUEST.** Let us likewise see this. **SOCRATES.** What? **GUEST.** Is there any science among those whose action consists in composing, which would willingly construct any work of its own, even the most worthless, out of both bad and good materials? Or rather, does every 
<margin>Every science rejects the bad and seizes the useful.</margin>
science always avoid the wicked as much as it can, but capture the fit and useful? And from these—partly similar, partly dissimilar—all collected into one, does it not forge one certain power and idea? **SOCRATES.** That rather. **GUEST.** Never, therefore, will a true skill in civil affairs according to nature 
E willingly constitute any city out of bad and good men: but it will explore each one by discipline and some trial, and the examination having been made, it will afterward commit that same duty to those who can both teach others and themselves obey: over whom it will diligently preside and command, just as the art of weaving presides over the carders and other preparers of wool-work, prescribing such things to each as it thinks conducive to its weaving. **SOCRATES.** Entirely so. **GUEST.** By the same reasoning, royal majesty seems to me to preside over all those 
<margin>Certain duties of royal majesty.</margin>
who imbue and educate others according to the institutes of the laws, permitting them to exercise and teach only that which, pertaining to its own reason, induces decorous manners: 
F but those who cannot attain the power of fortitude, temperance, or the other virtues, but are drawn by the depravity of nature to impiety, petulance, and injustice, it ejects from the assembly of citizens, and damns them by exile, death, and extreme disgrace. **SOCRATES.** So it is handed down in a way. **GUEST.** But the ignorant and small-minded little men it subjects to servile ministry <note>slavery</note>. **SOCRATES.** Very skillfully. **GUEST.** The rest, however, whose characters can be raised to a noble habit through discipline, and permit themselves to be tempered together by art, it elevates and protects. From these, indeed, those which verge more toward 
G fortitude, it deems to be in the place of the **warp** because of their solid manners: but those which verge toward modesty, similar to soft and tender material, it deems to have the image of a **woof of saffron color**. Finally, those things which by nature tend in a contrary and different direction, it strives to bind together in turn and to weave. **SOCRATES.** How? **GUEST.** First, indeed, according to the reason of kinship, it binds the eternal part of the soul with a **divine bond**: after the divine, however, it binds that which is of an animal nature with **human bonds**. **SOCRATES.** How is that? **GUEST.** Whenever there is in souls a true and stable opinion concerning the beautiful, just, and good, or their contraries, I assert that it becomes divine in the daemonic genus <note>meaning the "divine" or "superior" part of the soul</note>, that is, the wise and happy part. **SOCRATES.** It is truly fitting. **GUEST.** 
H Do we know that it behooves the civil man and good law-giver, alone by the "royal muse," to be able to insert this into those who are rightly partakers of discipline as is fitting, whom we just mentioned? **SOCRATES.** That is also consistent. **GUEST.** But he who is unable to do that, Socrates, ought not to be called by the names we were just seeking. **SOCRATES.** Certainly not. **GUEST.** Is not a brave soul, if it be a partaker of truth of this kind, made gentle, and thus most greatly desires to live and act justly among others? But if it be altogether without it, it returns again to ferocity...

<summary>In this passage from Plato's Statesman, the Guest explains that the art of politics is like weaving, where the ruler must harmonize the conflicting "warp" of courageous citizens and the "woof" of temperate citizens. This is achieved by a "divine bond" of shared moral values (truth, justice, and goodness) and by weeding out irredeemable elements from the state.</summary>

# THE STATESMAN <note>original: "PLATONIS POLITICVS"</note>

GUEST: ...falls into a beast-like nature. SOCRATES: Undoubtedly. GUEST: But a soul that is modest by nature, when imbued with these opinions, becomes truly temperate and moderate, so as to be useful to the state. However, the soul devoid of them rightly earns the shameful reputation of stupidity and cowardice. SOCRATES: Very true. GUEST: Must we not say that a connection and bond of this kind—among the wicked themselves, or between the good and the wicked—can never be stable? And that no science would ever industriously use it to bind such people together? SOCRATES: Exactly. GUEST: But for those whom nature has gifted with noble characters, and whom custom has educated according to nature's norm, this bond alone is instilled through the laws. In these people, that civil art <note>the art of statesmanship</note> acts as a remedy; and for this reason, as we said before, the reconciliation of those parts of virtue which are naturally contrary and clashing is a kind of divine work. SOCRATES: These things are true. GUEST: Where this divine bond is established, it is easy to both find and perfect the human bonds. SOCRATES: In what way, and which ones especially? GUEST: The necessities of kinship and the sharing of children, and those matters involving betrothals and marriages. For most people do not couple correctly for the procreation of children in these affairs. SOCRATES: Why so? GUEST: As for how greedily they pursue wealth and power in these matters—what is the point of recounting that more diligently in speech? SOCRATES: None. GUEST: But it is better to speak of those who make lineage their concern, in case they perhaps act beyond measure. SOCRATES: That is fair. GUEST: They act without any right reason, following immediate pleasure; and because they delight only in those similar to themselves, and reject those who are different, they cause a great deal of difficulty. SOCRATES: In what way? GUEST: For modest men seek characters similar to their own; as far as they are able, they marry from such stock and give their daughters to such men. In the same way, the brave type seeks out those similar to themselves, whereas it ought to be done entirely the opposite way by both types.

<margin>The condition of the brave nature.</margin>

SOCRATES: How? And for what cause? GUEST: Because this is the condition of the brave nature: if it remains devoid of temperance <note>self-control/moderation</note> through many generations, it becomes stronger at first, but finally turns to madness and fails. SOCRATES: That is likely. GUEST: Again, a soul full of excessive modesty, but entirely lacking the audacity of courage, if it passes through many similar generations, becomes more sluggish than is fitting, and at last is submerged in a certain extreme lethargy. SOCRATES: It is clear that this also happens. GUEST: We can easily bind both types of men with these bonds, as we said, if both have the same opinion regarding what is beautiful and good. This is the one and complete work of the royal weaving: that it never permits moderate characters to be separate from brave ones, but weaves both natures together through the consensus of the same opinion, through honors and reproaches, and through alternating marriages, creating from these a smooth and excellently coherent web. To these types, the statesman should always commit the public offices and duties in common. SOCRATES: In what way? GUEST: Where the government of one man suffices, he shall put a man endowed with both characters in charge. Where more are needed, he will mix parts of each type. For the characters of temperate rulers are very cautious, just, and stable, but they lack the sharp readiness and a certain vehemence suitable for acting. SOCRATES: So it seems regarding these as well. GUEST: Courage, on the other hand, yields to the others in caution and justice, but excels greatly in getting things done. Truly, all things in the city cannot be done well, privately or publicly, unless both of these are present. SOCRATES: Certainly not. GUEST: Therefore, let us say that the end of the civil action is woven with a right public policy when, by reconciling the natures of the brave and the temperate in harmony and friendship, it makes their life common. This context is truly the most magnificent and best of all webs, protecting and embracing all others in the city, both slaves and free men, comprehending them in this texture and sequence. And so the statesman dominates and presides over the city, so that he omits nothing of those things which, as far as possible, make a city happy. SOCRATES: Indeed, Guest, you have excellently defined for us the royal and civil man.

<column-break/>

GUEST: ...into a certain beast-like nature? SOCRATES: How could it be otherwise? GUEST: And what of the well-ordered nature? Does it not, by sharing in these opinions, become truly temperate and orderly, at least as far as is possible in a state? But if it does not share in what we are talking about, does it not most justly receive a shameful reputation for ignorance? SOCRATES: Entirely so. GUEST: Therefore, let us say that a weaving and bond of this sort never becomes permanent for the wicked among themselves, nor for the good toward the wicked; nor would any science ever seriously use it for such people. SOCRATES: How could it? GUEST: But for those characters that are noble from the start and have been nurtured according to nature, we say this bond alone is implanted through the laws by the art of the statesman. This is the remedy, and as we said, this divine bond brings together the parts of virtue which are unlike and moving in opposite directions. SOCRATES: Most true. GUEST: Since this divine bond exists, there is no difficulty in perceiving the remaining human bonds, nor in completing them once perceived. SOCRATES: How so? And which ones do you mean? GUEST: Those of intermarriages and the sharing of children, and matters regarding private betrothals and weddings. For most people do not bind these things correctly for the procreation of children. SOCRATES: Why is that? GUEST: Why would anyone seriously complain about the pursuit of wealth and power in such things, as if they were worthy of speech? SOCRATES: Not at all. GUEST: It is more just to speak of those who take care of their lineage, if they happen to act in a way that is not right. SOCRATES: That is likely. GUEST: They act without a single right reason, pursuing immediate ease; and by welcoming those like themselves and rejecting those unlike them, they assign themselves the greatest discomfort. SOCRATES: How? GUEST: The orderly people seek their own character; they marry from such as these and give their daughters back to them. And likewise, the courageous character acts in the same way, pursuing its own nature; whereas both types ought to do the exact opposite. SOCRATES: How, and for what reason? GUEST: Because courage, when it is bred for many generations without being mixed with a temperate nature, flourishes with strength at first, but in the end breaks out into total madness. SOCRATES: That is likely. GUEST: On the other hand, the soul that is too full of modesty and unmixed with courageous daring, when it repeats this through many generations, is born more sluggish than is proper and finally becomes completely crippled. SOCRATES: That also is likely to happen. GUEST: I said that these bonds are not difficult to tie, provided that both types have one and the same opinion about what is beautiful and good. For this was the whole task of the royal weaving: never to allow the temperate characters to stand apart from the courageous, but to shuttle them together with shared opinions, honors, dishonors, reputations, and the giving of pledges to one another. Thus, he produces what is called a smooth and "well-woven" fabric out of them, and always entrusts the offices in the cities to these types in common. SOCRATES: How? GUEST: Where there is a need for one ruler, he chooses a leader who possesses both qualities; where there is need for many, he mixes a portion of each. For the characters of temperate rulers are very cautious, just, and preserving, but they lack sharpness and a certain quick, practical boldness. SOCRATES: That is my view as well. GUEST: Courageous characters, in turn, are inferior to the others in justice and caution, but they are superior in actions. It is impossible for all things in cities, both private and public, to go well unless both qualities are present. SOCRATES: How could they not be? GUEST: Let us say, then, that this is the end of the web of political action: the character of courageous and temperate men, woven together in a straight weave, when the royal art brings their life together in harmony and friendship, completing the most magnificent and best of all fabrics. It covers all other people in the cities, both slaves and free men, holding them together with this weave; and insofar as it belongs to a city to become happy, it leaves nothing out, but rules and presides. SOCRATES: You have most beautifully completed for us, Guest, the definition of the royal and political man.

# PROTAGORAS, OR
## THE SOPHISTS.

->A style intended for demonstration.<- <note>original: "Ad ostentationem comparatus / Ἐνδεικτικός"</note>

<column-break/>

# ΠΡΩΤΑΓΟΡΑΣ, Η,
## ΣΟΦΙΣΤΑΙ.

->Ἐνδεικτικός.<-

<sig>h</sig>

---

### SUMMARY OF THE DIALOGUE.

The goal and argument of this discussion is the same as that of the *Euthydemus*: namely, to uncover the empty speculations of the **Sophists**, so that their pride and vanity may be exposed, despised, and cast far away. Some opinions drawn from the storehouse of true philosophy are proposed here, but in such a way that they are tainted with certain counterfeit colorings. The primary question is: **Whether virtue can be learned**, which Protagoras indeed affirms. But while he prepares to prove his opinion, he acts in such a way that he leads himself into various narrow straits of contradiction, and rashly mixes everything with fruitless disputes; thus, he rightly seems not a master of true knowledge, but a creator of futile trifles. For it was Plato’s plan to mock the nonsense of the sophists with these examples, so that we might detest them as corrupters of true philosophy and completely abhor them. From here, one may also draw certain excellent lessons, among which are these: that **Wisdom** is not a bare or imaginary knowledge of things, nor that which acts wrongly and viciously; that nothing is pleasant which is not also good...

<summary>This page concludes Plato's Statesman by defining the ideal ruler as a "weaver" who unites the contrasting virtues of courage and moderation through social bonds and shared values, then transitions to the Protagoras, a dialogue aimed at debunking the false wisdom of the Sophists.</summary>

COMPANION: From where do you appear, Socrates? Surely it is from your usual hunt for the youthful beauty of Alcibiades? <note>Alcibiades was a prominent and wealthy Athenian citizen known for his beauty and controversial political career; Socrates was famously his mentor.</note> Indeed, when I saw him just the other day, he seemed a handsome man—a man indeed, Socrates (if I may say so among ourselves), and one whose beard is already filling out. SOCRATES: So what of it? Are you not an admirer of Homer, who
<margin>Homer said: "the most graceful youth..."</margin>said that the most graceful prime of youth is that of the "first beard," <note>original: "χαριεστάτην ἥβην εἶ" - a reference to Homer's Odyssey, describing the god Hermes.</note> such as Alcibiades has now? COMPANION: What of it now, then? Are you coming from him? And how is the young man disposed toward you? SOCRATES: Well, I thought, and especially so today. For he spoke much on my behalf, coming to my aid; and so I have just now come from him. However, I want to tell you something strange. Though he was present, I hardly paid him any mind, and I frequently forgot he was there. COMPANION: And what could have happened to
<margin>B</margin>
distract you so much? For surely you haven't met anyone more beautiful than him, at least not in this city. SOCRATES: Much more beautiful, in fact. COMPANION: What are you saying? A citizen or a foreigner? SOCRATES: A foreigner. COMPANION: From where? SOCRATES: From Abdera. <note>Abdera was a city in Thrace, known as the home of Protagoras.</note> COMPANION: And did this foreigner seem so beautiful to you that he appeared more handsome than the son of Clinias <note>referring to Alcibiades</note>? SOCRATES: How could he not, my dear friend? For is not that which is wisest always more beautiful? COMPANION: But have you really just come from meeting a wise man, Socrates? SOCRATES: Indeed, from the wisest of all men now living—if, that is, you consider Protagoras <note>A famous Sophist, one of the "professional teachers" of the 5th century BC who claimed to teach virtue for a fee.</note> to be the wisest. COMPANION: Oh! What are you saying? Has Protagoras arrived in town? SOCRATES: He has been here for three
<margin>C</margin>
days already. COMPANION: And you have just now come from being with him? SOCRATES: Certainly, and I have heard and said a great deal. COMPANION: Why then do you not relate the conversation to us? Unless something prevents you, sit here and let this boy make room for you. SOCRATES: Certainly, and I shall be grateful to you if you listen. COMPANION: And we to you, if you tell it. SOCRATES: Then the gratitude shall be doubled. Listen, then. Last night, while it was still deep dawn, Hippocrates, the son of Apollodorus and brother of Phason, knocked very violently at my door with his staff. As soon as someone opened it for him, he rushed straight in, calling out in a loud voice, "Socrates, are you awake or sleeping?" And I, 
<margin>D</margin>
recognizing his voice, said, "This is Hippocrates. Are you bringing some news?" "Nothing," he said, "except good news." "That is well," I said. "But what is it? What cause brings you here?" "Protagoras has arrived," he said, standing beside me. "He arrived the day before yesterday," I said. "Have you only just heard?" "By the gods," he said, "only yesterday evening." And feeling for my bed in the dark, he sat down at my feet and said, "Indeed, it was late in the evening when I returned from Oenoe. For my slave, Satyrus, had run away; I intended to tell you I was going after him, but I forgot due to another matter. When I came back and we had eaten and were about to rest, then my brother told me that Protagoras had come. I immediately tried to come to you, but then 
<margin>E</margin>
it seemed too late in the night. But as soon as sleep released me from my fatigue, I rose at once and came straight here." And I, knowing his courage and his excitement, asked, "What is this to you? Has Protagoras done you some wrong?" He laughed and said, "By the gods, Socrates, yes—because he alone is wise, and he does not make me wise!" "But by Zeus," I said, "if you give him money and persuade him, he will make you wise too." "If only, O Zeus and gods," he said, "it were a matter of that! I would not spare anything of my own property nor that of my friends. But for this very reason I have come to you now, so that you might speak to him on my behalf. For I am quite young, 
<margin>F</margin>
and I have never seen Protagoras nor heard him speak. I was still a child when he was here before. But, Socrates, everyone praises the man and says he is the wisest at speaking. Why do we not go to him, so we may find him at home? He is staying, so I heard, with Callias the son of Hipponicus. Let us go." And I said, "Not yet, my good man, let us not go there yet (for it is too early). Instead, let us get up and go into the courtyard, and spend time walking there until it is light. Then we shall go. For Protagoras spends most of his time indoors. So be confident, we will likely find him inside." After this, we rose and went into the courtyard; and I, testing the strength of Hippocrates’ intent, began to examine him and asked: "Tell me, Hippocrates, you are now preparing to go to Protagoras to pay him a fee for yourself. To what kind of person do you think you are going? And what do you expect to become? It is as if 
<margin>G</margin>
you intended to go to your namesake, Hippocrates of Cos, the descendant of Asclepius, <note>Hippocrates of Cos was the most famous physician of antiquity; Asclepius was the god of medicine.</note> to pay him a fee for yourself. If someone asked you: 'Tell me, Hippocrates, you are going to pay a fee to Hippocrates—in what capacity?' What would you answer?" "I would say," he replied, "as to a doctor." "And what would you expect to become?" "A doctor," he said. "And if you went to Polyclitus the Argive or Phidias the Athenian..." <note>Famous sculptors of the 5th century BC.</note> "If someone asked, 'Tell me Hippocrates, you will give a fee to Hippocrates: To what kind of man, and for what reason?' What would you respond? Namely, as to a doctor. In what way will you turn out? That is, as one who will emerge as a doctor. But if you went to Polyclitus the Argive, or Phidias..."

FROM WHERE, O Socrates, do you come? Are you returning, perhaps, from that hunt to which the beauty of Alcibiades usually provokes you? For lately, as I was watching, he seemed a handsome man to me—a man, I say, who might indeed be counted among us, since the first down is already 
<margin>SOCRATES</margin>
spreading across his cheeks. SOCRATES: So be it, what of it? Do you not approve of Homer, who said that the most pleasing age is that of the first down? That is the age Alcibiades is now in. COMPANION: But at present, are you not coming from him? And how is the youth now affected toward you? SOCRATES: 
Well indeed; he seemed especially well today, for he helped me many times today in speaking, and I have just now come from him. And I will tell you something wonderful: although he was present, I barely looked at him; my mind was elsewhere and I hardly noticed him. COMPANION: What was
so great that it diverted you from him? For no one more beautiful from among our citizens could have been there. SOCRATES: On the contrary, there was someone much more beautiful. COMPANION: What are you saying? A citizen? Or a foreigner? SOCRATES: A foreigner. COMPANION: From where? SOCRATES: From Abdera. COMPANION: Was that foreigner really seen by you as being endowed with such remarkable beauty that he seemed more handsome to you than the son of Clinias? SOCRATES: What prevents it, O blessed one, from that which is wiser being also more beautiful? COMPANION: Are you perhaps coming from a conversation with some wise man? SOCRATES: From the wisest, indeed, of all the men of our age—if indeed Protagoras seems to you to be the wisest of all others. COMPANION: Look, what are you saying? Has Protagoras arrived here? SOCRATES: Three days ago. COMPANION: Have you just been with him? SOCRATES: Just now, and I spoke much, and I also heard much. COMPANION: Won't you relate those things to us? Unless something prevents you, we may sit here. This boy will give his place to you. SOCRATES: I will indeed relate them, and I will be grateful besides if you listen. COMPANION: And we to you, if you speak. SOCRATES: A double grace it shall be then. Listen, therefore. Last night, before the rising of the light, Hippocrates the son of Apollodorus, brother of Phason, 
<margin>Occasion of the dialogue.</margin>
knocked loudly at my door with his staff. And when someone had opened the door, he suddenly entered in a hurry and cried out in a loud voice: "Are you sleeping, O Socrates, or are you awake?" I, recognizing his voice, said: "This is Hippocrates. O Hippocrates, is there any news?" "Nothing," he said, "except I come to bring pleasant news." "Excellent," I said. "But what is it? What cause brought you here?" "Protagoras has come," he said, "he is staying near me." Then I said: "He arrived some time ago; have you only just heard?" "Yesterday evening, certainly," he said. And feeling for a stool in the darkness with his hand, he sat down at my feet and added: "Late yesterday evening, having returned from Oenoe—for my boy Satyrus had fled from me. And when I wanted to signal to you that I would pursue him, I forgot because something else intervened. But when I had come back, and we had dined and wanted to give ourselves to sleep, then for the first time my brother announced that Protagoras had arrived. I tried to hurry to you immediately, but the unseasonable night held me back. But having woken from sleep and been relieved of my labor, I have come here to you at once." I, however, noticing the man's great spirit and his amazement, said: "What is this to you? Does Protagoras affect you with some injury?" Then he, smiling, said: "Indeed, it is because he alone is wise, but he does not make me wise." SOCRATES: On the contrary, he will certainly make you wise too, if you persuade him by offering a fee. HIPPOCRATES: O Jupiter and the other gods! I would spare neither my own things nor those of my friends, if only I were confident I would achieve that. And for that reason I come to you now, so that you may intercede for me with him. For I am both younger, and I have never seen nor heard Protagoras; for I was a child then, when he first arrived here. All men indeed, O Socrates, praise this man, and they say he is the wisest in speaking. But why do we not hasten to him, so that we may meet him at home? He is staying, so I heard, at the house of Callias the son of Hipponicus. Let us go now. SOCRATES: Not yet, O good man, I said, we must not go there yet. For it is still very early morning. But let us go to the courtyard, where we will walk until the dawn shines; afterwards we will go to Protagoras himself. For indeed Protagoras spends a great deal of time at home. Therefore be confident, for we shall find him at home. With these things said, we rose and went into the courtyard, and I, wishing to make a test of his confidence, looked at him carefully, and interrogated him thus: "Come tell me, O Hippocrates, you wish to go to Protagoras now to give him a fee for yourself. To what kind of man are you going? And you yourself, what kind of man do you expect to emerge from him? Just as if you wished to set out to your namesake, Hippocrates of Cos, that man born of the stock of Asclepius, to pay him a fee for yourself, and someone..."

The narrative begins with a young man named Hippocrates excitedly waking Socrates early in the morning, eager to pay Protagoras to teach him wisdom.</summary>

...to the Athenian <note>Referring to the master sculptor Phidias.</note>, with a fee offered on your behalf to them, and someone asked you what kind of men they were and for what reason you offer money to Polyclitus <note>Polyclitus was a famous Greek sculptor known for his bronze statues and his 'Canon' of proportions.</note> and Phidias: what would you say to this? **Hippocrates:** As to sculptors. **Socrates:** And what would you yourself become? **Hippocrates:** A sculptor, clearly. **Socrates:** Pay attention, please: you and I are now setting out to Protagoras, and for your sake we are prepared to give him money, if only our funds are sufficient and we can persuade him; if not, we will expend our friends' money as well. If anyone, seeing us so eager in this, were to ask: "Tell me, Socrates and Hippocrates, to what kind of man and for what reason do you intend to give money to Protagoras?" how would we answer him?
<margin>A</margin> What specific title have we heard for Protagoras? They call Phidias a sculptor and Homer a poet; but what do they call Protagoras? **Hippocrates:** They call this man a <term>Sophist</term> <note>original: "Sophistam." A Sophist was a professional teacher in Ancient Greece who traveled to cities to teach rhetoric and virtue for a fee.</note>, Socrates. **Socrates:** So we are going to him as to a Sophist to hire him? **Hippocrates:** Exactly. **Socrates:** If someone asked you with what intention and what you yourself expect to become by going to Protagoras, what would you say? At this, Hippocrates blushed—for dawn was just beginning to break, enough that his face was visible—and then he answered: "If we follow the previous logic, I would surely become a Sophist myself." **Socrates:** By the gods, would you not be ashamed to present yourself as a Sophist among the Greeks? **Hippocrates:** Strongly so, Socrates, if I must speak what I truly feel.
<margin>B</margin> **Socrates:** But look, Hippocrates, perhaps your study of this Protagorean art is not meant to make you a Sophist. Perhaps it is like your education with a grammarian, a lyre-player, or a wrestling coach, which you attended not to learn the profession itself, but for the sake of education <note>original: "παιδείᾳ" (paideia). This refers to the general cultivation of a citizen rather than specialized professional training.</note>, as befits a private and free man. **Hippocrates:** That seems to be exactly the nature of my study with Protagoras. **Socrates:** Do you know what you are about to do now, or does it escape you? **Hippocrates:** About what? **Socrates:** That you are about to commit the care of your soul to a man who is, as you say, a Sophist. I would be very surprised if you actually knew what a Sophist is. If you are ignorant of this, you do not know to what you are devoting your efforts, whether it is good or bad.
<margin>C</margin> **Hippocrates:** I think I know. **Socrates:** Tell me then, what do you think a Sophist is? **Hippocrates:** I think, as the name implies, he is one who understands matters pertaining to wisdom. **Socrates:** One could say the same of painters and carpenters, that they are those who understand matters of wisdom. But if someone asked about painters, "Wisdom in what matters?" we would answer "In the wisdom of making images," and similarly for others. And if we were asked in the same way about a Sophist, what would we say his wisdom is?
<margin>D</margin> Of what art is he a teacher? **Hippocrates:** A teacher of eloquence and the power of speaking, Socrates. **Socrates:** Perhaps we would be speaking the truth, but not sufficiently. For that answer requires another question: about what subjects does the Sophist make men skilled in speaking? A lyre-player makes them skilled in speaking about the same things in which he makes them learned, namely, playing the lyre, does he not? **Hippocrates:** Certainly. **Socrates:** But the Sophist—what power of speaking does he provide? On what subjects? Clearly on those which he understands. **Hippocrates:** That is likely. **Socrates:** What then is it that the Sophist understands and teaches others? **Hippocrates:** By Hercules <note>original: "Her-cle." A common Romanized oath used here to translate the Greek "Ma Di'" (By Zeus).</note>, I do not know.
<margin>E</margin> **Socrates:** Do you not see what a great danger you are subjecting your soul to? If you were going to put your body at such a risk, where it might turn out for better or worse, would you not first consider carefully whether to commit it to such danger, and consult your friends and relatives for a long time? Yet you value your soul more than your body, and your whole well-being—whether things go poorly or well—depends on its health or sickness; yet regarding whether your soul should be committed to this visiting stranger, you have consulted neither your father, nor your brother, nor any of us who are your friends and family. Instead, having heard of his arrival yesterday evening, you hurry here at early dawn, without taking counsel on whether you ought to trust yourself to him. Rather, you are ready to spend all your own money and your friends' money, as if you had already decided that you must adhere to Protagoras—whom you say you have never seen or spoken to.
<margin>F</margin> You call him a Sophist, yet you clearly do not know what a Sophist is, to whom you are about to surrender yourself. **Hippocrates:** You seem to speak the truth, Socrates. **Socrates:** Is a Sophist not, Hippocrates, a kind of merchant or a retailer of the provisions by which the soul is nourished? **Hippocrates:** He certainly seems so to me; but what nourishes the soul? **Socrates:** Learning <note>original: "Disciplinis" (Latin) / "Μαθήμασι" (Greek).</note>. But we must be careful, my friend, that the Sophist does not deceive us while praising what he sells, just as those who sell food for the body—the merchants and retailers—do. For they praise everything they bring, and they do not understand whether what they sell is healthy or harmful for the body;
<margin>G</margin> and those who buy from them are also ignorant, unless one happens to be a doctor or a trainer. In the same way, those who carry various learnings through the cities for sale, retailing them to anyone who desires to buy, praise everything they sell. And perhaps some of them, my good friend, are ignorant of whether what they sell is useful or harmful to the soul; and similarly those who buy from them, unless one of them happens to be a physician of the soul. If therefore you understand what is profitable or harmful among these, you may buy safely...

<column-break/>

...the Athenian <note>original: "τὸν Ἀθηναῖον" (ton Athenaion).</note>, to pay a fee on your behalf to them, if someone asked you, "To what kind of person are you paying money when you pay it to Polyclitus and Phidias?" what would you answer? "I would say: to statue-makers." "And what would you yourself become?" "Clearly a statue-maker." Very well, but now you and I are going to Protagoras, and we are ready to pay him a fee on your behalf; if our own money is enough, we will persuade him with that; but if not, we will spend that of our friends as well. If anyone, seeing us so eager in this, were to ask: "Tell me, Socrates and Hippocrates, to what kind of man do you intend to pay money when you pay it to Protagoras?" what would we answer him?
<margin>A</margin> What other name have we heard used of Protagoras, as we hear Phidias called a statue-maker and Homer a poet? What such thing do we hear of Protagoras? "They call the man a <term>Sophist</term>, Socrates," he said. "Then we are going to pay money to him as a Sophist?" "Exactly." If he were to ask you this too: "And what do you expect to become yourself by going to Protagoras?" And he said, blushing (for by now a little light of day was appearing, so that he was visible): "If this is at all like the previous cases, it is clear that I am to become a Sophist." "And you," I said, "by the gods, would you not be ashamed to present yourself as a Sophist to the Greeks?" "By Zeus, Socrates, if I must say what I really think." "But perhaps, Hippocrates,
<margin>B</margin> you do not suppose your learning from Protagoras will be of that sort, but rather like that you had from the grammarian, the lyre-player, and the trainer. For you did not learn each of these to be a professional, but for education, as befits a private citizen and a free man." "Indeed, it seems to me," he said, "that the learning from Protagoras is more of that sort." "Do you know then what you are about to do, or does it escape you?" I asked. "About what?" "That you are about to offer your soul for treatment to a man who is, as you say, a Sophist; but what a Sophist is, I should be surprised if you know. Yet if you are ignorant of this, you do not even know to whom you are handing over your soul; whether to a good or a bad thing." "I think I know," he said. "Tell me then, what
<margin>C</margin> do you consider a Sophist to be?" "I think," he said, "as the name says, he is one who is knowledgeable in wise things." "Then," I said, "one can say this also of painters and carpenters, that they are knowledgeable in wise things. But if someone asked us in what things painters are wise, we would tell him: in matters of making images. And if he asked about the others, we would say the same. But if one asked, 'In what wise things is the Sophist wise?' what would we
<margin>D</margin> answer him? Of what craft is he the master?" "What else, Socrates, than that he is a master of making one a clever speaker?" "Perhaps," I said, "we would be telling the truth, but not yet sufficiently. For our answer still needs a question: about what does the Sophist make one a clever speaker? For instance, the lyre-player makes one a clever speaker about the very thing he is knowledgeable in, namely, playing the lyre. Is that not so?" "Yes." "Well then, about what does the Sophist make one a clever speaker? Clearly about that which he knows?" "Likely." "What then is this about which the Sophist is himself knowledgeable and makes his pupil so?" "By Zeus," he said, "I can no longer tell you." And I said after this, "What then? Do you know into what kind of danger you are going to put your soul? If you had to entrust your body to someone, at the risk of its becoming either sound or base, you would have looked into it many times whether to entrust it or not; and you would have called your friends and relatives for advice, considering it for many days. But that which you hold of more value than the body, the soul, and on which everything of yours depends, whether you fare well or ill, according to whether it becomes good or
<margin>E</margin> base—about this you have neither shared with your father, nor your brother, nor any of us your companions, whether or not to entrust your soul to this stranger who has arrived. But having heard of it in the evening, as you say, and coming at dawn, you make no mention or consultation of this, whether you ought to entrust yourself to him or not, but are ready to spend both your own and your friends' money, as if you had already decided that you must associate with Protagoras—whom you say you do not know and have never spoken with. You call him a Sophist, but you appear not to know what a Sophist is, to whom you are about to entrust yourself." And hearing this, he said, "It seems so, Socrates, from what you say." "Is it then, Hippocrates, that the Sophist happens to be a certain
<margin>F</margin> merchant or retailer of the wares from which the soul is nourished? For to me at least he appears to be such." "And with what is the soul nourished, Socrates?" "With learnings, surely," I said. "And see to it, friend, that the Sophist, in praising what he sells, does not deceive us, as do those who deal with the food of the body, the merchant and retailer. For these, of the wares they bring, do not themselves know what is good or bad for the body, but they praise everything they sell; nor do those who buy from them know, unless one happens to be a trainer or a doctor. So too those who carry learnings
<margin>G</margin> around the cities, selling and retailing them to whoever desires them, praise everything they sell. But perhaps some of these, my dear friend, are also ignorant of whether what they sell is good or bad for the soul; and likewise those who buy from them, unless one happens to be a physician of the soul. If then you happen to be knowledgeable of what is good or bad among these..."

# PROTAGORAS.

<margin>A</margin> ...it is safer for you to buy teachings from Protagoras or anyone else. Otherwise, take care, my dear youth <note>original: "ὦ μακάριε," literally "O blessed one," a common Socratic address</note>, lest you gamble and risk what is most dear to you. Indeed, there is a much greater danger in the purchase of teachings than in the purchase of food. When you buy food and drink from a merchant or a peddler, you can carry them away in other vessels. Before you receive them into your body by eating or drinking, you can set them down at home and call in an expert <note>original: "τὸν ἐπαΐοντα," one who understands or has specialized knowledge</note> to advise you on what should be eaten or drunk, and what should not, and how much, and when. Thus, the danger is not so great. But teachings cannot be carried away in another vessel; rather, once the price is paid, you must receive the teaching directly into your soul <note>original: "ἐν αὐτῇ τῇ ψυχῇ," in the soul itself</note>. Once learned, you depart either harmed or benefited. Let us, therefore, consider
<margin>B</margin> these things with those older than ourselves; for we are still too young to decide such a great matter. For now, however, let us proceed as we intended and listen to the man; then, having heard him, we can consult with others. For Protagoras is not there alone, but also Hippias of Elis and, I believe, Prodicus of Ceos, and many other wise men. This being our decision, we set out. When we reached the vestibule, we stood there discussing a certain point that had occurred to us on the way. So that the argument might not be left unfinished, but rather concluded before we entered, we stood in the vestibule talking until we reached an agreement. It seems to me that the
<margin>C</margin> porter, a certain eunuch, overheard us. He was likely annoyed by the multitude of Sophists <term>Sophists</term> <note>Professional teachers of rhetoric and "virtue" who charged high fees, often viewed with suspicion by Socrates for prioritizing persuasion over truth.</note> visiting the house. At any rate, when we knocked at the door, he opened it, saw us, and said, "Ha! More Sophists. He has no leisure!" And with both hands, he slammed the door shut as hard as he could. We knocked again. He answered through the closed door, "Men, have you not heard that he has no leisure?" "But my good man," I said, "we have not come to see Callias <note>The wealthy host of the Sophists.</note>, nor are we Sophists. Do not be afraid. We have come because we desire to see Protagoras. Please announce us." At last, the man reluctantly opened the door for us. When we entered, we found Protagoras walking in the portico.
<margin>D</margin> Walking with him in a line on one side were Callias, son of Hipponicus, his half-brother Paralus, son of Pericles, and Charmides, son of Glaucon. On the other side were Pericles’ other son, Xanthippus, Philippides, son of Philomelus, and Antimoerus of Mende, who is the most famous of Protagoras’ pupils and is studying professionally with the intention of becoming a Sophist himself. Behind them followed a crowd listening to their conversation. Most appeared to be foreigners whom Protagoras brings from every city he passes through, charming them with his voice like a modern Orpheus <note>A legendary musician of Greek myth who could charm all living things with his music.</note>; and they follow the sound of his voice, enchanted. There were also some locals in the choir. I was particularly delighted to observe this choir, seeing how gracefully they took care
<margin>E</margin> never to be in Protagoras’ way in front. Whenever he turned around with his companions, the listeners behind would part in a very orderly fashion to either side, and circling back, they always took their place behind him in the most beautiful manner. "Next I recognized" (as Homer says) <note>A reference to the *Odyssey*, where Odysseus describes the shades in the underworld.</note> Hippias of Elis, sitting on a high seat in the opposite portico. Seated around him on benches were Eryximachus, son of Acumenus, Phaedrus of Myrrhinus, and Andron, son of Androtion, along with some foreigners—both his fellow citizens and others. They appeared to be questioning Hippias on nature and
<margin>F</margin> astronomical matters concerning the heavens. He, sitting on his high seat, was explaining and settling their various difficulties. And indeed, "I also beheld Tantalus" <note>Another Homeric allusion to the underworld.</note>; for Prodicus of Ceos was also in town. He was in a certain room which Hipponicus used to use as a storeroom, but because of the multitude of guests, Callias had cleared it out and made it a lodging for foreigners. Prodicus was still in bed, wrapped in many fleeces and blankets, or so it seemed. Seated near him on the adjacent couches were Pausanias of Cerameis, and with Pausanias a lad who was still quite young—of a noble nature, I thought, and certainly very handsome. I believe I heard his name was
<margin>G</margin> Agathon <note>The future tragic poet and host of the *Symposium*.</note>; I would not be surprised if he were Pausanias’ beloved. There were also both Adeimantuses—the son of Cepis and the son of Leucolophides—and several others. I could not hear from the outside what they were discussing, though I was eager to hear Prodicus, for he seems to me a man of divine wisdom. However, because of the deepness of his voice, a certain booming sound in the room made his words indistinct. We had just entered when, behind us, came the beautiful Alcibiades (as you call him, and I agree) and Critias, son of Callaeschrus. After we entered and spent a little time observing these sights, we approached Protagoras. I said, "Protagoras, Hippocrates here and I have come to see you." "Do you wish to speak with me alone," he asked, "or in the presence of the others?" "It makes no difference to us," I replied. "Once you have heard why we have come, you can decide for yourself." "What is it then," he asked, "that brings you here?" "Hippocrates here is a local, the son of Apollodorus, from a great and wealthy house. He is thought to be a match for his peers in talent, and I believe he desires to become famous in the city. He thinks this is most likely to happen if he associates with you. Now, consider whether you think you should discuss this with us alone or with the others." "You are right to take such precautions on my behalf, Socrates," he said.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...from Protagoras and from anyone else you can. Otherwise, beware, O blessed youth, lest you bring your most precious things into the greatest risk of loss. For the danger is far more serious in purchasing teachings than in food. For he who buys food and drink from a shopkeeper or a merchant can, before he consumes them, carry them home in other vessels, and having put them away, he can carefully examine them. By calling in <gloss>him</gloss> who is an expert in such matters, he can deliberate what should be eaten or drunk, what should not, and how much, and when; therefore, the danger in buying is not heavy. But teachings cannot be transferred into another vessel; instead, it is necessary that he who buys them receives them in his mind. Having paid the price, he carries them within himself, having been either tainted or advanced toward better things.
<margin>B</margin> Therefore, let these matters be discussed by both of us with our seniors; for we are younger than the judgment of such a great matter requires. For the present, however, let us proceed as we began and hear this man, and after hearing him, we will communicate with others. For Protagoras is not present there alone, but also Hippias of Elis, and Prodicus of Ceos, as I believe, and many other men, and very wise ones at that. These things pleased us, and so we went on. Having entered the vestibule, we pursued a certain discourse which we had happened upon while walking. Lest it be left imperfect, we progressed in our conversation in the vestibule until we reached an agreement through our disputation.
<margin>C</margin> But I believe a certain eunuch, the porter, heard us; he was angry at those who came because of the frequency of those Sophists. We knocked; he opened. When he saw us, he said, "Ha, some people! He has no leisure." And at the same time, leaning with both hands, he shut the door. We knocked again, but he, with the doors closed, said, "Do you not hear that he has no leisure?" "O good man," I said, "we have not come to Callias, nor are we Sophists; but have confidence, we have need of Protagoras, we desire to see him." This having been announced, he finally opened the doors. Having entered, we found Protagoras walking in the vestibule of the portico. Many were following him, on this side
<margin>D</margin> Callias, son of Hipponicus, and his brother by the same mother, Paralus, born of Pericles, and Charmides, son of Glaucon. On the other side was Pericles' other son, Xanthippus, and Philippides, son of Philomelus, and Antimoerus of Mende, who was considered the most distinguished among all Protagoras’ listeners; he was learning that skill with the mind that he himself would one day profess as a future Sophist. Behind them followed others listening to Protagoras, most of whom appeared to be foreigners, whom he gathers from every city through which he travels, soothing them with his voice like a certain Orpheus, and alluring them. They follow his voice, charmed from every side. Some of our own countrymen were also in that choir. When I
<margin>E</margin> contemplated this choir, its order delighted me wonderfully. For with diligent caution, each one took care not to precede Protagoras by even a step. But when he turned his foot back, his listening followers followed him back quite aptly, and divided on both sides into a circle, they gave way so that they were always behind him. After this I saw, to speak in the words of Homer, Hippias of Elis sitting on a throne in the opposite vestibule of the portico. Around him, on benches, sat several others: Eryximachus, son of Acumenus, Phaedrus of Myrrhinus, Andron, son of Androtion, and some others, partly citizens and partly foreigners, who seemed to be asking Hippias about the sublime things of nature and
<margin>F</margin> the movements of the stars; he, sitting on his throne, explained the doubts of each. I saw Tantalus besides. Furthermore, Prodicus of Ceos was present, who had retired into a certain booth <note>original: "tabernaculum," often used for a tent or a small booth/room.</note> which Hipponicus had previously used as a larder; but so that the whole crowd of arriving guests might be received, Callias had removed the provisions and given that corner to the guests to inhabit. Prodicus, therefore, wrapped in shaggy blankets, and indeed many of them, as it seemed, was still reclining there. Sitting in the seats nearest to him were Pausanias of Cerameis, and near him a certain youth of excellent talent and generous nature, as it seems to me, named Agathon, as I heard. Nor
<margin>G</margin> should it seem a wonder if he is the beloved of Pausanias. Both Adeimantuses were also there, the son of Cepis and the son of Leucolophides, and many others. What they were debating among themselves I could not quite perceive from the outside, although I was vehemently eager to hear Prodicus. For he seems to me to be a most wise and divine man, but a certain sound from the gravity of his voice, continually rolling back under the archway, confused the individual words. Immediately after our entrance, Alcibiades entered—beautiful, as you say, and I believe it—and Critias, son of Callaeschrus. When we had entered and had not yet discussed certain things, and had contemplated those sights, we approached Protagoras. Then I said, "O Protagoras, for a certain reason Hippocrates and I have come here to you." <term>PROT.</term> Do you wish to speak with me privately, away from the others? Or in front of everyone? <term>SOCRAT.</term> To us it is all the same, but when you have heard why we have come, you shall see for yourself. <term>PROT.</term> What is it then, for whose sake you have come here? <term>SOCRAT.</term> This Hippocrates is our countryman, the son of Apollodorus, born of a noble and happy race. He himself contends with his equals for virtue.

<summary>Socrates and Hippocrates arrive at the house of Callias to meet Protagoras. The text vividly describes the theatrical atmosphere of the house, where several famous Sophists are holding court, and Socrates begins his inquiry by introducing Hippocrates as a potential student.</summary>

# OF PLATO

...moved by ambition, he desires to become an illustrious man in the state, <note>A</note> and he hopes to achieve this goal through your company. Consider whether it is better for us to consult with you about this alone, or in the presence of others. **PROTAGORAS:** You advise me rightly, Socrates: for a foreigner who travels through great cities and persuades the most excellent of the youth to leave the company of all others—whether their own kin or strangers, whether old or young—and adhere to him alone, as if they would become better men through his company than any other, must exercise a prudent caution. For great envy, much ill-will, and many <margin>Defense of the sophistic art.</margin>
plots arise against such a man. I, however, maintain that the sophistic art <note>original: "σοφιστικὴν τέχνην" (sophistikēn technēn), the professional craft of wisdom or teaching</note> is ancient, <note>B</note> but that those ancient men who practiced it, fearing this offense and envy, used other arts as a screen or a disguise. Some used poetry, as did Homer, Hesiod, and Simonides; others used the name of sacred rites and oracles, like Orpheus and Musaeus and their followers. I have heard that some even called it gymnastics, as Iccus of Tarentum seems to have done, and that Selybrian Herodicus—still living and a sophist second to none—who was originally of Megarian descent. Pythodes of Chios, a most learned sophist, and many others have hidden the sophistic <margin>Apparent reasons.</margin>
faculty under the veil of the musical art. All these men, as I have said, <note>C</note> strictly disguised the name to avoid envy, and hid the sophistic art under the pretext of other crafts. But I disagree with all of them in this regard, for I do not believe those clever tricks are beneficial. Nor do I think they achieve their desired end. For the leading men in the city see through all such disguises. The common people, in a way, do not notice, but simply praise whatever the leaders proclaim. But this effort to escape notice, when it fails to achieve its aim, only shows the one fleeing to be a fool, and makes people even more hostile. For they consider such a person to be a crafty deceiver <note>D</note> above all else. Therefore, I have taken a completely contrary path. I confess that I am a sophist and a teacher of men, and I believe this candid confession is a safer way to avoid envy than that disguise. Moreover, I have taken other precautions so that, by God's help, I have suffered no harm because of my profession as a sophist, though I have practiced this faculty for many years. Indeed, I am now advanced in years, and by age, I could be the father of any of you. Therefore, it will be most pleasing to me if you wish to speak about these matters while everyone inside is listening. Here, suspecting that he wished to show off and boast before Prodicus and Hippias—that we had come to hear him because we were inflamed by his reputation for wisdom—I said: "Why do we not call Prodicus and Hippias, and those with them, so that they too may hear us?" **PROTAGORAS:** <note>E</note> "Let us call them." Callias then said: "Should we prepare seats here, so that you may discuss while sitting?" We all agreed. Delighted at the thought of hearing wise men, we each grabbed benches and chairs and arranged them near Hippias, for the benches were already there. Then Callias and Alcibiades arrived, bringing Prodicus and his companions with them, having raised them from their beds. After we were all seated, Protagoras said: "Now, Socrates, <note>F</note> repeat in the presence of these men what you were asking me a moment ago on behalf of this youth." I replied: "Let us use the same beginning as before. Hippocrates here greatly desires to be your student; but he would gladly hear what he will carry away from your company. This was our question." **PROTAGORAS:** "Young man, you will never come to me without going away more learned, and every day you will progress more and more." **SOCRATES:** "That is not surprising, Protagoras; for it is fitting: since even you, at your age and with such wisdom, would go away better if someone taught you what you do not know. But that is not precisely what we are asking. Just as if Hippocrates here changed his mind <note>G</note> and wished to study with this youth who recently arrived, Zeuxippus of Heraclea, and approached him as he does you now, and heard from him that every day he spent with him, Zeuxippus would become better and progress—if he then asked, 'In what specifically will I become better, and in what will I progress?' Zeuxippus would reply: 'In the art of painting.' Or if he met Orthagoras of Thebes and heard the same things, and asked in what way he would become more excellent every day by associating with him, Orthagoras would reply: 'In the sound of the flutes.' In the same way, you also answer this youth and me asking on his behalf. <margin>What the sophist promises to teach.</margin>
For you say that Hippocrates, if he joins Protagoras, <note>H</note> will be more learned every day; in what, exactly? Declare it." Then Protagoras said: "You ask skillfully indeed, Socrates; and I rejoice in answering those who ask skillfully. Hippocrates, if he studies with me, will not fall into the error he would surely have suffered with other sophists. For others harm the youth. They force them back, against their will, into those arts they had fled, teaching them arithmetic, astronomy, geometry, and music." (And at the same time he looked toward Hippias).

<column-break/>

...to his peers. And he seems to me to desire to become famous in the city; <note>A</note> and he thinks this would most likely happen to him if he were to associate with you. So now you consider whether you think you should discuss these things alone or with others. "You are right," he said, "to take precautions, Socrates, on my behalf. For a man who is a foreigner, visiting great cities, and in them persuading the best of the young men to leave the company of others—both relatives and strangers, both older and younger—to associate with himself, on the grounds that they will be better because of his company, must be cautious in doing this. For no small <note>B</note> jealousies arise regarding these matters, as well as other ill-wills and plots. But I say that the sophistic art is old, but those of the ancient men who handled it, fearing its offensiveness, made a screen and a cover for it: some using poetry (such as Homer and Hesiod and Simonides), others, again, rites and oracles; those around Orpheus and Musaeus. And I have noticed some used even gymnastics; such as Iccus of Tarentum, and the one who is still now a sophist second to none, Herodicus of Selymbria, originally a Megarian. And your Agathocles made music a screen, being a great sophist, and <note>C</note> Pythocleides of Chios, and many others. All these (as I say), fearing envy, used these arts as defenses. I, however, do not agree with all of them in this. For I think they did not achieve at all what they intended. For they did not escape the notice of the men who are able to act in the cities, for whose sake these screens exist. Since the many, so to speak, perceive nothing; but whatever these leaders announce, they sing along with. To try to run away and not be able to run away, but to be caught, is great folly in the attempt, and necessarily makes men much more hostile. For they think such a person is a rogue in addition to everything else. I, <note>D</note> therefore, have gone a completely opposite way from these; and I confess both that I am a sophist, and that I educate men; and I think this caution is better than that one—to confess rather than to deny. And I have considered others in addition to this, so that (to speak with God's help) I suffer nothing terrible because of confessing that I am a sophist. Yet I have already been many years in the art. For indeed my total years are many; there is no one of whom I am not old enough to be the father. So it is much more pleasant for me, if you wish, to have the discussion about all these things in the presence of those within." And I (for I suspected he wanted to show off <note>E</note> and give himself airs before Prodicus and Hippias, because we had come as admirers of him) said, "Why then do we not also call Prodicus and Hippias, and those with them, so that they may listen?" "By all means," said Protagoras. "Would you like," said Callias, "us to prepare a seating area, so that you may sit while you discuss?" It seemed a good idea. And all of us, being glad as men who were about to hear wise men, ourselves took hold of the benches and the couches and arranged them near Hippias; for the benches were already there. In the meantime, Callias and Alcibiades arrived, bringing Prodicus, having raised him from his couch, and those who were with Prodicus. When we were all seated together, Protagoras said, "Now indeed, Socrates, <note>F</note> you may speak, since these men are also present, about the things you mentioned to me a little while ago on behalf of the young man." And I said that, "My starting point, Protagoras, is the same as just now, regarding the reasons I came. For Hippocrates here happens to be in a state of desiring your company. Whatever will result for him, then, if he associates with you, he says he would gladly learn. That is our speech." Taking it up, Protagoras said, "Young man, there will be for you then, if you associate with me, on the day you associate with me, the result of going home having become better, and on the next day these same things; and each day always to improve towards the better." And I, having heard this, said, "Protagoras, this which you say is nothing marvelous, but likely; since even you, although being of such an age and so wise, if someone were to teach you what you do not happen to know, you would become better. But not in this way; but just as if Hippocrates here, <note>G</note> changing his desire right now, should desire the company of this young man who has recently arrived, Zeuxippus of Heraclea, and coming to him, just as to you now, should hear from him these same things that he heard from you: that each day being with him, he will be better and will improve; if he asked him further, 'In what exactly do you say I will be better, and into what will I improve?' Zeuxippus would say to him, 'In painting.' And if associating with Orthagoras the Theban, and having heard from him these same things that he heard from you, he asked him in what he would be better each day associating with him, he would say 'In flute-playing.' Thus indeed you also say to the young man and to me asking on his behalf, 'Hippocrates here, associating with Protagoras, on the day he associates with him, <note>H</note> will go away having become better, and on each of the days he will improve.' Into what, Protagoras, and concerning what?" And Protagoras, having heard these things, said, "You ask well, Socrates, and I rejoice in answering those who ask well. For Hippocrates, coming to me, will not suffer what he would have suffered associating with any other of the sophists. For the others maltreat the young men. For they throw them back into the arts against their will..."

<summary>In this passage, the famous Sophist Protagoras defends his profession by arguing that it is more honest to openly admit to being a "Sophist" than to hide under the guise of poetry or music. Socrates then presses him to define exactly what practical benefit his students, such as young Hippocrates, will gain from his instruction.</summary>

# PROTAGORAS

"But whoever comes to me," <margin>A</margin> <note>These letters in the margin (A, B, C...) refer to the standard 'Stephanus' page numbers used by scholars to cite Plato's works.</note> said Protagoras, "will learn about nothing other than the very thing for which he came. That study is good counsel <note>original: 'εὐβουλία' (euboulia) — the ability to make sound decisions</note> regarding his own affairs, so that he may best manage his own household, and regarding the affairs of the city, so that he may be most capable in the state's business, both in speech and in action."

"Do I follow your meaning?" I asked. "For you seem to me to be describing the political art <note>original: 'πολιτικὴν τέχνην' (politikēn technēn) — the skill of being a citizen or statesman</note> and promising to make men into good citizens."

"That is exactly the profession I profess, Socrates," he replied.

"Then you possess a marvelous skill indeed," I said, "if indeed you truly possess it. For I will speak nothing to you but what I truly think. I did not believe, Protagoras, that this was something that could be taught; yet, when you say it is, I find I cannot distrust you. However, it is only right that I explain why I have always held it to be untaught, and not something provided by men to other men. For I—like all other Greeks—say that the Athenians are <margin>B</margin> <margin>It is shown by trial that virtue cannot be taught.</margin> wise. And I see that when we gather in the Assembly, whenever the city needs to undertake some building project, they send for the builders to act as advisors. When it concerns shipbuilding, they send for the shipwrights. They do this for all other matters that they believe can be learned and taught. But if anyone else attempts to advise them whom they do not consider a craftsman—even if he is remarkably handsome, wealthy, or of noble birth—they do not accept him. Instead, they laugh and jeer until the would-be speaker is shouted down and retreats, or until the archers <note>The 'archers' or Scythian guards served as the public security force in democratic Athens.</note> drag him away or remove him by order of the presiding officers. This is how they act in matters they consider to involve a technical skill. <margin>C</margin>

"But when it is necessary to deliberate on the administration of the city, any man may stand up and give advice: a carpenter, a blacksmith, a cobbler, a merchant, or a ship-master; the rich and the poor, the noble and the low-born alike. And no one reproaches them, as they did the others, by saying they attempt to give advice without having learned from anywhere or having had a teacher. Clearly, this is because the citizens do not believe this 'virtue' can be taught. And this is true not only in public, <margin>D</margin> but in our private lives as well. The wisest and best of our citizens are unable to hand down to others the very virtue they possess. For instance, Pericles, the father of these young men here, educated them well and properly in everything that requires a teacher; but in the wisdom he himself possesses, he neither educates them himself nor hands them over to another. Instead, they wander about, grazing as it were, like sacred cattle left to roam, to see if they might by chance stumble upon virtue on their own.

"If you prefer another example, this same man, Pericles, was the guardian of Clinias, the younger brother of Alcibiades here. Fearing that Clinias might be corrupted by Alcibiades, Pericles separated them and placed Clinias in the house of Ariphron to be educated. But before six months had passed, Ariphron returned the boy, <margin>E</margin> not knowing what to do with him. I could tell you of many others who, though they were good men themselves, never made anyone else better, whether among their own kin or among strangers. Looking at these examples, Protagoras, I do not think that virtue <note>original: 'ἀρετή' (aretē) — excellence or moral virtue</note> can be taught. But when I hear you saying these things, I am wavered, and I think there must be something in what you say, because I believe you are a man of great experience, who has learned much and discovered much for yourself. If, therefore, you can demonstrate to us more clearly that virtue is something that can be taught, do not begrudge us—please, demonstrate it."

"I will not begrudge you, Socrates," he said. "But should I demonstrate this to you as an elder speaking to his juniors, by telling a myth <note>original: 'μῦθον' (mython) — a story or fable</note>, <margin>F</margin> or should I proceed with a rational argument?"

Many of those sitting nearby told him to proceed in whichever way he preferred.

"I think," he said, "it would be more pleasant to tell you a myth."

"Once upon a time, there were gods, but no mortal races existed. But when the destined time for their birth arrived, <margin>This fable strives to demonstrate that virtue is taught.</margin> the gods fashioned them within the earth, mixing together earth and fire and all things that are blended with fire and earth. When they were about to bring them forth into the light, they charged Prometheus <note>Prometheus means 'Forethought'.</note> and Epimetheus <note>Epimetheus means 'Afterthought'.</note> to equip them and distribute powers to each as was fitting. Epimetheus begged Prometheus to let him make the distribution himself. 'When I have distributed them,' he said, 'you can inspect my work.' Having persuaded him, he began the distribution.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> "In his distribution, he gave strength without speed to some, while he equipped the weaker ones with swiftness. Some he armed; for others, he gave an unarmed nature but devised some other power for their safety. To those he made small, he gave winged flight or a dwelling beneath the earth. Those he made large, he protected by their very size. And so he distributed all other things, keeping a balance, taking care lest any race should be utterly extinguished.

"Once he had provided them with <margin>G</margin> means to escape mutual destruction, he devised protections against the seasons of Zeus, clothing them with thick hair and tough skins, sufficient to ward off the winter's cold and the summer's heat. He provided these as their own natural bedding when they went to their lairs. Beneath their feet, he gave some hooves, and others claws or tough, bloodless skin.

"Then he provided different foods for different creatures: for some, grass from the earth; for others, the fruits of trees or roots. To some, he granted that their food should be the flesh of other animals. To these predators, he gave a small offspring, but to those they consumed, he gave great fertility, ensuring the survival of the species.

"However, because Epimetheus was not entirely wise, he failed to notice that he had used up all the available powers on the <margin>H</margin> unreasoning animals. The race of humans was left unequipped and unadorned, and he was at a loss as to what to do..."
