<meta>Continuity: This page continues the "Great Speech" of the sophist Protagoras. Having been challenged by Socrates to prove that virtue can be taught, Protagoras begins a mythological story (a "mythos") explaining the origins of human civilization and the distribution of social virtues.</meta>

# PLATO

(nor did he <note>Referring to Epimetheus, whose name means 'afterthought'</note> notice that nothing would be left from such a great distribution with which to bestow thereafter upon our race). Therefore, the human race remained defenseless and empty: thus he doubted where to turn. To him in his doubt, Prometheus <note>Prometheus, whose name means 'foresight,' was the brother of Epimetheus.</note> stood by as a spectator of that division; he saw that the other animals were each supported by their own gifts and filled with good things, but that man was naked, unarmed, and lacking in shoes or bedding. Now indeed, the fatal day was looming which compelled man to go out from the earth into the light. And since Prometheus could find no other way for human safety, he stole the skilled wisdom of Vulcan <note>original: 'Vulcani' (Hephaestus), the god of fire and craftsmanship.</note> and Minerva <note>original: 'Mineruæ' (Athena), the goddess of wisdom and weaving.</note> along with fire. For it was not possible for anyone to obtain or even use that wisdom without fire. Thus, Prometheus brought it to the human race, and so we attained the wisdom that provides for life. Yet humans still lacked civil wisdom. For that was in the keeping of Jove <note>original: 'Iouem' (Zeus), king of the gods.</note>, whose citadel Prometheus was not permitted to ascend; the terrifying guards standing around the citadel of Jove deterred him. However, he secretly entered the shared workshop of Vulcan and Minerva in which they practiced their arts; he stole the fiery art of Vulcan and the other art of Minerva and handed them over to man, from which the faculty of living was obtained. Prometheus, as it is told, later paid the penalty for his theft because of Epimetheus <note>original: 'propter Epimetheum' — because of his brother's earlier mistake in the distribution.</note>. Since man was made a participant in a divine portion, at first—alone among animals because of this kinship—he believed there were gods, and dedicated altars and statues to them. Then, by his art, he quickly distinguished sounds and words into articulate speech, constructed houses, made clothes and shoes, fashioned bedding, and gathered food from the earth. Thus arranged from the beginning, men lived wandering and scattered, for they had not yet built cities. Consequently, since they were weaker, they were being slaughtered everywhere by wild beasts. For the faculty of the arts was sufficient for procuring food, but not at all for the struggle against savage beasts. For they were lacking in civil skill, of which the military art is a certain part. Therefore, so that they might fortify themselves against that plague, they gathered together by building cities. But once gathered, they committed injustices against one another, since they lacked the civil art; therefore, being dispersed again, they were torn apart by beasts. But Jove, taking thought for human safety, sent Mercury <note>original: 'Mercurium' (Hermes).</note> to bring shame <note>original: 'pudorem' (aidos) — a sense of respect or moral restraint.</note> and justice to the gatherings of men, so that these two might adorn cities and be the binding links of friendship, and reconcile the citizens with mutual goodwill. Mercury therefore asked on what condition he should hand over shame and justice to men. "Shall I distribute these," he said, "as the arts were distributed? For those were distributed such that one man skilled in the art of medicine is sufficient for many unskilled ones, and similarly for the other crafts. Shall I give shame and justice to men in this way? Or shall I bestow them upon all?" "Upon all," Jove replied, "indeed, let everyone be a participant in these. For no cities would stand if only a few shared in these as they do in the other arts. Furthermore, establish a law in my name: that whoever is entirely without a share of justice or shame should be put to death as a plague upon the city." For this reason, Socrates, all others as well as the Athenians, whenever a discussion is to be held about architecture or any other craft, they call upon a few as advisors and exclude the rest as unskilled, as you say and I agree. But whenever a council is begun concerning civil administration, which consists of the virtues of temperance and justice, they rightly admit everyone, since it is necessary for all to be participants in this virtue, or else no cities can exist. This, Socrates, is the cause of the matter you doubted. But so you do not suspect you are being deceived, accept this further proof: that clearly all mortals think every mortal is a participant in this civil virtue—that is, in temperance and justice. For in other faculties, as you say, if someone boasts—for instance, that he is an excellent flute-player when he is actually unskilled—those listening either laugh at him or are indignant. His relatives warn him as if he were insane and rebuke him. But the opposite happens in justice and other civil virtues; for even if they know someone is unjust, <margin>Aristotle in this opinion, Ethics Book 5.</margin> yet if he should confess the truth about this before those who do not know, they think he is insane. They do not think injustice should be made public; rather, they think one must always display justice, whether one possesses it or not. They think he who does not pretend to be just is out of his mind, as if it were necessary for every single person either to participate in civil virtue or to be exterminated from the company and life of men. From these things, I think it is sufficiently shown that they rightly admit anyone as a counselor on civil matters, because they judge that everyone possesses this virtue. Next, I will try to show you that they do not think virtue is innate or happens by chance, but is acquired through teaching and study. No one is angry at anyone for those evils which they think have happened by nature or by chance. Nor does anyone rebuke, teach, or punish those who are burdened by such evils so that they might not be that way; instead, we all rather pity them, whether they are deformed, small, or sickly. For who is so mindless as to try to do any of those things? They surely understand, I believe, that these evils and their opposites come to men by nature and by chance. On the contrary, when they judge that certain evils have been produced in someone by lack of study or training or teaching, then they are indignant, they rebuke, and they punish. Among their number is injustice, and impiety, and in short, whatever is contrary to civil virtue. Which, therefore, everyone...

<column-break/>

...irrational animals. Finally, the race of humans was still unadorned for him, and he did not know what to do. To him in his difficulty, Prometheus comes to inspect the distribution; and he sees the other animals fittingly provided with everything, but man naked, unshod, unbedded, and unarmed. And already the destined day was present, on which it was necessary for man to go out from the earth into the light. Prometheus, being gripped by the difficulty of finding what salvation he might find for man, steals the technical wisdom of Hephaestus and Athena along with fire (for it was impossible for it to be acquired or useful in any way without fire) and thus gives it as a gift to man. In this way, man possessed the wisdom concerning life; but he did not have political wisdom. For that was with Zeus. <margin>B</margin> And it was no longer permitted for Prometheus to enter the acropolis, the dwelling of Zeus (moreover, the guards of Zeus were fearsome); but he enters secretly into the shared dwelling of Athena and Hephaestus, in which they practiced their arts; and having stolen the fire-art of Hephaestus and the other art of Athena, he gives them to man. From this, the means of life became available to man; but later (as it is told) a trial for theft came upon Prometheus because of Epimetheus. Since man participated in a divine portion, first, because of his kinship with the god, he alone of animals believed in gods, and attempted to establish altars and images of gods. <margin>C</margin> Then he quickly articulated voice and names by his art; and he found dwellings, clothes, shoes, bedding, and food from the earth. Thus prepared at the beginning, men lived scattered, and there were no cities. They were being destroyed, therefore, by the wild beasts, because they were weaker than them in every way. And the demiurgic <note>original: 'δημιουργικὴ' (dēmiourgikē) — the "craft-working" or technical art.</note> art was a sufficient helper to them for food, but for the war against the beasts, it was lacking. For they did not yet have the political art, of which the military is a part. They sought, then, to gather together and be saved by founding cities. When, therefore, they were gathered, they did injustice to one another, because they did not have the political art. So, being scattered again, they were being destroyed. <margin>D</margin> Zeus, then, fearing for our race, lest it should entirely perish, sends Hermes bringing shame and justice to men, so that they might be the ornaments of cities and the gathering bonds of friendship. Hermes therefore asks Zeus in what manner he should give justice and shame to men. "Shall I distribute these in the same way the arts have been distributed? For they are distributed thus: one having the medical art is sufficient for many laypeople, and so with the other craftsmen. Shall I thus place justice and shame among men? Or shall I distribute them to all?" "To all," said Zeus, "and let all participate. For cities would not exist if only a few of them participated, as with the other arts. And set down a law from me: that he who is not able to participate in shame and justice is to be killed as a disease of the city." Thus indeed, Socrates, and for <margin>E</margin> these reasons, both others and the Athenians, when there is a talk about the virtue of carpentry or any other craft, they think only a few have a share in counsel; and if anyone outside the few gives advice, they do not tolerate it, as you say (and reasonably so, as I say). But when they go into a council for political virtue, which must proceed entirely through justice and temperance, they reasonably tolerate every man; as it is fitting for everyone to participate in this virtue, or else there are no cities. This, Socrates, is the cause of this. And so that you do not think you are being deceived that all men truly believe every man participates in justice and the rest of political virtue, take this as a further proof. For in the other virtues <margin>F</margin> (as you say), if someone says he is a good flute-player, or is good at any other art in which he is not, they either laugh at him or are angry, and his relatives come and rebuke him as if he were mad. But in justice and in the rest of political virtue, even if they know someone is unjust, if this man himself says the truth about himself against himself in front of many people—which in the other case they thought was temperance (to speak the truth)—here they think it is madness. And they say that everyone must say they are just, whether they are or not; or else the one who does not pretend to be just is mad. For it is necessary that there is no one who does not participate in it in some way or other, or else he would not be among men. That they reasonably accept every man as a counselor about this virtue, because they <margin>G</margin> believe it belongs to everyone, this is what I say. But that they do not believe it exists by nature, nor from chance, but that it is something taught and comes from care to whomever it comes, this I will try to demonstrate to you next. For as many evils as men believe they have from one another by nature or by chance, no one is angry at these, nor rebukes, nor teaches, nor punishes those who have them, so that they might not be such; rather, they pity them. For example, the ugly, or small, or weak—who is so mindless as to attempt to do any of these things to them? For they know, I think, that these things happen to men by nature and by chance, both the beautiful things and their opposites. But as many good things as they think come to men from care and practice and teaching, <margin>H</margin> if someone does not have these, but instead has the opposite evils, then surely anger occurs, and punishments, and rebukes. Of which one is injustice, and impiety, and in summary, everything contrary to political virtue. Wherefore everyone...

<summary>Protagoras recounts the myth of Prometheus, explaining that while humans have technical skills, they required the divinely-given gifts of justice and shame to form stable societies. He argues that because these virtues are essential for a city to exist, they are expected of all citizens and are therefore treated as subjects of education and social correction.</summary>
<keywords>Prometheus, Epimetheus, Zeus, Hermes, justice, shame, political virtue, civil art, teaching of virtue, Athens</keywords>

--- Page 231 ---
<meta>Continuity: This page continues Protagoras' "Great Speech." In the preceding section, Protagoras told a myth (mythos) about how Prometheus stole fire and the mechanical arts for humanity, and how Zeus later gave humans "shame" and "justice" so they could form cities. Now, Protagoras moves from myth to rational argument (logos) to prove to Socrates that virtue is something that can be taught and learned.</meta>

### PROTAGORAS

<margin>A</margin> He <note>Protagoras is referring to anyone who punishes an injustice.</note> everywhere condemns and reproves, because both wickedness and that civic virtue <note>original: "ἀρετή" (arete). In this context, it refers to the "excellence" required to be a good citizen.</note> proceed from industry and instruction. For if you are willing to consider, Socrates, what the power of punishing the unjust actually means, it will teach you that men believe virtue is something that can be acquired. For no one punishes the unjust simply because they have committed an injustice—unless they are like a beast, striking back irrationally in mere revenge. But one who undertakes to punish with reason does not punish for the sake of the past crime—for what has been done cannot be undone—but looks instead to the future, so that neither the culprit himself nor anyone else who sees him punished will sin again. <margin>B</margin> Anyone who holds this view and punishes with such a purpose clearly believes that virtue can be taught, for he punishes for the sake of deterrence. This is the opinion held by all who take vengeance upon wrongdoers, whether in private or in public. All men punish those they deem to be sinners, and your own fellow citizens, the Athenians, do so most of all. Therefore, it is clear from this reasoning that the Athenians are among those who believe that virtue can be taught and provided through effort. Thus, I have sufficiently demonstrated to you, Socrates—at least as it seems to me—that your citizens are right to accept the advice of a blacksmith or a cobbler on political matters, and that they consider virtue to be something that is taught and prepared.

<margin>C</margin> There remains, however, that doubt you raised regarding great men: why is it that these men teach their sons everything that can be learned from a teacher and make them wise in those things, yet in the specific virtue for which they themselves are famous, they make their sons no better than anyone else? For this, Socrates, I will no longer tell you a myth, but a reasoned argument <note>original: "λόγον" (logon). Protagoras is signaling a shift from storytelling to logical demonstration.</note>. Think of it this way: is there, or is there not, one single thing in which all citizens must participate if a city is to exist at all? For it is here that the solution to your doubt is found, and nowhere else. If there is indeed such a thing, and it is not the craft of the architect, or the blacksmith, or the potter, but rather justice, temperance <note>original: "σωφροσύνη" (sophrosyne), meaning moderation or self-control.</note>, and holiness—and if I may summarize it as the "virtue of a man"—if this is the thing <margin>D</margin> in which everyone must share, and if every man must act according to this (whatever else he wishes to learn or do), and if anyone who lacks it must be taught and corrected—whether child, man, or woman—until they are made better through such correction; and if anyone who does not submit to this punishment and instruction must be driven out of the city as incurable, or even put to death—if this is the case, then consider how strange it would be if good men taught their sons everything else but neglected to teach them this! For we have already shown that they believe virtue can be taught both privately and publicly. <margin>E</margin> Since it can be acquired through teaching and care, do they teach their sons things where the penalty for ignorance is not death, but then fail to teach them the very things where the penalty for their children is death, exile, the confiscation of property, or the total ruin of their houses? You must believe, Socrates, that they do teach them, and with the utmost diligence! Beginning from early childhood and continuing as long as they live, they teach and admonish them. As soon as a child understands what is said, his nurse, mother, tutor, and father all strive toward this one goal: that the child may become as good as possible. In every word and deed, they point out and demonstrate what is just and what is unjust, what is honorable <margin>F</margin> and what is shameful, what is holy and what is profane, what to do and what not to do. If the child obeys, it is well; if not, they straighten him with threats and blows, just as one would straighten a piece of warped and twisted wood.

After this, they send them to schoolmasters, and they charge the teachers to care far more for the good behavior of the children than for their letters or their music. The teachers do exactly this, and once the children have learned their letters and are ready to understand written words (just as they previously understood the spoken voice), the teachers set before them on their benches the works of great poets to read and learn by heart. In these works, there are many moral lessons, many stories, and many praises and encomiums of great men of old, <margin>G</margin> so that the child, being moved by emulation, may imitate them and long to become like them. The lyre players <note>original: "κιθαρισταί" (kitharistai), teachers of the kithara or lyre.</note> also do the same; they attend to temperance and see to it that the youths do nothing wrong. Furthermore, once they have learned to play the lyre, the teachers introduce them to the songs of other great lyric poets, setting these to music for the lyre. They compel the rhythms and harmonies to become familiar to the children’s souls, so that they may become more gentle, more rhythmic, and more harmonious, and thus be useful in both speech and action. For the whole life of man requires a certain rhythm and harmony. After this, parents send their sons to physical trainers <margin>H</margin>, so that by attaining a firm and fit body, they may better serve a virtuous mind, and not be forced to shrink from their duties in war or other actions because of physical weakness. Those who are most able to do this, do so most of all—and those who are most able are the wealthiest. Their sons start attending the schools of teachers at the earliest possible age and leave them the latest. Once they have left the schools, the city...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> He everywhere condemns and reproves the idea that either wickedness or civic virtue arises from anything other than industry and discipline. For if you wish to consider, Socrates, what force the punishment of the unjust has, you will understand from it that men believe virtue is acquired through effort. For no one punishes for the sake of the past, nor does he afflict the unjust with penalties simply because they have done wrong—unless one were to strike blindly like a brute without reason. But he who attempts to punish with reason does not punish because of a past crime (for he cannot make what is done undone), but looks toward the future, so that neither the culprit himself nor any other who is led by his example <margin>B</margin> will sin again. Whoever punishes with this purpose and such a judgment believes that virtue can be acquired through instruction. For he strikes for the sake of deterrence. This is the mindset and opinion with which everyone approaches punishment, both in public and in private life. Everyone punishes those they judge to be sinners, and most especially your fellow Athenian citizens. Therefore, it is established by this reasoning that the Athenians are also among those who believe virtue is taught. From these things, it is clearly shown, Socrates, as I believe, that your citizens do not wrongly accept the advice of blacksmiths and cobblers in civic administration, and that they believe virtue can be acquired through instruction and effort through practice.

<margin>C</margin> There remains that doubt you raised about men famous for virtue: for what reason do they educate their sons in everything that can be obtained from a teacher, yet in what pertains to their father's virtue, they make them no better than anyone else? To this I will bring a reason, Socrates, not a fable. For think of it this way: is there one thing, or is there not, of which it is necessary for all citizens to be participants, if indeed the city is to stand? For in this way your doubt is solved, and otherwise not at all. If this one thing exists, and it is not the craft of architects, nor the art of blacksmiths, nor the work of potters, but justice, temperance, holiness, and, to encompass it in a few words, the virtue proper to a man: if this <margin>D</margin> is, I say, that of which all must be participants, and with this to learn and do whatever else one pleases, but without this nothing at all; and if one who is void of this must be taught and reproved—whether child, man, or woman—until he is made better by correction; and if someone, having been punished and taught, does not obey, he should be driven from the cities or killed as incurable: if it is as we have said, and the prominent citizens in the republic educate their sons in other things, but in this not at all, notice how wonderfully they turn out to be excellent in that regard! For we have shown that they believe it can be taught both privately and publicly. <margin>E</margin> Since it can be acquired by both instruction and care, they teach their sons other things in which no death penalty is proposed for the ignorant; but in those things where death is the penalty for their children, as well as exile, and for those who are neither educated nor cultivated in virtue, and besides death, the confiscation of goods, and in short, the overturning of families—do they not teach these, nor apply all diligence and effort? It is right to think so, Socrates, that from tender years until the end of life they are instructed and admonished. For as soon as a child understands what is said, the nurse, mother, tutor, and father strive with all care and effort toward this: that the child might turn out best in every word and deed. Individually they show what is just, what is unjust, what is <margin>F</margin> honorable, what is base, what is holy, or what is profane, what is to be done, and what not. If the child obeys these things, they think it goes well; but if he resists, then they direct him with threats and blows like a warped and crooked piece of wood. After this, they hand the children over to be cared for by schoolmasters, and they demand from the masters a diligence for good behavior much more than for the teaching of letters and the lyre. The teachers, having taken them up, care for and cultivate them. And when they have learned their letters, they turn to understanding written things; they set before them to be read and learned the works of especially excellent poets, in which there are very many warnings, <margin>G</margin> and the deeds of ancient men outstanding in virtue are praised, so that the child, kindled by emulation, may imitate the noble deeds of his ancestors. Lyre players also study other things of this kind, especially temperance, and take care that the youths do nothing wrong. And when they have learned to strike the lyre, they again teach the songs of other poets outstanding in melody, which they sing to the lyre, and they strive to harmonize rhythms and melodies to the souls of the boys, so that having been made more gentle, modest, and harmonious, they might be useful both for acting and for speaking. For every life of man requires a certain rhythmic consonance. After this, parents send their sons to <margin>H</margin> masters of the gyms, so that having obtained a firm and fit habit of body, they might offer ministry to an excellent mind, lest they be forced to shrink back in wars and other actions, hindered by the fragility of their bodies. These things are observed most by those who are most able: and those most able are the wealthy—

<summary>Protagoras argues that the practice of punishment proves virtue is teachable, as its purpose is future deterrence rather than past revenge. He explains that education—from family guidance to school literature, music, and gymnastics—is a continuous social process designed to instill civic virtue in every citizen.</summary>
<keywords>deterrence, punishment, civic virtue, education, justice, temperance, harmony, Athenian assembly, Plato, Protagoras</keywords>

<meta>Continuity: This page continues Protagoras' "Great Speech" to Socrates. Having previously used a myth to show that all humans possess a sense of justice, Protagoras now uses rational arguments (logos) and analogies—such as children learning to write and the socialization of flute-players—to prove that virtue is taught by the entire community through laws and education.</meta>

# OF PLATO

### PROTAGORAS

...are they <note>Young citizens of the city.</note> compelled to learn the laws and live according to their example? It is so they do not act rashly by relying only on their own natural wit. Just as writing masters prescribe a certain model with a pen for boys who do not yet know how to write, and hand them the tablet, commanding them to imitate the trace of the letters as they write: so the city, prescribing laws—the inventions of the most prudent men of old who established them—compels everyone to rule and be ruled according to their standard. Furthermore, the city punishes those who wander from these laws. This punishment is called, both among you and many others, "corrections" or "rectifications," as if justice herself were setting things straight, which are termed <term>εὐθύναι</term> <note>original: "euthunai." In Athens, this specifically referred to the "accounting" or examination a magistrate underwent at the end of his term.</note>. Since there is such great care for virtue both privately and publicly, do you still doubt, O Socrates, and wonder if virtue can be taught? Indeed, no one ought to wonder at this; rather, it would be much more surprising if it could *not* be taught. 

Why then are the sons of good fathers often found to be wicked? Learn this, for it should not seem strange if what I have said is true: namely, that the care for virtue must belong not to one person alone, but to everyone, if a city is to endure. If it is as I say—and it certainly is—choose and consider any of the other skills or teachings. Suppose, for example, that a city could not exist unless we were all flute-players. If every person taught this skill to everyone else, both privately and publicly, and rebuked those who played poorly without any feeling of envy—just as now everyone proclaims what is just and lawful without envy, and does not hide these things as they might other crafts (for I believe the justice and virtue of others is profitable to us all)—if, then, we all most willingly showed everyone else what is just and lawful, and if we were to instruct each other in playing the flute with this same eagerness and charity, do you think, Socrates, that the sons of the best flute-players would turn out better than the sons of the worst? Not at all, I think. Rather, whoever was naturally gifted at the flute would make progress, and whoever was slow would make less; and often the son of a skilled player would turn out unskilled, while the son of an unskilled player would turn out gifted. Nevertheless, all of them would be sufficient flute-players compared to those who are totally ignorant of the art. 

In the same way, Socrates, you must consider that the man who seems the most unjust to you among those living under the law would be seen as just and a champion of right if he were compared to men who have neither education, nor courts, nor laws, nor any necessity in life to compel them to cultivate virtue. They would be savages, like those whom the poet Pherecrates brought on stage last year at the Lenaia <note>An Athenian festival involving dramatic competitions.</note>. If you were to fall among such men—those who hate humanity—you would think yourself well-off if you met even Eurybatus or Phrynondas <note>Two notoriously wicked men often mentioned in Greek comedy as the height of villainy.</note>, and you would bewail your luck, longing for the "wickedness" of our own people. But now you seem quite spoiled, Socrates, because everyone is a teacher of virtue to the best of their ability, and yet no one appears to be such a teacher to you. It is as if you were to ask who taught us to speak Greek; no one specific teacher would appear. Similarly, if you sought a teacher for the sons of craftsmen—someone to teach them the very craft they learned from their father and his fellow artisans—it would not be easy to find a single instructor, Socrates, though for those totally ignorant of the craft, it would be easy. 

So it must be said of virtue and other such things. We should think ourselves satisfied if someone can advance us even a little further toward virtue than others. Of these men, I profess to be one; I believe I know how to help a person become good and honorable more skillfully than other men, and in a way that is worthy of the fee I ask—indeed, even a greater fee, as my students themselves judge. This is the condition of my payment: after someone has learned from me, if he is willing, he pays the silver I demand. If not, he goes into a temple, takes an oath, and declares how much he thinks my lessons were worth, and pays that amount. 

Thus, Socrates, I have proven to you with both a story and a rational argument that virtue can be taught and learned. The Athenians themselves testify to this. We have also shown that it should not seem surprising if the sons of good fathers are wicked, or the sons of wicked fathers are good. Even the sons of the sculptor Polyclitus <note>A famous Greek sculptor of the 5th century BCE.</note>, who are the same age as Paralus and Xanthippus here, are nothing compared to their father; and the same is true of the sons of other craftsmen. But we should not yet condemn these young men, for they still offer some hope, being young.

When Protagoras had shown these and similar things, he made an end of speaking. But for a long time afterward, as if spellbound by his speech, I continued to gaze at him, longing to hear more. But when I perceived that he had truly finished, I finally recovered myself with some effort and, turning to Hippocrates, I said: "O son of Apollodorus, how great are the thanks I owe you for bringing me here today! For I value very highly having heard these things from Protagoras. Previously, I did not think it was through human care that good men become good, but now I am persuaded. Yet a small doubt remains which troubles me, which Protagoras will surely clear up easily, since he has explained so much already. For if one were to discuss these same things with any of our public orators, one might hear such speeches as Pericles or other capable speakers are accustomed to give."

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> "The city, in turn, compels them to learn the laws and to live according to them as a model, so that they do not act at random on their own, but strictly—just as writing masters, for those children not yet clever at writing, trace lines with the stylus and then give them the tablet, compelling them to write according to the guidance of those lines. So too the city, having traced out laws—the inventions of good and ancient lawgivers—compels them both to rule and be ruled according to these. Whoever goes outside of these, it punishes; and the name for this punishment, both among you and elsewhere in many places, <margin>B</margin> since justice keeps one straight, is 'straightenings' [accountings]. Since there is so much care concerning virtue both privately and publicly, do you wonder, Socrates, and are you at a loss as to whether virtue is teachable? But you should not wonder; rather, it would be much more a wonder if it were not teachable. Why then do many sons of good fathers turn out poorly? Learn this in turn. For it is nothing to wonder at, if what I said before was true: that for this thing, virtue, if a city is to exist, no one must be a private person [an amateur] in it. For if what I say is so (and it is so most of all things), consider it by choosing any other pursuit or study. For example, if what I say is true, it would not be possible for a city to exist unless we were all flute-players, each as he was able, and everyone taught this to everyone else both privately and publicly, and rebuked the one who did not play well, and did not begrudge <margin>C</margin> this—just as now no one begrudges or hides what is just and lawful, as they do with other crafts. For it is profitable for us, I think, that there be justice and virtue among one another. Because of this, everyone tells and teaches everyone else what is just and lawful with great eagerness. If, therefore, we also had all this eagerness and lack of grudge in teaching one another flute-playing, do you think, Socrates," he said, "that the sons of good flute-players would turn out to be good flute-players any more than the sons of poor ones? I think not. But whoever's son happened to be most naturally gifted for flute-playing, he would grow up to be famous; and whoever was <margin>D</margin> ungifted, would be without fame. Often the son of a good flute-player would turn out poor, and often the son of a poor one, good. But at any rate, they would all be sufficient flute-players compared to private persons who know nothing of flute-playing. In this way, think also now: whoever seems to you the most unjust man of those brought up in laws and human society, he is a just man and a craftsman of this thing, if he had to be judged against men who have neither education, nor courts, nor laws, nor any necessity whatsoever compelling them to care for virtue—but if they were some kind of savages, such as the poet Pherecrates taught [brought on stage] last year at the Lenaia. Surely, if you were to find yourself among such men, like the man-haters in that chorus, you would be glad if you happened upon Eurybatus and Phrynondas, and you would wail with longing <margin>E</margin> for the wickedness of the people here. But now you are spoiled, Socrates, because everyone is a teacher of virtue, as far as each is able, and yet no one appears so to you. It is as if you were to seek who is a teacher of the Greek language; not a single one would appear. Nor, I think, if you sought who would teach the sons of our craftsmen that very craft which they have learned from their father, so far as the father and the father's friends who are fellow craftsmen were able—who would still teach these? It is not easy, I think, Socrates, for a teacher of these to appear, but for those who are completely unskilled, it is easy. So it is with virtue and all other things. But if there is someone who <margin>F</margin> excels us even a little in leading us toward virtue, it is something to be welcomed. Of these men, I think I am one, and I would benefit someone more than other men toward becoming noble and good, and worthily of the fee which I charge—and even more, so that it seems so even to the student himself. Because of this, I have made the manner of the transaction of the fee like this: when someone has learned from me, if he wishes, he pays the silver I charge; but if not, he goes to a temple and, having sworn an oath as to how much he says the lessons are worth, he pays that much. Such, Socrates, is the story and the argument I have told you, to show that virtue is teachable, and the Athenians think so too; and that it is nothing to wonder at that good <margin>G</margin> fathers have poor sons, and poor fathers, good ones. Since even the sons of Polyclitus, the age-mates of Paralus and Xanthippus here, are nothing compared to their father, and so with the sons of other craftsmen. But it is not yet right to accuse these of that, for there are still hopes in them. For they are young." Protagoras, having displayed so many and such things, ceased from his speech. And I, for a long time, having been charmed, still looked at him as if he were going to say something, desiring to hear. But when I perceived that he had truly stopped, I somehow with difficulty gathered myself together and said, looking toward Hippocrates: "O son of Apollodorus, how I thank you that you urged me to come here. For I set great value on having heard what I heard from Protagoras. For I, in the time before this, thought that there was no human care by which <margin>H</margin> good men become good; but now I am persuaded. Except for a small thing in my way, which clearly Protagoras will easily explain, since he has explained these many things. For if someone were to meet with any of the public speakers about these same things, he might hear such speeches as from Pericles, or some other of those capable of speaking..."

<summary>Protagoras concludes his "Great Speech," arguing that virtue is taught by the whole of society through laws and social expectations, much like a native language. Socrates, though impressed, prepares to challenge Protagoras with a specific question about the unity of virtue.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: Following Protagoras’s "Great Speech" on how virtue is taught through social pressure and law, Socrates now begins his cross-examination (dialectic). He starts by praising Protagoras’s eloquence but notes a specific confusion regarding the nature of virtue itself.</meta>

# P R O T A G O R A S.

->A<-

...of eloquent men: but if one persists in questioning them further, like books, they have nothing to answer and no questions of their own to ask. If one asks even a small question about what has been said, like struck bronze which rings long and loud unless someone catches hold of it, these orators, when asked a brief question, draw out a long race of a speech. But Protagoras here is capable of speaking long and beautifully, as his previous speech shows, and is also capable, when questioned, of responding briefly and in summary. When he himself questions, he is able to wait and receive the answer—qualities found in few men. Now, therefore, Protagoras, I am in need of one small thing to have everything clear, if you would answer me this: you say that virtue is something that can be taught. And I, if I am to believe any man, believe you. 

->B<-

But there is something you said that I wondered at; I pray you, satisfy my soul on this point. <margin>He repeats certain sayings of Protagoras in order to convict him.</margin> For you said that Zeus sent justice and shame <note>original Greek: "αἰδῶ" (aidos) – a sense of shame or moral respect</note> to mankind. Then, as your speech proceeded, you frequently named justice, temperance, and holiness, as if all these were contained under one single thing called virtue, and that virtue itself is some one thing. I would like this explained clearly to me: is virtue some one thing, of which justice, temperance, and holiness are parts? Or are these things I have just mentioned merely names for one and the same existing thing? This is what I still desire to know. 
**PROTAGORAS:** That is an easy thing to answer, Socrates: virtue is indeed one thing, and the things you ask about are its parts. 

->C<-

**SOCRATES:** Are they parts in the way that the parts of a face are parts—the mouth, the nose, the eyes, and the ears? Or are they like the parts of gold, which do not differ from each other or from the whole, except in size and smallness? 
**PROTAGORAS:** It seems to me, Socrates, that they relate to virtue as the parts of the face relate to the whole face. 
**SOCRATES:** Do men, then, partake in these parts of virtue, some having one and some another? Or is it necessary that if a man possesses one, he must possess them all? 
**PROTAGORAS:** By no means, since 

->D<-

many are brave, yet unjust; and others are just, yet not at all wise. 
**SOCRATES:** Are wisdom and courage also parts of virtue? 
**PROTAGORAS:** Most certainly of all, and wisdom is the most excellent part of them all. 
**SOCRATES:** And is each of these something different from the others? 
**PROTAGORAS:** Yes. 
**SOCRATES:** Does each also have its own private power? Just as with the parts of the face, the eye is not like the ears, nor is its power the same; nor is any other part like another in power or in any other way. Is it the same with the parts of virtue, so that one is not like the other, neither in itself nor in its power? Is it not clear that it must be so, if it follows our example? 
**PROTAGORAS:** It is certainly so, Socrates. 

->E<-

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, no other part of virtue is like knowledge, nor like justice, nor like courage, nor like temperance, nor like holiness. 
**PROTAGORAS:** Certainly not. 
**SOCRATES:** Come then, let us consider together what sort of thing each of these is. First, like this: is justice a "thing," or no thing at all? To me it seems to be a thing. What do you think? 
**PROTAGORAS:** I think so too. 
**SOCRATES:** What then? If someone were to ask you and me: "Protagoras and Socrates, tell me please, this thing you just named, justice—is this thing itself just or unjust?" I would answer him that it is just. How would you cast your vote? The same as mine, or different? 
**PROTAGORAS:** The same. 

->F<-

**SOCRATES:** I would answer the questioner that justice is of such a nature as to be just; would you not also? 
**PROTAGORAS:** Yes. 
**SOCRATES:** If he then asked us: "Do you also say there is such a thing as holiness?" we would say yes, I suppose. 
**PROTAGORAS:** We would. 
**SOCRATES:** "And do you say this is also a 'thing'?" we would say yes, would we not? 
**PROTAGORAS:** We would. 
**SOCRATES:** "And do you think the nature of this thing is such as to be holy, or unholy?" I would be indignant at the question and say: "Watch your words, sir! How could anything else be holy if holiness itself were not holy?" What about you? Would you not answer the same? 
**PROTAGORAS:** Certainly. 
**SOCRATES:** If he then asked: "What was it you were saying a moment ago? Did I not hear you correctly? You seemed to say that the parts of virtue were so related to one another that one was not like the other." I would say to him: "You heard the rest correctly, but you are mistaken if you think *I* said that. For it was Protagoras here who answered, and I who only asked." If he then said: "Is he speaking the truth, 

->G<-

Protagoras? Do you say that one part of virtue is not like the other? Is this your statement?" What would you answer him? 
**PROTAGORAS:** I must necessarily admit it, Socrates. 
**SOCRATES:** Having admitted this, Protagoras, what shall we answer him if he asks further: "Is holiness then not of the nature of a just thing, nor justice of the nature of a holy thing? Is holiness then something 'not-just,' and justice something 'not-holy'? Is justice therefore unholy, and holiness unjust?" What shall we answer? For my own part, I would say that justice is holy and holiness is just. And for you, if you would let me, I would answer the same: that justice is either the same thing as holiness, or as similar as possible; and above all, that justice is like holiness, and holiness like justice. See if you would forbid me to answer this, or if you agree? 

->H<-

**PROTAGORAS:** It does not seem to me quite so simple, Socrates, that I can grant that holiness is just...

<summary>Socrates begins his cross-examination of Protagoras, questioning whether the various virtues (justice, wisdom, temperance, etc.) are distinct parts like the features of a face or unified like pieces of gold. Protagoras argues they are distinct, leading Socrates to a logical paradox regarding the relationship between justice and holiness.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: Following the previous page where Socrates began questioning Protagoras on whether the different virtues (justice, temperance, holiness, etc.) are distinct parts or one single thing, they are now debating the specific relationship between justice and holiness.</meta>

# PLATO

<page-num>202</page-num>

...or that justice is holy. But a certain difference seems to be present; yet what does that matter? If you wish, let holiness be just for us, and justice be holy. **SOCRATES:** Not for me, however. I have no need for this "if you wish" or "if it pleases you" to be the basis of our proof; rather, I want "you and me" to be the basis. By saying "you and me," I believe the argument is best examined if we remove that "if" from it. **PROTAGORAS:** Indeed, justice bears some resemblance to holiness. For in some way, anything resembles anything else. Even white resembles black in some respect, and hard resembles soft—and so too with other things that appear to be complete opposites. Even those things which we said before have different powers, <margin>B</margin> and where one is not like the other—such as the parts of a face—do have some resemblance to each other and are, in a certain way, like one another. By this reasoning, you could refute these points if you liked, on the grounds that all things are similar to one another. However, it is not right to call things "similar" just because they have some point of similarity, nor "dissimilar" if they have some point of dissimilarity, even if the similarity is very small. **SOCRATES:** I am surprised, Protagoras, if you think justice and holiness are related to each other in such a way that they have only a small resemblance. **PROTAGORAS:** Not entirely so, yet not exactly as you seem to think, either. **SOCRATES:** Since this topic seems to trouble you, let us set it aside; let us consider another of the things <margin>C</margin> you were saying. Do you call "folly" <note>original Latin: "insania"; Greek: "ἀφροσύνη" (aphrosyne) – lack of wisdom or senselessness</note> a certain thing? and do you say wisdom is its opposite? **PROTAGORAS:** I do. **SOCRATES:** Now, when men act rightly and usefully, do you think they act temperately <note>original Latin: "temperanter"; Greek: "σωφρονεῖν" (sophronein) – acting with self-control or sound-mindedness</note> in so doing, <margin>Interrogations through related terms and opposites, to prove that one thing has one opposite.</margin> or the opposite of how they should act? **PROTAGORAS:** They seem to me to act temperately when they act usefully and rightly. **SOCRATES:** And do they not act temperately by means of temperance? **PROTAGORAS:** Necessarily. **SOCRATES:** And do not those who act wrongly act foolishly, and in so acting, fail to act temperately? **PROTAGORAS:** So it seems. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, acting foolishly is the opposite of acting temperately. **PROTAGORAS:** It is indeed. **SOCRATES:** Then are not things done foolishly done by folly? and things done temperately, by temperance? <margin>D</margin> **PROTAGORAS:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** And whatever is done by strength, is it not done strongly? and whatever by weakness, weakly? **PROTAGORAS:** It appears so. **SOCRATES:** And whatever with speed, speedily? and whatever with slowness, slowly? **PROTAGORAS:** This too. **SOCRATES:** And that which is done in the same way is produced by the same cause? while that done in an opposite way is produced by an opposite cause? **PROTAGORAS:** I agree. **SOCRATES:** Tell me, then, is there such a thing as "the beautiful"? **PROTAGORAS:** There is indeed. **SOCRATES:** Is there any opposite to this other than "the ugly"? **PROTAGORAS:** Nothing else. **SOCRATES:** And is there something called "the good"? **PROTAGORAS:** There is. **SOCRATES:** And is there any other opposite <margin>E</margin> to it except "the evil"? **PROTAGORAS:** No other. **SOCRATES:** And in the voice, is there a "high pitch"? **PROTAGORAS:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** Is there any opposite to it other than "low pitch"? **PROTAGORAS:** That is the one. **SOCRATES:** Does not each of these opposites have only one opposite, and not many? **PROTAGORAS:** Only one. **SOCRATES:** Let us then recap what we have conceded so far. We have clearly conceded that for one thing there is only one opposite, and not more. **PROTAGORAS:** Truly. **SOCRATES:** Likewise, that what is done in an opposite way is produced by opposites. **PROTAGORAS:** This also. **SOCRATES:** Furthermore, we admitted that what is done foolishly is done in an opposite way to what is done temperately. **PROTAGORAS:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** And again, that what is acted temperately comes from temperance, <margin>F</margin> and what is acted foolishly comes from folly. **PROTAGORAS:** It is agreed. **SOCRATES:** Now, if it is done in an opposite way, must it not be done by an opposite? **PROTAGORAS:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** But one is done by temperance, the other by folly. **PROTAGORAS:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** In an opposite way? **PROTAGORAS:** In an opposite way. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, they are done by opposites? **PROTAGORAS:** Yes, by opposites. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, folly is the opposite of temperance? **PROTAGORAS:** It appears so. **SOCRATES:** Do we remember that we previously conceded that folly was the opposite of wisdom? **PROTAGORAS:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** And that for one thing there is only one opposite? **PROTAGORAS:** This too. **SOCRATES:** Which of these arguments, then, shall we reject, Protagoras? The one stating that one thing has only one opposite? Or the one that claimed wisdom differs from temperance, even though both were parts of virtue? And further, that they were not only distinct but also dissimilar in themselves and their powers, just like the parts of a face? <margin>G</margin> Which of these shall we refute? For the two statements together do not sound very harmonious; they do not chime or fit with one another. For how can they chime if it is necessary for one thing to have only one opposite and no more, yet for Folly—which is one—both Wisdom and Temperance appear to be its opposites? Is it so, Protagoras, or otherwise? **PROTAGORAS:** Let it be so, then; what follows? **SOCRATES:** By this reasoning, would not wisdom and temperance be one thing? Just as before, justice and holiness appeared to be roughly the same thing. Come now, Protagoras, do not grow weary, but let us proceed to the rest. Does an unjust man, in the act of doing injustice, seem to you to be acting temperately <margin>H</margin> and wisely? **PROTAGORAS:** I would not dare to confess this, Socrates, though many people assert it. **SOCRATES:** Shall I direct my words to them, then, or to you? **PROTAGORAS:** If you please, discuss this common opinion of the crowd first. **SOCRATES:** It makes no difference to me, provided that you yourself answer whether this seems true to you or not. For it is the argument itself that I am primarily examining. And that which happens through my questioning and your answering is perhaps incidental. — At this, Protagoras first showed off by complaining about the difficulty of the argument, but afterward he agreed to answer. — Come then, I said, answer me from the beginning. Do some people seem to you to be temperate while acting unjustly? **PROTAGORAS:** Let it be so. **SOCRATES:** And to be temperate is to be well-minded? **PROTAGORAS:** It is. **SOCRATES:** And to be well...

<column-break/>

<margin>Α</margin>...to separate justice, as much as he said, from holiness, saying it is "just." But he said, "Something in it seems to me to be different. But what does this matter?" he asked. "If you wish, let justice be holy for us, and holiness be just." "Not for me," I said. "For I have no need to have this 'if you wish' and 'if it seems so to you' refuted, but rather myself and you. And by 'myself and you,' I mean this: I think the argument would be best examined if someone took the 'if' away from it." "But truly," he said, "justice bears some resemblance to holiness. For indeed anything resembles anything else in some way or other. For white resembles black in some way, and hard resembles soft, and the other things that seem to be most opposite to each other. And those things which we said then had different powers, <margin>Β</margin> and that one was not like the other—the parts of the face—they resemble each other in some way, and one is like the other. So in this way you could refute these things, if you wished, on the grounds that all things are like each other. But it is not right to call things 'similar' that have some point of similarity, nor 'dissimilar' those that have some point of dissimilarity, even if the similarity is very small." And I, wondering, said to him, "Do justice and holiness really stand in such a relation to each other for you, that they have only some small similarity to each other?" "Not quite like that," he said, "but not again as you seem to think I mean." "Well then," I said, "since you seem <margin>Γ</margin> to be uneasy about this, let us let it go. But let us look at this other thing you were saying. What do you call 'folly'? Do you think wisdom is the opposite of this?" "I do," he said. "And when men act correctly and profitably, do they then seem to you to be temperate in acting so, or the opposite of how they acted?" "To be temperate," he said. "Do they not act temperately by temperance?" "Necessarily." "And those who do not act correctly act foolishly, and are not temperate in acting so?" "I agree," he said. "Then acting foolishly is the opposite of acting temperately?" He said yes. "Then things done foolishly are done by folly, and those <margin>Δ</margin> done temperately are done by temperance?" He agreed. "Then if something is done by strength, it is done strongly? and if by weakness, weakly?" He said yes. "And if something is done with speed, quickly? and if with slowness, slowly?" He said yes. "And if something is done in the same way, it is done by the same cause? and if in an opposite way, by an opposite cause?" He agreed. "Come then," I said, "is there something called 'the beautiful'?" He conceded. "Is there any opposite to this except 'the ugly'?" "There is not." "What then? Is there something called 'the good'?" "There is." "Is there any opposite to this except 'the evil'?" "There is not." "What then? Is there a 'high pitch' in the voice?" He said yes. "Is there any other opposite to this except 'the low'?" He said no. "Therefore," <margin>Ε</margin> I said, "to each of the opposites there is only one opposite, and not many?" He agreed. "Come then," I said, "let us recount what we have agreed upon. We agreed that one thing has only one opposite, and not more. We agreed. And that which is done foolishly is done in an opposite way. He said yes. And we agreed that what is done foolishly is done in an opposite way to what is done temperately. He said yes. And that which is done temperately is done by temperance, and what is done foolishly is done by folly. He conceded. Therefore, if it is done in an opposite way, it would be done by an opposite?" "Yes." "And one is done by temperance, and the other by folly?" "Yes." "In an opposite way?" "Quite so." "Therefore, by things that are opposites?" "Yes." "Therefore, folly is the opposite of temperance?" "It appears so." "Do you remember then that in what went before, it was agreed by us that folly is the opposite of wisdom?" He agreed. "And that one thing has only one opposite?" "I say so." "Which then, Protagoras, <margin>Ϛ</margin> shall we let go of? The argument that one thing has only one opposite, or that other one in which it was said that temperance is different from wisdom? And that each was a part of virtue? And besides being different, they were also unlike, both themselves and their powers, just like the parts of the face? Which then shall we let go of? For these two arguments are not stated in a very musical <note>original Greek: "μουσικῶς" (mousikos) – here meaning harmoniously or properly</note> way. For they do not chime together nor fit with each other. For how could they chime, if indeed it is necessary that for one thing there is only one opposite and not more, yet for Folly—being one—Wisdom and Temperance again appear as opposites? Is it so, Protagoras," I said, "or some other way?" He agreed, and very much against his will. "Therefore temperance and wisdom would be one thing? And before, justice and holiness <margin>Ζ</margin> appeared to us to be almost the same thing. Come then," I said, "Protagoras, let us not grow weary, but let us look into the rest. Does a man who acts unjustly seem to you to be temperate because he acts unjustly?" "I would be ashamed, Socrates," he said, "to agree to this; although many people say it." "Then shall I make the argument to them," I said, "or to you?" "If you wish," he said, "discuss this argument of the many first." "But it makes no difference to me, if only you will answer, whether these things seem so to you or not. For it is the argument that I am especially examining; however, it happens perhaps that both I the questioner and the one answering are being examined." At first <margin>Η</margin> Protagoras was making himself look grand <note>original Greek: "ἐκαλλωπίζετο" (ekallōpizeto) – to preen or give oneself airs</note> for us (for he was complaining that the argument was difficult), but then he conceded to answer. "Come then," I said, "answer me from the beginning. Do some people seem to you to be temperate when acting unjustly?" "Let it be so," he said. "And to be temperate is to be well-minded?" "He said yes." "And to be well-minded is to deliberate well..."

<summary>In this passage, Socrates uses logical deduction to force Protagoras to admit that different virtues, such as wisdom and temperance, may actually be the same thing, because they share the same opposite (folly). The dialogue highlights the tension between Protagoras’s view of virtues as distinct skills and Socrates’s pursuit of a unified moral truth.</summary>

-># PROTAGORAS. 203<-

<margin>A</margin> ...do they act wisely <note>The Greek term is "sophronein," which implies being of sound mind or acting with self-control</note> when they do wrong? "Let it be so," he said. "And do they act wisely," I asked, "if they fare well by doing wrong, or if they fare ill?" "If they fare well." "Do you then say that certain things are good?" "I do." "Then," I asked, "are those things good which are useful to humans?" "Indeed, by Zeus," he said, "I call things good even if they are not useful to humans."

And it seemed to me that Protagoras was already getting annoyed and starting to struggle, being prepared to resist in his answering. Therefore, seeing him in this state, I was cautious and asked him gently: "Protagoras, do you mean things that are useful to no human being, or things that are not useful at all? Do you call such things as these 'good'?" "By no means," he said. "But I,

<margin>B</margin> <margin>The sophist wanders.</margin> certainly know of many things that are useless to humans—foods, drinks, medicines, and a thousand other things—yet some are useful. Some are neither useful nor harmful to humans, but are so for horses; others only for oxen, and others for dogs. Some are useful for none of these, but rather for trees. Even among things for trees, some are good for the roots but harmful for the shoots. For instance, dung is a good thing when applied to the roots of all plants, but if you were to throw it upon the young branches and twigs, it destroys everything. Even oil is extremely bad for all plants and most hostile to the hair of all animals except for man. For the hair of man, it is a remedy, as it is for the rest of his body. Good is such a diverse and multifaceted thing that even here, it is a good thing for a man on the outside of his body,

<margin>C</margin> but the very same thing is most wicked for the internal parts. Because of this, all physicians forbid the sick from using oil, except in the smallest amounts in the foods they are about to eat—just enough to quench the unpleasantness that arises through the senses of the nose in foods and side-dishes."

When he had said these things, those present shouted their approval, saying he had spoken well. And I said: "Protagoras, I happen to be a forgetful sort of person; and if someone speaks to me at great length, I forget what the argument is about. Just as if I happened to be hard of hearing, you would think it necessary, if you intended to converse with me, to speak louder than to others; so now, since you have met a forgetful man, shorten your answers for me and make them briefer, if I am to follow you."

<margin>D</margin> "How then do you bid me to answer briefly? Shall I answer more briefly," he asked, "than is necessary?" "By no means," I said. "But as much as is necessary?" he asked. "Yes," I said. "Then shall I answer as briefly as *I* think is necessary, or as *you* do?" "I have heard," I said, "that you are able, both yourself and to teach another, to speak about the same things at great length if you wish, so that the speech never fails; or again so briefly that no one could say it in fewer words than you. If, therefore, you are going to converse with me, use the other method with me: brevity."

"Socrates," he said, "I have already come into many contests of words with men; and if I had done what you bid me—if I had conversed as my opponent commanded me—I would have appeared no better than anyone else, and the name of Protagoras would not be known among the Greeks."

<margin>E</margin> And I (for I realized that he was not pleased with his previous answers, and that he would not be willing to converse by answering of his own accord) thought it was no longer my business to be present at the gathering. "But truly, Protagoras," I said, "I do not stubbornly insist that our meeting happen contrary to what seems best to you; but whenever you wish to converse in such a way that I can follow, then I will converse with you. For you, as it is said of you and as you say yourself, are capable of meeting in both long speech and brevity—for you are a wise man—but I am unable to handle these long speeches, though I wish I were capable of it. But it was for you, who are capable of both, to yield to us, so that a conversation could take place.

<margin>F</margin> But now, since you are not willing, and I have some business and would not be able to remain with you while you stretch out long speeches (for I must go somewhere), I am leaving. Otherwise, I might have listened to these things of yours not without pleasure."

And as I said this, I stood up as if to depart; and as I was rising, Callias grabbed my right hand with his, and with his left he took hold of this old cloak <note>original Greek: "tribon"; a coarse, simple cloak worn by philosophers</note> of mine. And he said: "We will not let you go, Socrates! For if you leave, our dialogues will not be the same. I beg you, therefore, to stay with us; for I would not listen to anyone more gladly than you and Protagoras conversing. Do us all a favor."

<margin>G</margin> And I said (for I had already stood up to go): "O son of Hipponicus, I have always admired your love of wisdom, and now I praise and love it; so I would wish to do you a favor, if you asked of me things that were possible. But now it is as if you asked me to follow Crison of Himera <note>A famous Olympic runner known for his incredible speed</note>, a runner in his prime, or to keep pace and run with one of the long-distance runners or day-runners. I would tell you that I wish I could follow these runners even more than you do; but I cannot. But if you want to see me and Crison running in the same place, ask him to slow down. For I cannot run fast, but he can run slowly. If, therefore, you desire to hear me and Protagoras, ask him, just as he first answered me in brief and to the point of the questions,

<margin>H</margin> to answer in that way now. Otherwise, what will be the manner of our dialogue? For I thought that meeting together to converse with one another was a different thing from making a public speech."

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...or to be wise in that which others commit injury? <note>Translation of Latin: "autẽ ſapere conſulere in eo, in quo cæteri iniuriam exercent?"</note> **PROTAGORAS:** Let it be so. **SOCRATES:** Whether if they do well because they do injury, or if badly? **PROTAGORAS:** If well. **SOCRATES:** Do you say certain things are good? **PROTAGORAS:** I do. **SOCRATES:** Are those things good which are useful to men? **PROTAGORAS:** Nay, by Jove, I call certain things good, even if they are not useful to men. **SOCRATES:** But when it seemed to me that Protagoras was becoming angry and was descending to the answer unwillingly, I asked everything cautiously and step-by-step. "Do you mean, Protagoras, things which are useful to no man, or things which are in no way useful? And do you call such things good?" **PROTAGORAS:** Not at all. But I know many things that are useless to men: foods, drinks, medicines, and many other things;

<margin>B</margin> <margin>The sophist wanders.</margin> but others are useful. Some things which are the same for humans, bring a great weight of benefit to horses. And some to oxen only, some to dogs; some indeed to none of these, but rather to trees. And of those things for trees, some are such that they often benefit the roots but harm the shoots. Just as dung is useful to roots, but is quite noxious to the little branches and tender shoots. Oil also is most beneficial to all trees and herbs; but to the hair of all animals, human hair excepted, it is most harmful. For it benefits both the hair of men and the whole body. And so "the good" exists as a varied and multiform thing. Whence oil is best for the external parts of our body,

<margin>C</margin> but worst for the interior parts. For this reason, all doctors forbid the use of oil to the sick, nor do they permit them to use it, except very sparingly to reject the offensiveness of certain foul-smelling meats. When Protagoras had said these things, those present shouted with frequent applause, approving his words. But I said: "O Protagoras, I am indeed too forgetful, and if anyone protracts a speech into length, I immediately forget what the words are about. Truly, if I were somewhat deaf and you were to enter into conversation with me, you would think it necessary to shout louder to me than to others; so in the present case, since you speak to a forgetful man, act with more concise responses with me, if only you wish for me to follow you."

<margin>D</margin> **PROTAGORAS:** What brevity do you demand? Do you bid me to act with you in fewer words than is proper? **SOCRATES:** Not at all. **PROTAGORAS:** Or perhaps with as many words as are needed? **SOCRATES:** Exactly so. **PROTAGORAS:** Shall I then impose a limit on the speech by my own judgment, or will you rather establish the due boundary? **SOCRATES:** I have heard indeed that you are able to speak copiously whenever it is pleasing, so that speech never fails you, and also to touch upon the same things in fewer words than any mortal; and that you can teach that very power to others, as I hear. If therefore you are going to dispute with me, use I pray that brief and concise way of speaking. **PROTAGORAS:** O Socrates, I have long ago contended in speaking with many men. But if I had done what you advise—if, I say, I had spoken according to the rule prescribed to me by the listener—I would be no better than anyone else,

<margin>E</margin> nor would the name of Protagoras resound throughout all Greece. But I, when I realized that the previous mode of answering did not please Protagoras at all, and that he would by no means answer that way of his own will, judged it was by no means expedient for me to be present at those disputes; and therefore I said: "O Protagoras, I do not demand that we dispute together contrary to what is convenient for you; but if you wish to discourse so that I can follow, I will indeed stand by. For you indeed, as it is said of you and as you yourself profess, are equally able to both touch on things summarily and to discourse most amply; for you are a wise man. I, however, am unfit for a prolix speech;

<margin>F</margin> and I wish I were master of it. But it was in your interest to indulge us a little, since you are equally prepared for both, so that the dispute might be carried through. But since you are not willing, and business so urges me that I cannot linger here with you for long—though I would have heard those things gladly—I depart now whither the matter itself calls me." Having said these things, I rose immediately to depart. But as I was rising, Callias, catching me with his right hand and with his left this cloak, said: "We will not let you go, Socrates; for if you go out now, it will scarcely be possible for us to talk like this again. Stay, I beseech you; the speech of no one will delight me as much as yours there with Protagoras.

<margin>G</margin> Therefore, gratify both me and all these people." But I had already risen to go, and I said to Callias: "O son of Hipponicus, I have always admired your philosophy; now I praise and love it besides. Wherefore I would vehemently desire to gratify you, if you asked for possible things. But what you now ask is as if you were to pray that I should follow Crison of Himera, <margin>Crison of Himera, the runner.</margin> the runner and young man, with equal steps, or some of those who are accustomed to run the longest distance or to complete a day's course; for I would reply that I much more desire myself than you that I could equal these runners in the race,

<margin>H</margin> but I cannot. But if you wish to see me and this man, as if he were another Crison, running together, ask him to accompany me with equal steps. For I indeed cannot run quickly, but he can run slowly. Therefore if you desire to hear me and Protagoras disputing, entreat him that, just as he did from the beginning, he should now respond in few words and to the proposed question. Otherwise, what will be the mode of disputing? I certainly thought that being together to dispute with one another was separate from public speaking." But...
