-># OF PLATO<-

<columns>
...that it is one thing to converse by differing with one another, and another to deliver a public oration. But **A** look, Socrates," said Callias, "Protagoras seems to be making a fair request when he thinks he should be allowed to discuss as he pleases, just as you may as you please." At this, Alcibiades said, "You do not speak rightly, Callias. For our friend Socrates here confesses that he is powerless when it comes to long-winded speaking <note>original: "macrologia," referring to the Sophists' style of lengthy, rhetorical displays</note>, and in this he yields to Protagoras. However, if he were to yield to anyone in the art of disputation—in the giving and receiving of reasons—I would be greatly surprised. Therefore, if Protagoras confesses that he is inferior to Socrates in disputation, that is enough for Socrates. But if he claims this for himself as well, let him dispute by both questioning and answering, and let him not draw out his speech into a long **B** discourse at every single response, cutting off the argument so that no one else may speak. He is so wordy that the greater part of the listeners forgets what the original question was about—though I myself will vouch for Socrates that he will by no means forget what is said, even if he jests with us by claiming to be forgetful. To me, Socrates seems to be asking for much fairer terms. For it is proper for each man to express his own opinion." After Alcibiades, I believe it was Critias who spoke: "O Prodicus and Hippias, Callias seems to be strongly supporting Protagoras. But Alcibiades is always too contentious and persistent, whichever way he turns. It is not proper for us to favor one **C** more than the other, whether Socrates or Protagoras, but to ask both of them in common that they do not break off in the middle of their dispute once they have begun." When he had said this, Prodicus said, "You speak well, Critias. For it is proper for those who take part in these discussions to be 'common' listeners to both, but by no means 'equal' <note>Prodicus was famous for his hair-splitting distinctions between synonyms</note>. For these two things are not the same: it is proper to hear both in common, but not to attribute to each equally. To the wiser man, one should give more; to the more ignorant, less. For my part, Protagoras and Socrates, I think you ought to concede something to one another, and while you may 'dispute' with each other about what is said, you should by no means 'contend.' **D** Friends dispute with friends out of goodwill, but adversaries and enemies contend with one another. And in this way, our discussion would proceed most excellently. For if you disputed in this manner, you would be most highly 'esteemed' by us who listen, not 'praised,' I say. Listeners esteem with the judgment of the mind without deception; they praise with words, often falsely extolling something contrary to their true opinion. Likewise, we listeners would be filled with the greatest 'joy,' not 'pleasure.' **E** He is filled with joy who is delighted by learning and contemplation through intelligence itself; he is drenched in pleasure who, while eating or enjoying some other delight, is pleased by the physical sensation of the body." When Prodicus had said these things, many of those present agreed. Then Hippias the Wise began in this way: "O men present, I consider all of you to be kinsmen, relatives, and fellow citizens by nature, not by law. For like is kin to like by nature. But Law, being a tyrant over men, compels many things contrary to nature. It would be a shame, therefore, if we who understand the nature of things, and are the wisest of all the Greeks, and who have come together for this very purpose to this city—the very stronghold of Greek wisdom—and are gathered in this house, the largest and most magnificent in the whole city, should show nothing worthy of such greatness, but rather **F** dissent from one another, bickering in the manner of worthless little men. I, for my part, Socrates and Protagoras, exhort and entreat you to be willing to submit to us as if before arbiters who will lead you to a middle ground. Neither should you, Socrates, require that exact form of dialogue and that overly brief brevity of yours, since it is bothersome to Protagoras; rather, I pray, loosen the reins a little, so that your speeches may appear more magnificent and splendid. And you, Protagoras, I beg of you, do not run out into the high sea of speeches with all your ropes strained and sails full, until the land is nowhere to be seen; but both of you strive to keep to a middle course as much as you can. Therefore, do what I wish and obey: choose a staff-bearer, a president of the contest, and a judge who **G** shall set a limit to the words of each." This pleased those present, and all praised it. Callias told me he would not let me go, and they asked me to choose an arbiter. But I said, "It is not proper to put a judge over this dispute. For if the judge is more ignorant than we are, it will be unjust for an inferior to preside over his betters. If he is our equal, it will still not be right. For an equal will act as we do, and thus his selection will be superfluous. To choose someone truly better than us is impossible, I believe, since no one wiser than Protagoras here could be chosen. If you choose someone who is not at all more learned but you claim he is, this will be a disgrace to Protagoras—that you have appointed a judge over him as if he were an ignorant and ignoble person. For my part, it matters not. But so that we may proceed with the **H** dispute just as you wish, I propose this: If Protagoras does not wish to answer, let him at least ask the questions, and I will answer; and at the same time, I will try to show him in what manner, in my judgment, one ought to answer another. And when I have answered as many of his questions as he wishes, let him in turn promise to do the same for me. And if by chance he seems a little reluctant to answer, then both I and all of you together shall entreat the man, just as you are now entreating me, [not to spoil the gathering...]

<margin>The difference between 'common' and 'equal' listeners.</margin>

<margin>Between 'esteeming' and 'praising.'</margin>

<margin>Between 'rejoicing' and 'taking pleasure.'</margin>

<column-break/>

"You see, Socrates," he said, "Protagoras seems to be speaking fairly, claiming it should be permitted for him to discuss as he wishes, and for you as you wish."
Then Alcibiades took up the word and said, "You do not speak well, Callias. For Socrates here confesses that he has no part in long-speaking, and he yields to Protagoras in being able to carry out a long discourse; but in being able to give and receive an account <note>original: "logon," meaning an argument or rational account</note>, I would wonder if he yields to any man. If, then, Protagoras also confesses that he is inferior to Socrates in discussion, that is enough for Socrates; but if he contests it, let him discuss by asking and answering, not stretching out a long speech at every question, parrying the arguments and refusing to give an account, but drawing it out until most of the listeners have forgotten. For I will guarantee that Socrates will not forget, regardless of the fact that he plays and says he is forgetful. To me, then, Socrates seems to speak more reasonably. For it is necessary for each man to show his own opinion." After Alcibiades, I believe it was Critias who spoke: "O Prodicus and Hippias, Callias seems to me to be very much in a hurry to support Protagoras; but Alcibiades is always contentious toward whatever he sets his mind on. We, however, should not join the battle for either Socrates or Protagoras, but in common ask both of them not to break up the gathering in the middle." When he had said this, Prodicus said: "You seem to me to speak well, Critias. For it is necessary for those who are present at such discussions to be common listeners to both speakers, but not equal ones. For it is not the same thing. For it is necessary to hear both in common, but not to distribute equally to each; rather, to the wiser more, and to the more ignorant less. I then, Protagoras and Socrates, think you should agree to dispute with one another about the arguments, but not to contend. (For friends dispute even out of goodwill with friends, but those who are at variance and enemies contend with one another.) And thus our gathering would become most beautiful. For you who speak would thus be most highly esteemed among us who hear, and not praised. (For being esteemed is in the souls of the listeners without deception, but being praised is in words, often by those lying against their true opinion.) And we the listeners, in turn, would thus be most greatly gladdened, not pleased. For to be gladdened is to learn something and to share in wisdom by the mind itself; but to be pleased is to eat something or experience some other pleasure in the body itself."
When Prodicus had said these things, very many of those present accepted them. After Prodicus, Hippias the Wise said: "O men present, I consider you all to be kinsmen and relatives and citizens, by nature, not by law. For like is kin to like by nature; but law, being a tyrant of men, forces many things contrary to nature. For us, then, it is a shame to know the nature of things, and being the wisest of the Greeks, and for this very reason having now come together to the very town-hall <note>original: "prytaneion," the symbolic heart of the city</note> of wisdom of Greece, and to this greatest and most prosperous house of the city itself, to show nothing worthy of this dignity, but like the lowest of men to be at variance with one another. I therefore both ask and advise you, Protagoras and Socrates, to come to an agreement, as if we were arbiters bringing you together in the middle; and neither should you, Socrates, seek this exact form of dialogues that is too brief, if it is not pleasing to Protagoras, but let out and slacken the reins of the arguments, so that they may appear more magnificent and more graceful to us; nor again should Protagoras, stretching out every rope and letting out the favorable wind, flee into the sea of words, hiding the land; but both of you should cut a middle path. So do this, and obey me: choose a staff-bearer and an overseer and a presiding officer, who will guard the moderate length of the arguments for each of you." These things pleased those present, and everyone praised them. And Callias said he would not let me go, and they asked me to choose an overseer. I said then that it would be a shame to choose a referee for the arguments. For if the one chosen is worse than we are, it would not be right for the worse to oversee the better; if he is similar, it would not be right either; for he who is similar to us will do similar things, so that he will be chosen in vain. But indeed, you will choose someone better than us. In truth, as it seems, it is impossible for you to choose anyone wiser than this Protagoras. If you choose someone who is in no way better, but you say he is, this becomes a shame for him, as if an overseer were chosen for a common man. As for my part, it makes no difference to me; but I am willing to do it this way, so that the gathering and the dialogues you desire may happen. If Protagoras does not want to answer, let him ask questions himself, and I will answer; and at the same time I will try to show him how I say it is necessary for the one answering to answer. When I have answered as much as he wants to ask, in turn let him provide an account to me in the same way. If then he does not seem eager to answer the very thing asked, both I and you in common will ask him for the same things you asked of me: not to destroy the gathering. And there is no need of [an arbiter for this...]

<summary>The dialogue reaches a stalemate over the format of the debate, prompting the other guests (Alcibiades, Critias, Prodicus, and Hippias) to intervene with suggestions for moderation and arbitration. Socrates ultimately proposes a compromise where he and Protagoras trade roles as questioner and answerer.</summary>

# P R O T A G O R A S

<columns>
<margin>A</margin> ...for this purpose, so that whenever a dispute arises, you all may act together as judges. Everyone agreed that this was how it should be done. And although Protagoras was not very willing, he was nevertheless compelled to agree that he would ask questions; and after he had asked enough, he would in turn provide an answer and join those who respond. So, he began to ask questions in this way: "I believe, Socrates," he said, "that the greatest part of education for a man is to be skilled in poetry. This means being able to understand what is said by the poets—what is composed rightly and what is not—and to know how to distinguish between them and give a reason when questioned. And so, let the question now be about the very same subject that you and I are currently discussing: <margin>B</margin> virtue. However, since the discussion has been transferred to the realm of poetry, this will be the only difference. For Simonides says somewhere, addressing Scopas, the son of Creon the Thessalian: *For a man to become truly good is hard, four-square in hands and feet and mind, fashioned without a flaw.* Do you know this song, or shall I recite the whole thing to you?" And I said, "There is no need. For I know it, and it happens that I have studied the song quite carefully." "You speak well," he said. "Does it seem to you to be well and rightly composed, or not?" "Very well and rightly," I replied. "And does it seem to you to be well-composed if the poet contradicts himself?" "Not well at all," I said. "Look more closely then," he said. "But, my good man, I have examined it sufficiently." "Do you know then," he said, "that as the song proceeds, he says: <margin>C</margin> *Nor does the saying of Pittacus ring true to me, though spoken by a wise man: he said it is hard to be good.* <note>original: "ἐσθλὸν ἔμμεναι"</note> Do you realize that this same man says both these things and those earlier ones?" "I know it," I said. "Does it seem to you then," he asked, "that these later words agree with the former ones?" "It seems so to me." And yet at the same time, I was afraid he might be right. "But," I said, "does it not seem so to you?" "How could he seem to agree with himself when he says both things? First, he himself laid down that it is hard for a man to become truly good; then, proceeding a little further in the poem, he forgot this. He blames Pittacus, who says the same thing he did—that it is hard to be good—and says he does not accept the very thing he said himself. <margin>D</margin> And yet, when he blames the one who says the same things as he does, it is clear that he also blames himself. Therefore, either his first statement or his second is incorrect." Having said this, he provoked a great deal of noise and praise from the listeners. At first, I was like a man struck by a strong boxer; I was blinded and dizzy when he said these things and the others cheered. Then (to tell you the truth) in order to gain time to consider what the poet meant, I turned to Prodicus. Calling him, I said, "O Prodicus, Simonides is your fellow citizen; it is only right that you come to the man's aid. I think I shall call upon you just as Homer says the river Scamander, when besieged by Achilles, called upon the river Simois, saying:

<margin>E</margin> -> *Dear brother, let us both restrain the power of this man.* <-
-> *Let us hold him back.* <-

"And so I call upon you, lest Protagoras demolish our Simonides. For indeed, the correction of Simonides requires your 'musical' art <note>In this context, 'musical' refers to the arts of the Muses, specifically Prodicus's expertise in the precise meaning of words.</note>, by which you distinguish between 'wishing' and 'desiring' as not being the same, and many other fine things you mentioned just now. Consider now if you agree with me. For it does not seem that Simonides contradicts himself. You, Prodicus, declare your opinion: does *becoming* seem to be the same thing as *being* to you, or something different?" "Something different," said Prodicus. "Therefore," I said, "in the first part, Simonides himself declared his opinion: that for a man to *become* truly good is a hard thing?" "You speak the truth," said Prodicus. "But he blames Pittacus," I said, "not, as <margin>F</margin> Protagoras thinks, for saying the same thing as himself, but something else. For Pittacus did not say, as Simonides did, that it is hard *to become* good, but *to be* good. <note>original: "ἔμμεναι," an archaic form of "to be"</note> And it is not the same thing, O Protagoras (as Prodicus here says), to be and to become. If being is not the same as becoming, then Simonides does not contradict himself. And perhaps Prodicus here, and many others, might say according to Hesiod that it is hard to *become* good, for the gods placed sweat before virtue; but when one reaches the summit, it is then easy to possess, though it was hard to acquire." <note>Reference to Hesiod’s *Works and Days*.</note> Prodicus, having heard this, praised me. But Protagoras said, "Your correction, Socrates, contains a greater error than the one you are correcting." <margin>G</margin> And I said, "Then I have done a bad thing, it seems, O Protagoras; I am a ridiculous doctor who makes the disease worse while trying to cure it." "But that is how it is," he said. "How so?" I asked. "It would be a great ignorance on the part of the poet," he said, "if he said virtue is so cheap a thing to possess that it is easy, when it is the most difficult thing of all, as it seems to all men." And I said, "By Zeus, Prodicus here has intervened in our discussion at just the right moment. For it is likely, Protagoras, that the wisdom of Prodicus is an ancient, divine thing; either starting from Simonides or even older. But you, though experienced in many other things, seem to be inexperienced in this; unlike me, who am experienced because I am a disciple of this Prodicus. And now you do not seem to understand that perhaps Simonides did not understand this word 'hard' <margin>H</margin> in the way you do. Just as Prodicus here admonishes me every time I praise you or someone else and say that Protagoras is a wise and 'clever' <note>original: "δεινός" (deinos), which can mean 'clever' but also 'terrible' or 'dreadful'</note> man...

<meta>catchword: warns.</meta>

<column-break/>

...lest he dissolve the assembly. Nor is it necessary for you to appoint a single judge. For you shall all judge together. Everyone agreed that this was the way to act. Protagoras, however, seemed to enter into this unwillingly. At last, he was forced to concede that he would ask questions, and after he had asked enough, he would answer briefly. And so he began to question in this manner: "I believe, O Socrates, that the principal part of learning consists in this: that one should have as many poems as possible ready at hand. This means that one can understand the sayings of the poets—which ones are right and which are less so—and know how to discern them and give an account when questioned. And now, let someone ask about the very thing we are both now investigating: virtue. But there will be this difference: that the dispute has been transferred to poetry. For Simonides says to Scopas, the son of Creon the Thessalian, that it is difficult for a man to truly *become* good, four-square in hands, feet, and mind, perfectly fashioned. Do you remember the poem, or do you want me to explain it all?" Socrates: "There is no need. For I remember it, and I have taken diligent care of these verses." Protagoras: "You speak well. Does it seem to you that Simonides spoke well and rightly, or not?" Socrates: "Indeed, most excellently." Protagoras: "Does the poet seem to speak rightly if he contradicts himself?" Socrates: "Not at all." Protagoras: "Pay attention then more diligently." Socrates: "We are paying attention, good sir." Protagoras: "In the same poem he later says that the opinion of Pittacus—though he was a wise man—seems discordant to him, when he says: *It is difficult to remain good.* Do you see that the same Simonides said both this and the former things?" Socrates: "I do." Protagoras: "Are these things the same as those?" "The same," I said, "as it seems to me." And at the same time, fearing he might add something further, I asked whether it did not also seem so to him. "Do you ask," he said, "whether I think he is consistent with himself, he who said both these things? First, he proposed that it is truly difficult for a man to *become* good; but a little later, as if he had forgotten, he attacked Pittacus for saying the same thing—namely, that it is difficult for a man to *remain* good—rejecting his words even though he had said the same? Truly, when he accuses Pittacus, the author of the same opinion as his own, he condemns himself. Therefore, either the former or the latter is not said rightly." At these words, many listeners shouted and praised Protagoras. I, at first, as if struck by a robust boxer, was dizzy with blurred vision and staggered. For both his voice and the shouting of the others had utterly overwhelmed me. Then, to confess the truth to you honestly, in order to gain time to investigate the poet's mind, I turned to Prodicus and said: "Simonides was your fellow citizen, O Prodicus. Therefore, it is in your interest to bring him aid. I seem to be calling you just as in <margin>Iliad, Book 21</margin> Homer, when the Scamander was besieged by Achilles, called upon the Simois: *O sweet brother, let us both together restrain the force of this man.* In no different way do I now summon you, lest Protagoras conquer our Simonides. Truly, that Simonides may be rescued, there is need of that elegance of yours, by which you distinguish *wishing* and *desiring*, and those many excellent things you were saying a little while ago. And now see if you think the same as I do; for I do not think Simonides contradicts himself in his speech. But you, O Prodicus, expose your opinion first: does *to become* and *to be* seem the same to you, or something else?" "Something else, by Jove," said Prodicus. "Is it not true," I said, "that in the first part, Simonides explains his opinion, that it is difficult for a man to truly *become* good?" "You tell the truth," said Prodicus. "But he disapproves of Pittacus," I said, "not as Protagoras thinks, for saying the same thing, but something different. For Pittacus did not say it is difficult *to become* a good man, as Simonides did, but *to remain* one. But it is not the same thing, O Protagoras—as this Prodicus thinks—to *be* and to *become*; and if being and becoming are not the same, Simonides by no means states things contrary to himself. And perhaps it is permitted for this Prodicus and many others to cite that saying of Hesiod: that it is difficult to be made good, for he says the gods placed sweat before virtue <margin>In the work titled *Works and Days*</margin>. But when the highest peak has been reached, it is easy, though it was difficult to obtain." When Prodicus had heard these things, he praised me. But Protagoras said, "Socrates, that 'correction' of yours has more fault in it than the thing you are correcting." "Then things have gone poorly for me, O Protagoras, as it seems," I said, "and I am a ridiculous doctor: for while I strive to cure, I increase the disease." Protagoras: "Yet that is how it is." Socrates: "For what reason?" Protagoras: "For that poet would have been far too ignorant if he made virtue of so little value as to think its possession was easy, when it is the most difficult of all things, as it seems to all men." Socrates: "By Jove, this Prodicus has intervened opportunely in our conversations. For it seems, O Protagoras, that the divine wisdom of Prodicus is some ancient thing of long standing, either drawing its origin from Simonides or even older; you, however, although you are skilled in many other things, appear to be unskilled in this. I, however, have experience in it, having been a disciple of this Prodicus. And yet at present you do not seem to notice that perhaps Simonides did not use the word 'difficult' in the same way it is used by you; but Prodicus here frequently warns me that it is to be understood as something bad and heavy. For whenever I, praising either another or yourself, say: 'Protagoras is a wise and *deinos* man'—that is, powerful and grave..."

# OF PLATO
### PROTAGORAS

<columns>
<margin>A</margin>He <note>Prodicus, the specialist in synonyms</note> rebukes me immediately, and asks whether I am not ashamed to call what is "good" "dreadful": for what is "dreadful," he says, is "evil." No one, for instance, ever speaks of "dreadful wealth," or "dreadful peace," or "dreadful health"; rather, they speak of "dreadful disease," "dreadful war," or "dreadful poverty"—as if "dreadful" were synonymous with "evil." Perhaps, then, the Ceans <note>People from the island of Ceos, Simonides' home</note> and Simonides himself, when they say "difficult," mean either "evil" or something else that you do not understand.

Therefore, let us ask Prodicus. For it is fitting to consult him especially regarding the writings of Simonides. What, O Prodicus, did Simonides intend to be understood by the term "difficult"? <margin>PROD. Evil, certainly.</margin> PROD. Evil, certainly.

<margin>B</margin>For this reason, I suppose, Prodicus, he finds fault with Pittacus for saying that it is "difficult to remain good"—as if he had said it is "evil to remain good." PROD. And what else do you think Simonides intended, O Socrates, than to reproach Pittacus, because he did not know how to distinguish the correct meanings of names, seeing as he was a Lesbian <note>A native of the island of Lesbos</note> and was raised among barbarians? SOC. Do you hear, Protagoras, what Prodicus says? What do you say to this?

PROT. It is very far from being so, Prodicus. For I certainly know that Simonides, by the name "difficult," intended what others usually do—not "evil," but that which is "not easy," and which is acquired only through much labor.

<margin>C</margin>SOC. I also believe this is what Simonides intended, O Protagoras, and that Prodicus here understands it as well, but he is playing with you and testing whether you are able to defend your own argument. For that Simonides does not mean "evil" by "difficult" is evidenced by the words that follow; for he adds that "God alone is worthy to enjoy this gift." Surely he would not say that "to be good is evil" and then immediately add that God alone possesses this, attributing such a "gift" to God alone. Prodicus would then be calling Simonides a completely dissolute man, and in no way a true Cean.

But what I think Simonides actually felt in these verses, I will say, if you wish to put me to the test to see how I fare regarding poetry. Or, if you prefer, I will listen to you.

<margin>D</margin>When Protagoras heard this, he said, "As you please, Socrates." But Prodicus and Hippias and all the others urged me to proceed. I will try, then, to explain to you what I think about these verses. Philosophy is most ancient and most abundant among the Greeks in Crete and Lacedaemon <note>Sparta</note>, and more sophists <term>Sophists: professional teachers of wisdom and rhetoric</term> are found there than anywhere else. However, they deny it and pretend to be unlearned, so that they may not be discovered to surpass the rest of the Greeks in wisdom—exactly as Protagoras was saying earlier about the sophists. Instead, they wish to seem to excel the others in military skill and courage, fearing that if their true nature were revealed, everyone else would pursue the same study.

Therefore, they conceal it and deceive those who, in other cities, imitate the Lacedaemonian customs.

<margin>E</margin>For there are those who, because they have their ears boxed <note>from wrestling</note> and wrap themselves in thongs, and delight in exercises, and use short cloaks, wish to seem like Spartans—as if the Lacedaemonians surpassed the rest of the Greeks in these sorts of things.

But the Lacedaemonians, whenever they wish to converse more freely with their own sophists and grow weary of meeting in secret, expel all these "Laconizers" <note>imitators of Spartan ways</note> and any other foreigners who are visiting, and practice philosophy with their sophists in private. Furthermore, they and the Cretans forbid their young men to travel to other cities, lest they unlearn what is taught among them.

In these cities, there are found not only men who take great pride in their learning, but women as well.

<margin>F</margin>That I speak the truth, and that the Lacedaemonians are excellently educated in philosophy and discourse, you may observe most clearly from this: If someone converses with even the most ordinary of the Lacedaemonians, he will find him for the most part appearing crude in his speech. But then, whenever the opportunity of the matter demands it, like a powerful javelin-thrower, he hurls a short and coiled word, but one of great significance, so that the person talking with him seems no better than a child.

That the virtue of the Lacedaemonians consists more in the study of wisdom than in physical exercise is understood by some men of our age, and many in the past noticed the same, seeing that to be able to utter such words is the mark of a perfectly educated man.

<margin>The Sages of Greece. G</margin>From their number was Thales of Miletus, and Pittacus of Mitylene, Bias of Priene, our own Solon, Cleobulus of Lindus, Myson of Chenae, and the seventh of these was said to be Chilo the Lacedaemonian. All these were rivals and admirers of Lacedaemonian wisdom. We find that their wisdom was of such a kind: short words, worthy of being remembered by everyone. These men, having met together by common consent, dedicated the first-fruits of their wisdom to the temple of Apollo at Delphi, inscribing there what is now celebrated by all: **Know thyself** and **Nothing in excess.**

<margin>Lacedaemonian Wisdom.</margin>I mention these things for this reason: to make it clear that the character of ancient philosophy was a certain "Laconic" <note>Spartan</note> brevity, so to speak.

<margin>H</margin>And indeed, this particular saying of Pittacus was being circulated and celebrated by the wise: **It is difficult to remain good.** Simonides, therefore, since he desired the glory of wisdom, realized that if he could refute and overcome this proverb, just as one would a famous athlete, he himself would be held in high honor by all. For this reason, he composed those verses, intending, as I believe, to overthrow the words of the man whose glory he envied.

But let us all examine these things together and see whether I speak the truth. For first of all, the very beginning of the poem would seem like the work of a madman,

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>He asks if I am not ashamed to call good things "dreadful," for "dreadful" (he says) is "evil." At any rate, no one ever speaks of "dreadful wealth," nor of "dreadful peace," nor "dreadful health"; but of "dreadful disease," and "dreadful war," and "dreadful poverty"—as if "dreadful" were an evil thing. Perhaps, then, the Ceans and Simonides also understand "difficult" to be either "evil," or something else which you do not learn. Let us therefore ask Prodicus (for it is right to ask him about the voice of Simonides). What, O Prodicus, did Simonides mean by "difficult"? "Evil," he said.

<margin>B</margin>For this reason, then, I said, O Prodicus, he finds fault with Pittacus for saying, **It is difficult to be good**, just as if he had heard him saying that "it is evil to be good." "But what else do you think, Socrates," he said, "Simonides meant than this, to reproach Pittacus because he did not know how to distinguish names correctly, being a Lesbian and raised in a barbarian tongue?" "Do you hear then, Protagoras," I said, "this from Prodicus? Do you have anything to say to these things?"

And Protagoras said, "It is far from being so, Prodicus. But I know well that Simonides meant by 'difficult' the same as the rest of us: not 'evil,' but that which is not easy, but comes about through many troubles."

<margin>C</margin>"But I also think, Protagoras," I said, "that Simonides meant this, and that Prodicus here knows it; but he is playing, and seems to be testing you to see if you are able to come to the aid of your own argument. For that Simonides does not mean 'evil' by 'difficult' is a great proof in the very next phrase. For he says that 'God alone could have this prize.' Surely he is not saying this—that it is 'evil to be good.' Then he says God alone could have this, and assigned this prize to God alone. For Prodicus would be calling Simonides a certain licentious man, and in no way a Cean."

"But what Simonides seems to me to intend in this song, I am willing to tell you, if you wish to take a trial of me as to how I stand regarding what you say, the matter of verses; but if you wish, I will listen to you."

<margin>D</margin>Protagoras, having heard me saying these things, said, "If you wish, Socrates." And both Prodicus and Hippias urged me very much, as did the others. "I then," I said, "will try to go through for you what seems to me to be the case concerning this song. For philosophy is most ancient and most abundant among the Greeks in Crete and in Lacedaemon; and most sophists on earth are there. But they deny it, and pretend to be ignorant, so that they might not be revealed as excelling the Greeks in wisdom (just like those sophists Protagoras was speaking of); but rather that they might seem to excel in battle and in courage, thinking that if they were known for what they truly are, everyone would practice this. But now, having hidden that, they have deceived those who play the 'Laconizer' in the cities, and

<margin>E</margin>some have their ears broken, imitating them, and wrap thongs around themselves, and love gymnastics, and wear short cloaks—as if by these things the Lacedaemonians ruled the Greeks.

And the Lacedaemonians, whenever they wish to meet freely with the sophists among them, and are already annoyed at meeting in secret, make 'expulsions of foreigners' of these 'Laconizers' and any other stranger who is staying there, and meet with the sophists without the strangers knowing. And they themselves do not allow any of the young men to go out into other cities, just as the Cretans do not, so that they might not unlearn what they themselves teach.

And there are in these cities not only men who take pride in education, but also women.

<margin>F</margin>"And you might know that I speak the truth, and that the Lacedaemonians are best educated in philosophy and words, in this way: for if someone wishes to meet with the most ordinary of the Lacedaemonians, for the most part he will find him appearing as someone ordinary in words; then, wherever it happens in the conversation, he hurls a word worthy of mention, short and compressed, like a dreadful javelin-thrower, so that the one conversing appears no better than a child."

"This very thing, then, is what some of those now and those of old have understood: that to 'Laconize' is much more to philosophize than to love gymnastics; knowing that to be able to utter such words is the mark of a perfectly educated man."

<margin>G</margin>"Among these were Thales of Miletus, and Pittacus of Mitylene, and Bias of Priene, and our Solon, and Cleobulus of Lindus, and Myson of Chenae; and the seventh among these was said to be the Lacedaemonian Chilo. All these were zealots and lovers and students of the Lacedaemonian education. And one might learn that their wisdom was such a thing: short, memorable words spoken by each. These men also, having come together in common, dedicated the first-fruits of wisdom to Apollo in the temple at Delphi, writing these things which everyone hymns: **Know thyself, and Nothing in excess.**"

"Why then do I say these things? Because this was the manner of philosophy of the ancients, a certain Laconic brevity."

<margin>H</margin>"And indeed, this saying of Pittacus was circulated privately, being praised by the wise: **It is difficult to be good.** Simonides, then, being ambitious for wisdom, knew that if he could pull down this saying, like a famous athlete, and get the better of it, he himself would be famous among the men of that time."

"It was for this saying, then, and for this reason, that he has composed this whole song, as it seems to me. Let us all consider together whether I speak falsely, or if I say anything with truth. For immediately the first part of the song would appear mad,"
</columns>

<summary>Socrates engages in a playful linguistic debate with Prodicus and Protagoras over the meaning of "difficult" in a poem by Simonides. He then argues that true philosophy originates in the "Laconic brevity" of the Spartans and the Seven Sages.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: In the previous section, Socrates and the sophist Protagoras were debating the meaning of a poem by Simonides. Socrates, with the help of the linguist Prodicus, has begun a deep dive into the nuances of the word "difficult," arguing that Simonides used it specifically to refute a saying by the sage Pittacus.</meta>

# PROTAGORAS

<margin>A</margin> If he had intended to say that it is difficult for a man to become good, he would have inserted the particle "on the one hand" <note>original: "μέν" (men). Socrates is performing a close grammatical reading to show Simonides is contrasting his view with someone else's.</note>. For there seems to be no reason for its inclusion unless we say that Simonides is speaking in opposition to the words of Pittacus. When Pittacus said, "it is difficult to be good," Simonides objects: "No, Pittacus, it is not so; rather, it is truly <note>original: "ἀληθέως" (alētheōs). There is a play here on whether "truly" modifies "difficult" or "good."</note> difficult to *become* a good man," not "to be truly good." He does not use the word "truly" as if some people are "truly good" and others are good but "not truly"—for that would be foolish and unworthy of Simonides. Instead, we should say that there is a transposition in the poem. It is as if we imagine Pittacus saying, "O men, it is difficult to be good," and Simonides replying, <margin>B</margin> "O Pittacus, you are not speaking the truth. For it is not to *be*, but to *become* a good man—square in hands and feet and mind, fashioned without flaw <note>This "square" imagery refers to a person of perfect, unshakeable character, a common metaphor in Greek ethics.</note>—that is truly difficult." In this way, the particle "on the one hand" is inserted with reason, and the word "truly" is correctly placed at the end. All the lines that follow testify that it was spoken in this manner. Furthermore, there are many things in these verses that we could point out individually to show how beautifully they are written. They are composed with great skill and precision, but the discourse would be too long. Therefore, let us explain the general form and intent of the poet. He intends, throughout all these verses, to refute the saying of Pittacus. For he says a little later, almost in this way: <margin>C</margin> that to become a good man is truly difficult, yet for a certain time, it is possible. But once one has become good, to remain in that state and to *be* a good man—as you claim, Pittacus—is impossible and not for humans; only a God could possess this privilege. It is impossible for a man not to be bad if an irresistible misfortune strikes him down. Whom, then, does an unexpected disaster overwhelm in the steering of a ship? Clearly, not the unskilled man, for he is always down. Just as one cannot throw down a man who is already lying on the ground, but one can throw down a man who is standing and force him to lie down, so too can <margin>D</margin> an unexpected misfortune overcome a skillful and wise man. But it can never overcome the man who is always helpless. A great storm falling upon a pilot makes him helpless; a harsh season falling upon a farmer, or similar things upon a doctor, make them helpless. For it is possible for a good man to become bad (as is also testified by another poet who said, "A good man is at one time bad, and at another good"). But for a bad man to *become* bad is not possible, for he must always be so. Therefore, whenever an unexpected disaster invades a provident, wise, and good man, he becomes bad. But you say, <margin>E</margin> O Pittacus, that it is difficult to *be* good. The reality is this: to become good is possible, though difficult; but to remain good is entirely impossible. For anyone who acts well is good, and he who acts badly is bad. Now, what is a "good action" regarding letters? And what action makes a man "good" in them? Clearly, the learning of them. What action makes a man a good doctor? Evidently, the skill of curing the sick. He who cures well is a good doctor; he who cures badly is a bad one. Who then can become a bad doctor? Certainly the one who is first a doctor, and then a "good" doctor. For he is the one who could eventually become a bad doctor. But we, who are ignorant of the medical art, could never, by acting badly, become either doctors or carpenters or anything of the kind. Whoever does not become a doctor by performing his duty badly is also not a "bad" doctor. In the same way, a good man can sometimes become bad, either because of time, or labor, or disease, or some other accident. <margin>F</margin> For this alone is "bad action": to be deprived of knowledge. But a bad man could never "become" bad, for he is always bad. If he were to "become" bad, he would first have to have been good. Thus, these verses tend toward this point: that it is impossible for a man to remain always good, but it is possible to become good and then, the same man, to become bad again. For the most part, those whom the gods love are the best. All these things are said against Pittacus, as the following lines show even more clearly. "For this reason," he says, "I will never waste my life's portion on an empty, unachievable hope, seeking that which cannot be: a man entirely without flaw among all of us who eat the fruits of the wide earth. <margin>G</margin> If I find one, I shall tell you," he says. So vehemently and through the whole poem does he attack the saying of Pittacus. "But I praise and love everyone willingly who commits nothing shameful. Against necessity, not even the gods fight." This is said to the very same point. For Simonides was not so uneducated as to say he praised the man who "willingly" does no evil, as if there were some people who *do* act badly willingly. For I believe this: no wise man thinks that any human wanders astray or commits evil and shameful acts of his own will. They know well that all who commit shameful and evil acts do so against their will <note>This is a core "Socratic paradox": the idea that no one does evil knowingly, but only through ignorance of what is truly good.</note>. And so Simonides does not say he praises him <margin>H</margin> who does not do evil "willingly," but rather he uses the word "willingly" about himself—that he would willingly compel himself to be a friend and a praiser to someone...

<note>marginal note at bottom: ...he wished it to be understood, for he thought a distinguished and good man often [praises]... as when parents are moody and unjust...</note>

He introduces the famous philosophical claim that no one does evil voluntarily.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: In the previous section, Socrates has been providing a detailed, somewhat ironic interpretation of a poem by Simonides. He argued that the poet was intentionally critiquing the sage Pittacus’s claim that being good is difficult, suggesting instead that while "becoming" good is hard, "being" good is a state reserved for the gods.</meta>

# PLATONIS

<margin>A</margin> They are often accustomed to attacking the errors of his parents and country of their own accord, and to spread them everywhere, so that no one can criticize them for neglecting their parents and country. Therefore, they blame their parents and country, and unnecessarily provoke them with hatred and enmity. Truly good men, however, conceal the shames of their country instead, and force themselves to praise them. And if they have been affected by some injury that would justify being angry at their parents and country, they console themselves and reconcile themselves with their own people, and compel themselves, even against their will, to love and praise their ancestors. Often, I think, Simonides himself—not from his own heart's opinion, but against his will—approached some tyrant or other such person to praise and extol him.

<margin>B</margin> This, then, is what he says to Pittacus: "I do not rebuke you, O Pittacus, because I am by nature fond of disparaging others; for anyone is sufficient for me who is not evil, nor too shiftless. A healthy man who knows the justice that benefits the city will help it. Nor will I disparage him myself, for I do not delight in disparagement. For the race of fools is infinite, so that if one were to continue to blame them, he would necessarily become exhausted. Furthermore, all things are honorable in which base things are not mixed." He does not say this as if he were saying all things are white in which no black is mixed—for that would be ridiculous in many ways—but as if he were saying that he would tolerate those who are mediocre and would not blame them. "I do not seek," he says, "a blameless man among as many of us as

<margin>C</margin> reap the fruit of the broad earth." Then he announces to you what he has discovered: "namely, that I will praise no one for this reason. But it is enough for me if anyone holds the middle path and does nothing base. Thus I love all, thus I praise all." At this point, he used the Mitylenean dialect <note>original: "Mitylenæorum lingua." Simonides is subtly mimicking or addressing the local speech of Pittacus, who was from Mitylene.</note> as if speaking against Pittacus, saying, "Thus I praise all, thus I love all willingly." Here one ought to distinguish the word "willingly" from the following words: "whoever commits nothing base." For there are those whom I do not praise and love willingly. But if you, my Pittacus, had said even moderately consistent and true things, I would never have rebuked you. But now, since you utter false things about the greatest matters, which appear true to many, I am forced to rebuke you. This, O Prodicus and Protagoras,

<margin>D</margin> seems to me to have been the opinion of Simonides himself in those poems. Then Hippias said, "Well, O Socrates, you seem to have explained these poems well. I also have an interpretation suited to them, which I will show you if you wish." "Indeed," said Alcibiades, "but later; first it is proper to finish what was agreed between Socrates and Protagoras. And if Protagoras wishes to question further, Socrates should answer. But if Protagoras wishes to answer, Socrates should question." "Indeed, I concede," I said, "to Protagoras whichever of these will be more pleasing to him. But if it is agreeable, let us pass over the verses, and I will gladly finish with you, Protagoras, the things I first asked of you. For it seems to me

<margin>Discussion on poetic matters, of what sort it may be.</margin>
<margin>E</margin> that a discussion about poetic matters is very similar to the banquets of the ignorant and common people. These people, because of their ignorance, are unable to converse with one another using their own voices and their own discourse, so they hire flute-girls <note>original: "tibicines" / "αὐλητρίδας" (aulētridas). These were female musicians who played the aulos, a double-reeded instrument, often present at Greek drinking parties.</note> and conduct their banquet with an alien voice—that is, the blowing of flutes. But where noble, excellent, and educated guests gather, you would see neither flute-girls, nor dancing-girls, nor singing-girls, but they celebrate the banquet using their own voices, setting aside those trifles and jests, and debating modestly with alternate questions and answers, even

<margin>F</margin> if they drink wine in abundance. In the same way, if men such as most of us claim to be meet for discussions of this kind, there is no need at all for an alien voice or the words of poets, whom one cannot question about what they write. And those who bring their testimonies into the discussion say the poet means one thing, while others say he means another, yet they cannot prove the matter about which they differ or reach a conclusion. Therefore, wise men dismiss such conversations and talk among themselves, and in turn they test one another’s wit. Disputants of this kind,

<margin>Who are the true disputants.</margin>
<margin>G</margin> as I think, you and I ought now to imitate; and putting poets aside, we should discuss the matter itself with our own reasoning, making a trial both of our own wit and of the truth. If then you wish to question, I am ready to provide you with an answer; but if you wish otherwise, offer yourself to me and help me finish the things we have started. When I had brought forward these and other similar points, Protagoras did not clearly declare what he would rather do. Here Alcibiades, turning to Callias, said, "O Callias, does Protagoras seem to you to be doing the right thing now when he refuses to declare whether he wishes to answer or not? It does not seem so to me. But let him either debate now, or say that he does not wish to debate, so that we may know this about him. Then Socrates may debate with anyone else, or anyone else who wishes with someone else." Here Protagoras, as it seemed to me, moved by shame because of Alcibiades' speech and the prayers of Callias and the others present, finally descended to debating, and commanded Socrates himself to question, promising he would answer. "O Protagoras," I said, "do not think I am debating with you for any other reason than that I wish to discuss the things I doubt here and there. For I think it was not without cause that Homer said, 'If two go

<margin>Iliad book 10.</margin>
together, one might understand more than the other.' <note>original: "Σύν τε δύ᾽ ἐρχομένω" (Syn te dy' erchomenō). A famous Homeric line suggesting that intellectual collaboration is more effective than solitary thought.</note> For we are all more resourceful...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...in such a situation that they are glad to see it, and they show their parents' or country's faults and accuse them, so that people will not blame or reproach them for being negligent. Thus they blame them even more, and voluntarily wrap themselves in enmities out of necessity. But good men hide such things and force themselves to praise them; and if they are angry because they have been treated unjustly by their parents or country, they comfort themselves and reconcile themselves, forcing themselves to love and praise their own. Often, I think, even Simonides considered that he himself had praised and extolled a tyrant or someone else of that sort, not willingly, but because he was forced.

<margin>B</margin> These things he says to Pittacus: "I, O Pittacus, do not blame you for this reason, that I am a lover of blame. For it is enough for me if anyone is not bad, nor too helpless, a man who is sound and knows the justice that benefits the city. I will not find fault with him. For I am not a lover of fault-finding. For the tribe of fools is infinite. So if anyone delights in blaming, he would be satisfied by blaming them. All things are beautiful, indeed, with which ugly things are not mixed." He does not mean this as if he were saying, "All things are white with which black is not mixed" (for that would be ridiculous in many ways), but that he himself accepts the middle path, so as not to blame. "And I do not seek," he said, "a blameless man, among as many of us as reap the fruit of the

<margin>C</margin> earth. Then I will announce it to you when I see it. So for this reason I will praise no one; but it is enough for me if one is in the middle and does nothing evil. Thus I love and praise all." And he uses the dialect here of the Mityleneans, as if speaking to Pittacus when saying, "And I praise and love all willingly." Here one must distinguish the word "willingly," meaning, "whoever does nothing shameful," but "unwillingly I praise and love." "You then," he said, "if you had spoken moderately reasonable and true things, O Pittacus, I would never have blamed you; but now, since you are lying greatly and about the greatest things, and seem to be speaking the truth, for this reason I blame you." These things, O Prodicus and Protagoras (I said),

<margin>D</margin> Simonides seems to me to have had in mind when he made this song. And Hippias said, "You seem to me, Socrates, to have gone through the song well; however, I also have a well-reasoned account about it, which I will show you, if you wish." And Alcibiades said, "Yes, Hippias, another time; but now it is right to do what Protagoras and Socrates agreed with each other: if Protagoras wants to ask anything, Socrates should answer; and if he wants to answer Socrates, the other should ask." And I said, "I leave it to Protagoras, whichever is more pleasing to him; but if he wishes, let us leave the songs and verses alone; and about those things I first asked you, O Protagoras, I would gladly reach an end with you, considering them together. For it seems to me that debating about poetry

<margin>E</margin> is most like the banquets of base and common men. For these people, because they are unable to be with each other through themselves during the drinking, nor through their own voices and their own words, due to their lack of education, they pay for flute-girls, hiring at a great price an alien voice—the voice of flutes—and they are with each other through that voice. But where there are noble and good banquet-guests who are educated, you would not see flute-girls, nor dancing-girls, nor harpers, but they are capable of being with each other by themselves, without these trifles and playthings, speaking and listening in their own voices in an orderly way, even

<margin>F</margin> if they drink very much wine. In this way, such gatherings as this, if they take hold of men such as most of us say we are, have no need for an alien voice, nor of poets, whom it is not possible to question about what they say; and when the many bring them into their arguments, some say the poet intends this, and others say something else, debating about a matter which they are unable to prove. But they let such gatherings go, and are with each other by themselves, through their own words, giving and taking a trial of each other. It seems to me that you and I should rather imitate such people, and putting the poets aside, make our arguments to each other through ourselves, taking a trial of the truth and of ourselves.

<margin>G</margin> And if you still wish to ask, I am ready to provide myself to answer you; but if you wish, provide yourself to me, to put an end to the things we stopped in the middle of discussing." When I said these and other such things, Protagoras did not clearly show which of the two he would do. Then Alcibiades said, looking at Callias, "O Callias, does it seem to you that Protagoras is doing well now, not wishing to clarify whether he will give an account or not? For it does not seem so to me; but either let him debate, or let him say that he does not wish to debate; so that we may know this about him, and Socrates may debate with someone else, or whoever else wishes with another." And Protagoras, being ashamed (as it seemed to me) when Alcibiades said these things and Callias and almost all those present were entreating him, was with difficulty moved to debate, and he ordered me to ask him, promising that he would answer. I then said, "O Protagoras, do not think I am debating with you for any other reason than to examine those things about which I am personally in doubt; for I think Homer says something very true: 'When two go together, one might think of it before the other.' For we are all somewhat more resourceful in every work and word..."

<summary>Socrates concludes his critique of Simonides' poem, arguing that it is more important for intellectual men to converse directly than to interpret poetry, which he compares to low-class entertainment. After pressure from Alcibiades and Callias, Protagoras reluctantly agrees to stop interpreting verses and return to a direct dialectical debate with Socrates.</summary>

# PROTAGORAS

<margin>A</margin> "My dear friend," I said, "if someone thinks of something alone, they immediately go around seeking someone to show it to and someone to confirm it with, until they find them. For this reason, I would rather discuss these things with you than with anyone else, believing that you are best able to examine everything a person of quality <note>Greek: *epieikē*, referring to a reasonable or morally upright person.</note> ought to consider, and especially the nature of virtue. For who else but you? You not only believe yourself to be noble and good <note>Greek: *kalos kagathos*, the traditional Athenian ideal of a gentleman.</note>—as some others are who are themselves decent but cannot make others so—but you are both good yourself and capable of making others good. You have such confidence in yourself that, while others hide their art, you openly proclaim yourself throughout all of Greece, calling yourself a <margin>B</margin> Sophist <note>At this time, 'Sophist' was a relatively new term for a professional teacher of wisdom and rhetoric.</note> and declaring yourself a teacher of education and virtue, being the first to deem it right to demand a fee for it. How, then, should I not call upon you for the investigation of these matters, asking questions and sharing thoughts? It is unavoidable. And now, regarding the things I first asked about, I desire to have some points recalled to my mind by you from the beginning, and to examine others together with you. The question, I believe, was this: wisdom, temperance, courage, justice, and holiness—are these five names <margin>C</margin> for one single thing, or does each of these names have its own distinct underlying essence <note>original: *ousia*</note> and its own specific function, such that one is not like the other? You said then that they were not just names for one thing, but that each of these names applied to a distinct thing, and that all of these were 'parts' of virtue. You said they were not like parts of gold, which are similar to one another and to the whole, but like the parts of a face, which are dissimilar to the whole and to each other, each having its own unique power. If these things still seem the same to you as they did then, say so; but if they seem otherwise, define them for me now. I will not hold you to your previous account if you say something different now, for I would not be surprised if you said those things before merely to test me."

"But I tell you, Socrates," he said, "that all these are indeed parts of virtue. Four of them are reasonably close to one another, but courage <note>original: *andreia*</note> is very <margin>D</margin> different from all the rest. You will know I speak the truth by this: you will find many men who are extremely unjust, unholy, intemperate, and ignorant, yet who are pre-eminently courageous."

"Hold on," I said, "for what you say is worth examining. Do you mean that the courageous are 'bold,' <note>The Greek *tharraleos* implies confidence or daring, which Socrates will distinguish from true courage.</note> or something else?"

"I mean they are bold," he said, "and ready to rush into things that most people are afraid to approach."

"Tell me then, do you say virtue is something beautiful? And is it as something beautiful that you offer yourself as a teacher of it?"

"It is the most beautiful thing of all," he replied, "unless I am out of my mind."

"Is it, then, partly shameful and partly beautiful, <margin>E</margin> or is it entirely beautiful?"

"It is entirely beautiful, as much as anything can be."

"Do you know, then, who dives boldly into wells?"

"I do: divers."

"Is it because they have knowledge, or for some other reason?"

"Because they have knowledge."

"And who are bold in fighting from horseback? Is it the horsemen, or those who cannot ride?"

"The horsemen."

"And who are bold with light shields <note>The *peltasts* were light infantry named after their crescent-shaped shields.</note>? Those trained as light-infantry, or those who are not?"

"The light-infantry. And in all other things," he said, "if this is what you are seeking, those who have knowledge are bolder than those who do not, and they are bolder after they have learned than they were before they learned."

"But have you seen some," I asked, "who are ignorant of all these things, yet are bold regarding each of them?"

"I have indeed," he said, "and very bold indeed."

"Are these bold people, then, also courageous?"

<margin>F</margin> "If that were so," he said, "courage would be a shameful thing, for these people are acting like madmen."

"How then," I asked, "do you define the courageous? Did you not say they are the bold?"

"And I say so still," he replied.

"Then," I said, "do not these people who are bold in this way appear to be not courageous but mad? And on the other hand, in our previous examples, were not the wisest also the boldest? and being the boldest, were they not the most courageous? And according to this logic, would not wisdom be courage?"

"You do not remember well, Socrates, what I said and answered to you. When I was asked by you if the courageous are bold, I agreed. But I was not asked if the bold are also courageous. For if you had asked me that then, I would have said 'not all of them.' And as for my agreement that the courageous are bold, you have nowhere demonstrated that I was wrong to agree. Next, you show that those who have knowledge <margin>G</margin> are bolder than they were themselves when they lacked it, and bolder than others who lack it; and in this, you think courage and wisdom are the same. By following this method, you might as well think that physical strength <note>original: *ischyn*</note> is wisdom. For first, if you asked me in this way whether the strong are powerful, I would say yes. Then, if you asked whether those who know how to wrestle are more powerful than those who do not, and more powerful than they were themselves before they learned, I would say yes. If I agreed to these things, it would be open to you, using these same proofs, to say that according to my agreement, wisdom is strength. But I do not agree, either here or there, that the powerful are necessarily strong, though I do say the strong are powerful. For 'power' <note>original: *dynamin*</note> and 'strength' <note>original: *ischyn*</note> are not the same thing. Power comes from knowledge, or even from madness or passion; but strength <margin>H</margin> comes from nature and the proper nourishment of bodies. In the same way, over there, boldness and courage are not the same thing."

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...we are all equipped for any work, word, and sense to be investigated. But if a man thinks of something alone, he soon goes about everywhere seeking someone with whom he may communicate, and by whom he may be confirmed, until he finds them. For this reason, I myself now dispute with you more willingly than with any other, thinking that you will best judge all things—both concerning all other matters which pertain to the judgment of an upright man, and concerning these especially, which I was seeking: namely, virtue. For whom <margin>B</margin> could I hope would do this better than you? You who not only consider yourself upright—whereas some others are indeed upright themselves but cannot make others so. You, however, are not only endowed with virtue, but you also promise to adorn other men with the same. And so you trust in your own talent that, while all others conceal their art, you alone profess it, and you openly declare yourself a Sophist throughout all Greece, as if by some public proclamation, declaring yourself a teacher of doctrine and virtue, and you are the first to demand a fee for that craft. Why then does anything stand in the way of you being employed before others for the discussion of these matters, and for questioning, and why should not all things be communicated with you? Nothing at all stands in the way. And indeed, I myself now desire that those things about which I first asked be partly brought back to my mind by you, <margin>C</margin> and partly discussed by common judgment. The question was such as this, I think: whether wisdom, temperance, fortitude, justice, and holiness are five names of the same thing, or whether there is a certain proper essence underlying each of these names, and a certain thing having its own power, so that one is not like the other. You said then that these names were by no means for one thing, but that individual names were applied to individual things. Furthermore, that all these are parts of virtue, not indeed as parts of gold are similar to each other and to the whole, but as the parts of a face are mutually dissimilar to each other and to the whole, being distinct by their own power. And tell me if you still affirm these things now as <margin>D</margin> you did above. But if you now feel otherwise, distinguish everything clearly. Truly, I will not hold it against you if you say something else now. For I do not wonder if you said those things then for the sake of testing Socrates.

<term>prot.</term> I say that all these are parts of virtue, of which four are sufficiently similar to one another. Fortitude <note>In this Latin translation, *fortitudo* is used for the Greek *andreia* (courage).</note>, however, differs far from the others. That I speak truly, you will know in this way: you will find some men who are most unjust, most profane, most intemperate, and most ignorant, who nevertheless excel others in fortitude.

<term>soc.</term> Pay attention, please; what you say must be considered. Do you call the brave "bold," or something else?

<term>p.</term> Indeed, I call those bold who rush headlong into those things from which most would be deterred.

<term>socr.</term> Come then, do you assert <margin>E</margin> virtue to be something honorable and beautiful, and do you teach it as something beautiful?

<term>pro.</term> Most beautiful indeed, unless perhaps I am insane.

<term>soc.</term> Is a certain part of this base and a certain part beautiful? Or is it beautiful as a whole?

<term>prot.</term> It is as beautiful as it can possibly be.

<term>socr.</term> Do you know those who boldly dive into wells?

<term>pro.</term> Indeed I do. Divers.

<term>socr.</term> Is it because of what they know, or because of something else?

<term>port.</term> Because they know.

<term>soc.</term> Which men are bold enough to fight most bravely from horses? Horsemen, or those unskilled in equestrian industry?

<term>prot.</term> Horsemen.

<term>socr.</term> Who fights boldly with shields? Peltasts, or others?

<term>prot.</term> Those men indeed; and in all other things, if you ask that, those who know are more <margin>F</margin> bold than those who do not know; and the same men, after they have learned, are more vehemently bold than when they were ignorant.

<term>so.</term> Have you ever seen any who were ignorant of all these things, but who were nevertheless bold toward all these things?

<term>prot.</term> I have seen them, and they were bold in the extreme.

<term>socr.</term> Are those bold ones brave?

<term>prot.</term> Fortitude would be a base thing, since those bold ones are furious <note>The Latin *furiosi* here captures the sense of madness or irrationality.</note>.

<term>socr.</term> Do you not say the brave are themselves bold?

<term>pro.</term> I said so indeed, and I say so now.

<term>so.</term> Have not those who are thus bold appeared to be by no means brave, but rather raving? And above, again, the wisest appeared to us to be the boldest, and because they are the boldest, therefore they are also the bravest; and so according to this reasoning, would not wisdom itself be fortitude?

<term>prot.</term> <margin>G</margin> You do not well remember, O Socrates, what I said above and answered to you. Indeed, asked by you whether brave men are bold or not, I agreed. But whether the bold were also brave, you did not ask. If you had asked then, I would have answered, "certainly not all." But that brave men are not bold, you have never shown to be granted by me, nor would I have rightly granted it. Therefore, you show that men who know are bolder than the ignorant, and bolder than themselves [before learning], and therefore you think wisdom and fortitude are the same. By proceeding in this way, you could think that strength <note>Latin: *robur*</note> and wisdom are the same. For if you had similarly asked me in this way, whether robust men are powerful, I would have certainly asserted it. Then, whether those skilled in wrestling are <margin>H</margin> more powerful for competing than the unskilled, and they themselves after they have learned more than when they were ignorant, I would have admitted it again. With me confessing these things, it would have been permitted for you to infer in the same way, by my concession, that wisdom is strength. But I nowhere at present confess that powerful men are robust. I do say, however, that robust men are powerful. And I do not think strength and power are the same. For power can proceed from knowledge, and from madness, and from anger; but strength comes only from nature and the proper nutrition of bodies. Similarly in those other things, they are by no means the same...

<summary>Socrates and Protagoras debate the relationship between knowledge and courage, with Socrates attempting to equate courage with wisdom. Protagoras resists, arguing that while all courageous people are bold, not all bold people—such as the unskilled or the mad—possess the virtue of courage.</summary>
