# PLATO'S PROTAGORAS

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...should be considered to be courage and boldness <note>Latin: *audacia*; Greek: *tharsos*. This refers to mere daring or confidence, which Socrates distinguishes from true courage.</note>. Therefore, it happens that brave men are indeed bold, but not all bold men are brave. For boldness comes to men from skill, from anger, or from madness, just as we said regarding power; but courage arises from nature and the proper cultivation of souls.
**Socrates:** Do you say, Protagoras, that some men live well, and others live badly?
**Protagoras:** I certainly do.
**Socrates:** Does a man seem to you to live well if he lives in distress and pain?
**Protagoras:** Not at all.
**Socrates:** But if someone has lived pleasantly until the end of his life, would he be said to have lived well?
**Protagoras:** Certainly.
**Socrates:** Therefore, to live pleasantly is good, and to live distressingly is bad.
**Protagoras:** Provided that he takes pleasure in honorable things.
**Socrates:** What? Protagoras, do you—like many others—call certain pleasant things "bad" and certain painful things "good"?
**Protagoras:** I do.
**Socrates:** Insofar as they are pleasant, <margin>B</margin> are they not good? Unless something else results from them? And again, is it not the same way with painful things?
**Protagoras:** Just so.
**Socrates:** Is it not because they are painful that they are bad?
**Protagoras:** I do not know, Socrates, whether it is right for me to answer so simply to your question—that all pleasant things are good and all painful things are bad. Rather, it seems safer for me to answer, not only for the present question but for the whole course of my life, that there are some pleasant things that are not good, and some painful things that are not bad; and again, there are some which are neutral, being neither good nor bad.
**Socrates:** <margin>C</margin> Do you call "pleasant" those things which either participate in pleasure or produce pleasure?
**Protagoras:** Exactly.
**Socrates:** I am asking this, then: whether they are not good insofar as they are pleasant. I am asking if pleasure itself is not a good.
**Protagoras:** As you always say, Socrates, let us consider this. If the consideration seems to lead to the matter, and the pleasant and the good appear to be the same, we shall agree; if not, then we shall proceed to debate.
**Socrates:** Would you like to lead this discussion? Or do you bid me to lead?
**Protagoras:** It is fair that you <margin>D</margin> be the leader, for you began the discourse.
**Socrates:** Perhaps in this way what we seek will become clear: just as if someone, wanting to consider a man's health or some other physical condition or function, were to look at his face and his hands and say, "Come now, bare your chest and back for me so I may inspect them more clearly." In this way, I now require the same for this discussion. For since I have learned your opinion regarding the good and pleasure from your words, I must say something like this: "Come, Protagoras, and reveal your mind on this as well—what do you think about knowledge <note>original: *scientia* / *epistēmē*</note>? Do you hold the same view as most people, or something else?" For regarding knowledge, most people judge that it is not something robust, nor does it lead, nor does it rule. They do not think of it <margin>E</margin> as a leader or a ruler. Instead, they think that even when knowledge is present in a man, it is not knowledge that rules him, but something else—now anger, now pleasure, now pain, sometimes love, and often fear. They think of knowledge as if it were a slave <note>original: *mancipio* / *andrapodou*. Socrates uses a provocative image of knowledge being "dragged around" by the passions.</note> dragged about by all these other things. Do you feel the same? Or do you think knowledge is something noble and a ruler in man, so that if someone discerns good and evil, he could never be led by anything else to do anything other than what knowledge commands—and that wisdom <margin>F</margin> alone is a sufficient aid for a man?
**Protagoras:** It seems to me as you say, Socrates. For if it is shameful for any man to deny that wisdom and knowledge are the most powerful of all human things, it is certainly most shameful for me.
**Socrates:** You speak beautifully and truly. But do you know that many people do not believe you or me? They say that many who know what is best, though they could do it, are unwilling to do so, but do other things instead. And whenever I have asked what the cause of this is, they answer that they do these things because they are overcome by pleasure, or pain, or one of the other things we mentioned.
**Protagoras:** Men say many other things incorrectly as well, Socrates.
**Socrates:** Come then, try with me to persuade men and teach them what this experience is <margin>G</margin> that they call "being overcome by pleasures," and for which reason they do not do the good they know. For perhaps if we say to them, "You are wrong, O men, and you are deceived," they will ask, "If this is not, Protagoras and Socrates, 'being overcome by pleasure,' then what else is it? What do you say it is? Explain it to us."
**Protagoras:** But why, Socrates, should we attend to the opinion of the many, who speak however it happens?
**Socrates:** I think this will help us find how courage stands in relation to the other parts of virtue. Therefore, if you think we should stick to our previous agreement that I should lead in the way I think we can best find what we seek, follow me. But if you prefer not to, and wish to stop, I will stop.
**Protagoras:** You speak rightly; proceed as you began.
**Socrates:** I, if they were to ask us again, "What then do you say this is, which we called being <margin>H</margin> overcome by pleasures?" I would answer them thus: "Listen then; Protagoras and I will try to declare it to you. For do you say, O men, that anything else happens here except what often occurs—namely, that men, lured and conquered by the pleasure of food, drink, and sex, take those things for themselves even if they know they are bad?" They would agree.
But we would then ask them, "Why do you say those things are bad?"

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...confidence and courage. Thus it happens that the courageous are confident, but not all the confident are courageous. For confidence comes to men from art, and from spirit, and from madness, like power; but courage comes from nature and the good nurturing of souls. "Do you say," I said, "O Protagoras, that some men live well, and others badly?" He said he did. "Do you think a man would live well if he lived in distress and pain?" He said not. "What if he ended his life having lived pleasantly? Would he not seem to you to have lived well thus?" "I think so," he said. "To live pleasantly, then, is good; to live unpleasantly, bad." "If indeed," he said, "he lives taking pleasure in beautiful things." "What then, Protagoras? Do you, like the many, call some <margin>B</margin> pleasant things bad, and some painful things good?" "I do." "How so? Insofar as they are pleasant, are they for that reason not good? Unless something else results from them? and again, the painful in the same way?" "Thus." "And is it not also that insofar as they are painful, they are bad?" "I do not know, Socrates," he said, "simply as you ask, whether I should answer that all pleasant things are good and all painful things are bad. But it seems to me safer, not only for this present answer but for all the rest of my life, to answer that there are some pleasant things which are not good, and some painful things which are not bad; and there is a third kind, which are neither, neither bad nor good." "And do you call pleasant," I said, "not those <margin>C</margin> participating in pleasure or making pleasure?" "Certainly," he said. "This then I say, insofar as they are pleasant, whether they are not good; I am asking whether pleasure itself is not good." "As you say each time, Socrates," he said, "let us look into it. And if the inquiry seems to be to the point, and the same thing appears to be both pleasant and good, we will agree; but if not, then we will dispute." "Whether then," I said, "do you want to lead the inquiry, or shall I lead?" "It is just," he said, "that you lead. For you also began the discourse." "Perhaps then," I said, "it might become manifest to us in this way, just as if someone, looking at a man's form, either for health or for some other of the body's works, having seen <margin>D</margin> his face and the ends of his hands, should say, 'Come now, uncover for me also your chest and your back, show them, so that I may inspect more clearly.' I also desire something like this for the inquiry. Having seen that you hold this view regarding the good and the pleasant, I need to say something like this: 'Come now, Protagoras, and reveal this part of your thought to me: how do you stand regarding knowledge? Does this also seem to you as it does to the many men, or otherwise? The many think something like this about knowledge: that it is not strong, nor leading, nor ruling. They do not think of it as such; but rather that while knowledge is often in a man, knowledge does not rule him, but something else does: sometimes spirit, sometimes pleasure, sometimes pain, sometimes love, <margin>E</margin> and often fear. They think of knowledge simply as a slave, being dragged around by all the others. Does it seem like that to you too? Or is knowledge something beautiful and such as to rule the man, and if one knows the good and the bad, he would not be conquered by anything so as to do anything other than what knowledge commands, but that wisdom is sufficient to help the man?'" "It seems so," he said, "as you say, Socrates; and at the same time, if it is shameful for anyone else, it is certainly shameful for me not to say that wisdom and knowledge are the most powerful of all human affairs." "You speak well," I said, "and truly. <margin>F</margin> Do you know then that most men do not believe you and me? But they say many people, knowing the best things, are not willing to do them, though they could, but do other things. And as many as I have asked what the cause of this is, they say that those who do these things do them being overcome by pleasure or pain, or one of those things I just mentioned." "For I think," he said, "Socrates, that men say many other things also not correctly." "Come then, with me, try to persuade the men and teach them what this experience is, which they say is 'being overcome by pleasures' and not doing the best things because of these, though they know them. For perhaps if we said to them, 'You do not speak correctly, O men, but you lie,' <margin>G</margin> and asked what 'being overcome by pleasure' is—what is it really, and what do you yourselves say it is?—they would tell us." "But why, Socrates, must we consider the opinion of the many men, who say whatever they happen to say?" "I think," I said, "this is of some use to us for finding out about courage, how it stands in relation to the other parts of virtue. If then it seems good to you to abide by what we just decided, that I should lead where I think it will become most clearly manifest, follow. But if you do not want to, if it pleases you, let it go." "Nay, you speak most rightly," he said, "and finish as you began." "Again then," I said, "if they asked us, 'What then do you say this is, which we called being weaker than pleasures?' I would say to them thus: 'Listen then; for Protagoras and I <margin>H</margin> will try to tell you. For do you say, O men, that this happens to you in these cases: for example, being often conquered by food and drink and sex, which are pleasant, and knowing they are bad, you nevertheless do them?' They would say so. Then you and I would ask them again, 'In what way are they bad?'"

# PROTAGORAS

<column-break/>

**Socrates:** How do you say it is? Is it because these things provide a present pleasure and soothe with sweetness? Or is it because in the future they lead to diseases, poverty, and many other things of this kind? Or even if they bring nothing of the sort in the future, are they bad simply because they cause one to rejoice, <note>Greek: *chairein*; Latin: *gaudere*. This refers to the act of experiencing joy or delight.</note> because a man learns to take pleasure in them? Do you think, Protagoras, that they would answer in any other way than that these things are bad not because of the present pleasure they work, but because of the diseases and other things that follow?

<margin>A</margin> **Protagoras:** I believe the masses would answer in that way.

**Socrates:** And in bringing about diseases, do they not bring about pains? And in bringing about poverty, do they not bring about pain? They would agree, I think.

**Protagoras:** Certainly.

<margin>B</margin> **Socrates:** Therefore, O men, these things appear bad to you—as Protagoras and I also believe—for no other reason than that they end in pains and deprive one of other pleasures. They would confess it.

**Protagoras:** Without a doubt.

**Socrates:** If, on the other hand, we were to ask the opposite: "O men, you who say that painful things are also good, do you not mean things such as physical exercises, military service, and medical treatments performed by doctors through cutting, burning, drugs, or fasting? Do you say these are good, but painful?" They would agree.

**Protagoras:** They would.

**Socrates:** Do you call these things good because they inflict extreme pains and tortures at the moment? Or rather because health, a good bodily condition, <margin>C</margin> the safety of the country, power, and wealth follow from them in the future? They would say it is for that reason, I imagine.

**Protagoras:** I judge so as well.

**Socrates:** But are these things good for any other reason than that they result in pleasures and drive away or avoid troubles? Can you point to any other end <term>end (Latin: *finem*; Greek: *telos*): the ultimate goal or purpose of an action</term> toward which you look when you call these things good, other than pleasures and pains? They would say they cannot, I think.

**Protagoras:** I do not think they could either.

**Socrates:** Therefore, do you not pursue pleasure as a good and flee pain as an evil? They would concede.

**Protagoras:** Indeed.

**Socrates:** Consequently, you consider pain to be the evil and pleasure the good, since you say that even "rejoicing" <note>Greek: *to chairein*; Latin: *oblectationem*.</note> itself is bad only when it deprives one of greater pleasures than it offers, <margin>D</margin> or when it brings about pains more intense than the pleasures within it. For if you called rejoicing itself "bad" for some other reason, or by looking toward some other end, you would be able to show us. But you will not be able to.

**Protagoras:** They do not seem able to me either.

**Socrates:** Similarly, you say that pain itself is a good only when it drives away greater pains than it inflicts, or induces pleasures more intense than the pains. For if you judged pain to be a good by looking toward some other end, you could show us; but you will not be able to.

**Protagoras:** You speak the truth, Socrates.

<margin>E</margin> **Socrates:** If you were to ask me in turn, "O men, why do you speak so much and in so many ways about this?"—forgive me, I would answer immediately. For first, it is not easy to demonstrate what this experience is that you call "being overcome by pleasure." Second, all the proofs depend on this point. Even now, if you have some other way to say what the good is other than pleasure, or what the evil is other than pain, you are free to declare it. Is it enough for you to lead a pleasant life without distress? If it is enough, and you cannot name any other good or evil that does not end in these, listen to what follows. I tell you that if this is so, <margin>F</margin> your argument becomes ridiculous when you say that "a man, knowing that evil things are evil, nevertheless does them (when he could choose not to) because he is drawn and overcome by pleasure." And again you say that "a man, though conscious of what is good, is unwilling to do it because he is bound by a present pleasure."

That these claims are ridiculous will become clear if we stop using so many names—"pleasant," "painful," "good," and "evil." Since it has been established that there are only two things here, let us call them by only two names: first, "good" and "evil," and then "pleasant" and "painful." Having set this, let us say: "A man, knowing that evils are evil, nevertheless does them." If someone asks us "Why?", we will say "Because he was overcome." "By what?" he will ask. <margin>G</margin> But it is no longer permitted for us to say "by pleasure," for "good" has taken the place of the name "pleasure." So we answer him and say, "Because he was overcome." "By what?" he will ask. "By the good," we will answer, by Zeus!

Now, if the one questioning us happens to be a mocking man, he will surely laugh and say: "What an absurd thing you say! If someone does evil, knowing it is evil, when he ought not do it, because he was overcome by the good! Are these goods," he will ask, "not worthy of winning out over the evils, or are they worthy?" We will clearly answer that they were not worthy; for otherwise the man we say was "overcome by pleasures" would not have erred. "But in what way," he might ask, "are the goods unworthy of the evils, or the evils of the goods? Is it by any other measure than that some are greater and some are smaller? Or some are more and some are fewer?" <margin>H</margin> We certainly will have no other reason to give. He will then add: "It is clear then, that 'being overcome' means taking greater evils in exchange for smaller goods."

So much for that. Let us now switch the names back to "pleasant" and "painful" for these same things. We previously said a man does "evil" things; let us now say he does "painful" things, knowing they are painful, because he is overcome by "pleasant" things—which are clearly unworthy of victory. And what other "unworthiness" is there in a pleasure compared to a pain, except for an excess of...

<summary>Socrates uses a logical substitution to argue that "being overcome by pleasure" is an absurd concept if pleasure is the only good. He demonstrates that this phenomenon is actually a mistake in calculation, where a person chooses a small immediate pleasure at the cost of greater future pain.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: Socrates continues his dialogue with Protagoras and the gathered Sophists. Having established that "good" is essentially "pleasant" and "evil" is "painful," he is now deconstructing the common phrase "being overcome by pleasure."</meta>

# OF PLATO

...between themselves and their deficiencies? That is, when they become greater or smaller than one another, more or fewer, more intense or more relaxed. If someone should say: "But Socrates, there is a great difference between a present pleasure and a pleasure or pain that is yet to come," I would reply: "In any other way than by pleasure and pain? For it cannot be otherwise." It is just as if a man skilled in weighing were to collect the pleasant things on one side and the painful things on the other—those that are near as well as those that are far—and, placing them in the balance, say which are more. For if you weigh pleasures against pleasures, the greater and more numerous must always be chosen; if you compare pains to pains, the fewer and smaller; if you weigh delights against pains, then if the painful are outweighed by the pleasant—whether the near by the remote, or the remote by the near—one must choose that course of action in which the pleasures are found. <note>The Latin text here uses a Greek fragment; the full sense is: "one must perform that action in which these [pleasures] are present."</note> But if the pleasures are outweighed by the pains, that action is not to be done. Is it any other way, O men? I know they could bring no other answer. 

**Protagoras:** I myself am of the same opinion.

->**B**<-

**Socrates:** Since this is the case, I will ask them this: "Do the same masses appear larger to your eyes when close at hand, and smaller from a distance?" They will say yes, I think. And likewise with thickness and number? And do equal voices seem louder near at hand, but smaller from afar? They would agree. "If, then, our well-being and happiness consisted in this—that is, in constructing and accepting great masses while rejecting small ones—what would be the chief salvation of our lives? Would it be the art of measurement? Or rather the power of appearances, which shows how great a thing seems to be?" Surely the power of appearance would deceive us, and by confusing us with error, it would often force us to judge the same things differently at different times, causing us to change our minds repeatedly in our choices of great and small. But the faculty of measurement <note>Latin: *dimetiendi facultas*; Greek: *μετρητικὴ τέχνη* (metrētikē technē). Socrates argues that ethics is a form of calculation or "moral geometry."</note> would render this illusion void, and by revealing the truth, it would give peace to the soul resting upon that truth, and thus preserve our life. Would men agree to this or not? That we are saved by the art of measurement?

**Protagoras:** By that very art.

->**D**<-

**Socrates:** What further? If the salvation of our life consisted in the choice of even and odd—when it was necessary to correctly choose the more and when the less, whether comparing a thing to itself or one thing to another, whether near or far—what would chiefly save our lives? Would it not be knowledge? And specifically a kind of measurement, since that is the art of excess and defect? And since it concerns the even and the odd, would it be any other than the science of arithmetic? Would men grant us this, or not?

**Protagoras:** Without controversy.

**Socrates:** Come then, O men. Since it is certain that the salvation of life consists in the correct choice of pleasure and pain—that is, in the choice of the more and the fewer, the greater and the smaller, the nearer and the more remote—does it not follow that the faculty of measurement is primarily a consideration of excess, defect, and mutual equality? 

**Protagoras:** Necessarily. 

**Socrates:** And since it is a faculty of measurement, it must necessarily be an art and a science. 

**Protagoras:** They would grant it.

->**E**<-

**Socrates:** What specific science this may be, we shall consider another time. For now, it is enough that it is a science, regarding that demonstration which I and Protagoras were going to give to your question. This, if you remember, was the question: We agreed that nothing is more powerful than knowledge, and that wherever it is present, it always dominates pleasure and all other things. But you objected that pleasure often dominates even the man who knows. Since we did not grant this to you, you immediately asked: "If this is not 'being overcome by pleasures,' O Protagoras and Socrates, but something else, then declare what it is." If we had answered you then and there that it is "ignorance," <note>Latin: *inscitia*; Greek: *ἀμαθία* (amathia). In Socratic thought, no one does evil knowingly; they only do it because they miscalculate the "size" of the pleasure vs. the pain.</note> you would have laughed at us. But now, if you laugh at us, you will also be laughing at yourselves. For you yourselves confessed a little while ago that those who err in the choice of pleasure and pain do so from a defect of knowledge—and these are the "goods" and the "evils." Nor did you say it was merely a defect of knowledge, but specifically a defect of the science of measurement.

<margin>To be overcome by pleasures is extreme ignorance.</margin>

->**F**<-

An action that goes astray, and which knowledge does not rule—as you are well aware—comes from ignorance. Therefore, what is commonly called "being overcome by pleasures" is actually extreme ignorance. Of this disease, Protagoras here, and Prodicus, and Hippias <note>These are the three famous Sophists present. Socrates is playfully suggesting that if people realized their "vice" was just a lack of measurement-skills, they would pay these teachers to fix them.</note> profess themselves to be the doctors. But because you think this is something other than ignorance, you do not send yourselves or your children to be cured by these Sophists, who are the teachers of such matters, as if virtue could not be taught. Instead, because you are watchful of your money and do not give it to these instructors, you fail in both private and public life. This is plainly what we would have answered the common people.

->**G**<-

But now I ask you as well, O Prodicus and Hippias, along with Protagoras—for let this discourse be common to you all—whether I seem to speak the truth or falsehood? It seemed to all of them that what had been said was very true. "Do you agree then," I said, "that what is pleasant is good, and what is painful is evil? I reject that distinction of names which Prodicus here is accustomed to introduce, and I ask for his judgment. For whether you call it 'pleasurable,' or 'delightful,' or 'joyful,' or whatever name you please, my excellent Prodicus, answer me according to my intent." Smiling, Prodicus gave his assent, and the others likewise agreed. Then I said: "What of this, O men? Are not all actions that lead to a life free from pain and full of sweetness noble and useful? And is not a noble work both good and useful?" They agreed. "If then," I said, "the pleasant is good, no one who either knows or believes other things to be better...

<column-break/>

->**A**<-

...is there anything else but excess and defect of one another? These occur when they become greater or smaller than each other, more or fewer, more and less. For if someone should say, "But Socrates, the pleasure of the moment differs greatly from the pleasure and pain of the future," I would say, "In what other way does it differ than by pleasure and pain? For there is no other way." But like a man good at weighing, having put together the pleasant things and having put together the painful things, and having set both the near and the far in the balance, say which are more. For if you weigh pleasant things against pleasant, the greater and more numerous are always to be taken; if painful against painful, the fewer and smaller. If you weigh pleasant against painful, and the painful are exceeded by the pleasant—whether the near by the far or the far by the near—that action is to be done in which these are present; but if the pleasant are exceeded by the painful, it is not to be done. Does it stand any other way, O men? I know they could not say otherwise. He also agreed. "Since then this is so, answer me this," I shall say: "do the same magnitudes appear larger to your sight from near, but smaller from afar? Or not?" They will say yes. And thick things and many things likewise? and equal sounds are louder from near, but smaller from afar? They would say so. If then our well-doing depended on this, on performing and taking the large lengths and avoiding and not performing the small, what would have appeared as the salvation of our life? Would it be the art of measurement, or the power of appearance? Or did this [the power of appearance] lead us astray, and make us take and regret the same things many times over, both in our choices and in our actions concerning the large and small? While the art of measurement would have made this phantom of appearance powerless; and by showing the truth, would have made the soul have peace, remaining in the truth, and would have saved our life? Would men agree to these things, that the art of measurement would save us, or some other? He agreed it was the art of measurement. "What then, if the salvation of our life were in the choice of odd and even, when it was necessary to choose the 'more' correctly and when the 'less,' either itself against itself or one against the other, whether near or far? What would save our life? Would it not be knowledge? And some kind of measurement? Since the art is one of excess and defect? And since it is of odd and even, is it any other than arithmetic? Would men agree with us? Or not?" Protagoras also thought they would agree. "Very well, O men; since the salvation of our life has appeared to us to be in the correct choice of pleasure and pain, which is of the more and the less, and the greater and smaller, and the farther and nearer, does it not first appear to be measurement, being an inquiry into excess and defect and equality with one another?" "It must be so." "And since it is measurement, it must surely be an art and knowledge." They will agree. What this art and knowledge actually is, we shall inquire another time. But that it is knowledge is enough for the proof that I and Protagoras must give regarding what you asked us. [Addressing] Protagoras (since you mentioned it), when we were agreeing with one another that nothing is stronger than knowledge, but that it always rules wherever it is present, over both pleasure and all other things; and you said that pleasure often rules even the man who knows; and since we did not agree with you, you then asked us, "O Protagoras and Socrates, if this experience is not 'being overcome by pleasure,' then what is it, and what do you say it is? Tell us." If then we had told you immediately that it is ignorance, you would have laughed at us; but now if you laugh at us, you will also laugh at yourselves. For you have agreed that those who err concerning the choice of pleasures and pains (and these are goods and evils) err through a defect of knowledge; and not only of knowledge, but of that which you further agreed was measurement. And an action that is erred in without knowledge, you know yourselves that it is done through ignorance, so that this is what "being overcome by pleasure" is—the greatest ignorance; of which Protagoras here says he is a doctor, as do Prodicus and Hippias. But you, because you think it is something else than ignorance, neither go yourselves nor send your children to the teachers of these things, these Sophists, as though it were not a thing that can be taught; but being careful of your money and not giving it to them, you fare badly both in private and in public. These things we would have answered to the masses. But I ask you, Hippias and Prodicus, along with Protagoras (for let the discourse be shared among you), whether I seem to you to speak the truth or to lie. It seemed to all of them that what had been said was wonderfully true. "Do you agree then," I said, "that the pleasant is good, and the painful is evil? And I beg to be excused from the 'distinction of names' of Prodicus here; for whether you say 'pleasant,' or 'delightful,' or 'joyous,' or from whatever source and however you like to name such things, O best Prodicus, answer me this in the way I want." Prodicus laughed and agreed, and the others too. "What then?" I said, "O men, are not all the actions that are performed toward this end, that one may live without pain and pleasantly, are they not noble and useful? And is not the noble work both good and useful?" They agreed. "If then," I said, "the pleasant is good, no one either knowing or believing other things to be better than...

<margin>A</margin> ...better than those things he did or could have done; but rather, he does these things because he is able to, even though better options are available. Therefore, "to be overcome" is nothing other than <term>ignorance<note>Greek: *amathia*; Latin: *inscitia*. In Socratic philosophy, this refers to a fundamental lack of understanding regarding what is truly good for the soul.</note></term>, and "to master oneself" is nothing other than wisdom. Everyone agreed. "What then? Do you not say that ignorance is something of this sort: having a false opinion and being deceived about matters of great importance?" This also they all accepted. "What then?" (I said). "Is it not true that no one willingly goes toward what is evil, nor toward what he thinks is evil? It seems it is not in the nature of man to be willing to go toward what he thinks is evil instead of what is good. And when a man is forced to choose between two evils, no one will choose the greater if it is possible to choose the lesser." All these things seemed right to all of us. "What then?" (I said). "Do you call <term>dread<note>Greek: *deos*; Latin: *timor*.</note></term> something like fear? And is it—I am speaking to you, Prodicus—what I call an expectation of evil? "These things being so," (I said), "Prodicus and Hippias, let Protagoras here defend for us how his first answer can be correct—not the very first one, for then he said that of the five parts of virtue, no one was like the other, and each had its own power. By this you may know that courage differs greatly from the other parts of virtue.' And I was immediately astonished by that answer then, and even more so now that I have discussed these things with you. I asked him then if he called the courageous 'bold' or 'daring.' "Do cowards go toward what is bold, while the courageous go toward what is fearsome?" "So it is said by men, Socrates." "You speak the truth," (I said). "But that is not what I am asking. Rather, toward what do *you* say the courageous are headlong? Is it toward fearsome things, believing them to be fearsome? Or toward things that are not?" "But that," (he said), "was just shown to be impossible in the arguments you just gave." "And in this also you speak the truth," (I said). "So if this was correctly demonstrated, no one goes toward what he believes to be fearsome, since being 'overcome by oneself' was found to be ignorance." He admitted it. "Yet everyone goes toward what they feel confident about, both cowards and the <margin>E</margin> courageous; and in this sense, both cowards and courageous go toward the same things." "But nevertheless, Socrates," (he said), "the things toward which cowards and courageous men go are entirely opposite. For instance, the courageous are willing to go to war, but the cowards are not." "Is going to war noble," (I said), "or is it shameful?" "It is noble," he said. "And if it is noble, we agreed before it is also good. For we agreed that all noble actions are good." "You speak the truth," he said, "and it always seems so to me." "Rightly so," I said. "But which ones do you say are unwilling to go to war, when it is noble and good?" "The cowards," <margin>F</margin> he said. "And if it is noble and good," (I said), "is it not also pleasant?" "That was indeed agreed," he said. "Do the cowards then, knowing this, refuse to go toward that which is nobler, better, and more pleasant?" "But if I admit this," (he said), "I shall overturn our previous agreements." "And what of the courageous man? Does he not go toward what is nobler, better, and more pleasant?" "One must admit it," he said. "In short, then, the courageous do not fear shameful fears, when they fear, nor are they bold with shameful boldness." "True," he said. "And if not shameful, are they not noble?" He agreed. "And if noble, then also good?" "Yes." "And do not the cowards, the rash, and the <margin>G</margin> mad, on the contrary, fear shameful fears and show shameful boldness?" He agreed. "And do they show boldess in shameful and evil things for any other reason than through lack of knowledge and ignorance?" "It is so," he said. "What then? This thing by which cowards are cowards—do you call it cowardice or courage?" "Cowardice, surely," he said. "And did it not appear that they are cowards because of their ignorance of what is fearsome?" "Entirely so," he said. "It is through this ignorance, then, that they are cowards." He admitted it. "And that which makes them cowards is agreed by you to be cowardice?" He concurred. "Then the ignorance of what is fearsome and what is not fearsome would be cowardice?" He nodded. "But surely," (I said), "courage is the opposite of cowardice." "It is," he said. "Therefore, the <term>wisdom<note>Greek: *sophia*; Latin: *sapientia*. Here Socrates equates virtue with a specific type of expert knowledge.</note></term> regarding what is fearsome and what is not fearsome is the opposite of the ignorance of these things?" And here he still nodded. "And the ignorance of these things is cowardice?" With great difficulty, he nodded here. "Therefore, the wisdom of what is fearsome and what is not fearsome is courage, being the opposite of the ignorance of these things." At this, he would no longer nod, and he remained silent. And I said, "Why, Protagoras, will you neither say yes nor no to what I ask?" He said, "Finish it yourself."

<margin>A</margin> ...the better of those things he has done and can do: then he does these things when he could do better. But as for what is called <margin>Ignorance.</margin> "being overcome by passions," it is nothing other than ignorance; and to rule over passions is nothing but wisdom. This pleased everyone. For he said in what followed that four parts of virtue were close enough to one another, but one of them—namely, courage—differed far from the rest. He said this could be inferred from the fact that many men were found to be most courageous, who were nevertheless most profane, most unjust, most intemperate, and most ignorant; from which he wished it to be clear that courage differs most from all other parts of <margin>D</margin> virtue." I was immediately and vehemently astonished by his answer, and much more so after I treated these things with you. Therefore, I inquired of him whether he called the brave 'audacious.' He indeed added 'headlong' besides. "Do you remember, Protagoras, that you answered these things?" PROTAGORAS: "I remember." SOCRATES: "Tell us, I pray, toward what do you call headlong men brave? SOCRATES: "Do the timid approach things to be dared, and the brave things to be feared?" PROTAGORAS: "So it is said, Socrates." SOCRATES: "You tell the truth. But I do not ask this; rather, toward what do you call the headlong brave? SOCRATES: "Is it not true that if it is honorable, we agreed above that it is also <margin>F</margin> good? For it is agreed that all honorable and beautiful actions are also good." PROTAGORAS: "You speak the truth, and indeed it always seems so to me." SOCRATES: "Excellent. But whom do you say are unwilling to go into battle, when that journey is beautiful and good?" PROTAGORAS: "The timid." SOCRATES: "Is it not true that if it is beautiful and good, it is also pleasant?" PROTAGORAS: "It is conceded." SOCRATES: "Do the timid then, knowing this, refuse to proceed to that which is beautiful, better, and more pleasant?" PROTAGORAS: "But if we admit this, we shall pervert what was agreed upon above." SOCRATES: "What further? Does not the brave man tend toward what is beautiful, better, and more pleasant?" PROTAGORAS: "It is necessary to confess it." SOCRATES: "Altogether, therefore, brave men neither fear shamefully, if they ever fear, nor <margin>G</margin> are they bold shamefully." PROTAGORAS: "It is so." SOCRATES: "If not shamefully, then honorably and beautifully?" PROTAGORAS: "Certainly." SOCRATES: "And if honorably, then also well?" PROTAGORAS: "Indeed." SOCRATES: "Is it not true that the timid, the fierce, and the mad, on the contrary, are bold shamefully and fear shamefully?" PROTAGORAS: "That is true." SOCRATES: "But do they show boldness shamefully and badly for any other cause than through ignorance and lack of knowledge?" PROTAGORAS: "For this very reason." SOCRATES: "This thing by which they are timid, do you call it cowardice or courage?" PROTAGORAS: "Cowardice." SOCRATES: "And did not the timid appear to be so because of their ignorance of things to be feared?" PROTAGORAS: "Truly." SOCRATES: "Therefore, they are timid because of this ignorance?" PROTAGORAS: "Certainly." SOCRATES: "But you asserted that that which makes them timid is cowardice." PROTAGORAS: "I did." SOCRATES: "Therefore, is not the ignorance of things to be feared and things not to be feared, cowardice?" PROTAGORAS: "It will be." <margin>H</margin> SOCRATES: "Truly, courage is the opposite of cowardice." PROTAGORAS: "Without doubt." SOCRATES: "Is not the wisdom of things to be feared and not to be feared contrary to the ignorance of those same things?" PROTAGORAS: "Utterly." SOCRATES: "And the ignorance of these things is cowardice." PROTAGORAS: "Most certainly." SOCRATES: "The wisdom, therefore, of things to be feared and not to be feared is courage, existing as the opposite of the ignorance of these same things." No further would Protagoras nod, but he remained silent. Then I said: "Why are you silent, Protagoras? Why do you neither nod nor refuse?" "Finish the matter yourself," he said.

<summary>Socrates systematically breaks down Protagoras's claim that courage is distinct from knowledge, forcing him to admit that courage is the wisdom of knowing what truly deserves to be feared. The dialogue concludes that cowardice is simply a form of ignorance, effectively uniting all virtues under the umbrella of knowledge.</summary>

# PROTAGORAS

<margin>A</margin> I will conclude immediately, I said, if I may ask just this one thing: whether you still believe now, as you did before, that there are some people who are utterly ignorant and yet remain the most courageous. You seem, Socrates, he replied, to be contentiously striving to make me the one who answers. Therefore, I will gratify you. I say that it seems impossible, based on what we have previously conceded. I do not question you about all these things, I said, for any other reason than that I desire to know the nature of those things which pertain to virtue, or what virtue itself is. For I know that once this is declared, that matter will also be made known which both you and I have spent so many words upon: while I denied that virtue could be taught, and you, on the other hand, asserted that it could. But I think the outcome of our discussion, if it could use a human voice, would mock us and rebuke us in this way: "How foolish you both are, <margin>B</margin> Socrates and Protagoras! You, Socrates, were saying from the beginning that virtue could not be taught, yet now you strive to contradict yourself by showing that all these things—justice, temperance, and courage—are <term>knowledge<note>Greek: *episteme*; Latin: *scientia*. Socrates argues that if virtue is a form of knowledge, it must be teachable, contradicting his opening stance.</note></term>. By this reasoning, it is most clearly established that virtue can be taught. For if virtue were something other than knowledge, as Protagoras first asserted, it plainly could not be taught. But now if it appears to be knowledge, as you, Socrates, are trying to prove, it would be a wonder if virtue could not be acquired through instruction. Protagoras, however, originally wanted virtue to be teachable; now, conversely, he seems to struggle to make virtue appear to be anything rather than knowledge, <margin>C</margin> by which means it would be the least teachable of all." Indeed, Protagoras, seeing all these things so terribly overturned and confused, I am applying myself with great zeal so that they might come to light. And I would wish that, having run through these things together, we might show what virtue is, and likewise consider whether it can be taught or not—lest that famous <term>Epimetheus<note>Epimetheus (Afterthought) and Prometheus (Forethought) are brothers in Greek myth. Protagoras earlier told a myth where Epimetheus forgot to give humans survival traits, and Prometheus had to steal fire to save them.</note></term> deceive us again in our discussion, just as he neglected us in the distribution of traits, as you narrated. For Prometheus pleases me more than Epimetheus in the fable; and using his example, I handle all these matters by being "Promethean"—that is, looking forward—concerning my whole life. And if you are willing, as I said from the beginning, I would most gladly deliberate on these matters with you. Then Protagoras said, Socrates, I praise this zeal <margin>D</margin> of yours and the course of your discourse. For although other vices may be far from me, if my opinion does not deceive me, envy is certainly the furthest of all. Indeed, I have already said to many concerning you that I admire you most of all those I have met, certainly among your peers. I will go so far as to say it would not be a wonder to me if you became famous for your pursuit of wisdom. But we shall discuss these things another time, whenever you wish. For now, it is time for me to turn to other matters. So be it, I said, if it seems right to you, since for some time now it was time for me to depart; yet I remained to gratify Callias, that honorable young man. Having said and heard these things, we departed.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> "If," I said, "I might ask you just one more thing: whether it still seems to you, as it did then, that there are some men who are most ignorant, yet most courageous?" "You seem to me, Socrates," he said, "to still be fond of contention, wanting me to be the one answering. I will therefore gratify you, and I say that from what has been agreed upon, it seems to me to be impossible." "I am not," I said, "asking all these things for any other reason than wanting to examine how the matters of virtue stand, and what virtue itself is. For I know that if this were to become clear, that other thing would also become most evident, about which both you and I have drawn out a long discourse—I saying that virtue is not teachable, and you saying that it is. And it seems to me that the recent conclusion of our words, as if it were a person, would accuse and laugh at us. <margin>B</margin> And if it took a voice, it would say, 'You are strange men, Socrates and Protagoras! You, on the one hand, saying before that virtue is not teachable, are now hastening to the opposite, attempting to demonstrate that all things—justice, and temperance, and courage—are knowledge. In this way, virtue would most certainly appear to be teachable. For if virtue were something other than knowledge (as Protagoras was attempting to say), it would clearly not be teachable; but if it now appears to be entirely knowledge, as you are striving for, Socrates, it will be a wonder if it is not teachable. Protagoras, on the other hand, having then assumed it was teachable, now seems to be striving for the opposite, so that it might appear to be almost anything rather than knowledge; and thus it would be the least teachable of all.'" "I, therefore, Protagoras, seeing all these things terribly disturbed upside down, have every <margin>C</margin> eagerness for them to become clear; and I would wish us to go through these things and reach what virtue is, and then to examine it again, whether it is teachable or not teachable—lest that Epimetheus should trip us up and deceive us in our examination, just as he neglected us in the distribution, as you say. In the myth, Prometheus pleased me more than Epimetheus; and using him, and being 'promethean' <note>The Greek *promethoumenos* means "acting with forethought," a pun on the name Prometheus.</note> on behalf of my whole life, I busy myself with all these things; and, if you were willing, as I said at the beginning, I would most gladly look into these things together with you." And Protagoras said, "Socrates, I praise your eagerness and the way you go through your arguments. For I do not <margin>D</margin> think I am a bad man in other respects, and I am the least envious of men. Indeed, I have already said to many about you that of those I meet, I admire you by far the most, and of those your age, entirely so. And I say that I would not be surprised if you became one of the men distinguished for wisdom. But we shall go through these things another time, whenever you wish; for now it is already hour to turn to something else." "But," I said, "it is necessary to do so, if it seems right to you. For to me also it was time to go long ago, as I said; but I stayed to please the handsome Callias." Having said and heard these things, we went away.

# EUTHYDEMUS, OR, THE CONTENTIOUS.

> *SUMMARY OF THE DIALOGUE: In this, as in the previous dialogue, that question is treated: whether virtue can be taught. This is what the Sophists, with their haughty confidence, most strongly affirmed. Generally, the useless exhaustion of long-winded disputes is shown—about "goat's wool," as they say <note>Latin: *de lana caprina*. A proverb meaning a debate over something entirely worthless or non-existent.</note>—from which no fruit returns to mankind. The specific thesis of this disputation is concerning the false methods of acquiring knowledge, just as they are observed in the Sophists; and this is opposed to the teaching handed down in the 'Theages'. For having placed before our eyes their silly sophistical vanity, Plato demonstrates the emptiness of the Sophists, who professed themselves masters of learning. He teaches their foolish and insane ignorance, and their shameful greed, which even busies itself with making a profit from such great matters, so that the impure Sophists are merchants, or rather <term>hucksters<note>Latin: *caupones*. A derogatory term comparing Sophists to innkeepers who "water down" their goods for profit.</note></term>, of virtue and the soul. Having pointed out the vanity of the Sophists, Plato teaches in the conclusion of the speech that although the Sophists abuse the name and knowledge of philosophy, it is by no means to be allowed that the disgrace, which ought to remain with the authors alone, should result in hatred and envy toward true philosophy; which sufficiently protects itself against all the impostures of all Sophists with the certain and solid fruit of useful knowledge.*

CRITO, SOCRATES, EUTHYDEMUS, DIONYSODORUS, CLINIAS, CTESIPPUS.

# EUTHYDEMUS

<columns>
<margin>A</margin>
...I would simply cease. For my part, I did not even know before now that they were <term>pancratiasts<note>The *pancration* was an ancient Greek martial art combining wrestling and boxing; here Socrates uses it metaphorically for the sophists' "all-around" combat style in debate.</note></term>. These two are truly "all-fighters," quite unlike the two brothers from Acarnania who are pancratiasts. For those two are only able to fight with their bodies. But these two, first of all, are most formidable with their bodies in that kind of combat which is the most powerful of all—for they themselves are very skilled at fighting in armor, and they are able to make anyone else they teach similarly skilled. Furthermore, they are most powerful in the combat of the law courts, both in competing themselves and in teaching others to speak and to compose the kinds of speeches used in the courts. Previously, they were clever only in these matters, but now they have put the finishing touch on their "all-fighting" art. For they have now perfected that one remaining form of combat which was previously unmentioned, so that no one is able 
<margin>B</margin>
to stand against them. They have become so formidable at fighting in words, and at refuting whatever is said, whether it be false or true. Therefore, Crito, I have it in mind to hand myself over to these men. For they say that in a short time they can make anyone else formidable in these same skills.

**CRITO:** But what, Socrates? Are you not afraid of your age, that you might already be too old?

**SOCRATES:** Not at all, Crito; I have sufficient proof and encouragement not to be afraid. For these two, as the saying goes, were already old men when they began this wisdom which I desire—the <term>eristic<note>The art of verbal dispute or "wrangling," focused on winning an argument rather than discovering truth.</note></term> art. Only last year or the year before, they were not yet wise in it. I only fear one thing: that I might become a disgrace to these strangers, just as I have to Connus the son of Metrobius, the harp-player, who is still even now teaching me to play the harp. When the boys who are my fellow-students see me, 
<margin>C</margin>
they laugh at me and call Connus "the teacher of old men." I fear someone might level this same reproach against these strangers; and they, perhaps fearing this very thing, might not be willing to accept me. But I, Crito, have persuaded other old men to go there as fellow-students with me, and here I will try to persuade others. And why don't you also come along? We might even bring your sons to them as bait. For in their desire for the young men, they will surely be willing to educate us as well.

**CRITO:** Nothing prevents it, Socrates, if it seems best to you. But first, explain to me what the wisdom of these two men is, so that we may know what we are going to learn.

**SOCRATES:** You shall hear at once, for I cannot say that
<margin>D</margin>
I did not pay close attention to them. I attended very carefully and I remember it all; I will try to relate everything to you from the beginning. By some divine chance, I happened to be sitting alone in the place where the athletes undress, just where you saw me, and I was already intending to get up. But as I was rising, the usual <term>divine sign<note>Socrates' *daimonion*, an inner voice that often warned him against certain actions.</note></term> occurred. So I sat down again, and a little later these two entered—Euthydemus and Dionysodorus—and many other students with them, it seemed to me. Having entered, they began to walk about in the covered track. They had not yet completed two or three laps when Clinias entered, who you say has made such great progress—and you speak truly. Behind him were a great many lovers and others, including Ctesippus, a young man from the deme of Paeania, 
<margin>E</margin>
very handsome and noble, but somewhat insolent in his nature due to his youth. Clinias, seeing me from the entrance sitting alone, came straight toward me and sat down at my right, just as you say. When Dionysodorus and Euthydemus saw him, they first stood and talked with one another, glancing at us from time to time (for I was paying very close attention to them), and then they approached. Euthydemus sat down by the youth, and Dionysodorus sat by me on the left; the others sat wherever they happened to find a place. I greeted them, as I had not seen them for a long time. After this, I said to 
<margin>F</margin>
Clinias: "Clinias, these two men, Euthydemus and Dionysodorus, are wise not in small matters, but in great ones. For they know everything pertaining to war—all that a man who is to be a good general needs to know—both the tactics and the command of armies, and how to fight in armor. They are also able to make a man capable of defending himself in the law courts if anyone treats him unjustly." When I said this, they looked down on me. Both laughed, looking at one another, and Euthydemus said: "We no longer take those matters seriously, Socrates; we treat them as mere hobbies." I was amazed and said: "Your serious work must be beautiful indeed, if such great matters are mere hobbies to you. Tell me, by the gods, what is this beautiful work?" 

"Virtue," he said, "O Socrates; we believe we are 
<margin>G</margin>
able to transmit it better and more quickly than any other men." 

"O Zeus!" I said, "What a thing you say! Where did you find this <term>godsend<note>original: 'ἕρμαιον' (hermaion) - a stroke of luck or a gift from Hermes.</note></term>? I have always thought of you (as I was just saying) as being mostly formidable in armored combat, and that is what I said about you. For I remember that when you visited here before, this was what you proclaimed. But if you truly possess this knowledge now, be gracious to me—I simply address you as if you were gods, asking your pardon for my previous words. But see, Euthydemus and Dionysodorus, if you speak the truth. For because of the magnitude of the claim, it is no wonder if one is skeptical." 

"But rest assured, Socrates," they said, "that this is so." 

"Then I congratulate
<margin>H</margin>
you on this possession," I said, "much more than I would the Great King of Persia on his empire. But tell me this: do you intend to demonstrate this wisdom, or what have you decided?" 

"We are here for this very purpose, Socrates," they said, "to demonstrate..."

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
...until now I was truly ignorant that they were perfect athletes. For they are equipped for every kind of contest, not like the Acarnanian brothers who are athletes. Those men are strong only in body, but these are first of all strongest in speech, and in that kind of fighting by which all things are overcome. For they are highly skilled in arms, and they can make others skilled in arms if someone pays them a fee. Then they can handle judicial combat themselves with ease, and can instruct anyone else, both in writing and in pleading cases. And until now they were skilled only in these things, but now they have brought the perfect finish to their athletic faculty. 
<margin>B</margin>
For the kind of contest that was lacking, they have recently attained, so that no one is able to resist them, so strong are they in speaking, and they are prompt to refute any statement, whether true or false. Therefore, O Crito, I think of handing myself over to these men. For they promise to make any other person a master of these same things in a short time. 

**CRITO:** Does not your advanced age deter you, O Socrates? 

**SOCRATES:** Not at all, Crito. For there is that which comforts me, and does not let me distrust. For even these men, being now old, so to speak, have devoted themselves to this faculty which I now affect—namely, the contentious art. For in the previous year, or certainly three years ago, they were not yet skilled. But this one thing only I fear, lest I be a disgrace to these guests, just as I am to Connus the son of Metrobius, the harpist, who even 
<margin>C</margin>
now teaches me the strings. The boys, my fellow-students, therefore laugh at me daily, and call Connus himself "the teacher of old men." Lest, therefore, someone might object to this same thing with these guests, and they, deterred by that matter, might reject me, I have exhorted some others, O Crito, great in age, to go there with me for the sake of learning; and here likewise I will try to persuade some. Why don't you also be present? Indeed, let us even bring your sons as an enticement to them. For when they hope for the gathering of your sons as well, led by these as if by enticements, they will more willingly accept us to be taught. 

**CRITO:** Nothing prevents it, Socrates, if it seems good to you. But first, tell me what their wisdom is, so that I may know what we are to perceive. 
<margin>D</margin>

**SOCRATES:** You wait in vain for me to say I cannot tell you, as if I had not listened enough; on the contrary, I both listened diligently and I remember, and I will try to relate everything to you from the beginning. Indeed, by some divine chance, I was alone in the place where the athletes undress, where you saw me, when that accustomed sign of the <term>daemon<note>Socrates' personal guiding spirit or divine voice.</note></term> suddenly stopped me. So I stayed, and a little later Euthydemus and Dionysodorus entered, and with them many others, who seemed to me to be their disciples. Having entered, they walked about in the covered track itself. They had scarcely finished a second or third lap when that Clinias arrived, whom you say has profited greatly, and you speak truly. He was followed by friends and many others besides, then a certain youth, 
<margin>E</margin>
Ctesippus of Paeania, of good character and handsome, but rather playful by reason of his youth. Clinias, having observed me sitting alone from the entrance, came toward me and sat down at my right, as you yourself said. Dionysodorus and Euthydemus, having caught sight of him, first stood and discussed with each other, turning their eyes upon us here and there. For I was observing them most diligently. Then, approaching closer, they sat down: Euthydemus indeed next to the youth himself; Dionysodorus, however, next to me on the left, and others as each had a place. I therefore congratulated them, since I had not seen them for a long time. After these things, turning to 
<margin>F</margin>
Clinias: "These men, O Clinias," I said, "Euthydemus and Dionysodorus, are wise not in small matters, but in the greatest. They know all things that pertain to military matters, everything that becomes a future strenuous commander to know, of the line and orders, and the instructions of the army. Then also they can teach how someone may vindicate himself from injury in a judgment." But they despised me for speaking thus, and looking at each other, they both laughed. And Euthydemus said: "We no longer treat these things seriously, O Socrates, but as a hobby." But I, wondering, said: "Your studies must be excellent indeed, if your relaxations are so great. Tell me, I pray, what is this so excellent work of yours?" 
<margin>G</margin>

**EUTHYDEMUS:** Virtue, O Socrates, we persuade ourselves can be taught by us most easily and best of all men. 

**SOCRATES:** By Jupiter, what a precious thing you promise! By what chance especially did this gain come to you? Indeed, I thought of you thus, as I said, until now—namely, as men outstanding in military affairs, and I proclaimed that of you. For I remember when you first came here, you professed this alone; but if now you have truly attained this science, be propitious; I truly salute you just as gods, beseeching that you forgive what I said before. But see, O Euthydemus and Dionysodorus, whether you speak 
<margin>H</margin>
the truth. For it ought not to seem a wonder if someone, estimating the magnitude of this thing which you promise, finds it difficult to believe. 

**EUTHYDEMUS:** Know it to be so, O Socrates, absolutely. 

**SOCRATES:** I therefore judge you more blessed for the possession of this thing than that Great King for his kingdom. But tell me, I pray, whether you intend to exhibit this 

<margin>That advanced age should not deter one from learning.</margin>

wisdom of yours, or whether it is otherwise decreed among you? 

**EUTHYDEMUS:** To this very thing, O Socrates, we have come, to demonstrate...

# PLATO

<columns>
...and they will demonstrate and teach, if anyone wishes to learn. **A** Indeed, I myself stand as a guarantor for you—and I pledge for myself as well—that everyone who lacks this knowledge wishes to have it. I say this for myself, and for Clinias here, and for Ctesippus, and these others here (pointing to the admirers of Clinias who were standing near us). Ctesippus happened to be sitting far away from Clinias, but when Euthydemus leaned forward to speak to me, he blocked Ctesippus's view, as Clinias was sitting in the middle between us. Ctesippus, wanting to see his favorite youth <note>original: "παιδικά" (paidika), a term for a younger beloved in a pedagogical relationship</note> and being fond of listening, jumped up first and stood directly opposite us. **B** When the others saw this, they also gathered around: both the admirers of Clinias and the companions of Euthydemus and Dionysodorus. Pointing to them, I told Euthydemus that they were all ready to learn. Ctesippus and the others agreed very eagerly, and they all joined in urging him to demonstrate the power of his wisdom. 

I then said, "Euthydemus and Dionysodorus, please gratify these men and do this for my sake as well. Now, to demonstrate the bulk of your skills would clearly be a long task; but tell me this: can you only make a man good who is already persuaded that he ought to learn from you, or can you also persuade the man who is not yet convinced—either because he does not believe that virtue <note>original: "aretē" (virtue/excellence)</note> can be taught at all, or because he does not think you are its **C** teachers? Tell me, is it the task of this same art to persuade a man so disposed that virtue can be taught, and that you are the ones from whom he could best learn it?" 

"Indeed, Socrates," Dionysodorus replied, "it is the task of that very same art." 

"Then you," I said, "above all men now living, can best exhort people toward philosophy and the care of virtue?" 

"We certainly think so, Socrates." 

"Then put off the demonstration of your other skills for another time," I said, "and demonstrate this one thing now: persuade this youth here that he must pursue philosophy and care for virtue, and gratify me and all these others. For it has happened that we all feel this way about this lad: we desire **D** for him to become as good a man as possible. He is the son of Axiochus, who was the son of the elder <term>Alcibiades<note>The elder Alcibiades was the grandfather of the famous Athenian general; the youth Clinias is thus a cousin of the famous Alcibiades.</note></term>, and he is the cousin of the Alcibiades who is living now. His name is Clinias. He is young, and we are afraid for him—as is natural with the young—lest someone get to him first and turn his mind to some other pursuit, thereby corrupting him. You two have arrived at the perfect time. If it makes no difference to you, please test the boy and converse with him in our presence."

After I had said something like this, Euthydemus replied boldly and confidently, "It makes no difference at all, Socrates, provided the young man is willing to answer." 

"Oh, he is quite accustomed to that," I said. "For these friends of his are always coming to him and asking many questions and debating, **E** so I expect he will have the courage to answer."

What followed after this, Crito—how could I possibly describe it to you properly? For it is no small task to be able to recount such an impossible amount of wisdom. Therefore, I feel I must, like the poets, call upon the Muses and Memory to assist me as I begin the narrative. 

Euthydemus, as I recall, began in roughly this way: "Clinias, which of the two kinds of people are those who learn? Is it the wise, or the ignorant <note>original: "ἀμαθεῖς" (amatheis), meaning unlearned or lacking knowledge</note>?" 

The youth, seeing the weight of the question, blushed and looked at me in confusion. Seeing him troubled, I said, "Be brave, Clinias, and answer boldly whichever one you think it is. For perhaps you will receive the greatest benefit from it." **F** At that moment, Dionysodorus leaned toward my ear and said with a wide smile on his face, "I tell you beforehand, Socrates, that whichever way the lad answers, he will be refuted." 

While he was saying this, Clinias happened to give his answer, so I did not even have the chance to warn the boy. He answered that it was the wise who learn. 

And Euthydemus said, "Do you call some people 'teachers,' or not?" 
He agreed. 
"Are the teachers not the teachers of those who learn? Just as the lyre-player and the writing-master were teachers of you and the other boys, while you were the learners?" 
He agreed. 
"And when you were learning, did you not yet know the things you were learning?" 
**G** "We did not," he said. 
"Were you wise, then, when you did not know these things?" 
"Certainly not," he said. 
"Then if you were not wise, were you ignorant?" 
"Very much so." 
"Therefore, while you were learning what you did not know, you were learning while being ignorant." 
The youth nodded. 
"It follows then, Clinias, that it is the ignorant who learn, and not the wise as you supposed."

When he had said this, just like a chorus following the signal of their leader, the followers of Dionysodorus and Euthydemus broke into a great shout and laughter. And before the boy could catch his breath, Dionysodorus took up the argument and said, "What about this, Clinias? When the writing-master dictates something to you, which of the boys learn **H** what is dictated? The wise, or the ignorant?" 

"The wise," said Clinias. 
"Therefore it is the wise who learn, and not the ignorant. You did not answer Euthydemus correctly just now." 

At this, their admirers laughed and cheered very loudly, marvelling at the wisdom of the men. The rest of us sat silent and stunned. When Euthydemus saw that we were stunned, he did not let the boy go, but in order to make us wonder at him even more, he questioned him further. Like a skilled dancer in a chorus, he spun the question around to the same point from a different direction: "Do those..."
