<meta>catchword: "Do those..." (Greek: "Πότερα γὰρ οἱ μαν-")</meta>

<summary>Socrates introduces the young Clinias to the sophists Euthydemus and Dionysodorus, asking them to persuade him to pursue virtue. The sophists immediately trap Clinias in a series of logical paradoxes (eristic arguments) regarding whether the "wise" or the "ignorant" are the ones who learn.</summary>

<keywords>Plato, Socrates, Euthydemus, Dionysodorus, Clinias, sophistry, virtue, eristic argument, education, Alcibiades, logic traps</keywords>

--- Page 249 ---
<meta>Continuity: Socrates is observing the sophist brothers, Euthydemus and Dionysodorus, as they begin to question the young Clinias. On the previous page, the brothers had just claimed their ability to teach virtue and were asked by Socrates to demonstrate this skill on the youth.</meta>

### EUTHYDEMUS.

<margin>A</margin> "Therefore," he asked, "do those who learn, learn what they know, or what they do not know?"

Then Dionysodorus, whispering in my ear again, said, "And now, Socrates, this is another question just like the one before."

"By Zeus!" I said. "Indeed, the previous question seemed very fine to us."

"All of our questions," he replied, "are of this kind, Socrates—inescapable."

"That is exactly why," I said, "you seem to have such a great reputation among your students."

Meanwhile, Clinias answered Euthydemus that those who learn, learn what they do not know. Then Euthydemus asked him the same type of question as before: "What then? Do you know your letters?" <note>original: "γράμματα" (grammata), meaning letters of the alphabet or basic literacy</note>

"Yes," he said.

"All of them?"

He agreed.

"When someone recites anything, is he not reciting letters?"

He agreed.

<margin>B</margin> "Therefore," Euthydemus said, "he recites things that you know, if you indeed know all the letters."

He admitted this too.

"What then?" he asked. "Do you learn whatever someone recites, or does the person who does not know the letters learn?"

"No," he said, "I learn."

"Therefore, you learn what you already know, if indeed you know all the letters."

He agreed.

"Then you did not answer correctly," Euthydemus said.

Hardly had Euthydemus finished speaking when Dionysodorus, catching the argument like a ball, targeted the youth again. He said, "Euthydemus is deceiving you, Clinias. Tell me, is not 'learning' the act of receiving knowledge of that which one is learning?"

Clinias agreed.

"And 'knowing,'" he asked, "is that not already possessing the knowledge?"

He conceded.

<margin>C</margin> "Therefore, 'not knowing' is not yet possessing the knowledge?"

Clinias agreed with him.

"Now, which people receive a thing? Those who already have it, or those who do not?"

"Those who do not have it."

"Then have you not confessed that those who do not know are among those who receive knowledge?"

He nodded.

"Thus, those who learn are among those who receive, not those who already possess."

He agreed.

"Therefore, Clinias," he said, "those who do not know are the ones who learn, not those who know."

Euthydemus was rushing at the young man for a third bout <note>original: "πάλαισμα" (palaisma), a wrestling term used here for a round of verbal sparring</note>, but seeing that the boy was being overwhelmed—literally 'submerged'—and wanting to give him a rest so he would not lose heart, I began to comfort him.

I said, "Clinias, do not be surprised if these arguments seem strange to you. Perhaps you do not realize what these strangers <margin>D</margin> are doing to you. They are doing exactly what those in the Corybantic rites <note>The Corybantes were priests of Cybele known for ecstatic, rhythmic dancing and drumming</note> do when they perform the 'throning' ceremony for a person they are about to initiate. There is dancing and play there too, as you know if you have been initiated. And now these two are doing nothing but dancing around you and performing a kind of playful dance, as if they were purifying you before the actual initiation. 

So, for now, consider yourself to be hearing the first ceremonies of the sophist mysteries. First, as Prodicus <note>A famous contemporary sophist known for his precision in linguistics</note> says, one must learn about the 'correctness of names.' This is exactly what these strangers are showing you: that you did not realize that people use the word 'learning' in two ways. They use it first when someone, having no knowledge of a matter at the start, <margin>E</margin> later receives that knowledge. But they also use the same word when someone who already possesses knowledge uses that knowledge to examine the very same thing, whether it is being done or being said. They usually call this 'understanding' rather than 'learning,' but sometimes they call it 'learning' too. 

As these men have shown, it escaped your notice that the same name is applied to people in opposite states: both the one who knows and the one who does not. Something similar happened in the second question, where they asked whether people learn what they know or what they do not know. All of these things are merely games of instruction; that is why I say they are playing with you. I call it 'play' because <margin>F</margin> even if someone learned many such things, or even all of them, he would not know the nature of reality any better. He would only be able to play with people by tripping them up and overturning them through the differences in words—just like people who pull a stool out from under someone who is about to sit down, and then they laugh and rejoice when they see him lying on his back. 

So, consider these things from them to have been play. But next, they will clearly show you the serious matters they promised. I will guide them so they can pay me back what they promised; for they said they would demonstrate their 'protreptic' <note>exhortatory or encouraging</note> wisdom. But for now, it seems they thought they had to joke with you first. 

Therefore, Euthydemus and Dionysodorus, let this be the end of your play; perhaps it is enough. Now, demonstrate what follows next. It remains for you to show how you can lead this young man to the study of wisdom and virtue. But first, I will <margin>G</margin> show you how I understand this task and what I especially desire to hear. If I seem to do this in an amateurish or ridiculous way, please do not laugh at me. It is only out of an eagerness to hear your wisdom that I dare to improvise in front of you. So, both you and your students, endure listening to me without laughing. 

And you, son of Axiochus, answer me: Do we not all wish to do well? Or is this question one of those I just feared might be ridiculous? For it is probably foolish to even ask such a thing. Is there any human who does not wish to do well?"

"There is no one who does not," said Clinias.

"Very well," I said. "Next, since we wish to do well, how can we do well? Would it be if we had many good things? Or is this even more foolish to ask? For this is surely the case."

He agreed.

<margin>H</margin> "Come then," I said, "among the things that exist, which ones happen to be good for us? Or is this not a difficult thing to find, and not something a very dignified man needs to ponder? For everyone would tell us that being wealthy is a good thing. Is that not so?"

"Certainly," he said.

"And what about being healthy, and beautiful, and being sufficiently provided with other bodily advantages?"

He concurred.

"Furthermore, nobility, power, and honors in one's own city are surely good things."

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Therefore, he said, do they learn what they know, or what they do not know?
Then Dionysodorus again whispering in my ears, "Such a thing, O Socrates, is this also, as was brought up before." "By Jupiter," I said, "the previous one also seemed very fine to us." "Thus always," he said, "we propose inescapable questions." "Therefore you seem," I said, "to have no small authority among your disciples." Meanwhile Clinias responded to Euthydemus, that those who learn, learn what they are ignorant of. Immediately he questioned as above. "Do you yourself know your letters?" "I know them." "Surely all of them?" "And all." "When someone recites, does he not recite letters?" He granted it. "Therefore he recites those which you know, since you yourself know all the letters." He ad<margin>B</margin>mitted this also. "Surely you learn what someone recites?" He assented. "But truly being ignorant of letters, do you learn?" "Not at all." "Rather, knowing them, I learn." "Surely therefore you learn what you know? If indeed you know all the letters." He nodded. "Therefore you did not answer correctly." And Euthydemus had hardly said these things, when Dionysodorus, receiving the speech like a ball, thus attacked the youth. "Euthydemus deceives you, O Clinias. Tell me: Is not to learn to receive the knowledge of that which one learns?" Clinias admitted it. "But does to know mean anything else than already to have that knowledge?" He granted it. "To be ignorant, therefore, is <margin>C</margin> not yet to have knowledge?" He gave this also. "Which ones take up a thing? Those who have it, or those who do not have it?" "Those who do not have it." "And have you not confessed that ignorant men are of the number of those who do not have it?" He nodded. "Those learning therefore are of the number of those who take it up, not of those who have it." He proved it. "Therefore those who do not know, O Clinias, learn, not those who know." After these things, now seeking a third bout as if in a wrestling match, Euthydemus approached the youth. But I, pitying him as he was sinking, so that I might refresh him a little, lest perhaps he should be too terrified, began to console him in this manner. "Do not wonder, O Clinias, if these speeches are unusual to you: for perhaps you do not know what these guests mean. They <margin>D</margin> certainly do the same thing that the Corybantes are accustomed to do in the mysteries, when they place him whom they are about to initiate on a throne, they applaud, and lead dances nearby. I think you understand, if indeed you have been initiated. These men play similarly now, and lead dances and leap about, as if they were purifying the one whom they will soon initiate into the sacred rites. Therefore, for the present, think that some first ceremonies of the sophist rites are being celebrated. For in the beginning, just as Prodicus commands, it is fitting to learn the proper meanings of names: which also these guests show to you. For you did not know how people call 'learning' when they speak of these things. For they call it 'learning' both when someone attains a matter <margin>E</margin> which he did not hold before: and when, having obtained knowledge of it, he considers that same thing by that same knowledge, either when it is done or when it is said: which you might more correctly call 'understanding' than 'learning,' although it is not rarely called 'learning.' But that escaped you, as these men have shown, namely that the same name is attributed by men to contrary things, both to the knowing and to the ignorant. But similar to this is also that which they proposed in the second question, asking whether men learn what they know or what they do not know. All these things are certain games in disciplines, and I say these men are playing with you. But I call it play for this reason, because even if someone knew many or even all things of this kind, he would understand the nature of things <margin>F</margin> no more, yet he will be able to play with men from the diversity of names, as if tripping you up and throwing you down, in the manner of those who secretly pull away the benches from those wishing to sit, and laugh more profusely when they see him who fell lying on his back. Therefore, take these things also for games. But hereafter these men will treat serious matters for you, and I will demand from them what they promised: namely, in what way someone can be impelled toward wisdom. But now they seem to me to have thought that they should first jest with you. Therefore thus far, O Euthydemus and Dionysodorus, let it have been play for you. And perhaps it is enough. Show now what follows. For it remains for you to show in what way you might lead this youth to the study of virtue and wisdom. And I will say in the <margin>G</margin> beginning what seems to me, and what I most of all desire to hear. But if I do it unskillfully and ridiculously, do not, I pray, laugh. The desire for hearing your wisdom makes me not hesitate to bring forth my follies before you. You will therefore contain your laughter, you and your disciples. But you, son of Axiochus, answer me, whether we all desire to act well, that is, to live well. Or perhaps this question, as I feared, is of the number of those which are ridiculous? For it is of a madman, I think, to inquire after such things. For who is there of all people who does not desire to live well? "No one," said Clinias. "Come," I said, "since we wish to live well, in what way is it allowed to attain it? Surely if many good things were ours? Or is anyone foolish who would deny this?" "So it is agreed to be." "It is agreed," he said. "But of every kind <margin>H</margin> of thing, what are the good things?" I said. "Or perhaps that is not hard to find, nor to be doubted by an elegant man? For who is there who would deny that it is good to be rich? Is it not so?" "Most certainly," he said. "Is it not also to be healthy," I said, "and beautiful, and endowed with the other gifts of the body?" "Certainly," he said. "Furthermore, nobility, power, and honors in each one's city are good things."

<summary>Socrates comforts Clinias after the sophists confuse him with wordplay regarding the definition of "learning," explaining that they are merely playing a linguistic game before the "serious" instruction begins. Socrates then initiates a serious dialogue with Clinias to demonstrate the "protreptic" method, starting with the universal human desire for happiness and a list of commonly recognized goods.</summary>

# PLATO

"And those things too," he said. "What other goods," I asked, "remain? If we say that temperance, justice, and fortitude are goods, would we be speaking correctly? For perhaps someone might doubt it. But what do you say?" "They are surely goods," he replied. "And wisdom," I asked, "in what category shall we place it? Among the goods, or otherwise?" "Among the goods," he said. "Consider," I said, "whether we have overlooked any good worthy of mention." "It seems to me," he said, "that we have overlooked none." Here, thinking for a moment, I said, "O Clinias, we seem to have left out the greatest of all goods." "What is that?" he asked. "Good fortune," <note>original: "felicitatem" / "εὐτυχίαν" (eutychia). While often translated as 'happiness,' in this context it refers to 'success' or 'good luck.'</note> I said, "which everyone, even the most unlearned, calls the highest good." "You speak the truth," he said.

<margin>A certain definition of happiness</margin>
And I, changing my mind again, said, "O Clinias, we almost made ourselves a laughingstock to our guests." "Why so?" he asked. "Because having already placed happiness among the goods," I said, "we were just now speaking about the same thing again." "How so?" he asked. "It is ridiculous to propose again what was proposed before, and to recount the same things twice." "Why do you say that?" "Wisdom," I said, "is itself good fortune; even a child would know this." When he looked at me with wonder because of his youthful simplicity, and I noticed his amazement, I questioned him in this way: "Do you not know, O Clinias, that skilled flute players are the most successful of all in the use of the flute?" He agreed. "And that learned grammarians are the most successful in what pertains to writing and reading letters?" "Exactly," he said. "What about the dangers that occur at sea? Do not wise pilots achieve the desired harbor of navigation more successfully than others?" "That is so." "And does not a wise general lead a military campaign more safely, and will one not fight more safely with him than with an ignorant one?" "Without a doubt," he said. "And will a wise physician, I ask, lead you better to the desired health of the body than an unlearned one, and would you not more willingly commit yourself to him?" "Certainly," he said. "Is it because you think you would succeed more happily with a wise man than with a fool?"

<margin>Wisdom makes us happy</margin>
He agreed. "Wisdom, therefore, in all human affairs," I said, "makes us happy. For wisdom never errs nor is it deceived, but it performs its work rightly; otherwise, it would not even be wisdom." We eventually agreed, I know not how, to say in short that when wisdom is present, there is no need for further good fortune. When these things were granted, I asked him again what we should think about what had been granted above. "For we confessed," I said, "that if many goods were present to us, we would live well and blessedly." He admitted it. "Now, do we live blessedly because of the presence of goods if they do not benefit us, or if they do?" "If they benefit us," he said. "But do they contribute anything if we merely possess them, but do not use them? For instance, if we had many foods and drinks, but did not eat them, would they help us at all?" "Not at all," he said. "Furthermore, if all the materials were prepared and laid out for craftsmen to complete their work, but they did not use them, would they fare well because of the abundance of equipment and tools? As if all the tools and wood were prepared for a carpenter, but he built nothing—would he be helped, I ask, by the possession?" "In no way," he said. "What then? If someone acquired wealth and all the goods we mentioned, but never used them, would he be happy," I asked, "by the mere possession of those goods?" "Not at all, Socrates," he said. "It is necessary, then, for him who is to be happy," I said, "not only to possess such goods, but to use them. For possession alone helps nothing." "Right," he said. "But is the possession and use of goods, O Clinias," I asked, "enough for living blessedly?" "It seems so to me," he said. "Do you say so if one uses them rightly, or even if not rightly?" "If rightly," he said. "Good," I said. "For I think it is worse when someone misuses a thing than when he does not touch it at all. For the former is an evil, while the latter is neither good nor evil. Must we not say so?" He approved. "Now in the working and use of wood, does anything other than the knowledge of carpentry make it possible to use each thing rightly?" "Nothing else," he said. "Furthermore, regarding the making of vessels, does knowledge provide the right use?" He nodded. "And regarding the use of the goods we mentioned first—wealth, health, and beauty—was not knowledge itself the guide, teaching how to use these rightly and directing the work?" "Exactly," he said.
"Knowledge, then, provides men not only with success but also with good work, it seems, in every possession and action." He agreed. "Is there, I pray, any utility in all possessions without prudence and wisdom? Would a man gain more who lacks a mind, though he abounds in things and does much? Or he who does little and possesses little, but is of sound mind? Consider it this way. Does not he who acts less err less often? Erring less, he does less evil; doing less evil, he is less miserable?" "Entirely so," he said. "But in what way," I asked, "does someone do fewer things? Is it if he is poor, or if he is rich?" "If he is poor," he said. "If he is weak, or robust?" "If he is weak," he said. "If he is honored, or lowly?" "If he is lowly," he said. "If he is brave and temperate, or timid?" "If he is timid." "And does not a lazy man perform less than one prompt to act?" He admitted it. "And the slow more than the swift? The dull of sight and hearing more than the sharp?" All these things were agreed upon between us. Then I concluded in this manner:
"It seems that we have not been disputing about all those things we previously called goods, as to how they are good in their own nature,"

A He agreed. "What then," I said, "remains for us of the goods? Or are they all things such as being temperate, just, and brave? By Zeus, Clinias, do you think that if we posit these as goods, we shall be positing them correctly? For perhaps someone might dispute it with us. But how does it seem to you?" "Goods," Clinias said. "Well then," I said, "where shall we place wisdom? Among the goods? Or how do you say?" "Among the goods." "And consider whether we are leaving out any of the goods that are worthy of account." "But it seems to me," Clinias said, "none." And I, remembering, said, "By Zeus, we are in danger of leaving out the greatest of the goods." "What is that?" he said. "Good fortune, Clinias, which everyone says—even the very base—is the greatest of the goods." "You speak the truth," he said. And

"And when campaigning, with which would you more gladly share the danger and the fortune? With a wise general, or with an ignorant one?" "With a wise one." "And when ill, with which would you gladly risk the danger? With a wise doctor, or with an ignorant one?" "With a wise one." "Is it then," I said, "because you think you would be more fortunate doing things with a wise man than with an ignorant one?" He conceded. "Wisdom, then, everywhere makes men fortunate. For a man would never err when it is necessary to act rightly and to succeed. For then it would no longer be wisdom." We agreed

He agreed. "Would we then be happy because of the present goods, if they were to benefit us in some way, or if not at all?" "If they were to benefit us," he said. "Would they then benefit us at all if they were only present to us, but we did not use them? For example, if we had much food, but did not eat it, or drink, but did not drink it, would we be benefited?" "Certainly not," he said. "What about all craftsmen? If they had all the necessary things prepared for each for his own work, but did not use them, would they

For example, a carpenter: if all the tools and sufficient wood were prepared for him, but he built nothing, would he be benefited from the possession?" "In no way," he said. "What if someone had acquired wealth and all the goods we just mentioned, but used them not at all, would he be happy because of the possession of these goods?" "Certainly not, Socrates." "It is necessary then," I said, "as it seems, that he who is to be happy not only possess such goods, but also use them; for there is no benefit in the possession." "You speak the truth." "Is this then, Clinias, already sufficient to make someone happy: both to possess the goods and to use them?" "It seems so to me." "Whether," I said, "if one uses them rightly, or also if not?" "If rightly." "And indeed," I

He conceded. "What then? In the working and use regarding wood, is it anything other than the knowledge of carpentry that produces the right use?" "Certainly not," he said. "And indeed, in the working regarding vessels, it is knowledge that produces the right use." He agreed. "Is it then," I said, "also in the use of the goods we first mentioned—wealth, health, and beauty—that the right use of all such things was knowledge, which governed and set right the

"Is there then, by Zeus," I said, "any benefit in other possessions without prudence and wisdom? Would a man be profited by possessing much and doing much, if he has no mind? "Being brave and temperate, would he act less, or being a coward?" "A coward." "Therefore also

<margin>A</margin> "But as it seems, even those other things—unless wisdom <gloss>α</gloss> leads them—would not be goods, since <gloss>β</gloss> the leadership they follow determines their value. The <gloss>γ</gloss> more ignorantly they serve a leader, the worse they are; but if they serve prudence and wisdom, they are greater goods. He agreed. "Furthermore," I said, "let us examine what remains. Since <gloss>η</gloss> we all <gloss>θ</gloss> desire to be happy, and we appeared to become so by using things and using them rightly, and since it is knowledge that provides this rightness and success, it is necessary, as it seems, for <gloss>α</gloss> every man to <gloss>β</gloss> prepare himself in every way to become as wise as possible. <margin>B</margin> "Yes," he said. "And I suppose one should think it necessary to <gloss>γ</gloss> receive this from a father much more than money, and from guardians and friends, and others—especially those who claim to be lovers—and from strangers and citizens, begging and entreating them to share their wisdom. "If indeed, O Clinias," I said, "wisdom is <gloss>ζ</gloss> teachable, and does not <gloss>η</gloss> come to men of its own accord. For this

<margin>C</margin> is what we must still consider, as it has not yet been agreed between you and me." "But to me, Socrates," he said, "it seems to be teachable." And I, being pleased, said, "You speak beautifully, best of men! And you have done me a great favor by releasing me from a long inquiry into this very point—whether wisdom is teachable or not. Now then, since it seems to you to be teachable, and since it is the only thing that <gloss>α</gloss> makes a man <gloss>β</gloss> happy and fortunate, would you say anything else than that it is necessary to practice philosophy, and do you intend to do it yourself?" And when I heard this, I said, "My own example, O Dionysodorus and Euthydemus, of the kind of <gloss>δ</gloss> protreptic <note>The word 'protreptic' refers to a speech intended to exhort or persuade someone to a particular way of life, in this case, the pursuit of wisdom.</note> discourse I desire, is this: perhaps it is the work of an unpracticed layman and <gloss>ε</gloss> expressed with difficulty. But whichever of you wishes, show us this same thing by weaving it together with your art. Or if you do not wish to do that, then starting from where I left off, show the youth what follows: whether he must acquire every kind of knowledge, or if there is some one science that he must grasp to be <gloss>ζ</gloss> happy and a good man, and what that science is. For as I was saying at the start, it is very important to us that this <gloss>η</gloss> young man becomes wise and good."

So I said these things, O Crito. And <gloss>θ</gloss> I paid very close attention to what followed, and I watched to see in what way they would <gloss>ι</gloss> take up the argument and from where they would begin, <gloss>κ</gloss> since the young man was set on practicing wisdom and virtue. The elder of them, Dionysodorus, began the <gloss>λ</gloss> argument first. We all looked toward him, expecting to hear some marvelous words immediately—which is exactly what happened.

<margin>E</margin> For the man, O Crito, began a wonderful speech, which you ought to hear, for <gloss>μ</gloss> the argument was an unavoidable provocation toward virtue. "Tell me," he said, "Socrates and you others, who say you desire this youth to become wise: are you joking when you say this, or do you truly desire it and are you serious?" And I realized that they thought we had been joking before when we urged them to talk with the youth. Because they had now <gloss>ν</gloss> taken this seriously, I said even more emphatically that we were wonderfully serious. Then Dionysodorus said, <margin>F</margin> "Take care, Socrates, that you do not <gloss>ξ</gloss> deny what you are saying now." "I have considered it," I said, "for I shall never <gloss>ο</gloss> deny it." "What then?" he asked. "Do you say you want him to become wise?" "Certainly." "But now," he asked, "is Clinias wise or not?" "He says he is not yet," I replied, "for he <gloss>π</gloss> is not a boaster." "And you," he said, "want him to become wise, and not to be ignorant?" We agreed. "Therefore, you want him to become what he is not, and to no longer be what he is now." And when I heard this, I was troubled. And he, seeing me troubled, took up the argument: "Since you <gloss>ρ</gloss> want him to no longer be what he is now, you want him, as it seems, to perish. <note>This is a classic 'sophism' or logical trap. Dionysodorus argues that if you want someone to change their nature (from ignorant to wise), you are wishing for the 'destruction' of their current self.</note> Yet what fine friends and lovers they must be, who would desire above all else that their beloved should perish!"

<margin>G</margin> When Ctesippus heard this, he was indignant on behalf of <gloss>σ</gloss> his beloved, and said, "Stranger from Thurii, if it were not a bit <gloss>τ</gloss> rude to say so, I would say: 'May the consequences fall on your own head!' What has possessed you to <gloss>υ</gloss> speak such a lie against me and the others—a thing I think is <gloss>φ</gloss> unholy to say—that I would wish him to perish?" "But why," said Euthydemus, "Ctesippus, do you think it is possible <gloss>χ</gloss> to lie?" "By Zeus, I do," he replied, "unless I am out of my mind." "By speaking of the thing about which the speech is, or by not speaking of it?" "By speaking of it," he said. "Does he then, if he speaks of it, speak of any other of the things that are, except that very thing which he speaks of?" "How could he?" said Ctesippus. "And that thing which he speaks of is <gloss>ψ</gloss> one of the things that are, distinct from the others?" "Certainly." "Then does he who speaks that thing speak of that which is?" "Yes." "But surely he who speaks that which is, and things that are, <gloss>ω</gloss> speaks the truth. So Dionysodorus, if he speaks the things that are, speaks the truth and tells no lie against you." "Yes," said Ctesippus, <margin>A</margin> "but <gloss>α</gloss> in saying these things, Euthydemus, <gloss>β</gloss> he does not speak the things that are." <margin>A</margin> But as it appears, the matter stands thus: if ignorance presides over them, they are as much worse than their opposites as they can provide more abundant supports for crimes to a wicked leader. "It seems," he said, "to be as you say." "What else follows from these things," I said, "than that none of the other things is either good or evil; but of these two, wisdom is a good, and foolishness is an evil?" He approved. Now therefore let us consider what remains. Since we all desire to be happy, and we are made happy, as it appeared, by the fact that we <margin>B</margin> use things, and use them rightly: and since knowledge provides the rectitude of use and the prosperity of the outcome, everyone, setting aside all other things, must strive with all zeal to become as wise as possible. Is it not so? "Certainly," he said. Furthermore, everyone ought to think that this should be sought from parents, from tutors, and friends, and others—especially those who love them, whether they be guests or citizens—rather than great wealth, and all should be entreated to impart wisdom. Nor is it shameful or unworthy, Clinias, for the sake of wisdom to serve anyone, and to deserve well of everyone by honorable services. <margin>C</margin> "Do you feel the same?" "Entirely so," he said. "For you seem to speak rightly." "If only," I said, "wisdom can be taught, and does not come to men by chance and luck. For this is also to be tracked down: it is not yet established among us." Then he said, "To me indeed, O Socrates, it seems it can be taught." Delighted by this response, I said, "Well said, best of men! You have bestowed a very great benefit upon me, freeing me from a long discussion of whether wisdom can be taught or not. Now, however, since it seems to you that it can be acquired through teaching, and this alone of all things makes a man blessed and happy, what else would you say but that one must practice philosophy? Will you not do this?" "Most certainly," he said, "O Socrates, as much as that can be done." Having heard these things gladly, <margin>D</margin> I said, "O Dionysodorus and Euthydemus, you have here an example of an exhortation, such as I desire, collected by me at last, perhaps in unpolished and long-winded words. But whichever of you wishes, let him show this to us, weaving it together skillfully: or if this does not please you, at least pursue what is lacking in my speech for the youth's sake. Namely, whether it is necessary for him to prepare every kind of knowledge, or rather some one specific kind, who wishes to be a good and happy man; and then what this knowledge is. For as I said at the beginning, we vehemently desire this young man to turn out wise and good."

When I had said these things, O Crito, I was now intent on what followed, observing what kind of beginning of speaking they would make, and by what reason especially they would exhort Clinias to the study of wisdom and virtue. Here, he who is older in years, Dionysodorus, began first; and we indeed were all turned with our eyes toward him, about to hear some marvelous speech immediately: which also <margin>E</margin> happened. For he began a wonderful discourse, O Crito, worthy to be heard by you, seeing how beautifully he provokes one to virtue. "Tell me," he said, "O Socrates, and you others, whoever you are who want this youth to become wise, whether you are joking, or whether you are doing this seriously and truly desire it." Here, realizing that they had thought it was a game for themselves, when ordered to dispute with the youth, and therefore they themselves had played until now and had not treated serious matters: "We desire it most greatly," I said. Then Dionysodorus said, "See, O Socrates, lest you <margin>F</margin> at some time deny what you now bring forward." "I know," I said, "that I shall not deny it." "What then do you say?" he asked. "Do you want him to become wise?" "We want it," he said. "Is Clinias wise now, or not?" "Not yet," I said. "For he is not at all boastful." "But you," he said, "want him to become wise, and by no means to be ignorant?" We admitted it. "Therefore, what he is not," he said, "you desire him to become: and what he is now, you desire him no longer to be." When I had heard this, I was troubled; and he, noticing me troubled, said, "Since you want what he is now no longer to be, you want, as it seems, this boy to perish. Truly fine friends and lovers they are, who study with all care to destroy those they love!" Hearing these things, Ctesippus <margin>G</margin> took it badly for the sake of his beloved; and being indignant, said, "Guest from Thurii, if it were not a rustic thing to say, I would say to your face that you fasten a wicked and unworthy lie upon me and those others, namely that I desire him to perish." Here Euthydemus, turned toward Ctesippus, said, "Does it seem possible to you, that anyone should lie?" "By Jupiter," he said, "unless perhaps I am insane." "But he who lies," he said, "does he speak the thing itself about which the speech is, or does he not speak it?" "He speaks it," he said. "If he speaks the thing itself, he speaks nothing else besides that which he speaks. In what way," said Ctesippus, "could it be otherwise?" "Is there not some one thing," he said, "which he speaks, distinct from others?" "Certainly," said Ctesippus. "Is it not true that he who speaks that thing, brings forth that which is?" "So it is." "But surely whoever speaks that which is, or those things which are, speaks true things. Wherefore Dionysodorus, if he speaks the things that are, proclaims the truth, and we lie in nothing against you." "So it is," said Ctesippus. "But he who speaks these things, O Euthydemus, does not speak those things which are." To which Euthydemus replied: "Non-existent things, are they not nothing?" "No," he said. "But nowhere are those things which are not, things that exist?" "Nowhere." "Can it be that anyone should act concerning those things which are not..."

<summary>Socrates concludes his sincere exhortation to Clinias, establishing that wisdom is the only path to happiness, before the sophists Dionysodorus and Euthydemus take over. The sophists immediately employ eristic traps, arguing that wanting Clinias to become wise is equivalent to wanting his current self to die.</summary>

# OF PLATO

<margin>A</margin> "Or could someone prove that any person could make things that exist nowhere?" "By no means, in my opinion," said Ctesippus. "What then? When the orators harangue the people, do they do nothing?" "They do something," he replied. "If they act, then they also make?" "Yes." "Therefore, speaking itself is both acting and making." He agreed. "No one, therefore, speaks of non-existent things, for he would then be making something; and you, indeed," he said, "have confessed that it is impossible for anyone to make non-existent things. Therefore, according to your own argument, no one speaks falsely; rather, if Dionysodorus speaks, he speaks truths and things that exist." "By Zeus, Euthydemus," said Ctesippus, "he speaks of things that exist <margin>B</margin> in a certain way, but certainly not as they actually are." "How do you mean?" asked Dionysodorus. "Are there some people who speak of things as they are?" "There certainly are," he replied, "the good and noble men <note>original: "viri boni præclari" / "καλοὶ τε κἀγαθοὶ" — a standard Greek phrase for the ideal gentleman-citizen</note> who speak the truth." "What then?" said he, "do not good things belong to those who are well, and bad things to those who are ill?" He approved. "And you admit that good and noble men speak of things as they are?" "I admit it." "Therefore, O Ctesippus, good men speak badly of bad things, if indeed they speak of them as they are." <margin>C</margin> "Very much so," he said, "and they speak badly of bad men. If you take my advice, you will be careful, lest good men speak badly of you; for you know that the good speak badly of the bad." Here Euthydemus said: "And do they speak of the great greatly, and the hot hotly?" "Exceedingly so," said Ctesippus. "And of the cold they speak coldly, and say they argue coldly <note>The Latin 'differere frigidè' and Greek 'διαλέγεσθαι ψυχρῶς' play on a double meaning: 'coldly' in temperature and 'coldly' as in a dull or tedious style of speaking.</note>." Then Dionysodorus said, "You are being abusive, Ctesippus, you are being abusive!" "Not by Jove, Dionysodorus," he said, "for I love you; rather, I advise you as a friend, and I strive to persuade you never to speak so rudely in my presence as to say that I desire the destruction of those whom <margin>D</margin> I hold most dear." 

But I, perceiving they were becoming heated, joked with Ctesippus: "It seems to me, Ctesippus, that we ought to receive from these guests whatever they give, if they are willing to share anything, and not to quibble over names. For if they know how to 'destroy' men in such a way as to make them honest and prudent instead of evil and foolish—whether they are the inventors of this destruction themselves or learned it from another—so that by exterminating the bad man, they can restore him as a good one; it is clear they know how. For they said just now that they have recently acquired an art <margin>E</margin> by which they make good men out of bad ones. If they know this," I said, "let us permit them to destroy the youth, provided they make him wise; indeed, let us hand ourselves over to them to be cured in the same way. But if you young men are afraid, then let them try their art on me, as if on a Carian <note>original: "Care quoda" / "ἐν Καρὶ" — a reference to the proverb 'to take the risk on a Carian,' meaning to experiment on a person of little perceived value before trying it on someone important.</note>. Since I am an old man, I am ready to undergo the danger, and I give myself up to this Dionysodorus as if to Medea the Colchian <note>In Greek mythology, Medea was said to have the power to restore youth by cutting a person up and boiling them in a cauldron.</note>; let him destroy me, and if he wishes, let him boil me, or do whatever else he wants, provided he turns me into a good man." Ctesippus also said, "I likewise, O Socrates, commit myself to the will of our guests; and even if they wish to flay me more than they are flaying me now, I am willing, provided my skin is not turned into a wineskin like that of Marsyas <note>The satyr Marsyas was flayed alive by the god Apollo after losing a musical contest; his skin was said to have been made into a leather bottle or wineskin.</note>, but into virtue. And <margin>F</margin> Dionysodorus here thinks I am angry with him; I am not angry at all, but I oppose those things which he said incorrectly. But you, Dionysodorus, should not call my contradiction 'abuse.' For to abuse is one thing, and to contradict is another." 

Then Dionysodorus said, "I ask you, are you speaking about contradicting, as if you think contradicting is even a real thing at all?" "Certainly," said Ctesippus. "Or do you, O Dionysodorus, not think so?" "Indeed," said Dionysodorus, "you will never show that you have ever heard one person contradicting another." "You speak the truth?" he said. "Well, let us now hear if I can show you Ctesippus contradicting you, Dionysodorus." "Do you then promise this to us?" he asked. "Entirely," he replied. "Are there," he said, "accounts and reasons <note>original: "sermones ratiōnésque" / "λόγοι" — the word 'logos' can mean speech, account, reason, or definition.</note> for each thing that exists?" "There are," he said. "Does a person speak of a thing as it is, or as it is not?" "As it is," he said. "If you remember, Ctesippus," he said, "we showed a little while ago that no one speaks what is not. For it is established that no one can speak that which is not." "What of it?" asked Ctesippus. "Does that prevent you and me from contradicting each other?" Then he said, "Would we be contradicting if we both thought of the account of the same thing? Or would we not rather be saying the same thing?" He agreed. "But what if neither of us," he asked, "speaks the account of the thing? Are we then contradicting? Or do we then not have the matter in mind at all?" He admitted that also. <margin>G</margin> "Then is it when I speak the account of the thing, but you say something else, that we finally contradict? Or rather, when I say what the thing is, but you say something that is not the thing at all? And can one who does not speak contradict one who does?" At this, Ctesippus fell silent. 

But I, wondering at what was being said, asked: "In what way, Dionysodorus, do you say this? For indeed, having heard this kind of argument frequently from many people, I am always accustomed to wonder at it. For the followers of Protagoras <note>A famous sophist who taught that 'man is the measure of all things,' implying that there is no objective falsehood because everyone's perception is true to them.</note>, and those even more ancient than they, used it frequently. But to me it has always seemed wonderful, and such as to subvert both others and itself. I think, however, that I shall now hear the truth of it most clearly from you. Does it mean that it is impossible to speak falsely, and that he who speaks must either speak the truth or not speak at all?" He affirmed it. "But is it impossible to speak falsely," I asked, "yet possible to think falsely?" "Not even to think so," he said. "Therefore there is no such thing," I said, "as a false opinion." "None at all." "Neither is there ignorance," I said, "nor ignorant men; for would ignorance not be this: to be deceived about things?" "Entirely so," he said, "but this does not exist."

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> "Or would someone else refute it, so that he could make those things that are not? Not in my view," said Ctesippus. "What then? When the orators speak in the assembly, do they do nothing?" "They act indeed," he said. "And if they act, do they also make?" "Yes." "Is speaking both acting and making?" He agreed. "No one, therefore, speaks of that which is not, for he would then already be making something; and you have agreed that no one is able to make things that are not. <margin>B</margin> So according to your argument, no one speaks falsely; but if Dionysodorus speaks, he speaks the truth and things that are." "By Zeus," said Ctesippus, "O Euthydemus! But he speaks of things that are in a way, yet not as they truly are." "How do you say?" asked Dionysodorus, "O Ctesippus? Are there some who speak of things as they are?" "There are indeed," he said, "those who are good and noble, and those who speak the truth." "What then?" he said, "do not good things belong to those who are well, and bad things to those who are ill?" He concurred. "And do you agree that the good and noble speak of things as they are?" "I agree." "Then the good speak badly <margin>C</margin> of bad things, O Ctesippus, if indeed they speak of them as they are." "Yes, by Zeus," he said, "very much so, at least regarding bad men; and you (if you take my advice) will be careful, so that the good do not speak badly of you. For know well that the good speak badly of the bad." "And do they speak of the great greatly," said Euthydemus, "and the hot hotly?" "Certainly," said Ctesippus; "they speak of the cold coldly, and say they argue coldly." "You," said Dionysodorus, "are being abusive, O Ctesippus, you are being abusive!" "By Zeus, I am not," he said, "O Dionysodorus, since I am your friend; but I advise you as a companion, and I try <margin>D</margin> to persuade you never to speak so rudely in my presence, as to say that I wish those whom I value most to be destroyed." 

I then, since they seemed to me to be acting quite rudely toward each other, joked with Ctesippus and said, "O Ctesippus, it seems to me we should receive from the strangers what they say, if they are willing to share, and not to differ over a name. For if they know how to destroy men in such a way as to make them good and wise instead of wicked and foolish, and whether they found this themselves or learned such 'destruction' and 'ruin' from another, <margin>E</margin> so that having destroyed the wicked man, they show him forth as good again—if they know this (and it is clear they do, for they said their newly discovered art was making good men out of wicked ones)—let us then yield to them. Let them destroy the youth for us and make him wise, and all the rest of us as well. But if you young men are afraid, let the danger be on me, as if on a Carian. For I, since I am an old man, am ready to take the risk; and I hand myself over to this Dionysodorus, just as to Medea of Colchis. Let him destroy me; and if he wants, let him boil me; or let him do whatever he wishes, only let him <margin>F</margin> show me forth as good." And Ctesippus said, "I myself, O blessed Socrates, am ready to offer myself to the strangers, even if they want to flay me even more than they are flaying me now; if only my skin will not end up as a wineskin, like that of Marsyas, but in virtue. Yet this Dionysodorus here thinks I am angry with him; but I am not angry, I only contradict these things which seem to me to be spoken poorly. But you, Dionysodorus, do not call contradicting 'abuse.' For abuse is a different thing." And Dionysodorus said, "Do you speak of the 'account' <note>original: "λόγους" — here referring back to the argument or the possibility of speech.</note> as if contradicting exists, O Ctesippus?" "Absolutely," he said, "and very much so. Or do you not think, Dionysodorus, that there is such a thing as contradicting?" "Well, you," he said, "could not even demonstrate that you have ever heard anyone contradicting another." <margin>G</margin> "Are you telling the truth?" he said. "But let us hear now if I can demonstrate to you Ctesippus contradicting Dionysodorus." "Will you then promise <unclear>this very</unclear> argument?" "Quite so," he said. "What then?" he said; "are there accounts for each of the things that are?" "Certainly." "As each thing is, or as it is not?" "As it is." "For if you remember, Ctesippus," he said, "we just now demonstrated that no one speaks as it is not. For no one appeared to be speaking of that which is not." "What of that then?" said Ctesippus. "Do we contradict each other any less, you and I?" "Would we then be contradicting," he asked, "if both of us were speaking the account of the same thing? For thus we would surely be saying the same things?" He concurred. "But when neither of us," he asked, "speaks the account of the thing, would we then be contradicting? Or in that way would neither of us have mentioned the thing at all?" He agreed to this too. "But," he said, "when I speak the account of the thing, and you speak another account of something else, do we then contradict? Or do I speak the thing, while you do not speak at all? And how could he who does not speak contradict him who speaks?" 

And Ctesippus was silent; but I, marveling at the argument, said, "How do you mean this, Dionysodorus? For I have heard this argument in many places and many times, and I always wonder at it. For those around Protagoras <margin>H</margin> used it intensely, and those even more ancient; but to me it always seems to be something wonderful, that overturns both others and itself. I think I shall learn the truest version of it from you. Is it anything other than that it is impossible to speak falsely? For this is the power of the argument: that a speaker must either speak the truth or not speak?" He concurred. "Is it then that it is impossible to speak falsely, but possible to have a false opinion?" "Not even to have a false opinion," he said. "Then there is no false opinion at all," I said. "None," he said. "Then there is no ignorance, nor ignorant men? Or would this not be ignorance, if someone were to be false?" "Quite so," he said, "but this does not exist."

<summary>This page contains a classic sophistical debate from Plato's Euthydemus, where Dionysodorus argues that it is logically impossible to speak falsely or to contradict someone else, as all speech must be about "what is." Socrates ironically offers to let the sophists "destroy" his old self to rebuild him as a wise man, provided they can actually produce virtue.</summary>

<keywords>Protagorean paradox, impossibility of falsehood, contradiction, Marsyas, Medea of Colchis, Carian risk, sophistry, Socrates, Ctesippus, Dionysodorus, dialectic, virtue</keywords>

# EUTHYDEMUS

<columns>2</columns>
<sig>T iij</sig>

<margin>A</margin> "...people, or would this not be ignorance, if indeed lying is among the possible errors?" "Certainly," he said. "But does this error not exist?" I asked. "It does not," he said. "Are you saying this for the sake of the argument, Dionysodorus, so that you might say something strange? Or does it truly seem to you that no human being is ignorant?" "But you," he said, "refute it." "And is it even possible to refute according to your argument, if no one lies?" "It is not possible," said Euthydemus. "Neither then," said I, "did Dionysodorus just now bid me to refute him. For how could anyone command what does not exist?" "Euthydemus," I said, "I do not quite understand these clever and well-arranged things, but I grasp them only slowly. Perhaps I shall ask something a bit heavy <note>original: "φορτικώτερον" / "onerosum" — meaning something vulgar, burdensome, or socially awkward</note>; but forgive me. See here: if it is not possible to lie, nor to have a false opinion, nor to be ignorant, then it is also impossible to make a mistake when one acts. For in acting, one cannot fail in that which he does. Is this not what you say?" <margin>B</margin> "Quite so," he replied. "This now," I said, "is the heavy question. If we never err, whether in acting, speaking, or thinking—by Zeus!—if this is the case, what have you come here to teach? Did you not say just now that you could deliver virtue best of all men to anyone willing to learn?" "Socrates," Dionysodorus interrupted, "are you such a Cronus <note>original: "Κρόνος" — a reference to the ancient god, used here as a slang term for someone who is 'old-fashioned,' 'senile,' or a 'relic'</note> that you remember what we said at the beginning? Even if I said something last year, would you remember it now? But as for what is said in the present, will you have nothing to use?" "Because they are difficult," I said, "and not without reason. <margin>C</margin> For they come from wise men. Indeed, even this last thing you said is very difficult to deal with. For what do you mean by saying 'I have nothing to use,' Dionysodorus? Do you mean that I have no way to refute it? Tell me what else this phrase means, 'I have nothing to use to respond to these words'?" "But will you not answer," he said, "instead of saying it is difficult to deal with?" "Before you answer me?" I asked, "O Dionysodorus?" "Will you not answer?" he said. "Is it even just?" "It is just, indeed," he said. "On what grounds?" I asked. "Is it perhaps because you have arrived here as one all-wise in words, and you know when it is necessary to answer and when it is not? And now you will answer nothing at all, as you know you should not?" <margin>D</margin> "You are babbling," he said, "neglecting to answer. But, my good man, obey and answer, since you yourself admit I am wise." "I must obey, it seems," I said, "for you are in command. Ask then." "Do things that think have a soul?" he asked, "or do even soulless things think?" "Those with a soul." "Do you know," he asked, "any word that has a soul?" "By Zeus, not I." "Why then did you just ask me what my word meant?" "For no other reason," I said, "than my own stupidity, which led me to err. Or did I not err, but rather spoke correctly when I said that words 'mean' or 'think' something? Do you say I erred or not? For if I did not err, you will not refute me, even though you are wise, nor will you have anything to oppose to my speech. But if I did err, you are still not speaking correctly when you claim it is impossible to err. And these things I am saying are not from what you said last year! <margin>E</margin> But it seems to me," I continued, "O Dionysodorus and Euthydemus, that this argument revolves back to the same place; and now even, as it was formerly accustomed to do, it falls down even as it strikes. And your own art has not yet found a way to prevent this from happening to it, despite being so admirable for its precision in words." At this, Ctesippus said, "You say marvelous things, O men of Thurii <note>A Greek colony in Italy</note> or Chios <note>An island in the Aegean</note>, or wherever else you like to be named; it seems it is all the same to you to talk nonsense." <margin>F</margin> I, fearing that an insult might occur, again calmed Ctesippus, saying: "Ctesippus, I say the same to you that I said to Clinias. You do not know how wonderful the wisdom of these strangers is. They simply do not wish to show it to us in earnest, but like the Egyptian sophist Proteus <note>A sea god who changed shapes to avoid questioning</note>, they deceive us with tricks. Let us therefore imitate Menelaus and not let them go until they reveal what they truly intend. For I think they will show something quite beautiful if they begin to be serious. Therefore, let us beg them and pray that they manifest themselves. I think I will again lead the way in showing what sort of wisdom I pray they manifest to me. I will try to continue from where we left off before, <margin>G</margin> to see if I can provoke them by showing my pity, so that they might take the matter seriously. You, Clinias, remind me where we broke off our speech. For as I think, we stopped here, where we were agreeing that one must pursue philosophy. Is that not so?" "Certainly," he said. "And philosophy is the acquisition of knowledge," I said. "Yes," he said. "What knowledge then should we especially seek to acquire? Is it not, to put it simply, that which will benefit us?" "That very one," he said. "Would that knowledge benefit us most if we knew where the most gold is buried in the earth?" "Perhaps," he said. "But we refuted this long ago," I said, "because even if without labor and without digging the earth all things were made of gold for us, and we could even make the stones themselves gold, <margin>H</margin> even then this knowledge would be worthless and of no value. For if we do not know how to use the gold, it is of no use at all. Do you not remember?" "I remember," he said, "very much so." "Nor is any other knowledge of use, whether of money-making or medicine, or any other that teaches how to make something but does not teach how to use what is made. Is it not so?" He agreed. "Even if there were a knowledge that made us immortal, if it did not teach us how to use immortality, it would be of no benefit..."

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> is it possible for these things to be? "By all means," he said. "But that is not so," I said. "Certainly not," he replied. "Do you bring these things in for the sake of conversation, O Dionysodorus," I asked, "so that you might introduce something strange? Or truly, does no man seem to you to be ignorant?" "You, indeed," he said, "refute it." "Can anything be refuted," I said, "if, as you say, no one can lie?" "It cannot," said Euthydemus: "nor did Dionysodorus say that you should refute him. For in what way could anyone command what does not exist?" "I indeed, Euthydemus," I said, "do not very well learn these clever and distinguished things, but I touch on them in passing. Perhaps it will be burdensome what I ask, but forgive me, I pray. See, I beg you, if no one can lie, nor think false things, <margin>B</margin> nor be ignorant, then no one even while acting can err in anything. For he would not err from what he does. Is this what you say?" "Exactly so," he said. "This," I said, "is that heavy question. For if we never err, neither in acting, nor in speaking, nor even in thinking, what did you come here to teach? Did you not just now proclaim that you, above all others, could best deliver virtue to anyone who wished?" "To such an extent, O Socrates, are you a Cronus," said Dionysodorus, "that you remember now what we said at the beginning? And if I said anything last year, you will also remember it now; but as for these things which have been said in the present, you have nothing to answer." "Because they are difficult," I said, "and not without justice. <margin>C</margin> For they have proceeded from wise men. Indeed, even to that which you said last, it is most difficult to respond. For what do you mean, Dionysodorus, that I have nothing to answer? What do you wish to imply: that I have no way to convict that speech? For tell me what else that word means, that I have nothing with which those speeches might be answered by me? Do you mean anything else," he said, "than that it is difficult to answer? Surely answer before you yourself answer," I said, "Dionysodorus." "Why do you not answer?" he said. "Is it fair?" I asked. "Fair indeed," he said. "By what reason?" I asked. "Is it perhaps because you come to us endowed with the faculty of speaking, and you know when one must answer and when one must not, and therefore now you answer nothing, because it is not fitting to answer?" <margin>D</margin> To this he said, "You are trifiling, O Socrates, and you neglect to answer. But, O good man, obey, and answer him whom you yourself confess to be wise." "I must obey," I said, "for thus it is fitting to one who commands. Ask then." "Do those things have a soul," he asked, "whatever things understand anything? Or do they also lack a soul?" "They have one," I said. "Do you know," he asked, "any word having a soul?" "None indeed," I said. "Why then were you just now asking what the word meant?" "For no other reason," I said, "than because of my sluggishness, which forced me to err. But perhaps I did not err, but spoke rightly when I attributed thought to words. But do you say that I <margin>E</margin> erred or not? For if I did not err, neither will you now refute me, wise though you are, nor have you anything to oppose. But if I did err, not even then do you speak rightly when you say no one can err. And these things indeed I do not bring forward against those which you said last year. But it seems to me, O Dionysodorus and Euthydemus, this speech revolves to the same place; and now even, as was formerly accustomed to happen, when it strikes, it falls. And that this should not happen even to itself, it seems that your art, though admirable regarding the sharper diligence of speeches, has not yet provided." Here Ctesippus said, "You say marvelous things, O men of Thurii, or Chios, or whatever other name you please to claim: for whom to talk nonsense is all the same." <margin>F</margin> I, however, fearing lest it should come to insults, again mitigated Ctesippus thus: "The same things I say to you, O Ctesippus, I also said to Clinias. For you do not know how marvelous the wisdom of these guests is. But they do not wish to show it to us by choice, but after the manner of Proteus the Egyptian, that sophist, they deceive us with certain tricks. Let us therefore imitate Menelaus, and let them not go before they reveal what they have in mind. For they will exhibit something most beautiful, I think, if they bring it forth in truth. Wherefore let us exhort them and pray as suppliants that they exhibit it. But it seems I must again set forth what form of studies I require from them. I will endeavor from here, where we left off above, <margin>G</margin> to continue the speech, if in any way I might provoke them, so that pitying me, who am so heavily occupied, they might then treat the matter seriously. You, Clinias, tell me where we broke off the speech. For, as I think, we stuck here, where we were confessing that one must philosophize. Is it not so?" "Indeed," he said. "Philosophy is the acquisition of knowledge," I said. "Certainly," he said. "What knowledge then is it most fitting to acquire?" I asked. "Is it not, to say it briefly, that which benefits us?" "That very one," he said. "Would that knowledge benefit us most if we knew in what lands much gold is dug up?" "Surely," he said. "But we just now refuted that, because even if without labor, and without digging the earth, all things were golden for us, and we could even make the stones themselves golden, <margin>H</margin> yet this knowledge would be cheap and of no price. For if we do not know how to use gold, it is useful for nothing. Do you not remember?" "I remember," he said, "and most especially." "Nor is any knowledge of any thing, whether money-making, or medicine, or whatever else, useful," I said, "if it only teaches how to make, but does not teach how to use. Is it not so?" "Exactly," he said. "Even so," I said, "that if there were some knowledge that made us immortal, yet did not teach us how to use immortality..."

<summary>In this passage, Socrates challenges the sophists' claim that error is impossible, noting that if they cannot be wrong, they have nothing to teach. The dialogue then shifts to Socrates’ attempt to define the "kingly art" of philosophy as a type of knowledge that involves both the production and the correct use of things, such as gold or immortality.</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Dionysodorus, Euthydemus, sophistry, error, ignorance, Cronus, Proteus, philosophy, acquisition of knowledge, utility, immortality</keywords>

### OF PLATO

<columns>
<margin>A</margin>...would be entirely useless, if any faith is to be placed in the previous arguments. All these things seemed so to us. "Therefore, my dear boy," I said, "we have need of a science of such a kind that the making of a thing and the use of it should coincide." "It appears so," he said. "It seems then," I continued, "that there is a great difference between the art of the lyre-maker and the science of those who have attained the skill of playing the lyre. For one art is that which makes, and another is that which uses these things. For the art which fashions the lyre and that which plays the lyre differ greatly from one another. Do they not?" "It is so," he said. "Nor again," I said, "do we have need of the art of the flute-maker. For that art also differs from the one that uses it." "Certainly," he replied.

<margin>B</margin> "Perhaps then," I said, "the faculty of composing speeches is the one to be sought, so that you might become happy?" "I do not think so," he said. "What reason moves you to think this?" I asked. "I know indeed," he said, "certain authors of speeches who do not know how to use these very speeches they have composed, just as lyre-makers do not know how to use the lyres they have constructed for the use of others, who use them but do not know how to make them. It is clear, similarly, that regarding speeches there is one art that composes them, and another that uses what has been composed." "You seem to have pointed out with very clear evidence," I said, "that the art of those who compose speeches is by no means sufficient for happiness; although I was hoping that in this kind of science we would find what we have been seeking for so long."

<margin>C</margin> "Indeed, Clinia, these authors of speeches, as often as I have spoken with them, seem wise beyond all other mortals, and their art itself seems profoundly divine and sublime. And no wonder. For it is a certain part of the art of enchanters, and not much inferior to it. Furthermore, the faculty of enchanting is the soothing <note>original: "mitigatio" / "κήλησις" — a charming or spell-binding influence used to calm animals or people</note> of vipers, spiders, scorpions, and other wild beasts and diseases. But the oratorical art is a certain delighting and charming of judges, assemblymen, and other crowds. Or do you feel otherwise?" "Not otherwise," he said, "but exactly as you say." "Where then shall we turn," I asked, "and to what art?" "I am in doubt," he said. "But I think I have found it," I said. "Which one?" he asked. "The art of generalship <note>original: "Imperatoria" / "στρατηγική"</note> seems most of all to be the one which makes its possessor happy." "It does not seem so to me," he said.

<margin>D</margin> "For what reason?" I asked. "Because it seems to be a certain hunting art of men," he said. "What of it?" I asked. "Because," he said, "no hunter extends the work of hunting further than tracking and capturing; once they have seized what they were hunting, they are unable to use it. But those who hunt with dogs, and those who fish, hand over the prey to the cooks. Likewise, geometers, astronomers, and calculators <note>original: "logistæ" / "λογιστικοί"</note> are also hunters of a sort. For they do not make the figures and descriptions themselves, but they discover things as they are. Therefore, since they themselves do not know how to use them, they hunt only, and—provided they are not entirely lacking in mind—they hand over their discoveries to the dialecticians <note>original: "dialecticis" — those skilled in the art of logical discussion and the use of first principles</note> so that they may use them."

<margin>E</margin> "Well done, most beautiful and wise Clinia! Is it truly so?" "Exactly so," he said. "And by the same reasoning, the commanders of an army, after they have occupied either a city or an army, hand over the prey and spoils to the civil authorities. For they themselves do not know how to use these things they have seized, just as quail-catchers, after they have caught the quails, hand them over to the quail-breeders. If, therefore, you need that art which knows how to use what has been sought, whether by making it or by hunting it, and which makes its possessors happy, we must seek another art than the military one."

<margin>F</margin> CRITO: "What are you saying, Socrates? Did that youth say such things?" SOCRATES: "Do you not believe it, Crito?" CRITO: "By Jupiter, I do not. For I think if he said such things, he would no longer need the instruction of Euthydemus or any other man." SOCRATES: "Perhaps then it was Ctesippus who said these things, and I do not remember correctly." CRITO: "Which Ctesippus?" SOCRATES: "At least I remember this: it was neither Euthydemus nor Dionysodorus who brought these points forward. But, O blessed Crito, I suspect some more excellent person <note>original: "πράστιανότερον" / "prestantiorem" — Socrates suggests a divine or supernatural influence was speaking through the boy</note> present there said these things. For I do not doubt that I heard them." CRITO: "By Jupiter, Socrates, someone more excellent indeed seems to have produced those words. But after this, what art did you eventually examine? Did you find what you were seeking, or not?" SOCRATES: "How, O blessed one, could we have found it?"

<margin>G</margin> "Something ridiculous happened. For in the manner of children who chase larks <note>original: "galeritas" / "κορυδοὺς" — specifically the crested lark</note>, we were pursuing each of the sciences with a certain vehement passion, and always, just as we thought we were about to catch one, it would slip away and escape us. Why should I list them all to you? We approached the Royal Art <note>original: "Regiam artem" / "βασιλικὴν τέχνην"</note>, considering whether or not it was the one that makes men happy. But having fallen as if into a labyrinth, just when we hoped we were near the end, we turned back and were returned to the beginning again, finding ourselves in the same state as we were at the start of the dispute." CRITO: "How did this happen?" SOCRATES: "I will tell you. The royal faculty seemed to us to be the same as the civil or political art." CRITO: "In what way?" SOCRATES: "Since the military art and all other faculties seemed to submit the command of their works to the civil art, as if it were the only one that knows how to use them, we thought nothing would hinder this from being what we sought, being the cause of rightly administering the republic, and—according to that iambic line of Aeschylus—presiding alone at the helm of the city <note>original: "puppi sola ciuitatis præsidens" — a reference to Aeschylus' 'Seven Against Thebes'</note>, holding the rudders of the whole, ruling over all things, and making all things useful."

<margin>H</margin> CRITO: "And did this not seem right to you, Socrates?" SOCRATES: "You shall judge for yourself, Crito, if you hear what happened next. For we were seeking again in this manner: 'Come then, does that Royal Art, presiding over all things, produce some work or not?' 'Surely it does,'..."

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> "...nor does there seem to be any benefit from this art; if indeed we must obey what was previously agreed upon." These things seemed entirely so to us. "Therefore, my dear boy," I said, "we have need of a certain knowledge in which the making of a thing and the knowledge of how to use what one makes coincide." "It appears so," he said. "It seems then that the art of the lyre-maker is far from being such a knowledge. For here the art that makes and the art that uses are divided into separate things, even though they concern the same object; for the art of making lyres and the art of playing the cithara differ greatly from each other. Is it not so?" He agreed. "Nor indeed do we have any need of the art of flute-making. For this is another such art." It was agreed. "But by the gods," I said, "if we were to learn the art of speech-making, is this the one we should possess to be happy?"

<margin>B</margin> "I do not think so," said Clinia, interrupting. "What evidence do you use for this?" I asked. "I see," he said, "certain speech-makers who do not know how to use their own speeches which they themselves have made, just as lyre-makers do with lyres; but even here others are able to use what those men have crafted, though they are unable to make lyres themselves. It is clear then that regarding speeches, the art of making and the art of using are separate." "You seem to me," I said, "to state sufficient evidence that this art of the speech-makers is not the one which, if possessed, would make a person happy. And yet I thought that somewhere here would appear the science which we have been seeking for so long."

<margin>C</margin> "For indeed the men themselves, the speech-makers, whenever I associate with them, Clinia, seem to be super-wise; and their art itself is something wondrous and sublime. And indeed it is no wonder; for it is a part of the art of enchanters, and only slightly inferior to it. For the art of enchanters is the charming of vipers and spiders and scorpions and other beasts and diseases; while the other happens to be the charming and consolation of judges and assemblymen and other crowds. Or does it seem otherwise to you?" I asked. "No, but it appears to me just as you say," he said. "Where then," I asked, "should we turn? Toward what kind of art?" "I am not well-supplied with an answer," he said. "But," I said, "I think

<margin>D</margin> I have found it." "What is it?" asked Clinia. "The art of generalship seems to me," I said, "more than any other, to be the art which one might possess and be happy." "It does not seem so to me." "How so?" I asked. "This is a certain art of hunting humans," he said. "Why so?" I asked. "No part of hunting itself," he said, "goes further than hunting and capturing. But when they have captured that which they were hunting, they are not able to use it; instead, the hunters and the fishermen hand it over to the cooks. And again, the geometers and the astronomers and the calculators—for these too are hunters; for they do not make their diagrams, but discover the things that exist. Since, therefore, they do not know how to use these things themselves, but only how to hunt them, they hand them over,

<margin>E</margin> I suppose, to the dialecticians to make use of their discoveries, at least those of them who are not entirely foolish." "Very well," I said, "most beautiful and wise Clinia, is this how it is?" "Entirely so. And the generals," he said, "in the same way, whenever they have hunted a city or an army, they hand it over to the statesmen. For they themselves do not know how to use these things which they have hunted; just as, I think, quail-catchers hand them over to quail-breeders. If then," he said, "we need that art which, whatever it acquires either by making or by hunting, also knows how to use it, and such an art will make us blessed, then we must seek some other art," he said, "instead of

<margin>F</margin> generalship." CRITO: "What are you saying, Socrates? Did that youth utter such things?" SOCRATES: "Do you not think so, Crito?" CRITO: "By Zeus, certainly not. For I think that if he said these things, he would no longer need Euthydemus or anyone else for his education." SOCRATES: "But then, by Zeus, was it Ctesippus who said these things? For I do not remember." CRITO: "What Ctesippus?" SOCRATES: "But I do know this much: it was neither Euthydemus nor Dionysodorus who said these things. But, my dear Crito, perhaps some one of the higher powers present there uttered them? For that I heard these things, I know for certain." CRITO: "Yes, by Zeus, Socrates; some one of the higher powers indeed it seems to me, and very much so. But after this, what art did you seek? And did you find that one for the sake of which you were seeking?" SOCRATES: "From where, O blessed man, would we have found it? We were

<margin>G</margin> entirely ridiculous, just like children who chase larks; we always thought we were about to catch each of the sciences immediately, but they always slipped away. Why should I say more? When we came to the Royal Art and were examining it to see if this was the one that provides and produces happiness, then, as if falling into a labyrinth, just when we thought we were at the end, we turned back again and appeared to be right at the beginning of the search, needing just as much as when we first started seeking." CRITO: "How did this happen to you, Socrates?" SOCRATES: "I will tell you. For it seemed to us that the political art and the Royal Art were the same thing." CRITO: "Why so?" SOCRATES: "To this art, generalship and the others hand over the command of the works of which they themselves are the craftsmen, as it alone knows how to use them. It clearly seemed

<margin>H</margin> to us then that this was the one we were seeking, and the cause of acting rightly in the city; and simply, according to the iambic verse of Aeschylus, it alone sits at the helm of the city, steering all things and ruling all things, making all things useful." CRITO: "Did it not then seem well to you, Socrates?" SOCRATES: "You shall judge, Crito, if you are willing to hear what happened after this. For again we were looking at it somewhat in this way: 'Come, what does the Royal Art produce for us? It does work, I suppose?'"
</columns>

<summary>Socrates and Clinia conclude that generalship and rhetoric are merely forms of "hunting" or "making" that require a higher art to use their products; they identify this as the Royal or Political Art, but soon find themselves lost in a logical labyrinth.</summary>
