### EUTHYDEMUS

<margin>A</margin>
...we all agreed. For would you not also concede these things, Crito? CRITO: Without a doubt. SOCRATES: What then would you say is its work? As if I were to ask you: while Medicine governs all those things over which it is mistress, what work does it produce? Would you not rather answer "health"? CRITO: Certainly. SOCRATES: Likewise, what does your art of agriculture produce while it governs all those things over which it is mistress? Would you say it provides us with nourishment from the earth? CRITO: Indeed. SOCRATES: What work, then, does the **Royal Art** <note>original: "Regia facultas"; referring to the art of kingship or statesmanship</note> complete, since it governs all those things over which it is mistress? Perhaps the answer is not ready at hand. CRITO: By Hercules, it is not, Socrates. SOCRATES: Nor is it for us, 
<margin>B</margin>
Crito. But this much at least you know: if this is the art we desire, it must be useful. CRITO: Extremely so. SOCRATES: Is it not therefore necessary that it bring us some good? CRITO: It is altogether necessary. SOCRATES: Now, Clinias and I agreed that "good" is nothing other than a certain kind of knowledge. CRITO: So you certainly said. SOCRATES: Regarding the works of civil government, although everyone might especially grant that there are many—such as making the citizens wealthy, free, and in harmony—these things 
<margin>C</margin>
appeared to be neither good nor bad in themselves. But it is necessary, as was settled, that this art makes people wise and imparts knowledge, if indeed it is to be the one that profits us and makes us happy. CRITO: You speak the truth. For so it was settled between you then, just as you have recounted. SOCRATES: Does the royal discipline, then, make men wise and good? CRITO: What prevents it, Socrates? SOCRATES: But does it make *all* men good in *all* things, and does it provide *all* knowledge—the tanner's art, the carpenter's art, and all the rest? CRITO: I certainly do not think so, Socrates. SOCRATES: But then what knowledge is it? And in what way shall we be helped? It is not right for this art to be the producer of those works which are neither good nor bad. 
<margin>D</margin>
It is fitting that it provide no other knowledge than itself. Let us say then what this is, and how we are helped. Do you wish us to say, Crito, that it is the art by which we can make others good? CRITO: I certainly do. SOCRATES: And to what end will those "good" people lead? Or in what way will they be useful? Shall we say they will make others good? And those others will make yet more people good? But in what way they are actually "good" is nowhere apparent to us, since we have rejected those works called the "civil arts." Plainly—as the proverb goes—it has become a <margin>Proverb.</margin> "Corinth of Zeus" <note>original: "Iouis Corinthus"; a Greek proverb for something that repeats pointlessly or fails to reach a conclusion, like a circular argument</note>. And as I said before, we are just as far—indeed, even further than before—from finding that art which has the power to grant us happiness. CRITO: By Jove, Socrates, you seem to have fallen into a very great difficulty. 
<margin>E</margin>
SOCRATES: I indeed, Crito, when I was cast into this doubt, immediately cried out as loudly as I could, calling upon those strangers <note>The sophists Euthydemus and Dionysodorus</note> as if they were the **Dioscuri** <note>Castor and Pollux, the twin sons of Zeus, often called upon by sailors for rescue from storms</note>, begging them to snatch us—myself and the lad—from this turbulent surge of arguments. I asked them to set aside their joking and show us in earnest what that knowledge is, which, once acquired, would allow us to pass through the remainder of our lives happily. CRITO: And did Euthydemus wish to show you? SOCRATES: How could he not? And he began, my friend, to speak quite magnificently in this manner: "Shall I teach you, Socrates," he said, "this knowledge which you have long been seeking, or shall I demonstrate that you already possess it?" "O blessed man," I said, "are you able to do this?" "Very much so," he said. "Then demonstrate that I have it," I replied, "for that is much easier for me than learning it anew at my age." "Come then," he said, "answer me: do you know 
<margin>F</margin>
anything?" "I certainly know many things," I said, "though they are small." "That is enough," he said. "Do you think it possible for any existing thing *not* to be that very thing which it is?" "In no way," I said. "Do you not assert that you know something?" he asked. "Certainly." "Are you not then 'knowing' <note>original: "sciens"; possessing knowledge</note>, if indeed you know?" "I am, at least in regarding that which I know." "It makes no difference," he said. "Is it not necessary that you, being a 'knowing' person, know all things?" "No, by Jove," I said, "since there are many other things I do not know." "If there is something you do not know," he said, "are you not 'not-knowing'?" "Regarding that which I do not know, my friend," I said. "Nonetheless, you are 'not-knowing,'" he said, "yet you just now claimed to be 'knowing.' And so it happens that you are the very person who you are—both knowing and, again, not knowing, at the same time and in the same respect." "Very well, Euthydemus," I said. "For as the proverb goes, 'you say all things beautifully' <margin>Proverb</margin> 
<margin>G</margin>
<note>Equivalent to "you've said a mouthful"</note>. How then do I have that knowledge we were seeking? Because, evidently, it is impossible for a thing to be and not to be at the same time. Hence, if I know one thing, I know all things—for I cannot be 'knowing' and 'not-knowing' at once. And if I know all things, I also possess that knowledge we seek. Is that not what you are saying? And is this your wisdom?" "You are refuting yourself, Socrates," he said. "But what about you, Euthydemus?" I asked. "Has the same not happened to you? For I would not be at all bothered by whatever I might suffer alongside you and Dionysodorus here, this 'dear head' <note>A friendly Greek idiom for a person</note>. Tell me, do you two not know some things while not knowing others?" "Not at all, Socrates," said Dionysodorus. "What are you saying?" I asked. "Do you know nothing?" "Quite the contrary," he said. "Then you know all things," I said, "since you know anything at all." "All things," he said. "And you too know all things, if you know even one thing." "O Zeus!" I cried, "What a marvelous thing you say, and what a great blessing has appeared! Do all other men also know all things, or nothing?" "Surely," he said, "they cannot know some things and not know others, and thus be 'knowing' and 'not-knowing' at the same time." "What then?" I asked. <meta>Continuity: Following the search for the "Royal Art" or statesmanship, Socrates and Crito return to the demonstration by the sophists Euthydemus and Dionysodorus, who claim to possess a universal knowledge that makes all other learning unnecessary.</meta>

->OF PLATO<-

<margin>A</margin> Now at last, Dionysodorus, you seem to me to be speaking in earnest, and only with difficulty have I finally persuaded you to act seriously. Do you two truly know all things? For instance, the craft of carpentry and shoemaking? "Absolutely everything," he said. Do you also know how to sew with sinews <note>original: "neruis suere"; refers to the use of animal tendons as thread in shoemaking</note>? "Certainly," he replied, "and even how to cobble shoes." And do you know, I asked, the number of the stars and of the grains of sand? "Indeed," he said. "Do you think we would not admit to those as well?" Here Ctesippus, interrupting, said: "By Zeus, Dionysodorus, show us some such proof by which we may conclude that you are speaking the truth." "What sort of proof?" he asked. "Do you know," he said, "how many teeth Euthydemus has? And does Euthydemus know how many you have?" "Is it not enough for you," he replied, "to hear that we know all things?" "By no means," he said, "but show us this one thing only, that you speak the truth. For if you tell us how many teeth each of you has, and after we have counted them you are found to have spoken the truth, then we will believe you in everything else as well."

<margin>B</margin> But they, thinking that Ctesippus was trying to mock <note>original: "mordere" (to bite); here used metaphorically for verbal ribbing or biting wit</note> them, refused to answer anything else, except to repeat that they knew all things when questioned about particulars by Ctesippus. For Ctesippus questioned them quite openly about every single thing, even the most trivial or shameful matters, asking if they knew them. They, however, faced the questions with great courage, like wild boars <note>Plato often compares eristic or combative debaters to wild animals charging at their opponents</note> who charge against a blow, asserting that they understood everything.

<margin>C</margin> Therefore I too, O Crito, was finally compelled by my own disbelief to ask Euthydemus whether Dionysodorus also knew how to dance. He agreed that he did. "Surely not," I said, "to tumble over swords or turn upon a wheel at your age? Have you advanced so far in wisdom?" "There is nothing," he said, "that he does not know."

<margin>D</margin> Then I said: "Do you know all things only now? Or have you always known them?" "Always," they replied. "Did you know all things even from your tenderest age, and immediately when you were born?" "Everything," they both answered together. To us, this seemed an incredible thing. Then Euthydemus said, "Do you not believe it, Socrates?" "I would," I replied, "except for the fact that it is likely you are already wise." "And if you will answer me," he said, "I will show that you too admit to these wonderful things." "It would be most welcome," I said, "if you could convince me of this. For if I have been wise without knowing it, and you show that I know everything and have always known it, what greater windfall could I find in my whole life?" "Answer then," he said. "Ask," I replied, "as if I am ready to answer." "Are you a knower of something, Socrates, or of nothing?" "Of something," I said. "And do you know by that which makes you a knower, or by something else?" "By that which makes me a knower. For I suppose you mean the soul. Is that what you mean?" "Are you not ashamed, Socrates," he said, "to ask a question in return when you are being questioned?" "But what should I do?" I asked. "I will do whatever you command, though I do not know what you are asking. You order me to answer, but not to ask questions." "You surely conceive of something," he said, "by what I ask?" "I do," I replied. "Then answer according to what you conceive." "What then," I said, "if you ask with one meaning in mind, but I answer with another, having conceived something else? Will you be satisfied if I answer nothing to the point?" "It will be enough for me," he said, "though not for you, I think." Then I said, "By Jove, I will not answer until I hear more." "You will not answer," he said, "according to what you always conceive in your mind? You are talking nonsense, Socrates, and are far more unrefined than you ought to be." I realized then that he was a bit angry with me because I was making distinctions in the words with which he was trying to entangle me. I also remembered Connus <note>Socrates' music teacher, whom he frequently mentions as being frustrated by his slow learning</note>, who is often indignant with me whenever I do not yield to him, and then scorns me as if I were unlearned. Since I intended to give myself over to the teaching of these two, I thought I ought to be compliant, lest they reject me as a fool or an unteachable student.

<margin>F</margin> "Therefore," I said, "if it seems to you, Euthydemus, that this is how we must proceed, let it be so. For you understand the method of disputing much better than I, since you possess the art, while I am but a layman. Ask again from the beginning." "Answer again," he said, "whether you know what you know by something, or by nothing?" "By the soul," I said. "This man," he cried, "answers more than he is asked! I am not asking *by what* you know, but *whether* you know by something or not." "I have answered more than was proper," I said, "on account of my lack of education. Please forgive me. I will now answer simply that I always know whatever I know by something." "And is it always by this same thing," he asked, "or sometimes by this and sometimes by another?" "Always," I said, "when I know, I know by this."

<margin>G</margin> Here he said, "Will you not stop adding things beside the point?" "I answered this way," I said, "lest the word 'always' should deceive us." "It would not deceive us," he said, "but perhaps it deceives you. But answer: do you always know by this?" "Always," I replied, "since I must withdraw the 'whenever.'" "Do you not then always know by this? And since you always know, do you know some things by this by which you know, and others by something else, or all things by this same thing?" "All things," I said, "at least all that I know." "There it is again," he said, "the same qualification!" "I withdraw then," I said, "the phrase 'at least all that I know.'" "Do not withdraw a single thing," he said, "for I require nothing from you. But answer me: could you know all things unless you knew all things?" "That would be a marvel," I said. "Add now whatever you please," he said, "for you confess that you know all things. Is it so?" "It seems so," I said, "since my qualification 'whatever I know' has no weight; therefore I know all things." "And did you not also confess that you always know by that by which you know? Whether you know whenever, or however you please? For you have confessed that you always know, and all things at once. It is clear then that even when you were a child you knew, and when you were being conceived, and when you were born; indeed, even before you were born, and before the heaven and earth came to be, you knew all things, if indeed you always know."

<column-break/>

<margin>Α</margin> "O Dionysodorus," I said, "for it is clear to me now that you two are in earnest, and I have only with difficulty called upon you to be serious; do you both truly know all things, such as carpentry and shoemaking?" "Entirely," he replied. "And would you be able to sew with sinews?" "Yes, by Zeus, and cobble shoes." "And such things as the number of the stars, and the sand?" "Certainly," he said. "Or do you think we would not agree?" And Ctesippus, taking him up, said: "By Zeus, Dionysodorus, show me some proof of this, by which I shall know that you both speak the truth." "What shall I show?" he asked. "I know," he said, "how many teeth Euthydemus has; and Euthydemus knows how many you have." "Is it not enough for you," he said, "to hear that we know all things?" "Not at all," he replied, "but tell us this one thing more, and show that 
<margin>Β</margin> 
you speak the truth; and if you tell us how many each of you has, and we are seen to know it after we have counted, we will then believe you in the rest." Thinking they were being mocked, they were unwilling to do so, but they agreed that they knew all matters when asked about each one by Ctesippus. For Ctesippus, quite without concealment, asked about everything at the end, even the most shameful things, if they knew them. And they, most bravely meeting the questions, agreed that they knew; just like boars that charge against a blow. So that I myself, O Crito, falling at last into necessity through disbelief, asked Euthydemus if Dionysodorus also knew how to dance.
<margin>C</margin> 
And he said, "Entirely." "Surely not," I said, "to tumble among swords and turn upon a wheel at such an age? Have you come so far in wisdom?" "There is nothing," he said, "that he does not know." "And do you both," I asked, "know all things only now, or always?" "Always," he said. "And when you were children and immediately upon being born, did you know all things?" They both said yes at the same time. And to all of us, the matter seemed incredible. Then Euthydemus said, "Do you disbelieve, Socrates?" "Except," I said, "that it is likely you are wise." "But if," he said, "you will be willing to answer me, I will show that you also agree to these wonderful things." "Indeed," I said, "I will most gladly be refuted in this. For if I have been wise without knowing it, and you show this—that I know all things and always—what greater piece of luck <note>original: "hermaion"; literally a gift from Hermes, meaning a stroke of luck or a windfall</note> could I find in all my life?" "Answer then," he said. "Ask, as if I am going to answer." "Are you, then, Socrates," he asked, "a knower of something? Or not?" "I am." "Do you then know by that which makes you a knower, or by something else?" "By that which makes me a knower. For I think you mean the soul. Or do you not mean this?" "Are you not ashamed," he said, "O Socrates, being questioned, to ask a question in return?" "Very well," I said, "but how shall I act? For I will act as you command. When I do not know what you are asking, you nevertheless command me to answer, and not to ask again." "You surely conceive of something," he said, "in what I say?" "I do," I said. "To that, then, answer according to what you conceive." "What then," I said, "if you ask with one thing in mind 
<margin>Ε</margin> 
erringly, and I conceive it another way, and then I answer you according to that, will it satisfy you if I answer nothing to the point?" "To me, yes," he said, "but not to you, as I think." "By Zeus, I will not answer then," I said, "until I find out." "You will not answer," he said, "according to what you may always conceive, because you have nonsense to talk, and are more ancient than is fitting." And I knew that he was angry with me for distinguishing the things being said, wanting to hunt me down by surrounding me with names. I remembered then Connus, that he too is angry with me every time I do not yield to him; and then he takes less care of me, as being ignorant. Since then I was intending to attend these two as a pupil, I thought it necessary to yield, lest they, thinking me a clumsy student, should not receive me. I said therefore, "But if it seems best to you, Euthydemus, to do this, it must be done. For you 
<margin>F</margin> 
surely know better how to discourse than I, who have an art while I am a common man. Ask then again from the beginning." "Answer then again," he said, "whether you know what you know by something, or not?" "I do," I said, "by the soul." "This one again," he said, "answers more than what is asked. For I do not ask by what, but if you know something." "Again I have answered more than what is fitting," I said, "through lack of training; but forgive me. I will answer now simply that I know what I know by something always." "Is it," he said, "always by this same thing? Or is there a time when it is by this, and a time when it is by another?" "Always, whenever I know," I said, "it is by this." "Will you not again," he said, "stop adding qualifications?" "But only so that this 'always' does not trip us up." "Not us, certainly," he said, "but if anyone, you. But answer: do you always know by this?" "Always," I said, "since I must take away the 'whenever.'" 
<margin>G</margin> 
"Then you always know by this; and always knowing, do you know some things by this, and some things by another? Or all things by this?" "All things," I said, "at least those that I know." "There it is again," he said, "the same old qualification." "But I take away," I said, "the 'at least those that I know.'" "But do not take away even one thing," he said, "for I have no need of you. But answer me: could you know all things if you did not know all things?" "That would be a monster," I said. And he said, "Add then now whatever you wish. For you have agreed to know all things." "It seems so," I said, "since the 'what I know' has no power, I know all things." "Then you have also agreed that you always know by that by which you know; whether whenever you know, or however you please. For you have agreed to always know, and all things at the same time. It is clear then that even when you were a child you knew, and when you were being conceived, and when you were growing. And before heaven and earth themselves came to be, you knew all things, if indeed you always know."

<summary>In this passage from Plato's Euthydemus, the sophists use logical traps to argue that they and Socrates possess total omniscience, having known all things even before birth. The dialogue satirizes "eristic" reasoning—a combative style of argument focused on winning rather than finding the truth.</summary>

"And do you seem to be doing the same?" "Is it not impossible," Dionysodorus asked, "to speak while being silent?" "Impossible," Ctesippus said. <margin>E</margin> "But is it possible to be silent while speaking?" "Much less possible." "When you speak of stones, and wood, and iron, are you not speaking of silent things?" Ctesippus asked, "Are all things not silent?" "Certainly not," said Euthydemus. "Do all things speak then, my good man?" "Indeed, those that speak, do." "I was not asking that," he said, "but whether all things are silent or speak." Then, snatching the argument away, Dionysodorus said, "Neither and both. Clinias also laughed, being very delighted. Wherefore Ctesippus, exulting, grew more than ten times in his joy. It seemed to me that Ctesippus, like a crafty old fox, had wrung these very tricks from them by his own shrewdness. ...the other, or the same. "But for my part," I said, "I did not think even a child would suspect that 'the other' is not 'other.' But, O Dionysodorus, you have bypassed this point on purpose. "Do you know then," he asked, "what is appropriate for each craftsman? First, whom is it appropriate to work in bronze?" "I know indeed," I said, "the blacksmith." "And who is to work in clay?" "The potter." "And who is to slaughter, skin, chop into small pieces, boil, and roast?" "The cook," I replied. "Therefore," he said, "if someone does what is appropriate, will he act rightly?" "Most certainly." "And it is appropriate, as you say, for the cook to chop and skin. Did you agree to this, or not?" "I did," I said, "but please, have mercy on me." <margin>B</margin> "It is clear then," he said, "that if someone slaughters and chops up the cook, then boils and roasts him, he will be doing what is appropriate. And if someone hammers the blacksmith like bronze, or molds the potter like clay, he too will be doing what is appropriate." <margin>A</margin> "O Poseidon!" I cried, "you are now putting the <term>colophon</term><note>original: κολοφῶνα (kolophōna). A 'colophon' was a finishing stroke or a crowning touch to an argument.</note> on your wisdom. Will this skill ever be mine so that it becomes my own?" "Would you even recognize it, Socrates," he asked, "if it became your own?" "If you are willing," I said, "then clearly I would." "What then?" he asked. "Do you think you know what is your own?" "I do, unless you say otherwise. For I must begin with you and end with Euthydemus here." <margin>B</margin> "Do you then," he asked, "consider those things to be yours which you rule over, and which you are permitted to use however you wish? For example, cattle and sheep—would you consider those yours which you are permitted to sell, to give away, or to sacrifice to whichever of the gods you wish? And those things not so treated are not yours?" <margin>C</margin> And I—knowing that some beautiful point was about to emerge from these questions, and wishing to hear it as quickly as possible—said, "Certainly, it is exactly so; only such things are mine." "What then?" he asked. "Do you not call those things 'living beings' which have a soul?" "Yes," I said. "You agree then," he said, "that those living beings are yours which you have the power to do all these things with that I just mentioned?" "I agree." <margin>D</margin> And he, acting very ironically as if he were contemplating something great, said: "Tell me, Socrates, do you have a <term>paternal Zeus</term><note>original: Ζεὺς πατρῷος (Zeus Patrōos). A 'paternal' god is an ancestral deity of a family or tribe.</note>?" And I, suspecting the argument was headed exactly where it ended up, tried to dodge and turn like someone caught in a net. "I do not, Dionysodorus," I said. "Then you are a wretched man," he said, "and not even an Athenian, for you have no paternal gods, no sacred rites, nor anything else beautiful and good." "Hush, Dionysodorus," I said, "speak auspiciously and do not instruct me so harshly. For I do have altars and sacred rites, both domestic and paternal, and all other such things that other Athenians have." "Then for other Athenians," he said, "is there no paternal Zeus?" "There is not," I said. "This title is used by none of the <term>Ionians</term><note>The Ionians were one of the major linguistic and cultural divisions of the Greek world; Athens considered itself the mother city of the Ionians.</note>, neither those who migrated from this city nor by us. Instead, we have a <term>paternal Apollo</term>, because of the birth of Ion. <margin>E</margin> Zeus is not called 'paternal' by us, but <term>Herkeios</term><note>original: ἕρκειος. Meaning 'of the courtyard,' the protector of the household enclosure.</note> and <term>Phratrios</term><note>original: φράτριος. Meaning 'of the phratry' or kinship group.</note>, and Athena is also called Phratria." "Well, that is enough," said Dionysodorus. "For you have, as it seems, Apollo, Zeus, and Athena." "Certainly," I said. "Therefore, these would be your gods?" he asked. "Ancestors," I said, "and masters." "But they are yours, nonetheless," he said. "Did you not confess they are yours?" "I did," I said. "What else can I do?" "Are these gods not then living beings?" he asked. "For you agreed that whatever has a soul is a living being. Or do these gods not have a soul?" "They have one," I said. "Are they then living beings?" "They are," I said. "And you agreed," he said, "that of living beings, those are yours which you have the permission to give away, to sell, and to sacrifice to any god you wish." "I agreed," I said, "for I have been caught by you, Euthydemus!" <margin>F</margin> "Tell me then immediately," he said, "since you have admitted that Zeus and the other gods are yours, is it permitted for you to sell them, or give them away, or use them in any other way you wish, just like other living beings?" Then I, Crito, as if struck by the argument, lay there speechless. But Ctesippus came to my aid and said, "Bravo, O Hercules! What a fine argument!" And Dionysodorus replied, "Is Hercules 'Bravo,' or is 'Bravo' Hercules?" <margin>G</margin> And Ctesippus said, "O Poseidon! What terrifying arguments. I give up; these men are invincible." At that point, my dear Crito, there was no one present who did not praise the argument to the skies; laughing, clapping, and rejoicing, they were almost exhausted. For in the previous points, each time Euthydemus's followers alone had cheered quite beautifully; but here, even the columns in the <term>Lyceum</term><note>The Lyceum was a public gymnasium in Athens where philosophers and teachers gathered.</note> almost cheered for the two men and were delighted. I myself was so affected that I confessed I had never seen any men so wise; and being utterly enslaved by their wisdom, I turned to praising and eulogizing them, saying: "O happy pair, for your wonderful nature, who have perfected such a great matter so quickly and in such a short time! Your arguments contain many other beautiful things, Euthydemus and Dionysodorus; but among them, this is most magnificent: that you care nothing for the many, nor for the solemn men who think they are something, but only for those similar to yourselves. <margin>H</margin> And I know well that very few people like yourselves would be pleased by these arguments; but the rest are so ignorant of them that I know well they would be more ashamed..."

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...the same? But I did not think even a child would suspect this—that what is different is not different. Truly, O Dionysodorus, you have omitted this of your own accord. But you seem to me like craftsmen whose duty it is to finish each task, to pass through and deliver the method of disputation with decorum. "Do you know," he said, "what is appropriate for each craftsman to finish? First, do you know who should hammer bronze?" "The blacksmith," I said. "And who should mold clay?" "The potter." "And who again should slaughter and skin, and roast or boil meat cut into pieces?" "The cook." "Does not everyone who does what is appropriate, do rightly?" "Very much so," I said. "It is appropriate, as you say," he said, "for the cook to cut and skin. Have you granted this, or not?" *"I have granted it," I said, "but I pray you, forgive me."* <margin>B</margin> "It is established then," he said, "that if someone, in slaughtering and cutting up the cook, boils or roasts him, he does what is appropriate. Furthermore, if someone hammers the blacksmith with bronze, and molds the potter, he will likewise perform what is fitting." *"O Neptune," I said, "now you have placed the colophon on that wisdom of yours. Will this ever be present with me so that it becomes my own property?"* "Would you recognize it, Socrates," he asked, "now that it has been made your own?" *"If you yourself wish it," I said, "I certainly would."* "What further," he said, "do you think you recognize as your own?" *"Indeed," I said, "unless perhaps you say otherwise. For it is necessary to begin from you, but to end with this Euthydemus."* "Do you not think those things are yours," he asked, "of which you are <margin>C</margin> the master? And that you may use them at your will, like oxen and sheep? Do you think those are yours which you can sell and bestow, and vow to any of the gods? But those you cannot, are not yours?" *And I, thinking that some excellent question would arise from this, and being immediately inflamed with the greed of hearing it, said: "It is exactly so. Surely such things are mine."* "Do you not," he asked, "name those things 'animals' which have a soul?" *"Those very things," I said.* "Do you confess then that of animals, only those are yours concerning which you can do all these things that I just mentioned?" *"I confess it," I said.* At this, he restrained himself quite ironically, as if about to contemplate something great; then he said: "Come tell me, O Socrates. Is <margin>D</margin> there for you a paternal Jupiter?" *But I, suspecting the speech would return to where it arrived, and withdrawing through a certain ambiguous bypass, escaped the net in which I was already as if entangled, and I answered: "There is not, O Dionysodorus." "Wretched man you are," he said, "and not even an Athenian, for you have neither paternal gods, nor sacred rites, nor any other excellent and magnificent thing." "Cease those things, Dionysodorus," I said, "lest you speak ill omens, and do not instruct me so sharply. For I have both altars and domestic and paternal sacred rites, and whatever other things of that kind are present for Athenians."* "For the rest of the Athenians," he said, "is there a paternal Jupiter?" *"There is not," I said, "among the Ionians such a kinship, nor among those who flowed out from this city, nor among us, but a paternal Apollo because of the begetting of Ion. Jupiter is not called paternal by us, but he is called the protector of the city and the curator of the tribe, and Minerva is the curatrix of the tribe."* "It is enough," said Dionysodorus. "For there is for you, as it seems, Apollo, Jupiter, and Minerva." *"Altogether." "Will not those be your gods, namely as progenitors and masters? Are they not yours? Have you not confessed they are yours?" "I have confessed it," I said. "What then?"* "Are those gods not animals?" he said. *"You have further granted that whatever has a soul is an animal; but do these gods not have a soul?" "They certainly have," I said.* "Are they therefore animals?" *"They certainly are."* "But you said those of the animals were yours, over which you had power, so that you might at your will sell, bestow, and dedicate them to the gods." <margin>F</margin> *I cannot refuse Euthydemus, but that I granted those things.* Immediately he brought it in thus: "Since you confess that Jupiter is yours, and the other gods are yours, is it permitted for you to sell them and bestow them, and to treat them according to your lust as you do the other animals that are yours?" *I then, Crito, as if struck by the speech, fell silent. Ctesippus, however, attempting to help me, said, "Wow, by Hercules, what a magnificent speech!"* To which Dionysodorus said, "Is Hercules 'Wow,' or is 'Wow' Hercules?" *Then Ctesippus said, "By Neptune, what strong and hard speeches. I desist now."* These men are invincible. At this point truly, dear Crito, none of those present could contain themselves further from <margin>G</margin> extolling their speech with the highest praises. And those guests, Dionysodorus and Euthydemus, exulting and gesturing with laughter, applause, and joy, were almost undone. For in the earlier parts, while they brought forth individual points, only their followers immediately applauded. Here, however, almost the very columns of the Lyceum seemed to shout together, to applaud, and to rejoice. I indeed was so affected that I asserted I had never seen any men with equal wisdom. And being thoroughly enslaved to their wisdom, I began to praise and celebrate them exceedingly. "O men," I said, "blessed because of the wondrous gifts of nature: since you have finished so great a matter so easily and in so brief a time. Many other things indeed are excellent in your speeches, Euthydemus and Dionysodorus, in which this is especially <margin>H</margin> magnificent: that you have no care either for the common people or even for illustrious men, nor are they held in any value, but only those similar to you. I certainly know that there are few who would love this kind of speech, and those indeed similar to you; but the others are so ignorant of them and so [fear] them, that they would be more greatly ashamed..."

<summary>This page concludes a series of sophistic traps where Dionysodorus and Euthydemus use logical fallacies to argue that if Socrates owns his gods and they are "living things," he must be able to sell or sacrifice them like cattle. The scene ends with the crowd at the Lyceum erupting in ironic or overwhelmed applause at the absurdity.</summary>

-># PLATONIS<-

<margin>A</margin> ...if they should convince others with these arguments, rather than being convinced by others themselves. Moreover, your speeches have this popular and gentle quality: that you say nothing is either good or bad, nor white, nor any other such quality, nor absolutely anything distinct from another. In truth, as you boast, you effectively sew up men's mouths. Because you shut not only the mouths of others, but your own as well, it is a very charming thing, and you avoid the hatred and offense of those listening. But the greatest thing is that these things are so skillfully joined and established by you that you are able to pass them on to anyone in a short time. Indeed, I have noticed this and observed Ctesippus, seeing how suddenly he began to imitate you. <margin>B</margin> It is a fine thing to be able to teach the mystery of this matter as quickly as possible, yet it does not seem worthwhile for you to discourse in front of many people. Rather, if you believe me, you will take care not to speak in a large assembly, lest those who learn these things quickly feel no gratitude toward you. Therefore, communicate these things only among yourselves in turn, and let no one else hear them unless they lay down silver. If you are wise, you will give this same advice to your disciples: never to speak of these things with anyone except themselves and you. For that which is rare, Euthydemus, is honored. Water is bought at a very cheap price, though it is the most precious thing in nature, as **Pindar** <note>original: "Pindarus." Refers to the Greek lyric poet Pindar, who famously wrote "Water is best."</note> says. But come, I say, <margin>C</margin> take me and this young Clinias under your care. 

When we had discussed these and a few other brief matters, O Crito, we departed. Consider, then, how you might join me in attending these men. For they promise to teach anyone who is prepared to give silver, excluding no talent or age. And what is most profitable for you to hear, they say that the pursuit of accumulating money does not hinder anyone from easily perceiving their wisdom. 

**CRITO:** Indeed, Socrates, I am eager to hear and would most gladly learn. Yet I seem to be one of those who are not like Euthydemus, but rather like those you mentioned a little earlier, who prefer to be refuted by others with such catches of logic <note>original: "captiunculis" (little traps/syllogisms).</note> than to refute others. <margin>D</margin> Truly, it would be ridiculous if I were to continue to advise you. Nevertheless, nothing prevents me from relating to you what I heard from one of those who departed from you after the assembly broke up. 

As I was walking, I was met by one of those who are thought to excel greatly in judicial causes. "O Crito," he said, "did you hear nothing from those wise men?" "Nothing, by Jove," I said, "for the thick crowd and the noise prevented me from hearing, though I desired to." "Yet," he said, "it was worth hearing." "Why?" I asked. "So that you might have heard those men disputing, who excel all others in this kind of speech." To him I said, "What did you think of it?" "What else," he said, "than what is always heard from such men when they talk nonsense, <margin>E</margin> and with an unworthy zeal argue with one another about things of no importance?" He used these exact words. Then I said, "Nevertheless, philosophy is a graceful thing." "What grace, my blessed man," he said, "can there be in that which is of no value? But if you had been present a little earlier, I think you would have been ashamed for the sake of your friend, who was so foolish as to want to hand himself over to men who have no care for what they say, but catch at every single word and object. And yet these men, as I said before, excel others of our time." Truly, O Crito, both this study is most worthless, and those who are engaged in it are ridiculous.

<margin>F</margin> To me, Socrates, it did not seem right for that man—or whoever else—to disparage the matter itself. Yet, because he dared to dispute with such men in the presence of many people, he seemed to me to be rightly blamed. 

**SOCRATES:** O Crito, these men are worthy of wonder. But I do not yet know the nature of the man who met you. From which group was he who spoke ill of philosophy to you? Was he some orator, one of those who are powerful in judicial contests? Or one of those who produce and write such speeches with which the orators contend in court? 

**CRITO:** Not an orator at any rate, nor do I think he has ever spoken in court; but they say he understands the judicial business itself very well and <margin>G</margin> composes elegant speeches. 

**SOCRATES:** I understand now. I was just about to say the same thing. Surely these are the men, Crito, whom **Prodicus** <note>original: "Prodicus." A sophist famous for his focus on the precise meaning of words.</note> placed on the borders between the Philosopher and the Politician. These men think they are the wisest of all, and moreover, they think they appear so to the greatest number of people; they believe that only the philosophers stand in their way, preventing them from being equally approved by everyone. They judge, therefore, that if they spread this common opinion against philosophers—that they are of no value—they will carry off the highest glory of wisdom among all men without controversy. For they believe they are truly the wisest, but that in private conversations, when they encounter the followers of Euthydemus, they are hindered. They want it to seem reasonable that they are wise, because they hold they have enough of philosophy and enough of political skill, <margin>H</margin> and they participate in both as much as is necessary; being placed outside the turbulent storms of civil affairs, they may enjoy the fruits of wisdom pleasantly. 

**CRITO:** Does their speech then have some likeness to the truth? 

**SOCRATES:** It has, as you say, Crito, a likeness rather than the truth itself. For it is not easy to persuade them that both men and all other things which are halfway between two others, and share in both...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...they would rather be chosen to be refuted by others in speech than to be those who refute. And here again is another popular and mild thing in their speeches: whenever you say that nothing is beautiful or good, or white, or anything else of that sort, or that nothing is altogether different from another, you literally sew up men's mouths, just as you say. And because you seem to do this not only to others' mouths but even to your own, this is very charming and removes the offensiveness from your words. But the greatest thing is that these things are so technically discovered by you that anyone can learn them in a very short time. I myself realized this by paying attention to Ctesippus, seeing how quickly he was able to <margin>B</margin> imitate you on the spot. Now, while this ability to deliver wisdom instantly is a fine thing for quick transmission, it is not suitable for debating in front of people. But if you will take my advice, be careful not to speak in front of many, lest they learn it quickly and give you no thanks. Instead, let the two of you speak only to each other; or if you must speak before another, let it be only to someone who gives you silver. These same things, if you are prudent, you will advise your disciples: never to dispute with any man, but only with you and themselves. For that which is rare, Euthydemus, <margin>C</margin> is precious; but water is most cheap, even though it is best, as **Pindar** said. But come, I said, see that you receive both me and this Clinias. 

These things, Crito, and some other brief matters we discussed, and then we departed. Look, therefore, how you might go to school with these men. For they say they are able to teach anyone who is willing to give silver; and neither nature nor any age excludes anyone. And what is most fitting for you to hear is that they say even making money does not hinder anyone from easily taking up their wisdom. 

**CRITO:** Indeed, Socrates, I am a lover of hearing and would gladly learn. However, I am in danger of being one of those not like Euthydemus, but rather like those whom you were just mentioning: those who would rather be refuted by such arguments than to refute. Still, it seems ridiculous to me to be advising you; nevertheless, I want to report to you what I heard. As I was walking, one of those coming away from you approached me—a man who thinks himself very wise, one of those clever at the speeches used in the law courts. <margin>D</margin> "O Crito," he said, "do you not listen to these wise men?" "No, by Zeus," I said, "for I was not able to stand near enough to hear because of the crowd." "And yet," he said, "it was worth hearing." "What was it?" I asked. "So that you could have heard men debating who are now the wisest in such speeches." And I said, "What then did they seem to you?" "What else," he said, "than what one would always hear from such men talking nonsense and making an unworthy fuss about things of no value?" For that is roughly how he spoke in those words. And I said, "But surely philosophy is a charming thing." "What sort of 'charming,' my blessed man?" he said. "It is worth nothing. Indeed, if you had been present now, I think you would have been very ashamed for your companion. He was so strange, wanting to offer himself up to men who don't care at all what they say, but catch at every word. And these men (as I was just saying) are among the best of today. But really, Crito," he said, "the matter itself and the men who spend their time in it are altogether worthless and ridiculous." <margin>F</margin> Now to me, Socrates, he did not seem to be right in blaming the matter itself, nor would anyone else who blames it. However, in his blaming of the willingness to debate such men in front of many people, he seemed to me to be right. 

**SOCRATES:** O Crito, such men are wonderful. But I do not yet know what I am about to say. Was the one who approached you and blamed philosophy a lawyer, one of those clever at competing in the law courts, or one of those who send such men in—a composer of the speeches which the orators use for competition? 

**CRITO:** Not a lawyer at all, by Zeus; I don't think he has ever even gone up to a law court. But they say he understands the matter, by Zeus, and is clever and composes clever speeches. 

**SOCRATES:** Now I understand about these men; I was just now about to speak of them. For these are the ones, Crito, whom **Prodicus** said were the border-dwellers between a philosopher and a politician. They think they are the wisest of all <margin>G</margin> men, and besides being so, they think they appear so to many. Consequently, they believe that no others stand in the way of their being well-regarded by all except for those men concerned with philosophy. They think, therefore, that if they can establish a reputation for these men of seeming to be worth nothing, the prize for the reputation of wisdom will then be carried off by themselves among all men without dispute. For they think they are in truth the wisest; but in private discussions, whenever they are caught out, they are frustrated by the followers of Euthydemus. They believe they are wise, quite reasonably: for they have a moderate amount of philosophy, and a moderate amount of politics—a very reasonable argument. For they share in both as much as is needed, and being outside of dangers and contests, they reap the fruits of wisdom. 

**CRITO:** What then? Do they seem to you to say anything of sense, Socrates? 

**SOCRATES:** Hardly. 

**CRITO:** But this argument of these men has a certain plausibility. 

**SOCRATES:** <margin>H</margin> And indeed it does, Crito, have plausibility rather than truth. For it is not easy to persuade them that either men, or all other things that are between two things, and share in both...

<summary>Socrates and Crito discuss the public's perception of sophistry, specifically recounting a critic's dismissal of philosophy as "worthless nonsense." Socrates identifies these critics as "border-dwellers" who try to balance philosophy and politics to gain prestige without committing to either.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: This page follows the conclusion of Plato's *Euthydemus*, where Socrates has just finished mocking the linguistic tricks of the sophists. The conversation now shifts to a more serious discussion with his old friend Crito about the education of children and the reputation of philosophy, before transitioning into the beginning of a new dialogue, the *Hippias Minor*.</meta>

# HIPPIAS MINOR.

<margin>A</margin> ...two things were necessary, and participating in the grace of both, as many things as arise from both evil and good: one becomes better, the other worse. But as many things as arise from two goods that do not aim for the same thing together are worse than either, so that each of those from which they were composed was useful. But those things composed of two evils that do not even aim at the same thing, being in the middle, these alone are better than either of those of which both parts would participate. If, therefore, philosophy is a good thing because of its political actions, but each aims at something else, and these men <note>Socrates is likely referring to speechwriters or public intellectuals like Isocrates who tried to bridge the gap between philosophy and politics.</note> participating in both are in the middle of these, they say nothing of value; for they are inferior to both. But if one is good and the other evil, they are better than the one and worse than the other. If both are evil, then they might say something true, but otherwise not at all. Now I do not <margin>B</margin> think they would agree that both are evil, nor that one is not evil while the other is good. But in reality, these men, by participating in both, are inferior to both in respect to that for which both politics and philosophy are worthy of regard. Though they aim for the truth, they seek primarily to appear successful. We should not, therefore, resent their desires, but rather recognize them for what they are. For we must cherish every man who says anything at all that holds to a matter of wisdom and who works through it bravely and persistently.

**CRITO.** Indeed, Socrates, I myself am in a state of perplexity regarding my own affairs (as I always say to you), as to how I should deal with my sons. The younger one is still quite small, but Critobulus is already of age and needs someone who will be of benefit to him. Whenever I am with you, I am so affected that it seems to me a kind of madness to have taken such great care for <margin>C</margin> my children in so many other ways—regarding marriage, so that their mothers would be of noble birth, and regarding possessions, so that they might be as rich as possible—but to have neglected their education. Yet, whenever I look toward any of those who claim to educate men, I am struck with dismay. Every one of them, when I examine them, seems to me to be completely strange—to tell you the truth. Consequently, I do not know how I can turn the young man toward philosophy.

**SOCRATES.** My dear Crito, do you not know that in every pursuit, the common practitioners are many and worth nothing, while those who are serious are few and worth everything? Do you not think that gymnastics is a fine thing, as well as money-making, <margin>D</margin> rhetoric, and military leadership?

**CRITO.** Certainly, I do.

**SOCRATES.** What then? In each of these, do you not see that the majority are ridiculous in their performance of each task?

**CRITO.** Yes, by Zeus, you speak the absolute truth.

**SOCRATES.** Is it for this reason, then, that you will flee all these pursuits yourself and not entrust them to your son?

**CRITO.** That would not be just, Socrates.

**SOCRATES.** Then do not do what is not right, Crito. Rather, leave aside those who practice philosophy, whether they are good or bad, and examine the matter itself well and truly. If it appears to you to be a base thing, turn every man away from it, not just your sons; but if it appears to be as I think it is, then pursue and practice it confidently—as the saying goes—both yourself and your children.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...they participate; let them be such that those things which are made of evil and good become better than the former and worse than the latter. But those which come from two goods not leading to the same end are worse than both for the completion of the work for which both parts of the composition look. However, those things which are composed of two evils not tending toward the same end, these alone are better than both of those in which they participate. If, therefore, philosophy is good and political action is good, but each contributes to a different thing, and these men are participants in both, being placed in the middle of both, they conclude nothing. For they are worse than both. But if one of these is good and the other evil, they are <margin>B</margin> better than the one and worse than the other. If both were evil, only then would they speak the truth; otherwise, not at all. Nor do I think they would admit that both are evil, or that one is good and the other evil. But surely these men, by participating in both, are less fit for both that to which philosophy and political action pertain; and while they hold the third place, they do not hesitate to usurp the first. We must forgive their desire and not be indignant, yet they should be judged as they truly are. For we ought to love everyone who says something that shares in prudence and acts manfully.

**CRITO.** Indeed, Socrates, as I often speak with you, I am uncertain by what method I should educate my sons. The younger is still more tender <margin>C</margin> than discipline requires, but Critobulus is already an adult and needs someone by whose work he may profit. Whenever I speak with you, I am so moved that I think it is madness to be occupied with other things for the sake of one's sons—such as marriage, specifically that they might be born from the most noble mother, and then that an ample inheritance might be left to them—while neglecting their education. But when I look at those who profess to instruct men, I am frightened away, and to me, upon consideration, every one of them seems far removed from the thing they preach. And to tell you <margin>In any study, the base are very many, but the upright are few.</margin> the truth, I do not know how I may exhort and provoke my son toward philosophy.

**SOCRATES.** O friend Crito, are you unaware that in any pursuit, base men of no value are very many, <margin>D</margin> but the upright are few, and these are to be held in the highest value? Does it not seem to you that gymnastics, trade, rhetoric, and military affairs are fine things?

**CRITO.** To me, certainly.

**SOCRATES.** Do you not see in each of these arts that many are unfit and ridiculous in every task?

**CRITO.** It is so, and you speak only too truly.

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, for this reason, will you flee all studies and dissuade your son from them?

**CRITO.** It would not be fitting, Socrates.

**SOCRATES.** Beware then, Crito, lest you do what is unfitting. Cast aside this concern of whether the men who study philosophy are good or evil; examine the thing itself diligently. If upon inquiry the matter seems depraved to you, frighten away not only your sons but all men. But if it appears to you as it does to me, follow it manfully and practice it, and exhort your sons to the same study.

# HIPPIAS, OR, ON
# FALSEHOOD.
### Refutative.

# HIPPIAS, OR, ON
# FALSEHOOD.
### Prepared for Refutation.

---

-> **S U M M A R Y   O F   T H E   D I A L O G U E.** <-
The thesis of this particular dispute (the general one being the same as in the *Euthydemus* and *Protagoras*) concerns the backward manner of the Sophists in debating, both in the subject matter and in the mode of explaining it, just as Plato teaches in the established inquiry. For he introduces a certain Sophist, Hippias, speaking and arrogantly attributing everything to himself, claiming all law and authority over the Homeric writings, yet agitating inept little questions. The question is proposed: who is better, Achilles <note>The hero of the *Iliad*, famed for his strength and directness.</note> or Ulysses <note>Also known as Odysseus, the hero of the *Odyssey*, famed for his cunning and wit.</note>? Socrates, intentionally provoking the Sophist, says that Achilles is inferior to Ulysses; and by bringing certain reasons and comparing words from Homer, the topic of falsehood arises, which occupies the rest of the speech in various explanations. Socrates acts in such a way that he applies sophistic tricks against the empty Sophist, so that he may pierce him with his own weapons and entangle him in his own snares.

---

-> EUDICUS, SOCRATES, HIPPIAS. <-
<margin>E</margin> **EUDICUS.** But why are you silent, Socrates, after Hippias has displayed so much? Why do you not either praise something of what was said, or refute it if anything seems to you not to have been well spoken? Especially since we are left by ourselves—we who would most claim to have a share in the pursuit of philosophy.

**SOCRATES.** Indeed, Eudicus, there are some things I would gladly ask Hippias about regarding what he was just saying about Homer. For I used to hear from your father, Apemantus, that the *Iliad* was a finer poem by Homer than the *Odyssey*; and finer by as much as Achilles was better than Ulysses. For he said each of the poems was made for one of them: one for Ulysses, the other for Achilles. Regarding that, therefore, I would gladly <margin>F</margin> inquire (if Hippias is willing) how he feels about these two men, and which of them he says is better. For he has displayed many other things of all kinds to us, both about other poets and about Homer.

**EUDICUS.** It is clear that Hippias will not grudge answering if you ask him something. Is that not so, Hippias? If Socrates asks you something, will you answer? Or how will you act?

**HIPPIAS.** I would be acting strangely indeed, Eudicus...

<column-break/>

-> EUDICUS, SOCRATES, HIPPIAS. <-
<margin>E</margin> **EUDICUS.** But why indeed are you silent, Socrates, when Hippias here has shown so much? Why do you not either approve some of the things said, or argue if anything seems to you to have been said less than rightly? Especially when we who claim for ourselves no mediocre study of philosophy have come away as inferiors?

**SOCRATES.** Eudicus, there are some things among those which Hippias said about Homer that I desire to inquire about. I heard indeed from Apemantus your father that the *Iliad* of Homer was a more excellent poem than the *Odyssey*, because Achilles was more outstanding than Ulysses. For he said one poem was composed for Achilles and the other <margin>F</margin> for Ulysses. Concerning this, therefore, I am inclined to inquire of Hippias, if only it pleases him, which of those men he asserts to be more excellent, after so many other varied things about Homer and other poets have been shown to us.

**EUDICUS.** No grudge at all will prevent Hippias from responding to one who interrogates him. Will you respond or not, Hippias, if Socrates asks something?

**HIPPIAS.** I would hardly be acting rightly, Eudicus...

# PLATO

->A<- ...if I were now to flee from the questioning of Socrates—I, who have always been accustomed to travel from my homeland of Elis to the Olympic festivals <note>The ancient Olympic Games were a religious and athletic festival held in honor of Zeus.</note>, where the Greeks flock from all sides for the common celebration, and there at the temple to offer myself to anyone to explain whatever one might wish to have demonstrated, and to respond to every single question.

**SOCRATES:** O Hippias, what a happy lot has fallen to you, if you arrive at the sacred festival every Olympiad with such confidence in the wisdom of your mind. I would truly be amazed if any athlete, about to compete there in physical exercise, approached with as much confidence in his bodily strength as you do in the subtlety of your mind.

**HIPPIAS:** I am rightly so disposed, Socrates; for from the time I began to compete in the Olympics, I have not yet found anyone superior to me in any matter.

**SOCRATES:** ->B<- By Hercules, that is a magnificent thing you say, Hippias; this glory of yours will be a monument of wisdom both to the city of the Elians and to your parents. But what then do you judge concerning Achilles and Ulysses <note>original Latin: "Vlysse"; Greek: "Odyssea." The legendary hero Odysseus.</note>? Which of these do you think is better, and in what way? Furthermore, while many of us were inside and you were discoursing, some of your words escaped me. I was reluctant to inquire further, partly because there was a great crowd inside, and partly so that I would not be an obstacle to your oration. But now, since there are fewer of us and Eudicus here bids me ask, show us more clearly what you were saying about these lives, and in what way you distinguished between them.

**HIPPIAS:** I am indeed willing, Socrates, to report more openly than I did then ->C<- in the present moment, what I think about these men and others. I assert that Homer, of all those who went to Troy, depicted Achilles as the best man, Nestor as the wisest, and Ulysses as the most versatile <note>original: "versutùm multiformémq;" (Latin) / "polytropōtaton" (Greek). This word "polytropos" can mean many-turning, wily, or resourceful.</note> and wily.

**SOCRATES:** My goodness, O Hippias! Will you grant me this favor: namely, not to laugh at me if I am slow to understand and ask questions frequently? Deign to answer me, I pray, freely and easily.

**HIPPIAS:** It would indeed be shameful, O Socrates, since I teach these very things to others and demand money for them, if I did not indulge you when you ask, or did not answer with a cheerful mind.

**SOCRATES:** You speak very well indeed. Truly, when you said Achilles was depicted as the best man and Nestor as the wisest, I seemed to understand ->D<- what you were saying. But when you called Ulysses versatile and wily, to tell the truth, I did not understand what you meant to signify. Tell me—for perhaps from this I will perceive it better: was not Achilles also introduced by Homer as versatile and wily, or not?

**HIPPIAS:** Not at all, Socrates, but rather entirely simple <note>original: "simplex" (Latin) / "haploustatos" (Greek). In this context, it means straightforward or honest.</note>. For in the "Prayers" themselves <note>A reference to Book 9 of the Iliad, where an embassy is sent to pray for Achilles' return to battle.</note>, when he depicts them disputing, he makes Achilles speak thus to Ulysses:

<margin>Iliad, Book 9</margin>
->E<-
> O most noble Ulysses, weaver of deceits,
> It behooves me to refute your words intrepidly,
> Just as I think it must be done,
> Lest you sit here on this side and that and stun me with deceptive words.
> For that man is more hateful to me than the gates of black Hades,
> Who hides one thing in his heart,
> And then openly brings forth another, whatever it seems to be.
> But I will now speak as I believe it shall come to pass.

In these verses, he declares the character of both: that Achilles is truthful and simple, while Ulysses is wily and a liar. For here Achilles brings these charges against Ulysses.

**SOCRATES:** I seem now to understand what you say, Hippias. For by ->F<- "wily," you mean "a liar," as it appears.

**HIPPIAS:** Exactly, Socrates. For Homer depicts Ulysses as such in many places, both in the *Iliad* and in the *Odyssey*.

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, Homer thought that a truthful man was one thing, and a liar another, and that they were not both the same person?

**HIPPIAS:** How could it be otherwise, Socrates?

**SOCRATES:** And do you yourself think the same, Hippias?

**HIPPIAS:** Most certainly. For I would be very much in error if I thought otherwise.

**SOCRATES:** Let us then set aside Homer, since it is not possible to ask him what his intention was in composing these verses. But since you take up the cause, and those things which you assert Homer said seem right to you, answer for Homer and yourself at the same time.

**HIPPIAS:** It shall be done; ask briefly whatever you please.

**SOCRATES:** Do you call "liars" those who are unable to do anything, like the weak or the exhausted, or those who ->G<- are able to do something?

**HIPPIAS:** The powerful, and very much so—both in many other things, and especially in deceiving men.

**SOCRATES:** They are therefore powerful according to your speech; and wily, are they not?

**HIPPIAS:** Certainly.

**SOCRATES:** And are they wily and deceitful out of some kind of stupidity and imprudence, or rather through cunning and prudence?

**HIPPIAS:** Through cunning most of all, and prudence.

**SOCRATES:** They are prudent then, it seems.

**HIPPIAS:** Very much so, by Jove.

**SOCRATES:** Being prudent, do they not know what they are doing, or do they know?

**HIPPIAS:** On the contrary, they know it very well. For it is because of this that they mislead others.

**SOCRATES:** Since they have knowledge of these things which they know, are they ignorant, or rather wise?

**HIPPIAS:** Wise, evidently, in these very matters of deceiving.

**SOCRATES:** Stay, I pray you; let us repeat what has been said, so that we may examine what you are saying. You say that liars are powerful, prudent, knowledgeable, and wise in those things concerning which they are liars.

**HIPPIAS:** I do.

**SOCRATES:** And that others are truthful, while these on the contrary are liars, and that these two types are very much opposites?

**HIPPIAS:** I say that as well.

**SOCRATES:** From this it follows, then, that liars are among the number of the powerful and the wise.

**HIPPIAS:** Most certainly.

**SOCRATES:** But when you say the powerful and the wise are liars in this very...

<column-break/>

->A<- Always at the time of the Olympics, when the festival is held, I go up from my home in Elis to the sacred precinct, and I offer myself to speak on whatever anyone wishes of the things I have prepared for demonstration, and to answer whoever wishes whatever they may ask; and surely I would not flee the questions of Socrates.

**SOCRATES:** You have experienced a blessed state, Hippias, if every Olympiad you arrive at the temple with such good hope. I would be amazed if any of the athletes came there to compete with such fearlessness and confidence in their body as you say you have in your mind.

**HIPPIAS:** It is with good reason, Socrates, that I have this experience. For since I began to compete at the Olympics, I have never yet met anyone better than myself in anything.

**SOCRATES:** You speak beautifully, Hippias; your reputation is an offering of wisdom to the city of the Elians and to your parents. But what then do you tell us about Achilles and Odysseus? Which do you say is better, and in what respect? For when there were many of us inside and you were making your demonstration, I missed ->B<- what you were saying. I hesitated to ask further because there was a great crowd inside, and lest I be an obstacle to your demonstration by asking. But now, since we are fewer and Eudicus here urges me to ask, speak and teach us clearly what you were saying about these two men, and how you distinguished them.

**HIPPIAS:** Well, Socrates, I am willing to explain more clearly than I did then what I say about these and others. For I say that Homer made Achilles the best man of those who went to Troy, Nestor the wisest, and Odysseus the most wily <note>original: "polytropōtaton"</note>.

**SOCRATES:** Good heavens, Hippias! Grant me this favor: do not mock me if I struggle to learn what is said and ask many questions. But try to answer me mildly and easily.

**HIPPIAS:** For it would be shameful, Socrates, if I were to educate others in these very things and expect to receive money for them, yet I myself, when questioned by you, did not have indulgence and answer mildly.

**SOCRATES:** You speak quite well. For when you said Achilles was made the best, I thought I understood what you were saying, and also when you said Nestor was the wisest. But when you said the poet made Odysseus the most wily, this—to tell you the truth—I completely do not know what you mean. Tell me, so that I might learn better from this: has not Achilles been made wily by Homer?

**HIPPIAS:** Least of all, Socrates, but rather most simple. Since in the "Prayers," when he makes them speak to one another, Achilles says to Odysseus:

->E<-
> Divine son of Laertes, Odysseus of many devices,
> I must indeed speak my word without hesitation,
> Just as I think and as I believe it will be accomplished;
> For that man is as hateful to me as the gates of Hades,
> Who hides one thing in his heart and says another.
> But I will speak as it shall be accomplished for me.

In these verses he shows the character of each man: that Achilles is truthful and simple, while Odysseus is wily and false. For he makes Achilles say these verses to Odysseus.

**SOCRATES:** Now indeed, Hippias, I am likely to understand what you mean. By "wily," you mean "false," as it appears.

**HIPPIAS:** Exactly, Socrates. For Homer has made Odysseus such in many places, both in the *Iliad* and in the *Odyssey*.

**SOCRATES:** It seemed ->F<- then, as it appears, to Homer that one man was truthful and another false; but they were not the same.

**HIPPIAS:** How could it not be so, Socrates?

**SOCRATES:** And does it seem so to you as well, Hippias?

**HIPPIAS:** Most of all. For it would be strange if it were not so.

**SOCRATES:** Let us then leave Homer aside, since it is impossible to ask him what he was thinking when he composed these verses; but since you appear to accept the responsibility, and you agree with these things you say Homer said, answer for both Homer and yourself.

**HIPPIAS:** So it shall be. Ask briefly whatever you wish.

**SOCRATES:** Do you say the false are like those unable to do anything, such as the sick? Or like those able to do something?

**HIPPIAS:** Those able to do something, I say, and very much so—both many other things and specifically to deceive ->G<- men.

**SOCRATES:** They are then, as it seems, capable according to your word, and wily, are they not?

**HIPPIAS:** Yes.

**SOCRATES:** And are they wily and deceivers through foolishness and lack of sense? Or through villainy and a kind of prudence?

**HIPPIAS:** Through villainy most of all, and prudence.

**SOCRATES:** They are then prudent, it seems.

**HIPPIAS:** Yes, by Zeus, quite so.

**SOCRATES:** And being prudent, do they not know what they do, or do they know?

**HIPPIAS:** They know very well indeed; that is why they do evil.

**SOCRATES:** And knowing these things that they know, are they ignorant or wise?

**HIPPIAS:** Wise, surely, at least in deceiving.

**SOCRATES:** Hold on; let us remember what you said. You said the false are capable and prudent and knowledgeable and wise in the things they are false about?

**HIPPIAS:** I do say that.

**SOCRATES:** And that the truthful and the false are different, and most opposite to each other?

**HIPPIAS:** I say those things.

**SOCRATES:** Come then. It seems the false are capable and wise, according to your word.

**HIPPIAS:** Most certainly.

**SOCRATES:** When you say the false are capable and wise in...
