<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and the sophist Hippias. Hippias has just claimed to be the most skilled and knowledgeable person in all of Greece, particularly regarding the Homeric heroes Achilles and Odysseus. Socrates is now beginning his cross-examination to determine whether the "truthful man" and the "lying man" are truly different people.</meta>

### HIPPIAS MINOR.
V ij

<meta>catchword: poems, epic verses, tragedies, dithyrambs, and orations</meta>

<margin>A</margin> **Socrates:** On these very points, do you say that they are capable of lying if they wish, or incapable of the things about which they lie? **Hippias:** Capable, in my opinion. **Socrates:** To put it briefly then, those who are false are both wise and capable of lying. **Hippias:** Yes. **Socrates:** Therefore, a man who is incapable of lying and ignorant would not be a liar. **Hippias:** That is so. **Socrates:** And a "capable" person is one who can do what they wish, when they wish. I mean one who is not hindered by disease or such things; rather, just as you are capable of writing my name whenever you wish, that is how I mean it. Or do you not call a person so disposed "capable"? **Hippias:** Yes. **Socrates:** Tell me then, O Hippias, are you not indeed experienced in <margin>B</margin> calculation and the art of arithmetic? **Hippias:** Most of all men, Socrates. **Socrates:** Therefore, if someone were to ask you what the sum of three times seventy is, if you wished, would you not answer the truth about this most quickly and effectively of all? **Hippias:** Certainly. **Socrates:** And is that because you are the most capable and the wisest in these matters? **Hippias:** Yes. **Socrates:** Are you then only the wisest and most capable, or are you also the best in these matters in which you are most capable and wise—namely, calculation? **Hippias:** Also the best, surely, Socrates. **Socrates:** And you would be most capable of telling the truth about these things, would you not? **Hippias:** I believe so. **Socrates:** What then of false things regarding these same matters? Answer me now, Hippias, just as before, <margin>C</margin> plainly and magnificently. If someone asked you how much three times seventy is, would you be the most effective at lying, and would you always say false things regarding these numbers in the same way, if you wished to lie and never answer the truth? Or would someone ignorant of calculation be better able to lie than you if you wished to lie? Or might the ignorant person, while wishing to speak falsely, often tell the truth by accident if he didn't know the answer, whereas you, the wise man, if you wished to lie, would always lie in the same consistent way? **Hippias:** Yes, it is as you say. **Socrates:** Is the liar, then, a liar concerning other things, but not concerning numbers? Or would he never lie about number? **Hippias:** Nay, <margin>D</margin> by Zeus, he would lie about that most of all. **Socrates:** Let us assume this then, Hippias: that there is a certain kind of man who is a liar regarding calculation and number. **Hippias:** Certainly. **Socrates:** Who then would this be? Must he not have the power to lie, as you just agreed, if he is to be a liar? For it was said by you, if you remember, that he who is incapable of lying could never become a liar. **Hippias:** I remember, and it was said so. **Socrates:** Did you not just appear to be the most capable of lying about calculations? **Hippias:** Yes, that was also said. **Socrates:** Are you not also the most capable of speaking the truth about calculations? **Hippias:** Entirely so. **Socrates:** Therefore, the same person is most capable of speaking both falsely and truly about calculations. And this person is the one who is good at these things—the calculator. **Hippias:** Yes. **Socrates:** Who then, Hippias, becomes a liar regarding <margin>E</margin> calculation, other than the good man? For the same man is both capable and truthful. **Hippias:** It appears so. **Socrates:** Do you see then that the same man is both truthful and false regarding these matters? And the truthful man is no better than the liar? For they are surely the same person, and they do not have the most opposite characteristics, as you thought just now. **Hippias:** It does not appear so, at least in this case. **Socrates:** Do you wish, then, for us to look elsewhere? **Hippias:** If you wish to do otherwise. **Socrates:** Are you not also experienced in geometry? **Hippias:** I am. **Socrates:** Well then, is it not the same in geometry? Is the same man most capable of lying and telling the truth about geometric figures—that is, the geometer? **Hippias:** Yes. **Socrates:** And is anyone else good at these things besides him? **Hippias:** <margin>F</margin> No one else. **Socrates:** Therefore the good and wise geometer is most capable of both. And if anyone else were a liar regarding figures, it would be this man—the good one. For he is the capable one. But the bad man was incapable of lying. Thus, he who is not capable of lying could not become a liar, as has been agreed? **Hippias:** That is true. **Socrates:** Let us then look at a third: the astronomer. You believe yourself to be even more skilled in this art than in the previous ones. Is that not so, Hippias? **Hippias:** Yes. **Socrates:** Therefore in astronomy, too, these same things hold. **Hippias:** It is likely, Socrates. **Socrates:** In astronomy, then, if anyone is a liar, it will be the good astronomer—the one capable of lying. For it will not be the one who is incapable, as he is ignorant. **Hippias:** It appears so. **Socrates:** The same man, then, will be both truthful and false in astronomy. **Hippias:** It seems so. **Socrates:** <margin>G</margin> Come then, Hippias, let us look freely in this way through all the sciences, whether it is otherwise or thus. For you are surely the wisest of all men in the greatest number of arts; as I once heard you boasting of your great and enviable wisdom, when you were describing it in the marketplace near the tables <note>This refers to the money-changers' tables in the Athenian Agora.</note>. You said that you once went to Olympia having everything you wore about your body made by your own hands. First, the ring—for you began there—which you were wearing, was your own work, as you knew how to engrave rings. And another seal-stone <note>Used for stamping wax to seal documents.</note> was your work, and a <term>strigil</term> <note>original: "στλεγγίδα." A curved metal tool used by Greeks to scrape oil and dirt from the skin after exercise.</note>, and an oil-flask <note>original: "λήκυθον." A lekythos, a narrow-necked bottle for storing olive oil.</note>, which you made yourself. Then, the sandals you had on, you said you had cobbled them yourself, and you had woven your cloak and your tunic. And what <margin>H</margin> seemed most strange to everyone, and a display of the greatest wisdom, was when you said that the belt of your tunic, which you were wearing—which was like the expensive Persian ones—you had woven yourself. In addition to these things, you said you came having poems, both epic verses and tragedies, and <term>dithyrambs</term> <note>original: "διθυράμβους." Choral hymns sung in honor of Dionysus.</note>, and many diverse speeches composed in prose. And concerning the arts of which I was just speaking...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> **Socrates:** Regarding these same points, do you say they are powerful enough to lie if they wish, or are they powerless regarding the things about which they lie? **Hippias:** Powerful indeed. **Socrates:** So that we may speak summarily, liars are those who are powerful and wise enough to lie. **Hippias:** Plainly. **Socrates:** Therefore the man who cannot lie, and knows nothing, will not be a liar. **Hippias:** So it is. **Socrates:** Moreover, he is powerful who does what he wants, and when he wants. I do not mean one hindered by disease or some such thing, I say, but rather just as you can write my name whenever you wish—so now I ask. Do you not call a man so affected powerful? **Hippias:** Certainly. **Socrates:** Tell me, <margin>B</margin> O Hippias, are you not skilled in numbering and computing? **Hippias:** Most of all men. **Socrates:** If someone were to ask you, then, how much three times seven hundred <note>The Latin text here says "septingenta" (700), whereas the Greek says "70." This is likely a translation or printing error in the source manuscript.</note> amounts to, would you not, provided you wished, answer concerning these things as quickly and effectively as possible? **Hippias:** Precisely. **Socrates:** Is it not because you are most powerful and wise regarding those things? **Hippias:** Indeed. **Socrates:** Are you merely the wisest and most powerful? Or are you also the best regarding those same things in which you excel in wisdom and power, that is, in computing numbers? **Hippias:** And the best besides, Socrates. **Socrates:** Therefore you could speak the truth about these things most effectively above all others, could you not? <margin>C</margin> **Hippias:** I think so, truly. **Socrates:** And what of false things regarding the same? Come now, Hippias, answer as before, generously and magnificently. If someone were to ask how much three times seven hundred is, would you then lie more about these things, and always pronounce false things about them in the same way, wishing to lie and never bring forth the truth? Or would he who is ignorant of numbers be able to lie more than you, even if you wished to lie? Or on the contrary, would the ignorant man often bring forth the truth by accident while wishing to bring forth falsehoods, because he is ignorant of the matter itself? But you, since you are wise, whenever you wish to lie, will you lie consistently? **Hippias:** It is as you say. **Socrates:** Is the liar therefore a liar concerning other things, but not concerning numbers, nor <margin>D</margin> will he lie about number? **Hippias:** Nay, even concerning numbers. **Socrates:** Let us then posit this, Hippias, that concerning computation and number, some man is a liar. **Hippias:** Certainly. **Socrates:** Who then will this be? It is necessary that he be able to lie, as you yourself were saying, if he is to be a liar. For it was said by you, if you remember, that he who cannot lie is not a liar. **Hippias:** I remember indeed, and so it was said. **Socrates:** Did it not just now appear that you are the most powerful at lying in computing numbers? **Hippias:** That was also said. **Socrates:** Are you not also most powerful at bringing forth the truth about these same numbers? **Hippias:** Very much so. **Socrates:** Therefore the same person can <margin>E</margin> most effectively speak the truth and lie in computing: and that is he who is good at numbers, namely the calculator. **Hippias:** So it is, entirely. **Socrates:** Who then, Hippias, would be a liar in computing, unless it is he who is good at it? For he is powerful, and he is truthful. **Hippias:** It appears so. **Socrates:** You see that the same man is truthful in these things and a liar, and the truthful man is in no way better than the liar himself. For they are the same, and not very contrary, as you were recently thinking. **Hippias:** It certainly does not appear so now in these cases. **Socrates:** Do you wish us to consider other cases as well? **Hippias:** As you please. **Socrates:** Are you not also skilled in geometry? **Hippias:** I am. **Socrates:** Does not the same happen in geometry? The same man can pronounce false things most effectively concerning figures, and also true things. That man is the geometer. **Hippias:** Assuredly. **Socrates:** Is anyone else <margin>F</margin> good at these things besides him? **Hippias:** No other. **Socrates:** Does not the good and wise geometer have power over both? And if anyone else is a liar in figures, it is most of all he who is good at them: for he is powerful, whereas the bad man is powerless at lying. And he who is powerless at lying never becomes a liar, as has been confessed. **Hippias:** These things are so. **Socrates:** Let us look at a third besides, the astronomer, which art you, Hippias, are accustomed to profess even more than the previous ones; is it not so? **Hippias:** Certainly so. **Socrates:** Do not the same things happen in Astronomy? **Hippias:** It is consistent. **Socrates:** Wherefore in astronomy, if anyone else is a liar, it will be most of all he who is a good astronomer. For he is able to lie in the highest degree. For he who is powerless <margin>G</margin> is also ignorant. **Hippias:** So it appears. **Socrates:** Therefore the same man in astronomy will be both truthful and a liar. **Hippias:** It seems so. **Socrates:** Come, Hippias, consider this generally through all the sciences, whether it be so or otherwise. For before all others you are adorned with the most arts. Just as I heard you once boasting, that you abounded in much and desirable wisdom above others, walking and disputing in the marketplace among the tables: when you said that you once went to Olympia, and that all the ornaments you had on your body you had fashioned with your own hands. First indeed the ring which <margin>H</margin> <margin>The same things are found in Cicero, book 3 of "On the Orator."</margin> you had—for you began from there—was your own work, as if you were skilled in engraving. Furthermore, a certain seal was your work, and a strigil, and a small vessel for ointment <note>This is the translator's Latin gloss for the Greek 'lekythos'.</note> likewise your work, and even the shoes sewn by your own hands, and a cloak and an undergarment woven by you. And what seemed most wonderful, and a sign of singular wisdom, you said you had shown a belt as your own work, similar to the precious Persian ones. Likewise many and various poems of yours, composed in freer measures:

<summary>Socrates leads Hippias to admit that in technical fields like math, geometry, and astronomy, the "good" expert is the one most capable of both telling the truth and lying effectively. Socrates then reminds Hippias of his famous boast at the Olympic games, where he claimed to have handmade every item of his clothing and equipment.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and the sophist Hippias. Previously, Socrates argued that a person who is "capable" and "wise" in a specific field is the person best equipped to both tell the truth and tell a lie in that field. Hippias has struggled to find an example where the "truthful man" and the "liar" are two different people.</meta>

## OF PLATO

...furthermore, those things which I was mentioning earlier, you master more than all others: in rhythms and harmonies, the correct ratio of letters, and in very many other things of this kind, if I remember rightly. But indeed, I had overlooked your art of memory <note>original: *memorię artificium*</note>, in which you seem to me to be wonderfully strong. Perhaps I have forgotten many other things as well. But as I said, looking both at your arts (which are quite numerous) and those of others, tell me: have you ever found, among those things agreed upon between us, that the truthful man is different from the liar, and that they are not the same person? Look into any wisdom or cleverness, or whatever you please to call it. But you will never find it, my friend; for it does not exist anywhere. If it is elsewhere, tell me. **Hippias:** I cannot find it at this moment, Socrates. **Socrates:** Nor will you find it hereafter, I think. But if I speak the truth, remember, Hippias, what follows from our previous points. **Hippias:** I do not quite follow what you are saying, Socrates. **Socrates:** There is no need for your art of memory at the moment; for it is clear you do not think it necessary, but I will remind you. Do you remember saying that Achilles was a truthful man, while Odysseus <note>original: *Ulyfsem*</note> was lying and versatile? **Hippias:** Certainly. **Socrates:** But now you see that the same man has appeared to be both truthful and lying. Therefore, if Odysseus was a liar, he was also truthful. Likewise, if Achilles was truthful, he was also a liar; these men are neither different from each other nor opposites, but rather they turned out to be similar. **Hippias:** You always weave such little traps, Socrates, and seizing upon whatever is most troublesome in the discourse, you press on it and correct every tiny detail, rather than contending against the whole matter under discussion. For if you wish, I will now show you with many arguments and sufficient reason that Homer made Achilles better than Odysseus and truthful; while he made Odysseus crafty, lying in many things, and worse than Achilles. But if it pleases you, respond in turn, and compare your speech with mine, in which you may show the other to be better; and thus those present will better understand which of us has spoken more correctly. **Socrates:** I do not doubt, nor do I contend, Hippias, that you seem wiser than I. But I have always been accustomed, when someone disputes about a matter, to attend diligently, especially when the speaker seems to me to be wise. Then, indeed, being eager to understand what he says, I inquire, weigh, and estimate, so that I may perceive the things said more clearly. But if I think the speaker himself is of little account, I neither ask him anything nor attend to what he says. And by this very conjecture you will understand whom I estimate to be wise. For you will see me listening most accurately to their words and questioning them, so that I may profit in life by learning something. And now indeed, when I noticed your words, in which you showed Achilles' testimony from those poems against Odysseus as being boastful, it seemed a wonderful thing to me if you spoke the truth. Since Odysseus himself is crafty, he can be refuted by no lie; but Achilles seems to be crafty and shifting <note>original: *varius*</note> according to your own speech: for he lies. For when he had pronounced those verses, which you have just now reviewed,

<margin>Iliad 9</margin>
> That man is as hateful to me as the gates of black Hades
> Who hides one thing in his heart, and openly utters
> Something else, whatever it may be that he sees.

A little later he adds that he will be persuaded by neither Odysseus nor Agamemnon, and will not remain at Troy.

> But tomorrow, when I have performed the sacred rites to Jove
> and the other inhabitants of heaven, and have drawn the ships
> gathered on the curved shore into the sea, you will see them
> at first light sailing through the Hellespont, well-suited for fish.
> In which you will see, if you desire to look, brave
> and well-taught men leaning on their oars. For if
> Neptune fills the sails with favorable winds,
> the third light will find us on the fruitful shores of Phthia.

Likewise, earlier, while quarreling against Agamemnon, he says,

<margin>Iliad 1</margin>
> Behold, I shall depart for home in my black ships, for it is better
> to go to my fatherland Phthia: for my mind does not wish
> to fill you here with riches, while I remain inglorious in heavy arms.

Having said these things, now before the whole army and now to his friends, he nowhere appears to either prepare himself for the task or to draw down the ships, as if about to return home; rather, he cares very little that what he speaks should be true. Indeed, Hippias, I asked you from the beginning, when I was uncertain which of these was held more excellent by the poet, and I thought both were very good men, and it was difficult to know which of them excels in lying, and truth, and other virtue. For both are very similar in this. **Hippias:** You do not distinguish correctly, O Socrates. For the things Achilles lies about, he appears to lie not out of treachery, but unwillingly because of the army's misfortune, being forced to remain and bring help; but Odysseus lies willingly and by treachery. **Socrates:** You are deceiving me, my dearest Hippias, and you yourself are imitating Odysseus. **Hippias:** Not at all, Socrates, what are you saying? And for what reason? **Socrates:** Because you say Achilles does not lie out of treachery—he who was such a sorcerer <note>original: *gōēs*</note> and a deceiver in his boasting (as Homer has made him), that he appears so much more clever than Odysseus as to hide his own vanity from him, while in his presence he says things contrary to himself...

<column-break/>

**A** ...to arrive more exceptionally skilled than others, both regarding rhythms and harmonies and the correctness of letters; and many other things besides these, as I seem to remember. And yet I had forgotten your "mnemonic" <note>original: *mnēmonikon*</note> device (as it seems), by which you think you are most brilliant. I think I have forgotten very many other things as well. But as I say, looking at your arts (which are sufficient) and those of others, tell me if you find anywhere from what has been agreed between me and you, where the truthful man is one, and the lying man another, separate and not the same. Look for this in whatever wisdom you wish, or villainy, **B** or whatever you enjoy naming it. But you will not find it, friend. For it does not exist. Since you tell me. **Hippias:** I do not have it to tell, Socrates, at least not now. **Socrates:** Nor later, I think. But if I speak the truth, do you remember what happens to us from the argument, Hippias? **Hippias:** I do not quite understand what you are saying, Socrates. **Socrates:** For now perhaps you are not using your mnemonic device; for it is clear you do not think it necessary. But I will remind you. Do you know that you said Achilles was truthful, and Odysseus was lying and versatile? **Hippias:** Yes. **Socrates:** Now then, do you perceive that the same man has been shown to be both lying and truthful? So that if Odysseus was lying, he also becomes truthful; and if Achilles was truthful, he also becomes lying. And the men are not different from each other nor opposites, but similar. **C** **Hippias:** O Socrates, you always weave some such arguments, and picking out whatever is most difficult in the speech, you hold onto it, touching it bit by bit; and you do not contend with the whole matter about which the speech is made. Since even now, if you wish, I will demonstrate to you with many proofs and sufficient reason that Homer made Achilles better than Odysseus and without falsehood, but the other, both treacherous and lying in many things, and worse than Achilles. But if you wish, compare argument against argument, how the one is better; and these people will know better which of us speaks better. **D** **Socrates:** O Hippias, I do not dispute that you are wiser than I; but I am always accustomed, whenever someone says something, to pay attention; especially when the speaker seems to me to be wise, and desiring to learn what he says, I inquire and re-examine and bring together the things said, so that I may learn. But if the speaker seems to me to be trivial, I neither question him further, nor do I care what he says. And you will know by this those whom I consider to be wise; for you will find me being persistent about the things said by such a person, and inquiring from him, so that by learning I may be benefited. Since even now I noticed while you were speaking that in the verses which you just mentioned, pointing out that Achilles speaks to Odysseus as if he were a boaster, it seems strange to me if you speak the truth; because Odysseus, the versatile one, nowhere appears to have lied; but Achilles appears to be somewhat versatile according to **E** your speech. At any rate, he lies. For having said these verses beforehand, which you also just spoke,

> For that man is as hateful to me as the gates of Hades,
> Who hides one thing in his heart, but says another,

a little later he says that he would not be persuaded by both Odysseus and Agamemnon, nor would he stay at all in Troy; but

> Tomorrow, having performed sacrifices to Zeus (he says) and all the gods,
> having well-laden the ships, when I have dragged them to the sea,
> you shall see, if you wish and if these things concern you,
> my ships sailing very early over the fish-filled Hellespont,
> and men within them eager to row.
> And if the famous Earth-shaker <note>The god Poseidon or Neptune.</note> gives a fair voyage,
> on the third day I would reach deep-soiled Phthia.

**F** And even before these things, while reviling Agamemnon, he said,

> And now I go to Phthia; since it is much better
> to go home with the curved ships, nor do I think
> being dishonored here, I shall draw up wealth and riches for you.

Having said these things, sometimes in front of the whole army, and sometimes to his own companions, he nowhere appears either preparing or attempting to drag down the ships, as if about to sail home, but **G** quite nobly disregarding the truth. I therefore, Hippias, asked you from the beginning, being at a loss as to which of these two men was made better by the poet, and thinking both were best, and it was hard to judge which was better, both concerning falsehood and truth and other virtue. For both are nearly the same in this. **Hippias:** For you do not look at it well, Socrates. For what things Achilles lies about, he appears to lie not from design, but unwillingly, because of the misfortune of the camp, being forced to remain and help; but what Odysseus lies about, he does so both willingly and from design. **Socrates:** You are deceiving me, my dearest Hippias, and you yourself are imitating Odysseus. **Hippias:** Not at all, Socrates. What are you saying and in reference to what? **Socrates:** Because you say Achilles lies from design— **H** he who was such a sorcerer and a designer toward boasting (as Homer has made him) that he appears to be so much more prudent than Odysseus in easily escaping notice while boasting, that he escaped his own notice in saying the opposite things...

<summary>Socrates challenges Hippias’s claim that Achilles is purely truthful and Odysseus is a liar by citing passages from the Iliad where Achilles breaks his word. He argues that if Achilles says he will leave Troy but stays, he is just as "versatile" and "lying" as Odysseus.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Hippias, specifically investigating whether the hero Achilles is "simpler" (more honest) than the "crafty" Odysseus. Socrates is in the process of demonstrating that Achilles also says things that are not true.</meta>

### HIPPIAS MINOR

A ...to speak, and he escaped Odysseus’s notice; at least Odysseus does not seem to have said anything to him as if he sensed he was lying. **Hippias:** What is this you are saying, Socrates? **Socrates:** Do you not know that, while saying earlier that he would sail away at dawn, he later says to Ajax that he will not sail away, but says something different? **Hippias:** Where does he say this? **Socrates:** In those lines where he says:

B > For I will not think of bloody war,
> Until the son of wise Priam, noble Hector,
> Comes to the huts and ships of the Myrmidons,
> Killing the Argives and burning the ships with fire.
> But around my own hut and black ship,
> I think I shall hold Hector back, however eager he is for battle.

C Do you then, Hippias, think that the son of Thetis <note>The sea-nymph mother of Achilles.</note>, who was educated by the most wise Chiron <note>The centaur tutor of many Greek heroes.</note>, was so forgetful that, having just a moment before cursed those who are pretenders with the utmost abuse, he would himself appear to Odysseus to be planning to sail, yet appear to Ajax to be staying? Or did he think Odysseus was a simpleton and believe he could deceive him by this very art <note>original: *τέχνῃ*</note> and by lying? **Hippias:** It does not seem so to me, Socrates; rather, he was persuaded by his own simplicity <note>original: *ἁπλότητος*</note> to say one thing to Ajax and another to Odysseus. But Odysseus, whether he speaks the truth or lies, always acts by design <note>original: *δόλους*</note>. **Socrates:** Then it seems Odysseus is better than Achilles. **Hippias:** Not at all, surely, Socrates. **Socrates:** Why? Did it not just appear that those who lie voluntarily are better than those who do so involuntarily? **Hippias:** And how, Socrates, could those who do wrong voluntarily, and who voluntarily plot or work evil, be better than those who do so involuntarily? For whom there seems to be great forgiveness, if someone does wrong or lies or does some other evil without knowing it. And the laws, surely, are much harsher toward those who work evil and lie voluntarily than toward those who do so involuntarily.

D **Socrates:** Do you see, Hippias, that I speak the truth when I say I am persistent in questioning the wise? And I risk having only this one good thing, while all my other qualities are quite poor. For I am mistaken about how things actually are, and I do not know how they stand. I have sufficient proof of this: that whenever I am with one of you who are famous for wisdom, and to whose wisdom all the Greeks are witnesses, I appear to know nothing. For almost nothing seems the same to me as it does to you. And yet, what greater proof of ignorance is there than when someone disagrees with wise men? But I have this one wonderful good thing which saves me: I am not ashamed to learn. Instead, I inquire and I ask, and I feel great gratitude toward the one who answers, and I have never deprived anyone of gratitude. For I have never denied it when I have learned something, pretending the lesson was my own discovery; instead, I praise the one who taught me as being wise, declaring what I learned from him. And so even now, I do not agree with what you say, but I disagree very strongly. And I know well that this happens because of me—because I am the sort of man I am, to say nothing greater of myself. For it appears to me, Hippias, the exact opposite of what you say. I think those who harm people, who do wrong, who lie, who deceive, and who make mistakes voluntarily rather than involuntarily, are better than those who do so involuntarily. Sometimes, however, the opposite seems true to me as well, and I wander <note>Socrates uses the word *πλανῶμαι*, suggesting a state of intellectual wandering or confusion.</note> concerning these matters, clearly because I do not know.

E **Hippias:** It seems to me, Socrates, that never—

F ...but now, at the present moment, a sort of fit <note>original: *καταβολὴ*, a sudden onset or seizure.</note> has come over me, and those who sin voluntarily concerning something seem to me better than those who do so involuntarily. I blame the previous arguments for my present condition, making it appear that those who do each of these things involuntarily are worse than those who do them voluntarily. So do me a favor, and do not grudge me the healing of my soul. For you will perform a much greater good by stopping my soul from ignorance than by stopping my body from disease. If you wish to speak at length, I tell you beforehand that you would not cure me (for I could not follow); but if you are willing to answer me as you did just now, you will help me greatly. And I think you will not be harmed yourself. Rightly would I also call upon you, son of Apemantus; for you stirred me up to dispute with Hippias. Now, if Hippias is not willing to answer me, beg him on my behalf.

G **Eudicus:** But Socrates, I do not think we will need to beg Hippias; for his policy is not such that he would refuse, but rather that he would flee the question of no man. Is that not what you were saying, Hippias? **Hippias:** I was. But Socrates, Eudicus, always throws the arguments into confusion, and he seems to be acting like a trickster <note>original: *κακουργοῦντι* - one who works mischief or plays dirty tricks in an argument.</note>. **Socrates:** Most excellent Hippias, I do not do these things voluntarily (for then I would be wise and clever, according to your argument), but involuntarily, so have forgiveness for me. For you say that he who does mischief involuntarily ought to be forgiven. **Eudicus:** Do not do otherwise, Hippias; but for our sake and for the sake of your previous statements, answer what Socrates asks you. **Hippias:** Well, I will answer, since you command it. Ask what you wish.

H **Socrates:** I am very eager, Hippias, to examine what was just said: which are better, those who err voluntarily or those who do so involuntarily? I think the most correct way to approach the inquiry is like this:

<meta>catchword: the</meta>

<column-break/>

A ...he would dare to speak, and he would deceive Odysseus. Wherefore Odysseus seems to bring nothing against him, as one who did not notice the lie. **Hippias:** What are these things you say, Socrates? **Socrates:** Do you not know that afterward he said to Odysseus he would depart at first light; but to Ajax he said not so, but otherwise? **Hippias:** Where? **Socrates:** In these verses:

<margin>Iliad 9.</margin>
> No care for dire war shall hold me first,
> Until I hear that Hector, son of Priam, has come in arms
> Seeking the long tents and ships of the Myrmidons,
> He who oppresses the Argives conquered in battle,
> And who thereafter casts fire into the ships themselves.
> For I do not think that Hector, raging against my ships or camp,
> Will dare to touch them in the doubt of war.

B Or do you believe, Hippias, that the son of Thetis, educated by the most wise Chiron, was so forgetful that, although he had a little before attacked those vain boasters with a most vehement speech, he himself immediately told Odysseus—as if forgetful of himself—that he would sail, but told Ajax he would stay? Or rather was he plotting, since he knew Odysseus was older, and was far more powerful than him in devised machines and deceits? **Hippias:** It does not seem to me that Achilles said those things with deceit, but rather, persuaded by his very simplicity, he spoke differently to Ajax than to Odysseus. Odysseus, however, whether he speaks true or false things, is always stretching out snares.

C **Socrates:** Odysseus is better, then, as it seems, than Achilles. **Hippias:** Not at all, Socrates. **Socrates:** Did it not appear above that those who tell a lie of their own accord are better than those who do not? **Hippias:** In what way, Socrates, can those who knowingly do injury, who willingly plot and harm, be better than those who do these things contrary to their intention? Since much is forgiven to him who, through ignorance, brings injury, speaks a lie, or commits any other evil; and the laws punish more severely those who do evil and lie willingly than those who do so unwillingly.

D **Socrates:** You see, Hippias, that I speak the truth when I say that I am precise in the questioning of wise men; and while in other things I am very deficient, I have only this much of good. For what the nature of things itself is, I do not know—which can be guessed most of all from this: that as often as I speak with any of you who excel in the reputation of wisdom, and have all the Greeks as witnesses to your learning, I appear to know nothing. For never does the same thing seem to me, so to speak, as to you. What, however, is a more evident argument of ignorance <note>original: *inficitiæ*</note> than if one disagrees with wise men?

<margin>It is an argument of ignorance to disagree with the wise. The duties of learning and speaking.</margin>

E Yet I have this wonderful good which saves me, because without the blush of shame I prepare myself to learn. I ask and I inquire, and I have enormous gratitude for the one who answers, nor have I ever been ungrateful to anyone; nor among listeners do I ever claim for myself the discoveries of others, but I always extol the teacher with praise, and I attribute to him before all men the things that are his. And even now, what you say I do not at all admit—on the contrary, I far disagree, and I know certainly that this happens by my own fault; since I confess myself to be such as I am, lest I extol myself. To me indeed, Hippias, it seems altogether the opposite of how it seems to you. I think indeed that those who voluntarily harm men, do injury, lie, deceive, and fail are better than those who do so involuntarily. Sometimes, however, I judge otherwise, and I wander about these things, inasmuch as I am ignorant of the matter itself.

F Behold, now a certain disease of the mind has invaded me, and those who err with purpose regarding something seem to me better than those who err contrary to their intention. I consider the previous arguments to be the cause of this ill, by which it happens that for the present I think those who sin involuntarily are worse than those who do so voluntarily. Therefore, you shall forgive me, and let no envy keep you from curing my mind. You will confer a much greater benefit upon me if you free my mind of ignorance than if you free my body of sickness. If you wish to accomplish this with many words, I tell you beforehand that you will by no means cure me in this way, for I shall not follow. But if you are willing to answer as above, you will profit me greatly. I hope, moreover, that this will not be harmful to you. Truly I shall now invoke you, son of Apemantus; for you yourself induced me to dispute with Hippias. Therefore, if Hippias is now willing to answer, intercede on my behalf.

G **Eudicus:** I think there is no need for my prayers to Hippias, Socrates. For he did not propose that he would answer only under compulsion; rather, he promised he would answer everyone freely. Are these not the things you said, Hippias? **Hippias:** I did say them. But Socrates here, Eudicus, always disturbs those who are speaking, and seems to be a kind of juggler <note>original: *præstigiator*</note>. **Socrates:** O best of men, Hippias, I do not do these things voluntarily—otherwise I would be wise and clever according to your speech. But I act contrary to my intention; wherefore, forgive me. For you say that he who sins involuntarily must be forgiven.

H **Eudicus:** Do not do otherwise, Hippias, but for our sake and because of those things which were said by you above, answer to those things which Socrates asks. **Hippias:** I will answer indeed, since you ask it. Seek, therefore, what you please. **Socrates:** I vehemently desire, Hippias, to consider what was just said: which are better, those who sin voluntarily and of their own accord, or those who do the opposite? I hope, moreover, that it can be most rightly considered in this way.

<margin>Which are better: those who sin voluntarily of their own accord, or those who do the opposite?</margin>

<summary>Socrates challenges Hippias by pointing out that Achilles lied to his companions in the Iliad, using this to argue that a voluntary liar is more "capable" and thus better than an involuntary one. Hippias objects on moral and legal grounds, while Socrates admits to his own state of confusion and ignorance.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue of the *Hippias Minor*. Socrates is leading the sophist Hippias through a series of analogies regarding "doing wrong" vs "doing right" to explore the nature of the soul and excellence.</meta>

# PLATONIS <note>Plato's [Dialogue]</note>

<margin>A</margin> **Socrates:** Answer me now. Do you call someone a good runner?
**Hippias:** I do.
**Socrates:** And a bad one?
**Hippias:** Yes.
**Socrates:** Is the one who runs well not a good runner, and the one who runs poorly a bad one?
**Hippias:** Certainly.
**Socrates:** Does the one who runs slowly run poorly, and the one who runs quickly run well?
**Hippias:** Without a doubt.
**Socrates:** Therefore, in running, speed is a good thing, and slowness is an evil.
**Hippias:** What of it?
**Socrates:** Which runner, then, is better: the one who runs slowly on purpose, or the one who does so unintentionally?
**Hippias:** The one who does it voluntarily.
**Socrates:** Is running not "doing" something?
**Hippias:** It is doing, certainly.
**Socrates:** And is "doing" something not a form of work?
**Hippias:** Assuredly.
**Socrates:** Therefore, the one who runs poorly performs this bad and shameful work in the race.
**Hippias:** It is bad; how could it be otherwise?
**Socrates:** But the one who runs slowly runs poorly.
<margin>B</margin> **Hippias:** True.
**Socrates:** Does the good runner, then, perform this bad and shameful act by design, while the bad runner does it against his intent?
**Hippias:** So it seems.
**Socrates:** In a race, then, the one who does bad things unintentionally is worse than the one who does them willingly.
**Hippias:** In a race, clearly.
**Socrates:** What about in the wrestling school? <note>original: *palæstra* / *πάλη*</note> Which wrestler is better? Is it the one who falls by deliberate effort, or the one who falls unwillingly?
**Hippias:** The one who falls by deliberate effort.
**Socrates:** So it seems.
<margin>C</margin> In wrestling, is it worse and more shameful to fall, or to throw someone down?
**Hippias:** To fall.
**Socrates:** In wrestling, then, the one who does bad and shameful things by choice is a better wrestler than the one who does them out of weakness and lack of skill.
**Hippias:** So it seems.
**Socrates:** What about every other use of the body? Is not the person who is physically stronger and more fit able to do both things according to their will—both the things of a strong man and those of a weak man, both the beautiful and the shameful? Therefore, when one who has a superior physical condition does something poorly regarding the body, he does it willingly; but the weak man does it unwillingly.
**Hippias:** It seems the same thing applies to strength.
**Socrates:** And what should be said regarding the grace of one's appearance? Is it not the mark of a more beautiful and better body to assume shameful poses by great effort, while the deformed body does so by necessity? What do you think?
**Hippias:** I think the same as you.
**Socrates:** Therefore, <margin>D</margin> voluntary awkwardness pertains to the virtue <note>original: *virtutem* / *ἀρετῆς* — in this context, "excellence" or "functional power."</note> of the body, while the involuntary pertains to its defect.
**Hippias:** So it appears.
**Socrates:** And what do you say about the voice? Which do you say is better: the one that sings out of tune by the soul's will, or the one that does so out of lack of skill?
**Hippias:** The one that does so by the soul's will.
**Socrates:** And the other is worse?
**Hippias:** Without a doubt.
**Socrates:** Would you prefer to possess good things or bad things?
**Hippias:** Good things.
**Socrates:** Would you choose to have feet that limped by your own design, or those that did so unwillingly?
**Hippias:** Clearly those that did so by design.
**Socrates:** Is the limping of feet not a defect and a deformity?
**Hippias:** It is.
**Socrates:** And is dullness of vision not a defect <margin>E</margin> of the eyes?
**Hippias:** A defect.
**Socrates:** Which eyes would you rather choose, then? Those with which a person willingly sees blurredly or looks askance, or those with which one sees poorly against their will?
**Hippias:** Those with which one does so willingly.
**Socrates:** Therefore, of those things that are your own, you consider those that perform poorly by choice to be better than those that do so unintentionally?
**Hippias:** In such cases, yes.
**Socrates:** Does not one single logic encompass all the rest—ears, nose, mouth, and all the senses—which teaches that senses which fail against our intent are never to be chosen, as they are defective; while those that do so by design are to be chosen instead, as they are good?
**Hippias:** It seems so to me.
**Socrates:** And which use of tools is better? <margin>F</margin> Those with which a person errs willingly, or those with which one errs unwillingly? For example, regarding a rudder, is that one better with which a person steers poorly by design, or that with which one does so unwillingly?
**Hippias:** That with which one does so by design.
**Socrates:** Is it not the same for a bow, a lyre, pipes, and all other things?
**Hippias:** You speak the truth.
**Socrates:** Which soul <note>original: *anima* / *ψυχὴν*</note> of a horse is better to possess: one with which a person would ride poorly by choice, or one with which they would do so unwillingly?
**Hippias:** One with which they would do so by choice.
**Socrates:** Therefore, it is better.
**Hippias:** It is.
**Socrates:** With a better horse's soul, then, one will perform the bad works of that soul willingly, but the opposite works unwillingly.
**Hippias:** Entirely so.
**Socrates:** Does the same logic not apply to the soul of a dog and all other animals?
**Hippias:** The same.
<margin>G</margin> **Socrates:** And which archer's soul would you choose as being better? The one that willingly misses the target, or the one that misses unwillingly?
**Hippias:** The one that does so of its own accord.
**Socrates:** Is this soul not better for the art of archery?
**Hippias:** It is better.
**Socrates:** Therefore, the soul that misses unknowingly is worse than the one that misses knowingly.
**Hippias:** In the capacity of archery, yes.
**Socrates:** What about in the study of medicine? Is the soul which, in the act of healing, brings some harm to bodies by design not more skilled in the medical art than the one that errs through ignorance?
**Hippias:** Clearly.
**Socrates:** Therefore, the former is better in the art of medicine.
**Hippias:** Better.
**Socrates:** And what of the soul more skilled at playing the lyre or blowing the pipes, and in all other things; is it not better in these as well? And if it ever does something poorly against the art, it does so by design; whereas the inferior soul does so against its own judgment?
**Hippias:** It appears so.
**Socrates:** And regarding the souls of slaves, would we not rather choose to possess those that err and do harm <margin>H</margin> in their service knowingly, rather than those that do so through ignorance, as being better for these tasks?
**Hippias:** Truly.
**Socrates:** And our own soul—do we not desire to have it as good as possible?
**Hippias:** Indeed.
**Socrates:** Will it not be better if it does harm and errs willingly, rather than if it does so unknowingly?
**Hippias:** That would be a grave matter, O Socrates, if those who do injustice willingly were better than those who do so unwillingly.
**Socrates:** Yet from the things that have been said above, it seems to follow.
**Hippias:** Not to me, certainly.
**Socrates:** I thought, Hippias, that it would seem so to you as well. Answer me again, then. Is justice not either some kind of power, or knowledge, or both? Is it not necessary that justice be one of these?
**Hippias:** It is necessary.
**Socrates:** If justice is a power of the soul, will the more powerful soul not be the more just? For, my excellent man, such a soul appeared to us as better...

<column-break/>

**Socrates:** ...but answer me. Do you call someone a good runner?
**Hippias:** I do.
**Socrates:** And a bad one?
**Hippias:** Yes.
**Socrates:** Therefore, does the good runner run well, and the bad one run poorly?
**Hippias:** Yes.
**Socrates:** Does the one who runs slowly run poorly, and the one who runs quickly run well?
**Hippias:** Yes.
**Socrates:** In running, then, and in the act of running, speed is good, and slowness is bad?
**Hippias:** What else could it be?
**Socrates:** Which runner, then, is better: the one who runs slowly willingly, or the one who does so unwillingly?
**Hippias:** The one who does so willingly.
**Socrates:** Is running not "doing" something?
**Hippias:** It is doing, certainly.
**Socrates:** If it is doing, is it not also working at something?
**Hippias:** Yes.
**Socrates:** Therefore, the one who runs poorly performs this bad and shameful act in the race?
**Hippias:** Bad; for how could it not be?
**Socrates:** And the one who runs slowly runs poorly?
**Hippias:** Yes.
**Socrates:** Therefore, the good runner performs this bad and shameful act willingly, and the bad runner does so unwillingly?
**Hippias:** So it seems.
**Socrates:** In a race, then, the one who performs bad acts unwillingly is more wicked than the one who does so willingly.
**Hippias:** In a race, at least.
**Socrates:** What about in wrestling? Which wrestler is better: the one who falls willingly, or the one who falls unwillingly?
**Hippias:** The one who falls willingly, it seems.
**Socrates:** Is it more wicked and shameful in wrestling to fall, or to throw someone down?
**Hippias:** To fall.
**Socrates:** In wrestling, then, the one who performs shameful and wicked acts willingly is a better wrestler than the one who does so unwillingly.
**Hippias:** So it seems.
**Socrates:** What about in every other use of the body? Is not the person with the better body able to do more powerful things—both the strong and the weak, the shameful and the beautiful? Thus, when he performs poorly regarding the body, the one with the better body does so willingly; but the more wicked one does so unwillingly.
**Hippias:** It seems to be this way regarding strength as well.
**Socrates:** And what about awkwardness, O Hippias? Is it not the mark of the better body to assume shameful poses willingly, and the worse body to do so unwillingly? Or how does it seem to you?
**Hippias:** In that way.
**Socrates:** Therefore, voluntary awkwardness pertains to excellence <note>original: *ἀρετῆς*</note>, and the involuntary to the wickedness of the body.
**Hippias:** It appears so.
**Socrates:** And what do you say about the voice? Which do you say is better: the one that sings out of tune willingly, or the one that does so unwillingly?
**Hippias:** The one that does so willingly.
**Socrates:** And the one that does so unwillingly is more wretched?
**Hippias:** Yes.
**Socrates:** Would you prefer to possess good things or bad things?
**Hippias:** Good things.
**Socrates:** Would you prefer to possess feet that limp willingly, or unwillingly?
**Hippias:** Willingly.
**Socrates:** Is the limping of feet not a wickedness and awkwardness?
**Hippias:** Yes.
**Socrates:** And is poor vision not a wickedness of the eyes?
**Hippias:** Yes.
**Socrates:** Which eyes would you want to possess and be with? Those with which one would be dim-sighted and see poorly willingly, or unwillingly?
**Hippias:** Those with which one would do so willingly.
**Socrates:** Therefore, you consider those things that perform poorly willingly to be better than those that do so unwillingly.
**Hippias:** In such cases, yes.
**Socrates:** Does not one reason hold together the ears, the nose, the mouth, and all the senses: that those which perform poorly unwillingly are not to be possessed, as they are wicked; while those that do so willingly are to be possessed, as they are good?
**Hippias:** It seems so to me.
**Socrates:** What about tools? Which partnership is better? Those with which a person performs poorly willingly, or unwillingly? For example, a rudder with which one will steer poorly unwillingly—is it better than one with which one does so willingly?
**Hippias:** The one with which one does so willingly.
**Socrates:** Is it not the same with a bow, a lyre, pipes, and all other things?
**Hippias:** You speak the truth.
**Socrates:** What of this? Is possessing the soul of a horse with which one will ride poorly willingly better than one with which one does so unwillingly?
**Hippias:** Willingly.
**Socrates:** Therefore, it is better.
**Hippias:** Yes.
**Socrates:** With the better soul of a horse, then, one would perform the wicked works of this soul willingly, but those of wickedness unwillingly?
**Hippias:** Certainly.
**Socrates:** Does this not apply to a dog and all other animals?
**Hippias:** Yes.
**Socrates:** And what then? Regarding the soul of a man who is an archer, is the one better which misses the mark willingly, or the one which does so unwillingly?
**Hippias:** The one that does so willingly.
**Socrates:** Therefore, this soul is better at archery?
**Hippias:** Yes.
**Socrates:** And the soul that errs unwillingly is more wicked than the one that does so willingly.
**Hippias:** In archery, at least.
**Socrates:** What about in medicine? Is the one that performs poorly regarding bodies willingly not more medical?
**Hippias:** Yes.
**Socrates:** Therefore, this soul is better in this art than the one that is not medical.
**Hippias:** Better.
**Socrates:** And what about the soul more skilled at the lyre, and the one more skilled at the pipes, and all other things according to the arts and sciences—is the soul not better which, possessing them, performs poorly and shamefully and errs willingly, while the more wicked soul does so unwillingly?
**Hippias:** It appears so.
**Socrates:** But surely we would prefer to possess the souls of slaves that err and do harm willingly rather than unwillingly, as they are better for these things.
**Hippias:** Yes.
**Socrates:** And what of our own soul? Would we want to possess it in the best possible state?
**Hippias:** Yes.
**Socrates:** Will it not be better if it does harm and errs willingly, rather than if it does so unwillingly?
**Hippias:** It would be a terrible thing, O Socrates, if those who do injustice willingly were better than those who do so unwillingly.
**Socrates:** But it certainly appears so from what has been said.
**Hippias:** Not to me.
**Socrates:** I thought, Hippias, it would appear so to you as well. But answer me again: Is justice not some power or knowledge, or both? Or is it not necessary that justice be some of these?
**Hippias:** Yes.
**Socrates:** Therefore, if justice is a power of the soul, the more powerful soul is the more just. For it appeared to us that such a soul was better...

<summary>Socrates uses various analogies—from athletics to medicine and tools—to force Hippias into the paradoxical conclusion that the person who does wrong intentionally is "better" because they possess the skill and power to control their actions, whereas the one who does wrong unintentionally is simply incompetent.</summary>
<keywords>Plato, Socrates, Hippias, excellence, justice, intentionality, power, soul, skill, arts and sciences</keywords>

# CHARMIDES.

<margin>A</margin> ...appeared to us. **Hippias:** It did. **Socrates:** What then if knowledge is justice? Is the soul that is wiser not also more just? And the one that is more ignorant, more unjust? **Hippias:** That is so. **Socrates:** What if it possesses both? Will the soul that has both—that is, knowledge and power—not be more just? And the one lacking knowledge, more unjust? Must it not necessarily be so? **Hippias:** It appears so. **Socrates:** And the soul that is more powerful <margin>B</margin> and wiser appeared to be better, and more prepared for both beautiful and shameful actions in any task? **Hippias:** Certainly. **Socrates:** Whenever it does shameful things, then, it does them voluntarily because of its skill and power. These things—either both or one of them—pertain to justice. **Hippias:** So it seems. **Socrates:** Indeed, to do wrong is to do evil; to not do wrong is to do good. **Hippias:** That is right. **Socrates:** Therefore, the more powerful and better soul, whenever it acts unjustly, will do so by choice? But the wicked soul will act involuntarily? **Hippias:** It appeared so. **Socrates:** Is the good man not he who has a good soul? And the bad man he who has a bad one? **Hippias:** Without a doubt. **Socrates:** Therefore, it is the mark of a good man to do wrong voluntarily, and a bad man to do so involuntarily, provided that the good man has a good soul. **Hippias:** He certainly has one. **Socrates:** If there is any man, Hippias, who errs voluntarily and commits shameful and unjust acts, he could be none other than the good man. **Hippias:** I cannot agree with you on these points, Socrates. **Socrates:** Nor can I agree with myself, Hippias; nevertheless, based on our previous argument, it must <margin>C</margin> appear so to us for now. As I said before, I wander up and down on these matters and never stay of the same opinion. It is no wonder that I, or any other ordinary man, should wander so. But if you wise men also wander, that is a heavy evil for us, if we cannot cease our wandering even after coming to you.

---

## CHARMIDES, OR,
## ON TEMPERANCE,
## or Moderation.

->SUMMARY OF THE DIALOGUE<-

> *The title itself clearly declares the thesis of this discussion: namely, that it deals with temperance <note>Latin: "temperantia," translating the Greek "sōphrosunē," which implies moderation, self-control, or "soundness of mind."</note>. This is explained through various descriptions, though not strictly defined. The use of temperance is treated extensively, yet within the form of a dialogue from which solid doctrine can be drawn: that temperance extends widely through all parts of our life; it fortifies the knowledge of things with timely and fruitful judgment so that it is not some ineffective and empty theory; and finally, that it is entirely concerned with action and must be cultivated by those who desire to lead a happy life. There are also certain logical theorems here: that one should attend not to who is speaking, but to what is being said; that arts have certain defined subjects they deal with; and that it is false to claim there can be a "Science of sciences"—that is, a science which by itself governs the subjects and ends of all other sciences—since each science maintains itself by its own principles.*

---

SOCRATES, CHAEREPHON, CRITIAS,
CHARMIDES.

I RETURNED yesterday evening from the army at Potidaea <note>Potidaea was a Greek city-state where a famous siege took place during the Peloponnesian War (432–430 BCE).</note>; and having been away for a long time, I gladly returned to my usual haunts. In particular, I went into the wrestling school <note>original: "palæstra"</note> of Taureas, which is opposite the Royal Temple. There I found many people, some unknown to me, but most of them acquaintances. When they <margin>D</margin> saw me entering unexpectedly, they immediately greeted me from all sides. Chaerephon, especially, being a bit of a madman, jumped up from the middle and ran toward me; taking me by the hand, he said, "O Socrates, how did you survive the battle?" For shortly before we left, a battle had taken place at Potidaea, which those here had only just heard about. I answered him, "Just as you see." "It was reported here," he said, "that the battle was very fierce, and that many of our acquaintances fell in it." "The reports you heard were quite true," I said. "Were you present at the battle?" he asked. "I was." "Then sit here," he said, "and tell us about it, for we have not yet heard everything clearly." With these words, he led me to sit near Critias, the son of Callaeschrus. Sitting there, I greeted Critias and the others, and then I recounted what had happened in the military expedition, answering whatever anyone asked—for each was asking something different. When we had spoken enough of these things, I in turn questioned them about the state of affairs here: how philosophy was faring at present, and whether any of the youths had become distinguished for wisdom, or beauty, or both. Then Critias, looking toward the door and seeing some young men entering and teasing one another, with a crowd of others following behind, said, "Regarding the beautiful ones, Socrates, I think you will know soon enough. For those now entering are the forerunners and lovers of the one who <margin>E</margin> is judged to be the most beautiful and handsome of this time. He seems to be about to enter himself." "Who is he?" I asked, "and whose son?" "Perhaps you know him," he said, "though he was not yet of age before you left. You knew Charmides, the son of our uncle Glaucon, my cousin?" "I know him indeed," I said, "for even then he was not to be overlooked, though still a boy; now, I suppose, he must be quite a young man." "You will see immediately," he said, "how great and what sort of person he has become." While he was saying this, Charmides entered. As for me, my friend, I have no yardstick; <margin>F</margin> for I am simply a "white line on a white stone" <note>A proverb meaning someone who has no standard of judgment or is easily influenced; like a white chalk mark on a white stone, Socrates claims his judgment of beauty is indistinguishable because everyone appears beautiful to him.</note> when it comes to those who are beautiful.

<summary>Socrates concludes a debate with Hippias on the paradox of voluntary wrongdoing and begins the Charmides by returning from war and meeting a beautiful, promising youth in a wrestling school.</summary>

# PLATO

For nearly all the young men of that age seemed beautiful to me. But especially then, he [Charmides] appeared marvelous, both for his tall stature and his extraordinary natural disposition. All the others seemed captured by love for him; they were so struck and thrown into confusion by his entrance. Furthermore, many other admirers followed behind him. As far as the men were concerned, it was no wonder; but I also noticed the boys, none of whom—even the smallest—looked at anyone else, but all of them gazed at him as if he were a sacred image. Then Chaerephon turned to me and said, "How does the youth seem to you, Socrates? Is he not handsome of face?" "Wonderfully so," I replied. "And yet," he said, "if he were willing to strip, you would say his face was plain compared to the beauty that lies within." The others all agreed with Chaerephon on this point. "By Hercules," I said, "you describe an invincible man, if only one little thing were added to him." "What would that be?" asked Critias. "If," I replied, "he were naturally gifted with a soul of the highest quality—which is only fitting, Critias, as he is a descendant of your house." "Indeed," he said, "as far as his character is concerned, he is both most beautiful and most excellent." "Why then," I asked, "do we not strip his soul first and contemplate its interior form? For since he is now of such an age, I think he will be happy to engage in discussion." "Certainly," said Critias. "For he is a student of wisdom and, as it seems to both himself and others, quite a poet." "My dear friend Critias," I said, "this noble quality is drawn from the long line of your family, descending from Solon. <note>Solon was a famous Athenian lawmaker and poet, and an ancestor of both Critias and Charmides.</note> But why do you not show the young man to me now by calling him here? Even if he were younger, it would not be improper for him to discuss with us in your presence, as you are both his cousin and his guardian." "Rightly said," he replied. "He must be called now." And saying this, he turned to the attendant who followed behind and said, "Call Charmides. But look, tell him that I wish to introduce him to a certain physician regarding the illness he complained of recently." Then Critias said to me, "Recently, when Charmides rose in the morning, he complained of a headache. What is to stop you from pretending you have a remedy for a heavy head?" "Nothing stops me," I said, "provided he comes." "But he will come." And so it happened: for he came, and he provoked a great laugh from everyone. For each of us sitting together, wishing to yield a place for Charmides to sit, pushed his neighbor so purposefully that of those sitting at the ends, we forced one to stand up and knocked the other flat on the ground. He came and sat between me and Critias. Then, my friend, I was already in a state of confusion; the confidence I had just a moment ago—that I would easily dispute with him—deserted me. And after Critias said that I was the one who knew the remedy, he looked at me with his eyes in a way that was almost miraculous, and approached as if to ask a question. Everyone in the <term>palaestra</term> <note>A wrestling school or gymnasium, a common social hub for Athenian men.</note> immediately flocked toward us and surrounded us like a circle. Then, noble friend, when I looked at what was hidden beneath his cloak, I took fire and was no longer master of myself. I judged Critias to be most wise in matters of love; for while speaking of a beautiful boy, he used the comparison of another thing to warn me to look again and again, lest like a fawn coming into the sight of a lion, I should have a piece of my flesh torn away. For I certainly felt myself captured by that bait. However, when he asked if I knew the cure for a head, I finally managed to answer that I knew it. "What is it then?" he asked. "A certain leaf," I said. "But in addition, an incantation must be added; if one applies the charm while using the leaf, health is restored. Without the incantation, the leaf confers nothing." To this he replied, "I will indeed write down this incantation as you dictate it." "Whether you persuade me," I said, "or even if you do not?" He smiled and said, "If I persuade you, Socrates." "Aha," I said, "you clearly know my name too." "I do indeed," he said, "unless I am mistaken. For there is frequent talk of you among those of my age. I even remember when I was still a boy seeing you spend time with Critias here." "You are quite right," I said. "For I shall show you the manner of the incantation more boldly. Just a moment ago I did not know how to demonstrate its power to you.

<column-break/>

<margin>Precepts of medicine</margin> It is of such a kind, Charmides, that it cannot cure the head alone; just as you have often heard from skilled physicians, who, whenever someone suffering from eye pain consults them, say they cannot heal the eyes unless they first heal the head, nor can the head be cured without the treatment of the whole body. For this reason, they use certain rules that benefit the whole, and from the whole they proceed to restore the part. Have you not heard them speak this way, and that it is so?" "Entirely," he said. "Does it seem to you they speak correctly?" I asked, "and do you approve of this discourse?" "Most of all," he replied. Truly, when I heard that these things were approved by him, I regained my confidence, and my spirit was gradually stirred and refreshed again. "Such, Charmides, is the power of this incantation. I learned it there in the army from a certain physician of the Thracian followers of <term>Zalmoxis</term>, <note>A legendary social and religious reformer of the Thracians, often regarded as a god or a king who taught the immortality of the soul.</note> who are said even to bring about immortality. That Thracian physician added, moreover, that the Greek physicians preach what was just narrated. But Zalmoxis—"

<summary>In this opening scene of the Charmides, Socrates meets the exceptionally handsome youth Charmides and, under the guise of curing the boy's headache, introduces the philosophical principle of holism—that the part cannot be cured without the whole body and soul.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates, Critias, and the young Charmides. On the previous page, Socrates expressed admiration for Charmides' beauty and noble ancestry, leading to this discussion on the connection between the health of the body and the health of the soul.</meta>

# CHARMIDES.

<margin>A</margin> ...to attempt to heal, nor the head without the body, so also the body cannot be healed without the soul. And he said this was the very reason why many diseases escape the Greek physicians: because they are ignorant of the whole, which they ought to care for first. If the whole is not in good condition, it is impossible for the part to be well. For he said that everything springs from the soul—both the evils and the goods of the body and the whole man—and flows from there, just as everything flows from the head to the eyes. Therefore, one must first and most especially treat the soul if the head and the rest of the body are to be in good condition. He said, my dear friend, that the soul is treated with certain **incantations** <note>original: "epodai"</note>. And these incantations are **noble discourses** <note>original: "logoi kaloi"</note>. From such discourses, **temperance** <note>The Greek term is "sophrosyne," meaning moderation, self-control, or soundness of mind.</note> is born in the souls; and when it is born and
<margin>B</margin> present, it is then easy to provide health both to the head and to the rest of the body. So, while he was teaching me the remedy and the incantations, he said: "Let no one persuade you to treat his head with this remedy who does not first offer his soul to be treated by you with the incantation." For he said that this is the current error among men: that some attempt to be physicians of health or temperance separately from one another. And he strictly charged me that no one—no matter how rich, noble, or handsome—should persuade me to do otherwise. Therefore, since I swore an oath to him, I must obey, and I will obey. And if you are willing, according to the stranger’s commands, to first submit your soul to be charmed by the Thracian's incantations, I will then apply the remedy for the head. But if not, I would not know what to do for you, my dear Charmides. When Critias heard me say this, he said: "Socrates, this headache would be a stroke of luck <note>original: "Hermaion," a gift from Hermes.</note> for the youth, if he is compelled to improve his mind for the sake of his head. However, I tell you that Charmides is thought to excel his peers not only in appearance but also in that very thing for which you say you have the incantation: **temperance**."
<margin>D</margin> "Is that so?" I asked. "Indeed," he replied. "Then know well," he said, "that he is thought to be by far the most temperate person now living, and in all other things, for his age, he is second to none." "And indeed," I said, "it is only right, Charmides, that you should excel others in all such things. For I do not think anyone else here could easily show which two Athenian houses, by their union, would likely produce a nobler or better offspring than those from which you are born. For your father’s house, that of Critias the son of Dropides, has been handed down to us praised by Anacreon, Solon, and many other poets for its excellence in beauty, virtue, and all other so-called happiness. And your mother’s side is the same; for no man in all the continent <note>Referring to the Persian Empire or the mainland of Asia.</note> is said to have appeared more handsome or greater than your uncle Pyrilampes, whenever he went as an ambassador to the Great King or anyone else there.
<margin>E</margin> This whole house is in no way inferior to the other. Being born from such ancestors, it is likely that you would be first in all things. Regarding your visible form, dear son of Glaucon, you seem to me to shame none of your ancestors; but if you are also naturally gifted with temperance and these other virtues as Critias says, then your mother, dear Charmides, bore you to be a truly blessed man. The situation is this: if temperance is already present in you, as Critias here says, and you are sufficiently temperate, then you have no further need of the incantations of Zalmoxis or Abaris the Hyperborean <note>Mythical figures associated with Thracian and northern wisdom/healing.</note>, but the remedy for the head may be given to you at once. But if you seem to still lack these things, you must be charmed before receiving the remedy. Tell me yourself, do you agree with him, and do you say you already share sufficiently in temperance, or are you
<margin>F</margin> lacking in it?" Then Charmides blushed, and first he appeared even more handsome, for modesty <note>original: "aischyntelon"</note> becomes his age; then he answered quite nobly. He said it was not easy at the moment either to agree or to deny what was asked. "For if," he said, "I say I am not temperate, it would be a strange thing to say such things against myself, and I would also prove Critias to be a liar, along with many others who think I am temperate, as he said. But if I say I am, and praise myself, it will perhaps appear boastful. So I do not know how to answer you." And I said, "You seem to
<margin>G</margin> speak reasonably, Charmides. And it seems to me that we should examine this together, whether you possess what I am asking about or not; so that you are not forced to say what you do not wish, and I do not turn to medicine without due consideration. If it is pleasing to you, I wish to examine it with you; if not, we shall let it be." "Indeed," he said, "it is most pleasing of all. Therefore, as far as that is concerned, examine it in whatever way you think is best." "This then," I said, "seems to me the best way to investigate it. For it is clear that if temperance is present in you, you have some opinion about it. For it must be that, if it is within you, it provides a certain sensation from which you would have an opinion about what temperance is and what sort of thing it is. Do you not think so?" "I do," he said. "Therefore,"
<margin>H</margin> I said, "since you know how to speak Greek, could you not say what it appears to be to you?" "Perhaps," he said. "In order then that we may guess whether it is in you or not, tell me," I said, "what do you say temperance is, according to your opinion?" At first he hesitated and was not at all willing to answer; but finally, he answered...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> It is not fitting to treat you, nor the head without the rest of the body: so neither should the body be treated without the soul. And this is the cause why many diseases of the body remain hidden from Greek doctors, because they are ignorant of the whole itself, which ought to be cared for first; for if the whole is poorly affected, it is impossible for any part to be in good health. For all things, whether good or evil, flow from the soul into the body and the whole man, and from there they flow just as from the head into the eyes. Therefore, he commands that the soul be cared for first and most greatly, if indeed the head and the entire body are to be in good health. And he teaches, O blessed one, that the remedies of the soul are certain incantations. These are contained in noble discourses, by which temperance is granted to the soul: once it is inserted and present, it is easy to provide health to the head and the whole body. Therefore, when he taught the remedy
<margin>B</margin> and the incantation, he commanded that I should be moved by no prayers to provide a remedy for a head pain to anyone unless he had first committed his soul to be purged by those same incantations. Indeed, he said that the error of our times is that most people attempt to be doctors of health and temperance separately. Thus he warned me in a wonderful way and commanded that I take care that no one, whether rich or noble or beautiful, should ever persuade me to do otherwise. I bound myself to this by an oath; therefore, it is necessary that I obey, and I shall obey. But if you wish, according to the guest's precepts, to first subject your soul to all the
<margin>C</margin> incantations of that Thracian, I shall apply the remedy to your head. If not, I will not be able to help you, my friend Charmides. When Critias heard these things, he said: "This heaviness of the head will be a gain to the youth if he is compelled to become better in mind and soul because of his head. But I tell you that this Charmides excels all his equals not only in appearance, but even surpasses others in that very thing for which you said you have an incantation. Did you not speak of temperance above?" "Of that very thing," I said. "Know then that of all the youths of his age, he seems the most temperate,
<margin>D</margin> and in all other things according to the growth of his age, he is inferior to none." "It is fitting, O Charmides," I said, "in these things which Critias has said, that you should excel others. For no one, I think, could easily find a marriage of two Athenian families from which a more beautiful and honest offspring might likely be born than from the marriage of your ancestors. For the paternal line of this Critias, son of Dropides, has been made famous by Anacreon, Solon, and many other poets, as excelling in grace, virtue, and other happiness. And the glory of the maternal line is the same. For no one appeared either more beautiful or greater to all who inhabit the continent than your uncle Pyrilampes, whenever he
<margin>E</margin> went as an ambassador either to the Great King or to others inhabiting the continent. And in short, this entire house is in no way inferior to any other. Therefore it is probable that you, created from such a lineage, would hold the first parts in all things. As far as that appearance which is perceived by the eyes is concerned, O sweet son of Glaucon, you seem to me to have degenerated in nothing from your superiors. But if you are inclined by nature toward temperance and other things, as Critias here testifies, your mother bore you a blessed man, O dear Charmides. Therefore the matter stands thus: if temperance is in you, as Critias says, and you are sufficiently temperate, you have no need for the incantations of either Zalmoxis or Abaris the Hyperborean, but the remedy for the head must now be applied. But if temperance is lacking in you, the incantation must precede the remedy. Answer me yourself, therefore, whether you agree with Critias and claim to have enough temperance, or whether you recognize that something is lacking." Then the cheeks of Charmides were suffused with a blush, showing a
<margin>F</margin> more pleasing appearance. <margin>Modesty becomes the young.</margin> For modesty becomes that age. Then he responded quite nobly: "It is in no way easy to either admit or deny the things which have been asked at present. For if I deny that I am temperate, it will first seem shameful that I disparage myself; and then I would prove the opinion of Critias and many others, to whom I seem temperate, to be false. But if I affirm it, this boasting about myself will seem hateful. Therefore, I do not know which way to turn." "You seem to speak rightly, Charmides," I said; "therefore, I think we must
<margin>G</margin> investigate together whether you possess what I seek or not: so that you are not forced to speak otherwise than you wish, nor I hasten to heal rashly. If, therefore, it will be pleasing to you, I desire to investigate it together with you; if not, I think it should be dismissed." "Indeed, most pleasing of all," he said. "Therefore, as you yourself think best, so investigate." "In this way," I said, "the search seems likely to be more convenient. It is certainly established that if temperance is in you, you have something that you think about it. For it is necessary that, if it is within you, it provides some sense of itself, from which some opinion may arise concerning it, by which you might guess what and of what kind
<margin>H</margin> temperance is, do you not think so?" "I certainly think so." "Do you not believe this? Namely, since you know how to speak Greek, you could certainly say what it seems to you to be?" "Perhaps," he said. "So that we may guess whether temperance is in you or not, come tell me, what do you say temperance is, in your opinion?"
