# PLATO

<meta>The text below presents a parallel translation of the Latin and Greek columns found in the original manuscript. Both columns contain the same dialogue between Socrates and Charmides.</meta>

<margin>Sagacity is a certain quickness of the mind.</margin>

**A** ...Then he said with some hesitation that temperance <note>original: "temperantia" / "σωφροσύνη" (sophrosyne)</note> seems to him to be the act of doing all things in an orderly fashion, walking quietly and calmly along the way, speaking quietly, and doing all things in a similar manner. "And to put it briefly," he said, "quietness and a certain calmness seem to me to be what you are asking about." 

"You speak rightly," I said. "For they certainly say that quiet and placid men are temperate. But let us see if they speak the truth. Tell me then: is temperance not something noble?" <note>The Greek "kalon" and Latin "pulchrum" imply both physical beauty and moral nobility.</note>

"It certainly is," he replied.

"In the art of the grammarian, is it more noble to write the same letters quickly or slowly?"

"Quickly."

"And in reading, is it better to do so fast or slow?"

"Fast."

"And indeed, is it not more noble to strike the lyre quickly and to wrestle with agility," I asked, "than to do so quietly and slowly?"

"It is," he said.

**B** "And what about boxing and the pancratium? <note>A grueling ancient Greek sport combining boxing and wrestling.</note> Is it not the same? And in running and jumping, and all other bodily actions, if they are done swiftly and promptly, are they not considered noble? But if they are done slowly, with difficulty, placidly, or quietly, are they not considered shameful?"

"It appears so," he said.

"It is clear then, as far as the body is concerned," I said, "that not what is slow and quiet, but what is swiftest and most agile is the most noble. Is it not?"

"Entirely so," he said.

"And did we not agree that temperance is something noble?"

"We did."

"Therefore, regarding the body, quietness is not temperance, but rather speed would be more temperate, if indeed temperance is something noble."

"It seems so," he said.

**C** "And is not readiness in learning <note>original: "docilitas" / "εὐμαθία"</note> more noble than dullness?"

"It certainly is."

"But readiness in learning," I said, "is to learn quickly, while dullness is to learn late and slowly."

"Exactly," he said.

"And is it not more noble to teach another as swiftly as possible rather than hesitatingly and slowly?"

"Without a doubt."

"What about recollecting and remembering? Is it more noble to do so late and slowly, or easily and promptly?"

"Promptly," he said.

"And is not sagacity <note>original: "solertia" / "ἀγχίνοια"</note> a certain quickness of the mind," I asked, "rather than slowness?"

"It is," he said.

"Furthermore, to understand what is said in the schools of the grammarian or the lyre-player, and in all other things, is it not most noble to do so as swiftly as possible rather than as slowly as possible?"

"Yes," he said.

"And indeed, in the very investigations and deliberations of the mind, I think it is not the man who deliberates quietly and with difficulty who is to be praised, but the one who does so most easily and in a short time."

"That is true," he said.

**D** "From all this it follows, Charmides," I said, "that in matters of the body as well as those of the mind, swift and prompt things seem more noble than slow and quiet ones."

"So it appears," he said.

"Therefore, temperance is not a kind of quietness, nor is a quiet life a temperate one, as this reasoning suggests—seeing that what is temperate must also be noble. **E** For of these two options, either never or only very rarely in life have quiet actions appeared more noble to us than swift and vehement ones. But if, my friend, quiet actions were found to be no less noble than swift and vehement ones, even then temperance would not be 'acting quietly' any more than 'acting vehemently and quickly,' whether in walking, speaking, or anything else. Nor would a quiet life be more orderly and temperate than an unquiet one, since in our previous talk we assumed temperance is something noble, and we have confessed that swift things are no less noble than quiet ones."

"You seem to me to have spoken rightly, Socrates," he said.

"So then, Charmides," I said, "look at yourself more attentively again. Think about what sort of person temperance makes you when it is present, and what kind of thing it must be to make you so. Considering all these things, tell me well and manfully: what does it seem to be to you?"

**F** Collecting himself and contemplating more diligently, he said: "It seems to me that temperance makes a man feel a sense of shame or modesty, and that temperance is, in fact, **modesty**." <note>original: "pudor" / "αἰδὼς" (aidos). This term implies a sense of reverence, shame, or the social inhibition that prevents one from doing wrong.</note>

"What are you saying?" I asked. "Did you not just agree that temperance is something noble?"

"I did indeed," he said.

"And are not temperate men good men?"

"They are."

"Can that be good which does not produce good men?"

"By no means."

"So it is not only noble, but also good."

"So it seems to me."

"And do you not believe that Homer speaks rightly," I asked, "when he says that **shame is not good for a man in need**?"

<margin>Odyssey, Book 17.</margin>

**G** "I do believe it," he said.

"It appears then," I said, "that shame is both not good and good." <note>Socrates is pointing out a contradiction: if shame can be bad (as in Homer's example), but temperance is always good, then they cannot be the same thing.</note>

"It appears so."

"But temperance is only good, since it makes those to whom it is present good, and never bad."

"It seems to be exactly as you say."

"Therefore, temperance cannot be shame, since temperance is only good, while shame is no more good than it is evil."

"This seems rightly said to me, Socrates," he said. "But please consider this other definition I have just thought of. For I just remembered hearing someone say that temperance is **minding one's own business**. <note>original: "vt sua quisque agat" / "τὰ ἑαυτοῦ πράττειν"</note> See if you think the one who said this was speaking rightly."

"You rogue," I said, "did you hear this from Critias, or some other **H** wise man?"

"It seems," said Critias, "it was from someone else, for he certainly never heard it from me."

"What does it matter, Socrates," said Charmides, "from whom I heard it?"

"Not at all," I said, "for we should not consider *who* said it, but whether it is *true* or not."

"Now you are speaking rightly," he said.

"By Zeus, I am," I said. "Yet I would be surprised if we can figure out what this means, for it seems like a kind of riddle."

"Why so?" he asked.

"Because I do not think he meant the words...

<column-break/>

**A** ...Then with difficulty he said (that temperance seems to him to be) to do all things orderly, and to walk quietly on the roads, and to converse, and to do all other things in the same way. "And it seems to me," he said, "to put it concisely, that what you ask about is a certain quietness."

"Well then," I said, "are you right? At least they say, Charmides, that quiet people are temperate. Let us see if there is any truth in what they say. Tell me: is temperance not among the noble things?"

"Certainly," he said.

"In the school of the grammarian, is it most noble to write similar letters quickly or quietly?"

"Quickly."

"What about reading? Fast or slow?"

"Fast."

"And indeed, playing the lyre quickly and wrestling sharply is much more noble than doing so quietly and slowly?"

"Yes."

**B** "And what about boxing and the pancratium? Is it not the same?"

"Certainly."

"And running and jumping, and all the works of the body—are not those done sharply and quickly noble, while those done slowly, with difficulty, and quietly, are shameful?"

"It appears so."

"It appears to us then," I said, "that regarding the body, not the quiet, but the quickest and sharpest is most noble. Is it not?"

"Certainly."

"And temperance was something noble?"

"Yes."

"Therefore, regarding the body, not quietness, but speed would be more temperate, since temperance is noble."

"It seems so," he said.

"What then?" I asked. "Is quickness in learning <note>original: "eumathia"</note> more noble than slowness in learning?"

"Quickness in learning."

"And is quickness in learning to learn fast, while slowness in learning is to do so quietly and slowly?"

"Yes."

**C** "And to teach another—is it not more noble to do so quickly and forcefully rather than quietly and slowly?"

"Yes."

"What about recollecting and remembering? Is it more noble to do so quietly and slowly, or forcefully and quickly?"

"Forcefully and quickly," he said.

"And is not sagacity a certain sharpness of the soul, and not quietness?"

"True."

"Therefore, understanding what is said, whether at the grammarian's or the lyre-player's or anywhere else, is it not most noble to do so not as quietly as possible, but as quickly as possible?"

"Yes."

"And truly, in the soul's investigations and in deliberating, I think it is not the most quiet man—the one who deliberates and finds things out with difficulty—who is worthy of praise, but the one who does this most easily and quickly."

"That is so," he said.

**D** "Therefore, in all things, Charmides," I said, "both those concerning the soul and those concerning the body, things characterized by speed and sharpness appear more noble than those of slowness and quietness."

"It seems likely," he said.

"Temperance, then, would not be a kind of quietness, nor would the temperate life be a quiet one, at least by this reasoning, since it must be noble. For of the two, either never, or in very few instances, do quiet actions in life appear more noble than fast and strong ones. But even if, my friend, quiet actions happen to be no less noble than forceful and fast ones, even so, temperance would not be 'acting quietly' any more than acting forcefully and quickly—not in walking, not in speech, nor anywhere else. A quiet life would be no more orderly or temperate than a non-quiet one, since in our argument we assumed temperance is something noble. **E** And fast things have been shown to be no less noble than quiet ones."

"You seem to me to have spoken rightly, Socrates," he said.

"Once again then, Charmides," I said, "paying closer attention and looking into yourself, consider what sort of person temperance makes you when it is present, and what it must be to produce such an effect. Having gathered all this together, tell me well and manfully what it seems to be to you."

He paused, and having examined himself quite manfully, said: "It seems to me, then, that temperance makes a man feel shame, and makes him a modest man; and that temperance is exactly what **modesty** <note>original: "aidos"</note> is."

**F** "Well then," I said, "did you not just agree that temperance is noble?"

"Certainly," he said.

"And are temperate men not good?"

"Yes."

"Could that be good which does not produce good men?"

"Certainly not."

"Therefore, it is not only noble but also good."

"So it seems to me."

"What then?" I said. "Do you not believe Homer speaks well when he says that:
> Shame is not a good mate for a man in need to have present?"

"I do," he said.

"It seems then that shame is both not good and good."

"It appears so."

**G** "But temperance is good, if indeed it makes those in whom it is present good, and not bad."

"Truly, it seems to me to be as you say."

"Therefore, temperance cannot be shame, if the one happens to be good, while shame is no more good than it is also bad."

"That seems to me to be rightly said, Socrates," he said. "But consider this: what do you think of this definition of temperance? For I just remembered what I once heard someone saying: that temperance might be 'doing one's own business.' Consider whether you think the one who says this is speaking rightly."

"You rascal," I said, "have you heard this from Critias himself, or from some other wise man?"

"It seems," said Critias, "to be from someone else, for it was certainly not from me."

"But what does it matter, Charmides," I asked, "from whom you heard it?"

"Nothing," I said. "For in any case, we should not consider who said it, but whether it is spoken truly or not."

"Now you are speaking rightly," he said.

"By Zeus," I said, "but I would be surprised if we even find out how this stands. For it seems like a kind of **H** riddle."

"In what way?" he said.

"In what way? Surely not," I said, "in the way the words..."

# CHARMIDES

<margin>A</margin> "For he says—just as I was saying—that temperance <note>original: σωφροσύνη (sophrosyne)</note> is 'doing one's own business.' Do you think a scribe <note>original: γραμματιστής (grammatistēs), a teacher of letters or a clerk</note> is doing something, or even fearing something, when he writes or reads?" "By the gods, I do not," I said. "Does it seem to you that the scribe writes or reads only his own name, or do you children also learn this? Or did you write the names of your enemies no less than your own names and those of your friends?" "No less," he replied. "Were you then being meddlesome <note>The opposite of "doing one's own business."</note> and lacking in temperance while doing this?" "Not at all." "And yet, you were certainly not just 'doing your own business' if writing and reading are both forms of 'doing' or 'acting.'" "They are indeed." "And furthermore, my friend, would you say that practicing medicine, building houses, weaving, or performing any other craft is a form of 'doing'?" 
<margin>B</margin> "Certainly." "What then?" I said. "Does it seem to you that a city would be well-governed by a law that commanded everyone to weave and wash their own cloak, to make their own shoes, their own oil-flasks, their own scrapers <note>original: στλεγγίδα (stlengida) / strigilem; used by athletes to scrape oil and sweat from the skin</note>, and everything else by the same logic? That is, to never touch the belongings of others, but for each to work at and do only their own business?" "It does not seem so to me," he said. "And yet," I replied, "a city that is temperately managed would be well-governed." "How could it be otherwise?" he asked. "Therefore," I said, "it cannot be that temperance is 'doing one's own business' in this specific way." "It appears not." "Then it seems that the person who said temperance is 'doing one's own business' was speaking in riddles, just as I suspected just now. For surely he was not so foolish. Or did you hear this from some simpleton, Charmides?" "Least of all," he said, "since he seemed to be quite wise."
<margin>C</margin> "Then it seems more than likely to me that he wrapped his meaning in a riddle, because it is difficult to know what 'doing one's own business' actually is." "Perhaps," he said. "What then? Can you tell us what 'doing one's own business' might mean?" "By Zeus, I do not know," he replied. "But perhaps there is nothing to stop the one who said it from not knowing what he meant either." As he said this, he glanced slyly at Critias. Critias had clearly been anxious for some time, eager to prove himself before Charmides and those present. He had barely restrained himself before, but now he was no longer able to do so. It seemed to me—and I suspect I am right—that Charmides had heard this answer about temperance from Critias himself.
<margin>D</margin> Charmides, therefore, wanting Critias to take over the defense of the definition, nudged him and pointed out that he had been refuted. Critias could not bear this; indeed, he seemed to me to get angry with Charmides, much like a poet with an actor who performs his poems poorly. So, looking at him, he said: "Do you really think, Charmides, that if you do not understand what the person meant who said temperance is 'doing one's own business,' that he himself did not know either?" "My dear Critias," I said, "it is no wonder that this young man at his age does not know; but it is likely that you know, both because of your age and your studies. If you agree that temperance is what he says it is, and you accept the argument, I would much prefer to examine with you whether the statement is true or not." "I certainly agree," he said, "and I accept it." "You do well," I said. "Now tell me: do you agree with what I was asking just now—that craftsmen all 'make' something?" "I do." "And do they seem to you to make only their own things, or also the things of others?" "The things of others as well." "Are they then temperate, even though they do not 'make' only their own things?" "What prevents it?" he asked.
<margin>E</margin> "Nothing on my part, by Zeus," I said. "But see if there is something that prevents the man who proposed that temperance is 'doing one's own business' from then claiming that those who do the business of others can also be temperate." "Wait," he said, "did I admit that those who 'do' the business of others are temperate, or did I only admit that those who 'make' are?" "Tell me," I asked, "do you not call 'doing' and 'making' the same thing?" "Certainly not," he said, "nor is 'working' the same as 'making.' For I learned this from Hesiod, who said, 'Work is no disgrace.' <note>A famous line from Hesiod's *Works and Days*.</note> Do you think that if he called such tasks 'work' and 'doing'—the kind you were just talking about—that he would have said there is no disgrace for someone who is a shoemaker, or a seller of salted fish, or someone sitting in a brothel? You should not think so, Socrates. 
<margin>F</margin> "Rather, I believe he thought that 'making' <note>original: ποίησιν (poiesin)</note> is different from 'action' <note>original: πράξεως (praxeos)</note> and 'work.' A 'thing made' can sometimes be a reproach when it is not made with beauty; but 'work' is never a disgrace. For he called things that are made beautifully and usefully 'works,' and such 'makings' he called 'workings' and 'actions.' We must say that he considered only such things as 'one's own,' and all harmful things as 'belonging to others.' Therefore, you should believe that Hesiod, and any other man of sound mind, calls the one who does his own business 'temperate.'"
<margin>G</margin> "As soon as you began to speak, Critias," I said, "I perceived that you were calling 'one's own' and 'one's business' that which is good, and you were calling the 'makings' of good things 'actions.' For I have heard Prodicus <note>A Sophist famous for his focus on the precise meaning of synonyms.</note> distinguish between names in a thousand such ways. I will grant you that you may use any name however you wish, provided you clarify what you mean by the name you use. Now, then, define it more clearly from the beginning: do you say that temperance is the 'action' or 'making'—or however you wish to name it—of good things?" "I do," he said.
<margin>H</margin> "Then the person who does evil is not temperate, but only the one who does good." "And do you, my friend," he asked, "not think so?" "I agree..."

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> I said to him that, according to the sound of the words, temperance is indeed when anyone does his own business. "Do you think a scribe does nothing when he writes or reads?" "I think he does something," he said. "Does it seem to you that a scribe writes and reads only his own name? Or does he also instruct you boys? For you did not write the names of your enemies any less than those of your friends." "Certainly not less," he said. "When you did this," I asked, "were you being more meddlesome than is proper, and departing from the law of temperance?" "Not at all," he said. "But truly you were not doing only your own business, if writing and reading is 'doing' something." "That is so," he said. "Furthermore, my friend, is healing, building, weaving, or completing the work of any art doing something, or nothing?" "Something, certainly," he said.
<margin>B</margin> "Would it seem to you," I asked, "that a state was well-ordered in which the laws commanded that each man weave and wash his own garment, make his own shoes, his own oil-flask and scraper <note>original: strigilem</note>, his own oil vessels and ointments, and all his furniture; that he should never touch another's things, but always perform and complete his own?" "By no means," he said. "And yet, if a city is temperately disposed, it is well-ordered," I said. "Why not?" he said. "Therefore, temperance will not be doing such things, or doing 'one's own' in this manner?" "It appears not," he said. "Therefore, he was speaking in riddles," I said, "as I mentioned above, the one who declared that temperance is 'doing one's own business.' For he must not be thought to have been so foolish that his meaning was the same as the sound of the words."
<margin>C</margin> "Did some fool, O Charmides, hand this down to you?" "By no means," he said, "on the contrary, it was someone most wise in my judgment." "Then he altogether wrapped his opinion in obscure words," I said, "so that it is difficult to know what 'doing one's own' is." "Perhaps," he said. "Can you open for us what 'doing one's own' is?" I asked. "I truly do not know," he said. "Perhaps even the one who said these things did not sufficiently understand what he meant." While he was speaking thus, Charmides smiled and looked at Critias. Critias, although previously instigated by a desire for glory to argue against Charmides and others, had held himself back until now, but he could no longer contain himself. It seemed to me that what I had suspected was true: that Charmides had received that superior opinion about temperance from Critias.
<margin>D</margin> Therefore, Charmides, not wishing the answer to be disturbed and desiring to throw this labor back onto Critias, showed him as if he had been refuted. Critias by no means tolerated this; rather, he seemed to be no less indignant toward him than a poet toward an actor ineptly reciting his poems. And so, looking at him: "Do you think," he said, "O Charmides, that if you by no means understand what the sense was of the one who asserted that temperance is 'doing one's own,' that he himself did not understand it either?" "O best of men, Critias," I said, "it is no wonder that this young boy does not understand. But it is fitting for you to know these things, both because of your age and your study. If, therefore, you yourself also affirm that temperance is what he said, and you take up this discourse, I will more gladly investigate with you whether it is true or not." "I affirm it," he said, "and I take it up." "You do rightly," I said. "But tell me, I pray: Do you admit what I was asking a little while ago—that all craftsmen 'make' <note>original: facere</note> something?" "I do," he said. "Does it seem to you," I asked, "that they make only their own things, or others as well?" "Others as well," he said. "Do they act temperately, then, who do not make only their own things?" I asked. "What prevents it?" he said.
<margin>E</margin> "As far as I am concerned," I said, "nothing. But see if anything prevents it for him who, having supposed temperance to be 'doing one's own business' <note>original: agere fua</note>, then says there is no obstacle to those who do the business of others being temperate." "I conceded indeed," he said, "that those who do the business of others are temperate; but was it conceded that those who 'make' <note>original: faciunt</note> them are?" "Tell me," I said, "Critias, do you not call 'doing' <note>original: agere</note> and 'making' <note>original: facere</note> the same thing?" "Certainly not," he said, "nor the same as 'working' <note>original: operari</note>. For I learned that from Hesiod, who says, 'No work is a disgrace.' <margin>In the work *Works and Days* <note>original: ἔργα καὶ ἡμέραι</note>.</margin> Do you think that if he had called such works 'working' and 'doing' as you were describing above, he would have said no work is a disgrace to anyone—whether to a leather-cutter, or a tavern-keeper selling condiments and meat, or one sitting in a shop?" "It is not to be thought so, O Socrates."
<margin>F</margin> "Rather he, in my judgment, considered 'making' <note>original: effectionem</note> as something other than 'action' <note>original: actionem</note> and 'operation' <note>original: operationem</note>; and 'making' is sometimes a reproach when we do something apart from what is honorable, but 'work' is never a disgrace to us. For those things which are done honorably and usefully he called 'works,' and such 'makings' he called 'workings' and 'actions.' It should be thought, moreover, that he considered only these to be 'one's own,' and all harmful things to be altogether 'others'. Therefore, it is right to believe that Hesiod, and every other man of sound mind, calls the man 'temperate' who thus does his own business."
<margin>G</margin> "As soon as you began to speak, O Critias," I said, "I perceived that you call 'one's own' and 'proper' things good, and you name the 'makings' of good things 'actions.' For I have very often heard Prodicus distinguish names in this manner. I grant you indeed to use names at your pleasure, provided you declare what you wish to signify by each name. Now, therefore, define it more clearly again from the beginning: whether you say the action of good things, or the making, or however else you wish to name it, is temperance." "This very thing," he said. "He does not therefore act temperately," I said, "who does evil, but rather he who does good." "To you..."

<summary>In this passage, Socrates challenges the definition of temperance as "doing one's own business," leading Critias to intervene and refine the definition using a Sophistic distinction between "making" and "doing." Critias argues that temperance is specifically the "doing" of good and useful things.</summary>

# OF PLATO

<margin>A</margin> "O good man," he said, "does it not seem so? Let that go for the present," I said. "Let us consider not what seems to me, but what you yourself are now saying." "Indeed," he replied, "I would never say that he who does not do good things, but rather evil things, acts temperately. For I clearly define temperance <note>original: "σωφροσύνη" (sophrosyne)</note> as the performance of good deeds." "Perhaps," I replied, "nothing prevents you from speaking the truth; however, I wonder if you think that men acting temperately are ignorant of the fact that they are acting temperately." "I do not think so at all," he said. "Was it not said by you a little while ago," I asked, "that nothing prevents craftsmen <margin>B</margin> from living temperately even while they are doing the work of others?" "It was indeed said," you say, "but what follows from that?" "Nothing else," I said. "But tell me whether any doctor seems to you, while he makes someone healthy, to perform what is useful for himself and for the one he cures?" "He does to me," he said. "Does he not do what is fitting," I asked, "whoever does these things?" "Certainly," he said. "And he who does what is fitting, does he not also act temperately?" "He acts temperately," he said. "Is it necessary for the doctor to understand when he cures usefully and when he does not? And for every craftsman to know when the work he performs will be of benefit to him, and when it will not?" "Perhaps not," he said. "Sometimes, therefore," I said, "when a doctor has worked usefully or the opposite, he does not know himself how he has worked, even if he worked usefully, <margin>C</margin> as you yourself were admitting; and did you not say he acted temperately?" "I did," he said. "Is it not therefore," I said, "as it appears, that sometimes one who has worked usefully acts temperately and is temperate, but he himself is ignorant that he acts temperately and is being temperate?" "That," he said, "cannot happen, O Socrates. <margin>D</margin> Indeed, if anything was said in the previous discussion from which this necessarily follows, I would rather retract it; nor would I be ashamed to admit that I said something incorrectly, rather than agree that one who is ignorant of himself could be temperate. For I almost think that this very thing is temperance: to know oneself <note>original: "seipsum cognoscere" / "Γνῶθι σαυτὸν"</note>. And I agree with him who inscribed this precept on the temple of Apollo himself. For this inscription seems to be a kind of salutation from the God to the men who enter the temple, in place of the usual 'rejoice' <note>original: "gaudere" / "χαῖρε"; the standard Greek greeting</note>; as if it were not quite right to say 'rejoice,' nor should people command this of one another, but rather to live temperately. Thus the God addresses those entering the temple with a singular sentiment, and greets us differently than men do—as he intended, in my judgment, who set up the inscription. And to the one entering, he commands nothing else than to live temperately. But he interposes this precept in words more obscurely, like a prophet. For 'Know thyself' is the same as 'Live temperately,' as the letters testify and I interpret. But perhaps someone will think it is something else, which I believe happened to those who <margin>E</margin> added the subsequent sayings: 'Nothing in excess' <note>original: "Nihil nimis" / "Μηδὲν ἄγαν"</note> and 'Certainty brings ruin' <note>original: "Sponsionis comitem esse miseriam" / "Ἐγγύα, πάρα δ᾽ ἄτα" (literally: a pledge, then destruction)</note>. For they thought 'Know thyself' was a piece of advice, not the God’s own admonition to those entering. Then, so that they might hang up no less worthy advice, they added the rest. Therefore, Socrates, all these things are said by me because I will concede all the previous points to you without controversy. For perhaps you said something more correctly about them, or perhaps I did; yet nothing of what we said was clear. Now, however, I wish to give you an account of this, if you will not concede that temperance is to know oneself." "You deal with me," I said, "O Critias, as if I claimed to know the things I am asking; and you offer yourself to me, saying you will concede if I wish; but it is not so. For I seek with you always <margin>F</margin> concerning that which has been brought forward, precisely because I do not know it. I will see further whether I concede or not. Just wait while I consider these things." "Consider them," he said. "Behold, I am considering," I said. "If temperance is to know something, it is established that it must be some science <note>original: "scientia" / "ἐπιστήμη" (systematic knowledge or craft)</note> and a science of something. Is it not?" "It is indeed," he said, "of itself, evidently." "Is not medicine also the science of health?" "Entirely," he said. "If therefore you were asked: since medicine is the science of health, what does it confer upon us? Or what does it produce? I would respond that it benefits us greatly, for health is a beautiful work it performs for us. Do you accept this?" "I accept it," he said. "And if you asked again, <margin>G</margin> since architecture is the science of building, what work does it produce? I would answer 'houses,' and I would give an answer by the same reasoning for the other arts. Since you say temperance is the science of itself, it is your turn to answer if someone should ask in this manner: 'O Critias, since temperance is the science of itself, what beautiful work does it produce for us, worthy of the name?' Tell us, please." "You do not ask correctly, Socrates," he said. "For this science is not like the others, nor are the others like each other; yet you ask as if they were similar. For tell me, I pray: what work of the science of arithmetic <note>original: "computatricis" / "λογιστικῆς"</note> or geometry is such as a house is to architecture, or a cloak to the art of weaving, and many other such works which one could attribute to many arts? Can you show me any such work of these? You cannot." "You speak the truth," I said, "yet I can show this: what each of these sciences is the science *of*, which is something other than the science itself. Just as the skill of calculation is the science of the even and odd plurality, and how they relate to themselves and to each other, is it not?" "Certainly," he said. "Is not the even and odd something other than the science of calculation itself?" "It is," he said. "Furthermore—"

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> "Does it seem so to you? 'Wait,' I said, 'O good man, for let us not yet look at what seems to me, but at what you are saying now.' 'But truly,' he said, 'I do not say that he who does not do good things but evil acts temperately; but he who does good and not evil. For I clearly define for you that the practice of good things is temperance.' 'And perhaps nothing hinders you from speaking the truth. But this I wonder at,' I said, 'whether you think that men acting temperately are ignorant that they are being temperate.' 'I do not think so,' he said. 'Was it not said by you a little while ago,' I said, 'that nothing hinders craftsmen from being temperate even while they are doing the work of others?' 'It was said,' he replied, 'but what of it?' 'Nothing, but tell me if <margin>B</margin> a doctor seems to you, when he makes someone healthy, to do things useful both for himself and for the one he was healing.' 'To me he does.' 'Does he not do what is necessary, he who does these things?' 'Yes.' 'Does he who does what is necessary not act temperately?' 'He certainly acts temperately.' 'Is it then necessary for the doctor to know when he heals usefully and when not? And for each craftsman, when benefit is going to come from the work he does, and when not?' 'Perhaps not.' 'Sometimes then,' I said, 'having acted usefully or harmfully, the doctor does not know himself how he acted; yet having acted usefully (according to your argument), he acted temperately. Or did you not say so?' 'I did.' 'Does it not seem then,' <margin>C</margin> 'that sometimes having acted usefully, he acts temperately and is temperate, but is ignorant of himself that he is temperate?' 'But this, Socrates,' he said, 'could never happen. Rather, if you think anything I previously agreed to necessarily leads to this, I would rather retract some of those things, and I would not be ashamed to say I did not speak correctly, rather than ever concede that a man ignorant of himself could be temperate. For I say that this very thing is temperance: to know oneself. And I agree with the one who dedicated such an inscription at Delphi. For this inscription seems to me to be set up <margin>D</margin> as a greeting of the God to those entering, instead of "hail." As if this greeting "to rejoice" <note>original: "χαίρειν" (chairein)</note> were not correct, nor should people encourage this in one another, but rather to be temperate. In this way the God addresses those entering the temple. Differently than men do—such was the intention of the one who dedicated it, as it seems to me. And he says to the one who enters: "be temperate." But he says it somewhat enigmatically, like a prophet. For "Know thyself" and "Be temperate" are the same, as the letters say, and I do. But perhaps someone might think it is something else. Which is what I think happened to those who later dedicated the inscriptions "Nothing in excess" and "A pledge, then ruin." For these people thought "Know thyself" was a piece of advice, <margin>E</margin> but not the God's greeting. Therefore, so they might dedicate no less useful advice, they inscribed these. The reason I say all this, Socrates, is this: I give up all the previous points to you. For perhaps you said something more correctly about them, or perhaps I did; but nothing was at all clear in what we were saying. Now I am willing to give you an account of this, if you do not agree that temperance is to know oneself.' 'But,' I said, 'O Critias, you approach me as if I claimed to know about the things I ask, and as if I will agree with you if I wish. But it is not so; for I search with you always into what is proposed because I do not know it myself. Having considered it, then, I am willing to say whether I agree or not. But wait until I have considered it.' 'Consider then,' he said. 'And indeed,' I said, 'I am considering. If to know <margin>F</margin> something is temperance, it is clear that it would be some science, and of something. Or not?' 'It is,' he said, 'of oneself.' 'Is not medicine,' I said, 'the science of the healthy?' 'Certainly.' 'If then,' I said, 'you were to ask me: "since medicine is the science of the healthy, what is it useful for, and what does it produce?" I would say it is of no small benefit. For it produces health for us, a beautiful work, if you agree.' 'I agree.' 'And if you then asked me about architecture, which is the science of building, what work I say it produces, I would say "dwellings." And likewise for the other arts. It is necessary then for you also, on behalf of temperance, since you say it is the science of oneself, to be able to say when asked: "O Critias, what beautiful work does temperance, being the science of oneself, produce for us, that is worthy of the name?" Come then, speak.' 'But Socrates,' <margin>G</margin> he said, 'you do not search correctly. For this is not naturally similar to the other sciences, nor are the others to each other. But you make your inquiries as if they were similar. Since tell me,' he said, 'what is such a work of the art of calculation or geometry as a house is of architecture, or a garment of weaving, or other such works which one could show from many arts? Do you then have some such work of these to show me? You will not.' And I said: 'You speak the truth. But I have this to show you: what each of these sciences is the science of, which happens to be something other than the science itself. For example, the art of calculation is, I suppose, of the even and the odd plurality, and how they relate to themselves and to one another. Is it not?' 'Certainly,' he said. 'Is not the odd and even something other than the art of calculation itself?' 'How could it not be?' 'And yet—'"

<summary>Critias defines temperance as self-knowledge, linking it to the famous Delphic maxim "Know Thyself." Socrates challenges this by asking what specific "product" or "subject matter" self-knowledge possesses, comparing it to crafts like medicine or arithmetic.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from Plato’s *Charmides*. Socrates and Critias have just moved from discussing temperance as "doing one's own business" to a more abstract definition. Critias is now asserting that temperance is a unique form of knowledge that is self-referential—knowledge of knowledge itself.</meta>

### LACHES <note>Although the header reads "Laches," this text is actually from Plato's *Charmides* (166b–168c). This is a common error in early printed editions or mislabeled manuscripts.</note>

<margin>A</margin> ...itself, of the heavier and the lighter. But would not the art of weighing be something else? And the heavy and the light are the subjects of the art of weighing itself, I suppose.
Tell me then, what kind of knowledge is temperance <note>original: "σωφροσύνη" (sophrosyne)</note>, which results in something different from temperance itself?
"This is exactly the point," he said, "O Socrates: you have come in your search to the very thing by which temperance differs from all other forms of knowledge. You are seeking some similarity between it and the others. But it is not so. For while all the others are knowledges of something else, and not of themselves, this one alone is both a knowledge of the other knowledges and of itself. And this is far from being hidden from you. But I think you are doing exactly what you just said you were not doing: you are trying to refute me, leaving aside the matter under discussion."
"What a thing you are doing," I said, "supposing that if I refute you, I do it for any other reason than that for which I would examine myself—fearing that I might accidentally think I know something when I do not. And so now I say I am doing this: I am examining the argument, mainly for my own sake, but perhaps also for the sake of my other friends. Or do you not think it is a common good for almost all men that the nature of each existing thing should become clear?" "I certainly do," he said, "O Socrates."
<margin>B</margin> "Be of good courage then, my friend," I said, "and answer the question as it appears to you, and never mind whether it is Critias or Socrates who is being refuted. Pay attention only to the argument itself, and see what the result of the examination will be." "I will do so," he said, "for you seem to speak reasonably." "Tell me then," I said, "what you say about temperance." "I say then," he said, "that alone of all other knowledges, it is the knowledge of itself and of the other knowledges." "Would it not also then be the knowledge of ignorance," I asked, "if it is indeed the knowledge of knowledge?" "Certainly," he said.
<margin>C</margin> "Therefore the temperate man alone will know himself, and will be able to examine what he happens to know and what he does not. He will also be able to inspect others in the same way, to see what a man knows and thinks he knows—if indeed he knows it—and again what a man thinks he knows but does not. No one else can do this. And this is what it is to be temperate, and this is temperance: self-knowledge, or knowing what one knows and what one does not know. Is this what you are saying?" "It is," he said. "Then once again," I said, "let us offer a third libation to the Savior <note>A Greek idiom for a third and final attempt, referencing the custom of offering the third cup of wine at a banquet to Zeus the Savior.</note> and consider this from the beginning."
<margin>D</margin> "First, whether this is possible or not: to know that one knows what one knows, and that one knows what one does not know. Secondly, if it is perfectly possible, what benefit would there be for us in knowing this?" "We must indeed consider this," he said. "Come then, Critias," I said, "see if you appear more resourceful in these matters than I. For I am at a loss. Shall I tell you why?" "Certainly," he said. "Does it not seem," I asked, "that all these things are—if what you just said is true—a single knowledge that is the knowledge of nothing other than itself and the other knowledges, and that this same knowledge is also the knowledge of ignorance?" "Certainly."
<margin>E</margin> "See how strange an argument we are attempting to make, my friend. For if you consider this same thing in other cases, it will seem to you, I think, to be impossible." "How so? In what cases?" "In these: consider if you think there is a kind of sight which is not the sight of those things that other sights see, but is a sight of itself and of other sights, and even of the lack of sight; and which, although it is sight, sees no color, but only itself and other sights. Does any such sight seem to exist to you?" "By Zeus, not to me." "And what about hearing? Does it hear no sound, but only itself and other hearings, and even the lack of hearing?" "Not that either." "In short, consider all the senses: does any sense seem to you to be a sense of senses and of itself, but to perceive none of the things that the other senses perceive?" "Not to me." "And does there seem to be a desire which is not a desire for any pleasure, but is a desire for itself and for other desires?" "Certainly not."
<margin>F</margin> "Nor indeed a will, I think, which wills no good, but wills itself and other wills." "I say not." "And would you say there is a kind of love which happens to be a love of nothing beautiful, but is a love of itself and of other loves?" "Not I," he said. "Have you ever noticed a fear which fears itself and other fears, but fears nothing dangerous?" "I have not noticed such a thing," he said. "And an opinion, which is an opinion of itself and of other opinions, but which opines nothing of the things that other opinions opine?" "Not at all."
<margin>G</margin> "But it seems we are saying there is a kind of knowledge which is the knowledge of no subject of study, but is a knowledge of itself and of other knowledges." "So we are saying." "Is it not strange, then, if it actually exists? Let us not yet insist that it does not exist, but let us consider if it exists in this way. Tell me: is this knowledge a knowledge of *something*? And does it have a certain power so as to be of something?" "Certainly." "For we also say that 'the greater' has such a power that it is greater than something?" "It does." "Therefore it must be greater than something smaller, if it is indeed greater?" "Necessarily." "If then we should find something 'greater' which is greater than other greater things and greater than itself, but is greater than none of the things that other things are greater than—surely it would follow that if it were greater than itself, it must also be smaller than itself? Or not?"
<margin>H</margin> "It is quite necessary," he said, "O Socrates." "Therefore if something is double itself and of other doubles, must it not also be half of itself? For surely...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> The faculty of weighing is the balancing of a heavier and lighter weight. But the weight itself, both heavy and light, is something other than the art of weighing itself. I agree, he said. Speak then: what is temperance <note>original: "temperantia"</note> primarily the knowledge of, which makes it something other than temperance itself? "This indeed," he said, "which you now ask, is that very thing; by which temperance differs from all other knowledges <note>original: "scientiis"</note>. You, however, demand some similarity of this to the others. But the matter stands otherwise. Truly, all others are knowledges of some other thing, not at all of themselves. This alone is the knowledge of both other knowledges and of itself. You are far from being ignorant of these things: but I think you are doing what you a little while ago denied doing: for you are attempting to refute me, and you disregard that which is being discussed.
<margin>B</margin> "What are you doing?" I said. "Do you think that if I refute you, I do it for the sake of anything else than that for which I would examine myself—fearing lest I think I know what I do not know, and my ignorance should deceive me? And now indeed I assert that I am doing this most of all: weighing and examining the argument for my own sake first, and perhaps also for the sake of my close friends. Do you not think it is a common good for everyone that the condition of every matter should become known to all?" "Most certainly, O Socrates." "Boldly then, O blessed man," I said, "responding to the questions as your opinion leads you, do not care whether it is Critias or Socrates who is being refuted, but pay attention to the discourse itself, to see where it leads when examined." "I will do so," he said.
<margin>C</margin> "Regarding what you say about temperance," I said, "come, repeat it." "I say indeed," he said, "that of all other knowledges, this alone is the knowledge of both itself and the remaining knowledges." "Is it not also the knowledge of ignorance?" I asked. "If it is indeed the knowledge of knowledge." "Entirely so." "Therefore only the temperate man," I said, "will know himself, and will be able to examine what he knows and what he is ignorant of: he will be able to judge, moreover, among other men, what each one knows and thinks he knows (if indeed he knows it), and what each one is ignorant of while he thinks he knows it; but no one else will be able to do this. And this is what it is to be temperate, and this is temperance: to know oneself—that is, to understand what one knows and what one does not know. Are these the things you say?" "They are," he said.
<margin>D</margin> "Thirdly then," I said, "as they say, for the Savior, let us consider it as if from the beginning. First, whether this can be done or not: that what someone knows and what someone does not know, he can likewise know and recognize that he does not know. Then, if that can be done, what future utility will there be for those who understand it?" "It must be asked," he said. "Observe, Critias," I said, "whether you have anything certain in these matters: for I have nothing, and in what matter I doubt, if you wish, I will reveal it." "Indeed I wish it," he said. "These things follow," I said, "if what you yourself just said shall stand: Namely, that there is one certain knowledge which is the knowledge of nothing else than itself and of other knowledges: and that the same is again the knowledge of ignorance." "Precisely," he said.
<margin>E</margin> "See then, my friend," I said, "how absurd this our discourse becomes. Truly, if you consider this same thing in certain others, as I think, it will seem impossible to you." "By what reasoning?" he asked, "and where?" "Right here," I said. "Think whether it seems to you that there is any sight which is not the sight of those things of which other sights are, but is a vision of itself and of other visions, and likewise of non-vision; and that it sees no color at all, though it is a vision, but only looks into itself and other visions. Does any such vision seem to you to exist?" "None," he said. "Do you trust," I said, "that any power of hearing can be found which hears no voice, but perceives itself and other hearings, and non-hearings?" "That also is impossible," he said.
<margin>F</margin> "In short, scrutinize all the senses, and consider whether any sense can be found which perceives itself and the other senses, yet perceives none of those things which the other senses perceive." "I judge this also impossible," he said. "Or perhaps is there some desire <note>original: "cupiditatem"</note> of the senses, which affects no pleasure, but is a desire for itself and the remaining lusts?" "By no means," he said. "Nor a will <note>original: "voluntatem"</note>, I think," I said, "which desires no good, but seeks itself and other wills." "Not at all," he said. "Or would you even say that there is someone such that there is no love for anything beautiful, but rather his passion is for himself and other loves?" "I would not." "Have you ever devised any fear which is terrified of itself and other fears, but dreads nothing terrible or dangerous?" "Never at all," he said.
<margin>G</margin> "Furthermore, an opinion of such a kind that it is an opinion of other opinions and of itself, but opines nothing of those things which other opinions suspect?" "In no way." "Nevertheless, we have spoken of a certain knowledge of the kind we described, which is the knowledge of no dogma, but is a knowledge of itself and of other knowledges." "We have certainly said so," he said. "Is it not a certain wonder, if it exists? For let us not yet contend that it does not exist, but let us consider whether it is so." "You speak cleverly," he said. "Tell me now, is this knowledge the knowledge of *something*? And does it have a certain power of such a kind by which it is of something?" "Precisely," he said. "And do we not say it has a power by which it is greater than something?"
<margin>H</margin> "It is necessary," he said. "If we find something 'greater' which existed as greater than other greater things and itself, but yet was not greater than any of those things which others are greater than, would it not entirely follow that just as it is greater than itself, it is also smaller?" "It is entirely necessary, O Socrates." "Moreover, if anything is double," I said, "to other doubles and to itself, surely in being double to itself it will be half, and double to other halves?"

<summary>Socrates and Critias debate the possibility of "knowledge of knowledge" (temperance). Socrates challenges this definition by using analogies of the senses—such as a sight that sees only sight but no color—to argue that a faculty cannot be entirely self-referential without an external object.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from Plato’s Charmides. Socrates and Critias are examining whether "temperance" (sophrosyne) can be defined as "knowledge of knowledge." Socrates is using analogies of physical senses and mathematical relations to question if a power can be applied to itself.</meta>

Indeed, whatever is double is nothing other than the double of its half. "That is true," he said. Furthermore, that which is more than itself, is it not also less? And that which is heavier, is it also lighter? And that which is older, is it also younger? And in all other cases in the same way, whatever has its own power directed toward itself, will it not also possess that essence toward which its power is directed? I mean something like this: do we say that hearing is the hearing of anything other than a voice? "Certainly," he said. "If it hears itself," I said, "will it not hear itself having a voice? For otherwise it could not hear." "It follows necessarily," he said.

<margin>B</margin>
"And sight also, my best of men," I said, "if it sees itself, it will be necessary for it to have some color. For sight can perceive nothing without color." "It can perceive nothing," he said. "Do you see, Critias, that these things we have recounted appear to us partly as entirely impossible, and partly as highly doubtful whether they have their power directed toward themselves? For that magnitude and multitude and other things of this kind should have their power directed toward themselves is utterly impossible, is it not?" "That is absolutely so," he said. "But that sight and hearing," I said, "should perceive themselves, or that motion should move itself, or that heat should heat itself, and other such things, is not believed by some, though perhaps it seems believable to others. There is need of some great man, my friend, who can sufficiently distinguish in all these cases whether nothing at all has the power to act upon itself 

<margin>C</margin>
except knowledge, but only upon something else; or whether some things can and others cannot; and if there are some things which have power toward themselves, whether this knowledge which we call temperance <note>original: "temperantia" / "σωφροσύνη" (sophrosyne) — a complex Greek virtue involving moderation, self-control, and self-knowledge.</note> is among their number. For my part, I do not trust myself to be capable of discerning these things. Therefore, I cannot assert whether it is possible for there to be a 'knowledge of knowledge.' And even if this were granted, I would not yet agree that temperance is of this kind until I have investigated whether such a temperance would be of any benefit to us or not. For I prophesy that temperance is something useful and good. You then, son of Callaeschrus, since you define temperance as the knowledge of knowledge and of ignorance, show first that this which I was just saying is possible: 

<margin>D</margin>
next, besides being possible, that it is also beneficial. Thus perhaps you will satisfy me concerning the definition of temperance itself." When Critias heard this and saw me doubting, he seemed to be affected like those who, seeing others yawn, are themselves compelled to yawn; he appeared to be caught in a similar state of hesitation because I was hesitating. But as he was a man of high reputation, he was ashamed before those present, and he did not want to admit to me that he was unable to distinguish the points I had proposed, nor did he say anything clearly, but tried to hide his confusion. Then I, so that our discussion might proceed, said: "If it seems good to you, Critias, let us grant for now that there can be a 'knowledge of knowledge.' Whether it is possible or not, we will investigate at another time. But even if 

<margin>E</margin>
this were most possible, how does it make one more capable of knowing what one knows and what one does not know? For we said this was what it meant to know oneself and to be temperate. Is it not so?" "Most certainly," he said, "and it follows in a way, Socrates. For if someone has that knowledge which knows itself, he himself becomes such as that which he possesses: just as when one has speed, he is speedy; and when he has beauty, he is beautiful; and when he has cognition, he is a cognizer. Therefore, when someone possesses cognition itself of itself, he then becomes one who knows himself." "I do not doubt," I said, "that if someone possesses in himself something that knows itself, he would also know himself. But what necessity compels a man so affected to know what he knows and what he does not know?"

<margin>F</margin>
"Because," he said, "this and that are the same thing." "Perhaps so," I said, "but I seem to remain as I was, for I do not understand how knowing what one knows is the same as knowing what one does not know." "How can you say that?" he asked. "In this way," I replied. "If there is a knowledge of knowledge, will it be able to distinguish anything more than that, of these things, one is knowledge and the other is not knowledge?" "Nothing more, only that," he said. "Is it then the same to have knowledge and ignorance of health, as it is to have knowledge and ignorance of justice?" "By no means," he said. "For the one, I believe, is medicine, and the other is political skill; but this other is nothing but knowledge." "Of course," he said. "Unless 

<margin>G</margin>
someone knows health and justice in addition, but knows only knowledge, as one having the knowledge of this alone, he will recognize that he knows something, and that he has a certain knowledge, both in himself and in others. Is it not so?" "Yes." "But how will he understand by this knowledge *what* it is he knows? For medicine knows the healthy and the wholesome, not temperance; music knows harmony, not temperance; architecture knows buildings, not temperance; and so for all things, is it not so?" "It appears so," he said. "But if temperance is only the knowledge of knowledges, how will it understand what the healthy or the wholesome knows, or what the builder knows?" "In no way," he said. "Therefore, he who is ignorant of these things will not understand what he knows, but only *that* he knows something." "It seems so," he said. "Therefore, 

<margin>H</margin>
to be temperate will not be this, nor will temperance be the understanding of what one knows or what one does not know, but, as it seems, only that one knows and that one does not know." "It appears so," he said. "Nor will such a man be able to examine another who professes to know something, to see whether he knows what he claims to know or does not know it. Rather, as it seems," I said, "he will only recognize that the man has a certain knowledge; but of what thing it is a knowledge, temperance will not show him." "It does not seem so," he said. "Therefore, he will not be able to distinguish a physician who is a pretender <note>original: "simulantem" — one who fakes or imitates a profession.</note> from a true one, nor any other of those who possess knowledge from those who do not."

<margin>A</margin>
...of nothing else than its half. "True." And that which is more than itself will also be less, and being heavier, it will be lighter; and being older, it will be younger; and all other things in the same way, that whatever has its own power directed toward itself, will it not also have that essence toward which its power was directed? I mean this sort of thing: for example, hearing, we say, was the hearing of nothing else but a voice. Was it not? "Yes." Therefore, if it hears itself, it will hear itself having a voice; for it could not hear otherwise. "A great necessity." And sight too, my excellent man, if it sees itself, it must have some color. For no one would ever see a sight that had no color. "Certainly not." Do you see then, Critias,

<margin>B</margin>
that in all these things we have gone through, some appear to us entirely impossible, and others strongly provide a reason for disbelief that they have their own power toward themselves? For magnitudes and multitudes and such things are entirely impossible. Are they not? "Certainly." But hearing and sight, and even motion moving itself, and heat burning, and all such things, might provide disbelief to some, but perhaps not to others. There is need of a great man, my friend, who will sufficiently distinguish in all cases whether none of the things that exist has its own power toward itself by nature, but rather toward another, or some do and some do not; and if there are some that have it toward themselves, whether

<margin>C</margin>
knowledge is among these, which we say is temperance <note>original: "σωφροσύνην" (sophrosyne)</note>? I do not trust myself to be capable of distinguishing these things; therefore I cannot assert whether this is possible, for there to be a knowledge of knowledge, nor if it is most certainly so, do I accept it as being temperance until I have examined whether it would benefit us at all, being of such a kind, or not. For I judge temperance to be something beneficial and good. You then, son of Callaeschrus (since you propose that temperance is this, the knowledge of knowledge and also of ignorance), first show this, that what I was just saying is possible; then, in addition to being possible, that it is also beneficial.

<margin>D</margin>
And you might satisfy me that you are speaking correctly about what temperance is. And Critias, having heard these things and seeing me in difficulty—just as those who see people yawning opposite them suffer the same thing—he too seemed to be compelled by my being in difficulty to be caught by difficulty himself. Since he was always well-reputed, he was ashamed before those present; and he did not want to concede to me that he was unable to distinguish the things I challenged him with, but said nothing clear, covering up his difficulty. And I, so that the argument might proceed, said, "Well, if it seems so, Critias, let us now concede this, that it is possible for there to be a knowledge of knowledge; and later we will examine whether it is so or not. Come then, if this is most possible, why is it any more

<margin>E</margin>
possible to know what one knows and what one does not know? For we said this surely was to know oneself and to be temperate. Is it not?" "Certainly," he said, "and it follows, Socrates. For if someone has a knowledge which knows itself, he himself would be such as that which he possesses. Just as when someone has speed, he is speedy; and when beauty, beautiful; and when knowledge, knowing. And when someone has the knowledge of itself, he will then be one who knows himself." "I do not dispute this," I said, "that when one has that which knows itself, he will know himself; but having this, what necessity is there for him to know what he knows and what he does not know?" "Because, Socrates, this is the same as that." "Perhaps," I said, "but I am always likely to be the same. For I do not understand how it is the same thing to know what one knows and to know what one does not know."

<margin>F</margin>
"How do you mean?" he said. "In this way," I replied. "A knowledge being the knowledge of knowledge, will it be able to distinguish anything more than that of these things, this is knowledge and that is not knowledge?" "No; only that much." "Is it then the same, the knowledge and the ignorance of the healthy, and the knowledge and the ignorance of the just?" "By no means." "But the one, I think, is medicine, and the other is politics; but the other is nothing else than knowledge." "How could it not be?" "Therefore, if one does not also know the healthy and the just, but recognizes only knowledge, since he has only the knowledge that he knows these things and that he has a certain knowledge, he would likely recognize this about himself and others. Is it not so?" "Yes."

<margin>G</margin>
"But how will he know *that* he knows by this knowledge? For he knows the healthy by medicine, but not by temperance; and the harmonious by music, but not by temperance; and the building-art by architecture, but not by temperance; and so all things. Is it not so?" "It appears so." "And if temperance is only the knowledge of knowledges, how will he know that he knows the healthy or that he knows building?" "In no way." "Then the one who is ignorant of this will not know it, but only that he knows something." "It seems so." "Therefore, to be temperate would not be this, nor would temperance be knowing what one knows and what one does not know, but, as it seems, only that one knows and that one does not know."

<margin>H</margin>
"It is likely." "Neither then will this man be able to examine another who claims to know something, whether he knows what he says he knows or does not know it; but only this much, as it seems, will he know: that he has a certain knowledge. But of what it is, temperance will not make him know." "It does not appear so." "Neither then will he be able to distinguish the one who pretends to be a doctor, but is not, from the one who truly is, nor any other of the knowledgeable and the not."

<summary>In this passage from Plato's *Charmides*, Socrates questions whether temperance can be defined as "knowledge of knowledge." He argues that while one might know they possess "knowledge," this abstract self-awareness does not provide the specific expertise needed to distinguish a true professional, like a doctor, from a fraud.</summary>

<margin>A</margin>And let us not consider this: whether the temperate man, or anyone else for that matter, will truly distinguish the real doctor from the one who is not. Will he not proceed in this way? He will certainly not discuss the art of medicine with him. For, as we said, the doctor understands nothing but health and disease. Is that not so? "Yes, quite so." But as for <term>science</term><note>original: ἐπιστήμη (epistēmē) - a systematic branch of knowledge or craft</note>, he knew nothing of it; for we attributed this to temperance alone. "Yes." Therefore, the medical man does not even know about medicine, since medicine happens to be a science. "True." The temperate man will know that the doctor has *some* science; but to test what kind it is, the doctor must examine it. Is not each science defined not just as science, but as a specific kind by what it is about? Is not medicine therefore distinguished <margin>B</margin> from other sciences by being the science of the healthy and the diseased? "Yes." Is it not therefore necessary for anyone wishing to examine medicine to look at those things in which it exists? For surely it is not found in external things where it does not exist. "Certainly not." Therefore, one who examines the medical man as a medical man must look into matters of health and disease. "It seems so." Then, in what is said or done in these matters, he will examine whether what is said is true and what is done is done rightly? "Necessarily." But could anyone follow either of these without the art of medicine? "Certainly not." Nor could anyone else, as it seems, except a doctor—not even <margin>C</margin> the temperate man. For he would have to be a doctor in addition to being temperate. "That is so." Most of all, then, if temperance is only the science of science and of the lack of science, it will not be able to distinguish the skilled doctor from the unskilled one who pretends or thinks he is one; nor will it distinguish any other person who knows something from one who does not—except for a person of the same craft, just as with other artisans. "So it appears," he said.

"What then," I said, "O Critias, would be our benefit from temperance if it were like this? For if, as we assumed from the beginning, the temperate man knew what he knew and what he did not know—knowing the former and being aware of the latter—and was able to examine another person in the same state, we say it would be a great benefit to us to be <margin>D</margin> temperate. For we would live our lives without error, both ourselves and those who possess temperance, and all others ruled by us. For we would not ourselves attempt to do what we did not understand, but we would find those who did understand and hand the tasks over to them. Nor would we permit those under our rule to do anything except what they were likely to do rightly—which would be that for which they had knowledge. And thus, through temperance, a house would be well-managed, and a city well-governed, and everything else over which temperance ruled. For with error removed and rightness leading in every action, it is necessary for those so disposed to act honorably and well; and those who act well must be <margin>E</margin> happy. Did we not speak of temperance in this way, Critias," I said, "saying what a great good it would be to know what one knows and what one does not?" "Entirely so," he said. "But now," I said, "do you see that no such science has appeared anywhere?" "I see it," he said. 

"Does this temperance," I said, "which we now conceive to be the science of sciences and of the lack of science, have this good: that he who possesses it will learn whatever else he learns more easily, and everything will appear more clearly to him, since he sees the science itself in addition to each thing he learns? And will he examine others better regarding what he himself has learned, whereas those who examine without this will do so more weakly and poorly? Is it these sorts of things, my friend, that we will enjoy from temperance, while we are looking for something greater and seeking for it <margin>F</margin> to be something bigger than it is?" "Perhaps," he said, "it is so." "Perhaps," I said, "and perhaps we have sought for nothing useful at all. I suspect this because some strange things are appearing to me regarding temperance, if it is such a thing. For let us see, if you please, granting that it is possible for a science of science to exist, and let us not take away what we originally set down as the definition of temperance—knowing what one knows and does not know—but let us grant it. And having granted all this, let us look even more closely if it will actually benefit us as much as we said when we remarked what a great good temperance would be if it were like this, governing the management of a house or a city. For it seems to me, Critias, that we have not agreed rightly." "How so?" he asked. "Because," I said, "we easily agreed that it would be a <margin>G</margin> great good for humanity if each of us did what we knew, and turned over what we did not know to others who were experts." "Was that not a right agreement?" he asked. "It does not seem so to me," I said. "You speak truly strange things, Socrates," he said. "By the dog!"<note>original: νὴ τὸν κύνα (nē ton kyna) - a common Socratic oath</note> I said, "it seems so to me too. For looking back just now, I said that strange things were appearing to me and that I feared we were not looking at it correctly. For truly, if temperance is exactly like that, it is not even clear to me that it works any good for us." "How so?" he said, "Tell us, so we may know what you mean." "I think I am talking nonsense," I said, "yet it is necessary to examine what occurs to one, and not to pass it by in vain, if one cares even a little for himself." "You speak well," he said. "Listen then," I said, "to my dream,"

the one who knows from the one who does not. Let us consider it in this way: if a temperate man, or anyone else, is to judge between a true and a false doctor, will he not do it thus? He will not discuss the art of healing with him. For, as we were saying, a doctor understands nothing except what is healthy and what is sick, what is wholesome and what is harmful; is that not so? "Quite so," he said. "Furthermore, he knows nothing of science," I said, "for we attribute this to temperance alone." "So it is," he said. "Therefore, the doctor knows nothing of medicine either," I said, "inasmuch as medicine is a certain science." "You speak the truth," he said. "The temperate man will recognize that he [the doctor] has some science, but he will consider the doctor's skill as something else—namely, of what things and about what things it is. This becomes clear when it is known what things are the subject of that science. Is not every science defined not just by being a science, but by being a *specific* science? And is it not known what science it is by knowing those things which are the subject of that science?" "Exactly so," he said. "Medicine," I said, "is a science distinguished from other sciences by the fact that it is the skill of the healthy and the unhealthy?" "Certainly," he said. "Must not anyone who is going to consider medicine," I said, "examine it in those matters in which it is occupied? For it is not to be sought in extraneous things where it does not exist." "Certainly not," he said. "In healthy things and their opposites, therefore, he will consider the doctor insofar as he is a doctor, whoever investigates him rightly." "It seems so," he said. "Can anyone attain these things without skill in medicine?" "No one," he said. "Nor anyone else, as it seems, besides the doctor—and therefore not the temperate man. For he would have to be a doctor as well as temperate." "These things are true." "Altogether then, if temperance is the science of science or of ignorance, it will be able to discern neither the skilled doctor from the pretender who simulates medical skill or thinks he has it, nor anyone else among those who know something, except for a man who professes the same art, just as other artisans do." "So it appears." "What further benefit, O Critias, will come to us from temperance if it is such a thing? For if, as we supposed in the beginning, the temperate man knew what he knew and what he did not know—the former because he knows it, and the latter because he is ignorant of it—and could judge another man who was so affected, we would report a huge advantage for those endowed with temperance. For we would lead our lives without sin, both ourselves and whoever participated in temperance, and all others who were ruled by our authority. For we would not attempt things we were ignorant of, but having sought out knowledgeable men, we would yield to them. Nor would we allow others subject to our governance to do anything else except what they were likely to do rightly—that is, those things of which they had knowledge. And so through temperance, both the household would be rightly governed and the established city would be best ruled, and every other thing over which temperance itself presided. For with error removed and rectitude leading in every action, it is necessary for men so instructed to act honorably and well, and those acting well to be happy. "But now you see that no such science has appeared to us." "I see it indeed." "Does this temperance which we have now found—namely, being the science of knowing both science and ignorance—contain this good: that whoever is armed with it will learn whatever is to be learned more easily, and all things will offer themselves more clearly to him, since he sees the science itself regarding all things to be learned, and he will better examine others in these matters which he himself learns? Whereas those who examine without this will do it more weakly and ineptly. Are these the sorts of things, O friend, that temperance confers on us? Or are we imagining something greater and requiring it to be more than it is?" "Perhaps it is so," he said. "Perhaps," I said, "perhaps we have even hunted for something that confers nothing. I conjecture this because certain absurdities seem to follow concerning temperance if it is such a thing. Let us see then, if you please, granting that it is possible for it to be established that science is known; and let us not deprive temperance of what we set down in the beginning—namely, to know what someone knows or does not know—but let us rather grant it. And these things being granted, let us investigate even more diligently whether it helps us at present if it exists as such. For what we were saying just now—that temperance would be a huge good to us if it were such a thing, ruling over some administration, the house, and the city—we seem not to have granted correctly, O Critias." "Why so?" he asked. "Because we assert all too easily that it would be a huge good for men if each of us performed those things which they know, and left those things which they are ignorant of to certain others who know them."
