<meta>This page continues the dialogue in Plato's Charmides. Socrates is investigating whether "temperance" (sophrosyne), defined as "the science of science," actually benefits us, or if there is a more specific type of knowledge required for happiness.</meta>

# PLATONIS

<margin>A</margin> ...whether it has emerged through the gate of horn or the gate of ivory <note>A reference to Homer’s *Odyssey*; dreams passing through the gate of horn are true, while those through ivory are deceptive. Socrates is questioning the validity of their current argument.</note>. For if temperance, being such as we now define it, were to rule over us as much as possible, surely we would act according to the sciences. No one claiming to be a pilot when he is not would deceive us, nor would a doctor, nor a general, nor any other false professor of science escape our notice. With things arranged in this way, something else would follow for us: we would be physically healthier than we are now, and we would emerge safer from the dangers of the sea and war. Likewise, we would possess vessels, instruments, clothes, shoes, and all household goods manufactured more skillfully and conveniently, because we would be employing true craftsmen. If you also wish <term>vaticination</term><note>original: "vaticinationem" / "μαντικὴν" — the art of prophecy or divination</note> to be a science, let us grant that it is the knowledge of the future, and that temperance, presiding over it, would turn away vain pretenders and <margin>B</margin> choose true prophets for the prediction of things to come. I agree that the human race, thus established, would act and live skillfully. For temperance, acting as a guardian of human life, would never allow ignorance to creep in or permit it to use its own strength. However, my friend Critias, I cannot yet perceive that by acting according to science we would act *well* and be happy.

"You will not easily find another end for acting well and perfection," he said, "if you despise acting according to science."

"Explain a little more carefully," I said, "according to *which* science? Is it according to the science of shoemaking?"

"By Jove, no," he said.

"Is it perhaps the craft of the smith?"

"Not that either," he said.

"Is it according to the working of wool, or of wood, or something of that sort?"

"Not that," he said.

"It seems, then," I said, "that we should no longer stand by that speech <margin>C</margin> which asserted that he who lives according to science is happy. For you do not affirm that these people living according to science live happily; rather, you seem to define the happy man as one of those who lives scientifically regarding *certain* things. Perhaps you mean the one I mentioned just now: the prophet who knows all things to come. Is it this man, or another, you mean?"

"Both this man," he said, "and another."

"Whom?" I asked. <margin>D</margin> "Is it perhaps the man who knows not only the future, but also the past and the present, and is ignorant of nothing? Let us imagine someone of that kind. I think you would say no one else lives more scientifically than him."

"Certainly no one," he said.

"This too must be added: which of the sciences makes him most happy? Or do they all do so equally?"

"Not equally," he said.

"But which one especially? That by which he knows the present, past, and future? Is it the science of playing dice?"

"Why do you mention dice?" he said.

"Is it the science of calculation?"

"By no means."

"Is it the science of health?"

"That one more so," he said.

"But which is the one I mean most of all? The science of what?"

"The science of good and evil," he said.

"You rascal!" I said. "For a long time you have been leading me in a circle, hiding the fact that acting well <margin>E</margin> and being happy does not come from living scientifically or according to all other sciences, but according to this one single science of good and evil. Furthermore, Critias, if you chose to remove this science from the others, will medicine any less produce health? Will shoemaking any less provide shoes? Or weaving clothes? Will the art of the pilot any less avert the dangers of the sea, or the general any less avert the risks of war and save us?"

"Not at all," he said.

"But truly, my friend Critias," I said, "if this science of the good and the evil is taken away, none of these things will be done well or usefully."

"You speak the truth," he said.

"This, it seems, is not temperance, but the science whose work it is to benefit us. For temperance is not the science of sciences and ignorances, but the <margin>F</margin> knowledge of good and evil. Therefore, if temperance is useful to us, it must contribute to something else."

"But does this not also benefit us?" he asked. "For if temperance is the science of sciences and presides over the other sciences, it will also rule over this science of discerning good and evil, and thus it will benefit us."

"Does it provide good physical health," I asked, "rather than medicine? And will it perform the works of the other arts while the individual craftsmen cease their own work? Did we not long ago agree among ourselves that temperance is the science of science and ignorance, and not of any other faculty? Was it not so?"

"It certainly appears so," he said.

"Then it will not be the producer of health," I said.

"No," he said.

"For health is the work of another art."

"Certainly."

"Nor, then, is it the producer of utility, <margin>G</margin> my friend. For we attributed this work to another art just now, did we not?"

"Very much so."

"How then will temperance be useful to us, when it is the producer of no utility?"

"In no way, Socrates, does it seem to be."

"Do you see then, Critias, that I was right to fear earlier, and to blame myself, because I can perceive nothing great and useful concerning temperance? For never would that which is conceded by everyone to be the most beautiful of all things have appeared useless to us, if I were of any use myself in searching correctly. But now we are defeated on every side, and we are unable to find what on earth the author of names <note>A characteristic Platonic idea that names were originally given to things by a wise "legislator" or "name-giver" to reflect their true nature.</note> intended to signify by the name 'temperance.' And yet we have conceded many things that do not follow from our reasoning. For we conceded that there is a science of science, even though the argument did not allow it or say it was possible. <margin>H</margin> And further, we conceded that by this science one could know the works of the other sciences, even though the argument similarly opposed it—so that the temperate man might be such as to know what he knows, and to know again what he does not know. This we conceded quite magnificently and too freely, not noticing whether it was even possible..."

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...whether it has come through the horns or through the ivory. For if temperance, being such as we are now defining it, were to rule us as much as possible, what else would be done for us? No one, claiming to be a pilot when he is not, would deceive us; nor would a doctor, nor a general, nor anyone else pretending to know what he does not know, escape our notice. From these things being so, something else would happen to us: our bodies would be healthier, and those in danger at sea and in war would be saved; and our vessels, and our clothing, and all our footwear, and all our goods would be skillfully made for us <gloss>be]</gloss>, <gloss>and many other things, because we would use true craftsmen.</gloss> And if you wish, let us also grant that <term>prophecy</term><note>original: μαντικὴν (mantikēn)</note> is the <margin>B</margin> science of what is to be; and that temperance, presiding over it, would turn away the boasters and establish for us those who are truly prophets of the future. I follow you that the human race, thus prepared, would act and live scientifically. For temperance, acting as a guard, would not allow ignorance to fall in and become our helper <gloss>be]</gloss>. But that by acting scientifically we would act well and be happy—this, my dear Critias, we are not yet able to learn.

"But yet," I said, "you will not easily find any other end of acting well if you dishonor acting scientifically."

"Instruct me a little further," I said, <margin>C</margin> "concerning what you mean by 'scientifically.' Do you mean the science of cutting leather?"

"By Zeus, not I."

"But the working of bronze?"

"By no means."

"But of wool, or wood, or some <gloss>any</gloss> other such thing?"

"Certainly not."

"Then we no longer abide," I said, "by the speech that said he who lives scientifically is happy. For these who live scientifically are not admitted by you to be happy. But you seem to me to define the happy man as one who lives scientifically concerning certain things. And perhaps you mean the one I just mentioned: the one who knows everything that is to be, the prophet. Do you mean this man, or someone else?"

"Both him," he said, "and another."

"Whom?" I said. "Is it someone like this: if someone, in addition to the <margin>D</margin> future, also knew all things that have happened and things that now are, and was ignorant of nothing? "Certainly not."

"I still desire this: which of the sciences makes him happy? Or do they all do so equally?"

"By no means equally," he said.

"But which one most of all? Is it that by which he knows the things that are, and have been, and shall be? Is it the science of playing draughts?"

"What kind of draughts-playing?" he said.

"But is it the science of calculation?"

"By no means."

"But of health?"

"More so," he said.

"But that one which I mean most of all," I said, "is the science of what?"

"Of the good," he said, "and the evil."

"O you wretch!" I said. "You have been dragging me in a circle for a long time, hiding the fact that it is not living scientifically that makes us act well and be <margin>E</margin> happy, nor the sum of all other sciences, but this one alone, which is about the good and the evil. And since, Critias, if you wish to take this science out from the other sciences, will medicine any less produce health? Will shoemaking produce shoes? Or weaving produce clothes? Or the pilot's art prevent us from dying at sea, and the general's art in war?"

"None the less," he said.

"But, my dear Critias, for each of these things to be done well and usefully will have left us, if this science is absent."

"You speak the truth."

"But this, as it seems, is not temperance; but rather the science whose work it is to benefit us. For it is not the science of sciences and ignorances, but of the good and the evil. So if this temperance is useful, it must be something else."

"But why," he said, "would it not be useful? For if temperance is the science of sciences as much as possible, and it also presides over the other sciences, surely by ruling over this science <margin>F</margin> of the good, it would benefit us."

"Does it also make us healthy?" I said. "This, and not medicine? And would it perform the other things of the arts? And not the others, each doing its own work? Or did we not long ago disagree, that it is the science only of science and ignorance, and of nothing else? Is it not so?"

"So it appears."

"Then it will not be the producer of health."

"Certainly not."

"For health belonged to another art; did it not?"

"To another."

"Then it is not the producer of utility, my comrade. For we just now assigned this work to another art. Right?"

"Entirely so."

"How then will temperance be useful, being the producer of no utility?"

<margin>G</margin> "In no way, Socrates, does it seem so."

"Do you see then, Critias, how I was rightly afraid long ago, and justly blamed myself, that I was looking at nothing useful regarding temperance? For surely that which is agreed to be the most beautiful of all things would not have appeared useless to us, if I were of any use in searching well. But now we are defeated on every side, and we cannot find upon what existing thing the lawgiver placed this name, 'temperance.' And yet we have conceded many things in the argument that did not agree with us. For we conceded that science can be the science of science, though the argument did not allow it nor say it was possible. And again we conceded to this science that it could know the works of other sciences, though the argument did not allow this either, so <margin>H</margin> that the temperate man might be for us the one who knows what he knows, that he knows it, and what he does not know, that he does not know it. This we conceded altogether magnificently..."

<summary>Socrates and Critias conclude that "temperance," defined as the science of science, is useless for happiness unless it is combined with the specific science of good and evil. Socrates laments that they have failed to define temperance in a way that captures its presumed beauty and utility.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes Plato's dialogue "Charmides," which explores the nature of temperance (sophrosyne), and begins the dialogue "Laches," which investigates the nature of courage (andreia). The previous page ended with Socrates questioning if their definition of temperance as "the science of sciences" is actually useful for achieving happiness.</meta>

# LACHES.

<margin>A</margin> ...it would not be temperate at all to be in this state: to know, in a certain way, what one does not know at all. Yet we have agreed to this—namely, that a person who is ignorant of something can know that he does not know it—even though, in my opinion, nothing could appear more absurd than this. Nevertheless, this investigation has found us to be foolish rather than tough and persistent, and it is unable to find the truth. Instead, it has so thoroughly mocked itself that what we long ago agreed upon and established as being temperance has, in the end, insolently and quite insultingly appeared to be something entirely useless. 

For your sake, Charmides, rather than my own, I am deeply distressed if you, who are so excellent in both appearance and temperance of soul, are to gain nothing from such a great virtue, and if it is to be of no use to you in life. I am even more distressed on account of the incantation <note>original: "ἐπῳδῆς" / "incantationis" — Socrates previously claimed to have learned a medicinal charm for the soul from a Thracian physician.</note> which I learned from that Thracian, if I have applied so much zeal to learning something that is worth nothing. 

However, I do not quite believe this to be the case; rather, I think I am a poor investigator, since I consider temperance to be a great good. If you truly possess it, you are a blessed man. But consider whether you do possess it and have no need of the incantation. For if you have it, I would advise you to consider me a fool and incapable of seeking anything through reason, while you should consider yourself the more happy as you are the more temperate.

And Charmides said, "By Zeus, <margin>C</margin> Socrates, I do not know if I have it or not. For how could I know that which you two—as you say—are not yet able to discover? Indeed, I do not entirely believe you, Socrates. On the contrary, I think I do need the incantation, and as far as I am concerned, nothing prevents me from being treated by your incantations every day until you say I have had enough."

"Very well," said Critias, "but Charmides, if you do this, it will be proof to me that you are temperate: if you submit yourself to Socrates' incantations and never leave his side, whether in great matters or small."

"Expect me to follow and not fall behind," he said. "For I would be acting terribly if I did not obey you, my guardian, and do what you command."

"Indeed, I do command it," said Critias.

"Then I shall do so," he said, <margin>D</margin> "starting from this very day."

"What are you two planning to do?" I asked.

"Nothing else," said Charmides. "It is decided."

"Will you use force then," I said, "and not give me any choice in the matter?"

"Expect us to use force," he said, "since he commands it. Therefore, consider what you will do in response."

"There is no room for consideration," I said. "For when you are determined to do something and use force, no human being will be able to resist you."

"Then do not resist," he said.

"I will not resist then," I replied.

<margin>B</margin> <note>The Latin column (B-D) provides a parallel translation of the Greek text above. Socrates admits the failure of their logic but insists that temperance is a profound good, even if they cannot define it.</note>

# LACHES, OR, ON
# COURAGE.
->Obstetric.<- <note>original: "Μαιευτικός" / "Obstetricius" — Referring to the "Socratic Method" where Socrates acts as a midwife to help others give birth to their own ideas.</note>

**SUMMARY OF THE DIALOGUE.** *The dialogue deals with Courage, yet this is not its primary end. Plato’s purpose is to show that "civil men" (as he calls them)—against whom he struggled no less than against the Sophists—are ignorant of the true method of educating youth. They limit education to external and borrowed exercises, such as the handling of arms, horsemanship, and similar skills. However, they neglected virtue, which is the source and head of true education and to which all those skills ought to be referred. Plato represents the ill-considered concern of civil men for the education of their children through two old men, Lysimachus and Melesias. These men consult Laches and his friend Nicias (after whom the dialogue is named), who advise them to go to Socrates and rest in his counsel. That is, they suggest that a true knowledge of education <term>paideia</term><note>The holistic upbringing and moral education of a citizen.</note> must be drawn from the depths of philosophy—not randomly or indiscriminately, but from the mouths of prudent and sound teachers whose lives correspond to their words, rather than those who profess virtue with their lips but live basely and dissolutely.*

<column-break/>
*LYSIMACHUS, MELESIAS, NICIAS, LACHES, THE SONS OF NICIAS AND LACHES, SOCRATES.*

<margin>E</margin>
**Y**OU have seen the man fighting in armor, Nicias and Laches. But for what reason Melesias and I asked you to watch this with us, we did not say then, but we will say now. For we believe we ought to speak frankly with you. There are some who mock such things, and if someone consults them, they will not say what they truly think; instead, guessing at the mind of the one consulting them, they say things contrary to their own opinion. But we, believing you are both capable of judging and, once you have judged, will simply say what you think, have invited you to join us in deliberating on the matters we wish to communicate. 

The matter about which I have been making this long preamble is this: we have these sons here. This one is his son, named Thucydides after his grandfather; and this other is mine, also having his grandfather's name, for we call him Aristides. It has seemed best to us to care for them as much as possible, and not do what many people do—namely, once they become teenagers, to let them do whatever they want. Instead, we must now begin to care for them as much as we are able. Knowing that you also have sons, we thought that you, if anyone, must have considered how they might be cared for so as to become the best men. But if perhaps you have not often turned your...

**Y**OU have watched the man fighting in arms, Nicias and Laches. Why Melesias and I requested you to watch this together with us, we did not then declare. Now, however, we shall open the matter: for we think we must speak freely with you. There are some who laugh at these things; and if someone consults them, they do not express their own opinion, but thinking they understand the matter and the mind of the consultant, they bring forth things other than what they truly feel. But since we judge you to be sufficient both to understand and to simply explain what you know, we have summoned you as partners in the deliberation of those things we shall bring forward. The reason for my long beginning is this: these are our sons. This one is his son, called Thucydides by his grandfather's name; the other is mine, similarly keeping the grandfather's name: for we call him Aristides. It seems to us that the most diligent care must be taken of them, and we do not think we should do what many are accustomed to—who let their sons live according to their own lusts as soon as they have grown up—but rather, we must now begin to have a care for them, as much as we can. -># PLATO<-

<margin>A</margin> ...at the present moment we advise you that you should not neglect this, and we exhort you to deliberate with us concerning the education <note>original: "educatione" / "παιδείαν"</note> of our sons. As to why these things seem necessary to us, O Nicias and Laches, it is fitting that you hear, although the words that follow may be a little long. For Melesias here and I live together, and these young boys dine with us, taking part in our meals. Thus, as I indicated at the beginning of our talk, we speak to you freely and boldly. Truly, each of us can tell these boys many noble deeds performed by our own fathers both in peace and in war, by which they served either their own state or their allies; but we are unable to report any deeds performed by ourselves. Therefore, <margin>B</margin> we are ashamed before these boys, and we often blame our own fathers' negligence, because after we grew up, they permitted us to live in a certain softness and in luxury, while they were intent on the affairs of others. Showing these same things to these youths, we declare that if they neglect themselves and despise our precepts, they will become men of no reputation; but if they take care, they might perhaps turn out to be worthy of their ancestral names. They, for their part, respond that they will obey us. Now, as we were consulting with one another as to what discipline or habit they might best become the best of men, someone suggested that it is worthwhile for them to learn to fight in armor <note>original: "armis dimicare" / "έν όπλοις μάχεσθαι" — this refers to hoplite training, the heavy infantry style of Ancient Greece</note>, and he praised the man whom you just saw competing, and he urged us to turn our attention there. <margin>C</margin> Therefore, we thought it best that we should come to this spectacle, and that we should call you together both to watch it and also, if you are willing, to deliberate with a common purpose concerning the education of the young men. These are the matters we desired to discuss with you. It is now up to you to consult whether this thing ought to be learned or not, and to advise us if you have any other discipline or study worthy of praise for a young man; and then to declare what you will do regarding our request for counsel. NIC. I certainly approve of your intention, O Lysimachus and Melesias, and I am prepared to investigate this with you, and I believe Laches here is similarly inclined. LA. <margin>D</margin> You think rightly, O Nicias; for indeed, what Lysimachus was just reporting about his father and the father of Melesias seems most aptly said against those men and all who handle the affairs of the state. For, as Lysimachus complained, they neglect their sons as much as they do their other domestic matters. In these things, therefore, Lysimachus, you speak well; but I wonder that you call us to consult on the training of the youths yet do not invite Socrates here. First, he is a fellow-citizen; second, he is constantly occupied in the very places where you might find the kind of discipline or liberal study for the young that you require. LYS. What are you saying, Laches? Has Socrates here ever cared for such things? LA. Very much indeed, Lysimachus. <margin>E</margin> NIC. I too can be a witness to this fact no worse than Laches. For recently he brought a guest to me for the purpose of educating my son: Damon, a disciple of Agathocles, a teacher of music, a man more refined than others and skilled not only in music, but also in other faculties, so that he is certainly worthy for young men of this sort to be committed to his discipline and company. LYS. O Socrates, Nicias, and Laches, I and those of my age no longer know the younger men, as we mostly keep to our homes because of our age. But if you can give any good counsel to this fellow-citizen of yours, O son of Sophroniscus, then give it. For it is fitting: you are a friend to us through your father. For your father and I were always familiars and friends, and he departed from life before any quarrel <margin>F</margin> arose between us. To me, also, the name of Socrates still rings in my ears in a way, for these boys often use and celebrate it with great praise while arguing at home; I had not yet asked them whether they meant Socrates the son of Sophroniscus, or another. But, O boys, tell me: is this that Socrates whom you are so often accustomed to mention? BOY. That is undoubtedly him, father. LY. Well then, by Hera <note>original: "per Iunonem" / "νή την Η'ραν" — a common oath in Attic Greek, literally "by Hera"</note>, O Socrates, it is good that you uphold and honor your father, the best of men, and that our things shall be yours, and yours shall be ours. LA. Do not let this man go, Lysimachus; for I have observed him elsewhere as well, honoring not only his father but also his fatherland; for in the flight at Delium <note>original: "apud Delium" — referring to the Battle of Delium in 424 BCE, a significant Athenian defeat during the Peloponnesian War</note> <margin>G</margin> he retreated together with me, and I affirm this to you: that if the others had behaved in a similar manner, our city would be standing and would not have suffered such a great ruin. LY. This is the highest praise, O Socrates, which is now given to you by men worthy of trust, who are themselves to be praised in the very things for which they praise you. Know then that I rejoice in your reputation, and consider me bound to you with the greatest goodwill. It is necessary, therefore, that you first come to us and consider us as your household and friends, as is fitting. Therefore, from now on, since we have recognized one another, do not do otherwise; rather, embrace both us and these younger ones with a kind of domestic goodwill, so that mutual friendship may be preserved between us on both sides. This you will indeed do, and we shall again remind you of it hereafter. But concerning what we began to inquire: what do you say? Do you think it is beneficial for young men to have this discipline, to learn to fight in armor? SOCR. I will indeed try, O Lysimachus, if I can, to <margin>H</margin> give counsel on these matters, and to do all that you ask; but it seems most right to me that, since I am younger than these men and more inexperienced in these things myself, I should listen...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...bringing mind to such a thing <note>This continues the text from the preceding page</note>, reminding them that one must not neglect it, and calling upon you to make a joint inquiry with us concerning the sons. Why these things seemed good to us, O Nicias and Laches, you ought to hear, even if the account is a bit long. For Melesias here and I eat together, and the boys eat with us. Therefore, as I said at the start of the talk, we will speak with you with full freedom of speech. Each of us has many noble deeds to tell the boys about his own father, and how many things they performed in war, and how many in peace, managing both the affairs of the allies and those of the city; but neither of us has any deeds of our own to tell. <margin>B</margin> These things indeed make us feel ashamed before these boys, and we blame our fathers because they let us live in luxury when we became youths, while they attended to the affairs of others. And we point out these very things to these young men, saying that if they neglect themselves and do not obey us, they will become men of no fame; but if they take care, they might soon become worthy of the names they bear. These boys then say they will obey us. We ourselves are looking into what they might learn or practice to become the best possible men. Someone then introduced this subject to us: that it is a fine thing for a young man to learn to fight in armor; and he praised the one whom you watched performing. <margin>C</margin> It seemed then that we ought to come to see the man, and to take you along, both as fellow-spectators and as advisers and partners, if you wish, concerning the care of our sons. These are the things we wanted to communicate to you. Now it is your turn to advise both about this subject—whether it seems necessary to learn it or not—and about the others, if you have any subject or practice to praise for a young man, and to say what you will do regarding this partnership. NI. I, O Lysimachus and Melesias, praise your intention and am ready to partner with you; and I think Laches here is too. LA. You think truly, O Nicias. For what Lysimachus said just now about his father and that of Melesias seems to me very well said both against them, and us, and <margin>D</margin> all who manage the affairs of cities. For it happens to them, as he says, that both regarding children and other private matters, they are disregarded and handled negligently. You say these things well, Lysimachus. But that you call us as advisers for the education of the young men, yet do not call Socrates here, I wonder; first, because he is of your own district <note>original: "δημότην" / "demoten" — referring to the 'deme' or local administrative district of Athens</note>; second, because he always spends his time in places where there is some such study or practice that is noble for the young, such as you seek. LY. How do you mean, Laches? Has Socrates here made a study of any such thing? LA. Most certainly, Lysimachus. NI. And I too <margin>E</margin> could say this no worse than Laches. For he recently recommended to me a music teacher for my son: Damon, the student of Agathocles, the most graceful of men, worthy to spend time with young men of such an age not only in music but in all other things you might wish. LY. O Socrates, Nicias, and Laches, those of my age no longer know the younger ones, as they spend most of their time at home due to their age; but if you too, O son of Sophroniscus, have any good advice for this fellow-citizen of yours, you ought to give it. And it is just that you do so. For you happen to be a friend of our fathers. For I and your father were always companions and friends, and he died before any difference arose between us. And a memory of those who were just speaking brings his name to me. For these boys, <margin>F</margin> talking to each other at home, frequently mention Socrates and praise him greatly; however, I never yet asked them if they meant the son of Sophroniscus. But, O boys, tell me: is this the Socrates whom you mention each time? BOY. Certainly, father, this is he. LY. Well, by Hera, O Socrates, it is good that you uphold your father, who was the best of men; and that our affairs shall be familiar to you and yours to us. LA. And indeed, Lysimachus, do not let the man go. For I have seen him elsewhere as well, upholding not only his father but also his fatherland. For in the retreat from Delium he withdrew with me, <margin>G</margin> and I tell you, that if the others had been willing to be like him, our city would be upright and would not have fallen then into such a disaster. LY. O Socrates, this praise is noble, which you are now praised with by men worthy of being believed, and for those things for which they praise you. Know well then that I, hearing these things, rejoice that you are held in high regard. And consider me to be among those most well-disposed toward you. It was necessary even before this that you should visit us and consider us your own, as is just. But now, from this day, since we have recognized each other, do not do otherwise; but associate with and get to know both us and these younger men, so that you too may preserve our friendship. You will do these things, and we will remind you of them again. But concerning the things we began with, what do you say? What does it seem to you? Is the subject suitable for the boys, to learn to fight in armor? SOCR. Concerning these things too, O Lysimachus, I will try to advise <margin>H</margin> if I am able, and also to do all that you invite me to. But it seems most just to me that, being younger than these men and more inexperienced, I should hear from them...

<summary>Lysimachus and Melesias consult the generals Nicias and Laches on the military education of their sons, eventually realizing that Socrates, a friend of their fathers, is uniquely qualified to advise them. The passage highlights the Athenian concern with ancestral reputation and the perceived decline in the upbringing of the younger generation.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from the beginning of Plato's "Laches." In the previous section, the elderly fathers Lysimachus and Melesias asked the generals Nicias and Laches for advice on whether their sons should learn the art of "hoplomachia" (fighting in heavy armor). Socrates has just been invited to join the discussion as a moderator and advisor.</meta>

# LACHES.
X iiii

[Column 1 - translated from Greek]

A ...to hear what the younger men say, and to learn from them. If I have anything else to add beyond what they say, I will then teach and persuade both you and them. But O Nicias, why do you not speak to us both? NIC. There is nothing to hinder me, O Socrates. For it seems to me that this study is beneficial to the young in many ways. For it keeps them from spending time elsewhere, in those places where the young love to waste their leisure, and instead directs them to this, which necessarily makes the body better. For it is no worse than any other exercise, nor does it require less labor; and at the same time, this exercise and horsemanship <note>original: "ἡ ἱππική"</note> are most fitting for a free man. For we are in a true contest, and in those things for which a contest is proposed to us, only those who exercise in these instruments of war are truly training.

B Furthermore, this study will be of some benefit in the battle itself, when it is necessary to fight in a formation with many others. However, its greatest use is when the ranks are broken, and it becomes necessary to fight man-to-man, either to defend oneself while pursuing an attacker, or to repel someone attacking during a retreat. No man who is skilled in this art of fighting in armor <term>hoplomachia: the specialized art of fighting with heavy infantry equipment</term> would suffer anything at the hands of a single opponent, nor perhaps even from several, but would have the advantage everywhere. Moreover, such a thing calls forth a desire for another noble study.

C For every man, having learned how to fight in armor, would then desire the next study: that of military formations <note>tactics and troop movements</note>. And having mastered these, and being filled with a desire for glory in them, he would rush toward everything concerning the leadership of armies. It is already clear that the studies and practices following these are both noble and of great value for a man to learn and practice, and this study would lead the way to them. We shall add to it no small addition: that this knowledge itself would make any man in war both bolder and more courageous than he was before. Let us not disdain to say (even if it seems a smaller thing to some) that it also makes a man appear more graceful where it is needed, which at the same time makes him appear more formidable to his enemies because of that grace.

D For my part, O Lysimachus, as I say, I think we should teach the youths these things, and I have stated why I think so. But if Laches has anything to say contrary to this, I would gladly hear it. LA. But O Nicias, it is hard to say of any study whatsoever that it should not be learned. For it seems a good thing to know all things. And indeed, this art of arms, if it is a study (as those who teach it say, and as Nicias describes it), it ought to be learned; but if it is not a study, but those who promise it are deceiving us, or if it is a study but not a very serious one, why would one need to learn it? I say these things about it looking at this: I think that if this were something of value, it would not have escaped the notice of the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans, famous for their military prowess</note>, who care for nothing else in life but to seek and practice whatever learning would give them an advantage over others in war.

E And if it had escaped them, it certainly would not have escaped the teachers of this art themselves that the Spartans are the most earnest of the Greeks regarding such matters, and that a teacher honored among them for this would make the most money from others—just as a tragic poet who is honored among us makes his fortune. Therefore, whoever thinks he composes tragedy well does not wander outside Attica to show his skill in other cities, but hurries straight here and naturally shows it to us.

F But I see those who teach fighting in armor regarding Lacedaemon as an "inaccessible sanctuary" <note>An idiom meaning they are afraid to set foot there</note>, not even touching it with the tip of their foot, but circling around it and showing themselves to everyone else—especially to those who would themselves admit that many others are more youthful in the matters of war. Furthermore, O Lysimachus, I have been present with many of these men in actual action, and what sort of men they are, we can see for ourselves. For, as if by design, no man who practiced these arts of armor has ever become famous in war. Yet in all other skills, those who become famous are those who have practiced each one; but these men, it seems, have been so singularly unlucky in this compared to others.

G For even this Stesileus, whom you watched with me in such a large crowd when he was showing off and saying great things about himself, I saw elsewhere in a better light—showing his true self in reality, though not willingly. For when the ship on which he was serving as a marine attacked a merchant vessel, he fought with a "scythe-spear" <note>A long spear with a sickle-shaped blade attached to the tip</note>, a weapon as exceptional as he himself was meant to be. The other details of the man's deeds are not worth telling, but consider what became of his clever invention, the scythe on the spear-head. While he was fighting, it got caught in the ship's rigging and held fast. Stesileus pulled to release it, but he could not; meanwhile, his ship was passing the other. For a while, he ran along his own ship holding onto the spear; but when his ship moved past the other and the spear held him back, he let the spear slide through his hand until he was holding it by the very end of the butt-spike. There was laughter and clapping from those on the merchant ship at his ridiculous posture, and when someone threw a stone that landed at his feet on the deck, he let go of the spear entirely. Then even those on the trireme <note>The warship</note> could no longer hold back their laughter, seeing that famous scythe-spear hanging dangling from the merchant ship.

<column-break/>

[Column 2 - translated from Latin]

A ...first what they themselves think, and I shall learn; and if I have anything besides their opinions, I will then open it to you and these men. And why do you not speak first, O Nicias? <margin>Boys ought to learn the discipline of arms</margin> NIC. Nothing prevents it, Socrates. This skill seems to be useful to young men everywhere, and it is not something to be neglected, as young men are naturally accustomed to give themselves to it; rather, it is better to acquire that faculty through which a robust habit of the body is gained. For this exercise is inferior to no other, nor is it less laborious. Moreover, such exercise and skill in horsemanship especially become a free man. For in that contest of which we are the athletes, and in those things for which a contest is proposed to us, those alone fight who B exercise themselves in instruments of war of this kind. Furthermore, this skill will contribute in the battle itself, whenever it is necessary to fight in a line and order with many others. But it will be most profitable when the lines are dissolved, and it is necessary to engage in singular combat, either to pursue one who is resisting or to repel an attacker during flight. Surely, he who is instructed in this faculty will never succumb to one, and perhaps not even to many; rather, he will excel everywhere by this means. Furthermore, this faculty brings a desire for another noble discipline. For whoever has learned to fight with arms C will desire the discipline concerning the ordering of battle lines, which immediately follows. Having attained this, and being inflamed with a desire for glory in these things, he will betake himself to the command of armies, and in short, he will turn himself to all the noble institutions and studies concerning these things, which are worthy of knowledge, with that first skill leading the way. We shall also add something not to be despised: that this faculty would render each man in battle wonderfully bolder and braver. Nor should we remain silent on this point, although it might seem lighter: that you will make a man more fit and skilled there, where it is most necessary to be seen as fit and ready. D Certainly, in that place, he will appear more terrible to the enemies because of his very dexterity and skill. And so, O Lysimachus, it seems to me to be worth the effort that adolescents perceive these things; and I have explained the reason why I think so. Nevertheless, I would gladly hear if Laches wishes to bring forward anything besides these points. LACH. Indeed, Nicias, a speech would be considered absurd if anyone said that some discipline should not be acquired. For it seems better to know all things. Truly, this faculty concerning arms, if it is a discipline <margin>The discipline of arms is disparaged by reasons.</margin> (as those who teach it say, and such as Nicias proclaims it to be), then it must be learned. But if it is not a discipline, and those who promise it deceive us, or if it is indeed a discipline but of little value, why is it necessary to learn it? This E comes from the fact that, as I think, if this were of any value, it would never have escaped the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans</note>, who have no other care in all their life than to so prepare themselves in all things that they may excel all others in war. If by chance this thing escaped them, it would not have escaped the masters of this thing themselves, that the Spartans are most studious of arms, and whoever is held in price among them for this art would easily accumulate money there and elsewhere; just as a tragic poet is honored among us. For he who composes tragedies does not wander outside Attica, showing them in other cities, but immediately comes here and shows his works, not without reason, to these men. But those who are engaged in the exercise of arms, I see they consider Lacedaemon as if it were some inaccessible temple, and they never dare F even to ascend it with the tip of their foot. Instead, they wander around and boast among others, especially among those who would themselves confess they are inferior to many others in military matters. Furthermore, O Lysimachus, I have been present when not a few men of this kind were fighting, and I know what they are like. Although one may conjecture the matter for oneself: for, as if by deliberate effort, no one among those who have devoted themselves to these games has ever emerged illustrious in war, although in all other things those who exercise themselves frequently emerge as clear and famous; only these, compared to others, are so powerless of their wish that they seem utterly unfortunate. For G this Stesileus <margin>Stesileus the gladiator.</margin>, whom you saw with me showing himself off in such a crowd and professing too many wonders, I once looked upon elsewhere more certainly, when he was demonstrating himself to onlookers in truth, though not of his own will. For when the ship in which he was carried was attacking a merchant vessel, he was fighting with a scythe-tipped spear, a very great weapon, and he himself was very great. The other deeds of this man are hardly worthy of hearing, but this must not be passed over in silence: what happened from such a wonderful machine of this man, who added a scythe to his weapon. For while he was fighting, the scythe became entangled in the ship's supports. Stesileus was pulling to disentangle it, but he was unable; the ship, however, was passing by. Meanwhile, he accompanied the ship in its course, holding the spear. But when the ship had already passed the other ship, and he, holding the spear, was being pulled along, he finally came to the very end of the weapon with his hand. Therefore, laughter and a noise arose in the merchant ship because of Stesileus's appearance, and also because a stone was thrown at his feet on the deck, which forced him to let go of the spear. Then indeed, even those who were carried on the trireme could no longer contain themselves, seeing that scythe-tipped spear hanging from the ship.

<summary>Nicias and Laches debate the merits of military training for the youth. While Nicias argues it builds character and prepares one for war, Laches skeptically points out that the Spartans ignore it and shares a humorous story of a "professional" fighter failing ridiculously in actual combat.</summary>

# LACHES.
L
<meta>catchword: certainly</meta>

**A** However, I am not able to pay fees to the Sophists <note>Sophists: professional teachers in ancient Greece who charged for lessons in virtue and rhetoric</note>, who were the only ones claiming to be able to make me a "good and noble" man. As for myself, I am still unable to discover this art by my own talent. But if Nicias or Laches here has discovered it or learned it, I would not be surprised at all. For they are more abundant in wealth than I, so as to be able to learn from others, and they are older, so they have had time to find it. They seem to me capable of educating a man; for they would never have spoken so fearlessly about which youthful pursuits are good or bad if they did not believe they knew enough about it. In other matters, I certainly trust them; however, I was surprised that they disagreed with one another.

**B** Therefore, Lysimachus, just as Laches told you a moment ago not to let me go but to question me, I now in turn ask and command you, Lysimachus: do not let Laches or Nicias go. Instead, inquire of them, telling them that Socrates says he does not understand the matter, nor is he able to judge which of you speaks the truth, since he himself has never been an inventor of such things, nor has he learned them from any teacher. You, Laches and Nicias, tell each of us: who is the most learned person you have encountered regarding the education of youth? Do you know these things because you learned them from someone, or are you the discoverers yourselves? And if you did learn, who was the master for each of you? Or who are the other professors of this same art? So that, if you have little 

**C** leisure <note>original Latin: "otij"</note> remaining for these things because of the business of the Republic, we may go to those teachers and persuade them—whether by gifts, or by favor, or both—to take care of our sons and yours, so that they do not become wicked and bring disgrace upon their ancestors. But if you discovered this yourselves, give us an example: whom among others have you already made "good and noble" out of "base" men through your care? For if you are only now beginning to teach, you must be careful that the danger is not "risked on a Carian" (as they say) <note>original Greek: "ἐν τῷ Καρί"; a proverb meaning to perform a dangerous experiment on a person of little value before risking it on someone precious</note>, but rather on your own children and the children of your friends. Otherwise, what the proverb says might plainly happen: "to learn the potter's craft on a large jar" <note>original Latin: "In dolio figulariam experiri"; a proverb for trying a difficult task before mastering the basics</note>. Tell us, therefore, which of these things you claim for yourselves or deny?

**D** Ask them these things, Lysimachus, and do not let them go until they answer. 
**LYSIMACHUS:** Socrates seems to speak well, gentlemen. If, therefore, it would be pleasing to you, Nicias and Laches, to be questioned and to give an account, you must decide for yourselves. **E** For he was right to say that we are presently deliberating about the greatest of all our concerns. See then if you think it should be done this way.

to the temple or some other popular assembly, he stayed close to you. You have apparently not yet spoken with him since he has become a man.
**LYSIMACHUS:** Why is that, Nicias?
**NICIAS:** You seem not to know that whoever stays close to Socrates in conversation—as if joining his family—and clings to him in discussion, even if they started talking about something else entirely, is forced 

**F** at last, led around by Socrates' words, to give an account of his own life: what his current life is like, and how he has lived his past life. And once he has fallen into this, Socrates does not let him go until he has sufficiently examined all these things. I am familiar with this, and I know it is necessary to experience this from his words; I am well aware that I myself must undergo it now. I am quite delighted by his company, Lysimachus. I do not think it is a bad thing to be reminded if we have done or are doing anything incorrectly. On the contrary, it is necessary for one who does not flee these things to become more cautious for the future, believing according to that saying of Solon <note>Solon: an Athenian statesman and poet known for his wisdom</note> that one must learn as long as one lives,

and not hope that old age will bring us wisdom on its own. To me, therefore, it is neither 

**G** unusual nor unpleasant to be examined by Socrates. In fact, I knew long ago that if Socrates were present, our conversation would not be about the boys, but about ourselves. Therefore, nothing prevents me from discussing with Socrates however he wishes.
**LACHES:** My own feeling toward talk, Nicias, is simple—or if you prefer, not simple, but double. For I might seem to someone to be a lover of words, and at other times the opposite. **H** And such a man seems to me to be truly "musical," having tuned a most beautiful harmony—not on a lyre or some playful instrument, but having tuned his actual life so that his deeds are in concord with his words. This is truly in the "Doric" mode <note>Doric: a musical scale associated with bravery and tradition, which Laches considers the only truly Greek harmony</note>, and not the "Ionic," "Phrygian," or "Lydian." Such a man makes me rejoice...

# OF PLATO
<column-break/>

**NICIAS.** He delights me with his words and makes me appear to be a **lover of words** <note>original: "philologum" / "φιλόλογον"; one who enjoys intellectual discussion</note>; I receive his sayings with such great attention. Anyone who does the opposite offends my ears, and the more elegantly he seems to speak, the more he makes me appear to be a **hater of words** <note>original: "misologum" / "μισολόγον"</note>. I have not yet experienced Socrates’ words, but I have certainly experienced his deeds before, and I have found him to be worthy of noble speech and all freedom of expression. If, therefore, he possesses this quality as well, I completely agree with the man, and I will most gladly be examined by such a man, nor will it be troublesome for me to learn something from him.

Indeed, I also yield to Solon <note>Solon: An Athenian statesman and poet, one of the Seven Sages of Greece</note> (if he will allow this small addition), namely: "I wish to grow old learning many things," but only from good men. Let this much be granted to me: that the teacher himself be good, lest by chance I appear to be unteachable while learning against my will. Nor do I care whether the teacher is younger, or not yet famous in the opinion of men, or has some other such quality.

Therefore, Socrates, I declare to you that you may teach me and refute me however you wish, and you may learn what I myself might know. Certainly, I have been so disposed toward you since that day when you shared the danger with me and put your virtue to the test, showing such a character as anyone must exhibit who is to be justly tested. Therefore, say what you please, having no fear of our age.

**SOCRATES.** Then we shall not be able to accuse you as being unprepared for consulting and investigating.

**NICIAS.** But this is certainly our business, Socrates. For I consider you one of us. Consider on my behalf, for the sake of these youths, what we ought to ask of these men, and consult by discussing with them. For many things have already slipped from my memory because of my old age, including things I had intended to inquire about; nor shall I sufficiently remember what I hear if other conversations intervene. Therefore, run through the things we proposed among yourselves; I will listen, and when I have heard, I will perform whatever you and Melesias decide.

**SOCRATES.** Nicias and Laches, we must obey Lysimachus and Melesias. Perhaps it would not be bad to examine among ourselves those things we just now contended to investigate—namely, who were our teachers in such a discipline, or whom else we ourselves have made better. But such a consideration leads back to the same point; indeed, it will be the same as from the beginning. For if we happen to know about anything whatsoever that its presence makes that thing to which it is present better, and furthermore, if we are able to cause it to be present in that thing, it is clear that we know the thing itself about which we would be consultants: how one might acquire it most easily and best.

Perhaps you do not understand, but you will comprehend more easily this way. If we knew that **sight** <note>Latin: "visus", Greek: "ὄψις"</note> being present in the eyes makes those eyes in which it is present better, and furthermore, we were able to provide it to the eyes, it is clear that we would also know what sight itself is. Concerning this, we would sometimes have to consult on how one might acquire it most easily and conveniently. For if we were ignorant of what sight or hearing is, we would never be suitable consultants in medicine concerning the eyes or ears, investigating how one might best recover sight or hearing.

**LACHES.** You speak the truth, Socrates.

**SOCRATES.** Then, Laches, have these two men not called us to consultation at present, to ask in what way **virtue** <note>Latin: "virtus", Greek: "ἀρετὴ"</note>—if added to the souls of their sons—might make them better?

**LACHES.** Certainly.

**SOCRATES.** Then is it not necessary that this be established: namely, to understand what virtue itself is? For if we are entirely ignorant of what virtue is, how can we be consultants to anyone, and show the best and easiest way to attain virtue?

**LACHES.** In no way, Socrates.

**SOCRATES.** Do we say then, Laches, that we understand what virtue is?

**LACHES.** We certainly do.

**SOCRATES.** If we understand it, then surely we can also express what it is.

**LACHES.** Nothing prevents it.

**SOCRATES.** However, my good man, let us not immediately search for what all of virtue is. For that is a greater task. But let us first look at some part of it, to see if it is sufficiently clear to us; and in this way, our investigation will be easier.

**LACHES.** Let us do as you please.

**SOCRATES.** Which part of virtue then shall we choose? Is it not clearly that part to which the discipline of fighting in armor seems to look? It seems to many to look toward **courage** <note>Latin: "fortitudinem", Greek: "ἀνδρίαν"</note>, does it not?

**LACHES.** It certainly does.

**SOCRATES.** First, then, Laches, let us attempt to reveal what courage is; then after this, we will investigate in what way it may be acquired by the youths, so far as it can be produced by practice and study. Therefore, strive to explain to us what courage is.

**LACHES.** By Zeus, Socrates, that is not difficult to say! Know for certain that the brave man is he who, keeping his rank, stands his ground against the enemy and does not flee.

**SOCRATES.** You speak well, Laches. But perhaps because I asked you in somewhat obscure words, it caused you to answer something other than what I intended by my question.

**LACHES.** How do you mean that, Socrates?

**SOCRATES.** I will explain if I can. The brave man is indeed the one you describe, whoever fights against the enemy without deserting his rank.

**LACHES.** That is the one I mean.

**SOCRATES.** And I too. But what about the man who fights the enemy not by staying, but by fleeing?

**LACHES.** How "by fleeing"?

**SOCRATES.** Just as the Scythians <note>Scythians: Nomadic people from Central Asia known for their "Partian shot" or fighting while retreating</note> are said to fight no less by fleeing than by pursuing; and Homer, when praising the horses of Aeneas, says...

# LACHES

<margin>A</margin>
...the horses of Aeneas—"swiftly here and there"—he said they knew how to "pursue and flee." <note>Socrates is quoting Homer's *Iliad* 8.106-107</note> And he praised Aeneas himself for this very knowledge of fear, calling him a "counselor of fear." <note>original: "mēstōr phoboio" / "μήστωρ φόβοιο"</note> **LACHES:** And he was right to say so, Socrates, for he was speaking of chariots. You, however, are speaking of the Scythian horsemen. Their cavalry does indeed fight in that way, but the heavy infantry <note>term: "hoplitikon" / "ὁπλιτικὸν"; the heavily armed foot soldiers who were the backbone of Greek armies</note> of the Greeks fights as I described. **SOCRATES:** Except, perhaps, Laches, for the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans</note>. For they say that at the Battle of Plataea, when the Spartans came up against the soldiers with wicker shields, they were not willing to stand and fight them, but fled. But when the Persian ranks were broken, the Spartans turned back and fought like cavalry, and so they won that battle.

<margin>B</margin>
**SOCRATES:** I said this because I am the cause of your unsatisfactory answer, since I did not ask the question well. My intention was to ask you about those who are courageous not only in the heavy infantry, but also in the cavalry and in every branch of war; and not only those in war, but also those who are courageous in dangers at sea, and those who show courage in the face of disease, poverty, or political affairs. <margin>An enumeration is made so that courage may be sought in general.</margin> And further, I meant not only those who are courageous against pain or fear, but also those who are formidable at fighting against desires or pleasures, whether by standing their ground or by turning back. For surely there are some, Laches, who are courageous in such matters.

<margin>C</margin>
**LACHES:** Very much so, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Then all these men are courageous. Some possess courage in the face of pleasures, some in pains, some in desires, and some in fears. Others, I imagine, possess cowardice in these same things. **LACHES:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** I was asking what each of these two things is. So try again to say: first, what is courage, which is the same in all these cases? Or do you not yet understand what I mean? **LACHES:** Not quite.

<margin>D</margin>
**SOCRATES:** I mean it as if I were asking what "speed" is. It happens to be found in our running, and in playing the lyre, and in speaking, and in learning, and in many other things. We possess this quality, which is worth discussing, in the actions of the hands, the legs, the mouth and voice, or the mind. Do you not say so too? **LACHES:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** 
<margin>E</margin>
So if someone asked me, "Socrates, what is this thing which you call speed in all these activities?" <margin>The definition of speed.</margin> I would tell him that the power that accomplishes many things in a short time is what I call speed, whether in voice, or in running, or in all other things. **LACHES:** You would be speaking correctly. **SOCRATES:** Then you too, Laches, try to define courage in the same way. What power is it—the same in pleasure and in pain, and in all those things we just mentioned—that is called courage? <margin>A bad definition of courage.</margin> **LACHES:** It seems to me to be a certain **endurance of the soul** <note>original: "karteria tis tēs psychῆς" / "καρτερία τις τῆς ψυχῆς"</note>, if I must speak of the nature that runs through all these instances of courage. **SOCRATES:** But we must, if we are to answer the question for ourselves. Now, it seems to me that you do not consider every kind of endurance to be courage. <margin>Refutation.</margin> I conclude this from here: I am fairly certain, Laches, that you consider courage to be one of the very noble things. **LACHES:** You can be sure it is among the noblest. **SOCRATES:** Then endurance accompanied by wisdom <note>original: "phronēsis" / "φρόνησις"; practical wisdom or prudence</note> is noble and good? **LACHES:** Very much so. **SOCRATES:** But what about endurance with folly? Is it not the opposite—harmful and mischievous? **LACHES:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** Will you call something noble that is mischievous and harmful? **LACHES:** Surely not, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Then you will not admit that such endurance is courage, since it is not noble, while courage is noble. **LACHES:** You speak the truth. **SOCRATES:** Then, according to your argument, **wise endurance** would be courage. 

<margin>F</margin>
**LACHES:** It seems so. **SOCRATES:** Let us see, then: wise in what respect? Is it wisdom regarding all things, both great and small? For example, if someone endures in spending money wisely, knowing that by spending it he will gain more, would you call him courageous? **LACHES:** By Zeus, I would not. **SOCRATES:** Or suppose a doctor, when his son or someone else is suffering from inflammation of the lungs and begs for something to drink or eat, does not give in but endures? **LACHES:** Not at all; that is not courage either. **SOCRATES:** But what about a man enduring in war, willing to fight and calculating wisely, knowing that others will come to his aid, and that he will be fighting against fewer and inferior men than those on his side, and that he holds a better position? <margin>G</margin> Would you say that this man, who endures with such wisdom and preparation, is more courageous than the one in the opposite army who is willing to stand his ground and endure? **LACHES:** The one in the opposite army seems more courageous to me, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** And yet his endurance is more foolish than that of the other. **LACHES:** That is true. **SOCRATES:** Then you would say that the man who endures in a cavalry battle with knowledge of horsemanship is less courageous than the one who endures without such knowledge? **LACHES:** It seems so to me. **SOCRATES:** And the same for one who endures with skill in the sling or the bow, or any other art? **LACHES:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** And those who are willing to descend into a well and dive, enduring in this work though they are not experts in it—would you say they are more courageous than those who are experts? **LACHES:** What else could one say, Socrates? **SOCRATES:** Nothing, if that is what he thought. **LACHES:** Indeed, I do think so. **SOCRATES:** And...
<margin>H</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>Iliad. 8.</margin>
...to follow and flee very swiftly from here and there. And he once praised Aeneas himself similarly for his very knowledge of fearing; he said that he was skilled in fearing and fleeing. **LACHES:** And rightly so, O Socrates; for he was speaking of chariots, but you speak of the Scythian horsemen. Their cavalry indeed fights in that way, but those skilled in the Greek armor [hoplites] fight as I myself was saying. **SOCRATES:** Except perhaps for the Lacedaemonians, O Laches. For they say that the Lacedaemonians at Plataea, when they came upon the shield-bearers, did not at first withstand their attack nor persist, but rather fled. But after the Persian ranks were broken, they turned back in the manner of cavalry, and thus emerged victors in that battle. <margin>B</margin> **LACHES:** You tell the truth. **SOCRATES:** I was saying, therefore, that it happened because I had not questioned properly that you also did not answer correctly. For I wanted to ask not only about those who are brave regarding light armor, but also about the cavalry, and about all men simply brave in any kind of war; and not only on land, but in maritime storms, and even about those who are brave against diseases or poverty or civil affairs. And not only about those who are constant against pains or fears, but also about those who can fight bravely against pleasures and desires, whether persisting or even turning away. For there are, O Laches, some brave men in these matters as well. <margin>C</margin> **LACHES:** And very much so, O Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Are not all these brave? Nevertheless, some possess courage regarding pleasures, some regarding pains, some regarding desires, and some regarding fears; and those who are timid are timid, I suppose, regarding the same things. **LACHES:** It is entirely so. **SOCRATES:** I was asking what each of these two is. Therefore, express again to the best of your ability what courage itself is, which is found to be the same in all these. Do you not yet understand what I am saying? **LACHES:** Not sufficiently. **SOCRATES:** <margin>D</margin> I say it just as if I had asked: what is speed itself, which is present for us in running, in playing the cithara, in speaking, in learning, and in very many other things? Which indeed, as is worthy of mention, we possess in the movements of the hands, or the feet, or the mouth and voice, or the intellect. Do you not say the same? **LACHES:** Entirely. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, if someone were to ask me, "O Socrates, what do you say that thing is which you name as speed in all things?" I would certainly answer that a power performing many things in a short time, whether regarding the voice, or running, or all other things, seems so to me. **LACHES:** Correctly. **SOCRATES:** Try then, Laches, to define courage similarly: what is that power <margin>E</margin> in pleasure and pain and all the things we were just saying it belongs to, which is called the same "courage" through each instance. **LACHES:** It seems to me that courage is a certain endurance of the soul, if that which belongs to courage through all things must be told. **SOCRATES:** It must certainly be told, if we are to answer our own questions. But I think you do not consider just any endurance to be courage. I conjecture this from here: I know this much, Laches, that you think courage is a noble thing. **LACHES:** Nay, certainly the most noble. **SOCRATES:** Is not that endurance which wisdom accompanies both noble and good? **LACHES:** Entirely. **SOCRATES:** But that which folly [accompanies], is it not on the contrary harmful and noxious? **LACHES:** Surely. **SOCRATES:** Will you call noble that which is such—harmful and noxious? <margin>F</margin> **LACHES:** That would be a sin, O Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Then you will not call such endurance courage, since it is not noble, whereas courage itself is noble. **LACHES:** You speak the truth. **SOCRATES:** Prudent endurance, therefore, according to your speech, is courage. **LACHES:** It seems so. **SOCRATES:** Let us see, then, what kind of endurance, and in what matter it is prudent, that constitutes courage. Is it toward all things, both great and small? For instance, if someone endures while prudently spending money, knowing that from this expense he will gain, will you call him brave? **LACHES:** By no means. **SOCRATES:** Or if a doctor, when his son or anyone else is weighed down by a lung infection and asks for drink and food, endures and is not moved? **LACHES:** Nor will I call this endurance courage. <margin>G</margin> **SOCRATES:** But in war, would you call a man who is enduring and ready for battle—who prudently foresees everything, knowing that reinforcements will be present, and that he must fight against fewer and weaker men, and who uses a more advantageous position—would you call such a man, I say, enduring with such foresight and preparation, more brave than him who stands and endures in the opposite army? **LACHES:** Rather this one in the opposite army, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Yet the endurance of this one is more imprudent than that of the other. **LACHES:** You speak the truth. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, you will say that a man endowed with equestrian science and enduring in an equestrian contest is less brave than he who endures while devoid of this science? **LACHES:** So it seems to me. **SOCRATES:** And furthermore, him who knows how to throw with a sling <margin>H</margin> and draw a bow, or endures in any other thing, [is] less brave [than the unskillful]? **LACHES:** Entirely. **SOCRATES:** Likewise, whoever, without the art of swimming, dares to descend into a well and endure and persist in that work, or in any other work without art—will you say they are braver than those who are learned in those arts? **LACHES:** What else could one say, Socrates? **SOCRATES:** Nothing, if only one thinks so. **LACHES:** I certainly think so.

<summary>Socrates and Laches attempt to find a universal definition of courage, moving from specific military tactics to the proposal that courage is "wise endurance." However, they encounter a paradox where the person who endures without technical skill or knowledge (the "unwise") often seems more courageous than the expert.</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Laches, Plato, courage, andreia, endurance, karteria, wisdom, phronesis, military tactics, Plataea, definition of virtue</keywords>

**SOCRATES:** Yet those who face dangers without prudence do so more foolishly, and they endure them more recklessly than those who approach them with skill.
**LACHES:** So it seems.
**SOCRATES:** Did we not say earlier that imprudent boldness and endurance appeared to us to be shameful and harmful?
**LACHES:** Very much so.
**SOCRATES:** But we agreed that courage is something beautiful.
**LACHES:** We certainly did.
**SOCRATES:** Yet now, conversely, we are saying that this shameful, imprudent endurance is courage.
**LACHES:** That is how it appears.
**SOCRATES:** Does it seem to you that we are speaking correctly?
**LACHES:** By Zeus, Socrates, not at all.
**SOCRATES:** Therefore, to use your own phrase, you and I are not tuned to the "Doric harmony" <note>original: "Doricam harmoniam"; Socrates is using a musical metaphor. The Dorian mode was considered the most masculine and brave of Greek musical scales. He is teasing Laches, a man of action, that his words and his deeds are out of tune with each other.</note>. For our deeds do not harmonize with our words. In deed, someone might say we share in courage, but in speech, I think anyone who heard us disputing right now would say we do not.
**LACHES:** You speak the absolute truth.
**SOCRATES:** Does it seem good to you that we should be in this state?
**LACHES:** Not in the least.
**SOCRATES:** Are you willing, then, to trust the argument we have introduced, and to follow it?
**LACHES:** What argument, and which one in particular?
**SOCRATES:** The argument that commands us to endure. If you agree, let us stand firm and endure in this very inquiry, lest Courage herself mocks us for not searching for her courageously—if it is indeed the case that endurance itself is often courage.
**LACHES:** I am ready to persevere, Socrates, even though I am unaccustomed to such arguments. But a certain competitive spirit has seized me regarding what has been said, and I am truly annoyed that I am unable to express what I am thinking. I feel I understand what courage is, yet somehow it escaped me just now, so that I could not capture it in words or define its essence.
**SOCRATES:** Does it not behoove a good hunter to run along the trail and follow it shrewdly, rather than giving up lazily?
**LACHES:** It certainly does.
**SOCRATES:** Shall we then invite Nicias <note>Nicias was a prominent Athenian politician and general, known for his caution and piety.</note> to this hunt, to see if he is perhaps more shrewd than we are?
**LACHES:** Why wouldn't I want that?
**SOCRATES:** Come then, Nicias, come to the aid of your friends who are tossing and wavering in the waves of discourse. If you have any power, run to us and solve our difficulties.

**SOCRATES:** Why so?

**LACHES:** Certainly not.
