<meta>This page continues the dialogue in Plato's "Laches," where Socrates, Laches, and Nicias are attempting to define "courage." Nicias has just proposed that courage is a form of knowledge—specifically, the knowledge of what is to be feared and what is to be hoped for. This intellectual approach contrasts with Laches’ earlier view that courage is a physical or emotional persistence.</meta>

# LACHES

<margin>A</margin> **SOCRATES:** ...rather, my good man. For a prophet only needs to recognize the signs of things to come—whether there will be death, or disease, or loss of property, or victory, or defeat, whether in war or some other contest. But as to whether it is better for someone to suffer these things or not to suffer them, why does it belong more to a prophet to judge this than to anyone else?
**LACHES:** I really do not understand what he is trying to say, Socrates. For he shows us neither a prophet, nor a doctor, nor anyone else as the one he calls "courageous," unless he is saying that a courageous person is some kind of god. It seems to me that Nicias is simply unwilling to admit honestly that he is talking nonsense; instead, 
<margin>B</margin> he twists back and forth to hide his own confusion. Even you and I could have twisted like that just now, if we had wanted to avoid appearing to contradict ourselves. If we were arguing in a court of law, there might be some reason to do this; but in a gathering like this, why should anyone try to decorate themselves with empty words for no reason?
**SOCRATES:** I agree, Laches, it seems like nothing. But let us see if Nicias thinks he is actually saying something and is not just speaking for the sake of the argument. Let us ask him more clearly what he has in mind. If he is onto something, we will agree with him; if not, we will explain it to him.
**LACHES:** You ask him then, Socrates, if you want to know. I think I have questioned him enough.
**SOCRATES:** Nothing prevents me; the inquiry will be common to both you and me.
**LACHES:** By all means.
**SOCRATES:** Tell me then, Nicias—or rather, tell us, for Laches and I are sharing this argument together: do you say that courage is the knowledge <note>original: "ἐπιστήμην" (epistēmēn) - technical knowledge or science</note> of things that are fearful and things that are encouraging? 
**NICIAS:** I do.
<margin>C</margin> **SOCRATES:** And this knowledge is not something every man possesses, I suppose, since neither a doctor nor a prophet will know it, nor be courageous, unless they acquire this specific knowledge? Was that not what you were saying?
**NICIAS:** Exactly so.
**SOCRATES:** Then, as the proverb goes, "Not even any old pig would know this," and so a pig could not be courageous.
**NICIAS:** I think not.
**SOCRATES:** It is clear then, Nicias, that you do not believe even the Crommyonian sow <note>The Crommyonian sow was a legendary monstrous wild pig killed by the hero Theseus; Socrates is using a famous mythological beast to make a point about animal nature.</note> could have been courageous. I am not joking; I think it is necessary for someone who says what you do to either deny courage to any wild beast or else to concede that some beast is so wise that it knows things which only a few humans know because they are so difficult to grasp. 
<margin>D</margin> Indeed, the one who defines courage as you do must say that a lion, a leopard, a boar, and even a monkey are all equally courageous by nature. 
**NICIAS:** By the gods, Socrates, you speak well. 
**LACHES:** And truly, Nicias, answer this: do you say these wild animals are wiser than us—animals which we all agree are courageous—or do you dare to contradict everyone and say they are not courageous at all?
**NICIAS:** Indeed, Laches, I do not call wild beasts courageous, nor anything else that, because of its ignorance, does not fear things that are truly terrible; I call such things "fearless" and "foolish." Do you think I call all small children courageous, who fear nothing because they lack understanding? 
<margin>E</margin> I believe that being "fearless" and being "courageous" are not the same thing. I think courage and foresight <note>original: "προμηθείας" (promētheias) - literally "thinking ahead" or providence</note> belong to very few; but boldness, daring, and fearlessness without foresight belong to many—to men, women, children, and wild animals. So, the things you and most people call "courageous," I call "bold"; but "courageous" things are the wise ones I am speaking of.
**LACHES:** Look, Socrates, how well this man thinks he is decorating himself with words! Those whom everyone agrees are courageous, he tries to strip of this honor.
**NICIAS:** Not at all, Laches; be of good cheer. I say that you are wise, and Lamachus too, if indeed you are courageous—and many other Athenians as well.
**LACHES:** I will say nothing in response to that, though I could, lest you say I am truly a man from Aexone <note>Aexone was an Athenian district whose people were stereotypically known for being rude or abusive.</note>.
**SOCRATES:** Do not say it, Laches. Indeed, 
<margin>F</margin> you don't seem to have noticed that he has received this wisdom from our friend Damon <note>Damon was a famous music theorist and advisor to Pericles, often associated with sophisticated intellectual circles.</note>; and Damon spends a lot of time with Prodicus <note>Prodicus was a Sophist famous for his focus on the precise definition and distinction of words.</note>, who is considered the best of the Sophists at distinguishing such terms.
**LACHES:** And it is indeed appropriate, Socrates, for a Sophist to play at such cleverness rather than a man whom the city deems worthy to lead it.
**SOCRATES:** It is appropriate, my blessed friend, for one who presides over the greatest matters to possess the greatest prudence. But it seems to me that Nicias is worth investigating, to see what he is looking at when he defines courage this way.
**LACHES:** Then investigate him yourself, Socrates.
**SOCRATES:** That is what I intend to do, my best of men. But do not think I will let you out of our shared argument; pay attention and join me in examining what is being said.
**LACHES:** Let it be so, if you think it necessary.
**SOCRATES:** I do. But you, 
<margin>G</margin> Nicias, tell us again from the beginning: you know that at the start of our talk we were considering courage as a part of virtue?
**NICIAS:** Certainly.
**SOCRATES:** And did you not answer that it was a part—that there are other parts as well, which altogether are called "virtue"?
**NICIAS:** How could I not?
**SOCRATES:** Then do you name the same parts that I do? For besides courage, I call temperance, justice, and other similar things "parts." Do you not also?
**NICIAS:** Very much so.
**SOCRATES:** Wait there. We agree on these points. Now let us consider things that are "fearful" and "encouraging," so that you do not think they are one thing while we think they are another. 
<margin>H</margin> We will tell you what we think; if you do not agree, you must teach us.

<column-break/>

who else might it be? <margin>A</margin> **NICIAS:** Plainly the one I am describing, and much more so, my good man. For it belongs to the prophet only to foreknow the omens and signs of the future, whether death hangs over someone, or sickness, or loss of goods, or victory, or defeat in war, or any other contest. But as to which of these is better for a person to suffer or not to suffer, why would a prophet judge this more than anyone else?
**LACHES:** I do not know what this Socrates wants for himself; for he identifies neither a prophet, nor a doctor, nor anyone else as the one he calls brave, unless perhaps he says he is some kind of god. To me, Nicias seems 
<margin>B</margin> to be unwilling to admit honestly that he is saying nothing, and he is carried up and down, hiding his own ignorance. Truly, even we a little while ago—I mean you and I, Socrates—could have stalled in the same way, if we had wanted to pretend, so that we would not appear to contradict ourselves. If we had to plead in a court of law, it might be fitting to do this. But now, what is the use of decorating oneself with empty words in this gathering? 
**SOCRATES:** Nothing, as it seems to me, Laches. But let us see if perhaps Nicias thinks he is saying something, and is not just saying these things for the sake of the words. Therefore, let us learn more clearly from him what he feels; and if he seems to bring any truth, we will agree; if not, we will teach him.
**LACHES:** You ask him yourself, Socrates, if you wish. For I have questioned him enough.
**SOCRATES:** Nothing prevents me. For the questioning will be common to both me and you.
**LACHES:** By all means.
**SOCRATES:** Tell me, O Nicias—rather, tell us, for this question is common to both me and Laches: do you say that courage is the knowledge of things to be feared and things not to be feared?
**NICIAS:** Indeed.
**SOCRATES:** But to distinguish this is not the work of just any man, since neither 
<margin>C</margin> the doctor nor the prophet will know this, nor is he brave, unless he has attained this very knowledge? Did you not say so?
**NICIAS:** Exactly so.
**SOCRATES:** Therefore, as the proverb says, "Not any old pig would know this," <margin>D</margin> <margin>Proverb. See Plutarch in [Life of] Theseus.</margin> nor will it be brave. 
**NICIAS:** Certainly not, as it seems to me.
**SOCRATES:** It is certain then, Nicias, that you do not believe even the Crommyonian sow was brave. And I do not say these things for the sake of a joke, but I think that he who speaks this way admits the courage of no brute beast, nor concedes that any brute is so wise that it knows what very few men know because of the difficulty—the things a lion, or a leopard, or some boar might know. But it is necessary for him who defines courage as you have to say that the lion, the stag, the bull, and the monkey are all equally established by nature toward courage. 
**LACHES:** By the gods, you speak rightly, Socrates! And Nicias, answer us truly: do you say these beasts are wiser than us—beasts which we all admit are brave—or do you dare to deny they are brave, against everyone's opinion? 
<margin>E</margin> **NICIAS:** Indeed, Laches, I do not call brute beasts brave, nor anything else that, because of ignorance of terrible things, fears nothing—the intrepid and the fatuous. Or do you think I call all children brave, who fear nothing because of ignorance? I think, indeed, that being intrepid is not the same as being brave. For I think courage and foresight are found in very few; but ferocity and daring that lacks fear, and is entirely without foresight, is found in many—in men, women, children, and beasts. Therefore, the things that you and many others call "brave," I call "ferocious"; but "brave" things are those that prudently discern what is worthy of daring and what is worthy of fear.
**LACHES:** See, O Socrates, how beautifully this man, as he himself thinks, decorates himself with words. But he strives to deprive those of the honor of 
<margin>F</margin> courage whom all others agree are brave.
**SOCRATES:** I do not at all, O Laches; but be of good heart. For I say that you and Lamachus are wise, if indeed you are brave, and many others of the Athenians besides.
**LACHES:** I will offer nothing against these things, even if I were able, lest you say I am truly some kind of abusive slanderer.
**SOCRATES:** Do not say it, O Laches; for you do not seem to have noticed that he received this kind of wisdom from our friend Damon. And Damon is very devoted to Prodicus. Prodicus is said to be wonderful among the other Sophists in explaining and distinguishing the force of names.
**LACHES:** Truly, Socrates, it is more fitting for a Sophist to exalt himself with these studies than for a man whom the city judges worthy to lead it.
**SOCRATES:** It is fitting, Laches, for him who manages the greatest affairs to 
<margin>G</margin> also have the greatest prudence. But I think we must now inquire for what specific meaning Nicias established the name of "courage."
**LACHES:** You yourself inquire into these things, Socrates.
**SOCRATES:** I will do so, best of men; yet do not think you are excluded from the common discussion. You also apply your mind, and consider with us what is to be said.
**LACHES:** Let it be so, if it seems it must be done.
**SOCRATES:** Indeed it does. You, Nicias, tell us again from the beginning. You know that at the start of our speech we considered courage as if it were a certain part of virtue?
**NICIAS:** Indeed.
**SOCRATES:** And did you not respond to what was introduced above, that it was a certain part, as if there were also other parts, and all together 
<margin>H</margin> are called by the name of virtue?
**NICIAS:** Why not?
**SOCRATES:** Do you name the same parts that I do? For I, besides courage, name temperance, and justice, and certain such things. Do you also?
**NICIAS:** I also.
**SOCRATES:** Attend now. For we admit these things. But of those things which are worthy of fear and terrible, and of those things which are worthy of daring, let us next consider, lest perhaps you think they are one thing, and we think they are another. For the things we think, we will set out for you. You, indeed, if you disagree, teach us.

<summary>Socrates and Laches challenge Nicias’s intellectual definition of courage as the "knowledge of the fearful and the encouraging," leading Nicias to argue that true courage requires foresight and is distinct from mere animal fearlessness.</summary>
<keywords>Plato, Laches, Socrates, Nicias, courage, bravery, fearlessness, prudence, foresight, Sophists, Prodicus, Damon, Crommyonian sow</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue in Plato's "Laches." Previously, Nicias proposed that courage is the knowledge of what is to be feared and what is to be hoped for. Socrates is now testing whether this definition holds up by examining whether knowledge of the future (fear) can be separated from knowledge of the past and present.</meta>

# PLATO

<margin>A</margin> **SOCRATES:** We believe that "terrible" things are those that strike us with fear, while "daring" things are those that do not. But fear is not caused by past or present evils, but by those that are expected. For we call fear the expectation of a future evil. Do you not also feel the same, Laches? **LACHES:** Most certainly, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** You hear, Nicias, that we say "terrible" things are future evils, and "daring" things are future goods—or at least not evils. Is this how you think of them, or differently? **NICIAS:** Certainly in that way. **SOCRATES:** And do you call the knowledge of these things "courage"? **NICIAS:** Precisely. **SOCRATES:** <margin>B</margin> Let us see further if you agree with us on this third point. **NICIAS:** What is that? **SOCRATES:** I will tell you. To me and to this man <note>referring to Laches</note> it seems that for whatever there is a science or knowledge, there is not one knowledge of the past as it happened, another of the present as it happens, and another of the future as it might best happen; rather, it is the work of the same knowledge to know all these. Just as regarding health and the <term>salutary (that which promotes health)</term> at all times, no other science than medicine looks upon what is happening, what has happened, and what will happen, and how it will happen. And regarding the things that grow from the earth, agriculture is the same. Furthermore, in war, you yourselves will be witnesses that the military art subtly foresees all things, including the future. For you do not want it to be subject to <term>divination (the art of predicting the future through signs)</term>, but rather to command it, as it foresees more sharply what is happening or will happen in war. <margin>C</margin> And indeed the law so decrees: not that the seer should rule over the commander of the army, but that the commander of the army should rule over the seer. Shall we assert these things, Laches? **LACHES:** We shall. **SOCRATES:** Do you agree with us, Nicias, that it belongs to the same knowledge to understand the same things as they were in the past, as they are in the present, and as they will be in the future? **NICIAS:** Indeed, for so it seems to me, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Then, my good man, is not <term>courage (Latin: *fortitudo*)</term> the knowledge of things to be feared and their opposites, as you yourself proclaimed? **NICIAS:** It is indeed. **SOCRATES:** But it was established that the things we fear are future evils, and the things we dare are future goods. **NICIAS:** Plainly. **SOCRATES:** And the same knowledge covers the same things, whether past, present, or future. **NICIAS:** These things are true. <margin>D</margin> **SOCRATES:** Therefore, courage is not only the knowledge of things to be feared and their opposites; for it does not understand only future goods or evils, but also the present and the past, and simply all things, just as other sciences foresee. **NICIAS:** So it seems. **SOCRATES:** You have therefore answered us, Nicias, regarding about a third part of courage, although we asked what courage is as a whole. And indeed, as it seems for now, according to your argument, courage is not only the knowledge of things to be feared and their opposites, but of all goods and evils, and of all things simply (as follows from your words) regardless of how they stand. Do you judge it so now, Nicias, or otherwise? **NICIAS:** So it seems to me, Socrates. <margin>E</margin> **SOCRATES:** Do you think, blessed man, that such a man lacks any part of <term>virtue (Latin: *virtus*)</term>, who knows all goods exactly as they have been, are, and will be, and evils likewise? And do you think that man is in need of <term>temperance (moderation)</term>, and justice, or holiness, who alone is fit to prudently understand both divine and human goods and evils, to avoid the latter and seize the former, and who knows how to live rightly with all? **NICIAS:** You seem to speak the truth, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, that which was introduced by you, Nicias, is not a part of virtue, but the whole of virtue. **NICIAS:** So it appears. **SOCRATES:** However, we said that courage was a certain part of virtue. **NICIAS:** We plainly said so. **SOCRATES:** But what is now being said does not appear to be so. **NICIAS:** It does not. **SOCRATES:** We have not, therefore, found, Nicias, what courage itself is. **NICIAS:** We do not seem to have. <margin>F</margin> **LACHES:** And yet I thought, my friend Nicias, that you would find it, since you looked down on me as I was answering Socrates. I was hoping that you would declare these things to us from the wisdom of <note>Damon was a famous music theorist and advisor to Pericles, often associated with sophisticated intellectual views</note> Damon. **NICIAS:** You do well, Laches, to bravely mock me because you have been shown to be ignorant in this discussion; you care only whether I also appear as such, and you think it matters not at all if neither of us understands those things which anyone who wants to be someone ought to know. You seem to be truly suffering from a human failing, looking at others rather than at yourself. But I think I have spoken tolerably well about these matters. If anything was said less conveniently, I will correct them later with Damon himself, whom you think should be laughed at even though you have never seen him. <margin>G</margin> Moreover, when I am firmly settled in these things, I will also teach you, for you seem to be very much in need of instruction to overcome your envy. **LACHES:** You are indeed a wise one, Nicias; however, I advise Lysimachus and Melesias here not to require the efforts of myself or you regarding the education of their sons, but not to neglect this Socrates, just as I said from the beginning. If my sons were adults, I would have done the same. **NICIAS:** Indeed, I too agree that if Socrates is willing to take charge of the youths, no one else should be sought. I would most gladly entrust my son Niceratus to him, if he were willing. But as often as I speak to him about this, he points out others and refuses himself. Try then, Lysimachus, to see if Socrates might obey you more. **LYSIMACHUS:** It is only fair, Nicias, since I would be willing to do many things for him in return that I would not do for many others. What do you say, Socrates? Will you comply, and take care that these youths turn out as the best of men?

<column-break/>

**SOCRATES:** You judge correctly. We believe that "terrible" things are those that provide fear; "daring" things are those that do not provide fear. Fear is provided not by past evils or present ones, but by those that are expected. For fear is the expectation of a future evil. Does it not seem so to you as well, Laches? **LACHES:** Very much so, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** You hear our side then, Nicias, that we say "terrible" things are future evils; and "daring" things are future things that are not evil or are good. Do you set it down this way, or do you speak otherwise? **NICIAS:** In this way. **SOCRATES:** And do you call the knowledge of these things "courage"? **NICIAS:** Absolutely. **SOCRATES:** Let us consider a third point, whether it seems the same to you and to us. **NICIAS:** What sort of point is this? **SOCRATES:** I will explain. It seems to me and to this man that regarding whatever there is knowledge, it is not one knowledge for the past to know how it happened, another for the present to know how it happens, and another for how that which has not yet happened might best happen or will happen; rather, it is the same knowledge. For example, regarding health across all times, no other science but medicine, being one, oversees things happening, things past, and things to come, and how they will come to be. And regarding things growing from the earth, agriculture is the same. And surely you yourselves would testify that regarding war, <term>generalship (Greek: *stratēgia*)</term> provides for the future most excellently, along with everything else. Nor does it think it should serve divination, but rather rule it, as it knows better the things concerning war, both happening and about to happen. And the law decrees thus: not that the seer rule the general, but the general rule the seer. Shall we say these things, Laches? **LACHES:** We shall. **SOCRATES:** What then? Do you agree with us, Nicias, that regarding the same things, it is the same knowledge that understands the future, the present, and the past? **NICIAS:** I do. For it seems so to me, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Then, my best of men, <term>courage (Greek: *andreia*)</term> is the knowledge of terrible and daring things, as you say? Or is it not? **NICIAS:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** And it was agreed that terrible things and daring things are future goods and future evils. **NICIAS:** Very much so. **SOCRATES:** But the same knowledge is of the same things, whether future or existing in any way. **NICIAS:** These things are so. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, courage is not only the knowledge of terrible and daring things. For it understands not only future goods and evils, but also those happening and past, and those existing in any way, just like other sciences. **NICIAS:** It seems so. **SOCRATES:** You have answered us then, Nicias, regarding a part of courage—hardly a fifth—though we asked what courage was as a whole. And now again, it seems, according to your argument, courage is not only the knowledge of terrible and daring things, but it would be courage regarding almost all goods and evils, however they might be. Do you change your position to this, Nicias, or how do you say? **NICIAS:** It seems so to me, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Does it seem to you then, marvelous man, that such a person would lack any part of virtue, if he knew all the goods and how they happen, will happen, and have happened, and the evils likewise? And do you think this man is in need of <term>temperance (Greek: *sōphrosynē*)</term>, or justice and holiness, to whom alone it belongs to be careful regarding both gods and men concerning the terrible and the not terrible, and to provide goods, knowing how to associate with them correctly? **NICIAS:** You seem to me to be saying something, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, Nicias, what is now being said by you would not be a part of virtue, but the whole of virtue. **NICIAS:** It seems so. **SOCRATES:** And yet we said that courage was one part of the parts of virtue. **NICIAS:** We did say so. **SOCRATES:** But what is now being said does not appear to be that. **NICIAS:** It does not seem so. **SOCRATES:** Therefore we have not found, Nicias, what courage is. **NICIAS:** We do not appear to have. **LACHES:** And indeed I, my friend Nicias, thought you would find it, since you looked down on me when I was answering Socrates; I had a very great hope that you would find it by the wisdom of Damon. **NICIAS:** Excellent, Laches, that you think it is no longer a matter of concern that you yourself were just shown to know nothing about courage; but if I also appear as another such person, you look to that. And it will no longer matter (as it seems) to you that you know nothing with me of the things a man who thinks he is someone ought to have knowledge of. You seem to me to be truly doing a human thing, looking not at yourself but at others. But I think I have spoken reasonably well for myself about what we were just saying, and if any of it was not spoken sufficiently, I will correct it later both with Damon (whom you think you are laughing at, though perhaps you have never even seen him) and with others. And when I have confirmed these things, I will also teach you, and I will not be envious. For you seem to me to be very much in need of learning. **LACHES:** For you are wise, Nicias. But nevertheless, I advise Lysimachus and Melesias here to let you and me go regarding the education of the young men, and not to let go of this Socrates (as I was saying from the beginning). If my children were of age, I would do these very things. **NICIAS:** I also agree to these things. If Socrates is willing to take care of the youths, one should seek no one else. Since I would most gladly entrust Niceratus to him, if he were willing. But he always recommends others to me whenever I mention anything to him about this, and he himself is unwilling. But see, Lysimachus, if Socrates might listen to you more. **LYSIMACHUS:** It is right indeed, Nicias; since I would be willing to do many things for him, which I would not be willing to do for many others. What do you say then, Socrates? Will you listen at all, and join in the effort so that the youths might become the best they can be?

<meta>Catchword: at all, and</meta>

<summary>In this concluding movement of the dialogue, Socrates proves that Nicias' definition of courage as the "knowledge of fear and hope" implies a knowledge of all good and evil across all time, which is the definition of virtue itself rather than just the specific part called courage. The dialogue ends in an 'aporia' (a state of unresolved puzzle), with the characters agreeing that they all need further education and asking Socrates to teach their sons.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the dialogue "Laches" and begins the dialogue "Clitophon." In the previous section of the "Laches," Socrates and his companions reached a state of "aporia"—a philosophical crossroads where they realized they could not adequately define courage. They are now deciding on their next steps for the education of their sons.</meta>

C L I T O P H O.

<margin>A</margin> **SOCRATES:** It would indeed be a terrible thing, Lysimachus, to be unwilling to join in the effort to make ourselves as good as possible. If, in the discussion we just had, I had appeared to know the truth while these others did not, it would be right to call upon me especially for this task. But as it is, we have all fallen into the same difficulty <note>original: "aporia," a state of philosophical puzzlement</note>. Whom, then, could one of us prefer over another? In my view, no one. But since this is the case, see if you think my advice is sound. I say, gentlemen—and let this stay between us—that we should all search together for the best possible teacher, first for ourselves (for we truly need one) and then for these young men, sparing neither money nor anything else. If anyone laughs at us for choosing to attend a teacher's school at our age, I think we should quote Homer <note>Odyssey 17.347</note> against them, who said: "Shame is no good companion for a man in need." So, letting people say what they will, let us take care of ourselves and these youths together. **LYSIMACHUS:** I like what you say, Socrates. And as I am the oldest, I am the most eager to learn alongside the young men. But please, do this: come to my house tomorrow at dawn without fail, so that we may consult on these very matters. For now, let us end this gathering. **SOCRATES:** I will do exactly that, Lysimachus. I will come to you tomorrow, God willing.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> **SOCRATES:** <note>This column contains the contemporary Latin translation of the Greek text to the left.</note> It would certainly be a hard thing, Lysimachus, if anyone were to refuse such care. Therefore, if I had appeared skilled in the previous dispute and these others ignorant, I would rightly be the one called to this work. But since we are stuck in the same doubt, which of us should be chosen? It seems to me that no one in particular should be selected. However, as things stand, see if I advise us rightly. I believe, O men, (for I wish none of this to be voiced abroad) that we ought to seek together for the best teacher, first for ourselves, for we are in want; then for the youths, sparing neither money nor any other thing. To live as we live now, and to care for our sons in this way, I do not advise. <margin>B</margin> If anyone mocks us because we, at such an age, decide to enter a teacher's school, that saying of Homer <margin>Odyssey, Book 8 <note>Though the margin says Book 8, the quote is from Book 17</note></margin> should be thrown back at them. For he says that shame is of no use to a needy man. Therefore, despising all the words of detractors, let us take up the common care of ourselves and our youths. **LYSIMACHUS:** Your words please me, Socrates; and I determine that the older I am, the more studiously I shall learn together with the youths. But listen, do exactly this: come to my house at first light tomorrow, and do not neglect it, so that we may take counsel on these matters. For today’s meeting must now be dismissed. **SOCRATES:** I will do as you command, Lysimachus: and if God wills it, I shall come to you tomorrow.

<image-desc>Decorative historiated initial 'K' featuring a seated figure in a scholar's pose, framed by architectural or floral motifs.</image-desc>
**SOCRATES:** Someone recently reported to us that Clitophon, the son of Aristonymus, in a conversation with Lysias, was criticizing the time spent with Socrates and praising the company of Thrasymachus <note>A famous sophist and Socrates' antagonist in the Republic</note> beyond measure. **CLITOPHON:** Whoever it was, Socrates, they did not correctly report to you the words I spoke about you to Lysias. For in some things I was praising you, and in others I was not. But since it is clear you are blaming me, though you pretend to be indifferent, I would very gladly explain my views to you myself, especially since we happen to be alone. I want you to see that I do not hold you in low esteem. Perhaps you have heard an incorrect account, and so you appear more annoyed with me than is necessary. If you give me the freedom to speak plainly, I would gladly accept it, for I wish to speak. **SOCRATES:** Indeed, it would be shameful if I did not tolerate you when you are so eager to benefit me. For it is clear that once I have learned in what ways I am worse and in what ways better, I shall practice and pursue the latter, while fleeing the former with all my might. **CLITOPHON:** Listen then. For I, Socrates, when I was with you, was often struck with amazement as I listened; and you seemed to me to speak more beautifully than all other men when you rebuked people. Like a <term>god from a theatrical machine</term> <note>original: "deus ex machina," a stage device where a god appears to resolve a plot</note>, you would cry out: "Where are you rushing, O men? You are ignorant that you are doing nothing that you ought to do. You spend all your effort on how you might amass wealth, yet you neglect the sons to whom you will leave it, failing to find teachers of justice for them—if indeed justice can be taught—or those who can train and exercise them in it, if it is a matter of practice and habit. Nor did you ever take such care of yourselves in the past. But seeing that you and your children have learned letters, music, and gymnastics sufficiently (which you consider to be a complete education in virtue), you find yourselves no less wicked regarding money. Why do you not despise your current education, and seek those who will stop this <term>lack of harmony</term> <note>original: "amousia," a lack of cultivation or refinement</note>?" For it is because of this error and sloth—rather than any lack of rhythm between the foot and the lyre—that brother turns against brother, and cities against cities, becoming imbalanced and out of tune, falling into civil strife and suffering the worst extremes in war. You say, however, that it is not through lack of education or ignorance, but voluntarily, that the unjust are unjust. And yet you dare to say that injustice is a shameful thing, hated by the gods. How then could anyone choose such an evil voluntarily? "By being overcome by pleasures," you might say. But is not being "overcome" involuntary, if "overcoming" is voluntary? Thus, reason proves in every way that acting unjustly is involuntary, and that every man, both privately and publicly in the cities, ought to take more care than they currently do. These things, Socrates, when I hear you say them so often, I admire greatly and praise wonderfully. And when...

# C L I T O P H O N, O R, 
->T H E   E X H O R T A T I O N.<-

->S O C R A T E S, C L I T O P H O N.<-

<image-desc>Decorative historiated initial 'V' featuring floral and leafy scrollwork within a rectangular border.</image-desc>
**SOCRATES:** Recently a certain person reported to me that Clitophon, the son of Aristonymus, speaking with Lysias, was finding fault with Socrates’ company, but greatly praising that of Thrasymachus. **CLITOPHON:** Whoever that was, Socrates, he did not rightly narrate what I said of you with Lysias. For in certain things I praised you, in others not at all. But since you are clearly angry with me, although you pretend to care nothing for it, I will most gladly relate those things to you myself, especially since we are alone, so that you do not think I despise you so much. For perhaps you have heard an incorrect report, and thus you are rendered more hostile to me than is fitting. But if you give me the power to speak freely, I will most gladly tell you the matter. **SOCRATES:** Indeed it would be too shameful if I did not tolerate you when you wish to be of use to me. For it is established that when I understand in what way I am bad and in what way good, I shall turn away from the worse things with all my strength, and follow the better. **CLITOPHON:** Listen then. Indeed, while living with you, Socrates, I was many times vehemently astonished while I heard you speak, and you seemed to me to speak most excellently of all, whenever, rebuking men like a God suddenly appearing from a theatrical machine, you cried out: "Whither do you rush, O men? You know not where you are being carried, nor do you do anything that is required, <margin>A Proverb.</margin> you who lean with all your zeal toward piling up money, but neglect the sons to whom you will leave it. You do not commend them to teachers of justice who might show them how to use it justly—if justice can be taught—and if it is to be acquired by exercise and custom, who might diligently train them. Nor do you even care for yourselves. But when you see that you and your sons have attained a sufficiency of letters, music, and gymnastics, which you think to be a perfect discipline of virtue, and yet you are nonetheless wicked regarding money, why do you not despise this present education? Why do you not seek some who will free you from this lack of musical harmony? For because of this fault and sluggishness—more so than because of a foot moving out of sync with a lyre—brother turns against brother, and city against city in immoderate and discordant sedition, and they suffer and inflict the worst when battle is joined. But you say that it is not because of rudeness and ignorance, but by their own will, that those who are unjust are unjust. And again you do not hesitate to assert that injustice is a shameful thing, and odious to God. For what reason, then, would anyone choose such a great evil of his own will? You answer that a man undergoes this because he is overcome by pleasures. But is not being overcome against one's will, given that to overcome is from the will? Therefore, reason utterly convinces us that acting unjustly is against the will. Thus it is fitting that all men privately, and cities publicly, apply a more diligent care than is customary. <margin>It is fitting. Whenever I hear you saying these things, Socrates, I am wonderfully</margin> delighted and I praise you, and I do the same when I listen to what follows.

<meta>This page continues the dialogue "Clitophon," which is often attributed to Plato. In the previous section, Socrates was praising the pursuit of virtue. Here, Clitophon—a student of politics and a critic of Socrates's method—is responding. He recounts Socrates’s frequent arguments about the soul and body, but expresses frustration that Socrates only exhorts people to be virtuous without ever explaining what virtue actually *is* or how to achieve its specific results.</meta>

### OF PLATO

<margin>A</margin> **CLITOPHON:** You also say the following things in sequence: that those who exercise their bodies but neglect their souls are doing something similar to neglecting the ruler while being constantly busy with the subject <note>original: "subiectum," the part that is ruled</note>. Furthermore, you say that for anyone who does not know how to use a thing, it is better to let its use be. If, then, a person does not know how to use their eyes, or their ears, or their whole body, it is better for that person neither to hear, nor to see, nor to use their body in any other way, rather than to use it poorly. The same applies to the arts <note>original: "artibus" / "τέχναι" (techne), meaning skills or crafts</note>. For whoever does not know how to use their own lyre clearly does not know how to use their neighbor’s lyre either, as you yourself say. And whoever does not know how to use the instruments of others does not know how to use their own, nor any other tool or possession. And your argument finally proceeds beautifully to this conclusion: that for whoever does not know how to use their soul, it is better for that person to let their soul be at rest and not to live, rather than to live and be their own master in acting. If some necessity compels <margin>B</margin> such a person to live, it is better for them to lead their life as a slave rather than a free man. This is just like a ship: it is better to hand over the "rudders of thought" to someone else who has acquired the discipline of "piloting" human life—which you, Socrates, often call the Political art, and also identify as judgment and justice. To these speeches and many others of the same kind and great beauty—which assert that virtue can be taught and command a person to take care of themselves above all—I have almost never offered opposition, nor do I think I shall ever oppose them in the future. For I consider them extremely useful and highly effective for exhortation, serving to rouse men as if they were <margin>C</margin> sleeping. Therefore, I applied my mind as one who was about to hear what remained. I questioned not you first, O Socrates, but your equals, your companions, your associates, or whatever else they should be called. Of these, I questioned those who are held in highest regard by you before all others, asking what discourse would follow next. Following your custom, I set forth the question in this way: "O best of men, in what way," I said, "ought we now to receive Socrates's exhortations to virtue? Is this the only thing that exists, a mere walking forth, while the actual work and the completion of the thing are neglected? But surely this will be <margin>D</margin> our duty throughout our whole life: to provoke those who are not yet sufficiently stirred, and so always to exhort one another in turn. Or rather, since we and Socrates do not deny that this very thing must be done, should we inquire: what comes next? From where shall we begin the study of justice?" Suppose someone was exhorting us to care for the body—just as if we were children who paid no attention to gymnastics or medicine—and rebuked us because we were always thinking about wheat, barley, and vines, and all the things we seek for the sake of the body, yet we sought no art or industry by which the body's good condition is achieved, even though such an art exists. <margin>E</margin> Perhaps we would ask him what arts he says exist regarding the care of the body, and he would, I think, answer "medicine" and "gymnastics." In the same way now, let whoever seems to themselves to be most skilled in these matters answer: what art do we consider to be concerned with the virtue of the soul? One of those who seemed most robust answered me: "This art is no other than that which you heard from Socrates: know that it is justice." Then I said, "Do not merely bring me the name, but explain it further in this way: Medicine is called a certain art. From this, two things result: physicians are produced from physicians, and health is restored. One of these is no longer an art itself, but the 'work' <note>original: "opus" / "ἔργον" (ergon), the product or result of a skill</note> of the art being taught and perceived, which we call health. <margin>F</margin> Similarly, from architecture two things result: a building and the art of architecture; the former is the work, the latter is the teaching. Let justice likewise be the making of others to be just, as each of the previous craftsmen does. But what other *work* can the just man produce for us? Declare it." One person answered, I believe, "the contributing," another "the fitting," another "the conducive," and another "the useful." But I replied and objected that these same names exist in every art: for in each, things are said to be done and called useful, conducive, and other things of this kind. However, each art has its own specific goal toward which these names look. For example, in the craft of carpentry, what is said to be good, beautiful, and fitting tends toward this: that from wooden material, furniture is aptly made—which is not the art itself, but the work of the art. Let the work of justice itself be stated similarly." Here, <margin>G</margin> one of your associates, Socrates, answered—and he seemed to speak most elegantly. "The work specific to justice," he said, "which belongs to no other faculty, is to produce friendship in cities." He, in turn, being questioned, asserted that friendship was a certain good and never an evil. But when he was questioned about the "friendships" of children or animals, which we commonly call friendships, he denied that they were true friendships, since they often do more harm than good. He said those are falsely called friendships, for true friendship is undoubtedly concord <note>original: "consenſionem" / "ὁμόνοιαν" (homonoia), a 'oneness of mind'</note>. When he was then asked whether he called that concord a "concurrence of opinion" or "knowledge" <note>original: "ſcientiae" / "ἐπιστήμην" (episteme)</note>, he looked down upon opinion, because many concurrences of opinion among men are harmful. But he had confessed that friendship was an entirely good thing and the work of justice. Therefore, he said that concord and knowledge are the same thing, not opinion. <margin>H</margin> When we had been brought to this point in the conversation, the listeners, being in doubt, immediately cried out against him, saying that the argument had revolved back to the same place. For they said medicine is also concord...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> **CLITOPHON:** ...You further say that those who exercise the body but neglect the soul do something similar: they neglect the ruler and are always busy with the subject. You say that for anyone who does not know how to use a thing, it is better to leave off its use. If, then, a person does not know how to use their eyes, or their ears, or their whole body, it is better for that person neither to hear, nor to see, nor to use their body in any other way, rather than to use it poorly. The same applies to the arts. For whoever does not know how to use their own lyre clearly does not know how to use their neighbor’s lyre either. And whoever does not know how to use the instruments of others does not know how to use their own, nor any other tool or possession. And your argument finally proceeds beautifully to this conclusion: that for whoever does not know how to use their <margin>B</margin> soul, it is better for that person to let their soul be at rest and not to live, rather than to live and act on his own. If some necessity forces him to live, it is better for such a person to spend his life as a slave rather than a free man. Just as with a ship, it is better to hand over the rudders to the thought of another who has learned the art of piloting human life—which you, Socrates, often call the "Political art," and you say this same thing is judgment and justice. To these speeches and many others of the same kind and great beauty—which assert that virtue can be taught and command a person to take care of themselves above all—I have almost never offered opposition, nor do I think I shall ever oppose them in the future. For I consider them most clear and useful, and <margin>C</margin> truly capable of waking us as if we were sleeping. Therefore, I applied my mind to what would follow, as one who was about to hear. I questioned not you first, Socrates, but your equals, those who share your desires, your companions, or whatever else they should be called in relation to you. Of those who are most highly regarded by you, I first asked them what discourse would follow after this. And in your manner, I proposed the question to them: "O best of men," I said, "how are we to receive Socrates's exhortation to virtue? As if this were truly the only thing, but that we should never move on to the <margin>D</margin> actual practice and grasp it perfectly? Will this be our work throughout our whole life: to exhort those who are not yet turned toward virtue, and they in turn to others? Or should we ask Socrates and one another what follows this, once we agree that this is what a man must do? What comes after that? How do we say the learning of justice must begin?" It is as if someone were to exhort us to care for the body, seeing that we (like children) have no foresight of the fact that there are such things as gymnastics and medicine. Then he might reproach us, saying it is a shame to put all our care into wheat, barley, vines, and everything we labor for and acquire for the sake of the body, <margin>E</margin> while finding no art or device for the body itself so that it might be as good as possible—even though such an art exists. If we then asked the one exhorting us, "What arts are you talking about?" he would perhaps say "gymnastics" and "medicine." And now, let it be said: what do we say is the art that concerns the virtue of the soul? The one who seemed most robust among them, answering this, said to me: "This art is the very one you hear Socrates speaking of; what else is it but justice?" And when I said, "Do not tell me the name only, but tell me this: Medicine is an art. Its results are two-fold: one is to produce new physicians to join those who already exist; the other is health. <margin>F</margin> One of these is no longer the art itself, but the work of the art that teaches and is being learned—which we call health. Similarly, in carpentry there is a house and the art of carpentry; one is the work, the other is the teaching. So too with justice: one part is to make others just, just as the other arts make craftsmen. But what is the *other* work that the just man can perform for us? Tell us." This man, I believe, answered "the beneficial"; another "the fitting"; another "the useful"; another "the profitable." I then returned to the argument, saying that these names also exist in each of the arts—to act rightly, profitably, usefully, and so on. But each art will state its own *unique* goal toward which all these things tend. For example, in carpentry, acting well, beautifully, and as is fitting results in the natural creation of wooden vessels—which are not the art itself. Let the work of justice be stated in the same way." Finally, <margin>G</margin> one of your companions, Socrates (who seemed to speak most elegantly), answered me that this is the unique work of justice, belonging to no other faculty: to produce friendship in cities. When he was questioned further, he said that friendship was a good and never an evil. But when he was asked about the "friendships" of children or wild animals, which we call by this name, he would not accept them as friendships upon further questioning. For he said it happens that most such things are harmful rather than good. He said such things are not friendships at all, and those who name them so speak falsely. He said that true and real friendship is most clearly "concord" <note>original: "homonoia"</note>. When asked if he meant concord was "agreement in opinion" or "knowledge" <note>original: "episteme"</note>, he rejected agreement in opinion. For many harmful agreements in opinion arise among men. But he had agreed that friendship was entirely a good thing and the work of justice. Thus he said that concord and knowledge are the same thing, <margin>H</margin> not opinion. But at this point in the discourse, those present were at a loss and were able to seize upon the same point, saying that the argument had run around in a circle to the same point as the first people; they were saying that medicine is also a concord...

# CRATYLUS.

medicine, and the other arts, can declare what they are and what they deal with. But as for this thing you call justice, or harmony, it remains hidden where it leads or what its work is. I have asked you these same things, Socrates. At first, you said the work of justice was to benefit friends and harm enemies. But later, it seemed to you that a just man never harms anyone, but rather benefits everyone in everything. This has been tried not just once, Socrates, or twice; but having followed you as a persistent seeker for a long time, I have finally given up. I believe you are the best of men at inflaming people to take up the study of virtue. But of two things, one must be true: either you only have power up to this point and no further <note>Clitophon is suggesting Socrates is like a salesman who can praise a skill but doesn't actually possess the skill itself.</note>—which can happen in any art, such as a man who does not know how to steer a ship but has composed praises for the art of navigation to draw people to it—or you do not know justice yourself, despite your beautiful praises of it. I do not think this is the case, however. I think one of two other things: either you do not know, or you are unwilling to share it with me. For this reason, I will go to Thrasymachus <note>Thrasymachus was a famous Sophist known for his cynical view that "justice is the advantage of the stronger."</note>, I think, and anywhere else I can, hoping to be freed from my doubts. If you would be willing to stop these exhortations with me, I would listen. Just as if you had already urged me enough to care for the body through gymnastics, you would then explain what sort of condition my body is in and what treatment it needs; let the same happen now. Grant that Clitophon concedes it is ridiculous to put effort into other things while neglecting the soul, for whose sake everything else is labored. Consider me to have said all the other things that follow from this. I beg you, Socrates, do not do otherwise; lest, just as now, I must partly praise you and partly blame you before Lysias and others. For to a man who has not yet been exhorted toward virtue, you bring much help...

<column-break/>

and the remaining arts can declare what they are and what they revolve around. But indeed, this justice of yours, as you call it, or harmony—where it returns or what its work might be—remains hidden. I have finally asked you these same things, Socrates. You, indeed, immediately said that the work of justice is to benefit friends and to harm enemies. Afterwards, however, it seemed to you that a just man never harms anyone, but benefits each person in all things. These things, O Socrates, have been attempted not just once or twice; but since I have followed you for a long time as a suppliant, I have finally been exhausted, thinking that you are more fit than others for inflaming men so that they take up the study of virtue. But of two things, one is necessary: either you are only capable to that extent and nothing beyond—which can happen in any art, just as it can happen in the art of navigation that someone who does not know how to steer has devised certain praises of that art with which he may call men to it, as if it were most worthy—and in the other arts in the same way. Perhaps someone would attribute the same to you: as if you know justice itself no more than anyone else, even though you praise it excellently. However, I do not think so. For of two things, I say: either I think you do not know, or you are unwilling to communicate it with me. For which reason I shall betake myself to Thrasymachus, as I think, and to wherever else I can, and I shall hope to be freed from doubt. Nor would I betake myself elsewhere if you yourself were willing to make an end of those exhortations. Furthermore, just as if you had already sufficiently incited me to the care of the body which belongs to gymnastics, after such an exhortation you would open to me what the condition of my body might be and what kind of care it might need; so do in the present case. Assume that Clitophon concedes to you that it is ridiculous for someone to place effort in other things while neglecting the soul, for whose sake one labors in other things, and consider me to have repeated all the other things that follow after these and have just been said. I beseech you, Socrates, do not do otherwise, lest, as now, so also hereafter in the presence of Lysias and other men, it be necessary to partly praise you and partly to blame you. For to him who has not yet been exhorted toward virtue, you bring the greatest...

# CRATYLUS, OR, ON THE CORRECTNESS OF NAMES.
## Logical.

# CRATYLUS, OR, ON THE CORRECT RATIO OF NAMES.
## Concerning speech or reason.

> **SUMMARY OF THE DIALOGUE.** The thesis, as the title itself displays, is *On the correctness of names*, that is, from where names obtain their true and genuine calling. Two opinions are proposed concerning this correctness of names. First: That a natural ratio of names is innate and implanted in all men by nature; that is, that names are truly such as the nature of the things themselves was, and not from the constitution of men. Second: That names are imposed from the pacts and conventions of men, and are nothing other than what was established by the judgment and will of men. However, there exist certain primitive names which, established by those ancient authors and indeed by a power greater than is human, are the foundation of the rest of the words. From there, however, such a great confusion of words has arisen that, obscured by long spans of years, the traces of those first words are hardly recognized, if at all; these are seen better in certain barbarian <note>In the Greek context, "barbarian" simply referred to anyone who did not speak Greek.</note> languages than in Greek. Three of Plato’s own teachers dispute this: Hermogenes, Cratylus, and Socrates. Hermogenes (a most thoughtful follower of Parmenides and the Pythagoreans, who believe all things remain stable) thinks names have force by a certain natural reason. Cratylus, on the contrary (a follower of Heraclitus and other ancients who thought nothing is ever stable), thinks they are established by judgment alone. Socrates, however, to whose judgment they submit themselves, seems to lean more toward the opinion of Cratylus.

HERMOGENES, CRATYLUS, SOCRATES.

<margin>D</margin> **H**ERMOGENES: Is it your will, then, that we share our conversation with Socrates here? **CRATYLUS:** If it seems good to you. **HERMOGENES:** Cratylus here says, O Socrates, that there is a natural correctness of names for each of the things that exist; and that this is not a name—whatever some people, having agreed to call it, may call it, pronouncing a particle of their own voice—but that a certain correctness of names is innate to both Greeks and Barbarians, the same for all. I ask him, therefore, whether Cratylus is truly his name or not. He confesses it is. "And for Socrates," I said, "what name?" He says, "Socrates." "Is it not then for all others," I said, "that each name by which we call them is the name for each?" 
He replied, "But your name is not Hermogenes <note>The name "Hermogenes" literally means "born of Hermes." Hermes was the god of gain and luck; Hermogenes was famously poor/unlucky, which is why Cratylus says the name doesn't truly fit him.</note>, even if all men should call you so." And while I beseech him to open to me what he means by my questioning, he declares nothing at all, but playing with me, he pretends he is turning something over in his mind, as if he understands something about this matter which, if he wished to express it, would force me to confess that very thing and to say the same things he says. For which reason, I would gladly hear from you if you can guess the prophecy of Cratylus; yet I would more gladly hear your own opinion about the correctness of names, if indeed it pleases you.
<margin>E</margin> **SOCRATES:** O Hermogenes, son of Hipponicus, it is said in an old proverb that "Beautiful things are difficult to know." And indeed, that knowledge of names is no small matter. If I had already heard that fifty-drachma <note>A drachma was a significant unit of currency; fifty drachmae would be a very expensive, "premium" lecture.</note> demonstration from Prodicus, in whose teaching this was also included, as he himself testifies, nothing would prevent you from immediately understanding the truth about the correctness of names. But I have never heard it; I have only heard the one-drachma version. Therefore, I do not know what is true in these matters, but I am ready to investigate it together with you and with Cratylus. But as for what he says to you...

# PLATO

...that the name "Hermogenes" <note>The name Hermogenes literally means "born of Hermes." Hermes was the god of profit and luck; Socrates is teasing Hermogenes because, despite his name, he was famously unsuccessful in financial matters.</note> is not your name in reality, which is said to come from "gain," bites you, I think—as if you were greedy for money and failed to obtain it. But, as I was just saying, these things are difficult to know. However, it is necessary to investigate by bringing the arguments of both sides into the open, to see whether it is as you yourself say, or rather as Cratylus says. **HERMOGENES:** Indeed, Socrates, although I have already disputed this frequently with him and many others, I cannot yet be persuaded that there is any other "correctness" of a name than convention and agreement. It seems to me that whatever name anyone gives to a thing, that is the correct one. And if he changes it again and gives it another, the second name is no less correct than the first, just as we are accustomed to change the names of our servants. For no name belongs to any thing by nature, but only by the law and custom of those who have become used to calling it such. If the matter is otherwise, I am ready to listen and learn not only from Cratylus, but from anyone else. **SOCRATES:** Perhaps you have a point, Hermogenes. Let us consider: whatever name someone gives to a thing and calls it by, you assert that is its name? **HERMOGENES:** It certainly seems so to me. **SOCRATES:** And whether a private citizen calls it so, or a whole city? **HERMOGENES:** I assert it. **SOCRATES:** What then? If I myself call something—for instance, if what we now call a "man," I were to name a "horse," and what we call a "horse," I were to name a "man"—publicly the name for that thing would be "man," but privately it would be "horse," and then again privately "man" but publicly "horse." Is that how you speak? **HERMOGENES:** It seems so. **SOCRATES:** Tell me again, do you say that some speech is true, and some is false? **HERMOGENES:** I do indeed. **SOCRATES:** Would not that which speaks the truth be "true speech," and the other "false speech"? **HERMOGENES:** Exactly so. **SOCRATES:** And is the speech that describes things as they exist "true," and that which describes them as they do not exist "false"? **HERMOGENES:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** Is this then what it means—to say in speech those things that are and those that are not? **HERMOGENES:** That is it. **SOCRATES:** Regarding speech that is true: is it true as a whole, while its parts are not true? **HERMOGENES:** No, the parts are also true. **SOCRATES:** Are the large parts true, while the tiny little particles are false, or are they all true? **HERMOGENES:** All of them, I think. **SOCRATES:** Do you consider any part of speech smaller than the name? **HERMOGENES:** Not at all; this is the smallest part. **SOCRATES:** And this name is a part of true speech? **HERMOGENES:** Without a doubt. **SOCRATES:** Then it is a true part, as you say yourself. **HERMOGENES:** True. **SOCRATES:** And is the part of false speech not false? **HERMOGENES:** I say it is. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, it is permitted to call a name "true" and a name "false," if indeed one can say the same of speech. **HERMOGENES:** What prevents it? **SOCRATES:** Whatever name someone says a thing has, that is its name? **HERMOGENES:** That very thing. **SOCRATES:** Even if someone gives as many names to a thing as he likes, will it have that many? And also whenever he gives them? I have no other "correctness" of a name, Socrates, other than this: that it is permitted for me to call a thing by one name that I have given it, and for you to call it by another that you have given it. Thus I see in cities that some things have their own names, both among Greeks compared to other Greeks, and among Greeks compared to Barbarians <note>In this context, "Barbarian" refers to any non-Greek speaker.</note>. **SOCRATES:** Let us observe, Hermogenes, whether the things themselves seem to you to behave in such a way—that the essence of things is private to each person, as Protagoras taught. He said that "man is the measure of all things," <note>Protagoras (c. 490–420 BCE) was a Sophist philosopher who argued for relativism: that "truth" is merely what appears true to an individual.</note> so that as each thing appears to me, so it is for me; and as it appears to you, so it is for you. Or do you rather think that things have some firmness in their own essence? **HERMOGENES:** Sometimes, Socrates, in my doubts I have been led to what Protagoras taught. However, I am not quite persuaded that it is so. **SOCRATES:** Have you ever been led to the point where it seemed to you that no man was entirely evil? **HERMOGENES:** No, by Jove! Indeed, I have often been so affected as to think that some men were entirely evil, and quite many of them. **SOCRATES:** And have no men ever appeared entirely good to you? **HERMOGENES:** Very few. **SOCRATES:** But some have appeared so? **HERMOGENES:** Some. **SOCRATES:** On what basis do you judge this? On this basis: that some are entirely good and entirely wise, while others are altogether wicked and entirely unwise? **HERMOGENES:** It certainly seems so to me. **SOCRATES:** If Protagoras spoke the truth, and this is the "Truth" itself—that things are as they seem to each person—can it be possible that some men are wise and others unwise? **HERMOGENES:** Not at all. **SOCRATES:** And yet this, I think, would be unwise of you: to think Protagoras could speak the truth entirely. For one would not truly be wiser than another if what appears to each is true for each. **HERMOGENES:** That is so. **SOCRATES:** But neither do you agree with Euthydemus <note>Euthydemus was a Sophist who argued that all properties belong to all things at all times, making distinction impossible.</note>, I think, who says that all things belong to everyone similarly and always. For then some would not be good and others evil, if virtue and wickedness were present always and equally in everyone. **HERMOGENES:** You speak the truth. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, if neither do all things belong to everyone always and similarly, nor is each thing private to the individual, it is established that the things themselves have some firm essence within them. They are not dragged up and down by our imagination relative to us, but remain according to themselves in relation to their own essence, as they are established by nature. **HERMOGENES:** The same seems true to me as well, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Do the things themselves exist thus by nature, while their actions do not, but exist otherwise? Or are actions themselves also a certain species of things? **HERMOGENES:** They are entirely so. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, actions themselves are performed according to their own nature, not according to our opinion. Just as if we should decide to cut some object...

...the name Hermogenes in truth, just as if we were looking at what is just. It seems perhaps that you are longing for the acquisition of money, wherever you might have it in you.
