Setting it out for common consideration, we must look to see whether it is as you say, or as Cratylus says. **HERMOGENES:** And indeed, Socrates, having already spoken frequently with this man and many others, I cannot be persuaded that there is any other correctness of a name than agreement and convention. For it seems to me that whatever name anyone gives to something, that is the correct one; and if he then changes it to another, and no longer calls it by the first, the later one is no less correct than the former—just as we change the names of our servants. For no name has grown naturally for any individual thing, but rather by law and custom of those who have established the habit and the calling. If it is otherwise in any way, I am ready both to learn and to hear, not only from Cratylus, but from anyone else whatsoever. **SOCRATES:** Perhaps indeed you have a point, Hermogenes; let us examine it. Whatever one decides to call each thing, is that the name for each? **HERMOGENES:** It seems so to me. **SOCRATES:** And whether a private person calls it so, or a city? **HERMOGENES:** I say so. **SOCRATES:** What then? If I call any of the things that exist—for instance, that which we now call "man"—if I address this as "horse," and that which we now call "horse" as "man," will there be publicly the name "man" for the same thing, but privately "horse"? and privately "man," but publicly "horse"? Is that what you mean? **HERMOGENES:** It seems so to me. **SOCRATES:** Come then, tell me this: do you call something "speaking the truth" and "speaking falsely"? **HERMOGENES:** I do. **SOCRATES:** Then would there be a speech that is true, and one that is false? **HERMOGENES:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** Is that which says things as they are, "true"? And that which says them as they are not, "false"? **HERMOGENES:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** Is it possible, then, to say things that are and things that are not in speech? **HERMOGENES:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** Regarding true speech: is it true as a whole, while the parts of it are not true? **HERMOGENES:** No; the parts are also true. **SOCRATES:** Are the large parts true, while the small ones are not? Or are they all true? **HERMOGENES:** All of them, I think. **SOCRATES:** Is there any other part of speech you say is smaller than a name? **HERMOGENES:** No; this is the smallest. **SOCRATES:** And is the name also said to be part of the true speech? **HERMOGENES:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** And it is true, as you say? **HERMOGENES:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** And is the part of the false speech not false? **HERMOGENES:** I say so. **SOCRATES:** Is it possible then to speak of a false name and a true one, if indeed one can speak of a false and true speech? **HERMOGENES:** How could it not be? **SOCRATES:** Then whatever each person says is the name for something, that is the name for it? **HERMOGENES:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** And as many names as someone says belong to each thing, that many are there, and at the time when he says it? **HERMOGENES:** For I, Socrates, have no other correctness of a name but this: that for me it is one thing to call each thing by a name which I have established, and for you another, which you might establish. And so I see it with cities, that names are established privately for each for the same things—for Greeks compared to other Greeks, and for Greeks compared to barbarians. **SOCRATES:** Come then, let us see, Hermogenes, whether the things that exist also seem to you to be this way: that their essence is private to each person, as Protagoras said—saying that "man is the measure of all things." So that as things appear to me, such they are for me, and as they appear to you, such they are for you? Or do they seem to you to have some stability of their own essence? **HERMOGENES:** Already once before, Socrates, being at a loss, I was even carried away into what Protagoras says; however, it does not quite seem to me to be that way. **SOCRATES:** What then? Have you already been carried away to the point that it does not seem to you at all that there is such a thing as a wicked man? **HERMOGENES:** No, by Zeus! Rather, I have often experienced this, so that it seems to me there are some very wicked men, and in quite great numbers. **SOCRATES:** What then? Have very good men never yet seemed to exist to you? **HERMOGENES:** Very few. **SOCRATES:** But they have seemed to exist? **HERMOGENES:** To me, yes. **SOCRATES:** How then do you establish this? Is it thus: those who are very good are very wise, and those who are very wicked are very foolish? **HERMOGENES:** It seems so to me. **SOCRATES:** Is it possible then, if Protagoras spoke the truth and this is the "Truth"—that things are as they seem to each—that some of us are wise and others are foolish? **HERMOGENES:** Not at all. **SOCRATES:** And this (as I think) seems very clear to you: that if wisdom exists and also foolishness, it is not quite possible for Protagoras to be speaking the truth. For one person would not in truth be any wiser than another, if indeed whatever seems to each will be true for each. **HERMOGENES:** That is so. **SOCRATES:** But surely you do not think, according to Euthydemus, that all things are for everyone similarly at the same time and always. For then some would not be good and others wicked, if virtue and vice were similarly and always for everyone. **HERMOGENES:** You speak the truth. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, if neither are all things similarly for everyone at the same time and always, nor is each of the things that exist private to each person, it is clear then that the things themselves possess some stable essence of their own. They are not relative to us, nor are they dragged up and down by us by our own fancy, but they are also according to themselves, having their own essence as they are by nature. **HERMOGENES:** It seems to me, Socrates, to be so. **SOCRATES:** Would then the things themselves be this way by nature, while their actions would not be in the same manner? Or are actions themselves also one species of the things that exist? **HERMOGENES:** Certainly, they are too. **SOCRATES:** Then actions are performed according to their own nature as well, and not according to our opinion. For instance, if we should attempt to cut any of the things that exist...

<summary>Socrates and Hermogenes debate the nature of names, with Hermogenes arguing they are arbitrary conventions and Socrates suggesting they must correspond to the objective essence of things. Socrates refutes the radical relativism of Protagoras and Euthydemus to show that things (and actions) have a stable, natural reality independent of human opinion.</summary>
<keywords>Cratylus, Socrates, Hermogenes, Protagoras, Euthydemus, philosophy of language, relativism, essence, naming conventions, truth in speech</keywords>

--- Page 291 ---
<meta>Continuing from the previous discussion where Socrates and Hermogenes debated whether names are purely arbitrary conventions or have an inherent "correctness." Socrates now begins a series of analogies to show that naming is a practical skill governed by the nature of reality, not just personal whim.</meta>

# CRATYLVS.

<margin>A</margin> **SOCRATES:** Should each thing be divided as we ourselves wish, and by whatever means we wish? Or rather, if we wish to cut each thing according to its nature—to cut and be cut in the way that is natural, and with the tool that is natural—will we succeed and perform the action correctly? But if we act contrary to nature, will we fail and accomplish nothing?
**HERMOGENES:** It seems so to me.
**SOCRATES:** And so, if we attempt to burn something, we should not burn according to any random opinion, but according to the correct one? That is, in the way that each thing is naturally suited to burn and be burned, and with the natural tool.
**HERMOGENES:** That is true.
<margin>B</margin> **SOCRATES:** Does the same reasoning not apply to everything else?
**HERMOGENES:** Certainly.
**SOCRATES:** Is not speaking also one of these actions?
**HERMOGENES:** Yes.
**SOCRATES:** Then will a man speak correctly if he speaks as he thinks he should speak? Or rather, if he speaks in the way that nature requires things to be spoken and heard, and uses the tool that nature intended for it, will he succeed and truly say something? But if he does otherwise, will he fail and achieve nothing?
**HERMOGENES:** I believe it is as you say.
**SOCRATES:** Now, is not naming a part of speaking? For it is by naming that people carry out their speech.
**HERMOGENES:** Quite so.
**SOCRATES:** And is not naming also an action, if indeed speaking was an action concerning things?
**HERMOGENES:** Yes.
**SOCRATES:** But we have seen that actions do not depend on us, but possess a certain private nature of their own.
**HERMOGENES:** That is so.
**SOCRATES:** Therefore, we must name things in the way that <margin>C</margin> the nature of the things themselves requires them to be named, and with the proper tool—not according to our own will, if we are to remain consistent with what was said before. In this way, we might accomplish something and name things rightly, but not otherwise?
**HERMOGENES:** So it appears to me.
**SOCRATES:** Tell me then, that which was to be cut required something to cut with, did it not?
**HERMOGENES:** Yes.
**SOCRATES:** And that which was to be woven required something to weave with? And that which was to be bored required something to bore with?
**HERMOGENES:** Certainly.
**SOCRATES:** And that which was to be named required something to name with?
**HERMOGENES:** Indeed.
**SOCRATES:** What is the tool with which we bore?
**HERMOGENES:** A drill.
**SOCRATES:** And what is the tool with which we weave?
**HERMOGENES:** A shuttle. <note>The original Greek text uses 'kerkis' (κερκίς), while the Latin uses 'radius pecténque.' In ancient weaving, the shuttle or comb was used to separate the threads of the warp and press the weft together.</note>
<margin>D</margin> **SOCRATES:** And what is the tool with which we name?
**HERMOGENES:** A name.
**SOCRATES:** Well said. So the name is also a kind of tool.
**HERMOGENES:** It is.
**SOCRATES:** If I were to ask what kind of tool the shuttle is, would you not say it is that with which we weave?
**HERMOGENES:** Yes.
**SOCRATES:** And what do we do when we weave? Do we not separate the web and the warp that were tangled together?
**HERMOGENES:** Exactly.
**SOCRATES:** And you would say the same of the drill and other tools?
**HERMOGENES:** Certainly.
**SOCRATES:** Can you say the same about the name? Since the name is a tool, what do we do when we name?
**HERMOGENES:** I cannot say.
**SOCRATES:** Do we not teach one another something, and distinguish things according to how they are?
**HERMOGENES:** Indeed we do.
<margin>E</margin> **SOCRATES:** <margin>A name is an instrument for teaching and discerning the substance of things.</margin> A name, therefore, is an instrument for teaching and for distinguishing the nature <note>original: οὐσίας (ousia) / Latin: substantias. This refers to the true essence or "being" of a thing.</note> of things, just as the shuttle is for the fabric.
**HERMOGENES:** Yes.
**SOCRATES:** Now, the shuttle is a tool for weaving?
**HERMOGENES:** Of course.
**SOCRATES:** The weaver, then, will use the shuttle well—and "well" means in the manner of a weaver. And the teacher will use the name well—and "well" means in the manner of a teacher.
**HERMOGENES:** Yes.
**SOCRATES:** Whose work does the weaver use well when he uses the shuttle?
**HERMOGENES:** The carpenter's.
**SOCRATES:** And is every man a carpenter, or only he who possesses the craft?
**HERMOGENES:** Only he who possesses the craft.
**SOCRATES:** And whose work does the borer use well when he uses the drill?
**HERMOGENES:** The blacksmith's.
**SOCRATES:** And is every man a blacksmith, or only he who possesses the craft?
**HERMOGENES:** Only he who possesses the craft.
**SOCRATES:** Very well. And whose work will the teacher use when he uses the name?
**HERMOGENES:** I do not know that either.
**SOCRATES:** Can you not even say who provides us with the names we use?
**HERMOGENES:** Not at all.
**SOCRATES:** Does it not seem to you that the law provides them?
**HERMOGENES:** It <margin>F</margin> seems so.
**SOCRATES:** Therefore, the teacher will be using the work of the **lawgiver** <note>original: νομοθέτου (nomothetou). Socrates suggests language is a set of "laws" or "customs" established by a foundational creator.</note> when he uses a name.
**HERMOGENES:** I believe so.
**SOCRATES:** And does every man seem to you to be a lawgiver, or only he who possesses the craft?
**HERMOGENES:** Only he who possesses the craft.
**SOCRATES:** Then it is not the task of every man, Hermogenes, to establish a name, but only for a certain "maker of names." And this person, it seems, is the lawgiver—the rarest of all craftsmen among men.
**HERMOGENES:** So it seems.
**SOCRATES:** Come then, consider what the lawgiver looks toward when he establishes names. Look at the previous examples: what does the carpenter look toward when he makes a shuttle? Is it not toward something that is naturally suited for weaving?
**HERMOGENES:** Certainly.
**SOCRATES:** What if the shuttle breaks while he is making it? Will he make another by looking <margin>G</margin> at the broken one, or will he look toward that very **Form** <note>original: εἶδος (eidos). This is a central concept in Plato’s philosophy: the ideal, perfect version of an object that exists in the mind or a divine realm, which the craftsman tries to copy.</note> which he looked toward when he made the first one?
**HERMOGENES:** Toward that Form, I believe.
**SOCRATES:** And might we not most rightly call that "the Shuttle itself"?
**HERMOGENES:** I think so.
**SOCRATES:** Then, whenever it is necessary to make a shuttle for a fine garment, or a thick one, or for linen, or for wool, or for any other kind, must they not all possess the **Form** of the shuttle? Must he not give to each its natural character in the way that is best for its specific work?
**HERMOGENES:** Yes.
**SOCRATES:** And the same applies to all other tools. Once the tool that is naturally suited for each task is discovered, one must embody it in the material from which it is made—not however the craftsman might wish, but as nature itself requires. For he must know how to embody in iron the drill that is naturally suited <margin>H</margin> for each purpose.
**HERMOGENES:** Certainly.
**SOCRATES:** And the shuttle that is naturally suited for each task...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Is each thing to be divided as we wish and with what we wish? Or rather, if we divide each thing according to its nature—by which it is necessary to divide and be divided—and likewise with that by which a division ought to occur according to nature, will we not divide correctly and achieve something useful? But if we act against nature, will we go astray and achieve nothing? **HERMOGENES:** It seems so to me. **SOCRATES:** And if we attempt to burn something, we must not do it according to any random opinion, but according to the correct one—which is the manner in which a thing is naturally meant to burn and be burned, and with the proper tool. **HERMOGENES:** These things are true. <margin>B</margin> **SOCRATES:** Is not the same reasoning true for other things? **HERMOGENES:** The same. **SOCRATES:** And is not speaking also one of these operations? **HERMOGENES:** It certainly is. **SOCRATES:** Will he speak correctly who speaks as he thinks he should? Or rather he who speaks as the very nature of things requires them to be spoken and heard? If he speaks as nature demands, he will achieve something; if otherwise, he will err and accomplish nothing. **HERMOGENES:** I think as you say. **SOCRATES:** Is not a name a certain part of speaking? And do not those who name things speak in a certain way? **HERMOGENES:** Entirely. **SOCRATES:** And is naming not an action? Since speaking is an action concerning things. **HERMOGENES:** Exactly. **SOCRATES:** Actions, then, appeared to us not to look toward us, but to have a certain nature of their own. **HERMOGENES:** It is so. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, we must name according to the way the nature of the things themselves requires them to name and be named, and by the tool it requires—not according to the judgment of our own will, if we are to stand by what has been said. And thus we shall accomplish something and name things; otherwise, we shall not. **HERMOGENES:** It seems so to me. <margin>C</margin> **SOCRATES:** That which is to be cut, must it be cut with something? **HERMOGENES:** With something. **SOCRATES:** And that which is to be woven, must it be woven with something? And that which is to be bored, with something? **HERMOGENES:** Clearly. **SOCRATES:** Likewise, that which is to be named, must it be named with something? **HERMOGENES:** So it must be. **SOCRATES:** What is that with which one must bore? **HERMOGENES:** A drill. **SOCRATES:** What with which one weaves? **HERMOGENES:** The shuttle and comb. **SOCRATES:** What with which one names? **HERMOGENES:** A name. **SOCRATES:** Well spoken; therefore the name is a kind of instrument. **HERMOGENES:** It is. **SOCRATES:** If I asked what instrument the shuttle and comb are, you would answer: that with which we weave? **HERMOGENES:** Nothing else. **SOCRATES:** And what do we do when we weave? Do we not discern the threads of the warp and weft with the shuttle? **HERMOGENES:** That very thing. **SOCRATES:** Will you answer the same for the drill and the rest? **HERMOGENES:** The same. **SOCRATES:** Can you likewise declare concerning the name, what do we do when we name something with the name itself, which is an instrument? **HERMOGENES:** I cannot. <margin>D</margin> **SOCRATES:** Do we not teach one another something, and discern things as they are? **HERMOGENES:** Certainly. <margin>A name is an instrument for teaching and discerning the substance of things.</margin> **SOCRATES:** Therefore, a name is an instrument for teaching and discerning the substances of things, just as the comb and shuttle are for the web itself. **HERMOGENES:** So it must be said. **SOCRATES:** Furthermore, the shuttle is a tool for weaving. **HERMOGENES:** Why not? **SOCRATES:** The weaver, then, will use the shuttle and comb correctly—correctly, I say, according to the principle of weaving. But he who teaches will use a name, and correctly—correctly, clearly, according to the specific principle of teaching? **HERMOGENES:** Certainly. <margin>E</margin> **SOCRATES:** Whose work does the weaver use well when he uses the shuttle and comb? **HERMOGENES:** The carpenter's. **SOCRATES:** Any carpenter, or rather one who possesses the craft? **HERMOGENES:** One who has the craft. **SOCRATES:** Whose work does the borer use correctly when he uses the drill? **HERMOGENES:** The blacksmith's. **SOCRATES:** Is everyone a blacksmith? Or rather he who has the craft? **HERMOGENES:** He who has the craft. **SOCRATES:** Come then, say whose work the teacher himself uses whenever he uses a name. **HERMOGENES:** I do not know. **SOCRATES:** Do you not even know how to assign this? Who delivers to us the names we use? **HERMOGENES:** I am ignorant of this too. **SOCRATES:** Does it not seem to you that the law has established names for us? **HERMOGENES:** It seems so. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, the teacher will use the work of the **legislator** when he uses a name. **HERMOGENES:** I think so. **SOCRATES:** Does any man seem to you to be a maker of laws, or one endowed with the craft? **HERMOGENES:** One endowed with the craft. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, Hermogenes, it is not the part of just any man to impose a name, but of a certain <margin>F</margin> author of names. This person, as it seems, is the *institutor of names <margin>* Greek: legislator. Ficino: 'onomathetēs'. <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499) was the scholar who first translated Plato's complete works into Latin. Here the text notes his choice of the word 'onomathetēs' (name-giver).</note></margin>, who is found more rarely than any other craftsman among men. **HERMOGENES:** It appears so. **SOCRATES:** Observe, I pray, what the institutor of names looks toward <margin>G</margin> when he imposes names on things. Rather, judge by the previous examples: what does the carpenter look toward when he makes the shuttle and comb? Is it not toward something that is by nature fit for weaving? **HERMOGENES:** Entirely. **SOCRATES:** If in the very work this shuttle is broken, will he fashion another according to the image of the broken one? Or will he rather look toward the Form itself, according to whose exemplar he had made the shuttle that was broken? **HERMOGENES:** Toward the Form itself, as I judge. **SOCRATES:** And should we not rightly call that Form the very principle and the "shuttle" itself? **HERMOGENES:** I think so. **SOCRATES:** If it is ever necessary to prepare a shuttle for a garment that is thin or thick, of linen or of wool, <margin>H</margin> or of any other kind, all the shuttles must have the Form of the shuttle itself; but such a one as is naturally most suited for each, that one he must apply to perform the work as nature requires. **HERMOGENES:** It certainly must be so. **SOCRATES:** The same reasoning applies to other instruments. For that which fits each thing by nature, the instrument must be discovered and adapted to it—not just as the maker wishes, but as nature itself requires. For one must know how to produce in iron the drill suited to each thing. **HERMOGENES:** It is clear. **SOCRATES:** And likewise the shuttle suited to each...

<meta>catchword: singulis (to each)</meta>

<summary>Socrates argues that names are not arbitrary but are purposeful tools designed by a "Lawgiver" to teach and discern the true essence of things. He compares the name-maker to a craftsman who must look at the ideal "Form" of a tool to ensure it functions according to nature.</summary>
<keywords>Plato, Cratylus, Socrates, Hermogenes, philosophy of language, dialectic, Form, Idea, Lawgiver, naming, shuttle, Marsilio Ficino</keywords>

<meta>Continuing from the previous page, Socrates has established that actions—including speaking and naming—have their own inherent nature and are not merely subject to our whims. He is now using the analogy of tools, such as the weaver's shuttle, to explain how a "name-giver" must work.</meta>

Or do you not think he says something great and wonderful in these passages about the correctness of names? For it is clear, surely, that the gods call them with correctness, which are the names by nature. Or do you not think so? **HERMOGENES:** I well know for my part that if they call them anything, they call them correctly. Do you not think this is an impressive thing, to know in what way it is correct to call that river Xanthus rather than Scamander? Or if you wish, concerning the bird which the gods call Chalcis, but men Cymindis—is it a trivial thing to learn how much more correct it is to call the same bird Chalcis than Cymindis? Or regarding Batiea and Myrine, and many other things in this poet and others? But these things are perhaps too great for me and you to find out. But Scamandrius and Astyanax...

<summary>Socrates argues that naming is a specialized craft requiring a "legislator" who understands the natural forms of things, guided by a "dialectician" who knows how to use language correctly. He supports this by citing Homeric examples where gods and men use different names, implying a divinely correct natural vocabulary.</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Hermogenes, Cratylus, Homer, Protagoras, dialectics, natural names, Xanthus, Scamander, philosophy of language</keywords>

<meta>The dialogue continues between Socrates and Hermogenes. In the previous section, Socrates established that naming is an art performed by a "name-giver" who captures the essence of a thing. He now turns to specific examples from Homer’s *Iliad* to demonstrate how names can be "correct" regardless of their specific sounds.</meta>

### CRATYLUS. 261

Let us examine this in a more "human" way (as it seems to me) and more easily, looking at what Homer says names are for the son of Hector, and what he means by their "correctness." For you surely know these lines, or do you not? **HERMOGENES:** I certainly do. **SOCRATES:** Which of these two names do you think Homer thought was more correctly given to the child: "Astyanax" <note>From the Greek *asty* (city) and *anax* (lord/king), meaning "Lord of the City."</note> or "Scamandrius" <note>Named after the river Scamander near Troy.</note>? **HERMOGENES:** I cannot say. **SOCRATES:** Then consider it this way: if someone asked you whether you think the wiser or the less wise give names more correctly? **HERMOGENES:** Clearly, I would say the wiser. **SOCRATES:** And do you think the women in cities are wiser, or the men—speaking of the gender as a whole? **HERMOGENES:** The
<margin>B</margin>
men. **SOCRATES:** Then you know that Homer says the child of Hector was called Astyanax by the Trojans, but clearly he was called Scamandrius by the
<margin>Homer says Scamandrius was named by Hector: by others Astyanax.</margin>
women, since the men called him Astyanax. **HERMOGENES:** So it seems. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, Homer also considered the Trojans to be wiser than their wives. **HERMOGENES:** I suppose so. **SOCRATES:** He must have thought, then, that "Astyanax" was more correctly given to the child than "Scamandrius." **HERMOGENES:** That appears to be the case. **SOCRATES:** Let us then consider why that is. Does he not himself give us the best explanation of the "why"? For he says:

->For he alone protected their city and long walls.<-

Because of this, it seems, it is correct to call the son of the savior "Astyanax"—that is, the "Lord of the City" which his father was saving, as Homer says. **HERMOGENES:** So it
<margin>C</margin>
appears to me. **SOCRATES:** But why is that? For I myself do not yet understand it, Hermogenes. Do you? **HERMOGENES:** By Zeus, I do not. **SOCRATES:** But look, my good friend, Homer himself also gave the name to Hector. **HERMOGENES:** Why so? **SOCRATES:** Because it seems to me that the name "Hector" is very similar to "Astyanax," and both names seem Greek. For "Anax" (Lord) and "Hector" (Holder/Protector) <note>original: *Ἕκτωρ* (Hektor), related to *ekhein*, meaning to hold, possess, or check.</note> signify almost the same thing; both are royal names. For of whatever a man is an *Anax* (Lord), he is surely also the *Hector* (Holder) of it. It is clear that he dominates it, possesses it, and holds it. Or do I seem to be talking nonsense, and am I deceiving myself, thinking I have found some "trace" of Homer’s opinion regarding the correctness of names? **HERMOGENES:** By Zeus, not at all,
<margin>D</margin>
as it seems to me; perhaps you have touched upon something. **SOCRATES:** It is only right, it seems to me, to call the offspring of a lion a "lion," and the offspring of a horse a "horse." I do not mean if some monster is born from a horse—something other than a horse—but I mean that which is the natural offspring of the genus. If a cow, contrary to nature, should produce a horse, the offspring should not be called a calf, but a foal. And likewise, if a horse produces a calf contrary to nature, it should be called a calf. And if (I think) an offspring is born from a human that is not human, it should not be called a human. The same applies to trees and everything else. Do you agree? **HERMOGENES:** I agree. **SOCRATES:** You speak well.
<margin>E</margin>
Watch me now, lest I mislead you. By the same logic, if a king has offspring, the offspring should be called a "king." It makes no difference if the same meaning is expressed in different syllables, nor does it matter if a letter is added or taken away, as long as the <term>essence</term> <note>original: *ousia*. The fundamental nature or being of the thing.</note> of the thing remains dominant and is revealed in the name. **HERMOGENES:** How do you mean? **SOCRATES:** Nothing complicated. Just as we have names for the letters of the alphabet, but the names are not the letters themselves—except for four: *e*, *u*, *o*, and *omega*. For the other vowels and consonants, you know we wrap other letters around them to create names. But as long as we include the "power" <note>original: *dynamis*. Here, the phonetic value or functional essence of the letter.</note> of the letter, it is correct to call it by that name which signifies it. For example, "Beta" reveals the letter to us. You see that the addition of *e*, *t*, and
<margin>F</margin>
*a* does not prevent the nature of that letter from being shown by the whole name, just as the "name-giver" intended. He knew how to give names to letters correctly. **HERMOGENES:** That seems true to me. **SOCRATES:** Then will not the same logic apply to "King"? A king will be born from a king, a good man from a good man, a beautiful thing from a beautiful thing, and so on for every genus; unless a monster is born, the offspring should be called by the same name. However, the syllables can be varied so that to an untrained person, names that are the same appear different. It is like the medicines of doctors: when they are varied with colors or scents, they appear different to us, even though they are the same. But to the
<margin>G</margin>
doctor, who considers the "power" of the drugs, they appear the same, and he is not confused by the additions. So perhaps the man who understands names considers their "power" and is not confused if a letter is added, transposed, or removed, or even if the power of the name is expressed in entirely different letters. Just as we were saying: "Astyanax" and "Hector" share none of the same letters except for *t*, yet they mean the same thing. And what about "Archepolis" (Leader of the City)? What letters does it share with the others? Yet it signifies the same thing. And there are many other names that signify nothing but "King," and others that signify "General," such as "Agis," "Polemarchus," and "Eupolemus." Others signify the medical profession, like "Iatrocles" and
<margin>H</margin>
"Acesimbrotus." We might find many others that differ in syllables and letters but speak the same "power" in their meaning. Does it seem so, or not? **HERMOGENES:** Very much so. **SOCRATES:** To those...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
By human wit, as it seems to me, it can be understood and easily perceived (regarding what he says are the names of Hector’s son) what "correctness" Homer wishes there to be in these names. Do you know those poems in which the things I speak of are found? **HERMOGENES:** Entirely. **SOCRATES:** Which of those names do you think Homer thought more suitable for the boy: Astyanax or Scamandrius? **HERMOGENES:** I do not know. **SOCRATES:** Consider it thus: if someone asked you whether you think the wiser or the less wise impose names more correctly? **HERMOGENES:** I would certainly answer: the wiser. **SOCRATES:** Do the women in the cities seem wiser to you, or the men, as far as the gender is
<margin>B</margin>
concerned? **HERMOGENES:** The men. **SOCRATES:** Do you not know that Homer says Hector's son was called "Astyanax" by the Trojans, and "Scamandrius" by the women, since the men were accustomed to call him Astyanax? **HERMOGENES:** So it seems. **SOCRATES:** Did not Homer judge the Trojan men to be wiser than their women? **HERMOGENES:** Indeed, I think so. **SOCRATES:** He therefore judged that he was more correctly named Astyanax than Scamandrius. **HERMOGENES:** It is apparent. **SOCRATES:** Let us observe what cause he himself brings for this naming. "For he alone," he says, "protected the city and the wide walls for them." Therefore it is fitting, as it seems, to name the son of the Savior "Astyanax"—that is, the "King of the City"—of that city, I say, which his father saved, as Homer says. **HERMOGENES:** It seems the same to me. **SOCRATES:**
<margin>C</margin>
Moreover, I myself do not yet sufficiently understand why this is especially so, O Hermogenes. Do you perceive it? **HERMOGENES:** Not by Jove. **SOCRATES:** And yet, O good man, Homer himself imposed the name on Hector as well. **HERMOGENES:** For what reason? **SOCRATES:** Because that name "Hector" seems to me to be very close to "Astyanax"; for they signify almost the same thing, and the Greeks think both these names are royal. For of whomever one is an *anax* (that is, a king), of the same he is also an *hector* (that is, a possessor). For it is established that he dominates, possesses, and holds it. Or do I perhaps seem to you to be saying nothing? And am I deceived by an opinion in which I trusted I was reaching Homer’s knowledge about the correctness of names, as if by some tracks? **HERMOGENES:** Not at all,
<margin>D</margin>
as I judge; for perhaps you are touching upon something. **SOCRATES:** It is fitting, as it seems to me, to similarly name the son of a lion a "lion," and the son of a horse a "horse." I certainly do not mean if something is born from a horse as a monster—something other than a horse—but I mean that which is born according to the nature of the genus. For if, according to nature, the son of a cow should beget a horse, the one born is not a calf, but must be called a foal. And if a horse, contrary to nature, begets a calf, this is not to be called a foal, but a calf. Nor if another offspring than human is produced from a human, should that which is born be called a human. And the same must be judged concerning trees and all other things. Do you approve of these?
<margin>E</margin>
**HERMOGENES:** I certainly approve. **SOCRATES:** Watch me, lest I defraud you of anything. For by the same reasoning, if someone is born from a king, he is to be called a "king." But whether the same thing is signified in different syllables, it matters not; nor does it matter if a letter is added or even taken away, as long as the essence of the thing signified remains dominant, shining forth in the name itself. **HERMOGENES:** How do you say that? **SOCRATES:** I say nothing strange or new, but just as you see happen in the letters of the alphabet. For you know that we say the "names" of the letters, but by no means the letters themselves, except for four only. For we say *e*, *u* (simple), *o* (small), and *omega* (great). But for the others, both vowels and non-vowels, we add other letters and constitute names, such as "Beta," and so we pronounce them. But as long as we
<margin>F</margin>
insert the power of the letter itself shining through, it is fitting to call it that name which signifies the letter to us, as appears in "Beta," where with *e*, *t*, and *a* added, nothing prevented the nature of that letter from being shown by the whole name, as the author of names intended. He gave names to the letters quite skillfully. **HERMOGENES:** You seem to me to speak the truth. **SOCRATES:** Will not the same reasoning apply to "King"? A king will surely come from a king, a good man from a good man, a beautiful man from a beautiful man, and in all other things similarly: from any genus another such offspring, unless a monster is made, and the same names are to be said. But it is permitted to vary by syllables, so that to an unlearned man, those things which are the same may seem to be different. Just as the medicines of doctors, often varied by colors and scents although they are the same, seem different to us. But to a doctor
<margin>G</margin>
considering the "power" of the drugs, they are judged the same, nor do the additions disturb him. Similarly, perhaps, he who is learned in names considers their power, and his judgment is not disturbed if any letter is added, or transposed, or taken away, or if the same power of the name is found in other and many letters. As those names which we said above, "Astyanax" and "Hector," have entirely different letters except for *t* alone, yet they signify the same thing. Likewise, that "Archepolis" is said (that is, "Prince of the City"), what communion of letters does it have with the two above? Nevertheless, it signifies the same. And there are many other things which signify nothing else but "King." There are many besides which signify a leader of an army, such as "Agis," "Polemarchus," "Eupolemus." Likewise others which declare a professor of medicine, such as "Iatrocles," "Acesimbrotus." And many others can be
<margin>H</margin>
found, differing in syllables and letters, but thoroughly concordant in the power of their signification. Do you think so yourself, or otherwise? **HERMOGENES:** Certainly so. **SOCRATES:** To these...

<summary>Socrates argues that names like Hector and Astyanax are "correct" because they share a common "power" or meaning—leadership and protection—despite having different sounds. He explains that names are like biological offspring or technical terms: as long as the essential nature (the "power") is preserved, the specific letters or syllables used are secondary.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Hermogenes regarding the "correctness" of names. Having established that names should reflect the essence of the person or thing, Socrates begins a series of famous etymological analyses of Greek heroes and gods, often using puns or word-associations that were common in ancient linguistic theory.</meta>

# OF PLATO

### CRATYLUS. 262

Certainly, those things which come about according to nature should be given the same
<margin>A</margin> names. **HERMOGENES:** Entirely so. **SOCRATES:** But what about when some men are born contrary to nature in the form of a monster—for instance, when an impious man is born from a good and pious man? Should the one who is born not receive the name of the father, but rather the name of the genus to which he belongs? Just as we said before, if a horse produces the offspring of an ox, that offspring should not be called a horse, but an ox. **HERMOGENES:** That is so. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, to an impious man born of a pious one, we should attribute the name of his kind, not his parent. **HERMOGENES:** This is true. **SOCRATES:** Thus, it is not fitting to call such a son *Theophilus* <note>original: "θεόφιλον", meaning "Friend of God"</note> nor *Mnesitheus* <note>original: "μνησίθεον", meaning "Mindful of God"</note>, nor any such name; instead, he should be called by names signifying the opposite, if indeed names are to be correctly established. <margin>B</margin> **HERMOGENES:** That is exactly how it must be done, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Indeed, the name *Orestes* seems to have been correctly given, Hermogenes—whether by some chance or by some poet—signifying his fierce <note>original: "ferinam", referring to a beast-like nature</note>, wild, and mountain-dwelling nature by that name. <note>Socrates associates the name Orestes with the Greek word *oros*, meaning "mountain."</note> **HERMOGENES:** So it appears, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** It seems his father's name is also according to nature. **HERMOGENES:** It appears so. **SOCRATES:** It is evident that *Agamemnon* is the sort of man who thinks he must labor and endure, and persist through virtue in the things he has decreed. A proof of his endurance was his long stay at Troy with such a great army. That this man was of marvelous perseverance, then, <margin>C</margin> is signified by the name Agamemnon, as if it were "admirable in persistence." <note>original: "ἄγαστος κατὰ τὴν ἐπιμονήν" (agastos kata ten epimonen). Socrates breaks the name into *agan* (very much/admirable) and *memnon* (remaining/persisting).</note> Perhaps *Atreus* was also rightly named. For the murder of Chrysippus and the cruelty he practiced against Thyestes show him to be harmful and ruinous. For this reason, the name deviates slightly and secretly hints at his nature, so that it does not reveal the man's character to just anyone; but to those skilled in names, the meaning of *Atreus* is sufficiently clear. For it is said according to "stubborn," "fearless," and "ruinous," <note>original: "ἀτειρὲς, ἄτρεστον, ἀτηρὸν" (ateires, atreston, ateron). Socrates puns on the name Atreus sounding like these words for being unyielding or destructive.</note> as if he were indomitable, inexorable, harmful, and insolent. It seems the name *Pelops* was also appropriately given. For that name fittingly signifies a man who sees only what is near. **HERMOGENES:** How so? <margin>D</margin> **SOCRATES:** Because in the murder of Myrtilus, as the story goes, he could foresee nothing, nor look ahead from a distance to see what a great calamity would threaten his entire race. He looked only at what was before his feet and at the present—which is what "looking near" means—which he did when he strove with all his might to enter into marriage with Hippodamia. Hence the name Pelops comes from *pelas*, meaning "near," and *opsis*, which pertains to "vision." <note>Pelops' name is here derived from *pelas* (near) and *ops* (eye/face).</note> Furthermore, the name *Tantalus* seems rightly and naturally given, if the stories told about him are true. **HERMOGENES:** What stories? **SOCRATES:** That while he was still living, many grave misfortunes befell him, and finally his whole homeland was overturned. <margin>E</margin> Moreover, after his death, a stone hangs over his head—surely a most hard fate. These things entirely agree with the name, just as if someone wanted to name him "most wretched" <note>original: "ταλάντατον" (talantaton)</note>, but spoke a little more obscurely, putting *Tantalus* for *Talantatos*. Such a name his adverse fortune seems to have provided through the common report of the nations. Furthermore, the name of his father, *Zeus* <note>original: "Ioui" (Jove/Jupiter) in the Latin, "Διὶ" (Zeus) in the Greek.</note>, is correctly given, yet it is not easily understood. For the name of Zeus is like a complete sentence, which we use by dividing it into two parts. Some call him *Zena*, others *Dia*. <note>In Greek, the name Zeus has different forms (Zena, Dia) depending on the grammatical case.</note> These parts, when joined into one, reveal the nature of the God himself, which is exactly what a name ought to be able to accomplish. For there is no cause of living for us and all others more than the leader and king of all. <margin>F</margin> Therefore, this God is fittingly named "He through whom life (*zen*) always belongs to all living things." But the name is one, divided into two, as I said: *Dia* and *Zena*. Hearing that he is the son of *Saturn* <note>original: "Κρόνου" (Cronus)</note>, someone might think it insolent and insulting. But it is probable that Zeus is the offspring of some great intelligence. For what is called *koros* does not signify "boy," but the purity of his mind and his sincere integrity. <note>Socrates puns on *Cronus* sounding like *koros*, which can mean "boy" or "purity/satiety."</note> He is the son of *Ouranos* <note>original: "οὐρανοῦ", meaning "Heaven" or "Sky"</note>, as they say. Indeed, the act of looking at things above is rightly called *Ourania*, as if "looking at the things on high" <note>original: "ὁρῶσα τὰ ἄνω" (orosa ta ano)</note>. From this, they say, O Hermogenes—those who deal with sublime matters—that a pure mind is present, and that the name *Ouranos* was rightly imposed. <margin>G</margin> If I held in my mind the genealogy of the gods handed down by Hesiod, and could remember those whom he introduces as their progenitors, I would by no means cease to show you that names were correctly inscribed upon them, until I had made a trial of this wisdom to see if it accomplishes anything or fails—this wisdom which has so suddenly shone upon me, though I know not from where. **HERMOGENES:** Truly, Socrates, you seem to me like those who are seized by a divine spirit, suddenly pouring forth oracles. **SOCRATES:** I believe, <margin>H</margin> Hermogenes, that this wisdom has flowed into me from *Euthyphro*, the son of Pantias. For I have been with him since morning, listening intently. It seems, therefore, that being inspired by a divine spirit, he has not only filled my ears with blessed wisdom but has also taken possession of my soul. Thus I think we should act this way: today we shall use it and investigate the remaining things pertaining to names. But tomorrow, if you agree, we shall "purify" ourselves of it and renounce it, provided we find a man—either a priest or a sophist—skilled in such expiations. **HERMOGENES:** I greatly approve of this, Socrates, for I would most gladly hear what remains concerning names. **SOCRATES:** So be it.

<column-break/>

Names must be given according to the nature of those being born. <margin>A</margin> **HERMOGENES:** Quite so. **SOCRATES:** But what about those contrary to nature, who are born in the form of a monster? For instance, when an impious man is born from a good and god-fearing man, should he not—as we said before—not have the name of the parent, but of the genus to which he belongs? Just as if a horse should give birth to the offspring of an ox, the offspring should surely not have the name of the parent, but of its own kind? **HERMOGENES:** Quite so. **SOCRATES:** And so to the one born of the impious, the name "impious" should be given according to his kind. **HERMOGENES:** Let it be so. **SOCRATES:** Not *Theophilus*, as it seems, nor *Mnesitheus*, nor anything of that sort; but whatever signifies the opposite of these, if the names are to achieve correctness. **HERMOGENES:** Most certainly, Socrates. <margin>B</margin> **SOCRATES:** Just as *Orestes*, Hermogenes, seems to be rightly named; whether some chance gave him the name, or some poet, indicating the beast-like quality of his nature and his wild and mountain-dwelling character by the name. **HERMOGENES:** It appears so, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** And it seems his father's name is also according to nature. **HERMOGENES:** It appears so. **SOCRATES:** For *Agamemnon* seems to be the sort of man who decided to labor through and endure, putting an end to his purposes through virtue. The sign of his endurance was his staying at Troy with such a multitude. Does this man not signify, by the name *Agamemnon*, "admirable for his persistence"? Perhaps *Atreus* is also correct. For the murder of Chrysippus, and all those cruel things he did to Thyestes, were all ruinous and harmful to virtue. Therefore, the designation of the name <margin>C</margin> swerves a little and is hidden, so as not to reveal the man's nature to all; but to those who understand names, what *Atreus* wants to say is sufficiently clear. For according to "stubborn," and according to "fearless," and according to "ruinous," the name is correctly placed for him in every way. And it seems to me the name *Pelops* is also placed with measure. For this name signifies "one who sees what is near," and is worthy of this designation. **HERMOGENES:** How so? **SOCRATES:** As it is said of him regarding the things of the Peloponnese—it was impossible for him to foresee or provide for the whole boundary of the future, how much misfortune it would be filled with, seeing only what was near and at hand <margin>D</margin> (which is *pelas*), when he desired to obtain the marriage of Hippodamia by every means. And for *Tantalus*, everyone would think the name was placed correctly and according to nature, if what is said about him is true. **HERMOGENES:** What sort of things are these? **SOCRATES:** The many and terrible misfortunes that happened while he was still living, of which the end was that his whole homeland was overturned; and after he died, the "Tantalean" hanging of the stone over his head in Hades is wonderfully in harmony with the name. Just as if someone, wishing to name him "most wretched" (*talantaton*), named him secretively and said *Tantalus* instead—fortune seems to have provided such a name for him out of rumor. It appears also that the name of his father, <margin>E</margin> *Zeus*, is most beautifully placed. But it is not easy to understand. For the name of Zeus is literally like a sentence. Dividing it in two, some of us use one part, and some use the other. For some call him *Zena*, and others *Dia*. But put together into one, they show the nature of the god. Which is what we say a name should be able to achieve. For there is no one who is more the cause of living for us and all others than the ruler and king of all. It happens, then, that he is correctly named thus, being the god through whom living (*zen*) always belongs to all living things. But the name, being one, is divided in two (as I say), into *Dia* and *Zena*. And of this one, the son of *Cronus*—this might seem insulting to someone hearing it suddenly; but it is reasonable <margin>F</margin> that Zeus is the offspring of a certain great intellect. For *koros* signifies not "boy," but the pure and undefiled nature of his mind. And he is the son of *Ouranos*, as the story goes. And again, the looking upward is rightly called by this name, *Ourania*, "looking at things above"; from which they say, Hermogenes, that Cronus was born as a mind out of the undefiled and pure, and that the name *Ouranos* is correctly placed. And if I remembered the genealogies of Hesiod, and whom he says are the even older ancestors of these, I would not stop going through how correctly their names are placed, until I had made trial of this wisdom—whether it will do anything, or whether it fails—which has just now suddenly fallen upon me, I know not from where. <margin>G</margin> **HERMOGENES:** Indeed, Socrates, you truly seem to me like those who are inspired, suddenly giving oracles. **SOCRATES:** And I blame it, Hermogenes, mostly on it having fallen upon me from Euthyphro the son of Pantias. For since dawn I have been with him, and I gave him my ears. He seems, being inspired, not only to have filled my ears with divine wisdom, but also to have taken hold of my soul. It seems to me, then, that we should do this: for today, still use this same wisdom and examine the rest regarding names; but tomorrow, if it seems good to you too, we shall exorcise it and be purified, finding someone skilled in purifying such things, whether one of the priests or the sophists. **HERMOGENES:** I agree. <margin>H</margin> For I would very gladly hear the remaining things about names. **SOCRATES:** But...

<summary>In this passage, Socrates provides creative etymologies for the names of famous Greek heroes (Orestes, Agamemnon, Atreus, Pelops, Tantalus) and gods (Zeus, Cronus, Ouranos), arguing that their names reflect their histories or natures. He attributes his sudden linguistic insights to inspiration from the priest Euthyphro.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Hermogenes from the previous page. Having discussed the "correctness" of names based on a person's nature or ancestry, Socrates now moves toward investigating the etymologies of categories of beings—gods, demons, heroes, and humans—to see if their names reflect an underlying natural truth.</meta>

# CRATYLUS.

<margin>A</margin> ...is exactly how it must be done. Where, then, do you wish us to begin our inquiry? Since we have entered upon a certain pattern, let us see if the names themselves will serve as our guides, and whether everything is held together by mere chance or if the names possess some inherent correctness. Now, the names given to heroes and men before our time might perhaps deceive us. For many of them are established based on the names of ancestors, which, as we said at the start, may signify nothing about the individuals themselves. Many others are given as a sort of prayer, such as *Eutychides* <note>original: "Εὐτυχίδου", meaning "Son of Good Fortune"</note>, *Sosias* <note>original: "Σωσίαν", meaning "Saviour" or "Preserved"</note>, *Theophilus* <note>original: "Θεόφιλον", meaning "Loved by God"</note>, and many more. It seems to me that we should set such names aside.

<margin>B</margin> It is most likely that we will find correctly established names among those things that are eternal and follow the order of nature. Indeed, it is in these matters that the greatest care in the placement of names is most fitting. Perhaps some of them were even established by a power more divine than that of humans. **HERMOGENES:** You seem to me to speak well, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Is it not right, then, to begin with the gods, looking into how they were correctly called by this very name, "gods"? **HERMOGENES:** That is likely. **SOCRATES:** I suspect something of this sort: it seems to me that the first men in Greece considered only those to be gods whom many of the barbarians <note>A term used by Greeks for all non-Greek speakers.</note> still do today—the sun, the moon, the earth, the stars, and the sky. Since they saw all these things always moving in a race and "running," from this nature of "running" <note>original: "τοῦ θεῖν", *tou thein*</note>, they named them

<margin>C</margin> <margin>Gods</margin> "gods" <note>original: "θεούς", *theous*</note>. Later, as they became aware of other beings, they addressed them all by this same name. Does this account seem to have some truth to it, or none at all? **HERMOGENES:** It seems very much to be the case. **SOCRATES:** What, then, should we examine after this? **HERMOGENES:** Clearly, demons, heroes, and men. **SOCRATES:** "Demons"? <note>In the ancient sense, *daimones* were not necessarily evil, but intermediary spirits or wise souls.</note> Truly, Hermogenes, consider what the name "demons" might signify. See if what I say makes sense to you. **HERMOGENES:** Just speak. **SOCRATES:** Do you know who Hesiod says the demons are? **HERMOGENES:** I do not recall. **SOCRATES:** Not even that he says the first generation of men was a "golden race"? **HERMOGENES:** That, I do know. **SOCRATES:** He says of them: "But when this race was covered by fate, they were called holy demons upon the earth, noble, averters of evil, guardians

<margin>D</margin> of mortal men." **HERMOGENES:** What of it? **SOCRATES:** I think he calls it the "golden race" not because it was made of gold, but because it was good and beautiful. My evidence for this is that he also says our own race is "iron." **HERMOGENES:** You speak the truth. **SOCRATES:** Do you not think, then, that if someone today were good, Hesiod would say they belong to that golden race? **HERMOGENES:** It is likely. **SOCRATES:** And are the "good" anything other than the "wise"? **HERMOGENES:** They are the wise. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, he calls them "demons" above all because they were wise and "knowing" <note>original: "δαήμονες", *daēmones*</note>; he named them "demons" <note>original: "δαίμονας", *daimonas*</note> because of this. In our ancient tongue, this name and the word for "knowing" coincide. Thus, he and many other poets speak well when they

<margin>E</margin> say that when a good man dies, he receives a great fate and honor, and becomes a "demon," according to the title of wisdom. Therefore, I also maintain that every man who is wise and good is "demonic" <note>original: "δαιμόνιον", *daimonion*</note>, both while living and when dead; and he is correctly called a "demon." **HERMOGENES:** I find myself entirely in agreement with you on this, Socrates. But what then would a "hero" be? **SOCRATES:** That is not at all difficult to understand. Their name has been only slightly altered to show they were born from "love." **HERMOGENES:** How do you mean? **SOCRATES:** Do you not know that heroes are demigods? **HERMOGENES:** What of it? **SOCRATES:** Surely they were all born because a god fell in love with a mortal woman, or a mortal man with a goddess. If you examine this according to the ancient Attic dialect, you will understand it better. It will show you that the name is slightly derived from the word for "love" <note>original: "ἔρωτος", *erōtos*</note>, from which the heroes were born, for the sake of the name.

<margin>F</margin> <margin>From love</margin> Either this is what it means to be "heroes," or it is because they were wise, and rhetors <note>Public speakers or orators.</note>, and formidable at dialectic—being capable of "asking questions" <note>original: "ἐρωτᾶν", *erōtan*</note>. For "to speak" <note>original: "εἴρειν", *eirein*</note> is the same as "to say." Thus, as we were just saying, when spoken in the Attic dialect, the "heroes" turn out to be certain rhetors and questioners and lovers, so that the heroic tribe becomes a race of rhetors and sophists. But this is not hard to perceive. Rather, why on earth are men called "humans"? Can you say? **HERMOGENES:** From where would I know, my good friend? Even if I were able to find out, I would not try, because I believe you will be better able to find it than I. **SOCRATES:** You seem to trust in the inspiration of Euthyphro. **HERMOGENES:** Clearly. **SOCRATES:** And you are right to trust it. For even now I seem to have thought of it quite cleverly, and I run the risk, unless I am careful, of becoming wiser than is necessary this very day. Consider what I am saying. First,

<margin>G</margin> one must understand this about names: we often insert letters and take others out when naming things as we please, and we change the accents. For example, to make the phrase "Friend of Zeus" <note>original: "Διὶ φίλος", *Dii philos*</note> into a single name for us, we took out the second "iota" and pronounced the middle syllable with a grave accent instead of an acute one. In other cases, on the contrary, we insert letters, or speak with a heavier tone. **HERMOGENES:** You speak the truth. **SOCRATES:** This is exactly what has happened to the name "humans" <note>original: "ἀνθρώπων", *anthrōpōn*</note>, as it seems to me. It has become a name from a phrase, with one letter—the "alpha"—having been removed, and the ending made heavier. **HERMOGENES:** How do you mean? **SOCRATES:** Like this. The name "human" <note>original: "ἄνθρωπος", *anthrōpos*</note> signifies that while other beasts do not examine, nor reason, nor "look up at" <note>original: "ἀναθρεῖ", *anathrei*</note> what they see, the human...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...ought to proceed. From where, then, do you judge it best to begin? Now that we have prescribed a certain formula, let us find out if names themselves testify to us that they were not made by some chance, but truly contain some inherent correctness. The names of heroes and humans might perhaps deceive us. For many of these are placed according to the surnames of ancestors, and often do not fit at all, as we said at the beginning. Many people assign names as if they were making a wish, such as *Eutychides* <note>original: "εὐτυχίδου", Greek for "Son of Fortune"</note>, *Sosias* <note>original: "σωσίου", Greek for "Savior"</note>, and *Theophilus* <note>original: "θεοφίλου", Greek for "Friend of God"</note>, and many others. Such things

<margin>B</margin> I therefore judge should be passed over. For it is most decent and fitting for us to find those names which are correctly placed in eternal things and in the established order of nature. For it is in those things that the greatest care in creating names is most appropriate. Perhaps some of them were established by a certain divine power rather than a human one. **HERMOGENES:** You seem to me to speak excellently, O Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Is it not right to start from the gods themselves, and investigate the reason why they are called "gods" <note>original: "θεοὶ", *theoi*</note>? **HERMOGENES:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** This is how I conclude it. It seems to me that the ancient Greeks thought those were the only gods whom many of the Barbarians still consider so in these times: the sun, the moon, the earth, the stars, and the sky. Since they saw all these things always 

<margin>C</margin> <margin>Gods, from "running"</margin> in motion and running, they seem to have named them "gods" <note>original: "θεοὺς", *theous*</note> from this nature of "running" <note>original: "αἴθεῖν", *thein*</note>. Then, observing others, they called them all by the same name. Does what I say have some likelihood, or not? **HERMOGENES:** It certainly does. **SOCRATES:** What should be investigated next? **HERMOGENES:** It follows that we must ask about demons, heroes, and men. **SOCRATES:** About demons? And indeed the matter stands thus, O Hermogenes. What, then, does the name of "demons" mean? Notice if I say anything of value. **HERMOGENES:** Just speak. **SOCRATES:** Do you know those whom Hesiod says are demons? **HERMOGENES:** No. **SOCRATES:** Nor that <note>original: "ἐν ἔπεσι", in the verses; "ἔργα καὶ ἡμ.", Hesiod's *Works and Days*</note> he says a golden race of men existed in the beginning? **HERMOGENES:** This I do know. **SOCRATES:** For he says that from this race, after the

<margin>D</margin> fates of the present life, they become holy demons, dwelling on the earth, the best, the expellers of evils, and the guardians of men. **HERMOGENES:** What then? **SOCRATES:** Surely I think he calls them a "golden race," not because they were made of gold, but because they were good and excellent; which I gather from the fact that he says our own race is "iron." **HERMOGENES:** You tell the truth. **SOCRATES:** Do you not think that if any of our people were good now, they would be judged by Hesiod to be of the golden race? **HERMOGENES:** That is consistent. **SOCRATES:** But are the good anything other than the wise? **HERMOGENES:** The wise. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, as I judge, he calls them demons especially because they were wise and "knowing" <note>original: "δαίμονές", *daēmones*</note>. And from our ancient language, that

<margin>E</margin> name exists. For this reason, both he and many other poets speak excellently when they say that after a good person has finished their life, they obtain the greatest dignity and reward, and become a demon, according to the title of wisdom. Thus I also assert that a "demon" <note>original: "δάϊμονα", *daēmona*</note>—that is, a wise person—is every man who is good, and that he is "demonic"—that is, happy—living or dead, and is correctly called a demon. **HERMOGENES:** I seem to myself, O Socrates, to agree with you most strongly in this. But what does "hero" <note>original: "ἥρως", *hērōs*</note> mean? **SOCRATES:** That is not at all difficult to find; for the name of heroes differs only a little from its origin, indicating that their generation flowed from "love" <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ ἔρωτος", *apo tou erōtos*</note>. **HERMOGENES:**

<margin>F</margin> By what reason do you say that? **SOCRATES:** Do you not know that heroes are demigods? What then? **SOCRATES:** All heroes were certainly born either from the love of gods for human women, or the love of men for goddesses. Furthermore, if you consider this according to the ancient language of the Athenians, you will understand it better. For you will find that it is changed only slightly for the sake of the name from "love" <note>original: "ἔρωτος", *erōtos*</note>, from which the heroes were born; or else that the name of heroes was derived from this, or from the fact that they were wise, and rhetors, and eloquent—namely, very prompt at questioning and debating. For "to speak" <note>original: "εἴρειν", *eirein*</note> is to talk. Wherefore, as we were just saying, in the Attic voice "heroes" turn out to be certain rhetors, and disputants, and lovers. Thus the heroic offspring becomes a race of rhetors and sophists. But truly that is not difficult to know; rather, that is more obscure: for what reason

<margin>G</margin> are men called "humans" <note>original: "ἄνθρωποι", *anthrōpoi*</note>? Do you have anything to offer? **HERMOGENES:** From where would I have it, good man? Indeed, if I were able to find it in any way, I would not try, because I hope you will find it better and more easily than I. **SOCRATES:** You seem to me to trust in the inspiration of Euthyphro. **HERMOGENES:** Without a doubt. **SOCRATES:** And you trust rightly. For I seem to myself to have thought quite beautifully just now, and there is a danger, unless I am careful, that I might appear to have turned out wiser today than is proper. Attend to those things I shall say. It is fitting to notice this first about names: that we often add letters, often also take them away, while we name things at our will, and we frequently change the accents, as when we say "Friend of Zeus" <note>original: "Διὶ φίλος", *Dii philos*</note>. To make this a name for you, we removed the second "iota," and instead of an acute middle syllable, we pronounced it grave. In certain other things we insert letters, or we utter others more heavily. **HERMOGENES:** You report the truth. **SOCRATES:** This also happens in "human" <note>original: "ἄνθρωπος", *anthrōpos*</note>, as it seems to me. For...

For from a phrase a name was established, with one "alpha" removed, and a heavier ending produced. **HERMOGENES:** How do you say that? **SOCRATES:** Thus: the name "human" signifies that while other animals do not consider, nor notice, nor contemplate the things they see... <margin>the one who looks up at what he has seen</margin>
