# OF PLATO

->that of Saturn<- <note>original: "ὅτι Κρόνου" — This catchword indicates the first words of the following page.</note>

<margin>A</margin> But man both sees and contemplates, and reflects upon what he sees. Hence, man is rightly called <margin>human</margin> <note>original: "ἄνθρωπος" (anthrōpos)</note> alone among all living beings, as if he were <margin>contemplating what he has seen</margin> <note>original: "ἀναθρῶν ἃ ὄπωπεν" (anathrōn ha opōpe)</note>, that is, viewing what he has already looked upon. What shall I ask after this? Or is there something else you would gladly learn? **HERMOGENES:** Most definitely. **SOCRATES:** Immediately following the previous topics, a consideration of the soul and the body seems appropriate to me. For we call the combination of soul and body a "human." **HERMOGENES:** Without a doubt. **SOCRATES:** Let us try to distinguish these in the same way as the things above. Do you think we should first inquire about the soul, to see if it was rightly <margin>soul</margin> <note>original: "ψυχὴ" (psyche)</note> named? And then about the body? **HERMOGENES:** Indeed. **SOCRATES:** To express quickly what first occurs to me now, I believe those who named the soul in this way intended to convey that whenever it is present <margin>B</margin> in the body, it is the cause of its living, providing the power of breathing and cooling; and as soon as this cooling power ceases, the body is dissolved and perishes. Therefore, they seem to have named it <margin>soul</margin> <note>original: "ψυχὴ" (psyche)</note> as if it were <margin>cooling by breathing</margin> <note>original: "ἀναψῦχον" (anapsychon)</note>. But stay a moment, if you please. I seem to perceive something more probable among those who follow Euthyphro. For they would likely despise that first explanation and consider it somewhat crude. But see if this one will please you. **HERMOGENES:** Just say it. **SOCRATES:** What else but the soul do you think contains the body, carries it, and causes it to live and walk? **HERMOGENES:** Nothing else. **SOCRATES:** Do you not believe Anaxagoras, that the <margin>C</margin> nature of all things is organized and contained by a certain Mind and Soul? **HERMOGENES:** I do indeed. **SOCRATES:** It is fitting, therefore, to name that power <margin>nature-holder</margin> <note>original: "φυσέχην" (physechē)</note>, which <margin>carries and contains nature</margin> <note>original: "φύσιν, ὀχεῖ & ἔχει" (physis, ochei & echei)</note>. However, it is more elegantly pronounced as <margin>soul</margin> <note>original: "ψυχὴ" (psyche)</note>. **HERMOGENES:** It is certainly so. **SOCRATES:** And this seems to me more skillfully constructed. **HERMOGENES:** It truly is. **SOCRATES:** Yet it would appear ridiculous if it were named exactly as it was originally placed. **HERMOGENES:** But what follows after this, what do we say the nature of the next thing is? **SOCRATES:** Do you mean the <margin>body</margin> <term>soma</term>? <note>The Greek word for body.</note> **HERMOGENES:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** And yet it seems to me that in this name there is a slight deviation from its origin. For some teach that this body is the <margin>tomb</margin> <term>sema</term> <note>A pun on the phonetic similarity between "soma" (body) and "sema" (tomb).</note> of the soul, <margin>D</margin> as if the soul were buried in it for the present time. And also because the soul <margin>signifies</margin> <note>original: "σημαίνει" (semainei)</note> through the body whatever it can <margin>signify</margin> <note>original: "σημῇ" (semē)</note>, it is therefore rightly called a <margin>sign</margin> <term>sema</term>. Furthermore, it seems to me that the followers of Orpheus established this name for the primary reason that the soul pays the penalty for its sins in this body, and is enclosed within this surrounding wall like a prison, so that it may be <margin>saved</margin> <note>original: "σώζηται" (sōzētai)</note> or preserved. They wish it to be called just as it is, the <margin>body</margin> <term>soma</term>—a place of safekeeping for the soul until it pays all its debts—and they think not a single letter should be added. **HERMOGENES:** Enough has been said of these things, Socrates, I think. But could we consider the names of some of the gods, just as we did with Jupiter, to see by what correctness the names were established? **SOCRATES:** By Jupiter, <margin>E</margin> if we had any sense, Hermogenes, we would consider the foremost rule of correctness to be this: to confess that we know nothing of the gods, neither of themselves nor of the names by which they call themselves. For it is certain that they call themselves by true names. The second mode of correct naming, I believe, is to follow the law established for prayers: that we call them by whatever names it pleases them to be named, knowing nothing else. For this seems to me a well-decreed custom. Therefore, if you wish, let us proceed to this investigation, first prefacing to the gods that we will consider <margin>F</margin> nothing regarding them—for we do not trust ourselves to be able—but rather regarding humans, and what opinions they held when they established these names. For this is far from divine indignation. **HERMOGENES:** You seem to speak modestly, O Socrates, and we should proceed exactly so. **SOCRATES:** Should we not begin from Vesta, according to the custom? **HERMOGENES:** That is surely fitting. **SOCRATES:** By what reasoning shall we say she was named <margin>Hestia</margin> <term>hestia</term>? <note>The Greek goddess of the hearth, identified with the Roman Vesta.</note> **HERMOGENES:** By Jupiter, that is not easily found. **SOCRATES:** It truly seems, my good Hermogenes, that the first authors of names were not dull men, but rather acute investigators of sublime things. **HERMOGENES:** Why so? **SOCRATES:** The names appear to have been established by the invention of such men. And if one were to consider foreign names, he would nonetheless find what <margin>G</margin> each one means. Just as what we call <margin>essence</margin> <term>ousia</term>, some call <margin>esia</margin> <note>original: "ἐσίαν"</note>, and others <margin>osia</margin> <note>original: "ὠσίαν"</note>. First, according to one of those names, it seems not far from reason that the essence of things is called <margin>esia</margin>; and because we call that which partakes of essence <margin>participating in essence</margin> <note>original: "ἐσίαν"</note>, from this she could rightly be named <margin>Hestia</margin> <term>hestia</term>. Our ancestors also used to call <margin>essence</margin> <note>original: "οὐσίαν"</note> by the name <margin>osia</margin>. Furthermore, if one considers the sacrificial rites, he will think those who established these names thought this way. For it is fitting for those who named the essence of all things "Hestia" to sacrifice to Hestia before all other gods. Likewise, those who used the name <margin>osoun</margin> <note>original: "ὠσοῦν"</note> almost certainly agreed with Heraclitus that all things are always flowing and nothing stands still. They took the cause and origin of things to be the <margin>H</margin> <margin>pushing force</margin> <note>original: "ὠσοῦν" (osoun)</note> that impels. Therefore, it is rightly named <margin>osoun</margin>, the impelling cause. Let this be said of these things as if by those who understand nothing. After Vesta, it is appropriate to consider Rhea and Saturn, although we spoke of Saturn's name earlier. But perhaps I am saying nothing of value. **HERMOGENES:** Why so, Socrates? **SOCRATES:** My good man, I have noticed a certain swarm of wisdom. **HERMOGENES:** What kind of swarm? **SOCRATES:** It is ridiculous to say, yet it has something probable about it. **HERMOGENES:** What probability? **SOCRATES:** I seem to see Heraclitus, who long ago wisely handed down certain things concerning Saturn and Rhea,

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> But man, as soon as he has seen (and this is what "opope" means), also contemplates and reasons about this which he has seen. From this, alone among the animals, man was correctly named <note>original: "ἄνθρωπος" (anthrōpos)</note> "man," for "contemplating what he has seen" <note>original: "ἀναθρῶν ἃ ὄπωπεν" (anathrōn ha opōpe)</note>. What then shall I ask you after this? Or what would I gladly learn? **HERMOGENES:** By all means. **SOCRATES:** Just as if drinking, a second drink seems to me to follow in order. For we are speaking of soul and body, and nowhere else if not of man. **HERMOGENES:** How could it be otherwise? **SOCRATES:** Shall we try to distinguish these, just as we did those before? Do you speak of the soul first, how it reasonably obtains its name, and then the body? **HERMOGENES:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** To speak then of what I think, I believe those who named the soul intended something like this: that this, whenever it is present in the body, is the cause of its <margin>B</margin> living, providing the power to breathe and cooling it, and as soon as the cooling power fails, the body perishes and ends; whence they seem to have called it "psyche" <note>soul</note>. But if you wish, hold still a moment. For I seem to see something purer and more persuasive than this among the followers of Euthyphro. For they, as it seems to me, would have thought about this and considered it a vulgar explanation; but consider this and see if it pleases you too. **HERMOGENES:** Only tell it. **SOCRATES:** What else do you think holds and carries the nature of the whole body, so that it lives and goes about, other <margin>C</margin> than the soul? **HERMOGENES:** Nothing else. **SOCRATES:** What then? Do you not believe with Anaxagoras that mind and soul are what organize and hold the nature of all other things? **HERMOGENES:** I do. **SOCRATES:** This name "soul" would then be beautifully placed for this power, which carries and holds nature; one might call it "physeche" <note>nature-holder</note>. But it is possible to speak more elegantly by saying "psyche." **HERMOGENES:** Very much so. **SOCRATES:** And it seems to me that this is more technical than the other. **HERMOGENES:** Indeed it is. **SOCRATES:** Yet the name as it was originally placed appears truly ridiculous. **HERMOGENES:** But how do we say the next thing stands? **SOCRATES:** You mean the body? **HERMOGENES:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** This seems to me to be many-sided; if one deflects even a little, it is very much so. For some say it is the tomb <note>original: "σῆμα" (sēma)</note> of the soul, as if it were buried in the present; and because again by this the soul signifies whatever it signifies, for this reason it is rightly called a "sign" <note>original: "σῆμα" (sēma)</note>. However, it seems to me most likely that the followers of <margin>D</margin> Orpheus established this name, as the soul is paying a penalty for the things it owes. They believe it has this enclosure so that it may be saved <note>original: "σώζηται" (sōzētai)</note>, like the image of a prison. This very thing is therefore the "soma" <note>body</note> of the soul, as it is named, until it pays what is owed; and there is no need to change even a letter. **HERMOGENES:** These things seem to me to have been said sufficiently, Socrates. But regarding the names of the gods, such as you were just discussing about Jupiter, could we perhaps investigate them in the same way? What correctness is there in the names given to them? **SOCRATES:** Yes, by Jupiter, we indeed, O Hermogenes, if we have any sense, would know one most beautiful way: that we know nothing about the gods, neither of them themselves, nor of their names, whatever they call themselves. For it is clear that they call themselves by the true names. But the <margin>E</margin> second way of correctness is, just as it is the law for us to pray in our prayers, whoever they are and from wherever they rejoice in being named, these we also call them, as knowing nothing else. For this seems to me to be well-established. If you wish, then, let us look, having first said to the gods that we will examine nothing about them (for we do not think ourselves capable of such an examination) but rather about men, and what opinion they had when they established the names for them. For this is without blame. **HERMOGENES:** You seem to me, Socrates, to speak moderately; let us do so. **SOCRATES:** Shall we then begin from Hestia, according to the custom? **HERMOGENES:** It is only right. **SOCRATES:** What then would one say the namer was thinking when <margin>F</margin> he named Hestia? **HERMOGENES:** By Jupiter, I do not think this is easy either. **SOCRATES:** They run a risk, my good Hermogenes, those first established names, of not being base, but rather the work of certain lofty talkers and ponderers of the heavens. **HERMOGENES:** Why so? **SOCRATES:** The establishment of names appears to me to be the work of such men. And if one looks at foreign names, one would find no less what each one intends. For example, in this which we call "essence" <note>original: "οὐσίαν" (ousian)</note>, there are those who call it "esia" <note>original: "ἐσίαν"</note>, and others again "osia" <note>original: "ὠσίαν"</note>. First, then, according to the second of these names, the essence of things has a reason to be called Hestia; and because we say that which partakes of essence is "esia," according to this also it would be rightly called Hestia. For it seems we also anciently called <margin>G</margin> essence "esia." Furthermore, if one considers the sacrifices, one would think those who established these things thought thus. For it is likely that those who named the essence of all things Hestia would sacrifice to Hestia first before all the gods. But those who say "osia" would almost again, according to Heraclitus, think that all beings go along and nothing remains. The cause and leader of them, therefore, is that which pushes <note>original: "ὠθοῦν" (ōthoun)</note>; whence it is well for it to be named "osia." And let these things be said in this way as if to those who know nothing. After Hestia, it is right to investigate Rhea and Saturn. Although we have already gone through the name of Saturn. But perhaps I am saying nothing. **HERMOGENES:** Why, Socrates? **SOCRATES:** My good man, I have perceived a certain swarm of wisdom. **HERMOGENES:** What kind is this? **SOCRATES:** Very ridiculous to say, I think, however, it has a certain probability. **HERMOGENES:** What is it? **SOCRATES:** I seem to see Heraclitus saying some wise things of old, simply those <margin>H</margin> regarding Saturn...

He then transitions to the names of the gods, starting with Hestia, while humbly acknowledging that humans cannot know the true names used by the gods themselves.</summary>

# CRATYLUS

<margin>A</margin> ...concerning Kronos and Rhea, just as Homer used to say. **HERMOGENES:** What do you mean by that? **SOCRATES:** Heraclitus says somewhere that "everything moves and nothing remains"; and comparing existing things to the flow of a river, he says that you could not step into the same river twice. **HERMOGENES:** That is true. **SOCRATES:** What then? Does it seem to you that the person who gave the names Rhea and Kronos to the ancestors of the other gods thought differently from Heraclitus? Do you think it was by mere chance that he gave them both names related to streams? <note>Socrates is punning on the Greek names: Rhea is linked to *rhoē* (flow) and Kronos to *chronos* (time/duration).</note> Just as Homer speaks of Oceanus as the origin of the gods and Tethys as their mother. I believe Hesiod says the same. And Orpheus says somewhere that "Fair-flowing Oceanus was the first to begin marriage, he who wedded his sister Tethys, born of the same mother." See how these accounts agree with one another,
<margin>B</margin> and how they all tend toward the philosophy of Heraclitus. **HERMOGENES:** You seem to be making a good point, Socrates; however, I do not understand what the name "Tethys" is meant to signify. **SOCRATES:** But this name almost explains itself; it is a hidden name for a spring. For the words <note>original: "διαττόμενον" (diattomenon) and "ἠθούμενον" (ēthoumenon)</note> "that which is strained through" and "that which is filtered" are images of a spring. The name Tethys is composed of these two elements. **HERMOGENES:** That was well said, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Why shouldn't it be? But what comes after this? We have spoken of Zeus. **HERMOGENES:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** Let us then speak of his brothers, Poseidon and Pluto, and that other name by which they call him. **HERMOGENES:** By all means. **SOCRATES:** Now, it seems to me that Poseidon was named by the first name-giver because, as he was walking, 
<margin>C</margin> the nature of the sea held him back and no longer allowed him to proceed further, but acted like a shackle for his feet. He therefore named the god who rules this power "Poseidon," as being a "foot-shackle" <note>original: "ποσίδεσμον" (posidesmon)</note>. The letter 'e' was perhaps added for the sake of elegance. But perhaps that is not it; instead, in place of the 's', two 'l's were originally used, as if the god was "knowing many things" <note>original: "πολλά εἰδότος" (polla eidotos)</note>. Perhaps, though, he is named from "shaking" <note>original: "σείειν" (seiein)</note>, the "Shaker," with the 'p', 'o', and 'd' added to the name. As for "Pluto," he was so named according to the "giving of wealth" <note>original: "πλούτου" (ploutou)</note>, because wealth is sent up from the earth below. As for "Hades," most people seem to suppose that the name refers to the "unseen" <note>original: "ἀειδές" (aeides)</note>; and 
<margin>D</margin> being afraid of the name, they call him Pluto instead. **HERMOGENES:** And how does it appear to you, Socrates? **SOCRATES:** It seems to me that men have gone wrong in many ways concerning the power of this god, and they fear him without cause. They fear that once any of us dies, we remain there forever, and they are terrified that the soul goes to him naked of the body. But all these things—the god’s authority and his name—seem to me to point toward the same thing. **HERMOGENES:** How so? **SOCRATES:** I will tell you what I think. Tell me, for any living creature, which bond is stronger to make it stay in any place: necessity or desire? **HERMOGENES:** Desire is far superior, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Do you not think, then, that many would 
<margin>E</margin> escape from Hades if he did not bind those who go there with the strongest bond? **HERMOGENES:** Clearly so. **SOCRATES:** It must be, then, that he binds them with some desire, if indeed he is to bind them with the greatest bond of all. **HERMOGENES:** So it appears. **SOCRATES:** Are there not many desires? **HERMOGENES:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** What desire could be greater than when someone thinks that by associating with someone else, he will become a better man? **HERMOGENES:** By Zeus, none at all, Socrates! **SOCRATES:** For this reason, Hermogenes, we must believe that no one who has gone there ever wants to come back here—not even the Sirens themselves—but they and everyone else are enchanted
<margin>F</margin> by him. So beautiful are the words that Hades knows how to speak, it seems. And from this account, this god is a perfect sophist and a great benefactor to those with him, who also sends down so many good things to those of us here; such great abundance he has there. From this he received the name "Pluto" <note>the "Wealthy One"</note>. And his refusal to associate with men while they have bodies, but only when the soul is pure of all the evils and desires of the body—does this not seem to you to be the mark of a philosopher and someone who has thought things through well? He knows he can hold them fast by binding them with the desire for virtue, but while they possess the flutterings and madness of the body, not even his father Kronos could hold them with him, even if he bound them in those legendary chains. **HERMOGENES:** You certainly seem to be saying something,
<margin>G</margin> Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Indeed, Hermogenes, the name "Hades" is far from being derived from the "unseen" <note>original: "ἀειδές" (aeides)</note>; rather, it is much more likely that he was called Hades by the Lawgiver because he "knows all noble things" <note>original: "πάντα τὰ καλὰ εἰδέναι" (panta ta kala eidenai)</note>. **HERMOGENES:** Very well. What do we say of Demeter, Hera, Apollo, Athena, Hephaestus, Ares, and the other gods? **SOCRATES:** Demeter appears to be named after the "giving of food," as she gives like a "mother" <note>Socrates derives Demeter from *didousa mētēr*, "Giving Mother"</note>. Hera is named as the "Amiable one" <note>original: "ἐρατή" (erate)</note>, just as it is said that Zeus married her because he was "in love" <note>original: "ἐρασθεὶς" (erastheis)</note> with her. Or perhaps the Lawgiver was thinking of the heavens and named the "Air" <note>original: "ἀήρ" (aer)</note> Hera, disguising it by putting the beginning at the end. You would realize this if you said the name "Hera" many times over. As for "Pherrephatta" <note>Persephone</note>, many people also fear 
<margin>H</margin> this name, as they do "Apollo," through an ignorance of the correctness of names. They change it to "Persephone" to consider its meaning...

<column-break/>

...which even Homer had said. <term>HERMOGENES.</term> What is this you say? <term>SOCRATES.</term> For Heraclitus says that all things flow; nothing remains, and comparing the progress of things themselves to the flow of a river, he said it is not possible for you to dip yourself twice into the same water. <term>HERMOGENES.</term> These things are true. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Does he seem to you to differ from Heraclitus, he who inserted Rhea and Saturn <note>Greek: Kronos</note> as the progenitors of the other gods? Do you think he randomly imposed names of flowing things on both? Indeed, Homer established Oceanus as the origin of the gods, and Tethys as the mother. And Hesiod, I believe, intended the same. Furthermore, Orpheus said Oceanus first began the beautiful-flowing marriage, who <margin>B</margin> mixed with his own sister Tethys. See how greatly these things harmonize with one another, and all return to the opinion of Heraclitus. <term>HERMOGENES.</term> You seem to me to be saying something, Socrates. However, I do not sufficiently understand what the name of Tethys wants for itself. <term>SOCRATES.</term> This indeed signifies almost the same thing: since it is a hidden name for a spring. For <unclear>diattomenon and ethoumenon</unclear>, that is, "gushing forth" and "leaping across," present an image of a spring; and from both of these names the name <unclear>Tethys</unclear> is composed. <term>HERMOGENES.</term> This is indeed very fine, O Socrates. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Why not? But what follows: we have certainly spoken of Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note>. <term>HERMOGENES.</term> So it is. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Let us speak of his brothers, Neptune and Pluto, and the other name by which they call him. <term>HERMOGENES.</term> Certainly. <term>SOCRATES.</term> It seems Neptune 
<margin>C</margin> was called <unclear>Poseidon</unclear> by the one who first named him for this reason: because the nature of the sea detained him as he went, and did not permit him to go further, but threw shackles, as it were, upon his feet. And so he called the prince of the sea <unclear>Poseidon</unclear>, as if he were <unclear>posidesmon</unclear>, that is, having a shackle for the feet. The 'e' was perhaps added for the sake of beauty. Perhaps it does not mean this, but in place of 's', 'll' was first placed, as if he were called <unclear>polla eidos</unclear>, that is, a God "knowing many things." Perhaps from that which is said <unclear>seiein</unclear>, that is, "to shake," he was named <unclear>seion</unclear>, that is, "shaking," to which 'p' and 'd' were added. Pluto, moreover, we call as if <unclear>ploutou</unclear>, 
<margin>D</margin> that is, the "giver of riches," because riches are dug out from the bowels of the earth. <unclear>Hades</unclear>, indeed, the multitude interprets as <unclear>aeides</unclear>, "sad" or "dark." And shuddering at this name, they call him Pluto. <term>HERMOGENES.</term> But what do you feel, Socrates? <term>SOCRATES.</term> It seems to me that men have erred in many ways concerning the power of this God, and have always dreaded him, when it is least appropriate. Furthermore, everyone is terrified by this: that no one returns here after they have died, or that the soul, stripped of the body, goes there. But all these things, both the kingdom and the name of this god, seem to me to tend toward the same thing. <term>HERMOGENES.</term> In what way? <term>SOCRATES.</term> I will say what I feel; for I answer myself. Which of these is the more powerful bond for 
<margin>E</margin> detaining any animal anywhere: necessity or desire? <term>HERMOGENES.</term> By far, O Socrates, desire is superior. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Would not very many flee from the realm of Hades daily if he did not bind those who descend there with the strongest bond? <term>HERMOGENES.</term> Evidently. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Therefore, he binds them with a certain desire, as it seems, rather than by necessity, if indeed he binds with the strongest bond. <term>HERMOGENES.</term> It appears so. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Are there not again many desires? <term>HERMOGENES.</term> Many. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Therefore, he binds them with the most vehement desire of all, if indeed he must connect them with an insoluble knot. <term>HERMOGENES.</term> Certainly. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Is there any desire more vehement than that by which someone is affected when, through association with another, he hopes to emerge a better man? <term>HERMOGENES.</term> None, by Hercules, 
<margin>F</margin> Socrates. <term>SOCRATES.</term> For this reason it must be said, Hermogenes, that no one wants to return here from there, not even the Sirens themselves; rather, both they and all others are soothed and as if bound by the most sweet speeches of Pluto. And, as this reasoning testifies, that god is undoubtedly a most eloquent sophist, and confers immense benefits upon those who dwell in his presence: he who so abundantly overflows with riches that he supplies us with such great goods, whence he was also named Pluto. Does it not seem to you to be the duty of a philosopher and a man endowed with the lights of prudence and counsel, that he is unwilling to adhere to men having bodies, but only then admits them when their mind is purged of all bodily evils and lusts? This god surely devised that he would best retain souls by this method, if he bound them with a greed for virtue. But those who are infected by the stupor and insanity of the body, not even the father of Pluto, Saturn himself, is able to coerce with those bonds of his and keep with him. <term>HERMOGENES.</term> You seem to be saying something, 
<margin>G</margin> O Socrates. <term>SOCRATES.</term> It is far from the case, Hermogenes, that the name <unclear>Hades</unclear> was said as if it were <unclear>aeides</unclear>, that is, "sad" or "dark"; rather, it is much more derived from <unclear>to eidenai</unclear>, (that is, to know) all beautiful things. From this, therefore, that god was named <unclear>Hades</unclear> by the founder of names. <term>HERMOGENES.</term> Be it so. What besides do we say of the name of Ceres, and of Juno, Apollo and Minerva, Vulcan and Mars, and the other gods? <term>SOCRATES.</term> 
<margin>H</margin> Ceres indeed is called <unclear>Demeter</unclear> from the very distribution of grain <note>original: "σιτομέτρῳ" (sitometro)</note>, as if <unclear>didousa meter</unclear>, that is, the "exhibiting mother." <term>HERMOGENES.</term> True, that is Juno, as if <unclear>erate</unclear>, that is, "amiable," because of the love with which Jove is affected toward her. Perhaps also looking at the sublime, he who established this name called the "Air" <unclear>Hera</unclear>, and spoke obscurely, putting the beginning at the end. Which will indeed be clear to you if you pronounce that name frequently. <unclear>Pherrephatta</unclear>, that is Proserpina, and <unclear>Apollo</unclear>, some are afraid to name, because the correctness of names is unknown to them. Indeed, by changing it, they consider <unclear>Persephone</unclear> herself...

<summary>This page explores the etymological origins of the names of major Greek deities, connecting them to Heraclitean "flux" and the "desire for virtue" as the strongest bond in the afterlife. Socrates reinterprets Hades not as a place of darkness, but as a realm of profound knowledge and wisdom.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from the previous discussion on the names of the gods. Socrates and Hermogenes move from the elemental gods to the specific Olympian deities, examining how their names reflect their powers and natures according to the theory of "flux."</meta>

# 266 PLATO

### THE CRATYLUS

<margin>A</margin> And this appears grave <note>original: "grauéque"; here meaning serious or even frightening</note> to them. This, however, indicates the wisdom of the goddess herself. Wisdom, at any rate, is that which touches and is able to follow things as they flow. Therefore, this goddess would be rightly called Pherephapha <note>original: "Φερεπάφα"; Persephone</note> because of her wisdom and her contact <note>original: "ἐπαφήν" (epaphēn)</note> with that which is carried <note>original: "φερομένου" (pheromenou)</note>, or something of that sort. For this reason, the wise Hades himself associates with her because she is such a goddess. But now people distort this name, valuing the beauty of the sound more than the truth, so that they call her Pherephatta. The same thing has happened regarding the name of Apollo; for many dread that name as if it signifies something terrible. Have you not noticed this? **HERMOGENES:** I certainly have, and you speak the truth. **SOCRATES:** This name, however, as I think, is most perfectly suited to the power of the god.

<margin>B</margin> **HERMOGENES:** In what way? **SOCRATES:** I will try to express my opinion. Certainly no other single name could have been found more suitable to the four powers of this god, which would both encompass all of them and somehow declare his skill in music, prophecy, medicine, and archery. **HERMOGENES:** Explain it then. You say the name is something marvelous. **SOCRATES:** It is indeed harmoniously composed, as befits a musical god. First, purgation and purifications, both in medicine and in prophecy—as well as the purifications by the medicines of doctors or the incantations and expiations of prophets, the baths and sprinklings—all these have one single aim: to make a person pure in both body and soul. **HERMOGENES:** Exactly so. **SOCRATES:** Is not the god who purifies, then, the one who washes away <note>original: "ἀπολούων" (apolouon)</note> and releases <note>original: "ἀπολύων" (apolyon)</note> from such evils? **HERMOGENES:** Without a doubt. **SOCRATES:** Insofar as he washes and releases, as a physician of such things, he would rightly be called the Releaser <note>original: "Apolyōn"</note>. But regarding prophecy, and the true and the simple <note>original: "ἁπλοῦν" (haploun)</note>, which are the same, we can rightly call him as the Thessalians do; for all Thessalians call this god the Simple <note>original: "ἁπλῶν" (haplōn)</note>.

<margin>C</margin> Inasmuch as he is always in control of shooting arrows <note>original: "ἀεὶ βολῶν" (aei bolōn)</note> when he stretches the bow, he can be called "the Ever-Shooter" <note>original: "ἀεὶ βάλλων" (aei ballōn)</note>, that is, perpetually aiming and directing. Regarding music, however, one must think of it just as we think of the words "follower" <note>original: "ἀκόλουθος" (akolouthos)</note> and "spouse" <note>original: "ἄκοιτις" (akoitis)</note>, in which the letter *alpha* (a), as in many other words, signifies "together" <note>original: "ὁμοῦ" (homou)</note>. Here too, the *alpha* and the "turning" <note>original: "πόλησις" (polēsis)</note> signify a revolution that is performed together and at once: in the heavens, through those points we call "poles" <note>original: "πόλους" (polous)</note>, and in song, that "harmony" <note>original: "ἁρμονία"</note> which we call "consonance" <note>original: "συμφωνίαν"</note>. Because in these things, as those skilled in music and astronomy say, all things are turned together by a certain harmony. Now, this god presides over harmony, "turning all things together" <note>original: "ὁμοπολῶν" (homopolōn)</note>, both among gods and among men.

<margin>D</margin> Just as we called the "together-traveler" and "together-sleeper" a follower and a spouse, changing the "homo-" sound to "a-", so we called him Apollo who was the "together-turner" <note>original: "ὁμοπολῶν"</note>, inserting a second 'l' because the name would otherwise have sounded identical to a harsh word <note>original: "ἀπολλύων" (apollyōn) meaning 'destroying'</note>. It is this that people in these times suspect, and because they do not correctly perceive the power of the name, they fear it as if it signified some destruction. But in reality, this name encompasses all the powers of this god, as we said above. For it signifies the Simple, the Ever-Shooter, the Purifier, and the Together-Turner. As for the name of the Muses and music in general, it is drawn from the word "to seek" <note>original: "μῶσθαι" (mōsthai)</note>, and from the investigation and study of wisdom. Leto <note>original: "Λητώ"</note>, or Latona, is named from her mildness, because she is willing <note>original: "ἐθελήμων" (ethelēmōn)</note>, that is, prompt and exposed and ready to grant what anyone asks. Or perhaps, as foreigners call her—for many call her Letho—she seems to be named from the fact that her disposition is not rigid, but gentle and smooth <note>original: "λεῖον ἦθος" (leion ēthos)</note>. Artemis is named from being "sound" <note>original: "ἀρτεμές" (artemes)</note>, that is, whole and modest, because of her choice of virginity. Perhaps the giver of the name called her so as one who is "conscious of virtue" <note>original: "ἀρετῆς ἴστορα" (aretēs istora)</note>.

<margin>E</margin> Or perhaps Artemis was named as if she were "one who hates the birth-pains" <note>original: "μῖσον ἀποτόκους" (mison apotokous)</note>, as if she loathed the union of man and woman. For the name was established either because of one of these things, or because of all such things.

<margin>G</margin> **HERMOGENES:** But what about Dionysus and Aphrodite? **SOCRATES:** You ask great things, O son of Hipponicus. But there is a double reason for the names given to these gods: one serious and the other playful. Seek the serious one from others; however, nothing prevents us from recounting the playful one. Indeed, even the gods are fond of play. Dionysus is the "Giver of Wine" <note>original: "διδούς τὸν οἶνον" (didous ton oinon)</note>, playfully called "Didonysus." Wine itself could rightly be called "Think-Mind" <note>original: "οἰνόυς" (oinous)</note>, because it makes most people who drink it, though they are out of their minds, "think they have sense" <note>original: "οἴεσθαι νοῦν ἔχειν" (oiesthai noun echein)</note>. Regarding Venus <note>Aphrodite</note>, it is not fitting to disagree with Hesiod, but to concede that she is called Aphrodite because of her generation from "foam" <note>original: "ἀφροῦ" (aphrou)</note>. **HERMOGENES:** But surely, Socrates, since you are an Athenian, you will not pass over Athena in silence, nor Vulcan <note>Hephaestus</note> and Mars <note>Ares</note>. **SOCRATES:** That would hardly be fitting. **HERMOGENES:** Certainly not. **SOCRATES:** One of her names is not difficult to say why it was given. **HERMOGENES:** Which one? **SOCRATES:** We call her Pallas. **HERMOGENES:** Clearly. **SOCRATES:** We should consider the name to have been derived from dancing in arms; for to lift oneself or something else from the earth, or to carry something in one's hands, we call "to brandish" <note>original: "πάλλειν" (pallein)</note> and "to be brandished," to shake and to be shaken, and to perform a dance. **HERMOGENES:** Very much so. **SOCRATES:** We call her Pallas for this reason, then. **HERMOGENES:** And rightly so. But how do you interpret her other name? **SOCRATES:** You ask about Athena? **HERMOGENES:** That very one. **SOCRATES:** This is a weightier matter, my friend. The ancients seem to have thought of Athena...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...and it appears terrible to them. But this remains from the wisdom of the goddess. For since things are in flux, that which touches and can follow them must be wisdom. Thus Pherephapha <note>Persephone</note>, because of her wisdom and her "touching" <note>original: "ἐπαφήν"</note> of that which is "carried" <note>original: "φερομένου"</note>, would be correctly called by this name, or something similar. This is why Hades, being wise, dwells with her, because she is of such a nature. But today they distort her name, caring more for the pleasantness of the sound than the truth, so they call her Pherephatta. The same is true of Apollo, as I said; many have been frightened by the name of the god, as if it indicated something terrible. Or have you not noticed? **HERMOGENES:** Yes indeed; and what you say is true.

<margin>B</margin> **SOCRATES:** But it is (in my opinion) most beautifully established according to the power of the god. **HERMOGENES:** How so? **SOCRATES:** I will try to say what it seems to me. For there is no other single name that could have better fit the four powers of the god, so as to touch upon them all, and to show in a certain way music, prophecy, medicine, and archery. **HERMOGENES:** Tell me then. For you say the name is something strange. **SOCRATES:** On the contrary, it is well-harmonized, since the god is a musician. First, purification and cleansings, both in medical matters and prophetic ones, and the fumigations with medicinal drugs or prophetic rites, and the baths in such things, and the sprinklings—all these have one power: to make the person pure both in body and in soul. Is it not so? **HERMOGENES:** Very much so. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, the god who cleanses and "washes away" <note>original: "ἀπολούων"</note> and "releases" <note>original: "ἀπολύων"</note> from such evils would be this one. **HERMOGENES:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** According to these releases and washings, as a physician of such things, he would be rightly called "the Releaser" <note>original: "Apolyōn"</note>; but according to prophecy and the true and the simple—for they are the same—just as the Thessalians call him, he would be most correctly named. For all Thessalians call this god the "Simple" <note>original: "ἁπλῶν"</note>.

<margin>C</margin> And because he is always in control of shooting arrows <note>original: "ἀεὶ βολῶν"</note> in archery, he is the "Ever-shooter" <note>original: "ἀεὶ βάλλων"</note>. Regarding music, one must understand him as one does "follower" <note>original: "ἀκόλουθος"</note> and "spouse" <note>original: "ἄκοιτις"</note>, that the letter *alpha* signifies "together" in many places, and here it signifies "together-turning" <note>original: "ὁμοῦ πόλησιν"</note>, whether concerning the sky, which they call "poles," or the harmony in song, which is called "consonance" <note>original: "συμφωνία"</note>. Because all these things (as those refined in music and astronomy say) turn all together by a certain harmony. And this god presides over harmony, "turning them all together" <note>original: "ὁμοπολῶν"</note>, both among gods and among men.

<margin>D</margin> Just as we called the "together-traveler" and "together-sleeper" a follower and a spouse, changing the *omicron-upsilon* (ou) for an *alpha* (a), so we called him Apollo, he who "turns together" <note>original: "ὁμοπολῶν"</note>, inserting a second 'l' because it was becoming a namesake for a harsh word <note>original: "ἀπολλύων" - destroying</note>. This is what some people suspect today, because they do not correctly examine the power of the name, and they fear it as signifying some destruction. But the majority (as was just said) is established touching upon all the god's powers: the Simple, the Ever-shooter, the Washer, and the Together-turner. The Muses and music in general he named from the word "to seek" <note>original: "μῶσθαι"</note>, it seems, and from investigation and philosophy. Leto is named from the mildness of the goddess, in accordance with her being "willing" <note>original: "ἐθελήμονα"</note> of what anyone may ask. Perhaps, as foreigners call her—for many call her Letho—it seems she was called Letho by those who name her so because of her character, which is not rough but gentle and smooth <note>original: "λεῖον"</note>. Artemis seems to be named from "soundness" <note>original: "ἀρτεμές"</note> and "orderliness" <note>original: "κόσμιον"</note>, because of her desire for virginity. Perhaps the one who named her called the goddess "knower of virtue" <note>original: "ἀρετῆς ἴστορα"</note>. Or perhaps as one who "hates the plowing of a man in a woman" <note>meaning childbirth or intercourse</note>. Or for all these reasons, the name-giver gave this name to the goddess.

<margin>E</margin> **HERMOGENES:** What about Dionysus and Aphrodite?

<margin>G</margin> **SOCRATES:** You ask great things, O son of Hipponicus. But there is a serious way of explaining the names of these gods, and a playful one. Ask others for the serious one; but nothing prevents us from going through the playful one, for the gods too are fond of play. For Dionysus is the "Giver of Wine" <note>original: "ὁ διδοὺς τὸν οἶνον"</note>, called "Didonysos" in play. And wine <note>original: "οἶνος"</note>, because it makes most of those who drink it "think they have sense" <note>original: "οἴεσθαι νοῦν ἔχειν"</note> when they do not, could most justly be called "Think-sense" <note>original: "οἰόνους"</note>. About Aphrodite, it is not worth contradicting Hesiod, but rather agreeing that she was called Aphrodite because of her "birth from foam" <note>original: "ἀφροῦ γένεσιν"</note>. **HERMOGENES:** But surely you won't skip Athena, O Socrates, you who are an Athenian, nor Hephaestus and Ares. **SOCRATES:** That wouldn't be right. **HERMOGENES:** Indeed not. **SOCRATES:** It is not difficult to say why one of her names was established. **HERMOGENES:** Which one? **SOCRATES:** We call her Pallas, I believe. **HERMOGENES:** How could we not? **SOCRATES:** This name we consider to have been established from dancing in armor—and we think we are right. For "to lift up" <note>original: "μετεωρίζειν"</note> either oneself or something else, either from the earth or in one's hands, we call "to brandish" <note>original: "πάλλειν"</note> and "to be brandished," or to dance and be danced. **HERMOGENES:** Quite so. **SOCRATES:** So, Pallas for that reason. **HERMOGENES:** And correctly. But how do you explain the other name? **SOCRATES:** That of Athena? **HERMOGENES:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** This is a more stable matter, my friend. For the ancients seem to have considered Athena...

<summary>In this excerpt from Plato's Cratylus, Socrates provides etymological explanations for the names of various gods, arguing that names are not arbitrary but reflect the deities' inherent powers and characters, such as Apollo's association with purification and harmony.</summary>
<keywords>etymology, Apollo, Persephone, Artemis, Dionysus, Aphrodite, Athena, Plato, Cratylus, Greek mythology, linguistics, philosophy of language</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Socrates’ exploration of the etymologies of divine names. Having discussed the major gods in the previous section, he now turns to Athena, Hephaestus, Ares, Hermes, and the celestial bodies. Socrates uses these linguistic "histories" to argue that names reflect the fundamental nature or "flow" of the things they describe.</meta>

# CRATYLUS.

<margin>A</margin> Just like those today who are experts in the works of Homer. For many of them, in explaining the poet, say that he represented Athena as "mind" and "thought" <note>original: "νοῦν τε καὶ διάνοιαν"</note>. And the one who established her name seems to have had something similar in mind about her. Indeed, calling her the "mind of God" <note>original: "Θεονόη" (Theonoē)</note>, as if he were saying she is "Theonoē," he used an foreign dialect's "a" instead of the "e" and removed the "i" and the "s." Or perhaps not even that; rather, because she understands divine things <note>original: "θεῖα νοούσης" (theia noousēs)</note> better than all others, he called her "Theonoē." It is also not far off to say he wanted to call her "moral intelligence" <note>original: "Ἠθονόην" (Ethonoē)</note>, as she is intelligence in character <note>original: "ἐν τῷ ἤθει νόησιν"</note>. Then he himself, or some later people, changed it to the more beautiful name "Athena," as they thought. <margin>B</margin> **HERMOGENES:** What about Hephaestus? How do you explain that? **SOCRATES:** Are you asking about the noble "knower of light" <note>original: "φάεος ἵστορα" (phaeos histora)</note>? **HERMOGENES:** I believe so. **SOCRATES:** Is it not clear to everyone that he is "Phastos" <note>original: "Φάϊστος," meaning Shining One</note>, having pulled the "H" <note>original: "φ" (phi) here acting as an aspirate sound</note> to himself to become "Hephaestus"? **HERMOGENES:** That is likely, unless some other thought occurs to you. **SOCRATES:** Well, to keep that from happening, ask about Ares. **HERMOGENES:** I am asking. **SOCRATES:** If you like, his name "Ares" <note>original: "Ἄρης"</note> comes from his "masculine" <note>original: "ἄρρεν" (arren)</note> and "courageous" <note>original: "ἀνδρεῖον" (andreion)</note> nature. On the other hand, it could be because of his hard and unyielding nature, which they call "unbroken" <note>original: "ἄρρατον" (arraton)</note>; in every way, this name is fitting for a god of war. <margin>C</margin> **HERMOGENES:** Entirely so. **SOCRATES:** By the gods, let us leave the gods now; for I am afraid to speak about them. But propose any others you wish, so that you may see "what sort of horses those of Eryximachus are" <note>A proverbial expression meaning "to see what I can really do."</note>. **SOCRATES:** I will do that, but I have one more thing to ask you about Hermes, especially since Cratylus says I am not truly "Hermogenes" <note>Hermogenes' name literally means "Son of Hermes" or "Born of Hermes." Cratylus is teasing him that he lacks the eloquence associated with the god.</note>. Let us try to look at "Hermes" <note>original: "Ἑρμῆν"</note> and what the name means. He seems to have something to do with speech <note>original: "λόγον" (logos)</note>, in that he is an "interpreter" <note>original: "ἑρμηνέα" (hermenea)</note>, a messenger, a thief, a deceiver in words, and a bargainer; all this activity concerns the power of speech. As we said before, "to speak" <note>original: "εἴρειν" (eirein)</note> is the use of speech. And the divine Homer often says "he contrived" <note>original: "ἐμήσατο" (emēsato)</note>, which means to devise or plan. <margin>D</margin> From both of these, the lawgiver commands us, as it were: "O humans, he who contrived speech" <note>original: "τὸ εἴρειν ἐμήσατο"</note>—since "to speak" is "eirein"—should rightly be called by us "Eiremes." But now we, thinking we are making the name more elegant, call him "Hermes." Even "Iris" <note>The rainbow messenger goddess</note> seems to be named from "eirein" (to speak), because she was a messenger. **HERMOGENES:** By Zeus, it seems Cratylus was right to say I am no "Hermogenes," for I am certainly no clever "contriver of speech." **SOCRATES:** It is also likely, my friend, that Pan is the biform son of Hermes. **HERMOGENES:** How so? **SOCRATES:** You know that speech <note>original: "λόγος" (logos)</note> signifies "the whole" <note>original: "τὸ πᾶν" (to pan)</note>, and it revolves and circulates forever; and it is twofold: true and false. <margin>E</margin> **HERMOGENES:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** Now, the true part is smooth and divine, dwelling above among the gods; but the false part dwells below among the mass of men, and it is rough and "tragic" <note>original: "τραγικόν"; Socrates puns on the word for tragedy and the word for goat, "tragos."</note>. For it is there, in the tragic life, that the most myths and falsehoods are found. **HERMOGENES:** Quite so. **SOCRATES:** Rightly then, he who signifies "the whole" <note>original: "πᾶν"</note> and is "always moving" <note>original: "ἀεὶ πολῶν" (aei polon)</note> would be "Pan the goat-herd" <note>original: "Πὰν αἰπόλος" (Pan aipolos)</note>, the biform son of Hermes—smooth in his upper parts, but rough and goat-like in his lower parts. And Pan is either speech itself or the brother of speech, if he is the son of Hermes; and it is no wonder that a brother resembles a brother. But, as I was saying, my blessed man, let us be done with the gods. <margin>F</margin> **HERMOGENES:** With such gods as these, Socrates, if you wish. But what prevents you from discussing things like the sun, the moon, the stars, the earth, the ether, air, fire, water, the seasons, and the year? **SOCRATES:** You assign me many tasks! However, if it will please you, I am willing. **HERMOGENES:** It will indeed. **SOCRATES:** What then do you want first? Shall we discuss the "sun" <note>original: "ἥλιον" (helion)</note> as you said? **HERMOGENES:** By all means. **SOCRATES:** It seems it would be clearer if one used the Doric form of the name. The Dorians call it "Halios" <note>original: "ἅλιον"</note>. It would be "Halios" because it "gathers" <note>original: "ἁλίζειν" (halizein)</note> people into one place when it rises. Or perhaps because it "always revolves" <note>original: "ἀεὶ εἱλεῖ" (aei heilei)</note> around the earth in its course. Or because it "varies" <note>original: "αἰολεῖ" (aiolei)</note> the things produced by the earth as it moves. To "vary" and to "shift" are the same thing. <margin>G</margin> **HERMOGENES:** What about the moon <note>original: "σελήνη" (selēnē)</note>? **SOCRATES:** This name seems to put pressure on Anaxagoras. **HERMOGENES:** Why? **SOCRATES:** Because it seems to indicate something older than what he recently said: that the moon has its light from the sun. **HERMOGENES:** How so? **SOCRATES:** "Selas" <note>original: "σέλας"</note> and "light" are the same thing. **HERMOGENES:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** And this light is always "new" <note>original: "νέον" (neon)</note> and "old" <note>original: "ἕννον" (ennon)</note> around the moon, if what the followers of Anaxagoras say is true. For as it circles it forever, the sun always casts "new" light upon it, while the "old" light remains from the previous month. **HERMOGENES:** Exactly. **SOCRATES:** Many call her "Selanaia" <note>original: "σελαναία"</note>. **HERMOGENES:** True. **SOCRATES:** Because she always has light that is "new and old" <note>original: "σέλας νέον καὶ ἔννον"</note>, she would most rightly be called "Sela-eno-neia"; but it has been compressed into "Selanaia." **HERMOGENES:** That is a very dithyrambic <note>A high-flown, poetic style</note> name, Socrates! But what of the "month" and the "stars"? **SOCRATES:** "Month" <note>original: "μείς" (meis)</note> would be rightly called so from "diminishing" <note>original: "μειοῦσθαι" (meiousthai)</note>. The "stars" <note>original: "ἄστρα" (astra)</note> seem to take their name from "lightning" <note>original: "ἀστραπή" (astrapē)</note>. And lightning, because it "turns the eyes" <note>original: "τὰ ὦπας ἀναστρέφει"</note>, would be "anastrope"; but now it is called "astrapē" for elegance.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Just like those in these times who are learned in the interpretations of Homer. For most of them explain Homer by saying they devised Athena as "mind" and "thought." And whoever found the names seems to have felt something similar about her; or rather, extolling her even higher, he introduced her as the "mind of God," just as if he were saying, "Theonoē." This is done by using "a" for "o" in a certain foreign manner, and taking away the "l" and the "s." Perhaps it is not so, but "divine intelligence" <note>original: "θεία νόησις" (theia noēsis)</note>, that is, because she knows divine things above all others, he called her "Theonoē," meaning "one who knows divine things." Nor will it be beside the point if we say he wanted to call her "ethonoē," as if she were "intelligence in character." He himself later, or even those who came after, to produce something more beautiful <margin>B</margin> in appearance, named her Athena. **HERMOGENES:** What? About Vulcan, whom they name "Hephaestus," what do you say? **SOCRATES:** Do you ask about the noble "knower of light" <note>original: "φάεος ἵστορα"</note>, that is, the presiding officer of light? **HERMOGENES:** I seem to have asked about him. **SOCRATES:** It can be plain to anyone that he is "the one who is of light," and he claims the "k" for himself. Whence he is called "Hephaestus," that is, the presiding officer of light. Perhaps, unless it seems otherwise to you in some way. **SOCRATES:** See if it seems otherwise regarding Mars; ask. **HERMOGENES:** I am asking. **SOCRATES:** If you please, "Ares," that is Mars, is said according to "masculine" <note>original: "ἄρρεν"</note> and "strong" <note>original: "ἀνδρεῖον"</note>. Furthermore, if you wish, because of a certain rough, <margin>C</margin> hard, and unconquered nature—which is entirely called "unbroken" <note>original: "ἄρρατον"</note>—he was called "Ares"; this will also suit a thoroughly warlike god. **HERMOGENES:** Entirely. **SOCRATES:** Let us now dismiss the gods, by the gods, I beseech you. For I fear to discourse about them. But provoke me to any others you wish, so that you may know what sort of "horses of Euthyphro" <note>In the Latin translation, the name is given as Euthyphro, referencing the previous page where Socrates claimed he was inspired by him.</note> I have. **HERMOGENES:** I will do as you ask, if I may ask one thing of myself. For Cratylus denies that I am Hermogenes. Let us investigate, therefore, what the name "Hermes," that is Mercury, signifies, so that we may see if he speaks any truth here. **SOCRATES:** "Hermes," that is Mercury, seems to pertain to speech, insofar as he is an "interpreter" <note>original: "ἑρμηνεύς"</note>, that is, an interpreter and messenger, a thief-like seducer in speaking, and a vehement public speaker. All of that revolves around speech. Indeed, as we said in the earlier parts, "to speak" <note>original: "εἴρειν"</note> is the use of speech. Often, <margin>D</margin> however, Homer says of this: "he contrived" <note>original: "ἐμήσατο"</note>, that is, he machined or plotted. From both, therefore, the name of this god is composed: both from that which is "to speak," and from that which is "to machine" and "to devise things to be said," just as if the author of the name were commanding us. It is right, O men, that you call that god who "contrived to speak" <note>original: "εἴρειν ἐμήσατο"</note> "Eiremes." We, however, thinking it more elegant to speak thus, call him "Hermes." Furthermore, "Iris" seems to have her name from "eirein," that is to speak, because she is a messenger. **HERMOGENES:** By my faith, Cratylus seems to have rightly denied that I am Hermogenes. For I am dull at the invention of speech. **SOCRATES:** It is also fitting, my friend, that "Pan" the biform be the son of Mercury. **HERMOGENES:** By what reason? **SOCRATES:** You know that speech signifies "the whole" <note>original: "πᾶν"</note>, and it circles <margin>E</margin> and rolls forever, and it is twin: namely, true and false? **HERMOGENES:** Indeed. **SOCRATES:** Is not that which is true in speech smooth and divine, and dwelling above among the gods? On the contrary, is not that which is false below among the many of men, rough and tragic? For from here the fictions of fables and as many falsehoods as possible are found concerning the tragic life. **HERMOGENES:** It is entirely so. **SOCRATES:** Deservedly, therefore, he who is "announcing the whole" <note>original: "πᾶν"</note> and "always revolving" <note>original: "ἀεὶ πολῶν"</note> would be called "Pan the goat-herd," the biform son of Mercury: from his upper parts smooth and delicate, from his lower parts rough and goat-like. And Pan is either speech itself or the brother of speech, since he is the son of Mercury. And what wonder is it that a brother is like a brother? But <margin>F</margin> now, O blessed one, as I was asking a little while ago, let us break off this speech about the gods. **HERMOGENES:** Let us dismiss such gods, if you wish, O Socrates; but what prevents us from running through certain things of this sort? The sun, moon, stars, earth, ether, air, fire, water, spring, and the year? **SOCRATES:** These are many and great things you ask. Nevertheless, if it will be pleasing to you, I will comply. **HERMOGENES:** It will be plainly very pleasing. **SOCRATES:** What do you ask first? Or as you yourself were saying, first the "sun" <note>original: "ἥλιον"</note>? **HERMOGENES:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** It seems it would be more manifest if one used the Doric name. For the Dorians call it "Halion," and so it is named from "gathering" <note>original: "ἁλίζειν"</note>, that is, from the fact that it gathers men into one when it rises. Likewise from the fact that it "always revolves" <note>original: "ἀεὶ εἱλεῖ"</note> around the earth. Furthermore, because it varies in its circuit the things which are born of the earth. To vary and "to shift" <note>original: "αἰολεῖν"</note> are the same. <margin>G</margin> **HERMOGENES:** What indeed is to be said of "Selene," that is the moon? **SOCRATES:** This name seems to press upon Anaxagoras. **HERMOGENES:** Why? **SOCRATES:** Because it carries before it something older, which he said recently: that the moon draws its light from the sun. **HERMOGENES:** In what way? **SOCRATES:** Is "selas" the same as light? **HERMOGENES:** The same. **SOCRATES:** This light is perpetually "new" and "old" <note>original: "νέον & ἔννον"</note> around the moon, if only the followers of Anaxagoras speak the truth: for shining around it, it is continually renewed. The light of the past month, however, is old. **HERMOGENES:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** Many name the moon "Selanaia." **HERMOGENES:** Truly. **SOCRATES:** Since indeed it always has new and old light, it ought rightly to be called "Selaeno-eia." Now, however, with the word shortened, it is called "Selanaia." **HERMOGENES:** This is a dithyrambic name, O Socrates. But the "month" <note>original: "μῆνα"</note> and the "stars" <note>original: "ἄστρα"</note>, how do you interpret them? **SOCRATES:** The month "meis" indeed would be rightly named from "diminishing" <note>original: "μειοῦσθαι"</note>. The stars indeed have the surname of "lightning" <note>original: "ἀστράπη"</note>. "Astrape," however, because it "turns the sight" <note>original: "ὦπας ἀναστρέφει"</note>, that is, converts the vision to itself, ought to be called "anastrope." Now it is named "astrape" by a more elegant word.

<summary>Socrates provides etymological explanations for the names of Athena, Hermes, Pan, and celestial bodies like the Sun and Moon, often linking their names to their physical or philosophical functions. He highlights Anaxagoras’ then-recent theory that the moon reflects the sun's light as a basis for the moon's name.</summary>
<keywords>Athena, Hephaestus, Ares, Hermes, Pan, Helios, Selene, Anaxagoras, etymology, Greek philosophy, logos, speech, light</keywords>

--- Page 300 ---
<meta>This page continues Socrates' discussion of etymologies in Plato's Cratylus. Having previously discussed the names of gods and celestial bodies, Socrates now moves toward the names of the elements—fire, water, air—and the passage of time (the year and seasons). This transitions into an investigation of the names of the virtues, where Socrates introduces the "theory of flux" as the underlying logic used by the original name-givers.</meta>

# OF PLATO

<margin>A</margin> **HERMOGENES:** From where do the names "fire" <note>original: "πῦρ" (pyr)</note> and "water" <note>original: "ὕδωρ" (hydor)</note> derive? **SOCRATES:** I am truly at a loss. It seems either the Muse of Euthyphro has abandoned me, or this is a particularly difficult matter. Pay attention, I pray, to the trick I resort to in all things that I find doubtful. **HERMOGENES:** What trick is that? **SOCRATES:** I will tell you. Answer me this: do you know the reason why "fire" is so named? **HERMOGENES:** By Hercules, I do not. **SOCRATES:** See what I suspect about this. I believe the Greeks received many names from foreigners <note>original: "Barbaris," referring to non-Greek speakers</note>, especially those Greeks who live under foreign rule. **HERMOGENES:** What of it? **SOCRATES:** If someone seeks a proper explanation for these names according to the Greek tongue, and not according to the language from which the name was actually found, he will surely be at a loss. **HERMOGENES:** That is indeed likely. <margin>B</margin> **SOCRATES:** See then if this name "fire" is not of foreign origin. For it is not easy to fit it to the Greek language; it is well known that the Phrygians name it thus, with only a slight variation, as they also do with "water" and "dogs" <note>original: "κύνας" (kynas)</note>, and many other things. **HERMOGENES:** These things are true. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, one should not force an explanation for these, since no one can say anything certain about them. For this reason, I set aside these names of fire and water in this manner. But "aether" <note>original: "αἰθήρ"</note> was so named, Hermogenes, because it "always runs" <note>original: "ἀεὶ θεῖ" (aei thei)</note> around the things that are near the earth and elevates them. Or perhaps because it "always flows" <note>original: "αἰθεὶρ" interpreted as "semper fluit"</note>, or because a spirit is stirred by its flow. Poets indeed call blasts and winds "breaths" <note>original: "αὔτας"</note>. Perhaps then "air" <note>original: "ἀήρ"</note> is named as if it were a "flowing spirit" <note>original: "πνευματόρρουν"</note> or a "flowing blast." <margin>C</margin> Furthermore, I think "aether" should be explained because it "always runs around the flowing air" <note>original: "ἀεὶ θεῖ περὶ τὸν ἀέρα ῥέων"</note>; for this reason, it could be called "always-running-air" <note>original: "ἀειθεὴρ"</note>. "Earth" <note>original: "γῆ" (ge)</note>, however, expresses the sense more clearly if it is called "Gaia" <note>original: "γαῖα"</note>. For Gaia can rightly be called "the mother" <note>original: "γεννήτειρα" (genneteira)</note>, as Homer says. For when he says things "have been born" <note>original: "γεγάασι"</note>, he means they were generated within her. **HERMOGENES:** So be it. **SOCRATES:** What remains next? **HERMOGENES:** The seasons and the year. **SOCRATES:** "Seasons" <note>original: "ὧραι" (horai)</note> are indeed named by an ancient and Attic word, if you wish to know the likely truth. For they are called "Horai" because they "limit" <note>original: "ὁρίζουσι" (horizousi)</note> the winters and summers, the winds, and the fruits that grow from the earth. "Year" <note>original: "ἐνιαυτός" (eniautos)</note> and "time" <note>original: "ἔτος" (etos)</note> seem to be the same thing. <margin>D</margin> For that which in turn brings into the light all things that are born and produced from the earth, and which examines and discerns them within itself, is the year. And just as we said above that the name of Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note> was split in two—called "Zena" by some and "Dia" by others—so too some call the year "eniauton" because it is "within itself" <note>original: "ἐν ἑαυτῷ"</note>, and others "etos" because it "scrutinizes and examines." The full meaning is that which examines in itself. From this single phrase, two names were selected. For what is said together as "that which examines in itself" <note>original: "τὸ ἐν αὑτῷ ἐτάζον"</note>, is said distinctly as "eniautos" and "etos." <margin>E</margin> **HERMOGENES:** But truly, O Socrates, you are now moving quite far ahead. **SOCRATES:** I do seem to be wandering quite far into philosophy. **HERMOGENES:** Indeed. **SOCRATES:** Perhaps you will grant me even more. **HERMOGENES:** Truly, after this I would most gladly contemplate in what way those noble names of the virtues were properly given, such as "prudence" <note>original: "φρόνησις" (phronesis)</note>, "intelligence" <note>original: "σύνεσις" (synesis)</note>, "justice" <note>original: "δικαιοσύνη" (dikaiosyne)</note>, and all others of this kind. **SOCRATES:** You have taken up no small class of names, my friend. Nevertheless, since I have put on the lion's skin <note>A reference to Hercules, meaning he is preparing for a heroic or difficult task</note>, I must not be deterred, but rather consider those noble names of prudence, intelligence, thought, knowledge, and others of this sort. **HERMOGENES:** Certainly, we must by no means give up. **SOCRATES:** By the dog, I think I have a good suspicion about what I was just considering: it seems to me that those most ancient authors of names, like many of our own wise men, fell into a dizziness of the brain from their frequent turning around in the investigation of things. Because of this, they imagined that things themselves were being carried along and were wavering. They believe the cause of this opinion is not an internal dizziness, but an external circuit of the things themselves. They think nature is such that nothing in it is firm or stable, but all things flow and are carried along, being agitated in every way, always being born and passing away. This is what I see in the names that have just been mentioned. <margin>F</margin> **HERMOGENES:** In what way, Socrates? **SOCRATES:** Perhaps you did not notice that the previous names were given to things as if they were being carried, flowing, and moved by a perpetual generation? **HERMOGENES:** I did not quite perceive it. **SOCRATES:** First, the one we mentioned first pertains entirely to something of this kind. **HERMOGENES:** Which one is that? **SOCRATES:** "Prudence" <note>original: "φρόνησις"</note>. For it is the "perception of motion and flow" <note>original: "φορᾶς καὶ ῥοῦ νόησις" (phoras kai rhou noesis)</note>. <margin>G</margin> It can also signify the "utility of motion." Ultimately, it is concerned with agitation itself. Furthermore, if you like, "judgment" <note>original: "γνώμη" (gnome)</note> signifies the "consideration of generation" <note>original: "γονῆς νώμησιν"</note>. For to consider is to "examine" <note>original: "ναμᾶν"</note>. And if it pleases you, "intellection" <note>original: "νόησις" (noesis)</note> is the "desire for the new" <note>original: "νέου ἔσις" (neou esis)</note>. That things are "new" signifies they are always becoming; the one who invented the name indicates that the soul desires and approaches this. Originally "noesis" was called "no-esis," but two "e's" had to be pronounced, as in "noesis," as if it were "desire and approach for the new." "Temperance" <note>original: "σωφροσύνη" (sophrosyne)</note> is the safety and preservation of that "prudence" we just spoke of. "Knowledge" <note>original: "ἐπιστήμη" (episteme)</note> has this meaning: as if the soul, not to be looked down upon, follows flowing things, and neither leaves them far behind nor goes too far ahead. For this reason, with the letter "i" inserted, it is proper to call it "episteme." "Understanding" <note>original: "σύνεσις" (synesis)</note> seems to be like a "bringing together" <note>original: "συλλογισμός"</note>. When one is said "to understand" <note>original: "συνιέναι"</note>, it means the same as "to know." For "to understand" declares that the soul accompanies things and is at one with them.

<column-break/>

**HERMOGENES:** What about "fire" and "water"? **SOCRATES:** Regarding "fire," I am at a loss. It is likely that either the Muse of Euthyphro has again failed me, or this is very difficult. Consider then the machine <note>A "deus ex machina" or device</note> I bring in for all such things where I am at a loss. **HERMOGENES:** Tell me then. **SOCRATES:** I will tell you. Answer me: can you say in what way "fire" is named? **HERMOGENES:** By Zeus, I cannot. **SOCRATES:** Consider what I suspect about it. For I realize that the Greeks have taken many names from foreigners, especially those living under the foreigners. **HERMOGENES:** What then? **SOCRATES:** If someone seeks how these are reasonably placed according to the Greek language, and not according to that from which the name happens to come, you know he would be at a loss. **HERMOGENES:** Quite reasonably. **SOCRATES:** See then if the name "fire" is not a foreign one. For it is not easy to attach this to the Greek tongue, and it is clear that the Phrygians call it so, varying it only slightly; and also "water" and "dogs," and many other things. **HERMOGENES:** This is so. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, one must not force these, since anyone might say where "aether" comes from. Fire and water I give up in this way; but as for "air," O Hermogenes, is it called "aer" because it "lifts" <note>original: "αἴρει" (airei)</note> things from the earth, or because it "always flows" <note>original: "ἀεὶ ῥεῖ" (aei rhei)</note>? Or because a "flowing spirit" <note>original: "πνεῦμα ῥέον"</note> comes from it? For poets call the winds "breaths" <note>original: "αὔτας"</note>. Perhaps then it means, as if one were to say "flowing-spirit" or "flowing-breath"; he wants to say it thus, that it is "air." And "aether" I take to be this: because it "always runs around the air in a flow" <note>original: "ἀεὶ θεῖ περὶ τὸν ἀέρα ῥέων"</note>, it would rightly be called "always-runner" <note>original: "ἀειθεὴρ"</note>. "Earth" <note>original: "Γῆ"</note> more clearly signifies what it wants if one names it "Gaia." For "Gaia" would be correctly called "mother" <note>original: "γεννήτειρα"</note>, as Homer says. For "gegaasi" means to have been born. **HERMOGENES:** Good. **SOCRATES:** What then remains for us of such things? **HERMOGENES:** The "seasons," Socrates, and the "year," and "time." **SOCRATES:** "Seasons" <note>original: "ὧραι"</note> should be spoken of in the old Attic way, if you wish to know the likelihood. For they are "limiters" <note>original: "ὅραι" (horai), related to "horizein"</note> because they "limit" <note>original: "ὁρίζειν"</note> winters and summers and winds and the daily fruits of the earth. Because they limit, they are rightly called "Horai." "Year" <note>original: "Ἐνιαυτὸς"</note> and "time" <note>original: "ἔτος"</note> happen to be one thing. For that which brings each of the things that grow and are born into the light in its turn, and examines it within itself—this, just as the name of Zeus was divided in two before, some calling him "Zena" and others "Dia," so here too some say "eniautos" because it is "in itself" <note>original: "ἐν ἑαυτῷ"</note>, and others "etos" because it "examines" <note>original: "ἐτάζει"</note>. The whole account is "that which examines in itself." This being one thing is addressed as two. Thus two names have arisen, "eniautos" and "etos," from one account. **HERMOGENES:** By Zeus, Socrates, you are making great progress in these things. **SOCRATES:** I seem to be driving far into wisdom. **HERMOGENES:** Very much so. **SOCRATES:** Soon you will say so even more. **HERMOGENES:** But regarding this class of things, I would gladly behold these noble names, by what correctness the names regarding the virtues are placed; such as "prudence" and "intelligence," and "justice," and all other such things. **SOCRATES:** You stir up, my friend, no small class of names; but since I have put on the lion's skin, I must not be cowardly, but must examine (it seems) prudence, intelligence, judgment, knowledge, and all the other noble names you mention. **HERMOGENES:** Indeed, we must not stop. **SOCRATES:** And truly I think I am not divining badly regarding "vice"; what I just thought was that the very ancient people who established the names were, much like many of the current wise men, made dizzy by frequently turning around while seeking how things are, and then it seemed to them that things themselves were turning and being carried everywhere. They blame not their own internal state as the cause of this opinion, but that things themselves are naturally so, that none of them is permanent or stable, but they flow and are carried, and are full of every kind of motion and generation always. I say this having considered all the names just now. **HERMOGENES:** How so, Socrates? **SOCRATES:** Perhaps you did not notice what was just said, that names are placed upon things entirely as if they were being carried, flowing, and becoming? **HERMOGENES:** I did not quite realize. **SOCRATES:** And first, this which we first mentioned, is entirely regarding such things. **HERMOGENES:** Which one? **SOCRATES:** "Prudence." For it is the "perception of motion and flow." It could also be understood as "the advantage of motion." But at least it is "being carried." If you wish, "judgment" <note>original: "γνώμη"</note> entirely shows the "scrutiny of generation" <note>original: "γονῆς σκέψιν"</note> and "consideration" <note>original: "νώμησιν"</note>. For to consider and to look at are the same. If you wish, "intellection" <note>original: "νόησις"</note> itself is the "desire for the new" <note>original: "νέου ἔσις"</note>. That things are "new" means they are always becoming. That the soul desires this is indicated by the name-giver. For "noesis" was not called so anciently, but instead of the "eta," one had to say two "epsilons," "ne-esin." "Temperance" <note>original: "σωφροσύνη"</note> is the "salvation" <note>original: "σωτηρία"</note> of that "prudence" we were just looking at. And truly "knowledge" <note>original: "ἐπιστήμη"</note> indicates that the soul follows things that are carried, neither being left behind nor running ahead. Therefore we must name it "episteme" by inserting the "iota." "Understanding" <note>original: "σύνεσις"</note> in turn might seem to be like a "bringing together" <note>original: "συλλογισμός"</note>; but when one is said "to understand" <note>original: "συνιέναι"</note>, exactly the same thing happens as when one is said "to know." For it says the soul goes along with things...

<summary>Socrates argues that many fundamental names like fire and water are of foreign (barbarian) origin, while others are based on the Heraclitean idea that all things are in a state of flux or motion. He uses this "theory of motion" to explain the etymologies of virtues like prudence (phronesis) and intelligence (synesis).</summary>
<keywords>etymology, fire, water, aether, air, year, prudence, intelligence, Heraclitean flux, Phrygian language, Plato, Socrates</keywords>
