<meta>This page continues the etymological investigation led by Socrates. Having previously discussed the names of the gods and natural elements, Socrates now turns his attention to the names of the virtues and human qualities, attempting to show how these names reflect the philosophical theory of "universal flux"—the idea that everything in the universe is in constant motion.</meta>

# CRATYLUS.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...that is, wisdom <note>original: "σοφία" (sophia)</note>, is the "touching of agitation" <note>original: "φορᾶς ἐφάπτεσθαι" (phoras epaphesthai)</note>. This is somewhat obscure and foreign to us. However, we must recall from the poets that whenever they wish to express someone arriving or rushing forth, they say "eupit" or "leapt forth" <note>original: "ἰοῦν" (ioun)</note>. Furthermore, there was a famous man among the Lacedæmonians <note>the Spartans</note> named "Sous" <note>original: "Σοῦς"</note>, which means "headlong." This is how the Spartans indicate a sudden impulse of movement. Therefore, as all things are being carried along, "wisdom" demonstrates the "touching" <note>original: "ἐπαφή" (epaphe)</note> or perception of this very agitation, which is called "movement" <note>original: "σῶς" (sos)</note>. The word "good" <note>original: "ἀγαθὸν" (agathon)</note>, used for every nature, signifies that which is "admirable" <note>original: "ἀγαστόν" (agaston)</note>, or lovable and delightful. Indeed, since all things flow, some possess speed and others slowness. Therefore, not everything is swift, but there is something "admirable" in it. This "good" is thus declared by the name of the "admirable" itself.

<margin>B</margin> As for "justice" <note>original: "δικαιοσύνη" (dikaiosyne)</note>, we can easily guess that it implies the "understanding of the just" <note>original: "δικαίου σύνεσιν" (dikaiou synesin)</note>. But what the "just" <note>original: "δίκαιον" (dikaion)</note> itself means is difficult to know. It seems that many agree up to a point, but the rest is doubtful. For all those who believe the universe is in motion assume that most of it is agitated, and that something permeates through everything by which all things are made; this thing must be the thinnest and swiftest. For it could not run through all things unless it were so thin that nothing could resist its penetration, and so swift that it treats other things as if they were standing still. Since it governs all things by "running through" <note>original: "διαϊὸν" (diaïon)</note> and permeating them, it is rightly called "just" <note>original: "δίκαιον"</note>, with the letter "k" <note>original: "κ"</note> inserted for the sake of better pronunciation. So far, as we have just said, most people agree that this is what justice is. But I, Hermogenes, being eager for learning, have scrutinized all these things and perceived in secret what this "just" itself is, and its "cause." For that by which things are made is the cause; and someone once taught that this should be its proper name.

<margin>C</margin> But when, after hearing these things, I nevertheless ask little by little what "justice" itself is, since it behaves this way, I seem to be demanding more than is proper, and (as they say) I am "leaping over the fence and the rampart" <note>a Greek proverb for overstepping boundaries</note>. For they always respond that I have asked and heard enough; and wanting to satisfy me, one brings up one thing and another another, and they no longer agree. One says that "justice" is the sun. For the sun alone, by running through and heating all things, governs them. But when I joyfully tell this to someone as a wonderful thing I have heard, he immediately laughs at me and asks if I think no justice remains for men after the sun sets. So, when I press him to tell me what he thinks, he says that "fire" itself is justice. But that is not easy to understand. Therefore, another says it is not fire itself, but rather the heat innate in fire. Another holds all these things as nothing, saying that justice is that "Mind" <note>original: "νοῦς" (nous)</note> which Anaxagoras introduced. For he says that Mind, being mistress of its own nature and mixed with nothing, adorns all things by penetrating through all things. Here, my friend, I have fallen into greater ambiguity than before I sought to know anything about justice.

<margin>D</margin> However, to return to the purpose for which we are disputing, such a name as we have described was given to it for these reasons.

<term>HERMOGENES:</term> You seem, Socrates, to have heard these things from someone, rather than producing them crudely from your own workshop.

<term>SOCRATES:</term> What about the other things?

<term>HERMOGENES:</term> Not so.

<term>SOCRATES:</term> Attend then; for perhaps in the remaining things I might deceive you, as if I had not heard the things I bring forward. After justice, what remains for us? Courage <note>original: "ἀνδρίαν" (andreian)</note> we have not yet completed. "Injustice" is clearly an obstacle to that which runs through all things; "courage" <note>original: "ἀνδρία"</note> is engaged in "battle." In the nature of things, if they flow, a "battle" is nothing other than a "contrary flux" <note>original: "ἐναντίαν ῥοήν" (enantian rhoen)</note>. Therefore, if one subtracts the "d" <note>original: "δ"</note> from the name "courage" <note>original: "ἀνδρία"</note>, the remaining name "an-ria" <note>the Greek word for 'flow' is 'rhoe'</note> declares the action itself. It is plain that not every contrary flux is courage, but only that flux which is opposed to what is contrary to justice. For otherwise courage would not be praiseworthy. The words "male" <note>original: "ἄῤῥεν" (arrhen)</note> and "man" <note>original: "ἀνήρ" (aner)</note> derive from a similar origin, namely from "upward flux" <note>original: "ἄνω ῥοῇ" (ano rhoe)</note>.

<margin>E</margin> "Woman" <note>original: "γυνὴ" (gyne)</note>, however, seems to mean "offspring" <note>original: "γονή" (gone)</note>, that is, the fertile and procreative. "Female" <note>original: "θῆλυ" (thely)</note> is named from the "teat" <note>original: "θηλῆς" (theles)</note>. And "teat" seems, Hermogenes, to be so called because it makes things "thrive" <note>original: "τεθηλέναι" (tethelene)</note>, as if they were things being irrigated.

<term>HERMOGENES:</term> So it appears, Socrates.

<term>SOCRATES:</term> To "bloom" or "flourish" <note>original: "θάλλειν" (thallein)</note> represents the growth of the young, as something swift and sudden, which the one who fashioned the name suggested by "running" <note>original: "θεῖν" (thein)</note> and "leaping" <note>original: "ἅλλεσθαι" (hallesthai)</note>. Do you not notice me being carried, as it were, outside the course, now that I have found smooth and passable ground? Many things also remain that seem to pertain to serious matters.

<term>HERMOGENES:</term> You speak the truth. One of which is to see what "art" <note>original: "τέχνη" (techne)</note> signifies.

<term>SOCRATES:</term> Certainly. Does this not show the "possession of mind" <note>original: "ἔχειν νοῦν" (echein noun)</note>, if the "t" is removed and an "o" is inserted between the "ch" and "n," and between the "n" and "e"?

<margin>F</margin> <term>HERMOGENES:</term> That is a very strained and crude explanation, Socrates.

<term>SOCRATES:</term> Do you not know, blessed man, that the ancient names have now been buried by the study of tragic speech, as people add and subtract letters for the sake of elegance, changing them everywhere partly through length of time and partly through a desire for ornamentation? For example, in the word for "mirror" <note>original: "κάτοπτρῳ" (katoptro)</note>, how absurd is the addition of the "r" <note>original: "ρ"</note>? They do such things, I believe, because they value the artful shaping of the mouth more than the truth. Therefore, since they have added many things to the names themselves, they have finally brought it about that no one can understand the meaning of the names anymore.

<sig>Z iij</sig>
<meta>Catchword: uertentibus (turning/changing)</meta>

<summary>Socrates explores the etymological origins of virtues like wisdom, justice, and courage, arguing they are rooted in the concept of universal motion and flux. He concludes by warning that the original meanings of words are often obscured by poets and time through the addition or removal of letters for the sake of sound.</summary>
<keywords>etymology, Socrates, Justice, Courage, Flux, Wisdom, Anaxagoras, Mind, Linguistics, Plato</keywords>

--- Page 302 ---
<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Hermogenes regarding the "natural" origin of words. Socrates is currently demonstrating how names—specifically those related to moral virtues and vices—describe the state of the soul's motion, following the Heraclitean philosophy that all things are in a constant state of flux.</meta>

# OF PLATO

<margin>A</margin>
...one should notice. It is just as when people say "Sphinx" <note>original: "σφίγξ"</note>—that famous monster—when they ought to pronounce it "Phix," and in many other instances.
HERMOGENES: That is certainly how it is, Socrates.
SOCRATES: Truly, if everyone were allowed to add or take away letters at their own whim, there would be great liberty indeed, and anyone could assign any name to any thing.
HERMOGENES: You speak the truth.
SOCRATES: Plainly so. But it befits you, as a wise overseer, to observe a certain moderation and sense of propriety.
HERMOGENES: I truly wish I could.
SOCRATES: And I wish it for you, Hermogenes. But, my happy friend, do not demand too exact a discussion, lest you exhaust my strength entirely. For I am reaching the very peak of what has been said, now that we have considered "art" and are looking at **machine** <note>original: "μηχανή" (mechanē)</note>, that is, a clever device or invention.

<margin>B</margin>
It seems to signify the same as "reaching far" and "ascending." It is composed of two parts: "length" <note>original: "μήκους" (mēkous)</note>, meaning "far" or "much," and "to accomplish" or "to reach" <note>original: "ἄνειν" (anein)</note>. But as I was just saying, we must reach the summit of our speech and seek what these names signify: **virtue** <note>original: "ἀρετή" (aretē)</note> and **wickedness** <note>original: "κακία" (kakia)</note>. One of these I do not yet discover, but the other seems clear. For it harmonizes with all that came before: since all things are in motion, "wickedness" is "going badly" <note>original: "κακῶς ἰόν" (kakōs ion)</note>. Therefore, when the soul approaches things "badly," it is generally called wicked.

Specifically, this faculty of "bad proceeding" is most evident in **timidity** <note>original: "δειλίᾳ" (deilia)</note>, which we have not yet explained, having passed over it.

<margin>C</margin>
Indeed, we ought to have introduced it immediately after "fortitude." It seems we have bypassed many other things as well. A **bond** <note>original: "δεσμὸς" (desmos)</note> signifies a harsh fetter of the soul—for a bond is a restraint. But "pain" <note>original: "λύπη" (lupē)</note> perhaps signifies something harsh and heavy. Therefore, intense timidity is the greatest bond of the soul. Just as **difficulty** <note>original: "ἀπορία" (aporia)</note>—meaning a lack, want, or doubt—is an evil thing, and in short, any impediment to progress itself. This "going badly" seems to show that the soul is hindered and detained in its very motion.

<margin>D</margin>
When the soul undergoes this, it is said to be full of wickedness. But if the name "wickedness" applies to such things, its opposite, **virtue** <note>original: "ἀρετή" (aretē)</note>, will signify the contrary. First, it must be an easy and agile progress; second, it must be the free and unhindered impulse of a good soul. For this reason, that which is "always flowing" <note>original: "ἀεὶ ῥέον" (aei rheon)</note> without impediment or obstacle might rightly be called "ever-flowing" <note>original: "ἀειῤῥύτη" (aeirrute)</note>. Perhaps one might also call it "virtue" because it is "most choiceworthy" <note>original: "αἱρετωτάτης" (hairetotatēs)</note>; but through a compression of the word, it is called "virtue" <note>Socrates is suggesting *aretē* is a shortened version of *aeirrute* or *hairetē*</note>. You will say perhaps that I am making this up; but I maintain that if the name of wickedness I brought forward is correct, then this name of virtue is also correctly introduced.
HERMOGENES: But what does **evil** <note>original: "κακόν" (kakon)</note> mean, a word you used many times in the preceding section?
SOCRATES: By Jove, that is a strange thing and difficult to find, or so it seems to me. Therefore, I will apply that same "machine" I used before.
HERMOGENES: 

<margin>E</margin>
Which one?
SOCRATES: I will say that this name, too, is of **barbaric** <note>foreign</note> origin.
HERMOGENES: You seem to speak rightly.
SOCRATES: But let us leave these aside for now if you please, and consider how correctly these names **beautiful** <note>original: "καλὸν" (kalon)</note> and **ugly** <note>original: "αἰσχρόν" (aischron)</note> were fashioned. What "ugly" implies seems clear enough to me. Indeed, it agrees with what came before. It seems the one who fashioned names generally condemned any impediment to movement. For instance, to that which is "always holding the flow" <note>original: "ἀεὶ ἴσχοντα τὸν ῥοῦν" (aei ischonta ton rhoun)</note>, he gave the name "always-flow-holding" <note>original: "ἀεισχοροῦν" (aeischoroun)</note>. But now, by compressing it, people call it "ugly" <note>original: "αἰσχρόν"</note>.
HERMOGENES: And what of "beautiful"?

<margin>F</margin>
SOCRATES: This is harder to know, although it is derived in such a way that the letter *alpha* was lengthened only for the sake of harmony and meter.
HERMOGENES: In what way?
SOCRATES: This name seems to be a sort of nickname for **thought** <note>original: "διανοίας" (dianoias)</note>.
HERMOGENES: Why do you say that?
SOCRATES: What do you think is the cause of every thing being called by a name? Is it not the one who assigned the names?
HERMOGENES: Entirely so.
SOCRATES: And is this not "thought"—either of gods, or of men, or of both?
HERMOGENES: Certainly.
SOCRATES: Therefore, that which "calls" <note>original: "κάλουν" (kaloun)</note> things and "thought" <note>intellect</note> are the same.
HERMOGENES: It appears so.
SOCRATES: Whatever mind and thought produce are to be praised; what they do not produce are to be blamed.
HERMOGENES: Quite so.

<margin>G</margin>
SOCRATES: That which partakes of medicine produces medical works; that which partakes of the carpenter's art produces carpentry. What do you think?
HERMOGENES: I agree.
SOCRATES: Therefore, the "beautiful" produces beautiful things?
HERMOGENES: It must.
SOCRATES: And this producer is, as we said, "thought"?
HERMOGENES: Precisely.
SOCRATES: Therefore, the name "beautiful" <note>original: "καλόν"</note> is rightly a name for **wisdom** <note>prudence/prudentia</note>, for it performs such actions as we love and declare to be beautiful.
HERMOGENES: So it appears.
SOCRATES: What else of this kind remains to be investigated?
HERMOGENES: Those things that relate to the good and the beautiful: namely, the **expedient** <note>original: "συμφέρον" (sympheron)</note>, the **useful**, the **profitable**, and their opposites.
SOCRATES: You can find for yourself what "expedient" is if you consider what came before. For it appears to be a sibling of the word for "knowledge." It signifies nothing other than the "carrying along" <note>original: "συμφέρειν" (sympherein)</note> of the soul together with things; and the results of this are called "expedient" because they are "carried around together" <note>original: "συμπεριφέρεσθαι" (symperipheresthai)</note>.
HERMOGENES: It seems so.
SOCRATES: Now, **profitable** <note>original: "κερδαλέον" (kerdaleon)</note> comes from "gain" <note>original: "κέρδος" (kerdos)</note>. If one inserts a *delta* into this name, it expresses its meaning: for it names the "good" in another way. Because the good "is mixed" <note>original: "κεράννυται" (kerannutai)</note> into all things and diffuses its power through all, the name-giver signified this by using "gain."
HERMOGENES: But what of the **advantageous** <note>original: "λυσιτελοῦν" (lusiteloun)</note>?
SOCRATES: It seems, Hermogenes, it is not used as shopkeepers use it, meaning that which...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...the name implies, just as they call the "Sphinx" a "Sphinx" instead of a "Phix," and many other such things.
HERMOGENES: These things are so, Socrates.
SOCRATES: And again, if someone is allowed to add or remove whatever they wish from names, there will be great license, and one could fit any name to any thing.
HERMOGENES: You speak the truth.
SOCRATES: Indeed, the truth. But I think you, the wise supervisor, must guard the sense of measure and likelihood.
HERMOGENES: I would wish to.
SOCRATES: And I advise you, Hermogenes. But do not be too precise, my divine friend, lest you "strip me of my strength" <note>A Homeric idiom meaning to exhaust his inspiration</note>. For I am coming to the peak of what I have said, once I have touched upon "machine" <note>original: "μηχανήν"</note> after "art."

<margin>B</margin>
For "machine" seems to me to be a sign of "achieving much." For "length" <note>original: "μῆκος"</note> signifies "much." From both of these, "length" and "achieving," the name "machine" is composed. But as I just said, we must go to the peak of our discussion. We must seek what the names **virtue** <note>original: "ἀρετήν"</note> and **wickedness** <note>original: "κακίαν"</note> mean. One I do not yet see, but the other seems quite clear to me. For it agrees with all the previous names. Since all things are moving, everything that "goes badly" <note>original: "κακῶς ἰόν"</note> would be "wickedness." And when this "bad going" toward things is in the soul, it especially bears the name of wickedness. What this "going badly" is, seems to me to be revealed in **cowardice** <note>original: "δειλίᾳ"</note>, which we have not yet discussed but passed over, though we should have examined it after courage.

<margin>C</margin>
It seems to me we have left out many other things as well. Cowardice, then, signifies a "strong bond" <note>original: "δεσμὸν ἰσχυρόν"</note> of the soul. For the prefix "dei-" implies a kind of strength. Thus, cowardice would be the "greatest bond" of the soul; just as **difficulty** <note>original: "ἀπορία"</note> is an evil, and everything, it seems, that is an impediment to "going" and "proceeding." This "going badly," then, appears to signify being held back and hindered from proceeding, and when the soul has this, it becomes full of wickedness.

<margin>D</margin>
If "wickedness" is the name for these things, then **virtue** would be the opposite. It signifies first the absence of difficulty, and then the "ever-loosened flow" <note>original: "λελυμένην τὴν ῥοὴν"</note> of the good soul. Thus, that which is "always flowing" <note>original: "ἀεὶ ῥέον"</note> without being held or hindered has received this name. It is correct to call it "ever-flowing" <note>original: "ἀειῤῥύτην"</note>, though perhaps the name-giver meant "choiceworthy" <note>original: "αἱρετήν"</note>, as this state is most "choiceworthy." But the word has been clashed together and is called "virtue" <note>original: "ἀρετή"</note>. Perhaps you will again say I am inventing; but I say that if what I said before about "wickedness" is correct, then this name "virtue" is also correct.
HERMOGENES: And what about the word **evil** <note>original: "κακόν"</note>, through which you said much of what came before—what does that name mean?
SOCRATES: It seems to me a strange thing and difficult to grasp. So I apply that same "machine" to it as well.
HERMOGENES: Which one is that?

<margin>E</margin>
SOCRATES: The one of saying that this, too, is something "barbaric."
HERMOGENES: You seem to be right. But if it pleases you, let us leave those things. Let us try to see how the **beautiful** <note>original: "καλὸν"</note> and the **ugly** <note>original: "αἰσχρόν"</note> are not without reason.
SOCRATES: As for the "ugly," what it means already seems clear to me. This also agrees with the previous points. The one who established names seems to me to be disparaging that which hinders and "holds the flow" of all things. So he gave the name "ever-flow-holding" <note>original: "ἀεισχοῤῥουν"</note> to that which "always holds the flow" <note>original: "ἀεὶ ἴσχοντι τὸν ῥοῦν"</note>. But now, having clashed the letters together, they call it "ugly" <note>original: "αἰσχρόν"</note>.
HERMOGENES: And what of the "beautiful"?
SOCRATES: This is more difficult to understand. Yet they say it is shifted from its form only by harmony and the length of the "u" sound.
HERMOGENES: How so?
SOCRATES: This name seems to be a nickname for "thought" <note>original: "διανοίας"</note>.
HERMOGENES: How do you mean?
SOCRATES: Come then, what do you think is the cause of each of the things that exist being "called" by a name? Is it not that which established the names?
HERMOGENES: Certainly.
SOCRATES: And would this not be "thought," either of gods or men, or both?
HERMOGENES: Yes.
SOCRATES: Therefore, that which "calls" <note>original: "καλοῦν"</note> things and that which "thinks" <note>original: "νοῆσαν"</note> are the same: thought.

<margin>F</margin>
HERMOGENES: It appears so.
SOCRATES: And are not those things which mind and thought work out the very things that are "praiseworthy," while those they do not are "blameable"?
HERMOGENES: Very much so.
SOCRATES: Does not the medical art produce "medical" things? And the carpenter's art "carpentry" things? Or how do you say it?
HERMOGENES: That is what I say.
SOCRATES: And does not the "beautiful" then produce "beautiful" things?
HERMOGENES: It must.
SOCRATES: And this producer is, as we say, thought?
HERMOGENES: Yes.
SOCRATES: Correct then: the "beautiful" is a name for the **wisdom** <note>original: "φρονήσεως" (phroneseos)</note> that produces such things, which we welcome and declare to be beautiful.
HERMOGENES: It appears so.
SOCRATES: What then is still left for us of such things?
HERMOGENES: Those that relate to the good and the beautiful: the **advantageous** <note>original: "λυσιτελοῦντα"</note>, the **useful** <note>original: "ὠφέλιμα"</note>, the **profitable** <note>original: "κερδαλέα"</note>, and their opposites.
SOCRATES: The **expedient** <note>original: "συμφέρον"</note> you might find by looking at what went before.

<margin>G</margin>
For it appears to be a sibling of "knowledge." For it shows nothing other than the "simultaneous motion" <note>original: "ἅμα φορὰν"</note> of the soul with things. And the things done by such means are called "expedient" and "fitting" from the fact that they "are carried along together" <note>original: "συμπεριφέρεσθαι"</note>.
HERMOGENES: It seems so.
SOCRATES: And "profitable" <note>original: "κερδαλέον"</note> comes from "gain" <note>original: "κέρδους"</note>. And "gain," if you restore the *delta* to the name, shows what it intends. For it names the "good" in another way. Because the good "is mixed" <note>original: "κεράννυται"</note> into everything that passes through it, the name-giver called it by its power, but putting a *delta* in place of a *nu*, he pronounced it "gain" <note>original: "κέρδος"</note>.
HERMOGENES: And what of "advantageous" <note>original: "λυσιτελοῦν"</note>?
SOCRATES: It seems, Hermogenes, not to be used as the shopkeepers use it, meaning that which...

<summary>In this passage from the Cratylus, Socrates provides etymologies for moral and practical concepts, arguing that "virtue" reflects the soul's healthy, unhindered motion, while "vice" and "ugliness" represent the soul's motion being blocked or "going badly."</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Hermogenes from the previous page, where they were discussing the etymological origins of names related to "art" and "wickedness." Socrates is using the Heraclitean theory of universal flux—the idea that everything is in constant motion—to explain how words were originally constructed to describe the movement of the soul and the universe.</meta>

# CRATYLUS. 271

<margin>A</margin>Regarding "profitable" <note>original: "λυσιτελοῦν" (lysiteloun)</note>, it does not seem to me to mean the stopping of a gain. Rather, because the soul is the swiftest of all things, it does not allow things to stand still, nor does it permit their motion to reach an "end" <note>original: "τέλος" (telos)</note> so as to cease. Instead, it always "loosens" <note>original: "λύει" (lyei)</note> the end whenever it tries to settle, and provides an unceasing and immortal flow for things. It is in this way, I think, that the "good" was named "profitable"—because it "loosens the end" of the motion. As for "advantageous" <note>original: "ὠφέλιμον" (ōphelimon)</note>, it is a foreign-sounding name, and Homer often uses the word "to increase" <note>original: "ὠφέλλειν" (ōphellein)</note>. This refers to increasing and creating.
**HERMOGENES:** And what about the opposites of these?
**SOCRATES:** As for those that are merely negations, I do not think we need to go through them.

<margin>B</margin>**HERMOGENES:** Which ones do you mean?
**SOCRATES:** Words like "unsuitable," "unprofitable," "useless," and "gainless."
**HERMOGENES:** You are right.
**SOCRATES:** But we should look at "harmful" <note>original: "βλαβερόν" (blaberon)</note> and "damaging" <note>original: "ζημιῶδες" (zēmiōdes)</note>.
**HERMOGENES:** Yes.
**SOCRATES:** "Harmful" signifies that which "harms the flow" <note>original: "βλάπτον τὸν ῥοῦν" (blapton ton rhoun)</note>. Now, "to harm" implies "wanting to bind" <note>original: "βουλόμενον ἅπτειν" (boulomenon haptein)</note>. To "bind" and to "tie" are the same thing, and this is always a term of blame. Therefore, that which "wants to bind the flow" would most correctly be called "boulapherrhoun." But for the sake of elegance, it seems to me it has been called "harmful."
**HERMOGENES:** These names are turning out quite complex for you, Socrates! Just now, you sounded like you were chanting a prelude to a hymn to Athena when you pronounced that name "boulapherrhoun."
**SOCRATES:** It is not my fault, Hermogenes, but the fault of those who established the names.

<margin>C</margin>**HERMOGENES:** True. But what would "damaging" be?
**SOCRATES:** What could "damaging" possibly be? Look, Hermogenes, how I speak the truth when I say that by adding and removing letters, people greatly change the meanings of names; by shifting things just a little, they sometimes make them signify the exact opposite. We see this in the word "proper" <note>original: "δέον" (deon), meaning "necessary" or "binding"</note>. I just thought of it and was reminded of what I was about to tell you: our modern, "beautiful" way of speaking has twisted the meanings of "proper" and "damaging" into their opposites, hiding what they mean. But the ancient language reveals what both names intend.
**HERMOGENES:** How do you mean?
**SOCRATES:** I will tell you. You know that our ancestors

<margin>D</margin>made great use of the letters *iota* and *delta*. This is especially true of women, who are the best at preserving the ancient way of speaking. But now, instead of *iota*, they change it to *epsilon* or *eta*, and instead of *delta*, they use *zeta*, thinking these sound more grand.
**HERMOGENES:** In what way?
**SOCRATES:** For example, the very ancients called the "day" <note>original: "ἡμέραν" (hēmeran)</note> "himera," others called it "hemera," and now they say "hēmera."
**HERMOGENES:** That is true.
**SOCRATES:** You realize, then, that only the ancient name "himera" reveals the intent of the name-giver? Because men were glad and "longed" <note>original: "ἱμείρουσι" (himeirousi)</note> for the light to come out of the darkness, they named it "himera."
**HERMOGENES:** So it seems.
**SOCRATES:** But now, with the name all "tragicized" into "hēmera," you cannot understand what it wants to say. Though some think it is named that because it makes things "gentle" <note>original: "ἥμερα" (hēmera)</note>.

<margin>E</margin>**HERMOGENES:** So it seems to me.
**SOCRATES:** And do you know that the ancients called a "yoke" <note>original: "ζυγόν" (zygon)</note> a "duogon"?
**HERMOGENES:** Certainly.
**SOCRATES:** Now, "zygon" signifies nothing. But "duogon" was rightly named for the "binding of two" <note>original: "δυοῖν δέσεως" (dyoin deseōs)</note> for the sake of pulling together. Now it is "zygon." There are many other such cases.
**HERMOGENES:** It appears so.
**SOCRATES:** According to this logic, if we look at "proper" <note>term: "δέον" (deon) - literally that which is 'binding'</note> as it is currently spoken, it signifies the opposite of all the names associated with the "good." For "proper," being a form of the good, now appears to be a "bond" <note>original: "δεσμός" (desmos)</note> or a hindrance to motion, like a brother to "harmful."
**HERMOGENES:** It certainly appears that way, Socrates.
**SOCRATES:** But if you use the ancient name, it is much more likely to be correct than the current one. You will agree it aligns with the previous names for "good" if

<margin>F</margin>you restore the *iota* in place of the *epsilon*, as in the old days. For it was not "deon" (binding) but "dion" <note>original: "διὸν", from "διιέναι" (diiënai) - to go through</note>. This signifies the "good," which the name-giver always praises. In this way, the name-giver is consistent with himself: "dion" (going through), "advantageous," "profitable," "gainful," "good," "suitable," and "expedient" <note>original: "εὔπορον" (euporon) - easy to pass through</note> all appear to be the same thing. Through different names, they signify that which "arranges" and "goes through" <note>original: "διϊὸν" (diion)</note> all things, which is praised; while that which "holds" and "binds" is blamed. And indeed, if you look at "damaging" <note>original: "ζημιῶδες" (zēmiōdes)</note> according to the ancient speech, putting *delta* instead of *zeta*, the name will appear to be "demiōdes," given to that which "binds what goes" <note>original: "δοῦντι τὸ ἰόν" (dounti to ion)</note>.
**HERMOGENES:** What then of "pleasure," "pain," "desire," and such things, Socrates?
**SOCRATES:** They do not seem very difficult to me, Hermogenes. For

<margin>G</margin>"pleasure" <note>original: "ἡδονή" (hēdonē)</note> seems to get its name from the action that tends toward "benefit" <note>original: "ὄνησιν" (onēsin)</note>; the *delta* was added so it is called "hēdonē" instead of "hēonē." "Pain" <note>original: "λύπη" (lypē)</note> seems to be named from the "dissolution" <note>original: "διαλύσεως" (dialyseōs)</note> of the body which the body suffers in that state. "Sorrow" <note>original: "ἀνία" (ania)</note> is that which "hinders going" <note>original: "ἰέναι" (ienai)</note>. "Suffering" <note>original: "ἀλγηδών" (algēdōn)</note> seems like a foreign word to me, named from "painful." "Grief" <note>original: "ὀδύνη" (odynē)</note> is named from the "entry" <note>original: "ἔνδυσιν" (endysin)</note> of pain.
**HERMOGENES:** So it seems.
**SOCRATES:** "Distress" <note>original: "ἀχθηδών" (achthēdōn)</note> is a name clearly modeled on the "burden" <note>original: "ἄχθος" (achthos)</note> of motion. "Joy" <note>original: "χαρά" (chara)</note> seems named for the "outpouring" <note>original: "διαχύσει" (diachysē)</note> and ease of the flow of the soul. "Delight" <note>original: "τέρψις" (terpsis)</note> comes from "pleasant." And "pleasant" <note>original: "τερπνόν" (terpnon)</note> is named from the "soul's crawling" <note>original: "ἕρψεως" (herpseōs)</note>, to which it was compared; it was rightly called "herpnon," but over

<margin>H</margin>time was shifted to "terpnon." As for "merriment" <note>original: "εὐφροσύνη" (euphrosynē)</note>, no falsehood is needed to see...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>...to release <note>original: "Ἀπολὺν"</note>, that is, it avoids and diminishes expense; but because it is very swift, it does not let things stand, nor does it allow the motion to take an "end" <note>original: "τέλος"</note>—that is, the finish of progress—and cease. Rather, it always "releases" from that and puts it to flight if any limit approaches, and renders the thing unending and immortal. For this reason, I think the good is called "profitable" <note>original: "λυσιτελοῦν"</note>. For "releasing the end of motion" <note>original: "λύον τὸ τέλος"</note> is what it seems to be called. "Advantageous" <note>original: "ὠφέλειον"</note>, however, is a foreign name which Homer used many times. It is a title for increasing and making.
**HERMOGENES:** What should be said of their opposites?
**SOCRATES:**

<margin>B</margin>Those that are said through the negation of these, there is no need to treat.
**HERMOGENES:** Which ones?
**SOCRATES:** "Unsuitable," "unhelpful," "unprofitable," "unprofitable."
**HERMOGENES:** You speak the truth.
**SOCRATES:** But "harmful" <note>original: "βλαβερόν"</note> and "damaging" <note>original: "ζημιῶδες"</note>.
**HERMOGENES:** Certainly.
**SOCRATES:** "Harmful" indeed is said to be "harming the flow" <note>original: "βλάπτον τὸν ῥοῦν"</note>. Now "harming" signifies "wanting to bind" <note>original: "βουλόμενον ἅπτειν"</note>—that is, what wants to hinder and restrain—the "flow" <note>original: "τὸν ῥοῦν"</note>. This is used everywhere; and because it wants to "bind the flow," it would be correctly called "boulapherrhoun." But for the sake of ornament, I think it was named "harmful."
**HERMOGENES:** Various names occur to you, O Socrates. Indeed, you seem to me at present as if you were

<margin>C</margin>chanting some sort of prelude to the laws of Pallas Athena, while you pronounced this name "boulapherrhoun."
**SOCRATES:** I am not the cause, Hermogenes, but those who established the name itself.
**HERMOGENES:** You speak the truth. But what is "damaging" <note>original: "ζημιῶδες"</note>?
**SOCRATES:** What "damaging" ought to be, I will say, Hermogenes, and see how truly I speak when I say that by adding and taking away letters, they vary the sense of names greatly, so that often by changing a tiny thing, it induces a contrary meaning. This appears in this name "proper" <note>original: "δέον"</note>. This came to my mind recently while thinking of what I was to tell you. Indeed, that beautiful voice is new to us and forced a contrary sound

<margin>D</margin>upon us: "dion" and "damaging," confounding the sense itself. But the ancient name explains what each word wants.
**HERMOGENES:** How do you say that?
**SOCRATES:** I will say it indeed. It did not escape our ancestors to use *iota* and *delta* frequently, nor less the women, who especially preserve the ancient speech. But now, instead of *iota*, they use either *epsilon* or *eta*; and for *delta* they use *zeta*, as if these sound more magnificent.
**HERMOGENES:** In what way?
**SOCRATES:** As, behold, the most ancient men called "day" <note>original: "ἡμέραν"</note> "himera"; later ones partly "hemera," and partly, at this time, they call it "hēmera."
**HERMOGENES:** These things are true.
**SOCRATES:** You know then that by that ancient name only the mind of him who imposed the name is declared. For from the fact that they "longed" <note>original: "ἱμείρουσι"</note>—that is, for men desiring and welcoming the light that flashed out of the darkness—they named the day "himera."
**HERMOGENES:** It appears so.
**SOCRATES:** But now, you would by no means understand what that word "hēmera," chanted by the tragedians, wants for itself. Although some think "hēmera" is so called because it makes things "gentle" <note>original: "ἥμερα"</note>.
**HERMOGENES:** So it seems to me.
**SOCRATES:** Nor does it escape you that the ancients called a "yoke" <note>original: "ζυγόν"</note> a "duogon"?
**HERMOGENES:** Plainly.
**SOCRATES:** Truly "zygon" signifies nothing. But "duogon" shows the "bringing together of two" <note>original: "δυοῖν ἀγωγήν"</note> for the sake of binding them together. The same is to be judged of many others.
**HERMOGENES:** It is evident.
**SOCRATES:** By the same reason, "proper" <note>original: "δέον"</note> thus pronounced, shows the opposite of all names that look toward the good. For being a species of good, "deon" seems to be a "bond" <note>original: "δεσμός"</note>—that is, a certain chain and impediment to progress—as if it were something akin to "harmful" <note>original: "βλαβερόν"</note>.

<margin>F</margin>**HERMOGENES:** It appears so especially, O Socrates.
**SOCRATES:** But not so in the ancient name, which it is more likely was correctly established than ours. For you will agree with the former "goods" if you restore the ancient *iota* instead of *epsilon*. For not "deon" but "dion" signifies that good which the inventor of names always praises. And thus he does not disagree with himself; rather, they look to the same thing: "dion" (going through), "advantageous," "profitable," "gainful," "good," "suitable," "expedient" <note>original: "εὔπορον"</note>, that is, easy for progress. This whole set hints by different names at something penetrating through all things and adorning all things, which is everywhere praised; but that which stands in the way and detains, he disapproves. Furthermore, in this name "damaging" <note>original: "ζημιῶδες"</note>, if you place *delta* for *zeta* in the ancient manner, it will appear to you as a name imposed on that which "binds that which goes" <note>original: "δοῦν τι ἰόν"</note>; whence also it was called "demiōdes."
**HERMOGENES:** What of "pleasure," "pain," "desire"—namely "hēdonē," "lypē," "epithymia"—Socrates, and the rest of this kind?
**SOCRATES:** They seem not very obscure to me, Hermogenes. For "pleasure" <note>original: "ἡδονὴ"</note> is the name of that action which tends toward

<margin>G</margin>"benefit" <note>original: "ὄνησιν"</note>. But the *delta* was added so that instead of "hēonē," it is pronounced "hēdonē." "Pain" <note>original: "λύπη"</note> seems to be drawn from "dissolution" <note>original: "διαλύσεως"</note> of the body. For in a passion of this kind, the body is dissolved. "Sorrow" <note>original: "ἀνία"</note> demonstrates that which hinders "going" <note>original: "ἰέναι"</note>. "Cruciation" <note>original: "ἀλγηδών"</note> seems a foreign name, said from "painful." "Grief" <note>original: "ὀδύνη"</note> is named from the "ingression" <note>original: "ἐνδύσειας"</note> of pain.
**HERMOGENES:** It seems so.
**SOCRATES:** "Distress" <note>original: "ἀχθηδών"</note> signifies the heaviness and slowness of motion. For "achthos" is a burden, and "ion" is going. "Joy" <note>original: "χαρά"</note> is said from "profusion" <note>original: "διαχύσεως"</note> and "ease" <note>original: "ἀποριᾷ"</note> of the motion of the soul. "Delight" <note>original: "τέρψις"</note> is derived from "pleasant" <note>original: "τερπνοῦ"</note>. Now "pleasant" is "terpnon," that is, by the inspiration of delight into the soul. Wherefore it would be deservedly called "herpnon," that is, "breathing into." But in the interval of time, it came to be "terpnon." "Merriment" <note>original: "εὐφροσύνη"</note>, for what reason it is said, requires nothing false to assign...

<summary>In this segment of the Cratylus, Socrates provides etymological analyses of words related to benefit, harm, and emotion, arguing that their ancient forms reveal a worldview based on motion and flow. He illustrates how the shifting of letters over time has obscured these original meanings, sometimes making words for "good" things sound like words for "binding" or "stagnation."</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from the *Cratylus*, where Socrates provides etymologies for words related to emotions and states of mind. He continues to apply the "Heraclitean" principle that names reflect the internal "flow" and "motion" of the soul.</meta>

# PLATO'S

work. For every father [derives] this name from that which is called 
<margin>A</margin> "well" <note>original: "εὖ" (eu)</note> and "to come together" <note>original: "συμφέρεσθαι" (sympheresthai)</note>, as if to say the soul attains things well. For this reason, it ought to be called *Aphrophune* <note>original: "ἀφροφύνην" — Socrates is punning on "foam" and "wisdom" or "nature"</note>; though we now call it **Aphrodite**. But it is not difficult to assign what **desire** <note>original: "ἐπιθυμία" (epithymia)</note> means for itself. This name signifies a power tending toward the **spirit** <note>original: "θυμόν" (thymon)</note>, that is, the soul, anger, and fury. But *spirit* <note>original: "θυμός" (thymos)</note> comes from "raging" and "boiling" <note>original: "θύσεως καὶ ζέσεως" (thyseōs kai zeseōs)</note>, referring to the heat and impulse of the soul. Furthermore, **longing** <note>original: "ἵμερος" (himeros)</note> is a sweet and mild infusion, so named from the "flow" <note>original: "ῥοῦ" (rho)</note> that strongly draws the soul. Because it flows with an "impulse" <note>original: "ἱέμενος ῥεῖ" (hiemenos rhei)</note> and seeks after things, it strongly attracts the soul through the force or incitement of its flow. From this whole power, it was called *himeros*. Moreover, it is called **yearning** 
<margin>B</margin> <note>original: "πόθος" (pothos)</note>, which certainly does not signify a present sweetness like *himeros*, but burns for that which is absent. Hence *pothos* is named as the desire for the "absent" <note>original: "ἀπόντος" (apontos)</note>. The very same striving of the mind toward what is pleasing is called *himeros* when the object is present, and *pothos* when it is absent. **Love** <note>original: "ἔρως" (erōs)</note> is so called because it "flows in" <note>original: "εἰσρεῖ" (eisrei)</note> from the outside; this "flow" <note>original: "ῥοῦ" (rho)</note> is not internal to the one who has it, but is infused through the eyes. Therefore, from "flowing in" <note>original: "ἐσρεῖν" (esrein)</note>, it was called *esros* <note>original: "ἔσρος"</note> by our ancestors, for they used the letter *o* <note>omicron</note> instead of *ō* <note>omega</note>. Now it is called *erōs*, with the *ō* substituted for the *o*. But what do you command we consider next? <term>HERMOGENES.</term> 
<margin>C</margin> **Opinion** <note>original: "δόξα" (doxa)</note> and such things; from where do they have their names? <term>SOCRATES.</term> *Doxa* is named either from "pursuit" <note>original: "διώξει" (diōxei)</note>, by which the soul proceeds and follows, investigating the condition of things; or from the "shooting of a bow" <note>original: "τόξου βολῆς" (toxou bolēs)</note>. It seems rather to depend on the latter. **Estimation** <note>original: "οἴησις" (oiēsis)</note> agrees with this. Indeed, it shows the "entry" <note>original: "οἶσιν" (oisin)</note> of the soul into each thing to be considered, such as "what it is like." Just as **will** <note>original: "βουλή" (boulē)</note> is named from "shooting" <note>original: "βολῇ" (bolē)</note>, and **to wish** <note>original: "βούλεσθαι" (boulesthai)</note> signifies the very striving to reach something, it also means **to desire** <note>original: "ἐφίεσθαι" (ephiesthai)</note> and **to deliberate** <note>original: "βουλεύεσθαι" (bouleuesthai)</note>. All these things following after "opinion" appear to be images of the "shot" <note>original: "βολῆς" (bolēs)</note> and the striving itself. Just as the opposite, **lack of counsel** <note>original: "ἀβουλία" (aboulia)</note>, appears to be a certain failure or lack of power to attain, as if they do not strive, nor does one reach what they intend, wish, desire, or investigate. <term>HERMOGENES.</term> You seem to be gathering these more frequently, O Socrates. What might be the end now, God willing? I still wish **necessity** <note>original: "ἀνάγκην" (anankēn)</note> and the **voluntary** <note>original: "ἑκούσιον" (hekousion)</note> to be declared. For these surely follow the previous ones. <term>SOCRATES.</term> The *voluntary* is indeed that which is "yielding" <note>original: "εἶκον" (eikon)</note> and not resisting. By this name it is declared as "yielding to that which goes" <note>original: "εἶκον τῷ ἰόντι" (eikon tō ionti)</note>, or that which is performed by the will. But the **necessary** <note>original: "ἀναγκαῖον" (anankaion)</note> and resisting, since it happens against the will, involves error and ignorance. It is described from the process according to necessity, because in a rough and dense way they prohibit passage. Hence it is called *anankaion*, as if "going through a valley" <note>original: "ἄγκους ἰόν" (ankous ion)</note>. As long as our strength lasts, let us not give up. Therefore, please ask and do not stop. <term>HERMOGENES.</term> Behold, I ask about the greatest and most beautiful: **truth** <note>original: "ἀλήθεια" (alētheia)</note>, and **falsehood** <note>original: "ψεῦδος" (pseudos)</note>, and **being** <note>original: "ὄν" (on)</note>, and why this very thing we are discussing, a **name** <note>original: "ὄνομα" (onoma)</note>, is so called. <term>SOCRATES.</term> What do you 
<margin>D</margin> call "to seek" <note>original: "μάχεσθαι/μαίεσθαι" (maiesthai)</note>? <term>HERMOGENES.</term> I call it to inquire. <term>SOCRATES.</term> This word seems to be struck from that phrase which says it is "being" <note>original: "ὄν" (on)</note>, the name of which is an "inquiry." You will certainly understand this more clearly in what we call "notable" <note>original: "ὀνομαστόν" (onomaston)</note>; for here the name is expressed for what it is—namely, an inquiry into being. But *truth* <note>original: "ἀλήθεια" (alētheia)</note>, like the others, seems to be contracted and forged together. For the divine motion of being is included in this name, *aletheia*, as if it were "divine wandering" <note>original: "εἴη θείη ἄλη" (eiē theiē alē)</note>. But *falsehood* <note>original: "ψεῦδος" (pseudos)</note> is the opposite of motion. Again, here is used the obstacle to agitation, that which forces one to stand still. For it is said from "to sleep" <note>original: "καθεύδειν" (katheudein)</note>. But the *ps* <note>psi</note> added hides the sense of the name. *Being* <note>original: "ὄν" (on)</note> and **essence** <note>original: "οὐσία" (ousia)</note> agree with *truth* <note>original: "ἀληθείᾳ" (alētheia)</note> if the letter *i* <note>iota</note> is added; for it signifies "going" <note>original: "ἰόν" (ion)</note>. But **non-being** <note>original: "οὐκ ὄν" (ouk on)</note> some call "not going" <note>original: "οὐκ ἰόν" (ouk ion)</note>. <term>HERMOGENES.</term> These things you seem to me, O So-
<margin>E</margin> crates, to have discussed quite bravely. But if someone should ask you what the correct interpretation is of those words: "going" <note>original: "ἰόν" (ion)</note>, "flowing" <note>original: "ῥέον" (rheon)</note>, and "binding or detaining" <note>original: "δεσμόν" (desmon)</note>, what shall we best answer him? Do you have an answer? <term>SOCRATES.</term> I do indeed; something just occurred to us, by which answer we might seem to offer nothing at all. <term>HERMOGENES.</term> What sort of thing? <term>SOCRATES.</term> That we should say whatever we least understand is **foreign** <note>original: "barbaricum"</note>. For perhaps some are indeed such; or perhaps because of their antiquity, the primary names are inscrutable. For since words are pulled apart everywhere, it would be no wonder if the ancient language, compared with ours, differed in no way from a foreign tongue. <term>HERMOGENES.</term> What you say is not at all foreign to reason. <term>SOCRATES.</term> I bring forward reasonable things, yet the contest does not seem to admit an excuse on that account. But let us try to investigate these, and consider it thus: if someone always asked for the words through which a name is said, and again for those through which those words are said, and continued to inquire thus, would not the one who answers eventually be forced to tire and refuse? <term>HERMOGENES.</term> It certainly seems so to me. <term>SOCRATES.</term> When, therefore, will the one who denies an answer rightly cease? Is it not after he reaches those names which are the **elements** <note>original: "elementa"</note> of the other speeches and names? These, if they are elements, should not appear to be composed of other names. Just as above we said "good" <note>original: "ἀγαθὸν" (agathon)</note> was composed of "admirable" <note>original: "ἀγαστοῦ" (agastou)</note> and "swift" <note>original: "θοοῦ" (thoou)</note>. And again, we shall say those consist of others, and those of others still.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>...to be spoken. It is clear to everyone that from the soul "coming together well" <note>original: "εὖ... συμφέρεσθαι"</note> with things, it took this name, *Aphrophune*; yet we call it **Aphrodite**. Nor is **desire** <note>original: "ἐπιθυμία"</note> difficult, for the "power going toward the spirit" <note>original: "θυμὸν ἰοῦσα δύναμις"</note> was clearly called by this name. And **spirit** <note>original: "θυμός"</note> might have this name from the "raging and boiling" of the soul. But **longing** <note>original: "ἵμερος"</note> was named from the "flow" <note>original: "ῥοῦ"</note> that most draws the soul. For because it "flows while striving" <note>original: "ἑλμενος ῥεῖ"</note> and "desiring things" <note>original: "ἐφιέμενος τῶν πραγμάτων"</note>, it truly holds the soul fast through the striving of the flow; from this whole power, then, it was called *himeros*. 
<margin>B</margin> And indeed **yearning** <note>original: "πόθος"</note> is so called, signifying not the flow of the body already present, but that which is "elsewhere" and "absent" <note>original: "ἀπόντος"</note>. When that which one desired is present, it was called *himeros*; but when it is gone, this same thing is called *pothos*. **Love** <note>original: "ἔρως"</note> is so called because it "flows in from outside" <note>original: "εἰσρεῖ ἔξωθεν"</note>, and the flow is not internal to the possessor but is introduced through the eyes. For this reason, from "flowing in" <note>original: "ἐσρεῖν"</note>, it was called *esros* in the old days (when we used the *o* for *ō*), but now it is called *erōs* due to the change of *omega* for *omicron*. But what else do you say we should examine? <term>HERMOGENES.</term> **Opinion** <note>original: "δόξα"</note> and such things, how do they seem to you? <term>SOCRATES.</term> *Doxa*? It is named either from "pursuit" <note>original: "διώξει"</note>, which the soul performs in pursuing the knowledge of how things are, 
<margin>C</margin> or it seems to come from the "shooting of a bow." **Estimation** <note>original: "οἴησις"</note> agrees with this. For it signifies the "carrying" <note>original: "οἶσιν"</note> of the soul toward the whole of a thing, to see what each of the beings is. Just as **will** <note>original: "βουλή"</note> relates to "shooting" <note>original: "βολήν"</note>, and **to wish** <note>original: "βούλεσθαι"</note> signifies "to desire," and **to deliberate** <note>original: "βουλεύεσθαι"</note>. All these follow "opinion" and appear to be images of "shooting." Just as conversely, **lack of counsel** <note>original: "ἀβουλία"</note> seems to be "misfortune" <note>original: "ἀτυχία"</note>, as of one who did not shoot or hit that which he was shooting at, or wishing for, or deliberating about. <term>HERMOGENES.</term> These things now, Socrates, you seem to bring in more thickly. But I wish you to finish with **necessity** <note>original: "ἀνάγκην"</note>, which follows these, and the **voluntary** <note>original: "ἑκούσιον"</note>. <term>SOCRATES.</term> The *voluntary* <note>original: "ἑκούσιον"</note> is that which is "yielding" <note>original: "εἶκον"</note> and not resisting, but as I say, "yielding to that which goes" <note>original: "εἶκον τῷ ἰόντι"</note>. But the *necessary* <note>original: "ἀναγκαῖον"</note> and resisting, being against the will, would be about "error" and "ignorance." It is likened to a "journey through a valley" <note>original: "κατ’ ἄγκη πορείᾳ"</note>, because being difficult to pass, rough, and overgrown, it hinders one from going. Thence it was called *anankaion*, likened to the journey through the valley. As long as strength remains, let us not let it go, and do not you give up, but ask. <term>HERMOGENES.</term> I ask then about the greatest and most beautiful, concerning **truth** <note>original: "ἀλήθειαν"</note> and **falsehood** <note>original: "ψεῦδος"</note>, and **being** <note>original: "ὄν"</note>, and this very thing our talk is now about: **name** <note>original: "ὄνομα"</note>, why a "name" is a "name." <term>SOCRATES.</term> Do you call "to seek" <note>original: "μαίεσθαι"</note> something? <term>HERMOGENES.</term> I do; to inquire. <term>SOCRATES.</term> It seems then to have been struck from the phrase saying that "this is being" <note>original: "τοῦτ’ ὄν ἐστίν"</note>, of which the *name* is the search. You might know it better in what we call the "named" <note>original: "ὀνομαστόν"</note>. For there it clearly says it is a "name-giving" or search for being. **Truth** <note>original: "ἀλήθεια"</note> also seems to be forged like the others. For the divine motion of being seems to be addressed by this word *aletheia*, as being a "divine wandering" <note>original: "θεία ἄλη"</note>. But **falsehood** <note>original: "ψεῦδος"</note> is the opposite of the motion. For again it comes as a reproach to that which is "held back" and "forced to be quiet." It is likened to those who "sleep" <note>original: "καθεύδουσι"</note>. **Being** <note>original: "ὄν"</note> and **essence** <note>original: "οὐσία"</note> agree with the "true," having lost the *iota*; for it signifies "going" <note>original: "ἰόν"</note>. And **non-being** <note>original: "οὐκ ὄν"</note> again, as some even name it, "not going" <note>original: "οὐκ ἰόν"</note>. <term>HERMOGENES.</term> These things, Socrates, you seem 
<margin>F</margin> to have forged quite bravely. But if someone asked you, what correctness do these names have: "going" <note>original: "ἰόν"</note>, "flowing" <note>original: "ῥέον"</note>, and "binding" <note>original: "δεσμόν"</note>? What do you say one should answer? <term>HERMOGENES.</term> Quite so. <term>SOCRATES.</term> One thing we just now provided, so as to seem to say something in answering. <term>HERMOGENES.</term> What sort of thing? <term>SOCRATES.</term> To say that if we do not know, it is something "foreign" <note>original: "βαρβαρικόν"</note>. For this might perhaps be true. It might be that through antiquity the first of names are undiscoverable. For because names are twisted in every way, it would be 
<margin>F</margin> no wonder if the ancient voice compared to the current one differed in no way from a foreign one. <term>HERMOGENES.</term> You say nothing out of character. <term>SOCRATES.</term> I say it not unwillingly. However, the contest does not seem to me to admit excuses; we must be eager to examine them. Let us consider if someone always asks about the words through which a name is said, and again the words through which those words are said, and still does not stop; is it not necessary that in the end the answerer gives up? <term>HERMOGENES.</term> It seems so to me. <term>SOCRATES.</term> When would the one at a loss rightly stop? Would it not be when he arrives at those names which are "elements" <note>original: "στοιχεῖα"</note> of the other words or names? For these are no longer rightly shown to be composed of other names. Just as we said "good" <note>original: "ἀγαθὸν"</note> was composed of "admirable" and "swift"; we might say "swift" <note>original: "θοὸν"</note> consists of others, and those of yet others.

<summary>In this passage from Plato's Cratylus, Socrates uses etymology to argue that words like "love," "truth," and "desire" are derived from concepts of motion and flow, reflecting a Heraclitean worldview. He concludes by noting that etymological analysis must eventually reach "primary elements" or base words that cannot be further subdivided.</summary>

--- Page 305 ---
<meta>This page continues the dialogue of the *Cratylus*, moving from the specific etymologies of complex words (secondary names) to a deeper investigation into "primary names"—the fundamental building blocks of language. Socrates is beginning to argue that if words are composed of other words, there must eventually be "elements" that are not composed of anything else.</meta>

### CRATYLUS

<margin>A</margin> But once we have reached that which is no longer composed of other names, we shall rightly say we have reached an **element** <note>The Greek term *stoicheion* refers to both a physical element, like earth or fire, and a letter of the alphabet—the "atoms" of language.</note>, and we should no longer refer this to other names. HERMOGENES: You seem to speak skillfully to me. SOCRATES: Are not those names about which you were asking just now elements? And must we investigate their correct reasoning differently than the others? HERMOGENES: That is probable. SOCRATES: Probable indeed, Hermogenes. All the previous names seem to have been reduced to these. And if the matter stands as it seems to me, come again and consider this with me, lest I perhaps dote while I attempt to explain the correct reasoning of the primary names. HERMOGENES: Speak on; I shall meditate on it with all my strength.

<margin>B</margin> SOCRATES: I think you agree on this: there is one correct reasoning for any name, whether it is a primary name or a secondary one, and none of them differs from another in its nature as a name. HERMOGENES: Very much so. SOCRATES: Indeed, for all the names we discussed above, their correct reasoning consists in this: that the nature of each thing should be indicated. HERMOGENES: Without a doubt. SOCRATES: This surely must belong no less to the prior names than to the posterior ones, if they are to be names. HERMOGENES: Entirely. SOCRATES: And yet the posterior names were able to achieve this through the prior ones. HERMOGENES: It appears so.

SOCRATES: But the primary ones, which no others precede—in what way will they show us the things themselves as much as possible, if they are to be names? <margin>C</margin> Answer me this: if we lacked voice and tongue, and wanted to declare things to one another, would we not, just like those who are mute today, try to signify with our hands, head, and other members? HERMOGENES: Not otherwise, Socrates. SOCRATES: Therefore, if we were going to demonstrate something high and light, we would have raised our hand toward heaven, imitating the nature of the thing itself; but things low and heavy, we would have signaled toward the earth with a downward movement. Even to indicate a running horse or any other animal, each person would have shaped the gestures and figures of our bodies as closely as possible to their likeness. HERMOGENES: What you say seems necessary to me. SOCRATES: In this way, I think, a demonstration would be made with these parts of the body, <margin>D</margin> with the body clearly imitating what one wanted to show. HERMOGENES: Certainly.

SOCRATES: But since we want to declare things with voice, tongue, and mouth, will a demonstration through these not happen only if an imitation of whatever thing is made through them? HERMOGENES: I think it is necessary. SOCRATES: A name, then, as it appears, is an **imitation** <note>The Greek word *mimesis* means more than just "mimicry"; it suggests a representation that captures the essence of the subject.</note> of the voice, by which whoever imitates something, imitates and names it through the voice. HERMOGENES: It seems so to me too. SOCRATES: And yet, by Jupiter <note>original: "per Iouem" / "Μὰ Δί᾿" — a common oath in Greek and Latin dialogue.</note>, I do not yet think it has been said correctly, my friend. HERMOGENES: Why so? SOCRATES: Because we would be forced to admit that those who imitate sheep and roosters and other animals are "naming" the things they imitate. HERMOGENES: You speak the truth. SOCRATES: Do you think that is fitting? HERMOGENES: Not at all.

<margin>E</margin> SOCRATES: But what kind of imitation, Socrates, will a name be? SOCRATES: Not the kind of imitation that happens through music, even though that uses the voice; nor even of the same things that music imitates, for we do not seem to name through musical imitation. I mean it like this: voice and figure and color belong to most things. HERMOGENES: Entirely. SOCRATES: It seems to me that if someone imitates these, the faculty of naming does not consist in those imitations. For those are partly music and partly painting. Is it not so? HERMOGENES: Clearly. SOCRATES: What about this: do you not think there is an **essence** <note>original: "οὐσία" (ousia) / "essentia" — the fundamental "whatness" or being of a thing.</note> to each thing, just as there is to color and the others we mentioned? Does not an essence exist in color and voice themselves, and in everything else that is worthy of being called "a being"? HERMOGENES: It seems so to me.

<margin>F</margin> SOCRATES: If someone were able to imitate the essence of each thing with letters and syllables, would they not declare what each thing is? HERMOGENES: Most certainly. SOCRATES: What would you call such a person? You called the former ones "musician" and "painter"; what will you call this one? HERMOGENES: This person seems to me, Socrates, to be the one we have long been seeking: the **author of naming** <note>The "legislator" or "name-maker" (*onomastikos*).</note>. SOCRATES: If this is true, we must now consider those names you were asking about: *rhoēs*, that is, **flow** <note>original: "ῥοῆς" (rhoēs)</note>; *ienai*, that is, **to go** <note>original: "ἰέναι" (ienai)</note>; and *scheseōs*, that is, **retention** or **stoppage** <note>original: "σχέσεως" (scheseōs)</note>. We must see whether they really imitate the essence with their letters and syllables, or not. HERMOGENES: Indeed.

SOCRATES: Come, let us see whether these are the only primary names, or if there are many others besides these. <margin>G</margin> HERMOGENES: I think there are others. SOCRATES: It is likely. But what is the method of distinguishing where the imitator begins to imitate? Since the imitation of essence happens with letters and syllables, is it not best to first distinguish the elements? Just as those who study rhythms first distinguish the powers of the elements, then of the syllables, and only then approach the rhythms themselves, but never before? HERMOGENES: Certainly. SOCRATES: Should we not also first distinguish the vowel letters, and then the others according to their species—the mutes and semivowels? For that is how the men learned in these things speak. And again, distinguish the vowels that are not semivowels, and the different species of vowels from one another? And once we have distinguished all these things well, we must then bring in the names and consider <margin>H</margin> if they are the things to which everything is referred, like elements, from which one can recognize both the names themselves and whether species are contained within them.

<column-break/>

<summary>Socrates argues that naming is a form of vocal imitation of a thing's essence using letters and syllables, distinct from musical or artistic imitation. He proposes a systematic analysis of linguistic "elements" (vowels and consonants) to understand how primary names represent reality.</summary>
<keywords>elements, vocal imitation, essence, primary names, letters, syllables, mimesis, linguistics, Plato, Socrates</keywords>

--- Page 306 ---
<meta>This page continues Socrates' explanation of "primary names." He has just established that names are imitations of the essence of things, and now he is describing the "alphabet" of meaning—how individual letters and sounds were chosen by the original "name-giver" to reflect physical properties like motion, rest, or thinness.</meta>

-># OF PLATO<-

<margin>A</margin> ...in the same way as in the elements. Having carefully considered all these things, one must know how to apply each thing according to its likeness, whether one thing must be applied to one, or many mixed together: just as painters, wishing to express a likeness, sometimes apply only a purple color, sometimes any other color, and sometimes mix many together—for example, when they want to create a "man-likeness" <note>original: "andrikeolon," a skin-toned pigment or a realistic image of a person</note> or something of that sort—insofar as each image requires certain colors. In no other way shall we also adapt the elements to things: both one to one, wherever it seems most needed, <margin>B</margin> and when we have joined these, and from them established names and verbs, we shall again construct from those names and verbs something already large and beautiful and whole. And just as the art of painting calls that whole composite an "animal," so we call this whole fabric "discourse" <note>original: "orationem" (Latin) / "logon" (Greek)</note>, whether manufactured by the skill of naming, or rhetoric, or any other art that achieves this. Indeed, we ourselves shall not do this—for I have overstepped the bounds in speaking—because the ancients combined them in this way, if it was so established. But we, <margin>C</margin> if we are to consider it skillfully, must investigate all these things by distinguishing them, whether the primary and secondary names are placed as they should be, or not. Otherwise, we must see if we are connecting them poorly, O friend Hermogenes, lest there be an error. *HERMOGENES:* Perhaps, by Jove, O Socrates. *SOCRATES:* Do you yourself trust that you can distinguish these things in this way? For *I* distrust my own ability. *HERMOGENES:* I distrust my own much more. *SOCRATES:* Shall we let it go then? Or do you want us to try as best we can, and even if we can know only a little of these things, let us approach it—though first praying to the gods as we did a little while ago: that we, understanding nothing of the truth, are merely guessing at the opinions of men about them. So let us proceed now, similarly telling ourselves that if these things were to be distinguished in the best way, either by someone <margin>D</margin> else or by us, they certainly ought to have been distinguished thus. But now, as they say, we may treat these matters according to our strength. Do you admit this? Or what do you say? *HERMOGENES:* I think exactly so. *SOCRATES:* I think it will seem ridiculous, O Hermogenes, that things themselves become manifest through imitation by letters and syllables. Yet it is necessary; for we have nothing better than this to which we may look to judge the truth of the primary names—unless perhaps, <margin>E</margin> just as the Tragic poets flee to machines <note>referring to the "deus ex machina," where a god is lowered by a crane to resolve a plot</note> whenever they are in doubt, we too may expedite the matter by saying that the gods established the primary names, and therefore they were correctly instituted. Or is this the most powerful argument for us: that we received them from certain barbarians? For the barbarians are older than us; or perhaps because of their antiquity they cannot be discerned, and so are called "barbarous"? These are evasions, and very clever ones indeed, for those who do not wish to give a reason for the correct imposition of the primary names. For <margin>F</margin> whoever is ignorant of the correct reasoning of the primary names cannot know that of the secondary ones. Furthermore, the latter must be explained from the former, yet he is ignorant of those. Rather, it is necessary for one professing skill in the secondary names to have comprehended the antecedents much earlier and more perfectly, and to be able to demonstrate them. Otherwise, he should know that he will be babbling in the secondary ones. Or do you think otherwise? *HERMOGENES:* Not otherwise, Socrates. *SOCRATES:* What I have perceived about the primary names seems to me to be quite arrogant and ridiculous, and I will communicate them with you, if you wish. But if you find anything better, communicate it with me yourself. *HERMOGENES:* I will do so. But speak now with a brave spirit. *SOCRATES:* In the first place, the letter <term>ρ</term> <note>the letter rho (R)</note> seems to be like an instrument of all motion. But why motion is called <term>κίνησις</term> <note>original: "kinesis" (motion)</note>, we have not said, yet it is clear that it wants to be <term>ἵεσις</term> <note>original: "iesis" (sending or going)</note>. For we used to use <term>ε</term> <note>epsilon</note> instead of <term>ι</term> <note>iota</note>. The beginning is from <term>κίειν</term> <note>original: "kiein" (to go)</note>, which is a foreign word, and signifies "to go." Wherefore, if its ancient name were found translated into our voice, it would correctly be called <term>ἴεσις</term>. But now, from the foreign name <term>κίειν</term>, and by the changing of the <term>η</term> <note>eta</note>, and by the interposition of the <term>ν</term> <note>nu</note>, <margin>G</margin> it is named <term>κίνησις</term>. It ought to have been called <term>κείνησιν</term> or <term>ἔσιν</term>. <term>στάσις</term> <note>original: "stasis" (standing or rest)</note>, that is, station/rest, wants to be the negation of <term>ἰέναι</term> <note>original: "ienai" (to go)</note>. But for the sake of beauty, it is named <term>στάσις</term>. Therefore, the element <term>ρ</term> itself seemed a suitable instrument of motion to the author of names, as I was just saying, for expressing the likeness of movement. Everywhere, therefore, he uses <term>ρ</term> for the expression of motion. In the very first word, <term>ῥεῖν</term> and <term>ῥοή</term> <note>original: "rhein" (to flow) and "rhoe" (flux)</note>, he imitates movement through the letter <term>ρ</term>, then in <term>τρόμῳ</term> <note>original: "tromo" (trembling)</note>, and <term>τραχεῖ</term> <note>original: "trachei" (rough)</note>. Likewise in words of this sort: <term>κρούειν</term> <note>to strike</note>, <term>θραύειν</term> <note>to wound/break</note>, <term>ἐρύκειν</term> <note>to drag</note>, <term>ἐρύπτειν</term> <note>to shatter</note>, <term>κερματίζειν</term> <note>to cut into pieces</note>, <term>ῥυμβεῖν</term> <note>to whirl or stir up</note>. All these he fashions for the most part through <term>ρ</term> to create the likeness of motion. For I omit that the tongue, in pronouncing this letter, stays still the least, but rather is greatly agitated. Therefore, for the expression of these things, he used <term>ρ</term>. For all things that are most penetrating. Therefore, he imitates <term>ἰέναι</term> and <term>ἴεσθαι</term> <note>to go and to proceed</note> through <term>ι</term> <note>iota</note>. Just as through <term>φ, ψ, σ, ζ</term>, which are letters of more vehement breath, the author of names expresses such things as <term>ψυχρόν</term> <note>cold</note>, <term>ζέον</term> <note>fervent/boiling</note>, <term>σείεσθαι</term> <note>to be shaken</note>, and commonly <term>σεισμὸν</term> <note>concussion/shaking</note>; and whenever something vehement and full of breath is to be imitated, he seems to have especially used these. He also used <term>ι</term>, namely iota, for thin...

<column-break/>

...in the elements. Having well observed all these things, hoping to apply each one to its likeness, whether it is necessary to apply one to one, or to mix many together: just as the painters, wishing to make a likeness, sometimes apply only dark gray <note>original: "orphnon," a dark pigment</note>, and sometimes any other of the pigments; and there are times when they mix many, as when they prepare a "man-likeness" or any other such thing; as (I think) each image seems to require each pigment; so also we shall apply the elements to the things; <margin>B</margin> and applying one to one, where it seems necessary, and also making "tokens"—which indeed they call syllables—and again combining syllables, from which both names and verbs are composed; and again from names and verbs we shall construct something already great and beautiful and a whole, just as there the animal is created by the art of painting, so here discourse is created by the art of naming, or rhetoric, or whatever the art may be. Or rather, not we—but I was carried away in saying so. For the ancients combined them in the way they are composed. But we must, if we are to inspect them skillfully, consider all these things, having thus distinguished them, whether the primary names and the secondary ones are placed in the proper manner, or not, and thus observe them. For otherwise, to connect them might be a poor thing, and not according to the right way, O friend Hermogenes. *HERMOGENES:* Perhaps, by <margin>C</margin> Zeus, O Socrates. *SOCRATES:* What then? Do you believe in yourself that you are able to distinguish these things thus? *HERMOGENES:* Not I, certainly. *SOCRATES:* Then much is required for me, at least. *HERMOGENES:* Shall we then let it go? Or do you wish that as best we are able, even if we are able to see only a small part of them, we should attempt it; having first said (just as a little while ago) to the gods, that we, knowing nothing of the truth, are guessing at the opinions of men concerning it. And thus having spoken to ourselves again, let us go, because if it were possible to distinguish these things by any means, whether by anyone else or by us, it would be necessary to divide them thus. But now, as the saying goes, it will be necessary for us to busy ourselves with them according to our power. Does <margin>D</margin> this seem right? Or how do you say? *HERMOGENES:* It seems entirely so to me. *SOCRATES:* I think it will appear ridiculous, O Hermogenes, that things are made manifest by being imitated by letters and syllables. Nevertheless, it is necessary. For we have nothing better than this to which we may refer concerning the truth of the primary names; unless indeed, just as the tragedy-makers, whenever they are at a loss, flee to their machines, raising up gods, and <margin>E</margin> we too, having spoken thus, might be rid of it: that the gods established the primary names, and because of this they are correct. Is this the best of arguments for us? Or that other one, that we have received them from some barbarians? (For barbarians are older than us.) Or that because of antiquity it is impossible to inspect them, just like barbarian words. For these would all be evasions, and very elegant ones, for the one who does not wish to give an account of the primary names, how they are correctly placed. And yet, whoever does not know the correctness of the primary names, it is impossible for him to know the correctness of the secondary ones, which must be made manifest from those about which he knows nothing. But it is clear that the one who claims to be skillful about them must be able to demonstrate especially and most clearly concerning the primary names; or else know well that he will <margin>F</margin> already be talking nonsense about the secondary ones. Or does it seem otherwise to you? *HERMOGENES:* Not in any way otherwise, O Socrates. *SOCRATES:* What I then have in mind concerning the primary names seems to me to be quite insolent and ridiculous. Of these things I will share with you, if you wish; and you, in turn, if you have something better to get from somewhere, try to share it with me too. *HERMOGENES:* I will do so. But speak with confidence. *SOCRATES:* First, then, the letter <term>ρ</term> <note>rho</note> seems to me to be as it were an instrument of all motion, which I did not even say why it has this name. But it is clear that it wants to be <term>ἵεσις</term> <note>sending/going</note>. For we did not use <term>η</term>, but <term>ε</term>, in the old way. And the beginning is from <term>κίειν</term> <note>to go</note>. The name is foreign. And this is "to go" <note>original: "ienai"</note>. If then someone should find its ancient name coinciding with our voice, it would be correctly called <term>ἵεσις</term>. But now from the foreign <term>κίειν</term>, and from the change of the <term>η</term>, and the insertion of the <term>ν</term>, it is called <term>κίνησις</term> <note>motion</note>. But it should have been called <term>κείνησιν</term> or <term>ἔσιν</term>. And <term>στάσις</term> <note>rest</note> wants to be the negation of "to go" <note>original: "ienai"</note>. But for the sake of ornamentation, it has been named <term>στάσις</term>. Therefore, the element <term>ρ</term>, as I say, seemed a beautiful instrument of motion to the one who established names for the purpose of <margin>G</margin> imitating movement <note>original: "phora"</note>. At least in many places he uses it for this. First, in "flowing" <note>original: "rhein"</note> and "flux" <note>original: "rhoe"</note> he imitates the movement of this letter; then in "trembling" <note>original: "tromo"</note>, then in "rough" <note>original: "trachei"</note>; and again in such verbs as <term>κρούειν</term> <note>to strike</note>, <term>θραύειν</term> <note>to break</note>, <term>ἐρύκειν</term> <note>to drag</note>, <term>θρύπτειν</term> <note>to shatter</note>, <term>κερματίζειν</term> <note>to chop</note>, <term>ῥυμβεῖν</term> <note>to whirl</note>. All these he represents for the most part through the <term>ρ</term>. For (I think) the tongue in this remains still the least, and is shaken the most. Therefore it seems to me he used it for these things. And again, <term>ι</term> <note>iota</note> for all thin things, which indeed would go through all things most of all, for these reasons he imitates "to go" <note>original: "ienai"</note> and "to hasten" <note>original: "iesthai"</note> through the <term>ι</term>. Just as through <term>φ, χ, ψ</term>, and <term>σ</term>, and <term>ζῆτα</term> <note>zeta</note>, because the letters are breathy, he has imitated all such things in naming them: such as "cold" <note>original: "psychron"</note>, and "boiling" <note>original: "zeon"</note>, and "to be shaken" <note>original: "seiesthai"</note>, and altogether "shaking" <note>original: "seismon"</note>. And whenever he imitates the "windy" quality, everywhere there as...

<summary>In this passage from the Cratylus, Socrates explains his theory that individual letters (the "elements" of language) were chosen by the original name-giver to imitate the physical essence of things, such as the letter 'R' for motion and 'I' for penetration. He humorously dismisses common excuses for being unable to explain language, such as blaming "barbarians" or claiming divine intervention.</summary>
