-># CRATYLUS<-

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...the founder of all things <note>referring to the 'Legislator' or 'Name-giver'</note> intends, he employs such letters for the most part.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Furthermore, he seems to have considered the compression of the letter **s** <term>sigma</term> and the **t** <term>tau</term>, as well as the retraction of the tongue as if it were clinging, to be very suitable for expressing the power of "binding" and "station" <note>original Greek: *desmos* and *stasis*</note>. And because the tongue slips most of all in pronouncing the letter **l** <term>lambda</term>, he therefore named things by likeness through this letter, such as **smooth** <term>leia</term>, **to slip** <term>olisthanein</term>, **liquid** <term>kollodes</term>, **oily** <term>liparon</term>, and other such things. But where the power of the letter **g** <term>gamma</term> arrests the slipping tongue, by inserting it he formed **glutinous** <term>glischron</term>, **sweet** <term>gluku</term>, and **viscous** <term>gloiodes</term>. Observing also that the sound of the letter **n** <term>nu</term> is held deep in the throat, he used it to name **the inside** <term>to endon</term> and **the things within** <term>ta entos</term>, so that he might represent the things by the letters. He assigned the letter **a** <term>alpha</term> to **large things** <term>megala</term>, and the letter **e** <term>eta</term> to **length** <term>mekei</term>, because these are large letters. In the name for **round** <term>strongylon</term>, needing the letter **o** <term>omicron</term>, he mixed that letter in as much as possible. And by this same reasoning, the author of names seems to adapt all other things to individual objects according to letters and syllables, establishing both a sign and a name; from these, he then establishes the remaining forms through likeness. This, Hermogenes, seems to me to be the correct account of names, unless Cratylus here asserts something else.

<margin>C</margin> HERMOGENES: And truly, Socrates, Cratylus here often gives me trouble, as I said at the beginning, while he asserts there is some correct account of names, yet he does not explain what it is, so that I cannot discern whether he is being so obscure on purpose or not. Therefore, in the present moment, Cratylus, speak before Socrates: whether those things which Socrates says about names please you, or whether you can bring forward something more excellent. If you can, bring it into the open, so that you may either learn from Socrates, or instruct us both.

<margin>B</margin> CRATYLUS: Does it seem to you, Hermogenes, to be easy to perceive and teach any matter so quickly, let alone a matter so great, which is esteemed as one of the greatest of the great?

<margin>D</margin> HERMOGENES: By Jove, it does not seem so to me; rather, I think Hesiod spoke skillfully <margin>In book 1. <term>Odyssey</term> <note>This margin note likely refers to Hesiod's *Works and Days*, despite the "Odyssey" label</note></margin> when he said it is worthwhile to add "a little to a little." Therefore, if you are able to achieve anything, even if it is small, do not be burdened, but help this Socrates here, and me as well.

SOCRATES: Indeed, Cratylus, I myself would not assert any of those things I have mentioned above. To be sure, I have investigated this with Hermogenes in whatever way seemed best. Therefore, if you have anything better, dare to express it, as I will gladly receive whatever you say. For I would not be surprised if you yourself have considered such things and learned them from others. If, then, you say something more excellent, count me as one of your disciples regarding the correct account of names.

<margin>E</margin> CRATYLUS: Certainly, Socrates, as you say, these things have been my concern, and perhaps I might make a disciple of you. Yet I fear the matter may be quite the opposite. It occurs to me now to say the same thing to you that Achilles said to Ajax in the "Prayers" <margin>Iliad 9</margin>: "Ajax, son of Telamon, Zeus-born prince of the people, you have spoken everything according to my own mind." So you too, Socrates, seem to prophesy according to our own mind, whether you have been inspired by Euthyphro, or whether some Muse, dwelling within you for a long time, has until now remained hidden.

SOCRATES: O good Cratylus, I too have long wondered at my own wisdom, and I do not entirely trust it. Therefore, I think I must re-examine what I am saying. For to be deceived by oneself is the most difficult thing of all, for it is an exceedingly dangerous matter when the deceiver is never absent but always follows closely beside the one deceived. It is necessary, therefore, frequently to look back at what was said before, and as that poet says, "to look both forward and backward at once." And so, let us see now what has been said by us. We said the correctness of a name is that which shows what sort of thing each thing is. Shall we say that this has been stated sufficiently?

<margin>F</margin> CRATYLUS: To me, at least, it certainly seems so, Socrates.

SOCRATES: Are names, then, spoken for the sake of instruction?

CRATYLUS: Entirely.

SOCRATES: Shall we not also say that this is an art, and that there are practitioners of it?

CRATYLUS: Most certainly.

SOCRATES: Who are they?

CRATYLUS: Those whom you called from the beginning the "lawgivers" and "founders of names."

SOCRATES: Shall we consider this art to exist among men similarly to other arts, or <margin>G</margin> otherwise? This is what I mean: are some painters worse, and others more excellent?

CRATYLUS: They are.

SOCRATES: Do not the more excellent painters produce more beautiful works—namely, the figures of living creatures—while the others do the opposite? And likewise, do not builders make some houses more beautiful and others more ugly?

CRATYLUS: So it is.

SOCRATES: And do the authors of laws themselves produce some works that are more beautiful and others more ugly?

CRATYLUS: I no longer admit that point.

SOCRATES: Then some laws do not seem to you to be better and others worse?

CRATYLUS: Certainly not.

SOCRATES: Nor does it seem to you that one name is better imposed and another worse?

CRATYLUS: Not even that.

SOCRATES: Then all names are correctly established.

CRATYLUS: At least as many as are truly names.

SOCRATES: What about the name of our friend Hermogenes, which was mentioned a little while ago? Shall we say that this name was not given to him at all, unless he belongs to the **race of Hermes** <term>Hermou genesos</term>? Or was it given, but not correctly?

CRATYLUS: I do not even think it was given, Socrates, but only seems to be. It is actually the name of someone else, whose nature is that which is contained in the name.

SOCRATES: Does a person not even speak falsely when he says that this man is Hermogenes? For it must not be doubted that he is calling him Hermogenes, even though he is not.

CRATYLUS: How so?

SOCRATES: Is it because your argument stands on the idea that it is impossible to speak a falsehood at all? Is this...

--- Page 308 ---
<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Cratylus. Having explored how specific sounds (like the 'r' for motion or 'l' for smoothness) represent physical qualities, Socrates now turns to the philosophical problem of whether a name can be "false." Cratylus, following a popular Sophist view, argues that a name is either a perfect representation of a thing or it isn't a name at all.</meta>

-># PLATO<-

<margin>B</margin> ...and many people are currently saying this, friend Cratylus, just as they have asserted it in the past. **CRAT.** In what way, Socrates, when someone says what he says, can he be said to speak that which is not? Is "speaking falsely" anything other than saying things that are not? **SOCR.** That is a very clever argument, my friend, perhaps more suited for someone younger and sharper than myself. However, tell me this: do you think it is impossible to *speak* a falsehood, but possible to *state* one? **CRAT.** Neither is possible. **SOCR.** And is it also impossible to *utter* one, or even to *address* someone falsely? For instance, if someone met you in a gesture of hospitality, took your hand, and said: "Greetings, Athenian guest, Hermogenes, son of Smicrion." Would he be speaking these words, or stating them, or addressing you this way—not to you, in fact, but to this man Hermogenes, or perhaps to no one at all? **CRAT.** It seems to me, Socrates, that such a man would be making noise to no purpose. **SOCR.** I am satisfied with that. But does the man making such a noise utter what is true or what is false? Or is part of it true and part false? Even that would be enough for our argument. **CRAT.** I would say that such a person is just making a sound, moving himself in vain, as if he were striking a bronze pot. **SOCR.** Consider, Cratylus, if we might reach an agreement. Do you not say that the name is one thing, and the thing it names is another? **CRAT.** I do. **SOCR.** And you confess that a name is a kind of imitation <term>mimesis</term> of the thing itself? **CRAT.** Most certainly. **SOCR.** And that paintings <term>zographia</term> are imitations of certain things in another way? **CRAT.** Truly. <margin>C</margin> **SOC.** Come then—perhaps I do not fully grasp what you mean, though you may be speaking correctly. Can we distribute both of these imitations—paintings and names—to the things of which they are imitations, or not? **CRAT.** We can. **SOCR.** Observe this first: can someone attribute the image of a man to a man, and the image of a woman to a woman, and so on? **CRAT.** Certainly. **SOCR.** And what about the opposite? Attributing the image of a man to a woman, and that of a woman to a man? **CRAT.** That is also possible. **SOCR.** Are both of these distributions "right," or is only one of them right—the one that attributes the proper and similar image to each? **CRAT.** That is how it seems to me. **SOCR.** Then, so that you and I do not fight over words while being friends, listen to what I say. I call such a distribution "right" in both kinds of imitations—paintings and names. In the case of names, I call it not only "right," but "true." But the other kind, the distribution and application of the unlike, I call "not right," and in the case of names, "false." **CRAT.** <margin>D</margin> But see, Socrates, if perhaps this "wrong distribution" can only happen in paintings, and not at all in names; for names, it must always be necessary to assign them correctly. **SOC.** What do you mean? How does the one differ from the other? Is it not possible to approach a man and say, "This is your portrait," and show him either his own likeness or perhaps that of a woman? By "showing," I mean presenting it to his sense of sight. **CRAT.** Certainly. **SOC.** And what if you approach him again and say, "This is your name"? For a name is also a kind of imitation, <margin>E</margin> just as a portrait is. I put it like this: Could he not say, "This is your name," and then pour into his ear a sound—perhaps an imitation of a male, saying he is a "man," or perhaps an imitation of a female of the human race, saying she is a "woman"? Do you not think this can sometimes happen? **CRAT.** I am willing to concede this to you, Socrates; let it be so. **SOC.** You do well, my friend, if indeed this is the case. We need not fight too hard over it now. Furthermore, if there is such a thing as a "wrong distribution" here, we call one "speaking truly" and the other "speaking falsely." If this is so, and we can distribute names incorrectly—giving to things what does not belong to them—then it must be possible to do the same with verbs <term>rhemata</term>. And if names and verbs <margin>F</margin> can be arranged this way, it must also be true for whole sentences. For a sentence <term>logos</term>, I believe, is a composition of verbs and names. What do you say to that, Cratylus? **CRAT.** I agree with you, for you seem to speak rightly. **SOC.** Moreover, if we refer the first names back to the letters themselves through a kind of imitation, it can happen here just as in paintings. In a painting, we might apply all the fitting shapes and colors. Or we might not apply all of them, but add some things and take others away, making some parts more and others less. Is this not possible? **CRAT.** Without a doubt. **SOC.** He who attributes all that is fitting produces beautiful letters and images. But he who adds or takes away also makes letters and images, but bad ones. **CRAT.** Indeed. **SOC.** And what of the one who <margin>G</margin> imitates the essence of things through letters and syllables? By the same logic, if he attributes all that is fitting, will he not produce a beautiful image? And that image is a "name." But if he falls short in a few things, or sometimes exceeds them, an image will still be produced, but not a beautiful one. Therefore, some names will be well-constructed, and others the opposite? **CRAT.** Perhaps. **SOCRAT.** Perhaps, then, one man will be a "good craftsman" of names, and another a "bad" one. **CRATYL.** Certainly. **SOCRAT.** And did we not call this man the "Name-giver" <term>nomothetes</term>? **CRATYL.** Plainly. **SOCRAT.** Therefore, as in other arts, there will be one Name-giver who is good and another who is not, provided our previous points stand. **CRATYL.** That is true. But do you see, Socrates, whenever we attribute these letters—alpha and epsilon and any of the elements—to names through the art of grammar, if we take something away, or add something, or even fail to change it, the name we write...

<column-break/>

...do we think this argument is right? For there are quite a few who say this, friend Cratylus, both now and long ago. **CR.** How indeed, Socrates, could anyone, saying exactly what he says, say that which is not? Or is this not what "speaking falsely" is: to say things that are not real? **SO.** This argument is more elegant than suits my ability or my age, companion. Nevertheless, tell me this much: does it seem to you that one cannot *speak* a falsehood, but can *state* one? <note>original: "λέγειν" (speak/say) vs "φάναι" (state/assert)</note> **CR.** It does not seem to me that one can even state it. **SO.** Nor speak it, nor even address someone? As if someone meeting you while you were a guest, taking your hand, said: "Greetings, Athenian guest, son of Smicrion, Hermogenes." Would he be saying these things, or stating them, or speaking them? Or would he be addressing you this way—not you, but this man Hermogenes? Or no one? **CR.** It seems to me, Socrates, that he would be uttering these things in vain. **SO.** Even that is welcome. For would the one uttering these things be uttering what is true, or what is false? Or is one part of them true, and the other false? For even this would suffice. **CR.** I would say that such a man is making a noise, moving himself to no purpose, just as if one were to move a bronze vessel by striking it. **SO.** Come then, let us see if we can reach an agreement, Cratylus. Would you not say that the name is one thing, and that of which it is the name is another? **CR.** I would. **SO.** And do you not agree that the name is a kind of imitation <term>mimesis</term> of the thing? **CR.** Most certainly. **SO.** And do you not say that paintings are imitations of certain things in another way? **CR.** Yes. **SO.** Come then—perhaps I do not understand what you mean; but you might be speaking correctly. Is it possible to distribute <term>dianemai</term> and apply both of these imitations—both paintings and names—to the things of which they are imitations? Or not? **CR.** It is. **SO.** Look now. First consider this: could someone assign to a man the image of a man, and to a woman the image of a man, and to a woman the image of a man? **CR.** Very much so. **SO.** And also the opposite: the image of a man to a woman, and the image of a woman to a man? **CR.** These things are possible too. **SO.** Are both of these distributions right? Or only one? **CR.** Only the one. **SO.** The one that (I think) assigns to each thing that which is fitting and similar. **CR.** So it seems to me. **SO.** Then, so that you and I do not fight in our talk, being friends, accept what I say. For I call such a distribution, my companion, "right" in the case of both imitations—the paintings and the names. In the case of names, I call it not only "right" but "true." The other kind—the giving and applying of the unlike—is "not right," and "false" when it is done to names. **CR.** But see, Socrates, if this "not distributing rightly" is possible in paintings, but in names it is not, but is instead always necessarily right. **SO.** What do you mean? How does this differ from the other? Is it not possible to go up to some man and say, "This is your drawing," and show him, if it happens to be so, his own image, or if it happens to be so, that of a woman? By "show," I mean to bring it before the sense of his eyes. **CR.** Certainly. **SO.** What then? Again, approaching the same man, could one say, "This is your name"? For a name is also an imitation, just as a painting is. This is what I am saying: would it not be possible to say to him, "This is your name"? And after this, to bring it before his sense of hearing—if it happens to be his own imitation—by saying "man"? Or if it happens to be the imitation of the female of the human race, by saying "woman"? Does it not seem to you that this is possible and happens sometimes? **CR.** I am willing to concede it to you, Socrates; let it be so. **SO.** You do well, friend, if indeed it is so. For there is no need to fight intensely about it now. If, then, there is such a distribution here too, we wish to call one of these "speaking truth" and the other "speaking falsely." And if this is so, and it is possible to not distribute names rightly, nor to assign what is fitting to each, but sometimes what is not fitting, it would also be possible for verbs <term>rhemata</term> to do this same thing. And if verbs and names can be placed this way, sentences <term>logoi</term> must be as well. For sentences, I believe, are a composition of these. Is that not so, Cratylus? **CR.** It is so. You seem to me to speak well. **SO.** Therefore, if we were to make the first names like paintings, it is just as in paintings where one can assign all the fitting colors and shapes, or not all of them—leaving some out and adding others, making them more or larger. Is that not possible? **CR.** It is. **SO.** Then the one who assigns everything produces beautiful colors and images. But the one who adds or subtracts also produces drawings and images, but poor ones. **CR.** Yes. **SO.** What then? The one who imitates the essence <term>ousia</term> of beings through syllables and letters—by the same reasoning, if he assigns all that is fitting, will the image not be beautiful? (And this is a "name.") But if he leaves out a little or adds something sometimes, an image is made, but not a beautiful one; so that some names will be well-made, and others poorly? **CR.** Perhaps. **SO.** Perhaps then there will be a good craftsman <term>demiurgos</term> of names, and a bad one? **CR.** Yes. **SO.** And the name for this man was "Legislator." **CR.** Yes. **SO.** Then perhaps, by Zeus, it will be just as in the other arts: the Legislator will be sometimes good and sometimes bad, if what we agreed upon before holds true. **CR.** That is so. **SO.** But do you see, Socrates, whenever we assign these letters—alpha and beta and each of the elements—to names by the art of grammar, if we take anything away, or add anything, or change the position, we have written...

<summary>Socrates uses an analogy between painting and naming to convince Cratylus that names can be "false" if they are poorly distributed or incorrectly composed. He concludes that there are good and bad "Name-givers" (Legislators), just as there are good and bad artists.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from Plato’s Cratylus. In the preceding sections, Socrates and Cratylus have been discussing the "natural" origin of words—the idea that the sounds of letters inherently mimic the qualities of the things they name. This page marks a pivotal shift toward the role of "convention" and "custom" in language.</meta>

# PLATO'S WORKS

->Page 278<-

<column-break/>

[Socrates] ...to you if we are not [consistent], which the letter 'rho' <note>original: ρ (rho)</note> itself is consistent with flowing, motion, and hardness?
<margin>Crat.</margin> Right, at least to me.
<margin>Soc.</margin> And what about the letter 'lambda' <note>original: λ (lambda)</note>? Is it for the smooth and soft, as opposed to the others we just described?
<margin>Crat.</margin> Indeed.
<margin>Soc.</margin> Do you know that we call the same quality "hardness" <note>original: σκληρότης (sklērotēs)</note>, but the Eretrians <note>A Greek people from the island of Euboea, known in antiquity for their distinct dialect.</note> call it "hardner" <note>original: σκληρότηρ (sklērotēr)</note>?
<margin>Crat.</margin> Certainly.
<margin>Soc.</margin> Does it seem then that both these letters, 'rho' and 'sigma' <note>original: ρ and σ</note>, are similar to the same thing, and do they demonstrate the same thing to them through the ending in 'rho' as they do to us through 'sigma'? Or does one of the two signify nothing to the other?
<margin>Crat.</margin> They clearly demonstrate it to both.
<margin>Soc.</margin> Is this insofar as 'rho' and 'sigma' are similar, or insofar as they are dissimilar?
<margin>Crat.</margin> Insofar as they are similar.
<margin>Soc.</margin> Are they entirely similar?
<margin>Crat.</margin> At least for the purpose of signifying motion?
<margin>Soc.</margin> Well then, why does the 'lambda' <note>original: λ</note> inserted in the word not signify the opposite of hardness?
<margin>Crat.</margin> Perhaps it was not correctly inserted, Socrates, just as with the things you were treating earlier with Hermogenes, when you were removing and adding letters where it was most appropriate. And you seemed to me to be doing it correctly then; perhaps now 'rho' should be put in place of 'lambda.'
<margin>Soc.</margin> Well spoken. But what of this: as we are speaking now, do we not perceive one another's meaning when someone pronounces "hard" <note>original: σκληρὸν (sklēron)</note>? And do you not understand what I am saying right now?
<margin>Crat.</margin> I understand indeed, my dearest friend, because of custom.
<margin>Soc.</margin> When you say "custom," what else do you think you are saying besides "convention"? Or do you call "custom" something other than this: that when I pronounce this sound, I have that thought, and you also perceive what I am thinking? Is this not what you mean?
<margin>Crat.</margin> Exactly that.
<margin>Soc.</margin> If you recognize it when I pronounce it, then a declaration is made to you by me.
<margin>Crat.</margin> So it is.
<margin>Soc.</margin> And yet, I am uttering something dissimilar to what you yourself are thinking; since the letter 'lambda' is dissimilar to that which you call "hardness." If this is the case, you are surely accustoming yourself to it, and from this convention you establish the "correctness" of the name for yourself—since both dissimilar and similar letters represent the same thing to you because of the acquisition of custom and convention. But if custom is not convention, it can no longer be said that similarity is the means of declaration; rather, one must call it custom. For custom declares things through both similarity and dissimilarity. Since these things are granted, Cratylus (for I shall take your silence as a concession), it is necessary that custom and convention contribute something to the expression of those things we think and speak. For if you wish, my excellent man, to descend to the consideration of numbers, how do you hope to find proper names for them so that you can attribute a similar name to each individual number, if you do not allow your own concession and convention to have some authority regarding the logic of names? It pleases me, too, that names should be as similar to things as possible. Yet I fear that, as Hermogenes said, this "hauling" of similarity might be a bit slippery <note>Socrates uses a metaphor here suggesting that trying to force every word to sound like its meaning is an arduous or tenuous task.</note>, and we may be forced to use this "burdensome" thing, namely convention, for the correctness of names. For then perhaps one would speak best according to one's ability when one speaks with either entirely or mostly similar (that is, fitting) sounds, and most poorly when the opposite is true. But tell me one more thing after this: what power do names have for us, and what beauty do we assert is achieved through them?
<margin>Crat.</margin> They seem to me to teach everything, Socrates, and it should be simply asserted that whoever knows the names also knows the things themselves.
<margin>Soc.</margin> Perhaps, Cratylus, you mean something like this: that when someone knows what kind of thing a name is (and it is of the same kind as the thing itself), he will also recognize the thing itself, since the thing is similar to the name. This seems to be the one and the same art for all things similar to one another. Induced by this reasoning, you seem to have said that whoever knows names will also recognize the things themselves.
<margin>Crat.</margin> You speak the truth.
<margin>Soc.</margin> Come, let us see what this "method of teaching things" is that you now mention, and whether there is another besides it—though this one might be held as better—or if there is no other besides this one. Which of these do you think?
<margin>Crat.</margin> This one certainly; that there is evidently no other, but this one alone is best.
<margin>Soc.</margin> But do you think that things themselves are discovered in this way, so that whoever discovered names also found those things which the names belong to? Or must one rather seek and discover another method, and learn this one instead?
<margin>Crat.</margin> Most of all, according to those points, this very method must be both sought and discovered.
<margin>Soc.</margin> Come then, let us consider it this way, Cratylus: if someone, while investigating things, follows the names themselves and considers what each one wants to be, do you see how great a danger of deception he undergoes?
<margin>Crat.</margin> In what way?
<margin>Soc.</margin> Because the one who first established the names fashioned them, as we were saying, according to how he believed the things were. Is it not so?
<margin>Crat.</margin> Precisely so.
<margin>Soc.</margin> If, therefore, he did not perceive correctly, and established them as he perceived them, do you not think those following in his footsteps will be deceived?
<margin>Crat.</margin> It is not so, Socrates; rather, it was necessary for the one who established the names to have been a knower. Otherwise, as I said long ago, they would not be names at all. And the most evident proof for you that the author of names did not wander from the truth is that if he had perceived wrongly, everything would by no means be consistent for him. Or did you not notice yourself, when you were speaking, how all names tend toward the same goal?
<margin>Soc.</margin> That defense, my good Cratylus, is worth nothing. For what wonder is it if the first establisher of names, having been deceived, then dragged all subsequent things toward that first error by a certain force and compelled them to be consistent with it? Just as in geometric diagrams <note>Socrates compares language to a mathematical proof where one small error at the start makes the rest of the calculations consistently wrong.</note>, sometimes when a small, unknown, and false first premise exists, the many remaining parts follow and agree with one another. Therefore, everyone must debate many things concerning the establishment of any first principle, and consider most diligently whether he judges correctly or not.

<margin>One must debate many things concerning the establishment of a first principle.</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...to flowing and motion and hardness, or is it not well? <margin>Crat.</margin> Well indeed to me. <margin>Soc.</margin> And the 'lambda' <note>original: λ</note> for the smooth and soft, and those things we were just mentioning? <margin>Crat.</margin> Yes. <margin>Soc.</margin> Do you know then that we say the same thing is "hardness" <note>original: σκληρότης</note>, but the Eretrians say "hardner" <note>original: σκληρότηρ</note>? <margin>Crat.</margin> Quite so. <margin>Soc.</margin> Whether then do both the 'rho' and 'sigma' <note>original: ρ and ς</note> seem to be similar to the same thing, and do they show the same thing to them with the 'rho' ending, and to us with the 'sigma,' or does it show nothing to one of us? <margin>Crat.</margin> It shows it to both. <margin>Soc.</margin> Whether insofar as 'rho' and 'sigma' are similar, or insofar as they are not? <margin>Crat.</margin> Insofar as they are similar. <margin>Soc.</margin> In what way are they not similar in all respects? <margin>Crat.</margin> Perhaps toward the signifying of motion. <margin>Soc.</margin> And the 'lambda' <note>original: λ</note> lying within it, does it not signify the opposite of hardness? <margin>Crat.</margin> Perhaps it is not correctly placed, Socrates, just as <margin>B</margin> you were saying to Hermogenes, taking out and putting in letters where necessary; and you seemed right to me. And now perhaps instead of 'lambda' one should say 'rho.' <margin>Soc.</margin> Well said. What then now, as we were saying, do we not understand anything from each other when someone says "hard" <note>original: σκληρόν</note>? Do you not know what I am saying now? <margin>Crat.</margin> I do, by custom, my friend. <margin>Soc.</margin> In saying "custom," do you think you say anything different from "convention"? Or do you mean anything else by "custom" than that when I utter this, I think that; and you know that I think that? Is this not what you say? <margin>Crat.</margin> Yes. <margin>Soc.</margin> Therefore if you know it when I speak, a sign is made to you from me. <margin>Crat.</margin> Yes. <margin>Soc.</margin> From the dissimilar <margin>C) </margin> to that which I think and utter, if the 'lambda' is dissimilar to your "hardness." If this is so, what else is it than that you yourself have made a convention with yourself, and the correctness of the name becomes convention to you, since both similar and dissimilar letters show meaning, having met with custom and convention? If custom is not convention, it would no longer be possible to say that similarity is the indicator, but custom. For that, as it seems, indicates by both the similar and the dissimilar. Since we agree on these things, Cratylus (for I will take your silence as agreement), it is surely necessary for us to contribute something of convention and custom toward the indication of what we think when we speak. Since, best <margin>D</margin> of men, if you wish to come to number, from where do you think you will have names similar to each one of the numbers to apply to them, if you do not allow your own agreement and convention to have authority regarding the correctness of names? To me it is also pleasing that names should be as similar as possible to things; but truly, lest—as Hermogenes said—this dragging of similarity be a "sticky" <note>Socrates uses the word *glischra* (sticky/tenuous) to describe the difficulty of naturalistic etymology.</note> business, it is necessary to use this vulgar thing, convention, for the correctness of names. Since perhaps as far as possible, it would be most beautifully said when one speaks with all or as many similar sounds as possible (this is fitting) and most shamefully the opposite. Tell me this besides <margin>E</margin> these things: what power do names have for us, and what do we say is their beauty? <margin>Crat.</margin> To teach, it seems to me, Socrates, and this is quite simple: whoever knows the names, knows also the things. <margin>Soc.</margin> Perhaps, Cratylus, you mean something like this: that when someone knows the name, what kind of thing it is (and it is of the same kind as the thing), he will know the thing too, since it happens to be similar to the name. There is then one and the same art for all things similar to each other. And according to this you seem to me to say that whoever knows the names will know the things. <margin>Crat.</margin> You speak most truly. <margin>Soc.</margin> Hold then, let us see what this way of teaching beings is that you say; and whether there is another, and this one is better; or if there is no other but this one? <margin>Crat.</margin> So I <margin>F</margin> think, entirely so; this is the only and the best way. <margin>Soc.</margin> Whether the discovery of beings is the same as this: that he who found the names also found those things which the names are? Or must one seek and find in another way, but learn in this way? <margin>Crat.</margin> Most of all, to seek and find in the same way and according to the same things. <margin>Soc.</margin> Come then, let us consider, Cratylus, if someone seeking things follows names, looking at what each one wants to be, do you not think there is no small danger of being deceived? <margin>Crat.</margin> How? <margin>Soc.</margin> Clearly he who first established the names established them according to how he thought the things were, as we say. Is it not so? <margin>Crat.</margin> Yes. <margin>Soc.</margin> If then he did not think correctly, but established <margin>G</margin> them according to what he thought, what do you think we who follow him will suffer? Anything other than being deceived? <margin>Crat.</margin> But it is not so, Socrates; rather it is necessary that the one who establishes them knows what he is establishing; otherwise (as I said before) they would not be names. And let this be the greatest proof to you that the establisher did not miss the truth: for they would never have been so consistent with him. Or did you not notice yourself when saying that all names happened according to the same thing and for the same thing? <margin>Soc.</margin> But this, my good Cratylus, is no defense at all. For if the establisher slipped at the first point, and then forced the others to fit this and compelled them to agree with him, it is nothing strange; just as in diagrams when the first small and unclear falsehood occurs, the remaining many things follow and agree with each other. It is necessary then concerning the beginning of every word and every thing for every man to have much discourse and much consideration, whether the hypothesis holds correctly or not...

<summary>In this excerpt from Plato's Cratylus, Socrates challenges the idea that names have a purely "natural" origin. He argues that because we can understand words even when they contain "incorrect" sounds (like the 'l' in hardness), language must rely on human convention and custom rather than just physical similarity between sound and object.</summary>

<keywords>Socrates, Cratylus, Plato, linguistics, etymology, convention, custom, Greek language, Eretrian dialect, phonetics, philosophy of language</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue in Plato's Cratylus. Having previously explored how individual letters might mimic motion or rest, Socrates now challenges Cratylus by examining complex philosophical terms. He suggests that while many words seem to imply that everything is in "flux" (motion), other words of equal importance imply "stability" or "rest," creating a linguistic contradiction.</meta>

-># CRATYLUS<-

->Page 279<-

<margin>A</margin>
[Socrates]: ...will be examined; and if that is investigated, perhaps the rest will appear to follow from it. Yet names seem to be a strange thing, and they seem to agree with themselves. For if we return to what we discussed before, that the whole of reality is moving, carrying, and flowing, one might say that names indicate the essence of things to us in that way. But does it really seem so to you, or is that just how it appears?
<margin>Cratylus</margin>: It certainly seems so, and it signifies it correctly.
<margin>Soc.</margin>: Let us consider it by taking up the terms themselves. First, this name <term>Knowledge <note>original: ἐπιστήμη (epistēmē)</note></term> is ambiguous; it seems more to signify that it <term>stops <note>original: ἵστησιν (histēsin)</note></term> our soul at things, rather than that it is carried along with them. It is more correct to speak as we do now, keeping the beginning as it is, rather than dropping the "e" to say *pistēmē* <note>Socrates is playing with the word's sound: "epistēmē" sounds like "stopping" (histēmi), while "pistēmē" would imply "faith" or "trust."</note>. But one should insert the "i" instead of the "e" in *isen*. Next, <term>Understanding <note>original: σύνεσις (synesis)</note></term> would not
<margin>B</margin>
be a matter of tension for me, but of stability. Then <term>Inquiry <note>original: ἱστορία (historia)</note></term> signifies this very thing: that it <term>stops the flow <note>original: ἵστησι τὸν ῥοῦν (histēsi ton roun)</note></term>. And <term>Faithful <note>original: πιστὸν (piston)</note></term> absolutely signifies that which stops. Furthermore, <term>Memory <note>original: μνήμη (mnēmē)</note></term> indicates to everyone that there is a <term>stay <note>original: μονή (monē)</note></term> in the soul, not a motion. And if you wish, <term>Error <note>original: ἁμαρτία (hamartia)</note></term> and <term>Misfortune <note>original: συμφορά (symphora)</note></term>, if one follows the name, will appear the same as this "understanding" and "knowledge" and all other names associated with serious things. For even "error" and "licentiousness" are prepared in this way. For <term>Error <note>original: ἁμαρτία</note></term> appears to be a journey <term>along with God <note>original: ἅμα θεῷ (hama theō)</note></term>;
<margin>C</margin>
and <term>Licentiousness <note>original: ἀκολασία (akolasia)</note></term> appears to be an absolute <term>following <note>original: ἀκολουθία (akolouthia)</note></term> of things. And so, the names we think are for the worst things would appear most similar to those for the most beautiful things. I think many other names could be found (if one were to work at it) from which one might again think that the one who established names intended to signify that things are staying still, not moving or being carried.
<margin>Crat.</margin>: But Socrates, you see that the majority of names signify in that other way [the way of motion].
<margin>Soc.</margin>: What of it, Cratylus? Shall we count names like
<margin>D</margin>
voting stones? And is correctness found in this—that whichever side names appear to signify more often, those are the true ones?
<margin>Crat.</margin>: That doesn't seem likely.
<margin>Soc.</margin>: Not in the least, my friend. Let us leave those aside and consider if you will agree with me on this: we say that those who first established names, both the Greeks and the barbarians, were <term>Lawgivers <note>original: νομοθέτας (nomothetas) - here referring to those who set the laws of language</note></term>, and that the art of naming things is "legislative."
<margin>Crat.</margin>: Certainly.
<margin>Soc.</margin>: Tell me then, did the first lawgivers establish the first names knowing the things for which they set them, or in ignorance?
<margin>Crat.</margin>: I believe, Socrates, they did so knowing.
<margin>Soc.</margin>: Surely not, friend Cratylus, in ignorance?
<margin>Crat.</margin>: It does not seem so to me.
<margin>Soc.</margin>: Let us return to where we turned aside. If you remember, you said it was necessary that the one establishing names should do so knowing the things to which he gave them. Does that still seem so to you,
<margin>E</margin>
or not?
<margin>Crat.</margin>: It still does.
<margin>Soc.</margin>: And do you say the one who established the *first* names did so while knowing?
<margin>Crat.</margin>: While knowing.
<margin>Soc.</margin>: From what names, then, did they learn or find out the things that exist, if the first names had not yet been established? Since we said it is impossible to learn or find out things in any other way than by learning and being taught their names, or by finding them out for oneself?
<margin>Crat.</margin>: You seem to have a point, Socrates.
<margin>Soc.</margin>: In what way, then, shall we say they knew them? Or that they were lawgivers before any name at all was established and known to them, if indeed things cannot be learned except from names?
<margin>Crat.</margin>: I believe the truest explanation for these things, Socrates, is that a power greater than human
<margin>F</margin>
established the first names for things, so that it is necessary for them to be correct.
<margin>Soc.</margin>: Then do you think the creator of names—whether some spirit or a god—would establish names that contradict himself? Or did we seem to say nothing just now?
<margin>Crat.</margin>: But perhaps the other set are not names at all.
<margin>Soc.</margin>: Which ones, my excellent friend? Those that lead toward stability, or those toward motion? For it won't be decided by the greater number, as we just said.
<margin>Crat.</margin>: That is only fair, Socrates.
<margin>Soc.</margin>: Since names are in conflict, and some claim themselves to be like the truth, and others claim the same for themselves, by what shall we judge them? Or where shall we go? Surely not to other names, for there are none. It is clear that something other than names must be sought, which will show us without names which of these is the truth, demonstrating the truth of beings.
<margin>Crat.</margin>: It seems so to me.
<margin>Soc.</margin>: It is therefore possible, it seems, Cratylus, to learn about beings without names, if this is how it stands.
<margin>Crat.</margin>: So it appears.
<margin>Soc.</margin>: Through what else, then, would you expect to learn these things?
<margin>G</margin>
Is it through anything other than what is likely and most just—through one another, if they are related, and through the things themselves? For anything other than them would signify something else and different, but not the things themselves.
<margin>Crat.</margin>: You seem to speak the truth.
<margin>Soc.</margin>: Tell me, by Zeus: have we not often agreed that names correctly established are like those things for which the names are set, and are images of the things?
<margin>Crat.</margin>: Yes.
<margin>Soc.</margin>: If, therefore, it is possible to learn things through names, and also through the things themselves, which would be the better and clearer way of learning? To learn from the image
<margin>H</margin>
both the image itself—to see if it is beautifully made—and the truth of which it is an image?

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
From which, having been sufficiently examined, the rest must now follow the principle. I wonder, however, if they agree with the names themselves. Let us consider again what we reported above. We certainly said names signify essence in such a way as if all things run, are carried, and flow. Do you think they signify in this way?
<margin>Cratylus</margin>: Certainly so, and rightly indeed.
<margin>Socrates</margin>: Let us see, then, by repeating some of them. First, this name <term>Knowledge <note>original: ἐπιστήμη (epistēmē)</note></term>, that is *scientia*, is ambiguous, and seems rather to signify that it <term>stops <note>original: ἴστησιν (istēsin)</note></term>, that is, it stays the soul in things, rather than being carried around equally with things. And it seems to be more correct that we say its beginning as it is now, *epistēmē*, rather than by the ejection of the "e", *pistēmē*. And for "e", let us rather add "i". Next, <term>Understanding <note>original: σύνεσιν (synesin)</note></term>, that is,
<margin>B</margin>
it is called "firm," since it <term>sets <note>original: ἵστησιν (istēsin)</note></term> a base and standing; that is, it is an imitation of a foundation and status, rather than of motion. Furthermore, <term>Inquiry <note>original: ἱστορία (historia)</note></term> perhaps signifies this: that it <term>stops the flow <note>original: ἵστησι ἡ ῥοῦν (istēsi hē roun)</note></term>, and <term>Faithful <note>original: πιστὸν (piston)</note></term>, that is, what is to be believed, signifies to make entirely firm. Moreover, <term>Memory <note>original: μνήμη (mnēmē)</note></term> shows entirely that in the soul there is not motion or agitation, but <term>Stay <note>original: μονὴ (monē)</note></term>, that is, rest and stable permanence. And if anyone observes the names <term>Error <note>original: ἁμαρτία (hamartia)</note></term> and <term>Misfortune <note>original: συμφορά (symphora)</note></term>, they will seem to bring the same meaning as "understanding" and "knowledge," and the other names which are imposed on distinguished things. Likewise, <term>Ignorance <note>original: ἀμαθία (amathia)</note></term> and <term>Intemperance <note>original: ἀκολασία (akolasia)</note></term>
<margin>C</margin>
seem closest to these: *amathia* indeed seems to import "a progress going along with God" <note>original: ἅμα θεῷ ἰόντος πορείαν (hama theō iontos poreian)</note>. *Akolasia* truly signifies an absolute "perfection and assembly" <note>original: ἀκολουθίαν (akolouthian)</note> of the things themselves. And so, the names we think belong to the most shameful things will appear most similar to those names which concern the most beautiful things. I think many other things can be found, if someone applies himself to this, from which he will again judge that the author of names indicates things are stable, not running and carried away.
<margin>Crat.</margin>: However, Socrates, you see that he established
<margin>D</margin>
many according to the signification of agitation.
<margin>Soc.</margin>: What shall we do, Cratylus? Shall we count the names themselves like the votes of ballots? And shall we judge the correct reasoning of names by this rule, so that those are finally true for which the most significations of names vote?
<margin>Crat.</margin>: That is not fitting.
<margin>Soc.</margin>: Certainly not, friend. But leaving these things aside now, let us see whether you admit these things to us in that way, or not. Come, did we not a little while ago confess that those who imposed names in individual cities, both Greek and Barbarian, were <term>Onomatothetes <note>original: onomothetas</note></term>, that is, founders of names, and that the art which contained this faculty was the "founder of names"?
<margin>Crat.</margin>: Especially so.
<margin>Soc.</margin>: Now indeed, did the first onomatothetes establish the first names
<margin>E</margin>
knowing the things on which they were imposing names, or in ignorance?
<margin>Crat.</margin>: Knowing, as it indeed seems to me, Socrates.
<margin>Soc.</margin>: For they could not have done so in ignorance, friend Cratylus.
<margin>Crat.</margin>: Not in my opinion.
<margin>Soc.</margin>: Let us return to where we started. You said recently, if you remember, that it was necessary for him who established names to have foreknowledge of those things to which he granted names: do you still persist in that opinion, or not?
<margin>Crat.</margin>: Still.
<margin>Soc.</margin>: Do you say that even he who placed the first names knew them while he placed them?
<margin>Crat.</margin>: He knew them.
<margin>Soc.</margin>: From what names had he either learned or found the things out, when the first names had not yet been established? Since it has been said that it is impossible to either find or learn things unless we have learned what the names are, or have found them ourselves?
<margin>Crat.</margin>: You seem to me,
<margin>F</margin>
Socrates, to be saying something.
<margin>Soc.</margin>: In what way, then, shall we say they placed names while knowing? That founders of names existed before the placement of any name, and that they knew things beforehand, if indeed things cannot be learned otherwise than from names?
<margin>Crat.</margin>: I think indeed, Socrates, that the truest speech is that which says a certain power more excellent than human gave the first names to things, by which it was necessary that they were rightly distributed.
<margin>Soc.</margin>: Do you think the author of names—if some daemon or God existed—placed things contrary to himself? Or do we seem to have said nothing above?
<margin>Crat.</margin>: Perhaps the other set of these were not yet names.
<margin>Soc.</margin>: Which were they then, best of men? Those that turn toward
<margin>G</margin>
stability? Or those rather toward motion? For as we just said, it will not be judged by the multitude.
<margin>Crat.</margin>: So it is fitting, Socrates.
<margin>Soc.</margin>: Since names therefore disagree and contend with one another about the truth, and both these and those claim to be closer to the truth, by what rule shall we judge? Where shall we turn? For we shall not flee to other names, because there are none besides these. But certain other things besides names must be sought, which will show us without names which of these are true, namely, showing the truth of the things.
<margin>Crat.</margin>: So it seems to me.
<margin>Soc.</margin>: If these things are true, Cratylus, things can, as it seems, be perceived without names.
<margin>Crat.</margin>: It appears so.
<margin>Soc.</margin>: Through what else especially do you hope to perceive the things themselves? Is it not through what is agreeable and fitting? Through their mutual
<margin>H</margin>
communion, namely if they are in some way related to each other, and through the things themselves most of all. For that which is other than them signifies something else, not them.
<margin>Crat.</margin>: You seem to speak the truth.
<margin>Soc.</margin>: Tell me, I pray, have we not often conceded that names which are rightly placed are similar to those of which they are names, and are images of things?
<margin>Crat.</margin>: We have plainly conceded it.
<margin>Soc.</margin>: If therefore it is possible to learn things through names, and also through themselves, which will be the more excellent and clearer perception? To learn from the image and the image itself whether it be rightly expressed, and the truth of which this is an image?

<summary>Socrates argues that if language is the only way to learn about reality, the first "name-givers" could not have known what they were naming. He suggests that because names are contradictory (some implying motion and others rest), we must study reality directly through the things themselves rather than relying solely on words.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes Plato's Cratylus and begins the Gorgias. In the preceding text, Socrates and Cratylus discussed whether names accurately reflect the essence of things through their sounds. Socrates now moves to the ultimate philosophical question: whether reality is a constant "flux" of change or if there are stable, eternal Truths.</meta>

<page-num>280</page-num>
->OF PLATO<-

<margin>A</margin> [Socrates]: Or rather, if the truth itself and its image both arise from the truth, is it not more fitting that the image was established according to the truth?
CRATYLUS: It seems so to me, if it indeed comes from the truth.
SOCRATES: To judge the manner in which things must be understood, whether through instruction or discovery, is perhaps a greater task than for a mind like yours or mine. Let it suffice for us now to agree that things are to be learned and sought not from names, but rather from themselves.
CRATYLUS: So it appears, Socrates.
SOCRATES: Let us also consider this further: let not these many names, all tending toward the same point, deceive us—as if those who established them believed that all things are always running and flowing <note>original: ῥεόντων (rheontōn). This refers to the famous doctrine of Heraclitus that "everything flows."</note>, and established them with that consideration. Indeed, it seems to me they thought so; yet if such an opinion existed, it must be held as false. Truly, they have fallen as if into a whirlpool, and they themselves are wavering and tossed about, dragging us in and submerging us with them. Consider, wonderful Cratylus, what I often dream of: should we say there is something that is the <term>Beautiful itself <note>original: αὐτὸ τὸ καλὸν (auto to kalon); the "Form" or ideal essence of Beauty.</note></term> and the <term>Good itself</term>, and each of the things that exist in this way, or not?
CRATYLUS: It certainly seems so to me, Socrates.
SOCRATES: Let us then consider that very thing—not whether a certain face or something of that sort is beautiful, since all these things flow—but do we say that the Beautiful itself always remains such as it is?
CRATYLUS: It must be so.
SOCRATES: Is it possible to name it correctly if it always escapes, saying first what it is, and then what kind of thing it is? Or is it necessary that, while we are speaking, it immediately becomes something else and flees away, and is no longer the same?
CRATYLUS: It is necessary.
SOCRATES: In what way then will that thing exist, which never stays in the same state?
<margin>C</margin> For if it ever stays in the same state, it is clear that in that time in which it stays so, it does not change at all. But if it always stays in the same state and exists as the same, how could it transition or move, since it does not abandon its own <term>Idea <note>original: ἰδέας (ideas); the eternal blueprint or Form.</note></term>?
CRATYLUS: In no way.
SOCRATES: Furthermore, it could be known by no one. For while the power of knowing approached it, it would become something else and foreign; therefore, what it is or of what kind could not be known. For no knowledge perceives a thing in such a way that it perceives it as having no state at all.
CRATYLUS: It is as you say.
SOCRATES: But neither should we affirm that knowledge itself exists, Cratylus, if all things fall away and nothing remains. For if knowledge does not fall away from being knowledge, it will always remain, and will always be knowledge. But if the very form of knowledge departs, it will simultaneously fall into another form of knowledge, and it will not be knowledge.
<margin>D</margin> If it perpetually migrates, it will never be knowledge. And by this reasoning, neither that which is to know, nor that which is to be known, will ever exist. But if that which knows always exists, and that which is known exists, and the Beautiful exists, and the Good exists, and finally each of the things that exist, which we are now discussing, then they do not seem to me to be like a flux or a current. Now, whether these things are so, or as the followers of Heraclitus and many others say, is not easily discerned. Nor is it the part of a man of very sound mind to entrust himself and his soul to names, and to assert that the author of names was wise, and thus to think so poorly of all things as to believe nothing is whole or firm, but that all things flow and collapse like earthenware, and to judge that things are affected just as men suffering from <term>rheum <note>original: κατάῤῥῳ (katarrhō); a "runny nose" or discharge, used here as a metaphor for the universe "leaking" or "flowing" away.</note></term> of the head,
<margin>E</margin> so that all things are gripped by discharge and flux. Perhaps, Cratylus, it is so, and perhaps it is otherwise; therefore, the matter must be investigated with a brave spirit and diligent study, for one must not easily give assent. You are still young, and this age is sufficient for you. And if you find anything in your searching, you ought to share it with me as well.
CRATYLUS: I will do my best, Socrates. And know for certain that even now I am not idle; rather, to me as I think and revolve many things in my mind, it seems much more as Heraclitus says than as you were saying.
SOCRATES: Then later, my friend, after you have returned, teach me. But now, as you have decided, go into the countryside. And Hermogenes here will accompany you.
CRATYLUS: It shall be as you advise, Socrates. But you also, try now to think on these things.

<column-break/>

[Socrates]: ...or an image? Or if it is from the truth, is it not the case that both it and its image are correctly fashioned?
CRATYLUS: It seems to me that it must be from the truth.
SOCRATES: Therefore, the manner in which one must learn or discover existing things is perhaps a greater task to know than for me or you. But it is pleasing to agree on this: that not from names, but much rather from the things themselves, must they be learned and sought.
CRATYLUS: It appears so, Socrates.
SOCRATES: Furthermore, let us consider this: that these many names tending toward the same thing do not deceive us, even if those who established them did so because they thought all things were always going and flowing. For they seem to me to have thought so themselves.
<margin>B</margin> But if it happens that it is not so, then these men themselves, as if falling into some whirlpool, are stirred up and, dragging us along, throw us in too. For look, wonderful Cratylus, at what I often dream: do we say there is some "Beautiful itself" and "Good itself," and each one of the things that exist in this way, or not?
CRATYLUS: It seems so to me, Socrates, that there is.
SOCRATES: Let us then consider that very thing: not if some face is beautiful, or some such thing, for all these seem to flow; but the Beautiful itself, is it not always such as it is?
CRATYLUS: Necessarily.
SOCRATES: Is it then possible to address it correctly, if it is always passing away—first that it is *that*, then that it is *of such a kind*? Or is it necessary that, at the same moment we are speaking, it immediately becomes something else and passes away, and no longer holds its state?
CRATYLUS: Necessarily.
SOCRATES: How then could that be something which never stays the same?
<margin>C</margin> For if it ever stays the same, in that time it is clear that nothing changes. And if it is always the same and is the same thing, how could this change or move, never departing from its own form?
CRATYLUS: In no way.
SOCRATES: But surely it would not be known by anyone. For at the same time the knower approached it, it would become something else and of a different kind. So it would no longer be known what it is or how it is. And surely no knowledge knows that which it knows if it has no state at all.
CRATYLUS: It is as you say.
SOCRATES: But it is not likely that knowledge even exists, Cratylus, if all things are shifting and nothing remains. For if this very thing, knowledge, does not shift from being knowledge, then knowledge would always remain and be knowledge. But if the very form of knowledge shifts, it would simultaneously shift into another form of knowledge, and there would be no knowledge. If it is always shifting, there would always be no knowledge. And from this argument, neither the thing known nor the knower would exist.
<margin>D</margin> But if that which knows is always there, and that which is known is there, and the Beautiful is there, and the Good is there, and each of the things that exist is there, then it does not seem to me that these things we are now talking about are like a flux or a current. Whether these things are so, or in that way which the followers of Heraclitus and many others say, is not easy to examine. Nor is it the part of a very sensible man to entrust himself and his own soul to the care of names, trusting them and those who established them, asserting they know something; and to condemn himself and all existing things as if nothing were sound, but all things flow like earthenware, and just as men sick with rheum, to think that things are also so disposed:
<margin>E</margin> that all matters are held by a current and discharge. Perhaps then, Cratylus, it is so, and perhaps not. Therefore, one must look into it bravely and well, and not accept it easily. (For you are still young and have the age for it). And when you have looked, if you find it, share it with me too.
CRATYLUS: I will do these things. Know well, Socrates, that even now I am not without consideration; but to me, as I look and take trouble, it seems much more to be in that way which Heraclitus says.
SOCRATES: Another time then, my friend, you shall teach me when you have come back; but now, as you have prepared, go into the country; and Hermogenes here will also send you on your way.
CRATYLUS: These things shall be, Socrates; but you too, try to keep thinking on these things now.

# GORGIAS, OR, ON RHETORIC.
### Established for the purpose of refuting or overturning.

<column-break/>

# GORGIAS, OR, ON RHETORIC.
### Refutatory. <note>original: Ἀνατρεπικός (Anatreptikos); a term used by ancient editors to classify the dialogue's primary goal.</note>

---

### S U M M A R Y  O F  T H E  D I A L O G U E.

*Rhetoric is the subject here, both so that the inventions introduced into this art by the Sophists may be refuted, and so that its true nature may be taught. Therefore, the word **Refutatory** <note>original: ἀνατρεπικός (anatreptikos)</note> added to the title shows to what extent Plato primarily intends to deal with Rhetoric here: namely, to teach how wrongly the Sophists abuse Rhetoric; for they understood neither its true definition nor its true use: that is, neither its nature, nor the subject in which it is properly engaged, nor the end to which it ought to be directed. This refutation is contained in these two main points. Thus far, Plato condemns Rhetoric—not all Rhetoric simply, but that which was handed down by the Sophists and used by the majority of those men involved in the republic. Although he by no means hands down the precepts of Rhetoric as if repeating them from the very cradle of the art, he nevertheless teaches the true and genuine method of properly constructing a speech: namely, the use of Rhetoric without which it can in no way exist. Therefore, the thesis of this disputation is twofold: first, that it may overturn the phantoms of the Sophists, by which they would forge the name of Rhetoricians and sell their own smoke to the people under that beautiful title, while clearly perverting the true nature and true use of Rhetoric. The other part of the disputation is engaged in teaching, and teaches its nature from the opposite side. For as much as he takes away from that flattering Rhetoric, so much does he grant to that which he calls true and genuine.*

It then introduces the Gorgias, a dialogue focused on refuting the Sophists' empty rhetoric in favor of a true, ethical art of speech.</summary>

## CALLICLES, SOCRATES, CHAEREPHON, GORGIAS, POLUS.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'P' featuring leafy vine patterns in a square frame.</image-desc> **P**eople say, Socrates, that this is the way one should take part in war and battle <note>original: ΠOΛEMOY (Polemon). This is a play on words, as the dialogue begins with a reference to war, though they are attending a peaceful lecture.</note>. SOCRATES: Have we then, as the saying goes, arrived "after the feast" <note>An ancient Greek proverb meaning to arrive too late for the main event.</note> and missed out? CALLICLES: And a very charming feast it was indeed! For Gorgias has just recently finished giving us many beautiful demonstrations. SOCRATES: Truly, Callicles, the fault lies with Chaerephon here, who forced us to linger in the marketplace. CHAEREPHON: It is no matter, Socrates; for I will also provide the remedy. Since Gorgias is a friend of mine, he will give us a demonstration—now, if you like, or if you prefer, at another time. CALLICLES: What is this, Chaerephon? Does Socrates really desire to hear Gorgias? CHAEREPHON: That is the very reason we are here. CALLICLES: Then whenever you wish to come to my home—for Gorgias is staying with me—he will give a demonstration for you. SOCRATES: You speak well, Callicles. But would he be willing to converse with us? For I wish to learn from him what the power of the man’s <term>art <note>original: τέχνη (techne); meaning a craft, skill, or specialized system of knowledge.</note></term> is, and what it is that he professes and teaches. As for the rest of his demonstration, let him put it off until another time, as you suggest. CALLICLES: There is nothing like asking the man himself, Socrates. For that was one of the features of his demonstration. Just now, he invited everyone in the room to ask whatever they wished, and he said he would answer everything. SOCRATES: Truly, you speak well. Chaerephon, ask him. CHAEREPHON: What shall I ask? SOCRATES: Ask him who he is. CHAEREPHON: What do you mean? SOCRATES: Just as if he were a maker of shoes, he would surely answer you that he is a <term>cobbler <note>original: σκυτοτόμος (skytotomos). Socrates often uses humble professions to illustrate how a true "art" must have a specific subject matter.</note></term>. Or do you not understand what I mean? CHAEREPHON: I understand, and I will ask. Tell me, Gorgias, is what Callicles says true—that you profess to answer whatever anyone asks you? GORGIAS: It is true, Chaerephon. Indeed, I was just now making that very claim, and I say that no one has asked me anything new in many years. CHAEREPHON: Surely then you will answer easily, Gorgias. GORGIAS: You may make trial of that, Chaerephon. POLUS: By Zeus! If you wish, Chaerephon, try me instead. For Gorgias seems to me to be exhausted, as he has just now spoken at great length. CHAEREPHON: What, Polus? Do you think you can answer better than Gorgias? POLUS: What does that matter, so long as it is enough for you? CHAEREPHON: Not at all; since you wish it, answer. POLUS: Ask. CHAEREPHON: I am asking then: if Gorgias were skilled in the same art as his brother Herodicus, what would we rightly call him? Would it not be the same name as his brother? POLUS: Certainly. CHAEREPHON: Then we would speak correctly in calling him a physician? POLUS: Yes. CHAEREPHON: And if he were experienced in the art of Aristophon, son of Aglaophon, or his brother, what would we rightly call him? POLUS: Clearly, a painter. CHAEREPHON: But as it is, since he is skilled in some art, what should we call him to name him correctly? POLUS: O Chaerephon, there are many arts among men that have been discovered through experience. For experience makes our life proceed according to art, while inexperience leaves it to proceed according to chance. Of these arts, different men partake in different ways, and the best men partake of the best; among these is Gorgias here, who partakes in the most beautiful of the arts. SOCRATES: It seems, Gorgias, that Polus is well-prepared for making speeches; but he is not doing what he promised Chaerephon. GORGIAS: How so, Socrates? SOCRATES: He does not seem to me to be answering the question that was asked. GORGIAS: Then you, if you wish, ask him yourself. SOCRATES: No, not if you yourself are willing to answer. I would much rather ask you. For it is clear to me from what Polus has said that he has practiced the thing called <term>rhetoric <note>The art of persuasive speaking.</note></term> more than the art of dialogue. POLUS: Why so, Socrates? SOCRATES: Because, Polus, when Chaerephon asked what art Gorgias is skilled in, you praised his art as if someone were blaming it, but you did not say what it actually is. POLUS: Did I not answer that it was the most beautiful? SOCRATES: Indeed you did. But no one asked what the quality of Gorgias’s art was, but rather what it was, and what one ought to call Gorgias. Just as Chaerephon put the previous examples to you, and you answered him beautifully and briefly, speak now in the same way: what is the art, and what should we call Gorgias? Or rather, Gorgias, you tell us yourself: what should we call you, and in what art are you skilled? GORGIAS: Rhetoric, Socrates. SOCRATES: So we should call you an orator? GORGIAS: A good one, Socrates, if you wish to call me what I "boast myself to be," as Homer said. SOCRATES: I do wish it. GORGIAS: Then call me so. SOCRATES: And shall we say that you are able to make others so as well? GORGIAS: That is exactly what I profess, not only here, but elsewhere too. SOCRATES: Would you then be willing, Gorgias, to continue the way we are now conversing—questioning and answering—and put off until later this length of speech that Polus began? Do not fail in what you promised, but be willing to answer the question briefly. GORGIAS: There are some answers, Socrates, that necessarily require a long speech; nevertheless, I will try to be as brief as possible. For this is also one of my claims: that no one can say the same things

<margin>The occasion for the dialogue.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'S' featuring a figure seated in a landscape setting with trees and foliage, enclosed in a square border.</image-desc>**S**o to war and battle when one goes, O Socrates, they say one should delay. <margin>Proverb: We have come too late, after the feast.</margin> SOCRATES: Have we indeed come after the feast, as is commonly said, and are we present too late? B CALLICLES: What, O Chaerephon? Does Socrates desire to hear Gorgias? CHAEREPHON: It was for that very purpose that we were present. SOCRATES: Indeed, O Gorgias, Polus seems to be well-instructed for speaking.

GORGIAS: But you, if you wish, ask him again. SOCRATES: If you, Gorgias, would not disdain to answer me, I would inquire of yourself more willingly than of Polus. GORGIAS: There are indeed, O Socrates, certain answers which must necessarily be carried out in longer words; nevertheless, I will take care that you are answered as briefly as possible.
