# PLATO

...to be able to explain the same thing. **SOCRATES**: I have need of this brevity, Gorgias, and I pray that you might offer me an example of it; as for your abundance of words, put that off for another time. **GORGIAS**: Indeed, I shall do so, so that you may say you have never heard anyone more brief than me. **SOCRATES**: Come then, you say you possess the knowledge of the rhetorical <term>art <note>original Latin: *rhetoricæ artis*; Greek: *τέχνης* (techne). In ancient philosophy, a techne is a systematic craft or body of knowledge applied to a specific goal.</note></term>, and that you are able to make others into rhetoricians. Now, rhetoric itself is concerned with something, just as weaving is concerned with the manufacture of clothing. Is it not so? **GORGIAS**: It is. **SOCRATES**: And is not music concerned with the perfection of melody?
<margin>Music is concerned with the perfection of melody.</margin>
**GORGIAS**: It is. **SOCRATES**: By Jove <note>original: *Per Iouem*; a Latinization of the Greek oath "By Hera."</note>, Gorgias, these answers of yours delight me wonderfully, since you complete them with such brevity. **GORGIAS**: I hope I shall satisfy you in this wish of yours. **SOCRATES**: You say well. But answer similarly regarding rhetoric: what exactly is it the science of?
<margin>A bad first definition.</margin>
**GORGIAS**: Of speeches <note>original: *Sermonum*; Greek: *λόγους* (logos). This term can mean words, speeches, or rational arguments.</note>. **SOCRATES**: Of what kind of speeches, Gorgias? Is it those which show by what manner of diet the sick might recover? **GORGIAS**: No. **SOCRATES**: Then rhetoric is not concerned with all speeches. **GORGIAS**: Not at all. **SOCRATES**: Nevertheless, it is concerned with those that provide the faculty of speaking. **GORGIAS**: Yes. **SOCRATES**: And does rhetoric provide the power of understanding in the same matters in which it provides the power of speaking? **GORGIAS**: Why not? **SOCRATES**: Does not medicine, of which we were just speaking, make us able both to understand and to discourse upon the treatment of the sick? **GORGIAS**: It must. **SOCRATES**: And medicine therefore, it appears, is concerned with speeches. **GORGIAS**: It is so. **SOCRATES**: Namely, those pertaining to diseases. **GORGIAS**: Exactly. **SOCRATES**: And is not gymnastics also about speeches concerning the good or bad condition of bodies? **GORGIAS**: Certainly. **SOCRATES**: And so it is with other arts, Gorgias, by the same reasoning. For each of them is concerned with the speeches held regarding the matter in which that art is usually occupied. **GORGIAS**: It appears so. **SOCRATES**: Why then do you not call the other arts "rhetorical," since they are concerned with speeches? If, indeed, you define rhetoric as that which is concerned with speeches. **GORGIAS**: Because, Socrates, all the science of the other arts is concerned with manual works and actions of this kind, so to speak. But for rhetoric, there is no such manual work; rather, all its action and power consists in speaking. For this reason, I judge rhetoric to be the art concerned with speeches, and I affirm that I speak correctly. **SOCRATES**: I understand what you wish to call it; perhaps I shall comprehend it more clearly soon. But answer: we have arts, do we not? **GORGIAS**: We do. **SOCRATES**: From the whole number of arts, I think some are those which are mostly occupied with work, and require very few words; while others require none, but can even be perfected through silence: such as the art of painting, and sculpture, and many others. You seem to deny that rhetoric is of this number. **GORGIAS**: You take my meaning very well, Socrates. **SOCRATES**: Furthermore, there are other arts that perform everything through words, and have need of either no work, so to speak, or certainly very little. Such is arithmetic, calculation, geometry, and the game of dice and tables, and many other arts; in some of these, the words almost equal the actions, while in most, they exceed them, and all their action and power consists entirely in such words. You seem to me to say that rhetoric is something of this kind. **GORGIAS**: You speak the truth. **SOCRATES**: Yet I do not think you call any of these "rhetoric," although you said in word that the art having power in speaking is rhetoric. For if someone wished to be a caviller <note>A person who raises petty or trivial objections.</note>, he might take up the argument thus: "So, do you call arithmetic rhetoric, Gorgias?" But I do not think you call either arithmetic or geometry rhetoric. **GORGIAS**: You think truly, Socrates, and you grasp what I say correctly. **SOCRATES**: Come, now you also complete the answer I was seeking: since rhetoric is of the number of those arts that mostly use words, and there are others of this kind, try to express to us which art rhetoric is, and upon what subject it has its chief power in speaking. For instance, if someone should ask me about the arts I mentioned above, what arithmetic is called, I would answer as you just did, that it is one of those arts whose faculty is in words. And if he should ask again, "With what is it concerned?" I would say it is concerned with the knowledge of even and odd, and how many there are of each. Furthermore, if he asked again what I call the art of calculation, I will answer that this also is numbered among those arts whose whole faculty is placed in words. If he asks again what it is concerned with, I will answer in the manner of those who write decrees in the assembly: that in other respects, calculation differs not at all from arithmetic. Indeed, both are concerned with the same thing, namely the even and the odd; but they are dissimilar in this: that calculation considers how even and odd relate to themselves and to each other in terms of total quantity. Furthermore, if I were saying that astronomy is placed in that class of arts whose faculty is seen entirely in words, and someone asked again, "Toward what do the words of astronomy chiefly tend?" I would reply: "Toward the motion of the stars, the sun, and the moon, and how their courses relate to one another." **GORGIAS**: You would answer rightly indeed, Socrates. **SOCRATES**: Come then, you also, Gorgias. Certainly rhetoric is one of those arts that treat and perfect everything by word. Is it not? **GORGIAS**: Certainly. **SOCRATES**: Tell us then: what is it, of all things, which is the subject of these speeches used by rhetoric? **GORGIAS**: The greatest and best of human affairs, Socrates.

<column-break/>

**SOCRATES**: ...this same thing in brevity. **SOCRATES**: This is indeed necessary, Gorgias; and please provide me with a demonstration of this very thing, this brevity; as for long-windedness, save it for another time. **GORGIAS**: I shall do so; and you will say you have heard no one speak more briefly. **SOCRATES**: Come then (since you say you are an expert in the rhetorical art, and can make another a rhetorician): rhetoric happens to be about what existing thing? Just as weaving is about the making of clothes, is it not? **GORGIAS**: Yes. **SOCRATES**: And music about the making of melodies? **GORGIAS**: Yes. **SOCRATES**: By Hera, Gorgias, I admire your answers, because you answer in the briefest possible way. **GORGIAS**: Indeed, Socrates, I think I do this quite well. **SOCRATES**: You speak well. Come then, answer me in this way about rhetoric: what existing thing is it the knowledge of? **GORGIAS**: Speeches. **SOCRATES**: What kind of speeches, Gorgias? Is it those that show the sick how they might become healthy through their diet? **GORGIAS**: No. **SOCRATES**: Then rhetoric is not about all speeches. **GORGIAS**: Certainly not. **SOCRATES**: But it does make men able to speak? **GORGIAS**: Yes. **SOCRATES**: And also to think about what they say? **GORGIAS**: How could it not? **SOCRATES**: Does not medicine then, and also gymnastics, make men able to think and speak about the things they say? **GORGIAS**: Necessarily. **SOCRATES**: And medicine, then, it seems, is about speeches. **GORGIAS**: Yes. **SOCRATES**: Those regarding diseases? **GORGIAS**: Most certainly. **SOCRATES**: And is not gymnastics about speeches regarding the good and bad condition of bodies? **GORGIAS**: Quite so. **SOCRATES**: And indeed, the other arts, Gorgias, are the same; each of them is about those speeches that happen to be about the thing which each art is. **GORGIAS**: So it appears. **SOCRATES**: Why then do you not call the others "rhetorical," since they are about speeches, if indeed you call rhetoric that which is about speeches? **GORGIAS**: Because, Socrates, for the other arts, the knowledge is entirely about manual work and such actions (so to speak); but for rhetoric there is no such manual work, but all its action and authority is through speeches. For these reasons, I deem the rhetorical art to be about speeches; speaking correctly, as I claim. **SOCRATES**: Do I then understand what you wish to call it? Soon I shall know more clearly. But answer me: we have arts, do we not? **GORGIAS**: Yes. **SOCRATES**: Of all the arts, I think, for some the work is the main part, and they need few words; some need none at all, but the goal of the art is achieved through silence, such as painting and sculpture, and many others. It seems to me you are speaking of such arts when you say rhetoric is not among them. Is that not so? **GORGIAS**: You understand quite well, Socrates. **SOCRATES**: But there are other arts that achieve everything through speech, and require (so to speak) either no work or very little; such as arithmetic and calculation, and geometry, and even the game of draughts, and many other arts; in some of these the speeches are almost equal to the actions, and in many they are more; and altogether all their action and authority is through speeches. You seem to me to call rhetoric one of these. **GORGIAS**: You speak the truth. **SOCRATES**: But I do not think you wish to call any of these "rhetoric"; not that you said so in your phrase, "that which has its authority through speech is rhetoric"; and one might suppose, if he wished to be difficult in his words, "So, Gorgias, are you calling arithmetic rhetoric?" But I do not think you call either arithmetic or geometry rhetoric. **GORGIAS**: You think rightly, Socrates, and you understand correctly. **SOCRATES**: Come then, you also complete the answer I asked. Since rhetoric happens to be one of these arts that uses speech a great deal, and there happen to be others of this kind, try to say what rhetoric has its authority over in speeches. Just as if someone asked me about any of the arts I just mentioned: "Socrates, what is the art of arithmetic?" I would tell him, as you just did, that it is one of those that have their whole authority through speech. And if he asked me further, "About what?" I would say it is the knowledge of the even and the odd, and how many of each there happen to be. If he asked again, "And what do you call the art of calculation?" I would say that this too is one of those that are entirely authorized by speech. And if he asked further "About what?" I would say, like those who write motions in the assembly, that in other respects calculation is like arithmetic (for it is about the same thing, the even and the odd); but it differs in this much, that calculation examines how the even and the odd relate to themselves and to one another in quantity. And if someone asked about astronomy, when I said that it too is authorized entirely by speech, "But what are the speeches of astronomy about?" I would say, Socrates, I would say that they are about the motion of the stars, and the sun and the moon, and how they relate to one another in speed. **GORGIAS**: You would be speaking rightly, Socrates. **SOCRATES**: Come then, you too, Gorgias. For rhetoric happens to be one of those things that perform and authorize everything through speech. Is that not so? **GORGIAS**: It is. **SOCRATES**: Say then, what is it among existing things that these speeches, which rhetoric uses, are about? **GORGIAS**: The greatest of human affairs, Socrates, and the best.

<summary>In this segment of the dialogue, Socrates uses his characteristic method of inquiry to force Gorgias to move past a vague definition of rhetoric as "the art of speeches," noting that many specialized arts like medicine and arithmetic also rely on speech. Gorgias eventually defines rhetoric's unique domain as the mastery of the "greatest and best" of human affairs.</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Gorgias, rhetoric, dialectic, definition of art, techne, logos, arithmetic, calculation, human affairs</keywords>

# GORGIAS
Aa iiij

SOCRATES: But, Gorgias, this which you say is still debatable and not yet clear. For I think you have heard people at banquets singing that famous drinking song <note>original: "skolion" (Greek) / "cantilena" (Latin). A song sung by guests at a banquet while passing a lyre or branch.</note> in which the singers list the best things: first, to be healthy; second, to be beautiful; and third (as the poet of the song says), to be wealthy without deceit. GORGIAS: I have indeed heard it; but why do you mention this? SOCRATES: Because the craftsmen of these things praised by the poet—the physician, the trainer, and the money-maker—would immediately confront you. First, the physician would say: "Socrates, Gorgias is deceiving you. His art is not concerned with the greatest good for mankind; mine is." If I then asked him, "Who are you to say this?" he would likely say he is a physician. "What then? Do you say the work of your art is the greatest good?" "How could I not," he would perhaps say, "Socrates, since its work is health? What greater good is there for men than health?" And if after him the trainer should say: "I would be amazed, Socrates, if Gorgias could show you a greater good in his art than I can in mine." I would ask him in turn: "And you, man, who are you? What is your work?" "I am a trainer," he would say, "and my work is to make the bodies of men beautiful and strong." Following the trainer, the money-maker <note>original: "chrematistes" (Greek) / "nummator" (Latin). A person whose profession is the acquisition of wealth or finance.</note> would say, I imagine, looking down on everyone else: "Consider then, Socrates, if any good appears greater to you than wealth, whether it comes from Gorgias or anyone else." We would then say to him: "What is this? Are you the creator of this good?" He would say he is. "Who are you then?" "A money-maker." "Well? Do you judge wealth to be the greatest good?" "Of course," he will say. "And yet," we would say, "Gorgias here contends that his art is the cause of a greater good than yours." It is clear, then, that he would next ask: "And what is this good? Let Gorgias answer." Come then, Gorgias, imagine you are being questioned by them and by me; answer: what is this which you say is the greatest good for mankind, of which you are the creator?

GORGIAS: That which is, in truth, Socrates, the greatest good: the cause of freedom for men themselves, and at the same time the cause of each man being able to rule over others in his own city. SOCRATES: What then do you say this is?

GORGIAS: I mean the ability to persuade with words: to persuade the judges in the law court, the senators in the council, the citizens in the assembly, and in any other gathering which is a political gathering. And yet, with this power, you will have the physician as your slave, and the trainer as your slave; and this money-maker will be seen to be making money not for himself, but for another—for you, who have the power to speak and to persuade the multitudes. SOCRATES: Now you seem to me, Gorgias, to have shown most closely what kind of art you think rhetoric to be; and I think I have grasped it: that rhetoric is a creator of persuasion, and its entire practice and sum-total ends in this. Or can you say that rhetoric has any power beyond creating persuasion in the souls of the listeners? GORGIAS: Not at all, Socrates; you seem to me to have defined it sufficiently. For that is indeed its sum-total. SOCRATES: Listen then, Gorgias. For be assured that if anyone else disputes with another wanting to know the very thing the discussion is about, I believe myself to be such a person; and I judge you to be the same. GORGIAS: What then, Socrates? SOCRATES: I will tell you. I do not clearly know what kind of persuasion you say comes from rhetoric, or what matters it concerns—though I have a suspicion of what I think you mean and about what. Nevertheless, I will ask you what you say this persuasion from rhetoric is and what it is about. And why do I ask you when I already have a suspicion? Not for your sake, but for the sake of the argument, so that it may proceed in a way that makes the subject of our speech as clear as possible. Consider if I seem to be questioning you rightly. Just as if I happened to be asking you which of the painters Zeuxis <note>A famous Greek painter from the 5th century BCE, known for his realism.</note> was, and you told me "the one who paints animals," would I not rightly ask you, "what kind of animals does he paint, and in what way?" GORGIAS: Certainly. SOCRATES: And is this not because there are other painters who paint many other animals? GORGIAS: Yes. SOCRATES: But if no one else but Zeuxis painted, your answer would have been correct. GORGIAS: Of course. SOCRATES: Come then, speak also concerning rhetoric. Does it seem to you that rhetoric alone creates persuasion, or do other arts as well? I mean this: does whoever teaches anything persuade people of what he teaches, or not? GORGIAS: He certainly persuades them, Socrates, more than anyone. SOCRATES: Again, let us speak of the same arts we just mentioned. Does not arithmetic, and the arithmetician, teach us all that belongs to number? GORGIAS: Certainly. SOCRATES: Does it not also persuade? GORGIAS: Yes. SOCRATES: Therefore arithmetic is also a creator of persuasion. GORGIAS: It appears so. SOCRATES: Then if someone asks us what kind of persuasion and about what, we shall answer him that it is the teaching kind concerning the even and the odd, and how many there are of each. We could likewise show that all the other arts we just mentioned are creators of persuasion, and of what kind, and about what. Is it not so? GORGIAS: Yes. SOCRATES: Therefore rhetoric is not the only creator of persuasion.

<column-break/>

SOCR. But this too is ambiguous, Gorgias, and not clear in any way. I think indeed that you have heard that song which is sung in circles at banquets, in which the singers list things thus: The best of all things is to have prosperous health; <margin>The best is to be healthy.</margin> Second, an excellent form; <margin>Second, to be beautiful.</margin> Third, wealth, to use the words of the poet himself, acquired without fraud. <margin>Third, to have wealth acquired without fraud.</margin> GOR. I have heard it indeed: but to what purpose is this? SOCR. Because suddenly the craftsmen of the things praised in that song would encounter you: namely the physician, the trainer, and the money-maker. And first, the physician would immediately say: "Gorgias deceives you, O Socrates. For his art does not look to the greatest good of men, but mine does." Whereupon, if I were to ask him who he himself is, he would say perhaps that he is a physician. "What do you say then? Is the work of your art the greatest good?" "Why not?" he would respond: "since its work is health, and nothing is more excellent than health." After this, perhaps the trainer would greatly wonder if you could prove there is more good in your art than in his. If I asked him: "And you, who are you? What is your work?" "I am a trainer," he would say: "and it is my profession to make the bodies of men beautiful and strong." Then the money-maker or businessman, despising the others, I think, would object thus: "Observe, Socrates, whether you think any good is more excellent than riches, either with Gorgias or with anyone else." I would ask him in this manner: "Are you then the author of such a great good?" He would truly affirm he is. "Who are you then?" "I am a money-maker." "What then? Do you think the highest good for men is riches?" "Why wouldn't I think so?" he will say. I would then reply: "Yet this Gorgias here contends that his art is the cause of a greater good than yours." It is certain, therefore, that he will ask next: "What is that good? Let Gorgias himself demonstrate it." Therefore, come my Gorgias, imagine yourself to be questioned both by them and by me, and answer: what is that which you yourself judge to be the greatest good for men, and of which you profess yourself to be the author? GOR. That which is, O Socrates, the greatest good in reality, and the cause both that men retain their freedom, and that each one retains command and power in his own city over his own people. SOCR. What then do you say this is? GOR. To be able to persuade: both judges in a trial, and senators in the Senate, and listeners in an assembly, and in any other civil gathering. Now indeed, by this kind of faculty, the physician will serve you, the trainer will serve you: and even the money-maker himself will be found to have accumulated his riches not for himself, but for another—that is, for you, who are endowed with the art of speaking and of persuading the crowd. SOCR. Now you seem to me to have shown most closely what art you judge rhetoric to be. <margin>Another bad definition of Rhetoric.</margin> And if I understand you rightly, you say rhetoric is the creator of the art of persuasion, and that all its diligence and its sum-total is limited to this. Or have you anything further that you can relate concerning the faculty of this art, other than that it brings persuasion to the minds of the listeners? GOR. I have nothing else, Socrates; but you seem to me to have defined it abundantly. For this is its sum-total. SOCR. Listen, O Gorgias: be assured that if anyone else disputes with another, wishing to know that very thing about which they differ, I too, as I persuade myself, am such a person. Moreover, I judge that you also are so disposed. GOR. To what purpose is this? SOCR. I will say now: I do not yet know clearly enough what that persuasion is which you say proceeds from rhetoricians, or about what things it is. And although I may suspect what you intend to say and about what, I nonetheless ask of you what you say persuasion is and about what things it is made by rhetoric. But I ask this of you, even though I already suspect the cause of this thing, rather than expressing it myself: certainly not for your sake, but for the sake of the discourse itself, so that it may proceed in such a way that it explains to us most clearly that which is being discussed. <margin>A transition in the debate.</margin> Attend therefore whether I seem to ask you rightly again. Just as if I had asked who of the painters is Zeuxis: and you had responded "the one painting animals": would I not rightly ask, what kind of animals especially, and in what manner does he paint them? GOR. Quite rightly. SOCR. Is it not because there are also other painters, similarly painting many other animals? GOR. For that very reason. SOCR. But if no one else besides Zeuxis painted, you would have responded rightly in every way. GOR. Why not? SOCR. Come then, tell me also concerning rhetoric: whether this alone seems to persuade, or other arts as well. I mean something of this sort: whoever teaches anything, does he also persuade of that which he teaches, or not? GOR. He persuades, and most of all, O Socrates. SOCR. But again, let us consider in those same arts which we mentioned a little before. Does not Arithmetic teach whatever pertains to number; and the arithmetician likewise? GOR. Without a doubt. SOCR. Does it not also persuade? GOR. Certainly. SOCR. Therefore Arithmetic also effects persuasion. GOR. It appears so. SOCR. Furthermore, if someone were to ask what persuasion, and concerning what it effects it, we shall answer, namely the instructional kind concerning the even and the odd, and how many of each there are. We could similarly show the other arts which we just mentioned to be creators of persuasion, and of what and concerning what especially, could we not? GOR. Yes. SOCR. Wherefore rhetoric is not the only creator of persuasion.

<summary>Socrates challenges Gorgias to define the "greatest good" of rhetoric, leading Gorgias to define it as the "creator of persuasion" in political and legal settings. Socrates counters that many other arts, such as arithmetic, also produce persuasion within their own specific fields of knowledge.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and the famous orator Gorgias. # OF PLATO

<page-num>284</page-num>

<margin>A</margin> GORGIAS: You speak the truth. SOCRATES: Since, then, it is not the only art that does this, but others do as well, would it not be a fair question—just as we asked about the painter—to ask next about rhetoric: what kind of persuasion is it, and what is its subject matter? Does that seem like a fair question to you? GORGIAS: It does to me. SOCRATES: Answer then, <margin>B</margin> Gorgias, since it seems so to you. GORGIAS: I say, Socrates, that rhetoric is the mistress of that persuasion which takes place in courts of law and other gatherings, as I was saying just now, and it concerns matters of what is just and unjust. SOCRATES: I also suspected that you meant this kind of persuasion and these subjects, Gorgias. But so that you are not surprised if I ask you something similar again shortly—which might seem obvious, yet I ask it anyway—I do so, as I said, for the sake of completing the argument in its proper order. I do this so we do not get into the habit of guessing and snatching away each other’s words before they are finished; rather, you should complete your argument according to your own plan. GORGIAS: You seem to be acting quite rightly, Socrates. SOCRATES: Come then, let us consider this: do you call something "to have learned"? GORGIAS: I do. SOCRATES: And again, "to have believed"? GORGIAS: I do. SOCRATES: Do you think that learning and believing are the same thing, and that knowledge and belief <note>original: "disciplinam atque credulitatem" (Latin) / "mathēsis kai pistis" (Greek). Here, Socrates distinguishes between "knowledge" (which is always true) and "conviction/belief" (which can be true or false).</note> are the same, or are they different? GORGIAS: I certainly think they are different. <margin>C</margin> SOCRATES: You think correctly. You can tell from this: if someone asked you, "Is there such a thing as a false belief and a true belief?" you would say yes, I imagine. GORGIAS: Certainly. SOCRATES: But what about knowledge? Is there "false knowledge" and "true knowledge"? GORGIAS: Not at all. SOCRATES: It is clear, then, that they are not the same. GORGIAS: That is clear. SOCRATES: Nevertheless, both those who have learned and those who have believed have been persuaded. <margin>Persuasion is of two kinds. It is concluded that Rhetoric only creates belief, not teaching.</margin> GORGIAS: That is so. SOCRATES: Would you like us, then, to establish two types of persuasion: one which provides belief without knowledge, and another which provides knowledge? GORGIAS: By all means. SOCRATES: Which of these two types of persuasion does rhetoric produce in courts and other gatherings concerning just and unjust things? Is it the kind from which men believe without knowledge, or the kind from which they know? <margin>D</margin> GORGIAS: It is clear, Socrates, that it is the kind from which listeners are led to believe. SOCRATES: Therefore, as it seems, rhetoric is a craftsman of the persuasion that provides belief rather than instruction <note>original: "doctrinam" (Latin) / "didaskalikēs" (Greek). This is a central point in the dialogue: rhetoric makes people feel they understand something without actually giving them the underlying truth or expertise.</note> regarding the just or unjust. GORGIAS: Certainly. SOCRATES: An orator, then, does not teach courts and other crowds about just and unjust things, but merely induces belief. For he could not teach such a large crowd about such great matters in so short a time. GORGIAS: No, certainly not. SOCRATES: Come now, let us see what we should say about rhetoric. For I myself cannot yet fully understand what I am to say. When the city holds a meeting to elect physicians, or shipbuilders, or other craftsmen, <margin>E</margin> the orator will surely not be the one to give advice. For it is clear that in such elections, the person most skilled in that art must be chosen. Nor again, when the building of walls, the arrangement of harbors, or the equipping of a navy is discussed, will it be the orator’s duty to advise, but the architect’s. Furthermore, when there is deliberation about choosing a general, or arranging an army against enemies, or occupying locations, the military commanders will give advice, not the orators. What do you say to this, Gorgias? Since you claim to be an orator and to be able to make others orators, it is proper to ask you and learn from you the nature of your art. And consider that I am now acting in your interest. For perhaps among those here inside, <margin>F</margin> there is someone who wishes to become your student—as I notice some, indeed many, who might be deterred by shame from asking you these things. Therefore, consider that when I ask, they are also asking: "What will we gain if we submit ourselves to your teaching? On what subjects will we be able to advise the State? Only on the just and unjust? Or also on those things Socrates just mentioned?" Try, then, Gorgias, to answer them. GORGIAS: I will indeed try, Socrates, to explain the whole power of rhetoric clearly to you. For you have led us to it very well. You surely know that these dockyards and the walls of Athens, and the construction of the harbors, were built on the advice of Themistocles and Pericles, not by the advice of the craftsmen. SOCRATES: It is said so, <margin>G</margin> <margin>* Regarding the wall that faces south, see Suidas <note>original: "Suidas." Refers to the Suda, a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the Mediterranean world.</note>.</margin> Gorgias, regarding Themistocles. But I myself heard Pericles when he persuaded us to build the middle wall. GORGIAS: Moreover, whenever there is a deliberation about the elections you were just mentioning, you see that the orators are the ones who give advice, and it is their opinions that prevail in these matters. SOCRATES: It is because I marvel at this, Gorgias, that I have been asking for so long about the power of rhetoric. To me, when I think about it, the magnitude of its power seems almost divine. GORGIAS: Oh, if only you knew everything about the art, Socrates—you would see that it embraces almost all powers under itself. I will give you a great proof of this. Often, I have gone with my brother and other physicians to some sick person who refused to drink medicine or to allow the doctor to cut or burn him. <note>original: "secandum urendumve" (Latin) / "temein ē kausai" (Greek). This refers to ancient surgical practices of lancing and cauterizing wounds.</note> When the physician could not persuade him, I persuaded him by no other art than rhetoric. I say further, if an orator and a physician went to any city you like and had to compete in speech before the assembly or any other gathering to see which should be chosen as the physician, the orator or the doctor, the doctor would appear nowhere; the man skilled in speaking would be chosen, if he so wished. And in the same way, against any other craftsman, the orator...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> GORGIAS: You speak the truth. SOCRATES: Since, then, this art is not the only one that achieves this, but others do too, we would be right to ask, just as with the painter, what kind of persuasion and what subject of persuasion is rhetoric the art of. Or does it not seem right to you to ask? GORGIAS: It does to me. SOCRATES: Answer then, Gorgias, since it seems so to you. <margin>B</margin> GORGIAS: I am speaking, Socrates, of that persuasion in the courts and in other crowds, as I was just saying. And it is about those things that are just and unjust. SOCRATES: And I indeed suspected that you meant this persuasion and these subjects, Gorgias. But so that you do not wonder if, a little later, I ask you something of this sort again—which seems clear, yet I ask it repeatedly—as I say, I ask it for the sake of finishing the argument in order, not for your sake. It is so that we do not get used to snatching away what is said from each other by guessing; rather, you should finish your own points according to your premise however you wish. GORGIAS: And you seem to me to be doing rightly, Socrates. SOCRATES: Come then, let us examine this: do you call something "to have learned"? GORGIAS: I do. SOCRATES: What else? "To have believed"? GORGIAS: I do. SOCRATES: Does it seem to you that "to have learned" and "to have believed" are the same, and that "learning" and "belief" are the same? Or something else? GORGIAS: I think, Socrates, they are different. <margin>C</margin> SOCRATES: You think well; you will know it from this. For if someone asked you, "Is there, Gorgias, a belief that is false and one that is true?" you would say yes, I think? GORGIAS: Yes. SOCRATES: What then? Is there a knowledge that is false and true? GORGIAS: Not at all. SOCRATES: It is clear then that they are not the same. GORGIAS: You speak the truth. SOCRATES: But yet both those who have learned and those who have believed are persuaded. GORGIAS: That is so. SOCRATES: Do you wish then for us to set down two types of persuasion, one providing belief without knowing, and the other providing knowledge? GORGIAS: Certainly. SOCRATES: Which persuasion then does rhetoric produce in courts and other crowds, regarding just and unjust things? The one from which believing comes without knowing? Or the one from which knowing comes? GORGIAS: It is clear, Socrates, that it is the one from which believing comes. <margin>D</margin> SOCRATES: Rhetoric, then, as it seems, is a creator of persuasive belief, but not of teaching, concerning the just and unjust. GORGIAS: Yes. SOCRATES: Nor then is the orator a teacher of courts and other crowds regarding just and unjust things, but only persuasive. For surely he could not teach such a large crowd such great matters in so little time. GORGIAS: Certainly not. SOCRATES: Come then, let us see what we are actually saying about rhetoric. For I myself cannot yet understand what I am saying. When there is a gathering in the city about the choice of doctors, or shipbuilders, or any other professional group, will the orator then not give advice? For it is clear that in <margin>E</margin> each choice, the most technical person must be chosen. Nor when it is about the building of walls, or the construction of harbors, or dockyards; but the architects. Nor again when there is advice about the choice of generals, or some arrangement against enemies, or the taking of places; but the military experts will then give advice, and the orators will not. Or how do you say it, Gorgias? Since you say you are an orator yourself, and you make others orators, it is well to learn the things of your art from you. And think of me now as also looking out for your interest. For perhaps there is someone among those inside who wishes to become your student; as I perceive some, and quite a few, who perhaps <margin>F</margin> would be ashamed to ask you. Being asked by me, then, think that you are also being asked by them: "What will happen to us, Gorgias, if we associate with you? About what things will we be able to advise the city? Only about the just and unjust? Or also about those things Socrates was just saying?" Try then to answer them. GORGIAS: Well, I will try for you, Socrates, to clearly reveal the whole power of rhetoric. For you yourself guided us well. For you surely know that these dockyards and walls of the Athenians, and the construction of the harbors, happened from the advice of Themistocles; and others from Pericles; but not from the craftsmen. SOCRATES: These things are said, Gorgias, about Themistocles; but Pericles I myself heard when he advised us about the middle wall. <margin>G</margin> GORGIAS: And whenever there is a choice of those things you were saying, Socrates, you see that the orators are the ones who give advice, and they are the ones who win the opinions about these things. SOCRATES: Admiring these things, Gorgias, I have long been asking what the power of rhetoric is. For its magnitude appears to me to be something divine, when I look at it this way. GORGIAS: If you knew all, Socrates, that (so to speak) it holds all powers under itself. And I will tell you a great proof. For many times already I have gone with my brother, and with other doctors, to one of the sick who was not willing to drink medicine, or to allow the doctor to cut or burn, and when the doctor was unable to persuade him by medicine, I persuaded him, by no other art than rhetoric. and I say that in whatever city you wish to go, an orator and a doctor, if they had to compete in speech in an assembly, or in any other gathering, over which should be chosen as a doctor, the orator or the doctor, the doctor would appear nowhere, but the man able to speak would be chosen, if he wished. And against any other craftsman he might compete...

<summary>In this passage, Socrates leads Gorgias to admit that rhetoric produces "belief without knowledge" rather than true instruction. Gorgias defends the art by highlighting its immense power to persuade people on any subject, even technical ones like medicine or public works, far more effectively than actual experts.</summary>

# GORGIAS

<page-num>285</page-num>

[the orator] would persuade them, for the orator would be more capable than anyone else of being chosen. <margin>A</margin> For there is no subject on which the orator would not speak more persuasively than any other craftsman before a multitude. Such, then, is the power and the nature of this art. However, Socrates, one ought to use rhetoric just as one uses any other competitive skill. For in other competitive skills, one should not use them against everyone just because one has learned how to box, or to engage in the <term>pankration</term> <note>original: "παγκρατιαζειν" (Greek) / "pancratium" (Latin); an ancient Greek combat sport combining boxing and wrestling</note>, or to fight in armor so as to be superior to both friends and enemies. One should not, for this reason, strike one’s friends, or stab or kill them. Nor, by Zeus, if someone who has frequented the wrestling school and become a strong-bodied boxer then strikes his father or mother <margin>B</margin> or any other relative or friend, should we for that reason hate the physical trainers and those who teach fighting in armor and expel them from the cities. For they handed down these skills so that they might be used justly against enemies and wrongdoers—for defense, not for unprovoked attack. But these students pervert the skill and use their strength and art incorrectly. Therefore, it is not the teachers who are wicked, nor is the art to blame or wicked for this reason; rather, I believe, it is those who do not use it correctly. The same argument applies to rhetoric. For the orator is capable of speaking against everyone and about everything, so as to be more persuasive among the multitude—in short, about whatever he wishes. But he should no more for this reason strip the doctors of their reputation—just because he could do so—nor <margin>C</margin> the other craftsmen. Instead, one should use rhetoric justly, just as one uses competitive skills. But I think that if someone becomes an orator and then uses this power and art to do injustice, we should not hate the teacher and expel him from the city. For the teacher handed it over for a just use, but the student uses it in the opposite way. It is just, therefore, to hate, expel, and even kill the one who uses it incorrectly, but not the teacher.

SOCRATES: I think, Gorgias, that you too have experience with many discussions, and you have observed this in them: that people are not easily able to define the matters they undertake to discuss with one another, and so—having learned and taught each other—end their sessions in that way. Instead, if they <margin>D</margin> disagree about something, and one says the other is not speaking correctly or clearly, they grow angry and think the other is speaking out of envy, being more interested in "winning" the argument than in seeking the truth of the matter. And some, in the end, depart in a most shameful manner, having exchanged such insults and heard such things about themselves that even the bystanders are annoyed on their own behalf, regretting that they thought such men worth listening to. Why do I say this? Because right now, you do not seem to me to be saying things that are entirely consistent or harmonious with what you first said about rhetoric. I am afraid, then, to refute you, lest you suppose I speak not out of a desire for the matter to become clear, but out of a desire to win against you. Now, if you are the same kind of person I am, I would gladly question you; but if not, <margin>E</margin> I would let it be. And what kind of person am I? One of those who would gladly be refuted if I say anything untrue, and would gladly refute another if he says anything untrue—yet not less gladly be refuted than to refute. For I consider being refuted to be a greater good, insofar as it is a greater good for oneself to be delivered from the greatest evil than to deliver another. For I believe there is no evil so great for a man as a false opinion about the subjects we are discussing now. If, then, you say you are also such a person, let us discuss; but if you think we should stop, let us bid the argument farewell and break off the conversation.

GORGIAS: I claim, Socrates, that I am indeed such a person as you describe. Yet perhaps <margin>F</margin> we should also consider the interests of those present. For a long while now—even before you arrived—I have been demonstrating many things to those here, and perhaps we will draw this out too far if we continue the discussion. We must, therefore, look to their needs, lest we detain any of them who wish to do something else.

CHAEREPHON: You hear the noise for yourselves, Gorgias and Socrates, from these men who are eager to hear if you have anything to say. For my part, may I never have so much business that I would put anything else before a discussion of such importance and conducted in such a manner.

CALLICLES: By the gods, Chaerephon, I myself have been present at many discussions, but I do not know <margin>G</margin> if I have ever been as delighted as I am now. So, for my part, even if you wish to discuss all day long, you will be doing me a favor.

SOCRATES: Well, Callicles, for my part there is nothing to prevent it, if Gorgias is willing.

GORGIAS: It would be shameful for me, Socrates, to be unwilling hereafter, especially since I myself issued the invitation for anyone to ask whatever they wished. So, if it pleases these people, carry on the discussion and ask whatever you like.

SOCRATES: Listen then, Gorgias, to what I admired in what you were saying. For perhaps you were speaking correctly and I am taking it wrongly. You say you are able to make a man an orator if he wishes to learn from you? GORGIAS: Yes. SOCRATES: And so, regarding all things, he will be persuasive in a crowd—not by teaching them, but by persuading them? GORGIAS: Precisely so. SOCRATES: You were saying just now that even regarding health, the orator will be more persuasive than the doctor. GORGIAS: I did say that, at least in a crowd. SOCRATES: And does "in a crowd" mean "among those who do not know"? For surely among those who *do* know, he will not be more persuasive than the doctor. GORGIAS: You speak the truth.

<column-break/>

[The orator] will compete and obtain [the post], so that he himself rather than any other whatsoever is finally chosen. <margin>A</margin> For there is nothing about which the orator cannot speak with greater persuasion among the common people than any of the craftsmen. The power of this art is thus so great and of such a kind; nevertheless, it is proper to use rhetoric just as one uses any other faculty of combat. For one who has learned to fight with fists, limbs, and weapons so that he might emerge superior to friends and enemies ought not, because of this, to fight against everyone equally, so that he even strikes, wounds, or kills his friends. Nor, by Jove, if someone trained in the wrestling school as a boxer acquires bodily strength and then strikes his parents or some <margin>B</margin> other member of the household or friends, is it proper for that reason to hold the physical trainers and those who teach fighting with weapons in hatred and to expel them from the cities. For they handed down these things so that those who learned them might use them justly against enemies and those who would bring injury—turning them away, clearly, not inflicting them. Some, however, pervert these things and abuse their strength and art; but not for that reason should those who taught be judged wicked, nor should the art be blamed or held as evil, but rather, in my judgment, those who use it perversely. The same reasoning applies to rhetoric. For the orator can speak against everyone and about any matter whatsoever, so as to easily become superior in persuading the multitude about anything. Nevertheless, one should not for that reason deprive <margin>C</margin> doctors of their proper praise, even if they can perform this, nor other craftsmen; rather, one must use rhetoric rightly and with reason, just as one uses the faculty of combat. But if someone, having acquired rhetoric, then uses the faculty unjustly, it is not proper to hate and expel from the city the one who taught him; for the teacher handed it over for just use, while the student used it for the opposite purpose. Therefore, it is fair to hate, send into exile, and even put to death the one who abuses it, but by no means the teacher.

SOCRATES: I think, Gorgias, that you have been present at many disputes and have already discovered in them that those who dispute among themselves cannot easily, when they begin to differ, <margin>D</margin> depart in such a way that, by defining the matter itself, they only teach and learn from each other. Instead, if they contend over something and do not concede to one another that they are speaking either truly or clearly, they become inflamed with anger and think that what is said is born of envy—contending with each other rather than seeking out what was proposed. Sometimes they finally depart so shamefully, with mutual railings and curses, that even those listening are pained and annoyed that they thought such men worth hearing. But to what purpose do I say this? Because you do not seem to me now to be speaking in a way that is consistent and harmonious with what you previously brought forward concerning rhetoric. I fear, however, to refute you, lest you think I am contending not so much for the sake of declaring the truth as for your sake. If you are of the number of those to which I belong, I will gladly inquire into what you have proposed; if not, <margin>E</margin> I shall let it go. But if you ask of what number I am, I will answer: of those who gladly allow themselves to be refuted if they say anything false or foolish, and who also gladly refute others if something is said by another that is less than true; for whom it is no less pleasing to be corrected than to correct. <margin>The greatest evil for men is false opinion.</margin> For I consider it to be so much a greater good as it is a greater good to be freed from some greatest evil than to have freed others. For I think nothing is so destructive to men as a false opinion, especially in these matters concerning which our present discourse is established. Therefore, if you also affirm that you are such a person, let us carry on the dispute; but if you think it should be dropped, let us drop it now and dismiss the gathering.

GORGIAS: I say indeed, Socrates, that I also am of such a kind as you just described; but perhaps we must have regard for the others who are present. For long ago, <margin>F</margin> before you arrived, I related many things to these people. And now, perhaps, if we proceed to dispute, the delay will be drawn out longer. Therefore, we must be careful lest we detain them while they intend to do something else.

CHAEREPHON: You hear the shout, Gorgias and Socrates, of those desiring to be present for this discussion. To me, certainly, no business is of such importance that I would put anything else before this dispute established by you.

CALLICLES: By the Gods, Chaerephon, I too, though I have been present at many disputes, do not know if I have ever been <margin>G</margin> as delighted as I am now; and therefore, even if you spend the whole day disputing, it will be most pleasing to me.

SOCRATES: And yet, Callicles, as far as I am concerned, nothing will stand in the way, provided Gorgias is willing.

GORGIAS: It would indeed be shameful for me, Socrates, if I were to decline the dispute hereafter, especially since from the beginning I commanded all to ask about whatever anyone wished. Therefore, if it pleases those present, dispute and inquire into whatever you like.

SOCRATES: Hear now, Gorgias, what I wonder at in your words. For perhaps while you speak rightly, I perceive it otherwise. You say you are able to make a man an orator if he wishes to learn from you? GORGIAS: I do say so. SOCRATES: Not so that he may speak with knowledge about all things in a crowd, but with persuasion? GORGIAS: Exactly so. SOCRATES: You added, moreover, that the orator persuades more than the doctor concerning health. GORGIAS: I did say so, but in a crowd. SOCRATES: It is the same thing, therefore, to be "in a crowd" as to be "among the ignorant." For surely among those who know, he would not persuade more than the doctor concerning health. GORGIAS: You speak the truth.

<summary>Gorgias argues that rhetoric is a neutral tool that can be used for good or ill, and that the teacher should not be blamed for a student's misuse. Socrates and Gorgias agree to continue their dialogue, focusing on how rhetoric functions as a tool of persuasion among the ignorant rather than a tool of instruction among the knowledgeable.</summary>

# PLATO

soc. Therefore, if he is more persuasive than the doctor, does he not become more persuasive than the one who has knowledge? GOR. Certainly. soc. Even though he himself is not a doctor? GOR. Yes. soc. And if he is not a doctor, he is surely ignorant of those things that the doctor understands. GOR. Undoubtedly. soc. So, will the man who does not know be more persuasive than the one who knows when speaking among those who are also ignorant, since the orator excels the doctor in the power of persuasion? Is that what follows? GOR. In these cases, it certainly follows. soc. Is it not the same with all the other arts as well? That the orator and
<margin>B</margin>
rhetoric need not know the nature of the subjects themselves, but only need to have discovered a certain device of persuasion so as to appear to those who do not know to have more knowledge than those who actually know. GOR. Well, is it not a great relief, Socrates, that one does not need to learn the other arts, but only this single one, to be in no way inferior to the craftsmen?
soc. Whether the orator is inferior or not to others because of this situation, we shall examine shortly, if it seems to contribute anything to our discussion. But for now, let us first consider this: regarding the just and unjust, the honorable and the base, the good and the bad, is
<margin>C</margin>
the orator situated in the same way as he is toward health and the other subjects of the other arts? That is to say, does he not know what is good or bad, or what is beautiful or base, or just or unjust? Yet has he devised a kind of persuasion about such things so that, while he is ignorant himself, he appears among the ignorant to know more than those who actually know? Or is it necessary that he should know these things, and must anyone who intends to learn rhetoric from you already possess this knowledge before coming to you? And if not, will you, the teacher of rhetoric, teach none of these things to the newcomer (for that is not your job), but instead make him
<margin>D</margin>
appear to the many to know such things when he does not, and appear to be good and excellent when he is not at all? Or will you be completely unable to teach him rhetoric unless he has first grasped the truth of these matters? Or how do these things stand, Gorgias? I pray, by Zeus <note>original Latin: "per Iouem"; Greek: "πρὸς Διὸς"</note>, that you would finally reveal to us the power of rhetoric, as you just now began to do. GOR. Well, I suppose, Socrates, that if someone happens not to know these things, he will learn them from me as well. soc. Wait, you speak rightly. For if you make someone a rhetorician, he must know what is just and what is unjust, either by knowing it beforehand or by learning it from you afterward. GOR. Certainly. soc. What then? Is the man who has learned carpentry a carpenter? GOR. He is. soc. And the one who has learned music, a musician? GOR. Yes. soc. And the one who has learned medicine, a doctor? And in other matters in the same way: whoever has learned a subject becomes the kind of person that each branch of knowledge
<margin>E</margin>
produces? GOR. Certainly. soc. Therefore, by this reasoning, will not the man who has learned just things be just? GOR. Most certainly. soc. And the just man does just things. GOR. Yes. soc. Is it not then necessary that the rhetorician be just? And that the just man wishes to act justly? GOR. It appears so. soc. The just man, then, will never want to do wrong. GOR. Never. soc. It follows from the preceding argument that the rhetorician must be just. GOR. It must be so. soc. Therefore, the rhetorician will never want to do wrong. GOR. It seems not. soc. Remember that you said a little while ago that physical trainers should not be accused or expelled if a boxer uses his boxing skill badly and does wrong. And in the same
<margin>F</margin>
way, if an orator uses rhetoric unjustly, one should not accuse or expel the teacher, but rather the one who does the wrong and does not use rhetoric correctly. Were these things said or not? GOR. They were said. soc. But now it appears that this very same person, being a rhetorician, would never do wrong. GOR. It appears so. soc. And in our first discussions, Gorgias, it was said that rhetoric was about speech—not about even and odd numbers, but about the just and the unjust. GOR. Certainly. soc. While you were saying these things, I assumed that rhetoric could never be an unjust thing, since it always speaks about justice. But when you said shortly afterward that an orator might use rhetoric unjustly,
<margin>G</margin>
I was immediately astonished; and thinking that what you said was not consistent, I put forward these arguments: that if you thought it was a benefit to be refuted, just as I do, it would be worthwhile to continue our discussion; if not, we should let it go. But then, as we examined the matter more closely, as you well know, it was admitted that it is impossible for a rhetorician to use rhetoric unjustly or to wish to do wrong. To truly distinguish how these matters stand, by the dog <note>original Greek: "μὰ τὸν κύνα"; Socrates' characteristic oath</note>, Gorgias, would require no small amount of conversation and meeting.
POL. What is this, Socrates? Do you really hold this opinion of rhetoric that you are now stating? Or do you think Gorgias was led by a certain shame to concede to you that the rhetorician knows what is just, honorable, and good? And that if someone came to him ignorant of these things, he would teach them? From this concession, perhaps some contradiction
<margin>H</margin>
in the argument followed. You catch at such things with too much zeal, Socrates, while leading the respondent to such answers by your questioning. For who do you think would deny that he knows what is just and can teach it to others? But it is a great rudeness to lead an argument into such things. soc. For this very reason, my most excellent Polus, we purposely acquire friends and sons: so that when we ourselves, being older, may stumble, you younger men being present may correct our lives in both words and deeds. And now

SOC. Therefore, if he is to be more persuasive than the doctor, does he become more persuasive than the one who knows? GOR. Certainly. SOC. Without being a doctor himself? Or is that so? GOR. Yes. SOC. And he who is not a doctor is surely without the knowledge that the doctor possesses? GOR. Clearly so. SOC. Thus, the one who does not know will be more persuasive than the one who knows among those who do not know, whenever the orator is more persuasive than the doctor. Does this happen, or something else? GOR. This is what happens in this case. SOCRAT. Is it not then the same regarding all other arts
<margin>B</margin>
as well? Rhetoric and the orator need not know the things themselves and how they are; they only need to have found a device of persuasion so as to appear to those who do not know to have more knowledge than those who know. GOR. Is it not then a great ease, Socrates, not to have learned the other arts, but only this one, and yet be in no way inferior to the craftsmen? SOC. Whether the orator is inferior or not to others because of this, we shall look into presently, if it serves our argument; but now let us look at this: concerning health and injustice, and
the base and the beautiful, and the good and the bad, does the rhetorician stand in the same way as toward health and the subjects of the other arts? Not knowing the things themselves—what is good or what is bad, or what is beautiful or base, or just or

unjust—but having devised a persuasion about them so that he seems to know, though he does not know, among those who do not know, more than the one who knows? And by Zeus, as you just now said, reveal and tell us what the
<margin>D</margin>
power of rhetoric is. GOR. Well, I think, Socrates, that if he happens not to know, he will learn these things from me as well. SOC. Hold there; for you speak well. Is the one who has learned carpentry a carpenter? Or not? GOR. Yes. SOC. And the one who has learned music, a musician? GOR. Yes. SOC. And the one who has learned medicine, a doctor? And others in the same way; is the one who has learned each thing such as each branch of knowledge makes him? GOR. Certainly. SOC. And according to this, is the one who has learned just things just? GOR. Surely, by all means.
SOC. And the just man surely acts justly? GOR. Yes. SOC.

It is necessary. SOC. And the rhetorician must be just according to the argument. GOR. Yes. SOC. Therefore, the rhetorician will never want to act unjustly. GOR. It does not appear so. SOC. Do you remember saying a little while ago that one should not accuse the physical trainers, nor expel them from the cities, if the boxer does not use his boxing well and acts unjustly? <margin>F</margin>

And in our first words, Gorgias, it was said that rhetoric was about speech—not speech about the even and the odd, but about the just and the unjust. Was it not? GOR. Yes. SOC. While you were saying these things then, I understood that rhetoric could never be an unjust matter, since it always makes its arguments about justice. But when you said a little later that an orator might use rhetoric unjustly, I was astonished and, thinking that the things being said did not harmonize, I spoke those words: that if you thought it a gain to be refuted, as I do, it would be worth discussing; but if not, to let it be. <margin>G</margin>
rhetorician to use rhetoric unjustly and to want to do wrong. How these things truly stand, by the dog, Gorgias, is not a matter for a small conversation to adequately examine. POL. Perhaps from this agreement some contradiction followed in the arguments; which is exactly what you love, leading people to such questions. For who do you think will deny that he himself knows

<summary>Socrates leads Gorgias to a logical impasse, showing that if a rhetorician truly understands justice, they must act justly, contradicting Gorgias's earlier claim that rhetoric can be used for evil. Polus interjects, accusing Socrates of using Gorgias's sense of shame to trap him in a contradiction.</summary>

# GORGIAS

<page-num>287</page-num>

<margin>A</margin> in deeds and in words. And now, if Gorgias and I have stumbled in our reasoning, you who are present must set us right; indeed, it is only just. I am willing to take back anything we have agreed upon, if you think it was not well-settled—provided you observe one rule for me. <term>POLUS.</term> What rule do you mean? <term>SOCRATES.</term> Restrain that long-windedness, Polus <note>original: "makrologia"</note>, which you attempted to use at the start. <term>POLUS.</term> What? Am I not allowed to speak as much as I wish? <term>SOCRATES.</term> It would be a strange hardship indeed, my friend, if you came to Athens—the place in Greece where there is the greatest license of speech—and then you alone were denied it. But consider the alternative: if you speak at great length and refuse to answer what is asked, would I not also suffer a hardship if I were not allowed to leave and stop listening to you? If you care at all for the argument we have started and wish to set it right (as I was just saying), take back whatever you like; take your turn in asking and being asked, just as Gorgias and I did; refute me and be refuted. For you surely claim to know what Gorgias knows, do you not? <term>POLUS.</term>
<margin>B</margin> I do. <term>SOCRATES.</term> And do you not also invite people to ask you whatever they wish, as one who knows how to answer? <term>POLUS.</term> Certainly. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Well then, do whichever of these you prefer: ask or answer. <term>POLUS.</term> Very well, I will do so. And answer me, Socrates: since Gorgias seems to be at a loss to explain rhetoric to you, what do you say it is? <term>SOCRATES.</term> Are you asking what kind of art <note>original: "techne"</note> I claim it is? <term>POLUS.</term> I am. <term>SOCRATES.</term> To tell you the truth, Polus, I do not think it is an art at all. <term>POLUS.</term> Then what do you think rhetoric is? <term>SOCRATES.</term> A thing which you claim produced "art" in that book of yours I recently read. <term>POLUS.</term> What do you mean by that? <term>SOCRATES.</term> I call it a kind of knack <note>original: "empeiria", often translated as experience or routine</note>. <term>POLUS.</term>
<margin>C</margin> So rhetoric seems to be a knack to you? <term>SOCRATES.</term> To me, yes, unless you say otherwise. <term>POLUS.</term> A knack for what? <term>SOCRATES.</term> For producing a certain grace and pleasure. <term>POLUS.</term> Does rhetoric not then seem to be a beautiful thing, since it is capable of providing grace to men? <term>SOCRATES.</term> What, Polus? Have you already learned from me what I claim it is, that you should go on to ask if I think it is beautiful? <term>POLUS.</term> Have I not heard you say it is a kind of knack? <term>SOCRATES.</term> Since you value "giving grace" so much, would you like to do a small favor <note>Socrates is punning on the word "charis," which means both "grace/pleasure" and "favor"</note> for me? <term>POLUS.</term> I would. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Ask me now what kind of art I think cookery is. <term>POLUS.</term> I am asking: what art is cookery? <term>SOCRATES.</term>
<margin>D</margin> It is no art at all, Polus. <term>POLUS.</term> Then what is it? Tell me. <term>SOCRATES.</term> I say it is a kind of knack. <term>POLUS.</term> For what? Tell me. <term>SOCRATES.</term> I say it is for the production of a certain grace and pleasure, Polus. <term>POLUS.</term> Then are cookery and rhetoric the same thing? <term>SOCRATES.</term> Not at all; but they are both parts of the same pursuit. <term>POLUS.</term> What pursuit do you mean? <term>SOCRATES.</term> I fear it may be somewhat rude to speak the truth; I hesitate to say it for Gorgias's sake, lest he think I am mocking his own profession. Whether the rhetoric Gorgias practices is of this sort, I do not know—for our argument just now did not make it clear what he believes. But what I call rhetoric is a part of something that is not at all honorable. <term>GORGIAS.</term> What is it, Socrates? Speak; do not be ashamed on my account. <term>SOCRATES.</term> It seems to me then, Gorgias, to be a certain
<margin>E</margin> pursuit—not an artistic one, but one belonging to a shrewd and courageous soul, naturally clever at dealing with people. I call its sum total "flattery" <note>original: "kolakeia"</note>. This pursuit seems to me to have many other parts, and one of them is cookery. This is thought to be an art, but in my view it is not an art, but a knack and a routine. I call rhetoric a part of this as well, along with cosmetics <note>original: "kommotike", the art of dressing up/adornment</note> and sophistry—these four parts for four subjects. If Polus wants to find out more, let him; for he has not yet learned what part of flattery I claim rhetoric to be. He has not noticed that I haven't finished answering, yet he asks if
<margin>F</margin> I consider it beautiful. I will not answer him whether I think rhetoric is beautiful or ugly until I have first answered what it is. That would not be right, Polus. But if you want to know, ask me what part of flattery I say rhetoric is. <term>POLUS.</term> I am asking; answer which part it is. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Will you understand my answer? For rhetoric, in my account, is a phantom <note>original: "eidolon", an image or reflection</note> of a part of politics. <term>POLUS.</term> What then? Do you say it is beautiful or ugly? <term>SOCRATES.</term> Ugly, I say. For I call bad things ugly—since I must answer you as if you already understood what I am saying. <term>GORGIAS.</term> By Zeus, Socrates! I myself do not understand what you mean. <term>SOCRATES.</term>
<margin>G</margin> Reasonably so, Gorgias; for I have not yet spoken clearly. But this Polus here is young and sharp. <term>GORGIAS.</term> Well, leave him aside; tell me how you say rhetoric is a phantom of a part of politics. <term>SOCRATES.</term> I will try to explain what rhetoric seems to me to be. If it is not so, Polus here will refute me. You call something "body" and something "soul," do you not? <term>GORGIAS.</term> Of course. <term>SOCRATES.</term> And do you not believe there is a good condition for each of these? <term>GORGIAS.</term> I do. <term>SOCRATES.</term> And what of a condition that *appears* to be good, but is not? For example: many people seem to have healthy bodies, and no one would easily notice they are not healthy, except for a doctor or a trainer. <term>GORGIAS.</term> You are right. <term>SOCRATES.</term> I say there is such a thing in both the body and the soul, which makes... <margin>H</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> If anything escaped me or Gorgias in our discussion, you are present to correct it. For you ought to, and I gladly allow you, so that if you think any of the things conceded were not rightly conceded, you may change them as you wish, provided you avoid one thing. <term>POLUS.</term> What is that, Socrates? <term>SOCRATES.</term> That long-windedness of speech which you were starting from the very beginning of the discussion. <term>POLUS.</term> Why so? Shall I not be allowed to speak as much as I want? <term>SOCRATES.</term> You would be treated with a great injury indeed, most excellent man, if having come to Athens, where there is the greatest freedom of speech in all Greece, you alone should not have the power to speak as you please. But on the other hand, if you spoke at length and were unwilling to answer questions, would I not be treated with a great injury if I were not allowed to leave and refuse to listen to you? But if you have any care for this discussion and wish to correct it, as I was just saying, retract what seems to be retracted, asking and answering in turn, as Gorgias and I did; refute me and allow yourself to be refuted. Do you also claim to know what Gorgias professes to know? <term>POLUS.</term> I do say so. <term>SOCRATES.</term> And do you bid anyone to ask you whatever they wish, as a man who knows how to answer? <term>POLUS.</term> Certainly. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Now, therefore, do whichever you choose: either ask or answer. <margin>B</margin> <term>POLUS.</term> I will do so; and answer me, Socrates: since Gorgias seems to be unable to speak conveniently about rhetoric <margin>Rhetoric is no art.</margin>, what do you say it is? <term>SOCRATES.</term> Are you asking what art I think it is? <term>POLUS.</term> That is it. <term>SOCRATES.</term> None at all, Polus, to tell you the truth. <term>POLUS.</term> What then does rhetoric seem to you to be? <term>SOCRATES.</term> A thing which you say created "art" in that book I recently read. <term>POLUS.</term> What do you say? <term>SOCRATES.</term> A certain knack. <margin>C</margin> <term>POLUS.</term> Then rhetoric seems to you to be a knack? <margin>Rhetoric is a knack for producing a certain grace and pleasure.</margin> <term>SOCRATES.</term> To me, at least, unless you say otherwise. <term>POLUS.</term> A knack for what? <term>SOCRATES.</term> For producing a certain grace and pleasure. <term>POLUS.</term> Do you not then think rhetoric is something beautiful, since it can procure grace among men? <term>SOCRATES.</term> What, Polus? <margin>D</margin> Have you already heard what I say it is, that you next ask whether I think it is beautiful? <term>POLUS.</term> Have I not heard you say it is a certain knack? <term>SOCRATES.</term> Do you wish, then, since you value grace so much, to do me a little favor? <term>POLUS.</term> I do. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Ask me now what art I think cookery is. <term>POLUS.</term> Behold, I ask: what art is cookery? <term>SOCRATES.</term> None. <term>POLUS.</term> But what? <term>SOCRATES.</term> I say it is a certain knack. <term>POLUS.</term> What knack? <term>SOCRATES.</term> For producing grace and pleasure. <term>POLUS.</term> Is cookery the same as rhetoric? <term>SOCRATES.</term> In no way, but it is a part of the same pursuit. <term>POLUS.</term> What pursuit? <term>SOCRATES.</term> I fear it might be too harsh to speak the truth for Gorgias's sake, lest he think I am disparaging his pursuit. For I do not know whether this is the rhetoric Gorgias practices; for from this discussion, <margin>E</margin> nothing was made clear to us what he himself thinks. But what I call rhetoric is a part of a thing that is by no means honorable. <term>GORGIAS.</term> Of what part, Socrates? Speak, fearing nothing on my account. <term>SOCRATES.</term> It seems to me to be a certain pursuit, not <margin>A certain unartistic pursuit is described.</margin> artistic indeed, but belonging to a sagacious mind, naturally fit and powerful at winning over human society. I call its sum and head "flattery." Now, there seem to me to be many members of this pursuit. One indeed is <margin>Cookery, rhetoric, cosmetics, and sophistry are parts of the unartistic pursuit, whose head and sum is flattery.</margin> cookery, which although it seems to be an art, in my judgment is none, but a certain knack found by use. Furthermore, I say rhetoric is also a part of it, and cosmetics (which is called the trade of the fop), and sophistry. These four parts pertain to four things. If Polus wishes to ask, let him ask. For he has not yet heard what part <margin>F</margin> of flattery I say rhetoric is; nor has he noticed that I have not yet <margin>Rhetoric is a phantom of a part of politics.</margin> answered that. Therefore he asks whether I think it is beautiful or not. But I shall not answer whether I think rhetoric is something beautiful or shameful before I have opened up what it is. For it is not fitting to answer otherwise, Polus. But if you wish to hear, ask what part of flattery I say rhetoric is. <term>POLUS.</term> I ask now, what part? <term>SOCRATES.</term> Will you learn from my answer? It is, as I think, a phantom of a part of politics. <term>POLUS.</term> What then? Do you say it is something beautiful or shameful? <term>SOCRATES.</term> Shameful: since I say bad things are shameful; since it is necessary to answer you as one not ignorant of what I am now saying. <term>GORGIAS.</term> By Jove, I do not sufficiently understand what you are saying. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Nor indeed without cause, Gorgias; for I have not yet sufficiently expressed it. <margin>G</margin> But this Polus is young and sharp. <term>GORGIAS.</term> But let him be; answer me in what way you say rhetoric is a phantom of a part of politics. <term>SOCRATES.</term> I will attempt to express what rhetoric seems to me to be. But if the matter is otherwise, let this Polus refute me. Do you call something body and something soul? <term>GORGIAS.</term> Why not. <term>SOCRATES.</term> And do you not think there is some good condition for each of these? <term>GORGIAS.</term> I think so. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Moreover, does some condition appear good when it is not at all? I say something of this kind: many seem to have a well-affected body, whose bad health and condition no one would easily detect except a doctor or a master of gymnastics. <term>GORGIAS.</term> You tell the truth. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Something of this sort...

<summary>Socrates argues that rhetoric is not a true art but a "knack" for producing pleasure, categorizing it alongside cookery and cosmetics as forms of "flattery." He defines rhetoric as a "phantom" or false image of a part of politics, meant to deceive through appearance rather than truth.</summary>

<keywords>Socrates, Polus, Gorgias, flattery, rhetoric, cookery, knack vs art, appearance vs reality, politics, Athenian freedom of speech</keywords>
