# OF PLATO

<page-num>288</page-num>

<center>PLATONIS</center>

...I say this exists in both the body and the soul, making both the body and soul seem to be in good health when they are actually not. 
**GOR.** <note>Gorgias</note> It is so. 
**SOC.** <note>Socrates</note> Come then, if I can, I will explain more clearly what I have said. Since there are two distinct things, I believe there are two arts: the one pertaining to the soul I call the political art; the one pertaining to the body I cannot name with a single term, but for this single art that cares for the body, I set down two parts: one being gymnastics and the other medicine. In the political art, I place <term>legislation</term> <note>nomotheticam</note> as the counterpart to gymnastics, and <term>justice</term> <note>iudiciariam</note> as the counterpart to medicine. These communicate with one another because they deal with the same subjects—medicine with gymnastics, and justice with legislation—yet they still differ from each other. While these four arts exist, always caring for what is best—two for the body and two for the soul—the faculty of flattery <note>adulatoria</note> senses this. It does not truly know, but by guesswork, it divides itself into four, slipping under each of these parts and pretending to be what it has stepped into. It has no care for what is best, but always hunts after folly by means of what is most pleasant, deceiving the mind to such an extent that it seems to be of the greatest value. Under the guise of medicine, <term>cookery</term> <note>coquinaria</note> creeps in, pretending to know the best foods for the body. Therefore, if a cook and a physician had to compete before children, or before men as foolish and senseless as children, to decide which of them understands more about good or bad food, the physician would die of hunger. This, then, I call flattery, and I say it is a shameful thing, Polus—for I am saying this to you. I say this because it aims at pleasure without any <margin>That which lacks reason is not an art.</margin> regard for what is best. And I do not call it an art, but a certain knack <note>peritiam</note>, because it possesses no <margin>Every art is with reason.</margin> rational account of the nature of the things it offers, and thus cannot explain the cause <margin>Flatteries subvert the arts: Cookery, Cosmetics, Sophistry, Rhetoric. [Corresponding to] Medicine, Gymnastics, Legislation, Justice.</margin> of any of them. I do not give the name "art" to anything that lacks reason. If you doubt these things, I am willing to provide an explanation. So, as I said, cookery mimics medicine; and in the same way, <term>cosmetics</term> <note>fucatoria; the art of beautification through makeup and dress</note> mimics gymnastics. It is a harmful, deceptive, ignoble, and illiberal thing, deceiving through shapes, colors, smoothness, and outward appearance, so that by assuming a foreign beauty, people neglect the true beauty produced through gymnastics. To avoid being long-winded, I will speak in the manner of the geometers—for perhaps now you can follow: as cosmetics is to gymnastics, so is cookery to medicine; or rather, as cosmetics is to gymnastics, so is <term>sophistry</term> to legislation; and as cookery is to medicine, so is **rhetoric** to justice. However, as I was saying, they are naturally distinct in this way, yet because they are closely related, sophists and orators are mixed together in the same field and deal with the same things, and they do not know what to make of themselves, nor do other men know what to make of them. For if the soul did not rule the body, but the body ruled itself, and if the soul did not perceive and distinguish between cookery and medicine, but the body itself judged these things by the standard of its own pleasures, then the saying of <term>Anaxagoras</term> <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher who claimed "all things were together" in a chaotic mixture before Mind (Nous) ordered them.</note> would certainly apply, my friend Polus (for you are familiar with these matters): all things would be mixed together indiscriminately, and matters of medicine and health would be indistinguishable from matters of cookery. You have now heard what I claim rhetoric to be: it is the counterpart of cookery in the soul, just as cookery is in the body. Perhaps I have acted absurdly by stretching out a long speech after I forbade you from being long-winded. Yet I deserve pardon, for when I spoke briefly, you did not understand, nor were you able to make use of the answer I gave you, but you needed a full explanation. If I, in turn, cannot understand your answers, then you too may extend your speech. But if I can, let me use your answer or mine as I see fit. And now, if you can make use of this answer in any way, do so. 
**PO.** <note>Polus</note> What then do you say? Does rhetoric seem to be flattery to you? 
**SOC.** I said it was a *part* of flattery. Do you not remember, Polus, at your age? What will you do when you are older? 
**PO.** Do good orators seem to you to be held in low esteem in cities, like flatterers? 
**SOC.** Is this a question you are asking, or are you beginning a speech? 
**PO.** I am asking. 
**SOC.** They do not seem to me to be held in any esteem at all. 
**PO.** How can you say "no esteem"? Do they not have the greatest power in cities? 
**SOC.** Not if you say that power is something good for the one who possesses it. 
**PO.** I certainly say so. 
**SOC.** Then it seems to me that orators have the least power of anyone in a city. 
**PO.** What are you saying? Do they not, like tyrants, kill whomever they wish, and strip them of their property, and drive them out of the city? 
**SOC.** By the dog! <note>A common eccentric oath of Socrates.</note> I am in doubt, Polus, regarding each thing you say, whether you are expressing your own opinion or asking for mine. 
**PO.** I am asking for yours. 
**SOC.** Very well, my friend. But then you are asking me two questions at once. 
**PO.** How two? 
**SOC.** Did you not just say that orators kill whomever they wish, just like tyrants, and strip them of wealth and drive them into exile? 
**PO.** I did. 
**SOC.** I tell you, then, that these are two separate questions, and I shall answer both. I assert, Polus, that both orators and tyrants have the very least power in cities, as...

<column-break/>

...they seem to have the body and soul in good condition, but they have it no more than before. 
**GOR.** These things are so. 
**SOC.** Come then, let me show you more clearly what I mean, if I can. Since there are two distinct subjects, I say there are two arts. One, which concerns the soul, I call the political art; the other, which concerns the body, I cannot give a single name to, but though the care of the body is one, I say it has two parts: gymnastics and medicine. In the political art, the counterpart to gymnastics is legislation; and the counterpart to medicine is justice. They share with one another, being about the same thing, both medicine with gymnastics and justice with legislation. Yet they differ somewhat from each other. These being four, and always caring for the best—some for the body, others for the soul—the art of flattery, perceiving this—not by knowing, I say, but by aiming—divided itself into four, and slipping under each of the parts, pretends to be that which it has slipped under. It cares nothing for the best, but always hunts after ignorance with the most pleasant thing, and deceives, so as to seem to be of the greatest worth. Under medicine, cookery has slipped, and pretends to know the best foods for the body. So that if it were necessary for a cook and a physician to contend before children, or before men as senseless as children, as to which of them understands good and bad food, the physician or the cook, the physician would die of hunger. This then I call flattery, and I say such a thing is shameful, Polus. This I say to you: that it aims at the pleasant without the best. And I say it is not an art, but an experience <note>original: "empeirian"</note>. Because it has no rational account <note>original: "logon"</note> of the things it offers, of what nature they are, so that it cannot state the cause of each thing. I do not call an irrational thing an art. If you dispute these things, I am willing to submit to an argument. Under medicine, as I say, cookery-flattery is placed; under gymnastics, in the same way, is cosmetics. It is mischievous, deceptive, base, and illiberal, deceiving with shapes and colors and smoothness and appearance, so as to make people neglect their own beauty through gymnastics while drawing on a foreign beauty. So that I may not be long-winded, I am willing to speak to you like the geometers (for perhaps now you might follow): that what cosmetics is to gymnastics, cookery is to medicine. Or rather thus: what cosmetics is to gymnastics, sophistry is to legislation; and what cookery is to medicine, rhetoric is to justice. However, as I say, they are thus naturally distinct; but because they are near, sophists and orators are muddled together in the same place and about the same things, and they do not know what to do with themselves, nor do other men know what to do with them. For if the soul did not preside over the body, but the body over itself, and if cookery and medicine were not surveyed and distinguished by the soul, but the body itself judged them, weighing them by the delights it receives, the state of Anaxagoras would prevail, dear Polus (for you are experienced in these things): all things would be muddled together in the same place, and things of health and medicine and cookery would be undistinguished. What I say rhetoric is, you have heard: a counterpart of cookery in the soul, as that is in the body. Perhaps I have done something strange, in that while not allowing you to speak at length, I have extended a long speech myself. It is right to have forgiveness, for when I spoke briefly, you did not understand, nor were you able to use the answer I gave you, but you needed a narrative. If, therefore, when you answer I do not know what to do, you also stretch out a speech; but if I do know, let me use it. For that is just. And now, if you have anything to make of this answer, use it. 
**POL.** What then do you say? Does rhetoric seem to be flattery to you? 
**SOC.** I said it was a part of flattery. But do you not remember at your age, Polus? What will you do when you are older? 
**POL.** Do the good orators seem to you to be thought of as poor flatterers in the cities? 
**SOC.** Is this a question you ask, or are you speaking a beginning of a speech? 
**POL.** I am asking. 
**SOC.** They do not seem to me to be thought of at all. 
**POL.** How not thought of? Do they not have the greatest power in the cities? 
**SOC.** No, if you say that power is something good for the one who has power. 
**POL.** But I certainly do say so. 
**SOC.** Then the orators seem to me to have the least power of those in the city. 
**POL.** What? Do they not, like tyrants, kill whomever they wish, and take away property, and cast out from the cities whomever they see fit? 
**SOC.** By the dog, I am in doubt, Polus, at each of the things you say, whether you say these things yourself and show your own opinion, or whether you are asking me. 
**POL.** I am asking you. 
**SOC.** Well then, my friend. Then you ask me two things at once? 
**POL.** How two? 
**SOC.** Did you not just now say something like this: that orators kill whomever they wish, like tyrants, and take away property and drive from the cities whomever they see fit? 
**POL.** I did. 
**SOC.** I say to you then that these are two questions, and I will answer you both. For I say, Polus, that both the orators and the tyrants have the smallest power in the cities...

<summary>In this pivotal passage from Plato's Gorgias, Socrates defines rhetoric as a "flattery" that mimics justice, comparing it to how cookery mimics medicine by prioritizing pleasure over true health. He argues that orators and tyrants actually hold the least power in a city because they do not act according to rational will for the good, but merely follow what seems pleasant.</summary>

<keywords>Socrates, Polus, Rhetoric, Flattery, Justice, Medicine, Gymnastics, Legislation, Sophistry, Cookery, Cosmetics, Anaxagoras, Power vs. Will</keywords>

--- Page 321 ---
<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Polus. In the preceding section, Socrates argued that rhetoric is a form of flattery rather than a true art. Now, he moves to a paradoxical argument: that tyrants and orators, despite their apparent power to kill or exile anyone they wish, actually possess very little power because they do not do what they truly "want"—which is their own good.</meta>

<page-num>289</page-num>

<center># G O R G I A S.</center>

<margin>A</margin>...as I was just saying. For they do nothing that they *want*, so to speak; however, they do whatever *seems* best to them.
**POL.** <note>Polus</note> And isn't this what it means to have <term>great power</term>?
**SOC.** <note>Socrates</note> Not according to Polus, at least.
**POL.** I say it isn't? On the contrary, I certainly say it is!
**SOC.** By Zeus <note>original: "Μὰ τὸν" (Greek) / "Per Iouem" (Latin)</note>, no you don't. For you said that <term>great power</term> is a good thing for the person who has it.
**POL.** I certainly do say that.
**SOC.** Then do you think it is a good thing if someone does whatever seems best to him when he lacks <term>intelligence</term> <note>original: "νοῦν" / "mente"</note>? And do you call this having "great power"?
**POL.** I do not.
**SOC.** Then you must prove that orators possess intelligence, and that rhetoric is an art rather than a form of flattery, by refuting me. But if you leave me unrefuted, then the orators
<margin>B</margin> and the tyrants who do what seems best to them in their cities will have gained nothing good by it. Yet power, as you say, is a good thing; but doing what one thinks best without intelligence, even you admit is an evil. Is that not so?
**POL.** It is.
**SOC.** How then can orators or tyrants have great power in their cities, unless Socrates is refuted by Polus and forced to admit that they do what they *want*?
**POL.** What a man!
**SOC.** I deny they do what they want; go ahead and refute me.
**POL.** Did you not just admit a moment ago that they do what seems best to them?
**POL.** Certainly— <gloss>I indeed</gloss> —did.
**SOC.** And I admit it even now.
**POL.** Therefore, do they not do what they want?
**SOC.** I say they do not.
**POL.** Even though they do what seems best to them?
**SOC.** I say so.
**POL.** You say 
<margin>C</margin> shocking and monstrous things, Socrates!
**SOC.** Do not be so quick to accuse me, my dear Polus—to address you in your own style. But if you have questions for me, show me where I am lying; otherwise, answer the questions yourself.
**POL.** Indeed, I am willing to answer, so that I may finally know what you are talking about.
**SOC.** Do you think that when people do something, they want the action itself, or do they want that *for the sake of which* they perform the action? For example, those who drink medicine prescribed by doctors: do you think they want the thing they are doing—that is, to drink medicine and suffer pain—or do they want health, which is the reason they drink it?
**POL.** It is clearly health, the reason they drink it.
**POL.** <note>Socrates continues</note> And so it is with those who sail the seas or engage in other forms of business: they do not want the thing they do at each moment (for who wants to sail, face dangers, and suffer hardships?), but they want that for the sake of which they sail—to be wealthy. It is for wealth that they sail.
**POL.** Quite 
<margin>D</margin> so.
**SOC.** Is it not the same in all cases? If someone does something for the sake of a goal, they do not want the action they perform, but the goal for which they perform it?
**POL.** Yes.
**SOC.** Now, is there anything among existing things that is not either good, or bad, or intermediate between the two—neither good nor bad?
**POL.** It must be so, Socrates.
**SOC.** And you say that wisdom, health, wealth, and such things are "good," and their opposites are "bad"?
**POL.** I do.
**SOC.** And those things that are neither good nor bad, do you mean things like these: things that sometimes participate in the good, sometimes in the bad, and sometimes in neither—such as sitting, walking, running, and sailing; or again, things like stones and wood? Are these not the things you call neither good 
<margin>E</margin> nor bad?
**POL.** Indeed, those are the ones.
**SOC.** Then when people do these intermediate things, do they do them for the sake of the "good" things, or the "good" for the sake of the intermediate?
**POL.** The intermediate for the sake of the good, surely.
**SOC.** Therefore, it is in pursuit of the good that we walk when we walk, thinking it is better for us; and conversely, we stand still when we stand for the sake of the same thing: the good. Is it not so?
**POL.** Yes.
**SOC.** And if we kill someone, or exile them, or confiscate their property, do we not do it thinking it is better for us to do these things than not?
**POL.** Certainly.
**SOC.** Then it is for the sake of the good that people do all these things.
**POL.** I agree.
**SOC.** And did we not agree that we do not want the actions we take for the sake of something else, but we want the goal for which we take them?
**POL.** Absolutely.
<margin>F</margin> **SOC.** Therefore, we do not want to slaughter people, or exile them from cities, or take their money just for the sake of doing it. Rather, if these things are beneficial, we want to do them; but if they are harmful, we do not. For we want "good" things, as you say; but we do not want things that are neither good nor bad, nor those that are bad. Do you think I am telling the truth, Polus, or not? Why don't you answer?
**POL.** It is true.
**SOC.** Then if we agree on this, if someone kills another, or exiles him, or takes his money—whether he is a tyrant or an orator—thinking it is better for him when it actually happens to be worse, <insert>this man</insert> surely does what seems best to him. Is that not so?
**POL.** Yes.
**SOC.** But does he also do what he *wants*, if these things happen to be bad? Why don't you answer?
**POL.** No, it does not seem to me that he does what he wants.
**SOC.** Can such a man then have "great power" in that city, if indeed great power is something good according to
<margin>G</margin> your own admission?
**POL.** He cannot.
**SOC.** Then I was telling the truth when I said it is possible for a man to do what seems best to him in a city and yet not have great power, nor do what he wants.
**POL.** As if you, Socrates, would not choose to have the license to do whatever seems best to you in the city rather than not! Are you not jealous when you see someone who has killed whomever he pleased, or taken their property, or thrown them into chains?
**SOC.** Do you mean if he does so justly, or unjustly?
**POL.** Whichever way he does it, is it not enviable in both cases?
**SOC.** Hush, Polus!
**POL.** Why so?
**SOC.** Because one should not envy the unenviable or the miserable, but rather pity them.

<column-break/>

<margin>Whoever does something for the sake of something else does not want the action itself, but the goal for which he acts. A negative definition is used to inquire why something is not included in the disjunctive.</margin>

**Bb**

<summary>In this passage, Socrates leads Polus to admit that while tyrants may do "what seems best" to them, they do not do "what they want" because they desire the good but often act in ways that are harmful to themselves. Socrates establishes a hierarchy where actions (like drinking medicine) are only means to an end (like health), arguing that only beneficial actions constitute true power.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Polus from Plato’s *Gorgias*. Having previously established that "doing what one sees fit" is not true power unless it is guided by intelligence, Socrates now moves to the moral core of his argument: that it is better to suffer an injustice than to commit one. Polus attempts to counter this by citing the historical example of Archelaus of Macedonia, a man who rose to power through a series of brutal crimes and is, in Polus's view, obviously "happy" despite his injustice.</meta>

# PLATONIS

->**A**<- **POL.** <note>Polus</note> What then? Do you really believe that to be the case for the people I am talking about?
**SOC.** <note>Socrates</note> Why wouldn't I?
**POL.** So, anyone who kills whomever they see fit, and kills them justly, appears wretched and pitiable to you?
**SOC.** Not to me, certainly; however, his condition is not one to be envied.
**POL.** Didn't you say just a moment ago that such a man was wretched?
**SOC.** My friend, I was speaking of the man who kills *unjustly*—he is indeed wretched and, moreover, pitiable. But for the one who kills justly, his condition is simply not to be envied.
**POL.** Surely the one who is killed unjustly is pitiable and wretched?
**SOC.** Less so than his killer, Polus; and even less so than the one who is killed justly.
<margin>Committing an injustice is the greatest of all evils.</margin>
**POL.** How can that be, Socrates?
**SOC.** Because committing an injustice is the greatest of all evils.
**POL.** Is that really the greatest? Isn't suffering an injustice worse?
->**B**<- **SOC.** Not at all.
**POL.** Then you would prefer to suffer an injustice rather than commit one?
**SOC.** I would prefer neither. But if it were necessary either to do wrong or to suffer it, I would choose to suffer the injustice rather than commit it.
**POL.** Then you would not choose to be a tyrant.
**SOC.** Not if you define <term>tyranny</term> <note>original: "tyrannidem" (Latin) / "τυραννεῖν" (Greek); here meaning absolute power used for personal whim</note> the same way I do.
**POL.** I call it tyranny, as I said before: to have the license in the city to do whatever seems best, whether it pleases one to kill someone, or to drive them out, or to do anything else according to one's own lust.
**SOC.** But, my dear man, listen to what I say. If I were to go into the market when it is crowded with people, with a dagger tucked under my arm, and I boasted to you that I had recently acquired a wonderful power and tyranny—for if I thought any of these men you see ought to be killed, he would be struck down instantly; or if I thought someone's head should be
->**C**<- broken, it would be broken immediately; or if his cloak should be torn, it would be torn at once; such is my power in this city! But doing whatever one sees fit in this way is not "great power." Does it seem so to you?
**POL.** Certainly not in that sense.
->**D**<- **SOC.** Can you say why you do not approve of such power?
**POL.** I can indeed.
**SOC.** Why then? Tell me.

**SOC.** And to pay a penalty, is that not an evil?
**POL.** Entirely so.
**SOC.** Therefore, my wonderful man, do you not judge power to be "great" only when the person acting on their whims also acts *beneficially*, and thus achieves something good? That would be having great power. Otherwise, it is an evil and is actually "small power." But let us consider this: do we not agree that sometimes it is better to do those things we mentioned—to kill, exile, or seize property—and sometimes it is not?
**POL.** Absolutely.
**SOC.** Then it seems you and I are in agreement on this.
**POL.** Yes.
->**E**<- **SOC.** When, then, do you say it is better to do these things? Tell me, what boundary do you set?
**POL.** You should define it yourself, Socrates.
**SOC.** Then I say, Polus, if you would rather hear it from me: when someone does these things *justly*, it is better; but when *unjustly*, it is worse.
**POL.** It is very difficult to refute you, Socrates! Why, even a child could prove you wrong and show that what you say is false.
**SOC.** I would be very grateful to that child, and no less to you, if by refuting me you free me from such an error. I beg you, do not find it troublesome to bestow this benefit upon a friend; go ahead and refute me.
**POL.** Indeed, Socrates, there is no need to use ancient examples to refute you. Most recent events—things from only yesterday—are enough to prove you wrong and show that many unjust men are happy.
**SOC.** What events are these?
->**F**<- **POL.** Do you see Archelaus, the son of Perdiccas, ruling Macedonia?
**SOC.** Even if I do not see him, I have at least heard of him.
**POL.** Does he seem happy or wretched to you?
**SOC.** I do not know. I have never spoken with the man.
<margin>This is mentioned by Cicero in *Tusculan Disputations*, Book 5.</margin>
**POL.** Can you not know it any other way?
**SOC.** In no way.
**POL.** Then you will say you cannot even know if the Great King of the Persians is happy?
**SOC.** I would be telling the truth; for I do not know how he stands in terms of his education and whether he is a good man.
<margin>The just and good man is happy. The unjust man is base and wretched.</margin>
**POL.** What? Do you think the "happy life" is situated in that?
**SOC.** That is exactly what I believe: that the good are happy, and the wicked are wretched.
**POL.** Then Archelaus is wretched?
**SOC.** Certainly, if he is unjust.
**POL.** But how can that be denied? For he was born of a slave woman belonging to Alcetas, the brother of Perdiccas.
<margin>Archelaus was born from a handmaid of Alcetas.</margin>
By rights, he didn't deserve the kingdom of Macedonia he now holds; he was the slave of Alcetas by law. If he had wanted to do what was just, he would have served Alcetas and, by your reasoning, would be "happy." But now, look at the "wonderful" way he has been reduced to wretchedness after committing the greatest injustices! First, he summoned this very master and uncle of his, Alcetas, as if he were going to restore the kingdom that Perdiccas had taken. He feasted him and got him drunk; then he threw Alcetas and his son Alexander (Archelaus's own cousin and contemporary) into a wagon, took them away at night, slaughtered them, and made them disappear. Yet after doing this, he did not recognize his own wretchedness, nor did he repent. Instead, shortly afterward, he refused to let his legitimate brother (the son of Perdiccas), a boy of seven years to whom the kingdom rightfully belonged, live a "happy" life by raising him justly and returning the kingdom to him; instead, he threw him into a well and drowned him.

**SOC.** Not to me; but neither is he to be envied.

**SOC.** I meant the *unjust* man, my friend, who kills; and he is pitiable besides. But the one who kills justly is not to be envied.
**POL.** Surely the one who is killed unjustly is pitiable and wretched?

Polus attempts to refute this by citing Archelaus of Macedonia, whose successful but murderous rise to power he views as evidence that the unjust can be happy.</summary>

# GORGIAS.

[Polus continues his story about Archelaus:] ...to his mother Cleopatra, he claimed that the boy, while chasing a goose, fell into a well and died. <note>Archelaus had murdered his seven-year-old half-brother, the rightful heir, to secure his own power.</note> Therefore now, since he has committed the greatest injustices of anyone in Macedonia, he is the most wretched of all the Macedonians—but certainly not the "happiest." And perhaps there is some Athenian, starting with you, who would rather be any other Macedonian than Archelaus.

<margin>A</margin> **SOCRATES:** At the very beginning of our conversation, Polus, I praised you because you seemed to me to be well-trained in rhetoric, but to have neglected the art of dialectic <note>The Socratic method of cross-examination to find the truth, rather than just winning an argument.</note>. And now, is this the argument with which even a child could refute me? Do you think I have been refuted by you now, as you suppose, by your claim that the wrongdoer is not happy? How so, my good man? I do not agree with a single thing you say.

**POLUS:** That is because you are unwilling to agree, even though you likely think exactly as I do.

<margin>B</margin> **SOCRATES:** My dear friend, you are attempting to refute me "rhetorically," just as those in the law courts think they are refuting their opponents. For there, one side thinks they have refuted the other when they produce many famous witnesses for the claims they make, while the person speaking the opposite produces only one witness or none at all. But this kind of "refutation" is worth nothing in the pursuit of truth. Sometimes a man may be overwhelmed by the false testimony of many people who appear to be of high standing. And now, regarding what you say, almost everyone—Athenians and foreigners alike—will agree with you if you wish to produce witnesses against me to prove I am not telling the truth.

<margin>C</margin> They will testify for you: if you wish, Nicias the son of Niceratus and his brothers with him (whose dedicated tripods stand in a row in the <term>Dionysium</term> <note>The precinct of the temple of Dionysus in Athens.</note>); or if you wish, Aristocrates the son of Scellius, who dedicated that beautiful offering in the <term>Pythium</term> <note>The temple of Apollo Pythios.</note>. Or if you wish, the entire house of Pericles, or any other family you might choose from here in the city.

But I, though I stand alone, do not agree with you. You do not compel me by reason; instead, by producing many false witnesses against me, you attempt to cast me out of my "property"—which is the truth. 

<margin>D</margin> For my part, unless I can produce you, and you alone, as a witness who agrees with what I say, I consider that I have accomplished nothing of value in our discussion. And I think the same is true for you, unless I, a lone individual, testify for you and you let all those others go. This, then, is one way of refutation, as you and many others believe; but there is also another way, which I believe in. Let us compare them and see if they differ. For the things we are disputing are no small matter; they are, in fact, almost the very things which it is most honorable to know and most shameful not to know. The heart of the matter is to know or not to know who is happy and who is not.

To start with the current topic: you believe it is possible for a man who acts unjustly and is himself unjust to be happy, since you consider Archelaus to be unjust but happy. Are we to understand that this is your settled opinion?

**POLUS:** Certainly.

<margin>E</margin> **SOCRATES:** And I say it is impossible. This is the one point on which we disagree. Very well. Will the wrongdoer be happy if he meets with justice and punishment?

**POLUS:** Not at all; in that case, he would be the most wretched of men.

**SOCRATES:** But if the wrongdoer escapes justice, then according to your argument, he will be happy?

**POLUS:** That is what I say.

**SOCRATES:** But in my opinion, Polus, the man who does wrong and is unjust is wretched in any case. However, he is *more* wretched if he does not pay the penalty and does not meet with punishment for his crimes. He is *less* wretched if he pays the penalty and receives justice from both gods and men.

**POLUS:** You are attempting to say absurd things, Socrates!

**SOCRATES:** And I shall attempt to make you, my friend, say the same things as I do; for I consider you a friend. Now, these are the points on which we differ. Consider them yourself. I said earlier that doing wrong is worse than suffering it.

**POLUS:** Certainly you did.

**SOCRATES:** But you said suffering it is worse.

<margin>F</margin> **POLUS:** Yes.

**SOCRATES:** And I said those who do wrong are wretched, and you thought you refuted me?

**POLUS:** Yes, by Zeus, I did!

**SOCRATES:** In your own mind, at least, Polus.

**POLUS:** And perhaps I was right.

**SOCRATES:** But you said that wrongdoers are happy if they do not pay the penalty.

**POLUS:** Most certainly.

**SOCRATES:** And I say they are the most wretched of all, while those who pay the penalty are less so. Do you wish to refute this too?

**POLUS:** Why, this is even harder to refute than the first point, Socrates!

**SOCRATES:** Not at all, Polus; it is impossible. For the truth is never refuted.

**POLUS:** What are you saying? If a man is caught plotting to become a tyrant through injustice, and once caught he is stretched on the rack, castrated, has his eyes burned out, and after suffering many other great and <margin>G</margin> various outrages himself, and seeing his children and wife suffer the same, he is finally crucified or covered in pitch and burned alive—will *this* man be happier than if he had escaped, become the tyrant, and spent his life ruling the city, doing whatever he liked, envied and blessed by citizens and foreigners alike? Do you say it is impossible to refute that?

**SOCRATES:** You are trying to scare me with ghosts again, noble Polus, rather than refuting me; just a moment ago you were calling on witnesses. But remind me of one small thing: did you say "plotting for the tyranny *unjustly*"?

**POLUS:** I did.

<margin>H</margin> **SOCRATES:** In that case, neither of them will ever be "happier"—neither the one who unjustly seized the tyranny nor the one who was caught and punished. For between two wretched people, one cannot be happier; however, the one who escaped and became a tyrant is the more wretched of the two. Why are you laughing, Polus? Is this now a new form of refutation,

<margin>A</margin> **SOCRATES:** From the very beginning of the debate, Polus, I praised you as one well-instructed in Rhetoric, but I said you had neglected the art of reasoning. For often, because of a multitude of false witnesses, and even those who seem to be of some value and price, a person is unjustly oppressed. And yet, at present, if you wish to produce witnesses against me concerning these things you say, perhaps all the Athenians and foreigners will feel as you do. <margin>C</margin> But I alone do not agree with you. For you do not compel me with reasons, but by producing false witnesses against me, <margin>A point regarding witnesses and reasons.</margin> you strive to cast me down from the very substance of truth.

<margin>D</margin> I, however, unless I bring you yourself as a single witness agreeing with me, consider that I have accomplished nothing worthy of estimation in these matters we handle. For the head and sum of those things we investigate is either to know or to be ignorant of who is happy and who is miserable.

**POLUS:** Entirely.

**SOCRATES:** I, however, say that is impossible. This, then, is the one thing about which we are in doubt. So be it: will the unjust man be happy if he pays the penalty for his injustice?

**POLUS:** By no means; rather, he will be most wretched.

**SOCRATES:** But if the unjust man escapes punishment, as you say, he will be happy.

**POLUS:** Indeed I say so.

**SOCRATES:** But according to my opinion, Polus, he who does wrong and is unjust is altogether more miserable than others. He is more miserable if he never pays the penalty for his wrongs; but less miserable if he does pay, and receives just punishment from gods and men.

**POLUS:** How absurd are the things you dare to say!

<margin>F</margin> **SOCRATES:** I will give my effort, friend, so that you too may feel as I do; for I think you are a friend to me. **POLUS:** So you said.

**SOCRATES:** You, however, on the contrary, say to suffer it is worse than to do it. <margin>That it is worse to do wrong than to suffer it.</margin>

**POLUS:** Without a doubt.

**SOCRATES:** Moreover, I called those who do wrong miserable; and I was refuted by you.

**POLUS:** So you were, by Jove!

**SOCRATES:** In your judgment, at least.

**POLUS:** And perhaps in truth.

**SOCRATES:** You, however, said those doing wrong were happy when they did not pay the penalty.

<margin>G</margin> **POLUS:** Most especially.

**SOCRATES:** But I say those are the most wretched; while those who are punished are less wretched. Do you wish to refute that as well?

**POLUS:** But that is even more difficult than the other to refute!

**SOCRATES:** You should judge it not difficult, but impossible; for that which is true can never be refuted.

**POLUS:** I did indeed.

**SOCRATES:** Neither of them will ever be the happier: not the one who unjustly obtained the tyranny, nor the one who, being caught, paid the penalty. <meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Polus. In the previous section, Socrates argued that Polus's method of "refutation"—appealing to the opinions of the many—is useless for finding the truth, which requires only a single witness: the person one is actually talking to.</meta>

# OF PLATO

...to laugh when someone says something, rather than to refute it. <term>Polus</term> But Socrates, don't you think you have been refuted when you say things that no mortal would ever say? Just ask anyone present. <term>Socrates</term> O Polus, I am not one of those who are involved in the business of the state. In fact, last year, when I was chosen by lot to be on the Council <note>Original Latin: "in senatum." Socrates refers to the Council of 500, the governing body of Athens. I ask for the vote of only one person, and I do not say a single word to the crowd. See then if you are willing to give me my turn to refute you, and to answer what I ask. For I truly believe that both you and all other men think that doing an injury is worse than receiving one, and that escaping punishment is worse than undergoing it. <term>Polus</term> But I, for my part, do not think so, nor does any other person. <margin>The question is proposed for debate: whether it is worse to do an injury or to suffer one.</margin>
Which of the two do you think is worse? To do an injury, or to suffer one? <term>Polus</term> To suffer one. <term>Socrates</term> But which is more shameful? It seems you do not believe that "beautiful" and "good" are the same thing, nor that "shameful" and "bad" are the same. <note>In Greek thought, the "Beautiful" (kalon) often encompasses the noble or morally fine, while the "Shameful" (aischron) is the base or morally ugly.</note> <term>Polus</term> Certainly not.

<margin>Beautiful things are those which bring either utility, or pleasure, or both.</margin>
<term>Socrates</term> What about all beautiful things—for instance, bodies, colors, shapes, sounds, and ways of life? And you define it beautifully now, Socrates, by defining the "beautiful" by pleasure and the "good" that is beneficial. <term>Socrates</term> Then must we not define the "shameful" by the opposite: namely, by pain and by evil, which is to say, harm? <term>Polus</term> That must be so. <term>Socrates</term> Whenever, therefore, one of two beautiful things is more beautiful than the other, it is more beautiful because it exceeds the other in either pleasure, or utility, or both. <term>Polus</term> Precisely. <term>Socrates</term> And again, when one of two shameful things is more shameful, it must be more shameful because it exceeds the other in either pain or harm. Is that not necessary? <term>Polus</term> Yes. <term>Socrates</term> Come then, what was said a moment ago about doing and receiving an injury? Did you not say that suffering an injury is worse, but doing it is more shameful? <term>Polus</term> I did say that. <term>Socrates</term> Therefore, if doing wrong is more shameful than suffering it, is it not necessarily either more painful—and more shameful because it exceeds in pain—or in harm, or in both? <term>Polus</term> Why not? <term>Socrates</term> First, let us consider if doing an injury exceeds in pain: do those who do wrong feel more pain than those who suffer it? <term>Polus</term> Not at all, Socrates! <term>Socrates</term> So it does not exceed in pain. <term>Polus</term> It does not appear so. <term>Socrates</term> If not in pain, then it cannot be in both. <term>Polus</term> It seems not. <term>Socrates</term> Therefore, it must be the other. <term>Polus</term> The other. <term>Socrates</term> In evil and in harm, then. <term>Polus</term> It appears so. <term>Socrates</term> Because doing an injury exceeds in harm, it must be worse than suffering it. <term>Polus</term> That is manifest. <term>Socrates</term> And was it not conceded by the majority of men, and by you just now, that it is more shameful to do an injury than to receive one? <term>Polus</term> Yes. <term>Socrates</term> And now it has appeared to be worse as well? <term>Polus</term> It has. <term>Socrates</term> Would you then choose that which is worse and more shameful over that which is less so? Do not be afraid to answer, Polus. It will not hurt you; but submit yourself bravely to the argument as if to a doctor, and answer either "yes" or "no" to what I ask. <term>Polus</term> I would never choose that, Socrates. <term>Socrates</term> Do you think anyone else would? <term>Polus</term> According to this argument, it does not seem so to me.

<margin>Whether it is the greatest evil for one who commits injuries to be punished, or not to be punished.</margin>
<term>Socrates</term> Therefore I was speaking the truth when I said that neither I, nor you, nor any other man would choose to do an injury rather than suffer one, because it is worse. <term>Polus</term> It appears so. <term>Socrates</term> You see then, Polus, when we compare these arguments, they differ greatly from each other. For everyone else except me agrees with you; but for me, you alone are enough, by agreeing and testifying to my point. You are the only one whose vote and opinion I seek; the others I let go. Let this, then, be settled between us. Next, let us consider the second point we doubted: whether for a wrongdoer to pay the penalty is the greatest of evils, as you thought, or whether it is a greater evil not to pay it, which was my opinion. Let us consider it in this way...

<margin>A</margin> ...when someone says something, to laugh at them, but not to refute them. <term>Polus</term> Do you not think you have been refuted, Socrates, when you say things such as no man would ever say? <summary>In this passage from Plato's Gorgias, Socrates uses logical deduction to prove to Polus that doing an injustice is worse than suffering one, because it is more harmful, even if it is not more painful. This marks a turning point in the dialogue where Polus is forced to concede a major moral premise through the Socratic method.</summary>

# GORGIAS.

<margin>B</margin> **SOCRATES:** Do you call "paying the penalty" and "being justly punished" for doing wrong the same thing? **POLUS:** I do. **SOCRATES:** Can you say, then, that all just things are not fine, insofar as they are just? Consider carefully before you answer. <note>The Greek word used here is *kalos*, which can mean "beautiful," "noble," or "fine." Socrates is testing if Polus agrees that justice has an inherent moral beauty.</note> **POLUS:** It seems so to me, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Consider this too: if someone performs an action, must there be something that experiences the action from that person? **POLUS:** It seems so to me. **SOCRATES:** And does the thing experiencing the action experience exactly what the actor does? And in the same way? For example: if someone hits, must something be hit? **POLUS:** It must. **SOCRATES:** And if the hitter hits hard or fast, is the thing being hit likewise hit hard or fast? **POLUS:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, the experience of the thing being hit is of the same kind as the action of the hitter? **POLUS:** Entirely. **SOCRATES:** In the same way, if someone burns something, must something be burned? **POLUS:** How could it be otherwise? **SOCRATES:** And if he burns it intensely or painfully, the thing being burned is burned in exactly the same way as the burner burns it? **POLUS:** Entirely. **SOCRATES:** Does the same logic apply if someone cuts something? Something is cut. **POLUS:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** And if the cut is large or deep or painful, the thing being cut is cut in the same way as the cutter cuts it? **POLUS:** It appears so. **SOCRATES:** In short, see if you agree with what I was saying about everything: whatever the actor does, the "patient" <note>The "patient" refers to the person or thing receiving the action.</note> experiences that same thing. **POLUS:** I agree. **SOCRATES:** Given this agreement, is "paying the penalty" a matter of experiencing something, or doing something? **POLUS:** It is necessarily,

<margin>C</margin> Socrates, a matter of experiencing. **SOCRATES:** And must it not be by someone acting? **POLUS:** Certainly, by the one who punishes. **SOCRATES:** And does the one who punishes correctly punish justly? **POLUS:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** Does he act justly, or not? **POLUS:** Justly. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, the person being punished, in paying the penalty, experiences something just? **POLUS:** It appears so. **SOCRATES:** And have we not agreed that just things are fine? **POLUS:** Entirely. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, the one who punishes does something fine, and the one being punished experiences something fine. **POLUS:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** And if it is fine, it is also good? For a thing is "fine" if it is either pleasant or beneficial. **POLUS:** Necessarily. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, the person paying the penalty experiences something good. **POLUS:** It seems so. **SOCRATES:** Then he is benefited? **POLUS:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** Is the benefit what I suspect it is—that his soul becomes better if he is justly punished? **POLUS:** It is likely. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, the one paying the penalty is rid of a vice of the soul. **POLUS:** Yes. **SOCRATES:**

<margin>D</margin> Is he then rid of the greatest evil? Consider it this way: regarding a person’s wealth, do you see any evil other than poverty? **POLUS:** No, just poverty. **SOCRATES:** What about the body? Would you say its evils are weakness, disease, ugliness, and the like? **POLUS:** I would. **SOCRATES:** And do you believe there is a certain wickedness in the soul? **POLUS:** How could I not? **SOCRATES:** Do you call this injustice, ignorance, cowardice, and the like? **POLUS:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** Thus, for wealth, body, and soul—these three—you have named three types of wickedness: poverty, disease, and injustice. **POLUS:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** Which of these vices is the most shameful? Is it not injustice, and in short, the wickedness of the soul? **POLUS:** By far. **SOCRATES:** And if it is the most shameful, is it also the worst? **POLUS:** How do you mean that, Socrates? **SOCRATES:** This way: the most shameful thing is always so because it provides either the greatest pain, the greatest harm, or both, according to what we agreed earlier. <note>Socrates refers to a previous part of the dialogue where they defined the "fine" as the pleasant or useful, and the "shameful" as the painful or harmful.</note> **POLUS:** Quite so. **SOCRATES:** And have we not just agreed that injustice and all soul-wickedness is the most shameful? **POLUS:** We have. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, it is either the most painful—surpassing others in distress—or it is the most harmful, or both? **POLUS:** It must be. **SOCRATES:** Now, is being unjust, undisciplined, cowardly, or ignorant more painful than being poor or sick? **POLUS:** It does not seem so to me, Socrates, in that regard. **SOCRATES:** Then the vice of the soul surpasses the others in some extraordinary,

<margin>E</margin> wonderful magnitude of harm and amazing evil, and that is why it is the most shameful of all—since it is not surpassed in pain, according to your argument. **POLUS:** It appears so. **SOCRATES:** But surely, that which surpasses in the greatest harm must be the greatest evil in existence. **POLUS:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, injustice, lack of discipline, and other soul-wickedness is the greatest evil in existence? **POLUS:** It appears so. **SOCRATES:** Now, what art rids us of poverty? Is it not the art of money-making? **POLUS:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** And what rids us of disease? Is it not medicine? **POLUS:** Necessarily. **SOCRATES:** And what rids us of wickedness and injustice? If you don't have the answer ready, consider it this way: where and to whom do we take those whose bodies are sick? **POLUS:** To the doctors, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** And where do we take the unjust and the undisciplined? **POLUS:** You mean to the judges. **SOCRATES:** To pay the penalty, right? **POLUS:** I agree. **SOCRATES:** And is it not by using a certain kind of

<margin>G</margin> justice that those who punish correctly do their work? **POLUS:** Clearly. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, the art of money-making rids us of poverty; medicine rids us of disease; and the art of the courts rids us of lack of discipline and injustice. **POLUS:** It appears so. **SOCRATES:** Which of these, then, is the finest? **POLUS:** Which do you mean? **SOCRATES:** Money-making, medicine, or justice <note>Original Latin: *iudiciaria*. Socrates is comparing the professions that fix the three types of evil.</note>. **POLUS:** Justice is far superior, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Then it must either produce the most pleasure, the most benefit, or both, if it is the finest. **POLUS:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** Now, is being treated by a doctor pleasant? Do those being treated enjoy it? **POLUS:** I don't think so. **SOCRATES:** But it is beneficial, is it not? **POLUS:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** For the person is rid of a great evil; therefore, it is profitable to endure the pain and become healthy. **POLUS:** How could it be otherwise? **SOCRATES:** Would a person be

<margin>H</margin> happiest in their body if they were being treated, or if they had never been sick at all?

**SOCRATES:** Do you call "suffering punishment for injuries" and "being justly punished" for doing wrong the same thing? **POLUS:** The same. **SOCRATES:** Can you deny that all just things, insofar as they are just, are fine? And see that you respond prudently. **POLUS:** It seems so to me, just as it does to you. **SOCRATES:** Observe this as well: if someone acts upon something, must there be something that receives the action from the actor? **POLUS:** It seems so. **SOCRATES:** And must the receiver suffer that which the actor does? And must it be of the same quality as the action? For example: if someone hits, must something be hit? **POLUS:** It must. **SOCRATES:** And if he hits vehemently or swiftly, is the thing hit likewise hit? **POLUS:** Likewise. **SOCRATES:**

<margin>B</margin> Therefore, such a "passion" <note>In philosophy, a "passion" is simply the experience of being acted upon by an external force.</note> exists in the thing hit as the hitter produces? **POLUS:** Entirely. **SOCRATES:** And if someone burns something, must something be burned? **POLUS:** It must. **SOCRATES:** And if he burns it vehemently and, as I might say, with sharp pain, is the thing burned likewise burned in the same way as the burner burns it? **POLUS:** Exactly. **SOCRATES:** Similarly, if someone cuts, is something also cut? **POLUS:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** And if the cut is wide or deep or painful, must the thing being cut be cut by such a cut as the cutter himself makes? **POLUS:** It appears so. **SOCRATES:** Consider it summarily, then, whether you confess what I was just saying in all things: namely, that whatever the actor does, the "patient" suffers that very same thing.

<margin>C</margin> <margin>Whatever the actor does, the "patient" suffers that very same thing.</margin> **POLUS:** I confess it. **SOCRATES:** With these things conceded, answer me: is "paying the penalty" to suffer something, or to do something? **POLUS:** To suffer. **SOCRATES:** And is it not from some actor? **POLUS:** It is certain: from the one who punishes. **SOCRATES:** But does the one who punishes correctly not punish justly? **POLUS:** Justly. **SOCRATES:** Doing just things, or not? **POLUS:** Just things. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, he who is punished, while he pays the penalty for injustice, suffers just things. **POLUS:** It appears so. **SOCRATES:** And it was said that just things are fine. **POLUS:** Entirely. **SOCRATES:** Of these two, then, one does fine things, and the other—the one being punished—suffers fine things. **POLUS:** So it is. **SOCRATES:** And if they are fine, they are also good. For they are either pleasant or useful. **POLUS:** It must be so. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, he who is justly punished suffers good things. **POLUS:** It seems so. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, it is a benefit to him. **POLUS:** It is profitable. **SOCRATES:** And is it not—to explain my judgment—

<margin>D</margin> that he gains a better soul, provided he is justly punished? **POLUS:** It is consistent. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, he who pays the penalty is liberated from the depravity of the soul. **POLUS:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** Thus, he is liberated from the greatest evil. In the same way, consider: in the gathering of wealth, do you see any other evil for a man than poverty? **POLUS:** Only that. **SOCRATES:** And in the body, would you say the evil is weakness, disease, deformity, and other such things? **POLUS:** I would. **SOCRATES:** And do you not also think there is some evil in the soul? **POLUS:** Why not? **SOCRATES:** And do you not call this injustice, ignorance, cowardice, and others of that kind?

<margin>E</margin> **POLUS:** Most certainly. **SOCRATES:** Since there are these three—wealth, body, and soul—you have said there are three evils belonging to them: poverty, disease, and injustice. **POLUS:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** And of these evils, which is the most shameful? Is it not injustice? And, to speak summarily, the vice of the soul? **POLUS:** Most certainly. **SOCRATES:** But if the vice of the soul is the most shameful, then it is also the worst. **POLUS:** For what reason do you say this, O Socrates? **SOCRATES:** For this reason: that which is most shameful is so either because it causes the greatest pain, or because it brings the greatest harm, or because it does both—as appears from what was conceded earlier. **POLUS:** Truly. **SOCRATES:** And was it not conceded by us that injustice and every vice of the soul is the most shameful?

<margin>F</margin> **POLUS:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, either because it is the most troublesome, surpassing others in trouble, it is the most shameful of these; or because it brings harm; or because of both. **POLUS:** It must be so. **SOCRATES:** Is it then more troublesome to be unjust, undisciplined, cowardly, and ignorant than to be pressed by poverty and disease? **POLUS:** Certainly not, as far as can be gathered from these things. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, because the vice of the soul surpasses other evils by some incredible and wonderful magnitude of harm and evil, it is for that reason the most shameful of all; since it does not exceed them in pain, as you yourself say. **POLUS:** So it appears. **SOCRATES:** Now, that which exceeds in the greatest damage is the greatest of all evils. **POLUS:** It is so. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, injustice, lack of discipline, and other wickedness of the soul is the greatest

<margin>G</margin> evil of all. **POLUS:** It appears so. **SOCRATES:** Which art liberates us from poverty? Is it not money-making? **POLUS:** That very one. **SOCRATES:** And which from disease? Is it medicine? **POLUS:** That indeed. **SOCRATES:** But which from depravity and injustice? If that does not occur to you, consider it thus: to whom and to what place do we especially lead those laboring under bodily diseases? **POLUS:** To the doctors, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** And where do we lead the injurious and the dissolute? **POLUS:** To the judges. **SOCRATES:** To be punished, obviously. **POLUS:** I agree. **SOCRATES:** And do those who punish correctly not punish by relying on a certain justice? **POLUS:** Without a doubt. **SOCRATES:** Money-making, then, drives away poverty; Medicine drives away diseases; and the Judicial art removes lack of discipline and injustice. **POLUS:** So it appears. **SOCRATES:**

<margin>H</margin> Which of these, then, is the finest? **POLUS:** Which do you mean? **SOCRATES:** Money-making, medicine, or the judicial art. **POLUS:** The judicial art excels by far among these. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, it either brings the most pleasure, or the most utility, or both, if indeed it is the finest. **POLUS:** It is so. **SOCRATES:** Now, is being cured by a physician delightful? And do the sick take pleasure in the hands of the doctor while they are being cured? **POLUS:** It does not appear so. **SOCRATES:** Yet it is beneficial, is it not? **POLUS:** It is profitable. **SOCRATES:** Because, obviously, they are liberated from a great evil. For which reason it is useful to endure the pain, so that you may come out healthy.

<summary>Socrates uses the analogy of medical treatment to argue that just punishment is a "medicine for the soul," removing the greatest of all evils—injustice—which is more harmful than poverty or physical disease.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from the previous page where Socrates argued that it is better to suffer injustice than to commit it. Socrates and Polus are now exploring the nature of punishment as a "medicine" for the soul's diseases.</meta>

# PLATO'S [GORGIAS]

**POLUS:** Undoubtedly. **SOCRATES:** Then is the man who is cured through medicine and recovers his health the most happy regarding his body, or rather the man who never fell ill from the beginning? **POLUS:** Certainly the one who never fell ill. **SOCRATES:** For it seems that happiness does not consist in being freed from evils, but in being safe from them from the very start. **POLUS:** That is so. **SOCRATES:** Furthermore, if two people are in a bad state, either in body or soul, which of these is more miserable: the one who is treated and freed from the evil, or the one who is not? **POLUS:** The one who is not treated, in my opinion. **SOCRATES:** And wasn't being punished in a court of law a liberation from a certain very great evil—namely, from wickedness? **POLUS:** It was indeed. **SOCRATES:** Because a just penalty brings moderation <note>original: "moderetur"; the Greek "σωφρονίζει" implies making one self-controlled or "sound-minded".</note> and makes people more just, acting as a kind of medicine for wickedness. **POLUS:** That is so. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, the happiest person is the one who has no vice in their soul, since that appeared to be the greatest of all evils. **POLUS:** Without a doubt. **SOCRATES:** And second is the one who is freed from such an evil. **POLUS:** So it appears. **SOCRATES:** And that is the person who, having been caught and rebuked, has paid the penalty. **POLUS:** That very person. **SOCRATES:** The one who lives most poorly, then, is the one who is unjust and is not released from his injustice. **POLUS:** That is clear. **SOCRATES:** And is this not the person who, having committed the greatest injustices and used the greatest violence, manages to avoid being caught, punished, or made to pay the penalty—just as you say Archelaus <note>Archelaus was a King of Macedon whom Polus considers "happy" because he gained power through crimes but was never punished.</note> did, along with other tyrants, orators, and powerful men? **POLUS:** So it seems. **SOCRATES:** For men of this sort, my good friend, act almost exactly as if someone suffering from the gravest diseases should take care that he does not pay the penalty for the vices of his body to a doctor—that is, that he should not be cured. Like a child, he dreads surgery and cautery <note>Latin: "vltionem atque sectionem". The OCR "vltionem" is likely a misprint for "ustionem" (burning/cautery), matching the Greek "κάειν" (to burn).</note> as something painful. Does it not seem so to you? **POLUS:** It does to me. **SOCRATES:** Clearly because they are ignorant of the value of health and the virtue of the body. It appears from what we have just conceded, Polus, that those who flee from judgment do something similar: they look only at the pain of it, but are blind to its utility. They are ignorant of how much more miserable it is to live with a soul that is not healthy, but fractured, unjust, and impious, than to carry around a sick body. And so they take care not to undergo judgment, lest they be freed from the greatest evil. For this reason, they amass wealth, acquire friends, and study eloquence. But if we have confessed the truth to one another, do you see what follows from this discussion? Or do you want us to collect the points in order? **POLUS:** Unless you think otherwise. **SOCRATES:** Has it not been established that injustice and wrongdoing is the greatest evil? **POLUS:** It seems so. **SOCRATES:** And was it not shown that paying the penalty is the release from this evil? **POLUS:** So it appeared. **SOCRATES:** And that escaping the penalty is the persistence of the evil? **POLUS:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, doing injustice holds the second place among evils in terms of magnitude. But to do injustice and not pay the penalty is by its very nature the greatest and first of all evils. **POLUS:** It seems so. **SOCRATES:** This, then, my friend, is what we were disagreeing about. You were affirming that Archelaus was happy, because although he committed the greatest injustices, he paid no penalty. But I felt the opposite: that whether it be Archelaus or any other mortal who does not suffer punishment for his injustices, he is especially miserable. And I held that the one who inflicts injustice is always more miserable than the one who suffers it, and finally, that the one who does not pay the penalty is more miserable than the one who does. Were these not the things I was saying? **POLUS:** Those very things. **SOCRATES:** And has it not been demonstrated that these things were spoken truly? **POLUS:** It appears so. **SOCRATES:** Come then, Polus, if these things are established as true, of what great use is rhetoric? For surely it follows from what we have now agreed that we must watch ourselves most diligently: first, so that we do not commit injustice, as we would have enough evil from that alone. Is that not so? **POLUS:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** Second, if we or anyone else we care for commits an injustice, we should voluntarily offer ourselves to be punished, hurrying to the judge as if to a doctor, so that the disease of injustice does not become deep-seated and make the soul incurable. How else can we say it, Polus, if our previous agreements remain? Must these things not necessarily harmonize with those, and cannot be otherwise? <margin>Socrates wants us to accuse our friends of injustice and reveal them to the judge.</margin> **POLUS:** What else can we say, Socrates? **SOCRATES:** To defend or excuse our own injustice, then, or that of our parents, or friends, or children, or our wrongdoing country, rhetoric is of no use to us at all, Polus—unless one should judge that rhetoric ought to be used for the opposite purpose: for accusation! One should accuse oneself first, then one's family and friends, if any of them have committed an injustice. One should not hide their crimes, but bring them into the light so that they may pay the penalty and become healthy. Furthermore, one should compel oneself and others not to be cowardly, but to offer oneself bravely with eyes closed, as if to a doctor for cutting and burning, seeking the good and the honorable while disregarding the pain. Thus, if they have committed acts worthy of stripes, they should offer themselves to be beaten; if of bonds, to be bound; if of a fine, to pay it; if of exile, to be expelled; if of death, to be killed. In this matter, each person should be the accuser of themselves and their own kin, using the power of oratory for this purpose: that by revealing their injustices, they may be freed from the greatest evil of injustice. Shall we say this, Polus, or something else? **POLUS:** These things seem absurd to me, Socrates. Yet, perhaps they do harmonize with what was said before. **SOCRATES:** Is it not necessary either to pull down those previous conclusions, or to allow these following ones to stand? **POLUS:** That is how the matter stands. **SOCRATES:** On the contrary, if one must do harm to someone, whether an enemy or anyone else, provided only...

<column-break/>

**POLUS:** Clearly it is the one who is not even sick. **SOCRATES:** For happiness was not, it seems, the riddance of evil, but rather never possessing it in the first place. **POLUS:** That is so. **SOCRATES:** What then? Which of two people who have an evil, whether in body or soul, is more wretched? The one who is treated and rid of the evil, or the one who is not treated and keeps it? **POLUS:** It seems to me it is the one who is not treated.
**SOCRATES:** Then was not paying the penalty a riddance of the greatest evil, namely wickedness? **POLUS:** It was. **SOCRATES:** For punishment, I suppose, brings one to their senses <note>original: "Σωφρονίζει" (sophronizei); to make sound of mind or moderate.</note> and makes them more just, and justice becomes the medicine of wickedness. **POLUS:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** The happiest man, therefore, is he who has no vice in his soul, since this was shown to be the greatest of evils. **POLUS:** Clearly. **SOCRATES:** And the second, I suppose, is he who is being rid of it. **POLUS:** It seems so. **SOCRATES:** And this is the one who is admonished, rebuked, and pays the penalty. **POLUS:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** The one who has injustice and is not rid of it, therefore, lives the worst life. **POLUS:** It appears so. **SOCRATES:** And does this not happen to be the man who, committing the greatest crimes and practicing the greatest injustice, manages to avoid being admonished, or chastised, or paying the penalty—just as you say Archelaus has managed, and other tyrants, orators, and potentates? **POLUS:** It seems so. **SOCRATES:** For these people, my best of men, have achieved almost the same thing as if someone afflicted with the greatest diseases should manage not to give an account to the doctors for the errors of his body, and not be treated—fearing, as a child might, the burning and the cutting because it is painful. Or do you not also think so? **POLUS:** I do. **SOCRATES:** Being ignorant, as it seems, of what health and excellence of body is like. For they risk doing something of this sort, based on what we have now agreed, Polus: those who flee from the penalty look at its painfulness, but are blind to its benefit. They are ignorant of how much more wretched it is to live with a soul that is not healthy, but rotten, unjust, and unholy, than with an unhealthy body. Wherefore they do everything so as not to pay the penalty and be rid of the greatest evil, both amassing wealth and friends and ensuring they are as persuasive as possible in speaking. But if we have agreed to the truth, Polus, do you perceive the consequences of our argument? Or do you want us to sum them up? **POLUS:** Unless you think otherwise. **SOCRATES:** Does it then follow that injustice and doing wrong is the greatest evil? **POLUS:** It appears so. **SOCRATES:** And indeed, paying the penalty was shown to be a riddance of this evil. **POLUS:** Likely so. **SOCRATES:** And not paying it is a persistence of the evil? **POLUS:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** Because of these things, then, doing injustice is the second greatest evil; but doing injustice and not paying the penalty is by nature the greatest and first of all evils. **POLUS:** It seems so. **SOCRATES:** Was it not about this, my friend, that we were at odds? You were calling Archelaus happy, who does the greatest wrongs and pays no penalty; whereas I thought the opposite—that whether it be Archelaus or any other man who does not pay the penalty when he does wrong, it is his lot to be wretched beyond all other men; and that the one who does wrong is always more wretched than the one who is wronged, and the one who does not pay the penalty more than the one who does. Were these not the things I was saying? **POLUS:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** Has it not then been proven that what was said was true? **POLUS:** It appears so. **SOCRATES:** Very well. If these things are true, Polus, what then is the great use of rhetoric? For indeed, from our current agreements, one must most of all watch himself so that he does not do wrong, knowing he will have sufficient evil. Is that not so? **POLUS:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** And if he does wrong, either himself or anyone else for whom he cares, he should go of his own accord to where he will most quickly pay the penalty—to the judge, as if to a doctor—hurrying so that the disease of injustice does not become chronic and make the soul festering and incurable. Or how are we to say it, Polus, if our previous agreements still hold? Is it not necessary that these things harmonize with those in this way, and not otherwise? **POLUS:** What else are we to say, Socrates? **SOCRATES:** For the purpose of defending one's own injustice, then, or that of parents or companions or children or a wrongdoing country, rhetoric is of no use to us, Polus—unless one should suppose that one ought to accuse oneself most of all, and then one's kin and anyone else among one's friends who happens to do wrong; and not to hide it, but to bring the wrongdoing into the open so that he may pay the penalty and become healthy. One should compel both himself and others not to be a coward, but to offer himself with eyes shut and bravely, as if to a doctor for cutting and burning, pursuing the good and fine without calculating the pain. If he has done wrongs worthy of lashes, he should offer himself to be struck; if of bonds, to be bound; if of a fine, to pay it; if of exile, to be banished; if of death, to be executed—being himself the first accuser of both himself and his own kin; and not sparing them, but using rhetoric for this purpose: that by making the injustices manifest, they may be rid of the greatest evil, injustice. Shall we say this, or shall we not, Polus? **POLUS:** These things seem strange to me, Socrates; yet they perhaps harmonize with what you said before. **SOCRATES:** Then either those earlier points must be refuted, or these must necessarily follow. **POLUS:** Yes, that is how it is. **SOCRATES:** But turning it around, if one must indeed do harm to someone, whether an enemy or anyone else, provided only...

<summary>In this passage from Plato's Gorgias, Socrates argues that punishment is the medicine of the soul, and that the most wretched person is the one who commits a crime and escapes punishment. He concludes with the paradox that rhetoric should be used to ensure one is punished for their wrongs rather than to avoid justice.</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Polus, Archelaus, justice, medicine for the soul, rhetoric, punishment, moral philosophy, Gorgias, Plato</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue where Socrates argues that rhetoric's only true "use" for an unjust man is to ensure his enemies remain unpunished—and therefore "sick" in their souls—while ensuring he himself faces justice to be "cured."</meta>

# GORGIAS

### BB iiij

At the very least, one must take care that he himself does not suffer injustice from his enemy. But if his enemy has committed an injustice against others, he must provide by every means, in both word and deed, that the enemy does not pay the penalty, nor be brought before a judge. But if he is dragged there, he must perhaps strive to ensure that his enemy escapes and does not pay the price. Indeed, if he has stolen much gold, he should not return it, but keep it and spend it unjustly and impiously upon himself and his own. If he has committed crimes worthy of death, he should see to it that he never dies, if possible, but remains immortal in his wickedness. If that is not possible, he should at least live as long as possible in that depravity. For these things and others like them, Polus, rhetoric seems useful to me. But for the man who does not intend to do wrong, it does not seem to be of any great benefit—if indeed there is any benefit or utility in it at all. For in what was said previously, no such thing appeared.

**CALLICLES:** Tell me, Chaerephon, is Socrates speaking in earnest now, or is he joking?

**CHAEREPHON:** It seems to me, Callicles, that he is speaking quite seriously. However, there is nothing like asking the man himself.

**CALLICLES:** By the gods, I am eager to know. Tell me, Socrates, should we believe you are serious now, or joking? For if you are serious and these things you say are true, then the life of us humans would be turned upside down, and it seems we are doing exactly the opposite of what we ought to do.

**SOCRATES:** Callicles, if there were not a common experience <note>The Greek term is *pathos*, referring to a shared feeling or internal state.</note> among men—some having one and some another, yet the same in many—but if instead one of us had a unique and singular feeling different from the rest, it would not be easy to explain what one felt to others. Why do I say this? Because I notice that you and I are currently experiencing the same thing: we are two men, each in love with two things. I love Alcibiades, the son of Cleinias, and Philosophy; you love the Athenian people <note>original: "demum"; referring to the *Demos*, the citizen body of Athens.</note> and Pyrilampus. <note>Specifically, the handsome son of Pyrilampus, Demus.</note> I notice that in every instance, as clever as you are, you are unable to contradict your beloveds. Whatever they say and however they claim a thing to be, you cannot speak against it, but you are shifted up and down and changed. For in the assembly, if you are saying something and the Athenian people say it is not so, you change your opinion and say whatever you perceive will please them. You experience the same thing with that beautiful young son of Pyrilampus; you are unable to resist his will. Therefore, if anyone were to wonder at the absurdities you speak for their sake, you would perhaps answer him—if you wished to tell the truth—that unless your beloveds stop speaking this way, you will never stop either. Understand, then, that you must hear similar things from me, and do not wonder that I say them. Instead, make my mistress, Philosophy, cease saying them. For she always says, my dear friend, what you are hearing from me now. She is much less foolish and stubborn than my other beloved. For that son of Cleinias says one thing at one time and another at another, but Philosophy is always the same. She says the things that you now wonder at—and you were just now present to hear them. Either, then, refute her (as I was just saying) and prove that doing wrong and not paying the penalty for it is not the ultimate of all evils; or, if you let this stand unrefuted, then by the dog, the god of the Egyptians, <note>Socrates’ famous idiosyncratic oath, likely referring to the jackal-headed god Anubis.</note> Callicles will never agree with you, Callicles, but will be at odds with you for your whole life. And yet I think, my good man, that it would be better for my lyre to be out of tune and dissonant, or for a choir I was leading to be out of harmony, or for most men to disagree with me and speak against me, than for me, being one man, to be out of harmony with myself and contradict myself.

**CALLICLES:** O Socrates, you seem to be acting like a youthful braggart in your speeches, and you truly appear to be a demagogue <note>original: "concionator"; a public speaker who stirs up the crowd.</note>. And now you are playing the demagogue because the same thing happened to Polus that he accused Gorgias of suffering at your hands. For he said that when Gorgias was asked by you whether he would teach justice to someone who came to him to learn rhetoric but was ignorant of justice, Gorgias was moved by shame and said he would teach him, because of the habits of men who would be offended if someone refused. Because of this admission, Gorgias was forced to contradict himself—which is exactly what you love. Polus laughed at you then, and in my opinion, rightly so. But now he has suffered the same thing himself. And for this very reason, I do not admire Polus: because he conceded to you that doing wrong is more shameful <note>original: "turpius"</note> than suffering it. For by this concession, he was tied up by you in the argument and had his mouth shut, being ashamed to say what he really thought. For you, Socrates, truly lead people into such troublesome and populist traps—claiming all the while to be pursuing the truth—bringing up things that are not beautiful by nature, but only by law <term>Law vs. Nature: Callicles introduces the distinction between *Nomos* (human convention/law) and *Physis* (natural reality).</term>. For the most part, these two are contrary to each other: Law and Nature. If someone is overcome by shame and does not dare to speak what he thinks, he is compelled to contradict himself. You have noticed this clever trick and you use it maliciously in your arguments. If someone speaks according to law, you ask questions according to nature; if he speaks according to nature, you ask according to law. Just as you did now regarding doing and suffering injustice. For when Polus said that doing it was more shameful according to law, you pursued the argument as if it were according to nature. For by nature, whatever is worse is also more shameful, such as suffering injustice; but by law, doing it is more shameful. Indeed, suffering injustice is not even the experience of a real man, but of a slave, for whom it is better to be dead than to live—who, when he is insulted and wronged,

<summary>Callicles enters the debate, accusing Socrates of using intellectual "traps" and social shame to win arguments. He introduces the crucial distinction between "Nature" (where the strong dominate) and "Law" (which he claims is a tool used by the weak to restrain the strong).</summary>
