# OF PLATO

<margin>A</margin> ...he is affected, and can help neither himself nor his friends. But, as I think, those who establish the laws are the weak men and the masses. Therefore, looking to their own advantage, they establish these laws. Furthermore, they distribute praise and blame, being driven by a fear of the more powerful, lest they be surpassed in any matter. And so they say it is shameful and unjust for some to have more than others, and they define this as "doing wrong": namely, seeking to have more than others. For they think it is enough for them if, being inferior, they have an equal share. For this reason, then, it is said by law that it is unjust and shameful to seek to possess more than the rest; and this the common people name "injustice." But nature itself, 
<margin>B</margin> I believe, demonstrates that it is just for the better and more powerful to have more than the others. It shows this in many ways: both in other animals and in all cities and nations, where it is judged just that the more powerful should dominate the weaker and possess more. For by what right did Xerxes lead his army against the Greeks, or his father against the Scythians, or countless others one could mention? But these men, I believe, act according to the nature of right itself, and (by Jupiter) according to the law of nature itself; though perhaps not according to these laws established by us, through which we take the adolescents of the most excellent and strongest character from their cradles—binding them like lions—and fascinate them with certain magic spells <note>The Greek term is *epodais*, referring to incantations or charms used to "tame" the spirited youth.</note> and subdue them in a slave-like manner, saying that equality must be preserved, and that this is beautiful and just. But if a man of an excellent nature should arise, shaking off and tearing through and trampling underfoot all your writings, charms, incantations, and all the laws that depart from nature, he would stand up and appear as our master instead of our slave; and there the justice of nature itself would shine forth. It seems to me that Pindarus <note>Pindar, the lyric poet.</note> shows these same things in a certain song: where he says that law is the queen of all, mortals and immortals alike; and that she carries out justice by force with a most powerful hand.
<margin>D</margin> And he says he gathers this from the deeds done by Hercules: who—though I do not remember the poem well enough—I remember him saying that Hercules drove away the oxen of Geryon without having bought them or received them as a gift; as if by natural right itself it were dictated that both oxen and all other things possessed by men should belong to him who is more excellent and stronger. The truth, therefore, is this. And you would clearly recognize it if you would now turn to greater things, having dismissed your concern for philosophizing. For philosophy, O Socrates, is a graceful and charming thing if one touches upon it moderately in one's youth. But if one spends time in it 
<margin>E</margin> beyond measure, it is the ruin of men. For even if someone is endowed by nature with a good disposition, yet if he continues to philosophize late into life, he must necessarily turn out ignorant of all those things in which a man who intends to be distinguished, good, and excellent ought to be skilled. For they become ignorant of the laws of the city, and of the words which one must use in the customs and gatherings of men both publicly and privately, and furthermore of human pleasures and desires; and to put it briefly, they become altogether ignorant of morals. Therefore, whenever they turn to any business, whether public or private, they are held as ridiculous, just as public men are ridiculous when they descend into your exercises 
<margin>F</margin> and disputes. For that saying of Euripides happens to be true: *Each man shines in that, and hastens toward that, and devotes the greatest part of the day to that, wherein he may surpass himself.* But where he is inferior, he flees from it and disparages it; but he praises the other, out of a certain benevolence toward himself, thinking that he thus praises himself. But I think it is better to participate in both: in philosophy as far as is fitting for the sake of education <note>The original Latin uses *disciplinae gratia*, corresponding to the Greek *paideias charin*.</note>. Nor indeed is it shameful for a youth to philosophize. But when an older man is still leaning upon philosophy, the thing, Socrates, becomes truly ridiculous. Indeed, I 
<margin>G</margin> feel similarly toward those who give their effort to philosophy as I do toward those who lisp and play. For whenever I see a little child, for whom it is still decorous to speak, so lisping and playing, I am delighted; and it seems to me festive and liberal, and fitting for the age of a child. But whenever I hear a little boy expressing his words more precisely, it seems a bitter thing to me, and it offends my ears; it seems to show something slave-like. But when one hears a man lisping, or sees him playing, it appears truly ridiculous, and foreign to a man, and worthy of a beating. The same thing, therefore, happens to me regarding those who philosophize. For when I see philosophy in a young adolescent, I am greatly delighted, and I judge it fitting, and I consider this man to be free-born; but him who does not philosophize, I consider illiberal, and one who will never 
<margin>H</margin> present anything distinguished or noble concerning himself. But when I notice an older man still philosophizing and not yet putting away such studies, I think this man, Socrates, is now in need of lashes. For, as I was just saying, it happens to this man that even if he is well-born, he turns out idle and unmanly. For he flees the center of the city and the marketplaces, in which the poet says men become most illustrious; and he hides himself away with three or four boys, and spends his life whispering in corners.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...and unguarded, and unable to help himself, nor another, even if he cares for him. But I think the ones who make the laws are the weak men and the many. They establish laws for themselves and for their own advantage, and they distribute praises and 
reproaches, terrifying the stronger among men and those who are able to have more, so that they may not have more than themselves; they say that seeking to have more (pleonexia) <note>original: "πλεονεκτεῖν" (pleonektein) - to have more, often implying greed or overreaching.</note> is shameful and unjust. And this is what "doing injustice" is: seeking to have more than others. For they are content, I think, if they themselves have an equal share, being of the baser sort. Because of these things, by law, this is called unjust and shameful: seeking to have 
<margin>B</margin> more than the many; and they call it "doing injustice." But nature itself, I think, would show that it is just for the better man to have more than the worse, and the more powerful than the less powerful. It shows in many places that this is so, both among other animals and among men in whole cities and races: that justice is judged thus—for the stronger to rule the weaker and to have more. For by what justice did Xerxes campaign against Greece? Or his father against the Scythians? Or ten thousand other such things one could mention. But I think these men act according to the 
<margin>C</margin> nature of justice, and by Zeus, according to the law of nature; not perhaps according to this law which we establish, molding the best and strongest among us, taking them from youth like lions, and by charms and spells we enslave them, saying that they must have an equal share, and that this is the beautiful and the just. But I think if a man were to arise with a sufficient nature, shaking off all these things and breaking through them and escaping and trampling underfoot your writings and tricks and incantations and laws that are all against nature, he would rise up and be revealed as our master instead of our slave, and there 
<margin>D</margin> the justice of nature would shine out. It seems to me that Pindarus also indicates what I am saying in the song in which he says that law is the king of all mortals and immortals. And this law (he says) leads by force that which is most just with a supreme hand. He proves this by the deeds of Hercules. Since he says something like "unbought"—for I do not know the song perfectly—but he says that neither having bought them nor with Geryon giving them did he drive away the oxen; as this was justice by nature: that both oxen and all other possessions belong to the better and stronger, rather than the worse and weaker. This then is the truth, and you will know it if you come to greater things, leaving philosophy aside now. For 
philosophy, O Socrates, is a charming thing if one touches it moderately 
<margin>E</margin> in one's youth; but if one spends more time in it than is necessary, it is the destruction of men. For even if one is very gifted and philosophizes far into old age, he must necessarily become inexperienced in all things in which he who intends to be a beautiful, good, and famous man must be experienced. For they become inexperienced in the laws of the city, and in the words which one must use in dealing with men in contracts, both privately and publicly, and in human pleasures and desires; and in short, they become altogether inexperienced in characters. Therefore, whenever they come into some private or political business, they become ridiculous. Just as, I think, the 
<margin>F</margin> politicians are ridiculous when they come into your pastimes and your words. For that of Euripides happens: *Each man is brilliant in this, and toward this he presses, allotting the greatest part of his day to this, so that he may turn out to be at his best.* But wherever he is base, he flees from it and slanders it, but praises the other out of goodwill for himself, thinking that in this way he praises himself. But I think it is most correct to participate in both. It is beautiful to participate in philosophy for the sake of education, and it is not shameful for a youth to philosophize; but when a man is already older and still philosophizes, the thing, Socrates, becomes ridiculous. And I feel exactly the same toward those who philosophize as toward those who lisp and play. For when I see a child, to whom it still 
<margin>G</margin> belongs to speak thus, lisping and playing, I rejoice, and it seems charming to me and liberal and fitting for the child's age; but when I hear a little boy speaking clearly, it seems to me a bitter thing and it pains my ears, and seems to me to be something slave-like. But when one hears a man lisping or sees him playing, it appears ridiculous and unmanly and worthy of blows. I feel this same thing toward those who philosophize. For seeing philosophy in a young youth, I admire it, and it seems to me fitting, and I consider this man to be free; but him who does not philosophize, I consider unfree, and one who will never consider himself worthy 
of any beautiful or noble thing. But when I see an 
<margin>H</margin> older man still philosophizing and not being rid of it, this man, Socrates, seems to me to already need blows. For as I was just saying, even if he is very gifted, it happens to this man to become unmanly, fleeing the center of the city and the marketplaces in which the poet said men become most illustrious; and sinking down, he spends the rest of his life with youths in a corner, whispering with three or four.

<summary>Callicles delivers a provocative speech arguing that "justice" is merely a convention created by the weak to restrain the strong, whereas "natural justice" dictates that the superior should rule and possess more. He further mocks Socrates for his lifelong devotion to philosophy, calling it a childish pursuit that leaves grown men socially incompetent and unmanly.</summary>

-># GORGIAS.<-

A ...never utter anything noble or magnificent <note>original: "λυσιτελοῦντα... φθέγξασθαι"</note>. But I, Socrates, feel quite kindly and friendly toward you. I seem to have been affected toward you just as Zethus was toward Amphion in the play by Euripides, whom I mentioned earlier. Indeed, it comes to my mind to say to you the same sorts of things that he said to his brother: "Socrates, you neglect what you ought to care for; though you have a soul of such noble nature, you distinguish yourself with a certain boyish form. You could neither offer a word correctly in the councils of justice, nor could you grasp what is likely and persuasive, nor could you form a vigorous plan on behalf of another." And yet, my dear Socrates—and do not be angry with me, for I speak out of B goodwill for you—does it not seem shameful to you to be in the state I think you are in, along with all those others who constantly drive further into philosophy? For now, if someone were to seize you, or anyone else like you, and lead you away to prison, claiming you were doing wrong when you were doing no wrong at all, you know that you would not know what to do with yourself; you would reel and gape <note>original: "ἰλιγγιῴης ἂν καὶ χασμῷο" — a vivid description of a philosopher's confusion when faced with the harsh reality of the legal system.</note>, having nothing to say. And when you went up into the court, even if you met with a completely base and miserable accuser, you would die if he chose to seek the death penalty. And yet, how can this be wisdom, Socrates—if an art finds a man of naturally good character and makes him worse, C unable to help himself or to save himself or anyone else from the greatest dangers, but allows him to be stripped of all his property by his enemies, and literally to live as an outcast in the city? Toward such a man (if I may speak a bit crudely), it is permitted to strike him on the cheek without paying a penalty. But, my good friend, listen to me: stop your cross-examinations. Practice the music of great affairs <note>This is an allusion to the Euripidean debate between the brothers Zethus (the worker/politician) and Amphion (the musician/philosopher).</note>, and practice what will make you seem wise; leave these clever subtleties to others—whether they should be called nonsense or follies—

> from which you will come to dwell in empty houses.

Do not emulate men who cross-examine these trifles, but those who have a life and reputation and many other good things. **SOCRATES:** If I happened to have a golden soul, Callicles, do you not think I would be glad to find one of those D stones with which they test gold—the best one—against which I could bring my soul? If that stone agreed with me that my soul had been well cared for, I would then know for certain that I am in a good state and have no further need of another test. **CALLICLES:** Why do you ask this, Socrates? **SOCRATES:** I will tell you. I think that in meeting you, I have happened upon such a lucky find <note>original: "ἑρμαίῳ" — literally a "gift from Hermes," a stroke of good luck.</note>. **CALLICLES:** Why so? **SOCRATES:** I know well that if you agree with the opinions my soul holds, then those things are the very truth. For I realize that he who intends to sufficiently test a soul regarding whether it lives rightly or not must have three things, all of which you possess: knowledge, goodwill, and frankness <note>original: "ἐπιστήμην τε, καὶ εὔνοιαν, καὶ παῤῥησίαν"</note>. I meet many people who are not able to test me because they are not wise like you. E Others are wise, but they do not wish to tell me the truth because they do not care for me as you do. These two guests here, Gorgias and Polus, are both wise and my friends, but they are somewhat lacking in frankness and are more ashamed than they ought to be. How could they not be? They have come to such a point of shame that, because of it, each of them dares to contradict himself in front of many people, and that too regarding the most important matters. But you have all these things that the others lack: you are sufficiently educated, as many of the Athenians would say, and you are well-disposed toward me. What evidence do I have for this? I will tell you. I know, Callicles, that there are four of you who have become partners in wisdom: yourself, Tisandrus of Aphidnae, Andron the son of Androtion, and Nausicydes of Cholargos. Once I overheard you deliberating how far one should practice wisdom; and I know that a certain opinion prevailed among you: that one should not F be eager to philosophize with exactness. Instead, you exhorted one another to be careful lest, by becoming wiser than is proper, you should unknowingly become corrupted. Since, therefore, I hear you giving me the same advice you gave your closest companions, it is sufficient evidence for me that you are truly well-disposed toward me. And indeed, that you are the sort of man to speak frankly and not be ashamed, you say so yourself, and the speech you gave a little while ago agrees with you. It stands thus: clearly, if you agree with me on anything in our discussion, that point will have been sufficiently tested by you and me, and there will no longer be any need to refer it to another test. G For you would never have conceded it either through lack of wisdom or through an excess of shame; nor would you concede it to deceive me, for you are my friend, as you yourself say. Truly, then, your agreement and mine will reach the very goal of truth. And the investigation of these things about which you rebuked me is the most beautiful of all, Callicles: what sort of man one ought to be, what he should pursue, and to what extent, both when he is older and when he is young. For if I H do anything not rightly in my own life, be well assured that I do not err willingly, but through my own ignorance. You, then, just as you began to admonish me, do not stop; but show me clearly what this is that I should pursue, and in what way I might achieve it. And if you catch me now agreeing with you, but in later time not doing the same things I agreed to—

<column-break/>

A ...never to bring forth anything liberal or magnificent. Toward you, however, Socrates, I am well and kindly affected. Therefore, I think the same thing has happened to me regarding you as happened to Zethus regarding Amphion in Euripides, whom I mentioned just now. For certain such things come into my mind to say to you now, as he said to his brother. Truly, Socrates, you neglect those things which it was fitting for you to care for, and you even distort <note>original: "corformas" — likely a rendering of the Greek *diaprepeis*, implying a mis-shaping or peculiar appearance.</note> the excellence of a noble mind with a certain boyish appearance; as one who could neither speak words rightly in judgments or consultations if use required it, nor choose anything B suitable or probable, nor could you promptly consult for others. Therefore, friend Socrates, do not be angry with me. For my benevolence toward you now leads me to bring these things forward. Does it not seem shameful to you to be so disposed, as I think both you and all others are who pursue philosophy too long? For surely if someone were to seize you now, or anyone else from your group, and drag you into prison, and accuse you of inflicting some injury—even though you inflicted none—certainly you would not know what to do; but you would reel and gape, being entirely ignorant of your defense. Then, brought into judgment, even by a cowardly and abject accuser, you would be affected by the ultimate punishment <note>death</note>, if only it pleased him. Now truly, how does this pertain to wisdom, Socrates: if C any art, having found a man of noble mind, renders him worse, so that he is neither able to bring help to himself, nor to save himself or anyone else from the gravest dangers, but exposes him to the injuries of thieving enemies, living without honor in the city? Now indeed, it is permitted to strike such a man upon the cheek with impunity, even if it is a crude thing to say. Therefore, good man, listen to me, and cease now to be occupied in vain subtleties: practice the becoming duties of managing affairs, and those things from which you may seem to be wise. Leave those clever things—whether they ought to be called delusions or trifles—from which you will have empty houses to live in, to others. Finally, imitate not those who hunt for these small things, but those who have a livelihood, and glory, and many other very great goods. **SOCRATES:** If I had a golden soul, Callicles, D do you not think I would gladly find some one of those stones by which gold is usually tested—the best one—to which, applying my soul, if it were approved by it as if rightly educated, I would know for certain that I have enough, and do not require further proof?

<margin>
One who would test someone's soul ought to have three things: knowledge, benevolence, and boldness.
</margin>

**CALLICLES:** To what end is this, Socrates? **SOCRATES:** I will tell you. Indeed, I think that since I have found you, I have found this precious stone. **CALLICLES:** For what reason? **SOCRATES:** Because I know for certain that those things which you feel with me, among those which my mind thinks, will be true without a doubt. For I judge that in him who would test a soul, whether it is indeed rightly in justice or not, three things are chiefly required, all of which are in you: first knowledge, then opinion <note>In this context, *opinion* suggests a considered judgment.</note>—namely of a wise and E benevolent man—and thirdly, boldness <note>Latin: *audaciam*; Greek: *parrhesia*.</note>. For I find many who cannot test me rightly for this reason: because they are not wise, as you seem to be. Others are indeed wise, but they are unwilling to tell me the truth because they do not have a care for me as you do. But those foreigners, Gorgias and Polus, are indeed wise and they love me, but they lack boldness, and they are more modest than they ought to be. Indeed, to whom could this be a matter of doubt? For they have proceeded so far in modesty that both of them, on account of that very modesty, have dared to contradict themselves regarding the greatest matters in the presence of many men. While others lack all these things, F you have them. In the first place, you have been quite liberally educated, as many 

<margin>
The opinion of Callicles and his friends: One must not strive for an exact diligence in philosophy.
</margin>

Athenians would confirm, and you are benevolent toward me. By what conjecture I understand this, I will tell you. I know indeed, Callicles, that four of you were associates in the study of wisdom: you, of course, and Tisandrus of Aphidnae, and Andron the son of Androtion, and Nausicydes of Cholargos; and when once it was discussed among you how far one should study wisdom, I heard that such an opinion prevailed among you: that one should not strive for an exact diligence in philosophy, but one should beware lest, having become wise beyond what is fitting, you should secretly deprave yourselves. When, therefore, I hear you giving me the same G advice that you gave to your dearest friends, it is an abundantly great argument of your true love toward me. Lastly, that boldness is not lacking, and that shame does not hinder you, both you yourself affirm, and the speech which you held here a little while ago bears witness. Since these things are so, if you concede anything to me in disputing, it will have been sufficiently proven by us; nor will it be necessary to refer it to another test; otherwise you would never have conceded it to me, either from a defect of wisdom, or led by modesty, or for the sake of deceiving. For 

<margin>
A most beautiful agreement of things.
</margin>

you are a friend to me, as you yourself say. Truly, therefore, my confession and yours will now have the end of truth. But the consideration of these things in which you yourself rebuked me, Callicles, is the most beautiful of all: what sort of man it is fitting to be, and what and how far it is suitable to practice, as much in H youth as in old age. For I, indeed, if I do anything less rightly in my life, hold it certain that I wander not by my own will but rather by ignorance. Therefore, do you, as you began to admonish me, continue I pray, and clearly demonstrate to me what that very thing is, and by what way I may be able to follow that which you think I should seek. For if you find me consenting to you now, but afterwards you find me performing less than what I agreed to...

<summary>Callicles warns Socrates that his philosophical life makes him legally and politically vulnerable, comparing him to the impractical brother in a famous play. Socrates welcomes this critique, calling Callicles the perfect "touchstone" to test the truth because he possesses the rare combination of knowledge, friendship, and blunt honesty.</summary>

...think me altogether sluggish and lazy, and do not waste any more effort in admonishing me as if I were a lost cause. But resume for me from the beginning: how do you and Pindar <note>Pindar was a Greek lyric poet who famously wrote that "Law is king of all," a phrase Callicles interprets as the law of nature rather than man-made law.</note> say that justice stands according to nature? Is it that the more powerful should take by force what belongs to the weaker, and the better should rule the worse, and the more excellent should have more than the lowly? Do you say justice is anything else, or do I remember correctly?

<margin>A</margin>
CALLICLES. I was saying these things then, and I say them now. SOCRATES. But do you call the "better" and the "more powerful" the same thing? For I was not able to understand plainly then what you meant. Do you call the stronger "the more powerful," and is it necessary for the weaker to obey the stronger? You seemed to demonstrate this earlier when you said that large cities attack small ones by natural right because they are more powerful and stronger—as if being more powerful, stronger, and "better" were all the same. Or is it possible to be "better" but also inferior and weaker? And similarly, to be more powerful but "worse"? Or is the definition of "better" and "powerful" the same? Explain this to me more clearly: are "more powerful," "better," and "stronger" the same thing or different things?

<margin>B</margin>
CAL. Indeed, I clearly assert to you that they are the same. SOC. Is not the multitude <note>The "multitude" or "the many" (Greek: hoi polloi) refers to the general population or the masses.</note> itself naturally more powerful than a single person? It is they, after all, who establish the laws over the individual, as you were just saying. CAL. Of course. SOC. Therefore, the laws of the multitude are the laws of the "more powerful." CAL. Entirely so. SOC. Are they not also the laws of the "better"? For those who are more powerful, as you say, are much better. CAL. Certainly. SOC. Are not their institutions naturally "noble" <note>original: "καλὰ" (kala) — meaning beautiful, noble, or morally good</note>, since they are the more powerful?

<margin>C</margin>
CAL. I affirm it. SOC. Does not this multitude believe—as you were just saying—that it is just for equality to be maintained among all, and that it is more shameful to inflict an injury than to suffer one? Is it so or otherwise? And take care that you are not caught being "ashamed" <note>Socrates is teasing Callicles, suggesting he might be too embarrassed to admit that the "stronger" masses actually prefer equality.</note> here. Does this multitude believe or not that justice is maintaining equity, and not one person having more than another, and that doing wrong is more shameful than receiving it? Do not let any grudge, Callicles, keep you from answering this, so that if you agree with me, I may be confirmed by you as a man fully capable of judging.

<margin>D</margin>
CAL. The multitude certainly thinks so. SOC. Therefore, it is not by law alone that doing wrong is more shameful than suffering it, and that it is just to maintain equality, but also by nature itself. Therefore, you seem to have spoken untruly in your earlier remarks when you accused me, claiming that law and nature were opposites, and that I, realizing this, was playing a "crafty rogue" <note>original: "Veteratorem" / "κακουργῶ" — someone who uses deceptive tricks in an argument.</note> in our dispute: leading the argument toward "law" when someone speaks according to nature, and toward "nature" when someone speaks according to law. CAL. This man will never stop talking nonsense! Tell me, Socrates, are you not ashamed, at your age, to be hunting for names? <note>original: "ὀνόματα θηρεύων" — Callicles accuses Socrates of "word-hunting" or arguing over definitions rather than substance.</note> If someone trips over a word, do you treat it as a lucky find? Do you think I mean anything else by "more powerful" than "the better"? Haven't I been saying for a long time that "the better" and "the more powerful" are the same? Or do you think I am saying that if a rabble of slaves and all sorts of worthless men happens to congregate—men who are perhaps powerful only in physical strength—that whatever they decree are "laws"?

<margin>E</margin>
SOC. Very well, O most wise Callicles, is that what you mean? CAL. Most certainly. SOC. But I, blessed man, have long suspected you meant something of that sort, and I ask because I desire to know clearly what you mean. For surely you do not think two people are "better" than one, nor your slaves "better" than you, just because they are stronger? But tell me again from the beginning, who do you mean are the "better," since they are not the "stronger"? And please, wonderful man, teach me more gently, so that I do not run away from your school. CAL. You are being ironic, Socrates. SOC. No, by Zethus <note>A reference to the character Zethus from Euripides' play *Amphion*, whom Callicles cited earlier to criticize Socrates.</note>, Callicles, the very one you used to use so much irony against me just now! But come, tell me: whom do you call the "better"? CAL. I mean the more excellent. SOC. You see then, you are just uttering names, but showing nothing? Will you not explain if by "better" and "more powerful" you mean the "more prudent" <note>original: "φρονιμωτέρους" (phronimōterous) — meaning wiser, more sensible, or more practical.</note> or some others? CAL. By Jove, I mean these, and most emphatically so! SOC. Often, then, one prudent man is more powerful than ten thousand imprudent ones, according to your argument; and it is fitting for him to rule, and for the others to be subjects, and for the ruler to have more than those he rules. This is what you seem to want to say (and I am not "word-hunting") if one man is more powerful than ten thousand. CAL. That is exactly what I am saying. For I think this is natural justice: that he who is better and more prudent should rule and possess more than the inferior. SOC.

<margin>G</margin>
Stay a moment. What would you say if we were gathered in this place, as we are now, many of us together, and we had a common supply of much food and drink, and we were a mix of all sorts—some strong, some weak—but one of us was a physician, and thus more prudent than the rest regarding these things? He would be, as is likely, stronger than some and weaker than others. Would he not, being more prudent than us, be "better" and "more powerful" in this matter? CAL. Certainly. SOC. Should he then have more of this food than we do because he is better? Or should he, because of his excellence, distribute everything, but not retain more for himself in the distribution? Otherwise, he might be penalized. Instead, some should have more, and some less; and if he were the weakest of all, he, despite being the best, should have the least—

<summary>In this segment of the Gorgias, Socrates uses dialectic to dismantle Callicles' claim that "might makes right," forcing him to redefine "better" as "more prudent" rather than merely physically stronger. Socrates then begins a reductio ad absurdum argument using the example of a physician to question whether superior knowledge entitles one to a larger share of material goods.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the heated debate between Socrates and the young aristocrat Callicles. Previously, Callicles argued that the "stronger" should naturally possess more than the "weaker." Socrates is now pressing him to define what he means by "better" and "stronger," using his trademark method of comparing grand political ideas to humble everyday crafts.</meta>

-># GORGIAS<-

<margin>A</margin> ...the least of all to the best man, Callicles. Is it not so, my good friend? <margin>CALLICLES</margin> You are talking about food, drink, doctors, and nonsense; I am not talking about those things. <margin>SOCRATES</margin> Then do you say the "wiser" man is the "better" man? Say yes or no. <margin>CALL.</margin> I do. <margin>SOC.</margin> But should not the better man have more? <margin>CALL.</margin> Not of food or drink. <margin>SOC.</margin> I understand. Perhaps of clothes then? Should the most skilled weaver have the largest coat and go about dressed in the greatest number of the finest clothes? <margin>CALL.</margin> What do you mean, clothes? <margin>SOC.</margin> Well, in the matter of shoes, clearly the one who is wisest and best in that craft should have the advantage. Perhaps the cobbler should walk around with the largest shoes and the greatest number of them on his feet. <margin>CALL.</margin> What shoes? You are talking nonsense! <margin>SOC.</margin>
<margin>B</margin> If you don't mean those sorts of things, then perhaps these: a farmer, for instance, a man wise concerning the earth, noble and good; perhaps he should have the advantage in seeds and use the greatest amount of seed on his own land. <margin>CALL.</margin> How you always say the same things, Socrates! <margin>SOC.</margin> Not only that, Callicles, but also about the same subjects. <margin>CALL.</margin> By the gods, you literally never stop talking about cobblers, fullers <note>original: "κναφέας" (knapheas) - workers who cleaned and thickened cloth</note>, cooks, and doctors, as if our discussion were actually about them! <margin>SOC.</margin> Then will you say in what matters the "superior" and "wiser" man justly gets more by having the advantage? Or will you neither tolerate my suggestions nor tell me yourself? <margin>CALL.</margin>
<margin>C</margin> But I have been saying it for a long time! First, as to who the "superior" ones are: I do not mean cobblers or cooks, but those who are wise in the affairs of the city—regarding how it might be well-governed—and not only wise, but also courageous, being capable of carrying out what they have intended, and who do not give up through softness of soul. <margin>SOC.</margin> Do you see, my dear Callicles, that you and I do not make the same accusations against each other? For you claim that I always say the same things, and you reproach me for it; but I, on the contrary, reproach you because you never say the same thing about the same subjects. At one moment you defined the "better" and "superior" as the "stronger," and then again as the "wiser." And now you come with yet another definition: the "courageous"
<margin>D</margin> are now called by you the superior and the best. But, my good man, tell me once and for all: whom do you mean by the better and superior, and in what respect? <margin>CALL.</margin> I have already said: those who are wise in the affairs of the city and courageous. For it is fitting for these men to rule the cities; and justice consists in this: that these men, the rulers, have more than the others, the subjects. <margin>SOC.</margin> But what about themselves, my friend? <margin>CALL.</margin> What do you mean? <margin>SOC.</margin> I mean, are they rulers or subjects of themselves? <margin>CALL.</margin> What do you mean, "ruler of oneself"? <margin>SOC.</margin> Nothing complicated; just what the many mean: being temperate <note>original: "σώφρονα" (sōphrona) - often translated as self-controlled or moderate</note> and
<margin>E</margin> master of oneself, ruling the pleasures and desires within oneself. <margin>CALL.</margin> How charming you are! You call the simpletons "temperate." <margin>SOC.</margin> How so? There is no one who would not know that is not what I mean. <margin>CALL.</margin> Most certainly you do, Socrates! Since how could a man be happy if he is a slave to anyone at all? Rather, this is what is naturally beautiful and just, which I tell you now with all frankness: the man who is to live rightly must allow his desires to be as great as possible and not restrain them. When they are as great as possible, he must be capable of serving them through his courage and wisdom, and to satisfy whatever desire he may have. But this, I think, is not possible for the many. This is why they find fault with such men, hiding their own
<margin>F</margin> impotence out of shame. They say that lack of restraint is disgraceful, as I said before; they enslave those who are better by nature, and because they themselves are unable to satisfy their own pleasures, they praise temperance and justice because of their own unmanliness. For to those who had the advantage from the beginning—either being sons of kings or having the natural capacity to acquire some office, or a tyranny, or supreme power—what would truly be more disgraceful and worse than temperance for such men? For them, it is possible to enjoy good things with nothing standing in the way, yet they would invite as a master over themselves the laws, the talk, and the blame of the common people. Or how could they fail to be miserable under the "beauty" of justice and temperance, by distributing no more to their own friends than to their enemies,
<margin>G</margin> and that while being rulers in their own city? But in truth, Socrates—which you claim to pursue—it is like this: luxury, lack of restraint, and freedom, if they have support, this is virtue and happiness. All these other things—these fine-sounding, unnatural conventions—are the foolishness of men and worth nothing. <margin>SOC.</margin> You pursue your argument quite nobly, Callicles, by speaking frankly. For you are now clearly saying what others think but are unwilling to say. I beg you, therefore, not to give up in any way, so that it may truly become clear how one ought to live. Tell me: you say that desires must not be restrained if one intends to be what one should be? That by letting them grow as large as possible, one must prepare their satisfaction from somewhere or other? And that this is virtue? <margin>CALL.</margin> I say these things, yes. <margin>SOC.</margin> Then it is not correct to say that those
<margin>H</margin> who need nothing are happy. <margin>CALL.</margin> No, for in that case stones and the dead would be the happiest of all. <margin>SOC.</margin> But indeed, even as you say it, life is a strange thing.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...must be had [abounding], Callicles? Is it not thus to be called good? <margin>CALLICLES</margin> You speak of food, and drink, and doctors, and such trifles: but I do not speak of these. <margin>SOCRATES</margin> Whether therefore you say the wiser is the better, or not? Answer. <margin>CALL.</margin> I do. <margin>SOC.</margin> But is it not fitting that the better should receive more? <margin>CALL.</margin> Not of food and drink. <margin>SOC.</margin> I understand. Perhaps of clothes. And it would be fitting for him who is most skilled in making clothes to have a large cloak, and to go about adorned in many precious garments. <margin>CALL.</margin> What clothes are you telling me about? <margin>SOC.</margin> But perhaps in shoes it is fitting for him to receive more who is wiser and better in them: and perhaps the cobbler himself, being the <margin>B</margin> greatest, ought to have more shoes and carry many around on his feet. <margin>CALL.</margin> About what shoes are you raving now? <margin>SOC.</margin> But if you do not mean such things, at least you mean something of this sort: as a man wise in cultivating fields, both honest and good, ought to bring back more seed, and use the most in his own fields. <margin>CALL.</margin> How you always say the same things, O Socrates! <margin>SOC.</margin> Not only the same things, Callicles, but also about the same matters. <margin>CALL.</margin> By the gods, you always have cobblers, shoemakers, fullers, cooks, and doctors in your mouth, as if our discussion were established concerning these. <margin>SOC.</margin> Will you not therefore say at last, in what matters the more powerful and wiser <margin>C</margin> ought justly to possess more? Or will you neither permit me to say, nor will you say it yourself? <margin>CALL.</margin> But I have been saying it for a long time: first, indeed, who the more powerful are. For I do not mean cobblers, nor cooks, but those who are wise in administering the republic: and not wise only, but also brave, who are most fit for perfecting those things which they have thought out, and who do not succumb to any softness of mind. <margin>SOC.</margin> Do you see, Callicles, that I am not accused of the same by you as you are by me? You indeed accuse me as if I always repeat the same things: I, on the contrary, accuse you because you never bring forward the same things about the same matters. For at one time you <margin>D</margin> define the better and more powerful as the stronger, and at another time as the wiser. Now, moreover, you bring forward something else. For now certain "braver" ones are named by you as more powerful and better. But come, O good man, explain at last, whom especially and for what you call better and more powerful. <margin>CALL.</margin> I have already said: the wise in public affairs, namely, and the brave. For it befits these to command cities: and it is just that these have more than others—the rulers, namely, more than the subjects. <margin>SOC.</margin> But what of this? Does it befit them in any way to command themselves, or to obey themselves? <margin>CALL.</margin> In what way do you mean? <margin>SOC.</margin> I mean whether each one ought to rule himself: or is there no need that he should rule himself, but only others? <margin>CALL.</margin> How do you mean <margin>E</margin> ruling oneself? <margin>SOC.</margin> I say nothing obscure, but as many say: being temperate, and master of oneself, ruling one's own pleasures and desires. <margin>CALL.</margin> How festive you are, Socrates! You name stupid men "temperate." <margin>SOC.</margin> What do you say? There is no one who does not know that I least of all mean that. <margin>CALL.</margin> Indeed, very much so, O Socrates. For how can he be happy who serves anyone? But this is naturally just and beautiful, which I now tell you boldly: it is necessary for him who will lead his life rightly to permit his desires to be increased to the highest degree, and not to restrain them in any way: and to these, being as great as possible, to minister whatever they seek on account of fortitude and wisdom: and to fulfill entirely any of their passions. Which indeed, <margin>F</margin> because many are unable to achieve, they find fault with those who do attain it, hiding their own impotence out of shame: and they say that intemperance is base, just as I was saying in the preceding parts. Moreover, they lead men of a better nature into a slavish condition: and they themselves, since they cannot fulfill their own lusts, approve of temperance and justice on account of their own cowardice. But if it had happened to these from the beginning, that they were either the sons of kings, or their nature was sufficient for them to acquire some command, or tyranny, or power for themselves, surely it would be more base and worse for them to use temperance of this kind: who, when it was permitted to them to enjoy good things, and they were not hindered by any, <margin>G</margin> have set over themselves as a mistress the law and talk of the multitude, and their reproach. For in what way would they not be miserable? Since on account of a certain honesty of justice and temperance, they would grant nothing more to their friends than to their enemies, even while they were ruling in their own city. But, O Socrates, the truth itself which you claim to follow, holds itself thus: luxury, intemperance, and liberty—provided the means are supplied—is virtue and happiness. But those other fine things invented against nature are the delusions of men, and trifles entirely to be despised. <margin>SOC.</margin> Not ungenerously, O Callicles, do you proceed in the discussion using such boldness. Truly these things are now spoken openly by you, which others indeed think, <margin>H</margin> but are unwilling to say: wherefore I beseech you that you desist in no way, so that in truth we may be made more certain of the way in which we must live. Tell me then: you say desires are not to be coerced? If anyone wishes to be such as he ought to be: indeed, you say that permitting them to be at their height is virtue? <margin>CALL.</margin> I do say so. <margin>SOC.</margin> If it were so, it would not be rightly said that those are happy who need nothing. <margin>CALL.</margin> Otherwise stones and the dead would be the most happy. But nevertheless, even that which you say is a grave matter...

...to be increased to the highest degree; and you say that the fulfillment of these from elsewhere must be provided: and you say this is virtue? CALL. I do say so. SOC. If it were so, it would not be rightly said that those are happy who need nothing. CALL. Otherwise stones and the dead would be the most happy. But nevertheless, even that which you say is a grave matter.

<summary>In this pivotal exchange, Callicles rejects the traditional virtue of temperance (sophrosyne), arguing instead that true happiness and "natural justice" consist in having unrestrained desires and the power to satisfy them. Socrates challenges this by questioning if such a life is better than the state of a "stone or a corpse" which has no needs at all.</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Callicles, temperance, self-control, sophrosyne, desire, natural justice, ruling oneself, luxury, hedonism, virtue, arete, happiness, eudaimonia</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from page 299. Socrates is challenging Callicles's view that happiness consists of having massive, unrestrained desires and the power to satisfy them. Socrates begins to use various allegories—the leaky jar, the sieve, and the "itch"—to suggest that such a life is one of endless, miserable labor rather than fulfillment.</meta>

-># PLATO'S<-

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
...life. I would not be surprised if what Euripides said about this matter were true,
<margin>Euripides on life and death.</margin>
"Who knows if to live is really to die, and to die is to live?" <note>original: "Τίς δ᾽ οἶδεν εἰ τὸ ζῆν μέν ἐστι κατθανεῖν..." This famous quote from a lost play by Euripides suggests our physical life might be a spiritual death.</note> And perhaps we are actually dead right now. I once heard from a certain wise man that we are currently dead, and that our body is a tomb for us; and that part of the soul where the desires reside is of such a nature that it can be swayed and shifted back and forth. Thus, a clever man—perhaps a Sicilian or an Italian—telling a myth and playing on the name, called this part of the soul a "jar" <note>original: "pithon" / "pithos". Socrates is using a pun: the Greek word for "jar" (pithos) sounds like "persuadable" (pithanon).</note> because of its capacity for persuasion and belief. He called the foolish "uninitiated" <note>original: "amyētos" (uninitiated), which sounds like "un-sealed" or "leaky".</note>. He said that in these uninitiated people, that part of the soul where the lusts are—the intemperate and non-watertight part—is like a leaky jar, so described because of its insatiable nature. 
<margin>B</margin>
Therefore, this man shows you the opposite of your view: that among those in the unseen world <note>Hades, from "aeidēs," meaning unseen.</note>, the most miserable would be these uninitiated ones, who are forced to carry water into a leaky jar using a similarly leaky sieve. By the "sieve," he meant the soul—as the one who taught me said—the soul of the foolish. He compared the soul of the foolish to a sieve because it is full of holes, unable to hold anything due to a lack of faith and forgetfulness. These things might seem somewhat strange; nevertheless, they demonstrate what I want to persuade you of, if I am able: that instead of an insatiable and 
<margin>C</margin>
intemperate life, you should choose a moderate life that is satisfied and content with what is always at hand. But do I persuade you at all with this? Do you change your mind and think those who live temperately are happier than those who live intemperately? Or do I accomplish nothing, and even if I tell many more such stories, you are not going to change your mind? **CALL.** You have spoken the latter more truly, Socrates. **SOC.** Come then, let me bring another image from the same school of thought. Consider whether you would say the same of each life—the temperate and the intemperate—as if there were two men, each having many jars; and one has 
<margin>D</margin>
jars that are intact and full, some with wine, some with honey, some with milk, and many others with various things; but the sources of these liquids are rare, difficult to find, and acquired only through many painful labors. Now, the one who has filled his jars no longer needs to pour anything in or worry about it; as far as these are concerned, he is at rest. But for the other man, the sources are available just as they were for the first, though difficult to acquire; however, his jars are leaky and rotten, and he is forced to fill them constantly, day and night, or else suffer the most extreme pains. Since such is the life of each, do you say the life of the intemperate man is happier than that of the temperate? Does my argument persuade you to admit that the moderate life is better than the immoderate? Or do I still not persuade you? **CALL.** Not at all, Socrates. For the man who has filled everything has no more pleasure; rather, it is as I was just saying: he lives like a stone once he is full, feeling neither pleasure nor pain. But the sweetness of life consists in the constant and massive "in-flow." **SOC.** Is it not necessary that if much flows in, much must also flow out? And must there not be large holes for the outflow? **CALL.** Certainly. **SOC.** Then you are describing the life of a <term>Charadrius</term> <note>A bird (likely a plover) that was anciently believed to eat and excrete at the same time.</note>,
<margin>See Erasmus's proverbs: "Imitating the Charadrius."</margin>
not the life of a dead man or a stone. But tell me, do you mean something like being hungry and, while hungry, eating? **CALL.** I do. **SOC.** And being thirsty and, while thirsty, drinking? **CALL.** Indeed; and I affirm that having all other desires and being able to satisfy them with pleasure is the happy life. **SOC.** Well done, most excellent man! Continue as you have started, and do not be ashamed. It seems I too must not be held back by shame. First, tell me whether a man with the "itch" <note>original: "scabiosum". Likely referring to a skin condition like scabies or eczema.</note> who scratches himself, and can do so continually, should be thought to live happily. **CALL.** How absurd you are, Socrates, and truly a common rabble-rouser. **SOC.** Indeed, Callicles, I terrified Polus and Gorgias and made them feel ashamed. But you, see that you are not terrified or hindered by shame. For you are a brave man; just answer. **CALL.** I say then that the one who scratches also lives pleasantly. **SOC.** And if pleasantly, then also happily? **CALL.** Without a doubt. **SOC.** Is it so if he only scratches his head, or—I ask you—something more? See what you will answer, Callicles, if someone should ask you the things that follow in order. If these points are granted, would the life of those <term>lewd men</term> <note>original: "cinaedorum" / "κιναιδων". In Greek society, this referred to men who took a passive, submissive role in sexual acts for pleasure, a status considered highly shameful.</note> not be called terrible, foul, and miserable? Or will you dare to say they are happy, if they possess in abundance the things they desire? **CALL.** Are you not ashamed, Socrates, to lead the conversation to such things? **SOC.** Is it I who lead it there, noble sir? Or rather the one who so shamelessly asserts that those who are pleased, in whatever way they are pleased, are happy, and makes no distinction between which pleasures are good and which are bad? But tell me even now: do you assert that "pleasure" and "the good" are the same thing? Or is there some pleasure which is not good? **CALL.** So that my argument may not be inconsistent if I say they are different, I say they are the same. **SOC.** You are destroying your previous arguments, Callicles, and you will no longer be fit to examine the truth with me if you speak contrary to what you really think. **CALL.** You do the same, Socrates! **SOC.** Then I am not acting rightly if I do so, and neither are you. But, blessed man, consider whether "the good" is not simply "rejoicing in every way"; for if it were, many shameful things that were just hinted at would seem to follow.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
"For I would not wonder if Euripides speaks the truth in these lines, saying:
'Who knows if to live is actually to die, and to die is to live?' And perhaps we are in reality dead. This is something I have even heard from the wise: that we are now dead, and the body is our tomb; and that part of the soul in which the desires are, happens to be of a nature to be persuaded and to shift up and down. And so a certain clever man, telling a myth—perhaps a Sicilian or an Italian—playing on the word, because of its persuasibility and capacity for belief, called it a 'jar,' and the foolish he called the 'uninitiated.' Of the uninitiated, this part of the soul where the desires are—the intemperate and non-watertight part—he compared to a leaky jar because of its insatiability. He, on the contrary,
<margin>B</margin>
O Callicles, shows you that of those in Hades (meaning the 'unseen' realm), these would be the most wretched: the uninitiated, who carry water into the leaky jar with another such leaky thing, a sieve. By the 'sieve,' he means (as the one who spoke to me said) the soul; and he compared the soul of the foolish to a sieve as being leaky, because it is unable to hold anything due to its lack of faith and its forgetfulness. These things are fairly strange. However, they show what I want to point out to you, if I can somehow persuade you to change your mind: to choose, instead of the insatiable and intemperate life, the one that is orderly and content and satisfied with what is present. But do I
<margin>C</margin>
persuade you at all, and do you change your mind to think the orderly are happier than the intemperate? Or not at all? Even if I tell many such myths, will you not change your mind? **CALL.** You have said this more truly, Socrates. **SOC.** Come then, let me tell you another image from the same school as the current one. For consider if you speak of each life—the temperate and the intemperate—as if two men each had many jars; and for one, they were sound and full, one of wine, another of honey, another of milk, and many others of many things. But the sources of each of these were scarce and difficult, and provided only with much labor and difficulty. Now, one man,
<margin>D</margin>
having filled his jars, would no longer channel anything in or care about them, but as far as they are concerned, he would be at rest. But for the other, the sources—just like the first—would be possible to provide, but difficult; yet his vessels were leaky and rotten, and he would be forced to fill them always, day and night, or else suffer the extreme of pains. If such is the life of each, do you say the life of the intemperate is happier than that of the orderly? Do I persuade you at all, by saying this, to admit that the orderly life is better than the intemperate? Or do I not? **CALL.** You do not persuade me, Socrates. For that man who has filled his jars has no pleasure at all; but this is what I was just saying: to live like a stone once one is full, neither rejoicing any longer nor grieving. But in
<margin>E</margin>
this is the pleasant life: in the greatest possible inflow. **SOC.** Is it not then necessary, if much flows in, that what goes out must also be much? And must there not be large holes for the outflows? **CALL.** Very much so. **SOC.** You are describing the life of a Charadrius bird, then, but not of a corpse or a stone. And tell me, do you mean something like this: being hungry and eating when hungry? **CALL.** I do. **SOC.** And being thirsty, and drinking when thirsty? **CALL.** I say so; and having all the other desires, and being able to fill them, and rejoicing—that is living happily. **SOC.** Well done, my best of men! For continue as you began, and see that you do not feel ashamed. It seems that I too must not feel ashamed. And first, tell me if a man who has an itch and needs to scratch, having plenty of scratching to do, and passing his life scratching,
<margin>F</margin>
can live happily? **CALL.** How strange you are, Socrates, and a downright demagogue. **SOC.** That is why, Callicles, I startled Polus and Gorgias and made them ashamed. But you, do not be startled, nor be ashamed (for you are brave); just answer. **CALL.** I say then that even the man who scratches would live pleasantly. **SOC.** And if pleasantly, then also happily? **CALL.** Certainly. **SOC.** If he only scratches his head, or—what else shall I ask you? See, Callicles, what you will answer if someone asks you all the things that follow from this in order. For the sum of such things—the life of the *kinaidoi* <note>original: "κιναίδων". Men who took the passive role in sex, often for pleasure or money; seen as the ultimate symbol of lack of self-control.</note>—is that not terrible, shameful, and wretched? Or will you dare to say that these are happy, if they have an abundance of what they need? **CALL.** Are you not ashamed to lead the conversation to such things, Socrates? **SOC.**
<margin>G</margin>
Is it I who lead it there, noble sir? Or the one who says so shamelessly that those who rejoice, however they may rejoice, are happy, and does not distinguish which of the pleasures are good and which are bad? But even now, say: Do you say that the pleasant and the good are the same? Or is there something of the pleasant which is not good? **CALL.** So that my argument is not inconsistent if I say it is different, I say it is the same. **SOC.** You are ruining your first arguments, Callicles, and you can no longer properly examine the truth with me if you speak against your own opinions. **CALL.** You do the same, Socrates! **SOC.** Then neither do I do rightly, if I do this, nor do you. But, my dear man, look to see if the good is not just this: rejoicing in every way. For if it were, these things now being hinted at appear to result in many shameful things.

<summary>In this passage, Socrates uses the metaphors of leaky jars and sieves to argue that a life of unrestrained desire is a state of perpetual lack and misery, while Callicles insists that happiness is found only in the constant process of satisfying ever-larger appetites. Socrates pushes this logic to an uncomfortable extreme by asking if the life of someone constantly scratching an itch or a "kinaidos" (a socially stigmatized figure of pleasure) could be considered truly happy.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from page 300. Socrates is systematically dismantling Callicles's argument that pleasure and "the good" are identical. He has just finished a metaphorical discussion about "leaky jars" and is now moving into a formal logical proof based on the nature of opposites.</meta>

# GORGIAS.

<margin>A</margin>
...and many other consequences follow, if this is the case. 
**CALLICLES:** At least that is what you think, Socrates. 
**SOCRATES:** But what do you say? Do you agree to these things, Callicles? 
**CALLICLES:** I do. 
**SOCRATES:** Should we take up the argument as if you are speaking in earnest? 
**CALLICLES:** Very much so. 
**SOCRATES:** Come then, since you are of this mind, distinguish these things for me: do you call something "knowledge"? 
**CALLICLES:** I do. 
**SOCRATES:** And did you not just now say that "courage" was something different from "knowledge"? 
**CALLICLES:** I certainly did. 
**SOCRATES:** Did you speak of them as two distinct things, courage being different from knowledge? 
**CALLICLES:** Quite so. 
**SOCRATES:** And what about pleasure and knowledge? Are they the same thing, or different? 
<margin>B</margin>
**CALLICLES:** Different, surely, you most wise man. 
**SOCRATES:** And is courage also different from pleasure? 
**CALLICLES:** How could it not be? 
**SOCRATES:** Come then, let us remember this: Callicles of the district of Acharnae <note>original: "Ἀχαρνεὺς" (Acharnae). A large rural district of Athens.</note> says that the pleasant and the good are the same; but that knowledge and courage are different from each other and different from the good. But Socrates of the district of Alopece <note>original: "Ἀλωπεκῆθεν" (Alopece). Socrates's home district near the city walls of Athens.</note> does not agree with this. Or do you, Callicles? 
**CALLICLES:** He does not agree. 
**SOCRATES:** And I suspect Callicles won't either, once he examines himself rightly. Tell me: do you not think that those who fare well experience the opposite of those who fare ill? 
**CALLICLES:** I do. 
**SOCRATES:** Then if these things are opposites, must they not behave like health and disease? For surely a person is not healthy and sick at the same time, nor does he get rid of health and disease at the same time. 
**CALLICLES:** What do you mean by that? 
<margin>C</margin>
**SOCRATES:** Take any part of the body you like and consider it. Does a man's eye ever suffer from the disease called *ophthalmia* <note>original: "ὀφθαλμία". An ancient term for general eye inflammation or infection.</note>? 
**CALLICLES:** Of course. 
**SOCRATES:** But surely he is not healthy in that same eye at the same time? 
**CALLICLES:** Not in any way. 
**SOCRATES:** And what happens when he gets rid of the *ophthalmia*? Does he also get rid of his eye's health at that moment, so that he finally loses both together? 
**CALLICLES:** Not at all. 
**SOCRATES:** For that would be a marvelous and irrational thing, wouldn't it? 
**CALLICLES:** Very much so. 
**SOCRATES:** Rather, I think, he gains and loses each one in turn? 
**CALLICLES:** I agree. 
**SOCRATES:** And is it not the same with strength and weakness? 
**CALLICLES:** Yes. 
**SOCRATES:** And with speed and slowness? 
**CALLICLES:** Certainly. 
**SOCRATES:** Does he also gain and lose good things and happiness, and their opposites—bad things and misery—in turn? 
**CALLICLES:** Absolutely, I suppose. 
<margin>D</margin>
**SOCRATES:** If, then, we find things that a person both possesses and gets rid of at the same time, it is clear that these things cannot be "the good" and "the bad." Do we agree on this? Think carefully before you answer. 
**CALLICLES:** I agree most exceedingly. 
**SOCRATES:** Then go back to our earlier points. Did you say that hunger was pleasant or painful? I mean the hunger itself. 
**CALLICLES:** Painful, I say. 
**SOCRATES:** But eating while hungry is pleasant? 
**CALLICLES:** Yes. 
**SOCRATES:** I understand. But the hunger itself is painful, is it not? 
**CALLICLES:** I say so. 
**SOCRATES:** And is thirst not also painful? 
**CALLICLES:** Very much so. 
**SOCRATES:** Should I ask more questions, or do you admit that every deficiency and desire is painful? 
**CALLICLES:** I admit it; do not ask further. 
<margin>E</margin>
**SOCRATES:** Very well. But do you say that drinking when thirsty is anything other than pleasant? 
**CALLICLES:** I say it is pleasant. 
**SOCRATES:** Now, in this act you describe, the "being thirsty" is surely a state of pain? 
**CALLICLES:** Yes. 
**SOCRATES:** But "drinking" is the filling of the deficiency and is a pleasure? 
**CALLICLES:** Yes. 
**SOCRATES:** So you say that in the act of drinking, one feels joy? 
**CALLICLES:** Most certainly. 
**SOCRATES:** Even though one is thirsty—which is to say, in pain? 
**CALLICLES:** Yes. 
**SOCRATES:** Do you perceive the consequence? You are saying that you feel joy and pain simultaneously when you say someone drinks while thirsty. Does this not happen at the same time and in the same place, whether in the soul or the body? For I don't think it makes a difference. Is this true or not? 
**CALLICLES:** It is true. 
**SOCRATES:** Yet you said it was impossible to fare well (be happy) and fare ill (be miserable) at the same time. 
**CALLICLES:** And I still say so. 
**SOCRATES:** But you have just admitted that it is possible to feel joy while feeling pain. 
**CALLICLES:** So it appears. 
**SOCRATES:** Therefore, feeling joy is not the same as faring well, nor is feeling pain the same as faring ill. Consequently, the pleasant is different from the good. 
<margin>F</margin>
**CALLICLES:** I don't know what clever tricks you are playing, Socrates. 
**SOCRATES:** You know well enough, Callicles, but you are playing coy <note>original: "ἀκκίζῃ" (akkizē). From "Akkō," a figure in Greek folklore who was notoriously vain and pretended to reject things she actually wanted.</note>. Go a little further, so you can see how much nonsense you're talking, even while you're lecturing me as if you were wise. Does not each of us stop being thirsty and stop feeling the pleasure of drinking at the same time? 
**CALLICLES:** I don't know what you're talking about. 
**GORGIAS:** Don't be like that, Callicles. Answer for our sake too, so that the arguments may be finished. 
**CALLICLES:** But Socrates is always like this, Gorgias! He asks these tiny, worthless questions and refutes them. 
**GORGIAS:** What does that matter to you? Surely it's no skin off your back, Callicles. Just let Socrates cross-examine you however he likes. 
<margin>G</margin>
**CALLICLES:** Then ask your narrow little questions, since Gorgias wishes it. 
**SOCRATES:** You are a lucky man, Callicles, to have been initiated into the Great Mysteries before the Lesser ones <note>original: "τὰ μεγάλα... πρὶν τὰ σμικρά". A sarcastic reference to the Eleusinian Mysteries, where one usually had to complete the Lesser initiation before the Great one. Socrates suggests Callicles thinks he's too good for basic logic.</note>; I didn't think that was allowed. Answer then from where you left off: does one not stop being thirsty and stop feeling pleasure at the same time? 
**CALLICLES:** I say so. 
**SOCRATES:** And does one not stop being hungry and satisfy other desires and their pleasures at the same time? 
**CALLICLES:** That is so. 
**SOCRATES:** Does one not then stop the pains and the pleasures at the same time? 
**CALLICLES:** Yes. 
**SOCRATES:** But one does *not* stop experiencing the good and the bad at the same time, as you previously agreed. Do you not agree now? 
**CALLICLES:** I do. So what? 
**SOCRATES:** Simply this: 
<margin>H</margin>
that the good things are not the same as the pleasant things, my friend, nor are the bad things the same as the painful. For one pair ceases together, but the other does not, because they are different. How then...

<summary>In this passage, Socrates employs a logical argument to prove that pleasure and "the good" are not identical by showing that pleasure and pain can be felt simultaneously (such as drinking while thirsty), whereas a person cannot be "faring well" (happy) and "faring ill" (miserable) at the same time.</summary>
