# GORGIAS

...to us, and are you the third to agree? **CALLICLES:** I certainly am. **SOCRATES:** <margin>A</margin> Therefore, it is for the sake of good things that we ought to do everything else, including pleasant things, rather than doing good things for the sake of pleasant things. **CALLICLES:** Entirely so. **SOCRATES:** Is it then the task of any man to choose which of the pleasant things are good and which are bad? Or does one need a man of skill <term>techne; a systematic craft or science</term> for each? **CALLICLES:** A man of skill. **SOCRATES:** Let us then recall what I happened to be saying to Polus and Gorgias. I was saying (if you remember) that there were <insert>certain skills—some, on the one hand, reaching only as far as pleasure, producing only this and nothing else, being ignorant of what is better and worse; others, on the other hand, knowing what is good and what is bad. And I placed among those concerned with pleasures the skill of cookery—a mere knack <term>empeiria; a routine or experience gained by habit rather than scientific study</term> of the body, not a true art—while I called the one aiming at the good the art of medicine.</insert> And by the god of friendship, <margin>B</margin> Callicles, do not think you should play with me, nor answer whatever happens to come to mind contrary to your true opinion; nor, on the other hand, should you receive what I say as if I were playing. For you see that our argument is about this: and what could a man of even small intelligence be more serious about than this—the question of how one ought to live? Should it be the way you exhort me to—performing these "duties of a man," speaking before the people, practicing rhetoric, and engaging in politics in the manner you all do now? Or should it be this life in philosophy? And in what way does this life differ from that one? Perhaps, then, it is best to distinguish them, as I attempted to do just now; and having distinguished them and reached an agreement with one another, if these two lives really exist, we must consider how they differ from each other and which of them one <margin>C</margin> ought to live. Perhaps you do not yet know what I mean. **CALLICLES:** No, I certainly do not. **SOCRATES:** Well, I will tell you more clearly. Since you and I have agreed that there is something called "the good" and something called "the pleasant," and that the pleasant is different from the good, and that there is a certain study and preparation for the acquisition of each—one being the hunt for pleasure, the other for the good—first, either refute me on this very point or agree. **CALLICLES:** I agree. **SOCRATES:** Come then, agree with me also on what I was saying to our friends here, if I seemed to you to be speaking the truth then. I believe I was saying that <margin>D</margin> cookery does not seem to me to be an art, but a mere knack; whereas medicine is an art. I said this because medicine has investigated the nature of that which it treats and the cause of the things it does, and can give an account <term>logos; a rational explanation</term> of each of these. Medicine is like that. But the other, which is concerned with pleasure, toward which all its service is directed, approaches it in an entirely unscientific way, without having investigated either the nature of pleasure or its cause. It is entirely irrational (so to speak) and makes no precise distinctions, preserving only a memory of what usually happens through routine and experience, <insert>by which it provides</insert> its pleasures. First, then, consider if this seems to you to be stated adequately, and if there are certain <margin>E</margin> similar services regarding the soul. Some are artistic, having a certain foresight for what will be best for the soul; others, however, neglect this, but have investigated only the pleasure of the soul—just as in the case of the body—inquiring how it might be produced for it. They neither consider whether one pleasure is better or worse, nor do they care for anything other than simply gratifiying it, whether for better or for worse. For it seems to me, Callicles, that there are such services; and I say that such a thing is flattery, <note>original: "kolakeia"</note> whether it concerns the body or the soul or anything else where one serves pleasures without regard for the better and the worse. Do you now concur with us in having the same opinion on these matters, or do you disagree? **CALLICLES:** Not I; I agree, so that your argument may be finished and I may gratify Gorgias here. **SOCRATES:** And is this the case regarding only one soul, or is it not the case regarding two or many? **CALLICLES:** No, it is also <margin>F</margin> regarding two or many. **SOCRATES:** Is it not therefore possible to gratify them all at once, in a crowd, without considering what is best? **CALLICLES:** I should think so. **SOCRATES:** Can you then name which practices these are that do this? Or rather, if you prefer, as I ask the question, if any of these seem to you to be of this kind, say "yes," and if not, say "no." First, let us consider flute-playing. Does it not seem to you to be such a thing, Callicles, pursuing only our pleasure and caring for nothing else? **CALLICLES:** It seems so to me. **SOCRATES:** And are not all such things similar, such as lyre-playing in the contests? **CALLICLES:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** And what of the training of choruses and the poetry of dithyrambs? <note>Dithyrambs were hymns sung and danced in honor of Dionysus.</note> Does it not appear to you to be something of this sort? Or do you think Cinesias, the son of Meles, cares at all to say the kind of things that would make the listeners better? Or does he care only for what will gratify the crowd <margin>G</margin> of spectators? **CALLICLES:** That is clear enough, Socrates, at least concerning Cinesias. **SOCRATES:** And what of his father, Meles? Did he seem to you to look toward the best when he sang to the lyre? Or did he not even aim for the most pleasant? For he used to annoy the spectators with his singing. But consider: do you not think that all lyre-playing and the poetry of dithyrambs were invented for the sake of pleasure? **CALLICLES:** I do. **SOCRATES:** And what of this solemn and wondrous poetry of tragedy? Upon what has it set its heart? Is its effort and its purpose, as it seems, only to gratify the spectators? Or does it also struggle to avoid saying anything that might be pleasant and gratifying to them if it is wicked? But if something happens to be unpleasant yet beneficial, it will say and <margin>H</margin> sing this, whether they enjoy it or not? Which of these two does it seem to you that the poetry of tragedy is prepared for? **CALLICLES:** It is clear enough, Socrates, that...

<column-break/>

...agrees with us in this opinion? **CALLICLES:** I do indeed. **SOCRATES:** For <margin>A</margin> which reason, for the sake of good things, it is necessary to pursue both other things and pleasures, but not the good for the sake of pleasures. **CALLICLES:** Assuredly. **SOCRATES:** Is it then the part of any man to choose which of the things that delight are good, and which are bad? Or is the work of a man of skill rather needed for both? **CALLICLES:** Of a man of skill. **SOCRATES:** Let us therefore remember those things which I said to Polus and Gorgias. For if you remember, I was saying that there were certain preparatory faculties: some indeed reaching only as far as pleasure, being ignorant of what might be better or worse; others truly knowing what might be good or bad. I was placing, moreover, among those which are occupied with pleasures, the craft of cookery <margin>B</margin> regarding the body as a matter of experience, but not an art; but among those which aim at the good, the art of healing. And by friendly Jupiter <note>original: "Iouem amicabilem" (Zeus Philios)</note> I pray, O Callicles, that you do not joke against me: neither answer whatever occurs to you, nor again receive these things from me as if I were joking. For you see that our discourse is about that matter which a man of sound mind would strive to know more than anything else: namely, in what way one must live. Whether in the way you exhort, by doing those things which you say are the duties of a man: speaking to the people, practicing Rhetoric, and governing the republic just as you all govern at present; or rather, whether this philosophical life is to be taken up, and in what thing this life differs from that one. Perhaps indeed it is worthwhile, <margin>C</margin> as I had begun a little before, to distinguish them; and then when we have agreed upon the distinction, if this is a twofold life, to consider what the difference is, and in which one we ought rather to live. But perhaps you do not yet understand what I am saying. **CALLICLES:** Not yet, certainly. **SOCRATES:** But I shall speak more plainly. After we have both confessed that there is indeed something good and also something pleasant; but that the pleasant is something other than the good; and that there is a certain study and preparation of each for the sake of acquiring them: one being the hunting of the good, the other of pleasure. This very thing first, <margin>D</margin> before I proceed further, do you assent to me or not? **CALLICLES:** I assent. **SOCRATES:** Come then and assent to those things which I was saying to these men, if <margin>Why medicine is an art.</margin> only I seemed to you then to speak the truth. For I was constantly affirming that cookery did not seem to me to be an art, but a certain experience. But that medicine is an art, for the reason that the faculty of medicine considers both the nature of that which it cures and the cause of those things which it does; <margin>See what things are in experience itself.</margin> and of each of these it can give a reason. But the other faculty of pleasure proceeds toward that very pleasure about which its whole study is occupied entirely without art, neither considering the nature of the pleasure itself nor the cause: altogether reckless, as I might say, nor having any regard for anything, but relying only upon a certain use and experience and memory of that which has been accustomed to happen, it studiously prepares pleasures. <margin>E</margin> These things therefore first weigh, whether they seem sufficiently stated. Do you not moreover think there are certain such faculties regarding the soul—some indeed skillful, namely, having a care for that which is best for the soul; but others neglecting that, while they only think, as we have also said of the body, in what way they might be able to delight the soul. Which pleasures, whether they be better or worse, they by no means consider; nor do they care for anything else than that they may delight, whether it be for the better or for the worse. Indeed, such faculties seem to me to exist, and I call that whole <margin>F</margin> ministry "adulation" <note>original: "adulationem" (flattery)</note> both regarding the soul and regarding the body: and altogether regarding any other thing whose pleasure anyone affects, with no regard at all for the better or worse being applied. But do you indeed come into the same opinion with us, or do you disagree? **CALLICLES:** Not at all; on the contrary, I agree, so that your disputation may at some time be concluded, and I may gratify this Gorgias. **SOCRATES:** Is this then only regarding one soul? Is it not regarding two or many? **CALLICLES:** Not so, but also regarding two and regarding many. **SOCRATES:** Is it not possible to gratify many people meeting in one place without any regard for that which is best? **CALLICLES:** So I think. **SOCRATES:** Can you say which studies they are that <margin>G</margin> effect this? Or rather, if you wish me asking, that which seems to you to be such, concede to be such; but that which is not such, deny. First, let us consider the playing of the flute; does this not seem to you to be such that it cares for nothing else than to delight the ears? **CALLICLES:** It does to me. **SOCRATES:** And are not all others of the same kind, such as the lyre-playing which they use in contests? **CALLICLES:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** What of the teaching of the chorus and the poetry of dithyrambs? Does it not seem to you to be of the same kind? Or do you think Cinesias, the son of Meletus, looks toward saying something of the kind from which the listeners may be rendered better? Or rather, whence he may be able to please the crowd of followers? **CALLICLES:** This is indeed manifest, O Socrates, concerning Cinesias. **SOCRATES:** But his father Meles, did he seem to look toward that which was best when he sang to the lyre? Or did he <margin>Lyre-playing skill looks only to pleasure.</margin> indeed not even look to pleasure? For he was troublesome to those listening. <margin>H</margin> But consider: does not the whole skill of lyre-playing and the poetry of dithyrambs seem to you to be invented for the sake of delighting? **CALLICLES:** To me indeed. **SOCRATES:** But what does this noble tragedy and admirable poetry strive for? Is its study and effort toward only pleasing the listeners? And if there be anything which is pleasant and indeed welcome, but nevertheless evil, will it take care lest it ever say it? But on the contrary, if anything be troublesome, yet nevertheless useful, will it both say and sing it, whether the listeners be delighted or not? But what does the poetry of the tragedians seem to you to labor for most? **CALLICLES:** It is certain that it tends toward...

<summary>Socrates distinguishes between "arts" that aim at the good (like medicine) and "knacks" or "flatteries" that aim only at pleasure (like cookery and popular music). He argues that public performances like dithyrambs and tragedy are often merely forms of flattery designed to please the crowd rather than improve their souls.</summary>

Or do these men also hunt for the favor of their audience for the sake of their own private gain, neglecting the public good in the meantime? Do they treat the people like children, intent only on being agreeable, and caring nothing for whether the people are made better or worse by it? **CALLICLES:** Your question is not a simple one. For there are some who consult the welfare of the citizens when they speak, but there are others such as you describe. **SOCRATES:** That is enough. For if this is a dual thing, one part of it will be flattery and a shameful way of addressing the assembly, while the other will be beautiful—the effort to ensure that the souls of the citizens become as good as possible, always striving for the benefit of the listeners, whether what is said is pleasing or displeasing. But you have certainly never seen such oratory. Or if you can name such a person among the orators, why haven't you shown him to me? **CALLICLES:** By Jove, I cannot name a single one among the orators of today. **SOCRATES:** But can you point to any among the ancients through whom the Athenians became better after he began to speak, having been wicked before? But if it is otherwise, as we were compelled to admit later in the discussion—that those desires which make a man better should be fulfilled, and others not, and that there is a certain art for this—can you show me any such practitioner? **CALLICLES:** I truly have nothing to say. **SOCRATES:** But if you search properly, you will find one. Let us look at it calmly and quietly, considering whether any of these men was truly like that. Come, the good man who speaks toward what is best does not speak at random, but looks toward a specific goal. If you wish to look at painters, architects, shipbuilders, and all other craftsmen: any one of them arranges each part into a certain order, forcing one part to fit and harmonize with another until the whole is established as an ordered and arranged thing. Therefore, all craftsmen do this, and those we mentioned earlier—the physical trainers and doctors—do the same regarding the body. They arrange and compose it. Do we agree this is so, or not? **CALLICLES:** Let it be so. **SOCRATES:** A house that has achieved order and arrangement will be good; if not, it will be bad. **CALLICLES:** I agree. **SOCRATES:** And a ship in the same way. **CALLICLES:** The same. **SOCRATES:** And indeed our bodies as well. **CALLICLES:** Similarly. **SOCRATES:** What then of the soul? If it is devoid of order, will it be good? Or rather if it possesses order and arrangement? **CALLICLES:** It is necessary to admit this also from what was said before. **SOCRATES:** What then is the name for that which is produced in the body from order and arrangement? **CALLICLES:** Perhaps you mean health and strength. **SOCRATES:** I do indeed. Now try to find and state the name for that which is produced in the soul from order and arrangement, just as you did for the body. **CALLICLES:** Why do you not say it yourself, Socrates? **SOCRATES:** If it pleases you, I shall say it; and if I seem to speak the truth, you must grant it;

The "healthy" in the ordering of the body.
</margin>

</margin>

...they prefer pleasure and giving favor to the spectators. **SOCRATES:** Then such a thing, Callicles, we just now called flattery. **CALLICLES:** Entirely so. **SOCRATES:** Come then, if someone were to take away <gloss>original: "periele," a variant of "perieloito"</gloss> from all poetry its melody, rhythm, and meter, does anything remain besides speech? **CALLICLES:** Necessarily. **SOCRATES:** And these speeches are spoken to a great crowd and the common people. **CALLICLES:** I say so. **SOCRATES:** Poetry is therefore a kind of public speaking <term>demegoria; speaking to the 'demos' or people</term>. **CALLICLES:** So it appears. **SOCRATES:** Then rhetoric would be a kind of public speaking. For we say it is a form of flattery. **CALLICLES:** Entirely so. **SOCRATES:** Very well. For there are those who speak what they speak out of care for the citizens, but there are also those such as you describe. **SOCRATES:** That is enough. For if this is also two-fold, one part of it would be flattery and a shameful kind of public speaking; but the other is beautiful—the preparing of the souls of the citizens to be as good as possible. And it is always to struggle to say what is best, whether it will be pleasant or unpleasant to the listeners. But you have never yet seen this kind of rhetoric. Or if you can mention any such orator, why have you not told me who he is? **CALLICLES:** But by Zeus, I cannot tell you of any among the orators of today. **SOCRATES:** What then? Can you name any of the ancients through whom the Athenians are said to have become better, after that man began to speak in public, when they were worse before? For I do not know who this is. **CALLICLES:** What? Do you not hear that Themistocles was a good man, and Cimon, and Miltiades, and Pericles here, who has recently died, whom you also heard? **SOCRATES:** If indeed, Callicles, the virtue you mentioned earlier is true—the filling up of desires, both one's own and those of others. But if not this, but what we were forced to agree upon in the later argument—that those desires which, being fulfilled, make a man better, these we must satisfy, but those that make him worse, we must not—and that there is a certain art for this; can you say any such man has existed? **CALLICLES:** I have nothing I can say. **SOCRATES:** But if you seek well, you will find one. Let us look at it calmly, considering if any of these men was like that. For come, the good man, speaking for the sake of the best in whatever he says, does he not speak at random, but looking toward something? Just as all other craftsmen, each looking toward his own work, does not choose at random what he brings to his work, but so that what he works upon may have a certain form <note>original: "eidos"</note>. For instance, if you wish to look at painters, builders, shipwrights, or any other craftsman you like, see how each one places each thing he disposes into a certain order, and compels one thing to be fitting and to harmonize with the other, until he has constructed the whole as an ordered and arranged thing. And as for the other craftsmen, and those we just now mentioned—the trainers and doctors concerned with the body—they surely arrange and order the body. Do we agree this is so, or not? **CALLICLES:** Let this be so. **SOCRATES:** An ordered and arranged house, then, would be useful, but a disordered one, base? **CALLICLES:** I say so. **SOCRATES:** And a ship likewise? **CALLICLES:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** And indeed do we say the same of our bodies? **CALLICLES:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** And what of the soul? If it meets with disorder, will it be useful? Or if it meets with a certain order and arrangement? **CALLICLES:** It is necessary from the preceding to agree to this as well. **SOCRATES:** What then is the name for that which occurs in the body from order and arrangement? **CALLICLES:** Perhaps you mean health and strength. **SOCRATES:** I do. And what again is the name for that which is produced in the soul from order and arrangement? Try to find it and say it, just like the other name. **CALLICLES:** Why do you not say it yourself, Socrates? **SOCRATES:** But if it is more pleasing to you, I shall speak. And if I seem to you to speak well, say so; if not, refute me and do not permit it. It seems to me the name for the arrangements of the body is "healthy," from which health is produced in it and the other virtues of the body. Is this so, or is it not? **CALLICLES:** It is. **SOCRATES:** And for the arrangements and orderings of the soul, the name is "lawful" and "law," from which men become law-abiding and orderly. And these are justice and temperance. Do you say so, or not? **CALLICLES:** Let it be. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, the skilled and good rhetorician, looking toward these things, will apply whatever words he says and all his actions to the souls; and if he gives any gift, he will give it, or if he takes anything away, he will take it away; always keeping his mind on this: how justice may be produced in the souls of his citizens, and how injustice may be removed; and how temperance may be produced, and how lack of restraint may be...

<summary>Socrates argues that true rhetoric, like any craft, must aim at a specific "order" or "form." Just as a doctor aims for health in the body, a good statesman should aim for justice and temperance (order) in the souls of the citizens, rather than merely seeking to please them.</summary>

He is now pushing Callicles to admit that a disciplined soul is better than one that indulges every desire.</meta>

# GORGIAS

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...should be removed; instead, let temperance return, let intemperance be cast out, and let the other virtues be cultivated while wickedness is expelled? Do you agree or not? **CALLICLES:** I agree, certainly. **SOCRATES:** For what benefit is it, <margin>A</margin> O Callicles, to provide an ailing and badly affected body with many and most pleasant foods, or drink, or anything else that will not be of use—whether it be more or less, or the opposite of what right reason dictates? Are these things so, or not? **CALLICLES:** They are. **SOCRATES:** For I do not think it is profitable for a man to live in a diseased body. For in such a state, he must necessarily live poorly. Is it not so? **CALLICLES:** It is. **SOCRATES:** And as for satisfying desires—such as eating as much as one wants when hungry, or drinking as much as one pleases when thirsty—doctors usually permit a healthy <margin>B</margin> man to do so; but a sick man they never, so to speak, permit to fill himself with what he craves. Do you also agree to this? **CALLICLES:** I do. **SOCRATES:** As for the soul, my excellent friend, is the principle not the same? So long as it is corrupt, foolish, intemperate, unjust, and impious, it must surely be restrained from its desires and not permitted to do anything other than what will make it better. Do you agree or not? **CALLICLES:** I agree. **SOCRATES:** For is this not better for the soul itself? **CALLICLES:** Entirely so. **SOCRATES:** And is not restraining it from what it desires called "punishment" or "discipline" <note>original: "κολάζειν / coërcere"</note>? **CALLICLES:** Yes. **SOCRATES:**
<margin>C</margin> Discipline, therefore, is better for the soul than the lack of discipline <note>original: "ἀκολασία / incontinentia"</note> which you were just now preferring. **CALLICLES:** I do not know what you are saying, Socrates. Ask someone else. **SOCRATES:** This man cannot endure being helped, even when he himself is undergoing the very thing we are discussing: being disciplined by the argument. **CALLICLES:** I do not care at all for anything you say. I only answered you thus far for the sake of Gorgias. **SOCRATES:** Very well. What shall we do then? Shall we break off the argument in the middle? **CALLICLES:** You decide for yourself. **SOCRATES:** But they say it is not lawful to leave even stories unfinished <note>original: "μύθους / fabulas"</note>; rather, a "head" must be placed upon them <margin>It is a crime to leave stories unfinished. A Proverb.</margin> so they do not wander about headless. Answer the rest, then, so that our argument may attain its head <note>original: "κεφαλὴν / caput"</note>. **CALLICLES:** How violent you are, Socrates! If you take my advice, you will let this discussion go, or find someone else to talk with. **SOCRATES:** Who else is willing? We must not leave the argument incomplete. **CALLICLES:** Could you not go through the argument yourself, either speaking by yourself or answering your own questions? **SOCRATES:**
<margin>D</margin> So that the saying of Epicharmus <note>Epicharmus was a comic playwright; Socrates is jokingly saying he will have to play two parts at once.</note> might apply to me: "what two men spoke before, I alone am now sufficient for." However, it seems absolutely necessary to do so. If we do this, I think we all ought to strive competitively to know what is true and what is false regarding the things we discuss. For it is a common good for all that the truth be made manifest. I will therefore proceed with the argument as it seems to me to be. But if <margin>E</margin> any of you thinks I am conceding something to myself that is not true, you must challenge and refute me. For I do not speak as one who knows what I say, but I seek the truth together with you. Thus, if the one who challenges me appears to say something correct, I will be the first to agree. I say these things, however, if you think the argument ought to be completed; but if you do not wish it, let us drop it and go our way. **GORGIAS:** It does not seem to me, Socrates, that we should go yet; rather, you should finish the argument. I think the others agree. Indeed, I myself <margin>F</margin> wish to hear you go through the remainder. **SOCRATES:** Truly, Gorgias, I would have gladly continued to dispute with Callicles here until I had returned to him the speech of Amphion in exchange for that of Zethus <note>Socrates refers to a lost play by Euripides where two brothers, one a musician (Amphion) and one a man of action (Zethus), debate the best way of life.</note>. If you refute me, I will not be angry with you as you were with me; instead, you shall be recorded by me as my greatest benefactor. **CALLICLES:** Speak on, good man, and finish it. **SOCRATES:** Listen then as I resume the argument from the beginning. Are the pleasant and the good the same? They are not the same, as Callicles and I have agreed. Should we do pleasant things for the sake of the good, or good things for the sake of the pleasant? **CALLICLES:** Pleasant things for the sake of the good. **SOCRATES:** And is that "pleasant" by whose presence we feel pleasure, and "good" by whose presence we are good? **CALLICLES:** Entirely so. **SOCRATES:** But surely we are good, <margin>G</margin> and all other things are good, because of the presence of some virtue? This seems necessary to me, Callicles. But surely the virtue of each thing—whether of a tool, or the body, or the soul, or any living creature—does not come to it by mere chance, but by an order <note>original: "τάξει / ordine"</note>, a rightness, and an art that is assigned to each. Is this so? I say it is. Therefore, the virtue of each thing is a matter of being organized and ordered <note>original: "κεκοσμημένον / ornatum"</note>. I would say so. It is some order <note>original: "κόσμος / ornatus"</note>, then, proper to each thing and inherent in it, that makes each thing good. So it appears to me. Therefore, a soul that possesses its own proper order is better than one that lacks it. **CALLICLES:** It must be. But surely the soul that possesses order is orderly? **CALLICLES:** How could it be otherwise? And is the orderly soul <margin>H</margin> temperate <note>original: "σώφρων / temperatus"</note>? **CALLICLES:** Most necessarily. **SOCRATES:** Therefore the temperate soul is good. I have nothing else to say against this, my friend Callicles; but if you have, teach me. **CALLICLES:** Speak on, good man. **SOCRATES:** I say then that if the temperate soul is good, the soul in the opposite state is evil. And was this not the foolish and intemperate soul? Most certainly. **SOCRATES:** Furthermore, the temperate man would do what is fitting <note>original: "τὰ προσήκοντα / decentia"</note> toward both gods and men; for he would not be temperate if he did not do what is fitting. **CALLICLES:** That must be so. **SOCRATES:** Moreover, in doing what is fitting toward men, he would act justly; and toward the gods, piously.

<summary>Socrates argues that virtue in the soul, like health in the body, is the result of order and discipline. He concludes that a temperate soul is inherently good and will naturally act with justice and piety.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Callicles. In the previous section, Socrates established that the soul, like the body, requires discipline and restraint to be healthy. He now moves to demonstrate that the temperate person possesses all other virtues and that this order is reflected in the very structure of the universe.</meta>

### PLATO: GORGIAS

<column-break/>

towards the Gods, he acts piously. But he who acts justly and piously must necessarily be just and pious. <margin>A</margin> **CALLICLES:** That is the truth. **SOCRATES:** Furthermore, it is necessary that such a man be brave. For it is not the part of a temperate man to either pursue or flee what is not fitting. Instead, he ought to flee or pursue both individual things and people, as well as pleasures and pains, and even endure them when it is necessary. Therefore, it is absolutely necessary that the temperate man—since, as we have said, he is just, brave, and pious—be a perfectly good man. But the good man acts well and honorably in whatever he does. He who acts well is happy and blessed. The wicked man, however, who acts badly, is miserable. Such a person is one who is affected in the opposite way of the temperate man: namely, the intemperate man whom you were praising. I, therefore, establish these things as so, and I feel <margin>B</margin> them to be true. Wherefore, if this is the case, whoever wishes to be happy must follow and practice temperance; he must flee intemperance as fast as his feet can carry him. He must prepare himself so that he does not need castigation <note>original: "castigatione"; discipline or corrective punishment</note> and penalty. But if he, or anyone else close to him, whether a private citizen or the state itself, stands in need of it, he must be coerced by punishment if he is ever to be happy.

This seems to me the mark toward which we ought to look as we direct our lives, referring all things—both public and private—to this: that justice and temperance are present for him who is to be happy. One must not permit everything <margin>C</margin> to his own desires, for to try to satisfy them is an unquenchable evil, leading the life of a pirate. For such a man will never be dear to any human, nor to God, because there can be no fellowship <note>original: "societas"; the Greek "koinonia"</note> with him. And for him who has no fellowship, friendship can never be established. 

The wise men <note>likely referring to the Pythagoreans</note> teach that heaven and earth, gods and men, are held together by a certain fellowship and friendship, by modest order, and by temperance and justice. For this reason, they call this whole universe a "Cosmos" <note>original: "mundum / κόσμον"; meaning both "world" and "order/ornament"</note> <margin>D</margin> and an "order," not "disorder" <note>original: "immunditiam / ἀκοσμίαν"</note> or "intemperance." Although you are wise, you seem to me never to have noticed this. It has escaped your notice that "geometrical equality" <note>justice based on merit or proportion rather than simple arithmetic equality</note> has great power among both gods and men. But you think that *pleonexia* <note>original: "pleonexiam"; the desire to have more than others, or greed</note> (that is, excellence or taking the first part) should be practiced; for you neglect geometry.

Come then, either this argument of ours must be refuted—the claim that the happy become happy by the possession of justice and temperance, and the miserable become miserable through vice—or if it is true, we must consider what follows. <margin>E</margin> Surely all those earlier points will follow, about which you asked me if I was speaking seriously. I claimed that one should accuse oneself, one's son, and one's friend if any injustice has been committed, and that rhetoric should be used for that purpose. And those things which you thought Polus conceded out of shame were indeed true: namely, that doing an injury is as much worse as it is more shameful than suffering one. And he who intends to be a proper orator must be just and know what is just. This is what Polus said Gorgias conceded out of shame. 

Since these things are so, let us consider what those things are for which you reproach me: whether they are said correctly or not. You say that I am not able <margin>F</margin> to bring aid either to myself or to my friends and family, nor to liberate them from the greatest dangers; instead, I am at the mercy of anyone's whim like those who have been stripped of their rights—whether someone wants to strike me on the cheek (to use your boastful phrase), or take my money, or expel me from the city, or even put me to death. You said that to be in such a state is the most shameful thing of all. 

But my opinion, which has already been stated often and must be stated again since nothing prevents it, is the opposite: I say it is not the most shameful thing to be struck on the cheek unjustly, nor to have my body or purse cut, but that to strike and cut me and mine unjustly is more shameful and worse for the one doing it. Likewise, to steal, to lead into slavery, to break into <margin>G</margin> a house, and in short, to do any injury at all, is both worse and more shameful for the one who does it than for me who receives it. These things, having been conceded by us above as I bring them forward, are held and bound (even if it is a bit rustic to say so) by "iron and adamantine" arguments <note>original: "ferreis adamantinis’que rationibus"; unbreakable, diamond-hard logic</note>, as it would seem. Unless you, or someone stronger than you, can dissolve these, it is not possible to speak correctly in any way other than I am speaking now. 

For my argument always remains the same: I do not know how these things are in truth, but of all those I have spoken with until now, as I have just done with you, no one has been able to say otherwise without appearing <margin>G</margin> ridiculous. Therefore, I establish again that these things are so. And if they are so, and injustice is the greatest of evils for the one who commits it, then an even greater evil must be judged: namely, for the one who has committed it to never pay the penalty. What help, then, is that which, if a man cannot provide it for himself, makes him truly contemptible? Is it not that which removes the greatest harm from us? <margin>H</margin> Certainly, it must be the most shameful thing not to be able to provide this kind of aid to oneself, one's friends, and one's relatives. The second kind of aid is against the second-greatest evil, the third against the third, and so on, as the magnitude of each evil is naturally ordered. Is it any different than this, Callicles? **CALLICLES:** Not otherwise. **SOCRATES:** Since there are two things, doing injustice and suffering it, <margin>H</margin> we say doing it is the greater evil, and suffering it the lesser. What then should a man prepare for himself to help himself, so that he may have both benefits: that which comes from not doing injustice, and that from not suffering it? Is it power, or will? For instance, I ask: if he does not wish to be treated unjustly, will he not be treated unjustly? Or if he prepares for himself the *power* of not being treated unjustly, will he then not be treated unjustly? **CALLICLES:** It is clear, certainly, that it is power.

<column-break/>

...and the one who does what is just and holy must necessarily be just and holy. <margin>A</margin> **CALLICLES:** That is so. **SOCRATES:** And surely the brave man must be so too; for it is not the part of a temperate man to either pursue or flee what is not fitting; but one must flee and pursue the things, the people, the pleasures, and the pains that one ought, and endure and stand one's ground where one must. So there is a great necessity, Callicles, that the temperate man (as we have described), being just and brave and holy, is a perfectly good man. And the good man does well and beautifully whatever he does; and the one who does well is blessed and happy. But the wicked man who does poorly is miserable. This would be the one in the opposite state to the temperate man—the intemperate one, whom you were praising. I, then, set these things down thus, and I say they are true. And if they are true, the one who wishes, it seems, to be happy, <margin>B</margin> must pursue and practice temperance, and flee intemperance as fast as his feet can carry him. One must prepare himself above all not to need to be disciplined; but if he does need it, either himself or anyone else of his people, whether a private citizen or a city, he must submit to justice and be disciplined, if he is to be happy. 

This seems to me to be the goal toward which one should look in life; and to direct all his own affairs and those of the city to this end: that justice and temperance shall be present to him who is to be blessed. He must act thus, not allowing his desires to be intemperate, and trying to fill them—an unending evil, living the life of a robber. For such a man would not be <margin>C</margin> dear to any other man, nor to God; for he is incapable of fellowship. And for him in whom there is no fellowship, there can be no friendship. The wise say, Callicles, that heaven and earth, gods and men, are held together by fellowship, and friendship, and orderliness, and temperance, and justice. And the whole of this, for these reasons, they call "Cosmos," my friend, not "disorder" or "intemperance." 

But you seem to me not to pay attention to these things, though you are wise; but it has escaped you that "geometrical equality" is very powerful among both gods and men. You think one must practice *pleonexia* <note>original: "πλεονεξίαν"; greed or over-reaching</note>. For you neglect geometry. Well then. Either this argument of ours must be refuted—that it is not by the possession of justice <margin>D</margin> and temperance that the happy are happy, and by vice the miserable—or, if this is true, we must consider what follows. Those former things follow, Callicles, about which you asked me if I was speaking in earnest: namely, that one should accuse oneself, one's son, and one's companion, if he does any injustice; and that rhetoric should be used for this. And what you thought Polus conceded out of shame—that doing injustice is as much worse as it is more shameful than being treated unjustly—is true. And the one who is to be a correct orator must be just and knowledgeable in justice; which again Polus said Gorgias conceded through shame. 

These things being so, let us consider what those things are <margin>E</margin> for which you reproach me. Is it well said or not? That is, that I am not able to help either myself, or any of my friends or relatives, nor to save them from the greatest dangers; but I am at the mercy of anyone who wishes, like those without rights, whether someone wants to strike me (to use that youthful phrase of your speech) on the cheek, or take my money, or cast me out from the city, or, finally, to kill me. And to be in such a state is the most shameful of all, as your argument goes. But my own argument, which has been said many times already, but nothing prevents it being said yet again: I deny, Callicles, that being struck <margin>F</margin> on the cheek unjustly is the most shameful thing. Nor is having my body cut or my purse; but to strike and cut me and mine unjustly is both more shameful and worse. And stealing, and kidnapping, and house-breaking—in short, doing any injustice at all to me and mine, is both worse and more shameful for the doer than for me the victim. 

These things, which appeared so to us in our earlier discussions as I say, are held and bound (if it is somewhat rustic to say so) with iron and adamantine arguments, as it would at least seem. Which, unless you or someone more youthful than you can break them, it is not possible to speak correctly when saying anything other than what I say now. For my argument is always the same: that I do not know <margin>G</margin> how these things are; however, of those I have met, as now, no one is able to say otherwise without being ridiculous. I, then, set these things down as being so. 

And if it is so, and injustice is the greatest of evils to the doer; and even greater than this greatest, if possible, is for the doer not to pay the penalty; what kind of help is it that a man, being unable to provide for himself, would be truly ridiculous? Is it not that which will turn away the greatest harm from us? But there is a great necessity that this is the most shameful help: not to be able to help oneself, or one's own friends and relatives. Second is the help against the second evil; and third, the help against the third; and the others in the same way, as each magnitude of evil is by nature, so is the beauty of being able to help each, and the shame of not. Is it <margin>H</margin> otherwise or thus, Callicles? **CALLICLES:** Not otherwise. **SOCRATES:** Of the two then, doing injustice and suffering it, we say doing it is a greater evil, and suffering it is less. What then should a man prepare for himself to help himself, so as to have both benefits: the one from not doing injustice, and the one from not being treated unjustly? Is it power, or will? For instance, I ask: if he does not wish to be treated unjustly, will he not be treated unjustly? Or if he prepares a power for not being treated unjustly, will he not be treated unjustly? **CALLICLES:** This is certainly clear, that it is if he has power.

<summary>Socrates argues that the temperate soul is inherently virtuous and happy, connecting human morality to the "Cosmos" or universal order. He concludes that doing injustice is fundamentally worse than suffering it, an argument he claims is bound by "iron and adamantine" logic.</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Callicles, temperance, justice, Cosmos, geometrical equality, pleonexia, adamantine arguments, ethics, happiness</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Callicles. In the previous section, Socrates argued that the temperate man is necessarily just, brave, and pious, and thus happy, whereas the intemperate man is miserable. He now turns the conversation toward how one might practically protect oneself from suffering or committing injustice within a political system.</meta>

### ->GORGIAS<-

<margin>A</margin> ...to possess these benefits: namely, the benefit of not committing injustice and the benefit of not suffering it? Is it a matter of power or of will? Let me put it this way: if a man does not wish to be wronged, will he therefore not be wronged? Or must he provide himself with the power to ensure he is not wronged? **CALLICLES:** It is certainly clear that he needs power. **SOCRATES:** And what about committing injustice? Is it enough if a man simply does not wish to commit it? Will that suffice to prevent him from doing so? Or does this also require the provision of some power and skill <note>original: "techne"; a craft or systematic knowledge</note>, so that unless he learns and practices these things, he will commit injustice? Why don't you answer me on this point, Callicles? Do you think Polus and I were rightly forced to agree in our earlier discussion when we admitted that no one wishes to commit injustice, but that <margin>B</margin> all who do wrong do so against their own will? <note>This refers to the "Socratic Paradox," the idea that all wrongdoing stems from ignorance of what is truly good.</note> **CALLICLES:** Let it be so for you, Socrates, just so you can finish your argument. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, as it seems, we must also provide ourselves with some power and skill so that we do not commit injustice. **CALLICLES:** Quite so. **SOCRATES:** Then what is the skill that provides for suffering no injustice at all, or as little as possible? See if you agree with me. It seems to me that one must either rule in the city himself, or be a tyrant, or be a close associate of the existing government. **CALLICLES:** Do you see, Socrates, how ready I am to praise you when you say something well? You seem to me to have said this very well indeed. <margin>C</margin> **SOCRATES:** Consider this as well, and tell me if I am right. It seems to me that each man is a friend to another as much as possible in the way the ancient and wise proverbs say: "like is friend to like." <note>original: "homoios to homoio"; a common Greek proverb equivalent to "birds of a feather flock together."</note> Don't you agree? **CALLICLES:** I do. **SOCRATES:** So, where there is a tyrant who is a savage and uneducated ruler, if there were someone in the city much better than him, wouldn't the tyrant fear him? And could he ever be a true friend to such a man with all his heart? **CALLICLES:** That is true. **SOCRATES:** Nor would he be a friend to someone much inferior to himself, for the tyrant would despise him and never treat him with the seriousness due to a friend. **CALLICLES:** That is also true. **SOCRATES:** There remains, then, only one kind of friend worthy of the name for such a ruler: the man who is of the same character, who praises and blames the same things, and is willing to be ruled by and submissive to the ruler. Such a man will have great power in <margin>D</margin> that city, and no one will wrong him without paying for it. Is that not how it is? **CALLICLES:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** So if a young man in such a city thinks to himself, "How can I become very powerful and ensure no one wrongs me?" his path, it seems, is to accustom himself from his youth to enjoy and hate the same things as his master, and to make himself as much like the master as possible. Is that not so? **CALLICLES:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** And so, according to your argument, he will achieve the goal of not being wronged and having great power in the city. **CALLICLES:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** But will he also achieve the goal of not committing injustice? Or is he far from it? If he is to be like the ruler, who is unjust, he will surely have great power alongside him. On the contrary, I think his <margin>E</margin> preparation will be aimed at being able to commit as much injustice as possible and not paying the penalty for it. Is that not so? **CALLICLES:** It appears so. **SOCRATES:** Then he will possess the greatest of evils, having a soul that is wretched and mutilated because of his imitation of the master and his pursuit of power. **CALLICLES:** I don't know how you always twist these arguments up and down, Socrates! Don't you know that the imitator can kill the one who does not imitate, if he wishes, and strip him of his property? **SOCRATES:** I know it, my good Callicles—unless I am deaf—for I have heard it from you and Polus many times just now, and from almost everyone else in the city. <margin>F</margin> But you hear me too: he will kill him if he wishes, but it will be a wicked man killing a man who is honorable and good. **CALLICLES:** And isn't that the very thing that is so aggravating? **SOCRATES:** Not to a man of sense, as the argument shows. Or do you think a man should prepare himself to live as long as possible and study those arts that always save us from dangers, like that rhetoric you urge me to practice, which saves lives in the law courts? **CALLICLES:** Yes, by Zeus, and I am giving you good advice! **SOCRATES:** Tell me, then, my excellent friend, does the skill of swimming also seem to be a grand thing to you? **CALLICLES:** No, by Zeus, not to me. **SOCRATES:** And yet it also saves men from death when they fall into a situation where that skill is needed. If that seems trivial to you, I will tell you of a greater skill, <margin>G</margin> that of navigation <note>original: "kybernetike"; the art of the pilot or steersman</note>. It saves not only souls but also bodies and property from the extreme dangers, just as rhetoric does. But this skill is modest and orderly; it does not put on airs or act as if it were performing some magnificent feat. Yet, having achieved the same results as the legal skill—if it brings a man safely here from Aegina—it charges, I think, only two obols. And if it brings him from Egypt or the Pontus, having performed this great service of saving all those things I just mentioned—the man himself, his children, property, and wife—and landing them in the harbor, it charges at most two drachmas <note>The obol and drachma were standard Greek coins; the point is that the pilot's fee is remarkably small compared to the value of the lives saved.</note>. And the man who possesses this skill and has performed these tasks, once he has disembarked, walks along the shore by his ship in a humble manner. <margin>H</margin> For he calculates, I suppose, that it is uncertain which of his passengers he has benefited by not letting them drown, and which he has harmed, knowing that he has landed them no better in body or soul than when they first boarded his ship.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...would it follow that he neither inflicts injury nor receives it? Is this achieved through power or through will? I put it this way: if someone does not wish to suffer, will he not suffer injury? Or if he provides himself with power, will he only then avoid suffering it? **CALLICLES:** It is certainly established that it requires power. **SOCRATES:** And what about inflicting injury? Is it enough of a remedy if someone simply does not wish to be injurious? For then he will not inflict injury. Or must a certain power and skill <note>original: "ars"; translated from the Greek "techne," meaning a professional expertise.</note> be provided for this as well, which if one has not learned and practiced, he will do wrong? Why don't you at least answer me on this, Callicles? Do Polus and I seem to you to have been rightly compelled by the previous arguments or not? <margin>B</margin> For we confessed that no one wishes to do injury, but that those who inflict it do so unwillingly. **CALLICLES:** Let that be as you say, Socrates, so that you may conclude this dispute. **SOCRATES:** Does it seem then that a certain power and skill must be provided for this, so that we do not do injury to anyone? **CALLICLES:** Entirely so. **SOCRATES:** What then is the skill for providing the capacity by which one suffers either no injury at all or the very least? Consider whether the same thing occurs to you as to me. To me, it seems that one must either obtain the leadership in the state, or seize a tyranny, or have close dealings with the current government. **CALLICLES:** You see, O Socrates, how ready I am to approve if you say anything correctly. Truly, it seems to me that you have said this very rightly indeed. <margin>C</margin> **SOCRATES:** Consider this further, if I seem to speak rightly. It seems to me that each person is most a friend to someone who—as the ancient sages teach—is most like himself. Does it not seem so to you? **CALLICLES:** It does to me. **SOCRATES:** Where a fierce and unrefined tyrant rules, if there were someone in that city much better than him, wouldn't the tyrant fear him? And could he ever be a friend to him with all his heart? **CALLICLES:** That is how it happens. **SOCRATES:** Nor if someone were much worse? For the tyrant will despise him and will never be affected toward him as toward a friend. **CALLICLES:** You speak the truth. **SOCRATES:** Only that man, then, will be able to be a friend worthy of esteem to him, <margin>D</margin> who, being similar in character and praising and blaming the same things, is willing to be subject to and obey the master. This man will surely have great power in that city; no one will inflict injury upon him with impunity. Is it not so? **CALLICLES:** It is. **SOCRATES:** If then someone from among the youth in this city should think by what means he might best be able to obtain great power, so that no one could inflict injury upon him: the way, it seems to him, is this: from his very youth to accustom himself to rejoice and grieve at the same things as the master, and so to provide that he be as similar to him as possible. Is it not so? **CALLICLES:** It is. **SOCRATES:** This man then, as the present discourse indicates, will achieve the goal of not being able to have injury inflicted upon him, <margin>E</margin> and he will have great power in the city. **CALLICLES:** Entirely. **SOCRATES:** Will he also achieve the goal of inflicting injury on no one? Or is he far from it? Since he will be like an unjust ruler and have great authority with him. Truly, I think such a state of life is most adapted to this: that he be able to do as many injuries as possible and entirely escape the penalties for those injuries. Is it not so? **CALLICLES:** It appears so. **SOCRATES:** Will he not be occupied by the greatest evil, since he is wicked and has a soul infected by the imitation of his master and a similar power? **CALLICLES:** I do not know how, <margin>F</margin> O Socrates, you turn the discourse up and down. Do you not know that he who thus imitates can kill him who does not imitate, if only he wishes, and despoil him of his fortunes? **SOCRATES:** I know indeed, O good Callicles, unless I am deaf; since I have heard the same thing frequently not only from you but also from Polus a little while ago, and from almost everyone else in the city. But listen to me yourself: he will indeed kill him, if he wishes; but a wicked man will kill an honorable and good one. **CALLICLES:** But this is exactly what is so hard to bear. **SOCRATES:** Certainly not to a man endowed with mind and reason, as even your own discourse signifies. Or do you think a man must labor greatly at this very thing: to live as long as possible, and to practice those arts which can always keep us safe from dangers, such as rhetoric is, which you exhort me to take up, <margin>G</margin> because it often saves one in the courts. **CALLICLES:** By Jove, I am advising you rightly. **SOCRATES:** What then, O best of men? Does the skill of swimming seem remarkable to you? **CALLICLES:** No, by Jove. **SOCRATES:** Yet this saves men from destruction whenever they fall into a place where such an art is needed. But if this seems small to you, I will bring forward a greater one, namely the art of steering <note>original: "gubernatoriam"; navigation or the skill of a ship's pilot.</note>, which saves not only life but also bodies and money from extreme dangers, no differently than rhetoric. And yet this art is humble and modest, not boastful nor bombastic, as if it handled something magnificent and lofty. But although it performs the same things as rhetoric, if it brings one safely from Aegina to here, it demands only two coins <note>original: "numos"; here referring to the Greek obols.</note>. If indeed it has brought one back safely from Egypt or the <margin>H</margin> Pontus, as I was saying—ourselves, our children, wives, and riches—it demands two drachmas. And he who is endowed with this art, and who has performed these things, upon descending and walking on the shore by the sea and his ship, by no means carries himself high or is puffed up. For he notices, as I think, that it is uncertain whether he has benefited or harmed those whom he saved from being submerged in the waves: understanding that he has brought them back no better in body or soul than they were when they first entered the ship.

<summary>Socrates argues that to avoid suffering injustice in a corrupt state, one must become like the ruler, but warns that this imitation corrupts the soul. He compares rhetoric to the skill of a ship's pilot, noting that while both save lives, neither can improve the moral quality of the person saved.</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Callicles, Gorgias, justice, power, tyranny, Socratic Paradox, rhetoric, navigation, pilot, morality, soul</keywords>

--- Page 340 ---
<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Callicles. Previously, Socrates argued that power is only useful if it is used for justice. He now begins to deconstruct Callicles’ admiration for those who simply "save lives" or possess political power, using the analogy of the ship-pilot and the engineer.</meta>

### ->OF PLATO<-

<margin>A</margin> He thinks, therefore, that if someone pressed by great and incurable diseases of the body does not perish in the sea, this man is wretched for the very reason that he did not perish, and has received no benefit from the pilot. But if someone has many incurable diseases in his soul—which is more precious than the body—is it really right for this man to live? Will it bring him any benefit if someone saves him, whether from the sea, or from a court of justice, or from anywhere else? On the contrary, the pilot surely knows that it is not profitable for a wicked man to live, for he must necessarily live badly. For this reason, there is no law by which a pilot, although he saves us, can boast or be held in high honor. Furthermore, consider the <margin>B</margin> engineer <note>original: "machinarum faber" / "μηχανοποιόν"; a maker of engines or siege machines</note>, O marvelous man! He can sometimes save no less than a general or a pilot or anyone else, for he occasionally provides safety to entire cities. Does he seem to you to be comparable to a legal advocate? And yet, if he wanted to extol his own business as you people do, he would surely overwhelm you with words, exhorting everyone to become engineers, as if everything else were of no importance. He would not lack for material to say. Nevertheless, you would despise him and his art no less, and as if in insult you would call him a "mechanic," and you would not wish to give your daughter in marriage to his son, nor would you want to take his daughter for your own son. Although you praise your own status for certain reasons, by what right can you justly despise the engineer or the others I have just mentioned? <margin>C</margin> I know you would say that you are better and born of better stock. But if "better" is not what I say it is—if instead virtue is simply this: to save oneself and one's possessions, no matter what kind of person one is—then your censure of the engineer, the doctor, and all other arts invented for the sake of safety becomes ridiculous. But, O blessed man, see whether the noble and the good might be something other than saving and being saved. For a man who is truly a man should not desire to live for any length of time whatever, nor should he be in love with this life; rather, he should leave these cares to God and believe the <margin>Mulierum dictum, neminé vitare poſſe fatum.</margin> <margin>D</margin> women who say that no one can escape fate. <note>original: "fatun" / "εἱμαρμένην"; the predetermined destiny of a person</note> Instead, he should consider this above all: by what means he might live as well as possible during the time he is alive. Would this not happen if he makes himself as similar as possible to the citizens with whom he lives? And should you now strive to become as similar as possible to the Athenian people, if you are to be a friend to them and have great authority among them? Consider then whether this is profitable for you and me, O blessed man, lest that happens to us which they say happens to the Thessalian women <note>The witches of Thessaly were legendary for their ability to "draw down the moon," but the proverb suggests they did so at the cost of their own well-being or family.</note> when they draw down the moon: that our choice of this power in the city results in the loss of what is dearest to us. But if you think any man will hand over to you an art of such a kind that will make you powerful in this city while being unlike its government—whether for better or for worse—you do not, in my view, think correctly, O Callicles. For one must not be a mere imitator, but by one's very nature be similar to them, if <margin>E</margin> you are to achieve anything genuine toward the goodwill of the Athenian people, and by Zeus, toward Pyrilampes' son as well. Whoever makes you most like these people will make you a statesman and a rhetorician, just as you desire. For everyone delights in words that are consistent with their own character, and they are troubled by those that are different—unless you, O charming head, have something else to say. Shall we say anything to this, Callicles? <term>CALL.</term> I do not know how it is, Socrates, but you seem to speak well. Yet, I feel what happens to many others: I do not entirely believe you. <term>SOC.</term> The love for the people <note>original: "Amor populi" / "Ὁ δήμου ἔρως"; a play on the name of Callicles' lover, Demos</note>, O Callicles, dwelling in your soul, resists me. But if we consider these same things more often and more deeply, you <margin>F</margin> will perhaps be persuaded. Remember, then, that we said there are two ways of caring for both the body and the soul. One of these aims at pleasure, while the other aims at what is best, not showing favor but struggling for improvement. Did we not define these things earlier? <term>C.</term> Certainly. <term>S.</term> And that which leans toward pleasure is ignoble and is nothing other than flattery, is it not? <term>C.</term> Let it be so, if it pleases you. <term>S.</term> But the other strives to make whatever we care for, whether soul or body, as good as possible. <term>CAL.</term> Entirely so. <term>SOC.</term> Therefore, we must undertake the care of the state and its citizens in such a way that we make the citizens themselves good. Otherwise, <margin>G</margin> as we found earlier, it is of no use to bestow any other benefit unless the mind of those who are to receive it is honorable and good—whether they receive much money, or power, or any other authority. Shall we say this is so, or not? <term>CAL.</term> Entirely, if you like. <term>SOC.</term> If then, Callicles, we were encouraging one another to handle public affairs, such as the building of walls, or docks, or great temples, would we not need to consider and examine ourselves: first, whether we possess the skill of building or not, and from whom we learned it? Would it not be necessary <margin>H</margin> for this to be done? <term>CAL.</term> Certainly. <term>SOC.</term> And secondly, we would ask whether we have ever constructed any building privately, either for ourselves or for friends, and whether that building is beautiful or shameful. If we found upon examination that we had good and excellent teachers, and that many fine buildings had been built by us both with our teachers and privately by ourselves after we were free from our teachers—only then would it be consistent with reason to turn to public works. But if we could neither show who our teacher was, nor point to buildings...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...bodies or souls. He calculates, then, that if someone is held fast by great and incurable diseases in the body and did not drown, this man is miserable because he did not die, and has received no benefit from him. But if then someone has many and incurable diseases in that which is more precious than the body—the soul—must this man live? And would he benefit him, whether he saves him from the sea, or from the law court, or from any other place? No, for he knows that it is not better for the wicked man to live. For he must of necessity live badly. Therefore, it is not the custom for the pilot to be prideful, even though he saves us. Nor, O <margin>B</margin> wonderful man, should the engineer, who is able to save sometimes no less than a general—not to mention a pilot—or any other. For sometimes he saves whole cities. Does he seem to you to be on the level of the legal advocate? And yet, if he wished to speak, O Callicles, as you people do, dignifying his business, he would bury you in words, speaking and exhorting that it is necessary to become engineers, because all other things are nothing. For his argument would be sufficient for him. But you nonetheless look down on him and his art; and as an insult, you would call him an engineer; and you would not wish to give your son to his daughter, nor would you yourself take his. And yet, from the reasons you praise your own things, by what right do you look down on the engineer and the others I was just mentioning? I know you would say you are better and from better people. But if "better" is not what <margin>C</margin> I say, but this very thing is virtue: to save oneself and one's own, being whatever sort of person one happens to be, then your blame of the engineer, the doctor, and the other arts made for the sake of saving becomes laughable. But, O blessed man, see if the noble and the good are something other than saving and being saved. For this—living for however much time—should perhaps be dismissed by a man who is truly a man, and he should not be a lover of life; instead, having entrusted these things to God and having believed the women that no one could escape fate, he must consider what follows: in what way he might live best for this time which he is destined to live. Is it by making himself like the government in which <margin>D</margin> he lives? And so now, must you become as similar as possible to the people of Athens, if you are to be dear to them and be very powerful in the city? See if this is profitable for you and me; so that we do not, O strange man, suffer what they say the Thessalian women suffer who draw down the moon: our choice of this power in the city will be at the cost of what is dearest to us. But if you think any man will deliver to you such an art as will make you very powerful in this city while being unlike the government—whether for the better or for the worse—it seems to me, O Callicles, you are not deliberating rightly. For one must not be an imitator, but naturally similar to these people, if you are to produce anything genuine toward friendship with the Athenian people, and by Zeus, with the son of Pyrilampes as well. Whoever, therefore, will make you most similar to these people, he will <margin>E</margin> make you, as you desire to be a statesman, a statesman and a rhetorician. For everyone rejoices in speeches spoken in their own character, but they are annoyed by those of a foreign character—unless you say something else, O dear head. Shall we say something to these things, Callicles? <term>CALL.</term> I do not know how, Socrates, you seem to me to speak well. But the passion of the many has happened to me: I do not entirely believe you. <term>S.</term> For the love of the people, O Callicles, being in your soul, stands against me; but if perhaps we examine these same things many times and better, you will be persuaded. Remember, then, that we said there were two cares, tending <margin>F</margin> to each, both body and soul: one to associate for pleasure, and the other for the best, not being indulgent but struggling against it. Were these not the things we defined then? <term>K.</term> Certainly. <term>S.</term> Therefore, the one for pleasure is ignoble, and happens to be nothing other than flattery? <term>K.</term> Let it be so, if you wish it thus. <term>S.</term> But the other—how it shall be for the best—whether it happens to be body or soul, we tend to it. <term>K.</term> Certainly. <term>S.</term> Then must we not thus attempt to care for the city and the citizens, by making the citizens themselves as good as possible? For without this (as we found in the things before), there is no benefit in offering any other service, unless the mind of those who are about to receive either much money, or some rule, or any other power, is honorable. Shall we set it down that it is so? <margin>G</margin> <term>K.</term> Certainly, if it is more pleasing to you. <term>S.</term> If then we were exhorting one another, O Callicles, to act publicly in political affairs, regarding building—either of walls, or docks, or temples—concerning the greatest buildings, would we have to consider ourselves or examine, first if we understand the art or do not understand the art of building, and from whom we learned it? Would it be necessary, or not? <term>K.</term> Certainly. <term>S.</term> Then again, this second thing: whether we have ever built any building privately, either for some friend or for ourselves, and whether this building is beautiful or shameful. And if we found upon looking that we had teachers who were good and reputable, and <margin>H</margin> many and beautiful buildings built by us with the teachers, and many by ourselves privately after we were departed from the teachers—if things were thus, it would be the part of those with sense to go to public works. But if we had no teacher of ourselves to show, and no buildings...

<margin>A</margin> ...whether they were worth anything or nothing. Indeed, it would be foolish to attempt public works and to encourage one another to do so [without experience]. <margin>A</margin> they would not have been constructed poorly or not at all: it would certainly be foolish to undertake public works and to exhort one another to them. <meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Callicles in Plato's "Gorgias." Socrates is critiquing the famous Athenian statesmen of the past, arguing that they were merely "servants" who catered to the people's desires rather than true leaders who improved the citizens' souls.</meta>

### ->PLATONIS<-

<margin>A</margin> Or as you say, if they had been such [good] men, these things would never have happened to them. For good charioteers do not fall out of their chariots at the start, only to fall out later after they have trained their horses and become more skilled in their art. That does not happen in chariot-driving, nor in any other work; or does it seem so to you? <term>CAL.</term> <note>Callicles, Socrates' interlocutor who champions the "right of the stronger."</note> Not at all. <term>SOCRAT.</term> <note>Socrates, the philosopher.</note> Then what was said by us earlier appears to be true: that we know of no man in this city who has proven to be a good citizen in matters of state. You admitted that <margin>B</margin> none of those who are active now are such; but you claimed that among those who came before, some were, and you chose these men as the best among them. Yet these men have turned out to be no different in this matter than the orators of today. Therefore, if they were orators, they used neither the true art of rhetoric—otherwise they would never have fallen—nor the art of flattery. <term>CAL.</term> But it is far from the case, Socrates, that anyone today has performed such deeds as any one of those men performed. <term>SOCR.</term> My dear friend, I do not blame them insofar as they were servants of the city; indeed, in this respect, they seem to me to have been more diligent than our contemporaries, and better able to provide the city with those things it desired. But in the matter of redirecting the citizens' desires rather than giving in to them—using both persuasion and force to lead them toward that which would make the citizens better—there is, so to speak, no difference between these men and those of today. Yet this alone <margin>C</margin> is the duty of a good citizen. Nevertheless, I grant you that those men were more capable than these in providing the state with ships, dockyards, walls, and many other such things. Thus, we have come round to a ridiculous point in our discussion: for in all this time we have been talking, we never cease circling back to the same spot, unaware of what we are saying. I believe you have often admitted and recognized that there is a two-fold way of caring for both the body and the soul. One is a service, by which the things the body desires are provided: if it is hungry, food; if thirsty, drink; if cold, clothing, blankets, shoes, and other things required for bodily use. I <margin>D</margin> deliberately use these images for you so that you may understand more easily. For it is no wonder if a provider of these things—whether he be a tavern-keeper, a merchant, or a craftsman of any of these, such as a baker, a cook, a weaver, a shoemaker, or a leather-dresser—appears to be a caretaker of the body, both to himself and to others who are ignorant. But beyond all these, there is an art of gymnastics and medicine, in which the true care of the body consists. It is proper for these arts to command all the others and to use their products, because they possess the knowledge of what is good and bad for the body’s nourishment and health—something all the others are ignorant of. <margin>E</margin> For this reason, we must say that these other arts are servile, ministerial, and illiberal in the care of the body, while gymnastics and medicine are rightfully their masters. Now, you seem to me at times to recognize that these same principles apply to the soul, and you agree with me as if you understand what I am saying. But a little later, you bring forward the idea that there were once "noble and good" men in this city. And when I ask who they were, you seem to offer men who are quite the same in statecraft as if, when I asked who are or were good caretakers of the body in gymnastics, you were to answer me quite seriously: "Thearion the baker, and Mithaecus <note>Mithaecus was a famous chef from Sicily, known for writing a cookbook.</note> who wrote on the Sicilian art of cookery, and Sarambus the tavern-keeper"—as if these were wonderful <margin>F</margin> cultivators of the body: one for providing marvelous bread, the other for feasts, the other for wine. Perhaps you would be indignant if I told you that you do not understand gymnastics. For you are bringing forward servants and providers of desires, who understand nothing truly noble or good about the body; instead, they fill and fatten men's bodies as they see fit, and are praised by them even while they destroy their old health. And later, when diseases attack those who have been nourished this way, they do not accuse those who fed them out of ignorance; rather, they blame those who fed them for pleasure. When, I say, such immoderate filling finally brings on disease, they then criticize and find fault with their current advisors <margin>G</margin> and, if they can, they even harm them, while they heap praises on those earlier men who were the actual cause of the disease. And now, Callicles, you are doing something very similar when you praise those who nourished these citizens and filled them with the things they happened to desire. They say these men made the city great, but they do not perceive that it is now swollen and festering inside because of those men of old. For without temperance and justice, they have filled this city with harbors, dockyards, walls, tributes, revenues, and such trifles. When the outbreak of weakness finally comes, those who are governing the state at that moment are blamed. But Themistocles <note>The leader of Athens during the Persian Wars.</note> himself, and Cimon, and Pericles—who were the causes of the evils—are praised. <margin>H</margin> Therefore, unless you are careful, you may be caught, as may my friend Alcibiades, when you lose not only what was recently acquired but your old possessions as well, even though you were not the sole cause of the troubles, but perhaps only an accomplice. And yet, I see a foolish thing happening now, and I hear of it regarding those men of old. For I perceive that whenever the city treats one...
