<margin>Α</margin> ...as you say, if they had ever suffered these things. Surely good charioteers do not fall out of their chariots at the beginning, only to fall out after they have tended the horses and become better charioteers themselves? This is not the case in charioteering, nor in any other work. Or does it seem so to you? <term>CAL.</term> Not to me. <term>SOCR.</term> It seems, then, our previous words were true: that we know of no man who has proven to be a good statesman in this city. You agreed that none are so now, but you distinguished those of former times, and you selected these men. Yet they have been shown to be no different <margin>Β</margin> from those of the present. So, if they were orators, they used neither the true rhetoric (for they would not have fallen) nor the flattering kind. <term>CAL.</term> But surely, Socrates, it is a far cry from any of those today performing such works as any one of those men performed. <term>SOCR.</term> My dear fellow, I do not blame them as servants of the city; rather, they seem to me to have been more service-oriented than those now, and better able to provide the city with what it desired. But as for redirecting desires and not giving in—persuading and forcing the citizens toward that which would make them better—they were no different, so to speak, from the current ones. And that alone is the work of a good citizen. As for ships, walls, and dockyards, and many other such things, I agree with you that they were more clever at providing them than these men. But we are doing a ridiculous thing, you and I, in our discussion. <margin>C</margin> For in all the time we have been talking, we never stop circling back to the same point, ignorant of each other’s meaning. I think you have often admitted and recognized that this activity is twofold, concerning both the body and the soul. One part is servile, by which it is possible to provide—if our bodies are hungry—food; if thirsty, drink; if cold, clothing, bedding, shoes, and other things the body comes to desire. I am speaking to you through the same images on purpose so you may understand more easily. For it is nothing surprising that a provider of these things—whether a shopkeeper, a merchant, or a producer of the things themselves, like a baker, or a cook, or a weaver, or a shoemaker, or a tanner—should seem, being such as he is, both to himself and to others, to be a <margin>D</margin> caretaker of the body—at least to anyone who does not know that there is, besides all these, the art of gymnastics and medicine, which is truly the care of the body. It belongs to this art to rule over all these other arts and to use their works, because it knows what is useful and what is harmful in food and drink for the excellence of the body, while all these other arts are ignorant of it. Therefore, we must call these other arts slavish, servile, and illiberal in their concern for the body, but gymnastics and medicine are, by right, their mistresses. Now, that <margin>E</margin> these same things apply to the soul, you seem to me sometimes to understand; and you agree as if you know what I mean. But then a little later you come saying that "noble and good" citizens have existed in the city. And when I ask who they were, you seem to me to offer men for statecraft who are just like the people I would find if, when I asked about gymnastics—who had been or were good caretakers of bodies—you told me with great seriousness: "Thearion the baker, and Mithaecus who wrote the book on Sicilian cookery, and Sarambus the tavern-keeper"; saying that these had been wonderful caretakers of bodies—one for preparing wonderful bread, another for delicacies, another for wine. Perhaps you would be annoyed if I said to you: "My man, you understand nothing of gymnastics." <margin>F</margin> You tell me of servants and providers of desires—men who understand nothing noble or good regarding it; who, if it so happens, after filling and fattening the bodies of men and being praised by them, eventually destroy their original flesh as well. And they, in their inexperience, will not blame those who feasted them for their diseases and the loss of their original flesh; rather, they will blame whoever happens to be present and advising them at the time when the surfeit of that day finally brings disease much later. Because it was done without health, they will blame and reproach these people, and do them some harm if they can; but those former <margin>G</margin> men, the ones actually responsible for the evils, they will praise. And you now, Callicles, are doing something very similar: you praise men who feasted these people, entertaining them with the things they desired. And they say they made the city great; but they do not perceive that the city is swollen and festering because of those men of old. For without temperance and justice, they have filled the city with harbors, and dockyards, and walls, and tributes, and such nonsense. When, therefore, this fit of weakness comes, they will blame the advisors present at the time, but they will praise Themistocles and Cimon and Pericles, the ones responsible for the evils. And perhaps they will lay hold of you, if you are not careful, and my comrade Alcibiades, when they lose their old possessions in addition to what they gained—not that you are the primary causes of the evils, but perhaps <margin>H</margin> accomplices. And yet I see a foolish thing happening now, and I hear of it regarding the men of old. For I perceive that whenever the city treats someone...

<summary>In this passage, Socrates argues that the revered statesmen of Athens' past were merely providers of physical luxury rather than moral virtue. He compares them to bakers and cooks who fatten the body but destroy its health, contrasting them with true "doctors" of the soul.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Callicles in Plato’s "Gorgias." Socrates is extending his critique of Athenian statesmen, arguing that if they were truly "good" leaders, they would have improved the character of the citizens so much that the citizens would never turn against them. This parallels his critique of the Sophists, who claim to teach virtue but then complain when their students refuse to pay them.</meta>

### ->GORGIAS<-

...those who handle political affairs, when the city treats them unjustly, they become indignant and complain as if they are suffering terribly, despite having done many good deeds for the city. They claim, of course, that they are being destroyed unjustly by it. But this is an absolute falsehood. For no leader of a city could ever be destroyed unjustly by the very city he leads. It seems that the same thing happens to those who pretend to be statesmen as happens to those who are <term>Sophists</term> <note>Sophists were professional teachers in Ancient Greece who traveled from city to city, teaching rhetoric and "virtue" for a fee.</note>. For the Sophists, though they are wise in other matters, do a very absurd thing: while they claim to be teachers of virtue, they frequently accuse their own students of doing them wrong by depriving them of their fees and failing to show any other gratitude, despite having received benefits from them. What could be more irrational than this claim? That men who have become good and just—having been stripped of injustice by their teacher and having acquired justice—should act unjustly with the very thing they no longer possess? Does this not seem absurd to you, my friend? You have truly forced me to <note>original: "δημηγορεῖν" (demegorein)</note> make a public speech, Callicles, because you refuse to answer. <term>CAL.</term> And you, could you not speak unless someone answered you? <term>SOCR.</term> It seems I can; at least now I am drawing out long speeches since you do not wish to answer. But, my good man, tell me in the name of friendship: does it not seem irrational to you for a man to say he has made someone good, and then to complain that the student, having been made good by him and being good now, is subsequently wicked? <term>CAL.</term> It seems so to me. <term>SOCR.</term> And do you not hear those who profess to educate men in virtue saying such things? <term>CAL.</term> I do. But why would you talk about men who are worth nothing? <term>SOCR.</term> And what would you say about those who claim to lead the city and take care that it becomes as good as possible, but then turn around and accuse it, whenever the occasion arises, of being most wicked? Do you think these men differ at all from the others? The <term>Sophist</term> and the <term>Rhetor</term> <note>A Rhetor was a public speaker or politician.</note>, my dear fellow, are the same thing, or at least something very close and similar, as I was saying to Polus. But out of ignorance, you think one thing—Rhetoric—is something very beautiful, while you despise the other. In truth, however, the art of the Sophist is more beautiful than Rhetoric, just as the art of legislation is more beautiful than the judicial art, and gymnastics more beautiful than medicine. I used to think that only public speakers and Sophists were not permitted to complain about the very thing they teach—that their students are wicked toward them. Otherwise, by this very same argument, they would be accusing themselves at the same time of having provided no benefit to those they claim to have helped. Is this not how it is? <term>CAL.</term> Certainly. <term>SOCR.</term> And indeed, it is likely that only these people could afford to provide their service without a fixed fee, if what they said were true. For in the case of other benefits, if someone were made fast at running by a trainer, he might perhaps deprive the trainer of his gratitude if the trainer gave his service freely without making a contract for a fee, or if he gave the speed away before receiving the money. For it is not by slowness, I believe, that men act unjustly, but by injustice. Is that not so? <term>CAL.</term> Yes. <term>SOCR.</term> Therefore, if someone removes this very thing—injustice—there is no danger of him ever being treated unjustly. This is the only service that can be safely given away, provided one can actually make men good. Is it not so? <term>CAL.</term> I agree. <term>SOCR.</term> This is why, it seems, there is no shame in taking money for giving other kinds of advice, such as about building or other arts. <term>CAL.</term> So it seems. <term>SOCR.</term> But concerning this specific practice—how a person might become as good as possible and best manage his own household or the city—it is considered shameful to refuse to give advice unless someone gives him money. Is that not so? <term>CAL.</term> Yes. <term>SOCR.</term> The reason is clearly this: this is the only one of all benefits that makes the recipient desire to do good in return. Thus, it seems to be a good sign if someone, having performed this service, is treated well in return; but if not, then not. Is this the case? <term>CAL.</term> It is. <term>SOCR.</term> To which of these two types of service to the city do you then invite me? Define it for me: to the one where I struggle with the Athenians to make them as good as possible, like a doctor? Or to the one where I act as a servant and speak only to please them? Tell me the truth, Callicles. For it is only right that, since you began by speaking boldly to me, you should continue to say what you think. So speak now, well and nobly. <term>CAL.</term> I say then, that I invite you to act as a servant. <term>SOCR.</term> You are calling me to be a flatterer, then, my most noble friend. <term>CAL.</term> You may call it being a <term>Mysian</term> <note>The "Mysian" (Mysus) was a proverbially low, contemptible person, often used to mean the lowliest of the low.</note> if you prefer, Socrates; for if you do not do these things— <term>SOCR.</term> Do not say what you have said many times: that "whoever wishes will kill me," lest I should have to say in return, "Yes, a wicked man killing a good man." And do not say, "He will take away whatever I have," lest I should have to say, "But having taken it, he will not know how to use it; just as he took it unjustly, so having received it, he will use it unjustly; and if unjustly, then shamefully; and if shamefully, then badly." <term>CAL.</term> You seem to me, Socrates, to believe that you could never suffer any of these things, as if you lived out of harm's way and could not be brought into a court of law by some perhaps very wretched and low fellow. <term>SOCR.</term> I would be a fool indeed, Callicles, truly so, if I did not think that in this city anyone might suffer whatever happens to come along. But this I know well: that if I ever enter a court facing the danger of which you speak, he who brings me there will be a wicked man. For no good man would bring an innocent man to trial. Indeed, it would be nothing strange if I were put to death. Do you want me to tell you why I think this?

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Among those who are active in the republic, he attempts to condemn them for injustice; they take it heavily and are tormented in spirit, as if they were suffering unfair things—they who have conferred many benefits upon the republic. Certainly, they say they are being condemned unjustly by it. Which is entirely false. For a governor of a republic is never condemned unjustly by the city over which he presides. The same thing seems to happen to those involved in the republic as happens to the sophists. <margin>B</margin> For the sophists, although wise in other matters, act absurdly in this one thing: that while they claim to teach virtues, they often accuse their disciples of being ungrateful and unjust, who, though they have received good things from them, return no fee or gratitude. Than which speech nothing is further from reason: namely, that men who have been made good and just, and who have been removed from injustice by the work of the teacher, and endowed with justice, should inflict injuries on their teachers with that very injustice which they do not possess. Does it not seem to you, O friend, that this is absurd? In truth, you have forced me to play the orator, while you refuse to answer. <term>CA.</term> Can you not speak for yourself unless someone answers you? <term>SOC.</term> It seems I can; and now I am already extending my speeches at length, while you do not deign to answer me. But, O good man, tell me by Jupiter, the god of friendship: does it not seem beyond reason to you that he who says he has rendered someone good should complain about the same person, as if he who was made good by him is also evil? <margin>C</margin> <term>CAL.</term> It seems so to me. <term>SOC.</term> Do you not hear those who profess to teach virtue complaining of such things? <term>CAL.</term> I do indeed, but what can you say of men of no value? <term>SOC.</term> What indeed would you say of those who say they preside over the republic, and carefully devise how it may be the best possible, and then turn and accuse it as it happens, as if it were the worst? Do you think these differ from the others? Truly, O blessed one, a sophist and a rhetor are the same, or something very near and similar, as I was saying to Polus. But you, because of ignorance, think rhetoric is something excellent, but you despise the sophistical art. In truth, the sophistical art is more beautiful than rhetoric, just as the <margin>D</margin> making of laws is more beautiful than the judicial, and gymnastics than medicine. But only to the public speakers and sophists do I think it should not be granted to complain about that which they themselves teach, as if it were an evil to themselves. Otherwise, in that same accusation, they would equally incriminate themselves, as if they had profited nothing for those to whom they claim to have brought utility. Is it not so? <term>CAL.</term> Exactly so. <term>SOC.</term> And to have conferred a benefit without a fee, as is consistent, was fitting for these alone, if indeed they spoke the truth. For when someone has received other benefits—such as becoming fast through a master of gymnastics—perhaps he would not return gratitude unless he were cautioned to pay the fee as soon as he had escaped his slowness. <margin>E</margin> For it is not by slowness, I think, that men do injury, but by injustice. Is it not so? <term>CAL.</term> So it is. <term>SOC.</term> If anyone, therefore, takes away this very thing, namely injustice, he would have avoided the danger of injury. Truly, a benefit can be placed in safety through this alone: if one can truly make those on whom he confers it good. Is it not so? <term>CAL.</term> I agree. <term>SOC.</term> Therefore, it seems, in other contracts it is not shameful to look out for oneself, such as for buildings and other crafts. <term>CAL.</term> It appears so. <term>SOC.</term> But for this faculty—namely, that one becomes good and governs his family and the republic in the best way—it is considered shameful to be unwilling to teach anything before the money is secured. Is it not so? <term>CAL.</term> Certainly. <term>SOC.</term> <margin>F</margin> It is clear that this is the cause: because this alone of all benefits makes the one who has received it desirous of returning gratitude. Wherefore it seems to be an excellent proof: if he who has provided a service of this kind receives something in turn; but if not, by no means. Do these things stand so? <term>CAL.</term> They do. <term>SOC.</term> To which care of the city, then, do you exhort me? Come, define it for me: to that by which I may struggle with the Athenians and strive that they become as good as possible, like a doctor? Or to that by which I may become like a servant of pleasure and speak for the sake of favor? Tell me the truth, O Callicles; for it is fitting that you, as you began, should proceed boldly, expressing to me freely what you feel. And now, <margin>G</margin> therefore, answer well and nobly. <term>CAL.</term> I exhort you to the service. <term>SOC.</term> You provoke me, then, to flattery, O most noble man. <term>CAL.</term> If you prefer, O Socrates, to be called a <term>Mysian</term>, you shall be called so, unless you believe me. <term>SOC.</term> Do not object to me now what you have already often objected: namely, "whoever wishes will kill you, O Socrates," lest I should again answer: "but a bad man will kill a good one." Nor say again: "anyone will take from you, O Socrates, whatever you have," lest I also answer: "but truly he who takes it will not know how to use those things as useful to himself; but just as he took them unjustly from me, so he himself will use them unjustly; and if unjustly, <margin>H</margin> then also shamefully; and finally, if shamefully, then badly." <term>CAL.</term> You seem to me to think that nothing of this kind can happen to you, just as if you lived far from here; nor do you think you can be led into judgment by any

lazy and worthless man. <term>SOC.</term> I would certainly be a fool, O Callicles, if I did not think that in this city anyone could suffer anything of this kind. This, however, I know for certain: if I come into judgment, endangered by those things which you bring up, he who accuses me will be a wicked man. For no good man accuses an innocent man. Truly, it would be nothing strange if I were condemned to death. Do you wish me to tell you the reason why I [think] this?

<margin>No good man accuses the innocent.</margin>

<summary>Socrates argues that true statesmen and Sophists cannot logically complain about being mistreated by their followers, as their primary job is to instill the very justice that would prevent such mistreatment. He distinguishes between being a "servant" of the people's pleasures and a "doctor" of their souls, accepting that his commitment to the latter may lead to his death at the hands of a wicked accuser.</summary>

# ### ->OF PLATO<-

...expect? <term>CALL.</term> I certainly do. <term>SOC.</term> I believe that I, along with a few other Athenians—not to say alone—truly practice the <term>political art</term> <note>original: "civilem disciplinam." Socrates is claiming that true politics is the art of making souls better, not just managing the city's affairs.</note>, and that I alone among those now living exercise true statesmanship. This is because the words I speak at any time are not aimed at winning favor, but at what is best, rather than what is most pleasant. Because I am unwilling to do those "clever things" that you now advise and exhort me toward, I will have nothing to say in a court of justice. The same point occurs to me now that I said to <term>Polus</term> <note>A student of Gorgias who argued earlier in the dialogue that the powerful can do as they please.</note>. For I would be judged just as a doctor would be judged among children if a cook were to accuse him. Consider what sort of defense such a man could make if he were caught in such a situation and someone accused him in these words: "O children, this man has inflicted many evils upon you. He cuts and burns you <note>Referring to surgery and cautery, the harsh medical treatments of the time.</note>, and he twists you, making you waste away and choking you until you are at a loss; he gives you the most bitter potions and forces you to suffer hunger and thirst. I, however, provide you with many various and sweet treats." If a cook, as the accuser, brought these charges, what do you think a doctor caught in that trap would have to say? Or if perhaps he spoke the truth, saying: "All these things, O children, I did for the sake of your health"? How loudly do you think such judges would cry out? <term>CA.</term> One must assume they would cry out loudly indeed. <term>S.</term> Do you not think, then, that he would be held in the greatest confusion and at a total loss for a defense? <term>CA.</term> Entirely so. <term>S.</term> I know that the same thing would happen to me if I were dragged into court. For I would not be able to recount any pleasures I had discovered for their lusts—pleasures which they consider to be benefits and utilities—but I do not at all approve of those who invent them, nor do I consider those to whom they are provided to be any happier. Furthermore, if anyone should say that I either corrupt the youth by leading them into doubt and confusion, or that I rebuke and rail against my elders with bitter and biting words, whether in private or in public, I will not have the power to make them see that I say all these things justly—and that I consult only their own benefit—nor will I be able to bring forward anything else easily. For that reason, perhaps there is nothing that might not be decreed against me. <term>CALLIC.</term> Does it seem to you then, Socrates, that a man is in a good position in a city if he is such that he cannot protect himself? <term>SOCRAT.</term> If only he has this one thing in him, O <term>Callicles</term>, which you have often admitted: that he can provide that help to himself by which he has done or said nothing unjust against men or against the gods. For we have often agreed that this is the best kind of self-defense. If, therefore, someone should convict me of being unable to provide such help to myself or others, I would certainly be ashamed, whether I were refuted among many, or among a few, or alone by one person. And if I were to die because of this impotence, I would take it hard. But if I were to be put to death because of a lack of <term>flattering rhetoric</term> <note>Socrates distinguishes between true rhetoric (used for justice) and "flattery" (used to please the audience).</note>, I know for certain you would see me bearing death easily. For no one fears death itself, unless he is entirely devoid of reason and a coward; rather, he fears acting unjustly. For the soul to arrive in the underworld filled with many sins is the ultimate of all evils. Therefore, if you wish to know why this is so, I will offer you an account. <term>CA.</term> Indeed, since you have finished the rest, finish this as well. <term>SOC.</term> Listen then, as they say, to a very beautiful discourse, which I think you will consider a myth <note>original: "fabulam" / Greek "μῦθον"</note>, but I consider it a factual account. For I shall tell you what I am about to say as if it were the truth.

<margin>A</margin> ...expect? <term>CALL.</term> Very much so. <term>SOC.</term> I think that I, with a few other Athenians (lest I say alone), take up the truly political art, and alone among those now living I practice politics. Since, therefore, I do not speak the words I say on each occasion to win favor, but toward what is best, not what is most pleasant, and I am not willing to do those clever things you advise, I will not know what to say in the court of law. The same account comes to me as I told to <term>Polus</term>. For I shall be judged as a doctor would be judged among children, with a cook as the accuser. For consider what such a man could say in his defense if he were caught among them, <margin>B</margin> if someone accused him, saying: "O children, this man has worked many evils upon you; he destroys both you and the youngest among you by cutting and burning, and by wasting you away and choking you, he makes you at a loss; giving you the most bitter drinks and forcing you to hunger and thirst—not as I, who used to feast you on many sweet and varied things." What do you think a doctor, caught in such an evil situation, would have to say? Or if he told the truth, that "All these things I did, O children, for the sake of health"? How much do you think such judges would shout? Would it not be a great cry? <term>CALL.</term> Perhaps; one must certainly think so. <term>SOC.</term> Do you not think then that he would be in total confusion as to what he should say? <term>CALL.</term> Entirely so. <term>SOC.</term> I know that I too would suffer such a fate if I entered a court of law. <margin>C</margin> For I cannot tell them of the pleasures I have provided, which they consider to be benefits and utilities. But I do not envy those who provide them, nor those for whom they are provided. And if someone says that I either corrupt the youth by making them at a loss, or that I speak evil of the elders by saying bitter words either in private or in public, I will not be able to say the truth—that "I say and do all these things justly, for your own sake, O men of the jury"—nor will I be able to say anything else. So I shall likely suffer whatever happens. <term>CALL.</term> Does it seem to you then, O Socrates, that a man is well off in a city who is in such a state and is unable to help himself? <term>SOC.</term> If that one thing should be present in him, O <margin>D</margin> Callicles, which you have often agreed to: if he has helped himself by having said or done nothing unjust either concerning men or concerning the gods. For this has often been agreed by us to be the best kind of help for oneself. If, then, someone should refute me as being unable to provide this help to myself or another, I would be ashamed, whether refuted among many or few, or alone by one person; and if I should die because of this inability, I would be aggrieved. But if I should come to my end because of a lack of flattering rhetoric, I know well that you would see me bearing death easily. For no one fears dying itself, who is not altogether mindless and unmanly; but he fears acting unjustly. For to arrive in the underworld with a soul loaded with many <margin>E</margin> injustices is the last of all evils. And if you wish, I am willing to tell you an account of how this is so. <term>CALL.</term> Well, since you have finished the other things, finish this also. <term>SOC.</term> Listen then (as they say) to a very beautiful account, which you will think is a myth, as I suppose, but I think is a factual account. For I shall tell you what I am about to say as being true. For as Homer says, Zeus, Poseidon, and Pluto divided the rule among themselves when they received it from their father. There was this law concerning men in the time of Cronus, and it is still even now among the gods: that of men, he who has lived a just and holy life, when he dies, goes to the Isles of the Blessed to dwell in all happiness, outside of evils; but he who has lived unjustly and godlessly goes to the prison of payment and justice, which <margin>F</margin> they call Tartarus. In the time of Cronus, and even recently when Zeus had the rule, there were living judges of living men, judging them on that day when they were about to die. Therefore, the judgments were judged badly. So Pluto and the guardians from the Isles of the Blessed came and told Zeus that men were coming to them from both sides who were unworthy. So Zeus said: "Well, I," he said, "will stop this from happening. For now the judgments are judged badly. For those being judged," he said, "are judged while they are clothed. For they are judged while living. Many, then," he said, "having wicked souls, are dressed in beautiful bodies and noble birth and wealth; and when the judgment is, many witnesses come for them, to testify that they have lived justly. The <margin>G</margin> judges are dazed by these things, and at the same time they themselves judge while clothed, having eyes and ears and the whole body draped in front of their own souls. All these things stand in their way: their own clothing and the clothing of those being judged. First then," he said, "it must be stopped that they foresee their death; for now they foresee it. This, then, has already been told to Prometheus, that he should stop this in them. Next, they must be judged naked of all these things. For they must be judged after they have died. And the judge must be naked, dead, viewing with the soul itself the soul of each person, immediately after each has died, deserted by all his kin, leaving all that finery on the earth, so that the judgment may be just.

<summary>Socrates explains that his practice of true statesmanship makes him vulnerable in an Athenian court, as he refuses to use flattery. He concludes with a myth describing how Zeus established a post-mortem judgment of "naked" souls to ensure true justice, stripped of earthly status and deception.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the conclusion of the dialogue, where Socrates moves from the "doctor vs. cook" analogy to a formal myth regarding the final judgment of the soul. He describes how power on earth does not protect one from the scrutiny of the divine judges in the afterlife.</meta>

### ->GORGIAS.<-

<margin>A</margin> ...two from Asia, namely <term>Minos</term> and <term>Rhadamanthus</term>, and one from Europe, <term>Aeacus</term>. These men, therefore, after they have died, shall act as judges in a certain meadow, at the <term>crossroads</term> <note>original: "trivio," the place where three roads meet.</note> from which two paths lead: one toward <term>Tartarus</term> <note>The deep abyss used as a dungeon of torment and suffering for the wicked.</note>, and the other toward the <term>Isles of the Blessed</term>. Rhadamanthus shall judge those from Asia, while Aeacus shall judge those who come from Europe. To Minos, I shall assign the duty of being the final arbiter if anything remains ambiguous for the others, so that the judgment concerning the journey of souls may be as just and correct as possible. These are the things, O <term>Callicles</term>, which I have heard and which I believe to be true; and from these accounts, I have come to this conclusion: Death,
<margin>B</margin> as it seems to me, is nothing other than the dissolution of two things—the soul and the body—from one another. When these two have been separated, each of them retains much the same condition it possessed while the man was alive. At the start, the body displays its own nature, its care, and the marks of its experiences. For example, if someone had a large body, whether by nature, or through nourishment, or both, while he lived, his corpse will also be large after he dies. Likewise, if he was fat, he will be fat when dead, and so on for other traits. Furthermore, if a man took great care to wear his hair long, his corpse will retain that long hair. Again, if someone was a
<margin>C</margin> scoundrel <note>original: "verbero," referring to a slave or criminal who has been frequently whipped.</note> and had many marks of lashes impressed upon his body, either from whips or other wounds while he lived, we see that his dead body retains these same marks. And if any part of him was broken or twisted during life, these same things are apparent when he is dead. To put it briefly: whatever the condition of the body was during life, all or most of those features appear in the dead body for a time. The same thing, Callicles, seems to me to be true of the soul: everything is visible in the soul once it has stripped off the body—both its natural qualities and the impressions which the man contracted in his soul through his devotion to various pursuits. When, therefore, they arrive before the judge—those from Asia before Rhadamanthus—
<margin>D</margin> Rhadamanthus makes them stand before him and inspects each soul, though he does not know to whom the soul belongs. Often, encountering the soul of the <term>Great King of the Persians</term> <note>A common Greek archetype for the ultimate earthly power and luxury.</note>, or some other king or potentate, he finds nothing healthy in it. Instead, he sees it scourged and covered in scars from perjuries and injustice, marks which each of the man’s actions has impressed upon his soul. He sees everything twisted by lies and vanity, containing nothing straight because the man was raised without truth. Furthermore, because of the license to sin, and through petulance, soft luxury, and
<margin>E</margin> lack of restraint in individual actions, he sees a soul that is utterly disordered and foul. Having observed the soul in this state, he sends it in disgrace straight to the place of guarding, where it must undergo the punishments it deserves. It is appropriate that everyone who is rightly punished by another should either become better himself and receive some benefit, or serve as an example to others, so that those who see him suffering his punishment may become better through fear. Those who are punished by gods and men in a way that they derive some benefit are those who have committed remediable <note>original: "sanabilia," or curable.</note> sins; for them, pain and torment are profitable both among men and in the underworld. For there is no other way to be liberated from injustice. But those who are gripped by the most extreme injustice and have become incurable <note>original: "insanabiles"</note> because of such crimes, these are the ones from whom examples are made. They themselves no longer receive any benefit, being incurable;
<margin>F</margin> instead, they serve only as an example to others who behold them—punished for all time with the greatest, most bitter, and most terrifying agonies because of their crimes. They are displayed as a warning and a spectacle in the prison of the underworld for all the unjust who descend to those places. I say that <term>Archelaus</term> <note>The contemporary ruler of Macedon, whom Polus had previously cited as a "happy" man despite his crimes.</note> will be one of these, if what <term>Polus</term> says of him is true, as will any other tyrant of that sort. I believe that among those who serve only as examples, the majority are tyrants, kings, potentates, and rulers of cities. <margin>Odyssey, Book 11</margin> Indeed, because these men have the license to sin, they commit the gravest and most profane crimes. <term>Homer</term> bears witness to this, for he depicts kings and potentates as those who are punished for all time in the underworld, such as
<margin>G</margin> <term>Tantalus</term>, <term>Sisyphus</term>, and <term>Tityus</term>. <term>Thersites</term> <note>The "ugliest man who came to Troy," depicted by Homer as a low-ranking, loud-mouthed commoner.</note>, however, or anyone else who was wicked in a private capacity, no one has depicted as being tortured with great punishments as one who is incurable. I suppose this is because he lacked the license to do great evil, and for that reason, he was more fortunate than those who were granted the license to commit wickedness. Truly, Callicles, it is from the ranks of those who possess power and license that the most wicked men arise. Nevertheless, nothing prevents some good men from existing even among these; and certainly, anyone who remains good in such a position is wonderfully to be admired. For it is a difficult thing, O Callicles, and worthy of great praise, for someone who has achieved great license to do wrong to live a just life. Few such men are found. Yet there have been, both here and elsewhere,
<margin>H</margin> and I believe there will be, some excellent and good men endowed with this virtue: the ability to handle justly those things over which authority has been granted to them. One man in particular became most esteemed among all the Greeks: <term>Aristides</term>, son of Lysimachus. Most potentates, however, my good friend, are wicked. Therefore, as I
* was saying, when Rhadamanthus catches someone of that sort, he knows nothing else about him—neither who he is nor from whom he was born—only that he is wicked. And having discovered this, he dismisses him to Tartarus, marking whether he appears curable or incurable.

<summary>Socrates presents a myth of the afterlife where the soul is judged by Minos, Rhadamanthus, and Aeacus. He argues that while the body retains its physical scars after death, the soul retains the moral scars of its sins, and those who held great power are most likely to face eternal punishment as examples to others.</summary>

<margin>A</margin>He who is sent there suffers his deserved punishments. But at other times, having looked upon the soul of another—perhaps a private citizen or someone else who has lived piously and with integrity, which I believe happens most especially to **philosophers** who mind their own business and do not entangle themselves in many affairs—the judge is pleased and sends him to the **Isles of the Blessed**. <note>In Greek mythology, the Isles of the Blessed (Elysium) were a paradise reserved for those favored by the gods or the exceptionally virtuous.</note> Aeacus performs these same duties. Each of them holds a rod while he judges. But Minos sits alone in oversight, holding a **golden scepter**, just as Odysseus says of him in <margin>Odyssey, Book 11</margin> Homer: that he saw him holding a golden scepter and giving laws to the dead. I, therefore, O Callicles, am moved by these accounts, and I am already considering how I may show the judge a soul that is as healthy as possible. Therefore, scorning the honors of the common people and seeking the truth, I shall try to live as truly good a life as I can, and so to die when that time comes. I exhort all other men as much as I am able, and <margin>B</margin> I call you also to this kind of life and this contest, which I declare is a struggle greater than all other contests in this life. For this reason, I also reproach you, for you will not be able to bring help to yourself when you are judged, and when that sentence I just mentioned is passed upon you. But when you come before the judge, the son of Aegina <note>This refers to Aeacus, the son of Zeus and the nymph Aegina.</note>, and he takes hold of you to lead you away, you will gape and grow dizzy there no less than I do here before your judges. There, perhaps someone will strike you shamefully upon the cheek and treat you with utter insult and injury. Perhaps this seems to you like an old woman’s fable, and you despise what has been said; but indeed, it would be <margin>C</margin> no wonder to despise these things if, by searching, we could find something better and truer. But now you see that although you are three of the wisest Greeks living today—you, Polus, and Gorgias—you are still unable to show that one should live any other way than this, which also appears to be beneficial in that other world. Indeed, in so many discussions, while all other points have been refuted, this one alone remains firm: that one must be more careful to avoid doing an injury than suffering one; and that a man must meditate above all else not on *seeming* to be good, but on *actually being* good, both in public and in private. If someone should be found evil in some way, he must be punished. And this is the second best thing after being just: to become good again through correction and to pay the penalty for injustice. Furthermore, all flattery, whether <margin>D</margin> toward oneself or others, whether few or many, must be avoided. Finally, <term>Rhetoric</term> <note>The art of persuasive speaking.</note> and every other kind of action must be used only for the sake of justice. Therefore, believe me and follow me to that place where, when you arrive, you will be happy both living and dead, as your own speech indicates. And allow someone to despise you as a fool and to treat you with insults if he wishes; do not care if you are struck with ignominy. For you will suffer nothing grave if you are truly honorable and good, and if you practice virtue. But after we have exercised ourselves together in this way, then, if it seems worthwhile to you, we shall apply ourselves to public affairs, or to whatever else seems best to us then as we deliberate, when we are better able to deliberate than we are now. For it is a shameful thing for us, being such as we now appear to be, to boast in words as if we were something important, when we never hold the same opinions about the same things—even the most important things—so far have we sunk into ignorance. Let us therefore follow this reason, which has now been made known to us, as our guide, showing us that this is the best way of life: to live and die practicing justice and the other virtues. Let us obey this, and exhort others to do the same. But let us not obey that way of life in which you, trusting, exhort me; for it is worth nothing, O Callicles.

<column-break/>

He who arrives there suffers what is fitting. But at other times, looking upon another soul that has lived piously and with truth—the soul of a private man or some other (especially, I say, O Callicles, of a philosopher who has minded his own business and has not been a meddler in life)—the judge is filled with admiration and sends him to the **Isles of the Blessed**. Aeacus does these same things. Each of these judges holds a rod. But Minos sits in oversight alone, holding a golden scepter, as Odysseus says in Homer that he saw him:
->Holding a golden scepter, giving laws to the dead.<-
I, therefore, O Callicles, have been persuaded by these words, and I consider how I shall present my soul to the judge in its healthiest state. Thus, letting go of the honors sought by the many, and looking to the truth, I shall try to live as the best man I can be, and when I die, to die so. I exhort all other men as much as I can, and indeed I exhort you in turn to this life and this contest, which I say is instead of all the contests here. I reproach you because you will not be able to help yourself when your trial and judgment come, of which I spoke just now; but going before the judge, the son of Aegina, when he takes hold of you and leads you, you will gape and be dizzy there no less than I am here, and you there. And perhaps someone will strike you on the side of the head dishonorably, and will treat you with every kind of foul abuse. Perhaps these things seem to you to be a story told by an old woman, and you look down on them. And it would be nothing wonderful to look down on them if, by searching, we could find something better and truer than they are. But now you see that the three of you, who are the wisest of the Greeks today—you, Polus, and Gorgias—cannot demonstrate that one should live any other life than this, which is shown to be profitable even there. But in so many words, while the rest are refuted, this word alone remains steady: that doing wrong is to be more carefully avoided than suffering wrong, and that above all a man must practice not appearing to be good, but being so, both privately and publicly. And if anyone becomes evil in some respect, he must be punished. And this is the second good after being just: to become so, and being punished, to pay the penalty. And all flattery, both regarding oneself and regarding others, whether few or many, must be fled. And rhetoric must be used thus: always for what is just, as must every other action. Therefore, being persuaded by me, follow me to that place where, having arrived, you will be happy both living and having died, as the argument signifies. And let someone despise you as mindless, and let him foully abuse you if he wishes. And yes, by Zeus, do you yourself take courage and strike that shameful blow, for you will suffer nothing terrible if you are truly beautiful and good, practicing virtue. And then, having practiced thus in common, we shall then, if it seems we should, apply ourselves to politics, or we shall then deliberate on whatever seems best, being better at deliberating than we are now. For it is a shameful thing, being as we now appear to be, then to behave like youths as if we were something; we who never think the same about the same things, and those the greatest things—to such a point of uneducatedness have we come. Let us then use the argument that has now appeared to us as a leader, which signifies to us that this way of life is best: to live and to die practicing justice and the other virtue. Let us follow this, then, and exhort others to it, and not follow that which you, trusting in it, exhort me to. For it is worth nothing, O Callicles.

### ON LOVE.

### THE SYMPOSIUM, OR,
### ON LOVE.
->Ethical.<-

---

**SUMMARY OF THE DIALOGUE.**

This whole discussion is almost entirely allegorical and metaphysical. The summary is this: that **Love** is by no means a God, nor is it something most beautiful and excellent in itself (as Plato makes Phaedrus, Pausanias, Eryximachus, and the other partners in the discussion argue according to common and worn-out opinion). Rather, it is a certain desire in us that is neither beautiful nor ugly—that is, neither good nor bad in itself—but is such that it hungers for the good which it lacks, and is carried toward obtaining that good with the greatest force. The duty of this Love is to perform the office of an interpreter and a kind of carrier between God and men. He represents the origin of that middle nature between divine and mortal through a used image: namely, that Love was born from a father and mother of vastly different kinds. His father was **Porus**, the god of wealth, and his mother was **Penia**, that is, poverty. From the father’s side, he inclines toward skill; from the mother’s side, toward ignorance. Consequently, he is of a **philosophical nature**, which, through the consciousness of ignorance, is an investigator, so that the soul may attain true and solid knowledge by that divine power. The sparks of this philosophical nature are undoubtedly in all men, whom the ancient philosophers for that reason called <unclear>alochas</unclear>, <note>The Latin text defines this as "those born to find things through the guidance and auspices of investigation."</note> Thus, who Love is and what his origin is, is described here from the doctrine handed down by Plato. However, as for Plato mentioning <term>pederasty</term> <note>original: "παιδεραστίαν" (paiderastian); in the context of this Renaissance-era commentary, the author views the Greek cultural practice of relationships between men and youths with severe moral judgment.</note> so frequently, his audacity is to be abominated, unless he did it with the intention of showing his people that it ought to be detested. For in the first book of the <term>Laws</term> <note>original: "νόμοις" (nomois); Plato’s final and longest dialogue.</note>, he detests that baseness and calls it a "daring act against nature."

<summary>Socrates concludes the Gorgias by urging Callicles to prioritize justice over rhetoric, using the myth of the divine judges Minos, Aeacus, and Rhadamanthus to illustrate the soul's accountability. The page then transitions to the Symposium, introducing Love (Eros) as a philosophical intermediary born of Wealth and Poverty.</summary>

<meta>This page marks the transition from the end of the *Gorgias* (on the previous page) to the beginning of the *Symposium* (The Banquet). The dialogue opens with Apollodorus recounting a conversation he had with Glaucon regarding a famous dinner party held years earlier at the home of the poet Agathon.</meta>

# THE BANQUET

->APOLLODORUS, A COMPANION OF APOLLODORUS, GLAUCON, ARISTODEMUS, SOCRATES, AGATHON, PHAEDRUS, PAUSANIAS, ERYXIMACHUS, ARISTOPHANES, DIOTIMA, ALCIBIADES.<-

<margin>A</margin> I believe I am not unprepared regarding the things you ask about. For it so happened yesterday that I was coming up to the city from my home in Phaleron. <note>Phaleron was one of the ancient ports of Athens, about five miles from the city center.</note> Then one of my acquaintances, catching sight of me from behind at a distance, called out; and joking while he called, he said, "O you man of Phaleron! Apollodorus! Won't you wait?" And so I stopped and waited for him. <margin>B</margin> Then he said, "Apollodorus, I was just looking for you recently, wishing to learn about the gathering at Agathon's house with Socrates, Alcibiades, and the others who were present at the dinner then, to hear what the speeches on love were. For someone else was describing it to me, having heard it from Phoenix, the son of Philip; and he said that you also knew of it. But he was not able to say anything clearly. Therefore, you must describe it to me. For you are the most fit to report the words of your companion. But first tell me," he said, "were you yourself present at this gathering, or not?" And I said to him, "It seems your informant told you nothing clearly, if you think this gathering you ask about happened so recently <margin>C</margin> that I could have been present." "I did think so," he said. "How so, O Glaucon?" I asked. "Do you not know that it has been many years since Agathon has lived here? And it has not even been three years since I began spending time with Socrates, making it my care each day to know what he says or does. Before that, I used to run about at random, and while I thought I was doing something important, I was more wretched than anyone—no less than you are now, thinking you must do everything rather than study philosophy." And he said, "Do not mock me, but tell me when this gathering took place." And I told him, "When we were still children, when Agathon won the prize for his first tragedy, <note>Agathon won this victory at the Lenaea festival in 416 BCE.</note> on the day after he and his chorus-members performed the victory sacrifices." "That was quite <margin>D</margin> a long time ago, it seems," he said. "But who told it to you? Was it Socrates himself?" "No, by Zeus," I said, "it was the same man who told Phoenix. It was a certain Aristodemus, of the Cydathenaeum district—a small man, who always went about barefoot. <note>Aristodemus was a devoted follower of Socrates and imitated his habit of walking barefoot.</note> He had been present at the gathering, being one of the greatest lovers of Socrates at that time, as it seems to me. However, I have also already questioned Socrates himself about some of the things I heard from that man, and he confirmed them just as the other had described them." "Why then," he asked, "will you not describe it to me? Indeed, the road to the city is well-suited for those traveling to both speak and listen." So as we walked along together, we spoke of these things; so that (as I said at the beginning) <margin>E</margin> I am not unprepared. If, then, I must describe it to you as well, I must do so. For I myself, whenever I either make some speeches about philosophy or hear them from others, apart from thinking I am being benefited, I am wonderfully happy; but when I hear other kinds of talk, especially yours, the talk of wealthy men and money-makers, I am both annoyed and I pity you, my companions, because you think you are doing something when you are doing nothing. And perhaps, in turn, you think I am unfortunate, and I think you are right to think so; however, I do not just 'think' that about you—I know it for certain." **COMPANION:** "You are always the same, O Apollodorus. For you are always speaking ill of yourself and others; and you seem to me to simply think everyone is wretched except Socrates, starting with yourself. And where you ever got this nickname of being called 'the madman,' <note>original: "μανικὸς" (manikos). Apollodorus was known for his excitable and devoted temperament.</note> I do not know. For in your speech you are always like this—harsh toward yourself and others, except <margin>F</margin> Socrates." **APOLLODORUS:** "My dearest friend, it is clear then that by thinking this way about myself and about you, I am indeed mad and raving." **COMPANION:** "It is not worth arguing about these things now, Apollodorus; but do as we asked you, and explain what the speeches were." **APOLLODORUS:** "They were, then, something like this. Or rather, I will try to describe them to you from the beginning, just as he described them. For he said that he met Socrates, who had both bathed and put on his sandals—which he rarely did—and he asked him where he was going, having become so beautiful. And he said he was going to dinner at Agathon's. For yesterday he had avoided the victory celebration, fearing the crowd; but he had agreed to be present today. 'For this reason,' he said, 'I have made myself beautiful, <margin>G</margin> so that I may go as a beautiful man to a beautiful man.' <note>This is a play on words; Agathon's name in Greek is related to the word for "good" or "noble."</note> 'But you, Aristodemus,' he asked, 'how do you feel about being willing to go uninvited to dinner?' And I said," he reported, "that I would do whatever you command." "Follow me then," he said, "so that we may corrupt the proverb by changing it, showing that indeed 'Good men go to the feasts of the good uninvited.' <note>A play on a Greek proverb that usually said "Bad men go to the feasts of the good uninvited."</note> For Homer seems not <margin>Iliad, Book 2</margin> only to have disregarded this proverb, but even to have insulted it. For having made Agamemnon a man exceptionally good in military matters, and Menelaus a 'weak spearman,' when Agamemnon was making a sacrifice and hosting a feast, <margin>H</margin> he made Menelaus come to the banquet uninvited—a lesser man coming to the table of a better man." Hearing this, he said he replied, "Perhaps I will also be in danger, O Socrates—not as you say, but according to Homer—a common man going uninvited to the banquet of a wise man. So, if you lead me, what excuse will you give? For I will not admit that I came uninvited, but that I was invited by you." "'Two going together,'" he said, quoting Homer, "'we will deliberate on the way what we shall say.' But let us go."

<column-break/>

->APOLLODORUS, A COMPANION OF APOLLODORUS, GLAUCON, ARISTODEMUS, SOCRATES, AGATHON, PHAEDRUS, PAUSANIAS, ERYXIMACHUS, ARISTOPHANES, DIOTIMA, ALCIBIADES.<-

<margin>A</margin> I SEEM TO MYSELF to be sufficiently prepared in these matters which you seek. For yesterday, when I was returning home from Phaleron into the city, someone I knew, catching sight of me from behind, called out from a distance, and jokingly said as he called: "O man of Phaleron, Apollodorus, won't you wait?" I stood still and waited. <margin>B</margin> Then he said: "I was looking for you just now, desiring to hear what speeches were held concerning love at that dinner to which Agathon, Socrates, Alcibiades, and several others came together. For someone else also reported it to me, who had heard it from Phoenix the son of Philip, and he added that you knew of it. But he could bring nothing certain regarding the matter. Therefore, you should report it to me. For it concerns you to narrate the speeches of your friend. But first tell me: Were you yourself present when they debated, or not?" "Truly," I said, "it seems he reported nothing certain to you, if indeed you think they met so <margin>C</margin> recently that I could have been present." "I did think so indeed," he said. "From where did you get that?" I asked. "Do you not know, O Glaucon, that for many years now Agathon has not visited here? But from the time I began to associate with Socrates, and to observe his words and deeds more diligently every day, not yet three years have passed. Before that, I wandered wherever chance took me, and thinking I was doing something, I was the most miserable of all, just as you are now, who think anything should be done rather than philosophizing." "Do not bite," he said, "but teach me at what time the banquet was celebrated." To this I said, "While we were still boys, when Agathon reported a victory in his first contest of tragedy. On the following <margin>D</margin> day after the palm [of victory] and the sacrifices had been celebrated for the sake of the victory, the debate was instituted at a prepared banquet." "Certainly that is a long time ago," he said. "But who told you? Was it Socrates himself?" "No, by Jove," I said. "Rather, the same one who told Phoenix: a certain Aristodemus of Cydathenaeum, who was of small body and always went with bare feet. For he was present at the debate: since he, as it seems to me, loved Socrates more than all who were then present. Furthermore, I questioned Socrates himself about some things that man had reported, and he agreed with him in these things. Why then," he said, "do you not report it to me? Indeed, the way that leads into the city is suitable both for hearing and for speaking alike." So thus, as we went, we spoke of those things. Therefore, just as I said from the beginning, I am sufficiently <margin>E</margin> prepared in these matters. And if you wish these things to be recounted to you again, I will recount them again. For as often as I either have a speech about philosophy myself, or hear others speaking, besides the fact that I think it profits me, I rejoice wonderfully. But as often as I hear your other speeches—especially yours who always study to pile up money—I am both distressed and I pity you, because you think you are achieving something when you achieve nothing. Perhaps you also think me unhappy, which I suspect you think truly of me. However, I do not merely think it of you, but I know it for certain." **FRIEND:** "You are always like yourself, O Apollodorus: for you perpetually disparage yourself and others, and you seem without a doubt to think that you <margin>F</margin> especially, and then all others except Socrates alone, are unhappy. From where the nickname of 'madman' arose for you, I do not know. For in speaking you always treat yourself and others bitterly and harshly, approving Socrates alone." **APOLLODORUS:** "O most beloved man, it is established from this that I am mad and raving, because I think thus of myself and finally of you." <margin>F</margin> "It is by no means fitting to contend over these things at present, Apollodorus; but comply with our prayers, and set forth to us what those speeches were." **APOLLODORUS:** "They were indeed such as these. Or rather, I will now attempt to recount them to you from the beginning in the same order in which Aristodemus reported them. For he said that he met Socrates both washed and with his feet adorned with shoes, which he rarely did; and he asked him where he was going so adorned, and Socrates responded that he was going to Agathon's house to <margin>G</margin> dine; that he had avoided yesterday's dinner because he feared the gathering of the crowd on account of Agathon's palm [of victory], but he had promised that he would be present on the following day. For that reason he had adorned himself, so that he might go as a beautiful man to a beautiful man. He asked furthermore, 'By what means, Aristodemus, do you set out to dinner uninvited?' 'As you command,' I said. 'Follow me then,' he said, 'that we may lose that proverb by changing it in this manner: that even good men set out uninvited to the dinners of the good.' Homer indeed seems not <margin>Iliad, Book 2</margin> only not to observe, but even to violate the proverb. For when he had fashioned Agamemnon as a man strenuous in military affairs, and Menelaus indeed as soft, when Agamemnon was celebrating a banquet after a sacrifice, <margin>H</margin> he leads Menelaus to Agamemnon's table coming of his own accord. Where he made the worse man come uninvited to the table of the more excellent man." "Hearing these things, I said, 'Perhaps, O Socrates, I too shall seem not such as you say, but just as Homer led him: a cheap little man coming of his own accord to the banquet of a wise man. Therefore, since you lead me, see what reason you will assign for my arrival. For I will not confess that I come uninvited, but I will say I was invited by you.'" "'As two go together along the way,'" he said, "'we will perhaps consult what we shall say. But let us go now.'"

<meta>This page continues the narrative of the *Symposium* (The Banquet). In the previous section, Apollodorus began recounting the story told to him by Aristodemus. Aristodemus, an admirer of Socrates, had met the philosopher newly bathed and wearing sandals—a rare sight—and was invited to accompany him to a dinner party at the house of the poet Agathon to celebrate Agathon's recent victory in a dramatic competition.</meta>

### PLATO'S WORKS

<margin>A</margin> After they had discussed such things between themselves, Aristodemus said they set out. Socrates, however, was somehow turning his mind to himself, falling behind as they walked. When Aristodemus waited for him, Socrates told him to go on ahead. When he reached Agathon’s house, he found the door open, and he said a rather ridiculous thing happened there: a servant met him immediately upon his entrance and led him directly to where the others were reclining, for they were just about to begin dinner. As soon as Agathon saw him, he said, "O Aristodemus, you have come at a good time to dine with us. But if you came for some other reason, put it off for another time. Indeed, I was looking for you yesterday to invite you, but I saw you nowhere. But why do you not bring Socrates to us?" And I, he said, turning around, <margin>B</margin> saw Socrates nowhere following me. I answered Agathon that I had come with Socrates, having been invited here to dinner by him. "You did well," Agathon said, "but where is that man?" "He was walking just behind me a moment ago, but I myself wonder where he could be." "Boy," Agathon said, "go look for Socrates and bring him in to us. And you, Aristodemus, recline next to Eryximachus." Then he said a boy washed his feet so he could take his place. But another of the servants came back reporting that Socrates had withdrawn into the neighboring porch and stood there, and though called, he refused to enter. "You tell of an absurd thing," Agathon said. "Call him again, and do not let him go until he comes." But Aristodemus said he replied, "By no means, <margin>C</margin> O Agathon; rather, let him be. For this is a habit of his. Sometimes he withdraws and stands still wherever he happens to be. He will come soon, I think. Do not disturb him, but permit him to come at his own will." "If it seems so to you," Agathon said, "so it must be done. But you, boys, bring the feast to the others and set out whatever you please. For indeed, no one is presiding over us—a thing I have never done before. Therefore, considering that I and these others are now being received at a banquet by you, take care of everything diligently, so that we may approve of your service." After this, Aristodemus added that they began to dine, and though Socrates was often called at Agathon's command, he did not enter until he had exercised himself for a while in his usual manner, <margin>D</margin> arriving when the meal was half over. Agathon, who was sitting last and alone, said to him: "Here, O Socrates, recline next to me, so that by touching you I may enjoy that piece of wisdom which you discovered in the porch. For it is clear that you found it and have it, or you would not have stopped." Socrates sat down and said: <margin>E</margin> "Our affairs would be well, Agathon, if wisdom were such a thing that it flowed from the fuller man into the emptier one through contact, just as water flows from a full cup into an empty one through a strand of wool. For if wisdom is so, I value very much sitting next to you. For I think I shall be filled by you with a most abundant and excellent wisdom. Mine is indeed thin and ambiguous, like a sort of dream; but yours is quite brilliant and powerful, since in your youth it shone forth so clearly and flashed out only yesterday in the sight of more than <term>thirty thousand</term> Greeks." <note>original: "triginta milliū Gręcorū" / "τρισμυρίοις". This refers to the audience at the Theater of Dionysus during the Lenaia festival where Agathon's tragedy won.</note> "You are insulting, O Socrates," Agathon said. "But we two shall judge these things about wisdom later, with Dionysus as our judge; <note>Dionysus was the god of wine and theater. Agathon is suggesting that the wine they drink will eventually reveal who is truly wiser.</note> but for now, turn to the meal." After this, Aristodemus said, once Socrates had reclined and eaten, and the others had also finished their meal, they performed libations and tasted the wines in the manner of those sacrificing, and began to sing to the god and perform other customary acts. Then they turned to drinking, whereupon Pausanias began to speak in this way: "We must see, gentlemen, <margin>F</margin> by what means we may drink most lightly and pleasantly. For to confess the truth about myself first, I feel weighed down by yesterday's unmixed wine, and I need a certain intermission. I think most of you are similarly affected, for you were present yesterday. Consider, therefore, how we may drink most lightly and healthfully." To him Aristophanes soon replied: "You speak skillfully, Pausanias; a certain moderation in drinking ought to be applied. For I too am one of those who were drenched yesterday." When Eryximachus, the son of Acumenus, heard this, he said: "You speak rightly. And I desire to hear this from you in addition: how much strength does Agathon have for drinking?" "Not at all," Agathon said. "This is a stroke of luck for us," <margin>G</margin> said Eryximachus, "for me, I mean, and Aristodemus and Phaedrus, and these others, that you who are most capable of drinking are now weary of it. For we are always weak, except for Socrates, who is fit for both. Therefore, whatever we do will be the same to him. Since it seems to me that none of those present wish to drink heavily, perhaps if I speak the truth about drunkenness, I shall be less troublesome. For from my skill in medicine, it is clear to me that drunkenness is a troublesome thing for men. I would never willingly wish to drink to excess, nor would I advise another to do so, especially if someone is suffering from yesterday’s debauch." To him Phaedrus the Myrrhinusian said, as Aristodemus reported: "I have always trusted you, especially in matters of medicine; <margin>H</margin> and now similarly, provided the others also agree." When they had heard this, he said, they all agreed not to make the present gathering one of drunkenness, but to drink for pleasure. Then Eryximachus said: "Since it has been decided that it shall be in each man's discretion how much he drinks, and no one shall be forced to drink more than he wishes, I propose what remains: I think the flute-girl who just entered should be dismissed, to play the flute for herself or, if she wishes, for the women inside. But we..."

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> He said that after they had talked in some such way, they went on. Now Socrates, somehow attending to his own mind, lingered behind on the road as they walked. When Aristodemus waited for him, Socrates would bid him go on ahead. When he arrived at Agathon's house, he found the door open; and he said a funny thing happened to him there. For a boy coming from within met him and led him straight to where the others were reclining, and he found them just about to dine. As soon as Agathon saw him, he said, "O Aristodemus, you have come at a good time to dine with us; but if you came for something else, put it off for later. For I was looking for you yesterday to invite you, and was not able to see you. But how is it you did not bring Socrates to us?" And I, he said, turning around, <margin>B</margin> saw Socrates nowhere following. I said then that I had come with Socrates, having been invited by him here to dinner. "You do well," he said. "But where is he?" "He was just now coming in behind me, but I myself wonder where he could be." "Boy," said Agathon, "won't you look and bring Socrates in? And you," he said, "Aristodemus, recline next to Eryximachus." And he said a boy washed him so he could recline. Then another of the boys came with the news: "That Socrates has withdrawn and is standing in the neighbors' porch, and when I call him he will not come in." "You say a strange thing," he said; "surely you will call him and not let him go." And Aristodemus said he spoke up: "By no <margin>C</margin> means; let him be. For he has this habit. Sometimes he stands aside and stops wherever he happens to be. He will come soon, I think. Do not disturb him, but let him be." "Well, it must be done so if it seems best to you," said Agathon. "But you, boys, feast the rest of us; set out whatever you want, since no one is standing over you. This is something I have never done before—even when you were not thought to be invited by us, I call both myself to dine and these others. Serve us, so that we may praise you." After this, he said they dined, but Socrates did not enter. Agathon often ordered them to send for Socrates, but Aristodemus would not allow it. He came then, having spent not much time <margin>D</margin> as was his custom, but mostly when they were in the middle of dinner. Then Agathon (for he happened to be reclining last and alone) said, "Here, Socrates, recline next to me, so that by touching you I may enjoy the wise thing that came to you in the porch. For it is clear that you found it and have it; for you would not have moved away before." And Socrates sat down and said, <margin>E</margin> "It would be well, Agathon, if wisdom were such a thing as to flow from the fuller of us into the emptier, if we touch each other; like the water in the cups that flows through a strand of wool from the fuller into the emptier. For if wisdom is like that, I value very much reclining next to you. For I think I shall be filled from you with much and beautiful wisdom. For mine is poor and questionable, being like a dream; but yours is bright and has a great future, which from you, being young, shone out so strongly and became manifest the day before yesterday in the presence of more than thirty thousand Greeks." "You are an insolent man, Socrates," said Agathon. "But we will settle these things a little later, you and I, about our wisdom, using Dionysus as a judge; but now turn first to the dinner." After this, he said, when Socrates had reclined and dined, and the others as well, they made libations and sang to the god and did the other customary things, and turned to drinking. Then Pausanias, he said, began a speech of this sort: "Well, men, <margin>F</margin> in what way shall we drink most easily? I tell you that I really feel very badly from yesterday's drinking, and I need some refreshment; and I think most of you do too. For you were present yesterday. Consider then in what way we might drink most easily." Then Aristophanes said, "That is well said, Pausanias, that we should by all means prepare some ease from the drinking. For I too am one of those who were baptized yesterday." <note>Aristophanes uses the word "baptized" (βεβαπτισμένων) metaphorically to mean "soaked" or "drowned" in wine.</note> Hearing them, Eryximachus the son of Acumenus said, "You speak well. And I still need to hear from one of you: how does Agathon feel about being strong enough to drink?" "In no way," he said, "am I strong myself." "It would be a godsend for us," <margin>G</margin> he said, "it seems, for me and Aristodemus and Phaedrus and these here, if you who are most capable of drinking now give up. For we are always incapable. But I take Socrates out of the account; for he is sufficient for both, so that whichever we do will satisfy him. Since then it seems to me that no one present is eager to drink much wine, perhaps I, by telling the truth about what drunkenness is like, would be less unpleasant. For this at least has become clear to me from medicine, that drunkenness is a difficult thing for men; and I would not willingly wish to drink far, nor would I advise another, especially one who is still hungover from the day before." "Indeed," said Phaedrus the Myrrhinusian, interrupting, "I am accustomed to obey you, especially in what you say about medicine; and now <margin>H</margin> the rest also want to." Hearing this, they all agreed not to make the present gathering one of drunkenness, but to drink only for pleasure. "Since then," said Eryximachus, "this has been decided, that each should drink as much as he wishes and there be no compulsion, next I propose to let the flute-girl who just came in go away; let her play for herself, or if she wants, for the women inside. But we..."
