# THE BANQUET.

<margin>A</margin> "I judge that we ought to converse with one another today," <note>original: Ὁ γὰρ λόγων ἀλλήλοις συνεῖναι τετιμηκώς</note> he said. "And as to what kind of discourse we should have, if you are willing, I shall propose it." At this, everyone said they were pleased and ordered him to explain. Eryximachus then said, "The beginning of my speech is according to Euripides’ *Melanippe*: ‘The tale is not mine,’ <note>A reference to a lost play by Euripides where a character disclaims the source of their wisdom.</note> but comes from Phaedrus here, which I am about to tell. For Phaedrus frequently complains to me in annoyance, saying: 'Is it not a strange thing, Eryximachus, that while hymns and songs of praise have been composed by the poets for other gods, no poet among so many who have existed has ever composed a single encomium for Love <term>Eros</term>, who is so great and so powerful a god? And if you wish to consider the worthy sophists <note>Professional teachers and rhetoricians in ancient Greece.</note>,' he says, 'they write praises of Hercules and others in prose,

<margin>B</margin> just as the excellent Prodicus does. This is perhaps less surprising; but I once encountered a book by a wise man in which salt was praised with wonderful acclaim for its usefulness to life, and you might see many other such things celebrated with praises. To think that such things are treated with great zeal, but no man up to this day has dared to praise Love worthily—that so great a god is thus neglected!' These things Phaedrus says to me, and they seem to be well-spoken. Therefore, I desire both to offer him this contribution and to please him, and at the same time, I think it is fitting for us who are present to honor this god. If it seems good

<margin>C</margin> to you as well, we might find sufficient pastime in speeches. I think each of us should speak a discourse in praise of Love, going from left to right, as beautifully as we are able; and Phaedrus should begin first, since he is both the first in order and is, in a sense, the father of this discussion." Then Socrates said, "No one will vote against you, Eryximachus. For how could I refuse, I who claim to understand nothing other than the matters of love? Nor will Agathon and Pausanias oppose you, nor certainly Aristophanes, whose whole life is devoted to Dionysus <note>The god of wine and theater.</note> and Aphrodite <note>The goddess of love.</note>, nor any other of these whom I see here. Although the lot is not equal for us

<margin>D</margin> who are reclining at the end; but if those who go before speak sufficiently and beautifully, it will be enough for us. So, with good fortune, let Phaedrus begin and praise Love." All the others voted for this and gave the same order as Socrates. Now, Aristodemus did not remember everything that each person said, nor do I remember everything he told me; but I will tell you the speech of each of those whose words seemed to me most worth remembering. First, then, as I was saying, he said Phaedrus began from somewhere around here, saying that Love was a great god, and marvelous among both men and gods, for many reasons, but not least because of his birth. For it is a great honor, he said, for a god to be among the oldest. And as proof

<margin>E</margin> of this: parents of Love neither exist, nor are they mentioned by anyone, whether a common person or a poet. Rather, Hesiod says that first of all Chaos came into being, 'and then the broad-breasted Earth, the forever unshakable seat of all things, and Love.' <note>Phaedrus is quoting Hesiod’s *Theogony*, a foundational Greek poem about the origin of the gods.</note> He says that after Chaos, these two were born: Earth and Love. And Parmenides says of his generation: 'First of all the gods she devised Love.' Acusilaus also agrees with Hesiod. Thus it is agreed from many sides that Love is among the most ancient of beings. And being the oldest, he is the cause of the greatest goods for us. For I cannot say what greater good there is for a young man than a good lover, or for a lover than a beloved. For that which ought to guide men through their whole lives if they are to live honorably, this neither kinship can instill so well, nor honors,

<margin>F</margin> nor wealth, nor anything else, as can love. And what is this thing I mean? It is shame regarding shameful things, and the pursuit of honor in what is noble. For without these, neither a city nor a private citizen can accomplish great and noble works. I say, then, that if a man who is in love were caught doing something shameful, or suffering something shameful at the hands of another because he did not defend himself out of cowardice, he would not be so pained at being seen by his father, or by his companions, or by anyone else, as he would be if seen by his beloved. We see this same thing in the beloved as well: that he is especially ashamed before his lovers when he is seen involved in something shameful. If, therefore, there were some way for a city or an army to be composed of lovers and their beloveds, there is no way they could better

<margin>G</margin> dwell in their own land than by abstaining from all shameful things and competing with one another for honor. And such men, fighting alongside each other, would conquer almost all of mankind, even if they were few in number. For a man in love would surely rather be seen by all the world leaving his post or throwing away his arms than be seen by his beloved, and he would often choose to die many times over instead. Moreover, as for abandoning the beloved or failing to help him when he is in danger—no one is so cowardly that Love himself would not inspire him to virtue, making him like one who is best by nature. Truly, what Homer said—that a god 'breathed might' into some of the heroes—this is what Love provides to lovers, coming from himself. Furthermore, only those who love are willing to die for another—not only

<margin>H</margin> men, but also women. Alcestis, the daughter of Pelias, provides sufficient testimony of this speech to the Greeks, for she alone was willing to die for her husband, though he had both a father and a mother. She so surpassed them in affection because of her love that

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> I judge that we ought to converse with one another today. As to what our discussions should be, I will explain if you wish. To this, all said it pleased them and ordered him to explain. Eryximachus then said: "The beginning of my speech will be according to Euripides’ *Melanippe*. For the story I am about to begin is not mine, but that of Phaedrus: Phaedrus here often complains to me, asserting something absurd—that while poets have fashioned songs and hymns for the other gods, no poet among so many has ever written any praise for Love, who is yet so great and such a god.

<margin>B</margin> 'But if you wish, O Eryximachus, to search,' he says, 'you will surely find that eloquent Sophists have praised Hercules and others in prose, just as the most skilled Prodicus has; though this should perhaps seem less wonderful to anyone. But I myself have even read a book by a wise man in which salt was extolled with marvelous praises for its usefulness in diet; and one may find many other things of this kind celebrated with praises.' Is it not therefore unworthy that while people are studiously occupied with these things, no man has yet dared to praise Love worthily up to this day, but he is so utterly neglected, even though he is so great a God? To me, this speech of Phaedrus seems true. Therefore, I desire both to bestow this gift upon him

<margin>C</margin> and to gratify him, and I think it is fitting for us to honor this god. If it seems so to you as well, a suitable discussion will arise among us. Indeed, I think Love should be praised by each of us as skillfully and as excellently as we can. Let Phaedrus begin, since he sits first and is the author of this topic." Then Socrates said: "No one will resist you, Eryximachus. For how could I refuse, when I profess to know nothing except the art of love? Neither Agathon nor Pausanias will oppose you, and Aristophanes much less, for his whole study is centered around Dionysus and Venus <note>original: "Dionysium Venerémque" — the Roman names for Dionysus and Aphrodite.</note>, nor any

<margin>D</margin> other of those I now look upon. Although an equal lot has not fallen to us who recline at the end. For if the first ones depict him skillfully and abundantly, it will be enough for us. But let Phaedrus now begin with happy auspices and honor Love." All assented to these things Socrates said and gave the same order. Aristodemus did not remember the individual words of every man, nor do I remember every single thing he recounted. I will therefore report to you the speeches of those who said things worth remembering. In the beginning, they said Phaedrus started in this manner: "Love is a great god, and wonderful among gods and men, both for many other reasons and especially because of his origin. For since he is among the number of the most ancient gods, he appears worthy of honor.

<margin>E</margin> This we argue from the fact that the parents of Love neither exist nor are recorded by any poet or anyone else. But Hesiod asserts that in the beginning Chaos existed, and then: 'The broad and ever-stable Earth, the seat of all, and Love;' asserting that after Chaos, these two existed: Earth and Love. Parmenides, however, says of his generation: 'First of all the gods she generated Love.' Acusilaus also seems to agree with Hesiod. And so it is everywhere conceded that Love is among the most ancient. Since he is such, he is the cause of the greatest goods for us. For I do not find what better thing could happen to a youth than a most excellent lover, or to a lover than a most excellent beloved. There are indeed two things which from boyhood through all of life ought to lead

<margin>F</margin> the one who is to live excellently: shame in shameful matters, and the pursuit of glory and praise in honorable ones. These things neither lineage, nor riches, nor honors can provide to us more quickly or better than love can. Without these two, neither a city nor a private individual can ever accomplish anything noble and magnificent. I assert indeed that if a lover is caught doing something shameful or suffering it from another through cowardice, and not resisting or taking revenge, he is not so vehemently distressed if seen by his father, or by friends, or by any other man, as he would be if caught by his beloved. Similarly, we see the youth

<margin>G</margin> blush most especially when his lover finds him committing something shameful. If in some way a city or an army could be made partly of those who love and partly of those who are loved, they would act with bravery and manage all things beyond what can be said, while through shame they would abstain from shameful things and strive for honorable ones as if in a kind of rivalry; and such men, even few in number, would—to speak thus—surpass all men in battle. A lover would certainly blush more vehemently to desert his rank or throw away his arms in front of his beloved than in front of all other men. Indeed, he would often prefer to die than to desert the one he loves and not help him in dangers. Nor

<margin>H</margin> is anyone so cowardly that love does not inflame him and render him divine toward virtue, so that he becomes like the bravest man. <margin>Iliad, Book 10</margin> <note>original: "Iliad. υ." — referring to the 20th book (Upsilon) or 10th depending on the citation system; it refers to the divine inspiration of courage.</note> For what Homer said—that a god inspired force and fury into some of the heroes—this is what Love gives to lovers. Furthermore, lovers alone choose to die for another—not only men, but also women. ### OF PLATO

<margin>A</margin> ...showed that they were strangers and connected to their own son <note>Referring to the parents of Admetus, who refused to die for him, unlike his wife Alcestis.</note> by name only. This deed was judged so noble, not only by men but also by the gods, that although the gods have granted the gift of returning to life to only a very few among many who performed many great deeds, they immediately raised her from the dead, delighted by such an extraordinary act. Thus, the gods highly value zeal and virtue in matters of love.

<margin>Orpheus is sharply criticized.</margin> But Orpheus, the son of Oeagrus, they sent away from the underworld without his wish being granted. They did not restore the woman for whose sake he had descended, but showed him only a phantom of her <note>In this version of the myth, Orpheus is punished for his perceived cowardice.</note>, because he did not dare to die for the sake of love, as Alcestis did. Instead, being a mere cithara-player <term>citharoedus</term> <note>A professional singer who accompanies themselves on the lyre; here used as a slur for being "soft" or un-heroic.</note>, he was deterred by a certain softness and devised a scheme by which he might descend to the underworld while still living. For this crime, the gods decreed he should pay the penalty, <margin>B</margin> and they ordered that he be torn to pieces by women. 

Achilles, however, the son of Thetis, they honored and sent to the Isles of the Blessed. For he had learned from his mother that if he killed Hector, he would die immediately; if he did not, he would return to his homeland and die an old man. He boldly chose to fight for his lover Patroclus <margin>Iliad 18</margin> and to avenge his death—not only to die for him, but to be slain over his fallen body. Greatly approving of this, the gods decorated him with distinguished glory because he had valued his lover so highly. 

Aeschylus, however, talks utter nonsense <note>original: "delirat" / "φλυαρεῖ"</note> when he says that Patroclus was loved by Achilles; for Achilles surpassed not only Patroclus but all the heroes in beauty, <margin>C</margin> and was still beardless and much younger, as Homer says. Truly, the gods prize this virtue in love above all. Yet they admire and delight in it more, and bestow greater benefits, when the beloved <term>eromenos</term> <note>The younger beloved in a Greek relationship.</note> cherishes and loves the lover <term>erastes</term> <note>The older, active pursuer in a Greek relationship.</note>, than when the lover loves the beloved. For the lover is a more divine thing than the beloved, being seized by a divine madness. For this reason, they honored Achilles more than Alcestis, and indeed transported him to the Isles of the Blessed. 

From all this, I declare that Love <term>Eros</term> is the most ancient of all the gods, the most honored, and the most capable of all in helping men—both living and dead—to attain virtue and happiness.

<margin>D</margin> Such was the speech Phaedrus delivered, as was reported. After Phaedrus, certain others spoke, but their words had slipped from memory. Passing over them, the narrator related this speech of Pausanias:

<margin>E</margin> "It seems to me, Phaedrus, that the topic has not been properly set before us, in that we are commanded simply to praise Love. If there were only one Love, it would have been well said. But since Love is not just one, it is better to first define which one is to be praised. This, therefore, I shall attempt to correct. First, I will explain which Love it is proper to praise, and then I shall strive to extol him according to the dignity of that god. 

<margin>The double love.</margin> It escapes no one that without Love <term>Eros</term>, Venus <term>Aphrodite</term> never exists. <margin>The double Venus.</margin> Therefore, if there were only one Venus, there would be one Love. But since there are two Venuses, there must also be a double Love. Who would deny that there are two goddesses? One, surely, is the elder, who has no mother and is the daughter of Heaven <term>Uranus</term>, whom we call the Heavenly Venus <term>Aphrodite Urania</term>. The other is younger, the daughter of Jupiter <term>Zeus</term> and Dione, whom we call the Common or Vulgar Venus <term>Aphrodite Pandemos</term>. It follows that the Love who is the companion and helper of the former must be called Heavenly, and the latter Vulgar. 

It is proper to praise all gods, but the works of each Love must be distinguished. <margin>F</margin> Every action is such that, in its own nature, it is neither honorable nor shameful—such as what we are doing now: drinking, singing, or debating. None of these is shameful or honorable in itself. Rather, the *manner* of the action determines its name. That which is done well and rightly is honorable; that which is not right is shameful. By the same reasoning, not every love and not every manner of loving is honorable and worthy of praise, but only that Love which encourages us to love honorably. 

Indeed, the love of the Vulgar or Common Venus is truly vulgar and performs whatever it happens upon. This is the love by which base and low men love. Furthermore, they love women no less than males, and they love bodies more than souls, and they prefer those without intelligence to those who are prudent. They gape only at the fulfillment of their desire; whether they fulfill it honorably or not, they do not care at all. Thus it happens that they perform whatever chance offers them, whether good or evil. <margin>G</margin> For this affection flows from that Venus who is much younger than the other and who, in her birth, partakes of both the female and male sexes. 

But the Love that follows the Heavenly Venus—who partakes not of the female, but only of the male sex—is for boys <note>In the context of the Athenian social system of pederasty.</note>. Furthermore, because he is the companion of the elder Venus, he is free from all insolence. Therefore, those who are inspired by this love turn to the male gender, loving that which is naturally more robust and possesses more mind. One may recognize those who are moved purely and perfectly by this love even within the practice of loving boys: for they do not love young children, but adolescents, when they have begun to possess intelligence—which happens when they are close to growing a beard. Those who begin to love from this point are prepared, I believe, to live their whole lives together in a common life; they do not intend to deceive the beloved, taking advantage of their youth and foolishness, only to mock them and run off to another. There ought to be a law against loving young children, so that so much zeal is not wasted on an uncertain matter. For it is uncertain how the body or soul...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...of a boy will turn out in the end.

He is analyzing how various Greek city-states and foreign cultures regulate these relationships through their laws and customs.</meta>

->C O N V I V I V M.<-
->(THE SYMPOSIUM)<-

<margin>A</margin>
...of boys, according to whether it results in virtue or vice, in the soul or the body. Now, good men impose this law upon themselves voluntarily; however, it is necessary to compel the "common" <note>Greek: *pandēmos*; referring to the more base, physical form of attraction.</note> lovers to follow such a rule as well, just as we restrain them, as much as we are able, from pursuing free-born women. For these are the ones who have brought about the reproach that leads some to dare to say that it is a shameful thing to grant favors to lovers. They say this looking at these common lovers, seeing their untimeliness and injustice. Surely, nothing done in a moderate and lawful manner could justly bear such a reproach. Furthermore, the law concerning love in other cities is easy to understand, for it is simply defined; but the law here in Athens and in Lacedaemon <note>Sparta</note> is complex.

<margin>B</margin>
In Elis and among the Boeotians, and where men are not skilled in speech, the law simply states that it is noble to grant favors to lovers; no one, young or old, would call it shameful. This is, I believe, so that they do not have the trouble of trying to persuade the youth with words, being themselves incapable of speaking. But in Ionia and many other places under the rule of barbarians <note>In this context, "barbarian" refers to non-Greeks, specifically the Persian Empire.</note>, it is considered shameful. To the barbarians, because of their tyrannies, this is considered shameful, as are philosophy and the love of physical training. It does not, I think, benefit the rulers for great ideas to arise in their subjects, nor strong friendships and bonds of fellowship—all of which love, among other things, is especially prone to create. 

<margin>C</margin>
The tyrants who once ruled here learned this by experience. For the love between Aristogiton and the firm friendship of Harmodius <note>The "Tyrannicides" who were celebrated in Athens for overthrowing the sons of the tyrant Peisistratus.</note> became so strong that it destroyed their rule. Thus, wherever it has been established that it is shameful to grant favors to lovers, this is due to the wickedness of those who made the law—the greed of the rulers and the cowardice of the ruled. But where it was simply thought noble, it was because of the mental laziness of those who established it. Here in Athens, the law is established much more beautifully than those, though as I said, it is not easy to understand. For consider that it is said to be more noble to love openly than in secret, and especially to love those who are the most noble and best, even if they are less handsome than others. And further, the encouragement the lover receives from everyone is remarkable; it is not as if he were doing something shameful. If he succeeds in his pursuit, it is thought noble; if he fails, it is shameful. 

<margin>D</margin>
The law has given the lover the freedom to attempt to win his beloved by performing extraordinary deeds for which he is praised. If someone dared to do these same things while pursuing any other goal besides this—if he wished to gain money, or an office of power, or some other influence—he would reap the greatest reproaches of philosophy. For if, wanting to receive money from someone or to hold office, he chose to act as lovers do toward their favorites—making petitions and entreaties in his prayers, swearing oaths, sleeping on doorsteps, and being willing to endure a servitude that no slave would ever perform—he would be hindered from such actions by both friends and enemies. His enemies would reproach him for <margin>E</margin> his flattery and lack of a free man's spirit, while his friends would admonish him, feeling ashamed on his behalf. But for the lover who does all these things, a certain grace follows, and the law allows him to do them without reproach, as if he were accomplishing something quite noble. And what is most extraordinary, as the common people say, is that the gods grant pardon only to a lover who breaks an oath. For they say that a "lover's oath" <term>aphrodision horkon</term> <note>Literally "an oath of Aphrodite."</note> does not exist in the eyes of the gods. Thus, both gods and men have granted every liberty to the lover, as the law here says. By this reasoning, one might think that in this city, both loving and becoming friends with lovers are considered entirely noble. 

<margin>F</margin>
However, when fathers place tutors <term>paedagogi</term> <note>Slave-guardians who supervised boys' education and conduct.</note> over the beloved youths and do not allow them to talk with their lovers, and the tutor has orders to this effect, and their peers and companions reproach them if they see <margin>F</margin> <margin>The gods grant pardon only to lovers' perjuries. A lover's oath.</margin> such a thing happening, and the elders do not stop the mockers or scold them for speaking wrongly—looking at these things, one might conversely think that such behavior is considered most shameful here. But I believe the truth is this: it is not a simple matter. As was said from the beginning, no action is noble or shameful in itself. If it is done well, it is noble; if done badly, it is shameful. It is shameful to gratify a wicked man in a wicked way, but noble to gratify a good man in a noble way. The "common" lover is wicked—the one who loves the body more than the soul. He is not lasting, because he loves something that is not lasting. For as soon as the bloom of the body he loved fades, he "takes wing" and flies away, dishonoring all his many words and promises. But the one who loves a character that is good remains a lover throughout life, 

<margin>G</margin>
because he has fused himself to something that is lasting. Our law, then, wishes to test these men well and truly, to see whom one should gratify and whom one should flee. Therefore, it encourages the lover to pursue and the beloved to flee, acting as a judge of the contest to test which of the two the lover is, and which the beloved is. For this reason, first, it is considered shameful to be caught quickly (so that time may intervene, which seems to test most things well). Second, it is shameful to be caught by the influence of money or political power—whether one cowers under ill-treatment and does not endure, or whether one is benefited by money or political favors and does not despise them. For none of these things seem to be solid or lasting, apart from the fact that they do not spring from...

<meta>The text cuts off here, continuing the discussion of "Heavenly" vs "Common" love and the specific Athenian "test" of a lover's character on the following page.</meta>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
...of boys, whether it finally turns toward virtue or vice. Indeed, upright men propose this law to themselves voluntarily. It is also necessary to subject those common lovers to the same law by necessity, just as we prohibit those men, as much as possible, from loving free women. For these are the ones who have provided the occasion for reproach and for the opinions of certain people who say it is shameful to obey a lover. They speak such things regarding common lovers because they recognize and disapprove of their persistent annoyance and injustice. However, it is not fitting to disparage anything that is done modestly and lawfully. The law concerning love established in other cities is easy to understand because it is handed down simply. Among us and the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note>,

<margin>B</margin>
it exists in a varied form. For in Elis and among the Boeotians, and where men lack the art of speaking, it is simply decreed by law that one must grant favors to lovers; and among them, no one, whether young or old, declares it shameful. This was done by them, I believe, for the reason that they would not have to work hard at persuading adolescents, since they are inept at oratory. But in Ionia and among many others who are subject to the Barbarians, this is judged entirely shameful by law. For among the Barbarians, because of their tyrannies, this is considered shameful, as is the study of wisdom <margin>C</margin> and gymnastics. For those studies do not benefit tyrants, as they produce sharp and noble minds in their subjects, and give birth to indissoluble friendships and frequent societies among them—which are accustomed to be born from many things, but especially from love. Our own tyrants learned this from the facts themselves. For the love of Aristogiton and the confirmed friendship of Harmodius shattered their tyranny. And thus, wherever the indulgence of Love is fundamentally removed, it is forbidden by the wickedness of those who established the laws—namely, the greed of the princes and their desire to increase their power, and the cowardice of the subjects. But where it is permitted without limit, it is permitted because of the indolence and <margin>D</margin> sluggishness of those who so decreed it. 

Here, however, it is much more rightly established: but as I was saying, it is not easy to recognize. It seems clearly granted, if one considers what is said: that it is more excellent to love openly than secretly, and especially those who are noble and best, even if they seem less beautiful than others. The common encouragement of everyone also favors the lover greatly, as if he were attempting nothing shameful. For commonly, if someone captures his beloved, it is seen as something beautiful; if he does not capture him, it is shameful. And the law grants the lover wonderful devices to win his beloved over to himself and permits him to be praised for them; which, if someone ever <margin>E</margin> dared to attempt for the sake of anything else, he would incur the greatest reproaches from the philosophers. For if anyone—for the sake of receiving money from someone, or obtaining a magistracy or some other power—should attempt those things which lovers everywhere do toward their beloveds (offering supplications, entreating, lying at the doors at night, serving with a certain diligent observance, and obeying in all things which even a slave would not wish to do, nor even be compelled to do), he would be rebuked by enemies and friends alike. The former would disparage his slave-like flatteries and fawning, while the latter would correct him, and his friends would be ashamed of his servitude. But for the lover, while he does these things, he obtains grace; and as if he were doing something excellent, he is permitted by the law to do these things without any mark of infamy. And what is greatest of all, <margin>F</margin> <margin>The gods grant pardon only to lovers' perjuries. A lover's oath.</margin> it is commonly said that the gods grant pardon only to lovers' perjuries. For they say that a "Venereal oath" <note>An oath made in the name of Venus/Aphrodite.</note> has no power. Thus, both gods and men have granted every license to the lover, as our law testifies. If we look at these things that have been said, love will seem to be considered something most excellent in this city, and that the beloved should indulge the lover. If, on the other hand, we consider those things which I shall now say, we will think this is held to be most shameful among us. For parents entrust their sons to tutors, who prohibit the beloveds from speaking with their lovers. Their companions and peers also reproach them whenever they see such a thing, and the elders do not restrain them while they criticize such things, nor do they <margin>G</margin> correct them as if they were in error. 

Therefore, I believe the matter stands thus: as was said at the beginning, the act is not in itself either honest or shameful. For it is not simple; but if done rightly, it is honest; if otherwise, shameful. It is indeed shameful to obey a depraved person in a shameful manner. But it is honest to obey a good person in an honest manner. That "common" lover is depraved, who loves the body more than the soul. For he is not stable, since he loves a thing that is least stable; when that which he desired withers, he departs and flies away, keeping none of the things he had promised. But the lover of good character perseveres in friendship throughout his entire life, since he was pursuing something stable. Our law, in any case, commands us to examine these men diligently, <margin>H</margin> and to grant favors to the latter, but to flee the former. And it commands us to follow these for this reason, and to flee those, judging and examining what each person loves and what is loved in anyone. And for this cause, first, it is judged shameful to be captured easily and quickly, so that time may intervene, which is required for examining character; then, it is shameful to be captured either by an abundance of money or by the power of magistrates: whether he is ensnared by some fear rather than by will, or whether, having received money and acquired civil honors, he does not despise them. For none of these things seem to be solid or firm, except that which [comes] from...

<summary>Pausanias explains that Love is not inherently good or bad but depends on the lover's intent—loving the soul/virtue is noble, while loving only the body is "common" and shameful. He discusses how different cultures regulate these relationships and highlights the unique complexity of Athenian law, which uses time and social pressure to test the lover's sincerity.</summary>

# PLATONIS
## THE SYMPOSIUM

->A<- From such men, a noble friendship cannot arise. Therefore, according to our law, only one path remains by which those who are loved may rightfully grant favors to their lovers. For just as we have a law regarding lovers, which states that no voluntary service of a lover toward the beloved should be considered flattery or disgraceful, so too there remains another kind of voluntary servitude that incurs no infamy. This is the service which concerns itself with virtue. For it is established by our laws that if someone wishes to serve another, believing that through him he might advance in wisdom or in any other part of virtue, this voluntary servitude is neither unseemly for the servant nor should it be called flattery. It is necessary that these laws coincide: the one concerning lovers and the one written concerning philosophy and other virtues, if it is to be proper for the beloved to gratify their lovers.

->B<- For whenever the lover and the beloved come together in the same purpose, each having a law—the one prepared to justly serve the beloved in all things; the other, in turn, prepared to justly obey his teacher of wisdom and character—and when the former is able to contribute to wisdom and other virtues, while the latter is in need of education and wisdom; then, and only then, when these laws meet in one, does it happen that it is honorable for the beloved to gratify the lover, and in no other way. In this pursuit, even to be deceived is not shameful. In all other cases, such gratification is judged shameful, whether the opinion deceives the one obeying or not. For if someone gratifies a lover as if he were rich for the sake of wealth, and is deceived because the lover turns out to be poor, he is nonetheless blamed. For he appears to have revealed a servile habit of mind, showing that he would serve anyone in anything for the sake of money; which is by no means honorable.

->C<- By the same reasoning, if someone gratifies another as if he were a good man, hoping to become better himself through this association, and is deceived when that man is found to be wicked, this is a "noble deception." For he seems to have demonstrated his own disposition—that he was ready to endure all services for the sake of attaining virtue. This is surely judged most excellent. Thus, to gratify and serve for the sake of virtue is always honorable.

->D<- This is the Heavenly Love of the heavenly goddess herself: which is precious both privately and publicly, and compels both the lover and the beloved to take up the care and study of virtue. All other loves are the companions of the "Common" Venus <note>Latin: *Venus vulgaris*; refers to purely physical or base attraction.</note>. These things, O Phaedrus, I contribute to our discussion about Love as if on the spur of the moment. When Pausanias had made a "pause" <note>original: *pausam*, a pun on the speaker's name, Pausanias</note>—for so the wise teach me to play with words—

<margin>Aristophanes is teased and mocked.</margin>
->E<- Aristodemus said it was Aristophanes' turn to speak, but it happened that he was hindered by hiccups, either from overeating or some other cause. Therefore, he spoke to the physician Eryximachus, who was sitting next to him: "O Eryximachus, it is now your duty either to suppress my hiccups or to speak in my place until they stop." To this, Eryximachus replied: "I will do both. I will speak in your place, and you shall speak in mine after the hiccups have gone. Meanwhile, while I am speaking,

<margin>Remedies for hiccups.</margin>
->F<- if you wish to hold your breath for a long time, the hiccups will stop. If that does not please you, at least wash your throat with plenty of water. And if they are very violent, tickle your nostrils so that a sneeze is provoked. For if you do this once or twice, even if the hiccups are very violent, they will be removed." Aristophanes said, "Before you finish speaking, I will do as you command." Eryximachus then spoke: "It seems necessary to me, since Pausanias began his discourse well but did not finish it sufficiently, that I should now fulfill what is missing."

->G<- I certainly approve of that distinction by which Love was divided into two. However, I seem to have discovered through our art of medicine that Love exists not only in the souls of men toward beautiful things, but also toward many other things: in the bodies of all animals, in things that grow from the earth, and finally, in almost everything that exists in nature. This great and wonderful god extends himself most widely through all things, both human and divine. I shall first take an example from medical skill, so that I may honor my art. The nature of bodies contains this double Love. For that which is healthy in our bodies and that which is diseased are admittedly different and unlike. That which is unlike desires and loves unlike things. Therefore, there is one Love in a healthy body and another in a diseased one. And, as Pausanias was asserting a moment ago, just as it is honorable to gratify temperate men and not the intemperate, so too in bodies themselves, one must gratify good and healthy elements—in which the logic of medicine chiefly consists—but by no means the bad and diseased elements, if one wishes to be a skilled physician. To put it briefly,

<margin>Medicine.</margin>
medicine is the science of the body's love-impulses in relation to filling and emptying <note>This refers to the ancient medical theory of humors, where health was seen as a balance of bodily fluids.</note>. And whoever discerns the beautiful and the base Love in these matters is the most skilled physician. He who can change these things so that one Love grows in place of another, or who can implant Love where it is absent but needed, and remove it where it is harmful,

->H<- is a gifted craftsman. For it is necessary to be able to reconcile those things which are most hostile in the body and to plant a mutual Love between them.

<column-break/>

->A<- ...there would be no noble friendship for it. Thus, only one way remains in our law, if the beloved is to grant favors beautifully to the lover. For we have a law, just as there was for the lovers, that for any kind of voluntary service a beloved performs for a lover, it is not flattery, nor is it a matter of reproach. So too, there remains only one other voluntary servitude that is not a matter of reproach. This is the one concerning virtue. For it is our custom that if someone is willing to serve another, believing that through that person he will become better either in some kind of wisdom or in any other part of virtue, this voluntary servitude is not shameful, nor is it flattery.

->B<- It is necessary to bring these two laws together—the one concerning the love of boys and the one concerning philosophy and the rest of virtue—if it is to happen that it becomes a beautiful thing for the beloved to gratify the lover. For whenever the lover and the beloved come together in the same place, each following a law—the one prepared to serve the beloved who gratifies him in any way justly; the other, in turn, prepared to serve the one who makes him wise and good—and when the former is able to contribute to wisdom and the rest of virtue, and the latter is in need of education and the acquisition of other wisdom; then, when these laws coincide, only then does it happen that it is beautiful for the beloved to gratify the lover, and nowhere else.

->C<- In this situation, it is not even shameful to be deceived. But in all other cases, it brings shame whether one is deceived or not. For if someone gratifies a lover as if he were rich for the sake of wealth and is deceived, and does not receive money because the lover turns out to be poor, it is no less shameful. For such a person seems to have shown his own character—that for the sake of money, he would serve anyone in anything; and this is not beautiful. By the same logic, even if someone gratified another as if he were a good man, and expected to become better himself through the friendship of the lover, and is deceived because that man turns out to be bad and not possessing virtue, the deception is still beautiful. For he too seems to have revealed his own nature—that for the sake of virtue and becoming better, he would be eager for anything for anyone's sake; and this is the most beautiful thing of all.

->D<- Thus, it is altogether beautiful to grant favors for the sake of virtue. This is the Love of the Heavenly Goddess, and it is heavenly, and of great value both to the city and to individuals; for it compels the lover himself to take great care of his own virtue, and the beloved as well. All the others belong to the other goddess, the Common one. These things (he said), O Phaedrus, I contribute to you regarding Love on the spur of the moment. When Pausanias had "ceased" <note>Greek: *pausamenou*; a pun on Pausanias's name.</note> (for the wise teach me to speak in balanced phrases like this),

->E<- Aristodemus said it was Aristophanes' turn to speak, but it happened that a hiccup fell upon him, either from fullness or from some other cause. And he was not able to speak, but said (for the physician Eryximachus was lying next to him), "O Eryximachus, it is only right that you either stop my hiccups or speak on my behalf until I stop." And Eryximachus said, "I will do both of these. For I will speak in your turn, and you, when you have stopped, shall speak in mine. And while I am speaking, see if the hiccup will stop if you hold your breath for a long time; and if not, gargle with water. And if it is very strong, take something with which you might tickle your nose and sneeze; and if you do this once or twice, even if it is very strong, it will stop." Aristophanes said, "You shouldn't be long in starting your speech; I will do these things."

->F<- Then Eryximachus said: "It seems necessary to me then, since Pausanias, after starting his discourse beautifully, did not finish it sufficiently, that I must try to put an end <note>Greek: *telos*; meaning a conclusion or a goal.</note> to the discourse. For that Love is twofold seems to me a beautiful distinction. But that it is not only in the souls of men toward beautiful people, but also toward many other things, and in other things—in the bodies of all animals, and in things growing in the earth, and, so to speak, in all existing things—I believe I have observed from medicine, our art. And I see how great and wonderful the god is, and how he extends over everything, both in human and in divine matters."

->G<- "I will begin speaking from medicine, so that we may also honor the art. For the nature of bodies has this double Love. For the healthy part of the body and the diseased part are admittedly different and unlike; and the unlike desires and loves unlike things. Therefore, the Love in the healthy is one thing, and the Love in the diseased is another. It is (as Pausanias was just saying) a beautiful thing to gratify the good among men, but shameful to gratify the intemperate. So it is also in the bodies themselves: it is beautiful and necessary to gratify the good and healthy elements of each body, and this is what is called medicine; but to the bad and diseased elements, it is shameful and one must refuse gratification, if one is to be a skilled practitioner. For medicine is, to speak in a summary, the science of the body's love-inclinations toward filling and emptying. And the one who discerns the beautiful and shameful Love in these things is the most physician-like. And he who can produce a change so that one Love is acquired instead of the other, and knows how to implant Love in those who do not have it but need it, and how to remove it when it is there, would be a good craftsman."

->H<- "For it is necessary to be able to make the most hostile things in the body friendly and to make them love one another."

<meta>This page continues the speech of the physician Eryximachus, who has taken the place of the playwright Aristophanes while the latter recovers from a fit of hiccups. Eryximachus expands the previous definition of Love from a human emotion into a universal principle of harmony and balance that governs all sciences, including medicine, music, and astronomy.</meta>

# THE SYMPOSIUM

<margin>A</margin> The most hostile things are those that are most contrary to one another: the cold to the hot, the bitter to the sweet, the dry to the moist. It was by knowing how to instill mutual love and concord among these opposites that our ancestor Asclepius <note>The mythical founder of medicine and god of healing.</note> (as these poets say, and I believe them) established our medical art. Therefore, all medicine—as I am saying—is governed by this god; and likewise gymnastics and agriculture. That music is also governed by these same principles is clear to anyone who pays even the slightest attention, <margin>B</margin> just as Heraclitus <note>An early Greek philosopher known for the idea that the universe is in constant flux and defined by the "unity of opposites."</note> perhaps intended to say, though he did not express it well in words. For he says that "the One, being at variance with itself, is yet in agreement with itself, like the harmony of the bow and the lyre." Now, it is quite illogical to say that a harmony is "at variance," or that it consists of things that are still in disagreement. But perhaps he meant this: that from elements previously at variance—namely the high and the low pitch—harmony was later produced by the art of music through their agreement. For surely there could be no harmony if the high and low pitches were still in disagreement. Harmony is a consonance, and consonance is a kind of agreement; and it is impossible for an agreement to arise from things that disagree, as long as they are in disagreement. Conversely, that which is at variance and does not agree cannot be harmonized. In the same way, rhythm is created from the fast and the slow, which were formerly at variance but later came into agreement. And just as medicine does in its sphere, so here music instills agreement in all these things, creating a mutual love and concord between them. <margin>C</margin> Thus, music is the science of "erotic" matters concerning harmony and rhythm. In the actual structure of harmony and rhythm, it is not difficult to discern these erotic principles, nor does the "dual love" <note>Referring to the "Heavenly" and "Common" loves described by the previous speaker, Pausanias.</note> appear yet. But when it becomes necessary to apply rhythm and harmony to human affairs—either in composition (which is called melody-making) or in the correct use of melodies and measures already composed (which is called education)—then the task becomes difficult and requires a skilled craftsman. For here the same principle returns: we must gratify the orderly among men, and those who are not yet orderly so that they may become more so, <margin>D</margin> and we must preserve their love. This is the beautiful, the "Heavenly Love" of the Muse Urania <note>The Muse of Astronomy; "Urania" means "Heavenly."</note>. But the love belonging to Polyhymnia <note>The Muse of many songs; here representing a more "common" or vulgar variety of inspiration.</note> is the "Common Love," which one must apply with great caution to whomever it is offered, so that one may harvest its pleasure without instilling any excess. Similarly, in our own art of medicine, it is a great task to deal correctly with the desires concerning the art of cookery, so that one may harvest pleasure without disease. Therefore, in music, in medicine, and in all other things, both human and divine, we must observe both kinds of love as far as possible, for both are present. Even the constitution of the seasons of the year is full of both. For whenever the elements I just mentioned—the hot, the cold, the dry, and the moist—find a temperate love for one another and <margin>E</margin> receive a balanced harmony and mixture, they bring health and abundance to humans, other animals, and plants, and they do no harm. But when the Love characterized by excess and violence gains the upper hand in the seasons of the year, it destroys and injures many things. For plagues usually arise from such conditions, as well as many other diverse diseases in both beasts and plants. Indeed, frost, hail, and blight <note>original: "ἐρυσίβαι" / "rubigines" — a type of fungal disease affecting crops.</note> arise from the overabundance and disorder of such erotic impulses toward one another. The science of these things, concerning the movements of the stars and the seasons of the year, is called astronomy. <margin>F</margin> Furthermore, all sacrifices and the things over which divination <note>The practice of seeking knowledge of the future or the divine will.</note> presides—which involve the communion of gods and men with one another—are concerned with nothing else but the guarding and healing of Love. For all impiety tends to occur whenever one does not gratify the orderly Love, nor honors and respects it in every deed, but instead follows the other Love, whether regarding parents (living or dead) or regarding the gods. It is the task of divination to oversee these Loves and to heal them. Thus, divination is the craftsman of friendship between gods and men, because it understands which human erotic impulses tend toward divine law and which toward impiety. So great and mighty—or rather, all-powerful—is Love in its totality. <margin>G</margin> But the Love that is expressed in good deeds, accompanied by temperance and justice both among us and among the gods, possesses the greatest power and provides us with every happiness, making us able to associate with one another and be friends with the gods who are our superiors. Now, perhaps in my praise of Love, I have left much out, though not intentionally. If I have omitted anything, it is your job, Aristophanes, to fill it in—or, if you intend to praise the god in some other way, do so, since your hiccups have now ceased.

To this, Aristophanes replied (as the story goes) that the hiccups had indeed stopped, but not before he had applied a sneeze to them. "I wonder," he said, "if the 'orderly' part of the body desires such noises and ticklings as a sneeze produces, for it stopped immediately as soon as I applied the sneeze to it." <margin>H</margin> "My good Aristophanes," Eryximachus said, "watch what you are doing. You are playing the jester just as you are about to speak, and you are forcing me to be a guardian of your speech in case you say something ridiculous, when you could have spoken in peace." Aristophanes laughed and said, "You are right, Eryximachus. Let those words of mine be...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> But those things are most unfriendly which are most contrary: the cold to the hot, the bitter to the sweet, the moist to the dry, and others of this kind. Since our forefather Asclepius knew how to bring mutual love and concord to these things—as these poets testify, and I myself believe—he established our art. And so, all medicine is governed by this god in the way I have described. Similarly, agriculture and gymnastics are also governed by him. That the same principle applies to music is clear to anyone who pays even a little attention. <margin>B</margin> This is perhaps what Heraclitus felt, though he explained it poorly in words. He says that "the One, disagreeing with itself, comes together, like the harmony of the bow and the lyre." Yet it is an absurd statement to say that a harmony "disagrees," or that it exists from disagreeing parts while they are still out of tune. But perhaps he meant to signify that from things which previously disagreed—namely the low and the high pitch—harmony is composed through the musical art making them consonant. For harmony could never be composed from the low and the high while they are in disagreement. For harmony is a consonance, and consonance is a certain kind of concord. Concord cannot arise from disagreeing things as long as they disagree. That which disagrees and is not in concord cannot harmonize; just as rhythm is constituted from the fast and the slow, which previously disagreed but later harmonize. and just as medicine grants concord to the body, so music, by granting consonance <margin>C</margin> to voices, produces a mutual Love and consensus. Thus music is the science of harmony and rhythm, judging the erotic affections and powers. Truly, in the composition of harmony and rhythm itself, the nature of Love can easily be perceived; however, the "dual Love" is not yet distinguished here. But it is distinguished when rhythm and harmony must finally be used in relation to other people: either in creating it (which they call the making of melody) or in correctly using the melodies and meters already made (which they call education). Here the observation is difficult, and a skilled craftsman is needed. Now the previous argument returns: namely, that we must gratify modest men, and those <margin>D</margin> who are not yet sufficiently modest, so that they may become so, and their love must be preserved. And this is the decorous Love itself, the "Heavenly Love" of the Muse Urania. But the love of the Muse Polyhymnia is the "Common Love." This must be indulged with the greatest caution, so that men may draw pleasure from it while avoiding excess. Just as in our art it is a difficult task to use the desires that lure us to the sweet feasts of cooks correctly, so that we may eat pleasantly without damage to good health. Therefore, in music, in medicine, and in all other things, both human and divine, we must observe the presence of both Loves as much as we are able. Furthermore, the constitution of the seasons of the year is full of both. For whenever those things I just mentioned—the hot and the cold, the dry and the moist—obtain a compatible love for one another, and <margin>E</margin> take on a harmony and a timely balance, they bring a healthy and fertile year to humans, to all living things, and to plants, and they do no harm. On the contrary, when a petulant and insulting love prevails in the seasons of the year, it corrupts with much injury. Plagues are accustomed to arise from these, and many other diseases are born in various beasts and plants. For frost, ice, hail, and the rust and rot of crops proceed from an immoderate and exceeding love of qualities; the science of these things, and of the movement of the heavens and the seasons of the year, has been called astronomy. <margin>F</margin> Furthermore, all sacrifices and those things over which divination <margin>Divination.</margin> presides—namely the mutual communions of gods and men—are concerned with nothing other than the healing and guarding of Love. For all impiety is accustomed to arrive when one does not indulge modest Love, nor honors and venerates it in all things, but wanders about after the other Love, failing to behave correctly toward parents (living and dead) and toward the gods. To discern and heal these Loves is the purpose of divination. <margin>Divination.</margin> And moreover, divination is the craftsman of friendship between gods and men, because it understands which of the human loves touches upon what is sacred or what is profane. And so Love in its entirety contains much and ample—indeed, all—power. <margin>G</margin> But the Love that is concerned with good things, along with temperance and justice toward us as well as toward the gods, has the highest power and provides us with happiness. For it reconciles us to one another in a common life and makes us friends to the gods, who are superior to human nature. Perhaps I too am omitting many things that pertain to praising Love, yet not by choice. What is missing, it is your part, Aristophanes, to fulfill. Or, if you wish to honor this god in some other way, do so, now that your hiccups have ceased. Aristophanes then said that they were now calmed, though not before he was repressed by a sneeze. "Because of this," he said, "I wonder if the proper state of the body requires such noises and ridiculous sounds, such as a sneeze is. For as soon as the sneeze arose, the hiccups immediately stopped." "See, oh good Aristophanes, what you are doing," Eryximachus replied. "You are stirring up laughter against yourself just as you are about to speak, and you force me to become an observer of your speech to see if you bring forth anything laughable, when you could have spoken securely." <margin>H</margin> "You speak rightly, Eryximachus," Aristophanes interrupted. "Let those words be mine..."

# OF PLATO

...these things were not meant to be kept secret; but do not watch me too closely. For I do not fear that I might bring forth something that provokes laughter—for that would be the gain and proper business of our Muse—but I fear that I might say things that are truly ridiculous. Aristophanes, having shot your dart at us, do you hope to flee? <note>Eryximachus is teasing Aristophanes, who had previously been sidelined by hiccups.</note> But apply your mind to what you say, as if you must give an account for all your words; though perhaps, if I see fit, I shall let you off.

<margin>A</margin>
I intend to speak of Love in a different way than you and Pausanias. For it seems to me that humans have entirely failed to recognize the power of Love. For if they knew it, they would dedicate magnificent shrines, altars, and sacrifices to him; none of which is done in these times, though it would be most fitting to observe these things for him. For he is, above all other gods, most beneficial to the human race, a curator and protector of men, and a physician, through whose healing our race might attain the highest happiness. <margin>B</margin> I will therefore try to explain his power to you. You, in turn, will teach others what you learn from me today. First, it is necessary to learn what the nature of humans once was, and what its passions were. For it was not once as it is now, but far different. In the beginning, there were three kinds of humans, not only the two we have now, male and female, but also a third existed, composed of both. Only the name of this one remains to us; the thing itself has vanished.

<margin>C</margin>
It was then called **Androgynous** <term>Androgynous: From the Greek 'aner' (man) and 'gyne' (woman), signifying a person who is both.</term> in both form and name, a mixture of the male and female sex. Now the thing itself is gone, and only the name remains as a term of reproach. Furthermore, the whole form of each person was round, having a back and sides in a circle, four hands, and as many legs; likewise two faces on a rounded neck, and entirely alike. There was one head for both faces, which were turned in opposite directions. There were four ears, two sets of genitals, and everything else was as one might imagine from these details. They walked upright then, as now, in whichever direction they wished; and whenever they strove to go more quickly, like those who turn their legs upward and somersault in a circular dance, they were carried in a swift circle, leaning on their eight limbs. <margin>D</margin> The cause of these three kinds and such forms was this: the male was born from the Sun; the female from the Earth; and the mixed kind from the Moon. For the moon partakes of both <note>The Sun is traditionally male and the Earth female; the Moon, reflecting the sun onto the earth, was seen as intermediate.</note>. They were spherical in both shape and motion because they were like their parents. Hence they were of robust body and high spirit. For this reason, they attempted to fight the gods and ascend into heaven, just as Homer writes of Ephialtes and Otos <note>Twin giants from Greek mythology who attempted to storm Mount Olympus.</note>.

<margin>Iliad 11</margin>
<margin>E</margin>
Jupiter <note>The Latin text uses "Jupiter," while the Greek uses "Zeus." Both refer to the King of the Gods.</note> and the other gods therefore consulted on what should be done. In this matter, there was no small ambiguity. For they could find no way to kill them—as they had destroyed the race of the Giants with thunderbolts—for if the human race were extinguished, the worship and veneration of the gods by humans would perish; yet he did not think they should be permitted to continue in such insolence. At last, Jupiter explained his opinion. "I have found," he said, "a way by which it is possible for humans to exist and yet be more modest. And that will be if they are made weaker. I will now divide each one into two parts. From this, they will be both weaker and more useful to us. For there will be more in number who worship us. They shall walk upright on two legs. But if they seem to rise up impiously again, I will cut them in two once more, so that, leaning on a single leg, they will be forced to hop." Having said this, he divided each person in two, like those who divide eggs to pickle them, or who cut eggs with hairs. <margin>F</margin> He commanded Apollo that, as soon as the division was made, he should turn the face and half of the neck toward the side where the cut was made, so that by contemplating his own division, man might become more modest; and he ordered him to heal the rest. Apollo immediately turned the face, and drawing the skin together from all sides toward what is now called the belly—like a drawstring bag—he tied a single opening in the middle of the belly. This knot they call the navel. And he smoothed out most of the other wrinkles and shaped the breasts, using a tool such as cobblers use when they smooth the wrinkles of leather; but he left a few around the middle of the belly and the navel, to be a memorial of our ancient suffering. <margin>G</margin> After human nature was thus divided, since each desired his own half, they would run together and, throwing their arms around each other, they would embrace, longing to be fused into one. Consequently, they began to die from hunger and inactivity, because they never wanted to be separated. And when one half died and the other remained, the survivor would seek out another and embrace it—whether it were a half of a whole female (which we now call a woman) or a male. And so the human race was perishing.

<margin>H</margin>
Therefore, Jupiter took pity and devised another remedy: he moved the genitals to the front. For before this, they had these toward the back and did not procreate with each other, but by scattering seed into the earth like cicadas. But when he had moved them to the front, he caused generation to be fulfilled through these in one another: by the male in the female, for this reason: so that if a man met a woman in an embrace, they might produce offspring and the human species...

<summary>Aristophanes begins his speech by recounting a myth that humans were originally four-legged, four-armed, and spherical creatures of three genders who were split in two by Zeus as punishment for their pride. This act created the modern human form and the innate, desperate longing of individuals to find their "other half" through Love.</summary>

# THE SYMPOSIUM

<margin>A</margin> ...race. At the same time, if male should meet with male, they might find satisfaction in their embrace, find rest, and then turn to their labors and the other concerns of life. For love has been innate in humans for so long, a unifier of our ancient nature, attempting to make one out of two and to heal the human condition. Each of us, then, is a "tally" <note>original: *symbolon*, a broken object—like a coin or ring—split in two so that two people could later prove their connection by fitting the pieces together</note> of a human being, since we have been sliced like flatfish, two out of one. Each is forever seeking his own tally. Those men who are a section of that common gender (which was then called **Androgynous**) are lovers of women, and most adulterers come from this class. Similarly, those women who love men and are adulteresses come from this same class. But those women who are a section of the female gender do not pay much attention to men; <margin>B</margin> rather, they are turned toward women, and the "female-seekers" <term>hetairistriai</term> <note>A term for women who sought other women as companions or lovers</note> come from this class. Those who are a section of the male, however, pursue the male. While they are boys, being slices of the male, they love men and enjoy lying with and being embraced by men. These are the best of the boys and youths, being the most manly by nature. Some say they are shameless, but they lie. For they do this not from a lack of shame, but out of courage, manliness, and a masculine nature, welcoming what is similar to themselves. <margin>C</margin> A great proof of this is that when they reach maturity, only such men as these turn to political life. When they become men, they are lovers of youths, and by nature they do not pay attention to marriage or procreation, though they are compelled to do so by law. It is enough for them to live out their lives with one another, unmarried. Such a person becomes a lover of youths and a lover of his own admirers, always welcoming what is akin to him. When a lover of youths—or anyone else—happens upon his own particular half, they are struck by a wondrous sense <margin>D</margin> of friendship, intimacy, and love; they are unwilling, so to speak, to be separated from one another for even a moment. These are the ones who stay together through their whole lives, yet they could not even say what they want from each other. For it does not seem that the intimacy of sex is the reason one delights in the other’s company with such great earnestness; rather, it is clear that the soul of each desires something else, which it cannot describe, but rather senses through divination and riddles. If **Hephaestus** <note>The god of fire and craftsmanship (called Vulcan in the Latin column)</note> were to stand over them as they lay together, holding his tools, and ask: "What is it, O mortals, that you want from one another?" <margin>E</margin> and if, as they hesitated, he asked again: "Is this what you desire: to be joined together in the same place as much as possible, so that you are never apart from each other day or night? If you desire this, I am willing to melt you together and fuse you into the same being, so that the two of you become one. As long as you live, you shall live a common life as one; and when you die, there in the house of **Hades** <note>The underworld</note> you shall be one instead of two, having died together. See if this is what you long for, and if you would be satisfied to obtain it." We know that upon hearing this, not a single person would refuse or seem to want anything else. They would simply believe they had heard exactly what they had long desired: to come together and be melted with the beloved, becoming one out of two. The cause of this is that our ancient nature was as I described: we were once whole. **Love**, therefore, is the name for the desire and pursuit of the whole. <margin>F</margin> Formerly, as I say, we were one; but now, because of our wickedness, we have been split apart by the god, just as the **Arcadians** were by the **Lacedaemonians** <note>A historical reference to the Spartans breaking up the unified city of Mantinea in Arcadia into separate villages in 385 BCE</note>. There is a fear, then, that if we are not orderly toward the gods, we might be split again and go about like the figures carved in profile on tombstones, sliced through the nose, becoming like tallies <term>lispai</term> <note>Refers to a piece of bone or wood split down the middle</note>. For this reason, every man should encourage everyone to be pious toward the gods, so that we may escape the one fate and obtain the other, with Love as our leader and general. Let no one act against him—and he acts against Love who incurs the hatred of the gods. For if we become friends with and are reconciled to the god, we shall find and meet our own particular beloveds, which few do now. <margin>G</margin> And let not **Eryximachus** interrupt my speech to mock it, as if I were referring only to **Pausanias** and **Agathon** <note>Two of the guests at the banquet who were a well-known couple</note>. Perhaps they indeed happen to be among those who are male by nature. But I am speaking of all men and women generally: our race would be happy if we fulfilled our love and if each person found his own beloved, returning to his ancient nature. If this is the best, it follows that in our current circumstances, the closest thing to the best is also the best: to find a beloved who is naturally suited to one’s mind. If we praise the god who is responsible for this, we should rightly praise Love. In the present, he helps us most by leading us to what is our own; for the future, he provides the greatest hopes that if we offer piety to the gods, he will restore us to our ancient nature, heal us, and make us blessed and happy. <margin>H</margin> This, Eryximachus, is my speech about Love, different from yours. As I asked you before, do not mock it, so that we may hear what the rest have to say—or rather, what each of the remaining two has to say. For only Agathon and...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...they might propagate. But if male met with male, they might be moved from the embrace by satiety, and turning to active affairs, look after their livelihood. Hence, indeed, from that time a mutual love was born in humans, a reconciler of the ancient nature, striving to make one out of two, and to heal the nature of humans. Each of us is therefore a half-man, as if cut, just like those little fish called **Psittae** <note>original: *Psittae*, likely referring to flatfish like soles or turbots that look like half a fish</note>, which are made into two from one by cutting. Each person perpetually seeks his own half. Therefore, those men who are a portion of the mixed gender, which was once called **Androgynous**, are fond of women; adulterers, for the most part, are found among these. From this same kind, female adulterers take their origin. <margin>B</margin> On the other hand, those women who are a part of a woman do not greatly desire men, but are more inclined toward females; hence women who desire women are born from this line. But those who are a portion of the male follow males. While they are boys, being little particles of the male, they love men and rejoice in the constant familiarity and company of men. These are the most noble of boys and youths, for they are by nature more manly than all others. Some falsely call them "impudent." For it is not from any <margin>C</margin> lack of shame, but from a certain nobility, courage, and masculine spirit that they act this way, for they take joy in what is like themselves. A clear proof of this is that when they have matured, they alone turn to the administration of the state and emerge as excellent men. When they have reached manhood, they love youths; by nature they despise marriage and the procreation of children, but are forced into it by law. A celibate life is what pleases them. Entirely, therefore, such a man chooses males and becomes a studious seeker of friends, always rejoicing in what is kindred. Whenever he happens upon his own half (of whatever sex it may be), they are moved most vehemently <margin>D</margin> and are struck with awe; they burn with friendship, intimacy, and love, and do not permit themselves—if I may say so—to be separated for even a moment. These are the ones who continue to love through their whole life, yet they cannot express what they especially expect from one another. For it does not seem that sexual union is the reason why one is so greatly delighted by the company of the other. Truly it is something else that the soul of each desires, which it cannot express but rather prophesies and guesses at, marking its desire with obscure traces. And if, while they were lying together, **Vulcan** <note>Hephaestus</note> were to stand over them with his tools and ask: "What is it, O mortals, that you <margin>E</margin> require from each other?" and if, as they doubted, he asked again: "Is this what you long for: to be joined into one and the same thing everywhere as much as possible, so that you are separated neither by day nor by night? If you desire this, I will melt you together and pour you into the same mold, so that from two you may be made one, and remain one always, both in this life and among those below. See if this is what you burn for, and if it would be enough for you to be granted this." If Vulcan asked this, it is certain that no one would refuse, nor would they seem to desire anything else. For each would think he had heard what he had long ago desired: namely, through union and mixing with the beloved, to be made one out of two. The cause of this is that <margin>F</margin> the original nature of humans was this, and we were whole. The desire and effort to restore the whole, therefore, received the name of **Love**. Long ago, as I was saying, we were one. Then, because of our injustice, we were split by God, just as the **Arcadians** were by the **Lacedaemonians**. It is further to be feared that if we behave with less modesty toward the gods than is fitting, we may be divided again, and become like those figured on columns, with our noses sliced through, looking like those very thin creatures called **Lispae**. But for this reason, it is fitting for everyone to worship the gods with the highest piety and to exhort others to do the same, so that we may avoid those evils and obtain these goods, just as our leader and general **Love** <margin>G</margin> admonishes us. Let no one dare to resist him. For he who opposes the gods resists Love. But if, having been reconciled to God, we find Him favorable, we shall each find and obtain our longed-for half. This, indeed, few do in these times. And let not that **Eryximachus** carpers at this speech of mine, as if I were speaking of **Pausanias** and **Agathon**—for perhaps they are of this kind, and both are males by nature. I am speaking indeed of all men and women: that our race will only then be happy when we fulfill the impulse of love, and each obtains his own delights, restored fully to his ancient nature. If this is a most happy thing, it follows that among the things now granted to us, that which is closest to this is the best: that is, for everyone to obtain those who are naturally after his own heart. Praising God as the cause of this, we ought rightly to praise Love, who in the present time helps us greatly while he leads us to that which is each person's own, and for the future offers us the greatest hope that, if we piously worship the gods, he will restore us to our ancient form and, by healing us, make us most blessed. This, Eryximachus, is my discourse on Love, different from yours: which, as I prayed above, do not tear apart, so that we may hear what each of the others brings—or rather, what both bring.
