# OF PLATO

<page-num>324</page-num>

...Socrates remain. "I will yield to you," Eryximachus was saying. "For your speech pleases me. And if I did not know that Socrates and Agathon were so eloquent in matters of love, I would greatly doubt whether they would have words enough, given how many various things have already been said. But I still have confidence in them." "You yourself competed vigorously, Eryximachus," Socrates said. "But if you were in the position I am in now—or rather, in the position I will be in once Agathon has also spoken so skillfully—you would be just as terrified as I am now, and pressed on all sides by difficulties." "You wish to bewitch me, Socrates," Agathon replied, "so that I might be flustered in your presence, thinking that there is a great expectation among you—as if in a theater—that I am about to speak most elegantly."

#### B
"I would be very forgetful, Agathon," Socrates said, "if I thought you would be flustered now because of us few men, when I saw you ascend the tragic stage <note>Agathon had recently won a prize for his first tragedy; the "pulpitum" refers to the high platform where the poets and actors stood</note> so boldly and generously along with the actors, and deliver your poems without any sign of terror before such a vast multitude of spectators." "Do not think me so devoted to the theater and its favor," Agathon said, "that I am unaware 
<margin>A wise man should fear the judgment of a few wise people more than many fools.</margin>
that a wise man should fear the judgment of a few wise people more than many fools." "I would be judging unfairly, Agathon," Socrates said, "if I thought there was anything unrefined in you. I know well that if you encountered any whom you considered wise, you would care more for them than for the common crowd."

#### C
"But see that we ourselves are not such people. For we were present there too, counted among the common crowd. But if you were to meet other wise men, you would surely fear doing anything unseemly in their sight. Or do you say otherwise?" "No, you speak the truth," Agathon said. "But you would not feel shame before the crowd," Socrates said, "if you thought you were doing something unseemly." Here Phædrus interrupted, saying, "My friend Agathon, if you proceed to answer Socrates, he will not care how anything else here goes, so long as he has someone to dispute with, especially someone beautiful. I certainly enjoy hearing Socrates dispute. Nevertheless, I must ensure that love is praised by each person in a certain order. Therefore, you two must first praise the God, and afterwards you may dispute with each other as you please."

#### D
<margin>The right way of praising.</margin>
"You speak excellently, Phædrus," Agathon said, "and nothing prevents me from speaking. Indeed, I will be able to dispute with Socrates often at other times. But now I will first show how one ought to speak, and then I will speak. It seems to me that all who have spoken so far have not praised the God himself, but have recounted the benefits that are happily conferred by him upon men. But what he himself is like, who is the cause of these goods, no one has yet expressed. There is only one correct way of praising in all matters: to first show the nature of the subject being discussed, and then declare the things of which he is the cause. Thus, it is proper now to first show what kind of being Love is, and then explain his gifts."

#### E
"I assert that since all the gods are blessed, Love—if it is lawful and permissible to say so—is the most blessed of all, because he is the most beautiful and the best. That he is the most beautiful is clear first from this, Phædrus: that he is the youngest of all the gods. He himself provides clear proof of this by fleeing from old age—which is obviously swift, since it arrives sooner than it should. Love by nature hates old age and flees from it, but he mingles with the young."
<margin>Proverb: Like rejoices in like.</margin>
"It is skillfully said in the old proverb: 'like always clings to like.' And while I agree with Phædrus on many other points, I do not agree that Love is older than Saturn and Iapetus <note>Ancient Titans representing the oldest generation of gods</note>. Rather, I say that he is younger than the other gods, and always young. The ancient deeds of the gods, which Hesiod and Parmenides describe, must be attributed to Necessity rather than to Love, if they told the truth at all."

#### F
"For they would not have castrated or bound each other, nor would many other violent things have happened among the gods of old, if Love had been present with them. Instead, benevolence and the greatest peace would have reigned, just as they do now, since Love began to rule the gods. Therefore, he is young, and moreover, he is tender and soft. There is need of a poet such as Homer was to demonstrate the tender softness of Love."

#### G
"Homer says that Ate—that is, the goddess of Calamity—is soft. To show that her feet are tender, he says she never treads upon the ground, but walks upon the heads of men."
<margin>Iliad, Book 19</margin>
"It seems to be a clear deduction that she is tender because she does not walk on hard surfaces, but touches the soft. We should use the same argument for those wishing to show that Love is tender. For he does not go upon the earth, nor upon skulls (which are not very soft), but he fixes himself and remains in the softest of all things. For he establishes his seat in the characters and minds of gods and men. Yet he does not dwell in just any mind: for if he encounters a hard disposition, he flees; but if he finds one mild and soft, he moves in."

#### H
"Since, therefore, he always touches with his feet and his whole self the softest parts of the softest things, Love must be the most tender. For this reason, Love is both young and tender. Furthermore, he is fluid like water and slippery. For he could not flow around every part of the soul, nor enter and leave secretly, if he were hard and rigid. His beauty—that is, the harmony of his figure—can serve as proof of his well-proportioned and flexible form, with which Love is undoubtedly decorated more than all others. Furthermore, there is a perpetual battle between deformity and Love. Of his color...

<column-break/>

...and Socrates remained. "But I will obey you" (he said, meaning Eryximachus), "for the speech was pleasingly told. And if I were not aware that Socrates and Agathon were formidable in matters of love, I would be very afraid that they would run out of words, because of the many and various things already said. But nonetheless, I am confident."

#### B
Then Socrates said, "You fought well yourself, Eryximachus. But if you were where I am now—or rather, perhaps, where I will be once Agathon has spoken—you would be very much afraid and in every kind of trouble, just as I am now." "You want to bewitch me, Socrates," Agathon said, "so that I might be thrown into a state of confusion, because I think the theater has a great expectation that I will speak well." "I would be forgetful indeed, Agathon," Socrates said, "if, after seeing your courage and high-mindedness when you ascended the platform <note>original: *okribanta*, the wooden stage or platform for speakers/actors</note> with the actors, and looked out at such a large theater about to display your own words, and were not in the least bit dismayed, I now thought you would be flustered because of us few men." "What then, Socrates?" Agathon said. "Surely you don't think me so full of the theater that I don't even know that, to a man of sense, a few wise people are more fearsome than many fools?" "I would certainly not be doing well, Agathon," Socrates said, "if I thought of you so crudely. But I know well that if you met any whom you considered wise, you would care more for them than for the many. 

#### C
But let it not be that we are those people—for we were also present there, and were among the many. But if you were to meet other wise people, you would perhaps be ashamed before them if you thought you were doing something shameful. Or how do you say it?" "You speak the truth," he said. "But would you not be ashamed before the many if you thought you were doing something shameful?" And he said Phædrus interrupted, saying, "My friend Agathon, if you answer Socrates, it will no longer make any difference to him how things here happen, provided only that he has someone to talk with, especially someone beautiful. I also enjoy hearing Socrates talk, but I must take care of the eulogy for Love, and receive a speech from each one of you. So, after you have both paid your dues to the god, you may then talk." "You are right, Phædrus," Agathon said, "and nothing prevents me from speaking. For with Socrates, there will be many other occasions to talk."

#### D
"But I want first to say how I ought to speak, and then speak. For all those who have spoken before me seem to me not to be praising the god, but to be congratulating human beings for the goods of which the god is the cause. But what kind of being he is himself, who gave these gifts, no one has said. There is one right way of every praise concerning everything: to go through in speech what kind of being is the cause of what things concerning whatever the speech may be about. So then, it is right for us to praise Love first for what he is himself, and then for his gifts. I say then, that while all the gods are happy, Love—if it is holy and without offense to say so—is the most happy of them, being the most beautiful and the best."

#### E
"And he is the most beautiful, being such as this: first, he is the youngest of the gods, Phædrus. He himself provides a great proof for the argument, by fleeing in flight from old age, which is clearly swift. At any rate, it comes upon us faster than it should; which is why Love is by nature inclined to hate it, and not to come anywhere near it. But he is always with the young and is among them. For the old saying is right, that 'like always draws near to like.' But while I agree with Phædrus on many other things, I do not agree with this: that Love is older than Cronus and Iapetus. Instead, I say he is the youngest of the gods, and always young. Those old affairs concerning the gods, which Hesiod and Parmenides tell of, happened by Necessity and not by Love, if they told the truth. For there would have been no castrations or binding of one another, and many other violent things, if Love were among them, but friendship and peace, as there is now, ever since Love has ruled the gods."

#### F
"So he is young; and besides being young, he is tender. He is in need of a poet such as Homer was to show the tenderness of the god. For Homer says that Ate <note>original: *Atên*, the goddess of mischief, delusion, or calamity</note> is a god and is tender; at least he says her feet are tender, saying: 'her feet are tender; for she does not draw near the ground, but she walks upon the heads of men.' So he seems to me to show her tenderness by a fine proof, because she does not walk on what is hard, but on what is soft. We shall use the same proof concerning Love, that he is tender."

#### G
"For he does not walk on the earth, nor on skulls (which are not very soft), but he dwells and walks in the softest of things that exist. For he has established his dwelling in the characters and souls of gods and men; and again, not in all souls one after another, but whenever he meets a soul with a hard character, he goes away, and whenever he meets a soft one, he makes his home there. So, always touching with his feet and in every way the softest of the softest things, he must be the most tender. So he is the youngest and the most tender. In addition to these, he is fluid in form. For he would not be able to fold himself around everything, nor to go into every soul and at first escape notice, and then go out, if he were hard. A great proof of his well-proportioned and fluid form is his gracefulness, which Love is acknowledged to have pre-eminently among all."

#### H
"For there is always war between Love and gracelessness <note>original: *aschêmosynê*, lack of form, deformity, or indecency</note>."

# THE BANQUET

<margin>A</margin> The fact that this God dwells continuously among flowers signifies his beauty. For in that which lacks flowers, or where the bloom has faded—whether it be a body, a soul, or anything else—Love himself does not settle. But wherever there is a flowery and fragrant place, there he rests most pleasantly. Concerning the beauty of this god, many more things could be brought forward, but these shall suffice. Next, we must speak of the virtue of Love. This is of the greatest importance: Love neither inflicts injury upon a God or a man, nor does he suffer injury from a God or a man. For he does not suffer by force <note>The Greek term is *bia*, meaning literal physical violence or compulsion</note>, if indeed he suffers at all. For violence does not touch Love. Neither does he act by force, if he acts at all. For everyone willingly obeys Love in all things. Whatever agreements one person makes with another by mutual consent are held to be just, as the laws of the sovereign city state.

<margin>B</margin> Love participates not only in justice, but also in the highest temperance. For it is agreed among all that temperance consists in mastery over lusts and pleasures, and that no pleasure is more powerful than Love. If, therefore, all pleasures are weaker than Love, they are surely mastered by him, and he is their master. Thus, Love—since he masters lusts and pleasures—is wondrously temperate. Furthermore, regarding courage, not even Mars <note>The Roman name for the Greek god Ares</note> can resist Love. For Mars does not hold Love, but Love holds the love of Venus, as the story goes; and the one who holds is more powerful than the one who is held.
<margin>All pleasures are surpassed by love.</margin>

<margin>C</margin> Since Love masters the most courageous of all others, he must without doubt be judged the most courageous of all. Enough has been said of the justice, temperance, and courage of this god. It remains to speak of his wisdom, which must be pursued to the best of my ability. First, so that I may also honor my own art, just as Eryximachus honored his, I say this god is a poet so wise that he can make others poets as well. For anyone, even if they were previously unrefined, becomes a poet as soon as Love breathes upon them. From this we may clearly conclude that Love is a skilled poet, and that he possesses, in short, all the musical measures of poetry. For what a person does not have or does not know, they cannot give to another or show to another.
<margin>D</margin>
<margin>What one does not have or know, one cannot give or show to another.</margin>

Who would doubt that all animals are generated and born through the wisdom of Love? Furthermore, do we not see that the mastery of the arts is granted by this God? That the man who has Love as a teacher becomes eminent and famous in whatever art he pursues, while he who is not touched by Love remains in obscurity? For it was with desire as his guide and Love as his leader that Apollo discovered the skills of archery, healing, and divination; thus, even Apollo is a disciple of Love. Similarly, the Muses discovered music, Vulcan <note>Hephaestus</note> discovered the forging of bronze, Minerva <note>Athena</note> the art of weaving, and Jupiter <note>Zeus</note> the governance of gods and men.

<margin>E</margin> Because of this, the affairs of the gods were set in order when Love intervened—I mean, the love of beauty, for Love does not follow deformity. Previously, as I said at the beginning, many terrible things happened among the gods because of the reign of Necessity, as they say. But after this god was born from the desire for beautiful things, all good things came to both gods and men. So it seems to me, O Phaedrus, that Love is himself first the most beautiful and best, and then grants such qualities to all others. Something in verse occurs to me at this moment:

> This is the god who grants peace to the human race, 
> a calm face to the sea, rest to the winds, 
> a bed for man, and sleep granted to cares.

He removes all rusticity <note>original Greek: *allotriotes* (estrangement/alienation), Latin: *rusticitatem* (lack of refinement)</note> from us and unites us in intimacy, bringing together all such gatherings as these.

<margin>F</margin> On solemn and festive days, in dances, and in sacrifices, he is our leader and presiding officer. Providing gentleness and banishing wildness, he is the giver of benevolence and the expeller of all ill-will. He is gracious and kind, a sight for the wise to behold, pleasing to the gods, desired by those who lack him, and to be possessed and held fast by those who share in him. He is the father of delicacies, of soft allurements, of graces, of sweet outpouring, and of desire. He is the seeker of the good, the despiser of the evil. In labor, in fear, in desire, and in speech, he is the governor, the perfect helper, and the chief savior. He is the glory of all gods and men, the most beautiful and best leader. Truly every man ought to follow him, honoring him with noble hymns and participating in that song which Love himself sings, soothing the minds of gods and men. This speech of mine, Phaedrus, let it be dedicated to the god, filled partly with jests and partly with serious matters, according to the capacity of my talent.

<margin>G</margin> When Agathon had said these things, as Aristodemus related, all the guests approved the speech with a great round of applause, as it seemed to have been delivered in a manner worthy of both Agathon and the God. Therefore, Socrates, turning to Eryximachus, said: "O son of Acumenus, do I not now seem to have been rightly afraid before, and did I not truly prophesy that Agathon would speak most effectively, such that I thought I would be at a loss for words?" "In one thing," Eryximachus replied,

<column-break/>

<margin>H</margin> "I think you prophesied correctly, that Agathon would speak skillfully; but that eloquence would fail you, I do not believe at all." "And why," Socrates said, "O blessed one, should not I, or anyone else, be deterred from speaking when one has to talk after such a brilliant and copious oration? While the other parts were indeed aptly composed, they do not seem so miraculous; but the elegance of the nouns and verbs which he used at the conclusion of the speech—if anyone noticed it, they would be immediately stunned. For indeed, as I realized that I could not come close to such eloquence, I was moved by shame and was very nearly driven to flee from here, if I had any place to go. For the speech reminded me of Gorgias <note>Gorgias was a famous Sophist and rhetorician known for his rhythmic, highly ornamental style; Socrates is playfully suggesting Agathon’s speech was so "Gorgian" it turned him to stone like a Medusa head</note>..."

<meta>This page marks the transition from Agathon’s highly rhetorical and flowery speech to Socrates’ philosophical examination. On the previous page, Agathon concluded his praise of Love’s virtues (justice, temperance, and courage). Here, Socrates begins by playfully critiquing Agathon’s style before using his "Socratic method" to dissect the logic of what "Love" actually is.</meta>

-># PLATO<-

<insert>A</insert> I was reminded of that famous scene in Homer. I was truly afraid that, as Agathon finished his speech, he would cast the head of the eloquent Gorgias <note>original: "Gorgiae facundi caput." Socrates is making a pun. Gorgias was a famous teacher of rhetoric, but his name sounds like the "Gorgon" Medusa, who turned people to stone. Socrates jokes that Agathon’s eloquence was so powerful it might strike him dumb.</note> from his oration into mine, rendering me mute and turning me from a man into a stone. It was then that I realized I had been foolish to promise that I would join you in praising Love to the best of my ability, and that I was wrong to claim expertise in amorous matters, since I clearly did not know the proper way to praise anything. I had thought, in my ignorance, that when praising something, one ought to tell the truth about it, and that this truth should be the foundation; then, from those truths, one should select the most beautiful aspects and arrange them as gracefully as possible. I was quite <insert>B</insert> confident that I would speak well, since I believed I knew the "true" way to give praise.

However, it turns out that this was not the "proper" way to praise at all. Instead, it seems one is expected to attribute the greatest and most magnificent qualities to the subject being praised, whether they actually belong to it or not. If the claims are false, it apparently doesn't matter! For the goal was not to praise Love as he truly is, but to make everyone *believe* he is being praised as grandly as possible. This is why you stir up every possible argument and attribute them to Love, claiming he is "such a thing" and the "cause of such great things," so that he appears most beautiful and excellent—to those who don't know any better, of course. To those who actually know the truth, such praise would never be judged as right or pure. I was <insert>C</insert> completely ignorant of this method of praising. Therefore, I unintentionally agreed to join you in this exercise. My tongue promised, but my mind did not <note>This is a famous allusion to a line from the playwright Euripides: "My tongue swore, but my mind remains unsworn."</note>. Let such a style of praise be far from me! I cannot extol him in that way.

However, if you are willing, I am happy to speak the truth in my own fashion, rather than competing with your formal orations, which might make me look ridiculous. See then, Phaedrus, if you would like to hear a speech of this kind: one that tells only the truth about Love, with the words and phrases arranged simply, as they occur to me.

Phaedrus and the others then told him to speak in whatever way he thought best. 

<margin>Socrates directs Agathon so that he might speak with his confirmation.</margin>

<insert>D</insert> "Allow me, Phaedrus," Socrates said, "to ask Agathon a few small questions, so that I may speak with his agreement as my foundation."

"I allow it," Phaedrus replied. "Go ahead and ask."

Then, they say Socrates began his discourse something like this: 

"My dear friend Agathon, you seemed to lay down an excellent foundation for your speech when you said we must first show what Love is, and only then list his works. I greatly approve of that starting point. Come then, since you have spoken so elegantly and magnificently about the nature of Love, tell me this: Is Love the kind of thing that is the love *of* something, or is it the love of *nothing*? <insert>E</insert> I am not asking if he is the love of a mother or a father—that would be a ridiculous question, asking if 'Love' is the 'love of a mother.' But if I were to ask about a 'father,' and whether a father is the father of *someone* or not, you would surely answer—if you wished to speak correctly—that a father is the father of a son or a daughter. Is that not so?"

"Certainly," said Agathon.

"And is a mother not the mother of someone?" 

Agathon agreed to this as well.

"Answer me a little more," Socrates said, "so you can better understand my point. If I asked about a 'brother,' is he—by the very fact of being a brother—a brother to someone?"

Agathon said he was.

"Is he not the brother of a brother or a sister?"

"Indeed."

"Now, try to show us the same regarding Love. Is Love the love of nothing, or of something?"

"Of something, certainly."

"Keep that in mind then," Socrates said, "remembering what that 'something' is. But answer me this: <insert>F</insert> Does Love desire that thing of which he is the love, or not?"

"He certainly does."

"Does he have the thing he desires and loves in his possession while he desires it? Or does he not have it?"

"It is likely," Agathon said, "that he does not have it."

"Consider," said Socrates, "whether instead of 'likely,' it is actually *necessary* that the one who desires something lacks the thing he desires? And that if he does not lack it, he does not desire it? It seems wonderfully necessary to me. What do you think, Agathon?"

"I think so too," said Agathon.

"Good. Now, would someone who is already tall want to be tall? Or someone who is already strong want to be strong?"

<insert>G</insert> "That would be impossible, based on what we just agreed."

"For the one who already *is* those things would not be in lack of them."

"True."

"For if someone who is strong wanted to be strong," Socrates said, "or someone who is fast wanted to be fast, or someone healthy wanted to be healthy—for one might imagine that people who possess such qualities still desire the things they have—I say this so we aren't deceived. If you think about it, Agathon, those people *must* have those qualities in the present moment, whether they want to or not. Why would anyone desire what they already have? But when someone says, 'I, being healthy, want to be healthy,' or 'Being rich, I want to be rich; and therefore I desire the things I have,' we would answer them: 'My good man, you already possess wealth, health, and strength, <insert>H</insert> and you wish to possess them *in the future*, since in the present you have them regardless of your will.' Consider then, when you say, 'I desire what I have,' are you not really saying, 'I want the things I have now to also be present to me in the future'? Would he not agree?"

Agathon said he would.

"Is this not, then, a love for something that is not yet ready or held—namely, that these things be preserved for him in the time to follow?"

"Certainly."

"Therefore, he and everyone else who desires, desires that which is not yet...

<column-break/>

...reminded me, that I had truly suffered what Homer described. For I feared that at the end Agathon, by sending the head of Gorgias—so formidable in speaking—into his speech against mine, would make me a stone through speechlessness. I realized then how ridiculous I was when I agreed with you to take my turn in eulogizing Love, and claimed to be an expert in amorous matters, when in fact I knew nothing of the matter or how one ought to praise anything. For I, in my stupidity, thought one should tell the truths about each thing being praised; and that this should be the basis, and that from these truths the most beautiful should be selected and arranged as decorously as possible. And I was very proud of myself for speaking well, believing I knew the truth of how to praise anything. 

But it turns out, as it seems, that this was not the way to praise anything well, but rather to attribute the greatest and most beautiful things to the matter, whether they are so or not. And if they were false, it was nothing. For it was proposed, it seems, that each of us should *appear* to praise Love, not that we should actually praise him. For this reason, I think, you move every argument and attribute it to Love, and you say he is such a thing and the cause of such things, so that he may appear as beautiful and best as possible—clearly to those who do not know him. For surely not to those who know. And the praise is indeed beautiful and solemn. 

But I did not know the manner of the praise; and not knowing, I agreed with you to also take my turn in praising. My tongue then promised, but my mind did not. Let it go then; for I no longer praise in this manner, for I would not be able. Not indeed, but the truth, if you wish, I am willing to speak in my own way, not compared to your speeches, so that I do not incur laughter. See then, Phaedrus, if there is a need for such a speech, to hear the truths being told about Love, in such words and arrangement of phrases as might happen to occur." 

Then he said Phaedrus and the others ordered him to speak, in whatever way he himself thought he ought to speak. 

"Furthermore then," he said, "Phaedrus, allow me to ask Agathon a few more small things; so that having reached an agreement with him, I may then speak." 

"I allow it," said Phaedrus, "ask." 

After these things, he said Socrates began from somewhere here: 

"Indeed, my friend Agathon, you seemed to me to lead the way well in your speech, saying that first it was necessary to show what kind of thing Love is, and later his works. This beginning I altogether admire. Come then, tell me about Love—since you have also gone through the rest beautifully and magnificently—what he is like, and tell me this: is Love the kind of thing that is a love *of* something, or *of nothing*? I ask not if he is of some mother or father (for the question would be ridiculous, if Love is the love of a father or mother) but as if I were asking this very thing about a father: is a father the father of someone, or not? You would surely say to me (if you wished to answer well) that a father is the father of a son or a daughter. Or not?" 

"Certainly," said Agathon. 

"Is not the mother likewise?" 

He agreed to this also. 

"Furthermore then," said Socrates, "answer a few more things, so that you may better understand what I want. For if I were to ask: what then? A brother—this very thing that he is—is he a brother of someone, or not?" 

He said, "He is." 

"Is he not of a brother, or a sister?" He agreed. 

"Try then," he said, "to also speak of Love. Is Love the love of nothing, or of someone?" 

"Altogether of someone." 

"This indeed then," said Socrates, "keep within yourself, remembering of whom; but tell me this much: does Love desire that of which he is the love, or not?" 

"Certainly," he said. 

"Does he desire and love it while having that which he desires and loves? Or while not having it?" 

"While not having it, as is likely," he said. 

"Consider then," said Socrates, "instead of what is 'likely,' if it is a necessity that the desiring thing desires that which it lacks, or does not desire it, if it does not lack it. For to me, Agathon, it seems wonderfully to be a necessity. But how does it seem to you?" 

"To me also," he said, "it seems so." 

"You speak well. Would anyone, then, being great, wish to be great? Or being strong, be strong?" 

"Impossible, from what has been agreed." 

"For surely the one who *is* would not be in lack of these things." 

"You say the truth." 

"For if even one who is strong wished to be strong," said Socrates, "and one who is fast, to be fast; and one who is healthy, to be healthy—for perhaps someone might think these things and all such things, that those who are such and have these things, also desire these very things which they have. So that we are not deceived, I say this for this reason. For to these people, Agathon, if you consider, it is a necessity that they each have these things in the present, all that they have, whether they wish it or not. And of this indeed, who would desire it? But when someone says, 'I, being healthy, wish to be healthy, and being rich, wish to be rich, and I desire these very things which I have,' we would say to him, 'You, O man, possessing wealth and health and strength, wish also in the time to come to possess these things, since in the present now, whether you wish it or not, you have them.' Consider then, when you say this, 'I desire the things present,' if you say anything else than this: 'I wish the things now present to also be present in the time to come.' Would he not agree?" 

He said Agathon agreed. 

Then Socrates said, "Is this not, then, to love that which is not yet ready for him, nor which he has: the preservation of these things now present into the time to come?" 

"Certainly," he said. 

"And this man then, and anyone else..."

<summary>Socrates begins his critique of Agathon’s speech, arguing that true praise should be based on facts rather than mere rhetorical embellishment. He then initiates a dialectic examination to prove that Love is inherently a state of desire for what one does not currently possess or for the future security of what one has.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Agathon. Having established that Love is always "love of something," Socrates now moves to prove that Love is the desire for what one lacks, eventually leading into his recount of the teachings of Diotima.</meta>

->### THE SYMPOSIUM ###<-

<margin>A</margin> Everyone who desires, desires those things which are not at hand; that which he does not already have, or that which he is not, or that of which he is in need—these are the sorts of things that are the objects of desire and Love. "Quite so," said Socrates, "let us summarize what has been agreed. First, is Love not the love of certain things? And second, is it not the love of those things for which a person feels a lack?" "Yes," he replied. "Now, recall what you said in your speech about what the objects of Love are. If you like, I will remind you. I believe you said something like this: that the affairs of the gods were organized through the love of beautiful things, for there could be no love of ugly things. Did you not say something of the sort?" "I did say that," Agathon replied. "And you spoke quite well, my friend," said Socrates. "And if this is so, must Love not be the love of beauty, and not of ugliness?" He agreed. "Now, has it not been granted that one loves what one lacks <margin>B</margin> and does not possess?" "Yes," he said. "Therefore, Love lacks beauty and does not possess it." "That must be," he said. "What then? Do you call that which lacks beauty, and in no way possesses beauty, beautiful?" "Certainly not." "Then do you still maintain that Love is beautiful, if these things are so?" And Agathon said, "Socrates, it is likely that I knew nothing of what I said then." "And yet you spoke beautifully, Agathon," said Socrates. "But consider this one small thing further: Do not good things also seem beautiful to you?" "They do." "If, then, Love lacks beautiful things, and good things are beautiful, then he must also lack good things." "I cannot contradict you, Socrates," he said. "Let it be as you say." "It is the Truth, my dear Agathon, that you cannot contradict; for contradicting Socrates is not difficult at all."

"And now I will let you go. I will instead relate the discourse concerning <margin>C</margin> Love which I once heard from a prophetic woman named Diotima <note>Diotima of Mantinea is a perhaps-fictional priestess who serves as Socrates' instructor in the philosophy of Love. She represents a shift from male-centric rhetoric to a more mystical, divine understanding.</note>. She was wise in these matters and many others; once, when the Athenians offered sacrifices before a plague, she secured a ten-year delay of the disease. She is the one who taught me the science of love. I will try to recount to you the speech she gave, based on the points Agathon and I have already agreed upon, as best as I can by myself. It is necessary, Agathon, just as you described, to first explain who Love is and what he is like, and then to describe his works. It seems easiest to me to proceed in the same way the foreign woman did when she questioned me. For I said nearly the same things to <margin>D</margin> her that Agathon just said to me: that Love was a great god and was the love of beautiful things. But she proved to me, using the same arguments I used against Agathon, that according to my own logic, Love was neither beautiful nor good. 'How can you say this, Diotima?' I asked. 'Is Love then ugly and bad?' And she said, 'Hush! Do you think that anything which is not beautiful must necessarily be ugly?' 'Certainly,' I said. 'And that what is not wise must be ignorant? Have you not noticed that there is something between wisdom and ignorance?' 'What is that?' 'Right opinion,' she said. 'To hold a correct opinion without being able to give a reason for it—do you not realize that this is neither knowledge (for how could something without a reason be knowledge?) nor ignorance (for how can that which hits upon the truth be ignorance?). Right opinion is surely something like that, a middle ground between understanding <margin>E</margin> and ignorance.' 'You speak the truth,' I said. 'Then do not insist,' she said, 'that what is not beautiful must be ugly, or what is not good must be bad. In the same way, since you yourself admit that Love is neither good nor beautiful, do not think he must be ugly or bad, but rather something in between these two.'

'And yet,' I said, 'everyone agrees that he is a great god.' 'By "everyone,"' she asked, 'do you mean those who do not know, or those who do know?' 'I mean everyone together.' At this she laughed and said, 'And how, Socrates, could he be agreed to be a great god <margin>F</margin> by those who say he is not a god at all?' 'Who are they?' I asked. 'You are one,' she said, 'and I am another.' And I said, 'How can you say this?' 'Easily,' she replied. 'Tell me, do you not say that all gods are beautiful and happy? Or would you dare to say that any of the gods is not beautiful and happy?' 'By Zeus, not I,' I said. 'And do you not call those "happy" who possess good and beautiful things?' 'Certainly.' 'But you have already admitted that Love, because of his lack of good and beautiful things, desires those very things he lacks.' 'I have admitted it.' 'How then could he be a god, if he is stripped of beautiful and good things?' 'In no way, it seems.' 'Do you see <margin>G</margin> then,' she said, 'that you yourself do not consider Love a god?' 'What then could Love be?' I asked. 'A mortal?' 'Hardly.' 'What then?' 'As I said before,' she replied, 'something between a mortal and an immortal.' 'What is that, Diotima?' 'A great <term>spirit</term> <note>original Greek: "daimon." In Greek thought, a daimon was not an evil demon, but a spiritual intermediary or a guiding force that bridged the gap between the divine and the human.</note>, Socrates. For everything spiritual is between the divine and the mortal.'

'What power does it have?' I asked. 'It interprets and conveys things from men to gods and from gods to men,' she said. 'From men, it carries prayers and sacrifices; from gods, it brings commands and rewards for those sacrifices. Being in the middle of both, it fills the gap, so that the whole universe is bound together. Through this spirit, all prophecy proceeds, as well as the art of priests <margin>H</margin> regarding sacrifices, rituals, incantations, and all divination and sorcery. God does not mingle with man directly, but through this medium, all commerce and dialogue between gods and men occurs, whether we are awake or asleep. The man who is wise in such matters is a spiritual man; but he who is wise in other things, such as arts or manual crafts, is merely a <term>menial</term> <note>original Greek: "banausos." This term refers to a common laborer or artisan, often looked down upon by philosophers as being concerned only with material things rather than the soul.</note> worker. These spirits are many and of all kinds, and one of them is Love.' 'And who,' I asked, 'are his father and mother?' 'That is a longer story to tell,' she said, 'but I will tell it to you nonetheless. When Love was born...'

Whoever is skilled in these spiritual matters is a happy man and is called wise; but those who are skilled in other arts and capacities filled with empty things are called *banausi*, that is, hirelings. Indeed, these spirits are many and various. One of these is Love. "Who then," I asked, "are the parents of Love?" "Although it is a long story to tell," she said, "I will explain it nonetheless."

<column-break/>

...is already prepared and at hand, he desires that which is not present, which he does not have, which he himself is not, and which he lacks. Such are the things which are the objects of desire and Love. "Such they are, without a doubt." "Come," said Socrates, "let us repeat what was said above. First, Love was said to be the love of certain things, and second, specifically of those things which it lacks." "Certainly," I replied. "Remember, moreover, the assertion you made. I will bring it back to your memory if you wish. Indeed, I think you spoke thus: that all things were arranged by the gods because of the love of beautiful things. For of ugly things, there is no love at all. Did you not say so?" "I did indeed." "You speak plausibly, my friend. And if this is so, Love is certainly the love of beauty, but of ugliness, not at all." "I agree." "Has it not been granted that one loves that which one needs and does not have?" "Clearly granted." "Therefore Love lacks beauty, and does not have it." "It is necessary." "What then? Do you call that beautiful which is in need of beauty and does not have it?" "By no means." "Do you then further assert, if these things are so, that Love is beautiful?" "I seem to have understood nothing of what I said before." "You said it well. But answer a little further: do not good things themselves seem to be beautiful?" "They seem so to me." "If, therefore, Love lacks beautiful things, and good things are beautiful, he also lacks good things." "I could in no way fight against you, Socrates. Let it be, then, as you say." "You could never oppose the truth, my dear Agathon, though you might easily oppose Socrates."

<margin>Diotima the prophetess.</margin> But I will dismiss Agathon now, and I will relate to you, guests, the sermon on Love which I once received from a prophetic woman, Diotima, who was both skilled in these matters and understood many other things wisely; and who once, when the Athenians had performed sacrifices ten years before the plague, gave them a delay of the disease. She instructed me in the science of love. Therefore, what she said, I will attempt to express to you from myself, according to the points agreed upon between me and Agathon. It is necessary first, Agathon, as you also set out, to show what and of what kind Love is, and then to enumerate his works. It is better, as it seems to me, to relate it to you now in the same order in which that stranger treated it when she examined me. For I had told her almost the same things Agathon told me: that Love was a great god and looked toward beautiful things. And she refuted me with the same arguments by which I refuted him: that Love was neither beautiful, as I was saying, nor good. To which I then said, "What are you saying, Diotima? Is Love therefore ugly and bad?" And she: "Speak better, I pray. Do you think it necessary that whatever is not beautiful must be ugly?" "Certainly." "And that what is not wise is ignorant? Have you not noticed that there <margin>Between wisdom and ignorance, right opinion is the middle.</margin> is a certain middle ground between wisdom and ignorance?" "What is that?" "To think rightly—that is, to be a participant in the truth without a certain reason: for this is not knowledge, since knowledge is never without a reason. Nor, on the other hand, is it ignorance. For that which is composed of truth is not called ignorance. Right opinion is something of this kind, a middle between wisdom and ignorance." "You tell the truth," I was saying. "Do not force it then," she said, "that what is not beautiful must be ugly, or what is not good must be evil. By the same reasoning, although you may concede that Love is neither beautiful nor good, you should not therefore think he is necessarily ugly or bad, but a middle between those." <margin>Love is the middle between ugly and beautiful.</margin> "But truly, in this everyone agrees: that Love is a great god." "Do you mean the ignorant," she asked, "or the knowing?" "All of them," I said. "How in the world," she said laughing, "would those who do not even want him to be a god confess that he is a great god?" "Who are those people?" I asked. "You are one," she said. "I am the other." "How can you say that I asserted this?" "I will easily show you. Come, tell me: Do you not affirm that all gods are beautiful and blessed? Would you dare to say any of the gods is not beautiful or blessed?" "Not by Jove." "And do you not call those blessed who possess good and beautiful things?" "Them alone." "And yet you admitted earlier that Love, because of a lack of beautiful and good things, desires these very things of which he is in need." "I did admit it." "How then is he a god," she said, "who is devoid of beautiful and good things?" "In no way, as it seems," I said. "Do you see that you yourself do not think Love is a god?" "What then?" I asked. "Is Love mortal?" "Not at all." "What then?" "Like the things mentioned before, a middle between mortal and immortal." "What is it, Diotima?" "A great spirit, Socrates. For the entire nature of spirits is middle between mortals and gods." <margin>The nature of spirits.</margin> "What power does it have?" "It interprets," she said, "and carries human things to the gods, and divine things to humans: the prayers and sacrifices of the former, the commands and sacred solemn rituals, institutions, and order of the latter. <margin>The duties and offices of spirits.</margin> Positioned in the middle of both, it completes the whole, so that the universe is connected to itself by such a bond. Through this, every prophecy proceeds, and the diligence of priests concerning sacrifices and expiations, and incantations, and all divination, and <margin>Divination and magic are granted through spirits.</margin> magic. God indeed does not mingle with man, but through that middle ground, all commerce and conversation between gods and men is conducted, both while we are awake and while we sleep."

<margin>Love is one of the spirits.</margin> "One of these is Love." "Who then," I asked, "are the parents of Love?" "Although it is a long story to tell," she said, "I will explain it nonetheless. When [he] was born..."

# PLATO'S #

->### THE SYMPOSIUM ###<-

<margin>A</margin> When Venus <note>The Roman name for Aphrodite.</note> was born, the gods held a feast, and among them was Porus, the god of Abundance <gloss>Porus</gloss>, that is, the god of plenty, who is the son of Metis, or Counsel. When they had finished dining, Penia <gloss>Penia</gloss>, that is, poverty, came to beg for scraps, as happens where there is such abundance, and she waited by the doors. Now Porus, being drunk on nectar—for wine did not yet exist—entered the Garden of Jove <note>The Roman name for Zeus.</note> and, being heavy with sleep, began to slumber. Then Penia, driven by her own lack, devised a plan to have a child by Porus through a sort of trick. She lay down beside him and conceived Love. Thus Love was born as a follower and servant of Venus, because he was begotten on her birthday. Furthermore, by his very nature, he is captured by a desire for the beautiful, since Venus herself is beautiful. Because Love is the son of Resource and Poverty,

<margin>B</margin> he has obtained a fate of this kind. First, he is always poor, and he is far from being soft and beautiful, as most people think; instead, he is rough and squalid, barefoot, always wandering on the ground, without a home, without bedding or any covering, sleeping at doorways and on the road under the open sky, preserving his mother's nature and always living with want. Second, following his father’s nature, he schemes against the beautiful and the good; he is manly, bold, intense, and a keen hunter, always weaving new devices, a seeker of wisdom, eloquent, philosophizing throughout his entire life, a sorcerer, a powerful enchanter, a magician, and a sophist. He is neither entirely immortal by nature, nor is he mortal: but sometimes on the same day he flourishes and lives, as long as he has abundance; at other times he fails,

<margin>C</margin> and then lives again because of his father’s nature. Whatever he acquires continually flows away. Therefore, Love is never a beggar, nor is he wealthy. Furthermore, he is positioned between wisdom and ignorance. For the matter stands thus: None of the gods philosophizes or desires to become wise, for they already are. Nor does any other person who is wise philosophize. Neither do the entirely ignorant philosophize, nor do they desire to become wise. For this is the worst thing about ignorance: when someone who is neither beautiful nor good nor wise thinks himself to be sufficient in these things.

<margin>D</margin> Therefore, he never seeks after those things if he does not notice he is lacking them. "Who then, Diotima," I said, "are the ones who philosophize, if neither the wise nor the ignorant do so?" "Even a child would understand this by now," she said, "namely that it is those who are in the middle between these two, among whom is Love. For wisdom is indeed a most beautiful thing, and Love is concerned with the beautiful. From this it necessarily follows that Love is a philosopher; and since he is a philosopher, he holds the middle ground between the ignorant and the wise. The cause of this lies in his birth. For he was begotten from a father who is wise and resourceful, and a mother who is not at all wise and indeed poor. Such is the nature of this spirit <note>original: 'daemonis' — in Greek thought, a 'daemon' is a being between gods and mortals.</note>, my friend Socrates. It is no wonder that you imagined Love to be such as you did based on your opinion. For, as I gather from your words, you thought Love was the one being loved, not the one who loves, and for that reason Love seemed to you to be all-beautiful. That which is lovable is indeed truly beautiful, delicate, perfect, and most blessed. But the one who loves has another such form, as I have described above." "So be it, stranger," I said, "for you speak excellently.

<margin>E</margin> But since Love is such a thing, of what use is he to men?" "This next point, Socrates," she said, "I will endeavor to teach you. Such is Love, and thus was he born. He is concerned with beautiful things, as you say. But if someone were to ask: 'For what purpose is the love of beautiful things, Socrates and Diotima?' Or to speak more clearly: 'The one who loves beautiful things, what does he specifically seek?'"

<margin>F</margin> "What shall we answer?" "That they might be his own," I replied. "But this answer requires a further question: 'What will happen to the one who possesses beautiful things?'" "I have no ready answer," I said. "But," she said, "if someone were to change the terms, using 'the good' instead of 'the beautiful,' and ask: 'He who loves good things, what does he seek?'" "That they might be his own," I said. "And what will happen to the one who possesses good things?" "This answer is easier," I said. "He will be happy. For by the possession of good things, the happy are made happy; and there is no further need to ask why someone who wishes for happiness wants to be happy, for the answer seems to have reached its end." "You speak the truth," I said. "Now, do you think this will and this love are common to all men, and that all wish for good things to be their own always?" "Clearly, it is common," I said. "Why then, Socrates, do we not say that everyone loves, if indeed everyone loves the same things always? Why do we say some love and others do not?" "I wonder that myself," I said. "Do not wonder," she said. "For selecting one kind of lover, we call it 'Love,' giving it the name of the whole."

<margin>G</margin> "In other cases, we use other names." "Give me an example," I said. "As follows: You know that 'making' is something broad. Indeed, 'making' <note>The Greek term 'poiesis' literally means 'making' or 'creation' in a general sense.</note> in a general sense is the cause by which anything proceeds from non-being into being. Therefore, all actions of any art are 'makings,' and all craftsmen are 'poets,' that is, makers. "What you say is true," I said. "Yet you see that they are not called 'poets,' but are given other names. But from all making, one selected part, which is concerned with music and verse, is called by the name of the whole. For this alone is called 'poetry,' that is, making; and those who possess this part of making are called 'poets.'"

<margin>H</margin> "This is true," I said. "The same thing happens regarding Love. For in summary, every desire for good things and for happiness is a most great and treacherous Love in everyone. But those who turn toward the good through a devotion to money...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> When Aphrodite was born, the gods were feasting, including Porus, the son of Metis. When they had finished dinner, Penia came to beg, as there was a feast, and she was about the doors. Now Porus, being drunk on nectar (for wine was not yet known), went into the garden of Zeus and, being heavy, fell asleep. Then Penia, plotting because of her own poverty to have a child from Porus, lay down beside him and conceived Eros. For this reason, Eros has become an attendant and servant of Aphrodite, having been born on her birthday; and at the same time, he is by nature a lover of the beautiful, since Aphrodite is beautiful. Since, then, Eros is the son of Porus and Penia, he is in 

<margin>B</margin> such a condition as this. First, he is always poor, and he is far from being tender and beautiful (as many believe), but is instead hard and squalid, and barefoot, and homeless; always sleeping on the ground and without bedding, at doors and in the streets under the open sky; having his mother's nature; always dwelling with want. But according to his father, he is a plotter against the good and the beautiful, being brave, and bold, and intense; a clever hunter, always weaving some devices, and a desirer of wisdom, and resourceful; philosophizing through all his life; a clever sorcerer, and a magician, and a sophist. And he is not by nature either immortal or mortal; but sometimes on the same day 

<margin>C</margin> he flourishes and lives, whenever he is in resource, but at other times he dies; and then he comes back to life again, because of his father's nature. That which is provided always flows away. Thus Eros is never in want, nor is he wealthy. And again, he is in the middle between wisdom and ignorance. For it is thus: no one of the gods philosophizes, nor desires to become wise—for he is wise. Nor if anyone else is wise, does he philosophize. Nor again do the ignorant philosophize, nor desire to become wise. For this very thing is the difficulty of ignorance: that one who is not beautiful or good or wise thinks himself sufficient. 

<margin>D</margin> Therefore, the one who does not think himself in need does not desire that which he does not think he lacks. "Who then," I said, "are the ones who philosophize, if neither the wise nor the ignorant?" "It is clear," she said, "even to a child by now, that it would be those between both of these, of whom Eros is one. For wisdom is among the most beautiful things. Eros is love for the beautiful. Thus it is necessary for Eros to be a philosopher; and being a philosopher, to be between the wise and the ignorant. And the cause for him of these things is his birth. For he is from a wise and resourceful father, and a mother not wise and poor. Such then is the nature of the spirit, friend Socrates. But what you thought Eros to be, you suffered nothing wonderful. You thought, as it seems to me, judging from what you say, that Eros was the beloved, not the lover. Because of these things, I think, Eros appeared all-beautiful to you. For the lovable is truly beautiful and delicate and perfect and blessed; but the lover has another such form, such as I have described." And I said, "So be it, stranger. 

<margin>E</margin> Since Eros is such, what use has he for men?" "This then, after these things," she said, "O Socrates, I will try to teach you. For Eros is such and was thus born. And he is of beautiful things, as you say. But if someone should ask us, 'What is it of which Eros is, O Socrates and Diotima?' Or more clearly I will ask, 'The one who loves beautiful things, what does he love?'" And I said, "To possess them." "But the answer still desires," she said, "a question such as this: 'What will be to that one to whom the beautiful things come?'" 

<margin>F</margin> I said I did not have it quite ready to answer this question. "But," she said, "just as if someone, changing and using the 'good' instead of the 'beautiful,' should ask: 'Come, Socrates, the one who loves good things, what does he love?'" "To possess them," I said. "And what will be to that one to whom the good things come?" "This I am better able to answer," I said, "that he will be happy. For by the possession of good things, the happy are happy. And there is no longer need to ask further, 'For what does he wish to be happy, the one who wishes it?' but the answer seems to have an end." "You say the truth," I said. "Now this wishing and this love, do you think it is common to all men, and that all wish for good things to be to them always? Or how do you say?" "Thus," I said, "it is common." "Why then," she said, "Socrates, do we not say that all men love, if indeed all love the same things, and always? But we say some love, and others not?" "I wonder," I said, "myself." "But do not wonder," she said. "For having taken away one certain form, we name it 'love,' applying the name of the whole; 

<margin>G</margin> but for the others, we use other names." "Such as what?" I said. "Such as this. You know that 'poetry' is something great. For the cause of anything going from not-being into being is entirely 'poetry.' So that the works under all the arts are 'poetry,' and the craftsmen of these are all 'poets.'" "You say the truth." "But nevertheless," she said, "you know that they are not called poets, but have other names; and from all 'poetry' one part having been set apart, that concerning music and measures, is called by the name of the whole. For this alone is called 'poetry'; and those having this part of poetry are 'poets.'" 

<margin>H</margin> "These things are true," I said. "So then also concerning love; the main point is every desire for good things and for being happy, the greatest and treacherous love for everyone. But those turning in many other ways toward it, either according to money-making or according to love of gymnastics or according to...

It further defines Love as the universal human desire for the permanent possession of the "good," which leads to happiness.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the speech of Diotima of Mantinea as recounted by Socrates. In the previous section, she explained the mythical parentage of Love (Eros) as the child of Resource and Poverty. Now, she begins to define the true object of Love—not merely the search for one's "other half," but the pursuit of the Good and the desire for immortality through "birth in beauty."</meta>

# THE SYMPOSIUM #

<margin>A</margin> ...those who devote themselves to gymnastics or philosophy are neither said to "love" in this specific sense, nor are they called "lovers." But those who direct their devotion toward one specific form of it take the name of the whole: they are said to practice love, to love, and to be lovers. "You seem to speak the truth," I said. "And yet," she continued, "a certain story is told that those who seek their other half are the ones who love. But my argument says that love is neither for the half nor for the whole, unless, my friend, it happens to be something good. For men are even willing to have their own feet and hands cut off if they believe their own limbs to be diseased. I do not think each person clings to what is their own, unless one calls the 'good' their own and 'belonging to themselves,' while calling the 'evil' something 'alien.' Indeed, there is nothing else that human beings love except the Good. Or does it seem otherwise to you?" "By Zeus, not to me," I replied.

<margin>B</margin> "Can we then simply say," she asked, "that humans love the Good?" "Yes," I said. "What then? Must we not add," she asked, "that they love the Good to be *theirs*?" "We must add that." "And not only to be theirs," she said, "but to be theirs *forever*?" "That must be added too." "In summary, then," she said, "Love is the desire for the perpetual possession of the Good." "You speak most truly," I said. "Since Love is always this," she said, "in what way do those who pursue it act? In what activity would their zeal and effort be called 'Love'? What does this work happen to be? Can you say?" "I would not be admiring your wisdom, Diotima," I replied, "nor would I be coming to you to learn these very things, if I already knew the answer." "Then I shall tell you," she said. "It is a birth in beauty <note>original: "tokos en kalō"</note>, both according to the body and according to the soul." "What you say requires a diviner to interpret," I said, "for I do not understand." "Then I shall

<margin>C</margin> speak more clearly," she said. "All human beings, Socrates, are pregnant <gloss>kyousi</gloss> both in body and in soul. When they reach a certain age, our nature desires to give birth. But it cannot give birth in ugliness; it can only do so in beauty. The union of man and woman is a birth. This is a divine matter; in a living creature that is mortal, this is the immortal element: conception and generation. These cannot happen in that which is discordant. And the ugly is discordant with everything divine, while the beautiful is harmonious. Therefore, Beauty is both the Fate <gloss>Moira</gloss> and the goddess of childbirth <gloss>Eileithyia</gloss> <note>Eileithyia was the Greek goddess who presided over labor; Diotima is identifying the very concept of Beauty as the force that assists at the "birth" of ideas or children.</note> for generation. Because of this, whenever

<margin>D</margin> that which is pregnant approaches the beautiful, it becomes gentle and, overflowing with joy, it spills forth and gives birth and generates. But when it approaches the ugly, it turns away, sullen and pained; it shrivels up, it recoils and does not generate, but painfully labors while retaining its burden. Hence, in one who is pregnant and already swelling, there is a great flutter of excitement concerning the beautiful, because the beautiful person releases the possessor from great labor-pains. For Love, Socrates," she said, "is not a love of the beautiful, as you think." "What is it then?" I asked. "It is a love of generation and birth in the beautiful." "So be it," I said. "It certainly is so," she said. "And why of generation? Because generation is, as far as is possible for a mortal, something eternal and immortal. For it is

<margin>E</margin> necessary to desire immortality along with the Good, based on what we have agreed, if indeed Love is the desire for the Good to be one's own forever. It follows from this argument that Love is also a desire for immortality." She taught me all these things whenever she spoke on matters of love. Once, she asked: "What do you think, Socrates, is the cause of this love and desire? Do you not notice how strangely all animals are affected when they desire to give birth—both those that walk and those that fly? They are all sickly and 'lovesick,' first regarding their mating with one another, and then regarding the nourishment of their offspring. Even the weakest are ready to fight the strongest on behalf of their young, and even to die for them, or to waste away with hunger so that they may feed them, doing everything else besides. You might suppose," she said,

<margin>F</margin> "that humans do these things out of reason. But what is the cause of animals being so 'lovesick'? Can you say?" And I said again that I did not know. Then she said, "Do you intend to ever become an expert in matters of love if you do not understand this? For this reason, Diotima," I said, "I have come to you, knowing that I need teachers. Tell me the cause of these things and of other matters related to love." "If then," she said, "you believe that Love is by nature directed toward that which we have often agreed upon, do not wonder. For here, mortal nature seeks, as far as it can, to exist forever and to be immortal. And it can do so only by this means: by generation, because it always leaves behind another young one in place of the old. For even during the time in which each living creature

<margin>G</margin> is said to live and to 'be the same'—for instance, a man is said to be the same from childhood until he becomes an old man—he never actually possesses the same things in himself, even though he is called the same. He is always becoming new while losing parts of himself: his hair, his flesh, his bones, his blood, and his entire body. And not only in his body, but also in his soul: his habits, character, opinions, desires, pleasures, pains, and fears—none of these things ever stay the same in any individual, but some are born while others perish. But what is even stranger than these is that our knowledge <gloss>epistēmai</gloss> also changes; not only does some knowledge arrive while other knowledge is lost to us—so that we are never the same even regarding our knowledge—but even each single piece of knowledge suffers the same fate. For what is called 'studying' <gloss>meletan</gloss> exists because knowledge is departing.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...whether they proceed from gymnastics or wisdom, they are neither called "to love" nor "lovers." But those who strive toward it according to a certain specific form take the name of the whole: namely, "love," "to love," and "lovers." "You seem to speak rightly." Some say that those who seek their other half are "loving." I, however, assert that love is neither for the half nor for the whole, unless in some way it is good. For men are even willing to cut off their own hands and feet if they seem to be an evil and a ruin to themselves. For no one loves their own things, unless perhaps one calls what is good "one's own and proper" and what is evil "alien."

<margin>B</margin> Since indeed humans love nothing else besides the good. Does it not seem so to you also? "Certainly so." "Should it then be said simply that humans love the good?" "Without a doubt." "Should we not add that they desire the good to be present to them?" "That should be added." "And not only to be present, but to be present *always*?" "Always." "Love is, therefore, in sum, the appetite by which one desires the good to be always his." "You speak all too truly." "Since universal love is always of this kind, can you say what condition of seeking is most important, or what manner of pursuit, and in what action or study it is properly called 'Love'?" "If I had been able to show that, Diotima, I never would have wondered at your wisdom, nor would I have come to you for the sake of learning." "Then I shall tell you. It is," I say, "a birth in beauty, as much according to the soul as according to the body." "There is need of a prophecy to understand what you say; for I do not perceive this at all." "I shall speak more plainly.

<margin>C</margin> Every human body, O Socrates, is pregnant and heavy, and so is every soul. And as soon as we reach a certain age, our nature desires to bring forth. But it cannot bring forth in that which is foul; it can only in the beautiful. Truly, from the congress of man and woman, offspring and birth proceed. This work is divine; and in the mortal animal itself, this is the immortal thing: namely, conception and generation. These things, in that

<margin>D</margin> which is out of proportion and discordant, cannot be fulfilled. But the foul is discordant with everything that is divine, whereas the beautiful is in harmony with the divine. Beauty itself is therefore the Fate <note>original: "Parca"</note> and the Goddess of Childbirth <note>original: "Lucina"</note> for generation. For this reason, whenever that which is pregnant clings to the beautiful, it throbs with joy, it is spread abroad with cheer and pleasure, and it both brings forth and generates. Conversely, when it approaches the foul, it is contracted by a certain sadness and pain; it is frightened and restrained, and it does not give birth, but suffers, retaining the fetus. Wherefore, that which has conceived, and is already luxuriant and panting with the maturity of generation, lingers mostly around the beautiful, since it is relieved from sharp anxiety thereby. For Love, Socrates, is not of the beautiful, as you suppose." "But of what?" I asked. "Of generation and birth in the beautiful." "In truth." "In truth," I say. "Why of generation? Because love is an eternal and immortal thing, just as generation is in the mortal itself. It is necessary

<margin>E</margin> to desire immortality along with the good, from those things which we have previously granted, since love is the appetite <margin>Love is the desire for immortality.</margin> by which each person desires the good to be always present to himself. From these things, it is concluded that love is also a desire for immortality." Diotima delivered all these things to me when she spoke of matters of love. Furthermore, she asked: "What do you think is the cause of this love and desire, O Socrates? Do you not see how heavily all living things are affected—both those that walk and those that fly—when they are carried toward generation with their whole impulse, and they are maddened by the glow of love? First, for the sake of generation, how vehemently they desire to mate. Then, how much they labor concerning the nourishment of those born. For the sake of these, even weak animals demand battle against the strongest, and are ready to perish for them, and to fail from hunger, provided they may nourish their children, and they boldly approach any other danger. Humans, perhaps, one might think do these things by a discourse of reason; but for the beasts, what is the cause of such an ardent love? Can you assign this?" "Not at all," I said. "Do you believe," she said, "that you will be skilled in matters of love while you are ignorant of these things?" "For this reason, O Dio-

<margin>G</margin> tima, as I said above, I flee to you, because I recognize that I need a teacher. I pray, therefore, that you bring forth the cause of these and other things which pertain to love." "If you believe that love is of that nature of which we have now often spoken, do not wonder. For from this, just as from the previous points, mortal nature strives by its strength to be always and immortal. But it attains this only by generation, because it always substitutes another young one in place of the old. Indeed, in that very time <margin>Constant change in the body and soul.</margin> in which each of the animals is said to live and to be 'the same'—as from childhood to old age, although it is called the same, yet it never contains the same things in itself, but is always made new, and puts off the old, according to the hair, flesh, bones, and blood, and the entire body. And not only in the body, but also

in the soul this happens. Manners, customs, opinions, desires, pleasures, pains, and fears are continually changed. Nor does any of those things remain the same and similar, but the prior ones are abolished, and new ones succeed. Moreover, what is more wonderful, knowledge likewise not only vanishes and arises, and we are not always the same according to our knowledge, but also every single branch of knowledge suffers the same. For what is called "to meditate" or "to study" is said as if knowledge had departed...

# PLATO #

<margin>A</margin> For forgetfulness is the departure of knowledge. Meditation, however, by creating a new memory to replace the one that is fading, preserves that knowledge so that it seems to remain the same. This is the way every mortal thing is preserved—not by remaining entirely the same forever, like the divine, but because that which ages and departs leaves behind something new and similar to itself. By this mechanism, Socrates, she said, that which is mortal—whether it be the body or anything else—shares in immortality. But that which is divine and immortal does so in another way. Therefore, you should not wonder if every living thing naturally prizes its own offspring. For it is for the sake of immortality that this devotion and love follows everyone. When I heard this, I was moved by wonder and said: "Is this truly the case, O most wise Diotima?" And she, as the <term>perfect sophists</term><note>original: "perfecti sophistæ" / "τέλειοι σοφισταὶ". Here meaning highly skilled teachers of wisdom.</note> are accustomed to do, said:
<margin>B</margin> "Know it for certain, Socrates. For if you would consider the love of glory that resides in men, you would wonder at your own lack of reason regarding what I have said, unless you realize how vehemently they are affected by the desire to become famous, and to lay up an immortal glory for all time. For the sake of this, even more than for their own children, they are ready to undergo dangers, spend their wealth, endure any labors, and even die. Do you think," she asked, "that Alcestis would have died for Admetus, or Achilles would have died after Patroclus, or your own
<margin>Iliad, Book 1</margin>
<margin>C</margin> Codrus<note>Alcestis, Achilles, and Codrus were legendary figures who sacrificed their lives for love, friendship, or their kingdom, respectively.</note> would have died before his time for the sake of his children's kingdom, if they did not think an immortal memory of their virtue would remain—the very memory we still hold of them today? Far from it," she said. "Rather, for the sake of immortal virtue and such noble reputation, I believe everyone does everything—and the better they are, the more they strive. For they love immortality. Those who are pregnant in body," she said, "turn rather toward women and are lovers in that way, seeking through the procreation of children to provide for themselves immortality, remembrance, and happiness for all time to come. But there are those who are pregnant in soul—for there are indeed," she said, "those who conceive in their souls even more than in their bodies that which is fitting for a soul
<margin>D</margin> to conceive and bring forth. And what is fitting? Wisdom and every other virtue. Of these, all the poets are the parents, as are those craftsmen who are called inventors. But by far the greatest and most beautiful form of wisdom," she said, "is that which concerns the ordering of cities and households, the name of which is <term>temperance</term><note>original: "temperantia" / "σωφροσύνη". This refers to self-control and moderation.</note> and justice. When someone, therefore, is pregnant in soul with these virtues from their youth—being divine—and their maturity arrives, they then desire to give birth and procreate. Thus, I believe, such a person wanders about seeking the beauty in which they might procreate. For they will never procreate in what is ugly. Therefore, they embrace beautiful bodies rather than ugly ones, since they are 'pregnant.' And if they happen upon a soul that is beautiful, noble, and gifted, they embrace the combination of the two most gladly. To such a person, they are immediately well-supplied with words about virtue—what a good man ought to be, and what he should practice—and they attempt to educate him. For by clinging to the beautiful
<margin>E</margin> and associating with it, they give birth to and procreate what they had long ago conceived, remembering it both when present and absent. And that which is brought forth they nourish together with the other. Consequently, such people share a much greater communion with one another than that of physical children, and a firmer friendship, because they have shared in more beautiful and more immortal children. Everyone would rather have such children born to them than human ones; looking at Homer and Hesiod and the other good poets, they envy the offspring they left behind, which provide their parents with immortal glory and memory, being such as they are. Or if you wish," she said, "look at what kind of 'children' Lycurgus<note>The legendary lawgiver of Sparta.</note> left behind in Sparta as saviors of Sparta
<margin>F</margin> and, one might say, of all Greece. Among you, Solon<note>The famous Athenian lawmaker.</note> is also honored for his 'birth' of the laws; and there are many other men in many other places, both among the Greeks and the barbarians, who have displayed many noble deeds and fathered every kind of virtue. Many temples and sacred rites have already been dedicated to them because of such children, but for human children, this has never yet happened to anyone. Into these 'mysteries' of love, Socrates, even you might perhaps be initiated. But as for the final and highest revelations, for the sake of which these other things exist—if one pursues the path correctly—I do not know if you would be able to perceive them. I will tell you, however," she said, "and I will omit no effort of mine. You, for your part, try to follow me as best you can. It is necessary," she said, "for one who proceeds correctly in this matter to begin while young by going toward beautiful bodies. And first, if his guide directs him rightly,
<margin>G</margin> he should love one body and there generate beautiful discourses. Then he must realize that the beauty in any one body is brother to the beauty in any other body. And if it is right to pursue beauty of form, it is a great folly not to consider the beauty in all bodies to be one and the same. Once he has realized this, he must become a lover of all beautiful bodies, and slacken this intense devotion toward one, looking down upon it and considering it a small thing. After this, he should consider the beauty in souls to be more honorable than that in the body. So, if someone has a soul that is decent but has only a small physical bloom, it should be enough for him to love and care for that person, and to give birth to and seek out the kind of discourses
<margin>H</margin> that will make young men better. This is so that he may be compelled to see the beauty found in customs and laws...
