<meta>This page continues Diotima’s instruction to Socrates. Having explained that love is the desire for immortality through procreation, she now describes the "Ladder of Love"—the spiritual ascent from the love of physical bodies to the contemplation of the divine and absolute Form of Beauty itself.</meta>

# SYMPOSIUM #

<margin>A</margin> ...be led on, so that he may see that all beauty is akin to itself, and thus consider beauty in the body a small thing. After observing customs and laws, he should be led to the sciences, so that he might behold the beauty of knowledge; and looking now toward beauty in its abundance, he may no longer be a slave, like a servant devoted to the beauty of a single youth, or a single man, or one single practice, and thus be petty and small-minded. Instead, turning toward the vast sea of beauty and contemplating it, he may give birth to many noble and magnificent discourses and thoughts in abundant philosophy; until, strengthened and nourished there, he perceives a single knowledge of such a kind, which is the knowledge of Beauty.

<margin>B</margin> Try now, she said, to pay attention as closely as possible. For whoever is led this far in the matters of love, beholding beautiful things in the right order and correctly, will at last, coming to the end of the things of love, suddenly perceive a certain Beauty, marvelous in its nature. This, Socrates, is the very reason for all the previous labors: first, it always exists, neither coming to be nor perishing, neither increasing nor diminishing. Further, it is not beautiful in one part and ugly in another; nor beautiful at one time and not at another; nor beautiful in one relation and ugly in another; nor beautiful here and ugly there; as if it were beautiful to some and ugly to others. Nor will Beauty appear to him as a face, or hands, or anything else of which the body partakes; nor as a certain discourse, nor a certain science. Nor is it found anywhere in something else, such as in a living creature, or in the earth, or in the sky, or in anything else; but it is itself, by itself, with itself, always uniform in its essence.

<margin>C</margin> All other beautiful things participate in it in such a way that, while they come to be and perish, it becomes neither more nor less, nor suffers any change.

<margin>D</margin> When someone, ascending from these things through the right kind of love for youths, begins to perceive that Beauty, he has almost reached the goal. For this is the right way to approach the matters of love, or to be led by another: beginning from these beautiful things for the sake of that Beauty, to ever ascend, as if using stairs, from one to two, and from two to all beautiful bodies, and from beautiful bodies to beautiful practices, and from beautiful practices to beautiful lessons, until from these lessons he arrives at that final lesson, which is the knowledge of nothing other than that Beauty itself, and he finally knows what Beauty is. In this part of life, my dear Socrates, said the <term>woman from Mantinea</term><note>Referring to Diotima, a priestess or seer who serves as Socrates' teacher in the dialogue.</note>, if anywhere else, life is worth living for a man, as he contemplates Beauty itself.

<margin>E</margin> If you should ever see it, you will judge it to be beyond gold and garments and beautiful boys and youths. When you see them now, you and many others are so overwhelmed that you are ready to stop eating and drinking, if only it were possible, just to gaze upon them and be with them. What then, she said, would we think if it were granted to someone to see Beauty itself—pure, clear, unmixed, not clogged with human flesh and colors and other such mortal trifles, but to be able to see the divine Beauty itself in its unique form?

<margin>F</margin> Do you think, she said, that a life spent looking there, contemplating it with that by which it must be seen, and being with it, would be a poor life? Or do you not consider that there alone it will be possible for him—seeing Beauty with the eye that can see it—to give birth not to images of virtue (since he is not touching an image), but to true virtues, since he is touching the Truth? And having given birth to and nourished true virtue, it becomes possible for him to become dear to God; and if any man can be, he too becomes immortal. These things, Phaedrus and the rest of you, Diotima said, and I am persuaded by them. Being persuaded, I try to persuade others as well, that to achieve this possession, human nature could not easily find a better helper than Love <note>original: "Ἔρως" (Eros)</note>.

<margin>G</margin> Therefore, I say that every man ought to honor Love; I myself honor the matters of love and practice them exceedingly, and I exhort others to do the same. Both now and always, I praise the power and courage of Love as much as I am able. This speech, Phaedrus, if you wish, consider spoken as a tribute to Love; but if not, call it whatever and however you please.

When Socrates had said these things, the others praised him, but Aristophanes attempted to say something, because Socrates had mentioned him in his speech. Suddenly, there was a loud knocking at the outer door, making a great noise as of revelers, and the sound of a flute-girl was heard. Agathon said, "Boys, won't you go see? And if it is one of our friends, invite him in; but if not, tell them we are no longer drinking, but are already resting." Not long after, they heard the voice of Alcibiades in the courtyard, very drunk and shouting loudly, asking where Agathon was and demanding to be led to Agathon. So the flute-girl and some of his other followers led him to them, and he stood at the doors, crowned with a thick wreath of ivy and violets, and having very many ribbons upon his head. He said, "Greetings, gentlemen. Will you receive a very drunk man as a companion in drinking, or shall we go away after crowning...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...should be led, and let him understand that all beauty is uniform and related to itself, so that he may hold the beauty of the body in small regard. After duties and laws, let him pass to the sciences, so that he may contemplate the beauty of knowledge; and while he beholds that which overflows with abundant beauty, let him no longer admire the appearance of a single boy like a slave: nor let him be content with the beauty of one man or one duty. For whoever fails in this is a meager and abject servant. But let him plunge into the deep sea of beauty, where by that very sight he may give birth to many noble and magnificent reasons and understandings in abundant philosophy, until there, confirmed and strengthened, he may now behold one such science, which is the science of beauty.

<margin>B</margin> Now apply the sharp edge of your mind to me as best you can. Whoever is led step by step through the matters of love this far, having beheld beautiful things in the right order, reaching now the end of the amorous affection, will suddenly behold a beauty wonderful in its nature. This is that for whose sake we underwent all the preceding labors. In the beginning, indeed, it always is; it does not come to be, nor perish, nor ever grow, nor decrease: moreover, it is not beautiful in this part and ugly in that, or beautiful then and not at all at another time. Nor is it beautiful in relation to this, but ugly in relation to that. Or beautiful here, ugly there, as if it were beautiful to some, but by no means to others. Nor again will beauty itself be imagined as a beautiful face, or beautiful hands, or any other thing of which the body is a participant. Nor like a certain speech, nor like a certain science. Nor will it be thought to lie in another, such as in an animal, or the earth, or the sky, or any other thing, but it is itself through itself with itself, always existing as uniform.

<margin>C</margin> All other things that are beautiful are beautiful by participation in it, under that condition, namely, that while others are born and perish, nothing is subtracted from it or added, nor does it incur any suffering.

<margin>D</margin> When, however, someone ascending from these things by rightly loving boys begins to contemplate that very beauty, he has almost reached the end. This is indeed to proceed correctly toward the matters of love, or to be led by another, when namely one begins to ascend from these beautiful things for the sake of that beauty, using them as if they were certain steps, and passing first from one to two, and from two to all bodies that are beautiful, and from these to all beautiful duties, and from beautiful duties turned toward beautiful doctrines, and finally coming from many doctrines to that doctrine which is of nothing else than that very beauty: and so at last he contemplates what beauty itself is. In this state of life especially, O friend Socrates, says that prophetess guest, if anywhere else, life must be lived by a man, namely, in beholding beauty itself.

<margin>E</margin> Which if you ever see, you will judge it more precious than gold, more than can be said, or decorated garments, or beautiful boys and youths. Whom now both you and many others, while you watch, are exceedingly amazed by, and if it were possible, you would choose to live among them always, neglecting food and drink. How happy do we think that spectacle would be, if it should happen that he beholds beauty itself, <margin>Cicero, Book 2 of De Officiis</margin><note>The margin notes a parallel thought in Cicero's "On Duties."</note> sincere, whole, pure, simple, not contaminated with human flesh, colors, or other mortal trifles, but beholds the divine beauty itself according to itself.

<margin>F</margin> Would you make little of such a life? Namely, of the man who looks up there, who beholds so noble a spectacle, who clings to it. Do you not consider that he, seeing beauty with that eye by which it can be perceived, will bring forth not images of virtue any longer, but virtues themselves: since he touches not a phantom, but the thing itself. And when he brings forth and nourishes true virtue, he will be made a friend to God, and if any other of men is, he especially exists as immortal. These things, O Phaedrus, and other guests, Diotima told. To which I give credit, and I strive to persuade others, that human nature cannot easily find anything more conducive to the possession of blessed immortality than legitimate love.

<margin>G</margin> Wherefore I judge that love should be honored by all men. Indeed, I cultivate the matters of love, and I exercise myself in them most highly, and I exhort others. And now indeed and always, according to the faculty of my wit, I praise the power and fortitude of love. This speech, O Phaedrus, if you wish, consider as a certain praise of love: but if not, if it pleases you to call it otherwise, call it so. When Socrates had said these things, all the rest approved; Aristophanes, however, was attempting to say something: who, when Socrates was speaking, had made mention of his place at a certain point. But suddenly the door of the vestibule was struck and gave a sound, and the cry of revelling youths and a flute-player was heard. Then Agathon said, "Servants, see who has arrived, and if any friend of ours is among them, invite them to us. If none, announce that we are no longer drinking, but are now resting." But a little after, they heard the voice of Alcibiades, insulting in his drunkenness, and crying out loudly in the vestibule.

<margin>H</margin> And asking where Agathon was, and ordering that he be led to Agathon. Therefore, the flute-player and other companions led him, and they stood at the doors of the vestibule, crowned with a certain wreath of ivy and thick violets, and with many ribbons surrounding his head, and shouting, "I bid you hail, men; receive a very drunk man as a fellow-drinker. Or let us go away, having crowned Agathon..."

<meta>This page continues the narrative of Plato’s Symposium. On the previous page, Socrates finished recounting Diotima’s speech on the "Ladder of Love." Now, the scene shifts as Alcibiades, a charismatic but volatile Athenian statesman, bursts into the gathering while intoxicated.</meta>

# PLATO #

<margin>A</margin>
...only to crown him—the very reason I have come. Yesterday, indeed, I was unable to be present; but today I have come, wearing these ribbons on my head, so that from my own head I might bind the head of the wisest and most beautiful man, if I may put it that way. Will you laugh at me as if I am drunk? Even if you laugh, I know for certain that I speak the truth. Tell me clearly: will you permit me to enter on these terms? Will you drink with me, or not? Here, everyone shouted and ordered him to enter and take a seat. Agathon also called him over. His companions then led him in. While he was removing the ribbons to crown Agathon’s head, he held them before his eyes and did not see Socrates, even though he was right in his sight. He sat down next to Agathon, in the middle between him and Socrates, for Socrates had made room for him. When he had sat down, he congratulated Agathon and crowned him.

<margin>B</margin>
Agathon said, "Boys, take off Alcibiades' shoes, so that he may recline as the third person among us." Alcibiades replied, "By all means," and asked who the third guest was. Turning around, he saw Socrates, and jumping up, he cried, "By Hercules! What is this? Are you sitting here again, Socrates, lying in wait for me? You are always doing this—suddenly appearing where I least expect to find you. And why have you come here now? Why are you sitting here instead of next to Aristophanes <note>Aristophanes was the famous comic playwright of Athens, also a guest at this banquet.</note>, or someone else who is ridiculous and wants to be seen? You have cleverly devised a way to sit here next to the most beautiful of the guests!"

<margin>C</margin>
Socrates, turning to Agathon, said, "See, Agathon, if you can help me in some way. For the love of this man has turned out to be no light matter for me. Since the time I began to love him, I am no longer permitted to look at or speak to any beautiful person; this jealous man—seized by amorous suspicion and envy—does extraordinary things, insulting me and barely restraining himself from laying hands on me. See to it then that he does not do such a thing now, but reconcile us; or, if he tries to use force, help me. For I greatly fear his madness and his amorous impulses."

<margin>D</margin>
To this, Alcibiades said, "There can be no reconciliation between me and you, but I will take my revenge on you for this another time. For now, Agathon, give me some of those ribbons so that I may also decorate this man's marvelous head, lest he be angry with me for crowning you and not him—the man who conquers all people in speech, not just recently as you did, but always." Taking the ribbons, he crowned Socrates and sat down. Once seated, he said, "Come now, gentlemen, you seem too sober to me; I cannot allow this. You must drink, for that is what we agreed. Therefore, I appoint myself the ruler of the drinking <note>original: 'archon', the person chosen at a Greek symposium to decide how much wine everyone should drink.</note> until you have drunk enough."

<margin>E</margin>
"Agathon, order someone to bring a large cup, if there is one. But there is no need; boy, bring that wine-cooler instead!" He saw that it held more than eight *cotylae* <margin>* Cotylae, or Heminas.</margin> <note>A 'cotyla' or 'hemina' was a Greek unit of volume, roughly equal to half a pint. This vessel held about four liters.</note>. When he had filled the vessel, he drank it first, then ordered it to be poured for Socrates, saying, "Against Socrates, fellow guests, this trick gains me nothing. No matter how much someone orders him to drink, he will drain it, and you will never see him drunk." When the boy had poured it, Socrates drank.

<margin>F</margin>
Then Eryximachus <note>The doctor of the group, who previously suggested they give speeches instead of just drinking.</note> said, "What are we doing, Alcibiades? Are we neither to say anything over the cup, nor sing, but simply gulp it down as if we were parched?" To him, Alcibiades replied, "Greetings, excellent Eryximachus, son of an excellent and most prudent father." "Greetings to you as well," Eryximachus answered, "but what should we do?" "Whatever you command," said Alcibiades, "for we must obey you." <margin>Iliad 11</margin> <note>original: "Iliad. λ." quoting Homer: "A physician is worth many other men."</note> "Command, then, whatever you please." "Listen then," said Eryximachus. "Before you entered, it was decided that each person present, starting from the right, should praise Love to the best of his ability. We have each had our turn; but since you have not spoken and have already drunk, it is only right that you speak. When you have spoken, you may then command Socrates to do whatever you wish."

<margin>G</margin>
"Socrates likewise will command the one to his right, and so on for the rest." "You speak well, Eryximachus," said Alcibiades, "but it is not fair to expect a drunken man to match his words against the speeches of sober men. But, my dear friend, has Socrates persuaded you of anything he just said? Or do you know that the truth is entirely the opposite? For if I praise anyone—whether a god or another man—in his presence, he will not keep his hands off me." "Keep a civil tongue!" Socrates said. "By Neptune," replied Alcibiades, "say nothing to the contrary; for I will praise no one else while you are present." "Do that, then," said Eryximachus, "if you wish—praise Socrates." "What do you say?" asked Alcibiades. "Does it seem right, Eryximachus, that I should fall upon this man and take my revenge before you all?" "What are you thinking?" said Socrates. "Will you praise me through some ridiculous stories? What will you do?" "I will speak the truth," said Alcibiades. "Will you allow it?" "Indeed," said Socrates, "I not only allow you to speak the truth, I command it." "I shall obey," said Alcibiades, "as gladly as I can. But you must watch, and if I say anything that is not true, interrupt me as you please and prove me a liar. For I will not lie willingly. And do not be surprised if I recall things as they come to mind, out of order. For it is not easy for a man in my condition to recount your strange habits eloquently and in a precise sequence. I shall attempt, gentlemen, to praise Socrates through images. He will perhaps suspect that I am doing this for a laugh; but the image will be for the sake of the truth, not for mockery."

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
...only to crown him, which is why I came yesterday. For I tell you, yesterday I was not able to arrive, but now I have come with ribbons on my head, so that from my own head I might bind the head of the wisest and most beautiful man—if I may say so. Will you laugh at me as if I am drunk? Even if you laugh, I still know well that I speak the truth. But tell me right now, shall I come in on these terms? Will you drink with us, or not? Then everyone cheered and told him to enter and recline; and Agathon called him. And he came, led by his men; and while taking off the ribbons to bind him, he had them before his eyes and did not see Socrates, but sat down by Agathon, in the middle of Socrates and him. For Socrates had moved so that he might sit there. As he sat down, he greeted Agathon and bound him with ribbons.

<margin>B</margin>
Then Agathon said, "Boys, take off Alcibiades’ shoes, so that he may recline as a third." "By all means," said Alcibiades, "but who is this third drinking companion of ours?" And as he turned around, he saw Socrates; and seeing him, he jumped up and said, "O Hercules, what is this? Socrates here, lying in wait for me again? You were reclining here, just as you are used to appearing suddenly where I least thought you would be. And now why have you come? And why have you reclined here again? Not by Aristophanes, nor by anyone else who is and wants to be ridiculous; but you have managed to recline by the most beautiful of those inside."

<margin>C</margin>
And Socrates said, "Agathon, see if you can defend me. For my love for this man has become no small matter. From that time when I fell in love with him, it is no longer possible for me even to look at or talk to any beautiful person, or else he, being jealous and envious, does amazing things, and insults me, and hardly keeps his hands off me. See then that he does not do something now; but reconcile us, or if he tries to use force, defend me. For I greatly dread his madness and obsessive love."

<margin>D</margin>
"But," said Alcibiades, "there is no reconciliation for me and you. But I will punish you for these things later; for now, Agathon," he said, "give me some of the ribbons, so that I may bind this man’s amazing head—the head of the most temperate man—and so he may not blame me that I bound you, but did not bind him, who conquers all people in speeches, not just the day before yesterday like you, but always." And at the same time, taking the ribbons, he bound Socrates and reclined. When he had reclined, he said, "Well then, gentlemen. For you seem to me to be sober. This must not be allowed to you, but you must drink; for this was agreed upon by us. I therefore choose myself as the ruler of the drinking for you, until you have drunk enough."

<margin>E</margin>
"But let Agathon bring whatever large cup there is. Or rather, no need; but boy," he said, "bring that wine-cooler." Seeing that it held more than eight *cotylae*, he filled it, and first drank it himself, then ordered it to be poured for Socrates; and at the same time he said, "Toward Socrates, gentlemen, my trick is nothing. For however much one orders him to drink, he drinks that much, and will never be any the more drunk." So, when the boy poured it, Socrates drank.

<margin>F</margin>
Then Eryximachus said, "How then, Alcibiades, shall we do it? Shall we say nothing over the cup, nor sing? But simply drink like those who are thirsty?" Then Alcibiades said, "O Eryximachus, best son of the best and most temperate father, greetings." "And you," said Eryximachus, "but what shall we do?" "Whatever you command. For we must obey you. For a physician is worth many other men. Command, then, whatever you wish." "Listen then," said Eryximachus, "before you entered, it seemed best to us that each one in turn from left to right should speak about Love as beautifully as he could, in praise. All the rest of us have spoken; but since you have not spoken, and have drunk, it is right that you speak; and having spoken, command Socrates whatever you wish; and he the one to his right, and so the others."

<margin>G</margin>
"But," said Alcibiades, "O Eryximachus, you speak well; but to set a drunken man’s words against the speeches of sober men is not equal. And at the same time, my dear man, does Socrates persuade you of any of the things he just said? Or do you know that it is all the opposite of what he was saying? For this man, if I praise anyone in his presence, either a god or another man except him, will not keep his hands off me." "Will you not be quiet?" said Socrates. "By Poseidon," said Alcibiades, "say nothing against this; for I would not praise a single other person while you are present." "Then do so," said Eryximachus, "if you wish, praise Socrates." "How do you mean?" said Alcibiades. "Does it seem necessary, Eryximachus, to set upon the man and take revenge before you?" "You," said Socrates, "what do you have in mind? Will you praise me to make me ridiculous? Or what will you do?" "I will tell the truth. See if you allow it." "But indeed," he said, "I allow the truth, and command you to speak." "I will not delay," said Alcibiades. "And yet, do this: if I say anything not true, interrupt in the middle if you wish, and say that I am lying in this. For I will not lie willingly. If, however, as I remember I say one thing from one place and another from another, do not wonder. For it is not easy for someone in this state to count out your abundance of strange ways. I will attempt, gentlemen, to praise Socrates through images. It will be perhaps for the sake of making him ridiculous; but the image will be for the sake of the truth, not the ridiculous."

<meta>This page continues Alcibiades’ speech from Plato's *Symposium*. Having already disrupted the party and crowned Agathon, Alcibiades now turns his attention to Socrates. He begins a famous "praise" of Socrates that is both an admiration of his character and a confession of the emotional turmoil Socrates causes him.</meta>

# THE BANQUET #

I say that he is most like those statues of Silenus <note>Silenus was a rustic spirit of the forest, often depicted as a plump, elderly, and drunken satyr. These statues were hollow and could be opened.</note> found in the workshops of sculptors and stone-cutters, which the craftsmen make holding pipes or flutes; when they are opened in the middle, they are found to contain images of gods inside. And I say further that he is like the satyr Marsyas <note>Marsyas was a satyr who challenged the god Apollo to a musical contest. He was known for his incredible skill on the flute.</note>. Now, Socrates, even you would not dispute that you are like these figures in your outward appearance; but listen next to how you resemble them in other ways as well.

<margin>B</margin>
Are you not an insolent fellow? If you do not admit it, I will provide witnesses. Are you not a flute-player much more wonderful than Marsyas? He used to charm men through instruments by the power of his mouth—and even now, anyone who plays his music does the same. For the melodies that Olympus <note>A legendary musician said to be the pupil of Marsyas.</note> played, I say were taught to him by Marsyas. Those melodies, whether played by a skilled flute-player or a lowly flute-girl, are the only ones that truly possess the soul, revealing those who stand in need of the gods and sacred rites because the music itself is divine. You differ from him only in this: that you achieve the exact same effect with nothing but plain words, without any instruments. Certainly, when we hear any other great orator speaking, we hardly care at all; but when someone hears you, or even your words repeated by another—even if the speaker is quite poor at it—whether the listener is a woman, a man, or a youth, we are struck with awe and possessed. For my part, gentlemen, if I did not fear I would seem completely drunk, I would swear to you under oath what I have felt from this man’s words, and what I feel even now. For when I hear him, my heart leaps far more than the hearts of those in a religious frenzy <note>original: "Corybantes," followers of the goddess Cybele known for their wild, ecstatic dancing.</note>, and tears pour from me because of his words. I see many others suffering the same experience.

<margin>C</margin>
When I heard Pericles <note>The famous and powerful leader of Athens' Golden Age.</note> and other fine orators, I thought they spoke well, but I felt nothing like this; my soul was not thrown into turmoil, nor did it chafe at the thought that I was living like a slave. But by this Marsyas here, I have often been so affected that it seemed my life was not worth living in its current state. You will not say this is untrue, Socrates. Even now, I am conscious that if I chose to lend him my ears, I could not resist, but would suffer the same things again. For he compels me to admit that, while I am lacking in many things, I neglect myself while I attend to the affairs of the Athenians.

<margin>D</margin>
So, by force, I stop up my ears as if to escape the Sirens <note>Mythical creatures whose song lured sailors to their doom; Odysseus famously plugged his ears with wax to survive them.</note> and I run away, so that I do not grow old sitting here at his side. I suffer a feeling toward this man alone that no one would believe I possessed: a sense of shame. He is the only person who makes me feel ashamed. For I am conscious that I cannot argue against him or say that I should not do what he commands; yet when I leave him, I am overcome by the desire for the honors given by the crowd. So I play the runaway and flee from him; and whenever I see him, I am ashamed of what I have confessed. Often, I would even be glad to see him no longer among the living; yet if that were to happen, I know well that I would be much more grieved. Thus, I do not know how to deal with this man. And so, I and many others have suffered such things from the "flute-playing" of this satyr. But hear from me how like he is to the things I compared him to, and what a marvelous power he has.

<margin>E</margin>
For you should know well that none of you truly knows this man; but I will reveal him, since I have begun. You see that Socrates is transitionally attracted to beautiful people, and he is always with them and struck by them. Furthermore, he pretends to be ignorant of everything and to know nothing. Is this not his outward appearance? It is very much like a Silenus-statue. For this is the outer casing he has wrapped around himself, just like the carved Silenus.

<margin>F</margin>
But when he is opened up, fellow drinkers, how much temperance <note>original: "sophrosyne," a Greek term for self-control, moderation, and excellence of character.</note> do you think is inside? Know that he cares nothing for someone’s beauty—he despises it more than anyone could believe—nor for their wealth, nor for any other honor that the crowd considers a blessing. He considers all these possessions to be worth nothing, and he thinks we are nothing; I tell you, he spends his whole life being ironic <note>original: "eiron"—a person who downplays their own abilities or knowledge to provoke others to think.</note> and playing with people. But when he is serious and opened up, I do not know if anyone has seen the images inside. I, however, have seen them once; and they seemed to me so divine and golden and beautiful and wonderful, that I felt I must do whatever Socrates commanded.

<margin>G</margin>
Thinking that he was serious about my own youthful beauty, I thought this was a stroke of luck and a wonderful piece of good fortune; it seemed I had the opportunity, by gratifying Socrates, to hear everything he knew. For I was remarkably proud of my beauty. With this in mind, I once invited him to come along, and when I was alone with him—for I used to never be without a companion—I sent the companion away and stayed alone with him. I must tell you the whole truth. Pay attention; and if I lie, Socrates, you refute me. For I was alone with him, gentlemen, and I thought he would immediately speak to me the way a lover speaks to his beloved in private, and I was glad. But none of this happened at all; instead, he conversed with me as he usually did, and after spending the day with me, he went away. After this, I challenged him to exercise with me, and I exercised with him, thinking I would achieve something there. So he exercised with me and wrestled with me many times when no one else was present. And what can I say? I gained nothing by it. Since I had no success even then, I decided I must attack the man with stronger measures...

<column-break/>

<margin>See regarding this in the "Sileni of Alcibiades" by Erasmus. <note>Alcibiades’ comparison of Socrates to Silenus became a famous theme in Renaissance literature, particularly in the writings of Desiderius Erasmus.</note></margin>
I present Socrates as very similar to those Sileni, who are fashioned by sculptors sitting among other images, such that they hold pipes or flutes. If they are divided in two, they are found to have the images of the gods inside. I also say he is similar to the satyr Marsyas. And that in appearance you are very like them, O Socrates, not even you would deny. But that in other ways also you have a similarity to them, listen now. Are you not cheeky and insolent? If you do not confess it, I will bring forth witnesses. Are you not a flute-player? And a flute-player far more excellent than Marsyas. For he used to soothe men with certain instruments by the power of his mouth, and even now, if anyone uses his melodies—for I say it was Marsyas who taught the melodies that Olympus played. Therefore, whether a good man or a poor flute-girl uses his harmony, it alone draws souls, and because it is divine, it shows who has need of the gods and their mysteries. You, however, differ from him only in this: that without any instrument, with bare words, you achieve this same thing. We certainly, whenever we hear another person reporting the words of someone else, even a very good orator, we care nothing for them, so to speak. But when someone hears you, or hears your words reported by any other—even if the person reporting them is unskilled, and whether a man or a woman or a youth hears them—we are stunned, and gripped in our minds. Indeed, unless I suspected that I might seem too drunk, I would affirm with an oath what things have happened to me from this man's words, and happen even now. For whenever I hear him, much more than those who are carried away in the manner of the Corybantes, my heart is stirred within me at his words, and I shed tears, and I see this same thing happening to many others. And when I heard Pericles and other good orators, they seemed to me to speak excellently, but nothing like this happened to me, nor was my mind stirred, nor did it condemn itself as if living like a slave. But I am often swayed by our Marsyas here, so that I think I must in no way live in this state of life. Do not deny these things, O Socrates. Furthermore, I know for certain, if at this moment I were willing to lend him my ears, I could not endure it, but those same things would happen to me. For he compels me to confess that, though I myself am lacking in many things, yet I neglect myself and care for the business of the Athenian people. Therefore, by force, as if plugging my ears against the Sirens, I flee from him and avoid him, lest I grow old sitting by him. Moreover, I suffer toward him alone what no one would believe: that I am held back by shame and modesty before anyone. Yet I fear him alone. For I am conscious that I cannot defend myself, nor deny that I should do what he orders; but when I depart from him, I am overcome by popular ambition. Therefore I flee from him and avoid him, and whenever I look upon him, shame takes hold of me because I have not kept my promises, so that I often wish he would depart from this life; but then again, if that should happen, I know I would endure it with far more difficulty. Therefore, I do not know where to turn or how to deal with him. And such things have happened to me and many others from the melodies of this satyr. But hear the rest, how he is like those to whom I said he was similar, and behold what a wonderful power he has. Know that none of you knows Socrates. But I will show you, since I have already begun to speak. Do you see how vehemently Socrates is affected toward the beautiful? How he is always among them and is stunned? He ignores everything, he knows nothing. Certainly, this outward form is very like a Silenus. Know then that he is clothed in this outward form of habit like a certain carved Silenus. But inside, if he were opened, O men of the feast, what wonderful purity and integrity is within! He does not value the beauty of anyone's body at all, nor riches, nor honors, nor other things which the common people admire, but he despises all these things far more than can be believed and considers them as nothing. Wherefore, I tell you that we are of no account to him; yet he ironically pretends otherwise and never ceases to joke openly about these things. But when he acts seriously and is opened inside, I do not know whether any of you has ever looked upon the divine images that lie hidden within. I certainly have seen them at times, and they seemed to me so divine, and golden, and beautiful, and wonderful, that I thought it in no way right to act otherwise than as Socrates commands. I once, O men of the feast, thinking that Socrates was truly delighted by my appearance, thought I had found a wonderful and happy occasion for what I was aiming at. Indeed, I decided to gratify Socrates so that he might communicate to me whatever he knew. For I thought my beauty was something great and wonderful, and I trusted in it very much. And since I had never before been accustomed to speak with him without a companion, once, having dismissed my companion, I remained alone with him. All truths must be opened to you. Listen, I pray. If I lie, Socrates, refute it yourself. I remained indeed, O men of the feast, alone with him, hoping he would say the same things to me that lovers are accustomed to say to their beloved when they are alone. Which...

---

hope made me very glad, but none of these things was done, but as he was accustomed, when he had discussed things until evening, he went away. After this, I summoned him to the wrestling ground <term>palaestra: a public place for wrestling and athletics in ancient Greece</term> and exercised with him, as if I were going to achieve something in this. So we often exercised gymnastics together alone. Why is there need for many words? Nothing succeeded for me. But after this had in no way succeeded, I decided I must set more difficult traps for this man...

<meta>This page continues Alcibiades’ speech from the *Symposium*. Following his description of Socrates as a Silenus statue, Alcibiades now recounts a specific, failed attempt to seduce Socrates, using it to illustrate Socrates' extraordinary self-control and "inner beauty."</meta>

# OF PLATO #

I decided to make my move and not desist from what I had begun. Listen to how intensely I laid snares for him. I invited him to dinner, just as a lover might lay snares for the object of his affection. At first, he did not easily comply, but eventually, he gave in. He came: but having finished his food, he rose to leave immediately. At that time, held back by a sense of shame, I allowed him to go. But laying even more intense snares, I dragged out our conversation after dinner long into the night; and when he wished to depart, I used the lateness of the hour as an excuse and forced him to stay. He rested, therefore, on the couch next to me, the same one upon which he had sat for dinner; and no one else slept there that night besides us. What has been said so far could be told anywhere without a blush. But as for what follows, you shall not hear it <margin>Proverb.</margin> until I have invoked that proverb: "Wine—both with children and without children—is truthful." <note>original: "Vinum & cum pueritia, & sine pueritia est veridicum." A variation of "In vino veritas." In the Greek, it refers to the saying "Wine and children tell the truth."</note>
<margin>B</margin>
Indeed, it seems unjust that one who praises Socrates should pass over his proud and unconquerable deed in silence. Moreover, I am affected just like a man who has been bitten by a viper. They say that such a man is unwilling to reveal what his suffering is like except to those who have been bitten similarly, as if they alone—not being ignorant of the pain—would forgive him if, compelled by the agony, he should not hesitate to say or do anything. I, therefore, having been gripped by the even more vehement bite of philosophy—which is the sharpest of all—whether it be in the heart, or the soul, or whatever it should be called, have been wounded by a passion for philosophical discourse. These words bite more sharply than a viper and seize upon a young soul that is not entirely without talent, compelling it to do and say whatever may come. And seeing men like Phaedrus, Agathon, Eryximachus, <margin>C</margin> Pausanias, Aristodemus, Aristophanes, and finally Socrates himself, and the rest (for you have all shared with me in this philosophical madness and Bacchic frenzy), listen all of you. For you will give me pardon for the things I did then and for what I say now. But as for the servants, and any other profane or rustic person who may be present, let them stop up their ears.

When the lamp was extinguished and the servants were gone, it seemed to me, O fellow guests, that I should no longer hide or delay, but frankly open up what I felt. And so I nudged him and said, "Socrates, are you asleep?" "Not yet," he replied. "Do you know what I have been thinking?" I asked. "About <margin>D</margin> what?" he said. "You seem to me," I replied, "to be the only lover worthy of me, yet you seem too modest in your love. For my part, since things are as they are, I would consider it foolish <insert>not</insert> to gratify you in this, and in all other things, whether you might need my possessions or my friends. To me, nothing is more important than that I should become the best man possible. In this, no one can help me more than you. I would fear the reproaches of the wise far more for not obeying such a man, than I would fear the words of the foolish for obeying him." When he heard this, hiding behind his usual irony, he replied: "O friend Alcibiades, you seem truly to be no small or worthless man, if what you say about me is true, <margin>E</margin> and if there is in me some power through which you might be made better. You must see in me a wonderful beauty, far surpassing your own form. If, recognizing this, you seek to share it with me and to exchange beauty for beauty, you are trying to gain much more than I am, like a moneylender. For you are attempting to gain the truth of beautiful things in exchange for a mere reputation, and to receive gold for brass. <note>original: "aurum pro aurichalco." A reference to Homer's *Iliad*, where Glaucus foolishly exchanges his gold armor for the bronze armor of Diomedes.</note> But, O blessed one, look more carefully, lest my condition escapes you, since I am worth nothing. The eye of the mind begins to see more sharply only when the eye of the body begins to lose its bloom. But you are still far from that age." When I had heard this, I said, "My situation is as I have stated. I do not have one thing on my lips and another in my heart. You, then, decide what you think will be better for both you and me." "Well said," <margin>F</margin> he replied. "Therefore, in the future, we shall consult together and do what seems best for both of us, both in this and in all other matters." When I had heard and said these things, and having launched them like a spear, I thought I had wounded him. Rising, and not allowing him to speak a word further, I wrapped him in this cloak you see—for it was winter—and lying down under his old tattered coat, I threw my arms around this truly divine and marvelous man, and I lay there the whole night. These things, I know, you will not deny, O Socrates. Yet he entirely spurned my beauty, which I most relied upon, as if it were ridiculous, and he proudly despised it. I call all the gods and goddesses to witness, O judges—for you are the <margin>G</margin> judges of Socratic pride—that I rose from that bed having slept with Socrates no differently than if I had been lying with my father or an older brother.

What kind of mind do you think I had after this? I felt myself despised, yet I admired his nature, his temperance, and his courage, having found such a man as I never believed I would encounter in terms of wisdom and endurance. Consequently, I could find no reason to be angry with him or to leave him, nor could I find any lures by which I might win him over. For I knew that he was harder to conquer with money than <margin>H</margin> Ajax was with steel; and that by which I had hoped he would be most easily ensnared had failed me. I was at my wit's end, and I went about more enslaved by this man than anyone has ever been by another. All these things happened to me previously; and after this, it happened that we served together in the campaign at Potidaea...

<column-break/>

...I had attempted this, but now you must know what the matter is. I had besieged <margin>B</margin> him just as a lover laying snares for his beloved. Yet he did not quickly yield to this; however, in time he did. When he arrived, having dined with me, he wished to depart. And then, being ashamed, I let him go. But having laid snares again, after we had dined, I continued our discourse far into the night. And when he wished to go, I made the excuse that it was late and forced him to stay. He rested then on the bed next to mine, on which he had dined; and no one else was sleeping in the room but us. Up to this point in the story, it would be fine to speak to anyone. But as for what follows, you would not hear me speaking of it, if first of all, as the saying goes, "wine—both with children and without children—were not truthful." Furthermore, it seems to me unjust to pass over a proud deed of Socrates in silence when I have come here to praise him. Moreover, I suffer the same condition as one who has been bitten by a viper. For they say that one who has suffered this does not wish to tell what it was like except to those who have also been bitten, as they are the only ones who will understand and forgive him if he dared to do or say anything under the pressure of the pain. I, therefore, having been bitten by something more painful, and the most painful thing by which one could be bitten—for I have been struck and bitten in the heart, or the soul, or whatever it ought to be named, by the words of philosophy, which take hold more fiercely than a viper when they seize a young soul that is not untalented, and they make one do and <margin>C</margin> say anything whatsoever—and seeing Phaedrus, Agathon, Eryximachus, Pausanias, Aristodemus, and Aristophanes. And what need is there even to mention Socrates himself and the others? For you have all participated in the madness and Bacchic frenzy of philosophy. Therefore you shall all hear. For you will forgive both what was done then and what is said now. But as for the servants, and if there is anyone else profane and rustic, put very great gates upon your ears. For when the lamp was extinguished and the boys were outside, it seemed to me that I should not be subtle with him, but should say freely what I thought. And I said, nudging him, "Socrates, are you sleeping?" "Not at all," he said. "Do you know what I have decided?" "What is it especially?" he asked. "You seem to me," <margin>D</margin> I said, "to have been my only worthy lover; yet you seem to me to hesitate to mention it to me. But I, feeling this way, think it is very foolish of you not to gratify me in this and in anything else you might need from my property or my friends. For to me nothing is more important than becoming as good as possible. And I think I can have no more powerful helper in this than you. I would be much more ashamed before the wise for not gratifying such a man, than I would be before the many and the foolish for gratifying him." And when he heard me, he spoke very ironically and in his very usual manner, "O friend Alcibiades, you are likely not a worthless man indeed, if what you say about me happens to be true, and if there is in me some <margin>E</margin> power through which you might become better; for you must be seeing an incredible beauty in me, far different from the comeliness found in you. If indeed, seeing this, you are attempting to share it with me and to exchange beauty for beauty, you are intending to get much more than your fair share of me. You are attempting to acquire the truth of beautiful things in exchange for a reputation, and you are truly intending to exchange 'gold for bronze.' But, O blessed one, look more closely, lest I escape your notice as being nothing. Indeed, the sight of the mind begins to see sharply when the peak of the eyes' strength begins to fail; but you are still far from these things." And hearing this, I said, "As for my part, these things are as I have said; none of them have been said otherwise than as I intended. But you yourself deliberate on what you think is best for you and me." "Well," he said, "you <margin>F</margin> say this well. For in the time to come we shall deliberate and do what appears to us to be best for us both in these and in all other things." I, having heard and said these things, and having launched them like a bolt, thought I had wounded him. And rising up, and not allowing him to say anything more, I wrapped my own cloak around him (for it was winter) and lying down under his threadbare coat, throwing my arms around this truly divine and marvelous man, I lay there the whole night. And you will not say, O Socrates, that I am lying about these things either. But although I did these things, he so far triumphed over me and looked down upon and mocked my youthful beauty and <margin>G</margin> insulted it—and yet I thought that was something, O men of the jury. For you are the jury of Socratic pride. For know well, by the gods and goddesses, that I rose from my sleep with Socrates having slept no more remarkably than if I had slept with my father or an older brother. After this, what kind of mind do you think I had? On the one hand, I felt I had been dishonored, but on the other, I marveled at this man's nature, his temperance, and his courage, having met a man such as I never thought I would meet for wisdom and for endurance. So that I had no way to be angry, yet I was deprived of his company; nor did I have any means by which I might win him over. For I knew well that in terms of money <margin>H</margin> he was much more invulnerable than Ajax was to steel; and the only thing by which I thought he might be caught had escaped me. I was at a loss, and I went about enslaved by this man as no one ever was by any other. For all these things had happened to me before; and after this, the campaign at Potidaea happened to us...

<summary>Alcibiades recounts his failed attempt to seduce Socrates, describing how Socrates rejected his physical beauty in favor of seeking "true beauty." This story serves to illustrate Socrates' incredible self-control and his belief that philosophical wisdom is far more valuable than physical attraction.</summary>
<keywords>Alcibiades, Socrates, seduction, self-control, temperance, gold for bronze, philosophy, Potidaea, beauty, truth</keywords>

--- Page 367 ---
<meta>This page continues Alcibiades’ speech from the *Symposium*. Having previously described Socrates’ external appearance as a grotesque Silenus statue that hides divine images within, Alcibiades now recounts his personal experiences with Socrates on military campaigns to illustrate his incredible physical and mental endurance.</meta>

# THE BANQUET #

<margin>A</margin>But we were together in this way and took our meals together there. First of all, in his endurance of hardships, he surpassed not only me but everyone else. Whenever we were cut off somewhere—as often happens on a campaign—and were forced to go without food, the others were nothing compared to him in their ability to endure it. Again, in times of feasting, he was the only one who truly seemed to enjoy himself; and among other things, if he was ever compelled to drink, he conquered everyone at it. And what is most marvelous of all, no human being has ever seen Socrates drunk. This, I believe, will be proven shortly. <margin>B</margin>Furthermore, regarding his endurance of winter (for the winters there are terrible), he performed wonders. Once, during a most severe frost, when everyone else either stayed inside or, if they did go out, were bundled up in an extraordinary amount of clothing, with their feet bound and wrapped in felt and sheepskins, Socrates went out among them wearing only the same cloak he was accustomed to wearing before. Barefoot, he marched across the ice more easily than the others did in their shoes. The soldiers looked at him suspiciously, thinking he was showing contempt for them. But enough of that. There is another thing this hardy man did and endured there once on campaign that is well worth hearing. <margin>C</margin>Having been struck by some thought there at dawn, he stood still, contemplating it; and when he made no progress, he did not give up, but remained standing and searching. It was already midday, and people began to notice; they said to one another in wonder that Socrates had been standing there thinking since daybreak. Finally, in the evening, some of the Ionian soldiers, after they had finished dinner (for it was summer then), brought out their bedding and slept in the cool air, partly to watch him and see if he would stay standing all night. He remained standing until it was dawn and the sun rose; then he went on his way, after offering a prayer to the sun. <margin>D</margin>And if you wish to hear of him in battles—for it is only just to give him his due—when the battle took place for which the generals gave me the prize for valor, no one else saved my life but this man. He was unwilling to leave me when I was wounded, but saved both me and my armor. And I, Socrates, even then urged the generals to give the prize to you (and this you will neither blame me for nor say I am lying about), but because the generals looked to my social rank and wanted to give me the prize, you yourself were more eager than the generals that I should receive it rather than yourself. <margin>E</margin>Furthermore, gentlemen, it was a sight worth seeing when Socrates retreated with the army from the defeat at Delium. <note>Delium: A battle in 424 BCE where the Boeotians defeated the Athenians.</note> I happened to be there on horseback, while he was a heavy infantryman. When our men were already scattered, he and Laches were retreating together. I happened upon them and, seeing them, immediately urged them to take heart, saying I would not abandon them. There I saw Socrates even more clearly than at Potidaea <note>Potidaea: A city in northern Greece besieged by Athens (432–430 BCE); both Socrates and Alcibiades served there.</note> (for I was in less fear myself because I was on a horse). First, how much he surpassed Laches in presence of mind. <margin>F</margin>Then, it seemed to me, O Aristophanes—to use your own phrase—that even there he was walking just as he does here: "swaggering and casting his eyes side to side," <note>original: "βρενθυόμενος, καὶ τὼ ὀφθαλμὼ παραβάλλων." This is a direct quote from Aristophanes' play, *The Clouds*, which poked fun at Socrates.</note> calmly observing both friends and enemies. He made it clear to everyone, even from a great distance, that if anyone touched this man, he would defend himself very vigorously. Therefore, both he and his companion got away safely; for in war, people generally do not even touch those who carry themselves this way, but instead pursue those who flee headlong. One could praise Socrates for many other things, but while those things might perhaps be said of others, <margin>G</margin>this—that he is like no other human being, neither among the ancients nor among those now living—is worthy of all wonder. For as Achilles was, one might compare him to Brasidas <note>A famous Spartan general.</note> and others; and as Pericles was, one might compare him to Antenor or Nestor. There are others, too, who could be compared in the same way. But as for the strange nature of this man, both himself and his speeches, one could search and find nothing close, neither among those now living nor the ancients—unless, as I say, one compares him to no human, but to the Silenuses and satyrs, both him and his words. For indeed, I omitted this at the beginning: his speeches are most like those Silenus statues that open up. <margin>H</margin>For if anyone were to listen to Socrates’ speeches, they would seem quite ridiculous at first. They are wrapped in such words and phrases on the outside, like the hide of some insolent satyr. He speaks of pack-asses, and smiths, and cobblers, and tanners, and he always seems to say the same things in the same way, so that any inexperienced or foolish person would laugh at his words. But if one sees them being opened and gets inside them, he will find, first, that they are the only speeches that have sense within; then, that they are most divine, containing the most numerous images of virtue, and reaching toward the greatest heights—or rather, toward everything that it is proper for a man who intends to be noble and good to consider. These are the things, O fellow guests, for which I praise Socrates; and again, I have told you my complaints, mixing them in...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>And it happened to me against Potidaea; Socrates and I were tent-mates and companions in that army. First of all, in his endurance of labor, he far surpassed not only me but all others. If in any place, as is prone to happen in war, provisions failed, no one was found equal to him in enduring hunger and thirst. Again, in the abundance of things, in feasting and the military table, he alone seemed able to enjoy himself. And although he did not wish to drink, yet if he was forced to, he far surpassed all others in drinking; and what is most marvelous of all, no one ever saw him drunk. But this seems to be something that cannot yet be refuted for the future. <margin>B</margin>Against winters and frosts (which are very harsh in those places), he did wonderful things. For when a very great and intolerable frost occurred, so that no one dared to go out from their tents—or if any did go out, it was only if they were quite bundled up, their feet and legs carefully wrapped in skins and woolen cloths—Socrates went out during this very time with the other soldiers, yet adding nothing to that garment which he had been accustomed to wear before. Truly, with bare feet, he walked more easily through the ice than others did with shoes. The soldiers, seeing these things, suspected that they were being looked down upon by him. And in these matters, such was Socrates. But what this most tolerant man did in the same army is <margin>C</margin>worth hearing. For when some thought had once struck him, he stood thinking in the same spot from the morning time; and when it was not granted to him to unfold what he was thinking, he persisted in thinking, nor did he leave off. It was already noon, and the soldiers had noticed this and wondered, and one told another that Socrates had been standing since dawn thinking. Finally, some soldiers from Ionia, when night was already approaching, having already dined—for it was then summer—placed their bedding around him and lay in the cold, observing him to see if he would also persevere through the night. Socrates indeed stood until the following dawn and the rising of the sun. Afterward, he went away, once he had greeted the rising sun. <margin>D</margin>In battles also, what he was like must not be passed over in silence. For when that fight took place, from which the leaders of the army gave me the rewards as the best fighter, no one else saved me but Socrates. For seeing me gravely wounded, he by no means deserted me, but leaping forward before me, he protected both myself and my weapons, and saved me from the enemies. And I then, proclaiming these things, tried to ensure that those gifts were handed not to me, but to this Socrates, by whom I had been saved. You could not refute these things, nor deny them as false, Socrates. <margin>E</margin>Then indeed the leaders, looking to my dignity, preferred to give the gift to me, you especially, O Socrates, entreating them that the honor should be shown to me and not to you. But O men, it was a noble thing to see Socrates when our army fled from Delium. For I was also present at this battle, and indeed fighting from a horse, while Socrates himself was on foot. Our men being routed, and the flight of all now having occurred, Socrates and Laches retreated together. And when I had fallen upon them by chance, I told them to be of good heart, and said I would never desert them. <margin>F</margin>Here, therefore, I was able to look upon Socrates even better than at Potidaea, because I, relying on my horse, was less afraid. First, therefore, it was possible to see with how much caution and presence of mind he surpassed Laches. Then he seemed to me, O Aristophanes—what you also say he does here—to walk proudly, and with his eyes quietly surveying all things around him, and cautiously examining each detail. Indeed, he looked back at enemies and citizens in turn, showing by his eyes and look, and demonstrating even to those further off, that if anyone should attack him, it would not be done with impunity. Therefore, both he and the other departed safely; for almost no one attacks those who walk in this way, but rather those who are carried away in headlong flight. In many other things indeed Socrates can be wonderfully praised, but they are such that perhaps some others also deserve the same praise. <margin>G</margin>But those things are especially noteworthy in him, through which he is found to be similar to no other of men, neither of the ancients nor of the new. For what Achilles was like, someone might perhaps guess Brasidas to have been, and certain others; and what Pericles was like, such were Antenor and Nestor. There are others also who can be compared to each other in this way. But what Socrates is like, and what his wonderful manner of speaking is, almost no one approaches his likeness, neither of the old nor of those who are now, unless as I have now said and likened him. For indeed he is similar to no man, but to the Silenuses and Satyrs, both himself and his speeches. For this also had been omitted by me before: his speeches are very similar to opened Silenuses. For if anyone should hear his speeches, they seem at first, as is said, to be too absurd in appearance. Indeed, the names and <margin>H</margin>words on the exterior aspect bear the habit of some insulting Satyr. For he always has in his mouth pack-asses and blacksmiths, and shoemakers of boots, and tanners, and he seems to always say the same things about the same people, so that almost all who are less experienced or skilled would mock his words. But if anyone should look inside his speeches, he will first find that they alone of all others have a depth of meaning, and moreover are most divine, and contain very many most beautiful images of virtues, and extend themselves to very many things; indeed, they comprehend all precepts by which he ought to be instructed who is to live honorably and well. These are the things, O men of the banquet, for which I praise Socrates, and also those about which I complain. For you have heard meanwhile what [he did] to me...

<summary>Alcibiades recounts Socrates’ legendary physical endurance during the siege of Potidaea and his bravery during the retreat at Delium, concluding that Socrates is entirely unique among men, comparing his speech to Silenus statues that are humble on the outside but divine within.</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Alcibiades, Potidaea, Delium, military endurance, Silenus statues, Aristophanes, Laches, bravery, philosophical speech</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes the Symposium, where Alcibiades finishes his speech and the party dissolves at dawn. It then transitions into the beginning of the Phaedrus, including a scholarly introduction comparing the two dialogues' treatments of love and beauty.</meta>

# PLATO #

<margin>A</margin>He has inflicted injuries upon me. And he has behaved this way not only toward me, but also toward Charmides the son of Glaucon, and toward Euthydemus the son of Diocles, and many others whom he deceived under the guise of being their lover; for instead of the lover, he turned out to be the one they loved. Therefore, Agathon, I also warn you to beware of his pretenses and disguises, and by knowing him through what I have suffered, look after your own interests, and do not—as the proverb goes—be like the fools who only learn through their own misfortune. When Alcibiades had said this, Aristodemus reported that everyone laughed at his boldness and frankness of speech, since he still seemed to be captivated by his love for Socrates. Socrates then said: "You seem sober to me, Alcibiades. Otherwise, you would never have so artfully hidden the goal for which you said everything else by making such a roundabout circuit of words. At the very end of your speech, <margin>B</margin>as if it were an afterthought, you finally added your point: as though everything you said was for the sake of separating me from Agathon. You think that I ought to love no one but you, and that Agathon should be loved by no one but you. But your Satyr-like and Silenus-like <note>original: "Satyricum Silenicúmque"; referring to the grotesque but divine statues mentioned earlier in the speech</note> plot did not escape us. So, my dear Agathon, we must take care that his schemes do not succeed, and that no slander thrown between you and me causes a rift." Agathon replied, "Socrates, you seem to be speaking the truth. I suspect this because he sat down right between you and me to keep us apart. But this will gain him nothing; for I will get up and sit next to you." Socrates said, "Certainly, do so. Sit here below me." "O Jupiter!" Alcibiades exclaimed. "What things this man makes me endure! He wishes to overcome me in everything. But if nothing <margin>C</margin>else, you marvelous man, at least allow Agathon to sit here in the middle." "That would not be at all proper," Socrates replied. "For you have praised me. Now I must, in turn, praise the one sitting on my right. If Agathon stays behind you, surely he will not praise me again before he himself has been praised by me. So let him be, you happy man, and do not grudge the lad my praise. Indeed, I desire to praise him very much." "Aha!" Agathon said. "Alcibiades, there is no way I am staying here! I am moving at once so that Socrates may praise me." "That is how it always is," Alcibiades replied, "whenever Socrates is present; it is impossible for anyone else to win over the beautiful ones. See now how easily and with what probable reasoning he has drawn this one to himself." So Agathon got up to rest beside Socrates. Then, suddenly, a great crowd of <margin>D</margin>revelers reached the open doors—for someone had just gone out—and they entered and sat down among them. Everything was thrown into confusion by their noise, and from that point on, no order was observed in the drinking. Aristodemus recounted that Eryximachus, Phaedrus, and some others left, and that he himself fell into a deep sleep, for the nights were long then; he woke up around dawn as the roosters were already crowing. Having been woken, he found that the others were either sleeping or had departed. Only Agathon, Aristophanes, and Socrates were still awake, drinking from a large bowl and passing it to the right. Socrates was debating with them. Aristodemus said he did not remember the rest of the arguments, for he had not been there from the start and was heavy with sleep. But the main point of the discussion was that Socrates was forcing them to admit <margin>E</margin>that it belongs to the same man to know how to compose both tragedy and comedy, and that he who is a tragic poet by art is also a comic poet. When they had conceded this—driven by necessity rather than being fully persuaded—Aristophanes fell asleep first, and then Agathon, as the light was already breaking. Socrates, having put them to sleep, got up and departed, with Aristodemus following him as was his custom. Going to the Lyceum <note>A public gymnasium and garden in Athens where Socrates often taught</note> and washing himself as he usually did, he spent the whole day in his usual exercise, and finally, toward evening, went home to rest.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>He has treated me with insolence. And he has done these things not only to me, but also to Charmides the son of Glaucon, and Euthydemus the son of Diocles, and very many others, whom this man deceives as if he were their lover, yet he establishes himself as the beloved rather than the lover. I tell you this, Agathon, so that you are not deceived by him, but rather learn from our sufferings and be on your guard; do not, according to the proverb, be like the "child who learns only after he has suffered." When Alcibiades had said this, there was laughter at his frankness, because he seemed to still be in love with Socrates. Then Socrates said: "You seem sober to me, Alcibiades. For you would never have attempted to hide the reason you said all this by wrapping it in such a clever circuit, and then placing it at the very end as if it were a side-issue. As if you hadn't said everything for the purpose of slandering me and Agathon, thinking that I must love you and <margin>B</margin>no one else, and that Agathon must be loved by you and no one else. But you did not go unnoticed; this Satyr-play and Silenus-drama of yours has become plain. But, dear Agathon, let him gain nothing from it; instead, prepare yourself so that no one can drive a wedge between you and me." Agathon said, "Socrates, you are likely telling the truth. I judge this by the way he sat between us, so that he could keep us apart. He shall gain nothing from this; I will come and lie down next to you." "By all means," Socrates said, "lie down here below me." "O Zeus!" said Alcibiades, "What I suffer again from this man! He thinks he must prevail over me in every way. But if nothing else, you amazing man, let Agathon lie in the middle of us." "But that is impossible," said Socrates. "For you <margin>C</margin>have praised me, and I must in turn praise the one on my right. If Agathon lies below you, surely he will not praise me again before he is first praised by me. Let him be, you divine man, and do not grudge the youth being praised by me. For I very much desire to eulogize him." "Hooray, hooray!" said Agathon. "Alcibiades, there is no way I will stay here; I will move by all means, so that I may be praised by Socrates." "That is the usual way," said Alcibiades. "When Socrates is present, it is impossible for anyone else to share in the company of the beautiful. See how easily he found a persuasive reason for this one to lie beside him." So Agathon stood up to lie beside Socrates. But suddenly many revelers came to the doors, and finding them open because someone was going out, they made their way in and sat <margin>D</margin>down. Everything became full of noise, and no longer in any order, they were forced to drink a great deal of wine. Aristodemus said that Eryximachus and Phaedrus and some others went home. He himself fell asleep and slept a long time, as the nights were long. He woke up toward daybreak, as the roosters were singing. Upon waking, he saw that the others were sleeping or gone, but Agathon, Aristophanes, and Socrates were still awake, drinking from a large bowl from left to right. Socrates was talking to them. Aristodemus said he did not remember the other parts of the speech (for he had not been there from the beginning and was sleepy), but the main point was that Socrates was compelling them to agree that it is the task of the same man to understand how to make comedy and <margin>E</margin>tragedy, and that he who is a tragic poet by art is also a comic poet. As they were being forced to this, not quite following the argument, they began to nod. Aristophanes fell asleep first, and then Agathon as day was already coming. Socrates, having put them to sleep, got up and left, and Aristodemus followed him as was his habit. Having gone to the Lyceum and washed himself as at other times, he spent the rest of the whole day there. Having finished thus, he went home to rest in the evening.

# PHAEDRUS, OR,
## ON BEAUTY.

# ΦΑΙΔΡΟΣ, Η, ΠΕΡΙ
## ΚΑΛΟΥ.

| SUMMARY OF THE DIALOGUE. | SUMMARY OF THE DIALOGUE (GREEK). |
|-----------------|--------------------|
| This discussion is also, just like the one contained in the *Symposium*, entirely mystical, and it embraces a closely related subject, for both are about love, though directed toward different ends. The end of that one is the completion of happiness; the end of this one is the soul's freedom. | This discussion also, just like the things contained in the *Symposium*, is entirely mystical and contains a similar subject. For each is about love, though not toward the same end. For that one looks toward the fulfillment of happiness, while this one looks toward the freedom of the soul. |
| It explains nature: this one, its passions, among which the most excellent and effective is the desire for beauty. But since men err in various ways regarding that desire for beauty, pursuing shadows of things rather than the truth, and thus worshiping certain foul images instead of the true beautiful: for that reason, it had to be accurately discussed what true beauty is. This beauty is Reason, by which man is joined with God. Moreover, the interpreter of Reason is speech, a singular gift and ornament specially bestowed upon man. By its service and work, the beauty of Reason shines forth. Thus, the true beauty of man resides in both reason and speech. Since this beauty is fouled by man in many ways through the powerless intemperance of desires and lusts, there arise various and manifold types of ugliness, both in the soul itself and in speech. Plato chose these topics to teach how one errs in both. From there, he glides into a more copious and accurate explanation of the beautiful, learnedly discussing the nature, order, power, and faculty of Reason and speech. | And it shows the powers of love, and what are the modes of its madness; and what is the beauty of the soul; and how it is possible for human nature to contemplate this and be led back to God. In these matters, he also discusses rhetoric—that which is fitting for the wise man and that of the masses—and shows the difference between them, and carefully goes through the nature of the voice and the word, their order, power, and art. |
