--- Page 369 ---
<meta>This page marks the beginning of the *Phaedrus*, one of Plato’s most celebrated dialogues. It follows the transition from the *Symposium* (which ended on the previous page) to a new encounter between Socrates and a young man named Phaedrus. The setting shifts from a crowded banquet in the city to a tranquil walk along the Ilissus river in the countryside.</meta>

# PHAEDRUS

<margin>A</margin> <margin>The. sp.</margin> SOCRATES: Indeed, my friend, you speak well. But where has Lysias been? In the city, it seems.
PHAEDRUS: Yes, he was staying with Epicrates, in that house of Morychus <note>Morychus was an Athenian known for his luxurious lifestyle; Epicrates was a prominent politician.</note> near the temple of Olympian Zeus.
SOCRATES: And how did you spend your time? Surely Lysias feasted you with his speeches?
PHAEDRUS: You shall hear, if you have the leisure to walk along and listen.
SOCRATES: What? Do you not think that, in the words of Pindar <note>original: "κατὰ Πίνδαρον"; referring to the Greek lyric poet who wrote that business should be secondary to higher pursuits</note>, I would consider hearing your conversation with Lysias a matter of greater importance even than business?
PHAEDRUS: Lead on then.
SOCRATES: Please, tell me.
PHAEDRUS: Indeed, Socrates, the subject is well-suited for your ears. The discourse we were discussing was, in a certain way, about love. For Lysias has written about a beautiful youth being tempted, but not by a lover. He has managed this quite cleverly; for he argues that one should grant favors to a non-lover rather than to a lover.
SOCRATES: O, what a noble man! <margin>B</margin> If only he would write that one should favor the poor rather than the rich, and the old rather than the young, and all the other qualities that apply to me and the majority of us! Truly, his speeches would then be witty and of great public benefit. Indeed, I am so eager to hear it that even if you walk all the way to Megara, and following the method of Herodicus <note>Herodicus was a physician who recommended long walks to the city walls for health</note> you go to the wall and back again, I will not be left behind by you.
PHAEDRUS: What are you saying, my dear Socrates? Do you think that I, a mere amateur, could memorize in a way worthy of him what Lysias—the most skillful writer of our time—composed at his leisure over a long period? Far from it. Yet I would rather be able to do that than possess a great deal of gold.
SOCRATES: O Phaedrus, if I do not know Phaedrus, I have forgotten myself. <margin>C</margin> But neither of these is true. I know well that when he heard Lysias's speech, he did not hear it only once, but he kept asking him to repeat it many times, and Lysias willingly complied. But even this was not enough for him; finally, taking the book itself, he examined the parts he most desired. Doing this, sitting from early morning until he grew tired, he then went out for a walk—by the Dog! <note>original: "μὰ τὸν κύνα"; a characteristic oath of Socrates</note>—having memorized the speech, I believe, unless it was quite long. He was heading outside the walls to practice it. <margin>D</margin> Meeting a man who is sick with a passion for hearing speeches, he was glad to see him, because he would have a fellow-reveler in his ecstasy, and so he invited him to walk along. But when the lover of speeches asked him to speak, he pretended to be reluctant, as if he did not want to; yet in the end, he was going to speak even if one did not want to listen, perhaps even using force. So, Phaedrus, ask him to do now what he is going to do anyway.
PHAEDRUS: It is truly much better for me to speak as best I can. For you seem as though you will never let me go until I speak in one way or another.
SOCRATES: You have a very true perception of me.
PHAEDRUS: This, then, is what I shall do. For truly, Socrates, <margin>E</margin> I have not learned the words themselves by heart, but I have the general meaning of almost all the points by which he showed the difference between the lover and the non-lover; I will go through each of them in order, starting from the beginning.
SOCRATES: First, my dear friend, show me what you have in your left hand under your cloak. For I suspect you have the speech itself. If that is the case, understand this about me: though I love you dearly, while Lysias is present I have no intention of providing myself to you as a practice subject for your own performance. Come, show it!
PHAEDRUS: Stop! You have dashed the hope I had, Socrates, of practicing my memory on you. But where do you want us to sit and read?
SOCRATES: Let us turn aside and go along the Ilissus <note>The Ilissus is a small, sacred river in Athens</note>; then, wherever it seems quiet, we shall sit down.
PHAEDRUS: It seems I am lucky to be barefoot; you, of course, always are. <margin>F</margin> It will be easiest for us to walk along the stream with our feet in the water, and it is not unpleasant, especially at this time of year and day.
SOCRATES: Lead on, and look for a place where we might sit.
PHAEDRUS: Do you see that very tall plane tree?
SOCRATES: Of course.
PHAEDRUS: There is shade there, and a gentle breeze, and grass to sit on, or even to lie down on if we wish.
SOCRATES: Lead the way then.
PHAEDRUS: Tell me, Socrates, is it not from somewhere around here on the Ilissus that Boreas <note>The North Wind</note> is said to have carried off Orithyia?
SOCRATES: So it is said.
PHAEDRUS: Was it from this very spot? The water appears so lovely, pure, and clear, and it seems just the right place for young girls to play.
SOCRATES: No, it was further down, about two or three stades <note>A stade is roughly 600 feet</note>, where we cross over to the district of Agrae. There is even an altar of Boreas there.
PHAEDRUS: I hadn't noticed it. But tell me, by Zeus, Socrates, do you believe this myth is true?
SOCRATES: If I were to doubt it, as the wise men <note>referring to "Sophists" who tried to provide rational, scientific explanations for traditional myths</note> do, I would not be out of place. <margin>G</margin> Then I might rationalize it and say that a gust of the North Wind (Boreas) pushed her off the nearby rocks while she was playing with Pharmacia, and thus when she died, it was said she had been carried off by Boreas. Or perhaps it happened from the Areopagus <note>The "Hill of Ares" in Athens, where the high court sat</note>, for there is also a story that she was snatched from there and not from here. But I, Phaedrus, think such explanations are charming, but they belong to a man who is far too clever and industrious, and not entirely fortunate. For no other reason than that he must then go on to explain the form of the Centaurs, and then the Chimaera. And there follows a whole crowd of such Gorgons, and Pegasuses, and a multitude of other impossible and strange mythical <margin>H</margin> creatures. If someone, being skeptical, tries to bring each of these into a likely explanation, using a sort of rustic wisdom, he will need a great deal of leisure. But I have no leisure at all for these things. And the cause of it, my friend, is this: I am not yet able, according to the Delphic inscription, to know myself.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>...and he considers it more healthful than a running contest.
SOCRATES: Indeed he moves rightly, my friend. But where was Lysias? In the city, it seems.
PHAEDRUS: He was. For he is staying at the house of Morychus, which is near the temple of Olympian Zeus, with Epicrates.
SOCRATES: What was being done there? Was Lysias hosting you with a feast of oratory?
PHAEDRUS: You shall know, provided you have the leisure to listen while walking with me.
SOCRATES: What indeed? Do you not think that, according to Pindar, I would place hearing your conversation with Lysias even before business?
PHAEDRUS: Proceed then.
SOCRATES: You have only to speak.
PHAEDRUS: And yet that discussion, Socrates, is well-suited to your ears. For the speech that was delivered was, I know not how, about love. Lysias had written of a certain handsome youth being solicited, but not by a lover; and in this very thing he showed off his cleverness, by proving that a non-lover should be gratified more than a lover.
SOCRATES: O <margin>B</margin> noble man! I wish he would write that the poor man rather than the wealthy, and the old man rather than the youth, and all others affected as I and many of us are, should be gratified. Indeed, such a speech would be sophisticated and of public use. But such a great desire for hearing has seized me that if you should walk as far as Megara, and in the manner of Herodicus, once you have reached the wall, you immediately return, I would not leave you.
PHAEDRUS: What do you say, best <margin>C</margin> Socrates? Do you think that I, being unpracticed, could repeat those things which Lysias, the most eloquent of all who now write, composed over a long time at his leisure, in a way worthy of him? I am certainly very far from it. And yet I would rather have that ability than a great deal of gold.
SOCRATES: O Phaedrus, if I do not know Phaedrus, I have also forgotten myself. But neither of these is true. For I know for certain that he heard that speech of Lysias not once only, but he ordered it to be repeated often. And Lysias willingly obeyed. But even this was not enough for Phaedrus; finally taking the book, he considered the parts he most desired. When he had done this, sitting there from morning until he was tired, he went out for a walk—by the Dog!—as I indeed believe, committing it to memory, unless perhaps the speech was too long. And he was heading <margin>D</margin> just outside the walls to practice those very things. But meeting a man with an insane love of speeches, he rejoiced at the sight of him, because he would have someone to share in his excitement and exultation, and he invited him to go along. Then, being asked to speak by the man eager for speeches, he pretended to be burdened, as if he did not want to recount it; but finally, even if no one wanted to listen of their own accord, he was prepared to speak by force. I would therefore ask you, Phaedrus, to do for me now what you were going to do even without being asked.
PHAEDRUS: It is better, then, to speak as best I can. For you seem likely not to let me go until I have spoken to the best of my strength.
SOCRATES: You seem to see me quite truly.
PHAEDRUS: <margin>E</margin> Thus I shall do. But I have not learned the words themselves, Socrates; however, I hold the meanings of almost all of them, by which he shows the lover to differ from the non-lover, and I shall proceed to relate them to you briefly and in order, beginning from the start.
SOCRATES: Show me, I pray, first what you have in your left hand under your cloak. For I suspect you have the book itself. If this is so, think of it this way: I do indeed value you greatly, but while Lysias is present, I have no intention of offering myself to you as a listener. But come, show it.
PHAEDRUS: Cease. You have thrown me down from a great hope, Socrates, which I had in you, namely that I would exercise my talent along with you. But where do you wish us to sit and read?
SOCRATES: Let us turn aside here near the Ilissus river. Later, when it seems right, we shall rest <margin>F</margin> while sitting.
PHAEDRUS: I am very opportunely barefoot; for you always are. It will be easy for us to wade through the water itself, and not unpleasant, especially given the beauty of this time of year and day.
SOCRATES: Proceed then, and look for a place for us to sit.
PHAEDRUS: Do you see that very tall plane tree?
SOCRATES: I see it.
PHAEDRUS: There is shade, a moderate wind, and soft grass, wherever we might wish to sit or even lie down.
SOCRATES: Proceed then.
PHAEDRUS: Tell me, Socrates. Is it not said that Boreas once snatched Orithyia from the Ilissus here?
SOCRATES: So it is said.
PHAEDRUS: Was it not here? For the water appears pleasant, pure, and bright, and suitable for the games of girls.
SOCRATES: <margin>G</margin> Not at all, but a little further down by two or three stades, where we encounter the temple of Artemis <note>original: "Dianae"; using the Roman name for the Greek goddess Artemis</note>, and in that same place there is a certain altar to Boreas.
PHAEDRUS: I did not know it well. But tell me, by Jove <note>original: "Iouem"; Jupiter/Zeus</note>, Socrates, do you think this fable was true?
SOCRATES: Now, if I did not think so, like the wise men, I would not be absurd. Then, inventing a story, I would say that the wind of Boreas threw Orithyia from the nearby rocks while she was playing with Pharmacia, and so she died and was imagined to have been snatched by Boreas; or from the Areopagus. For there is another rumor that she was snatched from that place and not from here. But I, Phaedrus, consider these things pleasant indeed, but the work of a man too curious and anxious, and furthermore not a lucky man, for no other reason than that it is necessary for him to interpret the form of Centaurs and the Chimaera. And also <margin>H</margin> there flocks a crowd of Gorgons and Pegasuses, and a multitude of other monstrous forms. Therefore, if anyone does not believe these things are as they are told, but wishes to pull each one toward a suitable meaning, relying on a certain rustic wisdom, he will need too much leisure. But for me, there is no leisure for these things, for this reason, my friend: because I am not yet able, according to the Delphic precept, to know myself.

<summary>In this opening scene of the Phaedrus, Socrates meets Phaedrus and they decide to walk along the Ilissus river to read a speech by Lysias on the nature of love and the preference for non-lovers. Socrates dismisses the fashion of "rationalizing" ancient myths, stating that he must first fulfill the Delphic command to achieve self-knowledge.</summary>

# 338 PLATO

<margin>It is ridiculous when one ignores one's own business to investigate that of others.</margin>

**A** **Socrates:** Therefore, I think it is ridiculous, while I am still ignorant of myself, to want to investigate the business of others. So, letting these things be and believing the common opinion about them—as I was just saying—I consider not these things, but myself: whether I am some beast more complex than **Typhon** <note>A monstrous serpentine giant in Greek mythology, often associated with chaos and storms.</note> and more fiery and furious, or whether I am a gentler and simpler animal, sharing in some divine and modest nature. But, my friend, in the middle of our talk, was this not the tree to which you were leading us?
**Phaedrus:** This is certainly the one.
**Socrates:** By **Juno** <note>original: "Iunonem" / "Ἥραν" (Hera); Socrates often swore by the queen of the gods.</note>, a beautiful resting place! For this **Plane tree** <note>original: "Platanus" / "πλάτανος"; the Oriental Plane tree was prized for its shade.</note> has quite wide branches and is tall, and the height and shade of that **Chaste-tree** <note>original: "viticus" / "ἄγνου"; the *Agnus castus*, believed to preserve chastity and used in religious festivals.</note> is exceedingly beautiful and pleasant, and it is **B** now in the prime of its flowering, so that the whole place is filled with a sweet scent. A most clear spring also flows under the plane tree with very cold water, as one can judge by the touch of a foot. I gather it is sacred to certain **Nymphs** and to **Achelous** <note>Achelous was a major river god in Greece.</note> from these dolls and images. Do you not notice, moreover, how pleasant and sweet a breeze blows here? Something summery and musical resonates with the choir of **cicadas** <note>original: "cicadarum" / "τεττίγων"; insects famous for their "singing" in Greek literature.</note>. But most elegant of all is the grass itself, which grows on the gentle slope in such a way that it is perfectly suited for someone to lie down and rest their head softly. And so you have guided me, as if I were a stranger, quite excellently, my dear Phaedrus.
**Phaedrus:** O admirable man, you seem quite absurd indeed!

<margin>That one must live among men, not among trees.</margin>

**C** And truly, as you say, you are like a stranger being led about, not a local inhabitant: you appear as if you never cross our borders, nor even step outside the city walls.
**Socrates:** Forgive me, excellent Phaedrus. For I am a **lover of learning** <note>original: "discendi cupidus" / "φιλομαθὴς" (philomathes)</note>, and the fields and trees have nothing to teach me, but the men who live in the city do. You, however, seem to have found the medicine to make me go out. For just as people lead hungry animals by waving a branch or fruit before them, so you, by holding out a book of speeches, might lead me all over **Attica** and anywhere else you please. Now that we have arrived here,

<margin>The speech of Lysias against lovers.</margin>

**D** I think I shall lie down. You, however, choose whatever posture you think will be most comfortable for reading, and then read.
**Phaedrus:** Listen then. "You know the state of my affairs, and I think it would be to our mutual benefit, as you have heard, for these things to happen. I believe I should not fail to get what I ask for simply because I am not in love with you. For lovers, as soon as their desire is satisfied, regret the favors they have done; but for those who are not entangled in love, there is no reason they should ever feel regret. For they do not act out of necessity, but willingly, having consulted what is best for their own affairs, they bestow favors according to their means. Furthermore, lovers sometimes calculate how they have neglected their own business because of their love

**E** and what benefits they have bestowed to their own loss, and what labors they have undergone. Therefore, they think they have already returned a worthy gratitude to their beloveds. But those who are not deceived by love do not complain about neglecting their domestic affairs, nor about past labors, nor about falling into discord with their relatives for the sake of a friend. Therefore, since so many evils are removed, nothing remains but for them to be ready to do everything they believe will be a favor to the other. Most people say that lovers should be valued more because they are bound by the greatest affection for their beloveds, and are always ready to obey them in word and deed, even if they offend everyone else by doing so. It is easy to see that their claim is not true, because

**F** when their affection is transferred from one person to another, they will prefer their later beloveds to the former ones; and if the newer ones command it, they will even treat their former loves poorly. And yet, what reason is there to grant such a thing to a man who is afflicted with a calamity that no experienced person would even try to cure? Indeed, they themselves confess they are **mad** <note>original: "insanire" / "νοσεῖν" (sick/diseased)</note> rather than sane, and they know they are not in their right minds, but they cannot control themselves. So, how could they, once they return to their senses, think that those decisions they made in such a state were good? Furthermore, if you wish to choose the best from among lovers, your choice will be from a few; but if you seek the most suitable companion from among others, you may choose from many. There is much greater hope of finding a man worthy of your friendship among many than among few. If, therefore, you fear public infamy according to the laws, you must remember that lovers, who

**G** think they should be loved just as they love others, are accustomed to boast openly that their vigils were not in vain. But those who are not in love, because they can control themselves, prefer to seek what is best rather than the rumors of the crowd. Add to this that the common people, when they see lovers constantly following their beloveds and making a business of it, suspect that a shameful desire has seized them, or perhaps soon will. But they do not dare to disapprove of the familiarity of non-lovers. For they know it is necessary for men to associate with one another, either for the sake of friendship or for some other convenience. Furthermore, if fear has invaded you, thinking it will be difficult for the friendship to remain, or if a quarrel arises, a common loss to both occurs:

**H** and if you yield those things you value most, you will be greatly harmed; you will rightly fear lovers. For many things offend them, and

<column-break/>

**A** **Socrates:** It seems quite ridiculous to me, while I am still ignorant of this <note>Self-knowledge</note>, to look into things that do not belong to me. Therefore, letting these things go and following the custom regarding them, as I just said, I look not at them but at myself: whether I happen to be some beast more complex than **Typhon** and more full of passion, or a gentler and simpler animal, by nature sharing in some divine and modest lot. But, my friend, to interrupt our talk, was this not the tree to which you were leading us?
**Phaedrus:** This is the very one.
**Socrates:** By **Hera**, a beautiful resting place! For this **Plane tree** is very spreading and tall, and the height and shade of the **Chaste-tree** is beautiful; and since it is at the peak

**B** of its flowering, it provides the most fragrant scent to the place. Furthermore, a most charming spring flows under the plane tree with very cold water, as one may judge by the foot. From the figurines and images, it seems to be a sanctuary of certain **Nymphs** and of **Achelous**. If you wish, note also how pleasant and very sweet the air of the place is; it echoes with the summery and clear song of the choir of **cicadas**. But the most clever thing of all is the grass, because on a gentle slope it has grown enough to be perfectly comfortable for someone to lie down and rest their head. Thus, you have been an excellent guide for me, my dear Phaedrus.
**Phaedrus:** And you, O wonderful man, appear to be a most absurd person. For literally, as you say, you are like some stranger being guided and not a local. Thus, you do not travel out of the city across the border, nor

**C** do you seem to me to go outside the wall at all.
**Socrates:** Forgive me, my best of friends. For I am **fond of learning**. Now, the countryside and the trees are not willing to teach me anything, but the men in the city are. You, however, seem to me to have found the medicine to draw me out. For just as those who lead hungry cattle by waving a green branch or fruit, so you, by holding out speeches in books, seem likely to lead me around all of **Attica** and wherever else you please. Now, for the present, having arrived here, I think I shall lie down, and you, in whatever posture you think you can read most easily, choose that and read.
**Phaedrus:** Listen then. "Concerning my

**D** affairs, you know how they stand, and you have heard how I think it would be advantageous for us if these things happened. I claim that I should not fail to get what I ask for simply because I do not happen to be your lover. For to those [lovers], regret comes for the favors they have done whenever their desire ceases; but for the others, there is no time in which it is proper to change their minds. For not under necessity, but willingly, as they might best deliberate concerning their own interests, they do favors according to their own power. Furthermore, those who love look at the things of their own that they have managed badly because of their love, and the favors they have done; and adding the labor they have endured, they think they have long ago given a worthy return of gratitude to their beloveds. But for those who do not love, it is not possible to plead the neglect of their own affairs, nor

**E** to take into account past labors, nor to blame differences with their relatives. So, since so many evils have been cast aside, nothing is left but to do eagerly whatever they think they might do to please them. Furthermore, if it is worth valuing lovers highly for this reason—that they say they love most those they are in love with, and are ready both in words and in deeds to please their beloveds while making themselves hated by others—it is easy to know if they speak the truth, because whenever they later fall in love again, they will value those [new ones] more highly; and it is clear that if it seems good to those, they will even do evil to these [former ones]. And yet, how is it reasonable to grant such a thing to a man who has such a calamity, which

**F** no one with experience would even attempt to avert? For they themselves admit they are sick rather than of sound mind, and know that they think poorly but are unable to control themselves. So how, once they have become of sound mind, could they think those things were good which they desired while in such a state? And furthermore, if you were to choose the best from among the lovers, your choice would be from a few; but if from the others you chose the one most suitable for yourself, it would be from many. So there is much greater hope that among the many you will find the one worthy of your friendship. If, then, you fear the established custom, lest people find out and it becomes a reproach to you, it is likely that

**G** lovers—thinking that they will be envied by others just as they envy themselves—will be uplifted to speak and, being ambitious, will show off to everyone that their labor has not been in vain; but those who do not love, being masters of themselves, choose what is best instead of the reputation among men. Furthermore, many are bound to notice and see lovers following their beloveds and making this their business, so that when they are seen talking to each other, then people think they are together because their desire has been satisfied or is about to be; but they do not even attempt to blame those who do not love for their association, knowing that it is necessary to talk together either for the sake of some friendship or

**H** some other pleasure. And indeed, if fear has come upon you, thinking that it is difficult for friendship to last, and that if a difference arises in some other way, the calamity becomes common to both, but when you have surrendered what you value most, great harm comes to you, then you would reasonably fear lovers more. For there are many things that grieve them,

<meta>This page concludes the speech of the orator Lysias, which argues that a young man should grant his favors to a non-lover rather than a lover. It then begins the dialogue between Socrates and Phaedrus reflecting on the quality of the speech.</meta>

# 339 PHAEDRUS.

...and they think everything happens to their own harm. Therefore, they even turn others away from associating with the beloved, fearing those who possess wealth, lest they surpass them with money; or the educated, lest they prove superior in intelligence. They guard against the power of anyone possessing any other good. By persuading you to be hated by these people, they leave you destitute of friends. But if you, looking out for your own interests, are wiser than they are, you will come to a disagreement with them. Those who did not happen to be in love, however, but achieved what they desired through virtue, would not be jealous of those who are present, but would rather hate those who are unwilling to associate; thinking that they are looked down upon by the latter, but benefited by the former. Thus, there is much greater hope that friendship rather than enmity will come to them from this matter.

And indeed, many lovers desired the body before they knew the character or became experienced in other personal matters. So it is unclear if they will still wish to be friends then, once they have ceased their desire. But for non-lovers, who were friends to one another even before these things happened, it is not likely that these things will make their friendship less from what they have experienced, but that these things will be left as monuments of what is to come. And indeed, it is proper for you to become better by obeying me than a lover. For they praise both words and deeds even contrary to what is best; partly fearing they may be hated, and partly because they themselves judge worse due to their desire. For love displays such things: it makes the unfortunate believe that things which cause no pain to others are distressing; and it forces the fortunate to receive praise for things not worthy of pleasure. Therefore, it is much more fitting to pity the lovers than to envy them.

But if you listen to me, first, I will associate with you not by cultivating present pleasure, but the benefit that is to be in the future; not being overcome by love, but mastering myself; nor taking up strong enmity for small things, but slowly developing a little anger for great ones; having forgiveness for involuntary errors, and trying to turn you away from voluntary ones. For these are the signs of a friendship that will last a long time. But if it has occurred to you that it is impossible for a strong friendship to arise unless one happens to be in love, you must consider that we would not value our sons so much, nor our fathers and mothers, nor would we possess faithful friends, who have not come from such a desire, but from other pursuits. Furthermore, if one must gratify those who need it most, it is fitting to do good not to the best but to the most destitute of others. For being delivered from the greatest evils, they will feel the greatest gratitude toward them. And indeed, in one’s own private expenses, it is not worthy to invite friends, but those who are beggars and those who need to be filled. For they will both love and follow, and they will come to the doors, and will be most pleased, and will feel no small gratitude, and will pray for many good things for them. 

But perhaps it is fitting not to gratify those who are in extreme need, but those who are most able to return the favor; not the lovers only, but those worthy of the matter; not those who will enjoy your youth, but those who will share their own goods when you have become older; not those who, having succeeded, will boast to others, but those who, being ashamed, will be silent before all; not those who will be serious for a short time, but those who will be friends likewise throughout all of life; not those who, ceasing their desire, will seek an excuse for enmity, but those who, when your youth has faded, will then display their own virtue.

You, then, remember what has been said, and consider this: that friends admonish lovers that the practice is bad; but no relative has ever blamed non-lovers for taking bad counsel for themselves because of this. Perhaps you might ask me if I advise you to gratify all non-lovers. But I think not even a lover would tell you to have this mind toward all lovers. For it is not equally worthy of gratitude for the one receiving it, nor is it equally possible for you if you wish to keep it secret from others. There should be no harm from them, but benefit to both. I think, then, what has been said is sufficient for you; but if you desire anything else, thinking it has been left out, ask.

What does the speech seem to you, O Socrates? Has it not been spoken wonderfully both in other respects and in its words? **SOCRATES:** Divinely indeed, my friend, so that I was struck with amazement. And I suffered this because of you, O Phaedrus, looking at you, because you seemed to me to be delighted by the speech while reading it. For thinking that you understand such things better than I, I followed you, and following you, I shared your ecstatic frenzy <note>original: "συνεβάκχευσα" / "bacchatus sum"; referring to the divine madness or "Bacchic" possession inspired by a great speech.</note> along with you, O divine head. **PHAEDRUS:** Come now; is it thus you think you should joke? **SOCRATES [CRITIC]:** Do I seem to you to be joking and not to have been serious? **PHAEDRUS:** Not at all, Socrates; but tell the truth, by Zeus the god of friendship, do you think any other of the Greeks could say other things on this same subject, more and worthier of speech than these? **SOCRATES [CRITIC]:** What? Must the speech be praised by you and me in this way, as if the author had said what was necessary? And not in that way only, because each of the words has been turned clearly and roundly and accurately? For if it is necessary, it must be granted for your sake. Since it escaped me because of my own worthlessness, except that I paid attention only to its rhetorical character. For I would not have thought that even Lysias himself would consider himself sufficient...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> they prohibit those who are loved from being among others, fearing lest the wealthy surpass them in resources, or learned men in intelligence: and they try to keep those loved far away from anyone who seems to have anything remarkable in themselves. Persuading them to abstain from these, they deprive them of all friends. But if you, having taken account of your own affairs, have deliberated better than they, you will differ from them and depart. But those who are not captured by love of you, but for the sake of virtue, perform what is necessary, will by no means envy your familiarity with others: but rather they will hate those who wish to cling to you, thinking that you are despised by the former, but helped by your familiars.

<margin>B</margin> Wherefore there is much greater hope that friendships will come from this commerce rather than enmities. Added to these things is that most lovers desire the body before they have known either the character or anything else pertaining to the beloved. From which it follows that it is doubtful whether they will persevere in friendship once their desire is extinguished. To those who do not love, however, who were friends even before, and did not do everything for the sake of pleasure, it is consistent that their benevolence is not so ardently inflamed, but that their services are accepted as monuments of things to come.

Furthermore, you will turn out better if you believe me than if you give your ears to a lover. For lovers beyond measure extol your words and deeds <margin>C</margin> with praises, partly because they fear lest they offend you, partly because they are deceived in judging on account of the fire of desire. For love designates certain such things: it compels the unfortunate to think those things sad which offer no trouble to others: but it forces the fortunate and those who have obtained their wish to praise as pleasant those things which are not worthy of joy. Therefore, it is more fitting to pity them than to love them. But if you believe me, first indeed, I will be with you not for the sake of present pleasure, but for future utility, not enslaved to love, but commanding myself: nor will I ever undertake grave enmities for the smallest causes, but rather, being moved with difficulty for the greatest ones, I will forgive involuntary errors, and I will try to correct and <margin>D</margin> avoid voluntary ones. These are arguments for a friendship that will last for a long time. If, however, it seems to you that a firm friendship cannot be born except through love, you ought to notice that by this reasoning we would not value our sons much, nor our parents, nor would we have those faithful friends, who were not made friends from the heat of this love, but from any other pursuits. To these things, if the needy are to be gratified most of all, it is fitting by all means to help not the better men, but the poorest, for having been liberated from the greatest evils they will have immense gratitude. In one’s own and private expenses also, friends will not be those to be called together, but the hungry and the suppliants; for these will value the benefit most highly, they will follow you, they will wait <margin>E</margin> at your doors, they will applaud, they will give great thanks, and they will pour out prayers for you. But perhaps it is decent not to indulge the needy most, but those rather who can return the favor: nor lovers only, but those worthy of the benefit: nor those who are delighted by your beauty, but those who will be of use to you even when old: nor those who, having obtained their wish, will boast openly, but those who will be silent with modesty: nor those who will cultivate you for a short time, but those who will love you similarly through all your life: nor those who, when the heat of desire is extinguished, will seek occasions for enmities, but those who, as beauty fades, will show their virtue and constancy. You therefore remember what I have said, and think on this, that lovers are <margin>F</margin> rebuked by friends, as if love were a base thing. But no one of their familiars vituperates those who do not love on that account, as if they consulted poorly for themselves in this way. Perhaps you will ask me whether I advise you to obey all those who do not love. But I think not even the lover himself would order you to have this same mind toward all lovers. For it is not worthy of equal gratitude for the one receiving it, nor is it similarly easy for you who wish to remain hidden from the rest. It is necessary, however, that no loss should come from this, but some utility to both. I think the things already said are sufficient: but if anything seems to you to be added, ask.

What does it seem to you, O Socrates? Is not this speech <margin>G</margin> wonderfully composed in its other matters and its words? **SOCRATES:** In a marvelous way, O friend, so that I was stunned. And so, O Phaedrus, I was affected on your account, while I was looking back at you, because you seemed to me to exult in reading the speech. Thinking therefore that you know such things more than I, I followed you, O divine head, and I myself also was in ecstasy together with you. **PHAEDRUS:** Does it seem to you that you should joke in this way? **SOCRATES:** Do I seem to you to be joking? Or not to be speaking seriously? **PHAEDRUS:** By no means, O Socrates. But tell the truth by Jupiter <note>original: "Iouem"; Zeus.</note> who presides over friends, do you think anyone of the Greeks could say more and greater things about this same matter? **SOCRATES:** What indeed? Do we think the writer is to be praised on this account alone, because he said those things which were necessary? And not on this account alone, because he placed each word clearly and roundly and elegantly? For if you wish, it must be conceded for your sake. For indeed it escaped me on account of my laziness and lack of skill. For I intended only the eloquence of the one speaking, but for that, I thought that not even Lysias himself would consider himself sufficient.

-># PHÆDRUS.<-

<margin>A</margin> ...the substance of the matter. Therefore, as if they know it, they do not clarify it at the start of the inquiry. As they proceed, as is expected, it follows that they agree neither with themselves nor with others. Let you and I not suffer what we blame in others; since the question before us is whether one should enter into friendship with a lover or a non-lover, let us establish a definition by agreement on what love is and what power it has. Looking toward this and referring back to it, let us consider whether it brings benefit or harm. Now, it is clear to everyone that love is a kind of desire; but we also know that those who are not "in love" still desire what is beautiful. By what, then, shall we distinguish the lover from the non-lover? We must understand that in each of us there are two ruling and leading ideas <note>Socrates uses the term "idea" here to describe internal psychological forces or principles of action.</note> which we follow
<margin>B</margin> wherever they lead. One is an innate desire for pleasures; the other is an acquired opinion that strives for the best. These two within us sometimes agree, but at other times they are in a state of sedition and discord; and sometimes one prevails, and sometimes the other. When opinion leads by reason toward the best and gains the mastery, this power of living is called **temperance** <note>Original Greek: *sophrosyne*; a key Platonic virtue involving self-control and sound-mindedness.</note>. But when desire irrationally drags us toward pleasures and rules within us, this rule is called **wantonness** <note>Original Greek: *hybris*; here meaning an overstepping of bounds or lack of restraint.</note>. Now wantonness has many names, for it has many parts and forms. Whichever of these forms becomes most prominent in someone gives that person its name—a name that is neither honorable nor worthy to be held. For regarding food, when it overpowers the reason for what is best and dominates other desires, it is called gluttony, and it
<margin>C</margin> gives the person who possesses it that same name. Again, that form which exercises a tyranny over drunkenness and leads the one who possesses it there—it is clear what name it will receive. The same is true for the other names of these sister desires; whichever one is dominant at the time is the one it should be called. The reason why all the previous things were said is now almost clear; but everything is somehow clearer when spoken than when left unsaid. For the irrational desire which overcomes the opinion tending toward the right, and is driven toward the pleasure of beauty, and is strongly reinforced by its kindred desires toward the beauty of bodies—this dominant power, taking its name from its very strength <gloss>from its strength <note>original: "ἀπ’ αὐτῆς τῆς ῥώμης"</note></gloss>, is called **Love** <gloss>Love <note>original: "ἔρως"</note></gloss>. But, my dear friend Phaedrus, do I seem to you, as I do to myself, to have been affected by some divine possession?
<margin>D</margin> **PHAEDRUS.** Certainly, Socrates; an unusual flow of eloquence has taken hold of you. **SOCRATES.** Listen to me then in silence. For truly, this place seems to be divine. Therefore, if I should often be seized by the nymphs <note>Socrates refers to the local spirits of the stream where they are sitting; "nympholepsy" was a state of divine frenzy or inspiration.</note> as the speech proceeds, do not be surprised. For even now I am speaking in a way that is not far from dithyrambs <note>Dithyrambs were emotional, wild hymns sung in honor of Dionysus.</note>. **PHAEDRUS.** What you say is very true. **SOCRATES.** You, indeed, are the cause of these things. But hear the rest, for perhaps the coming inspiration may be averted. These things shall be God's concern; let us return in our speech to the boy. Come then, most excellent one: that which we had to deliberate upon has been said and defined. Looking toward this definition, let us say what remains: what benefit or harm will likely result from the lover and the non-lover to the one who grants them his favors.
<margin>E</margin> For a man who is enslaved to lust and serving pleasures, it is necessary that he make his beloved as pleasant to himself as possible. To a sick man, anything that does not resist him is pleasant, but anything better or equal is annoying. Therefore, the lover will never willingly endure a beloved who is superior or equal, but will always make him inferior and more deficient. Now, the ignorant is inferior to the wise, the coward to the brave, the one who cannot speak to the orator, the slow to the quick-witted. Since these and even more mental evils are either innate or created in the beloved, the lover is glad for them and seeks to foster them. Otherwise, he is deprived of his immediate pleasure.
<margin>F</margin> Therefore, the lover must be envious, and by keeping the beloved away from many other beneficial associations—which would most help him become a man—he causes great harm. But the greatest harm of all is keeping him from that which would make him most wise. This happens to be divine philosophy, from which the lover must keep his beloved far away, fearing that if the boy becomes wiser, he will be held in contempt. In short, he ensures that the beloved remains ignorant of all things and looks only to the lover; being such a person, he will be most pleasant to the lover, but most ruinous to himself. Thus, in matters pertaining to the mind, the companionship of a man who possesses this "love" is in no way beneficial.
<margin>G</margin> After this, we must see how he who is forced to prefer the sweet over the good will care for the body of the one he loves, if it is entrusted to him. He will surely be seen pursuing someone soft and not sturdy, not nourished in the bright sun but under mixed shade, inexperienced in manly labors and dry sweats, but experienced in a delicate and unmanly way of life, adorned with artificial colors and external ornaments for lack of his own, and accustomed to all other things that follow from these. These things are clear, and it is not worth going further; let us conclude them in summary before moving on. Such a body, in wars and other great necessities, gives confidence to enemies, while friends and even the lovers themselves fear for it.
<margin>H</margin> This, then, being manifest, let it be dismissed. Next, we must say what benefit or what harm the intimacy and guardianship of the lover will provide for our possessions. Now, this is clear to everyone, but especially to the lover,

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...the substance of the thing. As if they knew it, they do not declare it at the beginning of the inquiry. But as they proceed, it follows, as is fair, that they speak things consistent neither with themselves nor with others. Therefore, let it not happen to you and me what we condemn in others; since there is a dispute between us whether friendship should be entered into with a lover rather than a non-lover, let us understand what love itself is and what power it has, after a definition has been established by consensus. And looking toward this and referring back to it, let us consider whether it brings profit or detriment. That love is a certain desire is manifest to all; but we are not ignorant that even those who do not love desire beautiful or good things. Therefore, so that we may understand how a lover is discerned from a non-lover, it is necessary to know that there are two dominant and leading ideas in each of us,
<margin>B</margin> which we follow wherever they lead. One is the desire for pleasures innate in us. The other is an acquired opinion that is a seeker of the best. These either sometimes agree in us, or sometimes are in sedition and discord; and now this one, now the other, prevails. When, therefore, opinion leads by reason toward that which is best and overcomes, this very power of living is called **temperance**. But when desire draws us without reason toward pleasures and commands us, this command is called **lust** <note>Latin: *libido*.</note>.
<margin>C</margin> Now, since lust is multiform and has many parts, it has many names, and whichever of these forms is most exuberant in someone makes that person named by its own title; it does not grant him any graceful or worthy surname. For concerning food, that which overcomes reason and what is fair and good—and is moreover the desire of other desires—is called gluttony; and it makes the one who has it called by this very name. Again, that which exercises a tyranny concerning drunkenness and leads the one it possesses there—it is clear what name it will have, and other names related to these, and names of related desires, where one especially dominates, it is manifest how they should be applied. But the reason for which we have said all the above is now almost clear; yet whether it is said or not, it will be clearer than if it had been omitted. For the desire without reason which overcomes the opinion tending toward right, and snatches one toward the pleasure of form, and being vehemently strengthened by related desires concerning the form of the body, it overcomes and prevails—taking its name <gloss>from its very strength <note>original: "ἀπ’ αὐτῆς τῆς ῥώμης"</note></gloss>, that is, by force and vehemence, it is called <gloss>**Love** <note>original: "ἔρως"</note></gloss>. Does it seem to you, O friend Phaedrus, as it does to me, that I have suffered something divine?
<margin>D</margin> **PHAEDRUS.** Truly indeed, O Socrates, a certain unusual and flowing abundance has taken hold of you. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, hear me in silence. For in truth this place seems divine. Wherefore, if I am more frequently seized by nymphs as the speech proceeds, do not wonder. Surely those things which I just sang were not far distant from dithyrambs. **PHAEDRUS.** You tell the absolute truth. **SOCRATES.** You indeed are the cause of these things. But hear the rest, lest that which is coming upon me should depart. These things shall be a care to God. Let us return in our dispute to the boy.
<margin>E</margin> Come then, O best of men: what that thing is about which we consult has been said and defined. Looking, therefore, to this, let us see what remains: what profit or harm is likely to come from the lover and the non-lover to the one who complies. It is necessary that a man enslaved to lust and serving pleasures should render his beloved as pleasant to himself as possible. But to a sick man, whatever does not resist is pleasant; but that which is better or equal is troublesome. Wherefore, the lover will never willingly endure a beloved who is more excellent or equal. He will always make him inferior and more needy as far as he can. The ignorant is worse than the wise, the timid than the brave, the one inept at speaking than the orator, the dull than the sharp. These and more evils of the mind are naturally present or made in the beloved; the lover rejoices in them and tries to bring others upon him besides. Otherwise, he is deprived of pleasure.
<margin>F</margin> Therefore, the lover must be envious of the beloved, and by removing him from every association and study from which he might emerge excellent, he hinders him greatly. Most of all, he is harmful by depriving him of that which makes one most prudent. Now, divine philosophy makes one most prudent, from which the lover compels the beloved to be far removed, fearing lest he be held in contempt if the boy becomes wiser. Finally, he does everything so that the boy may emerge ignorant of all things and admire the lover. When he is such, he will be most pleasant to the lover, but most pernicious to himself. And thus in those things that pertain to intelligence, association with a lover is harmful.
<margin>G</margin> Hereafter, it must be seen in what way he who is forced to prefer the sweet before the good is going to care for the body of the one he loves, if it has been committed to him. He will surely desire a body not solid, but soft and delicate, nourished not under the sun, but in the shade. It will be educated far from dangers and labors and dry sweats, with a feminine and delicate diet, adorned with foreign colors and external ornaments due to a lack of its own, and accustomed to other things similar to these. Since it would be unworthy to recount all these things at length, we will conclude them briefly for the present, so that we may follow the rest. Truly, such a habit of body in battles and any other great necessity, enemies indeed boldly attack, while friends and the lovers themselves fear greatly for him.
<margin>H</margin> But this must now be dismissed as manifest. Next, it must be said what profit or what harm the familiarity and guardianship of a lover provides us in external things. But this is manifest to all, especially to the lover,

<meta>This page continues Socrates’ first speech in the *Phaedrus*. Having defined Love as a form of "irrational desire" or "madness" directed toward beauty, Socrates is now detailing the specific harms a "lover" (one consumed by this madness) inflicts upon the "beloved" (the youth he pursues), as opposed to a "non-lover" (a rational friend).</meta>

# OF PLATO

<margin>A</margin> ...because the lover desires his beloved to be bereft of his most dear, most precious, and most divine possessions. He actually prays for the youth to be deprived of parents, kin, and friends, believing they will be obstacles to that most sweet intimacy he shares with the beloved. Furthermore, he thinks a youth who possesses much gold or other property will neither be easily captured nor, once caught, easily managed. For this reason, it is necessary for a lover—out of envy—to grieve at the beloved’s prosperity and rejoice at his adversity. He even desires the young man to live for a long time without a wife, without children, and without a home, wishing to enjoy his own sweetness for as long as possible. There are other evils as well, but for many of these, some spirit <note>Original Latin: *daemon*; referring to a guiding spirit or supernatural force that influences human affairs.</note> has mixed in a bit of pleasure right at the beginning.
<margin>B</margin> Just as nature has provided a certain unrefined delight for the flatterer—that most dangerous beast and greatest of calamities—and just as one might criticize a courtesan as harmful, along with many other such creatures and pursuits that are accustomed to delighting us daily; yet the lover, besides being harmful, is also the most bothersome of all in his daily company. For "likes are most pleasantly gathered with likes," <margin>Proverb.</margin> according to the old proverb. Indeed, equality of age, leading to equal pleasures because of similarity, gives birth to friendship. Nevertheless, even these relationships can bring too much satiety <note>Over-fullness or boredom.</note>. Indeed, necessity is heavy for everyone in every thing; and this is especially true of the lover toward his
<margin>C</margin> beloved when there is a lack of similarity. For the senior, clinging to the junior, does not leave him willingly by day or night, but is driven by necessity and a "frenzy" <note>Original Latin: *furore*; a translation of the Greek *oistros*, the "stinging fly" of passion.</note>. This frenzy drags the lover along as he sees, hears, touches, and perceives the beloved with every sense, so that he follows him constantly with immense pleasure. But for the beloved, what pleasure or what consolation will keep him there for an equal time so that he is not distressed by extreme annoyance? He must look at a senile and deformed face, and other things like it, which are unpleasant not only to see but even to hear about; he is always faced with a certain necessity of being "captured," while being observed always and everywhere by suspicious guards. He hears 
<margin>D</margin> untimely and immoderate praises and reproaches from the lover; these are intolerable when the lover is sober, but when he is drunk, they are not only intolerable but also most shameful due to his excessive and open license in speaking to the point of exhaustion. Moreover, while he is in love, he is ruinous and burdensome. But when he ceases to love, he becomes unfaithful for the future toward the one whom he finally induced, with many oaths, prayers, and promises, to endure his hateful company in the hope of rewards. At last, when it is time to pay him back, he accepts another ruler and presiding officer within himself—namely, mind and temperance <note>Latin: *menté tēperantiámq*; meaning the return of his sanity and self-control.</note>—in place of love and madness. Now having become another person, he deceives the beloved. Then the beloved, 
<margin>E</margin> remembering the things once said and done, demands the favor of those benefits, thinking he is speaking to the same man. But the other, out of shame, neither dares to confess he has changed, nor does he find a way to fulfill the oaths and promises of that previous insane rule, now that he has regained his mind and temperance. He fears that if he does the same things as before, he will again become similar to what he once was. Thus it happens that the one who loved before now flees, and having changed, goes away—"as if the tile had fallen the other way" <note>A Greek proverb (*ostrakou metapestontos*) referring to a total reversal of fortune or a sudden change in sides, based on a game of chance played with a shell or tile.</note>. The other is forced to pursue him, taking it hard and turning to imprecations <note>Curses or bitter prayers.</note>. Truly, he was deceived from the beginning, since he did not know he should never have gratified the mind of a lover (who is necessarily insane), but rather a man who is free from love and possesses his mind. Otherwise, it would be 
<margin>F</margin> necessary to commit oneself to a man who is unfaithful, morose, envious, annoying, ruinous to one's possessions, ruinous to the condition of one's body, and by far most ruinous to the discipline of the soul—than which nothing is, or ever will be, more venerable among gods and men. These things, O boy, must be considered; and one must further notice that the lover’s friendship consists not of any benevolence, but of a certain greed for fulfillment, like hunger.

> As the wolf loves the lamb, so the lover loves the boy. <note>original: *Vt lupus ipſe agnum, puerum ſic ardet amator.*</note>

This is what I predicted, O Phaedrus. Do not expect to hear me further; let the speech have its end here. PHÆD. But I thought half the discussion was over, and that as much remained to be said about the non-lover—that one should favor him instead, and enumerating how many good things are in him. Why do you stop now, O Socrates? SO. Did you notice, Phaedrus, that 
<margin>G</margin> I am no longer singing dithyrambs <note>Dithyrambs were wild, passionate hymns; Socrates is joking that his speech is becoming too poetic and manic.</note>, even though my speech is in a critical mode? If I were to proceed to praise the other, what do you think I would do? Do you not perceive that I am clearly inspired by the Nymphs, both by your doing and by divine providence? Therefore, I say in summary: there are as many good things in the one as we have counted evils in the other. Why is there need for many words? Enough has been said about both. And so, the story will suffer what it must. I am now crossing the river and going away, before I am compelled by you to do something greater. PHÆD. Not yet, O Socrates, not before the heat passes. Do you not see that it is now almost noon—the hour they call "the stationary hour"? <note>The time of day when the sun seems to stand still; a moment of spiritual intensity in the dialogue.</note> Let us wait and talk about what has been said; then, as soon as it cools down, let us go.

<column-break/>

<margin>A-G</margin> <note>The right-hand column contains the original Ancient Greek text corresponding to the Latin/English translation provided in the left-hand column.</note>

SOCRAT. You are divine regarding speeches, O Phaedrus, and truly wonderful. I think, indeed, that of the orations held in these times, no one has been the author or cause of more than you...

He famously compares the lover's "affection" to a wolf's appetite for a lamb before attempting to flee the poetic frenzy brought on by the local spirits.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Phaedrus. Socrates has just finished a speech criticizing the "lover" in favor of the "non-lover," but he now feels a sense of religious dread, realizing he has insulted the god Love (Eros).</meta>

# PHÆDRUS.

...either by speaking yourself, or by somehow compelling others to do so. I except Simmias the Theban <note>A student of Socrates known for his prolific love of discourse.</note> from this account; but you, Phaedrus, far surpass everyone else. Now, you seem to have been the cause of yet another speech being delivered, and not a peaceful one at that. PHÆ. But how so, and what speech is this? SOC. My good friend, just as I was about to cross the river, the divine and customary sign <note>original: *daimonion*; Socrates frequently refers to an inner "divine voice" that warns him against certain actions.</note> that usually comes to me occurred. Whenever it happens, it forbids me from doing what I am about to do. I seemed to hear a voice from that very spot, which forbade me to depart until I had purified myself, as if I had committed some offense against the divine. I am indeed a seer <note>original: *mantis*</note>, though not a particularly excellent one—rather like those who are poor at writing, I am only sufficient for my own needs. So, I already clearly understand my error. For the soul itself, my friend, possesses a certain prophetic power. Indeed, I felt a bit troubled even while I was delivering that speech, and I was somehow bothered, as Ibycus <note>A Greek lyric poet.</note> says, "lest by sinning against the gods I should win honor among men." But now I realize my mistake. PHÆ. What do you mean? SOC. You have brought a terrible, Phaedrus—a terrible speech yourself, and you have forced me to speak one too. PHÆ. In what way? SOC. It was foolish and somewhat impious. What could be more terrible than that? PHÆ. Nothing, if what you say is true. SOC. Well then, do you not believe Love <note>original: *Eros*</note> to be the son of Aphrodite, and a certain god? PHÆ. So it is said. SOC. But it was not said by Lysias, nor by your speech, which was uttered through my mouth after you had enchanted it. If Love is a god or something divine, as he certainly is, he cannot be an evil thing. Yet the two speeches we just spoke treated him as if he were such. In this way, they sinned against Love. Furthermore, their foolishness was quite clever: while saying nothing sound or true, they acted solemn as if they were something great, in the hopes of deceiving some little men and winning their favor. Therefore, my friend, it is necessary for me to be purified. For those who sin in the telling of myths, there is an ancient purification <note>original: *katharmos*</note> which Homer did not know, but Stesichorus did. For when he was deprived of his sight because of his slander of Helen, he was not ignorant of the cause, as Homer was; rather, being a man of the Muses, he recognized the reason and immediately wrote:

> "That story was not true,
> Nor did you sail in the well-benched ships,
> Nor did you reach the towers of Troy." <note>This is the famous "Palinode of Stesichorus," where he recanted the traditional story of Helen of Troy to regain his sight.</note>

And having composed the whole poem, which is called a "palinode" <note>A "song sung again" or a formal retraction.</note>, he immediately recovered his lost sight. Now, I shall be wiser than those men in this one respect: before any evil befalls me for slandering Love, I shall attempt to offer him my palinode, and I will do so with my head bare, not veiled out of shame as I was before. PHÆ. Socrates, you could not say anything more pleasing to me than this. SOC. For you remember, my good Phaedrus, how shamelessly the two speeches were spoken—both the one read from the book and the one I spoke myself. If some noble and gentle man, who loved another of like character, or had ever loved one before, were to hear us saying that lovers stir up great enmities over small causes and are envious and harmful toward their beloveds—don't you think he would imagine he was hearing men raised among sailors who had never seen a noble love? Would he not utterly refuse to agree with our criticisms of Love? PHÆ. By Zeus, Socrates, he likely would. SOC. Out of shame before such a man, and out of fear of Love himself, I desire to wash out that "salty" <note>original: *halmyran*; a metaphor for the bitter or unpleasant taste of the previous speech.</note> discourse with a "potable" one. I also advise Lysias to write as soon as possible that one should grant favors to a lover rather than a non-lover, all else being equal. PHÆ. Be assured it shall be so. For once you have spoken the praise of the lover, I will certainly compel Lysias to write a speech on the same subject. SOC. I trust you in this, as long as you remain who you are. PHÆ. Speak then, with confidence. SOC. Where is that boy I was speaking to? Let him hear this speech too, so that he does not rashly grant favors to a non-lover before he hears what I have to say. PHÆ. He is right here at your side, whenever you wish. SOC. Understand then, my fair boy, that the previous speech was by Phaedrus, son of Pythocles, from the town of Myrrhinus; but the one I am about to speak is by Stesichorus, son of Euphemus, from Himera. And it must begin like this: "The story is not true which says that when a lover is present, one should rather grant favors to the non-lover because the lover is mad and the non-lover is sane." For if it were simply true that madness is an evil, the statement would be fine. But as it is, the greatest of blessings come to us through madness, provided it is given as a divine gift. For the prophetess at Delphi and the priestesses at Dodona, when they were mad, brought many noble things to Greece both in private and public life; but when they were sane, they achieved little or nothing. And if we were to mention the Sibyl and others who use inspired divination to predict many things for many people and guide them toward the future, we would be speaking at great length about what is obvious to everyone. This, however, is worth testifying: that the ancients who gave names to things did not consider madness <note>original: *mania*</note> to be something shameful or a reproach. Otherwise, they would not have connected this very name to the most beautiful art by which the future is discerned, calling it the "manic" <note>original: *manikē*</note> art. Rather, believing it to be a noble thing when it occurs by divine allotment, they gave it that name. But the people of today, tastelessly inserting the letter "t," call it the "mantic" <note>original: *mantikē*; the Greek word for prophecy.</note> art. In the same way, the investigation of the future by sane people through birds and other signs...

<column-break/>

...either of their own accord or by compelling others. I except Simmias the Theban. But you far excel others. And now you seem to have been the cause of some speech being delivered by me. PHÆ. You certainly do not declare war, but in what way, and what speech? SOC. When I was about to cross the river, the divine and customary sign happened to me; which, as often as it occurs, forbids me to do what I was about to do. Hence I seemed to hear a voice, which forbids me to depart before I have performed an expiation, as if I had offended against God. I am therefore a seer, though by no means a good one, but like those who know their letters poorly, I am sufficient for myself. Therefore, I now clearly understand my offense. Indeed, O friend, there is also something of prophecy in the soul. For it disturbed me even before while I was speaking; whence I somehow feared lest, as according to Ibycus, I might offend against the gods while attaining glory among men. Now I perceive in what I have offended. PHÆ. What is it? SOC. A grave, O Phaedrus, a grave speech, I say, you have brought, and you have compelled me to speak. PHÆ. In what way? SOC. A foolish and in a way impious one: what could be graver than that? PHÆ. None, if you tell the truth. SOC. What then of Love? Do you not think him the son of Venus, and some God? PHÆ. He is said to be. SOC. Yet not by Lysias, nor from your speech, which was brought forth through my mouth by you, as if drawn out by some incantation. But if Love is, as he certainly is, a God or something divine, he could not be evil. Yet the speeches about him were held as if he were evil. In this we have offended against Love. And yet these discussions of ours seem very inept, however polished they may be: for although they contain nothing sincere or true, they nevertheless boast as if they were of great value, if they should be approved by some deceived little men. Therefore, O friend, it is necessary for me to be purified. There is, moreover, for those who sin by storytelling, an ancient purification which Homer did not know, but Stesichorus did. For being deprived of his eyes on account of his disparagement of Helen, he was not ignorant of the cause of his blindness, like Homer, but as a man of the Muses, he recognized it. And so he immediately made those verses:

> "That story was not true, nor in the tall ships
> Did you depart in flight, nor did you reach the citadels of Troy."

And so, having published the poem which they call a *palinodia*, that is a recantation, he immediately recovered his lost sight. I, however, shall be wiser than both in this, that before any evil happens to me on account of the disparagement of Love, I will try to render a palinode to him, and indeed with an open head, not as above, veiled for shame. PHÆ. Truly, Socrates, you could do nothing more pleasing to me than this. SOC. For you remember, O Phaedrus, how impudently the speech was read from the book, and spoken by me also concerning the lover. For if some noble and modest man, who loves or has loved another like himself, should hear us when we say that lovers stir up the greatest enmities for the smallest causes, and are envious and harmful men to those they love, he would think he was hearing men educated on ships who had never seen any liberal love, nor would he in any way concede to us the things we bring forward in disparagement of Love. PHÆ. Perhaps, by Jove, Socrates. SOC. Fearing this man, and dreading Love himself, I desire to wash away that salty and noxious speech to our ears with a potable discourse. I advise Lysias also to write as soon as possible that one should indulge a lover rather than a non-lover, all else being equal. PHÆ. Know for certain that it will be so. For after you have praised the lover, it will be necessary for Lysias to be compelled by me to write the same. SOC. That I believe, as long as you are who you are now. PHÆ. Come, speak with a brave heart. SOC. Hey, where is that boy to whom I held the former speech, so that he may hear this one too, lest if he hears it not, he should rashly obey a non-lover. PHÆ. He is always close to you, as long as you desire. SOC. Thus then, O excellent boy, consider that the former speech was of Phaedrus the Myrrhinusian, son of Pythocles; but the following will be of Stesichorus son of Euphemus, the amiable man.

<margin>The greatest goods come through madness divinely granted.</margin>This will be the beginning of it: "That story is not true, which commands that favors be granted to the non-lover rather than the lover because the lover is mad and the non-lover is sane." For if it were simply true that madness is an evil, it would have been rightly said by us. But now the greatest of goods come to us through madness granted by a certain divine gift. For both the prophetess who predicted the future at Delphi, and the priests at Dodona, being mad indeed, brought many and great advantages privately and publicly to the Greek people; but truly while they are sane, few or none. And if we refer to the Sibyl, and others whoever have used divine prophecy, how many things predicting for the future they have profited, we would extend the speech too far, and bring forth a matter manifest to all. This, however, is worthy to be testified, that the ancients who imposed names on things did not think madness a foul thing, nor ignominious. For they would not have annexed this name to the most excellent art by which the future is discerned, calling it *manikē*, that is madness, but as if madness were some good thing when it proceeds from divine lot, they gave such a name to the honorable art. But now those juniors, having inserted the letter *t*, too unskillfully called it *mantikē*. Indeed, the investigations of the future by sane men through birds and other omens, as being from...

<summary>Socrates realizes that his previous speech slandering Love was an act of impiety and resolves to perform a "palinode" or recantation. He begins a new discourse arguing that Love is a form of "divine madness" which, like the inspiration of prophets at Delphi and Dodona, is a source of humanity's greatest blessings.</summary>
