<meta>This page continues Socrates' "Palinode" or retraction speech in the Phaedrus. Having previously spoken against love, he now argues that certain forms of "madness"—specifically those sent by the gods—are actually the source of our greatest blessings. He is currently distinguishing between human madness and divine inspiration.</meta>

# PLATO

...proceeding from the conjecture of human intelligence, they named it the mental and historical art of augury. <margin>Augury, Augury</margin> Later generations, changing a small letter to make it more honorable, adorned it with a nobler name <note>The Greek text plays on the words *oionoistike* (mental search) and *oionistike* (augury/prophecy). Socrates argues that the ancients valued divine prophecy higher than mere human prediction.</note>. Therefore, just as prophecy is more perfect and excellent than the conjecture of augury—in name as in truth—so the ancients testify that the madness proceeding from God is more noble than human prudence. Furthermore, when the greatest diseases and hardships loom over mortals due to ancient crimes and divine indignation, a certain madness has sometimes appeared to certain people; by prophesying to those in need, it found a remedy, fleeing to prayers and the service of the gods. From this, obtaining purifications and rites of atonement, it rendered the possessed person safe for both the present and the future, finding a release from present evils for the one who is rightly maddened and possessed.

The third type of possession and madness comes from the Muses. Taking a tender and untouched soul, it rouses and inspires it through songs and other poetry; by adorning the countless deeds of the ancients, it instructs future generations. But he who approaches the gates of poetry without the madness of the Muses, trusting that he will become a good poet through mere art, is himself empty, and his poetry vanishes before that which proceeds from madness—the poetry of the prudent man is eclipsed.

I can relate so many, and even more, noble works of divine madness. Therefore, let us not fear this, nor let any argument terrify us into thinking we should prefer a prudent and sane friend over an inspired one. Let our opponent show, if he can, and carry away the victory by proving that love is not granted by the gods for the benefit of the lover and the beloved. We, on the other hand, must now demonstrate that such madness is given by the gods to men for their greatest happiness. This demonstration will be unbelievable to the clever, but believable to the wise. However, we must first understand the truth regarding the nature of the divine and human soul by looking at its passions and works. Let this be the beginning of the demonstration:

<margin>On the immortality of the soul. This is taken from Cicero's Tusculan Disputations II, word for word.</margin> Every soul is immortal. For that which is always in motion is eternal. But that which brings motion to another, and which is itself moved from elsewhere, must necessarily have an end to living when it has an end to motion. Therefore, only that which moves itself—because it is never deserted by itself—never ceases to be moved. Moreover, for all other things that are moved, this is the fountain, the very principle of moving. There is no origin for a principle; for all things arise from a principle, but the principle itself cannot be born from anything. For it would not be a principle if it were generated from elsewhere. And if it never arises, it never dies either; for if the principle were extinguished, it could neither be reborn from another nor create another from itself, since all things must arise from a principle. Thus it is that the principle of motion comes from that which is moved by itself. This can neither be born nor die. Otherwise, the whole heaven would collapse and all nature would stand still, never finding any force by which it might be moved by a first impulse.

Since it appears that what moves itself is immortal, one will not feel ashamed to say that this is the very substance and definition of the soul. For every body that receives motion from the outside is inanimate (soulless). But that which possesses motion within itself and from itself is animate (souled), as if this were the very nature of the soul. If this is so—that there is nothing else that moves itself except the soul—then the soul is necessarily ungenerated and immortal. Enough has been said regarding the immortality of the soul.

<margin>On the idea of the soul.</margin> Regarding its "idea" <note>The "Idea" or form—the essential nature of the soul.</note>, we must speak in this way: To describe what it is entirely would require a divine and very long narrative; but to describe what it is *like* is a task for a human and shorter discourse. Let us speak then in this manner. Let the soul be likened to the combined power of a pair of winged horses and a charioteer. Now, the horses and charioteers of the gods are all good and of good descent, but those of others are mixed. <margin>How the living being is formed.</margin> In our case, the ruler of the soul drives a pair of horses; one of the horses is noble and beautiful and of such stock, but the other is the opposite and of opposite descent. Thus, the driving of our chariot is necessarily difficult and troublesome.

We must now attempt to explain how a living being is called "mortal" or "immortal." All soul has care of all that is inanimate, and it traverses the whole heaven, appearing now in one form, now in another. When it is perfect and winged, it soars on high and governs the whole world. But the soul that has lost its wings is carried along until it takes hold of something solid; there it finds a dwelling place and takes on an earthly body, which appears to move itself because of the soul's power. This whole complex—soul and body joined together—is called a living being, and is surnamed "mortal." "Immortal," on the other hand, is not a term we can grasp by any rational discourse, but rather something we imagine; for though we have never seen nor sufficiently understood God, we imagine an immortal living being that possesses a soul and possesses a body, joined together for all time. But let these things be as God pleases. Now, let us state the cause for the loss of wings, why they fall away from the soul. It is something like this: The natural power of a wing is to lift what is heavy into the heights where the race of gods dwells. Of all things related to the body, the soul participates most in the divine. The divine is beautiful, wise, and good, and everything of that sort. By these the wings of the soul are chiefly nourished and increased; but by the foul, the evil, and the opposite, the wing withers and perishes. Jupiter <note>original: Iupiter; Zeus in the Greek text.</note>, the great leader in heaven, driving his winged chariot, goes first, ordering all things and providing for them. Him follows...

<column-break/>

...from thought produced by human intelligence, they called the art of augury "oionistike." This term the moderns now call "oionistike," grandly lengthening the 'o'. How much more perfect and more honorable prophecy is than augury—both the name and the work—the ancients testify, stating that the madness from God is more beautiful than the sobriety that comes from men. Furthermore, for those suffering from the greatest diseases and labors due to ancient divine wrath, madness—having entered in and acted as a prophet for those in need—found a release, taking refuge in prayers and services to the gods. Thence, obtaining purifications and initiations, it made the one possessing it safe for the present and the future, finding a release from present evils for the one who is rightly maddened and possessed.

The third type is the possession and madness from the Muses, which, taking a tender and pathless soul, rouses and inspires it to frenzy in songs and other poetry; by adorning the ten thousand deeds of the ancients, it educates those who come after. But whoever comes to the gates of poetry without the madness of the Muses, persuaded that he will be an adequate poet by art alone, is himself incomplete, and the poetry of the sober man is eclipsed by that of the inspired. These and even more noble works of madness coming from the gods I can tell you. Therefore, let us not be afraid of this; nor let any speech disturb us, trying to frighten us into thinking that one should choose the sober man as a friend rather than the inspired. But let that man, in addition to this, show and carry away the victory by proving that love is not sent by the gods for the benefit of the lover and the beloved.

We, on the other hand, must demonstrate the opposite: that such madness is given by the gods for the greatest good fortune. The proof will be untrustworthy to the clever, but trustworthy to the wise. It is necessary first to understand the truth about the nature of the soul, both divine and human, by observing its passions and works. The beginning of the proof is this: All soul is immortal. For that which is always in motion is immortal. That which moves another and is moved by another, having a cessation of motion, has a cessation of life. Only that which moves itself, because it does not leave itself, never ceases being moved, but is also the fountain and beginning of motion for all other things that are moved.

A beginning is ungenerated. For it is necessary that everything that is generated be generated from a beginning, but the beginning itself from nothing. For if a beginning were generated from something, it would not be a beginning. Since it is ungenerated, it must also be indestructible. For if the beginning were destroyed, it could neither be generated from something else, nor could anything else be generated from it, since all things must be generated from a beginning. Thus the beginning of motion is that which moves itself. This can neither be destroyed nor generated; otherwise the whole heaven and all generation, collapsing, would stand still and never again have a source from which they would be moved and come to be.

Since it has been shown that what is moved by itself is immortal, one will not be ashamed to say that this is the essence and definition of the soul. For every body that is moved from the outside is soulless (inanimate); but that which is moved from within itself is ensouled (animate), as this is the nature of the soul. If this is so—that what moves itself is nothing other than the soul—then the soul would necessarily be ungenerated and immortal. Regarding its immortality, enough has been said.

Regarding its "idea," we must speak as follows: What it is like in every way would be a matter of a divine and long description; but what it resembles is a matter of a human and shorter one. Let us speak in this way: Let it be likened to the innate power of a pair of winged horses and a charioteer. Now, the horses and charioteers of the gods are all good themselves and of good descent; but the horses of the others are mixed. First, our ruler drives a pair of horses; then, of the horses, one is beautiful and good and of such descent, but the other is of opposite descent and is the opposite. Thus, the driving in our case is necessarily difficult and troublesome.

How a living being was called "mortal" and "immortal," we must try to say. All soul cares for all that is soulless; it patrols the whole heaven, appearing now in one form, now in another. When it is perfect and winged, it soars on high and governs the whole universe. But the soul that has shed its wings is carried along until it takes hold of something solid; there, having settled and taken an earthly body, which seems to move itself because of the soul's power, the whole is called a living being—soul and body joined—and receives the name "mortal." "Immortal" is not a name derived from any rational discourse, but we imagine it—having neither seen nor sufficiently understood God—as an immortal living being, having a soul and having a body, which are joined together for all time. But let these things be as God pleases, and let them be so described.

Let us grasp the cause of the loss of wings, why they fall away from the soul. It is something like this: The power of a wing is naturally to lead what is heavy upward, soaring to where the race of gods dwells. Of all things belonging to the body, the soul has shared most in the divine; and the divine is beautiful, wise, good, and everything of that sort. By these the wings of the soul are nourished and grow most, but by the ugly and the evil and the opposites, they wither and perish. Now the great leader in heaven, Zeus <note>original: Ζεὺς</note>, driving a winged chariot, goes first, ordering all things and caring for them; him follows an army...

<summary>In this passage, Socrates classifies three types of divine madness (prophetic, ritual, and poetic) and begins a philosophical proof for the immortality of the soul, describing it as a "self-mover" and utilizing the famous allegory of the winged chariot.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the famous "Chariot Allegory" from Plato’s dialogue on love and rhetoric, the Phaedrus. Socrates is describing the journey of the soul as a winged chariot, comparing the easy flight of the gods to the difficult struggle of human souls to perceive ultimate Truth.</meta>

# PHAEDRUS

The army of gods and demons, <insert>A</insert> which is ordered into eleven parts. For Hestia <note>The goddess of the hearth, who stays behind to maintain the divine home while the other gods travel.</note> alone remains in the house of the gods; but as for the others, all who are ranked in the number of the twelve ruling gods lead in the order to which each was assigned. Many and blessed are the divine sights and paths within the heavens, which the race of happy gods travels, each performing his own task; and whoever wishes and is able follows them, for envy <note>original: "phthónos"</note> stands far outside the divine choir. But when they go to the banquet and the feast, they travel upward to the highest peak of the sub-celestial vault. The chariots of the gods, being well-balanced and easy to guide, move easily, but the others travel with difficulty. For the horse of evil nature <note>original: "kakēs hippos"; this refers to the dark, unruly horse representing base desires.</note> is heavy, leaning toward the earth and weighing down the chariot, if it has not <insert>B</insert> been well trained by its charioteer. There, the final labor and contest lie before the soul. For those called immortal, when they reach the summit, go outside and stand upon the back of heaven; and as they stand, the revolution of the spheres carries them around, and they contemplate what lies outside of heaven. But that supracelestial place <note>The realm of pure Forms, existing beyond the physical universe.</note> no poet here has ever yet praised, nor ever will praise worthily. It is like this: for one must dare to speak the truth, especially when speaking about Truth itself. For the colorless, formless, and intangible essence—which truly exists—can be seen only by the mind, the governor of the soul; and around this essence, the genus of true knowledge has its <insert>C</insert> place. Therefore, since the divine mind is nourished by pure intellect and knowledge, and every soul that is destined to receive its due, seeing that which truly *is* through the passage of time, it is content and nourished by the contemplation of the truth, and is happy until the revolution carries it back to the same place. In this circuit, it beholds Justice itself, it beholds Temperance, it beholds Knowledge—not the kind that is subject to change, nor that which differs according to the various things we now call "realities," but the knowledge that exists in that which is truly real. And having likewise beheld all other true beings and been feasted, it sinks back into the interior of heaven and returns home. When it arrives, the charioteer stops the horses at the manger and gives them ambrosia and <insert>D</insert> nectar to drink. This is the life of the gods.

As for the other souls, the one that follows God best and becomes most like Him raises the head of its charioteer into the supracelestial place and is carried around in the revolution; yet it is troubled by its horses and barely beholds the true beings. Another soul sometimes raises its head and sometimes sinks; because of the violence of the horses, it sees some things but not others. The rest of the souls follow, all longing for the upper world, but being unable to reach it, they are carried around submerged, trampling and colliding with one another, each trying to get ahead of the other. Thus, there is a final tumult, struggle, and extreme sweat, where through the fault of the charioteers, many souls are lamed and many <insert>E</insert> have their wings broken; all, having endured great labor, depart without achieving the vision of reality, and after departing, they feed upon the food of mere opinion. The reason for this great effort to see the Plain of Truth is that the proper pasture for the best part of the soul happens to be in that meadow, and the nature of the wing, by which the soul is lifted up, is nourished by this. And this is the law of Adrasteia <note>A name for Nemesis or Necessity; here it represents the inescapable law governing the soul’s reincarnation.</note>: whatever soul, having accompanied a god, has caught sight of any of the true things, shall be free from harm until the next circuit; and if it can always do this, it shall always remain unharmed. But when, being unable to follow, it fails to see, and meeting with some misfortune, is filled with forgetfulness and vice and grows heavy, and being weighed down, loses its wings and falls to the earth, then the law forbids it to be planted in any brutal nature in its first <insert>F</insert> birth. Instead, it decrees that the soul which saw the most shall pass into the seed of a man who will become a philosopher, a lover of beauty, or someone musical and given to love; the second, into a lawful king or a warrior and ruler; the third, into a statesman, a household manager, or a merchant; the fourth, into a hardworking athlete or a physician of the body; the fifth, into a life of prophecy or some mystery-rite initiate; the sixth, into a poet or some other imitative artist; the seventh, into a craftsman or a farmer; the eighth, into a sophist or a demagogue; the ninth, into a tyrant. In all these, whoever lives justly receives a better lot, and whoever lives unjustly, a worse one. For each soul does not return to the same place from which it came for ten thousand years (for it does not grow wings before that time), except the <insert>G</insert> soul of one who has philosophized without guile, or who has loved youths with philosophy <note>original: "paiderastēsantos meta philosophias"; in the Athenian context, this referred to a mentored relationship aimed at cultivating virtue and wisdom.</note>. These souls, in the third thousand-year circuit, if they have chosen this life three times in succession, thus regain their wings and depart in the three-thousandth year. But the others, when they have finished their first life, receive judgment. Having been judged, some go to the places of correction beneath the earth and pay the penalty; others, lifted by Justice to some place in heaven, live in a manner worthy of the life they led in human form. In the thousandth year, both groups arrive at the lot and choice of their second life, and each chooses whatever life it wishes. There, a human soul may pass into the life of a beast, and from a beast, one who was once human may return again to a human. For a soul that has never seen the <insert>H</insert>...

<column-break/>

The army of gods and demons is ordered into eleven parts. But Hestia remains alone in the house of the gods. As for the other gods, whoever is counted in the number of the twelve, each presides over his own assigned function. Therefore, many and blessed are the sights and paths within heaven, upon which the race of blessed gods gazes, each performing his own duty. One who is willing and able always follows. For envy <note>original: "Liuor"</note> is far removed from the divine choir. But when they go to the banquet and feast, they go up to the highest summit of heaven. The vehicles of the gods, well-handled by the reins and equally balanced, move easily, but those of others move with difficulty. For the horse that shares in wickedness is heavy, leaning and pulling toward the earth, for whichever charioteer has not nourished his horse well. Here indeed the final labor and struggle is set before the soul. For those which are called immortal, when they have reached the summit, go forth and stand upon the back of heaven. Once positioned there, the very revolution carries them around, and they behold those things which are outside of heaven.

<margin>Note how Plato places something outside of heaven.</margin> But that supracelestial place no one of our poets has yet praised, nor ever praised according to its dignity. It is indeed in this manner. For one must dare to speak the truth, especially when speaking about the truth. Without color, without shape, without being touchable, the truly existing essence is perceived only by the intellect, the governor of the soul; around which the genus of true knowledge occupies this place.

<margin>The intellect is the governor of the soul.</margin> Therefore, just as the thought of God is nourished by intellect and pure knowledge, so too every thought of the soul which is about to receive its fitting condition, having gazed for a time upon that which is, is nourished and rejoices in the contemplation of truth, until the revolution brings the circle back to the same point. In this circuit, it beholds Justice itself, it beholds Temperance, it beholds Knowledge—not that which is subject to becoming, nor that which is one thing in one place and another in another, such as those things which we now call "beings"; but that knowledge which is truly in that which is real. And having similarly contemplated the other things which truly exist and being nourished by them, it goes back inside heaven and returns home. When it has returned, the charioteer, stopping the horses at the manger, sets before them ambrosia and gives them nectar to drink afterward. And this is the life of the gods.

As for the other souls, that which has followed God best and been made like Him, lifts the head of the charioteer into the supracelestial place and is carried along with the revolution, but is troubled by the horses and barely beholds those things which truly exist. Another sometimes lifts its head and sometimes lowers it; but because of the violence of the horses, it sees some things and does not see others. The other souls, though all desiring the higher place, follow along; but being unable to reach it, they are carried around submerged, trampling on one another and crowding, each striving to go before the other. Thus there is a tumult and a struggle and extreme sweat. Here indeed, through the fault of the charioteers, many are lamed, many have many feathers broken; and all, having been entangled in great labor, depart without the vision of that which truly is; and after their departure, they use the food of opinion. For the sake of this, there is much effort to behold where the Plain of Truth may be. For from such a meadow, the best power of the soul receives its fitting nourishment, and the nature of the wings by which the soul is raised is fed by this.

<margin>New conditions of the souls</margin> And the rule of Adrasteia is an inevitable law of the divine power, which is this: that whatever soul, having accompanied God, has seen any of the truths, shall be unharmed until another circuit; and if it can always do this, it shall always remain unhurt. But if, being unable to keep up, it does not see, and having met with some chance, is filled with forgetfulness and wickedness and grows heavy, and being weighed down has broken its wings and fallen to the earth, then the law forbids this soul in its first birth to go into any brutal nature. Instead, it commands that the one which has seen the most should go into the birth of a man who is a philosopher, or a lover of beauty, or a musician, or a lover. The one in the second place, into a legitimate king, or a man of war and command. The third, into a governor of a republic, or a manager of a household, or a merchant. The fourth, into a hardworking athlete, or one who will deal with the healing and care of the body. The fifth, into those who will be prophets or involved in certain mysteries. The sixth, into a poet, or any other of those who are properly engaged in imitation. The seventh, into a craftsman or <margin>*In Greek: Geometrium.</margin> *a farmer. The eighth, into a sophist or a demagogue. The ninth, into a tyranny. In all these, whoever has lived life justly obtains a better lot, but whoever lives unjustly, a worse one.

<margin>The soul returns to the same place after ten thousand years.</margin> For into the same place from which each soul set out, it does not return for ten thousand years. For it does not recover its wings before this space of time, except for the soul of him who has philosophized without guile, or who has loved youths together with the study of wisdom. These indeed, in the third circuit of a thousand years, if they have chosen this same life again in succession, having thus recovered their wings, fly away after three thousand years.

The other souls, having reached the end of their first life, are judged. Having been judged, some go into the place of judgment under the earth and suffer the punishments they deserve there. Others, raised into a certain place in heaven by judgment, live there as is worthy of that life which they lived in human form. In the thousandth year, both return to receive the lot and choice of a second life; each selects that life which it wishes. <margin>The transformation of the human soul.</margin> Here even a human soul passes into the life of a beast, and from a beast back into a man, provided that the soul was once that of a man.

<meta>This page continues the "Chariot Allegory" from Plato’s Phaedrus. Socrates is explaining how the human soul, having fallen from the divine procession of the gods, can regain its "wings" and return to the contemplation of ultimate Truth through the experience of beauty and love.</meta>

# PLATONIS

For that which has never beheld the truth shall never come into this human form. <note>original: "figuram"</note> But it is necessary for a human being to understand according to what is called a Form <term>eidos</term>, proceeding from many sensations into a single concept gathered by reasoning. This is the recollection <term>anamnesis</term> of those things which our soul once saw when traveling with God, looking down upon those things we now say exist, and looking upward toward that which truly *is*. Therefore, the mind of the philosopher alone deservedly recovers its wings. For his memory is always, as far as possible, dwelling upon those things in which God, being present, is divine. By the right use of such reminders, a man who is always initiated into the perfect mysteries <note>Plato uses the language of religious initiation (like the Eleusinian Mysteries) to describe the philosopher's journey to truth.</note> alone truly becomes perfect. But being separated from human strivings and clinging to the divine, he is rebuked by the multitude as if he were out of his mind; yet he is full of God, though the multitude does not notice.

->A<-

->B<-

Here, then, falls the whole discourse concerning the fourth madness <note>Socrates identifies four types of divine madness: prophetic, ritual, poetic, and finally, the madness of love.</note>, by which someone, when seeing some beauty here and remembering that true beauty, recovers his wings, and having recovered them, strives to fly away. But since he is unable to do so, looking upward like a bird and despising lower things, he is accused of being possessed by madness. Thus, this divine alienation is the best of all alienations, and it arises from the best things, both for the one who has it and the one who shares in it; and he who is held by this madness, when he loves beautiful things, is called a lover. For as has been said, every human soul has by nature gazed upon the things that truly are; otherwise, it would not have entered into this living being.

->C<-

But to remember those things from the things that are here is not easy for everyone; neither for those who saw those things there for only a short time, nor for those who, having descended here, were so unfortunate that, being corrupted by certain associations, they have forgotten the sacred things they once beheld. Therefore, few remain who have enough memory left. These, when they see here some likeness of those things they beheld there, are struck with awe and are, as it were, transported out of themselves; yet they do not know what this feeling is, because they do not fully perceive it.

->D<-

In the likenesses here, we see no splendor of justice, temperance, or any of the other things precious to souls; rather, through obscure instruments, barely a few, approaching these images, perceive the nature of that which is represented. But beauty we were then permitted to see most clearly, when with that blessed choir we saw a happy vision and followed in contemplation—we with Jupiter <note>original: "Ioue"; the Roman name for the Greek god Zeus.</note>, others with another of the gods—and were initiated into the rites which it is lawful to call the most blessed of all. These we performed while we were ourselves whole and untouched by the evils that awaited us in the future, as we gazed upon whole, simple, immovable, and blessed visions, initiated in pure light, being pure ourselves and unmarked by this which we now carry about and call a "body," bound to it like an oyster to its shell. <note>original: "in modum ostreæ"</note>

->E<-

<margin>The words of Cicero from Book 2 of *On Ends*.</margin>
But these things must be credited to memory, for whose sake, out of a longing for those things we once saw, we have now extended our discourse.
<margin>Beauty alone is the most lovable of all things.</margin>
Beauty, as we have said, both shone out then as it moved with those things, and having arrived here, we perceived it most clearly reflecting through our most piercing sense. For sight is the sharpest sense in us, though we do not see wisdom with it. What burning loves would wisdom excite for itself if it were seen! The same reasoning applies to the other things that are lovable. But only beauty has had this lot, to be the most manifest and most lovable of all.

->F<-

He, then, who was not recently initiated into the mysteries, or rather has been corrupted, is not quickly moved from here to there toward beauty itself, when he looks upon a certain likeness here which is named after it. Therefore, he does not feel reverence when he looks, but surrendered to the habit of a four-legged beast, he strives to approach and copulate for pleasure; and behaving with wantonness, he neither fears nor feels shame to pursue pleasure against nature. But he who was recently purified by the rites, or who once contemplated many things, when he sees a face of divine form graced with beauty, or some incorporeal form, first he shudders, and some old fear returns to him; then, looking upon it, he honors it as a god; and unless he feared the charge of intense madness, he would offer sacrifice to his beloved as to a statue or a god. As he gazes, he is seized by a change, a sweat, and an unusual heat, following the shudder. For when he receives the influx of beauty through his eyes, he grows warm, by which the nature of the wings is watered; but once he has grown warm, the parts concerning the sprouting melt, which for a long time, being hardened and closed up, prevented the shoot from germinating. When the nourishment has flowed in, the shafts of the wings, swelling from the very roots, strive to break out through the whole form of the soul. For once, the whole soul was supported by wings. At that time, it all seethes and leaps forward; and just as infants, when they are cutting teeth, are vexed by itching and pain in the gums, so the soul of one growing wings seethes and is affected by tickling and distress.

->G<-

Therefore, when it gazes upon the beauty of the boy, drinking in the desire flowing from there, it is watered and warmed; then it rests from its pain and rejoices. But when it is far away and the passages through which the wing strives to spring have dried up, being parched and constricted, they shut in the germ of the wings. This, being shut in together with that desire and the influx, leaping within like a pulse, pricks each of its own passages. Thus the whole soul, wounded on every side by the sting,

->H<-

<column-break/>

...never beheld the truth shall come into this form. For it is necessary for a man to understand according to what is called Form <term>eidos</term>, proceeding from many sensations into one concept gathered by reasoning. This is the recollection of those things which our soul once saw when traveling with God, looking down upon those things we now say exist, and looking up into that which truly *is*. Wherefore rightly the mind of the philosopher alone is winged. For it is always in memory, as far as possible, of those things in which God, being present, is divine. By the right use of such reminders, a man who is always initiated into the perfect mysteries alone truly becomes perfect. But standing aside from human strivings and becoming close to the divine, he is rebuked by the many as being disturbed, but he is full of god <term>enthousiazōn</term>, though the many do not notice.

->B<-

Here, then, comes the whole discourse concerning the fourth madness, which, when someone sees the beauty here, remembering the true beauty, grows wings and, being winged, is eager to fly away, but being unable, like a bird looking upward and neglecting the things below, is blamed for being in a mad state. Thus, this of all inspirations is the best and from the best, both for him who has it and him who shares it; and he who partakes of this madness and loves beautiful things is called a lover. For as has been said, every human soul has by nature gazed upon the things that are (or else it would not have come into this living being); but to remember those things from these things is not easy for every soul, neither for those who saw the things there briefly, nor for those who...

->C<-

...falling here were unfortunate, so that through certain associations turning toward injustice, they have forgotten the sacred things they then saw. Few indeed are left who have enough memory present. These, when they see some likeness of the things there, are struck with awe and are no longer masters of themselves. But they do not know what this passion is, because they do not perceive it sufficiently. In the likenesses here of justice and temperance and whatever else is precious to souls, there is no light; but through dull organs, barely a few, approaching the images, behold the nature of that which is imaged. But beauty was then bright to see, when with a happy choir we saw a blessed vision and...

->D<-

...spectacle, following—we with <gloss>as</gloss> Zeus, and others with another of the gods—they saw and were initiated into the mysteries which it is lawful to call most blessed; which we celebrated while being ourselves whole and untouched by the evils that awaited us in later time; gazing upon whole, simple, calm, and happy visions, being initiated and beholding them in pure light, being pure ourselves and unmarked by this which we now carry about and call a "body," bound to it like an oyster. These things, then, let us grant to memory, for whose sake we have now spoken at greater length out of longing for the things of then. But concerning beauty, as we said, it shone among those things. And having come here, we have grasped it...

->E<-

...shining most clearly through the clearest of our senses. For sight comes to us as the sharpest of the senses through the body, though wisdom <term>phronēsis</term> is not seen by it. For it would provide terrible loves if it provided any such clear image of itself coming to the sight, and so with all other lovable things. But now beauty alone has had this lot, to be most manifest and most lovable. He, then, who was not recently initiated, or who is corrupted, is not quickly carried from here to there toward beauty itself, when he gazes upon that which here bears its name. So he does not feel reverence when he sees it, but giving himself over to pleasure after the fashion of a four-legged beast, he attempts to mount and beget children; and consorting with insolence, he neither fears nor is ashamed to pursue pleasure against nature. But he who was recently initiated, who was a spectator of many things, when he...

->F<-

...sees a god-like face, beauty well-imitated, or some form of body, first he shudders, and some of the terrors of that time come over him; then looking upon it, he reverences it as a god, and if he did not fear the reputation of being utterly mad, he would sacrifice to his beloved as to a cult-image and a god. As he sees him, after the shudder, a change and sweat and unusual heat takes hold of him. For having received the emanation of beauty through his eyes, he grows warm, by which the nature of the wing is watered. When he has grown warm, the parts around the sprout melt, which for a long time, having been closed by hardness, prevented it from budding. When the nourishment has flowed in, the shaft of the wing swells and begins to grow from the root under the whole form of the soul. For it was once all winged. It seethes, then, in this state, and leaps up. And just as the condition of those...

->G<-

...cutting teeth always occurs around the teeth when they are just sprouting, itching and irritation always in the gums, so also does the soul suffer when it begins to grow wings. It seethes and is irritated and tickled while growing its wings. When, then, looking toward the beauty of the boy, receiving parts that come and flow from there (which for this reason are called "desire" <note>original: "himeros"; Plato makes a pun here on *himeros* and *mere*, meaning "parts" that flow into the lover.</note>), it is watered and warmed, it is relieved from the pain and rejoices; but when it is apart and grows dry, the mouths of the passages where the wing starts to grow, closing up, shut in the budding of the wing, and the budding shut in with desire, leaping like a pulse, pricks each passage for itself. <meta>This page continues Socrates's "Palinode" or speech on the divine nature of Love (Eros) from Plato’s Phaedrus. Having established that the soul is like a winged chariot, Socrates now describes the physical and psychological effects of "re-growing" those wings when one encounters beauty on earth.</meta>

# PHAEDRUS

<margin>B</margin> Stirred and tormented, the soul is again delighted when it remembers beauty. From the mixture of these two—the novelty and the vehemence of the passion—it is vexed, and in its anxiety, it rages and goes mad. Thus affected, it can neither sleep by night nor stay still by day because of its frenzy, but runs everywhere, struck by the desire to see the beautiful one. But when it sees him and drinks in that flow of longing, those parts that were previously obstructed and closed now open and release. As the soul breathes again, it is freed from these stings and pains. For the present, it is soothed by this most sweet pleasure, so that it never willingly leaves these charms behind. It values the beloved above all others; it consigns parents, brothers, and all friends to oblivion. It is not even moved when its inheritance is wasted through neglect. <margin>B</margin> It utterly despises the national customs and honors in which it used to take pride, and is ready to serve and sleep wherever it is permitted, as long as it is closest to the object of its desire. For it does not only worship and venerate the beautiful one, but has found in him the only physician for its most grievous troubles. This passion, O noble youth to whom I speak, men call <term>Eros</term> <note>original: "ἔρωτα", the Greek word for passionate love</note>. But if you were to hear what the gods call it, you would likely laugh because of your youth. Some of the "Sons of Homer" <note>The Homeridae were a group of rhapsodes or performers who claimed descent from the poet Homer and preserved "secret" or apocryphal verses.</note> pass down from their hidden poems two verses addressed to Love, one of which is quite insolent and not very metrical. They say:

> Mortals indeed call him "Eros," the winged one;
> But the Immortals call him "Pterota," because of the necessity of growing wings.

One may believe these verses or not, but <margin>C</margin> the cause and the condition of lovers is exactly this. Those who were followers of Zeus, when captured by love, can bear the burden of the "Winged One" <note>original: "pternonymon", a pun on Pterota/Eros</note> with greater constancy. But those who served Ares <note>The god of war.</note> and circled the heavens with him, when they are ensnared by love and think they are being wronged by the beloved, are easily provoked to slaughter <margin>D</margin> and are carried away headlong to kill both themselves and their beloveds. 

And so, according to which of the gods each person followed in the celestial dance, they honor and imitate that god as much as they can while they live and remain uncorrupted; in this manner, they conduct their lives and present themselves to their beloveds and others. Therefore, each person chooses a love from the ranks of the beautiful according to their own character, and as if that person were their own god, they fashion and adorn them like a statue, as if to honor and worship them. Those who follow Zeus seek a beloved whose soul is "Zeus-like." They consider whether the beloved is by nature inclined toward philosophy and leadership; and when they find such a one and love him, they do everything in their power to ensure he becomes so. If they have not previously entered into this pursuit, they apply themselves to learning it from wherever they can and proceed with the work themselves. Investigating the nature of their own god from within themselves, they finally achieve their goal because they are compelled to fix their mental gaze upon the god with intense focus. Then, when they touch him through memory, they are inspired by the divine and take from him their habits and pursuits, as far as a human can participate in God. Because they attribute the cause of all this to the beloved, they are even more ardently inflamed with affection. And if they draw from Zeus, like the priestesses of Bacchus <note>original: "bacchae", followers of Dionysus who were filled with divine madness.</note>, they pour it into the soul of the beloved, making him as similar as possible to their own god. <margin>E</margin> Those who followed Hera seek a royal soul; and having found him, they do the same things toward him. Likewise, the followers of Apollo and each of the other gods, imitating their respective deity, seek a youth who is naturally suited to that god. When they have gained him, they act by imitating the god themselves and by persuading and guiding the youth into the pursuits and character of that deity, as much as they are able. They do not use envy or ill-will toward their beloveds, but strive with all their might to form them into a perfect likeness of themselves and the god they worship. The care and the goal of true lovers, if they achieve what they desire, is indeed as I have described; and a noble and happy gift comes from the friend driven mad by love to his beloved, if he is captured. 

The person who is captured is caught in this way. At the beginning of this myth, we divided each soul into three parts: <margin>F</margin> we posited two forms of horses and a third form, the charioteer. Let these remain for us now. One of the horses, we say, is good, and the other is not. What the virtue of the good horse is, or the depravity of the bad one, we have not yet fully stated, but now we must. The good horse is of an excellent build, upright in appearance, with well-defined limbs, a high neck, a slightly hooked nose, white in color, with black eyes. He is a lover of honor with temperance and modesty, a companion to true glory; he needs no whip but is guided by command and reason alone. <margin>G</margin> The other horse is crooked, bulky, and haphazardly put together, with a stiff, thick neck and a short throat, a flat face, dark color, grey eyes shot with blood, insolent and arrogant, with shaggy, deaf ears, hardly obeying the whip and the spurs. 

Therefore, when the charioteer beholds the face of the beloved, and his whole soul is warmed through sensation and filled with the stings of tickling and desire, the horse that is obedient to the charioteer, constrained as usual by shame, holds himself back from leaping upon the beloved. But the other horse can no longer be restrained by spurs or whips, but leaps and, carried away by violence, torments his yoke-mate and the charioteer, dragging them toward the pleasures of Venus <note>original: "Veneris", referring to sexual desire or Aphrodite.</note>. At first, they resist him...

<summary>Socrates describes how lovers try to mold their beloveds into the likeness of the god they once followed in heaven, and introduces the physical characteristics of the two horses: the noble, white horse of self-control and the unruly, dark horse of lust.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Socrates's famous allegory of the soul as a chariot. We are currently witnessing the struggle between the charioteer (Reason) and the two horses—the white horse of Spirit and the black horse of Appetite—as they encounter a beautiful youth on earth.</meta>

# OF PLATO

...indignant that they are being dragged toward such heavy and unjust things. At last, when <margin>A</margin> this evil does not cease, they are driven forward and finally yield, agreeing to do what they are commanded. Thus they approach the glowing one and gaze upon his radiant face. When the charioteer beholds him, his memory is carried back to the very nature of Beauty itself; he sees it once more standing with Temperance <note>original: "σωφροσύνη" (sophrosyne), meaning moderation or self-control</note> upon a holy pedestal. Seeing this, he is struck with fear and falls backward in awe. At the same time, he is forced to pull the reins back so strongly that both horses are made to sit upon their haunches—the one horse willingly, because it does not struggle, but the insolent horse quite against its will. As they move further away, the one horse, <margin>B</margin> out of shame and wonder, wets the entire soul with sweat. But the other horse, once it is free from the pain caused by the bit and the fall, barely catches its breath before it breaks out in angry rebukes. It rails against the charioteer and its yoke-mate, accusing them of cowardice and for deserting their post and agreement out of fear. Again, it compels them to approach against their will, and only with difficulty does it grant their plea to put it off until later. When the appointed time comes, which the horses pretend to have forgotten, the charioteer reminds them; urging, neighing, and pulling, he compels them again to address the beloved with the same words. But when they have drawn near, the horse stoops down, extends its tail, bites the bit, and <margin>C</margin> pulls with utter shamelessness. But the charioteer, suffering the same shock as before, falls back as if from a starting-gate <note>The Latin "carcere" and Greek "ὑσπλήγος" refer to the starting barrier in a race-track.</note>; he pulls the bit back even more violently from the teeth of the wicked horse, covering its reviling tongue and jaws with blood, and forcing its legs and haunches to the ground, he compels it to suffer punishments. When this wicked horse has suffered such things many times, it finally abandons its insolence; now humbled, it follows the foresight of the charioteer. And when it sees the beautiful youth, it is consumed with fear, so that it eventually happens that the lover's soul follows the youth with a certain reverence and awe. Therefore, as the youth is tended with every service as if he were equal to a god by a lover who is not pretending, but is truly <margin>D</margin> affected in this way—and since the youth is by nature a friend to the one who honors him—he eventually enters into a shared friendship with the lover. Even if he had been deceived before by the slanders of his companions or others, who said it was shameful to associate with a lover and thus caused him to reject the lover, as time goes on, his age and the natural order of things lead him to welcome the lover into his company. For it is never decreed by fate that the evil should be a friend to the evil, nor that the good should not be a friend to the good. Once the youth has accepted the lover's conversation and company, the benevolence of the lover, now drawn closer, compels the beloved to marvel at him. He perceives that the goodwill of all his other friends and kinsmen is of no account when compared to this divinely inspired friend. <margin>E</margin> And as they continue this for a long time, drawing near to one another in the gymnasiums and other gatherings, then the fountain of that flowing stream—which Zeus, when he was captured by love for Ganymede <note>In Greek myth, the Trojan prince Ganymede was so beautiful that Zeus, in the form of an eagle, carried him to Olympus to be the cupbearer of the gods.</note>, called <term>imeros</term> <note>original: "ἵμερον", a term for the "fluid" or "flow" of desire</note>, that is, a flowing desire—pours abundantly upon the lover. Part of it is absorbed by him, and part of it flows out when he is full. Just as a breath of air or an echo bounces back from smooth and solid bodies to the place from which they came, so the stream of beauty reflects back into the beautiful youth through his eyes. It reaches the soul, where it is naturally inclined to go, and watering the passages of the wings, it causes them to sprout, filling the soul of the beloved with love in return. <margin>F</margin> He loves, then, but is uncertain what he loves; he neither knows his own state nor can he explain it. Just as one who has caught an eye infection from another cannot name the cause of his ailment, he does not realize that he is seeing himself in the lover as if in a mirror. Therefore, when the lover is present, the youth's pain ceases just as the lover's does; but when the lover is absent, he longs and is longed for in turn, possessing a "counter-love" <note>original: "ἀντέρωτα" (anterota), or reciprocal love</note> which is an image of love. He calls it, and believes it to be, not love, but friendship. His desire is much like the lover's, though weaker: he wants to see, touch, kiss, and lie down with him; and as is likely, he soon does these things. In their intimacy, the lover's <margin>G</margin> intemperate horse has much to say to the charioteer, demanding a small pleasure in exchange for many labors. But the youth's horse has nothing to say; though bursting with desire and confusion, it embraces the lover and kisses him, welcoming him as a most dear friend. When they lie together, it is not of a mind to refuse whatever favor the lover might ask. On the other hand, the yoke-mate and the charioteer resist these things with shame and reason. If, therefore, the better parts of their minds prevail, leading them to an ordered life and the study of philosophy, they spend their life here in happiness and harmony, masters of themselves and modest. They have enslaved that part of the soul in which vice dwelt and liberated that part where virtue resides. <margin>H</margin> At the end of this life, they fly away, light and winged, having won one of the three truly Olympic wrestling bouts. No greater good can be brought to man either by human temperance or divine madness. But if they follow a more worldly life, void of philosophy though ambitious, perhaps in a fit of drunkenness or some other careless license, their intemperate horses will catch their souls off guard...

<margin>And he makes mention of the favor of Aphrodite.</margin> <margin>A</margin> ...and they move forward, led on, yielding and agreeing to do what is commanded. And they came to the beloved and saw his flashing sight... <margin>B</margin> ...drenched the whole soul with sweat... <margin>C</margin> ...the charioteer, suffering the same passion, falling back as if from a starting barrier... <margin>D</margin> ...slandered by classmates... <margin>E</margin> ...which Zeus, loving Ganymede, called "longing" [imeros]... <margin>F</margin> ...possessing counter-love as an image of love... <margin>G</margin> ...if they win by leading the better parts of the mind toward an ordered life and philosophy... <margin>H</margin> ...they have won one of the three truly Olympic contests...

# PHAEDRUS

<margin>A</margin> ...driven by those unspoken longings they share, they choose the life of love which so many call blessed. When their time is finished, they live in a sweet harmony. For a long time, the soul remains rare and refined, though its lower parts were once enslaved to the beast. They are dear to one another, both while their love flourishes and after it has cooled, believing they have given and received the greatest pledges of faith from one another; they consider it a sin to break this trust and ever become enemies. At the end of their lives, they leave their bodies, though not yet fully fledged, having begun to grow the buds of their wings. Thus, they carry away <margin>B</margin> no small prize for their erotic madness. For the law <note>The divine law governing the cycle of reincarnation</note> forbids those who have already begun the journey beneath the heavens to descend into darkness or the journey under the earth; instead, they lead a bright life and are happy as they travel together, and for the sake of their love, they shall be granted wings together when the time comes. These things, O boy, are the divine gifts that the friendship of a lover will bestow upon you. But the intimacy of the non-lover, mixed as it is with mortal prudence, dealing in mortal and stingy things, breeds a lack of generosity in the beloved's soul—a quality praised by the masses as a virtue—and will cause the soul to wander for nine thousand years around the earth and under it in a state of foolishness. This, O dear Eros, is the recantation <note>original: "παλινῳδία" (palinodia), a song or poem retracting a previous statement</note> offered to you, given and paid as beautifully and perfectly as was in our power, especially in its poetic phrasing, which I was forced to use for Phaedrus's sake. But for my previous words, grant me pardon, and for these, give me thanks; be kind and propitious, and do not, in anger, take away or diminish the art of love which you have given me. Rather, grant that I may be held in even higher honor among the beautiful than I am now. And if in our previous discourse Phaedrus and I said anything discordant to you, lay the blame on Lysias, the father of that <margin>C</margin> speech. Turn him away from such talk and toward philosophy, just as his brother Polemarchus has been turned, so that his lover here, Phaedrus, may no longer waver as he does now, but may lead his life simply for the sake of Love and philosophical discourse. <term>Ph.</term> I join you in this prayer, Socrates, and if this is indeed better for us, may it come to pass. But I have long wondered at your speech, for you have fashioned it much more beautifully than the previous one. Indeed, I fear that Lysias may appear humble by comparison, if he should even wish to set another speech against it. For just lately, O wonderful man, one of the politicians was insulting him for this very thing, calling him a "speech-writer" <note>original: "λογογράφος" (logographos), a professional writer of legal or political speeches, often used as a slur against those who didn't speak their own heart</note> throughout his entire critique. So <margin>D</margin> perhaps, out of ambition, he might refrain from writing further. <term>S.</term> That is a laughable idea, young man, and you miss the mark regarding your friend if you think he is so easily frightened. Perhaps you also believe his critic actually meant what he said in his insults. <term>Ph.</term> It certainly seemed so, Socrates. And you yourself know that those with the greatest power and dignity in our cities are ashamed to write speeches or leave behind written works, fearing the judgment of later times, lest they be called "sophists." <note>professional teachers of rhetoric who charged fees, often viewed with suspicion by traditionalists</note> <term>S.</term> You are forgetting the "sweet bend" <note>An ancient proverb referring to a bypass or a pleasant detour, here likely referring to the Nile</note> of the Nile, Phaedrus. You fail to see that those politicians who think most highly of themselves are actually the ones who most love writing and leaving behind compositions. Indeed, <margin>E</margin> whenever they write a speech, they so love those who praise them that they write down first of all the names of those who approve of them in each instance. <term>Ph.</term> How do you mean? I do not understand. <term>S.</term> Do you not understand that at the beginning of a politician's writing, the name of his praiser is written first? <term>Ph.</term> How so? <term>S.</term> "It seemed good," the writing says, "to the Council, or to the People, or to both." And the writer mentions himself with great solemnity and praise, and then continues, showing off his own wisdom to his admirers, sometimes making his composition very long indeed. Does such a thing seem like anything other than a written speech to you? <term>Ph.</term> Not to me. <term>S.</term> Therefore, <margin>F</margin> if his speech remains in force, he departs the stage rejoicing like a poet. But if it is erased and he is deprived of this speech-writing and the dignity of being a writer, he and his friends go into mourning. <term>Ph.</term> Very much so. <term>S.</term> It is clear then that they do not look down upon the practice, but rather admire it. <term>Ph.</term> Entirely so. <term>S.</term> What then? When an orator or a king becomes so capable as to take on the power of a Lycurgus, a Solon, or a Darius <note>Famous lawgivers of Sparta, Athens, and Persia respectively</note>, becoming an immortal speech-writer in the state, does he not consider himself equal to a god while still living? And do not posterity, when they look upon his writings, judge him in the same way? <term>Ph.</term> They certainly do. <term>S.</term> Do you think, then, that any of these men, however much they might hate Lysias, would reproach him simply for the act of writing? <term>Ph.</term> <margin>G</margin> It is not likely, based on what you say. For they would be reproaching their own desires. <term>S.</term> This much, then, is clear to everyone: there is nothing shameful in the mere act of writing speeches. <term>Ph.</term> Why would there be? <term>S.</term> But this, I think, is where the shame begins: not in speaking or writing well, but in speaking and writing shamefully and badly. <term>Ph.</term> That is clear. What, then, is the method of writing well or poorly? <term>S.</term> Do we not need, Phaedrus, to examine Lysias on this point, or anyone else who has ever written or will write anything—whether it be a political treatise or a private work, in meter like a poet or without meter like a private citizen? <term>Ph.</term> You ask if we need to? <margin>H</margin> For what reason would a man live, so to speak, if not for such pleasures? Surely not for those pleasures that must be preceded by pain, which almost all...

<margin>A</margin> ...they are compelled to seek, and in the fulfillment of that desire, they are thereafter occupied. However, they use this path but rarely, for not every thought of the soul consents to it. These men are also friends, though less so than those mentioned before, both while enjoying their love and after it has been extinguished, believing they have both given and received the firmest pledges of faith to one another. They consider it a divine law that they must not break this faith and eventually turn from friends into enemies. Finally, when they have yielded to nature, they depart in such a state that although they are not yet winged, they have begun in some way to put forth feathers. Therefore, <margin>B</margin> they receive a prize for their erotic madness that is not small. For the law forbids those who had already begun their journey toward the heavens to descend into darkness and the place beneath the earth; instead, it commands that they lead a bright life and become blessed as they travel together, putting forth wings at the same time; and these things happen by the grace of love. Such and so great, O boy, and so divine are the things the friendship of a lover will bring you. But the familiarity of the one who does not love, joined with mortal temperance and devoted to mortal and meager duties, will generate in his companion’s soul that illiberality which is commonly regarded as virtue, and will cause him to wander foolishly for nine thousand years upon the earth and beneath it. This palinode for you, O beloved Love, we have sung as beautifully and best as we were able, driven by the poetic words and figures of Phaedrus. Therefore, <margin>C</margin> forgiving my previous words and receiving these from us with gratitude, be kind and propitious to me; and do not, in any indignation, take away or diminish the erotic art granted by you. Nor is that all, but it also escapes you that those among the administrators of the Republic who are the most prudent are exceedingly eager to compose and leave behind orations for posterity, and they so love those who praise their works that they list those who everywhere praise their writings as the first ones to be recorded. <term>P H.</term> How do you say that? For I do not understand. <term>S.</term> Do you not know that in the beginning of a book composed by a political man, the first name written is that of the praiser? <term>P H.</term> In what way? <term>S O C.</term> "It was approved," it says, written for the senate or the people, <margin>F</margin> or both; and the one who spoke, ambitiously naming himself and extolling the author of the opinion. Does that seem to be anything other than a written speech to you? <term>P H Æ.</term> Certainly nothing else. <term>S O.</term> But if it is approved, he leaves the theater rejoicing, just like a poet. But if it is rejected and he is excluded from writing his opinion, and not considered worthy for his opinion to be committed to letters, he himself and his friends mourn. <term>P H.</term> Most certainly. <term>S O C.</term> In this they clearly demonstrate that they do not despise this study, but value it highly. <term>P H Æ.</term> Exceedingly. <term>S O C.</term> What if some orator or king <margin>G</margin> has obtained such a faculty that, like Lycurgus, Solon, or Darius, he can be considered an immortal writer in the city? Does he not consider himself equal to a God even while living? And do not those who come after, considering his monuments, judge him similarly? <term>P H.</term> Vehemently. <term>S O C R.</term> Do you then think any such person, however malevolent toward Lysias, would reproach his study of writing? <term>P H Æ.</term> From what you say, that does not seem likely; for he would be reproaching his own study as well. <term>S O C R.</term> Therefore, it can be clear to anyone from this that a person is not to be reproached for the mere fact that he writes. <term>P H Æ.</term> <margin>H</margin> Why indeed? <term>S O C R.</term> But that is, as I judge, shameful: to speak and write shamefully and badly. <term>P H Æ D R.</term> That is manifest indeed.

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Phaedrus. body pleasures. Wherefore they are not wrongly called slavish. **SOCRATES.** We certainly have plenty of leisure, and it also seems to me that the cicadas, singing over our heads in the heat and talking to one another, are looking down at us. If they were to see us—just as they see many others at midday—not debating but rather dozing off, lulled by them because of our mental laziness, they would rightly laugh at us. They would think that some slaves had turned aside to their retreat, and like cattle, were caught in a midday sleep by the fountain in that very seclusion. But if they see us debating and not caught by their charms—as if they were Sirens <note>Mythical creatures whose song lured sailors to their doom; Socrates suggests the cicadas' song is a similar test of character</note>—sailing past them toward the harbor, they might perhaps very gladly grant us that reward which they are able to pass on to men by the gift of the gods. **PHAEDRUS.** And what is this gift they possess? For I do not think I have ever heard of it. **SOC.** It is not fitting for a man who is a lover of the Muses to be ignorant of such things. It is said that these cicadas were once human beings before the Muses were born. Then, when the Muses were born and song was revealed, some of those people were so overcome by the pleasure of singing that they neglected food and drink and died without realizing it. From them, the race of cicadas was later born, receiving this gift from the Muses: that they need no nourishment, but sing without food or drink as long as they live, and afterward go to the Muses to report which human here honors which Muse. So, when they report to Terpsichore <note>The Muse of dance and choral song</note> those who have honored her in dances and assemblies, they make her more favorable to them. To Erato <note>The Muse of love poetry</note>, they report those who have honored her in matters of love, and so on for the others according to the type of honor each receives. But to Calliope <note>The Muse of epic poetry, often considered the eldest and leader</note>, the eldest, and to Urania <note>The Muse of astronomy</note> who follows her, they report those who live in philosophy and honor their music; for these two Muses, more than the others, are concerned with the heavens and with discourses both divine and human, modulating their voices most beautifully. Therefore, for many reasons, we must speak of something and not sleep at midday. **PHAEDRUS.** We must certainly speak. **SOC.** Therefore, what we just proposed must now be considered: namely, by what reasoning a person speaks and writes either rightly or not rightly. **PH.** Without a doubt. **SOC.** Is it not necessary that he who is to speak rightly must have a true understanding of the matter about which he is to speak? **PHAEDRUS.** I have heard, my friend Socrates, that it is not necessary for a future orator to learn what is truly just, but rather what seems so to the multitude who will judge; nor what is truly good or honorable, but what appears to be so. For persuasion comes from these things rather than from the truth. **SOC.** One must never, O Phaedrus, despise the sayings of the wise; rather, one must diligently consider what they mean. Therefore, what you just said I do not think should be passed over. **PH.** You speak well. **SOC.** Let us consider it in this way. **PHAEDRUS.** In what way? **SOC.** If I were to persuade you that you should fight the enemy with a horse, and both of us were ignorant of what a horse is, but I knew only this much about you: that Phaedrus thinks a horse is that domestic animal which has the largest ears. **PHAEDRUS.** That would be ridiculous indeed, Socrates. **SOC.** Not yet; but suppose I were to earnestly try to persuade you with a speech composed in praise of a donkey, calling it a horse and asserting that the animal is of the highest value, useful at home and in the field, most prompt for war, fit for carrying baggage,
<margin>It is better to be a ridiculous friend than a heavy and hostile one.</margin>
and most convenient for many other things. **PHAEDRUS.** That would be utterly absurd. **SOCRATES.** Is it not better to be a ridiculous friend than a heavy and hostile one? **PHAEDRUS.** So it seems. **SOC.** When, therefore, an orator who is ignorant of good and evil similarly persuades a city—not indeed with a speech composed in praise of a "donkey's shadow" as if it were a horse, but discussing evil as if it were good, and having caught the opinions of the crowd, induces them to do evil instead of good—what kind of harvest do you think rhetoric of this sort will reap from what it has sown? **PHAEDRUS.** Surely not a good one. **SOC.** Have we, my good man, insulted the art of speaking more rudely than is fitting? She might perhaps say: "Why, O wonderful men, do you talk nonsense? For I compel no one who is ignorant of the truth to learn how to speak; but if anyone, having taken my advice, first perceives the truth and then takes me up: I certainly affirm this is a great thing, that without me, even if someone knows the facts, he will have no more power of persuasion." Would she not be right to say this? **PH.** I confess it, if only the following arguments testify that it is indeed an art. For I seem to hear some arguments asserting that she lies, and is not an art, but a practice without art. "The true art of speaking," says the
<margin>The art of speaking correctly is not without truth.</margin>
Spartan, "does not exist without a grasp of the truth, nor will it ever." O Socrates, bring these arguments here and examine what they say and how they say it. **SOC.** Come here, noble creatures, and persuade Phaedrus, the honorable youth, that unless he philosophizes sufficiently, he will never be able to speak sufficiently about anything. Let Phaedrus answer Socrates’s questioning. Would not rhetoric be, in its entirety, a certain <term>soul-leading</term> <note>original: "ψυχαγωγία" (psychagogia); literally a "leading of the soul," used here to describe how speech directs the listener's mind</note> through words, not only in courts and other public assemblies, but also in private gatherings, the same concerning both great and small things? For nothing is more honorable in great things than to conduct oneself according to the right method of art in small ones. Have you heard this? **PH.** Not quite, by Jove. Rather, this art is said to be used and written about primarily concerning court cases and public speeches; but I have not heard it extended further. **SOC.** But have you heard only of the arts of speaking by Nestor and Odysseus <note>Heroes of the Trojan War; Socrates uses them as archetypes for different styles of rhetoric</note>...

<column-break/>

[A] ...almost all the pleasures through the body have. Therefore, they are also rightly called slavish. **SOC.** We have leisure, it seems; and at the same time it seems to me as if the cicadas, singing over our heads in the heat and talking to one another, are looking at us too. If, then, they should see us two—just like the many—not talking at midday, but nodding off and being charmed by them through laziness of thought, they would rightly laugh at us, thinking that some slaves had come to them in their retreat, like sheep resting at noon around the fountain to sleep. But if they see us talking and [B] not being charmed by them, but remaining uncharmed as if by Sirens, they might perhaps give us the prize they have from the gods to give to men, being pleased with us. **PHAI.** And what is this they have? For I happen to be, it seems, one who has not heard. **SOK.** It is certainly not fitting for a man who loves the Muses to be one who has not heard such things. It is said that these were once humans before the Muses were born. But when the Muses were born and song appeared, some of those then were so struck by pleasure that, singing, they neglected food and drink, and they died without noticing it. From these, the race of cicadas was born after that, receiving this prize from the Muses: to need no food from birth, but without food or drink to sing straight away until they die; and after these things, going to the [C] Muses, to report who honors which of them among those here. To Terpsichore, then, reporting those who have honored her in dances, they make them more dear; and to Erato, those in matters of love; and to the others thus, according to the form of honor of each. But to the eldest, Calliope, and to the one after her, Urania, they report those who spend time in philosophy and honor their music; these indeed of the Muses, being especially concerned with heaven and with words both divine and human, send forth the most beautiful voice. For many reasons, then, we must speak of something, and not sleep in the midday. **PHAI.** We must indeed speak. **SOK.** Therefore, what we just proposed—to [D] examine the speech as to how it is good to speak and to write, and how not—must be examined. **PHAI.** Clearly. **SOK.** Must there not, then, be present in what is to be spoken well and beautifully the thought of the speaker, knowing the truth of what he is about to speak? **PHAI.** I have heard it this way about this, dear Socrates: that there is no necessity for the one who is to be an orator to learn what is truly just, but what would seem so to the multitude who will judge; nor the things that are truly good or beautiful, but whatever will seem so. For from these comes persuasion, but not from the truth. **SOK.** A word spoken by the wise must not be rejected, O Phaedrus, but we must see if they are saying something. And indeed, what has now been said must not be dismissed. **PHAI.** You speak rightly. **SOK.** Let us then examine it in this way. **PHAI.** How? **SOK.** If I should persuade you to repel the enemies by acquiring a horse; and both of us [E] were ignorant of a horse, but I happened to know this much about you: that Phaedrus believes a horse is the one of the domestic animals that has the largest ears. **PHAI.** That would be ridiculous, Socrates. **SOK.** Not yet; but when I should seriously persuade you, composing a speech, a praise of the donkey, calling it a horse; and saying that the creature is worth everything to possess both at home and on campaign; useful to fight from and capable of carrying equipment, and helpful for many other things. **PHAI.** It would be altogether ridiculous then. **SOK.** Is it not then better to be a ridiculous friend than a terrible and hostile one? **PHAI.** It seems so. **SOK.** When, therefore, the rhetorician, being ignorant of good and evil, taking a city in the same condition, persuades it—not making the praise about the "shadow of a donkey" as if it were a horse, but about evil as if it were good; and having studied the opinions of the multitude, persuades them to do evil instead [F] of good—what kind of fruit do you think rhetoric after that will harvest of what it sowed? **PHAI.** Not a very decent one. **SOK.** Have we then, my friend, reviled the art of words more rustically than is necessary? But she might perhaps say: "Why on earth, O wonderful men, do you talk nonsense? For I force no one who is ignorant of the truth to learn to speak; but if my advice is worth anything, having acquired that knowledge, then take me. This great thing then I say: that without me, there will be no more power of persuading by art for the one who knows the things that are." **PHAI.** Will she not speak justly, saying these things? **SOK.** I say so, if indeed the arguments that come upon her testify that she is an [G] art. For I seem to hear some arguments coming and testifying that she lies, and is not an art but an artless practice. "Of speaking," says the Spartan, "a true art, without having grasped the truth, neither exists nor will ever hereafter come to be." These arguments then, O Socrates, bring them here and examine what and how they say. **SOK.** Come here, noble creatures; and persuade Phaedrus the boy that unless he philosophizes sufficiently, he will never be sufficient to speak about anything. Let Phaedrus answer then; ask him. **PHAI.** Ask him. **SOK.** Would not rhetoric then, as a whole, be a certain soul-leading through words, not only in law-courts and whatever other public gatherings, but also in private? The same concerning small and great things? And nothing more [H] honorable when it happens rightly concerning serious or trivial matters? Or how have you heard these things? **PHAI.** No, by Zeus, not altogether so; but mostly how cases in law are spoken and written by art, and it is also spoken about public speaking; but further than that I have not heard. **SOK.** But have you heard only of the arts of Nestor and Odysseus...

<summary>Socrates shares the Myth of the Cicadas to emphasize the value of philosophical labor and argues that true rhetoric (the art of soul-leading) requires a foundation in truth rather than mere popular opinion.</summary>
