<meta>This page continues the conversation between Socrates and Phaedrus by the banks of the Ilissus. Having concluded his formal speeches on love, Socrates now begins a dialectical investigation into the nature of rhetoric itself, using Lysias’ speech as a case study for what constitutes "good" or "artful" writing.</meta>

# PHAEDRUS

<margin>A</margin> ...have you heard of the writings they used at Troy? <note>Socrates is playfully comparing contemporary rhetoricians to Homeric heroes: Nestor and Odysseus were famous for their persuasive speech in the *Iliad*.</note> Or have you never heard of the works of Palamedes? <margin>PH.</margin> By Zeus, I have heard of Nestor’s speeches—unless you are casting Gorgias <note>A famous traveling teacher of rhetoric from Sicily.</note> as a Nestor, or perhaps Thrasymachus and Theodorus as Odysseus. <margin>SOCR.</margin> Perhaps. But let us leave them aside. You tell me: what do opponents in a court of law actually do? Do they not practice the art of contradiction? Or what else shall we call it? <margin>PH.</margin> That is exactly what it is. <margin>SOCR.</margin> And is it about the just and the unjust? <margin>PH.</margin> Yes. <margin>SOCR.</margin> Then will not he who does this with art make the same thing appear to the same people at one time just, and when he wishes, unjust? <margin>PH.</margin> Certainly. <margin>SOCR.</margin> And in a public assembly, will he not make the same things appear to the city at one time good, and at another time the opposite? <margin>PH.</margin> Indeed. <margin>SOCR.</margin> Do we not also hear that the Eleatic Palamedes <note>This likely refers to Zeno of Elea, famous for his paradoxes (like Achilles and the Tortoise) which made the same thing seem both one and many, or at rest and in motion.</note> spoke with such art that <margin>B</margin> the same things appeared to his listeners both similar and dissimilar, both one and many, and both at rest and in motion? <margin>PH.</margin> Very much so. <margin>SOCR.</margin> Therefore, the art of contradiction is not limited to courts and public assemblies, but apparently, there is a single art—if indeed it is an art—concerning everything that is spoken, by which a man is able to make everything resemble everything else (within the limits of possibility), and to bring to light the attempts of others who try to hide their resemblances. <margin>PH.</margin> In what way do you mean this? <margin>SOCR.</margin> I think it will become clear if we look at it this way. Does deception occur more often in things that differ <margin>Deception in those things which differ little.</margin> greatly, or in things that differ only a little? <margin>PH.</margin> In those that differ a little. <margin>SOCR.</margin> Certainly, if you transition by small degrees, you are more likely to escape notice when arriving at the opposite than if you leap across in a single bound. <margin>PH.</margin> Of course. <margin>SOCR.</margin> Therefore, he who intends to deceive another, while remaining <margin>What one must know to deceive another.</margin> undecevied himself, must accurately discern the similarity and dissimilarity of things. <margin>C</margin> <margin>PH.</margin> That is necessary. <margin>SOCR.</margin> Is it possible, then, for someone who is ignorant of the truth of each thing to distinguish the small or large similarity of that unknown thing in relation to other things? <margin>PH.</margin> It is impossible. <margin>SOCR.</margin> It is clear, then, that for those who hold opinions contrary to reality and are deceived, this state of mind has slipped in through certain similarities. <margin>PH.</margin> That is how it happens. <margin>SOCR.</margin> Can anyone, then, possess the art of leading another person away from the truth by small steps through similarities, or avoid being led away himself, if he does not recognize what each thing truly is? <margin>PH.</margin> Never. <margin>SOCR.</margin> Therefore, my friend, the man who does not know the truth, but has <margin>It is concluded that rhetoric is to be despised without truth.</margin> hunted only after opinions, will provide an art of speaking that is, it seems, both ridiculous and artless. <margin>D</margin> <margin>PH.</margin> It seems likely. <margin>SOCR.</margin> Do you want us to look at the speech of Lysias, which you are carrying, and the speeches we ourselves gave, to see where we find "art" and where we find its absence? <margin>PH.</margin> More than anything; for as it is, we are speaking in bare terms without sufficient examples. <margin>SOCR.</margin> And indeed, by some stroke of luck, it seems these two speeches were spoken as examples of how one who knows the truth might, in play, lead his listeners astray. And I, for my part, O Phaedrus, blame the local gods of this place. Perhaps also the <margin>E</margin> prophets of the Muses <note>A reference back to the cicadas mentioned on the previous page.</note> singing above our heads have breathed this gift upon us; for I certainly do not possess any art of speaking. <margin>PH.</margin> Let it be as you say; only show me what you mean. <margin>SOCR.</margin> Come then, read me the beginning of Lysias' speech. <margin>PH.</margin> "You know how my affairs stand, and you have heard how I think it is to our advantage that these things happen. I claim that I should not fail in my request because I do not happen to be your lover. For lovers, when their desire ceases, regret the benefits they have bestowed..." <margin>SOCR.</margin> Stop. We must now say where he goes wrong and acts without art. Is that not so? <margin>PH.</margin> Yes. <margin>SOCR.</margin> Is it not clear to everyone that we agree about some things of this sort, but are in disagreement about others? <margin>PH.</margin> I think I understand what you mean, but say it more clearly. <margin>SOCR.</margin> When someone says the word "iron" or "silver," <margin>F</margin> do we not all think of the same thing? <margin>PH.</margin> Certainly. <margin>SOCR.</margin> But what when someone says "just" or "good"? Does not one person head in one direction and another elsewhere? And do we not disagree with each other and even within ourselves? <margin>PH.</margin> Most definitely. <margin>SOCR.</margin> So in some things we agree, and in others we do not. <margin>PH.</margin> True. <margin>SOCR.</margin> In which of these, then, are we more easily deceived? And in which does rhetoric have more power? <margin>PH.</margin> Clearly, in those things where we wander in uncertainty. <margin>SOCR.</margin> Therefore, the man who intends to pursue the art of rhetoric must first have methodically divided these two and grasped the characteristic <margin>G</margin> of each kind: the one in which the multitude must necessarily wander, and the one in which they do not. <margin>PH.</margin> He would indeed have grasped a beautiful principle, Socrates, who understands this. <margin>SOCR.</margin> Then, I think, when he comes to each specific case, he should not miss it, but acutely perceive which of the two classes the subject he is about to speak on belongs to. <margin>PH.</margin> Why not? <margin>SOCR.</margin> What then of "love"? Shall we say it belongs to the disputed class or the other? <margin>PH.</margin> To the disputed class, surely. <margin>SOCR.</margin> Or do you think it would have allowed you to say what you just said about it—that it is a harm to the beloved and the lover, and again that it is the greatest of goods? <margin>PH.</margin> You speak most rightly. <margin>SOCR.</margin> But tell me this also—for in my inspired state, I don't quite remember—whether I defined love at the beginning of my speech. <margin>PH.</margin> By Zeus, you did so most powerfully! <margin>SOCR.</margin> Oh, how much more skilled in speeches you show the nymphs of the Achelous and Pan, the son of Hermes, to be than Lysias, the son of Cephalus! Or am I wrong? <margin>H</margin> Did Lysias, at the beginning of his erotic speech, compel us to understand Love as some single thing that he himself intended? And did he then refer everything else to that?

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...which Ulysses used at Troy, you have heard; but that which Palamedes used, have you never heard? <margin>PH.</margin> And by Jove, I have heard the orations of Nestor; unless perhaps you imagine Gorgias to be Nestor, or Thrasymachus and Theodorus to be Ulysses. <margin>SOCR.</margin> Perhaps, but let us dismiss these. You, however, respond. What do adversaries do in the courts? Do they not contradict? Or shall we say they do something else? <margin>PH.</margin> This very thing. <margin>SOCR.</margin> Is it not about the just and the unjust? <margin>PH.</margin> So it is. <margin>SOCR.</margin> Will not he who does this by art bring it about that the same thing appears to the same person now just, now unjust? <margin>PH.</margin> What prevents it? <margin>SOCR.</margin> And in the assembly, so that the same things seem to the city now good, now the opposite? <margin>PH.</margin> Certainly. <margin>SOCR.</margin> Indeed, we have heard that the Eleatic Palamedes was accustomed by his art to make <margin>B</margin> the same things appear to his audience both similar and dissimilar, one and many, remaining and flowing. <margin>PH.</margin> Greatly so. <margin>SOCR.</margin> The contradictory faculty, therefore, is not only in the courts and assemblies, but in all things, as it appears, that are spoken; since there is one certain art by which one can make all things similar to all things—both what is possible and to whom it is possible—and bring into the light those similarities which another is hiding. <margin>PH.</margin> In what way do you say this? <margin>SOCR.</margin> In this way. Does deception happen in those <margin>Deception in those things which differ little.</margin> things which differ much, or those which differ little? <margin>PH.</margin> In those which differ little. <margin>SOCR.</margin> But if you transition by little bits, you will be more hidden when you come to the opposite than if you leap across suddenly. <margin>PH.</margin> Why not? <margin>SOCR.</margin> Therefore, <margin>What one must know to deceive another.</margin> he who is to deceive another while not being deceived himself must exquisitely distinguish the similarity and dissimilarity of things. <margin>C</margin> <margin>PHAE.</margin> It is necessary. <margin>SOCR.</margin> Can someone ignorant of the truth of individual things judge the small or great similarity of that which he ignores in the universe? <margin>PH.</margin> It is impossible indeed. <margin>SOCR.</margin> Therefore, those who hold opinions contrary to the nature of things and are mistaken, it is established that they are so affected because of certain similarities. <margin>PH.</margin> So it happens. <margin>SOCR.</margin> Can anyone, if he is ignorant of the matter, artificially and gradually lead someone by similarities away from the truth into the opposite? Or avoid this error in himself? <margin>D</margin> <margin>PH.</margin> Never. <margin>SOCR.</margin> Wherefore, O friend, whoever is ignorant of the truth and is led by opinions, exhibits a faculty of speaking that is, as it seems, clumsy and ridiculous. <margin>PH.</margin> So it seems. <margin>SOCR.</margin> Do you wish to see in the oration of Lysias, which you have in your hands, and in our discussion, where things are done artificially and where without art? <margin>PHAE.</margin> Most of all. For we are speaking nakedly at present, since we lack suitable examples. <margin>SOCR.</margin> But by some fortune, the arguments were spoken, as it seems, showing by example how a man possessing the truth, while playing with words, may draw his listeners. And I, O Phaedrus, think the local gods are the <margin>E</margin> causes of this. Perhaps even the prophets of the Muses singing over our heads have inspired us with this gift. For I have no art of speaking. <margin>PHAE.</margin> Let it be as you say. Only show what you are saying. <margin>SOCR.</margin> Come then, read the introduction of Lysias' oration. <margin>PHAE.</margin> "The status of my affairs is as you have understood. Therefore, since it is so, you have heard how I think it is conducive to our interests. I think indeed that I shall obtain what I seek from you no less because I am not captured by love for you. For lovers, as soon as they cease to love, repent of the benefits bestowed." <margin>SOCR.</margin> Stop. We must say in what he fails, and what he does without art. No? <margin>P.</margin> Certainly. <margin>SO.</margin> Is it not clear to anyone that in some things, while we speak, we all feel the same, but in others <margin>F</margin> not the same? <margin>PH.</margin> Although I seem to understand what you say, I desire you to speak more plainly. <margin>SOCR.</margin> When someone pronounces the name of iron or silver, do we not all immediately understand the same thing? <margin>PHAE.</margin> Exactly. <margin>SOCR.</margin> What when the name of the just or the good? Is not one person carried one way and another elsewhere? And do we not disagree with others and with ourselves? <margin>P.</margin> Greatly. <margin>SOCR.</margin> In some things therefore we agree, in others we disagree. <margin>PHAE.</margin> So it is. <margin>SOCR.</margin> Where then can we be more easily deceived? And in which of these does rhetoric have most power? <margin>PHAE.</margin> It is clear: in those in which we disagree. <margin>SOCR.</margin> Therefore it behooves him who is to master rhetoric first to have distinguished these in order, and to have perceived what the forms of each species <margin>G</margin> are, and where the multitude can most easily be deceived by ambiguity, and where not. <margin>PHAE.</margin> He would recognize a splendid form, O Socrates, who captured that in thought. <margin>SOCR.</margin> Next, I think, it behooves him that nothing escapes him when he comes to particulars, but that he acutely senses whether the thing about which he is to speak is of the one genus or the other. <margin>PHAE.</margin> Why not? <margin>SOCR.</margin> What then of love? Shall we say it is of the ambiguous genus or the other? <margin>PHAE.</margin> Of the ambiguous, certainly. <margin>SOCR.</margin> Or do you think it would allow you to say those things which you said above? That it is pernicious both to the beloved and to the lover, and again that it is the greatest <margin>H</margin> of goods. <margin>PH.</margin> You speak skillfully. <margin>SOCR.</margin> But you might also say this—for I, on account of that divine inspiration, do not quite remember—whether I defined love at the beginning of the dispute. <margin>PHAE.</margin> By Jove, wonderfully. <margin>SOCR.</margin> O, how much more skillful you show the nymphs of the Achelous, and Pan the son of Mercury, to be at composing orations than Lysias the son of Cephalus. Or will you say nothing? But Lysias at the beginning of his erotic discourse compelled us to understand Love as some certain thing which he himself wished, and referring the following things to that...

<summary>Socrates argues that true rhetoric requires knowing the truth of a subject to navigate the "similarities" that lead to deception, specifically distinguishing between agreed-upon terms (like iron) and disputed terms (like love or justice). He begins a critical analysis of Lysias' speech to demonstrate that it lacks this necessary logical foundation and definition.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Phaedrus. Socrates has just finished his "Palinode" or retraction speech in praise of Love (Eros). Now, he begins to analyze the structure of the previous speech by Lysias to demonstrate the principles of good rhetoric and the dialectical method of "Collection and Division."</meta>

# OF PLATO

**A** ...did he complete the whole speech? Or should we read the beginning again? *PHAED.* If you wish, though what you are looking for is not there. *SOCR.* Read it, so that I may hear the man himself. *PHAED.* "The state of my affairs is as you have understood; and since it is so, you have heard how I think it would benefit us. I believe I should not fail to get what I ask from you just because I am not captured by love for you. For lovers, as soon as their desire ceases, regret the benefits they have conferred." *SOCR.* It seems to be very far from doing what we seek. For he does not attempt to conduct his speech from the beginning, but from the end—upside down and backwards—and he starts with the very things a lover would say to his beloved after his love has already died. Or have I said nothing of substance, my dear Phaedrus? **B** *PHAED.* It is certainly the conclusion, Socrates, that he is speaking about. *SOCR.* And what about the rest? Do the other parts of the speech not seem to be thrown together at random? Or does it seem that what was placed second was joined there by some necessity? Or any other part of what was said? For to me, as one who knows nothing, it seemed that the writer said whatever happened to come into his head, quite freely. Do you have some "writer’s necessity" <note>Socrates uses the term "logographical necessity" to ask if there is a logical reason for the order of the sentences.</note> by which he arranged these things in such a sequence? *PHAED.* You are very kind, Socrates, if you think me capable of judging his writings with such precision. *SOCR.* But this **C** I think you would agree: every speech ought to be put together like a living creature <note>original: "animal quoddam" / "ζῶον". This is a famous Platonic metaphor: a good argument must have organic unity, with every part serving the whole.</note>, so that it has its own body, and is neither without a head nor lacking feet, but has a middle and extremities that are suited to each other and to the whole. *PHAED.* How could it be otherwise? *SOCR.* Consider then, I pray, whether your friend's speech is like that or otherwise. You will find it differs not at all from that epigram which some say was inscribed for Midas the Phrygian. <note>Midas was the legendary king who turned everything he touched to gold. The point here is that the poem's lines can be read in any order without changing the meaning.</note> *PHAED.* What is that, and what is it like? *SOCR.* Listen.

> I am a bronze maiden, I lie upon Midas’s tomb,
> And as long as the springs flow, and the tall trees grow green,
> Remaining here upon this much-wept-for grave,
> **D** I tell the passers-by that Midas is buried here.

That it makes no difference whether any part of it is placed first or last, I think you can see for yourself. *PHAED.* You are mocking our speech, Socrates. *SOCR.* Let us leave this one then, so as not to upset you, although it seems to contain many examples which we might inspect to our benefit—not to imitate them, of course. But let us move on to the other speeches; for they contained something, I think, that those who wish to study speaking should observe. *PHAED.* What was that? *SOCR.* They were surely opposites. For one asserted that the lover should be favored, the other that the non-lover should. *PHAED.* And quite vigorously too! **E** *SOCR.* I thought you were going to say, more truthfully, "quite madly." But that is the very thing I was looking for.

<margin>Types of madness</margin>
We called Love a certain kind of madness, did we not? *PHAED.* Certainly. *SOCR.* And we posited two types of madness: one resulting from human diseases, the other from a divine alienation <note>This refers to being "beside oneself" or "inspired."</note> which snatches a person out of the usual customs of life. *PHAED.* Entirely so. *SOCR.*

<margin>Four divine madnesses.</margin>
The divine parts we divided into four, presided over by four gods. We attributed the inspiration of prophecy to Apollo; the mysteries to Dionysus; the poetic to the Muses; and the madness of love to Aphrodite and Eros, which we said was the best of all. And I do not know how, while we were sketching the passion of love through certain images, we perhaps touched upon some truth, or perhaps were carried away elsewhere. **F** Thus, mixing a speech that was not entirely improbable, we composed a certain mythical hymn, and as if playing a game, we modestly praised my and your master, O Phaedrus—Love, the guardian of beautiful boys. *PHAED.* This was not unpleasant for me to hear. *SOCR.* Let us take this point from it: how the discussion transitioned from blame to praise. *PHAED.* How do you mean? *SOCR.* To me it seems that the rest was really just play. But if someone could grasp the power of two techniques <note>Socrates is introducing "Collection and Division," the core of his dialectic method.</note> that we stumbled upon by chance, it would be no thankless task. *PHAED.* Which techniques do you mean? *SOCR.* That one, looking toward a single Idea, might bring together things that are scattered in many places; **G** so that by defining each thing, he makes clear what it is he intends to teach. Just as we just now defined what Love is—whether it was done well or poorly. Certainly, because of this, our discussion possessed clarity and consistency with itself. *PHAED.* And what is the other technique you speak of, Socrates? *SOCR.* That one might be able to cut the subject back into its species, joint by joint, according to its natural growth, and not try to break any limb after the fashion of an unskillful cook <note>original: "imperiti coqui" / "κακοῦ μαγείρου". A good philosopher "carves" reality at its natural joints, whereas a bad one just smashes it.</note>. Instead, one should do as our recent speeches did, which took the frenzy of the mind as one common form. Just as in a single body the limbs grow in pairs with the same name—one called left, the other right—so the speech considered the form of madness as naturally **H** existing in us, and by cutting off the left-hand part, and cutting that again, it did not stop until it found a certain "left-handed" love, which it rightly insulted. The other speech led us to the right-hand side of madness, where it found a love that shared the same name but was divine; this it held up and praised as the cause of our greatest goods.

<column-break/>

**A** ...nevertheless, did he complete the whole of the latter speech? Do you wish for us to read its beginning again? *PH.* If it seems good to you; though what you seek is not there. *SOCR.* Speak it, so that I may hear the man himself. *PH.* "You know how my affairs stand; and I believe it is to our advantage if these things happen, as you have heard. I claim that I should not fail in what I ask because I do not happen to be your lover. For lovers later regret the good they have done when their desire ceases." *SOCR.* Truly, he seems to do much the opposite of what we seek; he attempts to run the speech not from the beginning but from the end, upside down; and he begins from where a lover who had already ceased loving would speak to his boy. Or have I said nothing, Phaedrus, my dear friend? **B** *PH.* It is certainly the end, Socrates, about which he makes his speech. *SOCR.* What then? Does not the rest of the speech seem to be cast down in a heap? Or does it appear that the second thing said had to be placed second by some necessity? Or any other of the things spoken? For to me it seemed, as one who knows nothing, that the writer said what came to him not ignobly. But do you have some speech-writing necessity, as to why he placed these things thus in sequence next to one another? *PH.* You are kind to think me capable of seeing his work so accurately. *SOCR.* But this much I think you would say is necessary: that every speech be composed like a living creature, having a body of its own; so that **C** it is neither headless nor footless, but has middle parts and extremities, written to be fitting to each other and to the whole. *PH.* How could it be otherwise? *SOCR.* Look then at your companion's speech, whether it is thus or otherwise; and you will find it differs not at all from the epigram which some say was inscribed for Midas the Phrygian. *PH.* Which one is that? And what is wrong with it? *SOCR.* It is this one, here:

> I am a bronze maiden; I lie on Midas’s tomb.
> As long as water flows and tall trees bloom,
> Remaining here on this much-wept-for grave,
**D** > I tell the passers-by that Midas is buried here.

That it makes no difference whether any part of it is said first or last, you surely perceive? So I think. *PH.* You are mocking our speech, Socrates. *SOCR.* This one then, so that you are not vexed, I will let be; (though it seems to me to have many examples which, by looking at them, one might benefit from imitating—though not entirely); let us go to the other speeches. For there was something in them, I think, which those who wish to examine speeches should see. *PH.* What sort of thing do you mean? *SOCR.* They were opposites, surely. One said that one should love; the other that one should not, as they spoke of how to grant favors. *PH.* And very manfully too. *SOCR.* I hoped you would say, "madly." For that is what I was seeking. We said that Love was a certain madness. Did we not? *PH.* Yes. *SOCR.* And of madness there are two kinds: one from human diseases; the other, arising from a divine change from the usual **E** customs. *PH.* Quite so. *SOCR.* And of the divine kind, we distinguished four parts belonging to four gods: prophetic inspiration we assigned to Apollo; the telestic <note>Refers to ritual initiation and purification.</note> to Dionysus; the poetic to the Muses; and the fourth, the madness of love, to Aphrodite and Eros. We said this was the best, and while we were likening the passion of love to something—perhaps touching upon some truth, though perhaps also being carried away elsewhere—we mixed a not altogether improbable speech, and played at a certain mythical hymn, moderately and piously, to my and your master Eros, O Phaedrus, the overseer of beautiful boys. *PH.* And it was very pleasant for me to hear. *SOCR.* Let us take this from it: how the speech was able to transition from blame to praise. *PH.* How then do you say that? *SOCR.* It seems to me that the **F** rest was truly played as a game; but of these things spoken by chance, if one were able to grasp the power of two forms by art, it would not be without grace. *PH.* What forms are these? *SOCR.* Bringing together things scattered in many places into one idea, looking at them together; so that by defining each, one makes clear whatever one wishes to teach. Just as now regarding Love: what it is was defined, whether it was said well or badly. At least the speech was able to speak with clarity and consistency because of this. *PH.* And what do you say the other form is, Socrates? *SOCR.* To be able to cut again according to species, at the joints, as it is naturally formed, and not to attempt to break any part like **G** a bad cook; but just as the two speeches just now took the unreason of the mind as one common form. Just as from one body there grow double and same-named parts, called left or right; so also the speech, having considered the form of madness as it is naturally in us, and cutting the part on the left side, and cutting this again, did not cease until it found a certain "left-handed" love among them, which it reviled quite justly. The other speech led us to the right-hand side of madness, and finding a certain divine love same-named with the other, and holding it forth, it praised it as the **H** cause of our greatest goods. *PH.* You speak most truly. *SOCR.* I myself am a lover of these divisions and collections, O Phaedrus, so that I may be able to...

---

...those speeches considered them as one. And the former, dividing the left-hand part and again dividing this, did not stop until it found a certain "left-handed" love there, and having found it, rightly condemned it. The second led us to the right-hand part, where finding Love similar in name to the first, yet divine, and magnifying it, it praised it as the cause of our greatest goods. *PHAED.* You speak very truly. *SOCR.* I love these divisions and collections, O Phaedrus, because they make me capable of both understanding and speaking.

<summary>Socrates explains the "Collection and Division" method of dialectic, using the metaphor of a cook carving a bird at its natural joints to describe how a speaker should structure an argument. He categorizes love as a form of "divine madness" divided into four types: prophetic, ritual, poetic, and erotic.</summary>
<keywords>dialectic, collection and division, divine madness, rhetoric, Midas, Eros, Apollo, Dionysus, Muses, Aphrodite, organic unity, speech-writing</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue where Socrates has just defined the two-fold method of "Collection" (bringing scattered particulars under one idea) and "Division" (dividing ideas into species at their natural joints). He now identifies those who practice this method as "dialecticians" and contrasts them with the famous teachers of rhetoric.</meta>

# PHAEDRUS

<margin>A</margin>
...and if I judge any other man to be capable of seeing both the One and the Many <note>original: "εἰς ἓν καὶ ἐπὶ πολλὰ" (into one and over many). This refers to the ability to see a universal concept and its specific sub-types.</note> as they are by nature, I follow behind him "in his footsteps as if he were a god." <note>A reference to Homer's Odyssey, describing following a divine path.</note> Whether the name I give to those who can do this is correct or not, God knows; but up until now, I have called them **dialecticians**. <note>In Plato's sense, a dialectician is one who uses logical analysis to reach the truth, rather than just using words to persuade.</note> But now, tell me what we should call the art learned from you and Lysias. Or is this that very "art of words" which Thrasymachus and the others use, by which they have become wise in speaking themselves and make others so, provided they are willing to bring them gifts as if to kings? *PHAEDRUS.* They are indeed kingly men, but they are certainly not knowledgeable in the things you are asking about. You seem to me to be right in calling this type of study "dialectics," but it seems to me that **rhetoric** still escapes us.

<margin>B</margin>
<margin>He who can divide according to the nature of things is a dialectician—that is, a metaphysician.</margin>
**SOCRATES.** How do you mean? Is there something beautiful which, though deprived of these dialectical methods, is nevertheless grasped by art? You and I must certainly not despise it; we must state what it is that remains of rhetoric. *PHAEDRUS.* There are a great many things, Socrates—at least the things written in the books on the "art of words." **SOCRATES.** You have reminded me well. First, I believe, an **introduction** <note>original: "προοίμιον" / "proœmium"</note> must be spoken at the beginning of the speech. These are the "refined" parts of the art you mean, are they not? *PHAEDRUS.* Yes. **SOCRATES.** And second is the **narration** <note>original: "διήγησιν" / "narratio"</note> and the evidence of witnesses; third, the **proofs**; fourth, **probabilities**. And I believe that most excellent "weaver of words" from Byzantium <note>Theodorus of Byzantium, a famous teacher of rhetoric known for his technical subdivisions of speeches.</note> introduced "confirmation" and "supplementary confirmation." *PHAEDRUS.* You mean the worthy **Theodorus**? **SOCRATES.** Who else?

<margin>C</margin>
And he also found how to produce "refutation" and "supplementary refutation," both in accusation and defense. And should we not bring into our midst the most excellent **Evenus of Paros**, who was the first to discover "sub-indications" and "incidental praise"? Some say he even put "incidental censures" into meter to help the memory; for he is a wise man. And shall we let **Tisias** and **Gorgias** <note>Tisias and Gorgias were pioneers of rhetoric in Sicily who claimed they could make the weaker argument seem the stronger.</note> sleep on, who saw that **probabilities** were to be honored more than truths? They make small things appear great and great things appear small through the power of words; they present new things in an old way and old things in a new way. They even discovered both concise brevity and infinite length on every subject. Once, when **Prodicus** <note>A Sophist known for his precision with synonyms.</note> heard me mention these things, he laughed, and said he alone had found what the art of words required: a speech should be neither long nor short, but of "moderate" length. *PHAEDRUS.* Most wise, Prodicus!

<margin>D</margin>
**SOCRATES.** And shall we not mention **Hippias**? For I think the stranger from Elis would vote with him. *PHAEDRUS.* Why not? **SOCRATES.** And how shall we describe the "shrines of words" belonging to **Polus**—such as his "repetition of words," his "maxims," his "imagery," and the "vocabulary of Licymnius" which he gave to him to produce "elegance of speech"? *PHAEDRUS.* And weren't there things like that by **Protagoras**, Socrates?

<margin>E</margin>
**SOCRATES.** Yes, my boy, a certain "correctness of diction" <note>original: "Ὀρθοέπειά" / "Orthoepeia"</note> and many other fine things. But in the art of speeches that drag out "pitiful laments" about old age and poverty, it seems to me the "strength of the Chalcedonian" <note>Thrasymachus of Chalcedon, famous for his emotional appeals in rhetoric.</note> has prevailed. He has become a man formidable at making many people angry at once, and then again, as he said, he can "charm" them out of their anger with incantations; he is the best at casting slanders and dissolving them, from whatever source they come. Regarding the **conclusion** <note>original: "τέλος" / "fine"</note> of speeches, everyone seems to agree, though some call it "recapitulation" <note>original: "ἐπάνοδον" / "repetitionem"</note> and others give it other names. *PHAEDRUS.* You mean reminding the listeners at the end, in summary, about what has been said? **SOCRATES.** That is what I mean—and anything else you might have to say about the art of words. *PHAEDRUS.* Only small things, not worth mentioning. **SOCRATES.** Then let us leave the small things aside and bring these others into the light to see what power of "art" they have and of what sort. *PHAEDRUS.* A very great power, Socrates, especially in gatherings of the crowd.

<margin>F</margin>
<margin>On the power and timing of speech.</margin>
**SOCRATES.** It has indeed. But, my friend, look and see if the weave of this "art" appears as thin and frayed to you as it does to me. *PHAEDRUS.* Just show me. **SOCRATES.** Tell me then: if someone went to your friend **Eryximachus** or his father **Acumenus** <note>Eryximachus and Acumenus were well-known physicians in Athens.</note> and said, "I know how to apply such things to the body so as to make it hot or cold as I wish, and if I choose, to make it vomit or have a bowel movement, and many other such things; and because I know these things, I claim to be a doctor and to be able to make a doctor of anyone to whom I hand down this knowledge"—what do you think they would say? *PHAEDRUS.* What else but to ask him if he also knows **to whom** and **when** and **to what extent** each of these things should be done?

<margin>G</margin>
**SOCRATES.** And if he said, "Not at all; but I claim that the one who has learned these things from me will be able to do what you ask for himself"? *PHAEDRUS.* They would say, I think, that the man is mad; he has heard something from a book or happened upon some medicines, and he thinks he has become a doctor, though he understands nothing of the art. **SOCRATES.** And what if someone went to **Sophocles** or **Euripides** <note>The two most famous tragic playwrights of the era.</note> and said he knew how to make very long speeches about a small matter and very short ones about a great matter, and could write pitiful speeches when he wished, or conversely, terrifying and threatening ones, and all such things? And by teaching these, he thought he was handing down the art of tragedy? *PHAEDRUS.* They too, Socrates, would laugh, I think, at anyone who thought tragedy was anything other than the **composition** of these elements, fitted to each other and to the whole.

<margin>H</margin>
**SOCRATES.** But they would not, I think, rebuke him rudely. It would be like a musician meeting a man who thinks he is a master of harmony because he knows how to produce the highest and lowest notes on a string. He would not say harshly, "You wretched madman!" but, being a musician, he would say more gently: "My good man, it is absolutely necessary for one who is to be a master of harmony to know these things; however, there is nothing to stop one who is in your condition from knowing nothing at all about harmony. You know the **preliminary** lessons necessary for harmony, but you do not know harmony itself." *PHAEDRUS.* Quite right.

<column-break/>

<note>The following section appears to be a printer's repetition or a catchword summary of the previous column's ending, common in early modern editions.</note>

**SOCRATES.** ...he would act just as a musician would when meeting a man who believes himself a musician because he knows how to produce the lowest and highest notes on a string. He would not say harshly, "You wretched madman!" but, being a musician, he would warn more mildly, "O best of men, it is necessary for anyone who would be a musician to hold these things. But nothing prevents one who is affected as you are from understanding absolutely nothing of harmony; for you recognize the things necessary *before* harmony, but you are entirely ignorant of harmony itself." *PHAEDRUS.* Most correct.

<summary>Socrates argues that technical rhetorical tricks (like introductions or emotional appeals) are merely "preliminaries" to the true art of rhetoric. He compares the popular rhetoricians to people who know how to use medicines but don't know the science of medicine, or those who know how to tune a string but do not understand harmony.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the conversation between Socrates and Phaedrus regarding the true nature of rhetoric. Socrates has just distinguished the "dialectician"—one who can divide and collect ideas according to their nature—from those who merely teach the tools of public speaking.</meta>

# OF PLATO

**SOCRATES.** In the same way, Sophocles would say to someone presenting him with the elements that precede a tragedy that he possesses the precursors to tragedy, but not the art of tragedy itself. And Acumenus the physician would say the same regarding the precursors of medicine, rather than medicine itself. **PHAEDRUS.** Quite right. **SOCRATES.** But what if the honey-toned Adrastus, <note>original: "mellifluus Adrastus." Adrastus was a legendary king of Argos, known in rhetorical tradition for his persuasive speech.</note> or even Pericles himself, heard of these wonderful "artifices of words" we were just recounting—the brief sayings, the use of images, and all those other things we thought should be examined in the light of day? Do we think they would be as harsh and rude as we are toward those who wrote and taught these things as if they were the "art of rhetoric"? Or would they, being wiser than us, rebuke us? Perhaps they would say: "O Phaedrus and Socrates, we should not be angry, but forgiving, if certain men who are ignorant of the art of logic <note>original: "differendi ignari" (ignorant of the way of distinguishing/disputing).</note> are unable to define what rhetoric actually is. Being in such a state, they possess only the necessary preliminary lessons of the art, yet they boast that they have discovered rhetoric itself. And by teaching these preliminaries to others, they claim to have handed over the complete art of oratory. They leave it to their students to acquire, through their own industry, the ability to arrange each of these elements persuasively and to weave together a whole speech, as if such things required no instruction." **PHAEDRUS.** Indeed, Socrates, that seems to be the nature of the "art" which these men teach and write about as rhetoric. And it seems to me you have spoken the truth. But how, and from where, can one acquire the art of the truly persuasive orator? **SOCRATES.** It is likely, Phaedrus—perhaps even necessary—that this contest, like any other, requires one to be perfected. If you have the natural talent to be an orator, you will become an excellent one if you add knowledge and practice. If you lack any of these, you will be incomplete. <margin>When one becomes an excellent orator.</margin> As for the true art of this kind, it does not seem to follow the path that Gorgias and Thrasymachus have taken, but another path entirely. **PHAEDRUS.** Which path is that? **SOCRATES.** It seems, my good man, that it was not without reason that Pericles became the most perfect of all orators. **PHAEDRUS.** Why so? **SOCRATES.** All the great arts require "idle talk" <note>original: "ἀδολεσχίας" (adoleschias). Socrates uses this term playfully to mean the deep, often seemingly pointless philosophical questioning of nature.</note> and the contemplation of the high things in nature. This loftiness of mind and the power to achieve one's goal in any matter seem to come from this source. This is what Pericles added to his natural talent. <margin>The great arts require dialectical exercise and contemplation. Pericles was a student of Anaxagoras.</margin> For by relying on his friendship with Anaxagoras, <note>Anaxagoras was a Pre-Socratic philosopher who taught that "Mind" (Nous) ordered the universe.</note> a man who investigated such things, Pericles gave himself over to contemplation. He came to understand the nature of the mind and of folly—the very things Anaxagoras discussed at length—and from that source, he drew into his art of speaking whatever he saw would be useful. **PHAEDRUS.** What do you mean by that? **SOCRATES.** The method of medicine is almost the same as the method of speaking. **PHAEDRUS.** In what way? **SOCRATES.** In both, it is necessary to divide nature: the nature of the body in the one, and of the soul in the other. If you intend to provide medicine and nourishment to the body not merely by routine and experience, but by art, you must do so to produce health and strength. Similarly, you must apply reasons and lawful institutions to the soul to impart whatever persuasion and virtue you desire. **PHAEDRUS.** That is very likely, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** Do you think it is possible to sufficiently understand the nature of the soul without understanding the nature of the whole? **PHAEDRUS.** If we are to believe Hippocrates, the successor of Asclepius, <note>Hippocrates is the famous "father of medicine"; the Asclepiads were a guild of physicians claiming descent from the god of healing.</note> we cannot even understand the nature of the body without this method. **SOCRATES.** Well said, my friend. But we must consider whether the reasoning of our discussion agrees with Hippocrates. **PHAEDRUS.** I agree. **SOCRATES.** Consider, then, what Hippocrates and true reason say about the investigation of nature. <margin>On the method of nature.</margin> Is this not how we must think about the nature of anything? First, we must ask whether the thing is simple or complex—the thing in which we wish to be experts ourselves and make others experts. Then, if it is simple, we must investigate its power: what action is it naturally suited to perform, and upon what? Or, what is it naturally suited to suffer, and by what? If it has many forms, we must count them and investigate each one as we did the single form: what does it naturally do, and what does it naturally suffer? **PHAEDRUS.** So it appears, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** To proceed without these steps is like the journey of a blind man. But one who treats something with art should not be compared to the blind or the deaf. It is clear that whoever teaches speeches with art will accurately demonstrate the essential nature of that thing to which he applies his speeches; and that thing, I suppose, is the soul. **PHAEDRUS.** Without a doubt. **SOCRATES.** Is not his whole effort directed toward this: to persuade the soul? **PHAEDRUS.** Exactly. **SOCRATES.** It is clear, then, that Thrasymachus—and anyone else who applies himself to teaching rhetoric—must first, with the greatest diligence, describe and declare whether the soul is by nature one and uniform, or complex like the form of the body. For this is what we mean by "showing its nature." **PHAEDRUS.** Entirely so. **SOCRATES.** Secondly, he must show what it can do to what, or what it can suffer from what. **PHAEDRUS.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** Thirdly, having classified the types of speeches and the types of souls, and their various states, he must run through all the causes, matching each speech to each soul. He must teach what kind of soul is necessarily moved to belief by what kind of speech, and for what reason, while another is not. **PHAEDRUS.** That would be most excellent, it seems...

<column-break/>

**A** **SOCRATES.** Therefore, Sophocles would also say of the man demonstrating to them the components of tragedy that he knows the things *around* tragedy, but not the tragic art itself; and Acumenus would say the same of the things *around* medicine, but not the medical art itself. **PHAEDRUS.** Entirely so. **SOCRATES.** And what of the honey-voiced Adrastus, or even Pericles? If they heard of the "all-beautiful" technical devices we just went through—the "brevity-of-speech" and "image-making" and all the other things we said should be examined "under the light"—would they be as harsh to the authors and teachers of these things as you and I were? Would they, out of a lack of refinement, speak uneducated words to those who wrote these as an "art of rhetoric"? Or, being wiser than us, would they rebuke us, saying: "O **B** Phaedrus and Socrates, one should not be angry but forgiving if some men, through an ignorance of dialectic, <note>original: "μὴ ἐπιστάμενοι διαλέγεσθαι" (not knowing how to engage in dialectic).</note> have been unable to define what rhetoric actually is. Because of this condition, possessing only the necessary preliminary studies of the art, they imagined they had discovered rhetoric itself; and by teaching these to others, they believe they have taught rhetoric perfectly. They think their students must provide for themselves the ability to speak each of these things persuasively and to construct the whole work from their own resources." **PHAEDRUS.** Indeed, Socrates, the "art" which these men teach and write about as rhetoric is likely something of that sort; and to me, **C** you seem to have spoken the truth. But as for the art of the truly rhetorical and persuasive man, how and from where might one be able to acquire it? **SOCRATES.** The ability, Phaedrus, to become a perfect competitor is likely—and perhaps even necessarily—the same here as in other things. If it is in your nature to be rhetorical, you will be a famous orator by adding knowledge and practice; but in whatever way you are lacking in these, in that way you will be incomplete. As for the "art" part of it, the method does not seem to me to be the path along which Lysias and Thrasymachus travel. **PHAEDRUS.** But which way, then? **SOCRATES.** It is likely, my best of men, that Pericles naturally became the most perfect of all in rhetoric. **PHAEDRUS.** Why so? **SOCRATES.** All the great **D** arts require "subtle chatter" and "high-altitude speculation" <note>original: "ἀδολεσχίας καὶ μετεωρολογίας φύσεως πέρι" (idle talk and meteorology/speculation about nature). Socrates is using the terminology of his critics to describe the value of philosophy.</note> about nature. For this loftiness of mind and all-round effectiveness seem to enter from some such source; and this is what Pericles acquired in addition to his natural talent. For I think that by falling in with Anaxagoras, who was that sort of man, Pericles was filled with "high-altitude speculation" and arrived at the nature of Mind and Folly (about which Anaxagoras made his long discourses); from there he drew into the art of words what was appropriate for it. **PHAEDRUS.** How do you mean this? **SOCRATES.** The method of the art of medicine is the same as that of rhetoric. **PHAEDRUS.** How so? **SOCRATES.** In both, one must analyze nature—the nature of the body in one, and of the soul in the other—if you intend, not by routine and experience alone, but by art, to impart health and strength to the body by applying medicines and nourishment, and to the soul, **E** by applying words and lawful practices, to hand over whatever persuasion and virtue you wish. **PHAEDRUS.** That is certainly likely, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** Do you then think it is possible to understand the nature of the soul in a way worthy of mention without understanding the nature of the whole? **PHAEDRUS.** If we are to believe Hippocrates of the house of Asclepius, we cannot even understand the body without this method. **SOCRATES.** He speaks well, my friend. However, in addition to Hippocrates, we must examine our reasoning to see if it agrees. **PHAEDRUS.** I agree. **SOCRATES.** Look then at what Hippocrates and true reason say about nature. Must we not think about the nature of anything in this way? First, is the thing about which we wish to be technical—and to make others so—simple or multiform? Then, if it is simple, we must look at its power: what is its natural capacity to act upon what, or what **F** is its capacity to be acted upon by what? And if it has many forms, we should count them and see in each one what we saw in the single case: what is its natural capacity to act, or to be acted upon by what? **PHAEDRUS.** It is likely, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** At any rate, the method without these steps is like the journey of a blind man. But one who pursues anything with art should not be likened to the blind or the deaf. It is clear that if one gives speeches to another with art, he will accurately demonstrate the essence of the nature of that thing to which he addresses the speeches; and this, surely, will be the soul. **PHAEDRUS.** Of course. **SOCRATES.** Is not his entire struggle directed toward persuasion? Or not? **PHAEDRUS.** Yes. **SOCRATES.** It is clear, then, that Thrasymachus **G** and whoever else teaches the art of rhetoric in earnest will first, with all accuracy, write and make the soul visible: whether it is by nature one and uniform, or multiform according to the shape of the body. For this is what we call "demonstrating its nature." **PHAEDRUS.** Entirely so. **SOCRATES.** Secondly, he must show what it is naturally suited to do or suffer from what. **PHAEDRUS.** Of course. **SOCRATES.** Thirdly, having classified the types of speeches and souls, and their various states, he will go through all the causes, fitting each speech to each soul, and teaching what kind of soul, under what kind of speeches, and for what cause, is necessarily persuaded, while another remains unpersuaded. **PHAEDRUS.** This would indeed, it seems, be the most beautiful way. **SOCRATES.** Indeed, my friend, nothing that is shown or spoken will ever be written or spoken with art in any other way—neither these things nor anything else. But the men who currently write "Arts of Words" (whom you have heard) are rogues and hide their knowledge, though they know all about the soul. Until they speak and write in this way, let us not be persuaded...

<summary>Socrates argues that true rhetoric is an art (techne) akin to medicine, requiring a deep philosophical understanding of the nature of the soul rather than just a collection of stylistic tricks. He highlights Pericles as a model orator who succeeded by combining natural talent with the philosophical contemplation of nature and the mind.</summary>
<keywords>Plato, Phaedrus, Socrates, rhetoric vs. dialectic, Pericles, Anaxagoras, Hippocrates, nature of the soul, persuasion, medical analogy</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Phaedrus. Socrates is transitioning from a critique of existing rhetorical manuals to defining a true "art" of rhetoric based on the nature of the soul and the principle of probability.</meta>

# PHAEDRUS

<margin>A</margin> ...we shall acknowledge that they write by art. PHAEDRUS. In what way do you mean?

<margin>How to speak with art.</margin> SOCRATES. I could not easily state the exact words. However, I am willing to explain how one ought to write, as far as possible, if it is to be done artistically. PHAEDRUS. Speak then. SOCRATES. Since the power of speech happens to be a way of <term>leading the soul</term> <note>original: "ψυχαγωγία" (psychagogia), literally "soul-leading" or "enchanting the soul."</note>, it is necessary for the one who intends to be an orator to know how many kinds of soul there are. These are of such and such a number, and of such and such a character; from which some people become of one sort, and others of another. Once these have been distinguished, there are in turn so many kinds of speeches, each of a certain character. Therefore, people of a certain sort are easily persuaded to certain things by certain kinds of speeches for a specific reason, while those of a different character are difficult to persuade for other reasons. After one has sufficiently understood these things, he must then observe them as they occur and are applied in actual affairs, and he must be able to follow them keenly with his perception. Otherwise, he still knows nothing more than the words he once heard from his teachers. But when he is sufficiently able to say what kind of person is persuaded by what kind of speech, and is able to perceive a person present before him and realize that "this is the man and this is the nature about which those lessons were concerned, now present in reality," to whom he must apply these specific speeches in this specific way to produce persuasion—when he possesses all these abilities, and has also grasped the <margin>B</margin> proper timing <note>original: "καιροὺς" (kairous), meaning the opportune or critical moment.</note> for when to speak and when to be silent, and understands the proper and improper use of brevity, of appeals to pity, of intensification, and all the various kinds of speeches he has learned—then, and not before, is his art beautifully and perfectly completed. But if anyone falls short in any of these points while speaking, teaching, or writing, yet claims to speak by art, the one who remains unpersuaded has the better of him. "What then?" the writer of such a manual might perhaps say, "O Phaedrus and Socrates, do you think the so-called art of speech should be accepted in this way, or in some other?" PHAEDRUS. It is impossible, Socrates, for it to be otherwise; yet it seems no small task.

SOCRATES. You speak the truth. For this reason, we ought to turn all these arguments upside down and examine whether some easier and shorter path to the art might appear, so that we do not wander in vain along a long and rough road when a short and smooth one is available. If you have any help to offer from what you have heard from Lysias or anyone else, try to remember and tell it. PHAEDRUS. For the <margin>D</margin> sake of trial I might, but not at this moment. SOCRATES. Shall I then tell you a story I heard from those who concern themselves with these matters? PHAEDRUS. Why not? SOCRATES. They say, Phaedrus, that it is only just to tell even the "wolf's side of the story." <note>A Greek proverb meaning that even the accused—or the unpopular side—deserves a hearing.</note> PHAEDRUS. And you should do just that. SOCRATES. They say, then, that there is no need to make such a grand affair of this, nor to trace the matter back so far to its high origins. For as we said at the beginning of this discussion, they claim that one who intends to be a sufficiently capable orator has no need to know the truth about what is just or good, whether in things or in men who are such by nature or education. They say that in the law courts, no one cares in the least for the truth of these matters, but only for what is <term>persuasive</term>. And this is the <term>probable</term> <note>original: "εἰκός" (eikos) or "verisimile," meaning what seems likely or credible to an audience, regardless of facts.</note>, to which the man who intends to speak with art must apply his mind. For they claim that sometimes one should not even relate what actually happened, if it does not seem probable, but rather what is probable, both in prosecution and in defense. In short, the speaker must pursue the probable and say a long farewell to the truth. For they believe that this principle, maintained throughout the entire speech, provides the complete art of rhetoric. PHAEDRUS. You have recounted exactly, Socrates, what those who profess to be masters of the art of speech say. I remember we touched on this briefly before. This seems to be a very great matter to those who spend their time on it. SOCRATES. But you have surely studied <margin>E</margin> Tisias <note>Tisias was one of the legendary founders of Greek rhetoric in Sicily.</note> himself with great care. Let Tisias tell us this then: does he define the "probable" as anything other than that which seems true to the crowd? PHAEDRUS. What else could it be? SOCRATES. It seems he discovered this clever and <margin>F</margin> artistic secret and wrote that if a weak but brave man, having beaten up a strong but cowardly man and stripped him of his cloak or something else, is brought into court, neither of them should tell the truth. The coward should say he was not beaten by the brave man alone, while the brave man should refute this by showing they were alone, and then use that famous argument: "How could a man as small as I am have attacked a man as strong as he is?" The strong man will not confess his own cowardice, but by attempting some other lie, he will perhaps provide his opponent with a way to refute him. And there are other such things said to be "by art" in other cases. Is it not so, Phaedrus? PHAEDRUS. Indeed it is. SOCRATES. Heavens! Tisias seems to have discovered a wonderfully hidden art, or whoever it was and wherever he likes to be named from. But, my friend, shall we say this to him or not? PHAEDRUS. Say what? SOCRATES. "O Tisias, long ago, before you came along, we happened to be saying that this 'probability' of yours occurs in the minds of the crowd because of its likeness to the truth. And we just now concluded that the one who knows the truth always knows best how to find these <margin>G</margin> likenesses. Therefore, if you have something else to say about the art of speech, we would listen; but if not, we will stand by what we have just discussed: that unless a man counts up the various natures of his future listeners, and is able to divide things into their kinds and encompass each individual thing under a single idea, he will never be an artist in words to the extent that it is possible for a human being. But <margin>H</margin> these things he will never acquire without much labor, which the wise man should undertake not for the sake of speaking and acting before men, but..."

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...we shall confess that they write by art. PHAEDRUS. What manner do you mean?
<margin>How to speak by art.</margin> SOCRATES. I could not easily speak the words themselves. But in what manner it is necessary to write, if we are to write by art, I will set forth as far as possible. PHAEDRUS. Speak, I pray. SOCRATES. Since the faculty of speaking is a certain drawing of the soul and a delight, the future orator must know how many species the soul has. For these are so many and of such a kind, from which some become of one sort, others of another. These being thus distinguished, of speeches also there are so many and of such kinds. Thus, souls of such a kind are easily persuaded to such things by such speeches for a certain cause; but those affected
<margin>B</margin> otherwise are not persuaded for some reason. Therefore, it is necessary for him who has sufficiently perceived these things, afterwards in actual business to be able to mark what is observed and caught in the moment, and to follow the senses; otherwise, he does not yet have anything more than the words formerly handed down to him by teachers. But when he can sufficiently say who is persuaded by what speeches, and keenly perceives the person present to be endowed with that character about which there was previously a discussion, and thus that he himself must be driven to such things by such speeches: he, thus instructed, will then at last have perfectly attained this art, when to these superior things he has added this: that he knows the opportunity for speaking and keeping silent, and the use or misuse of brevity, of pity, of sharper vehemence, and of amplification, and rightly knows the other parts of a speech handed down by teachers; but before this, by no means. But he who lacks any of these in speaking, or teaching, or writing, and says he speaks from art, the one who is not persuaded prevails. But perhaps a writer will thus address us: "O Phaedrus and Socrates, do you think the art of speaking is to be taken up thus entirely, or otherwise?" PHAEDRUS. It is impossible, O Socrates, otherwise, although that work appears not small. SOCRATES. You speak true things. And for the sake of these it is necessary, having revolved all speeches up and down, to search whether any easier and shorter way to it occurs, lest we wander blindly through a long and rough path when it is permitted to go through a short and level one. Wherefore, if you can bring any help through those things which you received from Lysias, or any other, recall it to memory, and set it forth. PHAEDRUS. For the sake of trying I could indeed, yet not at present. SOCRATES. Do you wish that I should also review for you a speech which I once heard about matters of this kind? PHAEDRUS. Why not? SOCRATES. They say therefore, O Phaedrus, it is just to narrate even that which is said of the wolf. <margin>Proverb.</margin> PHAEDRUS. And you should do so. SOCRATES. They say therefore there is no need to extol and magnify these things so much; nor to repeat the discussion from too high and far off. Indeed, as we said at the beginning of the discussion, it is not necessary for the future orator to know the truth about just and good things, whether of matters or of men, who are such by nature or education. For in judgments, they say, none of these care for the truth at all, but for persuasion. But that is the "probable" <note>original: "verisimile," literally "like the truth."</note>, to which he who is to speak by art ought to intend his mind. Nor are facts to be spoken sometimes, unless it is probable they were done; but both in accusation and defense, probabilities are always to be introduced: and entirely the speaker should pursue the probable, but the one speaking many things should neglect the truth. For if this is observed in every speech, they say the perfect art of oratory is exhibited. PHAEDRUS. You have narrated those things, O Socrates, which they say who profess the rhetorical art. For I remember we briefly touched on that in the things above. But this seems to be something great to those who are occupied in this art. SOCRATES. But you have also heavily trampled Tisias himself. SOCRATES. Let Tisias therefore also tell us this: does he call anything else "probable" and "likely" than that which seems so to the common people? PHAEDRUS. What else? SOCRATES. Besides, he seems to have discovered and written this clever and artificial thing: that if anyone weak and bold, when he has despoiled a certain strong and timid man, having beaten him with blows, is led into judgment, it is necessary for neither of these to confess the truth. But the timid one indeed should say he was not beaten by that bold one alone; but the bold one should refute this, showing they were alone, and take refuge in such a thing: "In what way, since I am weak, would I have attacked this strong man?" But he will not speak of his own timidity, but devising something false, perhaps he will prove his adversary wrong. And in other things also there are certain such things which are spoken by art. Is it not thus, O Phaedrus? PHAEDRUS. Entirely so. SOCRATES. How shrewdly Tisias seems to have invented an abstruse art, or whoever else it was, or by whatever other surname he is delighted. But shall we say this, O friend, or not? PHAEDRUS. What is that? SOCRATES. We were affirming to Tisias long before you approached, that this "probable" and "likely" happens to the common people not otherwise than through a likeness of the truth. But we were asserting that likenesses of the truth can be most aptly found everywhere by him who knows the truth. Wherefore, if you shall say anything else about this art, we will indeed listen; if less, we will grant faith to those things which we said a little before: namely, that unless someone knows and distinguishes the dispositions of the listeners, and separates the things themselves into their species, and again comprehends individuals in one idea, he will never attain the art of speaking as far as is permitted to man. But this he will never follow without long study. In which a prudent man will not sweat to the end that he may be able to speak and act toward men, but...

<sig>Gg iiij</sig>

<summary>Socrates argues that true rhetoric requires a deep understanding of human psychology (the soul) and its various types, rather than just memorized techniques. He critiques the Sophistic reliance on "probability" (eikos) over truth, using the example of Tisias to show how such an approach leads to deception rather than genuine art.</summary>

<keywords>Plato, Socrates, Phaedrus, Tisias, rhetoric, soul, psychagogia, probability, eikos, verisimile, persuasion, dialectic, truth vs. likelihood</keywords>

Socrates is now moving from the technical requirements of speaking to the nature of writing itself, introducing the famous myth of the invention of letters.</meta>

# OF PLATO

...so that they may rather be able to both speak and act, according to their capacity, in ways that are pleasing to the gods. For men wiser than us, O Tisias <note>Tisias was a pioneer of Greek rhetoric from Sicily, often associated with the idea that "probability" is more important than "truth."</note>, say that a man in his right mind ought not to study how to please his fellow-servants—except as a secondary matter—but how he may obey masters who are good and of good descent. For this reason, if the circuitous path is somewhat long, do not be surprised. For we must go around it, not as you suppose, but for the sake of great things. These things will be, as reason dictates, most beautifully accomplished from those efforts, if anyone is willing. PHAEDRUS. This seems to be very beautifully said, O Socrates, if only someone were able to achieve it. SOCRATES. But it is noble to always strive for noble things, and to endure whatever may happen to befall. PHAEDRUS. Very much so. SOCRATES. So much then for the art and lack of art in speaking. PHAEDRUS. Sufficiently so, indeed. SOCRATES.

<sig>B</sig> <margin>On the propriety of writing.</margin> It remains for us to say what is fitting and what is unfitting in writing. PHAEDRUS. Plainly. SOCRATES. Do you know in what way you can best please God by speaking or acting regarding discourses? PHAEDRUS. Not at all. Do you? SOCRATES. I have heard some things handed down by the ancients; but they themselves know the truth. If we could find that for ourselves, would we then have any concern for human opinions?

<sig>C</sig> PHAEDRUS. A ridiculous question indeed; but recite what you say you have heard. SOCRATES. I heard that near Naucratis in Egypt <note>Naucratis was an important Greek trading post in the Nile Delta.</note> there was one of the ancient gods of that place, to whom the bird called the Ibis was sacred; the name of the deity himself was Theuth <note>Theuth is the Greek name for the Egyptian god Thoth, the patron of scribes and wisdom.</note>. He was the first to invent numbers and the calculation of numbers, geometry, and astronomy, and further, the games of draughts and dice, and also letters. At that time Thamus was the king of all Egypt, living in the great city which the Greeks call Egyptian Thebes, and they call the god himself Ammon. Theuth went to him and showed him his arts, saying that they ought to be distributed to the rest of the Egyptians. But the king asked what the utility of each was; and as Theuth explained, the king praised what seemed well-said and blamed what was otherwise. Thamus is said to have shown many things to Theuth regarding each art in both directions, which would take a long speech to recount in detail.

<sig>D</sig> But when they came to the letters, Theuth said, "This discipline, O King, will make the Egyptians wiser and readier in memory. For a remedy <note>original: "remedium/φάρμακον" (pharmakon). In Greek, this word is famously ambiguous, meaning both "remedy" and "poison."</note> for memory and wisdom has been found." But the king replied, "O most ingenious Theuth, one man is able to give birth to the works of art, but another is better suited to judge what measure of harm or profit they will bring to those who use them. And now you, being the father of letters, have claimed the opposite of what they can do out of your benevolence toward them. For the use of them will breed forgetfulness in the souls of those who learn them, because of the neglect of memory; since, trusting in external written marks, they will not recall things from within themselves. Therefore, you have found a remedy not for memory, but for reminding. You offer your disciples a reputation for wisdom rather than the truth itself.

<sig>E</sig> For when they have read many things without the teaching of a master, they will seem to be experienced in many things while being, for the most part, ignorant. They will also be difficult to get along with, since they are not endowed with true wisdom, but are merely adorned with the opinion of wisdom." PHAEDRUS. You, O Socrates, easily make up stories of Egyptians or any other nation you please. SOCRATES. But, my friend, those who dwell in the temple of Zeus at Dodona <note>Dodona was an ancient oracle where the rustling leaves of sacred oak trees were interpreted as the voice of Zeus.</note> say that the first prophetic words broke forth from an oak. To those men of old, since they were not wise like you moderns, it was enough in their simplicity to listen to rocks and oaks, provided they spoke the truth. You, perhaps, think it matters who the speaker is and what land he comes from. For you do not consider only whether the things said are true or false.

<sig>F</sig> PHAEDRUS. You have rebuked me rightly, and it seems to me to be as the Theban king says regarding letters. SOCRATES. Therefore, whoever thinks he can leave an art behind in writing, or who receives it as something handed down in writing, as if something certain and firm would come from the letters, is very foolish; he truly ignores the prophecy of Ammon, believing that written words are anything more than a reminder to the one who already knows the things the letters signify. PHAEDRUS.

<sig>G</sig> Most rightly said. SOCRATES. For writing, Phaedrus, has this strange quality, and is truly very similar to painting. For the works of painting stand there as if living; but if you ask them anything, they maintain a very solemn silence. You might think that written discourses speak as if they had some understanding. But if you, being eager to learn, question them about anything they say, they always signify one and the same thing. And when a discourse is once written down, it is tossed about everywhere equally among those who understand it and those who have no business with it; it does not know to whom it ought to speak and to whom it ought not. When it is mistreated or unjustly insulted, it always needs its father's protection. For it can neither defend itself nor help itself. PHAEDRUS.

<sig>H</sig> These things also seem to be rightly said by you. SOCRATES. What further? Shall we look at another kind of discourse, the legitimate brother of this one, and see how it is born, and how much better and more powerful it is than the other? PHAEDRUS. What is this, and how do you say it comes to be? SOCRATES. It is the one, I say, which is written with knowledge in the soul of the learner, which is able to defend itself, and knows to whom it should speak and before whom it should be silent. PHAEDRUS. You mean the living and animate word of the man who knows, of which the written word may justly be called a kind of image. SOCRATES. Entirely so. But tell me this also: would a farmer of sound mind...

<column-break/>

<sig>A</sig> ...to speak and act before men, the temperate man must labor, but rather to speak things pleasing to the gods according to his power, and to do all things pleasingly according to his power. For as they say—O Tisias—the wiser among us say, that the man with mind should not study to please fellow-slaves, except as a side-task, but good masters and those of good stock. So if the circuit is long, do not wonder. For the sake of great things we must go around, not as you suppose. Yet these things shall be, as the argument says, if one is willing, the most beautiful results of those efforts. PHAEDRUS. Very beautifully said, I think, O Socrates, if only one were able. SOCRATES. But even in hunting for the beautiful, it is noble to suffer whatever may happen to befall. PHAEDRUS. Quite so. SOCRATES. Let this then be sufficient concerning the art and artlessness of speeches. PHAEDRUS.

<sig>B</sig> Why not? SOCRATES. The matter of propriety and impropriety in writing—how it might be done well, and what is improper—remains. Is it not so? PHAEDRUS. Yes. SOCRATES. Do you know, then, how you might best please God in the matter of speeches, whether acting or speaking? PHAEDRUS. Not at all. Do you? SOCRATES. I have a story I can tell from those of old; but they alone know the truth. If we could find this ourselves, would we still care for human opinions? PHAEDRUS. You ask a ridiculous thing; but tell what you say you have heard. SOCRATES. I heard then, that near Naucratis in Egypt was one of the ancient gods of that place, to whom the sacred bird which they call the Ibis belongs; and the name of the deity was Theuth. He was the first

<sig>C</sig> to invent number and calculation, and geometry and astronomy, and further, games of draughts and dice, and also letters. Now Thamus was king of all Egypt at that time, living in the great city of the upper region which the Greeks call Egyptian Thebes, and they call the god Ammon. Theuth went to him and showed him his arts, and said they ought to be given to the other Egyptians. The king asked what benefit each had. As he explained them, Thamus blamed some and praised others, according as he thought they were well or ill-said. Many things are said to have been declared by Thamus to Theuth about each art in both directions, which would be a long story to go through. But when he came to the letters, "This lesson, O King," said Theuth, "will make the

<sig>D</sig> Egyptians wiser and improve their memory. For a remedy for memory and wisdom has been found." But the king said, "O most technical Theuth, one man is able to give birth to the things of art, but another to judge what portion of harm and benefit they have for those who are going to use them. And now you, being the father of letters, have through benevolence said the opposite of what they can do. For this will produce forgetfulness in the souls of those who learn it, through neglect of memory, because through trust in writing they will be reminded from without by external marks, not from within by themselves. You have found a remedy not for memory, but for reminding. You provide your students with the appearance of wisdom, not the truth. For having become hearers of many things without being taught, they will seem to be multifaceted in knowledge, while being mostly

<sig>E</sig> ignorant and difficult to be with; having become 'seeming-wise' instead of wise." PHAEDRUS. O Socrates, you easily make up stories of Egypt and whatever land you please. SOCRATES. But, my friend, those in the temple of Zeus at Dodona said that the first prophetic words came from an oak. To the men of that time, since they were not wise like you young people, it was enough in their simplicity to listen to an oak and a rock, if only they spoke the truth. But to you, perhaps, it makes a difference who the speaker is and where he comes from. For you do not look only at whether the matter is so or otherwise. PHAEDRUS.

<sig>F</sig> You have rebuked me rightly. And it seems to me to be regarding letters just as the Theban says. SOCRATES. Therefore, he who thinks he can leave behind an art in writing, and he who receives it, thinking that something clear and solid will come from the writing, would be full of great simplicity; and he truly ignores the prophecy of Ammon, thinking that written words are anything more than a reminder to the one who knows the subject about which they were written. PHAEDRUS. Most rightly. SOCRATES. For writing, Phaedrus, has this strange quality, truly like painting. For the offspring of that art stand as if alive, but if you ask them anything, they maintain a very solemn silence. It is the same with written words; you might think they speak as if they had some intelligence, but if you ask them anything about what they say, wishing to learn, they signify only one and the same thing forever. And when it is once written, every discourse is rolled

<sig>G</sig> everywhere, equally among those who understand it and likewise among those to whom it does not belong; and it does not know to whom it should speak and to whom not. When it is ill-treated and unjustly reviled, it always needs its father to help it. For it is not able to defend or help itself. PHAEDRUS. These things also you have said most rightly. SOCRATES. What then? Shall we see another discourse, the legitimate brother of this one—how it is produced, and how much better and more powerful it is born than the other? PHAEDRUS. Which one is this, and how do you say it is produced? SOCRATES. The one that is written with knowledge in the soul of the learner, which is able to defend itself, and knows how to speak and when to be silent toward the right people. PHAEDRUS. You mean the living and breathing word of the one who knows; of which the written word might justly be called an image.

<sig>H</sig> SOCRATES. Entirely so. Tell me this: would a farmer who has sense...

<summary>Socrates recounts the myth of the Egyptian god Theuth and King Thamus to argue that writing is a "remedy for reminding" rather than a true path to wisdom. He characterizes written text as a silent, defenseless image of the "living" discourse that is written directly into a learner's soul.</summary>
