<meta>This page continues the discussion on the limitations of writing compared to the "living word" of spoken philosophy. Socrates has just introduced the idea that writing is a mere shadow of true knowledge, and now uses an agricultural metaphor to explain why a wise person would not rely solely on written texts.</meta>

# P H Æ D R V S. 357

<margin>A</margin>
Would a farmer who has sense, concerning the seeds he cares for and from which he wants fruit to be produced, plant them in the heat of summer in the **Gardens of Adonis** <note>The "Gardens of Adonis" were small pots or baskets filled with soil in which plants like lettuce or fennel were sown during the midsummer festival of Adonis. They sprouted rapidly but withered within eight days, symbolizing the short life of the god—and here, the superficial nature of writing.</note>, taking pleasure in seeing them become beautiful in only eight days? Or would he do such things only for the sake of amusement and for the festival, when he chose to do it at all? But for those seeds he was serious about, would he not use the art of agriculture, sowing them in suitable soil, and being content when what he sowed reached its fulfillment in the eighth month? PHAEDRUS: It is likely so, Socrates; he would do the one in earnest, and the other, as you say, in a very different way. SOCRATES: And shall we say that the man who possesses knowledge of what is just, beautiful, and good has less sense for his own "seeds" than a farmer does? PHAEDRUS: Not at all. SOCRATES: He will not, then, in earnest, "write them in water," sowing them with ink through a pen along with words—

<margin>B</margin>
words that are unable to defend themselves by speech, and unable to adequately teach the truth.

PHAEDRUS: No, that is certainly not likely. SOCRATES: Indeed not. But the "gardens of letters," it seems, he will sow and write for the sake of amusement; and whenever he writes, he will be storing up a treasury of reminders <note>original: "hypomnemata" (reminiscences or notebooks)</note> both for himself, against the forgetfulness of old age should he reach it, and for anyone else following the same track. He will be pleased to see them growing up tenderly; and while other men follow other amusements, refreshing themselves with drinking parties and other such brotherly pleasures, he, it seems, will spend his time "playing" with the things I mention instead. PHAEDRUS: You speak of a most noble pastime, Socrates, compared to a base one—the pastime of a man who is able to play with words, telling stories about justice and the other things you mention.

<margin>C</margin>
SOCRATES: It is so indeed, dear Phaedrus. But I believe a far more excellent earnestness arises concerning these matters when someone, using the **art of dialectic** <note>The method of logical inquiry through question and answer to reach a definition.</note> and taking a fitting soul, plants and sows words with knowledge. These words are able to help both themselves and the one who planted them; they are not fruitless, but contain a seed from which other words, springing up in other characters, are able to preserve this immortal seed forever, making the one who possesses it happy to the greatest extent possible for a human being. PHAEDRUS: What you say is indeed much more excellent.

<margin>D</margin>
SOCRATES: Now, then, Phaedrus, we are finally able to judge those other matters, since these have been agreed upon. PHAEDRUS: Which matters? SOCRATES: Those which we wished to see and which brought us to this point: so that we might examine the reproach against Lysias <note>A famous orator of the time whose written speech was criticized by Socrates earlier in the dialogue.</note> regarding the writing of speeches, and the speeches themselves—those written with art and those without it. Now, that which is artistic, and that which is not, seems to me to have been sufficiently explained.

PHAEDRUS: So it seemed, certainly. SOCRATES: But let us remind ourselves again: until a man knows the truth of each thing about which he speaks or writes, and becomes able to define the thing itself, and having defined it, knows how to divide it again by species until he reaches the indivisible; and until he has gained a clear view of the nature of the soul according to the same principles, finding the kind of speech that fits each nature, and so arranges and adorns his discourse—offering complex and harmoniously varied speeches to a complex soul, and simple speeches to a simple soul—until then, it will not be possible for the genus of speeches to be handled with art, as far as its nature allows, whether for the purpose of teaching or

<margin>E</margin>
for the purpose of persuasion, as our whole previous argument has signaled to us. PHAEDRUS: Entirely so; that is roughly how it appeared to us. SOCRATES: And what about the question of whether it is honorable or shameful to deliver and write speeches, and how this activity might justly be a matter of reproach? Have the things said a little while ago not made this clear? PHAEDRUS: Which things? SOCRATES: That if Lysias or anyone else ever wrote or will write, in private or in public, proposing laws—writing a political document—and thinking there is in it some great permanence and clarity, this is a reproach to the writer, whether anyone says so or not. For to be ignorant, whether waking or dreaming, of what is just and unjust, and bad and good, cannot truly escape being disgraceful, even if the whole crowd praises it. PHAEDRUS: Certainly not. SOCRATES: But consider the man who—

<margin>F</margin>
thinks that in a written speech on any subject, there is necessarily much that is "play," and that no speech ever written in meter or prose is worth great earnestness, nor any that is spoken like the recitations of rhapsodes <note>Performers who recited epic poetry, often without deep understanding.</note> which are delivered without examination or instruction for the sake of persuasion. Consider the man who believes that, in reality, the best of these serve only as a reminder to those who already know; but that in words spoken for the sake of instruction and learning—truly written in the soul concerning justice, beauty, and goodness—in these alone is there clarity, perfection, and something worth being earnest about. He thinks such words ought to be called his own "legitimate sons": first, the one found within himself, if it is there; and second, any offspring or brothers of it that have grown as they should in the souls of others. To other types of words, he says "farewell." 

<margin>G</margin>
Such a man as this, Phaedrus, is the kind of man that you and I might pray we both become. PHAEDRUS: I certainly wish and pray for the things you say. SOCRATES: Then let our "play" regarding speeches be considered sufficient. Go and tell Lysias that we went down to the stream of the Nymphs and the Muses and heard words which charged us to tell Lysias, and anyone else who composes speeches, and Homer, and anyone else who has composed poetry, whether plain or set to song; and thirdly, Solon <note>The famous lawgiver of Athens, representing the writers of laws.</note>, and whoever has written documents in political speeches, naming them laws:

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
Would he, with the greatest zeal and diligence, sow his most cherished seeds—from which he expects fruit—in the gardens of Adonis in the heat of summer, and rejoice to see them already made beautiful within eight days? Or would he rather do this, when he did it, for the sake of a festival and a game? But when acting in earnest, he would apply the study of agriculture, sowing where it is proper, and he will think it enough if, in an interval of eight months, his sowing reaches its harvest. PHAEDRUS: Exactly so, O Socrates; he will do those things in jest, as you say, but these in earnest. SOCRATES: And shall we think the man who possesses knowledge of things just, honorable, and good is more ignorant than a farmer regarding the sowing of his own seeds? PHAEDRUS: Least of all. SOCRATES: He will not, therefore,

<margin>B</margin>
studiously sow them in black water with a pen and with words, since he cannot help them when they are in danger, nor is he able to sufficiently demonstrate the truth from them. PHAEDRUS: Certainly that is not consistent with reason. SOCRATES: Truly not. But the gardens of letters, as it seems, he will sow and describe for the sake of play; and after he has written them as monuments and treasuries against the forgetfulness of his future old age, both for himself and for others who follow the same tracks, he will surely rejoice seeing his tender fruits already born, while other men follow other games and celebrate banquets and similar things. He, meanwhile, omitting these, will lead his life in the delights of discourse.

<margin>C</margin>
PHAEDRUS: You describe a most excellent game, Socrates, compared to that other very base one—the game of him who can play in discourses and converse about justice and the other things you speak of. SOCRATES: It is so indeed, friend Phaedrus. But in my opinion, the study in these matters is much more excellent when someone, using the art of dialectic and having found a suitable soul, plants and sows words with knowledge, which can bring help both to themselves and to their sower, and produce fruit and return seeds. From these, others being born in other characters can always preserve that immortal gift, and they make the one who has these things as happy as is possible for a man. PHAEDRUS: That too is much more excellent. SOCRATES: Now at last, O Phaedrus, having conceded these things, we can discern those others.

<margin>D</margin>
PHAEDRUS: Which ones? SOCRATES: Those, namely, for the sake of knowing which we have come down this far: that we might discuss the vituperation of Lysias in the art of writing itself, and those speeches themselves which are written either with art or without art. That which is artistic, and that which is void of art, we seem to have already sufficiently declared. PHAEDRUS: So it appears. SOCRATES: Again, it is necessary to remember that no one can possess the art of speaking to the highest degree for the purpose of persuading and teaching—as the superior reasoning has shown us—until he has known the truth of those things which he speaks or writes, and has learned to define the whole matter, and with the definition established, learned to divide it again according to species down to individuals. And by this reasoning, having contemplated the soul,

<margin>E</margin>
and having caught what is congruent to each nature, he so disposes and adorns the discourse, accommodating various speeches to a various soul, complex and manifold in harmony, but simple speeches to a simple soul. PHAEDRUS: So it has altogether appeared. SOCRATES: But what shall we say about that question we touched upon above? Whether it is honorable or base to pronounce and write orations, and how this study can be justly vituperated, and how not? Have the things above sufficiently declared this to us? PHAEDRUS: Which things? SOCRATES: Namely, that if Lysias, or anyone else, wrote at any time, or writes, or will write anything privately, or publicly regarding civil constitutions, in such a way—

<margin>F</margin>
—as to think that in his writings there is some great stability and certainty, that must be thought shameful for the writer, whether it is said by anyone or not. For to be ignorant of what is true and what is false, of the just and unjust, of the good and the evil—even if the whole common people should praise it—can never happen without being, in reality, most shameful. PHAEDRUS: Most shameful. SOCRATES: On the contrary, he who thinks that in a speech written about any matter there is a necessary element of play and jest, and who considers no speech, whether in prose or restricted by meter, to be worthy of great study in composition—like those who are accustomed to recite poems only for the sake of persuasion without judgment or teaching—but rather—

<margin>G</margin>
—considers that the best of those speeches were composed for the sake of being reminders to those who already know; and who thinks that in those speeches which are spoken for the sake of teaching and learning, and are truly written in the soul concerning things just, honorable, and good, there alone is there perspicuity and perfection and things worthy of study; and who judges that speeches of this kind are to be called his own legitimate sons—first of all the one that is within himself, if it be found, then whatever sons and brothers are born from this offspring in his own or in others' minds as is fitting, and postpones all others; this man, I say, such a one, O Phaedrus, seems to be the kind we would wish ourselves to become. PHAEDRUS: I for my part, as you say, desire it entirely and pray for it. SOCRATES: Let these things now be said by us concerning the art of speaking, as if spoken in play. Wherefore, you may tell Lysias that we, having gone to the flowing stream of the Nymphs and Muses, heard certain speeches which commanded us to tell Lysias and the other writers of orations, and Homer besides, and whoever else has composed naked poetry or poetry adorned with song, and lastly Solon and all who have committed civil institutions to writing:

<summary>In this concluding section of the Phaedrus, Socrates uses the metaphor of the "Gardens of Adonis" to argue that writing is a superficial pastime compared to "dialectic," which plants living knowledge in the soul. He concludes that a true master of rhetoric must know the truth, understand the nature of the soul, and view written texts only as reminders rather than sources of certainty.</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Phaedrus, Lysias, Gardens of Adonis, dialectic, rhetoric, writing vs speaking, soul, agriculture, Solon, Homer, philosophy</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes the dialogue of the *Phaedrus*, where Socrates and Phaedrus discuss the merits of speech over writing and the future of the orator Isocrates. It then transitions into the *Apology*, Plato’s account of Socrates’ defense speech during his trial for impiety and corrupting the youth.</meta>

<header>PLATONIS</header>

but if they have composed these works with a consciousness of the truth, and are able to defend what they have written when brought into discussion, and can show by speaking that their writings are of little value in comparison, then they should not be named for the things they toyed with using a pen, but rather for those things they have seriously thought out. PHAEDRUS: What names then, and how would you assign them? SOCRATES: To call them "Wise," <note>original: "Sapientis" / "σοφὸν". In the Greek tradition, a 'Sophist' claimed to possess wisdom, whereas a 'Philosopher' was merely a lover or seeker of it.</note> O Phaedrus, seems to me a great thing that belongs to God alone. But "Philosopher," or some similar name, would be more fitting and modest for such men as we have just described. PHAEDRUS: That is certainly not unbecoming. SOCRATES: Therefore, the man who has nothing more excellent than what he has written, and who has spent time turning it up and down, gluing pieces together or taking them away in his revisions, you would rightly call him a "poet" or a "writer of speeches" or a "law-writer," would you not? PHAEDRUS: Why not? SOCRATES: Tell these things, then, to your friend. PHAEDRUS: But what will you do? For your own friend must not be passed over. SOCRATES: Who is that? PHAEDRUS: The fair Isocrates <note>Isocrates was a famous Athenian orator and teacher. Plato often contrasted Socrates' philosophical method with the rhetorical training offered by Isocrates.</note>. What will you report to him? SOCRATES: What shall we say he is? SOCRATES: Isocrates is still young, O Phaedrus. But I wish to say what I prophesy for him. PHAEDRUS: What is that? SOCRATES: He seems to me to have a greater natural talent than could be compared to the speeches of Lysias. 
<margin>Cicero says this in his "The Orator" in these words.</margin> Furthermore, he has a more noble character toward virtue, so that it would not be at all surprising if, as he grows older, he should either surpass everyone who has ever touched a speech in this genre of oratory which he now studies—as if they were mere children—or, if he is not satisfied with these things, some more divine impulse might lead him to greater things. For there is, by nature, a certain philosophy in the mind of this man. This message, then, received from the gods of this place, I bring to Isocrates, my beloved; you bring yours to your Lysias. PHAEDRUS: It shall be so. But let us go from here, since the heat has now subsided. SOCRATES: We ought to offer a prayer to these gods before we go. PHAEDRUS: Why not? SOCRATES: O dear Pan <note>Pan was the god of the wild, shepherds, and flocks, often associated with the rustic setting of this dialogue.</note>, and all you other gods who dwell in this place, grant me that I may become beautiful within; and that whatever outward things I have may be at peace with those within. May I consider the wise man alone to be rich. And may I have only as much gold as a temperate man, and no other, could carry or drive away. Do you think we need to pray for anything else, Phaedrus? For me, the prayer is enough. PHAEDRUS: Make the same prayer for me as well. For the things of friends are common. SOCRATES: Let us go.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> If he has composed these things knowing where the truth lies, and is able to help his work when it is put to the test regarding what he wrote, being able himself to show that the written words are poor, such a man should not be addressed by a name derived from these writings, but from the things he was serious about. PHAEDRUS: What names then do you assign him? SOCRATES: To call him "wise," O Phaedrus, seems to me a great thing, and fitting for God alone; but to call him a "philosopher" <note>original: "φιλόσοφον" - literally 'wisdom-lover'.</note> or something of that sort would both fit him better and be in better taste. PHAEDRUS: And that would be not at all out of character. SOCRATES: Therefore, will you not rightly call him a poet, or a writer of speeches, or a drafter of laws, who has nothing more precious than the things he composed or wrote, turning them up and down over time, sticking them together and taking them away?
<margin>B</margin> PHAEDRUS: Of course. SOCRATES: Tell this then to your companion. PHAEDRUS: But what of you? What will you do? For your companion must not be overlooked either. SOCRATES: Who is he? PHAEDRUS: The beautiful Isocrates. What will you report to him, O Socrates? What shall we say he is? SOCRATES: Isocrates is still young, O Phaedrus. However, what I prophesy about him, I am willing to say. PHAEDRUS: What is that? SOCRATES: He seems to me to be better in his speeches than those of Lysias' circle, and to be tempered with a more noble nature. Thus it would be no wonder if, as he advances in age, he should excel more than children over all who have ever attempted speeches in the very works he now attempts; and further, if these things do not satisfy him, a more divine impulse might lead him to greater things.
<margin>C</margin> For by nature, my friend, there is a certain philosophy in the man’s intellect. These things, then, I announce from the gods here to Isocrates as my favorite; and you announce those things to Lysias as yours. PHAEDRUS: It shall be so. But let us go, since the stifling heat has become milder. SOCRATES: Should we not pray to these gods before we journey on? PHAEDRUS: Of course. SOCRATES: O dear Pan and all you other gods here, grant me to become beautiful in the inner self; and that my outer possessions be friendly to my inner ones. May I believe the wise man to be wealthy. And may I have a quantity of gold such as no one could carry or drive away except the temperate man. Do we need anything else, O Phaedrus? For me, the prayer is measured enough. PHAEDRUS: Pray for these same things for me too. For the affairs of friends are in common. SOCRATES: Let us go.

> *Socrates was accused by Meletus of investigating too curiously those things which are beneath the earth and in the heavens, and of teaching a certain more sublime science to others. In the forum, before the judges, Socrates began his defense for his life: yet in his own way, as a philosopher indeed, and one who intentionally recoils from an inflated and grand style of speaking.*

<meta>This page transitions from the end of the Phaedrus—a dialogue on love and rhetoric—to the beginning of the Apology. The Apology is Plato’s version of the speech Socrates gave in 399 BCE at his trial, where he faced charges of impiety and corrupting the youth of Athens.</meta>

# THE APOLOGY OF SOCRATES

<margin>A</margin> ...to pay attention to whether I speak what is just or not. For this is the excellence <note>original: "aretē" / "ἀρετή". Socrates suggests that just as a craftsman has a specific "excellence" (quality of work), a judge’s excellence is discerning justice.</note> of a judge, while that of an orator is to speak the truth. First, then, I must defend myself, men of Athens, against the first false accusations made against me and against my first accusers; and then against the later accusations and the later accusers. For many have accused me to you for many years now, saying nothing true. These I fear more than those around Anytus <note>Anytus was a prominent politician and one of the three official accusers in the trial.</note>, even though they too are formidable. But those others are more dangerous, men, who took hold of most of you from childhood and persuaded you with false accusations against me: 
<margin>B</margin> namely, that there is a certain Socrates, a "wise man," a thinker about the things in the heavens, who has searched into all things under the earth, and who makes the weaker argument the stronger <note>original: "ton hēttō logon, kreittō poiōn". This was a common slander against Sophists, implying they taught people how to win arguments regardless of the truth.</note>. Those who have spread this rumor, men of Athens, are my dangerous accusers; for those who hear them think that seekers of such things do not even believe in the gods. Moreover, these accusers are many and have been accusing me for a long time now; further, they spoke to you at an age when you were most trusting—when some of you were children or mere youths—accusing me in a case that went by default, as there was no one to defend me. 
<margin>C</margin> What is most unreasonable of all is that I cannot even know or tell you their names, unless one of them happens to be a comic poet <note>A reference to Aristophanes, whose play *The Clouds* (423 BCE) famously lampooned Socrates as a scientist-charlatan.</note>. All those who, using envy and slander, tried to persuade you—and those who, being persuaded themselves, then persuaded others—all these are the most difficult to deal with. For it is not possible to bring any of them here to court or to cross-examine them; one is forced to defend oneself as if shadow-boxing, and to argue when there is no one to answer. You must, therefore, accept that my accusers are of two kinds: those who have accused me recently, and those old ones I have just mentioned. You should think it right that I defend myself against the latter first, for you heard their accusations first, and much more often than those of the later ones. 
<margin>D</margin> Very well. I must make my defense, men of Athens, and I must attempt to remove from your minds in this very short time the slander which you have held for so long. I would wish for this to happen, if it is better for both you and me, and for my defense to be successful. But I think it is difficult, and I am not at all unaware of what kind of task it is. Nevertheless, let this proceed as God pleases; the law must be obeyed, and I must make my defense. Let us take up from the beginning what the accusation is from which this slander arose—the one that Melitus <note>Melitus was the primary individual who filed the formal legal charges against Socrates.</note> relied upon when he brought this indictment against me. 
<margin>E</margin> Very well. What did these slanderers say? We must read their "sworn statement" as if they were formal accusers: "Socrates acts unjustly and is meddlesome, by investigating things under the earth and in the heavens, by making the weaker argument the stronger, and by teaching these same things to others." It is something like that. For you yourselves saw these things in the comedy of Aristophanes: a certain Socrates being carried about there, claiming to walk on air and uttering a great deal of other nonsense, about which I know nothing, neither much nor little. I do not say this to disparage such knowledge, if anyone is wise in such matters—lest I be pursued by Melitus on even more charges—but indeed, men of Athens, I have no share in these things. 
<margin>F</margin> I offer most of you as witnesses, and I ask you to teach and tell one another, as many of you as have ever heard me conversing (and many of you have). Tell one another, then, if any of you ever heard me discussing such matters, either in a small way or a great way. From this you will recognize that the other things people say about me are of the same sort. But in fact, none of these things is true. And if you have heard from anyone that I attempt to educate people and charge a fee, that is not true either. Though I do think it is a fine thing if someone is able to educate people, like Gorgias of Leontini, Prodicus of Ceos, and Hippias of Elis <note>These were famous "Sophists," traveling teachers who charged large sums for lessons in rhetoric and virtue.</note>. 
<margin>G</margin> For each of them, men, is able to go into any of the cities and persuade the young men—who could associate for free with any of their own citizens they choose—to leave those associations and join them instead, paying them money and being grateful besides. There is also another wise man here from Paros, who I learned was in town. I happened to meet a man who has spent more money on Sophists than everyone else combined: Callias, the son of Hipponicus. I asked him (for he has two sons): "Callias," I said, "if your two sons had been born as colts or calves, we would be able to find and hire an overseer for them who would make them excellent in their proper virtue—and this would be some horse-trainer or farmer. But now, since they are human beings, whom do you have in mind to take as their overseer? Who is an expert in such virtue, that of a human being and a citizen? For I think you must have considered this, since you have sons. Is there such a person," I asked, "or not?" "Certainly," he said. "Who is he?" I asked, "and from where? And for how much does he teach?" "Evenus," he said, "Socrates; he is from Paros, and his fee is five minae <note>A 'mina' was a unit of currency; five minae was a substantial but relatively modest sum compared to the highest-priced Sophists.</note>." And I congratulated Evenus if he truly possessed this art and taught so 

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...and you should trust in this itself, and apply your mind to whether I say things that are just or unjust. For this is the duty of a judge, but the duty of an orator is to speak the truth. It is just, O men of Athens, for me to respond first to the first accusation falsely devised, and to the first accusers; then to the most recent ones. For many have falsely accused me before you for many years now, and I truly dread them more than the supporters of Anytus, although these too are powerful in persuasion. But those are more powerful, O men, who have occupied most of you from childhood, 
<margin>B</margin> accusing me far from the truth, and persuading you that there is a certain wise Socrates, a scrutinizer of those things above the air and those that happen beneath the earth, who is accustomed to make the worse cause appear the better by speaking. These men, O Athenians, who have spread this rumor about me, are my most powerful accusers. For those who hear these things think that scrutinizers of such matters do not believe there are gods. Indeed, accusers of this kind are very many, and they have been accusing me for a long time now; and they urged you at that age in which most of you were children or certainly young men and easily believed, in a deserted case where no one was defending me. 
<margin>C</margin> And that which is most alien to the reason of a defense is that it is not even permitted to know or speak their names, except if one of them happens to be a comic poet. However many, through envy and calumny, have persuaded you of these things, or those who, having been persuaded themselves, persuaded others—all these are entirely infinite, nor is it permitted to bring any of them into judgment, nor to refute them; but it is necessary to fight against them as if in the dark while defending myself, and to refute them when no one is responding. Therefore, you also consider, just as I was saying, that my accusers have been twofold: both those who have accused me recently, and those from long ago, of the kind I just described. And judge that I ought 
<margin>D</margin> to respond first to those whom you yourselves heard first, and much more often. Come, I must respond, O men of Athens, to those crimes, and I must strive in this so brief time to remove that opinion which you, deceived by calumnies, have conceived against me for a long time now. I wish, however, to refute the adversaries and prevail only if it would be better for you and for me. Although I think it will be difficult. Nor is it hidden from me what kind of thing it is. But, as it pleases God, so let it succeed. We, however, must obey the law and bring forward a defense for ourselves. Let us repeat from the beginning what the accusation is, from which that calumny against me was born, relying on which Melitus 
<margin>E</margin> indicted me. What then do my accusers say? For let their accusation be recited as if they were present in court, in which they swore to the slander: "Socrates acts unjustly, and too curiously searches into what is under the earth and what is in the heavens, and renders the inferior cause superior. Furthermore, he teaches the same things to others." Such indeed is the accusation. Certainly you saw such things in the comedy of Aristophanes: for a persona of Socrates is carried about there, affirming that he wanders through the air, and many trifles of that sort. Of which things I know nothing, neither much nor little. Nor do I say these things as if I make little of the science of such matters, if anyone is wise in such things, lest 
<margin>F</margin> I be accused of so great a crime by Melitus; but because in truth, O Athenians, I know nothing of these things. I bring forward most of you as witnesses of this. I pray you would be willing to teach and explain to each other, as many of you as have ever heard me talking—and most of you have heard me. Recount to each other, therefore, whether any of you ever heard me disputing about these things, whether much or little; and from this you will finally know that the other things which many spread about me are of the same sort. But indeed none of these things is true. Furthermore, if you have heard from anyone that I teach men and make money from it, that is not true either. And yet it seems a fine thing to me if someone could teach men, like Gorgias the Leontine, 
<margin>G</margin> and Prodicus the Chian, and Hippias the Elean. Each of whom, O men, has that faculty by which, having set out to individual cities, they persuade the youths—to whom it would be permitted in their own country to commend themselves to the discipline of their own citizens for free—to follow them instead, leaving behind the discipline of others, and having given money, to feel gratitude besides. There is also another wise man here, a Parian, whom I heard had come here. For it happened that I once fell upon that man who has spent more money on Sophists than all the others, I mean Callias, the son of Hipponicus. Him therefore I questioned. For he has two sons. "O Callias," I said, "if your sons 
<margin>H</margin> were colts or calves, we would have someone to set over them for a fee, who would make them both beautiful and excellent in their kind; such a person would be either some horseman or a farmer. But now, since your sons are human, whom do you think to set over them? And who has the knowledge of this human and civil virtue? I think you, since you have sons, have thought about this. Is there," I said, "such a person, or not?" "There is indeed," he said. "Who is he? From where? and for how much a fee does he teach?" "It is Evenus," he said, "O Socrates, a Parian; the fee is five minae." And I judged Evenus happy, if he truly has this art, and teaches it so diligently. For I myself also, if I knew such things, would be very proud, and greatly...

<summary>In this opening of the Apology, Socrates addresses the jury at his trial, distinguishing between his "old accusers" (long-standing rumors and theatrical caricatures) and his current accusers. He denies being a natural philosopher or a Sophist who charges money for teaching, contrasting himself with famous paid educators like Gorgias and Evenus.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Socrates' defense. On the previous page, he addressed the "old accusers" who claimed he was a natural philosopher or a teacher who took money. Here, he begins to explain the real origin of his unpopularity: a divine mission sparked by the Oracle at Delphi.</meta>

-># PLATO<-

<margin>A</margin> ...I would do. But certainly, men of Athens, I do not know these things. Someone might perhaps ask: "What then, Socrates, is your business? From where have these slanders against you arisen? For unless you were doing something different from the custom of others, such a great rumor would never have been stirred up about you. For from where would such frequent talk come, unless you had done something different from the rest? Tell us then what it is, so that we do not judge you rashly." This seems to me to be a fair question; and I will try to show you what it is that has earned me both this name and this slander. Hear me now; and though I fear I may seem to some of you to be joking, rest assured that I will tell you the whole truth.

<margin>B</margin> Indeed, men of Athens, I have gained this name for no other reason than a certain kind of wisdom. But what kind of wisdom? Perhaps that which is human wisdom <note>original: "humana sapientia". Socrates suggests his wisdom is limited to human affairs, unlike the "super-human" knowledge claimed by Sophists.</note>. For in this, I truly seem to be wise. But those whom I was mentioning a moment ago perhaps have a wisdom greater than human, or I do not know what to call it; for I certainly do not possess it. If anyone says I do, he lies and speaks to slander me. But do not be disturbed, men of Athens, and do not cry out even if I seem to say something boastful; for I will not speak my own words, but I will bring before you a witness worthy of credit. Indeed, if there is any wisdom in me, and of what kind it is, I will offer the god at Delphi as my witness.

<margin>C</margin> You certainly knew Chærephon. He was a friend of mine from youth, and a friend to the Athenian people; he fled into exile with you <note>A reference to the democratic citizens who fled Athens during the rule of the Thirty Tyrants in 404 BCE.</note> and returned with you. You clearly knew what kind of man Chærephon was, how vehement he was in whatever he turned his mind to. Once, having gone to Delphi, he dared to ask the oracle this question—again, men, do not be disturbed by what I am about to say. He asked if there was anyone wiser than I. The Pythia <note>The high priestess of Apollo at Delphi who delivered the prophecies.</note> responded that no one was wiser. His brother here will testify to these things, since Chærephon himself has passed away. Consider why I say these things: I must reveal to you from where this slander arose. Indeed, when I heard this, I thought to myself:

<margin>D</margin> "Whatever does the god mean? Or what is he signaling? For I am conscious that I am wise in nothing, great or small. What then does he mean when he asserts that I am the wisest? Surely the god does not lie, for that is not lawful for him." For a long time, I was at a loss as to what the oracle intended. At last, with great difficulty, I found a way to test it. I approached one of those who seemed to be wise, hoping that there, if anywhere, the prophecy could be refuted, and I could show the oracle: "This man is wiser than I, but you said I was." While I was examining him—there is no need to mention his name,

<margin>E</margin> but he was one of those who are active in public life—while I was examining him and conversing with him, men of Athens, I had this experience: this man seemed to be wise to many others, and especially to himself, but he was not. Then I tried to show him that he thought he was wise, but was not. Because of this, he became hateful toward me, as did many who were present. And so, returning to myself, I thought: I am certainly wiser than this man. For it appears that neither of us knows anything truly beautiful and good. But there is this difference: he, while knowing nothing, thinks he knows something; I, however, just as I do not know, do not think I know. I seem, therefore, in this small matter, to be wiser than this man, because **what I do not know, I do not even think I know.** After this, I went to another of those held to be even wiser than the first, and I judged exactly the same thing; and there I made him and many others hateful toward me. Then I proceeded to others in order, not unaware of how much hatred I was stirring up, and grieving and fearing because of it.

<margin>F</margin> Nevertheless, it seemed necessary to me to put the divine oracle before everything else, and to go everywhere searching for what the oracle meant, and for this reason, to approach all who seemed to know something. And **by the Dog** <note>original: "per Canem" / "νὴ τὸν κύνα". A common, eccentric oath used by Socrates, perhaps to avoid swearing by the major gods.</note>, men of Athens—for I must tell you the truth—I had an experience like this while searching according to the divine oracle: those who were most highly esteemed by human opinion, I found to be almost the most lacking; while others, who were considered inferior, were better off in terms of practical wisdom. It is worthwhile to tell you of my wanderings and the labors I endured so that the oracle might remain unrefuted for me.

<margin>G</margin> After the men in public life, I turned to the poets, the authors of tragedies and dithyrambs <note>Choral hymns sung in honor of Dionysus.</note> and other poems, thinking that here I would clearly catch myself being more ignorant than they. Taking up their books, in which they seemed to have labored most, I asked them their meaning, so that I might learn something from them. I am ashamed, men, to tell you the truth, but it must be said. Almost all others who were present, so to speak, could speak better about the things they themselves had written. I soon realized that poets do not create what they create by wisdom, but by a certain nature and divine inspiration, like those who prophesy in a divine frenzy. For these too say many fine things, but they understand nothing of what they say. It seemed to me that poets are affected in a similar way, and at the same time I noticed that because of their poetry, they thought

<column-break/>

...in such an orderly way I might be taught; for I certainly do not know these things. 
<margin>A</margin> I would have asked, if I understood these things. But I do not understand them, men of Athens. One of you might interrupt: "But Socrates, what is your business? From where have these slanders against you arisen? For surely, if you were not practicing something more extraordinary than others, so much talk and rumor would not have occurred, unless you were doing something different from the many. Tell us then what it is, so that we do not act rashly regarding you." This seems to me to be a just claim; and I will try to show you what it is that has produced for me both the name and the slander. Listen then. And perhaps I will seem to some of you to be playing, but know well, I will tell you the whole truth. 

<margin>B</margin> For I, men of Athens, have gained this name through nothing other than a certain wisdom. What kind of wisdom is this? That which is perhaps human wisdom. For in reality, I am likely to be wise in this. But these men whom I was just mentioning might be wise in some wisdom greater than human, or I do not know what to call it; for I certainly do not understand it. But whoever says I do, lies and speaks for the purpose of slandering me. And for me, men of Athens, do not make a disturbance, even if I seem to you to say something great. For I will not speak my own word, but I will refer the speaker to one who is credible to you. For of my wisdom, if indeed it is any and of what kind, I will offer the god at Delphi as a witness to you. 

<margin>C</margin> For you surely know Chærephon. He was my companion from youth and a companion to your multitude [the democracy], and he shared this exile with you and returned with you. And you know what kind of man Chærephon was, how vehement he was in whatever he would set out to do. And once, having gone to Delphi, he even dared to consult the oracle about this—as I say, do not make a disturbance, men—for he asked if anyone was wiser than I. The Pythia then replied that no one was wiser. And concerning these things, his brother here will testify to you, since he has died. Consider why I say these things; for I am going to teach you from where the slander against me has arisen. For when I heard these things, I pondered in this way: "Whatever does the god say? And whatever does he riddle? For I am conscious of being wise in nothing, great or small. What then does he mean by saying that I am the wisest? For surely he does not lie; for that is not lawful for him." And for a long time I was at a loss as to what 

<margin>D</margin> he meant. Then, with great difficulty, I turned to such an inquiry of him. I went to one of those who seemed to be wise, so that there, if anywhere, I might refute the prophecy and show the oracle that "This man is wiser than I, but you said it was I." Examining him then (for I have no need to speak his name)—he was one of the politicians—towards whom, when I examined him, I had such an experience, men of Athens: and in talking with him, this man seemed to me to seem wise to many other people and especially to himself, but to be so not at all. And then I tried to show him that he thought he was wise, but was not. From this, I became hated by him and by many of those present. So, going away to myself, I reasoned that I am wiser than this man. For likely neither of us knows anything noble or good; but he thinks he knows something, not knowing, while I, just as I do not know, do not even think I do. I seem, at any rate, to be a little bit wiser than this man in this very thing: that **what I do not know, I do not even think I know.** From there I went to another of those who seemed to be wiser than him, and the same things seemed to me, and there I became hated by him and by many others. After these things, I then went to one after another, perceiving and grieving and fearing that I 

<margin>E</margin> was becoming hated, but nevertheless it seemed to be necessary to consider the matter of the god of the highest importance. And I had to go, inquiring into what the oracle meant, to all those who seemed to know something. And by the dog, men of Athens (for I must tell you the truth), I truly had an experience like this: those who were most highly esteemed seemed to me to be almost the most deficient—to one searching according to the god—while others, who seemed more ordinary, were men more fit in respect to being prudent. I must indeed show you my wandering, like someone undergoing certain labors, so that the prophecy might be unrefuted for me. For after the politicians, I went to the poets, both those of tragedies and those of dithyrambs 

<margin>F</margin> and the others, so that there I would catch myself in the act of being more ignorant than they. Taking up their poems, which seemed to me to have been most carefully labored over by them, I would ask them what they meant, so that I might also learn something from them. I am ashamed, then, to tell you the truth, men; nevertheless, it must be told. For to speak plainly, almost all those present would have spoken better about the things they themselves had made. So I realized again concerning the poets, in a short time, this: that they do not create by wisdom, but by some nature and while being divinely inspired, just like the seers and the oracle-singers. For these too say many and fine things, but they know nothing of what they say. Some such experience appeared to me to have happened to the poets as well. And at the same time, I perceived that because of their poetry, they thought they were the wisest of men in other things as well, which they were not. So I went away...

<summary>Socrates recounts how his friend Chærephon visited the Oracle at Delphi, which declared Socrates the wisest of men. In his attempt to understand this riddle, Socrates began questioning politicians and poets, concluding that his wisdom lies solely in recognizing his own ignorance.</summary>

# APOLOGIA SOCR.
->361<-

from there, I went to the craftsmen, caught in the act of thinking I knew something. Finally, I went to the manual workers; for I was conscious that I knew nothing, so to speak; but I knew that I would find them knowing many and beautiful things. And in this I was not deceived, for they knew things which I did not know, and in this way they were wiser than I. But, O men of Athens, they seemed to me to have the same fault as the poets, even the good craftsmen. Because they practiced their craft well, each one claimed to be the wisest in other very great matters, and this discordance <note>original: "πλημμέλεια" (plēmmeleia), literally a false note in music; here meaning a character flaw or inconsistency</note> obscured that wisdom they did possess. So I asked myself on behalf of the oracle whether I would prefer to be as I am, neither wise with their wisdom nor ignorant with their ignorance, or to have both things that they have. I answered myself and the oracle that it was better for me to be as I am.

<margin>B</margin> From this investigation, O men of Athens, many enmities have arisen against me, and those of the most difficult and heavy kind, so that many slanders have come from them, and I have gained this name of being "wise." For those present always think that I myself am wise in those things in which I refute another. But the truth is likely, O men of Athens, that only the god is wise, and in this oracle he means this: that human wisdom is worth little or nothing. And he appears to be using the name of Socrates, making me an example, as if he were to say: "He among you, O humans, is wisest who, like Socrates, knows that he is truly worth nothing in respect to wisdom." These things

<margin>C</margin> I even now go about seeking and searching according to the god's will, both among citizens and strangers, if I think anyone is wise; and when he does not seem so to me, I assist the god by showing that he is not wise. And because of this occupation, I have had no leisure to do anything worth mentioning for the city's affairs, nor for my own; but I am in ten-thousandfold poverty because of my service to the god. Moreover, the young men following me (those who have the most leisure, the sons of the wealthiest) of their own accord enjoy hearing men being examined; and they themselves often imitate me, and then they attempt to examine others. And then, I think, they find

<margin>D</margin> a great abundance of men who think they know something, but know little or nothing. From this, those who are examined by them are angry at me, not at themselves; and they say that there is a certain Socrates, a most abominable man, who corrupts the young. And when someone asks them what he does and what he teaches, they have nothing to say, for they are ignorant; but so that they do not seem to be at a loss, they say these things that are ready at hand against all who philosophize: "things in the clouds and things under the earth," and "not believing in gods," and "making the weaker argument the stronger." For I think they would not wish to speak the truth—that they are clearly shown to be pretending to know, while knowing nothing. Since, therefore, I think they are ambitious and vehement and many, and they speak about me intensely and persuasively, they have filled your

<margin>E</margin> ears, both long ago and now, vehemently slandering me. From these men *Meletus* has attacked me, and *Anytus*, and *Lycon*: *Meletus* being aggrieved on behalf of the poets; *Anytus* on behalf of the craftsmen and the politicians; and *Lycon* on behalf of the orators. So that (as I said at the beginning) I should wonder if I were able to remove from you this slander, which has become so great in so short a time. This is the truth for you, O men of Athens; and I speak to you having hidden nothing, neither great nor small, nor having held anything back. And yet I know well enough that I am hated for these very same things, which is proof that I speak the truth, and that this is the slander against me, and these are its causes. And whether you seek these things now or later, you will find them so. Concerning the things which my first accusers charged, let this be a

<margin>F</margin> sufficient defense before you.
Against *Meletus*, the "good and patriotic man," as he says, and the later accusers, I will next attempt to defend myself. Again, then (as if these were a different set of accusers), let us take up their sworn deposition. It goes something like this: it says that *Socrates* does wrong by corrupting the young, and by not believing in the gods whom the city believes in, but in other new divinities <note>original: "δαιμόνια" (daimonia). This refers to Socrates' "divine sign" or inner voice, which his accusers framed as a strange new god.</note>. Such is the charge. Let us examine each part of this charge. He says that I do wrong by corrupting the young. But I, O men of Athens, say that *Meletus* does wrong, because he treats a serious matter as a joke, lightly bringing men to trial, pretending to be serious and to care about things for which he never had any concern. That this is

<margin>G</margin> so, I will try to demonstrate to you as well. Come here, *Meletus*, tell me:
Do you not consider it of the greatest importance that the youth should be as good as possible? I do. Come now, tell these men, who makes them better? For it is clear that you know, since it is a concern to you. For having found the corrupter, as you say—me—you bring me before these men and accuse me. Come, tell them and point out who it is that makes them better. Do you see, *Meletus*, that you are silent and have nothing to say? And yet does it not seem shameful to you, and a sufficient proof of what I say, that you have never cared about this? But tell me, my good man, who makes them better? The laws. But that is not

<column-break/>

that all men judge themselves to be the wisest, in matters where they are not wise.

<margin>A</margin> I went away, therefore, from there with the same opinion with which I had left the political men. But at last I betook myself to the craftsmen, as I was well conscious of how little I knew there, so to speak; I knew, however, that they knew many and beautiful things, and in this I was certainly not deceived. For they knew things which I myself did not know, and in this part they were wiser than I. But, O men of Athens, I found the skilled craftsmen in the same error as the poets. For because they performed their own craft rightly, each of them thought himself to be the wisest in other matters, even the greatest. And indeed, this error obscured that wisdom which was in them.

<margin>B</margin> Therefore, if I were to ask myself in the place of the oracle which I would choose: to remain as I am, neither knowing the things which they know, nor being ignorant of my own ignorance, or having both things which they have, I would plainly answer both myself and the oracle that it is better for me to remain as I am. Because of this inquiry of mine, O men of Athens, many enmities, most difficult and heavy, have been stirred up against me, from which many slanders have followed. Indeed, the name of "wise man" has arisen for me because of this, because those present think that I know those things in which I refute others. But it seems,

<margin>C</margin> O men of Athens, that in truth only god is wise, and in this oracle he wishes this: namely, that human wisdom is to be valued at little, or rather at nothing. And when he names *Socrates* as wise, he does so because he uses my name as a sort of example, as if he were to say: "He, O men, is wisest, who like *Socrates*, knows in truth that his wisdom is to be valued at nothing." These things, therefore, being so, even now I do not cease to search everywhere, obeying the god, and to examine whomever I think to be wise, whether of the citizens or of strangers.

<margin>D</margin> And if ever such a person does not seem so to me, then I myself, supporting and obeying [the god], demonstrate that he is not wise. And because of such occupations, almost no leisure is left to me either for performing anything public worthy of mention or privately, but I am established in extreme poverty because of the worship of God. Moreover, the young men who are most wealthy, who have leisure from business, follow me of their own accord and are delighted when they watch men being refuted by us. Furthermore, they themselves sometimes imitate me and then strive to confute others. In which matter they find a very great crowd of men who think they know something, when they either know nothing or very little. But those who are convinced by these youths are not so much angry with them as with me, and they cry out that there is a certain *Socrates*,

<margin>E</margin> a most wicked man and a corrupter of youth. But if anyone asks them what he does or what he teaches to corrupt them, they can assign nothing; indeed, they are completely ignorant. But so that they do not seem to lack material, they fly to those things which are commonly and easily thrown in the face of those who philosophize: namely, that he cares for things in the air and things under the earth. Indeed, he does not believe in the gods, and he persuades people that a bad cause is a good one. For they do not want to confess the truth, I think: namely, that they are indignant because they have been convicted of pretending to know things they do not know. Therefore, as they are ambitious and vehement and many, and as if by agreement, and persistently and with the diligent study of persuasion they accuse me, they have filled your ears, and for a long time

<margin>F</margin> and recently they have diligently fabricated slanders against me. From these *Meletus*, and *Anytus*, and *Lycon* have risen up against me: *Meletus* indeed being hostile to me on account of the poets, *Anytus* because of the craftsmen and the governors of the republic, and finally *Lycon* for the sake of the rhetoricians. Wherefore, as I said from the beginning, I would indeed wonder if I were able to remove from you this opinion conceived from such great slanders, and so long-established, now in such a short time. These things, O men of Athens, I speak truly to you, and I neither hide nor withdraw anything, whether great or small, although I know well enough that in saying these things I will be troublesome to them. Which indeed is an argument for you that I speak the truth, and that this slander has arisen against me, and its causes are of this kind. And whether in the present or

<margin>G</margin> in the future you inquire into these things, you will find it to be so. To those things, therefore, which the first accusers brought forward, let this be a sufficient defense before you. To *Meletus*, the good man and, as he says, a lover of his country, and to the remaining accusers I will next attempt to respond. But again, as if there were certain other accusers, let us bring into the midst the accusation undertaken with an oath to avoid the charge of slander. It is held in almost this way: *Socrates* acts unjustly, depraving the youth, and not believing in the gods whom the city believes in, but in certain other new divinities. The accusation is indeed of this kind: but let us discuss each part of this accusation. He charges me with depraving the young, and in this doing an injury; but I, O men of Athens, say on the contrary that *Meletus* does an injury, because he deliberately cavils and jokes, so easily dragging men into judgment, and pretending to be occupied with serious matters, and to have a care for those things which were never a care to him. That this is so I will try to show to you. Hey, *Meletus*, answer me: do you not yourself care most of all that the young men turn out as good as possible? I do indeed. Come then, tell these men now, who indeed makes the youths better. For it is certain that you know, since it is a care to you. You have already caught me as their corrupter, as you say, and having accused me to these men, you have dragged me into judgment. Therefore come, and tell them who makes them better, and show who he is. Why, O *Meletus*, are you silent? Do you see that you have nothing to say? And yet does that not seem shameful to you, and a sufficient proof of what I say, that you have never cared for these things? But tell me now, good man. Who makes them good? The laws. But I am not asking that.

<summary>Socrates describes how his search for wisdom led him to craftsmen, whose technical skill made them falsely believe they were wise in all things. He then begins his formal defense against Meletus, exposing Meletus's lack of genuine concern for the education of the youth he claims Socrates is corrupting.</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Meletus, Anytus, Lycon, artisans, human wisdom, Delphic Oracle, corruption of youth, legal charges, ignorance</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the trial of Socrates. Having established his own lack of "divine" wisdom, Socrates now directly cross-examines his accuser, Meletus, regarding the specific charges of corrupting the youth and impiety.</meta>

# OF PLATO
->362<-

<margin>A</margin> "O best of men. But what man [makes them better]? For it is clear you must know, since you have found their laws." 
"These men, Socrates—the judges." 
"What do you say, Meletus? Are these men able to instruct the youth and make them better?" 
"Most certainly." 
"All of them? Or can some do it and others not?" 
"All of them." 
"Well said, by Hera! <note>original: "Iunonem" in Latin; "Ἥραν" in Greek. Socrates often swore by Hera.</note> You speak of a great abundance of those who benefit the youth. But what of these listeners? Do they also make them better, or not?" 
"They too." 
"And what of the senators?" 
"The senators as well." 
"But then, Meletus, perhaps those in the assembly, the citizens, corrupt the young? Or do they all likewise make them better?" 
"They too." 
"All the 
<margin>B</margin> Athenians, then, it seems, make them noble and good <note>The Greek "kalos kagathos" refers to the ideal of a gentleman-citizen.</note> except for me alone. I alone am the one who corrupts them. Is this what you say?" 
"That is exactly what I say, and quite vehemently." 
"You truly condemn me to a great misfortune. But answer me: do you think the same is true of horses? That all men make them better, and only one person corrupts them? Or is it entirely the opposite—that there is only one, or very few, who are skilled in horsemanship and can make them better, while the majority, if they deal with and use horses, spoil them? Is this not how it stands, Meletus, both with horses and with all other living creatures? It certainly is, whether you and Anytus <note>Anytus was one of the primary prosecutors alongside Meletus.</note> deny it or admit it. For it would be a great stroke of luck for the youth if only one man corrupted them while everyone else benefited them. But indeed, Meletus, you show sufficiently that you have never cared for the youth; you plainly declare your own negligence, and that you have never meditated on the things for which you accuse me. Furthermore, I beseech you by Zeus, Meletus, answer us: is it better to live among good citizens or among bad ones? Answer, my friend. 
<margin>D</margin> I am asking you nothing difficult. Do not the wicked always do something bad to those they associate with, while the good do something good?" 
"Undoubtedly." 
"Is there anyone who wishes to be harmed rather than benefited by those he associates with? Answer, good man. For the law commands you to answer. Is there anyone who wants to be harmed?" 
"No one." 
"Come then, do you bring me here to court as one who corrupts the youth and makes them worse intentionally, or unintentionally?" 
"Intentionally, I say." 
"What? Are you, Meletus, at your young age, so much wiser than I am at my great age, that you clearly know that the wicked harm their associates and the good benefit them? And yet have I fallen into such a depth of folly that I do not even know that if I make one of my associates wicked, I run the risk of suffering some evil from him—and so I would bring this great evil upon myself intentionally, as you say? 
<margin>E</margin> I do not believe you in this, Meletus. And I think no other man will be convinced by you. Either I do not corrupt the youth, or if I do, I do it unwillingly. In both cases, you are lying. But if I corrupt them unwillingly, the law does not require me to be dragged into court for involuntary offenses, but rather to be taught and admonished privately. For it is clear that if I learn, I will stop doing what I did through ignorance. You, however, were unwilling to associate with me and instruct me; instead, you drag me into court, where the law commands those to be brought who need punishment rather than instruction. Now, men of Athens, it is clear from this what I was saying just now: that Meletus has never had any great or small concern for the education of the youth. Nevertheless, tell us, Meletus, in what way do you say I pervert the youth? Is it clearly, as you wrote in the indictment, by teaching them not to believe in the Gods the city believes in, but in other new daemons? <note>original: "dæmonia" (daimonia). In Greek thought, these were intermediate spirits, not necessarily "demons" in the modern sense.</note> Do you not claim that I corrupt the youth by teaching these things?" 
"I most certainly and vehemently claim this." 
"By those very Gods, Meletus, of whom we are now speaking, speak even more clearly to me and to these men. For I cannot yet plainly understand whether you mean I teach the youth to believe that *some* gods exist—and if so, then I believe in gods and am not entirely an atheist, nor am I unjust in this, even if I teach they are different from those the city recognizes—or is this what you accuse me of, that I introduce *other* gods? Or do you say that I altogether deny the existence of gods and teach others to deny them as well?" 
"I claim that you altogether deny the gods." 
"O marvelous Meletus, why do you say such things? Do I not even believe the sun or the moon to be gods, as other men do?" 
"By Zeus, no, O judges! For he says the sun is a stone, and the moon is earth." 
"Do you think you are accusing Anaxagoras, <note>Anaxagoras of Clazomenae was a pre-Socratic philosopher who was prosecuted for impiety decades earlier for these very views.</note> my dear Meletus? And do you so despise these men and think them so ignorant of letters that they do not know the books of Anaxagoras of Clazomenae are full of such claims? And so the youth are learning these things from me? Things which they could occasionally buy for a drachma at most from the orchestra <note>The "orchestra" here refers to a place in the Athenian marketplace or theater where books were sold.</note> and then laugh at Socrates if he pretended they were his own, especially since they are so absurd. But by God, Meletus, do you truly believe I think there is no god?" 
"None at all, by Zeus!" 
"You are untrustworthy, Meletus, even (as it seems to me) to yourself. For it appears to me, O men of Athens, that this man is very insolent and unrestrained, and that he has written this indictment out of a certain insolence, lack of restraint, and youthful rashness. For he seems to be composing a kind of riddle, testing whether 'Socrates the Wise' will catch him being witty and contradicting himself, or if he will deceive me and the other listeners. For he seems to me to contradict himself in the words of the indictment..."

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> "I am asking this, O best of men: what man knows the laws first and foremost?" 
"These men, Socrates, the judges." 
"How do you mean, Meletus? Are these men capable of educating the young and making them better?" 
"Very much so." 
"All of them? Or some of them, and others not?" 
"All of them." 
"Well said, by Hera! You speak of a great abundance of helpers. And what then? Do these listeners make them better, or not?" 
"These too." 
"And what about the councilors?" 
"The councilors as well." 
"But then, Meletus, do those in the assembly—the assemblymen—corrupt the younger ones? Or do they all make them better?" 
"They too." 
"All the Athenians, then (as it seems), make them 'noble and good,' except for me; I alone corrupt them. Is this what you say?" 
"That is exactly what I say." 
"You have truly found me in great misfortune. And answer me: does it 
<margin>B</margin> seem to you to be this way regarding horses? That those who make them better are all men, and there is only one who corrupts them? Or is it the opposite? That one man is capable of making them better, or very few—namely the horse-trainers—while the many, if they deal with and use horses, corrupt them? Is it not so, Meletus, both for horses and for all other animals? It certainly is, whether you and Anytus deny it or affirm it. For it would be a great state of happiness for the youth if only one man corrupted them while the others benefited them. But indeed, Meletus, you show sufficiently that you have never 
<margin>C</margin> cared for the youth; and you clearly reveal your own neglect, for you have no concern for the things for which you bring me here. Furthermore, tell us, by Zeus, Meletus, is it better to live among good citizens or wicked ones? Answer, my friend. For I am asking nothing difficult. Do not the wicked always do some evil to those who are nearest to them, while the good do something good?" 
"Certainly." 
"Is there anyone, then, who wants to be harmed by those he associates with rather than benefited? Answer, good man; for the law commands you to answer. 
<margin>D</margin> Is there anyone who wants to be harmed?" 
"Not at all." 
"Come then, do you bring me here as one who corrupts the youth and makes them more wicked intentionally or unintentionally?" 
"Intentionally, I say." 
"What then, Meletus? Are you at your age so much wiser than I am at mine, that you have recognized that the wicked always do something bad to those closest to them, while the good do something good? But I have come to such a point of ignorance that I do not even know this: that if I make any of my associates wretched, I will risk receiving some evil from him? So that I would do such a great evil intentionally, as you say? In this I do not believe you, Meletus, and I think no other human being does either. But either I do not corrupt them, or I corrupt them 
<margin>E</margin> unintentionally. So in both cases you are lying. And if I corrupt them unintentionally, for such involuntary errors the law is not to bring someone here to court, but to take them aside privately to teach and admonish them. For it is clear that if I learn, I will stop what I do unintentionally. But you avoided meeting with me and teaching me, and were unwilling; instead, you bring me here, where the law says to bring those in need of punishment, not instruction. But indeed, O men of Athens, this is already clear, as I was saying: that Meletus has never cared for these things, not even a little. Nevertheless, tell us how you say I corrupt the younger men, Meletus. Is it not clearly, according to the indictment you wrote, by teaching them not to believe in the gods whom the city believes in, but in other new spiritual things? Is it not by teaching these things that you say I corrupt them?" 
"I say that very strongly." 
"By these very 
<margin>F</margin> gods, Meletus, of whom we are now speaking, tell it even more clearly to me and to these men. For I cannot understand whether you say I teach them to believe that there are some gods (and thus I myself believe there are gods, and am not altogether an atheist, nor do I do wrong in this way), yet not the ones the city believes in, but others—and this is what you accuse me of, that they are *others*—or do you say that I myself do not believe in gods at all, and that I teach this to others?" 
"I say that you do not believe in gods at all." 
"O wonderful Meletus, why do you say this? Do I not even believe the sun or the moon are gods, as other men do?" 
"By Zeus, no, O judges! Since he says the sun is a stone and the moon is earth." 
"Do you think you are accusing Anaxagoras, my dear Meletus? Do you so look down on these men and think them so ignorant of letters that they do not know the books of Anaxagoras the Clazomenian are full of these ideas? And indeed, the youth learn these things from me, which they could sometimes buy—if the price were very high—for a drachma from the orchestra, 
<margin>G</margin> and then laugh at Socrates if he claimed they were his own, especially since they are so strange. But by Zeus, do I seem to you to believe there is no god?" 
"Not at all, by Zeus, not in any way." 
"You are unbelievable, Meletus, even (as it seems to me) to yourself. For this man seems to me, O men of Athens, to be very insolent and unrestrained, and to have written this indictment simply out of a kind of insolence, lack of restraint, and youthful rashness. For he is like someone composing a riddle, trying it out: 'Will Socrates the Wise realize that I am being clever and 
<margin>H</margin> saying things that contradict myself, or will I deceive him and the others who hear it?' For he seems to me to be saying contradictory things in the indictment itself..."

<summary>Socrates cross-examines Meletus, using the analogy of horse-training to argue that it is illogical to claim only one person corrupts the youth while the rest of society improves them. He further argues that the charge of atheism is contradictory and confuses his teachings with those of Anaxagoras.</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Meletus, cross-examination, corruption of youth, horse analogy, atheism, Anaxagoras, Athens, trial, daemons</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Socrates’s legal defense. Having previously argued that he does not corrupt the youth, he now turns to the charge of impiety—specifically the accusation that he introduces "new divinities" while not believing in the city's gods. He uses logical cross-examination to show the absurdity of his accuser's claims before transitioning into a moving defense of his philosophical mission as a divine duty.</meta>

# APOLOGY OF SOCRATES
->363<-

<margin>A</margin> It is as if he said: "Socrates acts against the laws by not believing in the Gods, yet believing in the Gods." This seems like the nonsense of someone joking and making clever, mocking quibbles. But now, men [of the jury], pay attention to how Meletus appears to me to be saying this. You, Meletus, answer us. And you all—as I requested at the beginning—do not be disturbed if I speak in my usual manner. Is there anyone, Meletus, who believes in human matters but does not believe there are humans? Let him answer me, men, and let him not keep creating disturbances. Is there anyone who does not believe in horses, but believes in things related to horsemanship? Or who does not believe in flute-players, but believes in the art of the flute? There is no such person, most excellent of men. If you do not wish to answer, I shall answer for you and for these others. But answer at least this next point, which is more relevant: Is there anyone who 
<margin>B</margin> believes in the works of spirits <note>The Greek "daimonia" refers to spiritual or divine things/actions; "daimones" refers to the spirits or minor deities themselves.</note> but does not believe in spirits? "No one." How slowly and reluctantly you answered, forced by the jury! Therefore, you admit that I believe in and teach of spiritual works, whether they be new or old; at any rate, according to your own statement, I believe in spiritual things, and you even swore to this in your indictment. But if I believe in spiritual things, it is absolutely necessary that I also believe in spirits. Is it not so? It is. I assume you agree, since you do not answer. And do we not think that spirits are either gods or the children of gods? Do you admit this, or not? "Certainly." Therefore, if I believe in spirits, as you yourself grant, 
<margin>C</margin> and if spirits are a kind of god, then this is what I meant when I said you were speaking in riddles and playing a joke on us: saying that I, who do not believe in gods, nevertheless believe in gods, since I believe in spirits. Again, if spirits are the children of gods—bastard sons, perhaps, born of nymphs or of others, as they are said to be—who among men could believe that children of the gods exist, but that gods do not? It would be just as absurd as if someone believed in the offspring of horses or donkeys—mules—but did not believe that horses and donkeys exist. But, Meletus, you undoubtedly brought this accusation either to test our wits, or because 
<margin>D</margin> you had no true crime of which to accuse me. By what logic could you persuade anyone with even a tiny bit of intelligence that the same man could believe in spiritual and divine things, and yet believe there are no spirits, no gods, and no heroes? It simply cannot be shown to be otherwise. Furthermore, men of Athens, that I have not committed the crime Meletus accuses me of does not seem to require a great defense; I judge that what has been said is enough. But what I said at the beginning—that great malice has been stirred up against me among the common people—is absolutely true. And this is what will destroy me, if 
<margin>E</margin> I am to be destroyed: not Meletus, nor Anytus, but the slander and envy of the many. These things have destroyed many other good men before, and I think they will continue to do so. There is nothing strange or surprising if it does not stop with me. Perhaps, then, someone might ask: "Are you not ashamed, Socrates, to have pursued such a path, from which you now run the risk of dying?" To this objection, I would give a just response: You do not speak well, sir, if you think a man who is of even a little use should weigh the risk of life or death; rather, he should consider only this whenever he acts: whether he is doing right or wrong, and whether his deeds are those of a good man or a bad one. Otherwise, by your logic, 
<margin>F</margin> all the demigods who fell at Troy would be considered worthless, especially the son of Thetis <note>Achilles, the hero of the Iliad.</note>, who so despised danger in comparison to enduring a shameful reputation. When his mother, a goddess, saw him eager to kill Hector, she said to him, I believe, something like this: "O son, if you avenge the death of your friend Patroclus by killing Hector, you yourself will die; for immediately after Hector," she said, "an unhappy fate awaits you." But when he heard this, he made light of the danger and death, fearing much more to live a shameful life and fail to avenge his friends. He immediately replied, "Let me die at once after I have punished the wrongdoer, rather than remain here as a laughingstock by the curved ships, a useless burden on the earth." <note>original: "telluris inutile pondus"; quoted from Homer's Iliad.</note> Who would say that he 
<margin>G</margin> had any care for danger or death? And truly, men of Athens, this is how it stands. Wherever a man has placed himself, judging it to be the best, or wherever he has been stationed by a superior, there, it seems to me, he must remain and face the danger, fearing neither death nor anything else more than shame. Indeed, men of Athens, I would have committed a grave error if, when those commanders whom you chose to lead me stationed me at Potidaea, Amphipolis, and Delium <note>Socrates served as a hoplite (infantryman) in these three major battles of the Peloponnesian War.</note>, I remained where they stationed me and faced the risk of death like anyone else; but when the God stationed me—as I believed and understood—commanding that I must live philosophizing and examining myself and others, I were to abandon my post for fear of death or any other thing. That would be a truly grave offense, and then indeed someone might justly bring me to court for not believing in the gods, since I would be disobeying the oracle, fearing death, and thinking myself wise when I am not. For to fear death, men, is nothing other than to seem wise when one is not. It is to seem to know what one does not know. For no one knows whether death might be the greatest of all goods for a man; yet men fear it as if they knew for certain it was the greatest of evils. And how can this not be the most blameworthy ignorance: thinking one knows what one does not know? But, men, I perhaps differ from most men in this one thing:
