# PLATONIS
->364<-

<margin>A</margin> And if I were to say that I am wiser than anyone in any respect, it would certainly be in this: that while I do not have sufficient knowledge of what happens in the underworld, I recognize that I do not know. But I do know that to commit injustice and to disobey a superior—whether God or man—is an evil and a shameful thing. Therefore, I will never fear or flee from those things which I do not know to be good, more than those things which I know to be evil. For this reason, if you should now acquit me, disregarding Anytus <note>Anytus was one of the three primary accusers of Socrates; he was a wealthy and influential politician.</note>, who said that either I should not have been brought to trial in the first place, or that having been brought, I must necessarily be condemned to death—telling you that if I were acquitted, your sons would all be utterly corrupted by following the teachings of Socrates—<margin>B</margin> if, I say, you were to tell me: "Socrates, we do not believe Anytus, and we acquit you on our own terms, but on this condition: that you no longer spend your time in this inquiry and in philosophy; and if you are caught doing so, you shall die." If, as I was saying, you should dismiss me on these conditions, I would reply to you: "O men of Athens, I hold you in high regard and I love you, but I will obey God rather than you. And as long as I draw breath and have the strength, I will not cease from practicing philosophy, exhorting and teaching anyone I happen to meet, in my accustomed way, saying: 'My excellent friend, since you are a citizen of Athens—the greatest city and the most famous for wisdom and <margin>C</margin> power—are you not ashamed to devote your whole effort to acquiring as much money, glory, and honor as possible? But as for wisdom, truth, and the best possible state of your soul, do you neither think of them nor care for them?'" And if any of you disputes this and claims to care for these things, I will not let him go at once, nor will I leave, but I will question, examine, and cross-examine him. And if he does not seem to me to possess virtue, even though he claims to, I will reproach him for setting the least value on things of the greatest worth, and the highest value on things that are most trivial. I will perform this duty for both young and old, whomever I meet, and for both stranger and citizen, but more so for you citizens, insofar as you are more closely related to me by birth. <margin>D</margin> For this is what God himself commands. And I believe that no greater good has yet happened to you in this city than this service of mine, which I perform in obedience to God. For I go about doing nothing else but persuading both young and old among you not to care for your bodies or your money first or more vehemently than for your soul, so that it may be as good as possible. I teach that virtue does not come from money, but that money and all other goods, both private and public, come to men from virtue. If, therefore, by teaching these things I corrupt the youth, these things would certainly be harmful. But if anyone says that I teach anything other than this, he says nothing at all. For the sake of <margin>E</margin> these things, O men of Athens, I declare—whether you believe Anytus or not, and whether you acquit me or not—I declare that I will do nothing else, even if I must die many times. Do not create a disturbance, O men of Athens! But, as I asked you at the beginning, listen to me with a calm mind; for it will be to your advantage, I think, if you listen to what I am about to say. Indeed, I am going to tell you some other things which, upon hearing, might provoke you to shout out; but do not do this. Know that if you kill me—being the kind of man I just described—you will not harm me more than you harm yourselves. Neither Meletus nor Anytus will ever harm me; they could not. For I do not think it is permitted <note>original: "nefas" (Latin) / "θεμιτὸν" (Greek), meaning "divinely sanctioned" or "right in the eyes of the gods."</note> for a better man to be harmed by a worse one. <margin>F</margin> He might, however, kill me, or drive me into exile, or strip me of my civil rights. And perhaps he or someone else might think these are great evils; but I do not think so. I think it is a much worse thing to do what he is doing now—attempting to kill a man unjustly. Therefore, O men of Athens, I am far from making a defense on my own behalf, as one might think; rather, I do it for your sake, so that you do not sin against the gift God has given you by condemning me. For if you kill me, you will not easily find another like me—truly, even if it sounds ridiculous to say—assigned to your city by God, as if to a large and noble horse which is somewhat sluggish because of its size and needs to be stirred up by a gadfly <note>Socrates famously compares himself to a gadfly (Latin: "calcaribus" / Greek: "μύωπός") that stings a lazy horse into action.</note>. Such a person, it seems, God has attached me to the city: one who never stops rousing, persuading, and reproaching each one of you throughout the whole day, everywhere I am with you. You will not easily find another such man, O men of Athens. Therefore, if you take my advice, you will spare me. But perhaps, like those who are drowsy and resent being woken up, you might strike out at me and, following Anytus, thoughtlessly and lightly kill me; then you would spend the rest of your time sleeping, unless God, looking out for you, should send someone else. <margin>G</margin> That I am indeed the kind of person who appears to have been given to the city by God, you can recognize from this: it does not seem like a human thing for me to have neglected all my own affairs and to have endured the neglect of my household for so many years now, while always being intent on your good, approaching each of you like a father or an older brother, persuading you to care for virtue. If I had received any payment for my service, or if I had demanded a wage while giving these exhortations, there would be some human reason for it. But now, as you can plainly see for yourselves, although my accusers have most shamelessly heaped all these other charges against me, they have not dared to be so shameless as to provide a witness to prove that I ever exacted or asked for any payment. <margin>H</margin> For this fact, I offer you, I think, a sufficient witness that I speak the truth: my poverty. But perhaps it may seem absurd to someone that I give this advice privately...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> and if indeed I should say I was wiser than anyone in anything, it would be in this: that not knowing sufficiently about the things in Hades, I also realize that I do not know. But to do injustice and to disobey one's superior, whether God or man, I know that this is evil and shameful. Therefore, in preference to the evils which I know to be evil, I shall never fear nor flee from those things which I do not know, as they may happen to be good. So that even if you let me go now (disbelieving Anytus, who said that either I should not have come here in the beginning, or since I did come, that it is impossible not to kill me, telling you that if I should escape, your sons, practicing what Socrates <margin>B</margin> teaches, will all be utterly corrupted)—if you were to say to me in response to this: "O Socrates, for now we will not obey Anytus, but we let you go; on this condition, however, that you no longer spend time in this search, nor practice philosophy; and if you are still caught doing this, you shall die." If, then, you should let me go (as I said) on these conditions, I would say to you: "I respect and love you, O men of Athens, but I shall obey the God rather than you; and as long as I breathe and am able, I shall certainly not stop practicing philosophy, and exhorting you and pointing out to whichever of you I happen to meet, saying what I usually do: 'O best of men, being an Athenian, of the greatest city and most renowned for wisdom and strength, are you not ashamed of caring for money, that you may have <margin>C</margin> as much as possible, and for reputation and honor, while for wisdom and truth, and for your soul, that it may be as good as possible, you do not care nor give it thought?'" And if any of you disputes this, and says he does care, I will not immediately let him go nor go away, but I will question him and examine him, and cross-examine him. And if he does not seem to me to possess virtue, but says he does, I will reproach him because he treats the things of most value as least important, and the paltrier things as more important. This I shall do for both younger and older, whomever I meet, both stranger and citizen; but more for the citizens, inasmuch as you are closer to me in kin. For these things the God commands, be well assured. And I think that no greater good has ever happened to you in the city than my service to the God. <margin>D</margin> For I go about doing nothing else but persuading both younger and older of you neither to care for your bodies nor for money more, nor as strongly, as for your soul, that it may be as good as possible; saying that virtue does not come from money, but from virtue comes money and all other good things for men, both privately and publicly. If then by saying these things I corrupt the young, these things would be harmful; but if anyone says that I say other things than these, he says nothing. In view of this I would say, O men of Athens, either obey Anytus or not; and either let me go or not; since I would not do otherwise, not even if I were to die many times. Do not make a disturbance, O men of Athens, but abide by my request not to make a disturbance at the things I say, but to listen. For indeed, as I think, you will be benefited by listening. For I am <margin>E</margin> about to say some other things to you at which you will perhaps cry out; but by no means do this. For be well assured, if you kill me, being such a man as I say I am, you will not harm me more than yourselves. For neither Meletus nor Anytus could harm me; for they would not be able to. For I do not think it is permitted for a better man to be harmed by a worse. He might indeed perhaps kill me or drive me out, or dishonor me; but these things this man perhaps thinks, and some other man likely does too, are great evils; but I do not think so, but rather much more to do what this man is now doing: attempting to kill a man unjustly. Now, therefore, O men of Athens, I am far from making a defense on my own behalf (as someone might think), but on your behalf, lest you should err at all concerning the gift of the God to you by voting against me. For if you kill me, you will not easily find another such man, simply <margin>F</margin> (even if it is rather ridiculous to say) attached to the city by the God, as if to a horse, large and well-bred, but rather sluggish because of its size, and needing to be awakened by some gadfly. Just so the God seems to me to have placed me in the city as such a one, who, awakening and persuading and reproaching each one of you, do not stop all day long settling everywhere. Such another will not easily come to be for you, O men, but if you obey me, you will spare me. But you, perhaps being vexed, like those who are drowsy when they are awakened, might strike me and, obeying Anytus, might easily kill me; then you would continue sleeping for the rest of time, <margin>G</margin> unless the God, caring for you, should send someone else to you. And that I happen to be such a one as to have been given by the God to the city, you might perceive from this. For it does not seem human that I should have neglected all my own affairs, and have tolerated the neglect of my household for so many years now, and always be doing your business, approaching each one privately like a father or an older brother, persuading you to care for virtue. And if indeed I got anything from these things, and was taking pay when I exhorted you, it would have some reason; but now you see yourselves that the accusers, though they accused me of all other things so shamelessly, were not able to be so shamelessly bold in this: to provide a witness that I ever either exacted or <margin>H</margin> asked for a fee from anyone. For I provide (I think) a sufficient witness that I speak the truth: my poverty. Perhaps, then, it might seem strange that I go around giving these...

<summary>Socrates explains that he fears wrongdoing more than death and refuses to stop philosophizing even under threat of execution. He famously characterizes himself as a "gadfly" sent by God to rouse the sluggish city of Athens to pursue virtue over wealth and status.</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Apology, gadfly metaphor, virtue vs wealth, divine mission, Anytus, Athenian trial, fear of death, soul, poverty as witness</keywords>

# APOLOGY OF SOCRATES
->365<-

<margin>A</margin> These things have advised me to avoid [public life] and remain quite still, and I do not dare to go up to your assembly to advise the city. The cause of this is what you have heard me say many times and in many places: that something **divine and spiritual** <note>original: "theion ti kai daimonion" — Socrates refers to his famous "daimonion," an inner voice or sign that warned him against certain actions.</note> comes to me as a voice. This is what Meletus mocked in his indictment. It began for me in childhood—a certain voice that, when it occurs, always turns me away from what I am about to do, but never encourages me. This is what opposes me entering politics. And it seems to me quite right to oppose it. For know well, men of Athens, if I had long ago attempted to engage in political affairs, I would have perished long ago, and I would have been of no use to you or to myself. And do not be angry with me for speaking the truth. For there is no man who will be saved, whether by you or <margin>B</margin> by any other multitude, if he honestly opposes you and prevents many unjust and illegal things from happening in the city. Rather, it is necessary for one who truly fights for justice, if he is to be saved even for a short time, to live as a **private citizen** <note>original: "idiōteuein" — the root of the word "idiot," but here meaning someone who does not hold public office.</note> and not as a public figure. I will provide you with great evidence of these things—not words, but (what you value more) deeds. Hear then what happened to me, so that you may know that I would not yield to anyone against what is right for fear of death; and by not yielding, I would have perished on the spot. I will tell you things that are perhaps tedious and "lawyerly," but they are true. For I, men of Athens, never held any other office in the city, but I did serve on the Council. It happened that our tribe, Antiochis, <margin>C</margin> held the presidency <note>The "prytanes" were the committee of the Council currently in charge of government business.</note> when you wanted to judge the ten generals who did not pick up the men from the naval battle <note>The Battle of Arginusae (406 BCE); the generals were illegally tried as a group rather than individually.</note>—judging them all together, which was illegal, as you all decided in later times. Then I alone of the presiding councilors opposed you, refusing to do anything against the laws, and I voted against it. Even though the orators were ready to indict me and arrest me, and you were all cheering them on and shouting, I thought I should rather run the risk with the law and justice than side with you in your unjust deliberations out of fear of imprisonment or death. These things happened while the city was still a democracy. <margin>D</margin> But when the oligarchy came to power, the **Thirty** <note>The Thirty Tyrants, a brutal pro-Spartan regime that ruled Athens for a year (404–403 BCE).</note> summoned me and four others to the Tholos <note>The Tholos was a round building in the Agora where the presiding officials ate and met.</note> and ordered us to bring Leon of Salamis from Salamis so that he might be put to death. They often gave such orders to many others, wanting to involve as many people as possible in their crimes. On that occasion, I showed again, not by words but by deeds, that I do not care about death at all (if it is not too rude to say so), but that my whole concern is to do nothing unjust or impious. For that government, powerful as it was, did not frighten me into doing anything unjust. But when we came out of the Tholos, the other four went to Salamis and brought Leon, while I simply went home. And perhaps I would have been put to death for this, had that government not been dissolved shortly thereafter. There will be many witnesses of these things for you. Do you then think I would have survived all these years if I had engaged in public affairs, and acting as a good man should, had supported what is just and, as <margin>E</margin> is necessary, made this the most important thing? Far from it, men of Athens; nor would any other man. But throughout my life, wherever I have engaged in public business, I will be seen to be such a man—and the same in private—never conceding anything to anyone against justice, neither to others nor to any of those whom my accusers say are my disciples. I, however, have never been anyone's teacher. But if anyone, whether young or old, desired to hear me speaking and going about my own business, I never begrudged it to anyone. Nor do I speak only when I receive money, and not when I do <margin>F</margin> not; but I offer myself to be questioned by rich and poor alike, and if anyone wants to listen to what I say while answering. And if any of these people becomes good or not, I cannot justly be held responsible, since I never promised or taught any kind of learning to anyone. If anyone says they ever learned or heard anything from me in private that everyone else did not also hear, know well that they do not speak the truth. But why then do some enjoy spending so much time with me? You have heard the whole truth from me, men of Athens: they enjoy hearing those who think they are wise, but are not, being cross-examined. For it is not unpleasant. This task, as I say, has been <margin>G</margin> commanded to me by God, through oracles and dreams, and in every way that any divine fate has ever commanded a man to do anything. These things, men of Athens, are both true and easy to prove. For if I am corrupting some of the youth, and have already corrupted others, it would surely follow that if some of them, having grown older, realized that I had ever given them bad advice when they were young, they would now come forward to accuse me and take revenge. And if they themselves were unwilling, some of their kinsmen—fathers, brothers, or other relatives—would now remember and take revenge if their family members had suffered any harm from me. In any case, many of them are present here, whom I can see: first...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...counseling individuals by going around too anxiously, yet not daring to advise the state publicly in the assemblies. The cause of this is that which you have often heard me say everywhere: namely, that a certain **divine and spiritual voice** <note>Latin: *divinum quiddam atque dæmonicum vocem*</note> is present with me. Meletus indeed mocked this in his accusation, but for me, this has been present since childhood—a certain voice which, as often as it occurs, forbids me to do what I was going to do, but never urges me on. This, I say, is what prevents me from applying myself to public affairs. And it seems to me quite right to oppose it. For it is certain, O men of Athens, if I had once undertaken public business, <margin>B</margin> I would have perished long ago; and so I would have brought no benefit either to you or to myself. Do not be angry with me, I pray, for speaking the truth. For no one can be safe for long if he honestly and bravely opposes either you or any other people, in order to prevent many unjust and wicked things that are accustomed to happen in the city. But it is necessary for him who truly fights for justice, if he is to be safe for even a short time, to live privately and not to touch the republic. I will bring you great proofs of these things—not words indeed, but (what you value highly) deeds. Hear now what has happened to me, so that you may more clearly see that I would have yielded <margin>C</margin> nothing against justice to anyone for fear of death, and that by not yielding, I would have perished. I will relate to you things that are somewhat troublesome and suited to a law court, yet true. For I, O men of Athens, have held no public office until now, except that I was elected to the Council. It happened that my tribe, Antiochis, was presiding at the time when you were in a hurry to condemn all ten commanders of the armies together, because they had not picked up those killed in the naval battle—unjustly indeed, as was afterwards known to you all. Then I alone of all the **prytanes** (that is, the senators) opposed you, so that you might do nothing contrary to the laws, and I resisted with my votes. At that time, while many orators were ready to report my name and <margin>D</margin> drag me into judgment, and you yourselves were ordering the same thing with a great shout, I judged that it was more fitting for me to undergo danger for the sake of the law and justice than to agree with you when you were not deciding what was just—out of fear of prison or death. And these things were done while the city was still established under the liberty of the people. But after it came to the power of a few, again those **Thirty** who occupied the republic, calling me with four others into the **Tholos**, ordered us to bring Leon of Salamis from Salamis so that he might be killed; such things as they <margin>E</margin> were then commanding to many others, so that they might involve as many as possible in their own crimes. Then I showed, not in words but in deed once again, that I care nothing at all for death—though it may seem a rustic thing to say—but that I care entirely for this: that I should do nothing unjust or impious. That terrible power did not frighten me in any way into doing anything unjustly. But when we departed from the Tholos, the remaining four went to Salamis and brought the captured Leon, while I went home; and perhaps for that reason they would have killed me, had their power not been dissolved shortly after. And of these things there will be many witnesses for you. <margin>F</margin> Do you therefore think I could have lived so many years if I had handled public affairs and, performing the duty of a good man, had supported justice and, as is proper, preferred that one duty above all others? Far from it, O men of Athens: for no other man could have remained safe for long by acting in such a way. But through all my life, if ever I handled public business, I proved myself to be such a man; and privately I am the same, never conceding to anyone anything beyond what is just—neither to others, nor to any of these whom those who accuse me claim are my disciples. I, however, was never anyone's teacher. But if anyone desired to hear <margin>G</margin> me speaking or acting, whether younger or older, I never denied it to anyone. Nor indeed am I one who disputes only when money is received, and is silent when it is not; but I offer myself to be questioned by the rich and the poor alike, and even if someone wants to hear what I say by responding. And whether any of these becomes upright or not, I could not justly be held to blame: seeing that I never either handed down or promised any teaching to anyone. But if anyone says that they learned or heard anything from me privately which I did not make common to all others, he does not speak the truth. But for what reason do some take delight in my company, O men of Athens? Hear the reason. It is exactly as I was telling you above: men take delight when they are present at the cross-examination of those who think they are wise when they are not. For it is an art that is not unpleasant. To me, however, as I said, this has been enjoined by God, both through prophecies and through dreams, and <meta>catchword: per</meta>

---

by every means in which any other divine fate has ever commanded any man to do anything. These things, O men of Athens, are both true and easily proven. For indeed, if I am now corrupting some of the young men, and have for a long time corrupted others, it would be consistent that now some of them, having become older, because they understood that I had advised them poorly when they were adolescents, would rise up against me and demand punishment. But if they themselves were unwilling, at least some of their relatives—fathers and brothers and other kinsmen—if their relatives had suffered any evil from me, would now commemorate it and demand punishment. <meta>This page continues the defense of Socrates during his trial in 339 BCE. Having previously explained his divine mission and why he avoided public politics, Socrates now addresses the presence of his supporters in the courtroom and his refusal to use emotional appeals to sway the jury.</meta>

# OF PLATO
->366<-

**A** This Crito is here, a man of my own age and from my own district, the father of Critobulus here. Then there is Lysanias of Sphettus, the father of Aeschines here. Furthermore, there is Antiphon of Cephisus, the father of Epigenes. There are others as well, whose fathers were my close associates: Nicostratus, the son of Theosdotides and brother of Theodotus. Theodotus himself is deceased, so he certainly could not have pressured his brother. Here also is Paralus, the son of Demodocus, whose brother was Theages. And Adeimantus, the son of Ariston, whose brother is this man, Plato. Finally, there is Aeantodorus, whose brother is Apollodorus here. I could mention many others, any one of whom Meletus ought to have produced as a witness during his speech. But if he forgot then, let him **B** produce one now—I will allow it. Let him speak, I say, if he has any such evidence. But you will find the truth is quite the opposite, men of Athens. For you see that everyone is ready to help me—the man who, according to Meletus and Anytus, has "corrupted" and brought "harm" to their own relatives. Now, perhaps those who were actually corrupted might have some reason to help me; but their uncorrupted relatives, men already of advanced age, what reason would they have to support me, unless it were for the sake of what is right and just? For they know well that Meletus is lying and that I am telling the truth. These things, then, men of Athens, and perhaps others like them, are what I have to say in my defense. But perhaps some among you, reflecting on your own habits, might be annoyed when you **C** remember how, even in less serious cases, a defendant often begs and entreats the judges with many tears, bringing his children and many other relatives and friends into court to stir up pity. Yet I will do none of these things, even though I am, as you see, facing the ultimate danger. Someone thinking of this might become more stubborn toward me and, being moved to anger by these very facts, might cast his vote in that anger. If any of you feels this way—though I do not believe you should—I think it would be fair to address him thus: "I too, my good man, <margin>Odyssey, Book 19</margin> have relatives. For, as Homer says, I was not born 'from an oak or a rock,' but from men." <note>original: "ex quercu vel petra" — a Greek idiom meaning he has a family and human origins, not a mythical or inanimate beginning.</note> Therefore, I too have relatives, **D** men of Athens, and three sons: one who is already an adolescent, and two who are still small children. Yet I will not bring any of them here to beg you for an acquittal. Why, then, will I do none of these things? Not out of any stubbornness, nor out of contempt for you, men of Athens—whether I am brave in the face of death or not is another matter. But for the sake of my reputation, and yours, and that of the whole city, I do not think it right for me to do such things at my age and with the name I have acquired, whether that reputation be true or false. For it is the general opinion that Socrates excels in some way above the common man. If, therefore, those among you who are thought to **E** excel in wisdom, or courage, or any other virtue, behave in such a way, it would be a great disgrace. I have often seen such men when they are being judged—men who were thought to be something special, but who performed extraordinary dramas as if they thought they would suffer something terrible if they died, as though they would be immortal if only you did not kill them. Such people seem to me to bring shame upon the city, so that a foreigner might suppose that those Athenians who excel in virtue, and whom the citizens prefer for high office and other honors, are no better than women. <note>In the cultural context of ancient Athens, public displays of excessive grief were often stereotyped as unmanly.</note> These things, men of Athens, you who are held in any regard should not do; and if we should try to do them, you should not permit it. Instead, you should show that you are far more likely to condemn a man who introduces these pathetic dramas and makes the city look ridiculous than a man who awaits the verdict in silence. Furthermore, **F** men of Athens, aside from reputation, it does not seem just to me to beg the judge, nor to be acquitted by begging, but rather to teach and persuade him. For a judge does not sit to grant justice as a personal favor, but to judge according to the laws. He has sworn an oath not to show favor to whomever he pleases, but to judge according to the laws. Therefore, we should not accustom you to breaking your oath, **G** nor should you become accustomed to it; for neither of us would then be acting piously. Do not, therefore, men of Athens, require me to do such things before you which I consider to be neither honorable, nor just, nor holy—especially when I am being accused of impiety by this man Meletus. For clearly, if I were to persuade you and force you by my entreaties to break your oath, I would be teaching you not to believe in the gods; and in my very defense, I would be accusing myself of not believing in them. But that is far from the truth. For I do believe that there are gods, **H** men of Athens, more than any of my accusers do; and I entrust to you and to God to judge concerning me in whatever way shall be best for me and for you.

<note>The text here shifts to the delivery of the verdict and Socrates' reaction to it.</note>

As to the fact that I am not distressed, men of Athens, at this result—that you have condemned me—many things contribute to this. Above all, it did not happen contrary to my expectation; rather, I am much more surprised by the number of votes on each side. For I did not think it would be by so small a margin, but by a large one. But now, **H** as it seems, if only three votes had fallen differently, I would have been acquitted. Indeed, it seems to me that I have already escaped Meletus; and not only escaped him, but it is clear to everyone that if Anytus and Lycon had not come forward to accuse me, he would have been fined a thousand drachmas <note>Under Athenian law, if a prosecutor failed to receive at least one-fifth of the jury's votes, they were heavily fined for bringing a frivolous lawsuit.</note> for not receiving a fifth part of the votes.

<column-break/>

**A** This Crito is here, my contemporary and fellow-villager, the father of this Critobulus. Then there is Lysanias of Sphettus, the father of this Aeschines. Also Antiphon of Cephisus is here, the father of Epigenes. Then there are these others, whose brothers have spent time in this pursuit: Nicostratus the son of Zotides, brother of Theodotus (and since Theodotus is dead, he at least could not entreat him to be silent); and here is Paralus, the son of Demodocus, whose brother was Theages. And here is Adeimantus, the son of Ariston, whose brother is Plato here; and Aeantodorus, whose brother is Apollodorus. And I have many others I could name for you, one of whom **B** Meletus especially ought to have produced as a witness in his own speech. But if he forgot then, let him produce one now—I yield the floor—and let him speak if he has any such witness. But you will find the very opposite, gentlemen: everyone is ready to help me, the "corruptor," the man who "works evil" upon their relatives, as Meletus and Anytus claim. Now, those who were actually corrupted might perhaps have a reason to help me, but the uncorrupted—men already older, who are the relatives of the former—what other reason would they have to help me but the correct and just one? Namely, that they know Meletus is lying and I am telling the truth. Well then, gentlemen, these are the sorts of things I might say in my defense, and perhaps others like them. **C** But perhaps one of you might be resentful, remembering himself: if he, while competing in a contest of less importance than this one, begged and supplicated the judges with many tears, bringing his children up to the stand so that he might be pitied as much as possible, along with many other relatives and friends; whereas I will do none of these things, even though I am, as I seem to be, facing the extreme danger. Perhaps someone, thinking of these things, might take a harder stance against me, and being angered by these very facts, might cast his vote in anger. If any of you is in this state—though I do not claim I deserve it—but if it were so, I think I would speak reasonably to him by saying: "I too, my good man, have certain relatives. For indeed, as Homer puts it, I was not born 'from an oak or a rock,' but from humans." So I too have relatives, and even sons, **D** men of Athens—three of them: one already a youth, and two who are children. But nevertheless, I will not bring any of them here to beg you to acquit me. Why then will I do none of these things? Not out of stubbornness, men of Athens, nor out of disrespect for you. Whether I am bold toward death or not is another story; but for the sake of reputation—mine, yours, and the whole city's—it does not seem honorable to me to do any of these things at my age and with this name I have, whether it be true or false. For it is at least believed that Socrates differs in some way from the mass of men. If, then, those of you who are thought to differ, whether in wisdom or courage or any other virtue, behave in such a way, it would be shameful. **E** I have often seen such men when they are on trial—men who are thought to be something, but who do amazing things, thinking they will suffer something terrible if they are put to death, as if they would be immortal if you did not kill them. They seem to me to attach shame to the city, so that a stranger might suppose that those Athenians who excel in virtue, whom the citizens themselves prefer for offices and other honors, are no different from women. These things, men of Athens, neither we who are thought to be anything at all should do, nor, if we do them, should you allow it. Rather, you should demonstrate this very thing: that you will much more likely condemn the one who introduces these pitiful dramas and makes the city ridiculous, than the one who keeps his peace. Aside from reputation, gentlemen, it does not **Ϛ** <note>original: "Ϛ" — the Greek numeral 6, used here as the section marker equivalent to "F".</note> seem just to me to beg the judge, nor to be acquitted by begging, but to teach and to persuade. For the judge does not sit for this purpose: to grant justice as a favor, but to judge what is so. And he has sworn an oath, not to show favor to whomever he likes, but to judge according to the laws. Therefore, we should not accustom you to perjure yourselves, nor should you become accustomed to it; for neither of us would then be acting piously. Do not, therefore, require me, men of Athens, to do such things toward you which I hold to be neither honorable, nor just, nor holy—especially, by Zeus, as I am being prosecuted for impiety by this Meletus. For clearly, if I should persuade you and force you by begging when you have **Ζ** sworn an oath, I would be teaching you not to believe that there are gods; and simply by defending myself, I would be accusing myself of not recognizing the gods. But it is far from being so. For I do recognize them, men of Athens, as none of my accusers do; and I entrust to you and to the god to judge concerning me in the way that is going to be best for me and for you.

As to my not being distressed, men of Athens, at this thing that has happened—that you voted to condemn me—many other things contribute to this, and also that what has happened was not unexpected by me. But I am much more surprised at the resulting number of votes on either side. For I, for my part, did not think it would be by so little, but by a lot. But now, **Η** as it seems, if only three of the votes had fallen differently, I would have been acquitted. Indeed, I have escaped Meletus, as it seems to me, even now; and not only have I escaped him, but it is clear to everyone that if Anytus and Lycon had not come up to accuse me, he would have had to pay a thousand drachmas, having not received a fifth part of the votes.

<summary>Socrates concludes his defense by refusing to beg for mercy, arguing that it would dishonor the city and force the judges to violate their oaths. After the verdict is delivered, he expresses surprise not at his conviction, but at the narrowness of the vote.</summary>

# THE APOLOGY OF SOCRATES
->366<-

...since he did not receive a fifth part of the votes. <note>original Greek: τὸ πέμπτον μέρος τῶν ψήφων. Under Athenian law, if a prosecutor failed to win at least 20% of the jury's votes, they were fined 1,000 drachmae to discourage frivolous lawsuits.</note> So, the man proposes the death penalty for me. Very well. And what counter-penalty shall I propose for you, men of Athens?
<margin>A</margin> Is it not clear that it should be what I deserve? What then? What do I deserve to suffer or to pay, because I did not lead a quiet life but instead neglected what most people care about—wealth, domestic affairs, military commands, public speaking, and the other offices, conspiracies, and factions that arise in the city? I considered myself truly too honest a man to survive if I entered into such things. Therefore, I did not go where I would be of no use to you or myself, but instead, I went to each of you privately to perform the greatest service, as I claim. I tried to persuade each of you not to care for any of his belongings before he cared for himself—to become as good and as wise as possible—
<margin>B</margin> nor to care for the city's affairs before caring for the city itself, and to care for other things in the same way. What then do I deserve for being such a man? Something good, men of Athens, if I am to be honored according to my true merit; and specifically, a good that is fitting for me. What then is fitting for a poor man who is a benefactor, who requires leisure so that he may exhort you? There is nothing more fitting, men of Athens, than for such a man to be maintained in the Prytaneum <note>original: Πρυτανείῳ. The Prytaneum was the seat of government where distinguished citizens and Olympic victors were fed at public expense.</note>—far more so than any of you who has won an Olympic victory with a single horse, a pair, or a chariot.
<margin>C</margin> For he only makes you *appear* to be happy, but I make you *actually* happy; and he does not need the food, but I do. If, then, I must propose a penalty according to justice and merit, I propose this: maintenance in the Prytaneum.

Perhaps in saying this, I seem to you to be speaking out of sheer arrogance, just as I spoke about appeals for pity. But that is not the case, men of Athens. Rather, it is because I am convinced that I have never intentionally wronged anyone. But I cannot convince you of this, because we have spoken together for only a short time. If you had a law, as other people do, that a trial involving the death penalty should last not just one day but many, I think you would have been convinced.
<margin>D</margin> But as it is, it is not easy to clear away great slanders in a short time. Being convinced that I have wronged no one, I am certainly not going to wrong myself by saying that I deserve something bad and proposing such a penalty for myself. What should I fear? That I should suffer the penalty Meletus proposes, which I say I do not know to be good or bad? Instead of that, should I choose something that I know for certain is bad? Should it be imprisonment? Why should I live in a prison, a slave to the "Eleven" <note>original: τοῖς ἕνδεκα. The Eleven were the officials in charge of the state prison and executions.</note> who are in power at any time? Or a fine, and stay in prison until I pay it? But that brings me back to what I just said: I have no money to pay it.
<margin>E</margin> Should I then propose exile? For perhaps you would accept that. I would be possessed by a great love of life, men of Athens, if I were so irrational as to be unable to reason that while you, my fellow citizens, were unable to endure my company and my words—finding them too burdensome and hateful, so that you now seek to be rid of them—others will somehow bear them easily. Far from it, men of Athens! A fine life it would be for a man of my age to go into exile, wandering from city to city, always being driven out. For I know well that wherever I go, the young men will listen to me just as they do here. If I drive them away, they themselves will persuade their elders to expel me; and if I do not
<margin>F</margin> drive them away, their fathers and relatives will expel me for their sake.

Perhaps someone might say: "Socrates, can you not go into exile and live quietly, keeping your mouth shut?" This is the hardest thing of all to make some of you believe. For if I say that this would be to disobey the god, and that for this reason I cannot keep quiet, you will not believe me, thinking I am being ironic. And if I say again that the greatest good for a man is this: to have conversations every day about virtue and the other things you hear me discussing when I examine myself and others—and that **the unexamined life is not worth living**—you will believe me even less. But the facts are as I say, men, though it is not easy to persuade you.
<margin>G</margin> At the same time, I am not accustomed to thinking I deserve any evil. If I had money, I would have proposed a fine of as much as I could pay, for that would not have harmed me. But I have none, unless you wish me to propose a penalty of what I can afford. I could perhaps pay you one mina <note>original: μνᾶν. A mina was a significant sum of silver for a commoner, though small for the wealthy.</note> of silver. So I propose that. But Plato here, men of Athens, and Crito, and Critobulus, and Apollodorus, tell me to propose thirty minae, and they say they will act as guarantors. So I propose that amount; these men will be sufficient guarantors of the money for you.

For the sake of a very short time, men of Athens, you will gain a reputation and be blamed by those who wish to revile the city, for having killed Socrates, a wise man.

<column-break/>

...since he had not received a fifth part of the voting pebbles. Therefore, that man makes me a defendant in a capital case. So be it. But I, O men of Athens, what penalty should I judge myself to deserve? Is it not clearly that of which I am worthy? What then? What is it right for me to suffer or pay, because I did not remain silent about what I learned, but neglected those things which the common crowd values—profit, household affairs, military commands, powers, and other magistracies—and moreover avoided the conspiracies and factions that occurred in the republic, judging myself in truth to be born for more equitable duties than to think my safety depended on these things? To these things, I say, I did not apply myself, for had I been occupied with them, I would have been of use neither to you nor to myself. Instead, I devoted myself to this one duty alone:
<margin>B</margin> applying myself privately to each one of you to bring the greatest utility, as I indeed believe, persuading each person that none of his possessions should be cared for before himself, so that he might turn out as good and as prudent as possible; nor should the affairs of the city be cared for before the city itself, and that care for other matters should be held in the same manner. What then, since I am such a man, am I worthy to receive from you? Surely something good, O men of Athens, if you truly judge according to merit, and indeed such a thing as would be suitable for me. What then is suitable for a man who is needy and a benefactor, for whom it is expedient to have leisure from other occupations
<margin>C</margin> so that he may exhort you toward virtue? There is certainly no other reward, O men of Athens, which more becomes such a man than to be nourished in the Prytaneum at public expense; and much more so than if any of you had conquered at Olympia with a horse, or a two-horse chariot, or a four-horse chariot. For that man indeed makes you *seem* to be happy, but I make you *actually* so. Furthermore, he does not lack for nourishment, but I do lack it. Therefore, if it is necessary to be valued according to merit and justice, I judge myself worthy of this: specifically, that public maintenance should be provided to me in the Prytaneum.

Perhaps in saying these things to you, I seem
<margin>D</margin> just as stubborn as I appeared earlier when I detested lamentations and supplications. But the matter is not like that, O men of Athens, but rather of this sort: I am persuaded that I have done no injury to anyone willingly. I do not persuade you of this because we have had a short time for speaking. But if there were such a law among you as there is among others, that where death is the penalty, the trial should be discussed not for one day but for many, I believe I would have persuaded you. Now, however, it was not easy to dissolve great slanders in so short a time. Since, therefore, I am persuaded that injury must be done to no one, I am far from about to do injury to myself and say that I
<margin>E</margin> am worthy of evil, and judge myself to have merited something of this kind. What then? Should I fear that I might undergo what Meletus thinks me worthy of—which I indeed say I do not know whether it is good or evil—so that to avoid this, I should choose one of those things which I know plainly to be evil, and judge myself worthy of that? Should it then be chains? Why should it be necessary for me to lead a life in prison, always serving the "Eleven-Men"? Should it be to pay money, and until it is paid, remain in chains? But that is the same as what I said above, since I lack the means to pay the money. Should it perhaps be exile? For perhaps I might be judged worthy of this.
<margin>F</margin> Yet a too great desire for life would possess me, O men of Athens, if I were so foolish as to not consider that if you, my citizens, were not able to bear my company and my speeches, but my conversation and speech were so heavy and hateful to you that you have now decreed to free yourselves from it, I might think others will easily tolerate me. I am far from that, O men of Athens. A fine life indeed would be mine, at this age, living as an exile and changing from one city to another, and living in continual rejection. For as I clearly understand, wherever I set out, the young men will follow and hear me just as they do here; and if I repel them, they in turn, persuading their elders of it, will repel me. If I do not repel them, their fathers and kinsmen will expel me because of them.

Perhaps someone will say: "Can you not, O Socrates,
<margin>G</margin> lead a life of silence and quiet in exile?" But this is the most difficult thing of all to persuade some of you. For if I respond that this is to not obey God, and therefore I cannot be quiet, you will not believe me, as if I were speaking with irony. Or if I say it is the greatest good to happen to a man to speak every day about virtue, and about other things concerning which you hear me daily speaking and thus examining myself and others, and that an unconsidered life is to be rejected, you will believe me even less in these things. But these things, O men of Athens, are as I say, though they can hardly be persuaded. And at the same time, I have never been accustomed to deem myself worthy of any evil. If I had money, I would have proposed a fine of as much as I could pay, nor would it have bothered me to lose it. Now, however, I have none, unless perhaps you wish me to be valued at as much as I am able to pay. I am able to pay nearly a mina of silver. For so much, then, I value the judgment. But Plato here, O men of Athens, and Crito, and Critobulus, and Apollodorus command me to propose thirty minae. They themselves will be the guarantors of so much money. Therefore, I value it at that much; these men will be sufficient guarantors of this silver for you.

Not for the sake of much time, O men of Athens, will you gain a reputation and provide material to those wishing to revile the city, because you have killed Socrates, a wise man.

<summary>Following his conviction, Socrates argues that instead of death, his "punishment" should be public maintenance as a benefactor of Athens. He famously declares that the unexamined life is not worth living and eventually offers a fine of thirty minae guaranteed by his friends.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the trial of Socrates. Having just been sentenced to death by the Athenian jury, Socrates offers his final reflections to the court, addressing both those who voted against him and those who voted for him.</meta>

# PLATO
->368<-

<margin>A</margin> For those who wish to reproach you will say that I am a wise man—even though I am not—in order to criticize you. If you had waited only a short time, this would have happened to you of its own accord. For you see my age, how far advanced it is in life and how close to death. I do not say this to all of you, but only to those who have condemned me to death. I say this also to these same men: perhaps you think, men of Athens, that I was convicted for a lack of words of the sort that might have persuaded you, had I thought it right to do or say anything possible to be acquitted by you. Far from it. I was indeed convicted for a lack—not of words, but of audacity and impudence, <margin>B</margin> and because I was unwilling to say to you the kinds of things that would have been most pleasant for you to hear: to hear me weeping and wailing, and doing and saying many other things unworthy of me (as I claim), the kind of things you are accustomed to hearing from others. But I did not think then that I should do anything unfree <note>original: "illiberale" / "ἀνελεύθερον." Referring to actions beneath the dignity of a free-born citizen.</note> on account of the danger, nor do I now repent having made my defense in this way. I much prefer to die having made such a defense than to live by the other kind. For neither in a trial nor in war should I or anyone else try to avoid death by doing anything and everything. In battle, it is often clear that a man could avoid death by throwing down his arms <margin>C</margin> and turning to beg for mercy from his pursuers. There are many other devices in every danger by which one might escape death, if one is shameless enough to do and say anything. But consider this, O men of Athens: it is not difficult to escape death, but it is much more difficult to escape wickedness. For wickedness runs faster than death. And now I, being slow and old, have been caught by the slower runner; but my accusers, being clever and swift, have been caught by the swifter: wickedness. And now I depart, condemned by you to the penalty of death; but they depart, condemned by truth <margin>D</margin> herself to wickedness and injustice. I abide by my penalty, and they by theirs. Perhaps these things were destined to be so, and I think they are for the best.

After this, I desire to make a prophecy to you who have condemned me. For I am now at that point where men are most likely to prophesy: when they are near death. I predict to you, O men of Athens, that if you kill me, a punishment will come upon you immediately after my death, far harsher, by Jove, than the one you have inflicted on me. You have done this now thinking that you will be released from giving an account of your lives. But the opposite will happen to you. There will be more who will hold you to account, whom I <margin>E</margin> used to restrain, though you did not realize it. They will be all the more troublesome as they are younger, and you will be more vexed by them. For if you think that by killing men you can stop someone from reproaching you for not living rightly, you are mistaken. This release is neither effective nor honorable. The easiest and best way is not to suppress others, but to prepare oneself to be as good as possible. Having prophesied these things to you who condemned me, I take my leave.

But to you who acquitted me, I would gladly speak about this thing that has happened, while the magistrates are busy and I have not yet gone to the place where I must die. Stay with me, my friends, for this short time. Nothing prevents us from conversing with one another while it is permitted. I want to show you, as my friends, what has just happened to me and what its meaning might be. For to me, O judges—for I may rightly call you judges <note>The "judges" (dikastai) here are the members of the jury who voted for his innocence, whom Socrates considers the only true judges.</note>—a wonderful thing has happened. <margin>These points are in Cicero’s first book on Divination.</margin> <margin>F</margin> That prophetic voice of the spirit <note>original: "dæmonis" / "δαιμονίου." This refers to Socrates' "daimonion," an inner divine sign or voice that warned him against certain actions.</note> has always been very frequent in the past, opposing me even in very small matters if I was about to do something incorrectly. But now, these things which you see have happened to me—things which one might certainly think and consider to be the extreme of evils. Yet the sign of the god did not oppose me when I left home this morning, nor when I came up here to the court, nor anywhere in my speech while I was talking, though in many other speeches it has often stopped me in the middle of a sentence. Now, in this matter, it has nowhere opposed me in any action or word. What do I take to be the cause of this? I will tell you. It appears to me that what has happened is a good thing. <margin>G</margin> And it is not possible that we judge correctly if we think death is an evil. I have a great proof of this: the sign would surely have opposed me, as it is accustomed to do, unless I were about to do something good.

Let us also consider it in this way, that there is much hope that it is a good thing. Death must be one of two things: either death removes all sensation entirely, or, as it is said, death is a certain <margin>Almost all of these things are described in Cicero’s Tusculan Disputations, Book 1.</margin> <margin>H</margin> migration of the soul from these places to another place. If sensation is extinguished and death is like a sleep which sometimes, even without dreams, brings the most peaceful rest—good gods, what a gain it is to die! For I think that if someone had to pick a night in which he slept so soundly that he did not even see a dream, and compared all the other nights and days of his whole life with that night, and had to say how many days and nights he lived better and more pleasantly than that night—I think that not only a private citizen, but even the Great King <note>The "Great King" was the common Greek title for the King of the Persian Empire, the wealthiest and most powerful man known to them.</note>—

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> A wise man. For they will say that I am wise, even if I am not, those who wish to reproach you. If you had waited a short time, this would have happened to you of its own accord. For you see my age, that it is already far along in life, and close to death. I say this not to all of you, but to those who voted for my death. And I say this also to these same men: Perhaps you think, O men of Athens, that I have been caught by a lack of the kind of words with which I could have persuaded you, if I thought I ought to do and say everything to escape the trial. Far from it. But I have been caught by a <margin>B</margin> lack, not of words, but of boldness and shamelessness, and of being unwilling to say such things to you as would have been most pleasant for you to hear: me wailing and lamenting, and doing and saying many other things unworthy of me, as I say—the kind of things you are used to hearing from others. But I did not then think I should do anything unfree because of the danger, nor do I now repent of having defended myself in this way. But I much prefer to die having defended myself thus, than to live in that way. For neither in court nor in war should I or anyone else devise how to escape death by doing anything and everything. For in battles it often becomes clear that one might escape dying by throwing away his <margin>C</margin> arms and turning to beg for mercy from his pursuers. And there are many other devices in each danger to avoid death, if one dares to do and say everything. But I suspect this is not the hard thing, O men of Athens—to escape death—but it is much harder to escape wickedness. For it runs faster than death. And now I, being slow and old, have been caught by the slower one. But my accusers, being clever and sharp, have been caught by the swifter one: wickedness. And now I go away, having been sentenced to death by you; but they have been sentenced by the truth <margin>D</margin> to villainy and injustice. And I abide by the penalty, and they do too. Perhaps these things were even meant to be this way, and I think they are well enough.

What comes after this, I desire to prophesy to you, O you who have condemned me. For I am now at that point where men most often prophesy, when they are about to die. For I say, O men who have killed me, that punishment will come to you immediately after my death, much harder, by Zeus, than the kind you killed me with. For you have done this now thinking you will be released from giving an account of your life. But it will turn out quite the opposite for you, as I say: those who will hold you to account will be more numerous, whom I was holding back, though you did not notice. And they will be <margin>E</margin> harder the younger they are, and you will be more angry. For if you think that by killing men you will restrain someone from reproaching you because you do not live correctly, you do not think well. For this release is neither entirely possible nor noble. But that other one is both noblest and easiest: not to cut off others, but to prepare oneself to be as good as possible. Having prophesied these things to you who condemned me, I depart.

But to those who voted to acquit me, I would gladly converse about this thing that has happened, while the officials are busy and I do not yet go where I must go to die. But stay with me, O men of Athens, for this much time. For nothing prevents us from telling stories to one another while it is allowed. For to you, as being friends, I want to show what has just happened to me and what it means. For to me, O judges (for by calling you <margin>F</margin> judges, I would call you correctly), something wonderful has happened. For my accustomed divination of the spirit, in all former time, was always very frequent, opposing me even in very small things if I was about to do something not correctly. But now, what you yourselves see has happened to me—things which someone might think, and are generally considered, to be the extremes of evils. But the sign of the god did not oppose me as I was leaving home in the morning, nor when I was coming up here to the court, nor anywhere in my speech when I was about to say something. And yet in other speeches it has often stopped me in the middle of speaking. But now, nowhere in this whole affair, neither in any deed nor in any word, has it opposed me. What then <margin>G</margin> do I take to be the cause? I will tell you. For it is likely that this thing that has happened to me is a good thing; and there is no way we can be right in our assumption, those of us who think that dying is an evil. A great proof of this has happened to me: for there is no way the accustomed sign would not have opposed me, if I were not about to do something good.

Let us also consider it in this way, that there is much hope that it is a good thing. For dying is one of two things: for either it is like being nothing, and the dead man has no sensation of anything; or, according to what is said, it happens to be a certain change and migration for the soul from this place here to another place. And if there is no sensation, but it is like a sleep when one sleeps and does not even see a dream, death would be a wonderful gain. For I <margin>H</margin> think, if someone had to pick out that night in which he slept so soundly that he did not even see a dream, and compared the other nights and days of his own life with this night, and had to say, after looking into it, how many days and nights he has lived better and more pleasantly than this night in his own life—I think that not only a private person, but even the Great King—

<summary>In this concluding portion of his defense, Socrates reflects on his death sentence, observing that his "divine sign" remained silent, which suggests his impending death is a benefit rather than an evil. He contrasts the difficulty of escaping death with the much greater difficulty of escaping wickedness, predicting that his execution will only bring more critics to Athens.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the "Apology," Socrates' defense speech at his trial, and begins the "Crito," a dialogue set in his prison cell. In the previous section, Socrates reflected on his conviction and the nature of death.</meta>

CRITO. 369

...for this [sleep] would be easily counted against all other days and nights. But if, on the other hand, death is like a journey from here to another place, and if what is said is true—that all the dead are indeed there—what greater good could there be than this, O judges? For if someone, arriving in the underworld <note>original: "ᾅδου" (Hades). In Greek thought, the realm of the dead, not necessarily a place of punishment.</note>, having been set free from these people who claim to be judges, finds those who are truly judges, who are said to preside there—Minos, Rhadamanthus, Aeacus, and Triptolemus, and all the other demigods who were righteous in their own lives—would that journey be a poor one? Or again, to keep company with Orpheus, Musaeus, Hesiod, and Homer; how much would any of you give for that? I, for my part, am willing to die many times over if these things are true. For me, the stay there would be wonderful, whenever I might meet Palamedes and Ajax, the son of Telamon, or anyone else of the ancients who died because of an unjust judgment. <note>Palamedes and Ajax were mythological heroes famously undone by legal trickery or unfair decisions.</note> Comparing my own experiences with theirs would, I think, be not unpleasant. And most importantly, I could spend my time examining and questioning those there, just as I do those here: which of them is wise, and which thinks he is, but is not. What would one give, O judges, to examine the man who led the great army against Troy, or Odysseus, or Sisyphus, or countless other men and women one could mention? To talk with them there, to be with them and examine them, would be an inconceivable happiness. Certainly, those there do not put people to death for doing such things. For in other respects, those there are happier than those here, and for the rest of time they are immortal, if indeed what is said is true. But you too, O judges, must be of good hope toward death; and you must keep this one truth in mind: that no evil can happen to a good man, either in life or in death, nor are his affairs neglected by the gods. My own situation now has not happened by chance; rather, it is clear to me that it was better for me to die now and be released from my troubles. For this reason, the divine sign <note>The "daimonion," an inner voice Socrates claimed warned him against wrong actions.</note> did not turn me back at any point, and I am not at all angry with those who condemned me or with my accusers. Yet, they did not condemn or accuse me with this intention, but thinking to harm me; for this they deserve blame. However, I ask this much of them: when my sons grow up, punish them, gentlemen, by troubling them with the same things I troubled you with, if they seem to care for money or anything else before virtue. And if they think they are something when they are nothing, reproach them as I reproached you—that they do not care for what they should, and they think they are something when they are worth nothing. If you do this, I will have received justice from you, both I and my sons. But now it is time to depart: I to die, and you to live. Which of us goes to a better thing is unclear to everyone except the god.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> <note>The initial letter 'M' was omitted by the printer, likely intended for a hand-painted red letter (rubrication).</note> [Indeed, it is] a great gain to be able to count [such a sleep] against the days. If, therefore, death is something of this sort, I truly call it a gain. For in this way, all time seems no longer than a single night. But if the things that are said are true—that death is a migration to those shores inhabited by those who have departed from this life—it is a much more blessed thing that you, when you have escaped from those who wish to be considered judges, should come to those who are truly called judges: Minos, Rhadamanthus, Aeacus, Triptolemus, and others, however many demigods lived justly. Can this journey seem mediocre to you? <margin>B</margin> To be able to speak with Orpheus, Musaeus, Hesiod, and Homer—at what price would you value that? Indeed, I would wish to die often, if it were possible, so that I might find the things of which I speak. For that dwelling and company would be wonderfully pleasing to me, since I would be with Palamedes, and Ajax the son of Telamon, and others of the ancients who died by a subverted judgment. I think it would not be unpleasant to compare my misfortunes with theirs. Furthermore, the greatest thing would be to spend time there searching and examining each person, just as I have done here: which of them is wise, and which, though he is not, yet thinks himself to be wise. Therefore, O judges, how much should one value the opportunity to test the wisdom of the great king who led the vast forces to Troy, or of Odysseus, or Sisyphus, and many others <margin>C</margin> of both men and women whom one could mention? To speak and associate with them in examination would be a completely inestimable happiness. For those who live there certainly do not put people to death for this reason; they are more blessed than we are in other things, and moreover, they remain immortal for the rest of time, if the things said are true. Nor should you, O judges—those of you who acquitted me—fear death. You should consider this one thing to be true: that nothing evil can happen to a good man, whether living or dead, and his affairs are never neglected by the immortal gods. Nor has this happened to me by chance; it is certain to me that to die now and be freed from labors was better for me. <margin>D</margin> For this reason, that divine sign did not oppose me. Truly, I have no reason to be angry with those by whom I was accused, or those by whom I was condemned, although they did not accuse or condemn me with this mind, but because they believed they were harming me. For this, they are certainly to be blamed. (But now, having returned to those same men, I speak to them thus:) I only pray this of you, O men: that you also treat my sons, when they have grown up, with the same punishments if they are as troublesome to you as I was, especially if they seem to you to have a greater care for money or any other thing than for virtue. And if they wish to seem to be something and think themselves of some value when <margin>E</margin> they are of none, rebuke them just as I did you, because they do not apply themselves to what they ought, and they think they are something when they are of no value. If you do this, I and my sons will have suffered what is just from you. But it is time to depart from here: I to die, you to live your lives. Which of the two is better, the immortal gods know; I believe that no man knows.

# CRITO, OR, ON WHAT IS TO BE DONE.
->Moral.<-

# CRITO, OR, ON WHAT IS TO BE DONE.
->Moral.<-

---

<margin>SUMMARY OF THE DIALOGUE.</margin> *Crito, a very close friend of Socrates, visits him in prison on the day his death is approaching. After having signaled to him many times to persuade him to let Crito lead him out of prison, he now especially urges him to allow it. He argues it is easy to do, as his friends' diligence has prepared everything. If Socrates does not do this, it will be both highly unbecoming for his friends and hateful to himself and his family. Socrates testifies that he will not do it until he has determined by certain arguments whether it can be done rightly. What he decides is easy to understand from his own words.*

---

->SOCRATES, CRITO.<-

<note>Decorative drop cap 'H'</note>
Why have you come at this hour, Crito? Or is it not still early?
<margin>F</margin> CRITO: It is indeed very early. SOCRATES: About what time?
CRITO: The first light of dawn. SOCRATES: I am surprised that the prison guard was willing to answer you.
CRITO: He is already familiar to me, Socrates, because I come here so often. Moreover, he has received some benefit from me. SOCRATES: Have you just arrived, or some time ago? CRITO: Quite some time ago. SOCRATES: Then why did you not wake me immediately, but sat there in silence? CRITO: No, by Zeus, Socrates, I myself would not have wished to be in such sleeplessness and grief for so long. But I have been wondering at you for a long time, seeing how sweetly you sleep. I intentionally did not wake you, so that you might pass the time as pleasantly as possible. I have often considered you happy in your character throughout your whole life, but especially so in this present misfortune, seeing how easily and calmly you bear it. SOCRATES: Truly, Crito, it would be absurd if a man of my age were to be distressed if he must now die. CRITO: Others, Socrates, of such an age are caught in similar misfortunes, but their age does not release them from being distressed by their present fate.

<column-break/>

->SOCRATES, CRITO.<-

<note>Decorative drop cap 'Q'</note>
Why have you come at this hour, O Crito? Is it not still very early? SOCRATES: Very early indeed. SOCRATES: How early, then? CRITO: The first dawn. SOCRATES: I wonder how the guard of the prison was willing to comply with you. CRITO: He is already <margin>F</margin> a friend to me, O Socrates, because I visit here frequently. Furthermore, he has received no small benefit from me. SOCRATES: Did you arrive just now, or a while ago? CRITO: A good while ago. SOCRATES: Then why did you not wake me at once, but sat by in silence? CRITO: Never, by Jove, O Socrates, would I have woken you. For I myself would not wish to remain for so long in wakefulness and pain. But I have been admiring you for some time <margin>G</margin> as I watch how sweetly you sleep. And I deliberately did not wake you, so that you might spend your time as peacefully as possible. Indeed, both often and truly throughout all your past life I have judged you blessed on account of your character, but especially in this present calamity, because you bear it so easily and clearly. SOCRATES: And yet it would be very absurd, O Crito, if someone of such a great age should take an imminent death hard. CRITO: Nevertheless, O Socrates, others equally old are overwhelmed by similar calamities, yet their age does not so help them that they do not take their present fortune heavily and...

### PLATO'S [WORKS]

A
...you bear it [sleep] so calmly. **SOCRATES:** Indeed I do. But why have you come so early? **CRITO:** I bring bitter news, O Socrates—not to you, it appears, but to me and all your friends; news both bitter and heavy. I believe I shall find it as difficult to bear as anything I have ever known. **SOCRATES:** What is this news? Has the ship from Delos <note>original: "nauis ex Delo". During the annual mission to Delos, Athens halted all executions. The return of the ship signaled that Socrates' death sentence could be carried out.</note> already returned, upon whose arrival I must die? **CRITO:** It has not yet arrived, but I believe it will come today, based on reports from men arriving from Sunium <note>A cape at the southern tip of the Attic peninsula.</note> who left it there. It is clear from these messengers that it will arrive today, and therefore it will be necessary for you, Socrates, to depart from this life tomorrow. **SOCRATES:**

With good fortune, Crito. If it pleases the gods, so be it. However, I do not think it will arrive today. **CRITO:** What do you base this guess on? **SOCRATES:** I will tell you. I must die on the day after the ship arrives. **CRITO:** So say those who have authority over these matters. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, I do not think it will come on this * following day, but the next.
<margin>* The following.</margin>

She called to me and said, "O Socrates,

on the third day hence, you shall reach fertile Phthia." <note>original: "Tertia hinc die Phthiam peruenies latiglebam." This is a reference to Homer's Iliad, where Achilles speaks of returning home. Though you could raise and educate them, you will abandon them entirely, and as far as you are concerned, their characters will be left to chance.

->H<-

They will likely suffer the fate that usually befalls orphans. Truly, one ought either not to have children at all, or else not refuse the labor of raising and educating them. You seem to me to be choosing the path of an idle and lazy man, whereas you should choose what a good and brave man would, especially one who has claimed to pursue virtue throughout his whole life. To me, it seems, it is among the heaviest things I could bear. **SOCRATES:** What is this news? It is clear from this that messengers will say it comes today, and it will be necessary tomorrow, O Socrates, for you to end your life. **SOCRATES:** Well, Crito, may it be

And it seems you did not wake me at an opportune time. **CRITO:** What was the dream? **SOCRATES:** A woman seemed to come to me, beautiful and well-formed, wearing white garments; she called me and said, "O Socrates, on the third day you would reach fertile Phthia." **CRITO:** How absurd the dream is, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Clear, rather, it seems to me, O Crito. **CRITO:** Too clear, it seems. But, O divine Socrates, even now trust me and be saved. For to me, if you die, it is not just one calamity; but apart from being deprived of you—such a companion as I shall never find again—I shall also seem to many, who do not know you and me clearly, that I was able to save you if I was willing to spend money, but that I was negligent. And yet what reputation could be more shameful than this: to seem to value money more than friends? For the many will not be persuaded that you yourself did not wish to leave here, even though we were eager for it. **SOCRATES:** But why, O blessed Crito, do we care so much for the opinion of the many? For the most decent men (whom it is more worthwhile to consider) will believe these things to have been done just as they were done. **CRITO:** But you see, Socrates, that it is necessary to care about the opinion of the many. These very present events show that the many are capable of working not the smallest of evils, but almost the greatest, if one is slandered among them. **SOCRATES:** If only, O Crito, the many were capable of working the greatest evils, so that they might also be capable of the greatest goods; then it would be well. But now they can do neither. For they are not able to make a man either wise or foolish. They do whatever they happen to do. **CRITO:** Let these things be so. But tell me this, Socrates: are you perhaps looking out for me and your other companions, lest, if you go out from here, the informers give us trouble for having smuggled you out? And we might be forced either to lose our entire property, or a great deal of money, or suffer something else in addition to these? For if you fear any such thing, let it go. For it is just that we, having saved you, should run this risk—and if necessary, even one greater than this. But trust me, and do not do otherwise. **SOCRATES:** I am looking out for these things, Crito, and many others. **CRITO:** Do not then fear these things. For the silver is not much which some are willing to take to save you and lead you out from here. Then, do you not see these informers, how cheap they are, and that there would be no need for much silver for them? My money is available to you, which I think is sufficient. Then, if out of concern for me you do not think you should spend my money, there are foreigners here ready to spend theirs. One has even brought sufficient silver for this very purpose, Simmias the Theban; Cebes is also ready, and many others. So (as I say) do not give up on saving yourself out of fear of these things, nor let what you said in the courtroom be a difficulty for you—that you would not know what to do with yourself if you left. For in many places and elsewhere, wherever you arrive, they will love you. And if you wish to go to Thessaly, I have guests there who will value you highly and provide safety for you, so that no one throughout Thessaly will trouble you. Furthermore, Socrates, you do not even seem to me to be attempting a just thing: betraying yourself when it is possible to be saved. You are hastening to have happen to yourself exactly what your enemies would hasten—and did hasten—wishing to destroy you. In addition to these things, you also seem to me to be betraying your sons, whom you might raise and educate, but you will go away and leave them, and for your part, they will fare however they happen to. And they will experience (as is likely) such things as usually happen to orphans in their orphanhood. Either one should not have children, or one should endure the hardship of both feeding and educating them. You seem to me to choose the most easy-going path. But one should choose what a good and brave man would choose, especially one claiming to care for virtue through his whole life. So I am ashamed for you and for us, your companions, lest this whole matter concerning you seem to have been handled with a certain unmanliness on our part: the entry of the case into the courtroom...
