Crito desperately attempts to persuade Socrates to escape, citing concerns for Socrates' children and his own reputation.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and his friend Crito in the Athenian prison. Crito is finishing his urgent appeal for Socrates to escape his death sentence, transitioning into Socrates’ philosophical defense of why he must remain and obey the law.</meta>

# CRITO

<margin>A</margin> ...that you entered the prison, when you might have chosen not to; then the trial itself and the way it was conducted; and finally this, the absurd ending of the whole affair, which seems to have escaped us through some lack of spirit and cowardice on our part. It will look as though we did not save you, nor did you save yourself, even though it was quite possible and doable if we had been of even the slightest use. See to it, Socrates, that these things do not bring shame upon both you and us, in addition to the harm they cause. Take counsel with yourself—or rather, the time for counsel is past; the decision should already be made. <margin>B</margin> There is only one plan: everything must be accomplished during this coming night. If we delay any longer, it will be impossible and no longer within our power. By all means, Socrates, take my advice and do not do otherwise.

**SOCRATES:** My dear Crito, your zeal is most valuable if it is joined with some degree of rightness. But if it is not, then the greater it is, the more troublesome it becomes. We must therefore consider whether these things ought to be done or not. For I am the kind of man who—not only now, but always—obeys nothing within me except the reason <note>original: "logos". Here meaning the rational argument or principle reached through logic.</note> which seems best to me upon reflection. The arguments I used in the past I cannot now cast away simply because this fortune has befallen me; they appear much the same to me now, and I honor and value the same principles I did before. <margin>C</margin> Unless we can find better arguments to bring forward at this moment, you may be sure I will not agree with you—not even if the power of the multitude tries to scare us like children with even more "bogeymen" <note>original: "mormolyttai". Mythical female nursing demons used to frighten children into behaving; Socrates uses this to describe the "scare tactics" of the Athenian public.</note> than they do now, threatening us with chains, death, and the loss of our property. 

How then might we consider these matters most fairly? Perhaps we should first take up the argument <margin>D</margin> you mentioned regarding public opinion. Was it always said correctly that we should pay attention to some opinions and not to others? Or was it said correctly only before I was condemned to die, but now it has become clear that it was said merely for the sake of talk, and was in truth only child’s play and nonsense? I desire, Crito, to examine this with you: whether the argument appears different to me now that I am in this situation, or whether it is the same. Shall we let it go, or shall we follow it? 

It used to be said (as I believe) by those who thought they were speaking sense—just as I was saying just now—that of the opinions men hold, some should be highly valued and others not. By the gods, Crito, does this not seem correctly said to you? <margin>E</margin> For you, in all human likelihood, are outside the danger of dying tomorrow, and your present calamity should not lead you astray. Consider then: does it not seem sufficient to say that one should not honor all the opinions of men, but some and not others? And not the opinions of everyone, but of some and not others? What do you say? Is this not correctly stated?

**CRITO:** It is correct.

**SOCRATES:** Then we should honor the good opinions and not the wicked ones?

**CRITO:** Yes.

**SOCRATES:** And are the good opinions those of the wise, while the wicked ones are those of the foolish?

**CRITO:** Of course.

**SOCRATES:** Come then, how were such things explained before? When a man is practicing gymnastics <note>original: "gymnazomenos". Physical training was a core part of Greek education and life.</note> and making it his business, does he pay attention to the praise, blame, and opinion of every man, or only to the one who happens to be a doctor or a trainer?

**CRITO:** To that one alone.

**SOCRATES:** <margin>F</margin> Therefore he should fear the blame and welcome the praise of that one man, rather than that of the multitude?

**CRITO:** Clearly.

**SOCRATES:** He must then act, exercise, eat, and drink in the way that seems right to the one who is the director and who understands, rather than the way it seems to everyone else.

**CRITO:** That is true.

**SOCRATES:** Well then. If he is disobedient to that one man and dishonors his opinion and his praises, but honors those of the many who understand nothing, will he not suffer some harm?

**CRITO:** Of course he will.

**SOCRATES:** And what is this harm? Where does it lead, and what part of the disobedient man does it affect?

**CRITO:** Clearly it affects the body, for it ruins it.

**SOCRATES:** You speak well. And is it not the same with other things, Crito, so that we need not go through them all? Regarding things that are just and unjust, shameful and honorable, <margin>G</margin> good and evil—the very things we are now consulting about—should we follow the opinion of the many and fear it, or the opinion of the one, if there is one who understands? Is he the one we should respect and fear more than all the others combined? If we do not follow him, we will damage and disfigure that part of us which is made better by justice and ruined by injustice. Or is there nothing to this?

**CRITO:** I believe there is, Socrates.

**SOCRATES:** Come then, if we ruin that which is made better by health and destroyed by disease because we did not follow the judgment of those who understand, is life worth living for us once it is ruined? This part is the body, is it not?

**CRITO:** Yes.

**SOCRATES:** <margin>H</margin> And is life worth living for us with a wretched and ruined body?

**CRITO:** In no way.

**SOCRATES:** Then is life worth living for us when that part is ruined which injustice harms and justice benefits? Or do we consider that part of us, whatever it may be, which is concerned with justice and injustice, to be of less value than the body?

**CRITO:** In no way.

**SOCRATES:** But rather more precious?

**CRITO:** Much more.

**SOCRATES:** Then, my excellent friend, we must not worry at all about what the many will say of us, but only what the one who understands justice and injustice will say, and the truth itself. Therefore, you were not correct in your first proposal when you suggested that we should consider the opinion of the multitude regarding...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...having entered, when it was permitted not to enter; then the contest of the trial itself conducted in this manner, and finally this extreme end—it will seem as if we have escaped through some vice of laziness or cowardice on our part, because we did not save you, nor did you save yourself, even though it could have been done without great difficulty if there had been even a small amount of industry in us. Therefore, O Socrates, consider whether these things, besides being evil, are also a disgrace to you and to us. Consult yourself. Indeed, it is no longer the time for consulting, but the time for the decision to have been made. There is only <margin>B</margin> one plan: namely, that all these things must be done this very next night. But if we delay any longer, nothing further can be done at all. Therefore, have faith in me entirely, Socrates, and do not act otherwise.

**SOCRATES:** O friend Crito, this zeal of yours would be worth a great deal if it were undertaken for some right reason. If not, the more vehement it is, the more troublesome. We must therefore consider whether these things ought to be done by us, or not. For I am a person—not only now, but always—who obeys nothing of mine except reason, which appears best to me as I reflect. Therefore, those reasons which I used in previous times, I cannot now reject even after I have fallen into this fortune; but they appear nearly the same to me, and I venerate and honor the same ones in the present as I did before. <margin>C</margin> So much so that unless we can bring forward better ones now, you should know clearly that I will not concede to you—not even if the power of the multitude tries to terrify us more than it does now, like children, with terrifying spectral masks <note>Latin: "larualis", referring to masks or ghosts (lares/larvae). Mirroring the Greek 'mormolyttai'.</note>, threatening chains and death and furthermore the deprivation of money.

**CRITO:** In what way then can we consider these things properly?

**SOCRATES:** In this way: if we take up again that which you were saying a little while ago about opinions. Whether it is always correctly held or not—namely, that it is necessary to take account of some opinions, but not at all of others. Or was it perhaps correctly said before it was necessary for me to die, but now it is established that it was said in vain for the sake of a dispute, <margin>D</margin> when in truth it was a kind of joke and nonsense? I desire indeed, O Crito, to consider with you whether that prior discourse appears different to me now that I am placed in this fortune, or exactly the same as before—and whether we should dismiss it or obey it. 

It used to be said, I believe, always by those who thought they were saying something meaningful—just as I was saying just now—that human opinions should partly be highly valued and followed, and partly not at all. This, by the Gods, O Crito, does it not seem to you to be correctly said? For you, as the condition of men goes, are so far from the danger of dying tomorrow that the present calamity does not lead you into error. Consider then whether it does not seem sufficiently stated to you that one <margin>E</margin> ought not to follow all the opinions of men, but to follow some and neglect others; and not those of everyone, but of some, and not others. What do you say then? Are these things not correctly stated?

**CRITO:** Correctly.

**SOCRATES:** Is it not proper to honor the good ones and despise the bad ones?

**CRITO:** It is proper.

**SOCRATES:** And are the good ones not those of the prudent? While the bad ones, on the contrary, are those of the imprudent?

**CRITO:** Why not?

**SOCRATES:** Come then, in what way were such things said again? A man who exercises in the gymnasiums and devotes effort to that matter—does he attend to the praise and blame and opinion of just any man, or only of that one who is a doctor or a master of the gymnasium?

**CRITO:** Of this man alone.

**SOCRATES:** Is it not proper to fear the blame and desire the praise of that one man rather than the many?

**CRITO:** Without doubt.

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, by this reasoning, he ought to act and exercise himself, and even eat and drink, as it seems best to that one who presides and understands, rather than as it seems to the common crowd.

**CRITO:** These things are true.

**SOCRATES:** What then if he does not obey that one man, and considers his opinion and commendations as nothing, <margin>F</margin> but honors the commendations of the ignorant crowd—will he be safe from harm?

**CRITO:** Not at all.

**SOCRATES:** But what sort of harm is it, and where does it lead, and into what part of the disobedient man?

**CRITO:** Into the body, obviously, for it corrupts it.

**SOCRATES:** You speak correctly. Is it not the same regarding other things, O Crito, if we run through them all? Concerning things just and unjust, shameful and honorable, <margin>G</margin> good and evil, about which our consultation is now concerned: should we follow and fear the opinion of the many, or rather that of the one who understands, whom it is proper to respect and fear more than all others? If we do not obey him, we will be hurt and corrupted in that part which is accustomed to be made better by the just and corrupted by the unjust. Or is that nothing?

**CRITO:** That is indeed what I think, O Socrates.

**SOCRATES:** Come then, if we have corrupted that which is made better by the healthy but corrupted by the unhealthy, by not following the judgments of the experts, will life be worth living for us with it destroyed? That is the body, is it not?

**CRITO:** That <margin>H</margin> very thing.

**SOCRATES:** Then is life worth living for us with a diseased and corrupted body?

**CRITO:** By no means.

**SOCRATES:** Or perhaps is life worth living for us when that part is corrupted which is harmed by the unjust but helped by the just? Or do we think that part is viler than the body—whatever it is of ours in which justice and injustice are concerned?

**CRITO:** By no means.

**SOCRATES:** But rather more precious?

**CRITO:** Greatly so.

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, O best of men, we must not care very much what the many say of us, but what that one says who understands things just and unjust, and truth itself. Therefore, in the first place, you did not correctly introduce the idea that we must consider the common opinion regarding...

...about just, honorable, and good things, and their opposites, that we should value the opinion of anyone. But indeed, someone might say: "Can the crowd kill us?" SOCRATES: And does this also hold: that living well, honorably, and justly are the same thing? CRITO: It holds. SOCRATES: Therefore, based on what we have agreed, we must consider this: whether it is just for me to try to go <margin>B</margin> out from here without the Athenians dismissing me, or unjust. As for the considerations you bring up regarding the spending of money, reputation, and the education of children—take care, Crito, that these are not really the concerns of "the many," <note>original: "vulgari" / "οἱ πολλοί". And if it appears that we are acting unfairly, we must not even think about whether we must die by remaining here and keeping quiet, or suffer anything else at all, before we do anything unfair. And if you can refute me in any part of what I say, refute me and I will agree with you. SOCRATES: Do we say that in no way should one do wrong <note>original: "iniuriam" / "ἀδικητέον". This refers to committing an injustice or a moral wrong.</note> willingly? Or rather, is it exactly <margin>E</margin> as we used to say: whether the multitude affirms it or denies it, and whether we are forced to undergo things more severe or lighter than these present ones? Nevertheless, do we admit that doing wrong is altogether an evil and a shameful thing for the one who does it, or not? CRITO: We certainly admit it. SOCRATES: In no way, then, must one do wrong? CRITO: In no way. SOCRATES: Nor, if one has suffered a wrong, should he retaliate, as the crowd thinks? Since one must in no way do wrong. CRITO: So it seems. SOCRATES: What then? Is it right to do evil to anyone, Crito, or not? CRITO: Certainly not, Socrates. SOCRATES: And what if someone who suffers evil returns evil to the one who inflicted it—would that be just, as the crowd says, or unjust? CRITO: Unjust. SOCRATES: For surely, inflicting evil upon <margin>F</margin> men is no different from doing them a wrong. CRITO: You speak the truth. SOCRATES: Therefore, one ought neither to retaliate nor to do evil to any man, no matter what you have suffered from them. And see to it, Crito, that while you grant these things, you do not agree with us against your own opinion. For I know that to only a few people does this seem true, or will it seem so. But those to whom it seems so, and those to whom it seems otherwise, have no common ground for deliberation; instead, it is necessary for them, when they look upon each other's counsels, to despise one another. Consider therefore very carefully whether you share this opinion with me and feel the same way. And let us deliberate by starting from this principle: that it is never right either to do wrong, or to retaliate for a wrong, or for one who has been treated badly to return the evil to the one who inflicted it. Or do you depart <margin>G</margin> from us and disagree with this principle? To me, it has seemed this way for a long time and still does now. But if it appears otherwise to you, speak and teach me. But if you stand by our former agreements, hear what follows. CRITO: I do stand by them and I agree with you; therefore, speak. SOCRATES: I say then next—or rather, I ask: should a person do those things which he has agreed with someone are just, or should he break his word? CRITO: He should do them. SOCRATES: From these things, then, consider this: if we depart from here without the city's consent, are we doing evil to some—and specifically to those whom it is least proper to harm—or not? And are we standing by those things we agreed were just, or the opposite? CRITO: I am unable, Socrates, to answer these questions. For I do not understand. <margin>H</margin> SOCRATES: Then consider it this way: suppose that as we were intending to either run away from here (or whatever this should be called), the Laws and the Commonwealth of this city were to come, stand before us, and ask: "Tell us, Socrates, what do you intend to do? Do you not understand that by this act you are attempting, you are plotting to destroy us—the Laws—and the entire city, so far as it lies in your power? Or do you think any city can still stand and not be overturned, in which public judgments have no force, but are made void and rescinded by private individuals?" What shall we say, Crito, to these and similar things? For anyone, and especially an orator, could say much on behalf of the law thus...

# CRITO.

<margin>
...under this law being destroyed, that the judgments rendered are valid? How indeed should they be valid if destroyed, or invalid?
</margin>
<margin>A</margin> ...under this law being destroyed, that the judgments rendered are valid? Or what shall we say to these things? That "the city wronged us, and did not judge the case correctly?" Shall we say these things, or what? CRITO: These things, by Zeus, O Socrates. SOCRATES: What then if the Laws should say: "O Socrates, was this not also agreed between us and you, to abide by the judgments which the city might decree?" If then we should wonder at them speaking, perhaps they would say: "O Socrates, do not wonder at what is said, but answer, since you are even accustomed to use the practice of questioning and answering. Come then, what charge do you bring against us and the city, that you attempt to destroy us? Did we not first give you birth? And through us did not your father take your mother, and beget you? Tell us then, for those of us <margin>B</margin> who are laws concerning marriages, do you find some fault, as if they were not well made?" "I find no fault," I would say. "But then for those laws concerning the child’s nourishment and education, in which you yourself were educated? Or did those of us appointed for this not command well, charging your father to educate you in music <note>In ancient Greece, "music" (mousikē) referred to all the arts overseen by the Muses, including literature and history, not just melody.</note> and gymnastics?" <note>Physical training or athletics.</note> "Well indeed," I would say. "Very well. Since you were born and nurtured and educated, could you say first that you were not our offspring and servant, both yourself and your ancestors? And if this is so, do you think justice is on an equal footing for you and us, and whatever we should attempt to do to you, do you think it is just for you to do these things back to us in turn? Or while toward your father justice was not <margin>C</margin> on an equal footing, nor toward a master (if you happened to have one) so that whatever you suffered, you could do the same in return—neither answering back when spoken to harshly, nor striking back when struck, nor many other such things—yet toward the fatherland and the laws it shall be permitted to you? So that if we attempt to destroy you, thinking it to be just, will you then attempt to destroy us, the laws and the fatherland, as much as you are able in return? And will you say, in doing these things, that you act justly, you who truly care for virtue? Or are you so wise that it has escaped your notice that more precious than mother and father and all other ancestors is the fatherland, and more venerable, and more holy, and held in higher honor both among gods and among men who have sense? And one must revere and yield more and <margin>D</margin> soothe a fatherland when it is angry than a father, and either persuade it, or do what it commands? And to suffer if it orders one to suffer anything, keeping quiet? Whether to be struck, or to be bound? Or if it leads you into war to be wounded or to die, these things must be done, and justice stands thus? And one must not give way, nor retreat, nor leave one’s post? But both in war and in court, and everywhere, one must do what the city and the fatherland command; or else persuade it of what is naturally just? But to use violence is not holy against either a mother or a father, and much less so against the fatherland?" What shall we say to these things, O Crito? That the laws speak the truth, or not? CRITO: It seems so to me. SOCRATES: "Consider then, O Socrates" (the laws might perhaps say) "if we speak these things truly, that you do not attempt to do just things <margin>E</margin> to us in what you now attempt. For we, having given you birth, nurtured you, educated you, and given you a share of all the beautiful things we were able to provide for you and all the other citizens—nevertheless, we proclaim that by having given permission to any of the Athenians who wishes, after he has been scrutinized <note>Likely referring to the "dokimasia," a formal check of a youth's status upon reaching adulthood.</note> and sees the affairs in the city and us, the Laws, that whoever among us does not please him, it is permitted for him to take his belongings and go wherever he wishes. And not one of us Laws stands in the way or forbids it, whether any of you wishes to go into a colony (if we and the city do not please him) or to migrate elsewhere having gone there, to go there wherever he wishes, keeping his own things. But whoever of you remains, seeing the way in which we judge cases and otherwise manage the city, we say that this man has already agreed by his action with us, that he will do those things which we command. And the one who does not obey, we say he does injustice in three ways: because he does not obey us who are his parents, <margin>F</margin> and because he does not obey his nurturers, and because having agreed to obey us, he neither obeys nor seeks to persuade us if we are doing something not well; though we propose our commands and do not cruelly order him to do what we command, but permit one of two things: either to persuade us, or to do it. He does neither of these. We say that you too, O Socrates, will be subject to these charges if you do what you intend; and not least of the Athenians you, but among those most especially." If then I should say, "Why so?" perhaps they would justly lay hold of me, saying that I happen to have agreed to this agreement more than any other of the Athenians. For they would say: "O Socrates, there are great proofs for us of these things, that we and the city pleased you. For you would never have stayed in it more than all the other <margin>G</margin> Athenians unless it pleased you exceptionally; and you never went out from the city for a festival <note>original: "theōrian" / "spectaculi gratia". This refers to official state pilgrimages to festivals like those at Delphi or Olympia.</note> except once to the Isthmus, <note>The Isthmian Games near Corinth.</note> nor anywhere else, except for military service; nor did you ever make another journey abroad like other men. Nor did a desire for another city or other laws seize you to know them; but we were sufficient for you, and our city. So strongly did you choose us, and you agreed to live as a citizen according to us; and among other things, you even begot children in the city, as it pleased you...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...declaring the law violated, which indeed orders that sentences passed by public judgment be ratified. Or shall we answer them that the city, by not judging correctly, brought an injury upon us? Is it thus or otherwise? CRITO: Thus, by Jove, O Socrates. SOCRATES: But indeed the laws themselves would respond thus: "O Socrates, was this not agreed between us and you, that you must stand by the judgments which the city has brought forth?" If you should wonder at the laws speaking so, perhaps they would say: "Do not wonder, Socrates, at what we have just said; rather, answer, since it is your custom both to question and to respond. Tell us then, what do you accuse in us and the city, that you strive to destroy us? In the first place, did we not beget you? and through us <margin>B</margin> did your father receive your mother and bring you forth? Tell us then, do you find fault with these laws among us which concern marriages, and are you angry with them as being in some part less than right?" "I am not angry," I would say. "But with these laws which provide for the education and instruction of children, in which you yourself were also instructed? Or did these laws, established for this duty, not arrange things rightly when they ordered your father to instruct you in music and gymnastics?" "They arranged it rightly," I would grant. "Come then, after you were born through us and nurtured and instructed, in the first place, can you deny that you are our offspring and servant, both yourself and your progenitors? Then since it is so, do you think right is on an equal footing for you and us, and that what we attempt to do to you, you may judge it just <margin>C</margin> to return the same to us in turn? Or since there is no equal right for you toward a father, nor toward a master if you had one—so that you might return upon them what you suffer from them, nor if they provoked you with a quarrel could you quarrel back, nor if they struck you could you strike back in turn, nor be permitted to attempt other such things against them—will it be permitted to you against the fatherland and the laws? To the extent that if we, judging it to be just, wish to kill you, you in turn would strive to destroy us, the laws and the fatherland, to the best of your strength, and say that you act justly in doing these things—you who profess to have a care for virtue in truth. Or are you so wise that it escaped you that the fatherland is to be preferred to father and mother and all progenitors, and that it is a more <margin>D</margin> venerable thing and more holy, and that the fatherland is to be placed in a higher position both among gods and among men of sound mind, and that it ought to be cherished more, and obeyed, and that one should be more submissive to it when it behaves more harshly and severely than to a father; and if it should command anything, either to dissuade it or to do it, and most patiently endure whatever it orders to be suffered? And whether it commands to be beaten, or to be cast into chains, or if it sends you into battle to receive wounds and undergo death, it must be obeyed entirely. For justice so dictates, and one must neither hesitate, nor flee, nor desert one's rank. But both in war, and in judgment, and everywhere, those things must be done which the republic and the fatherland <margin>E</margin> have ordered; or certainly you should persuade it and show it to what extent that which it commands is just; but to use force is a sin, whether against a mother or against a father, and most of all against the fatherland." What shall we say to these things, Crito—that the laws speak the truth, or otherwise? CRITO: It seems so to me. SOCRATES: Furthermore, the laws will perhaps say: "Observe, O Socrates, whether we speak truly that you attack us unjustly. For we who begat you, nurtured you, instituted you, and made both you and all other citizens partakers of all good things as far as we were able; <margin>F</margin> nevertheless, we permit any of the Athenians—once he has recognized and approved of the customs and laws of the city and the form of governing the republic—if we do not please someone, he may take his things and depart wherever it pleases him. Nor does any of us laws hinder or prohibit it, whether any of you, to whom we and the city are not at all pleasing, wishes to depart into some colony, or to transfer his habitation elsewhere; he may do so by his own judgment and carry his things with him. But whoever of you remains, after he has recognized in what manner we exercise judgments and rule the city in all other things, we now assert that he has agreed with us by the deed itself that he will do whatever we command. And he who does not obey, we affirm that he does injury in a threefold way: both because he does not obey us, his parents; and because he does not obey his nurturers; and because having pledged <margin>G</margin> to obey us, he neither obeys nor strives to persuade us if we seem to do something less than rightly. And since we propose our precepts freely and do not command rigidly, but permit one of two things—either to be persuaded by words or to fulfill the commands—he does neither of these. To these crimes, O Socrates, we judge you will be liable if you do what you contemplate; and not less so than the other Athenians, but most of all." And if I should ask the cause why I am liable above the others, perhaps they would justly bite back at me, saying that I more than any of the Athenians happened to have consented to the laws of the city. For they would say: "O Socrates, for us there are great proofs of these things, that we and the city pleased you. For you would never have inhabited it more than all other Athenians unless it had pleased you wonderfully. Therefore, you never left the city even for the sake of a spectacle, <note>original: "spectaculi gratia". See note on the left column.</note> except once to the Isthmus, nor anywhere else except into military service, nor did you ever make another pilgrimage as others are accustomed to do; nor did a desire for another city or for knowing other laws take you; but we and our city were sufficient for you, to such an extent did you vehemently approve of us, and you consented that you would live by our customs; then indeed, so that we may omit other things, you even procreated children in it, as if it..."

<summary>In this pivotal passage, Socrates personifies the Laws of Athens to argue that a citizen owes the state absolute obedience, similar to but greater than that owed to a parent, because the state provided the framework for his birth, education, and life. He emphasizes the 'social contract'—that by choosing to remain in Athens as an adult, Socrates has implicitly agreed to follow its laws and judgments.</summary>

# PLATO'S <note>original: PLATONIS</note>

<margin>A</margin>...if it should please you. Moreover, it was permitted to you in the trial itself to propose a penalty of exile if you had wished, and what you now attempt against the will of the city, you could have done then with its consent. But then you boasted in your words as if you did not take it hard if it were necessary for you to die. Rather, as you said, you chose death itself over exile. Now, however, you are neither ashamed of those words of yours, nor do you respect us, the laws, but you plot our destruction. You act as the basest slave would do, attempting to run away, contrary to the covenants and agreements in which you agreed with us to submit yourself to our governance. First, therefore, answer us this very thing: whether we speak truly in asserting that not in words, <margin>B</margin> but in the deed itself, you consented to be governed by our customs. Or are these things not true? What shall we say to this, Crito? Shall we not admit it?

CRIT. It is necessary, O Socrates.

SOC. What then (say the laws) are you doing anything other than transgressing the agreements and pacts made with us? You were not forced to enter into these with us, nor were you deceived, nor were you compelled to deliberate in a short time, but over seventy years; in which time it was permitted for you to depart, if we did not please you and the agreements did not seem just to you. Yet you did not prefer Lacedaemon <note>Sparta</note> or Crete, which cities you frequently proclaim to be well-governed, nor any other of the Greek or foreign cities. Rather, you traveled out from this city less often than the lame, the blind, and other crippled people. To such a degree did <margin>C</margin> this city please you above other Athenians, and we, the laws, likewise. For to whom can a city be pleasing whose laws do not please him? But now you do not abide by those things which have long been agreed upon between us and you. If you trust us, you will not commit an act that would cause everyone to mock you as you depart from the city. Consider again, if you should transgress these things and commit any of these sins, how will it profit either you or your kin? For it is almost certain that your kin will be in danger of being driven into exile themselves, deprived of their citizenship and stripped of their inheritance. But as for you, if you take yourself to some neighboring city, either Thebes or <margin>D</margin> Megara (for both are well-governed), you will arrive first as an enemy of their government; and all who care for their own country will look at you with suspicious eyes, regarding you as a corrupter of laws. And you will confirm the opinion of the judges, so that they will seem to have rendered their sentence against you correctly. For whoever is a corrupter of laws will most certainly seem to be a corrupter of both the young and the foolish. What then? Will you avoid the cities which are well-governed and the most moderate men? <margin>E</margin> And if you do this, will your life be worth living? Or perhaps you will shamelessly mingle with them, and not blush to discourse among them on the same subjects you were accustomed to here: namely, that virtue and justice, and laws and institutions, are to be valued above all else? Do you not think the behavior of Socrates will appear unseemly and least honorable? It must certainly be thought so. But perhaps, turning away from these cities, you will go off to Thessaly to Crito’s guests. For there, life is lived in a very disordered and intemperate manner. And perhaps they will gladly listen to you narrating how ridiculously you escaped from prison: how you threw some bundle over yourself, or put on a leather skin <note>Latin: *sagum coriaceum* - a rough cloak often used as a disguise</note>, or wrapped yourself in other things as those who take flight are accustomed to do, changing your habit and appearance. But do you think no one <margin>F</margin> will say how an old man, with so little time left to live, as is likely, dared to live with such sordid greed for life, having transgressed the greatest laws? Perhaps indeed, provided you do not offend anyone. Otherwise, Socrates, you will hear many things unworthy of you. You will live subject to all men and serving them. What will you do in Thessaly? Will you frequent banquets? As if you had traveled to Thessaly for the sake of a dinner. <margin>G</margin> Where will those discourses of ours concerning justice and the other virtues be? But indeed, you wish to live for the sake of your children, so that you may nourish and educate them. Will you then lead them into Thessaly to nourish and educate them there, making them foreigners, so they may carry away this benefit from you besides? Or will you not do that, but rather, left here while you are alive, they will be better nourished and educated by your kin in your absence? But will they care for them if you depart to Thessaly, but not if you depart to the other life? Surely, if there is any help in those who say they are your kin, it must be believed they will care for them. But, O Socrates, trust us, your nurturers, and value neither your children, nor life, nor anything else more than justice; so that when you have migrated to the other life, you may be able to give an account of all these things to those who rule there. For truly, if you do these things by transgressing the laws, it will happen neither better, nor more justly, nor more holily for you or yours; nor will it profit you there. Instead, you depart now having suffered injustice, if you depart, not from us the laws, but from men. But if you escape so shamefully, returning injury for injury and evil for evil, transgressing the agreements and promises made with us, and harming those whom you least ought to harm—namely yourself, your friends, your country, and us the laws—then we shall be angry with you while you live, and there the laws of the other life, which are

<column-break/>

...to you from the city. Moreover, in the trial itself, it was permitted to you to propose exile as a penalty, if you wished, and what you now attempt against the city’s will, you could have done then with its consent. But you then boasted as if you were not distressed if it were necessary for you to die, but you chose (as you said) death before exile. Now, however, you are neither ashamed of those words, nor do you respect us, the laws, by attempting to destroy us. You act as the most worthless slave would act, attempting to run away contrary to the contracts and agreements by which you agreed with us to live as a citizen. First, therefore, answer us this: whether we speak the truth in saying you agreed to live as a citizen according to us by your deeds, and not just in words. Or is it not true? What shall we say to this, Crito, other than that we agree? CRIT. It is necessary, Socrates. SOC. "Are you then," they would say, "doing anything other than transgressing the contracts and agreements made with us? You were not forced to agree, nor were you deceived, nor were you compelled to decide in a short time—but over seventy years, during which you could have left if we did not please you, or if the agreements did not seem just to you. But you did not prefer Lacedaemon or Crete, which you always say are well-governed, nor any other of the Greek cities or those of the barbarians. Instead, you stayed at home away from the city less than the lame, the blind, and the other disabled. Thus, the city and we, the laws, clearly pleased you more than other Athenians. For whom could a city please without laws? But now, will you not stand by what was agreed? You will, if you are persuaded by us, Socrates; and you will not be a laughingstock by leaving the city. For consider: by transgressing these things and failing in any of them, what good will you do yourself or your friends? For it is fairly clear that your friends will be in danger of being exiled themselves, deprived of their city, or losing their property. And as for you, if you go to one of the nearby cities, like Thebes or Megara (for both are well-governed), you will arrive as an enemy, Socrates, to their constitution; and all who care for their own cities will look at you with suspicion, thinking you a corrupter of the laws. And you will confirm the opinion of the judges, so that they seem to have judged the case correctly. For whoever is a corrupter of laws would certainly seem to be a corrupter of young and foolish men. Will you then flee the well-governed cities and the most orderly men? And if you do this, is it worth it for you to live? Or will you approach them and be so shameless as to carry on what discourses, Socrates? The same ones as here: that virtue and justice are most valuable to men, along with institutions and laws? And do you not think the conduct of Socrates will appear shameful? One must think so. But you will leave these cities and go to Thessaly to Crito’s friends. For there, there is the greatest disorder and license; and perhaps they would gladly hear you tell how ridiculously you ran away from prison, having put on some disguise, like a leather skin or other things that runaways usually put on, changing your own appearance. And will no one say that an old man, with so little time left in life, as is likely, dared to desire to live so greedily, transgressing the greatest laws? Perhaps, if you do not annoy anyone; otherwise, Socrates, you will hear many things unworthy of you. You will live by fawning on all men and being a slave. Doing what? Feasting in Thessaly? As if you had traveled to Thessaly for a dinner. And those discourses about justice and other virtues—where will they be for us? But you want to live for the sake of your children, to raise and educate them? What then? Will you take them to Thessaly and raise and educate them there, making them foreigners, so they might enjoy this benefit from you too? Or will they not have that, but being raised here while you are alive, will they be better raised and educated without you being with them? For will your friends take care of them? Will they take care of them if you travel to Thessaly, but not if you travel to Hades? If those who say they are your friends are of any use, one must think they will. But, O Socrates, be persuaded by us, your nurturers, and do not value children, or life, or anything else more than justice, so that when you arrive in Hades, you may have all these things to say in your defense to the rulers there. For it does not appear that doing these things is better, more just, or more holy for you here, or for any of your friends; nor will it be better for you when you arrive there. But now you depart having been wronged (if you depart), not by us the laws, but by men. But if you leave so shamefully, returning wrong for wrong and evil for evil, transgressing your own agreements and contracts with us, and doing evil to those you least should—yourself, your friends, your country, and us—we will be angry with you while you live, and there our brothers, the laws in Hades, will not receive you kindly...

<summary>The personified Laws of Athens argue that Socrates has a binding social contract with the state, and that escaping would be a shameful betrayal of his own principles, his family, and the justice system.</summary>

> Know well, my dear friend Crito, that I seem to hear these things, just as those in a religious frenzy <note>original: "κορυβαντιῶντες" (Corybantes). These were ecstatic worshippers of the goddess Cybele, known for hearing mystical flutes that others could not hear.</note> seem to hear the flutes; and in me, the echo of these words booms so loudly that I am unable to hear anything else. ...there [in the underworld] are our sisters, the Laws of Hades, who will by no means receive you kindly, knowing that you tried to destroy us to the best of your power. Therefore, take care that Crito does not persuade you otherwise than we do. Indeed, O sweet friend Crito, I seem to hear these things just as the Corybantes think they hear the flutes. And the sound of such speeches so echoes within me that I can hear no others. You see how things appear to me at present; if you attempt to contradict them, you will strive in vain. However, if you are confident you can accomplish anything, speak. CRITO: Truly, Socrates, I have nothing to say. SOCRATES: Stop then, Crito, and let us proceed this way, since God himself leads us this way.

# ## PHAEDO, OR, ON THE SOUL. <note>original: ΦΑΙΔΩΝ, Η, ΠΕΡΙ ΨΥΧΗΣ / PHÆDO, SIVE, DE ANIMO</note>

### SUMMARY OF THE DIALOGUE.
*Phaedo relates to Echecrates the conversations held by Socrates on that very day when he died after drinking poison. Through these, he demonstrated both his admirable and fearless constancy in undergoing death with a calm mind, and his certain and fixed opinion on the immortality of the soul. Therefore, using a fitting example from the mouth of Socrates himself—who was indeed dying and sealing his final thoughts as if in a last will and testament—Plato teaches that the soul is immortal. He also shows the soul's state and condition after the course of life is finished; and he does so in such a way as to demonstrate that death is least of all to be feared by a good man. Thus, the thesis of this dialogue is twofold. One, and indeed the primary one if you look at the aim of the speech, is "On Contemning Death"; the other, of the greatest importance, which is nevertheless used to prove the former, is "On the Immortality of the Soul." Hence the dialogue received its name from the more noble part. It is therefore partly moral, insofar as it deals with contemning death, and partly theological or (as they say) metaphysical, insofar as it treats the soul and God.*

-> ECHECRATES, PHAEDO, APOLLODORUS, SOCRATES, CEBES, SIMMIAS, CRITO, <-
-> THE SERVANT of the Eleven. <note>The "Eleven" were the Athenian magistrates in charge of the prison and executions.</note> <-

<margin>B</margin> Were you yourself present, O Phaedo, with Socrates on that day when he drank the poison in the prison, or did you hear it from someone else? PHAEDO: I was there myself, Echecrates. ECHECRATES: What then were the things the man said before his death? And how did he die? For I would gladly hear of it. For none of the citizens of Phlius <note>A city in the Peloponnese.</note> travel to Athens much these days, nor has any guest come from there for a long time who could bring us a clear report about these things, except only that he died by drinking poison; of other details, they had nothing to tell. PHAEDO: Did you not even learn about the trial and how it went? ECHECRATES: Yes, someone reported that to us; and we wondered why, although it took place long ago, he appears to have died much later. What was the reason for this, Phaedo? PHAEDO: A <margin>C</margin> certain piece of luck befell him, Echecrates. For it happened that on the day before the trial, the stern was crowned on the ship which the Athenians send every year to Delos. ECHECRATES: And what does this mean? PHAEDO: This is the ship, as the Athenians say, in which Theseus once went to Crete taking those "twice seven" <note>The seven youths and seven maidens sacrificed to the Minotaur.</note> and saved them, and was saved himself. They had vowed to Apollo, as the story goes, that if they were saved, they would send a sacred mission <note>original: θεωρίαν (theoria)</note> to Delos every year. And from that time even until now, they send it every year to the God. When they begin the mission, it is their law to keep the city pure during that time, and to execute no one by public decree until the ship reaches Delos and returns here again. This sometimes takes a long time, when the winds happen to hold them back. The beginning of the mission is when the priest of Apollo crowns the stern of the ship; and this <margin>D</margin> happened, as I say, on the day before the trial. For this reason, Socrates had a long time in the prison between his trial and his death. ECHECRATES: But what about the death itself, Phaedo? What was said and done, and which of his companions were present with the man? Or did the magistrates not allow them to be present, and did he die destitute of friends? PHAEDO: By no means; some were present, quite many in fact. ECHECRATES: Try then to report all these things to us as clearly as possible, unless you happen to be busy. PHAEDO: I am at leisure indeed, and I will try to narrate it for you. For to remember Socrates, whether I am speaking myself or hearing another, is always the most pleasant of all things to me. ECHECRATES: Indeed, Phaedo, those who are going to hear you feel the same way. So try to go through everything as accurately as you can. PHAEDO: I truly experienced a wonderful feeling being present there. For no pity entered into me <margin>E</margin> as one present at the death of a close friend. For the man appeared happy to me, Echecrates, both in his manner and his words, so fearlessly and nobly did he die. It occurred to me that even when going to the house of Hades, he did not go without a divine destiny, but that arriving there he would fare well, if anyone ever did. For these reasons, no pity at all entered into me, as might seem likely for someone present at a time of mourning; nor on the other hand did I feel pleasure, as we usually did when we were occupied with philosophy. For the conversations were of that kind. But a truly strange feeling came over me, an unusual mixture of pleasure and pain...

# OF PLATO

<margin>A</margin>
I was overcome as I considered that he was to die a little later. And all of us who were present were affected in nearly the same way, sometimes laughing, but at other times weeping. One man among us, however, stood out: Apollodorus—for you know the man and his character. <term>ECHEC.</term> How could I not? <term>PHÆD.</term> He was entirely overcome in that way, and I myself and all the others had our minds similarly distracted by distress. <term>ECHEC.</term> But who exactly was present, O Phaedo? <term>P.</term> Among the local citizens there were Apollodorus, and Critobulus, and his father Crito; also Hermogenes, Epigenes, Aeschines, and Antisthenes. Ctefippus of Paeania was there too, and Menexenus, and certain other locals. Plato, however, was ill, I believe.
<margin>B</margin>

prison. Therefore, while talking among ourselves, we always waited there until the prison was opened, for it did not open very early. We therefore told one another to return to the usual place as early as possible in the morning. The Eleven were the magistrates in Athens responsible for prisons and executions.</note> are releasing
<margin>D</margin>
Socrates from his chains and announcing to him that he must die today." Not long after, he returned and told us to enter. Thus, entering, we found Socrates just having been freed from his shackles, and Xanthippe—you know the woman—sitting near him, holding his young son in her arms. When she saw us, she began to wail and cry out as women are accustomed to do: "O Socrates," she said, "now your friends will speak to you for the last time, and you to them." But Socrates, looking at Crito, said, "O Crito, let someone take her home." And some of Crito's servants led her away, as she was shouting and beating her breast. Socrates, sitting up on the bed,
<margin>E</margin>
drew his leg toward him and rubbed it with his hand, and while rubbing it, he spoke thus: "How strange a thing it seems, O men, this thing which people call pleasure, and how wonderfully it is naturally related to pain itself, which seems to be its opposite. For they are unwilling to be present in a person at the same time. Yet, if someone pursues and catches one, he is almost always compelled to receive the other as well, as if they were both fastened together from a single peak. I believe that if Aesop had noticed this, he would have made a fable of it: namely, that God himself, wanting to reconcile these warring things but being unable to do so, joined their tips into one, and therefore, to whomever the one is present, the other follows soon after. This is exactly
<margin>F</margin>
what has happened to me now. Since my leg was just now suffering pain because of the chains, pleasure now seems to follow in its place." To this Cebes said, "By Jove, O Socrates, you have reminded me opportunely. For since you have composed poems—first a hymn in praise of Apollo, and then putting the fables of Aesop into verse—many others have asked me, and Evenus did so just recently, with what intention you did these things after coming to prison, things you had never done before. If, therefore, it matters to you that I have an answer for Evenus when he asks me again, as I know for certain he will, tell me, I pray, what should be answered."
<margin>G</margin>
"Tell him the truth, O Cebes," he said, "that I did this not because I wished to compete with him or his poems—for I knew that would not be easy—but to test certain dreams and not fail in my duty, if perhaps this was the 'music' they have so often commanded me to practice. They were of this sort: often in my past life the same dream has visited me, appearing in different forms at different times, but always giving the same command: 'Socrates, make music and practice it.' Therefore, what I did in former times, I thought was what the dream commanded; and just as we are accustomed to encourage runners, so I thought the dream was encouraging me in what I was already doing, as if philosophy were the greatest
<margin>H</margin>
music and I were working at it. But after the sentence was passed against me, and the festival of the God delayed my death, I thought that if perhaps the dream so often commanded it, I ought to practice this popular music and not resist it, but comply. For I thought it would be safer, before I departed from life, to discharge this duty and satisfy the dream by making poems. Thus, first I made verses in honor of the God whose festival was then being celebrated; and after the God, judging that he who is to be a poet ought to make fables and not just arguments, and I myself was not a storyteller,

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
...at once both pleasure and pain, as I reflected that he was about to die. And nearly all of us present were in such a state, at one moment laughing, and at another weeping; and one of us especially, Apollodorus—for you know the man and his manner. <term>EX.</term> How could I not? <term>PHAED.</term> He, then, was entirely in this state, and I myself was troubled, as were the others. <term>EX.</term> And who, O Phaedo, happened to be there? <term>PHAED.</term> This Apollodorus of the locals was present, and Critobulus, and his father Crito; and also Hermogenes, Epigenes, Aeschines, and Antisthenes. Ctesippus the Paeanian was also there, and Menexenus, and certain others of the locals. Plato, I believe, was ill. <term>EX.</term> Were any strangers
<margin>B</margin>
present? <term>PHAI.</term> Yes, Simmias the Theban, and Cebes, and Phaedondes; and from Megara, Euclides and Terpsion. <term>EX.</term> What then? Were Aristippus and Cleombrotus present? <term>PHAI.</term> Certainly not. For they were said to be in Aegina. <term>EX.</term> Was anyone else there? <term>PHAI.</term> I think these were nearly all who were present. <term>EX.</term> What then were the conversations you speak of? <term>PHAI.</term> I will try to narrate everything to you from the beginning. For indeed, on the preceding days, I and the others were accustomed to visit Socrates, gathering at dawn at the court in which the trial took place, for it was near the prison. We waited, therefore, each time until the prison was opened, spending time with one another. For it was not opened early. But when it was opened, we went in to Socrates, and we spent most of the day with him. And indeed, at that time we gathered earlier. For on the previous day, when we came out of the prison in the evening, we learned that the ship from Delos had arrived. We therefore charged one another to come as early as possible to the usual place. And we came; and the gatekeeper, who was accustomed to answer, coming out to us, told us to wait and not to go in before he himself gave the word. "For," he said, "the Eleven are releasing Socrates, and giving orders that he must die on this day." After waiting no long time, he came and told us to enter. Entering, then, we found Socrates just then released, and Xanthippe—for you know her—holding his little child and sitting by him. When Xanthippe saw us, she cried out and said such things as women are accustomed to say: "O Socrates, now for the last time your friends will speak to you, and you to them." And Socrates, looking at Crito, said, "O Crito, let someone lead her home." And some of Crito's people led her away, crying and beating herself. But Socrates, sitting up on the bed, bent his leg and rubbed it with his hand; and while rubbing it, he said, "How strange, O men, seems this thing which people call pleasure; how wonderfully it is related to what seems to be its opposite, pain; in that they will not both be present to a person at the same time. But if one pursues the one and takes it, he is almost always compelled to take the other as well, as if they were two joined from one head. And it seems to me," he said, "that if Aesop had thought of them, he would have composed a fable, how God, wishing to reconcile them when they were at war, since he could not do so, joined their heads together into the same point. And because of this, to whomever the one comes, the other follows after. Just as it seems to me myself, since there was pain in my leg because of the bond, now pleasure appears to follow it." Then Cebes, taking up the word, said, "By Zeus, O Socrates, you have done well to remind me. For concerning the poems you have made, putting into verse the stories of Aesop and the hymn to Apollo, some others have asked me already, and especially Evenus lately, what you had in mind that, after you came here, you made these, having never made anything before. If, then, it matters to you that I have an answer for Evenus when he asks me again (for I know well that he will ask), tell me what I must say." "Tell him then, O Cebes," he said, "the truth: that not wishing to be a rival to him or his poems did I make these (for I knew that would not be easy), but trying out what certain dreams might mean, and purifying myself, in case they should many times command me to make this music. For they were somewhat of this sort: often the same dream visited me in my past life, appearing at different times in different forms, saying the same things: 'O Socrates,' it said, 'make music and work at it.' And I, in the time before, supposed it was encouraging and urging me to do what I was already doing, just as those who encourage runners; and so the dream was urging me to do what I was doing, to make music—philosophy being the greatest music, and I doing this. But now, since the trial took place, and the festival of the God prevented me from dying, it seemed necessary, if indeed the dream should many times command me to make this common music, not to disobey it, but to do so. For it would be safer not to depart before purifying myself by making poems, in obedience to the dream. Thus, first I made a poem to the God whose sacrifice was then at hand; after the God, reflecting that a poet must, if he is to be a poet, make fables and not arguments, and I myself was not a storyteller...

<meta>This page continues the transition into the Phædo. Having introduced the friends present in the prison, the dialogue now turns to Socrates' final philosophical defense. He addresses why a philosopher, while forbidden from taking his own life, should nevertheless welcome the approach of death as a journey toward better masters and companions.</meta>

# PHÆDO.

For this reason, using the fables of Aesop that I had at hand and knew, I composed those I first encountered. Tell these things, then, to Cebes and Evenus <note>Evenus of Paros was a poet and sophist whom Socrates often mentioned with a touch of irony.</note>; bid him farewell, and tell him, if he is wise, to follow me. I am departing, it seems, today; for the Athenians so command. And Simmias said, <gloss>you are giving</gloss> what a command this is, O Socrates, to Evenus! For I have met the man many times; from what I have perceived, he will not at all <gloss>go</gloss> <note>The Greek text here is slightly ambiguous; the gloss refers to the act of following or obeying.</note> along with your advice willingly. Why? (said he) Is Evenus not a philosopher? He seems so to me, said Simmias. Then Evenus will be willing, as will everyone who worthily partakes in this matter. He will not, however, do violence to himself. For they say it is not lawful. And while <margin>A</margin> saying this, he lowered his legs from the bed to the ground; and sitting thus, he then discussed the rest. Cebes then asked him, How <margin>B</margin> do you say this, O Socrates, that it is not lawful to do violence to oneself, yet the philosopher would be willing to follow one who is dying? Why, O Cebes, have you and Simmias not heard about such things, having been companions of Philolaus <note>Philolaus was a famous Pythagorean philosopher; the Pythagoreans were known for their secretive doctrines on the soul.</note>? Nothing clear, O Socrates; but I too speak <gloss>about it</gloss> from hearsay. What I happen to have heard, however, there is no grudge against telling. For perhaps it is most fitting for one about to travel there to examine and tell stories about the journey there, what kind we think it is. For what else could one do in the time until sunset? Why then do they say it is not lawful for one to kill oneself, O Socrates? For I have already (just as you now asked) heard from Philolaus, when he <margin>C</margin> lived with us, and already from some others, that one ought not to do this; but I have never heard anything clear from anyone about it. But you must be eager, he said. For perhaps you might yet hear. Perhaps, however, it will seem strange to you if this alone of all other things is simple, and it never happens to a man—as with other things where death is sometimes better—to be worthy of death. And for those for whom it is better to die, it perhaps seems strange to you if it is not holy for these men to do themselves a kindness, but they must wait for another benefactor. <margin>D</margin> And Cebes, laughing softly, said "God knows," <note>original: "Ἴττω Ζεὺς." Cebes uses his native Boeotian dialect here, adding a touch of local flavor to his exclamation.</note> speaking in his own tongue. Indeed it might seem, said Socrates, to be irrational in this way; yet perhaps it has some reason. The doctrine spoken of in secret about these matters, that we humans are in a kind of guard-post <note>original: "φρουρᾷ." This term can mean either a prison or a soldier's watch-post, implying we are stationed here by a higher power.</note> and that one must not release oneself from it or run away, seems a great thing to me and not easy to see through; however, this at least seems to me, O Cebes, to be well said: that the gods are our caretakers, and that we humans are one of the possessions of the gods. Or does it not seem so to you? It does, said Cebes. Therefore (said he) would you not also, if one of your own possessions killed itself without you signaling that you wished it to die, be angry with it, and if you had any punishment, would you not punish it? Certainly, he said. Perhaps, then, in this way it is not irrational that one must not kill oneself before a god <margin>E</margin> sends some necessity, just like the one now present to us. That at least seems likely, said Cebes. But what you were just saying—that philosophers would easily be willing to die—that seems strange, O Socrates, if what we just said is reasonable: that God is the one taking care of us, and we are his possessions. For it is not reasonable that the wisest men should not be grieved to depart from this service in which they are governed by the gods, who are the best of all governors. For surely a wise man does not think he will take better care of himself when he has become free; but a foolish man might perhaps think these things—that one should flee from a master—and would not consider that one must not flee from the good, but stay as much as possible. Therefore he would flee irrationally; but he who has sense would surely desire to be always with one who is better than himself. And yet in this way, O Socrates, the opposite of what was just said is likely. For it is fitting for the wise to be grieved when dying, <margin>F</margin> while the foolish should rejoice. Upon hearing this, Socrates seemed to me to be pleased by Cebes' persistence; and looking at us, he said, Cebes is always searching out some arguments, and is not at all willing to be persuaded immediately by whatever one might say. And Simmias said, But indeed, O Socrates, now Cebes seems to me also to be saying something. For with what intent would truly wise men flee masters better than themselves and easily part from them? And Cebes seems to me to be aiming his argument at you, because you bear it so easily both leaving us and the gods, who are, as you yourself admit, good rulers. You speak justly, he said. For I think you are saying that I must make a defense as if in a court of law. Quite so, said Simmias. Come <margin>G</margin> then, <gloss>said he</gloss>, let me try to make a more persuasive defense to you than I did to the judges. For I, he said, O Simmias and Cebes, if I did not think I was going first to other gods who are both wise and good, and then also to dead men better than those here, I would be doing wrong not to be grieved by death; but as it is, be well assured that I hope to arrive among good men. And this I would not quite firmly insist upon; but that <margin>H</margin> I shall go to gods who are very good masters, be well assured that, if I would insist on anything else of such a kind, I would insist on this too. So for these reasons...

<column-break/>

From some of the fables of Aesop which I knew, and had more ready at hand, I composed them as I came upon each one first. Therefore, O Cebes, report these things to Evenus, and bid him to be well, and if he is wise, let him follow me. For I am migrating from here today, as it appears. For so the Athenians command. Then Simmias said, What kind of thing is it, O Socrates, that you command to Evenus? For I have often encountered him, and from what I perceive of him, in almost no way will he willingly obey you. Why indeed, he said; is Evenus not a philosopher? It seems so to me, said Simmias. Evenus will therefore wish it, as will whoever is worthily a participant in this matter. Yet perhaps he will not bring force upon himself. For they say it is not divinely lawful. And as he said these things, he lowered his legs from the bed to the ground. And sitting thus, he thereafter discussed the rest. Cebes then asked him, In what way do you say this, O Socrates? That it is not lawful to violate oneself, yet the philosopher desires to follow the dying? What, O Cebes, he said, have you and Simmias not heard such things from Philolaus, with whom you were familiar? Nothing manifest indeed, said Cebes. And yet I also, said Socrates, speak of these things from hearsay. Therefore, no envy will prevent me from relating to you what I myself have heard. For perhaps it is most fitting for one about to migrate there to consider and imagine in the mind what kind this migration itself should be thought to be. For what else should one do until the setting of the sun? For what cause, said Cebes, O Socrates, do they say it is a crime to lay hands upon oneself? For already, as you were just asking, I heard from Philolaus, when he was staying with us, and from some others besides, that it is not fitting to do it; yet I have never heard anything clear from anyone on this matter. But there is a need for attention, he said. For even if you have heard it, it might yet perhaps seem wonderful whether this alone of all others is simple: nor does it ever happen to a man as the rest, even when it is better to die than to live. Therefore, it will perhaps seem wonderful to you if to those for whom it is better to die, it is not permitted to benefit themselves, but they must wait for another who may benefit them. Then Cebes smiling said, "God knows," speaking in his own tongue. And yet it may indeed seem, said Socrates, to be so absurd. Perhaps, however, it has a certain reason. Truly that discourse which is held in secret concerning these matters—that we humans are in a certain custody, nor is it fitting for anyone to release himself from this, nor to flee—seems great to me, nor easy to know. Nevertheless, this seems to me, O Cebes, to be rightly said: that the gods have care for us; and that we humans are a certain one of the possessions of the gods. Or does it not seem so to you? To me indeed, said Cebes. Is it not therefore, he said, that you also, if any of your slaves should perish themselves, when you had by no means signaled that you wished him to depart from life, would be angry with him? And if you had the power, would you not inflict some punishment? Entirely so, he said. Perhaps therefore in this way it is not contrary to reason that it is not fitting to kill oneself before God has imposed some necessity, such as he has imposed on us in the present. That indeed appears consistent, said Cebes. But what you were just saying, that philosophers easily wish to die, seems absurd, O Socrates, if indeed what we have now said has reason: namely, that God carries out the care of us, and we are his possession. For it has no reason that the most prudent men should not take it poorly to be moved away from that care which the gods, the best governors of all things, provide. For a prudent man would never think that he himself will care for himself better if he should escape free; but some mindless person would perhaps think this, namely that one should flee from a master; nor would he reflect that it is not that which is good that is to be fled, but rather one should remain in it as much as possible. And so he would flee without reason. But he who has a mind desires to be always with him who is better. And thus, O Socrates, the opposite of what was said a little before is more probable. For it is fitting for the wise to bear death heavily, and the foolish indeed gladly. Socrates, therefore, when he had heard these things, seemed to me to be delighted by the cleverness of Cebes. And turning to us, he said, This Cebes is always searching out certain reasons, nor does he want to admit very easily what anyone says. Then Simmias said, To me also Cebes seems to be saying something. For by what counsel would wise men flee those who are truly better than themselves, and easily allow themselves to be without them? And yet Cebes seems to me to aim his speech at you, because you so easily leave both us and the gods, who are, as you yourself confess, good princes. You say just things, said Socrates. For I think you say that I ought to clear myself as if in a judgment. And most especially indeed, said Simmias. Come then, he said. I will now attempt among you to defend myself more accurately than I did before the judges. Indeed, O Simmias and Cebes, unless I thought I was about to migrate, first indeed to other wise and good gods, then to men who have died, better than those who are here, I would act unjustly in not being troubled...

Cebes challenges this, questioning why a wise man would ever want to leave such good masters as the gods in this life.</summary>

<meta>This page follows the opening of the dialogue in the prison where Socrates has just finished explaining that while suicide is forbidden, a philosopher should nonetheless be prepared to follow a dying person. Here, he begins his "second apology"—a defense of his cheerfulness in the face of death.</meta>

# PHÆDO

<margin>A</margin>
Therefore, I am by no means distressed by death, as I would be if things were otherwise; rather, I am of good heart, and I hope that there is something remaining for those who have died, and as it has been said for a long time, it will be much better for the good than for the evil. Simmias said: What then, O Socrates? Do you intend to depart from here holding this opinion yourself, or will you leave us as partakers of it? For I think this good is a common one for us as well. Furthermore, you will only have cleared yourself before us if you persuade us of what you say.

<margin>B</margin>
I will certainly give it my effort, he said. But first, let us listen to Crito. For it seems to me he has wanted to say something for some time. Crito said: What else, O Socrates, than what the one who is to give you the poison <note>The "poison" refers to hemlock, the standard method of execution in Athens for citizens. The jailer is concerned that Socrates's talking will interfere with the drug's effectiveness.</note> has been telling me for a long time? Namely, he says you must be warned to speak as little as possible; for he says that those who engage in dispute become too warm, and nothing of that sort is suitable for those about to drink the poison. Otherwise, those who do such things are sometimes forced to drink the poison twice, or even three times. Then Socrates said: Let him be. Let him simply prepare his duty, as if he were to provide it twice, or even three times if it should be necessary. Crito replied: I almost knew that you would answer that way. But he has been bothering me for a long time. Socrates said: Let him be. But to you, my judges, I wish now to give an account of why it seems to me that a man who has devoted himself to philosophy throughout his whole life rightly expects death with great confidence, and is of good hope that he will obtain the greatest goods there after he has migrated from here. How this is so, O Simmias and Cebes, I will certainly try to reveal. Whoever handles philosophy rightly seems to have hidden from other men that they are practicing nothing other than dying and being dead. <note>The famous Platonic definition of philosophy as "meditatio mortis" or a "rehearsal for death."</note> If this is true, it would be quite absurd if, when they have studied nothing but this throughout their whole life, they should be distressed when this very thing arrives which they have so long meditated upon and practiced.

<margin>C</margin>
At this, Simmias said, smiling: By Jove, Socrates, you have forced a laugh from me, though I was not at all wishing to laugh. For I think there will be many who, if they heard this, would think it was aptly said against philosophers; and our own people would agree, and quite strongly too, that philosophers are indeed dying, and that they are not at all ignorant that these men are worthy to suffer this very thing.

<margin>D</margin>
Perhaps they would be speaking rightly, O Simmias, except for the part where they say they are "not ignorant." For it is hidden from them in what way true philosophers both study to die and are worthy of death. But now let us leave them and speak to ourselves. Do we think death is something? Certainly something, said Simmias. Is it anything else, he said, than the release of the soul from the body? And is this what it means to be dead: that the body, released from the soul, exists by itself apart? And that the soul, released from the body, exists by itself apart? Is death anything other than this? Nothing else, said Simmias. Consider,

<margin>E</margin>
my good man, if the same thing seems so to you as it does to me. For from these things I think we will more clearly understand what we are investigating. Does it seem to you to be the duty of a philosopher to pursue those which are called pleasures, such as those of feasts and drinks? Not at all, Socrates, he said. But what of the pleasures of Venus <note>original: "venereorum" / "ἀφροδισίων" — referring to sexual pleasures.</note>? In no way, he said. What of the remaining care of the body—does it seem to you that the philosopher magnifies it? Such as having exquisite clothes, shoes, and other ornaments belonging to the body; do you think he values them highly, or counts them as nothing, except insofar as a great necessity forces him to use them? It seems to me the true philosopher counts all these as nothing, said Simmias. Does it not seem to you, he said, that such a man's study is not directed toward the body, but as much as possible departs from it and turns toward the soul? It seems so to me, said Simmias.

<margin>F</margin>
Therefore, in such things, does it not first appear clearly that the philosopher, more than other men, separates the soul as much as possible from communion with the body? It appears so, he said. But most people think, O Simmias, that a man for whom none of these things is sweet, and who does not enjoy them, is not worthy of living; that he is nearly dead, since he does not care for the pleasures of the body. You speak the absolute truth, he said.

<margin>G</margin>
But what about the acquisition of wisdom itself? he said. Is the body an impediment if one takes it along as a companion in the investigation, or not? I mean something like this: Do sight and hearing possess any truth for men? Or is it as the poets are always singing to us, that we hear nothing and see nothing clearly? <note>Referring to the idea that human senses are deceptive and "noisy" compared to pure reason.</note> And yet if these bodily senses are not clear or certain, neither are the others; for all the others are somewhat inferior to these. Do they not seem so to you? Entirely, he said. When then, he asked, does the soul touch the truth? For when it attempts to investigate anything with the body, it is clearly deceived by the body. You speak truly, he said. Is it not in reasoning, if anywhere at all, that some of the things that truly exist become manifest to it? It is so, he said. And it reasons best when none of these things disturb it, neither hearing, nor sight, nor pain, nor any pleasure; but when, drawing itself into itself as much as possible, it leaves the body behind and, communicating with it as little as possible and not touching it, it reaches out for that which truly is. It is so, he said. Does not the soul of the philosopher, in this case, most despise the body and flee from it, seeking to live by itself? It appears so, he said. What about these things, Simmias? Do we say
