<summary>Socrates defines philosophy as the "practice of death," arguing that a true philosopher seeks to separate the soul from the distractions and deceptions of the body to attain pure wisdom. He defends his calm acceptance of his impending execution by explaining that death is merely the final separation of soul and body which he has practiced his entire life.</summary>

<keywords>Socrates, Simmias, Crito, immortality of the soul, separation of soul and body, philosophy as preparation for death, bodily pleasures, senses as deception, hemlock, Phædo</keywords>

--- Page 411 ---
<meta>This page continues Socrates's "second apology" to his friends Simmias and Crito. He is explaining why a true philosopher does not fear death, but rather welcomes it as the culmination of a life's work. This section introduces the core Platonic idea that the body is a distraction to the soul's pursuit of truth.</meta>

# PHÆDO

<margin>A</margin>
"What then shall we say about Justice itself? Is it something, or nothing?"
"It is certainly something, by Zeus <note>original: "νὴ Δία". The Latin column uses "per Iovem" (by Jove).</note>," he said.
"And what of Beauty and Goodness?"
"Of course."
"Now, have you ever seen any of these things with your eyes?"
"Never," he replied.
"Or have you grasped them with any other bodily sense? I am speaking of all such things: of Magnitude, Health, Strength, and in short, of the essence of all things—what each one truly is. Is the truest nature of these things perceived through the body? Or is it rather that whoever among us prepares himself to think most deeply and accurately about the particular object he is examining will come closest to knowing it?"
"Certainly."
<margin>B</margin>
"And would he not do this most purely who approaches each thing with the mind alone, as much as possible, neither involving sight in his thinking nor dragging in any other sense to accompany his reasoning? Rather, using pure thought by itself, he would attempt to hunt down each pure reality as it is, having rid himself as much as possible of eyes and ears and, so to speak, the whole body, on the grounds that it disturbs the soul and does not allow it to acquire truth and wisdom when they are joined. Is it not this man, Simmias, if anyone, who will attain to what truly exists?"
"What you say is wonderfully true, Socrates," said Simmias.
"Then," he said, "from all this, a certain opinion must necessarily occur to genuine philosophers, such that they say things like this to one another: <margin>C</margin> 'There is a sort of narrow path that leads us, along with reason, in our investigation. For as long as we possess the body, and our soul is contaminated by such an evil, we shall never sufficiently attain what we desire—and we say this is the truth.' For the body provides us with countless distractions because of the necessity of its nourishment. Moreover, if any diseases fall upon us, they hinder our hunt for reality. It fills us with loves, desires, fears, all sorts of phantoms, and much nonsense, <margin>D</margin> so that, as the saying goes, in truth it never allows us to think about anything at all. For wars, factions, and battles are caused by nothing other than the body and its desires. All wars are fought for the sake of acquiring wealth, and we are forced to acquire wealth because of the body, being enslaved to its service. Because of all these things, we have no leisure for philosophy. And the final blow of all is that even if we do get some leisure from it and turn to examine something, it breaks in everywhere in our investigations, causing tumult and confusion and stunning us, so that we are unable to perceive the truth because of it. But it has been truly shown to us that if we are ever going to know anything purely, we must be rid of the body and must view things themselves with the soul itself. And then, it seems, we shall have that which we desire and of which we say we are lovers—wisdom—namely, after we have died, as the <margin>E</margin> argument indicates, but not while we live. For if it is impossible to know anything purely in the company of the body, then one of two things must be: either knowledge is nowhere to be gained, or else it is for the dead. For then the soul will be alone by itself, separate from the body, but not before. And while we live, we shall be closest to knowledge, as it seems, if we consort with the body as little as possible and have no commerce with it (except for what is strictly necessary), and do not allow ourselves to be filled with its nature, but remain pure from it until God himself releases us. And thus being pure and rid of the folly of the body, we shall likely be with others like ourselves and shall know through ourselves all that is pure. This is perhaps the truth itself; <margin>F</margin> for it may not be lawful for the impure to touch the pure. Such things, I think, Simmias, all right-minded lovers of learning must say to one another and believe. Or does it not seem so to you?"
"Most certainly, Socrates."
"Then," said Socrates, "if this is true, my friend, there is great hope that for one arriving where I am going, there, if anywhere else, he will sufficiently possess that for which we have taken so much trouble in our past life. So the journey now commanded of me is undertaken with good hope—as it would be for any other man who believes his mind has been prepared, as if purified."
"Exactly so," said Simmias.
"And does not purification <note>The Greek term here is *catharsis*, a central concept in Greek philosophy and drama meaning a cleansing or purging.</note> consist in this, as has been said for a long time in our discourse: the separating of the soul as much as possible <margin>G</margin> from the body, and the habituating of it to gather and collect itself from every part of the body, and to dwell, as far as it can, both now and in the hereafter, alone by itself, released from the body as if from chains?"
"Certainly," he said.
"And is not this called 'death'—the release and separation of the soul from the body?"
"Entirely so," he said.
"And to release it, as we say, is always the chief and only endeavor of those who philosophize rightly; and the very study of philosophers is this: the release and separation of the soul from the body. Is it not?"
"So it appears."
"Then, as I said at the beginning, it would be ridiculous if a man, having prepared himself throughout his life to live as close to death as possible, <margin>H</margin> should then be distressed when death arrives. Would it not be ridiculous?"

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
Is justice itself something, or nothing? "Something, by Jove," he said.
Again, are the beautiful itself and the good itself something? "Why not?"
Have you ever perceived any of these with your eyes? "Never," he said.
Or have you touched those things with any other sense of the body? I speak of all things, such as magnitude itself, health, strength itself, and in summary, of the essence of all other things, that is, what each thing is. Is that which is most true in these things perceived through the body? Or is it that whoever of us prepares himself to think most greatly and accurately with his mind, <margin>B</margin> approaching the very thing that is to be thought, comes closest to the knowledge of it? "By all means."
Would he not then do this most purely, whoever applied himself as much as possible to each thing with thought itself, neither using sight in his thinking nor joining any other sense at all to his reasoning? But using pure thought by itself, he would study to hunt down as much as possible each pure thing that exists, free from eyes, from ears, and—to speak summarily—from the whole body, as it disturbs the soul and does not permit it to attain truth and wisdom whenever it is received into fellowship. Will it not be this man, O Simmias, if anyone else ever will, who attains what truly is? "You speak wonderfully, O Socrates," said Simmias.
"Does it not then necessarily follow from all these things," he said, "that such an opinion must be established among true philosophers, so that they say such things among themselves? We seem to be led by a certain path of reason itself to consider this: as long as we have a body, and our soul is mixed with such an evil, we shall never abundantly attain that which we desire. For the body provides almost innumerable impediments <margin>D</margin> on account of its necessary nourishment. Furthermore, diseases falling upon us from this source hinder the investigation of truth; it fills us with loves, desires, fears, and various images, and finally with many trifles, so that it is most truly said that we are never permitted by it to understand anything rightly. For nothing else but the body and its desires impel us to wars, to seditions, and to fights. For all wars happen for the sake of money. We are forced to seek money for the sake of the body, serving its care. And so it happens that because of all these things, we are abstracted from the study of philosophy. But the extreme of all is that if any leisure happens to us from it, and we apply ourselves to consider something, it again opposes us everywhere as we investigate, disturbing the mind with a certain tumult, and as if striking us, it renders us stunned, so that hindered by this obstacle, we cannot perceive the truth. But it has been demonstrated to us in reality that if we are ever to understand anything purely, we must withdraw from the body and consider the things themselves with the soul itself. And then, as it appears, we shall become possessors of that which we affect and of which we profess ourselves to be lovers, namely wisdom, when we are dead, as our discourse indicates; but while we live, by no means. For if nothing can be purely discerned with the body, one of two things: either we can never attain knowledge, or after death. For then the soul itself will be by itself apart from the body, but before that, by no means. And while we live, as it seems, we shall come closest <margin>F</margin> to knowledge if we have as little commerce as possible with the body, nor communicate anything with it except as much as the greatest necessity compels; nor shall we be filled with its nature, but we shall beware of its contagion until God himself releases us. And thus pure, and freed from the foolishness of the body, as is consistent, we shall be with such as these, and we shall know through ourselves whatever is pure, that is, perhaps, the truth itself. For it is a crime for the impure to touch the pure. Such things, O Simmias, I judge it necessary for all who are rightly desirous of learning to say to one another and to think. Or does it not seem so to you?"
"And most especially of all, O Socrates."
"If these things are true then, O friend," he said, "there is great hope that he who <margin>G</margin> arrives there where I am now going will, if anywhere else, abundantly attain that for the sake of which we have undertaken so much business in this present life. This migration, therefore, imposed on me at present, I undertake with good hope; and likewise anyone else will undertake it who only thinks that a mind has been prepared for him as if purified."
"Quite so," said Simmias.
"And purification," he said, "does it not consist in this which we were saying a while ago, namely that as much as we can, we separate the soul from the body and accustom it to be withdrawn and collected by itself from the contagion of the body on all sides, and so to dwell (as far as possible), both in the present time and in the future, alone by itself <margin>H</margin> as if released from the chains of the body?"
"Most certainly," he said.
"Is not this then called death: the release and separation of the soul from the body?"
"Entirely," he said.
"But to release it, as we confess, at all times, he who philosophizes rightly strives most of all and alone. And this very thing is the meditation of philosophers: to release and separate the soul from the body. Is it not?"
"So it seems."
"Would it not then be, as I was saying in the beginning, ridiculous if a man who has so prepared himself in life as to come as close as possible to death, should then live so that when it finally arrives, he is indignant? Would it not?"

<summary>In this pivotal passage, Socrates defines philosophy as the "practice of dying," arguing that the body is a constant distraction to the soul's search for truth and that true wisdom can only be attained when the soul is separated from the flesh.</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Simmias, Forms, Justice, Beauty, body and soul, purification, catharsis, philosophy as preparation for death, Plato</keywords>

--- Page 412 ---
<meta>This page continues Socrates’s discourse in the "Phaedo." Previously, he described the pursuit of truth as a "narrow path" where the soul must detach itself from the body. Here, he concludes his "apology" by explaining why death is the ultimate goal of the philosopher and how true virtue differs from common social morality.</meta>

# OF PLATO

<margin>A</margin> "Is it not ridiculous? Why not? In reality then," he said, "O Simmias, those who philosophize rightly are practicing for death, and they are the least of all men to be terrified by it. Consider it in this way: since they are everywhere at odds with the body and desire to have the soul itself by itself, would it not be the height of absurdity if, when this finally happens, they should be frightened and troubled? Would they not go there gladly, where upon arriving, there is hope of attaining what they loved in life (namely, wisdom), and of being liberated from that companion whose company troubled them? Indeed, many have been willing to go to the underworld of their own accord upon the death of boyfriends, wives, or children, hoping to see those they loved there and to be with them. Shall a true lover <margin>B</margin> of wisdom, then, who has been strongly moved by this same hope—that he will find it worthily nowhere else but in the underworld—be distressed at dying and not go there gladly? We must believe, my friend, that if he is truly a philosopher, this opinion will weigh heavily with him: that he can reach pure wisdom nowhere else but there. And if this is so, as I was just saying, would it not be altogether against reason if such a man should fear death?" "By Zeus," said Simmias, "it would be against reason." "Therefore," he said, "it will be a sufficient proof that if you see a man troubled that he is about to die, he was not a philosopher, but a <term>φιλοσώματον</term> <note>original: "philosomaton," a lover of the body</note>, and likely also a <term>φιλοχρήματον</term> <note>original: "philochrematon," a lover of money</note> and a <term>φιλότιμον</term> <note>original: "philotimon," a lover of honor</note>: either one of these or both." 

<margin>C</margin> "It is exactly as you say," he said. "Then, Simmias, does not what is called courage belong most of all to men of this disposition?" "Most certainly," he replied. "And temperance—which even the many call temperance, meaning the quality of not being fluttered by desires but holding them in contempt and remaining orderly—does this not belong only to those who most of all despise the body and live in philosophy?" "It must be so," he said. "For if you wish to consider the courage and temperance of others, it will seem quite absurd to you." "In what way, Socrates?" "You know," he said, "that everyone else considers death to be one of the greatest evils." "Very much so," he said. 

<margin>D</margin> "Therefore, is it not out of fear of greater evils that those among them who are 'brave' endure death, when they do endure it?" "That is true." "So, it is through fearing and by fear that all men except philosophers are brave; yet it is absurd for someone to be brave through fear or cowardice." "Certainly." "And what of those among them called 'orderly'? Are they not affected in a similar way, being temperate through a kind of intemperance? Though we say this is impossible, nevertheless an affection similar to this happens to them in that foolish temperance of theirs. For fearing to be deprived of other pleasures, and desiring them, they abstain from some because they are overcome by others. Yet they call it 'intemperance' to be ruled by pleasures; nevertheless, it happens to them that by being mastered by pleasures, they master other pleasures. Now, this is similar to what was just said: that in a way, they have become temperate through intemperance." "It seems so." "But, blessed Simmias, I suspect this <margin>E</margin> is not the right path toward virtue—to exchange pleasures for pleasures, pains for pains, and fear for fear, the greater for the lesser, as if they were coins. Rather, the only right coin for which all these things ought to be exchanged is wisdom <note>original: "prudentia" in Latin / "phronesis" in Greek</note>. For this, and with this, all things are truly bought and sold: courage, temperance, justice, and in short, true virtue exists with wisdom, whether pleasures and fears and all such things are present or absent. But when separated from wisdom and exchanged for one another, such virtue is a mere shadow-painting, truly slavish, possessing nothing healthy or true. The truth of virtue actually consists in the purification of all such things; and temperance, justice, courage, and wisdom itself are a kind of purification. Therefore, those who established the mysteries <note>The "mysteries" refer to religious initiation rites, like those at Eleusis or the Orphic traditions, which promised a better lot in the afterlife.</note> for us seem to be no mean people, but in reality have long been hinting that whoever arrives in the underworld unpurified and uninitiated will lie in the mud; but he who arrives there purified and initiated will dwell with the gods. <margin>F</margin> For as they say in the mysteries: 'Many are the thyrsus-bearers, but few are the Bacchants.' <note>A "thyrsus" was a ritual staff. The proverb means many people perform the outward rituals, but few truly achieve the divine state of the god Bacchus (Dionysus).</note> These 'Bacchants' are, in my opinion, none other than those who have philosophized rightly. To be numbered among them, I have left nothing undone in my life, so far as I was able, but have striven in every way. Whether I have striven rightly or achieved anything, we shall know for certain when we arrive there, if God wills, in a little while, as it seems to me."

<margin>G</margin> "This, then, Simmias and Cebes, is the defense I offer as to why, when I leave you and the masters here, I am right not to be distressed or indignant. For I hope that there, no less than here, I shall find good masters and friends. But the many find this hard to believe. If, then, my defense has been more persuasive to you than it was to the Athenian judges, it is well." When Socrates had said this, Cebes took up the word and said, "Socrates, the rest seems to me to be well said, but what you said about the soul provides much doubt <margin>H</margin> to men; they fear that when the soul is separated from the body, it may no longer exist anywhere, but may be corrupted and perish on the very day a man dies..."

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> "Ridiculous? How could it not be? In truth then," he said, "O Simmias, those who practice philosophy in the right way are training to die, and to be dead is least fearful to them of all men. Look at it from this: if they are in every way at enmity with the body, and desire to have the soul itself by itself, but when this happens they should be afraid and resentful, would it not be a great inconsistency if they did not go gladly to that place where there is hope of attaining what they loved throughout life? And they loved wisdom, and sought to be rid of that which they were at enmity with while it was with them. Or is it that while many, upon the death of human loves, wives, and sons, have been willing to go to Hades of their own accord, led by this <margin>B</margin> hope of seeing and being with those they desired; yet one who truly loves wisdom, and has taken up this same strong hope—that he will meet it nowhere else worth mentioning except in Hades—will he then be resentful at dying and not go there gladly? One must think so, my friend, if he is truly a philosopher. For he will be strongly of this opinion: that he will meet with pure wisdom nowhere else but there. If this is so, as I was just saying, would it not be a great inconsistency if such a man feared death?" "A great one, by Zeus," he said. "Then is this not a sufficient proof to you," he said, "of a man whom you see resentful when he is about to die, that he was not after all a philosopher, but some 'body-lover' (*philosomatos*)? And this same man is probably <margin>C</margin> a 'money-lover' (*philochrematos*) and an 'honor-lover' (*philotimos*); either one of these, or both." "It is entirely as you say," he replied. "Does not then, Simmias, that which is called courage especially belong to those so disposed?" "Certainly," he said. "And also temperance—that which the many call temperance, which consists in not being excited by desires but being indifferent and orderly—does this not belong to those alone who most of all disregard the body and live in philosophy?" "Necessarily," he said. "For if you are willing," he said, "to consider the courage and temperance of others, it will seem strange to you." "How so, Socrates?" "You know," he said, "that all others consider death to be among the greatest evils?" "Very much so," he said. "Then it is through fear of greater evils that the brave among them endure death, <margin>D</margin> whenever they endure it?" "That is so." "Therefore, all are brave through fearing and fear, except for philosophers. And yet it is strange for someone to be brave through fear and cowardice." "It certainly is." "And what of the orderly among them? Have they not experienced the same thing? They are temperate because of a certain intemperance. Although we say this is impossible, nevertheless this affection happens to them in that simple-minded temperance. For fearing to be deprived of other pleasures, and desiring them, they abstain from some because they are mastered by others. And yet they call being ruled by pleasures 'intemperance'; but it happens to them to be mastered by pleasures while mastering other pleasures. This is similar to what was just said: that in a way, they have been made temperate through intemperance." <margin>E</margin> "So it seems." "O blessed Simmias, I suspect this is not the right exchange for virtue—to trade pleasures for pleasures, and pains for pains, and fear for fear, and the greater for the smaller, like coins. Rather, that alone is the right coin for which all these things must be exchanged: wisdom (*phronesis*). For this, and with this, all things are truly bought and sold: courage, and temperance, and justice; and in short, true virtue is with wisdom, whether pleasures and fears and all other such things are added or taken away. But when separated from wisdom and exchanged for one another, such virtue is a mere shadow-painting, and is in truth slavish, and has nothing <margin>F</margin> healthy or true about it. But the truth is really a purification from all such things, and temperance and justice and courage and wisdom itself are a kind of purification. And it seems that those who established the rites of initiation for us were no ordinary people, but were in truth long ago riddling that whoever arrives in Hades uninitiated and unperfected will lie in the mire; but he who has been purified and initiated, upon arriving there, will dwell with the gods. For as those concerned with the rites say: 'Many are the thyrsus-bearers, but few are the Bacchants.' And these are, in my opinion, none other than those who have practiced philosophy rightly. Among whom I have left nothing undone in my life, so far as I was able, <margin>G</margin> but have been eager in every way to become one of them. Whether I was rightly eager, and whether we achieved anything, we shall know clearly when we go there, if God wills, a little later, as it seems to me. This then," he said, "Simmias and Cebes, is the defense I offer: that in leaving you and my masters here, I am right not to take it hardly or be resentful, believing that there, no less than here, I shall meet with good masters and companions. But to the many this is a cause for disbelief. If then I am more persuasive to you in my defense than I was to the Athenian judges, it would be well." When Socrates had said these things, Cebes took up the argument and said, "O Socrates, the rest seems to me to be well said, but the things concerning the soul provide much disbelief to <margin>H</margin> men; they fear that when it is released from the body, it may no longer be anywhere, but may be destroyed and perish on that day when a man dies..."

<summary>Socrates argues that death is the goal of philosophy because it frees the soul to find pure wisdom. He contrasts the "slavish" virtue of the masses, based on trading fears and pleasures, with the "true coin" of wisdom-based virtue, and addresses the initiation mysteries.</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Simmias, Cebes, afterlife, soul, body, philosophy, courage, temperance, wisdom, purification, Bacchic mysteries, thyrsus-bearers</keywords>

--- Page 413 ---
<meta>This page follows Socrates’s explanation that a philosopher should not fear death. Here, Cebes introduces the primary counter-argument: the fear that the soul simply vanishes like smoke upon leaving the body. In response, Socrates begins his first formal proof for the immortality of the soul, known as the "Argument from Opposites."</meta>

# PHAEDO. 381

<margin>A</margin> "But," [said Cebes], "it is feared that when the soul is separated from the body, it may be dissolved and, upon departing, be scattered like a breath or smoke <note>The Greek uses 'pneuma' (breath/spirit) and 'kapnos' (smoke), reflecting a common ancient fear that the soul is a fragile, physical vapor.</note> and vanish, and no longer exist anywhere at all. Indeed, if it were to exist somewhere, gathered together within itself and liberated from those evils you have just described, there would be a great and noble hope, Socrates, that what you say is true. But this perhaps requires no small amount of persuasion and faith: to believe that the soul of a man exists after he has died, and that it possesses some power and intelligence." "You speak the truth, Cebes," said Socrates. "But what should we do? Do you wish for us to discourse <note>original: "diamythologōmen," meaning to discuss by telling stories or arguments.</note> upon these very matters, to see whether it is likely to be so or not?" "For my part," said Cebes, "I would gladly hear what opinion you hold about them." <margin>B</margin> "I do not think," said Socrates, "that anyone hearing us now, even if he were a comic poet, would say that I am babbling or talking about things that do not concern me. If it pleases you, then, we must look into it; let us consider it in this way: whether the souls of men who have died are in the underworld <note>original: "en Aidou," in the house of Hades.</note> or not. There is an ancient tradition <note>This likely refers to Orphic or Pythagorean teachings on reincarnation.</note> that we remember, which says that souls go from here to that place, and return here again, and are born from the dead. And if this is so—that the living are born again from the dead—what else could it be but that our souls are there? For they could not be born again if they did not exist. And this is a sufficient proof that these things are so, if it really becomes <margin>C</margin> clear that the living are born from nowhere else but from the dead. But if this is not the case, we would need another argument." "Quite so," said Cebes. "Now," said Socrates, "do not consider this only in relation to humans if you wish to understand it more easily, but in relation to all animals and plants, and in short, let us look at everything that has a birth. Let us see if all things are born in this way: opposites from opposites, and nowhere else, in all things that happen to have an opposite. For instance, the beautiful is the opposite of the ugly, and the just is the opposite of the unjust, and there are countless other such examples. Let us consider whether it is necessary that for anything that has an opposite, it must be born from nowhere else but from its own opposite. For example, when something becomes larger, is it not necessary that it was smaller before it became larger?" "Yes." "And if it becomes smaller, was it not larger before, and afterwards it became smaller?" "That is so," he said. <margin>D</margin> "And surely the weaker comes from the stronger, and the swifter from the slower?" "Certainly." "What then? If something becomes worse, does it not come from the better? And if more just, from the more unjust?" "How could it be otherwise?" "We have, then," he said, "sufficiently established this: that all things are born in this way, namely opposites from opposites." "Certainly." "What then? Is there something similar in them, such as a middle ground between both of any two opposites: two generations <note>original: "geneseis," processes of becoming or origins.</note>, one from the first to the second, and another from the second back to the first? Between a larger and a smaller thing, there is the middle ground of growth and decay; and so we call one 'to increase' and the other 'to decrease'." "Yes," he said. "And similarly, are there not processes such as being separated and being combined, or growing cold and <margin>E</margin> growing warm, and all things in the same way? Even if we do not use the names in every case, must it not in reality be so everywhere: that they are born from one another, and that there is a process of birth from each into the other?" "Certainly," he said. "What then?" said Socrates. "Is there something opposite to living, just as sleeping is the opposite of waking?" "Certainly," he said. "What is it?" "Being dead," he said. "Do these not then come from one another, since they are opposites, and since there are two processes of birth between them?" "How could it not be so?" "The one pair," said Socrates, "I will describe to you, both the state and the processes; you tell me the other. I say that one is sleeping and the other is waking; and from sleeping, waking is born, and from waking, sleeping is born. And their processes are, in the one case, falling asleep, and in the other, waking up. Is that sufficient for you, or not?" "Quite sufficient." "Now," he said, "you tell me in the same way about life and death. Do you not say that being dead is the opposite of living?" "I do." "And that they are born from one another?" "Yes." "What, then, is born from the living?" "The dead," he said. "And what," he asked, "is born from the dead?" "I must confess," he said, "that it is the living." "From the dead, then, O Cebes, living things and living men are born?" "It appears so," he said. "Therefore, our souls exist in the underworld." "It seems so." "Now, of these two processes, is not one of them clearly visible? For dying is surely clear, is it not?" "Certainly," he said. "What then shall we do?" he asked. "Shall we not provide the opposite process in return, or is nature to be lopsided in this respect? Or is it necessary to provide a process of birth opposite to dying?" "By all means," he said. "What is that process?" "Coming back to life <note>original: "anabiōskesthai," to return to life or be reborn.</note>." "Therefore," he said, "if there is such a thing as coming back to life, would this not be a birth from the dead into the living?" "Certainly." "It is agreed by us, then, in this way too, that the living are born from the dead no less than the dead from the living. And since this is so, it seems to be sufficient proof that the souls of the dead must necessarily exist somewhere, from whence they are born again." "It seems to me, Socrates," he said, "that this necessarily follows from what has been conceded." "Observe then, Cebes," he said, "that we have not conceded these things without reason, as it seems to me. For if the one set of things were not always returned in place of the others, as if traveling in a circle, but if birth were a straight line from one thing into its opposite only, and did not turn back again to the other, nor bend back—"

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> and immediately separated from the body it might be dissolved, and going out like wind or smoke might be dissipated and vanish, and no longer exist at all. Truly, if it were gathered together somewhere within itself, and liberated from those evils which you just related, there would be great and good hope, O Socrates, that what you were saying would come to pass. But for this, perhaps, no small amount of persuasion and faith is needed, so that it might be believed that the soul survives after the death of the man, and that it possesses some power and intelligence. "You speak the truth, O Cebes," said Socrates. "But what do you think should be done? Should we perhaps <margin>B</margin> converse about these very things, whether it is probable that it is so, or otherwise?" "I would certainly," said Cebes, "gladly hear what you think about these matters." "I do not think," said Socrates, "that anyone hearing this, even if he were a comic actor, would say that I am talking nonsense now, or speaking of things that are not fitting. If it pleases you, then, and if we ought to consider it, let us consider it in this way: whether indeed the souls of the dead are in the underworld or not. There exists an ancient saying, which we remember, that souls exist which have gone from here to that place, and return here again, and are made from the dead. And if this is true, that from the dead living people are made again, our souls must be there. For they would not be made again if they did not exist. And this is a sufficient conjecture <note>In the Latin column, 'coniectura' (conjecture/inference) is used to translate the Greek 'tekmērion' (proof/evidence).</note> that it is so, if it truly stands <margin>C</margin> that the living are made from nowhere else than from the dead. But if that is not so, another argument will be needed." "Entirely so," said Cebes. "Nor should you consider this only in men," he said, "if you wish to understand more clearly, but in all animals, and plants, and to speak briefly, in all things that are born, whether all things are made thus: namely, opposites from opposites, in whatever things such a thing occurs. Just as the beautiful is in a certain way the opposite of the ugly, and the just of the unjust, and we see many other such things. Let us consider whether it is necessary for whatever has an opposite, that it is made from nowhere else than from its own opposite? Just as when something is made larger, it is necessary that from that which was previously smaller, it afterwards becomes larger." "It is so." "And if something becomes smaller, will it not become smaller from that which was previously larger?" "Entirely so." "Furthermore, from the stronger comes the weaker, and from the slower <margin>D</margin> the swifter?" "Certainly." "What indeed? If something turns out worse, is it not from the better? And if more just, from the more unjust?" "Why not?" "In all things, therefore, we have sufficiently explored this: that all things are made thus, namely opposites from opposites." "Certainly." "What again? Is there also something of this sort in them, between two opposites? Namely, two generations between them, or progressions from one into the other, and into the other in turn from the first? For between larger and smaller, the middle ground is held by increase and decrease; and we say this one grows, but that one decreases." "So it is," he said. "And similarly, is it not in turn to be separated and to be mixed, to grow cold and <margin>E</margin> to grow warm, and all things in the same way? And even if names are lacking to us in some places, yet in reality itself it is necessary everywhere that all things are made from opposites in turn, and that there is a generation of each in turn into the other?" "Certainly," he said. "What indeed? To that which is 'to live,' is there something opposite? Just as to that which is 'to be awake,' 'to sleep' is the opposite?" "It is entirely so," he said. "What is it?" "To die," he said. "Do these not happen from one another? Since they are opposites. And since they are two, are there also two mutual generations between them?" "Nothing prevents it." "One pairing of them, which I was just mentioning, I will tell you," (said Socrates) "both the state itself and their generations. But you shall reveal the other to me. Now I say, that one is to sleep, the other to wake; and from sleep, waking is made, and from waking, sleep; and the generations of these are, the one to fall asleep, the other to wake up. Have I done enough or not?" "You have certainly satisfied me." "Tell me likewise about life and death. Do you not say that to live and to die are opposites?" "I do." "And that they are made from one another?" "Yes." "Therefore, from the living, what is made?" "The dead." "And what from the dead?" "It is necessary to confess: the living." "Therefore from the dead, O Cebes, living things and living people are made." "It appears so." "Are our souls, therefore, in the underworld?" "It seems so." "Is not, then, one of the generations concerning these things manifest? For to die is manifest, is it not?" "So it is indeed." "What then shall we do? Shall we not return a generation opposite to this in turn, but say that in this matter alone nature is maimed? Or is it truly necessary to return to that which is 'to die' a certain opposite generation?" "Certainly." "What is that one?" "To return to life <note>original: 'Reuiuiſcere' (reviviscere), the Latin equivalent of 'anabiōskesthai.'</note>." "Is it not therefore true that if there is a returning to life, this is a certain progression from the dead to the living?" "It is so." "It is agreed by us, therefore, by this further reason, that the living are made from the dead no less than the dead from the living. Which being so, a sufficient conjecture is held from this, that the souls of the dead necessarily exist somewhere, from whence they may return again." "It seems to me, O Socrates, that this necessarily follows from those things which were granted." "Observe then," he said, "O Cebes, that we have not granted these things without cause, as I think. For unless some things were continually returned for others in turn, as if returning in a circle, but there were a certain direct progression only from one into its opposite, and it did not reflect back...

<summary>Socrates introduces the Argument from Opposites, positing that since life and death are a pair of opposites, they must generate one another in a cyclic process, implying that the souls of the dead must exist in the underworld before being reborn.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the "Argument from Opposites," where Socrates posits that if life and death did not cycle into one another, the universe would eventually "run down" into a single state of death. Following this, Cebes introduces the "Theory of Recollection" (Anamnesis) as further proof of the soul's pre-existence.</meta>

...would turn back into the other, making a return, then all things—believe me—would eventually take on the same form and condition, and would cease to be created. "How do you mean that?" he asked. "It is not at all difficult to understand what I am saying," he replied. "For just as if one were to fall asleep, but never woke up again to be vigilant, you surely realize that all things would eventually come to such a point that the story of **Endymion** <note>In Greek mythology, Endymion was a youth granted eternal sleep by Zeus. Socrates uses him here to represent a universe where everything is 'asleep' or dead.</note> would seem like a silly tale, and he would appear nowhere, since all other things would likewise be overwhelmed by sleep. Furthermore, if all things were mixed together and <margin>B</margin> never separated, that famous saying of **Anaxagoras** <note>original: "Anaxagorae illud"; Anaxagoras was a philosopher who taught that originally "all things were together" in a chaotic mixture before Mind set them in order.</note> would suddenly come true: namely, that 'all things were together.' In the same way, my dear friend Cebes, if all things that have received life were to die, and having died, remained in that state of death and did not live again, is it not absolutely necessary that everything would eventually be destroyed and nothing would live? For if living things were created from other sources, but then died, what would prevent everything from being consumed by death?" "Nothing at all, Socrates," said Cebes, "it seems to me you speak the absolute truth." "It is certainly so, Cebes," he said, "as much as anything can be, in my opinion; and we have not admitted these things as if we were deceived, but in reality there is such a thing as returning to life, and the living are produced from the dead, and the souls of the dead exist. <margin>C</margin> And indeed, it is better for the good, and worse for the evil." "And," Cebes interrupted, "according to that argument, Socrates, which you are so fond of using—if it is indeed true—that our learning is nothing other than **recollection** <note>original: "reminiscentia"; the Greek term is 'anamnesis'. This is the theory that we do not learn new things, but rather remember truths our souls knew before birth.</note>: according to this, I say, it is necessary that we learned in some previous time those things which we now remember. But that would be impossible unless our soul had been somewhere before it came into this human form. Therefore, by this reasoning also, the soul seems to be something immortal." "But what are the proofs of this, <margin>D</margin> Cebes?" asked **Simmias**. "Bring them back to my memory, for I do not remember them well at present." "One argument is the most beautiful," said Cebes, "which is that when men are questioned—if one questions them rightly—they themselves answer everything just as it is. Yet they could never do this unless knowledge and right reason were already within them. Then, if one directs them to geometric figures and diagrams, or something similar, there he clearly discovers that this is the case." <note>This likely refers to Socrates's experiment in the 'Meno', where he guides a slave boy to solve a geometry problem to prove innate knowledge.</note> "If this reasoning, Simmias, does not satisfy you," said Socrates, "see if considering it in this way brings you to the same conclusion as us. For you are skeptical that what they call 'learning' can be recollection." "I am not exactly skeptical," said Simmias, "but I need to do the very thing we are talking about: to remember. <margin>E</margin> And indeed, from what Cebes has begun to say, I already remember and am persuaded. Nevertheless, I would very gladly hear from you the reasoning by which you were just now attempting to prove it yourself." "By this reasoning," said Socrates, "we surely agree in a way that if someone remembers something, he must have known it at some time before." "Quite so," he said. "Do we then also agree on this," he asked, "that whenever knowledge comes about in this manner, it is recollection? I mean it in this way: if someone, having seen or heard something, or perceived it by another sense, not only knows that thing but also recognizes something else, of which the knowledge is not the same but different, would we not rightly say that he remembers the thing which came into his mind?" "How do you mean that?" asked Simmias. <margin>F</margin> "This," said Socrates: "The knowledge of a man is one thing, and the knowledge of a **lyre** <note>A stringed musical instrument, common in ancient Greece.</note> is another." "Of course," said Simmias. "Do you not know, then, that this happens to lovers: when they see a lyre, or a garment, or anything else which their beloved boys were accustomed to use? For they recognize the lyre, and at the same time, they form in their mind the image of the boy to whom the lyre belonged. This is indeed recollection. Just as if someone sees Simmias often, he might be reminded of Cebes, and infinite other examples of the same kind." "Infinite, by Jove!" said Simmias. "Is it not, then," he asked, "a kind of recording or memory? Especially when it happens to us concerning things which, through length of time and neglect, we have already surrendered to oblivion?" "Certainly," said Simmias. <margin>G</margin> "What then?" asked Socrates. "Does it happen that one who sees a painted horse, or a painted lyre, remembers a man? And when he looks at a painting of Simmias, does Cebes come to his mind?" "Yes, indeed," he said. "Does it not even happen that he who looks at a painting of Simmias remembers Simmias himself?" "It certainly happens." "Does it not follow from all this that recollection arises sometimes from similar things and sometimes from dissimilar things?" "It does." "But whenever someone remembers something from similar things, is it not necessary to also notice whether this likeness falls short in any way, or not, from that of which the memory was revived?" "It is necessary." <margin>H</margin> "Consider then," he said, "if these things be so: we say there is such a thing as **Equality**. I do not mean one piece of wood being equal to another piece of wood, nor one stone to another stone, nor any other such thing, but beyond all these, we say that 'Equality itself' is something. Shall we say it is something, or nothing?" "We say so, by Jove," said Simmias, "and wonderfully so!" "And do we know what this Equality itself is?" "Certainly," he said. "From where did we receive the knowledge of it? Is it not from those things we just mentioned—namely, seeing woods, or stones, or other equal things—that from these we conceived that 'Equality' which is something other than them? Does it not seem to you to be something else? Consider it in this way: do not equal stones or woods, while remaining the same, sometimes appear equal to us, and sometimes unequal?"

<margin>A</margin> ...again back to the other, nor made a turn: you know that all things would finally have the same form, and suffer the same fate, and cease being born. "How do you say?" he asked. "It is not difficult (he said) to understand what I mean; just as if there were falling asleep, but waking up did not follow in turn, being produced from the sleeper—you know that in the end all things would make Endymion look like a trifle, and he would appear nowhere, because all other things would have suffered the same thing as him: sleep. And if all things were mixed together, but not separated, the condition described by Anaxagoras would quickly happen: 'all things together.' <margin>B</margin> In the same way, dear Cebes, even if all things that share in life were to die, and when they died, the dead remained in that form and did not live again—is there not a great necessity that in the end everything would be dead and nothing would live? For if living things were produced from other things, and the living died, what device could prevent all things from being consumed into being dead?" "Not a single one, it seems to me, Socrates," said Cebes; "rather, you seem to me to speak the absolute truth." "For it is (he said), O Cebes, as it seems to me, most of all so; and we do not agree on these very things while being deceived; but in reality there is both coming back to life, and the living being produced from the dead, and the souls of the dead existing; and for the good ones it is better, <margin>C</margin> and for the bad, worse." "And indeed (Cebes interrupted), also according to that argument, Socrates—if it is true—which you are accustomed to say frequently, that our learning happens to be nothing other than recollection, then according to this, we must have learned in some former time those things we now remember. And this is impossible unless our soul was somewhere before being born in this human form. So in this way too, the soul seems to be something immortal." "But, Cebes (Simmias interrupted), what are the proofs of these things? Remind me; for I do not remember very well at the moment." <margin>D</margin> "In one argument (said Cebes), and a most beautiful one: that when people are questioned, if someone questions them well, they themselves say everything as it is. Yet if there did not happen to be knowledge and right reason within them, they would not be able to do this. Then, if one brings them to diagrams or anything of that sort, there it shows most clearly that this is so." "But if you are not persuaded by this way, Simmias," said Socrates, "see if it seems so to you when considering it in this way. For you doubt how so-called 'learning' is recollection?" "I do not doubt it myself (said Simmias), but I need to do this very thing (he said) that the argument is about: to be reminded. And almost from what Cebes attempted to say, I already remember and am persuaded. None the less, I would hear now in what way you attempted to say it." <margin>E</margin> "In this way (he said). For we agree, I suppose, that if someone is to remember anything, he must have known it at some previous time." "Certainly (he said)." "Do we then also agree on this, that when knowledge comes in such a way, it is recollection? I mean a way like this: if someone, having seen or heard or received some other sensation of a thing, not only knows that, but also thinks of another thing of which the knowledge is not the same, but different. Do we not rightly say of this that he remembered that of which he got the thought?" "How do you mean?" "Examples like these: Surely the knowledge of a man and a lyre are different?" "How could they not be?" "Then you know that lovers, when they see a lyre or a cloak or anything else their beloveds are accustomed to use, experience this: they recognize the lyre and they take into their mind the form of the boy to whom the lyre belonged? And this is recollection. Just as someone seeing Simmias often remembers Cebes, and there are surely ten thousand other such things." <margin>F</margin> "Ten thousand indeed, by Jove!" said Simmias. "Is not then (he said) such a thing a kind of recollection? Especially when one experiences this concerning those things which, because of time and not looking at them, one had already forgotten?" "Very much so (he said)." "What then? (he said) Is it possible, upon seeing a horse in a picture or a lyre in a picture, to be reminded of a man?" "Certainly." "And seeing Simmias in a picture, to be reminded of Simmias himself?" "It is indeed (he said)." "Does it not then happen according to all these that recollection occurs, sometimes from similar things, and sometimes from dissimilar things?" "It happens." <margin>G</margin> "But when someone is reminded from similar things, is it not necessary to also experience this: to consider whether this falls short at all in its similarity, or not, from that which he remembered?" "It is necessary (he said)." "Consider then (he said) if these things are so. We say, I suppose, that there is something 'equal'; I do not mean a log to a log, nor a stone to a stone, nor any other such thing; but besides all these, something else: Equality itself. Shall we say it is something, or nothing?" "We shall say so, by Jove (said Simmias), most remarkably." "And do we know what it is?" "Certainly (he said)." "From where did we get the knowledge of it? Was it not from what we were just saying: seeing logs or stones or other equal things, from these we thought of that, though it is different from them? Or does it not seem different to you? <margin>H</margin> Consider it also in this way. Do not equal stones and logs, though being the same things, sometimes appear equal to one man..."

<meta>This page transitions from the general argument about the cycle of opposites (life and death) to the specific "Theory of Recollection." Socrates is now demonstrating that the soul must have existed before birth because we possess concepts—like "Equality"—that we could not have learned solely through the imperfect physical world.</meta>

# PHAEDO

<margin>A</margin> "...seem equal, or not?" "Quite so," he replied. "But what of this? Has the 'Equal itself' <note>Socrates refers to the "Form" or ideal concept of Equality, which is perfect, unlike physical objects.</note> ever appeared unequal to you, or has 'Equality' ever seemed to be 'Inequality'?" "Never, Socrates." "Then these equal things," he said, "are not the same as the Equal itself." "Not at all, in my view, Socrates." "Yet," he said, "is it not from these equal things—which are distinct from that 'Equal itself'—that you have conceived and grasped the knowledge of it?" "You speak most truly," he said. "And this is so whether it is similar to them or dissimilar?" "Certainly." "It makes no difference," he said. "As long as you see one thing and, from that sight, you contemplate another—whether similar or dissimilar—that process must necessarily be 'recollection' <note>original: "anamnesis"; the Platonic theory that all learning is actually the soul recovering knowledge it possessed before birth.</note>." "Very much so." "Now, what about this?" he asked. "Do we experience something like this regarding the pieces of wood and the equal things we were <margin>B</margin> just mentioning? Do they seem to us to be 'equal' in the same way as the 'Equal itself' is? Or do they fall short of being like the Equal, or not?" "They fall short by a great deal," he said. "Then do we agree that when someone sees a thing and thinks, 'This thing I see aims to be like some other reality, but it falls short and cannot be such as that, being instead inferior'—do we agree that the person thinking this must necessarily have prior knowledge of that which he says the object resembles but fails to match?" "Necessarily." "Well then, have we experienced <margin>C</margin> this same thing regarding equal things and the 'Equal itself'?" "Absolutely." "Therefore, we must have had knowledge of the 'Equal' before that time when we first saw equal things and realized that they all strive to be like the 'Equal,' but fall short of it." "That is so." "And we also agree on this: that we have not grasped this concept, nor is it possible to grasp it, except through sight or touch or some other sense. I treat all these senses as the same." "They are the same, Socrates, for the purpose of what our argument wants to prove." "But surely it is from the senses that we must realize that all things in the sensory world strive for that 'Equal' and yet are inferior to it. Or how do we put it?" "Just so. For before we began to see or hear or use our other senses, we must have <margin>D</margin> possessed knowledge of what the 'Equal itself' is, if we were going to refer the 'equals' from our senses to that standard—judging that they all eagerly desire to be such as it is, but are inferior to it." "This follows necessarily from what was said before, Socrates." "And did we not see and hear and exercise our other senses immediately upon being born?" "Certainly." "But we say we must have acquired the knowledge of the 'Equal' before these senses?" "Yes." "Therefore, it seems we must have acquired it before we were born." "So it seems." "Now, if we acquired <margin>E</margin> it before birth and were born possessing it, then we knew both before we were born and as soon as we were born—not only the 'Equal,' the 'Greater,' and the 'Smaller,' but all such things? For our argument now is not just about the 'Equal,' but also about the 'Beautiful itself,' the 'Good itself,' the 'Just,' the 'Holy,' and, as I say, about all those things which we mark with the seal of 'what it is' <note>This refers to the "Essence" or "Form" of a thing—its true, unchanging definition.</note> both in our questions and our answers. So it is necessary that we acquired knowledge of all these before birth." "That is so." "And if, having acquired these knowledges, we did not forget them each time, we would always be born knowing them and would know them throughout our lives. For to 'know' is <margin>F</margin> this: to keep a knowledge one has received and not to have lost it. Or do we not call the loss of knowledge 'forgetting'?" "By all means, Socrates," he said. "But if, I suppose, we lost at birth what we acquired before birth, and later, by using our senses on these things, we recover those knowledges we once held, would not what we call 'learning' be the recovery of our own knowledge? And would we not be right to call this 'recollection'?" "Rightly so." "For it has become <margin>G</margin> apparent that it is possible for someone, upon perceiving something—by seeing, hearing, or some other sense—to think of something else which he had forgotten, to which this object was related, whether it be dissimilar or similar. So, as I said, one of two things must be true: either we were born knowing them and we all know them throughout life, or those whom we say 'learn' are simply recollecting, and learning would be recollection." "That is exactly how it is, Socrates." "Which then do you choose, Simmias? That we are born with knowledge, or that we recollect later what we previously knew?" "I cannot choose at this moment, Socrates." "What about this? Can you choose, and what is your opinion on it: can a man <margin>G</margin> who knows a subject give an account <note>original: "logon"; a rational explanation or definition.</note> of what he knows, or not?" "He must be able to, Socrates." "And do you think everyone is able to give an account of these things we were just discussing?" "I wish they could," said Simmias, "but I fear much more that by this time tomorrow, there will be no one left alive <note>A somber reference to Socrates' impending execution the following day.</note> who is capable of doing so worthily." "Then you do not think, Simmias, that everyone knows these things?" "In no way." "Then they are recollecting what they once learned?" "It must be so." "When did our souls acquire this knowledge? Surely not since we became human beings." "Certainly not." "Before that, then?" "Yes." "Therefore, Simmias, souls existed before they were in human form, <margin>H</margin> apart from bodies, and they possessed intelligence." "Unless, Socrates, we acquire these knowledges at the very moment of birth; for that time is still left as an option."

<margin>A</margin> ...apparent? Absolutely. What about equal things themselves? Can they appear unequal to you, or can Equality itself appear to be Inequality? Never, O *Socrates*. Therefore, these equal things are not the same as the "Equal itself." In no way do they appear the same to me, O *Socrates*. Nevertheless, from these equal things, which are different from that "Equal itself," you have simultaneously contemplated and perceived the knowledge of it. You speak very truly. Whether it be similar to them or dissimilar? Entirely so. It certainly makes no difference; for as long as you have looked at one thing and, from this very sight, understood another—whether similar or dissimilar—it is necessary that recollection proceeds from this. And most especially. What then of this? Does it happen to us in this way regarding those things <margin>B</margin> we just spoke of, like pieces of wood and other things? Do these seem to be equal in the same way as the thing which is "Equal itself"? Or is there something lacking so that they are not such as the "Equal itself" is, or is there nothing lacking? Certainly, a great deal is lacking. Do we not confess that whenever someone, looking at a thing, perceives that this thing which he sees in the present desires to be such as something else among the things that are, but falls short and cannot be equal in the same way as that other thing, but is inferior—is it not necessary that he who perceives this must have previously known that thing which he says this object resembles in some way, though it does not reach full similarity? It is necessary. What then? Does something <margin>C</margin> like this happen to us or not, regarding equal things and the "Equal itself"? Very much so. It is necessary, therefore, that we possessed the knowledge of the "Equal itself" before that time in which, first seeing equal things, we recognized that all these things desire to be such as it is, yet fall short of its perfection. It is so. And yet we also confess this: that we have not recognized it from anywhere else, nor can we recognize it, except from sight, or touch, or some other sense. For I judge similarly of all these. Similarly, O *Socrates*, they serve to show the point at issue. And yet from the senses one must have understood that all things subject to the senses desire that "Equal," although they do not attain it. Or do we say otherwise? Not otherwise. For before we began to see, or hear, or use our other senses, it was necessary for us <margin>D</margin> to have possessed the knowledge of the "Equal itself"—specifically, what it is—if indeed we were going to refer these equal things which are subject to the senses back to it, judging that all these things strive to be such as it is, but are left behind as inferior. Necessarily, O *Socrates*, this follows from what was said before. Did we not, he said, see and hear and exercise our other senses immediately upon being born? Entirely so. But it was necessary, as we said, to have had the knowledge of the "Equal itself" before these. It was necessary. For which reason, as it seems, it is necessary that we grasped it before we were born. So it <margin>E</margin> appears. Is it not true that if, having obtained it before birth, we were born already possessing it, then we knew it both before birth and immediately upon being born—not only the "Equal itself," the greater and the lesser, but also all things of that same kind? For our discourse is not more about the "Equal" now than it is about the "Beautiful itself," the "Good itself," the "Just," and the "Holy," and as I say, about all those things to which we properly assign this "what it is" <note>Referring to the Form or Essence.</note>, both when asking questions and when giving answers; so that it is necessary for us to have had knowledge of all these before we were born. It is so. And if, after receiving these knowledges, we did not always forget them, it would be necessary to be born with them and to always know them throughout our entire life. For to know is <margin>F</margin> to retain the received knowledge of a thing and not to have lost it. Or do we not say that forgetting is the loss of knowledge? Exactly so, O *Socrates*. But if, having received knowledge before birth, we lost it while being born, and then later, by using our senses regarding those very knowledges, we receive back those which we had before: would not that which we call "learning" be the recovery of our own knowledge? And by naming this "Recollection," would we not be naming it correctly? Correct. For it appeared that this could happen: namely, that when someone has perceived something, either by seeing, or hearing, or perceiving in another way, he recognizes from this something else which he had forgotten, to which this thing in some way <margin>G</margin> was close, whether it be similar or dissimilar. Thus, as I have been saying for a while, one of two things is true: either we were born knowing them and we all know them through our whole life, or those who we then say are "learning" are only recollecting, and discipline is recollection. The matter stands entirely so, O *Socrates*. Which therefore do you choose, O *Simmias*? That we were born with knowledge, or that we recollect afterward those things of which we previously received knowledge? I am uncertain, *Socrates*, which I should choose at present. But what? Can you choose what seems right to you about this? Can a man who knows give an account of the things he knows, or the opposite? It is necessary, O *Socrates*, that he be able to. But do all people seem to you to be able to bring forward an account of those things we were just <margin>H</margin> treating? I would indeed wish it, said *Simmias*, but I fear much more that tomorrow there will be no man here who is able to do so with the proper dignity. You do not think then, O *Simmias*, that everyone understands this? In no way. They recollect then what they had once learned. It is necessary. But when did our souls receive this knowledge? Surely not after we were born as men. Certainly not. Therefore before. Yes. Souls existed, therefore, *Simmias*, even before they came into human form, separate from the body; and they possessed intelligence. Unless perhaps, O *Socrates*, we receive these knowledges at the moment we are born. For that time still remains as a possibility.

**They recollect then what they had once learned. It is necessary. But when did our souls receive this knowledge? Surely not after we were born as men. Certainly not. Therefore before. Yes. Souls existed, therefore, Simmias, even before they came into human form, separate from the body; and they possessed intelligence. Unless perhaps, O Socrates, we receive these knowledges at the moment we are born. For that time still remains as a possibility.**

<summary>Socrates presents the Theory of Recollection, arguing that since we can identify physical things as "imperfectly equal," we must have a prior, perfect knowledge of "Equality itself" from before birth. This implies that the human soul existed with intelligence before entering the body.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and his friends Simmias and Cebes. Having established that knowledge is "recollection," Socrates now moves to prove that if the soul existed before birth, it must also exist after death.</meta>

# PLATO

<margin>A</margin> "Let it be so, my friend. But at what other time do we lose them <note>The "them" refers to the perfect concepts or "Forms" like Equality, Beauty, and Goodness.</note>? For we are not born already possessing them, as we just agreed. Or do we lose them at the same moment we receive them? Or can you suggest another time?" "Not at all, Socrates," Simmias replied, "I did not realize I was saying nothing." "Is this then how it stands for us, Simmias? If those things we are always talking about truly exist—the Beautiful, the Good, and every such **essence** <term>Essence: The Latin 'essentia' or Greek 'ousia'; the true, unchanging nature of a thing</term> to which we refer all our sensory perceptions, finding them to have been ours previously—then it is necessary that just as these Forms exist, our soul must also have existed before we were born. But if these Forms do not exist, then this entire argument would be in vain. Is it not the case that it is equally necessary for these things to exist and for our souls to have existed before our birth; and if the former do not exist, neither do the latter?" "It seems to me, Socrates," said Simmias, "to be wonderfully the same necessity. The argument finds a beautiful refuge in the conclusion that our soul exists before we are born in the same way as the **essence** you just mentioned. For I hold nothing to be so certain as that all such things exist in the highest degree: the Beautiful, the Good, and all the others you spoke of. As far as I am concerned, it has been sufficiently demonstrated."

<margin>B</margin> "But how does it seem to Cebes?" asked Socrates. "For we must persuade him too." "I think he is sufficiently persuaded," said Simmias, "even though he is the most persistent of men in his doubt and the slowest to believe. Yet I believe it has been proven to him that our soul existed before our birth. However, whether it will still exist after we die does not yet seem to me, Socrates, to have been shown. That common doubt which Cebes brought up still stands: the fear that when a person dies, the soul is simultaneously scattered and thus ceases to exist. For what prevents it from being brought together from somewhere else and existing before it ever entered a human body, but then, after it leaves the body, having it then perish and be destroyed?" <margin>C</margin> "You speak well, Simmias," said Cebes. "For it seems only half of what is necessary has been proven—that our soul existed before we were born. It is also necessary to show that after we have died, it will exist no less than it did before we were born, if the demonstration is to be complete."

<margin>D</margin> "It has already been demonstrated, Simmias and Cebes," said Socrates, "even now, if you are willing to connect this current proof with the one we agreed upon earlier: that every living thing comes from the dead. For if the soul exists beforehand, and it is necessary for it, when entering life and being born, to come from nowhere else but from death and the state of being dead, how is it not necessary for it to exist also after death, since it must be born again? So, what you ask has been demonstrated even now. <margin>E</margin> Nevertheless, you and Simmias seem to wish to examine this argument even more diligently. You are afraid, in the manner of children, that as the soul exits the body, the wind might truly blow it apart and scatter it—especially if someone happens to die not in calm weather, but in a great gale." At this, Cebes laughed and said, "Try to persuade us, Socrates, as if we were afraid—or rather, not as if *we* were afraid, but perhaps there is a child within us who fears such things. Let us try to persuade him not to fear death as if it were a **bogeyman** <note>original: "laruas" (Latin) / "mormolukeia" (Greek); refers to mythical monsters used to frighten children.</note>."

<margin>F</margin> "Indeed," said Socrates, "you must sing charms to him every day until he is healed." "But where, Socrates," asked Cebes, "will we find such a good charmer <note>A 'charmer' here refers to a philosopher or teacher who can heal the soul's fears through reasoning.</note>, now that you are leaving us?" "Greece is large, Cebes," he replied, "and in it there are many good men; and there are also many foreign nations. You must search through all of them for such a charmer, sparing neither money nor labor. For there is nothing on which you could more opportunely spend your money. You must also search among yourselves; for perhaps you will not easily find anyone more capable of doing this than you are." "This shall be done," said Cebes. "But let us return to where we left off, if it pleases you." "It pleases me greatly," he said. "How could it not?" <margin>G</margin> "You speak well," said Cebes. "Should we not then," asked Socrates, "ask ourselves something like this: What kind of thing is liable to undergo this fate—namely, to be scattered? And for what kind of thing should we fear this might happen? And what kind of thing is not liable to it? And after this, should we not examine which of these the soul is? And from that, should we be confident or fearful for our own soul?" "You speak the truth," he said. "Does it not then belong to that which is **composite** <term>Composite: Something made of multiple parts</term>, and is by nature put together, to be dissolved in the same way it was put together? But if anything happens to be **uncompounded** <term>Simple/Uncompounded: Something made of a single, indivisible substance</term>, does it not belong to this alone, more than anything else, to not undergo this?" "It seems so to me," said Cebes. "Is it not then most likely that things which are always the same and in the same state are uncompounded, while things that are different at different times and never the same are composite?" "I think so, certainly." "Let us return to those things we discussed in the previous argument. Does **Essence itself**—the very being we define in our questions and answers—always remain the same and in the same state? Or does it change? Does the Equal itself, the Beautiful itself, each thing that truly *is*, ever admit of any change whatever? Or does each of them, being a **uniform** reality...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> "So be it, my friend. At what other time do we lose them? For we certainly do not possess them at the moment we are born, as we just agreed. Or do we lose them in the very moment we receive them? Or can you name another time?" "Not at all, Socrates; I realized I was speaking nonsense." "Does it then stand like this for us, Simmias?" he asked. "If those things exist which we are always talking about—the Beautiful and the Good and all such **essence**—and we refer all the things from our senses to this, discovering that it existed before as our own, and we compare these things to it, then it is a necessity that just as those things exist, so also our soul must exist before we were born. But if these things do not exist, would this argument not be spoken in vain? Is it so, that it is an equal necessity for these things to exist and for our souls to have existed before we were born; and if those do not, then neither do these?" "Exceedingly so, Socrates," said Simmias, "it seems to me to be the same necessity. The argument takes refuge in a good place: that our soul exists before we are born in the same way as the **essence** of which you now speak. For I have nothing so clear to me as this—that all such things exist as much as possible: the Beautiful and the Good and all the other things you just went through. For me, it has been sufficiently demonstrated."

<margin>B</margin> "But what about Cebes?" asked Socrates. "For we must persuade Cebes too." "It is sufficient," said Simmias, "as I believe; although he is the most forceful of men in disbelieving arguments. But I think he is persuaded of this: that before we were born, our soul existed. However, if it will still exist after we die, even to me, Socrates," he said, "it does not seem to have been demonstrated. That which Cebes just said still stands—the fear of the many—that when the person dies, the soul is scattered and this is the end of it. For what prevents it from coming into being and being put together from somewhere else, and existing before it comes into a human body; but then, after it arrives and is released from it, it then reaches its end and is destroyed?" <margin>C</margin> "You speak well, Simmias," said Cebes. "For it seems as if only half of what is needed has been demonstrated: that before we were born, our soul existed. But it is necessary to demonstrate in addition that after we die, it will exist no less than before we were born, if the proof is to have its completion."

<margin>D</margin> "It has been demonstrated, Simmias and Cebes," said Socrates, "even now, if you are willing to put this argument together with the one we agreed upon before it—that every living thing comes from that which is dead. For if the soul exists previously, and it is necessary for it, when going into life and being born, to come from nowhere else than from death and being dead, how is it not necessary for it to exist even after it dies, since it must be born again? So, it has been demonstrated even now, as has been said.

<margin>E</margin> "Nonetheless, you and Simmias seem to me to wish to work through this argument even more; and to fear, like children, that the wind might truly blow the soul apart and scatter it as it exits the body—especially whenever someone happens to die not in a calm, but in some great wind." And Cebes, laughing, said, "Try to persuade us, Socrates, as if we were afraid; or rather, not as if we were afraid, but perhaps there is some child in us who fears such things. Let us try to persuade him not to fear death like **bogeymen**."

<margin>F</margin> "But one must," said Socrates, "sing charms to him every day until he is healed." "Where then, Socrates," he asked, "shall we find a good charmer for such things, since you are leaving us?" "Greece is large, Cebes," he said, "in which there are surely good men; and there are many races of barbarians <note>original: "barbarōn"; to the Greeks, this meant anyone who did not speak Greek.</note>, all of whom you must search through, seeking such a charmer, sparing neither money nor labor. For there is nothing on which you could more timely spend your money. And you must seek among one another; for perhaps you would not easily find any more capable of doing this than yourselves." "Well, these things shall be done," said Cebes. "But let us return to where we left off, if it is pleasing to you." "It is indeed pleasing. How could it not be?" "Well said," he replied.

<margin>G</margin> "Therefore," said Socrates, "must we not ask ourselves something like this: To what kind of thing does it belong to undergo this fate—to be scattered? And for what kind of thing should we fear lest it undergo this? And for what kind not? And after this, let us again examine which of these the soul is; and from these things, let us either be confident or fear for our soul." "True," he said. "Does it then belong to that which has been put together and is **composite** by nature to undergo this—to be divided in the same way it was put together? And if there happens to be something **uncompounded**, does it belong to this alone to not undergo these things, if to anything else?" "It seems so to me," said Cebes. "Therefore, those things which are always the same and in the same state, these are most likely to be the uncompounded; but those things which are different at different times and never the same, these are the composite." "So it seems to me." "Let us then go," he said, "to those same things we went to in the previous argument. Does the **essence** itself, of whose being we give an account in our asking and answering, always remain the same and in the same state, or is it different at different times? Does the Equal itself, the Beautiful itself, each thing itself which *is*, ever admit of any change whatsoever? Or is each of them always what it is, being **uniform**...

<summary>Socrates argues that the soul's pre-existence is tied to the existence of eternal Forms (like Beauty and Truth), and attempts to soothe his friends' fears that the soul might "blow away" after death by distinguishing between composite things that break and simple things that are eternal.</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Simmias, Cebes, Forms, Essence, Immortality, Pre-existence, Death, Soul, Philosophy, Greece, Ancient Greek, Latin translation</keywords>
