<meta>This page continues the dialogue in Plato's Phaedo. Socrates is now leading Cebes through a series of logical steps to distinguish between the physical body and the non-physical soul, arguing that the soul's nature aligns it with the eternal and divine rather than the decaying material world.</meta>

# PHAEDO.

<margin>A</margin> "Does that which is itself in itself <note>original: 'αὐτὸ καθ᾽ αὑτὸ'—meaning the pure essence of a thing, like Beauty itself</note>, being always the same, never in any way admit any change?" "It must be so, Socrates," said Cebes. "What then of the many beautiful things—such as men, horses, garments, or anything else of that sort—whether they are equal or beautiful or share the same name as those pure essences? Do they remain the same, or are they the complete opposite, never being the same as themselves or as each other?" "These things," replied Cebes, "never remain the same." "And these things you can touch, see, and perceive with the other senses. But those that remain the same can only be grasped by the reasoning of the mind <term>Reasoning of the mind: 'διανοίας λογισμῷ' / 'intelligentiæ ratione'—the intellectual process of understanding truths that aren't visible to the eye</term>; such things are invisible and cannot be seen." "What you say is entirely true," he said. "Shall we then propose, if you like,"

<margin>B</margin> Socrates continued, "two kinds of beings: one visible, the other invisible?" "Let us propose it," he said. "And the invisible always remains the same, while the visible never does?" "Let us propose that too." "Now then, is there anything in ourselves other than the body and the soul?" "Nothing else," he said. "To which kind, then, do we say the body is more similar and more closely related?" "It is clear to everyone," he said, "that it is the visible." "And what of the soul? Is it visible or invisible?" "Not visible to humans, at least, Socrates." "But we were speaking of things visible or not according to human nature. Or do you think we meant some other nature?" "No, the human one." "What then do we say of the soul? That it is visible or invisible?" "Invisible." "It is, therefore, unseen <note>original: 'Ἀειδὲς' (Aeides)—a play on words in Greek, as the name 'Hades' was thought to be derived from 'unseen'</note>." 

<margin>C</margin> "Yes." "Therefore, the soul is more similar to the invisible, while the body is more similar to the visible." "It is entirely necessary, Socrates." "And did we not also say earlier that whenever the soul uses the body to examine something—whether through sight, or hearing, or another sense—it is dragged by the body toward things that never remain the same? Then the soul itself wanders and is troubled; it grows dizzy as if drunk <note>original: 'ὥσπερ μεθύουσα' / 'quasi ebria'</note>, because it has touched things of that nature." "Quite so." "But whenever the soul contemplates by itself, it departs to that which is pure, eternal, immortal, and unchanging. Because it is of a related nature, it stays with those things whenever it is by itself and is permitted to do so. Then it ceases its wandering and, in relation to those things, it always remains the same, for it has touched things that are like itself. And this state of the soul is called wisdom <term>Wisdom: 'φρόνησις' (phronesis)—a type of practical and moral wisdom or 'prudence'</term>." "You speak beautifully and most truly, Socrates."

<margin>D</margin> "Again, then, based on what was said before and what we are saying now, to which kind does the soul seem more similar and more closely related?" "I believe, Socrates," he said, "that even the most stubborn student would agree from this line of reasoning that the soul is in every way more similar to that which is always the same than to that which is not." "And the body?" "To the other kind." "Consider it also in this way: when soul and body are together, nature commands the body to serve and be ruled, and the soul to rule and lead. In this regard, 

<margin>E</margin> which of the two seems to you to be like the divine, and which like the mortal? Or do you not think the divine is naturally suited to rule and lead, while the mortal is suited to be ruled and to serve?" "I do." "To which, then, is the soul similar?" "It is clear, Socrates, that the soul is like the divine, and the body like the mortal." "Observe then, Cebes, if these are our conclusions from all that has been said: the soul is most like the divine, immortal, intellectual, uniform, indissoluble, and that which is always the same and consistent with itself. The body, in turn, is most like the human, mortal, unintellectual, multiform, dissoluble, and that which is never the same as itself. Can we, dear Cebes, argue otherwise?" "We cannot."

<margin>F</margin> "What then? Since this is so, is it not fitting for the body to dissolve quickly, but for the soul to be altogether indissoluble, or nearly so?" "How could it be otherwise?" "You notice then," he said, "that when a person dies, the visible part of him—the body—which is placed in the visible world and which we call a corpse, is meant to dissolve, fall away, and dissipate. Yet it does not suffer any of these things immediately, but remains for a considerable time. Indeed, if the person dies with their body in a graceful state and at a graceful age, it remains very much so. For the body, when shrunken and preserved—as they do in Egypt <note>A reference to the ancient Egyptian practice of mummification</note>—remains almost whole for an incredible amount of time. And even if some parts of the body rot, the bones and sinews and such parts are, so to speak, 

<margin>G</margin> immortal. Is that not so?" "Yes." "Then shall the soul—the 'unseen' which goes to another place that is noble, pure, and invisible, the true 'unseen' realm <note>A reference to Hades</note> to the presence of a good and wise God, where, if God wills, my own soul must soon go—shall this soul, being such and of such a nature, be scattered and destroyed as soon as it is released from the body, as many people say? Far from it, my dear Cebes and Simmias! Rather, the truth is much more like this: if it departs pure, dragging nothing of the body with it, since it had no willing commerce with the body during life, but rather fled from it..."

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Does that which is itself by itself <note>original: "Ipsum per seipsum"</note>, in the same manner and according to the same things, hold itself? And does it never, anywhere, nor in any way undergo any change? "It is necessary, Socrates," said Cebes, "that it always stays the same and according to the same things." "But what shall we say of the many," he asked, "which are similarly called beautiful—namely men, horses, garments, or any other such things—which are either called beautiful, or equal, or even of all those things which are synonyms of them: do these always stay according to the same things? Or rather, are they entirely contrary to those others, so that neither they themselves to themselves, nor to each other, ever—to speak simply—stay in any way 

<margin>B</margin> according to the same things and in the same manner?" "These, Socrates," said Cebes, "are never the same." "And these can indeed be touched, seen, and reached by the other senses. But those which always remain according to the same things are perceived in no other way than by the power of the mind alone; and those which are of such a kind are invisible and are not seen." "You speak entirely truly," he said. "Do you wish then that we set down two species of things: one of the visible, the other of the invisible?" "Let us set them down," he said. "And that the invisible is always in the same state, while the visible is never the same?" "Let us set this down also," he said. "Come now, is there anything else in us than this body and that soul?" "Nothing else," he said. "To which species do we say the body 

<margin>C</margin> is more similar and more related?" "To no one is it doubtful," he said, "that it is to the visible." "But what of the soul? Is it something visible, or the opposite?" "Not to men, at least, Socrates," he said. "And yet we were speaking only of those things which can be seen or not seen by the nature of men. Or were we discussing those which pertain to another nature?" "Only those which pertain to the human," he said. "What then did we say of the soul? That it is visible or invisible?" "Not visible." "Invisible, then?" "So it is." "The soul, therefore, is more similar to the invisible species than the body is; while the body is more similar to the visible." "That is entirely necessary." "And did we not also say this in the preceding arguments? That when the soul takes the body as a partner for considering something, either through sight, or through hearing, or through another sense 

<margin>D</margin> (for this is what it is to consider through the body, because it is done through the senses), then it is dragged by the body to those things which are never the same, and it wanders and is troubled, and staggers like a drunkard <note>original: "quasi ebria"</note>, inasmuch as it has touched such things." "Entirely." "But truly, as often as the mind itself thinks by itself, it brings itself thither to that which is pure, eternal, immortal, and always stays in the same manner: and as if it were a relative of it, it always clings to it, as often as it has returned into itself and is permitted to do so, and it ceases from error: and concerning those things it always stays according to the same things in the same manner, inasmuch as it has now touched such things. And this affection of it is named prudence <term>Prudence: 'prudentia' in Latin, translating the Greek 'phronesis'—the specialized wisdom of the soul</term>." "You speak excellently and entirely truly, 

<margin>E</margin> Socrates." "To which species, again, does the soul seem more similar and more related to you, from these things which were said both before and just now?" "I think indeed, Socrates," he said, "that anyone, even if entirely unteachable and stubborn, would concede from this discourse that the soul is in every way and in every part more similar to that which is always the same than to its opposite." "What about the body?" "To the other species." "Consider it again in this way. As long as the soul and the body are in the same place, nature commands the latter to serve and be subject, but the former to rule and dominate. According to these things, again, which seems to you to be like the divine, and which like the mortal? Or do you not think the divine is of such a nature that it rules and leads, while the mortal 

<margin>F</margin> is such that it is subjected and serves?" "I think so." "To which of these, then, is the soul similar?" "It is clear, Socrates, that the soul is similar to the divine, and the body to the mortal." "Observe now, Cebes, whether these things follow from all that has been said by us. Namely, that to the divine, immortal, intelligible, uniform, indissoluble, always in the same manner, and staying consistent with itself, the soul is most similar; but to the human, mortal, non-intelligible, multiform, dissoluble, and never staying the same as itself, the body is most similar. Can we, friend Cebes, bring forward anything else besides these things to show it is not so?" "We cannot." "What then? Since these things are so, is it not fitting for the 

<margin>G</margin> body that it be dissolved quickly? But for the soul, that it be entirely indissoluble, or something very close to an entirely indissoluble thing?" "Why not?" "You see, therefore, after a man has died, that which is the visible body in him, placed in a visible place, which we call a corpse, and which is suited to be dissolved, to fall, and to flow away—it undergoes none of these things suddenly, but if someone dies with his body in very good condition, it remains for a quite long time, and even continues in that very beauty. For the body, dried and preserved as they do in Egypt, remains almost whole for an incredible time. Indeed, even if it should rot, nevertheless

---

some parts of the body—namely the bones, the sinews, and similar things—remain, so to speak, immortal. Is it not so?" "Yes." "But the soul, which is something invisible, migrating into some similar and other place—excellent, pure, invisible, hidden from us—truly to the good and wise God, where, if God wills, my own soul must also migrate shortly: I say, such a soul, endowed with such a nature, will it not, as soon as it has been freed from the body, be dissipated and perish, as many people think? Far from it, O beloved Cebes and Simmias! Rather, the matter stands much more like this: if indeed it has departed pure, dragging nothing of the body with it, as one that has willingly shared nothing with it in life, but rather fled from it..."

<sig>K k</sig>

<summary>Socrates distinguishes between the visible, changing world of the body and the invisible, eternal world of the "Forms" and the soul. He argues that since the soul rules the body and seeks eternal truths, it is divine in nature and unlikely to simply dissipate upon death.</summary>
<keywords>Phaedo, Socrates, Cebes, Simmias, immortality of the soul, invisible vs visible, mummification, divine vs mortal, phronesis, wisdom, Hades</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue in Plato's Phaedo. Socrates is explaining to his friends that the goal of a philosopher is to prepare the soul for its eventual separation from the body, arguing that a life of physical indulgence traps the soul, while a life of reason liberates it.</meta>

# OF PLATO

Or is this not the meditation of death? It is entirely so. Therefore, will the soul, being in such a state, not depart to what is like itself—the divine? To the divine, the immortal, and the wise? When it arrives there, it becomes truly happy, being freed from error, ignorance, fears, wild loves, and all other human evils. And as is often said of the initiated <note>Socrates refers here to the mystery religions of ancient Greece, where participants believed they would dwell with the gods after death</note>, does it truly spend the rest of time living with the gods? These are the kinds of images produced by souls that did not depart purely from the body, but still carry something of the visible with them, which is why they can be seen. "In what way are these the happiest?" "But it is not permitted for any to reach the race of the gods except for those who, burning with the desire for learning, have practiced philosophy and departed entirely pure. It is for the sake of these things, my dear friends Simmias and Cebes, that those who rightly practice philosophy

"That would not be fitting, Socrates," said Cebes. "No, by Zeus," he replied. "Therefore, O Cebes, all those who care for their own soul and do not live merely to serve the body, bid farewell to all these others. They do not travel the same path as those who do not know where they are going. They themselves believe they should not act against philosophy and its release and

This is the famous 'soma-sema' (body-tomb) metaphor</note>, rather than through itself. They see it rolling in total ignorance, and philosophy observes that the strength of this prison comes from desire, so that the prisoner himself is the chief accomplice in his own binding. <column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
...when it is gathered together by itself, and always meditating on this. This is nothing else than correctly practicing philosophy, and in reality practicing how to die easily. Or would this not be the meditation on death? Entirely so. Therefore, if the soul is in this state, does it not depart to that which is similar to it, the divine? To the divine, and immortal, and wise? Where, having arrived, it is possible for it to be happy, having been released from wandering and ignorance and fears and wild loves and the other human evils; and just as it is said of the initiated, it truly spends the remaining time with the gods? Shall we say this, O Cebes, or otherwise? "Thus, by Zeus," said Cebes. But if (I think), having been defiled and
<margin>B</margin>
impure, it departs from the body, as one that was always with the body and served it and loved it, and was bewitched by it—both by desires and pleasures—so that nothing else seemed to be true except the corporeal, which one might touch and see, and drink and eat, and use for sexual purposes; but it was accustomed to hate and tremble at and flee that which is shadowy and invisible to the eyes, but intelligible and graspable by philosophy; being in such a state, do you think the soul will depart by itself in its purity? "Not in any way," he said. But I think it is caught by the corporeal; which its association and companionship with the body, through always
<margin>C</margin>
being together and through great practice, has made innate to it. "Certainly." And one must think, my friend, that this is heavy, and weighted, and earthy, and visible. And the soul that has this is weighed down and dragged back into the visible place, by fear of the invisible and of Hades, as it is said, rolling around monuments and tombs. Around which indeed have been seen certain shadowy phantoms of souls, such as these souls provide as images, those that have not been purely released, but participate in the visible; which is why they are seen. "It is likely, Socrates." "It is likely indeed, O Cebes. And these are not the souls of the good, but those of the worthless, which are forced
<margin>D</margin>
to wander around such things, paying the penalty for their former way of life, which was bad. And they wander until, by the desire of the corporeal nature that follows them, they are again bound into a body. And they are bound, as is likely, into such characters as they happened to have practiced in life." "What kind of things do you mean by these, Socrates?" "For example, those who have practiced gluttony and insolence and love of drinking, and have not been careful, are likely to enter into the races of asses and such beasts. Or don't you think so?" "What you say is very likely." "And those who have preferred injustice and tyrannies and robberies, into the races of wolves and hawks and kites. Or where else would we say such souls go?" "Doubtless," said Cebes, "into such as these." "Then," he said, "it is clear where the rest go, each according to
<margin>E</margin>
the similarities of their practice." "It is clear," he said, "how could it not be?" "Then are not the happiest of these," he said, "and those going to the best place, those who have practiced the popular and social virtue, which they call temperance and justice, which has come about from habit and practice, without philosophy and reason?" "In what way are these the happiest?" "Because it is likely these will arrive again into such a social and gentle race, perhaps of bees, or wasps, or ants, or even back into the same human race again, and that moderate men will be born from them." "It is likely." "But into the race of gods, it is not permitted for one who has not practiced philosophy and departed entirely pure to arrive, but only for the lover of learning. But for the sake of these things, my dear Simmias and Cebes,
<margin>F</margin>
the right philosophers abstain from all the desires of the body, and they endure, and do not give themselves over to them; not fearing the destruction of their home and poverty, like the many and the lovers of money; nor again fearing dishonor and the ill-repute of wickedness, like those who love power and those who love honor, and then abstain from them." "For it would not be fitting, Socrates," said Cebes. "Indeed not, by Zeus," he said. "Therefore, O Cebes, to all these things, those who have some care for their own soul, and do not live by molding their bodies, say farewell; they do not travel on the same path as them, as people who do not know where they are going. But they themselves, believing that one must not act contrary to philosophy and its release and
<margin>G</margin>
purification, turn this way, following it wherever it leads." "How, Socrates?" "I will tell you," he said. "For the lovers of learning know," he said, "that when philosophy takes over their soul, it is literally bound fast in the body and glued to it, forced to examine the things that are—as if through a prison—through the body, but not by itself through itself, and rolling in all ignorance. And philosophy, seeing the terribleness of the prison—that it is because of desire, so that the one who is bound might be the chief helper in his own binding—what I mean is, the lovers of learning know that philosophy, taking over
<margin>H</margin>
their soul in this state, gently encourages it and attempts to release it; showing that the investigation through the eyes is full of deceit, and deceitful is that through the ears and the other senses; and persuading the soul to withdraw from these...

<summary>In this passage from Plato's Phaedo, Socrates argues that philosophy is a "rehearsal for death" that purifies the soul. He describes how impure souls are reincarnated as animals reflecting their vices, while only philosophers can truly join the gods.</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Cebes, Simmias, Soul, Reincarnation, Philosophy, Asceticism, Afterlife, Virtue, Body vs Soul</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Socrates' argument about the soul's relationship to the body. Having previously discussed how the soul is polluted by physical desires, Socrates now explains how sensations of pleasure and pain act as physical "nails" that tether the soul to the material world, and uses the famous metaphor of the swan's song to describe his own peaceful approach to death.</meta>

# PHÆDO.

<column-break/>

<margin>having withdrawn</margin>
...to withdraw and collect itself, and to trust in nothing else but itself—whatever it understands by itself, of things that are in themselves. But whatever it considers through other means <note>original: "δι’ ἄλλων" (di’ allōn) — referring to the five senses</note>, being in other things <note>original: "ἐν ἄλλοις" (en allois) — referring to the changing physical world</note>, let it deem nothing true. For such a thing is sensible and visible, but what the soul itself sees is intelligible and invisible. Believing that it must not oppose this liberation, the soul of the true philosopher abstains from pleasures, desires, pains, and fears as much as possible, reasoning that when someone is intensely pleased, or afraid, or pained, or desirous, they suffer no such evil from them as one might suppose—such as falling ill or wasting money because of those desires. Rather, they suffer the greatest and most extreme of all evils, yet do not realize it. "What is this, Socrates?" asked Cebes. It is that the soul of every human is compelled, at the same time it feels intense pleasure or pain, to believe that the object of this feeling is the most vivid and true, <margin>A</margin> though it is not. These things are mostly visible objects, are they not? "Certainly." Is it not in this state of passion that the soul is most tightly bound by the body? "How so?" Because every pleasure and pain, as if holding a nail, <margin>B</margin> nails the soul to the body and pins it there, making it body-like <note>original: "σωματοειδῆ" (sōmatoeidē)</note>, so that it believes those things to be true which the body says are true. For by sharing the opinions of the body and finding joy in the same things, it is forced, I believe, <margin>C</margin> to become like the body in its ways and its nourishment, such that it can never arrive purely in the next life <note>original: "εἰς ᾅδου" (eis hadou) — literally "into Hades"</note>. Instead, it always departs full of the body's stain, and so quickly falls back into another body and grows there as if sown. Therefore, it remains entirely shut out from communion with the divine, the pure, and the uniform essence. "What you say is very true, Socrates," said Cebes. It is for these reasons, O Cebes, that those who truly love learning are orderly and brave—not for the reasons the common people claim. Or do you think otherwise? "Not at all." No, indeed. For the soul of a true philosopher would reason in this way: <margin>D</margin> it would not think that philosophy must set it free, only for it to surrender itself again to pleasures and pains and be bound once more, performing a useless task like Penelope unweaving her web <note>In Homer's Odyssey, Penelope avoided suitors by weaving a shroud by day and unweaving it by night; Socrates uses this to describe a soul that constantly undoes its own spiritual progress</note>. Rather, seeking a calm from these things and following reason, always remaining within it, the soul contemplates what is true, divine, and beyond mere opinion. Nourished by this, it believes it must live this way as long as it lives, and when it dies, it hopes to arrive at what is akin to itself, thus being freed from human evils. From such an upbringing and exercise, there is no reason to fear, O Simmias and Cebes, <margin>E</margin> that when it departs from the body it will be torn apart, scattered by the winds, and vanish so that it no longer exists anywhere.

---

When Socrates had said these things, a long silence followed. Socrates himself seemed to be reflecting on what had been said, as did most of us. But Cebes and Simmias were talking a little with each other. Socrates, seeing them, asked: "What? Do you think the things I said were spoken insufficiently? For there are still many doubts and objections, if one is to examine them thoroughly. If you are considering something else, I have nothing to say; but if you are in doubt about these matters, do not hesitate to speak and go through them yourselves, <margin>F</margin> if it seems to you that they could be stated better. And take me as a partner in the discussion, if you think you will fare better with me." And Simmias said: "To be honest, Socrates, I will tell you the truth. For a long time now, each of us has been in doubt and pushing the other to ask, because we desire to hear you, but we hesitate to cause you trouble, lest it be unpleasant for you <margin>G</margin> in your present misfortune." Hearing this, Socrates laughed gently and said: "My goodness, Simmias! It would be difficult indeed for me to persuade other men that I do not consider my present fate a misfortune, when I cannot even persuade you. You fear that I am in a more difficult and gloomy state now than I was in my earlier life. It seems I appear to you inferior to the swans in my power of prophecy. For they, when they perceive that they must die, having sung even in the time before, then sing most of all and most beautifully, rejoicing that they are about to go to the God whose servants they are. But humans, because of their own fear of death, tell lies about the swans and say they sing a dirge for their death, crying out of pain. They do not realize that no bird sings when it is hungry, or cold, or suffering any other pain—not the nightingale, nor the swallow, nor the hoopoe, which they say sing a mournful dirge. But it does not seem to me that these birds sing out of sorrow, nor do the swans. Rather, I believe, because they belong to Apollo <margin>H</margin>, they are gifted with prophecy; they foresee the good things in the afterlife, and so they sing and rejoice on that day more than ever before. Indeed, I think myself to be a fellow-servant of the swans, sacred to the same God, and I possess a gift of prophecy from my master no worse than theirs, nor do I depart from life with any less spirit. Therefore, you must speak and ask whatever you wish, as long as the Eleven <note>The "Eleven" were the Athenian officials responsible for prisoners and executions</note> allow it." "You speak well," said Simmias. "And so I will tell you..."

<meta>This page continues the dialogue in the prison cell on the day of Socrates' execution. Having discussed the soul’s purity, Socrates' students, Simmias and Cebes, now present their specific counter-arguments to his claims of immortality.</meta>

-># PLATO'S<-
# PHAEDO

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...about which I have doubts, and here again Cebes seems to find something in the previous argument difficult to accept. For it seems to me, Socrates, as perhaps it also seems to you, that to have certain knowledge of these matters in our present life is either impossible or extremely difficult. However, to fail to test what is said about them in every possible way—and to give up before one has exhausted every angle of investigation—seems to me the mark of a very weak man. For in these matters, one must achieve one of two things: either learn or discover the truth of how things are; or, if that is impossible, take the best and most resilient of human reasons <note>Simmias suggests that if we cannot have divine certainty, we must use the "raft" of the best logical theories available.</note> and, riding upon it as if on a raft, sail through the risks of this life. <margin>B</margin> This is necessary unless one could travel more safely and with less peril upon a sturdier vessel, perhaps some divine word <note>original: "λόγου θείου τινός" (logou theiou tinos) — Simmias hints at the longing for a revelation or higher truth beyond mere human logic.</note>. And so now, I will not be ashamed to ask my question, especially since you yourself encourage us to do so: I do not want to blame myself later for not having said what is on my mind now. Indeed, Socrates, when I consider what has been said alongside Cebes here, your arguments do not seem quite sufficient to me. Socrates replied, "Perhaps, my friend, your opinion is correct. But tell me, in what way do you think they are insufficient?"

<margin>C</margin> "In this way," said Simmias. "One might say the same thing about a harmony, a lyre, and its strings: that the harmony is something invisible, incorporeal, beautiful, and divine within the well-tuned lyre; but the lyre itself and its strings are bodies—physical, composite, earthy, and kin to what is mortal. Therefore, if someone were to break the lyre, or cut and snap the strings, one might argue by your same logic that the harmony must still exist and cannot have perished. For it would be impossible for the lyre and the strings (which are of a mortal nature) to still exist once the strings are broken, while the harmony (which is of a divine and immortal nature) perishes before that which is mortal. Rather, he would say that the harmony must still be somewhere, and that the wood and strings would rot away before the harmony suffered any harm. <margin>D</margin> I believe, Socrates, that you yourself have noticed that we usually conceive of the soul as something of this sort: that our body is held together in a state of tension by the hot, the cold, the dry, and the moist, and other such elements, and that our soul is a certain tempering <term>krasis|a blending or mixture</term> and harmony of these very things, resulting when they are well and moderately mixed with one another. If, then, the soul is a kind of harmony, it is clear that whenever our body is excessively relaxed or strained by diseases and other evils, the soul—despite being most divine—must immediately perish, just as other harmonies do, whether in musical sounds or in any of the works of craftsmen. Meanwhile, the remains of each body last for a long time, until they are either burned or rotted away. Consider then, what we shall say to this argument, if someone maintains that the soul is a mixture of the elements in the body and is the first to perish in what we call death."

<margin>E</margin> Then Socrates, as he often did, looked up sharply and smiled. "Simmias speaks fairly," he said. "If any of you is more ready to answer than I am, why does he not do so? For he seems to have handled the argument quite well. However, I think that before we answer him, we should first hear what Cebes objects to in the argument, so that in the intervening time we might have the opportunity to deliberate. <margin>F</margin> Then, after hearing them, we can either agree with them if they seem to speak in tune with the truth, or if not, we must defend and maintain our previous reasoning. Come then, Cebes, tell us what it is that troubles you and causes your doubt."

"I will tell you," said Cebes. <margin>G</margin> "It seems to me that the argument is still in the same place as before, and is subject to the same charge we made earlier. That our soul existed before it entered into this human form, I do not retract; that was very elegantly put and (if it is not too much to say) sufficiently demonstrated. However, that the soul continues to exist after we are dead does not seem proven to me. Yet I do not agree with Simmias's objection that the soul is not stronger and more long-lasting than the body. For it seems to me that the soul far excels all these things. 'Why then,' the argument might say to me, 'do you still doubt? Since you see that when a man dies, the weaker part of him still remains, does it not seem to you that the more long-lasting part must necessarily be preserved during this time?' To this, consider if there is any weight to my reply; for I too, like Simmias, need an analogy.

It seems to me that this is being said in much the same way as if someone were to speak about an old weaver who had died, saying that the man has not perished but is perhaps still safe somewhere. As evidence, he might offer the cloak that the man had woven for himself and wore, asserting that it is still sound and has not perished. And if someone did not believe him, he would ask which is more long-lasting: the race of men, or a cloak that is in daily use and worn. If the answer were that the human race is much more long-lasting, he would think it demonstrated that the man is much more likely to be safe, since that which was more fragile has not yet <margin>H</margin> perished. But I do not think this is the case, Simmias. Consider what I am saying. Anyone would understand that such an argument is foolish. For this weaver, having worn out and woven many such cloaks, died after many of them, though...

<column-break/>

...how, and whether he accepts what has been said. "For it seems to me, Socrates," [Simmias said], "that about such things—as perhaps it also seems to you—to know the clear truth in this present life is either impossible or very difficult. However, on the other hand, failing to test what is said about them in every way, and giving up before one has exhausted every perspective, is the mark of a very soft man. For regarding these matters, one must accomplish one of these things: either learn how they are, or find out; or, if these are impossible, take at least the best of human reasons and the hardest to refute, and riding upon it as if on a raft, risk the voyage through life; unless one could pass through more safely and with less danger upon a steadier vessel or some divine word. And so now, I will not be ashamed to ask, since you yourself say these things, nor will I blame myself in later time for not saying now what I think. For to me, Socrates—when I look at what has been said both by myself and with this man here—it does not seem to have been spoken sufficiently."

And Socrates said, "Perhaps, my friend, you are right; but tell me, in what way was it not sufficient?"

"In this way," he said, "one might say this same argument about a harmony and a lyre and its strings: that while the harmony is something invisible and incorporeal, and something very beautiful and divine in the tuned lyre; the lyre itself and the strings are bodies and body-like, composite and earthy, and kin to the mortal. Whenever, then, someone breaks the lyre, or cuts and snaps the strings, if one were to insist by the same argument as yours that the harmony must still exist and has not perished (for there would be no way that the lyre still exists when the strings are snapped, and that the strings, being of mortal nature, exist, but the harmony has perished—that which is of the same nature and kin to the divine and immortal perishing before the mortal), but should say that the harmony must still be somewhere, and the wood and strings must rot away before anything happens to it. For indeed, Socrates, I think you yourself have considered this: that we suppose the soul to be something of this kind—as our body is stretched and held together by the hot and cold, and dry and moist, the soul is a certain mixture and harmony of these very things, whenever they are mixed with one another beautifully and in due measure. If, then, the soul happens to be a kind of harmony, it is clear that when our body is slackened immoderately, or strained by diseases and other evils, the soul must immediately perish (even though it is most divine), just as other harmonies do, those in sounds and in all the works of craftsmen; but the remains of each body stay for a long time, until it is either burned or rots away. Look then to this argument, what we shall say if someone claims that the soul, being a mixture of the things in the body, is the first to perish in what is called death."

Socrates, having paused as he was often accustomed to do, and smiling, said, "Simmias speaks fairly. If any of you is more capable than I, why does he not answer? For he seems to have grasped the argument quite well. It seems to me, however, that before the answer, we should first hear from Cebes what he in turn finds fault with in the argument; so that when time has passed we may deliberate on what we shall say, and then, having heard them, either agree with them if they seem to be in tune, or if not, then at last defend the argument. But come," he said, "O Cebes, say what it was that was troubling you, causing your doubt."

"I am saying it," said Cebes. "For it seems to me the argument is still in the same place, and has the same charge as we said before. That our soul existed before it came into this form, I do not retract—it was very gracefully and (if it is not offensive to say) very sufficiently demonstrated. But that it still exists somewhere after we have died, that does not seem so to me. Not that I agree with Simmias’s objection that the soul is not stronger and more long-lasting than the body; for it seems to me to differ greatly in all these respects. 'Why then,' the argument might say, 'do you still doubt? Since you see that when the man has died, the weaker part still exists; does it not seem to you that the more long-lasting part must necessarily still be preserved during this time?' To this, then, consider if I am saying anything. For I too, as it seems, like Simmias, need an image. For it seems to me these things are said just as if one were to say this argument about an old weaver who had died: that the man has not perished, but is perhaps somewhere; and he might provide as evidence the cloak he wore, which he had woven himself, that it is sound and has not perished. And if someone doubted him, he would ask which is more long-lasting: the race of man or a cloak in use and being worn. If someone answered that the man's is much more so, he would think it demonstrated that beyond all doubt the man is sound, since the shorter-lived thing has not perished. But I think, Simmias, it is not so. For you too consider what I say. For anyone would take it that the one saying this says something foolish. For this weaver, having worn out and woven many such cloaks, [died] after them...

<summary>Simmias and Cebes present two famous objections to Socrates' theory of immortality: the "Harmony" argument (that the soul is merely the body's tuning) and the "Weaver" argument (that the soul might outlast some bodies but eventually wear out).</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue in the prison cell on the day of Socrates' execution. Having heard Simmias' objection that the soul is merely a "harmony" of the body, the group now listens to Cebes' final challenge: even if the soul is stronger than the body and outlasts many of them, it might eventually wear out and perish in a final death.</meta>

-># PHAEDO<-

...many there were," but the last (I think) weaver <note>Cebes' analogy: A weaver makes and wears out many cloaks in his life, but he eventually dies before his last cloak. Similarly, a soul might inhabit many bodies, but eventually perish before the last one.</note> and he is no more a man just because of this, nor is a garment something more trivial or weaker than he. I think the soul could receive this same image in relation to the body, and anyone saying these things would seem to me to speak reasonably: that the soul is long-lived, while the body is weaker and shorter-lived. But I would also say that each soul wears out many bodies, especially if it lives many years. For if the body flows and perishes while the man is still living, but the soul always weaves anew what is being worn out, it would be necessary that when the soul perishes, it would happen to have its last garment, and would perish before this one alone. But when the soul has perished, then at last the body would demonstrate the nature of its weakness, and quickly rotting, it would fall away. So, according to this argument, we cannot yet be confident and trust that when we die, our soul still exists somewhere. For if someone were to grant even more to the speaker than what you say, conceding to him not only that our soul existed in the time before we were born, but that nothing prevents some souls from still existing even after we die, and that they will be born many times and die again (for the soul is by nature so strong that it holds out through many births); even granting this, he might not yet concede that it does not suffer in these many births, and finally, in one of these deaths, it perishes completely. No one, he would say, knows which of these deaths and which dissolution of the body brings destruction to the soul (for it is impossible for any of us to perceive this). If this is the case, it is not fitting for anyone to face death with confidence—except a foolish confidence—unless he can prove that the soul is altogether immortal and indestructible; otherwise, it is necessary that he who is about to die must always fear for his own soul, lest in the current separation from the body it perish entirely. All of us, having heard them, were dismayed, as we later said to one another; for although we had been strongly persuaded by the previous argument, they seemed to disturb us again and cast us into a state of disbelief, not only regarding the arguments already spoken, but also concerning those yet to be said, lest we should be worthless judges or the matters themselves were inherently untrustworthy. **ECHE.** <note>Echecrates is the person listening to Phaedo's retelling of the story.</note> By the gods, Phaedo, I have sympathy for you. For even as I listen to you now, something like this occurs to me: "What argument shall we trust then?" For the argument that Socrates spoke, which was so very persuasive, has now fallen into disbelief. For this argument strangely takes hold of me, both now and always, that our soul is a kind of harmony; and as it was spoken, it reminded me that these things had already seemed true to me. And I very much need again (as if from the beginning) some other argument that will persuade me that the soul of the deceased does not die along with the body. Tell me then, by Zeus, how did Socrates pursue the argument? And did he also, as you say you did, appear clearly troubled, or not, but instead calmly come to the aid of the argument? And did he help it sufficiently or inadequately? Relate everything to us as accurately as you can. **PHAED.** Truly, Echecrates, though I have often admired Socrates, I never wondered at him more than when I was present then. That he had something to say in response was perhaps not strange; but I wondered at him most, first for this: how pleasantly, kindly, and admiringly he received the young men's argument; then, how sharply he perceived what we had suffered from the arguments; and finally, how well he healed us, and as if we were fleeing and defeated, he called us back and encouraged us to follow along and examine the argument with him. **ECHE.** How so? **PHAED.** I will tell you. I happened to be sitting to his right by the bed, on a certain low stool; he sat much higher than I. Stroking my head, then, and pressing together the hair on my neck (for he was accustomed, whenever it happened, to play with my hair), he said, "Tomorrow, perhaps, Phaedo, you will cut off these beautiful locks." <note>Cutting one's hair was a traditional sign of mourning in ancient Greece.</note> "It seems so, Socrates," I said. "Not if you listen to me," he said. "But why?" I asked. "Today," he said, "I will cut mine and you will cut yours, if our argument dies and we are not able to bring it back to life. And if I were you, and the argument escaped me, I would make an oath, like the Argives, <note>The Argives swore not to cut their hair until they regained the city of Thyrea.</note> not to let my hair grow long again until I had defeated the argument of Simmias and Cebes in a rematch." "But," I said, "against two, even Hercules is said not to be able to fight." "Then call upon me," he said, "as your Iolaus <note>Iolaus was the nephew and helper of Hercules.</note>, while it is still light." "I call upon you then," I said, "not as Hercules calls Iolaus, but as Iolaus calls Hercules." "It will make no difference," he said, "but first let us be careful that a certain fate does not befall us." "What kind?" I asked. "That we do not become misologists <note>original: "μισολόγοι" (misologoi) — haters of reason or arguments, similar to how a 'misanthrope' hates people.</note>," he said, "just as people become misanthropes. For there is no greater evil," he said, "that one could suffer than to hate arguments. Misology and misanthropy arise in the same way. For misanthropy sets in from trusting someone too much without skill <note>original: "ἄνευ τέχνης" (aneu technēs) — without the art of understanding human nature.</note>, and thinking the man to be altogether true and healthy and faithful, then a little later finding him to be wicked and unfaithful, and then another. And when this happens...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...were many, but the last indeed prior: nor for that reason does it follow more that a man is cheaper or weaker than a garment. I think the same comparison of the soul to the body can be made: and if someone brings forward these same things, he would seem to speak congruently: namely that the soul is indeed more long-lasting, but the body weaker and less long-lasting: but he would say that any of the souls consumes many bodies, especially if they live many years. For if the body flows, and is dissolved even while the man is living, the soul indeed re-weaves what is consumed continually; nevertheless it will be necessary when the soul has perished, then to have the last garment, and that it alone perishes before the last. But when the soul has perished, then at <margin>B</margin> last the body shows the weakness of its nature, quickly rotting and vanishing: so that by this reasoning we cannot yet be confident that even when we have departed our soul survives. For if someone granted even more than what you say to the speaker, and confessed not only that the soul existed before our birth, but even that nothing prevents some from remaining even after death, and admitted that it enters and leaves [the body] quite often: for the nature of the soul is so strong that having been placed in the body more often, it preserves itself and the body: yet with these things granted, he would not yet give this to you, that the soul is not exhausted in many generations, but would say at last it is entirely destroyed by some death out of many. Furthermore, he would add that no one can know that death and dissolution of the body which also brings <margin>C</margin> the destruction of the soul: for it is impossible that any of us should perceive it. If this indeed be so, there is no one who is not foolish to be confident in death, unless he can demonstrate that the soul is altogether immortal and indissoluble. Otherwise it is consistent and necessary that he who is about to die fears for his soul, and is always solicitous lest in that which is most imminently threatening—the disjunction of the body—it utterly perishes. All of us therefore, when we heard these things being said, were troubled, as we afterwards revealed among ourselves; because although we had been greatly persuaded by the previous disputation, they seemed to have disturbed us again, and cast us down into <margin>D</margin> doubt; so that we would not apply any faith either to the reasons already brought forward, or to those yet to be said, fearing lest either we were in no way good judges, or the matters themselves were unworthy of faith. **ECHEC.** By the gods, I grant you pardon indeed, O Phaedo. For to me indeed, just now listening to you, such a thing came into my mind. To what reason then shall I trust? Since that reason of Socrates, which was so very probable a little while ago, has now lost its credit. For it is a wonder how much that reason can do against me, and has always been able to do, which proves that our soul is a certain harmony: and now indeed having been heard, it suddenly recalled to my memory that the same thing had also seemed true to me before. Wherefore it happens that I stand in need of some other reason again as if <margin>E</margin> from the very beginning, which might persuade me that the soul does not perish with the body. Tell us therefore, I pray by Jove, in what way Socrates performed the disputation, and whether he himself also, just as you confess of yourselves, seemed to bear it heavily, or on the contrary, kindly defended his own reason: furthermore, whether he guarded it sufficiently or not: relate all these things to us as diligently as you can. **PHAED.** Truly, O Echecrates, having often admired Socrates, I never admired him with greater pleasure than then being present. That he had something with which to respond to the objections is perhaps not to be wondered at: but I admired these things in him most of all: first indeed, how pleasantly, <margin>F</margin> kindly, and in a friendly manner he received the words of the young men: then how sagaciously he sensed that we had been moved by their reasons: finally how opportunely he applied the medicine to us, and as if we were fleeing and conquered, he recalled us, and turned us back to following and considering the discourse together. **ECHEC.** In what way? **PHAE.** I was just saying. I happened to be sitting at his right hand on a certain low stool, next to the bed. He himself indeed sat far higher. Stroking my head therefore, and compressing the hairs upon my neck: (for he was accustomed sometimes, when the occasion brought it about, to play with my hair) "Tomorrow perhaps," he said, <margin>G</margin> "O Phaedo, you will cut these beautiful hairs." "So I think," I said, "O Socrates." "Certainly not, if you will listen to me," he said. "Why is this?" I said. "Rather today both I shall cut mine, and you yours, if our reason should die for us, and we ourselves cannot revive it. And yet if I were you, and the reason escaped me, I would swear in the manner of the Argives, not to nourish my hair before I had in turn conquered Simmias and Cebes. But truly," I said, "against two not even Hercules is said to have been sufficient." "But call me as your Iolaus, while there is light," he said. "I call you indeed," I said, "but not as Hercules calls Iolaus, rather as Iolaus calls Hercules." "It <margin>H</margin> matters nothing," he said. "In the first place indeed, we must take care lest something happens to us." "What then?" I said. "Lest we become haters of reason," he said, "just as some become haters of men. For no greater evil than this could happen to us, namely if we should hold reasons in hatred. But hatred arises in the same way both against reasons and against men. Hatred [of men comes from]... and that he is a sincere and faithful man, then indeed soon we find him wicked and unfaithful, and again another in the same way. Therefore when someone...

<margin>A</margin> ...it has often happened, especially by those whom he regarded as his most intimate and closest friends; at last, having been frequently offended, he hates **everyone**, and believes that there is no sincerity at all in anyone. Have you not noticed that this usually happens in this way? I replied, "I certainly have." "Is it not shameful," he said, "and clear that such a person attempts to deal with men without the <term>art of human affairs</term> <note>original: "humanarum rerum arte" / "technē tēs peri ta anthrōpeia"; Socrates suggests there is a specific skill or understanding required to navigate human relationships correctly</note>? For if he studied how to use this art, he would surely think of the matter as it truly is: namely, that those who are exceedingly good or bad are very few, but those in the middle are the most numerous." "In what way do you mean that?" I asked. "In the same way," he said, "as it happens with things that are very small or very large."

<margin>B</margin> "Do you think anything is rarer than finding a very large or very small man, or dog, or anything else? Or again, the swiftest and the slowest, the most beautiful and the ugliest, the whitest and the blackest? Do you not know that in all these things, the extremes are rare and few, while the middle ones are frequent and many?" "I think so," I said. "Therefore," he asked, "do you not think that if a contest of wickedness were proposed, very few would be found to be at the top of that category?" "That is likely," I said. "Likely indeed," he said, "but in this respect, arguments are not exactly like men—I was just following where you led. Rather, the similarity lies in this: when someone, without the <term>art of reasoning</term> <note>original: "rationum arte" / "technē tēs peri tous logous"; also known as logic or dialectic</note>, believes an argument to be true, but a little later it appears false—sometimes it is truly so, sometimes not—and then it happens again with one argument after another. This happens especially to those who spend their time in contradictory arguments."

<margin>C</margin> "For you know that these people think they have finally become the wisest of all, and that they alone have noticed that there is nothing healthy or firm in either things or arguments, but that everything is in reality tossed up and down as if in the <term>Euripus</term> <note>original: "Euripo"; refers to the Strait of Euripus between Euboea and Boeotia, famous for its violent and frequently changing currents</note>, and never stays in one state for any time." "You speak the truth," I said. "Then," he said, "would it not be a

<margin>D</margin> miserable condition, Phædo, if, when there is an argument that is true, firm, and capable of being understood, someone—after hearing such arguments that seem now true and now false—should not blame himself or his own lack of skill, but at last, out of pain, gladly shift all the blame from himself onto the arguments? And for the rest of his life, he would hate and revile them, deprived of the truth and knowledge of reality itself." "By Jove," I said, "it would be a miserable condition indeed." "First of all, then," he said, "let us be carefully on our guard against this, lest we persuade ourselves that there is nothing healthy in arguments; rather, let us believe that we ourselves are not yet healthy. Therefore, we must strive with all our strength to become healthy—you and the others for the sake of your whole remaining life, and I for the sake of death itself. For I am in danger at this very time of not

<margin>E</margin> behaving like a philosopher in this matter, but like a <term>contentious</term> <note>original: "contentiosum" / "philonikos"; literally 'victory-loving', describing someone who argues only to win rather than to find the truth</note> and stubborn man, as those who are strangers to learning are accustomed to do. For when there is a dispute about something, they do not care how the matter under discussion actually stands, but they strive stubbornly so that what they have proposed may seem true to those present. And I think that in the present moment I differ from them only in this: that I shall not strive to make what I say seem true to those present—unless that happens by accident—but rather that it may seem as true as possible to myself. For I reason thus, dear friend—and see how much I gain from this reasoning: If what I say happens to be true, it is worthwhile to believe it; but if nothing remains after death, at least in this time that remains of my life, I will be less bothersome to those present by my mourning. Moreover, this ignorance of mine will not persist with me—for that would be an evil—but it will be destroyed a little later. Thus prepared, Simmias and Cebes,

<margin>F</margin> I return to the discussion. But you, if you would listen to me, give no thought to Socrates, but much more to the truth; if I seem to speak the truth to you, agree with me; if not, oppose me with everything you have, taking care that I do not, out of excessive zeal, deceive both myself and you at the same time, and depart like a bee, leaving my sting behind."

"But now we must proceed," he said. "First, remind me of what you were saying, if I seem not to remember it. Simmias, as I think, distrusts and fears lest the soul, although it is more divine and beautiful than the body, should nevertheless perish first,

<margin>G</margin> insofar as it is a type of <term>harmony</term> <note>Simmias' earlier argument was that the soul is to the body as music/harmony is to a lyre; if the lyre breaks, the music vanishes</note>. But Cebes seemed to me to grant that the soul is more long-lasting than the body, yet he believes no one can know whether, after it has worn out many bodies many times, it might at last perish itself when it leaves the final body—and that death is precisely this: the destruction of the soul, since the body never stops perishing. Are these not the things, Simmias and Cebes, which we ought to consider?" Both confessed they were. "But do you reject all the arguments that were spoken previously? Or do you reject some but concede others?" "Some," they said, "and not others." "What then," he said, "about that argument in which we said that <term>learning is recollection</term> <note>original: "disciplinam reminiscentiam esse" / "mathēsin anamnesin einai"; the Platonic theory that we 'learn' by remembering knowledge our souls possessed before birth</note>? And if this is so, does it not necessarily follow that

<margin>H</margin> the soul was somewhere before it was enclosed in the body?" "To me," Cebes said, "that was wonderfully pleasing when you said it, and now I stand by that opinion more than any other." "I am affected in the same way," said Simmias, "and I would be very surprised if I ever felt otherwise about this matter." "But it is necessary..."

<margin>A</margin> "...often it happens to someone, and especially from those whom he might consider most intimate and suitable. "Therefore," he said, "is it not shameful, and clear that such a person attempts to deal with men without the art of human affairs? For if he dealt with them with art, he would believe things to be as they are: that the good and the very wicked are few on either side, and those in the middle are the most numerous." "How do you mean?" I asked. "Just as," he said, "concerning the very small and the very great. Do you think anything is rarer than to find a very large or very small man, or dog, or anything else? <margin>B</margin> slow, or beautiful or ugly, or white or black? "Therefore, do you think," he said, "if a contest of wickedness were proposed, very few would appear as the leaders even there?" "It is likely," I said. "It is likely," he said, "but in this way, arguments are not like men (though I was following you just now);

<margin>C</margin> rather, the similarity is there: when someone trusts an argument to be true, without the art of reasoning, and then a little later it seems false to him—sometimes being so and sometimes not—and again and again. "You certainly speak the truth," I said. "Then, O Phædo," he said, "it would be a piteous suffering if, there being some true and firm argument, and one capable of being understood, then

<margin>D</margin> because of encountering such arguments that sometimes seem true and sometimes not, someone should not blame himself or his own lack of skill, but at last, through pain, should gladly thrust the blame away from himself onto the arguments, and continue for the rest of his life hating and reviling the arguments, and be deprived of the truth and knowledge of reality." "First of all, then," he said, "let us be careful of this, and let us not let it enter our souls that there is likely nothing healthy in arguments; but much rather that we ourselves are not yet healthy, and we must act like men and be eager to become healthy—you and the others for the sake of all your life hereafter, and I for the sake of

<margin>E</margin> death itself. For I am in danger in the present moment of not being a philosopher regarding this, but like the very uneducated, being contentious. For they, when they dispute about something, do not care how the matter of the argument stands, but they are eager that what they have proposed should seem true to those present. And I think I shall differ from them in the present only by this much: for I shall not be eager that what I say seems true to those present (unless that were a side-issue), but that it should seem so as much as possible to myself. For I calculate, O dear companion (and see how selfishly), that if what I say happens to be true, it is well to be persuaded; but if there is nothing for one who has died, yet at least in the time before death I shall be less unpleasant to those present by my mourning. And this ignorance of mine does not persist with me (for that would be an evil), but will perish a little later. Thus prepared," I said, "O Simmias and Cebes, I come to the argument. You, however, if you are persuaded by me, giving little thought to

<margin>F</margin> Socrates, but much more to the truth, if I seem to you to say anything true, agree with me; but if not, resist with every argument, being careful lest I, out of zeal, deceive both myself and you at once, and like a bee depart leaving my sting behind."

"But we must go on," he said. "First, remind me of what you were saying, if I do not appear to remember. Simmias, as I think, both distrusts and fears lest the soul, although being more divine and beautiful than the body, should perish before it, being in the form of a harmony. But Cebes seemed to me to grant this: that the soul is more long-lasting than the body, but this is unclear to everyone:

<margin>G</margin> whether the soul, having worn out many bodies many times, might not now perish itself when it leaves the final body; and that this very thing is death: the destruction of the soul, since the body never ceases perishing. Is it anything other than these things, O Simmias and Cebes, that we must examine?" They both agreed to these things. "Do you then," he said, "accept all the previous arguments, or some but not others?" "Some," they said, "and not others." <margin>H</margin> persuaded by it, and now I stand by it as by no other argument." "And indeed," said Simmias, "I also feel this way, and I would very much wonder if I should ever think otherwise." # PHAEDO

<margin>A</margin> ...that it is a composite thing, and that the soul is a kind of harmony <note>original: "harmonia"; in Greek thought, this refers to the tuning or the mathematical ratio of a musical instrument</note> constituted from those elements stretched through the body. For surely you will not allow yourself to say that a composite harmony must exist before those elements from which it had to be composed. Or will you allow it? "In no way, Socrates," he said. "Do you perceive, then," Socrates said, "that this is what you happen to be saying when you claim that the soul exists even before it reaches human form and the body, yet you also say it is composed of things that do not yet exist? For a harmony is not at all like that which you compare it to; rather, the lyre, the strings, and the notes—still untuned—come into being first. <margin>B</margin> The harmony is the very last of all to be composed, and the first to be destroyed. How then will this argument harmonize with that one?" "In no way," replied Simmias. "And yet," said Socrates, "if any argument should be harmonious, it is surely one concerning harmony itself." "It should indeed," said Simmias. "This argument of yours, then," said Socrates, "does not harmonize. But see which of the two arguments you choose: that <term>learning is recollection</term> <note>original: "mathēsin anamnēsin einai"; the theory that the soul brings innate knowledge from a previous existence</note>, or that the soul is a harmony?"

"I much prefer the former, Socrates," he said. <margin>C</margin> "For this latter theory of harmony was accepted by me without demonstration, based on a certain likelihood and attractiveness—which is why it seems true to most people. But I am aware that arguments which base their proof on likelihoods are boasters; and if one is not on guard against them, they deceive us thoroughly, both in geometry and in everything else. But the argument concerning <term>recollection</term> and learning was stated through a hypothesis worthy of acceptance. For it was said that our soul exists before it enters the body, just as the essence itself exists which bears the name of 'that which is' <note>original: "hōper autēs estin hē ousia... to ho estin"; referring to the Forms or the true reality that the soul knows before birth</note>. I have accepted this, as I persuade myself, sufficiently and correctly. <margin>D</margin> It is therefore necessary, it seems, that I accept neither myself nor anyone else saying that the soul is a harmony."

"What then, Simmias," Socrates said, "does it seem to you to belong to a harmony, or any other composite thing, to be in any state other than that of the elements from which it is composed?" "In no way." "Nor surely to do anything, nor to suffer anything, other than what those elements do or suffer?" Simmias agreed. "It is not appropriate, then, for a harmony to lead the elements from which it is composed, but rather to follow them." He agreed. "Therefore, it is far from possible for a harmony to move in opposition, or to sound in opposition, or in any other way to be contrary to its own parts." "Far from it," he said. "What then? Is it not the nature of every harmony to be a harmony according to how it has been tuned?" <margin>E</margin> "I do not understand," he said. "Is it not the case," Socrates said, "that if it is tuned more and to a greater extent (if such a thing were possible), it would be more of a harmony and a greater one? But if it were tuned less and to a smaller extent, it would be a lesser and smaller harmony?" "Certainly." "Is this then true of the soul—that one soul can be, even in the slightest degree, more or to a greater extent, or less and to a smaller extent, this very thing: a soul?" "Not in any way," he said.

"Come then, by Zeus," he said. "Is it said that one soul possesses intellect and virtue and is good, while another possesses folly and wickedness and is evil? <margin>F</margin> Are these things said truly?" "Truly, indeed." "What then will those who maintain the soul is a harmony say these things are that exist in the souls—namely virtue and vice? Will they say they are yet another kind of harmony and disharmony? And that the good soul is tuned, and being itself a harmony, possesses within itself another harmony, while the bad soul is itself disharmonious and possesses no other harmony within it?" "I cannot say," replied Simmias. "But it is clear that the one who makes that hypothesis would say something of that sort."

"But it has already been agreed," Socrates said, "that one soul is not more or less a soul than another. And this agreement means that one harmony is not more, nor to a greater extent, nor less, nor to a smaller extent, a harmony than another. Is that not so?" "Certainly." <margin>G</margin> "And that which is neither more nor less a harmony is neither more nor less tuned. Is it so?" "It is." "And does that which is neither more nor less tuned participate more or less in harmony, or in an equal amount?" "An equal amount." "Therefore the soul, since it is not in any way more or less this very thing—a soul—than another, is also not more or less tuned?" "That is so." "And being in this state, it could not participate more in disharmony or harmony?" "No indeed." "And being in that state, could one soul participate more in vice or virtue than another, if vice is disharmony and virtue is harmony?" "Not at all." "Rather, Simmias, according to right reason, no soul will participate in vice if it is a harmony. For a harmony, being completely this very thing—a harmony—could never participate in disharmony." "Surely not." "Neither then could a soul, being completely a soul, participate in vice." "How could it, from what has been said?" <margin>H</margin> "From this argument, then, all souls of all living beings will be equally good, if souls are by nature equally this very thing: souls." "So it seems to me, Socrates," he said. "And does it seem to be correctly said," Socrates asked, "and would the argument have come to this if the hypothesis—that the soul is a harmony—were correct?" "In no way," he said.

"What then?" Socrates asked. "Of all the things in a human being, do you say anything else rules but the soul, especially the wise soul?" "I do not." "By yielding to the passions of the body, or by opposing them? I mean the passions,

<column-break/>

for example, when the body is thirsty, the soul pulls it back from drinking...

<summary>Socrates dismantles the "soul as harmony" theory by pointing out two contradictions: first, a harmony cannot exist before the instrument that creates it (violating the theory of Recollection), and second, if souls were harmonies, all souls would be equally virtuous, which contradicts the reality of human behavior.</summary>
