<meta>This page continues the dialogue in Socrates's prison cell on the day of his execution. Socrates is finishing his rebuttal to Simmias's "harmony" theory of the soul before addressing Cebes’s more difficult objection regarding the soul's endurance versus its immortality.</meta>

### PLATO'S WORKS

<margin>A</margin> But consider a case like this: if you are in the heat and thirst torments you, yet the soul pulls you in the opposite direction, urging you not to drink; or if hunger presses upon you, urging you not to eat. We see the soul opposing the physical impulses of the body in countless other ways, do we not? "Certainly," he said. And did we not agree earlier that the soul, if it were a harmony <note>original: "harmonia"; here Socrates refers to the tuning of a musical instrument</note>, would never sound a note in opposition to the tension, relaxation, vibration, or any other state of the elements from which it was composed? Did we not agree it would follow those elements, and never lead them? "We did agree," he said, "how could we not?" <margin>B</margin> But what now? Does the soul not seem to act in exactly the opposite way? It leads all those elements from which someone might say it is constituted. It opposes them in almost every way throughout life, ruling over them in every fashion—sometimes punishing them harshly and painfully through gymnastics and medicine, and sometimes more gently by rebuking or warning the desires, angers, and fears. It speaks to them as one thing addressing another, just as Homer wrote in the *Odyssey*:

<margin>Odyssey, Book 20</margin>
> *Then striking his breast, he rebuked his heart with these words:*
> *Endure, my heart; you have suffered even worse than this.* <note>original: "Tum pectus pulsans, cor sic affatur Ulysses, / Hoc quoque cor perfer, namque & graviora tulisti." Socrates uses this quote to show that Homer viewed the soul/mind as something that can command the physical heart/body.</note>

<margin>C</margin> Do you think Homer said this thinking that the soul was a harmony, the kind of thing to be subjected to the body's passions? Or did he think it was something far more divine than a harmony, something meant to lead and dominate? "By Zeus, Socrates, I believe the latter." Therefore, my good friend, it is not at all right for us to say the soul is a kind of harmony. If we did, it seems we would disagree both with the divine poet Homer and with ourselves. "That is so," he said. "Very well," said Socrates, "we have now, it seems, sufficiently appeased the 'Theban Harmony.' <note>The "Theban Harmony" refers to Simmias’s argument; Harmonia was the wife of Cadmus, the founder of Thebes.</note> But how, Cebes, shall we appease the 'Cadmean' argument <note>Referring to Cebes’s argument, named after Cadmus</note>, and by what reasoning?" "You seem to me," said Cebes, "likely to find a way. You devised this argument against the 'harmony' wonderfully and beyond my expectation. When I heard Simmias doubting, I <margin>D</margin> wondered if anyone could manage his argument. I was therefore greatly amazed that he could not withstand even the first onset of your reasoning. Thus, I would not be surprised if the 'Cadmean' argument suffered the same fate." "My good man," said Socrates, "do not speak so boldly, lest some 'evil eye' <note>original: "invidia"; likely referring to *baskania*, a Greek concept that over-confidence attracts bad luck or divine resentment</note> should overturn the argument that is to come. But that will be God's concern; let us, in the Homeric fashion, 'come close' and see if there is any truth in what you say. <margin>E</margin> The summary of what you seek is this: you demand it be demonstrated that our soul is neither subject to destruction nor mortal. You argue that if a philosopher, facing death with confidence and hoping to fare much better in the next life because of his study of philosophy, is not to be a fool, his confidence must be shown to be well-founded. You say that to show the soul is something strong and godlike, and that it existed even before we were born, does not necessarily prove immortality, but only that the soul is long-lasting and existed for countless ages before us, knowing and doing many things. Yet you believe this does not make it immortal; rather, you think its very entry into a human body is the beginning of its destruction, like a disease. Thus, it lives this life in misery and finally perishes in what we call death. You claim it makes no difference whether the soul enters a body once or many times; every one of us has reason to fear. For it is only right to fear death, unless one is a fool, if he does not know and cannot give a reason for the soul's immortality. This, I believe, is the substance of what you say, <margin>F</margin> Cebes. I am repeating it on purpose so that nothing escapes us, and so you may add to it or take away from it if you wish." "For the present," said Cebes, "I have nothing to add or take away. These are the things I am saying." Then Socrates, after pausing for a long time and reflecting within himself, said: "You are seeking no small thing, Cebes. For we must thoroughly discuss the cause of generation and corruption <note>The origins of life and the reasons for death/decay</note> in general. I will, if you like, relate to you my own experiences regarding these matters. Then, if anything I say seems useful for proving your point, you may use it." "I certainly do wish it," said Cebes. "Listen then to my story. <margin>G</margin> When I was young, Cebes, I was wonderfully eager for that wisdom which they call the 'inquiry into nature.' <note>original: "historia"; meaning a systematic investigation or account</note> For it seemed to me a magnificent thing to know the causes of everything—why each thing comes to be, why it perishes, and why it exists. I often turned myself upside down, first considering questions like these: Is it when heat and cold undergo a kind of putrefaction <note>An early Greek biological theory that life emerged from decaying matter</note>, as some have said, that living creatures are nurtured? And is it the blood with which we think, or air, or fire? Or is it none of these, but rather the brain that provides the senses of hearing, seeing, and smelling; and from these arise memory and opinion, and from memory and opinion, when they reach a state of rest, comes knowledge? Then again <margin>H</margin> I considered the destruction of these things, and the changes that occur in the heavens and the earth, until finally I seemed to myself to be so utterly unsuited for this kind of study that nothing could be more so. I will give you a sufficient proof: I was so blinded by these considerations that even those things which I previously

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...consider this then: for example, if there is heat and thirst within, the soul pulls in the opposite direction, toward not drinking; and if there is hunger, toward not eating. And in countless other things, we see the soul opposing the body’s conditions. Or do we not? "Completely so." Did we not also agree previously that the soul, being a harmony, would never sing in opposition to the tension, relaxation, vibration, or any other affection of the parts from which it happens to be made, but would follow them and never lead? "We agreed," he said, "for how could we not?" <margin>B</margin> What then? Does it not now appear to us to be doing the exact opposite—leading all those things from which someone says it is made, and opposing nearly all of them through all of life, mastering them in every way? Sometimes it punishes harshly and with pain, as in gymnastics and medicine, and sometimes more mildly, now threatening, now admonishing the desires, angers, and fears, as if it were one thing speaking to another? Just as Homer has portrayed in the *Odyssey*, where he says of Odysseus:

> *Striking his breast, he rebuked his heart with a word,*
> *Endure now, my heart; you have endured even more dog-like things than this.* <note>The Greek term translated here as "dog-like" (kynteron) implies something even more shameful or shameless than ordinary suffering.</note>

<margin>C</margin> Do you think he composed this while thinking that the soul was a harmony, such as would be led by the body’s passions, rather than something capable of leading and mastering them, being itself a much more divine thing than a harmony? "By Zeus, Socrates, that is my view." Therefore, my excellent friend, it is in no way right for us to say the soul is a kind of harmony. For we would agree neither with Homer, the divine poet, nor with our own selves. "That is so," he said.
"Very well then," said Socrates, "we have somehow made the Theban Harmony moderately propitious, as it seems. But what about the things of Cadmus, Cebes? How shall we appease them, and with what argument?" "You seem to me," said Cebes, "likely to find a way. Certainly, you spoke this argument against the 'harmony' to me with surprising success, beyond my expectation. For when Simmias was speaking of his doubt, I wondered <margin>D</margin> if anyone would be able to handle his reasoning. It seemed quite strange to me that his argument could not withstand the very first approach of your reasoning. I would not be surprised, then, if the argument of Cadmus suffered the same." "My good man," said Socrates, "do not speak so grandly, lest some malice <note>original: "baskania"; an 'evil eye' or malevolent influence that might spoil the discourse</note> overturn the argument that is about to be spoken. But these things will be the concern of God; let us, in the Homeric manner, go 'close in' and try to see if what you say has weight. The main point of <margin>E</margin> what you seek is this: you require it to be shown that our soul is indestructible and immortal. You argue that if a philosopher who is about to die is to be confident and believe that after death he will fare better there than if he had ended his life having lived in some other way, he must not be holding a foolish and senseless confidence. To show that the soul is something strong and god-like, and that it existed even before we were born, you say nothing prevents all these things from signifying not immortality, but only that the soul lasts a long time and existed somewhere before for an immense amount of time, and knew and did many things. But it was not for that reason any more immortal; rather, its very entry into a man's body was for it the beginning of destruction, like a disease. It would live this life in hardship and, in its end, perish in what is called death. You say it makes no difference whether it comes into a body once or many times, as far as the fear of each of us is concerned. For it is fitting to fear, unless one is a fool, if he does not know and cannot give an account of how the soul is immortal. Such things, I think, <margin>F</margin> are what you say, Cebes. And I am taking them up repeatedly on purpose, so that nothing may escape us; and if you wish to add or subtract anything, do so." And Cebes said, "But I do not at all need to subtract or add anything at the present. These are the things I am saying." Then Socrates, after waiting a considerable time and considering something within himself, said: "It is no small matter you are seeking, Cebes. For it is necessary to discuss thoroughly the cause of generation and destruction in general. I will therefore go through my own experiences regarding these things for you, if you wish. Then, if anything I say seems useful to you for persuasion regarding what you say, you may use it." "Indeed," said Cebes, "I do wish it." "Listen then to what I shall say. For I," he said, "O Cebes, when I was young, was wonderfully desirous of that wisdom which they call 'inquiry into nature.' For it seemed to me a magnificent thing <margin>G</margin> to know the causes of each thing—why each thing comes to be, why it perishes, and why it exists. And I often shifted myself up and down, considering first things like these: Is it when the hot and the cold undergo a kind of putrefaction, as some said, that then living things are nurtured? And is it the blood with which we think, or air, or fire? Or is it none of these, but the brain is that which provides the senses of hearing, seeing, and smelling? And from these would come memory and opinion; and from memory and opinion, once they have reached a state of rest, in this way knowledge comes to be. And again <margin>H</margin> considering the destructions of these things, and the events concerning the heavens and the earth, I finally seemed to myself so naturally unsuited for this inquiry as nothing else could be. I will tell you a sufficient proof: for those things which I even previously...

### PHAEDO.

<margin>A</margin> I once knew these things clearly—or so I thought, and so it seemed to others. But then I became so blinded by this kind of scientific inquiry that I "unlearned" even the things I previously thought I knew, including many other subjects and the very reason why a human being grows. Before this, I thought it was obvious to everyone that we grow because of eating and drinking. I believed that when, through food, flesh is added to flesh and bone to bone, and in the same way the appropriate matter is added to each part of the body, then the small mass later becomes large, and thus a small man becomes great. That is what I thought then; does it seem reasonable to you? "To me, certainly," said Cebes.

<margin>B</margin> Now consider these points as well. I thought I was satisfied with the view that whenever a tall man stood next to a short one, he appeared taller by a head, and one horse taller than another. Even clearer than that, it seemed to me that ten was more than eight because of the addition of two, and that a two-cubit measure was larger than a one-cubit measure because it exceeded it by half. "And now," asked Cebes, "what do you think about these things?" By Zeus <note>original: "nè Dia"; a common Greek oath</note>, I am far from thinking I know the cause of any of these things. I cannot even convince myself that when one is added to one, either the first one becomes two, or the added one becomes two, or that the two together become two simply because they were placed next to each other. I find it strange <margin>C</margin> that when they were apart, each was "one" and they were not "two," but as soon as they approached each other, this—the meeting and being placed near one another—became the cause of them becoming two. Nor can I still be persuaded that if someone divides "one," this division is the cause of it becoming "two." For that would be the opposite cause of becoming two than before: then it was because they were brought together and added; now it is because they are led away and separated. I no longer even believe I know why "one" becomes "one," or (in a word) why anything else comes to be, perishes, or exists, at least not by this method of inquiry.

Instead, I have a muddled way of my own, for I cannot accept the other way at all. But once I heard someone reading from a book, which he said was by Anaxagoras <note>Anaxagoras (c. 500–428 BC) was a Pre-Socratic philosopher who first introduced the concept of "Mind" as a cosmic force.</note>, <margin>D</margin> saying that Mind <note>original: "nous"</note> is the arranger and cause of all things. I was delighted with this cause, and it seemed to me somehow right that Mind should be the cause of everything. I thought that if this were so, the Mind that organizes everything would arrange each thing in the way that is best. Therefore, if anyone wanted to find the cause of how each thing comes to be, perishes, or exists, they would have to find what is best for that thing—how it is best for it to be, to act, or to be acted upon. From this reasoning, it followed that a person should look for nothing else, regarding themselves or others, <margin>E</margin> except what is most excellent and best. Necessarily, such a person would also know what is worse, since the knowledge of both is the same. 

As I reflected on this, I was happy to think I had found in Anaxagoras a teacher of the causes of existence after my own heart. I expected him to tell me first whether the earth is flat or round, and then explain the cause and the necessity of it, by stating what was "better" <note>original: "to ameinon"</note> and why it was better for the earth to be that way. And if he said it was in the center of the universe, he would further explain how it was better for it to be in the center. If he could show me these things, I was prepared to never again <margin>F</margin> desire any other kind of cause. I was similarly prepared to ask about the sun, the moon, and the other stars—about their relative speeds, their orbits, and their other properties—to understand how it is better for each of them to act and be acted upon as they are. I never would have thought that a man who claimed things were ordered by Mind would bring in any other cause for them than that it is best for them to be just as they are. I thought that by assigning a cause to each thing individually and to all things together, he would explain what is best for the individual and what is the common good for all.

I would not have traded these hopes for a great deal. I took up his books with great haste and read them as quickly as I could, so that I might know as soon as possible what is best and what is worse. But from this wonderful hope, my friend, I was swept away as I went on reading. I saw a man who made no use of Mind <margin>G</margin> and assigned no real causes to the arrangement of things, but instead blamed airs, ethers, waters, and many other strange things. To me, he seemed exactly like someone who might say: "Socrates does everything he does by Mind," but then, in trying to explain the causes of each of my actions, would say first that I am sitting here now because my body is composed of bones and sinews. He would say the bones are solid and have joints separating them, while the sinews are such that they can be tightened or relaxed, surrounding the bones along with the flesh and the skin that holds them together. Then, as the bones are lifted in their sockets, the sinews—by relaxing and contracting—make it possible for me to bend my limbs, and that is the cause of my sitting here in this slumped position. And again, regarding our conversation, he would offer other such "causes," like voices, air, and hearing, and ten thousand other things...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> I clearly knew, as it seemed to me and others, but I unlearned them, and many other things which I previously thought I knew, such as the reason why a human grows. For I used to think it was manifest to anyone that a human grows through food and drink. For when, through these, flesh is added to flesh and bones to bones, and in the same way in other parts when their own matter is applied, then surely a mass that was first small becomes large, and thus a small man is made great. That is what I thought then; do I not seem to have spoken well enough to you? "To me indeed," said Cebes. 

Take notice of these things further. For I thought I perceived correctly whenever I judged a man, or a large horse near a small one, <margin>B</margin> to be larger by a head itself. And much more evidently, ten appeared more to me than eight, because the number ten contained two more than the number eight. Furthermore, a two-cubit measure was larger than a one-cubit measure because it exceeded it by half. "But now," said Cebes, "what do you judge concerning these things?" By Jupiter <note>original Latin: "per Iouem"; translating the Greek "nè Dia"</note>, I seem to myself to be far from thinking I understand the cause of any of these things, I who cannot yet persuade myself that when someone adds one to one, either that one to which the one was added becomes two, or the one added and the one to which it was added become two because of the addition of one to the other. For I wonder <margin>C</margin> if, when each of these was separate, each was one and they were not then two; but after they were joined together, this very thing was the cause of them becoming two: namely, the meeting by which they are now placed closer. Nor even if someone divides one, can I still be persuaded that this very division is the cause of it becoming two. For then the cause of becoming two is the opposite of the previous one. Then it was because they were joined closer together and one was moved toward the other; now it is because one is moved away from the other and separated. 

Nor do I think I yet know why one becomes one, nor to put it briefly, do I profess to know anything else—why it comes to be, or perishes, or exists—through this very path. Instead, I myself vainly mix some other way, but this one I admit in no way. But when I once heard someone reading from a book of Anaxagoras (as he said), <margin>D</margin> this opinion of Anaxagoras himself: namely, that Mind orders all things and is the cause of all things. I was greatly delighted by this kind of cause, thinking it somehow consistent that Mind should be the cause of all. I thought that if this were so, so that Mind ordered all things, individual things were so disposed through it as they could be best disposed. Therefore, if anyone wished to find the cause by which individual things come to be, perish, or exist, this very thing must be found: namely, by what reason it is best for each thing either to be, or to suffer or do anything else. And by this logic, nothing else <margin>E</margin> should be considered by a man, either concerning himself or others, except what is most excellent and best. But it is necessary that he who knows this should also have known that which is worse. Since the science of these things is the same. 

Reflecting on these things within myself, I rejoiced, thinking I had found in Anaxagoras a teacher who would teach me the causes of things that I so greatly desired; and first he would tell me whether the earth is flat or round. And when he had said this, he would add the cause and the necessity, bringing forward namely that very thing which is better, and that it was better for it to be such. Furthermore, <margin>F</margin> if he said the earth was in the middle of the world, he would soon explain that it was better for it to be in the middle. If he showed me these things, I prepared myself as if I were going to posit no other kind of cause. Furthermore, concerning the sun and moon and the other stars, and their speed relative to each other, their rotations, and other things that usually happen to them, I had prepared myself to similarly seek and hear how and by what reason it is better for these individual things to either act or suffer, in whatever they do or suffer. For I did not think, since he had said from the beginning that they were ordered by that Mind, that he would later assign any other cause to things except that it is best for them to be as <margin>G</margin> they are. And so I thought that in rendering the causes of individuals, and then of all things in common, he would assign to individuals what is best for each, and to all the common good. 

Nor did I hold my hopes of little value, but with a certain supreme zeal I received the books and read them as quickly as I could, so that I might know as soon as possible what was best and what was worst. Led therefore by this marvelous hope, when I proceeded to read, I saw a man using Mind in no way, nor referring any cause to the ordering of things itself, but assigning aerial natures, and ethers, and waters, and many such incredible things as the causes of things. In which matter he seemed to me to act just as if someone said that Socrates does whatever he does by Mind; then, wanting to explain the causes of the individual things I do, he should say first that I now sit here because my body is composed of bones and sinews: and the bones indeed are solid, and have intervals of joints between them; but the sinews are of such a kind that they can be stretched and relaxed, and they embrace the bones with the flesh and skin which contains them. Therefore, when the bones are raised in their joints, the sinews, which both stretch and relax conveniently, make it so that I have the faculty of bending each limb, and for this cause I sit here bent. And again, regarding my disputation, he would say other such causes...

<summary>Socrates describes his early interest in natural science and his eventual disillusionment with purely material explanations. He recounts his excitement upon hearing Anaxagoras’s theory that Mind (Nous) orders the universe for the best, followed by his disappointment when Anaxagoras failed to provide purpose-driven (teleological) causes.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Socrates's famous "intellectual autobiography" in the Phaedo. Having found the materialist explanations of early scientists (like Anaxagoras) unsatisfying because they confused physical mechanisms with purposeful reasons, Socrates now describes his decision to seek the truth of things through "reasons" or "arguments" rather than direct physical observation.</meta>

### OF PLATO

<margin>A</margin> ...assigning as causes voices and air and hearing and countless other things of that kind, neglecting the truest causes: namely, because it seemed better to the Athenians to condemn me. And therefore it also seemed better to me to sit here, and I judged it more just to remain and undergo the punishment they might order. Indeed, **by the Dog** <note>original Latin: "per Canem"; Greek: "nè ton kyna." This was a characteristic, playful oath of Socrates.</note>, I think these sinews and these bones would have been long ago in Megara or Boeotia <note>neighboring cities where Socrates could have escaped to exile</note>, carried there by an opinion of what is best, if I had not judged it more just and honorable to pay the penalty the city demands of me, rather than to flee and live as an exile. But to call such things "causes" is utterly removed from reason. If someone were to say that without bones and sinews and such things I could not <margin>B</margin> do what I thought I must do, they would be right. However, to claim that I do what I do *because* of these things—while I act with my mind—rather than by the choice of what is best, would be a great and vast laziness of speech. For such a person is unable to distinguish that the true cause of a thing is one thing, and that without which the cause could not be a cause <note>Socrates is distinguishing between a "necessary condition" (physical body) and a "sufficient cause" (moral choice)</note> is another. It is this which many people, as if groping in the darkness, seem to call by a name not its own when they name it a "cause." Wherefore some, placing a vortex around the earth under the heavens, make the earth stay still; others, as if it were a broad kneading-trough for bread, <margin>C</margin> support it with air as a base. But they neither seek that very power by which things are now arranged as best they could be arranged, nor do they think it has any divine force. Instead, they believe they have found some **Atlas** <note>The Titan from Greek mythology who held up the sky; here used as a metaphor for a purely physical explanation of the universe's stability.</note> more robust and immortal, and more capable of holding all things together. But they think that the Good and the Fitting really connect and hold nothing together. Now, I would most gladly have become the disciple of anyone to learn how this cause works. But since I was deprived of this, and was unable to find it myself or learn it from another, I set out on a **second sailing** <term>second sailing</term> <note>original: "deuteros plous." A nautical term meaning to take up the oars when the wind fails; in philosophy, it refers to Socrates' shift from physical science to the study of "reasons" or "forms."</note> to investigate the cause. <margin>D</margin> Do you wish, O Cebes, for me to demonstrate this to you? "I desire it marvelously," said Cebes. At last, when I was exhausted from considering things, I decided I must be careful lest the same thing happen to me that happens to those who gaze at the sun during an eclipse. For they are sometimes robbed of their sight unless they look at its image in water or something of that kind. I considered something similar, and I feared my soul might be completely blinded if I looked at things with my eyes and tried to grasp them with any of my senses. Therefore, I decided it was worthwhile to take refuge in "reasons" <note>original: "rationes" / "logoi"; the logical arguments or definitions of things</note> and in them consider the truth of things. Perhaps this comparison of ours does not fit in every <margin>E</margin> respect. For I do not entirely agree that he who contemplates things in "reasons" is looking at images any more than he who looks at them in their physical effects. However, I directed my journey this way: always supposing the "reason" which I judge to be strongest, I set down as true whatever seems to harmonize with it, both regarding causes and all other things; and what does not harmonize, I set down as not true. But I wish to explain more clearly what I am saying. For I think you do not yet understand. "By Zeus, not much," said Cebes. But I am bringing nothing new, only what I have never stopped saying both elsewhere and in our previous discussion. I am going now to try to show you the kind of cause I have been dealing with, and I return to those <margin>F</margin> much-celebrated things, and I begin from them, supposing that there exists something that is **Beauty itself** by itself, and **Goodness**, and **Greatness**, and all the rest. If you grant me these and agree they exist, I hope from them to demonstrate the cause to you, and likewise to find that the soul is immortal. "But truly," said Cebes, "since I grant this to you, you should not delay in reaching your conclusion." Consider then, he said, what follows next, whether you agree with me. It seems to me that if there is anything else beautiful besides Beauty itself, it is beautiful for no other reason than because it participates in that Beauty. And I <margin>G</margin> say everything is like this. Do you accept this kind of cause? "I do indeed," he said. Therefore, I no longer perceive or am able to know those other "clever" causes. If someone tells me why any thing is beautiful—for instance, because it has a blooming color, or a shape, or any other such thing—I let those other things go, for I am usually confused by them. But this one thing I hold to myself, simply and truly, and perhaps foolishly: nothing else makes a thing beautiful except the presence of that Beauty, or a sharing in it, or in whatever way or manner it is communicated. For I would not yet affirm that; but <margin>H</margin> that all beautiful things are beautiful because of Beauty, this seems to me the safest answer to give both to myself and to others. And leaning upon this foundation,

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...assigning such causes; neglecting to state the truest causes: that since it seemed better to the Athenians to condemn me, for this reason it has also seemed better to me to sit here and more just to remain and undergo the penalty they may order. For, **by the Dog** <note>original Greek: "nè ton kyna."</note>, as I think, these sinews and bones would have been long ago either in Megara or among the Boeotians, carried by an opinion of what is best, if I had not thought it more just and honorable, rather than fleeing and running away, to undergo whatever penalty the city appoints. But to call such things causes is very strange. If someone were to say that without having such things—bones and sinews and whatever else I have—I would not be able to do what I decided, <margin>B</margin> he would speak the truth. However, to say that because of these things I do what I do, and that I act with my mind in this way, but not by the choice of what is best, would be a very great and long-lasting laziness of argument. For it is not being able to distinguish that the true cause is one thing, and that without which the cause would never be a cause is another. Which is exactly what the many seem to me to be groping at, as if in the dark, using a name that does not belong to it, calling it a "cause." Wherefore one man puts a vortex around the earth from the heavens and makes the earth stay still; another, like a broad kneading-trough, supports it with the air as a base. But the power of how these things are now placed as best as possible, <margin>C</margin> they neither seek, nor do they think it has any divine strength; but they believe they have found an **Atlas** more powerful and more immortal than this, and more capable of holding all things together, and they think that the truly Good and Binding does not bind or hold anything together. Now, I would gladly become a disciple of anyone to learn how such a cause is. But since I was deprived of this, and was unable to find it myself or learn it from another, I have performed a **second sailing** <term>second sailing</term> <note>original: "deuteron ploun."</note> in the search for the cause; do you want me to make a demonstration of it for you, O Cebes? "Most exceedingly," he said, <margin>D</margin> "is how I want it." It seemed to me then, he said, after this, when I was weary of examining things, that I must be careful lest I suffer what those who look at and examine an eclipse of the sun suffer. For some ruin their eyes unless they look at its image in water or something of that kind. I thought of something like this, and I feared lest my soul be altogether blinded, looking at things with my eyes and trying to grasp them with each of my senses. It seemed to me then that I must take refuge in "reasons" and examine in them the truth of things. Perhaps, then, the way I am comparing it is not entirely like it. For I do not at all concede that he who examines things in "reasons" is examining them in images more than he who examines them in physical works. But at any rate, I set out this way, and <margin>E</margin> having hypothesized on each occasion the reason I judge to be strongest, I set down as true whatever seems to me to harmonize with it, both about the cause and about all other things; and whatever does not, I set down as not true. I want to say more clearly to you what I mean. For I think you do not now understand. "No, by Zeus," said Cebes, "not very well." But, he said, I am saying nothing new, but exactly what I have always said at other times and in the past discussion. For I am going to try to show you the form of the cause I have been dealing with; and I will go back to those much-talked-about things, and I will start from them, hypothesizing that there is something **Beautiful itself** by itself, and **Good**, and **Great**, and all the rest. If you give and concede to me that these exist, I hope to show you the cause from them, and to find that the soul is immortal. "Well," said Cebes, "since I grant this to you, you cannot finish too soon." Consider then, he said, the things following from those, if you agree with me. For it seems to me, if there is anything else beautiful except Beauty itself, it is beautiful for no other reason than because it participates in that Beauty. And I say everything is like this. Do you agree with such a cause? "I agree," he said. "Then," he said, "I no longer understand nor am I able to know these other 'wise' causes; but if anyone tells me why anything is beautiful, either because it has a blooming color, or a shape, or anything else of that kind, I let the others go (for I am confused in all the others), but this <margin>G</margin> I hold to myself simply and artlessly, and perhaps foolishly: that nothing else makes it beautiful except either the presence or communion of that Beauty, or however and in whatever way it is added. For I do not yet insist on that, but only that by Beauty all beautiful things become beautiful. For this seems to me to be the safest thing to answer both to myself and to another; and holding to this, I think I shall never fall, but that it is safe for me and for anyone else to answer that by Beauty beautiful things become beautiful. Or does it not seem so to you?" "It does." "And by Greatness, then, great things are great, and greater things greater; and by Smallness, smaller things are smaller?" "Yes." "Then you would not accept it if someone said one person was greater than another by a head, and the smaller was <margin>H</margin> smaller by that same thing; but you would protest that you say nothing else..."

---

I think I shall never fall, but that I and anyone else can safely answer that whatever things are beautiful, become beautiful by Beauty itself. Do you not also agree? "I agree indeed." Therefore, also those things which are great, are great by Greatness itself; and those which are greater, are likewise greater; and those which are smaller, are smaller by Smallness. "So it is." Therefore you would not agree if someone said someone was greater than another by a head; and that he who is smaller is smaller by that same head; but you would testify that you would say nothing else...

<summary>Socrates explains his "second sailing," moving from physical explanations of the world to his theory of Forms, arguing that things possess qualities like beauty or greatness only by participating in the absolute Forms of Beauty or Greatness.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and his friends in his final hours. Socrates is explaining his "Safe Hypothesis"—the idea that things possess qualities (like being big or small) not because of physical reasons, but because they "participate" in abstract Forms like "Magnitude" or "Smallness."</meta>

### PHAEDO.

<margin>A</margin> ...than that everything greater than another is greater by nothing else than magnitude, and is greater for this very reason: because of magnitude. And the smaller is smaller by nothing else than smallness, and for this reason: because of smallness. You would perhaps fear (I think) that some opposing argument might meet you if you said someone was greater or smaller "by a head." First, that the greater would be greater and the smaller would be smaller by the same thing <note>the head</note>; and second, that the greater would be greater by a head which is small. It would indeed be a strange thing <note>original Greek: "teras" (a monster or marvel)</note> to say that someone is great because of something small. Would you not fear this? And Cebes, laughing, said, "I certainly would." <margin>B</margin> "Then," said Socrates, "would you not also fear to say that ten is more than eight by 'two,' and that this is the cause of it exceeding, rather than by 'multitude' <note>original Latin: "multitudine"; Greek: "plêthei"</note> and because of multitude? And that a two-cubit measure is greater than a one-cubit measure by 'half' rather than by 'magnitude'? For the same fear surely applies." "Absolutely," he said. "What then? If one is added to one, would you not be careful about saying that the addition is the cause of it becoming two, or if it is divided, that the division is the cause? You would cry out loudly that you know no other way for anything to come into being except by participating in the particular essence of each thing in which it participates. <margin>C</margin> In these cases, you have no other cause for it becoming two except the participation in **Duality** <note>original Latin: "duitatis"; Greek: "dyados"</note>, and that whatever is to be two must participate in this, and whatever is to be one must participate in **Unity** <note>original Latin: "vnitatis"; Greek: "monados"</note>. You would let those divisions and additions and other such 'clever subtleties' <note>original Latin: "argutias"; Greek: "kompseias" (literally 'refined things' or 'neatness')</note> go, leaving them for those wiser than you to answer. But you, fearing (as the saying goes) your own shadow and your inexperience, would cling to that 'safe' hypothesis <note>The "Safe Hypothesis" is Socrates' method of assuming the existence of the Forms (like Beauty or Magnitude) as the ultimate explanation for things.</note> of yours and answer in this way. But if anyone should lay hold of the hypothesis itself, you would let them be and not answer until you had considered the consequences of it, to see whether they agree or disagree with one another. And when you had to give an account of the hypothesis itself, you would do so in the same way, assuming another hypothesis—whichever seemed best of the higher ones—until you <margin>D</margin> reached something sufficient. You would not mix things together as the 'disputatious' <note>original Latin: "contentiosorum"; Greek: "antilogikoi." These were people who argued for victory rather than truth.</note> do, discussing the starting principle and the things that follow from it all at once, if you really wanted to find any of the things that truly exist. For those people perhaps have no thought or care for this; they are so clever that they can mix everything up together and still be pleased with themselves. But if you are one of the philosophers, I think you would do as I say." "What you say is very true," said Simmias and Cebes together.

**Echecrates:** By Jove, Phaedo, they were right to agree. It seems to me he explained these things with wonderful clarity, even to someone with very little sense.

**Phaedo:** <margin>E</margin> Indeed, Echecrates, it seemed so to everyone present at the time.

**Echecrates:** And so it seems to us who were not there, but are hearing it now. But what was said after that?

**Phaedo:** As I recall, after they had granted him this, and it was agreed that each of the **Forms** <note>original Latin: "speciem"; Greek: "eidon"</note> exists, and that other things get their names by participating in them, Socrates then asked: "If you say these things are so, when you say that Simmias is greater than Socrates but smaller than Phaedo, do you not then say that <margin>F</margin> both magnitude and smallness are in Simmias?" "I do." "But," said he, "you agree that Simmias exceeding Socrates is not actually as the words sound. For Simmias does not naturally exceed him by being Simmias, but by the magnitude which he happens to have. Nor does he exceed Socrates because Socrates is Socrates, but because Socrates has smallness relative to Simmias's magnitude." "True." "Nor is he exceeded by Phaedo because Phaedo is Phaedo, but because Phaedo has magnitude relative to Simmias's smallness?" "That is so." "Thus Simmias has the name of being both small and great, being in the middle of both: <margin>G</margin> surpassing the smallness of one with his magnitude, and granting to the other a magnitude that surpasses his own smallness." And smiling, he said, "I seem to be speaking like a book writer <note>original Latin: "expreſſius accuratiúſque"; Greek: "syngraphikōs." Socrates is teasing himself for being overly precise or technical.</note>, but it is as I say." Cebes agreed. "I say this because I want you to see it as I do. For it seems to me not only that Magnitude itself is never willing to be both great and small at the same time, but also that the 'magnitude in us' <note>the quality of bigness as it exists in a specific person</note> never admits the small, nor is it willing to be surpassed. Rather, one of two things must happen: either it flees and withdraws when its opposite, the small, approaches; or when it has approached, it perishes. It is not willing to stand its ground and receive smallness, and so become something other than what it was. Just as I, having received and stood my ground against smallness, am still the same person I am, even though I am small. But Magnitude, being great, has never dared to be small. In the same way, the small that is in us is never willing to become great; nor will any other of the opposites, while remaining what it was, become and be its own opposite at the same time. Rather, it either departs or perishes in this change." "I think exactly so," said Cebes. Then one of those present, hearing this (I do not clearly remember who it was), said: "By the gods! Was not the opposite of what is being said now agreed upon in our earlier discussion—that the greater comes from the smaller and the smaller from the greater, and that this is simply how opposites are generated from opposites? Now, it seems to me, it is being said that this could never happen." And Socrates, turning his head...

<column-break/>

<note>original Greek: "παραβαλὼν τὴν" (turning his...)</note>

<summary>Socrates explains the Theory of Forms, arguing that objects possess qualities like "greatness" or "twoness" by participating in abstract, unchanging Forms. He concludes that a Form (or the quality of a Form within an object) can never become its own opposite; it must either flee or perish when its opposite approaches.</summary>

<keywords>Plato, Socrates, Theory of Forms, Magnitude, Smallness, Participation, Duality, Unity, opposites, Phaedo, Cebes, Simmias</keywords>

Socrates has just been interrupted by an unnamed listener who reminds him of an earlier point in the discussion: that opposites arise from opposites (e.g., the living from the dead). Socrates is now clarifying the distinction between "opposite things" and "Opposites themselves" (the abstract Forms).</meta>

# PLATO

...had listened. "You have remembered that manfully," <note>original Latin: "Viriliter"; Greek: "Andrikos" — Socrates uses a term of praise for his friend's sharp memory</note> he said, "but you do not yet understand the difference between what was just said and what was said before. For then it was said that from a contrary thing, a contrary thing is born; but now we say that the contrary itself <note>the abstract Form</note> can never become contrary to itself, neither that which is within us, nor that which is in nature. For then, my friend, we were speaking of those things which *possess* contraries, calling them by the names of those qualities. But now we speak of those qualities themselves, by whose presence the things named get their names. We say that these qualities themselves would never be willing to undergo a mutual generation from one another." And at the same time, looking at Cebes, he said: "Did any of the things this man objected to trouble you also, Cebes?" "Not this time," said Cebes, "though I do not deny that many things do trouble me." "Then we have simply agreed on this," he said: "that a contrary will never be contrary to itself." "Entirely," he said. "Observe further if you agree with me on this as well. Do you call something 'heat' and 'cold'?" "I do indeed." "Are they the same as 'snow' and 'fire'?" "By Jove, certainly not." "So heat is something different from fire, and cold is something different from snow?" "Yes." "But I think you believe this: that snow, as long as it is snow, will never admit heat (as we were saying before) and still be what it was—snow and hot at the same time. Rather, upon the approach of heat, it will either retreat or perish." "Exactly." "Likewise fire, when cold approaches, will either move away or be extinguished; it will never dare to receive cold and still be what it was—fire and cold at the same time." <margin>C</margin> "You speak the truth," he said. "There are, then," he said, "some things of such a kind that they are not only entitled to their own name for all time, but also something else, which is not that first thing, but which always possesses its form as long as it exists. Perhaps what I am saying will be clearer in this example: the 'Odd' <note>original Latin: "Impar"; Greek: "peritton"</note> must always be called by this name which we now use. Must it not?" "Certainly." "Is it the only thing that is called so? For this is what I ask: is there not also something else, which is not the Odd itself, but which must nevertheless always be called by this name in addition to its own name, because it is so constituted by nature that it is never deserted by the Odd? I mean, for example, the number three <note>original Latin: "ternarium"; Greek: "trias"</note> and many others. Consider the case of three: does it not seem to you that it must always be called by its own name and also by the name of the 'Odd'? Yet 'Odd' is not the same thing as 'three.' Nevertheless, the number three, and five, and the whole half of the numbering system <note>meaning all odd numbers</note> are so constituted by nature that, although they are not the same as the 'Odd,' each of them is always odd. <margin>E</margin> Furthermore, two and four, and the whole other series of numbers, although they are not the same as 'the Even,' each of them is nevertheless always even. Do you agree or not?" "How could I not?" he said. "Then observe what I want to show. It is this: it appears that not only do those opposites not receive each other, but also those things which, although not opposites themselves, always *possess* opposites. These things do not seem to admit that Form which is contrary to the Form they hold within them; but when it approaches, they either perish or withdraw. Shall we not say that 'three' will perish first, or suffer anything else, before it stays to become 'even' while still being three?" "Absolutely," said Cebes. "And yet," he said, "the number two <note>original Latin: "binarius"</note> is not the opposite of three." "Certainly not." "Therefore, not only do the opposite Forms not admit each other's approach, but certain other things also do not admit the mutual entry of opposites." "You speak most truly," he said. "Would you like us, if we can, to define what these things are?" "I would indeed." "Then, Cebes, would they be those things which, whatever they occupy, compel that thing not only to retain its own idea, but also the idea of some opposite?" "How do you mean?" "Just as we were saying. For you know that whatever the 'idea of three' occupies must be not only three, but also odd." "Certainly." "To such a thing, then, we say the opposite idea to that which produces this result <note>the 'Even'</note> would never come." "Never." "But it was the 'idea of the Odd' that produced it?" "Yes." "And the opposite of this is the idea of the 'Even'?" "Yes." "Therefore, the idea of the 'Even' will never enter the number three." "Never." <margin>F</margin> "Consequently, the number three has no part in the even." "No part." "Therefore, the number three is necessarily odd." "It is." "What I was saying we must define—namely, what things they are which, although not opposite to something, nevertheless do not admit the opposite itself—is like the number Three. Although it is not the opposite of the 'Even,' it nonetheless does not accept it. For the number two always brings the opposite to the 'Odd,' and fire brings it to the 'Cold,' and many other things likewise. But see now if you define it this way: not only does a contrary not admit its contrary, but also that which brings a contrary to whatever it approaches never receives the form contrary to that which it brings. Recall it again; for it is not useless to hear it often. Five will not admit the form of the 'Even,' nor will ten—which is double—admit the form of the 'Odd.' This itself <note>ten</note> is the opposite of something else, yet it will never admit the form of the 'Odd.' Nor will the 'one-and-a-half' <note>original Latin: "sesquialter"</note>, nor other such things like the 'half,' receive the form of the 'Whole'; and similarly, the 'third part' and other such things, if you follow and agree with this." "I follow and agree entirely," he said. "Tell me then again from the beginning," he said, "and do not answer me with the same words I use in my question, but imitate me. I say...

<column-break/>

...his head, and having heard him, he said, "You have remembered that bravely. However, you do not perceive the difference between what is being said now and what was said then. For then it was said that from a contrary object, a contrary object is born; but now, that the contrary itself could never become contrary to itself, neither that which is in us nor that which is in nature. For then, my friend, we were speaking of those things which *have* contraries, calling them by the names of those contraries. But now we speak of those things themselves, by whose presence the things named get their names. We would never say that those things themselves would be willing to receive a generation from one another." And at the same time, looking at Cebes, he said: "Did any of the things this man said trouble you also, Cebes?" "Not this time," said Cebes, "though I do not deny that many things trouble me." <margin>B</margin> "Then we have agreed," he said, "simply on this: that a contrary will never be contrary to itself." "Altogether," he said. "Look at this for me as well," he said, "if you will agree. Do you call something 'hot' and 'cold'?" "I do." "Are they like 'snow' and 'fire'?" "By Zeus, I do not think so." "But is heat something other than fire, and snow something other than cold?" "Yes." "But this I think you believe: that snow, being snow, having received heat (as we said before) will no longer be what it was—snow and hot—but upon the approach of heat it will either withdraw from it or perish." "Certainly." "And fire too, when cold approaches it, will either withdraw or perish; it will never dare, having received coldness, to still be what it was—fire and cold." <margin>C</margin> "You speak the truth," he said. "It is then the case," he said, "concerning some such things, that not only is the Form itself worthy of its own name for all time, but also something else which is not that Form, but which always possesses the shape of that Form whenever it exists. Perhaps what I mean will be clearer in this: the 'Odd' must always meet with this name which we now say; or not?" "Certainly." "Is it the only one of existing things (for this I ask) or is there something else which is not the Odd itself, yet which must always be called by its name as well as its own, because it is so constituted that it is never left by the Odd? I mean something such as the 'triad' <note>the number three</note> experiences, and many others. Look at the triad. <margin>D</margin> Does it not seem to you that it must always be called by its own name and also by that of the 'Odd'—even though the Odd is not the same as the triad? Nevertheless, the triad and the pentad <note>the number five</note> and the whole half of number are so naturally constituted that, although not being the same as the Odd, each of them is always odd. And again, two and four and the whole other row of number, although not being the same as the 'Even,' each of them is always even. Do you agree or not?" "How could I not?" he said. "What I want to show, then," he said, "is this: that it appears not only that those opposites do not receive one another, but also all those things which, although not being opposites to each other, always possess the opposites. These too do not seem to receive that Idea which is opposite to the one within them, but when it comes upon them, they either perish or withdraw. Shall we not say that 'three' will perish first, and suffer anything else, before it stays to become 'even' while still being three?" "Most certainly," said Cebes. "And yet," he said, "the dyad <note>the number two</note> is not the opposite of the triad." "Indeed not." <margin>E</margin> "Therefore, not only do the opposite Forms not endure each other's approach, but certain other things do not endure the approach of opposites." "You speak most truly," he said. "Do you wish then," he said, "if we are able, that we define what these are?" "Certainly." "Would they be these, Cebes: those things which, whatever they occupy, compel it not only to have its own idea, but also never to receive the idea opposite to itself?" "How do you mean?" "Just as we were saying. For you know surely that whatever the 'idea of three' occupies, it is necessary for them to be not only three, but also odd?" "Certainly." "To such a thing, we say, the idea opposite to that form which produces this result would never come." "No." "And it was the 'Odd' that produced it?" "Yes." "And the opposite of this is the 'Even'?" "Yes." "Then to 'three,' the idea of the 'Even' will never come." "No indeed." "The number three, then, has no share in the even?" "No share." "The triad, then, is without-evenness <note>original Greek: "anartios" (not-even)</note>." "Yes." "What I was saying we should define, then, is what things—though not being opposite to a certain thing—nevertheless do not receive that opposite; as now the triad, though not being the opposite of the 'Even,' does not receive it any the more, for it always brings the opposite <note>the Odd</note> with it; and the dyad brings it to the 'Odd,' and fire to the 'Cold,' and very many others. But see if you define it thus: <margin>F</margin> not only does the opposite not receive the opposite, but also that which brings an opposite to whatever it goes to—the very thing that brings it never receives the oppositeness of that which is brought. Recall it again; for it is not worse to hear it many times. Five will not receive the idea of the 'Even'; nor will ten—the double—receive the idea of the 'Odd.' This itself <note>ten</note> is the opposite to something else, yet it will not receive the idea of the 'Odd'; nor will the 'one-and-a-half' <note>three-halves</note>, nor the others of that kind—the half—receive the idea of the 'Whole'; and the 'third part' again, and all such things, if you follow and agree with me." "I follow and agree very strongly," he said. "Tell me again," he said, <margin>G</margin> "from the beginning. and do not answer what I ask with the same words, but imitating me. I say...

<summary>Socrates distinguishes between abstract Forms and the physical things that participate in them. He explains that while a thing can change, the essential nature it holds (like the "Oddness" in the number Three) cannot admit its opposite (the "Even") without the thing itself perishing or retreating.</summary>

--- Page 429 ---
<meta>This page continues the logical proof for the immortality of the soul. Socrates is moving from the general theory of Forms to a specific application: because the soul is essentially linked to the Form of Life, it cannot admit its opposite (Death), making it both immortal and indestructible.</meta>

### 397

# PHAEDO

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> "I mean, besides that safe answer I gave at the beginning, I am now proposing a different one based on what we have just discussed. For if you were to ask me what must be present in a body for it to be hot, I would no longer give you that simple, ignorant <note>original Greek: ἀμαθῆ (amathe); Latin: rudem — Socrates refers to his earlier "safe but simple" explanation that things are hot because of Heat</note> answer that 'heat' must be present. Instead, I would give a more sophisticated answer based on our current talk: that 'fire' must be present. Nor, if you ask what must be in a body for it to be sick, will I say 'sickness,' but rather 'fever.' Nor, if you ask what must be in a number for it to be odd, will I say 'oddness,' but 'the unit' <note>original Greek: μονάς (monas); Latin: vnitas — the number one, which makes any set odd when added</note>; and so on for the rest. Now, see if you already understand well enough what I want." "Quite well enough," he said. "Answer then," said he, "what must be in a body for it to be living?" "The soul," he replied. "Is this always the case?" "How could it not be?" he said. "Does the soul, then, always bring life to whatever it occupies?" "It does indeed," he said. "Is there something
<margin>B</margin> opposite to life, or is there nothing?" "There is," he said. "What is it?" "Death." "Therefore, the soul will never admit the opposite of what it brings, as has been agreed in our previous points?" "Most certainly," said Cebes. "What then? That which does not admit the form of the 'even,' what do we now call it?" "The uneven (the odd)," he said. "And that which does not admit justice, and that which does not admit music?" "The unjust," he said, "and the unmusical." "Very well. And that which does not admit death, what do we call it?" "The immortal," he said. "Does the soul, then, not admit death?" "No." "Is the soul, then, immortal?" "It is immortal." "Well then," he said, "shall we say this has been demonstrated? Or how does it seem to you?" "Quite sufficiently, Socrates." "What then, Cebes?" he said. "If it were
<margin>C</margin> necessary for the 'un-even' to be indestructible, would the number three not be indestructible?" "How could it not be?" "Therefore, if the 'un-heated' were also necessarily indestructible, whenever someone brought heat to snow, would the snow not withdraw, safe and unmelted? For it would not perish, nor would it remain and admit the heat." "What you say is true," he said. "In the same way, I think, if the 'un-chilled' were indestructible, whenever something cold approached fire, the fire would never be extinguished or
<margin>D</margin> perish, but would go away safe." "Necessarily," he said. "So too," he said, "it is necessary to say this about the 'immortal.' If the immortal is indeed indestructible, it is impossible for the soul to perish when death comes upon it. For according to what has been said, it will not admit death, nor will it be dead; just as we said the number three will not be even, nor will the 'odd' itself be even; nor will fire be cold, nor the heat in the fire be coldness. But someone might say: 'What prevents the odd from not becoming even when the even approaches (as we agreed), but instead being destroyed, so that the even takes its place?' We could not argue against such a person that it is not destroyed, because the 'un-even' is not indestructible. If we had agreed on that, we could easily have argued that when the even approaches, the odd and the number three depart and go away. And we could argue the same for fire and heat and the rest, could we not?" "Certainly." "And so now regarding the immortal: if we agree that
<margin>E</margin> it is also indestructible, then the soul would be indestructible as well as immortal. If not, we would need another argument." "But there is no need for one," he said, "at least for this reason. For what else could escape destruction if the immortal, being eternal, could be destroyed?" "And God," said Socrates, "and the Form of life itself, and if there is anything else immortal—all would agree, I think, that these are never destroyed." "By Zeus, all men would indeed agree," he said, "and even more so, I think, the gods." "Since, then, the immortal is also incorruptible, what else follows but that the soul, if it happens to be immortal, must also be indestructible?" "It is a great necessity." "Therefore, when death comes to a man, the mortal part of him, it seems, dies; but the immortal part goes away safe and uncorrupted, withdrawing from death." "It appears so." "Above all
<margin>F</margin> things, then, Cebes," he said, "the soul is immortal and indestructible; and truly our souls will exist in Hades." "I, for my part, Socrates," he said, "have nothing else to say against this, nor can I doubt your arguments. But if Simmias here, or anyone else, has something to say, it would be well not to keep silent. For I do not know to what other time one could postpone speaking or hearing about such matters than the present moment." "Indeed,"
<margin>G</margin> said Simmias, "I myself have no reason to doubt, based on what has been said. However, because of the greatness of the subject we are discussing, and my low opinion of human weakness, I am forced to still feel some uncertainty within myself about what has been said." "Not only that, Simmias," said Socrates, "you are right to say this, but the first assumptions <note>original Latin: positiones primæ; Greek: ὑποθέσεις τὰς πρώτας (hypotheseis) — referring to the fundamental axioms the group agreed upon at the start of the logic</note>, even if they seem trustworthy to you, must nevertheless be examined more clearly. And if you analyze them sufficiently, I believe you will follow the argument as far as it is possible for a human to follow it. And if this itself becomes clear, you will seek nothing further." "You speak the truth," he said.

<margin>H</margin> "But this, my friends, it is right to consider: that if the soul is immortal, it requires care, not only for this time which we call 'living,' but for all time; and the danger would now seem to be truly terrible if one were to neglect it. For if death were a release from everything, it would be a stroke of luck for the wicked when they die to be rid of the body and their own wickedness along with the soul."

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Or besides that safe response placed at the beginning, there is another safe response found through those things which were just said. For if you ask me, O Socrates, what happens in a body to make it hot, I will not give you that simple and unlearned response—namely, if heat is present—but a more refined one from the present words: if fire enters. Similarly, if you ask me what happens in a body to make it sick: I will not answer if sickness is present, but if fever is. Again, if you inquire what happens to a number to make it odd: I will not say if oddness is present, but if the unit is; and in other matters in the same way. But see if you now clearly understand what I wish. "Most clearly." Answer then: what is it that, if it occurs in a body, will be living? "If the soul is." Does it not always hold itself so? "Always."
<margin>B</margin> Therefore, whatever the soul occupies, does it always bring life to it? "It brings it without doubt." Is there something contrary to life or not? "There is indeed." What is that? "Death." But the soul will never undergo the contrary of that which it always brings, just as has been granted from the previous points. "It is entirely so," said Cebes. What then of that which does not admit the idea of the even? How were we naming it a little while ago? "The uneven (the odd)." That which does not admit justice, or that which does not admit music? "The unjust," he said, "and the unmusical." Come now, that which does not undergo death, what do we call it? "The immortal."
<margin>C</margin> Therefore the soul does not admit death. "By no means." Therefore the soul is immortal. "Immortal indeed." Come then, shall we say this has now been demonstrated? Or does it seem otherwise to you? "And most sufficiently indeed, O Socrates." What then, Cebes? If it were necessary that whatever is entirely uneven were also not subject to destruction, would the number three not be free from destruction? "Why not?" Furthermore, if that which is not hot were necessarily not subject to destruction, whenever someone moved something hot toward snow, the snow would escape safe and un-melted; for it would neither perish nor admit the heat. "You tell the truth." In a similar way, I think, if anything were unable to grow cold, it also could not perish; whenever cold approached
<margin>D</margin> fire, the fire would not be extinguished or vanish, but would depart safe. "It is necessary." In the same way, it is necessary that we speak of the immortal. For if that which is immortal cannot perish, it is impossible for the soul to perish when death is imminent. For it will not receive death, just as is clear from the previous points, nor will it have perished; just as the number three will never be even, as we said, nor again will the even be odd; nor fire cold, nor the heat which is in fire ever be coldness. But someone will say: what prevents the uneven itself from not becoming even when the even approaches, as is agreed among us, but instead, with it being dissolved, the even succeeds in its
<margin>E</margin> place? We would not be able to argue against one speaking so, that it had not been destroyed—since the uneven and the indestructible are not the same. Otherwise, if this had been established by us, we would easily maintain that when the even approaches, the uneven three departs. And similarly we would bring the same argument concerning fire and heat and the rest. "Is it not so?" "Entirely." Now truly concerning the immortal: if it is established by us that what is immortal is also without destruction, it follows that the soul, besides being immortal, is also ignorant of destruction. But if this is not granted, there will be need for another argument. "But there is no need," he said, "so far as that is concerned, for another argument. For indeed, what else could be indestructible if the immortal and eternal itself were dissolved?"
<margin>F</margin> "God truly, and the very Form of life, and if there is anything else immortal, all would confess it to be indestructible." "By Jove, all men, and much more so, I think, the gods themselves." Since therefore that which is immortal is also incorruptible, what prevents the soul, if it shall be immortal, from also being incorruptible? "It follows necessarily." Therefore, when death is imminent for a man, that which is mortal in him perishes, as it appears; but that which is immortal, uncorrupted and safe, withdraws itself from death. "It is manifest." Therefore, most of all, O Cebes, the soul is immortal and incorruptible; and our souls will be among the spirits <note>original Latin: manes — the souls of the deceased in the underworld</note>. "I indeed, O Socrates, have nothing against these things by which I would not assent to your arguments. But if either Simmias here, or anyone else, has anything to say, it would be worth the effort not to have been silent. For I do not know to what other time anyone would put it off, if he desired either to say or hear anything concerning matters of this kind." "And yet," said Simmias, "neither do I have anything by which I would not assent to the previous arguments. Nevertheless, considering the magnitude of the matter itself which is being dealt with, and human weakness, I am forced within myself not yet to acquiesce to the things said." "On the contrary, you speak these things well, O Simmias, and the first positions, although they seem worthy of faith to you, must nevertheless be more diligently considered; and if you have discussed them sufficiently, as I think, you will follow this reasoning as far as it can be done by a man. And if this itself shall have been made manifest, you will seek nothing further." "You speak the truth," he said.

<margin>H</margin> "But this, O men, it is just to think: if the soul be immortal, it stands in need of the greatest care, not only for the sake of this time in which we are said to live, but even for the sake of the whole. For it must be thought that there will be a grave danger if anyone shall have neglected the soul. For if death were the dissolution of the whole, certainly the wicked would profit, since they would be liberated both from the body and from their own depravity along with the soul."

<summary>Socrates concludes the logical proof for the soul's immortality by arguing that since the soul is the principle of life, it cannot admit death, and if it is immortal, it must also be indestructible. He ends with a moral exhortation that because the soul survives death, we must prioritize its care and virtue.</summary>
<keywords>soul, immortality, indestructibility, Form of Life, Socrates, Cebes, Simmias, Hades, virtue, logic</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the final discourse of Socrates before his execution. Having "proven" the immortality of the soul, he now transitions into a "mythos" or a likely story about the soul's journey after death and the true nature of the Earth's geography.</meta>
