# PLATO
### PHAEDO

<margin>A</margin> But now, since the soul appears to be immortal, there remains no other escape from evils and no salvation, except for it to become as good and as wise as possible. For the soul, when it departs to the underworld <note>Latin: manes; Greek: hadou — the realm of the dead</note>, carries nothing else with it except its education and its upbringing. These things are said to either greatly benefit or greatly harm the one who has died, right at the very beginning of that journey. For they say that each person, when they depart from this life, is led by that guiding spirit <note>original: dæmone / δαίμων (daemon) — a personal spirit or guardian assigned to a person at birth</note> which had fallen to them by lot while living, to a certain place where all must be gathered together to be judged, and then proceed to the underworld with that guide who has been commanded to lead those departing from here to those places. But when they have received there what was their lot to receive, and have remained for the necessary time, they are led back here again by another guide after many and long cycles of time. However, the path is not such as
<margin>B</margin> Telephus says in the play by Aeschylus <note>Telephus was a king in Greek mythology; Aeschylus was a famous Athenian playwright</note>. For he says that a simple path leads to the underworld. But I think it is neither simple nor one-way. Otherwise, there would be no need for guides, since no one could lose their way if there were only one path. But now it seems to have many branches and many turnings. I say this, inferring it from the sacrifices and religious rites performed here. Therefore, the soul that is orderly and wise follows its guide willingly and is not ignorant of its surroundings. But the soul that is possessed by a desire for the body, as I said before, remains passionately attached to it for a long time; and after resisting in many ways and suffering much around the visible world, it is finally led away by force and with great difficulty by the guiding spirit appointed to care for it.
<margin>C</margin> When it arrives at the place where the other souls are, if it is found to be quite impure, having committed some crime, or having stained itself with unjust murders, or having performed other such deeds which are the works of similar souls, everyone flees and turns away from this soul, and no one is found who is willing to be its companion or its guide. Therefore, destitute of all help, it wanders about until certain cycles of time are fulfilled. When these are finally completed, it is carried by necessity
<margin>D</margin> into the habitation that befits it. But the soul that has passed through life in a pure and moderate way, having found gods as its companions and guides, dwells in the place that is suitable for each. There are indeed many and wonderful places on the earth, and the earth itself is neither of the kind nor of the size that those who usually discourse about the earth imagine it to be, as I have been persuaded by someone. Simmias then said, "In what way do you say this, Socrates? For I myself have heard many things about the earth, but not these things which you say you have accepted as true. Therefore, I would gladly
<margin>E</margin> hear them from you." "Indeed, Simmias, it does not seem to me to require the 'art of Glaucus' <note>original: ars Glauci / Γλαύκου τέχνη — a proverb for a very difficult task or rare skill, possibly referring to a legendary metalworker</note> to tell what these things are; but to prove that they are true seems to me to exceed the power of Glaucus's art. Moreover, I perhaps would not be sufficient for the task. Even if I knew how, Simmias, my remaining life does not seem long enough for such a long narration. However, nothing prevents me from saying what I believe the form of the earth to be and its various places." "That will be enough," said Simmias. "I am persuaded then," he said, "firstly, that if the earth is in the middle of the heaven and is round, it has no need of air or any other such necessity to keep it from falling. But it is sufficient to sustain it that the heaven is entirely uniform with itself in every direction, and that the earth itself is in equilibrium.
<margin>F</margin> For a thing in equilibrium, placed in the middle of something uniform, cannot be inclined more or less in any direction. Since it is balanced, it remains without leaning. First, then, I am persuaded of this." "And rightly so," said Simmias. "Furthermore," he said, "that the earth is something immense, and that we, from the Phasis <note>The Rioni River in modern Georgia, then considered the eastern limit of the known world</note> to the Pillars of Hercules <note>The Straits of Gibraltar, the western limit</note>, inhabit only a small portion of it, like ants or frogs around a pond, or around the sea. And that there are many others living in many other such places. For there are everywhere around the earth many hollows, varied both in their shapes and sizes, into which water, mist, and air flow together. But the earth itself is pure and lies in the pure heaven, in which the stars are, and which most of those who discourse on such things call the 'aether.'
<margin>G</margin> These things we see are like the dregs settling and always flowing into the hollow parts of the earth. We, therefore, dwelling in these hollows, are deceived into thinking that we dwell high up on the surface of the earth. It is as if someone dwelling at the very bottom of the sea were to think they inhabited the upper surface of the waters; and looking at the sun and the other stars through the water, they were to think the sea was the heaven. Because of their slowness and weakness, they would never have emerged to the top of the sea, nor have raised their head above the waves to see how much purer and more beautiful this place is than the depths where they are; nor would they have heard it from someone who had seen it.
<margin>H</margin> This same thing, then, happens to us. For dwelling in a certain hollow of the earth, we think we inhabit the upper surface, and we call the air 'heaven,' as if the stars moved through it as though it were the true heaven. This happens to us because, due to our weakness and slowness, we are unable to pass through to the uppermost limit of the air. But if someone were to reach the top, or fly up on wings, they would see what is there, just as fish emerging from the sea see our world. And if nature were sufficient to endure the sight, one would recognize immediately that that is the true heaven, the true light, and the true earth."

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> But now, since the soul is shown to be immortal, there would be no other escape from evils for it, nor salvation, except to become as good and as wise as possible. For the soul goes to the house of Hades holding nothing else but its education and upbringing; which indeed are said to be the greatest benefit or harm to the one who has died. At the start, the particular guiding spirit which fell to each while living, attempts to lead them to a certain place where those who have been gathered must be judged and then travel to the house of Hades, with that leader who has been appointed to convey those from here to there. Having obtained there what they must obtain, and having remained for the time they must remain, another leader brings them back here again, in many and long periods of time. But the journey is not as Aeschylus's Telephus says.
<margin>B</margin> For he says a simple path leads to the house of Hades; but it appears to me to be neither simple nor one. For then there would be no need of leaders; for surely no one would miss the way anywhere if there were only one road. But now it seems to have many partings and turnings. I say this, judging from the sacrifices and customs here. The orderly and wise soul follows and is not ignorant of its present circumstances; but the soul that desires the body (as I said before), being excited about it for a long time and about the visible place, after much resistance and much suffering, is led away by force and with difficulty by the appointed guiding spirit. When it arrives where the others are,
<margin>C</margin> the one that is impure and has done such things—either having touched unjust murders or having performed other such deeds which are brothers to these and the works of brother souls—everyone flees and turns away from it, and no one wishes to be its fellow-traveler or leader; but it wanders, held in every kind of distress, until certain times have passed; which having passed, it is carried by necessity into the dwelling place befitting it. But the one that has passed through life purely and moderately, and has obtained gods for fellow-travelers and leaders, dwells in the place proper to each.
<margin>D</margin> There are many and wonderful places of the earth; and the earth itself is neither in quality nor size such as it is supposed to be by those who are accustomed to speak about the earth, as I have been persuaded by someone. And Simmias said, "How do you mean this, Socrates? For concerning the earth I myself have heard many things; however, not these things of which you are persuaded. Therefore, I would gladly listen." "But indeed, Simmias, it does not seem to me to be the art of Glaucus to describe what it is; however, as to whether it is true, it seems more difficult to me than according to the art of Glaucus. And at the same time, I perhaps would not even be able; and at the same time, even if I knew, my life, Simmias, seems to me not to suffice for the length of the account. However, the form of the earth, as I am persuaded it is, and its places, nothing prevents me from
<margin>E</margin> telling." "But," Simmias said, "even these things are enough." "I am persuaded then," he said, "that first, if it is in the middle of the heaven being spherical, it needs nothing—neither air to prevent it from falling, nor any other such necessity; but the uniformity of the heaven itself with itself in every way is enough to hold it, and the equilibrium of the earth itself. For an equilibrated thing, placed in the middle of something uniform, will not be able to incline more or less in any direction; but being uniform, it will remain unbending. First then," he said, "I am persuaded of this." "And correctly," said
<margin>F</margin> Simmias. "Furthermore," he said, "that it is something very large; and that we inhabit the part from the Phasis to the Pillars of Hercules in some small portion, like ants or frogs dwelling around the sea; and that many others dwell elsewhere in many such places. For there are everywhere around the earth many hollows, of all kinds both in their forms and sizes; into which the water and the mist and the air have flowed together; but the earth itself, pure, lies in the pure heaven, in which are the stars, which most of those who are accustomed to speak about such things call 'aether.' Of which these things are the sediment, and they flow always into the hollows of the earth. We then, dwelling in its hollows, are unaware of it, and we think we dwell up on the earth. Just as if someone dwelling in the middle of the bottom of the deep sea should think he dwells
<margin>G</margin> on the sea, and seeing the sun and the other stars through the water, should think the sea is heaven; but through slowness and weakness, having never arrived at the surface of the sea, nor having seen—having emerged and poked his head out of the sea into the place here—how much purer and more beautiful it happens to be than those things with them, nor had he heard from another who had seen it. This same thing indeed we also have suffered. For dwelling in some hollow of the earth, we think we dwell above it, and we call the air heaven, as if through this being heaven
<margin>H</margin> the stars move. But the truth is the same: through weakness and slowness we are not able to pass through to the end of the air. Since, if someone should come to the top of it, or becoming winged should fly up, he would see—poking his head up, just as here the fish poking up from the sea see the things here—so someone would see the things there; and if nature were able to endure the sight, he would know that that is the truly heaven and the true light and the truly earth."

<summary>Socrates describes the soul's journey after death, guided by a personal spirit to judgment, while contrasting the "true" earth in the pure aether with the misty hollows where humans reside. He posits that the earth is a sphere held in equilibrium at the center of the universe.</summary>
<keywords>immortality, afterlife, guiding spirit, daemon, geography, spherical earth, equilibrium, aether, myth of the earth, Hades, judgment, Simmias, Socrates</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Socrates' final discourse in the Phaedo. Following his discussion on the soul's journey, he now provides a "likely story" (mythos) describing the physical nature of the Earth and the cosmos, shifting from abstract philosophy to a vivid, poetic geography of the afterlife and the "true" world above our own.</meta>

# PHAEDO

<margin>A</margin> If someone were to be led up to that height, they would recognize that there is the true heaven, the true light, and the truly real earth. For this earth of ours, and its stones and this whole region here, are corroded and eaten away, just as things in the sea are worn down by the brine. Nothing of any worth grows in the sea, nor is anything there perfect, so to speak; there are only caves, and sand, and immeasurable slime and mud wherever there is earth. These are not even remotely worthy of being compared to the beauties found with us. But the beauties of that higher place would seem even more superior to our own. If it is indeed right to tell a beautiful myth <note>Greek: mythos — Socrates uses "myth" here not as a "lie," but as a poetic way to describe truths that exceed human observation</note>, it is well worth hearing, Simmias, what the things upon the earth and beneath the sky are really like. "Indeed," said Simmias, "Socrates, we would very gladly hear this myth." "It is said then, my friend," he replied, "that first of all, the Earth itself, if one were to look at it from above, is seen to be like those twelve-patched leather balls <note>original: dodekaskytoi sphairai — these were balls made of twelve pentagonal pieces of leather, much like the construction of a modern soccer ball</note>, many-colored and distinguished by various hues, of which the colors our painters use here are like samples.

<margin>B</margin> There, the whole earth is made of such colors, and colors even more brilliant and pure than these. For one part is purple, of wonderful beauty; another is gold-colored; another, which is white, is whiter than chalk or snow; and it is composed of all the other colors in the same way, and indeed of more and more beautiful colors than those we have ever seen. For even these very hollows of the earth, being filled with water and air, provide a certain appearance of color, shining amidst the variety of the other colors, so that the earth's form appears as a single, continuous, multicolored surface.

<margin>C</margin> In this earth, being of such a nature, all things grow in proportion—trees, flowers, and fruits. Moreover, the mountains and the stones have, in the same proportion, their smoothness, transparency, and more beautiful colors. Our highly prized little stones here—sardius, jasper, emerald, and all such things—are but fragments of those. But there, there is nothing that is not like them, or even more beautiful. The reason for this is that those stones are pure, and not eaten away or corroded like ours by rot and brine from the things that flow together here, which bring ugliness and disease to stones, earth, and to other animals and plants.

<margin>D</margin> The Earth itself is adorned with all these things, and further with gold and silver and other such metals. For these are naturally visible, being many in number and large, and spread all over the earth, so that to see it is a sight for happy spectators <note>original: eudaimonōn theatōn — literally "blessed onlookers," suggesting the gods or perfected souls</note>. There are many other animals upon it, and men too—some living inland, some around the air as we live around the sea, and some on islands which the air flows around, being near the mainland. In a word, what water and the sea are to us for our needs, the air is to them; and what air is to us, the aether <note>original: aithēr — the "fifth element," a purer, higher form of air associated with the heavens</note> is to them.

<margin>E</margin> Their seasons are of such a temperament that the inhabitants are free from disease and live much longer than those here; in sight, hearing, wisdom, and all such things, they are as far removed from us as air is from water, and aether is from air, in terms of purity. Furthermore, they have groves and temples of the gods, in which the gods truly dwell, and voices, prophecies, and perceptions of the gods, and such direct interactions occur between them. They see the sun, moon, and stars as they truly are, and the rest of their happiness is in accordance with this. Such is the nature of the whole earth and the things around it. But there are also many places within it, in its hollows all around the whole sphere—some deeper and wider than the region we inhabit, others deeper but with a narrower opening than our own region, and some shallower in depth and broader.

<margin>F</margin> All of these are perforated into one another underground in many places, both by narrower and wider channels, and they have passages through which a great deal of water flows from one into another, as if into mixing bowls <note>original: kratēras — large vessels used for mixing wine and water</note>. There are also immeasurable magnitudes of ever-flowing rivers under the earth, both of hot and cold waters, and much fire, and great rivers of fire, and many of liquid mud—some purer and some more foul—like the rivers of mud that flow in Sicily before the lava stream, and the lava stream itself. Each of these places is filled with whatever happens to be flowing into them at any given time.

<margin>G</margin> All these things are moved up and down as if by a certain oscillation <note>original: aiōran — a swing or seesaw motion</note> existing within the earth. This oscillation is due to a certain natural cause: one of the chasms of the earth is remarkably the largest, and it is bored right through the entire earth. This is the one Homer spoke of, saying:

> ->Far, far away, where the deepest abyss lies beneath the earth.<-

This place he elsewhere, and many other poets, have called Tartarus. For into this chasm all the rivers flow together, and from it they flow out again. Each river becomes like the nature of the earth through which it flows. The cause for all the streams flowing out from there and flowing in is that this liquid has no bottom or foundation. Thus it oscillates and waves up and down, and the air and wind around it do the same. For they follow it both when the liquid rushes toward the far side of the earth and when it rushes toward this side. And just as with those who breathe...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...place, they are worn away and corrupted, like those things in the sea which are damaged by saltness. Nothing grows in the sea that is worthy of esteem; and, so to speak, there is nothing perfect in it, but only caverns, sand, incredible slime, and filth wherever there is earth. These things are in no way to be compared to our beauties. But the beauty of that other place will appear to far exceed our own. Therefore, if it is necessary to tell a most beautiful story, it is worthwhile, Simmias, to hear what those regions of the earth are like that lie beneath the heavens. "Indeed," said Simmias, "we would most gladly hear this story." They say then, my friend, he said,

<margin>B</margin> first of all, that the face of that earth, if one looks down from above, appears like those balls which are woven from twelve pieces of leather, distinct with various colors. Our colors here, which painters use, retain a certain likeness to them. But there, the entire earth is made of such colors, and of those much brighter and purer than these: part indeed is purple, endowed with wonderful beauty; part is of a golden color; part is whiter than plaster or snow. Moreover, it is composed similarly of other colors, and even more and more beautiful ones than have ever come to our knowledge. For indeed, these very hollows of the earth, being filled with water and air, bring a certain splendid appearance of color

<margin>C</margin> among the variety of the other colors, so that its appearance always seems as one varied whole. In such an earth, trees, flowers, and fruits grow in a similar, corresponding proportion. Moreover, the mountains and stones there have, in the same way, perfection and transparency, and more beautiful colors. Certain parts of these are the little stones which are held in high price among us—Sards, stones, Emeralds, and others of that kind. But there, there is nothing which is not such, or even more beautiful. The cause of this is that those stones are pure, and not, like ours, eaten and corrupted by rot and brine; for by these flowing together into this place, stones and the earth, animals and plants are infected and forced to become sick.

<margin>D</margin> The Earth itself is adorned with all these things, and also with gold and silver and other similar things. These shining things are born both numerous and large throughout the whole earth, so that to see it is a spectacle for happy spectators. Furthermore, there are many animals there, and men—some inhabiting the midland region, some around the air, just as we live around the shores of the sea, and some even on islands which, being placed not far from the continent, are surrounded by air. But to put it briefly, what water and the sea are to us for our use, the air is the same to them; and what air is to us, the aether is to them. The seasons among them have such a temperament that they live without disease continuously, and far longer than

<margin>E</margin> our people. Likewise, in sight, hearing, prudence, and other such things, they excel us as much as air excels water, and aether excels air in purity. Furthermore, there are temples and groves of the gods, in which the gods truly dwell as familiars, and there are oracles and divinations, and perceptions of the gods, and such familiarities of men with the gods. The sun, too, and the moon and other stars are seen by them as they truly are; and in other matters, they possess a happiness agreeable to these things. Thus, the entire earth is so prepared by nature, and those things which are around it. There are, moreover, in the earth itself, many places in a circle through its hollows, some indeed deeper and wider than the region inhabited by us, some

<margin>F</margin> deeper but having a narrower opening than this region of ours; and there are some elsewhere less deep but wider than ours. All these meet one another under the earth and break through in many ways from every side, both through narrower and wider passages, and have discourses and exits by which a great abundance of waters flows from some into others as if into mixing bowls. Likewise, there are incredible magnitudes of perennial rivers under the earth, of both hot and cold waters, and a great deal of fire, and huge rivers of fire; also many of muddy moisture, some indeed purer, some more filthy, like the torrent of mud which is in Sicily, and the muddy rivers flowing near it.

<margin>G</margin> Each place is filled by these, wherever it happens that they flow through. All these things are carried up and down as if in a hanging vessel placed in the earth (and so balanced that it inclines and raises each side in turn). That hanging vessel exists because of a certain nature of this kind. There is one among the chasms of the earth that is surely the greatest, and it is pierced and open through the entire earth. Concerning this, Homer says: "Far, far away, a deep pit stands beneath the earth." This, both he in other places and many of the poets have called Tartarus. For into this chasm all the rivers flow together, and from it they flow out again.

<margin>H</margin> Such indeed are the individual things, through whatever lands they glide. But the cause of all things flowing out from here and flowing back again is that this liquid has neither a bottom nor a foundation. Therefore, it is elevated and fluctuates up and down. The air and spirit which turn around it do the same. For it follows it both when it glides to the higher parts of the earth and when it glides to these of ours. And just as in those who breathe...

<sig>ll ij</sig>
<meta>catchword: For it follows (Latin: tur enim)</meta>

<summary>Socrates describes the "True Earth" as a vibrant, multicolored sphere where the inhabitants live in the air and aether just as humans live near the sea, contrasting this pure world with our own "corroded" hollows. He also begins a mythical geography of the underworld, describing the great chasm of Tartarus and the subterranean rivers that oscillate through the earth's interior.</summary>
<keywords>Phaedo, Socrates, True Earth, Aether, Tartarus, Myth of the Afterlife, Subterranean Rivers, Homeric Quote, Geography of the Soul</keywords>

--- Page 432 ---
<meta>This page continues Socrates’ mythical geography of the underworld from the previous page. Having described the "hollows" of the earth, he now details the movement of the subterranean waters and the four great rivers that govern the fate of souls after death.</meta>

# OF PLATO

<margin>A</margin> Just as the breath of a living creature continually exhales and inhales in a flowing stream, so there, the spirit <note>original: "spiritus" / "pneuma" — referring to the air or "breath" of the earth</note> being carried along with the moisture, produces certain terrible and incredible winds, whether it is flowing in or out. Therefore, when the water retreats into the place they call the "lower region," it flows into the channels of the earth along those streams and fills them up, much like those who pump water. But when it breaks forth from there and rushes back here, it fills these places once again. When they are full, the water flows through the conduits and the channels of the earth; and as the various fluids flow to those places toward which each has a path prepared, they create seas, lakes, rivers, and springs. <margin>B</margin> From there, they sink back again into the earth, some passing through longer and more numerous windings, others through fewer and shorter ones, and they discharge back into Tartarus <note>The deepest abyss of the underworld</note>: some certainly much deeper than they were drawn out, others only a little, but all flow back in at a lower point than they flowed out. Some flow out on the opposite side from where they entered, while others flow out on the same side. There are some that circle around entirely, coiling around the earth like snakes once or even many times, and having descended as far as possible, they discharge back into the depths. It is possible to descend in either direction as far as the center, but no further; for the descent from either side beyond that would be an uphill climb.

<margin>C</margin> Now, there are many other great and various streams, but among these many, there are four primary ones. The greatest and outermost of these, which flows in a circle around the earth, is called Oceanus <note>The Great Ocean</note>. Opposite this and flowing in the contrary direction is Acheron <note>The River of Woe</note>, which flows through various desert places and, passing under the earth, reaches the Acherusian Lake. This is where the souls of most of the dead arrive; and having stayed there for certain destined periods of time—some longer, some shorter—they are sent back again into the generations of living beings. The third river flows out between these two, and not far from its source, it falls into a vast place burning with much fire, creating a lake larger than our sea, boiling with water and mud. <margin>D</margin> From there, it moves in a circle, turbid and muddy, and winding around the earth, it reaches, among other places, the furthest edge of the Acherusian Lake, though it does not mix with its waters. After coiling many times under the earth, it discharges into a deeper part of Tartarus. This river they call Pyriphlegethon <note>original: "Pyriphlegethontem" — literally "Burning with Fire"</note>, and its fiery streams throw up fragments of lava wherever they happen to touch the earth. <margin>E</margin> Opposite this, the fourth river breaks out first into a place that is wild and savage (so they say), having a color throughout like dark blue <note>original: "cyaneus"</note>; this they call the Stygian region, and the river falling into it creates the Lake Styx. Having fallen here and received terrible powers in its water, it sinks beneath the earth and, coiling around, it moves in the opposite direction to Pyriphlegethon and meets it at the Acherusian Lake from the opposite side. Its water also mixes with no other, but having circled around, it discharges into Tartarus opposite Pyriphlegethon. The poets call this river Cocytus <note>The River of Wailing</note>.

When these things have been so arranged by nature, and the deceased arrive at the place where the guardian spirit <note>original: "daemon" — a guiding spirit assigned to each soul at birth</note> leads each one, they are first judged—both those who have lived noble, holy, and just lives, and those who have not. And so, those who are found to have lived a middle course, having set out for the Acheron and embarked on the vessels provided for them, arrive at the lake. There they dwell and are purified; by paying the penalty for their injustices, they are absolved, and each receives rewards for their good deeds according to their merit. <margin>F</margin> But those who, because of the greatness of their crimes, seem to be incurable—those who have committed many great acts of sacrilege, or many unjust and lawless murders, or other such deeds—these are cast by their fitting fate into Tartarus, from which they never emerge. Those, however, who have committed sins that are deemed great but curable—for instance, if in anger they have committed some act of violence against a father or mother, but have lived the rest of their lives in repentance, or if they have become manslayers in some similar manner—these must necessarily fall into Tartarus. But after they have fallen and stayed there for a year, the wave casts them out: the murderers by way of Cocytus, and the violators of parents by way of Pyriphlegethon. <margin>G</margin> After they have been carried along these rivers and reach the Acherusian Lake, they cry out and call to those whom they either killed or wronged; calling upon them, they beg and entreat that they be allowed to come out into the lake and be received. If they persuade them, they come out and their sufferings cease; but if not, they are carried back into Tartarus and from there into the rivers again, and they do not stop suffering these things until they have persuaded those they wronged. For this is the penalty imposed upon them by the judges.

But those who are found to have lived with exceptional holiness are freed and released from these regions within the earth as if from a prison; they rise to the pure dwelling place above and <margin>H</margin> inhabit the upper earth. Among these, those who have been sufficiently purified by philosophy live entirely without bodies for all time to come, and they reach even more beautiful dwellings than these. The beauty of these is not easy to describe, nor would the present time suffice to tell of it. But for the sake of these things which we have described, O Simmias, we must strive in every way to attain virtue and wisdom in this life; for the prize is beautiful, and the hope is great.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> The spirit breathes out and breathes in as it flows, and so there, the spirit suspended with the moisture produces certain terrible and irresistible winds, both entering and exiting. Whenever the water rushes and retreats into the place called "below," it flows through the earth into those streams and fills them, just like those who pump water. And when it leaves there and rushes back here, it fills the places here again. Once filled, it flows through the conduits and through the earth, and reaching each of the places to which a path is made for each, <margin>B</margin> it creates seas, lakes, rivers, and springs. From there, sinking again into the earth, some traveling through longer and more numerous places, others through fewer and shorter ones, they discharge again into Tartarus; some much lower than where they were pumped out, others only a little. But all flow in below their point of outflow. Some flow out directly opposite where they flow in, and some on the same side. There are some that go entirely in a circle, coiling around the earth once or even many times, like snakes; having wound downward as far as possible, they discharge again. It is possible to descend in either direction as far as the center, but no further, for the ground on either side rises steeply against both streams.

<margin>C</margin> Now there are many other great and varied streams; but among these many, there happen to be four such streams, of which the greatest and outermost, flowing in a circle, is the one called Oceanus. Opposite this and flowing in the contrary direction is the Acheron, which flows through other desert places and, especially, flowing under the earth, reaches the Acherusian Lake. This is where the souls of the many who have died arrive; and having waited for certain destined times, some longer and some shorter, they are sent out again into the births of living beings. A third river flows out between these, and near its point of outflow, it falls into a great place burning with much fire, and it creates a lake <margin>D</margin> larger than our sea, boiling with water and mud. From there it moves in a circle, turbid and muddy; winding around the earth, it reaches other places and also the edge of the Acherusian Lake, without mixing with the water. Having coiled many times under the earth, it discharges lower down than Tartarus. This is the one they call Pyriphlegethon, from which the lava streams blow off fragments wherever they happen to be on the earth. <margin>E</margin> Opposite this, the fourth river falls out into a place that is first terrible and wild (as it is said), having a color altogether like dark blue; this they call Stygian, and the river, falling into it, creates the lake Styx. Having fallen in there and taken on terrible powers in the water, it sinks into the earth and, coiling around, moves in the opposite direction to Pyriphlegethon and meets it in the Acherusian Lake from the opposite side. Its water also mixes with nothing, but this too, having gone around in a circle, discharges into Tartarus opposite Pyriphlegethon. The name for this (as the poets say) is Cocytus.

When these things are so by nature, and the deceased arrive at the place to which the spirit leads each one, they are first judged—those who lived well, holily, and justly, and those who did not. Those who are deemed to have lived a middle life, proceeding to the Acheron and embarking on the vehicles they have, arrive upon them at the lake. There they dwell, and being purified and paying the penalty for their injustices, they are released if anyone has committed an injustice; and they receive honors for their good deeds, each according to his merit. <margin>F</margin> But those who are deemed to be incurable because of the magnitude of their sins—either having committed many great acts of sacrilege, or many unjust and lawless murders, or any other such deeds—these their fitting fate throws into Tartarus, from which they never emerge. Those who are deemed to have committed sins that are curable but great—such as doing some act of violence against a father or mother in anger, and living the rest of their lives in repentance, or becoming murderers in some other such way—these must necessarily fall into Tartarus. Having fallen in and been there for a year, <margin>G</margin> the wave casts them out: the murderers by way of Cocytus, and the strikers of fathers and mothers by way of Pyriphlegethon. When, as they are being carried along, they reach the Acherusian Lake, they cry out and call—some to those they killed, others to those they wronged. Having called them, they supplicate and beg them to let them come out into the lake and to receive them. And if they persuade them, they come out and cease from their evils; but if not, they are carried back into Tartarus and from there again into the rivers. They do not stop suffering these things until they persuade those they wronged; for this was the justice set for them by the judges.

But those who are deemed to have lived exceptionally in holiness, these are the ones who are freed and released from these regions in the earth as if from prisons, and reaching the <margin>H</margin> pure dwelling above, they settle upon the earth. Among these, those who have been sufficiently purified by philosophy live entirely without bodies for the time to come, and they reach even more beautiful dwellings than these, which it is not easy to describe, nor is the time sufficient at present. But for the sake of these things we have discussed, Simmias, one must do everything so as to partake of virtue and wisdom in life; for the prize is beautiful, and the hope is great.

<summary>Socrates describes the subterranean rivers of the underworld (Oceanus, Acheron, Pyriphlegethon, and Cocytus) and the subsequent judgment of souls based on their earthly conduct. He concludes that the pursuit of philosophy and virtue is the only way to secure a blessed existence in the afterlife.</summary>

# PHAEDO

ll iij <note>This is a "signature mark," a printer's code used in early modern books to help binders assemble the pages in the correct order.</note>

<margin>A</margin> ...to share in such a life. For the prize is noble, and the hope is great. Now, to insist that these things are exactly as I have described them does not befit a man of sense. However, that either this or something very much like it is the truth regarding our souls and their habitations—since the soul clearly appears to be immortal—this, I think, is a fitting belief and a risk worth taking for one who thinks as I do. For the danger is a noble one, and one should, as it were, sing such truths to oneself like an incantation <note>original: "ἐπάδειν" (epadein) / "carmina". Socrates suggests that these philosophical myths act as "charms" to soothe the fear of death.</note>. This is why I have spent so much time lengthening this myth. But for these reasons, a man should be of good cheer regarding his own soul, if during his life he has said farewell to the other pleasures—those of the body and its adornments—viewing them as alien and thinking they do more harm than good. Instead, he should have busied himself with the pleasures of learning, <margin>B</margin> and having adorned his soul not with a borrowed beauty but with its own proper jewels—temperance, justice, courage, freedom, and truth—he thus awaits his journey to the underworld, ready to depart whenever fate calls. Now you, Simmias and Cebes and the rest, will each make this journey at some later time. But as for me, "fate now calls me" (as a tragic poet might say), and it is almost time for me to head to the bath. For it seems better to drink the poison after bathing, so as not to give the women the trouble of washing a corpse.

<margin>C</margin> When he had said this, Crito spoke: "Very well, Socrates. But what instructions do you have for these others or for me, concerning your children or anything else? What could we do that would be of most service to you?" "Nothing new, Crito," he replied, "just what I am always telling you: if you take care of yourselves, whatever you do will be a service to me and mine and to yourselves, even if you make no promises now. But if you neglect yourselves and are unwilling to live your lives following the tracks, so to speak, of what we have said both now and in the past, then no matter how many or how fervent the promises you make today, you will accomplish nothing." "We shall certainly strive to do as you say," Crito replied. "But in what manner shall we bury you?" <margin>D</margin> "However you like," said Socrates, "provided you can catch me and I do not escape you." Then, laughing quietly and looking at us, he said: "Friends, I cannot convince Crito that I am this Socrates who is now conversing and arranging each part of the argument. He thinks I am that one whom he will see as a corpse a little later, and so he asks how he should bury me. But the long argument I have been making—that when I drink the poison I will no longer remain with you, but will go away to some state of happiness belonging to the blessed—this, it seems to me, I say to him in vain, though I say it to comfort both you and <margin>E</margin> myself. You must therefore give a guarantee for me to Crito, the opposite of the guarantee he gave to the judges. He guaranteed that I would stay; but you must guarantee that I will not stay after I die, but will depart and go away. I want Crito to bear it more easily, and not to grieve for me as if I were suffering something terrible when he sees my body being burned or buried. Nor should he say at the funeral that he is laying out Socrates, or carrying him out, or interring him. For you should know well, my dear Crito, that to use words wrongly is not only a fault in itself, but it also creates some evil in our souls. No, you must be of good cheer and say you are burying my body; and you may bury it in whatever way is pleasing to you and which you think most lawful."

<margin>F</margin> Having said this, he rose and went into another room to bathe, and Crito followed him; but he told us to wait. So we waited, talking among ourselves about what had been said and examining it again. At other times we spoke of the misfortune that had befallen us, feeling quite simply as if we had been deprived of a father and would spend the rest of our lives as orphans. When he had bathed, his children were brought to him—he had two small sons and one grown—and the women of his household arrived. He spoke to them in Crito’s presence and gave them his final instructions, then he told the women and children to leave, and he returned to us. <margin>G</margin> It was now near sunset, for he had spent a long time inside. He came and sat down, freshly bathed, and not much was said after that. Then the officer of the Eleven <term>The Eleven</term> <note>The board of officials in Athens responsible for the prison and executions.</note> entered. He stood beside Socrates and said: "Socrates, I will not find the same fault in you that I find in others, who are angry with me and curse me when I announce, at the orders of the magistrates, that they must drink the poison. During this time I have found you to be the noblest, the gentlest, and the best man of all who have ever come to this place. And now, I am sure you are not angry with me—for you know who are really to blame—but with them. Now you know the message I have brought. Farewell, and try to bear what is necessary as easily as you can." And bursting into tears, he turned and went out. Socrates looked up at him and said: "Farewell to you, too; we will do as you say." Then, turning to us, he said: "What a charming man! Throughout my time here he has visited me and sometimes talked with me, and he has been the kindest of men. See how nobly he weeps for me now. <margin>H</margin> But come, Crito, let us obey him. Let someone bring the poison if it has been ground; if not, let the man grind it." But Crito said: "I think, Socrates, the sun is still on the mountains and has not yet set. I know of others who drink it quite late, long after the order has been given, having dined well..."

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> For the reward is indeed beautiful, and the hope is immense. To assert that these things are exactly as I have set them forth does not befit a man of sound mind; yet that either these things or something similar exists regarding our souls and their dwellings—since the soul itself appears immortal—seems to me both proper and worthy for one to believe, even as a risk. For the danger is honorable, and it is necessary to pour these things into our minds like certain great songs or incantations. For this reason, I have long protracted this story. But for the sake of these things, he who has neglected the pleasures and ornaments of the body as if they were alien, thinking he would accomplish something else more important, and has studiously followed the pleasures perceived in learning, ought to have good hope for his soul. <margin>B</margin> He will have decorated his soul not with a foreign ornament, but with its own: temperance, justice, fortitude, liberty, and truth. Thus he awaits the migration from this life, ready to depart whenever fate calls. You indeed, O Simmias and Cebes, and the others present, will each depart at some time in the future. But for me, as some tragic actor might say, fate now calls. And it is almost time that I turn to the bath. For it is better, I think, to bathe before drinking the poison, so that we do not cause trouble for the women in washing the corpse.

<margin>C</margin> When Socrates had said these things, Crito spoke thus: "Tell me, O Socrates, what do you command these others or me to do, either regarding your sons or concerning other matters? By doing what would we most gratify you?" "I prescribe nothing new," he said, "but what I always preach to you: namely, if you have a care for yourselves, whatever you do will turn out to be pleasing to me, to mine, and to yourselves, even if you do not promise it now. But if you neglect yourselves, being unwilling to direct your life according to those things which have been said now and in the time before, as if following tracks, you will accomplish nothing at all, even if you promise many things to us now." <margin>D</margin> Crito said, "Those things will indeed be our care. But in what way do you command that you be buried?" "As you please," he said, "if indeed you can catch me, and if I do not escape you." And smiling at the same time, and having turned toward us, he said, "I cannot persuade Crito that I am this Socrates who now disputes and arranges each spoken word. Rather, he thinks I am that which he will see a little later as a corpse. And so he asks how he should bury me. But that which I have long contended with many words—that after I drink the poison, I shall no longer be among you, but shall set out for the happiness of the blessed—this I seem to have said in vain to Crito, though I was consoling both you and <margin>E</margin> myself. Therefore, give a guarantee to Crito on my behalf, with a certain guarantee contrary to that which he himself gave to the judges. For he guaranteed that I would stand before the court; but you must guarantee that I will not remain once I have died, but will depart, so that Crito may bear my death more easily, and not lament me as if I were suffering dire things when he sees my body either being burned or buried. Nor should he say at the funeral that Socrates is being laid out, or carried out, or placed under the earth. For hold this as certain, most excellent Crito: that to not perceive correctly is not only to err in this very thing, but also to do some harm to souls. Instead, one must be confident and say that my body is being buried, and that it is buried in such a way as will please you and as you shall judge most just."

<margin>F</margin> Having said these things, he rose and entered a certain chamber as if to bathe. Crito followed him, but he ordered us to wait. We waited, therefore, talking among ourselves about those things which had been said, and considering them again. Moreover, we were recounting how great a calamity had befallen us: that we, as if deprived of a parent, were to spend the remainder of our lives as orphans. When Socrates had washed, his boys were brought to him (for he had two small sons, and one already grown). The women of the household also came. When Socrates had spoken to them in Crito's presence and had commanded what he wished, he ordered the women and boys to depart, and he himself returned to us. It was already around sunset, for he had stayed inside for a very long time. <margin>G</margin> When he had come to us having bathed, he sat down. Not many things were said after this before the officer of the Eleven came. Standing by him, he said, "O Socrates, I do not notice in you what I do in others. For they are indignant with me and curse me when I announce to them that the poison must be drunk as the magistrates compel. But I have known you, especially in this time, to be the most generous, the most gentle, and the best man of all who have ever come into this place. And now indeed I know for certain that you are not angry with me, but with those in whose hands you know the cause of this matter lies. Now therefore, you know what message I bring to you. Farewell, and strive to bear what is necessary as easily as your strength allows." And having said these things, he departed weeping. But Socrates, looking back at him, said: "Farewell to you also, and we shall do it." And at the same time, turning to us, he said: "How civil this man is! Not only in this, but in the time before he used to greet me and sometimes converse, and he was always the best of men. And now how nobly he laments me! <margin>H</margin> But come, O Crito, let us obey him, and let someone bring the poison here if it is already ground. If it is not yet ground, let that man grind it." "But I think indeed," Crito said, "O Socrates, that the sun has not yet left the mountains nor set. And I know others who, after it was announced to them, were accustomed to drink it very late, after they had dined sumptuously..."

# PLATO'S WORKS

<margin>A</margin>...and drinks, and sometimes even enjoying the company of those they happen to love. Therefore, do not hurry; there is still time." Then Socrates said, "Rightly indeed, O Crito, do those men act as they do. For they believe they gain something by doing so. And I, rightly, shall not do those things. For I expect to gain nothing by drinking the poison a little later, except to make myself ridiculous in my own eyes, as if I were clinging to life and being stingy with something of which nothing remains to me. But come now, obey me, and do not act otherwise." When Crito heard this, he signaled to the boy who was standing nearby. The boy went out and, after staying away for some time, returned, bringing with him the man who was to give the poison, which he carried ready-ground in a cup. Seeing him, Socrates said, "Well, my good man—for you have expertise in these matters—what must I do?" "Nothing else," he replied, "but to walk around after drinking until you feel a heaviness in your legs, and then lie down; and in this way, it will take effect." Saying this, he handed the cup to Socrates. Socrates took it quite cheerfully, O Echecrates, without trembling at all, and with no change in color or expression. But looking at the man with his usual bull-like gaze <note>original: "taurinè" / "ταυρηδὸν" (taurēdon). This describes Socrates’ habit of looking up from under his brow with a steady, intense stare.</note>, he asked, <margin>B</margin> "Is it permitted to pour a libation to someone from this drink?" "We have ground only as much, Socrates," he replied, "as we thought would be enough." "I understand," he said. "But it is both permitted and necessary to pray to the gods that our migration from here to there may be a happy one. This indeed I pray, and may it be so." And as he spoke these words, he raised the cup and drank it off right readily and calmly. Up until then, most of us had been able to hold back our tears reasonably well. But when we saw him drinking and having finished the drink, we could do so no longer; rather, in my case, grief so overcame me that my tears flowed in floods. Therefore, covering my face, I wept for myself—not for him, <margin>C</margin> indeed, but for my own fortune, in that I had been deprived of such a friend. Crito, even before me, had risen up when he could not contain his tears. But Apollodorus had never ceased weeping even in the time before this. Then, however, wailing aloud and grieving, he left no one present whose heart he did not break, except for Socrates himself. But Socrates, noticing this, said, "What are you doing, O wonderful men? Indeed, I sent the women away chiefly for this reason, that they might not do such things. For I have heard that one should die in peace and praise. Be quiet, therefore, and endure." When we heard this, we were ashamed and stopped weeping. But he, when he felt his legs grow heavy <margin>D</margin> while walking, lay down on his back; for so the man who gave the poison had directed. A little later, the man touched him and examined his feet and legs. Then, pressing his foot hard, he asked if he felt anything. Socrates said no. After this, he pressed the shins, and moving upward with his hand, he showed us that he was growing cold and stiff. And he touched him again, saying that when it reached his heart, then he would depart. Now his lower belly was almost cold when, uncovering himself—for he had been covered—he spoke what was his final word: "O Crito, we owe a cock to Asclepius; pay the debt, and do not neglect it." <note>Asclepius was the god of healing. By offering a rooster (cock), Socrates suggests that death is a "cure" for the sickness of earthly life.</note> <margin>E</margin> "It shall be done," said Crito, "as you command. But see if you wish for anything else." To this question, he answered nothing further. But after a short time had passed, he stirred. And the attendant uncovered him, and his eyes were fixed. When Crito saw this, he closed his mouth and eyes. This was the end of our friend, O Echecrates—a man who, in our judgment, was the best of all those we have ever known, and moreover, the wisest and most just.

# MENEXENUS, OR,
## THE FUNERAL ORATION.

**SUMMARY OF THE DIALOGUE.** Plato’s purpose is to exhort everyone to the highest love of their country; this he achieves in two ways. First, while he praises those who intrepidly undergo dangers and death for the safety of the fatherland. Second, while he himself extols the antiquity and virtues of his country with wondrous praises. The sum of the discourse, therefore, comes to this: that everyone should willingly prefer the safety and preservation of their country to all things, even to their own life, and should consider those blessed who have shed their blood for such causes, for whom both praise and eternal reward remain.

->SOCRATES, MENEXENUS.<-

<margin>F</margin><image-desc>An ornamental capital letter E showing a classical figure sitting in a landscape with Roman-style buildings in the background.</image-desc>Does Menexenus come from the forum? Or from where? "From the forum, Socrates, and from the Senate." SOCRATES: Why were you at the Senate? Is it perhaps because you think you have reached the end of your education and philosophy, and so you are eager to move on to greater things, and even though you are younger, to rule over us elders...

<column-break/>

...and drinkers, very much so, or having been with some of those they happened to desire. But do not hurry at all. For there is still time." And Socrates said, "Naturally, O Crito, those men do these things which you say (for they think they will gain by doing them), and I naturally will not do these things. For I think I will gain nothing by drinking a little later, other than to incur ridicule in my own eyes, by clinging to life and being sparing when nothing is left. But go," he said, "obey me and do not do otherwise." And Crito, hearing this, signaled to the boy standing nearby. And the boy, going out and spending a long time, came bringing the one who was to give the drug, carrying it ground in a cup. Seeing the man, Socrates said, "Well, my best man (for you are knowledgeable of these things), what must one do?" "Nothing else," he said, "than having drunk, walk around until a weight comes into your legs; then lie down." And so he will do it. And at the same time, he reached out the cup to Socrates. And taking it, and very graciously, O Echecrates, without trembling, and without changing either his color or his countenance, but as he was accustomed, looking bull-like at the man, he said, "What do you say about this drink, regarding making a libation to someone? Is it permitted or not?" "We grind just so much, Socrates," he said, "as we think to be the right amount." "I understand," he said; "but to pray to the gods is surely permitted and necessary, that the migration from here to there be fortunate; which indeed I pray, and may it be so." And at the same time as saying these things, holding it to his lips, very easily and calmly he drank it off. And most of us for a time were fairly able to hold back from weeping; but when we saw him drinking and having drunk, no longer. But for me, even against my will, the tears came in floods; so that covering myself, I wept for myself. For not indeed for him, but for my own fortune, of what a man and companion I had been deprived. Crito, even before me, since he was not able to hold back his tears, stood up. Apollodorus, even in the time before, had not ceased from weeping, and indeed then, crying out, weeping and grieving, there was no one of those present whom he did not break down, except for Socrates himself. But he said, "What things you are doing, O wonderful men. I indeed, not least for this reason, sent the women away, so that they might not misbehave in such a way. For I have heard that one must die in auspicious silence. But keep quiet and endure." And we, hearing this, were ashamed and held back from weeping. And he, having walked around, when he said his legs were heavy, lay down on his back. For so the man ordered. And at the same time, this man who gave the drug, touching him, after a period of time, examined his feet and legs. And then, pressing his foot hard, he asked if he perceived it. And he said he did not. And after this again the shins; and going up in this way, he showed us that he was becoming cold and stiff. And he himself touched him, and said that when it came to his heart, then he would be gone. Now already the parts around his abdomen were nearly cold; and uncovering himself (for he had been covered), he said what was indeed the last thing he uttered: "O Crito, we owe a cock to Asclepius. But pay it, and do not neglect it." "But these things shall be," said Crito. "But see if you have anything else to say." When he asked this, he answered nothing more; but after a short time, he stirred; and the man uncovered him; and his eyes were fixed. Seeing this, Crito closed his mouth and eyes. This was the end, O Echecrates, of our companion, a man, as we would say, of those then whom we experienced, the best, and otherwise the most prudent and most just.

# MENEXENUS.

<margin>A</margin>
...they have arrived so appropriately for themselves, so that your house may never lack someone to provide us with an advisor. If you yourself, O Socrates, allow me to lead and counsel, I shall strive to do so; but if not, I shall not. Now, however, I have come to the Council Chamber, having heard that the Council is about to choose someone to speak over those who have died. For you know they are intending to perform the funeral rites.
**SOCRATES.** Indeed, O Menexenus, it seems that in many ways it is a fine thing <note>original: "καλὸν εἶ" / "praeclarum esse". Socrates uses the word "kalon," meaning beautiful or noble, with a touch of his characteristic irony.</note> to die in war. For a man receives a funeral both beautiful and magnificent; and even if he dies as a poor man, he still obtains praise; and even if he were of little account, he is praised by wise men who do not offer praise randomly, but in speeches prepared over a long time. They praise so beautifully that, by describing both the qualities that belong to each man and those that do not, and by adorning them somehow most beautifully with words, they bewitch our souls. They praise the city in every way, and those who have died in the war, and all our ancestors of old, and even us who are still living, so that I myself, O Menexenus, feel quite noble when praised by them. Each time, I stand listening and enchanted, imagining myself in that moment to have become greater, more noble, and more beautiful. And as is often the case, some foreigners follow me and listen with me, in whose eyes I suddenly become more venerable. For they seem to me to feel the same way both toward me and toward the rest of the city, considering it more wonderful than before, being persuaded by the speaker. And this sense of dignity remains with me for more than three days; so vividly does the speech and the voice of the speaker ring in my ears and dwell there, that only on the fourth or fifth day do I remember myself and realize where on earth I am. Until then, I almost believe I am living in the Isles of the Blessed <note>original: "μακάρων νήσοις" / "beatorum insulas". In Greek mythology, this was the paradise reserved for heroes and the virtuous.</note>. Such is the skill of our rhetoricians.
<margin>C</margin>
**MENEXENUS.** You are always mocking the rhetoricians, Socrates. However, this time I think the one chosen will not be at all at a loss for what to say. For the choice has been made quite suddenly; therefore, the speaker will perhaps be forced to improvise. **SOCRATES.** Why, my good man? Each of them has speeches prepared long ago. Besides, it is not difficult to improvise on such subjects. If one had to speak well of Athenians among the Peloponnesians, or of Peloponnesians among Athenians, one would need a good rhetorician to persuade and be esteemed. But when someone competes among the very people he is praising, it is no great feat to seem to speak well. **MENEXENUS.** You do not think so, Socrates? **SOCRATES.** Not at all, by Zeus. **MENEXENUS.** Do you think you would be able to speak yourself, if it were necessary and the Council chose you? **SOCRATES.** For me, Menexenus, it would be no wonder to be able to speak, since I happen to have a teacher who is not at all mediocre in rhetoric, but the very one who has produced many other good speakers, and one who stands out among the Greeks: Pericles, the son of Xanthippus. **MENEXENUS.** Who is she? Surely you mean Aspasia? <note>Aspasia of Miletus was a highly educated woman and the partner of the statesman Pericles. She was famous for her intellectual brilliance, though as a woman and a foreigner, she could not hold political office herself.</note> **SOCRATES.** I do indeed; and also Connus, the son of Metrobius. For these are my two teachers: one of music, the other of rhetoric. It is no wonder that a man raised thus should be clever at speaking. Even someone educated less well than I—perhaps taught music by Lamprus and rhetoric by Antiphon the Rhamnusian—could still win esteem by praising Athenians among Athenians. **MENEXENUS.** And what would you have to say, if you were required to speak? **SOCRATES.** From myself, perhaps nothing; but only yesterday I heard Aspasia reciting a funeral oration for these very people. For she had heard what you say, that the Athenians were about to choose a speaker. Then she went over with me partly what should be said on the spot, and partly what she had considered before—when, I believe, she was composing the funeral oration which Pericles delivered, patching together some remnants from that one. **MENEXENUS.** Could you remember what Aspasia said? **SOCRATES.** I should hope so, unless I am mistaken. For I learned it from her, and I nearly received a beating whenever I forgot. **MENEXENUS.** Why then do you not recount it? **SOCRATES.** But I fear my teacher might be angry with me if I make her speech public. **MENEXENUS.** Not at all, Socrates; but speak, and you will do me a great favor, whether you wish to speak the words of Aspasia or of anyone else; only speak. **SOCRATES.** But perhaps you will laugh at me, if I seem to you, at my age, to be still playing. **MENEXENUS.** Not at all, Socrates; but speak by all means. **SOCRATES.** Indeed, I must gratify you; so much so that even if you ordered me to strip and dance, I would gratify you, since we are alone. But listen. For she began speaking, I believe, starting from the dead themselves, in this way:
"In deed, these men have what is fitting for them; having obtained which, they travel the fated journey, sent forth publicly by the city and privately by their kin. In word, the law commands that the remaining honor be paid to these men, and it is right to do so. For when deeds have been well performed, through a speech beautifully spoken, memory and honor are bestowed upon the doers..."

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
...to be in charge, so that your family, as it has always been accustomed, may always provide us with some counselor? **MENEXENUS.** If you yourself permit it, O Socrates, and advise that I should preside, I will give my effort; but if otherwise, by no means. Now, however, I have set out for the Senate <note>original: "Senatum". The Latin uses Roman political terminology for the Greek "Boule" (Council).</note>, because I had heard that someone must be chosen to adorn the deceased with praises. For, as you know, they are about to perform the funeral rites. **SOCRATES.** I have heard indeed, but whom especially have they chosen? **MENEXENUS.** No one. For they have postponed it until tomorrow. I think, however, that Archinus or Dion will be chosen.
<margin>B</margin>
**SOCRATES.** It seems, Menexenus, among many nations it is a very noble thing to fall in war. For he who thus departs from life is honored with a most magnificent funeral and tomb. And even if a poor man dies in this way, he does not lack a eulogy; or even if someone is lowly and cowardly, he is again extolled by wise men, who—not rashly, but with a speech composed and prepared over much time—praise so excellently that while they proclaim of someone both what is true and what is not, they deceive the minds of the listeners with the elegance of their words, as if by some sorcery or witchcraft. Meanwhile, they also adorn the City in every way, and they weave again the origin of our ancestors and those who fell in arms. They also extol us who are still living. For which reason, I myself, Menexenus, having been praised by them, somehow conceive something noble about myself: and when I give my ears to them everywhere, I am soothed by a wonderful sweetness, and immediately I consider myself greater, more noble, and more beautiful than before. And frequently some guests hear these things with me, and I am rendered more excellent in their presence than before. Indeed, the same thing seems to happen to them as to me, both toward me and toward the rest of the city. For, persuaded by the orator, they think the city more wonderful than before. And this glorious beauty remains with me for more than three days. So harmonious a speech and a melodious voice, flowing from the mouth of the orator, is poured into my ears, that only on the fourth
<margin>D</margin>
or fifth day afterward do I remember myself, and recognize where on earth I am. Then, however, I think myself all but inhabiting the Isles of the Blessed; so great is the dexterity with which our rhetoricians are endowed.
<margin>C</margin>
**MENEXENUS.** You always mock the rhetoricians, O Socrates. Now, however, I fear that for him who is chosen, the faculty of speaking may be lacking. For the choice has happened quite suddenly. Therefore, whoever is about to speak will perhaps be forced to make words somewhat unexpectedly. **SOCRATES.** Why, O good man? For each of them has had speeches composed for this purpose for a long time. Moreover, it is not difficult to speak of these matters without meditation. For if it were necessary to praise Athenians in the Peloponnese, or Peloponnesians in Athens, then an eloquent
<margin>E</margin>
orator would be needed, who would both persuade and be approved. But when someone exercises himself among those whom he also praises, it is certainly not difficult to speak well. **MENEXENUS.** Do you think that is easy, Socrates? **SOCRATES.** Indeed, by Jove! **MENEXENUS.** Do you hope that you could speak, if there were need, and you were chosen by a decree of the Senate? **SOCRATES.** What wonder, Menexenus, that I should be sufficient for speaking, who have obtained a mistress by no means unskilled in Rhetoric, who has rendered many other orators eloquent, and one the most excellent of all Greeks, the son of Xanthippus, Pericles? **MENEXENUS.** Who is that woman? Surely you mean Aspasia? **SOCRATES.** Both her I mean, and the son of Metrobius, Connus. For these two are my teachers:
<margin>F</margin>
Connus indeed of Music, but Aspasia of Rhetoric. Thus, therefore, it is no wonder for an erudite man to be eloquent. Nay, even if someone were less well-taught than I—having been taught music by Lamprus and rhetoric by Antiphon the Rhamnusian—he could still, by praising Athenians among Athenians themselves, so speak that his speech would be approved by the listeners. **MENEXENUS.** What do you have that you might bring forward, if you had to speak? **SOCRATES.** From myself, perhaps nothing. But yesterday I heard Aspasia herself dictating a funeral oration about these things. For she had heard what you yourself were saying, that the Athenians would choose someone to have a speech for them. Then, setting forth to me partly what was to be said unexpectedly, and partly, in my judgment, things premeditated, she wove together a funeral oration,
<margin>G</margin>
(which Pericles spoke) composing certain remains from that one. **MENEXENUS.** Would you not remember what Aspasia said? **SOCRATES.** Indeed, unless I were unjust. For I learned it from her, and it was nearly the case that she would have beaten me with blows on account of my forgetfulness. **MENEXENUS.** Why then do you not repeat it? **SOCRATES.** I fear lest my mistress be somewhat angry with me if I publish her speech. **MENEXENUS.** By no means, Socrates. But gratify me, whether it pleases you to say the speech of Aspasia or that of anyone else; only speak. **SOCRATES.** Perhaps you will laugh at me, if as an old man I still seem to be joking. **MENEXENUS.** By no means, O Socrates; but speak by all means. **SOCRATES.** I must yield to you. For almost if you ordered me to dance naked, since we are alone, I would obey. But hear now. For in this manner, as I think, she began to speak, taking the beginning from the deceased themselves.
"IN DEED itself, these just things have been done for them among us, which they having now attained, perform their fatal journey, sent forth as much publicly by the city as privately by their own with magnificent expense and a frequent gathering. But the law commands the praise of the city to be returned to them, and indeed it is fitting. For when deeds have been well performed, from the very adornment of words..."

Socrates ironically praises the power of such speeches to enchant the audience and claims that he could deliver one himself, having been taught by the famous intellectual Aspasia.</summary>
