<meta>This page continues the dialogue of the Menexenus, specifically the beginning of the "funeral oration" that Socrates claims to have learned from Aspasia. It transitions from the introductory remarks to the formal speech honoring the fallen soldiers of Athens.</meta>

# OF PLATO

...to those who have delivered it, lasting memory and splendor arise among the listeners. Such a speech is needed which sufficiently praises the deceased, kindly advises the survivors, and exhorts their children and brothers to the imitation of their virtue: and also consoles their parents and any other elders who may survive. What speech, then, will serve us in this way? Or from where shall we best begin to praise these noble men, who while living delighted their own people through their personal virtue, and did not hesitate to offer themselves to death for the safety of the living? It seems to me, therefore, appropriate to praise them according to their nature, just as they became good men; and they became good because they drew their origin from good ancestors. Therefore, let us first praise their noble lineage; then their education and discipline. Finally, let us recount that their deeds were performed in a manner most becoming to those who were of such descent and were subsequently so educated.

The first praise of their race is that the origin of their ancestors was not foreign, nor did it leave these successors here as if they were tenants or new men born from foreigners. Instead, they were indigenous <note>original: "indigenas" / "autochthones". This refers to the Athenian belief that they were born directly from the soil of their land, rather than migrating from elsewhere.</note> and truly dwelling in their fatherland, living and nourished not by a stepmother, as others are, but by their own mother—the very region which they inhabited. In this land they are now buried after completing their lives, resting in the bowels of her who bore them, nourished them, and received them back. For it is right to honor the mother herself before all things, for in this way their race is most greatly adorned. 

Furthermore, this region is to be celebrated not only by us but by all men, for many other reasons and especially because it is most dear to the Gods. The contest and judgment of the Gods concerning this land <note>Refers to the mythological contest between Athena and Poseidon for the patronage of Athens.</note> bears witness to this. Why should a land praised by the Gods not be praised by all mankind? Another praise for it is that at the time when the earth was producing all kinds of animals, both wild beasts and herds, our land alone was sterile of such things and free from wild animals. Instead, from all living creatures, it specifically brought forth man, who excels others in intelligence and alone observes justice and the Gods. 

That this region produced both our ancestors and those whom we celebrate in this assembly can be most evidently known from this: that everything which gives birth contains nourishment suitable for the offspring. By this, a woman who has given birth is clearly discerned from one who has substituted a child; for she who has given birth abounds in milk for the nourishment of the child, while the other does not. Our land and mother thus provides a clear proof that she procreated humans. For she alone and first at that time produced human nourishment—the fruits of wheat and barley—by which the human race is most conveniently fed, seeing that she truly produced that living being. It is more fitting to judge the earth by the woman than the woman by the earth; for the earth does not imitate the woman in conception and birth, but the woman imitates the earth. 

She did not distribute this fruit sparingly but shared it with other men as well. After this, she supplied oil to her children as a help for their labors. When her sons were nourished and grown to adulthood, she brought in Gods as rulers and teachers for them. Their names should be omitted for now; for we know well who they were that secured our life, both through the invention of arts for daily living and by the tradition and skill of arms for the protection of the region itself. Thus born and educated, their ancestors established a Commonwealth, of which it is right to speak briefly. For a commonwealth is the upbringing of men—a good one for the good, and the opposite for the bad. It must be shown, therefore, that our ancestors were nurtured in a noble Commonwealth, through which both they and these men were good, including those who have now departed from life. 

For the Commonwealth was the same then as it is now: an aristocracy <note>original: "aristocratia". Plato here provocatively describes the Athenian democracy as a "meritocracy" or "rule of the best" with the people's consent.</note>, under which we live in these times and nearly always since that period. Some call it a democracy, others whatever they please; but it is in truth a government by the best with the dignity of the people. For we always have leaders, sometimes created by succession of lineage, sometimes by election; but the greatest power in the city lies with the people, who always grant magistracies and power to those who are judged to be the best. Here, no one is rejected because of the weakness, poverty, or obscurity of their parents, nor honored for the opposite reasons as is common in other cities. But this is the rule: whoever is held to be wise or good, rules and commands. 

The cause of this government for us is the equality of our birth. For other cities are composed of various and dissimilar races; thus their governments are unequal—tyrannies and powers of the few. In those cities, men live regarding one another partly as masters and partly as slaves. But we and our people, all born as brothers from one mother, do not think ourselves to be masters or slaves of one another; but our equality of birth leads us to seek equality under the law, and to yield to nothing else except the reputation of virtue and wisdom. Therefore, both our parents and those of these men, being honorably born and nurtured in total liberty, performed many noble deeds known to all nations, both privately and publicly, thinking that for the sake of liberty they must fight against Greeks for the sake of other Greeks, and against barbarians for the sake of all the Greeks.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...becomes worthy in the eyes of the listeners. There is need of some such speech which will sufficiently praise those who have died, and will kindly exhort those who live—encouraging the descendants or brothers to imitate the virtue of these men, and consoling the fathers and mothers and any who are left of the older relatives. What speech, then, would appear to us to be of such a kind? Or from what point might we rightly begin praising good men, who while living gladdened their own people through virtue, and exchanged their end for the salvation of the living?

<margin>B</margin> It seems to me necessary, according to nature, just as they became good, so also to praise them. And they became good because they were born from good people. Let us therefore first extol their noble birth; second, their nourishment and education; and after these things, let us demonstrate the performance of their deeds, showing how nobly and worthily of these beginnings they displayed them. As for their noble birth, there was first the origin of their ancestors, which was not that of a foreigner, nor did it show these descendants to be mere residents in the land who had come from elsewhere, but rather indigenous ones (*autochthones*), truly living and dwelling in their fatherland, and being nourished not by a stepmother, as others are, but by the mother-land in which they lived, where they now lie in their own places after dying—the land that bore them, nourished them, and received them back. It is most just to first adorn their mother, for thus the noble birth of these men is adorned at the same time. And this

<margin>C</margin> land is worthy to be praised by all men, not only by us, for many other reasons, but first and greatest because she happens to be beloved by the gods. The strife and judgment of the gods who contended over her bears witness to our word. Which land the gods praised, how is she not justly praised by all mankind? A second praise would justly be hers because at that time when the whole earth was bringing forth and producing all kinds of living things, both beasts and plants, at that time our land appeared sterile and pure of wild beasts, but she chose and brought forth man, who excels the others in intelligence and alone acknowledges justice and gods. A great proof of this argument is that this earth bore the ancestors

<margin>D</margin> of these men and our own. For everything that gives birth has nourishment suitable for what it has brought forth. By this, a woman is also shown to have truly given birth or not—if she has no springs of nourishment for the child, she has substituted it. This our land and mother provides sufficient proof that she gave birth to humans. For she alone and first at that time bore human nourishment, the fruit of wheat and barley, by which the human race is most beautifully and best nourished, since she herself truly brought forth this living being. It is more appropriate to accept such proofs for the earth than for a woman. For the earth has not imitated the woman in pregnancy and birth, but the woman has imitated the earth. Of this fruit she was not envious, but

<margin>E</margin> shared it with others. After this, she brought forth for her descendants the birth of the olive, a help for labor. Having nourished and raised them to youth, she brought in gods as rulers and teachers for them; whose names it is fitting to omit in such a place, for we know those who established our life, being the first to teach the arts for daily living, and teaching the possession and use of arms for the guard of the land. Being thus born and educated, the ancestors of these men lived having established a constitution, which it is right to mention briefly. For a constitution is the nourishment of men—a noble one for the good, the opposite for the bad. As our predecessors were raised in a noble constitution, it is necessary to show that through this they were good, as are those now, among whom are these who have died.

<margin>F</margin> For the constitution then was the same as it is now, an aristocracy, in which we now live as citizens and have for all time since then for the most part. One man calls it a democracy, another something else, whatever he pleases; but it is in truth an aristocracy with the approval of the multitude. For we always have kings; these were sometimes by birth, sometimes by election. But for the most part, the multitude is in control of the city; it gives the offices and power to those who always seem to be the best. And no one is driven away by weakness, or poverty, or the obscurity of fathers, nor is anyone honored for the opposites, as in other cities; but there is one limit: he who is thought to be wise or good holds power and rules. The cause

<margin>G</margin> for us of this constitution is our equal birth. For other cities are composed of all kinds of men and are unequal; therefore their constitutions are also unequal, both tyrannies and oligarchies. They live, therefore, some considering each other slaves and others masters; but we and our people, all being brothers born of one mother, do not think it right to be slaves or masters of one another; but our natural equality of birth compels us to seek legal equality according to the law, and to yield to each other in nothing else except the reputation of virtue and wisdom. Whence it is that, having been raised in total liberty, the fathers of these men and our own, and these men themselves, being

<margin>H</margin> nobly born, displayed many noble deeds to all men both privately and publicly; thinking that they ought to fight for liberty both against Greeks for the sake of Greeks, and against barbarians for the sake of all the Greeks.

<summary>In this portion of the Menexenus, Socrates delivers a funeral oration celebrating the Athenian dead, emphasizing their "autochthony" (being born from the soil) and their meritocratic government as the sources of their superior virtue.</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Aspasia, Menexenus, funeral oration, epitaphios, autochthony, Athenian democracy, aristocracy, meritocracy, equality of birth, Greek patriotism</keywords>

--- Page 437 ---
<meta>This page continues the funeral oration attributed to Aspasia in Plato's Menexenus. The speaker moves from the origins of the Athenian people to their legendary and historical military achievements, specifically their role in defending Greece against the Persian Empire.</meta>

# MENEXENUS

<margin>A</margin> Indeed, regarding the time when Eumolpus and the Amazons invaded our land, and those even earlier who repelled them, and how our ancestors defended the Argives against the Cadmeans <note>The "Cadmeans" refers to the people of Thebes, founded by the mythical Cadmus.</note> and the Heraclidae <note>The "Heraclidae" were the descendants of Hercules who sought refuge in Athens.</note> against the Argives—the time is too short to recount these deeds as they deserve. The poets have already beautifully celebrated their virtue through music and song, making them known to everyone. Therefore, if we were to attempt to adorn these same deeds with bare prose, we might perhaps appear to take second place. For these reasons, I think it best to pass over those matters, especially since they have already received their due honor. <margin>B</margin> But regarding those deeds for which no poet has yet received worthy fame for worthy actions, and which still lie in the shadow of forgetfulness, it seems to me that I must make mention of them, praising them and introducing them to others, so that they might be set into songs and other forms of poetry in a manner befitting those who performed them.

Of the deeds I speak of, these are the first: the ancestors of this land, our own parents, were the first to restrain the Persians when they ruled over Asia and were enslaving Europe. It is both right and necessary to remember them first and to praise their virtue. One must look at that virtue as it was manifested in that time, when all of Asia was already enslaved to a third king. The first of these, <margin>C</margin> Cyrus, having freed his own fellow citizens, the Persians, by his own great spirit, simultaneously enslaved the Medes who had been their masters, and ruled the rest of Asia as far as Egypt. His son <note>This refers to Cambyses II, though he is not named here.</note> then advanced upon Egypt and as much of Libya as was possible to reach. The third king, Darius, defined his empire by land as far as the Scythians, and by sea he mastered both the waters and the islands, so that no one even presumed to be a rival to him. The very minds of all men had been enslaved; so many great and warlike nations had the Persian empire brought into subjection.

Darius then brought charges against us and the people of Eretria, using the pretext that we had plotted against Sardis. He sent five hundred thousand men in transports and ships, with three hundred warships, and appointed Datis as commander. <margin>D</margin> He told Datis to return bringing the Eretrians and Athenians as captives if he wished to keep his own head on his shoulders. Datis sailed to Eretria against men who were among the most famous of the Greeks of that time in matters of war, and who were not few in number. He overpowered them within three days. He searched their entire territory so that no one might escape, using this method: his soldiers, reaching the borders of Eretria and stretching from sea to sea, joined hands and passed through the entire land <note>This "netting" tactic involved soldiers forming a human chain to sweep an area and ensure no inhabitants were left behind.</note> so that they could report to the king that not a single person had escaped them. With this same intention, they landed from Eretria at Marathon, believing it was a simple matter for them to lead the Athenians away under the same yoke of necessity as the Eretrians.

While some of these deeds had been accomplished and others were being attempted, <margin>E</margin> no one among the Greeks came to the aid of either the Eretrians or the Athenians, except for the Lacedaemonians <note>The Lacedaemonians are the Spartans.</note>—and they arrived only on the day after the battle. All others were struck with terror, and being content with their own safety for the present moment, they remained still. In such a situation, one might recognize what kind of men they were in their virtue, those who received the force of the barbarians at Marathon and humbled the pride of all Asia. They were the first to set up trophies of victory over the barbarians, becoming leaders and teachers to others, showing that the power of the Persians was not invincible, but that every multitude and all wealth must yield to virtue. I say, then, <margin>F</margin> that those men were not only the fathers of our bodies, but also of our freedom and the freedom of all who live on this continent. For it was by looking back at that deed that the Greeks dared to risk the later battles for their safety, becoming the disciples of those who fought at Marathon.

The first prize of excellence in our speech must be awarded to them; the second prize to those who fought and won the sea-battles at Salamis and Artemisium. One could recount many things about these men—the kinds of dangers they endured by both land and sea, and how they repelled them. But I shall mention what seems to me the most beautiful thing about them: that they completed the work started by the men of Marathon. <margin>G</margin> For the men at Marathon had only demonstrated to the Greeks that it was possible to repel the barbarians by land, a few against many; but on the sea, it was still uncertain. The Persians held a reputation for being invincible at sea through their numbers, wealth, skill, and strength. Therefore, the men who fought the sea-battles then are worthy of praise for dissolving the innate fear of the Greeks and making them stop fearing the multitude of ships and men. It happened that through both groups—those who fought at Marathon and those who fought the sea-battle at Salamis—all other Greeks were educated: <margin>H</margin> they were taught and accustomed by the former on land, and by the latter on the sea, not to fear the barbarians.

I say that the deed at Plataea was the third in both number and virtue to bring about the safety of Greece, and this was now a shared achievement of the Lacedaemonians and the Athenians. All these men repelled the greatest and most difficult danger, and because of this virtue, they are now praised by us, and will be by those in the time to come. After this, however, many Greek cities were still under the barbarian, and it was reported that the King himself...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Truly, in what way they helped the Argives once against the Cadmeans, and the descendants of Hercules against the Argives, when Eumolpus and the Amazons, and even those before them, invaded the region—it is too narrow a time to report this according to its dignity. Their poets, elegantly celebrating their virtue through Music, have made it known among all nations. Therefore, if we were to attempt to repeat these same things in naked discourse <note>Latin: "nudo sermone," referring to prose as opposed to the "clothed" or adorned language of poetry.</note> now, we might perhaps seem to be second to them. Therefore, I think these things should be omitted for this reason, since <margin>B</margin> they already seem to be celebrated enough according to their dignity. But those things which have not yet been sung by any of the poets as the dignity of the events requires, and which no one has yet rescued from oblivion—these I think must now be proclaimed by us, so that we may praise them and help them, and provoke others to the same through odes and other poems, as is fitting to adorn them.

Of those things which I say, these are the first: when the Persians ruled Asia and were dominating Europe, the men of this region were the first to stop them—our ancestors. It is both necessary and becoming to remember them and to praise their virtue in the first place. It is especially necessary if anyone is to rightly praise the things done by them at that time, when all Asia already served a third king. The first of these, Cyrus, by a certain greatness <margin>C</margin> of spirit, restoring his fellow citizens the Persians to liberty, at the same time subjected their masters the Medes, and ruled over all Asia as far as Egypt. His son also ruled Egypt and Libya, as far as it was possible to advance. The third, Darius, extended his empire by a land battle as far as the Scythians. By naval force, he was master of the sea and the islands. Thus it happened that no one dared to resist him. Indeed, the minds of all men had already been cast down by a certain servile dread; so many, so great, and so warlike nations were held under the Persian empire.

Darius, however, accusing us and the Eretrians as if we were envious of Sardis, and having found this occasion for war, sent five hundred thousand men in fleets, and indeed three hundred ships; <margin>D</margin> he put Datis in charge of these, and commanded him to bring the Eretrians and Athenians to him as captives if he wished his own head to be safe. He, having been carried by ships to Eretria—where there were not a few men, and who moreover were numbered among the most illustrious of the Greeks of those times in warlike matters—made them captives in three days, and explored the whole region so that there was no place for anyone to escape; namely, in this way: His soldiers, having set out to the borders of Eretria and extending themselves from sea to sea, and running to meet each other with hands joined, traversed the entire region, so that they could report to the king that no one had escaped them. With the same plan, they descended from Eretria to Marathon, as it was most suitable to them for this: <margin>E</margin> that they might lead the Athenians away as captives together with the Eretrians, as if under the same yoke.

But while these things were partly accomplished and partly attempted, none of the Greeks except the Lacedaemonians brought aid to the Eretrians or Athenians. And they came on the day following the battle. All others were terrified, and thinking it went well with them if they escaped the present danger, they remained still. From this one may behold how great their virtue was, they who sustained the attack of the barbarians at Marathon and tamed the pride of all Asia. They were the first to triumph over the barbarians and showed by example to the rest that the force of the Persians was not at all invincible; rather, indeed, that every multitude <margin>F</margin> and abundance of riches obey virtue. I think those men existed not only as the parents of our bodies, but also as the authors of our liberty, both ours and of all who inhabit this region. For provoked by these examples, the later Greeks did not hesitate to undergo all dangers for their safety in the following wars, being truly the disciples of those who routed the Persians at Marathon.

Therefore, it is fitting to attribute the first palm of the oration to them, and the second to those who conquered the enemy in a naval battle around Salamis and Artemisium. Indeed, we could tell of many things done by these men—how many dangers they sustained and overcame, threatening by land and sea. But what I think is excellent above the others, <margin>G</margin> I will now report. For what remained after the Marathonian war, they perfected. Indeed, those who fought at Marathon only demonstrated this much to the Greeks: that in a land battle, a few Greeks could break the attack of many barbarians. But concerning a maritime victory, it was still uncertain. The Persians were thought to be invincible in maritime battles, both in multitude and riches, and in skill and strength. This, therefore, is worthy of praise in those who fought in ships then: that they utterly drove away the fear implanted in the Greeks, and made it so that they no longer feared the number of ships and men. By both of these groups it was brought about—as much by those fighting on land at Marathon as by those on the sea <margin>H</margin> afterwards around Salamis—that the rest of the Greeks were both taught and became accustomed, by the former on land and by the latter at sea, not to fear the barbarians.

I assert the third thing that was done at Plataea—which, in both number and virtue, stood as the cause of the safety of Greece. This is now common to both the Lacedaemonians and the Athenians. They performed the greatest and most difficult deed. On account of that virtue, they are praised both now by us and here...

<summary>In this portion of the funeral oration, the speaker recounts the heroic defense of Greece against the Persian Empire, highlighting the Battles of Marathon, Salamis, Artemisium, and Plataea as the foundation of Greek liberty. The text emphasizes that these victories proved that Persian wealth and numbers were no match for Athenian and Greek virtue.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the funeral oration in Plato's Menexenus. While the previous page focused on the Persian Wars (Marathon and Salamis), this page recounts the military history of Athens following those events, moving into the Peloponnesian War and the internal civil conflicts, emphasizing Athenian virtue even when fighting fellow Greeks.</meta>

-># PLATO<-

<margin>A</margin> ...about to invade the Greeks again. It is surely right to remember those men who put the finishing touch on the work of salvation started by their predecessors, having cleared and driven out every trace of the barbarians <note>original: "barbariem" / "τὸ βάρβαρον" - The Greeks used 'barbarian' to refer to any non-Greek speaker, specifically the Persians here.</note> from the sea. These were the men who fought the naval battle at the Eurymedon, those who campaigned in Cyprus, and those who sailed to Egypt and many other coastal lands. We must remember them and be grateful to them, for they compelled the terrified King <note>The King of Persia.</note> to look to his own safety rather than plot the destruction of the Greeks. This war was sustained by the whole city for the sake of themselves and all others who spoke the same language <note>original: "homines aduerfus barbaros" / "ὁμοφώνων" - highlighting the shared Greek language as a unifying factor against the Persians.</note> against the barbarians. <margin>B</margin> But when peace was finally made and the city was held in high honor, there arose against her that which usually falls upon successful men: first emulation, and from emulation, envy. This envy dragged our city, albeit unwillingly, into a war against fellow Greeks. After this war began, they clashed at Tanagra, fighting against the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans and their allies.</note> for the liberty of the Boeotians. Although the outcome of that battle was uncertain, the event that followed clarified the matter. For while many fled, deserting the Boeotians whom they were supposed to help, our men won a victory at Oenophyta on the third day and justly restored those who had been unjustly exiled. These were the first men after the Persian War to aid Greeks against Greeks for the sake of liberty; having proved themselves brave men and liberators of those they helped, they are the first to be honored by the city in these tombs for our remembrance. <margin>C</margin> After these events, as the war grew more intense and all the Greeks invaded and ravaged the land—returning an unworthy "thanks" to our city—our people defeated them in a naval battle and captured their leaders, the Lacedaemonians, at Sphagia <note>original: "Sphagia" / "Σφαγίᾳ" - likely referring to the victory at Sphacteria during the Peloponnesian War.</note>. Though they had the opportunity to put them to death, they spared them, gave them back, and made peace. They believed that against one's own race <note>original: "homines eiuſdem generis" / "τὸ ὁμόφυλον"</note>, one should fight only until victory is achieved, and that the common bond of the Greeks should not be destroyed because of the private anger of a city; but against the barbarians, the struggle should be to the death. <margin>D</margin> It is right, therefore, to praise these men who lie here after that war, because they showed that if anyone doubted Athenian virtue in the first war against the barbarians—thinking others were superior to the Athenians—their suspicions were false. For here it was demonstrated, when Greece was stirred by civil strife, that they overcame the leaders of the other Greeks in war, conquering by themselves those with whom they had previously conquered the barbarians together. <margin>E</margin> A third war, unexpected and severe, arose after this peace, in which many brave men fell who are buried here. Many of them raised numerous trophies of victory around Sicily, fighting for the liberty of the Leontines <note>Athens sent a massive expedition to Sicily (415–413 BCE) to aid the city of Leontini.</note>, whom they were bound by oath to help. But because of the length of the voyage, the city fell into difficulty and was unable to supply them; because of this failure of support, they met with misfortune. In this case, their enemies and opponents in war received more praise for their moderation and virtue than the friends of others usually do. Many others also fought in the naval battles at the Hellespont, capturing all the enemy's ships in a single day and winning many other victories. <margin>F</margin> I called this war "unexpected and severe" because no one would have believed that the rest of the Greeks would reach such a height of contention against our city as to dare to send ambassadors to that most hated barbarian King—whom they had once expelled with us—to bring him back to attack Greeks, and to gather all Greeks and barbarians alike to besiege this city. It was here that the power and virtue of this city shone most brightly. For when people thought she had already been defeated in war, and her ships were blockaded at Mitylene, our citizens went to their aid with sixty ships. Having boarded the ships themselves and proved themselves undeniably brave men, they defeated the enemy and liberated their friends. But because they met with an unworthy fate—not being recovered from the sea <note>referring to the aftermath of the Battle of Arginusae, where a storm prevented the rescue of sailors, leading to a famous trial in Athens.</note>—they lie here. <margin>G</margin> We must always remember and praise them. For by their virtue we won not only that naval battle, but the rest of the war as well. Because of them, our city gained such a reputation that it was believed she could never be conquered, not even by all mankind together. And indeed, that appeared to be true. For we were not overcome by the strength of others, but by our own internal dissensions. Even now we remain undefeated by foreigners; it was we who conquered ourselves and brought defeat upon ourselves. <margin>H</margin> After these times, when all was quiet and peace was made with others, a domestic civil war <note>original: "inteſtina ſeditio" / "ὁ οἰκεῖος ἡμῖν πόλεμος" - referring to the conflict between the supporters of the Thirty Tyrants and the democrats.</note> broke out among us. It was fought in such a way that, if it were fated for men to suffer from civil strife, no one would pray for their city to suffer in any other way. For how kindly and like kinsmen did the citizens from the Piraeus and those from the City mingle with one another, contrary to the expectations of the rest of the Greeks! And how moderately did they settle the war sparked against those at Eleusis! The cause of all this was nothing other than true kinship, which provides a firm and twin friendship not in words, but in deeds. We must also keep in memory those who fell by each other's hands in this war, and to reconcile...

<column-break/>

...about to set out again to attack the Greeks. It is right that we mention these men too, who placed the finishing touch of salvation upon the works of their predecessors by purging and driving out all the barbarians from the sea. These were those who fought at sea at the Eurymedon, and those who campaigned in Cyprus, and those who sailed to Egypt and many other places. We must remember them and be grateful to them because they made the King, out of fear, pay attention to his own safety rather than plot the destruction of the Greeks. And this war the city sustained throughout, for themselves and for others of the same speech against the barbarians. But when peace came and the city was honored, there came upon it what is prone to happen to men who are doing well: first zeal, and from zeal, envy. This placed even this city, against its will, in a state of war with the Greeks. After this, when war broke out, they joined battle at Tanagra, fighting against the Lacedaemonians for the liberty of the Boeotians; and the battle being contested, the later work decided it. For the others went away, leaving behind the Boeotians whom they were helping; but our men, winning on the third day at Oenophyta, justly restored those who were unjustly fleeing. These were the first after the Persian War to help Greeks for the sake of liberty against Greeks, and having become good men and having liberated those they helped, they lie in these tombs, being the first honored by the city in this remembrance. After these things, when a great war arose and all the Greeks invaded and cut up the land, paying back an unworthy "thanks" to the city, our men defeated them in a naval battle and took their leaders, the Lacedaemonians, at Sphagia. Although it was permitted to destroy them, they spared them and gave them back and made peace, thinking that against one's own race one should fight until victory, and not destroy the commonality of the Greeks because of a city's private anger; but against the barbarians, until destruction. These men are worthy of praise, who fought this war and lie here, because they showed—if anyone disputed whether in the previous war against the barbarians there were some others better than the Athenians—that they disputed what was not true. For these men were shown here, when Greece was in revolt, to be superior in the war, having subdued the leaders of the other Greeks, with whom they then conquered the barbarians in common, having now conquered them privately. A third war after this peace was both unexpected and terrible, in which many good men died and lie here; many having set up the most trophies around Sicily for the liberty of the Leontines, whom they sailed to those places to help because of oaths. But because of the length of the voyage, the city being placed in a state of difficulty and not being able to serve them, they were unfortunate, failing in this. Their enemies and those who fought against them have more praise for self-control and virtue than the friends of the others. And many were in the naval battle at the Hellespont, in one day taking all the ships of the enemies and defeating many others. What I said about the war being terrible and unexpected, I mean this: that the other Greeks came to such a point of rivalry against the city that they dared to send heralds to the most hateful King—whom they had cast out in common—to bring him back again privately against Greeks, a barbarian against Greeks, and to gather against the city all the Greeks and barbarians. Where indeed the strength and virtue of the city became manifest. For when people thought she was already fought down, and her ships were cut off in Mitylene, aiding with sixty ships, they themselves embarking on the ships and becoming admittedly the best men, winning against the enemies and releasing their friends, meeting with an unworthy fate and not being taken up from the sea, they lie here. Whom it is necessary to always remember and praise. For by their virtue we conquered not only the naval battle then, but also the rest of the war. For because of them the city had the reputation that she could never be fought down, not even by all men, and it seemed to be true. We were mastered by our own difference, not by others. For we are even now undefeated by them; but you yourselves both conquered us ourselves and we were defeated. After these things, when there was quiet and peace with the others, our domestic war was fought in such a way that if it were fated for men to revolt, no one would even pray for his own city to be sick in any other way. For from the Piraeus and from the city, how gladly and as kinsmen the citizens mixed with one another, and beyond the hope of the other Greeks, they settled the war against those in Eleusis with such moderation. And of all these things there is no other cause than the genuine kinship, providing a firm and racial friendship not in word but in deed. It is necessary also to have a memory of those who died in this war at each other's hands, and to reconcile...

It emphasizes that Athens fought for Greek liberty, spared fellow Greeks even in victory, and was ultimately only "defeated" by its own internal divisions rather than foreign enemies.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the funeral oration from Plato's Menexenus, moving from the victory over the Persians to the complex internal conflicts among the Greek city-states (such as the Peloponnesian and Corinthian Wars). The speaker highlights Athens’ role as a constant, if sometimes overly merciful, defender of Greek liberty against both Spartan aggression and Persian influence.</meta>

->## MENEXENUS<-

<margin>A</margin> ...in whatever way we can, just as we honor them with sacrifices at these ceremonies, since we ourselves have now been reconciled. For it was not through mutual malice that they fought, nor through hatred, but through misfortune. We who are still living are witnesses to this: being of the same nature as those who fell, we grant one another forgiveness for what we did and what we suffered. After this, when a total peace was established, our city remained quiet. She forgave the barbarians <note>The Persians.</note> because, having suffered enough at her hands, they had defended themselves quite vigorously. But she was indignant with the Greeks <note>Specifically the Spartans and their allies.</note>, remembering how they had been treated well by her and yet returned such "thanks"—joining with the barbarians, taking away the ships that had once saved them, and tearing down the walls <margin>B</margin> that we had built to prevent their own walls from falling. The city then resolved no longer to defend any Greeks who were being enslaved by one another or by barbarians. This was our state of mind. But while we were of this opinion, the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans.</note> believed that we, the guardians of liberty, had fallen, and that it was now their task to enslave the rest; and so they acted. Why should I make a long story of it? What followed are not ancient events, nor things done many generations ago. We ourselves know how the leading Greeks—the Argives, Boeotians, and Corinthians—came in terror to need the help of this city. And most miraculous of all, even the Great King <note>The King of Persia.</note> reached such a point of desperation that he feared his safety could come from nowhere else but this very city which he had so zealously tried to destroy. <margin>C</margin> Indeed, if anyone wished to bring a just accusation against the city, he could only rightly say this: that she is always too full of mercy and is a servant to the weaker side. In that time, she was unable to remain firm or hold to her previous resolution—to give no aid to those who had wronged her when they were being enslaved. Instead, she was moved, and she gave help. By her aid, she rescued the Greeks from slavery so that they were free until they enslaved themselves once again. To the Great King, however, she did not dare to give official aid, out of respect for the trophies of Marathon, Salamis, and Plataea <note>Famous Athenian victories over the Persians.</note>. But by allowing only exiles and volunteers to help him, she undeniably saved him. After rebuilding her walls and ships, and <margin>D</margin> accepting the war when she was forced to fight, she waged war against the Lacedaemonians on behalf of the Parians. But the Great King grew afraid of our city when he saw the Lacedaemonians giving up the war at sea. Wishing to desert his allies, he demanded the Greeks on the mainland—the very ones the Lacedaemonians had previously handed over to him in exchange for an alliance with us and the other allies. He thought we would refuse, giving him a pretext for his desertion. In this, he was deceived by his other allies; for the Corinthians, Argives, Boeotians, and other allies were willing to hand them over. They made an agreement and swore an oath to surrender the Greeks of the mainland if he would provide money. But we alone did not have the heart <margin>E</margin> to surrender them or to take that oath. Thus, the noble and free spirit of this city is firm and healthy, naturally hating the barbarian because we are pure Greeks, unmixed with barbarian blood. No descendants of Pelops, nor of Cadmus, nor of Egyptus or Danaus <note>Socrates lists mythological founders of other Greek cities who were said to have foreign/barbarian origins, contrasting them with the "pure" earth-born Athenians.</note>, nor many others who are barbarians by nature but Greeks by law, live among us. We are pure Greeks who live here, not of mixed-barbarian stock. Therefore, a pure hatred of alien natures has been bred into our city. Nevertheless, we were isolated once again because we refused to perform the shameful and unholy act of surrendering Greeks to barbarians. Yet, having fallen back into the same conditions that led to our previous defeat, <margin>F</margin> with God’s help, we concluded the war better than before. For we retained our ships, our walls, and our own colonies, and so we were freed from the war—a conclusion the enemy was also glad to accept. Yet we were deprived of brave men in this war too: those at Corinth who suffered from the difficult terrain, and those at Lechaeum who were lost through treachery. Brave, too, were those who liberated the Great King and drove the Lacedaemonians from the sea. I remind you of these men, and it is fitting that you join in praising and honoring such heroes.

These, then, were the deeds of the men lying here, and <margin>G</margin> of all the others who have died for the city. Many noble things have been said, but many more and even finer things remain; for many days and nights would not suffice for one who wished to recount everything. Remembering these things, every man must exhort the descendants of these heroes, as if in a battle, not to leave the rank of their ancestors nor to retreat through cowardice. I myself, therefore, O children of brave men, now exhort you, and in the future, whenever I meet any of you, I shall remind you and urge you to strive to be the best. <margin>H</margin> At present, it is my duty to say what our fathers commanded us to report to those they left behind, should anything happen to them, when they were about to face danger. I will tell you what I heard from them, and what they would now gladly...

<meta>The final lines of the left column bridge into the next page of the Latin translation, indicating a transition to the speech that the fallen soldiers would address to their sons.</meta>
...and it is right for you to repeat what your fathers commanded us... I will therefore recount to you at this time what [I heard] from those very men...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...as best we can, to reconcile them with one another through prayers and sacrifices performed for those who survived, since we too have been reconciled. For they did not join hands in battle out of wicked enmity, but out of a certain misfortune. Of this, we who survive are ourselves witnesses. Since we are joined to them by kin, we mutually give and receive forgiveness for whatever we either inflicted upon others or suffered from them. Then, when the city was resting in the greatest tranquility, she forgave the barbarians because, having been attacked by her, they had fought back bravely enough. But she was indignant with the Greeks because they had once returned injury for benefits received, entering into <margin>B</margin> alliances with the barbarians, plundering the ships by which they had been saved, and dismantling the walls by which we had once protected their own fortifications from falling. Thus the city decided she would no longer defend the Greeks if they were ever oppressed by other Greeks or by barbarians. While we were in this frame of mind, the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans.</note> thought that we, the defenders of liberty, had fallen, and that it would henceforth be their job to subjugate the others; and so they did. What need is there for many words? For I would not be speaking of ancient things or events from many centuries ago. It is no secret to us that the foremost of the Greeks—the Argives, Boeotians, and Corinthians—implored the help of this city in their terror. And what is most divine of all, <margin>C</margin> the King himself <note>The Persian King.</note> was reduced to such difficulty that he believed his safety could be secured from nowhere else but this city, which he had tried with all his might to destroy. Truly, if anyone wished to rightfully accuse this city, he could only object to this: that she is always moved by too much mercy and is too diligent in lifting up the fallen. In that crisis, she could not endure to keep to her previous resolution. She had indeed decreed that she would never help any of those from whom she had received injury when they were falling. Yet she changed her purpose and provided aid. Thus she liberated the Greeks from slavery with her help, so that they lived as free men until they subjugated each other once more. To the King, however, <margin>D</margin> she did not dare to bring aid; for she feared the triumphs previously reported from Marathon, Salamis, and Plataea. But while she allowed exiles and volunteers to favor him, she saved him too without controversy. Having built walls and constructed ships, and having undertaken the war when she was forced to wage it, she fought against the Lacedaemonians for the safety of the Parians. But the King, fearing our city after he saw the Lacedaemonians refusing the naval war, and wishing therefore to desert them, demanded the Greeks who were on the mainland—the very ones the Lacedaemonians had previously handed over so that he would fight with us and the other allies. He thought this would be denied him, giving him an opportunity to desert us. There he was deceived by his other allies; <margin>E</margin> for the Corinthians, Argives, Boeotians, and the rest of the allies were willing to hand them over, and they agreed by taking an oath that if he would give money, they would hand over those Greeks who were on the mainland. We alone, at that time, dared neither to hand them over nor to take the oath. So noble, free, constant, and pure is the custom of this city; and her nature is hostile to barbarians because these men are pure and whole Greeks without any mixture of barbarians. For there are no Pelopians, or Cadmians, or Egyptians, or Danaans mixed among us—those who are barbarians by nature and Greeks only by law—but we ourselves, being only Greeks, persist without any infection of barbarian confusion. <margin>F</margin> Indeed, this purity produced in this city a hatred against an alien race. We alone remained pure in this regard, because we refused to commit a base and profane deed by handing Greeks over to the hands of barbarians. Returning then to those matters from which we were first defeated, with God's favor, we waged war more successfully than before. For retaining our ships, walls, and colonies, we were freed from the war; even the enemies themselves ceased quite willingly. Nevertheless, we lost brave men in this war too, some intercepted at Corinth by the roughness and narrowness of the region, others defeated by treachery at Lechaeum. <margin>G</margin> Famous also were the men who liberated the King and expelled the Lacedaemonians from the sea. These I recall to your memory. It is fitting for you to praise and celebrate such men. And indeed, these deeds of the men lying here, and of all others who died for their country, which have been related, are many and noble; but those that remain are far more and more excellent. Indeed, many days and nights would hardly suffice if one wished to embrace them all. These things being recalled to memory, it is necessary for every man to constantly exhort the sons of these men to keep the rank of their ancestors as if in war, <margin>H</margin> and not to flee through cowardice. Indeed, O sons of excellent men, I myself both exhort you now and in the future, whenever I encounter any of you, I will always admonish and encourage you to strive to turn out as well as possible. Now, however, it is right for me to proclaim to those left behind what our fathers charged us to say, should anything happen when they were facing danger. I will therefore recount to you at this time what I heard from them, and what they would now gladly say to you themselves if the opportunity were given...

<summary>This page of the Menexenus recounts Athens' complex role in the post-Persian War era, emphasizing her "over-compassionate" nature in defending fellow Greeks—and even the Persian King—against Spartan hegemony, while boasting of the Athenians' "pure" non-barbarian lineage.</summary>
<keywords>Athenian exceptionalism, Corinthian War, Spartan aggression, Persian King, pure lineage, funeral oration, Marathon, Salamis, Plataea, Lechaeum</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the "speech of the dead" within Plato's Menexenus. In the previous section, the speaker recounted the history of Athenian military triumphs and sacrifices. Now, the orator adopts the persona of the fallen soldiers themselves, addressing their surviving children and parents with a final exhortation on virtue, honor, and the proper way to mourn.</meta>

# PLATO
## THE MENEXENUS

<margin>A</margin>
...they would command, at least as far as I can gather from what they used to say. Imagine now that you are hearing those very men speaking, or that they began their discourse in this way: "O children, the present circumstances bear witness that you are born of noble parents. Indeed, though it was permitted for us to live dishonorably, we preferred to die with honor, rather than subject you and our other descendants to any infamy, or bring disgrace upon our parents and ancestors—thinking that for a man who disgraces his own, life is not worth living. For such a man has no friend, neither among men nor gods, in life or after death. You must, therefore, be mindful of our words; if you practice anything else, practice it with virtue, knowing that without virtue, all pursuits and possessions are shameful and evil.
<margin>B</margin>
For riches bring no splendor to the one who possesses them with cowardice; such a man does not gain wealth for himself, but for another. Neither do beauty of body and strength, when they belong to the timid and base, appear as a grace. For they are unbecoming to him, making his cowardice more known and exposing it. Furthermore, knowledge that is removed from justice and other virtues is seen as cunning <note>original: "calliditas"</note>, not wisdom. For these reasons, first and last and through everything, strive with all zeal and diligence to surpass both us and our ancestors in the glory of virtue.
<margin>C</margin>
Otherwise, know that if we surpass you in virtue, this victory will bring us shame; but if we are surpassed by you, it will bring us happiness. We shall be most truly surpassed, and you shall be the victors, if you order your lives in such a way that you do not abuse the glory of your ancestors, nor, so to speak, squander it. For you must know that for a man who thinks himself to be something, nothing is more shameful than to offer himself to be honored not for his own virtue, but because of the glory of his predecessors. For the glory of parents is a noble and magnificent treasure for their children. But to use a treasure of money and honors, and not to hand it down to one's descendants through a lack of one's own possessions and glory, is shameful and utterly foreign to a man of noble character.
<margin>D</margin>
If you practice these things, then when the fates of your life are fulfilled, you will come to us as dear children to dear parents. But if you neglect these things and turn out to be wicked, no one will receive you gladly. Let these things be said to our children.
<margin>E</margin>
But as for our fathers and mothers, if any of ours survive and stand in need of consolation, it is right to comfort them, for it is proper to bear whatever happens with ease, and their lot must not be lamented with them. They will not need the lamentations of others, for their own fate will bring them enough sadness. Indeed, one must heal and soothe them, and above all remind them that the gods have already granted the greatest of the things they used to pray for. For they did not pray that their children be immortal, but that they be good and illustrious. They have obtained this wish, which must be considered the greatest good. It is not easy for a mortal man to have everything in life turn out according to his wish.
<margin>F</margin>
Yet, if they endure bravely with a brave heart, they will truly seem to be the parents of brave sons and to be brave themselves. But if they succumb to grief, they will lead people to suspect either that they are not our parents at all, or that those who praise us are lying. Neither of these should happen; rather, they should be our chief praisers in deed, showing themselves to be truly the fathers of men. Indeed, that ancient proverb, "Nothing in excess," <note>original: "Ne quid nimis" / "Μηδὲν ἄγαν". This was a famous maxim inscribed at the Temple of Apollo at Delphi, urging moderation.</note> seems to have been wisely spoken. For he who has all things necessary for living well dependent upon himself, and does not hang suspended upon others—neither wandering nor forced by the outcome of another's good or bad fortune—he has prepared the best way of living. This is the temperate man, this is the brave man, this is the wise man; he will obey that ancient precept most of all regarding children, whether they are born or pass away, as with all other worldly goods. He will never rejoice too much, nor mourn too much, who always places all the hope of his welfare in himself.
<margin>G</margin>
We judge and desire that our people should be like this. And indeed, in the present moment, we show ourselves to be such—certainly not troubled or terrified by excessive fear, even if we must now depart from life. We also pray that our fathers and mothers will spend their future lives in a similar state of mind, knowing that they will not please us most with lamentations and wailing. Rather, if there is any sense of the living among those who have died, we would be most troubled if they should destroy themselves and bear their lot with hardship. But if they bear it with moderation and lightness, they will please us most. Our lives have now reached that end which is most beautiful for men. Therefore, they should be praised rather than wept for. Truly, if they protect and nourish our wives and children, and devote themselves to them, they will best consign their misfortune to oblivion and lead lives that are more beautiful, more upright, and more pleasing to us.
<margin>H</margin>
It will suffice to proclaim these things to our families in our name. To the City, we command that it take care of our parents and our sons—that it educate the latter honorably and cherish the old age of the former with dignity. We know, however, even if we did not command these things, that you will take excellent care of them. These things, then, O children and parents of the dead, they have charged us to remind you. And I, as much as I am able, most diligently remind you, and in their name I beseech the younger ones to...

For the honors of parents are for their offspring a beautiful and magnificent treasure; but to use a treasure of wealth and honors and not to hand it down to one's offspring is shameful and unmanly, for lack of one's own possessions and good name.
<margin>D</margin>

<margin>E</margin>

Instead, by healing and soothing them, remind them that the gods have been listeners to the greatest of their prayers. For they did not pray that their children be born immortal, but good and famous; and these they have obtained, being the greatest of goods. It is not easy for a mortal man for everything to turn out according to his mind in his own life. And by bearing their misfortunes manfully, they will seem to be truly the fathers of manly sons, and to be such themselves. But by yielding, they will provide a suspicion that either they are not ours, or that we who praise them are lying. They should do neither of these; rather, they especially of all should be our praisers, showing themselves in deed to be men who are truly the fathers of men. For of old the saying "Nothing in excess" <note>original: "Μηδὲν ἄγαν"</note> was thought to be well said. For in truth it is well said.
<margin>F</margin>
For the man for whom all things leading to happiness depend upon himself, or nearly so, and do not hang upon other men—from whose good or bad actions his own affairs are forced to wander—for him the best way of life has been prepared. This is the temperate man, and this is the brave and prudent man. This man, when wealth and children come or are destroyed, will especially obey the proverb. For he will not appear either rejoicing or grieving in excess, because of his trust in himself. Such men we think our own should be, and we desire it, and we say so; and we now show ourselves to be such, not being vexed nor fearing in excess, if it is necessary to die at the present time. We beg of both fathers and mothers to spend the remainder of their lives with this same mindset; and to know that they will please us most, not by mourning nor by lamenting us. But if there is any perception among the dead of those who are living, they would be most ungrateful by harming themselves and bearing their misfortunes heavily. Unlike other citizens, she has appointed certain officials as a guard over the youths, so that their fathers and mothers shall not be wronged. She joins in raising the children herself, desiring that their orphancy be as hidden from them as possible. She stands in the place of a father to them while they are still children; and when they reach the age of manhood, she sends them to their own homes, having furnished them with a full suit of armor. She does this to point out and remind them of their father’s pursuits, giving them the tools of ancestral virtue. At the same time, for the sake of a good omen, she has them begin their journey to the ancestral hearth to take command, being already equipped with strength <margin>B</margin> and adorned with arms. She never ceases to honor the deceased themselves every year, performing the customary rites for all in common that are usually done privately for each. In addition to these things, she holds gymnastic and equestrian contests, and every kind of musical competition. To the dead, she stands in the place of an heir and a son; to the sons, she is a father; and to the parents and elders, she is a guardian. She provides all care for all people through all time. ## OR, CONCERNING JUSTICE.

<margin>D</margin> **I WENT DOWN** yesterday to the Piraeus with Glaucon, the son of Ariston, both to offer my prayers to the goddess <note>original: "τῇ θεῷ" (the goddess). This likely refers to Bendis, a Thracian deity whose cult was being introduced to Athens.</note> and at the same time wanting to see the festival, in what manner they would conduct it, since they were holding it now for the first time. The procession of the local inhabitants seemed beautiful to me, yet the one which the Thracians sent appeared no less fitting. After we had prayed and watched the spectacle, we were departing toward the city. Seeing us from a distance as we were starting for home, Polemarchus, the son of Cephalus, ordered his servant to run and tell us to wait for him. The boy caught hold of my cloak from behind and said, "Polemarchus orders you to wait." I turned around and asked where his master was. "He is coming up behind," he said, "just wait." "We will wait," <margin>E</margin> said Glaucon. A little later Polemarchus arrived, and with him Adeimantus, the brother of Glaucon, and Niceratus, the son of Nicias, and several others, apparently coming from the procession. Then Polemarchus said, "Socrates, you seem to me to have started for the city as if you are leaving." "You do not guess wrongly," I said. "Do you see," he said, "how many of us there are?" "How could I not?" "Either, then," he said, "become stronger than these men, or stay here." "Is there not one other option left," I said, "that we might persuade you that you ought to let us go?" "Could you really persuade us," he said...

<column-break/>

...that they may imitate the famous deeds of their kin, and the elders, that they may hope for the best for themselves. Truly, we shall nourish your old age both privately and publicly: and whomever of their progeny we encounter, we shall embrace with the greatest benevolence. You yourselves are by no means ignorant of the city’s providence, which, by established laws, protects the parents and children of those who have perished in war, and before other citizens, it ensures the care of such people is committed to the highest magistrate, lest the parents of these men should suffer any injury at all. Furthermore, the city itself educates the children, and strives so that their state of being orphaned is unknown to them. For she herself acts in the place of a parent; while they are boys, and when they have come to mature age, she sends them to their duties, adorned with full armor. she shows and reminds them of their father’s pursuits while she grants them the instruments of paternal virtue. And at the same time, for the sake of a favorable omen, she bids the son then first to enter his paternal home as if he were about to take command, adorned with arms and strength. Moreover, she honors those who have departed from life, renewing every year the ceremonies decreed by law for all in common, which are usually performed specifically for each individual in private. Likewise, she establishes gymnastic and equestrian contests, and various musical games. And indeed, as far as the deceased are concerned, she takes on the condition of an heir and a son; as for the sons, that of a father; as for the parents and others of this kind, that of a curator, always providing for everyone with all diligence. By the contemplation of these things, you ought to bear adverse events with a calm mind. For in this way you will be more pleasing to both the dead and the living, and you will care for others easily, and be easily cared for. But now, you and all the rest who have followed the law in common, depart. This, O Menexenus, is the speech of Aspasia of Miletus.
**MEN.** By Jove <note>original: "Per Iouem" (By Jupiter/Zeus)</note>, O Socrates, you say Aspasia is blessed, if, though she is a woman, she can compose such orations. **SOCR.** But if you believe it less, follow me, and you shall hear her speaking herself. **MEN.** Frequently I have been with Aspasia, Socrates, and I know what sort of person she is. **SOCR.** Why then do you not revere her? Why do you not have gratitude toward her on account of this oration? **MEN.** I certainly have great gratitude toward this woman—or toward the man, whoever it was who delivered this oration to you. And above many others, I have gratitude to the one narrating it. **SOCR.** Very well. But do not betray me, so that I may hereafter recount to you many of her excellent orations concerning civil matters. **MEN.** Be of good heart. I will not betray you. Only report them. **SOCR.** It shall be as you ask.

# PLATO ON THE REPUBLIC, OR CONCERNING JUSTICE,
### The first book of ten.

---

> *Plato's purpose in all these political books is to teach by what reasoning a Republic should be established opportunely and fruitfully, and with what laws it is agreeable to fortify it, so that the true method of establishing a society may be clear to men. The thesis and argument of the first book is the definition of Justice: which is proposed in such a way that what justice is not is taught rather than what it truly is. Moreover, he chose two descriptions of Justice on purpose, which he would refute in such a way that he might nevertheless scatter the seeds of an intact and full definition, which would represent the nature of the subject at hand. For a Republic consists of a magistrate and subjects: in the former, tyranny must be avoided, and in the latter, a certain promiscuous and unseemly <term>ataxia</term> <note>original: "ἀταξία" (disorder or lack of discipline)</note>. It is agreeable that the former should have regard not for private utility but for the safety and advantage of the subjects, and that the latter should render what they owe both to the magistrate and to each other, according to the formula of honesty.*

---

->SOCRATES, GLAUCON, POLEMARCHUS,<-
->THRASYMACHUS, ADEIMANTUS,<-
->CEPHALUS.<-

**I WENT DOWN** yesterday to the Piraeus together with Glaucon the son of Ariston, so that I might both pray to the Goddess and behold the celebration, in what way they would carry it out, which they were then doing for the first time. The local procession seemed beautiful to me: but nevertheless, as it appeared, that which the Thracians sent was decent. When we had both prayed and been present at the spectacle, we were returning to the city. But Polemarchus, the son of Cephalus, had seen us from afar returning home, and by sending a servant running, he ordered us to wait for him. Therefore, catching me by my clothing from behind, the servant said, "Polemarchus bids you stay." And I, turning toward him, asked where he himself was. "But he follows behind you," he said, "only wait." "We will wait," replied Glaucon. And a little later Polemarchus came, and with him Adeimantus the brother of Glaucon, and Niceratus the son of Nicias, and several others, who seemed to be coming from the procession. Therefore Polemarchus said, "You seem, O Socrates, to be hurrying toward the city as if about to depart." "You do not guess badly," I said. "Do you see," he said, "how many we are?" "Why not?" "Either, therefore, you must be stronger than these, or you must stay here." "You will grant this one thing," I said, "namely that you will permit us to depart, if we persuade you that we should be dismissed." "Could you persuade us," he said...

"Exactly so," said Polemarchus. <margin>Missing in the Greek manuscripts.</margin> "Therefore, you must either be stronger than we are, or you must stay here." "Furthermore," he continued, "they will perform a night festival <note>A "pannychis" or all-night celebration.</note> that is surely worth seeing. For we shall rise after dinner and go to see the rites, and we will meet many of the young men there and converse. So stay, and do not do otherwise." And Glaucon said, "It seems we must stay." "Well, if it seems so," I replied, "then so it must be done." We went, therefore, to the house of Polemarchus, and there we found both Euthydemus and Lysias, the brothers of Polemarchus, and Thrasymachus of Chalcedon, Charmantides of Paeania, and Cleitophon, the son of Aristonymus. Also inside was Cephalus, the father of Polemarchus, who seemed to me quite old; indeed, I had not seen him for a long time. He was sitting crowned with a wreath upon a certain cushion and chair. For he had just finished sacrificing in the courtyard. We sat down, therefore, next to him, for many seats were arranged there in a circle. As soon as Cephalus saw me, he greeted me and said: "O Socrates, you come down to the Piraeus to see us only rarely. You should not do so. For if I were still able to travel easily to the city, there would be no need for you to come here to us, but we would go to you. But now it is right for you to come here more frequently; for indeed, the more the other pleasures of the body fail me, the more the desire for conversation and the pleasure I receive from it increases. Therefore, do this: come to us here and be with these young men as if with friends and very close relatives." "And yet," I said, "O Cephalus, I am truly delighted <margin>Cicero’s *On Old Age*.</margin> to converse with very old men. For it seems to me that we should learn from those who have already completed a path that we too must perhaps travel, whether it be rough and difficult, or easy and passable. And I would gladly hear from you what you think about this matter, now that you have reached this time of life, which the poets call 'the threshold of old age' <note>original: "ἐπὶ γήραος οὐδῷ" (epi gēraos oudō). This is a traditional Homeric phrase.</note>—whether you call it a difficult part of life, or how you describe it." "I will tell you, by Jove," he said, "O Socrates, how it seems to me. Many of us of nearly the same age often gather together, preserving that ancient proverb. <note>The proverb "Like attracts like," or "The contemporary delights the contemporary."</note> Most of our group, when we meet, lament their lot, longing for the pleasures they enjoyed in youth, remembering sexual matters, drinking parties, feasts, and other things of that kind; they are aggrieved as if they had been deprived of great things. They say they lived well then, but now they do not even live at all. Some also deplore the insults and abuses of their relatives, and in this they especially blame old age, as if it were the cause of all their evils. But they do not seem to me to blame the true cause. For if old age were the cause, I would have suffered these same things on account of age, as would all others <margin>Cicero’s book *On Old Age*.</margin> who have reached this point in life. But I have found many who are not so affected, and I was once with Sophocles the poet when someone asked him if he still enjoyed sexual matters. 'The gods forbid!' <note>original: "Dij meliora" (Latin) / "εὐφήμει" (Greek). Sophocles' actual response implies "Hush, man!" or "Speak of better things!"</note> he replied; 'I have escaped those things most gladly, as if I had fled from a savage and furious master.' It seemed to me then that he spoke very well, and no less so now. For in old age, there is great peace and freedom from all such things. When the desires have cooled and ceased, that saying of Sophocles absolutely applies: we are set free from many and insane masters. But the blame for all these complaints lies in the character of men, not in their age. For moderate and easy-tempered men find even old age tolerable. But for the ill-tempered and unkind, any age is a burden." Then I, being wonderfully delighted by what he said and wanting to hear more, provoked him further, saying: "I think, O Cephalus, that many people, when you say these things, do not accept them; they think you bear old age easily because of your wealth rather than your character; for they say that the rich have many comforts." "What you say is true," he said. "They do not accept it; and there is something in what they say, but not nearly as much as they think. It is like the reply Themistocles is said to have given to a certain Seriphian <note>Seriphos was a tiny, insignificant Greek island.</note> who was insulting him, saying that he had achieved his glory not through his own merit but through that of his city. 'By Hercules,' he said, 'I would not have been famous if I were a Seriphian, nor would you have been, even if you were an Athenian.' The same can be said to those who are not wealthy and find old age difficult. For a good man could not bear old age easily in extreme poverty, but neither could a foolish man ever be at peace with himself even if he were wealthy." "But tell me," I said, "of the things you possess, were most of them left to you by your ancestors, or did you acquire them yourself?" "I have acquired some, Socrates," he said; "I am in the middle as a moneymaker between my father and my grandfather. For my grandfather, Cephalus, inheriting roughly as much wealth as I have now, increased it many times over. But my father, Lysanias, made it even less than it is now. I am satisfied if I leave these sons not less than I inherited, but perhaps a little more."

<column-break/>

And inside was also the father of Polemarchus, Cephalus. And he seemed to me to be very old. For it had been a long time since I had seen him. For if I were still in my strength to travel easily to the city, there would be no need for you to come here, but we would ->C<- go to you. But now you must come here more often. For you must know well that for me, as much as the other pleasures of the body wither away, so much the desires and pleasures concerning conversation increase. Do not do otherwise, then; but associate with these young men and come here to us, as to friends and very close family." "Indeed," I said, "O Cephalus, I rejoice in conversing with the very old. For it seems to me that we should learn from them, as from those who have gone before us on a certain road which we also will perhaps have to travel, what sort of road it is: whether rough and difficult, or easy and passable. And from you I would gladly learn what appears to you regarding this (since you are now at ->D<- that age which the poets say is 'at the threshold of old age'), whether it is a difficult part of life, or how you report it yourself." "I will tell you, by Zeus," he said, "O Socrates, how it appears to me. For often some of us who have a similar age come together, preserving the old proverb. Most of us, when we meet, lament, longing for the pleasures of youth and remembering sexual matters and drinking and feasting and other things that go with them. And they are indignant as if they had been robbed of some great things—and that then they lived well, but now they do not even live. Some also bewail the insults of their relatives against their old age, and because of this they sing a dirge for old age, saying how many evils it causes them. But to me, Socrates, these men do not seem to blame the right cause. For if this were the ->E<- cause, then I would have suffered these same things on account of old age, and all the others who have reached this age. But now I have already met others who are not so; and indeed I was once with Sophocles the poet when he was asked by someone, 'How,' he said, 'O Sophocles, do you stand toward sexual matters? Are you still capable of being with a woman?' And he said, 'Quiet, man! I have escaped it most gladly, as if I had escaped from some mad and savage master.' And then he seemed to me to have spoken well, and no less so now. For in old age there is altogether a great peace and freedom from such things. When the desires cease and slacken, then altogether what Sophocles said happens: it is a release from very many and mad masters. ->F<- But regarding these things, and those regarding relatives, there is one cause. Not old age, Socrates, but the character of the men. For if they are orderly and easy-tempered, even old age is only moderately painful; but if not, then both old age and youth, Socrates, turn out to be difficult for such a person." And I, admiring him for saying these things and wanting him to speak further, moved him on and said: "O Cephalus, I think that most people, when you say these things, do not accept them; but they think you bear old age easily not because of your character, but because you possess great wealth. For they say that the rich have many comforts." "You say the truth," he said. "They ->G<- do not accept it; and they say something, but not as much as they think. But the saying of Themistocles is good, who, when a Seriphian was insulting him and saying that he was famous not because of himself but because of his city, replied that neither would he himself, being a Seriphian, have become famous, nor would the other, being an Athenian. And for those who are not rich and bear old age with difficulty, the same logic holds: that neither would the good man bear old age with poverty very easily, nor would the bad man, even if he were rich, ever become easy-tempered with himself." "But did you," I said, "O Cephalus, receive the greater part of what you possess, or did you acquire it?" "What did I acquire, Socrates?" he said. ->H<- "I have been a sort of middle-ground moneymaker between my grandfather and my father. For my grandfather, who had the same name as I, having inherited nearly as much wealth as I now possess, made it many times as great; but Lysanias my father made it even less than it is now. I am content if I leave to these boys not less, but a little more than I received." "I asked for this reason," I said, "because..."
