<meta>This page continues the opening dialogue of Plato's "Republic" from the previous page. Having arrived at the house of the elderly Cephalus, Socrates begins to question him about the benefits of wealth and the nature of a well-lived life as one approaches the end.</meta>

# ON THE REPUBLIC BOOK I.

"It seemed to me," I said, "that you do not love money overmuch. This is generally the case with those who have not acquired wealth themselves. But those who have earned it are twice as fond of it as others. For just as poets love their own poems and fathers love their children, so too those who have made their own money are serious about it—as it is their own creation—as well as for its use, just like everyone else. Therefore, they are difficult company, for they are unwilling to praise anything except wealth." "You speak the truth," he replied. "Indeed I do," I said. "But tell me this further: what do you believe is the greatest good you have enjoyed from possessing a large fortune?"

<margin>B</margin>
"What I have to say," he replied, "is perhaps something I could not persuade many to believe. For you should know, Socrates, that when a man thinks he is near death, a fear and concern enters him regarding things that never entered his mind before. The myths told about those in the underworld—how one who has acted unjustly here must pay the penalty there—which were previously laughed at, then begin to turn his soul, fearing they might be true. And he himself, either because of the weakness of old age or because he is now closer to those things there, sees them more clearly. He becomes full of suspicion and dread; he begins to calculate and examine whether he has done any injustice to anyone.

<margin>C</margin>
The man who finds many injustices in his own life often wakes up from sleep in terror, as children do, and lives with a dark expectation. But for the man who is conscious of no injustice within himself, a sweet hope is always present—a 'good nurse of old age,' as Pindar says. For that poet expressed it elegantly when he said that for whoever leads a life of justice and holiness, 'sweet hope follows him, nourishing his heart and nursing his old age, she who most of all steers the shifting mind of mortals.' <note>Cephalus quotes the lyric poet Pindar (Fragment 214) to illustrate that a clear conscience brings peace in old age.</note> He speaks well indeed, marvelously so. It is for this reason that I consider the possession of wealth to be of the greatest value—not for every man, but for the decent one. Wealth contributes greatly to not having to deceive or lie to anyone, even unwillingly, and to not departing for the world below in fear because one owes sacrifices to a god or money to a man. It has many other uses, but comparing one thing against another, I would say that for a man of sense, Socrates, the possession of wealth is most useful for this purpose."

<margin>D</margin>
"You speak excellently, Cephalus," I said. "But as for this very thing, justice: shall we say it is simply telling the truth and returning what one has received from another? Or are these very actions sometimes just and sometimes unjust? For example, everyone would say that if someone received weapons from a friend who was in his right mind, and that friend then asked for them back while in a state of madness, one should not return such things, nor would the one who returned them be acting justly. Nor would someone be acting justly if he were willing to tell the whole truth to a person in such a state." "You speak correctly," he said. "Then this is not the definition of justice: to speak the truth and to return what one has received." "It certainly is, Socrates," Polemarchus interrupted, "at least if we are to believe Simonides." <note>Simonides of Ceos was a famous lyric poet often cited as an authority on wisdom and morality.</note> "And indeed," said Cephalus, "I now hand over the argument to you, for I must go now to attend to the sacrifices." "Is Polemarchus then the heir to your argument?" I asked. "Certainly," he said with a laugh, and at the same time he went off toward the sacrifices.

<margin>E</margin>
"Tell me then," I said, "you who are the heir to the argument: what do you say Simonides says that is correct concerning justice?" "That it is just to give back to each what is owed to him," he replied. "In saying this, he seems to me to speak well." "And yet," I said, "it is not easy to disbelieve Simonides, for he is a wise and divine man. But as for what he means by this, you, Polemarchus, perhaps understand it, but I am ignorant. For it is clear he does not mean what we were just saying—that one should return a deposit to someone who is not in his right mind when he asks for it. And yet, what was deposited is surely 'owed' in some sense, is it not?" "Yes." "But it is not to be given back under any circumstances when someone asks for it while not in his right mind?" "That is true," he said.

<margin>F</margin>
"Simonides, it seems, means something other than this when he says that it is just to give back what is owed." "He certainly does, by Zeus!" he said. "For he thinks that friends owe it to their friends to do some good, and no evil." "I understand," I said, "that he who returns gold to one who deposited it does not 'give back what is owed' if the returning and the receiving should prove harmful, and if the one receiving and the one returning are friends. Is this not what you say Simonides means?" "Exactly so."

<margin>G</margin>
"What then? Must we give back to enemies whatever happens to be owed to them?" "By all means," he said, "give them what is owed. And what is owed from an enemy to an enemy is, I think, what is also appropriate: some evil."

<margin>H</margin>
"It seems then," I said, "that Simonides, after the fashion of poets, gave a riddling definition of what justice is. For he intended to say, as it appears, that justice is giving to each what is appropriate, but he called this 'the debt' or 'what is owed'." "What else do you think?" he asked. "By Zeus," I said, "if someone were to ask him: 'Simonides, what does the art called medicine give back that is owed and appropriate, and to whom?' what do you think he would answer us?" "Clearly," he said, "it gives medicines, food, and drinks to bodies." "And what does the art called cookery give that is owed and appropriate, and to whom?" "It gives seasonings to meats." "Very well. Then what does the art called justice give, and to whom?" "If we are to follow the previous points, Socrates," he said, "it is the art that gives benefits to friends and harms to enemies."

<column-break/>

I asked him, I said, since you did not seem to me to value wealth overmuch—which is what those generally do who did not produce it for themselves. But those who have prepared it for themselves love it twice as much as others. For just as poets love their own poems and fathers love their sons, in the same way, those who have acquired money are devoted to it as their own work, not merely for its use and necessity like others. For this reason, their company is difficult, since they wish to praise nothing else besides riches. "You tell the truth," he said. "And very much so," I said. "But declare this also to me: What is the greatest good that you think you have attained from the possession of riches?"

<margin>B</margin>
"That," he said, "is something I might not easily persuade many of if I said it. Know for certain, Socrates, that after someone reaches the point where he thinks he is soon to die, fear and a certain care for those things he neglected in his earlier life fall upon him. For the stories told about the lower world—how those who have acted unjustly must pay the penalty there—though mocked until now, then move the soul, suspecting that they might perhaps be true. And the man himself, whether because of the weakness of old age or because he is closer to that other life, sees those things more sharply. He is rendered full of anxiety and fear, and he reflects upon and examines whether he has affected anyone with any injury.

<margin>C</margin>
He, therefore, who finds many iniquities in his life, frequently starts up out of his very sleep in terror like a child, and lives in the worst of hope. But he who is conscious of no injury done by him always has a pleasant hope present, the best nurse of old age, as Pindar says. For that poet sang skillfully, Socrates, when he said: 'Whoever leads a just and holy life, sweet hope accompanies him, nourishing his heart and fostering his old age, she who most of all governs the shifting mind of men.' He speaks well, then, and most admirably. To this, I think the possession of money contributes very much—not for just any man, but for the modest and fair man. The possession of riches contributes greatly to this: that one may depart for that place without fear, since you have neither cheated anyone against your will, nor lied, nor do you owe either sacrifices vowed to God or money to a man. It has other uses too, and indeed very many. But if one thing is compared to another, Socrates, I would not place it as the least benefit for a man of sense—rather, I would say riches confer a great deal toward this." "You speak excellently, Cephalus," I said. "But as for this very thing, namely justice: shall we say it is simply telling the truth and returning what one has received? Or is it that doing these same things is sometimes just and sometimes unjust? This is how it appears. Anyone would say that if a man of sound mind deposited a sword with you, and then, being insane, asked for it back, it would be a sin to return it, and he who returned it would not be just; nor would it be just if he told the whole truth to a man so affected." "You speak rightly," he said. "Therefore, this is not the definition of justice: to speak the truth and to return what was deposited." "You speak quite rightly, Socrates," said Polemarchus, taking up the discourse, "if it is right to believe Simonides in anything." At this, Cephalus said, "I hand over the discourse to you, for I must take care of the sacred rites." "Is Polemarchus then your heir?" I asked. And he, smiling, said, "He is indeed," and at once departed for the sacrificing.

<margin>F</margin>
"Tell me then," I said, "heir of the discourse, what do you assert is rightly said about justice by Simonides?" "That he says," he replied, "that it is just for what is owed to be returned to each. And in saying these things, he seems to speak rightly." "And yet," I said, "it is not easy to deny faith to Simonides. For he is a wise and divine man. But what he means, you perhaps understand, Polemarchus, but I am ignorant. For it is manifest that he does not mean what we were saying a little while ago—namely, to return a deposit to someone who is not sound of mind when he asks for it. And yet, that which was deposited is in some way 'owed.' Is it not?" "Certainly," he said. "Yet it must not be returned then, when someone asks for it who is not sound." "You speak the truth," he said. "Simonides, therefore, says something other than this when he asserts that it is just to return what is owed." "Something else, by Jove!" he said. "For he thinks that friends owe it to friends to do good, but not evil."

<margin>G</margin>
"I understand indeed that he would by no means be returning what is owed who returned gold to the one from whom he received the deposit, if the returning and the receiving should be harmful, and if they were friends, the one who receives and the one who returns. Do you not say that Simonides speaks thus?" "Exactly so." "What then? Must that which is owed be returned to enemies?" "Entirely what is owed to them," he said. "And what is owed to an enemy, I think, from an enemy, is what is fitting—namely, something evil."

<margin>H</margin>
"Then Simonides indicated poetically what justice is. For he judged, as it appears, that it is just to render what is fitting to each. But he called this 'what is owed.' But what do you think he would say if someone asked him: 'O Simonides, what faculty, and to whom, and giving what that is owed and fitting, is called medicine?' What do you think he would answer us?" "Doubtless, that which gives medicines, foods, and drinks to bodies." "Likewise, what art, and to whom, and providing what that is owed and fitting, is named cookery?" "That which gives sweet seasonings to meats." "Come then: what art, and to whom, and giving what, is that justice which returns benefits to friends and harms to enemies?"

Socrates has effectively dismantled the first common-sense definition (returning what is owed) by showing that context—specifically the sanity of the recipient—matters.</meta>

<summary>In this opening dialogue of The Republic, Socrates discusses the benefits of wealth with the elderly Cephalus, who argues that money helps a man maintain a clear conscience before death. The conversation shifts to defining justice, with Polemarchus defending the poet Simonides' view that justice consists of "giving each his due," eventually interpreted as helping friends and harming enemies.</summary>

<margin>A</margin> "Therefore, he defines justice as doing good to friends and evil to enemies?" "So it seems to me," he said. "Who then is most capable of doing good to friends who are suffering from disease, and evil to enemies, in respect to sickness and health?" <note>original: "morbo laborantes... ad bonam valetudinem, & ad malam"</note> "A physician." "And who is most capable for those sailing through the dangers of the sea?" "A pilot." "In what action and for what work, then, is the just man most capable of helping friends and harming enemies?" "In making war and in alliances <term>alliances: the Greek term 'xummacchein' refers specifically to fighting alongside someone in battle</term>, as it seems to me at least." "Very well. But to those who are not sick, my dear Polemarchus, a physician is useless." "True." "And a pilot to those who are not sailing." "Certainly." "Is the just man, then, also useless to those who are not at war?" "I do not think that is the case at all." "Justice, then, is also useful in peace?" <margin>B</margin> "It is useful." "Agriculture is also useful in peace, is it not?" "Yes." "For the gathering of crops?" "Certainly." "And also the craft of the shoemaker?" "Yes." "For the procurement of shoes, I suppose you would say." "Exactly." "What then of justice? For what use or acquisition would you say it is useful in peace?" <margin>C</margin> "For business dealings, Socrates." <note>original: "commercia" in Latin, "xymbolaia" in Greek, meaning contracts or social interactions</note> "By business dealings, do you mean partnerships, or something else?" "Partnerships, indeed." "Now, is the just man a good and useful partner in a game of checkers <note>original: "talis" / "petteia", an ancient board game often compared to checkers or chess</note>, or is the skilled player?" "The skilled player." "And in the laying of bricks and stones, is the just man a better and more useful partner than the builder?" "Not at all." "In what partnership, then, is the just man a better partner than the lyre-player, in the same way that the lyre-player is better than the just man for striking the strings?" "In matters of money, as it seems to me." "Except perhaps, Polemarchus, when it is necessary to *use* money—when it is necessary to buy or sell a horse in common. Then, I suppose, the horse-dealer <term>horse-dealer: the Latin 'mango' implies a trader or even a shifty salesman</term> would be more useful. Is that not so?" "It appears so." "And when a ship is needed, the shipbuilder or the pilot?" "It seems so." "In what common use of gold or silver, then, is the just man more useful than others?" "When we wish to deposit it and have it be safe, Socrates." "Do you mean, then, when there is no need to use it, but to let it lie?" "Exactly." "Then it is when money is *useless* that justice is useful in relation to it?" "It looks that way." "And when a pruning hook needs to be guarded, justice is useful both publicly and privately; but when it is to be used, the art of vine-dressing is useful?" "It appears so." "Will you also say that when a shield and a lyre must be guarded and not used, justice is useful; <margin>D</margin> but when they are to be used, the soldier's art and the musician's art are useful?" "Necessarily." "And so concerning all other things: is justice useless in their use, but useful in their non-use?" "It looks that way." "Justice, then, my friend, cannot be a very serious or important thing if it happens to be useful only for useless things. But let us consider this: is not the man most skilled at striking in a fight, whether in boxing or any other kind, also the best at guarding himself?" "Certainly." "And is not the man who is skilled at guarding against and escaping a disease also the most capable of inflicting it?" "So it seems to me." <margin>E</margin> "Furthermore, the best guard of an army is the one who can steal the enemy's plans and other actions." "Certainly." "Therefore, of whatever thing a man is a skilled guard, he is also a skilled thief." "It seems so." "If, then, the just man is skilled at guarding money, he is also skilled at stealing it." "So the argument indicates," he said. "The just man, then, has turned out to be a kind of thief, as it seems; and you likely learned this from Homer. For he admires Autolycus, the maternal grandfather of Odysseus, and says that he surpassed all men in thievery and in swearing oaths." <note>original: Odyssey, Book 19 (τ), line 395</note> "Justice, then, according to you and Homer and Simonides, seems to be a kind of art of stealing—<margin>F</margin> though for the benefit of friends and the harm of enemies. Was that not what you were saying?" "No, by Zeus!" he said. "But I no longer know what I was saying. However, this I still believe: that justice is to benefit friends and to harm enemies." "But by 'friends,' do you mean those who *seem* to be good and useful to each person, or those who *are* so, even if they do not seem so? And the same for enemies?" "It is likely," he said, "that one loves those he thinks are good and hates those he considers wicked." "But do men not make mistakes in this, so that many seem to them to be good who are not, and many the opposite?" "They do make mistakes." "To such people, then, the good are enemies and the wicked are friends?" "Very much so." "And yet, is it then 'just' for these people to benefit the wicked and harm the good?" <margin>G</margin> "It appears so." "But the good are just, and such as do no injustice." "True." "According to your argument, then, it is just to do harm to those who do no wrong." "Not at all, Socrates! For that seems to be a wicked argument." "Then it is just to harm the unjust and benefit the just?" "That argument appears better than the previous one." "It will follow, then, Polemarchus, for many who have erred in their judgment of men, that it is just for them to harm their friends (for their friends are wicked to them) and to benefit their enemies (for they are good). And thus we shall say the exact opposite of what we said Simonides meant." "It certainly happens that way," he said. "But let us change our definition. For we probably did not define 'friend' and 'enemy' correctly." "How did we define them, Polemarchus?" "That a friend is one who *seems* to be good and useful." <margin>H</margin> "How shall we correct it now?" "We shall say that a friend is one who both *seems* to be and *is* good. But the one who seems so, but is not, is a 'seeming' friend, but not a true friend. And the same definition shall hold for an enemy." "By this reasoning, then, the friend will be the good man, and the enemy will be the bad man." "Yes." "Do you then bid us add something to the definition of 'just' beyond what we said at first? # ON THE REPUBLIC, BOOK I.

<margin>A</margin> "...to do good to a friend and evil to an enemy; but now, in addition to this, should we say that it is just to do good to a friend who is good, and to harm an enemy who is evil?" "Certainly," he said, "that seems to me to be well stated." "Is it then," I asked, "the part of a just man to harm any human being at all?" "Most certainly," he replied, "he ought to harm those who are both wicked and enemies." <margin>B</margin> "But when horses are harmed, do they become better or worse?" "Worse." "Do they become worse in the excellence <note>original: 'aretē' (virtue/excellence)</note> of dogs, or that of horses?" "In that of horses." "And when dogs are harmed, do they become worse in the excellence of dogs, but not in that of horses?" "Necessarily." "Then must we not say, my friend, that when men are harmed, they become worse in human excellence?" "Certainly." "But is not justice a human excellence?" "That too is necessary." "And so, my friend, those men who are harmed must necessarily become more unjust." "It seems so." "Can musicians, then, by means of music, make men unmusical?" "Impossible." "Or can horsemen, by means of horsemanship, make men poor riders?" "No." "Then can the just, by means of justice, make men unjust? Or, in short, can the good, by means of excellence, make men bad?" "No, that is impossible." "For it is not the function of heat, I imagine, to make things cold, but of its opposite." "Yes." "Nor of dryness to make things wet, but of its opposite." "Certainly." "Nor is it the function of the good man to harm, but of his opposite." "So it appears." "And the just man is good?" "Certainly." "Then it is not the function of the just man, Polemarchus, to harm either a friend or anyone else, but of his opposite—the unjust man." "I think you speak the absolute truth, Socrates," he said. <margin>C</margin> "If, therefore, anyone says it is just to give each man what is owed to him—and by this he means that harm is owed to enemies from the just man, and benefit to friends—the one who said this was not wise. For he did not speak the truth. For it has become clear to us that it is never just to harm anyone." "I agree," he said. "Then we shall fight," I said, "as allies, you and I, if anyone claims that Simonides, or Bias, or Pittacus <note>Greek sages of the 6th century BCE</note>, or any other of the wise and blessed men said such a thing." "I for one," he said, "am ready to join you in the fight." "But do you know," I asked, "to whom I think that saying belongs—the claim that it is just to benefit friends and harm enemies?" "To whom?" he asked. "I think it belongs to Periander, or Perdiccas, or Xerxes, or Ismenias the Theban <note>historical figures associated with tyranny or great wealth</note>, or some other rich man who thought he had great power." "You speak most truly," he said. "Very well," I said, "since it has appeared that neither justice nor the just is this, what else might one say it is?"

<margin>D</margin> Now Thrasymachus <note>a Sophist known for his aggressive debating style</note> had often started to break in upon our argument while we were talking, but he had been prevented by those sitting near him who wanted to hear the discussion to the end. But when we paused, and I had said these things, he could no longer keep quiet. Gathering himself up like a wild beast, he lunged at us as if to tear us to pieces. Both Polemarchus and I were terrified and struck with fear. But he, shouting into our midst, said: "What nonsense has possessed you for so long, Socrates? And why do you act like simpletons with one another, giving way to each other? If you truly want to know what justice is, <margin>E</margin> do not only ask questions, nor pride yourself on refuting whatever someone answers—knowing this, that it is easier to ask than to answer—but answer yourself, and say what you claim justice to be. And do not tell me that it is the 'obligatory,' or the 'useful,' or the 'profitable,' or the 'gainful,' or the 'expedient.' Speak clearly and accurately, whatever you say. For I will not accept it if you talk such rubbish as that."

When I heard this, I was astonished, and looking at him, I was afraid. I think that if I had not looked at him before he looked at me, I would have been struck dumb. But as it was, when he began to grow wild at our argument, I looked at him first, so that I was able to answer him, and I said, trembling slightly: <margin>F</margin> "Thrasymachus, do not be hard on us. If we are making mistakes in the examination of these arguments, I and this man here, be assured that we err unwillingly. For do not suppose that if we were searching for gold, we would ever willingly give way to one another in the search and so ruin our chance of finding it; do not think then that while searching for justice, a thing more precious than much gold, we would then so foolishly yield to one another and not be as serious as possible about making it appear as it really is, my friend. But I suppose we are not able to find it. Therefore, it is surely much more reasonable for us to be pitied by you clever people than to be treated harshly." <margin>G</margin> And he, having heard this, laughed quite Sardonically <note>a bitter or mocking laugh</note> and said: "O Hercules! Here is that habitual irony of Socrates! I knew this, and I predicted to these people that you would refuse to answer, that you would play the ironist and do anything rather than answer if someone asked you something."

"That is because you are wise, Thrasymachus," I said. "You knew well that if you asked someone how many make twelve, and as you asked you cautioned him: 'My friend, do not tell me that twelve is twice six, or three times four, or six times two, or four times three; for I will not accept such nonsense from you'—it was clear to you, I imagine, that no one would answer a man who inquired in that way. But if he said to you, <margin>H</margin> 'Thrasymachus, what do you mean? Am I not to give any of the answers you mentioned? Even, you amazing man, if the truth happens to be one of them? Am I to say something other than the truth? Or what do you mean?' What would you have said to him in response?" "Well," he said, "how like the cases are!" "There is nothing to prevent it," I said. "For even if they are not alike..."

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...to benefit a friend and to harm an enemy. But now you wish us to say it is just that we should help a friend who is good, and conversely harm an enemy who is evil. It seems to me that this is stated very beautifully in this manner. Is it then the part of a just man to harm any human? One must indeed harm the wicked and enemies. If horses are harmed, do they become better or worse? Worse. Surely in respect to the excellence of horses, rather than that of dogs? In that of horses. And are not dogs, when harmed, made worse in the excellence of dogs and not in that of horses? Necessarily indeed. <margin>B</margin> Therefore, O friend, shall we not judge that men affected by detriment become worse in human virtue? Entirely so. And yet, is not justice a human virtue? Quite clearly. It will therefore be necessary for harmed men to become more unjust. It seems so. Is it possible then, I say, for musicians to make someone unmusical by music itself? By no means. Or for horsemen, by equestrian skill, to make men unskilled in horsemanship? It is not possible. Can just men, by justice itself, make men unjust? And in sum, can the good make men evil by virtue itself? Certainly not. For I do not think it is the work of heat to make anything cold, but of its opposite. It is so. Nor of dryness to make something wet, but of its opposite. Very much so. It is not therefore the part of the good man to harm, but of his opposite. It seems so. And the just man is good? Entirely. It is not therefore the work of the just man, O Polemarchus, to harm either a friend or anyone else, but of his opposite, the unjust man. <margin>C</margin> You seem to speak most truly, O Socrates. If someone then says it is just to give what is owed to each, and understands that damages are owed to enemies from a just man, and utility to friends, he who said this is by no means to be judged wise. For these things are not true. For it has been established that it is in no way just to harm anyone. I confess it indeed, he said. Therefore we shall fight, I and you together, if anyone should assert that either Simonides said this, or Bias, or Pittacus, or any other of the wise and blessed men. Indeed, I am ready to fight together with you against him. But do you know whose opinion this seems to me to be, by which it is asserted that it is just to benefit friends and to harm enemies? Whose then? he asked. I think it is of Periander, or Perdiccas, or Xerxes, or Ismenias the Theban, or some other wealthy man, thinking himself able to do the greatest things. You speak the truth, he said. After it appears that this is by no means justice or the just, what else would one say it is? <margin>D</margin> Now Thrasymachus had frequently desired to contradict us as we were disputing, but had been restrained by those present who wished to hear us. But after we had made an end of speaking, and I had said these things, he no longer contained himself; but gathering himself together like a certain wild beast, he made an onset upon us as if he were about to tear us apart immediately. Therefore both I and Polemarchus were terrified. But he cried out, "What trifles have occupied you until now, O Socrates? Why do you play the fool among yourselves, yielding to one <margin>E</margin> another? For if you truly desire to know what is just, do not only interrogate, nor desire to conquer by refuting after an answer has been given to you, observing that it is easier to interrogate than to answer. But you yourself answer what you think justice to be: and do not tell me that it is what is decent, nor what is useful, nor fruitful, nor conducive, nor conferring; but clearly and plainly declare to me what you say. For I will not admit it if you introduce trifles of this sort."

Hearing these things, I was terrified, and looking upon him, I feared: and as I think, unless I had looked at him before he looked at me, I would have become altogether mute. Now when he began to be exasperated by the discourse itself, <margin>F</margin> I looked back at him first, wherefore I was able to answer him, and trembling slightly I said, "O Thrasymachus, do not be fierce against us. For if we have slipped in considering these reasons, both I and this man, hold it for certain that we have erred unwillingly; surely if we were searching for gold, we would never spontaneously so yield to one another in inquiring that we would impede the discovery. Therefore do not think, since we are searching for justice in the present, a thing much more precious than gold, that we yield so foolishly among ourselves that we do not strive with all zeal whereby we may clearly find it. But as I think, we are not able to attain it. Wherefore it is much more fitting for you wise men to pity us than to urge us." Then he, hearing these things, laughed very Sardonically and profusely, <margin>G</margin> and "O Hercules," he said, "this is that accustomed irony of Socrates. But these things I knew and predicted to these people, that you would indeed be unwilling to answer, but would rather use irony, and finally do all things rather than answer anyone who interrogates." "You are wise, O Thrasymachus," I said, "and you know rightly, that if you were to ask someone how many are twelve, and in asking you should say beforehand, 'Do not tell me, friend, that twelve are twice six, nor three times four, nor six times two, nor four times three, otherwise I will by no means admit trifles of this sort,' no one would answer you thus interrogating. But if he should say to you, 'How, O <margin>H</margin> Thrasymachus, do you say? Should I not answer any of those things which you said beforehand? Whether, O wonderful man, even if it is one of these, but something foreign to the truth? Or in what way do you say that?' What would you say to him to these things?" "Be it so," he said. "But how is this like that?" "Nothing prohibits it," I said. "For even if it is not like..."

<summary>In this passage, Socrates concludes his refutation of Polemarchus's definition of justice, arguing that a just person never harms anyone because harming someone makes them less virtuous. The dialogue is then aggressively interrupted by Thrasymachus, who demands a positive definition of justice while forbidding Socrates from using his usual terminology.</summary>

<margin>A</margin> If, however, it seems so to the person being questioned, do you think he will answer any less according to what he believes, whether we forbid it or not? "Is that what you will do then?" he asked. "Will you give one of those answers I forbade?" "I would not be surprised," I said, "if after examining it, it seemed so to me." "How witty you are!" he said. "But besides this learning you speak of, you must also <margin>B</margin> pay money." "Of course, when I have some," I said. "I certainly believe you will," he said, "so that Socrates can carry out his usual habit: he will not answer himself, but will take the argument of the one responding and refute it." "My excellent friend," I said, "how can anyone answer, first, when he does not know, nor claims to know; and second, even if he has some opinion on these matters, he has been forbidden from saying what he thinks by a man of no small authority? When I had said this, Glaucon and the others begged him to do exactly that. It was obvious that Thrasymachus was possessed by a great desire to speak so that he might show off, for he believed he had an excellent answer; yet he pretended to insist that I should be the one to respond. Finally, he gave in. "This," he said, "is the wisdom of Socrates: he refuses to teach himself, but goes around learning from others, and returns no thanks for it." "That I learn from others," I said, "is true. But that I return no thanks is far from the truth. For I pay as much as I can; and I can only offer praise. <margin>D</margin> I have no money. But you will soon realize with what a ready will I do this, if someone seems to me to speak well, as soon as you have answered. For I expect you will speak well." "Listen then," he said. "For I affirm that justice is nothing other than the advantage of the stronger <note>original: 'quod potentiori vtile' / 'τὸ τοῦ κρείττονος συμφέρον' (the advantage of the stronger). This is one of the most famous challenges to traditional morality in Western philosophy.</note>. Why do you not praise me? I know you won't." "If only I first learn what you mean," I said. "For now I do not yet know, when you say justice is what is useful to the stronger, what you intend to imply, Thrasymachus. For surely you do not mean something like this: If Polydamas <note>A famous Greek athlete and Olympic champion known for his immense strength.</note> is a stronger athlete than us, and beef is useful for his body, that this food is also useful and just for us who are weaker than him." "You are a total scoundrel, Socrates," he said, "and you take my words in the way you can most deprave the argument." "Not at all, my <margin>E</margin> best of men," I said. "But explain this more clearly." "Are you unaware," he asked, "that of cities, some are governed by tyrants, others by the people, and some by the aristocrats?" "I know it well." "Is it not true that in every city, the ruling power is the one that is strongest?" "Certainly." "And each government makes laws for its own advantage: a democracy makes democratic laws, a tyranny makes tyrannical laws, and it happens similarly in the others. By establishing these laws, they declare that what is useful for themselves is 'just' for their subjects, and they punish anyone who transgresses this as a lawbreaker and an unjust person. This, then, my best of men, is what I say: that in all cities, 'justice' is the same thing—that which is advantageous to the established ruling power. The ruling power is everywhere the stronger. <margin>F</margin> Therefore, it is clear to one who reasons correctly that everywhere the same thing is 'just': that which is conducive to the stronger." "Now at last," I said, "I understand what you are saying. Whether it is true, however, I will try to learn. You have answered, Thrasymachus, that the 'useful' is justice, although you forbade me from giving that very answer. However, you have added that qualification: 'to the stronger.'" "A small addition, perhaps," he said. "It is not yet clear whether it is great or small," I replied. "But that we must investigate whether you speak the truth is plain. Since I myself confess that justice is something 'useful,' and you add 'useful to the stronger,' while I am ignorant of this, <margin>G</margin> it must be considered." "Consider it then," he said. "I will do so," I said. "Now tell me, do you assert that it is just to obey the rulers?" "I do." "Are the rulers in various cities always without error, or do they sometimes err?" "They can certainly err sometimes," he said. "Therefore, when they set out to make laws, do they make some rightly and others not rightly?" "I believe so." "To make them 'rightly' means to establish things useful to themselves; and 'not rightly' means things disadvantageous? Is that what you mean, or something else?" "Exactly that." "And whatever they establish must be observed by the subjects? And that is justice?" "Of course." "Then, according to your argument, it is not only just to do what is advantageous to the stronger, but also the opposite: what is disadvantageous. What are you saying?" <margin>H</margin> "What you yourself are saying, I think. But let us examine it more carefully. Have we not already agreed that the rulers sometimes command things that miss the mark of their own advantage? And that whatever they command, it is just for the subjects to observe? Have these things not been agreed upon between us?"

<summary>Thrasymachus defines justice as the "advantage of the stronger," claiming that rulers make laws solely for their own benefit. Socrates begins to dismantle this by pointing out that if rulers make mistakes and create laws that harm themselves, obeying those laws would actually be "unjust" by Thrasymachus's own definition.</summary>
<keywords>justice, advantage of the stronger, Socrates, Thrasymachus, Glaucon, tyranny, democracy, law-making, Polydamas</keywords>

# ON THE REPUBLIC, BOOK I.
Mm iiii

<margin>A</margin> "And you say it is just to do these things which are commanded by them. Then, oh most wise Thrasymachus, does it not necessarily follow that it is just to do the opposite of what you say? For the disadvantage of the stronger is surely what is commanded of the subjects to perform." "By Zeus," said Polemarchus, "that is very clear, Socrates." "Yes, if you bear witness for him," Cleitophon <note>Cleitophon was a political associate of Thrasymachus; his interruption attempts to legally 'save' the definition.</note> interrupted. "And why," he said, "is there a need for a witness? For Thrasymachus himself admits that rulers sometimes command things that are bad for themselves, yet it is just for the subjects to do these things. For Thrasymachus established that doing what is commanded by the rulers is just, Polemarchus." "Yes, Cleitophon, he also established that the advantage of the stronger is just. Having established both these points, he then admitted that sometimes the stronger command <margin>B</margin> the weaker and the subjects to do things that are disadvantageous to them. From these admissions, it follows that justice would be no more the advantage of the stronger than it is his disadvantage." "But," said Cleitophon, "by 'the advantage of the stronger' he meant what the stronger *believed* to be his advantage; this is what must be done by the weaker, and this is what he defined as justice." "But that was not how it was said," Polemarchus replied. "It makes no difference, Polemarchus," I said. "If Thrasymachus says it that way now, let us accept it that way. Tell me, Thrasymachus: was this what you intended justice to be—the *apparent* advantage of the stronger, whether it is actually advantageous or not? Is that how we should say you mean it?" "Not at all," he said. "Do you think I would call someone who makes a mistake 'the stronger' at the moment they are making the mistake?" "I certainly thought," I said, "that you meant this when you admitted that rulers are not infallible, but sometimes make mistakes." <margin>C</margin> "You are a trickster <note>original: "συκοφάντης" (sykophantes) - Socrates is accused of being a 'pettifogger' or a malicious verbal cheat.</note> in your arguments, Socrates! For instance, do you call someone a doctor who is mistaken about the sick, in the very respect that he is mistaken? Or a calculator, who makes an error in calculation, at the moment he errs, according to that error? Rather, I think, we use the expression 'the doctor made a mistake' or 'the calculator made a mistake,' or 'the grammarian.' But I believe that each of these, insofar as he is what we call him, never errs. So, according to precise reasoning—since you, too, are such a stickler for precision <margin>D</margin>—no craftsman ever errs. For he who errs does so through a failure of knowledge, in which respect he is not a craftsman. Therefore, no craftsman, wise man, or ruler ever errs at the moment he is a ruler. Yet everyone would say 'the doctor erred' or 'the ruler erred.' Understand, then, that this is the kind of answer I am giving you now. But the most precise truth is this: the ruler, insofar as he is a ruler, does not err; and not erring, he enacts what is best for himself. This is what must be done by the subject. So, as I said from the beginning, I say justice is to do what is to the advantage of the stronger." "Well then," I said, "Thrasymachus. Do I seem to you to be acting like a trickster?" "You certainly do," he said. <margin>E</margin> "Do you think I asked as I did because I was plotting to catch you out in the argument?" "I know it well!" he said, "but it will gain you nothing. For you will neither catch me by surprise with your tricks, nor will you be able to overpower me in the argument by force." "I wouldn't even dream of it, my dear man," I said. "But so that this doesn't happen to us again, define in which sense you mean the 'ruler' and 'the stronger'—is it the one commonly spoken of, or the one in the strict sense you just mentioned, whose advantage it will be just for the weaker to serve because he is stronger?" "The ruler in the most precise sense," he said. "Try your tricks and slanders against that, if you can. I ask for no quarter. But you won't be able to." <margin>F</margin> "Do you think," I said, "that I would be so mad as to try to 'shave a lion' <note>A Greek proverb meaning to attempt a dangerously impossible task.</note> and play tricks on Thrasymachus?" "You certainly tried just now," he said, "though you were a non-entity at it." "Enough of such talk," I said. "But tell me: the doctor in the strict sense, whom you just mentioned—is he a businessman, or a healer of the sick? And speak of the one who is truly a doctor." "A healer of the sick," he said. "And what of a pilot? Is the correct pilot a ruler of sailors, or a sailor?" "A ruler of sailors." "I think we should not take into account that he sails in the ship, nor should he be called a sailor. For he is not called a pilot because of his sailing, but because of his art <note>original: "τέχνη" (techne) - a craft, skill, or systematic branch of knowledge.</note> and his rule over the sailors." <margin>G</margin> "True," he said. "Now, for each of these, is there not something advantageous?" "Certainly." "And does not the art naturally exist for this purpose," I said, "to seek out and provide what is advantageous to each?" "For that purpose," he said. "Now, is there any other advantage for each of the arts, other than being as perfect as possible?" "How do you mean that?" "Just as if you were to ask me," I said, "if it is enough for the body to be a body, or if it needs something more. I would say it certainly does need something. For this reason, the art of medicine has now been invented, because the body is defective and it is not enough for it to be such as it is. Therefore, this art was provided to procure what is advantageous for it. Do I seem to you to speak correctly in saying this, or not?" "Correctly," he said. "What then? Is the art of medicine itself defective? Or does any other art need some excellence, as the eyes need sight or the ears hearing, so that for them there is a need for an art to look into and provide the advantage for these things? Is there some <margin>H</margin> defect in the art itself, such that each art needs another art to consider its advantage...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> But you affirm it is just to do those things which are commanded by them. Does it not then, oh most wise Thrasymachus, happen that justice is to do the opposite of what you said? For what is useless to the more powerful is somehow commanded of the subjects. At this, Polemarchus said, "By Jove, these things are most manifest, Socrates." "Exactly so, if you, Cleitophon," he said, "join as a witness." "What need is there," he replied, "for a witness? For Thrasymachus himself confesses that rulers sometimes command things that are not conducive to them: which things being performed by the inferiors, becomes just. For Thrasymachus established, oh Polemarchus, that to do what is commanded by the rulers is just," said Cleitophon. "And indeed, Cleitophon," said Polemarchus, "he established that the useful to the more powerful is just. <margin>B</margin> But putting forward both these points, he confessed again that sometimes the more powerful command things to the inferiors which are not useful to themselves. From these concessions, it follows that what is useful to the more powerful is no more just than what is useless." To this, Cleitophon said, "Thrasymachus called that 'useful to the stronger' which the stronger *judged* to be to his own benefit, and that this must be done by the subjects, and that this is justice." But Polemarchus said, "That was not what was said by Thrasymachus." "It matters nothing," I said, "oh Polemarchus. If Thrasymachus says it so now, let us also accept it so. And tell me, oh Thrasymachus, was this what you wished to call just: the useful to the stronger—that is, what *appears* useful to him, whether it benefits him or not? Is it so?" "Not at all," he said. "Do you think me the sort of man who would call someone who errs 'the more powerful' at the moment he sins?" "I thought," I said, "that you were saying so when you confessed that rulers were not entirely free from error, but sinned sometimes." "You are truly a trickster in your speeches, Socrates. <margin>C</margin> If someone errs regarding the sick, do you immediately call him a doctor insofar as he errs? Or a computer <note>A person who calculates or an accountant.</note> when he makes a mistake in setting down an account, then when he errs, according to this error? But as I think, we are accustomed to speak so: that the doctor, the accountant, and the grammarian errs. Yet I judge that none of these, insofar as he is what we call him, ever sins. Therefore, according to exact reasoning (since you also cut to the quick) <margin>D</margin> no craftsman sins. For whoever sins, sins by a deficiency of science, in which he is surely no craftsman. Wherefore no craftsman, or wise man, or ruler sins then when he is a ruler. But anyone might say both that the doctor sinned and the ruler sinned. Consider me, therefore, to have answered you in some such way. But that is to be said by exact reasoning: the ruler, insofar as he is ruler, does not sin; and not sinning, he commands those things which are best for himself. This must be done by those who are under his rule. For which reason, as I said from the beginning, I say it is just to do what is conducive to the more powerful. <margin>E</margin> "Do I seem to you, oh Thrasymachus, to be slandering you like a trickster?" "Most certainly." "For do you think I began to interrogate you in such a way as to lay an ambush, as I just now questioned?" "I know this well," he said. "But you will gain nothing. For neither do your ambushes escape me, nor when they are not hidden will you be able to bring force to your words." "I would not attempt this at all, oh blessed one," I said. "But lest anything like this happen to us again, distinguish whether you speak of the ruler and the more powerful according to the common people, or according to exact reasoning, which you also mentioned a little before: whose benefit, since he is more powerful, it is just to be carried out by the subjects." "I speak of the one ruling by the most exact reasoning," he said. "Pervert these things with those cavils of yours, if you can, Socrates. Indeed, I am surpassed by you in nothing, nor will you be able to." "Do you think," I said, <margin>F</margin> "I am so mad that I would dare to 'shave a lion' and lay traps for Thrasymachus?" "You certainly tried," he said, "though you could achieve nothing." "Let enough be said of these things," I said. "But tell me: he who is a doctor by right reasoning, just as you yourself said a little above, is he a seeker of money, or a curator of the sick? And speak of him who is a doctor in truth." "A curator of diseases, certainly," he said. "And the pilot, who is truly a pilot, is he the ruler of sailors, or a sailor?" "The ruler of sailors." "I think it is of no account that he sails in a ship, nor is he to be called a sailor. For he is not called a pilot because of <margin>G</margin> navigation, but because of the art itself and the rule over sailors." "You speak the truth," he said. "Is there not something useful for each of these?" "There is indeed." "And does not art tend toward this, that it should investigate and provide what is useful to each?" "Toward this very thing," he said. "Is there anything else useful for each art, except that it be as absolute as possible?" "How do you ask that?" "Just as if you asked me if it were enough for the body to be a body, or if it lacked some other thing. I would answer that it lacks entirely. And because of this, the art of medicine has now been found, because the body is weak and infirm, nor is it enough for it to be such. So that it may bring utility to this, the art itself was found. But do I seem to you to say true things?" "True indeed," he said. "What then? Does the art of medicine itself, or any other art, become so weak through itself that it lacks some virtue, as the eyes lack sight or the ears hearing, on account of which there is need in them for some art that investigates and provides those things which contribute to these same ends? Is there also in the art itself some defect, and does each art need another art..."

<summary>In this passage, Socrates maneuvers Thrasymachus into defining a ruler in the "strict sense" as an infallible expert. Socrates then uses the analogies of medicine and navigation to argue that every "art" or craft exists not for its own benefit, but to serve the needs of its subject (the patient or the sailors).</summary>
<keywords>justice, the stronger, craftsmanship, infallibility, medical art, navigation, political rule, sophistry, Socratic irony</keywords>

<meta>Continuity: On the previous page, Socrates and Thrasymachus were debating whether a ruler, when acting "precisely" as a ruler, ever makes a mistake by commanding something that is not to his own advantage. Socrates has just begun to argue that every "art" or "science" exists to serve its subject, not itself.</meta>

# OF PLATO
Mm iiii

...which considers what is useful to itself, and does that art in turn need another art, and so on to infinity? Or does each art look out for its own advantage? Or does it need neither itself nor another to investigate what might counteract its defects? For no defect or error exists in any art. Nor is it proper for an art to seek utility for anything other than the subject of that art. 
<margin>342</margin> 
The art itself is always whole and pure, so long as each remains entirely what it is. Consider this with that same exact reasoning: is this the case, or is it otherwise? "It is certainly so," he said. Therefore, medicine does not provide for medicine, but for the body. "That is true." Nor does horsemanship provide for horsemanship, but for horses; nor does any other art provide for itself—for it has no needs—but for that of which it is the art. "So it appears." But surely, Thrasymachus, the arts rule and have dominion over those things of which they are the arts. 
<margin>B</margin> 
He conceded this, though with great difficulty. Therefore, no science inquires after or commands the utility of the stronger, but rather that of the weaker, which is commanded by it. He did not deny this, though he prepared to fight against it. When he had confessed this, I added: No doctor, insofar as he is a doctor, seeks to provide for the doctor, or commands anything for his own sake, but for the sake of the patient. For it has been granted that he who is truly a doctor is a ruler of bodies, not a gatherer of money. Was that not granted? He agreed. And was it not also granted that the exact pilot of a ship is a ruler of sailors, not a sailor? This too. 
<margin>C</margin> 
Therefore, such a pilot and ruler does not inquire after and command what is beneficial to the pilot himself, but what is beneficial to the sailors who are ruled by him. This, too, he confessed with difficulty. And here I said: Nor does any other person, Thrasymachus, in any position of authority or power, insofar as he is a ruler, think of or command what is beneficial to himself, but what is beneficial to the subject; and everything he says and does, he says and does for the utility and dignity of that subject. When we reached this point, and it was clear to everyone that the definition of the just had been turned into its opposite, Thrasymachus did not respond as he should have, but said: "Tell me, Socrates, do you have a nurse?" 
<margin>D</margin> 
"What?" I said, "Should you not rather answer the question than ask such things?" "Because," he said, "she neglects you and does not wipe your dripping nose <note>original: "oppletas tibi nares non emungit" / "κορυζῶντα περιορᾷ." Thrasymachus uses a crude idiom to suggest Socrates is a simpleton or a child who needs his nose wiped because he is too naive to understand the world.</note> even though you need it, for you know nothing of sheep or shepherds." "Why do you say that?" I asked. "Because," he said, "you think that shepherds or herdsmen consider the good of the sheep or the oxen, and fatten and care for them, looking to anything other than the utility of their masters and themselves. And those who rule in cities, as they ought, you think look upon those who are under them in any other way than a shepherd looks upon his sheep; or that they think of anything else, day and night, than how utility might come to themselves. You are so far from understanding the just and justice, and the unjust and injustice, that you are ignorant that justice and the just
<margin>343</margin> 
are really another’s good—the advantage of the ruler and the stronger—but the personal loss of the one who obeys and serves. 
<margin>E</margin> 
Injustice, on the contrary, rules over those who are truly simple and just; those who obey do what is advantageous for the stronger ruler, and by their service make him happy, but they do not consult their own interest at all. You must consider it thus, oh most simple Socrates: a just man always has less than an unjust man. First, in private contracts, wherever a just man is a partner with an unjust man, you will find that when the partnership is dissolved, the just man always carries away less than the unjust. Then, in public matters, when taxes are to be paid, the just man pays more than his equals, and the unjust man less. And when something is to be received, the just man receives nothing, while the unjust man gains much. 
<margin>F</margin> 
Furthermore, whenever each of them holds some office, if no other loss falls upon the just man, at least his private affairs are neglected and fall into ruin, while he gains nothing from the public treasury because he is just. In addition to this, he becomes hated by his relatives and acquaintances because he refuses to serve them in anything beyond what is just. But for the unjust man, all the opposite occurs; I mean, as I said before, the one who is able to gain the most everywhere. Consider him, then, if you wish to judge how much more it profits him privately to be unjust than just. 
<margin>344</margin> 
You will learn this most easily if you look at the most perfect injustice, which makes the one who acts unjustly most happy, but those who suffer the injury, and would not wish to do injustice themselves, most miserable. 
<margin>G</margin> 
This is tyranny, which does not take the property of others bit by bit, but all at once, by fraud and by force: things sacred and holy, private and public. If someone commits a crime in any part of these and is caught, he is punished and subjected to the greatest disgrace. For those who commit such crimes in part are called temple-robbers, kidnappers, burglars, swindlers, and thieves. 
<margin>H</margin> 
But when someone, beyond stealing the money of the citizens, also kidnaps and enslaves the citizens themselves, instead of those shameful names, he is called happy and blessed, not only by his own citizens, but by all who hear that he has fulfilled the whole of injustice. For those who reproach injustice do not do so because they fear committing it, but because they fear suffering it.

<column-break/>

...will consider? And that which considers, will it in turn need another of the same kind? And is this without end, or will it consider its own advantage for itself? Or does it need neither itself nor another to consider the advantage for its own deficiency? For neither deficiency nor any error is present in any art, nor does it belong to an art to seek the advantage of anything other than that of which it is the art. But the art itself is unharmed and pure, being correct, so long as each remains precisely the whole that it is. And consider this according to that precise reasoning: is it so or otherwise? "It appears so," he said. "Therefore," I said, "medicine does not consider the advantage of medicine, but of the body." "Yes," he said. "Nor horsemanship for horsemanship, but for horses; nor any other art for itself (for it has no need), but for that of which it is the art." "It appears so," he said. "But surely, Thrasymachus, the arts rule and have power over that of which they are the arts." He conceded this also, but very reluctantly. "Therefore, no science considers the advantage of the stronger, nor commands it, but rather the advantage of the weaker and that which is ruled by itself." He eventually agreed to these things, though he attempted to fight against them. But when he had agreed, I said: "Is it not also true that no doctor, insofar as he is a doctor, considers or commands the advantage of the doctor, but that of the patient?" For it was agreed that the precise doctor is a ruler of bodies, but not a money-maker; or was it not agreed? He assented. "And also that the precise pilot is a ruler of sailors, but not a sailor?" It was agreed. "Therefore, such a pilot and ruler will not consider and prescribe the advantage of the pilot, but the advantage of the sailor and the subject." He agreed reluctantly. "Therefore," I said, "Thrasymachus, neither does anyone else in any position of rule, insofar as he is a ruler, consider or command his own advantage, but that of the subject, and that for which he himself works; and looking to that, and to what is advantageous and proper for it, he says all that he says and does all that he does." When we were at this point in the argument, and it was manifest to all that the definition of the just had turned into the opposite, Thrasymachus, instead of answering, said: "Tell me, Socrates, do you have a nurse?" "Why is that?" I said, "Should you not answer instead of asking such things?" "Because," he said, "she overlooks your dripping nose and does not wipe it when it is needed, for you do not even know sheep or shepherds." "Why specifically?" I asked. "Because you think the shepherds or the cowherds look to the good of the sheep or the cattle, and fatten them and care for them, looking to anything other than the good of the masters and themselves. And so you think those who rule in cities, those who truly rule, think of their subjects in any other way than one might be disposed toward sheep, and that they consider anything else day and night than that from which they themselves will benefit. And you are so far off concerning the just and justice, and the unjust and injustice, that you are ignorant that justice and the just are, in reality, another’s good—the advantage of the stronger and the ruler—but a personal harm to the one who obeys and serves. Injustice is the opposite, and it rules those who are truly simple and just; and the subjects do what is to the advantage of that man, since he is stronger; and by serving him, they make him happy, but themselves not at all. You must consider it thus, oh most simple Socrates: that a just man everywhere has less than an unjust man. First, in contracts with one another, wherever such a man is a partner with another, you would never find, upon the dissolution of the partnership, the just man having more than the unjust, but less. Then, in matters concerning the city, when there are taxes, the just man pays more from equal means, the other less; and when there are distributions, the one gains nothing, the other much. For even when each holds some office, to the just man it happens that, if no other loss occurs, his own affairs are in a worse state through neglect; and from the public he gains no benefit because he is just. Furthermore, he becomes hated by his relatives and acquaintances when he is unwilling to serve them in any way contrary to justice. To the unjust man, all these opposites belong. For I am speaking of the one I just mentioned, the one who is able to take great advantage. Consider him, then, if you wish to judge how much more it is to his own advantage to be unjust than to be just. You will learn this most easily of all if you go to the most perfect injustice, which makes the one who does wrong most happy, and those who are wronged, and would not wish to do wrong, most miserable. This is tyranny, which takes the property of others not little by little, but all at once, by stealth and by force, both sacred and holy, and private and public; for which, if someone does wrong in any one part and is not hidden, he is punished and has the greatest reproaches. For temple-robbers, kidnappers, burglars, swindlers, and thieves are the names called of those who do wrong in part of such crimes. But when someone, in addition to the money of the citizens, kidnaps and enslaves the citizens themselves, instead of these shameful names, they are called happy and blessed, not only by the citizens, but by all others who hear that he has committed the whole of injustice. For those who reproach injustice do so not because they fear doing unjust things, but because they fear suffering them. Thus, Socrates, injustice is something stronger, more free, and more masterful..."

<summary>Socrates argues that all arts, including ruling, serve the interest of their subjects, but Thrasymachus counters with the famous shepherd analogy, claiming that justice is merely the "good of another" and that perfect injustice, such as tyranny, brings the greatest happiness.</summary>

# ON THE REPUBLIC BOOK I.

<margin>A</margin> injustice is a more robust, free, and masterful thing than justice. As I said from the beginning: the interest of the stronger happens to be "the just," while "the unjust" is what is useful and profitable for oneself. Having said these things, Thrasymachus intended to leave, just like a bath-attendant <note>original: βαλανεὺς (balaneus); Socrates humorously compares Thrasymachus to a worker who douses customers with water all at once, just as Thrasymachus "drenched" them with a flood of words before trying to run away.</note> who has poured a great flood of words all at once into our ears. However, those present would not permit him to go, but forced him to stay and give an account of what he had said. I myself also requested it quite earnestly, saying: "O divine Thrasymachus, having tossed out such an argument, do you really intend to leave before you have sufficiently taught us, or learned yourself, whether this is the case or otherwise? <margin>B</margin> Or do you think it is a small matter to attempt to define the whole course of life? That is, to determine by what way of living each of us might lead the most profitable existence?" Thrasymachus replied, "Do I think it is otherwise?" "You seem," I said, "to have no care for us, nor any concern whether we shall live worse or better through our ignorance of what you claim to know. But, good sir, be eager to show it to us as well. It will not be a bad investment for you to benefit such a large group as we are. For I tell you my own view: I am not persuaded, nor do I think that injustice is more profitable than justice, even if one allows it to go on and does not hinder it from doing what it wishes. <margin>C</margin> Even if someone is unjust, my friend, and has the power to act unjustly either by secrecy or by force, he still does not persuade me that injustice is more profitable than justice. Perhaps someone else among us feels this way too, and not just I. Persuade us, then, blessed man, that we are not taking the right counsel when we value justice more than injustice." "And how," he asked, "shall I persuade you? If you are not persuaded by what I just said, what more can I do for you? Shall I take the argument and cram it into your soul?" "By Zeus, no!" I said, "Don't do that. But first, stand by whatever you say; or if you change your mind, change it openly and do not deceive us. <margin>D</margin> Now you see, Thrasymachus—for let us revisit what was said before—that when you first defined the true doctor, you later did not think it necessary to keep the same precision for the true shepherd. Instead, you think that he, insofar as he is a shepherd, tends the sheep not with a view to what is best for the sheep, but like a banquet-guest who is about to feast, looking toward the gluttony; or again, looking toward selling them, like a businessman rather than a shepherd. But surely the art of shepherding <note>term: techne; the Greek word for a specialized skill, craft, or branch of knowledge.</note> is concerned with nothing other than the good of what it is set over, to provide what is best for it. <margin>E</margin> For its own affairs are sufficiently provided for, so that it is the best possible art as long as it does not lack anything of being the art of shepherding. Thus, I thought just now that it was necessary for us to agree that every rule, insofar as it is a rule, considers what is best for nothing other than the one who is ruled and served, whether in a public or private office. But do you think that the rulers in cities—those who are truly rulers—exercise their office willingly?" "By Zeus," he said, "I don't just think it, I know it!" "What about other types of rule?" I asked. "Don't you realize that in the other arts, no one is willing to rule for their own sake? Instead, they demand wages, implying that the benefit of ruling will not come to themselves, but to those who are ruled. Tell me this: do we not say that each art is different from another because it has a different power? And, blessed man, do not answer contrary to your opinion, so that we may reach a conclusion." "Yes," he said, "that is what makes them different." "And does not each of these arts provide us with some specific benefit, rather than a general one? For example, medicine provides health, navigation provides safety at sea, and so on." "Certainly." "And does not the art of earning wages provide wages? For that is its specific power. <margin>F</margin> Do you call medicine and navigation the same thing? Or, if you wish to define them precisely as you proposed, if someone becomes healthy while acting as a pilot because sailing on the sea was good for his health, would you for that reason call his art medicine?" "Certainly not," he said. "Nor, I think, would you call the art of earning wages 'medicine' if someone becomes healthy while earning a wage." "No." "Well then, would you call medicine 'the art of earning wages' if someone earns a wage while practicing medicine?" "No," he said. "Now, we agreed that the benefit of each art is specific?" "Let it be so," he said. "Therefore, whatever benefit all craftsmen receive in common is clearly the result of their using some additional thing that is the same for all of them." "It seems so," he said. <margin>G</margin> "We say then that the benefit craftsmen receive by earning wages comes from their use of the additional art of earning wages." He agreed with difficulty. "Therefore, this benefit—the receiving of wages—does not come to each man from his own specific art. Rather, if we are to look at it precisely, the art of medicine produces health, while the art of earning produces a wage. The art of building produces a house, while the art of earning, following after it, produces a wage. And so it is with all the other arts: each performs its own work and benefits that over which it is set. But if a wage is not added to it, is there any benefit the craftsman receives from his art?" "It does not appear so," he said. "Does he then provide no benefit when he works for free?" "I think he does." "Then, Thrasymachus, it is now clear that no art or rule provides for its own benefit. Instead, as we were saying long ago, it provides for and commands the benefit of the subject; it considers the interest of the weaker, who is the subject, and not the interest of the stronger. For these reasons, dear Thrasymachus, I was saying just now that no one is willing to rule voluntarily, or to take up the task of correcting the evils of others, but instead they demand a wage; because the man who is going to practice his art beautifully never does what is best for himself...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...is something absolute, a bit more robust, more liberal, and more kingly than justice; and as I was saying from the beginning, that which is advantageous to the stronger is just, whereas the unjust is useful and advantageous to itself." When Thrasymachus had said these things, he had it in mind to depart, after he had poured a great flood of speech into our ears with the greatest force, like a bath-keeper. Those who were present, however, did not permit this, but compelled him both to stay and to offer a reason for the things he had said; and I in particular was vehemently asking: "O blessed Thrasymachus, having tossed out such a speech, do you hurry to depart before you have either fully taught us or learned yourself whether this matter is as you say, or otherwise? <margin>B</margin> Or do you perhaps think you have undertaken to define a small matter? Is it not rather the rule of life, by which if any of us receives it, he may live in the best possible way?" "Do I think," he said, "that the matter is otherwise?" "You seem," I said, "to have no care for us, nor to consider whether we live worse or better, being ignorant of that which you claim to know. But, O good man, show this to us willingly. For you will not have ill-placed a benefit which you bestow upon us, who are so many. I will indeed say what I feel. You by no means persuade me that injustice brings greater profit than justice, even if every license be granted to it so that it may effect whatever it desires. <margin>C</margin> But O good man, let there be someone who is unjust and who can do injury either by stealth or by force, yet you still do not persuade me that there is greater profit in injustice itself. In this opinion, perhaps, it is not only I, but some other of us who is of the same mind. Persuade us, therefore, blessed man, that we have not correctly valued justice more than injustice." "How," he said, "shall I further persuade you, if you are not persuaded by those things I was just saying? What further thing shall I do? Shall I thrust the speech into your mind?" "By no means," I said, "by Jupiter! <note>original: per Iovem; a common Latin oath translating the Greek "By Zeus."</note> But I would wish this first: that you stand by your words; or if you wish to change anything, make it known openly, and do not deceive us. <margin>D</margin> But then you see, Thrasymachus, so that we may resume the previous points: that when you first defined the true doctor as a healer of the sick, you did not afterwards think that the shepherd should be defined so purely, so that he guards only insofar as he is a shepherd. On the contrary, you think that he feeds the sheep, insofar as he is a shepherd, not for the benefit of the sheep, but for a devouring appetite, rather like a guest who is to eat them, or like a man fond of money who is going to sell them, rather than like a shepherd. Surely the pastoral art cares for nothing else except that what it guards be in the best condition. <margin>E</margin> For to the extent that it is a true pastoral faculty, nothing is lacking to it from being sufficient and the best. Thus I thought it necessary for us to confess that every headship, in that which is a headship, looks to the good of nothing else except that which is under it and cared for by it, whether it be private or public. But you, do you think that the princes in cities, who are truly princes, perform their magistracies willingly?" "I do not think so," he said, "but I know it for certain." "What then," I said, "of other headships? Do you not know that no one wants to take them up willingly, but they require a reward from them, as if no utility would come to themselves from such a command, but rather to those subject to them? Come, tell me," I said, "do we not say that any arts differ among themselves because they have a different power between them? Do not answer, O blessed man, contrary to your opinion, so that we may finish something." "By this very thing, clearly, they differ." "And does not each one provide some particular utility to us, and not one common with another? Just as medicine provides health, pilotage provides safety in sailing, and others similarly." <margin>F</margin> "Certainly." "And does not the mercenary art provide a price? For this is its power. Do you call medicine and pilotage the same? Or if you indeed wish to define and distinguish more absolutely as you established, even if someone steering a ship becomes healthy because the navigation is beneficial to him, you will not for this reason any more call pilotage itself 'medicine'?" "Certainly not." "Nor also, as I think, does a mercenary become healthy by the service itself." "Nor this." <margin>G</margin> "What further? Medicine is mercenary, if someone healing should make a profit?" "By no means." "And have we not conceded that the utility of any art is a certain particular one?" "Be it so." "If therefore all craftsmen commonly obtain some utility, it is clear that by using some one and the same common thing, they obtain a utility of this kind. We see that craftsmen receiving a reward follow a utility from the fact that they use the mercenary art." He barely assented. "Therefore this utility, namely the receiving of a reward, does not come to each from his own art. But if we wish to inquire diligently, medicine indeed produces health, the mercenary art produces profit; and architecture produces a building, while the mercenary art, having followed it, produces a reward; and all the others similarly. Each further perfects its own work, and benefits that for which it was invented. But if no reward be given to it, does the craftsman receive any utility from the art?" "None." "And does it not even then profit when he works for free?" "I think so." "Is it not therefore, O Thrasymachus, as is now manifest, that no art and no magistracy prepares utility for itself, but as we were saying in the previous points, it prepares and commands what is beneficial to the subject, always looking to the advantage of that inferior, not the superior. For these reasons, therefore, I was just now saying, O dear Thrasymachus, that no one approaches it, but they seek a reward; because he who wishes to undertake a command from a right art, and voluntarily the emendation of the evils of others...

<summary>In this passage from Plato's Republic, Socrates continues his debate with Thrasymachus, arguing that every true "art" (techne) exists to benefit its subject rather than the practitioner. He concludes that because ruling is an art that benefits the ruled, people only agree to rule if they are provided with wages or some form of compensation.</summary>
