Socrates now extends this logic to the "art of ruling," arguing that true leaders do not seek their own benefit, but the benefit of those they lead.</meta>

-># PLATO'S<-

<margin>A</margin> [A ruler] who is going to act according to the command of his own art, never acts for his own advantage, but for the utility of his subordinate. For this reason, it seems, a reward must be provided for those who are to be willing to govern—either money, or honor, or a penalty if they do not take up the command. "What do you mean by that, Socrates?" asked Glaucon. "I recognize the two rewards, but the 'penalty' you speak of, and how you place it in the category of a 'reward,' I do not understand." "Then you are unaware of the reward of the best men," I said, "for the sake of which the best men rule whenever they are willing to rule. Or are you unaware that being ambitious <note>original: φιλότιμόν (philotimon) - literally "honor-loving"</note> or being greedy <note>original: φιλάργυρον (philargyron) - "money-loving"</note> is considered a disgrace, and truly is one?" "I know that," said Glaucon. "For this reason, then," I said, "good men are not willing to rule for the sake of money or honor. For they do not wish to be called 'mercenaries' by openly receiving a wage for their office, <margin>B</margin> nor 'thieves' by secretly taking from the office. Nor, again, do they rule for honor’s sake, for they are not ambitious. It is necessary, therefore, that necessity and a penalty be imposed upon them if they are to be willing to take up office. This is why it is considered shameful for someone to seek office voluntarily without waiting for necessity. But the greatest of penalties is to be ruled by a worse man if one is not willing to rule himself. Fearing this very punishment, honest men seem to me to take up office when they do; and then they approach it not as if they were coming to something good, nor as if they were going to enjoy themselves in it, but as a necessary thing, since they have no better men, nor even equals, to whom they might entrust the task. Indeed, if there were a city of good men, <margin>C</margin> there would be as much struggle *not* to rule as there is now a desire to rule. There it would be clear that a truly legitimate prince does not look to his own advantage, but to that of his subject. Therefore, anyone who is not mindless would rather choose to be benefited by another than to be entangled in business while looking after others. I therefore in no way concede to Thrasymachus that justice is 'the interest of the stronger.' But this we shall consider hereafter. Much greater to me seems what Thrasymachus says now, when he asserts that the life of the unjust man is better than the life of the just. You, therefore, Glaucon, which of the two do you choose as being more true?" "I think the life of the just man is more profitable," said Glaucon. "Did you hear," I asked, "how many goods Thrasymachus just now enumerated as belonging to the unjust life?" "I heard," he said, "but I am not persuaded." "Do you want us to show him, <margin>D</margin> if we can find a way, that he is not speaking the truth?" "How could I not want that?" he replied. "If we were to speak against his speech, setting one argument against another, listing all the goods that the just man enjoys, and he in turn replied, and then we spoke again, it would be necessary for some third party to count and measure the goods we each collected for both sides; thus we would need certain judges to settle this dispute. But if, as we began just now, we discuss the matter by reaching mutual agreements, we ourselves will be both the advocates and the judges." "That is certainly so," he said. "Which method do you prefer?" "This one," he said. "Come then, Thrasymachus," I said, "answer us from the beginning. Do you assert that perfect injustice is more profitable than perfect justice?" "I certainly do," he replied, "and I have given the reasons why. What about this? Do you call one of these a virtue and the other a vice?" "Why not?" "Is justice, then, a virtue, and injustice a vice?" "Is that what I should confess, my charming friend, <note>original: ὦ ἥδιστε (o hediste) - a polite but slightly condescending 'most sweet' or 'dear sir'</note> when I say that injustice is profitable and justice is not?" "What then?" "The opposite," he said. <margin>E</margin> "Would you then call justice a vice?" "No, but a very noble simplicity." <note>original: εὐήθειαν (euetheian) - usually meaning 'good-naturedness' or 'simplicity,' but here Thrasymachus uses it to mean 'foolishness.'</note> "Then you call injustice 'wickedness'?" "No indeed. I call it good counsel <note>original: εὐβουλίαν (euboulian) - 'sagacity' or 'soundness of judgment.'</note> and wisdom." "Do unjust men, Thrasymachus, seem to you to be prudent and good?" "Yes, those who are able to do injustice perfectly—those who can bring cities and nations under their power. You perhaps think I am speaking of those who cut purses in secret; those things are profitable too, if they go unnoticed, but they are not worth mentioning. I mean what I just now said." "I understand what you mean," I replied. "But I wonder at this: if you place injustice in the category of virtue and wisdom, and justice in their opposites." "I certainly do." "This is now a more solid position, my friend, and it is no longer easy to find what one might say. For if you had asserted that injustice is profitable, yet confessed that it is a vice or something shameful (as some others do), <margin>G</margin> we could say something based on common opinions. But now it is clear you will say that injustice is something both beautiful and robust, and you will attribute to it all the other things we used to attribute to justice, since you have dared to place it among virtue and wisdom." "You prophesy most truly," he said. "Nonetheless, I must not shrink from inquiring further into this dispute, as long as I think you are saying what you really think. For you seem to me, Thrasymachus, to be not at all joking now, but to be putting forward what you believe to be the truth." "What does it matter to you whether I believe it or not, as long as you do not refute my argument?" "It matters nothing," I said. "But answer me this further: Does the just man seem to you to want to have more <note>original: πλέον ἔχειν (pleon echein) - 'to have more than one's share' or 'to outdo.'</note> than another just man?" "By no means. For then he would not be as 'civilized' and 'simple' as he is now." "What then? Would he want to outdo a just action?" "Not even a just action," he said. "Would he then think it worthy to have more than an unjust man, and would he think that to be just, or not?" "He would think it so," he said, "and he would think it worthy, but he would not

<meta>Continuity: On the previous page, Socrates argued that the best men rule not for profit or honor, but to avoid the penalty of being ruled by someone worse than themselves. # ON THE REPUBLIC, BOOK I.

<margin>A</margin>...would be able. "But that is not what I am asking," I said, "but whether the just man thinks he should have more than, or would wish to outdo <note>original: πλεονεκτεῖν (pleonektein) - to seek more than one's share or to outdo others</note>, another just man." "Not at all," he said. "And what about the unjust? Does he think he should outdo the just man and the just action?" "Of course," he said, "since he thinks he should have more than everyone else." <margin>B</margin> "Therefore, the unjust man will also outdo the unjust person and the unjust action, and he will strive to ensure he takes the most of everything for himself?" "That is so." "Let us put it this way then," I said: "The just man does not outdo his like, but his unlike; whereas the unjust man outdoes both his like and his unlike." "You have said it perfectly," he replied. "And yet," I said, "is the unjust man wise and good, while the just man is neither?" "That is also well said," he replied. "Therefore," I said, "the unjust man resembles the wise and the good, while the just man does not." "How could he not," he said, "being the sort of man he is, resemble those like himself? And the one who is not like them, does not?" "Excellent. So each of them is like those whom he resembles." "What else could he be?" he said. "Very well, <margin>C</margin> Thrasymachus; do you call someone 'musical' and another 'unmusical'?" "I do." "Which is wise and which is unwise?" "The musical man is surely wise, and the unmusical is unwise." "And in the things he is wise, is he also good? And in the things he is unwise, is he bad?" "Yes." "And what about the physician? Is it not the same?" "It is." "Does it seem to you then, my excellent friend, that a musical man, when tuning a lyre, would wish to outdo another musical man in the tightening and loosening of the strings, or think it right to have the better of him?" "Not in my view." "But would he outdo the unmusical man?" "Necessarily," he said. "And what of the physician? In the matter of food or drink, would he wish to outdo either another physician or a medical practice?" "Certainly not." "But would he outdo a non-physician?" "Yes." "Consider then, regarding every kind of knowledge and ignorance: does it seem to you that anyone who knows a subject would wish to choose to do or say more than what another who knows the subject would do or say, and not rather do the same things as his like in the same action?" "Perhaps," he said, "it must be so." "And what of the ignorant man? Would he not outdo both the man of knowledge and the ignorant man alike?" <margin>D</margin> "Perhaps." "But the man of knowledge is wise?" "I say so." "And the wise man is good?" "I say so." "Therefore, the good and wise man will not wish to outdo his like, but his unlike and opposite." "It seems so," he said. "But the bad and ignorant man will outdo both his like and his opposite." "So it appears." "Therefore, Thrasymachus," I said, "our unjust man outdoes both his like and his unlike? Was that not what you said?" "I did," he said. "And the just man will not outdo his like, but only his unlike?" "Yes." "It follows then," I said, "that the just man resembles the wise and good, while the unjust man resembles the bad and ignorant." "It's likely." "But we agreed that each is of the same character as the one he resembles." "We did indeed." "So, the just man has been revealed to us as good and wise, and the unjust as ignorant and bad." Now, Thrasymachus conceded all this—not as easily as I am now recounting it, but dragged along with difficulty, and with <margin>E</margin> a miraculous amount of sweat (it being summer, after all). It was then that I saw something I had never seen before: Thrasymachus blushing. When we had agreed that justice is virtue and wisdom, and injustice is vice and ignorance, I said, "Let that be settled for us. But we were also saying that injustice is something powerful. Or do you not remember, Thrasymachus?" "I remember," he said, "but I am not satisfied with what you are saying now, and I have arguments I could make about them. If I were to speak, I know well you would say I am 'making a public speech.' So either let me speak as much as I want, or if you wish to ask questions, ask; and I will say 'Very well' to you, as one does with old women telling stories, and I will nod 'yes' and 'no.'" "By no means," I said, "not against your own opinion." "To please you," he said, "since you will not let me speak. What else do you want?" "Nothing, by Zeus," I said, "but if you will do this, do it. I shall ask." "Ask then." "I ask this, then, which I asked <margin>F</margin> just now—so that we may examine the argument in order—what sort of thing justice is in relation to injustice. For it was said somewhere that injustice is both more capable and stronger than justice. But now," I said, "if justice is indeed wisdom and virtue, it will easily appear, I think, to be stronger than injustice, since injustice is ignorance; no one could still be unaware of that. But I do not desire to treat it so simply, Thrasymachus, but in this way: would you say a city could be unjust, and could attempt to enslave other cities unjustly, and have many already enslaved under its power?" "How could it not?" he said. "And the best city will do this most of all, being most perfectly unjust." "I understand," I said, "that this was your argument. But <margin>G</margin> I am considering this about it: whether the city that becomes superior to another city will have this power without justice, or if it must necessarily have it with justice." "If," he said, "it is as you were just saying—that justice is wisdom—then it will be with justice; but if it is as I was saying, it will be with injustice." "I am very delighted, Thrasymachus," I said, "that you are not merely nodding 'yes' and 'no,' but are also answering quite beautifully." "I am doing it to gratify you," he said. "That is good of you. But gratify me in this too, and tell me: do you think that a city, or an army, or robbers, or thieves, or any other group that jointly attempts something unjust, could accomplish anything if they were to act unjustly toward one another?" "Certainly not," he said. "What if they did not act unjustly? Would they not accomplish more?" "Quite so." For seditions...

<margin>A</margin> ...would be able. And I am not asking that, but whether the just man thinks he is worthy of having more than, or wishes to outdo, the just; and on the contrary, the unjust. It is certainly so. But what of the unjust? Does he think it fair to have more than both the just man and the just action? Why not? Since he thinks himself worthy of having more than everyone. Therefore, will the unjust man have more than the unjust person and the unjust action, and will he strive to surpass all in having? These things are true. What stands in the way, he said, of the one who is such being also like those who are such, and the one who is not such, not being like them? Very well. Surely. And in the same way we shall speak of the physician. In the same way. But I consider this about it: whether this city, which is more powerful than another city, will have this power without justice, or if it must necessarily have it with justice. If indeed, as you were saying a little before, justice itself is wisdom, it must be with justice. But if as I was saying, without justice. # PLATO

<margin>A</margin> "Thrasymachus, does not injustice produce enmities and battles among men, while justice produces harmony and friendship?" "Let it be so," he said, "so that I do not have to disagree with you." "You do well, my excellent friend. But tell me this also: if it is the work of injustice to implant hatred wherever it exists, then when it arises among free men and slaves, will it not make them hate one another and fall into strife, rendering them unable to achieve anything in common harmony?" "Certainly." "And what if it arises between two people? Will they not disagree, hate one another, and be enemies both to each other and to just men?" "They will indeed," he said. <margin>B</margin> "And if injustice resides in a single person, O wonderful man, will it not destroy his own power? Or will he retain it nonetheless?" "Let him retain it," he replied. "Does it not appear to have such a power that, in whatever it exists—whether a city, a tribe, an army, or anything else—it first renders that thing unable to act in cooperation with itself because of strife and disagreement? And furthermore, it makes that thing an enemy to itself, to every opponent, and to the just? Is it not so?" "It is." "And even in a single individual, I think, it will do all the things that it is by nature meant to do. First, it will make him unable to act because he is at odds with himself and lacks internal harmony. Then, it will make him an enemy both to himself and to just men. Is that not right?" "Yes." "And the gods, my friend, are they not also just?" "Let us suppose they are," he said. "Therefore, the unjust man will also be an enemy to the gods, Thrasymachus; but the just man will be their friend." "Feast on the discourse <note>original: "orationis epulo" / "ἑστιάσεως". Socrates uses a metaphor of a banquet, suggesting that the argument is a meal for the mind.</note> as you please," he said. "For I will not oppose you, lest I make these people here angry with me." <margin>C</margin> "Come then," I said, "and fulfill the rest of the feast for me by answering just as you have been doing. For it is clear that just men appear wiser, better, and more capable of action, while the unjust are unable to do anything together. In fact, when we say that any who are entirely unjust have ever vigorously accomplished anything together, we are not speaking the truth. For they would not have restrained themselves from harming one another if they were completely unjust. <margin>D</margin> But it is clear that some justice was in them, which made them at least refrain from injuring both each other and those they were attacking at the same time; and it was through this justice that they did what they did. They were only half-corrupted by injustice when they set out on their unjust deeds; for those who are thoroughly wicked and completely unjust are also completely incapable of acting. I understand that this is how things are, and not as you originally proposed. But whether the just also live better than the unjust and are happier <note>original: "feliciores" / "εὐδαιμονέστεροί". This refers to Eudaimonia, a state of flourishing or "living well."</note>—which is what we proposed to consider later—must now be examined. And, as it seems to me, this follows from what we have already said. Yet, we must consider it even more carefully. <margin>E</margin> For our discussion is not about some trivial or negligible matter, but about the very way in which one ought to live. Consider now." "Behold, I am considering," he said. "Tell me then: does it seem to you that a horse has a specific function?" "To me, yes." "Would you then define the <term>function</term> <note>original: "opus" / "ἔργον" (ergon). In Greek philosophy, the ergon is the specific work or purpose for which a thing is uniquely suited.</note> of a horse, or of anything else, as that which one can do only with that thing, or best with it?" "I do not understand," he said. "But look at it this way: could you see with anything other than your eyes?" "By no means." "What then? Could you hear with anything other than your ears?" "Not at all." "Therefore, we would be right to call these the 'functions' of those organs?" "Rightly so." "Could you not prune the shoots of a vine with a sword, or a carving knife, or many other tools?" "Why not?" "But I think you could not do it so well as with a pruning hook made for that purpose." "That is true." "Shall we then define this as the function of that tool?" "We shall indeed." <margin>F</margin> "Now I think you understand better what I was asking just now when I inquired whether the 'function' of each thing is that which it alone performs, or performs better than anything else." "I understand now," he said, "and it seems to me that this is the function of each thing." "Very well," I said. "Does it also seem to you that there is a <term>virtue</term> <note>original: "virtus" / "ἀρετή" (arete). This refers to the specific "excellence" that allows a thing to perform its function well.</note> for everything to which a function is assigned? Let us return to the same examples. We say the eyes have a function?" "They do." "Is there then also a virtue of the eyes?" "There is." "What about the ears? Was there a function?" "Yes." "And therefore a virtue?" "And a virtue." "And must we not say the same of all other things?" "The same." "Could the eyes ever perform their own function beautifully if they did not possess their own proper virtue, but had a vice instead of virtue?" "How could they? For you perhaps mean blindness instead of sight." <margin>G</margin> "Whatever their virtue may be—for I am not asking that yet—but whether they perform their function well by their own proper virtue, or badly by vice." "You speak the truth," he said. "And will the ears, if deprived of their own virtue, perform their function badly?" "Badly." "Shall we apply the same reasoning to all other things?" "It seems so to me." "Come then, and consider this next. Is there any function of the soul that you could not perform with anything else in existence—such as caring, ruling, deliberating, and all such things? Could we rightly attribute these to anything other than the soul, and say they are its own?" "To nothing else." "What about living itself? Shall we not say it is a function of the soul?" "Most certainly," he said. "And do we not say that there is also a certain virtue of the soul?" "We do." <margin>H</margin> "Will the soul ever, O Thrasymachus, perform its own functions well if deprived of its proper virtue? Or is that impossible?" "It is impossible." "It is necessary then that a bad soul rules and cares badly, while a good soul does all these things well." "Necessary." "Did we not agree that justice is the virtue of the soul, and injustice its vice?" "We did agree." "Therefore, the just soul and the just man will live well, but the unjust man will live badly." "So it appears according to your argument," he said. "But he who lives well is blessed and happy; and he who does not, is the opposite." "How could he not be?" "Therefore, the just man is happy, while the unjust man is miserable." "Let it be so," he said. "But surely..."

[The Greek text on this page is the original source for the Latin translation provided above. It follows the same dialogue: Socrates proves that injustice creates "strife and battles" (μάχας) while justice creates "harmony and friendship" (ὁμόνοιαν καὶ φιλίαν). He leads Thrasymachus through the logic of "function" (ἔργον) and "virtue" (ἀρετή), concluding that the soul’s function is "to care, rule, and deliberate" (ἐπιμελεῖσθαι καὶ ἄρχειν καὶ βουλεύεσθαι) and to "live" (ζῆν). Since justice is the soul's virtue, the just man lives well and is "happy" (εὐδαίμων), while the unjust man is "wretched" (ἄθλιος).]

ON THE REPUBLIC, BOOK II.

"But surely to be miserable is not profitable, my wonderful friend." "How could it be?" "Never then, O blessed Thrasymachus, is injustice more profitable than justice." "Let this be your feast, Socrates," he said, "at the festival of Bendis <note>original: "Βενδιδείοις" / "Dionysiis". Bendis was a Thracian goddess identified with Artemis/Diana; her festival involved a torch race.</note>." "A feast provided by you, Thrasymachus," I said, "since you have become gentle with me and have ceased to be difficult. However, I have not feasted well, though that is my own fault, not yours. Just as gluttons <note>original: "λίχνοι" / "auidiores"</note> snatch at every dish as it is carried past to taste it before they have properly enjoyed the previous one, so I seem to myself to have left the original object of our inquiry—what justice actually is—before finding it. Instead, I rushed off to consider whether it is a form of vice and ignorance, or wisdom and virtue. And when the later argument cropped up—that injustice is more profitable than justice—I could not refrain from moving from the former topic to this one. The result of our discussion for me, at present, is that I know nothing. For as long as I do not know what justice is, I shall hardly know whether it is a virtue or not, or whether the one who possesses it is happy or unhappy."

# PLATO'S REPUBLIC,
## OR, ON JUSTICE,
### THE SECOND DIALOGUE.

---

### SUMMARY OF THE DIALOGUE.

In the first book or dialogue, Plato laid the foundation of the dispute and represented the sum of the whole doctrine; now he descends to the specific parts. First, he illustrates the definition of Justice by its opposite, namely Injustice. For opposites become clear through their opposites. Then, he proposes a most beautiful beginning to a very rich discussion concerning the Republic, and deals distinctly with its members and its head—that is, the subjects and the magistracy. He describes the nature of the magistrate <note>The "Guardian" class</note> as being both spirited and perceptive: and therefore capable of repelling the force of enemies and inflicting punishment on wicked citizens with a certain great vehemence of mind; yet peaceably restraining his own people under the protection of the laws, and even establishing rewards for the good according to their merits. He makes two parts of that education: Music and Gymnastics, over which Religion is the mistress. He treats religion in such a way that he refutes the superstition of his own time, yet he does not teach the true religion, inasmuch as he was ignorant of it.

---

<margin>C</margin>
**When** I had said these things, I thought I was free from the discussion; but this, as it seems, was only the prelude. For Glaucon is always most courageous in all things, and particularly then he would not accept Thrasymachus’s withdrawal, but said: "Socrates, do you wish to merely *seem* to have persuaded us, or to *truly* persuade us that it is in every way better to be just than unjust?" "To truly persuade you," I said, "is what I would choose, if it were up to me." "Then," he said, "you are not doing what you wish. For tell me: does there seem to you to be a type of good which we would choose to have, not because we desire its consequences, but because we welcome it for its own sake? Such as joy, and all those pleasures that are harmless and bring nothing in the future except the delight of having them." <margin>D</margin> "To me at least," I said, "there seems to be such a thing." "And what of the type which we love both for its own sake and for what comes from it? Such as understanding, sight, and health. For we welcome such things for both reasons." "Certainly," I said. "And do you see a third kind of good," he asked, "which includes physical exercise, being treated when sick, the practice of medicine, and other ways of making money? For these we say are burdensome <note>original: "ἐπίπονα" / "laboriofa"</note> but beneficial to us. We would never choose to have them for their own sake, but only for the sake of the rewards and the other things that result from them." "Yes," I said, "there is this third kind. But what of it?" "In which of these," he asked, "do you place justice?" "In my opinion," I said, "it belongs in the finest category—the one which must be loved both for its own sake and for its consequences by anyone who intends to be truly blessed." <margin>E</margin> "That is not how it seems to the many," he said, "but they place it in the burdensome category, which must be practiced for the sake of rewards, reputation, and glory, but which should be avoided for its own sake as something difficult." "I know," I said, "that this is the common opinion, and for a long time now justice has been disparaged by Thrasymachus as being of this sort, while injustice is praised. But I, it seems, am a slow learner." "Come then," he said, "listen to me as well, to see if you still hold the same view. For Thrasymachus seems to me to have been charmed by you like a snake <note>original: "ὥσπερ ὄφις κηληθῆναι" / "tanquam ferpens... delinitus"</note> sooner than he should have been. But for me, the proof has not yet been demonstrated to my satisfaction for either side. I desire to hear what each of them is, and what power each has by itself when dwelling in the soul—letting the rewards and the consequences go for now. I will proceed in this way, if it pleases you: I will renew the argument of Thrasymachus. First, I will say what people say justice is and from where it originated. <margin>F</margin> Second, that everyone who practices it does so unwillingly, as something necessary but not as a good. Third, that they have good reason to do so; for the life of the unjust man is, as they say, much better than that of the just man. Although, Socrates, it does not seem so to me. Yet I am at a loss, for my ears are dinned by hearing Thrasymachus and countless others. But the argument on behalf of justice—that it is better than injustice—I have not yet heard from anyone in the way I want. I wish to hear justice praised for itself."

<margin>A</margin>But I think I would most like to hear this from you. Therefore, I will speak at length, praising the unjust life, and by speaking I will show you in what way I wish to hear you, in turn, blaming injustice and praising justice. But see if this pleases you. "Most of all," I said; "for regarding what subject would a person of sound mind more gladly listen and speak?" "You speak excellently," he said. "Now listen to what I first said I would speak of: what justice is and from where it arose. They say that by nature, to do injustice is a good thing, but to suffer injustice is an evil; yet there is far more evil in suffering injustice than there is good in doing it. Therefore, after they had both inflicted and suffered injustice, and had tasted both, those who were unable to avoid the one and achieve the other thought it would be profitable to enter into a contract <note>original: "pasciscantur" / "ξυνθέσθαι". This is an early description of what modern philosophers call the 'Social Contract'—the idea that laws exist to protect us from each other.</note> with one another, so that they would neither inflict nor suffer injustice. From this,
<margin>B</margin>they say, laws and their decrees began to be established, and the commands of the law were named 'lawful' and 'just.' This, then, they claim is the origin and essence of justice: it is a middle ground between the best, which is to do injustice without paying the penalty, and the worst, which is to suffer injustice without being able to take revenge. Therefore, justice is loved while in this middle position, not as a good thing, but because of the weakness of those who cannot do injustice; it is a barrier against the infliction of wrongs. For surely a man who had the power to do it, and was truly a man, would never enter into a contract with anyone to neither inflict nor suffer injustice; otherwise, he would be insane. This, Socrates, is the nature of justice, and it is from such things, as they say, that it was born. However, we would clearly see that those who observe justice do so unwillingly, because they lack the power to do injustice, if we were to imagine such a thing in our minds:
<margin>C</margin>if we gave both of them—the just and the unjust man—the liberty to do whatever they pleased, and then followed them, observing where their desire would lead each. We would surely catch the just man, driven by a greed for 'more' <note>original: "auiditate" / "πλεονεξίαν". Pleonexia is the Greek term for 'over-reaching' or the desire to have more than one's share.</note>, heading toward the same end as the unjust man. Every nature naturally pursues this as a good, but is led by law and force to respect equality. The liberty I speak of would be like the power they say was once given to the ancestor of Gyges the Lydian <note>Glaucon tells the famous legend of the Ring of Gyges, a story about the corrupting power of absolute anonymity.</note>. For they say he was a hired shepherd for the man who then ruled the Lydians. After a great storm of rain arose and the earth was shaken, they say the earth opened up a chasm in the region where he was grazing his flocks. When he saw this, wondering, he descended into the chasm and saw
<margin>D</margin>other marvelous things that they tell of in fables, and a hollow bronze horse, which had doors in its sides; having opened these, he saw the body of a dead man of unusual size. The body had nothing else on it except a golden ring on its finger. Having taken this, he left. Then he returned to the assembly of shepherds, which was held every month to report on the king's property. He sat down among the others, and it happened that when he by chance turned the bezel of the ring toward his palm, he was seen by no one, and the others spoke of him as if he were absent. Marveling at this, he touched the ring again and turned the bezel outward, and when he did so, he appeared again.
<margin>E</margin>Noticing this, he carefully tested whether the ring had this power, and it was found to be so: when the stone was turned toward himself, he was seen by no one; when turned toward others, he became visible. Having discovered this, he managed to be sent as one of the messengers to the king; upon arrival, he seduced the king's wife, and with her help, he plotted the death of the king, and having killed him, he seized the kingdom. Now, if there were two such rings, and the just man
<margin>F</margin>possessed one and the unjust man the other, no one would be found to be so 'adamantine' <note>original: "adamantinus" / "ἀδαμάντινος". In antiquity, 'adamant' referred to an impossibly hard, unbreakable substance like diamond.</note>, as it seems, that he would persist in justice and want to abstain from what belongs to others—when he could fearlessly take whatever he wanted from the marketplace, enter other people's houses, sleep with anyone he desired, kill, and release whomever he wished from prison, and do other things among men as if he were a god. In doing these things, the one would act no
<margin>G</margin>differently from the other; both would tend toward the same end. This is a great proof, one might say, that no one is just willingly, but only by necessity, as if justice were not a good for the individual privately. For wherever anyone thinks he can act unjustly, he does so at once; for every man thinks that injustice is much more profitable to him privately than justice. And whoever judges in this way thinks correctly, as the authors of this argument say. For if someone who obtained such power were unwilling to do any injustice and did not touch the property of others, he would be thought most miserable and most foolish by those who noticed it; yet they would praise him to each other's faces, deceiving one another because they greatly fear suffering injustice themselves. So much for that. But the life of each,
<margin>H</margin>the just and the unjust, we shall judge clearly if we distinguish the most just man and the most unjust man separately; otherwise, we cannot do it. Let the distinction be this: let us take nothing of injustice away from the unjust man, nor anything of justice from the just man, but let us place each as perfect in his own pursuit. First, then, let the unjust man act like a supreme pilot or a physician, who, as the most excellent craftsmen, senses what is
unjust <note>This is the catchword to bridge to the next page.</note>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin><margin>Discourse concerning justice</margin>...but I think I would most like to hear this from you. Therefore, I will speak at length, praising the unjust life, and by speaking I will show you in what way I wish to hear you, in turn, blaming injustice and praising justice. But see if this pleases you. "Most of all," I said; "for regarding what subject would a person of sound mind more gladly listen and speak?" "You speak excellently," he said. "Now listen to what I first said I would speak of: what justice is and from where it arose. They say that by nature, to do injustice is a good thing, but to suffer injustice is an evil; yet there is far more evil in suffering
<margin>B</margin>injustice than there is good in doing it. Therefore, after they had both inflicted and suffered injustice, and had tasted both, those who were unable to avoid the one and achieve the other thought it would be profitable to enter into a contract with one another, so that they would neither inflict nor suffer injustice. From this, they say, laws and their decrees began to be established, and the commands of the law were named 'lawful' and 'just.' This, then, they claim is the origin and essence of justice: it is a middle ground between the best, which is to do injustice without paying the penalty, and the worst, which is to suffer injustice without being able to take revenge. Therefore, justice is loved while in this middle position, not as a good thing, but because of the weakness of those who cannot do injustice. For surely a man who had the power to do it, and was truly a man, would never enter into a contract with anyone to neither inflict nor suffer injustice; otherwise, he would be insane. This, Socrates, is the nature of justice, and it is from such things, as they say, that it was born.
<margin>C</margin>However, we would clearly see that those who observe justice do so unwillingly, because they lack the power to do injustice, if we were to imagine such a thing in our minds: if we gave both of them the liberty to do whatever they pleased, the just and the unjust man, and then followed them, observing where their desire would lead each. We would surely catch the just man heading toward the same end as the unjust man, driven by greed—that which every nature naturally pursues as a good, but is led by law and force to respect equality. The liberty I speak of would be like the power they say was once given to the ancestor of Gyges the Lydian.
<margin>D</margin><margin>The Ring of Gyges</margin>For they say he was a shepherd serving the man who then ruled the Lydians. After a great storm of rain arose and an earthquake occurred, the earth was rent, and a chasm opened in the place where he was grazing his flocks. When he saw this, wondering, he descended and saw other marvelous things that they tell of in fables, and a hollow bronze horse, which had little windows; looking through these, he saw the body of a dead man, as it appeared, larger than a human. The body had nothing else on it except a golden ring on its hand; having taken this, he left. While he was sitting among the others, he happened to turn the collet of the ring toward himself, to the inside of his hand. When he did so, he became invisible to those sitting with him, and they spoke of him as if he were gone. He marveled at this, and touching the ring again,
<margin>E</margin>he turned the collet outward; and when he turned it, he became visible. <margin>F</margin>seized the throne. <meta>This page continues Glaucon’s challenge to Socrates. In the previous section, Glaucon argued that justice is merely a social contract created by the weak to protect themselves. Here, he proposes a thought experiment involving two "ideal" figures: the perfectly unjust man and the perfectly just man, to see which life is truly happier.</meta>

### ON THE REPUBLIC, BOOK II.

**A** He approaches his tasks, he leaves those things aside, and if he fails in any matter, he is able to correct it. In the same way, the unjust man, when he approaches his crimes correctly, must remain hidden if he is to be truly and supremely unjust. But if he is caught, he must be considered a failure. For the height of injustice is to seem just when one is not. Therefore, we must grant to the perfectly unjust man the most perfect injustice, and take nothing away. Instead, we must allow him, while committing the greatest injustices, to have prepared for himself the greatest reputation for justice. And if he should happen to trip up in any way, he should be able to set it right—being a man capable of speaking so as to persuade if any of his misdeeds are reported, and capable of using force **B** if force is required, through his courage and strength, and through his supply of friends and wealth.

When we have fashioned such a man, let us place beside him in our argument the just man: a simple and noble man who, as Aeschylus wrote, desires not to *seem* but to *be* good. We must certainly strip away this "seeming." For if he seems to be just, he will receive honors and gifts because people think he is such a man. It would then be unclear whether he is just for the sake of justice itself, or for the sake of the gifts and honors. He must be stripped of everything except justice, and placed in a state exactly opposite to the first man. Though doing no injustice, let him have the greatest reputation for injustice, so that he may be **C** tested in his justice, remaining unsoftened by his bad reputation and the things that follow from it. But let him remain immovable until death—seeming to be unjust through his whole life, yet being truly just. Thus, when both have reached the extreme—one of justice, the other of injustice—let them be judged as to which of them is the happier.

"My goodness!" I said, "my dear Glaucon, how vigorously you scrub each of these two men, just like a statue, to prepare them for our judgment."

"As much as I can," he said. "Since they are such as they are, it is no longer difficult, I think, to describe what kind of life awaits each of them. It must be told, then. And even if it is said somewhat crudely, do not **D** think that I am saying these things, Socrates, but rather those who praise injustice over justice. For they will say that the just man, being so disposed, will be scourged, tortured, and bound in chains. His eyes will be burned out, and finally, after suffering every evil, he will be impaled <note>original: "ανασχινδυλευθήσεται" / "suspendetur". In the Greek, this refers to a brutal form of execution similar to crucifixion or impalement, used here to show the ultimate worldly failure of the truly just man.</note>; he will then realize that one should not desire to *be* just, but only to *seem* so.

Indeed, the words of Aeschylus could be much more correctly applied to the unjust man. For they will say that the unjust man, because he pursues a reality consistent with truth and does not live according to the opinions of men, desires not to seem unjust, but to *be* so:

> Reaping the fruit of a deep and fertile furrow in his mind,
> From which noble counsels sprout.

First, he holds high office in his city because he appears to be just; then he marries from whatever family he wishes, and gives his children in marriage to whomever he chooses; he makes contracts **E** and associates with anyone he likes; and in all these things, he gains an advantage and makes a profit because he has no scruples about doing injustice. When entering into contests, whether public or private, he emerges superior and takes more than his share from his enemies. By taking more, he becomes rich, and can thus do good to his friends and harm his enemies. He offers sacrifices and dedications to the gods in abundance and magnificence, and he serves the gods (and whichever men he wishes) much better than the just man could. From this, they say it is likely that he is more beloved by the gods than the just man is. In this way, they say, Socrates, that both gods and men have prepared a better life for the unjust man than for the just."

When Glaucon had said these things, I was thinking of saying something in response, but his brother Adeimantus said, "Do you **F** think, Socrates, that enough has been said on this matter?"

"What else is there?" I asked.

"The very thing," he said, "that most needed to be said has not been mentioned."

"Well then," I said, "as the proverb goes, 'let a brother stand by a man.' So you, if he has left anything out, come to his aid—although what he has already said is enough to floor me and make it impossible for me to defend justice."

"That is nonsense," he said. "Listen to this as well. For we must also go through the arguments opposite to those he mentioned—those that praise justice and blame injustice—so that what I think Glaucon wants may be even clearer. **G** Parents certainly tell their sons, as do all those who have care of anyone, that it is necessary to be just; but they do not praise justice itself, but rather the reputation that comes from it. They want the man who is considered just to gain from that reputation the high offices, the marriages, and all the things Glaucon just listed.

But these people go even further with the benefits of reputation. For by bringing in the goodwill of the gods, they can list countless blessings for the holy, which they say the gods provide. <margin>*From the book titled Works and Days.*</margin> As the noble Hesiod and Homer testify: the former says the gods make the oaks for the just men bear acorns on their highest branches and bees in their middle, and their sheep are weighed down with wool, and many other goods of this kind. The other says things very similar. **H** 'Like a noble king,' he says, 'who is god-fearing and maintains justice: for him the black earth bears wheat and barley, the trees are weighed down with fruit, the flocks bring forth young without fail, and the sea provides fish.'

Musaeus and his son <note>referring to Eumolpus, a legendary figure associated with the Eleusinian Mysteries.</note> grant even more excellent goods to the just from the gods themselves. For in their account, they lead them into the underworld, seat them at a banquet of the holy, and make them spend all their time crowned with garlands and drinking—as if they considered eternal drunkenness to be the most beautiful reward for virtue. Others extend these rewards from the gods even further. For they say that the children of children, and an entire race, are left behind by the man who is holy and keeps his oaths.

<column-break/>

**A** <note>The Latin text here continues the same argument found in the Greek above.</note> He approaches [his crimes], he leaves [the mistakes] behind, and if he should slip up in anything else, he is able to correct it. Likewise, the unjust man who approaches his injuries correctly should remain hidden if he is to be supremely unjust. If he is caught, however, he should be considered unskilled. For the extreme of injustice is to be seen as just when one is not. Therefore, the most perfect injustice should be granted to the [seemingly] just man <note>The translator likely meant "unjust man" here, following the Greek.</note>, and nothing taken away. But it should be permitted that he who is most unjust holds the reputation of being just among all people. If he slips up in any way, he can correct it, being fit to persuade if any news of his evil deed is announced, and ready to use force **B** if necessary, through his courage, strength, and his abundance of wealth and friends.

Having fashioned such a man, let us place beside him the just man: a simple and noble man who, as it was written by Aeschylus, strives not to *seem* but to *be* good. Certainly, every opinion of justice must be removed from him, so that he does not seem just to anyone. For if he is seen as just, honors and rewards will be his. It will then be uncertain whether he is such a man for the sake of justice or for the sake of honors and gifts. He must therefore be deprived of all things except justice, and placed so as to be the opposite of the former man: doing nothing unjustly, let him be believed to be most unjust, so that he may be **C** tested for justice as if by an ordeal—so that he is not marked by infamy or the things that follow it, but remains immovable until death. While he is thought to be unjust throughout his whole life, he is nevertheless just. Thus, when both have reached the extreme—one of justice, the other of injustice—let it be judged which of them is more blessed.

"Goodness!" I said, "how vehemently, my friend Glaucon, you bring both men into clear judgment, like a statue."

"As much as I possibly can," he said. "Since they are such, it is no longer, I think, difficult to tell what kind of life awaits each. It must be said, then: if anything somewhat harsh is said, do not think, **D** Socrates, that I am saying it, but those who praise injustice over justice. For they will say that the just man, so afflicted, will be beaten, tortured, and endure chains. His eyes will be plucked out, and finally, having suffered all evils, he will be hanged <note>original: "suspendetur"</note>; and he will learn that one should desire not to *be* just, but to *seem* so."

Aeschylus's poem could be more correctly understood as referring to the unjust man. They will surely say that the unjust man, as one who follows things consistent with truth and does not live according to the opinion of men, desires not to seem but to be unjust: "Having in his mind a deep and fruitful furrow, from which excellent counsels sprout." First, he may take up magistracies in his city since he appears just; then marry from wherever he wishes, and marry off his own children to whomever he likes; he may meet and **E** communicate with anyone; and in addition to all this, he captures a profit by making a gain, since he does not fear at all to inflict injury. In contests, both public and private, he emerges superior and extracts more advantage than his adversaries. Thus he is made rich, whereby he may both hinder his enemies and help his friends. He worships the gods with gifts and sacrifices abundantly and magnificently, and can win over any man or god much better than the just man can. From this, they want it to follow that he is dearer to the gods than the just man. By this reasoning they say, O Socrates, that a life is better established for the unjust man among both gods and men than for the just man.

When Glaucon had said these things, and I was thinking of responding to them, his brother Adeimantus said, "Do you **F** not yet think, O Socrates, that enough has been said on this matter?"

"What then?" I said.

"Because," he said, "that which most needed to be said was not said."

"Brother," I said, "stand by the man, as the proverb goes. Therefore, if he has omitted anything here, you help; although the things said by him are enough to convict me and make me unable to defend justice."

Then he said, "That is nothing. Listen to these things besides. For it is fitting also to bring forward the contrary speeches to those he brought, by which justice is indeed praised and injustice, on the other hand, is blamed, so that what I think Glaucon wants may be more manifest. **G** Fathers indeed command their sons, and all who have the care of anyone, that it is necessary to be just; not praising justice itself, but the honors that follow from it: so that he who is held to be just may obtain from that reputation magistracies and marriages, and all those things which Glaucon said a little while ago about the man who is held to be just. Furthermore, they add glory to this. For mentioning the benevolence of the gods, they can report the highest benefits from the gods bestowed upon holy men. This is testified to by the noble Hesiod and Homer. The former asserts that the gods grant this to the just: that the oaks bear acorns on their higher branches, and in the middle, bees, and the sheep are burdened with wool, and many other goods of the same kind. The other says things similar to these: 'For as,' he says, 'to a good king who is like the gods, he brings a good name; the black **H** earth bears wheat and barley, the trees are burdened with fruit, the fertile cattle bring forth easily, and the sea provides fish.'

Musaeus likewise and his son wished even more excellent goods to be granted to the just by the gods themselves. For conducting them among the inhabitants of the underworld and placing them in the banquets of the holy, they make them crowned and always in great pleasure and drunkenness—thinking that the most beautiful reward of virtue is eternal intoxication. But others [say] that even longer-lasting rewards than these are given by the gods...

By these and similar means, they praise justice; but the profane and unjust they bury in a certain mire in the underworld, and force them to carry water in a sieve <note>This is a traditional Greek image of eternal futility in Hades, often associated with those who were never initiated into the mysteries</note>. They even mark the living with infamy. And finally, whatever punishments Glaucon recounted for those who are truly just but appear unjust, they recount the same for the unjust, and they have no others to tell. Such, then, is the praise and blame of both. Besides these things, Socrates, consider another kind of speech about justice and injustice, introduced both in private and by the poets. For everyone with one voice sings that **B** temperance and justice are noble things, but difficult and laborious; whereas intemperance and injustice are pleasant and easy to acquire, and are considered shameful only by opinion and law. They even say that unjust things are more profitable than just ones, as the common people say. And they readily honor the wicked who are rich and powerful, calling them happy both privately and publicly; but they despise those who are weak and poor, even though they concede that these men are better than the others. But of all these things, the most wonderful are the stories told about the gods and virtue: that the gods have given an unhappy life to many good men, and the opposite to the wicked. Furthermore, itinerant priests and soothsayers approach the doors of the rich, persuading them that they have power from the gods through **C** sacrifices and charms to expiate, in festivals and public games, any crime committed by them or their ancestors; and that they can harm any enemy they wish, whether just or unjust, at a small expense. Indeed, they assert that by certain incantations and binding-spells they can induce the gods to serve them in these matters.

Partly because the gods are moved by our prayers and gifts, they bring forward Homer as a witness, since **D** he himself says, "Even the gods themselves can be turned," and men turn them with sacrifices, vows, libations, and the smell of burnt offerings when anyone has transgressed and sinned. They circulate the books of Musæus and Orpheus, the offspring (as they say) of the Moon and the Muses, according to which they perform their rites, persuading not only individuals but even entire cities that absolutions and purifications of crimes are possible through sacrifices and the pleasures of games, for both the living and the dead. These they call *Teletas* <term>Teletas: ancient Greek initiation rites or expiatory sacrifices intended to purify the soul</term>, which liberate us from the evils that await us there; but for those who have neglected to sacrifice, terrible things remain. All these things, O Socrates, being of such a kind and so great concerning the rewards of virtue and vice, as **E** they pertain to gods and men, what do we think they will do to the minds of those young men who are clever by nature? They are able to fly, as it were, over all that is said and reason from it: what sort of person must one be, and what path should one enter to lead the best life? It is likely such a young man would revolve in his mind that saying of Pindar: "Shall I climb the high wall of justice, or enter the crooked ways of deceit, and so live my life fencing myself in?" For what has been said suggests that if I am just, yet do not seem so, there is no profit for me, but only certain labors and penalties. But to the unjust man who has attained the reputation of justice, a divine life is said to belong. Therefore, since the appearance of justice **F**—as the wise tell me—overpowers even the truth and is the master of happiness, must I not turn entirely toward it? I must, therefore, put on a mask and present a certain shadow-sketch of virtue, but behind me I must trail the cunning and versatile fox of the wise Archilochus <note>Archilochus was a Greek poet; the "fox" represents a clever, deceptive character</note>. But perhaps someone will say it is not easy for a wicked man to remain hidden forever. We shall answer that nothing great is easy. Nevertheless, if we wish to be happy, we must go where the tracks of these arguments lead. For to keep our wickedness hidden, we will form secret societies and clubs. There are also masters of persuasion who hand down the wisdom of the public assembly and the law courts; through these, we will partly persuade and partly **G** compel, so that while we take more for ourselves, we shall pay no penalty. But it is impossible, they say, either to hide from the gods or to compel them. Yet, if they do not exist, or if they care nothing for human affairs, we need not care about hiding from them. But if they do exist and do care for humans, we know it from no other source than the rumors and the poets who write their genealogies. These very same poets say that the gods can be turned by sacrifices, soothing prayers, and gifts. We must either believe both or neither. If we must believe them, we should act unjustly and then offer sacrifices to the gods from the fruits of our wrongdoing. For if we are just, we shall be unharmed by the **H** gods, but we shall lose the profits that come from injustice. But if we are unjust, we shall gain those profits, and by praying to them when we transgress and sin, we shall be delivered from punishment. But surely in the underworld we shall pay the penalty for the injustices we committed here, either ourselves or our children’s children. But, my friend, the reasoning goes: the initiations can do much, and the gods who release us are powerful, as the greatest cities say, and the children of the gods

from the gods. And they say that the children of children and the race following after remain for the holy and those who keep their oaths. These and other such things they say in praise of justice. But the unholy and unjust they bury in a certain mud in Hades, and they force them to carry water in a sieve. And even while they are living, they bring them into bad reputations; those very punishments which Glaucon went through regarding the just who are thought to be unjust, these they say regarding the unjust, and they have no others. Therefore, the praise and the blame for each is of this sort. In addition to these, consider, O Socrates, another kind of speech about justice and injustice, **B** spoken both in private and by the poets. For all sing from one mouth that temperance and justice are beautiful, but difficult and full of toil. But licentiousness and injustice are sweet and easy to acquire, and only in opinion and by law are they shameful. They say that unjust things are for the most part more profitable than just things. And they are willing to readily congratulate and honor the wicked who are rich and have other powers, both publicly and privately; but they dishonor and overlook those who are weak and poor, though they acknowledge that these are better than the others. But of all these, the stories told about the gods and virtue are the most wonderful: that even the gods have assigned misfortunes and a bad life to many good men, and the opposite fate to the opposite men. And beggars and soothsayers, going to the doors of the rich, **C** persuade them that there is a power among them provided by the gods through sacrifices and incantations—if any injustice has been committed by a man himself or his ancestors—to heal it with pleasures and festivals. And if he wishes to harm any enemy, at small expense he will hurt the just and the unjust alike; by certain inducements and binding-charms, they persuade the gods (as they say) to serve them. To all these speeches, they bring the poets as witnesses; some, giving examples of the ease of vice, say:
> "Wickedness can be seized even in abundance
> Easily; the way is smooth, and it dwells very near. **D**
> But before virtue the gods have placed sweat,"
and a path that is long and uphill. Others bring Homer as a witness to the turning of the gods by men; because he also said,
> "—the gods themselves are turnable."
And men turn them aside with sacrifices and soothing prayers, and libations and the steam of fat, entreating them when someone has overstepped and sinned. And they provide a hubbub of books by Musæus and Orpheus, the offspring of the Moon and the Muses, as they say; according to which they perform their sacrifices, persuading not only individuals but also cities, that there are indeed releases and purifications from injustices through sacrifices and the pleasures of play, both for the living and for those who have died; which indeed they call **E** initiations (*teletas*), which release us from the evils of that other place; but for those who have not sacrificed, terrible things wait. "All these things, my dear Socrates," he said, "being of such a kind and told in such quantity about virtue and vice—how men and gods regard them—what do we think they do to the souls of the young who hear them? Those who are naturally gifted and able, as if flitting over everything that is said, to gather from it what sort of person one should be, and in what way one should travel to pass through life as well as possible? For such a one would likely say to himself, according to Pindar: 'Whether shall I, by justice or by crooked deceits, climb the high wall and so live my life fencing myself in?' For the things said imply that if I am just, but do not also seem so, they say there is no benefit, but manifest toils and penalties. But for the unjust man who has **F** provided himself with a reputation for justice, a divine life is described. Since, then, 'seeming'—as the wise reveal to me—both overpowers the truth and is the master of happiness, I must turn entirely to this. I must draw a shadow-painting of virtue around me as a front and a facade, but I must trail behind me the fox of the most wise Archilochus, greedy and versatile. 'But surely,' someone will say, 'it is not easy to always remain hidden when one is wicked.' 'Neither is anything else easy,' we shall say, 'among great things. But nevertheless, if we are to be happy, we must go this way, as the tracks of the arguments lead.' For to remain hidden, we will organize conspiracies and clubs. And there are teachers of persuasion, granting the wisdom of the popular assembly and the law courts; from which we will partly persuade and partly **G** use force, so that by overreaching we may not pay the penalty. 'But surely the gods can neither be hidden from nor forced.' 'If then they do not exist, or if they have no care for human things, we need not care about being hidden. But if they both exist and take care, we know of them from no other source than what we have heard from the myths and the poets who have written their genealogies.' And these very ones say that the gods are such as to be turned aside by sacrifices and soothing prayers and offerings. We must believe either both or neither. If then we must believe, we should act unjustly and sacrifice from the fruits of the injustice. For if we are just, we shall be unpunished by the gods, but we shall push away the gains from injustice. But if we are unjust, we shall gain, and by entreating them, **H** when we overstep and sin, we shall get off unpunished. 'But surely in Hades we shall pay the penalty for the things we did unjustly here, either ourselves or our children’s children.' 'But, my friend,' he will say, calculating, 'the initiations again have great power, and the delivering gods, as the greatest cities say, and the children of the gods...'"

<summary>Adeimantus argues that people are taught to value justice only for its external rewards and reputation, rather than for its own sake. He cites poets like Homer and Hesiod to show how the youth are led to believe they can be unjust and simply "buy off" the gods with sacrifices.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the speech of Adeimantus, who is challenging Socrates to defend justice on its own merits. In the previous page, he discussed how parents and poets teach that justice is valuable only for the reputation and rewards it brings from gods and men. Here, he reaches the climax of his argument, demanding that Socrates prove justice is good for the soul itself, even if no one else ever sees it.</meta>

## ON THE REPUBLIC, BOOK II.

<margin>A</margin> Poets and seers, who are born of the gods, testify that these things are so. Therefore, by what logic should we be led further to prefer <term>justice</term><note>The Greek term is 'dikaiosyne,' which implies both legal righteousness and moral integrity.</note> over the greatest injustice? For if we hide our injustice under a false mask of respectability, we shall fare according to our desires among both gods and men, both in life and after death, as the speech of many excellent men testifies.

<margin>B</margin> From everything that has been said, O Socrates, who would believe that a man would ever wish to honor justice—if he possesses any power of spirit, or wealth, or body, or birth—and not rather laugh when he hears it praised? Indeed, even if someone could show that what we have said is false, and knows perfectly well that justice is the best thing, he would likely be very forgiving and not angry with the unjust. He understands that—unless a person avoids injustice through some divine nature or through the acquisition of knowledge—no one is truly just by choice. Rather, it is through cowardice, old age, or some other weakness that men find fault with injustice, simply because they lack the power to commit it.

<margin>C</margin> This is clear from the fact that as soon as such a person gains power, he is the first to act unjustly to the extent of his ability. And the cause of all this is nothing other than the very point from which this entire argument began, which both my brother and I have addressed to you, Socrates: "O wonderful man, among all of you who claim to be praisers of justice—beginning from the ancient heroes whose words remain with us down to the men of today—no one has ever blamed injustice or praised justice for any reason other than the reputations, honors, and gifts that come from them." But as for what each of them is in its own power, dwelling in the soul of the possessor and hidden from gods and men, no one has ever sufficiently explained in poetry or in private discourse—namely, that injustice is the greatest of all evils that the soul contains within itself, while justice is the greatest good.

<margin>D</margin> If this had been told to us by all of you from the beginning, and if we had been persuaded of it from our childhood, we would not be guarding one another against being wronged; rather, each man would be his own best guardian, fearing that by acting unjustly, he would be forced to live with the greatest of evils. These things, Socrates—and perhaps even more than these—Thrasymachus or someone else might say about justice and injustice, crudely overturning the power of each, in my opinion. But I, wishing to hear the opposite from you (for I have no desire to hide anything from you), speak with as much intensity as I can. Therefore, do not merely show us through your argument that justice is stronger than injustice, but show what each, by itself, does to the possessor, so that one is an evil and the other a good.

<margin>E</margin> Strip away their reputations, as Glaucon commanded. For if you do not take away the true reputations from both sides and add false ones, we will say you are not praising justice, but the *appearance* of it; and that you are not blaming being unjust, but the *appearance* of it; and that you are merely advising the unjust man to stay hidden, and agreeing with Thrasymachus that justice is "someone else's good"—that is, the advantage of the stronger—while injustice is an advantage and a profit to oneself, but a disadvantage to the weaker. Since you have agreed that justice is among the greatest goods—those which are worth possessing for the sake of their consequences, but much more for their own sake, such as sight, hearing, wisdom, health, and all other goods that are fertile by their own nature and not merely by opinion—praise this very thing about justice: how it benefits the one who has it by its own nature, while injustice harms him.

<margin>F</margin> Leave the praising of rewards and reputations to others. For I could tolerate others praising justice and blaming injustice in that way—extolling the reputations and rewards while reviling the opposite—but not you (unless you command it), because you have spent your entire life contemplating nothing other than this. Do not, therefore, merely show us by your argument that justice is better than injustice; rather, show what each does to its possessor by itself—whether it is hidden or not hidden from gods and men—so that one is a good and the other an evil.

When I had heard these things, I always admired the character of Glaucon and Adeimantus, but at that moment I was truly delighted and said: It was not badly written for you, O sons of that great man, by the lover of Glaucon at the beginning of his elegiac poems, when you distinguished yourselves in the battle at Megara <note>A reference to a real battle between Athens and Megara, highlighting the noble lineage of the brothers</note>: "O sons of Ariston <note>original: "Παῖδες Ἀρίστωνος" / "filij Aristonis." Ariston was the father of Plato, Glaucon, and Adeimantus.</note>, divine offspring of a famous man," and so on.

<margin>G</margin> This seems to me to be well said, my friends. For you have been affected in a truly divine way if you are not persuaded that injustice is better than justice, despite being able to speak so well on its behalf. I believe that you are indeed not persuaded. I judge this from your general character, for if I judged only by your words, I would not believe you. But the more I believe you, the more I am at a loss as to what to do. On the one hand, I do not know how to help (for I seem to be unable). The proof of my weakness is that you did not accept the arguments by which I thought I had sufficiently shown to Thrasymachus that justice is better than injustice.

<margin>H</margin> On the other hand, I do not know how I can *not* help. For I fear it would be a sin to stand by while justice is being slandered and to abandon her, failing to help while I am still breathing and have a voice. Therefore, it is best to defend her as well as I can. Then Glaucon and all the others begged me by all means to help, and not to let the argument drop, but to search out what each is and what the truth is regarding their respective benefits. I said, therefore, what seemed to me...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Poets and seers born of the gods testify that these things are so. Therefore, by what logic will we be led further to prefer justice over the greatest injustice, since if we hide our injustice under a deceptive appearance of honesty, everything will succeed for us according to our desire, both with the gods and with men, both while living and when deceased, as the speech of many excellent men testifies?

<margin>B</margin> From all that has now been said, O Socrates, who would believe that a man would wish to cultivate justice, if he has any power of fortune, or of wealth, or of body, or of family, and not rather laugh at it, if he hears it being praised? Indeed, if someone can show that what we have said is false, and correctly knows that justice is the best thing, he will be very forgiving and will not be angry with the unjust, since he understands that—unless someone hates unfairness by some divine nature, or abstains from injustice through learning—no one is just of his own will: but out of fear, or old age, or some other weakness, they find fault with injustice because they are unable to carry it out.

<margin>C</margin> This is indeed evident from the fact that as soon as someone has gained power, he is the first to act unjustly according to his strength: and of all these things there is no other cause than that from which this whole speech of mine and this man's [Glaucon's], O Socrates, proceeded against you. Since of you all, O wonderful Socrates, whoever professes the praises of justice—beginning from those ancient heroes of whom some memory exists down to our own men—no one has ever praised justice or blamed injustice otherwise than by looking toward the glory, gifts, or punishments which proceed from them. But as to what each of them does by its own nature, hidden in the soul of the possessor from gods and men, no one has ever sufficiently explained, either in poems or in other speech—namely, that injustice is the greatest of all evils which the soul contains in itself, while justice is the greatest good.

<margin>D</margin> For if it had been spoken thus by all of you from the beginning, and we had been persuaded of it from childhood, we would not be preventing one another from inflicting injury, but each would be his own guardian, fearing lest by acting unjustly, he should be joined to the greatest evil. These things, O Socrates, thus far—and perhaps even more—Thrasymachus or someone else might say about justice and injustice, inverting the power of each, and quite inappropriately, as it seems to me. But I, wishing nothing to be hidden from you, and desiring to hear the opposites from you, prolong the speech. Do not, therefore, only show us that justice is more excellent than injustice, but show how each, by itself affecting the soul, is an evil or a good.

<margin>E</margin> Take away opinions, as Glaucon also commanded. For if you do not take away the true ones from both sides, and put false ones in their place: we will not say that you are praising justice, but that which seems just; nor that you are blaming injustice, but that which seems unjust, and that you are ordering the unjust to remain hidden and agreeing with Thrasymachus: Justice indeed being another's good, conferred upon the more powerful; but injustice being conferred upon oneself and useful, yet useless to the weaker. Since therefore it is agreed that justice is numbered among the greatest goods, which are to be sought both for the sake of those things which follow and much more for themselves—namely, to see, to hear, to be wise, to be healthy, and whatever other goods are fertile by their own nature, not by opinion: praise this very thing in justice itself, that it helps the possessor by itself, while injustice harms. Leave opinions and rewards to be praised by others. For I could bear others, whenever they might praise justice or blame injustice in such a way as to seem to praise or blame opinions and rewards. But you,

<margin>F</margin> least of all—unless perhaps you command it—since you have consumed your whole life in no other thing than in this speculation. Do not, therefore, show us only in speech that justice is more excellent than injustice, but in what way each of them, affecting its participant—whether it is hidden or not hidden from gods and men—is either a good or an evil. When I had heard these things, although I had always loved the character of Glaucon and Adeimantus, then I was greatly in admiration, and I said: Not badly was the beginning of the elegiac poems written for you, O sons of that man, by the lover of Glaucon, who, when you had fought bravely in the Megarian battle, said:

<margin>G</margin> "O sons of Ariston, divine offspring of a famous man." This seems to be well said, friends. For you are divinely affected, if you are not persuaded that injustice is better than justice, since you can speak thus for it. But you seem to me not to be persuaded. I take the conjecture from your character, since according to the speech itself I would believe you least of all. But the more I believe, the more I am in doubt as to where I should turn. For how I may help, I know not. Indeed, I seem to be unable. That,

<margin>H</margin> however, is the sign: that you did not admit those things by which I thought I had sufficiently shown above, against Thrasymachus, that justice is better than injustice. Nor, again, do I find how I may now help, fearing lest perhaps it be a sin if he, who understands justice being blamed in his presence, should withdraw, nor speak for its defense as long as breathing and speaking are granted. It is better, therefore, to vote for it according to my strength. Then Glaucon and all the others asked that I should help with all my might, and not leave the dispute, but search out what each was, and what the true utility of each was. I said, therefore, as it seemed to me...

<sig>Nn iij</sig>

<summary>Adeimantus concludes his challenge to Socrates, demanding a proof that justice is inherently good for the soul regardless of external rewards. Socrates, impressed by their ability to argue against justice while remaining virtuous themselves, reluctantly agrees to take up the defense.</summary>
