<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion where Adeimantus challenged Socrates to define justice. Here, Socrates begins his famous "city-soul analogy," suggesting that justice might be easier to observe on a larger scale—in a city—before looking for it in an individual. This marks the transition from Book II's critique to the constructive phase of the Republic.</meta>

# OF PLATO

...it was my opinion that this question we are approaching is not to be looked down upon, but is the work of a man who sees keenly, as it seems to me. And since we are not so capable, we should investigate <term>justice</term><note>Latin: *iustitia*; Greek: *δικαιοσύνη* (dikaiosyne). In this context, it refers to the right ordering of a community or a soul.</note> just as if someone had ordered people who do not see keenly to read small letters placed far away, and then someone else noticed that those same letters existed elsewhere in a larger size and on a larger surface. It would be a stroke of luck, I think, to read the large ones first, and only then consider the smaller ones to see if they are indeed the same.

Exactly so, said Adeimantus. But what similarity do you see in this, Socrates, regarding the inquiry into justice?

I will tell you, I said. Do we say justice belongs to a single man? Or also to a whole city?

Certainly, he said.

And is not a city larger than one man?

It is larger, he said.

Perhaps then, justice is more ample in the larger thing, and easier to learn. Therefore, if you are willing, let us first seek what it is in cities. After that, we shall consider it in individuals, contemplating the likeness of the larger thing in the <term>form</term><note>Latin: *idea*; Greek: *ἰδέα*. Socrates is looking for the essential nature or "blueprint" of justice.</note> of the smaller.

You seem to speak skillfully, he said.

If we were to watch a city being established in speech, would we also see its justice and its injustice coming into being?

Perhaps, he said.

And so, once it is created, is there hope of more easily seeing what we seek?

Much more so.

It is necessary, then, to attempt to complete this. For I think it is no small task. Consider it, then.

It has already been considered, said Adeimantus. Do not do otherwise.

A city comes into existence, I think, because no one of us is self-sufficient, but stands in need of many things. Or do you think there is any other beginning for the founding of cities?

None other, he said.

Thus, one person joins another for one use, and another for another use; since we need many things, we have gathered many partners and helpers into one habitation. To this communal living we have given the name "city," have we not?

Entirely so.

They share their own goods with one another, and receive the goods of others in turn, believing this exchange to be to their advantage.

Precisely.

Come then, let us construct a city in our speech from the beginning. Our needs, as it seems, will create it.

Of course.

The first and greatest of all needs is the provision of food, so that we may exist and live.

Certainly.

The second is housing. The third is clothing <margin>Aristotle notes this in Politics, Book 4, Chapter 4.</margin> and such things.

It is as you say.

Come then. In what way will the city be sufficient for this preparation? Will there not be one farmer, another a builder, and another a weaver? Shall we also add a cobbler there, or some other person to care for the needs of the body?

By all means.

Therefore, the city itself would consist of at least four or five men.

So it appears.

What then? Must each of these men contribute his work to the community? For example, should the one farmer prepare food for four men, and spend four times the time and labor in farming to share it with the others? Or, neglecting the care of the others, should he prepare for himself only a fourth part of the food in a fourth part of his time? And of the remaining parts of his time, should he spend one in building a house, another in clothing, another in making shoes, not laboring to share his things with others, but providing for himself by himself without the help of others?

Perhaps in this way, O Socrates, said Adeimantus, it would be easier than the other.

Not by Jove! I said. That is absurd. For as you were speaking, I considered that we are not born particularly alike, but differing from one another, each produced by nature as being fit for different tasks. Does it not seem so to you?

To me, indeed.

Well then, would someone do better by practicing many arts at once, or if each individual practiced one?

Each practicing one.

And I think this too is manifest: that if someone misses the right moment for a task, the work is ruined.

That is clear.

For the thing to be done does not wish to wait for the leisure of the doer; rather, necessity compels the doer to follow the work itself, always observing the right occasion.

It must be so.

From this it is clear that more things are produced, and better, and more easily, when each person does one thing according to his nature, at the right time, and being free from other tasks.

That is absolutely so.

Therefore, O Adeimantus, we need more citizens than four to provide the things we have mentioned. For the farmer, it seems, will not make his own plow if it is to be useful for the work, nor his hoes and rakes, nor the other instruments which agriculture requires. Neither will the builder. For he also needs many tools. And the same must be said of the weaver and the cobbler. Is it not so?

The same.

Carpenters, then, and blacksmiths, and many other such craftsmen, becoming fellow citizens in our little town, will make it more crowded.

You speak the truth.

But this would not yet be large enough unless we added to them ox-herds, and shepherds, and other herdsmen, so that the farmers might have oxen for plowing, and the builders might use beasts of burden with the farmers for hauling materials, and the weavers and cobblers might have hides and wool.

Truly, it would not be a small city that had all these things.

And yet, to establish the city in a place where it will not need imports is almost impossible.

It is impossible.

It will therefore need still others, who will bring from another city what it lacks.

It will.

But a servant would be useless if he brought nothing to those from whom he receives what they need, would he not?

So it seems.

It is necessary, therefore, not only to produce enough for themselves, but also goods of the kind and quantity required by those from whom they receive what they need.

They must indeed.

<column-break/>

IT SEEMED [to me] that the inquiry we are attempting is no small thing, but for one who sees sharply, as it appears to me. Since, then, we are not clever, it seems to me (I said) that we should make such an investigation of it as if someone had ordered those who do not see very sharply to read small letters from a distance, and then someone noticed that the same letters exist somewhere else, larger and on a larger surface; it would have seemed a godsend, I think, to read those first and then examine the smaller ones, to see if they happen to be the same.

Quite so, said Adeimantus. But what do you see of that sort, Socrates, in the inquiry about justice?

I will tell you, I said. We say justice belongs to one man, and also, I suppose, to a whole city?

Certainly, he said.

And is not a city larger than one man?

Larger, he said.

Perhaps then, there might be more justice in the larger thing, and it might be easier to learn. So, if you wish, let us first inquire what it is like in cities. Then, let us examine it in each individual, looking for the likeness of the larger in the form of the smaller.

It seems to me, he said, that you speak well.

If, then, (I said) we should observe a city coming into being in speech, would we also see its justice and its injustice coming into being?

Perhaps, he said.

And when it has come into being, is there hope of more easily seeing what we seek?

Much more so.

Does it seem right, then, that we should attempt to carry this through? For I think it is no small labor. Consider it, then.

It has been considered, said Adeimantus; do not do otherwise.

A city comes into being, then (I said), as I believe, because each of us happens not to be self-sufficient, but in need of many things. Or what other beginning do you think there is for the founding of a city?

None other, he said.

So then, one person taking on another for one need, and another for another—needing many things, and gathering many partners and helpers into one settlement—to this common dwelling we give the name "city," do we not?

Quite so.

And one gives to another, if he gives anything, or receives, thinking it is better for himself.

Certainly.

Come then (I said), let us make a city in speech from the beginning. Our need, it seems, will make it.

How could it not?

But the first and greatest of needs is the provision of food, for the sake of existing and living.

By all means.

The second is for housing, and the third for clothing and such things.

That is so.

Come then (I said), how will the city suffice for so great a provision? Will there be one farmer, and one builder, and someone else a weaver? Or shall we add a cobbler there as well, or someone else of those who care for the body?

Certainly.

The most necessary city would consist of four or five men.

It appears so.

What then? Must each of these put his own work into a common fund for all? For instance, the farmer, being one, must he provide food for four, and spend four times the time and labor on the provision of food and share it with others? Or, neglecting them, should he make a fourth part of this food for himself alone in a fourth part of the time, and of the other three parts, spend one on the provision of a house, one on a garment, and one on shoes; and not have the trouble of sharing with others, but do his own business for himself?

And Adeimantus said: But perhaps, Socrates, it is easier in that way than the other.

Nothing [is easier], by Zeus! I said; it is absurd. For I myself realize, now that you have said it, that first of all, each of us is born not quite like each other, but differing in nature, one for the performance of one job, another for another. Or does it seem so to you?

To me, indeed.

What then? Would someone do better if he, as one man, worked at many arts, or when one man worked at one?

When one works at one, he said.

And yet, I think, it is clear that if someone lets the right time for a job pass by, it is ruined.

It is clear.

For the thing being done is not (I think) willing to wait for the leisure of the doer, but it is necessary for the doer to follow the thing being done, not as a secondary task.

It is necessary.

From this, more things are produced, and better and more easily, when one man does one thing according to his nature and at the right time, having leisure from other things.

By all means.

Then we need more citizens, Adeimantus, than four, for the provisions we were mentioning. For the farmer (as it seems) will not make his own plow himself, if it is to be a good one, nor his hoe, nor the other tools for farming. Nor, again, the builder; and he also needs many. And likewise the weaver and the cobbler. Is it not so?

True.

So carpenters and blacksmiths and many such craftsmen, becoming partners in our little town, make it crowded.

Quite so.

But it would not yet be very large, if we added to them ox-herds and shepherds and other herdsmen, so that the farmers might have oxen for plowing, and the builders might use beasts of burden with the farmers for hauling, and the weavers and cobblers might have hides and wool.

Nor (he said) would it be a small city, having all these.

And yet (I said), to settle the city itself in such a place where it will not need imports is almost impossible.

It is impossible.

There will be a need, then, for still others who will bring to it from another city what it needs.

There will be.

And yet, the servant would be empty-handed if he went bringing nothing that those people need from whom they are to get what they themselves require; he will come away empty. Will he not?

It seems so to me.

So they must produce at home not only enough for themselves, but also such things and in such quantity as are needed by those others.

They must.

<summary>Socrates introduces the analogy of the city and the soul, arguing that justice is more easily identified in a large-scale society. He then begins to "build" a city in speech, identifying the division of labor and mutual need as the foundational principles of a community.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Socrates’ construction of an "ideal city" in speech to better understand the nature of justice. Having established the basic necessities of food, shelter, and clothing, Socrates now expands the city’s population to include specialized labor and commerce.</meta>

## ON THE REPUBLIC, BOOK II

**P**lenty of farmers and other craftsmen will be needed for our city. Indeed, many more. And we will surely need other assistants who will import and export various goods. These are <term>merchants</term><note>Greek: *emporoi*; Latin: *mercatores*. These are international traders who travel between cities.</note>, are they not? Yes. So, we will also need merchants. Certainly. And if the trade is conducted by sea, we will need many others who are skilled in maritime labor. Many indeed. But what about within the city itself? How will they share the fruits of their labor with one another? This sharing, after all, was the reason we formed a community and founded a city. It is clear, I said, that they will do so by buying and selling. From this, we will require a marketplace and <term>currency</term><note>Greek: *nomisma*; Latin: *nummus*. Socrates views money as a "token for the sake of exchange."</note> as a token for the sake of exchange. Precisely. Now, if a farmer or any other craftsman brings his produce to the market, but does not arrive at the same time as those who wish to trade with him, will he sit idle in the marketplace, neglecting his own craft? Not at all, he said. There are those who, seeing this, take upon themselves this service. In well-ordered cities, these are usually those weakest in body and unfit for any other work. They must stay there in the marketplace to exchange goods for money with those who wish to sell, and then exchange that money for goods with those who wish to buy. This need, I said, gives rise to <term>shopkeepers</term><note>Greek: *kapeloi*; Latin: *caupones*. Unlike merchants who travel, these are local retailers who stay in the marketplace.</note> in our city. Do we not call "shopkeepers" those who are stationed in the marketplace to serve in buying and selling, while we call those who travel between cities "merchants"? Exactly. There are also, I believe, other assistants who may not be particularly worthy in their intellect for the community, but whose bodily strength is sufficient for labor. They sell the use of their strength, and calling the price of it "wages," they are named, I believe, <term>wage-earners</term><note>Greek: *misthotoi*; Latin: *mercenarij*. These represent the manual labor force of the city.</note>. Is that not so? Certainly. So wage-earners, it seems, complete the city. I think so. Well then, Adeimantus, has our city grown enough now to be complete? Perhaps. Where then would justice and injustice be found in it? And with which of these elements we have examined did they come into being? I do not know, Socrates, he said, unless it is in some need these people have for one another. Perhaps you are right, I said. We must look into it and not shrink from the task. First, then, let us consider how those thus prepared will live. Will they not produce grain, wine, clothes, and shoes? And having built themselves houses, in summer they will work mostly naked and barefoot, but in winter they will be sufficiently clothed and shod. They will nourish themselves by preparing meal from barley and flour from wheat, baking some and kneading others. They will serve noble cakes and loaves of bread upon reeds or clean leaves, and reclining on beds strewn with bryony and myrtle, they and their children will feast. They will drink wine, wear garlands, and sing hymns to the gods, living pleasantly with one another. They will not have more children than their means allow, guarding against poverty or war. And Glaucon interrupted, saying: You make these men feast without any <term>relishes</term><note>Greek: *opson*; Latin: *obsonio*. This refers to savory additions to bread, like meat or seasoned vegetables—essentially the "toppings" or "side dishes" that make a meal enjoyable.</note>, it seems. You speak the truth, I said. I forgot that they will also have relishes: salt, of course, and olives, and cheese; and they will boil onions and greens, such as are found in the fields. We will also set before them desserts of figs, chickpeas, and beans; and they will roast myrtle-berries and acorns at the fire, drinking in moderation. And so, spending their lives in peace and health, as is likely, they will die at an old age and pass on a similar life to their offspring. And he said: If you were founding a **city of pigs**<note>Greek: *hyon polin*; Latin: *suibus civitatem*. Glaucon argues that Socrates' simple city provides only for basic animal needs, not human refinement.</note>, Socrates, what else would you fodder them with but these things? But how should it be, Glaucon? I said. As is customary, he replied. They should recline on couches, I think, if they are not to be miserable, and dine from tables, and have the relishes and desserts that people have nowadays. Very well, I said, I understand. It seems we are not only considering how a city comes to be, but also a **luxurious city**<note>Greek: *tryphosan polin*; Latin: *delicatam urbem*. Socrates later calls this the "fevered" or "inflamed" city.</note>. Perhaps that is not a bad idea. For by looking at such a city, we might see where justice and injustice take root in cities. The true city, in my opinion, is the one we have described—the healthy one, as it were. But if you wish, let us also look at a fevered city; nothing prevents us. For some, it seems, these things will not suffice, nor will this simple way of life. They will want couches, tables, and other furniture, as well as relishes, perfumes, incense, courtesans, and pastries—and each of these in every variety. We must no longer limit ourselves to the necessities we first mentioned—houses, clothes, and shoes—but we must set in motion the arts of painting and embroidery, and acquire gold and ivory and all such things. Isn't that so? Yes, he said. Must we not then make the city larger? For that healthy one is no longer enough, but must now be filled with a multitude of things that are no longer in cities for the sake of necessity. For example, all kinds of hunters and imitators—many who work with shapes and colors, many who work with music: poets and their assistants, rhapsodes, actors, dancers, and contractors; and craftsmen of all sorts of vessels, especially those for feminine adornment...

<column-break/>

**P**lenty of farmers and other craftsmen are therefore necessary for us in the city. Plenty, certainly. And also, in addition, other assistants who may import and export individual goods. These, however, are merchants. Are they not? They are. We will therefore require merchants. Certainly. And if indeed there shall be maritime commerce, many will also be needed who are skilled in the things that pertain to navigation. Clearly many. But what about in the city itself? How will they share among themselves the things which each produces? For the sake of which sharing we introduced the community and constructed the city. It is evident, he said, that it is by buying and selling. Therefore, a marketplace and money will be established for us in commerce for the sake of this exchange? Altogether. Will a farmer, then, bringing into the marketplace something of those things which he produces, or some other craftsman, if he does not come at the same time as those with whom he is to exchange these things, cease from his work while standing in the market? By no means, he said. But there are those who, when they observe this, prepare themselves for this service. For in rightly instituted cities, certain men perform this who are weak in body and useless for other work; being stationed there around the marketplace, they partly exchange goods for silver with those who are about to sell, and partly give goods for silver to those who are about to buy. This necessity, therefore, produces for us the class of shopkeepers in the city. Do we not call "shopkeepers" those who station themselves in the market for selling and buying? But those who travel to foreign cities, "merchants"? Without a doubt. There are also others besides, as I judge, assistants, who though they can contribute little of mental strength to this society, have bodily strength sufficient for labors. These, then, selling the use of their strength—since they call the reward itself "wages"—are called wage-earners. Is it not so? Exactly so. Therefore, wage-earners are also a completion of the city. It seems so. Has the city now been so increased by us, O Adeimantus, that it is perfect? Perhaps. Where then in it will justice and injustice be, and in which of these things which we have treated is it simultaneously innate and implanted? Indeed, O Socrates, I do not know, unless perhaps it consists in a certain mutual use which we have mentioned. Perhaps, I said, you speak well. Nevertheless, it must be considered, and we must not desist. And first, indeed, let us look at the manner in which those citizens so instituted will use their livelihood. Will they not prepare food, and wine, and clothes, and shoes, and houses? In summer, for the most part, they will work without clothing and without shoes. In winter, however, they will be dressed in clothes and shoes as much as is sufficient. They will be nourished from barley and wheat, making flour, and partly indeed by kneading, partly by gathering it together, placing excellent cakes and breads upon reeds or clean leaves; and reclining upon beds made of herbs similar to myrtle, they themselves and their children will feast together, drinking wine, crowned with garlands, and praising the gods. They will live pleasantly together, nor will they beget children beyond their means, guarding against poverty and war. To this Glaucon responding, said: You make the guests feast without relish, as it seems. You speak the truth, I said. For I had forgotten this, that they will have relish: salt, namely, and olives, and cheese, and bulbs; moreover, they will cook greens as the pottage of the fields. And we will serve them desserts of figs, chickpeas, and beans; and they will roast myrtle berries and beech acorns on the coals, drinking moderately. And so, living quietly and healthily as is fitting, finishing their lives in old age, they will leave another such life to their posterity. If you had instituted a city of pigs, O Socrates, what other food would you have prepared for them? What then must be done, O Glaucon? I said. That which many are accustomed to, he said: they must recline upon couches, unless we wish to live miserably, and eat from a table, and have the relishes and desserts which they use in these times. So be it, Glaucon, I said. I understand: for we are not only considering, as it seems, how a city is made, but a delicate city. Perhaps, therefore, it will not be bad. For beholding this, we will perhaps discover where justice and injustice are born in cities. That which we have described seems to me to be the true city, as if it were a healthy one. But if you wish, let us also consider the swollen city. For nothing prohibits it. Truly these things, as it seems, will by no means suffice for some, and this diet will not please; but couches will be added, and tables, and other apparatus, and vessels, and relishes; and ointments, and perfumes, harlots, spices, seasonings, and delights—and each of these of every kind. Nor must only those things which we recounted above be placed as necessary—houses, clothes, and shoes—but painting must be added again, and the arts of variety, gold and ivory, and all other things of the same kind. Is it not so? Altogether, he said. Must not, therefore, the city be made larger? For that healthy one is no longer sufficient, but must be filled with a mass and a multitude of those who are no longer in cities for the sake of necessity: such as are all hunters, and mimes, and imitators, partly concerning figures and colors, partly concerning music; namely poets, and their assistants the rhapsodes, and reciters of poems, actors, singers, dancers, contractors, then of other things, and of those which pertain to women's...

<summary>Socrates describes the economic foundations of a city, moving from a simple "healthy" city based on necessity to a "luxurious" or "fevered" city demanded by Glaucon. This transition introduces specialized roles like merchants, shopkeepers, artists, and entertainers into the social structure.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Glaucon in Book II of the *Republic*. They are currently expanding their "city in speech" from a simple, healthy community into a "feverish" or luxurious city. This expansion necessitates new professions, more land, and ultimately, a professional class of soldiers.</meta>

### 428 PLATO

<margin>A</margin>...will belong to others. Furthermore, we shall require many more attendants. Do you not think we will need tutors, wet-nurses, nannies, <term>beauticians</term><note>Greek: *kommōtriai*; Latin: *compiatricibus*. These were specialists in hairstyles and cosmetics.</note>, barbers, and those who prepare delicacies and cook? Furthermore, we will also need swineherds. This profession was not in our earlier city—for there was no need—but in this one, we will require it. We will also need many other kinds of livestock if anyone is to eat them. Is that not so? Certainly. And will we not also require physicians much more, living in this way, than we did before? Much more indeed. And the land, which was once sufficient to feed those people, will become small instead of sufficient. Or how do we say it? It is as you say. Must we not then slice off a piece of our neighbors' land if we are to have enough for <margin>B</margin>pasture and plowing, and will they not do the same to ours if they also abandon themselves to the infinite accumulation of wealth, exceeding the limit of what is necessary? It will be quite necessary, Socrates. Shall we go to war then, or what shall we do? We shall go to war. And let us not yet say, I said, whether war brings anything bad or good; but only this, that we have found the origin of war: that from which great calamities, both public and private, befall the city when they occur. Quite so. Therefore, the city must be even larger, not by a little, but by a whole army, which can go out and fight on behalf of all our property and for the things we just mentioned <margin>C</margin>against invading enemies. What? he said. Are the citizens themselves not sufficient to fight? Not if you and all of us were right in what we agreed when we were molding the city. We agreed, if you remember, that it is impossible for one man to practice many arts well. You speak the truth, he said. Well then, I said, does not the struggle of war seem to be an art? Very much so, he said. Should we then care more for the <term>cobbler’s art</term><note>Socrates uses the humble example of shoemaking to show that even simple crafts require full-time dedication.</note> than for the art of war? Not at all. But we prohibited the cobbler from attempting to be a farmer, a weaver, or a builder at the same time, and we ordered him to work only at his own art, so that the work of cobbling might be done perfectly for us. To each of the others, we likewise assigned a single task for which his nature was suited, so that he might practice it throughout his life, free from other tasks, and not missing the right opportunities, <margin>D</margin>so as to perform it excellently. Now, does it not matter greatly whether the affairs of war are performed correctly? Or is this study so easy that someone can be a warrior and a farmer at the same time, or a cobbler, or some other craftsman? Yet no one could even become a proficient player of <term>draughts or dice</term><note>Latin: *talorum vel alearum*; Greek: *petteutikos ē kybeutikos*. Socrates argues that even games require more practice than most people give to military training.</note> if he did not apply himself to that art from childhood, but only treated it as a hobby. And will a man, merely by picking up a shield or other military weapons and instruments, become a sufficient soldier in any kind of combat in a single day? No other instrument makes a man a craftsman or an athlete just by taking it up, nor will it be useful to someone who has neither acquired the knowledge of that specific thing nor <margin>E</margin>provided himself with sufficient practice. These instruments would be precious indeed, he said. Therefore, I said, the greater the work of the Guardians, the more it requires freedom from other things, as well as the greatest art and diligence. I think so, he said. And does it not also require a nature suited for this pursuit? Why not? It will be our job then, it seems, if we are able, to select which and what kind of natures are suited for guarding the city. It is indeed our job. By Zeus, I said, we have taken up no small task; however, we must not be discouraged as far as our power allows. Certainly not. Do you think, I said, that the nature of a well-bred dog differs at all from that of a well-bred youth for the purpose of keeping guard? What do you mean? Each of them must be <margin>F</margin>keen to perceive, and swift to pursue what they perceive, and also strong, if it is necessary, to fight when they have caught it. All these are certainly needed. And he must be brave, if indeed he is to fight well. Why not? But will anyone be brave if he is not <term>high-spirited</term><note>Greek: *thymoeidēs*; Latin: *iracundus*. This refers to the spirited part of the soul—the seat of courage, anger, and pride.</note>, whether a horse, a dog, or any other animal? Or have you not noticed how an invincible and unconquerable thing is spirit? When it is present in the soul, every soul is fearless and indomitable against everything. I have noticed it. It is clear, then, what the guardian must be like in body. Yes. And also in soul: he must be high-spirited. That too. How then, Glaucon, I said, will they not be fierce toward one another and toward the other citizens, being of such a nature? By Zeus, he said, not easily. <margin>G</margin>Nevertheless, you say they must be gentle toward their own people but harsh toward enemies. Otherwise, they will not wait for others to destroy them, but they will do it to themselves first. True, he said. What then shall we do? Where shall we find a character that is at once gentle and high-spirited? For a gentle nature is surely the opposite of a spirited one. So it appears. But yet, if a man lacks either of these, he will not be a good guardian. These things seem impossible; and so it follows that a good guardian cannot be found. It seems so, he said. And I, being stuck, and revolving the previous points in my mind, said: We are rightly stuck, my friend. For we have wandered from the <margin>H</margin>comparison we introduced before. How do you mean? Have we not found that there are indeed such natures as we thought did not exist, having these opposite qualities? Where? One can see this in other animals, but not least in that guardian with which we compared our guardian. For you know that...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>...of others, including those concerning feminine adornment, and indeed we shall need more servants. Does it not seem to you that we will need tutors, wet-nurses, nannies, hair-dressers, barbers, and again, sauce-makers and cooks? Furthermore, we will need swineherds. This was not in our former city (for there was no need) but in this one, it will be needed besides. And we will need all the other types of cattle, if anyone is to eat them. Will we not? How could we not? Therefore, shall we not also be in need of doctors much more, living in this way, than we were before? Much more. And the land which was then sufficient to feed those then, will be small instead of sufficient. Or how do we say it? Thus, he said. Therefore, we must cut off a piece of the neighbors' land, if we are to have enough to pasture and <margin>B</margin>plow, and they in turn must cut from ours, if they also let themselves go to the unlimited acquisition of money, overstepping the boundary of what is necessary? There is a great necessity, Socrates, he said. Shall we go to war after this, Glaucon? Or how will it be? Thus, he said. And let us say nothing yet (I said) whether war works any evil or any good; but only this much, that we have found the origin of war, from which the most evils come to cities, both privately and publicly, whenever it occurs. Quite so. Furthermore, the city must be larger by no small amount, but by a whole army, which, going out, will fight on behalf of all our substance and on behalf of what we were just talking about <margin>C</margin>against those who come against us. Why? (he said) are they not themselves sufficient to fight? No, if (I said) you and we all agreed well when we were fashioning the city. We agreed surely, if you remember, that it is impossible for one man to work many arts well. You say the truth, he said. What then? (I said) the struggle concerning war, does it not seem to be an art? Very much so, he said. Should we then care more for the art of shoemaking than for the art of war? Not at all. But we forbade the shoemaker from even attempting to be a farmer at the same time, or a weaver, or a builder, but rather to just make shoes, so that the work of shoemaking would be done well for us; and to each of the others likewise we assigned one thing, toward which each was naturally suited, and at which he was to work, having leisure from other things, <margin>D</margin>working it through his life, not passing over the right moments, to work it well. But as for the things concerning war, is it not of the greatest importance that they be worked well? Or is it so easy that a farmer will also be a warrior, or a shoemaker, or one working any other art? But not even one man could become a sufficient player of draughts or dice if he did not practice this very thing from a child, but rather treated it as a side-task? And will he, by taking a shield or any other of the warlike weapons and instruments, on that very day be a sufficient competitor in heavy-armed combat or any other battle concerning war? None of the other instruments will make anyone a craftsman or an athlete by being taken up, nor will it be useful <margin>E</margin>to one who has neither taken up the knowledge of each nor provided sufficient practice? The instruments would be worth much then, he said. Therefore (I said), as the work of the Guardians is greatest, so it would require the most leisure from other things, and again the greatest art and diligence. I think so, he said. Does it not also require a nature suited to this very pursuit? How not? Our work then would be, it seems, if we are able, to pick out who and what kind of natures are suited for the guarding of the city. Our work indeed. By Zeus (I said), then we have taken up no slight matter; but nevertheless we must not shrink from it, as far as our power allows. No indeed, he said. Do you think (I said) there is any difference between the nature of a well-born puppy for guarding, and a well-born youth? What <margin>F</margin>do you mean? As in, both of them must be sharp to perceive, and light to pursue what they perceive; and strong again, if they must fight after catching it. They must indeed, he said, have all these. And surely he must be brave, if he is to fight well. How not? And will he be willing to be brave if he is not high-spirited, whether a horse or a dog or any other animal? Or have you not noticed how war-like and invincible spirit is? When it is present, every soul is fearless and indomitable toward everything? I have noticed. Now, as for the body, what the guardian should be like is clear. Yes. And as for the soul, that it be high-spirited. This too. How then, (I said) O Glaucon, will they not be savage to each other and to the other citizens, being such in their natures? By Zeus (he said), not easily. But nevertheless <margin>G</margin>one says they must be gentle to their own people, but harsh toward enemies. If not, they will not wait for others to destroy them, but they will be first to do it themselves. True, he said. What then (I said) shall we do? Where will we find a character at once gentle and great-spirited? For surely a gentle nature is the opposite of a high-spirited one. It appears so. But nevertheless, if he is deprived of either of these, he will not be a good guardian. These things seem like impossibilities; and so it turns out that it is impossible for a good guardian to exist. It is likely, he said. And I, being at a loss, and looking over what went before, said: Justly, O friend, are we at a loss. For we have left behind the comparison we brought in. <margin>H</margin>How do you say? Have we not noticed that there are after all such natures as we thought not, having these opposite things? Where? One could see it in other animals, and not least in the one to which we compared the guardian. For you know...

<summary>In this passage, Socrates and Glaucon discuss the transition to a "luxurious city," which requires a professional army (Guardians). Socrates argues that war is a specialized art requiring a specific nature—one that combines fierce spirit with gentleness—and compares this ideal nature to that of a well-bred guard dog.</summary>

# ON THE REPUBLIC, BOOK II

...Guardian. For you surely know that this is the natural character of well-bred dogs: to be as gentle as possible toward those they are familiar with and know, but the opposite toward those they do not know. I do know that. Therefore, I said, this is possible; and we are not seeking something contrary to nature when we look for such a guardian. It seems not. Does it seem to you then that one who is to be a guardian needs this further quality: in addition to being spirited, he must also be a <term>philosopher</term><note>The word "philosopher" here is used in its literal sense: "a lover of wisdom/learning" (philose-sophos).</note> by nature? How so? he asked; I do not understand. This too, I said, you will see in dogs, which is a trait in the animal worthy of wonder. What sort of trait? Whenever a dog sees someone it does not know, it is angry, even though it has suffered no harm before; but whenever it sees someone it knows, it welcomes them, even if it has never received any good from them. Have you never wondered at this? I have not paid much attention to it until now, he said; but it is clear that they do this. And yet, this seems to be a sophisticated quality of its nature, and truly philosophical. In what way? Because, I said, it distinguishes a friendly face from a hostile one by no other criterion than having learned the one and being ignorant of the other. And how can that which defines the familiar and the foreign by knowledge and ignorance not be a lover of learning? In no way, he said. But surely, I said, the lover of learning and the "philosopher" are the same thing? They are the same, he said. May we then confidently assume the same for a human being: if someone is to be gentle toward his relatives and acquaintances, he must by nature be a philosopher and a lover of learning? Let us assume so, he said. Then the one who is to be a fine and good guardian of the city will be philosophical, spirited, swift, and strong by nature. Entirely so, he said. 

Such, then, would be his nature. But in what way will these men be reared and educated by us? And does this investigation help us toward the goal for which we are considering everything—to see how justice and injustice arise in a city? We should consider this so that we do not omit a necessary argument or go through a redundant one. And Glaucon's brother <note>Adimantus</note> said: I certainly expect this inquiry will contribute greatly to that goal. By Zeus, I said, my dear Adimantus, then we must not give it up, even if it turns out to be rather long. No indeed, he said. Come then, like people telling stories in a fable and having leisure, let us educate these men in speech. We must. What then is the education? Is it hard to find a better one than that discovered over a long period of time? This consists of <term>gymnastics</term><note>Physical education and training.</note> for the body and <term>music</term><note>Greek: *mousike*. This includes not just music, but poetry, literature, and all the arts presided over by the Muses.</note> for the soul. It is. Shall we then begin educating them in music before gymnastics? Of course. When you say music, do you include stories, or not? I do. And there are two kinds of stories: one true, and the other false. Yes. They must be educated in both, but first in the false ones. I do not understand, he said, what you mean. Do you not understand, I said, that we first tell stories to children? These are, to put it simply, false, though there are true things in them. We use stories with children before gymnastics. That is true. This is what I meant when I said that music must be taken up before gymnastics. Correct, he said. Do you not know that the beginning of every work is the most important part, especially for anything young and tender? For that is when it is most easily molded and the shape that one wishes to impress upon each individual is taken in. Exactly so. Shall we then so easily allow children to hear any old stories fashioned by any old storytellers, and to take into their souls opinions that are mostly contrary to those we think they should have when they are grown? We shall not allow it at all. First then, it seems, we must supervise the makers of stories; and if they make a good story, we must accept it, but if not, we must reject it. We will persuade nurses and mothers to tell the accepted stories to the children, and to shape their souls with stories much more than their bodies with their hands. But most of the stories they tell now must be thrown out. Which ones? he asked. In the greater stories, I said, we shall also see the smaller ones. For there must be the same pattern and the same effect in both the greater and the smaller. Or don't you think so? I do, he said; but I do not understand which ones you call the greater. Those that Hesiod and Homer told us, and the other poets. For they composed false stories for mankind and told them, and they still tell them. Which ones, he asked, and what is it in them that you find fault with? That which, I said, ought to be blamed first and most of all, especially if someone does not lie well. What is that? When someone represents poorly in speech the nature of gods and heroes—like a painter who paints things not at all like the things he intends to copy. Indeed, he said, it is right to blame such things; but how do we mean this, and what kind of stories? First, I said, the greatest lie about the greatest things was not a fine lie: the one who said that <term>Uranus</term><note>Latin: *Cælum*. The primordial god of the Sky.</note> did what Hesiod says he did, and how <term>Cronus</term><note>Latin: *Saturnus*. Son of Uranus.</note> punished him. And the deeds of Cronus and what he suffered at the hands of his son <note>Zeus/Jupiter</note>—even if they were true, I would not think they should be told so easily to the thoughtless and the young; they should be kept silent. But if there were some necessity to tell them, they should be heard in secret by as few as possible, after they had sacrificed not a pig, but some great and rare victim, so that it would happen that as few as possible heard them. Indeed, he said, these stories are difficult. And they must not be told, Adimantus, in our ci—

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> A well-bred dog has this habit from nature: that it is very gentle toward its familiars and acquaintances, but on the contrary, harsh toward strangers. I certainly know this. Therefore, what we seek is neither impossible nor contrary to nature—namely, that a guardian should be such. So it appears. Does it seem to you, moreover, that the one who is to be a guardian needs to add to that ferocity a nature that is philosophical? How do you say this? For I do not understand. And yet, this can be observed in dogs, which is indeed a quality worthy of admiration in a beast. What sort of quality? When it sees a stranger, it takes it badly, even if it has suffered no harm from him. But it fawns upon an acquaintance, although it has received no good from him. Have you not yet wondered at this? I have not <margin>B</margin> noticed it much until now; but it is manifest that it does this. Yet this effect seems to be of nature itself—noble and truly philosophical. By what reasoning? Because it distinguishes a friend from an enemy by no other thing than sight, because it knows the former and is ignorant of the latter. Should we not, therefore, rightly call it a lover of learning and studious, since it distinguishes the domestic from the foreign by knowledge and ignorance? It should. Why not? Furthermore, the one who is studious of learning and the philosopher are the same. The same. Why then should we not boldly propose that in a human being also, if he is to be gentle toward his familiars and acquaintances, he must be a philosopher <margin>C</margin> and a lover of learning? Let us propose it. Therefore, he who is to be the best guardian of the city will be a philosopher, and spirited, and swift, and robust by nature. It is altogether so. Such a guardian let him be. But in what way will these guardians be nourished and educated by you? And will this consideration help us toward that for the sake of which we consider everything—to find out, namely, how justice and injustice arise in a city? This must certainly be thought about, lest we perhaps either omit the necessary or pursue the superfluous. I think indeed, said the brother of Glaucon, that this discussion contributes greatly to what has been proposed to us. So I myself think, by Jove, O friend Adimantus. We must not, therefore, desist, even if these things were to be rather long. Certainly not, he said. Come then, like people <margin>D</margin> passing leisure in telling fables, let us instruct these men in speech. Indeed, that is proper. What then will be the discipline? Will it be difficult to find a better one than that which has been found over a long time? This is gymnastics pertaining to the body, and music to the soul. It is clearly so. Should not this education begin with music rather than gymnastics? Certainly. When you say music, do you also include speeches, or not? I do. There are two kinds of speech: true and false. So it is. The future guardian must be educated in both, and first in the false. I do not understand, he said, what you are saying. Do you not know that we first tell stories to boys? <margin>E</margin> These, to speak simply, are false, yet there are also true things in them. We use stories for boys before gymnastics. It is as you say. This, therefore, is what I wanted when I said that music must be touched upon before gymnastics. Correctly so. Do you not know that in every thing, the beginning is the most important part, especially for the young and tender? For it is then most of all that the form is shaped and takes on the figure which one wishes to impress upon each person. Altogether so. Shall we then so easily permit children to hear any stories fashioned by anyone, and to drink into their souls opinions <margin>F</margin> that are for the most part contrary to those we think they ought to have when they have grown up? In no way will we permit it. First, therefore, as it seems, we must oversee the makers of fables; if they make any good fable, let them choose it, but let them reject the rest. Those which we have finally chosen, we shall take care to have told to the boys by nurses and mothers, so that their souls may be formed by fables much more than their bodies by hands. But of those stories they now tell, many will have to be rejected. Of what kind? he asked. In the greater, I said, we shall clearly see the lesser. For there must be the same figure and the same power in both the greater <margin>G</margin> and the lesser. Do you not think so? I do think so. But what you call the greater, I do not at all understand. Those which Hesiod and Homer and the rest of the poets wrote. For these have fashioned false stories for men, which are circulated daily. What stories do you mean? And what do you condemn in them? That which ought to be condemned first and most, especially when someone does not lie well. What is that? When someone poorly fashions in words what sort of gods and heroes they are, like a painter depicting things in no way similar to those he attempts to imitate. And yet such things are rightly blamed. But how and what kind do we mean? First of all, the greatest lie about the greatest things, which Hesiod did not tell well when he fashioned those deeds committed by <term>Uranus</term><note>Latin: *Cælus*. The Sky.</note>, and added how <term>Cronus</term><note>Latin: *Saturnus*.</note> punished him, and recounted what Cronus did and what he suffered from his son. Which things, even if they were true, I would not think should be brought so openly to men of little mind and to youths, but should rather be kept silent. But if a necessity of speaking were present, they should be heard in secret by a few, who had sacrificed not a pig, but some precious and rare victim, so that it might happen that as few as possible heard them. Truly these speeches are harsh. Nor are they to be told, O Adimantus, in our city.

<summary>Socrates argues that guardians must be both spirited and "philosophical" (like dogs who distinguish friends from strangers by knowledge). He then initiates a discussion on education, emphasizing the need to censor traditional myths by Homer and Hesiod that depict the gods as violent or immoral.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the education of the guardians. Having established that guardians must be both spirited and philosophical, Socrates now turns to the specific content of the stories and myths they should be told, arguing that traditional poetry often depicts the gods in ways that are morally corrupting.</meta>

# PLATO

<margin>A</margin> Nor should it be said to a young listener that if he commits the most extreme injustices, he is doing nothing remarkable; nor that if he punishes a father who has done wrong, he is not erring greatly, but rather doing exactly what the first and greatest of the gods did. <note>Socrates refers here to the myth of Cronus castrating his father Uranus, and Zeus later overthrowing Cronus.</note> "By Zeus," he said, "I also think these things are not fit to be told." Nor indeed, I said, should it be told at all that gods wage war against other gods, or plot and fight against one another. For these stories are not even true—if indeed those who are to guard our city for us ought to consider it the most shameful thing to be easily set at odds with one another.

<margin>B</margin> Therefore, the war of the giants must not be narrated to them in any way, nor the many various quarrels of gods and heroes with their own kin and relatives. Instead, if we are somehow to persuade them that no citizen was ever an enemy to another and that such a thing is not holy, then such stories should rather be told to them as children right from the start by the elders and the old women, and the poets must be compelled to direct their myths toward this end. But as for Hera being bound by her son, or Hephaestus <note>Latin: Vulcan</note> being hurled from heaven by his father when he intended to help his mother while she was being beaten, or the battles of the gods that Homer wrote about—these we must not admit into the city, whether they are composed with an <term>allegory</term><note>The original Greek uses "hyponoia," meaning a hidden or underlying meaning. Many ancient readers defended scandalous myths by saying they were symbolic.</note> or without one. For a young person is unable to distinguish what is an allegory and what is not; but whatever opinions one receives at that age tend to become difficult to wash away or change.

<margin>C</margin> For these reasons, perhaps, we must take every care that the first stories they hear are the best adapted to lead them toward virtue. "Your point is reasonable," he said. "But if someone were to ask us what these stories are, and what kind of myths they should be, what would we say?" Then I said, "O Adeimantus, you and I are not poets at this moment, but founders of a city. It is the duty of founders to know the <term>patterns</term><note>Greek: "typoi" (types or models). These are the theological standards the poets must follow.</note> within which the poets must compose their myths, and which they must not be permitted to overstep; however, the founders do not have to compose the myths themselves."

<margin>D</margin> "Right," he said. "But this is the very thing: what would be the patterns concerning <term>theology</term><note>Literally "discourse about the gods."</note>?" "Something like this," I said. "As God truly is, so must he always be described, whether he is described in epic verse, in song, or even in tragedy." "Indeed he must." "Is God not truly good, and must he not be called so?" "Of course." "But surely nothing good is harmful. Is it?" "I think not." "And that which is not harmful, does it do any harm?" "By no means." "And that which does no harm, does it do any evil?" "Not that either." "And that which does no evil could not be the cause of any evil?" "How could it be?" "Furthermore, is the good beneficial?" "Yes." "Therefore it is the cause of well-being?" "Yes." "The good, then, is not the cause of all things, but the cause of things that are well-off; of evil things, however, it is not the cause."

<margin>E</margin> "It is entirely so," he said. "Therefore," I said, "God, since he is good, would not be the cause of all things, as many people say, but the cause of a few things for human beings, and of many things he is not the cause. For our good things are far fewer than our evil ones. And for the good things, God alone must be called the cause; but for the evils, one must seek some other causes besides God."

<margin>Iliad 24</margin> "You seem to me to speak the truth," he said. "Therefore," I said, "we must not accept from Homer or any other poet the foolish error of saying about the gods that:
*Two jars lie in the threshold of Jove,* <note>original: "Iouis limine duo iacere dolia"</note>
*full of fates: one of good, the other of evil.*
And he to whom Jupiter gives a mixture of these meets sometimes with evil and sometimes with good; but he to whom he gives from the other jar alone—
*mad hunger drives him over the divine earth.*
Nor should we accept that Jupiter is for us the dispenser of both good and evil."

<margin>F</margin><margin>Iliad 4</margin><margin>Iliad 20</margin> Nor will we praise it if someone says that the violation of the oaths and truces by Pandarus was brought about through Athena and Zeus, or that the strife and judgment of the gods happened through Themis and Zeus. Nor, again, should we allow the young to hear what Aeschylus says: *God plants a cause for mortals, whenever he wishes to utterly destroy a house.* But if someone composes a poem in which these iambic verses appear—the sufferings of Niobe, or the house of Pelops, or the Trojan tales, or anything of that kind—we must either not allow him to say these are the works of a god, or if they are from a god, he must find a reason for them similar to the one we are now seeking: he must say that God did what was just and good, and that they were benefited by being punished. But the poet must not be permitted to say that those who pay the penalty are miserable, and that it was God who made them so.

<margin>G</margin> But if he were to say that the wicked were miserable because they needed punishment, and that in paying the penalty they were being helped by God, we should allow it. But to say that God, who is good, is the cause of evil to anyone—that we must fight against in every way. We must not allow anyone to say this in his own city, if it is to be governed by good laws, nor allow anyone to hear it, whether young or old, whether told in verse or in prose. For such things are neither holy to say, if they were said, nor useful to us, nor consistent with themselves. "I cast my vote with you for this law," he said, "and it pleases me." "This, then," I said, "would be one of the laws and patterns concerning the gods, to which speakers and poets will be required to conform: that God is not the cause of all things, but only of the good."

<margin>H</margin> "That is sufficient," he said. "What then about this second one? Do you think God is a sorcerer, appearing intentionally in different forms at different times—sometimes truly changing himself and altering his appearance into many shapes, and at other times deceiving us and presenting us with false images of himself?" Or...

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Adeimantus regarding the nature of the divine. In the previous section, they established that God must be the cause only of good, not of evil. Now, they examine whether the divine is unchanging and whether it ever uses deception.</meta>

# ON THE REPUBLIC, BOOK II.

...is something simple, and least of all likely to depart from its own form? "I hold it to be so," he said. "Yes, exactly so." "And what about this? Is it not necessary that if anything departs from its own form, it must be changed either by itself or by something else?" "It is necessary." "Then things that are in the best condition are least altered and moved by something else. For example, is not a body least altered by food, drink, and labor, and every plant by the heat of the sun, winds, and similar experiences—where the healthiest and strongest is changed the least?" "How could it be otherwise?" "And would not the bravest and wisest soul be least disturbed or altered by any external influence?" "Yes." "And indeed, by the same reasoning, all composite things—vessels, buildings, and garments—when they are well-made and in good condition, are least changed by time or other external influences." "That is so." "Therefore, everything that is in a good state, whether by nature, by art, or by both, admits the least change from another." "So it seems." "But surely God and the things of God are in every way in the best possible state." "How could they not be?" "In this way, then, God would least of all take on many forms." "Least of all indeed." "But would he change and alter himself?" "Clearly," he said, "if he is altered at all." "Does he then change himself into something better and more beautiful, or into something worse and uglier than himself?" "It must be for the worse," he said, "if he is altered at all. For surely we will not say that God is lacking in beauty or excellence." "You speak most correctly," I said. "And this being the case, Adeimantus, do you think anyone, whether god or human, would willingly make himself worse in any way?" "It is impossible," he said. "It is impossible then," I said, "for a god to wish to alter himself. Rather, as it seems, each of them, being as beautiful and as excellent as possible, remains forever simply in his own form." "That seems to me to be an absolute necessity," he said. "Then, my excellent friend," I said, "let none of the poets tell us that 'the gods, like strangers from far-off lands, taking all sorts of shapes, visit our cities.' <note>original: "θεοὶ ξείνοισιν ἐοικότες ἀλλοδαποῖσι..." A quote from Homer's Odyssey, 17.485-486.</note> And let no one tell lies about Proteus and Thetis; <note>Proteus and Thetis were sea deities famous for their ability to change shapes.</note> nor in tragedies or other poems let anyone introduce Hera disguised as a priestess, collecting life-giving gifts for the children of Inachus, the Argive river; <note>Inachus was a river god of Argos. This refers to a lost play where Hera appeared in disguise.</note> and let them not tell many other such lies to us. Nor again should mothers be persuaded by these poets to frighten their children by telling these stories badly—claiming that certain gods go about at night, appearing in the likeness of many strange guests—lest they both blaspheme against the gods and make their children more cowardly." "Let them not," he said. "But then," I said, "are the gods themselves such that they do not change, but they make us think they appear in all sorts of forms, deceiving and bewitching us?" "Perhaps," he said. "What?" I said, "would a god wish to lie, either in word or in deed, by putting forward a phantom?" "I do not know," he said. "Do you not know," I said, "that the true lie—if one may say such a thing—is hated by all gods and humans?" "What do you mean by that?" he said. "This," I said, "that no one willingly wishes to be deceived in the most vital part of themselves and about the most vital things, but everyone fears most of all to possess a lie there." "I still do not understand," he said. "That is because you think I am saying something profound," I said. "But I am saying that to be deceived in the soul about reality—to have been deceived and to be ignorant, and to hold and possess a lie there—is what everyone would least of all accept. They hate it most in that place." "Very much so," he said. "But surely it would be most correct to call what I just mentioned the 'true lie': the ignorance in the soul of the person who has been deceived. For the lie in words is a kind of imitation of the condition in the soul, an image that arises later, and not an entirely unmixed lie. Is it not so?" "Certainly." "The real lie, then, is hated not only by gods but also by humans." "I agree." "But what about the lie in words? When and for whom is it useful, so as not to be worthy of hatred? Is it not useful against enemies, or for those called friends when, through madness or some ignorance, they attempt to do something bad? In such a case, it becomes useful as a medicine to turn them away from it. And in the myths we were just discussing, because we do not know the truth about ancient things, do we not make the lie as useful as possible by making it as much like the truth as we can?" "It is very much so," he said. "In which of these ways, then, is a lie useful to God? Does he lie by making things like the truth because he does not know ancient things?" "That would be ridiculous," he said. "There is, then, no lying poet in God." "I think not." "Would he then lie because he fears his enemies?" "Far from it." "Because of the ignorance or madness of his friends?" "But no one who is ignorant or mad is a friend of God," he said. "There is, then, no reason why God would lie." "There is none." "Therefore, the divine and the spiritual are altogether free from falsehood." "Entirely," he said. "God is therefore altogether simple and true in both deed and word. He does not change himself, nor does he deceive others, neither by visions, nor by words, nor by the sending of signs, whether we are awake or dreaming." "So it seems to me also," he said, "now that you say it." "Do you agree then," I said, "that this is the second rule for speaking and writing about the gods: that they are not sorcerers who change themselves, nor do they mislead us with lies in word or deed?" "I agree." "Therefore, while we praise many other things in Homer, we shall not praise this: the sending of the dream by Zeus to Agamemnon..."

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...or rather a simple being, and least of all departing from his own form? I do not know what to say about these things at present. But what about this? Is it not necessary, if anything departs from its own form, that it is changed either by itself or by another? It is necessary. Things that are in the best condition are by no means changed or turned by another, just as the body is affected by food, drink, and labor, and all plants by heat and the storms of the winds, and similar sufferings; where that which is most sound and robust is least changed. Certainly so. Would not an external disturbance also least of all change a soul that is most brave and most wise? Indeed. <margin>B</margin> Furthermore, all composite things, such as vessels, buildings, and garments, when well-constructed and in good condition, are least changed by time or other sufferings. It is as you say. Whatever, therefore, is in a good state, whether by nature, by art, or by both, admits the least change from another. It seems so. But truly God himself, and the things that belong to God, are in every way in the best possible condition. Why not? By this reasoning, therefore, God would least of all take on multiple forms. Least of all. But would God turn or change himself? This is manifest, if indeed he were changed. Would he then change himself for the better and more beautiful, or for the worse and uglier than himself? It must be for the worse, if he is changed at all. For we do not say that God is unworthy of beauty and virtue. You speak most correctly. But since these things are so, do you believe, O Adeimantus, that anyone, whether god or human, would of his own will make himself worse? <margin>C</margin> That is certainly impossible. It is impossible, therefore, for God to wish to change himself. But as it seems, since each of the gods is most beautiful and best, as far as is possible, they all remain forever in their own simple form. I think this is entirely necessary. Therefore, let no poet tell us, O best of men, that the gods, like various strangers, visit cities in different forms. <margin>Odyssey 17.</margin> Nor let anyone lie about Proteus and Thetis in a similar way. Nor in tragedies or other poems should anyone introduce Juno <note>Hera</note> changed into the likeness of a priestess, collecting gifts for the children of Inachus, the river of Argos, to whom life has been given; and let no one dare to feign other such things. Nor let mothers terrify their children with these empty fables, saying that certain gods wander at night like certain strangers, under various forms, lest they both speak ill of the gods and make the children themselves more timid. By no means. <margin>D</margin> But are the gods themselves not immutable, yet by some deceptions do they seem to us to be changed into various forms? Perhaps so. But what? Does God wish to lie, either in word or by presenting a false image in reality? I do not know. Do you not know that everyone, both humans and gods, hates the lie itself in reality, if indeed it can be so called? What is this you say? I mean it thus: no one willingly wishes to lie in the most principal and excellent part of himself, and concerning the most principal and excellent things, <margin>E</margin> but dreads a lie there above all. Even now I do not understand. You think I am saying something great. But I am saying that no one would ever want the soul itself to lie about reality, to have been lied to, to be deceived by ignorance, and to have and receive a lie within it. For all men especially hate having a lie in the soul. Especially. And yet, what I was just saying would rightly be called a lie in reality: ignorance in the soul of the one who lies. Since a lie in speech is a certain imitation of that suffering which is in the soul, a later proceeding image, and not an entirely pure lie. <margin>F</margin> Is it not so? Entirely so. Therefore, the lie itself in reality is hateful not only to gods but also to humans. So it seems to me. But what about the lie in words? When and for whom is it so useful that it is not worthy of hatred? Is it not against enemies and those who are called friends, when because of madness or some ignorance they attempt some evil deed? Then, for the sake of averting them, it is useful as if it were a medicine. And in those myths we were just discussing, because we do not know wherein the truth of ancient things consists, we make the lie useful by assimilating it to the truth. It is exactly so. <margin>G</margin> According to which of these, then, is a lie useful to God? Is it because he does not know ancient things that he lies under the image of truth? That would indeed be ridiculous. A lying poet, therefore, is not in God. It does not seem so to me. Will he lie out of fear of enemies? Far from it. Or because of the dementia or insanity of his associates? But no one of the foolish or insane is a friend to God. There is, therefore, no reason why God should lie. None. Therefore, the nature of gods and spirits is entirely without a lie. Entirely. Therefore, God is altogether simple and true in words and deeds; he is not changed himself, nor does he deceive others, <margin>H</margin> neither through visions, nor through speeches, nor by sending signs, neither while we are sleeping nor while we are awake. It seems so to me as well, while you are speaking. Do you concede then that this is the second figure in which it is necessary to speak and feign concerning the gods—as those who are neither sorcerers, nor change themselves, nor seduce us with lies, either in word or deed?

<summary>In this passage, Socrates argues for the absolute immutability and truthfulness of the divine, concluding that God is simple, unchanging, and never deceptions. He rejects poetic accounts, like those of Homer, which depict gods changing shapes or lying to humans.</summary>

Nor will we praise Aeschylus when he introduces Thetis saying that 
<margin>A</margin> Apollo sang at her wedding, promising that her offspring would live a long life, free from disease. <note>original: "bonam Thetidis stirpem fore longæuam, morbisque intactam"</note> She says: "He sang that my fortunes would be dear to the gods, and his praise filled me with joy. I hoped that the divine mouth of Phoebus <note>An epithet for Apollo</note> was truthful and prophetic. Yet he, the very one who sang this, the one present at the feast, the one who said these things—he himself is the one who killed my son." Whenever such things are said about the gods, we will immediately protest and express our disapproval. We will not allow teachers to use these stories for the education of the youth, if our guardians are to be as god-fearing and divine as is possible for a human being. "I accept this model," he said, "and I will use it as a law everywhere."

# PLATO ON THE REPUBLIC,
->or,<-
## ON JUSTICE.
### THE THIRD DIALOGUE.

---

*SUMMARY OF THE DIALOGUE. Plato continues the same discourse on the training of the Magistrate, which he had divided into two parts: Music <note>In the Greek sense, "Music" (mousikē) refers to all the arts of the Muses, including literature and poetry</note> and Gymnastics. Having already dealt extensively with the former, he now pursues the remaining matters pertaining to it. Afterward, he treats Gymnastics. He then discusses the character, morals, training, and the method of testing lower magistrates to see how they might be placed in charge of public duties. Finally, from an explanation of what he calls a certain "Phoenician myth," he attaches a doctrine <note>original: "δόγμα"</note> regarding the community and total consensus of citizens as if they were blood relations and truly brothers in the same republic. This is the well-ordered arrangement <note>original: "εὐταξία"</note> of various men, so that some are like gold, others silver, and others iron and bronze; yet all are brought together to constitute the whole republic. Furthermore, since the teachings of the poets were granted too much authority by his people, he criticizes them, showing by the examples of famous men that they bring a plague and destruction to human morals; thus he creates a decree <note>original: "senatusconsultum"</note> to expel them from the republic, though honorably, so that their learning is given its due respect.*

---

These, then, are the things—as it seems to me—
<margin>B</margin> that should or should not be heard from childhood by those who are to honor the gods and their parents, and who will not think lightly of mutual friendship. "I think," said Adeimantus, "our view is correct." But what about those who are to be brave? Must we not tell them things that will make them fear death as little as possible? Or do you think anyone can ever be brave if they harbor such a fear? "Not at all, by Jove," he said. And what about those who believe the stories told about the underworld and think they are terrible—do you think such a person will be fearless in the face of death, and in battle will prefer death over slavery and captivity? "By no means." It is necessary then, 
<margin>C</margin> it seems, for us to give instructions also to those who tell these myths, and to ask them not to simply disparage the things in the underworld, but rather to praise them—as their stories are neither true nor useful to those who are to be warriors. "It is indeed necessary," he said. We shall therefore delete all such passages, starting with this verse: *I would rather serve as a laborer for another poor man on his farm than rule over all the dead who have perished.* <note>Homer, Odyssey 11.489</note> And this: *That the houses of the dead might appear to mortals and immortals alike as horrible, vast, and moldering, things which even the gods loathe.* <note>Homer, Iliad 20.64</note> And this: *O alas! Is there truly a soul and an image in the halls of Hades? But there is no mind within it.* <note>Homer, Iliad 23.103</note> And this: *That he alone should have wisdom; the rest flit about as shadows.* <note>Homer, Odyssey 10.495</note> Also, 
<margin>D</margin> *The soul, released from the limbs, flies to the underworld, bewailing its fate, leaving behind its strength and youth.* <note>Homer, Iliad 16.856</note> Also, *The soul went beneath the earth like smoke, squeaking as it went.* <note>Homer, Iliad 23.100</note> Also, *Just as bats <note>The Latin text uses "noctuae" (owls), but the Greek "νυκτερίδες" means bats</note> fly screeching in the depths of a vast cave, when one has fallen from the cluster on the rock where they clung to one another, so these went along gibbering together.* <note>Homer, Odyssey 24.6</note> These and all such things we will ask Homer and the other poets to forgive us for erasing—not because they are not poetic or pleasing to the ears of the many, but because the more poetic they are, the less they should be heard by boys and men who must be free, fearing slavery more than death. "Exactly so." Furthermore, shouldn't the 
<margin>E</margin> names given to these places—horrendous and terrifying—be cast out? I mean Cocytus <note>The river of wailing</note> and Styx <note>The river of hatred</note>, and terms like "those below" and "the dead," <note>original: "inferos, & mortuos"</note> and other names of this kind. They vehemently terrify everyone who hears them. Perhaps they serve some other purpose, but for our guardians, we fear such terror will make them softer and more fragile than they ought to be. "And we are right to fear it," he said. "They must be removed then." "They must." We must instead speak and introduce a form of speech contrary to these. "Clearly." Therefore, we shall also remove the 
lamentations and cries of pity of famous men. "It is necessary, if we remove what came before." Consider then if we are right to remove them. Do we not say that a moderate man will not think death a terrible thing for another moderate man who is his friend? "We do say that." He will not, then, lament for him as if he had suffered 
<margin>F</margin> something terrible. "No." Truly, we also say this: that such a man is sufficient unto himself for living well, and least of all men does he need anything else. "You speak the truth." It will be least distressing for him, then, to be deprived of children, or brothers, or riches, or anything else of that sort. "Least of all, certainly." Therefore, he will not 
<meta>catchword: lament</meta>

<column-break/>

...nor of Aeschylus, when Thetis says that Apollo, singing at her wedding, [spoke of] "my happy lot in offspring, free from disease and long-lived. Having said all this, he sang the Paean <note>A song of praise or triumph</note> over my god-blessed fortunes, gladdening my heart. And I hoped the divine mouth of Phoebus would be without falsehood, brimming with the prophetic art. But he, the very one who sang, he who was present at the feast, he who said these things, is the very one who killed my son." When someone says such things about the gods, we will be angry and will not grant a chorus <note>Refers to the state-sponsored theatrical production</note>, nor will we allow teachers to use such things for the education of the young, if our guardians are to be god-fearing and divine, as far as it is possible for a human being to be. "In every way," he said, "I agree with these models, and would use them as laws."
