# PLATO'S REPUBLIC,
->III,<-
## CONCERNING JUSTICE,
### THE THIRD DIALOGUE.

---

"As for the things concerning the gods," I said, "such things, it seems, should be heard and not heard from childhood by those who will honor the gods and their parents, and who will not value their friendship with one another as a small thing." "And I think," I said, "that our view appears correct." "What then? If they are to be brave, must not these things be said, and such things as will make them have the least fear of death? Or do you think anyone could ever be brave while having this fear within him?" "By Zeus," he said, "I certainly do not." "And what? Do you think someone who believes Hades exists and is a place of terror will be without fear of death, and in battles will choose death over defeat and slavery?" "Not at all." "We must then, as it seems, oversee those who take it upon themselves to tell these myths, and ask them not to simply revile the things in Hades, but rather to praise them, as they say things that are neither true nor useful to those who are to be warriors." "We must indeed," he said. "We shall then erase," I said, "beginning from this verse, all such things: *I would rather be on the land as a serf to another man, a portionless man who has not much livelihood, than to rule over all the perished dead.* And this: *And that the houses might appear to mortals and immortals, dreadful, dank, which even the gods loathe.* And: *O gods! Is there then even in the halls of Hades a soul and an image, but 
<margin>mind</margin> no mind <note>original: "φρένες"</note> in it at all?* And: *To him alone to be wise, while the others flit as shadows.* And: *The soul flying from the limbs went to Hades, wailing its fate, leaving behind manliness and youth.* And: *—and the soul went beneath the earth like smoke, twittering.* And: *As when bats in the corner of a wondrous cave fly twittering, when one falls from the string off the rock, and they hold onto one another; so these went along twittering together.* All these and such things we will ask Homer and the other poets not to be angry if we erase; not because they are not poetic and sweet for the many to hear, but because the more poetic they are, the less they should be heard by children and men who must be free, fearing slavery more than death." "By all means." "Must we not also discard all the names concerning these things that are dreadful and fearful: Cocytus and Styx, and those below, and the 'sapless ones' <note>original: "ἀλίβαντας" - a poetic term for the dead</note>, and all other such things named in this model, which make all who hear them shudder? And perhaps they are good for some other purpose; but we fear for our guardians, lest from such shuddering they become more feverish and soft than they ought to be." "And we are right to fear," he said. "They must be removed then." "Yes." "And the opposite model to these must be spoken and created." "Clearly." "And we shall also remove the wailings and the piteous cries of famous men." "It is necessary," he said, "if indeed we removed the former things." "Consider then," I said, "whether we shall remove them rightly or not. Do we not say that the good man will not think that for another good man, who is also his companion, dying is a terrible thing?" "We do say so." "Then he would not wail for him as if he had suffered something dreadful." "Certainly not." "And yet we also say this: that such a man is most self-sufficient for himself towards living well, and differs from others in needing another person least of all." "True," he said. "Least of all, then, is it a terrible thing for him to be deprived of a son, or a brother, or wealth, or any such thing." "Least of all indeed." "Least of all, then, would he wail, but he would bear it as mildly as possible when such a misfortune overtakes him." "Least of all..."
<meta>catchword: as mildly as possible</meta>

<summary>In this opening of Book III, Socrates and Adeimantus argue that poets like Homer and Aeschylus must be censored to prevent the youth from fearing death or believing the gods are the source of suffering. They list specific terrifying descriptions of the underworld that must be removed to ensure the guardians of the state remain brave and free.</summary>

# ON THE REPUBLIC, BOOK III.

<column-break/>

### ON THE REPUBLIC, BOOK III.

<margin>A</margin> ...that these things are false when such a calamity befalls someone. "Certainly," he said. We would be right, then, to remove the lamentations and the pitiful cries of famous men, and instead assign them to women—and not even the virtuous ones—and to base men. We do this so that those whom we say we are training for the protection of the country will find it beneath them to act in such a way. "That is correct," he replied. Again, we will ask Homer and the other poets not to depict Achilles, the son of a goddess, 

> Now lying on his side, then again
> On his back, and sometimes on his face; then starting up
> To wander, distracted, along the shore of the unharvested sea. <note>original: "Iliad 24.10–12"</note>

Nor should he be shown seizing the blackened dust with both hands and pouring it over his head, <note>original: "Iliad 18.23–24"</note> nor weeping and lamenting in all the various ways that Homer described. Nor should we see Priam, <margin>Iliad 22.414</margin> a man close to the gods, making supplications and rolling in the dung, calling out to each man by name. 

<margin>B</margin> We will ask them even more urgently not to represent the gods as lamenting and saying:

> Ah, miserable me! Ah, unhappy mother of the best of sons! <note>original: "Iliad 18.54"</note>

But if they must depict gods, at least let them not dare to represent the greatest of the gods in such an uncharacteristic likeness as to say:

> Alas! I see with my eyes a man dear to me
> Pursued around the city; and my heart grieves. <note>original: "Iliad 22.168–169"</note>

And likewise:

> Woe is me, for it is fated that Sarpedon, the dearest of men to me,
> Should be overcome by Patroclus, son of Menoetius. <note>original: "Iliad 16.433–434"</note>

<margin>C</margin> For if, my dear Adeimantus, our youth should listen to such things seriously instead of laughing at them as unworthy utterances, they would hardly consider such behavior unworthy of themselves, being mere humans. They would not restrain themselves if such a thought or action occurred to them; rather, without any shame or endurance, they would break into long laments and outcries over even the smallest misfortunes. "What you say is very true," he said. But this must not be, as our argument just now showed us; and we must follow that argument until someone convinces us with a better one. "It must not be." Furthermore, we should not be prone to excessive laughter; for generally, when someone gives themselves over to violent laughter, it seeks a violent reaction in return. "So it seems to me," he said. Therefore, we must not accept it if someone depicts men of high standing being overcome by laughter, and much less so if they are gods. "Much less indeed," he said.

<margin>D</margin> Therefore, we will not accept such things from Homer regarding the gods, such as:

> And unquenchable laughter <term>asbestos gelos</term> arose among the blessed gods
> As they saw Hephaestus bustling through the palace. <note>original: "Iliad 1.599–600"</note>

This is not to be accepted, according to your argument. "If you wish to attribute the argument to me," he said, "then certainly it is not to be accepted."

<margin>E</margin> Furthermore, truth must be held in high regard. For if we were right just now, and a lie <note>original: "ψεῦδος / mendacium"</note> is truly useless to the gods but useful to humans as a kind of medicine <term>pharmakon</term>, then it is clear that such a thing should be granted only to physicians, and private individuals should not touch it. "That is clear," he said. It belongs to the rulers of the city then, if to anyone, to lie for the benefit of the city, whether because of enemies or citizens; but all others must not touch it. For a private citizen to lie to such rulers is as great an error—or even greater—than for a sick man to lie to his physician, or an athlete to lie to his trainer about the condition of his own body, or for a sailor to lie to the pilot about the ship and the crew, regarding how things are with himself or his fellow sailors. "Very true," he said. If, then, the ruler catches anyone else lying in the city, 

> Any of those who are craftsmen,
> Whether a prophet, a healer of ills, or a builder of spears, <note>original: "Odyssey 17.383–384"</note>

he will punish him for introducing a practice that is as subversive and destructive to a city as it is to a ship. "He will," he said, "if indeed deeds are to follow words."

<margin>F</margin> What then? Will our young men not also need temperance <term>sophrosyne</term>? <note>A Greek virtue involving self-control and moderation</note> "How could they not?" And for the multitude, are not the main points of temperance these: to be obedient to their rulers, and to be rulers themselves over the pleasures of drink, sex, and food? "I think so." Then we shall say, I suppose, that such things are well-spoken, like what Diomedes says in Homer:

> Sit down in silence, and obey my word. <note>original: "Iliad 4.412"</note>

And what follows it:

> The Achaeans marched, breathing might,
> Silently fearing their leaders. <note>original: "Iliad 4.427, 3.8"</note>

And all other things of that kind. "They are well-spoken."

<margin>G</margin> But what about this:

> You drunkard, with the eyes of a dog and the heart of a deer! <note>original: "Iliad 1.225"</note>

And the lines following it? Are these well-spoken, or any other insults that private individuals might say to their rulers in prose or poetry? "They are not well-spoken." For I do not think they are suitable for young people to hear if they are to attain temperance; though if they provide some other pleasure, that is no surprise. How does it seem to you? "The same," he said.

<margin>H</margin> And what about making the wisest man say that it seems to him the finest thing of all when:

> The tables are full
> Of bread and meat, and the cup-bearer draws wine from the bowl
> And carries it around and pours it into the cups? <note>original: "Odyssey 9.8–10"</note>

Does it seem to you that hearing this is suitable for a young man's self-control? Or this:

> To die of hunger and meet one's fate is the most piteous thing? <note>original: "Odyssey 12.342"</note>

Or what about depicting Zeus, <insert>while other gods and men were sleeping, forgetting all the things he had planned while awake because of his desire for sex? He was so struck by the sight of Hera that he did not even wish to go into the chamber, but wanted to lie with her there on the ground, saying that he was gripped by a desire even stronger than when they first visited one another in secret from their parents.</insert> <note>original: "Iliad 14.315–328"</note>

# III PLATO

## ON THE REPUBLIC, BOOK III

<margin>a.</margin>Or when it [poetry] tells how Mars and Venus were bound by Vulcan <note>original: "Odyssey 8.266 ff." Mars and Venus are the Roman names used in this Latin translation for Ares and Aphrodite.</note> and other things of that sort? By Jove, it does not seem suitable to me. But wherever the deeds or words of excellent men are narrated with modesty and constancy, these are the things to be observed and heard. Just as when it is <margin>b.</margin>said: "Striking his breast, he rebuked his heart, saying: 'Endure, O heart, for you have suffered much worse than this before.'" <note>original: "Odyssey 20.17–18." This is a famous example of self-control.</note> This is exactly how one must act. <margin>c.</margin>Neither should we allow the citizens themselves to be corrupted by gifts, nor to be greedy for money. Not by any means. Therefore, it must not be sung that: "Gifts, believe me, please both men and gods." <note>A common Greek proverb often attributed to Hesiod.</note> Neither should <margin>d.</margin>Phoenix, the teacher of Achilles, be praised as if he spoke rightly when he advised Achilles to help the Achaeans if he received gifts, <margin>e.</margin>but if not receiving them, by no means to set aside his anger. Nor again shall we think Achilles himself worthy, or agree that he ought to be so greedy for money as to <margin>f.</margin>receive gifts from Agamemnon, or that he would refuse to return the corpse of Hector without a price. Certainly, it is not fitting to praise such things, he said. I truly fear, <margin>g.</margin>I said, to speak because of Homer—namely, that it is not right to assert these things about Achilles, or to believe others asserting them. And that he, in turn, said against Apollo: "You have hindered me, Apollo, most destructive of all gods; whom I would certainly take vengeance upon, if I <margin>h.</margin>had the power." Also, how stubbornly he behaved toward the river-god, even prepared to fight. Again, to the other river, <margin>i.</margin>Sperchius, regarding his sacred hair, he said: "To the hero Patroclus, now dead, I give my hair to be carried." <note>original: "Iliad 23.151." Achilles had vowed his hair to the river but gave it to his dead companion instead.</note> Nor is it to be believed that he did this. <margin>k.</margin>As for the dragging of Hector around the tomb of Patroclus and the slaughter of the captives upon the pyre, and all such things, we shall affirm neither <margin>l.</margin>that they are true, nor shall we allow our people to be persuaded that Achilles—the son of a goddess and of Peleus (a most temperate man and the grandson of Jove), educated by the most wise Chiron—was filled with such great turmoil that he suffered from two contrary diseases of the soul: <margin>m.</margin>meanness joined with greed, and likewise contempt for both gods and men. You speak very rightly. <margin>n.</margin>Again, let us neither believe these things, nor allow it to be said, that Theseus, the son of Neptune, and Pirithous, the son of Jove, rushed into such great robberies; nor that any other <margin>o.</margin>son of a god or hero ever dared to commit such grave and impious acts as they daily lie about. Rather, let us compel the poets <margin>p.</margin>either to deny that these were their deeds, or to not affirm that they are the sons of gods; but by no means to assert both at once, nor to give effort to persuade our youths <margin>q.</margin>that some evils arise from the gods, or that heroes are in no way better than men. For, as has already been said, these things are neither holy nor true. For we have shown that it is impossible for evils to proceed from the gods. <margin>r.</margin>We have clearly shown it. Furthermore, these things are harmful to those who hear them. For everyone will excuse his own wickedness, being persuaded that those who were the closest <margin>s.</margin>offspring of the gods, near to Jove, did and have done such things—those whose altar of ancestral Jove stands in the high air upon the peak of Mount Ida, and in whom <margin>t.</margin>the blood of the gods has not yet faded. Wherefore, such fables must be suppressed, lest they provide an easy occasion for wickedness to our <margin>u.</margin>youths. That is exactly how we must act. What species of discourse remains for us next, as we distinguish what things are to be narrated and what are not? For how one ought to speak <margin>x.</margin>concerning the gods has been said. Likewise concerning the spirits <term>daemons<gloss>In Greek thought, 'daemons' were intermediary spirits, not necessarily evil.</gloss></term> and heroes, and those who are in the underworld. Quite enough. Does it perhaps remain for us to speak about men? Certainly. <margin>y.</margin>It is impossible, my friend, to determine that at present. Why? Because I think we shall say that poets and storytellers speak wrongly concerning human beings regarding <margin>z.</margin>matters of the greatest importance: that many unjust men are happy, while the just are miserable; and that it is profitable to act unjustly if it remains hidden; but that justice itself is <margin>aa.</margin>useful to others, but harmful to the one who possesses it. These and other such things, I say, we shall forbid them to say; and we shall command them to sing and introduce into fables the opposites of these, shall we not? I certainly <margin>bb.</margin>know it. Therefore, if you confess that I speak rightly, shall I say that you have granted what we have been seeking for a long time? You judge rightly, he said. Shall we not <margin>cc.</margin>then grant that such discourse should be used regarding men once we have discovered what sort of thing justice is, and how by its own nature it <margin>dd.</margin>profits the one who possesses it, whether he seems to be just or does not seem so? You speak the truth. Concerning those things which are to be said, or not, enough has been disputed: next, as I think, we must discuss the manner of speaking <term>mimesis<gloss>The Greek word for imitation or representation.</gloss></term>: and thus we shall have found both what is to be said and how. I do not quite understand what you are saying, said Adeimantus. Yet it is necessary that you understand, I said, and thus perhaps you will understand this more clearly. Are not all things said by poets or makers of fables a narration of things either past, present, or future? What else? he said. Do they not then narrate either by simple narration, or by <term>imitation<gloss>Referring to the practice of a poet speaking in the voice of a character.</gloss></term>, or even by both modes? I require this also, he said, to be explained more clearly. I seem to be a ridiculous teacher, I said, and particularly obscure. Therefore, just as those who are less able in speaking are accustomed to do, so I now—not taking the whole matter, but taking a certain part—will try to show you in it what I want. And first tell me: do you know the beginnings of the *Iliad*, in which the poet says that Chryses supplicated Agamemnon

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>...leaving behind their dear parents; nor that Mars and Aphrodite were bound by Hephaestus, nor other such things. By Zeus, he said, it does not seem to me to be suitable. But if there are any <term>steadfast acts<gloss>Greek: karteriai</gloss></term> against all things both said and done by famous men, these must be seen and heard. Such as: "Striking his breast, he rebuked his heart with a word: 'Endure, O heart, for you have suffered even more dog-like things before.'" <note>The Greek text here corresponds exactly to the Latin column.</note> Entirely so, he said. Neither indeed must we allow these <margin>B</margin>men to be receivers of gifts, nor lovers of money. By no means. Nor should it be sung to them that "Gifts persuade gods, gifts persuade venerable kings." Nor should Phoenix, the tutor of Achilles, be praised as if he spoke moderately when advising him to help the Achaeans if he received gifts, but without gifts, not to be released from his wrath. Nor shall we deem Achilles himself worthy, or agree that he was a lover of money, such that he would receive gifts from Agamemnon, or again, having received a price for the corpse, release it; but otherwise would not be willing. It is not just, he said, to praise such things. I hesitate, <margin>C</margin>I said, to speak because of Homer—that it is not holy to say these things against Achilles, and to believe others saying them. And again, as he said to Apollo: "You have hindered me, Apollo, most destructive of all gods. Truly I would take vengeance on you, if I had the power." and how he behaved disobediently toward the river, being a god, and was ready to fight; and again, regarding the sacred hair of the other river, Sperchius, he said he would give the hair to the hero Patroclus, though he was already dead. And that he did this, we must not be persuaded. And the dragging of Hector around the tomb of Patroclus, and the slaughters of the captives upon the pyre—all these things we shall not say were spoken truly. Nor shall we allow our people to be persuaded that Achilles—being the son of a goddess and of Peleus (the most temperate of men and the third from Zeus), and having been reared by the most wise Chiron—was full of such great confusion as to have in himself two diseases contrary to one another: illiberalness joined with greed, and again, arrogance toward both gods and men. You speak <margin>D</margin>rightly, he said. Therefore, I said, let us not believe these things, nor allow them to be said: that Theseus, the son of Poseidon, and Pirithous, the son of Zeus, rushed upon such terrible robberies; nor that any other child of a god and hero would have dared to do terrible and impious things, such as they now lie about concerning them. But let us persuade the poets either to not say these are their deeds, or that these are not the children of gods. But to say both is not allowed; nor should they attempt to persuade our youth that the gods produce evils, and that heroes are no better than men. For as we said in the things before, these are neither holy nor true. For we have demonstrated that it is impossible for evils to be born from the gods. How could it be otherwise? And indeed, they are harmful to those who hear them. For every man will have an excuse for his own evil, being persuaded that even the near relatives of the gods, close to Zeus, do and did such things—those for whom <margin>E</margin>the altar of ancestral Zeus is in the high air on the Idean hill, and in whom the blood of the daemons has not yet faded. For which reasons, we must stop such myths, lest they plant in our youth a great ease for wickedness. Entirely so, he said. What species of discourse, I said, still remains for us in defining what things should be said and what should not? For regarding the gods, how one must speak has been said, and concerning the daemons and heroes, and those in Hades. Very much so. Therefore, would the remainder be concerning men? Obviously. It is impossible, O friend, for us to determine this at the present time. How so? Because I think we shall say that both poets and storytellers speak badly concerning men in the most important matters: that many unjust men are happy, but the just are wretched; and that it is profitable to do wrong if it is hidden; but <margin>F</margin>justice is another's good, but one's own loss. <note>This defines the "Sophist" view of justice that Socrates spends the rest of the book refuting.</note> Such things we shall forbid them to say, and we shall command them to sing and tell myths of the opposite things—or do you not think so? I know it well, he said. Therefore, if you agree that I speak rightly, shall I say that you have agreed to what we have been seeking for a long time? You have understood correctly, he said. Therefore, concerning men, we shall agree that such words must be spoken only when we find what justice is, and how by nature it is profitable to the one who has it, whether he seems to be just or not? Most true, he said. Let the matters concerning the content of stories have an end. But the matter of style <note>Greek: lexis</note> (as I think) must rather be considered after this; and then both what must be said and how it must be said will have been fully <margin>G</margin>considered. And Adeimantus said: I do not understand what you mean by this. But indeed, I said, you must. Perhaps then in this way you will understand it better. Is it not that all things said by mythologists or poets are a narration of things either past, present, or future? What else? he said. Do they not then accomplish this either by simple narration, or by means of imitation, or through both? I need to learn this also more clearly, he said. I seem, I said, to be a ridiculous and obscure teacher. Just as those who are unable to speak, I will not take the whole, but taking a part, I will try to show you in it what I want. Tell me: do you know the first parts of the *Iliad*, in which the poet says that Chryses requested of Agamemnon to release his daughter, and he [Agamemnon] was angry; and he [Chryses], since he did not succeed...

<summary>Socrates argues for the censorship of Homeric myths that depict heroes like Achilles as greedy or insolent, asserting that such stories corrupt the youth. He then transitions the discussion from the "content" of poetry to its "style," introducing the distinction between simple narrative and imitation (mimesis).</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion between Socrates and Adeimantus from the previous page. Having established what stories are acceptable for the education of the "guardians" (the protectors of the city), Socrates now turns to the "how"—the style or mode of the storytelling. He is specifically investigating the difference between simple narration and imitation (mimesis).</meta>

# ON THE REPUBLIC, BOOK III.

Did we not pray with the Achaeans to the god? I did. You know then that up to these lines—"and he entreated all the Achaeans,"—

->but especially the two sons of Atreus, the two marshals of the people,<-
<note>original: "Iliad 1.15-16"</note>

<margin>A</margin>the poet himself is speaking, and he does not try to turn our minds in any other direction, as if someone else were speaking but himself. But in what follows, he speaks as if he were Chryses himself, and tries his best to make us think that it is not Homer speaking, but the priest, who is an old man. And he has composed nearly all the rest of his narrative in this way, both regarding the events at Troy and those in Ithaca, and the whole of the *Odyssey* regarding the sufferings there. Certainly, he said. Now, is it not a "narration" when he delivers the speeches on each occasion, and also when he tells what <margin>B</margin>happens between the speeches? Of course. But when he delivers a speech as if he were someone else, shall we not say that he then makes his own style as similar as possible to that of the person he has announced as the speaker? We shall. Is not making oneself like another, either in voice or in gesture, the same as imitating the person one makes oneself like? Naturally. In such a case then (as it seems), this poet and the others perform their narration through imitation. Quite so. But if the poet never hid himself, his entire narrative and poetry would be made without imitation. So that you may not say you do not understand how this would be, I will explain. If Homer, after saying that Chryses came bringing a ransom for his daughter and as a suppliant of the Achaeans, and especially of the kings, had then spoken not as if he had become Chryses, but still as Homer, you know that it would not have been imitation, but simple narration. It would have gone something like this (and I shall speak without meter, for I am no poet): the priest came and prayed that the gods might grant to them, having captured Troy, to be saved themselves. But they should release his daughter to him, having accepted the ransom, and showing respect for the god. When he had said such things, the others showed reverence and agreed; but Agamemnon grew wild, commanding him to depart now and not to come back again, lest the scepter and the wreaths of the god should not protect him. He said that before his daughter was released, she would grow old in Argos with him. He ordered him to depart and not to provoke him, so that he might go home safe. The old man, hearing this, was afraid and went away in silence. But having <margin>C</margin>withdrawn from the camp, he prayed many things to Apollo, calling upon the titles of the god, and reminding him and demanding if he had ever given anything pleasing either in the building of temples or in the sacrifice of victims. For the sake of these things, he prayed that the Achaeans should pay for his tears with the god's arrows. In this way, my friend, I said, simple narration occurs without imitation. <margin>D</margin>I understand, he said. Understand then, I said, that the opposite of this happens when one removes the poet’s words between the speeches and leaves only the dialogue. This too, he said, I understand; it is the way tragedies work. You have grasped it most correctly, I said. And I think I can now <margin>E</margin>show you what I was unable to before: that of poetry and storytelling, one kind is entirely through imitation, as you say, which is tragedy and comedy; another kind is through the poet's own report—you would find this mostly in dithyrambs <note>Dithyrambs: Wild, choral hymns usually sung in honor of the god Dionysus.</note>; and still another kind uses both, as in epic poetry and in many other places, if you follow me. I understand, he said, what you meant then. Now remember what we said before: that we had already discussed *what* should be said, but we still had to consider *how* it should be said. I remember. This then was what I was saying: we need to agree whether we will allow the poets to make their narrations to us by imitating, or partly by imitating and partly not—and which parts of each—or whether they should not imitate at all. I <margin>F</margin>suspect, he said, that you are considering whether we will admit tragedy and comedy into the city, or not. Perhaps, I said, and even more than that. For I do not yet know myself; but wherever the argument, like a wind, carries us, there we must go. And you speak well, he said. Now consider this, Adeimantus: whether our guardians should be imitators or not. Or does this follow from our earlier points, that each man can practice one pursuit well, but not many? But if he tried this, taking on many things, he would fail in all of them, so as to be of no account in any. Why wouldn't it? Does the same logic not apply to imitation—that one man cannot imitate many things well, just as he can only do one thing well? Certainly not. He will hardly then practice any pursuit worthy of mention and at the same time imitate many things and be an imitator. Since <margin>G</margin>not even two forms of imitation that seem close to each other can be performed well by the same people at once; for example, writing both comedy and tragedy. Did you not just now call these two "imitations"? I did. And you are right that the same people cannot do both. Nor can rhapsodes <note>Rhapsodes: Professional performers who recited epic poetry, especially Homer.</note> and actors be the same people. True. But not even the actors for comedy and tragedy are the same. And all these are imitations, are they not? They are imitations. And besides these, Adeimantus, it seems to me that human nature is split into even smaller fragments; so that it is impossible to imitate many things well, or to do those very things of which the imitations are only likenesses. Very <margin>H</margin>true, he said. If then we are to preserve our first principle—that our guardians, being released from all other crafts, must be very precise craftsmen of the city’s freedom and practice nothing else that does not lead to this—then they should do nothing else,

<column-break/>

so that his daughter might be restored to him. But this man [Agamemnon] grew angry. Because of this, after he did not obtain his request, he called upon the God against the Achaeans? Indeed. And I believe you know this, that up to these verses, "He prayed to all the Achaeans, especially the sons of Atreus, the leaders of the nations," the poet himself speaks, and he does not try to turn our mind elsewhere, as if someone other than himself were speaking. But thereafter, he speaks as if he were Chryses himself, and he tries to show us not Homer, but that old priest. In the rest of the work, he always explains in this way, both in the deeds done at Troy, and in Ithaca, and in those things that happened in the *Odyssey*. It is entirely so. Is it not therefore a narration, both when he brings in continuous speeches, and when he speaks those things that come between them? Why not? But when he brings forth a speech as if he were someone else, shall we not say then that he makes his speech as similar as possible to the one whom he has introduced as speaking? Why should we not say so? Is it not true that to make oneself similar to another, either in form or in voice, is to imitate the one to whom he makes himself similar? Without doubt. In this, therefore, as it seems, both he and the other poets narrate through imitation. I agree. But where the poet does not hide himself, all that poetry and narration is without imitation. Lest you say that you do not understand even how this happens, I will tell you. For if Homer, when he said that Chryses had come to redeem his daughter, and had supplicated the Achaeans and especially the kings, had then spoken not as if he were Chryses, but as if he were Homer, you would know surely that imitation would not have existed, but only a simple narration. This is how it would have been. For I shall speak without verse, since I am not poetic. The priest, having set out, prayed that the gods would grant to them that they might take Troy safely, and that they should restore his daughter to him, having accepted the gifts, out of reverence for the god Apollo. When he had said these things, the rest approved the words of the priest. But Agamemnon, having become enraged, ordered him to depart immediately and not to return later; neither the god's crown nor the scepter would be of use to him: and he asserted that before he would return the daughter to him, it would happen that she would grow old with him in Argos. Therefore he ordered him to depart, and not to provoke him, so that he might depart in safety. When the old man had heard this, he was terrified, and departed in silence. But having left the camp, as a suppliant he prayed to Apollo with many words, calling upon his titles, that if he had ever done anything pleasing to him, either in building temples or in offering sacrifices, he should punish the Achaeans, and avenge his tears with his arrows. In this manner, O friend, a simple narration without imitation is made. I understand now. And know this besides, that the opposite of this occurs when the words of the poet, which are accustomed to come between speeches, are removed, and the speeches themselves are left continued in turn. I understand that also. For there is something similar in tragedies. You have understood quite rightly, and I think I can now reveal to you what I was not able to before: namely, that poetry and the fictions of stories are either entirely through imitation, as you yourself said of tragedy and comedy; or through the report of the poet himself, which is seen most of all in dithyrambs; or are composed of both, as appears in heroic poems and many others, if you understand. I understand now what you wished to say then. And yet, remember also before this, that we were saying that what had to be said has already been said: but in what manner it should be said must be considered next. I do remember. This then was it, which I said it was necessary for us to agree upon: whether we should allow the poets to use perpetual imitation, or to imitate in part and not at all in others, and what kind each might be: or to imitate nothing at all. I predict indeed that you will consider whether comedy and tragedy should be received into the city, or not. Perhaps, I said: and even more things than these. For I do not know yet: but where the argument, like a wind, carries us, there we must go. You speak excellently. Therefore, O Adeimantus, consider this: whether it is necessary for us to have our guardians be imitators, or not. Or does this depend on the things said above: that individuals can do single things rightly, but multiple things not at all; so that if anyone should attempt to handle more things, he fails in each, so that in none does he turn out excellent. So it would altogether happen. Is not the same reasoning true concerning imitation, that someone cannot imitate many things as well as he can one? Certainly not. Scarcely then will anyone apply himself to any pursuit worthy of esteem, and at the same time imitate many things, or be a suitable imitator, since not even two imitations, which seem to differ little from each other, can the same men handle well at once, such as comedy and tragedy together. Did you not say a little while ago that these were certain imitations? Indeed. And you say true things, that the same men are not able. Nor can rhapsodes (that is, singers of heroic poems) be actors at the same time. True. But neither are the actors the same for tragedy and comedy. All these things are certain imitations, are they not? Imitations. Furthermore, in smaller things than these, O Adeimantus, the nature of man seems to be divided, so that he can in no way imitate many things well, or even do those things of which the imitations themselves are certain likenesses. It is as you say. If therefore we wish the former reasoning to be held valid, our guardians, being far removed from all other crafts, must be the craftsmen of the fatherland's liberty, and very skillful indeed; nor should they care for anything else which does not tend toward this; they should do nothing else,

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Adeimantus from Book III of the *Republic*. They are discussing the education of the "guardians" (the protectors of the ideal city). Having previously decided which stories are moral enough for children, they are now debating whether these future leaders should be allowed to "imitate"—that is, to act out or perform—different types of characters in poetry and drama.</meta>

# OF PLATO

<margin>A</margin>...or they ought to imitate; or if they do imitate, they should imitate what is consistent with these virtues from their earliest childhood: specifically, men who are brave, temperate, holy, and free, and other such qualities. <note>The Greek term *eleutheros* (liberal/free) refers to the character of a free citizen as opposed to a slave.</note> They should neither perform nor be clever at imitating illiberal things, nor anything else that is shameful, lest from the imitation itself they begin to take on the reality of what they are mimicking. Have you not noticed that imitations, if they are practiced from a tender age and continue, settle into habits and become a second nature—affecting the body, the voice, and even the very way a person thinks? 

<margin>B</margin>Most certainly, he said. Therefore, I said, we will not allow those for whom we care, and who we say must become good men, to imitate a woman while they themselves are men—whether she is young or old, or a woman quarreling with her husband, or one contending against the gods and boasting because she thinks herself happy, or one caught in misfortunes, sorrows, and wailings. Much less will we allow them to imitate a woman who is ill, or in love, or in the pains of labor. Not at all, he replied. Nor should they imitate female or male slaves performing the duties of slaves. No, not that either. 

<margin>C</margin>Nor should they imitate bad men, it seems—those who are cowardly and do the opposite of what we have just described: men who revile and mock one another, using foul language, whether they are drunk or sober, or all the other ways such people sin against themselves and others in words and deeds. I also think they should not accustom themselves to making themselves like madmen in words or actions. For while they must recognize madmen and wicked people, both men and women, they must not perform or imitate any of their actions. Very true, he said. What then? I asked. Should they imitate blacksmiths <margin>D</margin> at their forges, or any other craftsmen, or those who row triremes <note>A trireme was an ancient warship with three banks of oars.</note>, or those who give them commands, or anything else related to these trades? How could they, he asked, when they are not even permitted to pay attention to any of these things? What about neighing horses, bellowing bulls, the roar of rivers, the crashing of the sea, thunder, and all such things? Will they imitate these? No, he said, for they are forbidden from being mad or making themselves like those who are mad. 

If I understand what you are saying, I replied, there is a certain style of speech and narration that the truly good and honorable man would use when he has something to say, and another style, quite unlike the first, which a man of the opposite nature and upbringing would always use. What kinds are these? he asked. It seems to me, I said, that the moderate man, when he comes to a passage in a narrative involving the words or actions of a good man, will be willing to report it as if he were that man himself; he will not be ashamed of such an imitation. He will especially imitate the good man acting firmly and wisely, but he will do so less often and to a lesser degree when the character is tripped up by disease, or love, or perhaps by drunkenness or some other misfortune. But when he comes across a character who is unworthy of him, he will be unwilling to seriously liken himself to his inferior, <margin>E</margin> except perhaps briefly when the character does something good. Instead, he will feel ashamed, both because he is unpracticed in imitating such types and because he finds it distasteful to mold and cast himself into the patterns of inferior men. In his mind, he despises this, unless it is done for the sake of a joke. 

Likely enough, he said. Therefore, will he not use the kind of narrative we described a little while ago regarding the verses of Homer? His speech will partake of both—of imitation and of simple narration—but there will be only a small portion of imitation in a long discourse. Am I right, or am I saying nothing? You are certainly right, he said; that is exactly the pattern such a speaker must follow. 

<margin>F</margin>On the other hand, I said, the man who is not of this character—the more inferior he is, the more he will narrate everything and think nothing is beneath him. He will attempt to imitate everything in earnest and in the sight of many: including those things we just mentioned, such as thunder, the noise of wind and hail, the sound of axles and pulleys, the calls of trumpets, flutes, pipes, and every kind of instrument; even the barking of dogs, the bleating of sheep, and the songs of birds. His entire style will consist of imitation in voice and gesture, with very little simple narration. That too is inevitable, he said. 

These then, I said, are the two types of speech. Indeed they are, he said. Now, does not one of these styles involve only small changes? And if one gives the speech an appropriate harmony and rhythm, does it not stay almost the same for the one speaking correctly, remaining within a single harmony? <margin>G</margin> For the changes are few, and the rhythm remains much the same. Entirely so, he said. But what about the other style? Does it not require the opposite—all harmonies and all rhythms—if it is to be spoken appropriately, because it contains so many varied forms of change? That is exactly how it is. 

Do not all poets and speakers hit upon one of these patterns of speech, or the other, or a mixture of both? They must, he said. What then shall we do? I asked. Shall we admit all of these into our city, or only one of the unmixed styles, or the mixed one? If my opinion prevails, he said, we should choose the unmixed imitator of the virtuous man. 

But surely, Adeimantus, the mixed style is also pleasing; and the style opposite to your choice is by far the most pleasing to children, their tutors, and the common crowd. It is indeed the most pleasing. But perhaps, I said, you would say it does not fit our republic, because with us, a man is not "double" or "multiple," since each person does only one job. No, it does not fit. Is it not for this reason that in such a city alone we will find the shoemaker to be a shoemaker and nothing else...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>...nor to imitate. But if they do imitate, they should imitate what is appropriate to them from above, right from childhood: the brave, the temperate, the pious, the free, and all such things. But they should neither do nor be clever at imitating illiberal things, nor anything else base, so that they do not reap the reality from the imitation. Or have you not noticed that imitations, if they continue from youth onward, settle into habits and nature, in body and voice and in the very mind? Most certainly, he said. 

We shall not then permit, I said, those for whom we claim to care, and who must become good men, to imitate a woman, being men themselves—whether she is young or older, or reviling a man, or striving and boasting against the gods, thinking herself a divine power, or <margin>B</margin> caught in misfortunes and griefs and lamentations. And as for her being sick, or in love, or in labor, we shall be far from allowing that. Entirely so, he said. 

Nor should they imitate female or male slaves performing the actions of slaves. No, not that either. Nor should they imitate bad men, as it seems—those who are cowardly and do the opposite of what we have just said: reviling and mocking one another, and using foul language, whether drunk or sober, or all the other ways such people sin in words and deeds against themselves and one another. I think they must not accustom themselves to likening themselves to madmen in words or deeds. For one must know madmen and wicked men and women, but one must do none of these things, nor imitate them. 

Most true, he said. What then? I said. Blacksmiths <margin>C</margin> or any others practicing a craft, or those rowing triremes, or those giving commands to them, or anything else of that sort—should they imitate these? And how could they, he said, since they are not even permitted to pay attention to any of these things? 

What then? Will they imitate neighing horses, or bellowing bulls, or sounding rivers, or the crashing sea, or thunder, and all such things? But it has been forbidden to them, he said, either to be mad or to make themselves like those who are mad. 

If then I understand what you are saying, there is a certain kind of speech and narration in which the truly "beautiful and good" man <note>original: *kalos kagathos* - the Greek ideal of a gentleman of perfect character.</note> would narrate whenever he had to say something; and there is another kind, unlike this one, which the man who is born and raised in the opposite way would always hold to and narrate in. 

<margin>D</margin> What kinds are these? he asked. It seems to me, I said, that the moderate man, when he comes in his narration to some speech or action of a good man, will be willing to report it as if he were that man himself, and will not be ashamed of such an imitation—especially when imitating the good man acting steadily and intelligently. But he will imitate less, and to a lesser degree, when the man is tripped up by diseases, or by loves, or even by drunkenness or some other misfortune. 

But when he comes to someone unworthy of himself, he will not be willing to seriously liken himself to his inferior, except perhaps for a brief moment when the man does something good. Instead, he will be ashamed, partly because he is unpracticed in imitating such people, and partly because he finds it difficult to mold and place himself into the types of worse men, <margin>E</margin> as he despises them in his mind, unless it is for the sake of play. 

It is likely, he said. Therefore, will he not use a narration such as we described a little while ago regarding the epic verses of Homer? And his speech will partake of both—of imitation and of the other kind of narration—but there will be only a small part of imitation in a long speech. Or am I saying nothing? You are saying quite a lot, he said; it must be the pattern for such a speaker. 

Will not the one who is not of this sort, I said, the more inferior he is, the more he will narrate everything, and think nothing is unworthy of himself? So he will attempt to imitate everything seriously and in front of many people—the very things we were just mentioning: thunders and the noises of winds <margin>F</margin> and hail, and of axles and pulleys, and of trumpets and flutes and pipes, and the sounds of all instruments, and even the cries of dogs and sheep and birds. And his speech will be entirely through imitation of voices and gestures, or will have only a tiny bit of narration. 

This too is necessary, he said. These then, I said, were the two kinds of speech I was talking about. And indeed they exist, he said. Now, does not one of them have few changes? And if one provides the proper harmony and rhythm to the speech, it becomes possible for the one speaking correctly to speak almost always in the same way and in a single harmony—for the changes are small—and likewise in a rhythm of a similar sort? 

<margin>G</margin> It is exactly so, he said. But what about the other kind? Does it not require the opposite—all harmonies and all rhythms—if it is to be spoken properly, because it has all kinds of forms of change? Very much so. 

Do not all poets and speakers hit upon one of these patterns of speech, or the other, or a mixture of both? They must, he said. What then shall we do? I asked. Shall we admit all of these into our city, or one of the unmixed kinds, or the mixed one? If my view wins, he said, we would admit the unmixed imitator of the decent man. 

But surely, Adeimantus, the mixed kind is pleasing; and by far the most pleasing to children and their tutors, and to the great mass of the crowd, is the opposite of the one you choose. Most pleasing indeed. But perhaps, I said, you would say it does not fit our regime, because there is no "double" or "multiple" man among us, since each person does one thing. It does not fit. Therefore, for these reasons, in such a city alone will we find the shoemaker to be a shoemaker,

<summary>Socrates argues that the city's guardians should only imitate virtuous men, as acting out bad or undignified roles can corrupt their character. He distinguishes between the "moderate" style of narration (minimal imitation of the good) and the "inferior" style (imitation of everything, including animals and noises), concluding that only the former fits a city based on specialization.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Glaucon regarding the censorship of the arts in the ideal city. The previous page discussed the dangers of "imitation" (acting out bad characters). Here, they move from the content of stories to the technical aspects of music—specifically, which musical modes, instruments, and rhythms are appropriate for training the souls of the "guardians" (the city's protectors).</meta>

# ON THE REPUBLIC, BOOK III.

<margin>A</margin> ...and not a pilot, in addition to shoemaking? And the farmer, a farmer only, and not a judge in addition to farming? And the soldier, a soldier only, and not a money-maker in addition to being a soldier? And everyone else in the same way? 
"That is true," he said.
"It seems, then, that if a man should arrive in our city who is so clever that he can transform himself into all shapes and imitate all things, and should want to show off himself and his poems, we would fall down and worship him as a holy, wonderful, and delightful being. But we would tell him that there is no such man in our city, nor is it permitted for such a person to exist here. We would send him away to another city, after pouring myrrh <note>A fragrant resin used as perfume or oil; here used as a gesture of high honor before an expulsion.</note> over his head and crowning him with wool. For ourselves, we shall make use of a more austere and less pleasing poet and storyteller for the sake of our benefit—one who would imitate the speech of a good man for us, and who would speak according to the models we established as laws from the beginning, when we first began to educate our soldiers."
<margin>B</margin> "We would certainly do that," he said, "if it were up to us."
"Now then, my friend," I said, "it seems that the part of music <note>In Ancient Greek, *mousikē* referred to all the arts of the Muses, including poetry and storytelling, not just instrumental sound.</note> involving speech and stories has been completely finished for us. For both what is to be said and how it is to be said have been discussed."
"I think so too," he said.
"Then after this," I said, "what remains is the matter of the style of song and melody."
"Clearly."
"Could not everyone already find what we ought to say about these things—what they must be like—if we are to stay in harmony with what has already been said?"
And Glaucon, laughing, said, "I, Socrates, seem to be left out of this 'everyone.' I cannot sufficiently grasp at this moment what sorts of things we ought to say, though I have my suspicions."
<margin>C</margin> "Surely," I said, "you can at least say this much: that a melody is composed of three things: the words, the harmony, and the rhythm." <note>original: "λόγου τε, καὶ ἁρμονίας, καὶ ῥυθμοῦ"</note>
"Yes," he said, "that much I can say."
"And as for the words, do they differ at all from words that are not set to music? Must they not be spoken according to the same models and in the same manner we just described?"
"That is true," he said.
"And indeed, the harmony and the rhythm must follow the words."
"Of course."
"But we said that we have no need of dirges and lamentations in our words."
"We do not."
"Which, then, are the mournful harmonies? <note>A "harmony" or "mode" (harmonia) in this context refers to a specific musical scale or tuning associated with certain emotional states.</note> Tell me, for you are a musician."
"The Mixed Lydian," he said, "and the 'Tight' Lydian, and others like them."
<margin>D</margin> "Should these not be removed then?" I asked. "For they are useless even for women who are to be decent, let alone for men."
"Certainly."
"Furthermore, drunkenness, softness, and idleness are most unbecoming for our guardians."
"How could they not be?"
"Which harmonies, then, are soft and fit for a drinking party?"
"The Ionian," he said, "and the Lydian—those that are called 'relaxed'."
"Then, my friend, could you use these for men who are warriors?"
"In no way," he said. "It seems you have only the Dorian and the Phrygian left."
"I do not know all the harmonies," I said, "but leave me the harmony that would fittingly imitate the tones and accents of a brave man in a state of war or any violent work; one who, if he fails, or meets wounds or death, or falls into any other misfortune, <margin>E</margin> fights against his fate with endurance and sobriety. And leave another harmony for a man engaged in a peaceful, non-violent, voluntary action—perhaps persuading someone or making a request, or praying to a god, or instructing and admonishing a man; or, on the other hand, a man who is listening to the requests or instructions or persuasion of another, and who, having succeeded in his goal, is not overbearing, but acts with temperance and moderation in all things and is content with the outcome. These two harmonies—the violent and the voluntary—which best imitate the tones of the unfortunate and the fortunate, the temperate and the brave—leave these!"
"But," he said, "you are asking for exactly the ones I just mentioned."
"Then," <margin>F</margin> I said, "we shall have no need of many-stringed instruments or 'pan-harmonic' instruments <note>Instruments capable of playing many different scales or complex, multi-tonal music, which Plato viewed as chaotic and corrupting.</note> in our songs and melodies."
"It seems not," he said.
"Then we shall not maintain makers of triangles, harps, or any instruments that have many strings and many harmonies?"
"We shall not, it seems."
"What then? Will you admit flute-makers or flute-players <term>aulos: a double-reed wind instrument, often translated as flute but more similar to an oboe or clarinet; it was associated with wild, Dionysian emotion.</term> into the city? Or is this not the most 'many-toned' of all? Even the pan-harmonic instruments are just imitations of the flute."
"Clearly," he said.
"There remain for you," I said, <margin>G</margin> "the lyre and the cithara <note>Stringed instruments associated with Apollo, the god of order and reason.</note> for use in the city; and for the shepherds in the fields, there might be some kind of pipe." <note>original: "σύριγξ" (syrinx/pan-pipes)</note>
"So the argument indicates," he said.
"We are doing nothing strange, my friend," I said, "in preferring Apollo and Apollo's instruments to Marsyas and his instruments." <note>Marsyas was a satyr who challenged Apollo to a musical contest using the flute/aulos; Apollo won and flayed Marsyas alive. This is a metaphor for choosing orderly music over ecstatic or "low" music.</note>
"By Zeus," he said, "I think not!"
"And by the dog!" I said. "We have been purging the city—the one we recently said was living in luxury—without even realizing it."
"And we are being wise to do so," he said.
"Come then," I said, "let us purge the rest. For following the harmonies, we must deal with rhythms. We should not pursue complex rhythms or all varieties of beats, but rather see which rhythms belong to a life that is orderly and brave. Having seen these, we must force the 'foot' <note>The metrical unit of rhythm.</note> and the melody to follow the words of such a life, not the words to follow the foot and melody. What these rhythms are is your job to say, just as you did with the harmonies."
"But by Zeus," he <margin>H</margin> said, "I cannot say. I can tell you from observation that there are three kinds of feet from which all the rhythms are woven—just as there are four notes from which all the harmonies are made—but which rhythms are imitations of which kind of life, I cannot say."
"Well," I said, "we shall consult with Damon <note>A famous 5th-century BCE music theorist and advisor to Pericles.</note> on this—which rhythms are suited to meanness and insolence, or madness and other vices..."

At this point we shall deliberate with Damon, as to which

<margin>A</margin> And not a pilot besides? And the farmer only a farmer, not also a judge; the soldier only a soldier, not also a money-changer? And the others in the same way? These things are true.
If, therefore, anyone should come into our city who, by the wisdom of his mind, is able to turn himself into all forms and imitate everything, and wishes to show off his poems, we would indeed worship him as something sacred, admirable, and pleasant. But we would say that there is no such man in our republic, nor is it right for him to be here. We would send him to another city, pouring ointment on his head and crowning him with wool. But we shall use a more austere and less pleasant <margin>B</margin> poet and storyteller for the sake of utility, who may express speech in a fitting way for us and say what is said in those formulas which we established as laws from the beginning, when we undertook to educate the soldiers. The same seems true to me as well.

Certainly.

"Which, then, are the soft and convivial harmonies?"
"The Ionian and Lydian, whichever are called 'loose' and 'remiss'."
"Will you then, my friend, use these in any way for the utility of soldiers?"
"In no way. But it seems to you that the remaining ones are the Dorian and Phrygian harmonies."
"I do not indeed know the harmonies," I said, "but leave that harmony which, as is fitting, imitates the voices and accents of one bravely going into battle and behaving manfully in any violent business—one who is in danger, whether rushing into wounds or death or falling into any other calamity, and in all those things constantly and manfully pushing back fortune. <margin>E</margin> And leave again another harmony, which imitates the voices and accents of a man engaged in a tranquil and non-violent but voluntary action: persuading someone of something, or entreating, or in prayers to God, or in the instruction and admonition of a man; or on the contrary, one who shows himself yielding to another who entreats or teaches or dissuades him; and who, although he has obtained his wish, is not puffed up with pride, but behaves temperately and modestly in all these things and rightly bears every fortune. Leave all these harmonies—these two that follow: the violent and the voluntary; the unfortunate and the fortunate; the temperate and the brave—and whichever most beautifully imitates their accents."
"But," <margin>F</margin> he said, "you do not command any others to be chosen than those I mentioned above."
"Now then, shall we have need in songs and melodies of a harmony that consists of many strings and all sorts of concerts?"
"Not as it seems to me."
"Therefore, we shall not nourish the makers of Triangles, Pectides <note>Types of ancient harps.</note>, and all instruments that consist of many strings and many consonances."
"It seems not."
"But what? Will you leave the makers of pipes and pipe-players in the city? Do not instruments of many strings and all harmonies imitate the pipe?"
"It is clear," he said.
"The lyre, therefore, remains, <margin>G</margin> and the cithara is useful in the city; and the pipe is convenient for shepherds in the fields."
"So the argument shows us."
"We are introducing nothing foreign, my friend, while we prefer Apollo and Apollo's instruments to Marsyas himself and his organs."
"By Jove, so it seems to me."
"By the Dog! For we have secretly begun to purge the city which we previously said was given over to excessive delights."
"And indeed, wisely."
"Come, let us purge the rest. It follows from those things said about harmonies that we should so pursue rhythms that we do not wander through too many variations, nor through just any movements, but discern what are the rhythms of a brave and temperate life. Which having been known, let us compel the foot and the song to follow such speech, not the speech to follow the foot and the song. But what such rhythms are, it is your part to declare, just as you explained the harmonies."
"By Jove," he said, "what I should say, <margin>H</margin> I do not have. For that there are three certain species from which these movements are woven—just as in voices there are four from which all harmonies are composed—I have observed and could say. But what kind are imitations of what kind of life, I am unable to open up."
"...foot movements are suited to illiberalness, petulance, madness..."

They also restrict musical instruments to the simple lyre and cithara, rejecting the flute and multi-stringed harps to ensure the citizens' souls remain disciplined.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Glaucon in Book III of Plato’s Republic. Having discussed the appropriate musical scales, they now move on to the morality of rhythms and the pervasive influence of the arts—including painting and architecture—on the souls of the young guardians. The Latin text is a Renaissance-era translation (likely by Marsilio Ficino), while the Greek is the original source text.</meta>

# OF PLATO

<margin>A</margin> ...and from other vices, and which rhythms agree with their opposites. However, I think I have heard, though not clearly enough, when he himself named a certain warlike, composite "dactyl" and a "heroic" rhythm; <note>The dactyl (long-short-short) was the standard meter of epic poetry like the Iliad.</note> I do not know quite how he arranged it, making it equal both up and down, turning it into short and long, and as I recall, he called another an "iamb" and another a "trochee." He also applied various lengths and brevities. In some of these, I believe he criticized or praised the movements of the foot no less than the rhythms themselves, or perhaps something composed of both. For I cannot explain these things clearly enough. But let these matters, as I was saying, be referred to Damon himself; for to distinguish them would require a lengthy discourse. Or do you think otherwise? "By Jove," he said, "it would be lengthy indeed." But this <margin>B</margin> you can discern: that elegance and unfitness follow the suitability and unsuitability of the rhythm. "How could they not?" But surely suitable rhythm follows beautiful speech and imitates it, as if it were similar; while unsuitable rhythm follows the opposite. Furthermore, harmony and dissonance act in the same way, since rhythm and harmony, as was said a little while ago, follow the speech, and the speech does not follow the rhythm and harmony. "Certainly," he said, "these things must follow the speech." But what of the style of speaking and the speech itself? Does it not follow the disposition of the soul? "Without a doubt." And do the other things follow the speech? "Of course." Therefore, grace of language, harmony, beauty, and <margin>C</margin> rhythmic suitability follow a moderated disposition of the soul, which they call <term>ἐυήθειαν</term> <note>original: "euetheian," literally "good-heartedness" or "simplicity." In Greek, it often meant "foolishness," but Socrates is reclaiming it here to mean a truly good and beautiful character.</note>. I do not mean the "good-heartedness" that we often use as a flattering term for a kind of ignorance; rather, I mean that "good-heartedness" in which the mind is truly provided with the best morals. "Exactly so," he said. Must not the young pursue these things everywhere, then, if they wish to do their own work? "They certainly must." For the whole art of painting is full of these things, and every such craftsmanship; the skill of weaving is full of it, as are embroidery, architecture, and the production of all other furniture and instruments; and even the nature of bodies and plants. Furthermore, in all these things there is either a certain <margin>D</margin> decency or indecency. And indeed, indecency, unsuitable rhythm, and dissonance are sisters to foul speech and wicked character; whereas their opposites are kindred and imitations of the opposite: a temperate and good character. "It is as you say." Is it only the poets we must urge and compel to express the image of good character in their poems, or else not write among us? Or shall we also prescribe to other craftsmen and forbid them from making any image of bad character—anything undisciplined, illiberal, or indecent—whether in the figures of animals, in buildings, or in any other craft? Or if someone cannot perform this, must he be prohibited from working among us, lest our guardians, nurtured on images of depravity as if on noxious grass, and daily <margin>E</margin> plucking and grazing on many things little by little, unknowingly contract one great evil in their souls? For this reason, those craftsmen must be sought out who, by a certain natural industry, can track down the nature of the beautiful and the graceful, so that the young, living as if in a healthy place, may be helped from every side; whenever something honorable reaches their eyes or ears from beautiful and honest works, like a breeze bringing health from healthy places—a breeze which, beginning to blow from their earliest years, gradually brings their minds into a likeness, friendship, and <margin>F</margin> harmony with honorable speech and reason. "They would be nurtured most excellently in that way," he said. "For this reason, then," I said, "O Glaucon, rhythm and harmony sink into the innermost parts of the soul through education in music; they strike the soul most vehemently, bringing a certain graceful form, through which a person becomes graceful and beautiful if he is rightly educated in music; but the contrary if he is educated otherwise. And because he would most sharply perceive whatever is neglected, not rightly crafted, or not well-born, he who has been nurtured there as he ought will rightly be pained by these things; he will praise beautiful things, and loving them and greedily seizing them, he will be nourished by them and become good and beautiful himself. But foul things he will rightly criticize <margin>G</margin> and hate, even at an age before he has received the power of reason. Finally, when reason arrives, he who has been thus nurtured will welcome it gladly, recognizing it through its familiarity and kinship." "It seems to me also," he said, "that nourishment in music is for the sake of these things." Just as we are sufficiently skilled in letters when the elements do not escape us, which are few and found in all things; and we do not despise them in small things or great, as if it were not necessary to understand them, but we strive to know them everywhere, since we will not be grammarians until we have prepared ourselves in this way. "You speak the truth." Furthermore, the images of letters, if they appear anywhere in water or in mirrors, we will not know until we know the letters themselves. For this is a matter of the same art and practice. "Entirely so." Is it then (by the gods) as I say? We shall not be musical—neither we nor those guardians we are educating for the city—until we know the forms of temperance, fortitude, liberality, and magnificence, and whatever are sisters to these, and their opposites, wherever they are found; so that we may perceive them and their images in whatever things they exist, and not despise them in small or great things, but think them to be a matter of the same art and study? "It is entirely necessary," he said.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...or what rhythms we must stop with that correspond to their opposites. But I think I have heard him naming, though not clearly, a certain "enoplion" <note>original: "ἐνόπλιόν," a warlike rhythm often used in armor-dances.</note> as a composite rhythm, and a dactyl, and a heroic one—I do not know how he arranged them, making the "up" and "down" equal, resulting in both short and long; and, as I recall, he named an iamb and another called a trochee, and assigned lengths and brevities to them. And in some of these, I think he blamed or praised the movements of the foot no less than the rhythms themselves, or some combination of both. For I cannot say for certain. But these matters, as we said, let us refer to Damon. For to distinguish them is no small task. Or do you think so? "By Zeus, not I!" But this at least <margin>B</margin> you can distinguish: that grace and ungracefulness follow good rhythm and bad rhythm? "How could I not?" But surely good and bad rhythm follow the style of speech—the one following the beautiful style, the other its opposite; and the same for good and bad harmony, if rhythm and harmony follow the words, as was just said, and not the words following them. "But indeed," he said, "these must follow the words." And what of the manner of speech and the words? Do they not follow the character of the soul? "How could they not?" and do the other things follow the speech? "Yes." Good speech, then, and good harmony, and grace, and good rhythm, follow "good-heartedness" (<term>ἐυήθειαν</term>). Not that "good-heartedness" which is a euphemism for folly, but that <margin>C</margin> mind which is truly and beautifully prepared in its character. "Entirely so," he said. "Must these things not be pursued everywhere by the young, if they are to do their own business?" "They must." And painting is full of them, as is every such craft; weaving is full of it, and embroidery, and architecture, and the making of all other vessels; and further, the nature of bodies and other plants. For in all these things there is grace or ungracefulness. And ungracefulness, bad rhythm, and bad harmony are sisters of bad speech and bad character; while their opposites are sisters and imitations of the opposite: the temperate and good character. "Certainly," he said. "Is it then only the poets we must supervise, compelling them to impress the image of the good character in their poems, or else not to write among us? Or must we also <margin>D</margin> supervise the other craftsmen and prevent this bad character—this undisciplined, illiberal, and ungraceful quality—from being impressed in the images of living things, or in buildings, or in any other manufactured thing? Or he who is not able to do this, shall we not allow him to craft among us? We must prevent this so that our guardians, being reared among images of vice as if in a bad pasture, grazing and plucking many things every day from many sources, do not unknowingly gather one great evil in their own souls. Rather, we must seek those craftsmen who are naturally gifted to track down the nature of the beautiful and the graceful, so that the young, dwelling as if in a healthy place, may be benefited by everything, wherever anything from beautiful works strikes their sight or hearing, like a breeze carrying health from good places, leading them straight from childhood, without their knowing it, into a likeness, friendship, and harmony with beautiful reason." "In this way," he said, "they would be most beautifully reared." "Is it not then for these reasons, Glaucon," I said, "that the most important part of education is in music, because rhythm and harmony sink most deeply into the interior of the soul and take hold of it most strongly, bringing gracefulness and making one graceful, if he is rightly reared; but if not, the opposite? And because he would most sharply perceive whatever is left out and not beautifully crafted, or not beautifully grown, he who has been reared there as he should would rightly feel disgust; he would praise beautiful things, and rejoicing and <margin>F</margin> welcoming them into his soul, he would be nourished by them and become both beautiful and good. But foul things he would rightly blame and hate while still young, before he is able to grasp reason. And when reason comes, he who has been so reared would welcome it, recognizing it most of all through its kinship." "It seems to me, at least," he said, "that education in music is for the sake of such things." Just as with letters, we are only sufficiently skilled when the elements do not escape us, being few in all the things they are carried around in; and we do not dishonor them in small or great things, as if it were not necessary to perceive them, but we are eager to distinguish them everywhere, knowing we shall not be grammarians until we have them so. "True." And therefore images of letters, if they should appear anywhere, <margin>G</margin> in water or in mirrors, we will not know them before we know the letters themselves? But it is a matter of the same art and study? "Entirely so." "Then, by the gods, is it as I say? We shall not be musical—neither we ourselves nor those guardians we say must be educated—until we recognize the forms of temperance, courage, liberality, magnificence, and whatever are sisters to these, and their opposites, carried around everywhere, and perceive them in the things in which they exist, both themselves and their images, and do not dishonor them in small or great things, but believe them to be a matter of the same art and study?" "There is great necessity," he said.

<summary>Socrates argues that because the soul absorbs the qualities of its environment, all arts and crafts in the ideal city—not just poetry—must be strictly regulated to reflect only beauty and virtuous character. Music is highlighted as the most potent educational tool because rhythm and harmony penetrate the soul directly, preparing it to recognize and love reason even before a child is old enough to understand it logically.</summary>
