<meta>This page continues the dialogue from Book III of Plato's Republic, where Socrates and Glaucon discuss the ideal education for the guardians of the state. Having established the proper musical modes and rhythms to shape the soul, they now address how music leads to the love of beauty and how physical training (gymnastics) must follow to care for the body.</meta>

### ON THE REPUBLIC, BOOK III.

"Therefore," I said, "to the one who is able to see, would it not be the most beautiful sight when someone happens to have beautiful character within their soul, and their physical form agrees and harmonizes with that character, both sharing the same pattern?" "Very much so," he replied. "And surely what is most beautiful is most lovable?" "How could it not be?" "The musical man, then, would love people who are like this to the greatest degree; but if someone were unharmonious, he would not love them." "Not if there were some defect in the soul," he said; "however, if it were some defect in the body, he might bear with it, so as to be willing to welcome them." "I understand," I said, "that you have or have had such a beloved <note>original: 'paidika'—referring to the Greek custom of mentorship and affection between an older man and a youth</note>, and I agree. But tell me this: is there any fellowship between self-control and excessive pleasure?" "How can there be," he asked, "since such pleasure unsettles the mind no less than grief does?" "But what about other virtues?" "None at all." "What then? Does it have fellowship with insolence and lack of restraint?" "Most of all." "Can you name a greater or sharper pleasure than that regarding sexual matters?" "I cannot," he replied, "nor can I name one more frenzied." "But is 'Right Love' <note>term: 'orthos eros'—a philosophical love focused on the intellectual and moral beauty of the beloved rather than physical gratification</note> by its nature a temperate and musical love of what is orderly and beautiful?" "Indeed it is," he said. "Therefore, nothing frenzied or related to lack of restraint should be brought near to right love?" "It should not." "And so, this pleasure must not be joined to it, nor should the lover and his beloved share in it if they love and are loved rightly." "By Jove, Socrates," he said, "it certainly must not be brought near." "Thus, it seems, you will legislate in the city we are founding that a lover may kiss and be with and touch his beloved as a son, for the sake of beauty, if he persuades him; but otherwise, his association with the one he cares for should be such that they are never thought to go further than this. If he acts otherwise, he shall undergo the reproach of being unmusical and lacking in taste." "So it shall be," he said. "Does it then seem to you, as it does to me, that our discourse on music has reached its end? For it has finished where it ought to finish: for music ought to end in the love of the beautiful." "I agree," he said. "After music, the young men must be trained in gymnastics." "Of course." "They must be carefully trained in this from childhood throughout their lives. The matter stands somewhat like this, I believe—and you should consider it as well. To me, it does not seem that a good body, by its own virtue, makes the soul good; but on the contrary, that a good soul, by its own virtue, renders the body as excellent as possible. How does it seem to you?" "To me also, it seems so." "Therefore, if we have sufficiently cultivated the mind and then hand over to it the detailed care of the body—providing only the general outlines so as not to be long-winded—would we be doing right?" "Entirely." "We said they must abstain from drunkenness. For it is more permissible for anyone else to be drunk than for a guardian, who, being weighed down by wine, would not know where on earth he is." "It would be ridiculous," he said, "for a guardian to need a guardian." "And what about food? For these men are athletes in the greatest of contests. Is that not so?" "Yes." "Would the habit of these professional athletes <note>Socrates compares the guardians to professional sports competitors, who were known for strict but often sluggish lifestyles</note> be suitable for them?" "Perhaps." "But," I said, "this habit is a sleepy one and precarious for health. Do you not see that they sleep their lives away, and if they depart even a little from their prescribed diet, these athletes become greatly and severely ill?" "I see that." "A more sophisticated training is needed for our military athletes," I said, "who must be like wakeful dogs, seeing and hearing as sharply as possible, and who, in their campaigns, must endure many changes of water and food, of sun and winter, so that they are not easily susceptible to illness." "So it seems to me." "Would not the best gymnastics be a sister to the simple music we described a moment ago?" "How do you mean?" "A simple and decent gymnastics, especially that of the soldiers." "In what way?" "One might learn such things even from Homer," I said. "For you know that in the campaigns, at the feasts of the heroes, he does not feast them on fish—even though they were by the sea at the Hellespont—nor on boiled meats, but only on roasted ones, which would be most accessible for soldiers. For everywhere, so to speak, it is easier to use fire itself than to carry around cooking vessels." "Very much so." <margin>Iliad. c.</margin> "Nor does Homer ever mention seasonings, as I recall. Even other athletes know this: that anyone who intends to have a body in good condition must abstain from all such things." "And they are right to know it and abstain," he said. "Then, my friend, it seems you do not praise a Syracusan table <note>Syracuse was legendary for its luxurious and decadent cuisine</note> and the Sicilian variety of side-dishes, if these things seem right to you." "I do not think I do." "Then you also disapprove of a Corinthian girl <note>gloss: a reference to the famous high-class prostitutes of Corinth</note> being a friend to men who intend to be in good physical condition." "By all means." "And also the Attic sweets that are thought to be so delightful?" "Necessarily." "For I think we would be right to compare this entire way of eating and living to the kind of melody and song composed in every harmony and in all rhythms." "How could we not?" "In the former case, variety produced lack of restraint; here, it produces disease. But simplicity in music produces temperance in the soul, and in gymnastics, it produces health in the body." "Most true," he said. "And when lack of restraint and diseases multiply in a city, are not many law courts and clinics opened? And then legal and medical arts begin to give themselves airs, especially when many free men...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Therefore, if in some man these things concur, so that in his soul beautiful habits reside, and in the physical appearance of his body each part corresponds and harmonizes with them, taking on the same form, this will be the most beautiful spectacle for the one who is able to observe it. Truly. And what is most beautiful is also most lovable. Certainly. A musical man would especially love such people; but if he perceived something dissonant, he would not. Not certainly if something were lacking in the soul; but if something were merely lacking in the body, he would endure it, even to the point of being willing to love and embrace them. <margin>B</margin> I understand indeed, because such people are either loved by you or have already been loved, and I agree. But tell me this. Is there any commerce between temperance and loose or excessive pleasure? In what way? Since pleasure of this sort moves the mind from its state no less than grief does. But with other virtues? Not at all. What then? Do insolence and lack of restraint (have communion with excessive pleasure?) Most of all. Have you any greater or more vehement pleasure than that which concerns sexual matters? I have no other more vehement, nor more frenzied. But right love is by its own nature temperately and musically in love with the beautiful and the decorous. Entirely. Therefore, nothing frenzied or belonging to lack of restraint is to be brought near to right love. Certainly not. Therefore, pleasure is not to be joined to it, nor should lovers share in it with the youths they legitimately love, nor should those who love and those who are loved. By Jove, in no way, O Socrates. <margin>C</margin> Thus then, as it seems, in the established city you will make a law that a lover may love, be with, and touch the beloved—if he persuades him—just as a son, for the sake of honorable things, and in all matters so conduct himself with the one he loves that he never allows it to be seen that he spent more time with him than this. Otherwise, let him undergo ignominy, as one who knows nothing at all of music or beauty. Thus indeed. Does it not seem to you that the discourse on music has now reached its goal? For where it ought to end, there it has now arrived. <margin>D</margin> For it is necessary that music end in the love of the beautiful. I agree indeed. After music, however, the young men are to be exercised in gymnastics. Why not? For it is necessary to be carefully educated in this also throughout the whole of life from childhood. This matter stands in this way, I think. Consider it yourself. To me indeed, it does not seem that a well-affected body, by its own power, makes a good soul, but on the contrary, a well-affected soul, by its own power, renders the body as good as possible. But what does it seem to you? The same as to you. If, after we have sufficiently cultivated the mind, we hand over to it the care of the things pertaining to the body, to inquire and care for them diligently and exactly—while we propose only certain general formulas, lest we be too long—shall we be doing right? Altogether. <margin>E</margin> We said, therefore, that they must abstain from drunkenness. For it is granted to anyone rather than a guardian that, being heavy with drunkenness, he should not know where on earth he is. Indeed, it would be ridiculous for a guardian to need a guardian. But what shall we say about foods? For these men are athletes, and indeed of the greatest contest. Is it not so? Most clearly. Would the habit of other athletes be suitable for them? Perhaps. But this is a sleepy habit, and doubtful for health. Or do you not see that they sleep through life? And if they depart even a little from their prescribed diet, these trainers become gravely ill. I see it indeed. Therefore, there is need of some more elegant exercise for warlike athletes, <margin>F</margin> whom it behooves to be like sleepless dogs, and to see and hear as sharply as possible, and to endure many changes of water and other foods, of heat and cold in the army, so that they do not easily fall into diseases. So it seems to me. Therefore, the best gymnastics would be a sister of the simple music about which we treated a little while ago. How so? A simple and suitable gymnastics, and especially the exercise of soldiers. In what way? <margin>Iliad. c.</margin> From Homer indeed we can say this. For you know how in the expeditions of war, in the feasts of the heroes, he does not prepare fish for them, although they were by the Hellespont sea, nor boiled meats, but roasted ones, which are more easily prepared by soldiers. For everywhere it is easier, to put it briefly, to use fire itself than to carry vessels around. Surely. <margin>G</margin> Nor does Homer ever mention various seasonings, as I believe. But this both others know and those who are exercised: that the one who must have a robust body must abstain from all such things. They know it rightly indeed, and they abstain. Therefore, O friend, you do not praise Syracusan tables and the variety of Sicilian dishes, as it seems; if indeed these things seem to you to be right. Not certainly, as it seems to me. You also censure the Corinthian luxury of flattering girls for those who are to be in the best physical condition. Entirely. Furthermore, the Attic sweets and seasonings, which seem pleasant and delicate to many. It is necessary. For I think that we would rightly compare all such food, if we said it was similar to the melody and song which are involved in every kind of harmony and all rhythms. Clearly. There indeed, variety produces lack of restraint; here, disease. But simplicity according to music produces temperance in souls, and according to gymnastics, health in bodies. You speak most truly. But when lack of restraint and diseases have multiplied in a city, both the courts and the doctors' shops are opened. Then the judiciary and medicine are held in high esteem, when even many free men...

<summary>Socrates and Glaucon conclude that musical education should lead to a love of beauty and be followed by a simple physical regimen. They argue that a healthy soul creates a healthy body and that guardians must avoid the decadent diets and lifestyles that lead to a reliance on doctors and lawyers.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Socrates' discourse with Glaucon regarding the physical education of the guardians. Having previously discussed music and the soul, they now critique the reliance on medicine and law as symptoms of a declining society where individuals lack self-discipline and purpose.</meta>

# PLATO'S [REPUBLIC]

<margin>A</margin> ...should they not strive for these things with the utmost effort? Why not? Therefore, you can take no greater sign of a poor and shameful education in a city than its need for supreme judges and physicians—not only for common people and laborers, but even for those who boast of having been raised in the liberal arts. Does it not seem shameful, and a great sign of a lack of training, to be forced to use the justice of others as if they were our masters and judges, because of our own lack of inner virtue? It is surely the most shameful of all things. Or do you not think this is even more shameful: when someone not only wastes a great portion of their life in courts, either accusing or defending, but is also carried away by a crude sort of boasting, glorying in the very fact <margin>B</margin> that they are powerful enough to inflict injury, and that they are so cunning in their evasions and tricks that they can find every loophole to escape punishment—and all for the sake of small and worthless things? They are ignorant of how much more noble and better it would be to arrange one's life so as not to require a sleepy judge. Certainly, this is even more shameful than the former. Furthermore, we must consider it absurd that men require doctors, not just for healing wounds or curing diseases that strike seasonally due to the weather, but because of laziness and that luxury in diet which we condemned <margin>C</margin> above. Like pools of stagnant water, they have filled themselves with fluids and vapors, forcing the noble successors of Asclepius <note>Asclepius was the Greek god of medicine; his "successors" are physicians.</note> to invent new names for diseases, calling them "flatulence" and "catarrhs." These are truly new names for diseases, he said, and quite absurd. I believe, I said, these did not exist in the time of Asclepius. I infer this because his sons at Troy did not find fault with the woman who offered a cup to the wounded Eurypylus at Patroclus's command, <margin>D</margin> even though it contained Pramnian wine mixed with flour and grated cheese—things which increase phlegm. <note>original: 'pituitam' / 'φλεγματώδη'—referring to the ancient theory of the Four Humors, where phlegm was associated with sluggishness and illness.</note> That cup was certainly absurd and hardly suitable for someone in that condition. No. Because if you notice, I said, the followers of Asclepius did not use this modern medical practice of "nursing" diseases before the time of Herodicus, as they say. Herodicus, being a trainer of youth and himself of sickly health, mixed gymnastics with medicine; he first wore himself out, and then many who came after him. In what way? By providing himself with a long death. For while he followed the course of his fatal disease, he could not, I think, cure himself; yet he was so occupied with his medical studies that, neglecting everything else, he wasted his life indulging his body. He suffered greatly if he departed even slightly from his accustomed diet, yet by this "wisdom" of his, he reached old age, dying with great difficulty. He won a remarkable <margin>E</margin> prize for his art, he said. Indeed, I said, it was the prize he deserved for not knowing that it was not through ignorance or lack of experience that Asclepius did not reveal this form of medicine to his descendants. Rather, he saw that in a well-governed city, a specific task is assigned to everyone which they must complete, and no one has the leisure to spend their whole life being a "professional patient" occupied with curing their body. This we notice, in a somewhat ridiculous way, among craftsmen, but we do not see it at all among those who are considered wealthy and happy. How is that? If a carpenter <margin>F</margin> falls ill, he demands from the doctor a quick remedy—either by vomiting, a purging of the bowels, or by cautery or the knife. But if someone prescribes a long regimen of diet, or wrapping the head in cloths and such things, he immediately says he has no leisure to be sick, and it is of no use to him to drag out his life by attending to constant treatments while neglecting his work. Then, bidding the doctor farewell, he returns to his usual way of life; if he recovers, he carries out his business, but if his body cannot endure the disease, he dies and is freed from his troubles. Thus, it seems fitting for a craftsman to use medicine in that way. And I said that his work was set before him because <margin>G</margin> if he does not perform it, it is not profitable for him to live. That is clear. But the rich man, as we said, has no such work set before him, which if he were forced to abstain from, life would no longer be worth living. None at all, as they say. Perhaps you have not heard Phocylides saying: "One ought to practice virtue as long as the means of living are supplied." <note>Phocylides was a 6th-century BC Greek gnomic poet famous for his maxims on ethics and practical living.</note> I think even before that, he said. Let us not argue with him about this, but let us teach ourselves whether a rich man ought to meditate on this, or if life is not worth living if he does not spend his time nursing diseases. For such care is an obstacle to the craft of the carpenter and other arts. It turns the mind away from work. But the precept of Phocylides is no obstacle. By Jove, he said, this excessive care of the body, which goes beyond simple gymnastics, is almost the greatest obstacle of all. For it is most troublesome to household management, military service, and all civil offices in the city. <margin>H</margin> What is greatest, however, is that it hinders the desire for learning and every diligence of understanding and meditation; for one is always suspecting headaches and dizziness, and blaming the study of philosophy as if these things were born from it. Therefore, it is entirely an obstacle to the exercise and testing of virtue. For it makes us think we are always sick, and we never cease complaining about the state of our body. That is likely. Seeing these things, I believe Asclepius showed medicine to those who were healthy by nature and upbringing, but who were suffering from some external and sudden disease; to these, he showed the way of medicine through drugs...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...should they not strive for these things? Why not? And regarding poor and shameful education in a city, could you find any greater evidence than the need for eminent doctors and judges, not only for the common folk and laborers, but even for those who pretend to have been brought up in a liberal fashion? Or does it not seem shameful, a great sign of a lack of culture, to be forced to use a justice imported from others as masters and judges, because of a lack of one's own? This is the most shameful thing of all, he said. Or does this seem even more shameful to you, I asked: when someone not only consumes much of his life in courtrooms, being the defendant or the prosecutor, but even, out of a lack of good taste, <margin>B</margin> is persuaded to pride himself on this very thing—as if he were clever at doing wrong and capable of twisting through all sorts of turns and escaping through every exit to avoid punishment? And all this for the sake of small and worthless things, being ignorant of how much more beautiful and better it is to arrange his life so as to never need a nodding judge. No, he said, that is even more shameful than the other. And as for needing medicine, I said, not for wounds or some seasonal diseases that strike, but because of idleness and the kind of diet we described, filling ourselves <margin>C</margin> like marshes with currents and vapors, and forcing the clever sons of Asclepius to give diseases names like "blows" and "catarrhs"—does that not seem shameful? It does indeed, I said, for these are truly strange and new names for diseases. Such things, I said, did not exist in the time of Asclepius, as I judge. I infer this because his sons at Troy did not blame the woman who gave the wounded Eurypylus a drink of Pramnian wine with much barley-meal and grated cheese sprinkled on it (which are thought to be phlegm-inducing) nor did they rebuke Patroclus who was treating him. And yet, he said, that drink is certainly strange for someone in such a state. Not if <margin>D</margin> you consider, I said, that the sons of Asclepius did not use this modern medical "nursing" of diseases, as they say, before the time of Herodicus. Herodicus, being a trainer of boys and becoming sickly himself, mixed gymnastics with medicine and wore out first and foremost himself, and then many others later. In what way? he asked. By making his death a long one, I said. For by following his disease, which was fatal, he was, I think, unable to cure himself, and being occupied with medical treatment to the exclusion of all else, he lived his life worn away, should he ever step out of his accustomed diet. Dying a hard death through his "wisdom," he reached old age. He certainly won a fine <margin>E</margin> prize for his art, he said. Just as one might expect, I said, from one who did not know that it was not through ignorance or inexperience with this form of medicine that Asclepius did not reveal it to his descendants. Rather, he knew that for all people in a well-governed city, a specific task is assigned to each, which they must perform; and no one has the leisure to be sick and under treatment throughout their life. We see this ridiculously in the case of a craftsman, though we do not notice it in those who are thought to be wealthy and happy. How so? he asked. When a carpenter <margin>F</margin> is ill, I said, he expects the doctor to give him a potion to vomit up the disease, or to be purged below, or to use cautery or the knife to be rid of it. But if someone prescribes him a long diet, putting little felt caps on his head and things following from that, he quickly says he has no leisure to be sick, nor is it profitable to live such a life, paying attention to a disease while neglecting his established work. And after that, bidding such a doctor farewell, he returns to his <margin>G</margin> usual diet, and becoming healthy, he lives doing his own business. But if his body is not capable of enduring it, he dies and is freed from his troubles. And for such a man, he said, it seems fitting to use medicine in this way. Is it not, I said, because he had a work which, if he did not do it, it was not profitable for him to live? Clearly, he said. But the rich man, as we say, has no such work set before him, which if he is forced to abstain from, life is not worth living. So it is not said. For you do not hear how Phocylides says one must, when one already has a livelihood, practice virtue. I think, he said, even before that. Let us not fight with him about this, I said; but let us teach ourselves whether the rich man must study this, and if life is not worth living for one who does not study it, <margin>H</margin> or if "nursing a disease" is an obstacle to the attention of the mind in carpentry and other arts, while the exhortation of Phocylides is no obstacle. Yes, by Zeus, he said; it is perhaps the greatest obstacle of all, if this redundant care of the body goes beyond gymnastics. For it is difficult for household management, for military campaigns, and for sedentary offices in the city. But the greatest thing is that it is hard for any kind of learning, or reflection and private study, as it is always suspecting certain tensions in the head and giddiness, and blaming them on philosophy. So wherever virtue is practiced and tested, this is an entire obstacle. For it makes one think one is always sick, and never to <margin>H</margin> cease from bodily pain. It is likely, he said. Therefore, knowing these things, let us say that Asclepius revealed medicine to those who were healthy in body by nature and diet, but who had some localized disease in them; for these people and for this condition, he revealed medicine...

<summary>Socrates argues that a society's reliance on lawyers and doctors indicates a lack of self-discipline and purpose, contrasting the productive life of a craftsman with the "prolonged death" of those who obsessively nurse chronic illnesses.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Glaucon regarding the ideal state. Having critiqued the over-reliance on medicine for those with poor self-discipline, Socrates now discusses the legendary physician Asclepius and the specific qualities required for doctors and judges in their Republic.</meta>

### ON THE REPUBLIC, BOOK III.

Weakness was removed by incisions <note>original: "a incisionibus"</note>, following the customary and usual diet, so that the affairs of the citizens would not be disrupted. However, for bodies that were thoroughly diseased with internal corruption, he [Asclepius] did not attempt to prolong a long and miserable life for the man—and consequently for his children—by gradually draining and then refilling the senses through a meticulous diet. He believed that one who could not live within the established and usual routine of life ought not to be treated, as such a person is of no use either to himself or to the city. You are saying, then, that Asclepius was a "statesman-like" physician. Certainly, and his sons prove that he was such a man. Or do you not see how they distinguished themselves in the Trojan War and practiced medicine in the way I describe? Do you not remember that when Menelaus was wounded by the hands of Pandarus, they wiped away the blood from the wound <margin>Iliad, Book 4</margin> and applied soothing ointments? Yet they prescribed no more of a specific rule for food and drink for him than they did for Eurypylus, as if the medicines were sufficient to cure men who, before receiving their wounds, had been of healthy body and moderate habits, even if they happened to drink a barley-mixture <note>original: "kykeon," a common ancient Greek beverage</note> at that very moment. But they believed that for those who were sickly by nature and lacked self-control, living was of no benefit to themselves or others; the art of medicine should not be practiced on them, nor should they be cured, even if they were wealthier than Midas <note>A mythical king famous for his "golden touch" and immense wealth.</note>.

->C<- You say the sons of Asclepius were quite clever men. And rightly so. Although the tragic poets and Pindar <note>An ancient Greek lyric poet known for his odes.</note> disagree with us; for they say that Asclepius was the son of Apollo, but was persuaded by a bribe of gold to cure a rich man who was already at the point of death, for which reason he was struck by a lightning bolt. But we, in accordance with what we said before, will not believe both of these claims: if he was the son of a god, we deny he was greedy for shameful profit; if he was greedy for profit, we reject the idea that he was the son of a god. That is very well said. But what do you say to this, O

->D<- Socrates? Is it not necessary to have good doctors in the city? And would they not be the best if they had dealt with the greatest number of healthy people and the greatest number of sick people? Likewise, would the best judges be those who have experience with all sorts of human characters? I certainly mean "good" ones. But do you understand whom I consider to be such? If you tell me. I will try. However, you are asking about two different things in the same breath. How so? Doctors would become most excellent if, starting from their youth, they not only studied their art but also interacted with as many sickly bodies as possible, and if they themselves had suffered from every kind of disease and were not entirely healthy by nature. For I do not think they cure the body with the body (for then it would be impossible for the doctor to ever be ill), but rather 

->E<- the soul cures the body. Is it not impossible for a soul that has been and remains evil to cure anything well? Rightly so. But the judge, my friend, rules the soul with the soul. Is it not impossible for a soul to have been raised among evil souls from youth, to have associated with them, and to have committed every sort of injustice itself, so that it might sharply deduce the crimes of others from its own experience, just as one knows diseases from one's own body? Instead, the soul must have been innocent and untainted by evil habits while it was young, if it is to be good and honorable and judge what is just with a healthy mind. For this reason, honest men, when they are young, appear foolish and are easily deceived by the unjust, because they do not have within themselves the patterns of evil emotions that the wicked possess. That is exactly what happens to them. Therefore, a good judge must not be a young man, but an old one, who has learned only late in life what injustice is. He should not have perceived it as a personal inhabitant of his own soul, but rather have observed it as something alien in the souls of others over a long time, and thus discern what kind of evil it is through knowledge, rather than through his own experience. Such a judge seems to be of the most noble sort. And a good one too, which is what you were asking; for he who has a good soul is good. 

->F<- But that cunning and villainous man, who has committed many injustices himself and thinks himself shrewd and wise, appears clever when he associates with his own kind, looking with suspicion and directing his mind toward the patterns within himself. But when he approaches those who are good and older, he appears foolish; he is distrustful at the wrong time and ignorant of healthy character, precisely because he has no internal pattern for it. But since he meets with the wicked more often than with the wise, he seems both to himself and to others to be more wise than ignorant. You speak the absolute truth. We should not, therefore, look for a good and wise judge in such a man, but in the former. For vice can never know both virtue and itself, but virtue, as nature is educated over time, will attain a knowledge of both itself and vice. Therefore, in my opinion, it is the virtuous man, not the wicked one, who becomes wise. I agree. Will you not then establish in the city a system of medicine such as we described, along with a system of justice that functions in this way? These will care for those citizens who are healthy in both body and soul; but as for the rest, those who are sickly in body they will allow to die, and those who are naturally evil and incurable in soul, they themselves will put to death. This has been shown to be the best for those who suffer and for the city itself. It is clear, then, that your youths will be careful not to fall into the need for the courtroom, since they practice that simple music <note>In the Platonic sense, "music" (mousike) refers to the entire education of the soul, including poetry and the arts, which produces "sophrosyne" or self-restraint.</note> which we said produces moderation. Why not? And will they not follow these same tracks...

<column-break/>

...so that weakness would be removed by treatments, while maintaining the usual and customary diet, lest civic duties be disturbed. But for bodies diseased to the core with internal corruption, he [the physician] by no means attempted to prolong life by a diligent diet—exhausting and refilling the senses—lest they should beget children who, as follows, would also be sickly. Nor did he think he should care for a person who could not live in the established and usual diet and rule, as it would benefit neither the man himself nor the city. You say Asclepius was a man of the state. It is clearly established, and his sons testify that he was so. Are you unaware that they were famous in the Trojan War? Although they also used the study of medicine, as I was saying. Do you not remember that for Menelaus, wounded by the hands of Pandarus, they wiped the blood from the wound <margin>Iliad, Book 4</margin> and smeared it with mitigating ointments? But they prescribed no fixed law regarding food and drink for him any more than for Eurypylus, as if drugs were sufficient to cure men who, before receiving wounds, had been of firm bodily habit and moderate in diet, even if they had drunk at that very moment. But men who were sickly both by nature and by lack of self-control, they thought it benefited neither themselves nor others to live; nor should the art be occupied with them, nor should they be cured, even if they were wealthier than Midas.

->C<- You claim that the sons of Asclepius were very skillful men. It is indeed fitting. Although the tragedians and Pindar do not agree with us. For they say that Asclepius was the son of Apollo, and was led by gold to cure a wealthy man when he was being overwhelmed by extreme sickness leading to death. For which reason he was also struck by a thunderbolt. But because of those things we said above, we do not grant them both of these things. Rather, if he was the son of a god, we will deny he was greedy for shameful gain; but if he was greedy for shameful gain, we will reject the idea that he was the son of a god. Those things are indeed well said. But what do you say about this, O

->D<- Socrates? Is it not necessary to have good doctors in the city? And such would be especially those who have been conversant with the greatest number of healthy and the greatest number of sick people. Likewise, judges who have experienced the various characters of men. And I say they are very good indeed. But do you now understand those whom I judge to be so? If you say it. I will certainly try. You, however, did not ask about a similar matter in the same way. By what reasoning? Doctors indeed would turn out most excellent if, from an early age, besides the study of learning their art, they were conversant among many with poorly affected bodies, and were themselves afflicted with every kind of disease and were of weak nature. For they do not, as I judge, cure the body with the body. For it would be impossible for those themselves ever to have been or to be ill. But

->E<- the soul cures the body. Can it not happen that a soul which has been and is evil might cure something well? Rightly indeed. But the judge, O friend, commands the soul itself with the soul. Is it not possible for some soul, from childhood conversant with evil souls and having performed unjust deeds, to finally coniecture the crimes of others acutely from itself, just as one knows diseases from the body itself? But it was necessary for the judge himself to have been innocent and ignorant of evil manners while he was young, if he, being good and honest, is to judge just things sincerely. Wherefore modest men, while they are young, seem to be dull-witted and those who can easily be deceived by the unjust, as those who do not have in themselves the same examples of evil affections as the wicked have. Certainly, that happens to them entirely. But indeed, the good judge ought not to be a young man, but an old one, who has learned late what sort of thing injustice is: as one who did not feel it as his own in his soul, but has known it as an alien thing in alien souls for a long time, and therefore discerns what kind of evil it is, judging by knowledge rather than by his own experience. Certainly, such a judge seems to be most noble. And good besides, which is what you were seeking. For he who has a good soul is good. But that versatile man and one suspecting evil, who has done many things unjustly and is held as shrewd and wise, when he is conversant with those like himself, he appears cautious and clever, for by directing his mind to the examples he has in himself, he is sufficiently cautious for himself. But when he stays close to good and older men, he seems a fool, since he is distrustful out of season and is ignorant of healthy and sincere character, inasmuch as he does not have examples of it. But since he is conversant more frequently with the evil than with the wise, he often seems more wise than foolish to himself and others. You speak the truth without a doubt. Therefore, one ought not to seek such a judge as being good and wise, but such a one as I was saying a little while ago. For wickedness will never know either itself or virtue. But virtue, with discipline added to nature over time, will understand both itself and wickedness. Therefore, it is not the evil man, as my opinion holds, but this man who turns out wise. It seems so to me too. Therefore, will you not establish medicine such as we said, together with this kind of judicial equity in the city, which indeed would punish with death those citizens who are [incurably] base in both soul and body? Thus it seems to be conducive both to those who suffer such things and to the city. It is established, furthermore, that they will take care that the youth do not fall into the use of the courts, by using that simple music from which we said they obtained temperance. Why not? And will they not follow these same tracks...

<summary>Socrates argues that the ideal state requires doctors who treat the treatable and judges who are old and virtuous, having learned of evil through observation rather than personal practice. He concludes that the incurably wicked should be put to death for the benefit of society.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Glaucon. Having previously discussed the limits of medicine and the physical care of the body, Socrates now shifts the conversation toward the integrated education of the "Guardians" (the protectors of the ideal city), focusing on the balance between physical training and the arts.</meta>

# PLATO

...the musician <note>In the Platonic sense, "music" or *musica* refers to all the arts governed by the Muses, including literature, poetry, and music itself.</note> who follows gymnastics will, if he wishes, act in such a way that he will have no need of medicine unless necessity compels him? I quite agree. He will exercise his body in the gymnasiums, looking more toward the strength of his spirited nature <note>original: "animi firmitatem naturae"; Greek: "τὸ θυμοειδὲς" (*to thymoeides*), the part of the soul associated with courage, anger, and spirit.</note> and arousing it, rather than seeking mere physical power. He will not, like other athletes, adopt a diet and undergo labors simply for the sake of brute strength. Quite right. Therefore, Glaucon, those who establish education in music and gymnastics do so not for the reason many suppose—to care for the body with one and the soul with the other. Why not? Because they seem to practice both primarily for the sake of the soul. In what way? Do you not see how the soul is affected by those who practice gymnastics throughout their entire life but never touch music, or by those who are affected in the opposite way?

<margin>B</margin> Of which people are you speaking? Of those characterized by a rustic harshness and ferocity, I said, and likewise of those characterized by softness and gentleness. I know indeed, he said, that those who use only gymnastics become more savage than is proper, while those who use only music become softer than is decent for them. And yet, I said, that savage quality belongs to the spirited part of our nature; if it is nourished correctly, it becomes brave, but if it is stretched further than is proper, it becomes fierce and hard, as is natural. I agree. But what about the mild and gentle quality? Does not the philosophical nature possess this? And if this is relaxed too much, does it not become softer than it should be, but if well-nourished, does it not become gentle and orderly? It is as you say. We said, then, that the guardians ought to possess both of these natures. They must indeed. And must these not be in harmony and accord with one another? Why not? And the soul in which they are in harmony is temperate and brave? Entirely so. But the soul in which they are discordant is cowardly and savage? Most certainly.

<margin>C</margin> Whoever permits music to surround and soothe his soul with constant sound, pouring into his ears (as if through a funnel) the harmonies we mentioned earlier—the sweet, the soft, and the mournful—and spends his whole life humming and being charmed by song, he first softens his spirited part <note>original: "iracundum"; Greek: "θυμοειδὲς"</note> like iron, making it useful from something that was useless and hard. But when he persists too long and is too much soothed, he then begins to melt and dissolve his spirit, until he has melted away all his vigor and cut out, as it were, the very sinews of his soul, making himself a "soft warrior." It is entirely so. And if, I said, he received from the beginning a nature lacking in spirit, he reaches this state quickly. But if he has a spirited nature, by weakening the strength of his soul, he makes it unstable—quickly irritated by the smallest trifles and just as quickly extinguished. Thus, instead of being spirited, such men become quick-tempered, moody, and full of discontent. That is exactly what happens.

<margin>D</margin> On the other hand, if a man devotes himself entirely to gymnastics and feasts well, but neglects music and philosophy, he first achieves a firm habit of body and is filled with spirit and greatness of mind, becoming braver than he was before. Very much so. But then, if he continues in this path and does nothing else, and never touches music at all, surely whatever desire for learning was in his soul becomes weak, deaf, and blind; for it has never tasted any doctrine, nor any investigation of things, nor any reason at all, nor any other music by which his senses could be awakened, nourished, or purified. That is clear. Such a man, I think, becomes an enemy of reason and of the Muses; he no longer uses persuasion through words but carries out everything by force and savage ferocity, like a wild beast, living in ignorance and clumsiness without harmony or grace. It is exactly as you say.

<margin>E</margin> For these two things, then, it seems a god has given two arts to men: music and gymnastics. These are for the spirited part and the philosophical part of the soul—not for the soul and body specifically, except as a side effect—but for these two parts of the soul, so that they may be harmonized with each other by being tightened or relaxed to the proper degree. So it appears. Therefore, we should rightly call him the most perfect musician and the one who possesses the greatest harmony who best blends gymnastics with music and applies them to the soul in the most moderate way, much more so than the man who merely tunes strings to one another. And rightly so, Socrates. Will we not then always need such a presiding officer in our city, Glaucon, if the republic is to be preserved? We shall need one most especially. These, then, would be the forms of discipline and education. For one might rightly say that dances of this kind, and hunting, and athletics, and horse-racing all follow these principles; they are not difficult to find. Perhaps they are not.

<margin>F</margin> Come then, I said. What must we distinguish next? Must it not be which of these very people should rule and which should be ruled? Why not? It is clear that the elders should rule and the younger should obey. It is indeed. And it is also clear that the best among them must be chosen. That is also clear. Are not the best of farmers those who have the greatest skill in farming? Certainly.

<margin>G</margin> Now, since we must choose the best from among the guardians, must we not choose those who are most skilled in guarding the city? Yes. They must therefore be wise in this matter, and powerful, and also full of care for the Republic. It is so. And a man cares most for that which he happens to love.

<column-break/>

the musician who pursues gymnastics will, if he wishes, choose to act so that he has no need of medicine, except when necessity demands. It seems so to me. He will perform these exercises and labors, looking to the spirited part of his nature and arousing it, rather than seeking strength; he does not, like other athletes, handle food and labor for the sake of mere power. Most rightly said, he replied. Then, Glaucon (I said), those who established education in music and gymnastics did not do so for the reason some think—namely, to treat the body with one and the soul with the other. But for what, then? he asked. It is likely (I said) that they established both primarily for the sake of the soul. How so? Do you not notice (I said) the disposition of the mind in those who have associated with gymnastics

<margin>B</margin> throughout their lives but have not touched music? Or those who are in the opposite state? About what are you speaking? he asked. About savagery and hardness, and on the other hand, about softness and gentleness, I replied. I myself have observed (he said) that those who use unmixed gymnastics turn out more savage than is proper, while those who use only music become softer than is good for them. And yet (I said), the savage quality is provided by the spirited part of one's nature; if correctly nurtured, it becomes brave, but if it is stretched more than is proper, it becomes hard and harsh, as is likely. So it seems to me, he said. And what of the gentle? Does not the philosophical nature possess this? And if it is relaxed too much, it becomes softer than it should be, but if well-nurtured, it is gentle and orderly? That is so. But we say the guardians must have both of these natures. They must. Therefore, these natures must be harmonized with one another. How could they not be? And the soul of the one who is harmonized is temperate and brave. Quite so. But of the one who is unharmonized, it is cowardly and rustic. Very much so. Therefore, whenever someone allows music to play upon him and pour into his soul through his ears, as if through a funnel (those sweet, soft, and mournful harmonies we were just mentioning), and spends his whole life warbling and being delighted by song, this man at first, if he had any spirit, softens it like iron and makes it useful instead of useless and hard. But when he persists and does not let go, but is charmed, he then begins to melt and dissolve his spirit, until he wastes away the spirit and cuts out, as it were, the sinews from the soul, making himself a "soft spearman." It is entirely so, he said. And if (I said) he starts with a nature that is naturally without spirit, he accomplishes this quickly; but if he has a spirited nature, he makes the spirit weak and easily moved, quickly irritated by small things and quickly extinguished. Such men become short-tempered and irritable instead of spirited, filled with ill-temper. Exactly so. What then? If a man labors much in gymnastics and feasts very well, but does not touch music or philosophy, does he not first, being in good bodily condition, become filled with pride and spirit, and become braver than himself? Very much so. What then? When he does nothing else and shares in no Muse anywhere, even if there was some love of learning in his soul, since it tastes no knowledge and takes no part in inquiry or reason or any other music, does it not become weak, deaf, and blind, since it is not awakened, nor fed, nor purified in its perceptions? It is so. Such a man, I think, becomes a hater of reason and unmusical; he no longer uses persuasion through words, but accomplishes everything by force and savagery, like a wild beast, and lives in ignorance and awkwardness, with a lack of rhythm and grace. Entirely so (he said), it is so.

<margin>E</margin> To these two parts, as it seems, I would say some god has given two arts to humans: music and gymnastics, for the spirited and the philosophical parts of the soul; not for the soul and body, unless as a secondary matter, but for those two parts, so that they may be harmonized with each other, being tightened and relaxed to the proper point. So it seems. Therefore, the one who best mingles gymnastics with music and brings them to the soul in the most measured way, we would most rightly call perfectly musical and most harmoniously composed, far more than the one who tunes strings to each other. Reasonably so, Socrates, he said. Will we not then, Glaucon, always need some such overseer in our city if the constitution is to be preserved? We shall indeed need one as much as possible. These, then, would be the patterns of education and nurture. For why should one go through the details of dances, or hunts and chases, or athletic and horse-racing contests? For it is fairly clear that these must follow the same patterns, and they are no longer difficult to find. Perhaps (he said) they are not difficult.

<margin>G</margin> Very well (I said). What must be divided by us after this? Is it not which of these same people shall rule and which shall be ruled? Why not? Is it not clear that the elders should be the rulers and the younger the subjects? It is clear. And that the best among them should rule? This also. Do not the best of farmers become the most skilled in farming? Yes. Now, since they must be the best guardians, must they not be the most skillful at guarding the city? Yes. Therefore, they must be wise in this, and capable, and moreover, they must care for the city? This is so. <margin>H</margin> And one cares most for that which one happens to love.

<summary>Socrates explains that a balanced education in both "music" (the arts) and gymnastics is essential to harmonize the "spirited" and "philosophical" parts of the soul. He concludes that the ideal rulers (Guardians) must be chosen from those who are most capable and most devoted to the city's welfare.</summary>

# ON THE REPUBLIC, BOOK III.

<margin>A</margin> It is necessary. And surely one loves most that which he thinks shares the same interests as himself; when he believes that if that person fares well, he himself fares well, and if not, the opposite. So it is, he said. We must, therefore, select from the other guardians such men who, as we observe them throughout their entire lives, appear most likely to do with all zeal what they consider to be for the city's benefit, and would in no way be willing to do what is not. They are indeed the most suitable, he said. It seems to me, then, that we must watch them at every age to see if they are guardians of this principle <note>original: "dogmatis"; the fundamental belief that one's interest is the city's interest.</note> and
<margin>B</margin> whether, neither by being enchanted nor by being forced, they cast out through forgetfulness the opinion that one must do what is best for the city. What do you mean by this "casting out"? I will tell you, I said. It seems to me that an opinion leaves the mind either voluntarily or involuntarily. Voluntarily, when a false opinion is discarded by one who learns better; involuntarily, when a true opinion is lost. I understand the voluntary loss, he said, but I need to learn about the involuntary. What? Do you not also think, I said, that men are deprived of good things against their will, but of evil things willingly? Or is it not an evil to be deceived about the truth, and a good to possess the truth? Or do you not think that to hold an opinion of things as they are is to possess the truth? You speak rightly, he said, and I believe men are deprived of a true opinion against their will. Do they not suffer this either by being stolen away, or
<margin>C</margin> enchanted, or forced? Again, I do not understand. I fear I am speaking like a tragic poet, I said. By "stolen away," I mean those who are persuaded to change their minds and those who forget; in the former case, logic, and in the latter, time, subtly removes the opinion. Do you understand now? Yes. By "forced," I mean those whom some pain or grief causes to change their opinion. This too I understand, he said, and you speak correctly. Furthermore, those who are "enchanted" are those, I believe you would say, who change their opinion because they are either charmed by pleasure or terrified by fear. It seems, he said, that everything which deceives enchants us. What I was saying just now, then, must be sought out: who are the best guardians of the principle within themselves, to do that which they judge best for the city.
<margin>D</margin> They must be observed from childhood, setting them tasks in which one would most likely forget such a principle or be deceived; the one who remembers and is hard to deceive should be chosen, and the one who is not should be rejected. Is that not so? Yes. And labors, pains, and contests must be set for them in which these same qualities are to be observed. Correct, he said. Must we not also, I said, create a trial for the third kind, enchantment, and observe them? Just as people lead young horses toward noise and tumult to see if they are easily frightened, so we must bring these men while they are young into scenes of terror, and then shift them again into pleasures—testing them much more than gold is tested in the fire—to see if the man is difficult to enchant and remains graceful in all circumstances, a good guardian
<margin>E</margin> of himself and of the music he has learned, showing himself rhythmic and harmonious throughout it all. Such a man would be most useful to himself and the city. And he who is tested in this way as a child, a youth, and a man, and comes out untainted, should be appointed as a ruler and guardian of the city. Honors should be given to him both in life and in death, and he should receive the greatest prizes of tombs and other monuments. But he who is not such a man should be rejected. Such, O Glaucon, I said, seems to me the selection and appointment of the rulers and guardians, described in outline and not with absolute precision. And so it seems to me, he said. Is it not then truly most correct to call these "Perfect Guardians" of
<margin>F</margin> enemies without and friends within, so that the latter will not wish to do harm and the former will not be able to? While the young men—whom we just now called guardians—will be called "Auxiliaries" and supporters of the rulers' decrees. I agree, he said. What device, then, I said, could we find for those necessary falsehoods we were talking about just now, so that by telling one noble lie we might persuade the rulers themselves if possible, or if not, the rest of the city? What sort of lie? he asked. Nothing new, I said, but a Phoenician tale <note>A reference to the myth of Cadmus and the dragon's teeth, where men were born directly from the earth.</note>, which has happened in many places before, as the poets say and have persuaded people to believe—though it has not happened among us, and I do not know if it could, but to persuade people of it requires a great deal of persuasion. You seem, he said, hesitant to speak. You will think it very natural
<margin>G</margin> for me to hesitate, I said, once I have told it. Speak, he said, and do not be afraid. I speak then, though I do not know with what boldness or with what words I shall use; I will attempt first to persuade the rulers themselves and the soldiers, and then the rest of the city, that the way we were nourishing and educating them was all like a dream that they seemed to experience. In truth, during that time they were being molded and nourished deep under the earth—they, their weapons, and the rest of their equipment being manufactured. When they were entirely finished, the earth, being their mother, delivered them. And now they must deliberate and defend the land in which they live as their mother and nurse, if anyone attacks it, and think of the other citizens as their brothers, also born of the earth. It was not without reason, he said, that you were ashamed to tell this lie. Quite
<margin>H</margin> naturally, I said; but hear the rest of the myth. "You are all, certainly, brothers in the city" (so we shall tell them as we tell our myth), "but God, in molding you, mixed gold in the generation of those of you who are fit to rule...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> It must be so. Furthermore, he loves this most who thinks the same things are advantageous to himself, and from whose happiness he judges his own happiness or unhappiness to depend. It is so. Therefore, those must be chosen from all the guardians who, upon our consideration, seem through their whole life to do with the greatest zeal those things which they lead themselves to believe are for the state; but on the other hand, to avoid what is contrary. Certainly, these are the most suitable. Therefore, they must be observed, as I think, in every age, whether they keep this precept, and neither as if deceived by some charms, nor compelled by any force, do they,
<margin>B</margin> forgetting themselves, cast out that opinion by which those things alone are judged to be done which are best for the state. What "casting out" do you speak of? I will tell you: it seems to me an opinion departs from the mind either voluntarily or involuntarily. Voluntarily indeed, a false one, in him who unlearns it. Involuntarily, however, every true opinion. What you say of the voluntary casting away, I understand; but as for the involuntary, I desire to learn. Do you not think men are deprived of good things involuntarily, but of evil things voluntarily? Is it not an evil to lie and to be ignorant of the truth; but to judge truly, a good? Does it not seem to you that to hold an opinion of things as they are is to think truly? You speak rightly, and it seems to me that men are deprived of a true opinion against their will. Do they not suffer this either by theft, or deception, or force? Neither
<margin>C</margin> do I understand this. I seem to speak like a tragic poet. For I say opinions are stolen from those whose minds are changed, either gradually obliterated by time, or secretly subtracted by an opposing reason. Now do you understand? I understand indeed. But force is brought upon those whom pain or torture compels to feel otherwise. That I understand indeed, and you speak rightly. Moreover, those are withdrawn as if by charms, I think, you also would say, who lay aside a former opinion, either smoothed by pleasure or terrified by fear. It seems truly that whatever deceives seduces us by charms. Therefore, what I was saying recently must be sought: who are those who constantly keep that opinion which is among them—namely, that that must always be done which they judge
<margin>D</margin> to be conducive to the state. They are to be observed, therefore, immediately from childhood, and those works are to be proposed to them from which one might most easily forget that precept and be deceived. And he who keeps himself mindful of it and is not deceived is to be chosen; he who is otherwise is to be rejected. Is it not so? Certainly. Therefore, both labors and pains and contests must be set before them, and in these, these same things are to be observed. Wisely. Must we not also fight according to that third kind of charm? And just as those who wish to inspect whether colts are fearful or not lead them into noise and
<margin>E</margin> tumult, so the younger ones must be driven into certain terrible things, and likewise into delights, and in these they must be examined much more than gold by fire: so that we may find out if there is any outsider among them who is not easily ensnared, and is composed in all things, the best guardian of himself and the preserver of that music which he learned, and shows himself graceful and harmonious in all these things. Such a man would be most useful to himself and his country. And he who has always been proved in childhood, youth, and mature age, and exists uncorrupted, is to be appointed guardian and prince of the city. Honors are to be paid to him both living and dead, and he shall obtain the greatest rewards of tombs and other monuments. He who is not such a man is to be rejected. Of this kind, therefore, O Glaucon,
<margin>F</margin> the choice and institution of the princes and guardians ought, it seems to me, to be, so that it is said summarily rather than accurately. The same seems to me. Therefore, most truly these shall be called guardians in every respect, both of external enemies and internal friends, so that the latter may not wish, and the former may not be able, to plot any evil. But the young men, whom we a little before called guardians, shall correctly be called auxiliaries and defenders of the institutions of the princes themselves. Thus I also feel. What, therefore, will be the way by which, from these lies which are sometimes fitting—as we were saying before—we may persuade them that there is something noble in lying, first to the princes; if not,
<margin>G</margin> at least to the remaining citizens? What sort of thing do you mean? Nothing good indeed, but a certain Phoenician thing: which was done before among many, as the poets have said and persuaded, but in our times not at all; nor do I know if it will ever be; certainly it is arduous to persuade. How sluggishly, he said, you seem to approach the speaking. I shall indeed seem so to you after I have spoken, and not without reason. Speak, come, and do not fear. Behold, now I speak, although I know not with what audacity and relying on what words I shall speak; and I will attempt first to persuade the princes themselves and the soldiers, and then also the remaining citizens, that those things with which we nourished and instructed them seemed to them like dreams happening around them. But they were then in truth under the earth, formed and nourished within, they themselves and their arms and all their furniture. But after they were altogether perfected, the earth brought them forth as a mother. And now indeed, as to a mother and nurse, they ought to consult for this region in which they are, and to succor it if anyone invades it, and to think
<margin>H</margin> of the other citizens as brothers born of the earth. Not without reason, he said, were you ashamed before to tell this lie. Rightly indeed, I say, but hear now the rest of the fable. You are all surely in the city as brothers (for so we shall say to them, telling the fable), but when God was forming you, those of you who...

<summary>This page describes the rigorous testing process for selecting city Rulers (Perfect Guardians) from the broader class of protectors, emphasizing their resistance to fear, pleasure, and deception. It also introduces the "Noble Lie," a foundational myth intended to foster civic unity by claiming all citizens are "earth-born" siblings with different metals in their souls.</summary>

# OF PLATO

<margin>Aristotle notes this in his *Politics*, Book 2, chapter 3.</margin>
**A** those of you born fit to rule, God mixed gold into their generation, which is why they are the most honored. To those who are born as helpers <note>The "auxiliaries" or military class.</note>, he mixed in silver. Finally, he mixed iron and bronze <note>original: "æs"; can refer to copper, bronze, or brass</note> for the farmers and other craftsmen. Because you are all of the same stock, you will mostly produce children like yourselves. However, it sometimes happens that a silver child is born from a golden parent, and likewise a golden child from a silver one, and so on with all the others in turn. Therefore, God commands the rulers first and foremost that they should be good guardians of nothing else—nor watch anything so vigilantly—as the children, to see which of these four metals has been mixed into their souls. And if a child of their own is born with a nature mixed with bronze or iron, they must show no pity, but instead assign the honor appropriate to that nature by

**B** <margin>Aristotle notes this passage in his *Politics*, Book 2, chapter 2.</margin> transferring them to the ranks of the craftsmen or farmers. Conversely, if a child is born among those classes with a nature of gold or silver, the rulers should honor them and promote them—the golden to the rank of guardians, and the silver to the helpers. For there is an oracle that the republic will be destroyed when a guardian of iron or bronze governs it. Do you have any way to make them believe this story? None at all, he said, at least not these men themselves; but I can see how their sons and those who come after, and the rest of posterity, might believe it. Even that, I said, would be well-suited to making them care more for the city and for one another.

**C** I think I understand what you mean. And this matter will go wherever the tradition <note>original: "fama" / "φήμη"; referring to the spread of the myth</note> leads it. But let us arm these "earth-born" men and lead them forth under the guidance of their rulers. Once they have gone forth, let them scout where in the city it is best to pitch their camp—a place from which they can best restrain those within, should anyone refuse to obey the laws, and repel those from without, if an enemy should invade like a wolf falling upon a flock. When they have pitched their camp and offered the proper sacrifices, let them build their dwellings. Is that right? It is, he said. And should these houses be of a sort that suffice against both winter and heat? Certainly, for you seem to be speaking of houses. Yes, I said, but houses for soldiers, not for money-makers.

**D** In what way, he asked, do you say the one differs from the other? I will try to explain, I said. For it would be the most terrible and shameful thing of all for shepherds to breed and keep dogs as helpers for their flocks in such a way that—through lack of discipline, or hunger, or some other bad habit—the dogs themselves would attempt to harm the sheep and become like wolves instead of dogs. Therefore, we must take every precaution that our helpers do not do such a thing to the citizens, since they are stronger than they, and instead of being benevolent allies, make themselves like savage masters. We must indeed take care. Would they not be provided with the greatest safeguard if they were truly well educated?

**E** But they already are, he said. I replied, that is not something we should dogmatically assert, my dear Glaucon; but what we were just saying is worth asserting: that they must receive the right education, whatever it may be, if they are to possess the most important quality for being gentle both to themselves and to those they guard. And that is quite right, he said. In addition to this education, any man of sound mind would say that their dwellings and other property should be arranged so as neither to prevent them from being the best possible guardians, nor to incite them to harm the other citizens. And he would speak truly. Consider then, I said, whether they ought to live and dwell in some such manner as this, if they are to be such men. First, no one shall possess any private property, unless it is absolutely necessary. Next, no one shall have a house or a storeroom that is not open for anyone who wishes to enter.

**F** As for their provisions—the things needed by temperate and brave warriors who are "athletes of war"—they should receive them from the other citizens as a fixed wage for their guarding, in such an amount that there is neither a surplus nor a deficit for the year. They shall live together, going to common meals <note>original: "comessationes" / "ξυσσίτια"; the Spartan-style communal mess halls</note> as if they were in a camp. We must tell them that they have divine gold and silver from the gods always within their souls, and they have no need of the human kind. Indeed, it is a sin to pollute the possession of that divine metal by mixing it with the possession of mortal gold; for many unholy things have come about for the sake of the common currency, but the gold within them is untainted. To them alone of all those in the city, it is forbidden <note>original: "nefas" / "οὐ θέμις"</note> to touch gold or silver, or to be under the same roof with it, or to wear it, or to drink from vessels of silver or gold.

**G** In this way, they would save both themselves and the city. But whenever they acquire land or houses or money of their own, they will be householders and farmers instead of guardians, and they will become hateful masters instead of allies to the other citizens. Hating and being hated, plotting and being plotted against, they will pass their whole lives in much greater fear of the internal enemies than the external ones; and then they and the rest of the city will be running very close to the brink of ruin. For all these reasons, then, I said, let us state that the guardians must be provided for in this way regarding their houses and all other things. And shall we establish this by law? By all means, said Glaucon.

<column-break/>

**A** mixed with them; for this reason they are most honored. To the helpers, he mixed silver; and iron and bronze to the farmers and other craftsmen. Since you are all kin, for the most part you will produce children like yourselves; but there are times when a silver child may be born from gold, and a golden offspring from silver, and all others from each other in the same way. Therefore, God commands the rulers first and most especially that they should be good guardians of nothing so much, nor watch anything so intently, as the children, to see what has been mixed into their souls. And if their own offspring is born with a nature of bronze or iron, they shall in no way have pity, but giving the honor due to its nature, they shall push it out among the craftsmen or the farmers. And if, in turn, one is born from these with a nature of gold or silver, they shall honor them and lead them up—the one to the guardianship, the other to the rank of helper. For there is an oracle that the city will be destroyed when iron or bronze guards it. Do you have any device to make them believe this myth? None at all, he said, at least not these men; but their sons and those who come after, and other men of later times, might. But even this, I said, would be good for making them care more for the city and for one another.

**C** For I almost understand what you are saying. And this matter will go wherever the rumor leads it. But let us, having armed these earth-born men, lead them forward under the guidance of the rulers. Let them go and observe where in the city is the best place to encamp, from which they might best control those within, if anyone should be unwilling to obey the laws, and ward off those from without, if an enemy, like a wolf, should come upon the flock. Having encamped and sacrificed to the proper gods, let them make their shelters. Or how should it be? So, he said. Dwellings of such a kind as to be sufficient to keep out the winter and the summer? Of course, for you seem to me, he said, to be speaking of houses. Yes, I said, but military ones, not for the purpose of making money.

**D** How, he asked, do you say this differs from the other? I will try to tell you, I said. For it is surely the most terrible and shameful of all things for shepherds to breed and keep such dogs as helpers for the flocks that, through lack of discipline or hunger or some other bad habit, the dogs themselves should attempt to do harm to the sheep and be made like wolves instead of dogs. Terrible, he said; how could it not be? Therefore, we must guard in every way against our helpers doing such a thing to the citizens, since they are stronger than they, and instead of being kindly allies, being made like savage masters. We must guard against it, he said. And would they not be prepared with the greatest caution if they are truly well educated?

**E** But indeed they are, he said. And I said, it is not worth insisting on this, dear Glaucon; but what we were just saying is worth it: that they must obtain the right education, whatever it is, if they are going to have the most important thing for being gentle both to themselves and to those guarded by them. And rightly so, he said. In addition to this education, a man of sense would say that their dwellings and other property must be so provided for them that it will neither prevent the guardians from being the best they can be, nor incite them to do harm to the other citizens. And he will speak truly. See then, I said, if they must live and dwell in some such way as this, if they are going to be such men. First, no one shall possess any private property, unless it is an absolute necessity; then, no one shall have a dwelling or a storehouse of such a kind that anyone who wishes cannot enter.

**F** And for provisions, as much as sober and brave athletes of war require, they shall receive a wage for their guarding from the other citizens, fixed so that there is neither a surplus for them for the year, nor a deficit. Going to common meals, as if they were in a camp, they shall live together. As for gold and silver, we shall tell them that they have divine metal from the gods always in their souls, and they have no need of the human kind; nor is it holy to pollute the possession of that divine gold by mixing it with the possession of mortal gold; because many unholy things have happened concerning the coinage of the masses, but the gold among them is untainted. But to them alone of those in the city, it is not lawful <note>original: "οὐ θέμις"</note> to handle or touch gold and silver, nor to go under the same roof with it, nor to wear it, nor to drink from silver or gold. And thus they would save themselves and save the city.

**G** But whenever they themselves acquire private land and houses and currency, they will be house-managers and farmers instead of guardians, and they will become hateful masters instead of allies of the other citizens. Hating and being hated, plotting and being plotted against, they will pass their whole life, fearing those within much more and more than the enemies from without, running even then very close to destruction, both themselves and the rest of the city. For the sake of all these things, then, I said, let us say that the guardians must be thus established, concerning their dwelling and the other matters. And shall we legislate these things, or not? By all means, said Glaucon.
