# PLATO’S REPUBLIC,
## Book IV, <note>The Greek text uses 'H', which usually signifies 8, but this is the start of Book 4.</note>
## ON JUSTICE,
### THE FOURTH DIALOGUE.

---

# PLATO’S REPUBLIC
## Or,
## ON JUSTICE,
### THE FOURTH DIALOGUE.

---

-> S U M M A R Y  O F  T H E  D I A L O G U E <-

> *After a precise discussion regarding the education of the guardians, at the end of the third book he began to treat the institution of the entire State, which he proceeds to explain diligently in this book. The thesis of this fourth dialogue, therefore, concerns the institution of the whole city, which he composes of Wisdom, Temperance, Fortitude, and Justice: so that by their power and efficacy, the Republic may be wise, temperate, courageous, and just. He treats the multifaceted conjunction and society of these virtues from the multiple faculties of the soul with great accuracy, so that from these, various modes of politics are composed, and some in such a way that they grow together harmoniously into one accord. From that harmony, he says, consists that Justice which is the foundation of the Republic. To these he opposes Injustice, the detriments of which he commemorates, just as he had taught the advantages of Justice. Furthermore, the name of Justice is taken here in various ways: now for the genus itself, now for a certain species within that common genus. Thus Aristotle in his Politics makes the name "Polity," which is said generally of every civil administration, the name of a species—specifically that form where the highest authority is in the hands of the people.*

---

<margin>A</margin> And Adimantus, interrupting, said: "What then, Socrates, will be your defense if someone should say that you are not making these men very happy? And this by their own doing, since the city truly belongs to them, yet they enjoy none of the city's goods—as others do, who possess lands, build beautiful and large houses, and acquire furnishings suitable to such homes; who offer private sacrifices to the gods and entertain guests; and indeed, who possess what you just mentioned, gold and silver, and everything else considered necessary for those who are to be blessed. But truly, he might say, they seem to be stationed in the city like hired helpers <margin>B</margin> <note>original: "auxiliarii"</note>, doing nothing else but standing guard." 

"Yes," I said, "and they do this for their food alone, receiving no pay beyond their provisions, unlike the others. Consequently, if they should wish to travel abroad privately, they will not be allowed; nor can they give gifts <note>original: "scortis largiri"; likely a reference to giving to mistresses or for private pleasures</note> or spend money on anything else they might wish, in the manner of those who are considered happy. You omit these and many other such points from your accusation." 

"Well," said Adimantus, "let these also be included in the charge." 

"What then shall we say in our defense?" I asked. "Yes. By following the same path," I said, "we shall find, I think, what must be said. We will say that it would be no wonder if these men, even as they are, were most happy. Nevertheless, we are not founding the city <margin>C</margin> with an eye to making one class among us exceptionally happy, but rather that the whole city should be as happy as possible. For we thought that in such a city we would most likely find justice, and conversely, in the worst-managed city, find injustice. Having observed these, we might judge what we have long been seeking. Now, then, as we believe, we are shaping the happy city—not by taking a few people in it and making them happy, but the whole. In a moment, we shall consider the opposite kind of city. 

It is as if someone came up to us while we were painting a statue and found fault, saying that we were not applying the most beautiful colors to the most beautiful parts of the animal. For the eyes, being the most beautiful part, <margin>D</margin> were not painted with purple <note>original: "ostreio" / "purpura"; the prized murex dye</note>, but with black. We would seem to answer him reasonably by saying: 'My dear fellow, do not think that we ought to paint the eyes so beautiful that they do not even look like eyes, nor the other parts likewise. But look and see whether, by giving each part its proper due, we make the whole thing beautiful.' 

And so now, do not force us to attach such happiness to the guardians that it will make them anything rather than guardians. For we know how to dress farmers in fine robes and gold and bid them work the land only for their pleasure; and to have potters recline from left to right <margin>E</margin> by the fire, drinking and feasting, with the wheel set aside to make pottery only as much as they desire; and to make all others blessed in such a way, so that the whole city might be happy. But do not advise us thus; for if we follow you, the farmer will not be a farmer, nor the potter a potter, nor will anyone else keep the form of those things from which a city is made. 

But for the others, the concern is less. For if cobblers become poor and corrupted, and pretend to be what they are not, it is no great disaster for the city. But if the guardians of the laws and the city are not what they seem to be, you see that they utterly destroy the entire city, just as they alone have the opportunity to manage it well and make it happy. Therefore, if we seek true guardians of the city, we must choose those who will least of all harm the city. But he who says such things makes them like farmers at a festival, feasting and happy, rather than citizens in a city; he would be speaking of something other than a city. 

We must consider, then, whether we appoint guardians with an eye to this—that they should have the greatest abundance of happiness—or whether we should look to the whole city <margin>F</margin> to see if happiness is found there. We must compel and persuade these helpers and guardians to do those things which will make them the best craftsmen of their own work, and all others likewise. And so, as the whole city grows and is rightly established, we must allow the several classes to participate in happiness as their nature allows."

"You seem to me," he said, "to speak well."

"And will the point that is sister to this one," I said, "also seem to you to be spoken rightly?"

"What point especially?"

"Consider whether these things corrupt the other craftsmen so as to make them bad."

"What things are these?"

"Wealth," I said, "and poverty."

"In what way?"

"In this way: if a potter becomes wealthy, does he seem to you to still be willing to care for his art?"

"Not at all," he said.

"He will certainly become more idle and negligent."

"Very much so."

"And therefore a worse craftsman..."

<margin>Does he seem to you even then to have care for his art? Not at all. He will certainly be rendered more idle and negligent. Very much so. Wherefore also worse...</margin>

"To speak briefly then," I said, "the overseers of the city must cling to this: they must not let it be destroyed without them noticing, but they must guard it through everything—that there be no innovation in gymnastics or music against the established order, but to guard it as much as possible. They should be afraid when someone says that men value the song more:

<note>original: "ἥ τις ἀειδόντεσσι νεωτάτη ἀμφιπέληται"</note>
*‘which circles newest to the singers,’* <note>A reference to Homer’s Odyssey, Book 1, line 351.</note>

lest anyone think the poet is speaking not of new songs, but of a new *style* of song, and praises this. One must neither praise such a thing nor accept it. For one must be cautious of changing to a new kind of music, as it risks the whole state. Nowhere are the modes of music changed without changing the greatest laws of the city, as Damon says, and I am persuaded." <note>Damon of Oa was an influential Greek music theorist and advisor to Pericles who believed music reflected and shaped a person's character (ethos).</note> "And B me then," said Adeimantus, "set me down as one of those who are persuaded." "Then the guardhouse," I said, "must, as it seems, be built by the guardians there in music." "Indeed," he said, "this lawlessness easily creeps in without being noticed."

"Yes," I said, "as if it were in the form of play, and as if it were doing no harm." "And it does no harm," he said, "except that, having settled in little by little, it flows quietly into the characters and the habits. From these, it emerges larger into the contracts men make with one another. And from the contracts, Socrates, it proceeds C to the laws and the constitutions with much insolence, until at last it overturns everything, both private and public." "Well then," I said, "is that how it is?" "It seems so to me," he said. "Therefore, as we said from the beginning, our children must participate in more lawful play immediately; for if play becomes lawless, and the children themselves likewise, it is impossible for them to grow into lawful and serious men." "How could it be otherwise?" he said. "Whenever, then, children start to play well and receive lawfulness through music, the opposite of the former case happens: it follows them into everything and grows, correcting anything in the city that was previously neglected." "True indeed," D he said. "And these men," I said, "will rediscover the seemingly small rules which those before them had completely destroyed." "What kind of rules?" "Things like this: the silence of the younger before the elder, which is proper; and sitting down, and rising to give place, and the care of parents; and the style of hair, and clothes, and shoes, and the whole outward appearance of the body, and all other such things. Or don't you think so?" "I do." "But to legislate these things would be foolish, I think. For they are not done, nor would they last, if they were legislated by word and in writing." "How could they?" "It seems then, Adeimantus," I said, "that the direction someone is pushed by their education determines what follows. Or does not like always call to like?" "Of course." "And finally, I think, we would say it ends in one perfect and vigorous result, E whether good or the opposite." "Indeed." "For these reasons then," I said, "I would not attempt to legislate such things." "And rightly so," he said.

"But by the gods," I said, "what about these market matters, regarding contracts and the dealings each man has with others in the market? Or, if you like, regarding the contracts of craftsmen, and insults, and physical injury, and the filing of lawsuits, and the appointment of judges, and wherever there are certain taxes to be collected or paid in markets or harbors, or generally market regulations, or city regulations, or harbor regulations, or any other such things—shall we dare to legislate any of these?" "It is not worth while," he said, "to dictate to good and honorable men. For most of the things that need to be F legislated they will easily find for themselves." "Yes, my friend," I said, "if God grants them the preservation of the laws we described before." "If not," he said, "they will spend their lives setting many such laws and correcting them, thinking they will reach what is best." "You are saying," I said, "that such people will live like those who are sick but, due to lack of self-control, are unwilling to leave their bad way of life." "Exactly so." "And indeed, these people live a charming life! For though they are being treated by doctors, they achieve nothing, except to make their illnesses more complex and greater; and they are always hoping that if someone suggests a medicine, they will be healthy because of it." "G Indeed," he said, "the condition of those who are sick is exactly like that." "And what about this?" I said. "Isn't it charming of them that they consider the man who tells them the truth to be their greatest enemy: that until they stop being drunk, and over-eating, and chasing sex, and being idle, neither medicines, nor cautery, nor surgery, nor charms, nor amulets, nor anything else of the sort will do them any good?" "Not very charming," he said. "For to be angry at someone who gives good advice has no charm." "You are not a praiser of such men, it seems," I said. "Certainly not, by Zeus!" "And even if the whole city," as we were just saying, "does such a thing, you will not praise it. Or don't they seem to you to be doing the same thing as these sick men—those cities that, being badly governed, warn the citizens not to move the whole constitution of the city, on pain of death to whoever does it? But whoever serves them most pleasantly while they are governed this way, and gratifies them by flattering them and knowing their wishes beforehand and being clever at fulfilling them—this man, then, will be the good man and H wise in great things, and will be honored by them." "They seem to me to be doing the same thing," he said, "and I do not praise it in any way." "But what about those who are willing to serve such cities and are eager to do so—don't you admire their courage and readiness?" "I do," he said, "except for those..."

One must neither praise such a thing, nor receive it. B One must certainly beware of introducing a new kind of music, as if it were a total shipwreck. "A certain citadel, then, as it seems, must be built for the sake of guarding by these same guardians around music." "Truly, such a sin creeps in secretly and easily." "It is not at all becoming to command good and distinguished men. For most of these, of what kind F and in what way they are to be established, they will easily find for themselves." "Certainly, friend, if God grants them the safety of those laws which we placed above. "Altogether such are the diseases of those laboring so. What then? Is this not charming in them? That they think him the most hostile of all who warns them of the truth, and says that neither drugs, nor burnings, nor incisions, nor incantations, nor those things which are applied from without, or any such things will be of use, until one stops indulging in drunkenness, gluttony, lust, and idleness?" "That is not at all charming. For to be angry against him who advises useful things has no charm. Therefore, you do not approve of men of this kind, as you seem." "Not at all, by Jove. On the contrary, whoever so treats those administering the Republic, and gratifies them, and creeps in, and assents to their will, and H behaves accordingly, he at last will be a good man, he wise in the greatest things, he will be affected by honor from them." "They seem to me to do exactly the same, nor do I praise it in any way. But what again? # PLATO'S REPUBLIC
## BOOK IV

<margin>A</margin> ...who are deceived by them, and believe themselves to be truly statesmen because they are praised by the masses. What do you say? Do you not forgive these men? Or do you think it possible for a man who is ignorant of measurement, when many others like himself tell him he is four cubits tall, not to believe this about himself? "No, not that," he said. Then do not be angry with them. For these are indeed the most ridiculous of all men, who pass laws concerning the matters we just described, and are always amending them, confident that they will find some end to the frauds committed in business and the things I was just speaking of—ignorant that they are, in truth, cutting off the heads of a <term>Hydra</term> <note>The Hydra was a mythological multi-headed water serpent; whenever one head was cut off, two more grew in its place. Socrates uses this as a metaphor for the futility of trying to fix a corrupt society through endless minor regulations rather than fundamental education.</note>. "Certainly," he said, "they are doing nothing else."

<margin>B</margin> "For my part," I said, "I do not think the true lawgiver should bother with this species of institutions and laws, whether in a ill-governed or a well-constituted city: in the former, because such regulations are useless and achieve nothing; in the latter, because some of them anyone could discover, while others follow naturally from the habits we established earlier." "What, then," he asked, "remains for us concerning the constitution of laws?" "For us," I said, "nothing."

<margin>C</margin> "But to the <term>Delphic Apollo</term> <note>Apollo’s oracle at Delphi was the highest religious authority in the Greek world. Socrates argues that the founding of temples and religious rites should be left to divine tradition rather than human invention.</note> belong the greatest, noblest, and first of institutions." "Which ones?" he asked. "The founding of temples and sacrifices, and other forms of worship for gods, spirits, and heroes; moreover, the graves of the dead and the services to be rendered to appease those in the world beyond. Such things as these we ourselves do not know, and in founding our city, we will obey no other, if we are wise, nor use any other interpreter than the ancestral one. For this god is surely the ancestral interpreter for all mankind in such matters, sitting at the center of the earth upon the <term>navel</term> <note>original: "umbilicum / ὀμφαλοῦ". The Greeks believed Delphi was the center (omphalos) of the world.</note> to give his guidance." "You speak well," he said, "and so it must be done." "The city, then, O son of Ariston, may now be said to be founded. Look now within it, having brought a great light from somewhere, and summon your brother, and Polemarchus, and the others, so that we may see if by any means we can discover where justice and injustice might be located—how they differ from one another, and

<margin>D</margin> which of the two he must possess who is to be happy, whether he is unnoticed or not by all gods and men." "You are talking nonsense," said Glaucon. "For you promised to investigate this yourself, saying it would be a sin if you did not bring aid to justice with all your might." "You remind me of the truth," I said, "and so I must do. But you all must assist me." "We will do so," he said. "I hope, then, to find it in this way. I think our city, if it has been rightly founded, is perfectly good." "It must be," he said. "It is clear, then, that it is wise, courageous, temperate, and just." "It is clear." "Whichever of these we find in the city, the remainder will be that which has not yet been found." "Why not?" he said. "Suppose there were four other things, and we were looking for one of them in some subject; if we recognized that one first, our search would be over. But if we found the other three first, by that very fact

<margin>E</margin> the one sought would be known, for it would clearly be nothing other than what remained." "You speak correctly," he said. "Should we not also seek in this same way concerning these virtues, since they are four?" "Clearly." "Now, among all these, <term>wisdom</term> seems to me the first to shine forth in the city; and something strange appears regarding it." "What is that?" he asked. "The city we have described seems to me to be truly wise. For it is 'good in counsel,' is it not?" "It is." "And this very faculty of good counsel is surely a kind of knowledge. For it is not through ignorance, but through knowledge, that men counsel well." "That is evident." "But there are many and various kinds of knowledge in the city." "There are."

<column-break/>

<margin>F</margin> "Is the city to be called wise and 'good in counsel' because of the knowledge of its carpenters?" "By no means because of that," he said, "but rather it is called skilled in carpentry." "Therefore, the city is not to be called wise because it counsels on how wooden vessels might be best produced." "Certainly not." "Is it then because of the knowledge that crafts works of bronze? Or any other such thing?" "Certainly because of none of these." "Nor is it because of the knowledge of producing fruits from the earth; that is called agriculture." "So I think." "What then?" I said. "Is there any knowledge in the city we have just founded, held by any of the citizens, which deliberates not about some private matter in the city, but about the city as a whole, and how it may best conduct itself toward itself and toward other

<margin>G</margin> cities?" "There is indeed." "What is it, and in whom does it reside?" "It is the very diligence of guarding, and it resides in those rulers whom we just now called 'perfect guardians'." "By reason of this knowledge, then, what do you call the city?" "Good in counsel," he said, "and truly wise." "Do you think there will be more blacksmiths in our city, or more of these true guardians?" "Many more blacksmiths," he said. "And among all those who are called by the name of some knowledge, will these guardians not be the fewest of all?" "By far." "Therefore, by the smallest group and part of itself, and by the knowledge that resides in its presiding and ruling part, the whole city is founded to be wise according to nature.

<margin>H</margin> And this, as it seems, is the class which is by nature the fewest and rarest, to whom it belongs to share in this knowledge, which alone of all other knowledges deserves to be called wisdom." "What you say is very true," he said. "This one of the four, then, we have somehow or other found—both what it is and in what part of the city it is located." "In my opinion, at least," he said, "it has been sufficiently explained." "But as for courage, both what it is and in what part of the city it resides, by which the city is to be called courageous, that is not very difficult to see." "How do you mean?"

# ON THE REPUBLIC, BOOK IV

<margin>A</margin> ...is not very hard to see. "How so?" "Who," I asked, "would look at anything else to call a city cowardly or brave, except to that part which fights and campaigns in its defense?" "No one," he said, "would look at anything else." "For I do not think," I said, "that the others in the city, by being either cowardly or brave, would have the authority to make the city itself one way or the other." "Certainly not." "Therefore, a city is brave because of a certain part of itself, because it possesses within that part a power that will preserve, through everything, the right opinion about what things are to be feared—namely, that they are the very things and types of things which the legislator proclaimed in their education. Or do you not call this courage?" "I did not quite understand what you said," he replied; "say it again." "I am saying," I said, "that courage is a kind of <term>preservation</term> <note>original: "σωτηρίαν" / "conseruationem". Socrates defines courage not just as an impulse, but as the ability to "save" or keep hold of one's educated convictions under pressure.</note>." "What kind of preservation?"
<margin>B</margin> "The preservation of the opinion formed by the law through education regarding what things are to be feared, and what they are like. And I called it preservation 'through everything' because one must preserve it while in the midst of pains, and in pleasures, and in desires, and in fears, and never cast it out. If you like, I am willing to use a comparison to show what it is like." "I do like." "You know, then," I said, "that when dyers want to dye wool so that it will be <term>sea-purple</term> <note>original: "ἁλουργὰ" / "purpureo". This refers to the expensive Tyrian purple dye derived from murex snails, famous for its permanence.</note>, they first select from many colors a single kind, which is white. Then they prepare it with no small amount of treatment, so that it will receive the 'bloom' or color as best as possible, and only then do they dye it. Whatever is dyed in this way becomes <term>fast-dyed</term> <note>original: "δευσοποιὸν" / "indelebile". Literally "steeped in the grain," meaning the color cannot be washed out.</note>, and washing, whether
<margin>C</margin> without soap or with soap, cannot take away its bloom. But you know what happens to wool that is not prepared this way, whether one dyes it in other colors or even in these, without prior treatment." "I know," he said, "that they look washed-out and ridiculous." "Understand then," I said, "that we were striving to do something similar, to the best of our power, when we selected the soldiers and educated them in music and gymnastics. You should think we were devising nothing else than that they, being persuaded, should receive the laws from us like a dye, so that their opinion about what is to be feared and about all other things might become fast-dyed through their having both the right nature and the right upbringing. Thus, their 'dye' would not be washed out by these 'detergents'—which are powerful at scouring things away—namely <term>pleasure</term>, which is more effective at this than any soda or lye;
<margin>D</margin> and pain, and fear, and desire, which are more powerful than any other scouring agent. This power, then, which preserves through everything the right and lawful opinion about what is to be feared and what is not, is what I call and define as courage—unless you have something else to say." "No, I have nothing else," he said. "For you seem to me to think that the right opinion about these same things that arises without education—such as in beasts or slaves—is not quite lawful, and you would call it something other than courage." "You speak most truly," I said. "I accept, then, that this is courage." "Accept it indeed," I said, "as <term>political courage</term> <note>Socrates distinguishes the bravery of a citizen-soldier (based on law and habit) from the higher philosophical courage he will discuss later.</note>, and you will accept it rightly. We shall discuss it more beautifully another time, if you wish; for now, we were not seeking this, but justice. For the purpose of that search, I think this is sufficient."
<margin>E</margin> "You speak well," he said. "Two virtues still remain," I said, "which we must see in the city: temperance, and that for the sake of which we are searching for everything: justice." "Exactly." "How then could we find justice so that we no longer have to trouble ourselves with temperance?" "For my part," he said, "I neither know how, nor would I wish justice to appear first if we were no longer to examine temperance. So, if you want to please me, consider this before that." "I certainly do wish to," I said, "unless I am to be unjust." "Consider it then," he said. "It must be considered," I replied. "And as it appears from here, it looks more like a certain concord and harmony than the previous virtues did."
<margin>F</margin> "How so?" "<term>Temperance</term> <note>original: "σωφροσύνη" / "temperantia". Also translated as self-control, moderation, or soundness of mind.</note>," I said, "is surely a kind of order and a mastery over certain pleasures and desires, as they say—using the phrase 'being master of oneself'—and I do not know in what way other such things are said as if they were tracks of it. Is that not so?" "Most certainly," he said. "Is not the phrase 'master of oneself' ridiculous? For he who is master of himself would surely also be subject to himself, and he who is subject would be master; for the same person is referred to in all these terms." "Of course." "But," I said, "this speech seems to me to want to say that in the human being himself, regarding the soul, there is a better part and a worse part.
<margin>G</margin> And whenever the part that is better by nature has mastery over the worse, this is what is meant by 'being master of oneself' (it is at least a term of praise). But whenever, due to bad upbringing or some bad company, the better part—which is smaller—is mastered by the multitude of the worse, this is blamed as a disgrace, and the person in this condition is called 'subject to himself' and 'unrestrained'." "So it seems," he said. "Look then," I said, "at our new city, and you will find one of these conditions existing in it. For you will say that it is justly called master of itself, if indeed that in which the better rules the worse is to be called temperate and 'master of itself'." "I am looking," he said, "and you speak the truth." "Furthermore, one would find the many and diverse desires, pleasures, and pains mostly in children, women, servants, and in the many and base of those who are called free men." "Certainly." "But the simple and moderate desires, which are led by the mind and right opinion with the help of reason, you will meet with only in the few—those who are best born and best <margin>H</margin> <column-break/> <margin>A</margin> ...educated."

<note>This translation combines the sense of both the Greek and Latin columns. The Latin text is a faithful Renaissance-era rendering of the Greek, and both preserve the standard Stephanus numbering (A, B, C, etc.) used for referencing Plato.</note>

<summary>Socrates defines courage as the lifelong preservation of lawful beliefs through education, using a metaphor of dyeing wool to describe how character is made permanent. He then introduces temperance as a harmony where the "better" part of a person or city rules over the "worse" part.</summary>

<keywords>courage, temperance, education, self-mastery, dyeing metaphor, soul, harmony, political virtue</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the four virtues of the ideal city. Having defined Wisdom (in the rulers) and Courage (in the soldiers), Socrates and Glaucon are now concluding their discussion on Temperance before beginning the "hunt" for the final virtue, Justice.</meta>

<margin>A</margin>...and the most excellently educated. "These things are true," he said. "Do you not see these things in this city? And do you not see that the desires of the common crowd and the lowly are mastered there by the desires and the wisdom of the few who are the better sort?" "I see it indeed," he said. "If, then, any city ought to be called the master of its pleasures and desires, and master of itself, this city must be so called." "Entirely so," he replied. "And should we not also call it <term>temperate</term> <note>original: "temperata" / "σώφρονα" (sophrone). This refers to self-control and moderation.</note>?" "Most certainly." "And furthermore, if there is any city where the rulers and the subjects share the same opinion about who ought to rule, it would be this one. Do you not think so?" "Most definitely," he said. "In which of the citizens, then, will you say temperance resides when they are so disposed? In the rulers, or in the subjects?" "In both, I suppose," he said.
<margin>B</margin> "Do you see then," I said, "that we were quite right in our prophecy just now when we said that temperance is like a kind of harmony?" "How so?" "Because, unlike wisdom and courage—each of which resides in a specific part and makes the city either wise or brave—this virtue does not act that way. Instead, it is literally stretched through the whole city, bringing into <term>unison</term> <note>original: "consonent" / "ξυνᾴδοντας". Socrates is using a musical metaphor where the different classes of society represent different notes in a chord.</note> the weakest, the strongest, and those in the middle, whether you measure by wisdom, strength, numbers, wealth, or anything else. Therefore, we would be most correct to say that this concord is temperance: a natural agreement between the worse and the better parts as to which should rule, both in the city and in each individual."
<margin>C</margin> "I entirely agree," he said. "Well then," I said, "three of the virtues in our city have been discovered, at least as they appear to us. What then is the remaining form through which the city would further participate in virtue? For it is clear that this must be Justice." "It is clear." "Now then, Glaucon, we must act like hunters surrounding a thicket. We must pay close attention so that Justice does not somehow escape us and vanish into obscurity. It is evident that she is somewhere here. Look closely and strive to catch sight of her; if you see her before I do, point her out to me!" "I wish I could," he said, "but you will find me a much more useful companion if you let me follow you and see what you point out." "Follow then," I said, "and <margin>D</margin> pray with me." "I will do so," he said, "only lead the way." "Truly," I said, "this place seems difficult to pass and full of shadows. It is certainly dark and hard to search through. Nevertheless, we must push on." "We must indeed," he said. And catching sight of something, I cried out, "Aha! Aha! Glaucon, we seem to have found a trail, and I do not think it will escape us for long." "Good news!" he said. "Truly," I said, "we are being quite sluggish." "In what way?" "For a long time now, my blessed friend, the thing we seek has been rolling around right before our feet from the very beginning, and we did not see it. We were quite ridiculous—like people who search for what they already have in their hands. We did not look at it, but <margin>E</margin> kept looking off into the distance, which is probably why it escaped our notice." "How do you mean?" he asked. "I mean," I said, "that it seems to me we have been speaking of it and hearing of it for a long time without realizing that we were, in a way, describing it ourselves." "This is a long introduction," he said, "for someone who is eager to hear the answer." "Listen then," I said, "to see if I am right. For that principle which we established at the very beginning as a necessity when we were founding the city—that, or some form of it, is Justice. We established, and have often said, if you remember, that each individual must practice the one occupation in the city for which his nature is best suited." "We did say that." "Furthermore, that Justice is the act of <term>doing one's own business</term> <note>original: "sua agere" / "τὸ τὰ αὑτοῦ πράττειν". This is the core of Plato's definition: justice is non-interference in the roles of others.</note> and not being a busybody in the affairs of others; this is something we have heard from many others and have often said ourselves." "We have indeed." "This, then, my friend," I said, "is what Justice likely is: doing one's own work. Do you know how I infer this?" "Not at all; tell me." "It seems to me," I said, "that the remaining virtue in the city, beyond those we have considered—temperance, courage, and wisdom—is that which provided the power for all of them to be born, and which preserves them once they are born, as long as it remains present. And we said that Justice would be what remained if we found the other three." "That is necessary," he said. "However," I said, "if we had to judge which of these virtues, by its presence, does the most to make our city good, it would be a difficult judgment. Is it the agreement between rulers and subjects? Is it the preservation of lawful opinion among the soldiers regarding what is to be feared? Is it <margin>G</margin> the wisdom and guardianship in the rulers? Or does this virtue contribute most to the city's goodness—the fact that in child and woman, slave and free, craftsman, ruler and subject, each one performs his own single task and does not meddle in others'?" "It is a difficult judgment, certainly," he said. "How could it not be?" "Therefore, it seems that the power of each person in the city doing their own work competes with wisdom, temperance, and courage in contributing to the virtue of the city." "Very much so," he said. "And would you not call this competing principle Justice?" "Absolutely." "Consider it also in this way, to see if you agree. <margin>H</margin> Will you not charge the rulers in the city with the duty of judging lawsuits?" "Of course." "And in their judging, will they aim at anything more than this: that no one shall grab what belongs to another, nor be deprived of what is his own?" "Nothing other than that." "Because that is just?" "Yes." "And so, by this reasoning also, the possession and practice of what is one's own and belongs to oneself would be acknowledged as Justice." "That is so." "See then if you agree with me on this next point."

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>...and the most excellently educated. "Truly," he said. "Do you not see these things existing in your city, where the desires of the many and the base are mastered by the desires and the wisdom of the fewer and better sort?" "I do," he said. "If, therefore, any city should be called superior to pleasures and desires, and master of itself, it is this one." "Entirely so," he said. "And should we not also call such a city temperate?" "Very much so," he said. "And if in any other city there is the same opinion among the rulers and the subjects about who should rule, it would be found in this one. Or does it not seem so?" "Quite strongly," he said. "In which of the citizens, then, will you say that being temperate resides, when they are so disposed? <margin>B</margin> In the rulers or the subjects?" "In both, I suppose," he said. "Do you see then," I said, "that we were quite right in our guessing just now that temperance is like a kind of harmony?" "Why so?" "Because, unlike courage and wisdom, which each exist in a part and make the city either wise or brave, this one does not act that way. It is stretched throughout the whole, producing a harmony among the weakest, the middle, and the strongest—whether you speak of their wisdom, their strength, their numbers, their wealth, or any other such thing. So that we might most rightly say that this concord is temperance: a natural unison between the worse and the better as to which should rule in the city and in every individual." <margin>C</margin> "I entirely agree," he said. "Well then," I said, "three things have been discovered in our city, or so it seems. What then is the remaining form through which the city might still share in virtue? For it is clear that this is Justice." "It is clear." "Now then, Glaucon, we must, like hunters, station ourselves around the thicket and pay attention lest Justice escape us and disappear into the unknown. For it is clear she is here somewhere. Look, therefore, and be eager to see her; if you see her before I do, tell me." "I wish I could," he said, "but if you use me as a follower who can see what is pointed out, you will be using me quite well enough." "Follow then," I said, <margin>D</margin> "praying with me." "I will do so," he said, "only lead." "And truly," I said, "the place seems difficult to tread and deeply shadowed. It is dark and hard to search. But nonetheless, we must go on." "We must," he said. And I, looking out, said "Aha! Aha! Glaucon, we may have a trail; I think it will not altogether escape us." "Good news," he said. "In truth," I said, "we have been quite stupid." "In what way?" "For a long time now, my good man, it has been rolling before our feet from the beginning, and we did not see it. We were most ridiculous, like people who hold something in their hands while searching for it. We did not look at it, <margin>E</margin> but looked off into the distance, and so it probably escaped us." "How do you mean?" he asked. "I mean," I said, "that we seem to have been speaking and hearing of it for a long time without realizing we were saying it in a way." "This is a long prologue," he said, "for one who wants to hear." "Well then," I said, "listen to see if I am making sense. What we established at the beginning as a universal requirement when we were founding the city—that, I think, or some form of it, is Justice. We established then, and have often said, if you remember, that each one must practice the one thing related to the city for which his nature is best fitted." "We did say that." "And further, that to do one's own business and not be a meddler is Justice; this we have heard from many others and have often said ourselves." "We have." "This, then," I said, "my friend, is likely what Justice is: the doing of one's own business. Do you know why I suspect this?" "No, tell me." "It seems to me," I said, "that the remainder of what we have examined in the city—temperance, courage, and wisdom—is this very thing: that which gave all of them the power to come into being, and when they have come into being, provides them with safety as long as it is present. And we said that Justice would be the remainder if we found the other three." "It must be," he said. "But indeed," I said, "if it were necessary to judge which of these makes the city most good, it would be a hard choice: whether it is the shared opinion of the rulers and subjects, or the preservation of the lawful opinion <margin>G</margin> among the soldiers about what is and is not to be feared, or the wisdom and guardianship in the rulers. Or is it this that most makes the city good: its presence in child, woman, slave, free man, craftsman, ruler, and subject—the fact that each one does his own work and does not meddle?" "Hard to judge," he said, "how could it not be?" "Therefore, it seems, the power of each person in the city doing his own business competes in terms of the city's virtue with its wisdom, temperance, and courage." "Very much so," he said. "And would you not then place Justice as the thing that competes with these for the city's virtue?" "Entirely so." "Look at it this way too, to see if it seems so: will you not enjoin the rulers in the city to judge lawsuits?" "Certainly." "And will they judge with any other aim <margin>H</margin> than this: that no one should have what belongs to others, nor be deprived of his own?" "No, only this." "As being just?" "Yes." "And so, in this way too, it would be agreed that the having and doing of what is one's own and one's proper business is Justice." "That is so." "See now if you agree with me."

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from Book IV of Plato’s Republic. Having identified wisdom, courage, and temperance in the ideal city, Socrates and Glaucon are now finalizing their definition of justice before applying that same definition to the individual human soul.</meta>

-># ON THE REPUBLIC, BOOK IV.<-

<margin>A</margin> "If a carpenter attempts to perform the work of a cobbler," I said, "or a cobbler the work of a carpenter, or if they swap their tools or their social status, or if the same person tries to do both jobs at once—if all these things are swapped around—do you think this would greatly harm the city?" "Not particularly," he replied. "But whenever, I suppose, someone who is by nature a craftsman or a common laborer is puffed up by wealth, or by a large following, or by strength, or any such thing, and then attempts to enter the rank of the <term>warrior</term> <note>original: "πολεμικοῦ" (polemikou). The 'Auxiliary' class responsible for defense.</note>; or if one of the warriors attempts to enter the rank of the counselor and <term>guardian</term> <note>original: "φύλακος" (phylakos). The ruling class of philosopher-kings.</note> when he is unworthy of it; and if these people swap their tools and their honors with one another; or when the same person tries to do all these things at once; then, I think you would agree, this kind of internal change and <term>meddling</term> <note>original: "πολυπραγμοσύνη" (polypragmosyne). Literally 'doing many things' or 'officiousness.' This is the opposite of sticking to one's own business.</note> is the absolute destruction of the city." "Most certainly," he said.

<margin>B</margin> "Therefore, since there are three classes, this meddling and the shifting between them is the greatest possible harm to the city and would most rightly be called a <term>great evil</term> <note>original: "κακουργία" (kakourgia). Mischief or criminal wrongdoing.</note>." "Exactly so." "And would you not say that the greatest evil against one's own city is <term>injustice</term> <note>original: "ἀδικία" (adikia).</note>?" "How could it be otherwise?" "This, then, is what injustice is. But let us state the opposite: when the money-making class, the auxiliary class, and the guardian class each perform their own work in the city—this is <term>justice</term> <note>original: "δικαιοσύνη" (dikaiosyne). For Socrates, justice is 'minding one's own business' and everyone playing their proper role.</note> and is what makes the city just." "It seems to me," he said, "that it is exactly as you say."

<margin>C</margin> "Let us not yet assert this with total certainty," I said. "Rather, if this same principle is applied to each individual human being and is agreed to be justice there as well, then we shall give our consent. For what else could we say? But if not, then we shall look for something else. For now, let us complete the inquiry we began: we thought that if we could first observe justice in something larger that possesses it, it would be easier to see what it is like in a single person. And it seemed to us that this larger thing was the city. And so we constructed it as best we could, knowing well that justice would be found in a <margin>D</margin> good city. Therefore, what appeared to us there, let us now apply to the individual. If the two agree, that will be well. But if something different appears in the individual, we will return to the city to test it. By looking at them side-by-side and rubbing them together like fire-sticks, we might make justice shine forth; and once it is visible, we can fix it firmly in our own minds." "You speak with good sense," he said, "and that is how we must act."

"Therefore," I said, "if we call two things by the same name—one larger and one smaller—are they unlike in respect to that which makes them the same, or are they alike?" "They are alike," he said. "Then a just man will not differ at all from a just city in respect to the very form of justice, but will be like it." "He will be like it," he said.

<margin>E</margin> "But truly, the city was seen to be just when the three types of natures within it each performed their own work. Furthermore, it was seen to be temperate, brave, and wise because of certain conditions and habits of these same three classes." "That is true," he said. "And so, my friend, we shall expect that the individual—having these same three forms in his own soul—will rightly be called by the same names as the city, because they are affected in the same way." "That is absolutely necessary," he said. "Now we have stumbled upon a small matter!" I said. "The question of whether the soul possesses these three forms within itself or not." "It does not seem like a small matter to me," he said. "Perhaps, Socrates, the old saying is true: 'Fine things are difficult.'" <margin>F</margin> "So it seems," I said. "And you should know, Glaucon, that in my opinion, we will never grasp this accurately using the methods we are currently using in our discussion. The road that leads there is longer and more demanding. However, perhaps we can proceed in a way that is worthy of what we have already discussed and examined."

"Is that not enough?" he asked. "For me, at least for the present, it would be sufficient." "And for me," I said, "it will be quite enough." "Then do not grow weary," he said, "but continue the search." "Is it not then quite necessary for us to agree," I said, "that the same forms and characters that are in the city are also in each of us? For they could not have come there from anywhere else. It would be ridiculous if someone thought that the quality of <term>spirit</term> <note>original: "θυμοειδές" (thymoeides). The 'spirited' or 'lion-like' part of the soul associated with anger and honor.</note> did not come from the individual citizens—those who are famous for it, <margin>G</margin> such as the people of Thrace and Scythia and generally the northern regions; or the <term>love of learning</term> <note>original: "φιλομαθές" (philomathes). The desire for knowledge.</note>, which one might mostly attribute to our own region; or the <term>love of money</term> <note>original: "φιλοχρήματον" (philochrematon), which one might say is found most among the Phoenicians and the Egyptians." "Very true," he said.

"This is indeed the case," I said, "and it is not hard to recognize." "Not at all." "But this is the difficult part: do we perform each of these actions with the same part of ourselves, or are there three parts, one for each action? Do we learn with one part, feel anger with another, and with a third part desire the pleasures of food and procreation and their relatives? Or do we act with the soul as a whole whenever we set ourselves toward something? These are the things that will be difficult to define in a way that is worthy of the subject." "I think so too," he said. "Then let us try to define them in this way: are they the same as one another, or different?" "How?" "It is clear that the same thing will not be willing to do or undergo opposite things at the same time, in the same part of itself, and in relation to the same object. So, if we find these opposites occurring in these parts, we will know they were not the same thing, but many." "Very well." "Consider then what I say." "Speak on," he said. "Is it possible for the same thing to stand still and move at the same time in the same respect?" "By no means." "Now, let us be even more precise—"

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> If a craftsman should attempt the work of a leather-worker, or a leather-worker that of a craftsman, or if they should exchange their tools or their rewards, or if the same man strives to practice both, and all such things are exchanged among them, do you think this exchange affects the city with any great loss? "Certainly not," he said. But whenever some artisan or someone else who is by nature a money-maker, puffed up by riches, or by a great multitude, or by strength, or some other such thing, tries to cross over into the rank of the military man, or a soldier who is unworthy strives to ascend to the dignity of a counselor and guardian, and these people exchange their tools and rewards in turn, or the same man attempts to do all these things at once, then I think <margin>B</margin> you will see the destruction of the whole city. "And most especially so." Since there are therefore three classes in the city, the meddling in many affairs and the exchange of one for another is the ultimate calamity of the city, and it will most rightly be called its ruin. "It is so." And will you not say that the greatest ruin of your city is injustice? "Why not?" This, therefore, is injustice. But on the other hand, we say this: the proper action of the money-making, auxiliary, and guardian classes—each one performing its own work in the city—is the opposite of that confusion mentioned above; it will be justice and will make the city just. "It seems to <margin>C</margin> be no other way than this." We ought not to assert this entirely yet. But if the same form is affirmed to be justice when we consider it in the soul of each individual man, then at last we shall agree. For what else should we say? Otherwise, we will then think of something else. But now let us put an end to this discussion, according to which we thought that if we first contemplated justice in some larger thing that possessed it, we would then more easily inspect what kind of thing it is in a single man. And it seemed to us that this larger thing was the city itself, and so we founded it as best we could, knowing that <margin>D</margin> justice exists in a good republic. Therefore, that which appeared to us in the city, let us refer to the individual; and if the same thing holds there, it will be enough for us. But if something else should appear in the individual, we shall turn back to the city and examine these things; and perhaps by considering and striking them together like flints, we will strike out the spark of justice, and once it has shone clearly, we will establish it among ourselves. "You speak skillfully, and it must be done that way." Now, is that which we call the 'same,' whether it be larger or smaller, dissimilar insofar as it is called the same, or is it similar? "Similar, certainly." Therefore, a just man, as far as the form of justice is concerned, differs in no way from a just city, but will be similar. "Similar." But a city was seen to be just when <margin>E</margin> the three classes of men performed their own work according to the nature of each. It was also temperate, brave, and wise because of the dispositions and habits of these same classes, and not because of others. "These things are true." And so, my friend, we shall judge that the individual, having these same forms in his soul, deserves to share the same names with the city because of those same dispositions. "It is entirely necessary." Have we then fallen back, O marvelous one, into a slight thought about the soul—whether it has these three forms in itself or not? "It does not seem to me that we have slipped into a slight discussion. For perhaps what is said is true, O Socrates: that beautiful things are difficult." "It certainly appears so. And know for certain, O Glaucon, that in my opinion, <margin>F</margin> we shall never exactly comprehend this from such discourses as we are using in the present dispute; for the way that leads there is longer. Perhaps, however, it could be discussed worthily according to those things that were said and considered above." "Should that not seem enough?" "It will certainly suffice for me at present." "It will be quite enough for me as well." "Then let it not irk you, but consider. Truly it is necessary for us to confess that the same forms and characters exist in us as exist in the city. For they did not come into the city from anywhere else. Indeed, it would be ridiculous if someone thought that an angry spirit was not brought into cities by private individuals—those who have the same nature, such as the Thracians, the Scythians, and the northern nations; or <margin>G</margin> the study of wisdom, brought by the instinct of private men such as our own people are naturally gifted with; or the greed for gain, from that desire of individual men which the Phoenicians and the Egyptians are especially said to be affected by." "And most especially so." "This is indeed the case, and it is not difficult to know." "Certainly not difficult. But this is the difficult part: whether we do each of these things with one and the same part, or rather have three things in us, by each of which we perform one action: with one we learn, with another we are angry, and with a third we desire those pleasures which pertain to nutrition and procreation, and other things of this sort; or whether we fulfill each of these with the whole soul when we set about a thing. These things would not easily be discerned in a way worthy of the subject." "It seems so to me as well." "Let us then attempt to define these things, whether they are the same among themselves or different." "In what way?" "It is clearly established that the same thing cannot do or suffer opposites according to the same respect and in relation to the same thing at the same time. Therefore, if we ever find these things happening in them, we will understand that they are not one and the same, but many." "So be it." "Observe what I say." "Speak." "Is it possible for the same thing to stand still and be moved at the same time in the same respect?" "In no way." "Furthermore, let us consider these things more diligently—"

<summary>Socrates and Glaucon define justice as "minding one's own business"—each class in the city or each part of the soul performing its proper role. They introduce the principle of non-contradiction to prove the soul has distinct parts: the rational, the spirited, and the appetitive.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Glaucon in Book IV of Plato's Republic. Previously, Socrates defined justice in the city as each class performing its own specific function. Now, he begins to apply this logic to the human soul, establishing the principle of non-contradiction to prove the soul has distinct parts.</meta>

-># OF PLATO<-

<margin>A</margin> "...let us confirm this, lest any ambiguity perhaps arise for us as we proceed. For if someone should say of a man who is standing still, but moving his hands and head, that the same person is both standing and moving at the same time, we would not, I think, consider it right to speak this way. Instead, we would say that one part of him stands, while another part moves. Is that not so?" "It is indeed." "And if the person making these points should become even more clever and witty, playfully arguing that **spinning tops** <note>original: "turbinem trochúmque" in Latin; "στρόβιλοι" in Greek. A common toy used as a physical analogy for complex motion.</note> as a whole both stand still and move at the same time when they are fixed on a single point and revolve around their center—or anything else that moves in a circle while remaining in the same place—we would not accept his argument. We would say that such objects are not standing and moving in the same respect. 
<margin>B</margin> Instead, we would say that they have both a straight axis and a circumference; in respect to the straight axis they stand still (since they do not lean in any direction), but in respect to the circumference they move in a circle. However, whenever the axis itself inclines to the right or left, forward or backward while it is revolving, then it is in no way standing still." "Quite right," he said. "Therefore, no such objections will disturb us or persuade us that the same thing, at the same time, in the same respect, and in relation to the same object, could ever act or be acted upon in contrary ways." "They certainly will not move me," he said. "Nevertheless," I said, "so that we are not <margin>C</margin> forced to linger too long in refuting all these false objections, let us proceed on the assumption that this principle is correct. We will agree that if these things should ever appear otherwise than they do now, all the conclusions we draw from them will be considered void." "That is certainly the right way to proceed," he said. "Now," I said, "would you not categorize nodding and shaking the head, desiring to take something and refusing it, or drawing something toward oneself and repelling it, as being opposites of one another, whether you call them actions or passions?" "It makes no difference," he said, "they are opposites." "What then," <margin>D</margin> I said, "about hunger, thirst, and the desires in general, as well as wishing and willing? Would you not place all of these in the categories we just mentioned? For instance, would you not say that the soul of one who desires always either seeks that which it appetites, or draws to itself that which it wishes to have? Or again, insofar as it wants something to be provided for it, does it not nod 'yes' to itself, as if in answer to a question, reaching out for the fulfillment of its desire?" "I would." "But what about not-wishing, being unwilling, and not-desiring? Shall we not place these in the category of repelling and driving away from the soul, and generally in the category of opposites?" "Of course." "Since this is so, shall we say there is a specific class of desires, and that the most obvious of these are what we call thirst and hunger?" "We shall," he said. "And one is for drink, the other for food?" "Yes." "Now, insofar as it is thirst, is it a desire in the soul for anything more than that? For instance, is thirst a desire for <term>hot drink</term> <note>Socrates is distinguishing between a simple desire and a qualified desire.</note> or cold, or much or little, or in a word, for a drink of a certain quality? Or rather, if heat is present in the thirsty person, does it induce a desire for the cold? And if 
<margin>E</margin> cold is present, a desire for the hot? And if the thirst is great due to a large presence of need, will it produce a desire for much? But if the need is small, a desire for little? But the act of thirsting itself is never a desire for anything else than its own natural object, which is drink; and likewise, hunger is for food?" "Just so," he said, "each desire itself is only for its own natural object. The desire for a drink of a certain kind or quality is an addition." "Now," I said, "let no one catch us off guard or disturb us with the claim that no one desires 'drink,' but rather 'good drink,' or not 'food,' but 'good food,' since everyone desires good things. Thus, if thirst is a desire, it must be for something good—whether drink or whatever else it happens to be. And the same for other desires." 
<margin>F</margin> "Perhaps," he said, "the person who said that might seem to have a point." "Nevertheless," I said, "whatever things are of such a nature as to be 'of' something, those that are of a certain quality are 'of' an object of a certain quality, I believe; but those that are just themselves are 'of' an object that is just itself." "I do not quite understand," he said. "Do you not understand," I said, "that the 'greater' is such as to be greater than something?" "Certainly." "Namely, greater than the smaller?" "Yes." "And the 'much greater' than the 'much smaller,' is it not?" "Yes." "And the 'once greater' than the 'once smaller,' and the 'future greater' than the 'future smaller'?" "Of course," he said. "And the same applies to 'more' in relation to 'fewer,' and 'double' to 'half,' and all such things; and also 'heavier' to 'lighter,' 'faster' to 'slower,' and 'hot' to 'cold,' and all things similar to these; is it not so?" "Certainly." <margin>G</margin> "And what about the various branches of knowledge? Is the principle not the same? **Knowledge** <note>original: "Scientia" / "ἐπιστήμη".</note> itself is knowledge of the 'knowable' itself, or whatever we should designate as the object of knowledge. But a particular kind of knowledge, of a certain quality, is of a particular kind of object. For example: when the knowledge of building houses arose, it was distinguished from other kinds of knowledge, and so was called **architecture** <note>original: "ædificatoria" / "οἰκοδομική".</note>." "Why not?" "Was it not because it was of a certain quality, which no other branch of knowledge possessed?" "Yes." "Therefore, because it was of a certain kind of object, it became a certain kind of knowledge itself. And is this not the case for all other arts and sciences?" "It is so." "This, then," I said, "is what I wanted to say earlier—if you understand now—that things which are 'of' something are, if taken alone, only of the object alone; but if they are of a certain quality, they are of a certain kind of object. I do not mean that they are of the same quality as their objects <margin>H</margin> (as if the knowledge of health and disease were itself healthy and diseased, or the knowledge of evil and good were itself evil and good). Rather, since knowledge is not of the object itself..."

<column-break/>

"...let us come to an agreement, so that we do not disagree as we go further. For if someone should say of a man standing still, but moving his hands and his head, that the same man stands and moves at the same time, we would not, I think, agree that one should speak this way; rather, that some part of him stands, and another moves. Is it not so?" "It is." "Therefore, even if the one saying these things should become more sophisticated and witty, playing the part of a clever person, saying that **spinning tops** <note>original: "στρόβιλοι".</note> as a whole both stand and move at the same time whenever they revolve with their center fixed in the same place; or that anything else moving in a circle in the same spot does this, we would not accept it, because such things do not stand and move in respect to the same parts of themselves. Rather, we would say that they have both a straight line and a circumference in themselves; and in respect to the straight line they stand (for they do not incline in any way), but in respect to the circumference they move in a circle. But when the straight axis inclines either to the right or to the left, or to the front or the back while it is revolving, then it is in no way standing." "And quite rightly," he said. "Nothing, then, of such things being said will frighten us; nor will it persuade us any more that anything being the same at the same time, in the same respect, and in relation to the same object, could suffer or even do contrary things." "Not me, at least," he said. "But nevertheless," I said, "in order that we are not compelled to go through all such disputes and confirm that they are not true—which would make our speech long—let us hypothesize that this is so and proceed forward, having agreed that if these things should ever appear otherwise than this, all the things that follow for us from this will be undone." "Indeed," he said, "it is necessary to do this." "Therefore," I said, "nodding in agreement and shaking the head in denial, and the desiring to take something and the refusing of it, and the drawing toward oneself and the repelling—would you place all such things as being opposites to one another, whether they are actions or passions? For it will make no difference in this respect." "Nay," he said, "they are opposites." "What then?" I said, "thirsting and hungering, and generally the desires, and again willing and wishing, would you not place all these into those forms which were just mentioned? For example, will you not say that the soul of one who desires always either seeks that which he desires, or draws to himself that which he wishes to happen to him? Or again, insofar as he wishes something to be provided for him, he nods 'yes' to this toward himself, as if answering someone who asked, reaching out toward the realization of it?" "I would." "But what? To not-wish, and to not-will, and to not-desire, shall we not say these belong to repelling and driving away from the soul, and to all the opposites of the former?" "How could we not?" "This being the case, shall we say there is a kind of desires? And that the most manifest of these are what we call thirst and hunger?" "We shall say so," he said. "Is not one for drink, and the other for food?" "Yes." "Therefore, insofar as it is thirst, do we say it is a desire in the soul for anything more than what it is? For example, is thirst a thirst for a hot drink or a cold one, or much or little, or in a single word, for a drink of a certain quality? Or if some heat is added to the thirst, might it provide the desire for something cold? And if coldness, the desire for something hot? And if the thirst is great due to the presence of quantity, will it provide the desire for much? And if little, for little? But the act of thirsting itself will never be a desire for anything other than its natural object: drink itself; and again, hungering for food?" "Thus," he said, "each desire itself is only for that which it is by nature; the desire for this or that kind of object is an addition." "Lest anyone," I said, "should disturb us when we are off our guard, claiming that no one desires drink, but good drink, and not food, but good food. For everyone, it seems, desires good things. If, then, thirst is a desire, it would be for something good, whether of drink or whatever else it is a desire for; and the others likewise." "Perhaps," he said, "the one saying these things would seem to be saying something." "But nevertheless," I said, "whatever things are such as to be 'of' something, those that are of a certain quality are of a certain kind of object, as it seems to me; but the things themselves are each of the object itself alone." "I did not learn your meaning," he said. "Did you not learn," I said, "that the 'greater' is such as to be greater than something?" "Certainly." "Is it not greater than the smaller?" "Yes." "And the 'much greater' than the 'smaller'? Is it not?" "Yes." "Therefore, also the 'once greater' than the 'once smaller'? And the 'future greater' than the 'future smaller'?" "What else?" he said. "And 'more' to 'fewer,' and 'double' to 'half,' and all such things; and again 'heavier' to 'lighter,' and 'faster' to 'slower'; and furthermore 'hot' to 'cold,' and all things similar to these; do they not stand so?" "Certainly." "What about things concerning knowledge? Is it not the same way? Knowledge itself is knowledge of the 'learnable' itself, or whatever knowledge should be placed upon. But a certain knowledge and of a certain quality is of a certain kind and a certain object. I mean something like this: when the knowledge of house-building arose, it differed from other knowledges, so that it was called **architecture** <note>original: "οἰκοδομική".</note>?" "Of course." "Was it not by being a certain kind, such as no other of the others was?" "Yes." "Therefore, since it was of a certain kind of object, it also became a certain kind of knowledge? And the other arts and knowledges likewise?" "It is so." "This then," I said, "say that I wanted to say then, if you have now learned that whatever things are such as to be 'of' something, those that are alone are of the object alone, but those of a certain kind are of a certain kind of object. And I do not say that of whatever kind they may be, they are also such (as that the knowledge of the healthy and the diseased is itself healthy and diseased; and that of the bad and the good is itself bad and good); but because it was not of that itself of which knowledge is..."

<summary>Socrates establishes the principle of non-contradiction—that one thing cannot be in opposite states in the same respect—using the analogy of a spinning top. He then applies this to human psychology, arguing that basic desires like thirst are for their natural objects alone, unless specifically qualified.</summary>
<keywords>non-contradiction, spinning top analogy, psychology of desire, thirst, hunger, relativity, specific knowledge, architecture, Socrates, Glaucon</keywords>
