<meta>This page continues the dialogue from the previous section where Socrates uses the principle of non-contradiction to analyze the soul. Having established that the same thing cannot act in contrary ways at the same time, he now applies this to the conflict between desire and reason, eventually identifying three distinct parts of the human soul.</meta>

-># ON THE REPUBLIC, BOOK IV.<-

"So then, as I said regarding knowledge," I began, "would I be right to say that <margin>A</margin> when it becomes associated with things like health and disease, a specific kind of knowledge arises? This is why it is no longer called simply 'knowledge,' but because a certain quality was added, it is called **medical science**." "I understand," he said, "and it seems to me to be so." "And thirst, then," I said, "would you not place it among those things that are what they are in relation to something else? Thirst is, presumably, thirst for...?" "I would indeed," he said, "it is for **drink**." "Therefore, for a certain kind of drink, there is a certain kind of thirst? But thirst itself is neither for much nor little, <margin>B</margin> nor for good nor bad, nor, in a word, for any specific quality; rather, is it not the nature of thirst itself to be only for drink itself?" "Exactly so." "Now, let no one catch us off guard or disturb us with the claim that no one desires 'drink' but rather 'good drink,' or not 'food' but 'good food.' For everyone, they say, desires **good things**. If thirst is a desire, it would be for something good—whether drink or whatever else it is a desire for—and the same for the others." "Perhaps," he said, "the person saying that might seem to have a point." <margin>C</margin> "But surely," I said, "whenever things are such as to be 'of something,' those that have a specific quality are of a specific kind of object, while those that are just themselves are only of the object itself." "I don't understand," he said. "Do you not understand," I asked, "that the 'greater' is such as to be greater than something?" "Certainly." "Than the 'smaller'?" "Yes." "And the 'much greater' is than the 'much smaller'?" "Yes." "And the 'once greater' than the 'once smaller'? And the 'future greater' than the 'future smaller'?" <margin>D</margin> "Of course." "And so it is with 'more' in relation to 'fewer,' and 'double' to 'half,' and all such things; and again, 'heavier' to 'lighter,' and 'faster' to 'slower'; and even 'hot' to 'cold,' and all similar things—is it not so?" "Certainly." "And what about the branches of knowledge? Is it not the same way? Knowledge itself is knowledge of the 'learnable' itself, or whatever we should designate as the object of knowledge. But a specific kind of knowledge is of a specific kind of object. I mean it like this: <margin>E</margin> when the knowledge of building houses arose, did it not differ from other knowledges by being a specific kind?" "How could it not?" "And was it not because it was of a specific kind of thing?" "Yes." "And as shipbuilding is for ships, and so on for the rest?" "Certainly." "Therefore," I said, "say the same of thirst: in itself it is what it is by nature—it is of 'drink' itself. But if a specific quality is added, it becomes a specific kind of thirst. Yet thirst itself is neither for much, nor little, nor good, nor bad, nor in a word for any quality, but thirst itself is by nature for drink alone." "Exactly so." <margin>F</margin> "Now," I said, "the soul of the thirsty person, insofar as it thirsts, wishes for nothing other than to drink; it reaches for this and is driven toward it." "That is clear." "Therefore, if something ever pulls the soul back when it is thirsty, would there not be something else in it, different from the part that thirsts and leads it like a beast toward drink? For we say that the same thing cannot perform contrary actions with the same part of itself toward the same object at the same time." "It cannot." "Just as," I said, "it is not right to say of an **archer** <margin>G</margin> that his hands are simultaneously pushing the bow away and pulling it toward him; rather, one hand is the one pushing, and the other is the one pulling." "Absolutely," he said. "Now, can we say that there are sometimes people who are thirsty but do not wish to drink?" "Indeed," he said, "many people, and many times." "What then," I asked, "should one say about them? Is there not something in their soul commanding them to drink, and something forbidding them to drink, which is different from and masters the commander?" <margin>H</margin> "So it seems to me." "Does it not happen that the forbidding element arises, when it does, from **reasoning** <note>original: "logismou" (λογισμοῦ). This refers to the logical, calculating part of the mind.</note>, while the forces that lead and pull arise from passions and diseases?" "It appears so." "We shall not be unreasonable," I said, "if we claim these are two distinct parts. We shall call that by which the soul reasons the **Rational** <note>original: "logistikon" (λογιστικόν)</note> part; and that with which it loves, hungers, thirsts, and is fluttered by other desires, we shall call the **Irrational** and **Appetitive** <note>original: "epithymetikon" (ἐπιθυμητικόν)</note> part, a companion to certain fulfillments and pleasures." "No, it is only natural," he said, "for us to think so." "Let these two types, then, be defined as existing in the soul. But what about **Spirit** <note>original: "thymou" (θυμοῦ). This is the 'spirited' part related to anger, honor, and courage.</note>, or that by which we get angry—is it a third part? Or would it be of the same nature as one of the others?" "Perhaps," he said, "as the appetitive part." "But," I said, "I once heard a story that I believe: that **Leontius** <note>Leontius, son of Aglaion, is a classic example used to show the conflict between the three parts of the soul: desire (to look), reason (it's wrong), and spirit (anger at his own failure).</note>, the son of Aglaion, was coming up from the Piraeus under the outside of the Northern Wall when he noticed corpses lying by the public executioner. He desired to see them, but at the same time he was disgusted and turned himself away. For a while he fought and covered his eyes, but finally, overcome by the desire, he forced his eyes wide open, ran toward the corpses, and said, 'Look for yourselves, you miserable wretches, take your fill of the beautiful sight!'" "I have heard it too," he said. "This story, however," I said, "indicates that **anger** <note>original: "orgen" (ὀργήν)</note> sometimes fights against the desires, as if they were two different things." "It does indicate that," he said. "And do we not notice elsewhere," I said, "that often when desires force someone against their reason, the person reviles himself and is angry at the thing within him that forces him? And just as if there were two factions at war, the spirit becomes an ally to the reason? But as for the spirit making common cause with the desires when reason forbids it—I don't think you would say you have ever perceived such a thing happening in yourself, nor, I think, in anyone else." "No, by Zeus," he said. "And what happens," I asked, "when someone thinks he is being treated unjustly? Is it not true that the more noble he is, the less he is able to be angry—even if he suffers hunger, cold, or any other such thing at the hands of one whom he thinks is acting justly? And as I say, his spirit refuses to be roused against such a person." "That is true," he said. "But what when he thinks he is being wronged? Does he not then boil and chafe, and fight for what he thinks is just? And though he suffers hunger and cold and all such things, he endures and is victorious, and does not cease from his noble efforts until he either achieves his end, or dies, or is called back and calmed by the **reason** within him, like a dog by a shepherd?" "Exactly," he said, "it is like the comparison you make. Indeed, in our city, we established the **auxiliaries** <note>The soldier/guardian class in Plato's ideal city.</note> as dogs, obedient to the rulers as if to the shepherds of the city." "You understand perfectly what I mean to say," I replied. "But do you also consider this?" "What?" "That our view of the spirited part is now the opposite of what it was before. For then we thought it was something appetitive; but now we say it is far from that, and that in the soul's civil war, it takes up arms on the side of the rational part." "Entirely so," he said. "Is it then different from the rational part as well, so that there are not three but only two types in the soul, the rational and the appetitive? Or, just as there were three classes that held the city together—the money-makers, the auxiliaries, and the counselors—is there likewise this third 'spirited' part in the soul, which is the natural helper of the rational part, unless it is corrupted by bad upbringing?" "It must be a third," he said. "Yes," I said, "provided it appears to be something other than the rational part, just as it appeared to be different from the appetitive." "But that is not hard to show," he said. "For one can see this even in small children: from the moment they are born they are full of spirit, yet some never seem to me to partake in reasoning, and most do so only late in life." "By Zeus," I said, "you have put it well. And one can see what you say in beasts as well. Moreover, the verse from **Homer** <note>Odyssey 20.17</note> that we quoted earlier will bear witness, where he says:

> He struck his chest and rebuked his heart with a word.

For there, Homer clearly shows one part rebuking another—the part that has reasoned about what is better and worse rebuking the part that is irrationally angry." "You are absolutely right," he said.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...it became a specific kind of knowledge; or rather, it turned out to be knowledge of a specific kind of thing, namely health and sickness. From this, it happened that it was no longer called simply "knowledge," but with a certain quality added, it was called **medical science**. I understand now, and these things seem to me to be so. But thirst—would you not number it among those things that exist in relation to something else? For what is thirst? I would certainly number it so, and I say that it is a thirst for **drink**. Is it not a thirst for a certain kind of drink? Therefore, thirst itself is neither for much nor little, nor good nor bad, nor to embrace it in a single word, of any specific quality, but is by nature purely a thirst for drink itself? <margin>B</margin> It is entirely so. The soul of the thirsty person, then, insofar as it thirsts, desires nothing other than to drink, and it affects this and is carried toward it. It is established. If, therefore, something ever pulls the thirsty person back, it must be something in the soul distinct from that part which thirsts, which drives it toward drink like a beast. For we say it is impossible for the same thing, in the same part of itself, to act in contrary ways toward the same thing at the same time. Certainly not—just as it would be absurd to say that the hands of the same **archer** simultaneously push the bow away and pull it back. Rather, one must say that one hand pushes and the other hand pulls. Quite so. Do we <margin>C</margin> admit that there are some who, though they thirst, are sometimes unwilling to drink? Many, and often. What shall one say of these: is there not something in their soul that allures them to drink, and something else that prohibits it? Which is indeed different and dominates the alluring part. So it seems to me. Does it not then follow that the part which prohibits these things is in the soul by **reason** <note>original: "ex ratione"</note> whenever it acts? While the things that incite and pull are from the passions and disturbances? It appears so. <margin>D</margin> We shall therefore rightly consider these two to be different from each other. That by which the soul reasons, we shall call its **Rational** part. But that by which it loves, hungers, and thirsts, and falls more prone to other lusts, we shall call the **Irrational**, the greedy companion of certain fulfillments and pleasures. Certainly they are different, he said. And we shall rightly judge them so. Let these two species in the soul, then, I said, be distinct. But as for that which pertains to anger, or by which we are angered—is it some third thing? Or is it kindred to one of these two? <margin>E</margin> Perhaps, he said, it is kindred to the part that desires pleasures. And yet I believe this on account of what I once heard: namely, that when **Leontius**, son of Aglaion, was ascending from the Piraeus under the northern wall (to the city), he sensed corpses lying in the city's pit and public sewer; at once he desired to look, yet he was horrified and turned away, covering his face, fighting with himself. Finally, overcome by desire, he ran to the corpses with wide eyes, saying: 'Behold, now you may, oh unhappy ones, satisfy your desire with this "beautiful" sight.' I have heard it myself. Therefore, this story testifies that **anger** often fights against concupiscence, as if these were different things from each other. It certainly signifies that. Do we not also frequently observe elsewhere, when desires do violence to someone against reason, that they rebuke themselves and are indignant against that part of themselves which does the violence? And as if two were dissenting, the anger runs to help the reason? But as for being joined to the desires, to move against the will of reason—I do not think you have ever claimed to have caught such a thing in yourself or in another. <margin>F</margin> Never, by Jove. What then? I said. When someone thinks he is committing an injustice, is it not true that the more noble he is, the less he is able to be angry, even while he hungers and freezes and suffers any other such thing from the one he thinks acts justly? And as I have said, the anger of such a man is not roused against him? You speak the truth. But what when someone thinks he is suffering an injury? Does he not then boil and rage, and offer help to that which seems just, enduring hunger, cold, and other such things? And he contends for victory, nor does he cease from his noble <margin>G</margin> efforts, until he either succeeds, or dies, or like a dog by a shepherd, is finally called back by the **reason** within him and becomes mild? Entirely so; this power is like the one you compare it to. For in our city we placed the **auxiliaries** themselves as dogs, obeying the princes as if they were the shepherds of the city. You have understood very well what I wished to say. But do you notice this one thing more? What is that? That at present we judge the opposite of what we did above concerning irascibility. For then we referred the power of anger to the nature of concupiscence. But now we say there is a great difference, and we claim much more that anger takes up arms for reason when the parts of the soul are at odds. Quite so. <margin>H</margin> Is the power of anger also different from reason, or is it a species of reason, so that there are not three, but only two species in the soul—the rational and the appetitive? Or rather, just as three classes contained the city—the money-making, the auxiliary, and the consultative—so also in the soul is there a certain third power, namely irascibility, which by its own nature protects the parts of reason, unless it has been depraved by wicked education? It must be that it is a third. Truly, even if it appears to be something other than reason, just as it was seen above to differ from concupiscence. But indeed, that can easily be made clear. For anyone may understand this in children, who are full of irascibility as soon as they are born. But of reason, some seem to me never to become masters, and many only late in life. By Jove...

<summary>Socrates establishes the tripartite division of the soul—Rational, Appetitive, and Spirited—using the principle of internal conflict and the illustrative story of Leontius. He concludes that Spirit (Thymos) is a natural ally to Reason, distinct from the base desires.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from the previous section where Socrates and Glaucon established that the human soul consists of three distinct parts: the rational, the spirited (or "irascible"), and the appetitive. This mimics the three-class structure of their ideal city.</meta>

->### OF PLATO<-

I said, you speak most excellently. Furthermore, one can see that this is the case even in beasts, <margin>Odyssey, Book 20</margin> as you yourself say. Homer also bears witness to this in the passage we quoted earlier: *Striking his breast, he rebuked his heart with words.* <note>original: "Pectora percutiens monitis affatur acerbis." This is a Latin translation of Homer, Odyssey 20.17.</note> <margin>A</margin> For here, Homer clearly depicts one part of the soul rebuking the other—namely, the part that reasons about what is better and worse rebuking the irrational impulse of anger. You speak quite rightly, he said. 

And so, I said, we have finally reached the shore with difficulty; we have fairly well agreed that the same classes that exist in the city also exist in the soul of every individual, and that they are equal in number. This is so. Must it not then follow that the individual is wise in the same way and by the same part that the city was wise? Certainly. And that <margin>B</margin> the individual is brave in the same way and by the same part that the city is brave, and that in all other matters of virtue, both the individual and the city stand in the same relation? It must be so. And we shall say, O Glaucon, that a man is **just** in the same way that a city was just. That too is entirely necessary. 

But we have not forgotten that the city was seen to be just because each of the three classes within it performed its own specific function. I do not think we have forgotten, he said. We must therefore remember that <margin>C</margin> each of us will be just—doing his own work—when each part of his soul performs its own proper task. We must certainly remember that. Does it not belong to the **rational part** <note>original Latin: "rationali potentiæ"</note> to rule, since it is wise and exercises foresight for the whole soul? And does it not belong to the **spirited part** <note>original Latin: "iraſcendi naturæ," referring to the part of the soul responsible for anger, courage, and "will-power"</note> to be its subject and ally? Entirely so. 

And as we said before, will not a blending of music and gymnastics <note>In a Platonic context, "music" refers to all the arts and sciences (the Muses), and "gymnastics" to physical training.</note> bring these two into harmony? It will strengthen and nourish the rational part with noble words and teachings, while it will relax, soothe, and tame the spirited part through harmony and rhythm. Most certainly, he said. And when these two have been so nurtured and have truly learned their own roles and been educated, they will preside over the **appetitive part** <note>The "concupiscent" part that desires food, sex, and money.</note> which is the largest part of the soul in every man and is by nature insatiably greedy for wealth. They will watch over it, lest it become gorged on the so-called pleasures of the body and, growing large and strong, it no longer performs its own task <margin>D</margin> but attempts to enslave and rule over those things it is not suited by nature to rule, thereby overturning the entire life of the soul. 

Quite so, he said. And would these two parts not also be the best defenders of the whole soul and body against external enemies? The one part takes counsel with foresight, while the other fights, following the leader and carrying out the plans through its courage. That is true. And we call an individual **brave**, I think, because of this spirited part, when it preserves the commands of reason regarding what is and is not to be feared, through both pains and pleasures. Correct, he said. And we call him **wise** because of that small part which rules within him and gives those commands, possessing within itself the knowledge <margin>E</margin> of what is beneficial for each part and for the whole community of the three parts together. Certainly. 

And do we not call him **temperate** <note>original Latin: "temperantem," translating the Greek "sophrosyne," meaning self-control or moderation.</note> because of the friendship and harmony of these same parts? That is, when the ruling part and the two subject parts agree that the rational part ought to rule, and they do not rebel against it. Temperance, he said, is surely nothing other than this, whether in a city or an individual. And finally, a man will be **just** because of that principle we have stated so often and in such detail. It is entirely necessary, he said. 

What then? I asked. Is there anything that blurs our view so that justice seems to be something different <margin>F</margin> from what it appeared to be in the city? It does not seem so to me, he said. We can confirm this completely, I said, if there is still any doubt in our minds, by applying common or "vulgar" tests to it. What kind of tests? For instance, if we had to deliberate about this city and a man who is born and raised in the same way, whether such a man, if he received a deposit of gold or silver, would be thought likely to embezzle it. Do you think anyone would judge such a man more likely to commit a fraud than those who are not like him? No one at all. And will he not also be free from sacrilege, theft, and betrayals, whether privately against his companions or publicly against the state? <margin>G</margin> Certainly. Moreover, he would never be unfaithful to his oaths or other agreements. By no means. Adultery, neglect of parents, and lack of religious devotion to the Gods are more suited to anyone else than to a man of this character. Entirely so. 

And is the cause of all this not that each part within him performs its own work, whether in ruling or in being ruled? That is surely the cause, and nothing else. Do you then seek any other definition of justice than this power which produces such men and such cities? Not I, by Zeus, he said. 

At last, that **dream** of ours is fulfilled, which we said we suspected: that from the very beginning of our founding of the city, by some divine favor, we had likely stumbled upon a starting point and a model of justice. Quite so. For it was, O Glaucon, a sort of image of justice—which is why it was useful—that the man who is a cobbler by nature should practice the craft of cobbling and do nothing else, and the carpenter should build. And so on for the others. It appears so. 

In truth, justice is such a thing, but it is not concerned with the external actions of a man, but with his internal action—truly concerning himself and his own parts. It does not allow any of the parts within him to do the work of another, nor does it let the various classes of the soul 

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> I said, you have spoken well. Furthermore, one might see this in beasts as well, proving that what you say is true. To these things, we may add the testimony of Homer which we mentioned somewhere above: *Striking his chest, he rebuked his heart with words.* <note>Greek: "Στῆθος δὲ πλήξας, κραδίην ἠνίπαπε μύθῳ." From Odyssey 20.17.</note> For here clearly, Homer has depicted one thing rebuking another—the part that has calculated about better and worse rebuking the part that is irrationally angry. You are absolutely right, he said. 

These things, I said, we have finally reached by swimming through them with difficulty; and we have fairly well agreed that the same kinds of parts that are in the city are also in the soul of each individual, and are equal in number. This is so. Must it not then follow that, just as the city was wise, and by the same principle, the individual is also wise? Why not? And that by which the <margin>B</margin> individual is brave, and in the same way, by that the city is also brave? And in everything else regarding virtue, both have the same relation. It is necessary. And we shall say, O Glaucon, I think, that a man is **just** in the same way that a city was just. This too is quite necessary. 

But we have not forgotten this, surely: that the city was just because each of the three groups within it performed its own tasks. I do not think we have forgotten, he said. We must therefore remember that each of us, when the parts within him each do their own work, will be just and a doer of his own work. We must certainly remember that, he said. Does it not then belong to the **reasoning part** <margin>C</margin> to rule, being wise and having the foresight for the whole soul, while the **spirited part** is to be its subject and ally? Certainly. 

And will not, as we were saying, the mixture of music and gymnastics make them harmonious, by stretching and nourishing the one with noble words and lessons, and by relaxing, comforting, and taming the other with harmony and rhythm? Quite so, he said. And these two, having been so reared and having truly learned their own roles and been educated, will preside over the **appetitive part**, which is the largest part of the soul in each person, and is by nature most insatiable for money. They will watch over it, lest it be filled with the so-called pleasures of the body and, becoming large and strong, no longer performs its own task, but attempts to enslave and rule over those it is not suited to by its nature, and so overturns the whole life of all. Entirely so, <margin>D</margin> he said. 

And would these two not also most beautifully guard against enemies from without, on behalf of the whole soul and body, the one part taking counsel, and the other fighting, following the ruler and through its courage carrying out what has been counseled? These things are so. And we call a person **brave**, I think, by this part, when his spirited part preserves through both pains and pleasures the command of reason about what is to be feared and what is not. Correct, he said. 

And we call him **wise** by that small part that ruled in him and gave these commands, it also possessing within itself the knowledge of what is beneficial to each part and to the whole community of these three parts. Quite so. And what of **temperance**? Is it not by the friendship and harmony of these same <margin>E</margin> parts, when the ruler and the two ruled parts agree in the opinion that the reasoning part must rule, and they do not rebel against it? Temperance indeed, he said, is nothing else but this, in both city and individual. 

And surely he will be **just** by that which we have often said, and in this way. There is much necessity for it. What then? I said. Does justice in any way seem blurred to us, or to be something other than what it appeared to be in the city? Not to me, he said. In this way, I said, <margin>F</margin> we might confirm it altogether, if anything still disputes it in our soul, by bringing common tests to it. What kind? For example, if we had to agree, concerning that city and the man who is naturally like it and has been so reared, whether such a man, having received a deposit of gold or silver, would seem likely to embezzle it. Who do you think would believe he would do this rather than those who are not of his kind? No one, he said. 

And would he not be far from sacrilege, theft, and betrayals, either privately of companions or publicly of cities? Far from it. And he would not be in any way unfaithful to oaths or other agreements. How could he be? Adulteries, and neglect of parents, and lack of service to the gods belong to any other man rather than such a one. To any other indeed, he said. And is the cause of all this not that each of the parts within him performs its own work regarding ruling and being ruled? This, and nothing else. Do you then still look for justice to be something other <margin>G</margin> than this power which makes such men and cities? By Zeus, he said, not I. 

Therefore, our dream has been perfectly fulfilled, which we said we suspected: that as soon as we began to found our city, by some god’s help, we had likely stepped into a beginning and a pattern of justice. Altogether so. And that was, O Glaucon—which is also why it is beneficial—a kind of image of justice: that the man who is a cobbler by nature should rightly be a cobbler and do nothing else, and the carpenter a carpenter, and so on for the others. It appears so. 

But justice was in truth, it seems, something of this sort, yet not concerning the external performance of one's own tasks, but concerning the internal performance, truly involving oneself and one's own parts, not allowing the parts within him to do the work of others, nor allowing the kinds of parts in the soul to meddle in many things...

<summary>This page concludes the definition of the four cardinal virtues—wisdom, courage, temperance, and justice—within the individual soul, mirroring the structure of the ideal city. Justice is defined not as an external rule, but as the internal harmony where each part of the soul (reason, spirit, and appetite) performs its own proper function.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the conclusion of Book IV of Plato’s Republic. Socrates and Glaucon have just identified the four virtues (wisdom, courage, temperance, and justice) within the ideal city and are now finalizing the definition of justice within the individual soul. The text concludes by transitioning into the different types of political regimes and their corresponding character types.</meta>

# ON THE REPUBLIC, BOOK IV.

<margin>A</margin> ...nor to allow the parts of the soul to meddle with one another; rather, he has set his own internal house in order. He has become master of himself, orderly and a friend to himself. He has harmonized the three parts of his soul just like the three intervals of a musical scale—the low, the high, and the middle <note>original: "νεάτης τε καὶ ὑπάτης καὶ μέσης" (neates, hypates, meses). These refer to the strings of a lyre: the 'lowest' in pitch (but highest on the instrument), the 'highest' in pitch, and the middle.</note>—and if there are any other parts in between, he binds them all together. He becomes entirely one out of many, temperate and harmonized. Only then does he act, if he must perform any action—whether it concerns the acquisition of wealth, the care of his body, <margin>B</margin> or some political matter or private contract. In all these affairs, he considers and names that action "just and beautiful" which preserves and helps to complete this internal harmony. He considers "wisdom" to be the knowledge that presides over such action. Conversely, he considers an "unjust action" to be that which always dissolves this harmony, and "ignorance" to be the opinion that presides over such an action. "Socrates," he said, "what you say is entirely true." "Very well," I said, "we might say we have found the just man, the just city, and the justice that exists within them—and we would not be lying." "By Zeus, no indeed!" he replied. "Shall we affirm it then?" "Let us affirm it." "So be it," I said. "Next, I believe, we must consider injustice." "Clearly." "Must it not be a kind of civil war <note>original: "στάσιν" (stasin). A technical term for internal political strife or revolution.</note> between these same three parts, a meddlesomeness and interference in others' business, and a rebellion <margin>C</margin> of a certain part against the whole soul? It seeks to rule when it is not fitting, being of such a nature that it ought to be a slave to the ruling class of the soul. We shall say, I suppose, that such internal turmoil and wandering is what constitutes injustice, licentiousness, cowardice, ignorance, and in short, all vice." "That is exactly what they are," he said. "Then," I said, "to act unjustly and to do wrong, and conversely to act justly—all these are now clearly evident, if indeed injustice and justice are also clear." "How so?" "Because," I said, "they are no different from healthy and diseased things; as those are in the body, so these are in the soul." "In what way?" he asked. "Healthy things produce health; diseased things produce disease." "Yes." <margin>D</margin> "Therefore, just actions produce justice, and unjust actions produce injustice." "Necessarily." "Now, to produce health is to establish the parts of the body according to nature, so that they dominate and are dominated by one another in turn. To produce disease is to have them rule or be ruled by one another contrary to nature." "It is so." "Therefore," I said, "to produce justice is to establish the parts of the soul according to nature, so that they rule and are ruled by one another. To produce injustice is to have them rule and be ruled contrary to nature." "Exactly," he said. "Virtue, then, would seem to be a kind of health, beauty, and well-being of the soul; vice is a disease, deformity, and weakness." "That is true." "And do <margin>E</margin> noble practices lead to the acquisition of virtue, while base ones lead to vice?" "Necessarily." "What remains now, it seems, is for us to consider whether it is profitable to act justly, to practice noble habits, and to be just—whether one is known to be such or not—or to do injustice and be unjust, provided one does not pay the penalty and become better through punishment." "But Socrates," he said, "this inquiry now seems to me to be ridiculous. If life is thought not to be worth living when the nature of the body is ruined, even with all kinds of food and drink and all wealth and power; then when the nature of that very thing by which we live <note>referring to the soul</note> is troubled and ruined, shall life be worth living? Even if a man does whatever he wishes, except for that which will rid him of vice and injustice and gain him justice and virtue—now that both have been shown to be as we have described them?" "It is indeed ridiculous," I said. "But nevertheless, since we have <margin>F</margin> come to a point where we can see as clearly as possible that these things are so, we must not grow weary." "Least of all, by Zeus," he said, "we must not hesitate." "Come here then," I said, "so that you may see how many forms vice has—at least the ones I think are worth seeing." "I follow," he said, "only tell me." "In fact," I said, "just as if from a watchtower, since we have climbed to this point in our argument, it appears to me that there is only one form of virtue, but infinite forms of vice. However, four of them are worth mentioning." <margin>G</margin> "How do you mean?" he asked. "As many types of political constitutions as there are that have distinct forms, so many types of soul there are likely to be." "How many then?" "Five types of constitutions," I said, "and five of the soul." "Tell me," he said, "which are they?" I replied: "One is the one we have just described. It could be called by two names: if one man stands out among the rulers, it is called a Monarchy; if there are many, it is called an Aristocracy." "True," he said. "I call this one form," I said. "For whether there are many or only one, they would not change the significant laws of the city, provided they have been raised and educated as we described." "That is not likely," he said.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...to treat duties that are mutually confusing: but in truth, he rightly arranges his own affairs, and is master over them; he adorns himself and becomes his own friend, contemplating these three parts within himself as if they were three musical terms—the lowest, the highest, and the middle—or whatever other middle there might be. Therefore, binding all these together, and having become entirely one out of many, tempered and composed, he finally acts (if he acts at all), whether concerning the acquisition of money, the care of the body, or even civil or private business. In all these, he considers <margin>B</margin> and calls that action "just and noble" which fulfills and preserves this internal state. But he calls the "wisdom" presiding over this action "knowledge." On the other hand, he calls an "unjust action" that which dissolves this state, and "ignorance" the opinion that leads this action. "You speak entirely truly, O Socrates." "If, therefore, we say we have found the just man and the just city, and what justice is in each of them, we shall not, I think, be far from the truth." "By Jove, no." "Must it be asserted then?" "Undoubtedly." "So be it. Indeed, next it seems we must consider injustice." "Plainly." "It is fitting to call injustice a certain sedition <note>original: "Seditionem." Latin for internal discord or insurrection.</note> of these three parts, a meddlesome and varied <margin>C</margin> usurpation of another's work, and an insolent rebellion of a certain part against the whole soul—rising up to command the royal class of the soul, which nature commands it to serve. Such things, I think, and the disturbance and error of these parts, we shall call injustice, intemperance, cowardice, ignorance, and finally, all wickedness." "These things are exactly so." "Is it not now clear enough what it means to do unjust things and to inflict injury, and conversely, what it is to act justly, since justice and injustice are clear?" "In what way?" "Because they differ in no way from things that are healthy or unhealthy. For as those are in the body, so these are in the soul." "In what way?" <margin>D</margin> "Healthy things bring health; unhealthy things bring disease." "Plainly." "Similarly, to act justly produces justice in the soul; to do unjust things produces injustice." "It must be so." "Now, to bring health is to arrange the things in the body so that they are mastered by or master one another according to the order of nature. Disease, however, is when one part rules or obeys another contrary to nature." "It is so." "By the same logic, to provide justice is nothing other than to arrange the parts of the soul in their proper order, so that they obey and command according to the norm of nature. Injustice, however, is when one part commands or obeys another contrary to nature." "Exactly." "Virtue, therefore, as it appears, is a kind of health, beauty, and good constitution of the soul. <margin>E</margin> Wickedness, on the contrary, is disease, deformity, and weakness." "It is as you say." "Do not noble exercises lead to the acquisition of virtue, and base ones to wickedness?" "It must be so." "It remains, as it seems, to be discussed whether it is profitable to act justly, to cultivate noble things, and to be just—whether it be hidden or not—or to inflict injury and be unjust, provided one is not punished nor made better by chastisement." "To me, O Socrates, that discussion seems ridiculous. If, when the nature of the body is corrupted, it seems that life is not worth living, even in the greatest abundance of food and drink, all riches, and the empire of the whole world; <margin>F</margin> then when the nature of that by which we live is disturbed and corrupted, shall life be worth living? Even if someone does whatever he pleases, doing anything other than that by which he might be freed from wickedness and inequity, and obtain justice and probity—now that both have appeared as we have described them." "Truly ridiculous," I said. "But since we have come this far, so that we may see as clearly as possible that these things are so, we must not be lazy." "By Jove, least of all." "Come then," I said, "approach here, so that you may see how many species vice has, as it seems to me. Attend now; these are worthy of being seen." "I follow indeed; only speak." "And yet, as if from a watchtower, since we have climbed here by reasoning, one species of virtue occurs to me; but of vice, there are innumerable forms. From these, there are <margin>G</margin> four certain ones which ought to be remembered." "How do you say that?" "Just as there are modes of republics having their own species, so many appear to be the modes of the soul itself." "How many?" "Five of republics, and again five of the soul." "Say which they are." "I assert that one mode of the republic is this one which we have set forth. It can be called by two names. For if among the leaders of the city there is one who is most excellent of all, it will be called a Kingdom. But if there are many, it will be called a Government of the Best <note>original: "gubernatio optimatum," translating the Greek "aristokratia."</note>." "You tell the truth." "I say this is one species because, whether many govern or one, no one who has been educated and instructed as we have said will change anything worthy of regard in the laws of the republic." "For that would not be reasonable," he said.

-> PLATO <-

<summary>Socrates and Glaucon define justice as the natural harmony of the soul's three parts (reason, spirit, and appetite) and injustice as internal "civil war." They conclude that virtue is the soul's health, making the just life inherently more profitable than the unjust one, regardless of external rewards.</summary>

<meta>This page marks the beginning of Book V (the "Fifth Dialogue"). On the previous page, Socrates had just finished defining justice in the soul and was about to describe the four types of defective regimes. This page captures the famous "interruption" where his companions demand more detail on the social arrangements of the ideal city.</meta>

<header>PLATO’S</header>

# PLATO'S REPUBLIC,
## Or,
### ON JUSTICE,
#### THE FIFTH DIALOGUE.

->SUMMARY OF THE DIALOGUE. THE FIFTH DIALOGUE.<-

Plato teaches here the reason why a Magistrate must be established so that the Republic may be happy: namely, through true philosophy, which is not superficial and does not merely pursue some external ornament of life and speech, but turns the soul away from these created and fleeting things toward that which truly is—the solid and genuine knowledge of God <note>In the original Latin, the translator uses "Dei" (God) to represent Plato's concept of "The Good."</note>. Therefore, taking up the matter from a slightly deeper perspective, he extensively pursues the subject, nature, and utility of Philosophy. He establishes that philosophy is the knowledge of the highest good—that is, God—and that the utility of the republic stands upon that foundation. Furthermore, he argues that the state will only then be happy when either philosophers rule in it, or kings practice philosophy; and that there will be no rest from evils for humanity before then. However, since he had said the best republic consists of the highest community of both souls and all things, he defines the manner of that community thus: that duties in the republic should be common to women just as to men, and that wives, children, and goods should likewise be common to the citizens. This opinion is rightly criticized by Aristotle, who indeed wants the republic to be one, yet only to the extent that the greatest account be taken of the differing natures suited to different men, so that <term>good order</term> <note>original Greek: εὐταξία (eutaxia)</note> may be preserved in all things, and all confusion and <term>excessive meddling</term> <note>original Greek: πολυταραμοσύνη (polytaramosyne), referring to a state of great disorder or being "much-disturbed."</note>—the certain ruin of a republic—may be avoided.

---

<margin>A</margin>
I call, therefore, a city of this kind and such a Republic "good" and "upright," and I say that such a man is "good." And if this republic is upright, I call the others "depraved," insofar as they wander astray regarding the governance of the city itself and the discipline of private individuals—which indeed exist in four forms of depravity. "Which ones are those?" he asked. Then I was proceeding to relate in what manner each seemed to me to depend upon the others in turn. But Polemarchus—for he sat a little further from me than Adeimantus—sitting behind Adeimantus’s back, stretched out his hand and caught Adeimantus’s cloak from above around the shoulders; he drew him toward himself, leaned in, and moved his mouth to his ear. Of the things he said, we perceived nothing except this one thing: "Shall we let him go? Or what shall we do?" To which Adeimantus responded more loudly, "Not at all," he said. At this I said, "What is it that you will not permit?" "You," he said. <margin>B</margin> "Why so?" I asked. "You seem to us to be shrinking back," he said, "and to be keeping silent about an entire section of this discussion—and not the least part—so as not to explain it to us, and thus to steal it away. You think it escapes us what you said poorly regarding wives and children: namely, that it is clear to everyone that 'all things should be common among friends.'" "Was I not right to say that, Adeimantus?" I asked. "Right, to be sure," he said, "but just as in other matters, so in this it is necessary to explain in what manner it is 'right,' <margin>C</margin> and what the mode of this community is to be. For there could be many ways. Do not, therefore, skip over this, lest you fail to reveal to us which one you specifically mean. For we have been waiting a long time, hoping that you would explain both the condition of generation regarding the procreation of children, and the method of education regarding their nutrition—and what this whole community of wives and children you speak of ought to be. For we consider this to be of great, or rather, total importance to the republic, whether it be done rightly or not. Now, therefore, since you are attacking another form of republic before you have sufficiently and conveniently treated these things, we have resolved—as you yourself heard—not to permit you to move on to anything else until you have explained all these things just as you did the others." "Consider me too," said <margin>D</margin> Glaucon, "to be a sharer in this vote." "In this," said Thrasymachus, "you may certainly assume, Socrates, that we are all in agreement." "What are you doing?" I cried. "Why do you call me back like this? What a heavy discussion about the Republic you have stirred up again, as if from the very beginning! Indeed, I was rejoicing as if I had already finished this part, thinking it was enough if anyone accepted these things as they were said. By demanding these things now, you do not know what a 'swarm' of arguments you are inciting. Foreseeing this then, I passed it over, lest it stir up much trouble for us." "What?" said Thrasymachus, "Do you think these men have come here to smelt gold <note>A Greek proverb for a futile or greedy search; here meaning 'to waste time' instead of seeking wisdom.</note>, rather than to hear arguments?" "To hear arguments, certainly," I said, <margin>E</margin> "but in moderation." "But the measure and limit for hearing such arguments, Socrates," said Glaucon, "is the whole of life for men who have understanding. But never mind our part; do not grow weary, if it seems good to you, in declaring those things we seek: what this community of wives and children will be for our guardians, and what system of nursing the children is to be applied in that very time that falls between birth and education, which indeed seems most laborious; try to open these things to us." "It is not easy, blessed man," I said, "to explain these things, for there are more ambiguities in them than in the previous ones. First, indeed, it might be doubted whether these things are possible. Furthermore, even if they were possible, it will be doubted whether they are <margin>F</margin> for the best, and in what way. Therefore, this difficulty discourages me; I fear, my dearest friend, lest this speech of mine seem to be a mere wish." "Do not hesitate," he said, "I beg you; for you do not have listeners who are ungrateful, or incredulous, or ill-willed." "O best of men," I said, "do you say this to encourage me?" "Certainly," he said. "You do," I said, "the exact opposite. For if I were persuaded that I knew what I am saying, this encouragement would be well-timed. For it is safe and daring to pronounce the truths one knows about the greatest and most precious things among wise and friendly men. But to speak with distrust and ambiguity, as I am doing, is a thing to be guarded against and dangerous—not because I fear moving the listeners to laughter (for that would be childish)—but lest, wandering far from the truth, I myself fall into falsehood and drag my friends down into ruin with me, and we be deceived together in those matters where it least of all befits one to err. Therefore, as a suppliant, I adore Adrasteia <note>Adrasteia was a goddess often identified with Nemesis or Inevitable Fate; Socrates invokes her to avoid the "hubris" of speaking on things he does not fully understand.</note> for the things I am about to say, Glaucon. For I believe it is less...

<margin>B</margin>
...of which we heard nothing else. But this: "Shall we then let him go," he said, "or what shall we do?" Adeimantus laughed softly, speaking now aloud... <meta>This page follows the introduction to Book V. Socrates is being pressured by his friends to explain the controversial social structures of his ideal city, specifically the role of women and children, which he had previously mentioned only in passing.</meta>

<header>ON THE REPUBLIC BOOK V.</header>

<margin>A</margin>
...for I suspect that it is a lesser fault <note>original Greek: ἁμάρτημα (hamartēma)</note> to be an involuntary killer of someone than to be a deceiver regarding the beautiful, the good, the just, and the legal institutions. Therefore, it is better to run this <margin>at risk</margin> risk among enemies than among friends. So, you encourage me well. 

And Glaucon, laughing, said: "But Socrates, if we suffer anything untoward from this argument, we release you as one clean of murder <note>Glaucon is jokingly using the language of a law court to put Socrates at ease about the radical ideas he is about to propose.</note>, and not as a deceiver of us. So speak with courage." 

"Well then," I said, "the person who has been released is considered 'clean' in that world, as the law says. And if it is likely there, it is likely here too." 

"Speak, then," he said, "for that reason."

"I must now," I said, "say in reverse what perhaps should have been said in its proper sequence. But perhaps it might be right this way: after the male drama has been completely finished, 
<margin>B</margin>
to perform the female drama in its turn—especially since you challenge me so. For men born and educated as we have described, in my opinion, there is no other correct way to possess and use children and wives than to follow the path we first started upon. We attempted, did we not, to establish the men as guardians <note>The "Guardians" are the ruling and soldier class of Plato's ideal city.</note> of the flock in our argument?" 

"Yes." 

"Let us follow that, then, and assign a birth and upbringing that is very similar; and let us see if it suits us or not." 

"How?" he asked. 

"In this way: 
<margin>C</margin>
do we think the female guardian dogs <margin>but much greater</margin> ought to guard the same things that the males guard, and hunt with them, and do everything else in common? Or should the females stay indoors as if they were unable to work because of the birth and nursing of puppies, while the males do the labor and have all the care of the flocks?" 

"In common," he said, "they do everything. Except that we treat the females as the weaker and the males as the stronger." 

"Is it possible," I asked, "to use any animal for the same tasks if you do not give it the same food and education?" 

"It is not possible." 

"If, then, we are to use the women for the same tasks as the men, must they be taught the same things?" 

"Yes." 

"Were not music and gymnastics <note>In ancient Greece, "Music" referred to all the arts of the Muses (literature, history, music), while "Gymnastics" referred to physical training.</note> given to the men?" 

"Yes." 

"Then these two arts, and the things pertaining to war, must also be assigned to the women, and they must be used in the same way?" 

"It seems likely from what you say," he said. 

"Perhaps then," I said, "many of the things being said now would appear ridiculous because they are contrary to custom, if they are practiced as they are being described." 

"Very much so," he said. 

"What," I asked, "do you see as the most ridiculous 
<margin>D</margin>
of them? Is it clearly the sight of naked women exercising in the wrestling schools with the men—not only the young ones, but even the older women? Just like the old men in the gymnasiums, when they are wrinkled and not pleasant to look at, yet still love their exercise?" 

"By Zeus," he said, "that would indeed appear ridiculous, at least as things stand now." 

"Therefore," I said, "since we have started to speak, we must not fear the jests of the 'refined' folk, nor how many or what kind of jokes they might make about such a change occurring in gymnastics and music, and not least in the wearing of armor and the riding of horses." 

"You speak correctly," he said. 

"But since we have begun the argument, we must travel 
<margin>E</margin> <margin>towards the harshness of the law</margin> 
toward the harshness of the law. We must ask these people not to do as they usually do, but to be serious, and remind them that it was not long ago that it seemed shameful and ridiculous to the Greeks—as it does now to many of the barbarians—to see naked men. And when the Cretans first began these exercises, and then the Lacedaemonians <note>The Lacedaemonians are the Spartans, known for their rigorous physical training.</note>, it was possible for the witty men of that time to mock all such things. Or don't you think so?" 

"I do." 

"But when, I think, it appeared better to those practicing it to be naked than to cover all such parts, the ridiculousness in the eyes faded away before the excellence revealed by reason. This showed that he is a fool who thinks anything is ridiculous except what is bad; or who attempts to raise a laugh by looking at any other sight as ridiculous than that of the foolish and the bad; or who, being serious, aims at any other target than that of the good." 

"Absolutely," he said. 

"Should we not then 
<margin>F</margin> <margin>must be agreed upon</margin> 
first agree upon this: whether these things are possible or not? And we must grant a debate to anyone who wants to argue, whether in jest or in earnest, whether female human nature is able to share with the male sex in all tasks, or in none at all, or whether it is capable of some but not others—and in which category the business of war falls. Would not someone starting this way, as is fitting, also finish in the best way?" 

"By far," he said. 

"Do you want us," I asked, "to argue against ourselves on behalf of others, so that the opposing side's argument is not besieged while left undefended?" 

"Nothing prevents it," he said. 

"Let us say then on their behalf: 'Socrates and Glaucon, there is no need for others to dispute with you. For you yourselves, at the beginning of the settlement 
<margin>G</margin> <margin>if according to nature</margin> 
of the city you were founding, agreed that it was necessary for each one to do his own single task according to his nature <note>This refers to the core principle of the Republic established in earlier books: "One man, one job."</note>.'" 

"We did agree, I think; for how could we not?" 

"Is there not, then, a vast difference between a woman and a man in their nature?" 

"How could there not be a difference?" 

"Is it not then proper to assign a different task to each, according to their own nature?" 

"Certainly." 

"How then are you not in error now, and contradicting yourselves, by saying that men and women ought to do the same things, when they have natures that are so widely separated? Do you have, my amazing friend, any defense against this?" 

"As it comes so suddenly," he said, "it is not very easy. But I will ask you, and we do ask you, to explain the argument on our behalf..."

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...that he commits a fault who unintentionally kills someone, more than he who deceives regarding the constitutions of honorable, good, and just things. However, it is better to undergo this risk among enemies than among friends. Therefore, O Glaucon, encourage me better. 

"But indeed, O Socrates," says Glaucon, "if by any means we happen to err in this dispute, we absolve you as if from homicide, and we pronounce you innocent of this deception. Therefore, enter the dispute boldly." 

"Furthermore, he is innocent," I said, "who is absolved there, as the laws teach. Therefore, he who is absolved here is also innocent." 

"Speak, therefore," he said, "for this reason." 

"It is necessary 
<margin>B</margin> 
to speak again now," I said, "of things which perhaps should have been said next in order. But perhaps it is worthwhile, after the things pertaining to men have, as it were, had their own act, to report next the things of women, especially since you yourself exhort me to this. For people born and educated as we have described above, as my opinion goes, there is no other right acquisition and use of children and women than by walking that path which we ourselves entered from the beginning. For we attempted to make the men, in our speech, as if they were guardians of the flock." 

"Certainly," he said. 

"Let us follow this then, applying a birth and nutrition as similar as possible, and let us consider whether it is fitting or not." 

"In what way?" he asked. 

<margin>C</margin> 
"In this way: whether among guardian dogs, we think the females themselves ought to guard the same things as the males, and hunt together, and do all other things in common. Or should the females stay inside and keep the domestic things, as if they were weak because of the birth and nutrition of the puppies themselves; while the males undergo the labors and carry out all the care of the herd?" 

"We assign all things to them in common," he said, "except that we use the females as the weaker, and the males as the stronger." 

"Is it possible to use any animal for the same things unless you have nourished and educated it in the same manner?" 

"In no way." 

"If therefore we will use the females for the same things as the men, it is fitting to educate them in the same things." 

"Certainly." 

"Moreover, we assigned music and gymnastics to the men." 

"Indeed." 

"To the women, therefore, these arts and military matters must be assigned similarly, and it is fitting to use them for these same things." 

"That is consistent with what you say." 

"Perhaps many things, contrary to 
<margin>D</margin> 
custom, will seem ridiculous among the things now being said, if they are done as they are described." 

"And most especially that." 

"What in these do you see as most ridiculous? Or is it because you are to see naked women in the wrestling schools contending with men—not only the young, but also the old women—just as the old men in the gymnasiums, when they are exercised together, even though they are now wrinkled and not pleasant in appearance?" 

"So by Jove <note>Latin: "Iovem" (Jupiter). The translator uses Roman deities to replace Greek ones (Zeus).</note>. For that would indeed seem laughable, as things are now." 

"We, therefore, since we have begun to speak, ought by no means to fear the ridicules of witty 
<margin>E</margin> 
men, however many and of whatever kind they may cast against a change of this sort, which we introduce regarding music and gymnastics, and no less regarding armor and the equestrian faculty." 

"You speak rightly." 

"Therefore, since we have begun to speak, let us proceed to the severity of the law, asking those people not to act in their usual way but to think seriously, and reminding them that not a long time has passed since it seemed base and ridiculous to the Greeks—what today seems ridiculous to most of the barbarians—namely, to see naked men. And when they first attacked such exercises, first indeed the Cretans, then also the Lacedaemonians, it was surely permitted to the urban and witty men who then were, to carp at all these things—don't you think so?" 

"Indeed." 

"But after, as I think, it seemed more advantageous to those using it that the body be naked rather than 
<margin>F</margin> 
covered while being exercised, it happened that because the best thing had been indicated by reason, it appeared by no means ridiculous to the eyes. From which it is clear that that man is vain who thinks anything is to be laughed at except what is evil, and attempts to mock, proposing to himself any other cause of derision than what is tasteless and evil, or thinks anything honorable and worthy of study while looking elsewhere than toward the good." 

"It is entirely so." 

"Must we not first agree on this: whether these things are possible or not? And grant moreover to everyone that they may doubt against these things according to their judgment, whether in jest or in earnest—whoever wishes to doubt—whether in the nature of humans the female is able to communicate with the male in all works, or in none, or in 
<margin>G</margin> 
which of them she may be capable, and in others not at all; and the military matter itself, in which of these two kinds it may be. Would not anyone who has thus rightly begun, as is decent, also rightly finish?" 

"Most especially." 

"Do you wish, therefore, that we, for the sake of others, oppose ourselves with doubts, lest without a defense, which might belong to the other side's reasoning, they be attacked?" 

"Nothing prohibits it." 

"Let us speak, therefore, under their person in this manner: 'There is no need, O Socrates and Glaucon, for others to resist us. For among ourselves from the very beginning of the founding of the city, it was established that it is necessary according to nature for each one...'"

**A** ...that a defense might be brought forward, you may explain. "These things indeed, O Glaucon," I said, "and many others of the same kind, I have been foreseeing for a long time; I was timid and unwilling to descend to this law concerning the possession and upbringing of women and children." "By Zeus," he said, "it certainly does not appear to be a light matter." "Quite so." "And must we not also swim and try to escape safely from the waves of this discussion, hoping that either some dolphin might pick us up <note>A reference to the legend of Arion, a poet saved from drowning by a dolphin.</note> or some other unexpected and sudden cause of safety might be ours?" "So it seems," he said. **B** "Look around, I pray, if we might find an exit. For it was agreed among us that one nature should handle one type of work, and another nature another; but that the nature of a woman and a man are different. Now, we are commanding these different natures to apply themselves to the same things. In this, we are being accused by you." "Indeed." "How noble, O Glaucon, is the power of the art of contradiction!" <note>The Latin 'contradictoriæ artis' refers to *eristic*, a style of argument focused on winning rather than finding the truth.</note> "Why?" he asked. "Because it seems to me that many people fall into it even against their will, and they think they are not quarreling but debating, because they are unable to divide the subject according to its types <note>original: 'secundum species'</note>, but instead they pursue the contradiction of the proposal according to the name itself, using contention against one another rather than discussion." "That does happen to many," he said, "but does the same thing now happen to us?" **C** "Very much so," I said. "We seem to be touching upon contradiction against our will." "In what way?" "Because we are contending quite strongly and contentiously—if you look at the words—that a nature that is not the same ought not to handle the same tasks. But we have in no way considered what kind of 'nature' is the 'different' or 'the same,' or toward what we were looking when we defined them, when we assigned different studies to different natures and the same to the same." "Certainly we have not considered that," he said. **D** "Yet it is permitted for us, as it seems, to inquire of ourselves: whether the nature of bald men and hairy men is the same, or rather the opposite. And after we have conceded that it is opposite, if bald men should cut leather and make shoes, we would in no way allow hairy men to do the same; or if the hairy men do it, we would not allow the bald." "That would be ridiculous," he said. "And is it ridiculous for any other reason than that we did not then establish nature as being 'the same' or 'different' in an absolute sense, but we observed only that species of difference and similarity which pertained to the pursuits themselves? Just as we said a doctor and a man having a soul suited to the study of medicine have the same nature. Do you not think so?" "I do." "But a man suited for medicine and another man ready for carpentry have different natures?" "Entirely." "Therefore," I said, "if the race of men and the race of women appear to differ in some art or pursuit, we will say that this must be assigned to each; but if they appear to differ in this alone <insert>† (at least)</insert> <margin>*† This is missing in the Greek, yet it must be read.*</margin>, that the female bears children and the male begets them, we will say it has not yet been demonstrated that a woman differs from a man regarding what we are now talking about, but we will still judge that both our guardians and their women ought to practice the same things." **E** "Quite right." "After this, do we not command the one who says the opposite to teach us this very thing: for which art or which duty among those which conduct the state is the nature of a man and a woman not the same, but different?" "That is indeed proper." "Perhaps as you were saying a little while ago, someone else might say: it is not easy to say enough on the spot, but if it is thought out, it is not at all difficult." "He would say that." "Do you wish then that we ask the one who opposes us these things to listen to us and attend, to see if we can show him in any way that there is no pursuit proper to a woman in the administration of the city?" "By all means." **F** "Come then, let us say to him: Answer, did you not say that someone is endowed by nature with a talent or lack of talent for some work based on this: that one perceives something easily, and another with difficulty; and that if one learns a small thing from someone, he finds out a great deal from it himself, while another, though he has learned and practiced many things, does not even preserve what he has learned; and for one, the members of the body sufficiently serve the mind, while for the other they are resistant? Are there any other things besides these by which you distinguish a man naturally well-suited for something from one poorly suited?" "No one will say otherwise." "Do you know of anything practiced by humans in which the race of men does not have all these things in a more excellent degree than the race of women? Or shall we wander far in words, mentioning the art of weaving, and the preparation of cakes and preserves, in which the female race seems to be something <note>Socrates is being somewhat ironic here, acknowledging traditional gender roles only to dismiss them as proof of essential nature.</note>—where it appears truly ridiculous when it is beaten?" "You speak the truth," he said, "because in almost all things, so to speak, one race is far surpassed by the other. However, many women are superior to many men in many things. But the whole matter is as you say." "There is no duty, therefore, O friend, among those who administer the city, which is proper to a woman because she is a woman, or to a man because he is a man, **G** but natures are equally dispersed among the living beings of both: and the female is a partaker of all

duties according to nature, and the man in all; but in all things the woman is weaker than the man." "It is entirely so." "Shall we then enjoin all things on the men, and nothing on the woman?" "How could we?" "For there is, I think, as we shall say, even among women one suited for medicine, and another not; one for music, and another by nature a stranger to music." "Of course." "And another indeed is ready for gymnastic exercises and military matters, while another is unfit for these." "So I believe."

And for the one, the things of the body sufficiently serve the mind, while for the other they oppose it? He dismantles the idea that biological differences in reproduction (bearing vs. begetting) dictate professional or social roles, using the analogy of "bald vs. hairy" shoemakers to show that only relevant natural talents matter for one's "nature."</summary>

# ON THE REPUBLIC, BOOK V

<margin>A</margin> ...is one woman musical, and another not? "I believe so." And what of this: is one a lover of wisdom <note>original: "philó-sophos"</note>, and another a hater of it? And is one high-spirited, and another spiritless? "That is also true." Is there, then, a woman capable of being a Guardian? Or did we not choose such a nature for the male Guardians as well? "We did indeed." Therefore, the nature of both woman and man is the same in respect to guarding the city, except in that the one is weaker and the other stronger. "So it appears." These women, then, must be chosen to live with such men and to guard the city with them, since they are capable and share a similar nature of soul. "Quite so."

<margin>B</margin> Must not the same pursuits be assigned to the same natures? "The same." We have at last come back around to our earlier point, and we agree that it is not against nature to assign music and gymnastics to the wives of the Guardians. "Entirely so." We were not, then, legislating impossibilities or mere dreams, since we established the law according to nature; rather, the way things are done now—contrary to these principles—is much more a violation of nature, as it seems. "So it seems." Now, was our inquiry not whether what we said was both possible and for the best? "It was." And that it is possible has now been agreed? "Yes." Next, must we agree that it is for the best? "That is clear."

<margin>C</margin> Therefore, to make a woman a Guardian, will one education produce the man and another the woman, especially since it takes hold of the same nature? "No, it will not be different." What is your opinion on this matter? "What matter?" The belief that one man is better and another worse, or do you think all are equal? "By no means." In the city we are founding, do you think we have produced better men in the Guardians, who received the education we described, or in the shoemakers, who were educated in the craft of leatherworking? "You ask a ridiculous question," he said. "I understand," I replied. "But what of this? Are these Guardians not the best of all the citizens?" "By far." "And what then? Will these women not be the best of all women?" "They will be, by far."

<margin>D</margin> Is there anything better for a city than for the best possible men and women to be produced within it? "There is not." And will music and gymnastics, applied as we described, achieve this? "How could they not?" We have therefore established a law for the city that is not only possible but also the very best. "That is so." The wives of the Guardians must therefore strip for exercise, since they will clothe themselves in virtue <term>virtue (aretē): Socrates uses the metaphor of "clothing oneself in excellence" to argue that physical modesty should not prevent women from the training required to protect the state.</term> instead of garments. They must share in war and the rest of the city’s defense, and do nothing else. However, the lighter parts of these duties must be assigned to the women rather than the men, because of the weakness of their sex. But the man who laughs at naked women, exercising for the sake of what is best, "plucks the fruit of a wisdom that is unripe" <note>Socrates suggests that such a mocker doesn't understand the true nature of the ridiculous.</note>, and knows neither what he laughs at nor what he does. For it is most beautifully said—and will continue to be said—that the useful is beautiful, and the harmful is shameful. "Completely so."

<margin>E</margin> Let us say, then, that we have escaped this one "wave" of the law concerning women without being completely submerged, having established that our male and female Guardians must perform all duties in common. Our argument is consistent with itself, showing that what we propose is both possible and beneficial. "Indeed," he said, "it is no small wave you are escaping." "You will not call it a great one," I said, "when you see the one that follows." "Speak then, so I may see it," he said.

<margin>F</margin> This law follows the others, as I think: That these women shall all be common to all these men, and that no woman shall live privately with any man; and further, that the children shall be common, so that no parent shall know his own offspring, nor any child his parent. "This," he said, "is a much greater cause for disbelief than the former, both regarding its possibility and its utility." "I do not think," I said, "that the utility of it—that it is the greatest good for women and children to be common, if it were possible—would be disputed. But I think the question of whether it is possible or not will provide the greatest dispute." "One might very well argue both points," he said.

<margin>G</margin> "You are speaking of a conspiracy of arguments!" I said. "I thought I should escape from one of them if you agreed it was useful, and then I would only have to discuss whether it was possible or not." "But," he said, "you did not go unnoticed while trying to escape. Give an account of both." "I must submit to the penalty," I said. "But grant me this favor: let me feast my mind, as those who are lazy in thought are accustomed to banquet themselves whenever they walk alone.

<margin>H</margin> For such people, before they have found out how what they desire might come to be, they set that question aside so they do not tire themselves out deliberating about the possible and impossible. Assuming what they want already exists, they then arrange the rest and take delight in recounting what they will do when it happens, making a soul that is already idle even lazier. I too am becoming soft now, and I desire to postpone that inquiry into how these things are possible until later. For now, assuming they are possible, I will examine—if you permit—how the rulers will arrange these matters when they happen, and how this will be the most advantageous of all things for the city and the Guardians. This I will try to consider with you first, and the other things later, if you allow." "I do allow it," he said, "so proceed." "I think then," I said, "that if the rulers are to be worthy of the name..."
