# PLATONIS <note>original: "of Plato"</note>

In the same way, their assistants <note>Referring to the younger guardians or subordinates</note> will wish to carry out what is commanded, while the others will give orders, partly obeying the laws themselves and partly imitating the spirit of the laws, insofar as we have permitted them. "That seems likely," he said. You, therefore, as the lawgiver, just as you chose the men, so by choosing the women, you will provide those who are as similar in nature as possible. Since they will have common houses and common meals, and none of them will possess anything of their own, they will live together. And by mingling with one another in the gymnasiums and in the rest of their upbringing, they will be drawn, I think, by an innate necessity to mutual union. Do I not seem to speak of things that are necessary? "Not by a geometric necessity," he said, "but by an <term>erotic necessity</term><note>Plato contrasts mathematical certainty with the powerful, natural drive of human attraction</note>, which is much sharper than the other for persuading and drawing the common people." "Indeed, very much so," I said. 

But after this, Glaucon, to mingle without order, or to do anything else of that kind, is neither holy in a city of happy men, nor will the rulers permit it. "For it would not be just," he said. It is clear, then, that we shall next establish marriages that are as sacred as possible. And the most beneficial marriages would be the most sacred. "Entirely so." Tell me then, Glaucon, how they will be most beneficial. For I see in your house hunting dogs and many fine birds. Have you ever noticed anything regarding their mating and the production of offspring? "What sort of thing?" he asked. First, even among these noble animals, are there not some who are the very best? "There are." Do you permit them to breed indiscriminately? Or do you take care that the offspring come from the best? "From the best." And do you breed from the very young, or the very old, or those in the prime of their life? "From those in their prime." And if they were not bred in this way, do you think the breed of birds and dogs would be much worse? "I do," he said. Do you think it is any different for horses or other animals? "That would be absurd." 

"Good heavens!" I said, "My dear friend, how much we need the highest caliber of rulers, if the same holds true for the human race." "It certainly does," he said, "but what of it?" Because it is necessary, I said, for them to use many <term>medicines</term><note>Plato uses the word 'pharmakon', which can mean medicine, poison, or a 'noble lie' used for the benefit of the state</note>. When bodies do not need medicine but are willing to follow a disciplined diet, we think a lesser doctor is sufficient. But when medicine must be administered, we know a more courageous doctor is required. "True," he said, "but what is the point?" It seems it will be necessary for the rulers to use frequent lies and deception for the benefit of their subjects. We said above that all such things are useful in the manner of a medicine. "And rightly so," he said. It seems this "right way" will occur not least in marriages and the procreation of children. "How so?" 

It is necessary, according to what we have agreed, that the best men should mate with the best women as often as possible, and the inferior men with the inferior women as rarely as possible. We must also rear the offspring of the former, but not the latter, if the flock is to be of the highest quality. And all these things must be done without anyone knowing, except the rulers, if the "herd" of Guardians is to remain free from internal conflict. "Very right," he said. Therefore, certain festivals will be established by law, in which we will bring together the brides and grooms; there will be sacrifices and hymns composed by our poets, suitable for the marriages taking place. But the number of marriages we will leave to the discretion of the rulers, so that, taking into account wars, diseases, and other such things, they may maintain the same number of citizens as much as possible, so that the city does not become too large or too small. "Correct," he said. 

Certain <insert>clever</insert> lotteries must be devised, I think, so that the inferior man, in each mating, blames his luck and not the rulers. "Indeed," he said. And to those young men who excel in war or other things, rewards and prizes must be given, and many such things; and they should have more frequent permission to sleep with women, so that from this pretext as many children as possible may be fathered by such men. "Right." Therefore, the children who are born from these unions will be taken by the officials appointed for this—whether men or women, or both, for the offices are common to both men and women. "It is so." Taking the offspring of the good parents, they will carry them to the nursery, to certain nurses living apart in some area of the city. But the children of the inferior parents, or any of the others born with a deformity, they will hide away in secret and obscure places, as is fitting, if the race of Guardians is to remain pure. "It must be so," he said, "if the breed of Guardians is to be kept clean." 

These officials will also take care of the nursing. They will bring the mothers to the nursery when their breasts are full, using every device to ensure that no mother recognizes her own child; and they will provide other women who have milk, if the mothers are not sufficient. They will also see that the time for breastfeeding is kept moderate. The vigils and other labors will be handed over to the wet-nurses and caregivers. "You are giving the wives of the Guardians a great deal of ease in child-bearing," he said. "It is fitting," I replied. "But come, let us follow the next part of our plan." We said that children should be produced by those in the prime of life. "We did." Does it not also seem to you that the prime of life is twenty years for a woman and thirty for a man? "Which years are these?" he asked. For a woman, I said, starting from her twentieth year until her fortieth...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...of name, those who will assist them in these things, and will be willing to do what is commanded, while the others will give orders, partly obeying the laws themselves and partly imitating whatever we permit them. "It is likely," he said. "You, then, the lawgiver," I said, "having chosen the women just as you chose the men, will hand them over to be as similar in nature as possible. Since they possess common houses and common meals, and no one owns anything of that sort individually, they will be together. And being mixed together both in the gymnasiums and in the rest of their upbringing, they will be led, I think, by an innate necessity toward union with one another. Or do I not seem to speak of things that are necessary?" "Not by geometric necessities," he said, "but by erotic ones; which are likely <margin>B</margin> sharper than those for persuading and drawing the common people." "Quite so," I said. "But after this, Glaucon, to mate in a disorderly fashion, or to do anything else, is neither holy in a city of happy people, nor will the rulers permit it." "For it would not be just," he said. "It is clear then that after this we shall make marriages as sacred as possible; and the most beneficial would be the sacred ones." "By all means." "How then will they be most beneficial? Tell me this, Glaucon. For I see in your house hunting dogs and a great many noble birds. Have you then, by Zeus, paid attention to their matings and procreations?" "In what way?" he asked. <margin>C</margin> "First, among these themselves, even though they are noble, are there not some who prove to be the best?" "There are." "Do you then breed from all of them alike? Or are you eager to breed as much as possible from the best?" "From the best." "And what of this? From the youngest, or the oldest, or those in their prime as much as possible?" "From those in their prime." "And if they are not bred in this way, do you think the race of birds and dogs will be much worse for you?" "I do," he said. "And what do you think of horses and other animals? Is it any different?" "It would be strange indeed," he said. "Aha!" I said, "my dear friend, how very much we need the most excellent rulers, if it is the same with the race of humans." "It is indeed so," he said. "But why?" "Because it is necessary for them," I said, "to use many <term>medicines</term>. We think a lesser doctor is sufficient for bodies that do not need medicines but are willing to follow a diet; but when it is necessary <margin>D</margin> to use medicines, we know a more courageous doctor is needed." "True. But to what do you refer?" "To this," I said: "the rulers will likely have to use a great deal of falsehood and deception for the benefit of the ruled. And we said somewhere that all such things are useful in the form of a medicine." "And rightly so," he said. "In marriages then and procreations, this 'rightly' seems to occur in no small way." "How so?" "It is necessary," I said, "from our agreements, that the best men sleep with the best women as often as possible, but the most inferior men with the most inferior women the opposite; and to rear the offspring of the former, <margin>E</margin> but not of the latter, if the flock is to be of the highest quality. And all these things happening must be hidden from all except the rulers themselves, if the herd of Guardians is to be as free from faction as possible." "Most right," he said. "Therefore, certain festivals must be established by law, in which we will bring together the brides and the bridegrooms; and sacrifices and hymns must be made by our poets, suitable for the marriages being made. But the number of marriages we will leave to the rulers, so that they may preserve the same number of men as much as possible, looking toward wars and diseases and all such things; and so that the city does not become either great or small for us, as far as possible." "Right," he said. "Certain <insert>clever</insert> lotteries, I think, must be made, so that the inferior man may blame chance for each union, but not the rulers." "Quite so," he said. "And to the good among the young in war or elsewhere, honors must be given and prizes, <margin>F</margin> and the more unrestricted authority to sleep with women, so that at the same time, with this pretext, as many of the children as possible may be sown from such men." "Right." "Therefore, the officials appointed over these things—whether women or men, or both, for offices are common to women and men—will receive the offspring as they are born." "Yes." "The children of the good, I think, they will take and carry to the fold, to certain nurses who dwell separately in a certain part of the city; but the children of the inferior, and if any of the others are born deformed, they will hide in a secret and hidden place, as is fitting." "If indeed," he said, "the race of Guardians is to be pure." "Therefore they will also take care of the nursing, bringing the mothers to the fold <margin>G</margin> when their breasts are full, using every device so that no one will recognize her own child, and providing other women who have milk, if these are not sufficient. And they will see to it that the nursing itself lasts for a moderate time; and the sleepless nights and the other labor they will hand over to the wet-nurses and caregivers." "You speak of a great ease of child-bearing," he said, "for the women of the Guardians." "For it is fitting," I said. "But let us go through the next part of what we intended. For we said that offspring must be born from those in their prime." "True." "Does a moderate time of prime seem to you to be twenty years for a woman, and thirty for a man?" "Which years are they?" he asked. "For a woman," I said, "beginning from her twentieth year until her fortieth..."

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from Book V of the Republic. Socrates has just described the "mating lotteries" and is now detailing the specific ages for procreation and the resulting social structure where all children are held in common by the Guardian class.</meta>

# ON THE REPUBLIC, BOOK V.

<margin>A</margin> ...to be born to the city. For a man, once he has passed the peak of his fastest running <note>original: "τοῦ ὀξυτάτου δρόμου ἀκμὴν"</note>, he shall father children for the city from that time until he is fifty-five years old. "In both cases," he said, "this is the prime of both body and mind." Therefore, if anyone either older or younger than these ages involves himself in procreation for the community, we shall say his offense is neither holy nor just, as he begets a child for the city who, being born in secret, will not be the product of sacrifices and prayers (which the priestesses, priests, and the entire city offer at every wedding, praying that from the good, better descendants may always be born, and from the useful, more useful ones), but rather is born in darkness and through terrible lack of self-control.

<margin>B</margin> "You are right," he said. "The same law will apply," I said, "if any man who is still of the age for procreation touches a woman of child-bearing age without the ruler having joined them. For we shall say he presents the city with a child who is a bastard, unauthorized, and unholy." "Very true," he said. "But I think that when the women and men have passed the age for procreation, we shall leave them free to associate with whomever they wish—except for a daughter, a mother, the children of daughters, or the ancestors of a mother; and for women, likewise, anyone except a son, a father, or their descendants and ancestors. And after we have given all these instructions, we must charge them to be careful, above all, not to bring any fetus into the light of day, should one be conceived; but if one should be forced to birth, they must dispose of it on the understanding that there is no food for such a one." <note>This is a reference to the ancient practice of 'exposure,' where infants were left in the elements if they were not sanctioned by the state or family.</note>

<margin>C</margin> "That also is reasonably said," he said. "But how will they distinguish their fathers and daughters and the others you just mentioned?" "Not at all," I said. "But from the day a man becomes a bridegroom, all children born in the tenth or seventh month after that day will be addressed by him—the males as sons and the females as daughters; and they will call him father. Likewise, he will call their descendants 'grandchildren,' and they in turn will call the first group grandfathers and grandmothers. Those born during the time in which their mothers and fathers were procreating will be called sisters and brothers; so that, as we were just saying, they may not touch one another. However, the law will allow brothers and sisters to live together if the lot falls that way and the <term>Pythia</term> <note>The priestess of Apollo at Delphi who gave oracular pronouncements.</note> approves." "Very true," he said.

<margin>D</margin> "This, then, Glaucon, is the community of wives and children for the Guardians of your city. That it follows from the rest of our constitution and is by far the best, we must next confirm by argument. Or what shall we do?" "That, by Zeus!" he said. "Is not this, then, the beginning of our agreement: to ask ourselves what we can say is the greatest good for the construction of a city, at which the legislator must aim in making laws, and what is the greatest evil? Then we should examine whether what we have just described fits the track of the good for us and is far removed from the track of the evil." "By all means," he said.

<margin>E</margin> "Can we name any greater evil for a city than that which pulls it apart and makes it many instead of one? Or any greater good than that which binds it together and makes it one?" "We cannot." "Does not the community of pleasure and pain bind them together, when all the citizens, as much as possible, rejoice and grieve in the same way at the same successes and failures?" "Certainly," he said. "But the privatization of such feelings dissolves the bond, when some are overwhelmed with grief and others are overjoyed at the very same experiences of the city and its people." "Of course."

<margin>F</margin> "Does this not happen when the citizens do not say these words in unison: 'mine' and 'not mine,' and similarly concerning what belongs to another?" "Exactly so." "In whichever city the greatest number of people say 'mine' and 'not mine' about the same things in the same way, is that city not best governed?" "Very much so." "And is it not the city that is closest to the condition of a single human being? For instance, when a finger of one of us is hit, the whole community of the body, stretching to the soul and reaching that single arrangement of the ruler within it, feels the pain and all suffers together as a whole when the part is hurt. And so we say that the *man* has a pain in his finger. The same logic applies to any other part of a person, both regarding pain when a part suffers, and pleasure when it finds relief." "The same indeed," he said. "And to answer your question, the best-governed city lives closest to this condition. I suppose that when any one of its citizens suffers anything, whether good or bad, such a city will most of all say that the suffering is its own, and the whole city will either rejoice or grieve together." "It must be so," he said, "in a city with good laws."

<margin>G</margin> "It is time then," I said, "for us to return to our own city and look for the things we have agreed upon in this discussion, to see if she possesses them more than any other." "We must do so," he said. "What then? Are there not rulers and a common people in other cities just as there are in this one?" "There are." "And will they all address one another as citizens?" "How could they not?" "But besides the name 'citizen,' what does the people call the rulers in other cities?" "In most, they call them 'masters' <note>original: "δεσπότας"</note>; but in democracies, they call them by this very name: 'rulers.'" "And what does the people in our city call the rulers?" "Saviors and helpers," he said. "And what do the rulers call the people?" "Paymasters and providers." "And in other cities, what do the rulers call the people?" "Slaves," he said. "And what do the rulers call one another?" "Co-rulers," he said. "And what do ours call one another?" "Fellow-guardians," he said.

<margin>H</margin> "Can you say whether any of the rulers in other cities addresses one of his co-rulers as a kinsman and another as a stranger?" "Yes, many do."

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...shall give birth, but a man, after he has passed the highest flower of his course (that is, thirty years), shall procreate until he is fifty-five years old. "Truly," he said, "the vigor of mind and body consists in those states." If, therefore, anyone older than these, or younger, touches procreation in common, we shall judge this to be a profane and iniquous crime, as if a fetus is being brought into the city which, if it remains hidden, will be born not under the sacrifices and vows that the priests and priestesses and the whole city perform at each wedding—praying that from the good, better ones may be born, and from the useful, more useful ones—but rather born in darkness out of a certain grave incontinence. "You speak rightly."

<margin>B</margin> The same reasoning must also be held concerning that man who, while he is still in the age for begetting, but has not yet been joined by the prince <note>original: "à principe copulatus"</note>, touches a woman of legal age. Surely we shall assert that he begets a child who is a bastard, incestuous, and profane. "Quite cleverly put." Therefore, when the women and men have passed the age fit for procreation, we shall say it is permitted for the men to be joined with whomever they wish, except for a daughter and a mother, and the children of daughters, or the elders of a mother; it is also permitted for women to be joined with anyone except for a son and a father, and those above and below them.

<margin>C</margin> When we have commanded all these things, we shall forbid such a fetus (if it should happen) from being brought forth into the light. If anything should force a mother to give birth, we shall instruct that it be exposed, as if there were no nourishment for it. "These things are also well said. But the fathers and daughters and the others you mentioned, how will they know one another?" In no way; but all who are born in the tenth month, or the seventh, from that day on which someone applied himself to the work of children, the males shall be named his sons, and the females his daughters. And those born shall call him father, and similarly he shall say the children of those born are his grandchildren, while they in turn shall call those above them grandfathers and grandmothers; and those who are born at the same time in which their fathers and mothers were begetting, they shall call brothers and sisters. And thus, as I was just saying, they would in no way touch each other. However, the law will grant cohabitation to brothers and sisters if the lot gives it, and the Pythia confirms it through her responses. "Quite rightly."

<margin>D</margin> Such then, O Glaucon, will be the community of wives and children among the guardians of the city. That it agrees with the rest of the city's order, and is by far the best, must next be confirmed by reason; or what shall we do? "This, by Jove," he said. "Is not this the beginning of our agreement, that we ask ourselves what is the greatest good we can find for the constitution of a city, toward which the legislator, looking upon it, ought to establish laws, and what is the greatest evil?"

<margin>E</margin> "Let us consider then, whether the things we have just narrated agree with the investigation of the good itself, and are dissonant with the track of evil." "Most of all." <margin>Aristotle notes this in Politics, Book 2, Chapter 2.</margin> "Do we have any evil more ruinous to a city than that which divides it and makes many out of one? Or anything better than that which binds it together and makes it one?" "We do not." "Now the community of pleasure and pain unites it, when all citizens rejoice and grieve equally at the arrival or departure of the same things?" "Most certainly." "But a diversity in these things dissolves it, when some grieve vehemently and others rejoice over the same events of the city and of those who are in the city." "Why not?"

<margin>F</margin> "From this, such a thing follows: when these words are not said together in the city, 'Mine' and 'Not Mine,' and 'Another's' in the same way." <margin>See another manuscript here, unlike the Aldine edition in which this place is corrupted.</margin> "Very much so. In whatever city most people say this—'Mine' and 'Not Mine'—about the same thing in the same way, that city is best governed." "Precisely; and whichever is affected as nearly as possible like a single man, as whenever a finger of one of us is struck, the whole community of the body, reaching to the soul, in one coordination of that which rules in the soul itself, felt it immediately, and the whole suffered together with the afflicted part. And for that reason we say the man's finger hurts. And the same reasoning applies to any other part of a man: both that which is afflicted by pain, and that which is refreshed by pleasure."

<margin>G</margin> "The same reasoning certainly: and as you ask, the city which is best ruled comes closest to this. Whenever, as I think, anything good or evil happens to any of the citizens, such a city will cry out that the one so affected is its own, and therefore the whole will either rejoice together or grieve together." "It must be that this happens in a city governed by the best laws. But it is now time for us to return to our city and inquire whether the things now established among us agree most with this city, or rather with another." "By all means." "Are there not princes and people in other cities, and similarly in this one?" "There are." "And will all these call one another citizens?" "Why not?" "But besides the name of citizen, how does the people call the princes in other cities?" "In most indeed, masters; but in a popular government, princes." "But the people of our city, how will they name the princes beyond the name of citizen?" "Saviors and helpers," he said. "And in what way will those call the people?" "Payers of wages and nurturers."

<margin>H</margin> "Who indeed among the princes of other cities would call one of his colleagues his kinsman, and another a stranger?" "Many indeed." "A kinsman..."

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from Book V of Plato’s Republic. Socrates has just established the laws regarding the ages for procreation and is now explaining the social consequences of the "community of women and children" among the Guardian class, specifically how it fosters total unity within the state.</meta>

# PLATO'S [REPUBLIC]

<margin>A</margin> ...therefore he both thinks of and speaks of his own as his own; but of the stranger, as not his own. "Exactly." But among your guardians, is there any who would consider or address any of his fellow-guardians as a stranger? "Not at all," he said. "For in whomever he meets, he will believe he is meeting either a brother, or a sister, or a father, or a mother, or a son, or a daughter, or the children or ancestors of these." You speak excellently; but tell me this too: will you only establish the names of kinship by law, or must they also perform all the duties associated with those names? Regarding fathers, must they show the reverence, care, and obedience that the law prescribes for parents? Otherwise, they might face the anger of both gods and men, as those who act neither holily nor justly if they do otherwise. <margin>B</margin> Will these words, or others, ring in the ears of the children from all the citizens, both concerning those pointed out to them as parents and concerning other relatives? "These very words," he said. "For it would be absurd if the names of kinship were uttered only by the mouth without the performance of duties." In this city, then, more than any other, when one person fares well or ill, they will all cry out with one voice, as we were just saying: "Mine is doing well," or "Mine is doing poorly." "Very true," he said. And we said that along with this opinion and these words, common pleasures and <margin>C</margin> pains would follow. "And we were right to say so." Therefore, our citizens will most especially share in that thing which they call "mine"; and sharing in this, they will thus share most fully in common pleasures and pains. "Deeply so." And the cause of these things, along with the rest of the city's constitution, is the community of wives and children among the guardians. "It is so, entirely." Indeed, we confessed this to be the greatest good for a city when we said that a well-governed city is like a body, which shares in the pleasure and pain of any of its individual parts. "And we were right to concede that." Therefore, the cause of the greatest good for the city has been shown to us to be the community of children and women among the auxiliary class. "Completely." And this is consistent with what was said before. For we said that they should have neither private houses, nor <margin>D</margin> lands, nor any possession, but should receive their nourishment from others as a reward for their guardianship, and all consume it in common, if they are to be true guardians. "Correct," he said. Do not both the things said before and the things said now make them even more into true guardians, and prevent them from tearing the city apart by calling "mine" not the same thing for everyone, but different things for different people? One person dragging to his own house whatever he could acquire apart from the others, another into his separate house; and with separate wives and children, each would feel individual pleasures and pains. Instead, with one common opinion of what is "their own," and all tending toward the same goal as far as possible, they will be affected by similar pleasures and pains if anything happens. "Most certainly." And what of lawsuits and mutual accusations? Will they not <margin>E</margin> all but vanish, since no one will possess anything of his own except his body, the rest being common? From this it follows that they will be free from civil strife, at least regarding those disputes that usually arise over money, children, or relatives. "It is absolutely necessary that these be absent." Furthermore, they will not contend with one another over acts of violence. For we shall assert that it is honorable and just for equals to defend themselves against equals, imposing the duty of physical care for their bodies. "Correct." And this law also contains a right principle: that if someone is angry with another and seeks to satisfy his anger, he will be less likely to provoke greater civil strife. "Exactly so." Our law will appoint the elder to rule over all the younger, and to correct them. "That is clear." Furthermore, it is certain that a younger man will never attempt to violate or strike an elder unless the rulers command it, nor will he likely treat him with any dishonor. For two guardians are sufficient to prevent this: fear and shame. Shame will not permit them to violate those they suspect are their parents; <margin>G</margin> and fear will deter anyone from injury, fearing that all the others—some as sons, some as brothers, some as fathers—will come to the aid of the one oppressed. "It happens exactly so." In every way, then, the men will live in peace with one another according to these laws. "Very much so." And since these men do not engage in civil strife among themselves, there is no fear that the rest of the city will ever move against them or against each other. "Certainly not." I hesitate to mention the most trivial of the evils they will be free from, as it is somewhat unbecoming. Flattery of the rich by the poor will surely be absent, as will the anxieties and pains of the needy when they struggle to nourish children and seek money for the necessary support of household servants—now borrowing, now denying what they received, and striving for profit by any means. They also set aside many things with their wives and servants to store for a time. For how many and what kind of things men suffer in these matters, O friend; they are both servile and illiberal, and not worth describing. "It is clear even to a blind man," he said. They will be free from all these things, and will live a life more blessed than those who win at Olympia. "In what way?" Because those victors are considered happy for a small part of what these men possess. <margin>H</margin> For the victory of these guardians is more noble, and their public nourishment more complete...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...to consider and speak of what is kindred <note>original: "oikeion"</note> as his own, and what is alien <note>original: "allotrion"</note> as not his own. "Just so." What then of the guardians in your city? Is there any who would consider or address any of his fellow-guardians as a stranger? "Not at all," he said. "For in whomever he meets, he will believe he is meeting either a brother, or a sister, or a father, or a mother, or a son, or a daughter, or the children or ancestors of these." "You speak most beautifully," I said. "But tell me this further: will you only legislate that these names of kinship be used, or must they also perform all their actions in accordance with the names? Toward their fathers, they must show all the reverence the law requires for fathers, as well as care and the duty of being obedient to parents. Otherwise, it will be better for him neither before the gods nor before men, as he would be acting neither holily nor justly if he did anything other than this. <margin>B</margin> Will these sayings, or others, be sung by all the citizens directly into the ears of the children, both concerning those pointed out to them as fathers and concerning other relatives?" "These," he said. "For it would be ridiculous if they only uttered the names of kinship through their mouths without deeds." "Therefore, of all cities, this one will most perfectly agree when any one person fares either well or ill; they will say that phrase we just mentioned: 'What is mine is doing well,' or 'What is mine is doing poorly.'" "Most true," he said. "And did we not say that with this belief and this phrase, common pleasures and pains would follow?" "And we were right to say so." <margin>C</margin> "Will not our citizens, then, most especially share in that thing which they call 'mine'? And sharing in this, will they not thus share most fully in pleasure and pain?" "Quite so." "And is not the cause of this, in addition to the rest of the constitution, the community of women and children for the guardians?" "It is the greatest cause," he said. "And yet, we agreed this was the greatest good for a city, comparing a well-ordered city to a body in respect to how it feels the pleasure and pain of its parts." "And we were right to agree," he said. "So the cause of the greatest good for the city has appeared to us to be the community of wives and children among the auxiliaries." "Certainly," he said. "And indeed, we were in agreement with the previous points. For we said somewhere that they must have neither private houses nor land, nor any possession, but should receive nourishment from the others as a reward for their guarding, and all consume it in common, <margin>D</margin> if they are to be truly guardians." "Correct," he said. "Does not then what I am saying, both the things mentioned before and what is being said now, make them still more into true guardians, and prevent them from tearing the city apart by calling 'mine' not the same thing, but different things for different people? One man dragging to his own house whatever he can acquire apart from the others, another to his house, which is different; and having different wives and children, producing individual pleasures and pains that are private to them? Instead, they should all tend toward the same thing as their own, and as far as possible, all feel the same pleasures and pains together." "Precisely," he said. "What then? Will not lawsuits and accusations against one another vanish from among them, so to speak, because no one possesses anything private except his body, while everything else is <margin>E</margin> common? From this it follows that they will be free from civil strife, as much as people usually fight over the possession of money, or children, or relatives." "It is a great necessity," he said, "that they be rid of these." "And indeed, there would not even be lawsuits for violence and assault among them. For we shall say it is noble and just for those of the same age to defend themselves against those of the same age, placing the necessity of caring for their bodies upon them." "Correct," he said. "And this law is also right," I said: "if someone is angry at anyone, by satisfying his anger in such a way, he would be less likely to move toward greater civil strife." "Certainly." "The elder will be commanded to rule over and punish all the younger." "Clearly." "And it is also clear that a younger man will never attempt to use violence against or strike an elder, unless the rulers command it; nor do I think he will dishonor him in any other way. For two guardians are sufficient to prevent it: fear and shame. Shame, on the one hand, preventing him from touching those he considers parents; fear, on the other, that the others will come to the aid of the one suffering—some as sons, some as brothers, some as fathers." "It happens that way," he said. "Then in every way, because of the laws, the men will have peace with one another." "Very much so." "And if they do not strive among themselves, there is no danger that the rest of the city will ever be at odds with them or with each other." "Indeed not." "I hesitate even to mention the smallest of evils because of their <margin>G</margin> unseemliness, from which they would be delivered: the flattery of the rich by the poor, and the difficulties and pains they have in rearing children and making money for the necessary food for servants—now borrowing, now denying, now getting it by any means, and giving it to their wives and servants to manage. How many such things there are, my friend, and what terrible and ignoble things they suffer, not even worth mentioning." "They are clear," he said, "even to a blind man." "They will be delivered from all these things, and will live a life more blessed than that which the Olympic victors live." "How?" "Because those men are deemed happy for a small part of what is available to these." <margin>H</margin> "For the victory of these men is more noble, and their public nourishment more perfect..."

<margin>A</margin> ...moreover, for their victory, they win the salvation of the entire city. For their sustenance and all other necessities of life, they and their children receive a crown <note>Original: "ἀναδοῦνται," referring to being crowned like an athlete.</note>, and they receive prizes of honor from their own city while living; and when they have died, they share in a worthy burial. "These are very beautiful things indeed," he said. "Do you remember then," I asked, "that in our earlier discussion, I know not whose argument <note>This refers to Adeimantus's objection at the beginning of Book IV.</note> reproached us, saying that we were not making the guardians happy? For though it was in their power to have everything belonging to the citizens, they had nothing. We said then, I believe, that we would look into this another time if it were convenient; but for the present, we were making the guardians truly guardians, and the city as happy as possible—not looking at one specific class within it to mold their happiness." "I remember," he said. "What <margin>B</margin> then? Does the life of these auxiliaries <term>auxiliaries: the soldier class within the Guardians</term> appear to us now to be far more noble and better than that of Olympic victors? It does not seem to be at all like the life of cobblers, or other craftsmen, or farmers." "It does not seem so to me," he said. "Yet truly, what I said then is right to repeat here: that if the guardian should strive to become happy in such a way that he is no longer a guardian, and he is not satisfied with a life so moderate and stable—and, as we say, the best—but a foolish and childish opinion of happiness should seize him, driving him by his power to claim everything in the city as his own, he will come to know that Hesiod was truly wise when he said that, in a way, <margin>C</margin> <margin>Hesiod, Works and Days</margin> 'the half is more than the whole.' <note>original: "πλέον εἶναί πως ἥμισυ παντός"</note> If he takes me as his counselor, he will remain in this life."

"Do you then agree," I said, "to this community of women with men which we have described, regarding education, the bearing of children, and the guarding of other citizens? That whether they stay in the city or go out to war, they must guard together and hunt together like dogs, and in every way participate in everything according to their ability? And by doing these things, they will act for the best, and not contrary to the nature of the female toward the male, by which nature they were meant to share with one another?" "I agree," he said. "Is it not then remaining," I asked, "to determine if such a community is possible among humans, just as it is <margin>D</margin> among other animals, and in what way it is possible?" "You have anticipated," he said, "the very question I was going to ask." "Regarding their conduct in war," I said, "it is quite clear, I think, how they will fight." "How?" he asked. "They will go on campaigns together, and moreover, they will bring those of their children who are sturdy into the war, so that like the children of other craftsmen, they may observe those things which they will have to craft when they are grown. Besides observing, they shall assist and serve in all things pertaining to war, and look after their fathers and mothers. Or have you not noticed what happens in the arts—for example, how the children of potters observe for a long time as assistants before they ever touch the clay?" "I have indeed." "Should these potters then be more careful in educating their own children through experience and observation of their future duties than the guardians? That would be <margin>E</margin> ridiculous," he said. "Furthermore, every creature fights more fiercely when its offspring are present." "That is so. But there is a danger, Socrates, and no small one, that if they suffer a defeat (as often happens in war), they may lose their children along with themselves, making it impossible for the rest of the city to recover." "What you say is true," I replied. "But do you think our first priority should be to ensure they never face any danger?" "By no means." "Well then, if they must face danger, should it not be in those instances where they will become better men if they succeed?" "Clearly so." "And do you think it makes only a small difference, not worth the risk, whether children who are to be warriors observe the business of war or not?" "No, it makes a great difference for the purpose you mention." "We must, therefore, make the children observers of war as a starting point, but we must also devise safety for them; then all will be well. Is that not so?" "Yes." "First, then," I said, "their fathers, so far as humans can, will not be ignorant but knowledgeable about which campaigns are dangerous and which are not." "That is likely," he said. "Into some they will take them, but of others, they will be cautious." "Rightly so." "And they will surely," I said, "place over them as commanders not the most worthless men, but those who by experience and age are fit to be leaders and tutors." "That is appropriate." "Yet we must admit that many things happen to many people contrary to expectation." "Very much so." "To guard against such things, then, my friend, we must <margin>G</margin> give the children wings <note>A metaphor for providing them with the means of swift escape.</note> from the very beginning, so that if need be, they may fly away and escape." "What do you mean?" he asked. "They must be mounted on horses," I said, "at the youngest possible age, and when they have been taught to ride, they must be taken to the spectacle not on high-spirited or aggressive horses, but on those that are the swiftest and most obedient. For in this way, they will best observe their future work, and most safely escape, if necessary, by following their elder leaders." "I think you speak rightly," he said. "Now, what about the business of war? <margin>H</margin> How should your soldiers behave toward one another and toward the enemy? Does my view seem right or not?" "Tell me," he said, "what is it?" "If any of them," I said, "should desert his rank, or throw away his arms, or do any such thing out of cowardice, should we not demote him to the status of a craftsman or a farmer?" "Certainly." ### PLATO'S [REPUBLIC]

...should be crowned by each of the youths and boys in turn while on campaign, does it not seem so to you? Indeed it does. And what of this: should they not also join right hands? This as well. But perhaps this further point does not yet seem right to you? What is it? That he should receive and give a kiss to anyone he wishes. On the contrary, I think this most important of all. And I believe this law should be added: that as long as they are on that expedition, no one whom he wishes to kiss may refuse him; thus, if anyone is seized by love for someone, whether male or female, he will be more eager to achieve victory. This is excellent; for it has already been said that marriages will be more readily available to brave men than to others, and such selections will be more frequent, so that as many children as possible may be born from such men. We certainly said that. Indeed, according to Homer, it is just to honor such young men in this way. For he said that Ajax, who excelled in war, was "honored with long chines" <note>original: "assiduis ab humeris" / "νώτοισιν... διηνεκέεσσι". This refers to the choice cut of meat from the back of an ox, a traditional hero's reward in the Iliad.</note>, as if this were a fitting honor for a vigorous and brave man, by which both his honor and his strength might be increased together. Quite right. In these matters, then, we shall follow Homer. For in our sacrifices and all such occasions, we shall honor good men—in proportion to how good they appear to be—with hymns and the things we just mentioned, and also with seats of honor, meats, and "full cups," so that we may simultaneously honor and train these excellent men and women. You speak most beautifully. And as for him who dies in battle after conducting himself bravely, shall we not say first that he belongs to the <margin>Hesiod, *Works and Days*, Book 1.</margin> golden race? Most certainly. Then, placing our faith in Hesiod, we shall assert that whenever any of this race die, "they become holy terrestrial guardian spirits <note>original: "dæmones" / "δαίμονες". In Greek thought, these are not "demons" in the modern sense, but protective spirits or intermediaries between gods and men.</note>, excellent ones, averters of evil, and guardians of mortal men." We shall certainly believe so. We shall therefore consult the oracle to learn how we ought to bury these blessed and godlike men, and with what special marks of distinction; and so we shall bury them as the god directs. Without a doubt. And for all time thereafter, we shall care for and worship their tombs as those of guardian spirits. We shall likewise observe these same rites for those who, having been judged to have lived with exceptional virtue, die of old age or in some other manner. That is surely fitting. But how will our soldiers conduct themselves toward their enemies? In what regard? First, concerning slavery: do you think it just that Greeks should reduce Greek cities to slavery? Or rather, should they not permit this to be done by others, and oppose it as far as they can, and make it a habit to spare the Greek race, fearing lest they themselves be forced into slavery by the barbarians? <note>The term "barbarians" was used by Greeks to refer to anyone who did not speak Greek.</note> It is entirely and in every way better to spare them; no Greek should be made a slave by our men, and they should advise other Greeks to be careful of this as well. Exactly; for in this way they would turn more readily and strongly against the barbarians and refrain from fighting one another. What else? Is it honorable to strip the dead of anything except their weapons after a victory, or not? Does this not provide a pretext for cowards not to face the enemy, as if they were doing something significant while they are actually stooping over a corpse? For many armies have already perished because of this greed for looting. Very much so. Does it not seem illiberal, greedy, and characteristic of a small, womanly mind to strip a corpse and to think the dead body is an enemy when the adversary himself has flown away, leaving behind the instrument with which he fought? Do you think those who do this differ at all from dogs who snap at the stones thrown at them, but do not touch the person who threw them? I think they do not differ in the least. Therefore, we must abstain from such looting, for it hinders victory. We must abstain entirely. Nor shall we bring captured weapons into the temples to dedicate them to God—especially the weapons of Greeks—if indeed we care for the goodwill of other Greeks. Rather, we shall fear lest it be an unholy pollution <note>original: "scelus impium" / "μίασμα". This refers to ritual or religious defilement.</note> to bring such things from our own people into a sacred place, unless the god says otherwise. Quite right. And will your soldiers ravage the lands of the Greeks with whom they fight, or burn their houses? I would gladly hear what you think of this. To me, it seems that neither should be done, but only the annual harvest should be taken. Shall I tell you why? Certainly. It seems to me that just as these two names exist—"War" and "Civil Strife" <note>original: "Bellum ac Seditio" / "πόλεμός τε καὶ στάσις". Socrates distinguishes between external war and internal conflict.</note>—so there are two distinct things underlying these two differences. I say these two are: one being internal and related, the other being foreign and strange. Enmity among our own kind is called civil strife; that against foreigners is called war. What you say is not at all out of place. Consider whether this is also to the point: I assert that all Greeks are of one kin and related to each other by race, but are foreign and strange to the barbarians. You speak excellently. Whenever, then, Greeks fight against barbarians, or barbarians against Greeks, we shall say they are at war, and are enemies by nature, and this enmity shall be called "war." But when Greeks act in such a way against Greeks, we shall say that they are friends by nature, but that Greece is in this case sick and in a state of discord, and this enmity should be called "civil strife." I agree to view it this way. Consider then, I said, that in what is now agreed to be civil strife, wherever such a thing occurs and a city is divided, if both sides ravage the fields and burn the houses of the others, how ruinous the strife appears to be, and neither side seems to love their country. For they would never dare to ravage their nurse and mother; rather, it is sufficient for the victors to take the crops from the vanquished,

<column-break/>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Glaucon in Book V of Plato's Republic. Having discussed the shared lives of the Guardians, they now conclude their rules for "Greek-on-Greek" warfare before addressing the most difficult challenge: whether such an ideal city can actually exist in the physical world.</meta>

# ON THE REPUBLIC, BOOK V.

<margin>A</margin> ...thinking that they will one day be reconciled and will not be at war forever.
"Their mindset," he said, "is certainly much gentler than the other."
"What then?" I asked. "In this city you are founding, will the citizens not be Greeks?"
"They must be," he replied.
"And will they not then be good and gentle?"
"Very much so."
"And will they not be <term>Philhellenes</term> <note>original: "φιλέλληνες"; literally 'lovers of Greeks.' In the ancient world, this implied a shared cultural and religious identity that transcended individual city-state loyalties.</note>? Will they not consider all Greece their own, and share in the same sacred rites as the other Greeks?"
"Most certainly."
"Therefore, they will consider any disagreement with Greeks—their own kin—to be factional strife, and they will not even call it war?"
"Indeed not."
"And they will disagree as those who intend to be reconciled?"
"Absolutely."
"Thus they will correct them in a kindly way, <margin>B</margin> not punishing them with slavery or seeking their destruction; they will be correctors, not enemies."
"Exactly so," he said.
"As Greeks, then, they will not ravage Greece, nor will they burn houses. Nor will they agree that every person in a city—men, women, and children—is their enemy; rather, they will hold that only the few who caused the disagreement are enemies. For all these reasons, they will not be willing to waste the land, since the majority of the people are friends, nor will they overturn houses. They will carry the dispute only as far as is needed until the innocent sufferers force those responsible to pay the penalty."
"I agree," he said, "that our citizens must behave this way toward their Greek rivals; but toward the <term>barbarians</term> <note>original: "βαρβάρους"; to the Greeks, this meant anyone who did not speak Greek, though here it specifically refers to foreign enemies like the Persians.</note>, they should behave as <margin>C</margin> the Greeks now do toward one another."
"Let us then establish this law for our Guardians: they are neither to waste the land nor burn houses."
"Let us establish it," he said, "and agree that this and our previous rules are well-settled. But Socrates, it seems to me that if one allows you to speak on such things, you will never remember the point you pushed aside to say all this: how is it possible for this constitution to come into being, and in what way is it possible? I grant that if it did exist, it would bring all manner of good to the city where it happened. I will even add what you left out: they would fight their enemies most effectively because they would never abandon one another, knowing and calling each other by these names: <margin>D</margin> brothers, fathers, and sons. And if their women joined the campaign—whether in the same rank or stationed behind to terrify the enemy and provide aid if needed—I know they would be entirely invincible. I also see all the domestic benefits you have omitted. But since I admit that all these things, and ten thousand others, would exist if this constitution were realized, say no more about them. Instead, let us now try to convince ourselves of this: is it possible? And if so, how? Let the other matters go."
"You have made a sudden assault upon my argument," I said, "and you show no mercy to a man on campaign! Perhaps you do not realize that I have barely escaped the first two waves, and now you are bringing upon me the greatest and most <margin>E</margin> difficult <term>third wave</term> <note>original: "τρικυμίας"; the 'triple wave' was a common Greek metaphor for a series of increasing challenges. Here, Socrates refers to his three most controversial proposals: equal education for women, the abolition of the private family, and (the upcoming) rule by philosopher-kings.</note>. When you see and hear it, you will surely grant me your sympathy, realizing that I had good reason to hesitate and fear to speak such a paradoxical argument or attempt to examine it."
"The more you say such things," he replied, "the less we will let you off from explaining how this constitution can become possible. So speak, and do not delay."
"Well then," I said, "we must first remember that we came to this point while searching for the nature of justice and injustice."
"We must," he said, "but what of it?"
"Nothing. But if we discover what justice is, shall we require that the just man differ in no way from justice itself, but be in every way exactly like justice? Or shall we be satisfied if he is <margin>F</margin> as close to it as possible and partakes of it more than anyone else?"
"We shall be satisfied with that," he said.
"Then it was for the sake of a model," I said, "that we were seeking the nature of justice itself and what a perfectly just man would be like, if he could exist. And likewise for injustice and the most unjust man. This was so that by looking at them—seeing how they appeared to us in terms of happiness and its opposite—we would be forced to admit regarding ourselves that whoever is most like them will have a fate most like theirs. We did not do this to prove that these things can actually happen."
"That is true," he said.
"Do you think a painter is any less good if, after painting a model of the most beautiful human being <margin>G</margin> and rendering every detail in the picture perfectly, he could not prove that such a man could actually exist?"
"By Zeus, I do not," he replied.
"Well then? Did we not say we were constructing a model in speech of a good city?"
"Certainly."
"Do you think we spoke any less well, then, if we cannot prove that it is possible to inhabit a city exactly as we have described it?"
"Not at all," he said.
"That is the truth of the matter," I said. "But if I must also strive to please you by showing how and in what way it might be most possible, you must agree with me again on these same points for the sake of the demonstration."
"Which points?"
"Is it possible for anything to be practiced exactly as it is described? Or is it the nature of practice to grasp truth less than speech does, even if some think otherwise? Do you agree or not?"
"I agree," he said.
"Then do not force me to prove that the things we have described in speech must happen exactly so in deed. But if we are able to find how a city might be inhabited as closely as possible to what has been said, you must admit that we have discovered how these things you command can be possible. Would you not be satisfied if you achieved this? For I certainly would be."

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...thinking that they will not always be at war with one another, but will eventually be reconciled. This is surely the sentiment of gentler men.
"This city you are founding, is it not Greek?"
"It is."
"Therefore, the citizens in it will be both good and gentle?"
"Greatly so."
"Wherefore they are lovers of the Greeks. Surely they will consider all Greece to be joined to them, and they will hold sacred rites in common with others, as is the custom."
"Most definitely."
"Thus, they will consider a contention arising against other Greeks as if it were conducted with their own people; they will call it a factional dispute, not a war."
"They will act exactly so."
"Therefore, they will argue as those who must one day be reconciled."
"Certainly."
"They will act, then, with a benevolent and temperate mind, <margin>B</margin> not looking toward slavery or death, as they are not enemies in the least."
"In this way, indeed."
"Since they are Greeks, they will not destroy Greece, nor will they burn houses, nor will they believe that in every city everyone is against them—men, women, and children—but only the very few who were the authors of the discord. For this reason, they will neither devastate the region of those who are mostly friends, nor will they subvert their homes; they will struggle only so far as to ensure that those who gave cause for the discord pay a just and fair penalty."
"I agree indeed that Greeks should fight in this way, but against barbarians they <margin>C</margin> ought to be minded as the Greeks are currently minded toward one another."
"Let us then establish this law for the Guardians: that they neither plunder the fields nor consume the houses with fire."
"Let us establish it," he said, "and let us assert that this, along with what came before, is correctly settled."
"But it seems to me, O Socrates, that if one allows you to go on recounting other things, you will never remember that point which you pushed aside to bring all this into the open: namely, whether it is possible for this republic to exist, and in what way it can exist. For if it were to exist, I do not doubt that all good things would come to the city itself. I also see what you left out: that those citizens would fight most strenuously against enemies, because they would never desert one another, knowing <margin>D</margin> each other to be kinsmen and calling one another by these names: brothers, fathers, sons. And if the women were to serve in the military as well—whether in the same rank or in the rear—to terrify the enemy and to bring help to the men when necessity demands, I know for certain they would be invincible. And I understand how many good things would follow them at home, even if all have not been said. But since I concede that all these and many other benefits would come if this republic were to exist, do not mention more about it. Instead, let us now endeavor to persuade ourselves that it is possible, and by what reason it is possible for this republic to stand. Let us leave the other matters aside."
"With a sudden incursion, you have again invaded my discourse, and you do not forgive a man on campaign. Perhaps you do not notice <margin>E</margin> that I have barely emerged from two waves, and now you thrust me back into a third, the greatest and most difficult. After you have seen and heard it, you will surely grant me pardon, recognizing that it was not without cause that I feared to enter upon a discourse so far removed from the common opinion of men."
"The more things of this kind you gather," he said, "the less you will be released by us from showing in what way this republic can come to be. Therefore, speak now, and do not delay."
"First of all," I said, "one must remember that we have come to this point while inquiring into the nature of justice and injustice."
"Certainly we must, but where does this lead?"
"Well, if we have beheld the nature of justice, shall we judge the just man to be in no way different <margin>F</margin> from it, but to be entirely such as justice itself is? Or shall we think it sufficient if he approaches it as closely as possible and partakes of it more than all others?"
"We shall think that is quite enough."
"It was for the sake of an example, then, that we sought the nature of justice and the character of the perfectly just man, if he should exist. And likewise for injustice and the most unjust man. This was so that as we looked upon them—seeing what they appeared to be regarding happiness and misery—we would be forced to confess about ourselves that whatever lot each of us has, it will be such as he who shows himself most similar to them. We did not investigate these things to show that they could actually happen."
"These things are true."
"Do you judge that a painter would be any less good because, after he has produced an absolute model of human beauty <margin>G</margin> and omitted nothing from the appearance, he is unable to demonstrate that such a man can be found?"
"By no means."
"And did we not likewise fashion a model of the most excellent city in our discourse?"
"Indeed."
"Do you then think we have spoken any less correctly if we cannot show that such a city can exist as we have depicted in our speech?"
"Not at all."
"That is indeed the truth of it. But if, for your sake, it must also be demonstrated how and according to what it might most be achieved, you must again grant me these same points for the demonstration."
"Which points?"
"Can anything be done exactly as it is said? Or is it ordained by nature that action should reach the truth less than speech, even if it does not seem so to some? Do you indeed grant this, or not?"
"I grant it."
"Then do not compel me to demonstrate that these things we have run through in words must be realized entirely in fact. But if we are able to find by what reason the institution of a Republic may come as close as possible to these things, it must be confessed that we have discovered how the things you command can be achieved. Will you not consider this to be enough, if you achieve this much? For I indeed would be satisfied."

### OF PLATO

<margin>A</margin> "And I too," I said. "Next, as it seems, let us try to seek and show what is currently done poorly in cities, which prevents them from being governed in this way; and whether by the change of one small thing a city might be brought to this form of government; and if not one, then two; or if not two, then by the fewest possible changes and those of the least significance."
"By all means," he said.
"I think I can show," I said, "that by one single change it can be transformed. It is certainly not a small or easy change, but it is possible."
"What is it?" he asked.
"I am coming now," I said, "to what we compared to the greatest wave. It shall be spoken, even if—just like a wave breaking into laughter—it should utterly overwhelm me with ridicule and contempt. Consider what I am about to say."
"Speak on," he said.
"Unless," I said, "either **philosophers rule as kings** in cities, or those who are now called kings and potentates **philosophize genuinely and sufficiently**, and these two things—political power and philosophy—coincide in the same person, while the many natures of those who currently pursue one without the other are forcibly excluded, there will be no rest from evils, my dear Glaucon, for cities, nor, I think, for the human race. Nor will this republic, which we have described in words, ever be born to the extent possible and see the light of the sun. This is what I have long hesitated to say, seeing how much it goes against common opinion. For it is difficult to see that no other city, whether private or public, could ever be happy."
And he replied, "O Socrates, you have let fall such a statement and such an argument that you must expect many people—and not insignificant ones—to immediately throw off their cloaks, as it were, and stripping naked, seize whatever weapon happens to be at hand and run at you in full force, prepared to do terrible things. Unless you defend yourself with argument and escape them, you will truly pay the penalty of being mocked."
"Are you not the cause of this?" I asked.
"And I was right to be!" he said. "But I will not betray you; I will defend you with what I can. I can offer goodwill and encouragement, and perhaps I can answer you more fittingly than another. Therefore, since you have such a helper, try to show these skeptics that things are as you say."
"I must try," I said, "since you offer such great an alliance. It seems necessary to me, if we are to escape those you mention, to define for them who we mean when we dare to say that philosophers must rule. Thus, when they are made clear, one can defend oneself by showing that it belongs to their nature to both study philosophy and lead the city, while it belongs to others not to touch it, but to follow the leader."
"It is time," he said, "to define them."
"Come then, follow me this way, so that we may explain it sufficiently in some manner."
"Lead on," he said.
"Do I need to remind you," I said, "or do you remember yourself, that when we say someone loves something, if it is said truly, he must not love one part of it and not another, but must be devoted to the whole?"
"I need a reminder, it seems," he said, "for I do not quite understand."
"It would be more fitting for another to say that, O Glaucon," I replied. "But it is not fitting for a man who is a lover to forget that all boys in their bloom sting and stir the lover of boys, appearing worthy of care and affection. Is this not how you act toward beautiful youths? One, because he is snub-nosed, is praised as 'charming' by you; another’s hook-nose you call 'regal'; and the one between these two you say is of 'perfect proportions.' Those who are dark you call 'manly' to look upon, and the fair-skinned you say are 'children of the gods.' As for the 'honey-colored' <note>original: "μελιχλώρους" (melichlōrous); a term used by lovers to flatter a youth who was actually pale or sallow.</note>, do you think that name is anything other than the creation of a lover who makes light of paleness and bears it easily if it is found in one who is in his bloom? In a word, you find every excuse and use every turn of phrase so as not to reject anyone who is in the flower of youth."
"If you wish to use me as an example of how lovers behave," he said, "I grant it for the sake of the argument."
"What about lovers of wine?" I asked. "Do you not see them doing the same things? They welcome any wine on any pretext?"
"Quite so."
"And indeed, you see that ambitious men <note>original: "φιλοτίμους" (philotimous); literally 'lovers of honor.'</note>, if they cannot lead the whole army, will lead a squad; and if they are not honored by great and venerable men, they are content to be honored by the small and base, because they are entirely desirous of honor."
"Precisely."
"Then say yes or no to this: when we say someone is a desirer of something, shall we say he desires the whole of that kind, or one part but not another?"
"The whole," he said.
"Shall we not then also say that the philosopher is a desirer of wisdom <note>original: "σοφίας" (sophias)</note>, not of one part and not another, but of all wisdom?"
"True."
"The one, then, who is picky about his studies, especially while he is young and does not yet have a rational understanding of what is useful and what is not, we shall not say is a lover of learning <term>philomathē</term> <note>original: "φιλομαθῆ"; one who loves to learn.</note>, nor a philosopher. Just as we say that one who is picky about food is neither hungry nor a lover of food, but a poor eater."
"And we would be right to say so."
"But the man who is willing to taste every kind of learning, who goes joyfully to learn and is insatiable in it—this man we shall rightly call a philosopher. Shall we not?"
To this Glaucon agreed. "But then," he said, "many strange people will be found to be such. For those who are lovers of sights <note>original: "φιλοθεάμονες" (philotheamones); those who attend festivals and theaters just for the spectacle.</note> all seem to be such because they delight in learning; and it is strange to call 'philosophers' those who are curious to hear...

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Glaucon in Book V of Plato's Republic. In the previous section, Socrates began his famous "third wave" of the argument: the claim that philosophers must become kings or kings must become philosophers for a city to find rest from its troubles.
