### ON THE REPUBLIC, BOOK V.

<margin>A</margin> ...to such discourses and such a way of life? Instead, as if they had hired out their ears to listen to every chorus, they are found at the Dionysian festivals <note>The Dionysia were major religious festivals in Athens honoring Dionysus, involving theatrical performances.</note>, missing none, neither in the cities nor in the villages. Shall we say that all these, and others who learn such things, and those of the minor arts, are philosophers? By no means, I said; but they are similar to philosophers. And the true ones, he said, who do you say they are? The ones who love the sight of truth, I said. That is indeed correct, he said, but what do you mean by it? It is not at all easy, I said, to explain to another. But you, I think, will agree with me on this. On what? Since beauty is the opposite of ugliness, they are two.
<margin>B</margin> Of course. And since they are two, each is one? That as well. And about justice and injustice, good and evil, and all <gloss>the same</gloss> <note>original: "autōn"</note> forms, the same account holds: each itself is one, but because they appear everywhere in community with actions and bodies and each other, each appears to be many. You speak correctly, he said. In this way, then, I said, I distinguish those you were just calling "lovers of sights," "lovers of arts," and "men of action," and separately again those about whom we are speaking, who alone might correctly be called philosophers. How do you mean? Those, I said, who love hearing and sights are fond of beautiful sounds and colors and shapes, and everything created from such things, but their intellect is unable to see and be fond of the nature of the beautiful itself.
<margin>C</margin> That is certainly how it is, he said. But those who are able to approach the beautiful itself and see it by itself—would they not be rare? Very much so. The one, then, who acknowledges beautiful things but does not acknowledge beauty itself, and is not able to follow if someone leads him to the knowledge of it—does he seem to you to live in a dream or awake? Consider: does dreaming not consist in this, whether one is asleep or awake, in thinking that a likeness is not a likeness but rather the thing itself that it resembles? I would certainly say, he said, that such a person is dreaming. What then? The one who holds the opposite of these, who acknowledges beauty itself and is able to see both it and the things that participate in it, and does not think that the participants are beauty itself, nor that beauty itself is the participants—does he seem to you to live awake or in a dream? Very much awake, he said. Would we not then correctly call the <gloss>form</gloss> <note>original: "eidos"</note> of his thought "knowledge," because he knows; and the other's "opinion," because he opines? Entirely so.
<margin>D</margin> What then? If the one whom we say opines but does not know is angry with us and disputes that what we say is not true, will we have some way to soothe him and gently persuade him, while hiding that he is not in a healthy state? We must, he said. Come then, consider what <gloss>ask</gloss> <note>original: "erōta"</note> we shall say to him. Or would you like us to inquire of him in this way, saying that if he knows anything, there is no grudge against him, but we would gladly see him knowing something. But tell us this: Does the one who knows, know something or nothing? You answer me on his behalf. I will answer, he said, that he knows something. Does he know what is, or what is not? What is. For how could what is not be known?
<margin>E</margin> We are sufficiently sure of this, then, even if we looked at it from many angles: that which entirely "is" is entirely knowable; and that which in no way "is" is in every way unknowable. Most sufficiently, he said. Very well. If anything, then, is so constituted as both to be and not to be, would it not lie between that which purely is and that which in no way is? It would be in between. Therefore, since knowledge is directed at what is, and ignorance of necessity at what is not, then for this "in-between" we must seek something in between ignorance and knowledge, if there happens to be such a thing. Entirely so. Do we say then that "opinion" is something? Of course. Is it a different power from knowledge, or the same? Different.
<margin>F</margin> Therefore opinion is set over one thing and knowledge over another, each according to its own power. It is so. Does knowledge not naturally know what is, to know what "that which is" is? But rather, it seems to me necessary to distinguish it this way first. How? We shall say that powers <note>Plato uses the term "powers" (dynameis) to refer to the capacities of the soul, like sight or hearing.</note> are a certain class of things by which we are able to do what we can do, and everything else does whatever it can. For example, I say sight and hearing are among the powers, if you understand the form I want to describe. I understand, he said. Listen then to what they seem to me to be. For I do not see any color of a power, nor a shape, nor any such thing as I do in many other cases, looking at which I distinguish for myself that some are one thing and some another. In the case of a power, I look only at that which it is directed toward and what it <margin>G</margin> accomplishes. And in this way, <gloss>or by the form</gloss> <note>original: "ē tō eidei"</note> I have called each of them a power. That which is directed toward the same thing and accomplishes the same thing, I call the same power; and that which is directed toward something else and accomplishes something else, I call another power. What about you? What do you do? The same, he said. Come back here again then, my best of men. Do you say that knowledge itself is a certain power? Or in what class do you place it? Into this one, he said, as the most robust of all powers. What then? Shall we bring "opinion" into the class of power, or into some other form? Not at all, he said. For that by which we are able to opine is nothing other than opinion. But a little while ago you agreed that knowledge and opinion were not the same. How, he said, could any man of sense put the fallible in the same place as the infallible? Excellent, I said. And it is clear that we agree that
<margin>H</margin> opinion is something different from knowledge. Different. Each of them, therefore, being a different power, is naturally directed toward a different object. It is necessary. Knowledge is directed toward what is, to know "being" as it is. Certainly...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...They do not willingly approach the reasoning of speaking and debating: but to hear all the choruses immediately, as if with ears hired for pay, they are observed in the Bacchanalia, and they desire to hear all of them, whether they are performed in the city or in the countryside. Shall we call all these, and others eager to perceive such things, and those devoted to the most base arts, philosophers? By no means, but similar to philosophers. But the true philosophers, whom do you call? The ones eager to behold the truth. That is right, but how do you say it? I would not easily say it to another. But I think you will grant this to me. What
<margin>B</margin> most of all? Since beauty is the opposite of ugliness, these are two things. Why not? And since these are two, each will be one. And this also. Concerning the just and the unjust, the good and the bad, and all forms, the same reasoning holds. For each of these is one itself: but appearing everywhere by the communication of actions and bodies and alternating with each other, each appears to be many. You speak skillfully. I distinguish these by this logic: separately those whom you just spoke of, the lovers of living <note>The Latin text here uses "viuendi" (living), though the context suggests "seeing" or "spectacles."</note> and the studious of arts and actions, and separately also those of whom we speak, whom alone one will rightly call philosophers. How do you say this? Men eager for hearing and seeing are greatly
<margin>C</margin> delighted by beautiful voices, colors, and figures, and all things that consist of such; but their thought cannot reach the nature of the beautiful itself. It is so. But those who are able to ascend to the beautiful itself, and to behold it according to itself, are they not rare? Very rare indeed. He who thinks these things are beautiful, but does not think beauty itself exists, nor, if anyone should lead him to the perception of it, can reach it—does he seem to you to truly know, or to play in dreams? Consider then, is not dreaming this: when someone, whether sleeping or waking, thinks that which is similar to something is not similar, but is the very thing itself which it resembles? I would say this man sees dreams. What then? He who is affected to the contrary, and understands
<margin>D</margin> what the beautiful itself is, and is able to discern both it and those things which participate in it, so that he thinks neither that it is those things, nor those things are it—does he live awake, or sleeping? Certainly wide awake. Therefore we shall rightly call the cognition of this one "knowledge," as of one who knows; and of the other "opinion," as of one who opines. Entirely. If he should be angry with us, he whom we say opines and does not know, and should deny that we speak the truth, by what reasoning shall we mitigate him, and gradually and mildly persuade him that he is not of sound mind? It is indeed necessary. Observe what we shall say to him. If you wish, we will certainly inquire of him in this way, saying that if he knows anything, <margin>or, Let us not change</margin> <note>These marginal notes "vel, Non matamus" suggest a textual variation or correction in the manuscript's source.</note> there is no envy: but it will be pleasing to us both that he knows something, and to have known what he knows. But
<margin>E</margin> tell me this. Whoever knows, does he know something or nothing? But you, answer in his place. Something, certainly. Whether what is, or what is not? What is. For in what way could that which is not be known? This will sufficiently stand, if it is investigated under various reasoning: that clearly what is altogether "being," can also be altogether known; what is in no way "being," is in no way known. Most sufficiently. Come, if anything then is so situated that it both is and is not, will it not be a medium between that which is altogether, and that which is in no way? A medium. About that which is, knowledge itself is occupied. Ignorance of necessity is about that which is not. About the medium of these,
<margin>F</margin> some medium must be investigated, between science <note>In this context, "science" is used as a synonym for "systematic knowledge" (scientia).</note> and ignorance, if anything of this sort is found. Altogether. Do we say that opinion is something? Why not? Whether the same power as science, or a different one? Different. Therefore opinion is occupied with one thing, and science with another, either according to the same power, or each according to its own power. It is so. Does not science indeed know about that which is, by that reason in which it is being? Rather, I think it is necessary that I first distinguish these. How? We will say surely that powers are a certain genus of those things that are, by which we also can do whatever we can, and anything else, whatever it can. Just as I call sight and hearing certain powers, if only you
<margin>G</margin> understand what I am saying. I understand indeed. Hear what seems to me concerning these. For I indeed see neither any color of the power itself, nor a figure, nor any of such things, such as of many other things, looking at which I distinguish some things among myself, that these are one thing, those are another. But in a power, I only look at that toward which it is and what it performs: and by this reasoning, I have called each of them a power: and that indeed which tends toward the same, and performs the same, I call the same; but another which looks toward another thing, and works another thing. But what do you do in these? The same as you. Come, turn back again to these, O best man, whether you say science is a certain
<margin>H</margin> power? Or do you refer it to another genus? A power, and surely the most valid of all powers. But opinion, shall we refer it to a power, or to some other form? To a power, certainly. For that by which we can opine is nothing other than opinion. But a little before you were confessing <note>original: "confitebaris"</note> that science and opinion were not the same. For how, he said, could anyone having a mind assert that the thing which can fail and that which cannot fail are the same? Very well indeed. It is established therefore that knowledge is something different for us from opinion. Plainly different. Each therefore can work one thing or another by its own nature. It is necessary. Science, which is for that which is, knows the being itself as it is. Certainly.

<meta>The catchword "confitebaris" at the bottom of the Latin column matches the start of the final paragraph's realization that knowledge and opinion are distinct.</meta>

<summary>This page defines the true philosopher as a "lover of the sight of truth," distinguishing them from "lovers of sights and sounds" who only appreciate beautiful objects rather than Beauty itself. It establishes the ontological framework that Knowledge corresponds to "Being," Ignorance to "Non-being," and Opinion to the intermediate state between them.</summary>
<keywords>Plato, Republic, Socrates, Glaucon, knowledge, opinion, Being, Non-being, Forms, Powers, Beauty, Dionysia, philosophy, intellect</keywords>

--- Page 500 ---
<meta>This page continues the dialogue in Book V of the Republic. Socrates is leading Glaucon through a logical proof to distinguish between "Knowledge" (which deals with what truly is) and "Opinion" (which deals with things that both are and are not). This distinction is crucial for Plato's definition of the true philosopher.</meta>

### ->PLATONIS<-
### ->(OF PLATO)<-

<margin>A</margin> Does opinion, then, form opinions? Yes. Is it the same thing that knowledge knows? Or is it that which is perceived by opinion and that which is known by knowledge the same, or is it rather impossible? It is certainly impossible based on what we have already granted: if indeed different powers are by nature directed toward different things, and both knowledge and opinion are powers, each different from the other, as we said. From these points, it is impossible for the object of knowledge and the object of opinion to be the same. 

Now then, if that which "is" <note>Being, or the realm of unchanging Truth</note> is perceived by knowledge, must we not say that what is perceived by opinion is something other than that which "is"? It must be something else. Does one then form an opinion about that which "is not"? Or is it impossible to form an opinion about what "is not"? Think about it this way: Does not everyone who forms an opinion direct his opinion toward something? Or is it possible to form an opinion, yet form an opinion about nothing? That is impossible. But whoever forms an opinion, opines some one thing? Without a doubt. Yet that which "is not" should not be called "one thing," but rather "nothing." Exactly. We necessarily attribute ignorance to that which "is not," but knowledge to that which "is." Quite right. Therefore, one opines neither that which "is" nor that which "is not." That is so. Consequently, opinion will be neither ignorance nor knowledge. So it seems.

Is it then outside of these, exceeding knowledge in clarity or ignorance in obscurity? Neither of these. Does it then seem to you that opinion is darker than knowledge, but <margin>B</margin> clearer than ignorance? Very much so. It lies, then, between both? Certainly. Therefore, opinion will be the midpoint between them. A midpoint indeed. 

Did we not say earlier that if anything should appear such that it both "is" and "is not" at the same time, such a thing would be placed between that which truly "is" and that which entirely "is not"? And that neither knowledge nor ignorance would pertain to it, but rather that which appeared to be between ignorance and knowledge? Rightly so. And now it has appeared that what we call "opinion" is the midpoint between these two. It has indeed. 

Therefore, it remains for us to find, I think, that which participates in both—that is, in both "being" and "not being"—and which cannot be purely called either one; so that if it appears to us, we may justly call it the "opinable" <note>That which can be the subject of opinion</note>, <margin>C</margin> attributing the extremes to the extremes and the middle to the middle. Is it not so? Exactly so. 

These things being established, I shall ask him—that man who denies that the Beautiful itself and the one Form <note>The "Idea" or "Form," the perfect version of a concept</note> of beauty exists, which always remains the same in the same way, but who believes there are many beautiful things. This "lover of sights" <note>The philotheamōn, who loves the physical world but not the underlying truth</note> will in no way admit that the Beautiful is one, or the Just is one, and so on for the rest. I shall ask him: "Of all these many beautiful things, my good man, is there any that will not also appear ugly? And of the just things, any that will not appear unjust? And of the holy things, any that will not appear unholy?" No, he said, but it is necessary that these beautiful things will also appear ugly in some way, as will the others you ask about. 

What about the many double things? Do they seem any less half than they do double? Not at all. And the large and the small, or the light and the heavy—will they be called these things any more than they will be called their opposites? No, he said, but each will always participate in both. Is each of these many things, then, more than it is not that which someone says it is? This is like those double-meaning jokes told at banquets, or the <margin>D</margin> children’s riddle about the eunuch <note>The riddle of the eunuch who hit a bat: A man who was not a man (a eunuch), seeing and not seeing (having poor sight) a bird that was not a bird (a bat), sitting on a branch that was not a branch (a reed), hit it and did not hit it (with a stone that was not a stone, a pumice stone).</note> and his aim at the bat—about how and with what he hit it. For these things are ambiguous; it is not possible to firmly understand any of them as either "being" or "not being," nor as both, nor as neither. 

Do you know how to treat them? Can you find a better place for them than the middle between essence and non-being? For they will appear neither darker than "not being" (so as to "be" less), nor clearer than "being" (so as to "be" more). You speak very truly. 

We have found then, it seems, that the many conventional views held by the many <note>The masses or the unphilosophical</note> about beauty and other things, are rolling around somewhere in the middle between that which entirely "is not" and that which entirely "is." We have found it indeed. And we previously agreed that if such a thing appeared, it should be called "perceived by opinion" rather than "known by knowledge," since it wanders in the middle and is caught by the intermediate power. It was so agreed. 

Therefore, those who look upon these many beautiful things, but do not see the Beautiful itself, and are unable to follow anyone who would lead them to it—and those who look upon many just things, but not Justice itself, and so on—we shall say that they "opine" all these things, but "know" nothing of what they opine. It must be so. But what of those who contemplate the things themselves <note>The unchanging Forms</note>, which always remain the same in the same way? Do they not know rather than opine? That is also necessary. Shall we not say that these people love and admire the things that are the objects of knowledge, while the others love the things that are the objects of opinion? Do we not remember that we said these latter people love and look upon beautiful voices and colors and such things, but do not admit that the Beautiful itself is anything? We remember. Therefore, we will not be mistaken if we call them <margin>F</margin> lovers of opinion <note>original: "φιλοδόξους" (philodoxous)</note> rather than "philosophers" <note>original: "φιλοσόφους" (philosophous)</note>, even though they will be very angry with us if we say so. Not if they listen to me, he said; for it is not right to be angry with the truth. Therefore, those who admire and love each thing that truly "is" <margin>G</margin> we shall call "philosophers" and not "lovers of opinion." By all means, he said.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> These things, then, do you understand how they stand? Yes. And do we say that opinion opines something? Yes. Is it the same thing that knowledge knows? Or is the object of knowledge and the object of opinion the same? Or is it impossible? It is impossible, he said, based on the agreements; if indeed different powers are by nature directed toward different things, and both are powers—opinion and knowledge—and each is different, as we said. From these, then, it does not allow the object of knowledge and the object of opinion to be the same. Therefore, if that which "is" is known, will something else be opined, other than that which "is"? Something else. Does one then opine that which "is not"? Or is it impossible even to opine that which "is not"? Consider it: does not he who opines direct his opinion toward something? Or is it possible to opine, yet opine nothing? Impossible. But <margin>B</margin> he who opines opines at least some one thing? Yes. But surely that which "is not" would most correctly be addressed not as one thing, but as nothing. Quite so. We assigned ignorance to that which "is not" of necessity, but knowledge to that which "is." Correct, he said. Therefore, one opines neither that which "is," nor that which "is not." No. Neither ignorance nor knowledge, then, would be opinion. It does not seem so. Is it then outside of these, exceeding knowledge in clarity, or ignorance in lack of clarity? Neither. But then, I said, does opinion appear to you darker than knowledge, but brighter than ignorance? Very much so, he said. And if it lies between both? Yes. Opinion then would be between these two. Entirely so. Did we not say in what went before, that if something should appear <margin>C</margin> as both "being" and "not being" at the same time, such a thing lies between the purely "being" and the totally "not being"? And that neither knowledge nor ignorance would be over it, but that which appeared between ignorance and knowledge? Correct. And now there has appeared between these two that which we call opinion. It has appeared. 

That, then, would remain for us to find, as it seems: that which partakes of both, of "being" and "not being," and which could be called neither one purely; so that if it appears as the "opinable," we may justly address it as such, assigning the extremes to the extremes and the middle to the middle. Or not so? So. 

These things being assumed, let him tell me, I shall say, and let him answer—<margin>D</margin> that good man who does not believe in the Beautiful itself, and no Idea of beauty itself always remaining the same in the same way; but he believes in many beautiful things, that "lover of sights," who would in no way endure it if someone said the Beautiful is one, and the Just is one, and so on. For of these many beautiful things, we shall say, "Most excellent man, is there any that will not appear ugly? And of the just, which will not appear unjust? And of the holy, which will not appear unholy?" "No," he said, "but they must appear both beautiful and ugly in a way, and all the other things you ask." What then? Do the many double things appear any less half than double? Nothing. And great and small, and light and heavy, will they be called these things <margin>E</margin> any more than their opposites? "No," he said, "but each will always have something of both." Is each of the many things, then, this [which it is called] more than it is not? It is like the puns at banquets, he said, and the children’s riddle about the eunuch and his aim at the bat, and what they riddle he hit it with. For these too are double-edged, and it is not possible to firmly think of any of them as either "being" or "not being," nor both, nor neither. 

"Do you have then," I said, "what to do with them? Or where will you put them in a better place than between essence and not-being? For they will not appear darker than 'not-being' so as to not-be more, nor clearer than 'being' so as to be more." "Most true," he said. We have found then, as it seems, that the many conventions of the many about beauty and other things roll around somewhere <margin>F</margin> between "not-being" and "being." We have found it purely. And we agreed before that if any such thing appeared, it must be called "opinable" but not "known," the intermediate wanderer being caught by the intermediate power. We agreed. 

Therefore, those who look upon many beautiful things, but do not see the Beautiful itself, nor are they able to follow another who leads them to it, and see many just things, but not Justice itself, and all things so, we shall say that they "opine" all things, but "know" none of the things they opine. "Necessity," he said. But what of those who look upon the things themselves, and those that are always the same in the same way—do they not know, and not opine? "Necessity for these too." Shall we not then say that these people embrace and love the things of which there is knowledge, and the others, those of which there is opinion? Or do we not remember <margin>G</margin> that we said they love and look upon beautiful voices and colors and such things, but do not endure the Beautiful itself as being anything? "We remember." Shall we then commit any error in calling them "lovers of opinion" rather than "philosophers"? And would they be very angry with us if we said so? "Not if they are persuaded by me," he said, "for it is not lawful to be angry with the truth." Those then who embrace each thing that truly "is," must be called philosophers and not lovers of opinion. "By all means."

<summary>In this concluding section of Book V, Socrates defines the "opinable" as a middle state between being and non-being, corresponding to the "lover of sights" who sees many beautiful things but cannot grasp the singular Form of Beauty. He concludes that such people are "lovers of opinion" (philodoxoi) rather than "philosophers" (philosophers), who love the unchanging truth of Being.</summary>

--- Page 501 ---
<meta>This page marks the beginning of Book VI of Plato's Republic. In the previous page (the end of Book V), Socrates established the distinction between knowledge (of what is) and opinion (of what both is and is not). He now transitions into defining the character and education of the "philosopher-king" who is fit to rule the ideal city.</meta>

# OF THE REPUBLIC, BOOK VI.

-> SUMMARY OF THE DIALOGUE. <-

> Near the end of the previous book, Plato progressed into a very serious discussion regarding true philosophy, its purpose, and its utility for the proper governance of the state. He taught the distinction between the true and the false <note>original: "adulterini"</note> philosopher, so that the hatred and envy resulting from the disgrace of "stolen" philosophy would not fall upon this most noble science. Now, in these next two books, he diligently pursues that same discourse on philosophy, so that the theorem "The Republic shall be happy when philosophers are its magistrates" may be found true through solid arguments. Therefore, he brilliantly teaches the true subject of genuine philosophy and the method and reason for defining it. The summary is this: The Guardian of the Republic must be equipped with the protections of the best sciences—not so that he may feed his mind on fruitless contemplations, but so that he may direct all the principles of that erudition and virtue (which he has acquired through study) toward the common utility of human society. He shows that the subject of philosophy is the "Idea of the Good" <note>original Latin: "Idea boni"</note>, which is truly Being, and "Himself" <note>original Greek: "αὐτοὶν", by which name he signifies God</note>. Plato eloquently testifies that this is his own opinion regarding that supreme Idea. Having thus indicated the subject, he begins to explain the method of knowing, which he pursues accurately in the seventh book.

---

# PLATO’S REPUBLIC,
-> OR, <-
-> CONCERNING JUSTICE, <-
-> SIXTH DIALOGUE. <-

<image-desc>Decorative initial O featuring a floral or scrollwork design.</image-desc>

<margin>A</margin> "So then, Glaucon," I said, "after a long and tedious discourse, we have at last, with some difficulty, revealed who are the true philosophers and who are not." "Perhaps," he said, "it was not easy to do so in brief." "It does not seem so," I replied. "At least, I think it would have been shown even better if we had only needed to speak of this one thing, and did not have to go through many other remaining points in order to see how a just life differs from an unjust one. What, then, is our next task?" "What else," he said, "but that which follows in order?" "Since philosophers are those who are able <margin>B</margin> to grasp that which is always the same and unchanging, while those who cannot—but instead wander among many and various things—are not philosophers, which of these two should be the leaders of the city?" "How should we state this to speak reasonably?" he asked. "Whichever of them appear capable of guarding the laws and customs of cities," I said, "those we should appoint as Guardians." "Correct," he said. "Now then," I said, "is it clear whether a guardian who is to keep watch over anything should be blind or sharp-sighted?" "How could it not be clear?" he said. "Do those who are truly deprived of the knowledge of each thing that *is* <note>meaning the unchanging Reality or Forms</note> seem to you to differ at all from the blind? They have no clear model <term>paradigm (παράδειγμα)</term> in their soul, and they cannot, like painters looking toward the truest model, <margin>C</margin> always refer to it and contemplate it as accurately as possible. Thus, they cannot establish here the laws concerning things beautiful, just, and good, if they need to be established, or guard and preserve those already laid down." "By Zeus," he said, "they do not differ much at all." "Shall we then appoint these men as guardians rather than those who have come to know each thing that truly is, and who are in no way inferior to the others in experience or any other part of virtue?" "It would be absurd," he said, "to choose others, provided they are not lacking in those other qualities; for in this very point, which is the greatest, they would excel." "Shall we then discuss in what way the same men will be able to possess both these sets of qualities?" "Certainly." "As we said at the beginning of this discourse, <margin>D</margin> we must first learn their nature. I think if we sufficiently agree on that, we will also agree that the same people can possess these qualities, and that no others should be leaders of cities but them." "How so?" "Let this first be agreed upon by us concerning philosophical natures: that they are always in love with learning <note>original: "μαθήματός"</note>, which reveals to them that essence <term>ousia (οὐσίας)</term> which always exists and is not driven wandering by birth and decay." "Let it be agreed." "And furthermore," I said, "that they desire the whole of that essence, and do not willingly give up any part of it, whether small or large, more or less honored, just as we described before concerning the ambitious and those in love." "You are right," he said. "Consider then what follows next: is it not necessary that those who are to be as we described have this further quality in their nature?" <margin>E</margin> "What quality?" "Truthfulness—the refusal to ever willingly accept falsehood, but rather to hate it and love the truth." "It is likely," he said. "It is not only likely, my friend, but entirely necessary that one who is naturally in love with something should cherish everything that is kin and belongs to his beloved." "Correct," he said. "And could you find anything more akin to wisdom than truth?" "How could I?" he asked. "Is it then possible for the same nature to be both a lover of wisdom and a lover of falsehood?" "In no way." "Therefore, the true lover of learning must, from youth upward, strive as much as possible for all truth." "Completely so." "But we know that when a person's desires flow strongly toward one thing, they are weaker in other directions, like a stream diverted into another channel." "Of course." "So, when one's desires have flowed toward learning <margin>F</margin> and everything of that kind, they would be concerned, I think, with the pleasure of the soul itself, and would leave behind the pleasures of the body—if, that is, one is a true and not a sham philosopher." "That is a great necessity." "Such a man is temperate and in no way a lover of money; for the things for which money is sought with great expense are more properly the concern of anyone rather than him." "That is so." "And certainly, you must also consider this when you are to judge a philosophical nature from one that is not." "What is that?" "Take care that a certain lack of generosity <note>original: "ἀνελευθερίας", meaning a narrowness or meanness of spirit</note> does not escape your notice. For small-mindedness is most opposed to a soul that is always going to reach for the whole and the sum of everything divine and human." "Most true," he said. "To a mind that possesses magnificence and the contemplation of all time and all essence, do you think human life can seem to be anything great?" "Impossible," he said. "Therefore, such a man will not consider death to be something terrible either."

<column-break/>

# THE REPUBLIC OF PLATO,
-> OR, <-
-> CONCERNING JUSTICE, <-
-> SIXTH DIALOGUE. <-

<image-desc>Decorative initial Q featuring a floral design within a square frame.</image-desc>

<margin>A</margin> "What sort of men philosophers are," I said, "and what sort those are who are strangers to philosophy, O Glaucon, has finally been established through a long discourse." "It was perhaps not easy," he said, "to explain it in fewer words." "Not so that it would be clear. But it would shine more plainly, I think, if we only had to relate this one thing and not wander through many other matters, if one wishes to show how much a just life differs from an unjust one. What remains for us to do after this? What else but that which follows in sequence? Since philosophers are those who can reach that which always <margin>B</margin> remains the same in the same way, while those who cannot, but instead wander through many changeable things, are not philosophers: which of these should be the leaders of the city?" "How can we answer this correctly?" "Whichever ones can guard the laws and duties of the city, to these the rudders of the republic must be committed." "Rightly so." "But it is obvious whether a blind man or one who sees sharply should be the one to whom we entrust something to be kept safe. Why would it not be obvious? Do they seem to you to differ from the blind, those who lack knowledge of each thing that truly exists, and have no clear model in their minds? Nor can they, like painters looking toward the truest model, <margin>C</margin> and referring to it and gazing upon it as accurately as possible, only then establish laws here concerning what is beautiful, just, and good (if necessary), and guard and preserve the laws once they are established?" "Certainly, they do not differ much. Shall we then choose these as guardians rather than those who know each thing that truly is, and who are in no way inferior in experience or any other part of virtue?" "It would certainly be absurd for any others to be chosen, especially if the other qualities are not lacking. In this, they certainly excel by far. Shall we not now say in what way these same men can possess both these and those qualities?" "By all means." "What we said at the beginning of this discussion, <margin>D</margin> we must first learn their nature; and I think, if we agree sufficiently on that, we will also agree that it is possible for the same men to achieve these things, and that no others besides these ought to be leaders of the city." "In what way?" "Let this first be established between us concerning the talents of philosophers: that they always love that discipline by which that nature which always exists, and is not changed by birth and corruption, becomes better known to them." "Let it be established." "Furthermore, that they desire it in its entirety, and do not willingly scorn any part of it, neither small nor large, neither honored nor base, just as we said above concerning the ambitious and those captured by love." "Correct." "Besides this, notice whether it is necessary for this to be in the nature of those who will be such as we have described." "What is that?" "That they be devoid of the nature of all lying, <margin>E</margin> and never lie willingly; but rather hate all falsehood and love the truth." "It is probable." "Not only is it probable, O friend, but altogether necessary, that he who is naturally moved by love for something should cherish whatever is akin and familiar to the beloved." "Wisely said. Is anything more familiar to wisdom than truth?" "Nothing. Is it then possible for the same nature to be both philosophical and deceitful?" "In no way. Therefore, it is necessary for one truly desirous of learning to seek all truth with the utmost effort from childhood." "Entirely so. But for one whose desires are carried ardently toward a certain thing, his desires for other things are weaker, since they flow elsewhere like little streams." "No doubt. Whoever, therefore, burns with all desire for the disciplines <margin>F</margin> and other such things, seeks the pure pleasure of the soul itself, and despises the pleasures of the body—unless he be a fake and in no way a true philosopher." "That is most necessary. Such a man will also be temperate, and not a lover of money. For it belongs to anyone rather than him to gape after the accumulation of money, for the sake of which others toil in seeking wealth with the greatest loss." "It is so. Furthermore, this must be considered whenever you wish to discern the nature of one who becomes a philosopher and one who does not." "What is it?" "Lest perhaps some hidden lack of generosity <note>original: "illiberalitas"</note> be present. For small-mindedness is altogether contrary to a soul <note>The Latin text here has a slight break or omission</note> which possesses magnificence of thought, and is always ready to investigate the whole of time and the universe, both divine and human." "You speak the truth." "In the contemplation of such magnificent substance, human life cannot seem to be anything great." "Certainly not. Will he then consider death to be a terrible thing?"

<summary>This page introduces Book VI of the Republic, where Socrates defines the "philosopher-king" as one who possesses knowledge of eternal truths and moral virtues, arguing they are the only ones fit to guard the laws of a city. Socrates emphasizes that true philosophers must love truth, hate falsehood, and possess a "magnificence" of mind that values the eternal over the transitory.</summary>

--- Page 502 ---
<meta>This page continues the dialogue from the end of Book V, where Socrates and Adimantus have been discussing the qualities required for the guardians of the ideal city. Socrates is now refining the definition of the "true philosopher" as someone who possesses both intellectual brilliance and moral excellence, preparing to address why such people are often viewed as useless by society.</meta>

# PLATO

<margin>A</margin> By no means. Therefore, a fearful and illiberal <note>The Latin 'illiberalis' and Greek 'ἀνελεύθερος' refer to a person lacking the free, generous spirit of a gentleman.</note> nature does not suit true philosophy. It does not, as it seems to me. But will a man who is modest, not greedy for gain, not illiberal, not proud, and not fearful, be difficult in his dealings or unjust? Not at all. Furthermore, when you wish to discern which soul is philosophical and which is not, you will observe this immediately from their tender years: whether he is just and mild, or unjust and savage. Most certainly. Nor, I think, will you overlook this. What? Whether he is quick or slow to perceive. Do you think anyone could ever love something that he does with great difficulty and, after much effort, achieves only a little? Never, indeed. What if he should retain nothing <margin>B</margin> of what he learns, forgetting everything? Would he not be void of knowledge? Void. And when he undertakes all that fruitless labor, will he not be forced in the end to hate himself and such an activity? Nothing prevents it. Therefore, let us by no means think that a forgetful soul belongs to the nature of true philosophers, but rather let us seek one with a very good memory. Quite so. Furthermore, we would say that an uncultured and awkward nature always leads toward a lack of moderation. Always. And do you think truth is compatible with a lack of moderation and excess, or rather with moderation? With moderation. Therefore, let us grant to this nature a mind that is well-proportioned and graceful above all others, which we wish to be naturally inclined toward beholding the "Idea" <note>The "Idea" or "Form" is Plato's term for the perfect, eternal reality of a thing, of which earthly things are mere shadows.</note> of each thing as it truly is. Certainly. Does it not <margin>C</margin> seem to you that we have run through each quality in a necessary, continuous series—qualities that must belong to a soul that has perfectly attained the truth of things? Most certainly, he said. Can you in any way find fault with a study that no one can sufficiently pursue unless he is by nature sharp-witted, possessing a good memory, magnificent, graceful, and a friend and kinsman of truth, justice, courage, and temperance? Not even Momus <note>Momus was the Greek god of mockery and criticism; the phrase implies even the harshest critic could find no flaw.</note> could carp at such a thing. Would you not commit the administration of the state to such men alone, once they have finally advanced in education and age? To this Adimantus replied: No one, O Socrates, could contradict you. But indeed, those who hear what you say are affected in this way: they think that through their lack of skill in questioning and <margin>D</margin> answering, they are led a little astray by the argument at each question, and when these small errors are finally gathered together, they assert a massive error and something contrary to what they first asserted. Just as those who do not know how to play the game of "Calculi" <note>original: 'calculis' (Latin) / 'ψήφοις' (Greek). This refers to Petteia, an ancient board game similar to checkers or chess, played with stones or tokens.</note> are eventually blocked and hemmed in by those who are skilled in that game, having nowhere to move, so they also think themselves finally forced and hemmed in, having nothing to say, being checkmated by words as if by stones—even though the truth is not necessarily on that side. I say this looking at the present situation. For someone might say to you that he cannot oppose your words in each point, but that in actual fact, he sees that whoever applies themselves to the study of philosophy <margin>E</margin>—not merely tasting it for the sake of education while they are young and then departing from it, but lingering in it a long time—for the most part turn out quite absurd <note>original: 'absurdos' (Latin) / 'ἀλλοκότους' (Greek). This suggests they become "strange" or "eccentric."</note>, not to say entirely wicked. And even those who seem the most respectable are nonetheless so tainted by this study you praise that they become useless for governing the state. When I heard this, I said: Do you think those who say these things are lying? I do not know, he said, but I would gladly hear what you think. You will certainly hear, if you ask, that they seem to me to speak the truth. How then, he asked, can it be right to say that <margin>F</margin> there will be no rest from evils for cities until philosophers rule in them, when we admit they are useless to the state? The question you ask requires an answer given through a certain image <note>original: 'imaginem' / 'εἰκόνος'. Socrates is famously known for using analogies and parables.</note>. But you, I think, are not accustomed to speaking in parables. "Be that as it may," I said. "Are you mocking me, now that you have pushed me into a discourse so difficult to demonstrate? Hear then the image, so that you may more clearly see how greedily I use analogies. For the suffering that the best men endure in relation to the state is so harsh that there is no other single thing like it. Therefore, it is necessary to gather it from many sources and compare it, and so give an account of them. Just as when painters depict 'Goat-stags' <note>original: 'tragelaphos' / 'τραγελάφους'. A mythical creature combining a goat and a deer, used here to represent something unnaturally composite.</note> and other <margin>G</margin> such mixed fictions. Imagine in your mind a certain captain of a ship or a fleet who exceeds the rest of the sailors in stature and bodily strength, but who is somewhat deaf and short-sighted, and whose mind is ignorant of navigation. Imagine the sailors quarreling among themselves about the steering, while each one thinks he is worthy of the command, although he has never learned the art, nor can he point to any teacher in that matter, nor state the time when he learned it. They even deny that the art can be taught, and they are ready to cut to pieces anyone who contends that it can. They themselves <margin>H</margin> crowd around the captain, pleading and striving with all their might for him to hand over the helm to them. If they do not persuade him, but others do, they either kill the others or throw them overboard. Then, having first bound the noble captain with 'Mandrake' <note>original: 'mandragora'. A plant used in antiquity as a powerful sedative or anesthetic.</note> or wine, they seize the government of the ship, use its supplies, indulge in wine and feasting, and navigate as such men are likely to do. Furthermore, they praise anyone who is clever at helping them usurp the command of the ship, calling him a true sailor and navigator,

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Not at all. A cowardly and unfree nature, as it seems, would have no part in true philosophy. I do not think so. What then? Can the man who is orderly, not a lover of money, not unfree, not a boaster, and not a coward, ever be difficult to deal with or unjust? It is impossible. And this too, when you are looking for the philosophical soul and the one that is not, you will examine from the very beginning while he is still young: whether he is just and gentle, or unsociable and savage. Quite so. Nor indeed will you overlook this, as I believe. What sort of thing? Whether he is a quick learner or a slow learner. Or do you ever expect anyone to love a thing sufficiently if he does it in pain, and achieves <margin>B</margin> only a little with great difficulty? It could not happen. What if he could save nothing of what he learns, being full of forgetfulness? Would he not be unable to avoid being empty of knowledge? How could he not be? Laboring thus in vain, do you not think he will be forced in the end to hate both himself and such a habit? Of course. Let us never, then, judge a forgetful soul to be among those sufficiently philosophical; let us rather seek one that is mindful by nature. Absolutely. But indeed, we would say that an unmusical and graceless nature draws one nowhere else than toward a lack of proportion. Certainly. And do you think truth is related to lack of proportion, or to proportion? To proportion. Let us seek, then, in addition to the other qualities, a mind that is by nature well-proportioned and graceful, whose own nature will make it easily led toward the "Idea" of each being. How could we not? What then? Do we not seem to you to have <margin>C</margin> discussed each point as necessary and following one from the other for the soul that intends to partake in Being sufficiently and perfectly? Most necessary indeed, he said. Is there any way, then, that you can find fault with such a pursuit, which no one could ever sufficiently pursue unless he were by nature mindful, a quick learner, high-minded, graceful, and a friend and kinsman of truth, justice, courage, and temperance? Not even Momus himself, he said, could find fault with such a thing. Then, to such men as these, perfected by education and age, would you not alone entrust the city? And Adimantus said: O Socrates, no one could be able to speak against these things. But indeed, those who hear what you say each time are affected in this way: they think that through inexperience in asking and answering, they are led a <margin>D</margin> little astray by the argument at each question, and when these small points are added up at the end of the discussion, a great error appears, which is the opposite of what they first said. And just as those who are not clever at playing draughts <note>original: 'πεττεύειν' (petteuein), the Greek game of petteia mentioned above.</note> are finally blocked by those who are, and have nothing to move, so they too are finally blocked and have nothing to say by this other kind of "draughts" played not with stones, but with words. Yet the truth is not at all more on that side. I say this looking at the present situation. For now, someone might say to you that in word he cannot oppose you on each question, but in fact he sees that as many as start out upon philosophy—not touching it for the sake of being educated while they are young and then letting it go, but spending a longer time in it—the majority <margin>E</margin> become quite eccentric (not to say altogether wicked), while those who seem most respectable nonetheless suffer this from the pursuit you praise: they become useless to cities. And I, having heard this, said: Do you think those who say these things are lying? I do not know, he said, but I would gladly hear your opinion. You would hear that they seem to me to speak the truth. How then, he said, is it well to say that cities will not stop from evils until the philosophers rule in them, whom we agree are useless to them? You ask a question, I said, that needs an answer spoken through an image. And you, he said, I think, are not accustomed to speaking through images! "Well then," I said, "are you mocking me after having cast me into an argument so difficult to prove? Hear then the image, so that you may see even more <margin>F</margin> how greedily I make comparisons. For the condition of the most respectable men, which they suffer in relation to their cities, is so hard that there is not even one other thing like it. But one must gather it from many things to make the comparison and speak in their defense, just as painters paint 'Goat-stags' and such things by mixing them together. For imagine such a thing happening either concerning many ships or one: a shipmaster, in height and strength exceeding all those in the ship, but somewhat deaf and seeing likewise but a little, and knowing other such things about nautical matters. And the sailors quarreling with one another about the steering, each thinking he ought to steer, though he has never <margin>G</margin> learned the art, nor can he show a teacher of himself, nor a time in which he was learning. And besides these things, they say it is not even teachable; they are even ready to cut to pieces the one who says it is teachable. They themselves are always crowded around the shipmaster, begging and doing everything so that he might entrust the helm to them. And sometimes, if they do not persuade him, but others do more so, they kill the others or throw them out of the ship. And having hobbled the noble shipmaster with mandrake or wine or some other thing, they rule the ship, using the things within it; and drinking and feasting, they sail as is likely for such people. Besides these things, they praise and call a 'nautical man' and a 'pilot' and <margin>H</margin> 'one who knows the things of the ship' whoever is clever at assisting them in how they shall rule...

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Adeimantus from Book VI of the Republic. Having established the virtues of the philosophical nature (memory, courage, and greatness of soul), Socrates now uses the famous "Ship of State" allegory to explain why such individuals are dismissed by society as "useless."</meta>

# ON THE REPUBLIC, BOOK VI.

<margin>A</margin> ...either by persuasion or by force, they may take over the shipowner. They disparage anyone who does not join them as "useless" or as someone who merely has experience in being "unserviceable," but they do not understand that the true pilot must necessarily pay attention to the year, the seasons, the sky, the stars, and the winds, and all things pertaining to his craft, if he is to be a true master of a ship. They do not believe it is possible to acquire the art and practice of how to steer a ship—whether some people want him to or not—alongside the skill of navigation. Since these things happen on ships, do you not think that the true pilot would be called a "star-gazer" <note>original: "μετεωροσκόπον"</note>, a "babbler," and "useless" to them by the sailors on ships so poorly managed? "Indeed," said Adeimantus.

<margin>B</margin> "I do not think," I said, "that you need to see the image examined in detail to understand that this is how cities are disposed toward true philosophers; you surely understand what I am saying." "I certainly do," he replied. "First, then, teach this image to that man who wonders why philosophers are not honored in cities, and try to persuade him that it would be much more wonderful if they were honored." "I will teach him," he said.

<margin>C</margin> "And tell him that you are speaking the truth when you say that the most excellent of those in philosophy are useless to the many; however, tell him to blame those who do not use them for their uselessness, and not the excellent men themselves. For it is not in the nature of things for a pilot to beg sailors to be ruled by him, nor for the wise to go to the doors of the rich—the man who came up with that clever saying was lying. The truth of the matter is that whether a man be rich or poor, if he is sick, he must go to the doors of physicians; and everyone who needs to be ruled must go to the doors of the one capable of ruling. It is not for the ruler, if he is truly of any use, to beg the subjects to be ruled. If you compare the political rulers of today to those sailors we just mentioned, and those called 'useless star-gazers' <note>original: "μετεωρολέσχας"</note> to the true pilots, you will not be far from the truth." "Quite right," he said.

<margin>D</margin> "For these reasons and in these circumstances, it is not easy for the best pursuit to be highly esteemed by those who pursue the opposite. But by far the greatest and most powerful slander against philosophy arises because of those who claim to pursue such things—those of whom you say the critic of philosophy claims that most who approach it are wicked, and the best of them are useless. And I agreed that you were speaking the truth, did I not?" "Yes." "Therefore, have we explained the cause of the uselessness of the excellent?" "We certainly have." "Do you want us next to explain the necessity of the wickedness of the many, and try to show, if we can, that philosophy is not responsible for this either?" "By all means." "Let us listen and speak, reminding ourselves from where we started: the nature that one must necessarily have to become a 'noble and good' <note>original: "καλὸν τε κἀγαθὸν"</note> man. First of all, if you remember, truth led him, which he had to pursue entirely and everywhere; otherwise, if he were a boaster, he would have no part in true philosophy." "That is how it was said." "Is this one point not very much contrary to the current opinion of her?" "Very much so," he said.

<margin>E</margin> "Shall we not, then, reasonably defend him by saying that a true lover of learning is naturally inclined to strive for that which *is* <note>meaning: true reality or being</note>, and does not stay among the many particular things that are merely thought to exist? Rather, he moves forward, and his passion is not blunted or ceased until he touches the nature of each thing as it truly is, with that part of the soul which is suited to touch such a thing. And it is suited because it is of the same kin. Approaching this and mingling with true being, having given birth to intelligence and truth, he might then truly know and live and be nourished; and only then would he find rest from his labor, and not before." "As clearly as possible," he said. "Well then, will it be part of this man to love falsehood, or quite the opposite, to hate it?" "To hate it," he said.

<margin>F</margin> "And where truth leads, I think we would never say that a choir of evils follows her." "How could it?" "Instead, there follows a healthy and just character, which is followed by moderation." "Correct," he said. "And why is it necessary to arrange the rest of the choir of the philosophical nature again from the beginning? For you surely remember that courage, magnificence, quickness of learning, and memory belonged to them. But when you objected that everyone would be forced to agree with what we said, yet if they looked away from the words and at the people themselves, they would say they see some as useless and the many as corrupt with every vice—we are now examining the cause of this slander: why are the many wicked? For this reason, we have again taken up the nature of true philosophers and necessarily defined it." "That is so," he said.

<margin>G</margin> "We must now," I said, "behold the destructions of this nature: how it is destroyed in many people, while only a small few escape—those whom people call not wicked, but useless. After that, we must look at the natures that imitate this and establish themselves in its pursuit—natures whose souls arrive at a pursuit that is unworthy of them and beyond their strength, where they stumble in many ways and attach to philosophy that reputation which you described."

<margin>H</margin> "What are these destructions you speak of?" he asked. "I will try to explain them to you if I can," I said. "Now, I think everyone will agree with us on this: such a nature..."

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...either by persuasion or by force, once the owner has been removed, they may assist themselves. But the man who is unable to do this, they disparage as useless; they do not even consider the duty of a true pilot: that it clearly belongs to him to take account of the year, the seasons of the sky, the stars, and the winds, and all those things that belong to that art, if he is truly to be the pilot of a ship. They think it impossible to receive the art of steering—whether some are willing or unwilling—at the same time as the faculty of navigation. If things are so on a ship, do you not think the true pilot would be called an empty and curious inspector of sublime things, and useless to the ship itself, by those who sail in such ships? "Very much so," said Adeimantus.

<margin>B</margin> "I do not think it necessary," I said, "that I explain to you at greater length how the citizens in cities are affected toward true philosophers, just as the sailors in such ships are toward the true pilot; for I think you understand what I am saying."

<margin>C</margin> "Exceedingly so. First, therefore, to the man who wonders that philosophers are least honored in cities, explain this image, and try to persuade him that it would be much more wonderful if they were honored." "I shall indeed do so." "And you may add this besides: that those who say the best philosophers are useless to the common people speak the truth. But say that they themselves are not the cause of their uselessness, but rather those who do not make use of these philosophers. For it is not agreeable to nature that a pilot should beg sailors to commit themselves to his direction, or that the wise should approach the doors of the rich. But whoever first boasted of this, surely lied."

<margin>D</margin> "In truth, however, nature is so arranged that whether a rich man or a poor man be held by ill health, he must necessarily seek the doors of physicians; and all who need the direction of a superior should go to the houses of men capable of governing, not that the governors—if they are of any value—should beg that they might govern their inferiors. Indeed, if you compare those who administer the Republic in these times with those sailors we just mentioned, you will not err; and if you compare those who are called useless and vain, and superstitious searchers of hidden things, to true pilots, you will do rightly." "Rightly indeed," he said. "For these reasons, therefore, it is not easy for an honest study to be approved by those who are accustomed to contrary habits. But the greatest and most vehement slander of philosophy arises because of the morals of those who profess the studies of philosophy. For those who accuse philosophy say, as you mention, that most of those who take themselves to philosophy are very wicked; or if some of them excel the rest, they are useless. And I have conceded these things to you, have I not?"

<margin>E</margin> "Certainly. Have we not explained the cause why the best philosophers seem to be useless?" "Certainly." "But why the many are also wicked, shall we next open up? And shall we declare, according to our strength, that there is no fault in philosophy?" "I certainly wish it." "Let us proceed to these things, repeating what we introduced above: what sort of nature he must have who is to be honest and good. His leader first of all, if you have committed it to memory, was truth, which he must follow altogether and everywhere; or if he be vain, he must also be devoid of true philosophy." "It was exactly so stated." "This one thing, therefore, is entirely foreign to those things which are now thought of him." "Most foreign. Shall we not decently defend his cause in this manner?"

<margin>F</margin> "We shall say that a man desirous of knowledge is so fashioned by nature that he always strives for that which truly exists, nor does he linger in those single and many things about which opinion is concerned, but proceeding further, he is not fatigued or ceases from his desire until he has touched the proper nature of each thing with that power of the mind by which it is fitting to apprehend it. Moreover, it is fitting through a certain kindred power. When he has adhered with this, and has joined and mixed himself with that which truly exists, and has from there truly generated intelligence and truth, he will surely know the truth, and truly live and be nourished. From this birth at last all his distress shall cease, but before this, by no means."

<margin>G</margin> "Those things are very well said. Will such a man in any way love a lie? Or rather, will he entirely hate it?" "He will hate it, certainly. Truly, where truth is the leader, I do not think we will say that a choir of evils follows her." "For how could it?" "Nay, rather a sincere and just habit follows. This we shall also say is followed by temperance." "Wisely." "Furthermore, what need is there to recount the rest of the philosophical choir from the beginning? For you remember that with these agree, as I was saying, courage, magnificence, sharpness of wit, and memory. But when you objected—what anyone would necessarily be forced to confess to what we were saying—that omitting our words and turning to those of whom the speech was about, he said he saw them partly useless, partly corrupted by all wickedness: now indeed we have begun to search out the cause of this

<margin>H</margin> slander, and why many of them are evil; and for this cause we have again sought the legitimate nature of philosophers, and necessarily defined it." "It is so." "Next we must seek by what reasoning the nature of the philosopher is depraved in many (though a small thing escaped us); indeed, this also must be noticed: those whom he calls not bad indeed, but useless. Then also what sort of dispositions of men those are which imitate this nature and usurp its work, and attempting a study unworthy of them and beyond their strength, they often fail, and induce everywhere that opinion of philosophy which you were relating." "But what depravations do you mean?" "I will show you if I can. Truly I think anyone will grant us this: that such a nature as we have described..."

<summary>In this passage from Book VI of the Republic, Socrates uses the "Ship of State" allegory to explain that philosophers are perceived as useless because society (the sailors) lacks the wisdom to value true navigation (knowledge of the forms). He further argues that the bad reputation of philosophy comes from those who are not true philosophers but corruptions of that noble nature.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Socrates’ argument from the previous page regarding the "uselessness" of philosophers. He is now moving into the more dangerous territory of how society corrupts the few naturally gifted souls who could have become true philosophers.</meta>

# OF PLATO

& and [being] endowed with all these things, which a future perfect philosopher requires, to arise rarely and among few. Do you not think so? Most certainly. And see how many and how great are the destructions of even these few. Which ones? That which is most wonderful of all to hear: that every single one of those traits which we recently approved in the nature of the philosopher actually corrupts the soul that possesses them, and mostly twists it away from philosophy; I speak of courage, and temperance, and all the others we recounted. This is indeed absurd to hear. Furthermore, all those things which are commonly called "goods" deprave and hinder the soul: beauty, wealth, physical strength, and a powerful lineage in the city, and other things of this kind. For you have the general pattern of what I am saying. I do indeed, and I would gladly hear more exactly what you mean. Grasp the whole matter correctly, and it will appear clear to you; nor will what has been said about these things seem absurd to you. How do you instruct me in this? We know that every seed, whether of plants or of animals, which has not obtained the nutrition appropriate to each—neither in the right time nor the right place—the more vigorous and vehement it is, the more it lacks its proper advantages. For evil is more contrary to the good than to the non-good. Why not? It is therefore, I think, consistent that the best nature, if nourished by a foreign diet, turns out worse than a weak nature. It is so indeed.

<margin>B</margin>
By this reasoning, then, we say, *Adeimantus*, that souls endowed with the most excellent nature become the worst if they have been badly educated. Or do you think that unspeakable crimes and extreme wickedness proceed from a weak nature rather than from a noble nature corrupted by education? Will a feeble nature ever be the cause of either great goods or great evils? Certainly not. If, therefore, the nature of the philosopher itself attains the appropriate discipline, it must necessarily reach every virtue by always progressing. But if it is sown, born, and nourished perversely, it falls back into all the opposite traits, unless perhaps some one of the gods should help it. Or do you also think, as many do, that it is true as they say, that certain youths are corrupted by sophists <note>Sophists were professional teachers in Ancient Greece often accused of prioritizing rhetorical victory over truth</note>, and that these corruptors are certain private sophists, and should we not rather believe that those who speak this way are themselves the greatest sophists? For they teach and render every one of the youths, men, and women exactly as they wish. When does this happen most of all? he asked. When, I said, many people are crowded together either in assemblies, or courts, or theaters, or camps, or any other huge gathering of men, and they confidently disapprove of some of the things said or done and praise others, being carried away with great tumult in both cases as they hiss and applaud with a great noise and shouting. Then the walls and the places where they are, echoing, give out a noise twice as great as those who are praising and blaming. In such a situation, what kind of heart <note>original: "quo animo / τίνα καρδίαν"</note> do you think a young man has? Or what private education do you think can withstand these acclamations, so that it is not overwhelmed by such blame and praise and carried away by the current wherever the wave drifts? So that he will approve of the same things they do, calling them honorable, and likewise reject the same things as base. He will moreover apply himself to the same studies as they do, and turn out just like them.

<margin>C</margin>
<margin>D</margin>
<margin>E</margin>
That is absolutely necessary, O *Socrates*. Yet we have not yet introduced the greatest necessity. Which one? That which these teachers and sophists impose by their deeds when they cannot persuade with words. Do you not see that they mark a man who does not obey them with infamy? They condemn him to the loss of money and to the punishment of death. Most certainly. What other sophist, then, do you think, or what other private discourses could oppose and resist these? Surely none, he said. None indeed. Nay, to resist these is the height of folly. For there never was, nor is, nor will there be any other character, humanly speaking, trained toward virtue against the discipline of these men, O friend. For the divine, according to the proverb, we must except from the account. For know this for certain: whoever escapes and turns out as he should in such a constitution of public affairs, you would not be speaking wrongly to say that he escaped by divine help <note>original: "divino auxilio / θεοῦ μοῖραν"</note>.

<margin>F</margin>
It seems no different to me. This too you ought to think. What is it? Each of those private wage-earners whom these people call sophists, and consider rivals in their art, thinks he should teach nothing other than the opinions of the many which they hold when they are gathered together, and he calls this wisdom. It is as if someone had observed the rages and desires of a vast, strong brute <note>original: "vastis cuiusdam animalis bruti / θρέμματος μεγάλου"</note> that was being nourished—how it should be approached and how touched; also when it is most fierce or most mild, and from what causes it becomes so. Likewise the sounds which it is accustomed to utter in each case. And by what sounds of others the animal is excited or soothed. After he has learned all these things by long association, he calls this experience "wisdom," and having systematized it as a kind of art, he turns to teaching it, though in truth he knows nothing of which of these opinions and desires is honorable or base, good or evil, just or unjust. But he names all these things according to the opinions of that great beast: calling the things in which it delights "good," and the things by which it is offended "evil." Nor can he give any other reason for them, but he calls "just" and "honorable" the things that are necessary. But as to how the nature of the "necessary" and the "good" actually differ, he has never seen...

<margin>G</margin>
<margin>H</margin>

<column-break/>

...all these things or they use as many as were just mentioned, if he is to become a perfect philosopher, it happens rarely among men and to few. Or do you not think so? Very much so. Of these few, see how many are the destructions and how great. Which ones? What is most wonderful of all to hear, that each one of the things we praised in that nature destroys the soul that has it, and pulls it away from philosophy. I mean courage, temperance, and all the things we went through. It is strange (he said) to hear. Furthermore (said I), in addition to these, all the so-called "goods" corrupt and pull it away: beauty, and wealth, and strength of body, and powerful kinship in the city, and all the things related to these. For you have the type of what I mean. I have it, he said; and I would gladly learn more accurately what you are saying. Grasp it then (said I) as a whole correctly; and something clear will appear to you, and what was said before about it will not seem strange. How then, he said, do you command? Of every seed (said I) or plant, whether of the earth or of animals, we know that that which does not find the seat which befits each, nor the season, nor the place—the more vigorous it is, the more it lacks what is appropriate. For evil is more opposite to the good, I suppose, than to the not-good. How not? It has then (I think) reason, that the best nature, being in an alien nourishment, comes off worse than the base nature. It has. Is it not then (said I), O Adeimantus, that we should say the most gifted souls likewise, if they meet with bad upbringing, become exceptionally bad? Or do you think that great injustices and unmixed wickedness come from a base nature, and not from a vigorous nature ruined by upbringing? And that a weak nature will ever be the cause of great goods or great evils? No, but (said he) it is thus. Then the nature which we set down for the philosopher, if, I think, it meets with appropriate learning, must necessarily grow and reach every virtue; but if, being sown and planted in what is not appropriate, it is nourished there, it falls back into all the opposites, unless some one of the gods happens to help it. Or do you also think, as the many do, that some young men are corrupted by sophists; and that certain private sophists are the corruptors, to any degree worth mentioning? But is it not rather those who say these very things who are the greatest sophists, educating most perfectly and turning out as they wish both young and old, men and women? When? he said. When (I said) many are seated together in a crowd in assemblies, or in law-courts, or theaters, or camps, or some other common gathering of a multitude, and with much noise they blame some of the things said or done and praise others, both in excess, shouting and clapping; and besides them the rocks and the place in which they are, echoing, provide a double noise of the blame and praise. In such a thing, what kind of heart do you think the young man has, as the saying goes? Or what private education will hold out for him, which will not be washed away by such blame or praise, and go drifting down the stream wherever it carries him? And he will say the same things are honorable and base as they do, and he will practice what they do, and be such as they are? There is (said he), O Socrates, great necessity. And yet (said I) we have not yet mentioned the greatest necessity. What kind? That which these educators and sophists add by deed, when they do not persuade by word. Or do you not know that the one who is not persuaded they punish with loss of rights and money and death? Indeed (he said) very much so. What other sophist then do you think, or what kind of private words, stretching in opposition to these, will prevail? I think none (said he). No (said I), but even the attempt is great folly. For there does not arise, nor has there been, nor indeed will there be a different character toward virtue, having been educated against the education of these people. A human one, O companion; but a divine one, according to the proverb, let us take out of the account. For one must know well, that whatever is saved and becomes as it should, in such a state of political affairs, you will not speak badly if you say a divine portion <note>original: "θεοῦ μοῖραν"</note> saved it. It does not seem otherwise to me (he said). Furthermore then (said I), let this also seem so to you. What is that? Each of the wage-earners, whom these people call sophists and consider rivals in art, teaches nothing other than these dogmas of the many, which they hold when they are gathered together, and they call this wisdom. Just as if someone were learning the moods and desires of a great and strong brute being nourished—how it is necessary to approach it and how to touch it, and when it is most difficult or most gentle and from what causes it becomes so, and the voices which it is accustomed to utter in each case, and again what voices of another make it tame or wild. And having learned all these things, by association and a long time spent, he should call it wisdom, and having organized it as an art, should turn to teaching, knowing nothing in truth of these dogmas and desires, as to what is honorable or base, or good or evil, or just or unjust; but should name all these things according to the opinions of the great animal; calling the things it rejoiced in good, and the things it was vexed by evil. And he should have no other account of them; but the things that are necessary, he calls just and honorable; but the nature of the necessary and the good, how much they differ in reality, he has neither seen...
