<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Adeimantus regarding why naturally gifted individuals—those with the potential to be true philosophers—are often corrupted by society. It transitions from the general influence of the public to the specific ways a gifted youth is targeted by flatterers and the resulting "void" in philosophy that is filled by unworthy pretenders.</meta>

# ON THE REPUBLIC, BOOK VI.

...nor could he show it to others. If someone were so disposed, I ask, by Zeus, would he not seem to you to be an absurd teacher? <margin>A</margin> To me, certainly. And does he seem to you to differ at all from the one who considers it "wisdom" to have understood the angers and pleasures of a crowd of many diverse people gathered together—whether in painting, music, or the administration of the state? For it is clear that if someone associates with them and displays a work of poetry, or some other craft, or a service to the state, and grants the public the authority to judge his work beyond what is necessary, the "Diomedean necessity," <note>original: "Διομήδεια ἀνάγκη" — a proverbial expression meaning a "compelling necessity" or being forced to do something against one's better judgment, named after the hero Diomedes.</note> as they say, will force him to do the very things they approve. But as to these things being truly good and noble, have you ever heard one of them give a reason that was not ridiculous? I have never heard one, he said, nor do I think I ever will. Therefore, keeping all this in mind, remember this as well: <margin>B</margin> Can the multitude ever admit, or even grasp, the concept of the "Beautiful itself" as opposed to "many beautiful things"? Or the essence of any thing as opposed to its many instances? Not at all. Therefore, it is impossible for a multitude to be a philosopher. It is impossible. And so, those who practice philosophy are necessarily blamed by the many. Necessarily. And also by those private individuals who, desiring to please the crowd, mingle with them. That is clear. From this, what way do you see to save a philosophical nature, so that it might stay in its pursuit and reach the goal of philosophy? Consider it from what we said before. It was agreed that a quickness at learning, memory, courage, and magnificence of spirit belong to this nature. Yes. <margin>C</margin> Will not such a person, from the start, be first among all his peers, especially if his body is naturally suited to his soul? How could he not be? Therefore, his relatives and fellow citizens will surely want to make use of him for their own affairs when he grows older. Certainly. They will lie at his feet, then, with prayers, honors, and flatteries, trying to seize for themselves his future power. That is what usually happens, he said. What then, I asked, do you think such a man will do in such circumstances? Especially if he happens to be from a great city, and is wealthy, noble, handsome, and tall? <margin>D</margin> Will he not be filled with boundless hope, thinking himself capable of managing the affairs of both the Greeks and the Barbarians? <note>By "Barbarians," Plato refers to any non-Greek speaking peoples, such as the Persians.</note> And so he will lift himself up with empty pride and senseless arrogance. Very much so. If someone were to approach a man in this state and gently tell him the truth—that he has no mind in him, though he needs it, and that it cannot be acquired except by a slave-like devotion to its pursuit—do you think it would be easy for him to listen through such a cloud of evils? Far from it, he said. But if, I said, because of a good natural disposition and a certain innate kinship with reason, he does listen and is drawn toward philosophy, what do we think those will do who believe they are losing his usefulness and companionship? <margin>E</margin> Will they not do and say anything, through private plots and public accusations, to ensure that he is not persuaded, and that his persuader is unable to succeed? That is quite certain. Is there any way, then, for such a man to practice philosophy? Not at all. Do you see then, I said, that we were not wrong when we said that the very parts of the philosopher's nature, when poorly nurtured, are in a way the cause of his falling away from the pursuit? And even the so-called "goods"—wealth and all such equipment—act as hindrances? Indeed, it was rightly said. This then, oh wonderful man, is the destruction and corruption of the best nature for the most excellent pursuit—a nature that is rare enough as it is. From these men come those who work the greatest evils upon cities and individuals, as well as those who do great good, if they happen to be drawn that way. But a small nature never does anything great for anyone, whether a private person or a city. Most true, he said. <margin>F</margin> So those who fall away—the very ones most suited for philosophy—leave her desolate and unfinished, and they themselves live a life that is neither proper nor true. Then others, unworthy of her, rush in as if she were an orphan abandoned by her kin, and they bring shame upon her and cover her with the very reproaches you mentioned: that of those who keep company with her, some are worth nothing, and many are worthy of many evils. Yes, that is what is said. And it is said with good reason, I replied. For other little men, seeing this place empty, though still full of noble names and titles, leap from their crafts into philosophy, <margin>G</margin> like prisoners who flee from jail to take sanctuary in temples—those who happen to be the most clever at their own little trade. For even in this state, the prestige of philosophy still remains more magnificent than that of the other arts. This is what many desire whose natures are imperfect; their souls are cramped and broken by their mechanical trades and crafts, just as their bodies are marred by their manual labor. Is this not inevitable? Quite so. Do you think, I asked, they look any different to the eye than a little bald-headed smith who has come into some money, just released from his chains, washed in a bath, wearing a new cloak, and dressed up like a bridegroom, <margin>H</margin> about to marry his master’s daughter because she is poor and has no one to care for her? Not very different at all. What kind of offspring are such people likely to produce?

<column-break/>

...nor can he show it to others. If someone, I say, were so disposed, would he not seem to you, by Jove, <note>Latin: "Iouem" (Jupiter). The translator uses the Roman equivalent of the Greek "Zeus."</note> to be an absurd teacher? To me indeed. Does he seem to you to differ from the one who considers it wisdom to have mastered the angers and pleasures of many various men coming together in one place, whether in painting, music, or the discipline of administering the republic? For it is clear that if someone spends time with these people and shows them a work of poetry, or of another art, or a service pertaining to the republic, and gives the public the authority to judge the work beyond what is necessary, he will be compelled by "Diomedean necessity," as they say, to do the things they approve. But as to these things being truly good and honorable, have you ever heard one of them assign a reason that was not ridiculous? I have never even heard one, nor, as I think, will I hear one. Therefore, imagining all these things in your mind, remember this as well: Can the public ever admit, even if someone else says it, or reach by themselves, the concept of the "Beautiful itself," and not just these many beautiful things—and the same for other things—not indeed these many individual things which are apparent, but the one nature of each thing? Not at all. Therefore, a philosopher cannot be of the multitude. No. Furthermore, it is necessary that those practicing philosophy be blamed by them. Necessary. And by all those wishing to please the people. It is clear. From these things, then, what way do you see for preserving the philosophical nature, so that, persisting in its study, it may reach the end of philosophizing? Think of it from what has been said. It was granted that sharpness in learning, memory, fortitude, and magnificence belong to this nature. Plainly. Will not such a person immediately be first among all in everything, especially if he has obtained a body by nature conforming to his soul? Certainly, nothing prevents it. Therefore, all his relatives and citizens will want to use him to conduct their own business when he has grown up. Certainly. Therefore, they will preoccupy his future virtue and power with prayers, supplications, honors, and flatteries. That is how it usually happens. What do you think such a man will do then? Especially if he was born in a great city, and is distinguished in it by wealth and lineage, and is moreover of honorable form and tall. Do you not think he will be elated by immense hope? Thinking himself sufficient to manage the affairs of both the Greeks and the Barbarians. Whence he will extol himself, sporting a haughty manner, full of empty pride and insane arrogance. Vehemently. If someone should in a friendly way warn a man so disposed, saying that he has no mind at all, yet needs it; but that it can be acquired by no one unless he subjects himself to its acquisition, do you think that he, occupied by such great evils, will easily lend his ears to the one warning him? Far from it. But if, by the goodness of nature and a certain innate affection for reason, someone should listen and be moved and drawn to philosophy, what do we think those will do who believe that the youth's use and companionship are being corrupted by that person's merit? Will they not strive with all zeal, both in speaking and in acting, so that the youth does not obey the warnings, and that the exhorter cannot persuade him, pursuing him with both private snares and public accusations? It is very necessary. Will any faculty for philosophizing remain to him? Plainly, very little. Do you see then that we were not wrong to say above that the parts of the philosophical nature, if a perverse education is applied, are in a way the causes of one being turned away from that study? And moreover, those things which are commonly thought of as goods—namely wealth and all such furniture—are an impediment? It was indeed rightly said. This, O wonderful man, is the ruin and corruption of such and so great a nature for the most excellent duty, which is indeed found quite rarely, as we said. And from this talent come those men who commit heinous crimes, both privately and publicly; and likewise those who are authors of great goods for both individuals and states. But a meager talent never performs anything great, either privately or publicly. You speak truly indeed. Since many who are naturally fit for philosophizing are twisted away from this study and leave philosophy unfinished and desolate, they lead a life neither decent nor true; while others, certainly unworthy of it, approaching philosophy as if it were orphaned of its kin, disgrace it excessively and affect it with that infamy by which you mentioned it was noted by detractors, who object that of those who give their labor to philosophy, some are worthy of nothing, and many are worthy of many evils. These things were certainly said. And deservedly said. For many other little men, seeing this seat empty, though distinguished by famous names and dignity, like those who flee from prison to temples, gladly leap from the arts to philosophy—especially those who excel in their own little craft. For truly philosophy, although she is in this state, yet surpasses the other arts in dignity and magnificence. Which many affect who are naturally imperfect, and just as their bodies are damaged by arts and trades, so also are their souls depressed and broken by mechanical services. Is it not necessary? Most of all. Do you think they differ at all in appearance from a blacksmith, rich, small, and bald, who has come out of chains, washed himself in the baths, and adorned himself with a new garment like a bridegroom, about to marry the daughter of his master who is pressed by poverty and has no one else to give her to? I think they do not differ much. What sort of offspring must we think will be born from these?

# OF PLATO

<margin>A</margin> Is it not then, I asked, truly bastardized and base? It absolutely must be so. What kind of thoughts and opinions should we say are produced when men unworthy of education approach it and associate with it in a way they do not deserve? Shall we not call them, as is fitting, <term>sophisms</term> <note>original: "sophismata" — deceptive arguments that sound clever but lack true wisdom.</note>? Are they not things with nothing legitimate about them, nothing worthy of true wisdom? They certainly are, he replied. Therefore, Adeimantus, very few men remain who are worthy to dwell in the company of philosophy. These are perhaps those born with a noble character and well-bred, who, having been caught in exile, remain with philosophy because there are no corrupters around; or perhaps a great soul born in a small city, who looks down on the affairs of the state with contempt. There might also be a few who come to it from another craft which they have rightly despised as being beneath their natural talents. <margin>B</margin> Furthermore, the "bridle of our companion Theages" <note>The "Bridle of Theages" became a proverbial expression for a physical disability that prevents someone from entering the "corrupting" world of politics, thereby "reining them in" toward a life of thought.</note> might be enough to hold someone back. For our friend Theages was prepared in every way to fall away from philosophy, but the poor health of his body, by excluding him from political affairs, keeps him close to it. Regarding my own case, the "divine sign" <note>original: "Dæmonis / τὸ δαιμόνιον" — Socrates often referred to a "daimonion" or divine voice that warned him against certain actions.</note> is not worth mentioning, for it has happened to perhaps only one other person, or no one at all before me. Now, those few who belong to this group and have tasted how sweet and blessed a possession philosophy is, and have seen clearly enough the madness of the many, realize that no one, <margin>C</margin> to put it briefly and simply, does anything healthy in the affairs of cities. They see there is no ally with whom one could go to the aid of justice and survive. Instead, such a man is like someone fallen among wild beasts: he is unwilling to join in their injustice, yet he is not strong enough to resist all the savages alone. He would perish before he could help his city or his friends, becoming useless to himself and others. Taking all this into account, he keeps quiet and minds his own business. Like a traveler in a storm, when the dust and rain are driven by the wind, he stands aside under the shelter of a wall. Seeing others filled with lawlessness, he is content if he can somehow live his life here pure from injustice and unholy deeds, and depart from life with good hope, serene and satisfied. <margin>D</margin> Truly, he said, such a man would depart having accomplished no small thing. But not the greatest thing, I said, unless he finds a state that is suitable for him. For in a suitable state, he will grow more himself, and preserve both his private interests and the public good. I believe enough has been said regarding why philosophy has been slandered and why that slander is unjust, unless you have something else to add. I have nothing more to say on that, he replied. But which of the current governments do you think is best suited for a philosopher? None at all, I said. That is exactly my complaint: that no existing constitution of a city is worthy of the philosopher's nature. Therefore, this nature is twisted and changed. <margin>E</margin> Just as a foreign seed sown in an alien soil loses its strength and tends to take on the nature of the local plants, so this kind of soul loses its own power and falls into a foreign character. But if it should find the best form of government—just as it is itself the best—then it will show that it was indeed something divine, while all other things, whether characters or pursuits, are merely human. Now, you are clearly about to ask me what this form of government is. You guessed wrongly, he said. For I was not going to ask that, but rather whether it is this very state we have just finished founding, or another. In most respects, I said, it is this one. But this was also said back then: that there must always be something in the city that possesses the same understanding of the constitution that you, the legislator, had when you established the laws. It was indeed said, he replied. But it was not sufficiently explained, <margin>F</margin> because I was deterred by your objections, which showed that the demonstration would be long and difficult. For what remains is not easy to describe at all. What is that? In what way a city should handle philosophy so that it is not destroyed. For all great things are precarious, and as the proverb truly says, "beautiful things are difficult." Nevertheless, he said, let the demonstration reach its end by making this clear. It will not be a lack of will, I said, but perhaps a lack of ability that hinders me. You will see my eagerness for yourself. Observe even now how readily and boldly I am going to say that the city should approach this study in the opposite way than it does now. How so? At present, I said, those who do touch it are young men just out of childhood. They approach the most difficult part of it—I mean the skill of debating—in the midst of managing their households and businesses, and then they abandon it. Even those who are considered most inclined toward wisdom do this. Later, if they are invited by others who are practicing it, they might agree to be listeners, and they think this is a great thing, believing it should be treated as a mere side-hobby. <margin>G</margin> By old age, with the exception of a few, they are extinguished much more than the Heraclitean sun, <note>The philosopher Heraclitus famously said the sun is new every day; Socrates suggests these men go out and are never rekindled.</note> because they are never lit again. Then what should they do? he asked. Entirely the opposite. While they are boys and youths, they should engage in youthful education and philosophy, taking good care of their bodies while they are growing and strengthening, as a service to philosophy. As age progresses and the soul begins to reach maturity, they should increase its exercises. But when their strength fails and they are released from political and military duties, then they should be allowed to roam free and do nothing else—except as a sideline—those who are to live happily and, after the migration of the soul, 

<column-break/>

…not bastardized and base? There is great necessity. What then? Those unworthy of education, <margin>A</margin> when they approach it and keep company with it undeservingly, what kind of thoughts and opinions shall we say they generate? Are they not truly what we should call sophisms, nothing genuine, nothing possessing the value of true wisdom? Entirely so, he said. A very small number, I said, O Adeimantus, is left of those who associate with philosophy worthily: perhaps a noble and well-reared character caught in exile, who has remained with her according to his nature for lack of corrupters; or when a great soul is born in a small city and, despising the affairs of the city, looks away from them; or perhaps a small few who might come to it from another craft, having rightly despised it as being without talent. <margin>B</margin> And the "bridle of our companion Theages" might also be the sort of thing to restrain someone. For in the case of Theages, all other things were prepared for his falling away from philosophy, but the nursing of a sickly body, by excluding him from politics, holds him back. My own case, the "divine sign," is not worth speaking of, for it has happened to perhaps one other, or to no one at all before. And of these few, those who have become philosophers and have tasted how sweet and blessed a possession it is, and have also seen sufficiently the madness of the many—and that no one does anything healthy, so to speak, regarding the affairs of cities, and that there is no ally with whom one could go to the aid of the just and be saved—but like a man fallen among wild beasts, <margin>C</margin> neither willing to join in injustice nor being capable, as one man, to hold out against all the savages, he would perish before he could benefit the city or his friends, becoming useless to himself and others. Reasoning these things out, he keeps quiet and minds his own business, like someone in a storm of dust and sleet driven by the wind, standing under a small wall. Seeing others filled with lawlessness, he is content if he himself can somehow live his life here pure of injustice and unholy deeds, and make his departure from it with good hope, gracious and well-pleasing. But indeed, he said, he would depart having accomplished not the least of things. Nor yet the greatest, I said, not having met with a suitable constitution. For in a suitable one he himself will grow more, and will save the private along with the public. Regarding <margin>D</margin> why philosophy has received slander, and that it was not just, I think it has been said moderately well, unless you have something else to say. But I have nothing more to say about this, he said. But which of the current constitutions do you mean? None at all, I said. But this is my complaint: that no current state of a city is worthy of a philosophical nature. Therefore it is turned and altered; just as a foreign seed sown in another land tends to lose its strength and pass into the local type, so this race now does not keep its own power but falls away into <margin>E</margin> a foreign character. But if it should take the best constitution, just as it is itself best, then it will show that this was indeed divine, while the others were human—both the natures and the pursuits. So it is clear that after this you will ask what this constitution is. You did not guess right, he said. For I was not going to ask that, but whether it is this one which we described in founding the city, or another. In other respects, I said, it is this one. But this very thing was said even then: that there would always need to be something in the city that has the same understanding of the constitution that you, the legislator, had when you were setting down the laws. It was said, he replied. But it was not sufficiently shown, I said, for fear of what you all might object to, having shown that the demonstration of it would be long and difficult. Since what remains is not at all the easiest to go through. What is that? In what way a city handling philosophy will not be destroyed. For all great things are precarious <margin>F</margin> and, as the saying goes, "the beautiful is truly difficult." But nonetheless, he said, let the demonstration take its end, this having become clear. It is not the lack of will, I said, but if anything, the lack of power that will hinder. Being present, you will know my eagerness. Look even now how eagerly and riskily I am about to say that, contrary to now, the city must touch this pursuit. How? Now, I said, those who do touch it are mere striplings, just out of childhood, who approach the most difficult part of it in the midst of housekeeping and moneymaking, and then they depart—those considered most philosophical. I mean by the most difficult part, that concerning arguments. In the time after that, if they are called by others who are doing this and they wish to be <margin>G</margin> listeners, they think it a great thing, believing it should be done as a side-task. Toward old age, with the exception of some few, they are extinguished much more than the Heraclitean sun, in as much as they are never rekindled. How then should it be? he said. Entirely the opposite. While they are striplings and children, they should handle a boyish education and philosophy; they should take very good care of their bodies while they are sprouting and ripening, acquiring them as a service to philosophy. As age proceeds, in which the soul begins to be perfected, they should intensify her exercises. But when strength fails and they are outside of political and military duties, then they should be let out to pasture and do nothing else, except as a side-task—those who are going to live happily, and having died,

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Book VI of Plato’s Republic. Having discussed why philosophers are currently seen as useless or wicked by the public, Socrates now moves to argue that a perfect state is only possible if true philosophers are compelled to rule or if rulers are divinely inspired to become philosophers. This leads into the famous metaphor of the philosopher as a "painter" of the constitution.</meta>

# ON THE REPUBLIC, BOOK VI.

...expecting a portion of that life there <note>Referring to the afterlife or the realm of ideal forms.</note> which is fitting for those who have bettered themselves. "Truly, Socrates," he said, "you seem to speak with great enthusiasm. However, I think that most people, if they hear this, will resist even more vigorously and will not be persuaded at all, starting with Thrasymachus." "Do not try to make trouble," I said, "between me and Thrasymachus, who have just become friends—though we were not really enemies before. For we shall not slacken our efforts until we either persuade him and the others, or at least achieve something that will be of use for that future life when, born again, they happen upon such discourses as these." "You speak of a short time," he said. "It is nothing," I replied, "compared to all of time. But that the many are not persuaded by what we say is no wonder. For they have never yet seen that which we are now describing actually happen. Instead, they have heard only clever phrases <note>original: "ῥήματα" (rhemata)</note> designedly balanced against one another, not occurring by chance as they do now. But a man who is as perfectly equated and likened to virtue as possible, and who rules by deed and word in a city of like character—this is something they have never seen, whether in one man or many. Or do you think they have?" "Not at all." "Nor, my blessed friend, have they been listeners to noble and free discourses, such as those where the truth is sought intensely and in every way for the sake of knowledge. They have only encountered those clever and contentious arguments that aim at nothing but reputation and strife, whether in the courts or in private gatherings, which they shun from a distance." "No, they have not seen these either," he said. "For these reasons," I said, "and because we foresaw these things then and were afraid, we were nevertheless compelled by the truth to say that neither city, nor constitution, nor even a man will ever be perfect until these few philosophers—those who are not wicked but are now called useless—are forced by some chance necessity, whether they wish it or not, to take charge of the city and the city is made to obey them; or until a true passion for true philosophy falls by some divine inspiration upon those who are now in power or upon their sons. To say that either of these things, or both, is impossible, I say is not reasonable. If it were, we would rightly be laughed at for speaking of things that are merely like empty wishes. Is it not so?" "It is so." "If, then, there has been some necessity in the infinite time of the past for those who are supreme in philosophy to take charge of a city, or if there is such a necessity now in some barbarian land <note>In the Greek context, "barbarian" simply meant any non-Greek speaking culture.</note> far beyond our sight, or if it shall happen hereafter, we are ready to contend in argument that the constitution we described has existed, does exist, and will exist, whenever this Muse <note>The Muse of Philosophy.</note> gains control of a city. For its birth is not impossible, nor do we speak of impossibilities; though we ourselves admit that they are difficult." "I agree," he said. "But the many," I said, "you will say do not agree." "Perhaps," he said. "My dear friend," I said, "do not bring such a heavy charge against the many. They will surely hold a different opinion if, instead of being contentious with them, you gently encourage them and remove the slander against the love of learning. Show them whom you mean by philosophers, and define, as we did just now, their nature and their practice, so they do not think you are talking about the people they have in mind. Or if they see them in this light, will you not say they will take a different view and give different answers? Or do you think anyone who is not himself envious and harsh will be angry with one who is not harsh, or feel envy toward one who is not envious, but is instead gentle? I will say it first: I think such a harsh nature exists only in a few, and not in the multitude." "I certainly agree with you," he said. "And do you also agree with this? The cause of the many being ill-disposed toward philosophy is those outsiders who have burst in like rioters where they do not belong, insulting one another and being full of hostility, always making their talk about people—doing what is least becoming to philosophy." "Very much so," he said. "For indeed, Adeimantus, the man whose mind is truly fixed on the things that *are* <note>The eternal Forms or Truths.</note> has no leisure to look down at the affairs of men, and by fighting with them, to be filled with envy and ill-will. Instead, he keeps his eyes fixed upon things that are ordered and always remain the same, which neither wrong nor are wronged by one another, but are all ordered and according to reason; these he imitates and tries to liken himself to as much as possible. Or do you think there is any way to prevent someone from imitating that which he admires and associates with?" "It is impossible," he said. "Then the philosopher, by associating with what is divine and orderly, becomes as orderly and divine as is possible for a human; though slander is plentiful everywhere." "Absolutely." "If then," I said, "some necessity arises for him to practice bringing what he sees there <note>In the divine realm of forms.</note> into the habits of men, both in private and public, and not just to mold himself, do you think he will be a poor craftsman of temperance, justice, and all popular virtue?" "Least of all," he said. "But if the many perceive that what we say about him is true, will they still be angry with the philosophers and disbelieve us when we say that a city can never be happy unless it is drawn by those painters who use the divine pattern?" "They will not be angry," he said, "if they perceive it. But what is this 'manner of drawing' you mean?" "Taking the city and the characters of men like a tablet," I said, "they would first of all make it clean. This is not at all easy; but you know that this is how they would immediately differ from all others..."

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...about to take up a lot in life fitting for their past actions. You seem to me, O Socrates, to speak quite readily indeed. I think, however, that most people, once they have heard these things, will resist you even more promptly and will be by no means persuaded. And I believe Thrasymachus will be among the first to act so. Do not, I said, plot against the mutual goodwill between me and Thrasymachus. For we have recently become friends, nor were we enemies before. Nor truly shall we cease until we persuade both him and others, or at least achieve something contributing to that life which, when they have reached it, they will find these words again. "You have spoken of a brief time," he said. "On the contrary," I said, "it is as nothing if compared to the whole of time." But that the many do not offer their trust to these things that have been said is no wonder. For they have never seen that which was just said <margin>B</margin> come to pass; instead, they have seen certain words of this kind, composed with industry into a sort of resemblance, not meeting by chance as they do now. But a man perfected in virtue as far as can be, and most powerful in deeds and words in such a city—they have never beheld either one or many such men. Or do you think so? "In no way." Nor have they ever, O blessed man, lent their ears to honest and free discourses, by which truth is sought with persistence and every zeal for the sake of knowing. But these things full of craftiness and contention, desiring nothing other than opinion and strife, both in the courts and in private conversations, are omitted. "Not <margin>C</margin> indeed." Therefore, when we ourselves foresaw and feared these things, we were compelled by the truth to say that neither any city, nor republic, nor man will be perfect before some necessity happens by chance to these few philosophers—who are neither evil nor useless, as is commonly thought—so that whether they wish it or not, they undertake the care of the city, or are heard by the citizens; or at least until a true love of true philosophy, by some divine inspiration, takes hold of those who rule, or their sons. That either one of these, or both, are impossible, I do not think can be demonstrated. Otherwise, we are rightly <margin>D</margin> mocked, as if we were fashioning things according to our own heart's desire. Is it not so? "Exactly so." If, therefore, at some time in the infinite past, men outstanding in philosophy were driven by necessity to govern the republic, or if in these times they govern in some barbarian region very far removed from our sight, or if they shall govern in the future, in this state of affairs we certainly affirm that the republic described above has been, is, and shall be. Whenever this Muse presides over the city, it can certainly happen; nor do we fashion impossibilities. However, that these things are difficult has also been conceded by us. "It seems so to me as well." You will add, perhaps, that this does not seem so to the common people. "Perhaps." Do not blame the common people so much, O <margin>E</margin> blessed man. But what do you think they will believe if, not with the zeal of contention, but with friendly admonitions—having dissolved the slander against philosophy—you show them whom you specifically call philosophers? And as you recently distinguished, show both their nature and their study, lest they suspect you are speaking of those whom they themselves imagine. Or if they have conceived it so, you would say they were deceived by a false opinion and did not respond to what was proposed. Do you think, I say, that anyone is provoked against a mild man? Or that a man without envy and malice would envy a man who is not envious? I respond for you: that in the multitude of men, such a harsh nature exists in only a very few. "I think the same myself." And do you think this also? The cause <margin>F</margin> for which the multitude bears philosophy with an unfavorable mind is those who, though they are unfit for philosophy, have professed it, and harass men everywhere with insults, and as if delighted by enmities, always speak ill of men, doing a thing least fitting for philosophy. "Altogether." For indeed, O Adeimantus, for that man who has directed every sharp focus of his mind toward those things which truly are, no leisure remains to look back at the inferior affairs of men, and by fighting with them, to stir up envy and malevolence for himself. But he contemplates those things which always keep the same order, which neither inflict nor suffer injury from one another, but all are adorned and arranged according to reason. And these things he imi-<margin>G</margin>tates, and makes himself as similar to them as possible. Or do you think it can happen that someone does not imitate that to which he clings with admiring love? "In no way." Wherefore, since the philosopher frequently clings to the divine and the decorous, he himself becomes divine and decorous as far as is possible for a man. But slander is great in all things. "It is so entirely." If, therefore, he is induced by some necessity to transfer those things which he beholds there into the habits of men, both privately and publicly, and to form not only himself but others, do you think he will be an unskillful craftsman of temperance, justice, and all popular virtue? "By no means." If the common people perceive that we are telling the truth about this, will they be angry with the philosophers? And will they not believe us when we say that a city will not otherwise be happy than if those who use a divine example, like painters, form it? "They will by no means be angry," he said, "if they perceive it. But what manner of painting do you mean?" "When painters—these, I say—have received the city and the habits of men like a certain tablet, they will first of all purge it, which is by no means easy. Do you not know that in this especially the philosophers differ from others..."

He argues that a perfect state is possible if true philosophers, who model themselves on divine order, are given the chance to "paint" a new society on a clean slate.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Socrates' argument in Book VI of the Republic, where he describes the philosopher as a craftsman of the soul and the state. He has just explained that the public’s hostility toward philosophy can be softened if they realize the true nature of a philosopher's work.</meta>

# PLATO'S [WORKS]

<margin>A</margin>...because they would not be willing to touch either a private person or a state, nor to draft laws, until they have either received a clean canvas <note>original: "purgata" / "καθαρὰν"; Socrates suggests the state must be wiped clean of corrupt habits before the philosopher begins.</note> or made it so themselves. And they would be right. Do you not think that after this they would sketch out the form of the constitution? Of course. Then, in doing this work, I believe they would look frequently in both directions: towards that which is naturally just, beautiful, and temperate, and all such things, and again towards the human realm. They would arrange human affairs according to that higher model, observing human nature through human duties, aiming for that figure which Homer also called the "divine form and image" <note>original: "Dei speciem & imaginem" / "θεοειδές τε καὶ θεοείκελον"; a reference to Homeric descriptions of heroes.</note> when it appears among men. Quite right. <margin>B</margin> Part they would erase, I suppose, and part they would paint in again, until they have made human characters as dear to God as is possible. It would indeed, he said, be a most beautiful painting. Shall we then persuade those men, I said—the ones you said were ready to attack us—that such a man is the "painter of constitutions"? This is the man we praised to them earlier, for whose sake they were angry because we were entrusting the government of the city to him. Do they hear this now with a calmer mind? Very much so, he said, if they are wise. In what part now will they oppose us? <margin>C</margin> Will they claim that philosophers are not lovers of truth and of that which truly exists? That would be absurd. Or perhaps they will deny that the nature of philosophers, as we have described it, is familiar with the best? Not even that. What then? Will they deny that such a nature, if it receives the proper duties, will be perfectly good and, more than any other, close to wisdom? Or will they prefer those whom we ourselves set aside? Not at all. Will they still be angry when we say that unless the race of philosophers takes the helm of the state, there will be no rest from evils for either the state or its citizens? And that the republic we are describing in words will never see the light of day? <margin>D</margin> Perhaps less so. Do you wish, then, I said, for us to say that they are not just "less" angry, but altogether softened and persuaded? Lest they perhaps confess it only out of shame. By all means. Let them then be persuaded of this. But as for this next point, who would doubt that children of kings or powerful men could be born as philosophers? No one. And one might add that even if such are born, they must necessarily be corrupted. For we also concede that it is difficult for them to be preserved <note>kept pure from the "stains" of power or vice.</note>. But who will add further that in all of time, out of all men, not even one has ever been preserved? No one would say that. Yet surely one such nature, if it finds an obedient city, is sufficient to accomplish all these things which now lack belief. Sufficient indeed. I suppose, I said, if a ruler commands the laws and duties we have described, it is not impossible that the citizens would be willing to obey. Certainly not. And is it a wonder, or impossible, that others should think the same things we think? I do not think so. And that these things are the best, if indeed they are possible, has been sufficiently discussed above, I believe. <margin>E</margin> Sufficiently. Therefore, from what has been said, it follows that the things we have predicted concerning the making of laws would be best if they were done; they are difficult to achieve, but not impossible. It clearly follows. Since we have finally reached the end of these matters, we must now move on to the rest: namely, in what manner, and through what studies and disciplines, the "Saviors" <term>Saviors: "σωτῆρες" (soteres), referring here to the elite guardians who preserve the state's integrity.</term> of our republic will be trained, and at what age each will take up their various tasks. We must certainly speak of these things now. <margin>F</margin> I did not act very wisely when, in the previous parts, I left out the difficulty and trouble of marriages, the procreation of children, and the appointment of rulers. For I knew how envious a thing it was, and how difficult to speak of, or even to make true. But now we are nevertheless compelled to deal with these things. Those matters pertaining to women and children we have already completed; but those regarding the rulers must be examined again as if from the beginning. We said, if you remember, that they must show themselves to be lovers of the city, tested in both pleasures and pains, and that they must not be moved from this conviction by labors, or by fear of dangers, or by any other change. But the one who is unable to do this must be rejected; while the one who emerges everywhere sincere and incorrupt, like gold tested in the trial of fire, should be set as a ruler over the city, and honored with rewards both in life and after death. Such rewards should be as we have commonly stated, briefly passing over this and almost turning the discourse aside; for we were afraid to move things as they are now. You speak the truth, he said; I remember. For I was hesitant, my friend, to say the things I have now dared to say. But let us now dare to assert this: that the most diligent guardians must be philosophers. Let that be settled. Notice how few such men there will be. For the parts of that nature which we said must be in them rarely occur together; for the most part, they are born divided. How do you mean? Do you not know that those same men who are quick to learn, have good memories, are ingenious and sharp, and possess those traits that follow from these, are not also usually strong and high-minded enough to live in a moderate, quiet, and constant way? For such men of keen intellect are carried away by their own sharpness wherever it may lead, and are void of all stability and gravity. You speak the truth.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...to differ from the others in that they would not be willing to touch either an individual or a city, nor to write laws, before they either received it clean or made it so themselves. And rightly so, he said. Therefore, after these things, do you think they would sketch the outline of the constitution? Why not? Working it out, I think, they would look frequently in both directions: towards that which is naturally just and beautiful and temperate, and all such things, and again towards that which they would produce among men, mixing and blending from their practices the "human image" <note>original: "ἀνδρείκελον" (andreikelon); literally "man-colored" or "the human likeness."</note>, taking as their mark that which Homer called the "god-like and god-resembling" among men. Correct, <margin>B</margin> he said. And one part they would erase, I think, and another they would write in again, until they have made human characters as dear to God as they can possibly be. That would be the most beautiful painting, he said. Shall we then somehow persuade those who you said were coming at us in battle-array that such a man is a "painter of constitutions"? Is it the one whom we were praising to them then—the one for whose sake they were angry that we were handing over the cities to him? And are they even more soothed now when they hear it? Much more so, he said, if they are sensible. For in what way will they find reason to dispute it? <margin>C</margin> Will they deny that philosophers are lovers of reality and truth? That would be strange, he said. Or that their nature, which we have described, is akin to the best? Not that either. What then? That such a nature, having met with the appropriate practices, will not be perfectly good and philosophical—if indeed any other is? Or that it belongs more to those natures whom we set apart? Surely not. Will they then still be wild with anger when we say that, until the philosophical race gains power over the city, there will be no end of evils for the city or the citizens? Nor will the constitution which we are telling as a story in words reach its completion in deed? Perhaps less so, he said. Do you wish then, I said, that we do not say they are "less" angry, but that they have become altogether gentle and persuaded, so that if nothing else, they may agree out of shame? By all means, he said. <margin>D</margin> Let these people, then, I said, be persuaded of this. But will anyone dispute this next: that children of kings or dynasts could be born with philosophical natures? Not even one person, he said. And that such being born, there is a great necessity for them to be corrupted? Even we concede that it is hard for them to be saved <note>meaning: to keep their philosophical integrity.</note>. But that in all of time, out of all men, not even one could ever be saved—is there anyone who would dispute that? How could they? But surely, I said, one who is sufficient, having a city that obeys him, can bring to completion all those things which are now disbelieved. For he is sufficient, he said. For I suppose, I said, if a ruler establishes the laws and practices we have described, it is surely not impossible for the citizens to be willing to follow them. Not at all. But is it a marvel and impossible that what seems good to us should also seem so to others? I do not think so, he said. And surely that these things are best, if they are possible, has been sufficiently described in what came before, as I think. Sufficiently indeed. Now, it seems, we have come to this conclusion regarding legislation: that what we say is best, if it could happen; but that for it to happen is difficult, though not impossible. That is the conclusion, he said. <margin>E</margin> Therefore, since this has with difficulty reached an end, the things remaining must be spoken of next: in what way and from what studies and practices the "Saviors" of the constitution will be produced, and at what ages each will take up each task. It must be spoken of, he said. Nothing wise came of me, I said, when I previously left aside the difficulty of the possession of women and the procreation of children, and the appointment of the rulers— <margin>F</margin> knowing how envious and difficult a task it becomes, even if entirely true. For now the necessity to go through them has come nonetheless. The matters of the women and children have been finished; but the matter of the rulers must be pursued as if from the beginning. We were saying, if you remember, that they must appear as lovers of the city, being tested in pleasures and pains, and that they must not appear to cast out this conviction in labors, or in fears, or in any other change. The one who is unable must be rejected; but the one who comes out pure in every way, like gold tested in fire, must be appointed as a ruler, and honors must be given to him while living and after he has died, and prizes as well. Such were the things being said, while the argument passed by and hid its face, fearing to disturb the present state of things. Most true, <margin>G</margin> he said, for I remember. For I was hesitant, my friend, I said, to say the things that have now been dared. But now let this be dared: to say that the most precise guardians must be established as philosophers. Let it be said, he said. Consider then how few they will likely be for you. For the nature we described them as needing to have—its parts only rarely wish to grow together into the same person; for the most part, they grow torn apart. How, he said, do you mean? Those who are quick to learn and have good memories, and are sharp-witted and quick, and all other such things—you know that they do not often also wish to grow up together with souls that are energetic and magnificent, such as are orderly and wish to live with quietness and stability; rather, such men are carried by their quickness wherever it may chance, and all stability departs from them. You speak the truth, he said. Therefore, these stable characters again...

<meta>This page continues the dialogue in Book VI of Plato's Republic, where Socrates is detailing the rigorous training required for the "guardians" or philosopher-kings. On the previous page, Socrates argued that the public could be reconciled to philosophy if they saw the philosopher as a divine painter of the constitution.</meta>

# ON THE REPUBLIC, BOOK VI.

<margin>A</margin> ...and stability, which are traits one might rely on as trustworthy—those who are intrepid in the face of fears during war—likewise act the same way toward learning. They are slow to move and hard to teach, as if numbed; they are filled with sleep and yawning whenever they must labor at such a task. This is true, he said. But we said that a person must share well and beautifully in both <note>That is, the guardian must possess both a quick mind and a steady, reliable character—traits that rarely appear together.</note>, or else they should not be given the most precise education, nor honors, nor authority. Correct, he said. Do you not think this combination will be rare? How could it not be? <margin>β'</margin> We must therefore test them in the labors, fears, and pleasures we mentioned before; and we must also add what we then passed over but now state: that they must be exercised in many branches of study, observing whether the soul is capable of enduring the greatest studies <margin>B</margin> <note>original: "μέγιστα μαθήματα"; literally the "greatest things to be learned."</note>, or whether it will flinch, as those who flinch in other types of struggles. It is certainly fitting to observe them in this way, he said. <margin>γ'</margin> But what do you mean by the "greatest studies"? You surely remember, I said, that after we distinguished three forms of the soul <note>The "tripartite soul": reason, spirit (thirst for honor), and appetite.</note>, we reached conclusions about the nature of justice, temperance, courage, and wisdom. If I did not remember, he said, I would not be worthy to hear the rest. Do you also remember what was said before those definitions? What was that? It was said that it was possible to see these virtues in their finest form, but that there was a longer circuit <note>original: "μακροτέρα περίοδος"; Socrates suggests that the quick definitions they gave earlier were insufficient and that a more circular, arduous path of reasoning is required for true understanding.</note> which one must travel to make them clearly manifest. We said it was possible to attach proofs to the previous arguments, and you said that would be sufficient. And so we spoke then in a way that seemed to me to be lacking in truth—but if it pleased you, that is for you to say. To me, it seemed moderate enough, he said; and the others thought so too. <margin>δ'</margin> But, my friend, I said, a measure of such things that falls short of the truth in any way is not a "moderate" measure at all. For nothing incomplete is a measure of anything. Yet it sometimes seems to people that they have done enough and that there is no need to seek further. Many feel this way, he said, because of laziness. But this is a feeling, I said, that a guardian of a city and its laws should least of all possess. That is likely, he said. <margin>D</margin> Therefore, my friend, I said, such a person must travel the "longer circuit," and must labor no less in learning than in physical exercise. Otherwise, as we were just saying, they will never reach the goal of the greatest and most fitting study. Are these virtues not the greatest? he asked. Is there something even greater than justice and those things we described? There is something greater, I said. Even of these virtues, we must not look at a mere sketch, as we are doing now, but we must not neglect their most perfect realization. Or is it not ridiculous to put every effort into other things of little value, striving for them to be as precise and pure as possible, while not demanding the greatest precision for the greatest things? <margin>E</margin> A very worthy thought, he said. But as for what this "greatest study" is, and what you say it concerns, do you think anyone would let you go without asking what it is? Not at all, I said. Ask away. You have certainly heard it not <margin>ε'</margin> a few times; but now you either do not understand, or you intend to give me trouble by being contentious. I suspect the latter. For you have often heard that the Idea of the Good <note>original: "ἡ τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ ἰδέα"; the supreme reality in Plato's thought, which makes all other things knowable and useful.</note> is the greatest study; it is by this that just things and the rest become useful and beneficial. And now you almost certainly know that I am going to say this, and furthermore, that we do not know it sufficiently. But if we do not know it, even if we knew everything else as well as possible without it, you know that it would be of no benefit to us—just as if we possessed something without the Good. Or do you think it is any advantage to possess all things, if they are not good? Or to understand everything else without understanding the Good, while understanding nothing beautiful or good? By Zeus, I do not, he said. But you also know this: that to the many, the Good seems to be pleasure, while to the more refined, it seems to be wisdom <note>original: "φρόνησις"; often translated as practical wisdom or intelligence.</note>. How could I not? And you know, <margin>F</margin> my friend, that those who hold this view cannot show what kind of wisdom it is, but are finally forced to say it is "the wisdom of the good." And quite ridiculously, too, he said. <margin>ζ'</margin> How is it not? I said, if they reproach us for not knowing the good, and then speak to us as if we did know it. For they say it is "wisdom of the good," as if we understood what they meant when they utter the name of "the good." Very true, he said. What about those who define pleasure as the good? Are they any less full of error than the others? Are they not also forced to admit that there are bad pleasures? Certainly. It happens then, I think, <margin>G</margin> that they admit the same things are both good and bad. Is it not so? Of course. It is clear then that there are many great disputes about this? How could there not be? <margin>η'</margin> And is this not also clear: that many would choose to do, possess, and seem to have things that are considered just and beautiful, even if they are not; yet when it comes to the good, no one is satisfied to possess what only seems so, but they seek what really is, and here everyone despises mere opinion? Very much so, he said. This, then, is what every soul pursues, and for the sake of which it does everything, divining that it is something, but being at a loss and unable to grasp sufficiently what it is, nor to use any stable faith such as it has about other things. Because of this, the soul misses the benefit of anything else. Should we say that such a great and vital thing must be left in darkness for the best men in the city, to whom we will entrust everything? <margin>H</margin> Least of all, he said. I think, then, I said, that when justice and

<column-break/>

Others, in whose stability one must place the greatest trust—as they are intrepid in war—just as they are immovable in these matters, so they are slower and duller toward learning. They are indeed sluggish and drowse whenever they must be vigilant in contemplation. It is as you say. But we stated in earlier parts that the leader ought to participate in both qualities in the best possible way. Otherwise, the highest learning should not be offered to him, nor honors or offices bestowed. Correct. Do you not think this will happen only rarely? Very rarely. It is necessary, therefore, to examine the character of the future leader in those things we mentioned above: in labors, fears, and pleasures. We add further—what we omitted then—that it is necessary to exercise him in many studies: so that it may be clear whether he is capable of grasping the greatest learning, or whether he fails instead, just like someone who trembles and fails in other works. It is certainly fitting to investigate in this way. But what do you call the "greatest learning"? I think you remember when we established three species in the soul, that justice, temperance, fortitude, and wisdom were defined by us as being in agreement with one another? If I did not remember, I would not be worthy to hear the rest from you. Do you also hold in memory what was said before these things? What was that? We said certainly that by a somewhat wider circuit of speech <note>original: "orationis circuitu"; reflecting the "longer road" mentioned in the Greek.</note>, these things could be known more exactly: but that it was more convenient to introduce demonstrations more consistent with what had gone before. To which you responded that this was sufficient. And so at that time these things were treated with a "crude Minerva" <note>original: "pingui Minerua"; a Latin idiom for doing something plainly, roughly, or without much refinement.</note>, as it seemed to me. But if it pleases you, say so yourself. It seemed both to me and to the others to have been said sufficiently and moderately. But in these matters, O friend, a measure that omits any part of the truth is not done very moderately. For nothing imperfect is the measure of anything. Although it sometimes seems to some that a matter has been sufficiently treated immediately, and that there is no need for a longer inquiry. This happens to very many because of laziness. This vice ought to be most foreign to a guardian of the city and the laws. Agreed. Therefore, friend, a wider circuit must be traveled by this man, and no less effort must be spent on learning than on exercising. Otherwise, as we said a little while ago, he will never arrive at the end of the highest and most necessary learning. Are these not the greatest things? And is there something else besides justice and the others we have narrated that is more excellent? Indeed, I say, there is something more excellent, and it is by no means fitting to look at a mere sketch <note>original: "adumbrationem"; a shadow or outline.</note> of these very things as we do now: but one must grasp their absolute reason. Is it not ridiculous to place all zeal in the smallest things, and to strive vehemently so they are performed as diligently and sincerely as possible, but to think a light effort is enough for the greatest things? Completely ridiculous. But do you think anyone will rest unless he now asks of you what that learning is which you call the greatest, and what it is concerned with? Not at all, I say: but you yourself ask, although I think you have heard it many times. Now, however, you either do not notice, or you rather intend to disturb me with your scruples. I suspect the latter. For you have often heard that the Idea of the Good is the greatest learning. By using this, both just things and other things become useful and profitable. And know that I want to say almost this, and furthermore, that we do not know it sufficiently. But if we do not know it, and if we should know all other things as well as possible without it, know that there would be no utility for us from the others: just as nothing would profit us if we possessed it without the Good. Or do you think it is anything more to possess all other things without the possession of the Good, than to understand all else without the understanding of the Good and the Beautiful themselves? Certainly not. To many, indeed, the Good seems to be pleasure, and to the more refined, wisdom. Without a doubt. Furthermore, you know this: that those who think wisdom is the Good, if they are asked what wisdom specifically, they are unable to declare it, but are forced at last to say "the wisdom of the Good." What a ridiculous response. Why should it not seem ridiculous, if while they reproach us for being ignorant of the Good, they speak of the Good to us again as if we were people who understood it? For they say the Good is the wisdom of the Good, as if we knew what they meant when they pronounce the name of the Good. You speak the truth. But those who define the Good as pleasure, do they err any less than the others? Are they not also forced to admit that there are bad pleasures? Greatly so. They are forced to admit, therefore, that the same things are both good and bad. Are they not? Plainly. Is it not clear that many and great ambiguities arise concerning this? It is clear. Is this not also manifest: that while many would prefer to do, possess, and seem to be what appears just and honest even if they are not, no one thinks he has enough if he possesses only what *seems* good, but everyone seeks those things which are truly good, and in these matters everyone despises mere opinion? Most especially. The soul of every man seeks the Good, and for its sake does all things, sensing that it is something: yet it is in doubt, nor can it

---

sufficiently grasp what it is, nor does it have such a certain and explored knowledge as it has of other things: and for that reason it fails in other things when it proceeds to judge what is useful. In a matter that is such and so great, shall we say that those most excellent men in the city, to whom we commit all things, ought to be similarly blind? Not in the least. I certainly think that the guardian who [is ignorant of] just and

<column-break/>

beautiful things when they are unknown, and in what way they are good, would be a guardian worth nothing if he is ignorant of this; I suspect that no one will know them sufficiently before knowing this. And you suspect well, he said. Therefore, our constitution will be perfectly ordered, if such a guardian oversees it, one who is a knower of these things. It must be so, he said. But how...

<meta>Catchword: fufficienter</meta>

<summary>Socrates identifies the "Idea of the Good" as the ultimate subject of study for the philosopher-king, arguing that without knowledge of the Good, all other virtues and possessions are useless. He explains that while people might settle for the appearance of justice, everyone demands the reality of the Good.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue in Book VI of Plato's Republic. Socrates and Glaucon are discussing the "greatest study"—the Form of the Good—and how the guardians of the state must understand it to truly govern effectively.</meta>

# ->PLATO’S<-

<margin>A</margin> ...possess honorable things, yet be ignorant of the reason why they are good, it is of little value. Indeed, it is likely that one who is ignorant of this cannot sufficiently know the things themselves. I suspect that no one will know them properly until the Good itself is sufficiently understood. You suspect rightly, he said. Therefore, our Republic will be perfectly ordered for us if a guardian who is skilled in these matters governs it. It must be so. But you, O Socrates, do you say the Good itself is knowledge, or pleasure, or something else besides these? Then I said: Truly, you are an upright man; I have known for a long time that it would not be enough for you to merely report the opinions of others. <margin>B</margin> It does not seem right to me, O Socrates, he said, to be able to report the opinions of others but not one’s own, especially for a man who has spent so much time occupied with these matters. Do you think it right, I asked, for someone to speak of things they do not know as if they were an expert? By no means as an expert, he said, but as one who is willing to set forth what he thinks based on opinion. What? I said. Do you not realize that all opinions without knowledge are shameful, even the best of which are blind? Or do you think those who form a true opinion without understanding <note>original: "sine intelligentia" / "ἄνευ νοῦ"; referring to 'doxa' or right opinion without the rational 'logos' to back it up.</note> differ at all from blind men who happen to walk the right path? Not at all. Do you wish, then, to behold shameful, blind, and crooked things, when you might hear of clear and beautiful things from others? <margin>C</margin> Come, by Zeus, Socrates! Glaucon said. Do not stop now, when you have almost reached the goal. For it will be enough for us if you treat the Good in the same way you treated justice, temperance, and the other virtues. It would also be very much enough for me, my friend, I said. But I fear my strength will fail, and by daring beyond my power, I shall appear foolish and move the listeners to laughter. However, O happy men, let us set aside for the present what the Good itself is. For it seems to me to be beyond our current inquiry. But I am willing to tell you of what appears to be the "offspring" <note>original: "prolem" / "ἔκγονος"; Socrates uses a financial metaphor here, where the "offspring" is the interest on a debt of knowledge.</note> of the Good, and what is most similar to it, if it pleases you; if not, I shall let it be. Speak then, he said. You shall settle the account of the "father" another time. I wish indeed, I said, that I were able to explain it and you were able to receive it—not just the offspring, as now, but both the offspring and the ancestors of the Good. Receive then this "interest" and "offspring" of the Good itself. <margin>D</margin> Yet take care that I do not unintentionally deceive you by giving a false account of this offspring. We shall take care as best we can, he said. Just speak. I shall speak, indeed, if we first agree and recall what was mentioned above and has been said many times elsewhere. What is that? he asked. We say there are many beautiful things, and many good things, and we distinguish them in our speech. We do indeed. But we also speak of Beauty itself and the Good itself, and similarly concerning all things that we previously posited as many; we now posit them according to a single Form <term>Idea: the eternal, unchanging essence of a thing</term> for each, as if there were only one, and we call it "that which each thing is." These things are true. <margin>E</margin> And we say that the many things are seen but not "thought" <note>original: "intelligi" / "νοεῖσθαι"; meaning grasped by the intellect.</note>, whereas the Forms are thought but not seen. That is exactly right. By what power within us do we see the things that are visible to the eyes? By sight. And is it not by hearing that things are heard, and by the other senses that all sensible things are perceived? Why not? Have you noticed how the Creator of the senses fashioned the power of seeing and being seen with such great perfection? Not entirely. Consider it this way: Do hearing and sound need some other kind of thing in order for the one to hear and the other to be heard? That is, if a third thing is absent, will the one not hear and the other not be heard? Not at all. I think, indeed, that many others—not to say all other senses—require no such thing. Or can you name one that does? I cannot. <margin>F</margin> Do you not notice that the power of sight and that which is subject to sight require such a thing? In what way? Though sight is present in the eyes and the one possessing it tries to use it, and though color is present in the objects, unless a third kind of thing is present, which is naturally suited for this very purpose, you know that sight will see nothing and colors will remain invisible. What is this thing you speak of? That which you call light. You speak the truth. Therefore, the sense of sight and the power of being seen are joined together by a bond far more honorable than all other such pairings—if indeed light is not to be despised. It is far from being despised. <margin>G</margin> Which of the celestial gods do you consider the cause of this, whose light makes our sight see most perfectly and makes the objects seen? The same one you and others do; for you are clearly asking about the Sun. Is it not the nature of sight to be related to this god? How? Sight is not the Sun, nor is the eye in which sight resides the Sun. Certainly not. But I think the eye is the most "sun-like" of all the organs of sense. Very much so. And does it not possess the power it has as something dispensed from the Sun, like an overflow? Exactly. Therefore, the Sun is not sight, but since it is the cause of sight, it is seen by sight itself. Quite so. <margin>H</margin> Say then, I said, that this is what I call the "offspring of the Good," which the Good generated to be analogous to itself: what the Good is in the intelligible realm <note>original: "loco intelligibili" / "νοητῷ τόπῳ"; the realm of pure thought and Forms.</note> in relation to the intellect and the things understood, the Sun is in the visible realm in relation to sight and the things seen. In what way? he asked. Explain further. You know, I said, that when the eyes are no longer turned toward those things whose colors the light of day illuminates, but toward those things touched by the rays of night, they grow dim and seem almost blind, as if pure sight were not in them. So it happens. But when they turn toward things the Sun illustrates, they see clearly, and in those same eyes...

<column-break/>

...things that are beautiful, if it is unknown in what way they are good; it is a guardian of great value to possess, if he is likely to know these things. I suspect no one will know them sufficiently before that. For you suspect well, he said. Will our city not be perfectly ordered, then, if such a guardian oversees it, one who is a knower of these things? It is necessary, he said. But you, Socrates, do you say the good is knowledge, or pleasure? Or something else besides these? This man (I said) is noble and has long been clear that he would not be satisfied with what others think about these things. For it does not seem just to me, Socrates, he said, to be able to state the dogmas of others, but not one's own, after having spent so much time occupied with these matters. What then? I said, does it seem just to you to speak about what one does not know as if one knew it? By no means as if knowing, he said; however, as one who has an opinion, he should be willing to say what he thinks. What then? (I said) have you not perceived that opinions without knowledge are all base? The best of which are blind? Or do they seem to you to differ at all from blind men walking the right path, those who opine something true without the mind? In no way, he said. Do you wish then to behold base things, blind and crooked, when it is possible to hear from others things that are clear and beautiful? By Zeus, Socrates, said Glaucon, do not stop as if you were at the end. For it will suffice for us if, just as you went through justice and temperance and the others, you likewise go through the Good. And for me too (I said) O companion, it will be very much enough; but I fear I shall not be able, and in my eagerness, I shall act unseemly and incur laughter. But, O blessed ones, let us let be for now what the Good itself is. (For it seems to me to be more than what can be reached by our present impulse, at least according to what I think now) but I am willing to speak of what appears to be an offspring of the Good and most like it, if it is pleasing to you; if not, let it be. But, he said, speak. For another time you will pay the narrative of the father. I would wish (I said) that I were able to pay it back, and you to receive it; but not, as now, just the interest <note>original: "τόκους"; here 'tokos' means both 'child/offspring' and 'financial interest'.</note>. Take then this interest and offspring of the Good itself. Be careful, however, lest I somehow deceive you unwillingly, giving a counterfeit account of the interest. We shall be careful, he said, as much as possible; but only speak. Having come to an agreement, I said, and having reminded you of what was said before, and has already been said many other times. What kind of things? he said. Many beautiful things (I said) and many good things, and we say each is so and we define them in speech. For we say so. And Beauty itself, and Goodness itself, and so concerning all the things we then posited as many, we now posit again according to one idea for each, as being one, and we address it as "that which each is." And we say the former are seen, but not thought; but the ideas are thought, but not seen. Entirely so. By what then of ourselves do we see the things seen? By sight, he said. And so (I said) by hearing, the things heard? and by the other senses, all the sensible things? Of course. Have you then (I said) considered the craftsman of the senses, by how much he crafted the power of seeing and being seen as the most costly? Not quite, he said. But look at it this way. Is there anything hearing and voice need of another kind in order for the one to hear and the other to be heard? Which, if a third thing does not come to them, the one will not hear, and the other will not be heard? Nothing, he said. And I think (I said) not many others (so as not to say none) need any such thing; or can you say of any? Not I, he said. But do you not perceive that the sense of sight and the visible need it? How? Sight being in the eyes, and the one having it attempting to use it, and color being present in them, if the third kind of thing does not come, which is naturally suited for this very purpose, you know that sight will see nothing, and the colors will be invisible. Of what then do you speak? (he said). That which you call (I said) light. True (he said) you speak. By no small idea then the sense of seeing, and the power of being seen, were yoked together by a more honorable yoke than other pairings; if indeed light is not unhonored. But indeed (he said) it is far from being unhonored. Which then can you name as the cause of this among the gods in heaven, whose light makes our sight see most beautifully, and the things seen to be seen? The very one you (he said) and others do, for clearly you are asking about the Sun. Is then sight naturally related to this god in this way? How? Sight is not the sun, neither itself nor that in which it occurs, which we call the eye. Not indeed. But it is the most sun-like, I think, of the organs concerning the senses. By far. Does it not also possess the power it has, dispensed from this as if flowing in? Quite so. Is then the sun not sight, but being the cause of it, is seen by it? So it is, he said. This then (I said) say that I call the offspring of the Good, which the Good generated analogous to itself, what it is in the intelligible region towards the mind and the things thought, this is in the visible region towards sight and the things seen. How? (he said) explain it further to me. Eyes (I said) you know that when one no longer turns them to those things whose colors the daylight covers, but those which the night-lights cover, they are dimmed and appear near to blind, as if pure sight were not in them? And very much so, he said. But when, I think, they see clearly the things the sun shines upon, and sight appears to be in these very eyes. Of course. Thus then consider also the part of the soul. # ->ON THE REPUBLIC, BOOK VI.<-
