<margin>A</margin> Understand the soul in this way: when it focuses on that which is illuminated by truth and being, it understands and knows it, and appears to possess intelligence. But when it turns toward that which is mixed with darkness—that which is born and passes away <note>original: "τὸ γιγνόμενόν τε καὶ ἀπολλύμενον" / "generatur atque corrumpitur"; referring to the physical world of change</note>—its sight is dimmed, it holds only changing opinions, and it seems to lack a mind. So it appears. Therefore, you must say that the "Idea of the Good" is what provides truth to the things known and gives the power of knowing to the one who knows. Understand it as the cause of science <note>original: "ἐπιστήμη" / "scientia"; here meaning certain, demonstrable knowledge</note> and of truth as it is perceived by the mind. Even though both of these—knowledge and truth—are beautiful, you will be right to judge that the Good is something different and even more beautiful than they are. Just as in the visible world it is right to
<margin>B</margin> think of light and sight as "sun-like," but wrong to think they are the sun itself, so here it is right to think of these two—knowledge and truth—as "good-like," but it is wrong to think that either of them is the Good itself. The state of the Good must be honored even more highly. You speak of an inconceivable beauty, he said, if it provides knowledge and truth but is itself superior to them in beauty. You certainly aren't saying it is "pleasure," are you? Hush! I said. Rather, examine its image in this way. How? You will say, I think, that the sun provides those things which are seen not only with the power to be seen, but also with their generation, growth, and nourishment, though the sun itself is not "generation." How could it be? In the same way, you should say that the things known receive from the Good not only
<margin>C</margin> their being known, but also their very existence and essence <note>original: "οὐσία" / "essentia"; the fundamental reality or 'being' of a thing</note>, though the Good is not essence, but rather surpasses essence in dignity and power. Then Glaucon said quite laughingly: By Apollo! What a divine excess! You are the cause, I said, for forcing me to say what I think about it. And please do not stop, he said, until you have finished the comparison with the sun, if anything has been left out. Indeed, I said, many things are left out. Then do not omit even a small thing, he said. I think many things will be left aside, I said; nonetheless, as far as is possible at present, I will not willingly leave anything out. Do not, he said. Think then, as we were saying, that there are these two rulers: one reigns over the intelligible realm and place, the other over the visible realm—I will not say "the heavens" 
<margin>D</margin> lest you think I am playing word games with the name. You have these two forms then: the visible and the intelligible. I have them. Now, take a line and cut it into two unequal segments. Divide each of those segments again in the same ratio—one for the visible world and one for the intelligible—and you will have them distinguished by their clarity and obscurity. In the visible segment, one part contains images. By "images," I mean first shadows, then reflections in water and in things that are dense, smooth, and bright, and everything of that sort, if you understand. I understand. In the other part, place the things that these images resemble: the animals around us, everything that grows, and the whole class of 
<margin>E</margin> manufactured things. I place them, he said. Would you also be willing to say, I asked, that this division represents the distinction between truth and its lack? As the object of opinion is to the object of knowledge, so is the image to the thing it represents? I would, very much so. Now consider how the intelligible segment must be cut. How? In one part of it, the soul is forced to investigate using the things previously divided as images; it proceeds from hypotheses <note>original: "ὑποθέσεων"; assumptions or starting points taken for granted</note> not toward a first principle, but toward a conclusion. In the other part, the soul moves from a hypothesis toward a "non-hypothetical" first principle, without using the images used in the first part, making its way through the Forms themselves. I do not quite understand what you mean, he said. Well, try again, I said; it will be 
<margin>F</margin> easier to understand once this is said first. I think you know that those who deal with geometry, arithmetic, and such things, assume the "odd" and the "even," the figures, and the three kinds of angles, and other related things for each method. They treat these things as known, making them their "hypotheses," and they do not think they owe any explanation of them either to themselves or to others, as if they were obvious to everyone. Starting from these, they go through the rest of the steps and end up consistently at the point they intended to investigate. I certainly know that, he said. And you also know 
<margin>G</margin> that they use visible forms and speak about them, though they are not thinking about these specific drawings, but about the things they resemble. For instance, they argue about the "Square Itself" and the "Diameter Itself," not the one they actually draw. And so it is with other things: these very things they mold and draw, which have their own shadows and reflections in water, they use as images, seeking to see those things themselves which can only be seen with the mind. You speak the truth, he said. This, then, was the form of the intelligible I was talking about. The soul is forced to use hypotheses in its search for it, not traveling toward a first principle because it cannot rise above its
<margin>H</margin> hypotheses, but using as images those very things which were represented by the lower objects—things which, compared to the objects below them, are considered distinct and are honored as being clear. I understand, he said, that you are speaking of what happens in geometry and its sister arts. Then understand that by the other segment of the intelligible, I mean that which Reason itself grasps by the power of dialectic <note>The art of logical conversation and investigation to reach the highest truths</note>. It does not treat hypotheses as first principles, but truly as hypotheses—that is, as stepping stones and springboards—so that it may go as far as the "non-hypothetical," <column-break/> <margin>A</margin> For when the soul clings to that in which truth and being itself shine forth, it understands and knows it, and appears to have intellect. But when it is carried toward that which is mixed with darkness—namely, that which is born and decays—its edge is blunted, it turns over various opinions, and it seems to be without a mind. So it appears. Therefore, you must say that the Idea of the Good is that which provides truth to the things understood and gives the power to understand to the one who understands, being the cause of science and truth, which is perceived through the intellect. Since these two—knowledge and truth—are so beautiful, if you judge the Good itself to be something other and even more beautiful than they are, you will judge rightly. And just as it is proper to think that light and 
<margin>B</margin> the power of sight have a certain "sun-like" quality, but not that they are the sun itself: so it is right to think that knowledge and truth have a certain "good-like" quality, but it is not right to think they are the Good itself. For the majesty of the Good itself is more venerable. You describe an inestimable beauty, he said, if it provides science and truth, yet surpasses them in beauty. For surely you are not saying it is pleasure. God forbid, I said. Rather, contemplate its image more clearly in this way. How? You will say, I think, that the sun provides those things that are seen not only with the power of being seen, but also with their generation, growth, and nourishment, though it is not itself "generation." How so? In the same way, you should say that the Good 
<margin>C</margin> gives to those things which are known not only that they are known, but also bestows their being and essence, although the Good itself is not essence, but exceeds essence in dignity and power. Then Glaucon said, laughing, "By Hercules, this is a marvelous excess!" You are certainly the cause of this, I said, you who compelled me to open up what I thought about this. Do not stop yet, he said, but finish the comparison of the sun especially, if anything was omitted. Many things are indeed omitted. Do not omit even the smallest thing. I think indeed that many things will remain, nevertheless, as many as can be related at present, I will not willingly let go. So I pray. Think of these two things: one reigns in the 
<margin>D</margin> intelligible class and place, the other in the invisible <note>likely a slip in the Latin text for "visible"</note>, lest I seem to deceive you about the name by saying "the heavens." However, hold these two species: the visible and the intelligible. I hold them. Just as if you took a line cut into two unequal portions, and divided each part again by a similar ratio: so now distinguish the one visible class offered to you, and the other intelligible class, according to clarity and obscurity. In the visible class, one portion will contain images. I call images, first, shadows; then, the likenesses that appear in water, and in bodies that are dense, smooth, and bright, and every such thing, if you understand. I understand. The other 
<margin>E</margin> portion will encompass those things of which these are likenesses: namely, the animals among us, plants, and the entire class of manufactured things. Thus I place them. Do you wish further to say that this class is distinguished according to truth and non-truth: so that as that which is fashioned by opinion is to that which is known by science, so is the likeness to that of which it is a likeness? Very much so. Consider again the division of the intelligible. In what way? One class of it is that which the soul investigates by using those things previously divided as if they were images, compelled to proceed from positions <note>hypotheses</note> not toward a principle, but toward an end. The other, which the mind thinks out, proceeds from a supposition toward a 
<margin>F</margin> non-supposed principle, not using the images which we used for the other class, but progressing in the Forms themselves through them. I do not sufficiently understand what you say. But you will understand more easily through this. I think it is not hidden from you that those who are occupied with geometry and arithmetic and other things of that kind, suppose the even and the odd and figures and three species of angles, and similar things in each of their arguments; and having placed these as if they were manifest to anyone, they think no explanation needs to be given for them. And starting from here, they descend to other things, and finally reach that which they were seeking. I know that entirely. 
<margin>G</margin> Truly you also know that they use forms that fall into sight, and they speak about them; although they do not direct their mind to these, but rather to those things of which these are likenesses—namely, to the Square itself and the Diameter itself, not to those which they draw. And in other things in the same way, they use these species which they describe and figure—of which there are shadows and images in water—as images, striving to behold those things which are not perceived otherwise than by knowledge. You speak the truth. I was calling this a species of the intelligible class, to the investigation of which the soul is compelled to use 
<margin>H</margin> suppositions, not going toward a principle because it cannot ascend above 
suppositions, and it uses these images which are from the lower things, compared to the likeness of the higher, and thus they are conceived and distinguished by opinion as if they contributed clearly to those things. I understand indeed that you speak of what is usually done in geometry and its sister arts. <summary>In this passage from Republic Book VI, Socrates explains the "Idea of the Good" as the ultimate source of truth and being, using the Sun as a metaphor. He then introduces the "Divided Line" to categorize reality into four levels: shadows/reflections, physical objects, mathematical truths, and the ultimate Forms reached through dialectic.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes Book VI of Plato's Republic, finishing the "Analogy of the Divided Line," and begins Book VII with the famous "Allegory of the Cave." These passages explore how the human soul moves from perceiving mere shadows of reality to grasping the highest forms of truth.</meta>

...using certain steps and supports <note>original: "gradibus quibusdam & adminiculis" / "ἐπιβάσεσί τε καὶ ὁρμαῖς"; referring to hypotheses as stepping stones</note>, until it reaches that which is not a hypothesis <note>original: "quod nõ supponitur" / "τὸ ἀνυπόθετον"; the unhypothetical first principle</note>, namely the first principle of the universe. Having touched this, it turns back and clings to those things which depend on that principle, and so descends to the conclusion, using nothing sensible at all, but only the Forms themselves, proceeding through them and toward them. 
I understand at last, Glaucon said, though not as well as I would wish. You seem to be proposing a great task. You intend to distinguish that part of truly existing and intelligible being, which we contemplate through the science of demonstration <note>the "Dialectic"</note>, as being clearer than that which we investigate through those sciences called "arts" <note>referring to technical sciences like geometry and arithmetic</note>. In these arts, hypotheses are taken as principles, and those who consider them are forced to observe with thought <note>original: "dianoia"; a middle stage of reasoning</note> rather than the senses. However, because they do not ascend to the first principle but search from hypotheses, they do not seem to you to have true intellect <note>original: "nous"; intuitive understanding</note> concerning these things, even though they are intelligible when joined with the principle. You seem to me to call the state of geometricians and such "thought" rather than "intellect," as if thought held a middle place between opinion and intellect.
<margin>B</margin> You have understood it quite well, I said. And for these four proportions, accept these four affections of the soul: **Intelligence** <note>original: "noesis"</note> for the highest, **thought** <note>original: "dianoia"</note> for the second, **faith** <note>original: "pistis"; conviction regarding physical objects</note> for the third, and for the last, **representation** or **imagination** <note>original: "eikasia"; the perception of shadows and reflections</note>. Arrange them in a ratio, so that they participate in clarity just as the objects they concern participate in truth. 
I understand, he said, and I agree with what you say, and I arrange them as you command.

# PLATO'S REPUBLIC
## Or,
## ON JUSTICE,
### THE SEVENTH DIALOGUE.

->SUMMARY OF THE DIALOGUE.<-
Having explained the subject of true philosophy, Socrates now diligently pursues the method of learning it. He teaches the way and reasoning by which we reach that highest point, and how, once instructed in that noble science, we may approach the serious and sober practice <note>original: "πρᾶξιν"</note> of life and the republic. He carefully fits this teaching to his purpose: that the discipline required of a Guardian is not some empty contemplation, but a prudent and effective knowledge of things adapted to the duties of life and human society. Thus, the "philosophical Magistrate" should be instructed in the knowledge of divine and human things, which is the true and primary philosophy. This he calls **Dialectic**, whose handmaidens are **Physics**, which deals with the generation of things, and the **Mathematical** disciplines, which are intermediaries between physical things and the highest science. He treats all these matters diligently and at length.

After these things, I said, picture our nature, in respect to its education and its ignorance, by such an image as this. Imagine in your mind a subterranean dwelling, like a cave, with a very long entrance open to the light throughout the whole cavern. In this cave, men have been raised from childhood with their necks and legs so bound that they are forced to remain still and look only forward, unable to turn their heads because of the chains. Behind their backs, high up and far off, a fire's flame is burning. Between the fire and the chained men, there is a raised path, alongside which a low wall has been built, like the screens puppeteers use to show their wonders to the spectators. 
"I see it," he said. 
Imagine also men behind the wall carrying various vessels that rise above the wall, and stone and wooden statues of men and other animals, crafted in various ways. As is natural, some of those carrying these things are silent, while others speak. 
"What a strange image you describe, and what strange captives!" 
They are just like us, I said. For first, do you think such people see anything of themselves or of the men next to them, except the shadows cast by the fire onto the opposite wall of the cave? 
"Nothing else," he said, "since they have never been able to move their heads in their whole lives." 
And what about the objects being carried? Do they not see only their shadows? 
"Of course." 
If they were able to talk to one another, don't we believe they would think the things they saw should be called by the names of the real objects? 
"Necessarily." 
And if an echo resonated from the opposite side of the prison, whenever one of the passersby spoke, do you think they would believe anything else was speaking except the passing shadows? 
"By Jupiter, no!" 
In every way, then, such people would judge nothing to be true except the shadows of crafted objects. 
"It is absolutely necessary." 
Conversely, consider what their release from chains and the cure of their ignorance would be like. If one of them were released and suddenly forced to stand up, turn his neck, walk, and look toward the light itself, he would suffer immediate pain and, because of the brightness, would be unable to look at the things whose shadows he saw before. If someone told him that what he saw before were mere trifles, but that now he was closer to true things and, turned toward more real objects, he saw more correctly—and if the person pointed out each of the passing objects and asked him what it was—don't you think he would be at a loss and believe that the things he saw before were truer than the ones being shown to him now? 
"Much truer." 
And if he forced him to look at the light itself, wouldn't his eyes suffer...

<column-break/>

...going toward the principle of the whole, and having grasped it, again clinging to those things that cling to it, he thus descends to the end, making use of nothing sensible at all, but of the Forms themselves, through them, into them, and ending in the Forms. 
I understand, he said, though not sufficiently. For you seem to me to be describing a massive task; yet you wish to define that part of being and the intelligible which is contemplated by the science of dialectic as being clearer than that which is contemplated by the so-called arts, for which hypotheses are principles. Those who contemplate these things are forced to use thought but not the senses. Yet because they do not ascend to a first principle when they investigate, but start from hypotheses, they do not seem to you to possess intellect <note>nous</note> <margin>B</margin> regarding them, although they are intelligible when paired with a first principle. You seem to call the habit of geometricians and the like "thought" <note>dianoia</note> but not "intellect," as if thought were something between opinion and intellect. 
You have understood most sufficiently, I said. And apply these four states occurring in the soul to the four sections: intelligence <note>noesis</note> for the highest; thought <note>dianoia</note> for the second; assign faith <note>pistis</note> to the third, and to the last imagination <note>eikasia</note>. Arrange them proportionately, considering that as they participate in truth, so do they participate in clarity. 
I understand, he said, and I agree, and I arrange them as you say.

# PLATO'S REPUBLIC,
## VII,
## ON JUSTICE,
### THE SEVENTH DIALOGUE.

After these things, I said, compare our nature, in respect to education and the lack of it, to a condition like this. See: men as if in a subterranean cave-like dwelling, having its entrance open to the light and extending long along the whole cave. In this, they have been from childhood in chains, both their legs and necks, so as to remain there and look only toward the front, unable to turn their heads around because of the chain. And light from a fire, burning above and from a distance, is behind them. Between the fire and the prisoners, there is a path above, along which see a low wall built, just as the screens stand before men in the shows of puppet-players, over which they show their wonders. 
"I see," he said. 
See then also men carrying all sorts of vessels along the wall, which reach above the wall, and statues of men and other animals made of stone and wood and all kinds of materials; as is likely, some of the carriers are speaking and some are silent. 
"A strange image," he said, "and strange prisoners." 
Like us, I said. For first, do you think such men have seen anything of themselves and of each other except the shadows cast by the fire onto the part of the cave opposite them? 
"How could they," he said, "if they were forced to keep their heads unmoved throughout life?" 
And what of the things being carried past? Is it not the same? 
"What else?" 
If, then, they were able to converse with one another, do you not think they would believe they were naming the actual things that were present which they saw? 
"Necessarily." 
And what if the prison also had an echo from the opposite side? Whenever one of the passersby spoke, do you think they would believe anything else was speaking than the passing shadow? 
"By Zeus, not I," he said. 
In every way, then, I said, such people would believe nothing else to be the truth than the shadows of the artifacts. 
"Most necessarily," he said. 
Consider then, I said, their release and healing from their chains and their foolishness, what it would be like if such a thing happened to them by nature. Whenever one was released, and forced suddenly to stand up and turn his neck and walk and look up toward the light, and doing all these things he was in pain and, because of the flickering brightness, was unable to see those things whose shadows he saw then—what do you think he would say, if someone told him that then he saw nonsense, but now he was somewhat nearer to being and, turned toward more real things, he saw more correctly? And if, pointing out each of the passing objects, he forced him to answer what it is? Do you not think he would be at a loss, and believe that the things seen then were truer than the things shown now? 
"By far," he said. 
And if he forced him to [look] toward the light itself...

<meta>This page continues the "Allegory of the Cave" from Book VII of Plato's Republic. Having previously described the prisoners chained in an underground cavern seeing only shadows, Socrates now describes what happens when a prisoner is liberated and forced into the light of the sun.</meta>

# ON THE REPUBLIC, BOOK VII.

<margin>A</margin> Don't you think he would be blinded, and turn his eyes away toward the things he was able to see before, believing those shadows to be truly clearer than the things being shown to him now? "Exactly so," he said. And if, I said, someone were to drag him by force up that rough and steep ascent, and not let go until he had been hauled out into the light of the sun, would he not be in pain and feel a great deal of resentment at being so treated? And when he finally came into the light, with his eyes filled with the glare, would he be able to see even one of the things we now call true? "Not at first," he replied.

<margin>B</margin> He would need to grow accustomed to it, I think, if he were to see the things above. First, he would most easily perceive the shadows; after that, the reflections of men and other things in the water; and later, the objects themselves. From there, he would find it easier to gaze upon the heavenly bodies and the sky itself at night—looking at the light of the stars and the moon—rather than looking at the sun and its brilliance by day. "How could it be otherwise?" Finally, I think, he would be able to look upon the sun itself—not just its reflections in the water or in some other alien place, but the sun as it is, in its own domain. "That is inevitable," he said. And after this, he would finally conclude that the sun is the source of the seasons and the years, the guardian of everything in the visible world, and in a certain way, the cause of all those things he and his companions used to see in the cave. "It is clear," he said, "that he would arrive at these conclusions after seeing those things."

<margin>C</margin> What then? When he recalls his first home, the "wisdom" found there, and his former fellow-prisoners, don't you think he would consider himself happy for the change and pity the others? "Very much so." And if there were any honors, praises, or prizes exchanged among the prisoners for the one who could most sharply perceive the passing shadows, or who best remembered which shadows usually came first, which followed, and which appeared together—and who was therefore best able to predict what was coming next—do you think he would desire those honors or envy those who are powerful and respected in the cave? Or would he feel as Homer did, and greatly prefer to be a "serf to another man, a landless laborer," <note>original: "ἐπάρουρον ἐόντα θητευέμεν ἄλλῳ ἀνδρὶ παρ’ ἀκλήρῳ"; a quote from the Odyssey (11.489) where the ghost of Achilles says he would rather be the lowest servant on earth than king of the dead</note>

<margin>D</margin> and endure anything else in the world rather than hold those old opinions and live in that way? "Yes," he said, "I think he would choose to suffer anything rather than live like that." Now consider this: if such a man were to go back down and sit in his old seat, would his eyes not be filled with darkness, coming suddenly out of the sunlight? "Certainly," he said.

<margin>E</margin> And if he had to compete again with those perpetual prisoners in recognizing those shadows—while his vision was still dim and before his eyes had adjusted (and the time required to get used to the dark might be quite long)—would he not be a laughingstock? Would they not say of him that he had gone up only to come back with his eyes ruined, and that it wasn't even worth trying to go up? And as for anyone who tried to free the prisoners and lead them up, if they could only lay their hands on him, wouldn't they kill him? "They certainly would," he said. <note>This is a poignant reference to the trial and execution of Socrates, Plato’s teacher, who was put to death by the citizens of Athens.</note>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> What do you think? Would he not turn his eyes back to those things which he had easily seen before, judging them to be more certain than the things which were then suddenly being presented? "Undoubtedly so." But if someone were to violently pull him up through the rough and difficult places, and not allow him to look at anything until he had been drawn out to the light of the sun, do you not think he would suffer and take it ill while he was being snatched away? And when he was brought out to the light, his eyes being clouded by the brightness, he would be able to see none of those things which are now considered true by men. "Certainly nothing, at least not suddenly."

<margin>B</margin> Habituation, therefore, is the first requirement if he is to inspect the things above. First, he will more easily behold the shadows, then the images of men and other things in the waters. Afterward, however, he will be able to contemplate the things in the heavens, and the heaven itself more easily at night, while looking at the light of the stars and the moon, than if he were to gaze at the sun itself and the glare of the sun by day. "Without a doubt." And so finally he will look up at the sun itself—not as its image appears in the water or in a foreign region, but he will contemplate it as it is in its own place, and be able to know its nature. "It must be so." He will at last realize that it is the sun that regulates the seasons and the years, that rules all things in the visible world, and is, in a certain way, the author of all those things they saw before.

<margin>C</margin> It is certain he would ascend to this by these steps. What if he recalls his former dwelling, the "wisdom" of those people, and his chains? Do you not think he would consider himself blessed by the change of place, and pity them? "Most certainly." Furthermore, if any honors and praises were mutually bestowed, and rewards given to the one who most keenly discerned whatever passed by, and best remembered which of them were prior, which posterior, and which were accustomed to move together, and from these things best predicted the future—do you think he would long for these? Would he think those men blessed who are honored and hold power among them? Or would he choose, as Homer says, to be the servant of some landless man in a foreign field <note>original: "in alieno scilicet rure serui alicuius extorris mancipium effici"</note>

<margin>D</margin> and to endure anything rather than be deceived by those opinions and live in misery? "I believe he would choose anything else rather than a life of that kind." Then consider this also: if he were to descend again and reach the seat he had before, would he not be overwhelmed by darkness, having suddenly departed from the sun? "Vehemently."

<margin>E</margin> But if he had to discern those shadows again, and argue about them with those who are held by perpetual chains—and his opinion had to be offered at that very time when his eyes are hallucinating, before his sight is cleared (which would not happen quickly)—would he not provoke laughter? Would it not be a disgrace for him in the eyes of everyone, that after he went up, he returned with ruined eyes? Would they not say that one should never strive for the heights, and that if the one who tried to loose them and lead them up were caught, he should be killed immediately? "Killed indeed," he said.

<margin>F</margin> This entire image, my friend Glaucon, must be applied to what was said before. The prison is the world seen by the eyes; the light of the fire in the cave is the power of the sun. Finally, if you interpret the ascent to the heights and the sight of them as the soul’s journey to the intelligible realm <note>term: "intelligible region" / "νοητὸν τόπον"; the realm of abstract truths and Forms that can only be understood by the mind, not the senses</note>, you will not wander from my own hope, since you wish to hear my opinion. God knows whether it is true. This, then, is how it appears to me: in the intelligible order, the Form of the Good is the ultimate thing, and is seen only with difficulty. But once it is seen, one must conclude that it is the cause of all things right and beautiful; in the visible world it created light and the master of light <note>the sun</note>, while in the intelligible world it is itself the sovereign, producing truth and reason. This is what anyone who is to act wisely, whether in private or in public, must see. "I also think this," he said, "so far as I am able."

<margin>G</margin> Come then, and consider this as well: do not wonder that those who reach this place are unwilling to handle human affairs, but their minds' eyes are always directed toward the heights. For that is probable, if indeed it follows the image described above. "Quite probable," he said. And what of this? Do you think it a wonder if someone, falling from divine spectacles to these human evils, appears clumsy and is laughed at—especially if, before he is accustomed to the present darkness and while still dim-sighted, he is forced to contend in courts or elsewhere about the shadows of justice, or those statues of which these are shadows, and to argue about the perception and judgments of those who have never seen Justice itself? "Not at all a wonder," he said.

<margin>H</margin> But if someone has a mind, he will remember that the eyes are usually troubled in two ways and for two reasons: both when we descend from light into shadow, and when we go from darkness into light. Recognizing that the soul is affected in the same way whenever he sees it troubled and hindered in seeing something, he will not break out into laughter thoughtlessly. Instead, he will carefully inquire whether it is overwhelmed by new darkness from descending from a brighter life, or whether, rising from great ignorance to a radiant spectacle, it is failing under the excessive flash of brightness. And thus he would judge the state and life of the one to be blessed, and pity the other. Or, if he wished to laugh at that life, his laughter would be less foolish than laughter directed at the one who had fallen from the light above. "That is very reasonably said."

<summary>This page presents the climax of the Allegory of the Cave, describing the painful transition from the cave's shadows to the sun's light, which represents the "Idea of the Good." Socrates explains that the philosopher who has seen the truth will struggle to adjust back to the "shadows" of human politics and law, often appearing foolish to those who have never left the cave.</summary>

-># OF PLATO<-

<margin>A</margin> Therefore, if these things are true, we must conclude that education is not what some people proclaim it to be. They claim that they can put knowledge into a soul that lacks it, as if they were putting sight into blind eyes. They certainly make such a profession. But our present argument indicates that this power is already present in everyone's soul, along with the instrument by which each person learns. Just as an eye cannot be turned from darkness to light unless the whole body turns with it, so too must the entire soul be turned away from the world of becoming <note>original: "ex obscuro" / "ἐκ τοῦ σκοτώδους" - referring to the world of sensory experience</note> until it is able to endure the contemplation of true being and the brightest part of being—which we call the Good. Isn't that so? Yes. <margin>B</margin> For this very purpose, then, education would be a certain skill in directing the soul: a method for turning it around as easily and effectively as possible. Its goal is not to grant the eye the power of sight—for it already possesses that—but rather to ensure that, since the eye is currently turned the wrong way and not looking where it should, it be redirected through every possible means. So it seems. Now, the other qualities referred to as "virtues of the soul" seem to be similar to the virtues of the body; for even if they are not present by nature, they seem to be acquired later through habit and practice. <margin>C</margin> Wisdom, however, is a much more divine virtue than all the others, for it never loses its power. Depending on which way the soul is turned, it becomes either useful and beneficial or, conversely, useless and harmful. Have you not yet noticed how sharply the "little souls" of those who are considered clever but wicked can see? How quickly they discern the things toward which they are turned? Their vision is by no means dim, but it is forced to serve their malice; thus, the more acutely they see, the more evil they perform. Certainly. However, if such a nature were pruned from childhood—if the "lead weights" <note>original: "plumbea pondera" / "μολυβδίδας" - a metaphor for heavy, grounding desires</note> associated with the world of becoming were cut away—those weights which, through gluttony and similar pleasures and lusts, cling to the soul and drag its vision downward—then that same soul, once freed and turned toward the truth, would see those higher things just as sharply as it sees the things it is currently focused on. That is probable. <margin>D</margin> What about this? Is it not both probable and necessary from what has been said that neither the uneducated who are ignorant of the truth, nor those who are permitted to spend their entire lives in study, can adequately govern the state? The former lack a single fixed goal in life at which they must aim in all their private and public actions. The latter will not take up the tasks of a citizen of their own accord, believing that they already inhabit the "Isles of the Blessed" <note>A mythological paradise for the virtuous, used here to describe the ivory tower of pure academic life</note> while still living this life. True, he said. It is therefore our task as founders of the city to compel the best natures to reach that highest knowledge we mentioned—to see the Good and to make that ascent. And once they have ascended and seen enough, we must not permit them what is currently allowed. What is that? <margin>E</margin> Namely, we must not allow them to remain there and refuse to descend again to those prisoners in the cave, nor to share in their labors and honors, whether those honors be trivial or significant. "But," he asked, "shall we do them an injustice and force them to live a worse life when they could enjoy a better one?" You have forgotten again, my friend, that the legislator's concern is not that any one class in the city should be exceptionally happy, but rather the whole city. <margin>F</margin> Indeed, he brings the citizens together through persuasion and necessity, making them share with one another the benefits that each is able to contribute to the common good. The legislator produces such men in the city not to let them turn wherever each one pleases, but to use them as a bond for the state. You speak the truth, he said; I had forgotten that. Consider then, Glaucon, that we will not be doing an injustice to the philosophers who arise among us. Rather, we shall be speaking justly to them when we compel them to care for and guard others. We will say: "Those who become philosophers in other cities are justified in avoiding the labors of the state, because they grow up on their own, regardless of the government in each city. <margin>G</margin> It is only fair that something which grows by itself, owing its nourishment to no one, should not feel obligated to pay anyone back for its upbringing. But we have bred you to be leaders and kings in the hive, both for yourselves and for the rest of the city. You have been educated more perfectly and thoroughly than those others, and you are more capable of participating in both worlds <note>The world of contemplation and the world of political action</note>. You must, therefore, each in turn descend into the habitation of the others and grow accustomed to seeing in the dark. For once you are accustomed to it, you will see ten thousand times better than those who live there; you will recognize what the various shadows are and what they represent, because you have seen the truth of what is beautiful, just, and good. And so, our city will be governed by us and by you as a place of waking reality, not as a dream—unlike most cities today, which are inhabited by people who fight over shadows and contend for power as if it were some great good." <margin>H</margin> But the truth is this: the city in which those who are to rule are least eager to hold office is necessarily the one governed best and most free from civil strife; whereas the city that has the opposite kind of rulers will be the opposite. Quite so, he said. Will our foster-children refuse us when they hear this? Will they be unwilling to take their turn in sharing the labors of the state,

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> We must (I said) think this way about these matters, if these things are true: that education is not as some who profess it claim it to be. For they say that, where knowledge is not present in the soul, they put it in, much like putting sight into blind eyes. For so they say, he replied. But our current argument (I said) signifies that this power exists in everyone's soul, and the instrument by which each person learns—much as if an eye were unable to turn from the dark to the light except with the whole body—so must the whole soul be turned away from that which is coming-into-being until it is able to endure the contemplation of being and the brightest part of being. And this, we say, is the Good. Is it not? Yes. <margin>B</margin> Of this very thing (I said) there would be an art of turning: the manner in which one might be converted as easily and effectively as possible. This is not the art of producing sight in the soul, but rather, since it already possesses sight but is not correctly turned, nor looking where it ought, it is the art of contriving this redirection. So it seems, he said. Now, the other so-called virtues of the soul appear to be close to those of the body; (for not being present before, they are later produced by habits and exercises) but the virtue of wisdom, more than any other, seems to belong to something more divine, which never loses its power, but by being turned becomes either useful and beneficial, or again useless and harmful. Or have you not yet noticed those who are said to be wicked but wise, how sharply their "little soul" <note>original: "ψυχάριον" (psycharion) - a diminutive, mocking term for a clever but petty mind</note> looks, and how keenly it discerns the things to which it is turned? It does not have poor vision, but it is forced to serve vice, so that the more sharply it sees, the more evils it accomplishes. Quite so, he said. <margin>C</margin> If, however (I said), this part of such a nature had been trimmed from childhood—if the attachments to "becoming" had been cut away, like leaden weights, which, through eating and similar pleasures and gluttonies, become attached and turn the soul's vision toward things below; if, being freed from these, it were turned toward the truth, that same soul in those same men would see those things most sharply, just as it sees the things it is now turned toward. <margin>D</margin> That is likely, he said. What then? Is this not likely (I said), and necessary from what has been said, that neither the uneducated and those inexperienced in the truth could ever sufficiently manage a city, nor those who are permitted to spend their lives in study until the end? The former, because they have no single goal in life at which they ought to aim in all they do, both privately and publicly; the latter, because they will not act of their own free will, thinking they are already settled in the Isles of the Blessed while still living. True, he said. It is our task then (I said) as founders to compel the best natures to reach the study which we previously said was the greatest: to see the Good and to make that ascent; and when they have ascended and seen enough, not to permit them what is now permitted. <margin>E</margin> What is that? To remain there (I said), and not be willing to descend again to those prisoners, nor to share in their labors and honors, whether they be meaner or more serious. "Then," he said, "shall we wrong them? And make them live a worse life, when a better one is possible for them?" You have forgotten (I said) again, my friend, that the law is not concerned with this—how any one class in the city shall fare exceptionally well—but it contrives to bring this about in the whole city, harmonizing the citizens by persuasion and necessity, making them share with one another the benefit which each is able to bring to the community; and it produces such men in the city, not to let them turn wherever each wants, but so that it may use them for the binding together of the city. <margin>F</margin> True, he said. I had forgotten. Observe then (I said), O Glaucon, that we will not be wronging the philosophers who arise among us, but we shall say just things to them when we compel them to care for and guard the others. We shall say that those who become such in other cities naturally do not share in the labors of those cities; (for they grow up spontaneously, against the will of the government in each. And it is just that the self-grown, owing no one for its nourishment, should not be eager to pay back the price of its upbringing) <margin>G</margin> but you we have begotten for yourselves and for the rest of the city, like leaders and kings in a hive, having been educated better and more perfectly than those others, and being more capable of sharing in both. You must therefore descend in turn into the habitation of the others, and grow accustomed to seeing the dark things. For when you are accustomed, you will see ten thousand times better than those there, and you will know what each of the images is and what they are images of, because you have seen the truth concerning the beautiful, the just, and the good. And thus the city will be inhabited as a waking reality for us and for you, and not as a dream, as most are now inhabited by those who fight shadows with one another and quarrel over ruling as if it were some great good. But the truth is surely this: in the city where those who are destined to rule are least eager to rule, that city is necessarily inhabited best and with the least faction; but the city that has the opposite kind of rulers, the opposite. Quite so, he said. <margin>H</margin> Will our foster-children then (do you think) disobey us when they hear this, and be unwilling to labor together in the city, each in their turn,

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Glaucon in Book VII of the Republic. Having established that the philosopher who has seen the "Sun" (the Good) must return to the "Cave" to rule, Socrates now begins to identify the specific curriculum—beginning with arithmetic—that will lead the future rulers from the world of shadows to the world of true being.</meta>

-># ON THE REPUBLIC, BOOK VII.<-

<margin>A</margin> ...or is it possible for them to remain together in that pure state? It is impossible, he said. For we shall be imposing just duties upon just men. However, each of them will approach the task of ruling as a necessity—the exact opposite of those who currently hold power in every city.

Indeed, my friend, I said, the matter stands thus: if you can discover a life for those who are to rule that is better than ruling itself, then it is possible for you to have a well-ordered city. For in such a city alone will those who are truly rich hold power—not rich in gold, but rich in the things a happy man must possess: a good and wise life. But if beggars, men hungry for their own private goods, approach public affairs thinking they must snatch their share of "the good" from there, it can never be. For when the right to rule becomes an object of competition, such a domestic and internal war destroys both the rulers themselves and the rest of the city.

<margin>B</margin> Most true, he said.

Do you know of any other life, I asked, that looks down upon political office other than the life of true philosophy? 

No, by Zeus, he replied.

But surely it is necessary that those who are not lovers of ruling should approach it; otherwise, their rivals for that love will fight them.

How could it be otherwise?

Whom else, then, will you compel to undertake the guardianship of the city, if not those who are most prudent concerning the means by which a city is best governed, and who possess other honors and a life superior to that of the politician?

None others, he said.

Would you like us now to consider in what way such men will be produced, and how someone might lead them up into the light—just as some are said to have ascended from the underworld <note>original: "ex inferis" / "ἐξ ᾅδου"</note> to the gods?

How could I not? he replied.

This matter, it seems, is not merely the "flipping of a shell" <note>An ancient Greek game called *ostrakinda* where a shell was flipped to determine which team fled and which pursued. Socrates means education is not a game of chance but a serious transformation.</note>, but a turning of the soul around: from a day that is like night toward the true day of being—an ascent which we shall call true philosophy.

Quite so.

Must we not, therefore, examine which of the subjects of study has such power?

<margin>C</margin> Of course.

What subject then, Glaucon, would be a draw for the soul, pulling it from the world of "becoming" <term>becoming: the physical world of change and decay</term> toward "being" <term>being: the eternal, unchanging world of forms</term>? And I am thinking of this as I speak: did we not say it was necessary for these men to be athletes of war while they were young?

We did say that.

Therefore, this subject we are seeking must have this additional quality as well.

What quality?

That it is not useless to military men.

It must be so, he said, if it is at all possible.

Now, in our earlier discussion, we educated them in gymnastics and music.

That was the case, he said.

<margin>D</margin> Gymnastics, I suppose, is concerned with that which grows and decays, for it presides over the growth and wasting of the body.

So it appears.

Then this would not be the study we are seeking.

No.

But what about music, as far as we described it before?

But that, he said, was the counterpart to gymnastics (if you remember); it educated the guardians through habits, providing a certain harmony of character—not knowledge—and a certain rhythmic grace. Even in the stories they told, whether fables or truer accounts, there were habits akin to these. But as for a subject of study that leads toward the kind of "good" you are now seeking, <margin>E</margin> there was nothing of that sort in it.

You remind me most accurately, I said. For in truth, it contained nothing of the kind. But, my dear Glaucon, what would such a subject be? For the mechanical arts <note>original: "artes mechanicae" / "τέχναι βάναυσοι" - Socrates refers to crafts and physical trades which were often considered "low" or "illiberal" because they did not involve abstract reasoning.</note> all seemed to us to be somewhat vulgar.

How could they not?

Well then, what other study is left, once music, gymnastics, and the mechanical arts are set aside?

Come, I said, if we can find nothing else outside of these, let us take something that applies to them all.

What do you mean?

For instance, that common thing which all arts, thought processes, and sciences use—and which everyone must learn among the very first things.

What is that? he asked.

This trifling matter, I said: the ability to distinguish the one, the two, and the three. I mean, in short, number and calculation. Is it not the case that every art and science is forced to participate in these?

Most certainly, he said.

<margin>F</margin> Is not the art of war included?

It is absolutely necessary, he said.

In the tragedies, Palamedes <note>A Greek hero of the Trojan War credited with inventing various things, including the alphabet and numbers.</note> is always making Agamemnon look like a ridiculous general. Have you not noticed that he claims that, by inventing number, he organized the ranks of the army at Troy and counted the ships and everything else? This implies that before this, they were uncounted, and Agamemnon, it seems, did not even know how many feet he had, since he did not know how to count! What kind of general do you think he was then?

A strange one indeed, he said, if that were true.

Shall we not then conclude, I said, that the ability to calculate and count is a necessary study for a soldier?

More than anything else, he said, if he is to understand anything at all about military formations—or rather, if he is to be a human being.

Do you perceive in this study the same thing that I do?

<margin>G</margin> What is that?

It seems to be one of those things that by its nature leads toward the intellect—the very thing we are seeking. Yet no one seems to use it correctly, though it is entirely capable of drawing the mind toward true essence <note>original: "essentia" / "οὐσία"</note>.

How do you mean? he asked.

I will try, I said, to make my opinion clear to you. Observe how I distinguish in my own mind those things which lead toward the goal we mentioned and those which do not. Look along with me and either agree or disagree, so that we may see more clearly if this is as I suspect.

Show me, he said.

I am showing you then, I said: if you can see that some things perceived by the senses do not summon the intellect to further inquiry, because they are sufficiently judged by the senses themselves; while other things altogether command the intellect to investigate,

<summary>Socrates explains that future rulers must be motivated by a love of philosophy rather than a desire for power. He identifies arithmetic as the first subject of higher education because it is both practically useful for military commanders and intellectually stimulating, drawing the soul away from the physical world toward the realm of abstract truth.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Book VII of Plato’s Republic. Socrates and Glaucon have just agreed that the future rulers of the city must be philosophers who are "compelled" to lead. Socrates now begins to outline the specific education required to turn the soul from the world of "becoming" (sensory experience) toward the world of "being" (eternal truth), starting with the role of perception and the study of arithmetic.</meta>

# THE WORKS OF PLATO

<margin>A</margin>...as if the sense in them judges nothing soundly. <note>original: "quasi sensus in eis nihil syncere dijudicet" / "ὡς τῆς αἰσθήσεως οὐδὲν ὑγιὲς ποιούσης"</note> You are speaking, he said, of things seen from a great distance, or those sketched in a play of shadows. You haven't quite grasped what I meant, I said. What do you mean then? I said: those things do not provoke the intellect which do not result in a contrary sensation at the same time. But those that do result in a contrary sensation, I define as "provocatives," since the sense indicates one thing no more than its opposite, whether it is seen from near or far. What I mean will be clearer to you this way: we say these are three fingers—the pinky, the second, and the middle. <margin>B</margin> Certainly. Imagine me speaking of them as being seen from close up. Now consider this about them: Each of them appears equally to be a finger, and in this respect, it makes no difference whether it is seen in the middle or at the end, whether it is white or black, thick or thin, or anything of that sort. In all such cases, the common soul is not compelled to summon the <term>intelligence</term> <note>Greek: "noēsis," the highest form of rational insight</note> to ask what a finger is. For sight itself never signaled to the soul that a finger was simultaneously the opposite of a finger. Certainly not, he said. It is reasonable then, I said, that such a thing would neither provoke nor wake the mind.

<margin>C</margin> But what about their size and smallness? Does sight see them sufficiently? Does it matter if one lies in the middle or at the end? And likewise with thickness and thinness, or softness and hardness for the sense of touch? Do the other senses not declare such things imperfectly? Or does each of them act in this way: first, the sense assigned to hardness is also forced to deal with softness, and it reports to the soul that it has perceived the same thing to be both hard and soft. Certainly, he said. Is it not then necessary in such things for the soul to be at a loss <note>Socrates uses the term "aporia," a state of productive confusion</note> as to what this sense of "hard" signifies, if it calls the same thing "soft" as well? Likewise with the sense of heavy and light—what are "heavy" and "light" if the sense signifies that the heavy is light and the light is heavy? These interpretations come to the soul as absurdities and require investigation. Therefore, it is reasonable that in these matters, <margin>D</margin> the soul first tries to summon <term>reason</term> <note>Latin: "rationem," Greek: "logismos," referring to calculation or logical grouping</note> and intelligence to consider whether each of the things reported is one or two. How could it be otherwise?

And if they appear as two, does not each appear as one and distinct? Yes. If each is one, and both are two, the soul will understand the two as separate. For if it perceived them as indistinct, it would understand them not as two, but as one. Right. We say sight sees "great" and "small," not as something distinct, but as something confused. Is it not so? Plainly. Because of this lack of clarity, the intelligence is forced to look at the great and small again, not as confused, but as distinct—the opposite of the way sight saw them. You speak the truth. <margin>E</margin> From here, we are first prompted to ask: what then is "the great" and what is "the small"? Exactly. And so we called one the "intelligible" and the other the "visible." Most correctly.

This is what I was trying to say just now: that some things stir the soul toward intelligence, and some do not. I defined as "provocative" those things that strike the senses along with their opposites; those that do not, do not wake the mind. I understand now, he said, and it seems so to me. What then about number and "the one"? In which class do they seem to be? I do not understand. But consider it from what was said before. For if "the one" is sufficiently seen by itself, or grasped by some other sense, it would not lead the mind toward <term>essence</term> <note>Latin: "essentiam," Greek: "ousia," referring to true, unchanging reality</note>, just as we said regarding the finger. But if some contradiction is always seen along with it, so that it appears no more one than its opposite, then it would need a judge, and the soul would be forced to be at a loss and to seek, moving its internal understanding, and asking what "the one" itself is. In this way, the study of "the one" would be among those things that lead the soul and turn it toward the contemplation of that which truly is.

Indeed, he said, the sight of "the one" has this quality. For we see the same thing at once as "one" and as an infinite multitude. If this happens to "the one," the same will happen to every number? Without doubt. And yet, the whole science of <term>calculation and arithmetic</term> <note>Greek: "logistikē te kai arithmētikē"</note> is about number. Very much so. And these seem to lead toward truth. Marvellously so. <margin>G</margin> This discipline, then, would be among those we seek—most necessary for a soldier to know for arranging his ranks, and for a philosopher to emerge from the waves of <term>generation</term> <note>The physical world of birth, death, and change</note> and touch essence, without which discipline they will not be able to calculate or reason. That is so. But our guardian is both a soldier and a philosopher. Indeed. It would be appropriate then, Glaucon, to legislate this and persuade those who are to perform the greatest duties in the city to turn to the science of calculation, and not to touch it lightly, but to pursue it until they reach the contemplation of the nature of numbers with the mind itself—not for the sake of buying and selling like merchants or shopkeepers, but for the sake of war and to easily turn the soul from change toward truth and essence. You speak excellently. And yet, now that this study of calculation has been mentioned, I think to myself how fine it is and how useful it is to us everywhere for what follows... <margin>H</note> In what way? This very thing I just said...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>...as if the sense in them judges nothing soundly. You are speaking, he said, of things seen from a great distance, or those sketched in a play of shadows. You haven't quite grasped what I meant, I said. What do you mean then? I said: those things do not provoke the intellect which do not result in a contrary sensation at the same time. But those that do result in a contrary sensation, I define as "provocatives," since the sense indicates one thing no more than its opposite, whether it is seen from near or far. What I mean will be clearer to you this way: we say these are three fingers—the pinky, the second, and the middle. <margin>B</margin> Certainly. Imagine me speaking of them as being seen from close up. Now consider this about them: Each of them appears equally to be a finger, and in this respect, it makes no difference whether it is seen in the middle or at the end, whether it is white or black, thick or thin, or anything of that sort. In all such cases, the common soul is not compelled to summon the intelligence to ask what a finger is. For sight itself never signaled to the soul that a finger was simultaneously the opposite of a finger. Certainly not, he said. It is reasonable then, I said, that such a thing would neither provoke nor wake the mind.

<margin>C</margin> But what about their size and smallness? Does sight see them sufficiently? Does it matter if one lies in the middle or at the end? And likewise with thickness and thinness, or softness and hardness for the sense of touch? Do the other senses not declare such things imperfectly? Or does each of them act in this way: first, the sense assigned to hardness is also forced to deal with softness, and it reports to the soul that it has perceived the same thing to be both hard and soft. Certainly, he said. Is it not then necessary in such things for the soul to be at a loss as to what this sense of "hard" signifies, if it calls the same thing "soft" as well? Likewise with the sense of heavy and light—what are "heavy" and "light" if the sense signifies that the light is heavy and the heavy is light? These interpretations come to the soul as absurdities and require investigation. Therefore, it is reasonable that in these matters, <margin>D</margin> the soul first tries to summon reason and intelligence to consider whether each of the things reported is one or two. How could it be otherwise?

And if they appear as two, does not each appear as one and distinct? Yes. If each is one, and both are two, the soul will understand the two as separate. For if it perceived them as indistinct, it would understand them not as two, but as one. Right. We say sight sees "great" and "small," not as something distinct, but as something confused. Is it not so? Plainly. Because of this lack of clarity, the intelligence is forced to look at the great and small again, not as confused, but as distinct—the opposite of the way sight saw them. You speak the truth. <margin>E</margin> From here, we are first prompted to ask: what then is "the great" and what is "the small"? Exactly. And so we called one the "intelligible" and the other the "visible." Most correctly.

This is what I was trying to say just now: that some things stir the soul toward intelligence, and some do not. I defined as "provocative" those things that strike the senses along with their opposites; those that do not, do not wake the mind. I understand now, he said, and it seems so to me. What then about number and "the one"? In which class do they seem to be? I do not understand. But consider it from what was said before. For if "the one" is sufficiently seen by itself, or grasped by some other sense, it would not lead the mind toward essence, just as we said regarding the finger. In this way, the study of "the one" would be among those things that lead the soul and turn it toward the contemplation of that which truly is.

Marvellously so. <margin>G</margin> This discipline, then, would be among those we seek—most necessary for a soldier to know for arranging his ranks, and for a philosopher to emerge from the waves of generation and touch essence, without which discipline they will not be able to calculate or reason. <summary>Socrates explains that while simple objects like a finger do not provoke deep thought, contradictory sensations—such as things being both large and small or one and many—force the soul to use reason to understand truth. This paradox makes the study of arithmetic essential for philosopher-kings, as it directs the mind toward the eternal nature of being.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue in Book VII of Plato's Republic. Socrates and Glaucon are discussing the specific mathematical disciplines required to train the "guardians" (the future philosopher-kings) of their ideal city. They have just moved from basic perception to the study of arithmetic.</meta>

### ON THE REPUBLIC, BOOK VII

<margin>Arithmetic compels the soul to use the intellect</margin>
...compels one to reason about numbers. It in no way accepts it if someone, in the course of a discussion, introduces numbers that have visible or tangible bodies. For you surely know that those who are skilled in these matters laugh at and refuse to accept it if anyone attempts to divide "the One" itself in argument. Instead, if you try to break it into small pieces, they multiply it, taking care that the "One" never appears to be not one, but many parts. <note>The Greek mathematicians treated "The One" (unity) as an indivisible principle. If you "divide" 1 into fractions, they see it as "multiplying" the number of units to maintain the integrity of the concept.</note> You speak very truly, he said. What then, Glaucon, if someone were to ask them: "You wonderful men, what sort of numbers are you talking about, in which the 'one' is as you claim it to be—each unit entirely equal to every other, not differing in the slightest, and containing no parts within itself?" What do you think they would answer? I think they would say they are speaking of those things which can only be grasped by the mind, and cannot be handled in any other way. You see then, my friend, I said, that this study really does seem to be necessary for us, since it clearly compels the soul to use the
<margin>The soul toward truth itself</margin>
intelligence to reach truth itself. It certainly does that, he said, and very powerfully. And what about this? Have you noticed that those who are naturally gifted in calculation appear to be sharp in almost all studies? Even those who are slow, if they are educated and exercised in this, even if they gain nothing else from it, still improve by becoming sharper than they were before. That is true, he said. And indeed, I think you would not easily find many studies that require more effort for the learner or practitioner than this one. Certainly not. For all these reasons, then, this study must not be neglected, but the best natures must be educated in it. I agree, he said. Let this then, I said, be our first established point. Second, let us consider the study that follows it, to see if it concerns us. What is that? he asked. Do you mean geometry? That very one, I said.

<margin>On geometry</margin>
Insofar as it pertains to war, he said, it is clearly suitable. For in pitching camp, occupying positions, concentrating or deploying troops, and all the other maneuvers that armies perform in battle or on the march, it makes all the difference whether a commander is a geometrician or not. However, I said, for such purposes, a small portion of geometry and calculation would suffice. We must investigate whether the greater and more advanced part of it tends toward that goal:
<margin>Toward the idea of the good</margin>
making it easier to perceive the <term>Idea of the Good</term> <note>The highest form of knowledge in Plato's philosophy, representing ultimate truth and purpose.</note>. We say that everything tends toward this which compels the soul to turn toward that region where the most blessed part of "Being" exists, which the soul must see by all means. You are right, he said. Therefore, if it compels the soul to contemplate "Being" (the eternal), it is suitable; but if it forces it toward "Becoming" (the changing world), it is not. So we say. Indeed, I said, those who have even a little experience in geometry will not dispute this with us: that this science is entirely the opposite of the language used by its practitioners. How so? he asked. They speak in a very ridiculous and restricted way; for they speak as if they were "doing" something and as if all their words were for the sake of action—using terms like "squaring," "extending," and "adding."
<margin>Geometry</margin>
But in fact, this entire study is pursued for the sake of knowledge. Entirely so, he said. Must we not also agree on this? What? That it is for the sake of knowing that which always is, not that which at some time comes into being and then perishes. That is easily granted, he said; for geometry is knowledge of what eternally exists. It would then, my noble friend, be something that draws the soul toward truth and produces a philosophical mind, directing upward those thoughts which we now improperly cast downward. As much as is possible, he said. As much as is possible, then, I said, we must command that those in your "Most Beautiful City" <note>original: "kallipoli" / "καλλίστῃ πόλει"</note> in no way neglect geometry. For even its secondary benefits are not
<margin>Geometry</margin>
small. What are they? he asked. Those you mentioned concerning war, I said; and indeed, for the better reception of all studies, we know that there is a world of difference between one who has grasped geometry and one who has not. A total difference, indeed, he said. Let us then set this down as the second study for the youth. Let us, he said. What then? Shall we set down astronomy as the third? Or do you disagree? I agree, he said. For being more sensitive to the seasons, months, and years is suitable not only for agriculture and navigation, but no less so for the art of command in war. 
<margin>Astronomy</margin>
You are amusing, I said, for you seem to fear the "many," lest you be thought to be prescribing useless studies. Yet it is no simple thing—indeed, it is difficult—to believe that in these studies an instrument of the soul is purified and rekindled, which had been destroyed and blinded by other pursuits—an instrument more precious to save than ten thousand eyes. For by this alone is truth seen. To those who agree with this, you will seem to speak with incredible wisdom; but those who have never perceived this will naturally think you are saying nothing at all. For they see no other benefit from these studies worth mentioning. Consider now, then, with which group you are debating; or are you debating with neither, but conducting the argument chiefly for your own sake? Though you would not grudge anyone else if they could gain some benefit from it. I prefer, he said, to speak, ask, and answer mostly for my own sake. Well then, I said, we must move back a step. For just now we did not
<margin>Stereometry</margin>
take the correct order following geometry. How so? he asked. After plane surfaces, I said, we took up solids already in motion...

<meta>catchword: than (Latin: quam),</meta>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
...compels one to reason about numbers, it in no way admits it if someone, by arguing, introduces for the sake of numbers bodies that are both seen and felt. For you know how those skilled in these matters, whenever someone strives to divide "the One" itself in words, they immediately resist and do not tolerate this. But if you break it, they multiply it, being careful lest "the One" should ever appear not as one, but as many small parts. You speak the truth. What then do you think, O Glaucon, if someone were to ask them: "O wonderful men, what sort of numbers are you discussing, in which such a 'One' exists as you describe, where each
<margin>B</margin>
unit is equal, and everything is entirely equal to everything else, not differing in the slightest, yet containing no part within itself?" What, I say, do you think they would answer to this? I truly believe they would answer that they are speaking of those numbers which can only be thought of, but can in no way be handled. You see then, O friend, that this skill in this discipline is truly necessary to us: since, as it appears, it leads the mind to this—that it uses intelligence itself for perceiving truth itself. It does so vehemently. But what of this: have you also noticed that
<margin>C</margin>
men who are calculators by nature seem sharp, so to speak, in all doctrines? Moreover, if any who are slower in intellect give themselves to this study, even if they receive no other benefit, they at least achieve this: that they are sharper than they were before. It is so. But indeed, you will not easily find many things, I believe, which are learned with greater difficulty than these. Certainly not. For all these reasons we have brought forward, these things must by no means be neglected, but those who are of the best disposition should be especially instructed in them. I agree indeed. Let this then be settled for us: after this, let us consider what is next, whether it is of use to us. What is that? Do you mean Geometry? This very thing. For insofar
<margin>D</margin>
as it contributes to military affairs, it certainly suits us. For in pitching camp, occupying a region, gathering troops, or even spreading them out, and for every method of organizing an army both in the fight itself and on the march, it is of great importance whether someone is a geometrician or not. For these things, a certain small part of Geometry and Arithmetic suffices. But we must inquire whether a longer study and more fruitful perception contributes to the easy distinguishing of the "Idea of the Good." Indeed, all things contribute to this which turn the mind toward that place where there is the most blessed of essence, which must be fully known by the soul. Rightly so. Therefore, if the study of Geometry compels one to gaze upon essence, it is suitable; but if it forces one toward "becoming," it is not. So we say. Certainly, those who have tasted even a little bit of Geometry will not deny this to us: that this science behaves in a way entirely contrary to how those who
<margin>E</margin>
work in it speak. In what way? Because they speak quite ridiculously and as if they were forced. For like certain laborers, they make their words for the sake of the work, saying "to square," "to extend," and "to add," and other similar things. Yet this whole doctrine is sought for the sake of knowledge. It is entirely so. And must we not also grant this? What? That it is sought for the sake of knowing that which always is, not that which arises at some time and perishes. It must plainly be granted: for Geometry is the knowledge of that which is always. It will, therefore, O noble man, lift the soul toward truth, and so prepare the thought for philosophizing that we turn toward higher things what we now,
<margin>F</margin>
contrary to what is proper, cast down to lower things. As much as is possible. As much as possible, then, it must be commanded that those who inhabit this most excellent city should in no way despise Geometry: for even those things which seem to be somewhat outside its purpose are not small. Of what kind? Those you mentioned concerning the matter of war. We know, moreover, that for all disciplines to be more easily perceived, it makes a total difference whether someone has touched Geometry or not. Entirely. Let us therefore propose this doctrine to be learned in the second place by the youth. Shall we then put Astronomy in the third place? What do you think? It should be put there. For to perceive the opportunities of months and years
<margin>G</margin>
is no less suitable for military affairs than for agriculture and navigation. How pleasing you are to me. For you seem to fear lest many people think you are introducing useless disciplines. But it is no light thing, but rather very difficult to persuade people that from such disciplines a certain instrument of the soul is purged and brought back to life, which before had been infected and blinded by other studies—an instrument that should be preserved more than ten thousand eyes of the body. For by this alone is truth inspected. Therefore, to those who feel the same, you will seem to speak wonderfully well. But those who have never thought of this will rightly think you are saying nothing. For they see no other utility in them worthy of esteem. Here then, you must see with which group you
<margin>H</margin>
prefer to discuss. Or perhaps with neither, but you speak chiefly for your own sake; yet you are not held by any envy if someone else were able to gain something from them by asking and answering. Come then, I say, go back: for just now we did not correctly take up what follows Geometry. Why? Because after the plane, we immediately took up that solid...

<summary>Socrates argues that arithmetic and geometry are essential for the education of the soul because they turn the mind away from the changing world of the senses toward eternal truth and the Idea of the Good. He identifies the "eye of the soul" as the only faculty capable of perceiving ultimate truth, which mathematical study purifies.</summary>
