<meta>This page continues the curriculum for the philosopher-kings. Having discussed arithmetic and plane geometry, Socrates and Glaucon now move toward the study of three-dimensional objects (stereometry) and astronomy. The translation covers both the Latin and Greek columns, which provide the same text.</meta>

-># OF PLATO<-

...which is circulated, we received before we grasped it for itself. <margin>A</margin> It is right, then, to take up the third increase immediately after the second. This third study concerns the increase of cubes and that which partakes of depth. <note>original Latin: "cuborum augmentum"; Greek: "κύβων αὔξην." This refers to Stereometry, or solid geometry, which deals with three-dimensional shapes.</note> "It certainly is," he said. "But these things, O Socrates, do not yet seem to have been discovered." There are two causes for this: first, because no city holds these studies in honor, they are sought after with little energy because they are difficult; and second, those who do search for them need a leader, without whom they would hardly find anything. To find such a leader is difficult; and even if one were found, as things stand now, those who investigate these matters are too arrogant to obey him. But if the whole city were to preside over this work and hold it in honor, these seekers would obey, and these matters, being discussed continuously and with great effort, would become clear. <margin>B</margin> For even now, although the common people despise and restrict these studies, and though the researchers themselves do not understand how they are useful, they still grow in strength through a certain inherent charm. <note>original: "vi gratiæ cuiusdam" / "ὑπὸ χάριτος." Socrates suggests that the beauty of mathematics is so great that the science progresses even without state support.</note> Nor is it a wonder that they appear this way. "Indeed," he said, "that charm is very great. But explain more clearly what you were just saying. The study concerning the plane surface you called Geometry." "I did," I said. "Next," he said, "you first placed Astronomy after Geometry, but a little later you drew back." "In my haste to go through everything quickly," I said, "I am actually moving slower. For the method of the increase in depth came next, but because its investigation is in a ridiculous state, I passed over it <margin>C</margin> and, after Geometry, I immediately touched upon Astronomy, which consists of the motion of depth itself." <note>By "motion of depth," Socrates means the motion of solid bodies—the planets and stars.</note> "You speak rightly," he said. "Therefore, let us place Astronomy in the fourth place, as if the science we just skipped over existed, provided that the city takes it up." "That is fitting," he said. "And as for the praise of Astronomy, Socrates, which you previously rebuked me for as being a vulgar way to extol it, I now follow your lead. For I think it is clear to anyone that this study compels the soul to look toward higher things and leads it from here to there." "Perhaps it is clear to everyone except me," I said. <margin>D</margin> "For it does not seem so to me." "But how then?" he asked. "As those who now join it to philosophy handle it, they seem to me to make the soul look downward." "In what way do you say that?" he asked. "You seem to me," I said, "to define the understanding of 'higher things' quite generously. For you would likely believe that if someone were to look up at a ceiling decorated with various colors and perceive something, he was not looking with his eyes but with his intellect. Perhaps you are right and I am foolish; but I, for my part, cannot think of any other discipline that makes the soul look upward except that which deals with Being and the invisible. <margin>E</margin> But if someone, gaping upward or squinting downward, tries to perceive something through the senses, I deny that he ever learns; for there is no science of such things. I say his soul is not looking up, but down, even if he were floating on his back on land or in the sea while learning." "I have been justly rebuked," he said. "But how then do you say Astronomy should be learned, contrary to how they learn it now, if its knowledge is to be useful for what we are discussing?" "In this way," I said. <margin>F</margin> "We must think of these ornaments in the heavens—since they are set in the visible realm—as being the most beautiful and perfect of their kind, but far inferior to the true ones. I mean the true movements and true speeds, which are carried in true number and in all true figures, both in relation to each other and in moving the things within them. These things are grasped by reason and thought, but not by sight. Or do you think otherwise?" "Not at all," he said. <margin>G</margin> "Therefore," I said, "we must use the ornaments of the heavens as a model for the contemplation of higher things, just as if one were to see diagrams by Daedalus <note>Daedalus was a mythical master craftsman and inventor. Socrates uses his "diagrams" as a metaphor for beautiful but ultimately physical representations of mathematical truth.</note> or some other artist or painter exquisitely composed. For a person skilled in geometry, seeing such things, would think the craftsmanship beautiful, but would think it ridiculous to study them seriously as if to find in them the absolute truth of equals, or doubles, or any other proportion. Why would that not be absurd?" "How could it not be?" he said. "Think then," I said, "that the true astronomer will feel the same when he looks at the movements of the stars. <margin>G</margin> He will think that the heaven itself and the things in it have been crafted by the Creator of the heavens as beautifully as such works can be; but he will think it absurd for anyone to believe that the ratio of night to day, or of these to the month, or of the month to the year, or of the other stars to these and to each other, always remains the same and never changes in any way—since they have a body and are visible—and to seek with all his effort to find the absolute truth in them." "As I listen to you now," he said, "I agree." "Therefore," I said, "we shall use problems, as in Geometry, and so we shall pursue Astronomy; but the things in the heavens <margin>H</margin> we shall leave alone, if we intend to truly partake in Astronomy and make the natural wisdom of our soul useful instead of useless." "You impose a much greater task on the astronomer," he said, "than is currently required." "I think," I said, "that we must also prescribe other things in the same way, if we are to be of any use as lawmakers. But what other suitable discipline can you remember?" "I have none to mention at present," he said. "Yet," I said, "motion does not provide us with just one species, but many, as I think."

<summary>Socrates argues that astronomy should not be studied by simply looking at the stars, but through mathematical problems that lead the soul to understand invisible truths. He also highlights the neglected field of solid geometry (stereometry) as a necessary step between plane geometry and astronomy.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the curriculum for the philosopher-kings in Plato’s Republic. Having discussed solid geometry and astronomy, Socrates now transitions to the final mathematical science: harmonics (music theory). He critiques those who focus only on what they hear, rather than the underlying mathematical principles, before finally introducing "Dialectic"—the ultimate philosophical method of reasoning.</meta>

->### ON THE REPUBLIC, BOOK VII.###<-

<margin>A</margin>Perhaps a wise man could explain all things; but as for what concerns us, what are they? I said: besides that, there is a counterpart to it. What kind? It seems, I said, that as the eyes are fixed upon astronomy, so the ears are fixed upon the motion of harmony; and these sciences are sisters to one another, as the Pythagoreans <note>The Pythagoreans were a school of philosophers who believed that the universe was built on mathematical ratios and that the "music of the spheres" governed the heavens.</note> say, and we, O Glaucon, agree—or how shall we do it? Just so, he said. Therefore, I said, since the work is great, we shall ask them how they speak of these things, and if there is anything else besides them; but through all this, we shall guard our own principle. Which one? <margin>B</margin>That those whom we nourish <note>Socrates refers to the "alumni" or students being trained to lead the city.</note> should never attempt to learn anything imperfect, or anything that does not reach that goal where all things ought to arrive, as we were just saying about astronomy. Or do you not know that they do something similar regarding harmony? For while they measure and compare the chords and tones heard by the ears, they labor in vain, just like the astronomers. By the gods, he said, and quite ridiculously too! They speak of certain "densities" <note>original Greek: "πυκνώματ’" (pyknomata). In ancient music theory, these were small intervals or "condensations" of notes.</note> and press their ears close as if trying to catch a voice from a neighbor's house. Some say they can still hear a small sound in between, which is the smallest interval by which they must measure; others disagree, saying the notes now sound the same—both groups putting their ears before their minds. You, I said, are speaking of those fine musicians who cause trouble for the strings and torture them, twisting them upon the pegs. But so the metaphor does not become too long—concerning the blows of the plectrum <note>A plectrum is a small tool, like a modern guitar pick, used to pluck strings.</note> and the accusations and denials of the strings—I will end the image here. I am not speaking of these men, but of those whom we said we would ask about harmony. For they do the same as those in astronomy: they seek the numbers within these audible harmonies, but they do not rise to the level of problems, to investigate which numbers are harmonious and which are not, and for what reason. You speak of a divine matter, he said. It is useful, indeed, I said, for the <margin>C</margin>search for the Beautiful and the Good; but if pursued otherwise, it is useless. That is likely, he said. And I think, I said, that the method of all these studies we have gone through, if it reaches their mutual communication and kinship, and considers how they are related to one another, contributes something to what we desire, and our labor is not without profit; otherwise, it is in vain. I also divine it so, he said; but you speak of a very great work, O Socrates. Of the prelude, I said, or of what? Do we not know that all these things are but the preludes to the law <note>The Greek word "nomos" means both "law" and "musical melody," a pun Socrates uses to bridge music and philosophy.</note> itself which must be learned? For surely those skilled in these matters do not seem to be "dialecticians" to you. No, by Zeus, he said; except for a very few whom I have met. But then, I said, if they are <margin>D</margin>unable to give and receive a reason, will they ever know anything of what we say must be known? Not at all, he said. Is this not then, O Glaucon, I said, the law itself which the power of dialectic performs? Which, being intelligible, the power of sight would imitate—that power which we said attempts to look at animals themselves, and at the stars, and finally at the sun itself. So too, when one attempts to use dialectic, without any of the senses, but through reason alone, to rush toward that which each thing is; and if he does not stop until he grasps what the Good itself is through the intellect, <margin>E</margin>then he arrives at the very end of the intelligible, just as the other man then reached the end of the visible. Entirely so, he said. What then? Do you not call this journey "dialectic"? <note>Dialectic is the process of dialogue and logical analysis used to reach ultimate truths.</note> Indeed, I do. But, I said, this release from bonds, and the turning away from shadows toward the images and the light, and the ascent from the underground cave to the sun; and there, <margin>F</margin>while still being unable to look at animals and plants and the light of the sun, looking instead at the divine reflections in the water and the shadows of real things—not the shadows of images cast by another such light as if it were the sun—all this study of the arts we have gone through has this power: it leads the best part of the soul up to the contemplation of the best among existing things, just as then the clearest part of the body was led to the brightest thing in the physical and visible region. <margin>G</margin>I accept it so, he said. Although it seems very difficult to accept in one way, it is also difficult not to accept in another. Nevertheless—for these things are not only to be heard now, but must be returned to many times—assuming these things are as we have said, let us proceed to the law itself, and go through it as we went through the prelude. Tell me then, what is the manner of the power of dialectic, and into what types is it divided, and what are its paths? For these, it seems, would be the ones leading to that place where, for the one who arrives, there would be a rest from the journey and an end to the path. You will no longer, I said, O dear Glaucon, be able to follow; for on my part, there would be no lack of eagerness. You would no longer see an image of what we are speaking of, but the truth itself—at least as it appears to me. Whether it is truly so or not, it is no longer right to insist; but that it is something like this, must be insisted. Is it not so? Indeed. Therefore, the power of dialectic alone for us in these things... <margin>H</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>Everyone who is wise will indeed be able to bring these things forth. But those which occur to me are two. Of what kind? One indeed is very similar and equivalent to Astronomy. Of what kind, I say? Just as the eyes were made for Astronomy, so the ears seem to have been fashioned for harmonic motion. Whence also the Pythagoreans think these are sister sciences, and we, O Glaucon, agree. Or what shall we do, I said? Just so, he said. Since this is a grand work, shall we not ask them how they speak of these things, and whether there is anything else besides them? But through all these, shall we <margin>B</margin>not preserve our own purpose? What is that? That our students should never at any time give effort to learning anything less than perfect from these studies, which does not tend toward that place where all things ought to proceed, as we recently narrated concerning Astronomy. Are you ignorant that they do something similar regarding harmony? For while they measure and compare the concords and tones perceived by the ears, they waste their time in useless labor, just like the astronomers. By the gods, those men are quite ridiculous! They repeat and double their sounds more frequently, and bring their ears closer, as if to hunt the voice itself from a nearby place. And some of them say they hear some sound still in the middle, and that this is the smallest interval by which one ought to measure; but others disagree, as if a similar sound is already heard. And both prefer their ears to their minds. But you, I said, do you call those common musicians who both twist and vex the strings, and violently stretch them upon the tuning pegs (both by tightening and loosening)? But lest the comparison be carried too far into the striking done with the plectrum, and that boastful and stubborn accusing of the strings, I will put an end to this image: and I say that not these, but those others rather, should be asked to speak about harmony. For they do the same as those who are engaged in Astronomy. Namely, they pursue those numbers which are in the harmonies pertaining to the ears. But they do not pass from there to investigating which numbers are consonant, which are not, and for what reason both are so. You narrate an excellent thing. Add also that it is useful for the investigation of the good and the beautiful itself, which, if sought otherwise, would be altogether useless. That is indeed probable. I think, moreover, that the treatment of all the aforementioned things, if it touches upon <margin>C</margin>their mutual communion and kinship, and investigates by what reason they cohere with one another, will lead toward those things which we seek, and men will engage in these things not in vain, but quite usefully; but uselessly, if it is done otherwise. And I also prophesy thus, but what you command is a great thing, O Socrates. What, he said, do you say, or something else? Are we <margin>D</margin>ignorant that all these things are the beginning of the law itself, which it is fitting to learn? For those who are skilled in these things do not yet seem to you to be able to discourse upon them. Not by Jove, except for a certain very few of all those whom I have ever known. But indeed, unless one, I said, can both receive and give a reason, he will never know anything of those things which we say must be known. Never at all. Is this not <margin>E</margin>now the law, O Glaucon, I said, which is shown through the art of discourse, when again, since it is intelligible, that power imitates the sight, which we said above now turns itself toward the animals themselves, and toward the stars, and finally toward the sun itself? Not otherwise, when one betakes himself to discoursing without any senses, by reason alone he strives toward that which anything is: who, if he does not <margin>F</margin>stop until he has perceived by intelligence itself that which is good, only then arrives at the end of the intelligible itself, just as that other man ascended to the end of the visible. It altogether happens thus. Do you not call this progression "dialectic"? What prevents it? And yet, just as that release from chains, and the turning from shadows to the images and the light, and the exit from the cave to the light of the sun, and there the inspection of animals and plants, and the looking at the sun and stars in water because of the weakness of the eyes, turns that which is clearest in bodies <margin>G</margin>toward that which is most radiant in the corporeal and visible region of all things. So the study of all the aforementioned arts leads the soul through the shadows, not of images, but rather of those things which truly are; and it makes the soul judge them, and leads the soul to another thing, to the sun, and has a certain power of exalting that which is most excellent in the soul to the contemplation of that which is best in the order of things. I indeed accept it thus: although such things seem to me to be such that they can neither easily be admitted nor easily rejected. Nevertheless, since they must be heard not only for the present, but repeatedly thereafter, these things having been so placed as they are now delivered, let us come to the law itself, and let us run through it just as we have already completed the prelude. Therefore, tell me, I pray, what is the mode of the power of discourse, and <margin>H</margin>into what species it is distributed, and what are the paths. For these are, it seems, what lead thither where whoever has arrived will at last rest as if at the end of a journey. Not yet, O friend Glaucon, will you be able to follow. Truly, as far as is in me, no zeal will be lacking to you, by which you may become possessed of your wish. Nor will you see any longer the image of that which we are dealing with, but the true thing itself as it appears to me. But whether it is really such or not, it is by no means fitting to affirm. But that at least must be asserted, that such a thing is to be known. Is it not so? Nothing prevents it. Furthermore, also this: that only the faculty of discourse to a man in those things which we have said...

He uses the allegory of the cave to describe how Dialectic leads the soul from the shadows of sensory perception to the ultimate truth of the "Good."</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the education of the philosopher-kings from Book VII of Plato’s Republic. Having dismissed the lower mathematical arts as mere preliminaries, Socrates now defines "Dialectic"—the highest form of reasoning—and begins to describe the character traits required of those chosen for this rigorous training.</meta>

## OF PLATO ##

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...show this to one who is learned. Otherwise, it is truly impossible to know it thoroughly. This also must be asserted: no one will oppose us when we say that the faculty of discourse <note>Latin: *differendi facultas*; Greek: *dialektikē*. This refers to Dialectic, the art of logical discussion and the highest branch of philosophy.</note> alone attempts, by a certain order, to find out what each thing is in itself. Indeed, all other arts look either toward human opinions and desires, or toward the generation and composition of things, or toward the cultivation of those things which are generated and composed. As for the rest, which we said participated in some way in true reality—namely Geometry and its companions—they merely dream about being; it is impossible for them to see anything clearly so long as they use suppositions <note>Latin: *suppositionibus*; Greek: *hypothesibus*. These are "hypotheses" or unproven starting points.</note> <margin>B</margin> and keep them so fixed and immovable that they cannot give an account of them. For where the principle is something unknown, and the end and the middle are drawn from that unknown thing, by what means can we call such a connected assertion "science"? By none. 

Only Dialectic, truly, proceeds by doing away with all suppositions, moving toward the first principle itself so that it may be firmly grasped. It slowly draws and leads upward the eye of the soul, which was buried in a barbaric mud <note>original: "coeno barbarico". A famous Platonic metaphor for the ignorance and sensory confusion of the uneducated mind.</note>, using those arts we have described as assistants and servants. We have often called these "sciences" out of habit, but they require another name, clearer than "opinion" but more obscure than "science." <margin>C</margin> In our previous discussions, we called this "thought" <term>Dianoia: the type of reasoning used in mathematics, which sits between mere belief and pure intellectual understanding</term>. However, there is no controversy over the name among those who investigate such great things as we are currently discussing. Not at all; for they only require the expression of internal concepts regarding the state of things. 

It is pleasing, then, as before, to call the first part **science**, the second **thought**, the third **faith**, and the last **imagination** or **assimilation**. And both of the first together we call **intelligence**, while both of the latter together we call **opinion**. Opinion is concerned with generation <note>The physical world of change and "becoming."</note>, while intelligence is concerned with essence <note>The eternal world of "being."</note>. As essence is to generation, so is intelligence to opinion. And as intelligence is to opinion, so is science to faith, and <margin>D</margin> thought to imagination. 

But let us omit, O Glaucon, the comparison of the things these deal with, and the twofold division of each—namely the "opinable" and the "intelligible"—lest this discourse become more prolix than those that came before. 

Indeed, as far as my mind is able, I wish to follow the rest. 

Do you not call a "dialectician" one who grasps the reason for the essence of each thing? And would you not say that he who has no such reason, insofar as he can give no account to himself or to another, lacks intelligence regarding that thing? 

Certainly, one must say so. 

The same must be judged concerning **the Good**. For whoever cannot define the Idea of the Good by reason, distinguishing it from all other things—passing through all tests as if in a battle, refuting things not according to opinion but according to substance, and proceeding through all these with stable and unshakable reason—you would say that such a man knows neither the Good itself nor any other good thing. Rather, if he happens to touch upon some phantom <note>original: "simulacrum". A mere shadow or imitation of the truth.</note> of it, he touches it by opinion rather than science; <margin>E</margin> he slumbers through this life in dreams, and before he can wake up, he descends to the underworld to be occupied finally by total sleep. 

By Jove, I shall assert all these things exactly so! 

However, as for your own children, whom you are now nourishing and instructing in words: if you were ever to educate them in reality, I do not think you would permit them to hold power over the greatest things in the city while they were as devoid of reason as mere lines. 

Certainly not. 

You will therefore make a law <margin>F</margin> that they should especially apply themselves to that discipline by which they will be most fit to ask and answer questions in a scientific manner. 

I shall prescribe that together with you. 

Does it then seem to you that Dialectic is placed above all other teachings like an apex <note>original: "thrigkos". This refers to the "copestone" or finishing stone at the very top of a wall, signifying completion.</note>, and that no other teaching can be found higher or more eminent, but that this is now the end of all learning? 

It seems so to me. 

It remains, then, to disclose to whom these disciplines should be distributed, and in what manner. 

Evidently. 

Do you remember in our first selection of leaders, what kind of people we chose? 

How could I not? 

Think, then, that those same natures ought to be chosen for these other things. For the most steadfast and the bravest men should be selected, and as far as possible, the most handsome. Not only must we seek men who are noble and formidable in character, but those who additionally possess the natural gifts that this discipline requires. 

Which ones? 

Sharpness, I say; a facility of intellect must be present for the perception of these teachings. For the soul is more easily deterred by the difficulty of <margin>G</margin> learning than by physical exercise, since labor is more the soul's own when it is done alone, rather than shared with the body. 

You speak the truth. 

We must also seek a man with a strong memory, who is most upright and most enduring. For how else do you think anyone would willingly undergo the labors of the body and also complete such an arduous study of meditation? 

No one could, unless he were endowed with the best nature. It is from that error, as I said before, that infamy has arisen against philosophy—because men do not approach her according to her dignity. For she should be handled not by bastards, but by legitimate sons. 

In what way? 

First, a man must not be "lame" in his love of labor...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...only the power [of dialectic] will reveal this to one who is experienced, but it is not possible in any other way. And then he said, it is worthy to be defined. 

What then? I said. No one will dispute with us when we say that this method alone attempts to grasp what each thing is in itself. But all other arts are either directed toward the opinions and desires of men, or toward generations and compositions, or toward the care of things that grow and are composed. As for the rest, which we said catch hold of something of reality—geometry and those following it—we see that they dream about being, but it is impossible for them to see it in a waking state as long as they use hypotheses <margin>B</margin> and leave them unmoved, being unable to give an account of them. For where the beginning is what one does not know, and the end and the middle are woven together from what one does not know, what mechanism can ever turn such an agreement into science? 

None, he said. 

Therefore, I said, the dialectic method alone proceeds in this way, doing away with hypotheses, toward the principle itself, in order to be certain. And it gently draws and leads upward the eye of the soul, which is buried in a certain "barbaric mud," using as assistants and companions the arts we have gone through. These we have often called "sciences" because of custom, but they need another name, clearer than opinion but more dim than science. We defined it as "thought" somewhere earlier. But it is not, as it seems to me, a dispute over a name for those who have a search before them for such great things as we have. 

No, indeed, he said. 

It is pleasing then, I said, as before, to call the first part **science**, the second **thought**, the third **faith**, and the fourth **imagination**. And both of these together, **opinion**, and both of those together, **intellection**. Opinion is about generation, and intellection is about essence; and as essence is to generation, so is intellection to opinion, science to faith, and thought to imagination. But let us leave aside the analogy of the things these are over, and the twofold division of each—the opinable and the intelligible—O Glaucon, lest it fill us with many more words than those we have already gone through. 

But for my part, he said, I agree with the other things as far as I am able. 

Do you then call a "dialectician" one who grasps the reason for the essence of each thing? And as for him <margin>D</margin> who does not have it, insofar as he cannot give a reason to himself and to another, will you not say he lacks intelligence regarding it? 

How could I not say so? 

Then it is the same concerning the Good: whoever cannot define the Idea of the Good by reason, separating it from all other things, and as if in a battle passing through all tests, eager to refute not according to opinion but according to essence, and who goes through all these with an unshakable reason—will you not say that such a one knows neither the Good itself, nor any other good? But if he happens to lay hold of some image of it, he lays hold of it by opinion, not by science; and he dreams and slumbers through his present life, and before <margin>E</margin> waking up here, he arrives first in Hades to fall completely asleep. 

By Zeus! he said, I will certainly say all these things. 

But as for your own children, whom you are nourishing and educating in speech: if you were ever to nourish them in deed, you would not (I think) allow them to be rulers in the city, being the masters of the greatest things, while they are as irrational as "lines." <note>A mathematical pun: "irrational lines" were a known concept in Greek geometry, here used to describe people who cannot give a rational account (logos).</note> 

No indeed, he said. 

Will you then legislate for them to lay hold of this education most of all, from which they will be able to ask and answer in the most scientific way? 

I will legislate it, he said, along with you. 

Does it then seem to you, I said, that dialectic lies above our studies like a copestone, and that no other study could rightly be placed above it, but that it is the end of all studies? 

It seems so to me, he said. 

The distribution, therefore, I said, remains <margin>F</margin> for you: to whom we shall give these studies, and in what manner. 

Clearly, he said. 

Do you remember the former selection of rulers, what kind we chose? 

How could I not? 

For the rest, then, I said, consider that those natures must be chosen. For the most steady and the most courageous must be preferred, and as far as possible, the most well-formed. In addition to these, we must seek those who are not only noble and grave in their characters, but who also possess the qualities of nature that fit this education. 

What kind are they? 

Sharpness, O blessed one, I said, must be present in them for their studies, and they must not learn with difficulty. For souls are far more likely to lose heart in difficult studies than in gymnastic exercises; for the labor is more <margin>G</margin> their own, being private to the soul and not shared with the body. 

True, he said. 

And we must seek one who is mindful, unstinting, and in every way a lover of labor. Or in what way do you think someone would be willing to work through the labors of the body and also complete such great learning and practice? 

No one would, he said, unless he were altogether well-gifted by nature. 

At least the current error, I said, and the dishonor that has fallen upon philosophy, happened because of these things (as we said before): that people do not lay hold of her according to her merit. For it should not be bastards who lay hold of her, but the legitimate. 

How? he said. 

First, I said, in the love of labor, the one who is not a lover of philosophy must not be "lame"—that is, being only half-loving of labor...

<summary>This page defines Dialectic as the supreme science that moves beyond mathematical hypotheses to grasp the first principle of reality. It outlines the four levels of the human mind (Knowledge, Thought, Faith, and Imagination) and lists the rigorous intellectual and moral qualities required of future philosopher-kings.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the ideal education for philosopher-kings. Having previously defined Dialectic, Socrates now focuses on the character requirements for students and the timeline for their training, moving from childhood play to the rigors of military service and eventually to the highest forms of abstract reasoning.</meta>

## BOOK VII OF THE REPUBLIC ##

<column-break/>

...half of his nature, he is lazy. This occurs whenever someone is a lover of gymnastics and hunting, and exerts himself in all physical labors, but is not a lover of learning, nor a listener, nor an inquirer; instead, he hates all such effort. And he is likewise "lame" who has shifted his diligence in the opposite direction. "You speak most truly," he said. Therefore, in terms of truth (I said), shall we not likewise consider that soul to be mutilated <note>Latin: *mancum*; Greek: *anapēron*. Refers to a soul that is functionally disabled because it lacks a part of virtue.</note> which hates the intentional lie, and takes it hard in itself and is infuriated when others lie, but easily tolerates the unintentional lie? And if it is caught being ignorant somewhere, it is not angry, but contentedly wallows in its ignorance like a pig in the mud? "Absolutely," he said. And regarding temperance (I said), and courage, and magnificence, and all parts of virtue, one must no less observe who is legitimate and who is a bastard. For when someone—whether an individual or a city—does not know how to examine such things, they unknowingly employ the "lame" and the "bastard" for whatever purpose happens to be at hand; individuals use them as friends, and the Republic uses them as its leaders. "It happens exactly so," he said. We must take precaution in all these matters. For if we bring those who are sound in body and mind to such great learning and such great exercise and educate them, then Justice herself will not find fault with us, and we shall preserve the city and the Republic. But if we bring those of a different disposition to these things, we shall do the opposite in all things, and we shall pour even more ridicule upon philosophy. "That would indeed be shameful," he said. "It certainly would," I said. "But I seem to have been affected by something ridiculous in the present moment." "What is that?" he asked. "I forgot (I said) that we were playing, and so I spoke with more intensity than was proper. For while speaking, I looked toward Philosophy herself, and seeing her unworthily and shamefully insulted, I seem to have been moved to anger; and as if indignant at those responsible, I spoke more seriously than I intended." <margin>D</margin> "By Jove, no," he said, "at least not to me as a listener." "But to me as the speaker, it seemed so," I said. "But let us not forget this: that in our earlier selection, we chose old men; but in this selection, that will not be permitted. We must not believe Solon <note>Solon was a famous Athenian lawmaker and poet who famously said, "I grow old ever learning many things." Socrates disagrees, arguing that intense mental labor is for the young.</note> when he says that an old man can learn many things; he can do so no more than he can run. For all great and frequent labors belong to the young." "Necessarily," he said. "Therefore, matters of arithmetic, and geometry, and all that preliminary education which must precede dialectic, should be set before them while they are still children, yet the manner of teaching should be such that they do not seem forced to learn." <margin>E</margin> "Why is that?" "Because (I said) a free man should not learn any discipline with the spirit of a slave. For physical labors, undertaken by force, do not make the body any worse; but no forced discipline in the soul is lasting." "You speak the truth," he said. "Therefore, do not nourish the children in their disciplines by force, O best of men, but as if they were playing, so that you may better be able to perceive what each one is naturally suited for." "What you say (he said) is reasonable." <margin>F</margin> "Do you not remember (I said) that we said the children should even be led to war on horses as spectators, and if it could be done safely, they should be brought close and given a taste of blood, like young hounds?" "I remember," he said. "And in all these things (I said)—in labors, studies, and dangers—whoever appears most ready and sharp must be selected for a certain list." "At what age?" he asked. "When they are released from the necessary gymnastics. For in that time, whether it be two or three years, they can do nothing else. For exhaustion and sleep are enemies to learning. And at the same time, this test is not the least important: how each person appears in their gymnastics." "Certainly," he said. <margin>G</margin> "After this time (I said), those who are chosen from the age of twenty shall receive greater honors than the others; and the disciplines which were shown to them in a scattered way during childhood must be brought together into a 'synoptic' view <note>original: "synopsin". This is a "global" or unified view where the student sees how all sciences relate to one another and to reality.</note> of the kinship of the disciplines with one another and with the nature of that which truly exists." "Only this kind of knowledge (he said) remains stable in those who receive it." "And it is also the greatest test (I said) of a dialectical nature. For he who sees the whole is a dialectician; he who does not, is not." "I agree," he said. "Therefore (I said), you will need to watch for those who are most like this, who are steadfast in their studies, steadfast in war, and in other legal duties; and when they have passed their thirtieth year, you must select them from the chosen ones <margin>H</margin> and appoint them to even greater honors. You must examine them by the power of dialectic to see who is able, letting go of the eyes and the other senses, to move toward that which truly exists, along with the truth. And here, my friend, is a task requiring great caution." "Why especially?" he asked. "Do you not notice (I said) how great an evil currently surrounds dialectic?" "What kind of evil?" he said. "It is surely filled with lawlessness <note>Greek: *paranomias*. Socrates warns that young people who learn to argue before they have character may use their skills to destroy traditional morality without finding true justice.</note>," I said. "Very much so," he said. "Do you think it is anything surprising that they suffer this, and do you not sympathize?" "In what way especially?" he asked. "It is as if (I said) a supposititious child <note>original: "supposititius". A child secretly substituted for another at birth; a foster child who doesn't know their true parents.</note> were brought up in great wealth and a large, noble family, surrounded by many flatterers; but upon becoming a man, he perceived that he was not the son of those who called themselves his parents, yet he could not find those who actually sired him. Can you guess how he would be disposed toward the flatterers and toward those who substituted him, during the time...

<summary>Socrates outlines the physical and mental traits of the ideal student, emphasizing that education should be non-compulsory "play" for children and that only those who show a unified "synoptic" understanding of the sciences should progress to Dialectic after age thirty.</summary>
<keywords>Plato, Republic, education of children, dialectic, gymnastics, Solon, synoptic view, philosopher-kings, non-compulsory learning, nature vs nurture</keywords>

--- Page 522 ---
<meta>This page continues the curriculum for the philosopher-kings of the Republic. Having discussed the "lame" or "mutilated" soul on the previous page, Socrates now introduces a cautionary analogy regarding the study of Dialectic. He warns that if young people are introduced to philosophical questioning before they are mature, they may lose their moral compass, much like a child who discovers they are adopted and loses respect for their foster parents.</meta>

# PLATO’S REPUBLIC #

<margin>A</margin> ...both at that time when he suspected nothing of the substitution <note original: "suppositione/hypobolēs">A reference to an analogy of a child who discovers they were "substituted" or adopted, and thus loses respect for their foster parents.</note>, as well as after he recognized the reality of the matter? Or do you wish to hear my prophecy? "I certainly do," he said. I prophesy, therefore, that while he is entirely ignorant of the substitution, he will honor those he considers his parents and relatives more than he honors flatterers. He will be less likely to neglect them if they are in need, less likely to do or say anything unlawful against them, and in serious matters, he will obey them more than he obeys the sycophants. "That is quite likely," he said. But if he should perceive the truth, he will surely honor and care for these parents less, and will cultivate the flatterers more than before. He will obey them more closely, model his life after theirs, and converse with them openly and freely. But for those he once thought were his parents and kin, he will have no <margin>B</margin> concern at all, unless he happens to be of an exceptionally noble nature. "Everything would happen exactly as you say," he replied. But how does this comparison apply to those who pursue philosophical disputations? "Listen now," I said. We have held certain opinions since childhood about noble and just duties, under which we were educated as if by parents; we obey these, and we honor them above all others. "Quite so." There are also pleasures that present themselves to us, which entice us toward their opposites; they flatter the soul and try to pull us toward them. Yet those who are even slightly more moderate than the rest are not swayed by these, but instead honor those ancestral traditions and obey them. "That is how it happens." Now, if the power of Dialectic <note>The art of logical investigation and questioning used to find the truth.</note> should approach someone so disposed and ask them what is "noble," <margin>C</margin> and when they respond with what they learned from the lawmaker, the argument refutes them—and through frequent and varied rebuttals leads them to believe that this thing is no more noble than it is shameful—and if the argument does the same regarding the "just" and the "good," and the other things they previously held in highest honor, how do you think they will treat that honor and obedience thereafter? "Necessarily," he said, "they will no longer honor or obey them in the same way." Therefore, when someone no longer considers these domestic traditions to be honorable or familiar as before, and yet does not find the true ones, to what other life will he likely turn than to one of flattery and pleasure? <margin>D</margin> "That is likely indeed." Thus, from being a just man, he will become lawless. "It is inevitable." Is it not reasonable then, as I was just saying, that the condition of those who prepare themselves for such disputation deserves great indulgence? "And mercy as well," he said. Therefore, to avoid this pitiable outcome, only those who have reached thirty years of age should cautiously taste these dialectical arguments. "Exactly so." Is it not a prudent caution to ensure that younger men do not touch them? For it is not hidden from us, I think, that when youths first taste the art of disputation, they immediately use it as a kind of game for refutation. <margin>E</margin> Zealously imitating those who refute others, they themselves redargue <note>A formal word for "refute" or "disprove."</note> everyone else, and they take delight, in the manner of puppies, in perpetually pulling and tearing at those near them with their arguments. "Wonderfully so," he said. But when they have refuted many, and have been refuted by many themselves, they quickly fall into a state where they hold none of their former opinions to be certain. And because of this, both they and the whole of philosophy are brought into ill repute among others. "You speak very truly," he said. But an older man will more carefully decline such madness, and will instead imitate one who engages in discussion for the sake of investigating the truth, rather than one who devotes himself to cleverness and "catch-questions" for the sake of a game. Furthermore, he will behave more modestly, and will turn the pursuit of disputation from something infamous into something illustrious. All our previous statements were made with this very caution in mind: namely, that those admitted to the study of disputation must be moderate and serious, and that it should not be shared with unfit men, as is currently done <margin>F</margin> with anyone whom chance presents. "By all means." If one gives himself diligently and assiduously to disputation, doing nothing else except perhaps exercising the body in the gymnasiums, five years should be sufficient for the soul to perceive these things. "Do you say six? Or four?" Make it five. Then they must be led down into that Cave <note>A reference back to the "Allegory of the Cave," where prisoners see only shadows. Here, it refers to practical public life and military service.</note> again, and forced to take up those commands that pertain to war and whatever other offices belong to the young, so that they do not fall behind others in practical experience. And in these tasks, they must also be tested to see if they remain constant while being pulled in every direction, or if they waver. "How many years <margin>G</margin> do you assign to this?" Fifteen. But when they reach their fiftieth year, those who have remained sound and have excelled in all deeds and sciences are finally to be led to the goal. They must be compelled to turn the "eye of the soul" <note original: "animi radium">Literally "the ray of the soul."</note> upward to look upon that which provides light to all; and when they have known the Good itself, they shall use it as a pattern to bring order to the city, to private citizens, and to themselves for the rest of their lives, each in their turn. They shall spend most of their time in philosophy, but when their turn comes, they shall keep watch over civil affairs and govern for the sake of the Republic, performing this service not as something noble or desirable, but <margin>H</margin> rather as a necessity. And thus, when they have similarly instructed others, they will leave behind such men as guardians of the Republic in their place, and they themselves will depart to dwell in the Isles of the Blessed. Public monuments and sacrifices shall be dedicated to them as if to semi-divine spirits <note original: "daemonibus">In the ancient sense: benevolent guardian spirits or intermediaries between gods and men.</note> if the Pythian oracle confirms it; if not, at least as to blessed and divine men. "Socrates," he said, "like a sculptor, you have shaped our rulers to be entirely magnificent." And what I have said of men, the same...

<column-break/>

...in that time in which he did not know about the substitution, and when he already knew? Or do you wish to hear me prophesying? "I wish it," he said. I prophesy then (I said) that he would honor his father and mother and his other apparent relatives more than the flatterers; and he would be less likely to see them in need, less likely to act or speak lawlessly against them, and less likely to disobey them in great matters than the flatterers, during the time he did not know the truth. "Likely," he said. But upon perceiving the reality, I suspect he would then slacken in his honor and devotion toward them, and would instead attach himself to the flatterers and obey them more than before. He would live according to their way, associating with them openly; but for that father and the others who were considered relatives, unless he were by nature exceptionally fair, he would care nothing. "You say everything as it would happen," he said; "but how does this image apply to those who handle arguments?" In this way: we have, I suppose, certain doctrines from childhood about things just and noble, in which we have been brought up as by parents, obeying and honoring them. "We do." And there are other practices opposite to these, which hold pleasures that flatter our soul and pull it toward themselves, but they do not persuade those who are even moderately balanced; instead, they honor the ancestral ways and obey them. "This is so." What then? (I said) when a question comes to someone in such a state, asking "What is the noble?" and when he answers what he heard from the lawgiver, the argument refutes him. Refuting him many times and in many ways, it casts him into the opinion that this is no more noble than it is base; and similarly regarding the just and the good, and the things he held in highest honor. After this, what do you think he will do regarding their honor and obedience? "Necessarily," he said, "he will no longer honor them or obey them in the same way." When, therefore, (I said) he no longer considers these things honorable or his own as before, and does not find the truth, is there any other life he will likely turn to than the one that flatters him? "There is not," he said. "He will seem, I think, to have become lawless instead of law-abiding." "Necessarily." "Therefore," I said, "it is likely that this is the condition of those who handle arguments in this way, and as I said just now, it is worthy of much indulgence." "And of pity, too," he said. "Therefore, so that this pity does not arise concerning your thirty-year-olds, you must handle the argument in every way cautiously." "Very much so," he said. "Is not this one great safeguard: that they do not taste these things while they are young? For I think you have noticed that youngsters, when they first get a taste of arguments, use them as a game, always using them for contradiction. Imitating those who refute, they themselves refute others, rejoicing like puppies in pulling and tearing with words at those nearby." "Exceedingly so," he said. "Then when they have refuted many and been refuted by many, they fall vehemently and quickly into believing nothing of what they believed before. From this, they themselves and the whole of philosophy are slandered among others." "Most true," he said. "But an older man," (I said) "would not wish to share in such madness. He will instead imitate the one who wishes to engage in dialectic and consider the truth, rather than the one who plays and contradicts for the sake of a game. He will be more moderate himself, and will make the pursuit more honorable instead of more dishonorable." "Rightly so," he said. "And all the things said before this were said by way of precaution: that those to whom one will impart arguments should be of a balanced and steady nature, and not, as is now the case, that any chance person with no fitness comes to it." "By all means," he said. "Is it enough then to stay in the study of argument continuously and intensely, doing nothing else but exercising in a corresponding way with physical exercises, for twice as many years as before?" "Six?" he asked, "or do you mean four?" "Let it be five," I said. "For after this, you must lead them down into that cave again, and compel them to hold offices relating to war and such offices as belong to the young, so that they do not fall behind the others in experience. And in these things too, they must be tested to see if they will remain firm while being pulled in every direction, or if they will be shifted." "And how much time," he asked, "do you set for this?" "Fifteen years," I said. "And when they have become fifty years old, those who have come through safely and excelled in every way, both in deeds and in sciences, must finally be led to the goal and compelled to incline the ray of their soul to look toward that which provides light for all. Having seen the Good itself, they must use it as a pattern, and order the city and private individuals and themselves for the remainder of their lives, each in their turn. For the most part, they will spend their time in philosophy; but when their turn comes, they will toil in political matters and rule, each for the sake of the city, doing this not as something noble, but as something necessary. And thus, having always educated others like themselves and leaving them behind as guardians of the city, they will go away to dwell in the Isles of the Blessed. The city will make monuments and sacrifices to them publicly (if the Pythia concurs) as to divine spirits; or if not, as to happy and divine men." "Most beautiful, Socrates," he said, "you have finished the rulers, just like a sculptor." "And the women, too..."

He outlines a rigorous 50-year path from study to military service, culminating in the vision of "The Good" and the duty to rule the state.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the discussion of the ideal state in Book VII and begins Book VIII of Plato's Republic. # ON THE REPUBLIC, BOOK VIII #

<margin>A</margin> ...and this must also be understood regarding women. Do not think, Glaucon, that I have been speaking more about men than about women—at least those among them whose natures are found to be sufficiently capable of these duties. "That is right," he said, "if indeed they are to share all things equally with the men, as we have described." Do you then agree <note original: "Num concedis">Socrates is asking for a final consensus on the feasibility of their thought experiment.</note> that our words concerning the city and its constitution were not merely a collection of prayers or wishes, but things that are difficult to achieve yet possible, provided they are done in the way we have stated? This occurs when true philosophers—whether one or many—gain power in a city and look down upon the current honors, considering them illiberal and worthless. Instead, they will value what is right and the honors that proceed from it as most important, and they will regard <margin>B</margin> Justice <note original: "quod iustum">The central theme of the entire work.</note> as the greatest and most necessary thing. By serving justice and increasing its influence, they will properly set their own city in order. "In what way?" he asked. All those in the city who have reached the age of ten will be sent out into the fields. Taking their children, the philosophers will raise them far away from the habits their parents currently practice, educating them in their own customs and laws, which we have already described. And in this way, that city and constitution we spoke of will arise most quickly and easily; if it should ever exist, it will be blessed, and it will bring the greatest benefit to the people among whom it is established. "Quite so," he said. "And as for how such a city might be constituted, if it ever were to be, Socrates, you seem to me to have discovered it well." Have we not then spoken enough both about this city <margin>C</margin> and the man who is similar to it? For it is clear what sort of person we will say he ought to be. "It is clear indeed," he replied, "and as for what you ask, I believe we have reached the end of this topic."

# PLATO ON THE REPUBLIC, #
-> Or, <-
-> ON JUSTICE, <-
# THE EIGHTH DIALOGUE. #

> SUMMARY OF THE DIALOGUE. *Having explained the republic under right administration, he now consequently deals with the vicious forms, which he has hitherto designated by the name of Injustice. He had established three modes of right governance: monarchy, aristocracy, and "polity" (the latter name noting a popular governance, commonly called Democracy). He now explains the excesses and failings of those three forms of public administration. He pursues this doctrine in the next two books, namely the eighth and ninth. He considers these failings or excesses both in the republic and in the character of the citizens, from which the character of the city is shaped. He notes four excesses: in Aristocracy, he finds oligarchy; in Polity, democracy; and in Kingship, timarchy and tyranny. He deals with all of these individually in this dialogue. He does not finish the discussion of Tyranny here but defers it to the following book.*

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'E' featuring a classical figure, matching the style of the Greek side.</image-desc>

SO BE IT, I said. It has been agreed between us, Glaucon, that in a city that is to be perfectly established, women and children must be held in common; so too must all education. Similarly, all duties, whether in war or in peace, are to be shared. Their kings must be those men who have proven to be the most excellent in both the study of philosophy and in military matters. "It is fully agreed," he said. Furthermore, we conceded this: that when such rulers have been established, they will lead the soldiers and assign them to habi-<margin>D</margin>tations such as we described before—common to all, where nothing belongs to any individual. And not only regarding housing, but also regarding furniture and possessions; if you recall, we agreed on what sort these ought to be. "I certainly remember," he said, "that we judged no one should possess any of the things that others now own. Instead, like athletes of war and guardians, they should receive an annual wage for their protection from the others in the form of food, and they must look after both themselves and the rest of the city." "Rightly said," I replied. "But come now, since we have finished this, let us recall where we turned aside to reach this point, so that we may travel the same path again." "That is not difficult," he said. "For almost exactly as you have just done, <margin>E</margin> you spoke as if you had completed the discussion of the city, stating that you would call such a city 'good' (the one you described), and also the man who was similar to it—even though, as it appeared, you could have described an even better city and man. You said, moreover, that if this republic is the right one, the others are deviations. Of the remaining forms of government, as I recall, you said there were four species worth speaking of, whose defects we should inspect, along with the men who resemble them. Thus, having looked at them all and declaring who is the best man and who is the worst, we might consider whether the best man is the happiest and the worst the most miserable, or if the matter stands otherwise. But when I asked you which four republics you meant, Pole-<margin>F</margin>marchus and Adeimantus interrupted the conversation; and taking up the discourse from there, you have finally arrived here." "You remember quite correctly," I said. "Therefore, like a wrestler, offer me the same grip again; and when I ask the same question, try now to say what you were then about to declare." "If indeed I am able," I replied. "I myself am very eager to hear," he said, "which four republics you were speaking of." "It is not difficult for you to hear them," I said. "For those I speak of are the ones that actually have names: first, that which is praised by many, the Cretan and Laconian <note original: "Cretenſis & Laconica">Referring to the systems of Crete and Sparta, often admired for their discipline.</note>. Second, and praised in the second place, is that which is called the power of the few (Oligarchy), a republic full of many evils. Then there is that which differs greatly from it and follows it, the popular government (Democracy)..."

--- Page 524 ---
<meta>This page continues from the end of Book VII of Plato's Republic. Socrates has just finished describing the ideal city and the philosopher-king. He now transitions into Book VIII, where he examines the four "diseased" or corrupt forms of government and the corresponding character types of the individuals who live within them.</meta>

# OF PLATO #

<margin>A</margin> Furthermore, the noble **tyranny**, which differs from all of these, is the fourth and final disease of the city. Or do you have another form of the republic that is situated in some clear and distinct category? For there are also certain minor principalities, purchased kingdoms, and similar forms of civil power that hold a kind of middle ground between these. Among these, no fewer are found among the Barbarians <note>In this context, "Barbarians" refers to any non-Greek speaking peoples, such as the Persians or Scythians.</note> than among the Greeks. Many of them are certainly reported to be strange. In the same way, there are as many species of human character and habits. Do you think that republics are made from an oak tree or a rock, perhaps, rather than from the characters of the citizens? For wherever these characters flow, they drag everything else along with them. "From the characters, without a doubt," he said. Therefore, if there are five species of government, there will also be five dispositions of the private souls.

<margin>B</margin> "Nothing stands in the way of that." We have certainly seen the man who is similar to the **aristocracy** <note>The "rule of the best," which Socrates has been describing in the previous books.</note> (the government of the best), whom we rightly asserted to be good and just. "We have seen him." Next, it is fitting to describe the inferior types: the contentious and ambitious man, formed according to the **Lacedaemonian** <note>The Lacedaemonian or Spartan republic, known for its focus on military honor and discipline.</note> republic; then the man who desires the rule of the few (**oligarchy**), the **popular** (democratic) man, and the **tyrannical** man. This is so that, by discerning the most unjust man, we may compare him with the most just, and perfectly understand how pure and absolute justice relates to pure and absolute injustice, in terms of the happiness or misery of the just or unjust man. Thus, we may either follow the advice of **Thrasymachus** <note>Thrasymachus was the sophist in Book I who argued that "might makes right" and that injustice is more profitable than justice.</note> and pursue injustice, or be persuaded by our present reasoning and pursue justice. "That is exactly how we must proceed," he said.

<margin>C</margin> Should we not observe the characters in republics before we look at them in private persons, just as we began before, because they are more obvious there? Thus, we should first consider the **ambitious republic** (for which I have no name other than "ambitious power" or "timarchy"); after that, we will consider such a man. Then we shall look at the power of the few (**oligarchy**) and such a man; afterward, the government of the multitude (**democracy**) and the popular man; and finally, considering the city oppressed by **tyranny** and recognizing the tyrannical soul within it, we shall attempt to judge sufficiently what we have proposed. "The inspection and judgment would proceed rightly in this way," he said. Come then, let us try to explain how an ambitious empire arises from the government of the best (aristocracy).

<margin>D</margin> Is it not simply true that every republic changes because of the ruling class itself, specifically when strife or sedition arises within it? But as long as it is in agreement with itself, even if it is very small, it is impossible for it to be moved. "That is so." But in what way, O **Glaucon**, will this city of ours be moved from its state? How will the leaders and defenders disagree with one another and among themselves? Do you wish, like **Homer**, that we pray to the **Muses** to explain to us how sedition first fell upon them? Shall we say they speak to us in the "tragic" style <note>Socrates suggests the Muses are speaking in a grand, theatrical manner, as if playing a game with children while actually being serious.</note>, as if playing and joking with us like children, speaking of grand things? <margin>E</margin> "In what way?" Almost like this: It is difficult for a city so constituted to be moved from its state. But since everything that is born is subject to corruption, even such a constitution cannot remain forever, but will be dissolved.

The dissolution is this: Not only for plants in the ground, but also for animals on the earth, there is a season of fertility and sterility of both soul and body. This occurs whenever the revolutions of the circles join together for each species—shorter cycles for those that are short-lived, and the opposite for those that live longer. Those whom you have educated to lead the city, although they are wise, will not be able to grasp the fertility or sterility of your race through reason combined with sense; rather, it will escape them, <margin>F</margin> and they will occasionally beget children when it is not the opportune time. For that which is divinely generated, there is a cycle contained by a perfect number. For human generation, however, there is a number <note>This is the famous "Platonic Number" or "Marriage Number," one of the most notoriously difficult and debated mathematical passages in ancient literature.</note> in which first the increases, both mastering and mastered, taking three distances and four terms—of things like and unlike, increasing and decreasing—make all things correspond and commensurable with one another. The 4:3 ratio joined with five and increased three times provides two harmonies. One is a square, a hundred times a hundred. <margin>G</margin> The other is of equal length but oblong, consisting of a hundred numbers from the commensurable diameters of five, each lacking one, and two that cannot be expressed, and a hundred cubes of three.

This entire geometric number, having such authority, holds the power over better and worse generations. If your guardians are ignorant of this and join brides and grooms at the wrong time, the children born will be neither talented nor fortunate. The predecessors will appoint the best of these as leaders, but because they are unworthy of the succession of their parents, they will begin to neglect their subjects once they are in office. They will not care for **Music** <note>In the Greek sense, "Music" refers to all the arts of the Muses, including literature and philosophy.</note> as they should, nor for gymnastics, which will make the young more "unmusical" and uncultured. From these, leaders will be appointed who are less careful than they should be in <margin>H</margin> examining those "Generations" of which **Hesiod** <note>The poet Hesiod described the decline of humanity through five ages: Gold, Silver, Bronze, Heroes, and Iron.</note> speaks and which we also mentioned: the golden, silver, bronze, and iron races. But when iron is mixed with silver, and bronze with gold, a discordant inequality and lack of harmony will arise. Wherever these are born, they always produce war and enmity. Wherever such a race of men is present, it is always shaken by sedition. We must say that the Muses answer rightly. "And they must," he said, "since they are Muses."

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...next in order, democracy; and finally the noble tyranny, differing from all these, the fourth and final sickness of the city. Or do you have another form of government which lies in some other distinct form? For dynasties and purchased kingdoms and other such states are somewhere between these. You would find no fewer of them among the barbarians than among the Greeks. "Many strange ones are spoken of," he said. "Do you know then," I said, "that there must be as many types of human character as there are forms of government? Or do you think governments grow from an oak or a rock, and not from the habits of the people in the cities, which, as if by their weight, drag everything else after them?" "Not at all from anywhere else," he said. <margin>B</margin> "Therefore, if there are five types of cities, the arrangements of the individual soul must also be five." "Certainly." "We have already described the man who is like the aristocracy, whom we rightly call good and just." "We have." "Should we then go through the worse types: the one who is contentious and loves honor, standing according to the Laconian (Spartan) constitution; and then the oligarchical, the democratic, and the tyrannical? This is so that having seen the most unjust, we may contrast him with the most just, and our inquiry may be complete: how pure justice relates to pure injustice regarding the happiness and misery of the possessor. Thus we may either follow Thrasymachus and pursue injustice, or follow the argument now appearing and pursue justice." "By all means," <margin>C</margin> he said, "we must do it this way."

"Shall we then, as we began by looking at habits in governments before looking at them in individuals because it was clearer, now first look at the honor-loving (ambitious) government? (For I have no other name in common use; it must be called either timocracy or timarchy). We will examine such a man in relation to it; then oligarchy and the oligarchical man; then looking toward democracy we will view the democratic man; and fourth, going to the city under tyranny and seeing it, we will then look into the tyrannical soul and try to become capable judges of what we proposed." "In that way," he said, "the viewing and the judgment would happen reasonably." "Come then," I said, "let us try to say in what way a timocracy would arise out of an aristocracy. <margin>D</margin> Is it not a simple rule that every government changes because of the ruling class itself, when strife arises within that very group? But if they are of one mind, even if the group is very small, it is impossible for it to be moved?" "That is so." "How then, O Glaucon, will our city be moved, and in what way will the auxiliaries and the rulers fall into strife with each other and themselves? Or do you wish, like Homer, that we pray to the Muses to tell us how strife first fell upon them? And shall we say they speak 'tragically,' as if playing and mocking us as children, yet speaking in a high style as if in earnest?" "How?" <margin>E</margin> "In this way. It is difficult for a city so established to be moved. But since there is decay for everything that is born, even such a constitution will not remain for all time, but will be dissolved.

The dissolution is this: Not only for plants in the earth but also for animals on the earth, there is a season of fertility and sterility of both soul and bodies, whenever the revolutions join the cycles for each; short cycles for the short-lived, and the opposite for the opposite. Regarding the fertility and sterility of your own race, even though the leaders you have educated for the city are wise, they will not attain it by calculation combined with sense; it will escape them, and they will sometimes beget children when they should not. For a divine birth, there is a period which a perfect number encompasses; <margin>F</margin> but for a human birth, it is the first number in which the increases... <note>The text continues with the same complex mathematical description of the "Marriage Number" found in the Latin column, involving geometric ratios and harmonies.</note> ...This whole geometric number is master over better and worse births. When your guardians, being ignorant of this, join brides and grooms out of season, the children will be neither naturally gifted nor lucky. The predecessors will appoint the best of these, but they, being unworthy, <margin>G</margin> will come into the powers of their fathers and will begin to neglect us, even though they are guardians, first considering music of less value than they should, and second, gymnastics. Thus your young people will become more uncultured. From them will be appointed rulers who are not very guardian-like in testing the races of Hesiod and those among us—the gold, silver, bronze, and iron. When iron is mixed with silver and bronze with gold, an unharmonious inequality and irregularity will arise; and wherever these arise, they always breed war and enmity. We must say <margin>H</margin> that this is the origin of strife, wherever it occurs." "And we shall say they answer rightly," he said. "For they must," I said, "being Muses."

<meta>The catchword at the bottom of the Greek column is "Τί οὖν;" (Ti oun?), meaning "What then?" or "So what?"</meta>

<summary>In this opening of Book VIII, Socrates describes the decline of the ideal aristocracy into timocracy (rule of honor), triggered by a failure of the rulers to correctly calculate the "Marriage Number," leading to the birth of inferior children and the mixing of social classes.</summary>
