<meta>This page transitions from the description of the ideal Aristocracy in Book VII to the first stage of political decline in Book VIII: Timocracy. This occurs when the "perfect number" for breeding the guardian class is missed, leading to a "mixture of metals" in the soul.</meta>

### ON THE REPUBLIC, BOOK VIII ###

<margin>A</margin> "How then," I said, "shall the Muses speak of it? Once sedition <note>original: Στάσεως (staseōs); refers to civil strife or internal conflict within the ruling class.</note> has arisen, both classes will be pulled in different directions: the iron and bronze natures toward gain, the acquisition of land and houses, and the abundance of gold and silver. But those natures containing gold and silver, not being poor but naturally wealthy in their souls, lead toward virtue and the ancient establishment. As they struggle and pull against one another, they finally reach a middle ground: they agree to divide the land and houses for private possession. Those they formerly guarded as free men, friends, and providers, they now reduce to servitude, holding them as subjects and servants, while they themselves attend to war and their own protection." "This seems to me," he said, "to be the origin of the transition."

<margin>B</margin> "Therefore," I said, "this government will be a middle point between the rule of the best <note>Aristocracy</note> and the power of the few <note>Oligarchy</note>." "Certainly." "So it will change in this way. But once changed, how will it be governed? Is it not clear that in some ways it will imitate the former republic, and in others the power of the few, since it stands in the middle? Yet it will also have something unique to itself?" "Exactly so," he said. "In honoring the rulers, and in having its warriors abstain from farming, manual arts, and other money-making; in establishing communal meals, and in focusing on gymnastics and the contests of war—in all these ways it will imitate the former state." "Yes."

"However, in its fear of bringing the wise to power—because it no longer possesses men who are simple and sincere, but rather those of mixed character—it will incline toward the spirited <note>original: θυμοειδεῖς (thymoeideis); those dominated by "thymos" or the "spirited" part of the soul associated with anger and honor.</note> and simpler men, born more for war than for peace. It will value the deceits and stratagems of war, spending all its time in conflict. Will these not be its unique features?" "Yes."

<margin>C</margin> "And such men," I said, "will be greedy for money, just like those in oligarchies. They will fiercely worship gold and silver in secret, possessing private storehouses and domestic treasuries where they can hide them. They will have walled houses—veritable private nests—in which they spend a great deal on women and whomever else they please."

<margin>D</column> "Very true," he said. "Will they not also be stingy with their own money, since they prize it and do not acquire it openly? Yet they will be profuse in spending the money of others to satisfy their desires, harvesting pleasures in secret, running away from the law like children from a father. They have been educated not by persuasion, but by force, because they neglected the true Muse <note>Philosophy and reasoned culture.</note> who is joined with speech and philosophy, and they honored gymnastics more highly than music <note>In the Greek sense, "Music" includes all the arts and sciences overseen by the Muses.</note>." "You describe a republic," he said, "entirely mixed of good and evil." "It is indeed mixed," I said. "But one single thing is most apparent in it, caused by the rule of the spirited element: the love of contention and the love of honor <note>original: φιλονεικίαι καὶ φιλοτιμίαι (philoneikiai kai philotimiai).</note>." "Very much so," he said.

"This, then, is how this republic would be born and what it would be like—to sketch the form of a government in words without working out every detail accurately. It is enough to see from the sketch both the most just man and the most unjust. It would be an endless task to go through every form of government and every character without leaving anything out." "Rightly said," he replied. "Who, then, is the man corresponding to this republic? How is he formed, and what is his nature?" "I think," said Adimantus, "he comes close to being like Glaucon here, at least in his love of contention." "Perhaps in that," I said, "but in these other ways his nature seems different." "In what ways?"

<margin>E</margin> "He must be more self-willed," I said, "and somewhat less cultured, though a lover of the Muses and a lover of listening, yet not at all a rhetorician. Such a man would be harsh toward slaves—not despising them as a well-educated man would, but being gentle toward free men. He would be highly obedient to rulers, yet ambitious for power and honor, thinking he deserves to rule not because of his eloquence or anything of that sort, but because of his military deeds and things related to war. He would also be a lover of gymnastics and hunting." "That is indeed," he said, "the character of that republic."

<margin>F</margin> "And such a man," I said, "would despise money while he is young, but the older he grows, the more he would always embrace it, because he shares in the money-loving nature and is not pure in his pursuit of virtue, <margin>G</margin> having been abandoned by the best guardian." "What guardian is that?" Adimantus asked. "Reason," I said, "mixed with music. This alone, when it resides within a man, is the lifelong savior of virtue." "Well said," he replied. "And such a timocratic youth," I said, "is like such a city." "Certainly."

"And he is formed," I said, "in this way: sometimes he is the young son of a good father who lives in a poorly governed city, avoiding honors, offices, lawsuits, and all such busybodying, and who is willing to be at a disadvantage so as not to have trouble." "How does he become this way?" he asked. "When he first hears his mother complaining that her husband is not among the rulers, and that she is therefore looked down upon among other women. Then she sees that he is not very concerned with money, nor does he fight and insult people in private in the courts or in public, but bears all such things with indifference. She notices that he is always attentive to his own mind, yet neither values her very much nor treats her with dishonor..."

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...they may be. What then will the Muses be said to say hereafter? After sedition has arisen, both kinds of natures will be carried away: the iron and bronze indeed toward the pursuit of gain, the possession of fields and houses, and an abundance of gold and silver. But that which is in the golden and silver natures, as if not of a poor but of a wealthy nature, leads toward virtue and the pristine state. But fighting against each other and pulling in opposite directions, they finally come to an agreement in the middle, so that having divided the fields and houses, each may possess them privately. Those who were previously preserved by them as free men, friends, and nourishers are reduced to servitude, and as subjects and slaves, they are compelled to take care of the war and the guarding of them. From this, it certainly seems to me, this change happens.

<margin>B</margin> This government will surely be in the middle between the rule of the best and the power of the few. It certainly will. It will be changed in this way. But when it has been changed into that, what mode of governing will it primarily keep? Is it not clear that it will partly imitate the former republic, and partly the power of the few, inasmuch as it is located in the middle, and partly also it will possess something of its own? Entirely so. And it will imitate the former in this: that the rulers will be honored, and the soldiers will abstain from agriculture, mechanical arts, and other pursuits, and there will be communal banquets, and gymnastic games and military contests will be frequented. Certainly. But it will have some things peculiar to itself, such as <margin>C</margin> it will fear to admit the wise to leadership, because it does not possess men of this kind who are simple or pure, but those of a mixed sort. It will rather choose more spirited and simpler men for governing, who seem born for war rather than for peace. It will also make much of deceits and the machines of war, and will always be at war. Certainly. Yet these men will be greedy for money, just like those who live in the power of the few, and being overwhelmed by darkness, they will honor gold and silver more rudely, as those who have treasuries and their own storehouses in which to hide these things, and also walled houses like private nests in which they spend much on women and others according to their pleasure.

<margin>D</margin> You speak the truth. Will they not also be more stingy in their own affairs than is fitting? Seeing as they magnify money and do not acquire it openly; but they will be more profuse in the affairs of others because of their lust, and they will secretly indulge in pleasures, fleeing the law everywhere, just as children avoid their father’s sight; not educated by persuasion, but by force, because they neglected true music which is joined with speech and philosophy, and honored gymnastics much more and before music. You describe a republic mixed of evil and good. It is indeed mixed: but before others, because of the empire of spiritedness and anger, the studies of contention and ambition grow strong in it. Vehemently. Will not this republic so grow together and be such as it is permitted to describe the figure of a republic in speech, though not with the highest diligence, because it suffices from the description itself to discern the most just and most unjust man, and it would be an inextricable work if anyone should undertake to narrate all republics and all manners, omitting nothing at all. Rightly. Who then is the man according to this republic? How is he made? What sort of man exists? I think indeed, said Adimantus, he is similar to this Glaucon, for the sake of contention. Perhaps, I said, in this he is similar. But in these things his nature does not seem to be similar. In what?

<margin>E</margin> Surely it is necessary for him to be more stubborn, and in a way more estranged from music, yet a lover of music; and studious of hearing, but by no means a rhetorician. And toward slaves such a man will be harsh, not despising slaves like a moderately learned man; but toward free men he will be mild; toward rulers indeed very obedient, but also more greedy for leadership and honors; thinking it necessary to excel and lead others not by the art of speaking or any other similar faculty, but by warlike and civil deeds, since he is also very studious of gymnastics and hunting. This is certainly, he said, the custom <margin>F</margin> of that republic. Will not that man also despise money in his youth; but the more he ages, the more he will love money, because he is a participant in an avaricious nature, and is not pure toward virtue, <margin>G</margin> because he lacks the best guardian? Which one? asked Adimantus. Reason and the operation of music mixed together, which alone when it is present, preserves virtue throughout all of life in the one who leads. You speak excellently, he said. Such a youth is indeed a lover of ambitious command, similar to such a city. Entirely. But he becomes such in this manner: sometimes, for instance, when some youth is the son of a good father living in a city not well governed, fleeing honors, leaderships, and judgments, and the rest of this kind of care for business, and gladly subjecting himself so that he may avoid labors. In what way does he become so? When, for instance, he hears his mother bearing it poorly that her husband does not at all perform the duties of a magistrate, and therefore she is held in contempt among other women; then being indignant whenever she beholds her husband solicitous in money, judgments, and public contention, but toward all these things rather negligent, and such a one as to live with himself for the most part, and neither to despise his wife, nor yet to greatly cherish her...

<summary>This page describes the transition from the ideal Aristocracy to a Timocracy, characterized by a love of honor and military spirit. It details how the ruling class begins to value private property and secret wealth, and describes the "Timocratic man" as being shaped by a spirited nature and a lack of philosophical education.</summary>
<keywords>Timocracy, Republic, Plato, Socrates, Adimantus, spiritedness, ambition, degeneration of the state, honor-loving, martial virtue</keywords>

--- Page 526 ---
<meta>This page continues the dialogue from Book VIII of Plato's Republic. Having previously described the Timocracy (a state based on honor), Socrates now describes how the Timocratic man is formed and how that state inevitably decays into an Oligarchy (a state based on wealth).</meta>

->### PLATO'S REPUBLIC###<-

<margin>A</margin> "From all these things, a mother often complains to her son that his father is unmanly <note>original: ἀνάνδριος (anandrios); literally "without manliness," suggesting a lack of political ambition.</note> and too easy-going, along with all the other things women are accustomed to gossip about regarding such men." "Indeed," said Adeimantus, "women often say many such things." "And you know," I said, "that even the servants of such families—those who seem most loyal—sometimes whisper similar things to the boys in secret. If they see someone who owes money to the father whom the father does not pursue in court, or someone else who wrongs him, they urge the son that when he grows up, he must take revenge on all such people and be more of a man than his father was. The son hears and sees other similar things when he goes out: those who mind their own business in the city are called fools and held in low esteem, while those who do not are honored and praised. When the youth hears and sees all this, and on the other hand hears his father's reason and sees his father's way of life up close in contrast to the others, he is pulled in two directions. His father’s influence nourishes and increases the **rational faculty** <note>original: λογιστικόν (logistikon); the part of the soul that calculates and reasons.</note> of his soul, while the others nourish the natures of **desire** and **anger**."

<margin>B</margin> "Therefore, since he is not born with a bad nature but has been influenced by the bad habits of others, and is pulled by both, he submits to a middle power—the contentious and angry part of himself—and becomes a man of high spirit and a lover of honor <note>This describes the Timocratic man.</note>." "You seem to me to have described his nature accurately," he said. "We have, then," I said, "the second form of government and the second type of man." "We have indeed." "Should we not then say, as Aeschylus did, 'Another man suited to another city'? Or rather, according to our plan, should we describe the city first?" "Certainly," he said. "And the one that follows such a republic is, I believe, **Oligarchy**."

<margin>C</margin> "What sort of constitution do you specifically call an Oligarchy?" "The one based on a **property assessment** <term>original: τιμημάτων (timēmatōn); a census or valuation of property used to determine political eligibility.</term>," I said, "in which the rich rule, and the poor man has no share in the government." "I understand," he said. "Must we not first say how the transition from an ambitious government to this one occurs?" "Certainly." "Indeed, even to a blind man, it is clear how the change happens." "How?" "That **treasury** <note>original: Ταμεῖον (tameion); a private storehouse or treasury.</note> full of gold which each man possesses ruins such a republic. For first, they find new ways to spend money and they pervert the laws for this purpose, as neither they nor their wives obey them."

<margin>D</margin> "That is likely," he said. "Then, I suppose, as one sees another and enters into competition, the majority of them become like this." "Likely." "From there, as they proceed further into the pursuit of wealth, the more they value it, the more they devalue **virtue**. Is it not true that virtue and wealth differ as if they were placed in the opposite pans of a balance scale, always tipping in opposite directions?" "Exactly so," he said. "Therefore, when wealth and the wealthy are honored in a city, virtue and good men are despised." "That is clear." "And people always practice what is honored and neglect what is dishonored."

<margin>E</margin> "So it is. Thus, instead of being men who love victory and honor, they finally become lovers of trade and money. They praise and admire the rich man and raise him to office, but they despise the poor man." "Entirely so." "And then they establish a law which is the hallmark of an oligarchic constitution: they set a required amount of money—greater where the oligarchy is more intense, and lesser where it is less so—and they proclaim that no one may hold office whose property does not reach the fixed assessment. They achieve this either by force of arms or by instilling fear before they establish such a government. Is it not so?" "It is indeed." "This, then, is the constitution." "Yes," he said.

<margin>F</margin> "But what is the character of this republic? And what are the defects we said it would have?" "First," I said, "consider the very nature of its defining limit. Look: if someone were to choose the pilots of ships based on their property assessment, but would never admit a poor man even if he were a more skillful pilot, what do you think would follow?" "That they would navigate the ship poorly," he said. "Is it not the same for any other position of authority?" "I believe so." "Is it so for everything except a city? Or for a city as well?" "Much more so for a city," he said, "since its government is the most difficult and the greatest." "This, then, is one such great defect that Oligarchy suffers." "It appears so."

<margin>G</margin> "And what of this? Is this any less serious?" "What is it?" "That such a city is necessarily not one, but two: one of the poor and one of the rich, living in the same place and always plotting against one another." "By Zeus, that is not a lesser evil." "Furthermore, it is not a good thing that they are unable to wage war. This is because they are forced either to use the armed populace—whom they fear more than the enemy—or, if they do not use them, they appear as true 'oligarchs' <note>A pun on the word, implying they are 'few' even on the battlefield.</note> in the heat of the fight. Moreover, they are unwilling to pay money for the war because they are lovers of wealth. Is that honorable?" "Certainly not." "And what of that which we criticized before: that the same people in such a city perform many different roles at once—farming, trading, and fighting? Does that seem right?" "In no way." "See then if this is the greatest of all these evils, which this state is the first to admit." "What is that?" "That it is permitted for a man to sell all his possessions, and for another to acquire them, and for the seller to live in the city while being no part of the state at all—neither a trader, nor a craftsman, nor a knight, nor a foot-soldier, but only called a pauper and destitute."

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Distressed by all these things, and because his mother says his father is unmanly and too remiss, and says all the other things that women are accustomed to sing about regarding such matters. "And very much so," said Adeimantus, "many such things and similar to themselves." "You know then," I said, "that even the servants of such men sometimes secretly say such things to the sons—those who seem well-intentioned—and if they see someone who either owes money that the father does not pursue, or is doing some other wrong, they urge the sons that when they become men, they should take revenge on all such people, and be more of a man than their father?" "And he hears and sees other such things; those who do their own business in the city are called private citizens and are of small account; but those who do not are honored and praised. Then indeed the youth, hearing and seeing all such things, and again hearing his father's words and seeing his father's pursuits from close by alongside those of others, is pulled by both these: by the father, who waters and increases the rational part in his soul; and by the others, who water the desiring and spirited parts. Since he was not born with the nature of a bad man, but has kept bad company with others, being pulled into the middle by both of these, he came to hand over the rule within himself to the middle, the contentious

<margin>C</margin> and spirited part; and he became a high-minded and honor-loving man." "You seem to me," he said, "to have completely gone through his nature." "We have, then," I said, "the second republic and the second man." "We have," he said. "Should we not after this say, as Aeschylus does: 'Another man stationed at another city?' or rather, according to our hypothesis, the city first?" "By all means," he said. "And it would be, as I think, Oligarchy, which follows such a republic." "What sort of arrangement," he said, "do you call Oligarchy?" "The republic based on property assessments," I said, "in which the rich rule, and the poor have no part in the rule." "I understand," he said. "Must we not then say how it first transitions from Timocracy into Oligarchy?" "Yes." "And indeed,"

<margin>D</margin> I said, "it is clear even to a blind man how it transitions." "How?" "That treasury," I said, "filled with gold for each of those men, ruins such a republic. For first they find expenditures for themselves, and they bring the laws to this end, disobeying them themselves and their wives." "Likely," he said. "Then, I think, as one sees another and goes into jealousy, they make the multitude like themselves." "Likely." "From there then," I said, "proceeding further into the making of money, by as much as they lead this to be more honored, by so much is virtue more dishonored. Or does virtue not stand apart from wealth in such a way, as if they were lying in the pans of a balance, each always weighing toward the opposite?" "Very much so," he said. "When wealth is honored in a city and the wealthy,

<margin>E</margin> virtue and the good are more dishonored." "Clear." "What is always honored is practiced, and what is dishonored is neglected." "Thus." "Instead of contentious and honor-loving men, they finally become lovers of money-making and lovers of money; and the rich man they praise and admire, and they lead him into office, but the poor man they dishonor." "Quite so." "Then indeed they place laws as the boundary of an oligarchic republic, having ordered a quantity of money: for one more, a greater oligarchy; for another less, a lesser; having proclaimed not to participate in offices for whomsoever there is not property reaching the set assessment. These things they accomplish either by force with arms, or even before that by causing fear they establish such a republic. Or is it not so?" "Thus indeed." "The

<margin>F</margin> establishment, so to speak, is this." "Yes," he said. "But what is the manner of the republic? And what sort of faults does it have that we said it had?" "First," I said, "is this very thing: what its boundary is like. For consider: if someone should make pilots of ships thus by property assessments, and not entrust it to the poor man, even if he were more skillful at piloting." "A wretched voyage," he said, "they would sail." "Is it not also about any other thing, or any rule?" "I think so." "Except a city?" I said, "or also concerning a city?" "Much more," he said, "most of all, by as much as the rule is most difficult and greatest." "One indeed, this so great a fault, Oligarchy would have." "It appears." "What then? Is this anything

<margin>G</margin> less than that?" "What sort of thing?" "That such a city is not one but two by necessity: one of poor men, the other of rich men; dwelling in the same place, always plotting against one another." "Not at all, by Zeus," he said, "is it less." "But neither is this fine: being unable to fight any war, because of being forced either to use the armed multitude and fear them more than the enemies; or not using them, to appear truly as oligarchs in the fighting itself; and at the same time not being willing to contribute money, being lovers of money." "Not fine." "What then? That which we long ago rebuked: the doing of many things—farming and money-making and fighting at the same time—the same people in such a republic; or does it seem to be right?" "In no way whatsoever." "See then, if of all these evils this is the greatest which this city first admits." "What sort?" "The being allowed to sell all of one's own, and for another to acquire his things, and having sold them, to dwell in the city being none of the parts of the city: neither a money-maker, nor a craftsman, nor a knight, nor a foot-soldier, but called a pauper and indigent."

<summary>This page describes the shift from a Timocracy (honor-based) to an Oligarchy (wealth-based), focusing on how the love of money inevitably devalues virtue and splits the city into two warring factions of rich and poor.</summary>
<keywords>Plato, Republic, Oligarchy, property assessment, census, virtue vs. wealth, social decay, political philosophy, Socrates, Adeimantus</keywords>

--- Page 527 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion from Book VIII of Plato's Republic. Socrates and Adeimantus are identifying the flaws of an Oligarchy (a government based on wealth) and describing the "Oligarchic man" who values money above all else. This follows the description of the Timocratic man (who values honor) from the previous page.</meta>

# ON THE REPUBLIC, BOOK VIII.

<margin>A</margin> "This is the first flaw, certainly," he said. "Moreover, this sort of thing is not forbidden in cities governed by the few. If it were, some would not be excessively wealthy while others were completely destitute." "You are right." "Now consider this: when such a wealthy man was spending his money, was he of any more use to the city for the purposes we just mentioned? Or did he only *seem* to be one of the rulers, while in truth he was neither a ruler nor a servant of the state, but merely a consumer of his own resources?" "That is how it seemed," he said; "he was nothing but a consumer." "Do you wish, then," I asked, "for us to say that just as a **drone** <note>original: κηφήν (kēphēn) / fucus; a male bee that does not work but eats the honey. Plato uses this as a metaphor for people who live off the wealth of a community without contributing to it.</note> is born in a hive as a disease of the swarm, so too such a man is born in a house as a pestilence to the city?" "Quite so, Socrates," he replied.

<margin>B</margin> "Now, Adeimantus, has God not made all the winged drones stingless? But among these 'pedestrian' drones, have we not seen that some are stingless, while others are armed with terrible stings? From the stingless ones come those who end their old age as beggars; but from those with stings come all who are called criminals." "Most true," he said. "It is clear then," I said, "that in any city where you see beggars, there are also thieves, cut-purses, temple-robbers, and craftsmen of all such evils hidden away in that place." "It is clear," he said. "What then? In cities ruled by an oligarchy, do you not see beggars present?" "Nearly everyone," he said, "except for the rulers themselves." "Should we not then assume," I said, "that there are also many criminals among them, armed with stings, whom the authorities must diligently restrain by force?" "We should indeed," he said.

<margin>C</margin> "Shall we not say that such people arise there due to a lack of education, a bad upbringing, and a corrupt arrangement of the state?" "We shall." "Such then is the city ruled by an oligarchy, and it is burdened by these evils, and perhaps even more." "Nearly so," he said. "Let this finish our description of the state they call an **Oligarchy** <note>original: ὀλιγαρχία; rule by the few, specifically based on a property qualification.</note>, which chooses its rulers based on a <term>census</term> <note>original: τιμημάτων (timēmatōn) / census; a legal assessment of a person's property and wealth to determine their status.</note>. Next, let us investigate how a man becomes like this state, and what he is like once he has been formed." "By all means," he said. "Does he not change from that 'spirited' youth into an oligarchic one in this way?" "How?" "When a son is born to him, at first the boy admires his father and follows in his footsteps. But then he sees his father suddenly stumble—

<margin>D</margin> as if hitting a reef—against the city, and sees him pour out all his belongings and his very self. This happens after his father has served as a general or held some other high office, only to be dragged into court by informants, ruined by false accusers, disgraced, and stripped of his entire estate." "That is likely," he said. "Seeing and suffering these things, my friend, and having lost his inheritance, he becomes afraid. I imagine he immediately topples **Ambition** and that **Spirited** quality <note>original: θυμοειδές (thymoeides); the part of the soul associated with anger, courage, and the desire for honor.</note> from the throne of his soul. Humbled by poverty, he turns to profit-making; living greedily, stingily, and sparingly, he works hard to heap up money. Do you not think that such a man then

<margin>E</margin> seats **Avarice** and the love of wealth upon that empty throne? Does he not create a 'Great King' within himself, adorning it with tiaras, golden collars, and Persian swords?" <note>A metaphor for how the desire for money becomes an absolute, tyrannical ruler over the man's inner life.</note> "I do," he said. "And as for the **Rational** and **Spirited** parts of his soul, I believe he forces them to sit on the ground at the feet of this King as slaves. He forbids the rational part to calculate or consider anything except how to turn a small amount of money into a larger sum. He allows the spirited part to admire and honor nothing but wealth and the wealthy, and to take pride in nothing except the possession of money or whatever leads to it." "There is no other change," he said, "so swift and powerful as that of a youth who loved honor becoming a man who loves money."

<margin>F</margin> "Is this man then the 'Oligarchic' type?" I asked. "At least his transformation is from a man who resembles the state from which Oligarchy itself arose." "Let us see if he is truly like it." "Let us see." "First, is he not like it in the way he prizes money above all else?" "How could he not be?" "And further, is he not like it in being stingy and hard-working, satisfying only his necessary desires and refusing all other expenses, enslaving his other appetites as being 'vain'?" "Precisely." "He is a squalid man," I said, "who makes a profit from everything and hoarsely scrapes together a hoard—the very kind of man the multitude praises. Is this not the man who resembles such a state?" "It seems so to me," he said. "Wealth is the thing most honored both by that city and by such a man." "That is because, I think," I said, "such a man has never applied his mind to education."

<margin>G</margin> "I think not," he said, "for if he had, he would not have appointed a blind leader for his chorus." <note>A reference to Plutus, the Greek god of wealth, who was traditionally depicted as blind.</note> "Very well," I said, "now consider this: because of his lack of education, do we not say that 'drone-like' desires exist within him—some like beggars and others like criminals—held down by force through his other preoccupations?" "Certainly," he said. "Do you know where to look to see his criminality?" "Where?" he asked. "Look at his guardianship of orphans, or any similar situation that gives him a great deal of power to act unjustly." "True." "Is it not clear then, that in his other business dealings where he has a good reputation and appears to be just, he is only restraining his other evil desires through a certain forced 'decency'? He does not restrain them because he is convinced it is better to do so, nor does he calm them with reason, but through necessity and fear, trembling for the rest of his possessions." "Quite so," he said. "And by Zeus," I said, "my friend, you will find those drone-like desires within many of them whenever they have the chance to spend someone else's money." "Very much so."

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> This is the first, certainly. This is not forbidden in cities that are subjected to the rule of the few. For otherwise, some would not be more opulent than is fitting, and others would not be utterly beggars. You speak correctly. But consider this: when a wealthy man of this kind was spending his means, was he of any more use to the city for those things we were speaking of just now? Or did he only seem to be among the number of the rulers, while in truth he was neither a ruler nor a servant, but a consumer of his own resources? So it certainly seemed. He was, however, nothing other than a consumer. Or do we wish to say that, just as a drone born in a honeycomb is a disease of the swarm of bees, so too such a man

<margin>B</margin> born in a home will be a plague to the republic? "Precisely," said Socrates. Does not God make all winged drones without stings? But these terrestrial ones we see are partly without stings, and partly armed with dire stings. And from those who do not have stings, they eventually become paupers in their old age; but those equipped with stings are those who are called criminals. You speak the truth. It is established, therefore, that in a city where you see beggars, there are also thieves hiding in secret, and cut-purses, and temple-robbers, and the architects of all these crimes. It is certainly established. Do you not see that in cities governed by the few, there are destitute people? Nearly all of them, except for the rulers. Do we not therefore think that there are many criminals in such a city, armed with those very stings, whom the diligence and force of the government keep in check? We plainly think so. Is it not on account of

<margin>C</margin> a depraved education, a lack of discipline, and an unfair arrangement of the republic that we shall assert such men turn out that way? We shall. Such, then, will be the city subjected to the rule of the few, and it will be pressed by all these evils, and perhaps even more. Nearly so. Now let us consider the republic we have established, which they call the power of the few, which elects its rulers from a property assessment. After this, let us investigate how a man is made similar to it, and after he is made similar, what he is like. Just so. Is it not by this reason that he passes mostly from being ambitious to being a lover of the rule of the few? How? When some youth there first imitates his father and follows in his footsteps; then he sees him as one who has struck the city

<margin>D</margin> like a reef, suddenly fallen from the peak of dignity and scattering himself and all his things—whether after the dignity of a general and leader, or some other greatest magistracy—dragged into judgment by plotters, circumvented by false accusers, oppressed, cast out, and spoiled of his honors and patrimony. It is a likely thing. That man, O friend, having looked upon and endured these things, and having lost his patrimony, because of fear, immediately casts down from the throne of his soul that ambition and boldness, and having been made humble because of poverty, turns himself to profit-making. Living very meagerly, dryly, and sparingly, and vexing himself in going about his business, he gathers money. Do you not think such a

<margin>E</margin> man then places avarice and the desire for gain in that seat of the soul? And fashions within himself some "Great King"? And adorns him with royal ornaments: crowns, belts, buckles, fringes, and a Persian sword? Indeed. And here, he forces the rational power and the heat of spiritedness, cast down on the ground here and there, to serve this king. He permits them to inquire into and consider nothing else except how the most money can be gathered from the least. This part admires and honors nothing else except riches and the wealthy, nor does it seek dignity from any other thing than money, or if anything else contributes to that end. There is certainly no other change so swift and vehement as that of a youth from being ambitious to being a lover of

<margin>F</margin> money. Is not this man, then, a student of the rule of the few? The change of the man himself is similar to that of the Republic from which the power of the few emerged. Let us consider, then, whether he is similar. Let us consider. First, in that he makes much of money, he will be similar. Why not? Furthermore, also in that he is more parsimonious and intent on work, and satisfies only his necessary desires, but by no means indulges in other expenses, but restrains other appetites as if they were superfluous. Greatly so. Thus he lives more dryly and squalidly, increasing his family estate from all sides with the greatest parsimony, intent on heaping up a treasure, which kind of men the common people approve of. Will not this man be similar to that flawed Republic? It seems so to me. Money, therefore, is most honored both by every city of this kind and by this man. For neither has this man,

<margin>G</margin> as I think, applied his mind to discipline. Not as I think; for otherwise he would not have set a blind leader over himself. Very well, then. But notice this: do we not say that desires similar to the nature of drones are in him because of a lack of discipline—partly beggarly, partly criminal—held in check by force and other diligence? And most certainly. Do you know where to look to see their crimes? Where? At the guardianships of orphans, and if anything of that sort happens to them, where they might obtain the greatest license for injury. You tell the truth. Is it not established that in other business dealings, where such a man is held to be honest, while he seems to be just, he restrains the other depraved desires within himself with a certain equity of life? He does not obey for the reason that it is not better, nor does he tame them with reason, but trembles with necessity and fear concerning his remaining substance. In many cases, O friend, you will find, when it is necessary to spend another's money, desires very similar to a drone's. Most especially.

<meta>catchword: Most especially. Indeed, O friend, you will find in many, when...</meta>

<summary>Socrates describes the decay of the Timocratic man into the Oligarchic man, driven by the trauma of seeing his father lose his status and wealth. This new character prioritizes the accumulation of money above all else, suppressing his reason and honor in favor of miserly greed.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the transition in Book VIII of Plato's Republic, moving from the description of the "Oligarchic man" (who values wealth above all) to the birth of Democracy and the "Democratic man." In the previous page, Socrates established that a city ruled by the wealthy eventually produces "drones"—people who have lost their property and have nothing left but their "stings" (their resentment and debt).</meta>

# OF PLATO

<margin>A</margin> "Therefore, such a man will not be free from internal strife; he will not be a single individual, but a double one, possessing desires where the better ones generally dominate the worse." "That is so." "For this reason, I think he will be more composed than many others. However, the true virtue of a harmonious and consistent mind will fly far from him." "So it seems to me." "Furthermore, this parsimonious man will be a poor competitor in the city when it comes to any private victory or honorable ambition, since he is unwilling to spend money for the sake of fame or such contests. He fears awakening his expensive desires or calling them into the fight. By fighting with only a small portion of his resources, <margin>B</margin> in the manner of an oligarch, he is usually defeated, though he keeps his wealth." "Very much so." "Can we still doubt, then, that the parsimonious man and the money-maker is modeled after the city governed by the few?" "In no way." "After this, it seems we must investigate how a popular government <note>original: "popularis gubernatio" / δημοκρατία (dēmokratia); what we call Democracy.</note> is established and what its condition is, so that, recognizing the same condition in such a person, we may bring him to judgment." "Indeed, we shall continue our journey in that way." "Does the city not change from an oligarchy into a popular government in this way: because the citizens have proposed that the greatest good is to be as wealthy as possible?" <margin>C</margin> "How so?" "Because the rulers in such a state, dominating through their riches, neglect to pass laws restraining the profligacy and ruin of dissolute young men. They do this so that by buying up the property of such youths and lending to them at interest, they themselves may become even wealthier and more honored." "Most certainly." "It is therefore clear that it is impossible in a city to honor wealth and at the same time possess temperance <note>original: "temperantiam" / σωφροσύνη (sōphrosynē); a core Greek virtue meaning moderation, self-control, or soundness of mind.</note> among the citizens; of necessity, one is always neglected in favor of the other." "That is quite clear." "While they neglect the education of the youth in an oligarchy and allow them to live for pleasure, they often force <margin>D</margin> men who are not ungenerous to be reduced to poverty." "Indeed." "These people sit in the city, I believe, armed with stings <note>original: "aculeis armati" / κεκεντρωμένοι (kekentrōmenoi); referring back to the "drones" mentioned on the previous page—citizens who have lost their status and now seek revolution.</note>; some are burdened with debt, some are stripped of their honors, and some are oppressed by both evils. They lie in wait for those who they know have possessed their goods, and for others, and thus they plot revolution every day." "That is so." "But the money-makers, bent over their profits, seem not to notice these people. Instead, they wound anyone else who yields to them by injecting their silver, and by bringing back a massive offspring of interest <note>original: "fœnúfque" / τόκους (tokous); in Greek and Latin, the word for "interest" on a loan is the same as the word for "offspring" or "children." Plato is playing on the idea of money 'breeding' more money.</note> from the father, they fill the city with drones and beggars." "Most definitely." "Nor are they willing <margin>E</margin> to extinguish the fire of such a great evil by forbidding each person to deal with his own property as he pleases. Nor, on the other hand, do they prohibit such things through a second law." "According to which law?" "The one that follows closely after that, which forces citizens to take care for virtue. For if someone were to command that most voluntary contracts be made at the lender's own risk, they would gather money less shamelessly in the city, and fewer evils such as we have described would be born." "Entirely so." "But as it is, for these reasons, the rulers treat their subjects in this way in the city. As for themselves and their own children, they make the young ones delicate, soft, and idle, unable to endure any labor of mind or body, and succumbing to pleasures and pains." "Precisely." "And they themselves become such that they value nothing but profit, and have no more care for virtue than do the beggars." "Certainly." <margin>F</margin> "Therefore, when they are so prepared—whenever the rulers and the subjects meet one another, whether on journeys or in some other common business, or at public spectacles, or serving in the army together, whether sailing or fighting, or even watching one another in the midst of danger—the poor are by no means despised by the rich in these situations. On the contrary, frequently a poor man, lean and bronzed by the sun, when stationed in battle next to a wealthy man who has been nourished in the shade and is burdened with excess flesh—when he sees him out of breath and full of anxiety—will he not think that such men are rich only through our own cowardice, and will they not say to one another when they meet in private: 'Our masters are worth nothing'?" "I know well that they are accustomed to do so." <margin>G</margin> "Therefore, just as a weak and sickly body needs only a slight nudge from the outside to fall into disease, and sometimes even without any external cause it turns against itself, so too a city affected by these same evils, at the slightest provocation—whether one side brings in help from an oligarchy or the other from a democracy—falls sick and fights with itself. Often it is agitated by sedition even without external help." "Precisely." "Democracy, I believe, comes into being when the poor, having gained the victory, kill some of the wealthy and drive others into exile. To the rest, they grant an equal share of the government and offices; and for the most part, the magistrates in it are chosen by lot." <note>In ancient Athens, many government officials were chosen by a "lottery" (sortition) rather than election, to ensure equality among citizens.</note> "That is certainly the constitution of a democratic city, whether it is established by arms or by others leaving out of fear. What, then, will be the life of these citizens? What <margin>H</margin> kind of government will it be? For it is clear that a certain kind of democratic man will appear." "Clear indeed." "Will they not first of all be free, and the city be full of freedom and frankness of speech, and will there not be license for everyone to do whatever they wish?" "So it is said." "And where there is license,

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> (he said) "Very much so. Therefore, such a person would not be free from internal strife, nor would he be a single individual, but a double one. He would possess desires that, for the most part, have the better ones ruling over the worse." "It is so." "Because of these things, I think, such a person would be more self-controlled than many; however, the true virtue of a harmonious and tuned soul would escape far from him." "It seems so to me." "And indeed, the parsimonious man is a poor competitor in a city for any private victory or other fine ambition. He is unwilling to spend money for the sake of a good reputation or for such contests, fearing to awaken expensive desires and to call them into alliance and rivalry. <margin>B</margin> Fighting in the manner of an oligarch with only a few of his resources, he is mostly defeated, and yet he stays rich." "And very much so," he said. "Do we still doubt then," I said, "that the parsimonious man and the money-maker is ranked according to his similarity to the city governed by an oligarchy?" "Not at all," he said. "Next, it seems, we must consider democracy: in what manner it arises, and once it has arisen, what sort of character it has; so that we may in turn know the life of such a man and bring him before us for judgment." "Thus we shall proceed as we began." "Does it not change," I said, "in some such way from oligarchy to democracy, because of the greed for the proposed good—that one must become as rich as possible?" "How so?" "Since <margin>C</margin> the rulers in it are rulers because they possess much, they are unwilling to restrain by law those of the youth who become dissolute, preventing them from spending and destroying their own property. They do this so that by buying the belongings of such people and lending to them at interest, they may become even richer and more honored." "More than anything." "Is it not already clear in the city that it is impossible to honor wealth and at the same time sufficiently acquire self-control among the citizens, but it is necessary either to neglect the one or the other?" "It is fairly clear," he said. "By neglecting things in oligarchies and allowing people to become dissolute, they have sometimes forced men who are not without talent to become poor." "Very much so." <margin>D</margin> "These men sit, I think, in the city, both stung and armed—some owing debts, others having lost their citizen rights, and others both—hating and plotting against those who acquired their property and against the rest, being in love with revolution." "That is so." "But the money-makers, with their heads down, pretending not to see these people, continue to inject their silver into any of the remainder who yield to them. By bringing back the offspring of the debt—interest many times the principal—they create a great number of drones and beggars in the city." "How could they not?" he said. "And they are not willing," I said, "to extinguish such an evil as it spreads, either by preventing a person from <margin>E</margin> turning his property whatever way he wishes, or by this other law which dissolves such things." "By what law?" "The one that is second after that, forcing the citizens to care for virtue. For if it were commanded that a person enters into most voluntary contracts at his own risk, they would make money less shamelessly in the city, and fewer such evils as we have just mentioned would grow in it." "And much fewer," he said. "But now," I said, "for all these reasons, the rulers treat the subjects in the city in this way; and as for themselves and their own, do they not make the young men luxurious and idle toward the labors of both body and soul, and soft in resisting pleasures and pains, and lazy?" "What else?" "And they themselves, neglecting everything except money-making, have made <margin>F</margin> no more care for virtue than have the poor." "No indeed." "Thus prepared, whenever the rulers and the subjects encounter one another, either on journeys or in other associations, whether at festivals or on campaigns, or as shipmates or fellow soldiers, or when they observe one another in actual dangers, the poor are in no way despised by the rich. Instead, often a lean, poor man, tanned by the sun, stationed in battle beside a rich man who has been brought up in the shade and possesses much superfluous flesh, sees him full of shortness of breath and confusion. Do you not think he believes that such people are rich only through their own cowardice, and that they pass the word to one another when they meet in private: 'Our men are worth nothing'?" "I know well," he said, "that they do so." "Therefore, just as <margin>G</margin> a sickly body needs only a small push from outside to fall into illness, and sometimes even without external things it is at strife with itself, so also the city that is in that same state, from a small pretext brought from outside—either one side bringing in an alliance from an oligarchic city or the other from a democratic one—falls sick and fights with itself, and sometimes even without external help it is in a state of sedition?" "And very much so." "Democracy, I think, arises when the poor are victorious, killing some of the others and exiling others. To the rest, they give an equal share of the constitution and the offices, and for the most part, the offices in it are distributed by lot." "For that is," he said, "the establishment of democracy, whether it happens through arms or through the fear of those who have withdrawn. What then," I said, "is the manner in which these people live? And what sort of constitution is this? For it is clear that such a man will appear to be a democratic one." "Clear," he said. "First then, are they not free, and the city becomes full of freedom and frankness of speech; and there is license in it to do whatever one wants?" "So it is said, at least," he said. "And where there is <margin>H</margin> license, it is clear that each man would arrange his own life in the city in whatever way he chooses." "It appears so."

This creates a class of resentful poor who, realizing the rich are physically and morally weak, eventually overthrow them to establish a state based on total freedom and equality by lot.</summary>

# ON THE REPUBLIC, BOOK VIII

<margin>A</margin> ...are born in this city-state. "Very much so." "It seems, then, that this is the most beautiful of all constitutions; and like a cloak embroidered with every kind of flower <note>original: "pallium variis depictum coloribus" / ἱμάτιον ποικίλον (himation poikilon). Plato uses the metaphor of a multi-colored or 'dappled' garment to describe the chaotic variety of democracy.</note>, so this city, decorated with every kind of character, appears most beautiful indeed. And just as children and women delight in things that are multi-colored and diverse, so many people would judge this city to be the most beautiful because of its variety." "And they certainly would," he said. "Moreover, my blessed friend, it is a convenient place to look for a constitution." "Why so?" "Because it contains every kind of government within itself due to its liberty. It seems necessary for anyone who wishes to establish a city—<margin>B</margin> just as we were doing just now—to enter a democratic city and choose the constitutional arrangement that pleases him most, as if he had gone to a marketplace <note>original: "nundinas" / παντοπώλιον (pantopōlion). A 'general store' or 'fair' where one can shop for any style of life.</note> of constitutions, and having made his choice, he may then establish his own city." "Perhaps," he said, "he would not be at a loss for models." "And what of this? Is it not a sweet and divine life at first glance? You are not compelled to hold office in this city, even if you are qualified for it, nor to obey if you do not wish to, nor to go to war when others are at war, nor to keep the peace when others do, unless you desire peace? And even if some law forbids you from ruling or serving as a judge, you may nonetheless rule and judge if <margin>C</margin> it happens to please you?" "Perhaps it seems so at first," he said. "And what about the mildness shown to certain condemned men? Is it not elegant? Or have you not yet seen in such a city men condemned to death or exile who nevertheless remain and walk about in the open? And as if no one noticed or cared, they wander through the city like heroes <note>original: "instar heroum" / ὥσπερ ἥρως (hōsper hērōs). Here, 'hero' refers to the spirits of the dead who were thought to walk among the living unseen.</note> returning from the afterlife." "I have seen many," he said. "And the excessive indulgence of such a city, and its utter lack of small-mindedness—indeed, its contempt for the things we spoke of so solemnly when we were founding our city! We said that unless a man had a truly transcendent nature, he would never become a good man unless from his earliest childhood he played among beautiful things and practiced all such noble habits. But this city <margin>D</margin> tramples all that underfoot with a lofty spirit; it does not care what kind of pursuits a man comes from when he enters politics, but honors him simply if he says he is a friend to the masses." "A very generous spirit indeed," he said. "These and similar traits," I said, "are what democracy would have. It would be, as it seems, a pleasant form of government, without a master, and varied, distributing a certain equality to both equals and unequals alike." "You describe what is very well known." "Now consider," I said, "who such a man is in private. Or should we first investigate, as we did with the city, how he comes to be?" "Yes, certainly." "Does it not happen in this way? I suppose he would be the son of that parsimonious <term>parsimonious: extremely frugal or stingy, specifically referring here to the 'Oligarchic man' who only values money.</term> and oligarchic father, raised <margin>E</margin> under his father’s habits." "Why not?" "This son, by force, restrains those pleasures within himself that are spendthrift but not profit-making—those which are called 'unnecessary' desires." "That is clear," he said. "So that we do not speak in shadows, shall we first define which desires are necessary and which are not?" "I would like that," he said.

<margin>Which pleasures are necessary and which are not.</margin> "Those which we are unable to turn away would rightly be called necessary, as would those which benefit us when they are fulfilled. For it is necessary by our nature to seek both of these. Is it not?" "Entirely so." "Therefore, we shall rightly call them necessary." "Rightly." "And what of those that a man could rid himself of if he practiced from his <margin>F</margin> youth, and which, while present, do no good—or even do the opposite of good? If we said all these were unnecessary, would we not be speaking well?" "Very well." "Let us take an example of each so we may grasp them in general outline." "We should." "Would not the desire for eating—specifically for simple food and seasonings—so far as it leads to health and a good condition of the body, be necessary?" "I think so." "The use of basic food is necessary for two reasons: because it is beneficial and because life cannot continue without it." "Yes." "And the desire for seasoning is necessary insofar as it contributes to the body’s well-being." "Certainly." "But what of the desire that goes beyond these—for other kinds of food—which can be restrained from youth and, through education, be removed from most people? This desire is harmful to the body and harmful to the soul’s wisdom and temperance. Would it not rightly be called unnecessary?" "Most rightly." "And we can say that these latter desires are 'spendthrift,' while the former are <margin>G</margin> 'profit-making' because they are useful for our work." "Indeed." "And we shall say the same regarding sexual desires and the others." "The same." "And so, the man we recently called a 'drone' <note>original: "fucum" / κηφῆνα (kēphēna). In Plato's metaphor, a drone is a member of society who consumes resources without producing anything, often driven by unnecessary appetites.</note> is the one who is enslaved to such unnecessary pleasures and desires, while the man ruled by necessary ones is the parsimonious and oligarchic man." "Undoubtedly." "Now," I said, "let us say again how the democratic man comes from the oligarchic one. It seems to me it happens mostly in this way." "How?" "When a young man, raised—as we just said—without education and in a stingy manner, tastes the honey of the drones and associates with fierce and dangerous creatures who can provide all sorts of varied <margin>H</margin> and manifold pleasures. This, you must realize, is the origin of the change within him, from the oligarchic nature to the democratic one." "It must be so," he said. "And just as the city changed when one party received help from an outside alliance—like joining like—does the young man also change when a species of desires from the outside comes to the aid of one of the factions within him, being akin and similar to it?"

# THE WORKS OF PLATO

<page-num>498</page-num>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> "Quite so! And if some support for the oligarchic <term>Oligarchic: Relating to the rule of the few, usually defined by wealth and frugality.</term> part of his nature should come from his father or other relatives, through their warnings and rebukes, then a state of sedition, resistance, and an internal struggle against himself arises." "Indeed." "And sometimes, I believe, the democratic condition yields to the oligarchic state, and some of his desires either perish or are cast out because a certain sense of shame arises in the youth’s soul, through which order is restored." "That does happen sometimes." "But then, I suppose, other desires akin to those cast out are secretly nurtured, and because of the father's ignorance in education, they become many and powerful." "That is certainly the way it happens." "These then pull him back to the same old associations and, through secret connections, they breed a great multitude." "What is to stop them?" <margin>B</margin> "At last, I believe, they occupy the acropolis <note>original: "arcem" / ἀκρόπολιν. Plato uses the image of the 'high city' or 'citadel' to represent the seat of reason in the soul.</note> of the young man’s soul, sensing that it is empty of noble studies, honorable practices, and true principles—which are the best guardians and protectors in the minds of men beloved by the gods." "Most certainly." "Then, in their place, false and arrogant reasons and opinions rush up and seize that same location within him." "Very much so." "Does he not then return to those Lotus-eaters <note>original: "Lotophagos". A reference to Homer’s Odyssey; those who eat the lotus flower forget their home and purpose, much like the youth forgets his duty for pleasure.</note> and openly make his home there? And if any help for the frugal part of his soul should come from his family, those arrogant reasons bar the gates of the royal wall within him. They neither admit the supporting force itself, nor do they receive the 'ambassadors'—the warnings of older, private individuals. They themselves prevail in the battle. <margin>C</margin> Calling shame 'folly,' they drive it out as a dishonored exile; they call temperance 'cowardice,' and after insulting it, they cast it out. Modesty and moderation in spending they treat as 'rusticity' and 'meanness,' and they banish them beyond the borders with the help of many futile desires." "Most certainly." "When they have emptied and purged the soul of the man they have seized and initiated into these great mysteries, they then lead in Insolence, Anarchy, Prodigality, and Impudence, all shining and crowned with a great throng of followers. They praise and flatter them, <margin>D</margin> calling Insolence 'good breeding,' Anarchy 'liberty,' Prodigality 'magnificence,' and Impudence 'manhood.' Is it not in some such way," I asked, "that a young man changes from one nurtured on necessary desires to the liberation and release of unnecessary and futile pleasures?" "Yes, that is quite clear," he said. "After this, such a man lives on, I think, spending his money, labor, and time no more on necessary pleasures than on unnecessary ones. But if he is lucky and his madness does not go too far, and as he grows older the great tumult passes, he may readmit parts of the exiled virtues and not give himself entirely to the new arrivals. He establishes a sort of equality among his pleasures. <margin>E</margin> He hands over the command of himself to whichever pleasure happens to turn up, as if by lot, until it is satisfied, and then to another, neglecting none but nurturing all equally." "Indeed, that is how it happens." "But he does not accept true reason, nor does he admit it into his 'acropolis.' If anyone tells him that some pleasures belong to good and noble desires, while others belong to evil ones, and that the former should be practiced and honored while the latter should be restrained and mastered, he shakes his head at all this. He claims they are all alike and should be honored equally." "Indeed, a man in that state does exactly that." <margin>F</margin> "Does he not live from day to day, indulging the desire that happens to be present? At one time he is drunk and enchanted by the flute; then he drinks only water and starves himself; at another time he exercises in the gymnasium; then again he is idle and neglects everything; and sometimes he even dabbles in philosophy. Often he turns to politics and, jumping up, says and does whatever comes into his head. If he happens to admire soldiers, he is carried in that direction; if he admires merchants, he goes toward them. There is no order or necessity in his life; yet he calls this life pleasant, free, and blessed, and he follows it to the end." <margin>G</margin> "You have perfectly described the life of a man who makes no distinction in his way of living." "I believe," I said, "that this man is multifaceted and full of many different characters—beautiful and many-colored, just like that city-state we described. Many men and women would envy his life, as it contains so many models of constitutions and characters within itself." "That is it exactly." "Then let this man be set alongside democracy, as he may rightly be called the democratic man." "Let it be so." "It remains for us to discuss the most 'excellent' constitution and the most 'excellent' man: tyranny and the tyrant." "Quite so." "Come then, dear friend, let us see how tyranny arises. That it changes from democracy is almost obvious." "It is." "Does tyranny arise from democracy in the same way that democracy arose from oligarchy?" "How?" "The 'good' that they proposed to themselves in oligarchy—the thing that established it—was an excess of wealth. Was it not?" "Yes." <margin>H</margin> "An insatiable thirst for wealth and the neglect of everything else for the sake of making money is what destroyed it." "True." "And so, does the insatiable desire for what democracy defines as 'good' also destroy it?" "What do you say it defines as good?" "Liberty," I replied. "For in a democratic city, you would hear that this is the best of things..."

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> "Exactly so. And if some aid should come to the oligarchic element in him, perhaps from his father or other relatives, advising and reproaching him, then a factional split, a counter-resistance, and a battle within himself arises." "Indeed." "And sometimes, I think, the democratic part yields to the oligarchic; and some of the desires are destroyed, while others are cast out, as a kind of shame is born in the soul of the youth; and order is restored again." "It happens sometimes," he said. "But then, I think, other desires akin to those cast out are nurtured, and because of the father's lack of knowledge in upbringing, they become many and strong." "It usually happens that way," he said. "Therefore, they drew him back to the same companions, and by consorting with them in secret, they bred a multitude." "What then?" <margin>B</margin> "Finally, I believe, they seized the acropolis of the young man’s soul, perceiving it to be empty of knowledge, fine pursuits, and true words—which are the best sentinels and guardians in the minds of men dear to the gods." "Very much so," he said. "Then false and boastful words and opinions, I think, rushing up in their place, occupied that same spot in such a man." "Quite so," he said. "Does he not then go back to those Lotus-eaters and live there openly? And if any help for the frugal part of his soul arrives from his relatives, those boastful words close the gates of the royal wall within him, and they neither let in the alliance itself, nor do they receive the 'ambassadors'—the words of older private men. <margin>C</margin> They themselves hold power, having won the battle. Calling shame 'silliness,' they thrust it out as a dishonored exile; calling temperance 'unmanliness' and insulting it, they cast it out. Persuading him that moderation and orderly expenditure are 'rusticity' and 'illiberal' <term>Illiberal: Meaning 'not fitting for a free person'; stingy or unrefined.</term>, they banish them across the borders with many useless desires." "Very much so." "Having emptied and purged the soul of the one they have seized and are initiating into great rites, they then bring in Insolence, Anarchy, Wastefulness, and Impudence, brilliant and crowned with a great multitude, praising them and using soft names: calling Insolence 'education,' Anarchy 'liberty,' Wastefulness 'magnificence,' <margin>D</margin> and Impudence 'courage.' Is it not in this way," I asked, "that a young man changes from being raised in necessary desires to the liberation and relaxation of unnecessary and useless pleasures?" "Most clearly," he said. "After this, I think, such a man lives, spending his money, labor, and time no more on necessary than on unnecessary pleasures. But if he is lucky and is not driven beyond the point of Bacchic madness <note>original: "ekbakcheuthe" / ἐκβακχευθῇ. Refers to the wild, frenzied worship of Bacchus (Dionysus), god of wine.</note>, and as he grows older and the great tumult has passed, he may accept back some of the exiled virtues and not give himself entirely to the invaders. Instead, he places his pleasures on an equal footing <margin>E</margin> and lives, handing over the rule of himself to whichever pleasure happens along, as if by the lot, until it is satisfied, and then to another; he dishonors none, but feeds them all equally." "Entirely so." "And he does not accept true reason," I said, "nor does he let it into the citadel, even if someone says that some pleasures are of the noble and good desires, and others of the wicked; and that some should be practiced and honored, but others disciplined and enslaved. To all this he shakes his head and says that they are all alike and to be honored equally." "Indeed," he said, "he does that, being in such a state." <margin>F</margin> "And so," I said, "he lives his life day by day, indulging the desire that falls his way: now getting drunk to the sound of the flute, then drinking only water and slimming down; now exercising, then being idle and neglecting everything; then passing the time as if in philosophy. Often he plays the politician and, jumping up, says and does whatever happens to occur to him. And if he ever envies any military men, he is carried that way; or if he envies businessmen, he goes that way. No order or necessity is upon his life, but he calls this life pleasant, free, and blessed, and he uses it throughout." "You have certainly," he said, "described the life of a man of equal rights <term>Isonomikos: A man of 'equal law' or 'equal rights,' here used to mean a man who treats all his whims as equally valid.</term>." <margin>G</margin> "I believe," I said, "that this man is multifaceted, full of the most varied characters, and beautiful and many-colored like that city-state. Many men and women would envy him for his life, as he contains within himself the greatest number of examples of constitutions and manners." "That is how it is," he said. "Well then, shall such a man be ranked with democracy, since he would correctly be called a democratic man?" "Let him be so ranked," he said. "The most beautiful constitution and the most beautiful man remain for us to discuss: tyranny and the tyrant." "Absolutely," he said. "Come then, what is the manner of tyranny's birth, my dear friend? That it changes from democracy is fairly clear." "Clear." "Then does tyranny arise from democracy in some way the same as democracy did from oligarchy?" <margin>H</margin> "How?" "That which they proposed as 'good,'" I said, "and through which oligarchy was established—this was an excess of wealth. Was it not?" "Yes." "Therefore, the insatiable desire for wealth, and the neglect of everything else because of money-making, destroyed it." "True," he said. "Does then the insatiable desire for that which democracy defines as 'good' also dissolve it?" "What do you say it defines as such?" "Liberty," I said. "For in a city under a democracy..."

<summary>Socrates describes the "democratic man" as a person who lacks internal discipline, treating all desires as equal and shifting between various hobbies and lifestyles. He concludes by suggesting that the same insatiable desire for "liberty" that defines democracy eventually leads to its collapse into tyranny.</summary>
