<meta>This page continues the discussion from Book VIII of Plato's Republic, where Socrates and Glaucon examine the transition from a democratic state to tyranny. The previous page detailed the rise of the "democratic man" and his embrace of varied, unnecessary pleasures; here, the focus shifts to how the excess of liberty within the city itself causes its eventual collapse.</meta>

# ON THE REPUBLIC, BOOK VIII.

<page-num>499</page-num>

<margin>A</margin> "You will hear that this is the most beautiful state, and for this reason, it is the only one in which a man who is naturally free <note>Socrates is being ironic here, suggesting that while democracy seems "beautiful" and "free," its lack of structure is its downfall.</note> would find it worthy to live." "Indeed," he said, "that is a very common saying." <margin>B</margin> "Is it not then," I asked, "as I was about to say, that the insatiable desire for this very thing—liberty—and the neglect of all other things, changes this form of government and prepares it to need a tyranny?" "How so?" he asked. "Whenever, I believe, a democratic city, thirsting for liberty, happens to get bad cup-bearers <note>original: "κακῶν οἰνοχόων" / "malos pincernas". Leaders who provide the people with too much "unmixed" freedom, leading to a kind of political drunkenness.</note> as its leaders, and it becomes intoxicated with more unmixed freedom than is proper, it then punishes its rulers unless they are very mild and grant a great deal of license, accusing them of being foul and oligarchic <term>Oligarchic: Favoring the rule of a wealthy few over the many.</term>." "They certainly do that," he said. <margin>B</margin> "Furthermore, it insults those who are obedient to the rulers as being servile and worthless men. It praises and honors, both privately and publicly, the rulers who act like subjects and the subjects who act like rulers. Is it not inevitable that in such a city, the spirit of liberty goes to every extreme?" "How could it not?" "And this lack of authority, my friend," I said, "creeps into private homes and finally even spreads among the animals." "How do we mean such a thing?" he asked. "For instance," I said, "a father becomes accustomed to being like a child and fears his sons, while the son becomes like a father and neither feels shame nor fears his parents, all so that he may be 'free.' The resident alien <margin>C</margin> is made equal to the citizen, and the citizen to the alien, and the stranger likewise." "That is what happens," he said. "These and other similar small things occur," I said. "In such a city, the teacher fears and flatters the students, while the students despise their teachers and likewise their tutors. To put it briefly, the young compare themselves to their elders and contend with them in words and deeds, while the old men, stooping to the level of the young, are filled with playfulness and wit, imitating the youth so that they do not appear unpleasant or authoritative." "Most certainly," he said. <margin>D</margin> "But the ultimate extreme of liberty for the multitude, my friend, occurs in such a city when the purchased slaves, both male and female, are no less free than those who bought them. And we almost forgot to mention how much equality and liberty exists between women and men, and men and women." "Shall we not say, according to Aeschylus <note>Aeschylus was a famous Greek tragic playwright; the phrase "whatever comes to the mouth" refers to speaking one's mind freely.</note>, 'what now comes to our lips'?" "Certainly," I said, "and that is what I am saying. Indeed, no one who has not experienced it would believe how much more free the domestic animals are here than elsewhere. For truly, even the dogs, according to the proverb, become <margin>Proverb</margin> like their mistresses; and even the horses and donkeys are accustomed to walk with great freedom and dignity along the roads, bumping into anyone they meet if he does not step aside. Everything is thus filled with the spirit of liberty." "You are telling me my own dream," he said, "for I often experience this myself when traveling to the countryside." <margin>E</margin> "Do you see then," I said, "the sum total of all these things gathered together? It makes the souls of the citizens so tender that if anyone suggests even a little bit of servitude, they become angry and cannot endure it. For in the end, as you know, they disregard even the laws, written or unwritten, so that no one may be a master over them in any way." "I know it well," he said. "This then, my friend," I said, "is that beautiful and youthful beginning from which tyranny is born, as it seems to me." "Youthful indeed," he said, "but what follows this?" "The same disease," I said, "which broke out in the oligarchy and destroyed it, also breaks out here, but with more power and strength due to the excessive license, and it enslaves the democracy. In truth, any excess usually leads to a great change in the opposite direction—in the seasons, in plants, in bodies, and <margin>F</margin> most of all in political systems." "That is likely," he said. "For excessive liberty seems to change into nothing else but excessive slavery, both for the individual and the city." "That is likely." "Thus, it is natural," I said, "that tyranny is established from no other system than democracy; from the highest liberty, the greatest and most savage slavery arises." "That follows reason," he said. "But that was not, I think, what you were asking. You asked what the disease is that grows in both oligarchy and democracy and reduces the latter to slavery." "You speak the truth," he said. <margin>G</margin> "I was speaking," I said, "of that class of idle and extravagant men—the most courageous of them being the leaders and the more cowardly being the followers. We compared them to drones <term>Drones: Socrates uses the metaphor of "drones" (unproductive bees) to describe citizens who do not contribute to society but instead agitate or consume its resources.</term>, some with stings and others without." "And rightly so," he said. "These two types," I said, "disturb every political system they enter, just as phlegm and bile <note>original: "pituita ac bilis". Ancient medicine viewed health as a balance of fluids; an excess of phlegm or bile caused disease.</note> disturb the body. A good physician and lawgiver of a city must take precautions against them beforehand, no less than a wise beekeeper—first, so that they do not arise in the city, and if they do, so that they are cut out as quickly as possible, along with their honeycombs." "Yes, by Zeus," he said, "entirely so." <margin>H</margin> "Now then," I said, "let us take it this way, so that we may see more clearly what we desire." "How?" "Let us divide the democratic city into three parts in our argument, just as it is in reality. One part is this class of 'drones' which grows through license no less than in the oligarchy." "It is so." "But it is much fiercer in this city than in the other." "In what way?" "There, because it is held in contempt and excluded from office, it becomes weak and unexercised. But in a democracy, this class is the one that presides over almost everything. The fiercest part of it speaks and acts, while the rest sits buzzing around the platforms and does not tolerate anyone who speaks otherwise. Consequently, all things—"

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> "You will hear, and therefore in this city alone it is fitting for that man to live who is free by nature. Certainly that name 'liberty' is praised more frequently in this city. Is it not what I was going to say—that the insatiable desire for this very thing, and the neglect of others, changes this republic and forces it to stand in need of tyranny?" "By what means?" "When, namely, a popular state thirsting for liberty finds bad cup-bearers presiding over it, and it gorges itself more profusely than is proper and becomes drunken, and it punishes the leaders as if they were too rigid and desiring the rule of the few, unless they are very mild and grant a great deal of license. Thus it truly happens. <margin>B</margin> And yet it rebukes those who obey the leaders as if they were servile men of no value; but leaders who are equal to subjects, and subjects equal to leaders, it praises and honors both privately and publicly. Is it not necessary in such a city for men to reach the summit of liberty?" "Without a doubt." "And does this ingrained license, impatient of obedience, my friend, creep into private homes and extend even all the way to the beasts? In what way do we say this? For example, if a father becomes like his son and fears his sons, and the son is equal to the father, neither respecting his parents nor fearing them, so that he may be most free; <margin>C</margin> furthermore, the resident alien is made equal to the citizen, and the citizen to the resident alien, and the stranger likewise." "So it happens. These and other similar minor things occur. Truly, in that city the teacher fears his students and flatters them, the students despise the teachers and similarly the tutors. And to speak briefly, the younger make themselves equal to the elders. The elders, moreover, sitting together with the younger and on equal footing, oppose them with both words and deeds; like jesters, they delight them with witticisms, lest they appear severe and too imperious." "Very much so." <margin>D</margin> "But the extreme liberty of the common people, my friend, is how great in such a city, when even the purchased slaves are no less free than the buyers; and how much equality and liberty there is for women toward men, and men toward women, we have almost forgotten to say. Shall we not say, according to Aeschylus, what now comes to our mouth? Just so, I say, and I indeed say this: truly the beasts which are nourished by men, how much freer they are in this city than elsewhere, no one would believe unless they had experienced it. For even the little dogs, as the proverb has it, are such as their mistresses are. <margin>Proverb</margin> And the horses and donkeys are rendered such, having been accustomed to walk very freely and haughtily through the streets, so that they make a charge against anyone they meet, unless he yields. And all other things are done with the greatest license." "You are telling me my own dream; for these things frequently happen to me as I am setting out for the countryside." <margin>E</margin> "Do you see where the sum of all these things mentioned above finally tends? Thus, indeed, the delicate mind of the citizens is rendered such that if anyone brings even a little bit of servitude, they bear it poorly and do not tolerate it. At last, they truly despise all laws, both written and unwritten, lest any master preside over them. That is indeed manifest. This, my friend, is that remarkable and elegant republic from which, as it seems to me, tyranny is born." "Elegant indeed, but to what end is this?" "Furthermore, the disease which, creeping into the power of the few, undermined it—the same disease, budding and increasing in this state from excessive license, brings the popular city under the yoke of slavery. And in summary, every excess is accustomed to turn completely into its opposite, in seasons, in trees, in animals, and <margin>F</margin> most of all in republics." "Not without justice." "For excessive liberty seems to turn into nothing else than excessive slavery, both privately and publicly." "Certainly that is consistent. Therefore, I was not speaking without reason when I said that tyranny arises from no other republic than the popular one: from extreme liberty, the most grave and most savage slavery." "So reason shows. But not this, I believe, were you asking, but rather what is that same disease born in the power of the few and in the popular government that reduces it to slavery." "You tell the truth." <margin>G</margin> "I was speaking of the race of idle and prodigal men, part of whom are stronger and more manly, part more cowardly; and the former indeed lead, while the latter follow—these men we compared to drones in the previous parts: those indeed to stinging drones, these to drones lacking stings." "And deservedly. These indeed, in whatever city they may be, disturb it, just as phlegm and bile disturb the body. These a good physician and founder of laws must take precaution against from afar, no less than a skillful tender of bees: first, so that they do not arise in the city; but if they do arise, that they are cut out immediately along with the honeycombs themselves." "Thus it must be done. Let us then take it so, that what we seek may be more clearly understood." "In what way? Let us divide the popular city, as it is in reality, into three parts. One indeed is this genus which is born in it because of license, no less than in the power of the few." <margin>H</margin> "It is so." "But it is far more fierce in this city than in that one. For what reason? There, because it is held in contempt and repelled from magistracies, it becomes weak because of idleness. But in the popular city, that whole genus, with few exceptions, presides, and the fiercest part of it speaks and acts; the other part, clinging near the tribunals, whispers and does not tolerate it if anyone has said otherwise. Wherefore all things—"

<summary>Socrates describes how an obsession with absolute liberty in a democracy leads to a total collapse of social order—affecting families, schools, and even animals—which inevitably results in the rise of tyranny as "extreme liberty" transforms into "extreme slavery." He introduces the metaphor of "drones" (idle, agitating men) as the social disease that destabilizes both oligarchies and democracies.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from Book VIII of the Republic. Having established that democracy's obsession with "unmixed" liberty leads to chaos, Socrates now describes the three classes that emerge in such a state and how the "protector of the people" inevitably transforms into a tyrant.</meta>

# PLATO'S WORKS

<margin>A</margin> ...with few exceptions, are administered in a city of this kind. "Exactly so," he said. Now, another such group is always being separated from the multitude. "Which one?" Since everyone is pursuing profit, those who are naturally most orderly generally become the wealthiest. "That is likely." It is from these, I believe, that the greatest and easiest supply of "honey" <note>original: "mellis" / "μέλι". Plato uses honey as a metaphor for the wealth or capital accumulated by the industrious class, which the "drones" seek to harvest.</note> is squeezed for the drones. "How indeed," he asked, "could one squeeze honey from those who possess so little?" Such wealthy people, I think, are called the "drones' pasture." "Almost certainly," he said. The people would be the third class, consisting of those who work for themselves, stay out of trouble, and do not possess very much. This class is the most numerous and the most powerful in a democracy whenever it is assembled. "It is," he said, "but it does not often wish to do so unless it gets a share of the
<margin>B</margin> honey." Does it not always get a share, I asked, insofar as those in power are able to despoil the wealthy and distribute the spoils to the people, while keeping the most for themselves? "Indeed, in that way it does get a share," he said. Those who are thus plundered are forced to defend themselves by speaking before the people and acting as best they can. "Of course." They are then accused by the others—even if they have no desire for revolution—of plotting against the people and being oligarchs <term>Oligarchs: Those who believe power should rest with a small, wealthy elite.</term>. "What else?" Finally, when they see the people attempting to do them wrong—not willingly, but through ignorance and being deceived by the slanderers—then indeed, whether they want to or not, they truly become oligarchic. It is not of their own accord, but because that stinging drone <note>The "drone" here refers to the parasitic political agitator who goads the classes against one another.</note> implants this evil in them. "Very much so." Then come accusations, lawsuits, and mutual struggles. "Exactly." And the people are always accustomed to set up one man as their special protector, and to nurture him and make him grow great. "They are." It is clear then, I said,
<margin>C</margin> that whenever a tyrant arises, he sprouts from this "root of protection" and from nowhere else. "That is quite clear." What then is the beginning of the change from a protector into a tyrant? Is it not clear that it happens when the protector begins to do what is told in the myth concerning the temple of Lycaean Jove <note>original: "Iouis Lycæi" / "Διὸς τοῦ Λυκαίου". This refers to the cult of Zeus on Mount Lykaion in Arcadia, where legend claimed that one who tasted human flesh mixed with animal sacrifice would be turned into a wolf.</note> in Arcadia? "What is that?" he asked. The story goes that whoever tastes human entrails, chopped up with those of other victims, is of necessity turned into a wolf. Have you not heard the story? "I have." In the same way, when this leader of the people, finding the crowd entirely obedient to him, does not abstain from the blood of his own tribe, but brings men to trial on false charges (as they are fond of doing) and stains himself with unholy murder, extinguishing a man's life and tasting with unholy tongue and mouth the blood of his kinsmen—he then exiles some, kills others, and hints at the abolition of debts and the redistribution of land. Is it not then necessary and fated that such a man either be destroyed by his enemies or become a tyrant,
<margin>D A wolf from a man.</margin> and turn from a man into a wolf? "It is absolutely necessary." This is the man, I said, who becomes the leader of the faction against the wealthy. "The very one." Does he not then, having been driven out and returning despite his enemies, return as a finished tyrant? "Clearly." And if they
<margin>E</margin> are unable to expel him or kill him by slandering him to the city, they then plot to do away with him by a violent and secret death. "That is certainly how it usually happens," he said. Hence follows that famous tyrannical request which all who have reached this stage devise: they ask the people for certain bodyguards, so that the "helper of the people" may be safe for them. "Exactly," he said. And the people give them, I believe, being afraid for him but quite secure for themselves. "Very much so." When a man of wealth—who, because of his money, is considered an enemy of the people—notices this, then indeed, my friend, according to the oracle given to Croesus <note>Croesus was the King of Lydia; the oracle told him that if he crossed the river Hermus to attack the Persians, he would destroy a great empire (which turned out to be his own).</note>, "he flees to the pebbly Hermus, nor does he stay, nor is he ashamed to be called a coward." "He certainly wouldn't be ashamed a second time," he said. And if anyone
<margin>F</margin> is caught, I believe, he is put to death. "Necessarily." But that protector of the state does not lie "great in his greatness," <note>original: "magnus magnificè" / "μέγας μεγαλωστὶ". A Homeric allusion to a fallen hero; Plato is saying the tyrant does not fall heroically but stands tall over the ruins of others.</note> but having overthrown many others, he stands in the chariot of the state, a finished tyrant instead of a protector. "How could he not?" he said. Shall we then describe the happiness of this man, and of the city in which such a mortal arises? "By all means,"
<margin>G</margin> he said, "let us do so." In the first days and for some time, does he not smile and greet everyone he meets? He says he is no tyrant, and promises many things both privately and publicly; he frees people from debts, distributes land to the people and to those around him, and pretends to be gracious and fatherly to everyone. "He must," he said. But once he has reconciled with some of his external enemies and destroyed others, and there is quiet from them, his first act is always to stir up some war, so that the people may be in need of a leader. "That is likely." And also so that, by paying war taxes, they may become poor and be forced to attend to their daily needs, and thus plot against him less. "Clearly." And if he suspects any of having free spirits and not being likely to allow his rule, he can find a pretext to destroy them by exposing them to the enemy. For all these reasons, it is necessary for a tyrant
<margin>H</margin> to be always stirring up new wars. "Necessary." In doing this, he is bound to become more hated by the citizens. "How could he not?" And is it not likely that some of those who helped set him up and who are in power—those who happen to be the most courageous—will speak out both to him and to one another, criticizing what is happening?

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...by such [men] is administered in such a state, with few exceptions. "Quite so," he said. Something else of this sort is always separated from the multitude. "What sort?" When all are engaged in money-making, those who are most orderly by nature generally become the wealthiest. "Likely." It is from these, I think, that the most "honey" is harvested for the drones, and it is most easily squeezed from them. "How indeed," he said, "could one squeeze it from those who have little?" Such people, I think, are called "the wealthy," the pasture of the drones. "Pretty much," he said. The people would be the third class, as many as are manual laborers and stay out of politics, not possessing very much; which is the most numerous and most sovereign class in a democracy, whenever it is assembled. "It is," he said, "but it does not often wish to do this unless it receives some share of the honey." Does it not always receive a share, I said, insofar as
<margin>B</margin> those who stand at the head are able to take away the property of those who have it, and by distributing it to the people, keep the most for themselves? "It does indeed receive a share," he said, "in that way." Those from whom it is taken are forced, I think, to defend themselves by speaking before the people and acting as they are able. "Of course." Then they are accused by the others, even if they do not desire revolution, of plotting against the people and being oligarchs. "What then?" And so finally, when they see the people attempting to do them wrong—not willingly, but out of ignorance and being deceived by the slanderers—then indeed, whether they wish it or not, they become truly oligarchic. Not willingly, but this evil is also planted in them by that drone, who stings them. "Exactly so." Then come impeachments and trials and struggles against one another. "Very much so." Is it not then the custom of the people always to set up one man as their special leader, and to nurture him and make him great? "It is the custom." This then is clear, I said,
<margin>C</margin> that whenever a tyrant grows, he sprouts from a "protector" root and from nowhere else. "Very clear." What then is the beginning of the change from protector to tyrant? Is it not clear that it is when the protector begins to do the same thing as in the myth told about the temple of Lycaean Zeus in Arcadia? "What is that?" he said. That whoever tastes of human entrails, when one piece is mixed in with those of other victims, must of necessity become a wolf. Or have you not heard the story? "I have." Is it not then the same with one who, as leader of the people, taking hold of a very compliant mob, does not keep himself from kindred blood, but by unjustly accusing them (as they are wont to do) and bringing them into court, commits murder, doing away with a man's life, and with unholy tongue and mouth tastes the blood of a kinsman, and exiles men and kills them, and hints at the abolition of debts and redistribution of land—is it not then necessary for such a man after this, and his fate, either to be destroyed by his enemies or to be a tyrant and become a wolf from a man? "Very much so," he said.
<margin>D</margin> This is the man, I said, who becomes the faction-leader against those who have property. "This is he." Does he then, having been driven out and returning in spite of his enemies, return as a finished tyrant? "Clearly." But if they are unable to drive him out, or
<margin>E</margin> kill him by slandering him to the city, they plot to kill him by a secret, violent death. "It usually happens that way," he said. Then those who have advanced to this point all devise that notorious tyrannical request—to ask the people for certain bodyguards of his person, so that the "helper of the people" may be safe for them. "Quite so," he said. And they give them, I think, fearing for him but confident for themselves. "Very much so." And when a man who has money sees this, and along with his money the reputation of being a hater of the people, then indeed, my friend, according to the oracle given to Croesus, "he flees to the pebbly Hermus, and does not stay, nor is he ashamed to be a coward." "For he would not," he said, "be ashamed a second time." But
<margin>F</margin> he who is caught, I think, I said, is given over to death. "Necessarily." But that protector himself of the city—it is clear that he does not "lie in his great majesty," but having cast down many others, he stands in the chariot of the city, a finished tyrant instead of a protector. "What else could happen?" he said. Let us then describe the happiness, I said, of the man and of the city in which such a mortal arises.
<margin>G</margin> "By all means," he said, "let us describe it." Does he not then, I said, in the first days and for a time, smile upon and greet everyone he meets, and say he is no tyrant, and promise many things both privately and publicly? And he frees men from debts and distributes land to the people and to those around him, and pretends to be gracious and fatherly to all? "He must," he said. But when, I think, he is reconciled with his external enemies—having destroyed some and come to terms with others—and there is quiet from them, he first of all always stirs up some wars, so that the people may be in need of a leader. "That is likely." And also so that by paying contributions they may become poor and be forced to attend to their daily needs, and thus plot against him less. "Clearly." And if he suspects any, I think, of having free thoughts and not being likely to allow him to rule, he can destroy them with a pretext by giving them up to the enemy. For all these reasons, it is always necessary for a tyrant to stir up war. "It is
<margin>H</margin> necessary." And while doing this, he is more ready to be hated by the citizens. "How could he not be?" And do not some of those who helped set him up and who are in power speak out boldly both to him and to one another, rebuking the...

<summary>This page describes the transition from a democratic protector to a tyrant, utilizing the metaphor of "drones" feeding on "honey" (wealth) and the mythological transformation of a man into a wolf. It highlights how the tyrant creates a cycle of war and paranoia to maintain control over the populace.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from Book VIII of the Republic. Socrates is describing how the "protector of the people" becomes a tyrant by systematically eliminating those who might oppose him, eventually turning even on the people who brought him to power.</meta>

# ON THE REPUBLIC BOOK VIII.

<margin>A</margin> ...we might recognize those who happen to be the most courageous. "It is likely," he said. The tyrant must then remove all of these people from the scene if he intends to rule, until he leaves behind no one—friend or foe—who is of any worth. "That is clear." He must therefore keep a sharp eye out to see who is brave, who is high-minded, who is wise, and who is rich. Such is his "happiness" <note>original: "εὐδαίμων" / "beatus". Socrates uses this ironically; the tyrant's life is actually one of constant fear.</note> that he is forced, whether he wants to or not, to be an enemy to all these and to plot against them until he has "purged" the city. "A fine purgation indeed!" he remarked. "Yes," I said, "but the opposite of what doctors do to the body. For doctors remove the worst and leave the best, but the tyrant does the opposite." "It seems he must," he said, "if he is to remain in power." "Then he is bound by a blessed necessity," I said, "which commands him either to live amongst a crowd of worthless people—and be hated by them—or not to live at all." "Such is his condition," he replied.

<margin>B</margin> "Is it not true, then, that the more he is hated by the citizens for doing these things, the more numerous and faithful bodyguards <term>Bodyguards: original "δορυφόρων" / "satellitibus", literally 'spear-bearers'. In a Greek context, this was the hallmark of a tyrant.</term> he will require?" "How could he not?" "Who then are these faithful ones, and from where will he summon them?" "Many will come flying to him of their own accord," he said, "if he offers them pay." "By the dog!" <note>A common oath of Socrates, used here to express astonishment or emphasis.</note> I exclaimed, "you seem to be talking about more 'drones' again—foreigners from all over the place." "You have the truth of it," he said.

<margin>C</margin> "But would he not also want people from right here?" "How?" "By taking the slaves away from the citizens, granting them freedom, and making them part of his own bodyguard." "Most certainly," he said, "since these are his most faithful followers." "What a blessed thing a tyrant is," I said, "if he uses such friends and faithful men after having destroyed those former citizens." "Indeed," he said, "he uses such as these." "And these companions admire him," I said, "and the new citizens <note>In this context, the freed slaves and mercenaries who replaced the old citizen body.</note> associate with him, while the decent men hate and avoid him." "Why wouldn't they?" "It is not for nothing," I said, "that tragedy is thought to be a wise art, and Euripides to be excellent in it." "Why is that?" "Because he uttered this phrase of deep meaning: 'Tyrants are wise through the company of the wise' <note>original: "σοφοὶ τύραννοί εἰσι τῇ τῶν σοφῶν συνουσίᾳ". This was a well-known line from a lost play, often used to mock the way poets flattered rulers.</note>. He clearly meant that these 'wise' ones are the people he associates with." "And he praises tyranny as something god-like," he said, "along with many other things said by him and the other poets." "Therefore," I said, "since the tragic poets are wise, they will forgive us—and those who govern as we do—if we do not admit them into our state, because they are singers of the praises of tyranny."

<margin>D</margin> "I think," he said, "that those among them who are more refined will forgive us. But," I said, "they go around to other cities, gathering crowds, hiring great, loud, and persuasive voices, and they draw the states toward tyranny and democracy." "Very much so." "And furthermore, they receive pay and are honored, most of all, as is expected, by tyrants, and secondly by democracy. But the higher they go up the steep slope of political systems, the more their honor fails, as if it were unable to proceed from shortness of breath." "Exactly so."

<margin>E</margin> "But now," I said, "we have wandered from the point. Let us speak again of that 'fine' and numerous and diverse army of the tyrant, which is never the same: how will it be fed?" "It is clear," he said, "that if there are sacred treasures in the city, he will spend them, as long as the proceeds from what is sold last, requiring the people to pay fewer taxes." "And what happens when these funds fail?" "Clearly," he said, "he and his drinking companions, his associates, and his mistresses will be fed from his father’s estate." "I understand," I said, "the people who gave birth to the tyrant will feed him and his companions." "They must." "What do you mean?" I asked. "What if the people are indignant and say that it is not right for a grown son to be fed by his father, but rather the opposite, for the father to be fed by the son? And that they did not give birth to him and set him up for this: so that when he grew up, they themselves would be enslaved to their own slaves, along with these others? Instead, they intended to be set free from the wealthy and 'the good and beautiful' <term>The good and beautiful: original "καλῶν κἀγαθῶν", a Greek idiom for the aristocratic upper class.</term> by his leadership. And now they command him and his companions to leave the city, just as a father might drive a son and his rowdy drinking buddies out of the house!"

<margin>F</margin> "By Zeus!" he said, "the people will then finally realize what kind of creature they have been raising, embracing, and increasing; and they will see that they are the weaker ones trying to drive out the stronger."

<margin>G</margin> "What are you saying?" I asked. "Will the tyrant dare to use force against his 'father,' and if he does not obey, will he strike him?" "Yes," he said, "after he has taken away his weapons." "You are describing the tyrant as a patricide," I said, "and a harsh caretaker of the elderly. And, as it seems, this would now be tyranny in its admitted form. As the saying goes, the people, in fleeing the smoke of the slavery of free men, have fallen into the fire of the mastery of slaves. Instead of that great and untimely liberty, they have put on the harshest and bitterest of slaveries—the slavery to slaves." "That is exactly how it happens," he said. "Well then," I said, "shall we not have spoken appropriately if we say we have sufficiently explained how tyranny arises from democracy, and what it is like when it has arisen?" "Very sufficiently," he said.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...disapprove, especially those who are of a more high-minded spirit. It is likely. It follows that the tyrant must remove all these people from the midst if he is to rule, until he leaves no one among his friends or enemies who is of any importance. This is indeed manifest. It is necessary, therefore, for him to keenly inspect who is brave, who is magnanimous, who is wise, or who is wealthy. Indeed, he is so "blessed" that, whether he wants to or not, he will be an enemy to these and plot against them until he has purged the city. You describe a truly remarkable purgation. It is clearly the opposite of the purgation used by doctors. For doctors cleanse from the body that which is the worst and leave that which is best. The tyrant does the opposite. He is indeed
<margin>B</margin> forced to act this way if he is to rule. He is bound by a truly "blessed" necessity which commands him either to live his life with many wicked people—and even be hated by them—or not to live at all. Such is indeed his condition. Is it not true that the more he is hated by the citizens while doing these things, the more numerous and faithful guards he requires? What prevents it? Who then are most faithful to him? From where will he summon them? Many will fly to him from everywhere, lured by pay. You seem to be talking about "drones" again, by the Dog—some foreigners flowing together from various nations. You see it correctly. But who from among the locals? Would there not be some, if he 
<margin>C</margin> wished? How? Namely, if he takes the slaves away from the citizens, grants them liberty, and enlists them into the bodyguard of his own service. Very much so, since these are the most faithful to him. What a magnificent possession of a tyrant you describe, if indeed he uses such friends and faithful men after he has destroyed those former ones. Nevertheless, he uses such as these. And his associates admire him, and new citizens converse with him, but good men hate and flee from him. What forbids it? It is not without reason, then, that tragedy seems to be a wise craft, and in it Euripides seems to excel. For what reason? Because he sang this with a profound mind: "Tyrants are wise by the company of the wise," and he said these are the wise ones who associate with them. Furthermore, he extols tyranny as if it were a divine thing; and many other things are said by him and the other poets. Truly,
<margin>D</margin> the tragic poets, as wise men, will forgive us, I think, and those who govern the republic just as we do, if we do not admit them into our republic, being as they are the praisers of tyranny. They will forgive us, I suppose, whoever among them are more refined men. But they go around other cities, gathering a crowd with excellent, grand, and plausible voices for which there is no lack of reward; they drag republics toward tyranny and the popular state. Forcefully. Do they not receive a price for these things and are honored, first as is likely by tyrants, and then also by that popular republic? But truly, the higher they ascend toward the steep summit of republics, the more their honor fails, like one who is exhausted by frequent panting and is unable to proceed. So it is, indeed. But lest we wander further now that we have digressed, let us say from where the tyrant shall feed that "fine" army of his, so
<margin>E</margin> numerous, diverse, and always changing. It is established first that if there are any sacred riches in the city, he will seize them and consume them as long as those things which are sold suffice, while he demands lighter tributes from the common people. What if these riches fail? It is clear that he himself, his colleagues, his companions, and his harlots—both boys and women—will be fed from his father's estate. I understand indeed that the people who fathered the tyrant will nourish him and his friends. So it is forced. But what if the
<margin>F</margin> people are angered and say that it is not fair for a grown son to be nourished any longer by his father, but on the contrary, the father by the son; and that they did not create him for this, so that when the son was grown, the father himself, serving his own slave, should nourish both him and his slaves, and all the others flowing in from everywhere as his supporters? Rather, they intended that by his leadership they should be freed from those wealthy men who are considered "the good and beautiful" in the city. And thus the people might order him to depart from the city, along with his friends, just as a father might drive a son from the house together with a crowd of revelers. By Jove, the people will then finally recognize what they are, and in what kind of beast they took delight while they were fathering and educating it, and how they—though weaker—try to cast out one who is more powerful. What do you say?
<margin>G</margin> Will the tyrant dare to bring force against his father, and if he does not obey, to strike him? Yes indeed, for he will take away his weapons. You say then that the tyrant is a patricide and a harsh nurturer of old age. And as it seems, this is specifically tyranny. And as it is said, the people, fleeing the smoke of the slavery of free men, fall into the flame of servile domination, undergoing the harshest and bitterest slavery of slaves in place of that immense and unseasonable liberty. So it happens, indeed. Shall we not then have correctly stated that we have sufficiently discussed how tyranny is born from popular government, and what it is like when it is born? Very sufficiently indeed.

<summary>Socrates describes the final descent of a democracy into tyranny, where the tyrant purges the city of all virtuous men, frees slaves to serve as his guards, and eventually turns violently against the people who first empowered him.</summary>

<meta>This page marks the beginning of Book IX of Plato's Republic. It follows the conclusion of Book VIII, where Socrates described the transition from democracy to tyranny. Here, the focus shifts from the political state to the individual soul of the tyrant.</meta>

# OF PLATO ON THE REPUBLIC
## Or,
## ON JUSTICE,
### THE NINTH DIALOGUE.

# OF PLATO ON THE REPUBLIC,
## OR,
## ON JUSTICE,
### THE NINTH DIALOGUE.

> SUMMARY OF THE DIALOGUE. *The discussion concerning Tyranny, begun in the previous dialogue, is here completed: he diligently pursues its origin from the license of the people, and finally all its passions <note>original: "πάθη" (pathē)</note>. And just as he had taught that the state of a right republic is the most fortunate, and the condition of a man accustomed to its laws is the most happy; so he graphically represents the most unhappy condition of a corrupt republic, and of the man accustomed to it—namely, the Tyranny and the tyrannical character. He treats, moreover, of the faculties of the soul, and of those desires and pleasures which fall upon them in various and manifold ways: for subduing these, he brings forward an opportune remedy, namely, the rule of Reason.*

---

<image-desc>Two large decorative woodcut initials. The letter 'D' on the left contains a detailed scene of a village or town. The letter 'O' on the right is similarly ornate with botanical patterns.</image-desc>

<margin>A distinction concerning pleasures.</margin>
**D**einceps <note>The Latin and Greek columns are parallel versions of the same text. I have translated both into English to maintain the layout.</note> It remains next to be considered, I said, in what manner the tyrannical man is made from the democratic one, what sort of man he is, and whether he leads a miserable or a happy life. "Certainly that is what remains," he said. Do you know what I still feel is missing? "What?" We do not yet seem to have sufficiently distinguished how many and of what kind the desires <term>Desires: original "cupiditates" / "ἐπιθυμιῶν". In Plato's psychology, these are the irrational urges of the lowest part of the soul.</term> are. And unless that is clear, the investigation of what we seek will be more obscure. "It will still be opportune." Assuredly; and see what I wish to know about them, for it is this. Of those pleasures and desires which are not necessary, some seem to me to be lawless. These appear to be present in everyone; but when they are punished by the laws and by better desires together with reason, in some men they either disappear entirely or are so repressed that they are rendered very rare and weak; in others, however, they turn out to become more violent and frequent. "Which ones do you especially call by that name?" Those which are more often excited in sleep. When we are sleeping, that part of the soul which partakes of mind and reason lies dormant and weak; but that part in which there is a certain wildness and savage cruelty, when it is immoderately deprived of food, leaps up in sleep and tosses itself about immoderately. Thus, all things are presented to this part's sight, being void of mind and reason: so that it seems to mingle the body with its mother <note>original: "cum matre corpus miscere" / "μητρί τε γὰρ ἐπιχειρεῖν μίγνυσθαι". This is a famous early reference to what would later be called Oedipal desires—taboos that Plato argues exist in the subconscious.</note>, or with any other whatever, whether man, god, or often a beast; and also to slaughter someone and to be impiously reckless, and to do many things impurely and foully, with rashness and impudence. But he who has given himself to rest with a healthy and moderate cultivation and diet, having stirred up and erected that part of his soul which is of mind and counsel, and having saturated it with a feast of good thoughts; and having neither killed that part of the soul which is nourished by pleasure through want, nor let it overflow with satiety (either of which is accustomed to blunt the edge of the mind, whether something is lacking to nature or abounds and overflows); and also having calmed and extinguished that third part of the soul in which the fire of anger exists—then it will happen, the two rash parts of the soul being suppressed, that the third part of reason and mind will shine forth, and show itself vigorous and sharp for dreaming; then the visions of his rest will meet him as tranquil and true. "I think entirely so." What more? We wish to know this in summary: that there is in everyone a certain species of desires that is dire, savage, and unjust, even in those who seem most moderate among men. This becomes manifest in sleep. See then if I seem to say anything of worth, and whether you agree. "I certainly agree." Remember, then, what kind of man we said the democratic one was. He was the one who, from his early years, was brought up under a thrifty father who indulged only the desire for profit, but despised the others which were not necessary, but were the companions of play and ornament. "Was it not so?" "Entirely so." Having then associated with more elevated men, full of those lusts which we have just described, he began to turn aside toward all insolence and their manners, out of hatred for his father's parsimony. But since he was of a better nature than his corrupters, being pulled from both sides, he reached a middle ground between both manners, being moderately affected by each, as he thought, leading a life neither illiberal nor dissipated, having changed from a lover of the power of the few into a democrat. "That was certainly, and is, the opinion concerning such a man." Suppose again that this man is now older, and has a young son brought up in his own manners. "I suppose it." Suppose further that the same things happen to him which had happened to his father: that he is drawn toward every disgrace and the license of a wanton life, which those who lead it nevertheless call "complete liberty." His father and other relatives support those middle desires we spoke of, while others, on the contrary, lend their aid to the opposite. When those terrible enchanters and tyrant-makers have no other hope of holding the youth, they devise a way to excite a certain love in him, to be a protector and guardian of the idle and those desires that minister to his lust—a winged and surely giant drone <term>Drone: original "fucus" / "κηφῆνα". A drone is a male bee that does no work and lives off the hive's labor; Plato uses this to describe the parasitic nature of the tyrant's central lust.</term>. Do you think the love of such things is anything else? "Nothing else." When the other desires come buzzing around him, full of incense, perfumes, crowns, and unmixed wine, and the pleasures of such company, having been released to the ultimate degree, they increase and nourish that longing, and thus add a sting to the drone: then this...

<margin>This is from Cicero’s "On Divination."</margin>

<column-break/>

**H**e <note>The Greek text corresponds exactly to the Latin translation provided on the left.</note> then remains (I said), this tyrannical man, to be examined: how he changes from a democrat, what kind of person he becomes when he has arisen, and in what manner he lives, whether miserable or blessed. "He is indeed what remains," he said. Do you know then (I said) what I still desire? "What is that?" The matter of desires—what they are and how many—we do not seem to have sufficiently divided. While this is lacking, the inquiry into what we are seeking will be more obscure. "Is it not then (he said) still a good time?" "Certainly. And look at what I want to see in them. It is this: of the pleasures and desires that are not necessary, some seem to me to be lawless. These appear to be born in everyone, but being restrained by the laws and by the better desires with reason, in some men they are either completely gotten rid of, or a few remain and are weak; but in others, they are stronger and more numerous." "What are these (he said) that you speak of?" "Those (I said) that are awakened during sleep. When the rest of the soul is asleep—the rational and gentle part, the one that rules the other—but the beastly and savage part, being gorged with food or drink, leaps up, and having pushed away sleep, seeks to go and satisfy its own habits. You know that in such a state it dares to do everything, as if it were released and set free from all shame and prudence. For it does not shrink from attempting to mingle with a mother, as it thinks, or with any other man, or god, or beast; or from any murder; or from abstaining from no food; and in a word, it lacks nothing of folly or impudence." "You speak (he said) most truly." "But whenever (I think) a man is healthy in himself and temperate, and goes to sleep having awakened his rational part, and having feasted it on fair words and contemplations, coming to a consistency with himself; and having given his desiring part neither want nor satiety, so that it may fall asleep and not cause trouble to the best part by its joy or its grief, but allow it, alone by itself and pure, to examine and reach for the perception of something it does not know, whether of things past, or present, or even to come; and likewise having calmed the spirited part <note>original: "θυμοειδὲς". The "middle" part of the soul associated with anger, courage, and honor.</note>, and not going to sleep with his spirit moved by anger against anyone; but having quieted two of the forms, and moved the third, in which wisdom is born, he thus takes his rest—you know that in such a state he especially touches the truth, and least of all do lawless visions appear in his dreams." "I think (he said) it is entirely so." "These things, then, we have been led to speak of at greater length than intended. But what we wish to recognize is this: that a certain terrible, savage, and lawless form of desires exists in everyone, even in some of us who seem to be moderate. And this becomes manifest in sleep. See then if I seem to be saying something, and if you agree." "I do agree." "Then remember (I said) what kind of man we said the man of the people <note>The "democratic man".</note> was. He was born, I believe, and brought up from his youth under a thrifty father, who honored only the money-making desires, but dishonored those that were not necessary but existed for the sake of play and finery. Was it not so?" "Yes." "But having associated with more sophisticated men, full of those desires we just went through, he rushed into every kind of insolence and into their way of life, out of hatred for his father's thrift. But having a better nature than those who were corrupting him, and being drawn both ways, he settled into a middle ground between the two manners; and enjoying each moderately, as he thought, he lived a life neither illiberal nor lawless, having become a man of the people from having been a man of the oligarchy." "For that (he said) was and is the opinion regarding such a man." "Suppose then (I said) again that this man has now become older, and has a young son brought up in his habits." "I suppose it." "Suppose then also that the same things happen to him as happened to his father: that he is led into every lawlessness, which is called 'total liberty' by those leading him. Suppose his father and other relatives help those middle desires, while others help the opposite side. When those clever magicians and tyrant-makers hope they will not hold the youth in any other way, they plot to implant in him a certain love to be a leader of his idle and spendthrift desires—a winged and great drone. Or what else do you think the love of such things is?" "Nothing else (he said) but that." "Then, when the other desires come buzzing around it, full of incense and perfumes and crowns and wine, and the pleasures that are released in such gatherings to the extreme, they increase and nourish it, and implant a sting of longing in the drone; then it is surrounded by madness as its bodyguard..."

<summary>Socrates begins Book IX by explaining that even moderate people possess "lawless" desires that appear in dreams, and argues that the tyrannical man is born when these desires are fanned into a "giant drone" of lust and madness.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the beginning of Book IX of Plato's Republic. Socrates and Adeimantus are defining the "tyrannical man"—the individual whose soul is governed not by reason, but by a single, lawless master-passion.</meta>

<page-num>503</page-num>
<header>ON THE REPUBLIC, BOOK IX.</header>

<margin>A</margin>
...and in whomsoever this master-passion dwells, it rages entirely and seethes with madness. Then, surrounded by its bodyguards <note>original: "δορυφόρους" (doryphorous) – literally "spear-bearers," referring to the desires that protect the master-passion</note>, and driven by a sting, if it finds within him any opinions or desires that are useful or still feel shame, it immediately roots them out and drives them away, until it has purged the soul of temperance and filled it with an imported madness. "You are describing the origin of a tyrannical man perfectly," he said. "Is it not also for this reason," I asked, "that Love <note>original: "Ἔρως" (Eros) – here referring to an overwhelming, lawless desire rather than romantic affection</note> has long been called a tyrant?" "It certainly seems so," he replied. "And does not a drunken man, my friend, also possess a tyrannical mindset?" "He does indeed." "Furthermore, one who is mad and out of his mind attempts and expects to be able to rule not only over men, but even over the gods." "Most certainly," he said. "Then a tyrannical man, my dear friend," I said, 
<margin>B</margin> "truly comes into being when he becomes—either by nature, by habit, or by both—drunken, erotic, and melancholic <note>original: "μελαγχολικὸς" (melancholikos) – in ancient medicine, this referred to an excess of 'black bile' leading to erratic or intense behavior</note>." "That is exactly how it is." "This, it seems, is how such a man is produced. But how does he live?" "As the saying goes among those who joke," he said, "you will have to tell me that." "I shall," I replied. "For I believe that after this, feasts follow among them, and revelries, banquets, and courtesans, and all such things as happen when Love the Tyrant, dwelling within and navigating the soul, steers everything." "Necessarily so," he said. "Do not many and terrible desires then sprout up beside him every day and night, in need of many things?" "Many indeed." "Therefore, any income they have is quickly consumed." "How could it not be?" "And after this come loans and the stripping away of one's property." "Surely." "And when everything fails, is it not necessary for the 
<margin>C</margin> desires—frequent and fierce, nesting like young birds—to cry out? And they, driven as if by stings—namely by other lusts, and especially by Love itself, which leads all the others like bodyguards—will run wild and search for who has anything that can be taken away either by fraud or by force." "Very much so," he said. "Therefore, they are compelled to snatch from everywhere, or else be gripped by great pangs and pains." "They are indeed compelled." "And just as the new pleasures arising within him have surpassed the old ones and taken what was theirs, will he not likewise deem it right, though he is younger, to have more than his father and mother, and to take from them? And if he has spent his own portion, will he not spend his parents' wealth besides?" 
<margin>D</margin> "Why would he not?" he said. "And if they do not permit it, will he not first attempt to steal from and deceive his parents?" "Entirely." "And whenever he cannot do that, would he then snatch it and use force against them?" "I believe so," he said. "And if the old man and the old woman resist and fight back, O wonderful man, would he be cautious and spare himself from doing anything tyrannical?" "I am not at all confident," he said, "regarding the parents of such a man." "But by Zeus, Adeimantus," I said, "for the sake of a newly-found, unnecessary mistress, do you think such a man would strike his long-beloved and necessary mother? Or for the sake of a newly-found, unnecessary, blooming youth, would he strike his aged, necessary father, the oldest of his friends, 
<margin>E</margin> and make them slaves to those others if he brought them into the same house?" "By Zeus, he would," he said. "How very blessed it seems," I said, "to have fathered a tyrannical son." "Not at all," he said. "What then? When the resources of his father and mother fail him, and there is already a great swarm of pleasures gathered within him, will he not first break into someone's house or snatch someone's cloak late at night? And after that, will he not rob some temple? And in all these acts, the opinions he held from childhood regarding what is honorable or shameful—those which were the judges of his conduct—will be overcome by those opinions that have recently been freed from slavery and now serve as Love’s bodyguards. 
<margin>F</margin> Those desires which were formerly released only in dreams during sleep—while he was still living under the laws and the democratic rule of his father within himself—will now, when he is tyrannized by Love, be his constant waking state. For he will abstain from no foul murder, nor any food, nor any deed. Rather, Love living tyrannically within him in total anarchy and lawlessness, being the sole monarch, will lead the man who possesses it (just as if he were a city) into every daring act, to sustain himself and the riotous mob around him—partly those desires that entered from without through evil company, 
<margin>G</margin> and partly those from within that were released and set free by his own habits. Is this not the life of such a man?" "It is indeed," he said. "And if there are only a few such men in a city," I said, "and the rest of the multitude is temperate, they will go abroad and serve some other tyrant as bodyguards, or serve for hire if there is a war. But if they remain in peace and quiet, they commit many small evils right there in the city." "What kind do you mean?" "They steal, break into houses, cut purses, strip people of their clothes, rob temples, and kidnap people. Sometimes, if they are good at speaking, they become false informers, bear false witness, and take bribes." 
<margin>H</margin> "You call these small evils," he said, "if there are only a few such men?" "These are small," I said, "when compared to the great ones. Indeed, all these things, when compared to the tyrant, do not even come close to the 'mark' (as the proverb says) regarding the wickedness and misery of a city. For whenever many such men appear in a city, followed by many others, and they realize their own great number, then they are the ones who create the tyrant—aided by the folly of the people—choosing that one among them who has the greatest and most potent tyrant within his own soul." "That is consistent," he said. 

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
...this master-passion rages entirely, and seethes with madness: and then, crowded by bodyguards, and goaded by a sting, if it finds any frugal and modest opinions or desires within him, it immediately roots them out and expels them, until it casts out all temperance from the soul and refills it with a new insanity. "You describe the origin of a tyrannical man excellently." "Was it not for this reason that love was called a tyrant long ago?" "It clearly seems so." "And a drunken man, my friend, does he not bear a tyrannical spirit?" "Certainly." "Moreover, the furious man who is out of his mind strives to command not only men, but even the gods, and hopes that he will achieve it." "Most vehemently." "A tyrannical man, O blessed man, 
<margin>B</margin> truly becomes so when, either by nature or by studies or by both, he becomes intoxicated, subject to love, and furious." "The matter stands exactly so." "Thus such a man, as it appears, is produced. But in what manner does he live?" "That, as those who joke say, you will tell me." "I say indeed: after these things, as I think, they indulge in feasts, revelries, gatherings, and assemblies, with harlots and all other things of this sort—those whose tyrant Love, dwelling within the inner chambers of the soul, rules everything." "It is necessary." "Therefore many vehement desires, lacking many things, sprout up every day and night." "Many indeed." "Quickly, then, if any revenues existed, they are consumed." "Why not?" "After this come usury and the dissipation of the patrimony." "Without a doubt." "But when everything fails, it is necessary for the 
<margin>C</margin> desires to cry out and complain, which indeed hide in the nest of the soul, frequent and burning. They, struck as if by certain stings—by other lusts, and especially with love as the leader of all others like bodyguards—are tossed and carried away to explore if anyone possesses anything that can be stolen by fraud or snatched by force." "Very much so." "Therefore they are compelled to seize from everywhere, or to be tortured by huge stings and pains." "They are clearly compelled." "Now, just as his new and adult pleasures have surpassed the former ones and have taken what was theirs for their own use, will he not also judge it to be just that he, being younger, should have more than his parents and take from them? And if 
<margin>D</margin> he has consumed his own portion, will he not spend the paternal wealth besides?" "Why not?" "But if those parents do not permit it, he will first attempt to steal and deceive them." "Entirely." "But if he cannot do that, he will then snatch and bring force upon his parents." "So I think." "And if the father and mother are old, O wonderful man, and they resist and fight back, will he respect them, and so restrain himself that he does nothing tyrannical?" "I fear for the father and mother of a man so affected." "By Jupiter, O Adeimantus," I said, "for the sake of a recently beloved and unnecessary concubine, do you think such a man will strike his long-time 
<margin>E</margin> and necessary mother? Or for the sake of some beautiful, recently-armed unnecessary youth, will he strike his deformed and necessary old father, the oldest of all his friends, and subject them to those others if he brings them into the same house?" "By Jupiter, entirely." "How blessed it seems to have fathered a tyrannical son." "Not very." "What then? When his parents' wealth fails him, and the swarm of pleasures within him is now most crowded, will he not first dig through the wall of some house, or late at night snatch the cloak from someone? Then he will even despoil a temple. And in all these things, the opinions he had held since childhood about what is honorable and base—which were the laws by which he was judged—will now be overcome by those that recently escaped from slavery and now serve as bodyguards surrounding love. 
<margin>F</margin> These were formerly released only during sleep through dreams, while he was still established in a popular <note>original: "populari" (the Latin translator's term for the 'democratic' state of the soul)</note> condition under the laws and his father's precepts. But finally, ensnared by the tyranny of love, as he rarely was in his sleep, so he will always be while awake. For he will abstain from no impious slaughter, nor from gluttony, nor from any crime. Rather, love living tyrannically within him with all license and transgression, being the sole master, will shamelessly drag the man subjected to it (as if he were a city) to all things. From this he will nourish himself and the crowd of his bodyguards, partly those who entered from without from some wicked habit, 
<margin>G</margin> and partly those from within, released and manumitted by him from those same morals. Is this not the life of such a man?" "Exactly so." "And if there are only a few such men in the city, and all the rest of the multitude is modest, because there is no place for them there, they depart and guard another tyrant. Having accepted pay, if there is a war anywhere, they help; but if they can be in peace and quiet, they commit many, many small crimes there in that city." "Of what kind?" "They will steal, dig through walls, cut purses, despoil and plunder, snatch sacred things, force captured men into slavery, and also bring false accusations whenever they are strong in speaking, give false testimony, and corrupt judges with gifts." 
<margin>H</margin> "You call these small evils, if there are only a few such men?" "These, if compared to the greater ones, are called small. And all these things, compared to the 

---

tyrant, do not at all reach the mark (as the proverb says) regarding the malice and misery of the city. For as often as many such men are found in the city, and many others follow them, and they perceive the huge number of their own, they give birth to a tyrant through the ignorance of the common people—him especially, who among them is so affected that he has the most powerful tyrant within his own soul. "That is indeed consistent."

# PLATO'S [REPUBLIC]

...indeed, he will be most powerful. Would this not be easy if everyone yielded to him? But if the city resists this tyrant, then just as he previously violated his father and mother, he will again violate his country to the best of his ability, bringing in new young companions. He will compel his once-dear country and "mother-land"—to use the Cretan expression <note>original: "matriámque" / "μητρίδα" (metrida). The Cretans used this term to emphasize the land that birthed them, rather than the "father-land" (patria).</note>—to serve these newcomers, both in their upbringing and their way of life. This will be the ultimate goal of that man’s desire. "Exactly so," he said. Do such men not behave this way in private before they gain power? First, they associate mostly with those who flatter and fawn over them, obeying them in everything and serving them. If they need something, they themselves submit, playing whatever part is necessary like domestic servants. But once they have achieved their goal, they show themselves as strangers. Indeed, they spend their whole lives this way: never a friend to anyone, always either ruling over someone or serving someone. The tyrannical nature never tastes true freedom or true friendship. "Quite so." Shall we not rightly call such men untrustworthy? "Rightly so." And furthermore, they are as unjust as possible, if we were correct in our earlier agreement about the nature of justice. "We were certainly correct," he said. Let us conclude, then, who is the worst man: he is the one who, while awake, is exactly like the man we described earlier in his dreams. "Absolutely." This is what becomes of a man who is naturally tyrannical and attains sole rule; the longer he lives in his tyranny, the more he becomes this way. "It is necessary," said Glaucon, taking up the argument. Whoever appears most wicked will also appear most miserable; and whoever holds power as a tyrant for the longest time and in the greatest degree is, in truth, the most unjust and most miserable for the longest time. However, many people will have many different opinions on this. "That must be the case," he said. Is the tyrannical man not similar to a city oppressed by tyranny? And the democratic man to a democratic city, and so on? "Why not?" Just as city compares to city in virtue and happiness, so does man compare to man. "Nothing prevents it." How then does a city subjected to a tyrant compare to one ruled by a king, such as the one we first described? "They are total opposites," he said. "For one is the best, and the other the worst." I will not ask which you mean, for that is clear. But regarding happiness and misery, do you judge in the same way or differently? Let us not be dazzled by the outward appearance of the tyrannical city, looking only at the tyrant himself or the few who hold power with him; rather, as is proper, let us enter into the depths of the entire city, survey every part, and only then deliver our verdict. "You advise me well," he said, "for it is clear to everyone that no city is more miserable than one oppressed by tyranny, and none is happier than one governed by a king." If I were to demand the same observation regarding the men themselves, would I be right? That is, if I judged that the verdict should be given by someone who can, in his mind, creep into the tyrant's character and see through his habits—someone who is not like a child, stunned by the outward display and theatrical pomp <note>original: "tragico apparatu" / "τραγικῆς σκευῆς". This refers to the elaborate costumes and masks worn by actors in Greek tragedies, suggesting the tyrant’s public persona is merely a mask.</note> which they put on for those watching from the outside, but can judge with insight. If I say we should listen to one who is able to discern, who has lived with the tyrant and witnessed his actions at home, seeing how he behaves toward each of his family members—for it is in these private moments that a man is seen stripped of his tragic costume—and who has also seen him in public dangers; if I asked such a witness to declare how the tyrant compares to others in terms of happiness and misery, would I be right? "You would be very right to ask that." Shall we pretend, then, that we are among those who are able to judge and who have encountered such men, so that we have someone to answer our questions? "I am willing." Come then, consider the comparison this way, recalling the likeness between the city and the man, and observe the conditions of each one by one. "Tell me which ones," he said. First, regarding the city, would you call the tyrannical city free or enslaved? "The most enslaved of all," he said. Yet you see masters and free men within it. "I do," he said, "but that is only a small part; the whole, so to speak, and the best part of it, is in shameful and wretched slavery." If, therefore, the man is like the city, must not the same order exist in him, and his soul be filled with much lack of freedom and servitude? Must not those parts of his soul which are best be enslaved, while a small, most wicked and most demented part plays the master? "It is necessary," he said. What then? Will you call such a soul enslaved or free? "Enslaved, surely." But an enslaved city under a tyrant does not do what it wants. "Hardly at all." Therefore, a tyrannical soul will also not do what it wants—speaking of the soul as a whole—but, always driven by a violent sting <note>original: "stimulo" / "οἴστρου" (oistros). Originally meaning a horsefly, this term was used metaphorically for a maddening or divine sting that drives one to frenzy.</note>, it will be full of confusion and regret. "Why not?" Must the tyrannical city be rich or poor? "Poor." Then the tyrannical soul must also be impoverished and insatiable. "It is as you say." And is it not necessary for such a city and such a man to be filled with fear? "Very much so." Furthermore, will you find more lamentations, sighs, weeping, and distress in any other city? "In no way." And do you think such things exist more in any other man than in

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...most [powerful]. But if the city does not yield, then just as he once punished his mother and father, he will now punish his country if he is able, bringing in new companions. He will keep and nourish his once-dear "mother-land"—as the Cretans call it—and his fatherland in a state of slavery under these people. And this would be the end of such a man's desire. "Exactly so," he said. <margin>B</margin> Do such men not become like this in private before they rule? First, they associate with people who flatter them or are prepared to serve them in everything. If they need something, they themselves fall at the feet of others, daring to assume every posture as if they were close kin; but once they have gained what they want, they act as strangers. They live their whole lives never being a friend to anyone, but always either mastering someone or being enslaved to another. A tyrannical nature never tastes true freedom or true friendship. "Quite so." Then would we be right to call such men untrustworthy? "How could we not?" And indeed, they are as unjust as possible, if we were right in what we previously agreed about the nature of justice. "Indeed we were," he said. Let us summarize then, I said, the worst man: he is likely the one who, when awake, is such as we described a man being in his dreams. "Precisely." This is the man who becomes most tyrannical by nature and attains monarchy; and the more time he spends in his tyranny, the more he becomes this way. "It is necessary," Glaucon said, taking up the argument. <margin>C</margin> Then will the one who appears most wicked also appear most miserable? And will the one who has been a tyrant for the longest time and in the greatest degree be, in truth, most miserable for the longest time? Though many people think many different things. "It is necessary," he said, "that these things be so." Is the tyrannical man not like the tyrannical city in his resemblance, and the democratic man like the democratic city, and so on for the others? "Of course." Then whatever a city is to a city in virtue and happiness, a man is to a man? "How could it be otherwise?" What then? How is the tyrannical city compared to the kingly city we first described? "The complete opposite," he said. "For one is the best, the other the worst." <margin>D</margin> I will not ask which you mean, for it is clear. But regarding happiness and misery, do you judge them in the same way or differently? And let us not be overwhelmed by looking at the tyrant as a single person, nor at the few around him, but let us enter into the whole city as one should, sinking down into every part and seeing it all; then we shall declare our opinion. "Your challenge is fair," he said. "And it is clear to everyone that there is no city more miserable than a tyrannical one, and none happier than a kingly one." <margin>E</margin> If I were to make the same challenge regarding the men, would I be right to demand that the judgment be made by someone who can, in his thought, enter into a man’s character and see through it? Someone who is not, like a child, struck with awe by the outward facade that tyrants put on for those outside, but can see through it sufficiently? If I thought we should all listen to that man—the one who is able to judge because he has lived in the same house and witnessed the tyrant's actions at home, seeing how he treats each member of his household (where one would most likely be seen stripped of his tragic costume), and who has also seen him in public dangers—and if we told him to report how the tyrant compares to others in happiness and misery? "You would be perfectly right in that challenge," he said. <margin>F</margin> Do you want us to pretend that we are among those who are able to judge and who have already encountered such people, so that we may have someone to answer our questions? "By all means." Come then, I said, consider it this way: remembering the likeness of the city and the man, look at the suffering of each in turn. "What kind of suffering?" he asked. First, I said, speaking of the city, will you say the tyrannical one is free or a slave? "The most enslaved possible," he said. And yet you see masters and free people in it. "I see a small part that is so," he said, "but the whole, so to speak, and the most decent part of it, is in dishonorable and wretched slavery." <margin>G</margin> If then the man is like the city, is it not necessary that the same arrangement exist in him, and his soul be full of much slavery and lack of freedom? Must not those parts of it be enslaved which were most decent, while a small, most wretched and most mad part acts as master? "It is necessary," he said. What then? Will you say such a soul is a slave or free? "A slave, surely." And the enslaved and tyrannical city does the least of what it wants. "Very much so." And the tyrannical soul, therefore, will do the least of what it wants—to speak of the soul as a whole. Always dragged by a violent sting, it will be full of turmoil and regret. "How could it not be?" Is it necessary for the tyrannical city to be rich or poor? "Poor." And the tyrannical soul, then, must be impoverished and insatiable. "So it is," he said. <margin>H</margin> What then? Is it not necessary for such a city and such a man to be full of fear? "Most certainly." And as for wailing, groaning, lamenting, and grieving—do you think you will find more in any other city? "In no way." And in any other man, do you think there are more such things than in this tyrannical one, who is maddened by his lusts and desires? "How could there be?" he said. Looking at all these things and others like them, you have judged the city to be the most miserable of cities. "Was I not right?" he asked. "Very much so," I said. But regarding...

Socrates argues that just as a tyrannical city is enslaved, poor, and fearful, the tyrannical soul is dominated by its lowest desires and remains perpetually unsatisfied and restless.</summary>
