<meta>This page continues the dialogue from Book IX of Plato’s Republic. Having established the character of the "tyrannical man" as one ruled by lusts, Socrates now leads Glaucon to judge the relative happiness or misery of such a life, specifically comparing a private individual to a ruler.</meta>

### ON THE REPUBLIC, BOOK IX.

And of the man again, I said, looking back at what you were saying, "By far," he said, "he is the most wretched of all." "This," I said, "you say correctly. But how?" he asked. "Not yet," I said, "do I think this man is the *most* wretched." "But who then?" "Perhaps you will think this next man is even more wretched than him." "Which one?" "The one," I said, "who, being tyrannical by nature, does not live out a private life, but is unfortunate, and by some ill-luck is provided the opportunity to become an actual tyrant." "I suspect," he said, "from what has been said before, that you speak the truth." "Yes," I said. "But one must not merely *opine* about such things, but rather examine them very well with such reasoning. For the investigation concerns the greatest matter: a good life and a bad one." "Most right," he said.

<margin>B</margin>
"Consider then whether I am saying anything of substance. For it seems to me we must understand it from this, if we are to look at it clearly." "From what?" "From each one of the private individuals, those who are wealthy in cities and possess many slaves; for these men have this at least in common with tyrants: the ruling over many. The difference is only in the number of subjects." "It is indeed a difference." "Do you know then that these men live without fear, and do not fear their domestic servants?" "What would they have to fear?" "Nothing," I said, "but do you understand the reason?" "Yes. It is because the whole city helps each individual private citizen." "You speak well," I said. "But what if some god were to lift a single man, who has fifty or even more slaves, out of the city—himself, his wife, and his children—and set him in a wilderness with the rest of his property and his servants, where no free man was likely to help him? In what kind of fear, and how much, do you think he would be?"

<margin>C</margin>
"In the greatest fear," he said, "at least I think so." "Would he not then be forced to flatter all of his own slaves, and make many promises, and set them free, though he had no desire to do so? And would he not appear as a fawning servant to his own attendants?" "He would be under a great necessity," he said, "or else he would perish." "What if the god," I said, "were to settle many other neighbors around him in a circle, who would not tolerate anyone claiming to be the master of another, but if they caught such a person, would punish him with the ultimate penalties?" "He would be," he said, "I think, even more in a state of total evil, being guarded in a circle by nothing but enemies."

<margin>D</margin>
"I have described," I said, "all such things; he is like a man trapped in a prison, being of such a nature as we have described, full of many and various fears and lusts. Though he has a greedy soul, he alone in the city is not permitted to travel anywhere, nor to see the sights that other free men desire. Instead, he lives mostly lurking in his house like a woman, envying the other citizens if any of them travel abroad and see anything good." "Exactly so," he said. "Therefore, the man who is poorly governed within himself—whom you just now judged most wretched, the tyrannical man—reaps even more of these evils if he does not live as a private person, but is compelled by some fortune to play the tyrant, and being unable to control himself, attempts to rule others; just as if someone with a sick body, unable to control itself, were forced to spend his life not in private, but always competing and fighting against other bodies."

<margin>E</margin>
"You speak entirely in a way that is most similar to the truth, Socrates," he said. "Therefore," I said, "dear Glaucon, is this condition not altogether wretched? And does the one acting as tyrant not live even more harshly than the life you previously judged most difficult?" "Quite so," he said. "It is then the truth, even if it does not seem so to some, that the real tyrant is a real slave, subject to the greatest flatteries and slaveries, and a fawner of the most wicked men. He never satisfies his desires in any way, but is seen to be in the greatest need and truly poor, if one knows how to look at his whole soul. He is full of fear throughout his whole life, full of convulsions and pains—if indeed he resembles the state of the city over which he rules. And he does resemble it, does he not?" "Very much so," he said.

<margin>F</margin>
"Therefore, we shall also assign to the man those things we mentioned before: that he must be, and even more so than before because of his rule, envious, faithless, unjust, friendless, unholy, and a host and nourisher of every vice. From all these things, he is most of all unfortunate himself, and next, he makes those near him just like himself." "No one," he said, "with a mind will contradict you." "Come then," I said, "now just as the final judge <note>This refers to the official who awarded prizes in Athenian dramatic or athletic contests.</note> declares the winner, so you do the same: who is first in your opinion in happiness, and who is second? Judge the five in order: the Kingly, the Timocratic <note>original: "timokratikon" / "τιμοκρατικὸν". A regime based on honor and military glory.</note>, the Oligarchic, the Democratic, and the Tyrannical."

<margin>G</margin>
"The judgment is easy," he said. "For I judge them as they entered, like choruses, by virtue and vice, by happiness and its opposite." "Shall we hire a herald then," I said, "or shall I myself announce it? That the son of Ariston <note>Ariston was the father of Glaucon and Plato; Socrates is giving Glaucon the honor of the final verdict.</note> has judged that the best and most just man is the happiest (this being the most kingly man, who is king over himself), while the worst and most unjust is the most wretched; and this happens to be the one who, being most tyrannical, is a tyrant over himself and over the city." "Let it be so proclaimed by you," he said. "Shall I add," I said, "whether they remain hidden as such, or not, from all men and gods?" "Add it," he said.

<column-break/>

[The following is the English translation of the Latin column, which mirrors the Greek text above.]

From that tyrannical one, who is insane with desires and loves? In what way? Truly, looking back at all these things, and the other types of the same, you have judged the tyrannical city to be the most miserable of all cities. Is it not so? Most certainly. But what do you say again about the tyrannical man, whenever you observe these same things? By far, I say, he is the most miserable of all. This you do not say correctly. Why? This man is not yet, as I think, the most miserable. Who then? This one perhaps will seem to you more miserable than him. Who, I say? He who, while being tyrannical by nature, does not lead a private life, but is unhappy, and by some chance is led to the point where he possesses a tyranny. From those things that have been said, I guess you speak the truth. It is so. But one ought not to merely opine such things, but rather investigate them most diligently with such a reason. For our dispute is about a very great matter: namely, a good life and a bad one. Expertly said.

<margin>B</margin>
Pay attention, therefore, if I may say something. For it seems to me we must consider this from these things. From what? From each of the private citizens, namely, those who so abound in riches that they have many slaves. For they have this in common with tyrants: that they command many. But the difference is that a tyrant rules over many more. It is a difference indeed. Do you know that these men live securely with their household, and do not fear their servants? Why would they fear them? Nothing. But do you understand the cause? Certainly, because obviously the whole city succumbs to the aid of each of the private citizens. You speak excellently.

<margin>Why the father of the family fears nothing from a multitude of slaves.</margin>
<margin>C</margin>
What if some god were to take one who had fifty or more slaves, out of the city together with his wife and children, and set him in a solitude, with all his things and slaves, where no free men could bring him help? With what and how great a fear do you think he would be vexed, lest by chance the slaves should kill him and his children and wife? The greatest, as I think. Will he not be forced to flatter certain slaves, and promise many things, and set them free, though he has no need to do so? Whence he himself will be a flatterer to his own ministers. He will be compelled either to do so, or to perish. What if the god placed many others nearby in that region, who would by no means tolerate that one should rule another, and if they caught anyone claiming lordship for himself, they would afflict him with extreme punishments? I think his condition would be much worse, if he were enclosed by a wall of enemies.

<margin>D</margin>
Is not the tyrant closed in such a prison, being such by nature as we explained in the previous parts, agitated by many and diverse fears and loves? But since he is of a soul exceedingly greedy, to him alone it is neither permitted to go out anywhere, nor to look at what is pleasing to free men: but within the walls of the house, he stays fearful like a woman, envying other citizens if anyone walks outside the walls and sees anything good. Exactly so.

<margin>E</margin>
Does that man not incur many more such things besides, who, governing himself badly—whom you also just now judged most miserable, the tyrannical man—by no means lives a private life, but by some force of fortune is compelled to exercise tyranny: and since he cannot command himself, he strives to command others? Just as if someone with a weak body, not sustaining itself by its own strength, were forced not to lead a quiet life, but to strive and fight against other bodies. You bring in very similar things, O Socrates, and very true ones.

<margin>The most wretched thing is a tyrant who has obtained a tyranny.</margin>
<margin>F</margin>
Is this not therefore, O friend Glaucon, an altogether miserable condition, and is the life of a man who has obtained a tyranny harder than that life which you judged hardest above? Greatly. But he is in fact, although it may not seem so to someone, a true tyrant and a true slave, bound to extreme flattery and slavery, a flatterer of the most wicked men: who never fills his appetites, but always lacks many things, and appears truly needy, if someone looks into the inner parts of his soul. He is terrified by perpetual dread, and vexed by anxiety and anguish, if he is similar to the state of the city which he heads. But he is similar. Is he not? And most greatly indeed.

<margin>G</margin>
Besides these things, we shall also attribute to this man those things which we mentioned before: that it is necessary for him to be, both before and much more after he has obtained the tyranny, envious, faithless, unjust, void of benevolence, impious, and to become the sink and fuel of every wickedness, and from all these to be most miserable, and also to render others who adhere to him similar. No one of sound mind will contradict this. Come, just as a judge looking around at everything judges concerning individuals, so may you bring forth in the present: who in your judgment is first in happiness, who is second: and narrate the others gradually who are five in number. The Kingly, the one studious of the Republic in which the magistrate is created from the census <note>This refers to Timocracy.</note>, the one desirous of the power of the few <note>Oligarchy</note>, the popular <note>Democracy</note>, and the tyrannical. And that judgment is easy. For as if I had entered, I compare and judge those as if they were choruses in virtue and depravity, happiness, and its opposite. Shall we hire a herald? Or shall I rather pronounce these things? That the son of Ariston judged the best and most just man to be the happiest, and he said that he was the man most kingly of all, and ruling himself: but the worst and most unjust to be the most miserable, and that such a one is he who is most a tyrant, and presses himself and the city with tyranny. So let it be proclaimed. Shall I add, whether such men are hidden, or are not hidden from men and gods alike? Add it. Let it be so then. Indeed, together...

<summary>Socrates and Glaucon conclude that the tyrannical man is the most miserable of all, especially if he is forced to actually rule a city, which acts as a prison for his fears. They formally rank the five types of souls, placing the "Kingly" self-ruler at the peak of happiness and the tyrant at the bottom.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Socrates’ argument from Book IX of the Republic. In the preceding section, Socrates described the wretchedness of the tyrannical man. Here, he begins a second proof for the superiority of the just life by dividing the soul into three parts and examining the specific pleasures associated with each.</meta>

# OF PLATO

<margin>A</margin>
Let this be our first demonstration; but let us look at a second, if it seems right. What is it? Since the city is divided into three classes, so also, I believe, the soul of every individual is divided into three parts; and from this, a second proof will be born. What is it? This: since there are three parts of the soul, there appear also to be three pleasures, each one being proper to its own part. There are also as many desires and forms of rule. How so? We say one part is that by which a man <term>learns<note>Referring to the rational part of the soul, the *logistikon*.</note></term>. Another is that by which he is <term>spirited<note>Latin: *irascitur*; Greek: *thymoeides*. This refers to the part of the soul associated with anger, courage, and the drive for honor.</note></term>. But for the third, because of its variety, we could not name it with a single proper word of its own; instead, we have named it after that which is greatest and most violent within it. We have called it the 
<margin>B</margin>
<term>appetitive<note>Latin: *concupiscibile*; Greek: *epithymētikon*. The part of the soul driven by physical needs.</note></term> because of the intensity of those desires for food, drink, and sex, and those things which follow them. We have also called it "money-loving," since such desires are satisfied primarily through money. Rightly so. And if we say that its pleasure and affection are for gain, we shall best reduce our speech to a single summary, so that we signify something certain to ourselves whenever we speak of this part of the soul. And if we call this whole part "wealth-loving" and "greedy for gain," we shall name it quite correctly. So it seems to me. What then? Does not the spirited nature draw one entirely toward power, victory, and glory? Greatly so. If then we call it "contentious" and "ambitious," 
<margin>C</margin>
would we not be right? Most rightly. But as for that part by which we learn, it is clear to everyone that it always strives to investigate the truth of all things, and has the least concern for money and glory. Entirely so. If we call this third part "desirous of learning" and "philosophical," the name will be appropriately bestowed. It is as you say. Now, do we not say that in the souls of some men one of these parts dominates, while in others another part rules, whichever it may be? We do. For this reason, we say there are three primary classes of men: the philosopher, the contentious, and the greedy. Exactly. And there are also three types of pleasure underlying these, each belonging to its own. Entirely so. If you should ask each of these men separately which of these lives is the
<margin>D</margin>
sweetest, each will prefer his own to the others. The greedy man, in comparison with gain itself, will judge the delights of honors or learning to be worth nothing, unless perhaps they bring in some money. You speak the truth. But the ambitious man considers the pleasure perceived from money to be heavy and troublesome, and again considers that which is perceived by learning to be mere smoke and trifles, because such study does not bring honor. That is how it stands. Let us also suppose the philosopher counts the other pleasures as worth a straw when compared to that constant joy of learning in which he delights while investigating the truth; he calls the others "necessary" because he would not pursue them unless necessity compelled him. We must know this well. 
<margin>E</margin>
When, therefore, the pleasures of each life and the life itself come into dispute—not regarding which way of living is more honorable or base, or better or worse, but concerning which is sweeter and more peaceful—by what reasoning shall we discern whose opinion is truer? I do not quite know what to answer. Look at it this way: by what standard ought one to judge things that are to be correctly decided? Is it not by experience, wisdom, and reason? Or does anyone have better tools for judging? By no means. Attend then: Since there are three men, which of them is most experienced in all the pleasures we have described? Does the greedy man, in learning what the truth is, 
<margin>F</margin>
seem to you more experienced in the sweetness of learning than the philosopher is in gain, or is it rather the opposite? There is a vast difference. For it is necessary for the philosopher to have tasted the pleasure of the other from his childhood. But it is by no means necessary for the greedy man to have perceived or experienced how much delight there is in the investigation of truth. Indeed, even if he tried, he would not easily achieve it. Therefore, the philosopher far exceeds the greedy man in his experience of both pleasures. Far. And is the ambitious man any less ignorant of the pleasure perceived from honor than the philosopher is of that which comes from wisdom? Honor indeed follows all of them if they perform their proposed duty. For the rich man is honored by the multitude, as are the brave and the wise. Therefore, everyone understands through use itself how much pleasure comes from honor. But the sweetness found in the contemplation of truth, the philosopher alone feels. 
<margin>G</margin>
Therefore, as far as experience is concerned, the philosopher judges best among the others. Very much so. Furthermore, he alone will have experienced it alongside wisdom. Surely. Moreover, that organ through which judgment must be made is not the instrument of the greedy or ambitious man, but of the philosopher. What sort of instrument is that? We said that judgment must be made through <term>reasoning<note>Latin: *rationes*; Greek: *logoi*. Refers to rational arguments or discourse.</note></term>. We did. And reasoning is especially the philosopher's instrument. Clearly. If wealth and gain were the best way to judge things, the things praised or disapproved of by the man devoted to profit would necessarily be the truest. Completely. Or if it were by honor, victory, and courage, it would be what the ambitious and
<margin>H</margin>
victory-loving man judged. But since it is by experience, wisdom, and reason, it is necessary that what the philosopher and the lover of reason praise must be truest. Therefore, since there are three pleasures, the pleasure of that part by which we learn will be the sweetest, and the life in which this part rules will be the most delightful. Nothing stands in the way. Certainly, the philosopher, in whom rests the authority to judge truly, praises his own life. And what life does he say is second?

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
This then is one proof. But we must see a second, if in some way it seems right. What is this? Since the city (I said) was divided according to three forms, so also the soul of each individual is divided threefold; thus, it seems to me, another demonstration is possible. What is it? This. As there are three parts, three pleasures also appear to me, one unique to each; and likewise three desires and ruling principles. How do you mean? he asked. One part, we say, was that by which a man learns; the second, that by which he is spirited; the third, because of its multi-form nature, we could not name with a single proper name, but we named it by the greatest and strongest thing it had within it. For we have called it "appetitive" because of the intensity of the desires for food, drink, sex, and all other things that follow these, and also 
<margin>B</margin>
"money-loving," because such desires are primarily fulfilled through money. And rightly so, he said. If then we should say that its pleasure and its love is for "gain," would we not best bring our argument to a single head, so that we might clarify something to ourselves whenever we speak of this part of the soul? And would we be right to call it money-loving and gain-loving? It seems so to me, he said. What about the spirited part? Do we not say it is always wholly set on mastery, victory, and good reputation? Very much so. If then we called it "victory-loving" and "honor-loving," 
<margin>C</margin>
would it be appropriate? Most appropriate. But surely, as for the part with which we learn, it is obvious to everyone that it is always entirely directed toward knowing the truth of how things are, and it cares least of all for money and glory. Very much so. If we call it "learning-loving" and "philosophical," we should be calling it by its proper character. Surely. And so (I said), it rules in the souls of men—in one person this part, in another that, whichever it happens to be. Thus it is, he said. For these reasons, we say that the primary classes of men are three: the philosopher, the victory-lover, and the gain-lover. Exactly. And so there are three kinds of pleasure, one underlying each of these. Certainly. You know then (I said) that if you wished to ask three 
<margin>D</margin>
such men in turn, each of them which of these lives is the sweetest, each would most praise his own. The money-maker will say that, compared to the pleasure of gaining, the pleasure of being honored or of learning is worth nothing, unless one of them produces silver. True, he said. And what about the honor-lover? (I said). Does he not consider the pleasure from money to be vulgar, and again the pleasure of learning—unless the study brings honor—to be nothing but smoke and nonsense? It is so, he said. And the philosopher (I said), we may assume, considers the other pleasures to be nothing compared to knowing the truth of how things are, and being always in such a state of learning; he is never far from such pleasure. But the others he calls truly 
<margin>E</margin>
"necessary," since he would have no need of the others unless there were a necessity. We must know this well, he said. Since therefore (I said) there is a dispute about the pleasures of each type and the life itself—not merely as to living more beautifully or basely, or worse or better, but regarding the very thing of being sweeter and more painless—how might we know which of them speaks most truly? I am not quite able to say, he said. But look at it this way: by what must one judge what is to be judged well? Is it not by experience, and wisdom, and reason? Or could one have a better criterion than these? How could he? he said. Consider then: of the three men, who is the most experienced in all the pleasures we mentioned? Does the gain-lover, in learning the truth of 
<margin>F</margin>
what it is, seem to you more experienced in the pleasure of knowing than the philosopher is in the pleasure of gaining? There is a great difference, he said. For the philosopher must of necessity taste the others from childhood; but for the gain-lover, there is no necessity to taste the pleasure of learning the truth—to know how sweet it is—nor to become experienced in it. Rather, even if he were eager, it would not be easy. Therefore (I said), the philosopher far exceeds the gain-lover in his experience of both pleasures. Very much so. And what about the honor-lover? Is he more experienced in the pleasure of learning than the philosopher is in the pleasure of being honored? But (he said) if they all achieve what they are set upon, honor follows them all. For the wealthy man is honored by many, as is the brave man and the wise; so that from the experience of being honored, they all know what kind of pleasure it is. But as for the vision of what *is*, and the pleasure it holds, it is impossible for anyone to taste it except the philosopher. 
<margin>G</margin>
Then for the sake of experience (I said), this man judges best of all. Much so. And indeed, he alone will have experience joined with wisdom. Certainly. But also, the very instrument through which one must judge is not the instrument of the gain-lover, nor of the honor-lover, but of the philosopher. What kind is that? We said judgment must be made through reasons, did we not? Yes. And reasons are the philosopher’s primary instrument. Of course. Now, if wealth and gain were the best things by which to judge, the things praised and blamed by the gain-lover would necessarily be the most true. Quite so. And if honor, victory, and courage? Would it not be the honor-lover and victory-lover? Clearly. But since it is by experience, wisdom, and reason? Necessarily (he said), the things which the philosopher and the lover of reason praise are 
<margin>H</margin>
the sweetest. Since then there are three pleasures, the pleasure of this part of the soul with which we learn would be the sweetest, and the life of that man in whom this part rules is the most pleasant. How could it be otherwise? he said. At any rate, being a competent praiser, the wise man praises his own life. And which life (I said) does he say is second, and which pleasure is second? <gloss>himself like the prudent man.</gloss>

<summary>In this section of Plato's Republic Book IX, Socrates divides the soul into three parts—Rational, Spirited, and Appetitive—and argues that the philosopher is the most qualified judge of true happiness because he alone has experienced the pleasures of all three types of life.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Book IX of Plato’s Republic. Having identified three parts of the soul—the rational, the spirited, and the appetitive—Socrates is now leading Glaucon through a series of proofs to demonstrate that the pleasure of the philosopher (the rational part) is the most "true" and "pure," whereas the pleasures of the tyrant are merely shadows or the absence of pain.</meta>

Vv ij

<margin>A</margin>
Which pleasure does the judge rank first? Is it not clearly that of the warrior and the lover of honor? For even the pleasure of the money-maker has some value. But the pleasures of the lover of gain seem to be exceeded. What does it matter? he asked. These things, then, would have been settled through examination, and the just man has already twice defeated the unjust man. For the third bout, in the <term>Olympic fashion<note>original: "ὀλυμπικῶς" (olympikōs). In Greek banquets, the third libation was traditionally offered to "Zeus the Savior" (Zeus Soter). Socrates uses this as a metaphor for his third and final "saving" argument.</note></term>, dedicated to the Savior and to Olympic Zeus, observe that the pleasure of the others is not even entirely true, nor pure, but is a kind of <term>shadow-painting<note>original: "ἐσκιαγραφημένη" (eskiagraphēmenē). A technique in Greek art using light and shadow to create an illusion of depth; here, it means the pleasures are illusory.</note></term>, as I think I have heard from some wise man. Yet this would be the greatest and most decisive of falls. Great indeed; but how do you mean? If I search it out this way, I will seek while you answer. Ask then. Tell me, do we not say that pleasure is the opposite of pain? We do. And is there a certain middle state of quietude of the 
<margin>B</margin>
soul between both, which is neither joy nor pain? There is. Do you not remember, I said, the words of the sick, which they say when they are ill? Which words? That nothing is sweeter than being healthy, but it had escaped them how sweet it was before they fell ill. I remember, he said. And do you not also hear those who are held by some great pain saying that nothing is sweeter than to cease from suffering? I do. And in many other such circumstances, I believe, you perceive men who, when they are in pain, praise the absence of pain and the quietude of such a state as being the sweetest thing, rather than actually feeling joy. 
<margin>C</margin>
For then, he said, quietude perhaps becomes sweet and desirable. And when someone ceases to feel joy, I said, the quietude of pleasure will be painful. Perhaps, he said. Therefore, that which we just said was the middle between both—quietude—will at some time be both pain and pleasure. It seems so. And is it possible for that which is neither to become both? It does not seem so to me. And yet, when pleasure and pain arise in the soul, are they not both a kind of motion? Yes. But did not that which is neither painful nor pleasant just now appear to be quietude and in the middle of these? It did. How then is it right to think that not suffering is sweet, or that not rejoicing is bitter? In no way. Therefore this is not really so, I said, but it only appears so: pleasure appears sweet compared to the painful, and pain appears bitter compared to the pleasant, when in that state of quiet; there is nothing healthy in these <term>phantasms<note>original: "φαντασμάτων" (phantasmatōn). Visions or appearances that lack true substance.</note></term> of true pleasure, but they are a kind of 
<margin>D</margin>
sorcery. So the argument signifies, he said. Look now, I said, at pleasures that do not come out of pains; so that you do not often think in the present discussion that it is naturally ordained that pleasure is the cessation of pain, and pain the cessation of pleasure. Where, he asked, and what pleasures do you mean? There are many others, I said, but consider especially the pleasures of smell. For these, without any prior pain, suddenly become immense in greatness; and when they cease, they leave no pain behind. This is very true, he said. Let us not believe, then, that pure pleasure is the release from pain, nor that pain is the absence of pleasure. No indeed. Yet, I said, those pleasures that reach the soul through the body, and are called pleasures, are almost all of this type—they are releases from pains. They are. And do the <term>pre-joys<note>original: "προχαίρησις" (prochairēsis). The anticipation or "tasting beforehand" of a pleasure.</note></term> and pre-pains that arise from the expectation of these future things behave in the same way? In the same way. Do you know, I said, what they are like and what they most resemble? What? he asked. 
<margin>E</margin>
Do you believe, I said, that there is in nature an "up," a "down," and a "middle"? I do. Do you think, then, that anyone being carried from the bottom to the middle would think anything else than that he was being carried up? And standing in the middle, looking back at where he was brought from, would he believe he was anywhere else but "up," having never seen the truly "up"? By Zeus, I said, I do not think such a person would think otherwise. But if he were carried back down again, I said, he would think he was being carried down, and he would think truly? How could he not? And would he not suffer all this because he is inexperienced with what is truly up, middle, and down? Clearly. 
<margin>F</margin>
Would you wonder, then, if those who are unskilled in the truth have unhealthy opinions about many other things, and are so disposed toward pleasure and pain and the middle between them, that when they are brought toward the painful they think truly and are really in pain; but when they move from pain to the middle, they strongly believe they have reached fulfillment and pleasure? Just as those who look at gray next to black, because they have not seen white, are deceived, so also those who compare the absence of pain with pain, because they have not experienced true pleasure, are they not deceived? By Zeus, he said, I would not wonder; rather, I would wonder much more if it were not so. 
<margin>G</margin>
Consider it thus, I said. Are not hunger and thirst and such things certain "emptyings" of the state of the body? What else? And are not ignorance and folly an emptiness of the state of the soul? Very much so. And would not he who partakes of nourishment and he who gains intellect be filled? How could they not? And is the truer filling that of the less real or the more real? Clearly that of the more real. Which kinds do you think participate more in pure essence? Those such as bread, drink, meat, and nourishment in general, or the species of true opinion, knowledge, intellect, and in short, all virtue? Judge it this way: that which belongs to the always-similar, the immortal, and the truth, and is itself such and arises in such a thing—does that seem more real to you than that which belongs to the never-similar and the mortal, and is itself such and arises in such a thing? The one belonging to the always-similar differs greatly, he said.

<column-break/>

Or which pleasure would that judge put first? It is agreed that he would place the warrior’s and the ambitious man’s first. For the pleasure of the money-maker is closer to him than it is to others. Finally, therefore, he seems to place the life of the one greedy for gain last. Why not? These two then succeed each other in turn, and the <margin>Proverb.</margin> just man has now twice defeated the unjust. But for the third, in the <term>Olympic<note>Referring again to the "third pour" for Zeus the Savior.</note></term> rite, giving it to the Savior and to Olympic Zeus, consider that no pleasure except that of the prudent man is truly real or pure, but is shadowy and empty; as I seem to have heard from some wise man: and this will be the most heavy fall and ruin of the unjust man. Truly a wonder. But in what way do you say this? I will find out, searching it out while you respond. Ask. Tell me, I pray, do we not say pleasure is contrary to pain? We do. Do we not place a certain middle state of rest, <margin>Concerning the middle between pleasure and pain.</margin> which is neither to rejoice nor to grieve? We do. And since it is a middle, is it a rest and a vacation of the mind from both? Do you not say it is so? Quite so. Do you remember what the words of the sick are wont to be while they labor under disease? What do you say they are? That nothing is sweeter than health, but it escaped them how sweet it was before they were sick. I remember indeed. And do you not hear men vexed by the most bitter pains exclaiming that nothing is sweeter than to be free from that affliction? I hear them. Furthermore, you hear men tortured by very many other such afflictions, while they are tortured, shouting and asserting that it is sweetest to be affected by no pain, and to be free from present trouble; they do not say, however, that it is sweetest to rejoice. For this rest is then perhaps most pleasing to them. But truly, when someone ceases to rejoice, will he think that cessation of pleasure is troublesome? Perhaps. Therefore, that rest which we said a little before was the middle of both, will sometimes be both: then pain, and then pleasure. It seems so. Is it possible for that which is neither to be both? Not, as I think. And yet, when there is pleasure or pain in the mind, are they not both certain motions? Certainly. But that third thing which is neither pain nor pleasure, did it not just appear to be a certain rest and the middle of those? Clearly. In what way then shall we rightly think that not grieving is sweet, and not rejoicing is bitter? In no way. Therefore that is not so, but it appears so, if you compare the pleasant to the troublesome, and the troublesome to the pleasant: and that is then the middle, and rest. Nor do any of these offer us anything of true pleasure, but they arise from certain deceptions. So the reason shows. See then the pleasures that follow no pain, lest you more often think in the present dispute that it is so arranged by nature that pleasure is the privation of pain, and pain the privation of pleasure. Where, you ask, and which pleasures do you mean? There are many and others, but especially, if you wish to observe, the pleasures that occur around smell: for these, with no pain preceding, suddenly come forth as great; and when they cease, no pain follows them. You tell the truest things. Let us not believe, therefore, that the cessation of pain is pure pleasure: nor that pain is the absence of pleasure. No. But truly of those things which enter the mind through the body, and are called pleasures, almost the greatest and most numerous are such that they are liberations from pains. They are indeed. And those which are born from the expectation of these future things, certain <term>pre-tastes<note>Latin: *prægultationes*. A literal "tasting beforehand."</note></term> of pleasure and pain, have themselves in the same way. In the same way. Do you know what kind these pleasures are, and to what they are most similar? To what? he said. Do you think there is anything in nature that is highest, lowest, and middle? I do. Do you think that someone, when he is carried from the lowest to the middle, thinks anything else than that he is ascending to the summit? and while he stands in the middle, and turns his eyes back thither from whence he had come, does he think he is anywhere else than in the highest, since he does not see that which is truly the summit? By Zeus, I do not think such a man would think otherwise. If he were brought down again, he would think he was being carried downward, and he would think truly? Why not? Do not all these things happen to him for this reason: because he has not yet experienced what is truly the highest, what the middle, and what the lowest? It is indeed manifest. Will you then wonder if men unskilled in truth have incorrect opinions about many other things, and are also so affected regarding pleasure and pain, and the middle between them, that as often as they fall into pain, they judge truly and truly grieve: but as often as they rise from pain into the middle, they think they have followed fulfillment and pleasure? And just as those who, next to black, look only at gray, because they do not see white, think that gray is the brightest thing; so also those who compare the vacancy of pain with pain, but have not experienced true pleasure—are they not deceived in judging? By Zeus, I shall not wonder at that. Indeed, if it happened otherwise, I would rather wonder. But consider it thus. Are not hunger and thirst and other things of the same kind certain vacancies of the habit of the body itself? Why not? But ignorance and imprudence are a certain vacancy of the habit of the mind. Most of all. But that one is filled while he takes food, and this one while he takes intelligence. Why not? Which filling is truer? That which occurs through things that are more and more truly real, or that through others? That through things that are more real. Which things do you think are of a purer substance? Are they kinds of food, drink, meat, and all nourishments; or the species of true opinion, science, and mind, and in short, universal virtue? Judge in this way: that which always adheres to the similar, the immortal, and the truth, and is itself such...

<summary>Socrates argues that most people mistake the "middle state" of rest (the absence of pain) for true pleasure, using the analogy of someone who thinks they are at the "top" simply because they have moved from the "bottom" to the "middle." He concludes that intellectual and virtuous pursuits provide "truer" fulfillment because they fill the soul with immortal truths rather than perishable food.</summary>

### Page 508

...exists, and is in such a thing, does it seem to you to have more <term>being<note>original: "esse" / "εἶναι". In Platonic philosophy, "Being" refers to the eternal, unchanging reality, while "Becoming" refers to the physical, changing world.</note></term>? Or rather that which is never similar or mortal, yet is of such a nature and produced in such a thing? The latter, which is kindred to what is always similar, is far superior. Does the essence of a thing that is always similar participate more in being than in knowledge? No. Or in truth? Not that either. And if it has less of truth, does it not also have less of being? It must. Is it not generally true that all the kinds of things concerning the care of the body participate less in truth and being than the kinds of things concerning the care of the soul? Far less. And do you not think the body itself participates less than the soul? I do. Therefore, that which is filled with things that have more "being," and which itself has more "being," is more truly filled than that which is filled with things that have less "being," and which itself has less? Why not? If, therefore, to be filled with things according to nature is pleasant, then that which is truly filled with more real things would more naturally and truly cause a man to rejoice with true pleasure. But that which partakes of things that have less "being" and are less true is less truly or firmly filled, and partakes of a more untrustworthy and less true pleasure. It is absolutely necessary. Therefore, those men who are inexperienced in wisdom and virtue, and are always devoted to banquets and similar things, are carried downward, and then back again to the middle, and wander there throughout their lives. They never emerge above this, nor do they ever look up toward that which is truly high, nor are they ever truly filled with "being," nor do they taste any stable or pure pleasure. Like cattle, they always look downward toward the ground and toward their tables; they feed, fatten, and mate, and for the sake of getting more of these things, they kick and butt each other with iron horns and hooves, killing one another out of insatiable greed, because they are not filling the real and stable part of themselves with real food. Entirely so, Socrates, Glaucon replied; you describe the life of the common people like an <term>oracle<note>original: "χρησμῳδεῖς" (chrēsmōdeis). Glaucon suggests Socrates is speaking with the poetic and prophetic weight of a divine revelation.</note></term>. Is it not then necessary that they live with pleasures mixed with pains, which are mere images and <term>shadow-paintings<note>original: "ἐσκιαγραφημένη" (eskiagraphēmenē). An artistic technique using light and shadow to create illusion; Socrates uses it to mean pleasures that are not real but depend on their contrast with pain.</note></term> of true pleasure? They are so stained by comparison with one another that both the pleasures and the pains appear more intense, and they breed a mad passion for themselves in the foolish, and they are fought over, just as <term>Stesichorus<note>Stesichorus was a Greek poet who famously claimed that the Greeks and Trojans fought over a phantom (eidolon) of Helen, while the real Helen remained in Egypt.</note></term> says the Trojans fought over the phantom of Helen in ignorance of the truth. It is absolutely necessary that it be so. And what about the <term>spirited part<note>original: "θυμοειδὲς" (thymoeides). The part of the soul associated with anger, ambition, and the pursuit of honor.</note></term> of the soul? Must not similar things happen when someone pursues the fulfillment of honor, victory, and anger without reason or sense, whether through envy because of ambition, or violence because of a love of strife, or anger because of a difficult temper? Such things must happen here as well. Let us then boldly assert that even regarding the part that is greedy for gain and the other part that is fond of victory: whichever desires follow knowledge and reason, and pursue and take those pleasures which reason allows, will attain the truest pleasures possible for them, because they follow truth, and they will perceive their own proper pleasures—since what is best for each is also most "proper" to it.

<margin>
What is best for each is most proper to it.
</margin>

Most proper indeed. Therefore, when the whole soul follows the part in which philosophy resides, and is far from all internal strife, then it happens that each part performs its own office and is just; moreover, each part reaps its own pleasures, which are the best and, as far as possible, the truest. Precisely. But when one of the other parts rules, it happens that it neither finds its own proper pleasure, and it forces the other parts to pursue an alien and untrue pleasure. That is how it happens. Do not those things which are furthest from philosophy and reason most especially produce such effects? Indeed. And is not that which is furthest from law and order also furthest from reason? Obviously. And those desires that were seen to be burning with love and <term>tyrannical<note>Socrates refers to the "Tyrannical man" described earlier in Book IX, who is a slave to his lowest lusts.</note></term> appeared to be separated by the greatest interval? Entirely so. And the kingly and moderate desires appeared to differ by the least? Yes. The tyrant, therefore, will be very far from true and proper pleasure, while the King will be closest to it. Necessarily.

<margin>
How much the just man exceeds the unjust in pleasure.
</margin>

The tyrant, then, will lead the most bitter life, and the king the sweetest. That is absolutely necessary. Do you know by how much more sadly the tyrant lives than the king? I shall know, if you tell me. Since there are three kinds of desires—one legitimate and two bastard—the tyrant, having crossed the highest peaks of the bastard ones, as he flees law and reason, lives with certain slave-like and bodyguard pleasures. How much he is inferior is not easy to say, except perhaps in this way. How? From the <term>oligarch<note>A man ruled by the desire for wealth.</note></term>, the tyrant was third in line; for the <term>democrat<note>A man ruled by a variety of unnecessary desires.</note></term> was in the middle of them. Yes. Does he not then live with a third image of pleasure from that man, if what we said before is true? So it must be said. And the oligarch is third from the kingly man, if we place the aristocratic and the kingly in the same category. Third indeed. Therefore, the tyrant is separated from true pleasure by a number that is three times three. It appears so. Therefore, the image of tyrannical pleasure, it seems, is a plane number according to its length. Precisely. But according to its power and the third increase, it is manifest how great an interval it is distant. It is manifest to a calculator. If someone, reversing the order, should ask how much the king exceeds the tyrant in the truth of pleasure, having completed the multiplication, he will find that the king exceeds the tyrant in the sweetness of life, and...

<column-break/>

<note>The right column contains the original Greek text of the same dialogue translated above.</note>

Whether it exists, and is in such a thing, does it seem to you to be more, or that which is never similar and mortal, being itself of such a nature and produced in such a thing? Far different, he said, is that which is always similar. Does the essence which is always similar participate more in being than in knowledge? Not at all. And in truth? Nor this. And if it is less in truth, is it not also less in being? Necessarily. In general, do not the classes of things concerning the care of the body participate less in truth and being than the classes concerning the care of the soul? By far. And do you not think the body itself is less than the soul? I do. Therefore, that which is filled with things that are more "being," and which is itself more "being," is more truly filled than that which is filled with things that have less "being," and is itself less "being"? How could it not be? If, therefore, to be filled with things that are naturally fitting is pleasant, that which is filled with "being" and with things that are more "being" would make one rejoice more truly and more really with true pleasure. But that which partakes of things that have less "being" would be less truly and firmly filled, and would partake of a more untrustworthy and less true pleasure. Most necessarily, he said. Therefore, those who are inexperienced in wisdom and virtue, and are always with banquets and such things, are carried downward, it seems, and back again to the middle, and wander in this way through life. Above this, toward that which is truly upward, they never looked nor were they ever carried; nor were they filled with the "being" of "being," nor did they taste stable and pure pleasure. But like cattle, always looking downward and stooped toward the ground and toward tables, they feed, fattening themselves and mating; and for the sake of the greed for these things, kicking and butting one another with iron horns and hooves, they kill each other out of insatiability, as they are not filling themselves with "being" nor filling the part of themselves that can hold it. Entirely, Glaucon said, Socrates, you speak of the life of the many as if by an oracle. Is it not then necessary that they also live with pleasures mixed with pains, which are images of true pleasure and shadow-paintings, colored by their position next to one another, so that each appears intense, and they breed mad passions for themselves in the foolish and are fought over, just as Stesichorus says the phantom of Helen was fought over by those in Troy, in ignorance of the truth? It is very necessary, he said, that it be something of that sort. And what about the spirited part? Must not other such things happen, whenever someone pursues this very thing, either through envy because of ambition, or violence because of a love of strife, or anger because of a difficult temper, pursuing a surfeit of honor and victory and anger without reason and mind? Such things, he said, must necessarily be about this part too. What then? I said. Let us boldly say that even concerning the love of gain and the love of strife, whichever desires follow knowledge and reason, and with those pursue the pleasures which wisdom leads, will take the truest pleasures as far as it is possible for them to take true ones, as they follow truth, and they will take their own proper ones, if indeed what is best for each is also most proper. But indeed, he said, it is most proper. Therefore, when the whole soul follows the philosopher, and does not stir up strife, each part can do its own work and be just, and especially each part can reap its own pleasures and the best ones, and as far as possible the truest. Absolutely. But when one of the others rules, it happens that it does not find its own pleasure, and it forces the others to pursue an alien and untrue pleasure. Thus, he said. Therefore, would not those things which are furthest from philosophy and reason most likely work such effects? By far. And is not that which is furthest from reason also that which is furthest from law and order? Clearly. And did not the erotic and tyrannical desires appear to be furthest removed? By far. And the kingly and orderly ones the least? Yes. Therefore, I think, the tyrant will be furthest from true and proper pleasure, and the king the least. Necessarily. And the tyrant, I said, will live most unpleasantly, and the king most pleasantly. Very necessarily. Do you know, then, I said, by how much more unpleasantly the tyrant lives than the king? If you tell me, he said. There are three pleasures, it seems, in essence: one legitimate, two bastard. Having overstepped the bounds beyond the beyond, the tyrant, fleeing law and reason, dwells with certain slave-like bodyguard pleasures, and how much he is inferior is not at all easy to say, except perhaps in this way. How? he said. From the oligarch, the tyrant was third; for the democrat was in the middle of them. Yes. Therefore, he would also dwell with a third image of pleasure from that one, if the previous things were true. Thus. And the oligarch, in turn, is third from the kingly man, if we place the aristocratic and kingly in the same category. Third indeed. Therefore, I said, the tyrant is distant from true pleasure by a number that is three times three. It appears so. The image of tyrannical pleasure, it seems, would be a plane number according to the number. Absolutely. But according to the power and the third increase, it is clearly how great a distance he is removed. It is clear, he said, to the calculator. Therefore, if one, having turned it around, and now returning...

<meta>This page continues Socrates’s mathematical and metaphorical proof of the superiority of the just life over the unjust life. Having just calculated that a king lives 729 times more pleasantly than a tyrant, the dialogue now shifts to a famous psychological allegory: the tripartite soul represented as a multi-headed beast, a lion, and a man.</meta>

# OF THE REPUBLIC, BOOK IX.

<margin>A</margin> ...if one says the king is removed from the tyrant by a distance of seven hundred and twenty-nine times <note>original: "ἑπτακοσιοπλασιάκις" / "septingentis". Plato uses the number 729 (which is 9 cubed or 27 squared) to represent the massive numerical gulf between the happiness of a just ruler and the misery of a tyrant, roughly corresponding to the number of days and nights in a year.</note> in terms of healthy pleasure, he will define it as a completed multiplication; while the tyrant is removed by this same distance in terms of misery. "A marvelous calculation," he said, "you have poured out regarding the difference between the two men, the just and the unjust, in relation to pleasure and pain." And yet, I said, it is a true number and one appropriate to human lives, if indeed days, nights, months, and years are appropriate to them. "They certainly are," he said. Therefore, if the good and just man surpasses the wicked and unjust man by so much in pleasure, it is incredible by how much more he will surpass him in the grace, beauty, and virtue of his life. "Incredible indeed, by Zeus!" he said.
<margin>B</margin> "Very well then," I said, "since we have reached this point in our argument, let us take up again the first things said <note>This refers back to the beginning of the *Republic*, where the character Thrasymachus argued that injustice is more profitable than justice.</note> which brought us here. It was said somewhere that it is profitable to act unjustly for the man who is perfectly unjust, but who is thought to be just. Was that not the argument?" "It was indeed." "Now then," I said, "let us reason with him, since we have now agreed upon what power both unjust and just actions possess." "How?" he asked. "By fashioning an image of the soul in words, so that the one who said those things may recognize what he was saying." "What kind of image?" he asked. "One of those creatures," I said, "such as the ancient myths tell us used to exist, like the <term>Chimera<note>A fire-breathing monster with a lion's head, goat's body, and serpent's tail.</note></term>, <term>Scylla<note>A sea monster with many heads.</note></term>, <term>Cerberus<note>The three-headed hound of Hades.</note></term>, and many other forms that are said to have grown together, many ideas becoming one." "They are so described," he said. "Fashion, then, a single idea 
<margin>C</margin> of a manifold and many-headed beast, having heads of domestic and wild animals in a circle, and being able to change and grow all these from itself." "That is the work of a skillful fashioner," he said, "but since words are easier to mold than wax, consider it fashioned." "Now, fashion one other idea of a lion, and one of a man. Let the first be by far the largest, and the second the next largest." "These are easier," he said, "and they are fashioned." "Now join these three into one, so that they are somehow grown together with one another." "They are joined," he said. "Now fashion around them from the outside the image of a single being, that of the man; so that to someone who cannot see what is inside, but sees only the outer shell, it appears to be a single animal: a man." "I have fashioned the shell," he said. "Let us say then to the person who claims that 
<margin>D</margin> it is profitable for this man to act unjustly, and that doing justice does not benefit him, that he is saying nothing other than that it is profitable for him to feast the manifold beast and make it strong, along with the lion and the things belonging to the lion; but to starve the man and make him weak, so that he is dragged wherever either of those others leads him; and that he should not accustom one part to the other nor make them friends, but rather allow them to bite and fight and devour one another." "That is exactly what the one who praises injustice would be saying," he said. "On the other hand, the one who says that just things are profitable would say that we should act and 
<margin>E</margin> speak in such a way that the 'inner man' <note>original: "ὁ ἐντὸς ἄνθρωπος" / "interior homo". This is Plato's famous term for the rational part of the soul (Reason/Logos) which distinguishes humans from beasts.</note> within the man shall have the greatest mastery; and he will take care of the many-headed creature like a farmer, nourishing and taming the domestic heads, while preventing the wild ones from growing, making the nature of the lion his ally, and caring for all of them in common, making them friends with each other and with himself, and so he will nourish them." "Exactly so," he said, "this is what the one who praises justice says." "In every way, then, the one who praises justice would be speaking the truth, while the one who praises injustice would be lying. For whether one looks at pleasure, reputation, or utility, the praiser of the just is truthful, while the critic has nothing sound to say, nor does he even know what he is criticizing." "It seems so to me, at least," he said, "not in any way." "Let us therefore persuade him gently—for 
<margin>F</margin> he does not err willingly—by asking him: 'O blessed man, do we not say that the standards of the noble and the base have been established for these reasons: the noble things are those that subject the bestial parts of our nature to the human—or rather, perhaps, to the divine—while the base are those that enslave the gentle part to the wild?' Will he agree, or what?" "He will agree," he said, "if he listens to me." "Is there anyone then," I said, "whom it profits from this argument to take gold unjustly, if it happens that, while taking the gold, he simultaneously enslaves the best part of himself to the most wretched? Or, if by taking gold he enslaved his son or daughter to wild and evil men, it would not profit him, even if he took a vast amount for it; and if he enslaves the most 
<margin>G</margin> divine part of himself to the most godless and polluted part, and feels no pity, is he not then wretched? Is he not taking a bribe of gold for a much more terrible destruction than <term>Eriphyle<note>In Greek myth, Eriphyle was bribed with a golden necklace to persuade her husband, Amphiaraus, to join the fatal expedition against Thebes.</note></term>, who accepted the necklace in exchange for her husband’s soul?" "Much more indeed," said Glaucon, "for I will answer you on his behalf." "And do you not think that intemperance has long been blamed for such reasons, because in such a state that terrible, great, and manifold beast is let loose further than it should be?" "It is clear," he said. "And are not stubbornness and irritability blamed when 
the lion-like and serpent-like part increases and is stretched out of harmony?" "Certainly." "And are not luxury and softness 
<margin>H</margin> blamed for the loosening and relaxation of this same part, when they produce cowardice in it?" "Of course." "And flattery and illiberality, when someone subjects this same spirited part to the 
multitudinous beast, and for the sake of money and its insatiable greed, accustoms it from youth to be insulted and to become a monkey instead of a lion?"

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...the king, in bitterness of life, is removed from the tyrant by seven hundred and twenty-nine steps. This is a truly wonderful interval you have piled up between the just and unjust man in terms of pleasure and pain. This number is certainly true and appropriate for the lives of men, if indeed days, nights, months, and years are appropriate to them. They certainly are. And yet, if the good and just man exceeds the evil and unjust man by so much in pleasure, it is truly marvelous by how much more he will exceed him in ornament, beauty, and virtue. Truly marvelous indeed. But after we have come this far in our discussion, let us repeat what was said at the beginning, from which we were led to these points. It was 
<margin>B</margin> said at one time that acting unjustly was profitable for him who, though he is entirely unjust, is nevertheless thought to be just. Was it not said so? It was. To these things, therefore, let us now speak, since we have agreed among ourselves what power both just and unjust operation possesses. In what way? Let us figure an image of the soul in words, so that he who said those things may recognize what he said. What kind? Such a one as those natures said to have existed in former times, like the Chimera, Scylla, and Cerberus, and many others in which various forms are said to have been born together in the same being. They are so described. Fashion, therefore, one figure 
of a very varied beast, having many heads in a circle—heads, I say, partly of domestic animals and partly of 
<margin>C</margin> wild ones—which can change and produce all these things from itself. You describe the skill of a new kind of painter; nevertheless, since speech is easier to mold than wax, let it be fashioned. Add to these, moreover, one form of a lion on top, and on top of this, one of a man. And let the first be the most ample, the second more narrow, and the third narrowest. These are easy things, and thus they are formed. Join these three, therefore, so that they grow together with one another to form one. They are joined. Place around them on the outside the image of a single man, so that to him who cannot look into the interior, but sees only the outer covering, it appears to be one 
animal, namely a man. I have placed it around. Let us say, then, to him who asserts that it is profitable for this man to act unjustly, but to live 
<margin>D</margin> justly is in no way profitable, that he asserts nothing other than that it is profitable for him to feed that manifold beast and the lion, and to make that lion stronger, but to let the man perish from hunger and to weaken him, even to the point that because of his feebleness he is dragged wherever those others snatch him; nor does he make one part tame with the other, nor reconcile them, but rather allows each to tear the other with bites and to devour each other while fighting. Whoever would praise injury would say exactly these things. Therefore, if someone says that just duties are profitable, he will advise that these things should be done and said, by which that "inner man" of this kind of 
<margin>E</margin> animal may obtain the highest power; and that he should have care for that beast with many heads, like a farmer, nourishing, watering, and fostering the domestic heads, but immediately cutting off the wild ones, while he takes the nature of the lion as a helper for this and cares for all things in common; and reconciles them to each other and to himself with mutual goodwill. Surely he says these things, who praises the just. In every way, therefore, he who praises just things speaks the truth; but he who praises unjust things lies. For both in regard to pleasure, and in regard to beauty, and in regard to profit, the praiser of the just pronounces true things. The critic, however, brings nothing of the truth, nor does he know what he disapproves of. In no way, as it 
<margin>F</margin> seems to me at least. Let us therefore persuade him with gentle words (for he does not err of his own will), asking him thus: "O blessed man, do we not say that both honorable and shameful institutions of life exist because of certain things like these? Honorable things, indeed, which subject the bestial part of nature to the human—or perhaps rather to the divine—while shameful things are those that enslave the tame part to the wild master." Will he agree, or not? He will agree, if he believes me. "Is there anyone then whom it profits by this reasoning to take gold unjustly, if indeed it happens that while he receives the gold, he compels the most excellent part of himself to serve the most ignoble? For if, by 
taking gold, he made his son or daughter a slave to 
<margin>G</margin> wild and wicked men, it would in no way profit him to have received it, even if he took a great deal. But if he compels the most divine part of himself to serve the most profane and wicked part, and is not touched by mercy, will he not be wretched? He is corrupted by gifts of gold with much more grievous destruction to himself than Eriphyle, who received that necklace in order to betray her husband's life." "Very much so," as I respond to you on his behalf. "And do you not think that intemperance was once called such for a certain reason, because in it, that dire, huge, and manifold beast wanders further than is proper?" It is clear. "And are not contumacy and insolence disapproved of, when 
that lion-like and serpent-like kind so prevails that it grows strong beyond all modesty?" Entirely. "And is not delicate 
<margin>H</margin> softness reprehended in the too-free relaxation of this same part, when it procreates fear and idleness in him?" Why not? "And flattery and illiberality, when someone submits this same vigor of spirit to the turbulent and manifold beast, and for the sake of gain and its insatiable desire, casts it down and thus from its first years accustoms it so that it is turned from a lion into a monkey?"

He depicts the human soul as a composite of a multi-headed beast (desires), a lion (spirit), and an inner man (reason), arguing that the just man ensures reason governs the whole.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the ninth book of Plato’s Republic and introduces the final book. In the preceding text, Socrates argued that the philosopher-king is the happiest of men because his soul is governed by reason, whereas the tyrant is the most miserable because his soul is enslaved to chaotic desires. This page explores how an individual should govern their "inner republic," even if the ideal city does not exist on earth.</meta>

<margin>A</margin> "Very much so," he said. And why, do you think, are mechanical and manual arts <note>original: "βαναυσία" / "mechanica" — referring to trades involving physical labor, which were often looked down upon by the Greek aristocracy as "base" because they left little time for civic or intellectual life.</note> considered a reproach? Is it for any other reason than when the best part of someone’s nature is so weak that it cannot rule the beasts within him, but can only serve them and study how to flatter them? "It seems likely," he said. Therefore, so that such a person may be ruled by a guide similar to the one who rules the best man, do we not say he ought to be the servant <note>original: "δοῦλον" / "seruum"</note> of that best man, who has the divine element as a ruler within himself? We do not think he should be ruled to his own detriment (as Thrasymachus believed of subjects), 
<margin>B</margin> but because it is better for everyone to be ruled by a divine and wise prince—ideally one who has this ruler within themselves, but if not, then by one imposed from without. In this way, we may all be as similar and friendly as possible, being subjects of the same ruler. "And rightly so," he said. Indeed, the law clearly shows this is its intention, as it looks out for all citizens. This is also demonstrated by the rule over children, who are not permitted to be free until we have established a 'republic' within them as we have in the city. By cultivating their best part, we create a guardian and ruler within them similar to our own, and only then do we let them go free.
<margin>C</margin> "That is quite clear." In what way then, O Glaucon, shall we say it profits anyone to act unjustly, or without restraint, or basely? For through such works he becomes a worse person, even if he acquires more money or any other power. "In no way," he said. And how could it profit the wrongdoer to go undetected and escape punishment? Does not the one who remains hidden become even more wicked? But when a man is caught and punished, the beast-like part of him is calmed and tamed, and the gentle part is set free. His whole soul is restored to its best nature, taking on a more precious habit by gaining temperance <note>original: "σωφροσύνην" / "temperantiam" — often translated as self-control or moderation.</note> 
<margin>D</margin> and justice together with wisdom. This state is more precious than when the body attains strength, beauty, and health, insofar as the soul is more precious than the body. "Absolutely so," he said. Therefore, any man of sound mind will direct his whole life toward this goal. Primarily, he will value those studies that make his soul such as this, while scorning others. "Manifestly," he said. Furthermore, he will not pamper and nourish his body to indulge beastly and irrational pleasures, nor will he prioritize health, strength, or beauty unless they also lead to temperance. He will always be seen tuning the harmony of his body for the sake of the symphony of his soul. "Indeed," he said, "if he is truly to be a musician." <note>The term "musician" here is metaphorical, referring to someone who creates harmony between their physical and spiritual lives.</note> But he will not be dazzled by the crowd's estimation of wealth, 
<margin>E</margin> nor will he pile up riches to an infinite degree, inviting infinite evils upon himself. "Certainly not, I think." Rather, always looking toward the republic within himself <note>original: "πολιτείαν" / "Respublic." — Plato uses the same word for a political state and the internal organization of the soul.</note>, he will take care not to disturb its balance through either the lack or the excess of money. Governing himself in this way, he will act to increase or spend his wealth only as far as he is able. "Entirely so," he said. Moreover, he will look to the same standard regarding honors. He will gladly taste and partake of those that he hopes will make him a better man; but he will flee, both in private and in public, those honors that he fears might overturn his present state of mind. "Then he will never want to engage in politics," he said, "if that is his care." 
<margin>F</margin> "By the dog <note>original: "νὴ τὸν κύνα" — Socrates’ famous favorite oath.</note>, I will!" I said. "He certainly will in his own city. But perhaps not in his fatherland, unless some divine chance should occur." "I understand," he said, "you mean in the city we have just founded in our discussion—which exists only in words, for I do not think it exists anywhere on earth." "But perhaps," I said, "a model <note>original: "παράδειγμα" / "exemplar"</note> of it exists in heaven for the one who wishes to see it and, seeing it, to establish himself there."

# PLATO’S REPUBLIC,
## BOOK X,
## ON JUSTICE,
### THE TENTH DIALOGUE.

->It matters not whether it exists anywhere or will exist. For he will perform the duties of that city alone, and no other. "That is likely," he said.<-

---

**SUMMARY OF THE DIALOGUE.** Plato having brought this most noble dispute to an end, he does two things in this tenth book. First, he explains more clearly the reasoning by which he had hitherto banished poetry from the community of his republic. He gave the reason for this new decree so successfully because, in his time and among his people, poetry was held in the highest esteem; thus, he was under a heavy necessity to avoid resentment. However, he grants a place for "chaste poetry" in the republic—namely, for hymns to the Gods and for celebrating the praises of illustrious men. Then, he places a beautiful "colophon" <note>A finishing stroke or crowning conclusion.</note> upon this beautiful discourse regarding the rewards that accompany justice both in this life and the next, and the punishments that follow injustice, of which he represents a certain horrible description <note>original: "ὑπόστασιν"</note>; and conversely, a most pleasant and desirable description of that happiness which the just will enjoy in the second life.

<summary>This page concludes Book IX of the Republic, asserting that a wise man governs his life according to an internal "heavenly model" of justice, and introduces Book X, which discusses the banishment of poetry and the immortality of the soul.</summary>
