<meta>This page transitions from the end of Book IX into the beginning of Book X of Plato's Republic. In the previous page, Socrates discussed the internal "republic" of the soul and the importance of reason ruling over the lower appetites. Here, he returns to the critique of poetry, specifically its "imitative" nature, which he argues can lead the soul away from truth.</meta>

# ON THE REPUBLIC, BOOK 10.

<column-break/>

### THE BEGINNING OF BOOK X

<margin>A</margin> "And truly," I said, "while I think of many other reasons why we were entirely right in how we founded our city, I say this especially when considering the matter of poetry." "In what way?" he asked. "In our refusal to admit any part of it that is imitative <note>original: "μιμητική" (mimētikē) / "imitatione" — the act of representing or mimicking reality through art.</note>. For it is now even more clear to me, I believe, that such things must not be accepted, especially now that we have distinguished the different parts of the soul." "What do you mean by that?" "To speak plainly among ourselves—for you will not denounce me to the tragic poets and all the other imitators—all such things seem to be a corruption of the mind <note>original: "λώβη... τῆς... διανοίας" / "corruptela... mentis"</note> for those who hear them, unless they possess the antidote <note>original: "φάρμακον" (pharmakon) — a medicinal cure or a protective charm.</note>, which is the knowledge of what these things actually are." "In what sense are you saying this?" he asked.

<margin>B</margin> "I must speak," I said, "even though a certain friendship and reverence for Homer, which I have had since childhood, holds me back from speaking. For he seems to have been the first teacher and leader of all these beautiful tragic things. But one must not honor a man above the truth. Therefore, what I began to say must be spoken." "By all means," he replied. "Listen then, or rather, answer me." "Ask away." "Could you explain to me generally what imitation is? For I myself do not entirely understand what it aims to be." "Is it likely then," he said, "that I would understand it?" "That would not be strange," I said, "since those with duller vision often see things before those with sharper eyes." "That is true," he said. "But in your presence, I would not dare to say what I think, even if I saw something. So, you look for it yourself." "Do you want us to begin our inquiry from here, using our usual method? For we are accustomed to posit a single 'Form' <note>original: "εἶδος" (eidos) / "speciem" — often translated as 'Idea,' the perfect, eternal blueprint of an object in Plato's philosophy.</note> for each group of many things to which we give the same name. Do you understand?" "I do." "Let us then take any of these 'many things' you like. For instance, if you wish, there are surely many beds and tables." "Of course."

<margin>D</margin> "But for these two items of furniture, there are only two Ideas: one of the Bed, and one of the Table." "Yes." "And are we not accustomed to say that the craftsman <note>original: "δημιουργὸς" (demiourgos) — literally a 'worker for the people'; an artisan.</note> of each piece of furniture looks toward the Idea when he makes the beds or the tables that we use, and so on for other things? For surely no craftsman makes the Idea itself. How could he?" "He could not." "Now, see what you would call this other kind of craftsman." "Which one?" "The one who makes all the things that every single manual laborer makes." "You are describing a very powerful and marvelous man!" "Not yet; soon you will say so even more. For this same artisan is not only able to make all kinds of furniture, but he also makes everything that grows from the earth, produces all living creatures, including himself, and besides these, he fashions the earth, the heavens, the gods, and everything in heaven and in the underworld beneath the earth." "You are describing a truly marvelous sophist <note>original: "σοφιστήν" (sophistēn) — here used to mean a 'clever maker' or 'wonder-worker,' though often carrying a negative connotation of trickery.</note>," he said. "You don't believe me?" I asked. "Tell me, do you think such a craftsman simply does not exist? Or that in one sense there could be a maker of all these things, but in another sense there could not?

<margin>E</margin> Or do you not perceive that you yourself could make all these things in a certain way?" "And what is that way?" he asked. "It is not difficult," I said, "but is done in many places and very quickly. Most quickly, I think, if you take a mirror <note>original: "κάτοπτρον" / "speculum"</note> and carry it around everywhere. You will soon 'make' the sun and the things in the heavens; you will soon 'make' the earth, and soon yourself and the other animals, and the furniture and plants, and all the things we just mentioned." "Yes," he said, "I could make them 'appear,' but they would not be things that truly exist." "Excellent!" I said, "you have come to exactly the point I needed for the argument. For the painter, I believe, is also this kind of craftsman. Is he not?" "How could he not be?" "But you will say, I think, that what he makes is not 'true,' even though in a certain way the painter also makes a bed. Or does he not?" "Yes," 

<margin>F</margin> he said, "he makes an appearing bed." "And what of the bed-maker? Did you not just say that he does not make the 'Form' (which we say is the essence of the Bed), but only a particular bed?" "I did say that." "Therefore, if he does not make the essence, he does not make that which 'is,' but something that resembles what 'is,' yet is not the reality itself. And if anyone were to say that the work of the bed-maker or any other artisan was perfectly real, they would likely be mistaken, wouldn't they?" "At least according to those who spend their time in these kinds of arguments," he said. "We should not be surprised then if this, too, turns out to be a dim thing compared to the truth." "Certainly not." "Shall we then," I said, "look for who this 'imitator' is based on these examples?" 

<margin>G</margin> "If you wish," he said. "Then there turn out to be three kinds of beds. One is the one existing in nature, which we would say, I think, that God produced. Or would anyone else?" "No one, I think." "And one is the one the carpenter made." "Yes," he said. "And one is the one the painter made. Is that right?" "Let it be so." "Painter, bed-maker, God: these are the three masters of three species of beds." "Yes, three." "Now God, whether because he did not want to, or because there was some necessity that he not make more than one Bed in nature, made only that one which is the essential Bed. Two such beds, or more, were never created by God, nor will they ever be." "How so?" he asked. "Because," I said, "if he were to make only two, then yet another one would appear, whose Form those two would both share; and *that* would be the essential Bed, not those two." "Rightly so,"

<margin>H</margin> he said. "Knowing this, I believe, and wishing to be the real maker of a real Bed, and not just a particular maker of a particular bed, God produced only one Bed, unique by its nature." "It seems so." "Do you want us, then, to call Him the 'Natural Producer' <note>original: "φυτουργὸν" (phytourgon) — literally 'one who plants' or 'begets by nature.'</note> of this, or something similar?" "That would be just, since He has produced this and everything else by nature." *It seems so. Do you wish, then, that we call him the planter of this...*

<summary>Socrates begins Book X by justifying the exclusion of imitative poetry from the ideal city, introducing the famous 'Three Beds' analogy to show that art is three steps removed from truth. He argues that God creates the ideal Form, the artisan creates a physical copy, and the artist merely imitates the appearance of that copy.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from the beginning of Book X of Plato’s Republic. Having established that poetry is imitative, Socrates and Glaucon now delve into the specific nature of the "imitator" by comparing the painter, the craftsman, and the creator of natural forms. They are about to apply this hierarchy to Homer and the tragic poets.</meta>

# PLATO'S REPUBLIC

*Translation of the Latin and Greek Columns:*

->A<-

<margin>The Imitator.</margin>
...he made this and all other things. But what of the carpenter? Is he not the craftsman of the bed? Yes. And what of the painter? Is he also a creator and maker of such a work? Not at all. But how would you say he relates to the bed? It seems to me he is most aptly called the **imitator** <note>original: "imitator" / "μιμητής" (mimētēs)</note> of that which those others produce. Therefore, do you call him an imitator who produces a work three levels removed from nature? Certainly. Such then will be the tragic poet, if indeed he is an imitator, being someone at the third remove from the king <note>In Plato's hierarchy, the "king" or "god" creates the ideal Form, the artisan creates the physical object, and the artist creates the image.</note> and the truth; and likewise all other imitators. That appears to be so. We are agreed, then, on the imitator. But tell me this about the painter: does he attempt to imitate each thing as it exists in nature, or the works of the craftsmen? The works of the craftsmen. And does he imitate them as they actually are, or as they appear?

->B<-

Distinguish this further for me. How do you mean? Like this: if a bed is viewed from the side, or from the front, or from any other angle, does it differ from itself? Or does it not differ at all, but only *appears* different to those looking at it? And so with other things. It appears so, but it does not actually differ. Consider this as well: at what does the painter’s industry aim in each case? Is it to imitate the reality of each thing as it is? Or rather to imitate the appearance, as it appears? Is it an imitation of an appearing image <note>original: "phantasmatis" / "φαντάσματος" — a mere phantom or superficial appearance.</note> or of the truth? Of the appearing image. Imitation, therefore, is far removed from the truth; and, as it seems, it can produce all things for this reason: because it touches only a small part of each thing, and that part is a mere shadow. In this way, a painter will paint us a cobbler, a carpenter, or other craftsmen, though he understands nothing of these arts; nevertheless, if he is a skilled painter and displays his image of a carpenter from a distance, he will deceive children and foolish men into thinking he is a true carpenter.

->C<-

What then? Furthermore, my friend, we must consider this in all such cases. Whenever someone tells us of such a person—that he has met a man learned in all crafts, and who understands everything more perfectly than any other person—we must reply to him that he is a fool. He has likely encountered some <term>sorcerer</term> <note>original: "praestigiatorem" / "γόητί" (goēti) — a juggler or charlatan who uses illusions to trick the eye.</note> and imitator by whose deceptions he was misled; he thought the man was all-wise because he himself was unable to distinguish knowledge from ignorance and imitation from reality itself. You speak most truly.

->D<-

<margin>The Tragedians are criticized.</margin>
Is it not fitting, after this, to discuss tragedy and its leader, Homer? For we have heard from some that tragic poets understand all arts, and all human things pertaining to both virtue and vice, and even divine things. For they say a good poet, if he is to compose well, must have knowledge of his subjects, or else he could compose nothing. Therefore we must consider whether those who praise them have been deceived by the imitative industry of the poets, and whether, looking upon their works, they fail to perceive that these are at the third remove from reality, and are easy to make even for a man ignorant of the truth. For they create shadows, not real things. Or

->E<-

perhaps there is something in what they say, and good poets truly understand those things about which they seem to the common people to speak so well? This must be thoroughly distinguished. If someone were able to produce both—the thing to be imitated and its image—do you think he would devote himself to the creation of images? Would he set this work before himself as the best thing in his life? Not at all. Surely, if he had true skill in the things he imitates, he would much rather apply himself to the real works than to their imitations; he would strive to leave many noble works as monuments of himself to posterity, and would be more eager to be the one praised by others than to be always the praiser of other men's works. I certainly think so; for the honor and the benefit are not equal.

->F<-

Furthermore, let us not demand an account of other matters from Homer or any other poet, asking if any of them was truly a physician and not merely an imitator of medical discourse—whom among the ancients or the moderns has a poet made healthy, as Asclepius <note>The Greek god of healing and medicine.</note> did, or what disciples of the medical art did he leave behind, as he left his descendants? Nor let us ask them about the other arts; let us pass over the rest. But concerning those greatest 

->G<-

and most noble things which Homer attempts to treat—wars, commands, republics, and the education of men—it is right to question him thus: "Friend Homer, if you are not at the third remove from the truth concerning virtue—a mere creator of an image (whom we defined as an imitator)—but are instead at the second, and are able to say what pursuits make men better or worse in private and public life, tell us, please, which city has been better governed because of you? Just as Sparta was because of Lycurgus, and many other cities, large and small, were because of others. Which city acknowledges you as its best lawgiver and benefactor? Italy and Sicily celebrate Charondas, and we celebrate Solon. But who celebrates you, and for what?" None, I believe, says Glaucon, mentions his benefits. Indeed, not even the followers of Homer <note>original: "Homeridae" — a guild or family of poets who claimed descent from Homer and performed his epics.</note> dare to claim this.

->H<-

What war is remembered to have been successfully waged in Homer’s time under his counsel or leadership? None. Furthermore, what inventions <note>original: "inventa" / "ἐπίνοιαι"</note> of a wise man are attributed to him for the duties of life and art? Such as those of Thales of Miletus, and Anacharsis the Scythian? Nothing of the sort. If not publicly, then at least privately: is it said that Homer himself, while he lived, was a leader in education

<column-break/>

<summary>In this passage from Book X of the Republic, Socrates argues that artists and poets like Homer are merely "imitators" of appearances, positioned at a third remove from the ultimate truth. He challenges the idea of Homer's supreme wisdom by noting that Homer never governed a city, won a war, or founded a way of life.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Socrates’ argument in Book X of the Republic, where he critiques the value of imitative poetry. Having previously established that a painter only copies the appearance of a craftsman's work, Socrates now applies this logic to Homer and the great poets, arguing that they lack the practical knowledge possessed by those who actually use or create tools.</meta>

### ON THE REPUBLIC, BOOK X.

Those who came after Pythagoras <note>A famous Greek philosopher and mathematician (c. 570–495 BCE) who founded a way of life based on asceticism and communal study.</note> passed down a certain "Pythagorean way of life," for which he was uniquely beloved. Even now, his successors who follow this way appear distinct from the rest of the world. But no such thing is told of **Homer**. <margin>A</margin> For **Creophilus** <note>A legendary early poet, sometimes called Homer's companion or son-in-law. His name suggests "meat-lover."</note>, Socrates, that companion of Homer, would perhaps appear even more ridiculous in his education than in his name, if the stories told about Homer are true. For it is said that he was greatly neglected by his companions even while he was still alive.

It is indeed said so, I replied. But do you think, Glaucon, that if Homer had truly been able to educate men and make them better—meaning he possessed actual knowledge rather than just the ability to imitate—he would not have gained many companions and been honored and loved by them? <margin>B</margin> Indeed, **Protagoras of Abdera** and **Prodicus of Ceos** <note>Famous Sophists, or professional teachers, who charged high fees to teach rhetoric and virtue.</note> and many others are able to convince their contemporaries in private that they will never be able to manage their own households or their city unless these teachers oversee their education. For this wisdom, they are so intensely loved that their followers almost carry them around on their heads.

If Homer or **Hesiod** <note>An early Greek poet, author of "Theogony" and "Works and Days."</note> had truly been able to help men toward virtue, would their contemporaries have allowed them to wander about reciting poems? <margin>C</margin> Would they not have clung to them more tightly than to gold, and forced them to stay at home? Or, if they could not persuade them to stay, would they not have followed them wherever they went until they had received a sufficient education?

You seem to me, Socrates, to speak the absolute truth.

Then let us establish that all the poets, beginning with Homer, are merely **imitators of images of virtue** <note>original: "imitatores... virtutis imaginum" / "μιμητὰς εἰδώλων ἀρετῆς"</note> and of the other things they write about, but they never lay hold of the truth. Just as we said before, a painter will depict a shoemaker who *appears* to be real to those who know nothing of shoemaking, even though the painter himself understands nothing of the craft; he relies only on colors and shapes. <margin>D</margin> In the same way, we shall say the poet uses "musical colors"—names and phrases—to paint a picture of each craft, though he understands nothing but how to imitate. To others like himself, who judge only by words, it seems he speaks beautifully, whether he talks of shoemaking, military command, or anything else in meter, rhythm, and harmony. Such a powerful charm do these things naturally possess. For I think you know what the works of the poets look like when they are stripped of their musical coloring and read by themselves. You have surely seen them?

I have, he said.

Do they not, I said, resemble the faces of those who are youthful but not truly handsome, when the bloom of youth has left them?

Exactly so, he said.

Now consider this: the creator of the image—the imitator, as we call him—understands nothing of reality, only appearance. Is that not so? Yes. Then let us not leave this half-said, but look at it clearly. <margin>E</margin> A painter, we say, will paint a bridle and a bit? Yes. But the shoemaker and the blacksmith will actually make them? Certainly. Does the painter understand how the bridle and bit ought to be shaped? Or does even the maker—the blacksmith or the leatherworker—understand this? Is it not rather the one who knows how to *use* them, the horseman, who truly knows?

That is most true.

Shall we not say then that this applies to everything? How? That for each object, there are three distinct arts: the one that **uses** it, the one that **makes** it, and the one that **imitates** it? <margin>F</margin> Yes. Therefore, the excellence, beauty, and correctness of every instrument, living creature, and action are determined solely by the **use** for which each was made or designed by nature.

That is so.

It is therefore necessary that the **user** of each thing be the most experienced, and that he report to the maker which features are good or bad in actual use. For example, a flute-player reports to the flute-maker about the flutes, specifying how they should perform while playing, and the maker follows his instructions. How could it be otherwise? <margin>G</margin> Thus, the one who knows reports on the quality of the flutes, and the other, trusting him, produces them. Yes. Regarding the same instrument, then, the maker has a **correct belief** <note>original: "rectam fidem" / "πίστιν ὀρθὴν" — a level of conviction based on following an expert's guidance.</note> about its beauty or flaws because he associates with the one who knows; but the user has **knowledge** <note>original: "scientiam" / "ἐπιστήμην" — direct, certain understanding gained through use.</note>.

Certainly.

But what of the imitator? Will he have knowledge from using the things he paints, to know whether they are good and correct? Or will he have correct belief because he is forced to associate with the one who knows? Neither. Then the imitator will neither know nor have a correct belief regarding the quality of what he imitates. It seems not. The imitator is a charming fellow, then, in his "wisdom" regarding his subjects! Not at all. Nevertheless, he will go on imitating, even without knowing whether a thing is good or bad; he will likely imitate whatever *appears* beautiful to the ignorant multitude. What else?

We have, it seems, reached a fair agreement: the imitator knows nothing of value about the things he imitates. Imitation is a kind of **play** <note>original: "iocum" / "παιδιάν" (paidian) — a game or amusement, as opposed to serious work.</note>, not a serious pursuit. And those who take up tragic poetry, whether in iambic or heroic verse, are all imitators in the highest degree.

Absolutely.

By Zeus! I said, is this imitation not something removed to the third degree from the truth? Yes. To which part of the human soul, then, does it belong?

<column-break/>

As the successors of Homer handed down a certain way of life: Just as **Pythagoras** lived with the highest authority in this regard, and his followers even in these times are held as illustrious among others for celebrating the Pythagorean life. Yet no such thing is told of **Homer**. <margin>A</margin> For **Creophilus**, O Socrates, perhaps a friend of **Homer**, will appear even more ridiculous in his discipline than in his name, if the things told about Homer are true. For it is said he was quite negligent toward him while he was alive. It is indeed said. But surely, O Glaucon, if **Homer** was truly able to instruct men and make them better, as one who possessed not only imitation but also understanding <margin>B</margin> in these matters, why did he not acquire many friends? Why was he not honored while alive? Why not loved? Surely **Protagoras of Abdera**, and **Prodicus of Ceos**, and many others can persuade the men of their time, approaching them privately, that they will never manage their family or public affairs rightly unless they themselves educate them: and for this wisdom they are so ardently loved, that their followers can scarcely restrain themselves from carrying them about on their heads. But **Homer** or **Hesiod**, the men of those times, if indeed those poets were able to help them toward virtue, would they have permitted them to wander about everywhere singing poems? <margin>C</margin> Would they not rather have embraced them more than gold, and brought them into their domestic and familiar company? And if they could not persuade them, would they not have followed them everywhere, until they were sufficiently imbued with those same studies?

You seem to me to speak quite truly, O Socrates. Let us therefore suppose that all the poetic men, beginning with **Homer**, are imitators of the images of virtue, and similarly of the other things they sing, but they by no means touch the truth. But as we said a little before, the painter will paint a visible image of a shoemaker, though he himself understands nothing of shoemaking, and that image appears to be the shoemaker himself to those who understand nothing of the thing itself, but look only at colors and shapes. <margin>D</margin> Entirely so. We shall say the poet no differently expresses certain colors of the individual arts with names and words, though he understands none of these things himself, but only imitates, so that to those who judge these things from words, he seems to speak well, whether he speaks of shoemaking in verse, rhythm, and harmony, or of military affairs, or of any other things. To such an extent do those poetic things naturally soothe the ears. But I think you know what these works of the poets look like when they are considered stripped of the colors of music. Have you ever noticed? I have. Do they not look just like the faces of those who are pretty rather than beautiful because of their youth: such as they appear after the bloom itself has left them? Altogether. Come then and notice this. The imitator, the author of the image, understands the thing itself not at all, but only the apparent image of the thing. It is so. Let us not leave it imperfect, then, but <margin>E</margin> contemplate it sufficiently. Speak, he said. A painter will paint reins and a bit. Plainly. But a leatherworker and a blacksmith will make them. Certainly. Does the painter understand what kind the reins and bit should be? Or does even the maker, whether the blacksmith or the leatherworker, not know, but only he who knows how to use them, the horseman? You speak the truth. Shall we not say it is so regarding everything? How? Regarding everything there are these three arts: the using, the making, and the imitating? Certainly. The virtue, beauty, and correctness of every instrument, animal, and action, are referred to nothing other than the use, for the <margin>F</margin> sake of which each thing is either made or born. It is so. It is necessary, therefore, that he who uses a thing be the most skillful, and signify to the maker of the work what good or bad qualities it has in the use of that which he uses. Just as a flute-player shows the flute-maker which flutes are most fit for use, and commands what kind he ought to make: and the latter provides himself as a servant, and does not command. Why not? Does not the one who understands pronounce to the other about fit and unfit flutes? And the other, believing, produces them? Plainly. Regarding the same instrument, therefore, the maker has a right faith about its beauty and wickedness, adhering to the one who understands, and being compelled to hear from the one who understands: but the one who uses it has knowledge. <margin>G</margin> Entirely. But will the imitator have knowledge from the use of those things which he paints, whether they be beautiful and right, or the contrary? Or a right opinion, from the fact that he necessarily adheres to the one who understands, and is instructed by him as to what kind of things are to be painted? Neither. Therefore the imitator will neither understand nor rightly opine regarding the beauty or contrary of those things which he imitates? It does not seem so. The imitator will be fine in his depiction as far as wisdom is concerned, in the things he makes? Not much. Nevertheless he will imitate, not understanding in what way each thing is either rightly held or the contrary. But as it appears, whatever he believes to be beautiful to the many and the ignorant, this he will imitate. What else? These things seem sufficiently confessed by us, namely that imitators understand nothing worthy of esteem regarding those things which they imitate: but that imitation is a certain joke rather than a serious matter: and that all those who handle tragic poetry in iambics and heroic songs are imitators above all others. And especially so. By **Jupiter** <note>original: "Iouem" / "Διός" (Zeus)</note>, I said. But this imitation is distant by a third degree from the truth. Is it not? It is as you say. To which of those things that are in man does it belong?

<summary>Socrates argues that poets like Homer are mere imitators who lack the practical knowledge of the craftsman or the specialized knowledge of the user. He concludes that imitation is a "third-hand" version of reality, appealing to the ignorant rather than the wise.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue in Book X of the Republic, where Socrates moves from discussing the physical imitation of craftsmen’s tools to the psychological effects of imitative art on the human soul. This follows the argument that poets, like painters, produce works that are "three removes from the truth."</meta>

->### OF PLATO<-

<margin>A</margin> ...insofar as it has power of this kind: Of what sort do you ask? Of this sort. The same magnitude seen from afar and from nearby does not appear equal. It does not. The same objects also appear crooked and straight when viewed in water and out of it, and again both concave and convex because of the sight's error regarding colors. Every such confusion is found within our soul. The power of <term>shadow-painting</term> <note>original: *skia-graphia*; a technique using light and shade to create an illusion of three-dimensionality, which Plato viewed as a form of visual deception.</note>, having attacked this weakness of our nature, leaves no trickery of magic untried, as does the art of wonder-working and many other such devices. You speak the truth. Are not the disciplines of measuring, counting, and weighing the most welcome aids for a human against these things, so that what appears larger or smaller, or more, or heavier, does not prevail within us, but rather that which is grasped by number, measure, and scale? How could it be otherwise? <margin>B</margin> And yet, this is the duty of the rational part of the soul. Of this very part. But often, while this part measures and indicates that some things are larger or smaller than others, or equal, the opposite appearances appear to us at the same time regarding these same things. So it happens. Did we not say elsewhere that it is impossible for the same part of the soul to hold contrary opinions at the same time about the same things? And we said so rightly. Therefore, the power of the soul which opines contrary to measurement will not be the same as that which opines according to measurement. Certainly not. But indeed, that which trusts in measurement and calculation is the best part of the soul. Nothing prevents it. Therefore, that which opposes it will be some noble-less part of us. It must be so. Wanting to express this very confession, I was saying above that painting and the whole power of imitation perform their work far from the truth; and again, it joins with and enters into friendship with a part of us that is entirely devoid of <term>prudence</term> <note>original: *prudentia/phronesis*; practical wisdom or the ability to discern the true nature of things.</note>, aiming at nothing healthy or true. Most certainly. <margin>D</margin> Therefore, a base power of imitation, mingling with a base part, procreates base things. So it appears. Is this so only for that which pertains to sight? Or also for that which pertains to hearing, which we call poetry? It is probable that this is also the case. Let us not, therefore, trust only in the likeness that appears to us from painting, but let us come to that very nature of thought to which poetic imitation accommodates itself, and let us see whether it is something base or precious. So we must. Let us propose it in this way. Poetry imitates men acting either by force or voluntarily, and thinking, as a result of their actions, that they have fared either well or ill, and therefore being affected either by pain or by pleasure. Is there anything else? Nothing else. In all these things, does a man agree with himself? Or rather, just as he was at odds regarding sight, as we related, and held contrary opinions in himself at the same time about the same things, does he also in action be at odds and fight with himself? But now it comes to my mind that there is no need for us to dispute this at present. For in the previous discussion we sufficiently agreed on these things: namely, confessing that our soul is agitated by thousands of such varied contentions opposing themselves at the same time. Rightly. Rightly indeed. But <margin>On the upright man, that he should endure grief.</margin> <margin>E</margin> that which was then omitted by us, now seems to me necessary to be cleared up. What is that? An upright man, endowed with such a mind, if he loses a son or something else most dear to him, will bear it more easily than others, as we said. Clearly. But now let us also consider this: whether he will not grieve at all. Even this would be impossible; but he will moderate his grief in some way. This is certainly truer. Tell me this about him for the present: whether you think he will resist grief more when he is seen by his fellow men, or when he is alone, deprived of the company of others. It makes a great difference if he is in the sight of others. Furthermore, when he is alone, he will dare to say many things which he would be ashamed to utter before others. He will do many things which he would never wish to be seen by others. It is so. That which commands him to resist is reason and law; but that which drags him toward grief is the <term>affliction</term> <note>original: *perturbatio/pathos*; an uncontrolled emotional state or suffering.</note>. You speak the truth. When a man is agitated by contrary impulses concerning the same thing at the same time, we say those must necessarily be two distinct things. Without a doubt. <margin>F</margin> One part, indeed, is ready to obey the law, however it may enjoin. In what way? The law surely dictates that it is best in adversities to keep as quiet as possible and not to complain; because it is uncertain whether the event is good or evil, and because grieving contributes nothing to the future, nor is any of human affairs to be weighed heavily; and grief is an impediment to that which can be of immediate assistance. To what do you refer? <margin>G</margin> I say it is necessary to deliberate about the things that have happened, and as in a throw of the <term>dice</term> <note>original: *talorum/kybon*; knucklebones or gaming dice.</note>, according to how they fall, to arrange one's affairs in whatever way reason says would be best. Nor indeed, if any adversity happens, should we prostrate ourselves and, as children are wont to do when they stumble against a stone, linger in wailing, clinging to the part that was hurt; but we must accustom the soul to be ready to heal and to correct whatever is sick and fallen, dismissing lamentations. This is indeed an opportune remedy against the blows of fortune. That which is indeed best, willingly obeys this reason. It is certain. <margin>H</margin> But that which drags us toward the remembrance of the affliction and toward mourning, and keeps us longer in them, is irrational, lazy, and fearful. So it must be said. That which is complaining admits of much and varied imitation. But the prudent and quiet...

<column-break/>

...insofar as it is well-disposed regarding power? Of what sort of thing do you speak? Of this sort. The same size, I suppose, does not appear equal to us through sight when seen from near and from far. No indeed. And things appear both crooked and straight when viewed in water and out of it, and both concave and convex, because of the error of sight regarding colors; and every such confusion is clearly present in our soul; this affection of our nature, which shadow-painting attacks, leaves nothing of sorcery undone, as do wonder-working and many other such devices. True. Have not measuring, counting, and weighing appeared to be the most graceful aids against these? So that what appears larger or smaller, or more or heavier, does not rule in us, but rather that which has calculated, measured, or weighed? How could it not? <margin>B</margin> But surely this would be the work of the rational part in the soul. Of this part indeed. But to this part, though it has often measured and signaled that some things are larger or smaller than others, or equal, the opposite appears at the same time regarding the same things. Yes. Did we not say it is impossible to have contrary opinions at the same time about the same things? And we spoke rightly. Therefore, the part of the soul that opines contrary to the measures would not be the same as that which opines according to the measures. No indeed. But surely that which trusts in measure and calculation would be the best part of the soul. Why not? And that which opposes this would be one of the base things in us. Necessarily. Wishing to agree on this, then, I said that painting and imitation in general, being far from the truth, performs its own work, and it associates with and is a mistress and friend to that part in us which is far from prudence, for no healthy or true purpose. Entirely so, he said. <margin>D</margin> Therefore, imitation, being base and associating with a base part, generates base things. It seems so. Is it (I said) only that which concerns sight, or also that which concerns hearing, which we call poetry? It is likely, he said, that this also is so. Let us not then (I said) trust only in the likelihood from painting, but let us also go to that part of the intellect with which poetic imitation associates, and see whether it is base or serious. We must do so. <margin>D</margin> Let us put it this way. Imitation, we say, imitates men performing forced or voluntary actions; and from the acting, thinking they have fared well or ill; and in all these things, either grieving or rejoicing. Was there anything else besides these? Nothing. Is a man, then, in all these things, in a state of internal harmony? Or just as he was at odds regarding sight, and had contrary opinions in himself at the same time about the same things, does he also in his actions be at odds and fight with himself? But I remember that there is no need for us to agree on this now; for in the earlier arguments we sufficiently agreed on all these things: that our soul is full of thousands of such contradictions occurring at the same time. Rightly, he said. Rightly indeed (I said); but what we then left out, now seems to me necessary to go through. What is that? he said. <margin>E</margin> A decent man (I said), having shared in such a fortune as losing a son, or something else he holds most dear, we said somewhere even then that he will bear it more easily than others. Certainly. But now let us examine this: whether he will not be distressed at all, or if this is impossible, but he will be moderate in some way toward grief. Thus rather (he said) is the truth. Tell me this about him: whether you think he will fight and resist his grief more when he is seen by his peers, or when he is alone by himself in solitude? Much indeed (he said) will it differ when he is seen. But when left alone, I think, he will venture to utter many things which, if anyone heard him, he would be ashamed of; and he will do many things which he would not accept anyone seeing him do. It is so (he said). Is it not that reason and law are what command him to resist, but the passion itself is what drags him toward the griefs? True. When contrary pulls occur in a man regarding the same thing at the same time, we say it is necessary for there to be two parts in him. How not? <margin>F</margin> Therefore, the one part is ready to obey the law, as the law leads the way. How? The law says somewhere that it is best to keep quiet as much as possible in misfortunes and not to be vexed; as it is not clear what is good and bad in such things, and nothing is gained for the future by taking it hard, nor is anything of human affairs worth great seriousness; and that which ought to be present to us in them as quickly as possible, the act of grieving becomes an impediment to it. To what (he said) do you refer? <margin>G</margin> To deliberating (I said) about what has happened, and as in a fall of dice, to set one's affairs in relation to the things that have fallen, in whatever way reason determines would be best; but not like children, having stumbled, and like children, holding onto the part that was struck, to waste time in crying; but always to habituate the soul as quickly as possible to turn toward healing and restoring what has fallen and is sick, doing away with lamentation by a medicinal power. Most rightly (he said) would someone bear up against fortunes in this way. We say, then, that the best part is willing to follow this rational part. Clearly. <margin>H</margin> But that which leads toward the memories of the suffering and toward lamentations, and is insatiable for them, shall we not say it is irrational and lazy, and a friend of cowardice? We shall say so indeed. Therefore, the fretful part admits of much and varied imitation; but the prudent...

<summary>Socrates argues that the soul has a rational part that uses measurement to overcome sensory illusions and an irrational, base part that succumbs to them. He then applies this to the "affliction" of grief, arguing that law and reason demand a quiet, medicinal response to tragedy, while imitative poetry appeals to the irrational part of the soul that prefers to dwell on suffering.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument from Book X of the Republic, where Socrates explains why imitative art (poetry and painting) appeals to the lower, irrational parts of the human soul rather than the rational part.</meta>

->### ON THE REPUBLIC, BOOK X.<-

<margin>A</margin> ...the calm and quiet character, being nearly always consistent with itself, is neither easy to imitate, nor—when imitated—easy to understand, especially by a crowd gathered at a festival or by all sorts of people flocking to the theaters. For the imitation they witness is of a state of mind that is foreign to them. <note>Plato argues that rational, steady behavior makes for "boring" drama; audiences prefer seeing wild emotional swings.</note> It is entirely so. Clearly, then, the imitative poet is not naturally inclined toward this part of the soul, nor is his wisdom designed to please it, if he intends to be popular with the masses. Instead, he focuses on the irritable and fickle character, because it is so easy to imitate. It is clear. Therefore, we would be justified in taking hold of him and placing him as the counterpart to the painter. He resembles the painter in that he produces things that are base in relation to the truth. He also resembles him in that he communicates with a similar part of the soul—not the best part, but an inferior one. And so, we would <margin>B</margin> be right not to <unclear>admit</unclear> <note>original: *paradechoimetha* / *recipiemus*</note> him into a city that is to be well-governed. This is because he rouses and nurtures this part of the soul, and by making it strong, he destroys the rational part. Just as in a city, when one hands over power to wicked men and betrays the city while destroying the more refined citizens, so we shall say that the imitative poet instills an evil "constitution" <note>original: *politeian*; here referring to the internal governance of the soul.</note> in the soul of each individual by pleasing the foolish part. This part cannot distinguish the greater from the smaller but thinks the same things are sometimes large and sometimes small; he is a creator of phantoms, standing far removed from the truth. Quite so. However, we have not yet brought the greatest accusation against poetry. For the fact that it is <margin>C</margin> capable of corrupting even the virtuous, with the exception of a very few, is surely a terrible thing. How could it not be, if it actually does this? Listen and consider. When the best of us hear Homer, or some other tragic poet, imitating one of the heroes in mourning, delivering a long speech of lamentation, or even singing and beating their breasts, you know that we feel pleasure. Giving ourselves over to it, we follow along in sympathy, and in earnest we praise as a good poet whoever can affect us in this way as much as possible. I know, of course. But when a domestic grief actually befalls one of us, you notice that we pride ourselves on the opposite—if we are able to keep quiet and endure. We consider this the behavior <margin>D</margin> of a man, while that which we praised before in the theater is the behavior of a woman. <note>In the Greek context, public displays of excessive grief were often culturally coded as "unmanly" or "feminine," whereas the "Stoic" ideal of the citizen was one of self-restraint.</note> I do notice it, he said. Is this praise then well-placed? (I asked). Is it right for a man to see someone behaving in a way he would not deign to behave himself—and would indeed be ashamed of—and yet not feel disgust, but instead feel joy and offer praise? No, by Zeus, he said, it does not seem reasonable. Indeed (I said), if you look at it in this way. In what way? If you consider that the part of the soul which is forcibly held back during our own misfortunes—which hungers for tears and a good cry to satisfy its natural desire—is the very part that is filled and delighted by the poets. That part of us which is by nature the best, because it has not been sufficiently educated by reason or habit, relaxes its guard over this wailing part. It thinks it is merely watching the suffering of others, and that there is no shame for itself if another man, who claims to be good, grieves immoderately; it praises and pities him. It thinks it gains a profit of pleasure there, and would not want to be deprived of it by <margin>E</margin> despising the whole poem. For few people, I think, are capable of reflecting that what we enjoy in others must inevitably be reflected in ourselves. For if we nurture the "pitiable" element into something strong by feeding it on the sorrows of others, it is not easy to restrain it during our own sufferings. Most true, he said. Does the same logic not apply to the laughable? If there is a joke you would be ashamed to make yourself, yet you enjoy hearing it in a comic imitation or in private conversation and do not hate it as something base, you are doing the same thing as in the case of the pathetic. For that impulse in yourself which wanted to play the buffoon, but which you held back by reason because you feared a reputation for vulgarity, you now let loose. Having made that part of you vigorous at the theater, you often fail to notice that you have been carried away in your private life until you become a comic poet yourself. <note>Plato warns that "harmless" entertainment habituates the soul to vice.</note> Very much so, he said. And the same applies to lust, anger, and all the desires, pains, and pleasures in the soul, which we say accompany every action of ours; <margin>F</margin> poetic imitation has this effect on us. It nurtures them by watering them when they ought to be withered; it sets them up as rulers over us, when they ought to be ruled, so that we might become better and happier rather than worse and more miserable. I cannot say otherwise, he said. Therefore (I said), Glaucon, when you meet with admirers of Homer who say that this poet has educated Greece, and that for the management and education of human affairs he is a poet worth taking up to learn from, and that one should arrange one's whole life according to this poet—you should indeed be friendly and embrace them, <margin>G</margin> as they are the best men they are able to be. You should even concede that Homer is the most poetic of all and the first of the tragic poets. But you must know that only hymns to the gods and praises of good men are to be admitted into the city. For if you admit the "honeyed Muse" in lyrics or epic poems, then pleasure and pain will be the kings of your city, instead of law and the principle that has always been deemed best by the community: reason. Most true, he said. Let this, then (I said), be our defense, now that we have reminded ourselves about poetry—that we were right to banish it from the city, given its nature. For reason constrained us. But let us also say to her, lest she charge us with a certain harshness and rusticity, that there is an ancient quarrel between poetry...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...a character that is always similar to itself is not easily imitated, nor, if imitated, is it easily perceived, especially by a crowd of various peoples flowing together into a theater. For the imitation is of an affection foreign to them. It is entirely so. It is clear that the imitative poet does not intend his wisdom to please this nature of the soul, if he wishes to please the common people; rather, he observes the querulous and varied character of the soul, which can be easily portrayed through imitation. It is evident. Therefore, we rightly criticize poetic imitation and say it corresponds exactly to the imitation of the painter. First, because both produce things that are worthless if you look at the truth. Second, because they similarly support the part of the soul that lacks reason and <margin>B</margin> <margin>Similarity</margin> disregard the best part. And for that reason, we shall by no means receive it into a legitimately governed state, because it arouses and feeds this part of the soul; while it strengthens this, it destroys the power of reason. Just as one who, in a city, by making the most powerful men wicked, would betray the city and destroy the upright; so also the imitative poet induces a perverse "republic" in the soul of each person, while he flatters that part of the soul which is without mind, and which distinguishes neither greater nor smaller things, but thinks the same things are sometimes small and sometimes great, and fashions images for it, being vehemently alienated from the truth. By far. We have not yet described the <margin>C</margin> <margin>The great evil of poetry</margin> greatest evil that comes from it. Indeed, this must be considered the greatest harm: that it can corrupt even upright men, with very few exceptions. Why could it not, if indeed it does so? Listen, I say, and see. Do not even the best of us, when we hear Homer, or any other tragic poet, imitating some hero involved in grief, crying out, and bewailing his fortune in querulous melodies, and striking his breast with his fists, feel delighted in a certain way? Gaping at those things, we follow them and are affected together with them, and with serious zeal we praise him as a good poet who moves us so vehemently. I have noticed it. But whenever <margin>D</margin> <margin>Book 3 of the Republic</margin> a domestic and true sorrow invades one of us, you know how we glory in the opposite: namely, if in some way we are able to keep quiet and tolerate the pain—as if this were the part of a man, while that which we previously praised was the part of a woman. Plainly. How excellent is this praise! Indeed, it is absurd that someone who watches such a man—the kind he would least want to be himself, and of which he would be most ashamed—does not loathe it, but is delighted and praises it. It is altogether absurd. Certainly, if you also observe it in this way. In what way? Because clearly that which is forcibly restrained in our own calamities, and prohibited from breaking out into tears and weeping, and from indulging its nature which is greedy for tears, is the very thing that the poets satisfy, and which they thoroughly flatter. Then certainly, that which is best by nature in us, being instructed neither by reason nor by experience, ceases to guard that querulous part, as if it were watching the <margin>E</margin> <margin>The misfortunes of others are transferred to one's own</margin> disturbances of another, and as if it were no disgrace to itself if, while another man who proclaims himself to be excellent in virtue weeps immoderately, it should praise and pity him. Rather, it thinks it gains that pleasure, and would by no means wish to be deprived of it out of contempt for that poetry. Few indeed notice, as I believe, that it is necessary for something to be transferred from others into one's own affairs. For if you nourish that mournful disposition in the misfortunes of others and make it stronger, you will not easily stop it in your own. You speak too much truth. Is not the same reasoning true regarding laughter? <margin>F</margin> <margin>On laughter</margin> For what you would be most ashamed to do for the sake of provoking laughter, when you hear it in a comedy or a private imitation, you listen to most willingly as something ridiculous, and you do the same here as we said happened in the mournful imitation. For that disposition of yours, prone to laughter, which you yourself contained within you for fear of the crime of buffoonery, you now release into jokes; and by gradually making the affection of laughter itself more vehement, you begin to be carried away in your own gestures into laughter more than is becoming, and you emerge as a ridiculous buffoon excited by the jokes of comedy. Vehemently indeed. We say the same also about lust and anger, and about all the desires and affections of the soul, both sad and pleasant, which we said follow us in every action; poetic imitation fashions such things in us. <margin>G</margin> <margin>Hymns to the gods</margin> For it nourishes them while it fosters and waters them, when they ought rather to be thinned out by dryness; and it brings it about that these rule in us, when they ought rather to be subjects, so that we may become better and happier instead of worse and more miserable. I cannot say otherwise. Whenever, therefore, Glaucon, you encounter praisers of Homer, and you hear them saying that Homer has educated all of Greece, and that for the government and discipline of human affairs this poet ought to be adopted, and all life should be instructed according to his institutions, remember that they are to be tolerated and loved as men who are the best according to their capacity. And concede that Homer is the most excellent poet and the chief of the tragedians. But know that only hymns to the gods and praises of excellent men ought to be admitted from poetry into the city. For if you accept the voluptuous Muse in songs and poems, pleasure and pain will rule in the city instead of the law and that which has always seemed best: namely, reason. You speak the truth. Let these things be said by us to that effect: that we rightly expelled poetry of such a kind from the city. For reason so compelled us. Let us also add this, lest she accuse us of rigidity and rusticity, because a certain ancient quarrel exists between poetry...

<summary>This page concludes Plato’s argument that imitative poetry is psychologically damaging because it feeds the irrational, emotional parts of the soul while bypassing reason, eventually corrupting even virtuous citizens. Socrates maintains that while Homer is a great poet, only hymns to gods and praises of heroes can be allowed in a just city to ensure that reason, not pleasure or pain, remains the ruler.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Book X of Plato's Republic, moving from the critique of imitative poetry to the defense of poetry's potential utility, and finally transitioning into the famous argument for the immortality of the human soul.</meta>

# PLATO

<margin>Absent from the Greek.</margin>
<margin>A</margin>
...and the disagreement with philosophy. (Certainly, the following sayings and many others can be taken as evidence of this old contention: namely, "that talkative dog barking at her master" <note>original: "canis illa garrula ad aures domini latrans." This and the following phrases were likely insults hurled by poets at philosophers.</note>; and "that great man in the empty talk of fools"; and "the crowd of over-wise men who have the upper hand." Also, "those who meditate on thin and trivial things because they are pressed by poverty." And countless other signs of that ancient grudge.) Nevertheless, let it be said that if poetry, the servant of pleasure and imitation, can bring any argument to show that she ought to be received into a well-ordered state, we shall gladly receive her, so that we may enjoy her delights. For we are <margin>B</margin> well aware of her charms. But it is a sin to betray what appears to be the truth. For tell me, my friend, are you not also soothed by her? Especially when you view her through Homer? "Very much so." Is it not then fair that she should return from exile to make her defense, whether in song or in another meter? "Entirely so." Let us also grant to her defenders—those who are not poets themselves but lovers of poetry—the chance to speak on her behalf in prose, to show that she is not only pleasant but also useful for the commonwealth and for the conduct of human life. And we shall listen with a favorable mind, for we shall surely gain if she appears not only sweet but also useful. <margin>C</margin> "What stands in the way of such a gain?" Otherwise, my dear friend, just as those who have once fallen in love, if they find the love is not beneficial, they force themselves to stay away, even if it is painful to stop loving; so we too, because of the love for such poetry that has been bred in us by our education in beautiful republics, shall certainly hope that she appears as excellent and as true as possible. But as long as she is unable to make her defense, we shall listen to her while repeating to ourselves the arguments we have set forth as a kind of incantation against the dangers that threaten us, taking care not to fall back into those childish loves of the masses. We shall remain mindful that one should not take such poetry seriously, as if it were a matter of truth or a serious pursuit. Rather, the listener must be on guard, fearing for the "republic" <margin>D</margin> within his own soul. And what we have said of poetry must be held to firmly. "I certainly agree." For the contest is great, my friend Glaucon—great, and not as small as it seems—to become either good or evil. Therefore, one should not neglect justice and the other virtues for the sake of money, honor, power, or even for any delight of poetry. "I agree with these reasons we have discussed, and I think anyone else would confess the same." <margin>E</margin> And yet, we have not even mentioned the greatest rewards of virtue and the prizes laid out for her. "You speak of immense rewards, if there are any greater than those we have already named." What can be truly great in a short span of time? For this entire time from childhood to the end of old age is but a tiny thing compared to the whole of eternity. "Indeed, it is nothing." Do you then think an immortal thing should be concerned for this brief time, rather than for the whole of eternity? <margin>Demonstration of the immortality of the soul.</margin> "Certainly for the whole. But what is the point of this?" Are you unaware that the human soul is immortal and free from destruction? Then Glaucon, looking at me with wonder, said: "By Jove, I certainly do not know that. But can you show it to be so?" Indeed I can, unless I wish to be unjust. And I think you can too, for it is not difficult. "It seems difficult to me. But I would gladly hear you explain what you say is not difficult." <margin>F</margin> You shall hear it now. "Speak." Do you call something 'good' and something 'evil'? "I do." And do you see them in the same way I do? "In what way?" I think that everything which dissolves and corrupts is 'evil,' while that which preserves and benefits is 'good.' "I agree." And do you say there is a specific good and a specific evil for each thing? For example, ophthalmia for the eyes, disease for the whole body, blight for grain, rot for wood, and rust for bronze and iron—and as I say, almost everything has a specific evil and "sickness" <term>sickness</term><note>original: *morbum* / *nosēma*; here referring to the internal corruption of a thing's nature.</note> natural to it? "I agree." And whenever one of these attaches to a thing, does it not make the thing it touches worse, and finally dissolve and destroy it entirely? "How could it not?" Therefore, its own specific evil and its own depravity is what corrupts each thing. And unless that specific evil corrupts it, nothing else ever will. For that which is good never destroys anything, nor does that which is neither good nor evil. "How could they?" If, therefore, we find <margin>G</margin> something that has an evil which makes it worse, yet is unable to dissolve or destroy it, will we not then know that a thing so naturally constituted cannot be subject to death? "That seems likely." What then? Is there anything that makes the soul depraved? "Yes, certainly those things we mentioned: injustice, intemperance, cowardice, and ignorance." Does any of these dissolve and destroy it? And take care that we are not deceived into thinking that an unjust and foolish man, when he is caught in his crime, is then destroyed by his injustice, which is the vice of the soul. "Speak on." Does not the specific vice of the body, which is disease, waste it away and dissolve it until it is no longer a body? And all the things we just mentioned, do they not cease to be when their own specific evil takes hold and stains them? "Yes, exactly." Does the soul not then follow the same pattern—does injustice and the rest of vice, when present, dissipate and waste it away until, dragging it toward death, it separates it from the body? "Not at all." Yet it is surely absurd to think that the vice of another thing could destroy something when its own vice does not bring it to an end. "That is indeed irrational." Pay attention then, Glaucon. From the specific badness of food, which

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
...there is an ancient quarrel between philosophy and poetry. For there is that "yelping hound barking at her master," and that "great man in the empty talk of fools," and "the crowd of over-wise men who hold sway," and "those who worry over thin things because they are poor," and ten thousand other signs of the ancient opposition between them. Nevertheless, let it be said that if imitative poetry, which aims at pleasure, can provide an argument that she belongs in a well-governed city, we would gladly welcome her back, for we are conscious of being charmed by her ourselves. But it is not holy to betray what seems to be the truth. For, <margin>B</margin> my friend, are you not also charmed by her, especially when you contemplate her through Homer? "Very much so." Is it not then just that she should return only after having made her defense, whether in song or some other meter? "Quite so." And we would surely grant her defenders—those who are not poets, but lovers of poetry—the chance to speak for her in prose without meter, to show that she is not only pleasant but also beneficial to constitutions and to human life; and we shall listen favorably. For we shall surely profit if she is shown to be not only pleasant but also beneficial. "How could we not profit?" But if not, my dear companion, then just like those who were once in love, if they think their love is not beneficial, they stay away—by force, perhaps, but they stay away nonetheless. So we too, because of the love for such poetry that has been implanted in us by our upbringing in beautiful constitutions, will be well-disposed <margin>C</margin> toward her appearing as the best and truest possible. But as long as she is unable to defend herself, we shall listen to her while chanting to ourselves this argument we are making, this incantation, fearing that we might fall back into that childish love and the love of the many. We shall perceive that we must not take such poetry seriously, as if it laid hold of truth and were a serious matter; instead, the listener must be cautious of her, fearing for the "constitution" <note>original: *politeias*; the internal order of the soul.</note> within himself, and must believe what we have said about poetry. "I entirely agree," he said. For the struggle is great, my friend <margin>D</margin> Glaucon, great—not as small as it seems—to become a good man rather than a bad one. So one should not be moved by honor, nor by money, nor by any office, nor even by poetry, to neglect justice and the rest of virtue. "I agree with you based on what we have discussed, and I think anyone else would too." And yet, <margin>E</margin> I said, we have not even discussed the greatest rewards of virtue and the prizes proposed for her. "You speak of an unthinkable magnitude," he said, "if there are other things greater than those already mentioned." For what can be great in a short time? For this whole time from childhood to old age is but a small thing compared to the whole of time. "It is nothing," he said. What then? Do you think an immortal thing should be serious about such a short time, and not about the whole? "I think so," he said, "but why do you say this?" Have you not perceived, I asked, that our soul is immortal and never perishes? And he, looking at me with wonder, said, "By Jove, not I! But are you able to say this?" "If I am not being unjust," I said, "and I think you can too; for it is nothing difficult." "It is to me," he said, "but I would gladly hear from you this 'nothing difficult' thing." "You shall hear it," I said. "Speak <margin>F</margin> then." Do you call something 'good' and 'evil'? "I do." Do you then think of them as I do? "In what way?" That which destroys and corrupts everything is the evil; and that which preserves and benefits is the good. "I do," he said. What then? Do you say there is an evil and a good for each thing? For example, ophthalmia for the eyes, and disease for the whole body, and blight for grain, and rot for wood, and rust for bronze and iron—and as I say, almost every thing has an innate evil and sickness? "I do." Then whenever one of these is added to something, does it not make that to which it is added wretched, and in the end, dissolve and destroy the whole thing? "How could it not?" Thus, the innate evil and the depravity of each thing destroys it; or, if this does not destroy it, nothing else can ever corrupt it. For that which is good will never destroy anything, nor will that which is neither evil nor good. "How could it?" he said. If, then, we find something among existing things that has an evil which makes it base, yet is not able to dissolve it and destroy it, will we not then know that there was no destruction for a thing so naturally constituted? "That is likely," he said. What then? I asked. Is there not that which makes the soul evil? "Certainly," he said, "all those things we just went through: injustice, intemperance, cowardice, and ignorance." Does any of these dissolve and destroy it? And consider this, lest we be deceived into thinking that the unjust and foolish man, when he is caught acting unjustly, is then destroyed by injustice, which is the depravity <margin>G</margin> of the soul. Rather, look at it this way: just as the depravity of the body, which is disease, wastes and destroys it and leads it to no longer be a body, and all the things we just listed reach the point of non-existence because their own specific evil settles in and corrupts them—is that not so? "Yes." Come then, and consider the soul in the same way. Does the injustice and other vice present in it, by being within and clinging to it, corrupt and wither it until it leads it to death and separates it from the body? "In no way," he said. But it is surely irrational, I said, for the depravity of another thing to destroy something, while its own depravity does not. "Irrational." For consider, Glaucon, that not even by the badness of food, which is...
