<meta>This page continues the logical proof for the immortality of the soul from the previous discussion in Book X. Having established that each thing is destroyed by its own specific "evil" or "disease," Socrates now argues that because the soul’s specific evil—injustice—does not actually kill it, the soul must be indestructible.</meta>

# ON THE REPUBLIC, BOOK X.

<margin>A</margin> ...due to age, or rottenness, or any other quality, do we think the body must perish for that reason? No; unless the badness of the food itself produces a bodily defect within the body, we will say that the body has perished from its own internal evil, which is disease. But as long as the body is one thing and the food is another, we will never believe that the body is destroyed by an external evil—the badness of the food—unless that external evil produces the internal evil natural to the body. "You are perfectly right," he said. Following the same logic, then, I said: unless a defect of the body produces a defect in the soul, we should never believe that the soul perishes from an external evil without its own internal defect—that is, one thing perishing from the evil of another. "That makes sense," he said.

<margin>B</margin> Therefore, we must either disprove this and show our reasoning is wrong, or, as long as it remains unrefuted, let us never say that a soul perishes because of a fever, or any other disease, or even by the sword; not even if someone were to cut the entire body into the smallest possible pieces. Let no one say the soul is any more destroyed for these reasons until it can be proven that because of these bodily sufferings, the soul itself becomes more unjust or more unholy. While an external evil exists in something else, but the internal evil proper to a thing does not arise within it, we must not allow anyone to say that the soul, or anything else, is destroyed.

"But surely," he said, "no one will ever show that the souls of the dying become more unjust because of death itself."

But if anyone, I said, dares to face the argument and say that the dying man becomes more wicked and unjust so that he doesn't have to admit the soul is immortal, <margin>C</margin> we will surely demand that—if he is telling the truth—injustice must be as fatal to its possessor as a disease. We would expect those who catch it to die from it by its very nature, the most unjust dying quickly and the less unjust more slowly. This is not how it works now, where the unjust only die when others inflict capital punishment upon them. "By Zeus!" he exclaimed, "injustice will not seem like such a terrible thing then, if it is fatal to the one who catches it, for that would be a release from evils! <note>The irony here is that if injustice killed the wicked man instantly, it would be a "mercy" by ending his capacity to do evil.</note> On the contrary, I think it will appear quite the opposite: killing others if it can, but rendering the possessor very much alive—and not just alive, but intensely alert. That is how far it is from being fatal."

<margin>D</margin> "You speak well," I said. Since the soul’s own internal wickedness and its own evil are not enough to kill or destroy it, it is hardly likely that an evil intended for the destruction of something else—the body—will destroy the soul or anything other than what it was specifically meant for. "Hardly likely indeed," he said.

Therefore, since it is not destroyed by any evil at all, whether internal or external, it is clear that the soul must necessarily exist forever; and if it exists forever, it is immortal. "It must be so," he said.

"Let this then be established," I said. "And if it is so, you realize that the same souls would always exist. They could not become fewer, since none are destroyed, nor could they become more numerous. For if any immortal thing were to increase, you know it would have to come from something mortal, and eventually everything would end up being immortal." "That is true," he said.

"But," I said, "let us not believe <margin>E</margin> that—for the argument will not allow it—nor should we think that the soul in its truest nature is the kind of thing that is full of great variety, internal contradiction, and change." "What do you mean?" he asked. "It is not easy," I replied, "for something to be eternal if it is composed of many parts and lacks the most perfect composition, as the soul appeared to us just now." <note>Socrates refers to the "tripartite soul" (reason, spirit, appetite) discussed earlier; he suggests the "true" soul might be simpler or more unified than it appears when trapped in a body.</note> "That is not likely."

Now, that the soul is immortal is forced upon us both by the recent argument and by others. But to see it as it truly is, we must not look at it as it is now, damaged by its association with the body and other evils. Instead, we must carefully contemplate it with the eye of reason as it is when it becomes pure. Then one will find it far more beautiful and will more clearly discern <margin>F</margin> justice, injustice, and everything we have discussed. We have spoken the truth about it as it appears in the present, but we have looked at it like those who see the sea-god Glaucus <note>A mythological fisherman who became an immortal sea-god; his body was said to be encrusted with sea-life after centuries in the ocean.</note>. They cannot easily see his original nature because the old parts of his body have been broken off or worn away and entirely disfigured by the waves, while other things have grown onto him—shells, seaweed, and stones—so that he looks more like a wild beast than his natural self. This is how we see the soul, disfigured by countless evils. But we must look elsewhere, Glaucon. "Where?" he asked.

To its love of wisdom <note>original: "philosophia"</note>, <margin>G</margin> and consider what it clings to and what kind of company it seeks, because it is akin to the divine, the immortal, and the eternal. Think what it would become if it followed such a nature entirely, and was lifted by this impulse out of the sea in which it now lives, shaking off the stones and shells. For now, because it feasts upon the earth, it is encrusted with earthy, stony, and wild things from those so-called "happy feasts." Then one might see its true nature, whether it is multiform or uniform, or however it may be. But for now, I believe we have sufficiently described the conditions and forms it takes in human life. "Most certainly," he said.

"Have we not then cleared away the other points in the argument?..."

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...when things are said to be corrupted by age, or rotten, or changed in any other way, we do not think the body can perish merely from that. But if the defect of the food introduces the body's own specific defect, we will say the body is destroyed by its own defect—namely, disease—through the food. But since the body is one thing and food another, we will never think that it can be dissipated by an external failure of food (which has a different nature) unless it brings in its own internal failure. You speak correctly indeed. By the same reasoning, unless the detriment of the body introduces a detriment to the soul itself, we ought by no means to think that the soul perishes from an external evil without its own depravity; nor is one thing dissipated by the evil of another. So reason advises.

<margin>B</margin> Therefore, let us either refute these points as not being correctly stated, or, as long as they remain unshaken, let us not grant that the soul is dissipated by fever or any other disease, or by the cutting of the throat, or even if someone should cut the body into the smallest pieces—not until someone has shown that because of these passions of the body, the soul itself becomes more unjust and more profane. But as long as an external evil is present to one thing, while its own internal evil does not take hold, let us by no means grant that anything can be corrupted.

"But indeed," he said, "no one will ever show that the souls of the dying are made more unjust because of death."

"But if anyone," I said, "dares to object to us that the one who dies becomes worse and more unjust—lest he be forced to confess that souls are immortal— <margin>C</margin> we shall say it is necessary, if he speaks the truth, that injustice is a deadly vice (just like a disease) to the one who has it. And by this very killing power of its own nature, those who take it up would be killed: those who have it most would die quickly, and those who have it less would die more slowly. It would not be as it is now, where the unjust only die because others inflict punishment on them." "By Jupiter!" he said, "then injustice will not seem to be a very grave evil if it is deadly to the unjust man. For it would be a liberation from evils! But I think, on the contrary, that it entirely kills others as much as it can, but makes the man who shares in it very much alive, and remarkably vigilant; it is so very far from being <margin>D</margin> deadly." "You speak cleverly."

For when its own depravity and its own evil cannot kill the soul, an evil arising from the destruction of something else, and directed toward another thing, will never dissolve either the soul or anything else beyond that to which it properly belongs. "Never, as is probable."

Since it is destroyed by no evil at all, whether its own or external, it is clear that it always exists, and that it is necessary. And if it always exists, it exists as an immortal thing. "Necessarily."

"Let this, therefore, be so. And if it is so, you should observe that souls will always be the same. For they will never be fewer, since none perish. Nor again will they be more. For if anything immortal were to be made more, it would be made from the mortal, and eventually all things would be immortal." "You speak the truth."

<margin>E</margin> "But truly we do not think that, for reason forbids it. Nor again do we believe that the soul in its truest nature is such that it is varied, dissimilar, and differing within itself." "How do you mean this?" "It is not easy for something to be eternal which is composed of many parts and has not obtained the best composition, as the soul has now appeared to us." "That is consistent."

That the soul is immortal, both the present reasoning and others besides can convince us. But if someone truly desires to see what it is like in reality, he must by no means look at it as we do now, <margin>F</margin> defiled by the communion of the body and other evils, but he must diligently discern with reason what it is like when it has become pure. There, certainly, it will appear much more beautiful, and when it is such, it will judge more clearly what is just and what is not, and the other things we have said above. We have indeed spoken the truth about it as it appears at present. But we have seen it no differently than many might look upon the sea-god Glaucus. For they cannot easily consider the ancient nature of Glaucus, because the ancient parts of his body are partly broken, partly worn away, and thoroughly dissipated by the waves, while other things—shells, seaweed, and stones—cling to him in turn, from which he presents the image of a beast much more than the appearance of his former nature.

<margin>G</margin> So also we always see the soul defiled by innumerable evils. But indeed, one ought to turn one's eyes elsewhere, O Glaucon. "Where?" "To its philosophy," I said, "and concerning that, one must observe what the soul touches, and what company it affects and strives for, as one that is kindred to the divine, the immortal, and the eternal. And what it would be further if it should entirely follow such a nature, being led by this affection and effort out of the sea in which it is presently submerged, and emerging naked after shaking off the sand and shells which now—as if nourished by the earth—cling to it as many earthy, stony, and wild things because of it.

Then at last we shall contemplate the true nature of the soul itself, and we shall recognize whether it is varied or simple, and what its whole condition is. But for now, I believe we have declared the affects and forms of the soul in human life well enough." "Quite so," he said. "Have we not then expelled the other things in this dispute?..."

He concludes by illustrating the soul's current "encrusted" state with the metaphor of the sea-god Glaucus, urging Glaucon to look toward philosophy to see the soul's true, divine nature.</summary>

<meta>This page marks a major transition in Book X of the Republic. Having concluded the logical proof that the soul is immortal, Socrates shifts from discussing the internal nature of justice to its external rewards. He moves from the "loaned" philosophical abstraction (where the just man was assumed to appear unjust) back to the reality of how the just are treated by gods and men, eventually introducing the famous Myth of Er to describe the soul’s journey after death.</meta>

# OF PLATO

...but we have by no means brought forward the rewards and honors of justice, in the way that you said Homer and Hesiod did. Instead, we have found that justice itself is the best reward for the soul itself, and we have shown that one must act justly, whether one possesses the Ring of Gyges <note>A mythical ring that granted invisibility, allowing its owner to act unjustly without being seen.</note> or even the helmet of Pluto <note>Latin: *Plutonis galeam*; Greek: *Ἄϊδος κυνῆν* (the helmet of Hades). Like the ring, this mythological helmet rendered the wearer invisible.</note>. "You speak the truth," he said. Furthermore, even now, there is no harm in restoring to justice and the rest of virtue those rewards which she provides to the soul, both from men and from the gods, while the person is still alive and after they have died. "By all means," he said. Will you then restore to me what you "borrowed" in the discussion? "What in particular?" 

<margin>B</margin> I granted to you that the just man should appear unjust, and the unjust man just. For you requested that, even if it were impossible for these things to be hidden from gods and men, it should nonetheless be granted for the sake of argument, so that justice itself might be judged against injustice itself. "Do you not remember?" "I would be acting unfairly if I did not," he said. Now that the judgment has been rendered, I demand back, on behalf of justice, the reputation she enjoys from gods and men; let us agree that she is esteemed as such, so that she may carry off the prizes of victory which she gains from appearing just and bestows upon those who possess her. For she has already been shown to grant the true benefits that come from actually being just, and she does not deceive those who truly lay hold of her. "You ask what is fair," he said. First, then, 

<margin>C</margin> you will grant me this: that the nature of each man, both the just and the unjust, is not hidden from the gods. "We grant it." If they are not hidden, then one will be loved by God and the other hated, just as we agreed at the beginning. "That is so." And for the one who is a friend of the gods, shall we not agree that all things which come from the gods are the best possible, unless some necessary evil remains for him from a former sin? "Certainly." Thus, we must think this of the just man: whether he falls into poverty, or disease, or any other of those things that seem to be evils, these things will eventually lead to some good for him, either in life or in death. For he is never neglected by the gods, whoever earnestly desires to become just and, by practicing virtue as far as is possible for a man, strives to become like God. "It is likely," he said, "that such a man would not be neglected by one who is like him." But regarding the unjust man, we must think the opposite. "Completely so." 

<margin>D</margin> These, then, are the prizes of victory that the just man receives from the gods. "So I believe," he said. But what does he receive from men? Does it not happen thus, if we must speak the truth? Do not the clever but wicked men act like those runners who run well from the lower end <note>The start of the race</note>, but not from the upper end? At first they leap away swiftly, but at the end they are laughed at, slinking away with their ears hanging down and departing without a crown. But the true runners reach the finish, receive the prize, and are crowned. Does it not generally happen the same way for just men? At the end of every action, association, and of life itself, they are held in high esteem and carry off the prizes from men. "Very much so." 

<margin>E</margin> Will you then tolerate me saying of them what you yourself said of the unjust? For I shall say that the just, when they have reached a mature age, hold office in their own city if they wish, and enter into marriages with whomever they please, both giving and receiving in marriage. In short, everything you said of the unjust, I now affirm of the just. Conversely, I say of the unjust men that most of them, even if they hide their vices for a time, are caught at the end of the race and become utterly ridiculous; in their old age, they are wretchedly insulted by both strangers and citizens, scourged, and they suffer all those things you truly described as being harsh—they will be tortured and burned. Imagine that you have heard me repeating all those things you listed. But as I was saying, see if you will tolerate this. "I will indeed," he said, "for what you say is fair." 

<margin>F</margin> These, then, I said, are the rewards, wages, and gifts which are given to the just man by gods and men, in addition to those good things which justice herself contains within herself. "They are very excellent and certain," he said. But these are nothing in number or magnitude compared to those things which await each man after death. And these things must be heard, so that each may receive in full what the argument owes them. "Speak on," he said, "for there are not many things I would hear more gladly." I will not tell you a "Tale of Alcinous" <note>original: *Alcini Apologum*. This refers to the long, elaborate stories Odysseus told to King Alcinous in the *Odyssey*. Socrates is punning on the word "Alcinous" and the word "Alkimos," which means brave.</note>, but the tale of a brave man, Er, son of Armenius, a Pamphylian by birth. He once died in 

<margin>G</margin> battle, and when the bodies were taken up on the tenth day, the others being already decayed, he was found whole and undecayed. Having been carried home to be buried, on the twelfth day after his death, while he was laid upon the funeral pyre, he returned to life; and having revived, he told what he had seen in the world beyond. He said that after his soul had departed from his body, it traveled with many others until they arrived at a certain mysterious place, in which there were two openings in the earth close to one another, and two others opposite them above in the region of heaven. Between these openings sat judges. When they had rendered judgment, they commanded the just to proceed to the right and upwards through heaven, binding the signs of the judgment they had received onto their fronts; but the unjust they ordered to the left and downwards, these also carrying behind them the signs of everything they had done in life. When Er himself approached, they told him that he must become a messenger to men concerning the things there, and they commanded him to listen and observe everything that happened in that place. He saw there...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...and we did not bring forward the rewards or the reputations of justice, just as you said Hesiod and Homer did; but we found that justice itself is best for the soul itself, and that the soul must do what is just, whether it has the Ring of Gyges or not, and even if it has the helmet of Hades in addition to such a ring. "You speak most truly," he said. "Is it then, Glaucon," I said, "now no longer a cause for offense to restore to justice and the rest of virtue the rewards, both in their number and kind, which it provides to the soul from both men and gods, both while the man is still living and after he has died?" "Certainly," he said. "Will you then restore to me what you borrowed 

<margin>B</margin> in the argument?" "What in particular?" "I granted to you that the just man should seem to be unjust, and the unjust man just. For you requested that even if it were not possible for these things to be hidden from both gods and men, it should nonetheless be granted for the sake of the argument, so that justice itself might be judged against injustice itself. Or do you not remember?" "I would be doing wrong," he said, "if I did not." "Since, therefore, they have been judged, I demand back on behalf of justice the reputation which it has from both gods and men, and that we agree it is so esteemed; so that it may also carry off the prizes of victory which it gains from 'seeming' and gives to those who possess it, since it has already been shown to give the good things that come from 'being' and does not deceive those who truly receive it." "You ask for what is just," he said. "Therefore," 

<margin>C</margin> I said, "first you will restore this: that it is not hidden from the gods what sort of person each of them is." "We will restore it," he said. "And if they are not hidden, the one would be a friend of the gods, and the other a hater of the gods, as we also agreed at the beginning." "That is so." "And for the friend of the gods, shall we not agree that whatever comes from the gods, all of it is the best possible, unless some necessary evil from a former sin was already present to him?" "By all means." "So it must be assumed for the just man, whether he is in poverty, or in diseases, or in any other of the things that seem to be evils, that for him these things will end in something good, either while living or even when dead. For surely he is never neglected by the gods, whoever wishes to be eager to become just and, by practicing virtue, to become like God as much as is possible for a man." "It is likely," he said, "that such a one would not be 

<margin>D</margin> neglected by the one who is like him." "Then must we not think the opposite about the unjust man?" "Very much so." "Such, then, would be the prizes of victory from the gods for the just man." "According to my opinion, at least," he said. "And what," I said, "from men? Is it not thus? (If we must set down the reality). Do not the clever and unjust men do exactly what runners do—those who run well from the lower part of the course, but not from the upper? At first they leap away sharply, but at the end they become ridiculous, slinking off with their ears on their shoulders and departing without a crown. But those who are truly runners, coming to the end, both receive the prizes and are crowned. Does it not happen thus for the just as well for the most part? 

<margin>E</margin> Toward the end of every action and association and of life itself, they are held in high esteem and carry away the prizes from men?" "Very much so." "Will you then tolerate me saying about these men what you yourself said about the unjust? For I will say that the just, when they become older, hold office in their own city if they wish, and marry from wherever they wish, and give their children in marriage to whomever they want; and all the things you said about those men, I now say about these. and again about the unjust: that many of them, even if they are hidden while they are young, are caught at the end of the race and are ridiculous; and becoming old men, they are wretchedly insulted by both strangers and citizens, being scourged and racked, which you said were 'boorish' <note>original: *ἄγροικα* (agroika) - meaning rustic, crude, or uncivilized.</note>, speaking the truth; then they will be racked and burned. Suppose that you have 

<margin>F</margin> heard from me that they suffer all these things. But see if you will tolerate what I say." "Certainly," he said, "for you speak justly." "The things, therefore," I said, "that come to the just man while living from both gods and men—prizes and wages and gifts—in addition to those good things which justice itself provided, would be such as these." "And very beautiful and firm they are," he said. "These things, then," I said, "are nothing in number or magnitude compared to those things which await each man after death. And it is necessary to hear them, so that each of them may have received in full what is owed by the argument to be heard." "You may speak," he said, "as there are not many other things I would hear more pleasantly." "But I will not tell you," I said, "a tale of Alcinous, but of a brave man, Er the son of Armenius, a Pamphylian by race. Who once, 

<margin>G</margin> having died in war, when the dead were taken up on the tenth day, already decayed, was taken up whole; and being carried home, he was about to be buried on the twelfth day, but lying on the pyre, he returned to life. And having returned to life, he told what he had seen there. He said that when his soul went out, it traveled with many, and they arrived at a certain demonic place, in which there were two chasms of the earth held next to one another, and of the heaven again other ones in the upper part opposite them. Who, when they had judged, commanded the just to proceed the way to the right and upwards through the heaven, having signs of the judgments bound on their front; but the unjust, the way to the left and downwards, these also having signs on their back of all the things they had done. <margin>B</margin> ...to possess the most brilliant white. The fourth is somewhat reddish. The second, however, exceeds the sixth in whiteness. The entire spindle is turned in a circular motion; but while the whole is being revolved, the seven interior circles are turned in the opposite direction to the whole, more slowly. Of these, the eighth is moved with the swiftest motion; then the seventh, sixth, and fifth follow one another. The third moves with such a motion that it seems to carry the fourth around with it. The fourth carries the third, and the fifth carries the second. The spindle itself turns upon the knees of Necessity. Above, upon each of its circles, a Siren stands, being carried around with the globe, emitting a single sound, or rather a single note. From all eight, however, a single harmony resounds. <margin>B</margin> Furthermore, three others sit at equal intervals, each upon a throne: the daughters of Necessity, the Fates <note>The Moerae or Fates are the personifications of destiny.</note>, clothed in white robes and with garlands upon their heads: Lachesis, Clotho, and Atropos. They sing to the harmony of the Sirens: Lachesis sings of things past, Clotho of things present, and Atropos of things to come. And Clotho, with her right hand, touches the outer circumference of the spindle and helps to turn it, at intervals of time. Atropos, with her left hand, does the same for the inner circles. Lachesis, in turn, touches both the inner and outer with each hand alternately. Therefore, when the souls arrive, they must immediately go before Lachesis. <margin>C</margin> There, a certain prophet first arranges them in order; then, having taken from the knees of Lachesis the lots and the models of lives, he ascends a high platform and speaks thus: "The word of the maiden Lachesis, daughter of Necessity: O souls of a day, this is the beginning of another cycle of a mortal and death-bringing race. A guardian spirit <note>original: "daemon" — here meaning a guiding destiny or tutelary spirit, not an evil entity.</note> will not be allotted to you, but you shall choose your own guardian spirit. Let him who draws the first lot be the first to choose a life, to which he shall be bound by necessity. Virtue has no master <note>original: "Virtus inviolabilis ac libera" / "ἀρετὴ δὲ ἀδέσποτον" (arete de adespoto) — implying virtue is free and belongs to no one but the one who honors it.</note>. As each man honors or neglects her, so shall he possess more or less of her. The blame lies with the chooser; God is blameless." Having said this, he cast the lots among them all; each soul took up the lot that fell near him. Nor is anyone allowed to know his place in the order until he has taken it. For only then does he understand which number he has drawn. <margin>D</margin> After this, he placed the models of lives upon the ground before them: far more numerous than those who were present. He said there were lives of all kinds of men and of all animals. For there were tyrannies <term>Tyrannides: absolute rule or dictatorships</term> among them: some lasting a lifetime, others interrupted in the middle, ending in poverty, exile, and beggary. There were also lives of famous men, some renowned for their appearance, beauty, strength, and athletic skill; others for their noble ancestry and the virtues of their forefathers. There were lives of women in the same manner. But there was no fixed rank for the soul, because it is necessary that by choosing another life, the soul becomes of a different character. All other things were mixed with one another: some with wealth and poverty, some with sickness and health, and some occupying a middle state between these. <margin>E</margin> This, indeed, O Glaucon, is where the whole danger for a human being lies. For this reason, we must take every care that each of us, neglecting other studies, seeks out and follows this study: to see if he can somehow learn and discover who will make him able and knowledgeable enough to discern a good life from a bad one, and always and everywhere to choose the better from among the possible choices. He must consider all the things we have mentioned, both joined together and separated, and how they relate to the virtue of a life. He must understand what beauty mixed with poverty or wealth, and joined with what habit of soul, works evil or good; and what nobility or low birth, private life or public office, strength or weakness, quickness of mind or slowness, and all such things that are either natural to the soul or acquired, do when they are blended together. So that from all these things, he may be able to conclude and choose, looking toward the nature of the soul, between the worse and the better life. Calling that life "worse" which makes the soul more unjust, and that life "better" which makes it more just; and let him disregard all else. For we have seen that this choice is the best both for the living and the dead. Holding this opinion with adamantine firmness, he must go to the house of Hades <note>The underworld or afterlife.</note>, so that even there he may be undazzled by riches and such evils; and not, by falling into tyrannies and other such actions, commit many and incurable crimes and suffer even worse himself. <margin>G</margin> Indeed, he should know how to always choose the middle life between such extremes, and to flee from excess in either direction, both in this life and in the future. For thus a human being becomes most blessed. And indeed, the messenger from that place reported that the prophet added this to his decree: "Even for the one who comes last, if he chooses wisely and lives consistently, there is a desirable life, not an evil one. Let not the first be careless in his choice, nor the last despair." When he had said this, he said that the one who had drawn the first lot immediately ran forward and chose the greatest tyranny; through folly and greed, he had not sufficiently examined everything before choosing. Thus, he failed to notice that in that life it was fated for him to devour his own children and suffer many other evils. But later, when he had considered the chosen life at leisure, he beat his breast and lamented his choice, not abiding by the warnings of the prophet. For he did not blame himself for these evils, but fortune, the spirits <note>original: "daemones"</note>, and everything else...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...to have color; fourth, reddish; second, to surpass the sixth in whiteness. The spindle itself turns in a circle, the whole having the same motion; but within the whole as it revolves, the seven inner circles revolve slowly in the opposite direction to the whole. Of these, the eighth goes the fastest, and second and together with each other, the seventh, sixth, and fifth. The third goes with a motion that makes the fourth appear to be revolving back upon it; the fourth carries the third; the fifth, the second. The spindle turns on the knees of Necessity. Upon each of its circles, a Siren stands above, being carried around with it, uttering a single voice of one tone; but from all eight, a single harmony <margin>B</margin> resounds. Others sit around at equal intervals, each on a throne, the daughters of Necessity, the Fates, in white robes, with garlands on their heads, Lachesis and Clotho and Atropos, singing to the harmony of the Sirens, Lachesis of things that have been, Clotho of things that are, Atropos of things that are to be. And Clotho with her right hand touches the outer circumference of the spindle and helps to turn it, following a period of time; Atropos with her left hand does the same to the inner ones; Lachesis touches each in turn with either hand. When they arrived, they had to go straight to Lachesis. A certain prophet first set them in order; then, taking from the knees of Lachesis <margin>C</margin> lots and models of lives, and ascending a high platform, he said: "The word of the maiden Lachesis, daughter of Necessity. Souls of a day, the beginning of another period of a mortal race that brings death. A guardian spirit <note>original: "daimon"</note> will not draw lots for you, but you shall choose a guardian spirit. Let him who draws the first lot first choose a life, to which he shall be bound by necessity. Virtue is without a master; as each honors or dishonors her, he will have more or less of her. The fault is the chooser's; God is blameless." Having said this, he threw the lots to everyone. Each took up the one that fell by him, except for Er himself. It was clear to the one who took it what order he had drawn. After this, he again placed the models of lives on the ground before them, many more than those present. They were of all kinds; for there were lives of all animals and indeed all <margin>D</margin> human lives. For there were tyrannies among them, some lasting through life, others being destroyed in the middle and ending in poverty and exile and beggary. There were also lives of famous men, some for their form and beauty and other strength and athletic skill, others for their birth and the virtues of their ancestors; and famous men in these respects likewise; and similarly of women. But there was no fixed rank of the soul, because of the necessity that by choosing a different life, it becomes different; but other things were mixed with one another and with wealth and poverty, some with disease, some with health; and some in the middle of these. There indeed (as it seems), dear Glaucon, is the <margin>E</margin> whole danger for a man. And for this reason, we must especially take care that each of us, neglecting other studies, shall be a seeker and a student of this study: if from somewhere he might be able to learn and discover who will make him capable and knowledgeable, discerning a good and a bad life, to choose the better from the possibilities always and everywhere; reasoning out all the things mentioned, both being joined together and divided, how they relate to the virtue of a life; and to know what beauty mixed with poverty or wealth, and with what habit of soul, works evil or good; and what noble birth and low birth, and private life and office, and strength and weakness, and quickness of mind and slowness, and all such things of those being by nature concerning the soul, and of those acquired, works by being blended with one another. So that from all these things he is able, by reasoning, to choose, looking <margin>F</margin> away to the nature of the soul, both the worse and the better life. Calling 'worse' that which will lead it there to becoming more unjust, and 'better' that which leads it to becoming more just. But all other things he will let go. For we have seen that for one living and for one having died, this is the best choice. One must go to Hades having this opinion like adamant, so that he may be undazzled even there by riches and such evils; and not, falling into tyrannies and other such actions, work many and incurable evils, and still himself suffer greater ones; but know to choose the middle life of such things always, and to flee the excesses in either direction, both in this <margin>G</margin> life, as far as possible, and in all that follows. For thus a man becomes most divinely happy. And indeed, then the messenger from there said the prophet spoke thus: "Even for the last comer, choosing with mind, living intensely, there lies a life to be loved, not an evil one. Let not the leader of the choice be careless, nor the last despair." When he had said this, he said the one who drew the first lot immediately came forward and chose the greatest tyranny, and through folly and greed, chose without having sufficiently examined everything; but it escaped him that there was in it the fate of eating his own children, and other evils; but when he examined it at leisure, he beat himself and lamented the choice, not abiding by the things proclaimed by the prophet. For he did not blame himself for the evils, but fortune and the spirit <note>The Greek text cuts off here at "daimona" (spirit/destiny).</note>...

<summary>This page presents the climactic moral lesson of the Myth of Er, describing the "Spindle of Necessity" that governs the cosmos and the ritual where souls must choose their next lives. Plato emphasizes that individuals are responsible for their own destinies, as the "prophet" declares that virtue is free and the choice belongs to the soul, not to the divine.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the Myth of Er from the conclusion of Plato's Republic. The narrator, Er, describes the souls' process of choosing their next incarnations after their time in the afterlife. This follows the introduction of the Fates—Lachesis, Clotho, and Atropos—who oversee the destiny of every soul.</meta>

# ON THE REPUBLIC, BOOK 10

...rather than himself. <margin>A</margin> He said that among those who had come from heaven, there was one who had lived his previous life in a well-ordered state, participating in virtue by habit, but without the foundation of philosophy. To put it simply, no fewer of those caught in such mistakes were those who had come from heaven, for they were untrained in hardships. However, many of those from the earth—having suffered themselves and seen others suffer—did not make their choices in a hurry. For this reason, and also because of the luck of the draw, there was an exchange of good and evil for most of the souls. Yet, if someone, whenever he arrives in this life here, pursues philosophy in a healthy way, and if the lot of his choice does not fall among the very last, it is likely—from what is reported from there—that <margin>B</margin> he would not only be happy here, but his journey from here to there and back again would not be a rough, earthly one, but smooth and heavenly. For he said this spectacle was worth seeing: how the various souls chose their lives. Indeed, it was a sight that was pitiful, ridiculous, and wonderful. For the most part, they chose according to the habits of their former life. He said he saw the soul that had once belonged to Orpheus choosing the life of a swan; because of his hatred for the race of women due to his death at their hands, he was unwilling to be conceived and born of a woman. He saw the soul of Thamyris <note>A legendary singer who challenged the Muses.</note> choosing the life of a nightingale. He also saw a swan changing its lot to choose a human life, and other musical animals doing the same, as is natural. The twentieth soul to draw a lot chose the life of a lion; this was the soul of Ajax, son of Telamon, who fled from becoming a man because he remembered the judgment of the arms <note>Ajax committed suicide after the armor of Achilles was awarded to Odysseus instead of him.</note>. After him came the soul of Agamemnon; he too, out of hatred for the human race because of his sufferings, exchanged his lot for the life of an eagle. The soul of Atalanta <note>A famous huntress and athlete.</note>, falling in the middle of the lots, saw the great honors of a male athlete and could not pass them by, but took that life. After her, he saw the soul of Epeius, son of Panopeus <note>The craftsman who built the Trojan Horse.</note>, passing into the nature of a craftswoman. Far off, among the very last, he saw the soul of the buffoon Thersites <note>The ugliest and most foul-mouthed soldier in the Iliad.</note> putting on the form of an ape. By chance, the soul of Odysseus, having drawn the very last lot, came forward to choose. Because he remembered his former <margin>D</margin> labors, he had recovered from all ambition. For a long time, he went about seeking the life of an ordinary, private man who had nothing to do with public affairs. At last, he found it lying somewhere, neglected by all the others. When he saw it, he said he would have done the same even if he had drawn the first lot, and he chose it gladly. Likewise, from the other animals, they passed into humans and into one another—the unjust into wild beasts, the just into tame ones—and every kind of mixture occurred. Now, when all the souls had chosen their lives, according to the order in which they had drawn their lots, they went forward to Lachesis. She sent with each soul the guardian spirit <note>original: "daimon"</note> it had chosen, to be the protector of its life and the fulfiller of its choices. This spirit first led the soul to Clotho, under her hand and the turning of the spindle's whorl, to ratify the fate it had chosen by lot. After touching this, the spirit led the soul again to the spinning of Atropos <note>Atropos means "Inflexible" or "Unturning," signifying that the destiny is now fixed.</note>, to make the web of destiny irreversible. From there, without turning back, they went under the throne of Necessity. When all had passed through it, they marched to the Plain of Oblivion <note>original: "Lethe"</note> through a terrible, stifling heat. For the plain was empty of trees and anything that grows from the earth. When evening came, they camped by the River of Unheeding <note>original: "Ameles"</note>, whose water no vessel can hold. It is necessary for everyone to drink a certain measure of this water, but those who are not saved by wisdom drink more than the measure. As each person drinks, they forget <margin>F</margin> everything. When they had fallen asleep and it was midnight, there was thunder and an earthquake, and suddenly they were carried upward to their birth, some one way and some another, shooting like stars. Er himself was forbidden from drinking the water. In what way and how he returned to his body, he did not know; but suddenly opening his eyes at dawn, he saw himself already lying upon the funeral pyre. And so, O Glaucon, the myth was saved and did not perish; and it will save us if we are persuaded by it. We shall cross the River of Oblivion well, and we shall not defile our souls.

But if we are persuaded by me, believing the soul to be immortal and <margin>G</margin> able to endure all evils and all goods, we shall always hold to the upward path. We shall practice justice with wisdom in every way, so that we may be friends both to ourselves and to the gods—both while we remain here and when we receive the prizes of virtue, like victors in the games being led around to collect their rewards. Thus, both here and in the thousand-year journey we have described, may we fare well.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Everything rather than himself. Indeed, he was one of those who had descended from heaven, who had lived his former life in a well-ordered state, having exercised virtue by habit rather than by the study of philosophy. Nor were there fewer of those who fall from on high than of the others who were deceived in their selection, as they were ignorant of hardships. But of those who came from the earth, most—because they had both labored in calamities themselves and seen others laboring—did not choose a life at random. For this reason, and also due to the fortune of the lot, an exchange of goods and evils happened to many souls. Furthermore, if anyone, whenever he comes into this life, philosophizes sincerely, and the lot of choice does not <margin>B</margin> fall to him last, it appears from what is reported from that place that he will not only be happy here, but his journey from here to there and his return here again will not be earthly and rough, but smooth and heavenly. He said this spectacle was also a sight worthy of consideration: how the individual souls chose their individual lives. It was indeed a miserable, ridiculous, and wonderful sight—making their choice, as they did for the most part, according to the habit of their prior life. For he said he saw the soul that had once been Orpheus's choosing the life of a swan out of hatred for the race of women; because he was killed by them, he was unwilling to be born from women. He saw the soul of Thamyris choosing that of a nightingale. He also saw a swan turn to the choice of a human life, and other musical animals, as is consistent, did the same. He said that a certain soul, when the lots were offered, chose the life of a lion; this was the soul of Ajax, son of Telamon, detesting the nature of men whenever the memory of that judgment—where he contended with Odysseus for the arms—came into his mind. After him, the soul of Agamemnon, because of his miseries, assumed the life of an eagle out of hatred for the human race. Then the soul of Atalanta, who had received a middle lot, saw how a male athlete is affected with the greatest honors; she could not <margin>D</margin> restrain herself from choosing the life of an athlete. Then the soul of Epeius, son of Panopeus, moved straight away into the nature of an artistic woman. Far off, among the very last, the soul of the ridiculous Thersites put on the form of an ape. By chance, he said, the soul of Odysseus arrived to take the very last lot. From the memory of past labors, having ceased from ambition, he went around for a long time before choosing, seeking the life of a private man who was most alienated from the management of affairs. He found it at last, lying somewhere and neglected by the others, and said he would not have chosen any other life even if he had obtained the first lot; therefore, he embraced that life gladly. He asserted that likewise, from other wild beasts, souls passed into men, and they were changed in turn: the unjust into fierce wild beasts, while the just took up the life of gentle animals; and in this manner, all the mixtures were completed. When all the souls had chosen their lives in order, as the lot had given, he recounted that they approached Lachesis in a long line. Lachesis assigned to each the guardian spirit <note>original: "daemon"</note> they had taken, to be the guardian of their life and the executor of the works they had chosen. This spirit first leads the soul to Clotho, and under her hand and the revolution and whirlpool of the spindle, it approves the fortune which the soul had chosen by lot. When the soul has touched this, it is led from here to the spinning of Atropos, which makes the threads unchangeable. From there, they quickly go to the throne of Necessity, through which when they all have passed, they go forward under a vehement heat and <margin>F</margin> glow into the Plain of Oblivion <note>original: "Letheum"</note>, which is entirely destitute of trees and everything that is born of the earth. He said they lay down as night approached near the River of Negligence <note>original: "Amelitem"</note>, whose water no vessel can hold. It is necessary for each to drink some of this water. But those who do not have wisdom as their leader drink more than is proper. He who drinks always forgets all things. When they had slept until midnight, they were suddenly awakened by thunder and an earthquake, and they sprang up, some one way and some another, upward toward generation, darting forth like stars. He related that he himself had been forbidden from drinking of that river. But how he returned into his body, he did not know; but when he suddenly <margin>G</margin> looked around at dawn, he noticed himself placed upon the pyre. And so, O Glaucon, the story was saved and did not perish, and it will save us likewise if we obey it, and we shall cross the River of Oblivion well, and we shall not infect the soul with any stain. Wherefore, if we comply with my words, believing the soul to be immortal and such that it can sustain all evils and all goods, we shall always follow the way leading to the higher things, and we shall cultivate justice with wisdom by every means, so that we may be friends to ourselves and to the gods while we lead this life, and after we have carried back the rewards of virtue, as if having obtained victory and triumphs, both here and in the thousand-year journey of which we have spoken, may we fare happily.

<summary>This page concludes the Myth of Er, describing how souls choose their next lives based on past experiences and then pass through the Fates and the River of Oblivion before being reborn. Socrates ends the Republic by exhorting Glaucon to pursue justice and wisdom so that the soul may fare well in both this life and the next.</summary>

# PLATO’S
## TIMAEUS, OR, ON NATURE,
### Or on the universe.

# TIMAEUS, OR, ON
## NATURE.

->SUMMARY OF THE DIALOGUE.<-
> The thesis or aim of the discussion is apparent from the title itself: On the Nature of the Universe. It encompasses Plato’s eternal doctrine regarding the nature of things—that is, the creation, causes, and powers of the Universe and all its parts. Thus, the subject of the discussion is an explanation of Physics <note>original: "Physices explicatio"</note>. For the philosopher teaches by what principle and origin the Universe and its individual parts both came to exist and continue to subsist and be preserved: by whose power and virtue they do so. Specifically, he shows that the world was created by God, and is powerfully maintained by that same force and efficacy with which He created and founded it, through natural causes created and ordained by Him for that end. Therefore, the World did not exist from eternity by chance, without a preceding cause, or by its own power; rather, it began to exist at a certain beginning by the definite decree and effective power of God. God, having delineated the image of the World in His own mind, created and founded it at the appointed time so that it might truly exist in a certain and stable manner. Furthermore, he explains the wonderful force, powers, and effects of Nature. He teaches that Nature was created by God, and that Time, the first <unclear>all-encompassing measure</unclear> <note>original: "πᾶνος"</note> of all created things, was also created by that same architect; this is meant to strike down the profane philosophies that argue for the eternity of time and an eternal world, which is a reproach to the creator. Having explained the power and efficacy of the Universe, he then deals specifically with Man, the most excellent of all living beings and thus the most significant part of the world, whose craftsmanship—of both body and soul—he pursues diligently. <gloss>7</gloss>

<margin>A</margin>
->SOCRATES, TIMAEUS, CRITIAS, HERMOCRATES.<-

->SOCRATES, TIMAEUS, CRITIAS, HERMOCRATES.<-

One, two, three. But where, my dear Timaeus, is the fourth of those who were my guests at yesterday's feast, and who should now be my hosts in turn? TIMAEUS. He has fallen ill, Socrates. For he would not willingly have stayed away from this gathering and discussion. SOCRATES. Then it will be your duty, Timaeus, and the duty of those present, to fill the role of that absent fourth man. TIMAEUS. Certainly. We shall omit nothing that is within our power. Since we were so sumptuously entertained by you yesterday, it would be unjust if those of us here did not host you in return with equal alacrity. SOCRATES. Do you remember how many topics I proposed for you to discuss, and what they were? <margin>B</margin> TIMAEUS. We remember some of them; but for those we have forgotten, you are here to remind us. Or rather, if it is not too much trouble, please repeat them briefly from the beginning, so that they may be more firmly fixed in our minds. SOCRATES. I will do so. The summary of yesterday’s discussion was about what kind of Republic <note>original: "Resp." / "πολιτειας"</note> seemed to me to be the best, and from what kind of men it should be composed. TIMAEUS. Indeed, Socrates, what you said was very much to all our liking. SOCRATES. Did we not first separate the farmers and other artisans from the class of those who are to fight in war? TIMAEUS. Certainly. SOCRATES. And since we assigned to each person only one single duty in the arts, giving each what was most suited to their natural instinct, we also commanded those who would wage war above all others to have this one task alone: to be the guardians of the city, protecting it against both external enemies and those within who would overturn the state. <margin>C</margin> We said they should be mild toward those subject to them, who are friends by nature, but most fierce in battle against enemies. TIMAEUS. Just so. SOCRATES. We said that a double nature must exist in the souls of the guardians: they must be both spirited <note>The "irascible" or "thumos" part of the soul, responsible for courage.</note> and particularly suited to a philosophical disposition, so that they may be rightly gentle to their own and fierce toward strangers. TIMAEUS. Without a doubt. SOCRATES. And what did we say about their education? Were they not trained by us in gymnastic exercises, and music, and all other fitting disciplines? TIMAEUS. Most certainly. SOCRATES. <margin>D</margin> We established that men so educated should not have—nor even consider having—gold, silver, or any other private property; instead, as helpers and public servants, they should be content with a wage alone, provided by those they protect, in such an amount as seems sufficient for those living moderately. We also wanted them to use a public stipend in common, and to spend it on a common life together, so that having set aside all other concerns, they might care only for virtue and the guardianship of the state. TIMAEUS. These things were also said by you in that way. SOCRATES. Furthermore, we prescribed that the nature of women should be fashioned no differently than that of men, and that all pursuits, both of war and of peace, should be common to both women and men. TIMAEUS. That too was stated in the same manner. SOCRATES. Do you hold in your memory what we said about the procreation of children? Perhaps you remember it firmly because of the novelty of the idea. We established a community of marriages and children, so that no one might distinguish his own offspring, but all should be considered kinsmen by everyone. Those of roughly the same age would consider one another brothers and sisters, while they would show the reverence of parents or grandparents to their elders, and be moved toward their juniors as if toward children and grandchildren. TIMAEUS. These things are also easy to remember. SOCRATES. <margin>E</margin> In order that the best possible children might be born from the very start, we placed magistrates of both sexes in charge of marriages. These officials would secretly arrange the unions so that the brave would be paired with the brave, and the base with the base, and yet no discord would arise from this; for in an unlucky pairing, each person would blame fortune rather than the plan of the leaders. SOCRATES. We remember. SOCRATES. Furthermore, we ordained that the offspring of the good should be reared in the fatherland, while the others should be sent secretly to other places. Finally, both groups should be carefully observed as they grow up: if any among those sent away show a good disposition, they should be recalled to the fatherland; but if any among those kept at home seem poorly disposed, they should likewise be sent away. TIMAEUS. <margin>F</margin> So it was decided. SOCRATES. Have we now recounted yesterday's discussion sufficiently, as much as a summary allows? Or is there anything else I have omitted, my friend Timaeus, that you wish to review? TIMAEUS. Nothing at all; these are exactly the things you were discussing, Socrates.

<column-break/>

One, two, three. But where, my dear Timaeus, is the fourth of our guests of yesterday, who should now be our host? TIMAEUS. A certain illness has befallen him, Socrates. For he would not have willingly missed this gathering. SOCRATES. Then it is your task, and the task of these others present, to fulfill his part. TIMAEUS. By all means; and as far as we are able, we shall leave nothing out. For it would not be right, after being entertained by you yesterday with such hospitality as was fitting, if the rest of us did not eagerly host you in return. SOCRATES. Do you then remember how much and about what things I charged you to speak? TIMAEUS. Some we remember; and whatever we do not, you being present will remind us. Or rather, if it is not a burden to you, go over them again briefly from the beginning, so that they may be more firmly established among us. SOCRATES. It shall be done. Yesterday, the main point of the words spoken by me concerning the state <note>original: "πολιτειας"</note> was what kind of city would appear to me to be the best, and from what kind of men it would be composed. TIMAEUS. And it was very much spoken to our minds, Socrates. SOCRATES. Did we not first separate the class of those who are to fight for the city from the farmers and the other crafts? TIMAEUS. Yes. SOCRATES. And giving to each that which was appropriate according to his nature, and only one occupation for each craft, we said that those who must fight before all others should be only guardians of the city; whether someone from without or even from within should come to do harm, they are to judge mildly those who are ruled by them, as being friends by nature, but to be harsh in battles with those enemies they encounter. TIMAEUS. Entirely so. SOCRATES. For I think we said that the soul of the guardians must be at once spirited and uniquely philosophical, so that they might be able to be rightly mild and harsh to each group. TIMAEUS. Yes. SOCRATES. And what of their upbringing? Was it not that they should be reared in gymnastics and music, and in all the disciplines that are fitting for them? TIMAEUS. Certainly. SOCRATES. And it was said that those so reared should not consider gold, nor silver, nor any other possession to be their own; but as assistants receiving a wage for their guardianship from those they save—as much as is moderate for sober men—they should spend it in common, and live together with one another, having a constant care for virtue and enjoying leisure from all other pursuits. TIMAEUS. These things were also said in this way. SOCRATES. And indeed we also mentioned women: that their natures must be harmonized to be very similar to those of the men, and that all pursuits must be given to them all in common, both in war and in other modes of life. TIMAEUS. This too was said. SOCRATES. What about the matter of child-rearing? Or is this easy to remember because of the unusual nature of what was said: that we made the marriages and children common to all, contriving that no one should ever recognize his own offspring as his own, but that all should consider all others to be their kin? Sisters and brothers for those who fall within the fitting age of birth; and those before and above them, parents and ancestors of parents; and those below, descendants and children of descendants. TIMAEUS. Yes, these things you say are also easy to remember. SOCRATES. And in order that they might be as excellent as possible in their natures right from the start, do we not remember how we said the male and female rulers must secretly contrive the joining of marriages with certain lots? Thus the bad and the good will be paired with those like themselves, and no one will feel hatred because of this, thinking that chance was the cause of the pairing. TIMAEUS. We remember. SOCRATES. And indeed we said that the children of the good must be reared, but those of the base must be secretly distributed to the rest of the city; and as they grow, the rulers must always watch those who are worthy and bring them back, and exchange those among themselves who are unworthy for the place of those returning. TIMAEUS. So it was. SOCRATES. Have we then gone through it already, just as we did yesterday, so as to return again to the main points of what was said, or do we still miss anything, friend Timaeus? TIMAEUS. Not at all; these were the very things that were said, Socrates.

### TIMAEUS. 523

...always toward the constitution which we described, I happen to feel somewhat like this. My feeling is similar to that of someone who has looked upon beautiful animals somewhere—whether they are depicted in a painting or are truly alive but remaining at rest—and who then arrives at a desire to see them moving and engaged in some competition that seems to suit their bodies. I have felt this same thing toward the city we described. For I would gladly listen to someone describing the contests that a city undergoes, struggling against other cities in a fitting manner when it comes to war; and how, in its warring, it delivers what is appropriate to its education and upbringing, both in its actions during deeds and in its negotiations in words <note>original: "λόγοις διερμηνεύσεις"</note> toward each of the cities. Now, these things, <margin>B</margin> O Critias and Hermocrates, I have judged myself as never being capable of praising the men and the city sufficiently. And my own inability is no surprise; but I have formed the same opinion even about the poets of old and those of the present day—not that I dishonor the race of poets, but it is clear to all that the tribe of imitators will most easily and best imitate those things in which they have been brought up. But that which falls outside of each person’s upbringing is difficult to imitate well in deeds, and even more difficult in words. Furthermore, as for the tribe of Sophists <note>Professional teachers of rhetoric and philosophy who traveled between cities, often criticized by Socrates for prioritizing style over truth.</note>, I consider them experienced in many fine words, but I fear that—since they are a wandering tribe throughout the cities and have nowhere established their own dwellings—they might miss the mark regarding philosophers and statesmen: specifically, how many and what sort of things they might do and say in war and battles, in their actions and in their verbal dealings with others. There remains <margin>D</margin> then only the group of your own standing, which shares in both natures by temperament and education. For Timaeus here is from a most law-abiding city, Locri in Italy, and being inferior to no one there in wealth or birth, he has held the greatest offices and honors in the city, and in my opinion has reached the very summit of all philosophy. And as for Critias, we all here know that he is no amateur in any of the things we are discussing. Regarding the nature and education of Hermocrates, we must believe the many testimonies that he is sufficient for all these tasks. Therefore, yesterday, when I realized you were thinking of asking me to describe the constitution, I readily obliged, knowing that no one would be more capable than you of taking up the next part of the discourse, if you were willing. For once you have placed the city in a fitting war, you alone of those now living could provide it with everything that is appropriate to it. Having said what was commanded of me, I in turn commanded you what I am saying now. You agreed, after consulting together among yourselves, to repay me now with the "guest-gifts" <term>xenia</term> <note>The traditional Greek concept of hospitality where gifts or favors are exchanged between host and guest.</note> of your discourse. So here I am, dressed up for the occasion and most ready of all to receive them.

HERMOCRATES: And indeed, Socrates, as Timaeus here said, we shall not lack any zeal, nor is there any excuse for us not to do this. Thus, even yesterday, as soon as we arrived from here at the guest-quarters of Critias where we are staying, and even before that on the road, we were considering these very things. He then introduced us to a story from ancient hearsay; tell it now, Critias, to him, so that he may judge whether it is suitable for his command or not.

CRITIAS: This must be done, if it also seems right to our third partner, Timaeus.

TIMAEUS: It seems right indeed.

CRITIAS: Listen then, Socrates, to a story that is very strange, yet entirely true, as Solon, the wisest of the Seven Sages, once said. He was a relative and a very great friend of our great-grandfather Dropides, as <margin>F</margin> he himself says in many places in his poetry. He told our grandfather Critias (as the old man in turn remembered and told us) that there were great and wonderful ancient deeds of this city that had disappeared through time and the destruction of men. One was the greatest of all, which it would now be fitting for us to bring to mind, both to repay our debt of gratitude to you and at the same time to praise the goddess justly and truly during this festival, as if we were singing a hymn to her.

SOCRATES: You speak well. But what was this deed that Critias described, not as a mere story, but as something truly performed by this city in ancient times according to what Solon heard?

CRITIAS: I will tell you, having heard an old story from a man who was no longer young. For at that time, Critias (as he said) was already nearly <margin>G</margin> ninety years old, and I was roughly ten. It happened to be the "Youth's Day" <note>original: "Κουρεῶτις" (Koureotis), the third day of the Apaturia festival when children were registered into their kinship groups.</note> of the Apaturia festival. The custom of the feast for the boys occurred then as it always does: our fathers set up contests for the recitation of epic poetry. Many poems by many poets were recited, and since the poems of Solon were new at that time, many of us children sang them. Then one of the clansmen said—whether he truly thought so then or was just trying to please Critias—that it seemed to him that Solon was not only the wisest of men in other respects, but also the most noble of all poets in his poetry. The old man (for I remember it very well) was greatly pleased and said with a smile: "If only, O Amynander, <margin>H</margin> he had not used poetry merely as a pastime, but had taken it seriously as others do, and had finished the story which he brought here from Egypt—and if he had not been forced to neglect it because of the factions and other evils he found here upon his return—in my opinion, neither Hesiod nor Homer...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...I am thus affected by the republic we have described. I will reveal it to you plainly by comparison. Just as if someone, having looked upon animals of extraordinary beauty, whether painted or alive but motionless, should desire to see the movements and gestures of the living creatures and some contest of theirs; so I would now gladly hear someone narrating in what way the city described above might struggle with neighboring cities, and what things worthy of such an education and discipline it might demonstrate toward individual cities, whether in war or in peace, both in speaking and in acting. Truly, O Critias and Hermocrates, <margin>B</margin> I am conscious within myself that I cannot praise that city and its men according to their dignity. That I cannot is no wonder, but I think the same of the ancient poets and those of this century: not that I would disparage the poetic race, but because it is evident to anyone that those who study imitation easily and best imitate those things in which they were educated. But things foreign and far removed from their upbringing are difficult to emulate properly in deeds, and even more difficult in words. As for the Sophists, I consider them skilled in speaking and in almost all other very noble arts; but because they wander daily through many cities and have no fixed homes of their own, I fear they cannot even attain by conjecture <margin>C</margin> how many and what kind of things philosophical and civil men might do toward individuals in words and deeds, both in war and in peace. Therefore, only your profession remains, powerful both by nature and by the discipline of philosophy and the study of managing affairs. Timaeus here, from Locri—which is governed most justly of all cities in Italy—is most outstanding at home in nobility and wealth, has performed the highest magistracies and honors, and has ascended, in my opinion, to the highest peaks of all philosophy. We all know that Critias also has attained both of these. That the nature and education of Hermocrates are also suited to handling all these things we have mentioned, <margin>D</margin> we cannot doubt, as we are reminded by many testimonies. Therefore, when you asked me yesterday to dispute concerning the republic, I most gladly obeyed, thinking that what remained for the established work could be handled by no one more conveniently than by you, if only you were willing. For since you have established a city fit for war, you alone of all men will, in turn, bestow upon it all the things that become it. When, in the previous parts, I had finished what had been enjoined upon me, I committed to you the things just mentioned to be handled; and you, by common consent, took up the task commanded of me to prepare in return a banquet of discourses. I am therefore present, most ready for the promised feast.

HERMOCRATES: We also, O Socrates, as Timaeus just promised, will execute what you command to the best of our strength, especially since there is no reason for excusing ourselves from doing so. For yesterday, when the dispute was finished and we soon returned to the lodging where we were received at the house of Critias, we spoke of these things first during the walk, and again at home. He therefore told us an ancient history, which I would wish you, O Critias, to recount now to Socrates, so that when he has heard it, he may judge whether it seems to contribute to that matter which he commanded us to execute.

CRITIAS: It must be done, if it so seems to Timaeus <margin>E</margin> also, the third participant in this dispute.

TIMAEUS: It seems so indeed.

CRITIAS: Hear, Socrates, a story that is wonderful indeed, but full of truth, which Solon, the wisest of the seven wise men, used to recount. For he was a very close domestic friend <margin>F</margin> of our great-grandfather Dropides, as he himself often testifies in his poems. To our grandfather Critias, as the old man himself afterwards related to us, he once told the memorable deeds of this city, which had been obliterated by the length of time and the death of men. He recounted one deed especially remarkable above the others, which I think should be told to you now, so that we may both comply with your custom and honor the goddess to whom today's procession is dedicated with this narration, as if with a kind of singing of hymns, as is right.

SOCRATES: You speak rightly. But what, finally, is that thing which Critias revealed to you from the narration of Solon—not as if described in words, but as if once performed by this city?

CRITIAS: I will relate the ancient <margin>G</margin> history passed down to me as a boy by my grandfather. When Critias was about ninety years old, as he himself used to say, and I was ten, and that solemn day was being celebrated on which boys are accustomed to be called together to sing poems, we were assembled; and not only with the nearest and best-known boys, but a contest of singing poems was enjoined upon us by our parents. There, not a few poems of many poets were pronounced from memory, and the verses of Solon were sung by most of the boys, who admired the novelty of the poetry. Then a certain fellow-clansman, whether because he judged it so or because he wished to flatter Critias, said it seemed to him that Solon was both the wisest in other things and <margin>H</margin> the most noble of all poets in his songs. At these words, as I rightly remember, the old man was greatly delighted, and laughing thus, he said: "If only, O Amynander, Solon had followed poetry not just for the sake of relaxing his mind, but with devoted and serious effort as others do, and had finished the history which he had begun after returning from Egypt—from which indeed he was turned away in mid-course, disturbed by seditions and other fluctuations of the city—neither Homer nor Hesiod..."
