# OF PLATO

### 524

...nor would he have been inferior to any other of the poets, in my opinion. To <margin>A</margin> this, Socrates said: "What was the subject, O Critias, that Solon intended to treat?" "Concerning the greatest matters," he replied, "which were once performed by this city, the memory of which has been extinguished among us by the long passage of time and the death of men. Tell us, I pray," he said, "O Critias, what was that work, and how was it performed, and from whom did Solon hear it and recount it as a truth?" He said: "There is an Egyptian region called the Delta, from whose summit the streams of the Nile are split. Its fields are named the Saitic prefecture. In these fields is a very great city, which they call Sais, from which King Amasis came. The foundress of that city was a goddess whom the Egyptians call Neith <note>original: "Neithen"</note>, and the Greeks call Athena <note>original: "Athenan"</note>. Furthermore, these men are friends of the Athenians, and they claim to be <margin>B</margin> joined to them by a certain kinship. Solon related that when he arrived there, he was received with great honor. And when he inquired about the memory of ancient times from those priests who were most skilled in this matter, he said he discovered that neither he himself nor any other of the Greeks had any real knowledge of antiquity. On one occasion, in the presence of the priests, in order to provoke them into telling their own stories, he began to speak of the most ancient events of Athens: of the first Phoroneus and Niobe, and after the world-flood, of Pyrrha and Deucalion <note>Greek mythological figures associated with the origins of humanity and the great deluge</note>, and of their descendants, and the times in which each event occurred. Then one of the priests, a man of great age, said: 'O Solon, Solon, you Greeks <margin>C</margin> are always children, and there is no such thing as an old man from Greece.' When Solon asked why he said this, the priest replied: 'Because your souls are always young; in them is no ancient opinion derived from the commemoration of old times, no knowledge gray with age. This happens to you because there have been, and will be, many and varied destructions of men. The greatest of these must necessarily occur either by a conflagration of fire or by floods of water; lesser ones occur by countless other calamities. For what is told among you—that Phaethon <note>The son of Helios who lost control of the sun chariot</note>, the son of the Sun, once ascended his father’s chariot and, failing to keep his father’s course, scorched the earth and was himself consumed by celestial flames—though it seems like a fable, is to be thought <margin>D</margin> true in a certain way. For after a long interval of time, there occurs a certain shift in the celestial circuit, which is necessarily followed by a vast inflammation. Then those who inhabit high and arid places perish more than those near the sea and rivers. To us, however, the Nile is not only a savior in many other things, but also wards off this kind of destruction. But when the gods cleanse the earth by a deluge of water, the shepherds and herdsmen who live on the mountain ridges escape that danger, while your cities located in the plains are swept into the sea by the force of the rivers. But in this region of ours, neither then nor <margin>E</margin> at any other time does water descend upon the fields from above; on the contrary, it gushes upward from the bowels of the earth. For this reason, the monuments of the most ancient things are preserved among us. Therefore, wherever neither excessive rainstorms nor immense fires occur, men are always present, though at times they are fewer and at others more numerous. Whatever deeds have been performed by our nation, or by yours, or by others, that are worthy of memory—if they have come to our ears—they are preserved in our temples, having been written down. Among you and other nations, however, achievements are only recently recorded in letters and monuments, but at certain cycles of time, a deluge sent from <margin>F</margin> heaven devastates everything. Thus, those who succeed you are left bereft of both letters and the Muses. The result is that you become like youths again, unrefined and entirely ignorant of all past events. For even those things which you just recounted from your histories, O Solon, differ little from childish fables. First, because you remember only one flood, though many preceded it. Second, because you are ignorant of the most illustrious and excellent race of your ancestors in your own region, from whom you and all the other Athenians are descended, born from a small seed that once survived the public disaster. This has remained hidden from you because those survivors and their descendants lacked the use of <margin>G</margin> letters for many centuries. For before that fatal deluge of the earth, O Solon, the city of the Athenians was most excellent in the duties of both war and peace; its works and laws excelled all those whose memory has reached us under heaven.' Then Solon, having marveled, said that he earnestly entreated the priests to reveal all the works of the ancient citizens in detail. And one of the priests replied: 'No envy prevents this, Solon. I will speak willingly for your sake and for that of your city; but especially for the sake of the goddess who founded, nurtured, and instructed both your city and ours—taking the seeds of your city a thousand years earlier from the Earth and Vulcan <note>Hephaestus</note>. The history of this our later city, spanning eight thousand <margin>H</margin> years, is contained in our sacred writings. Therefore, I will briefly sketch for you now the institutions and the noble deeds of those citizens who existed nine thousand years before us. Later, when more leisure is given, we will explain everything more broadly by taking up the book of histories. First, consider their laws and how they agree with ours. For you will find many similarities here to those of that time. To begin with, the priests are separated...'

<column-break/>

...nor would any other poet ever have achieved a greater end for a fee. "What <margin>A</margin> was the story," he said, "O Critias?" "Concerning the greatest," he replied, "and most famous deed, which would most justly be carried out by all, which this city performed, but through time and the destruction of those who worked it, the story did not endure to the present." "Tell it from the beginning," he said, "both what it was and how, and from whom Solon heard it and told it as the truth." "There is a certain place in Egypt," he said, "in the Delta, around which the stream of the Nile splits at its head, called the Saitic district; of this district the greatest city is Sais; from where King Amasis also came. The presiding deity of the city is a goddess, whose name in Egyptian is Neith <note>original: "Νηΐθ"</note>, and in Greek, as their story goes, Athena <note>original: "Ἀθηνᾶ"</note>. They are very great friends of the Athenians and <margin>B</margin> they say they are in some way related to those here. Solon said that when he arrived there he was held in great honor among them, and indeed, when he asked about ancient things of those priests most experienced in these matters, he found that neither he himself nor any other Greek knew anything (so to speak) about such things. And once, wishing to lead them into a discussion about the ancients of this place, he attempted to speak of the most ancient things—about Phoroneus, who was called the first, and Niobe, and after the flood again about Deucalion and Pyrrha, and he went through the genealogy of their descendants, and tried to calculate the times by remembering how many years had passed for the things he spoke of. And a certain one of the priests, who was very old, said: 'O Solon, Solon, <margin>C</margin> you Greeks are always children, and there is no such thing as an old Greek.' Having heard this, he asked: 'How so? What do you mean by this?' 'You are all young in your souls,' he said. 'For you have in them no ancient tradition based on old hearsay, nor any learning gray with time. And the cause of these things is this: many and various destructions of men have occurred, and will occur—the greatest by fire and water, and others lesser by countless other things. For that which is also told among you—how once Phaethon, the son of the Sun, having yoked his father’s chariot, because he was not able to drive along his father’s path, burnt up things on the earth and was himself destroyed by a thunderbolt—this is told in the form of a myth, but the truth is a shifting <margin>D</margin> of the things moving in the heavens around the earth, and through long intervals of time, a destruction by much fire of the things on the earth occurs. Then, therefore, as many as live in mountains and in high places and in dry places perish more than those dwelling near rivers and the sea. And to us the Nile is a savior in other things and then saves us from this difficulty by being released. But when again the gods, cleansing the earth with waters, deluge it, those in the mountains are saved, the herdsmen and shepherds; but those in the cities among you are carried into the sea by the rivers. In this land, neither then nor at any other time does water flow from above upon the fields; on the contrary, it is its nature to come up from below. For which reasons the things preserved here are said to be the most ancient. But the truth is, in all <margin>E</margin> places where excessive storm or heat does not prevent it, there is always a race of men, sometimes more, sometimes fewer. And whatever has happened either among us, or here, or in another place which we know by hearsay—if anything noble or great has occurred, or anything else involving destruction—all these things have been written down from of old here in the temples and preserved. But the things among you and other people happen to be recently equipped each time with letters and everything a city needs; and again, after the usual cycle of years, like a disease, a heavenly stream comes sweeping down upon them, leaving only the illiterate and uncultured among you. So you <margin>F</margin> become young again from the beginning, knowing nothing of the things here, nor of the things among yourselves, as many as were in ancient times. For indeed, the genealogies which you just went through, O Solon, concerning those among you, differ little from the myths of children. For first, you remember only one flood of the earth, though many happened before; and further, you do not know that the most beautiful and best race among men once existed in your land, from whom you and your whole city now are, a small seed having once been left behind. But this has escaped you because the survivors for many generations died without the use of letters. For there was once, O Solon, before the greatest destruction by waters, the city now belonging to the Athenians, which was best both in war and in all things most exceptionally well-ordered; to which the most beautiful deeds and the most beautiful constitutions are said to have belonged, <margin>G</margin> of all those under heaven of which we have received hearsay.' Having heard this, Solon said he marveled, and showed every eagerness, asking the priests to go through everything accurately in order concerning the ancient citizens. Then the priest said: 'There is no envy, O Solon; but I will tell it for your sake and for that of your city, and especially for the sake of the goddess who was allotted and nurtured and educated both your city and this one—yours being former by a thousand years, having received your seed from Earth and Hephaestus, and this one later. And the number of years of the arrangement of things here is written in our sacred letters as eight thousand. Concerning the citizens <margin>H</margin> who lived nine thousand years ago, I will show you briefly their laws and the most beautiful deed performed by them. We will go through the details about everything in order hereafter at our leisure, taking up the writings themselves. Consider their laws first in relation to those here. For you will find many examples here of those then existing among you. First, the class of...'

# TIMAEUS

### 525

<margin>A</margin> ...the class of priests, set apart and separated from the rest. After this, the class of craftsmen, where each performs his own craft by himself without mixing with others. Then there are the classes of shepherds, hunters, and farmers. Furthermore, you have surely noticed that the warrior class here is separated from all other classes, to whom the law permits no concern other than the matters of war. Additionally, there is the manner of their equipment with shields and spears, which we were the first in Asia <note>In antiquity, "Asia" often referred specifically to Asia Minor (modern-day Turkey).</note> to take up, for the goddess showed these things to us first, just as she did to you in those regions. As for the matter of wisdom, you surely see how much care the law has taken here from the very beginning, regarding the whole order of the world, down to divination and medicine for the sake of health; from these divine things, the law discovered how to apply them to human affairs, along with all the other branches of learning that follow from them. <margin>B</margin> At that time, the goddess established this whole system and order when she first founded your city. She chose the place in which you were born because she saw that the well-tempered seasons there would produce the most prudent and wise men. Since the goddess was both a lover of war and a lover of wisdom, she chose the location that would likely produce men most like herself, and there she founded her first city. You lived then under such laws, and even better ones, surpassing all mankind in every virtue, as is fitting for those who are the offspring and pupils of gods. Many <margin>C</margin> great and wonderful deeds of your city are recorded here and admired, but one stands out above all others in greatness and excellence. For the records tell of a great power that your city once stopped, a power that was insolently advancing against all of Europe and Asia at once, having set out from the Atlantic sea. For at that time, that sea was navigable. It had an island in front of the mouth which you call (as you say) the Pillars of Hercules <note>The Strait of Gibraltar.</note>. This island was larger than Libya <note>In this context, Libya refers to North Africa.</note> and Asia combined, and from it, travelers of that time could cross to the other islands. From those islands, they could reach the entire opposite continent which surrounds that true ocean. For all these things inside the mouth of which we speak appear to be only a harbor with a narrow entrance; <margin>D</margin> but that other is truly a sea, and the land surrounding it may most rightly be called a continent. On this island of Atlantis, a great and marvelous power of kings had arisen, ruling over the whole island, many other islands, and parts of the continent. Furthermore, they ruled the regions inside the mouth as far as Libya up to the borders of Egypt, and Europe as far as Tyrrhenia <note>The land of the Etruscans in central Italy.</note>. This entire power, gathered into one, once attempted to enslave your region, our region, and everything inside the mouth with a single assault. Then, O Solon, the power of your city became manifest to all mankind in its excellence and strength. <margin>E</margin> For it stood foremost in courage and all the arts of war; at times leading the Greeks, and at other times forced to stand alone when the others fell away. Having reached the extremes of danger, it defeated the invaders and raised a trophy of victory. It prevented those not yet enslaved from being subjugated, and it generously liberated all of us who dwell within the borders of Hercules. But in later times, there occurred extraordinary earthquakes and floods; and when one difficult day and night came, your entire warrior class was swallowed up by the earth all at once, and the island of Atlantis likewise sank beneath the sea and vanished. This is why that sea is even now impassable and unsearchable, being blocked by the shallow mud produced by the sinking island. These things, O Socrates, <margin>F</margin> are the summary of what was told by the elder Critias, according to what he heard from Solon. While you were speaking yesterday about the republic and the men you described, I was amazed as I remembered these very things I am now saying; I noted how divinely, by some chance, you coincided in most respects with what Solon said. I did not wish to speak of it immediately, for after so much time, I did not remember it sufficiently. I decided, therefore, that I must first go over everything thoroughly in my own mind before speaking. This is why I quickly agreed to the tasks you set yesterday, thinking that I would not be at a loss to provide a discourse fitting for our purposes, which is the greatest task in all such matters. <margin>G</margin> And so, just as he said, as soon as I left here yesterday, I began to relate these things to these men as I remembered them, and after I went home, I spent almost the whole night recovering the details. Truly, as the saying goes, the lessons of childhood have a wonderful way of staying in the memory. I do not know if I could recall everything I heard yesterday, but I would be entirely surprised if any part of what I heard a very long time ago has escaped me. At that time, I listened with great pleasure and playfulness, and the old man taught me eagerly, as I asked him many questions; thus, the story remains in me like the indelible marks of a brand <note>Original Greek: "egkaumata," referring to encaustic painting or branding, suggesting the memories are "burnt-in."</note>. Indeed, I told these men these very things at dawn, so that they might have a subject for discussion with me. Now, therefore, as I have <margin>H</margin> said, I am ready to speak, O Socrates, not only in summary but in detail, just as I heard it. We will transfer the citizens and the city that you described to us yesterday as a myth into the sphere of reality; we will take those ancient Athenians of the priest's story to be the true citizens of your ideal state. They will harmonize perfectly, and we shall not be out of tune if we say that your citizens are those very people who lived in that...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> They lead their lives apart from the whole crowd. Next, the various kinds of craftsmen are so distinguished among themselves that each performs his own work, and no one works promiscuously. Similarly, the tasks of shepherds, hunters, and farmers are distinct from one another. The soldiers also here, as you know, are segregated from all others, and are commanded by the laws to handle only matters of war. Their armor, such as the use of shields and spears, is very similar in both places; we were the first to use them in Asia, and the goddess delivered these to you first, just as she did in those places. Great care was also given to wisdom and moderation by our laws from the beginning, as you see, and additionally to divination and medicine; and health was <margin>B</margin> procured for us through these divine means. Finally, whatever disciplines pertain to these are found to be diligently established by the law. The goddess adorned your city first from its origins with this kind of institution and order, when she chose that region for the founding of the city which, because of the temperament of the air, would procreate the most prudent minds. For as a goddess who is both warlike and wise, she decided to choose such a region that would produce men similar to herself. Therefore, the ancient Athenians, formed by these laws or even more honorable institutions, excelled all others in every kind of virtue, as was fitting for those who were born and raised by gods. Many <margin>C</margin> and wonderful deeds of your city are read in our monuments, but one deed is outstanding in magnitude and virtue. For it is handed down that your city once resisted innumerable forces of enemies, which, having set out from the Atlantic sea, had already properly besieged all of Europe and Asia. For at that time that strait was navigable, having in its mouth and as if in its vestibule an island, which you call the Pillars of Hercules. It is said that the island was larger than Libya and Asia together, through which there was a path to other nearby islands, and from the islands to the entire continent lying in sight, bordering the sea. But inside the mouth itself, a harbor is said to have existed in a narrow bay. That ocean was a true sea, <margin>D</margin> and that land was truly a continent. In this island of Atlantis, there existed a very great and admirable power of kings, who ruled over that whole island, many others, and a great part of the mainland continent; moreover, they dominated those regions which are near us. <margin>On the ancient Athenians and Egyptian histories.</margin> Indeed, they ruled over the third part of the world, which is called Libya, as far as Egypt, and over Europe as far as the Tyrrhenian Sea. All their power, collected into one, invaded our region, O Solon, and your region, and whatever was contained within the pillars of Hercules. Then the virtue of your city shone forth among all nations. Since it excelled all in magnanimity and the arts of war, partly with other Greeks and partly alone when the others deserted, it underwent extreme dangers <margin>E</margin> and conquered the enemy. It prohibited those who had not yet come under their sway and power from being conquered; others, namely all of us who live this side of the pillars of Hercules, it saved without exception. After this, by a huge earthquake and a vast flood of one day and night, it happened that the earth, gaping open, absorbed all those warlike men of yours at once, and the island of Atlantis was merged under a vast whirlpool. For this reason, that sea was left unnavigable because of the mud of the absorbed island. This, O Socrates, is the summary of those things which the elder Critias narrated as received from Solon. But while you were discussing the republic and its citizens yesterday, a certain <margin>F</margin> admiration came to me from memory, reflecting that by a certain divine fate it happened that you related things very similar to Solon's history. For that reason, I brought forward nothing then, since from long neglect I did not sufficiently remember. Therefore, I judged it better that before I began to relate it to you, I should repeat it to myself. Thus, I immediately consented to your command, because I was confident that, as is most fitting in matters of this kind, I would find something that would agree with the proposed subject. So yesterday, as he says, immediately after leaving here, I recounted these things to them as I then remembered. Then, by staying awake through the night, I recovered almost everything. Truly, we are able to remember for a longer time and more firmly those things which we learn in childhood, as it is said. And I do not know whether I could now correctly relate all that I heard yesterday; <margin>G</margin> but I would indeed be surprised if any of the things I received as a boy had escaped my memory. For I heard those things with pleasure and jest, since that old man taught me willingly, and I asked and inquired of him repeatedly. Therefore, like certain marks of letters burnt in indelibly, all those things remained fixed in my memory. And I even narrated these things to them before sunrise, so that together with me they might be better prepared for this speech. But to bring myself to that point where all these things are heading, I am ready, O Socrates, to narrate everything not only in summary but in detail as I heard it. The city and the citizens which you fashioned yesterday in your discussion as if through a fable, <margin>H</margin> we shall now set down as a true thing. We will consider that city to be this city of Athens. We will judge that the citizens whom you yourself devised were those true ancestors of ours narrated by the priest. Certainly these things will agree entirely, nor will it be out of place if we say that your citizens are... <note>original: "θεοὺς θήσομεν"</note> <gloss>we shall place them as gods</gloss>... those very ones in that...

# PLATO

### 526

<margin>A</margin> ...truly we should say those ancient people existed. Therefore, by sharing the task among us, we will all try to fulfill the duty you have imposed on us to the best of our abilities. But see, O Socrates, whether we should approve this discourse or demand another. **SOCRATES.** And what discourse, O Critias, should we approve more than this? It is wonderfully suited to the current sacrifice for the goddess <note>original: "deæ sacris" refers to the festival of Athena/Neith.</note> because of its close connection. The greatest point, indeed, is that this is not a made-up fable, but a true history being told. By what means or from where, then, should we start another discussion if we rejected this one? Certainly, we must not. Therefore, with good fortune, you must now speak, while I, in exchange for yesterday’s narration, listen to you today in silence. <margin>B</margin> **CRITIAS.** Consider, Socrates, whether we have arranged this mutual banquet of words conveniently for you. It seemed best to us that Timaeus—since he is the most skilled of all of us in Astronomy and has spent the most effort in understanding the nature of the universe—should speak first. He will begin from the generation of the world and continue down to the nature of mankind. And then I, taking over the men who were generated by Timaeus’s account and then educated by yours, shall bring them before your judgment according to the word and law of Solon. I will make them citizens of this city, regarding them as those ancient Athenians who were once forgotten, but whom the sacred <margin>C</margin> records of the Egyptians have brought out of the darkness and into the light. Thus, from then on, we shall speak of them as the original Athenians. **SOCRATES.** You seem to have prepared a rich and splendid feast of discussion for me. It is your duty then, O Timaeus, to begin the discourse now, having called upon the gods according to custom. **TIMAEUS.** You advise well, Socrates. For all those who possess even a small amount of wisdom are accustomed to call upon God at the beginning of any work, whether great or small. How much more is it right for us—who are about to discuss the universe, whether it was created or is uncreated—to call for divine help, unless we are completely foolish? Therefore, we pray to all the gods and goddesses: first, that what we say may please them; and second, that we may remain consistent with ourselves. As far as the gods are concerned, let our prayer be finished. But as for ourselves, we must pray <margin>D</margin> that you may easily follow and that I may explain the matter at hand according to my mind’s purpose. At the start, it seems to me that I must make this distinction: what is that which always *is* and has no beginning, and what is that which *becomes* but never truly *is*? The first is perceptible by the intellect through the path of reason, as it is always the same. The second is grasped by opinion through irrational sensation, as it is born and dies and never truly exists. Furthermore, whatever is born must necessarily be born from some cause. For it is impossible for anything to arise without a cause. Whenever the craftsman <note>term: "opifex" (Latin) or "demiurgos" (Greek), referring to the divine architect or maker of the universe.</note> looks toward that which is always the same in the construction of some work, and using such an eternal model, brings its form and power into his work, then <margin>E</margin> the whole work must necessarily be beautiful. But whenever he looks toward that which is created, using a generated model, it is not beautiful at all. Now, let us name this whole Universe—whether "Heaven" or "World" or whatever other name it prefers. Concerning this, we must first consider what should be investigated at the start of every inquiry: whether it has always existed without any beginning of generation, or whether it was created, taking its start from some beginning. It is surely seen and touched, and it has a body. All such things move the senses. What moves the senses is grasped by opinion through sensation. It is clear that such things are born and are generated. Moreover, we have stated that whatever is born must necessarily be born from some cause. <margin>F</margin> It is difficult to find the maker and father of this universe, and once you have found him, it is forbidden to speak of him to the common people. Again, we must consider which model the builder of the world imitated: that which is always the same and similar to itself, or that which was created? Yet if this world is beautiful and its maker good, he certainly preferred to imitate the eternal model. If it were otherwise—which is not even lawful to say—he would have followed a created model instead of an eternal one. But since the world is the most beautiful of all generated things, and its author is the best of all causes, there is no doubt that he followed the eternal model. Being thus created, it was made according to that which can be grasped only by reason and wisdom and remains unchangeable. From this it follows that this world must necessarily be <margin>G</margin> an image of something. However, to explain the nature of its origin is very difficult. Therefore, let us distinguish between the image and the model in this way: words seem to have a certain kinship with the things they express. Therefore, when discussing that which is firm, stable, and grasped by the mind, the words should likewise be stable, unchangeable, and as far as possible, undeniable. But when discussing the image of that firm and stable reality, "likely" <note>original: "verisimiles" or "eikotas" (Greek), meaning probable or likeness-like. Timaeus is establishing that human science is a "likely story" rather than absolute certainty.</note> accounts are sufficient. These stand in the same relation to the higher truths as the image stands to the model. Indeed, what *being* is to *becoming*, *truth* is to *belief*. Therefore, O Socrates, if many people have said many things about the gods and the generation of the universe, do not wonder, I pray, if I cannot provide accounts that are perfectly consistent and exact. It should be enough if I provide accounts no less probable than anyone else’s. It is right to remember that both I who speak and you who judge are only human: so if probable things are said, you should require nothing further. **SOCRATES.** Well said, O Timaeus. Therefore, as you command...

<column-break/>

...at that time. Sharing the task together, we will try to fulfill the assignment you gave us to the best of our ability. We must consider, Socrates, whether this account is to our mind, or if we should seek another in its place. **SOCRATES.** And what account, Critias, could we take in exchange for this one? It would be most fitting for the present sacrifice to the goddess due to its kinship; and the fact that it is not a fabricated myth but a true story is a very great thing. For how and from where else shall we find others, if we abandon these? It is not possible. So, with good luck, you must speak, and I, in return for yesterday's talk, will now keep quiet and listen. **CRITIAS.** See then, Socrates, the arrangement of the hospitality we have set for you. For it seemed to us that Timaeus—since he is the most knowledgeable among us in astronomy and has made it his chief work to know the nature of the universe—should speak first, beginning from the generation of the world and ending with the nature of humans. I will follow him, having received from him humans who have been created in speech, and from you those who have been exceptionally educated. According to Solon's account and law, I will bring them before us as if before judges, making them citizens of this city, as being those Athenians of that time whom the report of the sacred writings revealed to be vanished. For the rest, we will make our arguments as if concerning citizens and Athenians who already exist. **SOCRATES.** I seem to be about to receive a complete and splendid feast of words in return. It would be your job to speak, Timaeus, after calling upon the gods according to the law, as is fitting. **TIMAEUS.** But Socrates, everyone who shares even a small part of sound mind always calls upon a god at the start of any undertaking, small or great. For us, who are about to make arguments about the universe—whether it has been created or is uncreated—unless we are completely out of our minds, it is necessary to call upon the gods and goddesses and pray that all things be said according to their mind especially, and following that, according to ours. Let this be our invocation to the gods; but we must also call upon our own efforts, so that you may learn most easily, and I may best demonstrate what I have in mind regarding the subjects before us. In my opinion, then, we must first distinguish these things: what is that which always is and has no becoming, and what is that which is always becoming but never is? The one is grasped by thought with reason, being always the same; the other is grasped by opinion with unreasoning sensation, being something that becomes and perishes, but never really is. Now, everything that becomes must necessarily become by some cause; for it is impossible for anything to have a beginning of becoming without a cause. Now, whenever the craftsman, looking always to that which is the same, using such a thing as a model, works out its form and power, everything so completed is necessarily beautiful; but that which is done looking to what has become, using a created model, is not beautiful. Now, the whole heaven—or world, or whatever other name it might most especially accept—let it be named by us thus. We must first consider about it what lies at the beginning of any inquiry: whether it always was, having no beginning of generation, or whether it has become, starting from some beginning. It has become; for it is visible and tangible and has a body, and all such things are sensible; and sensible things, grasped by opinion with sensation, appear to be becoming and generated. Now, we say that what is becoming must necessarily become by some cause. To find the maker and father of this universe is a task, and having found him, it is impossible to speak of him to everyone. This, then, we must again consider about him: according to which of the models did the builder work it out? Was it toward that which is always the same and in the same state, or toward that which has become? If this world is beautiful and the craftsman is good, it is clear that he looked to the eternal; but if (which is not lawful for anyone even to say) he looked to what has become, it is clear to everyone that he looked to the eternal. For the world is the most beautiful of generated things, and he is the best of causes. Having been generated in this way, it has been crafted according to that which is grasped by reason and wisdom and which is always the same. These things being so, it is also a complete necessity that this world is an image of something. Now, it is most important to begin every subject according to its natural beginning. Thus, we must distinguish concerning the image and its model, that words are akin to the things which they explain. Therefore, concerning what is stable and certain and manifest with the aid of reason, the words must be stable and unchanging, and as far as it is possible for words to be irrefutable and immovable, they must fall short in nothing. But those words spoken of that which is likeness-like and which is an image must be likely, and stand in proportion to the former words. For what essence is to generation, truth is to belief. If then, Socrates, after many people have said many things about the gods and the generation of the universe, we are not able to provide accounts that are in every way completely consistent and accurate, do not be surprised. But if we provide accounts no less likely than others, we ought to be content, remembering that I who speak and you who judge have a human nature; so that accepting the likely story concerning these things, it is fitting to seek nothing further. **SOCRATES.** Excellent, Timaeus, and entirely as you suggest...

# TIMÆUS.

...should be accepted. We have indeed wonderfully accepted your preamble; now, perform the rest of the discourse for us in order. TIMAEUS: Let us then state for what reason the one who composed the universe <note>original: "ξυνιστὰς" (the Composer/Architect), often referred to as the Demiurge.</note> did so. He was good, and in one who is good, no envy ever arises regarding anything. Being entirely free from such a feeling, he wished for all things to become as much like himself as possible. If one accepts this as the primary and most sovereign principle of the world's generation from wise men, they would be accepting it most correctly. For God, wishing all things to be good and, as far as possible, nothing to be flawed, took all that was visible—which was not at rest but moving in a discordant and disorderly fashion—and brought it from disorder into order, judging that order was in every way better than the other. <margin>A</margin> <margin>To provide order within the disordered.</margin> It was not, nor is it now, permitted for the best of all beings to do anything except what is most beautiful. Therefore, after calculating, he found that among things naturally visible, no work that is void of intelligence would ever be more beautiful as a whole than one that possesses intelligence. Furthermore, it is impossible for intelligence to be present in anything without a soul. Because of this calculation, by placing intelligence within the soul and the soul within the body, he fashioned the universe so that his finished work might be the most beautiful and best by nature. Thus, according to probable reasoning, we must say that this world became a living being <note>original: "ζῶον," literally a "living creature" or "animal."</note> endowed with soul and intelligence in truth through the providence of God. <margin>B</margin> <margin>Definition of the world.</margin> Having established this, we must next say what follows: in the likeness of which living being did the Composer establish it? We should not deign to compare it to any species of creature that exists as a part; for nothing that resembles an incomplete thing could ever be beautiful. <margin>C</margin> <margin>Regarding the exemplary cause.</margin> Rather, let us posit that it is most like that Living Being of which all other living beings are parts, both individually and by their kinds. For that intelligible Being contains within itself all living things, just as this world contains us and all other visible creatures that have been formed. For God, wishing to make this world most similar to the most beautiful and perfectly complete of intelligible beings, established it as a single visible living being, containing within itself all the living creatures that are by nature related to it. Have we then correctly called the heaven "one," or would it be more correct to say there are many or infinite heavens? One it must be, if indeed it is to be fashioned according to the model. <margin>D</margin> <margin>Concerning the unity of the intelligible world.</margin> For that which contains all intelligible living beings could never be one of a pair; for if it were, there would have to be another living being containing those two, of which they would both be parts. In that case, this world would be more correctly called a likeness not of those two, but of that third one which contains them. Therefore, so that this world might be like the perfect Living Being in its uniqueness, the Creator made neither two nor infinite worlds; rather, this one unique world was born, and is, and shall be. <margin>Vnus an plures mundi.</margin> Now, that which is generated must be bodily, visible, and touchable. Without fire, nothing could ever become visible; nor touchable without something solid; and nothing is solid without earth. Therefore, at the beginning of constructing the body of the universe, God made fire and earth. <margin>E</margin> <margin>The power of earth and fire.</margin> But it is not possible for two things alone to be joined together without a third; for there must be some bond in the middle to bring the two together. The most beautiful of bonds is that which makes itself and the things it binds into a single unit as much as possible. This is naturally achieved most beautifully by proportion. For whenever, among three numbers—whether they be volumes or powers—the middle term is such that as the first is to it, so it is to the last; and conversely, as the last is to the middle, so the middle is to the first; then the middle becomes both first and last, and the last and first both become the middle. In this way, all will necessarily result in being the same. And by becoming the same as one other, they will all be one. If, then, the body of the universe were required to be a plane without depth, a single middle term would have sufficed to bind itself and its neighbors together. <margin>F</margin> But since it was appropriate for the world to be solid, and solids are never joined by one middle term but always by two, God placed air and water in the middle between fire and earth. He established them in the same proportion to one another as much as possible: so that as fire is to air, air is to water; and as air is to water, water is to earth. Thus he bound together and established a heaven that is visible and touchable. For these reasons, and from such things being four in number, the body of the world was generated, brought into harmony through proportion. From these it gained a spirit of friendship, so that having come together into a unity with itself, it cannot be dissolved by any other except by the one who bound it together. The composition of the world took the whole of each of these four elements. <margin>G</margin> <margin>The world consists of the whole of matter. Aging and disease come from external causes: from which you see that the world is eternal due to the lack of a cause for its decay, not because of its matter.</margin> For the Composer established it out of all the fire, water, air, and earth that existed, leaving no part or power of any of them outside. He designed this, first, so that it might be a whole living being, as perfect as possible, made of perfect parts; second, so that it might be one, since nothing was left over from which another such thing could be born; and finally, so that it might be free from old age and disease. He realized that for a body, when hot and cold things and all things that have strong powers surround it from the outside and strike it unseasonably, they dissolve it and, by bringing on diseases and old age, cause it to waste away. For this reason and by this logic, he fashioned the world as a single whole, made of all wholes, perfect, and free from disease and old age. And he gave it the shape that was most appropriate and akin to its nature. For...

<meta>This page continues the speech of Timaeus regarding the creation of the world. ->528 PLATO<-

A
Indeed, for this living being <note>original: "Animal" / "ζῷον" (Living Being/Animal). Plato views the entire universe as a single, living, breathing entity.</note> which was intended to contain all other living beings within its scope, it required that specific shape in which all other shapes are contained. For this reason, he made it **spherical**: in which every extremity is reached by equal rays from the center. He fashioned it so perfectly <note>original: "tornauit", literally "turned on a lathe", suggesting the precision of a craftsman.</note> that nothing could be more round, and all parts were most similar to one another. For he thought that what is similar is far more beautiful than what is dissimilar. Furthermore, he polished this globe to be smooth all around the outside. And not without reason. For it had no need for **eyes**, since nothing was left outside that could be seen. Nor for **ears**, since there was nothing outside to be heard. Nor was the exterior of the world surrounded by air so as to require **breathing**. Nor indeed was there any need for members through which
B
it might receive new **food**, or expel the waste of digested food: no loss could occur, and no addition. For there was neither a place nor a source from which such things could come. For the world nourishes itself through its own consumption and aging. Indeed, the world was fabricated by divine art in such a way that it suffers and acts all things within itself and by itself. For that Author reckoned that if the world were self-sufficient, it would be more excellent than if it required the assistance of others. He did not think hands were necessary for it, because there was nothing to be grasped or pushed away. Nor did it need feet or other members for progress or standing.
<margin>Seven types of local motion</margin>
C
For he attributed to it the motion appropriate to its body, which, out of the seven types of motion, pertains most to the **mind** and **intelligence**. Therefore, when he had led it around through the same points, and in the same way, and within itself, he caused it to move in a **circular revolution**. He separated the six other motions <note>These are up, down, forwards, backwards, left, and right.</note> from it, and entirely freed it from their wandering and straying. For this rotation, which did not require feet, he gave it neither legs nor feet. Therefore, when that God who always exists <note>The eternal Creator or Demiurge.</note> thought about the god that was one day to exist <note>The created universe, which Plato considers a "secondary" or "visible" god.</note>, he made it smooth and even, and equal in every direction from the middle to the summit, a whole and perfect body made from whole and perfect bodies.
D
Moreover, he placed the **Soul** in its center, and stretched it through the whole, and even covered the body itself from the outside with it. He established this world as one, and only, and solitary, and revolving in a circle, which by its own virtue could easily sustain itself, needing no other, being sufficiently known and a friend to itself. Therefore, for all these reasons, the Maker made the world a blessed god. But he did not create the soul in the way we have just begun to describe—that is, after he had finished the body. For he who joined these would not have permitted the older to obey the younger. But we, being participants in chance, often speak thoughtlessly and at random. But he, 
<margin>Parts of the substance of the soul.</margin>
E
by both generation and virtue, established the soul as prior to and older than the body, as that which was to rule over an obedient body, made specifically from these things and in this manner. From the substance that is **indivisible** and always the same, and from that which is **divisible** among bodies, he mixed a third type of substance in the middle, which would participate in the nature of the "Same" and the nature of the "Other." He placed this middle substance between the indivisible substance and that which is divided among bodies. When he had taken these three, he tempered them all into one form. He forcibly reconciled the nature of the "Other" <note>original: "alterum" / "θατέρου" (the Different/Other), which is naturally resistant to mixing.</note>, which was reluctant to blend, with that which is called the "Same." After he had mixed these with the substance and made one out of the three, he again divided this whole into as many members as were fitting, each consisting of the Same, the Other, and the Substance. The division was as follows. First, he took one portion from the whole.
Second, double the first part. Then a third, which was one-and-a-half times the second, and triple the first. After that a fourth, double the second. Fifth, triple the third. Sixth, eight times the first. Finally, the seventh, which exceeded the first by twenty-six parts <note>This creates two mathematical series: 1, 2, 4, 8 and 1, 3, 9, 27. These are the "Lambda" proportions representing the harmony of the universe.</note>.
F
After this, he filled the double and triple intervals, cutting off parts again from the whole. These he placed in the intervals so that there were two means <note>term: "medietates" (means). In music and math, these are the arithmetic and harmonic means used to create a scale.</note> in each: one which exceeds one extreme by the same proportion as it is exceeded by the other; the other which exceeds one extreme by the same number as it is exceeded by the other. When he had taken the intervals of 3/2, 4/3, and 9/8, he filled all the 4/3 intervals with the 9/8 interval in the first spaces, leaving a small portion of each. The ratio of the remaining portion of this interval, compared number to number, was that between 256 and 243 <note>In music theory, this is known as a "limma" or Pythagorean semitone.</note>. And so the whole mixture from which he was cutting these was now
G
consumed. Then he cut this entire series lengthwise into two, and joined them to each other middle-to-middle in the shape of the letter **X** <note>original: "Græcæ literæ" (the Greek letter Chi). This represents the intersection of the celestial equator and the ecliptic.</note>, so that their ends met, and the lines themselves crossed each other.

<column-break/>

A To the living being that was to contain all living beings within it, it would be a fitting shape to have that which encompasses within itself all possible shapes. Therefore, he fashioned it into a **spherical** form, equal in every direction from the center to the extremities, circular and round, the most perfect of all shapes and the most similar to itself; for he considered the similar to be infinitely more beautiful than the dissimilar. He made it perfectly smooth all around the outside, for many reasons. For it had no need for eyes (since nothing visible was left outside), nor for hearing (for there was nothing to be heard). Nor was there any breath of air needing to be inhaled. Nor did it require any organ
B
through which it might receive food into itself, or again discharge it after it had been digested. For nothing went out from it, nor did anything enter it from anywhere. For it provided its own wasting away as its own food, and performing and suffering all things within itself and by itself, it was created by art. For he who composed it thought that if it were self-sufficient, it would be better than if it were in need of others. He did not think it necessary to attach hands to it in vain, with which it would have no need to take anything or defend itself; nor feet, nor any of the apparatus for walking. For he assigned to it the motion proper to its body, out of the seven motions that which is most concerned with **mind** and **intelligence**. Therefore, leading it around in the same way, in the same place, and within itself, he made it 
C
move in a spinning circle. He took away all the other six motions and made it wanderless in respect to them. Since for this revolution there was no need of feet, he generated it without legs and without feet. This, then, was the whole plan of the god who always is, reasoned out for the god who was one day to be; he made it smooth and even, equal in every direction from the center, a body whole and perfect, made out of perfect bodies. And placing the **Soul** in the middle of it, he stretched it through the whole, and further wrapped the body around with it on the outside; and establishing a circle revolving in a circle, he set up the Heaven as one, unique, and solitary, able by its own virtue to be with itself and needing no other, but being sufficiently known and a friend to itself. For all these reasons, he generated it as a blessed god. But as for the soul, it is not as we are now attempting to say, 
D
that the god designed it to be younger than the body. For he would not have allowed the older to be ruled by the younger after joining them together. But we, participating much in the accidental and the random, speak in such a way. But he made the soul prior to and older than the body in both birth and virtue, as the mistress and ruler of the subject, out of these things and in this manner: from the **indivisible** and eternally unchanging substance, and from the **divisible** substance that comes to be in bodies, he mixed a third form of substance from both in the middle, pertaining to the nature of the "Same" and the nature of the "Other," and he established it in the middle between the indivisible and the bodily divisible. And taking these three, he mixed them all into one idea, fitting the nature of the "Other,"
E
which was hard to mix, into the "Same" by force. And mixing them with the substance, and making one out of the three, he again divided this whole into as many portions as was fitting; and each portion was mixed from the Same, the Other, and the Substance. He began to divide thus: first, he took one portion from the whole. After this, he took one double the size of the first. Then a third, which was one-and-a-half times the second and triple the first. The fourth was double the second. The fifth was triple the third. The sixth was eight times the first. The seventh was twenty-seven times the first. After this, he filled up the double and triple intervals, cutting off yet more portions from there and placing them in the spaces between, so that
F
in each interval there were two means: one exceeding and being exceeded by the same part of the extremes themselves, the other exceeding and being exceeded by an equal number. From these links within the previous intervals, 3/2, 4/3, and 9/8 intervals were formed; he filled up all the 4/3 intervals with the 9/8 interval, leaving a small part of each. This remaining part of the interval had the ratio of number to number of 256 to 243. And indeed, the mixture from which he cut these things was now all used up. This entire composition, then, he cut in two along its length, and joined the two at their centers to each other
G
like the letter **Chi**, and bent them into a circle, joining them to themselves and to each other at the point opposite the intersection; and he encompassed them with the motion that revolves in the same way and in the same place; and he made one of the circles the outer and the other the inner. He named the outer motion that of the nature of the "Same," and the inner that of the "Other." The motion of the "Same" he led around to the right by the side; the motion of the "Other" he led diagonally to the left. But he gave the dominion to the revolution of the "Same" and the "Similar." For he left that one alone and undivided, but the inner one he divided six times, into seven unequal circles according to the double and triple intervals, seven me...

Then he twisted them into a circle, so that they were joined together at the region opposite the intersection: and he embraced them on all sides with that motion which is always revolved in the same way and similarly: and he made one of the circles outer, and the other inner. The outer motion he named of the same nature, but the inner of the other nature. And he turned that which was kindred to the nature of the same toward the side to the right: but that of the other, through the diameter to the left. But he gave the leadership to the agitation of the same and the similar. For that alone he left undivided. But the interior, when he had divided it six times, and seven...

# TIMAEUS

<note>Plato continues describing the mathematical division of the World-Soul into specific ratios.</note>
He fashioned these in intervals of double and triple, three of each. He commanded the circles to move in directions contrary to one another: three of them <note>The Sun, Venus, and Mercury</note> to move with similar speed, while the other four <note>The Moon, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note> were to move at speeds dissimilar to each other and to the first three, yet always maintaining a definite proportion. 

When the entire composition of the Soul had been completed according to the mind of the Composer, he then fashioned the whole of the bodily realm within it, and drawing them together center to center, he fitted them together. The Soul, woven throughout from the center even to the farthest reaches of heaven and covering the exterior in a circle, turned within herself and began a divine beginning of unceasing and intelligent life for all time. Indeed, the body of the heaven was made visible, but the Soul remains invisible—partaking in reason and harmony, having been made the best of all created things by the best of eternal beings. 

Since the Soul is composed of the natures of "The Same," "The Other," and "Essence" <note>These are Plato's three primary categories of being</note>, and has been divided and bound together in proportion, she turns back upon herself. Whenever she touches anything that has a divisible nature or an indivisible one, she moves through her whole self and declares what that thing is identical to and what it is different from. She identifies in what relation, where, how, and when it happens that each thing exists or is acted upon, both in the realm of things that are born and in the realm of things that are always the same. 

This internal reason <note>original: "λόγος" (logos)</note> becomes true when it concerns both "The Other" and "The Same." It is carried on without speech or sound within that which is self-moved. When it concerns a sensible object, and the circle of "The Other" <note>The realm of change and physical things</note> moving correctly reports it to the whole Soul, then firm and true opinions and beliefs arise. But when it concerns the rational realm, and the circle of "The Same" <note>The realm of eternal truth</note> running smoothly declares it, then understanding and knowledge are necessarily perfected. If anyone should say that these two things <note>understanding and knowledge</note> exist in anything other than a Soul, they speak everything but the truth.

As the Father who begat the world <note>The Demiurge or Creator</note> perceived that this created image of the eternal gods was moving and living, he was delighted. In his joy, he planned to make his work even more like its original model. Since that model is an eternal living being, he attempted to make this universe as similar to it as possible. Now, the nature of that original living being was eternal, and it was not possible to bestow this quality fully upon a created thing. Therefore, he resolved to make a moving image of eternity. 

While he was setting the heavens in order, he created an eternal image moving according to number—an image of that eternity which remains in unity. This image is what we have named "Time." For days and nights, months and years, which did not exist before the heavens were born, he devised at the same moment the heavens were constructed. These are all parts of Time; and "was" and "will be" are forms of Time that have come into being. We often incorrectly apply these terms to the eternal essence. For we say that it "was," "is," and "will be," but in truth, only "is" <note>original: "ἔστι" (esti)</note> properly belongs to it. 

"Was" and "will be" should only be said of the process of birth that proceeds in time, for they are both movements. But that which is always the same and unmoved should not become older or younger through time; it never "was" in the past, nor "will be" in the future. In short, it is subject to none of those conditions which birth has attached to the things we perceive through our senses. These are merely forms of Time which mimic Eternity and circle according to number. Furthermore, we use phrases like "that which has happened *is* happened" or "that which is happening *is* happening," and "that which will be *is* that which will be," or "the non-existent *is* non-existent." None of these expressions are accurate. However, this may not be the right time to argue over such precision.

Time, then, was created together with the heavens, so that having been born together, they might also be dissolved together, if ever such a dissolution should occur. It was made according to the model of the eternal nature, so that it might be as similar to it as possible. For the model exists for all eternity, while the heaven has been, is, and shall be for all time. 

Based on this plan and thought of God regarding the birth of Time—so that Time might be brought into being—the Sun, the Moon, and five other stars, which are called "planets" <note>original: "πλανητὰ" (planeta), meaning "wanderers"</note>, were created to define and preserve the numbers of Time. After God had made the bodies of each of them, he placed them into the orbits in which the revolution of "The Other" was moving, seven in total. He placed the Moon in the first orbit around the Earth, and the Sun in the second orbit above the Earth. Then he placed the Morning Star <note>original: "Ἑωσφόρον" / "Luciferi" (Venus)</note> and the star sacred to Mercury <note>original: "Ἑρμοῦ" / "Mercurij"</note> in orbits that move with a speed equal to the Sun, but which possess a contrary power. Because of this, the Sun, Mercury, and the Morning Star continually overtake and are overtaken by one another. As for the other planets, if one were to describe the reasons why he established them all, the explanation—being a secondary matter—would require more labor than the subject for which it is told. Perhaps these things will receive the explanation they deserve later, if we have the leisure.

Once each of the stars necessary for the creation of Time had reached its proper orbit, and their bodies had been bound with living souls and become living beings, they learned their appointed tasks. According to the oblique motion of "The Other," which travels through and is dominated by the motion of "The Same," some moved in larger circles and some in smaller. Those in the smaller circles moved faster, and those in the larger moved more slowly.

<column-break/>

A
He had created unequal orbits in double and triple intervals, and since there are three of each kind, he commanded the orbits to complete their courses in contrary directions to one another. Out of the seven interior orbits, he commanded three to turn with equal speed, but the other four to turn with a speed that was unequal both to themselves and to the first three, yet always in a proper ratio. After the entire constitution of the soul was finished according to the mind of that creator, he immediately fashioned all that is bodily within it, and fitting the center to the center, he joined them with a suitable harmony. And the soul, stretching from the middle through everything to the farthest ends of heaven, and wrapped around it from the outside, turning back into herself, gave a divine beginning to a perpetual and wise life for all time. And the body of the heaven was made visible, but the soul 
B
escaped the sight of eyes. Being composed of reason and harmony by its author—who is the best of all eternal and intelligible things—the soul was herself made the best of all things that have been generated. Since she was conflated from three parts—namely, "The Same," "The Other," and "Essence"—and was distinguished and compacted by the rule of proportion, and is reflected in a circle upon herself, whenever she touches anything that has a divisible or an indivisible essence, she turns entirely within herself and discerns what each thing is. she determines to what a thing is the same, from what it is different, and in what way, where, how, and when it happens that such a thing exists or is acted upon, both in those things that are born and in those that are always the same.
C
Furthermore, Reason, turning toward that which is "The Same" and being verified, deals with both "The Other" and "The Same." Carried around without sound or any noise in that which is moved by itself, when it turns toward something sensible, and if the circle of the different and "Other" nature correctly announces the matter through the whole soul, it produces firm and true opinions and assents of faith. When, on the other hand, it deals with the rational, and the circle of "The Same" revolving fitly announces the matter, then understanding and knowledge are necessarily perfected. Whoever says these things happen in anything other than a soul will wander far from the truth.
D
When that Father who begat the world perceived that this beautiful image of the eternal gods <note>The universe</note>, which he had made, was moving and living, he was delighted with his work. Led by this joy, he thought to make his work even more like that first exemplar. Therefore, just as that exemplar is an eternal living being, he resolved to make this universe such a thing as far as he was able. The nature of that living being is eternal: a quality that cannot be entirely granted to a created work. *Therefore*, he decreed that a moving image of eternity should be fashioned. While he adorned the heaven, he made an eternal image of that eternity which remains in unity, an image that flows according to number, which we have called Time.
E
Furthermore, he commanded that days and nights, months and years—which did not exist before the heaven—should be born at the same time the world was born. All these are parts of Time. However, we incorrectly assign "was" and "will be," which are species of created time, to the eternal substance. For we say of the eternal that it "is," "was," and "will be." But in truth, only "is" belongs to it. Having been and being about to be must be referred to the generation that proceeds in time. For those two are certain movements. But the eternal substance remains always the same and immovable; it never becomes older or younger than itself, nor was it so until now, nor will it be in the future, nor does it receive any of those things which corporeal and mobile things are subject to by the very condition of their birth.
F
*Truly*, all these are species of Time which imitates eternity and revolves according to number. We also often say that what has been done *is* done; that what is happening *is* in the process of birth; that what will be *is* to be done; and that what is not *is* non-existent. We say none of these things correctly or with exact reason. But the present discussion does not require an exquisite debate on these matters. Time was made together with the heaven, so that having risen together, they might also be dissolved together, if any dissolution should ever happen to them. And it was made according to the pattern of the eternal nature so that the world might be as similar to that more excellent model as possible. For that world <note>The world of Forms/Ideas</note> is the exemplar for all eternity. But this world has been, is, and shall be throughout all time.
<margin>
Here again begins the interpretation of Cicero, which you will find until the end.
</margin>
G
By this reason and plan of God, who wished to create time, the Sun and Moon, and five other stars which are called "erratic" <note>planets</note>, were made so that the number of time might be distinguished and observed. When God had made the bodies of seven such stars, he applied them to the seven orbits which are turned by the circuit of "The Other" and different nature. He placed the Moon in the first circuit above the earth. In the second, the Sun. Then he fixed the globe of the Morning Star <note>Venus</note> and the sacred star of Mercury (as it is called) to orbits equal in speed to the Sun, but contrary to it in power. By this, it happens that they overtake one another, and are in turn overtaken by one another similarly—these stars: the Sun, the Morning Star, and Mercury. As for the orders, progresses, and reasons of the other stars, if anyone wished to run through them all, there would be more labor in the telling than in the work for whose sake it is undertaken. Perhaps these things will be treated by us with the 

dignity they deserve at another time, if leisure is granted. After each of the things belonging to the series of time had obtained a progress suitable to it, and their bodies—compacted by vital bonds—became living beings, they held to their prescribed tenor and established order. Namely, that according to the oblique agitation of "The Other" and different nature, which is subject to the agitation of "The Same," those orbits should perform some a larger and some a narrower circle: and those which performed a smaller circle moved more swiftly, while those with a larger circle moved more slowly.
