# OF PLATO

<margin>A</margin>...were to revolve more slowly. But according to the motion of the "Same," <note>The "Same" refers to the outer, uniform rotation of the heavens (the celestial equator), while the "Other" refers to the diagonal path of the planets (the ecliptic).</note> those which travel most quickly appeared to be overtaken by those that were actually slower. For the supreme rotation <note>The daily rotation of the fixed stars.</note> turned all their circles into a spiral, and because these bodies are moved by two contrary forces at once, the body that receded most slowly from the swiftest rotation appeared to be the closest to it. To ensure there was a certain and clear measure of their relative speed and slowness, and so that the dance of all eight motions might come to light, God kindled a most brilliant light in the second circle from the earth, which we have just now called the Sun. <margin>B</margin> By its splendor, the entire heaven might be illuminated, and all living beings capable of understanding number might participate in it, learning the art of counting from the revolution of the "Same" and the "Similar." <note>The "Same" provides the regular cycle of day and night.</note> From this also arose the variety of night and day. Because of this, the revolution of the single, most wise circuit was established. A month is completed when the Moon, having finished its own circle, catches up to the Sun. A year is completed when the Sun has traversed its own orbit. As for the paths of the other stars, men—except for a very few—remain ignorant of them; they neither call them by fixed names nor measure them against one another with distinct numbers. <margin>C</margin> Thus, so to speak, they do not know that the wanderings of these stars actually constitute what is rightly called "Time," though these paths are infinite in number and wonderful in their variety. It is, however, easy to understand that the "Perfect Number of Time" <note>The "Great Year," a cycle in which all planets return to their starting positions relative to the fixed stars.</note> completes a Perfect Year only when all eight circuits, having finished their courses—which the ever-identical and similar movement measures—return to their original starting point. For these reasons were created those stars that travel through the heaven and have turning points, so that this entire visible world might be most like that perfect, intelligible Living Being <note>The "Archetype" or divine model used by the Creator.</note> in its imitation of eternity. Now, up until the birth of Time, <margin>Classes of living beings.</margin><margin>D</margin> he had fashioned the rest of the world in the image of the proposed model. But because this world did not yet contain all living beings within its circuit, the likeness of this image to its model was deficient in that regard. Therefore, God began to fill up what was lacking, following the example of that supreme model. <margin>Four forms of living beings.</margin> In whatever number and of whatever kind the Mind perceives the "Ideas" to be in the original Living Being, he thought that this world should contain just as many and of the same kind. There are four such forms: one is the race of celestial gods <note>The stars and planets.</note>; the second is the winged and air-traveling race; the third is suited to the waters; and the fourth is the race of terrestrial animals. <margin>E</margin> He composed the form of the divine beings mostly from fire, so that they would be most brilliant and beautiful to behold. And because he wished them to be similar to the form of the whole, he made them round; he placed them in the wisdom of the Best Being, commanded them to follow it, and distributed them throughout the whole heaven, so that a true adornment <note>original: "ornatus," translating the Greek "cosmos."</note> might be added to it everywhere from this variety. He gave the divine beings two kinds of motion: one by which they always turn in the same place and in the same way, as they always think the same thoughts about the same things; the other by which they are led forward by the rotation of the "Same" and "Similar." But he willed that they be free from the other five motions, <note>Up, down, left, right, forward, backward.</note> so that each of them might be as excellent as possible. For this reason, those stars were made that do not wander—which are divine living beings—and are therefore always carried along in the same circuit. But those that wander and glide with a changeable logic <margin>The Earth, most ancient of the gods within the heaven.</margin><margin>F</margin> were generated thereafter, as we said above. The Earth, our nourisher, wound around the pole stretched through the whole universe, he willed to be the maker and guardian of day and night, and the first and oldest of all the gods who were born within the heaven. But as for the dances of these gods, their conjunctions with one another, the various revolutions of their circles and their approaches—how they are joined or opposed to each other, whether moving forward or backward, what results from their sequence for us, at what times and in what manner they are hidden or emerge, and what omens they bring when rising to strike fear into men unskilled in these matters: to try to explain all this without a careful inspection of their physical models would be a vain labor. But let this suffice; and now let what had to be said about the nature of those visible and generated gods reach its end. As for the others <margin>G</margin> who are called "daemons," <note>Lower divine beings or traditional mythological gods.</note> to know and declare their origin is a task greater than our genius can report. We must, therefore, believe those men of old who, being the offspring of gods as they themselves said, knew their own parents best. It is surely impossible not to have faith in the children of gods, even if their speech is not confirmed by necessary or probable reasons. But because they claimed to speak of their own family matters, we shall follow the law and grant them our belief. Thus, as handed down by them, let the generation of these gods be understood and described: Oceanus and Tethys are said to have been the children of Earth and Heaven. From these were born Phorcys, Saturn, and Rhea, and the rest of their siblings. From Saturn and Rhea were born Jupiter and Juno, and all those whom we daily hear mentioned as their brothers. From these, in turn, others were born. After all were brought forth—both those who revolve visibly in the heaven and those who appear to us only when they wish—the Generator of the world spoke to them thus: "Gods, born of gods, of whom I am the maker and father, attend to these things. Those works which were made by me

<column-break/>

...traveling seemed to overtake and be overtaken. It [the rotation of the Same] turned all their circles into a spiral, because they were being carried in two opposite directions at once; thus the one departing most slowly from it, though it was the swiftest, appeared to be the closest. In order that there might be a clear measure of their relative slowness and speed, and that they might proceed in their eight orbits, God kindled a light in the second circuit from the earth, which we now call the Sun; so that it might shine as much as possible throughout the whole heaven, and that living beings, as many as was fitting, might participate in number, learning it from the revolution of the Same and the Similar. Thus night and day came to be, and for these reasons the period of the one and most intelligent circuit was established. A month occurs when the Moon, having traveled around her own circle, overtakes the Sun. A year occurs whenever the Sun has traveled around his own circle. As for the periods of the others, men—except for a few out of many—have not observed them, nor do they give them names, nor do they measure them against one another by observing them with numbers. So, to speak plainly, they do not know that Time consists of the wanderings of these, which are of an incalculable multitude and wonderfully varied. Yet it is nonetheless possible to perceive that the "Perfect Number of Time" fulfills the Perfect Year then, when the speeds of all the eight circuits, having finished their courses together, are measured by the circuit of the Same and the Similar. In this way and for these reasons were generated all the stars that have turnings as they travel through heaven, so that this world might be as similar as possible to the most perfect and intelligible Living Being, in imitation of its eternal nature. And indeed, the other forms were completed up to the birth of Time, in likeness to the model to which it was being compared; but because it did not yet contain all living beings generated within itself, in this respect it was still dissimilar. This remainder he proceeded to work out, molding it to the nature of the model. Therefore, just as the Mind perceives Ideas present in the absolute Living Being—what kinds they are and how many it sees—so he thought that this world should also have such and so many. There are four: one, the heavenly race of gods; another, the winged and air-traveling; third, the water-dwelling kind; and fourth, the pedestrian and land-dwelling. Now, he made the form of the divine kind mostly out of fire, so that it might be most brilliant and beautiful to look upon. Making it like the whole, he made it well-rounded. He placed it in the intelligence of the Best Being, following it, and distributed it in a circle around the whole heaven, to be a true adornment <note>original: "κόσμον" (cosmos), meaning both order and beauty.</note> for it throughout the whole. He assigned two motions to each: one, in the same place and in the same way, always thinking the same thoughts about the same things within itself; the other, forward, being mastered by the revolution of the Same and the Similar. But for the other five motions he made them motionless and stationary, so that each of them might be as excellent as possible. For this reason have come to be all the stars that do not wander, being divine living beings; and because of this, they always remain turning in the same place. But those that turn and have such a wandering, as was said before, came to be in that way. And the Earth, our nourisher, which is wound around the pole stretched through the whole, he devised to be the guardian and creator of night and day, the first and eldest of the bodies that have come to be within the heaven. But the dances of these very gods and their juxtapositions with one another, and the revolutions of their circles back upon themselves and their progressions, and in their conjunctions, which of the gods come to be near one another and which are in opposition, and in what order they pass in front of one another, and at what times they are hidden from us and then reappear, sending terrors and signs of things to come to those who are able to calculate them—to describe these things without a visible model <note>original: "μιμημάτων" (mimematon), referring to astronomical instruments or orreries.</note> would be a vain labor. But let this be enough for us on this subject, and let our account of the nature of the visible and generated gods reach its end. Concerning the other daemons, to speak and to know their generation is beyond our power; but we must believe those who have spoken before, being the descendants of gods, as they said, and who surely knew their own ancestors. It is impossible, then, to disbelieve the children of the gods, even if they speak without probable or necessary proofs; but as they claim to be reporting family matters, we must believe them in obedience to the law. Thus then, according to them, let the generation of these gods be and be described: Oceanus and Tethys were the children of Earth and Heaven; from these, Phorcys and Cronus and Rhea and those with them; and from Cronus and Rhea, Zeus and Hera and all those whom we know are called their brothers; and still others, the descendants of these. When, therefore, all the gods were generated—both those who revolve visibly and those who appear only as far as they wish—the Generator of this universe spoke to them as follows: "Gods, sons of gods, of whom I am the maker and father, and of whose works I am the author, which, having been brought into being by me, are indissoluble as long as I so will. Everything that is bound can be dissolved; but to wish to dissolve that which is well-harmonized and in good condition is the act of an evil being. Therefore, since you have been generated, you are not entirely immortal nor indissoluble; yet you shall not be dissolved, nor shall you meet the fate of death, because you have received the benefit of my will, which is a bond even greater and more sovereign than those by which you were bound together at your birth. Now, therefore, learn what I show to you. There are still three mortal races to be generated. If these are not brought into being, the heaven will be incomplete. For it will not contain all the kinds of living beings within itself; but it must, if it is to be sufficiently perfect. But through me..."

### TIMÆUS

...these things having come into being and having shared in life, would be made equal to the gods. Therefore, so that mortal beings may exist, and that the All may truly be the All, turn yourselves according to nature to the crafting of living beings, imitating my power used in your own generation. <margin>A</margin> And as for that part of them which is fit to share the same name as the immortals—that which is called divine and which leads those among them who are willing to follow justice and you—I will deliver the seed and the beginning, having sown it myself. For the rest, you must weave the mortal to the immortal, crafting and giving birth to living beings; give them food to make them grow, and receive them again when they perish.

He spoke; and into the same mixing bowl <note>original: "krater." This refers to the vessel used for mixing wine and water, here used as a metaphor for the container in which the substances of the soul are blended.</note> in which he had previously blended and tempered the soul of the universe, he poured the remains of the earlier mixture. He mixed them in much the same way, <margin>B</margin> yet they were no longer as pure as before, but of a second and third degree of purity. When he had compounded the whole, he divided it into souls equal in number to the stars and assigned each soul to a star. Having mounted them as if on a chariot, he showed them the nature of the universe and declared to them the laws of fate: that the first birth would be ordained as one and the same for all, so that no one should be disadvantaged by him. They were to be sown into the instruments of time <note>The planets and stars, which "measure" time through their movement.</note> appropriate to each, and from this would grow the most god-fearing of living beings.

Since human nature is twofold, the better kind would be that which would hereafter be called "man." Whenever they were of necessity implanted in bodies, and as one part of the body was added and another taken away, first, there must be a single innate sense-perception common to all, arising from violent impressions. Second, there would be love mixed with pleasure and pain, and besides these, fear and anger, and all the emotions that follow them or are naturally opposed to them. If they could master these, <margin>C</margin> they would live in justice; but if they were mastered by them, they would live in injustice. He who lived well for his appointed time would return again to the habitation of his kindred star and lead a blessed life. But he who failed in this would be changed into the nature of a woman in his second birth.

If even then he did not cease from wickedness, he would be changed into some such beastly nature <margin>D</margin> resembling the character of his depravity. He would not cease from his labors and transformations until, by following the revolution of the "Same" and the "Similar" within himself, he had overcome by reason that turbulent and irrational mass of fire, water, air, and earth that later clung to him, and so return to the form of his first and best condition.

When he had enacted all these laws for them, so that he might be blameless for the future wickedness of any of them, he sowed some of them into the Sun, some into the Moon, and some into the other instruments of time. After this sowing, he handed over to the junior gods the task of fashioning mortal bodies, <margin>E</margin> and of crafting the remainder of the human soul that was still required, along with all that follows it. He commanded them to rule over and govern the mortal creature as nobly and as well as possible, except insofar as it might become the cause of its own evils.

After he had arranged all these things, he remained in his own customary nature. And as he remained, his children <note>The lesser or "junior" gods created by the Demiurge.</note> understood their father’s order and obeyed it. Taking the immortal principle of a mortal living being, and imitating their own craftsman, they borrowed from the cosmos portions of fire and earth, water and air, which were to be restored again. These they fastened together, not with the indissoluble bonds with which they themselves were held, but welding them with numerous invisible pegs because of their smallness, making of all the parts a single body for each individual. Then they bound the circuits of the immortal <margin>F</margin> soul into the body, which is subject to a constant flow of arrival and departure.

These souls, being bound into a great river, neither mastered it nor were mastered by it, but were borne along by force and also bore others by force. Consequently, the whole living creature moved, but in a disordered fashion, proceeding haphazardly and without reason, having all six types of motion. It moved forward and backward, and again to the right and to the left, and downward and upward, wandering in every way through the six regions of space. For though the flood that provided nourishment was great, <margin>G</margin> a still greater tumult was caused by the impressions of things falling upon them: when the body happened upon some external fire, or a solid mass of earth, or the slippery moisture of waters, or was caught by a storm of winds carried through the air, and the motions from all these things were carried through the body to the soul. For this reason, these motions were then—and are still now—called "sensations" <note>original: "aistheseis."</note>. At that time, these sensations produced a very great and intense motion, and moving together with the constantly flowing stream, they shook the circuits of the soul violently. They completely fettered the circuit of the "Same" by flowing against it...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> **By my** will, these things are indissoluble. Indeed, everything that is bound can be loosed. But it is the mark of an evil will to wish to dissolve that which has been beautifully composed and is well-ordered. Therefore, because you have been generated, you are not entirely immortal nor indissoluble. Yet you shall never be dissolved, nor shall you undergo the fate of death. For my will is for you a greater and more powerful bond for the preservation of your life than those knots by which you were bound when you were being born. But now, listen to what I command. Three types of mortals still remain for us to generate; without their generation, the heaven will be imperfect. <margin>B</margin> For it will not contain within its circle all types of living beings. But it must contain them if the world is to be entirely perfect. Yet if these were created by me alone and granted life, they would be made equal to the gods. Therefore, turn yourselves according to nature to the generation of animals, so that you may imitate my power which I used in your own origin. And as for that part of the animal which is such that it is fit to share a name with the immortals, and be called divine, and hold the sovereignty, and worship justice and you of its own accord, I will deliver the seed and the beginning to you. <margin>C</margin> It is right for you to execute the rest, so that weaving the mortal to the immortal nature, you may make and give birth to living beings, provide them with food to grow, and receive them back again when they are consumed.

Having said this, he poured the remains of the previous mixing into the same bowl in which he had tempered the soul of the whole world. He mixed them in a similar way, yet they were not similarly perfect, but were of a second and third degree of descent from the first. Finally, when he had established the universe, he distributed a number of souls equal to the stars, assigning each soul to each star. Placing them upon these as if upon a vehicle, he showed them the nature of the universe and declared the laws of fate to them: showing that the first generation <margin>To each kind of soul, one star is assigned.</margin> <margin>D</margin> would be one and the same for all in a certain order, so that no one should receive less than another. After the souls were sown, as it were, through the instruments of time appropriate to each, it was destined that a living being should be born which, of all animals, would be most devoted to divine worship.

Human nature is twofold: that kind would be more excellent which was to be called by the name of "man." When the souls were implanted in bodies by necessity, and as something was added to their bodies and in turn taken away, it was necessary that first, one inward sense, common to all and joined to their nature, should be excited by violent passions; then love mixed with pleasure and pain, and after these fear and anger, and whatever either follows these or is <margin>E</margin> contrary to them. Those who master these shall live justly, but those who are mastered by them shall live unjustly. And he who rightly completes the race of living granted by nature shall return to that star to which he was suited and lead a blessed life. But he who acts to the contrary shall be forced in his second birth to become a woman, with his sex changed. And he who even then does not make an end to sinning shall be transformed into the nature of brutes similar to his own character, in proportion to how much he is depraved. Nor shall he cease from labors and transformations until, having followed that rotation of his own same and similar nature implanted within him, and having subdued those turbulent and manifold affections later contracted from fire, water, air, and earth, he has calmed them through reason <margin>Love mixed with pleasure and pain.</margin> <margin>F</margin> and returned to his first and best state of being.

When he had designated these things for them—so that the cause of future depravity should not rest with him—he sowed some into the earth, some into the moon, and others into the markers established for the signaling of the spans of time. After this sowing, he mandated the remaining tasks to the junior gods: that they should fashion mortal bodies, and whatever remained of the human soul that ought to be added, they should join all this and its consequences together. They were to rule and govern the nature of the mortal animal as excellently and beautifully as possible, unless the creature should be the cause of evils to itself.

And he who disposed all these things remained rightly in his own state. While he remained so, his children, having recognized their father's order, immediately followed it. Thus, having received from him the immortal principle of a mortal animal, they imitated their own maker. They borrowed from the world particles of fire, air, water, and earth, which they were to restore again, and they joined them together—not with those same indissoluble bonds with which they themselves were bound, but with such as could not be seen because of their smallness. By joining many such "pegs," they made one body out of all the parts, and into this body, as it was both flowing in and flowing out, <margin>G</margin> they bound the circuits of the divine soul.

Therefore, these circuits, immersed in a deep river, neither held nor were held, but were carried along by force and also carried things with them. From this it happened that the entire animal moved, yet without order and with a certain accidental tossing. For it happens that it wanders through six motions, everywhere through the six differences of place, proceeding namely: forward and backward, to the right and to the left, upward and downward. Since a great flood washed in and flowed out from which the animal was nourished, a much greater tumult was caused by passions brought in from the outside: as when some body encountered the shock of an external fire, or was harmed by the solidity of earth, or the moisture of water, or the blast of air. Furthermore, the motions from all these things pass through the body to the soul, which for that reason were called "sensations" both in the beginning and now. In the beginning, these sensations continually excited many and very great motions, as that river flowed constantly, and with these floods, they violently shook the circuits of the soul. Indeed, they entirely hindered that circuit of the "Same" nature in its very course...

# OF PLATO

...they pull apart the circuit of the other <note>In Plato's cosmology, the soul is composed of two circles: the "Same" (fixed stars) and the "Other" (the planets). Here, physical embodiment disrupts these cosmic motions.</note>, to such an extent that those double and triple intervals arranged on both sides—the three intervals, and the intermediate connections of the ratios of four-to-three, three-to-two, and nine-to-eight <note>original: "sesquitertia, sesquialtera, sesquioctaua." These are the mathematical ratios (4:3, 3:2, and 9:8) that create musical harmony and, for Plato, the structure of the soul.</note>, which can be dissolved by no one except the one who joined them—are twisted in every kind of revolution. They induce all sorts of fractures and variations in the orbits, as many as can possibly occur. Thus, the circuits themselves, barely held together, are carried along, but they are carried along without reason, sometimes in reverse, sometimes at an angle, and sometimes in a sort of upside-down arrangement. It is as if someone were to fix their head on the ground and raise their feet high in the air; in such a state, it seems to the one affected, as well as to the spectators, that the right side is the left and the left is the right. Therefore, when the circuits of the soul suffer this or other similar disruptions, whenever they encounter something from the outside—whether of the "same" or the "other" kind—they judge what is "the same" or "the other" falsely. For this reason, they are then deceptive and mindless, and there is no ruling or leading circuit within them. And when external senses strike the soul with great force and take possession of it entirely, then those who are actually subjugated and serving seem to be the masters. On account of these things, at the beginning, when the soul is first enclosed in the bonds of a mortal body, it is rendered mindless.

<margin>Why the elderly are wise.</margin>
But after the "river" of nutrition and growth flows more gently and decreases, and the circuits of the soul perform their journey with more tranquil motion, becoming more settled as time passes and returning to the shape appropriate to their nature, then the direct revolutions of each circle discern the nature of the "same" and the "other" correctly, and they make the person thus instructed prudent. If someone joins appropriate discipline and education to a right upbringing, they will escape the most serious "disease" <note>Here, "disease" refers to ignorance or a lack of philosophical understanding.</note> and emerge entirely healthy and whole. But if one neglects this, they enter upon a "lame" path of life and, being like someone crippled and altogether useless, they fall back down to the underworld. However, these things happen after birth.

But now we must discuss the first composition of man more precisely, and show by probable reasoning for what cause and by what providence of the gods each member of the body was adapted to the specific duties of the soul. In the beginning, the gods fashioned the shape of the head to the roundness of the world, and in it they placed those two divine circuits of the soul.

<margin>The head is the most divine member.</margin>
The head is, moreover, the most divine member of the body and the ruler of the rest of the members, to which the gods commanded the whole joined body to be subject and to obey. For they devised that it should possess all the movements that could possibly exist. Since, however, the earth is unequal and rough, partly sloping upward and partly downward, if the head were to crawl upon the ground or roll across the surface of the earth, it would not be able to pass through these twists and turns without injury. To avoid this evil, the gods placed this tall habit of the body

<margin>Tallness.</margin>
under the head as a vehicle for easier progress. Furthermore, they attached four limbs to the body, stretched out in length and flexible, by which the divine providence might easily move, namely to grasp objects, to stand, and to stay firm, through all of which the head might travel, staying on top as the dwelling place of the most divine and sacred part. For this reason, therefore, they gave us legs and hands. Deeming the front parts to be more excellent than the back and more fit for commanding, they willed that we should move for the most part in a forward direction. Furthermore, it was necessary for the

<margin>On the many eyes. 12.</margin>
front parts to be distinct and different. Therefore, they first added the face to the globe of the head, and in the face they assigned all the instruments that might assist the soul's providence, and they decreed that the natural command of man should consist in this front and foremost part. But of all the parts of the face, the "light-bringing" circles of the eyes shine first, given for this reason: The gods made the circles of the eyes partakers of that fire which does not burn, but which brings the day to the world by sweetly illuminating it. For they willed that the internal fire of our body, which is a pure sibling of this external fire, should flow out through the eyes. In the eyes, there is a gentle and dense collection of this kind of fire, but the purer fire flies out only through the more solid and narrow middle of the eye, while the thicker fire is held back. Thus, when the light of day applies itself to the ray of vision, then those two similar things—meeting and mixing together where the keenness of the eyes is directed—coalesce into the form of a single "domestic" body <note>original: "domestici corporis." This refers to the "body" of light formed when the light from the eye and the light from the sun combine.</note>, wherever the meeting of the internal and external light occurs. Therefore, this whole, having obtained the same quality because of its similarity, whenever it touches anything else or is touched by another thing, diffuses the motion of this touch to the whole body and through it to the soul, producing that sensation which is called sight. But after the kindred fire has departed into the night, the ray of vision vanishes. For, breaking out into air that is unlike itself, it is changed and extinguished, since it has no natural communion with the nearby air, which lacks the splendor of fire. Therefore, it stops seeing and induces sleep. For the gods devised the eyelids as a salutary covering for the eyes; when these are closed, that power of the internal fire is restrained by the fitting cover, and once compressed, it spreads through and soothes the internal motions, and once these are relaxed, a soft rest creeps in. If deep sleep occupies us because of great quiet, few dreams follow. But if some more violent motions are left behind like the remnants of wakefulness, depending on the nature and location of those remnants, such and so many

<column-break/>

...flow, and they held back the ruling and going [circuits]. And regarding the passage of the "Other," they twisted them so that the three intervals of the double and triple [ratios], and the means and bonds of the three-halves, four-thirds, and nine-eighths <note>original: "ἡμιολίων καὶ ἐπιτρίτων καὶ ἐπογδόων." These are the Greek terms for the musical ratios 3:2, 4:3, and 9:8.</note>—since they were not entirely dissolvable except by the one who bound them—made all sorts of turns, all sorts of fractures and corruptions of the circles, in every way possible. Thus, being barely held together with one another, they were carried along, but they were carried along without reason, sometimes in opposite directions, sometimes sideways, sometimes upside-down. Just as when someone, having leaned their head upon the ground and thrust their feet upward against something, is upside-down; then in this state, both to the sufferer and to the onlookers, the right side appears left and the left side appears right to each other. When the revolutions [of the soul] suffer this same thing and other such things violently, whenever they encounter anything of the "Same" or the "Other" kind from the outside, they then address the "same" as "other" and the "other" as "same" in contradiction of the truth, and they become false and mindless. No period or leader is in them at that time. And when certain external sensations, being carried along and falling upon them, draw the whole vessel <note>original: "κύτος" (kutos). Literally a hollow vessel or container, here referring to the soul's housing.</note> of the soul along with them, then these [sensations], although they are mastered, seem to master. And because of all these conditions, now at the beginning, a soul first becomes mindless whenever it is bound into a mortal body. But when the "river" of growth and nutrition flows in less, and the periods once again attaining calm go their own way and become more settled as time goes on, then the revolutions of each of the circles are straightened out according to their natural shape. Addressing the "other" and the "same" correctly, they make the one possessing them a sensible person. If, then, a right upbringing of education also assists, a person becomes entirely whole and healthy, having escaped the greatest disease. But if he is negligent, having traveled a "lame" life, he returns to the House of Hades <note>original: "Ἅιδου." The Greek underworld.</note> incomplete and mindless. But these things happen later.

We must now discuss more accurately the things proposed before: the generation of bodies part by part, and of the soul, and for what causes and providences of the gods they came to be. We must proceed by holding fast to the most likely account. Imitating the shape of the universe, which is round, the gods bound the two divine revolutions into a spherical body—this which we now call the "head"—which is the most divine thing in us and the master of all that is within us. To it the gods handed over the whole body they had assembled for its service, having perceived that it should participate in all the motions that were to be. So that it might not roll upon the earth—which has all sorts of heights and depths—and be at a loss how to climb over the one or get out of the other, they gave it this [body] as a vehicle and a means of ease. From this the body acquired its length, and grew four limbs that can be extended and bent, the god having engineered a way of travel. By grasping and bracing itself with these, it was able to travel through all places, carrying on high the dwelling place of our most divine and sacred part. For this reason, then, legs and hands were attached to all. Deeming the front to be more honorable and more fit for leading than the back, the gods gave us the majority of our movement in this direction. It was necessary, then, that man should have the front distinguished and unlike the back. Therefore, having first placed the sight around the vessel of the head, they bound into it the face, and in this they bound instruments for all the providence of the soul, and they ordained that this, which is naturally the front, should partake in leadership.

Of the instruments, they first fashioned the "light-bearing" eyes <note>original: "φωσφόρα ... ὄμματα" (phosphora ommata). Phosphoros means bringing light; it is also the name of the Morning Star (Venus).</note>, binding them in for such a cause: they engineered a body to come into being from that kind of fire which does not have the power of burning, but which provides a gentle light, proper to each day. For they made the pure fire within us, which is a sibling to this [daylight], to flow through the eyes, smooth and dense; they compressed the whole eye, but especially the middle, so that it would keep out everything thicker and allow only such pure fire to filter through. Whenever, therefore, there is daylight, then the stream of vision, going out and being similar meeting similar, is compacted and coalesces into a single kindred body in the direct line of the eyes, wherever the light traveling from within strikes against that which meets it from without. Thus, the whole being affected similarly due to its similarity, whenever it touches anything or anything else touches it, it passes on the motions of these through the whole body unto the soul and provides this sensation which we call "seeing." But when the kindred fire departs into the night, the stream is cut off. For going out into what is unlike, it is changed and extinguished, as it is no longer of one nature with the neighboring air, since the air lacks fire. It stops seeing, and moreover, it becomes an inducer of sleep. For the protection which the gods engineered for the sake of sight, the nature of the eyelids—whenever these close, they shut in the power of the fire within. This fire then diffuses and smooths the internal motions; once they are smoothed, quiet occurs. When much quiet has occurred, sleep with few dreams falls upon us. But if some greater motions are left behind, according to their nature and the places where they are left, they produce such and so many...

<meta>This page continues Plato's dialogue, the *Timaeus*, moving from the mathematical construction of the soul to the physical mechanisms of the body, specifically optics and the purpose of the senses. It bridges the "works of Intellect" with the "works of Necessity."</meta>

# TIMAEUS

...it provides representations of dreams which, when we are awakened, are remembered as images. Regarding the production of images in mirrors, and all things that are visible and smooth, it is no longer difficult to understand. For from the communion of the internal and external fire with one another, and again from the union of a single fire at the smooth surface—which occurs and is reshaped in many ways—all such appearances necessarily occur. This happens when the fire of the face and the fire of the sight congeal around the smooth and bright surface. Things on the right appear to be on the left, because the opposite parts of the sight come into contact with the opposite parts of the mirror, contrary to the usual habit of impact. However, the right appears right and the left appears left when the light of the vision, as it is being joined, shifts. This occurs when the smoothness of the mirrors, taking on a curved shape on either side, pushes the right part of the sight to the left side, and the other to the other. <margin>B</margin> If the mirror is turned to the length of the face, it makes the whole thing appear upside-down, pushing the bottom of the light toward the top and the top toward the bottom. All these things are among the auxiliary causes <note>original: "ξυμαιτίων" / "adjunct causes." Plato distinguishes between the mechanical "how" and the divine "why."</note> which God uses as ministers to achieve, as far as possible, the Idea of the Best. But they are thought by most people not to be auxiliary causes, but the primary causes of all things—chilling and heating, solidifying and dissolving, and performing all such effects. But such things are capable of having no reason or intellect for any purpose. For of all things that exist, the only one which is fitting to possess intellect is the soul. And this is invisible. But fire, water, air, and earth are all visible bodies. The lover of mind and knowledge must necessarily pursue the first causes of an intelligent nature. <margin>C</margin> But those causes which are moved by others and which of necessity move other things must be considered second causes. Therefore, we must speak of both kinds of causes, but separately: those which are the craftsmen of beautiful and good things with the aid of intellect, and those which, when isolated from wisdom, produce disorderly and random effects each time. Let this be enough said regarding the auxiliary causes of the eyes in order that they might have the power they now possess. But their greatest work for our benefit, for which God gave them to us, must be told next. Sight, in my opinion, has become the cause of the greatest benefit to us; for of the words now being spoken about the universe, none could ever have been <margin>D</margin> uttered if we had never seen the stars, or the sun, or the heavens. But now, the sight of day and night, months and the revolutions of the years, have created number, given us the conception of time, and the ability to search into the nature of the universe. From these things we have acquired the genus of philosophy, than which no greater good has ever come nor will ever come to the mortal race as a gift from the gods. This, I say, is the greatest benefit of the eyes. Why should we celebrate the other lesser ones? If a man who is not a philosopher were blinded and lost them, he would lament and mourn in vain. But let this be said by us: this is the cause, and for this purpose God found and gave us sight: so that by observing the circuits of the mind in heaven, we might use them for the revolutions <margin>E</margin> of our own thinking, which are kindred to those—the disturbed to the undisturbed. By learning these, and participating in the natural correctness of reasoning, and by imitating the entirely unerring revolutions of God, we might stabilize the wandering revolutions within ourselves. Regarding voice and hearing, the same account applies: they were given by the gods for the same purposes. For speech is appointed for this very purpose, contributing the greatest part to it; and likewise, whatever part of musical voice is useful for hearing was given for the sake of harmony. And harmony, having motions kindred to the circuits of our soul, is seen by the one who uses the Muses with intellect not to be useful for irrational <margin>F</margin> pleasure—as it is thought to be now—but as an ally given by the Muses to the discordant circuit of the soul within us, to bring it into order and symphony with itself. Rhythm also, because our condition is mostly immoderate and lacking in grace, was given by the same gods as a help for the same purpose. Thus, the things that have been spoken of previously, with few exceptions, have shown the things crafted through intellect. But we must also place beside them in our account the things that come about through necessity. For the generation of this world was mixed, arising from the composition of both necessity and intellect. Since intellect was ruling <note>original: "ἄρχοντος." Here, Intellect "persuades" Necessity to order the world for the best.</note> necessity by persuading it to lead most of the things that come into being toward the best, in this way, by necessity yielding to wise persuasion, this universe was first constructed. If anyone <margin>G</margin> then will truly tell how it was made, they must also mix in the form of the "errant cause," in the way that its nature is to act. Thus we must return again and, taking a suitable starting point for these things in turn, we must begin once more from the beginning, just as we did with the previous topics. We must consider the nature of fire, water, air, and earth before the generation of the heavens, and the conditions that existed before this. For until now, no one has revealed their generation, but we speak as if people know what fire and each of the others are, calling them "principles" and assuming they are the "elements" <note>original: "στοιχεῖα." It is not even fitting for them to be compared to the form of syllables by anyone who has even a little sense. For now, however...

Indeed, things on the right seem to be on the left, because by an unusual manner we touch the contrary parts of the eyes with contrary parts. But the right corresponds to the right, and the left to the left, when the light, having been mixed with that which it is mingled, leaps across. This happens when the smoothness of the mirrors has assumed a depth on this side and that, and thus turned the right part of the eyes into the left of the mirror, and the left into the right. <insert>B</insert> But if the mirror is turned to the length of the face, it renders the face turned upward, when the superior part of the light is turned to the inferior, and the inferior to the superior. And all these are of that kind which assist the causes of things, which God uses as ministers to perfect the idea of the best, as far as it can be done. But most people think these are not the helpers of the governance of causes, but are the causes of all things themselves—things which have the nature of cold and heat, rare and dense, and other similar things, <insert>C</insert> but possess no reason or mind at all. It is necessary, however, for a lover of mind and science to seek the principal causes of a wise nature; <margin>Why eyes were given to humans.</margin> and to judge those which are necessarily moved by others, but move other things, as secondary causes. Therefore, we must judge thus, that we distinguish between both kinds of causes, and speak separately about those which are the makers of beautiful and good things with intelligence, and about those again which, being void of prudence, do whatever they do at random and without order. And concerning the secondary causes of the eyes, leading to that power which they have, <insert>D</insert> I think enough has been said. But the greatest work for whose sake they were usefully given to us by God must next be explained. For the knowledge of the best things, as I judge, the eyes have brought to us. For these things which are discussed concerning the world would never have been discovered if neither the stars, nor the sun, nor the heaven could have been looked upon. But the knowledge of day and night, arising from the eyes, has caused us to measure the circuits of months and years by a certain counting, to know time, and to scrutinize the order of the universal nature. From which things we have attained philosophy. No greater gift than this has ever been <insert>E</insert> given to the mortal race by the gift of the gods, nor will be given. This, therefore, I say is the greatest benefit of the eyes. I pass over other minor things. For which, those who are strangers to philosophy, if they were deprived of them and should complain, would complain in vain. And when we have recognized them, and have perceived the order of each according to the right reason of nature, <insert>F</insert> we should imitate the revolutions of God which are performed without any error, and according to their example, compose our own wandering and erratic thoughts. I believe the gods have also given us voice and hearing for the sake of the same thing. For speech pertains to these very things and is of great benefit, and every use of the musical voice is granted for the sake of <margin>Concerning voice and rhythm.</margin> harmony. And harmony, which has motions congruent and kindred to the wanderings of our soul, is useful to a man using the Muses with prudence, not for a pleasure void of reason—as it seems now—but was given by the Muses for this: that through it we might compose the dissonant circuit of the soul and bring it back to a concord congruent with itself. Rhythm also seems to have been granted for this: that we might most aptly temper the immoderate habit within us which lacks grace. <insert>G</insert> Thus far we have treated the works of the mind, with a few exceptions. Therefore, it is necessary for one who will truly narrate the constitution of the world to also mix in the species of the "errant cause," according to the instinct of its own nature. This will be done conveniently if, a suitable principle of these things themselves being taken, we discuss them again from their very origin, just as we did concerning the superior things. No one indeed until this time has shown their generation, but we speak of them as if it were known what fire and the rest are, and we constitute them the first principles of the world, when they ought not to be considered by men of any mind even as the equivalent of syllables, let alone elements. <meta>This page marks a pivotal shift in the *Timaeus*. Having discussed the "Works of Intellect," Plato now introduces the "Works of Necessity," requiring a more complex framework that includes a "third genus" or "receptacle" to explain the physical world's constant flux.</meta>

**A** But for now, we do not think we should speak of the first principle of all things, or their principles, or however they may be called. We refrain from this discussion for no other reason than that it is difficult, in our present mode of inquiry, to express what we think about these matters. Therefore, you should not expect me to speak of them, nor could I persuade myself that I could rightly undertake such a great task. However, as I said from the beginning, we will maintain the power of **likelihood** <note>original: "verisimilitudinis" / "eikotōn logōn" — Plato often uses "likely stories" to describe the physical world, which cannot be known with the absolute certainty of mathematics.</note>, and we shall strive to yield to no one in assigning probable reasons concerning these things. Thus, we shall explain both individual things and the whole from the beginning. Let us now, at the start of our discourse, pray to God as our Savior, asking that He lead us from a strange and unusual exposition toward a doctrine of likelihood, and so let us begin our inquiry. But we must draw this discussion of the universe from a broader division than before. Previously, we made a division into two species. Now, a **third genus** must be added. For two were sufficient in the previous parts: one as a model, which is always the same and grasped only by the intellect; the other as an image derived from this model, subject to generation and visible to the eyes. Since we thought these two were sufficient, we did not add a third. But now, reason seems to compel us to try to explain a difficult and obscure species. What power and what nature should we consider it to possess? This above all: that it is the **receptacle** <note>original: "receptaculum" / "hypodochē"</note> and, as it were, the **nurse** of all generation.

**B** Although this is stated truly, it must be spoken of more clearly. This is an arduous task, especially because to demonstrate this thing, it is first necessary to doubt and inquire about fire and the other things called **elements** <note>original: "elementa" / "stoicheia"</note>—to ask which of these should be called "water" rather than "fire," or "air" rather than "earth," or why any one thing should be called by a specific name rather than by all names together. It is truly difficult to assert anything certain and firm about them. In what way, then, and by what reason, and with what probability shall we speak in such an inquiry?

**C** First, that body which we just now called "water," when it congeals into solid matter, appears to become stone and earth; but when it melts and flows away, it becomes spirit and air. Likewise, air when burnt becomes fire. Fire, when extinguished and made more "thick," creates air. Again, air when made denser congeals into mist and clouds. When these are further compressed, rain flows down. From water, earth and stones are born again. And so we see all these things, in a kind of cycle, giving to one another their powers and nourishment for generation in turn. Since these things never appear to remain the same, who could, without blushing or fear of 

**D** <margin>That fire and others are not truly "this thing" but "of such a kind."</margin>suspicion of being refuted, call any one of these things by a certain and firm name rather than another? Surely no one. Therefore, the safest way of speaking in these matters will be this: That which we see always becoming different at different times—for example, in the likeness of fire—we should not call "this thing" as if it were fire, but rather "of such a kind," that is, something "fiery." Nor should we call water "this thing," but something "watery," nor anything else as if it possessed stability. Indeed, not even by 

**E** <margin>See how the things called elements cannot even be pointed out with pronouns.</margin>any pronouns should these things be designated—the words we usually use when we point to a thing and say "this" or "that." For they flee, and do not wait for that demonstration which designates "this" and "of this" and "to this," nor for any name that treats them as existing and stable. Therefore, we should not call all such things "this" or "that," but rather "such a thing," or "like this" because of some similarity. We should call fire everywhere "such," and the same for all other things that are generated. But that in which each of these appears to come into being, and then to dissolve, is the only thing that should be called by those pronouns by which we signify "this" or "that." However, that which is of a certain quality—such as hot, or white, or any of the opposites, or anything composed of opposites—should by no means be called by those names.

**F** <margin>See how the analogy of matter is shown.</margin>But let us explain what we mean more clearly. If someone were to mold all kinds of figures out of a single piece of gold, and never ceased reshaping each one into others, and if someone were to point at one of them and ask what it is, we could most truly and safely respond that it is "gold." But to say that it is a "triangle" or some other figure that has been impressed upon it and 

**G** <margin>Matter never recedes from its potential.</margin><margin>Things in matter are images of true things.</margin><margin>See how matter is formless.</margin>is constantly changing, as if these things truly existed, is not permitted. We must be content with that single response as the safest. The same reasoning applies to that nature which receives all bodies: it must always be called the same. For it never recedes from its own potential. It always receives all things, and it never assumes any form similar to those that enter it in any way. Every nature is subject to being molded, and being moved and shaped by the things that enter it, it appears different at different times. But the things that enter and exit are **images** of things that truly and always exist, shaped by those very things that truly are in a wondrous and hardly explainable way, as we shall narrate hereafter. For the present, three genera must be assumed: one which is generated; another in which it is generated; and a third from which that which is born draws its likeness. Therefore, it is fitting to compare these thus: the **receiver** to a **mother**; the **source** to a **father**; and the **nature between them** to an **offspring**. But it must be understood that since there must be an image of things distinguished by every variety of form, that womb of formation will never be well-prepared unless it is **formless**, and by its own nature lacks all the forms it is about to receive. For if it were similar to any of those things it receives into itself, then when it received things of an opposite or entirely different nature...

**A** ...let it be thus with us: why we should not now speak about the first principle of all things, or their principles, or whatever seems right concerning them—for no other reason than the difficulty of showing our current views according to our present method of exposition. Therefore, neither should you think I ought to speak, nor could I persuade myself that I would be able to handle it rightly by taking on such a great task. But preserving what was said at the beginning—the power of **likely accounts**—I will try to speak about each and every thing in a way that is no less likely, but rather more so, than what has come before. Having now called upon God at the beginning of our words, as a Savior to deliver us from a strange and unusual narrative to the doctrine of likelihood, let us begin to speak again. Our new beginning concerning the whole must now be divided more broadly than before. For then we distinguished two kinds, but now a third genus must be revealed by us. Two were sufficient for what was said previously: one being proposed as a model, intelligible and always existing in the same way; and the second being a copy of the model, having generation and being visible. A third we did not then distinguish, thinking the two would be sufficient. But now the argument seems to compel us to attempt to make visible in words a difficult and dim kind. What power and nature should we assume it has? Primarily this: that it is the **receptacle** of all generation, like a **nurse**.

**B** The truth has been stated, but it must be spoken of more clearly. This is difficult, especially because it is necessary to first raise doubts about fire and the things associated with fire for this purpose. For it is difficult to say which of these one should call "water" rather than "fire," and what any one of them should be called rather than all of them together—to speak of each in such a way as to use a trustworthy and certain account. How then, and where, and what likely thing shall we say after having raised these doubts? 

**C** First, that which we have just now named "water," we see (as we think) becoming stones and earth when it congeals. But when it melts and dissolves, this same thing becomes breath and air; (and air when ignited becomes fire); and conversely, fire when contracted and extinguished returns again to the form of air; and again air, coming together and thickening, becomes cloud and 

**D** mist. And from these, being still more compressed, flows water; and from water, earth and stones again. Thus they pass on generation to one another in a cycle, as it appears. Since these things never appear as the same individuals, who would not be ashamed of himself for firmly asserting that any one of them is "this" and not something else? No one. Rather, by far the safest course when we make assumptions about these things is to speak thus: that which we always see becoming different at different times, such as fire, we should not call "this," but we should address fire as "the suchlike" in each case; nor water as "this," but always "the suchlike"; nor anything else as having any stability, among all the things we think we indicate by using the words "this" and "that," 

**E** as if we were showing something. For it flees, not awaiting the expression of "this" or "that" or "to this," or any phrase that points them out as being permanent. But one should not speak of each of these things in that way; rather, one should call "the suchlike"—that which always moves about as similar—in respect to each and all of them. Thus, fire is that which is "such" through everything, and so is everything that has generation. But that in which each of them appears to come into being, and from which they again perish—only that should be addressed by using the names "this" and "that." But that which is of any quality—hot or white or any of the opposites, and everything derived from these—none of these should that receptacle be called. But we must strive to speak of it 

**F** more clearly again. For if someone, having molded all figures out of gold, should never stop remolding each into all the others, and if someone were to point to one of them and ask what it is, it is by far safest for the truth to say that it is "gold." But the triangle and all the other figures that were coming into being—one should never speak of these as "being," since they change while one is making the assertion. But if the questioner is willing to accept "of such a kind" with safety, one should be satisfied. The same account applies to the nature that receives all bodies: it must always be addressed by the same name. For it never departs from its own power. It always receives all things, and it has never taken any shape similar to any of the things that enter it in any way or at any time. 

**G** For it is laid down by nature as an **impressible mass** <note>original: "ekmageion" — This term refers to a material like wax or clay that can receive a stamp or impression.</note> for everything, being moved and reshaped by the things that enter it. It appears different at different times because of them. But the things that enter and exit are imitations of the things that always are, having been stamped from them in a way that is difficult to describe and wondrous, which we shall pursue hereafter. In the present, then, we must conceive of three kinds: that which comes into being, that in which it comes into being, and that from which the thing coming into being grows as an imitation. And indeed, it is fitting to compare the **receiver** to a **mother**, the **source** to a **father**, and the **nature between them** to an **offspring**. We must understand that if there is to be an impression to be seen that is varied with all varieties, this very thing in which the impression is set would not be well-prepared unless it were **formless** of all those ideas which it is about to receive from somewhere. For if it were like any of the things entering into it, when it received things of an opposite nature or of a completely different kind, it would...

<meta>This page continues Plato’s investigation into the "third genus"—the Receptacle or "Space"—which acts as the container for all physical creation. It follows the previous discussion where the need for a medium between the eternal Forms and the changing physical world was established.</meta>

...would represent it poorly, showing its own appearance. Therefore, it is necessary for that which is to receive all kinds of things into itself to be outside of all forms; just as in the case of ointments, those who prepare them through art first seek a certain smoothness in the liquids that are to receive the fragrant scents. Or as those who attempt to imprint shapes in soft materials, they allow no previous shape to be visible at all, but instead they make the surface as smooth and level as possible. In the same way, that which is intended to repeatedly and well receive the likenesses of the things that always exist throughout its whole self, must naturally be outside of all forms. Therefore, let us not call the mother and receptacle of that which has become visible and entirely sensible either earth, or air, or fire, or water, nor anything composed of these, nor that from which these have come. Rather, if we say it is an invisible and formless species <note>original: "eidos" — here referring to a "kind" or "nature" rather than a perfect Form.</note>, all-receiving, and participating in the most difficult way in the intelligible <note>The "intelligible" refers to the realm of perfect, unchanging ideas that can only be understood by the mind, not the senses.</note>, and most hard to grasp, we shall not be lying. But as far as it is possible to reach its nature from what has been said, one might most correctly say this: that a part of it appears as fire whenever it is ignited; a part as water when it is moistened; and as earth and air insofar as it receives the imitations of these. But we must consider this more precisely by defining it through reason: is there such a thing as "fire itself" in and of itself, and all those things which we always say exist as things in themselves? Or are these things which we see, and as many others as we perceive through the body, the only things that possess such truth, and there is nothing else besides these anywhere or in any way? And do we say in vain each time that there is an intelligible form of each thing, when it was actually nothing but a word? It is not right to leave the present matter unexamined and unjudged, asserting only that it is so; nor should we add another long digression to a discourse that is already long. But if some great definition could be shown briefly, that would be most helpful. Thus, I give my own vote: If mind <note>original: "nous"</note> and true opinion are two distinct kinds, then these self-existing forms must absolutely exist—things which we cannot perceive but only understand. But if, as it seems to some, true opinion differs in no way from mind, then everything we perceive through the body must be considered most certain. But we must say they are two, because they have come to be separately and are unlike. For the one is produced in us by instruction, the other by persuasion; the one is always accompanied by true reason, the other is irrational; the one is unmoved by persuasion, the other is subject to it. And we must say that every man shares in true opinion, but of mind, only the gods and a very small race of men partake. Since these things are so, we must agree that there is one species that stays the same: unbegotten and indestructible, neither receiving anything else into itself from elsewhere, nor itself going into anything else; invisible and otherwise imperceptible, which is what the intellect has been allotted to look upon. But the second is that which bears the same name and is similar to it, sensible, generated, always in motion, coming to be in some place and again perishing from there; it is grasped by opinion with the help of sensation. The third genus is that of space, which never admits destruction but provides a home for all things that have birth; it is grasped without sensation by a sort of "bastard reasoning" <note>original: "logismō tini nothō" — Plato means we cannot "see" space, but we infer it must be there to hold objects.</note> and is hardly trustworthy. When we look at this, we dream and say it is necessary for everything that exists to be in some place and occupy some space, and that which is neither on earth nor in heaven is nothing. Because of this dreaming state, we are unable to wake up and distinguish the truth of these and related things regarding the sleepless and truly existing nature—that since an image is not even the owner of that for which it was created, but is always the phantom of something else, it must therefore come to be in something else, clinging to existence in some way, or else be nothing at all. But to that which truly exists, true and accurate reason comes as a witness: that as long as one thing is one thing and another is another, neither will ever come to be in the other so as to be both one and two at the same time. This then is my summary judgment: that there were three things in three ways even before the heaven was made—Being, Space, and Becoming. And the nurse of becoming, being moistened and ignited, and receiving the forms of earth and air, and suffering all the other experiences that follow these, appeared varied to the sight. But because she was filled with powers that were neither similar nor balanced, she was not in equilibrium in any part, but being swayed unevenly in every direction, she was shaken by those things and, in turn, shook them. And they, being moved, were carried in different directions, separated like things that are shaken and winnowed by baskets and tools for the cleaning of grain; the dense and heavy things fall in one place, while the rare and light are carried to another seat. So then the four kinds, being shaken by the receptacle—which itself moved like a winnowing tool—separated the most dissimilar things far from each other and pushed the most similar together. Thus, these things occupied different places even before the whole universe was organized from them.

<column-break/>

This is why that which is to receive all kinds must have no form of its own. Just as those who are about to make sweet-smelling ointments prepare the liquid material they wish to scent so that it has no smell of its own; and those who wish to imprint figures into soft materials do not allow any prior figure to appear in them, but polish them with an exact smoothness. So <margin>B</margin> that which is to be correctly shaped into the various likenesses of all eternal things must by its own nature lack all these forms. For this reason, let us say that the mother and receptacle of this entire universe—which is both created and manifest to all senses—is neither earth, nor air, nor fire, nor water, nor again anything composed of these, nor those things from which these themselves consist. Rather, it is a certain invisible and formless species, capable of receiving all things, which in a certain ambiguous and scarcely explicable way participates in the divine and intelligible nature. It cannot be grasped by itself in any way, but as much as its nature can be touched from what has been said, we can say this: that the part of it which is ignited appears as fire; the part that is moistened as water; and earth and air similarly, insofar as it receives their images. But we must consider these things by distinguishing them through reason: is there some fire that exists by itself, separate from matter, and those other things which we often say remain by themselves? Or are these only the things we perceive by the senses of the body, and do they contain such truth in themselves that there are no others anywhere besides these? Do we say in vain that there is an intelligible species of each thing, when these are nothing but words? <margin>D</margin> Indeed, this should not be asserted blindly or without examination, nor should we add a long digression to the present discussion, which is already long by nature. <margin>He briefly proves that the Forms exist.</margin> But a brief summary that encompasses great things will seem very timely. Thus, I will give my own opinion on this matter. If intellect and true opinion are two different kinds, it is necessary that there be species of this sort which exist by themselves and are grasped by intelligence rather than the senses. But if, as it seems to some, true opinion differs not at all from intellect, then all things which the bodily sense touches must be held as certain. But I believe we must say they are two, because they are made separately and are dissimilar. For <margin>E</margin> instruction introduces the one to us, but persuasion the other; the former is always with true reason, the latter without reason; the former is not changeable by any persuasion, while the latter is subject to this change. Every man is a partaker of true opinion. But of intelligence, <margin>That few men are partakers of intelligence.</margin> all the gods indeed, but very few men, are partakers. Since these things are so, we must admit there is a species which is always the same, without birth or death, which neither receives anything else into itself from elsewhere nor goes out into anything else, and is perceived by no sense of the body; this is what belongs to intelligence alone. But there is something after this which agrees with it not in nature but in name, and bears its likeness: it is generated, <margin>F</margin> manifest to the senses, always moving and sustained by another, born in some place and then receding from it, to be grasped by opinion through the senses. <margin>That matter is place.</margin> The third kind is space, which never perishes but provides a seat for all things that are born. This is touched without the sense of touch, by a certain "adulterous reason," and is scarcely believable. Finally, when we look toward this with our mind, we dream in a way, and think it necessary that whatever exists must be placed in some location and occupy some region; and that which is neither on earth nor in heaven, we believe <margin>G</margin> does not exist at all. Because we are occupied by these dreams, we are unable to discern all these and similar states from the sleepless and truly existing nature. Therefore, we cannot even discern that since an image does not belong to itself (after that thing in which it was made), but is always the phantom of another, it is not unfitting that it should be in something else, and so in a certain way participate in essence, for otherwise it could not exist at all. But to that which truly exists, this true and exquisite reason gives support, teaching that as long as a thing is such that this is one thing and that is another, neither will ever be in the other so as to become one and two at the same time. This then is the summary of my mind's opinion: that there exist, even before the birth of heaven, these three things in a threefold way—Being, Space, and Becoming. And the nurse of becoming, ignited and moistened, receiving the forms of earth and air, and suffering the experiences that follow these, appeared all-form to the sight. But because it was filled with forces that were neither similar nor equal in weight, it was in no part balanced, but swaying and declining unevenly in every direction, it was shaken by those things we mentioned, and it in turn shook them. By this impulse, they were driven and separated in different ways, just as we see things separated in the cleaning of grain by winnowing tools, where the solid and heavy are carried one way, and the light and rare another. The arrangements and origins of the elements.
