origin of these things one by one, using a new and unaccustomed <note>original: "inusitato" — Plato warns that his mathematical explanation of the elements is a novel theory.</note> kind of demonstration; yet to you, who have traveled all the paths of noble learning, it shall be plain and clear.

<margin>B</margin>

In the first place, no one will doubt that fire, earth, water, and air are bodies. Now, every kind of body has depth. And it is necessary that depth consists of planes. Furthermore, the straightness of a plane base is constructed from triangles, and all triangles have their beginning from two types, each having one right angle and two acute angles. One of these triangles has an equal part of the right angle on both sides, being defined by equal sides <note>This is the 45-45-90 or Isosceles right triangle.</note>; but in the other, unequal parts are distributed to unequal sides <note>This is the Scalene right triangle, specifically the 30-60-90 triangle.</note>. Therefore, proceeding by probable reasons joined to necessity, let us lay down the origin

<margin>C</margin>

of fire and the other bodies in this way. The principles higher than these are known only to God, and to whoever is a friend of God. We must see, then, by what most powerful reason the four most beautiful bodies are made—dissimilar indeed to one another, but such that they may be dissolved into each other and generated from one another. If we grasp this, we shall hold the truth itself concerning the generation of fire and earth, and of those things which are made as intermediates between them according to a preserved proportion. For then we shall grant to no one that there are anywhere more beautiful bodies visible to the eyes than these, of which each belongs to a single genus. We must therefore attempt to arrange the

<margin>D</margin>

four genera of bodies that excel in beauty, and thus assert that we have sufficiently grasped their nature. Of the two triangles, the Isosceles (that is, the equal-sided) has but a single nature; but the triangle that is longer on one side <note>The Scalene.</note> has infinite natures. Therefore, if we wish to begin correctly, we must choose the most beautiful of these infinite types. And if anyone wishes to bring forth a more beautiful one chosen by himself for the constitution of these things, his opinion shall prevail not as an adversary’s, but as a friend’s. We set aside the others, therefore, and posit one most beautiful among the many triangles, from which an equilateral triangle is constructed from three parts <note>original: "ex tertio" — likely referring to the 30-60-90 triangle which, when doubled, forms an equilateral triangle.</note>. The reason why this is so would be

<margin>E</margin>

rather long to explain. But for him who finds it to be so by diligent investigation, a sweet prize of victory awaits. Let there be proposed to us, then, two triangles from among many, out of which the bodies of fire and the rest are composed. One of these is the Isosceles, consisting of equal sides. The other is that which always has its longer side three times greater in power <note>original: "potentia triplo maius" — in geometry, "power" refers to the square of the side. A 30-60-90 triangle has sides in ratio 1 : √3 : 2; the square of √3 is 3.</note> than the shorter side. But what we said too carelessly in the previous section must now be more clearly distinguished. It seemed to us—and not quite correctly—that all four genera were generated from one another in turn. In truth, the four genera are generated from the triangles we have chosen. Three of them indeed come from the one having unequal sides <note>Fire, Air, and Water.</note>. But the fourth unique genus

<margin>F</margin>

is composed from the Isosceles triangle <note>Earth.</note>. Therefore, it is not possible for all of them to be so resolved and changed into each other that a few large things are made from many small ones, or the reverse. Three of them certainly can be. For since all these are made from one type, when the larger ones are dissolved, many small ones are formed from them, having obtained small and fitting shapes for themselves. Again, when many small ones are dispersed through their triangles and amplified, they make the number of a single mass, and they complete another single great species. Let these things be said thus far concerning their mutual generation. It remains for us to say what kind of species each of them has become, and from what concurrent numbers they have been accumulated. There will be, then, a first species, which has been composed of the fewest parts;

<margin>G</margin>

its element is that triangle which has its longer side twice as large as its shorter side <note>Referring to the hypotenuse being twice the length of the shortest side in a 30-60-90 triangle.</note>. When two of this kind are joined across a diameter, and this is done three times, and the shorter sides of the diameters are led to the same point as a center, one equilateral triangle is finished from six triangles in number. Then, four equilateral triangles composed according to three plane angles make one solid angle; this follows in birth immediately after the most obtuse of all plane angles. And when four such solid angles have been born, the first solid species <note>The Tetrahedron, which represents Fire.</note> arises, capable of distributing the whole circumference into equal and similar parts.

<margin>H</margin>

The second species indeed is made from the same triangles, but constructed according to eight equilateral triangles, making one solid angle from four planes; and six such angles being made, the second body <note>The Octahedron, representing Air.</note> is completed. And the third is born from twice sixty elements joined together, and twelve solid angles, each of which is contained by five plane equilateral triangles, having twenty equilateral bases <note>The Icosahedron, representing Water.</note>. Now, one of the elements has thus far produced these things. But the Isosceles triangle generated the nature of the fourth genus, being arranged according to four triangles, and bringing the right angles together at the center, making one equilateral quadrangle <note>A square.</note>. Six of these joined together produced eight solid angles, each of which is fitted together by three plane right angles. The shape of the body

<column-break/>

Indeed, these things which, having been ordered, will be known. And before this, all these things were held without reason and without measure. But when the whole was first attempted to be ordered, fire first, and earth, and air, and water—having certain traces of themselves—were altogether in such a condition as it is likely for everything to have when God is absent from it. Being such by nature at that time, he first shaped them with forms and numbers. And that God composed them to be as beautiful and as excellent as possible from things that were not so, let this be laid down by us as a saying always to be maintained. Now, therefore, we must attempt to tell you the arrangement and generation of each of them by an unusual <note>original: "ἀήθει" — unaccustomed or strange.</note> argument. But because you participate in those paths of education through which the things being said are necessarily demonstrated, you will follow. First, indeed, it is surely clear to everyone that fire and earth and water and air are bodies. Every form of body also has depth. And it is an absolute necessity that depth should encompass a plane nature. The straightness of the plane base is composed of triangles. All triangles begin from two types, each having one right angle and two acute angles. Of these, one part has on either side a portion of a right angle, divided by equal sides; the other part has unequal portions distributed to unequal sides. This we posit as the beginning of fire and the other bodies, proceeding according to the likely account joined with necessity. But the principles of these from further above are known to God, and to whichever of men is a friend to him. It must be said what four most beautiful bodies might be made, which are dissimilar to themselves but able to be generated from one another when some of them are dissolved. For if we attain this, we have the truth of generation concerning earth and fire, and the things that are in the middle according to proportion. For then we will concede to no one that there are more beautiful bodies to be seen than these, each existing as a single genus. We must therefore be eager to fit together the four genera of bodies that differ in beauty, and to say that we have sufficiently grasped their nature. Of the two triangles, the Isosceles has been allotted one nature, but the Scalene <term>Scalene <note>A triangle with three unequal sides.</note></term> has infinite natures. We must choose again the most beautiful of the infinite, if we are to begin in an orderly way. If, then, anyone is able to speak having chosen a more beautiful one for the composition of these, he, being not an enemy but a friend, prevails. We posit, then, one most beautiful among the many triangles, passing over the others, out of which the equilateral triangle is constructed from three parts. The reason why is a longer story. But for him who tests this and finds it to be not so, the prizes of friendship lie as his reward. Let two triangles be chosen, out of which the body of fire and the other bodies have been manufactured: one, the Isosceles; the other, that which always has the longer side triple in power to the lesser. But what was not securely stated before must now be more clearly defined. For all four genera appeared to have generation into one another, but this was not correctly imagined. For four genera are produced from the triangles we have chosen: three from the one having unequal sides, but the fourth alone is fitted together from the Isosceles triangle. Therefore, not all are able, when dissolved into one another, to become a few large things from many small ones, and the reverse. But some are able. For as many as are born from one, when the larger ones are dissolved, many small ones are composed from the same parts, receiving the shapes appropriate to them; and again, when many small ones are scattered according to triangles, becoming one number, they might complete another single large form of one mass. Let these things be said concerning their nature into one another. Next, it would be for us to say what kind of form each of them has become, and from what numbers falling together. The first form and smallest to be composed shall lead the way. Its element is that which has the hypotenuse twice the length of the lesser side. When two of these are joined together across a diameter, and this happens three times, and they lean the diameters and the short sides into the same point as a center, one equilateral triangle has been made out of six in number. When four equilateral triangles are composed, they make one solid angle at every three plane angles, which is born following the most obtuse of plane angles. When four such angles are completed, the first solid form <note>The Tetrahedron.</note>, which is distributive of the whole circumference into equal and similar parts, is composed. The second is from the same triangles, but composed according to eight equilateral triangles, having worked out one solid angle from four planes; and six such being made, the second body was thus finished. The third is from twice sixty of the elements joined together, with twelve solid angles, each being encompassed by five plane equilateral triangles, and it has become a thing having twenty equilateral bases. And the one part of the elements was done with these, having generated them. But the Isosceles triangle brought forth the nature of the fourth, being composed according to four, bringing the right angles together into the center, and working out one equilateral quadrangle. Six such being joined together completed eight solid angles, each being fitted together according to three plane right angles. The shape of the composed body...

-># TIMAEUS. #<-

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> <note>Plato is describing the dodecahedron, the fifth solid, which represents the cosmos itself.</note> of the body, it became an image, having been composed of an equilateral square base. Furthermore, there being a certain fifth composition, God used it for the whole, painting it as a representation of the universe. If anyone, considering these things carefully, wonders whether one should say there are infinite worlds or a finite number, he would think that believing in infinite worlds belongs to someone truly unlearned in matters where experience is required. But whether it is right to say there is one world or five is a more reasonable question. Our argument indeed indicates that there is one world naturally formed according to a likely account; but another person, looking elsewhere, will think otherwise. These matters, however, we must let pass. But we must now distribute the things that have come into being in our discourse into fire, earth, water, and air. To earth let us give the cubic form. For <margin>B</margin> of the four kinds, earth is the most immobile, and of bodies, it is the most plastic <note>original: "πλαστικωτάτη" (plastikōtatē) — meaning the most capable of being molded or shaped, like clay.</note>. It is most necessary that such a thing be that which possesses the most stable bases. Of the triangles we laid down at the beginning, the base of the equilateral ones is naturally more stable than that of the unequal ones; and the square surface composed of each, being equilateral, necessarily stands more firmly than a triangle, both in its parts and as a whole. Therefore, by assigning this to earth, we preserve the likely account. To water, in turn, we give the least mobile form; <margin>C</margin> to fire, the most mobile; and to air, the middle. And the smallest body we give to fire; the largest to water; and the middle to air. Again, the sharpest form to fire; the second to air; and the third to water. Now, of all these, that which has the fewest bases must necessarily be the most mobile <note>Plato means the tetrahedron (pyramid), which has only four faces.</note>, as well as the most cutting and the sharpest of all in every way; and also the lightest, being composed of the fewest identical parts. The second must have these qualities in the second degree, and the third in the third. Let it be then, according to right reason and the likely account, that the solid form of the pyramid is the element and seed of fire; the second according to its generation we call air; and the third, water. All these must be imagined as being so small that for each individual part of each kind, <margin>D</margin> nothing is seen by us because of its smallness; but when many are gathered together, their masses are seen. And indeed, God harmonized these in proportion everywhere, regarding their quantities, motions, and other powers, exactly as the nature of Necessity, being willingly persuaded, yielded; in this way, he finished them all with accuracy. From all these kinds which we have previously mentioned, things would most likely be as follows: Earth, meeting with fire and being dissolved by its sharpness, would be carried about, whether it were dissolved in fire itself, or in a mass of air or water, until its parts, meeting somewhere and being harmonized again with themselves, become earth again. For they could never <margin>E</margin> pass into another form. But water, being divided by fire or even by air, can become, when its parts are reorganized, one body of fire and two of air. And the segments of air from one dissolved part could become two bodies of fire. And again, when fire is caught in air or water or some earth, being a small amount moving in many, and is crushed while fighting in those moving things, two bodies of fire are combined into one form of air; and if air is conquered and broken into small pieces, from two whole parts and a half, one whole form of water will be compacted. Let us reason about them again in this way: whenever one of the other kinds is caught in fire and is cut by the sharpness of its angles and sides, <margin>F</margin> it stops being cut only when it has entirely turned into the nature of fire. For a thing that is similar and identical to itself cannot cause any change in, nor suffer anything from, that which is in the same state as itself; but as long as it is becoming something else and is weaker while fighting a stronger, it does not stop being dissolved. Again, when fewer small things are caught in many larger ones and are torn apart and extinguished, if they are willing to be composed into the idea of the victor, they stop being extinguished; and so fire becomes air, and air becomes water. But if they go into these or any other of the kinds and fight, they do not stop being dissolved until either, being entirely pushed and dissolved, they escape to their kindred, or being conquered, they become one similar to the victor and remain as a fellow-dweller with it. And indeed, <margin>G</margin> through these sufferings, they all change their places. For the masses of each kind are kept separate in their own place by the motion of the receiver; but the things that become unlike are carried by the shaking toward the place of those things they have been made like. Thus, as many as are pure and primary bodies were created through such causes. But that other kinds are produced within their forms must be attributed to the composition of each of the elements: for the original growth did not produce a triangle of only one size for each, but smaller and larger ones, as many in number as there are kinds within the forms. Therefore, when these are mixed with themselves and with one another, there is an infinite variety, <margin>H</margin> which those who intend to be observers of nature must use in their likely account. Now, concerning motion and composition, in what way and with what things they came to be, if one does not reach an agreement, there would be much to <note>Original Latin note: "ta [the catchword below] seems likely to be an impediment to the discussion that remains on the back." This refers to a printing error where the catchword 'ta' doesn't match the next page perfectly.</note> hinder the subsequent reasoning. These things have now been mostly said; but let us follow those and come to these: it is agreed that motion never wishes to exist...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Thus constituted, the cubic figure was made, having obtained six equilateral square bases. There is also a certain fifth composition, which God used for the constitution of the universe, and with it he described and figured it. Looking at this, someone might not absurdly doubt whether one should think there are infinite worlds or finite ones: to say they are infinite he will think belongs to one who has no skill or knowledge worthy of things. But to inquire whether one world or five have truly been born, he will think is less absurd. Our reason indeed asserts by a probable proof that one world was born. But another person, looking to other things, will think otherwise. But these matters are to be dismissed. And now <margin>B</margin> the four kinds recently arranged by us, let us distribute into fire, earth, water, and air. To earth let us assign the cubic species. For of all four, earth is the most immobile, and of all bodily things, the most firmly compacted. And it is necessary that such a thing be produced especially because it possesses the firmest and safest bases. Furthermore, among the triangles placed from the beginning, those that are equilateral possess a firmer and safer base than the scalene ones. And the plane square composed of equilateral triangles is certainly necessarily more stable than a triangle, both as to the whole and as to the parts. Wherefore, if we wish to follow a convenient and probable reason, <margin>C</margin> let us attribute this to earth: then to water, that which is more immobile than the remaining three: to fire, that which is most mobile: to air, the middle. And the smallest body to fire, the largest to water, the middle to air: also the sharpest to fire, the second from this to air, the third to water. From all these, that which has the fewest bases must necessarily be the most rapid. For it is the most ready for penetrating, since it is truly the sharpest of all. Also the lightest, since it consists of the fewest parts of the same kind. That which is second must have these qualities in the second place. The third in the third. Therefore, according to right and probable reason, let the solid species of the pyramid be the element and seed of fire. The second species in generation let us give to air, the third to water. Concerning all these <margin>D</margin> things so small, it must be thought that if individual parts of individual kinds are taken, none of them can be seen by us because of their smallness: but if many are gathered together, their masses and magnitudes are seen. Moreover, all these things were connected by God everywhere with such proportion regarding their quantities, motions, and powers, exactly as the nature of Necessity, being willing and persuaded, could receive. From all those whose kinds we have narrated above, the matter seems to hold itself thus by merit. Earth, when it falls into fire, being dissolved by its sharpness, is carried about, resolved into fire, or air, or water, until its parts, gathered again and joined to one another, <margin>E</margin> rebuild the earth. For it would never migrate into another species. Water, moreover, divided into parts by fire or air, makes, when its parts are reconciled, one body of fire and two of air: but portions of air from one dissolved part make two bodies of fire. Again, when fire is occupied by air or water or some earth, and it being few is moved among many, and fights in those that are agitated, and being tossed is distracted, the bodies of fire will convert into one species of air: then when air is overcome and dispersed, from two whole parts and a half, one whole species of water coalesces. Finally, let us consider them again thus: as often as any other kind is caught by fire and is cut by the sharpness of its angles and sides, <margin>F</margin> it then finally ceases to be dispersed when it has passed into the nature of fire. For no kind suffers anything from a similar and identical kind; but as long as it is changed into another, and being weaker struggles with a more powerful one, it does not cease to be dissolved. Again, when smaller things are surrounded by many larger ones, and being few and torn apart they are extinguished, when they wish to be established in the idea of the victor, they cease to be extinguished, and air is made from fire, and water from air. But if a transition is made into these, and some other kind attacks, they do not cease to be dissolved while agitated, until either they are completely dissolved and flee to their kin, or being conquered <margin>G</margin> they finally turn into one thing similar to the victor and remain familiarly with the conqueror. Indeed, through these passions, they all change their seats in turn. For the multitudes of any kind are distinguished by their own place, because of the agitation of the receptacle itself. But those things which have become unlike each other are carried, because of the wave and concussion, to the place of those they have become like. Therefore, unmixed and primary bodies were fabricated from causes of this sort. But that other kinds are innate in their species is because of the constitution of each element, which from the beginning brought forth not only one triangle with one magnitude, but also larger and smaller ones, as many in number as there are kinds in the species. Wherefore, these mixed in themselves and with one another <margin>H</margin> have infinite variety: of which those who are to give a probable reason for nature ought to be experts. Therefore, unless one certainly understands in what way and with what things motion and constitution occur, much has been said of one part, but much remains to be said. In itself...

<summary>This page details the geometric "atomism" of Plato's Timaeus, assigning the five Platonic solids to the elements (Earth as cube, Fire as pyramid, etc.) and explaining how they can break apart and transform into one another.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the physical elements and their properties. The previous page established the geometric forms of earth (the cube) and the other elements. Here, Timaeus discusses the mechanics of motion, the compression of matter, and the specific varieties of fire, air, and water—including the formation of metals like gold and copper, and meteorological phenomena like hail and snow.</meta>

-># 538 OF PLATO #<-

<column-break/>

Motion never tends to arise from nature alone. For it is difficult, or rather impossible, to find that which is to be moved without a mover, or a mover without that which is to be moved. Motion is the least present in these things <note>referring to the state of balance</note>. Indeed, these things can never be smooth and level. Thus, we shall always place rest in uniformity and smoothness, and motion, on the contrary, in nature's inequality. Furthermore, inequality is the cause of this nature, which is the opposite of the smooth and level. We have already discussed the generation of inequality. But in what way the individual elements, according to their kinds, do not cease to be moved and carried through one another once they are divided, we have by no means explained. Therefore, we shall explain it next as follows.

The circuit of the entire nature, since it has embraced all kinds in its circular span and strives to unite with itself, constrains all things and allows no empty space to be left anywhere. On this account, fire has penetrated most through all things, then air, as it is closest to fire in its thinness, and the others follow in similar fashion. For those things composed of the largest parts leave the greatest vacuum in their constitution, while the smallest leave the least. The pressure of this compression thrusts the small parts into the voids of the large ones. Therefore, when the small are worked into the large, and the small parts themselves separate the large, while the larger ones coerce the smaller, all are carried up or down into their own places. For anything changes its seat when its magnitude is altered.

Thus, for these reasons, the generation of the nature contrary to smoothness is always preserved, exhibiting a perpetual motion of these things both in the present and the future. After this, it must be known that there are many <margin>Many kinds of fire.</margin> kinds of fire: namely, flame; and that which is kindled by it, which burns indeed but brings no light to the eyes; and that which remains within the things that were kindled after the flame is extinguished. Similarly, of the <margin>Many kinds of air.</margin> genus of air, one is the purest and most agile, which they call <term>aether<note>The "upper air" or fifth element, thought by the Greeks to be what the gods breathe and what fills space.</note></term>; another is the most turbulent, obscured by mist and clouds; and other species must be thought to exist without names, due to the inequality of the <term>triangles<note>Plato’s theory posits that the elements are composed of microscopic geometric triangles.</note></term>. There are two principal <margin>The generations of metals and adamant.</margin> kinds of water. One is liquid, the other is fusible <note>original: "fusile" — meaning "meltable," referring to metals.</note>. The liquid kind, because it consists of small and unequal types of water, is easily moved by itself and by others due to the condition of its inequality and the appearance of its shape. But that which is composed of larger, equal, and smooth parts is more stable than the former. It is compact and heavy due to its smooth equality, but because of the onset of fire penetrating and dissolving it, it loses its equality and partakes in motion. Having become agile and mobile, pushed by the neighboring air and spread through the earth, it undergoes two things: it liquefies and falls into the earth. The first is called the purging of the mass, the latter is called flowing. Again, as the fire flies out from there—since there is no exit into a vacuum—the neighboring air pushes the still mobile liquid mass into the seats of the fire and mixes it with itself. Finally, the mass, being compressed and having again obtained smooth equality (since the fire, the architect of inequality, has now departed), gathers itself into the same state. We call the departure of fire "cooling," and the bond and meeting that occurs when the fire leaves, we call "congealing" and "icy rigidity."

Of these waters we have called fusible, that which becomes most dense from the thinnest and smoothest parts—uniform, splendid, and yellow—is a most precious thing: gold, which has been compacted through rock as it flourished. But a branch of gold, which is the hardest due to its density and is also tinged with a black color, is called <term>adamant<note>original: "adamas" — likely referring here to a dark, ultra-hard mineral or perhaps hematite, though often translated as diamond.</note></term>. But that which has parts close to gold, but contains more than one species and is denser than gold, partaking of a small and thin portion of earth so that it is harsher and harder, but lighter because it has large intervals inside—this is one kind of shining, congealed waters, and it is named copper. But when the earthy part mixed with it is separated from its other parts due to age, and being sent to the outer surface becomes visible by itself, rust is then born. It is by no means laborious to pursue the rest of this kind through likely reasoning. For if someone, for the sake of relaxing his study, sets aside the reasoning of those things which are eternal and considers the likely proofs concerning generation, and is delighted by such consideration without any regret, he will achieve a moderate and wise play in life.

Having granted these things now, those which seem probable concerning the same matters should be run through as follows. A thin part of water is often mixed with fire; it is liquid and fluid, so named because it flows around the slippery earth, and is also soft for the reason that its bases, being less firm and stable than those of earth, easily yield and slide. When this water is deprived of fire and deserted by air, it becomes more uniform and is forced into itself by the expulsion of the foreign parts. Thus compacted, if this happens above the earth, it becomes hail; if on the earth, ice. These things occur when it is frozen and coheres most greatly by cold; but when it is less frozen, if it happens above the earth, it is snow; if on the earth, having become thicker from dew, it is called frost. But when many species of water are mixed together, another entire genus straining from the earth through trees is called liquor or humor. Because of the dissimilarity of the mixture, the individual liquors produce many other kinds without names, but four fiery species, being most evident and clear, have obtained names. That which warms the soul along with the body is called wine.

<column-break/>

...that there is motion. For it is difficult, or rather impossible, for that which is to be moved to exist without that which will move it, or the mover without that which is to be moved. It is impossible for motion to exist when these things are absent, or for these things ever to be uniform. Thus, let us always place rest in uniformity and motion in non-uniformity. The cause of the non-uniform nature is, again, inequality. We have already analyzed the generation of inequality; but how it is that each of these, having been separated into their kinds, have not ceased their motion and passage through one another, we have not yet said. Thus, we shall speak again. The revolution of the whole, since it has embraced the kinds, being circular and naturally tending to want to come together with itself, squeezes everything and allows no empty space to be left. Therefore, fire has permeated through all things most of all, and air second, as it is second in thinness; and the others in this way. For the things made of the largest parts have left the largest emptiness in their composition, and the smallest, the least. The meeting of the compression pushes the small things into the gaps of the large ones. Therefore, when the small are placed beside the large, and the smaller ones divide the larger, and the larger ones compress the smaller, all are carried up and down toward their own places. For each thing, changing its size, also changes the position of its places. In this way and for these reasons, the generation of inequality being preserved always provides the motion that these things have, both now and in the future, continually.

After these things, one must realize that many kinds of fire have been produced: such as flame, and that which comes from flame, which does not burn but provides light to the eyes, and that which is left of the fire itself in the glowing embers after the flame has been extinguished. In the same way, of air, there is the most translucent kind, called by the name aether; and the most turbid, mist and darkness. And there are other nameless species produced through the inequality of the triangles. Of water, there are first two kinds: the liquid and the fusible kind. The liquid kind, because it partakes of the kinds of water that are small, is mobile, both by itself and by another, because of the inequality and the idea of its shape; but that which is made of large and uniform parts is more stable than that and heavy, being compacted by uniformity. But when fire enters and dissolves it, losing its uniformity, it partakes more of motion; and having become immobile <note>The Greek text "ἀκινήτου" (immobile) here seems to contrast with the Latin "agile," though the context suggests the transition to a fluid state</note>, being pushed by the neighboring air and spread out upon the earth, it is said to melt (the reduction of the mass) and to flow (the movement toward a state on the earth); each name was taken from the experience. Again, as the fire falls out from there, since it does not go out into a vacuum, the neighboring air is pushed, thrusting the still liquid mass into the seats of the fire and mixing it with itself. The mass, being pushed together and regaining its uniformity—since the fire, the craftsman of inequality, is absent—settles into the same state as itself. The departure of the fire is called cooling; and the coming together after it has gone, being a congealed kind, is so named.

Of all these which we have called fusible waters, that which becomes densest from the thinnest and most uniform parts, a unique kind, shared with the glint of a yellow color, is a most highly valued possession: gold, which was solidified as it was filtered through rock. And a shoot of gold, which is very hard because of its density and is black, was called adamant. That which is close to gold in its parts, but has more species, being denser than gold in its density, and partaking of a small and thin portion of earth so as to be harder; but having large gaps within itself, it is lighter; this shining, congealed kind of water is copper. And the part from the earth mixed with it, when they are separated from one another again as it grows old, becoming visible by itself, is called rust. It is no longer complicated to reason out the other such things, following the form of likely myths; whenever someone, for the sake of rest, sets aside the arguments concerning eternal things and pursues the likely accounts concerning generation, he acquires a pleasure that brings no regret, making for himself a moderate and wise play in his life. Letting this be so now, we shall go through the likely accounts of these things in order. The water mixed with fire, as much as is thin and liquid, is called liquid because of its motion and the way it rolls upon the earth; and again it is soft because its bases are less stable than those of earth, so it yields. When this is separated from fire and isolated from air, it becomes more uniform and is compressed by the departure of those things into itself. Being thus frozen, that which suffers this most above the earth is hail; and on the earth, ice; and that which is less so, being half-frozen above the earth, is snow; and that which is compacted upon the earth from dew is called frost. Most species of water mixed with one another, the whole kind being filtered through the plants from the earth, are called juices; because of the mixtures having the dissimilarity of each, they provide many other nameless kinds, but four fiery species, becoming most transparent, have received their names: that which warms the soul along with the body [is wine]...

<summary>Timaeus explains that motion is caused by physical inequality and the constant compression of the universe, which prevents a vacuum. He then categorizes various states of matter, describing how metals like gold and copper are "fusible water" and how weather patterns like snow and hail are formed by the interaction of elements.</summary>

<keywords>Timaeus, Plato, physics, elements, motion, inequality, vacuum, fire, aether, water, gold, copper, rust, hail, ice, snow, frost, wine</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discourse of Timaeus regarding the composition of the physical world. Following the discussion on the motion of elements and the pressure of the cosmic sphere from the previous page, the text now classifies specific substances—oils, stones, salts, and clays—based on their elemental mixtures. It then transitions into the physiological explanation of sensations, specifically how the geometric shapes of elements interact with the human body to produce feelings of heat, cold, hardness, and softness.</meta>

-># TIMAEUS. TIMAEUS. #<-

<column-break/>

That which is smooth and disperses the sight, and is therefore bright and glistening to the eye, appearing as an oily form, is pitch, castor oil <note>original: "kiki"</note>, and oil itself, and all other things of the same power. But that which, through its fluidity, penetrates the narrow passages of the mouth to the very seat of nature, and by this power provides sweetness, is commonly called honey. Finally, that which dissolves the flesh by its sharpness, a foamy kind separated from all juices by its fermentation, is named sap <note>original: "chymosis"</note>. Of the types of earth, that which emerges through water in this way becomes a stony body. For when the condensed water is diminished in the mixture, it passes into the form of air; this air then returns to its own place, but as there was no vacuum within them, it pushes the neighboring air. If this air is heavy, it is pushed and poured around the mass of earth, crushing it vehemently and driving it into the seats from which the new air ascended. Thus, earth compacted by air so that it cannot be dissolved by water forms stones; the more beautiful ones are those that shine transparently from equal and smooth parts, while the base ones are the opposite. But when all moisture is snatched away by the sharpness of fire, and the body is rendered more brittle than before, that species remains which is named pottery <note>original: "keramon"</note>. Sometimes, when moisture is left behind and the earth becomes fusible through fire, and then black stone is formed when it is cooled. But when that same substance, in a similar way, is deprived of much moisture from a mixture, but consists of finer parts of earth and is salty, becoming semi-solid and emerging through water, it is called <term>nitrum<note>A naturally occurring mineral soda (natron) used for cleaning, not modern chemical nitrogen.</note></term>, a kind that purifies oil and earth; and that which is most suitable for the common needs of daily life, according to right reason and law, is salt, a body dear to the gods. But as for those things common to both, they are not soluble by water, but are so bonded by fire for such a reason. Fire and air do not liquefy the masses of earth. For since these two are the thinnest and smaller than the voids of the earth, they pass through its most capacious passages without any violence, so that they neither dissolve nor liquefy it. But the parts of water, because they are larger, cause liquefaction by a violent flow. Thus water alone dissolves earth that is poorly compacted, but only fire dissolves it when it is well compacted; for nothing except fire can penetrate it. Again, regarding the condensation of water, only fire dissolves the most violent kind, but both fire and air dissolve the weaker kind—air through the voids, and fire even through the <term>triangles<note>Plato theorized that the elements were composed of microscopic geometric shapes (triangles) that fit together.</note></term>. But nothing dissolves air that is violently constricted except through its own element; fire alone dissolves that which coheres without violence. Bodies composed of water and earth are so arranged that as long as water occupies the constricted voids of the earth, parts of water coming from outside cannot enter, and thus do not liquefy it; but the parts of fire, entering the passages of the water—just as water enters the earth—and affecting the water as fire affects air, cause the common body to flow. These substances partly contain less water than earth, such as the whole genus of glass and those stones called fusible; and partly they contain more water, such as all those things that are compacted into wax-like bodies and emit vapors. Thus far, we have nearly demonstrated those species which vary by shapes, combinations, and mutual changes; we shall next attempt to show for what reasons their sensations <note>original: "passiones"</note> arise. First, there must always be a sense present in what is said. But we have not yet explained the generation of the flesh and what pertains to the flesh, nor the mortal part of the soul. For these things cannot be sufficiently explained without the sensations, nor the sensations without these; yet it is nearly impossible to explain both at once. Therefore, one must be assumed first, and the other discussed later. So that the sensations may follow the kinds in order, let those things pertaining to the body and soul stand first. First, then, let us see in what way fire is called hot; we shall perceive this if we consider the separation and cutting made by it in our body. For that this sensation is a certain sharpness is manifest to nearly everyone. But we must consider the thinness of its angles, the sharpness of its sides, the smallness of its particles, and the velocity of its motion—by all of which it is vehement and penetrating, always quickly cutting and dissipating whatever it encounters—recalling the generation of its shape. For that nature, and no other, dividing our bodies and paring them into small parts, rightly induces that sensation which is properly named heat. The sensation contrary to this, though manifest to all, should not lack its own explanation. For the moist parts of bodies larger than our own, when they flow into the body, push out the smaller parts, but cannot enter their seats; instead, they coagulate our moisture, and from being unequal and agitated, they make it immobile through equality and contraction, forcing it into a narrow space. But that which is contracted against nature, according to nature resists and pulls itself back in the opposite direction. In this struggle and shaking, trembling and shivering consist; and this entire sensation is called cold, and that which causes it is named "the cold." We call "hard" that to which our flesh yields, and "soft" that which yields to the flesh; and we name things hard and soft in relation to each other in the same way. Whatever rests on a small base yields. But that which is made of square <note>Referring to the cubic shape of earth.</note> bases and firmaments, being very firmly set, is the most resistant form; and whatever is extremely dense, vehemently resists anything coming against it.

<meta>This page continues the discourse of Timaeus regarding the composition of the physical world. Following the discussion on the chemical and elemental nature of substances like oils and stones, the text transitions into a physical and philosophical analysis of weight and direction. It challenges the common understanding of "up" and "down" by applying the logic of a spherical universe, eventually moving into the physiological causes of sensory perception, specifically pleasure and pain.</meta>

-># OF PLATO #<-

...rebounds. Moreover, the nature of heavy and light, together with that which is called <margin>Upward and downward</margin> upward and downward, will be most conveniently explained. However, it is an absurd thing to say that there are two places in nature distinct from each other by a great distance: one called "downward," to which all things possessing a certain bodily mass are carried, and another called "upward," toward which all things are moved by force. For since the entire heaven is round, all the extremities, being equally distant from the center, must be extremities in the same way. The center also, being at an equal distance from the extremities in all directions by equal lines, looks toward all of them equally from its region. Since, therefore, the world is arranged in this way, if anyone says that any of these parts are "up" or "down," he will be seen to err, and not without reason. **A** For the middle place in it ought to be called neither upward nor downward, but the center. That which, in turn, circles around it in every direction is neither the middle, **B** nor does it have one part differing from another in relation to the center or anything located in the opposite region. Indeed, no one would rightly attribute contrary names to that which is most similar to itself. For if there were something solid and balanced in the center of the universe, it would not incline toward any part of the extremities because of their perfect similarity; but if someone were to walk around it, he would often stand with his feet opposite <note>original: "plantis oppositis", referring to the concept of the Antipodes, or people living on the opposite side of the globe</note> his previous position, and he would call the same part of it now "upward" and now "downward." Therefore, since the universe is round, as we said a little while ago, a wise man will by no means affirm that it has a "superior" or "inferior" place. **C** But let us investigate where these names come from and in what context we have observed them so as to transfer them to the whole world. Suppose someone were to reside in that region of the world which fire has obtained as its lot for the most part, and toward which fire is carried from all sides; and suppose he gained some power by which he could seize and weigh parts of the fire, or place them in the pans of a scale to drag them into the dissimilar air below. It is quite clear that a smaller portion of fire would be more easily forced than a larger one. For when two things are suspended together by a single force, the smaller yields more to the force, while the larger yields less. And one is said to be "heavy" and carried "downward," while the other is called "upward" and "light." The same thing happens to us who inhabit the earth. **D** For while standing on the earth and walking through it, we separate and distinguish types of earth from one another, and often throw earth into the dissimilar air by force and against its nature; here, a smaller portion thrown into a dissimilar place yields more quickly to the violence than a larger one, and we have named it "light," and the place toward which we compel it "upward." The contrary condition we call "heavy" and "downward." It is necessary that these should differ from each other because the masses of the elements occupy places contrary to one another. For what is light in one place is contrary to what is light in the opposite place; and similarly, heavy to heavy, and what is called downward to downward, and upward to upward. **E** For all these will be found to be transverse to each other, contrary, and entirely different. Yet one thing must be thought concerning all of them: that the path and journey of each thing toward its like and kin makes that which is carried "heavy," and the place into which it is carried "downward." Things that are otherwise produce different results. Let these be the causes mentioned for these experiences. As for the causes of <margin>On smooth and rough</margin> smooth and rough experiences, anyone who looks closely will be able to reveal them to others. For hardness mixed with inequality produces the latter, while equality combined with density produces the former. But of those experiences which happen commonly to the whole body, **F** <margin>On pleasure and pain</margin> there remains the greatest, which is the cause of pleasure and pain in the things we have discussed. Similarly, those things which are accessible to the senses through the parts of the body move both pains and pleasures. Thus, let us accept the causes of every experience, both perceptible and imperceptible, first calling to memory what we defined above concerning the nature that moves easily and that which moves with difficulty; for in this way we ought to pursue all things we desire to comprehend. When some experience, even a brief one, falls upon that which is easily moved, any part of it transfers that very experience to the following parts in every direction, until it reaches the seat of wisdom <note>original: "prudentiae sedem", the Greek uses 'phronimon', referring to the conscious or rational part of the soul/brain</note>; there, through these messengers as it were, the thing that brought the experience is recognized. **G** But that which is affected in the opposite way, and remains in some way immobile, does not have that circular transfer; it alone suffers, but does not move the nearest parts. Therefore, when the parts do not impart the first experience to one another, and the whole animal is not agitated by this, it remains devoid of sensation toward what it suffers. This certainly happens concerning the bones, the hair, and the other parts which are mostly made of earth within us. But the instruments of sight and hearing act entirely differently because the greatest power of fire and air is in them. Furthermore, as pertains to pleasure and pain, let it be considered thus: an experience brought upon us abundantly and all at once, violently and against nature, is painful. Conversely, that which returns to its nature abundantly and all at once is sweet; and the opposite is the opposite. But an experience brought with great ease is felt most strongly, yet is least a participant in pleasure and pain. Such are those things which arise from sight. We have said above that our body becomes akin to sight every day; to this, burns or cuts and any such experiences do not bring pain, nor is there pleasure when it is restored to its own form...

<column-break/>

...gathering the most density, itself where it is most [dense]; as for heavy and light, this can be shown most clearly if examined along with what is called the nature of "up" and "down." For it is not at all right to think that there are naturally two places, dividing the whole into two opposites—the one "down," to which everything is carried that has any bodily bulk, and the other "up," where everything goes only by compulsion. For since the whole heaven is spherical, all parts that are at an equal distance from the center must be extremities in the same way. The center, being distant by the same measures from the extremities, must be thought of as being opposite to all of them. **A** With the world being naturally such, if someone places anything as "up" or "down," he will not be seen to use the name justly, as it does not belong. For the middle place in it is not naturally "down" or "up," but is justly called the "middle"; **B** and the circumference is neither the middle, nor does it have one part differing from another in relation to the center more than any other part on the opposite side. To that which is naturally similar in every way, what contrary names could one apply, and how could he think he speaks well? For even if there were something solid at the center of the universe in perfect balance, it would never be carried toward any of the extremities because of its absolute similarity in every direction. But even if one were to travel around it in a circle, often standing as an antipode <term>antipodes<note>meaning those with "feet opposite" on a sphere</note></term>, he would call the same part of it "down" and "up." For the whole (as has been said) being spherical, it is not the part of a wise man to say that it has a place called "down" and another "up." **C** But where these names came from, and in what things they exist, so that we have learned to divide the whole heaven in this way—these things we must agree upon, based on our following hypotheses. If someone were in that place of the universe where the nature of fire has mostly been allotted, and where most of it would be gathered, and if he were to climb upon it or have the power to do so, taking portions of the fire and putting them into the pans of a scale, and lifting the balance-beam and dragging the fire into the dissimilar air by force, it is clear that the smaller portion is more easily forced than the larger. For when two things are raised at once by a single strength, the smaller must yield more to the force, and the larger less; and the larger is called "heavy" and "moving downward," while the small is called "light" and "upward." **D** We must detect ourselves doing this very same thing in this region. For standing on the earth, distinguishing types of earth, and sometimes dragging the earth itself into the dissimilar air by force and against nature, we cling to the kinship of the element. The smaller part yields more easily than the larger when we force it into the dissimilar; we have therefore called it "light," and the place into which we force it "upward." The opposite experience to these is "heavy" and "downward." These must necessarily differ from one another because the multitudes of the earth-like elements occupy a place opposite to each other. For what is light in one place is contrary to what is light in the opposite place, and the heavy to the heavy; the down to the down, and the up to the up. **E** All will be seen to be contrary and transverse and in every way different from each other. But this one thing must be understood about all of them: that the path of each toward its kindred element makes the thing carried "heavy," and the place toward which such a thing is carried "down"; and those things having the opposite relation are called the other names. Let these be called the causes of such experiences. Anyone could see the cause of the smooth and rough experience and be able to tell another. For hardness mixed with irregularity produces the one, while smoothness with density produces the other. **F** The greatest remaining of the experiences common to the body is the cause of pleasures and pains in those things we have gone through; and whatever things have acquired sensations through the parts of the body, and have pains and pleasures following within them. Thus, let us grasp the causes of every sensible and non-sensible experience, remembering how we distinguished the nature of what moves easily and what moves with difficulty in the preceding parts. For in this way we must pursue everything we intend to explain. For that which is naturally easy to move, when even a brief experience falls upon it, passes it on in a circle, one part to another, producing the same effect, until it comes to the thinking part <note>original: "phronimon", the mind or seat of consciousness</note> and announces the power of the thing that produced it. **G** But the opposite, being stable and not moving in any circle, only suffers the effect, but does not move what is near it. Thus, as parts do not pass it to other parts, the first experience in them remains unmoved in the whole animal, rendering the part that suffered it without sensation. These things happen regarding bones and hair and whatever other parts we have within us that are mostly of earth. But the parts before these, especially sight and hearing, act differently because there is the greatest power of fire and air in them. This is how one must think about pleasure and pain: an experience produced within us that is against nature and violent and sudden is painful; but that which returns back to nature all at once is pleasant. The opposite of these is the opposite. But that which happens quietly or entirely is without sensation and not painful, not participating in pain or pleasure—such as the experiences regarding sight itself; for it was said in the preceding parts that this body becomes akin to us daily. In this, cuts and burns and whatever else it suffers do not produce pains, nor pleasures in turn, when it returns to...

<summary>Timaeus explains that in a spherical universe, "up" and "down" are relative terms based on the movement of elements toward their kindred masses. He then defines the physiological mechanisms of pleasure and pain as violent disruptions or smooth restorations of the body's natural state.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Timaeus's explanation of the physical world, moving from the physics of weight and space to the physiology of the senses. It specifically addresses how the physical structure of elements affects the human body to produce sensations of pleasure, pain, taste, smell, and sound. It bridges the gap between the "macro" world of the four elements and the "micro" world of human perception.</meta>

-># TIMÆUS #<-

<margin>A</margin> ...the same form being absent. However, the greatest and clearest sensations occur according to how much a person is affected by them, or how they encounter and touch them. For there is no inherent violence in their composition or separation. But those bodies composed of larger parts, which yield only with difficulty to the agent and transmit their motions to the whole, possess pleasures and pains: pains when they are moved out of their natural state, and pleasures when they are restored to it again. Whatever parts undergo departures and emptyings <note>original: κενώσεις (kenoseis) - the process of being emptied of a substance</note> gradually, but receive their replenishments all at once and in great abundance—such as being unaware of the emptying but sensitive to the filling—do not provide pain to the mortal part of the soul, but rather provide the greatest pleasures. This is clearly seen in the case of sweet smells. But whatever parts are moved out of their natural state all at once, and are only with difficulty and gradually restored to the same state, produce the opposite of the former effects. <margin>B</margin> These things are evident in the case of burns and cuts to the body. We have now nearly discussed the common affections of the whole body and the names given to the things that produce them.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Next, we must try to explain, as far as we are able, the affections that occur in specific parts of our bodies, both the sensations themselves and their causes. First, we must reveal as best we can those things concerning flavors <note>original: χυμῶν (chymon) - juices or flavors</note> which we omitted previously, being specific affections of the tongue. It appears that these also, like many other things, <margin>C</margin> arise through certain contractions and separations, and they also employ roughness and smoothness more than other things. For all those earthy parts that enter through the small veins—which are like the tongue’s testing-grounds, stretching toward the heart—and fall upon the moist and tender parts of the flesh, as they melt down, they contract and dry the veins. If they are rougher, they appear harsh <note>original: στρυφνὰ (stryphna) - astringent, like an unripe fruit</note>; if they are less rough, they appear austere. Those things which cleanse these parts and wash away everything around the tongue, if they do so excessively and fasten upon the tongue so as to melt away some of its very nature—such as the power of nitre <note>term: nitre — a naturally occurring mineral (sodium carbonate/soda), used here as a cleansing agent</note>—are all called bitter. Those things that are less potent than the nitre-like quality and cleanse with moderation appear salty to us, without a harsh bitterness, and are rather more agreeable. Those things that share in the body's heat <margin>D</margin> and are smoothed by it, becoming inflamed and in turn burning the part that heated them, and being carried upward by their lightness toward the senses of the head, cutting through everything they encounter by these powers—all such things are called pungent. But when these same parts have been refined by decay and enter into the narrow veins, and find there earthy parts and parts of air in proper proportion, so that they cause them to move and swirl around one another, and as they swirl they fall upon each other and enter into different parts, creating hollows that stretch out around the entering parts; these, when a moist film of air is stretched out (sometimes earthy, sometimes pure), become moist vessels of air—hollow and round waters. Those made of pure air are transparent and are called <margin>E</margin> bubbles <note>original: πομφόλυγας (pompholyges)</note>; but those made of the earthy moisture, being moved and raised up together, are called boiling and fermentation. The cause of all these affections is named acidic. An affection contrary to all these described things arises from a contrary cause: whenever the composition of the parts entering in liquids is naturally suited to the condition of the tongue, it smooths and oils the parts that were roughened, and it relaxes or contracts those that were unnaturally constricted or dispersed. In short, it settles everything back into its natural state; such a remedy for violent <margin>F</margin> affections is pleasant and agreeable to everyone, and is called sweet. So much for these things. Concerning the power of the nostrils, there are no distinct types. For the whole nature of smells is <term>half-formed</term> <note>Plato argues that smells are transitional states between air and water, and thus lack the distinct "forms" that the four primary elements possess</note>. No element has a proportion suited to having a particular smell. Rather, our veins in these parts are too narrow for the types of earth and water, but too wide for those of fire and air. Because of this, no one ever perceives an odor of any of those elements themselves, but odors always arise from things being moistened, or rotting, or melting, or evaporating. For they arise in the middle state, when water is changing into air or air into water. All smells are either smoke or mist. Of these, the transition from air to water is mist; that from water to air is smoke. From this it follows that all smells are <margin>G</margin> thinner than water, but thicker than air. This is clearly shown whenever someone's breath is obstructed and they draw in the air by force; then, no smell is filtered through, but the breath, stripped of the smell, follows alone. For these reasons, the various complexities of these things have no names, as they are not composed of many or simple types; rather, let them be called only by the two distinct names of pleasant and painful. The one disturbs and acts violently upon the whole cavity of the body that lies between the top of the head and the navel; the other soothes this same part and restore it with love to its natural state. Third, we must consider the sensory part within us concerning hearing, and we must <margin>H</margin> explain the causes through which its affections occur. In general, let us define sound as a stroke <note>original: πληγή (plege) - a blow or impact</note> transmitted by the air, through the ears, the brain, and the blood, as far as the soul. And the motion caused by it, beginning from the head and ending in the seat...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...pleasure. However, strong and clear senses belong to it insofar as it suffers something, or encounters and touches something. For no violence at all exists in this separation or composition. But bodies constituted from larger parts, which yield only with difficulty to the agent, when they transmit the motions brought upon them to the whole body, contain both pleasures and pains: when, to be sure, they are moved out of their state, they are pains; when they return, they are pleasures. Whatever parts suffer their own departures and emptyings gradually, but their replenishments all at once and abundantly, although they have no sense of the emptying, they do have a sense of the replenishment. Because of the mortality of that power, they bring no pains, but <margin>B</margin> the greatest pleasures. This is known from the perception of sweet odors. And those things which are driven out from their nature all at once and abundantly, but are only gradually and with difficulty restored to it, are affected in a manner contrary to those mentioned above. This is clearly seen in the cutting and burning of limbs. Now we have discussed the common passions of the whole body and the names of those things that bring them about. Now, therefore, let us explain according to our strength those things that happen to specific parts of our body, from where they arise, and by what causes they are brought about. First, those things which we left behind earlier when we were dealing with the humors, since they are affections of the tongue, let us declare them in whatever way we can. They seem, moreover, <margin>C</margin> to occur just like many other things by certain separations and compositions, and furthermore to employ smoothness and roughness more than other things. Veins are stretched from the tongue to the seat of the heart, as messengers of flavors: if anything falls into these so as to penetrate the moist softness of the flesh and, being somewhat liquefied by its earthy nature, they contract and dry those veins, they produce flavors of this kind. To be sure, if they are rougher, they are "acerbic" and "sharp"; but if they are less rough, they are "austere." Those things which both purge the veins and, if anything clings to the tongue, wash it away—if they do this beyond measure and liquefy something of the nature itself, such as is the power in nitre—are all named bitter. But if they have a power more tempered than nitre and wipe away more gently, they appear salty to us without the roughness of bitterness, and more friendly. Those things, however, which are applied to the heat of the mouth and are <margin>D</margin> softened and made to glow by it, in turn make the mouth itself glow, and by their lightness are raised upward to the senses of the head, and by their attraction divide each thing, because of these kinds of powers they are called "acute" or "sharp." Sometimes, moreover, these same things, having been thinned out by putrefaction, enter the narrow veins and compel the interior parts—both the earthy and in some way the airy—to be mixed together as they are tossed about, and once mixed to circulate, some entering others; and by their entry they cause the penetrated parts to become hollow and distended, where the moisture surrounds the air in a hollow and bubble-like way. This moisture is sometimes earthy in whatever way, and sometimes pure, and a moist and clear vessel of air is made from the hollow water. <margin>E</margin> But that which is born from pure water is transparent on all sides and is called a "bubble." But that which is made from a more muddy moisture, being agitated, carried along, and surrounded, is called "ebullition," "a bubble," or "fermentation." The cause of all these affections is called the "acid" quality. For all these things that have been said, a contrary affection proceeds from a contrary cause. But when the quality of the entering things is moist and naturally concordant and agreeable to the quality of the tongue, it smooths and softens it, and it soothes the contracted roughness; and those things which were contracted or scattered in us contrary to nature, it relaxes or collects, and in summary restores the natural habit to each. Everything of this kind is pleasant and <margin>F</margin> friendly to all, a medicine and remedy for violent passions, and it is called sweet. Regarding the power of the nostrils, there are no distinct species. For the nature of odors is half-formed. Indeed, it belongs to no species to have any odor. But our veins regarding these things are too narrow for the types of earth and water, but wider for the types of fire and air. On which account no one ever smelled any of those. But odors are produced in the moistening of certain things, or in putrefaction, or liquefaction, or evaporation. For when water passes into air, or air into water, odors arise in the middle of these; and every odor is either smoke or mist. But of these, that which is changed from air into water is mist; but that which is changed from water into air is smoke. Hence it happens that odors are thinner than water but thicker <margin>G</margin> than air. This becomes most clear when, some certain thing obstructing the nostrils, someone violently draws breath into himself. Then surely no odor flows in at the same time, but the breath alone follows, stripped of the odor. Therefore, these two varieties among these things are without a name, being neither from many nor from simple species; but two names only are manifest there, namely, pleasant and troublesome. The latter indeed disturbs and violates all that capacity which extends from the highest point of the head to the navel. <note>About hearing.</note> But the former soothes the same, and by a friendly entry preserves its natural habit. Furthermore, we ought to consider the third power of sensing, namely hearing, so that we may explain from what causes its affections proceed. <margin>H</margin> Therefore, let us altogether define voice as a certain pulsation from the air, penetrating through the ears, the brain, and the blood all the way to the soul. Also, the motion born from it, beginning from the head and in the seat...
