-># OF PLATO #<-

...seat of the liver, let us call it hearing. A swift motion produces a sharp <note>original: "acuta" - high-pitched</note> sound; a slow one, a deep <note>original: "grauis" - low-pitched</note> sound. A uniform and smooth motion is even, while the opposite is rough. A great motion produces a loud sound, and a small one produces a soft sound. The harmony and consonance of these sounds we shall explain in what follows.

<margin>A</margin> Next follows the fourth kind of sensation to be explained, which contains within itself a very great variety; all the things falling under it are called colors. <margin>On colors.</margin> Color is like a small flame or an effulgence emanating from individual bodies, having parts adapted to the sight for the purpose of sensing. We have previously treated the causes from which vision is produced. Now, concerning colors, it seems appropriate to speak of what is probable in this manner. Of those particles brought from other parts that fall upon the sight, some are smaller, some larger, and some are equal to the parts of the sight itself. Those that are equal cannot be felt, and are called "diaphanous" <note>original: "diaphana" - transparent</note>, that is, clear from both sides. Those that are smaller or larger, however, we say either "discern" <note>original: "discernere" - to separate or dilate</note> or "contract" the vision, just as heat and cold affect the flesh, or as those things which are pungent or sharp affect the tongue by contracting or separating it. And those things which affect the vision in this way, we call white or black; these are indeed the passions of those things I was just describing, and are in a sense kindred and the same, though they seem different in another category for these reasons.

<margin>B</margin> Thus they are to be named: that which "disaggregates" the vision is white; that which "aggregates" <note>original: "congregat" - brings together or contracts</note> it is black. Indeed, we say that fire is a sharper motion of another kind, falling upon and dispersing the vision all the way to the eyes, violently disturbing and liquefying the very passages and channels of the eyes. <margin>C</margin> We say this is fire meeting it from the opposite direction, and from this encounter, tears—a body mixed from fire and water—are poured out. And while one fire leaps out like a flash of lightning, and another enters and is extinguished by the moisture, various colors are created from a mixture of this kind; we call the passion itself "glittering" or "flashing," and that which causes it, "bright" or "radiant." A medium kind of fire, reaching the moisture of the eyes and mixing with it, is not at all radiant, but from the very admixture of the fiery ray with the moisture, it creates a blood-like color, which we have named "red." <margin>D</margin> Bright and white mixed with red produces "yellow" <note>original: "flauum"</note>. However, in what measure these individual things are mixed with one another, even if someone knew, it would not be the mark of a wise man to tell, especially since he could not in any way offer a necessary or even a probable account of them.

<margin>E</margin> Red mixed with white and black generates "purple." A slightly darker "murex" <note>original: a purple-red dye from sea snails</note> and a "muddy" <note>original: "lutheolus"</note> color are made when these are blended together and burned, and more blackness is added. "Tawny" is produced by the tempering of yellow and brown. Brown is produced by the confusion of white and black. The coupling of white and yellow generates "pallor." Brightness added to white and steeped in much blackness produces "dark blue" <note>original: "cæruleum"</note>. Dark blue with white creates "grey-blue" <note>original: "glaucum"</note>. From the tempering of tawny and black, the color "green" is born. Nearly all other colors become manifest from these. For if anyone, imitating the superior mixtures, pursues the remaining colors, he will be disputing with probable reasons. But if anyone attempts the discussion and proof of these things by the work itself, he will seem to be ignorant of the difference between human and divine nature. Truly, God is sufficient to collect many things into one, and again to lead one out into many; for He knows and is able at the same time. But no man is able to do either, nor is there any now, nor will there ever be. All these things, thus naturally disposed by necessity, the <term>Fabricator</term> <note>The Demiurge or Creator-Craftsman</note> of the most beautiful and best work assumed in those things being born, when He generated a God sufficient in Himself and most perfect: using causes as ministers for these things, but acting Himself in each part for that which was good. For it is fitting to distinguish two species of causes. <margin>F</margin> <margin>Two species of causes.</margin> One is "necessary," the other "divine." And we must seek the divine in all things, so that we may attain a blessed life as far as is possible for our nature. We must also investigate the "necessary" cause for the sake of those divine ones. For one must consider that without these necessary things, those others upon which we place our study cannot be understood, comprehended, or perceived in any other way.

<margin>G</margin> Since, therefore, the material now lies before us as if before craftsmen—namely, the types of causes holding the place of prepared material from which the following discussion is to be woven—let us return briefly to the beginning, and quickly go back to the place from which we have proceeded thus far. And so finally, let us place an end and a crown upon the discussion, such as the previous matters require. As we said from the beginning, when these things lacked order, God instilled in each thing, both toward itself and toward others, a measure and a ratio of proportion, to the extent that each was able to receive it. At that time, surely nothing participated in order, except perhaps by some chance; nor was there anything then that could rightly be called water or fire or any of the other things now named among us. But He first adorned all these things, and then from them He constituted this universe as a single living being, containing within itself all mortal and immortal animals. And of the divine things He Himself is the author, but He handed over the generation of mortals to His own offspring to be completed. They, therefore, imitating their parent and receiving the immortal principle of the soul, enclosed that soul in a mortal body, and subjected the whole body to the soul as if it were a vehicle, and in it they fabricated another species of soul, which is mortal, having...

<column-break/>

...concerning the seat of the liver, let us follow. Whatever part of it is fast, we call "high-pitched"; whatever is slower, "lower-pitched." That which is uniform, we call "smooth"; that which is the opposite, "rough." The great, we call "loud"; and that which is the opposite, "small." Regarding their harmonies, it is necessary to speak in what will be said hereafter. There remains a fourth sensory type which we must distinguish, possessing many variations within itself; all of these we collectively call "colors," a flame flowing off from each body, having particles symmetrical with the sight for the purpose of perception. We have already stated the origin of the causes of vision in the previous sections; here, therefore, it is most fitting to go through an account of colors that is reasonable and likely. Of the particles carried from other parts and falling into the sight, some are smaller, some larger, and some are equal to the parts of the sight itself. Those that are equal are imperceptible; these we call "transparent." Those that are larger and smaller, some contract and some dilate the vision, just as the hot and cold affect the flesh, or as the astringent and whatever are heating and sharp affect the tongue. White and black are the affections caused by these, being the same in another genus, yet appearing different for these other reasons. Thus they must be named: that which dilates the vision is "white," and its opposite is "black." A sharper motion, falling upon and dilating the vision as far as the eyes, and violently pushing through and melting the very passages of the eyes, is a mass of fire, like a lightning bolt, which we call "tears" as it pours out from there; being itself fire meeting fire from the opposite direction, and as one fire leaps out as from lightning and the other enters and is quenched in the moisture, all sorts of colors are produced in this movement. We call this affection "dazzling," and that which produces it we have named "bright" and "shining." That kind of fire between these, reaching the moisture of the eyes and mixing with it, not shining but through the moisture mixing with the fire of the blood, produces a "red" color; we call its name "red." Bright mixed with red and white becomes "yellow." But as for the measure in which these are mixed, even if one knew, he would not have the sense to say it; for one could not state any necessity or likely account of them even moderately. Red blended with black and white makes "purple." It becomes "dark" when these are mixed and burned, and more black is blended in. "Flame-colored" comes from the mixing of yellow and grey; grey comes from white and black. "Ocher" comes from white mixed with yellow. Bright falling upon white and falling into a saturated black results in a "dark blue" color. Dark blue mixed with white becomes "grey-blue"; flame-colored with black becomes "leek-green." The rest are nearly all clear from these, as to which mixtures they should be likened to preserve the likely story. But if someone, by looking at the works themselves, should try to put these to the test, he would be ignorant of the difference between human and divine nature: that God is capable of mixing many into one and again dissolving one into many, being both knowledgeable and powerful; but of men, no one is capable of either of these things, neither now nor ever in the future. All these things being then such by nature, the Creator of the most beautiful and best work took them up by necessity among things being born, when He generated the self-sufficient and most perfect God <note>The Universe</note>; using the causes concerning these as servants, while He Himself fashioned the good in all things being born. Therefore, one must distinguish two kinds of causes: the one "necessary," the other "divine." And the divine must be sought in all things for the sake of attaining a happy life, as far as our nature admits; but the necessary for the sake of those others, reckoning that without these, those very things we strive for cannot be understood, nor grasped, nor in any way shared. Since, then, the kinds of causes now lie before us like timber for craftsmen, from which the rest of the discourse must be woven together, let us return briefly to the beginning and quickly travel back to the same point from which we arrived here, and try to put an appropriate end and head to our story to fit what went before. Just as was said at the beginning, when these things were in disorder, God instilled in each thing symmetry, both toward itself and toward others, as much as was possible for them to be proportionate and symmetrical. For then they participated in nothing except by chance, nor was there anything at all worthy of the names we now use, such as fire and water and the rest. But He first ordered all these, then from them He constructed this universe, one living being, containing all living things within it, both mortal and immortal. And of the divine, He Himself became the <term>Demiurge</term> <note>Craftsman</note>, but the generation of mortals He assigned to His own offspring to craft. They, imitating Him, and receiving the immortal principle of the soul, <margin>H</margin> next fashioned around it a mortal body; they gave the whole body to it as a vehicle, and they built within it another form of soul, the mortal one, having terrible...

<meta>This page continues the physical and metaphysical description of the human body from the previous section. While the previous page discussed the senses and light, this page moves into the "anatomy of the soul," explaining how the gods housed different parts of human nature—reason, spirit, and desire—within specific organs like the heart, lungs, and liver.</meta>

-># TIMAEUS #<-

...and having within it necessary passions. <margin>Passions.</margin> <margin>A</margin> The first of these is pleasure, the greatest lure of evil; then pain, which puts good things to flight. Furthermore, there are boldness and fear, those two foolish counselors; and anger, which is hard to appease; and hope, which is easily led astray by irrational sensation and all-consuming love. By mixing these together, they [the gods] necessarily composed the mortal race. And for this reason, fearing to defile the divine part <note>The "divine part" refers to the rational soul located in the head.</note> more than was absolutely necessary, they housed the mortal part separately in another dwelling-place of the body. They built an isthmus and boundary between the head and the chest by placing the neck between them, so that they might be kept apart. Within the chest and what is called the thorax, they bound the mortal kind of soul. <margin>B</margin> And since one part of it was naturally better and the other worse, they divided the cavity of the thorax, separating it as one might divide the quarters of men from the quarters of women. <margin>The Diaphragm.</margin> They placed the midriff <note>original: "phrenas" / "diaphragma"</note> as a partition between them in the middle. That part of the soul which participates in courage and spirit <note>original: "thumos" - often translated as "spiritedness" or "righteous anger."</note>, being fond of contention, they housed closer to the head, between the midriff and the neck. This was so that it might listen to reason and, joining with it, forcibly restrain the tribe of desires whenever they should refuse to obey the command and word from the citadel <note>The "citadel" is a metaphor for the brain/head, where reason resides.</note> of their own will. The heart, which is the origin of the veins <margin>C</margin> <margin>The heart is the origin of the veins and the fount of blood.</margin> and the fountain of the blood that moves impetuously through all the limbs, they established in the guardhouse. They did this so that when the fire of anger boils up—either because reason announces that some unjust action is being committed against them from without, or by some desire from within—the whole sensing part of the body might quickly perceive the commands and threats through all the narrow channels. Thus, it might become obedient and follow in every way, allowing the best part <note>Reason</note> to lead among them all. But because the gods knew that the heart would throb in the expectation of danger and the arousal of spirit, and that all such swelling of the passionate parts would happen through fire, they sought a remedy for it. They planted the form of the lung <margin>Lungs.</margin> nearby. First, they made it soft and bloodless, then they provided it with small perforated cavities inside, like a sponge. This was so that by receiving breath and drink, it might provide cooling and relief from the internal heat. <margin>D</margin> For this reason, they cut the passages of the windpipe <note>original: "arterias" - here referring to the bronchial tubes or air passages.</note> toward the lung and wrapped the lung around the heart like a soft cushion. Thus, when anger reaches its peak within the heart, it might leap against a yielding substance, be cooled down, and—feeling less distress—be better able to join with spirit in serving the commands of reason. Finally, that part of the soul which desires food and drink, and all things that the nature of the body requires, they housed in the region between the midriff and the boundary of the navel. There, they constructed a sort of manger for the nourishment of the whole body, and they tied this part of the soul there like a wild animal. They believed it was necessary to keep it tethered if the mortal race was ever to exist. <margin>E</margin> They placed it there so that it might always feed at its manger and dwell as far as possible from the seat of counsel <note>The head</note>. By causing as little noise and shouting as possible, it allows the best part of us to consult in quiet for the common benefit of all. Now, the gods knew that this part of the soul would not understand reason, and that even if it did perceive something through the senses, it would not naturally care for rational words. Instead, it would be led away by images and phantoms both by night and by day. To address this, God designed the form of the liver and placed it in that soul-part's dwelling. He made it dense, smooth, <margin>F</margin> bright, and sweet, though not without a share of bitterness. This was so that the power of thoughts descending from the mind might act upon the liver like a mirror that receives shapes and gives back images to be seen. When the mind uses a portion of the liver's bitterness, it can strike fear into that part of the soul. By moving harshly and mixing bitterness throughout the liver, it produces bilious colors and contracts the whole organ, making it wrinkled and rough. It twists the lobe and the vessels, <note>original: "fibras... gall-bladder... and the portal veins."</note> blocking and closing them to cause pain and distress. But when a breath of gentleness from the mind paints the opposite images, it provides a rest from bitterness by refusing to move or touch what is contrary to its nature. Instead, it uses the sweetness innate to the liver to make everything straight, smooth, and free. <margin>G</margin> It makes that part of the soul dwelling around the liver peaceful and cheerful, allowing it to pass the night in moderation and practice divination through dreams, since it has no share in reason or wisdom. For those who fashioned us remembered the command of their father <note>The Creator or Demiurge</note> to make the mortal race as good as possible. Thus, they established the power of prophecy even in this lower part of us, so that it might touch upon the truth in some way. It is a sufficient sign that God gave the power of divination to human foolishness: for no one in their right mind achieves true and inspired prophecy. This happens only when the power of wisdom is fettered by sleep, or hindered by disease, or some divine possession. However, it belongs only to the wise person to understand the things spoken or remembered from a dream or a waking state produced by this prophetic and inspired nature.

<column-break/>

disturbed by heavy and necessary perturbations. Of these <margin>Perturbations.</margin> <margin>A</margin> the first would be pleasure, the greatest bait of evil; then pain, a flight from and hindrance to good. Besides these, there is audacity and fear, those two mindless counselors; added to these is implacable wrath, and hope, that seductive mistress, along with irrational sense and all-invading love. Mixing these together, they of necessity composed the mortal race. But lest the divine part be polluted by any mortal contagion, except as much as supreme necessity required, they placed the mortal part separately in another seat of the body. They separated the head from the breast by interposing the neck and throat. In the breast and thorax, therefore, they placed the mortal kind of soul. <margin>B</margin> And since that part was by nature partly better and partly worse, they arranged the capacity of the thorax again, discerning the seats as if one were for men and the other for women. <margin>Diaphragm.</margin> For they interjected a certain cartilage called the diaphragm (which they also call the *phrenas*) as a medium between these. The part of the soul that participates in fortitude and anger, and is contentious, they made closer to the head, between the diaphragm and the middle of the neck. This was so that, being obedient to reason, it might—together with reason—restrain the tribe of desires by force, whenever desire might reject the orders of reason dwelling in the citadel of the head. But the heart, the origin of the veins <margin>C</margin> <margin>The heart is the origin of the veins and the fount of blood.</margin> and the fountain of blood flowing with a certain impetus through the whole body, they wished to suspend in the region of the bodyguards. This was so that when the force of anger blazes up—reason announcing if any injury is done unjustly from without, or if any concupiscence disturbs from within—then quickly through all the narrow passages, whatever in the body participates in sense might feel the orders and threats. Thus, it would obey and follow entirely, and endure in all things the command of that most excellent ruler. <margin>Pulmo [Lung].</margin> But when they recognized that the heart would tremble at the sight of terrible things and would often burn with anger, and that all this work would be done through fire, they applied the covering of the lungs to the heart for the sake of tempering such heat. The lung is first soft and bloodless, then distinguished by hollow tubes within like a sponge. Thus, by drawing in breath and drink, it might cool the heat of the heart by this kind of respiration and <margin>D</margin> refreshment. For this reason, they derived the arteries like aqueducts through the substance of the lungs and wrapped them around the heart like a soft cushion. This was so that when excessive anger boils, it might cool down, tempered toward easier obedience. Once the tumult is settled, the spirit might more easily serve and obey reason as a minister. Finally, that part of the soul which desires food and drink, and all other things the body lacks, they applied to the middle region between the diaphragm and the navel. There they wished a certain manger to exist for the nourishment of the whole body, and there they bound that force of the soul like a wild animal. Here, truly, it is necessary for it to nourish its body, if the mortal race is ever to be. <margin>E</margin> So that it might always feed at the manger and dwell far from the counselor, and therefore might not disturb him with its clamor and noise, but permit the chief leader of our nature to consult in tranquil leisure for the common utility of all, the gods seem to have given it this inferior region to inhabit. But because God saw that this part of the soul would be such that it would not listen to reason—and if it were struck by any sense, it would in no way obey reasons, but would be mostly snatched away by images and visions by night and day—for this reason he created the nature of the liver and placed it in its dwelling. I say he made it dense in nature, smooth, clear, sweet, and not without a share of bitterness. This was so that the power of thoughts descending from the mind might be received in the liver as if in a mirror that takes in shapes and returns images to the sight. Sometimes, it terrifies the soul when it uses the bitter part of its nature, intending threats and suddenly suffusing the whole liver with bile and terrible colors. It renders it contracted, wrinkled, and rough, and affects its fibers, its bile, its gallbladder, and the veins called the "gates" <note>original: "portae" - the portal veins of the liver.</note> in such a way that, partly by twisting them from their right habit and partly by obstructing and closing them, it provides pains and detriments. But again, when an inspiration of gentleness from the mind portrays contrary <margin>G</margin> visions, it calms the bitterness because it wishes neither to move nor touch a nature contrary to itself. Using the sweetness innate to it, it directs all things to be straight, smooth, and free. Then it makes the peaceful and mild part of the soul inhabiting the liver so that even in sleep it is moderately affected and uses prophecy, since it is void of reason and prudence. For those who composed us, mindful of that paternal mandate by which he had commanded the mortal race to be made as good as possible, so established the worse part of us that it too might be in some way a participant in truth. Clearly, they established prophecy in it. That God gave the power of divining to human madness can be an argument for us: for no one while in a sound mind attains divine and true prophecy, but

---

only when the power of prudence is hindered by sleep, or oppressed by disease, or moved out of its state by some divine transport, does divination usually occur. It is the duty only of the prudent man to understand those things which have been pronounced by a prophetic and raging nature, whether sleeping or waking.

<meta>This page continues Plato’s detailed anatomical and physiological "myth," specifically explaining the purpose of the internal organs and the physical composition of the body. Having previously discussed the placement of the soul's parts, he now moves to the biological function of the liver, spleen, and the "bonds of life" found in the marrow.</meta>

-># OF PLATO #<-

...and whatever visions have shone forth, to discern them by reasoning in such a way that he may explain by what logic, and for whom, some future, past, or present good or evil seems to be portended. However, it is not the duty of one who has been in a frenzy, and remains in it still, <margin>The work of a prudent man.</margin> to judge what he has seen or uttered. Indeed, that ancient saying is well known: "To do one’s own business and to know oneself is the work of the prudent man alone." <note>This refers to the Socratic/Platonic ideal of "sophrosyne," often translated as temperance or self-knowledge.</note> Hence, the law commands that prophets be appointed as judges over divine divinations. Some people call these men "seers," <note>original: "vates"</note> being entirely ignorant that they are actually the interpreters of the cryptic utterances and visions wrapped in obscure volumes, and are not seers themselves. For this reason, they should be called interpreters and announcers of the things foretold.

And indeed, the nature <margin>The liver.</margin> of the liver was made such for this very reason, and placed in the seat we have described, specifically for the sake of divination. Furthermore, while each person is still alive, the signs of such things are expressed more clearly; but when one is deprived of life, blindness occurs, and there is no clear sign of divination. Located next to this on the left is a member [the spleen] for the sake of the liver, so that it may always keep the liver pure and bright—shining and clear like a mirror, and suited for reflecting images. Therefore, when the liver abounds with filth due to some <margin>Concerning the spleen.</margin> bodily disease, the porousness of the spleen, acting as a cleanser, drinks those impurities up, since this member is hollow and bloodless. Thus, being filled with these cleansings, it grows and swells with corruption. And again, when the body is cleansed, the spleen shrinks back into itself and subsides.

We have now described what parts of the soul are mortal, what is divine, where they reside, with what they are associated, and why they are separated from one another. But whether it truly is as we have said, we shall only assert if a divine oracle confirms it; however, we do not hesitate to maintain that it is *likely* to be so, and will continue to assert it even more diligently through investigation. For now, let us take this as our assertion. That which follows must be treated in a similar way. It remains, then, to describe the logic by which the other members of the body were arranged. It is most fitting that they consist of this reasoning: those fabricators of our race knew that we would be intemperate regarding food and drink, and because of gluttony we would consume more than measure or <margin>Concerning the intestines and their spirit.</margin> necessity required. Therefore, lest a sudden death occur due to diseases, and the mortal race thus perish prematurely and incomplete, they fashioned the lower belly to receive the abundance of food and drink. Furthermore, they wrapped the coils of the intestines around it, so that the nourishment we take in would not pass through us too quickly, immediately forcing a new necessity for food upon us. For if we suffered from that unfillable and perpetual abyss [of hunger], our race would have been left devoid of philosophy, music, and all moderation, and would have been utterly disobedient to that part in us which is most divine.

The nature of the bones and flesh and other such things was composed in this way. <margin>Concerning the bones and flesh.</margin> Truly, the generation of the marrow provided the beginning for all of these. For the bonds of that life which the soul leads when joined to the body are attached to the marrow, and being drawn from it through the whole body, they bind and support the construction of our frame. The marrow itself was generated from other things. There were certain primary triangles, unbent and smooth, most suited for the exact generation of fire, air, water, and earth. <note>In the *Timaeus*, Plato argues that the four elements are composed of microscopic geometric shapes, specifically triangles.</note> From each of these kinds, God separated individuals, and mixing them in due proportion with one another, he established a seed-bank and a fuel for the entire generation of mortals while he procreated the substance of the marrow from them. Afterward, sowing in it, he bound the different kinds of souls. Furthermore, he distinguished right away in that first distribution as many and as various figures as the marrow ought to have from each species. And that part of the marrow which was to receive the divine seed, as if into a field—he made it globular and smooth on all sides; and he willed it to be named the <term>ἐγκέφαλον</term> (enkephalon), that is, the **brain**, because when each animal was finally completed, the vessel capable of holding the brain was to be called the <term>κεφαλὴ</term> (kephale), that is, the **head**. However, that which was to contain the remaining and mortal powers of the soul, he shaped into forms that were both round and oblong, and he willed all of it to be called "marrow." And casting from these the bonds of the whole soul as if from anchors, he then completed our entire body around them, and supported them from the outside with a texture of bones.

As for the bone itself, he composed it thus: sifting pure and smooth earth, he mixed and moistened it with marrow. Afterward, he cast it into fire, then dipped it in water, then back into fire, and again into water. And by thus transferring it often into each, he rendered it such that it could be melted by neither. Using this, he enclosed the brain in a bony sphere as if made on a lathe. He left narrow passages here, and around the marrow of both the neck and the back, he fashioned "little wheels" and "pivots" <note>original: "rotulas vertiginesque" - describing the vertebrae.</note> from the bone itself, which he placed as hinges, extending from the head through the whole trunk. Thus he protected all the seed by walling it in with a stony circuit. <margin>Concerning the nerves.</margin> Furthermore, he added joints, using the nature of "the Other" <note>A reference to the "Same" and the "Other," metaphysical principles Plato uses to explain movement and difference.</note> within them as a kind of mediating power for the sake of movement and bending. But judging that the nature of the bone would be drier and more rigid than it ought to be, and that when heated and then cooled it would quickly decay and corrupt the seed within, he fashioned the kind of nerves and flesh: so that with the nerves binding the other members...

<column-break/>

...and as many visions as appear correctly, to discern them all by reasoning—how they signify something and to whom, whether of a future, past, or present evil or good. But for one who is in a frenzy, or who remains in it, it is not his task to judge the things seen or spoken by himself. On the contrary, it has been well said of old that to do and to know one's own business and oneself belongs to the temperate man alone. Whence indeed it is the law to appoint the race of prophets as judges over inspired divinations. Some call these men "seers," <note>original: "manteis"</note> being altogether ignorant that they are the interpreters of the enigmatic speech and vision; they should not be called seers at all, but most justly "prophets" <note>original: "prophetai" - literally 'forth-tellers' or 'interpreters'.</note> of things divined. 

The nature of the liver, then, for these reasons, is such as it is and is born in the place we mentioned, for the sake of divination. And indeed, while each such creature is alive, it has clearer signs; but deprived of life, it becomes blind, and the divinations it offers are too dim to signify anything clearly. Again, the composition and seat of its neighbor, the internal organ [the spleen], was placed on the left, for the sake of the liver: to keep it always bright and pure, prepared like a mirror and ready, always lying beside it as a cleansing cloth. Wherefore indeed, whenever certain impurities arise around the liver due to a disease of the body, the spleen, being of a porous nature, cleanses them all and receives them, woven as it is of a hollow and bloodless fabric. Whence, being filled with the things it cleanses away, it grows large and swollen with festering; and again, when the body is cleansed, it subsides and sinks back into the same state.

Now, regarding the soul—how much of it is mortal and how much divine, and where, and with what, and for what reasons they were housed separately—if God were to agree, only then could we insist that this is the absolute truth. But that what we have said is *probable*, we must venture to say now and even more so as we look into it further; and so let it be asserted. That which follows these things must be pursued in the same way: how the remainder of the body came to be. From a reasoning such as this, it would most of all be fitting for it to be composed: those who were putting our race together knew the intemperance regarding drink and food that would be in us, and that we would fill ourselves with more than the moderate and necessary amount due to a love of gorging. Therefore, lest swift destruction occur through diseases, and the mortal race reach an end immediately and incomplete, they foresaw this and placed the lower belly as a receptacle for the excess of food and drink, named the "exit" <note>The Greek "exeilo" suggests a place of winding or exit.</note> for the surplus. They wound the coil of the intestines around it, so that the food would not pass through quickly and force the body to need more food again too soon; for by providing insatiability through gluttony, it would make the whole race devoid of philosophy and music, and unheeding of the most divine part among us.

Regarding the bones and flesh and all such nature, it was as follows. For all of these, the beginning was the generation of the marrow. For the bonds of life, while the soul is bound together with the body, are fastened in this, and they root the mortal race. The marrow itself was made from other things. For of the triangles, those which were first, being unbent and smooth, and were most capable of producing fire, water, air, and earth with accuracy—God, separating these from their own respective kinds and mixing them in proportion to one another, fashioned the marrow out of them, devising a "universal seed-bed" <note>original: "panspermian"</note> for every mortal race. And after this, planting the soul-types within it, he bound them down. As for the shapes which the marrow was to have, and what kinds of forms, he divided it into just as many and such shapes right at the beginning in the first distribution. And that part which, like a field, was to contain within it the divine seed—having fashioned it round on all sides, he named this portion of the marrow the "brain" <term>ἐγκέφαλον</term>; for when each animal was completed, the vessel around it was to become the "head" <term>κεφαλὴ</term>. But that part which was to hold the remaining and mortal part of the soul, he divided into shapes that were both round and elongated. He called it all "marrow"; and, as if casting anchors from these, he fastened the bonds of the whole soul and then fashioned our whole body around it. First, he constructed a covering for it all around, made of bone.

He composed the bone in this way: sifting pure and smooth earth, he kneaded and moistened it with marrow. After this, he placed it in fire. After that, he dipped it in water, then again in fire, and again in water. By transferring it thus many times from one to the other, he made it insoluble by both. Using this, he fashioned a bony sphere around the brain, and in this he left a narrow passage. And around the marrow of the neck and the back, he fashioned vertebrae from them, extending them like hinges, beginning from the head and through the whole cavity. And so, preserving the whole seed, he enclosed it in a stony circuit, adding joints, and using the nature of "the Other" within them as a power standing in the middle for the sake of motion and bending. But thinking that the condition of the bony nature was more brittle and rigid than it ought to be, and that when heated and then cooled it would become diseased and quickly destroy the seed within it, for these reasons he devised the race of nerves and flesh, so that by binding all the other members with the nerve, which can be tightened and loosened...

<meta>This page continues the anatomical discourse in Plato's Timaeus, transitioning from the internal organs (liver and spleen) and marrow to the outer structures of the body: flesh, sinews, skin, and hair. It explores the teleological reasoning—the "why"—behind the human form's physical vulnerabilities and strengths.</meta>

-># TIMÆUS #<-

<margin>A</margin> ...provides for the body as it is violently bent or stretched. Of the flesh, he made it a defense against the heat and a protection against the storms of winter, and furthermore against falls, much like padded garments <note>The Greek compares flesh to felted or quilted clothes that absorb impact.</note>, yielding softly and gently to the body. He placed a warm moisture within it so that in the summer, as it perspires and becomes damp on the outside, it provides a natural cooling for the whole body; and through the winter, it might moderately repel the frost that approaches from the outside and surrounds the body with its own internal fire. Thinking on these things, our **Craftsman** <note>original: "κηροπλάστης" (keroplastes) – literally a "wax-molder," referring to the divine creator.</note> mixed and joined together water, fire, and earth, composing a ferment from sharp and salty elements, and mixing these in, he established a juicy and soft flesh. But the nature of the **sinews** <note>The Greek "neura" refers to what we now distinguish as nerves, tendons, and ligaments; here it implies the binding cords of the body.</note>, he tempered from a mixture of bone and unfermented flesh, creating a single power midway between the two, <margin>B</margin> staining it with a yellow color. Hence, it became more tense and tougher than flesh, but softer and more flexible than bone. With these sinews, God bound the bones and the marrow together, tying them to one another, and afterwards shaded them all from above with flesh. Those bones that were the most "animated" <note>Containing the most marrow/soul-substance.</note> he covered with the least flesh, but those that were "inanimate" on the inside, he covered with the most and thickest. And indeed, at the joints of the bones, wherever reason did not show a necessity for them to be covered, he grew little flesh. He did this so that they would not hinder the bending of the limbs or make the bodies difficult to move, and so that many thick layers, packed tightly together, would not cause a lack of sensation through their density, making the things of the **intellect** <margin>C</margin> harder to remember and duller. Therefore, the bones of the forearm and the shin, those around the nature of the hips, the bones of the upper arms and the forearms, and all our other parts without joints, as well as the internal bones—which are void of wisdom due to the small amount of soul in their marrow—all these are filled with flesh. But those parts that are wise have less. This is true unless he perhaps established flesh itself for the sake of the senses, such as the form of the tongue. But for the most part, it is as described. For the nature that is born and nourished by necessity in no way admits both dense bone and much flesh <margin>D</margin> along with keen sensation. This composition would have belonged most of all to the head, if the two had been willing to coincide. If the human race had possessed a fleshy, sinewy, and powerful head, it would have enjoyed a life twice as long, or even many times longer, more robust and painless than it is now. But the **Creators** of our birth, calculating whether they should make a longer-lived but inferior creature, or a shorter-lived but superior one, decided that the shorter but better life was in every way preferable to the longer but worse. Hence, they did not cover the head with flesh or sinews, since it has no joints. And so, for all these reasons, the head was placed upon the body as something more sensitive and wise, but much weaker than the rest of a man. <margin>E</margin> For these reasons and in this way, God placed the sinews at the extremity of the head, gluing them in a circle around the neck by way of similarity, and bound the jaws to them under the face. The rest he dispersed through all the limbs, joining joint to joint. Those who ordered us also adorned the power of our mouth with teeth, tongue, and lips, for the sake of things both necessary and best, just as it is now arranged: the entrance was devised for the sake of necessary things, but the exit for the sake of the best. For everything that enters to provide nourishment to the body is necessary; but the stream of words flowing out and serving <margin>F</margin> **wisdom** is the fairest and best of all streams. Furthermore, the head could not be left as bare bone alone, due to the extremes of the seasons; nor could it be covered and become dull and insensitive due to the burden of flesh. Therefore, a remaining fleshy nature was left, not entirely dried up, forming what we now call the skin. This skin, because of the moisture in the brain, grew and circled the head; where the sutures meet, the moisture rising up watered it and closed it at the crown, as if gathering it into a knot. The variety of the forms of the sutures occurred because of the power of the soul's circuits and the nourishment—the more they clash with one another, the more sutures there are; the less, the fewer. <margin>G</margin> The Divine then pricked this whole skin all around with fire. As it was pierced and the moisture was carried out through it, the pure liquid and heat escaped; but the mixed part, from which the skin itself was made, was lifted by the outward motion and stretched out long, having a fineness equal to the puncture. But because of its slowness, it was pushed back by the surrounding air outside and coiled back under the skin, where it took root. Through these processes, hair grows in the skin; it is a thread-like thing of the same nature as the skin, but harder and denser due to the cooling of the air. As each hair is separated from the skin, it is cooled and becomes dense. <margin>H</margin> By this means, the Creator made our head hairy, using the causes mentioned, but intending it to be a covering instead of flesh for the safety of the brain—being lightweight and sufficient to provide shade in summer and shelter in winter, without hindering sensation...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...both tightened and loosened around the joints themselves, it might render the body prompt and agile for every flexion and tension. Flesh indeed would be a covering against cold and heat; and as the external supports of the body are wont to be, a defense against various falls: especially because it was to be such that it would yield softly and gently to bodies. To this he added a warm humor, so that in summer, being moist and damp on the outside, it might provide a natural cooling to the whole body; but in winter, it might conversely repel the exterior ice with its own fire in a moderate way. When the **molder** of our body thought on these things, he fashioned soft flesh full of juice from a certain mixture tempered from water, fire, and earth, applying a sharp and salty ferment to them. <margin>B</margin> But the nature of the **sinews** he tempered into one middle power from both bone and unfermented flesh, and stained it with a yellow color. Hence it is that the substance of the sinews is more tense and dry than flesh, but more agile and softer than bone. With these, God bound the marrow and the bones together, and covered all these things with flesh. Therefore, those bones which were most "animated" he covered with the fewest fleshes; but those which were least so, on the contrary, with the most and thickest. Furthermore, at the joints of the bones, except where the reason of necessity demanded otherwise, he added few fleshes, lest they be an impediment to flexions and make the bodies slow to move, or lest by their <margin>C</margin> solid thickness and mass they should dull the edge of the senses, hinder memory, or blunt the sharpness of the intellect. For this reason, the bones of the groin, shins, hips, arms, and shoulders, and all others that lack joints, or those hidden internal bones which are void of prudence because of the small amount of soul in the marrow, are covered with much flesh. But those that have prudence have fewer, unless perhaps a certain fleshy mass was specifically adapted for some sense, such as the tongue is. In others, it is as we have said. For nature, born and nourished of necessity, in no way admits compact bone and much flesh together with <margin>D</margin> acute sensation. For the composition of the head would have had these most of all, if they had wished to coincide: and the race of men, having a fat, sinewy, and robust head, would have possessed a life double or even much longer, stronger, and more peaceful than ours. But it seemed to our fabricators, when consulting about our race whether they should make it longer-lived but worse, or of a shorter life but better, that a short and better life was entirely to be preferred to a long and worse one. Therefore, they wove the head with thin bone, and did not support it with flesh and sinews because it was not going to have flexions. For all these reasons, the head was constituted more acute for sensing and more prudent than all members, but <margin>E</margin> more weak. For this reason and in this manner, God, placing the sinews around the extreme part of the head, wrapped them around the spine with a certain similarity, and bound the upper jaws to them under the face, and disseminated the rest through all the members, connecting joint to joint. Furthermore, those adorners of ours decorated the nature of the mouth with teeth, tongue, and lips, just as we now see, for the sake of things both necessary and best. For they devised the entrance for the sake of necessary things, but the exit for the sake of the best. Certainly, whatever is admitted into the body for nourishment is necessary. <margin>F</margin> But the outflow of words, the minister of prudence, is the best and fairest of all outflows. Moreover, the head could not be left naked and destitute of all other covering, because of the excess of heat and cold; nor, on the other hand, was it to be rendered void of sense and dull, weighed down by the weight of flesh. Therefore, where the flesh was not entirely lacking, the larger residue that remained was segregated, and the skin itself, joined to the humor around the brain and germinating, clothed the head. The moisture gushing out under the joints irrigated it and fastened it at the crown. The species of sutures were made varied because of the power of the soul's circuits and nourishment: and for those that fought more against each other, there were more; for those that fought less, fewer. <margin>G</margin> <margin>On hair.</margin> God pricked and struck all this skin on every side with fire. Through the little cracks of the skin, as if through vents, the moisture flowed out; but that which was mixed from the same things as the skin, being pushed out by the force of the emanation, was extended in length, having the same thinness as the puncture. But being pushed back by the surrounding spirit, and revolving again under the skin, it took root. For these reasons, hair grew in the skin, similar to the skin in nature, but harder and denser than the skin because of the coagulation made by the cold. Indeed, the hair, having been produced outside the skin, stiffened from the cold. <margin>H</margin> In this way, God established for us a crowded and hairy head, using those causes which we have mentioned: he wished the covering itself for the protection of the brain to be not heavy with flesh, but light, sufficient to repel the intemperance of cold and heat.

<meta>This page continues the anatomical and teleological description of the human body from Plato’s Timaeus. -># OF PLATO #<-

...so that it might not in the least hinder the sharpness of the senses. However, that combination of **sinew** <note>original: "nerui" / "νεύρου" — referring here to the connective tissues</note>, skin, and bone which exists in the fingers, having been dried out, was covered by a single common and harder layer of skin. The **accessory cause** <note>The physical mechanism of formation.</note> of this consists in those things we have mentioned; but the **principal cause** <note>The divine intent or "why."</note> lies in that intelligence which fashioned it for the sake of future benefit. For those makers of ours were not ignorant that women and other animals would one day be produced from men. They understood, moreover, that the use of **nails** <note>original: "vnguium" / "ὀνύχων"</note> would be necessary for many tasks even for the beasts. Where-
<margin>B</margin>
-fore, they armed humans with nails immediately at their birth. By this reasoning and for these causes, they covered the extremities of the limbs with skin, hair, and nails. Since all the parts and limbs of the mortal living being were created in a mutual kinship, and necessarily possessed life through fire and breath, the gods provided this plan so that the animal itself would not quickly fail, dissolved and exhausted by these elements. Indeed, mixing the nature of the human race with other forms and senses, they planted as it were another kind of living being. Such are the domestic
<margin>C</margin>
trees, plants, and seeds which, having been sown and cultivated by art, are now mild toward us; whereas without cultivation, they are wild. For whatever participates in life may rightly be called a **living being** <note>original: "animal" / "ζῶον"</note>. That which we now speak of participates in the **third species of soul** <note>The vegetative or appetitive soul.</note>, which we have placed between the diaphragm and the navel. In this soul, there is no place for opinion, reason, or mind at all. However, it feels the sensation of pleasure and pain along with desires. For it suffers all things continually. Yet, since it turns within itself and upon itself, rejecting external motion and using its own domestic movement, nature did not grant it the power to consider its own affairs by means of reason. Therefore, it indeed lives and
<margin>D</margin>
is no different from a living animal; but because it was deprived of that power by which something moves itself from place to place, it remained rigid and fixed, clinging by its roots. When those superior creators of ours had supplied all these things for our nourishment, they led various channels through our body like **aqueducts** <note>original: "meatus veluti aquæductus" / "ὀχετοὺς"</note> in a garden, so that it might be irrigated by the derivation of liquid. First, they cut two hidden channels beneath the junction of the skin and the flesh—namely, two veins along the back, following the twofold shape of the body itself, to the right and to the left. These they sent down along the spine, enclosing the generative **marrow** <note>The "genital marrow" refers to the spinal cord, thought to be the source of life-seed.</note> between them, so that this might flourish as much as possible, and that the overflow from here, as if running downhill, might provide a balanced irrigation to other parts.
<margin>E</margin>
After this, splitting the veins around the head and weaving them together from opposite sides, they distributed them partly from the right to the left and partly from the left to the right of the body, so that there might be a connection from the head to the rest of the body along with the skin (since it was not bound and separated by sinews in a circle around the crown); and also so that the power of sensation from both sides might flow throughout the whole body. From here, they led the aqueduct in this order, which we shall clearly perceive if we first affirm this: whatever is composed of smaller parts can hold larger things, but those made of larger parts cannot contain the smaller. **Fire**, above
<margin>F</margin>
all other kinds, consists of the smallest particles. Therefore, it penetrates water, air, earth, and all things composed of them, passing through to such an extent that nothing can contain it. The same must be thought regarding our **belly** <note>original: "vtero" / "κοιλίας" — referring to the digestive cavity.</note>. Indeed, it retains the food and drink cast into it. But it cannot hold back breath and fire, because they are of a thinner composition than the belly itself. Therefore, God used these for the purpose of completing the irrigation from the belly into the veins. For he wove a certain **net** <note>original: "Rete" / "πλέγμα"</note> made of air and fire, like a **wicker creel** <note>original: "sagenæ" / "κύρτοι" — a bulbous fish trap made of reeds.</note>. In this net, there are two bulbous entrances: one of which he again split into two parts, and from these bulbous parts he stretched out something like ropes throughout the entire body to the ends of that texture. All the inner parts of the mesh he composed of fire, but the bulbs and the outer
<margin>G</margin>
container itself he made of air. Finally, taking these and applying them to the formed animal, he arranged them in this way. He directed the bulbs into the mouth. Since the bulbous part is double, he sent one through the **arteries** <note>In ancient anatomy, the "arteries" often referred to the windpipe/bronchi.</note> into the lungs, and the other alongside the arteries into the belly. The other part he divided and led both sections to the channels of the nose in common, so that when one does not reach the mouth, all its flows and passages might be filled from this source. The other capacity of the creel he wished to be around the hollow parts of the body. And he caused all of this to flow softly into the curved and bulbous parts at one time, as if air were there; and at other times, those same curved parts flow back. Since the net is porous, it penetrates the body and emerges again. The rays of internal fire follow in continuous succession as the air passes in either direction. This never ceases to happen as long as the mortal animal exists. This kind of agitation we believe was rightly named **expiration and respiration**. All this work and this entire process in our body occurs through a kind of irrigation and cooling for the sake of life and nourishment. For when, as the breath goes out and in, the internal fire follows it...

<column-break/>

...hindrance in the way. But that which is in the joining of the sinew, skin, and bone around the fingers, having been mixed from three and dried out, became one common hard skin—working together as an auxiliary cause in these things, but fashioned by the most sovereign Mind for the sake of things that would be hereafter. For those who established us knew that women and other beasts would one day be born from men. And indeed, they knew the use of nails, that many of the creatures would need them for many purposes. Hence, in humans at their very birth, they sketched out the origin of nails. For this reason and by these pretexts, they grew skin, hair, and nails at the ends of the limbs. Since all the parts and members of the mortal living being were grown together, and it happened by necessity that it had its life in fire and breath, and because of this it was wasting away being melted and emptied by them, the gods devised a help for it. For mixing a nature related to human nature with other forms and sensations, so as to be another living being, they planted those things which are now domestic trees, plants, and seeds, which having been planted by agriculture, have been educated toward us. Previously, there were only the wild kinds, being older than the domestic ones. For everything that participates in living may most rightly be called a living being.
<margin>C</margin>
However, that of which we now speak participates in the third kind of soul, which is said to be seated between the diaphragm and the navel. This has no part in opinion, reasoning, or intellect, but in the sensation of pleasure and pain, along with desires. For it continues suffering all things. But in turning about itself within itself, pushing away external motion and using its own, nature has not granted it the power to perceive its own nature by any reasoning or insight. Wherefore it indeed lives, but is not other than a living animal. It is fixed, remaining rooted, because it is deprived of the motion of itself by itself. These kinds having been planted by the superior ones for us, the inferior ones, they channeled conduits in our body, cutting them as if they were channels in gardens,
<margin>D</margin>
so that it might be watered as if from an inflowing stream. And first, they cut two hidden channels under the joining of the skin and the flesh, two veins along the back, twofold as the body happened to be, both right and left. These they let down along the spine, taking the generative marrow in between, so that this might flourish as much as possible, and that the inflow happening from there, as if downhill, might be well-protected and provide an even watering to the rest. After this, having split the veins about the head and woven them through one another from opposite directions, they let them through, inclining those from the right to the left of the body, and those from the left to the right; so that there might be a bond of the head to the body along with the skin, since it was not separated by sinews from those around the crown; and also so that the experience of the
<margin>E</margin>
senses might be distributed from both parts to the whole body. From here, they then prepared the water-way in such a manner, which we may more easily understand if we first agree on the following: that all things which are composed of smaller parts hold the larger, but those from larger parts cannot hold the smaller. Fire is the smallest-parted of all kinds. Whence it passes through water, earth, and air, and whatever is composed of these, and nothing is able to hold it. The same must be thought about the belly in us: that it holds the food and drink falling into it, but it cannot hold air and fire, which are smaller-parted than its own constitution. These, then, God used for the watering from the belly to the veins; weaving a mesh of air and fire, like a wicker creel, having double inner-creels at the entrance. One of these he again wove as a fork. And from the inner-creels he stretched out as it were ropes in a circle through everything to the ends of the mesh. All the inner parts of the weaving he composed of fire. The inner-creels and the container he made air-like. And taking them, he placed them against the fashioned animal in such a way: the part of the inner-creels he let down into the mouth; it being double, he let one part down through the arteries into the lungs, and the other into the belly, alongside the arteries. The other, having split
<margin>G</margin>
each part, he let go in common through the channels of the nose; so that when the one does not go through the mouth, all the streams of that part might be filled from this. The other container of the creel he grew around the whole hollow of our body. And all this, he made to flow together softly into the inner-creels at one time, as they are air; and at another time, the inner-creels flow back, and the mesh, as the body is porous, sinks inward through it and back out again. The rays of fire within follow the air as it goes in either direction; and this, as long as the mortal living being is constituted, does not cease to happen. To this kind of motion, the one who gave names, we say, gave the names of inspiration and expiration. All this work and experience happened to our body so that it might be watered and cooled, and thus be nourished and live. For whenever the breath goes in and out, the fire joined within follows...

<meta>This page continues the physiological discourse of the Timaeus. Having previously discussed the outer layers of the body (skin, hair, and nails) and the "net-like" structure of the internal organs, Plato now explains the mechanics of digestion and respiration. He uses the principle of "circular thrusting" (antiperistasis) to deny the existence of a vacuum, applying this theory to various physical phenomena like magnetism and acoustics, before concluding with the nature of blood and the geometric basis of growth.</meta>

# TIMAEUS #

<margin>
How food is
dissolved.
</margin>
<margin>A</margin> ...and as it moves through the belly, it encounters the food and drink, dissolves them, and by dividing them into small parts, leads them through the pathways of its progress. Just as one draws water from a spring into channels, it pumps these nutrients into the veins, making the streams of the veins flow through the body as if through a conduit. Now, let us consider the process of respiration again, looking at the causes that made it function as it does now. It is thus: since there is no vacuum <note>Plato adheres to the "plenum" theory, where all space is filled with matter; therefore, motion requires one thing to push another out of its place.</note> into which any moving thing could enter, and the breath is carried outward from us, it is clear to everyone that it does not go into a void, but pushes the neighboring air from its seat. That which is pushed always drives its neighbor, and by this necessity, everything is driven around into the seat from which the
<margin>

occurs.
</margin>
<margin>B</margin> breath went out. Entering there and filling it, it follows the breath. This whole process occurs at once, like a revolving wheel, because there is no vacuum. Therefore, when the chest and lungs let the breath out, they are filled again by the air around the body, which enters through the porous flesh and is driven around in a circle. Again, when this air is sent back and goes out through the body, it pushes the respiration inward through the passages of the mouth and nostrils. We must assume the primary cause of these things is this: every living animal has heat within its blood and veins, like a spring of fire residing within it. This is what we compared to the mesh of a **weir** <note>original: "κύρτου" / "sagenae" — a wicker fish-trap or basket-net used as a metaphor for the respiratory and circulatory systems.</note>, extending through the middle and
<margin>C</margin> woven entirely of fire, while the other parts on the outside are of air. Now, it must be granted that heat, by its nature, moves outward to its own region toward what is akin to it. Since there are two outlets—one through the body to the outside, and the other through the mouth and nose—whenever it rushes toward one, it pushes the air around toward the other. That which is pushed, falling into the fire, is heated, while that which goes out is cooled. As the heat changes and the parts at the other outlet become hotter, that warmer part inclines back again toward its own nature, pushing the air at the other side. This side, suffering the same and returning the same effect, creates a constant oscillation like a swaying circle, which results in
<margin>
Concerning

and
attraction.
</margin>
<margin>D</margin> inspiration and expiration. Furthermore, we must seek the causes of the effects of medical **cupping glasses** <note>A common ancient medical tool where a vacuum was created in a glass to draw blood or "humors" to the surface.</note> in this same way, as well as the mechanism of swallowing, and of projectiles—whether they are thrown high in the air or travel along the ground. This also explains why sounds seem fast or slow, shrill or deep; sometimes they are discordant because the motion they produce in us is uneven, and sometimes they are harmonious because of their similarity. For the slower sounds catch up with the motions of the earlier, faster sounds when the latter are already dying down and have reached a similarity with them. Upon catching up, they do not disturb them by introducing a different motion, but instead join the beginning of a slower motion to the end of the faster one. By attaching this similarity to the fading motion, they blend a single experience from shrill and deep. Hence, they provide
<margin>E</margin> pleasure to the simple-minded, and joy to the wise, through the imitation of **divine harmony** <note>A central theme in the Timaeus: the physical world imitates the mathematical and musical order of the cosmos.</note> found in mortal motions. The same is true for all flows of water, the falling of thunderbolts, and the wondered-at "attraction" of amber and the **Heraclean stones** <note>original: "Ἡρακλείας λίθων" — magnetite or lodestone (magnets).</note>. In truth, there is no such thing as "attraction" in any of these. Rather, because there is no vacuum and these things push one another around, they separate or combine as each moves toward its own proper seat. To anyone who investigates in the proper manner, these wonders will appear as the result of these interconnected experiences. Indeed, the process of respiration (from which this discussion started) occurred through these
<margin>F</margin> causes, as was said before: fire cuts the food, and as it rises within, following the breath, it fills the veins from the belly by pumping up the cut pieces from there. Because of this, the streams of nourishment have become so abundant throughout the entire body of all animals. These nutrients—freshly cut and derived from kindred things, some from fruits and some from herbs which God planted for this very purpose to be our food—take on all sorts of colors because of their mixing. But a red color is most prevalent, a nature fashioned by the fire's cutting and its "imprinting" on the moisture. Therefore, the color of that which flows through the body has the appearance we have described, which we call
<margin>
Concerning
the blood.
</margin>
<margin>G</margin> **blood** <note>Plato views blood as the final product of digestion, essentially liquefied food turned red by internal fire.</note>, the "pasture" of the flesh and the whole body. From this, each part is irrigated and fills the base of whatever has been emptied. The manner of this filling and emptying is the same as the motion of everything in the universe: every kindred thing is carried toward itself. For the things that surround us on the outside are always dissolving us and distributing each kind of matter by sending it away to its own species. The blood-nutrients within us, having been broken into small pieces and contained within the living being—which is held together like a mini-universe—are compelled to imitate the motion of the whole. Therefore, each of the parts within, being carried toward its own kind, fills again what was just emptied. When more flows out than flows in, the whole creature declines; when more flows in, it grows.

Concerning

</margin>
<margin>H</margin> When the composition of the whole animal is young, it has its **triangles** <note>Plato’s physics posits that the elements are made of microscopic triangles. In youth, these are "sharp" and strong.</note> new, as if still fresh from the shipyard's stocks; their interlocking with one another is strong, and the whole body is tender, having been recently formed from marrow...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...it follows, and being diffused through the belly, it encounters food and drink. It immediately liquefies them and divides them into the smallest parts. Through the exits where progress is open, as if drawing from a certain spring, it carries them out: namely, it transfers whatever it has exhausted into the passages of the veins, and distributes the flows of the veins through the body as if through a valley. But let us look again at the causes by which respiration was instituted in this manner which we now perceive. The consideration of this matter will be as follows. Since a vacuum exists nowhere into which anything being carried might enter, and the breath flies out from us, it is established that this breath does not fly out into a vacuum, but displaces the air nearest to it from its seat. That which is displaced always
<margin>B</margin> pushes the next air, and by a necessity of this kind, whatever is struck and driven into that seat from which the breath was excluded, enters there and, by filling it, follows the breath itself. And this whole thing happens simultaneously by a certain revolution in which there is nowhere a vacuum. For this reason, when the chest and lungs have exhaled the breath, it is soon filled by the air surrounding the body, which penetrates the passages of the body. And again, the air flying from the body and the emitted breath forces the inspiration to be drawn back inside through the passages of the mouth and nostrils. We posit the causes that give a beginning to these things in this way. Every animal of this universe possesses heat in its veins and blood, like some spring of fire.
<margin>C</margin> And we compared this to a "net-trap," extended through the middle and entirely woven from fire, while all the exterior parts are of air. Truly, it must be thought that heat, by its nature, emanates outward in its own region toward that which is kindred to it. Since there are two outlets, one outward through the body and the other back through the mouth and nostrils, when the breath makes an impetus toward one side and thrusts it out, it conversely draws back and strikes against the other. That which is drawn back, running into the fire, grows hot; that which has exhaled grows cold. Therefore, while the heat is exchanged, and those parts using the other passage grow warm, and again that which boils moves toward its own nature, and by this moving out it strikes the other into the other path—and again these things
<margin>D</margin> perpetually suffer and do the same—certainly this breath, continually fluctuating here and there in a certain circle, contains expiration and inspiration. Furthermore, the causes of the effects that happen from the "suction" of **cupping glasses** by physicians, and also of drinking, and moreover of those things which are thrown—whether they are sent high up or carried on the ground—must certainly be treated by this reasoning. Moreover, voices, whichever are heard as fast or slow, high-pitched or deep, are sometimes dissonant because of the unlikeness of the motion produced in us by them, and sometimes consonant because of their likeness. For the voices that are themselves slower, succeeding those earlier and faster motions which are now ceasing and have already progressed to something similar, catch up with them. In catching them, they do not disturb them
<margin>E</margin> by throwing in another motion, but introduce the beginning of a slower movement according to the start of the faster one. While it adapts a certain likeness of the ending motion to itself, they temper one concord out of the high and the deep. Whence they grant pleasure to the foolish and joy to the wise, because of the imitation of **divine harmony** found in mortal movements. The same reasoning applies to the flows of waters, the impetus of thunderbolts, and that wondrous "attraction" of amber or of that stone which is named the **Heraclean stone**. In truth, no attraction of these things happens: but since there is nowhere a vacuum, and these things push one another in turn, and being
<margin>F</margin> compressed or separated, each seeks its own place, these wonderful events will appear to a diligent investigator of these things to happen from these mutual interactions. And yet respiration, from which we digressed to this point, proceeds from these causes and in this manner, as we said above. Namely, while the fire divides the food and is raised internally, it fills the veins from the belly by a common elevation of this kind, from the fact that it draws the worn-down pieces from there. For this reason, the liquids of the nutrients are thoroughly diffused through the whole body of all animals. Immediately, the things worn down and taken from their kin—partly from fruits, partly from
<margin>G</margin> herbs, which God produced for the nourishment of our body—possess entirely various colors because of the mixing. But a red color prevails most in these, whose nature comes from a portion of fire and a "wiping away" performed in the moisture. Therefore, the color of that which flows through the whole body is such in appearance as we have said. We have named it **blood**, the food of the flesh and the entire body. From there, the irrigation distributed everywhere fills all that has been exhausted. Moreover, the mode of filling or emptying is such as the motion of anything in the universe, through which whatever is kindred brings itself to itself. For the things that are poured around us from the outside dissolve us continually, and send out each portion of us to its own kind.
<margin>H</margin> The bloody parts within us, worn down and enclosed in the viscera—as is right to happen in any animal situated under heaven—are forced to imitate the motion of the whole. Therefore, when any worn-down parts in us seek their kin, they fill whatever has been exhausted. Furthermore, when more leaves than has been added, the animal decreases; when the opposite happens, it grows. Therefore, the recent composition of any animal, since it has new **triangles** as if from a wooden frame, possesses a strong structure of them...

<summary>This page explains Plato’s theories on digestion and respiration as a circular mechanical process where "fire" breaks down food into blood. It also notably argues against the existence of a vacuum, explaining physical phenomena like magnetism, suction, and sound as results of "circular pushing" rather than attraction.</summary>
