<meta>This page continues the physiological discourse of the Timaeus (81A-83C). Having previously discussed the mechanics of digestion and respiration, Plato now transitions into the geometric theory of growth and aging, the nature of a natural death, and the pathological origins of disease through the imbalance of elements and humors.</meta>

# PLATO #

<margin>A</margin> ...possesses; however, its whole mass is quite tender, having been recently formed from the straightest marrow and nourished upon milk. Therefore, when this young body receives the triangles <note>Plato believes the four elements are made of tiny geometric triangles. In a young person, these triangles are "sharp" and can easily cut through the triangles of food to provide nourishment.</note> that fall upon it from the outside—from which food and drink are composed—it overcomes and grinds them down with its own triangles, which are newer and stronger than those old and weak ones entering from without. Thus, it makes the animal large by nourishing it with many similar parts. But when the "root" and bond of its own triangles begins to loosen—because they have been exhausted and tamed by long labor and many struggles over time—the body can no longer reduce the incoming nutrients into its own likeness through grinding. Instead, its own members are easily dissolved by the triangles entering from outside. <margin>B</margin> From this point, the whole animal begins to waste away and fail as it is overcome; this loss of strength is called old age. The end truly comes when the bonds of those triangles which form the marrow are no longer able to hold together, but, relaxed by exhaustion, they release the bonds of the soul. The soul, once released according to nature, flies away with pleasure. For anything that happens against nature is painful, but that which happens according to nature is pleasant. Likewise, death brought on by disease and wounds is violent and painful; but the death that creeps in naturally as old age leads to the end is the lightest of all types of death, occurring with pleasure rather than pain. But as for where diseases arise, who could doubt it? <margin>C</margin> For since there are four elements from which the body is compacted—Earth, Fire, Water, and Air—an unnatural abundance or deficiency of these, or their displacement from their proper place to a foreign one (where they do not hold what is suitable for them), causes an internal rebellion and diseases. For whenever any of these is produced or moved contrary to nature, parts that were previously cold become hot, dry parts become moist, light parts become heavy, and all other qualities are similarly changed. Only when the same thing is added to or taken from the same thing in the same way and in due proportion will it allow itself to remain safe and whole. <margin>D</margin> But whatever goes astray, whether by addition or subtraction, induces various changes, diseases, and infinite corruptions. From the secondary compositions formed according to nature, a second way of understanding good or bad health will be given to anyone who seeks it. For since marrow, bone, flesh, and nerves consist of those elements, and blood has also been formed from them (though in a different way), most other conditions happen as described above; however, the greatest and most severe diseases arise in this way: namely, when these substances are formed from each other in a reversed order, they are undoubtedly corrupted. According to nature, flesh and nerves are generated from blood: the nerves from the fibers <note original: "villis">The "villis" or fibers are the clotting agents in the blood that Plato believes form the structural parts of the body.</note> and ligaments because of their kinship, and the flesh from the coagulation of that which is separated from the fibers. That which emanates from the nerves and flesh is sticky and fatty; it glues the flesh to the bones and nourishes the bone itself surrounding the marrow. <margin>E</margin> Furthermore, the purest kind of triangles, the smoothest and most fatty, which filters through the thickness of the bones and drops down, waters the marrow. As long as each part is formed in this manner, good health is maintained. But ill health follows when the opposite occurs. For whenever melted flesh sends its waste back into the veins, the blood in the veins becomes thick and varied with breath, infected with diverse colors, bitterness, and acidic or salty flavors, generating bile, blood-serum, and much phlegm. All these things, once generated and corrupted, first infect the blood itself, and providing no nourishment to the body, are carried everywhere through the veins without observing any order of natural circulation. <margin>F</margin> These substances are truly enemies among themselves because they offer no use to one another. Furthermore, they are hostile to the established habit of the body, dissolving and liquefying its stable state. When the oldest portion of the flesh liquefies, it is most difficult to digest and turns black from being "burnt" for so long; because it has wasted away and is thoroughly eaten through, it acquires a bitterness that is hostile to all other parts of the body not yet contaminated. Sometimes that black color, instead of bitterness, has a sharp acidity when the bitter quality has become more refined. Other times, the bitterness is tinged with blood and takes on a reddish color, but when mixed with the black, it looks like bile. Furthermore, a yellow color joins with the bitterness when new flesh is liquefied by the heat of fire. <margin>G</margin> And indeed, some physician, or perhaps someone gifted with the talent to see one genus within many things, gave the common name "bile" to all of these. But the various species of bile received their own names according to their variety of colors. Ichor <note original: "cruor">The Latin uses 'cruor' (blood/gore), but the Greek 'ichôr' refers to the thin, watery part of blood or discharge.</note> is also present: the serum of the blood is mild, but that of black and sharp bile is wild and aggressive when mixed with salty flavors due to heat; such a thing is called "acid phlegm." Often, a portion of thin and fresh flesh liquefies along with air, and being inflated by the trapped wind and surrounded by moisture, it forms bubbles <note original: "ampullæ">Plato describes these as microscopic bubbles in the blood that, when clustered, become visible.</note> which cannot be seen individually because of their smallness; but when joined together and swollen into a larger mass, they become visible...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...possesses; and the whole structure is tender, as it has been newly formed from marrow and nourished on milk. When the triangles <note original: "trigona">The basic geometric building blocks of matter in Plato's physics.</note> contained within the body encounter the external triangles from food and drink—which are older and weaker than its own—the body's new triangles overcome and cut them, making the animal grow large by nourishing it from many similar parts. But when the "root" of the triangles relaxes, because it has struggled against many things over a long time, it can no longer cut the incoming food into its own likeness, and the body itself is easily divided by those things entering from outside. <margin>B</margin> In this state, every animal wastes away and is overcome; this affliction is named "old age." Finally, when the joined bonds of the triangles around the marrow no longer hold, they drift apart through exhaustion and let go of the bonds of the soul. The soul, thus released according to its nature, flies away with joy. For everything that is contrary to nature is painful, but that which happens according to nature is pleasant. Death, therefore, by this same logic—when caused by disease or wounds—is painful and violent; but the death that comes at the end of old age according to nature is the most painless of deaths, occurring with pleasure rather than grief. Where diseases originate is surely clear to everyone. Since there are four kinds of elements from which the body is compacted—Earth, Fire, Water, and Air—an unnatural excess or deficiency of these, or a <margin>C</margin> displacement from their own place to another, causes rebellion. Fire and the others, when they are present in a way that is not fitting, produce sedition and disease. For when each thing is produced or moved contrary to nature, those things that were previously cool become hot; those that were dry later become moist; and likewise the light and the heavy; and they undergo all manner of changes. For we say that only when the same thing is added to or taken from the same thing in the same way and in proportion, will it allow that thing to remain safe and healthy within itself. But whatever fails in any of these—whether by leaving or arriving—will cause all kinds of alterations, diseases, and infinite destructions. Again, after the primary structures formed according to nature, a second understanding of diseases <margin>D</margin> becomes available to whoever wishes to consider it. For since marrow, bone, flesh, and nerve are compacted from those elements, and blood is also produced from them in another way, most other things occur as they should, but the greatest and most difficult diseases happen this way: when the generation of these substances moves in reverse, then they are destroyed. For by nature, flesh and nerves come from blood: the nerve from the fibers <note original: "inôn">The internal threads or fibers that Plato believes give blood its structure.</note> because of their kinship, and the flesh from the thickening of that which is separated from the fibers. That which comes from the nerves and flesh, being sticky and oily, both glues the flesh to the nature of the bones and nourishes the bone itself <margin>E</margin> that surrounds the marrow. Furthermore, that which is filtered through the density of the bones—the purest kind of triangles, smoothest and most oily—leaks and drops from the bones to water the marrow. When each of these happens according to this order, health generally results; but when in the opposite way, disease follows. For when melting flesh sends its liquefaction back into the veins, then the blood in the veins, mixed with breath, becomes much and varied, diversified by colors and densities, and furthermore by sharp and salty powers, producing biles, ichors, and phlegms of all kinds. For all these things, being produced in reverse and corrupted, first destroy the blood itself, and providing no further nourishment to the body, are carried everywhere <margin>F</margin> through the veins, losing the order of their natural cycles. These are enemies to themselves because they can enjoy nothing of one another, and they are hostile to the established state of the body, destroying and melting it. When the oldest part of the flesh melts, it becomes difficult to digest and turns black from long burning; because it is thoroughly eaten away and bitter, it is dangerous to every part of the body that is not yet corrupted. And sometimes, instead of bitterness, the black color has an acidity, the bitterness having become more refined; but sometimes the bitterness, being dyed with blood, takes on a redder color; and when the black is mixed with this, it becomes bile-like. Furthermore, a yellow color is mixed with the bitterness when new flesh is melted by the fire of the internal flame. And <margin>G</margin> either some physicians have given the common name "bile" to all these, or perhaps someone capable of looking at many dissimilar things and seeing one class within them, worthy of a single name, did so. All other things called types of bile have their own specific definitions according to their color. Ichor <note original: "ichôr">The watery discharge or serum of the blood.</note> of one kind, the serum of the blood, is mild; but that of black and sharp bile is savage, when it is mixed with salty powers due to heat. Such a thing is called "acid phlegm." Again, that which is melted from new and tender flesh along with air, when this is puffed up and enclosed by moisture, bubbles are formed from this condition—each invisible due to smallness, but collectively providing a visible mass—having a color...

<summary>Plato explains that growth and aging are determined by the strength of the "geometric triangles" that make up the body, and defines disease as a "rebellion" where tissues like flesh and nerve break down back into the blood, creating harmful humors like bile and phlegm.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the transition from the physics of the human body to its pathology. On the previous page, Plato discussed how the "triangles" of the body break down in old age; here, he explores how the liquefaction of tissues (flesh, sinews, and marrow) creates the "humors"—phlegm and bile—which lead to various diseases. This marks the beginning of the Timaeus’s medical treatise (82d–85e).</meta>

# TIMAEUS #

...and that which is cast off is white. This entire liquefaction of soft flesh, when mixed with air and not being of great age, we call "white phlegm." <note>Plato views phlegm not just as mucus, but as a byproduct of decomposing tissue.</note> From this newly formed phlegm come sweat and tears, and all other such fluids that the body pours out as it purifies itself every day. All these things become the instruments of disease when the blood is not replenished from food and drink according to nature, but instead gains its mass from contrary sources, violating the laws of nature. <margin>A</margin> Now, when any part of the flesh is dissolved but the foundations of it remain, the power of the misfortune is only half as great, for a recovery can still be easily achieved. But when the substance that binds the flesh to the bone becomes diseased—namely, when that bond no longer separates from the bone and the <term>nerve</term> <note>In antiquity, "nerve" (neuron) referred to tendons and ligaments as well as what we now call nerves.</note> to nourish it and bind the flesh, but instead of being oily, smooth, and sticky, it becomes rough and salty, parched by a poor diet— <margin>B</margin> then all that part so affected, being detached from the bones, withers away again under the flesh and the nerves. The flesh, falling away from its roots, leaves the nerves bare and full of salty brine. These substances then fall back into the circulation of the blood and increase the number of diseases previously mentioned. While these bodily sufferings are severe, those that follow are even greater. <margin>C</margin> This occurs when the bone, due to the density of the flesh, cannot breathe sufficiently and becomes heated by decay; it then develops gangrene <note>original: "sphakelisan," referring to necrosis or bone decay</note> and refuses to accept nourishment. Instead, the bone itself begins to crumble and falls back into the flesh, and the flesh falls into the blood, making the earlier diseases much more acute. But the ultimate stage of all is when the nature of the marrow becomes diseased through some deficiency or excess; this produces the most severe and sovereign diseases, leading inevitably to death, as the entire nature of the body is forced to flow in reverse. <margin>D</margin> A third class of diseases must be considered as arising in three ways: from wind, from phlegm, or from bile. When the lungs—which are the stewards of breath for the body—do not provide clean passages because they are blocked by rheum, the breath cannot go where it should in some places, while in others it enters in greater volume than is proper. Consequently, the parts that are not cooled begin to rot, while the breath that forces its way through the veins twists them and dissolves the body, becoming trapped in its center at the diaphragm. From this, countless painful diseases arise, often accompanied by heavy sweating. Often, when the flesh is dissolved within the body, air is generated there; unable to escape, it causes the same agonies as air that has entered from the outside. <margin>E</margin> These pains are greatest when the air surrounds the nerves and small veins, causing them to swell and violently stretching the tendons and the continuous nerves backward. These diseases, named from the very "tension" of the suffering, are called <term>tetanus</term> and <term>opisthotonos</term> <note>These are conditions involving severe muscle spasms and backward arching of the spine.</note>. For these, a cure is difficult; indeed, it is primarily the onset of fevers that resolves such conditions. White phlegm is also dangerous when trapped inside because of the air in its bubbles; if it has a way to breathe outside the body, it is milder, but it mottles the body by producing <margin>F</margin> white leprosy, dull-white leprosy, and related diseases. When phlegm is mixed with black bile and is spread over the "divine circuits" of the head <note>The "divine circuits" refer to the circular motions of the soul within the brain.</note> and disturbs them, it is more manageable if it occurs during sleep, but if it attacks those who are awake, it is harder to shake off. Because it affects the nature of that which is sacred, it is most justly called the "Sacred Disease" <note>This is the ancient term for epilepsy.</note>. Acid and salty phlegm is the source of all diseases that involve catarrh (running fluids); and because of the variety of places into which it flows, it has received many different names. All parts of the body that are said to be "inflamed" are so named because of the burning and fire caused by bile. If bile finds a way to breathe out, it sends up various kinds of eruptions as it boils; but if it is shut inside, it produces many inflammatory diseases. <margin>G</margin> The worst occurs when bile is mixed with pure blood and disrupts the order of the <term>fibers</term> <note>original: "ines," referring to fibrin, the component of blood responsible for clotting.</note>. These fibers are distributed in the blood so that it may maintain a proper balance of thinness and thickness, so that it neither flows out of the porous body because of heat, nor becomes so dense and sluggish that it can hardly circulate in the veins. The fibers preserve the right measure of these qualities. If someone collects these fibers from the blood of even a dead body as it cools, the rest of the blood remains fluid; but if the fibers are left, they quickly congeal the blood in the presence of cold. Since the fibers have this power in the blood, bile—which is naturally "old blood" and has been melted back into it from the flesh—initially enters the blood while hot and moist in small amounts, and is congealed by the power of the fibers. <margin>H</margin> As it congeals and is violently extinguished, it causes an internal chill and shivering. But when more bile flows in, it overcomes the fibers with its own heat, sets them boiling in disorder, and shakes them; and if it is strong enough to prevail to the end, it penetrates the substance of the marrow, burns it, and looses the bonds of the soul—like the cables of a ship—and sets it free. But when there is less bile, the body itself resists the melting; the bile, being overcome, either is expelled throughout the body or is driven through the veins into the lower or upper belly, like...

<column-break/>

...and because of the foam, its generation has a white color. All this thinning of the more tender flesh, occurring together with the spirit <note>original: "spiritus," here meaning air or breath within the tissues</note> which swells as it is surrounded by wind from the moisture, we call "white phlegm." Likewise, the residue and overflow of recent phlegm are tears and sweat, and whatever other fluids into which the body is daily resolved. And all these are the instruments of diseases, specifically when the blood is increased not from food and drink according to nature, but from contrary sources against the laws of nature. <margin>A</margin> Therefore, when any flesh is cut away, and its root remains, the power of the calamity is only half-total. For it is easily restored. But when that which binds the flesh to the bones becomes diseased, and the blood flowing from those nerves <note>tendons/ligaments</note> no longer nourishes the bones or binds the flesh, but instead—through an injustice of diet—has become rough, salty, dry, and scaly from being fatty and sticky, then surely all that is attacked by these things, having been cut off from the bones, <margin>B</margin> stiffens under the nerves. The flesh also, falling away from its roots, leaves the nerves bare and covered in salty humor; and flowing into the streams of the blood, it makes the diseases we mentioned above even more numerous. These are indeed grave sufferings for bodies. But those that precede these are quite more severe: <margin>C</margin> namely, when the bone, due to the thickness of the flesh, does not have sufficient respiration, and is therefore vexed and constricted by the heat of putrefaction, it does not receive nourishment, but instead, the bone itself falls back into the flesh as it is cooled. That flesh then falls back into blood, and the blood into flesh. From this, diseases more acute than the previous ones are born. The extreme of all, however, is when the nature of the marrow becomes diseased due to some defect or excess; for from this come the most violent and most dangerous diseases leading toward death, for then the entire structural framework of the body is necessarily dissolved. <margin>D</margin> After this, we divide the third species of diseases into three parts. For one is created by spirit (wind), another by phlegm, and another by bile. For when the lung—the guardian and, as it were, the storehouse of the spirit—does not provide us with free and unhindered breathing passages because they are blocked by distillation, then in one part no spirit is sent, while in another more than is proper is received; then those parts that lack respiration and cooling begin to waste away. But that which is received in excess, being carried through the veins, twists them and dissolves the body, occupying the diaphragm in the middle—that is, the partition placed in between; from this, innumerable and extremely troublesome diseases arise with much sweating. Often, also, within the body, spirit is born when the flesh is separated and thinned; since it cannot escape outside, it causes the same pains as the spirit that entered from elsewhere. But it afflicts one with massive pains when, surrounded by the nerves and nearby small veins, it inflates them and stretches and twists the ligaments and continuous nerves from behind. These diseases, indeed, from the very tension and inflating passion, are named "tensions" <note>tetanus</note> and "back-twists" <margin>E</margin> <note>opisthotonos</note>, for which the remedy is difficult. For the fevers that arise are the primary things that resolve these. White phlegm, however, because of the spirit of the bubbles trapped inside, is difficult when it descends to the outer skin; it is milder, but it sprinkles the body with various filth and infects it with white spots, and generates other diseases of that kind. But when mixed with black bile, and it glides into the most divine passages of the head, it is accustomed to dissipate and disturb them. If this happens to those who are sleeping, it is milder; but if to those who are awake, it is more difficult to expel. Since this is a languor of a "sacred nature," it is called the "sacred disease" not without reason. Furthermore, acid and salty phlegm is the origin of all the languors that occur by distillation; but because it glides into many places, it generates many evil states of health. <margin>F</margin> Whatever parts of the body are said to swell are vexed by the fire and combustion of bile, which, when it exhales, produces various tumors on the outside by its heat; but when restrained on the inside, it procreates many burning and devouring diseases. But it is worst of all when, mixed with pure blood, it moves the threads of the fibers and ligaments out of their order, which were led and scattered into the blood for the purpose of achieving a moderate habit of thinness and thickness, <margin>G</margin> so that the blood should not flow out of the body easily because of heat (since it is slippery), nor, if it were thicker, should it become inept for movement and flow and reflow with difficulty through the veins. For this convenience of nature, ligaments of this kind are very opportune; if someone should draw and contract them together even in a dead man, when the blood is cold with the chill of death, all the rest of the blood is diffused. But when they are released, they are immediately constricted with the preceding cold. Since, therefore, these fibers have this power in the blood, when the nature of bile has become old blood, and has been resolved again from the flesh into this blood, falling in little by little at first, being warm and moist, it is constricted by the force of those fibers. <margin>H</margin> And being constricted and violently extinguished, it stirs up a storm and trembling within. But when it flows in more abundantly, overcoming the ligaments with its own heat and boiling beyond measure, it simmers indeed; and if it be suitable for victory continuously even to the end, it penetrates into the marrows, and having burned the roots, it then dissolves and cuts away the bonds of the soul, like the ropes of a ship, and dismisses it free. But when less bile is present, and the liquefying body resists it, the bile itself being bound, either it is cast out through the whole body, or being driven through the veins into the lower or upper belly, just as...

<meta>This page continues Plato’s medical discourse in the Timaeus. Having previously discussed how the breakdown of tissues creates corrupt humors, he now categorizes specific physical ailments like fevers according to the four elements, before transitioning into "diseases of the soul." This section is famous for the Platonic doctrine that "no one is willingly evil," attributing moral failings to physiological imbalances and poor education.</meta>

# PLATO #

<margin>A</margin> ...like a fugitive from a seditious city, [the soul] thus escapes from the body, bringing on those diseases which they call Diarrheas and Dysenteries—
<margin>Diarrhea & Dysentery.</margin>
that is, slippery fluxes of the belly and corrosive discharges—as well as many other similar troubles of the same kind. Thus, when the body suffers most from an <term>excess of fire</term> <note>Plato associates the four elements with specific fever cycles based on their mobility.</note>, it labors under a continuous fever. When it suffers from an excess of air, it produces a daily (quotidian) fever. From water comes a tertian fever, because water is more sluggish than fire and air. Finally, from an excess of earth comes a quartan fever.
<margin>On fevers.</margin>
Since earth is the slowest of all elements, being of the fourth degree, it burns and recedes in a four-fold circuit of time; hence it brings on quartan fevers, which are cured only with great difficulty and after a long time.

<margin>B</margin> In this manner, then, the diseases of the body occur. But the diseases of the soul arise from the habit of the body in the following way. We consider the disease of the soul to be <term>dementia</term> <note>original: "dementiam" (Latin) / "anoian" (Greek). In this context, it refers to a lack of reason or "mindlessness."</note>. Of this, we posit two kinds: Insanity and Ignorance. Therefore, whatever passion brings on either of these must be called a sickness of the soul. For this reason,
<margin>Violent pleasures and pains are the gravest diseases of the soul.</margin>
excessive pleasures and pains must be judged the most serious of all soul-diseases. For whoever exults in excessive joy or is depressed by excessive pain, while greedily and unseasonably striving to seize the former or obstinately trying to avoid the latter, can neither see nor hear anything correctly; he rages with madness and, in such a state, is least capable of reason.

<margin>C</margin> He who possesses an abundance of fluid and sluggish seed around the <term>marrow</term> <note>Plato believed the marrow was the physical substance that anchored the soul to the body and was the source of reproductive seed.</note>, and who, like a tree weighted down with more fruit than is appropriate, luxuriates in excessive abundance, will certainly experience many pains and many pleasures in his lusts and their "offspring" and "fruits." Throughout his entire life, he is driven to madness and fury by these immense pleasures and pains. Although his soul is sick and foolish because of his body, the common people do not consider him sick, but rather think he is acting of his own free will—an assessment that is false. The truth is this: sexual incontinence is for the most part a weakness of the soul caused by the condition of a single substance—namely, the porousness of the bones, which creates a slippery and moist condition in the body.

<margin>D</margin> Indeed, almost all lack of restraint regarding pleasures—which is usually criticized as if we were wicked by choice—is not correctly blamed in that way. For <term>no one is evil willingly</term> <note>original: "Nemo enim sponte malus." This is a central tenet of Socratic and Platonic philosophy: people only do "evil" because they are mistaken about what is truly "good," often due to physical or educational defects.</note>, but every evil man becomes evil because of some faulty habit of the body and an unrefined education. To everyone, these things are hostile and inimical, and they happen as harmful evils. Again, a soul afflicted by pain falls into much wickedness in a similar way because of the body. For when sharp and hostile phlegm, or bitter and bilious humors, wander through the body and do not find a way out, but are coiled within the viscera, they pour their vapor into the inner chambers of the soul itself, creating various languors of the soul—some greater, some lesser, sometimes more frequent, sometimes fewer.

<margin>E</margin> These humors and vapors are carried to the <term>three seats of the soul</term> <note>The rational soul (head), the spirited soul (chest), and the appetitive soul (belly).</note>, and according to the diversity of the location, each generates various types of difficulty and distress: sometimes audacity, sometimes cowardice; and furthermore, forgetfulness and dullness of mind. Often, to this faulty habit of the physical frame and disposition, there are added the unjust customs of the city and speech—both private and public—that are not a little harmful. Nor are any doctrines learned from a tender age as remedies for such great evils. And so, whichever of us are wicked, we become wicked for two causes that occur most especially against our will; the blame for these evils should be attributed to the "planters" rather than the "planted," and to the educators rather than the educated.

<margin>F</margin> Nevertheless, one must strive with all one’s might, through the diligence of education, pursuits, and doctrines, to reject wickedness and embrace virtue through one’s disposition. But the treatment of these matters belongs to another mode of discourse. Now, conversely, it is proper to explain by what care or causes we may attain health of the body and soul. For it is more just to speak of good things than of evil things. Everything good is beautiful; and the beautiful cannot exist without measure and moderation. Therefore, a living being that is to be good must be moderated by a fitting measure. Of those things which are called "commensurate" or "proportioned," we perceive and judge the small ones,
<margin>G</margin> but the most important and greatest we ignore. Furthermore, for good and bad health, for virtues and vices, no proportion or lack thereof is of greater moment than that of the soul to the body itself. We consider none of these things, nor do we notice that when a weaker and inferior frame carries a robust and great soul, or when these are joined in the opposite way, the whole living being cannot be beautiful, for it lacks the greatest measure and proportion. But the opposite condition is, to anyone capable of seeing it, the most beautiful and lovely of all spectacles. A body that disagrees with itself because of legs that are too large or some other limb exceeding the proper limit is both ugly and, in performing labors, becomes distorted, stumbles, grows weary, falls, and provides the cause of innumerable evils for itself. The same must be judged regarding that composite of soul and body which we call a "living being." For when the soul is much more powerful than the body, it exults in it and carries it away, filling the whole interior with shaking languors. When it also contends in some ambitious competition for learning and investigation, whether privately or publicly, it inflames the body and dissolves it. Sometimes also, by stirring up distillations and fluxes, it deceives most physicians and forces them to judge the causes to be the opposite of what they are.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...or like a fugitive from a city in revolt, falling out of the body, it produces diarrheas and dysenteries, and all such diseases. Thus, the body that is sick mostly from an excess of fire produces continuous heat and fevers; that from air, daily fevers; tertian fevers from water, because it is more sluggish than air and fire; and that from earth—being the most sluggish of these and being purged in four-fold periods of time—produces quartan fevers and is relieved with difficulty. And these are the ways in which bodily diseases occur.

<margin>B</margin> Those regarding the soul, through the habit of the body, are as follows. We must agree that the disease of the soul is <term>folly</term> <note>original: "anoian."</note>. There are two kinds of folly: one is madness, the other is ignorance. Therefore, whatever condition a person falls into that causes either of these must be called a disease of the soul. We must posit that excessive pleasures and pains are the greatest disease for the soul. For a man in excessive joy, or suffering the opposite from pain, hastening unseasonably to seize the one or flee the other, is able neither to see nor to hear anything correctly; he raves and is then least able to partake of reason.

Whoever has seed that is plentiful and flowing about the marrow, like a tree that is naturally more fruitful than is proportionate, acquires many pangs and many pleasures in his desires and in
<margin>C</margin> the "births" concerning such things. Being for the most part of his life driven to madness through these greatest pleasures and pains—having a soul rendered sick and mindless by the body—he is wrongly thought to be evil not as one who is sick, but as one who is evil willingly. But the truth is, lack of restraint in sexual matters has become a disease of the soul, largely due to the condition of a single type of substance, caused by the porousness of the bones making the body fluid and moist. And indeed, almost all things for which lack of control over pleasures is blamed, as if the wicked were so willingly, are not correctly blamed. For no one is evil willingly; but through some wicked habit of the body and an uneducated upbringing, the evil man becomes evil. To every man, these things are hateful and
<margin>D</margin> will turn out to be an evil. And again, concerning pains, the soul likewise acquires much wickedness because of the body. For wherever the humors of sharp and salty phlegm, and all those that are bitter and bilious, wander through the body and do not find a breath-hole outward, but are coiled within, they mix their own vapor with the movement of the soul and are blended with it, producing all kinds of soul-diseases, to a greater or lesser degree, and more or fewer. For being carried to the three regions of the soul, whichever one they fall upon, they diversify the forms of peevishness and despondency of all kinds, and they diversify both audacity and cowardice; and still further, forgetfulness as well as difficulty in learning.

In addition to these things, when men are thus in a bad state of composition, and bad forms of government and bad speeches are spoken in cities both privately and publicly, and further, no medicinal studies for these things are learned from youth, in this way all of us who are evil become evil through two most involuntary causes. Of these, one must always blame the "planters" more than the "planted," and those who nurture more than those who are nurtured. One must strive, however one can, through both upbringing and pursuits and studies, to flee wickedness and seize the opposite. But these things belong to another type of discourse.

Now we must return to the opposite of these: the treatment of bodies and minds, by what causes they are preserved. For it is more just to hold a discourse concerning good things than concerning evil. Everything good is beautiful; and the beautiful is not without measure; therefore, the living being that is to be such must be posited as proportionate. Of things that are proportionate, we perceive and reason about the small ones,
<margin>F</margin> but regarding the most sovereign and greatest, we are without reason. For in respect to health and diseases, virtues and vices, no proportion or lack of measure is greater than that of the soul itself toward the body itself. Of these things we consider nothing, nor do we realize that when a weaker or smaller form carries a soul that is strong and in every way great, or when again the opposite of these are joined together, the whole living being is not beautiful. For it is disproportionate in the greatest proportions. But that which is in the opposite state is, to him who is able to discern it, the most beautiful and lovely of all sights. Just as a body that is over-legged, or has some other disproportionate part in itself, is both ugly and, in its participation in labors, produces much fatigue and many convulsions, and through its
<margin>G</margin> instability causes falls, it is the cause of ten thousand evils to itself.

The same must be thought concerning the "both-together," the living being which we call so: that whenever in it the soul, being stronger than the body, is in a state of high passion, it shakes the whole of it from within and fills it with diseases. And when it goes intensely into certain studies and investigations, it wastes the body away. And again, when it engages in teachings and battles in words publicly and privately through strife and contention, it makes the body inflamed and dissolves it; and by bringing on rheums, it deceives most of those called physicians and makes them blame the opposite causes.

<summary>Plato describes how physical elements cause specific fevers and argues that "no one is evil willingly," as moral failings (like sexual incontinence or anger) are actually diseases caused by bodily imbalances, poor education, and bad societal influences. He emphasizes the necessity of "symmetry" or proportion between a strong soul and a healthy body to achieve true beauty and virtue.</summary>
<keywords>fever, diarrhea, dysentery, dementia, ignorance, insanity, marrow, incontinence, involuntary evil, humors, symmetry, soul-body relationship, education, Timaeus</keywords>

Having established that "no one is willingly evil," Plato now transitions into the practical remedies for these imbalances: the proportional exercise of both body and soul to achieve a state of "beauty and goodness."</meta>

# TIMEO V. S. #

<margin>A</margin> Again, when a body that is great and superior in its sluggish mass is joined to a small and feeble mind, there are two types of natural desires in humans: one for the body, which is for food, and another for the most divine part within us, which is for wisdom. In such a case, the movements of the more powerful part prevail and increase what belongs to it; however, they render the soul's part dull, slow to learn, and forgetful, thereby creating the greatest disease of all: <term>ignorance</term> <note>original: "amathian" (Greek) / "imperitiam" (Latin). Plato views ignorance not just as a lack of data, but as a structural failure of the soul's reasoning ability.</note>. There is but one salvation for both: neither to move the soul without the body, nor the body without the soul, so that by resisting one another they may become balanced and healthy. Therefore, the mathematician or anyone else who intensely works his mind on some other study must also grant movement to his body and engage in <term>gymnastics</term> <note>Broadly referring to physical education and athletics.</note>. <margin>B</margin> Conversely, he who diligently forms and strengthens his body must in turn provide movements to the soul, making use of <term>music</term> <note>In the Greek sense, "Music" includes all the arts overseen by the Muses, including literature and history.</note> and all philosophy, if he is to be rightly called both "beautiful and good" <term>kalos kagathos</term> <note>A central Greek ideal of a "gentleman" who possesses both physical beauty and moral excellence.</note>. One must care for the parts of the body in the same way, imitating the form of the Universe. For since the body is burned within by the things that enter it, or chilled, <margin>C</margin> and is again dried or moistened by things from the outside, and suffers the consequences of both these motions, if a person remains at rest and abandons the body to these movements, he will be overcome and destroyed. But if one imitates that nature which we call the "Nurturer of the Universe" <note>A reference to the *Receptacle* or the underlying nurse of all generation discussed earlier in the dialogue.</note>—never allowing the body to be completely still, but moving it always—one can resist the internal and external motions by a constant shaking. By this moderate agitation, one brings the wandering passions and parts of the body into order and arrangement with one another, according to their kinship. This follows the principle we discussed earlier regarding the Universe: by not placing enemy next to enemy, one will not allow <margin>D</margin> wars and diseases to be stirred up in the body, but rather, by placing friend next to friend, health will be produced and maintained. 

<margin>Which motion is best.</margin>
Of all movements, the best is that which is produced within itself by itself, for this is most akin to the intellectual motion of the Universe. Motion produced by another is inferior. But the worst motion is that which, while the body lies still and at rest, moves the body in parts by the agency of others. Therefore, <margin>D</margin> of all the ways to purge and strengthen the body, that which occurs through gymnastic exercise is the most healthful. Second to this is a gentle transport, whether by ship or any other vehicle that does not cause fatigue. A third species of motion is useful only when extreme necessity compels it, but should otherwise never be accepted by a person of sound mind: <margin>On purgations.</margin> that is the medical purgation performed through <term>pharmaceuticals</term> <note>Drugs or medicinal potions.</note>. <margin>E</margin> For diseases, unless they are very dangerous, should not be provoked by drugs. Indeed, the constitution of diseases resembles, in a way, the nature of living beings. For the composition of animals is limited by specific cycles of time according to their kind; every individual animal is born with a fated lifespan, unless necessary accidents intervene. For the <term>triangles</term> <note>Plato’s physics posits that the elements and tissues are composed of geometric triangles. Aging occurs when these triangles can no longer lock together.</note> of each person possess from the very start a power to endure for a certain time, <margin>E</margin> beyond which no one can extend their life. The same holds true for the constitution of illnesses: if someone tries to cut them short with drugs before their destined course of time, small diseases tend to become great, and few become many. Therefore, one should govern all such things through careful diet and regimen, <margin>Correcting disease through careful diet.</margin> as far as leisure permits, and not provoke a difficult and irritable evil by drugging it. 

Let this be what we have to say concerning the living being as a whole, and its bodily part, and how one might live most rationally by governing oneself and being governed by reason. But that part which is to do the governing must be even more carefully prepared, to the best of one's power, so that it might be as beautiful and excellent as possible for the task of leadership. <margin>F</margin> To discuss this subject with exact precision would be a task in its own right. However, following the tracks of what we have said before, one might reach a suitable conclusion by considering the matter in this way: as we have said many times, there are three types of soul dwelling within us in three locations, and each happens to have its own movements. Now, to speak as briefly as possible, whatever part of these remains idle and keeps still from its own movements must necessarily become very weak, while that which is constantly exercised becomes very strong. Therefore, care must be taken that they keep their movements proportional to one another. 

Regarding the most sovereign part of our soul, we should think of it in this way: that God has given it to each of us as a <term>guiding spirit</term> <note>original: "daimona" (Greek/Latin). Here referring to the highest, rational part of the soul.</note>. <margin>G</margin> We say that this spirit dwells in the highest citadel of our body and lifts us up from the earth toward our kinship in heaven, for we are not an earthly plant, but a heavenly one. And this is most rightly said. For from that place where the first generation of the soul arose, the Divine hangs our head as a root, and thus keeps the whole body upright. Now, for the man who is engrossed in his appetites or ambitions and labors at them intensely, all his thoughts must necessarily become mortal; and as much as it is possible to become entirely mortal, he will fall not a bit short of it, having increased his mortal nature. But for him who has been zealous for the love of learning and true wisdom, and has exercised these parts of himself most, he must—if he lays hold of truth—think thoughts that are immortal and divine. Indeed, it is necessary that... <margin>H</margin>

<column-break/>

A Again, when a body is large and exceeds its small and weak soul in sluggish mass, there are two types of desires natural to man: one through the body for nourishment, the other through that which is most divine in us, for prudence. In this case, the more powerful movements of the body prevail and increase what belongs to them, but they render the soul's part dull, unteachable, and forgetful, and thus they generate the greatest infirmity, which is ignorance. There is finally only one salvation for both: that we move neither the soul without the body, nor the body without the soul, so that in mutual contention, with their powers equalized, they may protect the good health of the whole. Therefore, whoever gives his effort to B mathematical doctrines or any other intense mental investigation must also employ the motion of the body and engage in gymnastic exercise. And again, he who forms and strengthens the body with the greatest diligence must in turn add the movements of the soul, using music and all the studies of philosophy, if indeed one is to be rightly called both good and beautiful. In like manner, we ought to care for the parts, imitating the appearance of the whole. For since the body is burned within by things entering it, or becomes cold, C and again is rendered dry or moist by external things, and suffers what follows from these, when someone leads a life of leisure and commits the body to these motions, he is overcome by them and dissolved. But if one, in caring for the body, imitates that nature which we call the "nurturer of the universe," so that he never allows it to be sluggish but moves it always, and with a perpetual agitation resists both the internal and external motions according to nature, and by a certain moderate commotion brings the wandering passions and parts of the body back into order and adornment by preserving the ratio of their kinship, following that higher discourse we had concerning the universe, he will by no means allow enemy to stir up battles and diseases against enemy D in the body, but will instead ensure that friend clinging to friend protects the health of the body. <margin>Which of the motions is best.</margin> Of all motions, the best is that which occurs in itself from itself. For it is most akin to the motion of the mind and the universe itself. That which is produced by another is inferior. The worst motion, however, is when the body lies at rest and quiet and is moved by others in its parts. Therefore, of all the purifications and constitutions of the body, that which is done through gymnastic exercise is the most healthful. Closely following this is an easy transport, whether performed by ship or any other vehicle. A third species of commotion is only then to be used when extreme necessity compels it, but should in no way be undertaken by a man of sound mind. <margin>Concerning purifications.</margin> That is the physicians' purification, which is usually done with drugs, E that is, loosening medicines. For unless diseases are very dangerous, they are not to be provoked with drugs. For every constitution of diseases is in some way similar to the nature of living beings. Indeed, the composition of animals is bounded by certain cycles of time from the very beginning of their generation: and this the whole genus suffers, and every single animal contains within itself from its birth a fated span of living, except for necessary passions. For the triangles possessing power from the very beginning of each individual cohere sufficiently for the use of life until a certain time, beyond which life is prolonged for no one. The same mode of constitution applies to illnesses. If anyone strives to amputate these with drugs before such a course of time, they are accustomed to turn from small to great, and from few to many. Therefore, diseases are to be corrected and governed by diligence of diet, <margin>Diseases are to be corrected by diligence of diet.</margin> as leisure is given to each, and this difficult and weapon-like evil is not to be provoked with drugs. And concerning the common living being and its bodily part—by what diligence they are to be ruled and governed so that the rational way of living is preserved—let these things be said. But that which is to govern must itself be instructed much more and much earlier, according to its powers, so that it is prepared as excellently and beautifully as possible for ruling. An exact discussion of this matter would require its own complete dispute. However, as far as it pertains to what we are dealing with, if one walks through the tracks of what came before, he will arrive at the proper end of these things most profitably. We have often said in what preceded that there are three species of soul in us distributed in three ways, and each has its own movements. So now let us conclude in a few words: whichever of them is sluggish and acts at leisure from its own movements, is necessarily rendered most weak; but that which acts assiduously is made most robust. Therefore, work must be given so that each species preserves its movements among themselves, moderated with a suitable tenor. Concerning the most excellent species of our soul, we must think thus: namely, that God gave this to each as our guiding spirit; we say this has its seat in the highest H citadel of the body, and lifts us from the earth to our kinship with heaven, as beings born of a heavenly rather than an earthly seed. Which indeed is very rightly said. For from where the first origin of the soul was given, from there the divine power, suspending our head as our root and origin, directs the whole body. In him, therefore, who is occupied in fulfilling the passions of desire and ambitious anger, all opinions must necessarily become mortal, and he will even become as mortal as it is possible to be, since he has increased his mortal nature to his utmost power. But he who has been entirely inflamed with the desire for learning truth, and all his...

# PLATO'S #

<column-break/>

...has focused his efforts primarily on this one thing, it is entirely necessary—provided he touches the truth—that he comprehend things immortal and divine. Insofar as human nature is capable of attaining immortality, he should become fully immortal, leaving no part of immortality behind. Moreover, since he always cultivates the divine and keeps the <term>daemon</term> <note>original: "daemonem" (Latin) / "daimona" (Greek). Here, Plato refers to the highest part of the soul, the intellect, which acts as a personal guardian spirit or inner divinity.</note> within himself in perfect order, he shall be exceptionally blessed. Now, the cultivation of everything is always one: to provide each with its proper nourishment and motion. To the divine part within us, the kindred motions are the thoughts and revolutions of the universe itself. Following these, each of us ought to correct those circuits in our head that were corrupted at the time of our first birth, by learning the harmonies and revolutions of the world. Through this understanding, we should make the thinking subject similar to the object of thought, according to its original nature. By achieving this likeness, we fulfill the goal of the best life set before us by the Gods, both for the present and the future. But now, that discussion of the universe, which we proposed to carry through to the generation of mankind, seems to have nearly reached its end.

<margin>
On the generation of women.
</margin>
As for the generation of the other living creatures, we shall touch upon them briefly, only so far as necessity requires. In this way, one may seem to maintain a proper measure in this discussion. Let us speak of them thus: All those men who lived unjustly or cowardly, as a probable account shows us, were transformed into women in their second birth <note>Plato presents a theory of "devolution" or reincarnation, where your form in the next life depends on your conduct in this one.</note>. It was at that time, and for this reason, that the gods fashioned the love of sexual intercourse. Thus, they composed one living being endowed with soul in men, and another in women. The gods derived the passage for drink—which flows through the lungs, beneath the kidneys, into the bladder, and is discharged with the breath—and channeled it like a pipe into the compacted marrow that runs from the head down the neck and spine, which in our previous discussions we called <term>Sperma</term> <note>original: "Sperma" (Greek/Latin for "seed"). Plato views semen as a portion of the brain/spinal marrow.</note>.

<margin>
On the seed.
</margin>
This marrow, being alive and possessing a "breath" <note>The "pneuma" or vital spirit.</note>, creates a vital desire for discharge at the point where it breathes out, and thus implanted in us the love of procreation.

<margin>
The desire for procreation.
</margin>
Wherefore, the nature of the private parts in men is stubborn and self-willed, like a creature that does not listen to reason, and it attempts to dominate everything through the violence of its frenzied lusts. In the same way, what are called the <term>vulva</term> and <term>matrix</term> <note>Terms for the womb.</note> in women are like a living animal within them that is eager to bear children. When it remains without fruit for a long time beyond its proper season, it becomes distressed and highly indignant. Wandering everywhere throughout the body, it blocks the passages of the breath, prevents respiration, afflicts the body with extreme distress, and burdens it with all kinds of diseases <note>This describes the "Wandering Womb," a common medical theory in antiquity used to explain what was then called "hysteria."</note>, until the desire and love of both sexes bring them together to pluck the fruit from the tree, as it were. They then sow into the womb—as if into a field—living creatures that are at first invisible due to their smallness and unformed state; soon they unfold what they had joined together, nourish them until they are large within, and finally bring them out into the light, thus completing the generation of animals.

<margin>
The generation of birds.
</margin>
In this manner, women and all that is female were created. The race of birds was refashioned from our own type, but with feathers instead of hair. Into these were transformed those men who were simple and innocent, but light-minded—those who were curious about things in the heavens but were so foolish as to believe that the most certain proofs of such things could be demonstrated solely through the judgment of the eyes <note>i.e., people who relied on mere appearance rather than mathematical/philosophical reasoning.</note>.

<margin>
The generation of wild beasts.
</margin>
The race of land animals and wild beasts was born from those men who, being entirely alien to philosophy, never turned their eyes toward the heavens because they no longer used the intellectual revolutions in their heads, but followed the parts of the soul dominant in the belly and chest. Because of these habits, their front limbs and heads were drawn toward the ground by their natural kinship; they developed elongated and various-shaped skulls where the circuits of their souls were crushed and broken through inactivity. Their race was made four-footed or even many-footed, as God provided more points of support for the more foolish ones, so they might be even more drawn toward the earth. Those who were the most foolish of all, who stretched their whole bodies upon the ground as if they had no further need of feet, were changed into footless creatures that crawl upon the earth.

<margin>
The generation of aquatic animals.
</margin>
The fourth kind is the aquatic race, born from those who were the most mindless and ignorant of all. Those who transformed them did not even deem them worthy of breathing pure air, because they possessed souls made utterly impure by all sorts of transgressions. Therefore, instead of the thin and pure breathing of air, they were thrust into the deep and murky breathing of water. From this arose the multitude of fish, oysters, and all aquatic creatures, who received the lowest habitations as a penalty for their extreme ignorance. In this way, both then and now, living creatures change into one another, being transformed as they lose or gain mind and folly. Let our discussion of the universe now have its end. For this world, having received both mortal and immortal living things and being filled with them, has at last become a visible animal containing all visible things—an image of the intelligible God, a perceptible god, greatest, best, most beautiful, and most perfect: this one, only-begotten Heaven.

<column-break/>

->A<-

...to partake of immortality as much as human nature allows, leaving no part of it behind. And because he is always attending to the divine, and has the <term>daemon</term> dwelling within him well-ordered, he must be supremely happy. Now there is but one way to care for everything: to assign to each its proper nourishment and motions. The motions akin to the divine part in us are the thoughts and revolutions of the universe. These every man ought to follow, correcting the revolutions in the head which were damaged at birth, by learning the harmonies and revolutions of the universe. By this learning, he should make the seer like the thing seen, according to his original nature; and having made them alike, he attains the goal of the best life offered to men by the gods, for the present and the future. And so, the task assigned to us at the beginning—to describe the universe down to the generation of man—seems now to have reached its end. For we must mention briefly how the other animals came to be, unless there is a need to be lengthy. In this way, one might seem to strike the right balance. Let it be told as follows: Of the men who were born, those who were cowards and lived unjustly were transformed into women in the second generation. At that time, for this reason, the gods devised the love of intercourse, fashioning an animate creature, one in us and one in women. They did this in the following way: the passage for drink, where it receives liquid through the lungs under the kidneys into the bladder and emits it with the pressure of the breath, they connected to the marrow that had been solidified from the head through the neck and along the spine—which we called "seed" in our previous accounts. This seed, being alive and having found an outlet, created a vital desire for discharge at the place where it breathed, and so produced the love of procreation. Wherefore in men, the nature of the genitals, being disobedient and self-willed, like a creature that will not listen to reason, attempts to master everything with its stinging lusts. Likewise in women, the so-called womb and matrix, for the same reason, is an animal within them desiring child-bearing; when it remains unfruitful for a long time beyond its season, it becomes disgruntled and angry, and wandering all over the body, it blocks the air passages and prevents breathing, bringing on extreme distress and all kinds of diseases, until the desire and love of both, like fruit from a tree, pluck and sow into the womb as into a field invisible and unformed animals, which they then distinguish and nourish until they are large, finally bringing them to light and completing the generation of animals. Thus women and the whole female sex were born. The race of birds was remolded, growing feathers instead of hair, from men who were innocent but light-minded—those who studied the heavens but thought that the most solid proofs of these things were through sight, because of their simple-mindedness. The land-dwelling and wild animals came from those who made no use of philosophy and never looked at the nature of the heavens, because they no longer used the circuits in their heads but followed the parts of the soul in the chest. From these practices, they had their front limbs and heads drawn to the earth by their natural affinity and fixed there; and they grew elongated or various shapes of heads, wherever the revolutions of each were crushed through idleness. The four-footed race was produced from this, as god gave more feet to the more mindless, to draw them more toward the earth. To the most mindless of these, whose bodies were stretched entirely on the ground as if they had no more need for feet, they gave birth to footless things that crawl on the earth. The fourth race, the aquatic ones, came from those who were the most senseless and ignorant, whom the transformers no longer thought worthy of pure breath, as they had souls made impure by all sorts of errors; instead of the thin and pure breathing of air, they were pushed into the murky and deep breathing of water. Hence the race of fish and oysters and all water creatures arose, having received the furthest dwellings as a punishment for the furthest ignorance. According to these things, all animals then and now change into one another, being transformed by the loss or gain of intellect and folly. And now let us say that our account of the universe has its end. For having received both mortal and immortal animals, and having been filled with them, this world has thus become a visible animal containing the visible, the image of the intelligible god, perceptible, greatest and best, most beautiful and most perfect, this one heaven, being only-begotten.

<meta>This page transitions from the conclusion of Plato’s dialogue *Timaeus* to a supplemental treatise attributed to Timaeus of Locri himself. While the previous page ended Plato's "likely account" of the cosmos, this text—titled *On the Soul of the World and Nature*—was historically believed to be the original Pythagorean source that Plato used as his model, though modern scholars often view it as a later work written in the Pythagorean style.</meta>

# TIMAEUS OF LOCRI
## ON THE SOUL OF THE WORLD,
### and Nature.

# OF TIMAEUS OF LOCRI
## ON THE SOUL OF THE WORLD,
### That is, Nature.

> *We have inserted this small book, which was missing from the copies of Ficino <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the influential Renaissance scholar who translated Plato into Latin.</note>, having borrowed it from elsewhere. This Timaeus of Locri was a Pythagorean philosopher and, as it appears, most skilled in a purer form of philosophy; thus, Plato not undeservedly set him before himself as a sort of archetype in explaining physical matters. Regarding the time in which he lived, there is doubt: some believe he was older than Plato, others that he was his contemporary <note>original: "σύγχρονον" (synchronon)</note>.*

---

<margin>A</margin>
Timaeus of Locri said these things: That there are two causes of all things. One is Mind, which governs things that come to be according to reason; the other is Necessity, which governs things that exist by force, according to the powers and faculties of bodies. Of these, he said that the one belonging to the nature of the Good is called God, the principle of the best things; but those things which follow and act as assisting causes are reduced to Necessity. He taught that the universe consists of the Idea, Matter, and the Sensible <note>The "Sensible" refers to the physical world we can perceive with our senses.</note>, which is like the offspring of the first two. The Idea is unbegotten, immobile, and constant; it belongs to the nature of the "Same" and is the intelligible model for all generated things that exist in a state of change. For such a thing is what the <term>Idea</term> <note>In this context, an Idea is an eternal, perfect blueprint or pattern in the divine mind.</note> is said to be and is understood to be. Matter, however, is the impression-bearer, the mother, the nurse, and the receptable for the generation of the third essence. For by receiving the likenesses into itself and, as it were, taking their impress, it brings all generated things to completion.
<margin>B</margin>
He said that this Matter is eternal, yet not immobile; by itself it is formless and without shape, yet it is capable of receiving every form. Regarding bodies, it is divisible and partakes in the nature of the "Other." They call Matter both "Place" and "Space." These two, then, are contrary principles. The Idea (or Form) holds the role of the male and the father, while Matter holds the role of the female and the mother. The third things are the offspring born from these. Since there are these three, they are known in three ways: the Form is known by the mind and through science; Matter is known by a kind of "bastard reasoning" <note>original: "λογισμῷ νόθῳ" (logismō nothō). This refers to a type of intuition that tries to grasp something (like pure space or matter) that has no qualities of its own.</note>, because it is not perceived directly but through a kind of analogy; and the offspring are known through sensation and opinion. Before the Heavens existed, the Form and Matter existed in reason, and God was the craftsman of the better state. Since that which is older is superior to the younger, and order is superior to disorder, God—being good—saw that Matter was receiving the Form and changing in various but disordered ways. He saw that it was necessary to bring it into order, leading it from undefined changes to a fixed state, so that the distinctions between bodies might correspond to one another and not receive changes by mere chance. He created this world out of the whole of Matter, making it the boundary of the nature of all things, because it contains all other things within itself. It is one, unique, perfect, endowed with a soul and reason (for a nature with soul and reason is better than one without) and it has a spherical body, for this shape is more perfect than all others. Because he wished to produce the most beautiful offspring, he made this a "generated god," never to be destroyed by any cause other than the God who composed it, should He ever wish to dissolve it. But it is not the nature of a good parent to be driven to the destruction of a most beautiful offspring.
<margin>D</margin>
Therefore, the world remains constantly as it was created by God: free from corruption and death, blessed, the best of all generated things. It came from the best cause, which did not look toward models made by human hands, but toward that Idea and intelligible essence. When things are modeled after such a pattern with exquisite reason, they become most beautiful and do not need to be improved by new efforts. The world is always perfect in comparison to sensible things. Because the Model contains all living beings within itself, it left nothing else outside; this Model is the perfect boundary of intelligible things, just as this world is the boundary of sensible things. Furthermore, it is solid, and of such a kind that it can be touched and seen; therefore, it has been allotted Earth and Fire, and those which come between earth and fire, Air and Water. It is composed of perfect bodies, which exist entirely within it, so that no part is left outside. Thus, the body of the universe is most absolute, so that nothing may be lacking within it, and it is in no way liable to destruction from external causes. For there are no other things apart from earth, fire, and the two intermediate elements. These are held together by a formula of the best proportion, in a kind of equal power, so that they neither dominate one another nor are dominated by one another in parts, such that some would increase and others diminish; rather, they remain bound by an indissoluble framework, constricted by the bond of the highest reason. For when there are three terms and the intervals are distant from each other by that same ratio, then we see the middle term acts like a ray: as the first is to the second, so the second is to the third. This works conversely and when the intervals are swapped, provided the order of places is preserved.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
Timaeus of Locri said these things: That there are two causes of all things: Mind, for those things which are born through reason, and Necessity for those things that exist by force, according to the powers and faculties of bodies. Of these things—that is, the nature of the goods—the best is a certain principle of the best things, and it is called God. But those things which follow and come as helping causes are reduced to Necessity. For all things are Idea, Matter, and the Sensible, which is like their offspring. This [the Idea] is indeed unbegotten and immobile. There is, moreover, in this totality of nature, something that remains and is intelligible—a model for generated things, which indeed exist in a certain perpetual flux of changes. In these successions of individual things, such a constant and perpetual model is called the Idea and is comprehended by the mind. Matter, however, is the expressed likeness of things, both mother and nurse, and fit for the generation of the third essence. For when it has received the forms of things into itself and, as it were, imprinted them, it produces these offspring. He said that this Matter is eternal, but not immobile; it is free and exempt from every form and figure by itself, yet it receives any forms whatsoever. Concerning bodies, it is divisible and partakes of the nature of the "Other." They call Matter both "Place" and "Seat." These two are therefore contrary principles. The Idea (that is, the Form) has the ratio of the male and the father; Matter has that of the female and the mother. The third is the essence of those things which, like offspring, are born from these. Since these three exist, they are also known in three ways:
<margin>C</margin>
The Form is known by the mind and by science; Matter by a certain "adulterous" ratiocination (because it is understood not by a straight and equal observation of the thing, but from a certain proportion and comparison); and the offspring which are born from them are known by sense and opinion. Before the Heaven existed, there were by reason the Form and the Matter, and indeed that God was the maker of the better. Since, therefore, the older is more excellent than the younger, and that which is ordered more than the disordered, God—since he is indeed good—saw Matter receiving the form and being altered, variously indeed, but nevertheless inordinately. He saw also that it was necessary that he himself should reduce it into order, and establish it from undefined changes to a certain and defined state: so that the distinctions of the bodies might correspond to each other by mutual reason, and not receive changes haphazardly back and forth. God created this world out of all the matter, and circumscribed and defined the nature of the universe as the limit itself: because indeed it embraces all other things in itself, being that it is one, only-begotten, perfect, endowed with soul and reason (for thus it was going to be better than that which is void of soul and reason) with a spherical body (for this figure is more perfect than all other figures). Therefore, since God wished to produce the most beautiful offspring, he made this a "generated God," never to be corrupted by another cause, except by the God who composed it, if ever he should wish to dissolve it. But it is not the part of a good parent to be driven to the destruction of his own offspring, and that a most beautiful one.
<margin>E</margin>
Therefore, the world remains constantly such as it was created by God: free from all corruption and death, blessed, the best of all generated things. Since it existed from the best cause, which proposed to itself not certain models produced by the handiwork of hands, but that intelligible Idea and essence: to which, indeed, when things themselves were made by a certain exquisite reason, they became most beautiful, and of such a kind that they ought not to be amended by any new work. The world is always perfect in comparison to sensible things: because also that Model, which embraces all living animals in itself, left nothing else outside. This Model is the perfect limit of intelligible things, just as this world is the limit of sensible things. Furthermore, it is solid, and of such a kind that it can both be touched and seen: and accordingly it has been allotted Earth and Fire, and those which come in between earth and fire, Air and Water. It is constituted of perfect bodies, which exist entirely within it, so that no part is left outside of it: so that it may be the most absolute body of the universe, so that nothing can be desired in it, and it is in no way subject to destruction, beyond all harm of death. For there are no other things separately from earth and fire, and the two other intermediate elements. For they themselves, from the formula of the best proportion, are contained by a certain equal power among themselves, so that they neither contain nor are contained by part among themselves mutually, so that some take increase and others diminution, but indeed they remain constricted by a certain indissoluble frame, the bond of a certain best reason. For when there are three terms, and the intervals also are distant from each other by that same reason: then indeed we see the middle like a ray to the first, as the third is to itself: and by a contrary turn, and with the intervals changed, they will be joined, the order of places being preserved.
