<meta>This page continues the Pythagorean treatise on "The Soul of the World and Nature," attributed to Timaeus of Locri. Having established the primary causes of the universe, the text now transitions into the mathematical and geometrical construction of the cosmos, specifically the creation of the World Soul and the mechanics of celestial motion. This mirrors the complex "Lambda" proportions found in Plato's Timaeus.</meta>

# TIMAEUS OF LOCRI

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> To recount these things in such a way that the numbers and, as it were, the joints <note>The author uses "articuli" (Latin) or "ἄρθρα" (Greek) to describe the mathematical ratios as the 'joints' or 'limbs' of the soul's structure.</note> of these proportions are understood is impossible unless the things, endowed with an equal power, are set before the eyes in a descriptive diagram. Such a method of teaching is suitable for representing both the logic of the world's shape and its motion. Insofar as the World is a spherical shape—and thus similar to itself in every direction—it is certainly capable of containing all other shapes of the same kind. Furthermore, it maintains a certain perpetual tenor through its circular motion. Only a spherical or circular shape is able, whether resting or moving, to be composed in the same place with a fitting measure, so that it never fails or <margin>B</margin> moves into any other place; this is because all parts are at equal distances from the center itself. Since it is perfectly smooth and entirely uniform, so that nothing is lacking for total and perfect equality, it does not require the mortal instruments <note>original: "mortalibus instrumentis" / "θνατῷ ὀργάνων" – referring to limbs like arms or legs.</note> that are fitted and adapted for the practical use of other living creatures.

God placed the Soul of the world in its center and extended it outward; he covered the entire universe with it, having mixed it with a certain temperament. This was composed of an indivisible form and a divisible <margin>C</margin> essence, so that a single temperament exists from these two. Into this mixture, he blended two powers as the principles of motion: the "Same" and the "Other." <note>The "Same" (Idem) refers to the uniform motion of the fixed stars, while the "Other" (Alterum) refers to the diverse motions of the planets.</note> This Soul, because it does not easily accept being mixed, did not readily coalesce into the formula of this temperament. All these ratios are blended according to harmonic numbers, which the Maker distinguished appropriately with certain signs of knowledge, so that the constitution of this world-soul would not be unknown.

God did not arrange this Soul to come after the bodily essence, as we might say—for that which is more honorable and august in both power and time is prior—but he created it as the elder. He did so in this order: since there were four primary units, he took one from them, reaching toward eight tens and three hundreds. <note>This refers to a complex Pythagorean calculation involving the sum of the geometric and harmonic progressions used to "map" the soul.</note> It is easy to gather the double and triple of this once the first number is established. All these numbers, with their supplements and "sesquioctaves" <note>A sesquioctave (9:8 ratio) corresponds to a whole tone in musical theory.</note>, must be <margin>D</margin> thirty-six terms; the entire number becomes one hundred and fourteen thousand, six hundred and ninety-five. These divisions are as follows: 114,695.

In this manner, he divided the soul of the universe. Furthermore, only the Mind sees God as the chief author and parent of all these sacred things. But that which is generated, we see with our eyes: this world and its parts. The chief parts are the Heavens, which are themselves divided in two: some are of the nature of the "Same," and some of the "Other." Some of these lead all internal things from the outside, moving from East to West in a universal <margin>E</margin> motion. Those which belong to the motion of the "Other" return from West to East within, moving with their own peculiar motion. They are rotated accidentally by the motion of the "Same," which has the more dominant power in the world.

This motion of the "Other," distributed through harmonic ratios, is distinguished by seven circular ranks. The Moon, being the lowest of all and approaching closer to the earth, completes its circle monthly. The Sun completes its circle in a year's time. Two others travel at a pace equal to the Sun: the stars of Mercury and Juno—which the common people call Venus or the Morning Star <note>original: "Luciferum" / "φωσφόρον" (Phosphorus)</note>. For not every group of men is educated in the laws of astronomical knowledge, nor <margin>F</margin> do they skillfully know the differences between the risings and settings of stars. For the same star is sometimes the Evening Star <gloss>.i. the setting one</gloss> <note>original: "Vesperus" / "ἕσπερος" (Hesperus)</note> when it follows the Sun so that it is visible to us while the Sun hides its own light; and sometimes it is called the Morning Star <gloss>.i. the eastern one</gloss> when it precedes the approaching Sun and rises first at dawn. Therefore, the star of Venus is often the Morning Star because it is carried in the same course as the Sun. Yet it is not the only "Lucifer," for many stars, both fixed and wandering, perform this role. Indeed, every star of sufficient magnitude that stands above the horizon before the Sun announces the day.

Now, the other three planets—namely Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn—have their own unique speeds and unequal years. They finish their courses in proper spaces so they can be perceived with certain knowledge, appearing, hiding, and failing <note>This refers to planetary "stations" and retrograde motion where a planet seems to stop or disappear.</note> at fixed times, creating true risings and settings. They perform clear appearances in the East and West relative to the Sun, which provides the day by its course from east to west, and the night in the opposite way, from west to east. The Sun is carried by that motion of the "Same," but the year is defined by its own peculiar motion. From these two motions, <margin>G</margin> the Sun completes a double course: while it is carried around by the universal motion of the heavens, it also involves itself in a spiral and a circle by an oblique motion. This oblique motion designates the seasons and differences of the days; but while it is swept around by the rapid motion of the fixed stars, it creates Night and Day with every circuit.

These are the parts of time, which he calls "circuits." God ordered time along with the world itself. For the stars did not exist before time, nor consequently did the year, nor the seasons of the year distinguished by certain circuits, by which this generated time is defined. Time is the image of ungenerated time, which we call Eternity. For just as this Universe was created according to the model of the intelligible world, so this time was established with the world by the Maker according to the model of Eternity.

Furthermore, the Earth is established in the middle, the hearth of the gods, the boundary of night and day; it generates settings and risings according to the sections of the horizons... <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence, continuing on the next page.</note>

<summary>This page describes the geometrical and mathematical creation of the World Soul using harmonic ratios, explaining why the universe is spherical and how the seven planets move. It establishes Time as a "moving image of Eternity," created simultaneously with the physical world.</summary>
<keywords>World Soul, Harmony, Spherical Geometry, Same and Other, Astronomy, Venus, Lucifer, Hesperus, Time, Eternity, Timaeus of Locri</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the technical description of the world's physical construction. Having previously discussed the World Soul, the text now shifts to the "building blocks" of matter—geometric triangles—and how they form the four elements (Earth, Water, Air, and Fire). This follows the Pythagorean and Platonic tradition of seeing the universe as a mathematical masterpiece.</meta>

### ON THE SOUL OF THE WORLD.

Earth is the most ancient of the bodies within the heavens. Water never comes into being without Earth, nor does Air without moisture. Fire, too, if deprived of moisture and the matter it burns, could not be expected to sustain itself. Thus, Earth was firmly established at the very center as the root and foundation of all things. Of all things that are created, <term>Matter</term><note>The underlying "stuff" of the universe, which has no shape of its own.</note> acts as the subject, while the <term>Idea</term><note>The divine blueprint or formal cause.</note> acts as the ratio of form. From these are born the bodies: Earth, Water, Air, and Fire. Their nature is as follows: every body is composed of planes, and these planes are made of triangles. 

One of these is the right-angled isosceles triangle, which is half of a square. The other is a scalene triangle, which has its larger side triple the power of the smaller side. Its smallest angle is one-third of a right angle; the middle angle is double that (two-thirds of a right angle); and the largest is a right angle itself. This scalene triangle is half of an equilateral triangle, formed when an equilateral triangle is cut down the middle from its vertex to its base. In this triangle, the sides are unequal. Let this be called the <term>Scalene</term><note>Literally "crooked" or "uneven" in the original Greek.</note> triangle. The half-square, on the other hand, was the origin for the construction of Earth; for a square is composed of four of these half-squares joined together. 

From the square is generated the <term>Cube</term>, the most stable of all bodies, having six sides and eight angles. Because of this, Earth is the heaviest element and the hardest to move; it cannot be transformed into any other element because it does not share the same triangular "DNA" as the others. Only Earth has the half-square as its unique element. The element for the other bodies—Fire, Air, and Water—is the half-equilateral triangle; when six of these are joined, they form an equilateral triangle. From this, the <term>Pyramid</term><note>In modern geometry, we call this a tetrahedron.</note> is constructed, having four bases and equal angles—this is the form of Fire, which is the most mobile and has the finest parts. After this is the <term>Octahedron</term>, with eight bases and six angles, which is the element of Air. The third is the <term>Icosahedron</term>, with twenty bases and twelve angles, the element of Water, which has many parts and is heavy. 

Since these three are composed of the same basic triangle, they can be transformed into one another. However, the <term>Dodecahedron</term><note>A twelve-sided solid.</note> was used as the image of the Universe itself, as it most closely resembles a sphere. Because of its fine parts, Fire penetrates through everything; Air penetrates the others except Fire; and Water penetrates through the Earth. All things are full, leaving no vacuum. These bodies are swept along by the rotation of the universe, rubbing against and alternating with one another, providing a constant change of birth and decay.

Using these materials, God constructed this world. It can be felt because of Earth and seen because of Fire—these are the two extremes. Through Air and Water, he bound the world together with the strongest bond: <term>Proportion</term><note>original: "harmonia" / "ἁρμονίᾳ". In this context, it refers to mathematical ratios that hold the elements in balance.</note>. This bond holds both itself and the things it masters together. If the thing to be bound were a simple plane, one middle term would be enough; but since it is a solid, it requires two middle terms. Thus, he arranged the two extremes with two means: as Fire is to Air, Air is to Water; and as Air is to Water, Water is to Earth. This works in reverse and in alternation as well: as Earth is to Air, Water is to Fire. Since all are equal in power, their ratios exist in a state of equal law. Thus, this world is a single entity, held together by a divine bond of proportion.

Each of the four bodies has many species. Fire appears as flame, light, and radiance, due to the inequality of the triangles within each. Air is sometimes pure and dry, and sometimes cloudy and misty. Water can be fluid or frozen—such as snow, frost, hail, and ice. Of liquids, some are thin like honey or oil, others are thick like pitch or wax. Of the solid species, some are meltable, like gold, silver, copper, tin, lead, and <term>Sagona</term><note>A term for refined or "purified" iron.</note>; others are brittle, like sulfur, bitumen, nitre, salt, alum, and similar stones.

After the world was constructed, God planned the creation of mortal living beings, so that the world might be perfect, having been made fully according to the divine Image. He tempered and divided the human soul from the same ratios and powers as the World Soul, but he handed over the task of making it to <term>Nature</term><note>The "changing" or "mortal" creative force.</note>, which receives and passes on what is perishable. Nature took up the task of making mortal and short-lived creatures, bringing in their souls as a kind of "flow"—some from the Moon, some from the Sun, and some from the other planets wandering in the region of the "Other." He reserved one part of the soul, endowed with the power of the "Same," which he mixed into the rational part as an image of wisdom for those who are fortunate. For in the human soul, one part is rational and intelligent, while the other is irrational and unthinking. Of the rational part, the better portion comes from the nature of the "Same," while the lesser comes from the "Other." Both are seated in the head, so that the other parts of the soul and body may serve this part, just as the rest of a ship is subject to the captain.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Indeed, the most ancient of all things in this universe is the body of Earth; for Water was not born without Earth, nor was Air born without moisture. Fire, being destitute of moisture as the material by which it is inflamed, could by no means subsist. Therefore, Earth, the root of all and the firmament of the others, was stabilized at the same moment. Of created things, then, the subject is Matter; but the ratio and proportion of form is the Idea. Their offspring are the Bodies: namely Earth, Water, Air, and Fire. Their generation and production are of this kind. Every body consists of planes; and these consist of Triangles. One is a right-angled triangle of equal sides, a half-square. The other is of unequal <margin>B</margin> sides, having its larger angle triple in power to the smaller. The smallest angle in it is the third part of a right angle; the middle is double this, being two third-parts; the largest is a right angle, having a <term>sesquialter</term><note>A ratio of 1.5 to 1 (or 3:2).</note> proportion to the middle and being triple the minimum. This triangle is a half-equilateral triangle, insofar as it is compared with an equilateral triangle cut in two by a perpendicular line from the vertex to the bottom into equal parts. There are two right-angled triangles in each; but in one, only the two sides forming the right angle are equal, while in the other, all three sides are unequal. This figure may be called "Oblique." The half-square was the principle for the <margin>C</margin> constitution of Earth. For a square is composed of these four squares. From the square, the <term>Cube</term> is generated, the most firm and stationary of all bodies, so that it cannot be moved in any direction; it has six sides and eight angles. This is certainly the element for the constitution of Earth: heaviest and difficult to move, such that it cannot be transmuted into any other body because it has no community with any other kind of triangle. For Earth alone has the half-square as its own peculiar element. This is further the element of other bodies: Fire, Air, and Water. For when the half-equilateral is combined six times, <margin>D</margin> a triangle of equal legs is formed from it; from this the pyramid, which has four bases and equal angles, is composed—the species of fire, most mobile and of the thinnest parts. After this, that which consists of eight seats, having eight bases and [six] angles, is the element of Air. The third, which has twenty sides, twenty bases, and twelve angles, is the element of Water, of the most numerous and heaviest parts. These, being composed of the same element, are changed into one another. But that which consists of twelve seats established the image of the Universe, as it most closely <margin>E</margin> approaches a spherical figure. Fire, therefore, because of the thinness of its parts, penetrates through all things; Air likewise through other elements, except fire; Water, however, through the earth. All things are therefore full, and they leave nothing of a vacuum. They are whirled around by that rapid motion of the universe, and being firmed, they are rubbed against one another in turn, and perform an unending alteration toward birth and destruction. Using the ministry and work of these, God constructed this world. This world can be touched because of Earth and seen because of Fire: which two are the extremes. Through Air and Water, by the proportion of a certain very firm bond, he bound the world together, which constrains both itself and those things which are contained by it. If, therefore, <margin>F</margin> that which is bound were a plane, one middle term would be enough; but if a solid, it requires two. Therefore, he adapted the two extremes to the two means, so that they were as Fire is to Air, Air is to Water, and Water is to Earth; and conversely, as Fire is to Water, Air is to Earth; and conversely, as Earth is to Water, Water is to Air, and Air is to Fire; and conversely, as Earth is to Air, Water is to Fire. Since all things are equal in power, their whole ratios are in equality. Thus, this one world consists by the proportion of a certain happy and clearly divine bond. Furthermore, each of these four bodies has many species. Fire indeed <margin>G</margin> has flame, light, and splendor, because of the inequality of the triangles which are in each of them. In the same way also Air: part is pure and dry, part is humid and cloudy. Water also: some is fluid, some is congealed, such as snow, hail, and ice. Of moisture, some is thin, like honey or oil; another is compact, like pitch or wax. Of the compact species, one is fusile (meltable), like gold, silver, copper, tin, lead, and a kind of refined iron which they call <term>Sagona</term>; another is fragile, like sulfur, bitumen, nitre, salt, alum, and stones of the same kind. Now, after the constitution of the world, God strived for the generation of mortal animals, so that it might be perfect and absolute according to that image. He distributed the human soul, tempered and divided from the same ratios and powers, assigning this ministry to the "altering" Nature. Nature, having received the commands of these things, took the place of the Creator himself in making mortal and ephemeral animals, into which it instilled souls as if by a certain flux. Thus it led some from the Moon, some from the Sun, and some from the other stars that wander in the part of the "Other." He excepted one soul, which is endowed with the power of the "Same," which he mixed in that part which participates in reason, an image of wisdom for those who enjoy a good fate. For of the human soul, one part participates in reason and is intelligent; the other is void of reason and unseeing. Of that which participates in reason, the better and more powerful part is of the nature of the "Same"; the worse, however, is of the "Other." Both have their seat around the head, so that the remaining parts of both soul and body serve this, just as all things are under the hull of the ship itself.

<meta>This page continues the exposition of Platonic-Pythagorean natural philosophy, transitioning from the mathematical construction of the elements to the biological and sensory architecture of the human body. # PLATONIC PHILOSOPHY

<margin>A</margin>As for the part of the soul that lacks reason, that portion prone to anger is located around the heart; the portion that feels desire has its seat around the liver. Truly, the Brain is the source and root of the marrow, and in it also resides the sovereignty of the soul. From this, a certain diffusion flows through the vertebrae of the back, like a downward-sloping channel, so that from there, material for seed and generation may be supplied. The bones are the protections for the marrow, while the flesh is their cover and wrapping. He joined the joints with nerves <note>original Latin: *neruis*; likely referring to tendons or ligaments in this context</note> through bonds to allow for movement. Among the internal instruments, he made some for the sake of nourishment and others for safety.

<margin>B</margin>Of the motions that proceed from external things, those attributed to that "place of wisdom" <note>the brain</note> are categorized as senses. Those that do not fall under perception escape the senses, either because the affected bodies are too earthy or because the motions are too weak. Therefore, whatever motions exceed nature produce pain, while those restored to nature are called Pleasures. Of the senses, God kindled sight for us for the contemplation of heavenly things and the acquisition of knowledge. He created hearing as a fit instrument for perceiving speech and harmony; if a person were deprived of this sense from birth, they would also be deprived of the faculty of emitting speech. Thus, they say this sense is most closely related to speech.

<margin>C</margin>Whatever are called "affections of bodies" receive their names based on the logic of touch. Indeed, by their own inclination toward the place of touch, the vital faculties distinguish heat, cold, dryness, moisture, smoothness, roughness, yielding, resisting, soft, and hard. Touch also judges heavy and light; however, reason defines and determines these by the inclination that tends toward the center or away from the center. They say "downward" and "the center" are entirely the same thing; for the center of a sphere is itself "downward," while that which is above this, up to the circumference, they call "upward." Heat, therefore, consists of the thinnest parts

<margin>D</margin>and has the power and faculty of separating bodies. Cold, however, consists of thicker parts and constricts the passages. Taste is similar to touch; for by thickening and separating, and also by a certain subtle entry into the passages and by their shapes, things pertaining to taste are either harsh or smooth. For those things that have the power to induce a stupor in the tongue and wipe it clean are perceived as Harsh; those that wipe the tongue moderately are Salty; but those that inflame the tongue and penetrate deep into the flesh are Acrid. Their opposites, the smooth and sweet, melt into juice.

<margin>E</margin>Furthermore, the types of odor are not distinct. They are filtered through narrow passages that are too solid to be contracted or dispersed by the putrefactions and "cooking" of the earth and earthy things. They are either of a pleasant or unpleasant smell. Voice, moreover, is a stroke in the air reaching the soul through the ears; the passages of these ears extend until they reach the liver. In these is the spirit <note>original Latin: *spiritus*; here meaning breath or vital air</note>, the motion of which is hearing. Of voice and hearing, one type is swift and sharp <note>high-pitched</note>, another is slow and deep <note>low-pitched</note>, and a middle type is defined by no certain measure of boundaries. One type is large, being much and diffused; another is small, being few and contracted. That which is ordered according to musical ratios is harmonious; that which is confused and foreign to reason is absurd and intemperate.

<margin>F</margin>The fourth genus of things that fall under the senses has various and manifold species. These are called visibles; in this genus, various colors and many colored things are included. The primary colors are four: White, black, bright <note>original Latin: *splendidus*</note>, and red <note>original Latin: *puniceus*</note>. The rest are generated from these being mixed. White color, then, disperses the sight, while black composes and joins it together—just as Heat diffuses touch, while cold, by contrast, can contract it; and just as a harsh taste contracts, while an acrid taste tends to pull apart by a certain natural faculty. Furthermore, of those animals that breathe air, the body is both nourished and preserved while nourishment is distributed through the veins into the entire mass of the body,

<margin>G</margin>and is derived by a certain downward flow as if through canals, and is irrigated by the spirit, which diffuses it with an effective motion even to the furthest ends. Respiration occurs because there is no vacuum in nature; air is both attracted through invisible pores and flows in to replace that which has flowed out. From those same passages, moisture and sweat clearly emerge on the uppermost part of the skin. Now, since something of the body itself is consumed by natural heat, it is necessary for an equal motion of that which was consumed to be introduced in turn. Unless this happened, a vacuum would occur in the nature of things, which can happen in no way. For the animal could not repair and restore its strength by that perpetual motion of flowing unless the "tent of the body" were separated from a vacuum. A similar mechanism usually occurs in instruments—even inanimate ones—from that reciprocal proportion of respiration: the cupping glass <note>a medical tool used to create suction</note> and amber <note>known for its static attraction</note> are images of respiration. For spirits flow out through the body, and in turn are introduced through respiration by both the mouth and nostrils. Then again, like the Euripus <note>a strait in Greece famous for its changing currents</note>, they are carried in turn into the body. The body is distended according to these inflows. But the cupping glass, once the air is consumed by fire, attracts moisture; amber, once the spirit is excreted, receives a similar body. All nourishment is brought into the body from the root of the heart and the fountain of the stomach. If the inflow is greater than the outflow, it is called Growth; if less, Diminution. Vigor consists at the boundary of these and is understood as the equality of the outflow and inflow. But when the joints of the constitution are dissolved, if there is no longer a passage for the spirit, or if nourishment is no longer distributed—

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Of the irrational part [of the soul], the spirited part is around the heart, and the desiring part is around the liver. Of the body, the sources and the root of the marrow are the brain, in which is the ruling power. From this, a flow runs through the remaining vertebrae, from which the seed and offspring are released. The bones are the coverings of the marrow. Of these, the flesh is the shelter and wrap, and he joined the limbs at the knees with faithful bonds for movement. Of the internal parts, some are for the sake of food, and some for safety.

<margin>B</margin> Of motions, those caused by external things, which are transmitted to the seat of wisdom, are called sensations. Those that do not fall under perception are unperceived, either because the affected bodies are too earthy or because the motions are too weak to be felt. Whatever things, therefore, displace nature are painful; whatever things restore it to its state are named pleasures. Of the sensations, God kindled sight for us for the vision of heavenly things and the gathering of knowledge. Hearing he produced for the perception of words and melodies; if a man is deprived of this by nature, he will not be able to use speech for his benefit. Therefore, they say this sense is most closely related to reason.

<margin>C</margin> Whatever affections of bodies are named, they are referred to touch, and their inclination to their place. For touch judges the vital powers: the hottest, coldest, driest, wettest, smoothest, roughest, yielding, resisting, soft, and hard. Touch judges heavy and light, but reason defines them by their flow toward the center and away from the center. For they say "down" and "center" are the same. For that which is of the sphere is "down," and that which is above this, up to the circumference, is "up." Heat, then, seems to be fine-grained and dispersive of bodies;

<margin>D</margin> cold is thick-grained and constrictive of the pores. Those things regarding taste are like touch. For by composition and division, and also by entry into the pores and by their shapes, things are either harsh or smooth. Those that grip and cleanse the tongue appear harsh; those that cleanse moderately are salty; those that are burning and dissolve the flesh are acrid. Their opposites, smooth and sweet, are flavorful. Of smell, the kinds are not distinguished. For it is filtered through narrow pores, being more solid than can be contracted or diffused by the rot and ripening of earth and earthy things. They are pleasant and foul-smelling.

<margin>E</margin> Voice is a strike in the air, reaching to the soul through the ears, the pores of which reach down to the liver, containing spirit, the motion of which is hearing. Of voice and hearing, one is fast and high-pitched, one is slow; the most proportional is in the middle. And that which is much and diffused is loud; that which is little and gathered is small. That which is ordered according to musical ratios is harmonious; that which is disordered and without flow is unharmonious and discordant.

<margin>F</margin> The fourth kind of sensible thing is many-formed and most varied. These are called visibles, in which are colors of all kinds and many colored things. Of these, there are four: white, black, bright, and red. The others are produced from the mixing of these. White, then, diffuses the sight, and black composes it; just as heat diffuses touch, and cold contracts it; and as the harsh contracts taste, and the acrid naturally diffuses it. The frame of air-breathing animals is nourished and held together by the food distributed through the veins to the whole mass, by an inflow; as if irrigated through channels and watered by the spirit, which diffuses them, carrying them to the extremities.

<margin>G</margin> Respiration occurs because there is no vacuum in nature, air flowing in and being drawn in place of that which flows out through the invisible cuts through which the moisture also appears, and some being consumed by natural heat. It is necessary, therefore, that an equal amount to what was consumed enters in return; otherwise, there would be a vacuum, which is impossible. For the animal would not be a single flowing whole if the frame were interrupted by a vacuum. A similar mechanical action happens in inanimate things, following the analogy of respiration. For the cupping glass and amber are images of respiration. For the spirits flow out through the body, and in return through respiration they enter by the mouth and nostrils; then again, like the Euripus, they are carried back into the drink, and it distends. For this reason, the cupping glass, when the air is consumed by fire, draws in the liquid; and amber, when the spirit is expelled, takes up a similar body. All food is brought to the body from the root of the heart and the spring of the belly; if the passage is greater than the outflow, it is called growth; if less, decay. Maturity is the middle of these, and is understood in the equality of outflow and inflow. When the bonds of the constitution are dissolved, if there is no longer a passage for the spirit, or if food is not distributed, the animal perishes. Many are the fates that cause life and death. In the flesh, this is called disease.

<summary>This page details the physiology of the human body and the nature of the five senses according to Platonic thought, explaining how the soul is seated in organs like the heart and liver and how biological processes like respiration and growth function through the movement of "spirit" and nourishment.</summary>
<keywords>physiology, tripartite soul, anatomy, brain, marrow, five senses, color theory, respiration, vacuum, cupping glass, amber, nutrition</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of human physiology from page 336, moving from the physical structure of the organs to the origins of disease in both the body and the soul, and the methods (medicine and philosophy) used to restore harmony.</meta>

# ON THE NATURE OF THE WORLD

<margin>A</margin> The origins of diseases are the asymmetries of the bodies, occurring whenever the elements derived from the blood—heat, cold, moisture, or dryness—either exceed or fall short of their proper proportions. These imbalances are caused by turns and alterations in the blood, for from its corruption arise the decaying movements of the flesh. These changes happen because the blood becomes acidic, salty, or sharp, leading to the wasting away of the flesh. From this, the discharges of bile <note>original Greek: *cholas*; one of the four vital fluids or 'humors' believed to govern health</note> and phlegm <note>original Greek: *phlegmatos*; considered a cold, moist humor</note> arise.

<margin>B</margin> For when the humors <term>humors|The vital fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) that ancient doctors believed must remain balanced for health</term> suffer and the fluids putrefy, they cause various ailments. Those deep within are mild, but those originating in the bones are difficult, and those affecting the marrow are agonizing. The final stages of diseases involve breath <note>original Greek: *pneuma*</note>, bile, and phlegm, which increase and flow into alien regions or elongated spaces. When they occupy the territory of their betters and drive out the kindred elements, they settle in and harm the body, dissolving it into these very substances. These are the afflictions of the body, and from the soul also come many diseases. Different parts of the soul suffer different ailments: in the sensory part, a loss of sensation; in the memory, forgetfulness; in the impulsive part, a lack of appetite and <unclear>apathy</unclear>; in the emotional part, wild passions and frantic rages; and in the rational part, ignorance and folly.

The origins of vice are pleasures and pains, because they tempt and terrify us. They are sparked in the body but mixed into the soul, and are reported from the soul by various names: for there are loves, longings, unrestrained desires, fuming angers, <margin>C</margin> heavy tempers, diverse cravings, and immoderate pleasures. Simply put, to be inappropriately disposed toward the passions and their origins is the boundary between virtue and vice. For an excess in these, or the ability to master them, renders us either well or poorly disposed. Regarding these impulses, the temperaments of our bodies can provide great assistance—whether they are sharp or hot, or causing other types of madness, they can lead us toward melancholy <note>original: *melancholias*; literally 'black bile', associated with both genius and profound sadness</note> and the most extreme lusts. Parts of the living being, through their vigor, make the forms of inflamed bodies appear more than healthy ones; from these come all despondencies, forgetfulness, and follies.

Daily habits are also sufficient factors—the environment in which one is raised, whether in a city or a home, and the daily diet, which either weakens the soul <margin>D</margin> or strengthens it toward courage. For bad living conditions, lack of education, the things we hear praised, and the habits of those we drink with have the greatest power toward virtue or vice. These causes originate from our parents and the fundamental elements more than from ourselves, provided that we do not fall into laziness by withdrawing from our proper duties. To ensure the well-being of the living creature, the body must possess its subordinate virtues: health, keen senses, strength, and beauty. The origin of beauty is the symmetry of the parts toward each other and toward the soul. For nature joined the frame as an instrument, intended to be obedient and harmonious with the purpose of life. One must also harmonize the soul toward its corresponding <margin>E</margin> virtues: toward temperance (as if it were the health of the body), toward prudence (as if it were the keenness of the senses), toward courage (like strength or vigor), and toward justice (like the beauty of the body). The seeds of these are in nature, but their middle stages and completion come from care: for the body, through gymnastics and medicine; for the soul, through education and philosophy. For these powers nourish and labor over both bodies and souls through toil, exercise, and the purest diet—the former through medicines, and the latter by educating the soul through punishments and rebukes. For they strengthen those in whom they create a purposeful impulse, urging them toward a favorable reputation.

Therefore, the art of physical training, and its relative, medicine, being assigned to treat bodies, lead their powers into the most excellent harmony, making the blood and the breath flow together. If any morbid parts should arise, the strength of the blood and breath has the power to overcome them. Furthermore, music and its leader, philosophy, which were established by the gods and the laws for the correction of the soul, use habit and persuasion—and sometimes even compulsion—to make the irrational part of the soul obey the rational. They ensure the irrational part is no longer unruly, but settled in a quiet state, so that it does not move against the impulse of reason, nor fail to remain still when commanded, whether in action or in the enjoyment of pleasures. For this is the limit of temperance: obedience and endurance. And faith, and the most ancient philosophy, having purged away falsehoods, have instilled knowledge, calling the mind back from great ignorance and opening it to the vision of divine things. To dwell among these with self-sufficiency and cooperation, judging life by a balanced standard, is happiness. He to whom the divine has allotted this portion is led by the truest opinion toward the most blessed life. But if someone is harsh and disobedient,

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...the animal perishes. There are many plagues and harms to life, and causes of death, but one general kind is called Disease. The ruler and primary cause of diseases is the intemperance and disturbance of the primary faculties: namely, if the simple faculties—heat, cold, moisture, or dryness—either overflow or fail. After these come the changes and alterations of the blood from corruption, and the depravations of wasting flesh: if, through the alternation of shifts toward the acidic, the salty, or the sharp, alterations of the blood or wasting of the flesh occur. For from these come the origins of bile and phlegm <note>original Latin: *pituitae*</note>, morbid humors, and the putrefaction of fluids—thin indeed, if they are deep-seated, but <margin>B</margin> difficult to cure if their origins are generated from the bones; and truly troublesome [to the senses] are those ignited from the marrow. Last are the diseases of the spirit, bile, and phlegm: while they increase and flow into foreign seats or the principal locations of the body. Then they occupy a better place, and having driven out the kindred elements, they fix their seat there, and once the bodies are afflicted, they are dissolved into these very things.

These are the affections of the body, and from them many diseases of the soul arise: but different ones have different powers. Over the faculty of sensation, stupor; over the power of memory, forgetfulness; over appetite, a loathing of the stomach or an excessive fire of craving; over the emotional part, wild affections and rages <margin>C</margin> spurred by a "gadfly" <note>original: *oestro*; a metaphor for a stinging passion that drives one mad</note>; and over the rational faculty of the soul, unteachability, ignorance, and foolishness. The principles of vice, however, are pleasures and pains, desires and fears—kindled from the body, but as if mixed into the soul; and therefore from various effects they receive various names. For loves, longings, dissolved desires, stirred-up angers, heavy outbursts, and finally infinite cravings arise in the soul from these movements. In short, for the soul to be subjected to an improper and absurd command of cravings is the boundary between Virtue and Vice. For being either steeped in these or superior to them renders us either well or poorly affected.

<margin>D</margin> To these impulses of the soul, the temperaments of the body bring much assistance; whether they are vehement and glowing, or affected and composed in some other way, as the movements are various and manifold, they carry us away toward "black bile" <note>Latin: *atras biles*; melancholy</note> and the most effusive lusts. Moreover, certain parts, irritated by those flows, bring on sharp bites and the forms of swelling rather than healthy bodies; through these, sadness, forgetfulness, foolishness, and consternation fall upon us. Habits also have great power—those by which one conforms oneself in the city or family in which one was born and raised. Added to this is the daily way of living, <margin>E</margin> either breaking and effeminating the soul, or on the contrary, corroborating it toward gravity and strength. For living under the open sky, a simple and thin diet, exercises, and finally the character of those with whom you associate, have great momentum toward either virtue or vice.

Vice, however, arises from our parents and the elements rather than from neglect and the intemperance of public morals: [namely, since we are so composed] that we never depart from those actions which lead us to those primeval stains of our parents. Furthermore, for the animal to be well, it must be endowed with a body that fully embraces those virtues by which health, subtlety of the senses, strength, and finally beauty can be established. <margin>F</margin> The principles of beauty are the congruence and elegance of the parts, which harmoniously conspire and agree both with themselves and with the soul itself. For Nature composed this tabernacle of the body as an instrument, so that it might be both obedient and fit for all the reasons of life in a harmonious and apt way. The soul also must be conformed and instructed toward the fitting virtues: surely toward temperance, just as the body is toward health; toward prudence, as if toward the subtlety of the senses; toward fortitude, as if toward strength and power; and toward justice, as the body is toward beauty.

The first seeds of these virtues are from nature; the <margin>G</margin> middle and the ends are from diligence: in the body, through the help of gymnastics and medicine; in the soul, through the benefit of erudition and philosophy. For these faculties nourish and strengthen both souls and bodies through labors, exercises, and a pure way of life: employing partly medicines to refresh and restore the body, and partly the instruction of the soul through chastenings and rebukes. For they strengthen the soul while they rouse its impulse with the stings of exhortation and drive it toward suitable and fruitful actions. Therefore, the unifying art <note>Gymnastics</note> and its kinsman Medicine are destined for caring for bodies; bringing those faculties to the best harmony, they render the blood pure and the spirit flowing freely: so that if anything morbid lies beneath, they may prevail over and banish it with those strong faculties of the blood and spirit.

Now indeed Music and its leader Philosophy, established by the gods and laws for the amendment of the soul, accustom, persuade, and compel the part of the soul void of reason to obey reason: and they ensure that for that part which is void of reason, Anger is mild and secure, and Desire is quiet; to the extent that they themselves are neither moved without reason, nor on the contrary remain still when the Mind has provoked them to actions or the fruit of pleasure. For that is the limit of temperance: Obedience and endurance. But also intelligence and that ancient and majestic philosophy, having purged the mind of lying and vain opinions and recalled it from great ignorance, have dedicated it to Knowledge, and raised it to the contemplation of divine things. In the cognition of which things, if anyone so engages that he bears a soul content with his lot, and holds human accidents placed under his feet, and in this equity of soul aspires as if by a favorable river to a moderate and tempered life, he has reached certain happiness. And certainly he to whom God has attributed these lots, is led through the truest opinion to the most blessed life. If, on the contrary, someone should be hard and stubborn...

<summary>This page discusses the dual nature of health and disease, explaining that physical ailments arise from humoral imbalances while mental vices stem from unmastered passions. It proposes a holistic cure where Medicine and Gymnastics treat the body, while Philosophy and Music harmonize the soul, leading to a state of blessedness.</summary>

<keywords>humoral theory, bile, phlegm, pneuma, virtue, vice, melancholy, temperance, gymnastics, medicine, philosophy, symmetry, harmony, soul and body</keywords>

<meta>This page transitions from the metaphysical and physiological conclusions of the Timaeus into the historical and political narrative of the Critias. It concludes the discussion on the cycle of the soul and the justice of the universe before introducing the legendary account of ancient Athens and Atlantis.</meta>

If one refuses to obey those most holy precepts, punishment will follow him, both from the laws and from the voices of those discourses that proclaim both heavenly and infernal penalties. Namely, that unhappy spirits <note>original: "manes"; the souls of the deceased</note> await implacable punishments, and other things which the Ionic poet <note>original: "Ionicus poëta"; likely referring to Homer</note> wrote, recalled from ancient memory. By the hearing of these things, he wished to shape the minds of men toward religion and purity. Indeed, I approve of his counsel in this name; for just as we heal diseased bodies with certain remedies if they do not yield to the most healthful ones, so we restrain souls with false stories if they are not led by true ones.

<margin>B</margin> For this reason, let it be granted that foreign punishments are necessarily commemorated—as if souls migrate back and forth into various bodies: those of the cowardly into female bodies, assigned to them for leur ignominy; of murderers into the bodies of wild beasts for penalty and punishment; of the lewd into the forms of swine or boars; of light and rash men into the species of winged creatures that dwell in the air; and finally, of the sluggish, idle, ignorant, and stupid into the form of aquatic creatures.

All these things, in the second circuit, Nemesis <note>The goddess of divine retribution and vengeance</note> willed to be ratified and fixed by a certain judgment, along with the names of those infernal furies to whom the highest God, the commander and president of all, attributed the inspection of human affairs, and to whom he also committed the government of the world. This world indeed consists of gods, men, and other living creatures, perfected by a reason that is absolutely complete in all its parts. And all these things were created according to that best image of the unbegotten, eternal, and intelligible Form <note>Referring to Plato's Theory of Forms, the perfect templates of reality</note>.

<column-break/>

And let him be persuaded of this punishment, both that which comes from the laws and that which is brought by the discourses themselves: terrors both heavenly and in the house of Hades, that unappeasable punishments lie in store for the spirits below. And other such things as the Ionic poets sang of old, making them for the accursed. For as we heal diseased bodies with bitter medicines, even if they do not yield to the healthiest ones, so we restrain souls with false words if they are not led by the truth. 

These things might be called "foreign stories" <note>original: "xenai"; strange or foreign myths</note>, told for our benefit, such as that the soul changes its dress: that of cowards into female vessels <note>original: "skafea"; literally hulls or vessels, meaning bodies</note>, given over to insult; that of murderers into the bodies of wild beasts for punishment; that of the gluttonous or the rapacious into the forms of swine; that of the light-headed and high-flying into the forms of air-roaming birds; and that of the idle, the unshielded, the ignorant, and the foolish into the form of those in the water. 

All these things in the second period Nemesis judged together with the vengeful earthly spirits, the overseers of human things. To these, the God who is leader of all entrusted the administration of the world, which is filled with gods, humans, and other living things, as many as have been crafted according to the best image of the unbegotten and eternal form.

## PLATO'S CRITIAS,
->Or,<-
## THE ATLANTIC.

**SUMMARY OF THE DIALOGUE.** *This dialogue is an appendix to the greater Timaeus. It concerns the ancient history of the world. Therefore, the entire discourse of this dispute is clearly historical: its end and subject is the commemoration of that primeval age. It deals specifically with the Athenians, who boasted that they were the most ancient of all Greeks, claiming for themselves the majestic title of Autochthones* <note>original Greek: "αὐτόχθονων"; meaning "born from the soil itself"</note> *to testify that they had held their lands constantly. This pertained greatly to the domestic praise of the Athenians; therefore, it was most accurately written down by Plato out of love for his fatherland. It is likely, however, that this entire narration was taken from the monuments of the Egyptians, who, above all other nations, claimed the right and dignity of antiquity for themselves.*

### TIMAEUS, CRITIAS, SOCRATES, HERMOCRATES.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'Q' featuring a man's face and leafy flourishes.</image-desc>
**H**ow grateful is rest to one weary after a long journey, O Socrates; so to me, after the long windings of this dispute, silence is sweet. Now I pray to this world—which has long been a god in reality, but has recently become one in my speech—that if anything has been said rightly, he himself may preserve and guard it for us. But if we have brought forth anything unbecoming in the preceding words, even unintentionally, let him exact the fitting penalty from us. The proper penalty for one who has erred through ignorance or negligence is that he be made knowledgeable and diligent. Therefore, so that hereafter we may speak more rightly concerning the generation of the gods, we pray that the most perfect and healthful medicine of all, knowledge, be given to us by the God of medicines. Having finished my part, I now grant the following dispute to Critias, as was agreed between us. <margin>D</margin> CRI. I accept it, Timaeus; and just as you asked for indulgence <note>original: "veniam"; pardon or grace in speaking</note> at the beginning, as one about to speak of great things, I now ask for the same. Indeed, I believe an even greater indulgence should be granted for the things that remain. Although I know this request of mine might seem somewhat bold and rustic, it must nonetheless be said. For no one of sound mind would object that what you said previously was not well spoken; but I will try to show that what remains to be said, being more difficult, requires greater indulgence. For it is easier for one who discourses about the gods to men to seem to speak adequately, than for one who speaks about mortals to you. For the lack of skill and the ignorance of the listeners provides a great <margin>E</margin> abundance for those who describe unknown things. How we might know and have acquaintance with the nature of the gods, we are not ignorant. But so that I may open my meaning more clearly to you, attend to this. Whatever is said by us, we ought to regard as a certain imitation and expression of a likeness. Nor is it hidden from us what ease or difficulty there is in the work of painters concerning divine or human bodies, so that they may seem to represent them sufficiently to those who look upon them. Truly, when they paint the earth and mountains, rivers, woods, and the whole sky, and those things which consist and wander around the sky, <margin>F</margin> first we think it is enough if someone can return even a tiny image of those things; then, being entirely ignorant of such things, we neither examine the works of the painters nor refute them, but we use a certain obscure and deceptive sketch. But when someone attempts to fashion the likeness of our own bodies, then, because of our familiar observation of our own affairs, we more sharply perceive the errors and are severe and sharp judges and exactors against him who has not expressed every lineament and color. The same may be seen to happen in speeches. For we think it is enough if, concerning heavenly things...

### CRITIAS.

<margin>A</margin> ...we are satisfied with divine things even if they are spoken of with only a slight resemblance to the truth, but we examine mortal and human things with exact precision. Therefore, if we are not able to perfectly render what is fitting in our immediate speech, it is right to forgive us. For one must consider that mortal things are not easy, but difficult to represent through imitation to the satisfaction of opinion. I have said all this, O Socrates, wishing to remind you and to ask for a pardon that is not less, but rather greater, for what I am about to say. If I seem to ask for what is just, grant me this favor willingly.
SOCRATES: Why should we not grant it, Critias? Furthermore, let us give the same to Hermocrates as a third gift. For it is clear that a little later, when it is his turn to speak, he will make the same <margin>B</margin> request as you. Therefore, so that he may provide a different beginning and not be forced to say the same things, let him know that pardon is already granted to him, and let him speak accordingly. However, I warn you, dear Critias, of the mindset of this theater <note>original: "theatrou"; referring here to the audience or the gathering of listeners</note>: the previous poet <note>Referring to Timaeus, whose discourse preceded this one</note> was wonderfully successful in his speech. Therefore, you will need a great deal of pardon if you are to be capable of taking over the task.
HERMOCRATES: You give the same warning to me, Socrates, as you do to him. But men who lose heart, Critias, never yet set up a trophy <note>A monument of victory in battle</note>. One must go forward to the argument bravely, calling upon both the Paean <note>A title for Apollo as a healer or protector</note> and the Muses to reveal and sing of those ancient citizens who were good men.
CRITIAS: O friend Hermocrates, you are assigned for the following <margin>C</margin> day, and having another speaker before you, you still feel bold. However, what the task is like will perhaps soon be clear to you. Nevertheless, I must obey your persuasion and encouragement. In addition to the gods you mentioned, others must be invoked, and especially Mnemosyne <note>The goddess of Memory and mother of the Muses</note>. For almost all the most important parts of our story depend upon this goddess. For if we remember sufficiently and report the things once told by the priests and brought here by Solon <note>The famous Athenian lawmaker and poet</note>, I know that we will seem to this theater to have performed our duty moderately well. This, then, must be done now, and there must be no further delay.
First of all, let us remember that the total was nine thousand years since the war was reported to have occurred between those living outside the Pillars of Heracles <margin>D</margin> <note>The Strait of Gibraltar</note> and all those living within them; this war we must now describe. Of the one side, it was said that this city [Athens] was the leader and fought through the entire war; of the other side, the leaders were the kings of the island of Atlantis, which we said was once an island larger than Libya and Asia combined, but now, due to earthquakes, it is an impassable barrier of mud for those who sail out from here into the open sea, so that they can no longer pass through. The many barbarian nations and all the tribes of the Greeks that existed then, the course of the story will reveal in each place as it unfolds; but the Athenians of that time and the enemies they fought must necessarily be described first—the power of both and their forms of government. Of these, <margin>E</margin> we must give priority to our own affairs here.
For the gods once divided the entire earth by regions through lots, not by strife (for it would not be a correct argument to say that the gods were ignorant of what was fitting for each of them, or that knowing what belonged more to others, they would try to acquire it for themselves through contention). Receiving their own beloved lands by the lots of justice, they settled the regions. Having settled them, they raised us as their possessions and flocks, just as shepherds do; except they did not use physical violence on our bodies, like shepherds driving cattle with blows, but rather they governed us as an easily led creature, directing all that is mortal. Some gods, having been allotted different places, adorned them; but Hephaestus and Athena <note>Gods of craftsmanship and wisdom respectively</note>, <margin>F</margin> having a common nature—both being siblings from the same father, and both arriving at the same goals through the love of wisdom and the love of art—both received this land [Attica] as their single, common lot, as it was naturally suited and favorable to virtue and wisdom. Having produced good men as indigenous inhabitants of the soil, they put into their minds the order of government. Their names have been preserved, but their deeds, because of the destruction of those who succeeded them and the length of time, have vanished. For the surviving race (as was said before) was always left as mountain-dwellers and unlettered, having heard only the names of the rulers in the land and very little of their deeds. They gave these names to their offspring out of affection; but they did not know the virtues and the laws of those who lived before <margin>G</margin> them, except for some obscure rumors about each. Being in want of the necessities of life for many generations, they and their children focused their minds on their immediate needs and spoke only of these, neglecting the memory of ancient things. For mythology and the investigation of the past come to cities along with leisure, when they see that the necessities of life are already provided; but not before. In this way, the names of the ancients have been preserved without their deeds. I say this, judging by the fact that Solon said those priests, in their narration of the ancient war, included many names similar to those of later times, such as Cecrops, Erechtheus, and Erichthonius...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...nothing should be brought forth concerning divine things that is little fitting. Indeed, we are accustomed to examine mortal and human works with great exactness. Therefore, if we handle those things which must be said immediately with less than their proper dignity, it is right to forgive us. For it must not be thought that mortal things can be easily expressed—indeed, they are certainly difficult—by imitation according to common opinion. For this reason I have said all these things, O Socrates, desiring both to remind you and to seek a greater pardon from you for the things that remain. If I seem to seek what is just, grant this pardon willingly.
SOCRATES: Why, O Critias, should we not give it to you? Furthermore, let this same thing be given by us a third time to Hermocrates. For it is certain that a little later, when he is about to speak, he will pray <margin>B</margin> for the same. So that he may begin in another way and not be forced to repeat the same things, let him know that pardon has been granted to him: and as if that were certain, let him immediately prepare himself to speak. I forewarn you, however, friend Critias, of the mind and judgment of the listeners: for the first poet who spoke in this gathering was wonderfully approved. Therefore, you will have great need of pardon if you are to rightly fulfill the duty of a successor.
HERMOCRATES: You send the same message to me, O Socrates, as you do to him. But the sluggish and the faint-hearted have never attained the palm of victory, Critias. It is fitting, therefore, to approach the discourse with a brave heart, and having called upon Apollo and the Muses, to illustrate the ancient citizens—excellent men—with the highest praises.
CRITIAS: O friend Hermocrates, because the following <margin>C</margin> day has been assigned to you, and you are to follow another speaker, you are therefore confident. But what sort of task it is, the reality itself will perhaps declare. I must obey your exhortation and your thorough encouragement. And besides the gods whom you mentioned, it is fitting to invoke others in addition, and especially Mnemosyne—that is, Memory—in which goddess the most important moments of our speech are placed. Surely, if we sufficiently remember and now recount for you what was once handed down by the priests and brought here by Solon, we shall seem to this theater, as I think, to have fulfilled our duty well enough. This, therefore, must be done now, and there must be no further delay.
First, let us commemorate that the sum of years is nine thousand since the time it was handed down that war existed among all those who <margin>D</margin> lived beyond and those who lived around the Pillars of Hercules, which we are now about to narrate. Of these, the leader was this city, and it finished the whole war, as it is said. Of the others, the leaders were the kings of the Atlantic island, which island we stated was at one time larger than Libya and Asia, but afterward a pathless mud was left there when the island was submerged by a concussion of the earth, which indeed stands in the way of those sailing from here into the deep sea, so that it is not permitted to sail further. The barbarian nations which then existed, and the Greeks generally, the progress of the discourse itself will narrate everywhere as the occasion is given; but it is fitting to set forth first the powers and republics of the Athenians who then existed, and of their adversaries, and the order and success of the war. Of these same people, <margin>E</margin> we will first narrate our own.
The gods once allotted the circle of the whole earth to themselves individually, distributed into single regions. Nor did contention cause this partition. For it would be far from reason that the gods should be ignorant of what is fitting for each of them, or that knowing what belongs rather to others, they should contend to usurp the rights of others in turn. But taking up their own regions according to their wishes by the lots of judgment and law, and caring for each like friends, they arranged the regions to be inhabited. And they nourished us like their own flocks and possessions and herds, with this exception: that they did not wish to compel our bodies with bodies, <margin>F</margin> in the manner that shepherds are accustomed to do to cattle and beasts with blows. But as if directing a docile and obedient animal, and as if steering an agile ship from the stern, they used persuasion as a rudder, and with that they touched the soul, and so according to their will they governed the whole mortal race. And some gods, having been allotted the government of other places, established those things; but Vulcan and Minerva <note>Latin names for Hephaestus and Athena</note>, having a common nature—both because they are from the same father, and because they tend toward the same things through the study of wisdom and the diligence of the arts—thus obtained this region as a common lot, as it was <margin>G</margin> naturally proper and congruent to virtue and prudence. And they procreated in it indigenous men, exceedingly noble, and infused the order of a republic into their minds. Only their names survive; but their works have been deleted from the memory of men by the destruction of those who succeeded them and by the long interval of time. For the race of men that always survived, as we said in the previous sections, was mountain-wandering and unrefined, to whom only the names of the powerful men in the region had been heard. But besides these, there were only certain meager traces of their deeds. Therefore, the descendants imposed the names of the ancients upon their children with a certain affection of love, being ignorant of the virtues and laws of their predecessors; for they had nothing of these except rumor, and that not sufficiently certain. But when for many ages they were in need of the things necessary for food, and they and their children applied their minds to these things by whose poverty they were pressed, and spoke about these, they neglected the memory of ancient things. For storytelling and the investigation of ancient things are accustomed to arise in cities only when leisure is present, when the necessities of life are already prepared, but never before. And so the names of the ancients have been preserved without their works. I say these things thus conjecturing, since Solon said those priests inserted very many names similar to those of later generations into the narration of the ancient war, such as Cecrops, Erechtheus, and Erichthonius...

# PLATO’S WORKS

<margin>A</margin> ...Erichthonius <note>A legendary early king of Athens, said to have been born from the earth itself.</note>, and many of the other names recorded before the time of Theseus. The names and deeds of the women were similar, as was the figure and statue of the goddess Pallas Athena. At that time, the pursuits of war were common to both men and women. Indeed, the goddess was then depicted in armor, serving as an example to all that among all species of animals that live in groups, the nature of both the male and the female is such that they are capable of practicing the virtue appropriate to their kind in common. 

In those days, there lived in this region various classes of citizens who were occupied with crafts and agriculture. But the warrior class, having been set apart from the beginning by divine men, lived separately, possessing everything 
<margin>B</margin> necessary for their sustenance and education. None of them possessed any private property, for they considered all things to be held in common. Beyond what was sufficient for their needs, they required nothing from the other citizens, and they practiced all those customs which were described yesterday regarding the "guardians" <term>Guardians: The elite warrior-ruler class in Plato's ideal city, as discussed in his earlier work, the *Republic*.</term> we discussed. 

Furthermore, what has been said about our land is both true and probable. First, in those times, its borders stretched on one side toward the Isthmus, and on the other toward the mainland as far as the heights of Cithaeron and Parnes. These borders descended on the right toward Oropia and on the left toward the sea, with the Asopus river 
<margin>C</margin> marking the boundary. It is said that this land then surpassed all others in fertility. For this reason, the region was then able to support the vast army of those who lived around it. 

The clearest evidence of this fertility is that what remains of the land today can still compete with any other in the variety and quality of its fruits and its abundant pastures for every kind of animal. But in those days, it produced all these things not only in great beauty but in the greatest abundance. By what reasoning is this probable? Or by what signs can one conjecture the remains of that ancient land? The whole territory lies like a long promontory stretching from the mainland into the sea, and the surrounding basin of the sea is everywhere very deep. 
<margin>D</margin> Since many great floods have occurred during the interval of nine thousand years (for that is the number of years that have passed from that time to the present), the soil that washed down from the higher places during these times and catastrophes did not accumulate into a significant mound as it does elsewhere, but was always carried away and disappeared into the depths. 

Therefore, compared to what it once was, the present land is like the skeleton of a body wasted by disease; the soft and rich soil has been washed away, and only the thin, emaciated body of the land remains. Once, the land was intact and had high hills, and the plains now called 
<margin>E</margin> Phelleus <note>A Greek term for "stony ground," used here as a proper name for the rocky regions of Attica.</note> were filled with rich soil. There were thick forests on the mountain tops, of which even now traces appear. For there are some mountains which now only provide food for bees, but in times not so long ago, huge trees were cut from them for the roofs and timbering of the largest buildings, the structures of which still stand. There were also many other cultivated trees, tall and fruit-bearing, and the pastures for cattle were incredibly rich. 

Furthermore, this region enjoyed the annual rain from Zeus <note>original: "Ioue" (Jove/Zeus)</note>, which did not run off the bare earth into the sea as it does now. Instead, the land held the water, absorbing it into its "clay" <note>likely referring to the deep soil layers</note> and storing it, sending the water that had soaked down from the heights into the hollows, thus providing an abundance of springs and rivers in all places. Even now, sacred monuments remain at these ancient springs, proving that what we are telling you is true. 

Such was the natural condition of the land. Moreover, it was cultivated by true farmers who were dedicated to this very task—men of noble character and natural talent, who possessed the finest soil, the most abundant water, and a climate perfectly tempered for the seasons of the year. 

As for the city, it was arranged in the following way at that time. First, the Acropolis <term>Acropolis: The "high city" or fortified citadel of Athens.</term> was not as it is now. For now, a single night of torrential rain has washed away the soil and left it bare, occurring during an earthquake and the third disastrous flood before the great destruction of Deucalion <note>Deucalion was the survivor of a great flood in Greek mythology, similar to Noah.</note>. 
<margin>G</margin> But in former times, the Acropolis was so large that it reached to the Eridanus and Ilissus rivers and included the Pnyx and Lycabettus <note>Significant hills and landmarks in ancient and modern Athens.</note>, with the boundary being opposite the Pnyx. It was all covered in soil and, except for a few places, was level on top. 

Outside the citadel, on its slopes, lived the craftsmen and those farmers who worked the nearby fields. But on the summit, the warrior class lived alone around the temple of Athena and Hephaestus, enclosed by a single wall like the garden of a single house. On the northern side, they had built common houses and winter dining halls, and all that was necessary for their communal life, including temples—all built without the use of gold or silver. 
<margin>H</margin> For they never made use of these metals for any purpose. Instead, following a middle path between pride and meanness, they built modest houses in which they and their children's children grew old, always handing them down to others like themselves. In the summer, they used the southern side of the citadel, leaving aside their dining halls and focusing on their gardens and gymnasiums.

<column-break/>

...and Erichthonius, and most of those other names that are remembered before the time of Theseus. Solon said that the priests, in recounting the war of that time, used these names for the people of that era. And so it was with the women: the fashion and statue of the goddess 
<margin>A</margin> showed that in those days, military pursuits were shared by women and men alike. This custom of representing the goddess in armor was a sign to the people of that time that among all creatures that pair together, both female and male have the natural capacity to practice the virtue appropriate to their species in common.

At that time, various other classes of citizens lived in this land, occupied with crafts and producing food from the earth. 
<margin>B</margin> But the warrior class, having been separated from the beginning by divine men, lived apart, having all things necessary for their food and education. None of them possessed anything of their own, but they considered all things to be held in common by everyone. They did not think it right to receive anything from the other citizens beyond sufficient food. They practiced all the customs we spoke of yesterday when we described those who were proposed to be "guardians."

And indeed, what was said about our land was both plausible and true. First, its boundaries were then defined as extending toward the Isthmus, and on the other part of the mainland, 
<margin>C</margin> as far as the peaks of Cithaeron and Parnes. The boundaries descended on the right, including the territory of Oropia, and on the left toward the sea by the Asopus. In excellence, this land surpassed all others, and was thus able to support the vast army of the surrounding inhabitants. 

A great proof of its excellence is this: what is now left of it can compete with any other land in being all-productive and fertile, and it provides good pasture for all animals. But then, in addition to its beauty, it produced these things in vast quantities. How then is this credible? And what remnant of the land of that time could be rightly described? The whole territory lies stretching out long into the 
<margin>D</margin> sea like a promontory. The basin of the sea that surrounds it is everywhere deep. 

Many great floods having occurred during the nine thousand years (for that is the number of years that have passed from that time until now), the earth that washed down from the heights during these times and through these events did not settle as a mound in other places, as is worth mentioning, but always flowing around in a circle, it vanished into the depths. What remains now, compared to what existed then, is like the bones of a 
diseased body, as in small islands; the soil, which was once rich and soft, having fallen away, and only the thin body of the land being left. 

But at that time, the land was unharmed and had high hills, and the plains now called 
<margin>E</margin> Phelleus were full of rich earth. It had much timber in the mountains, of which there are even now visible proofs. For there are mountains which now provide food only for bees, but it is not a very long time since trees were cut from there for the roofing of the largest buildings, and these roof beams are still sound. There were also many other tall, cultivated trees, and it produced unspeakable pasture for flocks. 

Furthermore, the land enjoyed the annual water from Zeus, not losing it as it does now by letting it flow off the bare earth into the sea. Instead, having much soil and receiving the water into itself, storing it in the covering clay, and letting the water it had absorbed from the heights flow into the hollows, it provided all places with 
<margin>F</margin> abundant flows of springs and rivers. The remnants of these are still preserved at all the ancient springs, which are signs that what is now said about the land is true.

Such was the nature of the rest of the country, and it was arranged as was likely by true farmers, who were actually practicing this craft—men who loved beauty and were naturally gifted, possessing the best soil and most abundant water, and a climate of the most moderately tempered seasons. 

The city at that time was settled in this way: First, the condition of the Acropolis was not as it is now. For now, a single rainy night of extraordinary force has washed the soil away and left it bare, while an earthquake occurred at the same time—this was the third disastrous flood before the destruction of Deucalion. 
<margin>G</margin> But in the former time, its size reached down toward the Eridanus and the Ilissus, and it encompassed the Pnyx and the Lycabettus, having the boundary opposite the Pnyx. It was all covered with earth, and except for a few places, it was flat on top. 

It was inhabited on the outside, along its slopes, by the craftsmen and those farmers who farmed nearby. But on the heights, the warrior class lived by itself around the temple of Athena and Hephaestus, enclosed by a single wall like the garden of one house. They lived on the northern side, having built common houses and winter dining halls, and all the buildings that were necessary for their communal life 
and for the temples, without the use of gold or silver. They made no use of these anywhere, but pursuing the middle path 
<margin>H</margin> between arrogance and meanness, they built decent houses in which they and their descendants grew old and handed them down, always the same, to others like them. On the southern side, they gave up their dining halls for the summer and made use of gardens and gymnasiums.
