# CRITIAS

<margin>A</margin> There was once a single spring located where the citadel now stands. After it was choked off by earthquakes, only the small trickles that remain today were left. But in those days, it provided an abundant flow for everyone, being well-tempered for both winter and summer. They lived in this fashion: the guardians <note>The warrior class of ancient Athens.</note> dwelt on the heights around the spring, while they acted as leaders of the other Greeks with their consent. They were careful to keep their population of men and women who were already fit for war, or soon to be, at a constant number—roughly twenty thousand. These people were of such a character, and they governed their own land and Greece with justice in this manner forever. Throughout all of Europe and Asia, they were the most famous and renowned of all people of that time, both for the beauty of their bodies and the many virtues of their souls. <margin>B</margin> As for the affairs of those who fought against them, I will now share with you, my friends, the details as they were set forth from the beginning—unless the memories of what we heard as children have escaped me. 

But before I begin the account, I must clarify a small point so that you are not surprised to hear Greek names given to barbarian men. You shall now learn the reason for this. Solon, intending to use this account for his own poetry, inquired into the meaning of the names and found that those first Egyptians who wrote them down had translated them into their own language. Solon himself, taking up the sense of each name, translated them back again and recorded them in our own tongue. <margin>C</margin> These writings were in the possession of my grandfather, and they are still with me today; I studied them carefully when I was a child. Therefore, if you hear names similar to ours, do not let it wonder you, for you now know the cause. 

The story was long, beginning as was said before concerning the lot of the gods: how they distributed the whole earth among themselves, some in larger portions and others in smaller, and established temples and sacrifices for themselves. Thus Poseidon, having received the island of Atlantis as his lot, settled the children he had fathered by a mortal woman in a certain place on the island, described as follows. <margin>D</margin> Toward the sea, but in the center of the whole island, there was a plain, which is said to have been the most beautiful of all plains and possessed of excellent fertility. Near this plain, and again in the center of the island about fifty stadia <note>A stadium was roughly 600 feet; 50 stadia is approximately 5.7 miles.</note> away, was a mountain of low height on all sides. On this mountain lived one of the men who had originally been born from the earth there, named Evenor, who lived with his wife Leucippe. They had an only daughter, Cleito. When the girl reached marriageable age, her mother and father died. Poseidon, falling in love with her, had intercourse with her; and the hill on which she lived he made strong and fortified, breaking it off in a circle, creating alternating rings of sea and land—some smaller, some larger—one after another. There were two rings of land and three of sea, as if turned on a lathe from the center of the island, each equidistant from the other, so that the hill was inaccessible to men. For in those days, ships and sailing did not yet exist. <margin>E</margin> He himself, as a god, easily adorned the central island, bringing up two springs of water from beneath the earth—one warm and the other flowing cold from a fountain—and causing the earth to yield various and sufficient food. He fathered and raised five pairs of twin male children. Having divided the whole island of Atlantis into ten parts, he gave the eldest son his mother’s dwelling and the surrounding allotment, which was the largest and best. He appointed him king over the others, and the others he made governors, giving each of them dominion over many people and a large territory. He gave names to them all: to the eldest, the king, from whom the whole island and the sea took the name "Atlantic," for the name of that first king was Atlas. <margin>F</margin> To his twin brother, who was born immediately after him and who was allotted the extremity of the island toward the Pillars of Hercules <note>The Strait of Gibraltar.</note>, reaching toward the region now called Gadeira in that place, he gave the Greek name Eumelus, but in the native tongue, Gadeirus—which may have provided the name for that region. Of the second pair born, he called one Ampheres and the other Evaemon. Of the third, he called the first-born Mneseus and the one after him Autochthon. Of the fourth, the first was Elasippus and the later one Mestor. Of the fifth pair, the first was named Azaes and the second Diaprepes. All these men and their descendants lived there for many generations, ruling over many other islands in the sea and also, as was said before, over the regions within the strait as far as Egypt and Tyrrhenia <note>Ancient Etruria/Italy.</note>. <margin>G</margin> From Atlas, a great and honorable race descended. The eldest king always handed down the leadership to his eldest son, and they preserved the kingdom for many generations, possessing such a wealth of riches as had never been seen before in any dynasty of kings, nor is likely to be easily seen again. All things were provided for them, both in the city and throughout the rest of the country, for their use. Many things were brought to them from abroad because of their empire, but the island itself provided the most for the needs of life. <margin>H</margin> First, whatever is mined from the earth, both solid and fusible metals; and that which is now only a name, but was then more than a name—Orichalcum <term>Orichalcum: A legendary reddish metal, considered second in value only to gold in antiquity; likely a natural alloy of copper and zinc.</term>—was dug out of the earth in many parts of the island, being the most precious of the metals existing at that time, except for gold. And the forests provided timber in abundance for the works of carpenters. Furthermore, the land produced enough for animals, both wild and domestic.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> There was one spring in the place where the citadel is now. When it was exhausted due to an earthquake, only small rivulets were left around it. At that time, however, it supplied a flowing liquid abundantly to all: its temperature was healthy in both summer and winter. In this manner they inhabited these places, as guardians of their own citizens and leaders of the rest of the Greeks who followed them willingly, observing above all that their number should always remain the same—that is, men and women already strong in warfare. Nor was the number of soldiers ever fewer than twenty thousand. Since they were such people, and always administered their own fatherland and all of Greece justly in this manner, they were considered the most proven and famous of all who lived then throughout all Europe and Asia, as much for their noble physical build as for the innumerable gifts of their minds. <margin>B</margin> Next, we shall communicate with you, as friends, what the affairs of their adversaries were like from the beginning, unless perhaps what we heard as children has slipped from memory. But before I relate this, you must be cautioned not to wonder if you now hear many names of barbarian men in Greek. This happened because Solon, when he thought to insert them into his poems, investigated the very force of the names and found that those first Egyptians, the writers of these things, had translated the names into their own language. Wherefore he himself, again taking up the sense of each name, converted it into our own tongue. <margin>C</margin> These writings were with my grandfather, and are now with me; I took care of them long ago as a boy. If, therefore, you hear such names now as are found among us, do not wonder: for you understand the cause of this. There is need for a long discourse if I am to narrate from the beginning that which I said before: regarding the lot of the gods, how they distributed the entire earth among themselves—some into larger portions, some narrower—and established temples and sacred rites for themselves. Truly Neptune <note>original: "Neptunus" - the Roman name for Poseidon.</note> was allotted the Atlantic island and fathered sons from a mortal woman in a certain place on the island of this sort. <margin>D</margin> Beside the sea, but in the very middle of the island, there was a plain, which is said to have been the most spacious and fertile of all. Near the plain, again in the center, there was a short mountain, fifty stadia distant. Here lived one of those who were born from the earth in the beginning, named Evenor. He, from his wife Leucippe, had fathered an only daughter, Cleito. Their parents having died and the girl being now mature, Neptune, captured by desire for her, united with her and surrounded the hill where she lived with flowing coils of water and zones of land alternately—some wider, some narrower. Of these, two were of land and three were of sea, which, as if described by a lathe, were distant from the middle of the island by an equal interval on all sides, and rendered the hill itself inaccessible to men. For at that time there were no ships, nor any skill in navigation. He himself, as a God, easily adorned the middle island and ordered springs of two-fold water, cold and hot, to break out from the hidden depths of the earth through exterior fountains; likewise, he ordered various and abundant foods to sprout through the lands. <margin>E</margin> Furthermore, he fathered and raised five pairs of twin male offspring. And having divided the whole Atlantic island into ten regions, he granted to the first-born his mother's habitation and the region that was around it—truly the largest and most powerful portion. He appointed him king of the rest, and the others as princes of many nations and regions. He imposed names on each. <margin>F</margin> The first-born he called Atlas, king of the whole island. Whence also the sea is called the Atlantic. The one who immediately followed him in the same birth, he called Gadirus in the native tongue, whom we call Eumelus in Greek. He was allotted the extreme parts of the island toward the pillars of Hercules and named the place Gadiricum after his own name. Of the second birth, he named one Ampheres, the other Evaemon. of the third, the first-born Mneseus, the second Autochthon. Of the fourth, Elasippus the former, and Mestor the latter. Of the fifth, finally, Azaes the first, and Diaprepes the second. All these and their descendants lived there for many centuries, ruling over many other islands throughout the sea, and even over those which are inhabited as far as Egypt and Tyrrhenia, as we said before. <margin>G</margin> Truly, in the greatest generation was the whole race of Atlas, and always the older king left the kingdom to the first-born; they preserved this empire for many centuries. Indeed, they had such a great abundance of wealth as had belonged to no kings before them, nor will easily be compared to any of those who come after. All things in the city and the whole kingdom were built and organized for them as utility required. Many things were brought to them from the outside because of their empire; very many things also the island itself produced pertaining to every use of life. First, all things whatever are dug from the bowels of the earth—both those that remain solid and those that are melted—and that which is now only named, but was then certainly <margin>H</margin> dug up the most: Orichalcum, a remarkable metal from many places on the island, then among them most precious except for gold. And whatever the forest produces for architects, it bore in abundance. It even supplied pasture for animals, both wild and domestic.

<summary>Critias recounts the divine origins of Atlantis, describing how Poseidon established a dynasty with his ten sons on a fertile, fortified island. He explains the lineage of King Atlas and the immense natural resources, including the legendary metal orichalcum, that fueled the empire's wealth.</summary>
<keywords>Atlantis, Poseidon, Atlas, Orichalcum, Solon, Cleito, Gadeirus, Pillars of Hercules, ancient history, mythology</keywords>

# OF PLATO

<margin>B</margin>
Moreover, there was a vast abundance of elephants there. For the land provided sufficient pasture for all animals—those that feed in marshes, lakes, and rivers, as well as those that graze on mountains or in the plains. This included this vast and most voracious kind of animal <note>Referring to the elephant's massive appetite.</note>. Furthermore, the earth produced all the fragrant things it nurtures today: roots, grasses, woods, flowing saps, flowers, and fruits. It also yielded the sweet moisture of the vine and the solid food upon which we ourselves are nourished <note>Likely referring to grains or cereals.</note>. There were also those foods we use for sustenance and for flavoring, which we call legumes. There were also liquid extracts from trees and foods to quench thirst and satisfy hunger. Nor were perfumes <note>original: "vnguenta"</note> lacking. Added to these were the most copious fruits of various trees for the sake of luxury. There were also the delights of desserts <note>original: "bellaria"</note>, which are pleasant to those who have labored. All these things were produced by that island which once existed: sacred, beautiful, wondrous, and most fertile. And gathering these things from the earth, they built temples, royal palaces, harbors, shipyards, and the entire region, arranging in this manner those rings of sea which surrounded the ancient capital. First, by constructing bridges, they provided a passage to the exterior and to the royal seat, where they built royal dwellings in the very beginning, on the seats of the god himself and of their ancestors.

<margin>C</margin>
Receiving the palace adorned by one ruler after another in continuous succession, each king strove to surpass his predecessor in decoration as much as he was able, until they had constructed a mass of buildings wondrous in both size and beauty. Furthermore, they drew a trench from the sea to the outermost circle, extending three <term>plethra</term> <note>A Greek unit of measurement, roughly 100 feet or 30 meters.</note> in width, one hundred feet in depth, and fifty <term>stadia</term> <note>A stadium is roughly 600 feet; 50 stadia is approximately 6 miles or 9 kilometers.</note> in length. And so that ships could reach that circle from this sea as if entering a harbor, they opened its mouth so that it could receive the largest vessels. Likewise, they made bridges over the zones of land that separated the rings of the sea, so that one could sail from one ring to another in a single <term>trireme</term> <note>An ancient galley with three banks of oars.</note>; but they covered these from above, so that the passage below was navigable by ship.

<margin>D</margin>
For the banks of the land zones were high, rising above the sea. The largest circuit, through which the sea flowed, was three stadia in width; the next ring of land was exactly equal to it. Of the following two, the water ring was two stadia wide, while the land ring was again equal to the preceding water ring. Finally, there was one stadium of water that surrounded the island positioned in the center. The diameter of the island where the palace stood was five stadia. They enclosed this island, the rings, and the bridge (which was a plethrum in width) on both sides with a stone wall, building towers and gates at each of the bridges according to the passages of the sea.

<margin>E</margin>
Stone was quarried from beneath the island, both from the central buildings and from those rings, inside and out—some was black, some white, and some red. Because of the cavities in the rock, these quarries provided two excellent shipyards. Some buildings were simple, while others they constructed from stones of various colors, seeking pleasure through variety itself. Furthermore, they coated the entire surface of the wall that enclosed the outermost ring with thin bronze; the inner wall they coated with tin; and the wall surrounding the citadel itself they coated with <term>orichalcum</term> <note>A legendary metal mentioned in ancient writings, described as a gold-colored alloy of copper, perhaps brass.</note>, which shimmered with a fiery glow.

<margin>F</margin>
The royal palace within the citadel was constructed as follows: In the center was a sacred and inaccessible temple of <term>Cleito</term> <note>The mortal woman who, according to the myth, bore Poseidon's children.</note> and Neptune <note>original: "Neptuníque"; Plato uses the Greek name Poseidon.</note>, surrounded by a golden enclosure. There, from the beginning, the lineage of the ten kings was born, and there every year people gathered from the ten regions to perform sacred solemnities for each of them. The temple of Neptune was one stadium long, three plethra wide, and of a height that seemed appropriate to its length and width. Its appearance and style were <term>barbaric</term> <note>original: "barbarica"; in this context, it means "foreign" or "non-Greek" rather than "primitive."</note>.

<margin>G</margin>
They adorned the entire exterior of the temple with silver, except for the highest pinnacles; for the gables and peaks themselves were adorned with gold. Inside, the entire ceiling was seen to be ivory, variously carved with gold, silver, and orichalcum. However, they adorned the walls, columns, and floors with orichalcum. There was a statue of the God standing in a chariot, holding the reins of winged horses, and so tall that his head touched the high ceiling. Around him were a hundred <term>Nereids</term> <note>Sea nymphs of Greek mythology.</note> sitting upon dolphins; for that was how many they believed there to be at that time. There were also many other statues and offerings from private citizens. Outside stood golden images of all the royal women and of all the men who had descended from the ten lineages, as well as many other great statues and offerings from both the kings and private individuals, both from the city itself and from others subject to their empire. There was also an altar appropriate in size and craftsmanship to the rest of the display. In the same way, the palace was suited both to the greatness of the kingdom and to the sacred ornaments.

<margin>H</margin>
They also made use of springs, both hot and cold, which flowed with an inexhaustible stream, and which possessed a wonderful healthfulness and pleasantness for either use. Furthermore, dwellings were constructed around the springs, and trees were planted there; water reservoirs were also placed around them, some open to the sky, and others covered to serve as warm baths in the winter time—some for the royals, others for private citizens, some for women, and others for horses and other beasts of burden. A fitting and appropriate arrangement was maintained for each.

<column-break/>

<margin>B</margin>
It supported wild animals, and indeed, the race of elephants was most numerous there. For there was pasture for all other animals, those that live in marshes, lakes, and rivers, as well as those that graze on mountains and in the plains. But this animal was particularly noted as being the largest and most voracious of all. In addition to these, whatever fragrant things the earth nurtures now—roots, herbs, woods, saps, or distillations, whether of flowers or fruits—it bore and nourished well. Furthermore, there was the cultivated fruit, both the dry kind <note>Grains.</note> which we use for food, and all those which we use for the sake of the meal (all parts of which we call legumes), and the woody kind <note>Tree fruits.</note> which provides drinks, food, and ointments; and the fruit of trees produced for the sake of play and pleasure, which is hard to store; and all those we offer after dinner as welcome relief from fullness for one who is weary. All these things that island, then existing under the sun, produced: sacred, beautiful, wondrous, and infinite in quantity. Taking all these things from the earth, they constructed the temples, the royal dwellings, the harbors, the shipyards, and all the rest of the country, arranging them in this order. The channels of the sea, which were around the ancient mother-city, they first bridged, making a way out and toward the palace.

<margin>C</margin>
They built the palace at the very beginning in this habitation of the god and their ancestors. One receiving it from another, and adorning what was already adorned, each always surpassed his predecessor in power, until they produced a dwelling to behold that was astonishing for its size and the beauty of its workmanship. For starting from the sea, they dug a canal three plethra wide, one hundred feet deep, and fifty stadia long, reaching to the outermost ring, and they made the passage up from the sea into it as into a harbor, opening a mouth sufficient for the largest ships to sail in. Moreover, the rings of land which separated those of the sea, they cut through at the bridges enough for one trireme to sail through from one to another; and they roofed them over from above, so that the passage was underneath.

<margin>D</margin>
For the lips of the land were high enough above the sea. The largest of the rings into which the sea was let was three stadia in width; the next land ring was equal to it. Of the second pair, the water ring was two stadia in width, and the dry one was again equal to the preceding water ring; and the one around the island itself in the center was one stadium. The island on which the palace stood was five stadia in diameter. This island, the rings, and the bridge (which was a plethrum in width) they surrounded on both sides with a stone wall, placing towers and gates on the bridges at all the passages of the sea.

<margin>E</margin>
They quarried the stone from under the island in the center and from under the rings, both on the outside and the inside; some was white, some black, and some red. As they quarried, they also fashioned double hollowed-out ship-houses within, roofed over by the native rock itself. Of the buildings, some were simple, while others they wove together from different stones, making them variegated for the sake of play, bestowing on them a natural pleasure. They covered the entire circuit of the wall around the outermost ring with bronze, using it like a coating; that of the inner one they covered with tin; and that around the citadel itself with orichalcum, which had fiery reflections.

<margin>F</margin>
The palace within the citadel was arranged thus: In the center there was a sacred area, inaccessible, dedicated to Cleito and Poseidon, surrounded by a golden enclosure—the very place where, in the beginning, they had generated the race of the ten kings. There also, every year, people from all the ten provinces sent seasonal offerings to each of those kings. The temple of Poseidon himself was one stadium in length, three plethra in width, and of a height proportionate to these dimensions to the eye; it had a certain barbaric appearance.

<margin>G</margin>
They coated the entire exterior of the temple with silver, except for the pinnacles; but the pinnacles were coated with gold. As for the interior, the ceiling was seen to be all ivory, variegated with gold, silver, and orichalcum; and all the other parts—the walls, the columns, and the floor—they covered with orichalcum. They set up golden statues: the god himself standing on a chariot, the charioteer of six winged horses, himself so large that he touched the roof with the top of his head; and a hundred Nereids on dolphins around him, for people of that time believed them to be that many. There were many other statues within, dedicated by private individuals. Around the temple on the outside stood golden images of all the women and all the men who were descended from the ten kings; and many other great offerings of both kings and private persons, both from the city itself and from the foreign nations over which they ruled. There was an altar which corresponded to this greatness and workmanship in its construction; and the palace, in the same way, was suited to the greatness of the empire and to the splendor of the temples.

<margin>H</margin>
They used springs, one of cold and one of hot water, both having a generous abundance, and both wonderfully suited by the nature of their waters for use because of their pleasantness and excellence. They used them by building houses and plantations of trees suited to the waters; and they placed around them reservoirs, some open to the air, and others covered for warm baths in the winter—separate ones for the royals, and separate ones for private individuals; and still others for women, and others for horses and other beasts of burden, giving to each its appropriate decoration.

<summary>This page describes the legendary natural wealth and architectural wonders of Atlantis, detailing its concentric rings of land and water, its multicolored stone buildings, and the opulent gold and silver temple of Poseidon.</summary>

-># CRITIAS<-

<margin>A</margin> They led the flowing and irrigation water into the grove of Poseidon <note>original: "Neptuni"</note>. Because of the fertility of the soil, it was filled with trees of many kinds, wondrous in their height and beauty. From there, they diverted the water into the outer circles through aqueducts running alongside the bridges. In these circles, many temples and sanctuaries to various gods were built, along with gardens and gymnasia—some for men and others for horses—separately on each of the circular islands. Among these facilities, there was a magnificent hippodrome <term>hippodromus: an ancient stadium for horse and chariot racing</term> reserved for the citizens, situated in the middle of the largest island. Its width was one stade <term>stade: a unit of length, approximately 600 feet or 185 meters</term>, while its length stretched around the entire circuit, providing space for the horses to compete. Surrounding the hippodrome on both sides were houses for the guards and attendants. <margin>B</margin> The most faithful soldiers were assigned guard duty within the smaller ring, closer to the citadel; however, to those who surpassed all others in loyalty, quarters were granted within the citadel itself, near the kings. The shipyards were full of triremes <term>trireme: a warship with three banks of oars</term> and all the equipment necessary for them, everything being sufficiently prepared. Such was the arrangement of the royal dwellings. Passing through the three outer harbors, one came to a wall that began at the sea and ran in a circle, standing fifty stades away from the largest circle and harbor. This wall closed in on itself at the mouth of the channel that faced the sea. This whole area <margin>C</margin> was densely populated with many houses. The harbor and the largest basin were full of ships and merchants arriving from all directions, whose great numbers created a constant shouting, diverse noise, and clamor both day and night. Now, we have recalled the city and the layout of the ancient seat nearly as it was described then. Next, we must try to recount the nature and the cultivation of the rest of the region. First, the entire area was said to be very high and steep from the sea. But all the land around the city was a plain, which itself was surrounded by mountains that reached down to the sea, being smooth and level. <margin>D</margin> Its total length on one side was three thousand stades, and from the center upwards from the sea, it was two thousand stades. This part of the island faced south and was sheltered from the north winds. The mountains surrounding it were celebrated at that time as surpassing all that now exist in number, size, and beauty. They contained many wealthy villages of inhabitants, as well as rivers, lakes, and meadows providing sufficient nourishment for all animals, both wild and domestic. There was also a vast amount of timber, varied in its species, providing an abundant supply for every kind of work. Thus, this plain was shaped by nature and cultivated by many kings over a long period of time. <margin>E</margin> It was rectangular in shape, mostly straight and long, but where it deviated, they followed the circuit of the trench they dug around it. The depth, width, and length of this trench were incredible to hear of, considering it was a man-made work compared to other labors; however, we must report what we heard. It was dug to a depth of one plethron <term>plethron: approximately 100 feet</term>, and its width was a stade everywhere. Since it was dug around the entire plain, its length happened to be ten thousand stades. It received the streams coming down from the mountains, and after circling the plain and reaching the city from both sides, it finally flowed out into the sea. From the upper part of this trench, straight canals <margin>F</margin> one hundred feet wide were cut through the plain and led back into the trench near the sea. These canals were separated from one another by a distance of one hundred stades. They used these to bring timber down from the mountains to the city and to transport other seasonal products by boat, cutting cross-channels into one another and toward the city. They harvested the land twice a year: in winter, they used the rains provided by Zeus, and in summer, they brought the water from the canals to irrigate what the earth produced. As for the number of men in the plain useful for war, it was ordered that each lot of land should provide one leader. The size of a lot was ten times ten stades, and the total number of lots was sixty thousand. Of those who lived in the mountains and the rest <margin>G</margin> of the country, there was said to be an infinite number; according to their locations and villages, they were all distributed among these lots under their leaders. The law required each leader to provide a sixth part of a war chariot—up to ten thousand chariots—two horses and their riders, and a pair of horses without a seat, which included a soldier who could dismount and fight with a small shield and a driver to manage both horses. They also provided two heavy infantrymen, two archers, two slingers, and three light-armed stone-throwers and three javelin-throwers. Finally, they provided four sailors to make up the complement of one thousand two hundred ships. This was the military preparation of the royal city; the arrangements for the other nine <margin>H</margin> cities were different, and it would take a long time to describe them. The offices and honors were established from the beginning in this way: each of the ten kings in his own province and city held power over the men and most of the laws, punishing and putting to death whomever he wished. Their authority over one another and their communal relations were governed by the commands of Poseidon, as the law handed down to them and the records written by the first kings on a column of orichalcum <term>orichalcum: a legendary metal, possibly a gold-copper alloy, considered second only to gold in value</term>, which stood in the center...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> They led the flowing and irrigation water into the place of Neptune <note>original: "Neptuni"</note>, which was filled with various trees of marvelous height and appearance due to the fertility of the soil. And from there, they diverted it into the outer circuit through aqueducts near the bridges. There were many temples and shrines of the gods, gardens, and gymnasia—some for men, some for horses—separately in each of the circular islands. But around the middle of the largest island of all, there was a principal hippodrome. Its width was one stade, and its length stretched through the whole circle for equestrian competition. Around the hippodrome on both sides were houses arranged for the guards and attendants. <margin>B</margin> To the soldiers of proven faith, the guardianship was committed within the narrower circuit closest to the citadel; to those who surpassed all others in loyalty, habitations were granted in the citadel itself, near the kings. The shipyards were full of triremes and all the instruments pertaining to them, each being sufficiently laid out. And this was the equipment of the royal palaces. Passing through the harbors, of which there were three outer ones, a wall appeared all around, beginning from the sea like a rampart, and standing at every point fifty stades from the largest circle and harbor, which returned to the mouth of the trench that was toward the sea. All of that <margin>C</margin> was inhabited, and the royal space abounded with many and frequent buildings; the basin itself and the widest harbor were full of ships and merchants flocking from everywhere. There, because of the frequent crowd, a continuous clamor and huge noise were heard day and night. And so, concerning the arrangement of the city and the ancient seat, as was formerly handed down, we have now reported for the present. Next, we shall attempt to commemorate what the nature or the cultivation of the rest of the region was. At first, the whole place was very elevated, abrupt near the sea. But the region around the city was entirely level, surrounding the city; yet it was itself surrounded by mountains rising from the sea, being easy and uniform. Its <margin>D</margin> total length on one side was three thousand stades; from the middle above, even to the sea, two thousand. The site of the island verged toward the south, exposed to the North Wind from the higher places. Its mountains surpassed all that now exist in number, height, and beauty. In them were many villages of inhabitants, and very wealthy ones. Nor were there lacking rivers, lakes, and meadows, by which animals both wild and domestic were abundantly nourished. Likewise, the forest was thick and varied, supplying material in plenty for individual works. And so that place was as much arranged by nature as it was cultivated <margin>E</margin> by the diligence and wealth of many kings over a long time. The region was square, for the most part stretching straight in length, but because of the trench dug around it, it lost its straight shape. Its depth, length, and breadth were incredible to say. For it seems impossible that so vast a work, compared with other works, was made by the hands of men. Yet we must say what we have heard. The depth was of one acre <note>original: "Iugeris"</note>, the width everywhere was a stade; and since it was driven through the whole plain, its length was ten thousand stades. It certainly received the streams flowing down from the mountains, and revolving through the fields to the city, arriving here and there, it finally broke out into the sea. From above, from the trench itself, canals one hundred feet wide and cut straight through the field were led <margin>F</margin> back into the trench nearest the sea. One was separated from another by one hundred stades. They brought timber from the forests into the city, and other things collected in their own seasons, by ships through the double canals; for the tracts of the canals intersected each other obliquely all the way to the city. They gathered twin fruits and crops from the earth every year: in winter, the earth was moistened by rains through the favor of Jove <note>original: "Iouis," referring to Zeus</note>, and in summer it was irrigated by streams from the aqueducts. Concerning the number of men in the level region useful for military affairs, this was the order: each part chose and provided its own leader. The size of each part was ten times ten stades; the total number of all was sixty thousand. But of those who inhabited the mountains and other <margin>G</margin> places, the number was infinite; through the places and tracts into such lots, all were distributed according to the leaders. Therefore, it was instituted that a leader should bring into war a sixth part of the war chariots, up to ten thousand chariots, two horses, and riders, and again a pair of horses without a saddle. Where there would also be one who, armed with a small shield, would descend, and one who would rule both horses in turn with the reins. Likewise two armor-bearers, and archers and slingers, two on each side; light-armed soldiers, stone-throwers, and javelin-throwers, three of each. Four sailors, for the complement of one thousand two hundred ships. In this way, then, were military affairs prepared in the royal city. But the equipment of the remaining nine <margin>H</margin> cities was held differently in different places, of which things the narration would be too long. The magistrates and honors were thus instituted from the beginning. Each of the ten kings in his own province and in his own city dominated the men, and also most of the laws, and punished according to his will and condemned each one to death. Indeed, the empire and communion among them were directed according to the mandates of Neptune, just as the laws and letters announced to them by their ancestors on a certain column made of orichalcum near the middle of the island, in the temple...

<summary>This page provides a meticulous description of Atlantis’s urban planning, advanced irrigation systems, and massive military organization. It highlights the central role of Poseidon’s laws, which were physically inscribed on a column of orichalcum to govern the ten kings.</summary>

<header>OF PLATO</header>

<margin>A</margin> ...were inscribed by Poseidon <note>original: "Neptuni"</note> himself. They used to gather every fifth and, in turn, every sixth year, alternating between even and odd numbers to give an equal part to both. When they were assembled, they deliberated on public affairs and, after a diligent examination, they would pass judgment if any among them had committed a transgression. Whenever a judgment was to be rendered, they bound one another with the following oath. While bulls were left roaming free in the temple of Poseidon, the ten kings, being left alone, would make a vow to the god to capture a victim pleasing to him without the use of iron. Thus, they hunted using only wooden staves and nooses. Whichever bull they captured, they led to the column and, at the very top of that pillar, they cut its throat exactly as the written laws commanded. Upon the column, in addition to the laws, there was an oath and terrible curses <margin>B</margin> invoked against those who did not obey. When they had prepared the sacrifices according to custom and were ready to burn the limbs of the bull, they filled a bowl and cast in a clot of blood for each of them. The rest of the carcass they gave to the fire, after purifying the column. Finally, drawing from the bowl with golden vials and pouring libations over the fire, they swore an oath, promising that they would judge according to the laws inscribed on the column and punish anyone who had previously transgressed. Furthermore, they swore never to willfully depart from the standard of those writings, nor to rule or obey any ruler except in accordance with the laws of their father. After each of them had made this prayer for himself and his descendants, he drank and <margin>C</margin> offered the vial to the temple of the god. As night approached, they turned their attention to the banquet and necessary matters. When the fire of the sacrifices had nearly died out, each king put on a most beautiful robe of dark blue <term>ceruleam: a deep, sea-blue color associated with Poseidon</term> and sat upon the ground in the darkness near the embers of the oath-offerings. Extinguishing every other fire in the sanctuary, they were judged and gave judgment if any among them had accused another of breaking the laws. After they had judged, and as soon as the light of day appeared, they inscribed their sentences on a golden tablet and hung them up, together with their robes, as a memorial for posterity. There were many other laws concerning the sacred rites of the individual kings, but these were the most important: that they should <margin>D</margin> never take up arms against one another, and instead, all should come to the aid of any royal house if someone in any city attempted to eradicate their lineage. Deliberating in common—as their ancestors did—concerning war and other actions, they granted the right of leadership to the lineage of Atlas <note>original: "Atlantico generi"</note>. However, the king was not granted the authority of life and death over any of his kinsmen unless more than five of the ten kings agreed to the same sentence. This power, so great and of such a kind as then existed in those places, the god brought back to these regions of ours on a certain occasion, as the story goes. For many ages, as long as the divine nature <margin>E</margin> within them endured, they were obedient to the laws and well-disposed toward the divine race to which they were related. For they possessed magnificent and true thoughts in their souls. Thus, they practiced moderation and prudence both in the face of external events and in their dealings with one another. Because of this, they looked down upon everything except virtue and made little account of their present wealth. They bore the weight of their gold and other possessions as if it were a burden. They were not intoxicated by luxury, nor did they lose their self-control through wealth; rather, being sober, they saw clearly that all these things increase through common friendship joined with virtue, but through the pursuit and excessive honoring of such goods, these very things perish, and virtue and friendship are destroyed along with them. As long as such reason and divine nature flourished in them, all the things we described before increased. But when the divine portion within them began to fade away through long abuse and became tainted by frequent mingling with the mortal nature of men, and the human character prevailed, they—no longer able to bear their prosperity—fell into disgrace. For to those who had eyes to see, they appeared shameful, having lost the most beautiful of their most precious qualities. But to those who were unable to perceive the true path to a happy life, they then appeared most excellent and blessed, even as they were filled with an unjust greed for "more" and with violent power. Then, indeed, Zeus <note>original: "Jupiter"</note>, the god of gods who rules all by law, perceiving these things and wishing to punish these men so that they might become more temperate and harmonious by being disciplined, summoned all the gods to their most honored seat, which stands in the center of the entire world and looks down upon all things that participate in generation. And having gathered them, he spoke as follows:

<column-break/>

In the center of the island stood the temple of Poseidon. Every fifth or, alternating, every sixth year, they gathered, assigning an equal share to both even and odd numbers. When gathered, they consulted on common matters and examined if anyone was transgressing, and they gave judgment. When they were about to judge, they gave each other pledges of this sort: while bulls were roaming free in the temple of Poseidon, the ten kings, being alone, prayed to the god to catch a victim pleasing to him without iron, and they hunted with wooden staves and nooses. The bull they caught they led to the column and slaughtered it against the top of the pillar, according to the writings. On the column, in addition to the laws, was an oath calling down great curses upon those who were disobedient. When they had sacrificed according to their laws and were hallowing all the limbs of the bull, they mixed a bowl of wine and cast in a clot of blood for each man. The rest they cast into the fire, after purifying the column. After this, drawing from the bowl with golden vials and pouring a libation upon the fire, they swore to judge according to the laws on the column and to punish any who had transgressed before, and that in the future they would not willfully transgress the writings, nor rule or obey a ruler except according to the laws of their father. After each had prayed these things for himself and his lineage, he drank and dedicated the vial in the temple of the god, then occupied himself with dinner and necessary things. When darkness came and the fire around the sacrifices died down, they all put on most beautiful dark blue robes and sat on the ground at night near the embers of the oath-sacrifices, extinguishing all fire around the temple, and they were judged or judged others if anyone accused another of transgressing. Having judged, they wrote the judgments on a golden tablet when light came and dedicated them with the robes as memorials. There were many other laws concerning the rituals of the individual kings, but the greatest were: never to bear arms against each other, to help one another if someone tried to overthrow the royal line in any city, and deliberating in common, as did those before them, on war and other matters, giving the leadership to the race of Atlas. The king had no power over the life of any kinsman unless it seemed right to more than half of the ten. This power, so great and of such a kind as then existed in those places, the god organized and brought against these places of ours for some such reason (as the story goes). For many generations, as long as the nature of the god was sufficient for them, they were obedient to the laws and kindly disposed to the divine kinsman. For they possessed true and entirely great spirits, practicing mildness with wisdom toward the chances of life and toward one another. Therefore, looking down on everything except virtue, they thought little of their present circumstances and bore easily, as a burden, the mass of gold and other possessions. They were not drunk with luxury, nor did they stumble in lack of self-control because of wealth, knowing that all these things increase from common friendship with virtue, but by the pursuit and honor of these things, they themselves waste away and virtue perishes with them. From such reasoning and the divine nature remaining, all we described before increased. But when the portion of the god began to vanish in them, being mixed often with much mortal element, and the human character prevailed, then, no longer able to bear their prosperity, they behaved unseemly, and to one able to see, they appeared shameful, losing the most beautiful of their most precious things. To those unable to see the true life for happiness, they then seemed most beautiful and blessed, being full of unjust greed and power. But Zeus, the god of gods, reigning by law, since he is able to see such things, noticing a noble race in a wretched state and wishing to impose a penalty on them so they might become more disciplined and harmonious, gathered all the gods to their most honored dwelling, which, situated in the center of the whole universe, looks down on all things that have partaken in generation. And having gathered them, he said:

# PLATO’S LAWS, OR,

-> The first of the twelve discourses or dialogues. <-

---

-> **SUMMARY OF THE DIALOGUE** <-
In setting out to discuss the laws, Plato begins appropriately with their cause and foundation. He notes a twofold cause: the primary and highest is God; the second and intermediary is Virtue—not just some part of it, but the whole of virtue, perfect and absolute in all its parts. This is the bond by which the society of the human race can be held together. He also teaches that human nature is the subject of the laws, though it is a nature that is corrupt and contaminated by various vices. Thus, Reason itself has as many enemies as there are desires in man, the battle of which is expressed through <meta>continuity with next page</meta> images...

While the previous page dealt with the divine origins and eventual corruption of a legendary kingdom, this text moves into practical political philosophy, examining the origins and purpose of legislation through a conversation between three elderly men: an Athenian, a Cretan, and a Spartan.</meta>

# ON THE LAWS, BOOK I.

...he describes with images. He does this for the purpose of letting the legislator understand how much diligence and how much judgment he must apply in establishing laws—laws in which that insane sequence of human desires may be restrained. Therefore, the thesis of this dialogue is: the Causes, the Subject, and the Goal of Laws. This goal is defined such that the citizens and the republic are composed of a temperament of virtues, and thus true happiness may be established for them.

->THE ATHENIAN STRANGER, CLEINIAS THE CRETAN, MEGILLUS THE LACEDAEMONIAN.<-

->THE ATHENIAN STRANGER, CLEINIAS THE CRETAN, MEGILLUS THE LACEDAEMONIAN.<-

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
<image-desc>A large ornamental woodcut initial 'Theta' (Θ) containing a figure seated in a pastoral landscape with a tree.</image-desc>
**ATHENIAN:** Was it a god or some man, O strangers, whom you take to be the cause of the arrangement of your laws? **CLEINIAS:** A god, stranger, a god—to speak in the most just way. Among us, it was Zeus; but among the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note>, from where this man comes, I believe they say it was Apollo. Is that not so? **MEGILLUS:** Yes. **ATHENIAN:** Do you speak then according to Homer, saying that Minos <note>The legendary first King of Crete</note> visited his father <note>Zeus</note> every ninth year for consultation, and that he established the laws for your cities based on those divine voices? **CLEINIAS:** So it is said among us. And they also say that his brother, Rhadamanthys—you have heard the name—was the most just of men. We Cretans would say he earned this praise because he administered justice so rightly in those times. **ATHENIAN:** It is indeed a noble reputation, and one most fitting for a son of Zeus. Since you both have been brought up in such legal customs, I expect it would not be unpleasant for us to pass the time during our journey by speaking and listening to one another about the constitution of states and their laws. Certainly, the road from Knossos <note>The capital of ancient Crete</note> to the cave and temple of Zeus is, as we hear, quite long; and there are resting places along the way, as is natural in this current stifling heat, shaded beneath high trees.

<margin>C</margin>
It would be fitting for our age to rest frequently in them and, by exchanging words with one another, to complete the whole journey in comfort. **CLEINIAS:** Indeed, stranger, as we go further, there are cypress trees in the groves of wonderful height and beauty, and meadows too, where we might linger and rest. **ATHENIAN:** You speak rightly. **CLEINIAS:** Entirely so; but once we see them, we shall say so with even more certainty. Let us go, then, with good fortune. **ATHENIAN:** So be it. And tell me, why has your law established for you the communal meals <note>original: "syssitia"; these were public mess halls intended to foster civic unity and military discipline</note>, the gymnasia, and the style of your weaponry? **CLEINIAS:** I believe, stranger, that our customs are easy for anyone to understand. You see the nature of the whole land of Crete: it is not flat like the land of the Thessalians.

<margin>D</margin>
For that reason, they use horses more, while we use our own feet for running. Our land is uneven and better suited for the practice of foot-racing. It is necessary in such a place to possess light armor and not to run while carrying a heavy weight. Thus, the lightness of bows and arrows seems to be most fitting. All these things of ours are prepared with a view toward war; and the legislator, as it seems to me, arranged everything looking toward this end. He likely instituted the communal meals because he saw that all men, whenever they are on a campaign, are forced by the circumstances of the action to eat together for the sake of their own protection. He seems to me to have condemned the foolishness of the masses, who do not understand that for everyone, there is a continuous war throughout life against all other states.

<margin>E</margin>
If indeed, during a time of war, it is necessary to eat together for protection and to have certain officers and subordinates organized as guards, then this same thing must also be done in time of peace. For what most men call "peace" is only a name; in reality, by nature, there is always an undeclared war of every state against every other state. If you look at it this way, you will find that the Cretan legislator arranged all our legal customs, both public and private, with an eye toward war. He handed down the laws for us to guard in this way, believing that nothing else—neither possessions nor pursuits—is of any benefit unless one prevails in war; for all the goods of the vanquished become the property of the victors.

<margin>F</margin>
**ATHENIAN:** You seem to me, stranger, to be well-trained in explaining the Cretan customs. But tell me this more clearly: you seem to define a well-governed city as one that is organized in such a way as to defeat other cities in war. Is that right? **CLEINIAS:** Certainly. And I believe our friend here <note>Megillus</note> agrees. **MEGILLUS:** How else, O divine man, would any Lacedaemonian answer? **ATHENIAN:** Is this principle right for a city against a city, but different for a village against a village? **CLEINIAS:** Not at all. **ATHENIAN:** Is it the same? **CLEINIAS:** Yes. **ATHENIAN:** And what about one household against another in the same village, or one man against another man? Is it still the same? **CLEINIAS:** The same. **ATHENIAN:** And what of a man against himself? Must we think of him as an enemy against an enemy? Or how shall we say it?

<margin>G</margin>
**CLEINIAS:** O Athenian stranger! I would not want to call you merely a man of Attica, for you seem to me rather to be worthy of the name of the goddess <note>Athena, the goddess of wisdom</note>. By leading the argument back to its first principle, you have made it clearer. Thus, you will more easily discover that we were correct just now in saying that everyone is an enemy to everyone else, both in public and in private, and each individual is an enemy to himself. **ATHENIAN:** How do you mean, marvelous man? **CLEINIAS:** In this case too, stranger, for a man to conquer himself is the first and best of all victories; but to be defeated by himself is the most shameful and worst of all things.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
<image-desc>A large ornamental woodcut initial 'N' containing a figure playing a lyre in a landscape.</image-desc>
**DO YOU BELIEVE** that some man, O strangers, is the cause of your established laws? **CLEINIAS:** A God, O stranger, a God, I say, as it is proper to assert: among us indeed Zeus, but among the Lacedaemonians from where this man comes, I believe they would say Apollo.

<margin>B</margin>
Is it not so? **MEGILLUS:** Certainly. **ATHENIAN:** Do you say this following Homer? Namely, that Minos used to seek a meeting with his father every nine years, and according to his advice, he placed the laws for your cities just as that poet sings. **CLEINIAS:** So our people say. They also say his brother Rhadamanthys (for you have heard the name) was most just. And we Cretans judge that he attained this praise because at that time he correctly distributed justice to each person. **ATHENIAN:** Truly, that is an excellent praise and most worthy of a son of Zeus. But because both of you have been educated in such customs and laws—you, of course, and this man here—I hope it will not be unpleasant for us if we discuss the constitution of cities and laws while we walk. Moreover, the way from Knossos to the cave and temple of Zeus is, as we have heard, long enough, and there are shady spots along it under tall trees, as is suitable in the heat.

<margin>C</margin>
It will therefore be fitting for our age to rest frequently in these, and to complete this whole journey without trouble through the mutual comfort of conversation. **CLEINIAS:** And yet, stranger, as we proceed, we shall come upon cypresses in the groves of wonderful height and beauty, and also pleasant meadows, in which we may gladly linger while resting. **ATHENIAN:** You speak rightly indeed. **CLEINIAS:** Entirely. But we shall affirm these things more once we have seen them. For now, let us go with good omens.

<margin>D</margin>
**ATHENIAN:** Let it be so. But tell me, I pray, for what reason did the law establish for you public banquets, gymnasia, and the art of weaponry? **CLEINIAS:** I think, O stranger, that these things of ours are very easy to understand. For you see the nature of the entire Cretan region; it is not, like Thessaly, flat. Therefore, they use horses more, and we use running. This inequality of places is better suited for pedestrian exercise and running. For this reason, it is also necessary that the armor be lighter, so that it does not hinder the run by its own weight. The lightness of bows and arrows, therefore, is most suitable. All these things, then, are adapted for us for war; and looking toward that, the legislator, as it seems to me, instituted everything. Indeed, for this reason he even seems to have ordained the law of meeting together, because he saw that all men in military service are forced by the situation itself to have communal meals for the sake of their own protection. In this, I certainly think he condemned many people for the crime of foolishness, because they do not at all understand that there is a continuous and perpetual war for all cities against all others.

<margin>E</margin>
For if, while there is war, communal meals are celebrated for the sake of protection, and it is necessary for some leaders together with their subjects to have been armed to protect the rest, that very thing must also be done in time of peace. For what many people call "peace," that should be considered to be a name only. In reality, there is by nature an undeclared war for all cities against all others, and you will find, if you consider it, that the Cretan legislator wrote all laws for us, both privately and publicly, as if he were looking toward war, and he ordered us to obey them as if there were no use for other things—neither possessions nor arts—unless one prevails in war; since all the goods of those who are defeated pass over to the victors.

<margin>F</margin>
**ATHENIAN:** Well said, O stranger; you seem to me to be well-practiced in explaining the Cretan laws. But you should say this more clearly. For you seemed to say that a city is correctly arranged only if it is so instituted that it can defeat other cities in war. Is it so? **CLEINIAS:** Exactly so. I think this man will also agree. **MEGILLUS:** How else, O divine man, would any of the Lacedaemonians answer? **ATHENIAN:** Does this apply to a city against a city, but differently to a village against a village? **CLEINIAS:** Not otherwise. **ATHENIAN:** Therefore they are in a similar state. **CLEINIAS:** Similar. **ATHENIAN:** What further is to be said about any neighborhood against itself? Shall we say that anyone must meditate and prepare against himself as an enemy against an enemy?

<margin>G</margin>
Or otherwise? **CLEINIAS:** Athenian stranger—for I do not wish to call you merely "Attic." You seem to be more worthy of the name of the goddess of Athens herself, that is, Pallas. Indeed, you have made this whole reasoning plain by reducing it to its principle, whereby it may more easily be found that it has already been correctly said: namely, that all are enemies to all, both publicly and privately, and individuals are enemies to themselves. **ATHENIAN:** How do you say that, O wonderful man? **CLEINIAS:** Here too, O stranger, I say that to conquer oneself is the first and best victory; but to be conquered by oneself is something most shameful and worst.

<summary>This page introduces Plato's *Laws*, opening with a dialogue between an Athenian, a Cretan, and a Spartan who discuss the divine origins of their laws (Zeus and Apollo). The Cretan protagonist argues that all social institutions, including communal meals and physical training, are designed for a state of perpetual war, leading to the philosophical claim that the greatest victory is self-conquest.</summary>

--- Page 598 ---
<meta>This page continues the opening dialogue of Plato's *Laws*. Having established that the Lacedaemonian (Spartan) and Cretan laws seem focused entirely on preparing for war, the Athenian Stranger now pushes his companions to consider whether "victory over oneself" is the true goal of a city, just as it is for an individual.</meta>

<page-num>566</page-num>
<header>PLATO'S [WORKS]</header>

<margin>A</margin>And all these things signify that there is a war within every individual against themselves. <term>ATHENIAN:</term> Let us, therefore, take up that argument again. For since each of us is either a master of himself or inferior to himself, must we say that a household, a village, and a city have this same condition within them? Or should we say otherwise? <term>CLEINIAS:</term> Are you asking if some are masters of themselves and others are inferior to themselves? <term>ATHENIAN:</term> Exactly. <term>CLEINIAS:</term> You have asked this rightly too. For this happens no less in cities; indeed, they observe this most clearly in them. For where the better people overcome the multitude and the worse people, that city is truly and rightly said to be a master of itself, and it will be praised for this victory quite justly. But on the contrary, when the opposite occurs.

<margin>B</margin><term>ATHENIAN:</term> But whether the worse is ever superior to and more powerful than the better, let that be set aside for the present; for it requires a longer discussion. But what you have said, I understand in this way: that sometimes citizens who are kin and of the same city—many and wicked—will conspire against those few who are just, and they will use force to subject them. And if they prevail, that city will be called inferior to itself and wicked; but if they are defeated, it will be called superior and virtuous.
<term>CLEINIAS:</term> What you say is strange, stranger; yet it must be admitted as such.
<term>ATHENIAN:</term> Come now, and let us consider this again. Many brothers might be born from one father and the same mother; and it is no wonder if most of them turn out unjust, and only a few turn out just. <term>CLEINIAS:</term> It is not a wonder at all.

<margin>C</margin><term>ATHENIAN:</term> Nor is it fitting, I think, for me or for you to hunt after this point—namely, whether a household and an entire kinship appears "inferior to itself" if the wicked prevail, or "superior" if they are defeated. For we are not doing this to observe the elegance or crudeness of words, as many are accustomed to do, but rather to track down what the right principle is according to nature in laws, and what the error might be. <term>CLEINIAS:</term> You speak the truth, stranger. <term>MEGILLUS:</term> Truly, it seems to me also that what has been said so far is sound. <term>ATHENIAN:</term> Let us consider this further. Could some judge be placed in charge of those brothers we just mentioned? <term>CLEINIAS:</term> Undoubtedly.

<margin>D</margin><term>ATHENIAN:</term> Which judge, then, will be better? The one who destroys the wicked and makes it so that the virtuous rule themselves? Or the one who makes the virtuous rule, but allows the wicked to live after persuading them to submit voluntarily to being ruled? Let us add a third judge in terms of excellence to these, if such a man can be found: one who, taking over a quarreling kinship, would destroy no one, but by reconciling them would write laws for them by which they might be friends with each other forever. <term>CLEINIAS:</term> Such a judge and legislator would be far better.

<margin>E</margin><term>ATHENIAN:</term> And yet, he will write laws for them looking toward the opposite of war. <term>CLEINIAS:</term> You speak the truth. <term>ATHENIAN:</term> What then? He who organizes a city with an eye toward war—will he look toward external wars and direct the life of the citizens to those, or toward internal ones, which are called <term>seditiones</term> <note>original Latin: *seditiones*, Greek: *stasis* — meaning internal civil strife or factional conflict</note>, which any man would least of all want to exist in his city, and if they do exist, would want to abolish as quickly as possible? <term>CLEINIAS:</term> Clearly toward these internal ones. <term>ATHENIAN:</term> And would anyone prefer to achieve peace from civil strife by the destruction of one part of the citizens when the other part has gained victory, or rather that peace be made through reconciliation and friendship strengthened, so that the mind of the whole city might then turn toward external wars? <term>CLEINIAS:</term> Everyone would surely opt for the latter rather than the former to happen to their own city. <term>ATHENIAN:</term> And would not the legislator do the same? <term>CLEINIAS:</term> Likewise.

<margin>F</margin><term>ATHENIAN:</term> Must not all laws be made for the sake of the best thing? <term>CLEINIAS:</term> Certainly for that. <term>ATHENIAN:</term> Yet the best thing is neither war nor civil strife—for everyone prays that they might never have to enter into these—but rather peace and mutual goodwill. But neither is that victory by which a city overcomes itself a truly "best" thing, but rather a necessary one. To think that the best state of a city consists in fighting and winning is like someone thinking that a sick person is doing best while being treated, but not even thinking about the one who never fell ill in the first place. And if someone thinks similarly about the happiness of a city or a private individual, he will never truly be a statesman—looking only and primarily toward external wars—nor will he be an exquisite maker of laws, unless he writes laws about war for the sake of peace, rather than writing laws about peace for the sake of war. <term>CLEINIAS:</term> These things seem to be rightly said, stranger. Yet I would be surprised if our laws, as well as those of the Lacedaemonians, were not diligently established for the sake of war.

<margin>G</margin><term>ATHENIAN:</term> Perhaps that is so. However, we ought not to investigate the matter contentiously, but quietly, with as much zeal as possible applied to such things by both you and them. I beg you to pay attention, then. Let us begin with <term>Tyrtæus</term> <note>A 7th-century BCE Greek poet known for his military elegies</note>, who was an Athenian by nature but later a citizen of the Lacedaemonians, and who applied himself to these matters more than other men. He said: *Not if he should surpass all in riches, and alone possess the most goods* (for he enumerates nearly everything), *will a man depart as worthy of the name in my eyes, who is not fit for handling arms.* Perhaps you also have heard these poems. For I think this man [Megillus] is already weary from hearing them. <term>MEGILLUS:</term> These are most common among us. <term>CLEINIAS:</term> These have also reached us, brought from Lacedaemon. <term>ATHENIAN:</term> Let us, therefore, question this poet together in this way: "O most divine poet <term>Tyrtæus</term>, you certainly seem to us to be wise and good, since you have extolled with excellent praise those who have excelled in war." Regarding this, now, I and he and Cleinias—

<column-break/>

<margin>Α</margin> For these things signify that there is a war in each of us against ourselves. <term>ATHENIAN:</term> Let us then turn the argument back again. For since each one of us is either master of himself or inferior to himself, shall we say that a house, a village, and a city have this same thing in themselves, or shall we not? <term>CLEINIAS:</term> You speak well of someone being "master of himself," but what do you mean? <term>ATHENIAN:</term> Yes. <term>CLEINIAS:</term> And you asked this correctly. For such a thing is very intense, especially in cities. In those where the better men defeat the multitude and the worse, that city would rightly be called master of itself, and it would be praised most justly for such a victory; but the opposite where the opposite happens. <term>ATHENIAN:</term> Whether the worse is ever master of the better, let us leave aside (for it is a longer <margin>Β</margin> discussion); but what you say I now understand: that sometimes fellow citizens of the same city, being many and unjust, come together and force the just, who are fewer, into slavery. And whenever they prevail, the city would rightly be called both inferior to itself and bad; but where they are defeated, it is master of itself and good. <term>CLEINIAS:</term> And what is now being said is very strange, stranger; yet it is most necessary to agree it is so. <term>ATHENIAN:</term> Hold on, then, and let us consider this again. Many brothers could be sons of one man and one mother. And it is not surprising at all that the majority <margin>C</margin> of them become unjust, and the fewer, just. <term>CLEINIAS:</term> Not at all. <term>ATHENIAN:</term> And it would not be fitting for me and you to hunt for this: that if the wicked win, this house and kinship would be called inferior to itself, but master of itself if they are defeated. For we are not now considering this for the sake of the elegance or ungracefulness of words according to the talk of the many, but for the sake of correctness and error concerning laws, whatever their nature may be. <term>CLEINIAS:</term> You speak most truly, stranger. <term>MEGILLUS:</term> It seems well to me also, as far as this goes now. <term>ATHENIAN:</term> Let us see this too. For these <margin>D</margin> brothers just mentioned, would there be some judge? <term>CLEINIAS:</term> Certainly. <term>ATHENIAN:</term> Which one, then, is better? The one who would destroy all those among them who are bad, and set the better to rule themselves? Or the one who would make the good rule, but letting the worse live, would make them be ruled voluntarily? Thirdly, let us mention a judge in respect to virtue, if there were such a one, who, having taken over one kinship that was in conflict, would neither destroy anyone, but having reconciled them for the future, would lay down laws for them so that they could preserve friendship for one another and be friends. <term>CLEINIAS:</term> Such a judge and legislator would be by far the better. <term>ATHENIAN:</term> And yet, he would lay down laws for them looking toward the opposite of war. <term>CLEINIAS:</term> That is true. <term>ATHENIAN:</term> And what of the one who harmonizes the city? Would he organize its life looking toward its external war more than toward the war that happens within it at various times, which is called <term>stasis</term> <note>civil strife</note>? Which every man would most wish never to happen in his own city, and if it did happen, to be rid of it as quickly as possible. <term>CLEINIAS:</term> Clearly toward the latter. <term>ATHENIAN:</term> And would one prefer peace from the strife to come by the destruction of one group and the victory of the other, or rather that after reconciliation, friendship and peace were established, so that they might then be forced to turn their attention toward external enemies? <term>CLEINIAS:</term> Everyone would prefer it to happen to his own city in this way rather than that. <term>ATHENIAN:</term> And the legislator likewise? <term>CLEINIAS:</term> Of course. <term>ATHENIAN:</term> Does not everyone establish all laws for the sake of the best? <term>CLEINIAS:</term> How could they not? <term>ATHENIAN:</term> But the best is neither war nor civil strife (it is to be prayed that there be no need of these), but peace toward one another and friendliness. And so it seems that for a city to conquer itself was not among the best things, but among the necessary ones. It is as if someone thought a sick body, happening upon a medical purging, was then doing best, but paid no mind to the body that needed it not at all. Likewise, if someone thinks this way about the happiness of a city or an individual, he would never be a true statesman, looking correctly only and primarily toward external matters of war, nor would he be an accurate legislator, unless he legislated the things of war for the sake of peace rather than the things of peace for the sake of war. <term>CLEINIAS:</term> This argument, stranger, seems somehow to have been rightly spoken; yet I wonder if our laws and those in Lacedaemon have not made all their effort for the sake of these [war-like] things. <term>ATHENIAN:</term> Perhaps they have. <margin>G</margin> But we must not fight harshly among ourselves now; rather, we must ask quietly, as both we and they are always most serious about these things. Follow me in the argument. Let us take <term>Tyrtæus</term>, by nature an Athenian, but now having become a citizen [of Sparta], who indeed of all men was most serious about these things, saying that:
> I would neither mention nor take account of a man,
> not even if he were the richest of men, he says, nor if he possessed many good things (mentioning nearly all of them), who did not always prove best in war
<margin>H</margin> against himself. <note>original: *autou* — here suggesting the internal battle for excellence</note>. You have surely heard his poems. For this man, I think, is sated with them. <term>MEGILLUS:</term> Quite so. <term>CLEINIAS:</term> Indeed, they have come to us as well, brought from Lacedaemon. <term>ATHENIAN:</term> Come now, let us question this poet together as if in this way: "O <term>Tyrtæus</term>, most divine poet; for you seem to us to be wise and good, because you have exceptionally praised those who excel in war. Now then, I and he and <term>Cleinias</term>—

<summary>This page contains a dialogue exploring the philosophical definition of "victory" for a city and an individual, arguing that peace and internal harmony (mastery of self) are superior to success in war. The Athenian Stranger challenges the Spartan and Cretan focus on military law, suggesting that the best legislator acts as a reconciler rather than a conqueror.</summary>
