<meta>This page continues the dialogue from the beginning of Book I of Plato’s Laws. The Athenian Stranger is leading Clinias (the Cretan) and Megillus (the Spartan) to realize that laws should not be designed solely for victory in war, but for the cultivation of all virtues, especially justice and wisdom during times of internal peace.</meta>

# ON THE LAWS, BOOK I.

<margin>A</margin> **ATHENIAN:** This man from Knossos <note>original: "ὁ Κνώσιος," referring to Clinias</note> seems to agree with me very much on this, as I see it. But whether we are speaking of the same men or not, we should like to know clearly. Tell us, then: do you believe there are two kinds of war, just as we have clearly supposed? Or how do you see it? To this, I think, even a man far less skilled than the poet **Tyrtaeus** <note>A Spartan poet famous for his war songs emphasizing courage in battle</note> would immediately answer the truth: that there are two. One is what we all call civil war <note>original: "στάσιν" (stasis) / "seditionem"</note>, which is the most difficult of all wars, as we just agreed. The other kind of war, I think we would all agree, is much milder than that, which we use against external enemies and foreigners when we are at odds. <term>CLINIAS:</term> Who could doubt that? <term>ATHENIAN:</term>

<margin>B</margin> Come then, tell us: regarding which men and which kind of war were you praising so highly when you spoke, and whom were you blaming? You seem to have praised those who wage external wars with great spirit. For you said in your poems that you cannot endure those "who do not dare to behold bloody slaughter, and reach out to strike the enemy from close at hand." <note>The Athenian is quoting Tyrtaeus's poetry to challenge the narrow focus on battlefield bravery.</note> From this, we would conclude, Tyrtaeus, that you especially praise those who distinguish themselves in external and foreign wars. He would surely admit this, wouldn't he? <term>CLINIAS:</term> Of course. <term>ATHENIAN:</term> But we, while admitting these men are good, still claim that those who prove themselves best in the greatest war are far better. And we too have a poet as a witness, **Theognis** <note>An elegiac poet from Megara known for his moral maxims</note>, a citizen of the Megarians in Sicily, who says: "A faithful man is worth his weight in gold and silver, Cyrnus, in the midst of terrible

<margin>C</margin> civil strife." We say that such a man, in a much more difficult war, is as much better than the other as justice, temperance, and wisdom, when joined with courage, are better than courage alone. For a man can never be truly "faithful and sound" in times of civil war without possessing the sum of all virtues. Yet there are many mercenaries—as Tyrtaeus would not deny—who are willing to die while fighting in external wars, most of whom are bold, unjust, insolent, and the most senseless of almost all men. To what end does this argument lead?

<margin>D</margin> Where does it finish? Is the argument sound? What was it trying to make clear? It is this: that both the lawgiver here in Crete who received laws from Zeus, and any other lawgiver worth anything at all, will always establish laws looking toward the greatest virtue. This virtue is, as Theognis says, "faithfulness in times of danger," which one might call "perfect justice." But that which Tyrtaeus praised so highly, though beautiful and fittingly celebrated by the poet, is nonetheless rightly ranked only fourth in importance and power. <term>CLINIAS:</term> O Stranger, are we then casting our own lawgiver down among the lowest of lawgivers? <term>ATHENIAN:</term> Not him, my excellent friend, but ourselves, if we think that Lycurgus and Minos established the laws in Lacedaemon <note>Sparta</note> and here in Crete

<margin>E</margin> primarily with a view toward war. <term>CLINIAS:</term> How then should we have spoken? <term>ATHENIAN:</term> As truth and justice require when speaking of divine matters: we must believe they looked not to a mere fragment of virtue—and the least fragment at that—but to the whole of virtue, and that they sought out laws according to all its forms. They did not do as people do today, who seek only what they happen to need; for one man seeks laws concerning inheritance and heiresses, another concerning assault, and others about thousands of such matters. But we say that the proper inquiry into laws, conducted by those who seek well, should begin as we have just begun. I entirely admire your attempt to explain the laws; for to begin with virtue, saying the laws were made for its sake, is surely the right approach.

<margin>F</margin> But because you claimed the lawgiver legislated by looking only at a small fragment of virtue, you seemed to me to be speaking incorrectly, and for that reason I have spoken at such length. Now, do you wish for me to tell you how I would have preferred you to distinguish these things? <term>CLINIAS:</term> Certainly. <term>ATHENIAN:</term> You should have said: "Stranger, the laws of the Cretans are not admired among all the Greeks without reason. They are correctly established because they make those who use them happy; for they provide all good things." Now, goods are of two kinds: some are *human*, and others are *divine*. The human goods depend upon the divine ones. If a city receives the greater goods, it also possesses the lesser; but if not, it is deprived of both. Among the lesser goods, the first is health; the second is beauty; the third is

<margin>G</margin> strength, for running and all other bodily movements; and the fourth is wealth—not "blind" wealth, but wealth that sees clearly, provided it follows wisdom. Among the divine goods, the leader is **wisdom** <note>original: "φρόνησις" (phronesis), practical wisdom</note>; second is a **temperate** state of the soul joined with intellect; third, from these two mixed with courage, is **justice**; and fourth is **courage**. All these are naturally ranked before those human goods, and the lawgiver must also rank them so. After these, he must command the citizens to keep their other instructions focused on these goals. The human goods should look to the divine, and all the divine goods should look to the leading Intellect <note>original: "νοῦν" (noun)</note>. This includes how they join together in marriage. Next, it concerns the birth and upbringing of children, both

<margin>H</margin> male and female, from their youth through their older years into old age. The lawgiver must rightly care for these by bestowing honors or dishonors in all their social interactions, observing their pains, pleasures, and desires. He must carefully examine the intensities of all their loves...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> <note>The Latin column replicates the Greek content translated above.</note> The man of Knossos seems to agree with you strongly. But whether we speak of the same men or not, we would wish to know plainly. Therefore explain to us, do you also, like us, think there are two kinds of war, or otherwise? To this, I think, not only Tyrtaeus, but anyone far more lowly than he, would immediately answer: two. One which we call civil war, and we just admitted it is the most serious of all. The other kind of war, which we all place as much milder than that, which we use against outsiders and foreigners. <term>CLINIAS:</term> Who could doubt it? <term>ATHENIAN:</term>

<margin>B</margin> Tell us then, which men in which kind of war did you praise so much, and which did you so greatly blame? For you seem to have praised those who wage external wars with great courage. For you said in your poems, "I despise anyone who does not dare to look upon bloody slaughter, and provoke harsh Mars hand to hand." From this, we gather, O Tyrtaeus, that you praise those who are famous above others in waging external wars. Tyrtaeus would concede this. <term>CLINIAS:</term> Why not? <term>ATHENIAN:</term> But we, while these are outstanding, think those who excel in the greatest war are far more outstanding. And we have the poet Theognis, a citizen of Megara in Sicily, as a witness, who says: "A faithful man would be equal to yellow silver and gold,

<margin>C</margin> remaining firm in insane civil strife." This man, therefore, we say is as much better in the most serious war as justice, temperance, and wisdom, joined with courage, are better than courage alone. For no one can be found whole and faithful in civil wars without the full number of all virtues. However, many mercenaries are found—which Tyrtaeus will not deny—who fight intrepidly in external war: most of whom are fierce, unjust, insolent, and except for a few, the most senseless of all. To what purpose is this? And what did he want declared from these things when he said them? That clearly, both he who gave laws here from Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note>, as well as any other lawmaker,

<margin>D</margin> if he brings forth anything at all, will establish laws in such a way that he looks to nothing else but the most ample virtue. But there is, as Theognis says, that "faith" which shines most in dangers. Which one will call perfect justice. That virtue which Tyrtaeus praised so greatly, although it is beautiful and seasonably praised by the poet, nonetheless in virtue (by which it is called the honorable kind), is most rightly honored in the fourth place by number and power. <term>CLINIAS:</term> Therefore, stranger, do we reject the founder of our laws among the last of lawgivers? <term>ATHENIAN:</term> Not him, O best of men, but ourselves, if we think that here among the Lacedaemonians Lycurgus, and Minos [in Crete], established the laws looking toward war. <term>CLINIAS:</term> How then ought we to have spoken of this? <term>ATHENIAN:</term> As truth and justice demand of those who discuss a divine republic: it must be thought that they looked not to a part of virtue, and especially to the lowlier part, but to universal virtue itself, and sought the laws through each of its species, not investigating those species which many people now propose and seek. For each man usually seeks that which he most lacks: one concerning inheritance and women left as sole heirs to be taken as wives, another concerning injury, another concerning many other such things. But we think the inquiry into laws is well done when it is sought just as we have now begun. And I indeed greatly approve of your entrance into explaining the laws. For by making the beginning from virtue, saying the laws were established for the sake of virtue, you seem to have approached it correctly.

<margin>F</margin> But because you affirmed that the founder of the laws looked toward a part of virtue, and that the smallest part, you seemed to me to speak incorrectly, and therefore I used a longer speech afterward. But how I would have wished you to distinguish this for us, if you wish, I will tell you. <term>CLINIAS:</term> I certainly wish it. <term>ATHENIAN:</term> It was necessary to speak in this manner, O stranger: "The laws of the Cretans are not without reason approved by all, especially the Greeks. For they are correctly placed, since they make those using them happy. For they offer all good things to them." Now goods are twofold: some are human, others divine; and human goods depend on the divine. If any city receives the greater, it also possesses the lesser; but if it lacks those, it is deprived of both. Of the lesser, the first is health, the second beauty, the third strength for running and other motions of the body, the fourth riches, which are not blind, but see sharply if they follow wisdom. Which wisdom indeed exists as the first leader of divine goods. Then, after the mind, a temperate habit of the soul. From these two mixed with courage, justice emerges third. Courage holds the fourth place. All these are by nature preferred to those human ones. Wherefore it is necessary that the lawgiver himself also follow this order, and command everyone that they should always act in individual matters looking toward these very things: for human things are to be referred to the divine, and divine things to the Mind as the leader. He ought to care, furthermore, for marriages among citizens, and the generations and educations of children, males and females alike, both the young and those advanced in age: and those who conduct themselves correctly in these things, as is fitting, he should honor; on the contrary, he should blame pains, pleasures, and desires in all conversation. He will also consider and diligently observe toward which studies...

<summary>In this passage, the Athenian Stranger argues that laws should be designed to foster "perfect justice" and all virtues, rather than just military courage. He establishes a hierarchy of "Divine Goods" (Wisdom, Temperance, Justice, Courage) which are superior to "Human Goods" (Health, Beauty, Strength, Wealth).</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue in Book I of Plato's Laws, where the Athenian Stranger is examining the legal systems of Crete and Sparta. They have just moved from discussing the general purpose of laws—to instill virtue—to the specific ways a legislator regulates the life of the city.</meta>

### PLATO'S LAWS

<margin>A</margin> ...everyone is seized by love; the legislator will praise upright duties through laws and will condemn their opposites. He will likewise teach and define what is honorable and what is shameful in each person's passions—namely, concerning anger and fear, and whatever other disturbances occur in times of adversity, or delights in times of prosperity. He will do this regarding all movements of the soul that vex men due to disease, war, poverty, or their opposites. After this, it is necessary for the legislator to diligently observe the gains and expenses of the citizens and recognize how they occur. Furthermore, he must watch over their associations and dissolutions, whether they enter into them voluntarily or involuntarily. He should notice wherever justice is present or absent in these dealings. To those who are obedient to the laws, he should assign honors; to those who are disobedient, he should establish due punishments.

<margin>B</margin> Finally, having handled all things until the end of the Republic, he must necessarily observe and decree how monuments are to be built for the dead, and what honors should be paid to each of the deceased. Once these things are declared, the legislator will appoint guardians over all of them: some administering through wisdom, others through true opinion, so that the mind, gathering all these things into one, may lead them toward the pursuit of temperance <note>Latin: *temperantiam*; Greek: *σωφροσύνῃ* (sophrosyne), often translated as self-control or moderation</note> and justice, rather than riches or ambition. In this way, guests, I would have wished—and still wish—for you to explain how all these things are present in the laws of Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note> and Pythian Apollo, which Minos and Lycurgus wrote. I want to know in what order they are made manifest to one who has skill in laws by art or practice, though to the rest of us they are in no way apparent.

**CLINIAS:** How then, guest, should we treat the matters that follow?

**ATHENIAN:** It seems to me that we should treat things from the beginning again, as we started above. First, we should handle those things pertaining to fortitude <note>manly courage</note>; then we shall go through one species of virtue after another, if that pleases you. Let us deal with the first one now, and use it as a model for the rest, so that our conversation may provide a relief for our journey. Finally, when we have treated all virtue, we shall show, if God wills, that those things we just mentioned look toward that goal.

<margin>C</margin> **CLINIAS:** You speak well; let us first try to examine this praiser of Jove <note>referring to the Spartan/Cretan tradition of divine law</note>.

**ATHENIAN:** I shall try—for both you and myself. For this discourse pertains to us both. Tell me then: did we say that the common meals <note>original: *syssitia*</note> and the gymnasia were invented by the legislator for the purpose of war?

**CLINIAS:** Indeed.

**ATHENIAN:** And is there a third or fourth thing to be said for the same purpose? For perhaps it is necessary to number them this way, both in this kind of virtue and in the other parts of virtue—or whatever else it might be proper to call them for the sake of explanation.

<margin>E</margin> **MEGILLUS:** I would say the third is hunting, and no Lacedaemonian <note>Spartan</note> would deny it. Let us try to find the fourth and fifth. I place the fourth as the most important among my people: namely, the endurance of pain. This is practiced daily in hand-to-hand fights and certain robberies, which result in many wounds. Added to these is a certain "remarkable concealment" <term>Krypteia</term> <note>A Spartan institution where young men lived in the wild, often patrolling for rebellious serfs</note>, which is a powerful exercise in endurance; it is told how they wander through the whole region day and night without servants, with bare feet in winter and often with the rest of their body naked. Furthermore, in the exercises of our naked youths <term>Gymnopaedia</term> <note>An annual Spartan festival involving athletic competitions and choral dances</note>, there is a remarkable endurance when they must resist the force of intense heat. There are many other such things among us that one could not easily enumerate.

**ATHENIAN:** You speak well, Lacedaemonian guest. But is the fight of fortitude only against fears and pains? Or is it also against desires and pleasures, and certain vehement flatteries which bend the minds even of those who seem honorable, making them like wax?

**MEGILLUS:** It is against all these things.

**ATHENIAN:** If we remember what was said above, someone here said that a city could be "inferior to itself," and a man could be "inferior to himself." Isn't that so, Knossian guest?

**CLINIAS:** Exactly so.

**ATHENIAN:** Which one, then, should we call "worse": the one who is broken by pain, or the one who is overcome by pleasure?

**CLINIAS:** I think the one who is overcome by pleasure. And everyone considers a man ensnared by pleasure to be more "inferior to himself"—and indeed with more disgrace—than one demolished by pain.

<margin>G</margin> **ATHENIAN:** Then did the legislators of Jove and Apollo establish a "lame" fortitude, which can resist adversity on the left, but on the right succumbs to prosperity, joy, and flatteries? Or is it sufficient for both?

**CLINIAS:** I believe it is for both.

**ATHENIAN:** Let us then explain what customs there are in your cities which taste of pleasures, rather than fleeing them entirely—just as they do not flee pains. Instead, just as is done with pains, let them be led into the midst of pleasures, so that men may be partly driven by force and partly invited by honors to overcome them. Where in your laws is this seen, which makes men equally brave against pleasures as against pains? Where does it show them to be victors over what they ought to conquer, and in no way allow them to be overcome by those most grave enemies within themselves? Tell me, I pray, what is there among you of this sort?

**MEGILLUS:** It is not as easy, guest, to produce many laws opposed to pleasure as I could for pain. I do not have great and clear sections against pleasures, though perhaps I might find small ones.

**CLINIAS:** Nor could I similarly show this in the laws of the Cretans.

**ATHENIAN:** And it is no wonder, my best guests...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...and to keep watch over them, and to correctly blame and praise their thoughts through the laws. Again, in fits of anger and in fears, and all those disturbances that occur in the soul through shame, and those escapes from such things in misfortunes, and those things that happen in sickness, or in wars, or in poverty, or their opposites—concerning all these human sufferings, their dispositions must be taught and defined as either noble or not. After these things, it is necessary for the legislator to watch over the possessions of the citizens and their expenditures, in whatever way they may occur, and their social interactions and dissolutions in all forms, both voluntary and involuntary.

<margin>B</margin> He must consider, in each of these interactions with one another, what is just and what is not, where the holy is present and where it is lacking. He must assign honors to those who are obedient to the laws, and impose fixed penalties on the disobedient, until he has gone through to the end of the entire state's constitution. Furthermore, he must determine the manner in which burials should take place for each, and what honors should be paid to them. Once the one who establishes the laws has seen all this, he will set guardians over them all: some proceeding through wisdom, others through true opinion. Thus mind, binding all these things together, may show them following temperance and justice, rather than wealth or ambition. In this way, strangers, I would have wished—and still wish now—for you to go through how all these things are in the laws said to be of Zeus, and those of Pythian Apollo, which Minos and Lycurgus established; and that, having taken a certain order, they are manifest to one skilled in the art of laws, whether by some habit, though to the rest of us they are in no way clear.

**CLINIAS:** How then, stranger, should we speak of the things after this?

**ATHENIAN:** It seems to me we should go through it again from the beginning (just as we started) with the practices of fortitude first. Then we will go through one and then another form of virtue, if you wish. But so that we may go through the first, we will try to set it out as a model, discussing the other things in the same way to make the path pleasant <margin>C</margin> like a story. Later, we shall go through all virtue; for we must go through it now, and looking toward that, we shall show it, if God wills.

**CLINIAS:** You speak well, and try first to judge this praiser of Zeus for us.

**ATHENIAN:** I will try, for both you and myself. For the argument is common. Tell me then: do we say the common meals and the gymnasia were invented for war by the legislator?

**CLINIAS:** Yes.

**ATHENIAN:** And a third thing, or a fourth? For perhaps it would be necessary to go through the other parts of virtue in this way—whether they be parts, or whatever they should be called—the logic alone makes it clear.

**MEGILLUS:** I would say the third is hunting, and any of the Lacedaemonians would say so. Let us try to say a fourth or fifth, if we can.

<margin>E</margin> I would try to say the fourth is the endurance of pain, which happens much among us, both in hand-to-hand fights and in certain robberies where many blows are given each time. Furthermore, there is a thing called the <term>Krypteia</term>, which is wonderfully laborious for endurance; there is the lack of shoes in winters and the lack of bedding; and they serve themselves without attendants, wandering through the whole country by night and by day. Furthermore, in the <term>Gymnopaedia</term> festivals, terrible endurances occur among us, as they fight against the strength of the heat, and many other things, almost as many as one could not stop going through each time.

**CLINIAS:** You speak well, Lacedaemonian stranger. But as for fortitude, is it simply that one must only fight against fears and pains? Or also against desires and pleasures, and certain dangerous flatteries of fawning? These soften the spirits even of those who think themselves solemn, and make them do all sorts of things.

**MEGILLUS:** I think it is against all these things.

**ATHENIAN:** If we remember the previous discourse, somewhere there it was said a city and a man could be "inferior to themselves." Or not, Knossian stranger?

**CLINIAS:** Quite so.

**ATHENIAN:** Now then, which do we say is worse: the one who is "inferior" to pain, or the one who is more so to pleasures?

**CLINIAS:** It seems to me, the one of pleasures. And we all say that the one mastered by pleasure is more shamefully "inferior to himself" <margin>G</margin> than the one mastered by pains.

**ATHENIAN:** Then surely the legislator of Zeus and the Pythian one did not legislate a "lame" fortitude, capable of resisting only on the left <note>the side of pain/adversity</note>, but unable to resist on the right, which is elegant and flattering? Or is it for both?

**CLINIAS:** I claim it is for both.

**ATHENIAN:** Let us say again, then: what practices are there in both your cities which taste of pleasures and do not flee them, just as they did not flee pains, but leading them into the midst of pleasures, they were charmed and persuaded so as to master them? Where then is there the same thing arranged concerning pleasures as is said in the laws concerning pains? What is it then that works for you equally against both pains and pleasures, making the same men brave, conquering what they must conquer, and in no way being inferior to enemies that are closest to them and most difficult?

**MEGILLUS:** In this way, stranger, just as I had laws to set against pains, of which I could tell many, I might perhaps be at a loss to speak of large and clear parts concerning pleasures; but concerning small ones, I might perhaps find some.

**CLINIAS:** Nor would I myself be able to show such a thing clearly in the laws of Crete.

**ATHENIAN:** O best of strangers...

<summary>In this passage, the Athenian Stranger argues that a complete legal system must cultivate fortitude not only against pain and fear (through military training and endurance) but also against the allurements of pleasure. The Spartan and Cretan speakers admit their laws focus heavily on physical endurance (like the Krypteia and Gymnopaedia) but lack robust training for self-control against desire.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue in Book I of Plato's Laws. The Athenian Stranger, Clinias the Cretan, and Megillus the Spartan are discussing how a society should handle criticism of its own laws and how it should train citizens to handle both pain and pleasure.</meta>

# ON THE LAWS, BOOK I.

**Athenian.** It is no wonder. But if any of us, wishing to see both the truth and what is best, finds something to criticize in the laws of our respective homes, you should accept this from one another not with bitterness but with mildness. **Clinias.** You have spoken rightly, Athenian guest; we must follow your lead. **Athenian.** Indeed we must. **Clinias.** It would not be right for anyone to criticize the Lacedæmonian <note>Spartan</note> or Cretan constitutions without reason. Perhaps I might have something more encouraging to say to both of you. For if your laws are even moderately well-ordered, one of the finest laws you could have is the one that forbids any young person from searching for what might be good or bad in them; instead, with one voice and from one mouth, everyone should agree that all the laws are well-established by the gods. If anyone says otherwise, the listeners should not tolerate it at all. However, if an old man sees something in your laws worth discussing, he should address such talk to a ruler or a peer, ensuring no young person is present to hear. **Clinias.** You speak most correctly, guest. Like a prophet, even though you were not there when our laws were founded, you seem to have guessed the mind of the legislator quite well and speak the absolute truth. **Athenian.** Since there are no young people with us now, and we ourselves are permitted by the lawgiver to discuss these matters privately due to our age, we should not be doing anything wrong. **Clinias.** That is so. Therefore, do not hesitate to criticize our laws. For it is not dishonorable to recognize something that is not good; rather, it leads to a remedy if the words are received with goodwill instead of envy. **Athenian.** Excellent. I will not speak to criticize the laws until I have examined them as thoroughly as I can, or rather, until I have explored my doubts. For your lawgiver, alone among the Greeks and barbarians of whom we have word, commanded you to abstain from the greatest pleasures and amusements, and not even to taste them. Regarding pains and fears (which we just discussed), he believed that if anyone flees from them consistently from childhood, then when they encounter unavoidable labor, fear, and pain, they will flee before those who have been trained in them, and will become their slaves. I believe the same legislator should have thought the same regarding pleasures, saying to himself: if our citizens remain inexperienced in the greatest pleasures from youth, and are untrained in enduring through pleasures and refusing to do shameful things for the sake of the sweetness of desire, they will suffer the same fate as those defeated by fear. They will be enslaved in another, even more shameful way by those who can endure in the face of pleasure and those who possess the means to provide it—who are sometimes entirely wicked people. Their souls will be partly enslaved and partly free, and they will not deserve to be called simply brave and free. Consider then if any of what I have said seems right to you. **Clinias.** It seems so to us, at least while you are speaking. But to believe such a significant point so easily might be the mark of the young and foolish. **Athenian.** But if we proceed to the next topics we proposed, Clinias and my Lacedæmonian guest—for after courage we should speak of temperance <note>Latin: *moderatione*; Greek: *σωφρονύνης* (sophrosyne)</note>—what difference is there between these constitutions and those of men who live haphazardly, just as we discussed regarding war? **Megillus.** Almost none. **Clinias.** But it seems that our common meals and gymnasiums were well-invented for both virtues. **Athenian.** It truly seems, guests, that it is difficult for constitutions to be beyond dispute in both deed and word. For just as with bodies, it is impossible to prescribe a single practice for a single body without it appearing that this same thing harms some parts of our bodies while helping others. These gymnasiums and common meals now benefit cities in many ways, but they are difficult regarding civil strife. This is shown by the youth of the Milesians, Boeotians, and Thurians. Furthermore, this practice seems ancient and natural, yet it has corrupted the pleasures of sex not only for humans but also for beasts. Your cities would be the first one might accuse of this, as would any others that are most devoted to gymnasiums. Whether one should think of such things in jest or in earnest, it must be noted that when the female and male natures come together for procreation, the pleasure in this seems to be granted according to nature; but the union of male with male or female with female is against nature <note>Latin: *praeter naturam*; Greek: *παρὰ φύσιν*</note>. Such audacity first arose from an incontinence of pleasure. We all blame the Cretans for the myth of Ganymede <note>A Trojan prince abducted by Zeus. The Athenian suggests the Cretans invented this myth to justify their own behavior by attributing it to a god.</note>, claiming they composed it; since they believed their laws came from Zeus, they added this myth about Zeus so that, by following the god, they might enjoy this pleasure as well. But let the myth be gone. When men examine laws, almost their entire inquiry is about pleasures and pains, both in cities and in private characters. For these are two fountains released by nature to flow: he who draws from them from the right source, at the right time, and in the right amount, is happy—whether it be a city, an individual, or any living creature. But he who draws ignorantly and outside of the proper moments, lives the opposite life.

<column-break/>

**A** Best of guests. Truly, if any diligent investigator of the truth and the best among us should find something to criticize in the ancestral laws of each of us, we ought to bear it in turn, not with a heavy heart, but with a fair mind. **Clinias.** You speak rightly, Athenian guest. Therefore, I judge that you should be obeyed. **Athenian.** Certainly, Clinias, it is not fitting for men of this age and condition, such as you are, to do otherwise. **Clinias.** Certainly not. **Athenian.** Whether rightly or not someone might criticize the Spartan and Cretan Republics is another question. But what is said by many, I could perhaps report better than either of you. To you, indeed, whether the laws are rightly established or not, <margin>The best law.</margin> **B** there is certainly one law that is best: the one which forbids any of the young to dare to ask whether the laws are right or otherwise, but commands that with one mouth of all and one voice they be conceded as rightly established by the gods; nor should it allow anyone to say anything otherwise. However, if an old man has thought of something, he should report it to the leaders and his peers, with no young person listening. **Clinias.** You speak rightly, guest; and although you were absent then from the mind of the founder, yet like a prophet you seem to have cleverly guessed those things now and to speak the deep truth. **Athenian.** Therefore, since no young people are present with us now, we are permitted by the legislator to discuss these things among ourselves without sin because of our old age. **Clinias.** It is as you say. Therefore, do not spare us, but freely criticize our laws. For it is not **C** unbecoming to know if something is not rightly handled. For if someone receives it not with envy, but with a benevolent mind, a remedy is found. **Athenian.** You speak excellently. I indeed shall not criticize before I have considered it diligently according to my strength; rather, I shall speak by way of doubting. For to you alone of all Greeks and barbarians of whom we have knowledge, the legislator commands you to beware of the greatest pleasures and the most pleasant games, and not to taste anything of them. But concerning pains and fears, of which we just spoke, he judged thus: if someone becomes accustomed to declining them from their early years, it happens that whenever it is necessary to undergo inevitable pains, fears, and labors, he flees from those who are practiced in these things **D** and serves them. This very thing, as I judge, he ought to have thought about pleasure also, and thought this to himself: if from an early age the citizens are without experience of the greatest pleasures, and are not taught to contain themselves in pleasure, and to do nothing shameful for the sake of pleasurable delight, they will succumb just as those who are conquered by fear, and they will serve in a certain other and more shameful way than those who are accustomed to containing themselves in the midst of pleasures, and who, living among pleasures, can supply themselves with amusements—perhaps the worst of men. And so they will have a soul partly slave and partly free, nor ought they to be called entirely brave and free. Consider therefore if anything from what has been said **E** seems to be spoken rightly to you. **Clinias.** It seems so indeed. For thus is the discourse. But it would be the part of the young, or rather the completely insane, to assent immediately and easily to such great matters. **Athenian.** What then? Shall we now pursue what we proposed, O Clinias and Lacedæmonian guest? For after fortitude, let us speak of moderation <note>Latin: *moderatione*</note>, and what difference there is between these and the rest of the Republics, or those which seem to be governed by chance and not by law, just as we did now concerning war? **Megillus.** That is almost not easy. **Clinias.** Yet the common banquets and gymnastic contests seem to have been conveniently invented for both. **Athenian.** It seems indeed, O guests, [that it is difficult] **F** to introduce something certain and fixed. For just as in bodies it cannot happen that any one pursuit is adapted to one body which does not seem to benefit some and harm others, so also in the city. Truly, gymnasiums and fellowships benefit cities in some places, but in seditions they are entirely harmful. Of which matter the Milesians, Boeotians, and Thurians are an example to us. And yet these ancient studies seem to have perverted the old and natural pleasures concerning sexual matters <note>Latin: *venerea*</note> not only in men, but also in beasts. In which matter your primary cities could be accused, and all others who had the greatest care for gymnastic exercises. And whether one ought to think of it in jest or in earnest, **G** it must be considered that when the female and the male come together for procreation, this kind of pleasure seems attributed to them according to nature. But that males are mixed with males or females with females, that pleasure is against nature. And those who first dared such a deed did it through the incontinence of pleasure. Furthermore, we all vehemently blame the Cretan fable about Ganymede, that it was fashioned against Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note>; so that, since their laws were believed to have had their origin from him, by imitating that god who delivered the laws, they might also enjoy this pleasure. But let the fable be gone: the thought of those who consider laws ought to be almost entirely about pleasures and <margin>Two sources: pain and pleasure</margin> pains, as much concerning public as concerning private morals of each. For these two fountains bubble up from nature: from which he who draws from where, when, and as much as is proper, is happy—the private person, namely, and the city and every animal; but he who lives ignorantly and against opportunity to the contrary, is unhappy. **Megillus.** ...

<sig>Bbb iij</sig>
<meta>The final word "infipienter" (unwisely/ignorantly) is a catchword for the next page.</meta>

<summary>This page discusses the proper way to critique laws—arguing that only the elderly should do so in private—and explores the moral challenges of pleasure and pain. The Athenian criticizes the Cretan and Spartan focus on gymnasiums for potentially encouraging same-sex relationships, which he classifies as "against nature" and justified by myths like Ganymede.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from Book I of Plato's Laws. Following the discussion on how laws should handle pain and pleasure, the Spartan Megillus now defends the strict discipline of his homeland against the perceived "softness" of other cultures, specifically regarding the use of alcohol.</meta>

# PLATO'S [LAWS]

<margin>A</margin> **Megillus.** What you say is quite right, guest, and we see nothing that can be said against it. It seems to me that the lawgiver of the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans</note> correctly commanded that pleasures should be avoided. As for the laws of Knossos, our friend Clinias here will assist them if he wishes. But in Sparta, I believe the regulations regarding pleasures are the best among all men. For our law has banished from the entire region that which leads all men into the greatest pleasures, insolence, and all kinds of madness; you will see no drinking parties <note>original: "compotationes"; these were the Greek *symposia*, formal drinking gatherings</note> either in the fields or in the cities governed by Spartans, nor any of the things associated with such parties that stir us toward every pleasure. Nor is there anyone who, meeting someone acting out in drunkenness, would not immediately inflict the greatest punishment upon him; not even the excuse of the festival of Bacchus <note>The Dionysia, a festival honoring the god of wine</note> <margin>B</margin> would free him. It is quite unlike what I saw among your people in your carriages, or among the Tarentines (who are our colonists), where I saw the whole city drunk during the Bacchanals. Among us, however, nothing of the sort is seen. **Athenian.** O Lacedaemonian guest, all such things are praiseworthy where there is a certain endurance or restraint; but where they are entirely permitted, they become softening. For someone defending our ways might quickly find fault with you by pointing out the license and freedom of the women in your country. In all such cases—whether in Tarentum, or among us, or indeed among you—there is one answer that seems to clear the matter: that these customs are not bad, but right. For anyone can answer a surprised foreigner who sees unfamiliar customs: <margin>C</margin> "Do not wonder, guest; this is the law among us. Perhaps among you, there is a different law regarding these same matters." But for us now, my dear friends, the conversation is not about other men, but about the virtue and vice of the lawgivers themselves. Let us speak more broadly about the whole subject of drunkenness. For it is no small matter, nor is the judgment of it a trivial task for a lawgiver. I am not asking whether one should drink wine or not, but about drunkenness itself: whether we should use it <margin>D</margin> as the Scythians and Persians do, and also the Carthaginians, Gauls, Iberians, and Thracians (all of whom are very warlike nations), or whether we should act like you, who abstain entirely. The Scythians and Thracians use wine entirely unmixed <note>original: "mero"; drinking wine without water was considered barbaric by the Greeks</note>, both men and women, and they pour it over their clothes, thinking this a noble and happy way of life. The Persians also indulge greatly in other luxuries that you despise, though more moderately than those others, my good man. **Megillus.** But we rout and put to flight all those people whenever we take up arms! **Athenian.** My dear friend, do not say that. For many flights and pursuits have <margin>E</margin> happened and will happen, for which no certain cause of this kind can be given. Therefore, we should not take victory or defeat in war as a certain argument for whether a practice is honorable or the opposite, especially since smaller cities are often reduced to slavery by larger ones in battle. We can see this with the Locrians, who were considered to have the best laws in their region but were conquered by the Syracusans, and the people of Ceos by the Athenians, and many other such examples. Therefore, setting aside victory and defeat in war, let us try to persuade ourselves by considering each practice in its own right, finding what is true in each. Let us say how this thing is good, and that thing is not good. But first, listen to me on how <margin>F</margin> good and evil ought to be considered in these matters. **Megillus.** How do you mean? **Athenian.** It seems to me that everyone who immediately praises or blames a practice as soon as it is proposed in a discussion is making a mistake. It is as if someone, upon hearing bread praised as a good food, immediately criticized it before perceiving its effects—without asking how it is prepared, for whom, with what, or in what physical condition it should be offered. This is what we seem to be doing now in our debate. As soon as drunkenness was mentioned, some of us immediately blamed it and others praised it, which is quite absurd. By bringing in witnesses and supporters on each side, <margin>G</margin> some of us think we are saying something credible because we have many examples, while others think they are right because those who abstain from wine win in battle—which, as I said, is an ambiguous point. If we proceed this way with other laws as well, we will achieve nothing in my opinion. But I will try, if I can, to show us the right way and method for all such things using the example of drunkenness itself; for countless nations, doubting these same things, would contend with your two cities in argument. **Megillus.** We must certainly listen if a right way of considering these things can be found. **Athenian.** Let us consider it this way. Suppose someone praised the care and keeping of goats as a fine thing to possess, while another person, having seen goats grazing without a shepherd through planted fields and causing damage, criticized them. If that person blamed every herd he saw that was either without a leader or governed by bad leaders, would we consider his criticism to be sound? **Megillus.** Not at all.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> **Megillus.** These things are well said, guest, yet a certain speechlessness takes hold of us as to what should be said in response. Nonetheless, it seems to me that the lawgiver in Lacedaemon correctly commanded us to flee pleasures. As for the laws in Knossos, our friend here [Clinias] will help them if he wishes. But the matters in Sparta concerning pleasures seem to me to be the best established among men. For our law has driven out from our whole land that which men fall into—the greatest pleasures, insolence, and every kind of folly. You would not see, either in the fields or in the cities that Spartans care for, any symposia <note>original: "συμπόσια"; drinking parties</note>, nor any of those things that follow them <margin>B</margin> and stir up every pleasure to the best of their power. There is no one who, meeting a person reveling in drunkenness, would not immediately impose the greatest penalty; nor would the excuse of the Dionysia <note>The festival of Dionysus</note> free him, as I once saw among your people in your wagons, and as I saw in Tarentum among our colonists, where the whole city was drunk during the Dionysia. Among us, however, there is nothing of the sort. **Athenian.** O Lacedaemonian guest, all such things are praiseworthy where there is some form of endurance; but where they are relaxed, people become more sluggish. For someone defending our ways might quickly catch you by showing the lack of restraint among your women. For all <margin>C</margin> such things—in Tarentum, among us, and among you—one answer seems to settle the matter: that it is not bad, but right. For everyone answering a wondering stranger who sees unfamiliar customs in their land will say: "Do not wonder, guest; this is our law, and perhaps you have a different one regarding these same things." But our discussion now, dear friends, is not about other men, but about the vice and virtue of the lawgivers themselves. So let us speak more about the whole of drunkenness. For it is no small practice, nor is it the task of a trivial lawgiver to judge it. I am not speaking of the drinking of wine in general, but of drunkenness itself: whether <margin>D</margin> we should use it as the Scythians and Persians do, and also the Carthaginians, Celts, Iberians, and Thracians—these being warlike races—or as you do. For you, as you say, abstain entirely. But the Scythians and Thracians, using unmixed wine <note>original: "ἀκράτῳ"; wine not diluted with water</note> entirely—both the women and the men—and pouring it over their clothes, believe they are following a beautiful and happy practice. The Persians also use other luxuries that you reject, though they do so in a more orderly fashion than those others, my good man. **Megillus.** But we pursue and rout all these people whenever we take weapons into our hands. **Athenian.** My friend, do not say these things. For many flights and pursuits have occurred and will occur that are without clear proof. Therefore, it is clear <margin>E</margin> that we should never call a practice beautiful or not beautiful based on victory or defeat in battle. Since larger cities conquer and enslave smaller ones in fighting—as the Syracusans did to the Locrians, who were thought to be the most well-governed of the people in that region, or the Athenians to the Ceans; and we could find ten thousand other such examples. Instead, let us try to persuade ourselves by speaking of each practice itself; let us set aside the talk of victory and defeat for now. Let us say that this kind of thing is toward the beautiful, while that kind is not. But first, hear from me how one should look at these things to determine what is useful and what is not. **Megillus.** How do you mean? **Athenian.** It seems to me that all those who take up a practice in speech and set out to blame it or praise it immediately are not acting in the right way. It is the <margin>F</margin> same as if someone, when another person praised wheat as a good food, immediately blamed it without asking about its preparation or its consumption—in what manner, for whom, how, with what, and in what state of the body it should be offered. We seem to be doing the same thing now in our conversation. For having heard only the name of "drunkenness," some of us immediately blame it and others praise it, which is very strange. For each side uses witnesses and praisers; some of us claim to say something significant because we can point to many examples, while others point to the fact that we see those who do not use it conquering in battle. But this point is also disputed by us. If we <margin>G</margin> go through each of the other laws in this way, it would not be to my liking. I want to speak of this very thing, drunkenness, in another way, trying if I can to show the right method for all such things; since ten thousand times ten thousand nations would dispute these things with our two cities in argument. **Megillus.** Indeed, if we have any right way of examining such things, we must not hesitate to listen. **Athenian.** Let us look at it this way. Suppose someone praised the keeping of goats and the animal itself as a fine possession, while another person, having seen goats without a goatherd doing damage in cultivated fields, blamed them. If he looked at every herd that was without a leader or had bad leaders and thus found fault, do we think his blame of such a thing would ever be healthy? **Megillus.** How could it be?

<summary>Megillus defends Spartan sobriety against the perceived "barbaric" drunkenness of other nations, but the Athenian Stranger argues that military victory is a poor measure of a law's quality. He proposes a more systematic method for evaluating social practices, using the analogy of a shepherd to argue that the failure of a practice often lies in a lack of proper leadership rather than the practice itself.</summary>
<keywords>Plato, Laws, Megillus, Spartan discipline, drunkenness, symposia, Dionysia, Scythians, Persians, military victory, Locri, Ceos, social philosophy, leadership, goatherd analogy</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from Book I of Plato's Laws. Previously, Megillus the Spartan praised his city's strict prohibition of drinking parties. The Athenian Guest now begins to challenge this by comparing the "governance" of a drinking party to the command of a ship or an army, suggesting that even wine-drinking can be a tool for education if properly led.</meta>

# ON THE LAWS, BOOK I.

<margin>A</margin> <term>The Athenian.</term> Would a pilot of a ship be good in our eyes if he possessed only the technical skill of navigation, regardless of whether he suffered from seasickness <note>original: "nausia"; the Athenian uses this as a metaphor for being overwhelmed by a condition</note> or not? Or how else should we put it? <term>Megillus.</term> Not at all; he must have the skill and also be free from the condition you mention. <term>The Athenian.</term> And what of the leader of an army? If he possesses the science of warfare, is he fit to lead even if he is a coward and, in times of danger, becomes "seasick" with a drunkenness born of fear? <term>Megillus.</term> Certainly not. <term>The Athenian.</term> And what if he lacks the skill and is also a coward? <term>Megillus.</term> You are describing a completely worthless man, a ruler not of men, but of some very lowly women. <term>The Athenian.</term> Now, consider someone who praises or blames any kind of social gathering that requires a leader to be useful. Suppose this critic has never seen such a gathering <margin>B</margin> conducted correctly under a proper leader, but has only seen them leaderless or with bad leaders. Do we think such a person's judgment—whether they blame or praise these gatherings—carries any weight? <term>Megillus.</term> How could it? For can a person ever truly observe such a gathering if they have never seen it functioning correctly? <term>The Athenian.</term> Stay a moment. Of the many types of social gatherings, shall we count "drinking-together" <note>original: "sympotas"; refers to the Greek symposium or drinking party</note> and drinking parties as one specific kind of association? <term>Megillus.</term> Most certainly. <term>The Athenian.</term> Has anyone ever seen this particular association conducted correctly? It is easy for you Spartans to say you have never seen it, as it is neither your custom nor your law. But I have encountered many such parties in many places, and I have, so to speak, investigated them all. I have seen or heard of almost none that were conducted entirely correctly. I have seen small parts and few details handled well, but for the most part, they are—to put it simply—total failures. <margin>C</margin> <term>Clinias.</term> What do you mean by this, Guest? Explain yourself more clearly. Since we lack experience in these matters, as you said, we would not even know what is right or wrong in such gatherings even if we were present. <term>The Athenian.</term> That is likely. But try to learn from my description. Do you understand that in every meeting and association for any action whatsoever, there must be a ruler if it is to be correct? <term>Clinias.</term> Of course. <term>The Athenian.</term> And we were just saying that the ruler of those fighting in war must be brave. <term>Clinias.</term> Certainly. <term>The Athenian.</term> A brave man is less disturbed by fears than a coward. <term>Clinias.</term> That is also true. <term>The Athenian.</term> If there were a way to put a general in charge of an army who was entirely fearless and undisturbed, wouldn't we do so by every possible means? <term>Clinias.</term> Most definitely. <term>The Athenian.</term> But now we are not <margin>D</margin> speaking of a leader of an army, nor of men facing enemies in war, but of friends in peace joining with friends for the sake of goodwill. <term>Clinias.</term> Correct. <term>The Athenian.</term> Such a gathering, if it involves wine, will not be without disturbance. Is that not so? <term>Clinias.</term> Far from it! I imagine it would be quite the opposite. <term>The Athenian.</term> So, first of all, do these men not also need a ruler? <term>Clinias.</term> More than anyone. <term>The Athenian.</term> Should we then provide such a ruler who is, if possible, undisturbed himself? <term>Clinias.</term> Of course. <margin>E</margin> <term>The Athenian.</term> Moreover, he must be wise regarding social gatherings. For it is his duty to be the guardian of the friendship they already have, and to take care that it becomes even greater through their time together. <term>Clinias.</term> Very true. <term>The Athenian.</term> Therefore, a sober and wise ruler should be appointed over those who are drinking, not the opposite. For if a young or unwise ruler, himself drunk, were to lead drunken men, he would need great "good luck" not to cause some massive disaster. <term>Clinias.</term> Great luck indeed. <term>The Athenian.</term> So, if someone were to criticize these gatherings in cities where they are conducted as well as possible, taking issue with the practice itself, they might perhaps be right. But if someone sees a practice that is conducted poorly and then slanders it, <margin>F</margin> it is clear that they do not realize it is being done incorrectly. They do not see that anything, when performed without a sober master and ruler, will appear bad. Do you not realize that a drunken pilot, or any leader of anything, will overturn everything—whether it be ships, chariots, armies, or whatever else he is supposed to be steering? <term>Clinias.</term> What you say is entirely true, Guest. But tell us this: if this custom regarding drinking were conducted correctly, what good would it do us? To use your example, an army correctly led brings victory in war to its followers, which is no small good; and so with the others. But what great benefit would a correctly guided drinking party bring to individuals or to the city? <margin>G</margin> <term>The Athenian.</term> Well, what great benefit would we say comes to a city from one child, or even one choir, being correctly educated? If asked this way, we might say that the benefit from one individual is small. But if you ask in general what great benefit the education of educated people brings to the city, it is not difficult to say: being well-educated, they become good men, and being such, they act nobly in all things and defeat their enemies in battle. Education brings victory, though victory sometimes brings a lack of education <note>original: "apaideusian"; victory can lead to pride and the loss of the discipline that earned it</note>. For many men, becoming more insolent because of victories in war, have been filled with countless other evils through that insolence. While education has never been a "Cadmean" thing <note>original: "Kadmeia"; a Cadmean victory is one where the victor is ruined as much as the defeated</note>, victories for men <margin>H</margin> have often been so, and will be again. <term>Clinias.</term> You seem to be saying, friend, that social interaction over wine is a significant part of education, if it is done correctly. <term>The Athenian.</term> Indeed I am. <term>Clinias.</term> Can you then explain...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> <term>The Athenian.</term> Truly, would a pilot of a ship be considered good if he only had the art of steering, but was overwhelmed by seasickness <note>original: "nausea"</note>? Or how should he be called good? <term>Megillus.</term> Seasickness contributes nothing to his skill. <term>The Athenian.</term> What about a leader of an army? If he holds the art of warfare well, should he be considered a sufficient leader for that reason, even if he is fearful, and in dangers, his fear flows over him like a kind of drunkenness? <term>Megillus.</term> In what way could he be? <term>The Athenian.</term> What further if he neither has the skill nor is brave? <term>Megillus.</term> You describe someone completely lazy and useless, a leader not of men, but of some worthless women. <term>The Athenian.</term> He who praises or vituperates any society <note>original: "societatem"; here meaning a group or gathering</note> over which someone might be a leader—and which is a useful society <margin>B</margin> whenever it finds its proper pilot—but who has never seen it correctly governed, but always either without leaders or with wicked ones: can he ever correctly blame or praise it? <term>Megillus.</term> How can he do so, having never seen a society correctly governed? <term>The Athenian.</term> Come now, pay attention. Shall we not say that drinkers and drinking-parties are one kind of society among many? <term>Megillus.</term> Most certainly. <term>The Athenian.</term> But has anyone ever seen this society correctly governed? It is very easy for you to answer that you have never seen it. For it is not customary for you according to your ancestral laws. But I have been present at many, and have diligently sought out <margin>C</margin> information on all of them; and I have seen or heard of almost none that were administered correctly as a whole, but only small parts, here and there, and few at that. Most, I might say, I have known to go completely astray. <term>Clinias.</term> Why do you say these things, O Guest? Explain it more clearly. For we, as you were saying, since we have no experience in this matter, cannot immediately know what is done correctly or what is done poorly in it. <term>The Athenian.</term> That is reasonable indeed; but try to learn as I speak. In every assembly and community of any affairs whatsoever, do you admit there ought to be a leader? <term>Clinias.</term> Without a doubt. <term>The Athenian.</term> And yet we were saying a little while ago that the leader of those fighting ought to be brave. <margin>D</margin> <term>Clinias.</term> We were saying that. <term>The Athenian.</term> Now, a brave man is less disturbed by fear than a fearful one. <term>Clinias.</term> It is so. <term>The Athenian.</term> If any way could be found to put a completely intrepid leader over an army, would we not strive for it with all our zeal? <term>Clinias.</term> Greatly so. <term>The Athenian.</term> But now we speak not of an army, nor of one who is to command against enemies in war, but of one who is to govern in peace the pleasant social gathering of friends among themselves. <term>Clinias.</term> That is right. <term>The Athenian.</term> That society, if indeed drunkenness is present, will it be without tumult? <term>Clinias.</term> How? I think it would be the opposite. <term>The Athenian.</term> Therefore, these also have need of a leader first. <term>Clinias.</term> Most of all. <term>The Athenian.</term> Should we then choose a leader who is not himself disturbed, if that were possible? <margin>E</margin> It is indeed necessary. <term>The Athenian.</term> This leader ought to be skilled in reconciling the society; for it ought to be his office to preserve their present friendship and to ensure that a greater friendship grows out of that fellowship. <term>Clinias.</term> You speak the truth. <term>The Athenian.</term> Should not, therefore, a sober and wise leader of the drunk be appointed, and not the opposite? For if a young man, not wise but drunk, were the leader of the drunk, it would be credited to good luck, not to counsel, if he did not overturn everything by his rashness. <term>Clinias.</term> Most excellently put. <term>The Athenian.</term> If anyone, therefore, were to accuse drinking parties—even when they were arranged as correctly as possible in a city—he might perhaps be right in accusing the thing itself. But if, because of <margin>F</margin> one turbulent drinking party he has seen, he vituperates all drinking parties, it is first of all clear that he is ignorant that it was not correctly arranged; and secondly, it is certain that everything will appear wicked in the same way, even if done by a sober master and leader. Have you not noticed that a drunken pilot of a ship, or of any other thing, overturns everything, whether they be ships, or chariots, or armies, or whatever else is ruled by him? <term>Clinias.</term> You have said this quite truly, Guest; but explain this for us also. What would these drinking parties, if correctly conducted, confer upon us? Just as we were saying, an army correctly led would bring victory in war, a <margin>G</margin> benefit certainly not small. The same is to be judged of others; but from a drinking party correctly governed, what great thing would come to the city or to private citizens? <term>The Athenian.</term> Well, what great thing will the city obtain from one boy, or one certain group, being correctly instructed? If we are asked this, we will reply that only a small utility comes to the city from the education of just one. But if you ask what the education of well-instructed youths confers upon the republic in general, it will not be difficult to say. For those well-instructed will turn out to be good men. And being made good, they will then conduct other things well, and will also defeat their enemies in fighting. Discipline surely provides victory; victory sometimes <margin>H</margin> produces negligence and rudeness. For many, elated in victory, have contracted many other vices through insolence. And indeed, no discipline was ever "Cadmean." But there have been and will be many such victories. <term>Clinias.</term> You seem, O friend, to praise the common custom of wine-drinking as if it were a great part of discipline, if it be done correctly. <term>The Athenian.</term> Indeed. <term>Clinias.</term> You will be able, then, to explain the truth of this...

<summary>In this passage, the Athenian argues that drinking parties (symposia) are social institutions that require wise, sober leadership to be beneficial. He suggests that, like military training, the proper governance of social pleasure is a vital component of a citizen's education and character-building.</summary>

# OF PLATO

...to show that this is so? THE ATHENIAN: To prove that these things are truly as they are, O guest, when many harbor doubts, is for God alone. However, if I say what I feel, I think no ill-will shall stand in the way; for we have decided for the present to speak of laws and the republic. CLINIAS: Come, let us try to learn what your view is regarding these ambiguities. THE ATHENIAN: That is only right. It is necessary that you turn your whole mind to learning, and I to teaching. But first, hear this: All the Greeks regard our city as both a lover of words <note>original: "philologos"</note> and talkative. Lacedaemon <note>Sparta</note> and Crete, however, are different: the former is brief of speech <note>original: "brachylogos"</note>, while the latter practices depth of thought more than many words. I am careful lest I seem to speak many words about a small matter—drunkenness—by using such a long oration. But the correct arrangement of a drinking-party, according to nature, can never be clearly or sufficiently treated in speech without the right rule of music, nor can music be treated without the whole of discipline <note>original: "paideia," referring to the upbringing and education of a child</note>. All these things surely require many words. See, therefore, what must be done. Should we pass over these things for the present and move on to some other question regarding the laws? MEGILLUS: You are perhaps unaware, Athenian guest, that our family is the public host <note>original: "proxenos," a local representative of another city's interests</note> of your city. And just as happens to all boys, I think, who hear that they are the hosts of a certain city, a certain benevolence toward it—as if it were a second fatherland—immediately flows into them from their tender years; so it happened to me. Indeed, as a boy I used to hear the Lacedaemonian children, whenever they were either angry with or praising the Athenians, say: "Megillus, your city has brought us this evil or this good." Hearing these things, and feeling great benevolence toward you, I would fight against those who disparaged you. To me, your voice is now very pleasant, <margin>A good Athenian, very good indeed.</margin> and that which is commonly said—that good Athenians are exceptionally good—seems to me to be spoken quite truly. For they alone are good by their own nature, by a certain divine lot, not by compulsion or artifice, but truly. Therefore, as far as I am concerned, you may speak freely, guest; recount whatever you wish. CLINIAS: You shall also be heard by me, guest; whatever comes into your mind, bring it forth with the greatest confidence. For perhaps <margin>Epimenides.</margin> you have heard that Epimenides was a divine man: he was of our family, and ten years before the Persian War, warned by a divine oracle, he came to you and performed certain sacrifices. When the Athenians were fearing the Persian fleet, he predicted that the Persians would by no means come for ten years; and even when they did come, they would depart without accomplishing their goal, having suffered more evils than they inflicted. At that time, our ancestors were joined with yours in the bond of hospitality, and from that time our parents and I have been well-disposed toward you. THE ATHENIAN: You are ready to listen, as it seems. I, for my part, am ready in will rather than prepared in faculty. I shall try, however, as best I can. First, then, regarding this discourse, let us define what education <note>original: "disciplina," translating "paideia"</note> is, and what power it has. For our present discussion must travel through this subject until it reaches God himself. CLINIAS: That is certainly what must be done, if it pleases you. THE ATHENIAN: While I say what education is, consider whether my opinion pleases you. CLINIAS: Speak on. THE ATHENIAN: I assert, indeed, that those who are to become outstanding men in any field must practice that very thing from early childhood, as much in play as in study, in every detail fitting to the business. For instance, if someone is to be a skilled farmer or builder, he must play at either tilling the earth or building certain childish houses from his earliest age; and the one who raises him must provide small tools for each, which are images of the real tools. They ought also to learn beforehand the lessons necessary for their craft. For example, a future carpenter should learn to measure and use a rule; a future horseman should play at riding, or do something of that kind. In all things we should try through play to turn the pleasures and desires of children toward that goal which we wish them to reach at last. We say the head of education is right upbringing, which leads the soul of the child in play toward a love of that thing which he must do perfectly when he reaches manhood, through the virtue of his art. But consider now, as I was saying, if what has been said so far meets with your approval. CLINIAS: Why should it not? THE ATHENIAN: However, it should not be left undetermined what we mean by "education." For when we blame or praise the upbringings of individuals, we are accustomed to say that one man is educated and another is uneducated, even though the latter may be very skilled in trade or navigation or other such things. Indeed, we do not think of that as "education," but rather that which makes a person desire and love virtue from childhood: specifically, that which makes a man a perfect citizen, knowing how to rule and be ruled with justice. This upbringing alone is what this discourse calls "education." But that training which tends toward amassing money, or increasing bodily strength, or seeking some other skill without mind and justice, it deems mechanical <note>original: "mechanicam," translating "banauson," a term for lowly or manual labor</note> and illiberal, and unworthy of the name of education.

<column-break/>

...to say that what has just been said is true? **A** ATHENIAN: To strongly affirm, O guest, that these things are so—given how many people dispute them—is the task of a god. But if I must say what appears to me, there is no reason not to, since we have set out at this time to make our discourse concerning laws and the constitution. **CLINIAS:** Let us try then to understand this very thing: what you think about these matters currently in dispute. **A** ATHENIAN: Well, we must do so; both you who are trying to learn and I who am trying to explain must together strain our discourse toward the goal. But first, hear this from me: all the Greeks suppose our city to be a lover of words and a speaker of many words; but Lacedaemon and Crete they suppose, the one to be brief-speaking, and the other **B** to practice many-mindedness rather than many-wordedness. I am considering then whether I might give you the impression of saying much about a small thing—about drunkenness—by spinning out an endless speech about a minor matter. But its correction according to nature could never be made clear or sufficient in words without the correctness of music; and music again could never be understood without the whole of education. These things require a very great deal of speaking. See then what we should do: should we leave these things for the present and move on to another discourse concerning laws? **MEGILLUS:** O Athenian guest, you perhaps do not know that our house happens to be the host of your city. Just as perhaps happens to all children, when they hear they are the hosts of some city, each of us feels a certain goodwill toward that host-city from youth, **C** as if it were a second fatherland after our own. And indeed this very thing has happened to me. For hearing from children, whenever the Lacedaemonians found fault with or praised the Athenians, they would say: "Your city, Megillus, has done us a bad or a good turn." Hearing these things and fighting against them on your behalf against those who brought the city into reproach, I conceived all goodwill for you. And to me now your voice is dear, and that which is said by many—that as many Athenians as are good are exceptionally so—seems to be spoken most truly. For they alone are good without necessity, by their own nature, by a divine lot, truly and not by artifice. Therefore, as far as I am concerned, you may confidently say as much **D** as is pleasing to you. **CLINIAS:** And indeed, O guest, after you have heard and accepted my word as well, speak as confidently as you wish. For you have perhaps heard that Epimenides was a divine man, who was a relative of ours; having come to you ten years before the Persian wars, according to the oracle of the god, he performed certain sacrifices which the god commanded. And when the Athenians were fearing the Persian fleet, he said that they would not come for ten years; and when they did come, they would depart having accomplished nothing of what they hoped, and having suffered more evils than they had done. At that time our ancestors entered into a guest-friendship with you; and from that, both our parents and we have goodwill toward you. **A** ATHENIAN: It seems then that you are ready to listen; but as for my part, though I am ready to wish it, it is not altogether easy to accomplish. Nevertheless, it must be tried. First, then, letting the discourse go, let us observe what education is and what power it has. For we say that our present discourse must proceed through this, until it arrives at the god. **CLINIAS:** Let us by all means do so, if it is pleasing to you. **A** ATHENIAN: While I am saying then what one must declare education to be, consider if the statement pleases you. **CLINIAS:** Speak on. **A** ATHENIAN: I say then: I affirm that whoever is to be a good man at anything must practice this very thing immediately from childhood, both in play and in earnest, in each of the particulars belonging to the matter. For example, the one who is to be a good farmer or again a builder, the one must play at building some of the toy buildings; the other **E** at farming; and the one who nurtures them must provide each with small tools, imitations of the true ones. And indeed they must learn beforehand those lessons that are necessary to have learned: for instance, a carpenter should learn to measure or use a plumb-line, and a warrior should play at riding or doing some other such thing. One must try through play to turn the pleasures and desires of the children toward that place where, having arrived, they must have their end. We say then that the summary of education is right upbringing: that which, through play, will lead the soul of the child most toward a love of that which he will need to be perfect in when he becomes a man—the virtue of the craft. See then if up to this point (as I said) the statement pleases you. **CLINIAS:** How could it not? **A** ATHENIAN: Let us not then allow what we call education to be undefined. For now, when we disparage or praise the upbringings of various people, we say that one of us is educated and another uneducated, even though the latter is sometimes very well "educated" in the business of shop-keeping or ship-owning and other such things. For we do not consider these things to be education, as it seems, but that which makes a citizen desire and love to become perfect, knowing both how to rule and be ruled with justice. This upbringing, having set it apart, this discourse, as it seems to me, would now wish to call **H** education alone; but that which tends toward money, or toward some strength, or even toward some other wisdom without mind and justice, it considers to be mechanical and illiberal, and not worthy at all to be called education.

<summary>The Athenian Guest defines true education (paideia) as the cultivation of virtue and citizenship from childhood through play, distinguishing it from mere technical or "mechanical" training. Megillus and Clinias affirm their families' long-standing diplomatic and religious ties to Athens, establishing a bond of trust for the dialogue.</summary>
