### ON THE LAWS, BOOK I

<margin>A</margin> But let us not differ with them about a name; rather, let the argument we just agreed upon hold: that those who have been rightly educated <note>original: "pepaideumenoi"</note> generally become good men. We must never disparage education, as it is the first of the most beautiful things that come to the best of men. And if it ever goes astray, but is capable of being corrected, one must always strive to do so throughout their whole life to the best of their ability. CLINIAS: You are right; we agree with what you say. ATHENIAN: Furthermore, we agreed long ago that those capable of ruling themselves are good, while those who cannot are bad. CLINIAS: You speak most correctly. ATHENIAN: Let us, then, take this up again more clearly, to see what we mean by it. And please, accept an image <note>original: "eikonos"</note> from me, if I am somehow able to clarify such a thing for you. <margin>B</margin> CLINIAS: Just speak. ATHENIAN: Shall we assume that each one of us is a single person? CLINIAS: Yes. ATHENIAN: And that each possesses within himself two counselors, both foolish and opposing one another, which we call pleasure and pain? CLINIAS: That is so. ATHENIAN: And in addition to these two, there are expectations of the future, the common name for which is "hope." Specifically, the expectation before pain is called "fear," while the expectation before its opposite is called "confidence." Above all these is "reasoning" <note>original: "logismos"</note>, determining which of them is better or worse; and when this reasoning becomes a common decree of the city, it is named "law" <note>original: "nomos"</note>. CLINIAS: I follow you, though with some difficulty; nonetheless, speak what follows as if I were keeping up. ATHENIAN: And indeed, I find myself in the same state of mind. ATHENIAN: Let us think about these things in this way: <margin>C</margin> let us consider each of us living beings to be a divine wonder <note>The Greek "thauma" can mean a wonder, a marvel, or a string-controlled puppet.</note>, whether we were constructed as a toy for the gods or for some serious purpose. For this we do not know; but this we do know: that these passions in us are like nerves or strings that pull us, and they tug against one another, being opposite, toward opposite actions, where the distinction between virtue and vice lies. For the argument says that one must always follow one of these pulls and never let go of it, but must pull against the other "nerves." And this, it says, is the golden and sacred guidance of reasoning, which is called the common law of the city. The other cords are hard and made of iron, while this one is soft, as it is made of gold; the others resemble all sorts of different forms. One must always cooperate with the most beautiful guidance <margin>D</margin> of the law. For because the reasoning is beautiful, but also gentle and not violent, its guidance requires assistants, so that the golden element in us may overcome the other types. And thus the myth concerning us being "wonders" would be saved by virtue; and the meaning of being "superior to oneself" or "inferior to oneself" would become more evident. It would also be clear that both the individual, by grasping the true reasoning within himself regarding these pulls, must live following it; and the city, whether receiving the reasoning from a god or from this person who has come to know these things, must establish it as law and conduct its own affairs and its dealings with other cities accordingly. In this way, vice and virtue would be more clearly distinguished for us; and as this becomes more evident, <margin>E</margin> education and other practices will perhaps become more apparent. And indeed, as for the practice of wine-drinking, which might seem a trivial thing to spend so much time discussing... CLINIAS: It might perhaps turn out that the length of the discussion is not unworthy of it. ATHENIAN: Well said; let us complete whatever is worth discussing in this current pursuit. CLINIAS: Speak then. ATHENIAN: If we apply "drunkenness" to this "wonder" <note>the human puppet</note>, what sort of effect will we produce in it? CLINIAS: To what end do you ask this? ATHENIAN: Nothing specific yet; but I am asking what sort of thing it becomes when it joins with this state. I will try to speak even more clearly. I am <margin>F</margin> asking this: Does the drinking of wine intensify pleasures, pains, angers, and loves? CLINIAS: Very much so. ATHENIAN: And what about the senses, memories, opinions, and wisdom? Does it likewise make them more intense? Or do these entirely desert a person if they become saturated with drunkenness? CLINIAS: Yes, they entirely desert him. ATHENIAN: Does he not then arrive at the same state of soul as when he was a young child? CLINIAS: Certainly. ATHENIAN: At that moment, he would be least in control of himself. CLINIAS: Least of all. ATHENIAN: And do we not say such a man is at his worst? CLINIAS: Very much so. ATHENIAN: Not only, then, does the old man become a child for a second time, it seems, but also <margin>G</margin> the drunkard. CLINIAS: You have spoken excellently, stranger. ATHENIAN: Is there any argument that will attempt to persuade us that this practice should be tasted, and not fled from with all one's strength according to one's power? CLINIAS: It seems there is. At least, you say so, and you were ready to speak of it just now. ATHENIAN: You remember correctly. And I am ready now, since you both said you were eager to listen. CLINIAS: How could we not listen? If for no other reason, then for the sake of the wonder and the strangeness of it—if a man must ever willingly throw himself into such total depravity. ATHENIAN: You mean depravity of the soul, do you not? CLINIAS: Yes. ATHENIAN: But what about this, my friend? Would we not wonder if someone willingly arrived at a depravity <margin>H</margin> of the body—I mean thinness, ugliness, and weakness? CLINIAS: How could we not? ATHENIAN: What then? Do we think that those who walk themselves into doctors' offices to drink medicine are unaware that a little later, and for many days, they will have their body in such a state that, if they were to have it that way forever, they would not choose to live? Or do we not know that those who go to gyms and take on labors are made weak by exhaustion in the moment...

<column-break/>

But let us not contend over the word: but let this, which was asserted a little before, be agreed upon between us: that those who have obtained right discipline, almost all turn out upright; those on the contrary, turn out wicked. Wherefore in no matter is discipline to be neglected, which is present as the first of the most excellent things to distinguished men. And if anyone has failed in any matter, and it can be corrected, let him amend himself, and let him do this throughout his whole life according to his strength. <margin>A</margin> CLINIAS: You speak rightly. Therefore, what you say must be granted. ATHENIAN: But we confessed long ago that those who are able to command themselves are good, but those who cannot are bad. CLINIAS: Quite skillfully. ATHENIAN: Let us resume therefore that very thing, so that what we say may become more clearly known. And <margin>B</margin> you should receive this through an image so that it may be clear, if in any way I am able to open this matter to you. CLINIAS: Speak now. ATHENIAN: Do we not think any one of us is one? CLINIAS: One. ATHENIAN: Having, namely, within himself two counselors, contrary and mindless, whom we call pleasure and pain. CLINIAS: This also. ATHENIAN: To these are added opinions of future things, for which the common name is hope: but properly that which presents itself before pain is fear, and that before its opposite, confidence. To all these the judgment of reason is added, dictating what of these is better, what worse. If this is made a common decree of the city, it is named law. <margin>C</margin> CLINIAS: I follow you with difficulty. Speak however what remains, just as if I were following. MEGILLUS: The same has happened to me as well. ATHENIAN: Let us think of these things thus: that we should consider each of us in the race of living beings as a certain divine wonder, whether established by those above for sport or in earnest (for we do not know that). This however we are not ignorant of, that these affections in us, like inborn nerves or ropes, pull us in turn and pull us back to contrary actions, where virtue and vice exist separately. For reason declares that one pull is always to be followed, and never to be abandoned, but by this one all others must be resisted; and that this is the leadership of reason, golden and sacred, which <margin>D</margin> is called the common law of the city. And that the others are hard and made of iron, but this one soft, because it is golden: and uniform moreover, the others multiform. It is necessary therefore that we always follow the most beautiful leadership of the law, and favor it. For since the judgment of reason is an honorable thing, and mild rather than violent, its leadership stands in need of ministers, so that the golden race in us may overcome the other races. And thus the fable, because man is said to be a wonderful thing, will be preserved by virtue: and by what reason anyone is called superior or inferior to himself in a certain way, will be more plainly known: and that it is necessary for each one, having perceived true reason in himself concerning these pulls, to have it as a law and to direct himself toward it: and that the City, <margin>E</margin> having received the reason either from some one of the gods, or from this very person who has known this, should have it as a law, and according to its norm institute its duties with itself, and with other cities: and thus virtue and vice will lie open to us more clearly distinguished, which being plainly perceived, both discipline and the rest of studies will perhaps shine forth more. And that custom now received in drinking-bouts, concerning which it will perhaps be thought of little value if I speak at length. CLINIAS: Perhaps it will not seem unworthy of a long speech. ATHENIAN: You speak well, wherefore let us say what seems most worthy in it. CLINIAS: Proceed now. ATHENIAN: If we add drunkenness to this wonderful thing, what sort of thing shall we make it? <margin>F</margin> CLINIAS: To what purpose do you ask that? ATHENIAN: I do not yet say. But if this wonderful thing should mix itself with that, what sort of thing is it rendered? Indeed I will attempt to say what I want more openly. I ask something of this sort. <margin>Lessons from wine.</margin> Whether the use of wine excites pleasures, pains, angers, loves, more vehemently. CLINIAS: Very much so indeed. ATHENIAN: Whether it also makes the senses, memory, opinion, and intelligence similarly more vehement. Or does it altogether extinguish them, if anyone has been occupied by drunkenness. CLINIAS: It certainly altogether extinguishes them. ATHENIAN: To that habit of mind, therefore, he returns, which the boy had in his first years. CLINIAS: Indeed. ATHENIAN: Wherefore he will then be least master of himself. CLINIAS: Least of all. ATHENIAN: He will therefore be the worst. CLINIAS: Greatly. ATHENIAN: Not only therefore, as it seems, will the old man <margin>G</margin> be a boy twice, but also the drunken man himself. <margin>A drunkard is also twice a child.</margin> CLINIAS: That was very well said, guest. ATHENIAN: Will any reason be able to persuade us that this thing must in some way be tasted: and is not to be fled from with all one's strength? CLINIAS: It will perhaps be able, as you say, and you were just now showing yourself ready to speak. ATHENIAN: You remember very well. Truly I am ready even now, since both of you have promised to listen not unwillingly. CLINIAS: Why should we not listen, even if for no other reason, yet because it seems a wonderful and absurd thing, if it shall behoove a man sometimes of his own accord to cast himself away into all depravity? ATHENIAN: Do you say of the soul? CLINIAS: Of the soul. ATHENIAN: Shall we then wonder, O friend, if anyone should come <margin>H</margin> of his own accord into depravity of the body—I mean thinness, deformity, weakness? CLINIAS: Why not? ATHENIAN: Do we then think those who of their own accord take the drugs of physicians are ignorant that they will have their body so affected a little after for several days, that if they were to have it similarly affected forever, [they would not wish to live]? Or are we also ignorant that those who go to gyms and undergo labors, become weak with weariness immediately?

<summary>In this passage, Plato uses the famous "puppet" analogy to describe the human soul as being pulled by various cords of emotion (pleasure, pain, fear), while emphasizing that the "golden cord" of reason—translated into law—is the only one a virtuous person should follow. He also begins to argue that while wine-drinking seems to degrade a person to the state of a child, it may have a specific pedagogical or medical utility when properly understood.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the Athenian Guest’s dialogue with Clinias the Cretan. Having established that education is the foundation of virtue, the Athenian now begins to argue for the practical utility of communal drinking. He introduces a thought experiment about two kinds of fear and a hypothetical "fear potion" to demonstrate how wine can serve as a safe training ground for character.</meta>

### PLATO'S WORKS

<margin>A</margin> **CLINIAS:** We are well aware of all these things. **ATHENIAN:** And surely we also know that everyone pursues these activities willingly for the sake of future benefit. **CLINIAS:** Precisely. **ATHENIAN:** Should we not think about other practices in the same way? **CLINIAS:** In exactly the same way. **ATHENIAN:** Then we must also consider the practice of wine-drinking in this manner, if indeed it is right to consider it among these other things. **CLINIAS:** Certainly so. **ATHENIAN:** If it is seen to provide a benefit no less than that found in physical exercise, then it is well. However, it initially surpasses physical exercise in this: exercise involves pain, while drinking does not. **CLINIAS:** That is correct. But I would be amazed if we could actually perceive such a benefit in it. **ATHENIAN:** That is exactly what we must now try to explain. Tell me: can we conceive of two species of fear that are nearly opposites of one another? **CLINIAS:**
<margin>B</margin> Which ones do you mean? **ATHENIAN:** These: surely we fear evils when we expect them to happen in the future. **CLINIAS:** We do. **ATHENIAN:** But we also frequently fear the opinion of others, when we dread that by saying or doing something dishonorable, we might appear wicked. This specific fear we—and indeed everyone, I believe—call shame <note>original: "pudorem" (Latin) / "αἰσχύνην" (Greek). This refers to a sense of modesty or moral dread regarding one's reputation.</note>. **CLINIAS:** Who could doubt that? **ATHENIAN:** These are the two fears I was speaking of. One of them is contrary to pains and other terrors, and it is also contrary to most of the greatest pleasures. **CLINIAS:** Quite right. **ATHENIAN:** Is it not
<margin>C</margin> the case, then, that a legislator, or anyone else who wishes to be of use to men, should hold this fear in the highest honor and call it modesty <note>original: "pudorem" / "αἰδῶ". In Ancient Greek culture, "aidos" was the virtue of being restrained by a sense of shame or respect for others.</note>? And would he not call its opposite—confidence—"impudence," and consider it the greatest evil for men, both privately and publicly? **CLINIAS:** Well said. **ATHENIAN:** This fear preserves us in many other great matters; and in war, if one thing is compared to another, nothing grants us victory and safety as much as this does. For there are two things that produce victory: boldness toward enemies, and fear of shameful disgrace toward friends. **CLINIAS:** That is true. **ATHENIAN:** Therefore, each of us must become both fearless and fearful. We have already distinguished the reasons why both are necessary. **CLINIAS:** Entirely. **ATHENIAN:** Furthermore, whenever we wish to make someone fearless—by leading them, under the impulse of law, into the terror of many fears—that is how we
<margin>D</margin> achieve it. **CLINIAS:** So it seems. **ATHENIAN:** But when we want to lead someone to fear the things that *should* be feared, must we not test them against things that incline toward impudence? We must train them in the struggle against internal pleasures, or in the habits of their past life, and urge them toward victory. Only by conquering these things can a person become truly brave. For one who has never tested himself, nor been trained in these contests, will not possess even half of the strength required for virtue. How can anyone be perfectly temperate unless he has strongly resisted the many pleasures and desires that compel him toward impudence and injustice? Must he not overcome them through reason, action, and skill, in both play and serious matters? Can a man be temperate, I ask, if he has suffered none of this? **CLINIAS:** That does not seem likely.
<margin>E</margin> **ATHENIAN:** But tell me, I pray, has some god given a "fear-medicine" <note>original: "pharmaeum" / "φάρμακον". This refers to a medicinal potion or drug.</note> to mankind, such that the more someone drinks of it, the more miserable he thinks he becomes with every draught? One where he fears everything, both present and future, and eventually falls into utter dread, even if he is the bravest of men? And then, when he has slept it off and been freed from the potion, he returns to his usual self? **CLINIAS:** And what kind of potion, my friend, could we ever say has existed in human life? **ATHENIAN:** None, certainly. Yet if such a potion were found, would it be useful to a lawgiver for the sake of courage? Could we say the following to the maker of the laws: "Come now, lawgiver—whether you write laws for the Cretans or anyone else—would you wish to be able to test the courage and cowardice of your citizens?" **CLINIAS:** Anyone would surely answer that he would wish to. **ATHENIAN:** And then, would you wish to do so safely and without great
<margin>G</margin> imminent danger, or the opposite? **CLINIAS:** Anyone would admit they prefer to do it safely and securely. **ATHENIAN:** Would you then use this potion, leading them into these terrors and testing them in the midst of their disturbances? Would you use your commands and warnings to make your citizens fearless, honoring some and rebuking others if they do not obey your warnings? And would you leave those who performed strenuously in the exercise unpunished, while punishing those who did the opposite? Or would you not use it at all, even if you had no other complaint against the potion? **CLINIAS:** Why would he not use it, Guest? **ATHENIAN:** Such an exercise, my friend, would be wonderfully easy compared to our current ones, and could be used by one person, or a few, or however many you wished. And if someone, alone in a solitary place, puts shame before his eyes—
<margin>H</margin> because he does not wish to be seen before he has made progress—and así trains himself against fear with only this potion prepared (instead of many other things), he would surely achieve something worthwhile. Or if someone, trusting in his nature and well-prepared by practice, does not fear to exercise with many drinking companions, he could show—by inevitably draining and consuming the wine in the cup—that he is so powerful and superior that he commits no great error through impudence. Because of his virtue, his character remains unmoved, and he departs after the final drink before drunkenness sets in, being especially wary of the violence that pure wine works on all men. **CLINIAS:** Certainly, Guest, a man who conducts himself in this way would emerge as truly moderate. **ATHENIAN:** Again, let us return to...

<column-break/>

<margin>Α</margin> ...they happen, etc. We know all these things. **ATHENIAN:** And surely they travel this path for the sake of its utility? **CLINIAS:** Most excellently. **ATHENIAN:** Therefore, must we not think about other practices in the same way? **CLINIAS:** Certainly. **ATHENIAN:** Or should we also think of the pastimes of wine in the same way, if we are to think rightly about these matters? **CLINIAS:** How could we not? **ATHENIAN:** If, then, it appears to have some benefit for us, no less than that regarding the body, it would initially surpass music; for while one involves pains, the other does not. **CLINIAS:** You speak rightly. But I would wonder if we could learn any such thing in it. **ATHENIAN:** This is exactly what
<margin>Β</margin> we must now, as it seems, try to tell you. Tell me: can we understand two nearly opposite forms of fear? **CLINIAS:** What kinds? **ATHENIAN:** Such as these: do we not fear evils, expecting them to happen? **CLINIAS:** Yes. **ATHENIAN:** And do we not often fear reputation, thinking that we will be thought evil if we say or do something not beautiful? This fear we call—and I think everyone else does too—shame. **CLINIAS:** Why not? **ATHENIAN:** These are the two fears I spoke of; one of which is opposite to pains and other fears, and opposite again to the most and greatest pleasures. **CLINIAS:** You speak most rightly. **ATHENIAN:** Would not a lawgiver, and anyone of even slight use, hold this fear in the greatest honor and
<margin>Γ</margin> call it modesty? And would he not call the boldness opposite to this "impudence," and consider it the greatest evil for all, both privately and publicly? **CLINIAS:** You speak rightly. **ATHENIAN:** Does not this fear save us in many other great things? And in war, nothing works so powerfully for our victory and safety, one for one. For there are two things that produce victory: boldness toward enemies, and fear toward friends concerning wicked shame. **CLINIAS:** That is so. **ATHENIAN:** Therefore, each of us must become fearless and fearful; we have distinguished why each is necessary. **CLINIAS:** Entirely so. **ATHENIAN:** And indeed, when we wish to make each person
<margin>Δ</margin> fearless, we lead them into fear of many things under the law and produce such a result. **CLINIAS:** So it appears. **ATHENIAN:** But what when we need to make someone fear what is shameful? Must we not, by instilling shame in him and exercising him in fear, make him overcome his pleasures in the struggle? Or must a man become perfect in courage by fighting against and conquering himself? If any man is inexperienced and untrained in such contests, he would not become even half-finished in virtue. Will he ever be perfectly temperate if he has not fought against many pleasures and desires that lead to impudence and injustice, and conquered them with reason, deed, and skill, in play and in earnest, but has instead remained untouched by all such things? **CLINIAS:** That
<margin>Ε</margin> would be a likely argument. **ATHENIAN:** What then? Has some god given a medicine for fear to men, so that the more someone drinks of it, the more he thinks himself to become miserable with every draught, and fears all things present and future? And eventually, even the bravest of men enters into utter dread, but after sleeping it off and being freed from the drink, he becomes the same person again each time? **CLINIAS:** And what such drink, Guest, do we say has ever existed among men? **ATHENIAN:** None. But if it did exist somewhere, would it be
<margin>Ϛ</margin> useful to a lawgiver for courage? For instance: we might speak to him thus: "Come, Lawgiver—whether you legislate for Cretans or anyone else—would you first of all desire to be able to take a test of your citizens regarding courage and cowardice?" **CLINIAS:** Everyone would clearly say yes. **ATHENIAN:** What then? With safety, or with great dangers, or with their opposites? **CLINIAS:** Everyone will agree to do it with safety. **ATHENIAN:** And would you use it, leading them into these fears, and testing them in their sufferings, so as to compel them to become fearless, encouraging or admonishing them, and honoring them? And the one who is disobedient—the one who does not become such as you ordain in all things and who is not healthy and brave after the exercise—would you dismiss him without a penalty, or
<margin>Ζ</margin> would you impose a punishment? Or would you not use it at all, having nothing else to charge against the drink? **CLINIAS:** And how could he not use it, Guest? **ATHENIAN:** Such an exercise, my friend, would be a marvelous ease compared to current practices, whether for one person, a few, or however many one wished. And if someone, alone in solitude, putting shame first and thinking he should not be seen before he is in good condition, were thus to exercise himself in fears, having prepared only the drink for himself, he would be doing something right. Or if someone, trusting in his nature and practice to be well-prepared, had no hesitation in exercising with many fellow-drinkers, showing his power in the necessary trial of the drink, prevailing and conquering so as not to stumble into any great unseemliness, nor to be altered in his virtue, but departed after the final drink before arriving at that which he fears above all: the defeat of all men by the drink. **CLINIAS:** Yes,
<margin>Η</margin> such a man, Guest, would be acting temperately by doing so. **ATHENIAN:** Again, then, to...

<summary>The Athenian Guest explores the dual nature of fear—dread of future harm versus the fear of shame (modesty)—and proposes that virtue must be tested through exposure to pleasure and fear. He introduces the hypothetical "fear potion" to illustrate how wine, which induces boldness, can be used as a safe tool to train and test a person's self-control and courage.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the Athenian Guest's argument regarding the utility of wine as a psychological "test" (basanos). In the previous section, they discussed the two types of fear: the fear of expected evils and the fear of social disgrace (shame). Now, the Athenian explains how wine acts as a safe training ground for the soul.</meta>

<margin>A</margin> Let us speak to the lawgiver in this way: "Well then, O lawgiver, neither has a god given such a medicine <note>original: "pharmacum" (Latin) / "φάρμακον" (Greek); a term that can mean both a medicine and a poison</note> against fear to humans, nor have we ourselves devised one. (For I do not include sorcerers among our company). However, regarding the opposite—the lack of fear, and the tendency to be overly confident and bold when one should not be—is there a potion for this? Or how do we describe it?" **CLINIAS:** He will likely say that wine is such a thing. **ATHENIAN:** And does it not have the opposite effect of the potion we just mentioned? For when a man drinks it, he first becomes more cheerful than he was before; then, the more he tastes of it, the more he is filled with good hopes and a sense of power in his own reputation. Finally, such a man becomes full of "free speech" <note>original: "παῤῥησίας" (parrhesia); the Greek concept of frank and bold speech</note> and liberty, as if he were a wise man, and is filled with a total lack of fear, so that he speaks and acts without hesitation. **CLINIAS:** I believe everyone would agree with that. **MEGILLUS:** Certainly.

<margin>B</margin> **ATHENIAN:** Let us then recall this: we said there are two things in our souls that must be cultivated. One is that we should be as confident as possible; the other, on the contrary, is that we should be as fearful as possible. **CLINIAS:** You seem to be speaking of those things related to shame <note>original: "pudore" (Latin) / "αἰδοῦς" (Greek)</note>, as we understood it. **ATHENIAN:** You remember well. But since courage and a fearless disposition must be practiced in the midst of fears, we must consider whether the opposite quality ought to be cultivated in opposite circumstances. **CLINIAS:** That seems likely. **ATHENIAN:** Therefore, in those situations where we are naturally inclined to become excessively bold and daring, we should practice being as little impudent and audacious as possible. On the contrary, we should be fearful when it comes to speaking, enduring, or doing anything shameful. **CLINIAS:** So it seems.

<margin>C</margin> **ATHENIAN:** And are these not the conditions in which we find ourselves so affected: anger, love, pride, ignorance, greed, and cowardice? And also those things like wealth, beauty, and strength—anything that makes men lose their minds through a sort of intoxication of pleasure? For the sake of testing all these things lightly and without harm, and for introducing practice, what more convenient pleasure can we name than the one that examines character through drinking—provided a prudent caution is applied? Let us consider: if we have a soul that is harsh and wild, from which a thousand injustices spring, where is it safer to take a trial of it? Is it in business dealings, where the risk to oneself is great? Or is it more dangerous <margin>D</margin> to test the soul during the festivals of Dionysus <note>The god of wine and theater</note>, or when a soul is overcome by sexual desire, exposing the modesty of one’s daughters, sons, or wives to danger among those dearest to us, just to see the character of the soul? One could say a thousand things in praise of how much better it is to observe characters through the playfulness of the cup, which is without penalty, provided it is done with shame <note>sense of propriety</note>. Regarding this, we believe neither the Cretans nor any other men would ever doubt that this is a suitable examination of character—and indeed, superior to others for being easy, safe, and swift. **CLINIAS:** That is certainly true. **ATHENIAN:** This would then be something most useful: to know the natures and habits of souls through that art whose task it is to care for them. And this, I believe, is the duty of the political faculty <note>The art of statesmanship or citizenship</note>. Is it not? **CLINIAS:** It is exactly so.

<margin>E</margin> # PLATO ON THE LAWS, OR,
## ON THE INSTITUTION OF LAWS,
### THE SECOND DIALOGUE.

> **SUMMARY OF THE DIALOGUE.** *Having laid the foundation of the laws, Plato has also noted their subject, namely human nature. A legislator must take the greatest account of this when instituting laws. Since two passions primarily dominate human desires—Pain and Pleasure—he taught that diligent caution must be applied to them, lest there be either too much license or too much severity. Therefore, the circumstances of various natures must be considered so that laws can be prudently adapted according to their character. This question, begun in the first book, is diligently pursued in this second book: namely, the method of adapting laws to the circumstances of persons. He teaches how much discipline contributes to memory, specifically in the minds of children, and that there is a certain becoming harmony—like rhythm, dance, and melody—for all ages, so that the various habits of both mind and body may be shaped by it.*

<margin>D</margin> **N**ext, however, we must consider this concerning these matters: whether they possess only this good—that we may perceive the state of our natures—or whether there is also some great utility, worthy of much study, in the drinking of wine, if it is done correctly. What then do we say? There is indeed, as this reasoning seems to suggest. Where and how it is so, let us, I pray, listen attentively, lest we be hindered by it. **CLINIAS:** Speak then. **ATHENIAN:** I desire, therefore, to recall to memory what we mean by "correct discipline" <note>or education</note>. For, as I conjecture at present, the preservation of this duty lies in it being correctly instituted. **CLINIAS:** You speak of a great thing. **ATHENIAN:** I say, first of all, <margin>The first sense of children is pleasure and pain.</margin> that the first sense of children is that of pleasure and pain; and these are the two things in which virtue and vice first arise in the soul. Happy is he to whom it happens even in old age that he can attain wisdom and true opinions. <margin>This is from Cicero's book "On Ends," 5.</margin> Furthermore, the perfect man is he who possesses these and all the goods that are in them. I call "discipline" that virtue which first comes to children. If pleasure, love, pain, and hatred are correctly instilled into their souls before they are moved by reason, and then, when reason is present, they consent to reason because of the superior habit of good character—this very consensus is, in its entirety, virtue. But the proper habituation regarding pleasures and pains, through which men from the beginning until the end of life...

<column-break/>

<summary>The Athenian Guest explains that wine acts as a safe, cost-effective "touchstone" for testing human character, and Book II begins by defining education as the correct habituation of a child's feelings of pleasure and pain before they reach the age of reason.</summary>
<keywords>Plato, Laws, education, virtue, pleasure, pain, wine, character testing, Dionysus, legislation, Cicero, habituation, Greek philosophy</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Book II of Plato's Laws. Having established wine as a tool for testing a person's character, the Athenian Guest now moves to define the broader concept of education (paideia) as the proper training of the soul's feelings of pleasure and pain, specifically through the divine gifts of song and dance.</meta>

# PLATONIS

...that they should hate what ought to be hated, and love what ought to be loved—if you should take this training <note>original: "disciplinam" (Latin) / "παιδείαν" (Greek); usually translated as "education"</note> by itself, set apart and considered according to reason, you would, in my opinion, call it by its right name. **CLINIAS:** Indeed, Guest, both what you said previously regarding education and what you have said now seem well-spoken. **ATHENIAN:** Very well then. However, in the course of life, men often overstep and pervert this right institution of pleasures and pains, which we call education. But the Gods, pitying the human race, which is naturally weighed down by labor, have established for them periods of relaxation from their toils, namely by instituting the rotation of solemn festivals in honor of the gods. Furthermore, they have given the Muses, and Apollo the leader of the Muses, and Bacchus <note>Dionysus</note> as fellow-celebrants, along with the council of gods, to be correctors of our behavior during these solemnities.

->**B**<-

<margin>Cite Cicero: On Ends, Book 5 for this sentiment.</margin>
We must consider, therefore, whether this discourse is natural and true to us, which says that all young creatures—to put it in a word—are unable to keep their bodies or their voices quiet; they are always seeking to move and wanting to speak. Some leap and skip, as if dancing and playing with pleasure, while others shout with various voices. Other animals, however, have no sense of the order or disorder in these movements, which order is called <term>rhythm</term> and <term>harmony</term>. 

->**C**<-

<margin>What rhythm and harmony are.</margin>
But to us, a sense shared with rhythm and harmony has been granted by those gods whom we said were given to us as fellow-celebrants. They move us with pleasure and lead our choir, binding us together with songs and dances. This "choir" <note>original: "chorum" (Latin) / "χορός" (Greek)</note> they named from the word for "joy" <note>original: "ἀπὸ τῆς χαρᾶς" (Greek), a folk etymology linking 'chorus' to 'chara' (joy)</note>. First, let us consider: do we agree that the primary education is through the Muses and Apollo? Or how do we see it? **CLINIAS:** Exactly so. **ATHENIAN:** Therefore, the uneducated man must be called "one who has not practiced the dance" <note>original: "achoreutos" (Greek)</note>. Conversely, the educated man is one who has practiced it sufficiently. **CLINIAS:** That is how we define it. **ATHENIAN:** Now, the whole of the dance <note>original: "chorea"</note> is both rhythmic movement and vocal harmony <note>original: "concentus"</note>. **CLINIAS:** Necessarily. **ATHENIAN:** Whoever, then, is well-instructed in education is able both to dance and to sing well. **CLINIAS:** So it seems.

->**D**<-

<margin>What constitutes a dance.</margin>
**ATHENIAN:** But let us see what it is we just said. **CLINIAS:** What do you mean? **ATHENIAN:** When we say someone sings well and dances well, must we add "provided they sing good things and dance good things," or not? **CLINIAS:** We must add that. **ATHENIAN:** What then? If someone considers honorable things to be honorable as they truly are, and shameful things to be shameful likewise, and uses them accordingly—will such a man be a better master of the dance and music than one who can sufficiently execute with body and voice what he *thinks* is honorable, yet does not take joy in honorable things, nor feel disgust at shameful ones? Or is it the man who, although he cannot perfectly succeed with his voice and body as is fitting, yet succeeds in his sense of pleasure and pain, so that he rejoices in the good and hates the wicked? **CLINIAS:** You describe a great difference in education, O Guest.

->**E**<-

**ATHENIAN:** If, then, the three of us are not ignorant of what is good in song and dance, we certainly recognize who has rightly attained education and who has not. But if we are ignorant of this, we shall never be able to know if there is any preservation of education, or where it might be. Is it not so? **CLINIAS:** Quite so. **ATHENIAN:** Next, then, like dogs following a scent, let us track down the proper figure, melody, song, and dance. For if these escape us, we shall dispute in vain about right education, whether Greek or barbarian. **CLINIAS:** I believe so. **ATHENIAN:** What figure and melody, then, is it fitting to call "good"? Are the figures and voices of a brave soul in times of trial similar to those of a cowardly soul? **CLINIAS:** How could they be similar, when not even their complexions are the same?

->**F**<-

**ATHENIAN:** Well said, my friend. But in Music, there are both figures and harmonies, since it is concerned with rhythm and harmony. Therefore, one may speak of the "figure" and "song" of a good rhythm and harmony; but we cannot correctly speak of a "good color," as dance-masters are sometimes accustomed to imagine. Rather, there is a certain figure or song for the cowardly man and another for the brave; and these are rightly called honorable in brave men and shameful in the cowardly. But not to be too long-winded, let us simply say: all figures and harmonies that attach themselves to virtue of soul or body—or to an image of virtue—are honorable; those of the contrary sort are shameful. **CLINIAS:** You are right, and we judge these things to be so for the present.

->**G**<-

**ATHENIAN:** Furthermore, we must consider this: do we all take pleasure in all dances equally, or is there a great difference? **CLINIAS:** A very great difference. **ATHENIAN:** What then shall we say has led us into error? Is it that the same things are not honorable and good to all of us? Or are they the same, but they do not seem so? For surely no one will dare to say that a vicious dance is better than one that participates in virtue. Nor will anyone ever admit that he himself rejoices in shameful figures while others enjoy a different kind of Muse. Although many claim that the right standard of music consists in its power to bring pleasure to the soul. That, however, is neither to be tolerated nor spoken at all—for it is an impiety. This, rather, is the cause of the error. **CLINIAS:** Which one? **ATHENIAN:** Since in the dance, imitations are made of various characters and various things performed in various fortunes and habits, those who speak, sing, or express these things through the appearance of dance—either by nature, by custom, or both—approve of them and find they suit their own spirits. Thus they rejoice in them and praise them as honorable...

<column-break/>

...not what one ought to hate, but having gone from the beginning to the end, to love what one ought to love—if you were to cut this out with reason and address it as education <note>original: "παιδείαν" (paideia)</note>, in my opinion at least, you would be addressing it correctly. **CLINIAS:** Both previously, O Guest, and now, what you have said concerning education seems to us to have been said rightly. **ATHENIAN:** Well then. Since education consists of these correctly nurtured pleasures and pains, it often happens that for men in the course of life, these are loosened and destroyed in many ways. But the gods, pitying the naturally labor-prone race of men, appointed for them rests from their toils, namely the exchanges of festivals for the gods, and gave the Muses, and Apollo the leader of the Muses, and Dionysus as fellow-celebrants, so that our nurtures might be set right during the festivals with the help of the gods. We must see, then, whether the account we are singing is true to nature, or how. It says that every young creature, so to speak, is unable to keep its body and voice quiet, but always seeks to move and to utter sound—some leaping and skipping, as if dancing with pleasure and playing, while others utter all sorts of sounds. Now, other animals do not have a perception of the order or lack of order in movements, which we call rhythm and harmony. But to us, the gods whom we said were given as fellow-dancers are the ones who have given the rhythmic and harmonic sense accompanied by pleasure, by which they move us and lead our choirs, joining us together with songs and dances; and they have named the choirs "chorous" from the innate name of "joy" <note>original: "χαρᾶς" (charas)</note>. First, then, let us accept this: shall we grant that education is first through the Muses and Apollo, or how? **CLINIAS:** Thus. **ATHENIAN:** Then the uneducated man will be for us "one who has not danced"; while the educated man must be positioned as "one who has danced sufficiently." **CLINIAS:** Of course. **ATHENIAN:** And the dance-ensemble <note>original: "χορεία" (chorea)</note> is, as a whole, both dance and song. **CLINIAS:** Necessarily. **ATHENIAN:** Then the man who is well educated would be able both to sing and to dance well. **CLINIAS:** So it seems. **ATHENIAN:** Let us see then what is being said now. **CLINIAS:** What sort of thing? **ATHENIAN:** "To sing well" (we say) and "to dance well." Should we add "and to sing good things and dance good things," or not? **CLINIAS:** Let us add it. **ATHENIAN:** What then of the man who, thinking good things to be good and shameful things to be shameful, uses them accordingly? Will such a person be better educated for us than if, although he is able to serve sufficiently with his body and voice that which he thinks to be good, he does not take joy in all good things, nor hate what is not good? Or is it that man who might not be entirely able to succeed with his voice and body in his thinking, yet succeeds in his pleasure and pain, welcoming whatever is good and being distressed by whatever is not good? **CLINIAS:** You are describing a great difference, O Guest, in education. **ATHENIAN:** Therefore, if we three recognize what is good in song and dance, being three ourselves, we also know who is rightly educated and who is uneducated. But if we are ignorant of this, we could never distinguish what is the safeguard of education and where it is. Is it not so? **CLINIAS:** So it is. **ATHENIAN:** Therefore, now again, like dogs on a scent, let us search out the good figure, the melody, the song, and the dance. If these things escape us, our discourse about education—whether Greek or barbarian—will be in vain. **CLINIAS:** Yes. **ATHENIAN:** Very well. What do we say the good figure or melody is? Come now, for a brave soul held in labors and a cowardly soul in the same and equal labors, do their figures and sounds happen to be similar? **CLINIAS:** How could they be, when not even their colors are? **ATHENIAN:** Well said, O companion. But in music, there are both figures and melodies, as music is composed of rhythms and harmonies. Thus there is a rhythmic and harmonic melody or figure, but there is no such thing as a "well-colored" one as the dance-teachers imagine when they say one "sounds correctly." But the figure or melody of the coward and the brave man does exist, and it is right to call them so: those of the brave are good, those of the cowardly are shameful. And so that we do not have a great deal of long-windedness about these things, let it simply be that all figures and melodies associated with virtue of soul or body—whether they are themselves or some image of them—are good; those of vice, on the contrary, are all the opposite. **CLINIAS:** You propose this rightly, and let this be our answer for now. **ATHENIAN:** Furthermore, this: do all of us take joy in all dances equally, or is there much lack thereof? **CLINIAS:** More than anything. **ATHENIAN:** What then do we say is the cause of our having wandered? Is it that the same things are not good to us everywhere? Does it seem that, being the same, they do not seem the same? For surely no one will say that the dances of vice are ever better than those of virtue; nor that he himself rejoices in the figures of wickedness, while others do so with some contrary Muse. Yet most people say the correctness of music is the power providing pleasure to souls. But this is neither tolerable nor pious to utter at all. This rather is more likely to lead us astray. **CLINIAS:** What sort of thing? **ATHENIAN:** Since the matters concerning the dance are imitations of characters, occurring in all sorts of actions and fortunes, with each person going through them with habits and imitations, those for whom the things said or sung, or however danced, are according to their character, either by nature or...

<summary>This page defines education (paideia) as the proper alignment of a person's feelings of pleasure and pain with virtue, primarily through the divine gifts of song and dance (the "chorea"). It argues that while all youth are naturally restless, only humans possess the sense of rhythm and harmony given by the gods to turn this movement into a moral exercise.</summary>
<keywords>education, paideia, rhythm, harmony, Muses, Apollo, Dionysus, dance, song, virtue, brave vs. cowardly, imitation, pleasure vs. truth</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from Book II of Plato’s Laws. Having previously discussed the divine origin of festivals and the role of the Muses, Apollo, and Dionysus, the Athenian Guest now examines how the internal character of a person interacts with external music and dance, and introduces the famous example of Egyptian artistic stability.</meta>

# ON THE LAWS, BOOK II. 577

<margin>A</margin> ...and habit, or even both, it is inevitable that they will find joy in these things, praise them, and address them as beautiful. But for those to whom these things occur contrary to their nature, character, or some habit, they can neither find joy in them nor praise them, but must instead call them "cold" <note>original: "ψυχρὰ" (Greek) / "turpia" (Latin, meaning shameful). In Greek, calling a work "cold" meant it lacked soul or inspiration.</note>. In cases where nature is right but habit is contrary, or habit is right but nature is contrary, people offer praises that are at odds with their pleasures. They claim each of these things is "pleasant but wicked." In the presence of others whom they consider wise, they are ashamed to move their bodies in such ways or to sing them aloud as if they were seriously declaring them to be beautiful; but in private, they delight in them.

**CLINIAS:** You speak most truly. **ATHENIAN:** Now, does any harm come to the one who finds joy in wicked postures or melodies, or does any benefit come <margin>B</margin> to those who accept pleasures of the opposite kind? **CLINIAS:** That seems likely. **ATHENIAN:** Is it merely likely, or is it also necessary? Is it not the same as when someone associates with the wicked characters of evil men and, rather than hating them, finds joy in accepting them—perhaps even reproaching them only in jest, as if dreaming of his own wickedness? In such a case, it is absolutely necessary that the one who rejoices becomes like that in which he finds joy, even if he is ashamed to praise it. And what greater good or evil could we say falls upon us by necessity than this? **CLINIAS:** I think none. **ATHENIAN:** Where laws are well-established, <margin>C</margin> or will be in the future, do we think the poetic license regarding the <term>Muses</term> <note>mousike: the combined arts of music, poetry, and dance</note> and education will be such that the poet can teach the children and youth in the choirs whatever rhythm, melody, or word happens to please the poet himself in his work, regardless of whether it leads toward virtue or vice? **CLINIAS:** Certainly, that would be irrational. **MEGILLUS:** How could it be otherwise? **ATHENIAN:** But yet, today, this is exactly what is permitted to be done in almost every city—except in Egypt. **CLINIAS:** And in Egypt, how do you say such a thing has been legislated? **ATHENIAN:** It is a wonder to hear. Long ago, it seems, they recognized the principle we are now discussing: that the youth in cities must be accustomed to beautiful postures and beautiful melodies. Having determined what these are and of what sort, they displayed them in the temples. Beyond these, it was not permitted for painters or any others <margin>D</margin> who produce postures and such things to innovate, or to invent anything other than the ancestral forms. Nor is it permitted today, either in these arts or in music as a whole. If you look, you will find there works painted or sculpted ten thousand years ago <note>Plato uses "ten thousand years" as a rhetorical figure to mean "time immemorial."</note>—not just "so to speak" ten thousand, but literally—that are neither more beautiful nor more ugly than those produced today, but are crafted with the very same skill. **CLINIAS:** What you say is marvelous. **ATHENIAN:** Rather, it is the height of statesmanship and legislation. You might find other things there that are trivial, but this fact about music is true and worthy of consideration: that it was possible to legislate concerning such matters with confidence, establishing melodies that possess a natural correctness. <margin>E</margin> This, however, would be the work of a god or some divine man. Just as they say there that the melodies preserved for all this time are actually the poems of Isis <note>In Egyptian mythology, Isis was the goddess of magic and motherhood; here, Plato credits her with the invention of sacred music.</note>. Therefore, as I was saying, if someone were able to grasp their correctness in any way at all, he should have the courage to reduce them to law and order. For the craving for pleasure and pain—the desire to always seek out new music—does not actually have great power to corrupt the consecrated <term>choreia</term> <note>A combination of dance and song performed by a choir</note> by accusing it of being "old-fashioned." At least in Egypt, it seems it was not at all able to corrupt it, but quite the opposite. **CLINIAS:** It seems things would be as you say based on your words. **ATHENIAN:** Can we then confidently say that the use of music and play within the choir is correct <margin>F</margin> in the following way? We rejoice whenever we think we are doing well, and whenever we rejoice, we think in turn that we are doing well. Is it not so? **CLINIAS:** It is exactly so. **ATHENIAN:** And indeed, when we are rejoicing in such a state, we are unable to keep still. **CLINIAS:** That is true. **ATHENIAN:** Are not the young among us ready to dance? And we, the elders, considering it proper to watch them, find joy in their play and celebration—especially since our own youthful agility is now failing us. Out of longing for that agility, we establish contests for those who are best able to awaken the memory of youth within us. **CLINIAS:** Very true. <margin>G</margin> **ATHENIAN:** Should we think it is entirely in vain that common people say of those performing in the festivals: "The one who makes us rejoice the most and provides the greatest pleasure is to be considered the wisest and judged the winner"? For indeed, since we are permitted to play at such times, the one who makes the most people rejoice should be most honored and—as I just said—carry away the prize. Is this not a right thing to say, and would it not be right if it were done? **CLINIAS:** Perhaps. **ATHENIAN:** But, my blessed friend, let us not judge such a thing too hastily. Instead, let us distinguish it into parts and consider it this way: what if someone were to propose a contest of any kind whatsoever, without defining it as gymnastic, or equestrian, or musical? If he gathered all the citizens together and, for the sake of pleasure alone, established a contest with prizes for whoever could delight the spectators most—without specifying by what means—

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...it is necessary to name them so. But to those for whom these things happen contrary to nature, or custom, or some habit, they are unable to rejoice in them, nor can they praise them; indeed, they must call them shameful. But truly, for those to whom these things happen rightly by nature but contrary to custom—or rightly by custom but contrary to nature—they offer praises that are the opposite of their pleasures. For they say that each of these things brings joy, yet they concede they are wicked. And for that reason, in the presence of others whom they think are of sound mind, they fear to move their body in that way; they also fear to sing those things, and to declare them honorable and worthy of study. But in private, they delight in all of them. 
**CLINIAS:** You speak very true things. **ATHENIAN:** Is any damage brought <margin>B</margin> to him who delights in wicked figures or songs, or any utility to those who take pleasure in their opposites? **CLINIAS:** That seems likely. **ATHENIAN:** Is it only likely, or is it even necessary that it be so? Just as when someone associates with wicked men and does not hate their characters, but rather delights in them and indulges them—even if he censures them as a joke, as if seeing their wickedness in himself during a dream. Then indeed it is necessary that he become similar to those in whom he rejoices, even if he is afraid to praise them. In this matter, what greater thing, either good or evil, should we think must necessarily happen to us? **CLINIAS:** I think nothing. **ATHENIAN:** Do we <margin>C</margin> suppose that where laws are well-constituted, or will be in the future, there will be such license in the poetic arts—in the teachings and games of the Muses—that whatever delights the poet, whether in rhythm, song, or poetic word, he is allowed to teach the same? And to bend the boys and youths of well-educated citizens in the choirs toward either virtue or vice, whichever happens? **CLINIAS:** That is contrary to reason. **MEGILLUS:** Certainly. **ATHENIAN:** But this, to speak briefly, is allowed almost everywhere except in Egypt. **CLINIAS:** In what way do you say this law was sanctioned in Egypt? **ATHENIAN:** This is a wonder to hear. For long ago, as it seems to me, they recognized that which we have now said: that in cities, the young must be accustomed to good figures and good songs. What <margin>D</margin> and of what sort these things are was established by them in their sacred rites, and beyond those, neither painters nor other makers of figures or any kind of craftsmen were allowed to introduce any innovations, nor even to think of others besides the ancestral ones. Nor is it permitted today, either in these or in music in general. Therefore, if you observe, you will find there things depicted or shaped in whatever way ten thousand years ago—not just ten thousand years old, so to speak, but truly so—that are no more beautiful nor more shameful than those which are painted today, but are crafted with the same art. **CLINIAS:** What you say is marvelous to hear. **ATHENIAN:** Rather, it is extremely statesmanlike and most fitting for the establishing of laws. You will find other trivial things there, but this regarding music is true and <margin>E</margin> worthy of notice: namely, that it was possible to provide a certain and stable law for such things, and that the legislator intended to introduce such harmonies as displayed a natural rectitude. This indeed is the work of a god or some divine man. Just as they say there that those most ancient harmonies among them are the poems of Isis. Wherefore, as I was saying, if anyone is able in any way to understand the rectitude of these things, he must dare to reduce them to order and law. For the constant new affection of the appetite regarding pleasure and pain, which always strives to use new music, perhaps does not have great power to corrupt those choirs by the insistence of antiquity which were established by <margin>F</margin> sacred laws. Certainly, it seems that it has not been able to corrupt the Egyptian choirs in all that time, but quite the opposite. **CLINIAS:** The matter stands as it is gathered from your words. **ATHENIAN:** Let us say then confidently that the choir is rightly connected with games and music. We rejoice as often as we believe we are living happily; and as often as we rejoice, we again judge that we are living happily. Is it not so? **CLINIAS:** Exactly so. **ATHENIAN:** And while we rejoice, we are not able to keep still. **CLINIAS:** It is as you say. **ATHENIAN:** Is it not therefore that the youths among us are fit for dancing? We who are older, however, think it proper to be occupied in watching them while we rejoice in their games and celebration, since the lightness of the body fails us. Out of a desire for that agility, we set up contests for those who are most able to recall that youthful age to our memory. **CLINIAS:** You tell the truth. **ATHENIAN:** Do we then think it is entirely in vain that it is said by many concerning people performing sacred games, that he must be judged the wisest and the master of victory who makes us rejoice and be glad the most? For after it is permitted to play in these things, it seems fitting that we especially honor him who provokes as many as possible and to the greatest degree to joy, and—as I was saying—declare him the winner. Is that rightly said? And would it be rightly done if it were so? **CLINIAS:** Perhaps. **ATHENIAN:** But, O blessed man, let us not give our sentence so precipitously, but let us consider this very thing by distinguishing it into parts in this way. If someone should at some time propose any kind of contest, but specifies neither gymnastic, nor musical, nor equestrian, but having gathered all the citizens, should establish a contest for the sake of pleasure alone, and propose prizes to him who delights the spectators most, and is judged to have done it best of all,

<summary>The Athenian Guest explains that music and art have the power to mold character, arguing that Egypt's "ten thousand years" of unchanging, divinely-inspired artistic standards prove that states can and should legislate cultural aesthetics to prevent moral decay. He questions whether pleasure should be the only metric for judging artistic success in public contests.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the Athenian Guest’s argument regarding the standard of beauty in art. Having previously noted that people often praise what they do not actually enjoy, he now moves to a thought experiment about a general competition to determine what truly constitutes "pleasure" and who is fit to judge it.</meta>

# PLATO'S LAWS

<margin>A</margin> ...and since no specific motive for delight has been defined, what do we think would result from such a proclamation? **CLINIAS:** What are you referring to? **ATHENIAN:** Suppose someone, like Homer, were to perform a Rhapsody <note>The rhythmic recitation of epic poetry, usually from memory.</note>; another, a song on the Cithara; another, a Tragedy; and yet another, a Comedy. It would not be surprising if someone even thought they could win by showing some marvelous puppet-show. When many such contestants of various kinds have gathered, can we say who would rightly be the winner? **CLINIAS:** You ask an absurd question. For who could answer skillfully before they had been present to hear each of the competitors for themselves?

<margin>B</margin> **ATHENIAN:** Would you like me to provide an answer to this "absurd" question? **CLINIAS:** Why not? **ATHENIAN:** If very small children were to give the verdict, they would judge the puppet-showman <note>original: "praestigiatorum" (Latin) / "θαύματα ἐπιδεικνύντα" (Greek, meaning "one who shows wonders"). Referring to magicians or puppeteers.</note> to have defeated all the others. Would they not? **CLINIAS:** Of course. **ATHENIAN:** But older children would prefer the comic poet. Educated women, the young men, and perhaps the entire multitude of the crowd would likely praise Tragedy. **CLINIAS:** That is likely how it would happen. **ATHENIAN:** However, we older men would perhaps listen with the greatest pleasure to a Rhapsode who sang well from Homer—the *Iliad* or the *Odyssey*—or something from Hesiod, and we would declare him the winner over everyone. Does it not remain, then, to declare who would be the winner *by right*? **CLINIAS:** Certainly. **ATHENIAN:** It is clear to me, and you must also grant it, that the true winner is the one judged to have won by men of our own age. For the experience we gain with age is everywhere a great and excellent thing in all civil matters.

<margin>C</margin> **CLINIAS:** Undoubtedly. **ATHENIAN:** I concede this much to the masses: that music must be judged by the pleasure it provides. However, I do not mean the pleasure of just any person. I say that the most beautiful Muse is the one that delights the best and sufficiently educated people—especially the one that delights a man preeminent in virtue and discipline. For this reason, we affirm that the judges of these matters must possess virtue. They must participate in both wisdom and courage. Wisdom, because a true judge must not learn how to determine a judgment from the crowd, nor should he be so stunned by the noise of the multitude and his own ignorance as to deliver a verdict in that state.

<margin>D</margin> He must have courage because, even if he understands the truth in his own mind, he must not, through laziness or fear, allow his mouth—which invoked the gods before he sat to judge—to lazily pronounce a false and unjust judgment. For the judge sits not as a student of the spectators, but as their teacher, as is right, intended to oppose the unseemly pleasures of the audience. This was permitted by the ancient Greek law, just as it is now by the Sicilian and Italian law; but that law, by leaving the matter to the multitude of spectators and declaring the winner by a show of hands, has corrupted the poets themselves. They now compose everything to suit the base pleasure of the judges, so that the spectators are essentially teaching the poets, rather than the poets teaching them. 

<margin>E</margin> It has also corrupted the pleasures of the performance itself. For while those who attend should always hear things better than their own habits so as to attain a higher pleasure, the opposite now happens to them in the theater. What, then, is the point of what we have said? See if it is this. **CLINIAS:** What is it? **ATHENIAN:** It seems to me that our argument has come back for the third or fourth time to the same point: that discipline <note>original: "disciplinam" (Latin) / "παιδεία" (Greek: Paideia). This encompasses the whole education and upbringing of a citizen.</note> is the drawing and leading of children toward that right reason which the law declares to be correct, and which the most equitable and experienced elders have confirmed as truly right. In order, then, that the soul of the child may not become accustomed to feeling joy or pain in opposition to the law, but may follow the law by rejoicing in and grieving at the same things as the old man, the lawmaker will use persuasion. If necessary, he will compel the poet to describe the deeds of the temperate, brave, and good in noble words—shaping their figures through rhythm and their tones through harmony as is fitting, through those songs which we call Odes, but which are in reality <gloss>incantations</gloss> <note>original: "ἐπῳδαί" (epōdai). In Greek, this word refers to magical spells or charms; Plato uses it to describe how music "charms" the soul into a state of virtue.</note> for the soul, intentionally composed so that human souls may follow the laws through their joys and sorrows.

<margin>F</margin> Since young souls cannot endure serious study, these things are spoken and performed as games and songs. In this, the same effect is achieved as by those who care for people with sick bodies: they smear healthy food with sweet seasonings, but coat harmful things in bitter ones, so that the patients grow accustomed to accepting the one and rejecting the other. **CLINIAS:** Do you think, Guest, that these rules are observed in other cities? For as far as I know, the things you prescribe are done nowhere except among us and the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans.</note>. Elsewhere, they are always inventing new things in dancing and all other music, changed not by laws, but by certain wandering pleasures which are never the same nor remain in the same state, but are always changing—contrary to those Egyptian customs you described.

<margin>G</margin> **ATHENIAN:** You are quite right, Clinias. If I seemed to say earlier that the things you mention were happening everywhere, I would not be surprised if I expressed my thoughts unclearly. I was stating what I *wish* to happen in music, and I seemed to you to be saying they *were* happening. For to rebuke things that are incurable and far-gone in error is never pleasant, though sometimes necessary. But since we agree on these points, do you not assert that such things are practiced among you and the Spartans more than among other Greeks? **CLINIAS:** How could we not?

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...and if he should win, having achieved this most of all, and be judged the most pleasant among the contestants: what do we think would result from this proclamation? **CLINIAS:** Regarding what? **ATHENIAN:** It is likely that one person might display Rhapsody, like Homer; another, a performance on the Cithara; another, Tragedy; another, Comedy. It would not be strange if someone, by displaying marvels <note>Greek: *thaumata*, referring to wonders or puppet-shows.</note>, believed they should win most of all. If these and ten thousand other such contestants came forward, could we say who would win by right? **CLINIAS:** You have asked a strange thing. For who could answer as though they knew, before hearing and becoming an audience to each of the athletes themselves?

<margin>B</margin> **ATHENIAN:** What then? Do you want me to answer this strange answer for you both? **CLINIAS:** Certainly. **ATHENIAN:** If, then, the very small children were to judge, they would judge the one showing the marvels; is that not so? **CLINIAS:** How could they not? **ATHENIAN:** And if the older boys judged, they would pick the one who does comedies; and tragedy would be the choice of the educated women, and the young men, and perhaps nearly the whole multitude. **CLINIAS:** Perhaps so. **ATHENIAN:** But we old men would probably listen with the greatest pleasure to a Rhapsode setting forth the *Iliad* or the *Odyssey* or something of Hesiod, and we would say he won by a great deal. Who, then, would have won correctly? That is the next question, is it not? **CLINIAS:** Yes. **ATHENIAN:** It is clear that I and you must say that those judged by our contemporaries would win correctly. For our habit <note>The Latin version translates the Greek *ethos* as "use of things" or "experience."</note> seems to us to be by far the best in all cities and everywhere.

<margin>C</margin> **CLINIAS:** Certainly. **ATHENIAN:** I also concede this much to the many, that music should be judged by pleasure—not, however, by the pleasure of just anyone. Rather, that Muse is most beautiful which delights the best people and those sufficiently educated; and most of all, the one that delights the single man who excels in virtue and education. For this reason, we say the judges of these things need virtue, because they must share in other wisdom and especially in courage. For the true judge must not judge by learning from the theater, being struck out of his senses by the noise of the many and his own lack of education.

<margin>D</margin> Nor, on the other hand, if he does know, should he—through unmanliness and cowardice—lazily announce a false judgment from the very same mouth with which he called upon the gods when he was about to judge. For the judge sits not as a disciple, but as a teacher of the spectators (at least if justice is to be served), and to stand in opposition to those spectators who do not offer pleasure in a fitting or correct way. For it was permitted by the ancient and Greek law—unlike the Sicilian and Italian law, which now leaves it to the multitude of spectators and decides the winner by a show of hands—which has corrupted the poets themselves. (For they compose for the pleasure of the judges, so that the spectators, being base, are the ones who educate the poets.) It has also corrupted the pleasures of the spectators. For while they ought to always be hearing things better than their own pleasures, so that they may have a better pleasure, they now do the exact opposite.

<margin>E</margin> What, then, does our argument wish to signify to us now that it has been completed? Consider this. **CLINIAS:** What sort of thing? **ATHENIAN:** It seems to me that the argument has come around to the same thing for a third or fourth time: that education <note>Greek: *paideia*.</note> is the drawing and leading of children toward the reason that is called "right" by the law, and which is agreed to be truly right by the most equitable and oldest men through their experience. So that the soul of the child may not be habituated to feel joy and pain in opposition to the law and those persuaded by the law, but may follow along, feeling joy and pain at the same things as the old man. For the sake of these things, what we call songs are truly <gloss>incantations</gloss> for the souls, having been seriously created for the purpose of such a symphony <note>A "symphony" or "concord" between the soul's feelings and the law's commands.</note> as we describe.

<margin>F</margin> But because the souls of the young cannot bear seriousness, they are called "games" and "songs" and are practiced as such. Just as those who care for people with sick and weak bodies try to offer useful nourishment in pleasant drinks and foods, but harmful things in unpleasant ones—so that they may welcome the one and correctly be habituated to hate the other. In the same way, the correct lawmaker will persuade the poet, and if he cannot persuade he will compel him, to correctly create in noble and praiseworthy words the postures of the temperate and brave and all-around good men, in both rhythms and melodies in harmonies. **CLINIAS:** By Zeus, Guest, do you think they do this now in the other cities? For I, as far as I

<margin>G</margin> perceive, do not know of these things being practiced except among us or the Lacedaemonians. Instead, certain new things are always happening in dances and all other music, changed not by laws but by certain disorderly pleasures, which are far from being the same or constant in the way you described regarding the Egyptians; rather, they are never the same. **ATHENIAN:** Excellent, Clinias! If I seemed to you to be saying the things you mention are happening now, I would not wonder if I did so because I was not speaking clearly what I intended. But I was saying what I *wish* would happen regarding music; perhaps I spoke such things that it seemed to you I was saying they were so. For to find fault with things that are incurable and far advanced in error is in no way pleasant, though sometimes it is necessary. But since these things seem the same to you as well, come, do you say that such things happen among you and these others more than among the other Greeks? **CLINIAS:** How could we not?

<summary>The Athenian Guest argues that art should be judged by the pleasure of the most virtuous and educated elders rather than the masses. He defines education as a system of "incantations" (songs) that train a child's emotions to align with the law's definition of right and wrong.</summary>
