<meta>This page continues the Athenian Guest’s dialogue with Clinias of Crete. Having established that judges of the arts should be those of superior virtue and education, the Athenian now argues that the content of poetry and music must be regulated by law to ensure it promotes the idea that a just life is necessarily a happy and pleasant one.</meta>

# ON THE LAWS, BOOK II.

ATHENIAN: If these things were handled similarly among other peoples, would they not be conducted better than they are now?
CLINIAS: Certainly, it would be much better if they were arranged in the way they are among those people and among us, and just as you prescribed a moment ago.

<margin>A</margin> <margin>What the poets ought to sing.</margin> ATHENIAN: Come then, let us see if these are the things that are proclaimed among you in all your education and music. You compel the poets to say in their songs that the good man—who is temperate and just—is fortunate and blessed, whether he is large and robust, or small and weak, and whether he is poor or wealthy. But the unjust man, even if he were wealthier than Cinyras or Midas <note>Cinyras was a legendary king of Cyprus known for his wealth, and Midas was the mythical king whose touch turned everything to gold.</note>, is miserable and leads a life of sorrow.

<margin>B</margin> Therefore, if your poet speaks rightly, he will say: "I would never mention, nor account as a man, one who did not possess and manage everything called 'good' alongside justice." He would say that such a man, adorned with justice, should delight in fighting the enemy hand-to-hand. But the unjust man should not dare to look upon bloody slaughter, nor be able to outrun the Thracian North Wind <note>original: "Thracium... Boream" (Latin) / "Θρηΐκιον βορέην" (Greek). Boreas was the Greek god of the cold North Wind.</note>, nor should he ever possess any of those things called "goods." For the things the common people call "goods" are not correctly named.

<margin>C</margin> Indeed, they say the greatest good is health; the next is beauty; the third is strength; and the fourth is wealth. They list countless other things as "goods" of this kind. To see and hear sharply, and to use the other senses fully, are seen as goods; and alongside these, the power of a tyrant to do whatever you desire. They say the pinnacle of all happiness is to gain immortality immediately while possessing all these things.

<margin>D</margin> But you and I are in agreement on this: for just and holy men, the possession of all these things is the best, but for the unjust, the possession of them all is the worst, starting with health itself. For to be healthy, to see, to hear, to perceive everything easily, and simply to live—even to live forever—is the greatest evil if one lives always devoid of justice and all other virtues. It is a lesser evil if someone in such a state finishes their life in the shortest possible time. These are the things you will encourage and compel your poets to say, and you will educate your youth using rhythms and harmonies that agree with these ideas. Do you yourselves recognize this? For I assert that what are commonly called "evils" are actually "goods" for the unjust, but "evils" for the just. And those things called "goods" are truly good for the good, but evil for the evil. Do we agree then on the point we were investigating, or not?

<margin>E</margin> CLINIAS: In part we seem to agree, but in part, not at all.
ATHENIAN: Perhaps I have not persuaded you that the man who is unjust and insolent is not blessed, but miserable—even if he has health, wealth, perpetual power as a tyrant, and possesses invincible physical strength, spirit, and immortality, and suffers none of the things commonly called "evils."
CLINIAS: You speak the truth <note>Clinias is likely agreeing with the Athenian's description of his own doubt, rather than the Athenian's conclusion.</note>.
ATHENIAN: Very well, but what should be said next? If a man is strong, beautiful, and rich, and does whatever he desires through his whole life, doesn't it seem to you that if he is unjust and insolent, he must necessarily live a shameful life? Will you at least concede that he lives shamefully?
CLINIAS: Certainly.
ATHENIAN: And does he not also live badly?
CLINIAS: I wouldn't agree with that in the same way.
ATHENIAN: And what about "unpleasantly" or "disadvantageously" to himself? Do you not concede those?
CLINIAS: How could we concede those?

<margin>F</margin> <margin>Whether the unjust man is unhappy even if he possesses everything called good, simply because he is unjust.</margin> ATHENIAN: How? If a god, my friends, would grant us a shared agreement of mind; for as it stands, we are in disagreement. To me, these points seem as certain and necessary, my friend Clinias, as the fact that Crete is an island. And if I were the one establishing laws for the Cretans, I would compel both the poets and all the other citizens to speak in this way. I would impose nearly the greatest of all punishments if anyone in the land asserted that there were ever any wicked men who live pleasantly, or that some things are "useful" and "profitable" while other things are "more just." I would persuade my citizens to say many things contrary to what is currently said by the Cretans and Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans.</note>, and indeed by the rest of humanity. Come now, by Jupiter and Apollo, you excellent men, if we were to ask these very gods who gave us our laws: "Is the most just life the most pleasant, or are there two lives, one being the most pleasant and the other being the most just?" If they were to answer that there are two, we might perhaps ask them again, if we wished to inquire correctly, "Which ones should be called the happier: those living most justly, or those living most pleasantly?" If they were to answer "those living most pleasantly," their response would be shameful.

<margin>G</margin> I would rather such a thing be said by fathers and legislators than by the gods. Therefore, let it be assumed that I have asked these questions of a father and a legislator, and the answer given to me was: the one who lives most pleasantly is the most blessed. I would then counter: "O Father, did you not want me to live as happily as possible? Certainly. But you never stopped commanding me to live as justly as possible." Whoever grants both these things at once—whether a legislator or a father—speaks absurdly and is inconsistent with himself. But if he were to answer that the most just life is the most happy, anyone who hears this would ask, I think: "What good and beautiful thing does the law praise in that life that is better than pleasure?" For what good can be present in a just man that is separated from pleasure?

<margin>H</margin> Tell me, I pray: are praise and glory from both men and gods something good and honorable, yet unpleasant? And is infamy the opposite?

<summary>The Athenian Guest argues that the law must compel poets to teach that justice and happiness are inseparable, contending that "goods" like wealth or health are actually harmful to the unjust man.</summary>

# OF PLATO

ATHENIAN: We would say least of all, O legislator. But is it true that neither committing nor suffering injury is pleasant, while being good and honorable is something else? Or are the other things pleasant, but shameful and bad? CLINIAS: How can you say that? ATHENIAN: Therefore, a line of reasoning that does not separate the pleasant from the just, nor the good from the honorable, is persuasive—if for no other reason, then at least to make someone willing to live a holy and just life. Therefore, to a legislator, the most shameful and contrary speech is one that denies these things are so. For no one would willingly choose to do that which does not bring him more joy than pain.
<margin>B</margin>
Indeed, things seen from a distance often cause a dizzying blur <note>original: "caliginosam affert vertiginem" / "σκοτοδινιᾶν". This refers to the optical illusion where objects far away look different than they do up close; Plato uses this as a metaphor for how people misjudge the pleasure of justice vs. injustice.</note> to everyone, especially to children. Therefore, the legislator will lead the citizens' opinions to the opposite view, removing the darkness and the dizziness. Through praises, customs, and arguments, he will somehow persuade them that just and unjust things are like shadow-paintings: that unjust things appear pleasant and just things appear most unpleasant when viewed by an unjust and wicked man; but when viewed by a just man, everything appears exactly the opposite. CLINIAS: So it appears. ATHENIAN: But in truth, which judgment shall we consider superior? That of the better soul or that of the worse? CLINIAS: Necessarily that of the better. ATHENIAN: It is necessary, then, that the unjust life is not only more shameful and worse, but in truth even more unpleasant than the just and holy life.
<margin>C</margin>
CLINIAS: So it certainly seems, my friend, according to this reasoning. ATHENIAN: Even if this were not the case—as our argument has just shown it to be—a legislator of even small benefit would venture to tell a "useful lie" to the youth for their own good, if ever a lie should be told. For what lie could be more useful than this one, which is able to lead those who hear it to embrace justice not by force, but of their own free will? CLINIAS: Truth, O guest, is a beautiful and lasting thing. Yet it seems it is not always easy to persuade people of it. ATHENIAN: Be that as it may. But that Sidonian fable <note>The "Sidonian fable" refers to the myth of Cadmus, who sowed dragon's teeth in the ground from which armed soldiers were born.</note>, though it lacked all probability, was easily believed, as were many others. CLINIAS: Which ones? ATHENIAN: That from teeth
<margin>D</margin>
sown in the earth, fully armed soldiers were once born. This is a great example for a legislator that he can persuade the souls of the young of whatever he wishes. Therefore, he ought to investigate nothing else except what things, if believed, would bring the greatest good to the city. He should apply all his effort to ensure that the entire community sings of these things with one and the same voice, as much as possible, always in their songs, myths, and discourses. This is my view. If you feel differently, feel free to contradict me. CLINIAS: Neither of us seems able to doubt these points. ATHENIAN:
<margin>E</margin>
I shall proceed then, asserting that all the choirs—which are three in number—ought to enchant the still tender and soft souls of children with all the good things we have discussed and whatever else we might tell. The main point should be this: that if we declare the best and most pleasant life to be judged the same by the gods, we shall speak the truth and be more likely to persuade those we need to than if we spoke otherwise. CLINIAS: What you say must be granted. ATHENIAN: Therefore, let the first choir, the <term>Children's Choir (chorus puerilis)</term> of the Muses, enter first to sing these things with great zeal to the whole city. The second choir, those up to thirty years of age, shall invoke <term>Apollo Paean</term> <note>Apollo in his role as a healer and protector, often invoked with a "Paean" or hymn of praise.</note> as a witness to the truth of these words, and suppliantly pray that he be favorable to the youth. The third shall be the choir of those between thirty and sixty years of age. Those older than this, who can no longer sing songs about these same customs, we judge should be left as tellers of myths by divine inspiration. CLINIAS: Who are these third choirs you speak of, guest? For we do not clearly understand what you mean by them.
<margin>F</margin>
ATHENIAN: These are the very ones for whose sake most of the previous discussion was introduced. CLINIAS: We do not yet understand. Try to speak more clearly. ATHENIAN: It was said at the beginning of our talk, if we remember, that the nature of all young people is so fiery that it cannot keep still in body or voice, but always cries out and leaps without order. We said no other animal has a sense of order in these things, except for human nature. The name for the order seen in movement is <term>Rhythm (Rhythmus)</term>; but the order in the voice, where high and low pitches are blended together, is called
<margin>G</margin>
<term>Harmony (Harmonia)</term>. Both together were called <term>Choral Art (Chorea)</term>. We also said the gods, pitying us, gave us Apollo and the Muses as fellow-dancers and leaders. And if we remember, we counted <term>Dionysus</term> <note>Dionysus is the god of wine and festivity; here, he is associated with the older choir, perhaps because wine helps older men find the courage to sing.</note> as the third. CLINIAS: How could we not remember? ATHENIAN: The choirs of Apollo and the Muses have already been mentioned. But the third and remaining choir must necessarily be attributed to Dionysus. CLINIAS: How so? Explain further. For at first hearing, a "Dionysian choir of elders"—those over thirty and even up to sixty—seems very strange. ATHENIAN: You speak truly. But I think reason is needed here to show how this can be done appropriately. CLINIAS: What then? ATHENIAN: Do we agree on those previous points? CLINIAS: Which ones? ATHENIAN: That every man and child, free and slave, male and female, and the entire city should never stop singing to the entire city in various ways the things we have described...

<column-break/>

ATHENIAN: Least of all, my dear legislator, would I say so. But is it not true that not doing wrong at all, nor being wronged by anyone, is not just good or honorable, but the other things are pleasant, while these are shameful and bad? CLINIAS: And how could that be? ATHENIAN: Therefore, the argument that does not separate the pleasant from the just, and the good from the honorable, is persuasive—if nothing else—toward making someone willing to live the holy and just life. Thus, to a legislator, it is the most shameful of speeches and the most contrary to say that these things are not so. For no one would willingly be persuaded to do that which is not followed by more joy than pain. Now, things seen from afar provide everyone, so to speak—and especially children—with a "shadow-dizziness" <note>original: "σκοτοδινιᾶν". This refers to the blurred vision or vertigo caused by looking into darkness or at distant things.</note>. But the legislator will establish an opinion contrary to this, removing the darkness,
<margin>B</margin>
and he will persuade them somehow through customs, praises, and arguments, that just and unjust things are like shadow-paintings; and that unjust things appear the opposite of just things—appearing pleasant to the unjust and wicked man, while just things appear most unpleasant; but from the perspective of the just man, everything appears exactly the opposite in both cases. CLINIAS: So it appears. ATHENIAN: And which of these two judgments shall we say is more authoritative? That of the inferior soul, or that of the better? CLINIAS: Necessarily that of the better. ATHENIAN: It is necessary then that the unjust life is not only more shameful and wretched, but in truth also more unpleasant than the just and holy life. CLINIAS: It seems likely, my friend, according to our current argument. ATHENIAN: And a legislator who is of any small use, even if
<margin>C</margin>
this were not the case—as the argument now holds it to be—would he not have dared to lie to the youth for their own good? Is there any lie more profitable than this one, which could make everyone do all just things not by force, but willingly? CLINIAS: Truth is a beautiful thing, O guest, and a lasting one; yet it seems not easy to persuade people of it. ATHENIAN: Very well. But the Sidonian myth was easy to believe, as improbable as it was, and ten thousand others like it. CLINIAS: What kind? ATHENIAN: That teeth were once sown and that armed men grew out of them. This is a great
<margin>D</margin>
example for a legislator of how he can persuade the souls of the young of whatever he attempts. Therefore, he needs to find out nothing else in his investigation except what, if he persuaded them of it, would work the greatest good for the city. He must consider every art and every device to ensure that such a community always speaks one and the same thing about these matters as much as possible throughout their whole life, in songs, myths, and discourses. If it seems otherwise to anyone, let them not hesitate to challenge the argument. CLINIAS: But it does not seem to me that either of us will ever be able to challenge these points. ATHENIAN: It would be my turn then to speak of what follows. I say that everyone must sing—the three choirs being there—to the souls of children while they are still young and tender, telling them all the other beautiful things we have gone through and may still go through. Let this be the summary of them: by saying that the same life is both most pleasant and best in the eyes of the gods, we shall speak most truly and, at the same time, we shall persuade those we must persuade more effectively than if we spoke in any other way.
<margin>E</margin>
CLINIAS: It must be as you say. ATHENIAN: First, then, the <term>Childhood Choir (παιδικὸς χορὸς)</term> of the Muses would most rightly enter first to sing such things into the midst of the whole city with all earnestness. Second is the choir of those up to thirty years old, who, calling upon the <term>Paean</term> as a witness to the truth of what is said, will come with a prayer, asking him to be gracious and persuasive to the youth. It is also necessary for those who are thirty up to sixty years of age to sing. As for those after that (who are no longer able to sustain songs), they should be left as myth-tellers of the same moral characters through divine inspiration. CLINIAS: But O guest, who are these third choirs you speak of? For we do not quite
<margin>F</margin>
clearly understand what you wish to say about them. ATHENIAN: Indeed, these are the very ones for whose sake most of the preceding arguments were spoken. CLINIAS: We haven't learned it yet; try to speak even more clearly. ATHENIAN: We said (if we remember) at the beginning of the discourse, that the nature of all young things is fiery and unable to keep quiet in body or voice, but is always shouting and jumping in a disorderly way. We said that no other animal has a sense of order in both these things, but the human nature alone possesses this. To the order of movement the name <term>Rhythm (ῥυθμὸς)</term> was given; and to the order of the voice (the blending of high and low pitches), the name <term>Harmony (ἁρμονία)</term> was given, and the two together were called <term>Choral Art (χορεία)</term>. We said that the gods pitied us and gave us fellow-dancers and choir-leaders:
<margin>G</margin>
Apollo and the Muses. And indeed, we mentioned a third (if we remember), Dionysus. CLINIAS: How could we not remember? ATHENIAN: Now, the choir of Apollo and the Muses has been discussed; the third and remaining choir must necessarily be called the choir of Dionysus. CLINIAS: How so? Tell us. For a "choir of elderly men" dedicated to Dionysus would seem very strange to someone hearing it suddenly—if men over thirty, and even fifty, and up to sixty, are to dance in his honor. ATHENIAN: You speak most truly. But I believe an argument is needed for these things, to show how it could be done appropriately. CLINIAS: Certainly. ATHENIAN: Do we then agree on what was said before? CLINIAS: Which things? ATHENIAN: That every man and child, free and slave, female and male, and the whole city to the whole city, should never cease singing to itself those things we have gone through...

<summary>The Athenian argues that a legislator must use music and myths, like the story of Cadmus and the dragon's teeth, to convince citizens that a just life is the most pleasant. He proposes three civic choirs: one for children (Muses), one for young adults (Apollo), and one for elders (Dionysus).</summary>

<meta>Continuity: This page continues the dialogue from the previous discussion on the psychological influence of music and poetry. Having established that the legislator must align justice with pleasure, the Athenian Stranger now addresses how to engage the most respected, older citizens in the city's musical education through the "Chorus of Dionysus" and the regulated use of wine.</meta>

# BOOK II OF THE LAWS

### Ccc iij

<column-break/>

<margin>ἃ διειληλυθάμεν... <note>original: "ἃ διειληλυθάμεν, ἀμουσότατος..." / The Greek text begins by discussing how the lack of musical harmony in a soul makes it unrefined.</note></margin> ...so that they might be affected by singing together with pleasure. <term>CLINIAS:</term> There is nothing to prevent us from agreeing that it ought to be so. <term>ATHENIAN:</term> But since this is the best part of the city—those who, by reason of their age and wisdom, possess the greatest authority for persuasion—will they not, by singing the best songs, be the cause of the greatest goods? Or shall we foolishly neglect that which contains the primary power of the best and most useful songs? <term>CLINIAS:</term> It is impossible to neglect it, as it now appears. <term>ATHENIAN:</term> How then might this be done decently? Look and see if it might be this way. <term>CLINIAS:</term> In what way? <term>ATHENIAN:</term> Every older man is full of hesitation toward singing, and he takes less delight in doing so; when the situation requires him to sing, the older and more moderate he becomes, the more he is ashamed to sing. Is it not so?

<margin>B</margin>
<term>CLINIAS:</term> It is exactly so. <term>ATHENIAN:</term> But he will be even more ashamed to stand upright and sing in a theater before a diverse multitude. This is especially true if these older men are forced to sing like competitive choirs striving for victory—becoming thin and fasting <note>Greek: ἄσιτοι / Latin: ieiuni; referring to the rigorous physical preparation and dieting required for professional choral competitions.</note> so that their voices might be clearer. Such men would sing with pain and shame, and would approach the task quite reluctantly. <term>CLINIAS:</term> What you say is very necessary. <term>ATHENIAN:</term> How then shall we make them willing to take up singing? Shall we not first pass a law that children, until the age of eighteen, should not taste wine at all? We shall teach them that one must not pour fire upon fire <note>original: "πῦρ ἐπὶ πῦρ" / "ignem igni". A proverbial expression suggesting that adding the "heat" of wine to the natural "heat" of youth leads to madness or excess.</note> into the body and soul, before they begin to undergo labors. We must guard against the manic habit of youth.

<margin>C</margin>
After this, they may taste wine in moderation until the age of thirty; but the young man must entirely abstain from drunkenness and excessive drinking. But when a man reaches forty years of age, he may feast at the common tables and call upon the other gods, and especially invite **Dionysus** to the mystery and play of the elders. For Dionysus gave wine to mankind as a remedy <note>original: "φάρμακον" / "remedy" or "medicine".</note> against the harshness of old age, so that we might grow young again and forget our despondency. Thus, the character of the soul, like iron placed in the fire, is led from hardness into softness and becomes more flexible. First, then, each man so disposed would be less ashamed and more willing to sing—not before many, but among a moderate number; not among strangers, but among his own; and to perform what we have often called "incantations."

<margin>D</margin>
<term>CLINIAS:</term> Yes, very much so. <term>ATHENIAN:</term> Therefore, to lead them to participate in song, this method would not be at all unbecoming. <term>CLINIAS:</term> Certainly not. <term>ATHENIAN:</term> But with what voice and what "muse" <note>In this context, "muse" refers to the specific style or genre of music and poetry.</note> will these men sing? Is it not clear that it must be one that suits them? <term>CLINIAS:</term> Of course. <term>ATHENIAN:</term> Which style, then, would suit divine men? Would it be the style of the public choirs? <term>CLINIAS:</term> We ourselves, O Guest, and these men here, are able to sing nothing other than what we learned in the choirs when we became accustomed to singing. <term>ATHENIAN:</term> Naturally so. For you have never truly attained the most beautiful song. You possess a government of a military camp rather than one of city-dwellers. You keep your young men like a herd of colts grazing together in a pack.

<margin>E</margin>
None of you takes his own youth and, to restrain his ferocity, puts him in the hands of a private trainer of horses, who might educate him by stroking him gently and taming him, performing all things suitable for education. From such a process, he would become not only a good soldier, but also one capable of governing cities and towns—the one we said at the beginning was more warlike than the soldiers of **Tyrtaeus** <note>A Spartan poet famous for his war songs. Plato argues that true "warlikeness" includes the virtue of justice, not just courage.</note>, honoring the gift of courage as the fourth part of virtue, and not the first, always and everywhere, both privately and publicly. <term>CLINIAS:</term> I do not know how it is, Guest, that you are once again disparaging our legislators. <term>ATHENIAN:</term> I do not do so with intent, my good man, if indeed I do it at all; but let us go where the argument leads, if you wish. For if we have a music that is better than that of the choirs and the common theaters, let us try to offer it to those whom we said are ashamed of the latter and seek a better kind.

<margin>F</margin>
<term>CLINIAS:</term> By all means. <term>ATHENIAN:</term> In all things followed by a certain grace, is it not necessary that there be present either that grace itself as its primary attraction, or a certain correctness, or thirdly, a utility? For example, I say that food and drink and all nourishment have a grace which we call pleasure; but their correctness and utility is that which we call the healthfulness of the things provided. <term>CLINIAS:</term> Quite so. <term>ATHENIAN:</term> So too in learning, there is a grace which is called pleasure; but correctness and utility, along with goodness and beauty, are produced by the truth itself. <term>CLINIAS:</term> It is so.

<margin>G</margin>
<term>ATHENIAN:</term> What then of the arts that produce likenesses—the imitative arts? If they produce pleasure, is it not right to call that pleasure "grace"? <term>CLINIAS:</term> Yes. <term>ATHENIAN:</term> But the correctness of such things, generally speaking, would be produced by equality: achieving the proper quantity and quality, rather than by pleasure. <term>CLINIAS:</term> Excellent. <term>ATHENIAN:</term> Therefore, only that thing can be rightly judged by pleasure which produces neither utility, nor truth, nor likeness, nor again any harm, but exists solely for the sake of that grace which accompanies it—which may be most beautifully named "pleasure" when none of these other things follow it. <term>CLINIAS:</term> You speak only of harmless pleasure. <term>ATHENIAN:</term> Yes, and I also call it "play" or "amusement" <note>original: "παιδιάν" / "ludum".</note> when it brings neither harm nor any utility worthy of serious consideration. <term>CLINIAS:</term> You speak most truly. <term>ATHENIAN:</term> From what has been said, should we not then say that all imitation is least suited to be judged by pleasure? <gloss>from these same arguments then, when it does not harm, nor benefit... <note>original: "ἐξ' τῶν ἀντῶν πωτ' λω λόγω τότε ὅτ' αν μή τι π' ἀλλη, μήτε ὠφελῇ"</note></gloss>

<meta>catchword: συνορᾷν (to see together / perceive)</meta>

<summary>In this passage, the Athenian Stranger proposes regulating wine to "soften" the souls of older citizens, making them willing to participate in the "Chorus of Dionysus" to educate the city through song. He further distinguishes between art judged by mere pleasure ("play") and art judged by its "correctness" and "truth."</summary>

<meta>This page follows the discussion on the moral purpose of music. The Athenian Stranger continues to argue that the quality of art should be judged by its truth and the excellence of its imitation, rather than the mere pleasure it provides to the audience.</meta>

# OF PLATO

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...that it must not be judged by what is not true. Similarly, this applies to equality as well. For it is not because something seems equal to one person, or because another person finds joy in it, that the thing itself is equal, or that the <term>commensurable</term> <note>Latin: *commensurabile*; Greek: *σύμμετρον* (symmetron). Refers to things having a common measure or being in proper proportion to one another.</note> is truly commensurable; rather, it is so by truth alone, and by nothing else. **CLINIAS:** That is absolutely true. **ATHENIAN:** And yet we say that all music is an art of imitation and of producing likenesses. **CLINIAS:** Who could doubt that? **ATHENIAN:** Therefore, when someone asserts that music is to be judged by pleasure alone, he is not to be listened to at all. Such music, if it is practiced anywhere, is not the kind we should seek; instead, we must seek that which possesses a likeness to the good through imitation. **CLINIAS:** These words are very true. **ATHENIAN:** Thus, those who seek the best kind of song and the best <term>Muse</term> <note>The "Muse" here refers generally to the arts of music, poetry, and dance over which the Muses presided.</note> should not seek that which is pleasant, but <margin>B</margin> that which is correct. For the correctness of imitation consists in this: as we were saying, that the thing being expressed by imitation is produced in such a quantity and quality as it is in itself. **CLINIAS:** Who could doubt it? **ATHENIAN:** And yet everyone would concede this about music: that all its poems are imitations and likenesses. All poets, listeners, and actors alike would surely agree on this. **CLINIAS:** Very much so. **ATHENIAN:** It is necessary, then, that regarding every poem and artistic creation, the person who is not going to make a mistake must know what the thing being depicted actually is. For if he does not know what its essence is intended to be, or of what it is an image, he will never understand whether it is correct or contains errors. **CLINIAS:** <margin>C</margin> Never, certainly. **ATHENIAN:** But can someone who does not understand the correctness of a work ever know whether it is well or poorly made? I am speaking somewhat obscurely; perhaps I can say it more clearly this way. **CLINIAS:** In what way? **ATHENIAN:** There are many likenesses made that pertain to the sight. **CLINIAS:** Certainly. **ATHENIAN:** If someone does not understand the proportions of the body being depicted, will he ever know whether it has been painted correctly? For instance, whether it has the proper joints of the body and each individual part, as well as the number, quality, and location of each as is fitting, and further, the colors and shapes? Or, on the contrary, whether all these things have been painted in a confused manner? Do you think anyone could judge these things if he did not know the animal being painted? **CLINIAS:** <margin>D</margin> In no way. **ATHENIAN:** But what if someone knows that the thing painted or shaped in some way is a human being, and that all its parts, shapes, and colors have been rendered by art? Is it necessary that such a person will also immediately recognize if there is some defect of beauty in it? **CLINIAS:** Nearly all of us, Guest, would recognize what is beautiful in living creatures. **ATHENIAN:** You speak rightly. Therefore, in every image—whether made through painting, or through music, or in any other way—must not the <margin>The things that pertain to a prudent judge.</margin> <margin>E</margin> prudent judge possess these three things? First, he must know what the subject of the imitation is; second, that it is imitated correctly; and third, that any likeness produced in words, melodies, or rhythms has been made well. **CLINIAS:** So it seems. **ATHENIAN:** Let us not grow weary, then, of explaining the difficulty found in music. Furthermore, since music is celebrated more than other kinds of likenesses, it requires greater diligence than the others. For the person who goes astray in this is harmed the most, as he drinks in bad character under the guise of sweetness. This is difficult to perceive because poets are not as skilled in the poetic art as the Muses themselves. For the Muses would never make such an error as to assign the colors and melodies of women to the words of men; nor in the melodies and figures of free men would they fit the <margin>F</margin> rhythms of slaves and the illiberal; nor in the rhythms and figures of free men would they provide a melody or speech contrary to those rhythms. Furthermore, they would never confuse the voices of wild beasts and humans, nor the sounds of instruments and all sorts of noises as if they were imitating a single thing. Human poets, however, often throw many such things into confusion and mix them without reason, providing laughter for those men whom Orpheus says have "attained the hour of delight." For they see all these things confused, and the poets themselves pull things apart, separating rhythm and gestures from melody, composing bare speeches in meter without melody, and also adapting melodies and <margin>G</margin> rhythms without words to the bare playing of the lyre and the sound of the flute. In this matter, it is extremely difficult to know what the rhythm and melody mean when they are without words, and what worthy imitation they resemble. One must consider that everything of this sort is full of crudeness—whatever follows too closely after speed, smoothness, or the voices of wild beasts—such that you use the flute or lyre for anything other than dance and song. To use either of them bare <note>Meaning instrumental music without vocals.</note> is a misuse, much like the deceptive displays of a magician, and is entirely foreign to the Muses. But this is the reason for these things. We, however, are considering not that those thirty or fifty years old and older should not use our Muses, but rather how they *ought* to use them. From these points, our argument seems to signify that for those advanced toward their fiftieth year who must sing, it is necessary for them to possess the Muse of the chorus better than others. For it is necessary that they acutely perceive and know melodies and rhythms. For how else will anyone know the correctness of a song—whether the <term>Doric mode</term> <note>The Doric mode was considered by Plato to be the most stable, courageous, and "manly" of the Greek musical scales.</note> is appropriate or not, or whether the rhythm the poet has joined to it was joined correctly or not? **CLINIAS:** Certainly in no other way. **ATHENIAN:** But the common people are to be laughed at when they think they can sufficiently distinguish what is well-harmonized and rhythmic from what is not.

<summary>The Athenian Stranger argues that music should be judged by its "truth" or accuracy of imitation rather than the pleasure it gives. He emphasizes that a proper judge must know the subject being imitated, whether it is rendered correctly, and whether it is beautiful, noting that instrumental music without words is particularly prone to being meaningless or "crude."</summary>
<keywords>Plato, Laws, music, imitation, mimesis, Doric mode, aesthetics, rhythm, harmony, education, the Chorus of Dionysus</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between the Athenian Stranger and Clinias regarding the regulation of music and drinking parties. It focuses on the "Chorus of Dionysus," composed of older men, and how wine can be used as a tool for moral education and character formation.</meta>

# ON THE LAWS, BOOK II

### THE SECOND BOOK OF THE LAWS BY PLATO

<margin>A</margin> For my part, those who have long been compelled to sing and dance to rhythms, but who are ignorant of the specific details of these things, do not consider this: that any song is correctly composed if it contains all that is fitting to it; and if it does not, it is the opposite. <margin>B</margin> **CLINIAS:** That is certainly necessary. **ATHENIAN:** What then? If someone does not understand the reason for it, or what it contains, will he ever recognize how it is correctly formed in any instance, as we have said? **CLINIAS:** How could that be possible? **ATHENIAN:** It seems, then, that we have discovered this regarding those elder singers whom we previously called upon—who may at first be unwilling but are encouraged to sing gladly—that it is necessary for them to have learned these things to such an extent that each of them can follow the progression and weights of the rhythms as well as the harmonic sounds of the strings. In this way, by understanding the harmonies and rhythms, they may be able to select those songs which are fitting for men of such age and character to sing. Thus, while singing, they may immediately perceive innocent pleasures themselves and lead the youth toward virtuous characters through songs and delights. Having been taught to this extent, they will possess a more exquisite discipline than the common crowd or even the poets themselves. As for that third point—whether the imitation is good or bad—it is not strictly necessary for the poet to know it, but he must know the harmony and the rhythm. These men, however, must know all three so that they can choose the best and the second-best. Otherwise, they will never be sufficiently able to use <term>incantations</term> <note>original Greek: ἐπῳδός (epōdos). Here used metaphorically for songs that "charm" or "enchant" the soul toward virtue.</note> to attract the souls of the young toward excellence. <margin>C</margin> Indeed, what we intended from the beginning—to show that our discourse brings proper aid to the <term>Chorus of Dionysus</term> <note>A group of older citizens (over 60) who, in Plato's ideal state, participate in controlled drinking parties to maintain their spirits and model proper behavior.</note>—has been stated to the best of our ability. But let us consider if this has truly been accomplished. Such a gathering of men necessarily becomes more turbulent as the exchange progresses. This is what we supposed from the start must happen in the gatherings that take place today. **CLINIAS:** It is necessary. **ATHENIAN:** In such a state, every man is lifted up, becoming lighter than himself; he exults and is filled with boldness. He no longer listens to his neighbor, but considers himself a sufficient leader for both himself and everyone else. **CLINIAS:** Without a doubt. **ATHENIAN:** And did we not say that whenever this happens, the souls of those drinking—just like iron in a fire—become hot with wine and thus grow softer and more youthful? <margin>D</margin> <margin>Just as iron is softened by fire, so the bodies of the elderly are softened by wine.</margin> Therefore, they are more easily led by someone who has the power and knowledge to instruct and mold them, just as when they were young? And this "molder" is the same person we then called the good legislator. For him, a method of calculation must be prescribed in the laws, so that these laws may restrain the man who has become confident, bold, and more impudent than is proper—who refuses to observe the order of silence, speech, drinking, and music in their proper turns. The laws must instruct him so that he wishes to do the opposite of what he currently does, introducing the best kind of fear along with justice against that rising and shameful confidence. This fear we have named "divine fear," "modesty," and "shame." **CLINIAS:** It is as you say. **ATHENIAN:** The authors and guardians of these laws must themselves be free from disturbance and drunkenness, <margin>E</margin> serving as "sober generals" over those who are intoxicated. For to fight against drunkenness without prudent and composed leaders is harder than to battle enemies without brave commanders. If anyone refuses to obey these leaders—the directors of Dionysus who are over sixty years of age—he should bear equal or even greater disgrace than one who disobeys the leaders of <term>Mars</term> <note>original Latin: Martis; Greek: Ἄρεως (Areōs). Referring to military commanders or the god of war.</note>. **CLINIAS:** Correct. **ATHENIAN:** Therefore, if such drunkenness and such play were employed, would not the participants gain great benefit from it? They would depart from one another joined by greater goodwill than before, rather than as enemies as they do now, having conversed together according to the law and having obeyed the rules when the sober lead the intoxicated. **CLINIAS:** Certainly, if such drinking were of the kind you now describe. <margin>F</margin> **ATHENIAN:** Let us no longer, then, simply disparage the gift of the <term>Liber Pater</term> <note>A Roman name for Dionysus/Bacchus, the "Free Father."</note> as if it were an evil thing or unworthy of being received into the city. Indeed, many more things could be said in this vein, though I hesitate to proclaim that greatest good which Dionysus grants to the many, because people, when they hear of it, might not receive or understand it correctly. **CLINIAS:** What is that? **ATHENIAN:** A certain rumor and fame has flowed down to us that this god was once deprived of his mind by <term>Juno</term> <note>The Roman name for Hera, who in myth drove Dionysus mad.</note>, and that for the sake of vengeance he introduced the Bacchic dance and all madness, and gave wine for this very purpose. However, I leave such stories to those who think it safe to say such things about the gods. But this much I know: <margin>G</margin> no animal is born with as much intelligence as it will have when it is fully grown. Furthermore, in that time when it does not yet possess its own wisdom, every creature raves and cries out without order, and as soon as it can stand, it leaps about in a disorganized fashion. Let us remember that we said these are the principles of music and gymnastics. **CLINIAS:** We remember. **ATHENIAN:** And did we not also say that the sense of rhythm and harmony is unique to us humans, and that <margin>H</margin> Apollo, the Muses, and Dionysus were given to us as leaders for these things? **CLINIAS:** Certainly. **ATHENIAN:** Wine, then, as many say, was given to men for vengeance, so that they might go mad. But according to our discourse, it is a remedy and a medicine for the opposite: <margin>Why wine was given to humans.</margin> so that the soul may acquire modesty, and the body may gain health and strength.

<column-break/>

<summary>This page argues that controlled drinking parties, led by sober elders, act as a "medicine" to soften the rigid souls of the elderly and instill modesty and social harmony through music and rhythm.</summary>
<keywords>Plato, Laws, music education, Dionysus, wine, rhythm, harmony, moral discipline, sober leaders, divine fear, modesty</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 583 regarding the education of the "Chorus of Dionysus." Having discussed the role of music and wine in training the soul, the Athenian Stranger now transitions to the second part of education: gymnastics, while concluding his strict recommendations for the regulation of wine.</meta>

<page-num>584</page-num>
<header>OF PLATO</header>

<margin>The whole choral dance and its parts.</margin> **CLINIAS:** You have recalled the previous argument excellently, guest. **ATHENIAN:** We have now discussed half of what pertains to the <term>choral art<note>Latin: "chorea"; Greek: "choreia." This refers to the combined art of song and dance, which Plato views as the foundation of all education.</note></term>. Shall we complete the remaining part, as it seems, or shall we pass over it? **CLINIAS:** What parts do you mean, and how do you divide them? **ATHENIAN:** Indeed, we said that the whole choral art constitutes our entire system of education. One part of this choral art consists of the voice, expressed through rhythm and harmony. **CLINIAS:** That is so. <margin>A</margin> **ATHENIAN:** The other part consists of the movement of the body, expressed through rhythm and posture. While it shares rhythm in common with the movement of the voice, posture is its own unique characteristic. In that first part, the movement of the voice is song itself. **CLINIAS:** What you say is very true. **ATHENIAN:** Now, the training of the voice which leads to the virtue of the soul, we have somehow named "music." **CLINIAS:** Quite rightly. <margin>B</margin> **ATHENIAN:** Furthermore, if the movement of the body in play—which we have called "dance"—attains the virtue of the body, let us call this skillful guidance toward that end "gymnastics." **CLINIAS:** Most correctly. **ATHENIAN:** As for music, which we called half of the choral art, let us consider it sufficiently discussed; and so let it be settled. Therefore, let us now speak of the remaining part—or what should we do? **CLINIAS:** O best of men, you are speaking with Cretans and Lacedæmonians <note>Lacedæmonians are Spartans; both cultures were famous in the ancient world for prioritizing physical training (gymnastics) over almost everything else.</note>. Since we have treated music sufficiently, but gymnastics not at all, which of us do you think would respond to such a question? <margin>C</margin> **ATHENIAN:** I would say that by asking this, you have already clearly answered. For I perceive that this question of yours is a kind of response, as I said, and simultaneously a command to go through the matters pertaining to gymnastics. **CLINIAS:** You have understood me perfectly; please do so. **ATHENIAN:** I must do it, for it is not difficult to explain things that are very well known to both of you. Truly, both of you are far more experienced in this art than in the former one. **CLINIAS:** You speak nearly the truth. **ATHENIAN:** Is there not also a beginning to this "play"? It is that every animal is naturally accustomed to leap. But man, as we touched upon, having received a sense of rhythm, generated and gave birth to dance. Song then arouses rhythm. These two, joined together, gave birth to the choral art and play. <margin>D</margin> **CLINIAS:** That is so. **ATHENIAN:** We have already finished one part of this, and we shall proceed to the other next. **CLINIAS:** By all means. **ATHENIAN:** Let us first conclude our discourse on the "choral art of drunkenness" <note>The Athenian refers to the regulated drinking parties discussed in the previous pages as a "choral art" because they were intended to be rhythmic, harmonious, and educational.</note> with this sentiment, if it pleases you. **CLINIAS:** In what way? **ATHENIAN:** If a city uses these drinking regulations as a serious matter, observing the order of laws for the sake of practicing temperance, and does not flee from other pleasures but practices them in the same way so as to overcome them—then all these things should be used in this manner. But if a city uses these gatherings merely as play, and it is permitted for anyone to drink whenever they wish, with whomever they wish, and to practice any other whims, I would not be of the opinion that such a city or such a man should ever indulge in drunkenness. <margin>E</margin> Rather, I would approve of the Carthaginian law <note>The Carthaginians were known for their strict military discipline and laws regarding sobriety.</note> far more than the custom of the Cretans or Lacedæmonians. This law dictates that no one should ever dare to taste wine while in a military camp, but should drink water for that entire time; and that in the city, no male or female slave should ever be allowed the use of wine; nor should magistrates during the year they hold office. I would also entirely prohibit pilots and judges on duty from tasting wine, as well as those about to deliberate on important matters. I would allow no one at all to have wine during the day, unless it were necessary for bodily exercise or on account of illness; nor even at night for a man or woman when they intend to procreate children. <margin>F</margin> Many more instances could be listed in which men who possess a right mind and respect the law would abstain from wine. Therefore, according to this reasoning, a city would not need many vineyards. Rather, other agriculture and the whole standard of living would maintain its proper order, and the use of wine would be the most moderate and sparing of nearly all things. So, my guests, if it seems right to you as well, let this be the <term>colophon<note>Original: "colophon." A traditional term meaning the finishing touch or the final crowning stroke to a work.</note></term> placed upon our discourse regarding wine. **CLINIAS:** Well said. It seems so to us as well.

<column-break/>

<columns>2</columns>

# THE LAWS OF PLATO, OR, ON THE INSTITUTION OF LAWS,
## THE THIRD DIALOGUE.

<column-break/>

# ΠΛΑΤΩΝΟΣ ΝΟΜΩΝ, Η, ΠΕΡΙ ΝΟΜΟΘΕΣΙΑΣ,
## ΔΙΑΛΟΓΟΣ ΤΡΙΤΟΣ.

<column-break/>

SUMMARY OF THE DIALOGUE. Having established the foundation of laws, he now deals with their origin: he teaches when, at what time, and for what causes men began to establish laws. He traces their infancy back to the time that existed after a certain universal flood <note>Latin: "diluvium." This refers to the myth of Deucalion's flood, the Greek equivalent of the story of Noah.</note>, when human society was almost destroyed—the whole world having been surrounded and overwhelmed by waters—and had to be restored from those remnants of men who had been preserved from that devastation on the higher peaks of mountains. Therefore, in that beginning of a world being born again, he explains that a certain simplicity and equity served as the most sacred law, since neither poverty incited anyone to inflict injury, nor did abundance and plenty incite them to greed. But as the human race grew day by day, laws began to be applied like bonds, so that the lack of restraint of the powerful might be checked, and the weaker might be kept to their duty. Thus, he establishes necessity as the cause for composing laws and constituting a state: and he shows that various occasions gave the beginnings to various laws and political systems.

<summary>This page concludes the discussion on the educational value of wine and the choral arts, introducing the strict Carthaginian laws on sobriety, before transitioning into Book III, which examines the post-flood origins of human civilization and law.</summary>
<keywords>choral art, gymnastics, music, temperance, Carthaginian law, wine regulation, universal flood, origin of laws, simplicity, equity</keywords>

--- Page 617 ---
<meta>This page marks the beginning of Book III of Plato’s Laws. Having concluded the discussion on the education of the soul and the body (music and gymnastics) in the previous books, the Athenian Stranger now shifts the focus to the historical origins of political systems and the development of civilization from its most primitive states.</meta>

# ON THE LAWS, BOOK III

<page-num>585</page-num>
<header>ON THE LAWS, BOOK III</header>

<margin>A</margin> **ATHENIAN STRANGER:** So much, then, for those matters. But what shall we say was the beginning of a <term>political system<note>Greek: "politeia." This refers to the constitution, the form of government, or the general way of life in a city-state.</note></term>? Might one not see it most easily and clearly from this perspective? **CLEINIAS:** From where? **ATHENIAN:** From the same point where one must observe the progress of cities as they shift, at various times, toward either virtue or vice. **CLEINIAS:** And what point is that? **ATHENIAN:** I believe it is from the vast length and infinity of time, and the changes that occur within such a span. **CLEINIAS:** How do you mean? **ATHENIAN:** Tell me, from the time that cities have existed and men have lived as citizens, do you think you could ever grasp how much time has passed? **CLEINIAS:** That would not be easy at all. <margin>B</margin> **ATHENIAN:** At the very least, it would be something infinite and impossible to calculate. **CLEINIAS:** Indeed, that is certainly true. **ATHENIAN:** Have not countless thousands upon thousands of cities come into being during this time? And by the same logic of number, have not just as many been destroyed? Have they not been governed under every kind of political system many times in every place? Have they not sometimes grown larger from smaller beginnings, and at other times smaller from larger ones? And have they not become worse from better, and better from worse? **CLEINIAS:** Necessarily so. **ATHENIAN:** Let us, if we can, find the cause of this change. For perhaps it might show us the first <margin>C</margin> birth and transformation of political systems. **CLEINIAS:** You speak well. You must be eager to show us what you think about it, and we must follow along. **ATHENIAN:** Do the ancient stories seem to you to hold any truth? **CLEINIAS:** Which stories? **ATHENIAN:** That many destructions of mankind have occurred through <term>floods<note>Greek: "kataklysmois." Plato refers to the recurring ancient belief that human civilization is periodically wiped out by natural disasters.</note></term>, diseases, and many other causes, in which only a small remnant of the human race was left behind. **CLEINIAS:** Such a thing seems very persuasive to everyone. **ATHENIAN:** Come then, let us consider one of these many destructions—specifically, the one that occurred long ago by the great deluge. **CLEINIAS:** What should we keep in mind regarding it? <margin>D</margin> **ATHENIAN:** That those who then escaped the destruction would likely have been some mountain-dwelling shepherds, small sparks of the human race preserved on the peaks. **CLEINIAS:** Clearly. **ATHENIAN:** And such men must necessarily have been inexperienced in other arts, and especially in the schemes that men in cities use against one another for greed and rivalry, and all the other evils they devise. **CLEINIAS:** That is likely. **ATHENIAN:** Let us assume, then, that the cities situated in the plains and by the sea were completely destroyed at that time? **CLEINIAS:** Let us assume it. **ATHENIAN:** Shall we say, then, that all tools were lost, and if there was any important invention concerning the arts, or politics, or any other kind of wisdom, all these things vanished in that era? <margin>E</margin> **CLEINIAS:** For how, my friend, could anything new ever have been invented if these things had remained as they are now organized for all time? It would have been impossible for these things to have remained hidden from those people for ten thousand times ten thousand years; rather, what we have now has been discovered recently—either a thousand or two thousand years ago—some by <term>Daedalus<note>A mythical inventor and architect.</note></term>, some by <term>Orpheus<note>A legendary musician and poet.</note></term>, some by <term>Palamedes<note>A Greek hero credited with inventing writing and numbers.</note></term>. Musical matters were found by Marsyas and Olympus, and the lyre by Amphion; and many other things by others, discovered, so to speak, only "yesterday and the day before." **ATHENIAN:** Do you realize, Cleinias, that you have left out your friend who was truly born "yesterday"? **CLEINIAS:** Do you mean <term>Epimenides<note>A semi-mythical Cretan seer and philosopher.</note></term>? **ATHENIAN:** Yes, him. For he surpassed all of you in his inventions, my friend. What <term>Hesiod<note>An early Greek poet.</note></term> prophesied long ago in word, that man actually performed in deed, as you people say. **CLEINIAS:** We do indeed say so. <margin>F</margin> **ATHENIAN:** Let us then say that this was the state of human affairs at the time the destruction occurred: a vast and terrifying desolation, but a great abundance of land. Of the other animals that had perished, some herds of cattle and perhaps a few goats might have been left, and these were the rare resources men had for grazing at the beginning. **CLEINIAS:** Certainly. **ATHENIAN:** But as for cities, political systems, and legislation—the subjects of our present discussion—do we think any memory of them remained at all? **CLEINIAS:** Not in the least. **ATHENIAN:** Is it not, then, from those conditions that all our current affairs have arisen—cities, political systems, arts, laws, and much vice as well as much virtue? **CLEINIAS:** How so? **ATHENIAN:** Do we believe, wonderful man, that those people of old—being inexperienced in the many fine things of the city, as well as the many opposites—could have been perfect in either virtue or vice? <margin>G</margin> **CLEINIAS:** A fair question; we understand what you mean. **ATHENIAN:** Therefore, as time progressed and our race multiplied, all things advanced to the state they are in now. **CLEINIAS:** Most correctly. **ATHENIAN:** Not suddenly, as is likely, but little by little over an immense span of time. **CLEINIAS:** That is very fitting. **ATHENIAN:** For a fresh fear of descending from the heights to the plains had, I think, taken hold of everyone. **CLEINIAS:** Of course. **ATHENIAN:** Did they not see each other with pleasure because of their small numbers in those times? Yet, traveling to one another by land or sea was nearly impossible, for almost all the arts used for travel had perished along with the other skills. Therefore, I think they could not easily mingle with one another. Iron, bronze, and all metals had vanished in the confusion, so there was no way to extract or refine them; thus, there was no work for woodsmen. For even if some tool had been left behind in the mountains, it was quickly worn away and disappeared, and no others could be made until the art of metallurgy was rediscovered by men. **CLEINIAS:** How could it be otherwise? **ATHENIAN:** At that time—

<column-break/>

<margin>The beginning of political science.</margin>
<margin>A</margin> **ATHENIAN:** Let these things indeed be so. But what shall we say was the beginning of <term>political science<note>Latin: "civilis disciplinae." The study and practice of governing a state.</note></term>? Or would someone not see this most easily and best from this point? **CLEINIAS:** From where? **ATHENIAN:** From where the growth of cities towards both virtue and vice can also be observed. **CLEINIAS:** From where do you say? **ATHENIAN:** I believe, in fact, from the length and infinity of time, and the changes of things within it. **CLEINIAS:** In what way do you say this? **ATHENIAN:** Come, tell me, if you can: since cities and political institutions began among men, how great a span of time has preceded us? **CLEINIAS:** That is by no means easy to say. <margin>B</margin> **ATHENIAN:** It is certainly infinite and impossible to think upon. **CLEINIAS:** So it is entirely. **ATHENIAN:** Have not innumerable cities been founded in this time, and just as many destroyed? Cities that have experienced every condition of political life everywhere, made now larger from smaller, now smaller from larger, worse from better, and conversely, better from worse? **CLEINIAS:** That is indeed necessary. **ATHENIAN:** Therefore, let us think out the cause of this change, if we can. For perhaps it will show us the first cause and transformation of political life. **CLEINIAS:** You speak rightly. Therefore, you must <margin>C</margin> diligently explain what you think about this matter, and we must listen attentively. **ATHENIAN:** Do the ancient discourses then seem to possess some truth? **CLEINIAS:** Which ones? **ATHENIAN:** Namely, that many destructions of men from floods, diseases, and many other things have happened in the past, from which only a few men survived. **CLEINIAS:** That seems very likely to anyone. **ATHENIAN:** Come now, of many, let us look at this one destruction which was caused by the deluge. **CLEINIAS:** What do you command us to think about this? **ATHENIAN:** Surely that those who then escaped the disaster were certain mountain shepherds, few seeds preserved on the peaks of mountains for the propagation of the human race. **CLEINIAS:** It is clear. **ATHENIAN:** And yet it is necessary that they were both unskilled in other arts and ignorant of the pursuits of <margin>D</margin> greed and contention among citizens, and the other cunning deeds against others. **CLEINIAS:** That is indeed consistent. **ATHENIAN:** Let us also assume that the cities of the plains and the coast perished utterly at that time. **CLEINIAS:** Let us assume it. **ATHENIAN:** Therefore, all tools and whatever arts—whether pertaining to political science or to another faculty—that existed as inventions, we shall assert collapsed in those times. **CLEINIAS:** For how, O best of men, if these things had remained forever as they are now, would anything have been a new invention to anyone? Clearly because an innumerable multitude of years was unknown to them. Only a thousand or two thousand years have passed since anything is said to have been invented—partly by Daedalus, partly by Orpheus, partly by Palamedes. <margin>E</margin> Just as those things pertaining to music are attributed to Marsyas and Olympus, and those pertaining to the lyre to Amphion; and many other things to others, invented, so to speak, "yesterday and the day before." **ATHENIAN:** Do you see, Cleinias, that a friend has been omitted by you, who was truly of yesterday? **CLEINIAS:** Do you mean Epimenides? **ATHENIAN:** This man indeed. For he excelled everyone among you by far in the invention of new things, O friend. What Hesiod once divined in words, Epimenides himself perfected in fact, as you assert. **CLEINIAS:** We certainly assert it. **ATHENIAN:** From that devastation, we think a great and terrible desolation occurred then in human affairs. A vastness of fertile fields was deserted, and the other animals having been <margin>F</margin> destroyed, barely the kind of oxen and goats remained—and that indeed was rare—by the grazing of which men then led their lives. **CLEINIAS:** Who doubts it? **ATHENIAN:** But of the city and of political science and laws, about which our present discourse is held, do we think there was even any memory of them, so to speak? **CLEINIAS:** None at all. **ATHENIAN:** Did not all these things—cities, political sciences, arts, laws, and a no small supply of vice and virtue—proceed to us from those who were so disposed? **CLEINIAS:** In what way do you say this? **ATHENIAN:** Do we think, O wondrous man, that those men, since they were ignorant of many things held as honorable or shameful among citizens, stood at the summit of either virtue or vice? **CLEINIAS:** You have spoken well, and we understand what you wish. **ATHENIAN:** In the <margin>G</margin> progress of time, then, and the human race being multiplied, all things were advanced to the condition we see now. **CLEINIAS:** Quite rightly. **ATHENIAN:** Yet not suddenly, as is likely, but gradually and in a long time. **CLEINIAS:** That is very appropriate. **ATHENIAN:** For a fresh dread prohibited them from descending into the plains from the mountain peaks. **CLEINIAS:** Certainly. **ATHENIAN:** And because of their scarcity in those times, did they not rejoice at the sight of one another? Especially since a passage to others was easy neither by land nor by sea, as almost all tools for passage had been destroyed along with the arts. Wherefore, I think, they could not very well meet together. For iron and all metals had perished in the confusion, so that they could not be found or dug out into the light; hence there were also no carpenters. For even if some tool survived, having been left at some time in the mountains, it quickly vanished, being worn out; nor could others be made before the art of metallurgy was again discovered by men. **CLEINIAS:** For how else could it have happened? **ATHENIAN:** And how many—

<summary>This page explores the speculative history of human civilization, proposing that periodic cataclysms like floods destroy advanced societies, leaving only primitive mountain shepherds to restart humanity. Plato uses this to explain why political systems and arts appear relatively "new" in history and how they develop slowly from a state of simple survival.</summary>

# PLATO'S LAWS

<page-num>586</page-num>
<header>PLATO'S LAWS</header>

<margin>A</margin> do we think this happened afterward? **CLEINIAS:** To many, surely. **ATHENIAN:** I suppose, then, that all the arts that require iron, bronze, and all such materials would have been forgotten during that same period—or even longer—shrouded in the darkness of ignorance. **CLEINIAS:** That is certainly true. **ATHENIAN:** Furthermore, at that time, there was neither sedition nor war. **CLEINIAS:** For what reason? **ATHENIAN:** First, because of their isolation, they embraced one another with a warm-hearted goodwill. Second, food did not provoke conflict; for there was no lack of pasture, except perhaps for a few at the very beginning. In those times, they lived mostly on the products of their herds. There was no lack of milk <margin>B</margin> and meat. Moreover, hunting provided them with a ready supply of food, and not of poor quality. They also had plenty of clothing, bedding, dwellings, and vessels—both those made with fire and those without. For the arts of pottery and weaving do not require iron; God granted these two arts to men so that, whenever they should fall into such a calamity, the human race might still be able to preserve and propagate itself. For this reason, they were not extremely poor, nor were they compelled by want to go to war. They could not possibly become wealthy either, since they had neither gold nor silver. In any gathering of men <margin>C</margin> where neither poverty nor wealth is present, the most just characters will be found. In such a place, neither insolence nor injustice has any room. Rivalry and envy are also far away. For these reasons, they were good men, and especially so because of their simplicity. For whatever they heard was honorable or shameful, they believed it to be the truth because of their simplicity and obeyed those warnings. Nor did anyone, out of a conceit of wisdom—as happens now—suspect a lie; but believing that what was said about gods and men was true, they established their lives in accordance with it. Therefore, they were altogether such as we described a moment ago. **CLEINIAS:** Both I and my friend here agree with you on these points. **ATHENIAN:** We said, furthermore, that many generations <margin>D</margin> living in this way were less skilled than those who lived before the flood, or than men of today. They were less experienced in the other arts and in the arts of war, whether practiced today by land or by sea. They also lacked knowledge of the legal judgments and seditions which, in cities, use both words and deeds to diligently strive to inflict injury on others. They were simpler, braver, more temperate, and in all ways more just. We have already stated the cause for this. **CLEINIAS:** You speak rightly. **ATHENIAN:** Let these things be said, then, and let all that follows be set forth, so that we may understand why those people <margin>E</margin> had need of laws, and who it was that established laws for them. **CLEINIAS:** You have spoken well. **ATHENIAN:** Did they then have no need of lawgivers, nor had such a practice yet become customary in those times? For the men of that time did not yet possess the art of writing, but lived following the customs and ancestral manners of their elders. **CLEINIAS:** That is likely. **ATHENIAN:** But what was the form of their civil discipline? **CLEINIAS:** Which form? **ATHENIAN:** It seems to me that everyone calls the civil discipline of that time <term>δυναστειάν<note>original Greek: "dynasteia." This refers to a form of governance where power is held by a family patriarch or a single powerful lord; a "lordship" or "chieftainship."</note></term>, that is, the rule of powers, which even now thrives in many places among both Greeks and Barbarians. Homer testifies that this existed in the dwelling of the <margin>Odyss. Book IX</margin> Cyclopes, saying: "They have no public assemblies for counsel, nor established laws; but they inhabit hollow caves on high mountains, and each one gives laws to his own wives and children, disregarding the affairs of others." **CLEINIAS:** This poet seems to have been a charming fellow to you. Indeed, we have seen some other very elegant verses of his, though not many. We Cretans do not make much use of foreign poetry. **MEGILLUS:** But we Spartans do use him. To us, the poet seems to have surpassed all others in this kind of thing, although he everywhere depicts an Ionian way of life rather than a Laconic <note>Laconic refers to the Spartan way of life—austere and brief—whereas Ionian refers to the more luxurious or expansive culture of the eastern Greeks.</note> one. He seems to testify well to your words here, as he has traced the antiquity of men back to a wild way of life through his stories. **CLEINIAS:** Indeed. **ATHENIAN:** He certainly testifies to it. Therefore, led by his testimony, let us believe that such forms of government did once exist. **MEGILLUS:** Correct. <margin>G</margin> **ATHENIAN:** Do not these governments arise from the people themselves who live scattered in individual dwellings and individual families, because of the poverty resulting from the destructions? In these groups, the eldest always rules, because their authority began with the father and mother. Following them like birds, they form a single flock, using the father's will as their law, and are governed in a most just kingdom of all. **MEGILLUS:** Exactly so. **ATHENIAN:** But afterward, when many come together in common, they establish larger cities. Turning first to agriculture at the base of mountains, they build enclosures of hedges like walls to protect themselves from wild beasts, constructing a single, large, and common dwelling. **MEGILLUS:** That seems very likely. **ATHENIAN:** And what of this: is it not also likely? **MEGILLUS:** What? **ATHENIAN:** When these larger dwellings are made from the smaller and first ones, each of the small groups arrives <margin>H</margin> bringing its own eldest ruler and its own particular customs, because they had lived apart. Thus, they had received different customs from different parents and teachers, by which each was accustomed to worship the gods and care for themselves—the more orderly customs from the orderly, and the more manly from the manly.

how we think this happened afterward? **CLEINIAS:** Clearly it happened in many ways. **ATHENIAN:** Therefore, all the arts that require iron and bronze and all such things would have vanished in that time and for even longer. **CLEINIAS:** Certainly. **ATHENIAN:** And furthermore, sedition and war had also perished <gloss>at that time<note>original: "x^v", likely a manuscript mark for "ton tote chronon" (that time).</note></gloss> in many places. **CLEINIAS:** How? **ATHENIAN:** First, because of their isolation, they were friendly to one another; and second, food was not a cause of contention for them. For there was no lack of pasture, except perhaps at the very beginning; for they lived mostly on that in those times. For they were in no way lacking in milk and meat; moreover, by hunting, they provided themselves with food that was neither poor nor scarce. Furthermore, they were not without clothing, bedding, houses, and vessels, both those made with fire and without. For the arts of pottery and weaving require no iron. God gave these two arts to men to produce these things, so that whenever they should come into such a state of need, the human race might have a way to grow and increase. All men, then, lived in this way, not being forced by poverty, and they did not fall into conflict among themselves. Nor could they ever become wealthy, being without gold and silver. And in whatever community neither wealth nor poverty dwells, there the most just characters would naturally arise. For neither insolence nor injustice, nor rivalries and envies, occur there. They were good, then, both for these reasons and because of their so-called "simplicity." For what they heard was beautiful or shameful, being simple-hearted, they thought these things were spoken most truly, and they obeyed. For no one knew how to suspect a lie out of wisdom, as people do today; but believing that what was said about gods and men was true, they lived according to it. Therefore, they were altogether such as we have just described. **CLEINIAS:** To me, at least, and to my friend here, these things seem right. **ATHENIAN:** Shall we not say, then, that many generations of those who lived then, after those who were before the flood, were more unskilled and more ignorant in other arts and in those of war—those which are practiced today by land and by sea, and those which are called legal judgments and seditions in cities, which use all sorts of devices in words and deeds to harm and wrong one another? They were simpler, braver, more temperate, and altogether more just. We have already explained the cause of this. **CLEINIAS:** You speak rightly. **ATHENIAN:** Let these things be said by us, then, and let us follow all the related consequences, so that we may understand what need for laws they had then, and who their lawgiver was. **CLEINIAS:** And you have spoken well. **ATHENIAN:** Did they then have no need for lawgivers, nor <gloss>in those times<note>original: "x^v", similar manuscript mark.</note></gloss> was such a thing customary? For there were not even letters yet for those who lived in this part of the cycle, but they lived following customs and what are called ancestral laws. **CLEINIAS:** That is likely. **ATHENIAN:** And yet, what was the manner and form of their government? **CLEINIAS:** What was it? **ATHENIAN:** It seems to me that everyone calls the government of that time "lordship" <note>Greek: "dynasteia"</note>, which even now still exists in many places among both Greeks and Barbarians. Homer says somewhere that it existed in the dwelling of the Cyclopes, saying:
> "To them there are no assemblies for counsel, nor laws;
> But they inhabit the peaks of high mountains,
> In hollow caves. Each one gives the law
> To his children and wives; nor do they care for one another."
**CLEINIAS:** Your poet seems to have been a graceful one. Indeed, we have gone through other very elegant parts of his work, though not many. For we Cretans do not make much use of foreign poems. **MEGILLUS:** But we Spartans do use them, and he seems to us to excel all such poets; however, he describes not a Laconian but rather an Ionian life every time. Now he seems to testify to your argument, having traced their ancient state back to a wild condition through his myths. **CLEINIAS:** Yes. **ATHENIAN:** He does indeed testify; let us take him as a witness that such governments once existed. **CLEINIAS:** Well said. **ATHENIAN:** Do they not arise from those people who lived scattered in single households and families because of the distress after the destructions? In these, the eldest rules, because the authority comes to them from their father and mother; following them like birds, they will form a single flock, living under paternal law and being ruled in the most just of all kingships. **CLEINIAS:** Very much so. **ATHENIAN:** After this, they come together in common to make larger cities, and many people flow together. They turn to some form of agriculture at the foot of the mountains, and they make enclosures of stones as defenses for their walls, for the sake of protection against wild beasts, creating one large and common house. **CLEINIAS:** It is likely that these things happened in this way. **ATHENIAN:** And what of this? Is it not likely? **CLEINIAS:** What? **ATHENIAN:** As these larger dwellings grew out of the smaller and original ones, each of the small ones <gloss>at that time<note>original: "x^v"</note></gloss> was present with its own eldest ruler and its own ancestral customs, because they had lived apart from one another. Having different parents and nurturers, they had different customs regarding the gods and themselves—the more orderly from the orderly, the more manly from the manly, and in the same way...

<summary>This page describes the primitive state of humanity after a global disaster, explaining how a lack of technology and wealth created a naturally virtuous, though simple, society governed by ancestral customs and patriarchal "lordship" (dynasteia) rather than written laws.</summary>
