# ON THE LAWS, BOOK III

<page-num>587</page-num>
<header>ON THE LAWS, BOOK III</header>

<margin>A</margin>
...in this way, each head of a household impresses their own preferences upon their children, and these children in turn—as we were saying—come to the larger settlement already possessing their own particular laws. **CLEINIAS:** How could it be otherwise? **ATHENIAN:** And it is surely inevitable that each group would be satisfied with its own laws first, and only secondarily with the laws of others. **CLEINIAS:** That is so. **ATHENIAN:** Have we not, then, as it seems, stumbled upon the very cradle of legislation? <note>original: "incunabula" (Latin) / "νομοθεσίας... ἐμβάντες" (Greek)</note> **CLEINIAS:** Very much so. **ATHENIAN:** After this, it becomes necessary for those who have come together to choose some representatives from among themselves to act in common. These men, having examined the customs of all the groups, will select those they most approve of and present them to the leaders and guides of the people—who are like kings—to be clearly displayed. These selectors will themselves be called "legislators." 
<margin>B</margin>
By establishing magistrates and forming a kind of aristocracy or even a kingship out of these various family powers, they will dwell within this new change of government. **CLEINIAS:** It would certainly happen in that sequence and in that manner. **ATHENIAN:** Let us then speak of a third form of government that arises, in which all types and conditions of states and cities happen to coincide. **CLEINIAS:** What sort of form is that? **ATHENIAN:** It is the one that <term>Homer</term> <note>The famous Greek epic poet</note> also pointed out as appearing after the second stage, when he says:
<margin>Iliad 20</margin>
"He founded <term>Dardania</term> <note>An ancient city near the site of Troy</note> (as he says somewhere), for as yet holy <term>Ilion</term> <note>The city of Troy</note> had not been built upon the plain, a city of mortal men, but they still dwelt on the slopes of many-fountained <term>Ida</term>." <note>original: "πολυπίδακος Ἴδης"</note> Indeed, he says these lines, as well as those he spoke concerning the Cyclopes, as if inspired by God and in accordance with nature. For the poetic race is indeed divine and inspired; when it sings, it touches upon many things that truly happen, aided by the <term>Graces</term> and the <term>Muses</term>. <note>The Greek goddesses of art, beauty, and inspiration</note> **CLEINIAS:** Very much so. **ATHENIAN:** Let us be drawn further along by the story that has just occurred to us; for perhaps it might signify something regarding our purpose. Ought we not to proceed? **CLEINIAS:** By all means. **ATHENIAN:** We say then that Ilion was settled, moving from the higher ground down into a large and beautiful plain, upon a certain hill that was not high, and which had many rivers flowing down from Ida. **CLEINIAS:** So they say. **ATHENIAN:** Do we not suppose that this happened a very long time after the flood? **CLEINIAS:** How could it not be a long time? **ATHENIAN:** They seem, at least, to have possessed a terrible forgetfulness regarding the destruction we were just speaking of, since they placed their city beneath so many rivers flowing from the heights, trusting in hills that were not particularly tall. <margin>D</margin> **CLEINIAS:** It is clear, then, that a vast and immeasurable amount of time must have passed for such a thing to occur. **ATHENIAN:** And many other cities, I believe, were already being inhabited then, as the human population increased. **CLEINIAS:** Certainly. **ATHENIAN:** And these were the cities that eventually campaigned against Troy, perhaps even by sea, as everyone was by then using the sea without fear. **CLEINIAS:** So it appears. **ATHENIAN:** And after remaining there for some ten years, the <term>Achaeans</term> <note>The name used by Homer for the Greeks</note> utterly destroyed Troy. **MEGILLUS:** Quite so. **ATHENIAN:** Now, during this ten-year period while Troy was being besieged, many evils happened to each of the besiegers at home due to the rebellions of the young men. <margin>Origin of the Dorians</margin> <margin>E</margin> When the soldiers returned to their own cities and homes, these youths did not receive them well or justly, but in such a way that many deaths, slaughters, and exiles resulted. Those who were driven out returned later under a different name, being called <term>Dorians</term> instead of Achaeans, because the man who gathered the exiles at that time was named <term>Dorieus</term>. And indeed, all these things are what you <term>Lacedaemonians</term> <note>The people of Sparta</note> tell in your stories and recount in detail. **MEGILLUS:** Certainly. **ATHENIAN:** Just as we were diverted at the beginning of our discussion about laws, falling into the topics of music and drinking, we have now returned to the same point as if by divine guidance. The argument itself gives us a handle, for it has come to the very settlement of Lacedaemon, which you correctly said was established under laws similar to those of its brother <term>Crete</term>. We have gained this much from the wandering of our discussion: by passing through various forms of government and settlements, we have observed a first, second, and third city, <margin>F</margin> following one another in the settlements over a vast length of time. And now this fourth city—or, if you prefer, this fourth nation—comes before us, which was settled once and is inhabited even now. If from all this we can understand what was settled well or poorly, and what kind of laws preserve those things that are preserved, and what kind destroy what is destroyed, <margin>G</margin> and what changes might make a city blessed, then, O Megillus and Cleinias, we must discuss these things again as if from the beginning—unless we have some complaint against what has already been said. **MEGILLUS:** If some god, my guest, were to promise us that, should we attempt a second examination of legislation, we would hear arguments no worse or shorter than those just spoken, I would travel a long way myself, and this present day would seem short to me, even though the sun is now turning from the summer toward the winter solstice. <margin>H</margin> **ATHENIAN:** It seems, then, that we must consider these things. **MEGILLUS:** Most certainly. **ATHENIAN:** Let us, then, place ourselves in thought at that time when Lacedaemon, <term>Argos</term>, and <term>Messene</term>, and the lands subject to them, were brought under the control of your ancestors, Megillus. For then, as the story goes, they decided to divide the army into three parts and settle three cities: Argos, Messene, and Lacedaemon. **MEGILLUS:** Very true. **ATHENIAN:** And <term>Temenus</term> became king of Argos, <term>Cresphontes</term> of Messene, and

# PLATO

<margin>A</margin> ...along with Patrocles. **MEGILLUS.** Certainly so. **ATHENIAN.** And all these men swore that they would be an enemy to anyone who attempted to devastate the kingdom of any one of them. **MEGILLUS.** Clearly. **ATHENIAN.** But tell me, by Jove, are any kingdoms or governments ever overthrown, or have any ever been overthrown by others, or rather by themselves? Or were we thinking that this was the case a little while ago when we fell into this discussion, but have now entirely forgotten? **MEGILLUS.** Not at all. **ATHENIAN.** Shall we not confirm the same thing even more now? For we are prompted to affirm this by the history of the events we have encountered. Therefore, we shall not revolve our discourse around something empty, since we are speaking of a true and historical event. <margin>B</margin> These were the facts: three kingdoms, and three cities governed by kings, swore to one another according to common laws established for both ruling and being ruled. The kings swore that they would not make their rule more violent as time and their lineage progressed; the people swore that if the kings kept their oath, they would never undermine the kingdoms, but would instead defend them if anyone ever attacked. The kings also bound themselves by oath to the other kings and peoples, and the peoples to other peoples and kings, to mutually repel any injuries inflicted. Is it not so? **MEGILLUS.** Precisely so. **ATHENIAN.** Now, that which is greatest in establishing a civil discipline was present in those three cities, whether the kings or others brought forth the laws. **MEGILLUS.** What was that? **ATHENIAN.** That two should rise up together against the one <margin>C</margin> which transgressed the established laws. **MEGILLUS.** That is certainly manifest. **ATHENIAN.** Many also charge legislators with this: that they should bring forth such laws as the multitude and the people will willingly accept—just as if one were to charge gymnastic masters or doctors to treat and heal bodies with pleasure and delight. **MEGILLUS.** Entirely so. **ATHENIAN.** Yet it is often a fine thing if one can restore bodies to a good habit and health even with a little discomfort. **MEGILLUS.** Why not? **ATHENIAN.** Furthermore, this other advantage was present for them, which was of no small help in the ease of establishing laws. **MEGILLUS.** What was that? **ATHENIAN.** Those legislators, in establishing an equality of goods, <margin>D</margin> did not face that greatest difficulty which usually happens in many cities when they come together under one law: if one seeks to disturb the possession of lands and introduce "new tablets" <note>original: "novas tabulas" — a Latin idiom for the cancellation of debts</note>, because they see that equality cannot be sufficiently achieved without these. For everyone cries out against anyone who tries to move such things, saying "do not move the immovable." Indeed, everyone openly curses the one who divides the lands and introduces the cancellation of debts, so that no one knows which way to turn. But for the Dorians <note>original: "Doris"</note>, this difficulty and disturbance did not exist. For they possessed the lands abundantly without controversy, and the great debts of old that had been built up <margin>E</margin> were not a burden to them. **MEGILLUS.** You speak the truth. **ATHENIAN.** Why then, best of men, did that constitution and its legislation turn out so badly? **MEGILLUS.** In what way? What was the fault? **ATHENIAN.** Because out of the three city constitutions, two quickly destroyed both their civil discipline and their laws, and only your city was left alone. **MEGILLUS.** What you ask is not easy to answer. **ATHENIAN.** And yet it is necessary for us to consider it now, and while discussing the laws in a kind of modest and elderly game, to complete this journey without distress, just as we said when we began to travel. **MEGILLUS.** Undoubtedly it must be done as you say. **ATHENIAN.** Can we then have a finer consideration of laws than of those laws <margin>F</margin> which adorned such cities? Or even think of any cities or institutions more honorable and greater than these? **MEGILLUS.** One would not easily prefer others to these. **ATHENIAN.** No one will doubt that those men, thus joined together, believed they could defend not only the Peloponnesus, but even all of Greece, if any Barbarian should inflict injury, just as they were stirred by the example of the Trojans, who, relying on the Assyrian power which took its origin from Ninus <note>The legendary founder of Nineveh</note>, had stirred up war against themselves. For the power of that empire was still not to be despised. Therefore, just as we now dread the Great King <note>Referring to the King of Persia</note>, so all men then <margin>G</margin> greatly feared the power of those nations conspiring as one. The second destruction of Troy had indeed brought great resentment against them. For the empire of the Assyrians was a certain small part of the power of Troy. Against all that power, therefore, the army divided into three cities by the brothers, the sons of Hercules who were then reigning, seemed to be in the best and most adorned condition, and much better equipped than the one that besieged Troy. For first, they considered themselves to have leaders, the Heraclidae <note>Descendants of Hercules</note>, who were more excellent than the Pelopidae <note>Descendants of Pelops, such as Agamemnon</note>; and second, they believed this army surpassed in virtue the one that went against Troy. For they had conquered those who had previously been the victors—that is, the Achaeans were defeated by the Dorians. Do we not believe they thought this way, and for that reason prepared themselves? **MEGILLUS.** Entirely so. **ATHENIAN.** It was likely, therefore, that they thought <margin>H</margin> this constitution of theirs would be firm and endure for a long time, especially because they had undergone many dangers and labors together, and were governed by kings who were brothers. Moreover, they had consulted many prophets, both others and especially the Delphic Apollo. **MEGILLUS.** That is very likely. **ATHENIAN.** Yet these things, which were expected to be so great, quickly vanished then, as it seems, except for a small part, as we just said...

<column-break/>

<margin>Α</margin> ...Patrocles and Eurymenes. **CLEINIAS.** How could it not be so? **ATHENIAN.** All these then swore to these men at that time to give aid if anyone should destroy their kingdom. **CLEINIAS.** Certainly. **ATHENIAN.** But is a kingdom destroyed, or has any rule ever been destroyed, by anyone other than by those themselves? Or did we, just a little while ago when touching upon these words, establish this, or have we now forgotten? **MEGILLUS.** How could we? **ATHENIAN.** Therefore, let us now confirm such a thing even more. Having gone over the deeds that occurred, it seems we have come to the same argument; so we shall not seek the same argument concerning something empty, but concerning what has happened and possesses truth. <margin>Β</margin> These things happened: three kingdoms swore to three cities governed by kings, each to the other, according to the laws they established, which were common for both ruling and being ruled. The rulers swore not to make their rule more violent as time and their lineage progressed; the others swore that if the rulers kept these promises, they themselves would never destroy the kingdoms, nor permit others to attempt it. The kings would help kings who were wronged, and the peoples would help both peoples and kings who were wronged. Was it not so? **MEGILLUS.** Thus it was. **ATHENIAN.** Therefore, that which was greatest was present in the establishments of the government legislated in the three cities, whether the kings <margin>C</margin> legislated or some others. **MEGILLUS.** What sort of thing? **ATHENIAN.** That two cities should always be helpers against the one city that was disobedient to the established laws. **MEGILLUS.** Clear. **ATHENIAN.** And indeed, many charge the legislators who arrange these things to make the laws such that the peoples and the multitudes will receive them willingly—just as if someone were to choose trainers or doctors to treat and heal the bodies being treated with pleasure. **MEGILLUS.** Entirely so. **ATHENIAN.** But how often must one be content if it is possible to produce healthy bodies that are free from disease even with no small amount of pain? **MEGILLUS.** Why not? **ATHENIAN.** And this other thing was also present for those men at that time, being no <margin>D</margin> small thing for the ease of the establishment of the laws. **MEGILLUS.** What sort of thing? **ATHENIAN.** The legislators did not face the greatest of reproaches: establishing a certain equality of property for everyone. This happens in many other cities being legislated, if anyone seeks to move the possession of land and the dissolution of debts. Seeing that equality could never sufficiently occur without these things, every man meets a legislator who attempts to move any such things with the cry "do not move the immovable," and he calls down curses on those introducing redistributions of land and cancellations of debts. Thus, every man is reduced to a state of helplessness. But for the Dorians, this was present in such a fine and blameless way: the land was divided without dispute, and there were no great and ancient debts. **MEGILLUS.** True. **ATHENIAN.** Why then, O best of men, did their <margin>E</margin> settlement and legislation turn out so badly for them? **MEGILLUS.** In what way and with what reproach do you say this? **ATHENIAN.** Because when three settlements were made, two parts of them quickly destroyed both the government and the laws, and only one remained—that of your city. **MEGILLUS.** You ask no easy thing. **ATHENIAN.** But yet we must now consider and examine this concerning laws, playing a prudent game of old men, and go through the path without pain as we said when we began to walk. **MEGILLUS.** Why not? And it must be done as you say. **ATHENIAN.** What better inquiry could we make concerning laws than about these which organized these cities? Or what cities or settlements could we look at that are more notable or larger? **MEGILLUS.** It is not easy to name others instead of these. **ATHENIAN.** Is it not clear that those men at that time intended <margin>F</margin> that the system they established would be a sufficient help not only to the Peloponnesus, but to all the Greeks, if any of the barbarians should wrong them? Just as those living around Ilion <note>Troy</note> then, trusting in the power of the Assyrians which existed around Ninus, were emboldened to stir up the war against Troy. For the form of that empire was still preserved in no small way. Just as we now fear the Great King, so those men then feared the organization that had been established. For the capture of Troy had become a great accusation against them, as it was a part <margin>G</margin> of that empire. Against all these things, the army of that time, divided into three cities under one arrangement by the brother kings, the sons of Hercules, seemed finely discovered and organized, and far superior to the one that went to Troy. For first, they thought they had the Heraclidae as better leaders than the Pelopidae; then, they say this army surpassed in virtue the one that went to Troy. For these had conquered again; those were the ones who had been defeated by these—namely, the Dorians defeated the Achaeans. Do we not think those men at that time prepared themselves with this intention? **MEGILLUS.** Entirely so. **ATHENIAN.** Therefore, it was also likely they held that it would be secure, and that they had a much longer story ahead, since they had shared many labors and dangers with one another, and were organized by one lineage <margin>H</margin> and by kings who were brothers. Moreover, they had used more prophets, both others and the Delphic Apollo. **MEGILLUS.** It is all very likely. **ATHENIAN.** These things, though so greatly expected, flew away then, as it seems, quickly.

<summary>The Athenian Stranger discusses the ancient Dorian alliance of three kingdoms, explaining that they were founded on mutual oaths and an ideal economic situation without debt or land disputes, yet two of the three failed due to internal collapse.</summary>

### ON THE LAWS, BOOK III.

<margin>A</margin> ...except for a small part near your own region. And the conflict between their two factions has never truly ceased, even until now. Indeed, if the original intention of that time had been realized and had harmonized into a single purpose, it would have possessed a power irresistible in war. **MEGILLUS.** How could it be otherwise? **ATHENIAN.** How then was it dissolved? Is it not worth investigating what kind of chance or fortune destroyed such a great and significant system? **MEGILLUS.** Certainly. If one were to examine other laws or constitutions to see what preserves great and beautiful things, or conversely what destroys everything, one could hardly ignore these events. **ATHENIAN.** It seems then that we have fortunately stumbled upon a very adequate subject for investigation. **MEGILLUS.** Entirely so. **ATHENIAN.** But tell me, <margin>B</margin> my marvelous friend, do all men—and we ourselves at this very moment—fail to notice that we often think we see something grand and wonderful being achieved, which would produce marvelous results if only someone knew how to use it correctly? Yet perhaps, in this very matter, we are not thinking rightly or according to nature. And is it not the same with all other things that we consider in this way? **MEGILLUS.** What do you mean? About what specifically is this observation made? **ATHENIAN.** My good man, I was just laughing at myself. For looking at that great military force we were discussing, it seemed to me to be a magnificent thing, a wonderful possession for the Greeks to have fallen into, as I said, if only someone had known how to use it well at the time. **MEGILLUS.** Did you not speak well and reasonably then, and did we not rightly praise you? **ATHENIAN.** <margin>C</margin> Perhaps. I am considering, however, that whenever anyone sees something great and possessed of much power and strength, a hope immediately charms them: that if the owner knew how to use such a great thing, he would achieve many wonderful things and be happy. **MEGILLUS.** And is this not correct? Or what do you mean? **ATHENIAN.** Consider what someone is looking at when they give such praise rightly. First, regarding what we were just saying: if those who then commanded the army had known how to organize it correctly, how would they have succeeded? Would they not have established it securely and preserved it forever, so that they themselves were free and ruled over whomever else they wished? And in short, they and their descendants would have <margin>D</margin> done whatever they desired among all men, both Greeks and barbarians? Was it not for the sake of this that they desired it? **MEGILLUS.** Entirely so. **ATHENIAN.** And if someone sees great wealth, or extraordinary family honors, or anything of that sort, and says the same thing, does he not say it while looking toward this—that through these things, all his desires (or at least the most significant ones) might be fulfilled? **MEGILLUS.** So it seems. **ATHENIAN.** Now, come: there is one common desire for all men, which is revealed by our current argument. **MEGILLUS.** What is that? **ATHENIAN.** That things should happen according to the command of one's own soul—all things if possible, but if not, at least human affairs. **MEGILLUS.** <margin>E</margin> Of course. **ATHENIAN.** Since we all wish for such a thing throughout our lives, as children, men, and old men, we necessarily pray for it continually. **MEGILLUS.** How could we not? **ATHENIAN.** And surely we would pray for our friends to have the same things they pray for themselves. **MEGILLUS.** Certainly. **ATHENIAN.** A son is a friend to a father, a boy to a man. **MEGILLUS.** Of course. **ATHENIAN.** Yet the father would often pray to the gods that the things his son prays for himself should in no way happen. **MEGILLUS.** You mean when the son is foolish and prays while still young? **ATHENIAN.** Yes, and also when the father—whether old or very young—knowing nothing of what is beautiful and just, prays with great fervor while in a state of passion <note>original: "παθήμασι" (pathemasi) - referring to intense emotions or suffering that cloud judgment.</note> similar to those of Theseus toward his son Hippolytus, who died so unhappily. <note>In Greek mythology, Theseus cursed his son Hippolytus based on a false accusation. The gods granted the wish, resulting in the son's tragic death. Plato uses this to show that a wish granted without wisdom is a disaster.</note> If the son then understood the situation, do you think he would join in his father's prayer? **MEGILLUS.** I understand what you are saying. You seem to be saying that we should not pray or strive for everything to follow our own will, but rather that our will should follow our <term>prudence</term> <note>original: "φρονήσει" (phronesei) - practical wisdom or the ability to discern the right course of action.</note>. Both the city and each one of us should pray and strive for one thing: how to possess mind and reason. **ATHENIAN.** Yes. And I myself remembered, and now wish to remind you, that a statesman and legislator should always keep this in view when establishing the orders of laws. In the beginning (if we remember), we said that you two praised the good legislator because he established all laws for the sake of war. I, however, said that this was looking toward only one virtue, and that the fourth one <note>The four cardinal virtues are Courage, Temperance, Justice, and Prudence. War primarily concerns Courage.</note>. I argued that one must look toward all virtue, and especially toward the first, which is the leader of all virtue. This is <term>prudence</term>, and mind, and opinion, followed by love and desire. Now our argument returns to the same point. And I say again what I said then—whether you wish to take it in jest or in earnest—that I claim it is dangerous to use prayer without mind; instead, the opposite of what one wishes will happen. If you are willing to believe that I am serious, please do so. For I fully expect you will now find, in following the argument about the laws we proposed earlier, that <margin>G</margin> the destruction of those kings and the ruin of their entire system was not caused by cowardice or ignorance of military matters by the rulers or their subjects; rather, they were destroyed by all other forms of vice, and especially by <term>ignorance</term> <note>original: "ἀμαθίᾳ" (amathia) - a "great ignorance" or folly where the soul's desires are not in harmony with reason.</note> concerning the greatest of human affairs. That this is how it happened then, and happens now if it happens anywhere, and will happen in the future, I will try to demonstrate in the following argument if you are willing.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...the part that inhabits your region. This part has never, even to this day, rested from the war undertaken against the other two parts. For if the constitution established then had remained in harmony, it would certainly have been invincible in war. **MEGILLUS.** Why not? **ATHENIAN.** In what way and by what reasoning was it dissolved? Does it not appear worthy of consideration what sort of fortune overturned so great and such a constitution? **MEGILLUS.** Surely no one could understand laws or other republics—through which great and beautiful things are preserved or, conversely, lost—if they neglected these things. **ATHENIAN.** We seem, then, to have happily stumbled upon a very suitable consideration. <margin>B</margin> **MEGILLUS.** Very much so. **ATHENIAN.** Does it not happen then, O marvelous man, that our error stays hidden from us all? Especially now, while we think we have perceived a singular thing, and how wonderful the results would be if someone did not ignore how to use it in the proper way? Yet perhaps we are currently thinking about this very thing neither rightly nor according to nature. And all others err in everything they think about in a similar way. **MEGILLUS.** What are you saying? And about what matter do you say this most specifically? **ATHENIAN.** I was certainly laughing at myself just now, my good man. For when I considered that army of which we just spoke, it seemed to me truly excellent and marvelous, and destined to achieve noble deeds for the Greeks, if someone had then used it well. **MEGILLUS.** <margin>C</margin> Did you not speak prudently in all things, and did we not praise you rightly? **ATHENIAN.** Perhaps. I think, however, that everyone who sees something great and endowed with huge power is immediately affected in such a way that they think: if the one who possesses it knew how to use such a great thing, he would be happy from the many noble deeds done through it. **MEGILLUS.** Is this not also correct? Or how do you mean? **ATHENIAN.** Consider now toward what the person is looking who praises each thing in this way, and if he speaks rightly. First, concerning what we were saying: in what way would they have used the opportunity happily if the leaders then had known how to order the army rightly? Would they not have preserved it forever if they had established it more securely at that time, so that they themselves were free and could subjugate others as they wished? And would they and their <margin>D</margin> descendants not have obtained whatever they desired among both Greeks and Barbarians? Did they not desire everything for the sake of this? **MEGILLUS.** Indeed, very much so. **ATHENIAN.** Therefore, whoever sees great riches, or excellent family honors, or anything of that sort, and says these same things, will say them looking toward this: as if through this, all things he desires (or at least the most and most powerful) will come to him. **MEGILLUS.** So it seems. **ATHENIAN.** There is certainly one desire common to all men, which the present discourse has signaled. **MEGILLUS.** What is it? **ATHENIAN.** That all things, or at least human things, should be carried out according to the desire of one's own soul. **MEGILLUS.** <margin>E</margin> Who could doubt it? **ATHENIAN.** Since we all always want this—in childhood, adulthood, and old age—we undoubtedly pray for it diligently. **MEGILLUS.** Certainly. **ATHENIAN.** We also pray for these things for our friends, which they themselves would pray for. **MEGILLUS.** This too. **ATHENIAN.** And a son is a friend to a father, when he is a boy to a man. **MEGILLUS.** Indeed. **ATHENIAN.** And yet, of those things the boy prays will happen to him, the father prays to the gods that many should not happen. **MEGILLUS.** Do you say that happens when the son who prays is young and senseless? **ATHENIAN.** Yes, and also when the father—whether old or quite young—knowing nothing of what is honest or just, is so affected that, like Theseus toward the unhappy Hippolytus, he prays too intensely; and if the son knows better, do you think the son will then pray for the same things as his father? **MEGILLUS.** I understand what you say. For you seem to me <margin>...that all things should follow our will, but rather that our will should follow our prudence.</margin> to be saying that we should not pray or strive for everything to follow our will, but rather that our will should follow our prudence. And that both a city and individuals should pray for and strive to have mind and reason. **ATHENIAN.** Precisely. Furthermore, I have remembered, and want you now to remember, that a statesman and legislator should always keep these things in view when making laws. Indeed, at the beginning of the discussion, you were saying that a good legislator should refer everything to war. I, however, said that he should look to only one virtue, even though there are four. One must look not to only one, but to <margin>G</margin> all: and especially to the first, which is the leader of all others—and this is prudence, and intellect, and opinion, together with the love and desire that follows them. Our speech now returns to the same point. And I, who said those things then, say the same things now, whether you wish it in jest or in earnest. I assert indeed that it is not safe to use a prayer, and to obtain a prayer, if you do not have mind; rather, it is better that the opposite of what you ask should happen. If you wish to consider these things said in earnest, do so. For I hope now to persuade you of what we proposed a little while ago: that the cause of the destruction of the kings and the dissolution of that entire constitution was not cowardice, nor ignorance of military affairs by either the leaders or subjects, but all the rest of depravity, and especially the greatest ignorance concerning human affairs. That these things happened so then, and happen now if they occur anywhere, or will happen in the future and not otherwise, I will endeavor to show, as the reasoning will next demonstrate.

<summary>The Athenian Stranger argues that the downfall of the Dorian kingdoms was caused not by military failure, but by "the greatest ignorance"—a lack of harmony between human desire and reason. He concludes that a legislator's primary goal must be the cultivation of prudence (phronesis) rather than just military strength.</summary>

# OF PLATO

...to find out, and to explain to you as friends, to the best of my ability.

<margin>A</margin> **CLINIAS.** It is a burden, O stranger, to praise you with words, but we shall praise you indeed by our actions, for we will listen eagerly to what you say; in this, the noble and true praiser is most clearly seen. **ATHENIAN.** You speak excellently, Clinias. Therefore, let us do as you say. **CLINIAS.** It shall be so, if God wills. You only speak. **ATHENIAN.** We claim then, proceeding through the remaining path of this discussion, that that great power <note>The military and political alliance of the Dorian states.</note> was lost through the greatest ignorance, and that even now similar outcomes proceed from the same cause. Therefore, if this is the case, the legislator ought to strive to give <margin>B</margin> wisdom to the citizens as much as possible, and to take away ignorance to the highest degree. **CLINIAS.** That is certainly evident. **ATHENIAN.** What then may be rightly called the greatest ignorance? Consider if you agree with me. For I judge it to be this. **CLINIAS.** What? **ATHENIAN.** When someone does not love what seems honorable or good to them, but hates it; and when they love and embrace what seems evil and unjust. I assert that this discord of pleasure and pain against the opinion that follows reason is the extreme ignorance, and I also call it the greatest, because it resides in the multitude of the soul. For that part of the soul which is subject to pain and pleasure is like the common people and the multitude of a city. When, <margin>C</margin> therefore, the soul opposes the knowledge, or opinion, or reason which by nature should rule, I call this ignorance: both in a city, when the multitude does not obey the rulers and the laws; and also in a single man, when although there are good reasons in the soul, nothing is done according to them, but everything is carried out to the contrary. These ignorances I assert are the most destructive for a city, and for any citizen, but not the ignorances of craftsmen <note>The Athenian distinguishes between moral ignorance and a simple lack of technical or trade skills.</note>, if indeed you guests understand what I am saying. **CLINIAS.** We both understand, O friend, and we grant these things. **ATHENIAN.** Let it then be established that to citizens who are ignorant in this way, nothing pertaining to leadership should be entrusted; rather, as ignorant men, they are to be rebuked, even if they are most sharp and eloquent, and have mastered everything pertaining to the ornament and sharpness of the mind. But those who are affected in the opposite way are to be held as wise, even if they "know neither letters," as the saying goes, "nor how to swim." <margin>D</margin> Offices of state must also be entrusted to these men as being prudent. For how, O friends, could even the smallest form of prudence exist without harmony? **CLINIAS.** In no way. **ATHENIAN.** But indeed, the most beautiful and greatest of all harmonies is rightly called the greatest <term>wisdom</term> <note>original: "sapientia" / "sophia"</note>. He who is to live according to reason must necessarily participate in this. But whoever is devoid of it will always seem to be a destroyer of his house, and never a savior of the city, but instead altogether ignorant in these matters. Let these things, therefore, be as we said a moment ago. **CLINIAS.** Exactly so. **ATHENIAN.** Now, must there not be rulers and subjects in cities? <margin>E</margin> **CLINIAS.** Certainly. **ATHENIAN.** So be it. But what and how many are the justifications <note>original: "rationes" / "axiomata"</note> for the dignity of ruling and obeying, both in cities, whether large or small, and similarly in private homes? Is not the first right justification of dignity that father and mother, and parents everywhere, should rule over their offspring? **CLINIAS.** Greatly so. **ATHENIAN.** The second, that the noble should rule the ignoble; the third, that the older should rule the younger. <margin>F</margin> **CLINIAS.** And this too. **ATHENIAN.** The fourth, that masters should rule slaves? **CLINIAS.** Without a doubt. **ATHENIAN.** The fifth, that the stronger should rule and the weaker obey? **CLINIAS.** You have just mentioned a most necessary form of rule. **ATHENIAN.** Indeed, it is the one most widely found among all animals, and "according to nature," as <note>original: "Thebanus Pindarus"</note> Pindar of Thebes once said. But the greatest dignity, it seems, should be placed sixth, by which the ignorant are ordered to follow, and the prudent to lead and rule. This rule, O most wise Pindar, I would affirm is not against nature, but according to the nature of the law, and is accepted willingly, not by violence. **CLINIAS.** Very well said. **ATHENIAN.** Let us bring forward a seventh form <margin>G</margin> of rule by some kind of lot, asserting that it is obtained by the grace of God and a certain good fortune: and let us consider it most just that he whom the lot has chosen should rule, and he whom it has rejected should obey. **CLINIAS.** You speak the truth. **ATHENIAN.** We shall say then, in a kind of jest, to someone who easily takes up the duty of making laws: "Do you see, O legislator, how many dignities concerning rulers must be weighed? And how they are opposed to one another? Truly, we have now found a certain source of civil strife, which you must guard against." First, consider carefully with us what those kings of Argos and Messene did wrong in these matters, so that they destroyed both themselves and the power of the Greeks, which was then marvelous. Was it not because they ignored the very correct saying of <note>original: "Hesiodo"</note> Hesiod, that "the half is often more than the whole"? When, for instance, taking the whole is harmful, but the half is moderate, then surely he judged the moderate to be more than the immoderate, as being better than the worse. **CLINIAS.** Most correctly. **ATHENIAN.** Do we believe this was destructive to the kings before <margin>H</margin> it was to the common people? **CLINIAS.** It is probable that this is mostly a disease of kings, who live proudly because of their luxuries. **ATHENIAN.** It is clear then that those kings first possessed this fault: they wanted to be able to grant more than the laws allowed, and they did not—

<column-break/>

...to find out, and to reveal it to you to the best of my power, as being friends. **CL.** To praise you in words, O stranger, would be rather tiresome; but we shall praise you in deed, for we will follow what you say with eagerness; in which the man who is free with his praise or not is most clearly manifest. **ATH.** Well spoken, Clinias; and let us do as you say. **CL.** These things shall be, if God is willing; only speak. **ATH.** We say then, exercising ourselves as we proceed through the rest of the discussion, that the greatest ignorance destroyed that power at that time; and that this same thing is by nature doing the same now. So that the legislator, since this is so, must try to instill in the cities as much wisdom as possible, and to remove folly to the highest degree. **CL.** That is clear. **ATH.** What then could rightly be called the greatest ignorance? See if you both agree with what is being said; for I, for my part, propose it to be this. **CL.** What kind? **ATH.** When someone, having an opinion that something is beautiful or good, does not love this, but hates it; and what seems to be wicked and unjust, he loves and embraces. This discord of pain and pleasure against the opinion according to reason, I say is the ultimate ignorance—and the greatest, because it belongs to the majority of the soul. For the part of it that feels pain and pleasure is what the common people and the multitude are in a city. When, therefore, the soul opposes the opinions or reason, which are by nature the rulers, this I call folly; and in a city, when the multitude does not obey the rulers and the laws; and the same for one man, whenever the beautiful reasons present in the soul produce nothing more, but rather everything is done to the contrary. All these ignorances I would set down as the most discordant for the city and for each one of the citizens, but not the ignorance of the craftsmen, if you indeed understand what I am saying. **CL.** We understand, O friend, and we agree with what you say. **ATH.** Let this, then, be laid down as decided and spoken: that to those of the citizens who are ignorant in these things, nothing involving rule is to be entrusted, and they are to be reproached as being ignorant, even if they are quite skilled in calculation, and have thoroughly labored at all the clever things and whatever is by nature for the speed of the soul; but those who have the opposite of these qualities, one should address as wise (even if, as the saying goes, they know neither letters nor how to swim) and the offices of rule are to be given to them as being sensible. For how, O friends, could there be even the smallest form of wisdom without harmony? It is not possible. But the most beautiful and greatest of harmonies would most justly be called the greatest wisdom; in which he who lives according to reason shares; but he who is deprived of it will appear to be a house-destroyer, and in no way a savior of the city, but, quite the opposite, always ignorant in these matters. Let these things, then, as we have just said, be laid down in this way. **CL.** Let them be so laid down. **ATH.** It is necessary, I suppose, for there to be rulers and subjects in cities? **CL.** Of course. **ATH.** Very well. What and how many are the justifications for both ruling and being ruled, in large and small cities alike, and likewise in households? Is not one the fact that fathers and mothers—and generally parents—rule over their offspring? Would not this be a correct justification everywhere? **CL.** Very much so. **ATH.** And following this, that the noble rule the ignoble; and third, following these, that the older should rule and the younger be ruled. **CL.** Of course. **ATH.** Fourth, that slaves should be ruled and masters rule. **CL.** How could it be otherwise? **ATH.** Fifth, I believe, that the stronger should rule and the weaker be ruled. **CL.** You have spoken of a very necessary rule. **ATH.** And indeed, it is the one most common among all living creatures, and is "according to nature," as the Theban Pindar once said. But the greatest justification, as it seems, would be the sixth: ordering not the one without knowledge, but the one who is sensible, to lead and to rule. And yet this, O most wise Pindar, I for my part would say does not happen against nature, but according to nature—the rule of the law over willing subjects, being natural and not forced. **CL.** You speak most correctly. **ATH.** Calling it god-beloved and a kind of good fortune, let us bring forward a seventh rule by lot; and we say it is most just that the one who wins the lot should rule, and the one who loses should be ruled and depart. **CL.** You speak most truly. **ATH.** "Do you see then," we might say, O legislator—playing with one of those who lightly undertake the laying down of laws—"how many justifications there are for rulers, and how they are by nature opposed to one another? For now we have discovered a source of factions, which you must heal. But first, examine with us how and in what way the kings of Argos and Messene at that time, by erring against these things, destroyed themselves and the power of the Greeks, which was marvelous at that time. Did they not fail to recognize that Hesiod spoke most correctly when he said that 'the half is often more than the whole'? Whenever taking the whole is harmful, but the half is moderate, then he considered the moderate to be more than the immoderate, being better than the worse." **CL.** Most correctly. **ATH.** Do we then think that this, occurring from time to time, destroyed the kings, or would it be in the common people? **CL.** It is likely, for the most part, that this is a disease of kings living arrogantly through luxury. **ATH.** Is it not clear, then, that those kings at that time were the first to have this desire to take more than the established laws; and what they had praised in word and by oath, they did not—

<summary>In this passage from Plato's Laws, the Athenian Stranger defines the "greatest ignorance" as a moral disharmony where the soul loves what it knows to be wrong. He outlines seven justifications for authority, emphasizing that the rule of the wise over the ignorant is the most natural, and warns that the neglect of moderation led to the downfall of ancient Greek kingdoms.</summary>
<keywords>Plato, Laws, political philosophy, ignorance, harmony, Pindar, Hesiod, authority, moderation, Argos, Messene, Dorian kings</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the Athenian Stranger’s analysis of the Dorian states. Having established that the collapse of the alliance was due to a lack of harmony between the rulers and the ruled—the "greatest ignorance"—he now examines the specific historical remedy found in Sparta: the introduction of constitutional checks and balances to prevent the "disease" of absolute power.</meta>

# ON THE LAWS, BOOK III.

<column-break/>

A They remained <note>Referring to the laws or agreements mentioned on the previous page.</note> as they had praised them in words and by oath. But the discord—which, as we say, is the greatest ignorance, though it appears to be wisdom—overthrew all those things through error and bitter lack of culture. **CLINIAS.** So it seems. **ATHENIAN.** Well then. What should the legislator have established then to guard against this disease? By the gods, is it not wise to say this now, nor is it difficult? But if someone had foreseen it then, he surely would have been wiser than we are. **MEGILLUS.** What do you mean by that? **ATHENIAN.** One can look at what happened among your people, Megillus, and from that knowledge, it is easy to say what <gloss>should have happened</gloss> then.

B **MEGILLUS.** Speak more clearly. **ATHENIAN.** It will certainly become very plain. **MEGILLUS.** In what way? **ATHENIAN.** If one gives too much power to things that are smaller, neglecting moderation—sails to ships, food to bodies, and authority to souls—everything is overturned. For when things are elevated beyond measure, they become insolent; some run into diseases, others into injustice, which is the child of insolence. What do we say then? Is it not this, my friends? That there is no mortal soul whose nature, if young and unaccountable to others, can bear the greatest authority among men without being filled with the greatest disease—folly—in its intellect, and thus incurring the hatred of its closest friends. When this happens, it quickly destroys the soul and vanishes all its power.

C To watch over this by observing moderation is the work of great legislators. Therefore, what happened then is now easy to see. **MEGILLUS.** What was it? **ATHENIAN.** A God, I believe, caring for you and looking into the future, planted for you a double line of kings from a single one <note>Sparta was unique in having two kings from two different royal houses, the Agiads and Eurypontids.</note>, and so contracted the power more toward moderation. After this, a certain human nature mixed with divine power <note>This refers to the legendary lawgiver Lycurgus.</note>, seeing your authority was still inflamed, mixed the sober power of old age <note>The "Gerontes" or Council of Elders.</note> with the stubborn strength of noble birth, making the vote of the twenty-eight elders equal to the power of the kings in the greatest matters. Then a third savior <note>King Theopompus.</note> appeared to you, seeing the authority still swelling and raging,

D and cast a bridle upon it—the power of the Ephors <note>The Ephors were five annually elected magistrates who acted as a check on the kings.</note>—bringing it close to the power of the lot <note>The "lot" refers to a democratic selection process, suggesting the Ephors represented the common people.</note>. By this reasoning, the kingship among you, composed of the necessary elements and possessing moderation, was itself saved and became the cause of safety for others. Since in the time of Temenus and Cresphontes <note>The original Dorian leaders of Argos and Messene.</note> and those who legislated for them, whoever they were, not even the faction of Aristodemus would have been saved. For they were not experienced enough in law-making. If they had been, they would never have thought to restrain a young soul with oaths when it had taken up an authority from which a tyranny could arise. But now God has shown what kind of authority <gloss>was then and is now</gloss>

E best to establish. That we should understand this after it has happened, as I said before, is nothing strange. For it is not hard to see a thing if you are shown an example. But if someone had foreseen it then, and had been able to moderate the authorities and make one out of three, he would have saved all the grand designs of that time, and neither the Persian fleet nor any other would ever have sailed against Greece, despising us as being of no account. **CLINIAS.** You speak the truth. **ATHENIAN.** They resisted them shamefully, Clinias. I say "shamefully," not because those of that time did not fight bravely on land and sea—for they won fine battles—but I say it was shameful because, of those three cities, only one defended Greece. The other two were so corrupted that one <note>Messene.</note> prevented Lacedaemon [Sparta]

F from helping by waging war against her with all her might. The other, Argos, which was ranked first in the original distribution, when called upon to repel the barbarian, did not listen or help. One could say many things about what happened then regarding that war that would be shameful to Greece. Nor would one be correct to say that "Greece" defended itself. For unless the common purpose of the Athenians and Lacedaemonians had repelled the impending slavery, almost all the Greek races would have been mixed together—barbarians among Greeks and Greeks among barbarians—just as those under the Persian tyranny are now scattered and poorly combined. We have these things, Clinias and Megillus, to blame

<margin>A city ought to be free, wise, and a friend to itself.</margin>

G on the so-called statesmen and legislators of old and of today, so that by searching for their causes, we may find what else should have been done. As we said just now: one should not legislate great and unmixed authorities, keeping in mind that a city must be free, wise, and a friend to itself. The legislator must look toward these goals. Do not wonder if we have often proposed various goals and said the legislator must look to them,

H and yet these goals do not seem the same to us each time. But one must consider that when we say we should look toward temperance, or wisdom, or friendship, the goal is not different, but the same. And if many such words confuse you, do not be disturbed. **CLINIAS.** We will try to do so, following the arguments. But now explain the point about friendship, freedom, and wisdom...

<summary>The Athenian Stranger explains that Sparta was saved from the tyranny and collapse that befell Argos and Messene because its power was moderated by three "saviors": the dual kingship, the Council of Elders (Gerousia), and the Ephors. This balance of power is presented as the essential goal of a legislator seeking to create a free and stable city.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the Athenian Stranger’s discourse on the balance of power. Having previously discussed the downfall of the Dorian kings due to their lack of "harmony," he now transitions to a broader historical and philosophical analysis of the two primary forms of government—Monarchy and Democracy—using Persia and Athens as his primary case studies.</meta>

# PLATO'S [LAWS]

<margin>Two mothers of civil governments</margin>
...you were saying the legislator ought to do. **ATHENIAN.** Listen to me then. There are two kinds of constitutions which are, as it were, the mothers from which all others may truly be said to have sprung. It is proper to call one **monarchy**, <note>original: "monarchiam"</note> that is, the rule of one; and the other **democracy**, <note>original: "democratiam"</note> that is, the rule of the people. One may say the Persian race holds the highest form of the former, and we [the Athenians] hold the highest of the latter. All other forms, as I said, are composed of a variety of these two. It is necessary for a city to participate in both of these if it is to possess liberty, friendship, and wisdom. This is what our argument intends to teach us when it says that a city can never be well governed if it is devoid of these things. **CLINIAS.** How so? **ATHENIAN.** Since one side [Persia] embraced **monarchy**—the rule of one—and the other [Athens] embraced **liberty** more than was appropriate, neither preserved a moderation <note>The Latin "mediocritatem" refers to the "golden mean" or a balanced middle ground, rather than poor quality.</note> between servitude and freedom. Your states, however—I speak of the Laconian [Spartan] and Cretan—did so to a greater degree. So did the Athenians and Persians in the past, though less so now. Shall we discuss the causes of this, or not?
<margin>Many things concerning the government of Cyrus, Cambyses, and Darius.</margin>
**CLINIAS.** By all means, if we wish to complete our proposed task. **ATHENIAN.** Let us listen then. In the time of **Cyrus**, when the Persians held to a greater moderation between servitude and liberty, they were first of all free themselves, and then they brought many others under their rule. For when the rulers shared liberty with their subjects and reduced things to a state of equality, the soldiers were more friendly to their generals and showed themselves ready in times of danger. And if there was any man among them who was wiser or capable in counsel, because the king was not envious but gave everyone the freedom to speak and honored those who shared his counsel, he brought his wisdom into the common light. Thus, through liberty, friendship, and a communion of minds, everything was made easy for them. **CLINIAS.** It seems that these things happened as you say. **ATHENIAN.** How then did that kingdom fall in the time of **Cambyses**, and was then restored in the time of **Darius**? Do you wish for us to speak as if by use of divination? <note>original: "vaticinor" / "μαντεύομαι". The Athenian suggests "divining" or "prophesying" the past—using philosophical reasoning to reconstruct historical motives.</note> **CLINIAS.** Why should we not? For this contributes to the goal we are pursuing. **ATHENIAN.** Thus I divine concerning Cyrus: in other matters he was a good leader and a friend to civil life, but he never touched upon right discipline, nor did he ever apply his mind to the administration of a household. **CLINIAS.** Why is that? **ATHENIAN.** From his youth, he was occupied with military service throughout his whole life and handed his sons over to women to be educated. These women raised them as if they were already "blessed" from childhood, lacking nothing; they prevented anyone from opposing them in any matter, as if their status required it, and forced everyone to praise whatever they said or did. Thus, they raised them to be such men as they were. **CLINIAS.** You seem to have described a "fine" education indeed! **ATHENIAN.** A feminine one, certainly, introduced by the royal women who were puffed up by new riches and left alone while the men were occupied with war and dangers. **CLINIAS.** That is consistent. **ATHENIAN.** Their father [Cyrus] possessed many herds of sheep, cattle, and men, but he did not realize that his sons, to whom he was to leave these things, were not being taught the ancestral Persian art—for the Persians were shepherds born in a harsh land, and the Persian art itself was hard, sufficient to make them robust shepherds who could stand guard, keep watch, and go to war if necessary. Instead, he permitted women and eunuchs to raise his sons in the Median fashion, and their education was corrupted by what is commonly thought to be "happiness." Thus they turned out as one would expect of those who had been raised in a state of total license. When, after the death of Cyrus, they took power, being full of luxury, impunity, and license, first one [Cambyses] killed the other because he could not bear equality; then, raging with ignorance and drunkenness, he lost the empire. For the Medes and a certain Eunuch then despised him as if he were a madman. **CLINIAS.** So it is said, and it seems to have happened nearly that way. **ATHENIAN.** And it is also said that the empire returned to the Persians through Darius and those seven men. **CLINIAS.** Plainly. **ATHENIAN.** Let us look then, following the argument. **Darius** was not the son of a king, nor was he nurtured in luxuries. When he came to power as the seventh of that group, he divided the empire into seven parts, of which some small dreams <note>A metaphor for the remnants of the original Persian system.</note> still remain today. He decided that they should live under laws that brought a certain common equality. He also sanctioned the distribution of land that Cyrus had promised the Persians, binding it by law, and offered friendship and community to all Persians, winning over the Persian people with money and gifts. Thus, being loved by his soldiers, he subjugated no fewer regions than Cyrus had left behind. After Darius came **Xerxes**, who was again educated in royal luxuries. But I now rightly call upon you, O Darius: you were not warned by the evil example of Cyrus, but you raised Xerxes in the same habits in which Cyrus had nurtured Cambyses. Xerxes, therefore, being raised in the same way, suffered similar misfortunes. From that time on, almost no King of the Persians has been truly "Great" except in name. I do not think fortune was the cause, but rather the bad life which the children of the exceedingly wealthy and of tyrants mostly live. For never can a boy, a man, or an old man turn out outstanding in virtue from such a life.

<column-break/>

**ATHENIAN.** Speak then of what you intended to say the legislator should have done.
**ATHENIAN.** Listen to me then. There are, as it were, two "mothers" of constitutions, from which one might say the others were born. It is right to call one **monarchy** and the other **democracy**. The Persian race represents the extreme of the former, and we [Athenians] the other. Almost all other forms, as I said, are woven together from these two. It is necessary to share in both of these if there is to be liberty and friendship combined with wisdom. **B** The argument intends to claim that a city can never be well governed if it is devoid of these elements. **CLINIAS.** For how could it be otherwise? **ATHENIAN.** One side loved the monarchical element, and the other loved the element of freedom more than was necessary; neither possessed the proper measure. Your states—the Laconian and Cretan—did so more successfully. The Athenians and Persians did so in the old days, but less so now. Let us go through the reasons. Shall we? **CLINIAS.** By all means, if we are to finish what we set out to do. **ATHENIAN.** Let us listen. For when the Persians, in the time of Cyrus, observed the proper measure between servitude and liberty, they first became free themselves, and then masters of many others. For as rulers they gave liberty to their subjects and led them toward equality; the soldiers were more friendly to their generals and showed themselves eager in dangers. And if there was anyone wise among them and able to give counsel, since the **C** king was not envious but gave freedom of speech and honored those who could offer advice, he contributed his power of wisdom to the common good. All things then flourished for them through liberty, friendship, and the communion of the mind. **CLINIAS.** It seems what you say is how it happened. **ATHENIAN.** How then did it perish under Cambyses and was saved again under Darius? Do you wish we use a kind of divination of the mind? **CLINIAS.** That will help our inquiry into the direction we have started. **ATHENIAN.** I divine now regarding Cyrus that, while in other respects he was a good general and a lover of his city, **D** he did not touch upon right education at all, and he paid no attention to the management of his household. **CLINIAS.** How should we say such a thing? **ATHENIAN.** It seems he campaigned for his whole life from his youth, handing over his children to the women to be raised. They raised them as if they were divine beings from childhood, already blessed and lacking in nothing. Since they were "sufficiently happy," the women prevented anyone from opposing them in anything, and forced everyone to praise everything they said or did; thus they raised them to be such as they were. **CLINIAS.** A "fine" upbringing you have described, it seems! **ATHENIAN.** A feminine one, let us say—of royal women who had recently become wealthy, raising the children in the absence of men who were away due to wars and many dangers. **CLINIAS.** That makes sense. **ATHENIAN.** The father [Cyrus] had flocks and sheep and herds of men and many other things; **E** but those to whom he was to leave them, he did not know were not being taught their father's own art, which was the Persian art—for Persians were shepherds, the offspring of a rough land, a harsh art capable of making them very good shepherds, able to live in the open, stay awake, and if necessary, go to war. But he allowed his sons to be corrupted by the so-called "happiness" of the Median education, being taught by women and eunuchs. Whence they became what they were likely to become, being raised with a "reproach-free" upbringing [meaning they were never corrected]. When the children came forth after the death of Cyrus, full of luxury and lack of restraint, first one killed the other, resenting equality; **F** after this, he himself [Cambyses], maddened by drink and lack of education, lost the rule to the Medes and the one then called the Eunuch, who despised Cambyses' folly. **CLINIAS.** These things are indeed said, and it seems they happened roughly in this way. **ATHENIAN.** Moreover, it is said that the rule came back to the Persians through Darius and the Seven. **CLINIAS.** Certainly. **ATHENIAN.** Let us observe, following the argument. Darius was not the son of a king, nor was he raised in a pampered education. When he came to the rule, being the seventh to take it, he divided it into seven parts, of which even now some small dreams remain. He established laws to live by, introducing a certain common equality; **G** and he incorporated into the law the tribute Cyrus had promised the Persians, providing friendship and community to all Persians, winning over the Persian people with money and gifts. Therefore, his armies with goodwill acquired for him lands no less than those Cyrus had left. After Darius came Xerxes, who was again raised in the royal and luxurious education. O Darius—it is perhaps most just to say—you did not learn from Cyrus's mistake, but you raised Xerxes in the same habits in which Cyrus had nurtured Cambyses. And he, being the offspring of the same education, performed deeds nearly identical to the sufferings of Cambyses. And from **H** that time on, almost no King in Persia has been truly Great, except in name. The cause, in my view, is not fortune, but the bad life which the children of the exceptionally wealthy and of tyrants for the most part live. For never will a child, a man, or an old man become outstanding in virtue from such an upbringing. These things, we say, the legislator must consider...

### ON THE LAWS BOOK III.

<margin>A</margin>
**ATHENIAN.** It is a task that should be considered by the legislator, and one we ought to observe in our present discussion. Indeed, Lacedaemonians <note>original: "Lacedaemonii," referring to the Spartans.</note>, it is only just to grant this to your city: that you do not entrust the highest offices to men simply because of their wealth, their royal blood, or their status as private citizens, unless the divine voice has commanded it from the beginning. For one must not confer the highest honors in a city upon anyone merely because they are preeminent in wealth, or because they are swift, or beautiful, or strong, if they lack virtue. Nor even if they possess some other virtue, but lack **temperance**. <note>original: "temperantiam" (Latin) / "sophrosyne" (Greek). This refers to self-control, moderation, and a sound mind.</note> **MEGILLUS.** How do you mean that, Stranger? **ATHENIAN.** Is not **courage** <note>original: "fortitudo"</note> one part of virtue? **MEGILLUS.** It is indeed. **ATHENIAN.** Judge for yourself, then, after you have heard my reasoning. Would you wish to have as a neighbor or a housemate someone who was exceedingly brave, but not at all temperate—rather, someone reckless and unrestrained in every vice? **MEGILLUS.** God forbid! **ATHENIAN.** What then of a man who is
<margin>B</margin>
skilled in many arts and wise in those things, but is **unjust**? <note>original: "iniustum"</note> **MEGILLUS.** Not in any way. **ATHENIAN.** Yet truly, justice cannot take root without temperance. **MEGILLUS.** How could it be otherwise? **ATHENIAN.** Nor, for that matter, can that man be called wise—whom we just now defined as one whose pleasures and pains are in harmony with and obedient to right reason. **MEGILLUS.** Certainly not. **ATHENIAN.** Let us further consider this, so that we may see how honors are distributed, correctly or incorrectly, among citizens. **MEGILLUS.** What do you mean? **ATHENIAN.** If temperance were to exist in someone's soul in isolation, stripped of every other kind of virtue, would it be rightly honored or not? **MEGILLUS.** I do not know how to answer. **ATHENIAN.** You have answered modestly enough. For if you had granted honor to either of those options, you would, I think, have spoken out of tune. **MEGILLUS.** Then it is well that I answered as I did. **ATHENIAN.** So be it. Indeed, this "addition" of honors and disgraces should be treated with a rational silence rather than a spoken answer.
<margin>C</margin>
**MEGILLUS.** You seem to be speaking of temperance itself. **ATHENIAN.** That is exactly what I mean. Therefore, that which benefits us most when added to other virtues should be honored most highly; and that which benefits us in the second degree should receive the second honor. And so, following this order of succession, each quality should receive the honors that follow in sequence. **MEGILLUS.** That is so. **ATHENIAN.** Furthermore, shall we say that these distributions also fall to the legislator? **MEGILLUS.** Most certainly. **ATHENIAN.** Do you wish that we leave to him the division of all things into every small and individual task? But since we ourselves are students of the law, let us attempt a three-fold division, separating them into the greatest, the middle, and the least. **MEGILLUS.**
<margin>D</margin>
By all means. **ATHENIAN.** We say, then, that a city which is to be saved and happy—so far as is possible for human power—must necessarily distribute honors and ignominies <note>original: "ignominias," meaning public disgrace or loss of status.</note> correctly. **MEGILLUS.** That is true. **ATHENIAN.** Now, a correct distribution is this: the primary and most highly honored goods are those of the **soul**, provided that temperance is present in it. In the second degree of dignity are placed the goods of the **body**. And in the third place are the external possessions and **wealth**. If any legislator or city oversteps these—perhaps by honoring wealth above all else, or by placing something that should be secondary in the first rank of honor—they will act neither holily nor as a true citizen. Shall we hold this as settled, or how? **MEGILLUS.** It is settled, quite clearly. **ATHENIAN.** It was our consideration of the Persian government that led us to speak of these things at greater length. We find that they have become even worse than before. And we say the cause is
<margin>E</margin>
that they took away too much of the people's liberty and increased the power of their masters beyond what was fitting, thereby destroying the fellowship and friendship within the city. When these are corrupted, the rulers no longer consult for the good of their subjects or the people, but only for their own power. Often, for the sake of some small advantage of their own, they do not care if they utterly ruin cities or destroy friendly nations with fire. Thus they hate with a hostile and merciless hatred, and are hated in return. And if ever a need arises for the people to fight on their behalf, the rulers find no common spirit or consensus among them, nor any willingness to face danger or fight for their masters with any heart. Instead, though they rule over almost countless thousands of men, they find them all
<margin>F</margin>
useless for war. And as if they were lacking in men, they hire others for pay, believing they will be saved by mercenaries and foreign soldiers. Furthermore, they are forced to act foolishly, since by their very deeds they proclaim that the things called honorable and noble in a city are mere trifles when compared to gold and silver. **MEGILLUS.** So it happens. **ATHENIAN.** But concerning the affairs of the Persians—how they are not well-managed now due to excessive domination and servitude—let enough have been said. **MEGILLUS.** Entirely so. **ATHENIAN.** Next, it is proper to run through the Athenian government in the same way, so it may be clear how a liberty that is subject to no magistrate is not much worse than that which follows a moderate rule. For at the time when the Persians
<margin>G</margin>
were attacking Greece—indeed, almost all of Europe—we had an ancient Republic, and there were certain magistrates based on a four-fold division of wealth. A certain **reverence** <note>original: "pudor" (Latin) / "aidos" (Greek). This refers to a sense of shame or respect that keeps people from breaking laws.</note> lived within us, acting like a master, because of which we were willing to live in subjection to the laws. Moreover, the sheer size of the forces by land and sea so terrified us that it compelled us to be even more observant of the laws and to obey our magistrates. For all these reasons, a great goodwill arose among us. It was nearly ten years before the naval battle fought at **Salamis**... <note>A decisive battle in 480 BCE where the Greeks defeated the Persian fleet.</note>
