# PLATONIS
## ON THE LAWS BOOK III

<margin>A</margin> **ATHENIAN.** Datis, dispatched by Darius, led the Persian fleet against the Athenians and the Eretrians. He was ordered by Darius, under penalty of death, to bring these people back as subjects to his rule. Datis, therefore, with a vast multitude of soldiers, completely conquered the Eretrians in a short time. From there, a terrifying rumor reached our city: that not a single Eretrian had escaped. It was said that the soldiers had joined hands and encircled the entire region of Eretria, capturing everyone as if in a net. <note>This "netting" (sageneuein) was a Persian tactic where soldiers formed a human chain to sweep an island of its inhabitants.</note> This rumor, whether true or not, terrified the other Greeks, and especially the Athenians. They sent embassies everywhere, pleading for help,
<margin>B</margin> but no one except the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans.</note> was willing to assist. These men, whether hindered by the war they were then waging against Messene, or for some other reason—for we do not know for certain—arrived only on the day after the Battle of Marathon. After this, it was said that the King <note>Darius I, and later his son Xerxes.</note> spent many days making massive preparations and issuing countless threats. Meanwhile, word arrived that Darius had died, and his son <note>Xerxes.</note>, a fierce young man, had taken up the empire and had no intention of abandoning his father's plans. The Athenians believed all these preparations were directed against them because of the slaughter at Marathon. Furthermore, hearing that Mount Athos was being dug through, the Hellespont bridged, and an immense fleet assembled, they realized there would be no safety for them by land or by sea.
<margin>C</margin> They felt this especially because they could rely on no one for protection. They remembered that when the Eretrians were first captured, no one had come to their aid or shared the danger for their sake. They expected the same outcome for themselves on land. By sea, they saw no hope of safety either, as more than a thousand ships were approaching. They saw only one hope, however thin and doubtful: looking back at their previous deeds, they saw that they had conquered even when hope seemed lost. Carried by this hope, they found that their only refuge would be in themselves and in the gods. All these
<margin>D</margin> factors bound them together with greater goodwill toward one another—I mean this present fear, and the fear that had long existed from the ancient laws, to which they were accustomed while serving them. This reverence <note>original Latin: "pudorem," Greek: "aidos." It refers to a sense of shame or respect for divine and human law.</note> we have often named in our previous discussions; we said that all who wish to be good must serve it. Whoever is possessed by this reverence is truly free and fearless. Had this present fear not been joined to that reverence, they never would have been provoked by such an attack to come together and defend the temples of the gods, the tombs of their ancestors, their fatherland, and their families and friends, as they are recorded to have done; instead, they would have scattered, each to a different place. **MEGILLUS.** You have spoken well, Stranger, and in a manner befitting both yourself and your country. **ATHENIAN.** That is true,
<margin>E</margin> Megillus. For it is right to recount these events to you, who share the nature of those ancestors. But both you and Clinias should consider whether what we are saying pertains to the making of laws. I am not telling these stories merely for the sake of conversation. See the purpose for which I say these things: so that we may understand that something similar happened to us as happened to the Persians; for while they dragged the people into total slavery, we, on the contrary, pushed the masses toward total liberty. How and why we say this will be shown by what follows. **MEGILLUS.** You speak well. But try to express more clearly what you were just saying. **ATHENIAN.** I will do so. Under our ancient laws, my friends, the
<margin>F</margin> common people were not masters of everything, but were, in a way, voluntary servants of the laws. **MEGILLUS.** What laws do you mean? **ATHENIAN.** I mean those which were established concerning **music**, so that we may trace from the beginning how this excessive liberty has gradually increased. For at that time, music was divided into distinct species and forms. One species was a song of prayer to the gods, which they called **hymns**. Opposite to this was another species of song, which one might best call **laments**. Another species was the **Paean** <note>A song of praise or healing, often dedicated to Apollo.</note>. Another concerned the birth of Dionysus, which I believe was called the **Dithyramb** <note>A wild, choral hymn.</note>. They even used this very word, "laws," <note>original Latin: "leges," Greek: "nomoi." In Greek, "nomos" means both "law" and "musical melody."</note> to name another type of song, specifically the **citharoedic** songs <note>Songs accompanied by the cithara or lyre.</note>. Once these and others had been established by law, it was not permitted to use one type of melody for another purpose. The authority to recognize, judge, and punish those who disobeyed
<margin>G</margin> did not belong to the whistling or the unrefined shouts of the crowd, as it does now, nor to the noisy applause of the mob. Instead, it was granted to men of distinguished learning to listen in silence until the end. Children, their teachers, and the general crowd were kept in order by the threat of the rod. While things were done in this orderly fashion, the multitude of citizens was willing to obey and did not dare to judge anything with a clamor. As time went on, the poets themselves became the authors of this unmusical lawlessness. They were naturally gifted poets, but they did not respect what was just and lawful in music,
<margin>H</margin> behaving like revelers and indulging in pleasure more than was proper. They mixed laments with hymns, and paeans with dithyrambs; they imitated the sounds of flutes with the lyre, mixing everything together. Unintentionally, through their ignorance, they lied about music, claiming that it possessed no inherent standard of rightness, but that it should be judged most correctly by the pleasure of the listener, whether that person be virtuous or otherwise.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Datis, leading the Persian fleet, was explicitly sent by Darius with orders to enslave the Athenians and Eretrians and bring them back, threatening him with death if he failed. Datis captured the Eretrians in a short time with his massive army, and a terrifying report reached our city: that none of the Eretrians had escaped him. For it was said that the soldiers of Datis, by joining hands, had netted the entire territory of Eretria. This story, whether true or however it arrived, terrified the other Greeks and especially the Athenians. When they sent ambassadors everywhere for help, no one was willing
<margin>B</margin> except the Lacedaemonians. They, however, were delayed—either by the war they were then fighting against Messene, or perhaps something else prevented them (for we do not know the reason)—and they arrived one day after the battle at Marathon had taken place. After this, reports of great preparations and ten thousand threats came from the King. As time passed, it was said that Darius had died, and that his son, young and impetuous, had taken over the rule and was in no way abandoning the drive. The Athenians thought all of this was being prepared against them because of what happened at Marathon. Hearing that Athos was being dug through and the Hellespont bridged, and seeing
<margin>C</margin> the multitude of ships, they felt there was no salvation for them either by land or by sea. For they knew no one would help them, remembering that even when the Persians first came and destroyed Eretria, no one helped them or risked fighting alongside them. They expected the same to happen then on land, and as for the sea, they saw a total lack of safety with more than a thousand ships attacking them. They could think of only one salvation, thin and desperate: they looked back at what had happened before, how victory in battle had seemed to come from hopeless circumstances. Riding on this hope, they found that their only refuge was in themselves and the gods.
<margin>D</margin> All these things created a friendship among them: the fear then present, and the fear born from the earlier laws—the fear they possessed by being slaves to the established laws, which we have often called "reverence" in our earlier words. We said that those who are to be good men must be slaves to this reverence; the man who lacks it is a coward, but the one who has it is free and fearless. If this fear had not taken hold then, they never would have come together to defend themselves, nor would they have defended the temples, the graves, the fatherland, and their other kinsmen and friends as they did then. Instead, each of us would have been scattered and dispersed little by little. **MEGILLUS.** You have spoken very rightly, Stranger, and in a way that is fitting for both yourself and your fatherland. **ATHENIAN.** This is so, Megillus. It is just to speak of these things that happened at that time to you,
<margin>E</margin> who are by nature a sharer in the character of those fathers. But you and Clinias should consider whether what we are saying is relevant to legislation. For I am not going through these things for the sake of stories, but for the reason I am stating. You see: in a certain way, the same experience has happened to us as to the Persians—they, by leading the people into total slavery, and we, on the contrary, by urging the masses toward total liberty. How and what we should say from this point on is, in a way, well-expressed by our previous words. **MEGILLUS.** You speak well. Try to show us even more clearly what you are saying now. **ATHENIAN.** It shall be so. Under the ancient laws, my friends, the
<margin>F</margin> people were not masters of their own votes, but in a certain way, they were willing slaves to the laws. **MEGILLUS.** What laws do you mean? **ATHENIAN.** First, those concerning the music of that time, so that we may trace from the beginning the excessive growth of the "free" life. For music was then divided into its own kinds and forms. One form of song was prayers to the gods, called by the name "hymns." Opposite to this was another kind of song, which one might best call "laments." Another was the "Paean," and another, I believe, called the "Dithyramb," which concerned the birth of Dionysus. They even used the word "laws" <note>Greek: *nomoi*.</note> for a specific kind of song, the "citharoedic" ones. Once these and others were firmly established, it was not permitted to misuse one kind of melody for another. The authority to know these, and having known them, to judge and punish the disobedient,
<margin>G</margin> was not the hiss or the unmusical shouts of the crowd, as it is now, nor the clapping that gives praise. Instead, for those who were educated, it was established to listen in silence until the end; for children and their attendants and the great mass of the crowd, the discipline was maintained by the rod of the supervisor. Thus, the mass of citizens was willing to be ruled in an orderly way and did not dare to judge by making a disturbance. But after this, as time went on, poets who were naturally poetic but ignorant of what is just and lawful in the Muse began to lead this unmusical lawlessness. They were driven by frenzy and possessed by pleasure more than was right, mixing laments with hymns,
<margin>H</margin> and paeans with dithyrambs. They imitated flute music with the lyre and brought everything together into everything else. Unintentionally, through their folly, they misrepresented music, as if it had no correctness at all, but should be judged most correctly by the pleasure of the one who enjoys it, whether that person is better or worse. By making such poems and adding such words...

<summary>This page discusses the historical role of fear and law-abiding reverence in saving Athens from the Persian invasions, and begins an analogy comparing political decline to the degradation of traditional musical standards.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from a historical analysis of the Persian Wars and the internal governance of Athens and Persia toward a practical application of these theories. The Athenian Stranger concludes the historical survey and begins a new phase of the dialogue where the characters decide to "found" a theoretical city to test their legislative ideas.</meta>

<margin>A</margin> **ATHENIAN.** ...they suggested, and thus rendered the common people so lawless and bold regarding music that they believed themselves fully capable of passing judgment on it. Because of this, theaters that were once silent began to erupt in shouting, as if the crowds understood what was beautiful or not in the arts of the Muses. Thus, the governance of music slipped from the rule of the best <note>Aristocracy</note> into a corrupt "rule of the theater" <note>original: "theatrocratia"</note>. If this had been merely a democracy of free men, no great harm would have come of it. But as it happened, this notion that everyone knows everything began with music, and lawlessness followed closely behind, disguised as "liberty." Men became fearless, thinking they possessed knowledge, and this lack of fear gave birth to impudence. Indeed, to not fear the opinion of a better man because of one's own audacity is almost the very definition of that ruinous impudence which springs from an excessive and reckless liberty. **MEGILLUS.** What you say is very true.

<margin>B</margin> **ATHENIAN.** Following this liberty comes the refusal to be subject to magistrates. From this source springs the desire to escape the service and admonition of father, mother, and elders. As men reach the extreme of this transgression, they seek to disobey the laws as well. At the very limit, they disregard oaths, pledges, and the gods themselves. They display and imitate what is called the "ancient Titanic nature," <note>Referring to the Titans who rebelled against the Olympian gods.</note> returning to those same old miseries, leading a life of hardship and finding no end to their evils. But why has all this been said? It seems to me the argument, like a horse, must be pulled back from all sides, lest it run away with its mouth unbridled and—as the proverb says—fall off a donkey. <note>A Greek idiom for making a fool of oneself or losing the thread of an argument.</note> We must ask, then, for what purpose was all this said? **MEGILLUS.** That is right.

<margin>C</margin> **ATHENIAN.** We said these things for the sake of the following. **MEGILLUS.** For what? **ATHENIAN.** We stated that a lawgiver must look toward three goals when establishing laws: that the city being organized should be free, friendly toward itself, and possess wisdom. Was this not what we said? **MEGILLUS.** Precisely. **ATHENIAN.** For this reason, we brought forward two types of government: one of extreme servitude <note>Persia</note> and the other of unrestrained liberty <note>Athens</note>. We considered which of these was governed correctly. We saw that when a moderate amount of authority and liberty were combined, both fared exceedingly well; but they fared poorly when either servitude or liberty was pushed to the extreme. **MEGILLUS.** You speak the truth.

<margin>D</margin> **ATHENIAN.** Moreover, it was for this same purpose that we considered the constitution of the Dorian armies, the settlements at the foot of Mount Dardanus, the coastal habitations, and those first survivors who remained after the devastation of the flood. For their sake, we discussed music, drunkenness, and all the subjects that came before. All these things were said so that we might understand how a city might best be governed, and how an individual might best order his own life. But if we have achieved anything worthwhile, what proof of it can we offer to ourselves, Megillus and Clinias?

<margin>E</margin> **CLINIAS.** Stranger, I think I see something. It seems quite providential that all these previous words of ours have been spoken. For I find myself in need of them now, and your arrival—yours and Megillus's—is most timely. I will not hide from you what has happened to me; indeed, I take it as a good omen. The greater part of Crete is attempting to establish a colony, and they have entrusted the care of this matter to the people of Knossos. The city of Knossos, in turn, has assigned the task to me and nine others. They have ordered us to establish laws, choosing those that please us from Cretan traditions or those gathered from elsewhere, telling us not to fear foreign laws if they appear superior.

<margin>F</margin> **CLINIAS.** Now, therefore, let us grant this favor to one another. Let us select from what has been said and, in speech, construct a city as if we were settling it from the beginning. In this way, we shall simultaneously examine the subject of our inquiry, and perhaps I may use this theoretical structure for the future city. **ATHENIAN.** This is no declaration of war you bring, Clinias! Therefore, unless it is inconvenient for Megillus, you may count on me to assist you to the best of my ability. **CLINIAS.** Well said. **MEGILLUS.** I am also ready. **CLINIAS.** You have both spoken excellently. Let us attempt, then, to first settle the city in speech.

## THE FOURTH DIALOGUE.

> *S U M M A R Y O F T H E D I A L O G V E. The author continues the explanation of the preface, which he pursues until nearly the middle of the fifth dialogue. In order to represent a true and consistent image of a Republic, he intentionally proposes a certain colony in the Cretan territory, to which the laws he delivers may be adapted. In the summary of that preface which he began from the very start of the discussion, he explains several illustrious chapters in this dialogue: namely, on the suitable site of a city (he does not approve of a maritime site, as it is more exposed to the trickeries of commerce); on the occasions for seeking settlements; on the form of the republic; and on the gods and the cult of parents. He also treats those most noble topics: the power and authority of laws; the necessity of prefaces before the legitimate and primary constitution of laws; and the rules by which these should be circumscribed.*

<meta>The dialogue continues from the previous discussion on the decline of civic order. ### PLATO'S LAWS

**ATHENIAN.** Come now, what kind of city should we imagine this to be? <insert>A</insert> I am not asking about its current name or what it might be called in the future—perhaps the act of colonization itself, or the specific site, or the name of a river, spring, or some local god will lend its fame to the new city. Rather, I am asking this: will it be a maritime city or located inland? **CLEINIAS.** The city we are discussing, stranger, is about eighty stades <note>About 9 miles or 15 kilometers.</note> from the sea. **ATHENIAN.** Are there harbors nearby, or is that coast entirely harborless? **CLEINIAS.** That region, stranger, has the best harbors possible. **ATHENIAN.** Goodness! What are you saying? And does the land bear all things, <insert>B</insert> or is it in need of some resources? **CLEINIAS.** It bears almost everything. **ATHENIAN.** Is there any city located near it? **CLEINIAS.** Not very close, which is exactly why we are settling it; due to an ancient expulsion of the inhabitants, the region has lain desolate for an immense amount of time. **ATHENIAN.** As for the plains, mountains, and forests, how is the land distributed? **CLEINIAS.** It is similar in nature to the rest of Crete. **ATHENIAN.** So you are saying it is rugged and wooded rather than a flat plain? **CLEINIAS.** I am indeed. **ATHENIAN.** Then it is not poorly suited for the acquisition of virtue. For if it were located on the coast, well-harbored, and not self-sufficient but in need of many imports, it would require a great savior and divine lawgivers
to ensure that <insert>C</insert> the nature of the region did not foster many varied and wicked customs. As it stands, there is comfort in the fact that it is eighty stades from the sea—though it is still closer to the coast than it ought to be, especially since you say it is so well-harbored. Nevertheless, we must be content with this. Proximity to the sea provides a city with daily pleasures, yet that neighborly sea is truly "salty" and bitter. For by filling the city with merchandise and the profits of retail trade, it breeds shifty and unfaithful characters in the soul, making the city distrustful and unfriendly toward itself and toward other nations. <insert>D</insert> However, the city has a remedy in that it produces all its own crops. Because the land is rugged, even though it produces everything, it does not produce a vast surplus. If it were fertile enough to produce a great excess, it would export much and receive a great influx of gold and silver in return. To speak plainly, there is nothing more ruinous than this for the development of noble and just character, as we said in our earlier discussions, if we remember correctly. **CLEINIAS.** We do remember, and we agree that what was said then and what is said now is correct. **ATHENIAN.** What about timber for shipbuilding? Is there an abundance there? **CLEINIAS.** There is no fir worth mentioning, nor any pine. <insert>E</insert> There is little cypress, and you will find very few larch or plane trees, which shipbuilders are forced to use for the interior parts of ships. **ATHENIAN.** In this regard too, the natural state of the region is not bad. **CLEINIAS.** Why so? **ATHENIAN.** Because it is better for a city to not be able to easily imitate the wicked practices of its enemies. **CLEINIAS.** Toward which of our previous points are you looking when you say this? **ATHENIAN.** Observe me closely, my excellent friend. I am looking back at what was said at the beginning regarding the Cretan laws—that they were aimed at a single goal: war. I said that such laws were well-placed insofar as they related to virtue, <insert>F</insert> but I did not entirely praise them because they focused only on a part of virtue, rather than the whole. Now, you must observe me in this present law-giving to see if I am ordaining anything that does not aim at virtue, or that aims only at a portion of it. I believe a true lawgiver should be like an archer, always aiming at that mark from which something good follows, while leaving aside all else—whether wealth or any other thing separated from virtue. I was saying that a "wicked imitation" of enemies occurs when people living by the sea are harassed by their foes. I will give an example, though I have no wish to dwell on past injuries.
<margin>Minos forced Attica to hand over seven youths.</margin>
Once, <insert>G</insert> Minos, relying on his great naval power, imposed a cruel tribute on the people of Attica. At that time, the Athenians did not yet have ships prepared for war as they do now, nor did their land have an abundance of timber to easily build a fleet. Therefore, they could not immediately avenge themselves by imitating the naval tactics of their enemies and becoming sailors themselves. It would have been better for them to have lost seven youths many times over than to have become sailors. For instead of remaining steady land-based soldiers <note>Hoplites</note>, they grew accustomed to leaping frequently onto ships and retreating quickly—thinking there was no shame in failing to withstand an enemy's charge or in refusing to die at their post. Instead, they found easy and ready excuses for throwing away their arms and engaging in what they call "not-shameful" flights. These are the kinds of words that usually result from naval warfare; they are not worthy of great praise, but rather the opposite. <insert>H</insert> One should never accustom the best part of the citizens to bad habits. We find this "refuge of ships" disapproved of even in Homer...

<column-break/>

**ATHENIAN.** Come then, what city shall we say this will be? I am not asking for its name now, nor what it might be called in the future (for perhaps the settlement itself, or the place, or some river or spring, or the name of a local god might give its own reputation to the new city). This is what I want to ask instead: will it be a coastal city or an inland one? **CLEINIAS.** The city about which we have just been speaking, stranger, is located about eighty stades from the sea. **ATHENIAN.** What of it? Is there a harbor near it, or is it completely without one? **CLEINIAS.** It is as well-harbored as possible in that area, stranger. **ATHENIAN.** Oh my, what a thing to say! What about the land itself? Does it bear all crops, or is it lacking in some? **CLEINIAS.** It is lacking in almost nothing. **ATHENIAN.** Is there any neighboring city nearby? **CLEINIAS.** Not at all; that is why it is being settled. An ancient migration from the place left this land desolate for an untold length of time. **ATHENIAN.** And how do the plains, mountains, and forests share the land? **CLEINIAS.** It resembles the nature of the rest of Crete as a whole. **ATHENIAN.** Would you call it more rugged than flat? **CLEINIAS.** Most certainly. **ATHENIAN.** Then it would not be unsuited for the acquisition of virtue. For if it were coastal and well-harbored, yet not self-sufficient but in need of many things, it would require some great savior and divine lawgivers to prevent it from having many diverse and petty characters, being such by nature. But now it is comforted by those eighty stades. It actually lies closer to the sea than it should, given that you say it is so well-harbored; nevertheless, even this is acceptable. For proximity to the sea is a "salty" and bitter neighbor, though it may be pleasant for daily life. Filling itself with commerce and money-making through retail trade, it breeds shifty and unfaithful habits in the souls, and makes the city itself unfaithful and unfriendly to itself and to other men. But a consolation for this is that it is self-sufficient. Since it is rugged, it is clear it would not produce a vast surplus while being self-sufficient. For if it had this, it would produce a large export and be filled in return with gold and silver currency—the greatest evil, so to speak, that can happen to a city for the birth and possession of just character, as we said (if we remember) in our previous words. **CLEINIAS.** We do remember, and we agree that we spoke rightly then and do so now. **ATHENIAN.** And what of the land’s supply of shipbuilding timber? **CLEINIAS.** There is no fir worth mentioning, nor pine; nor much cypress. One would find little larch or plane, which shipbuilders must use for the internal parts of vessels. **ATHENIAN.** This too would not be bad for the nature of the land. **CLEINIAS.** Why so? **ATHENIAN.** It is a good thing that a city cannot easily imitate the wicked imitations of its enemies. **CLEINIAS.** Looking at which of the things we've said do you say this? **ATHENIAN.** My good man, watch me, looking back at what was said at the beginning about the Cretan laws—that they looked to one thing. You two said that this one thing was war. I replied that if such laws were laid down looking toward virtue, it was well; but that they looked toward only a part, and not all of virtue, I could not quite agree. Now you two must watch me in return in this present lawgiving, to see if I legislate anything not tending toward virtue, or toward only a piece of virtue. For we assume that only that law is rightly laid down which, like an archer, aims at this: that which is always accompanied by something beautiful, while letting all other things pass—whether it be wealth or any other such thing separated from the aforementioned virtues. I was saying that the "wicked imitation" of enemies happens whenever one lives by the sea and is harassed by enemies, such as—I will tell you, not wishing to remind you of old grievances—Minos, who once forced the inhabitants of Attica to pay a harsh tribute, possessing great power at sea. They did not yet possess warships as they do now, nor did they have a land with shipbuilding timber to easily prepare a naval force. Thus, they were not able to become sailors themselves through imitation and immediately defend themselves against their enemies. For it would have been more to their advantage to lose seven children many times over than to become sailors instead of steady foot-soldiers, and to grow accustomed to leaping frequently and running back to the ships, thinking they were doing nothing shameful by not daring to die while staying to face the enemy's attack. Instead, they find plausible and very ready excuses for losing their arms and fleeing in what they say are "not-shameful" flights. For these are the words that they say result from naval infantry—words not often worthy of infinite praise, but the opposite. For one should never accustom people to bad habits, as we may also learn from Homer, that this practice...

<summary>The Athenian Stranger and Cleinias discuss the ideal location for a new Cretan colony, concluding that an inland, rugged, and self-sufficient site is best for fostering virtue. They argue that proximity to the sea and naval power leads to moral corruption, greed, and cowardice in warfare.</summary>
<keywords>Plato, Laws, Crete, geography, virtue, maritime trade, naval warfare, Minos, Attica, self-sufficiency, legislation</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from Book IV of Plato’s Laws. The Athenian Stranger is discussing the strategic and moral implications of a city's location. Having established that the new colony will be somewhat inland, he now critiques the influence of naval power on national character, citing Homer and the Persian Wars as examples. He then moves to the practical difficulties of founding a colony with a diverse population versus a homogenous one, before concluding that human legislation is often the result of necessity and chance.</meta>

# ON THE LAWS, BOOK IV

<margin>A</margin> ...such a thing is not good. Odysseus rebukes Agamemnon for this very reason, when the Greeks were being hard-pressed in battle by the Trojans and Agamemnon ordered them to drag the ships down into the sea. Odysseus grew angry with him and said:
> You who bid us, while the battle and the shout of war are joined,
> to drag the well-benched ships to the sea; so that even more
> the Trojans may have their prayers fulfilled, though they have already won much,
> and sheer destruction may fall upon us. For the Achaeans
> will not hold their ground in the war while the ships are being dragged to the sea,
> but will look away and cease from the joy of battle.
> Then your counsel will be a ruin, such as you speak.
<note>Homer, *Iliad* 14.96–102. Odysseus argues that if the ships are ready for a quick escape, the soldiers will lose their will to fight and instead flee.</note>

<margin>B</margin> So even he <note>Homer</note> recognized that it is an evil thing to have <term>triremes</term> <note>Ancient warships with three banks of oars.</note> stationed in the sea to provide an escape for those fighting; even lions would become accustomed to fleeing like deer if they adopted such habits. Furthermore, naval power does not usually grant honors to the most excellent part of the military, even though it provides safety. Since naval success is achieved through the skill of the pilot, the <term>penteconter</term> <note>A commander of fifty oarsmen.</note> captain, and the rowers—a diverse and not always distinguished group of men—no one could rightly distribute honors to the individuals involved. Yet how could a state still be well-ordered if it is deprived of the ability to honor its best citizens? <term>CLEINIAS.</term> It would be nearly impossible. And yet, stranger, we Cretans at least maintain that the naval battle of the Greeks against the barbarians at Salamis saved Greece. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> Indeed, many among the Greeks and barbarians say so. But I, my friend, and Megillus here, claim that the land battles—the one at Marathon and the one at Plataea—were the ones that began the salvation of the Greeks and brought it to completion. These battles made the Greeks better men, whereas the naval battles did not—to speak plainly about the battles that saved us then. For I would also add the sea battle at Artemisium to the one at Salamis. However, we are now looking toward the virtue of a political system and the nature of the land and the arrangement of laws. We do not believe that merely being saved and existing is the most precious thing for men (as the masses do), but rather becoming and being as virtuous as possible for as long as they live. I believe this has been stated by us previously. <term>CLEINIAS.</term> Certainly. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> Let us then consider this alone: whether we are following the same path, which is the best for cities regarding their settlement and the laying down of laws. <term>CLEINIAS.</term> By all means. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> Tell me then, what is the nature of your settlement? Is it anyone from all of Crete who wishes to join, as if a crowd had become too large in each city for the land to support? For surely you are not gathering any Greek who wishes to come. And yet I see some people from Argos and Aegina and elsewhere in Greece settled in your land. Tell me for the present case, <margin>D</margin> from where do you say the current citizen body for the state will come? <term>CLEINIAS.</term> It seems they will come from all of Crete; and of the other Greeks, those from the Peloponnese seem to me most likely to be welcomed as fellow-colonists. For what you just said is true: there are some from Argos. And the most highly regarded group here currently is the Gortynian, for it happens to have migrated here from Gortyn in the Peloponnese. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> It is not quite so easy for cities to settle in this way as it is for a swarm of bees—when a single race goes out from a single land to settle, as friends from among friends, perhaps squeezed out by a shortage of land or some other such necessity. Sometimes, too, a city is forced by civil strife to send out a portion of itself elsewhere. On other occasions, an entire city has fled, having been utterly defeated in a superior war. All these cases are easier to settle and legislate for in one way, but harder in another. For a single race that shares the same language and the same laws has a certain friendship, sharing in religious rites and all such things; however, it does not easily tolerate different laws and a political system that differs from its own. On the other hand, a group that has been in revolt due to the badness of its laws and seeks to maintain the same habits that led to its previous ruin makes it difficult and disobedient for the founder and legislator. But a diverse race that has flowed together into the same place <margin>G</margin> might perhaps be more willing to listen to new laws; however, to make them breathe together and, as the saying goes, pull together like a team of horses toward one and the same goal, takes a long time and is extremely difficult. Yet legislation and the settling of cities are the most perfect means for achieving virtue in men. <term>CLEINIAS.</term> That is likely. But tell me even more clearly what you are looking at when you say this. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> My good man, I was reflecting on the fact that when I look at legislators, I am afraid I might say something trivial. But if we speak to the point, it will be no trouble. And yet, why do I hesitate? For almost all human affairs seem to be in such a state. <term>CLEINIAS.</term> What do you mean? <term>ATHENIAN.</term> I was about to say that no human ever legislates anything, but that chances and various misfortunes falling in all sorts of ways legislate all things for us. For either a violent war <margin>H</margin> overturns a political system and changes the laws, or the distress of harsh poverty. Many things, too, such as diseases—when plagues fall upon a city and persist for a long time—force us to innovate. Looking at all these things, one would be justified in saying what I just said: that no mortal—

<column-break/>

...it seems. For Odysseus rebukes Agamemnon, who, <margin>A</margin> while the Greeks were occupied in battle against the Trojans, was ordering the ships to be led down into the sea. Being annoyed by this, Odysseus says:
> Do you order us, while the storm of war
> is pressing, to lead the well-decked ships into the deep,
> so that all things may succeed for the Trojans according to their wish,
> but for us, destructive slaughter and ruin may follow?
> For they will not commit themselves to a heavy fight
> when they see the ships ready for flight in the sea,
> but they will abandon the war and flee from there.
> Then it will be clear what kind of counsel yours was.

It is clear, therefore, that Homer also realized that triremes ready for the flight of those fighting are a hindrance. Indeed, even lions <margin>B</margin> used to such habits would become accustomed to fleeing like stags. Furthermore, the powers of states that rely on naval forces to achieve safety do not distribute honors to the best part of military affairs at all. For since naval matters are generated by the art of the pilot, the command of fifty men, the rowing, and the work of diverse and lowly men, one cannot rightly return honors to individuals. How can a state be in a right condition if it is deprived of this very thing? <term>CLEINIAS.</term> Nearly impossible. Nevertheless, stranger, we Cretans believe that the naval battle of the Greeks against the Barbarians at Salamis saved all of Greece. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> Indeed, many Greeks as well as Barbarians affirm this. But I, my friend, and Megillus here, say that the land battle at Marathon and the one at Plataea—one was the beginning of salvation, the other the end. And by these battles the Greeks were made better, but by the others they were not made better—to speak thus of the battles by which we were equally saved then. To the war waged at Salamis, I add that maritime battle which was committed at Artemisium. But looking now at the virtue of civil discipline, and the nature of the region, we consider the order of laws. For we do not think that being saved <margin>D</margin> and merely existing is to be held in the highest price by men, as the common people think, but that they should be as good as possible as long as they exist. This was also said by us in the previous parts, I believe. <term>CLEINIAS.</term> Plainly said. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> Let us therefore only observe whether we are following the same path which is best for cities in establishing a settlement and making laws. <term>CLEINIAS.</term> In a marvelous way. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> Tell me then what follows: what multitude will inhabit the colony? Is it whoever wishes from all of Crete, as if a great crowd were overflowing in individual cities? Or are they chosen for the strength and fertility of the land itself? For you do not gather all who wish from the Greeks, although I see some from Argos and Aegina and other parts of Greece inhabiting this region. But <margin>E</margin> at present you should tell me from where the multitude of these citizens will now come to you. <term>CLEINIAS.</term> I think it will be from all of Crete, and among other Greeks, those who come from the Peloponnese will, in my opinion, be most welcomed. What you were just saying is true, namely that they are from Argos. For that race which is now most praised here is Gortynian, which migrated here from Gortyn in the Peloponnese. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> But that migration into one city is not usually so easy for cities when it does not happen in the manner of swarms <note>original: *examinum*</note>, where one friendly race coming from a certain region—either pressed by the narrowness of the land or forced by some other such necessity—migrates into a foreign place. Sometimes <margin>F</margin> it happens that when a city is agitated by seditions, one part of the citizens withdraws elsewhere. Even an entire city, conquered in war, is sometimes found to have fled together. All these things are partly easy for being arranged in a new settlement and governed by newly placed laws, and partly difficult. For a race that is of one language and the same laws, since it has a community of sacred things and all such matters, is joined by some mutual friendship; but it does not easily accept other laws and a mode of government differing from its former one. But that which was stirred by seditions due to the wickedness of its own laws, since it desires those first <margin>G</margin> habits by which it was corrupted, shows itself hard and disobedient to the one governing and placing laws. That which has flowed together from various races will perhaps more willingly listen to new laws; but it is altogether arduous, and requires a long time, so that they can conspire and, like horses under one yoke, breathe one and the same thing, as the saying goes. But indeed, the sanction of laws and the constitution of a city is most perfect for the virtue of all men. <term>CLEINIAS.</term> That is probable indeed, but explain more clearly, good man, why you said that. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> While I wished to consider and praise legislators, I seem to have slipped into saying something trivial. However, if it is said opportunely, it will cause no trouble. And why do I hesitate, since almost all human things seem to be thus. <term>CLEINIAS.</term> Concerning what matter do you speak? <term>ATHENIAN.</term> I was about to say that no human ever <margin>H</margin> sanctions anything by law, but fortunes and various falling cases bring laws to us through all things. For either the violence of an imminent war overturns the prior republic and changes the laws, or some extreme poverty. Diseases also compel many to innovate. A long plague also, and the inconveniences of many years, and unseasonable weather. If anyone observes these things, he will not fear to exclaim the same thing I do now: that no mortal—

<summary>This page discusses the moral dangers of naval power, which Plato argues encourages cowardice and fails to reward virtue, and explores the challenges of founding a colony with mixed populations. It concludes with the philosophical observation that human laws are often dictated by external calamities like war, poverty, and disease rather than pure human agency.</summary>

# OF PLATO

<margin>
God and fortune, together with opportunity, govern all things, while art follows them.
</margin>

A ...that men do not establish laws, but that all human affairs are driven by fortunes. If someone were to assert this regarding navigation, piloting, medicine, or military command, they would seem to speak rightly. But then again, the following may also be said just as well concerning these same things. <term>CLINIAS.</term> <note>Clinias is a Cretan politician and one of the three main characters in this dialogue.</note> What is that? <term>ATHENIAN.</term> <note>The "Athenian Stranger" is the lead speaker, often thought to represent Plato’s own mature views.</note> That God indeed governs all things, and that fortune and opportunity govern all human affairs along with God. Yet, we must more gently allow a third factor to follow these: namely, art (or skill). For I believe that when a storm is imminent, it makes a great difference whether you possess the art of piloting or not. Is that not how we should put it? <term>CLINIAS.</term> Quite so. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> Does the same reasoning not apply to other things as well? And truly, the same must be granted to the laying down of laws: even if all other factors that lead to the happy settlement of a region coincide, a legislator who is a master of B truth should still be present for the state. <term>CLINIAS.</term> You speak the truth. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> Therefore, could not he who possesses the art in each of these cases rightly pray that something might be granted to him by fortune, so that he might need nothing other than his own skill? <term>CLINIAS.</term> Certainly. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> And all the others we just mentioned, if someone asked them, would they not reveal their own prayers and vows? <term>CLINIAS.</term> Clearly. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> The legislator, I believe, will do the same. <term>CLINIAS.</term> I think so. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> Come then, let us ask him: "O legislator, what kind of city do you wish to be handed over to you, so that you might thereafter be able to sufficiently organize it?" What would be C the right thing to say next? Should we provide the legislator’s answer? <term>CLINIAS.</term> By all means. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> He will say: "Give me a city ruled by a tyrant." <note>original: *Tyrannidi subiectam*. In this context, a "tyrant" refers to an absolute ruler with the power to make sweeping changes quickly, not necessarily an "evil" ruler in the modern sense.</note> And let the tyrant be young, possessing a strong memory, quick-witted, brave, and naturally magnificent. And that which we said earlier must follow all parts of virtue, let that also be present in the tyrant's soul, if indeed the other qualities are to be of any use. <term>CLINIAS.</term> It seems to me, Megillus, that the Stranger is saying that <term>temperance</term> <note>original: *Temperantiam* / *σωφροσύνην*. This refers to self-control, moderation, or "soundness of mind."</note> ought to be present in the soul of the tyrant. Is that not so? <term>ATHENIAN.</term> I mean the popular kind, Clinias—not that temperance which someone might solemnly call "wisdom," insisting that temperance is the same as being prudent—but that very D disposition which appears naturally at once in children and animals, so that some seem born more prone to pleasures, and others more continent. We said that this continence, when separated from the other goods, is of little value. Do you follow what I am saying? <term>CLINIAS.</term> Very much so. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> Let the tyrant, then, have this nature in addition to those other natural qualities, if the city is to achieve, as quickly and as well as possible, that government under which it may live most happily. For no swifter or better disposition of a city exists, or could ever exist. <term>CLINIAS.</term> But how, Stranger, and by what reasoning could anyone persuade himself that this is rightly said? <term>ATHENIAN.</term> It is easy to understand, Clinias, that this is the way it is by nature. <term>CLINIAS.</term> What do you mean? Are you asserting that this is the case if the tyrant is young, temperate, and excels in sharpness of mind and memory, being brave, magnificent, and fortunate? <term>ATHENIAN.</term> Add E nothing else, except that in his time a legislator worthy of praise is found, and some fortune brings them together. For if this happens, God has given nearly everything He usually gives whenever He wants a city to be exceptionally happy. Secondly, if there are two such rulers. Thirdly, if there are three. And in the same way for any succession, it becomes more difficult the more rulers there are; and conversely, the fewer there are, the easier it is. <term>CLINIAS.</term> You seem to affirm that the best republic is formed from a tyranny, provided there is a supreme legislator and a modest tyrant, and that the change from the former to the latter happens most easily and quickly. Second, from the power of a few (oligarchy). Third, from a popular power (democracy). Is it not so? <term>ATHENIAN.</term> Not at all. Rather, first from a tyranny. Next, F from a royal government (monarchy). Third, from a kind of democracy. Finally, the power of a few—oligarchy—undertakes the generation of the best republic with the greatest difficulty. For in an oligarchy, there are many powerful men. But we say these things happen when a true lawgiver is found by nature, and he happens to share a common power with those who have the most influence in the city. Where those in power are very few in number, but greatest in strength—as happens in a tyranny—there the change tends to be swift and easy. <term>CLINIAS.</term> How so? We do not understand. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> And yet, I think this has been said by us not once, but many times. But perhaps you have never seen a city weighed down by tyranny? <term>CLINIAS.</term> I have G no desire to see such a sight. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> Yet you would see in it what we have just described. <term>CLINIAS.</term> What is that? <term>ATHENIAN.</term> That a tyrant who wishes to change the customs of a city needs neither much labor nor a long time. For whether he wishes to lead the citizens toward the duties of virtue or the opposite, he must first enter upon the path himself for others to follow, and he must prescribe all things first by expressing them in his own actions—praising and honoring some things, while blaming others, and always disgracing those who do not obey in their individual actions. <term>CLINIAS.</term> But how can we believe that the citizens will quickly follow him everywhere, when he uses such persuasion and force? <term>ATHENIAN.</term> Let no one H persuade you, my friends, that there is any other way for the laws in a city to be changed more quickly and easily than by the example of those in power. Nor should you think it happens differently now, or will in the future. Certainly, this is neither impossible for us, nor difficult to do. But what is difficult to achieve, and has rarely happened...

<column-break/>

Α ...to legislate nothing strange, but that chance should bear all human things along. This is what one might say about navigation, piloting, medicine, and generalship, and seem to speak well. But indeed, one might also speak well in these same matters by saying this: <term>CLINIAS.</term> Saying what? <term>ATHENIAN.</term> That God indeed governs all, and with God, chance and opportunity steer all human affairs together. We must more gently grant that a third factor, art, should follow these; for I would consider it a great advantage to have the pilot's art during a winter storm, or not. Or what do you think? <term>CLINIAS.</term> Just so. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> Therefore, it is necessary that the same B reasoning holds for the others as well, and truly this same thing must be granted to legislation: that while all the other factors must coincide for a land to be fortunate—if it is ever to be lived in happily—the legislator must hold fast to the truth and attend to such a city in each instance. <term>CLINIAS.</term> You speak most truly. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> Therefore, would not he who possesses the art in each of the mentioned cases be able to pray rightly that something might be present to him through chance, so that he would only require his art? <term>CLINIAS.</term> Certainly. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> And all the others just now mentioned, if we commanded them to speak what they must, would they not do so? <term>CLINIAS.</term> Certainly. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> And the same thing, I think, the legislator would do. <term>CLINIAS.</term> I think so. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> Come then, legislator (let us say to him), what city and C in what condition shall we give you, which you, having received it, will then be able to sufficiently manage for the future? What is the right thing to say after this? Shall we state the legislator's words? Shall we not? <term>CLINIAS.</term> Yes. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> This: "Give me a city ruled by a tyrant," he will say. "And let the tyrant be young, and of good memory, and a quick learner, and brave, and magnificent by nature. And that which we said before must follow all the parts of virtue, let this now accompany the soul of the tyrant, if the other qualities of the rulers are to be of any benefit." <term>CLINIAS.</term> The Stranger seems to be saying, Megillus, that <term>temperance</term> <note>Greek: *sophrosyne*</note> must be well-present in the tyrant; is that not so? <term>ATHENIAN.</term> The popular kind, D Clinias, and not the kind someone would solemnly call "prudence," <note>Greek: *phronesis*</note> forcing the meaning of being temperate; but that which immediately blooms in children and animals—the innate quality where some are incontinent toward pleasures and others are continent. This, even when isolated from the many so-called goods, we said was not worth mentioning. Do you understand what I mean? <term>CLINIAS.</term> Certainly. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> Let the tyrant have this nature in addition to those other natures, if the city is to achieve as quickly and as best as possible the constitution which, having obtained it, it will live most happily. For there is not, nor could there ever be, a swifter and better arrangement for a constitution. <term>CLINIAS.</term> How indeed, and by what reasoning, Stranger, could someone say this and persuade himself that he is speaking rightly? <term>ATHENIAN.</term> It is easy to perceive this, Clinias, how this is so according to nature. <term>CLINIAS.</term> How do you mean? If a tyrant becomes (you say) young, E temperate, a quick learner, of good memory, brave, magnificent, and fortunate? <term>ATHENIAN.</term> Add also this: that in his time a legislator worthy of praise is born, and some chance brings them into the same place. For when this happens, everything has been nearly completed by God—the very things He does when He wishes a city to fare exceptionally well. Second, if ever such a thing happens with two rulers; third, by the same logic, it is harder the more there are; and the opposite, if the opposite. <term>CLINIAS.</term> You say the best city comes from a tyranny, provided there is a supreme legislator and an orderly tyrant; and that it would change most easily and quickly into this from such a state. Second, from an oligarchy—or how do you say? And third, from a democracy. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> Not at all; but from a tyranny first; F second, from a royal constitution; third, from some kind of democracy; and fourth, an oligarchy could only receive the birth of such things with the greatest difficulty. For many powerful men exist within it. We say these things happen when a true legislator is born by nature, and some common strength happens to be shared by him with those who are most powerful in the city. Where the rulers are fewest in number but strongest in power, as in a tyranny, there a swift and easy change usually occurs. <term>CLINIAS.</term> How? For we do not understand. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> And yet it has been said by us not once, but, I think, many times. But perhaps you G have never even beheld a city under a tyrant. <term>CLINIAS.</term> Nor am I a desirer of that sight. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> And yet you would see in it what was just now said. <term>CLINIAS.</term> What is that? <term>ATHENIAN.</term> The tyrant needs no labors, nor any vast amount of time, when he wishes to change the habits of a city. For he must first travel himself by the very path he wishes, whether he wants to exhort the citizens toward the practices of virtue or the opposite, by himself first sketching out everything by his own actions: praising and honoring some things, while leading others to reproach, and disgracing the one who does not obey in each action. <term>CLINIAS.</term> And how do we think the other citizens will quickly follow the one who has taken up such a means of persuasion and force at once? <term>ATHENIAN.</term> Let no one H persuade us, friends, that a city could ever change its laws more quickly and easily by any other way than by the leadership of those in power; nor that it happens now by any other way, or ever will. For this is not impossible for us, nor would it happen with difficulty; but this is the difficult thing to happen, and it has occurred only rarely...

<summary>In this passage, Plato explores the idea that the fastest way to establish a virtuous society is through the cooperation of a "temperate tyrant" and a wise legislator. He argues that because an absolute ruler can lead by example and has the power to enforce new customs, their influence is the most efficient catalyst for moral and legal reform.</summary>

# ON THE LAWS, BOOK IV.

...over a long period of time; but when it occurs, it works ten thousand blessings and every good in the city where it arises. **A** <term>CLINIAS.</term><note>A Cretan statesman helping to found a new colony.</note> What is this thing you are describing? <term>ATHENIAN.</term><note>The lead speaker of the dialogue, representing Plato’s mature philosophical views.</note> It is whenever a divine love for temperate and just practices arises in those who hold great power—whether they rule as a monarch, or excel through great wealth, or by the nobility of their family. It might also happen if someone could bring back the nature of <term>Nestor</term>,<note>A legendary Greek king from the Iliad, famous for his extreme age, wisdom, and persuasive speech.</note> who they say excelled all men in the power of his speech, but even more so in his temperance. Such a man, they say, existed in the time of Troy, but certainly not in our own. If, then, such a man has ever existed, or will exist, or is among us now, he **B** himself lives a blessed life, and blessed are those who hear the words flowing from his temperate mouth. The same logic applies to all forms of power: whenever the greatest power in a man coincides with wisdom and temperance, then the birth of the best constitution and the best laws occurs; but it can happen in no other way. Let this be spoken as a kind of oracular myth; let it be shown that, in one sense, it is difficult for a city to become well-governed, but in another sense—if what we say should occur—it is by far the quickest and easiest thing of all. <term>CLINIAS.</term> How so? <term>ATHENIAN.</term> Let us try, like old men playing a game with a child, **C** to mold the laws in our conversation. <term>CLINIAS.</term> Let us proceed then, and delay no longer. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> Let us invoke God at the beginning of our city’s construction. May He hear us, and having heard, may He come to us with favor and kindness to help us arrange the city and its laws. <term>CLINIAS.</term> May He indeed come. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> But what kind of constitution do we have in mind to give the city? <term>CLINIAS.</term> Tell me more clearly what you mean. Do you mean a democracy, an oligarchy, an aristocracy, or a kingship? For surely you do not mean a tyranny, as we might suppose. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> Come then, which of you two would like to answer first and tell me which of these your own **D** constitution at home is? <term>MEGILLUS.</term><note>A Spartan (Lacedaemonian) participant in the dialogue.</note> Is it not more just that I, being the elder, should speak first? <term>CLINIAS.</term> Perhaps. <term>MEGILLUS.</term> Truly, Stranger, when I consider the constitution in <term>Lacedaemon</term>,<note>The region of Greece where Sparta is located.</note> I cannot tell you what name it should be called. For it seems to me to resemble a tyranny, since the power of the <term>Ephors</term><note>original: "ἐφόρων" - Five powerful Spartan magistrates elected annually to oversee the kings and the state.</note> is wonderfully tyrannical. Yet at times it seems to me to be the most democratic of all cities. To say it is not an aristocracy would be completely absurd. Furthermore, it contains a kingship that lasts for life, which is the most ancient of all, as is said by all men and by ourselves. Thus, being asked so suddenly, I truly cannot define which of these constitutions it is. <term>CLINIAS.</term> I seem to suffer the same difficulty as you, **E** Megillus. For I am quite at a loss to say which of these the constitution of Knossos is. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> That is because, my excellent friends, you actually participate in true constitutions. But those we just named are not real constitutions; they are merely "settlements" of cities, where one part of the inhabitants is mastered by another part and serves it. Each of these is named after the power of the master. But if a city is to be named in such a way, it ought to be called by the name of the God who is the true master of those who possess reason. <term>CLINIAS.</term> And who is this God? <term>ATHENIAN.</term> Shall we use a little myth if we want to explain this question properly? <term>CLINIAS.</term> Certainly. **F** <term>ATHENIAN.</term> Long before those settlements of cities we discussed earlier, it is said that in the time of <term>Cronos</term><note>A Titan from Greek mythology (identified with the Roman Saturn) who ruled during a fabled "Golden Age" before the reign of Zeus.</note> there was a government and a settlement that was very happy. Any of our modern states that are well-governed are but an imitation of it. <term>MEGILLUS.</term> It seems we ought to hear more about this. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> I think so too, and that is why I brought it into the middle of our talk. <term>MEGILLUS.</term> You are doing exactly what is right; and by completing the myth in order, as is fitting for an old man, you would be doing very well indeed. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> I must do as you say. The tradition has handed down a report of that blessed life—how everything was provided in abundance and of its own accord. The cause is said to be this: Cronos knew (just as we have discussed) that no human nature is capable of **G** managing all human affairs with absolute power without being filled with arrogance and injustice. Considering this, he set over our cities as kings and rulers not men, but beings of a more divine and excellent race: <term>daimones</term>.<note>original: "δαίμονας" - In this context, these are not "demons" but intermediary divine spirits or guardians.</note> We do the same today with our flocks and herds of tame animals: we do not make bulls the rulers of bulls, nor goats the rulers of goats, but we—a better race—rule over them. In the same way, the God, who is a lover of mankind, set over us the race of spirits, which is better than our own. These spirits, with great ease to themselves and great care for us, provided peace, modesty, liberty, and an abundance **H** of justice, making the races of men free from civil strife and happy. This story, using the truth, tells us even today that for any city where not a God but some mortal rules, there is no relief from evils or labors. Rather, it suggests we must imitate by every means the life said to have existed under Cronos, and insofar as there is... ...there will be a rest from labors. But we must imitate with all zeal...

<column-break/>

...done over a long time; which if it should ever happen, it will produce **A** countless and immense goods for the city to which it occurs. <term>CLINIAS.</term> What is that? <term>ATHENIAN.</term> If ever a divine love of acting temperately and justly is born in a great power, which resides either in a single authority, or in the rule of several who excel in wealth or nobility of birth; or if ever someone should bring back the nature of Nestor, whom they say excelled all others much more in his eloquence of speech and temperance of life—such a man as is said to have lived in the times of Troy, but not at all in our own. If, I say, such a man was at some time, or will be, or is now among us, he **B** himself lives blessedly, and those too are blessed who hear the modest words flowing from his mouth. The same reasoning applies to all power: namely, that when the highest power meets with prudence and temperance in the same man, then finally the origin of the best government and the best laws will shine forth, but otherwise never. But let these things be spoken like a myth in the manner of oracles, and let it be shown, <margin>It is difficult to found a city with good laws.</margin> partly that it is difficult for a city to be founded with good laws, but partly that if that which we have said should happen, it is by far the easiest and shortest work of all. <term>CLINIAS.</term> In what way? <term>ATHENIAN.</term> Let us now attempt to adapt the whole matter to your city, just as **C** older men for children, fashioning laws through speech. <term>CLINIAS.</term> Let us approach it now without delay. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> In the first place, let us invoke God for the <margin>God must be invoked before all works are begun.</margin> constitution of the city. May He hear, and hearing, come to us propitious and kind, to adorn the city and the laws along with us. <term>CLINIAS.</term> I wish that He may come. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> But what kind of polity—that is, Republic—do we wish to deliver to the city? <term>CLINIAS.</term> Declare if you please what you mean: whether the power of the people, or of the few, or of the best men, or a kingdom. For we do not think you mean a tyranny. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> Come now, which of you wants to respond to me first: which of these is the republic of your own fatherland? **D** <term>MEGILLUS.</term> Is it not right, because I am older, that I should respond first? <term>CLINIAS.</term> Perhaps. <term>MEGILLUS.</term> When I revolve the Lacedaemonian republic in my mind, Stranger, I cannot easily tell you how it should be named. For it seems to be similar to a tyranny. For the power of the Ephors there is tyrannical in a wonderful way. Yet sometimes it appears most similar to a popular government above other cities. To deny that it is a republic of the best men (aristocracy) is altogether absurd. A kingdom also exists in it perpetually, which is said by others as well as ourselves to be the most ancient of all. Therefore, having been interrogated so suddenly, in truth, as I was saying, I cannot distinctly answer you at present which of those it is. <term>CLINIAS.</term> It seems to me, Megillus, **E** to have happened to me just as it did to you. For I do not know which of those I should affirm the Gnosian republic to be. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> For you are participants, O best of men, in true republics. But those which were just named are not republics, but certain habitations of cities, in which one part serves another dominant part, and the whole government takes its name from the power of the dominant part. But if a city were to be named in this way, it ought to be called by the name of God himself, who is the true lord of those who are composed of mind. <term>CLINIAS.</term> But who is that God? <term>ATHENIAN.</term> Must we use a myth for a little while, if we wish to declare **F** properly what was just asked? Or should we not do so? <term>CLINIAS.</term> By all means. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> Long before the habitations of cities, of which mention was made by us in the previous sections, it is said there was a certain principality and government under Saturn that was very happy. A certain imitation of this is held by that which is now governed by the best men. <term>CLINIAS.</term> Therefore, it seems, we must listen to this more attentively. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> It seems so to me, and for that reason I have just brought it forward. <term>MEGILLUS.</term> You do rightly indeed, and you will do well if you explain the following myth as far as is fitting. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> I will do as you say. The fame of that blessed life has indeed reached us, that it had all things in abundance and prepared of its own accord. The cause of this is handed down as follows: Since Saturn understood, **G** just as we have narrated, that no human nature can govern human affairs in such a way that, if he rules all things by his own will, he is not filled with wanton pride and injustice; since, I say, he was not ignorant of these things, he set over our cities as kings and princes not men, but demons of a more divine and excellent race, which we now do in flocks of sheep and herds of other tame animals. For we do not set bulls over bulls, nor goats over goats, but we ourselves, a better race, rule over them. Similarly, God, loving men, set over our race the race of demons, more excellent than us, which with the greatest ease—both their own and ours—took care of our affairs, and providing peace, **H** modesty, liberty, and an abundance of justice, made the race of men happy and far from sedition. This speech, using the truth, asserts that for all cities over which not God, but some mortal rules, there is never any quiet from evils, never any... ...commands that life which was under Saturn, and as much as is in us...

<summary>The Athenian Stranger explains that the ideal state arises when absolute power meets divine wisdom, using the "Myth of Cronos" to show that humans are unfit to rule other humans without divine guidance. He argues that modern "constitutions" are merely systems of partisan dominance, whereas a true state should be modeled after the rule of God or reason.</summary>
