<meta>This page continues the dialogue between the Athenian Stranger, Cleinias, and Megillus. In the previous section, they concluded that a great legislator needs a "divine love for temperance" to truly succeed. This page moves into the philosophical foundation of law: that law should be the "distribution of mind" rather than a tool for the powerful, and it concludes with a famous theological address on the nature of God and Justice.</meta>

-># OF PLATO<-

<margin>A</margin> ...of immortality; obeying this, they should govern their households and cities both privately and publicly, calling this distribution of the mind "Law." <note>The Athenian makes a linguistic connection: in Greek, the word for Law (*Nomos*) is nearly identical to the word for Distribution (*Dianome*), implying law is the way Mind/Intelligence is distributed into the world.</note> For if one man, or a power of a few, or even a democracy, has a soul devoted to pleasure and desire, and seeks to be filled with these—and since it can never achieve this, it is vexed by an insatiable, unquenchable fire and a terminal disease—and if such a power rules over a city or some private individuals while despising the laws, there is, as I was just saying, no hope of salvation. It is proper to consider, O Cleinias, whether we should believe this reasoning, or do otherwise. CLIN. We must believe it. <margin>B</margin> ATHEN. You perceive that some think there are as many types of laws as there are types of governments. We recently recounted how many types of governments most people propose. Do not think our current dispute is over a trivial matter, but rather over the greatest of things. For the question of what Justice and Injustice should look toward has fallen into ambiguity once again. For they say that laws should not refer to war, nor to virtue as a whole, but rather to whatever benefits the established state—whatever that state may be—so that it may always rule and never perish. They contend that the definition of Justice is best stated by nature in this way. <margin>C</margin> CLIN. In what way? ATHEN. That it is "whatever benefits the stronger." <note>This "Might makes Right" argument is a famous challenge Plato addresses in several works, most notably through the character Thrasymachus in the *Republic*.</note> CL. Speak more clearly. ATH. Take it this way: They say that whichever party rules the city always establishes the laws. Is that not so? CL. Certainly. ATH. Do you think (they ask) that either a victorious common people, or some other form of state, or even a tyrant, would willingly pass laws for any other reason than their own advantage—that is, the stability of their own rule? CL. For no other reason. ATHEN. And if anyone should transgress these laws once they are established, they will be punished as a lawbreaker by the one who introduced these institutions and calls them "Just." CL. So it appears. ATH. In this way, Justice will always be defined by that standard. CL. Indeed, this logic asserts that. ATH. This is surely one of those "wrongs" regarding the right to rule. CL. Which ones? <margin>D</margin> ATH. Those which we recounted above, explaining who ought to command whom. We said that parents should rule over children and grandchildren, elders over the younger, and the noble over the low-born. There were several others, if you remember, some of which stood in the way of others, and this was one of them. We added that Pindar <note>A famous Greek lyric poet.</note> considered it to be according to nature and just for the more powerful to rule over the weaker. CLIN. These things were certainly said then. ATHEN. Consider now to whom our city should be committed. For this has happened ten thousand times in various cities. CLIN. What has? <margin>E</margin> ATH. When there has been a struggle for rule, those who won seized control of the city’s affairs so entirely for themselves that they granted no office to the defeated or their descendants, always guarding against the possibility that one of the defeated might gain power and rise up, remembering past evils. We, of course, deny that these are true republics, nor do we think those laws are right which were not established for the sake of the whole city in common. Those who enact laws for the sake of a faction, we consider to be not citizens but partisans; and we think their claims of "Justice" are spoken in vain. We say these things because, in your city, we will not give office to someone because he is wealthy, or possesses anything of that sort—such as strength, size, or nobility of birth. Rather, we say that the one who most obeys the established laws, and in this way excels the others in the city, should be given the service and ministry of the gods: the highest office to the first, and the second office to him who excels in the second degree. And in the same way, we shall distribute each office in order according to worthiness. <margin>F</margin> I have called the magistrates "servants of the laws," not because I wish to invent new names, but because I believe the salvation of the city depends on this more than anything else—and the opposite leads to the opposite. For I see destruction is ready for that city in which the law is ruled by and lacks authority over the magistrates. But where the law is master over the magistrates, and the magistrates are servants of the law, I see salvation and all the good things that the gods provide to cities. CL. By Jove, Stranger, you see clearly for your age. For a young man sees such things quite dimly, but an old man sees them most sharply. MEGIL. You speak the truth. ATHEN. What then follows? Should we not assume the colonists have arrived and are present, and we should deliver the rest of our discourse to them? CL. What is stopping us? <margin>G</margin> ATHEN. Let us say this to them then: "O men, God—as the ancient saying witnesses—holding the beginning, the end, and the middle of all things, accomplishes his straight path by revolving according to nature. <note>The "ancient saying" likely refers to an Orphic or Pythagorean doctrine about the divine order of the universe.</note> Justice always accompanies Him, punishing those who fall away from the divine law. He who intends to be happy, clinging to this Justice, follows it with humility and order. But he who is lifted up by pride—whether he is puffed up by wealth or honors, or by beauty of body combined with the madness and insolence of youth—as if he needed no ruler or leader, but were himself a sufficient guide for others, is left behind, deserted by God. Being deserted, and finding others like himself, he skips about, throwing everything into confusion; and to many he seems to be someone of importance. Yet shortly after, suffering a punishment from Justice that cannot be faulted, he utterly overthrows himself, his house, and the entire city. Since these things are thus arranged, what ought a prudent man to do or think, or what should he avoid?" CLIN. There is no doubt that every man must think of how he might be among those who follow God.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...of immortality exists, obeying this, they should manage their households and cities in public and private life, naming the distribution of mind "Law." <note>original: "τὴν τοῦ νοῦ διανομὴν ἐπονομάζοντας νόμον" - the Greek highlights the pun on 'Nomos' (Law) and 'Nous' (Mind).</note> If, however, a single man, or some oligarchy, or even a democracy, possessing a soul that reaches out for pleasures and desires and needs to be filled with them—containing nothing, but being insatiable and filled with a wicked disease—should rule over a city or some individual, having trampled the laws; as I said, there is no means of salvation. We must consider this argument, O Cleinias, whether we shall be persuaded by it, or what we shall do. CL. It is necessary, I suppose, to be persuaded. <margin>B</margin> ATHEN. Do you perceive, then, that some say there are as many kinds of laws as there are of constitutions? We just went through as many constitutions as the many people describe. Do not think this is a trivial dispute, but one concerning the greatest matter. For the question of where Justice and Injustice ought to look has come back to us in dispute. For they say that laws should look neither toward war nor toward virtue as a whole, but rather toward whatever benefit the established constitution happens to have, so that it may always rule and not be dissolved. And they say the natural definition of Justice is best stated this way. CL. How? ATHEN. That it is "the advantage of the stronger." CL. Speak more clearly in this way. <margin>C</margin> ATH. They say, I suppose, that the ruling power in the city establishes the laws in each instance. Isn't that so? CLEIN. You speak the truth. ATHEN. Do you think, then (they say), that a victorious people, or any other constitution, or even a tyranny, would ever willingly establish anything as primary other than its own permanent interest in ruling? CLEIN. How could they not? ATHEN. And so, whoever transgresses these established things, the one who established them will punish him as a wrongdoer, naming these things "Just." CL. So it seems, at least. ATHEN. These things, then, would always and in this way be what Justice is. CL. At least, that is what this argument says. ATH. For this is one of those wrongs regarding ruling. CL. What kind, then? ATHEN. Those which we were examining then—who should rule over whom. And it appeared that parents should rule over offspring, the elder over the younger, the noble <margin>D</margin> over the ignoble, and there were many others which, if we remember, were sometimes in the way of each other. And indeed, one was this very thing, and we said somewhere that Pindar justifies the most violent thing as being "according to nature," as he said. CL. Yes, these were the things said then. ATHEN. Consider then to which of the two our city should be entrusted. For such a thing has happened ten thousand times already in some cities. CL. What kind of thing? ATHEN. When there have been battles over offices, those who won seized the affairs of the city so greedily for themselves that they shared no part of the rule with the defeated—neither with them nor their descendants. They live <margin>E</margin> suspecting one another, lest someone ever coming into office should rise up, remembering the past evils that occurred. We say now, I suppose, that these are not constitutions, nor are laws right that were not established for the sake of the whole city in common. But those enacted for the sake of some people, we call these "factions" but not "constitutions"; and their "Justices," they say, are spoken in vain. This is said for the sake of these things: for we shall not give offices in our city because someone is wealthy, nor because he possesses any other such thing like strength, or size, or birth. But whoever is most obedient to the established laws, and wins a victory in this over those in the city, to him we say the service of the gods should be given—the first and greatest service to the first, and let the second offices follow to the second in order. I have called those who are named "rulers" today "servants of the laws," not for the sake of innovating names, but because I believe that more than anything else, salvation or the opposite for a city depends on this. <margin>F</margin> For in whatever city the law is ruled and lacks authority, I see destruction ready for such a city; but in whatever city the law is master of the rulers, and the rulers are slaves to the law, I see salvation and every good thing that the gods have given to cities. CL. Yes, by Zeus, O Stranger. For you see clearly for your age. ATHEN. For every man, when he is young, sees such things most dimly, but as an old man, he sees them most sharply. CLEIN. Most true. ATHEN. What then is next? Should we not assume the settlers have already arrived and are present, and that we must finish the rest of the discourse for them? CL. How could we not? <margin>G</margin> ATHEN. "Men," we shall say to them, "God (as the ancient saying goes) holding the beginning and the end and the middle of all beings, completes his straight path, traveling according to nature. Justice always follows Him, the avenger of those who fall short of the divine law. He who intends to be happy, holding onto this Justice, follows it humble and orderly. But a certain person who is lifted up by arrogance, or raised up by wealth or honors, or even beauty of body, together with youth and folly, his soul burning with insolence, as if he needed neither a ruler nor any leader, but were capable even of leading others, is left behind, deserted by God. Being deserted, and taking to himself others of the same kind, he leaps about, throwing everything into confusion at once; and to many he seems to be someone of importance, but after not much time, suffering an undeniable punishment from Justice, he brings himself, his house, and his city to total ruin. In the face of these things thus arranged, what should the prudent man do or think, and what should he not?" CL. This is clear, that every one of those who will be must think that he must be of those who follow God...

<meta>This page continues the Athenian Stranger’s discourse on the divine foundation of the state. Having established that the law should be the "distribution of mind," he now addresses the moral character required of a citizen to be "dear to God."</meta>

### ON THE LAWS, BOOK IV.

<margin>A</margin> ...let us ask the man. ATHENIAN: What action then is dear to and follows God? One indeed, which has a single ancient and primary principle: that like is dear to like, provided it is moderate. <note>original: "τῷ μὲν ὁμοίῳ τὸ ὅμοιον ὄντι μέτριον φίλον ἂν εἴη"</note> But immoderate things are dear neither to each other nor to those that are moderate. For us, **God would be the measure of all things** in the highest degree—far more so than any man, as they say. <note>This is a direct rebuttal to the Sophist Protagoras, who famously claimed "Man is the measure of all things."</note> Therefore, he who intends to become dear to such a being must himself become like him to the best of his ability. According to this reasoning, the temperate man among us is dear to God, for he is like Him; while the intemperate man is unlike Him, different, and unjust; and the same applies to all other things. <margin>B</margin> Let us understand that the following principle follows these, being, I believe, the most beautiful and true of all: that for the good man to sacrifice and always commune with the gods through prayers, offerings, and every form of divine service is the most beautiful, best, and most effective way toward a happy life, and is especially fitting. But for the wicked man, the opposite is true. For the wicked man is impure in soul, whereas his opposite is pure. From the impure, it is never right for a good man or a God to accept gifts. Therefore, the great labor of the unholy concerning the gods is in vain, while for the holy, it is most timely and effective. <margin>C</margin> This then is the mark at which we ought to aim. But what are the "arrows," so to speak, and what is their proper flight, that we might speak most correctly? First, we say, after the honors of the Olympian and the presiding gods of the city, one would most correctly hit the mark of piety by assigning to the earthly gods <note>original: "χθονίοις... θεοῖς" — gods of the underworld or the earth, as opposed to the sky-dwelling Olympians.</note> even, second, and left-handed honors; and to those above them, the odd and the opposite honors to those just mentioned. After these gods, the man of sound mind would perform rites for the spirits <note>original: "δαίμοσιν" — daemons or divine intermediaries.</note>, and after them for the heroes. Following these come the private shrines of ancestral gods, consecrated according to the law. <margin>D</margin> After these come the honors for living parents, to whom it is right to pay the first and greatest of all debts, the oldest of all obligations. For one must believe that everything he possesses and has belongs to those who generated and nurtured him, so that he might provide these things for their service with all his strength: beginning first with <margin>D</margin> his property; second, the things of his body; and third, the things of his soul; thus repaying the debts of care and the ancient labor of birth-pains lent to him when young, and returning them to the old in their old age when they are in greatest need. Throughout one's entire life, one should maintain and have maintained an especially reverent speech toward his parents; for there is a very heavy penalty for light and winged words. For **Nemesis**, the messenger of Justice, is appointed as the overseer of all such matters. <note>Nemesis was the Greek goddess of retribution who punished arrogance and the neglect of duty.</note> One must, therefore, yield to them when they are angry and venting their wrath, whether they do so in word or deed, recognizing that a father who thinks he is being wronged by his son would naturally be exceedingly angry. When parents have died, the most moderate burial is the most beautiful; one should not exceed the customary monuments, nor fall short of what the ancestors provided for their own parents. One should also perform the annual rites of care for those who have already reached their end, which bring honor. By providing a continuous and unceasing memory, one honors them most of all, allotting a moderate portion of the wealth granted by fortune to the departed. Doing these things and living according to them at all times, we each would receive our worthy reward from the gods and those superior to us, spending the greatest part of our lives in good hope. <margin>E</margin> As for what one should do toward children, relatives, friends, citizens, and the hospitality and service of strangers commanded by the gods—completing one's own <margin>F</margin> life by brightening it with all these things—one must adorn it according to the law. The detailed treatment of the laws themselves, partly by persuading and partly by punishing through force and justice those who do not yield to persuasion, will render our city happy and blessed by the gods and spirits. But as for the things which it is both necessary and proper for a legislator to say—who thinks as I do—but which do not seem to fit conveniently into the form of a pure law, I believe it is necessary to provide an example of these first, both for the legislator himself and for those who are to be instructed by the law, and thereafter to begin the drafting of the laws, discussing all the rest to the best of one's ability. <margin>G</margin> How then might such things best be arranged? It is not at all easy to encompass them in a single formula; but let us take a certain approach to them, if we can affirm anything about them. CLIN. Tell me, what approach? ATHEN. I would wish them to be as persuasive as possible toward virtue; and it is clear the legislator will attempt this in his entire legislation. CLIN. Of course. ATHEN. Now, what has been said seems to me to contribute significantly to this: that the soul of the listener might not be entirely harsh, but rather milder and more benevolent in hearing the precepts. Thus, if it achieves even a little instead of a great deal, making the listener more benevolent and thus easier to teach, that is something to be welcomed. For there is no great ease or abundance of those who strive to become as good and as quickly as possible. Many declare **Hesiod** to be wise when he says that the road to wickedness is smooth and can be traveled without sweat, being very short:

> Before Virtue, the immortal gods have placed sweat;
> And the path to her is long and steep
> And rough at first; but when one reaches the summit,
> Then it becomes easy, though it was hard before.

<column-break/>

<margin>ATHENIAN</margin> What action then is loved by God, and follows Him? One indeed, certainly having one ancient and primary reason, that like is dear to like, provided it is moderate. Immoderate things, however, are dear neither to each other nor to those that are moderate. God truly would be for us the measure of all things in the highest degree, and much more so than any man, as they say. He who therefore desires to be a friend to such a being, it is necessary that he become such a man himself as much as possible. And according to this reasoning, whoever among men is temperate is dear to God. For he is like Him. But the intemperate man is unlike, different, and unjust, and other things similarly. <margin>B</margin> But let us understand that this reasoning follows all other reasonings, as I think, most beautiful and most true: that it befits a good man to sacrifice to the gods and to be present at divine matters. Truly to pursue them with prayers, gifts, and other divine worship is most beautiful, best, and most profitable for a blessed life, and it is decorous beyond all others. To the bad man, however, everything happens to the contrary. For the soul of the wicked is impure, but of the good, it is pure. From the impure, however, to receive gifts is becoming for neither a good man nor a God. In vain, therefore, do the profane labor regarding the gods, which all the holy do opportunely. And indeed, this is the mark toward which we must aim. <margin>C</margin> But what arrow is there for it, and what is their proper aim to speak most correctly? In the beginning, after the honors of the celestial gods and the gods presiding over the city, if anyone should grant to the earthly gods equal, fertile, and principal gifts, he will most correctly reach the mark of piety itself. But for those placed above these, the unequal and alternating ones responding to what was said above; after these gods, the man of sound mind will sacrifice to the spirits, and to the heroes after the spirits. There follow the statues of the ancestral gods, properly consecrated according to the law. Finally, the worship of living parents, to whom it is right to pay the first and greatest of all debts, the most ancient of obligations. <margin>D</margin> For everyone ought to think that all which he possesses belongs to those who begot and raised him, so that he ought to serve them in all these things according to his strength: first indeed with external goods, then also of the body, and finally those pertaining to the soul, obviously paying back all these things as borrowed, and in place of the cares and ancient pains of the parents, rendering new ones in their old age when they are most in need. Even in words, through the whole of life, it is most fitting to venerate parents. For a most heavy punishment hangs over light and winged words. For over all things is placed **Nemesis**, the messenger of judgment, the overseer of all such matters. It is necessary therefore to yield to them when they are angry and satisfying their wrath, whether they do it in words or deeds, not being ignorant that a father is quite rightly very angry with his son if at any time he thinks himself to be wronged by him. When parents are dead, the most becoming monuments are those most temperately constructed. It is not right to exceed the accustomed magnitude, nor to make them smaller than those which the ancestors built for their own parents. It is also fitting to renew the annual cares for the deceased which bring ornament, and with a new memory repeated daily, always to honor parents exceedingly, using a moderate expense according to fortune. If we observe these things, and as each of us always acts thus, we shall carry back worthy rewards from the gods and all others superior to our nature, living with great <margin>E</margin> good hope. <margin>F</margin> But what each ought to do toward children and grandchildren, kinsmen, friends, citizens, strangers, always worshiping the gods both in assembly and in all these dealings, and thus to illustrate his life according to the law, the treatment of the laws themselves will demonstrate, partly indeed by persuading, but partly by compelling harder characters with punishment; and thus it will make our city, with the gods favoring, happy and blessed. But what again is necessary and proper for the legislator, who agitates the same things as I do, to set forth, yet which do not seem to be able to be said conveniently under the form of law itself, an example of these I think must be brought forward first, as much for the legislator himself as for those who are to be instituted by law, and then the positioning of the laws should be begun, <margin>G</margin> discussing all the rest according to one's strength. How such things may best be held cannot easily be comprehended in one single formula. But thus let us take some measure concerning them, if we can affirm anything about them. CLIN. Tell me, what measure? ATHEN. I would wish them to be most persuaded and obedient to the duties of virtue, and the legislator will strive to do that everywhere. CLIN. Why not? ATHEN. The things which have been said seem to me to lead somewhat to that, so that if the mind of the hearer be not altogether raw, it may be made milder and more benevolent in hearing the precepts; but having been made more benevolent, it may learn more easily; and if this is not entirely achieved, it should be thought enough if it is done in at least some way. For there is no great abundance of those who strive to escape [wickedness] as best and as quickly as possible. Many preach that **Hesiod** is wise when he says that the way of vice is level, and is traveled without sweat because it is very short. But before virtue, he says, the immortal gods have placed sweat. And the way which leads to it is long, arduous, and rough at first; but after the highest summits have been reached, what had been an arduous way becomes easy.

<summary>In this passage, the Athenian Stranger explains that God, not man, is the measure of all things, and that a just society is built on a hierarchy of honors: first to the gods, then spirits, then heroes, and finally to living parents. He argues that laws should be preceded by persuasive "preambles" to make the citizens more willing to follow them, rather than relying solely on the threat of punishment.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the Athenian Stranger's argument regarding the moral and divine foundations of the law. Having discussed how a citizen should live to be dear to God, he now transitions into the practical methodology of law-making, specifically how a legislator should address the citizens—through either raw command or persuasive instruction.</meta>

# OF PLATO
## BOOK IV

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
...excels in the path. <term>CLINIAS.</term> He seems to speak well. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> That is certainly so. But I wish to place before you the direction in which our discourse was progressing. <term>CLINIAS.</term> Please do so. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> Let us turn our address to the legislator thus: "Tell us, O legislator, if you knew what we ought to do and say, would you not tell us?" <term>CLINIAS.</term> Necessarily. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> Did we not hear you saying a little while ago that the legislator should not permit poets to fashion whatever pleases them? For they do not understand which of their words, being contrary to the laws, might harm the city. <term>CLINIAS.</term> You speak the truth. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> If we were to say these things to him on behalf of the poets, would our words be modest? <term>CLINIAS.</term> Which words? <term>ATHENIAN.</term> "An ancient <margin>B</margin> story, O legislator, is commonly told by us and confirmed by everyone else: that when a poet sits upon the tripod of the Muse, <note>The "tripod" refers to the seat of the Pythia at Delphi, suggesting the poet acts as a divine medium rather than a rational composer.</note> he is not in his right mind, but flows like a fountain, and whatever flows in, he pours out. Since his art is a form of imitation, and he expresses the contrary passions of men, he is often compelled to say things that contradict himself, and he does not know which of these things is true. But it is not permitted for a legislator to say two different things about one matter in a law; rather, he must always announce one single thing about one thing." You will notice this from what you were just saying. Since some burials are excessive, others are deficient, and others hold the middle, you simply praised the moderate ones and ordered only them to be made. But if I had a very wealthy wife who ordered me to bury her magnificently, I would praise an excessive tomb in a poem; likewise, a poor and greedy man would praise a deficient one. But he who possesses moderate wealth and is himself moderate would praise the middle path. You, however, should not <margin>C</margin> speak as you did just now, merely saying "the moderate," but you must explain what the moderate is and how much it is. Otherwise, do not think such a speech is yet a law. <term>CLINIAS.</term> You speak most truly. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> Should the one who applies himself to establishing laws say nothing <margin>D</margin> of this sort in the beginning of the laws, but immediately set forth what must be done and what not, and having imposed the penalty, turn to another law, bringing no reasoning for exhortation or persuasion? Let us bring into the open two methods of healing, by which different doctors are accustomed to cure differently—just as children beg a doctor to cure them in the easiest way possible, let us ask the legislator. To make this clearer, do we not say that some are doctors, and others are assistants to doctors, whom we also call doctors? <term>CLINIAS.</term> Quite so. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> Whether they are free men or slaves, who possess the art by the command of their masters, by observation, use, and experience, but not according to nature—unlike the free doctors, who have both learned the art this way themselves and instruct their sons: do you posit these two kinds of doctors? <term>CLINIAS.</term> What forbids it? <term>ATHENIAN.</term> Do you then understand that since both slaves and free men <margin>E</margin> fall ill in the city, the slaves are mostly cured by slaves? These doctors run about the workshops and visit everyone; they neither give nor receive any rational account concerning the specific diseases of the servants. Instead, as if they knew exactly what they were doing, they give orders like proud and stubborn tyrants based on what seems useful from experience, and then fly off from one servant to another. In this way, they provide the master ease in caring for the sick. But the free doctor, for the most part, treats and considers the diseases of free men; he searches out the nature of the disease from its beginning, confers with the patient and his friends, and while learning something from them, he also teaches the sick person himself as much as possible. He does not issue any command until he has offered persuasion. And so, by always <margin>F</margin> persuading with gentleness, he attempts to lead the sick back to health. Which of the two is the better doctor or trainer: the one who heals and trains in this way, or the one who uses the other method? The one who performs a single task in a double way, or the one who does it simply, and follows the way which is the worse and more cruel of the two? <term>CLINIAS.</term> The double method is far superior, Guest. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> Do you wish then that we consider how this double and simple method occurs in the making of laws? <term>CLINIAS.</term> I certainly do. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> Tell me then, by the gods, what first law will the lawgiver write down? Will he not, according to nature, first adorn with regulations the very beginning of generation in the city? <term>CLINIAS.</term> Clearly. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> And the beginning of generation <margin>G</margin> for all cities is the union and communion of marriage. <term>CLINIAS.</term> Certainly. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> Therefore, if marriage laws are placed first, they will seem to be well placed for the right constitution of the whole city. <term>CLINIAS.</term> It is altogether so. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> Let us first state the simple law, which might perhaps be thus: "Every man shall marry between the age of thirty and thirty-five. If not, he shall be punished by a fine and dishonor; the fine shall be so much, and the dishonor of such a kind." This would be the simple law concerning marriage. But the double law would be thus: "A man should marry when he is thirty years old, up to thirty-five, reflecting that in a certain way the human race naturally partakes in immortality, <margin>H</margin> a thing for which everyone is by nature most desirous. For there is no one who <margin>Man is eternal through generation.</margin> does not desire to have a lasting name among posterity. The human race is thus immortal and persists for all time in this way: by leaving behind children's children, remaining one and the same always through generation..."

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> <term>CLINIAS.</term> And he seems to speak well. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> Entirely so. But the point to which the argument was leading and which it has worked out, I want to place in the midst for you. <term>CLINIAS.</term> Set it forth. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> Let us say then, speaking to the legislator: "Tell us, O legislator, <gloss>if indeed</gloss> you knew what we must do and say, is it not clear that you would also tell us?" <term>CLINIAS.</term> It is necessary. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> A little while ago, did we not hear you saying that the legislator must not allow the poets to say whatever is dear to them? For they would not know what they might say contrary to the laws that would harm the city. <term>CLINIAS.</term> You remember and speak the truth. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> If we were to say the following to him on behalf of the poets, would the things said be reasonable? <term>CLINIAS.</term> What things? <term>ATHENIAN.</term> "An old myth, O legislator, is always told by us, and is agreed upon by all others: that a poet, whenever he sits on the tripod of the Muse, is then not in his right mind, but like a fountain he readily allows what comes in to flow out. And since his art is imitation, he is forced, when making people with contrary dispositions, often to say things contrary to himself; and he does not know whether these or the other things said are true. But for the legislator, it is not possible to do this in the law—to say two things about one matter—but he must always declare one account about one thing. Consider this from the things just said by you. For regarding burial, there is the excessive, the deficient, and the moderate. Choosing one of these, the middle, you say this is to be appointed and you praised it simply. But I, if a woman were outstanding in wealth and ordered her own burial, I would praise the excessive tomb in a poem; and again, a stingy and poor man would praise the deficient; while a man possessing a middle estate and being moderate himself would praise the same. But you must not speak as you just did, merely saying 'moderate.' Rather, what the moderate is and how much, must be told; otherwise, do not yet consider such a speech of yours to be a law." <term>CLINIAS.</term> You speak most truly. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> Shall our appointed lawgiver address us with nothing of this sort at the beginning of the laws? But shall he straightway declare what must be done and what not, and having threatened the penalty, turn to another law, adding nothing of encouragement or persuasion to those for whom the laws are made? Just as there is a doctor such as we described, so there are those who treat us in each case in that way. Let us recall each way, so that we may beg the legislator, as children beg their fathers, to treat us in the gentlest way and persuade us. For example: we say there are some doctors, do we not, and some assistants of doctors? And do we not also call these men doctors? <term>CLINIAS.</term> Entirely so. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> Whether they are free or slaves, they acquire the art by the command of their masters and by observation and experience, but not according to nature, as the free men do, who have both learned it thus themselves and teach it to their own children. Would you posit these as two kinds of the so-called doctors? <term>CLINIAS.</term> How could I not? <term>ATHENIAN.</term> Do you also realize then that since there are slaves and free men among the sick in the cities, the slaves are mostly treated by slaves who run about or wait in the dispensaries? And none of these doctors gives or receives any account concerning each disease of each of the servants, but like a tyrant, having ordered what seems good to him from experience as if he knew it accurately, with arrogance, like a self-willed tyrant, he is off to another sick servant. In this way, he provides the master with ease in the care of the sick. But the free doctor for the most part treats and examines the diseases of free men; examining these from the beginning and according to nature, communicating with the sick person himself and his friends, he both learns something himself from the sick and, as far as he is able, teaches the patient himself. He does not issue a command until he has somehow persuaded him. Then, always making the sick person gentle with persuasion, leading him toward health, he tries to complete the cure. Is a doctor better who heals in this way or that, and a trainer who trains? By completing one power in a double way, or in a single way? And by working according to the worse and more savage of the two? <term>CLINIAS.</term> The double way, Guest, differs by far. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> Do you wish then that we observe this double and simple way occurring in the making of laws themselves? <term>CLINIAS.</term> How could I not wish it? <term>ATHENIAN.</term> Come then, by the gods, what first law would the lawgiver establish? Would he not, according to nature, first arrange the beginning of the generation of cities with regulations? <term>CLINIAS.</term> Of course. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> And is not the beginning of all generations in cities the mixing and communion of marriage? <term>CLINIAS.</term> How could it not be? <term>ATHENIAN.</term> It seems then that marriage laws, being established first, would be well established for the correctness of every city. <term>CLINIAS.</term> Entirely so. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> Let us then state the simple one first. It would perhaps go something like this: "A man shall marry when he is thirty years old, up to thirty-five years. If he does not, he must be punished by money and dishonor—by this much money, and by this or that dishonor." Let the simple one concerning marriage be of this sort. But the double one, thus: "A man shall marry when he is thirty years old, up to thirty-five, reflecting that there is a way in which the human race naturally partakes in immortality, for which everyone by nature has every desire. For to become famous, and not to lie nameless after death, is a desire for such a thing. Thus the race of men is naturally joined to all of time, which follows and will follow it to the end, being immortal in this way: by leaving behind children's children, being one and the same always by nature..."

<summary>The Athenian Stranger argues that laws should not be mere tyrannical commands, but should include persuasive preambles, comparing the ideal legislator to a "free" doctor who educates his patients rather than a "slave" doctor who merely dictates treatment. This principle is applied to the first law of the state—marriage—where the law encourages citizens to marry by explaining the role of procreation in human immortality.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the Athenian Stranger’s discourse on the nature of law. Having established that the goal of the city is virtue, he now moves into the specific method of legislating, using the example of marriage to distinguish between a law that simply commands and a law that seeks to persuade.</meta>

# ON THE LAWS, BOOK IV

...to partake in immortality. <note>Plato views the continuation of the species through children as a human way of sharing in divine immortality.</note> Truly, for a man to willingly deprive himself of this is never a holy act. <margin>A</margin> <margin>He deprives himself of the lineage of children if he neglects wife and offspring.</margin> If a man obeys the law, let him go unpunished; but if he does not obey, and remains unmarried at thirty-five years of age, let him be fined a certain amount annually, so that his solitary life does not seem to bring him profit or ease. Furthermore, let him have no share in the honors which the younger men in the city pay to their elders.

Hearing this law alongside the other, one might disagree on whether each law should be "double" in length at its shortest—by using persuasion and threats together—or whether it should be "single" in length by using threats alone.

<term>MEGILLUS</term> <note>Megillus is the Spartan (Lacedaemonian) representative in the dialogue, known for favoring brevity.</note>: The Laconian way, Stranger, is to always prefer the shorter version. However, if someone were to make me a judge of these writings, to choose which version I would want to have inscribed in my city, I would choose the longer one; and indeed, regarding every law, I would make the same choice following this example, if both versions were available. Yet, these laws must also please Clinias here, for it is his city that is now intending to use such laws.

<term>CLINIAS</term>: You have spoken well, Megillus.

<margin>B</margin> <term>ATHENIAN</term>: To make an argument about the length or shortness of writing is quite foolish. For I believe we should honor the best versions, not the shortest nor the longest. In the laws just mentioned, the one version does not merely differ from the other in being twice as long, but rather in what was said just now regarding the two types of doctors—this was very correctly applied. <note>Earlier, the Athenian compared "slave-doctors," who bark orders at patients, to "free-doctors," who explain the nature of the illness to the patient.</note> <margin>C</margin> It seems that no legislator has ever considered this: that while they might use two methods for legislation—persuasion and force—so far as is possible for the uneducated masses, they use only one. They do not mix persuasion into their law-making, but instead apply only pure force. 

But I, my friends, see a third thing that ought to happen regarding the laws, which is currently done nowhere.

<term>CLINIAS</term>: What is this thing you mean?

<term>ATHENIAN</term>: Something that has arisen from the very things we have been discussing, by some divine chance. For almost since the time we began speaking about the laws at dawn, it is now midday, and in this most beautiful resting place, we have done nothing else but <margin>D</margin> discuss laws. Yet it seems to me we are only now beginning to speak of the laws themselves; everything we said before was merely the **preambles** to the laws. 

Why do I say this? Because I wish to point out that all speech and every kind of vocal expression has its preambles and "preludes," which serve as a kind of artistic preparation, useful for what is about to be performed. Indeed, for the songs called "citharoedic <term>laws</term>" <note>In Greek, the word *nomos* meant both "law" and "musical melody." Plato is playing on this double meaning.</note> and for every kind of music, wonderfully crafted preambles are set forth. But for the actual laws—those we call political—no one has ever uttered a preamble, nor has any composer brought one into the light, as if such a thing did not exist by nature. <margin>E</margin> But our current conversation indicates to me that they do exist. 

The laws that seemed to me just now to be "double" are not simply double in a basic way; rather, they consist of two parts: the **law** itself and the **preamble** to the law. That which is a "tyrannical command"—which we compared to the orders of the slave-doctors—is the "pure law." But the part spoken before it, which was intended to be persuasive, has the power of a preamble in its speech. It was spoken so that the person to whom the legislator addresses the law might receive the command (which is the law) more benevolently and, because of that benevolence, be more ready to learn. Therefore, in my view, this entire persuasive speech should correctly be called the "preamble," not the law itself.

<margin>F</margin> Having said this, what do I wish to add? This: that the legislator should never make any law without its own preamble, and that each law should differ from the others by the degree to which these two parts we have discussed differ.

<term>CLINIAS</term>: For my part, I would not advise anyone knowledgeable in these matters to legislate in any other way.

<term>ATHENIAN</term>: You seem to have spoken well, Clinias, in saying that a preamble should precede all laws, and that at the start of all legislation, one must place the preamble that naturally fits each subject. For it is no small matter what follows, and it makes a great difference whether these things are remembered clearly or not. However, if we were to demand that preambles be crafted similarly for both major and minor laws, <margin>G</margin> we would not be speaking correctly. One does not do such a thing for every song or every speech. Although a preamble is naturally possible for all, it should not be used for all. We must leave this choice to the orator, the singer, and the legislator in each instance.

<term>CLINIAS</term>: You speak most truly. But let us no longer delay, Stranger; let us return to the argument and begin from those things you said before—not as if you were then making a preamble. Let us, as they say in the game, "start over from the beginning with better second tries," completing them as a preamble and not just as a random discourse. <margin>H</margin> Let us take our starting point by admitting it is a preamble. What we have said regarding the honor of the gods and the care of ancestors is sufficient. Let us try to speak of the next things in order, until the whole preamble seems to you to have been sufficiently stated.

<term>ATHENIAN</term>: In my view, it shall be so.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...attain immortality. It is a sin to willingly deprive oneself of immortality. Truly, he deprives himself of this from his heart who neglects children and a wife. Whoever obeys this law shall go unpunished. But he who does not obey, and is thirty-five years old without taking a wife, let him not think that a solitary life will bring him profit or pleasure; let him be fined a certain amount of money each year, and let him not share in those honors which the younger men in the city daily show to the elders. 

Comparing these two laws, one can judge whether it is better to write them double in length but as brief as possible, so that persuasion and threats are interjected together, or to use only threats and establish laws that are simple in length. 

<term>MEGILLUS</term>: It is the Laconian custom, Stranger, to always choose the shorter path. But if someone <margin>B</margin> were to make me the judge in these matters, allowing me to choose which law I would want in the city, I would choose the longer one; and in all other laws, if these two versions were proposed, I would do the same following this very example. However, the present laws must also be approved by Clinias; for his is the city for whose use these laws are being founded.

<term>CLINIAS</term>: You have spoken rightly, Megillus.

<term>ATHENIAN</term>: To care too much about the length or brevity of writing is quite foolish. For I believe the best versions, not the shortest or longest, are to be chosen. And yet, in the laws proposed just a moment ago, it is not only that one version <margin>C</margin> contributes more to virtue than the other; but what was said about the two types of doctors has been most correctly applied. It seems no legislator has ever thought of this. For although it is possible to use two methods—force and persuasion—to bring laws to the crowd that is unskilled in discipline, they use only one as far as they can. They do not join threats with persuasion, but instead bring only pure force. I, however, O blessed man, see a third thing that ought to happen in laws, which we see happening nowhere.

<term>CLINIAS</term>: What is that?

<term>ATHENIAN</term>: That which has been done by us, through a certain divine inspiration, through the things we have discussed. We began to debate the laws in the morning, and now it is noon; and in this pleasant place, we are most conveniently <margin>D</margin> resting, debating only about laws. And now for the first time we seem to be making a beginning of the laws that must be treated. All the previous things were actually the preambles of the laws. 

I wanted to say this because all speeches, and other things which involve the imitation of the voice, have preambles and certain "preludes," which contain an artistic and useful treatment of the matter to be spoken. Certainly, to those things which are called the "laws of citharoedic song" and to other music, wonderfully invented preambles are prefixed. But for true laws—which we say are civil laws—no one has ever pronounced or brought to light any preamble, as if none existed by nature. <margin>E</margin> To us, however, this delay and our discussion seem to signify that there is one. 

The laws which were just now called "double" are not simply double, but are two distinct things: the law and the preamble of the law. That which we compared to the tyrannical command and the service of slave-doctors is pure law. But that which was placed before it, called the persuasive part, truly looks toward persuasion, yet it has the force of a preamble. For so that the citizens may hear the legislator's command (which is the law) more benevolently, and because of this, respect it more easily, that entire speech was made to induce persuasion. Wherefore, in my opinion, this whole thing should rightly be called the preamble, not the reasoning of the law. After this, what else do I desire to be added? This, surely: <margin>F</margin> that the legislator must always prefix a preamble to every law, and show in each instance how they differ from themselves, just as those two parts were shown to differ.

<term>CLINIAS</term>: I would never desire a man skilled in these things to bring laws in any other way.

<term>ATHENIAN</term>: You have spoken well to me, O Clinias, in saying that a certain preamble shall precede all laws, and that it is necessary at the beginning of every legal writing to prefix to the whole discourse a preamble suited to each law. For it is no small thing that is said afterward, nor is it of small importance whether such things are commemorated clearly or obscurely. But if we should order that preambles of large and small laws be fashioned similarly, <margin>G</margin> we would not be ordering correctly. For that is not to be done in every song nor in every speech. For even if it can be found in all, it is not to be used in all. That, however, must always be granted to the orator, the singer, and the law-giver themselves.

<term>CLINIAS</term>: You speak the truth, Stranger. But let us delay no further; rather, let us now return to the proposed discourse, and let us begin from those things which you said above, not as if you were using a preamble. Therefore, as they say in the games, let us resume the better second tries from the beginning, as a certain preamble and not just any discourse as we were treating it just now. Let us begin <margin>H</margin> and profess to be starting a preamble. And concerning the honor of the gods and the care of our ancestors, let it be said that enough has been spoken; let us strive to finish the rest, until you think you have sufficiently completed the whole preamble. Finally, after the preamble, you will approach the laws.

<term>ATHENIAN</term>: Since regarding the gods and god...

<summary>This page presents a pivotal moment in Plato's Laws where the Athenian Stranger argues that laws should consist of two parts: a persuasive "preamble" to educate the citizen and the "pure law" or command itself. He uses the analogy of doctors to illustrate that law should treat citizens like free men to be reasoned with, rather than slaves to be commanded by force.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the Athenian Stranger's preamble to the legal code. Having discussed the duties toward the gods and ancestors, the dialogue now transitions into the "Fifth Dialogue" (Book V), focusing on the internal governance of the individual—specifically the cultivation and honoring of the soul as the foundation for any law-abiding society.</meta>

PLATO'S

...and regarding those who follow, and parents, whether living or deceased, as we have said in the introduction, and as we now affirm: what remains, as you seem to command, must be brought into the light. <note>original: "in lucem est educendum"</note> CLEINIAS: By all means. ATHENIAN: After those matters, indeed, which pertain to souls, to bodies, and to possessions, we must determine by common discussion with what zeal they are to be cultivated, so that both speakers and listeners may follow this discipline according to their strength. These things, therefore, truly must be spoken and heard by us after those others. CLEINIAS: You speak quite rightly.

## PLATO ON THE LAWS, OR, ON THE INSTITUTION OF LAWS, DIALOGUE FIVE.

#### SUMMARY OF THE DIALOGUE. *The first part of this dialogue encompasses several things that remained for completing the preface: and it treats that most beautiful topic, the True Cultivation of the Soul: that is, with how much zeal and labor a truly good citizen ought to cultivate his own soul, and what is the true and genuine manner of that cultivation; and furthermore, how much should be granted to the body, how much to money, and to all those external things. Thus Plato lays down the true foundation for the institution of laws. For laws would be instituted in vain, and would exert no efficacy, unless the soul of the one for whom they are established were first correctly formed, so that he himself might be a law unto himself. From there he approaches the legislation <note>original Greek: νομοθεσίαν (nomothesian)</note> itself, which is the second part of these twelve books.*

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial A featuring a classical figure, possibly a scholar or philosopher, seated in a landscape.</image-desc>
<margin>A</margin>
LET whoever just now heard concerning the gods and most dear parents now hear the rest. For each man’s soul, being most his own of all his possessions after the gods, is the most divine. Truly, those things which are one’s own are divided into two parts: the more powerful and better parts dominate, while the weaker and inferior parts serve. Surely, those which dominate must always be honored above those which serve. Wherefore, I rightly command that, after the dominant gods and those who follow them, our soul must be cultivated and held in the second place. But no one, <margin>B</margin> to speak briefly, honors his own soul rightly, though he may seem to. For honor is a divine good. But nothing of evil things is to be honored. Therefore, whoever thinks he can exalt his soul by certain speeches, or gifts, or obsequies, if he does not render the soul itself better from being worse—though he seems to honor it—he does not do so in the least. For immediately from childhood, every man thinks himself sufficient for knowing all things, and he believes he honors his soul by praising it and permitting it to do whatever it pleases. But we say that he who does these things does <margin>C</margin> <margin>True and false cultivation of the soul.</margin> not honor his soul, but harms it, which we nevertheless say must be honored in the second place after the gods. But neither does he honor it who, for his own sins and for his many and greatest crimes, considers others to be the cause rather than himself. He who, always excusing himself, seems to honor his soul, is yet far from it, since he harms it. Nor again, when someone indulges in pleasures contrary to the reason and praise of the legislator, does he honor his soul: for he casts it down, filling it with evils and repentance. Nor again does he honor it when he does not take up the labors praised by the law, or the fears and pains to be endured, but yields and succumbs. For in doing all these things, he disgraces his soul. But neither <margin>D</margin> when he deems this life the highest good does he honor it; rather, even then he disparages it. For he immediately assents to the soul that thinks all things in the underworld are evil, and he does not resist, teaching and refuting it, as if he were ignorant whether, on the contrary, the things which are with the gods of the underworld are the greatest of all goods for us. Furthermore, he who prefers the beauty of the body over virtue truly and most deeply disgraces the soul. For he judges the body more venerable than the soul. In this he certainly errs vehemently. For nothing of the earth is more venerable than heavenly things. And he who feels otherwise about the soul is utterly ignorant of how wonderful a thing he neglects. Nor again does he who desires money unjustly, or possessing it <margin>E</margin> unjustly does not grieve, adorn his soul with gifts; rather, he is furthest from this. For that which is venerable and beautiful in the soul, he betrays for a little gold; since all the gold that is above the earth or beneath the earth cannot be compensated for virtue. Finally, to speak summarily, whoever does not flee with all zeal from those things which the legislator thinks are base and evil, nor follows with all his strength those things which he has established as good and beautiful, does not see in all these how basely and foully he affects his most divine soul. For no one, to speak in a word, notices the greatest vengeance for acting badly according to justice. The greatest vengeance is that one is made similar to evil men, and being made similar, he flees good men and their conversations, and separates himself from them, but clings to the wicked and embraces their company. But he who has mixed himself with these <margin>F</margin> must necessarily suffer and do the same things which such men are accustomed to do and say among themselves. And such a passion is indeed not justice. For justice and the just are honorable. But vengeance is a passion following upon injustice, into which both he who does not fall and he who falls are miserable:

<column-break/>

ATHENIAN: Therefore, concerning the gods and those after the gods, and concerning parents both living <margin>A</margin> and deceased, we have adequately sketched out at that time what we now say. But that which remains yet of such a kind appears to me to be what you are now commanding, as if to bring it back into the light. CLEINIAS: Entirely so. ATHENIAN: But truly, after such things, it is fitting and most common for those who are being instructed—both the speaker and the listeners—to have zeal concerning their own souls and bodies and substances, and concerning relaxation, that they may become inhabitants of education according to their power. These things themselves, therefore, after those others, must truly be spoken and heard by us. CLEINIAS: You speak most rightly.

## OF PLATO ON THE LAWS,
## OR,
## CONCERNING LEGISLATION,
## THE FIFTH DIALOGUE.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial Alpha (A) featuring dense foliage and floral patterns.</image-desc>
<margin>A</margin>
LET every man now hear, who just now heard the things concerning the gods and our dear ancestors. For of all one’s own possessions, after the gods, the soul is the most divine, being most one's own. All things belonging to a person are entirely twofold for everyone: the better and more excellent are the masters, while the lesser and worse are the slaves. Therefore, those things of his which are the masters are always to be preferred over those that serve. Thus, in saying that one’s own soul, after the gods who are the masters and those who follow them, must be honored in the second place, I exhort you rightly. <margin>B</margin> But to speak as a word, no one of us honors it rightly; but it only seems so. For honor is surely a divine good; but of evil things, nothing is honorable. He who thinks either by some words or gifts to increase the soul, while making it nothing better from being worse, seems to honor it, but he does this in no way. For as soon as he is born, every man thinks himself capable of knowing all things, and he thinks he honors his soul by praising it, and by eagerly permitting it to do whatever it wishes. But what is now said by us is that these things harm and do not honor it. But it must be honored, as we say, in the second place after the gods. Nor, when a man does not consider himself the cause of his own <margin>C</margin> errors each time, and of the most and greatest evils, but blames others, and always removes himself as blameless, does he honor his soul, as it indeed seems. But he is far from doing this. For he harms it. Nor when he grants himself pleasures contrary to the reason and praise of the legislator, does he then in any way honor it; but he dishonors it, filling it with evils and regrets. Nor again, when he does not endure to the end the contrary labors that are praised, and fears and aches and griefs, but yields—then he does not honor it by yielding. For he renders it dishonorable by doing all such things. Nor when he considers that living is at all costs a good thing, does he honor it; but he dishonors it even then. For thinking that all things in the underworld are evil, the soul yields, and does not resist, <margin>D</margin> teaching and refuting itself, as if it does not know whether the things concerning the gods there are perhaps the greatest of all goods for us. Nor truly, when one prefers beauty before virtue, is this anything other than the truly and entirely dishonoring of the soul. For the argument says that the body is more honorable than the soul. Falsely: for that which is born of the earth is not more honorable than the Olympian things. But he who thinks otherwise about the soul is ignorant that he neglects this wonderful possession. Nor again, when someone loves to acquire money not beautifully, or does not take it hardly when acquiring it, does he then honor his soul with gifts; far from it. For that which is honorable and beautiful in it is given away for a little gold. For all the gold both upon the earth and under the earth is not worth as much as virtue. Nor <margin>E</margin> (to speak collectively) as many things as the legislator lists and sets down as being shameful and evil, and the contrary things as good and beautiful—if one does not wish to abstain from the former by every device, and to practice the latter with all his power—every man in all these things does not know that he is treating the soul, which is a most divine thing, most dishonorably and most unseemly. For of the greatest vengeance for wrongdoing, as one might say, no one takes account. But the greatest is this: to be made like unto evil men; and being made like them, to flee from good men and good words, and to be cut off from them, but to glue oneself to the others, pursuing them in their company. But being joined to such men, it is necessary to do and to suffer what such men are born to do and say to one another. This passion, therefore, is not justice (for justice and the just are beautiful), but it is retribution, <margin>F</margin> a suffering that follows injustice; from which both he who happens upon it and he who does not are wretched: the one because he is not healed, and the other because he himself perishes so that many others may be saved.

<summary>This page marks the beginning of Book V of the Laws, where the Athenian Stranger argues that the soul is man's most divine possession after the gods and must be honored through virtue rather than through self-indulgence or material wealth.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discourse on the proper hierarchy of values from the beginning of Book 5 of the "Laws." Having previously established that the soul is more honorable than the body, and the body more honorable than external possessions, Plato now turns to the character traits and internal dispositions required of a virtuous citizen.</meta>

-># PLATO<-
->### THE LAWS, BOOK 5<-

<margin>A</margin> A man of the highest character is to be honored. However, he who wishes to do so but lacks the power should be held in the second rank. But the envious man, who willfully contributes nothing of value to others for the sake of friendship, must be censured; yet we should not disparage the thing itself <note>Plato means we should not hate virtue or talent just because a bad person possesses it.</note> because of the man who possesses it poorly; rather, we should strive to acquire it with all our might. Furthermore, let every one of us compete for virtue without envy. For he who acts in this way enlarges his city, since he himself contends while not hindering others with slanders. The envious man, however, thinking he can excel by disparaging others, both fails to move correctly toward true virtue himself and makes his fellow competitors slower through unjust criticism. Thus, by removing the vigorous pursuit of acquiring virtue from the city, he deprives it, to the best of his ability, of its greatness and glory.

<margin>B</margin> It is necessary, moreover, for every man to be both high-spirited <term>high-spirited: from the Greek "thumoeides," referring to the part of the soul that feels righteous anger and the drive for honor</term> and as mild as possible. For we cannot escape the injuries of others which are either difficult or impossible to heal except through struggle, defense, victory, and the refusal to let any sin go unpunished—and no one can do this without a high-spirited soul. Regarding those injuries which are of such a kind that they can be healed, one must first recognize that no unjust man is voluntarily unjust. <note>This is a famous Platonic paradox: that people only do evil because they are ignorant of the true Good.</note> For no one would ever want to possess any of the greatest evils anywhere, and much less so in those things which are most precious to him. As we have said, the soul is truly the most precious thing belonging to everyone. Therefore, <margin>C</margin> since it is in the soul that one must be most honored, no one will voluntarily accept the greatest evil and wish to possess it through his whole life. Furthermore, every unjust man is entirely miserable, as is anyone who possesses any evil. It is right to pity those who are curable and to restrain one’s anger, so that the soul does not become wild with a womanish heat of rage or persist too harshly against them. However, for those who are so wicked as to be incurable, one must let anger take its full course. For this reason, we said that a good man must always be high-spirited—that is, not lacking a noble capacity for anger—and at the same time, mild. 

<margin>D</margin> Indeed, the greatest of all evils is innate in the souls of many men. Because they easily forgive themselves for it, they devise no remedy for it. This is what people mean when they say that "everyone is by nature a friend to himself," and that it is right for this to be so. But in truth, excessive love of oneself is always the cause of all sins in all men. For the lover is blinded regarding the beloved. Therefore, he who thinks he should honor himself more than the truth judges poorly what is just, good, and beautiful. Surely it becomes him who intends to be a great man to love neither himself nor his own things, but always to love just things, whether they are performed by himself or by another. From this very fault, it happens to everyone that they mistake their own ignorance for wisdom. Hence it happens that <margin>E</margin> although we know nothing (so to speak), we nevertheless believe we know everything. Since we do not allow others the opportunity to do the things we do not know how to do ourselves, we are forced to err by doing them ourselves. For this reason, everyone should flee from excessive self-love and follow those better than themselves, hindered by no blush of shame. 

There are also several other matters, smaller than these and often repeated, yet nonetheless useful and thus needing to be said. For there is a need for reminding. For just as something is always flowing out, something else must flow in. Remembrance <note>original: "recordatio" / "anamnesis"</note> is the influx of wisdom that has failed. Truly, one must abstain from excessive laughter and tears, and everyone should be instructed to restrain excessive joy and sorrow, maintaining themselves in a dignified manner: whether a divinity <term>divinity: "daemon," here referring to one's personal fortune or guiding spirit</term> places one in a state of prosperity, or whether, through the accidents of fortune, opposing spirits <margin>F</margin> rise up as if against those struggling toward steep and difficult works. Good men should always hope that the gifts God is accustomed to give to such men will not fail them. And if any heavy labors should fall upon them, God will make them lighter and change present circumstances for the better; conversely, all good things, together with good fortune, will be present for them. Let each person live with this hope, and let them diligently and accurately exhort themselves and others to the frequent remembrance of these things, both in jest and in earnest. 

Now, what each person ought to do and what sort of person he should be regarding divine duties has been said. But we have not yet explained human matters. They must be spoken of. <margin>G</margin> For we are giving instructions to men, not to gods. Furthermore, pleasures, pains, and desires are by nature most characteristic of humans. From these, every mortal animal is, as it were, necessarily suspended and hung with the greatest intensity. Certainly, the most honorable life is to be praised, not only because it excels in its outward form of glory, but also because if someone is willing to taste it and not flee from it immediately from youth, it also excels in that which we all seek: that we may rejoice more than we grieve throughout our whole life. That this is so will be easily and clearly revealed if one tastes it correctly. In what way this is done correctly must now be considered by reason, whether it is innate in us according to nature or otherwise contrary to nature. Thus, one ought to compare life to life, the more pleasant to the more painful, in this way: we wish for pleasure to be present for us. Pain, however, we neither choose nor wish for. A middle state we do not wish for in place of pleasure, yet we accept it in place of pain. We also wish for a smaller pain accompanied by a greater pleasure. A smaller pleasure accompanied by a greater pain, we do not wish for.

<column-break/>

...not sharing it, as if the honor were unworthy; but on the other hand, the man who is unable but willing, let him be ranked second. But as for the envious man who willfully shares none of his goods through friendship with anyone, he himself is to be blamed; but do not dishonor the possessions any more because of the possessor, but rather strive to acquire them according to your ability. Let everyone compete for virtue among us without envy. For such a man increases the city, contending himself but not hindering others with slanders. But the envious man, thinking he must excel by slandering others, himself exerts less effort toward true virtue and brings his competitors to discouragement by being unjustly blamed; and through these things, making the whole city unpracticed in the competition for virtue, he works to make it smaller in reputation for his own part. 

Truly, every man ought to be high-spirited, but as mild as possible. For it is not possible to escape the difficult and hard-to-heal, or even entirely incurable, injustices of others except by fighting and defending oneself and being victorious, and by punishing with no relenting. Every soul is incapable of doing this without noble spirit. Regarding those who commit injustices that are healable, one must recognize, first, that every unjust man is not voluntarily unjust; for no one anywhere would ever voluntarily possess any of the greatest evils, least of all in the most precious of his own things. The soul, as we said, is in truth the most precious thing to all. In the most precious thing, then, no one would ever voluntarily take the greatest evil and live possessing it through life. But the unjust man is altogether piteous, as is the one who has evils; it is permissible to pity the one who has curable things and to soften one's spirit by restraining it, and not to continue acting with sharp anger or womanish bitterness; but for him who offends in an unmixed and unappeasable way and is evil, one must let go of one's anger. Therefore we say that the good man must be high-spirited and mild on every occasion. 

The greatest evil of all is innate in the souls of most men, for which everyone, having forgiveness for himself, devises no escape. This is what they say: that every man is by nature a friend to himself, and that it is right that it should be so. But in truth, the cause of all errors for each person on every occasion is the excessive love of oneself. For the lover is blinded concerning the thing loved. So he judges the just, the good, and the beautiful poorly, thinking he must always honor his own interests before the truth. For he who is to be a great man must love neither himself nor his own things, but the just things, whether they happen to be done by himself or rather by another. From this same error comes the fact that thinking one's own ignorance is wisdom has happened to all. Whence, knowing nothing (so to speak), we think we know everything; and not permitting others to do what we do not understand, we are forced to err ourselves by doing them. Therefore every man must flee the excessive love of himself; and one must pursue the one who is better than oneself, putting no shame before such a thing. 

The things that are smaller than what has just been said, but no less useful than these, should be spoken, as a reminder to oneself. For just as something is always flowing in, the opposite must always flow in. Remembrance is the influx of wisdom that is failing. Therefore, one must refrain from excessive laughter and tears; and every man must instruct everyone else, and entirely concealing all excessive joy and excessive pain, try to behave with decorum, whether his fortune <note>original: "daimonos"</note> stands in prosperity or in those turns of fate where the divinities oppose some actions as if they were high and steep. One should always hope that for good men, God will provide what he gives; when labors fall upon them, he will make them smaller instead of larger, and change the present state of things for the better; and as for the good things, the opposites of these will always be present for them with good fortune. With these hopes every man should live, and with the reminders of all such things, sparing nothing, but always reminding another and himself clearly, both in play and in seriousness. 

Now, about the practices—what sort one should practice—and about each person himself—what sort he should be—nearly all the divine matters have been spoken. But the human matters have not yet been spoken by us. But they must be; for we are talking to men, not to gods. There are things most characteristic of human nature: pleasures, pains, and desires, from which every mortal living thing is absolutely suspended and hung with the greatest intensity. One must praise the most beautiful life, not only because it excels in form for the sake of good reputation, but also because if anyone is willing to taste it and does not become inexperienced with it from youth, it excels in this too, which we all seek: in rejoicing more and being pained less throughout all of life. That this is clear, if someone tastes it correctly, is readily and strongly apparent. What this correctness is, one must now consider by taking the argument to see whether it is innate in us according to nature, or otherwise against nature. One must consider life compared to life, the more pleasant and the more painful, in this way: we want pleasure for ourselves, but pain we do not choose nor want. The neutral state we do not want instead of pleasure, but we do want it in exchange for pain. We want less pain with greater pleasure, but we do not want less pleasure with greater pain.

<summary>Plato discusses the ethical character required of citizens, focusing on the dangers of excessive self-love and the importance of balancing righteous anger with mildness. He concludes by beginning an analysis of the human life based on the balance of pleasure and pain.</summary>
