<meta>This page continues the discussion on the pursuit of a virtuous life. Having established that virtue is superior to vice, the author now uses a "hedonistic calculus"—the balance of pleasure and pain—to prove that the virtuous life is not only more honorable but also more pleasant in the long run.</meta>

-># ON THE LAWS, BOOK 5<-

<column-break/>

A ...than. In the same way, we can declare that we do not wish to have both of these in equal measure. All these things—in terms of quantity, magnitude, intensity, and equality, as well as their opposites—differ or do not differ according to the choice and will of each person. Since these things are necessarily so, we desire that life in which both pleasure and pain occur in great number, size, and intensity, but where pleasures nevertheless exceed the pains. We do not desire the life in which the opposite occurs. Again, in a life where both are small, infrequent, and mild, we do not want it if the pains exceed the pleasures; but if the opposite is true, we do. Furthermore, we must consider the "balanced life" <note>A life where pleasure and pain are exactly equal.</note> as we did before: we desire it if it exceeds in what we love, and we do not desire it if it is surpassed by what we dislike. One must consider how all

B our lives are naturally bound up in these things, and which ones we naturally desire. If we say we desire anything other than these, we say so out of ignorance and a lack of experience with what these lives truly are. What, then, and how many are the lives in which we must recognize what is to be avoided and what is to be desired—what is voluntary and what is involuntary—and having recognized these, prescribe a law for oneself? From there, one should choose what is at once friendly, pleasant, best, and most beautiful, so that one may live as blessedly as is possible for a human being. Let us say that the temperate life is one, the prudent life another, the brave life a third, and finally the healthy life a fourth. And to these four

C let us set four others that are their opposites: the foolish, the cowardly, the intemperate, and the diseased. <margin>On the temperate and intemperate life.</margin> Whoever rightly knows the temperate life will describe it as mild in all things and moderate: it possesses quiet pains, mild pleasures, gentle desires, and loves that are not at all frantic. The intemperate life, however, is sharp in all things; it is agitated by vehement pains and vehement pleasures, by burning and frantic desires, and by loves that are strangely insane. But in the temperate life, pleasures exceed the pains, while in the intemperate life, the pleasures are exceeded by the pains in magnitude, number, and frequency. Thus it happens

D that by necessity, the one life is naturally more pleasant to us and the other more distressing. He who wishes to live pleasantly is not permitted to live intemperately by his own choice. Indeed, if what has just been said is correct, it follows that every intemperate person is such against his better judgment. <margin>The whole human crowd lives without temperance.</margin> For either through ignorance or lack of self-control, or both, the entire crowd of humanity lives without temperance <term>temperance: "sophrosyne" in Greek, meaning self-regulation or sound-mindedness</term>. We must think similarly about the healthy and the diseased life: both have pains and pleasures, but in health, pleasures exceed, while in sickness, pains exceed. Our will in choosing a way of life is never that pain should prevail. Where pain is overcome, we have judged <margin>Which type of life is chosen.</margin> that life to be more pleasant. The temperate man, therefore, compared to the intemperate—the prudent to the foolish, the brave to the coward—possesses each of these in smaller, fewer, and rarer

E amounts; one life exceeds in pleasures, the other in pains. Thus the brave man exceeds the coward, the prudent man exceeds the mindless, the temperate exceeds the reckless, and the healthy exceeds the sick in pleasure. To sum it up: the life that partakes in virtue—whether of body or soul—is more pleasant than the life that partakes in wickedness. Furthermore, it excels in beauty, correctness, power, and glory, so that he who is established in such a life lives more happily in all respects than his opposite. But let this preamble to the laws now come to an end. After the preamble, the law must necessarily follow. Or rather, the laws of the republic must now truly be written down. Just as in anything that is woven,

F the "woof" and the "warp" are not woven from the same materials <note>The "warp" (stamen) are the strong vertical threads; the "woof" or "trama" are the softer horizontal threads.</note>, but the type of thread for the warp is sturdier and firmer, while the woof is softer to yield more easily. In the same way, those who hold office in the city must always be distinguished from those who have given proof of themselves in some lesser capacity. There are two forms in a republic: one is the appointment of officials, the other is the constitution of the laws. But before all these things, one must consider this: when a shepherd, a cattle-herder, a horse-breeder, or any such person receives a flock or herd, they do not begin their care until they have applied a suitable purification to each individual.

G Furthermore, having separated the healthy from the sick and the well-born from the base, they will send some to other flocks and keep others for care. They know that otherwise, their labor would be in vain for both body and soul. For the depravity of nature and education corrupts to such an extent that unless one separates the healthy and uncorrupted type of character and body, they will perish from the contagion within the group. But for other animals, there is less concern, and they are mentioned only for the sake of example. Regarding humans, however, the legislator must apply the greatest diligence and search out everything carefully, so that he may write what is appropriate for each, both concerning purification <term>purification: "katharmos," here referring to the removal of "corrupt" individuals from the body politic</term> and all other actions. This is how the purification of a city stands: there are many types, some lighter and others more severe. If someone were both a tyrant and a legislator, he could use the difficult and best purifications. The law...

<summary>Plato concludes his philosophical introduction to the Laws by arguing that a virtuous life is mathematically more pleasant than a life of vice, and then transitions into the practicalities of statecraft using the metaphor of a weaver and a shepherd who must "purge" his flock before beginning his work.</summary>

# PLATO'S LAWS

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
However, for a lawgiver who establishes a new state and laws without the power of a tyrant, it will be sufficient if he applies the mildest form of purgation <note>original: "purgationem" / "καθαρμῷ". In this context, it refers to the "cleansing" of the citizen body by removing undesirable elements.</note>. For the most thorough purification—much like the strongest medicines applied to bodies—is full of pain; it brings punishment through just retribution, condemning the sinner to death or exile. For it is customary to entirely remove those who have committed the greatest sins, if they are incurable, since they cause the greatest harm to the city. But a milder purgation for us is of this sort: those who, due to a lack of food, seek leaders and offer themselves as willing followers out of need against those who have plenty—these he should kindly dispatch under the honorable name of a "colony," like a disease that weakens the city.

<margin>B</margin>
Every lawmaker must, in a certain way, do these things from the beginning, as we have said. However, some more difficult things have happened to us at present. For we ought not to devise either a colony or any selection for the sake of purgation at this moment; instead, just as water flows into the same basins from many springs and mountain torrents, we must observe that the liquid flowing together from all sides—partly by draining and pouring out, and partly by diverting and turning away—should be as pure as possible. Yet there is, as it seems, both labor and danger in every civil constitution.

<margin>C</margin>
Since we are now dealing with words and not deeds, let our selection be perfected and the purgation we desire be accomplished. For we shall prevent the wicked, who strive to enter and govern this city, from approaching by using every persuasion and examining them over a long enough time; but we shall entice the upright, making them as benevolent and propitious as possible according to our strength. But it should not be hidden how easily we have acted. Indeed, just as we said the colony of the Heraclidae <note>The descendants of Hercules, who historically resettled the Peloponnese, often cited as a model for a "fresh start" in Greek history.</note> was fortunate because it escaped the heavy and dangerous strife of dividing lands and cancelling debts—a matter which a city of old, forced to pass laws, can neither entirely omit nor easily change—so it seems to have happened to us as well.

<margin>D</margin>
There remains, therefore, only a prayer, so to speak, and a small, cautious change for those who are transforming over a long period. This change is that, in making these transitions, the citizens should possess many lands along with many debtors, and they should be willing to communicate humanely with the needy—partly by giving and partly by receiving—cultivating moderation <term>mediocritatem <gloss>the "Golden Mean" or middle path</gloss></term>, and believing that poverty consists not in the reduction of wealth, but in the insatiable desire for acquiring more. For this is the greatest beginning of safety for a city, upon which, as on a stable foundation, anyone can easily build whatever is decorous for the city and consistent with this constitution.

<margin>E</margin>
But if this foundation is weak and ruinous, no civil work will succeed prosperously thereafter. We indeed (as we say) flee from this, or if we do not flee, we show by words in what way it must be fled, saying that there is no other path—wide or narrow—of escape, except that we cultivate justice and do not follow the desire for acquisition. And let this now be established for us as a kind of support and protection for the city. For the wealth <note>original: "census" / "οὐσίας"</note> which the citizens have prepared for themselves must be free from reproach, or they should voluntarily cease from progressing further in acquisition, among whom old crimes are held in turn, and who are even slightly of sound mind. But those to whom God has given, as he has to us, the constitution of a new city in which there are no enmities—if they give themselves causes for enmity because of the distribution of houses and lands, they will be marked not by some human failing, but by the crime of the worst ignorance.

<margin>On the division of lands and the number of parts</margin>

<margin>F</margin>
What, then, will be the method of right distribution? First, I think, the number must be established: how large it ought to be. Then it must be asserted into how many and what kind of parts the distribution must be made for the citizens; finally, the lands and the houses themselves must be divided as equally as possible. But how great a multitude is sufficient cannot be rightly said other than by a comparison of the lands and the neighboring cities. Let the land be large enough to suffice for so many moderate men, and no larger a need. And there ought to be so many people that they can repel neighbors who do them wrong, and help those same neighbors when they suffer injury. Having inspected these things, we shall define both the land and the neighbors in deed and in word.

<margin>On the number suited to the most distributions, which is five thousand and forty.</margin>

<margin>G</margin>
Now, for the sake of example and description, so that the matter itself may be completed, let the discourse descend to the passing of the law. Let there be five thousand and forty <note>The number 5,040 is highly significant to Plato because it is a "highly composite number," divisible by every integer from 1 to 12 (except 11, which it nearly divides: 5040/11 = 458.18).</note> farmers because of the convenience of this number, and let them fight for the borders. Let the land and the houses likewise be distributed into the same parts, so that the man and the portion match in the distribution. And first, let a partition of the whole number be made into two parts, then into three; it is also possible into four, and into five, and so on up to ten in succession.

<margin>H</margin>
Certainly, every legislator must understand enough about numbers so that he is not ignorant of which number and what kind of number is most convenient for individual cities. Let us say that the number is more suitable which receives in itself the most distributions, and especially those arranged in successive order. For not every number has all sections into all things. But the number five thousand and forty—for war and for peace—

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
...if a lawgiver establishes a new constitution and laws without a tyranny, even if he cleanses the city with the mildest of purifications, he would be satisfied with such a result. The best purification is painful, much like certain medicines: it leads to punishment by way of justice and retribution, bringing death or exile as the end of the penalty. For it is accustomed to rid the city of those who have committed the greatest crimes and are incurable, as they are the greatest harm to the city. But the milder of the purifications is of this sort for us: as many as, through a lack of food, are ready to follow leaders against those who have property, these he sends away as a disease that has grown in the city, giving it the well-omened name of a "colony" and dismissing them as kindly as possible.

<margin>B</margin>
Every legislator must do this, however strangely, at the beginning. But for us, things even stranger than these have now occurred regarding this matter. For we need not devise a colony nor any selection for purification for the present; but as many streams of water from many sources and torrents flow into a single lake, it is necessary to keep watch with focused mind so that the water flowing together is as pure as possible—draining some, and diverting or turning away others. There is toil, as it seems, and danger in every political establishment.

<margin>C</margin>
But since we are now accomplishing this in speech and not in deed, let our collection be finished, and let its purification be considered completed now. For the wicked who attempt to come together into the present city to be citizens, we shall prevent from arriving by using every persuasion and testing them for a sufficient time; but all the good we shall receive with as much kindness and favor as we can. And let this stroke of luck not escape our notice: that, as we said, the colony of the Heraclidae was fortunate because it escaped a terrible and dangerous strife over the cutting of debts and the distribution of land. For when a city is forced to legislate, it is neither possible to leave the old order unmoved, nor is it possible to move everything.

<margin>D</margin>
Only a prayer, so to speak, remains, and a small, cautious transition, moving things a little over a long time. This is the transition that moves things: when those who possess plenty of land and have many debtors are willing, through their own fairness, to share reasonably with these people, partly by forgiving debts and partly by distributing land, clinging to moderation and considering poverty to be not the lessening of one's property, but the increasing of one's greed. For this is the greatest beginning of a city's salvation, and upon this, as on a lawful foundation <note>original: "κρηπῖδος"</note>, it is possible later to build the political order that is beneficial for such a state.

<margin>E</margin>
But if this transition is rotten, no subsequent political action will be easy for a city. We, as we say, escape this; yet let it be said more correctly that we do not escape it in whatever way we might make our flight from it. Let it be said now that it is through not being lovers of money combined with justice; for there is no other way, wide or narrow, to escape such a device. And let this be placed for us now as a stay of the city. For property must be established in some way without reproach among one another, or we should not proceed further forward voluntarily into another arrangement. For those who have old grievances against each other, even if they have only a small amount of sense, God has now given to us to settle a new city and not to have enmities against each other. To create causes for enmity through the distribution of land and houses would be a sign of total human ignorance and wickedness.

<margin>F</margin>
What then would be the method of right distribution? First, one must set the total number of the citizens: how many they shall be. After this, one must agree on the distribution for the constitution: into how many parts in number and of what size they must be divided. Following these things, the land and the houses must be divided as equally as possible. A sufficient number of people could not be rightly stated in any other way than in relation to the land and the neighboring cities. As for the land, let it be as much as is sufficient to feed so many people who are temperate; of more, there is no need. As for the number of people, let there be as many as are able to defend themselves against neighboring people who do them wrong, and who can help their own neighbors when they are wronged, not being entirely without resources. Having seen these things, we shall limit the territory and the neighbors in deed and in words.

<margin>G</margin>
And now, for the sake of form and a sketch, let the discourse proceed so that the legislation may be completed. Let there be five thousand and forty, for the sake of a certain fitting number, as land-holders and those who will defend the distribution. And let the land and the houses likewise be divided into the same parts, so that a man and his lot <note>original: "κλῆρος"</note> are joined in the distribution. First, let the two parts of every number be divided. After this, three in the same way. For it is naturally divisible by four and five and up to sixty <note>The Greek text here is more specific than the Latin, noting the number's divisibility up to 60.</note>.

<margin>H</margin>
Every child of legislation must always have the numbers in mind—what number and of what kind would be most useful for every city. Let us say that number is most suitable which has the most and most consecutive divisions within itself. For while not every number has every division into everything, the number of five thousand and forty—for war and for peace—

# ON THE LAWS, BOOK V

Regarding all peaceful agreements and associations, as well as taxes and distributions, the number of divisions should not exceed sixty parts. These parts should be further divided into ten continuous groups. These matters must be firmly grasped by those whom the law commands to manage them, for they cannot be handled otherwise. These things must be stated for the sake of anyone founding a city. Whether someone is building a new city from the start or considering the restoration of an old, ruined one, no person in their right mind will attempt to change the established traditions regarding the gods and sacred rites. This includes whatever has been received from Delphi, Dodona, or Ammon <note>Ammon refers to the oracle of Zeus-Ammon in Libya, which was highly respected in the Greek world alongside Delphi and Dodona.</note>, or ancient accounts that have persuaded people through visions or divine inspiration. Following these persuasions, people established sacrifices mixed with solemn rites, whether they originated locally or were brought from the Tyrrhenians <note>Etruscans</note>, from Cyprus, or elsewhere. By such accounts, they consecrated reputations, statues, altars, and temples, and marked out sacred groves for each of them. Not even the smallest detail of these should the lawgiver change; rather, he should assign a god, a spirit <note>original: "daimon" / "δαίμων". In Greek thought, these were intermediary beings between gods and humans, not necessarily evil.</note>, or some hero to each of the city's divisions. In the distribution of the land, the finest groves and all fitting things should be set aside first. This is so that the gatherings of each division, occurring at appointed times, may provide for every need and allow citizens to treat one another with kindness during sacrifices, fostering familiarity and mutual recognition. There is no greater good for a city than for citizens to be known to one another. For where there is no light between citizens regarding their character, but only darkness, no one will ever correctly receive the honor, the office, or the justice they deserve. Every man must strive in every city for one goal: that he never appears "counterfeit" <note>original: "kibdelos" / "κίβδηλός". This term usually refers to debased or fake coinage, applied here to human character.</note> to anyone, but remains always simple and true, and that no one else of that sort deceives him. The next move in the arrangement of the laws—like the "move from the sacred line" in a game of checkers <note>original: "πεττῶν ἀφ’ ἱεροῦ". A proverbial expression for a decisive, unusual, or final move in a game of skill.</note>—is unusual and might surprise the listener at first. However, upon reflection and experience, it will appear as the second-best way to inhabit a city. Perhaps someone will reject it because the lawgiver does not use the power of a tyrant in making the laws. But it is most correct to speak thus: to describe the best constitution, the second-best, and the third, and then give the choice to the one in charge of the settlement. Let us follow this method now, describing the constitution that is best in virtue, then the second, and then the third. We give the choice to Clinias now, and to anyone else who might wish to select from such models and assign to his own country what pleases him. The first city, constitution, and best laws are those where that ancient proverb is observed as much as possible throughout the entire city: the saying that "friends truly have all things in common." <note>original: "Amicorum omnia esse communia" / "κοινὰ τὰ φίλων". A central tenet of Plato’s ideal communal state.</note> Whether such a state exists now or will ever exist—where women, children, and all property are held in common, and every means is used to remove what is called "private" entirely from life—this is the peak of virtue. It is engineered so that even things naturally private become common in some way; for example, eyes, ears, and hands might seem to see, hear, and act for the common good. Everyone praises and blames the same things together, rejoicing and grieving over the same events. Whatever laws most effectively make a city "one," no one will ever set a better or more correct standard for virtue. Such a city, inhabited by gods or the children of gods, is a place of joy. Therefore, one should not look elsewhere for a model of a constitution, but cling to this one and seek it as much as possible. The one we have now undertaken would be the closest to immortality, and while it is the second-best, we shall, if God wills, complete the third after this. What then is this second state, and how does it come to be? First, let them distribute the land and the houses, and let them not farm the land in common. For such a practice is greater than what current birth, upbringing, and education can support. Let the distribution be made with the mindset that the person who receives a lot must consider it the common property of the whole city. Since the land is his fatherland, he must care for it more than a mother cares for her children; for the land is a goddess and the mistress of mortals. The same mindset must be held toward the local gods and spirits, so that these things may remain as they are for all time. To ensure this permanence, the number of hearths we have now distributed must always remain the same, neither increasing nor decreasing. This can be firmly established for the whole city if the one who receives the lot always leaves only one heir among his children—the one most dear to him—as his successor to care for the gods, the family, and the city, for both the living and the dead. As for the other children, if there are more than one, the females should be given in marriage according to the law that will be established, and the males should be given as adopted sons to those citizens who lack children of their own.

<column-break/>

Regarding all agreements, associations, taxes, and distributions, they should not be divided into more than one out of sixty parts.
<margin>A</margin>
From one up to ten, these divisions should be continuous. However, these matters should be carefully examined during leisure by those to whom the law has entrusted this task. And these things are exactly as they are described. These things must be stated for the sake of the one founding a city. Indeed, whether he founds a new one from the start or restores a scattered and ruined old one, concerning the gods and whatever sacred matters are appropriate to be established for individuals in the city, and by whatever names of gods or spirits <note>original: "daemonibus"</note> they are called, no one in his right mind will attempt to innovate. 
<margin>B</margin>
Whether these things were received from Delphi, Dodona, or Ammon, or asserted by some ancient fame as visions and inspirations of the gods: once these have been approved and the ancients have established sacrifices mixed with solemnities—whether they arose from the natives or are said to be Etruscan, or Cyprian, or from wherever you wish—and have handed down fame and consecrated statues through these accounts: they also established altars, temples, and sacred groves for each of them. In all these individual matters, the lawgiver shall not innovate even the smallest thing, but shall assign a god, a spirit, or some hero to each of the parts. In the distribution of the fields, he shall dedicate the first and most excellent groves and fields and all suitable things. 
<margin>C</margin>
Thus, the gatherings of the individual parts, made at fixed times, may more easily show their capacity for any use, and by sacrificing, they may kindly receive one another: whence they may also become familiar with each other and know one another. Indeed, nothing is better for a city than for citizens to know one another. For where there is no light among citizens in their characters, but darkness, there neither honors according to dignity nor magistracies will be correctly given, nor can his own right be rendered to each. There is nothing else, if you compare one man to another,
<margin>D</margin>
in which every person in all cities ought to place greater zeal than in this: that he himself never appears "adulterated" <note>original: "adulterinus". In the sense of being forged, fake, or dishonest.</note> to anyone, but always simple and true; and that no other such person deceives him. But the "throw" which now follows in the very positioning of the laws—as in the game of dice <note>original: "tesseris"</note>, as the proverb says, "from the sacred line"—since it is unusual, will perhaps at first cause the listener to wonder. To one who considers it and is experienced, however, it will seem that the city is best instituted in this second place. Perhaps someone will not accept it because the legislator does not use a tyrannical manner in bringing forth the laws. It will be handled rightly if the best republic, the second, and the third are proposed, and the choice is given to each to select whichever he wishes by his own judgment. 
<margin>E</margin>
Let us now do the same. And when we have set forth the first republic in virtue, and the second and third, let us give the choice to Clinias, and to anyone wishing to choose these according to his own custom, and to attribute to his own fatherland what pleases him. The first city and republic, therefore, and the best law, is where that ancient proverb holds place as much as possible throughout the entire city, which is truly said: 
<margin>The first city and republic where all things of friends are common.</margin>
"All things of friends are common." Certainly, the limit of virtue will be placed chiefly in this, than which no more correct one can be set: if somewhere either this exists, or ever will be, that wives are common, children are common, and all money is also common, and by every zeal that which is called "private" is removed from life on all sides: even to the extent that those things which are by nature private to individuals become in a certain way common, so that eyes, 
<margin>F</margin>
ears, and hands seem to see, hear, and act for the common use, and all similarly praise and blame the same things, rejoicing in the same things and grieving in the same things; and finally, that they live under these laws as much as possible, which make the city one. Such a city, whether gods or many children of gods inhabit it together, living thus and preserving it, they certainly live filled with all joy. Therefore, the model of a republic must not be looked for elsewhere, but having inspected this one, one must seek such a one as much as possible. That one, however, which 
<margin>G</margin>
we have approached here, if it should happen, will in a certain way come closest to immortality, and if not in the first place, at least it will be in the second. But concerning the third, we shall determine later if God wills. Now, however, let us consider what this one is and in what way it becomes such. First, therefore, let them lot out the houses and fields, 
<margin>The second unity and republic, that all things are common to the fatherland.</margin>
and let them not cultivate the fields in common. For this is greater than what this generation, nourishment, and education can bear. But let them distribute with this mind, that individuals think their lot is common to the whole city. 
<margin>H</margin>
Indeed, since that region is of the fatherland, they ought to cultivate it more than children a mother. For she, being a goddess, is the mistress of mortals. The same must be thought concerning the local gods and spirits. But to ensure that these things endure through all time, care must be taken that as many shares as are now distributed in number, so many they shall always be in the future, never more and never fewer. This will be firmly done in every city if each one, having obtained a lot, always leaves only one of his sons, whom he prefers, as the heir of that house and successor, a worshiper of the gods and the city, and of the family, and of the living and the dead; and of the other sons, if more than one are born to him, he shall place the females according to the law that shall be enacted; but the males he shall commit by adoption to those citizens who have no sons...

<summary>This page outlines the religious and administrative foundations of Plato's "second-best" city, emphasizing the importance of communal identity and social transparency. It famously defines the ideal state as one where all things are held in common, but acknowledges a more practical version based on private lots that are treated as a sacred trust for the fatherland.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plato's instructions for the internal management of the ideal city, following the division of land. Having established the "best" possible state where property is shared, he now moves to the "second-best" state, focusing on the strict regulation of population, currency, and the prohibition of usury to maintain social stability.</meta>

# PLATO'S LAWS

<columns>
...through favor <note>original: "per gratiam" / "χάριν". Here referring to natural luck or divine favor in birth rates.</note>. But if this favor fails some, or if more children are born—whether male or female—to individual families, or conversely if fewer are born because women happen not to be fertile, then the highest and most excellent magistrate must carefully consider what ought to be done. He should find a way, whether the birth of children is in excess or deficient, to ensure that the five thousand and forty households <note>Plato chose 5,040 because it is divisible by every number from 1 to 10, making it ideal for administrative and military divisions.</note> always remain exactly that number. There are many ways to do this: procreation can be restricted for those who are overly fertile, or conversely, care can be taken to increase the population when needed. Men can be encouraged toward this end through honors or marks of disgrace, and through the warnings given by the elderly to the young. Ultimately, all lack and poverty arise when the number of five thousand and forty homes is not preserved. But if, due to an excessive zeal for having children, the city increases so much that it exceeds the limit and is pressed by a scarcity of resources, that old advice often mentioned should be repeated: a colony of "dear friends sent from dear friends" should be dispatched to wherever seems most suitable. If, on the other hand, a plague of diseases or the calamity of war devastates the city like a flood, so that far fewer survivors remain than the statutory number, one should not—if it can be avoided—willingly admit citizens who have been raised in a foreign <note>original: "adulterina" / "νόθῳ" (bastard/adulterated). Plato is wary of people not raised under the city's specific educational laws.</note> discipline. 

<margin>Proverb.</margin>
But as the saying goes, not even God can compel necessity. Let us therefore consider that our present reasoning sounds in our ears in this way: "O best of men, honor likeness and equality, and that which is identical and harmonious according to nature. Never transgress this, whether in number or in power, regarding things that are good and beautiful. And now, above all, preserve throughout your whole lives the number we have prescribed. Furthermore, do not despise the measure of wealth you were initially allotted—which was a moderate amount—by buying or selling from one another. Otherwise, neither God himself, the distributor of lots, nor the lawgiver will favor you." For now, the law first commands the disobedient with this warning: if they are satisfied, they may keep their lot; if not, let the gods depart <note>original: "di cedant". This implies that the divine protection of the land is revoked if the sacred lots are traded like common goods.</note>, just as if the region itself were, in its first parts, sacred to all the gods. Next, all priests and priestesses shall pray during the first, second, and third sacrifices that both the buyer and seller of these inherited homes and lands suffer what is fitting. To instruct posterity, they shall write these deeds on monuments of cypress wood <note>Cypress was known for its durability, used here to emphasize the permanence of the law.</note> and place them in the temples for safekeeping. Furthermore, they shall entrust the guardianship of these records to the magistrate who seems most keen-sighted, so that no transactions made contrary to this reasoning escape them. Whoever does not obey the law and God shall be punished. How great a good this is for all republics that obey it, bringing order and preparation, 

<margin>Proverb.</margin>
no wicked man will ever understand, according to the ancient proverb, but only the experienced man of fair character.

<margin>On profit.</margin>
In this city, there shall not be much pursuit of profit. For no one should, nor is anyone permitted to, engage in illiberal <note>original: "illiberali" / "ἀνελεύθερον". Occupations considered "unfree" or beneath the dignity of a citizen, such as manual labor for hire.</note> profit-seeking, nor seek that infamous "mechanical" gain <term>Banausia <gloss>The Greek term for manual labor or craft-work performed for money, which Plato believed warped the soul and body.</gloss></term> which defiles noble character. Nor should anyone think that money is to be accumulated by any means from base and shameful things.

<margin>On possessing gold and coins.</margin>
To these is added another law: that no private person shall possess either gold or silver. But because currency is needed for the sake of daily exchange—which is essentially necessary for craftsmen and those of that sort, and so that wages may be paid to hirelings, slaves, and settlers—we therefore permit them to have such coins as are held in value among themselves, but are held in contempt by the rest of the world. However, since wars must often be waged and travel abroad is necessary, when ambassadors or messengers are sent to foreign nations, it is necessary that the city always possess common Greek currency <note>original: "communem Graeciae monetam". Standard silver coinage, like the Athenian drachma, recognized throughout the Mediterranean.</note>. If any necessity compels a private individual to travel abroad, he shall go with the permission of the magistrates. Upon his return, if he has an abundance of foreign coins, he shall exchange them for the city's currency and restore them to the state. If anyone is caught hiding them and converting them to private use, the hidden amount shall become public property. Those who were aware but did not report it shall be subject to curses and disgrace along with the offender, and shall be punished with a fine no less than the amount of foreign currency brought in.

<margin>On dowry and interest.</margin>
Furthermore, let no one be permitted to give or receive dowries, nor to deposit money with anyone he does not trust, nor to lend at interest. Indeed, if anyone accepts a loan at interest, it shall be lawful for the borrower to return neither the interest nor the principal. Anyone will judge these things to be best for the city if they always refer back to the primary intention of the righteous lawgiver. For the mind of a statesman does not have the desire—as many claim a good lawgiver ought to have—that he should wish the city to be as large and as rich as possible, filled with gold and silver, and ruling over as much land and sea as possible. They add that he should also want it to be as good and as happy as possible if he is to legislate correctly. But some of these things are possible, and others are not. Therefore, the founder of laws will wish for the possible; he will not wish for the impossible, for such a desire would be vain, nor would he...

<column-break/>

**A** ...through favor. But if favor fails some, or if more female offspring are born, or more males to each family, or on the contrary when they are fewer due to a failure of children, the magistrate who we said must be the greatest and most honored, seeing this, shall consider what must be done with the excess or the deficiency. He shall devise every means as much as possible so that the five thousand and forty households shall always remain only that many. There are many means. For there are restrictions on birth for those who are fertile, and on the contrary, there are cares and concerns for the abundance of children through honors and dishonors and the warnings of the elderly, meeting the young always through cautionary words—these would be able to achieve what we say. And indeed, **B** finally, if an absolute lack of means arises regarding the five thousand and forty households, and an overflow of citizens occurs because of the "mutual friendliness" <note>original: "ἀφιλοφροσύνην" - here used ironically or to mean a lack of space for the friendly co-dwellers.</note> of those living together, the old device which we have often mentioned shall be used: the sending out of a colony, which becomes "dear from those who are like them," to wherever it seems suitable. But if, on the contrary, a wave should ever come bringing a deluge of diseases or the destruction of wars, and the citizens become much fewer than the appointed number through bereavement, one should not—if possible—insert citizens who have been educated in a "bastard" <note>original: "νόθῳ" (illegitimate/foreign) education.</note> discipline. But as the saying goes, not even a god is said to be able to use force against necessity. Let us then say that the speech we have spoken remains with us, saying: **C** "O children of the best of men, do not slacken in honoring likeness and equality, and the same and the harmonious, according to nature and according to number and every power of beautiful and good things. And indeed now, first of all, guard throughout your life the number we have stated; then, do not dishonor the height and size of the property which you were initially allotted as a moderate amount, by buying and selling to one another. For neither the one who distributed the lot, being a god, is your ally, nor is the lawgiver." For now the law says it first appoints this for the disobedient, warning that it is permitted for whoever wishes to cast lots for these, or not to cast lots; as if the land were holy **D** and sacred to all the gods, then the priests and priestesses making prayers over the sacrifices of the hearth... and as far as the walls, the number or the foundations of the plots or lands they received, that they should suffer what is fitting. Having written down "cypress memories" in the sacred sacrifices <note>original: "κυπαρισσίνας μνήμας" - records on cypress wood.</note>, they shall place them for the time to come as a record of the years, and they shall establish guards of the faithful so that this may be maintained, choosing whoever seems most keen-sighted; so that the actions occurring contrary to these things each time do not escape them, but they may punish the one who is disobedient to the law and to God. How much good the current command may bring to all cities that obey it, having taken on the establishment of the cities, **E** according to the old proverb, no one who is wicked will ever know, but you will know through experience and equity. For profit-seeking is not much present in such a symmetry, nor should anyone be permitted to seek profit in an illiberal way, insofar as the so-called "dishonorable craftsmanship" <term>Banausia <gloss>Refers to manual trades that were thought to make the mind unfit for philosophy or politics.</gloss></term> turns away a free character, nor should one collect money from unworthy things of that sort. In addition to all these, a law follows that no private individual is permitted to possess gold or silver. Currency is for the sake of daily exchange, which is a necessity for craftsmen to exchange, and for all who have need of such things, to pay wages to hirelings, slaves, and settlers. For these reasons, we say currency must be possessed—**F** for the locals themselves, but for other men it is like a brother <note>original: "ἀδελφόν" - meaning it is only a "relative" or substitute for value elsewhere.</note>. But there shall be common Greek currency for the sake of military expeditions and travels to other men, such as embassies, or any other necessary city business. If a necessity ever arises for a private individual to travel abroad, let him travel after requesting permission from the rulers. If he returns with foreign currency left over, let him deposit it with the city, receiving the local currency in proportion. If anyone is seen keeping it for private use, let it become public, and the one who knows and does not tell shall be liable to a curse and disgrace along with the one who brought it, and in addition to a fine no less than the foreign currency brought in. In marrying and **G** giving in marriage, let no one give or receive a dowry, nor deposit money, nor lend at interest, as it is permitted to not return either the interest or the principal at all to the one who borrowed. Someone looking at it this way would judge these to be the best practices for a city, if he always refers back to the original intention of the lawgiver. The intention of a statesman having sense is, we say, not that which the many would say a good lawgiver ought to wish: that the city for which he legislates should be as large as possible and as rich as possible, possessing gold and silver, and ruling over as much land and sea as possible. They would say **H** further that he should wish the city to be as good and as happy as possible if he is to legislate correctly. Of these things, some are possible to happen, others are not. The one who organizes things would wish for the possible, but he would not wish for the impossible, nor would he...

</columns>

<summary>Plato outlines the socio-economic foundations of his "second-best" state, focusing on maintaining a fixed population of 5,040 households, prohibiting the private possession of precious metals, and outlawing usury. He argues that the goal of a true lawgiver is to ensure a city's goodness and happiness rather than its sheer size or wealth.</summary>

### ON THE LAWS, BOOK V.

<columns>

<margin>A</margin> ...and would likely desire that the citizens be both happy and good at the same time. However, it is impossible for those who are extremely wealthy to also be extremely good—at least if we define "the wealthy" as the common people do. For they call those men wealthy who possess, among a few individuals, property worth a great deal of money <note>original: "νομίσματος ἄξια κτήματα" / "money-worthy possessions"</note>, which even a wicked man might possess. If this is indeed the case, I would never agree with them that a wealthy man is truly happy unless he is also good. But it is impossible for someone to be exceptionally good and exceptionally wealthy at once. Why so? someone might ask. Because, we would say, the profit gained from both just and unjust sources is more than double that which comes from just sources alone; <margin>B</margin> furthermore, the expenses of those who refuse to spend either honorably or basely are half as much as the expenses of those who are willing to spend honorably and on honorable things. Therefore, a man who acts in the opposite way—earning twice as much and spending half as much—will always be wealthier than his counterpart. Of these two, one is a good man, while the other is not necessarily bad if he is merely frugal, though sometimes he is utterly wicked. But a good man, as we just said, can never be exceptionally wealthy. For the one who receives from both just and unjust sources and spends on neither just nor unjust things is wealthy, provided he is also frugal. The utterly wicked man, being for the most part a spendthrift <note>original: "ἄσωτος" / "prodigal" or "unsaved"</note>, is very poor. But he who spends on honorable things and acquires only from just sources is unlikely to ever excel in wealth, <margin>C</margin> nor will he be extremely poor. Thus, our argument is correct: the very wealthy are not good men, and if they are not good, they are not happy.

Now, the aim of our law here was that the citizens should be as happy as possible and as friendly to one another as possible. But citizens could never be "dear friends" where many lawsuits and injustices existed among them, but only where these are as small and few as possible. For this reason, we say that neither gold nor silver should exist in the city, nor should there be much money-making through menial trades <term>menial trades: <note>original: "διαβαναυσίας" / "banausia". Refers to manual labor or crafts that were thought to "vulgarize" the soul because they were done for pay rather than virtue.</note></term>, usury, or the shameful breeding of livestock. Instead, the city should rely on what agriculture yields and provides, and even then, only in such a measure that money-making does not force a man to neglect the things for which money exists. These things are <margin>D</margin> the soul and the body; which, without physical training <note>original: "γυμναστικῆς" / "gymnastics"</note> and the rest of education, would never become worth mentioning. This is why I have said more than once that the care of money should hold the last place in honor. Since there are three things in total that every man is serious about, the concern for money, if pursued correctly, is the third and last; the concern for the body is the middle; and the first is the concern for the soul. And indeed, the constitution we are now describing is only correctly legislated if it distributes honors in this order. But if any of the laws established therein appears to place health above temperance <note>original: "σωφρονεῖν" / "sophrosyne", meaning moderation or self-control</note>, or wealth above health and temperance, it will clearly be a law incorrectly placed. Therefore, the legislator must frequently remind himself: "What is it I want, and does this happen to me, or am I missing the mark?" In this way, perhaps, he might navigate through the task of legislation and set others free; <margin>E</margin> but in no other way could he ever do so.

Let the one who has received a lot <term>lot: <note>original: "κλῆρον" / "kleros". A portion of land assigned by lot to a citizen-family, intended to be inalienable.</note></term> possess it, we say, on the conditions we have stated. It would have been a fine thing if every person coming into the colony had all other things in equal measure. Since this is not possible, but one man will arrive possessing more money and another less, it is necessary for many reasons—and specifically for the sake of equal opportunity in the city's crises—that there be unequal property assessments. This is so that offices, taxes, and distributions may be assigned according to the value of each person's assessment, not only according to their own virtue and that of their ancestors, nor their bodily strength and beauty, but also according to their use of wealth and <margin>F</margin> poverty. By receiving honors and offices as equally as possible according to this proportional inequality, the citizens will not fall into discord.

For these reasons, it is necessary to establish four classes of property assessment: the first, second, third, and fourth—or whatever other names they may be called. This is so that they may remain in the same class, or, when the very wealthy become poor or the poor become wealthy, they may move into the assessment class that is appropriate for each.

Next, I would propose the following legal framework as a consequence: we say that in a city which is to be free from the greatest of diseases—which might more correctly be called "social division" or "sedition" <note>original: "στάσιν" / "stasis"</note>—neither harsh poverty nor, on the other hand, <margin>G</margin> enormous wealth should exist among any of the citizens. For both of these conditions breed one another. Therefore, the legislator must now state a limit for each of these. Let the limit of poverty be the value of the "lot," which must remain stable, and which no magistrate shall ever allow to become smaller for anyone; for this, the citizens who are ambitious for virtue will keep a watch over both their own property and that of others. Having established this measure, the legislator will allow a man to acquire twice this amount, or three times, or even up to four times. If anyone acquires more than this—whether by finding it, receiving it as a gift, making a profit, or by some other such stroke of luck—he should give the surplus to the city and the city's guardian gods. In doing so, he shall be held in high regard and remain free from penalty. But if someone <margin>H</margin> disobeys this law, anyone who wishes may inform on him, and the informant shall receive half of the amount, while the guilty party shall pay an equal amount out of his own property as a penalty, and the other half shall belong to the gods. All property, apart from the lot, should be written down openly before the magistrates appointed by law as guardians, so that all legal judgments regarding money may be easy and very clear. After this, the city first in...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...He will indeed wish them to be happy and good, which are two things that almost necessarily happen together. But for men to be very wealthy and simultaneously good is impossible. I speak of those who are wealthy as the many judge them, claiming those are wealthy who, being few among many, possess the most money—money which even any wicked person could possess. If this is so, I will never concede to them that a rich man is truly happy unless he is also good; but it cannot be that someone excels in wealth and goodness at the same time. Why is this? someone perhaps might ask. Because, we shall say, acquisition that is made both unjustly and justly <margin>B</margin> is more than double that which is made only justly. And the expenditures that are made neither honorably nor shamefully are half as large as those which are honorable and are honorably spent. Therefore, the man who acquires twice as much and spends half as much will never be richer than he who does the opposite. One of these is a good man; the other is not exactly bad when he is at least frugal, but sometimes he is entirely bad; a good man, however, as we have just said, is never exceptionally rich. For he who piles up money both justly and unjustly, and spends neither justly nor unjustly, becomes rich when he is frugal. But he who is entirely bad, since he is for the most part a spendthrift and a prodigal, becomes very poor. But he who spends honorably and acquires only justly will never easily excel in wealth, nor will he be pressed by poverty. Thus, our discourse <margin>C</margin> correctly asserts that the very wealthy are not good men; and if they are not good, they will not be happy either. 

Our legal sanction looks toward this goal: that the citizens may be most happy and especially friends among themselves. <margin>The very wealthy are not good.</margin> Certainly, they will never be friends if, being vexed by mutual injuries, they are forced to use many judgments in litigation; they will be friends if these are as small and few as possible. Therefore, we say it is necessary that there be neither gold nor silver in the city, nor much profit from mechanical works, inn-keeping, or usury, nor from livestock in a shameful way, but rather from those things which agriculture <margin>D</margin> offers and provides. And this in such a way that profit does not force one to neglect those things for the sake of which money is sought—these are the soul and the body, which without physical training and other discipline will never be of any <margin>Three things in which men place their zeal: goods of the soul, goods of the body, and money.</margin> value. Therefore, the care of money, as has already been said often, should hold the last place of honor. Indeed, since there are three things in which men place their zeal, the concern for money is the last and third, if it is held correctly; that of the body is the middle; and that of the soul is the first. And yet, this very republic which we are now founding is correctly ordered if it distributes honors in this way. If, however, any law established in it prefers the health of the body to temperance, or wealth to health and temperance, it seems not to have been correctly placed. Therefore, the legislator must often declare what he himself intends, and what, if it happens, will succeed well. If not, the hope of his institution will frustrate him. And thus perhaps he will deliver both himself <margin>E</margin> and others from the burden of bearing laws, but in no other way. 

He who has therefore drawn his portion by lot should possess it under the condition we have stated. It would be well done if all other things that come into the colony were possessed equally. But since that cannot be done, and one man coming will have more money and another less, it is necessary—for the sake of many things and for the opportunistic times of equality in the city—that unequal censuses be established in it. Thus, magistrates, taxes, and distributions may be received by each according to their dignity, not only because of their own virtue or that of their ancestors, or their beauty or the strength of their body, but also according to the use of wealth and poverty, as <margin>F</margin> equally as possible—that is, receiving in an unequal portion, but in a way that is easily made proportional—lest they should contend at all. For the sake of these things, it is necessary that four property censuses, differing in size, be made: First, Second, Third, and Fourth, or called by any other names. Thus some may remain in the same census, while others, having become richer or poorer, may pass into the census suitable for them. To these things, I will add the following form of law: namely, we say it is necessary that in a city which is to be free from the greatest disease (which I might more rightly call discord or sedition), there should be neither extreme want among any of the citizens, nor <margin>G</margin> immense wealth. For both of those are born from both of these. 

Wherefore, the limit of each must be established by the legislator. If, therefore, the limit of poverty is the census of the lot (which must be stable, and which no magistrate nor anyone else who cares for virtue shall suffer to be less for anyone), the legislator, having prescribed his measure for these, will permit them to possess double this amount, and triple, and quadruple. But if anyone possesses more, whether found, or given, or gained through profit, or acquired by any other such fortune, if he gives all that remains to the city and to the gods who are the guardians of the city, he shall be blameless and praiseworthy. But if he does not obey the law, whoever reports this <margin>H</margin> shall obtain half. The man himself shall be punished with an equal part of his own goods; but let the half-part be the gods'. Whatever things they possess beyond the lot should be openly written down before the magistrate who is the guardian of these things appointed by law, so that all judgments concerning money may be easy and very clear. After these things, the city first...

<margin>On the site of the city.</margin>

</columns>

<summary>Plato argues that extreme wealth is incompatible with virtue and happiness, as it often stems from unjust gain or a lack of honorable spending. He proposes a social structure with four property classes and a wealth cap set at four times the value of a citizen's basic land allotment to prevent the "disease" of civil discord.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the ideal city-state's physical and social organization. Having previously established the limit of 5,040 households, the text now details the geographic distribution of land and the importance of mathematical education for the citizenry.</meta>

# OF PLATO

<columns>

<margin>Division of the lands.</margin>
The city should be founded as close to the center of the region as possible, choosing a site that possesses all the other necessary conveniences for a city—things that are not difficult to understand or describe. Next, a division into twelve parts should be made. First, a sanctuary should be consecrated to Vesta <note>Greek: "Hestia"</note>, Jupiter <note>Greek: "Zeus"</note>, and Pallas <note>Greek: "Athena"</note>, and this area shall be called the "Acropolis" and enclosed by a circle. From this point, both the city itself and the entire region shall be divided into twelve sections. These parts must be made equal in value, so that sections with fertile soil are smaller in size, while those with poor soil are larger. Five thousand and forty lots <note>The number 5,040 was chosen by Plato because it is divisible by every number from 1 to 12 (except 11), making it ideal for administrative and military subdivisions.</note> are to be marked out, and each of these shall be divided into two portions. Every citizen shall receive a lot consisting of two parts joined by chance: one part near the city and one part farther away. Thus, the part nearest the city is paired with the part furthest away to form one lot; the second nearest with the second furthest, and so on for all the rest. <margin>B</margin> Care must also be taken in these dual divisions to address what I just mentioned regarding the fertility or poor quality of the soil, so that the distribution is made equal by adjusting the size of the plots. Furthermore, the citizens must be divided into twelve parts, just like the other goods, preserving an equality across all things, and everything must be recorded in a census. Then, the twelve lots shall be assigned to twelve gods. Each part shall be consecrated to its own god and be called a "tribe." Also, the twelve sections of the city must be divided into two dwellings each, just as was done for the rest of the region: one dwelling near the center and the other near the outskirts. <margin>C</margin> This concludes the order of settlement.

However, we must consider this above all: that the things we have described will likely never find such a perfect opportunity where everything coincides exactly as written. It is unlikely that men will easily tolerate such a settlement, or calmly endure having their wealth limited to a fixed and moderate amount throughout their lives, or follow our rules for the generation of children, or go without gold and silver, or accept all the other things the legislator is clearly going to command based on the principles above. Furthermore, they may not accept the placement of dwellings in the center and at the edges of the region as we have ordained. <margin>D</margin> All these things are spoken of as if they were dreams <note>original: "veluti somnia" / "just like dreams"</note>, or as if a city and its citizens were being molded out of wax. In a way, these ideas are not poorly expressed; but the legislator must also state what could be said in response. Do not think, my friends, that I am unaware that what has just been said is, in a sense, true. But it is right, I believe, that in every case, the person proposing a model <note>original: "exemplar" / "pattern"</note> to which a work should be compared should omit nothing that belongs to its highest beauty and truth. If someone is unable to achieve some of these things in practice because they are beyond human strength, he should leave them aside; <margin>E</margin> instead, he should pursue that which is closest to them and most akin to what ought to be done, while allowing the legislator to bring his vision to completion. Once that is done, the legislator and the citizen should together consider what part of the plan is useful and what might be impossible for the laws to sustain. For every craftsman, if he is to earn praise, must produce a work that is consistent with itself in every detail, even in the smallest matter.

Now, after the distribution of the twelve parts, we must observe that these twelve parts contain many further subdivisions, all the way down to the five thousand and forty lots. From these come the tribes, the clans, and the villages, as well as the military ranks and maneuvers. <margin>F</margin> Furthermore, the coinage, the measures for dry and liquid goods, and the weights must all be standardized and made harmonious with one another by the legislator. There is no need to fear that we will be thought too concerned with trifles or small details <margin>On the measurement of household goods.</margin> if someone commands that even the vessels and household furniture of the citizens should have their own measure, and that nothing should be possessed without a certain proportion. On a common level, the legislator should judge that the divisions and varieties of numbers are useful for everything—not only in their own internal relationships but also in lengths, depths, sounds, and movements, whether moving straight up or down or in a circle. <margin>G</margin> The legislator must look to all these things and command all citizens, as far as they are able, never to depart from this numerical order. For there is no other single branch of education in childhood that has as much power for domestic management, for politics, or for all the arts, as the study of numbers. Most importantly, it rouses those who are naturally sleepy and dull, making them quick to learn, mindful, and sharp-witted, improving them through a divine art <note>original: "divina arte"</note> beyond their natural state. All these things are good and proper institutions, provided that by other laws and duties, the spirit of meanness and greed <note>original: "illiberalitate & auaritia"</note> is rooted out of the souls of those who undertake them. If not, this study may produce cunning <note>Greek: "panourgia" / "knavery" or "villainy"</note> rather than wisdom. <margin>H</margin> We see this happening now with the Egyptians, the Phoenicians, and many other nations, due to the meanness of their other practices and possessions—whether this was caused by a bad legislator, an unlucky fate, or some other natural cause. For we must not forget, O Clinia and Megillus, that there is a great difference in locations for producing better or worse men...

<column-break/>

[The Greek text on the right column mirrors the Latin translation provided above, detailing the founding of the city in the center (μέσῳ) of the land, the dedication to Hestia, Zeus, and Athena, the division of the 5,040 lots (πεντακισχιλίους καὶ τετταράκοντα), and the pedagogical value of arithmetic in waking the "sleepy and ignorant" (νυστατὰ καὶ ἀμαθῆ) mind.]

<page-num>613</page-num>
<header>ON THE LAWS, BOOK VI.</header>

<columns>

<margin>A</margin>
...certain places differ from others in their power to produce better or worse men, and we must not legislate in opposition to these natural conditions. For some places, I suppose, are sunny or shaded due to various winds and atmospheres, while others differ because of their waters. Still others differ because of the food produced from the soil, which provides not only better or worse nourishment for the body, but is no less capable of producing all such effects in the soul. Of all these factors, the greatest differences occur in regions where there is a divine inspiration or where certain spirits <note>original: "daimones"</note> have their allotted portions, receiving those who settle there with favor or the opposite. A lawgiver of sound mind, having inspected these things as far as a human being is able to observe such matters, would then attempt to establish his laws accordingly. This is exactly what you must do, Cleinias; it is the first thing to turn your attention to when you are about to settle a territory. CLEINIAS: You speak excellently, Athenian guest; that is exactly how I must proceed.

# PLATO'S LAWS,
## OR,
### ON LEGISLATION,
### THE SIXTH DIALOGUE.

<margin>B</margin>
ATHENIAN: WELL THEN, after everything we have said up to this point, it would be nearly time for you to establish the government offices for your city. CLEINIAS: That is indeed the case. ATHENIAN: There are two parts to this that make up the orderly arrangement of a state. First, the establishment of the offices and the officials—how many there should be and in what manner they should be appointed. Second, we must assign the laws to each office, determining which laws, how many, and of what kind are appropriate for each. But let us pause for a moment before we begin the selection and say something relevant to the matter. CLEINIAS: What might that be? ATHENIAN: This: It is clear to everyone, I think, that although legislation is a great task, if a well-prepared city appoints unsuitable officials to oversee its well-made laws, not only will there be no benefit from those laws—and they might even become a laughingstock—but almost the greatest harm and ruin will come to cities because of them. CLEINIAS: How could it be otherwise?
<margin>C</margin>
ATHENIAN: Let us consider this, my friend, as it applies to your current state and city. You see that those who are to proceed correctly toward the powers of office must first have given a sufficient proof of themselves and their families from childhood until the time of their election. Secondly, those who are going to do the electing should have been raised and educated in the habits of the laws, so that they can properly judge and select those who are worthy or reject those who are not. But how could people who have only recently come together, who are strangers to one another and as yet uneducated, ever be able to choose officials without error? CLEINIAS: They almost never could.
<margin>D</margin>
ATHENIAN: Yet, as they say, "the contest does not easily admit excuses." This is the task you and I must now perform. Since you have undertaken to settle the city as one of ten representatives for the Knossians <note>Knossos was the major city of Crete; Cleinias is tasked with leading the colony of "Magnesia."</note>, as you say, and I have promised to help you with our present storytelling—well, I would not want to leave the story "headless" <note>An ancient idiom meaning an incomplete or unfinished work.</note> or mutilated; for if it wandered about in such a state, it would appear quite ugly. CLEINIAS: You have spoken very well, Guest. ATHENIAN: Not only spoken, but I will act accordingly to the best of my ability. CLEINIAS: Let us by all means do exactly as we say. ATHENIAN: So it shall be, if God wills it, and if we can overcome our old age to that extent. CLEINIAS: It is likely that God will so will. ATHENIAN: It is indeed likely. Following His lead, let us also consider this. CLEINIAS: Consider what?
<margin>E</margin>
ATHENIAN: How boldly and even dangerously our city will be settled at this time. CLEINIAS: What are you looking at, and why do you say this now? ATHENIAN: How easily and fearlessly we are legislating for inexperienced men, as if they will one day readily accept the laws we are now establishing. It is clear enough to almost anyone, even if they are not very wise, that no one will easily accept new laws at the start. However, if we could wait for a sufficient time—until children have tasted the laws, been raised under them, and become accustomed to them, taking part in the elections of the whole city—then, if this could be brought about correctly by some means, you would have great security. Indeed, time would be required to wait for a city to be so educated.
<margin>F</margin>
CLEINIAS: That certainly makes sense. ATHENIAN: Let us see then if we can find a suitable way to achieve this. I say, Cleinias, that the Knossians, above all other Cretans, should not only offer a ritual cleansing of the land you are now settling, but they should also take the utmost care to establish the first officials as securely and as excellently as possible.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
...for which different laws must be enacted as is expedient. For some places are difficult and unruly due to the variety and turbulence of the winds; others because of the waters; others because of the foods, which arise from the earth not only as advantageous or disadvantageous for bodies, but no less so for souls. Most of all, however, regions differ in whether there is a certain divine inspiration and what the local spirits <note>original: "daemones"</note> have allotted to them: those who dwell there are regarded by them either favorably or the opposite. Once these things have been considered according to human ability, a lawgiver in possession of his senses will turn his attention to making laws. This, O Cleinias, is what you must do. For you must turn your mind to these things before you cause the region to be inhabited. CLEINIAS: Excellently said, O Athenian guest. Therefore, this is what I must do.

---

# PLATO ON THE
## LAWS, OR, ON THE
### INSTITUTION OF
### LAWS, THE SIXTH DIALOGUE.

> SUMMARY OF THE DIALOGUE. This sixth book or dialogue deals with the most excellent part of the political order, namely the appointment of magistrates <note>original: "magistratuum"</note>. For it would be in vain to fortify a republic with laws unless there was an enforcement of those laws, which depends entirely on the foresight of the magistrates. He deals extensively and individually with the creation of all magistrates: the highest, middle, and lowest—those whose work and duties are variously employed in peace and in war, in the city and in the fields. And since marriage is the foundation of human society, he therefore deals with it here accurately, and even prescribes certain laws: on the manner of contracting marriage, on the procreation of children, on the law of dowries, and on divorces. He also corrects that foul <term>gloomy partnership</term> <note>original: "σκυθρωπὴν κοινωνίαν" (skythrōpēn koinōnian); likely referring to the communal family structures proposed in Plato's earlier work, the Republic.</note> which might have contaminated his distinguished discourse on the republic; he who is diligent must be corrected by this passage. He also deals with certain matters regarding slavery, which are the greatest part of <term>possessions</term> <note>original: "κτημάτων" (ktēmatōn)</note>, and therefore of great importance in the republic.

<margin>B</margin>
AFTER all the things we have said so far, it seems that the magistrates in the city must now be established. CLEINIAS: Certainly. ATHENIAN: There are indeed two aspects to the adornment of a republic. First, the constitution of the magistrates—how many are needed and by what means they are appointed. Second, concerning the laws to be assigned to the magistrate—how many and what kind are suitable for each. But for a little while before we elect the magistrates, let us pause to clarify some things pertaining to their election. CLEINIAS: Which things? ATHENIAN: These. Listen now.
<margin>C</margin>
No one doubts that since lawgiving is a great matter, if one establishes unsuitable magistrates for a city well-prepared by laws, then even though the laws are well-placed, it will not only be of no benefit and will provoke laughter, but it will even produce the greatest damage and calamities for cities. CLEINIAS: Plainly. ATHENIAN: This, therefore, must be considered, my friend: how this situation arises in this city and republic of yours. For you see that those who are to correctly receive a magistracy ought first to have been sufficiently tested since their youth—both they themselves and their families—right up until the election itself. Then, those who are to cast their votes must also have been educated in lawful customs, so that they can easily recognize those who should be admitted or rejected, and conduct themselves toward both according to their worth. But truly, those who have recently come together, since they neither know one another sufficiently nor are they yet educated, how can they ever correctly elect magistrates? CLEINIAS: In almost no way at all.
<margin>D</margin>
ATHENIAN: But indeed, the contest (as they say) does not easily accept excuses. This, however, must be done both by me now and by you: since you have also freely undertaken the duty of establishing a city for the Cretans, and are the tenth man in this work, as you yourself say; and I have promised to bring you help by this present conversation. Therefore, I will not allow this discourse of ours to be without a head and mutilated. For if it were to wander, it would appear ugly to everyone. CLEINIAS: You have spoken most excellently, Guest. ATHENIAN: Nay, I will even act thus to the best of my strength. CLEINIAS: Let us do exactly as we say. ATHENIAN: We shall do so indeed, if God wills, so that we may even overcome our old age in this part. CLEINIAS: But it must be believed that God wills it. ATHENIAN: It must be believed indeed. Therefore, following Him, let us say this as well. CLEINIAS: Say what?
<margin>E</margin>
ATHENIAN: How boldly and at the same time dangerously the city will be established by us at this time. CLEINIAS: To what end do you say this? ATHENIAN: Because we are easily and intrepidly giving laws to raw men, as if they would easily accept them. But if it were so, no one would easily accept new laws. If, however, we were to wait so long until children instructed by the laws, having lived together for a long time under those same laws, could cast their votes with the whole city, and if this were done correctly with all our strength, certainly both then and in the future, a city so instructed would remain far from error.
<margin>F</margin>
CLEINIAS: So reason advises. ATHENIAN: Let us see, then, if we can find some suitable way for these things. It is necessary, O Cleinias, that the Knossians, above all other Cretans, should not only begin by making a sort of libation for the republic you are now founding, but they should provide with all zeal that the first magistrates be established as safely and as excellently as possible.

<sig>Ff</sig>

</columns>

The Athenian Stranger warns that even perfect laws are useless or harmful without competent, well-educated officials to enforce them.</summary>
