# PLATO'S LAWS
## BOOK SIX (CONTINUED)

<columns>

<margin>A</margin> In establishing other offices, the work is shorter; but to appoint the guardians of the laws before all others is necessary with the greatest diligence. 
**CLINIAS.** In what way and by what reasoning shall we do this?
**ATHENIAN.** I say this, O men of Crete: Since the people of Knossos <note>original: "Gnofios"</note> take the lead among many cities, they must—together with those who have come to this colony—select thirty-seven men in total from among themselves and the colonists. 
<margin>B</margin> Nineteen shall be chosen from those who will inhabit the colony, and the remaining eighteen from Knossos itself. Let the Knossians grant these men to your city, and let them also make you yourself a citizen of this colony and one of the eighteen, either by persuasion or by a moderate degree of compulsion.
**CLINIAS.** But what of you, Guest, and Megillus? Will you not also participate in this Republic with us?
**ATHENIAN.** Athens thinks very highly of itself, O Clinias, and so does Sparta, and both are situated far away. But for you, everything is conveniently arranged: both for the other inhabitants and according to what has just been said about you, these things can be done most fittingly for you and them at this time. But as time goes on and the Republic remains established, let the designation of such magistrates be done in this way: Whoever is able to bear arms, whether cavalry or infantry, and who participated in war when their age permitted, shall enter their vote. They shall hold the assembly in the temple which the city deems most excellent. 
<margin>C</margin> Each man, from wherever he has come, shall place his name, his father’s name, his tribe, and his clan written on a tablet <note>original: "tabula"</note> upon the altar of the god. It shall be permitted for anyone who wishes, if he suspects a tablet is not correctly written, to take it away and place it in a public area, where it shall remain for no less than thirty days. The magistrates shall show to the whole city the three hundred tablets thus approved, and the city shall again accept or reject from these whomever it wishes. Then, one hundred selected a second time shall be shown again to everyone. For the third selection, anyone may name from the hundred men whomever he wishes. Then the thirty-seven men who receive the most votes shall be declared magistrates. 
<margin>D</margin> Who then, O Clinias and Megillus, will establish all these things concerning the magistrates and their probation in the city? Do we understand that in cities thus united from the beginning, there must be certain people to do this? Yet those who are to be chosen from all the magistrates are not yet to be found. However, it is necessary that they be not common men, but the highest 
<margin>Proverb.</margin> and most excellent. For it is said in the proverb: "The beginning is half of the whole work." <note>original: "Principium enim dimidium totius operis esse"</note> And we all everywhere praise him who has begun well. But to me, this seems to be more than half, and a right beginning has never been sufficiently praised by anyone.
**CLINIAS.** You speak rightly.
**ATHENIAN.** Therefore, since this is not hidden from us, let us not pass it over in silence; but let us clearly declare how it may be done, although I have nothing to say at present except this one necessary and useful thing.
**CLINIAS.** What is that?
**ATHENIAN.** Indeed, I say that for this city which we are about to found, 
<margin>E</margin> no one is either father or mother except that city which sends the colony. Nor am I ignorant that many colonies have been, and will be, torn apart by discord with the cities that sent them. But just as a son behaves toward his parents—who, although he may have opposed them at times, yet in the need of his childhood loves his parents and is loved in turn, and always fleeing to his own family finds protection in them alone—so also I think the new city will be affected toward its caretakers, the Knossians, and the Knossians toward the new city.
<margin>What is well said is not harmed by repetition.</margin> I repeat, therefore, what I just said. For it does no harm to say twice what is well said. It is necessary that the Knossians take care of all these things, and choose from the colonists the elder and best men, no fewer than one hundred, and another hundred from the Knossians themselves. I say that these men, having set out for the new city, must take care that the magistrates are established according to the laws and that those appointed are approved. Once these things are done, the Knossians may return to Knossos; but let the new city strive to preserve itself and live happily. Those who are numbered among the thirty-seven men shall take care of these matters now and forever after. First, let them be the guardians of the laws; then also of the records, where each man 
<margin>The maximum census of citizens, according to Plato.</margin>
<margin>G</margin> shall have written the size of his own property <note>original: "census"</note>. Let the maximum census be four minas; the second, three; the third, two; and the fourth, one. But if anyone is found to possess more than what is written on his tablet, let the surplus be made public property. Furthermore, let him be liable to anyone who wishes to accuse him as infamous, since he is found to despise the laws for the sake of gain. And anyone who wishes may accuse him before the guardians of the laws in the name of base gain. And he who is convicted shall be excluded from public possessions, and if any distribution of goods occurs in the city, he shall receive nothing beyond his original lot. It shall be written that he has been convicted for as long as he lives, where anyone who wishes may read it. 
<margin>H</margin> A Guardian of the Laws shall hold this office for no more than twenty years, and shall not hold it unless he is at least fifty years old. And if he has obtained this office while in his sixtieth year, let him preside for only ten years; in this way, he who has exceeded his seventieth year shall not hold such a great office.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Regarding other offices, the task is shorter; but for us to choose guardians of the laws is most necessary with all haste. **CLINIAS.** What then is the method and the plan we shall apply to this? **ATHENIAN.** I say this, O sons of the Cretans: the city of Knossos, because of its seniority among cities, should choose from those arriving at this settlement—both from its own people and from them—thirty-seven in total. Eighteen 
<margin>B</margin> shall be from the settlers, and the others from Knossos itself. These the Knossians shall give to the second city, and you yourself shall be a citizen of this colony, persuaded by new arguments or compelled by moderate force. **CLINIAS.** Why then, Guest, have you and Megillus not shared in this constitution with us? **ATHENIAN.** Athens thinks great things of itself, O Clinias, and so does Sparta, and both are far away. But for you, everything is in proper order, as it is for the other founders, just as we have recently discussed. Now, as to how the magistrates might best be chosen, let this be said: after time has passed and the constitution remains, let their selection be as follows: all those shall participate in the selection of magistrates who bear arms as cavalry or infantry, and who have shared in war during the strength of their age. The election shall be held in the temple which the city deems most honored. 
<margin>C</margin> Each man shall carry to the altar of the god a tablet on which is written his name, his father’s name, and the tribe and deme to which he belongs. He shall also write his own name alongside. It shall be permitted to anyone who wishes to take up any tablet that does not seem rightly written and place it in the marketplace for no less than thirty days. The magistrates shall then display to the whole city those tablets judged among the first three hundred for everyone to see. Then, in the same way, they shall bring back from these whomever each man wishes. Those chosen a second time from them—the one hundred—shall be shown again to all. For the third time, let anyone bring whomever he wishes from the hundred, proceeding through the same steps. Then the thirty-seven who receive the most votes, having been judged, shall be declared magistrates. 
<margin>D</margin> Who then, O Clinias and Megillus, will establish all these things in the city, the office and its examinations? Do we realize that for cities being founded in this way, there is a necessity for certain people to be there, but those who would first be their right rulers do not yet exist? They must be there somehow, and they should not be mediocre, but as far as possible the very best. For "the beginning" is said in proverbs to be "half of every work," and we all praise a good beginning every time. But it is (as it seems to me) more than half, and no one has yet praised a good beginning sufficiently. **CLINIAS.** You speak most correctly. **ATHENIAN.** Let us not, then, knowing this, 
<margin>E</margin> leave it unspoken, without clarifying to ourselves in what way it shall be. I for my part am in no way at a loss, except to say one thing that is necessary and useful for the present discussion. **CLINIAS.** What is that? **ATHENIAN.** I say that for this city we are settling, there is no father or mother except the city that is settling it. I am not unaware that many of those cities settled have often been at odds with their founders, and will be so in the future. But now, for the present, like a child—even if he is destined to differ from his parents later—in his current lack of education, he loves and is loved by his parents. Always fleeing to his relatives, he finds them his only necessary allies. This is what I say now exists for the Knossians because of their care for the new city, and for the new city toward Knossos. I say, just as I said just now (for a thing well said does no harm if repeated twice), that the Knossians must take care of all these things, choosing together from those arriving at the colony the eldest and the best they can, no fewer than one hundred; and let there be another hundred from the Knossians themselves. I say these men must go to the new city and help ensure that the offices are established according to the laws and are tested. When these things are done, let the Knossians inhabit Knossos, and let the new city attempt to preserve itself and be successful. Those who become the thirty-seven shall know now and for all time that they are chosen for these duties: first, let them be 
<margin>G</margin> guardians of the laws; next, of the written records where each man registers with the magistrates the amount of his property. Let the largest property-class be four minas; the second, three; the third, two; and the fourth, one. If anyone is found possessing more than what is written, let all such property become public. In addition, let him face a trial at the hands of anyone who wishes to prosecute him—not for a noble cause, but a 
<margin>H</margin> shameful one—if he is caught despising the laws for the sake of profit. Let anyone who wishes prosecute him for "shameful gain" before the guardians of the laws. If the defendant is convicted, let him not share in the common property. When there is a distribution in the city, let him have no share, except for his original lot. Let his conviction be recorded for as long as he lives, where anyone who wishes can read it. Let no one serve as a guardian of the laws for more than twenty years, and let him enter the office being no less than fifty years old. If he is appointed at sixty, let him rule for only ten years; and according to this logic, if he lives beyond seventy, let him no longer think of holding such a great office as if he were worthy.

# ON THE LAWS, BOOK VI.

<columns>

<margin>A</margin> Let these fifty-three matters concerning the guardians of the laws be concluded. As the laws move forward, whoever is able will provide instructions to these men, whose primary care—beyond what we have just stated—must be to oversee the current affairs. Now, let us speak in order about the election of the other magistrates. After these things, the leaders of the army must be chosen, along with their subordinates for war, such as masters of the horse <note>original: "hipparchs"</note>, tribal commanders <note>original: "phylarchs"</note>, and those who organize the infantry ranks. For the latter, the name "commanders of the ranks" <note>original: "taxiarchs," a term commonly used by the public</note> would be most fitting. For these positions, the guardians of the laws shall nominate certain citizens from this very city as future generals. Those who are either currently of the appropriate age to serve in war or have previously served shall then choose from those nominated. 
<margin>B</margin> If anyone believes that someone not nominated is better than one who was, he may name and nominate that person in place of the other, provided he confirms under oath that he truly judges the person to be better. Whichever of the two is chosen by a show of hands shall be entered into the selection process. The three who receive the most votes, after being scrutinized—just as the guardians of the laws were—shall be the generals and overseers of military affairs. These elected generals shall then nominate twelve "commanders of the ranks" <note>taxiarchs</note>, one for each tribe. The process for counter-nomination, the voting by show of hands, and the final judgment shall be the same as it was for the generals. 
<margin>C</margin> For the present, before the presiding officers <note>prytaneis</note> and the council have been chosen, the guardians of the laws shall gather the assembly in a place that is most sacred and suitable. The heavy infantry <note>hoplites</note> and the cavalry shall sit separately, and thirdly, all others who bear arms. In the election of generals and masters of the horse, everyone shall cast a vote; for the commanders of the ranks, only those who carry shields <note>hoplites</note> shall vote; for the tribal commanders, all the cavalry shall vote. As for the leaders of the light-armed troops, archers, or any other such units, the generals themselves shall appoint them for their own service. The designation of the masters of the horse <note>hipparchs</note> still remains. These shall be nominated by the same people who nominated the generals, and the selection and 
<margin>D</margin> counter-nomination shall proceed just as it did for the generals. The cavalry shall vote for them in the presence of the infantry. The two who receive the most votes shall lead all the cavalry. Disputes regarding the voting may be raised up to twice; if a third dispute arises, those who were responsible for the measure of the voting in each case shall decide. 

The Council <note>Boule</note> shall consist of three hundred and sixty members. This distribution is suitable as it can be divided into groups of twelve. If divided into four parts, there would be ninety members from each; thus, ninety councilmen shall be drawn from each of the property classes <note>census ranks</note>. First, all citizens are required to vote for representatives from the highest property class; 
<margin>E</margin> anyone who fails to do so shall be fined according to the determined penalty. Once these votes are cast, the names shall be recorded. On the following day, they shall vote for representatives from the second class in the same manner. On the third day, anyone who wishes may vote for representatives from the third class, but it shall be mandatory for those of the first three classes to do so. Those of the fourth and smallest class are free from the penalty if they do not wish to vote. On the fourth day, everyone shall vote for representatives from the fourth and smallest class. On this day, if a person from the third or fourth class does not vote, they shall not be fined; but if a person from the first or second class fails to vote, they shall be fined. The person from the second class shall be fined triple the initial amount, and the person from the first class quadruple. 
<margin>F</margin> On the fifth day, the magistrates shall display the names of all the nominees for all citizens to see. Everyone must then vote for individuals from this list or be fined the initial penalty. From those chosen out of all the property classes, half—that is, one hundred and eighty—shall be selected by lot to be confirmed for the annual order of the Council. 

In this way, the creation of the magistrates will be a middle ground between the power of a single ruler <note>monarchy</note> and the power of the people <note>democracy</note>. A republic should always maintain this middle path. For slaves and masters will never be friends, nor will the good and the bad be friends if they are granted equal honors. For when equal things are given to unequal people, they become unequal, unless they receive the proper measure. For because of both these extremes, republics are filled with civil strife. 
<margin>G</margin> There is an ancient and true saying that "equality creates friendship," which is stated quite rightly and harmoniously. However, because it is not entirely clear what kind of equality this is, it causes us great confusion. For there are two kinds of equality, called by the same name but in practice almost opposite. Any city or lawmaker can apply the first kind to the distribution of honors by using the lot—this is the equality of number, weight, and measure. But the truest and best equality is not easily seen by everyone. This is the "Judgment of Zeus" <note>a philosophical concept meaning giving to each what they deserve based on merit</note>. It is granted to humans only in small amounts, but wherever it is applied to cities or individuals, it brings all things good. It grants more to the greater and less to the lesser, giving to each according to their nature. Indeed, it always assigns greater honors to those with greater virtue, and to those of lesser virtue and education, it assigns what is fitting according to reason. This is indeed the essence of civil justice. This is what we must strive for; and looking toward this very equality, O Clinias, as we found this new city...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Let these three precepts regarding the guardians of the laws be established. As the laws progress, anyone will be able to instruct these men on what matters they should primarily care for, in addition to those we have just mentioned. Now, let us speak in turn of the selection of other magistrates. After these, the leaders of the army are to be chosen, as well as their subordinates in war: masters of the horse, tribal commanders, and organizers of the infantry, whom we shall rightly call "commanders of the ranks" according to common custom. Therefore, the guardians of the laws themselves shall nominate certain citizens of this city to be the future generals. All those who have served in wars at a suitable age, or who are now serving, shall either 
<margin>B</margin> approve or reject them. If anyone thinks that someone who has not been nominated is superior to one of the nominees, he may name and produce another in his place, provided he first confirms his judgment by oath. The one nominated by the greater number of votes shall be selected. The three who receive the most votes shall be approved as generals and overseers of military affairs, in the same manner as the guardians of the laws. They shall then nominate twelve "commanders of the ranks," one for each tribe. The right to nominate someone not already named and to prefer him over a nominee shall be permitted here too, just as we said regarding the soldiers. The assembly for this purpose, before the council is created, and the selection of the 
<margin>C</margin> commanders by the council, shall be held by the guardians of the laws in the most sacred and convenient location. There, the infantry and cavalry shall sit separately, and thirdly, everyone else who is under arms. In electing the leaders and masters of the horse, everyone shall cast a vote; for the commanders of the ranks, only those who carry shields <note>hoplites</note> shall vote; for the tribal commanders, all the cavalry. The generals themselves shall appoint the commanders of the light-armed troops, archers, and others of this sort. The designation of the masters of the horse remains. These shall be nominated by those who also nominated the generals of the army; the voting shall be conducted similarly, and 
<margin>D</margin> a similar comparison for nomination shall take place. The cavalry shall vote in the presence of the infantry. The two who are selected by the greater number of votes shall preside over all the cavalry. Disputes over votes may occur twice. If someone doubts a third time, those who established the manner of the assembly for each group shall judge the votes. 

The Council shall consist of three hundred and sixty men, divisible by twelve. For this distribution by sixty and three hundred men is fitting. It shall be divided into four parts of ninety each, so that ninety councilors are drawn from each of the property classes. First, all those of the highest class must necessarily vote; anyone who omits to vote shall be fined at the officials' discretion. After they have been nominated, they shall be recorded. On the following day, votes shall be cast 
<margin>E</margin> from the second class in the same way. On the third day, anyone who wishes may vote for the third class. It is mandatory, however, for men of the first three classes. The fourth and smallest class is free from penalty if any of them choose not to vote. On the fourth day, everyone shall vote from the fourth and smallest class, under the condition that if someone from the third or fourth class does not vote, he is not condemned. But if anyone from the first or second class neglects to vote, he shall be condemned: the one from the second class to triple the first penalty, and the one from the first class to quadruple. On the fifth day, the magistrates shall publish the recorded names for all citizens; all shall vote on these. Anyone who refuses shall be condemned to the first penalty. From those who 
<margin>F</margin> have been elected from all the property classes, half—that is, one hundred and eighty—shall be confirmed by lot to the order of the annual senate <note>Council</note>. 

Thus, the creation of magistrates will be a middle ground between the power of a single ruler and that of the people. It is necessary for a republic to always hold this middle. For slaves and masters will never be friends. Nor will the upright and the wicked, if they are treated with equal honors. For equals given to unequals become unequal, unless they receive their proper measure. It is because of both these things that republics are filled with sedition. For that ancient saying is very true: that friendship is born from equality. But because it is not clear enough what kind of equality achieves this, we are greatly troubled. Indeed, there are 
<margin>G</margin> two equalities called by the same name, but in effect almost opposite in many ways. One of these every city and lawmaker can apply in distributing honors by lot—I mean the equality of number, weight, and measure. But the truest and best equality is not easily seen by everyone: for it is the judgment of Zeus. It is always supplied to humans in small amounts, but as far as it is available, it brings all good things to both private individuals and cities. It gives more to the greater, less to the smaller, providing to each according to their nature. And it always assigns greater honors to those greater in virtue; but to those lesser in virtue and discipline, it assigns lesser honors. It imparts to each according to reason what is fitting. This is certainly our civil justice. We must desire this; and looking toward this very equality, O Clinias, while we found this new...

</columns>

<summary>This page outlines the specific electoral processes for military leaders and the Council in Plato's ideal city, detailing a system of tiered voting requirements based on wealth to balance democratic and aristocratic influences. It concludes with a philosophical defense of "proportional equality"—giving to each according to their merit—as the foundation of true justice and social harmony.</summary>

# OF PLATO

<columns>

<margin>A</margin> ...and we organize the city. Anyone else who establishes a city must look toward this same goal when making laws. One must not look toward a few tyrants, nor toward one man, nor toward the power of the people, but always toward justice. This justice is what we just described: the "equal distribution to unequal persons" according to their nature. Nevertheless, it is necessary for the whole city to use these two types of equality <note>Plato distinguishes between "arithmetic equality" (everyone gets the same) and "proportional equality" (everyone gets what they deserve based on virtue)</note> which are similar in name, if the whole city wishes to remain far from all internal strife. For that praiseworthy equality—the fair judgment of what is perfect and exact—is violated and broken when it departs from right judgment. Therefore, it is necessary to use the "equality of the lot" <note>selection by random chance</note> to completely avoid the indignation of the masses. In this matter, <margin>B</margin> one must invoke God and good fortune with prayers, so that the lot might be directed toward what is most just. Thus, we must necessarily use both types of equality: but we should use the equality that relies on luck only in very few cases. These things, my friends, must be observed for this reason by any city that expects to achieve safety. <margin>C</margin> Just as a ship in the middle of the sea requires guards both day and night, so too a city, placed in the middle of the surge of other cities, subject to various seditions and always close to the danger of being captured, needs a perpetual guard. Therefore, magistrates and guards ought to succeed one another from day into night and from night into day, so that the succession of those handing over and receiving the guard never ceases. A large crowd cannot do any of these things quickly. It is necessary, therefore, that the greatest part of the senators be allowed to spend most of their time in the administration of their own private affairs; however, a twelfth part of them—the distribution having been made into twelve months—should keep guard one after another, individually. This guard should be ready for anyone, whether from the city itself or coming from elsewhere, who wishes to report something or ask a question about those matters in which the city ought to either respond to other cities or receive answers to their questions from them. <margin>D</margin> This is also for the sake of the new plots that often tend to happen, primarily so they do not happen; but if they do occur, so that the city might sense it as quickly as possible and bring a remedy. This must always be done by the assembly of those presiding over the city, so that the difficulties that suddenly arise for the laws and the city may be resolved. This twelfth part of the council shall care for all these things, while the other eleven parts shall have their rest for those months. This part of the council must always perform this guardianship in the city together with the other magistrates. And the urban affairs will be properly ordered in this way. But what care and what order shall there be for the rest of the entire region? Since the whole city and the entire region have been divided into twelve parts, should we not appoint curators <margin>E</margin> of the roads, houses, buildings, ports, the market, fountains, sacred places, temples, and all other things of this kind within the city itself? <margin>CLINIAS.</margin> Why not? <margin>ATHENIAN.</margin> Let us say, then, that it is necessary to put temple-wardens and priests, both men and women, in charge. For the care of building and decorating roads so that men are not harmed and the animals themselves do not do damage, and so that everything appropriate for cities is handled both in the city's circuit and in the suburbs, three types of magistrates must be chosen. Those curators of the matters just mentioned shall be called "city-stewards" <note>original Latin: "ædiles"; original Greek: "astynomoi"</note>. <margin>City-stewards</margin> Those who will have care of the market and of selling shall be the "market-stewards" <note>original Greek: "agoranomoi"</note>. For sacred things, there shall be priests. <margin>Priests</margin> <margin>F</margin> And indeed, those priesthoods which have been handed down by succession from parents, whether to men or to women, should by no means be moved. But if there are no such priests, or only a few—which is likely to happen to those gathering to inhabit a new city—where these are lacking, priests and priestesses and temple-wardens must be appointed. All these appointments should be made partly by election and partly by lot. In every region and city, the common people <note>original Latin: "plebs"</note> must be joined with those who are not of the common people through friendship, so that there may be the greatest consensus in all these things. The matters pertaining to the creation of priests must be committed to God, so that just as it pleases Him, the divine fortune may bring the lots to those to whom it is granted. In the examination of those who have obtained the vote of the lot, that person must be approved who is sound and legitimate, and born from a house as clean as possible, free from slaughter and all such things committed against divine law; and his father and mother must have lived in the same way. <margin>G</margin> The laws concerning divine matters should be sought from Delphi <note>the famous Oracle of Apollo</note>, and "interpreters" <note>original Greek: "exegetai"; these were officials who explained sacred law</note> should be appointed for them, and these must be used. A priesthood should last no longer than a year. A person who is to handle divine matters sufficiently according to sacred laws must be no younger than sixty years old. Let the same regulations established for men be understood for sacred women [priestesses]. As for the Interpreters, the four tribes shall nominate three each; after three are approved from those chosen by the majority vote, they shall send the remaining nine to Delphi, so that one from each group of three may be selected by the oracle. Their approval and age shall be the same as was stated for the priests. These shall have the power of interpreting and explaining for their whole life. When one dies, the four tribes shall choose another from the same place where the previous one was from. There shall be "treasurers" <margin>Treasurers</margin> and keepers of the sacred money in each temple, who have authority over the profits, the fields dedicated to them, the fruits, and the leases and rentals...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...and we are now settling the city. If anyone ever settles another, we say it is necessary to legislate toward this same goal: not toward a few tyrants, or one, or some power of the people, but always toward justice. This is what was just now said: equality granted to each according to their nature, though they are unequal. It is necessary that these terms be used throughout the whole city if no part of it is ever to share in sedition. For fairness and forgiveness are departures from the perfect and exact when they occur contrary to right justice. Therefore, it is necessary to bring in the equality of the lot, for the sake of avoiding the difficulty of the many, <margin>B</margin> calling upon God and Good Fortune in prayers at that time to direct the lot toward the most just outcome. Thus it is necessary to use both equalities: but the one requiring luck should be used as little as possible. These things must be done, friends, by cities that intend to be preserved. Since a ship sailing at sea needs a guard always by day and night, so likewise a city situated in the surge of other cities, and living in danger of all kinds of plots, <margin>C</margin> might be captured. It is necessary then to join leaders to leaders from day to night and from night to day, always succeeding one another in guarding and being guarded; and those handing over should never cease. A multitude is not able to do any of these things quickly. It is necessary that most of the Council be allowed to remain for the greater part of the time at their own private affairs, managing them; hence, dividing the Council into twelve parts for twelve months, they should provide guards one by one. If someone comes from elsewhere, or even from the city itself, they should meet with them for questioning. Whether someone wishes to report something, or the city learns of things it is proper for a city to answer to other cities, or having asked others, to receive their answers. And indeed, for the sake of the various new things that are always accustomed to happen, <margin>D</margin> they must ensure as much as possible that they do not happen; or if they do, that the city, sensing it as quickly as possible, heals the occurrence. Because of this, this presiding part of the city must always have oversight and resolve whatever suddenly happens around the city. All these things should be the arrangement of the twelfth part of the Council, while the other eleven parts of the year take their rest. These guards must always be kept in the city by this portion of the Council in common with the other magistrates. And the city affairs would thus be properly arranged; but what care and what order shall there be for the rest of the whole region? When the whole city and the entire region have been divided into twelve parts, <margin>E</margin> should there not be certain appointed overseers of the roads of the city itself, and the houses, buildings, harbors, the market, fountains, and indeed the sacred precincts, temples, and all such things? <margin>KLINIAS.</margin> Of course. <margin>ATHENIAN.</margin> We say then that there must be temple-wardens and priests and priestesses for the temples. For the roads and buildings and the order concerning such things, and for men so they do not act unjustly, and for other animals, both in the city's surroundings and suburbs, so that things proper to cities might happen, three types of rulers must be chosen. Those just mentioned should be named "city-stewards" <note>astynomoi</note>, and those who always order the market, "market-stewards" <note>agoranomoi</note>. For the temples, priests; where there are ancestral priesthoods for men and women, do not move them. But if, as is likely for those <margin>F</margin> settling, there are vacancies in such houses, or no one or only a few have established priesthoods and priestesses, then temple-wardens must be made for the gods. Of all these, some must be elected and some must be by lot in their appointments; mixing the common people and those not of the common people in friendship in every region and city, so they might be in the greatest possible agreement. As for the matter of the temples, committing to God himself what is pleasing to Him, let the lot be cast, giving it over to divine fortune. One must examine the one who always gains the lot: first that he be whole and legitimate, then that he comes from as pure a house as possible; clean from murder and all such sins against divine things, both himself and his father and mother having lived the same way. <margin>G</margin> Taking the laws about divine things [from the Oracle], and having established "interpreters," use them. Priesthoods should be for a year and not longer. The one who is to excel sufficiently in divine matters according to sacred laws should be not less than sixty years old. Let the same laws apply to priestesses. For the Interpreters, after examining those who receive the most votes, send nine to Delphi, taking one from each triad. Their examination, time, and age should be the same as for the priests. These shall be Interpreters for life. When one leaves [dies], the four tribes shall choose another from where he left. Treasurers for the gods and sacred money for each of the temples, and for the precincts and fruits and the rents...

</columns>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of city administration from Plato's Laws, Book VI. The previous page ended with the need for perpetual guards in a city. This page details the specific selection of religious officials and the organization of the "agronomoi" (country-stewards) who serve as both regional guards and infrastructure managers.</meta>

### ON THE LAWS, BOOK VI.

...should be in charge, let three be chosen from the highest property classes <note>original: "maximis censibus"</note> for the greatest temples, two for the smaller ones, and one for the middle-sized and most graceful ones. These should be selected and approved in the same manner as the generals of the army. And let these matters concerning sacred things be carried out as we have described.

**A** Truly, effort must be made so that, as far as possible, nothing remains without a guard. The city itself shall be overseen by the army commanders, the leaders of the ranks, the masters of the horse, the tribunes, the leaders of the council, the city-stewards <note>original: "ædiles"</note>, and the overseers of the markets, once they have been elected in their proper order. As for the rest of the territory, let it be guarded in this way: the entire region has been divided into twelve parts, as equal as possible.

**B** Thus, one tribe being assigned to each part by lot, it shall select five men per year to serve as country-stewards <note>original Greek: "agronomoi"; Latin: "agrorum curatores"</note> and leaders of the tribes. Each of these five shall choose twelve young men from his own tribe, no younger than twenty-five years old and no older than thirty. To these individuals, parts of each region shall be assigned by lot every month, so that all of them may gain experience and knowledge of the entire territory. <margin>Boundaries of the region.</margin> These leaders and guards shall hold their office and care for two years. When they have first drawn lots for the parts to be guarded, they shall change locations every month; the leaders of the guards shall lead them to the next adjacent location in a circle toward the right. By "the right," I mean the direction facing the rising sun. Then,

**C** in the second year, they shall be shifted toward the left, so that they do not become familiar with the region only during one season of the year, but may recognize what happens in every part of the region at any time. In the third year, five other country-stewards and leaders of the guards shall be selected by the tribal heads, along with their twelve caretakers. The care and labor in each location shall be as follows: first, the region must be fortified as much as possible against the attacks of enemies. By digging ditches wherever necessary and surrounding the area with towers and enclosures to the best of their strength, they shall keep out those wishing to do harm. For these tasks, they shall use the local pack animals and servants whenever they are not occupied with their own work,

**D** appointing some men over them to arrange all places so that it is difficult for enemies to pass through, but easy for friends, cattle, and draft animals, making the region as accessible as possible. They shall diligently ensure that rainwater not only does no harm to the land but actually benefits it, flowing from the high mountains into the hollow valleys. There, they shall force the water to gather by means of ditches and walls, so that the rainwater, being absorbed into the ground, creates springs and fountains in all the lower fields and places, thus irrigating even the driest areas with much healthy moisture.

**E** They shall decorate the springs and rivers with trees and buildings. Furthermore, they shall care for the groves and the lands dedicated to the gods, making them fertile by constant irrigation and directing water to them, and they shall provide moisture and springs to the mines. In this way, they shall make everything abundant and the temples of the gods more beautiful. Everywhere in these places, the young men shall prepare gymnasia <note>educational and athletic centers</note> for themselves as well as for the elderly, establishing hot baths and providing an abundance of dry wood, so that a remedy for the sick and a soothing relief for farmers exhausted by labor may be kindly offered. This type of care is far better than the medicine of an unskilled doctor. All these things, and others of this kind, serve as an ornament and a utility to these places, providing a pleasant sort of recreation. In short, the zeal regarding these matters

**F** <margin>Market-stewards.</margin> should be of this kind: each of the sixty men <note>The 5 leaders and 12 youths from each of the 12 districts make up the larger guard force, though the "sixty" refers specifically to the 5 leaders per 12 districts.</note> shall guard the location assigned to him, not only for the sake of enemies, but also for those who call themselves friends. And if any person among neighbors or citizens, whether slave or free, should do an injury to another, the five leaders themselves shall judge in small matters; but in larger matters, the seventeen <note>The 5 leaders plus the 12 youths</note> together shall judge up to the value of three minae <note>An ancient unit of currency; 3 minae was a significant sum, roughly 300 drachmae.</note> concerning whatever complaint one has against another. No one shall be a judge or a magistrate who is not subject to giving an account of his performed office, except for those who, like kings, bring an end to affairs.

**G** Furthermore, if they receive anything from the farmers, or if they are corrupted by the gifts of flatterers to pervert judgment, let them be covered in disgrace throughout the entire city for being captured by gifts and flattery. In other injuries, up to the value of one mina, let them voluntarily pay a fine to the neighbors and inhabitants. But if they refuse to pay what they owe in larger or smaller injuries, hoping to escape judgment and punishment because they move from place to place every month, they shall be accused in the public court. Whoever is convicted shall pay double to the person he oppressed with injury. Both the leaders and the other country-stewards shall live for these two years in the following manner: first, they shall have common meals <note>original: "convivia"</note> in each of their locations. Anyone who is absent for one day or night, or eats elsewhere without the leaders' order or without any pressing necessity, if the five men condemn him and post his name in the forum as having deserted his guard, he shall be treated with great disgrace...

<meta>This page continues the administrative regulations from Book VI of Plato's Laws. The previous page detailed the selection of the "agronomoi" or country-stewards and their initial assignments. # THE WORKS OF PLATO
## ON THE LAWS, BOOK VI.

->A<-
...as one who, as far as it lies within him, has betrayed the state <note>original Latin: "rempublicam prodidit"; Greek: "τὴν πολιτείαν... προδιδούς". Plato views the neglect of civic duty as a form of treason.</note>. And he may be struck with impunity by anyone he happens to meet who is willing to strike him. All sixty of the senior men shall observe whether any of the leaders commit such a fault; and anyone who perceives or hears of it and does not bring an accusation shall be liable under the same law as the offender, and shall be punished with a harsher censure by the youth, being held in contempt in all youthful magistracies. The guardians of the laws shall diligently observe all these matters: first, that they do not happen at all; and second, that if they do, they are punished as justice demands.

->B<-
<margin>He who has not served cannot be a praised master</margin>
Every man should hold this view concerning all people: that he who has never served can never be a master worthy of praise. Therefore, one ought to take more pride in having served well than in having ruled well; first, serving the laws (for to serve them is to serve the gods), and secondly, serving the elders who have lived honorably. Finally, throughout this two-year period, the country-stewards <note>original Greek: "agronomoi"</note> shall adopt a very humble and simple way of life. Thus, when the twelve men are assembled with the five leaders, they shall consult among themselves as if they were servants who will have no other attendants or slaves of their own. For they shall not use the farmers or villagers for their own private service, but only for public duties.

->C<-
In all other matters, they should plan to live as if serving themselves; furthermore, they must always be armed, both in summer and winter, patrolling the entire region to guard it more diligently until they know every location. Indeed, no knowledge seems of less importance than this: that the entire region be known exquisitely by all. For the sake of this knowledge, no less than for pleasure or other utility, the young men should devote themselves to breeding dogs and to the rest of the hunt. They ought to practice that pursuit which some call "secret service" <note>original Greek: "kryptous", referring to the "Krypteia," a Spartan tradition of sending youths out to live off the land.</note>; but whether it is called that, or "country-guarding," or whatever else anyone wishes, it is necessary that those who desire the safety of their city exercise themselves diligently in this matter to the best of their strength.

->D<-
<margin>On the selection of city-stewards.</margin>
It follows that we should speak of the election of the city-stewards <note>original Greek: "astynomoi"</note> and their commanders. Following the sixty country-stewards are three city-stewards, who divide the twelve parts of the city into three and imitate the others in their duties. They shall have care of the city streets and the public roads that lead from the countryside into the city; they also oversee buildings to ensure they are constructed according to the laws. Furthermore, they care for the water which the guards bring into the city, ensuring it is led into the fountains as clear and sufficient as possible, to both assist and adorn the city. It is necessary that these men be of such a sort that, setting aside their private cares, they have the leisure to manage public affairs.

->E<-
Therefore, let every man nominate as a prospective official whomever he wishes from the highest property class <note>original Latin: "maximo censu"; Greek: "μεγίστων τιμημάτων". Athenian society was divided into classes based on wealth.</note>. From the six who receive the most votes, three shall be chosen by lot to take up these cares. Finally, once they have been approved, they shall perform their magistracy according to the laws prescribed for them. Next, five market-stewards <note>original Greek: "agoranomoi"; Latin: "aediles"</note>, who are the overseers of goods for sale, shall be chosen from the first and second property classes. Their election shall be carried out in nearly the same manner as that of the city-stewards. From the ten who surpass the others in votes, five shall be designated by lot, and after being approved, they shall be declared magistrates. Everyone shall nominate a candidate. Anyone who refuses to do so, if he is accused before the leaders, shall be fined fifty drachmas <note>A drachma was a standard Greek silver coin; fifty drachmas was a significant sum, roughly two months' wages for a laborer.</note> and shall also be considered a poor citizen.

->F<-
Any who wish may enter the assembly and the common gathering; and all members of the first and second property classes shall be compelled to attend. Furthermore, anyone from these classes who is absent shall be fined ten drachmas. Men of the third and fourth classes, however, shall not be compelled to attend. Therefore, whoever from these classes is not present shall be free from penalty, unless the leaders, due to some urgent necessity, command everyone to be present. It is the duty of the market-stewards to maintain the order of the marketplace as established by law. They shall also have care of the fountains and temples in that location, so that no one acts injuriously there; if someone does, a slave or a foreigner shall suffer punishment by lashes and chains. A citizen, however, shall be fined up to one hundred drachmas by them. For a larger fine, up to double this amount, they may not condemn the offender unless the city-stewards are also present. The city-stewards shall have the same condition for fining and punishing in their own magistracy. For they themselves shall have the power to fine up to one mina <note>A mina was equal to 100 drachmas.</note>. For a double fine, the authority of the censors shall also be required.

->G<-
<margin>Teachers of the arts.</margin>
After this, dual magistrates for music and gymnastics shall be established for each faculty: some for the sake of education <note>original Latin: "disciplinae"; Greek: "παιδείας"</note> and others for the sake of competition. Those in charge of education shall oversee the equipment of the gymnasia and schools, as well as the order of learning; they shall see to it that both males and females in their youth proceed to these things honorably and remain in them honorably. In gymnastics, the athletes themselves who assign the tasks shall have care of the training, and they shall announce the rules to the athletes, that is, to the competitors. And these likewise ought to be dual: some regarding music, others regarding gymnastics. And in gymnastics, the same men shall oversee both human and horse competitions.

->H<-
In music, however, some shall oversee solo performances <note>original Greek: "monodia"</note>—that is, song and funeral orations—and the art of imitation itself, such as that of the rhapsodes (those who compose or recite epic poetry), cithara players, flute players, and all such others; while others shall oversee the choral song. First, therefore, regarding the choral play, where men, boys, and girls...

<column-break/>

->A<-
...and let him bear the reproach of having betrayed the constitution as far as his own part is concerned, and let him be punished with blows by anyone who meets him and wishes to punish him, with impunity. The officials should perceive such things regarding such men... those who perceive or learn of it, if they do not proceed against him, let them be held under the same laws, and let them be penalized more than the youths; let them always be held in dishonor by all the youthful offices. Let the guardians of the laws be strict overseers of these things, so that either the offense does not happen at all, or if it happens, it meets its deserved justice. Every man must think concerning all men, that he who has not served as a slave would never...

->B<-
...become a master worthy of praise; and one should take pride in having served well rather than in having ruled well: first to the laws (as this is service to the gods), then the young serving the elders and those who have lived honorably. After this, it is necessary for one who has become a country-steward to have tasted that humble and poor way of daily life for these two years. Whenever the twelve are enrolled, coming together with the five, let them deliberate as those who will have no other servants or slaves for themselves, nor will they use the other farmers or villagers as attendants for their private needs, but only for what concerns public matters; for other things, they should think to live by doing for themselves and serving one another...

->C<-
...in addition to these things, exploring the whole country in summer and winter with their weapons, for the sake of guarding and knowing all the places always. For it seems to be a lesson second to none, that all should know their own country with accuracy. For the sake of this, the young man should practice hunting with dogs and other kinds of hunting no less than any other pleasure, for the sake of the benefit that comes to all from such things. Therefore, whether someone calls this practice "the hidden ones" <note>Greek: "kryptous"</note> or "country-stewards" or whatever name they delight in calling it, every man should practice it to the best of his ability...

->D<-
...insofar as they intend to sufficiently save their own city. Next after this, the selection of officials—market-stewards <note>Greek: "agoranomoi"</note> and city-stewards <note>Greek: "astynomoi"</note>—follows for us. There follow the country-stewards three city-stewards, out of sixty, having divided the walls into twelve parts of the city, imitating those others; taking care of the roads in the town, and the highways from the country always leading into the city; and of the buildings, so that they all happen according to laws; and indeed of the waters, so that those guarding them may send them and keep them well-tended, so that they go into the fountains sufficient and clean, and both adorn and benefit the city. It is necessary for these men to be capable and to have leisure to care for public affairs.

->E<-
Therefore, let every man propose from the highest property classes whichever city-steward he wishes; and after voting by show of hands and arriving at the six who have the most, having chosen the three by lot, those to whom these things are a care. After being approved, they shall rule according to the laws set for them. Next to these, five market-stewards are to be chosen from the second and first property classes; for the rest, their selection shall happen just as that of the city-stewards: ten others having been voted by show of hands, they shall choose the five by lot; and after being approved, they shall be the officials. Let everyone vote for all. He who is not willing, if he is reported to the officials, let him be fined fifty drachmas, in addition to...

->F<-
...seeming to be a bad citizen. Let whoever wishes go to the assembly and the common gathering, but let it be compulsory for those of the second and first property classes, being fined ten drachmas if they are not present; but let it be allowed for those of the third and fourth classes not to be compelled; rather, let them be released without fine, unless the officials announce for everyone to meet due to some necessity. The market-stewards must guard the order concerning the market arranged by laws; and they shall care for the temples and fountains in the market, so that no one does any wrong. Let them punish the one doing wrong with blows and bonds if he is a slave or a foreigner; but if someone who is a local is disorderly about such things, they shall be sovereign judges up to one hundred drachmas of currency, but for double this, together with the city-stewards...

->G<-
...judging the one doing wrong. And let the same fines and punishments be for the city-stewards in their own office, fining up to a mina, but for double this, together with the country-stewards. After this, let dual officials of music and gymnastics be established for each; some for the sake of education itself, others for the sake of competition. By "education," the law intends to say overseers of the gymnasia and schools, of order and teaching at the same time, and of the care concerning these things, and concerning the attendance and housing of males and female maidens. Of "competition," there shall be judges of contests in both gymnastic and always in music for the athletes. Dual indeed for these: always some for music, others for competition. Of...

->H<-
...competition indeed, both of men and of horses, the same man; but of music, it would be fitting for others to become judges of contests for those concerning solo song and imitation—such as rhapsodes and cithara players and flute players and all such—and others for those concerning choral song. First indeed concerning the play of the choirs, of children and men and females...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of civic offices in Plato’s Laws. Having previously discussed the country-stewards (agronomoi), the text now moves to the selection of officials responsible for cultural life—music, choruses, and gymnastics—and the most critical office of all: the Supervisor of Education. It also introduces the basic structure of the judicial system.</meta>

# ON THE LAWS, BOOK VI.

<margin>A</margin> ...leaders must be chosen for the choruses involved in dancing and the entire arrangement of music. A single leader is sufficient for them, provided he is not less than forty years of age. One leader is also sufficient for solo singing <note>original Greek: "monodia"; Latin: "monodia". This refers to a single voice performing without a chorus, often in competition.</note>, provided he is not less than thirty years of age; he shall introduce the performers and provide a sufficient judgment for those competing. The leader and arranger of the choruses should be chosen in the following manner: those who are devoted to such matters shall go to the assembly, and if they do not go, they shall be fined—the guardians of the laws shall be the judges of this. For others, attendance shall not be compulsory if they do not wish it. The election shall be made by those who are experienced in these arts. During the scrutiny <note>original: "dokimasia". This was a formal investigation into a candidate's fitness for office in ancient Greece.</note>, let there be both accusation and defense: on one side that the candidate is inexperienced, and on the other that he is experienced.

<margin>B</margin> Whoever is chosen by show of hands and passes the scrutiny shall serve as leader of the choruses for one year according to the law. In the same way, the person chosen for that year to judge solo singing and flute-playing <note>original Latin: "tibicinio"; Greek: "synaulion". This refers to performances accompanied by the aulos, a double-reed woodwind instrument.</note> shall preside over the judges and deliver the verdict. Next, it is necessary to choose directors of the contests <note>original Greek: "athlothetes". These were officials who managed games and awarded prizes.</note> for the gymnasia, involving both horses and men. The election shall be open to the first three property classes, but the smallest class shall be free from any penalty for not attending. Twenty men shall be pre-elected by show of hands; from these twenty, three shall be chosen by lot, provided they also pass the scrutiny of the judges. If anyone is rejected during any stage of the selection or judgment, another shall be chosen in the same manner and undergo the same scrutiny.

<margin>C</margin> There remains one official who will oversee the cultivation <note>original Greek: "georgikon" (farming/cultivating); Latin: "disciplinae". Plato uses a metaphor of agriculture for education.</note> of all our education, for both females and males. Let there be one person to lead these according to the laws, not less than fifty years of age, and the father of legitimate children—preferably both sons and daughters, but at least one or the other. Both the one who chooses and the one chosen must realize that this office is by far the greatest of all the highest offices in the city. For in every living thing, the first growth, if it starts well toward the excellence of its own nature, has the greatest power to achieve its proper end—this is true for plants, for animals (both wild and tame), and for humans.

<margin>D</margin> Now, man, as we say, is a gentle animal <note>original Latin: "mansuetum animal"; Greek: "hemeron". Plato argues that while humans are naturally social and gentle, their behavior depends entirely on their upbringing.</note>. Indeed, if he attains a right education and possesses a fortunate nature, he becomes the most divine and gentle of animals; but if he is not sufficiently or well-reared, he becomes the wildest of all things that the earth produces. For these reasons, the lawgiver must not treat the education and rearing of children as a secondary matter or a side-project. He must first begin by choosing, with great care, the man who is to be in charge of it: he who is the best in all respects among the citizens. This man, to the best of his ability, shall be appointed as the protector and supervisor of education.

<margin>E</margin> Therefore, all the magistrates, except for the council and the presiding officers <note>original Greek: "prytaneis". These were the executive committee of the council.</note>, shall go to the Temple of Apollo and cast a secret ballot before the guardians of the laws, each selecting the person he believes would most excellently govern educational matters. Whoever receives the most votes and is approved by the other electing magistrates (excluding the guardians of the laws) shall serve for five years. In the sixth year, another shall be appointed to this office in the same way. If any public official dies more than thirty days before his term expires, those responsible shall appoint another in the same manner. Furthermore, if a guardian of orphans <note>original Latin: "orphanorum tutor"</note> <margin>Guardians/Tutors.</margin> dies, the relatives and kinsmen on both the father's and mother's side, as far as first cousins, who are present in the city, shall appoint another within ten days. Otherwise, each shall be fined one drachma per day until they appoint a guardian for the orphans.

<margin>F</margin> Now, any city would surely cease to be a city in which courts of law were not established in a proper manner. <margin>Method of judgments and the forum. The Judge.</margin> On the other hand, a "mute judge" <note>original Latin: "Iudex autem mutus". A judge who does not actively question the parties to uncover the truth.</note>—one who, in the preliminary hearings, says no more than the litigants, as if he were a mere arbitrator—would never be sufficient for the declaration of justice. For this reason, it is not easy for a great number of people to judge well, nor for a few if they are negligent. The matter in dispute must always be made clear by both sides.

<margin>G</margin> Time, slow deliberation, and frequent questioning are useful for making the controversy plain. Therefore, those who have a grievance <margin>Arbitrators.</margin> against one another should first go to their neighbors and friends, and especially to those who best know the facts of the disputed actions. If a sufficient judgment is not obtained through them, the party shall go to another court.

<margin>H</margin> Thirdly, if the two previous courts cannot reconcile them, a final end shall be put to the suit. In a certain way, the establishment of courts is like the election of magistrates. For every magistrate must necessarily be a judge of certain things. However, not every judge is necessarily a magistrate or a leader; nonetheless, a judge is, in a way, a magistrate of no small importance on the day he concludes a trial.

Let us then, treating judges as magistrates, discuss who would be suitable, what matters they should judge, and how many should be assigned to each case. Let the most authoritative court be that which the parties appoint for themselves, choosing certain judges by common consent.

Of the remaining matters, let there be two types of tribunals. One is when a private citizen accuses another private citizen of a wrong and brings him to trial. The other is when the public interest is harmed by one of the citizens...

# PLATO'S LAWS

<margin>A</margin> If anyone believes that a public injury is being committed by some citizen and attempts to assist the common wealth, he must speak. We must state, therefore, what kind of judges there ought to be. First, let there be a court common to all private citizens who are litigating for a third time among themselves, formed in this way: let all the magistrates, both those serving for a year and those for a longer term, on the day before the first of the month <note>original Latin: "pridie calendas"; Greek: "τῇ πρὸ τῶν καλανδῶν". This is the eve of the new year.</note> in which the new year begins after the summer solstice, assemble in a single temple. There, having taken an oath, they shall select one judge from each magistracy—offering them as a kind of first-fruits to the god—one who seems to be the best and likely to deliver judgments to the citizens in the most excellent and holy manner during that year. And after the judges have been designated, they shall be scrutinized by the very ones who designated them. If any are rejected, another shall be chosen in a similar fashion.

<margin>B</margin> Those who are approved shall deliver judgments for those who were not reconciled through the preceding courts, and they shall cast their votes openly. The consultants and the other magistrates who declared them must necessarily be present as listeners and spectators. Anyone else who wishes may also attend. If anyone accuses a judge of having voluntarily given an unjust sentence, he shall do so before the guardians of the laws. If the judge is condemned, he shall pay half the damage to the person who suffered the injury. If he seems worthy of a greater penalty, the judges who condemned him shall decide what he ought to suffer or pay, either to the state or to the injured party. In public accusations, however, it is necessary first of all to make the multitude a participant in the judgment.

<margin>C</margin> For when a sin is committed against the city, everyone is injured. Therefore, people are rightly aggrieved if they are not admitted to the act of judging. But the beginning and the end of such a trial ought to be referred to the people, while the examination and approval should be given to the three greatest magistrates, upon whom the litigants agree. If they cannot agree, the council itself shall recognize and judge the choice of each. Furthermore, it is necessary for all to participate in private judgments to the best of their ability. For he who is entirely excluded from the power of judging thinks himself completely alienated from the state. For these reasons, it is necessary that judgments also be made by tribes, and that judges chosen by lot should immediately judge, uncorrupted by prayers.

<margin>D</margin> And finally, that court shall define everything which we have said must be as entirely untainted as is possible in human affairs, to determine those disputes which could be settled neither by neighbors nor by fellow tribesmen. Truly, regarding the courts—which no one can easily affirm or deny are magistracies without controversy—this description, drawn as if from the outside, has embraced some things and seems to have left others behind. For the exact positioning and division of judicial laws will be placed much more correctly at the end of the law-giving process. Therefore, let us defer these until that time. Most of the other magistrates have now been arranged. But the total and accurate civil

<margin>E</margin> distribution, whether it pertains to one or to all, cannot be clearly declared before the treatment itself has reached its conclusion, having embraced its beginnings, following parts, middle, and all its members. This treatment, having progressed at present as far as the creation of magistrates, is a sufficient end to what preceded it, and a beginning for the laying down of laws, admitting no further delay or sluggishness. <margin>CLI.</margin> **Cleinias:** Although you have spoken everything to my satisfaction, Stranger, it is much more pleasing to me at present that you have joined the end of what has been said with the beginning of what is to be said. <margin>ATH.</margin> **Athenian:** Well then, let this wise game of old men <note>original Latin: "seniorum ludus"; Greek: "πρεσβυτῶν... παιδιά". Plato often characterizes his philosophical dialogues as a form of serious "play."</note> be played out by us this far. <margin>CLI.</margin> **Cleinias:** You seem to indicate a truly beautiful pursuit for men. <margin>ATH.</margin> **Athenian:** It is only fitting. But let us

<margin>F</margin> notice if this seems the same to you as it does to me. **Cleinias:** What exactly? And concerning what matters? **Athenian:** Do you not know that the same thing happens in this matter as in the skill of painters? For that art seems to have no limit in painting living creatures, but always by shading and un-shading <note>original Latin: "inunbrando, & deumbrando"; Greek: "χραίνειν ἢ ἀποχραίνειν". This refers to the technique of adding highlights and shadows to create depth.</note>—or whatever else it may be called by painters—it strives to decorate and never ceases. For it is impossible that there should not be an increase toward more beautiful and more expressive things. **Cleinias:** I almost understand what you are saying as I listen, though I have no experience in such an art. **Athenian:** That has not hindered you. But let us use this comparison that has happened upon us.

<margin>G</margin> If someone wished to paint a most beautiful creature, which should always progress toward the better rather than the worse in future time, do you not see that, since he is mortal, unless he leaves behind some successor in the art who can restore anything abolished from the creature by time, or add what was omitted by the artist through weakness of skill—and thus make the creature more radiant day by day—that laborious work would last but a short time? **Cleinias:** Entirely so. **Athenian:** Does not the will of the legislator seem to you to be the same? First, that the laws be written as sufficiently and exquisitely as possible; then, as time proceeds and the reality of things is tested, do you think any legislator is so foolish as to be ignorant that it is necessary for many such things to be left behind which require amendment by some successor, so that the republic always becomes not worse, but better and more adorned?

# OF PLATO

### BOOK VI

<margin>A</margin>
This correction through experience, while the legislator is alive, should be done in common with him. If he passes away, the individual magistrates should report any defects in their respective offices to the Guardians of the Laws and make corrections until each detail seems to have reached its final point of approval. Only then should they consider these laws ratified, and they shall use them alongside the others that the legislator wrote from the beginning. In these matters, they shall never change anything of their own accord. If, however, some necessity should ever seem to be pressing, all the magistrates and the entire people must consult together on this, and all the oracles of the gods must be sought. If there is a single consensus among all of them, they may make the change; otherwise, they never shall, but the one who prohibits the change shall prevail according to the law.

<margin>B</margin>
Whenever, therefore, someone has reached the age of twenty-five, having looked upon others and being looked upon by others, and believes he has found a partner suitable to his soul and a fitting society for the sharing and procreation of children, he should marry before he is thirty-five years old. But first, let him hear how that which is fitting and appropriate should be sought. For, as Clinias says, it is necessary to place a proper preamble before each individual law. 
CLINIAS: You have remembered well, Stranger, and you have chosen a time for your speech that is most appropriate. 
ATHENIAN: You speak rightly.

<margin>What marriages are to be contracted.</margin>
<margin>C</margin>
Let us speak thus: O son, who is born of good parents, you ought to contract those marriages which prudent men deem honorable. Such men would advise that one should neither flee the kinship of the poor nor specifically pursue that of the rich; but, all else being equal, one should always honor the poorer party and enter into a partnership with them. For this is beneficial both to the city and to the families being joined. Indeed, that which is moderate and balanced is wonderfully superior to the immoderate and excessive in terms of virtue. Therefore, whoever is conscious in himself of a spirit more fierce or swift in action than is proper, he ought to take care to marry the daughter of the quietest possible parents; and he who is naturally disposed to the opposite should seek out the opposite kinship. But let there finally be one common principle for marriage: that each person enter into a marriage that is useful to the city, not merely the one most pleasant to himself.

<margin>D</margin>
For individuals are always drawn by nature toward those similar to themselves. From this, the entire city becomes as unequal as possible in both wealth and character—the very things we least want to happen, yet which happen most frequently in many cities. But if we were to establish this as a law through reason—that the rich should not join with the rich, nor the powerful with the powerful, but that we should force the swifter spirits to be coupled with the slower, and the slower conversely with the swifter—not only would our speech seem ridiculous, but it would also provoke anger in many people. For it is not easy to understand by the intellect alone that a city ought to be like a mixing bowl <note>original: "paterae" in Latin, "κρατῆρος" (krater) in Greek. This refers to the large vessel used to mix wine with water.</note>, in which the pure wine, which bubbles when first poured in, is immediately chastened by the sobriety of another god <note>The "sober god" is a poetic reference to water, which tempers the "madness" of Dionysus (wine).</note>, and, being excellently tempered, becomes a good and moderate drink.

<margin>E</margin>
But how this might occur in the mixed procreation of children, no one, to speak briefly, can easily perceive. For this reason, we should not compel citizens by law, but rather lead them by persuasion, so that they value the equal and balanced generation of their children more than the equality of a most wealthy kinship. And him who gapes after money in marriage, we should not bar by written law, but rather deter with disgrace and reproaches. Thus, these things are urged for the proper celebration of marriage, along with what we said previously: that by leaving behind children's children—who are, of course, our successors in divine service—we may attain nature’s immortality.

<margin>F</margin>
All these things and more, someone might rightly say as a preamble to entering marriage. But if anyone does not obey of his own accord, and lives in the city as a stranger to this partnership, and has spent thirty-five years without marriage, let him be fined each year. If he is from the highest property class, 

<margin>How great a penalty is fined to him who refuses to take a wife.</margin>
let him be fined one hundred drachmas; if from the second, seventy; if from the third, sixty; if from the fourth, thirty. This money is to be consecrated to the goddess Juno <note>original: "Iunoni" (Juno) in Latin, "Ἥρας" (Hera) in Greek.</note>. If anyone does not pay in a given year, he shall owe tenfold. The collector of this money shall be the treasurer of the goddess herself; if he does not collect it, he himself shall owe it, and each must render an account of this. Thus let the man who refuses to marry be fined in money, and in honor as follows: First, let him receive no honors from the younger men, and let no youth obey him in anything of his own accord. Then, if he dares to strike anyone, let anyone present rise up against him and bring aid to the one who received the injury. If anyone present does not do this,

<margin>On dowries.</margin>
he shall be considered a cowardly and bad citizen by the laws. Regarding the dowry, it was spoken of before, and let it be said again now: that there should be an exchange of equals for equals, so that neither the one who receives nor the one who gives shall grow old in a lack of money. For the necessities of life are abundantly available to everyone in this city. Furthermore, there will be less insulting arrogance among the women, and less humble and ungenerous slavery for the husbands on account of money. He who obeys will certainly do this one thing excellently. But he who does not obey, but either gives or receives anything that exceeds fifty drachmas in value for the sake of clothing—one paying a mina, another three half-minas, another two minas—and he who belongs to the highest 

<margin>H</margin>
property class shall pay an equal amount again to the treasury, and whatever was given or received shall be consecrated to Jupiter <note>original: "Ioui" (Jove/Jupiter) in Latin, "Διός" (Zeus) in Greek.</note> and Juno. We wish the treasurers of these gods to be the collectors of this money,
