A
...having been assigned to each. While the legislator who arranged them is alive, the end of these things should be pursued in common. If he reaches the end of his life, those offices should bring what is lacking to the Guardians of the Laws, assisting them until each of the well-wrought works seems to have reached its completion. Then, having established them as unchangeable, they shall use them along with the other laws which the legislator established for them at the beginning. Concerning these, they shall never move anything willingly; but if a necessity should ever seem to take hold, all the magistrates must be counselors, and all the people and all the oracles of the gods must be consulted. If they all agree, then they may move them; but otherwise never and in no way, but the one who prevents it shall always prevail according to the law. Whenever someone, having reached 

B
twenty-five years of age, looking about and being looked upon by others, believes he has found for himself a fitting partner for the communion and birth of children, let every man marry within thirty-five years. But first, let him hear how it is necessary to seek what is fitting and harmonious. For it is necessary (as Clinias says) to set before the law a preamble proper to each. CLINIAS: You have remembered most beautifully, Stranger; you have seized the right moment for the discourse, and one very much suited to the proportion of the matter. ATHENIAN: You speak well. Let us say then, O youth, to one born of good fathers, that it is necessary to marry from among the marriages held in good repute by those with sense, who would advise one not to flee the marriage of the poor nor to pursue especially the marriage of the rich; but 

C
if other things are equal, always honoring the lesser, to come together into partnership. For this would be advantageous to the city and to the households living together. For the even and the proportional is ten thousand times better than the unmixed in respect to virtue. One who is conscious of being too impetuous and swifter than is necessary in all his actions should be eager to become the kinsman of balanced parents; and he who is naturally the opposite should proceed to opposite kinships. Let there be one story concerning all marriage: each man must seek the marriage that is advantageous to the city, not the one that is most pleasant to himself. For everyone is always carried by nature toward what is most similar to himself. Whence the whole city becomes unequal, both in wealth and in the habits of character. From which 

D
the things we do not wish to happen to us do indeed happen, and most of all in the majority of cities. Now, to legislate these things by a verbal law—that the rich should not marry the rich, nor the powerful the daughter of the powerful, but to compel those of swifter characters to proceed toward the slower, and the slower toward the swifter in the communion of marriage—would be ridiculous and would arouse anger in many. For it is not easy to perceive that a city must be mixed like a wine-bowl; where the mad wine, being poured in, boils, but being chastened by another sober god and receiving a beautiful communion, it produces a good and moderate drink. That this is what happens in the mixing of children, no one, so to speak, is able to see. For the sake of these things, if 

E
one were to compel such things by law, one should try instead to use enchantments to persuade them, making them value the balance of their children more than the insatiable equality of wealth in marriage; and by reproach, one should turn away the man who is always serious about money in marriages, rather than forcing him by written law. Let these be the encouraging things said concerning marriages. And indeed, those things said before these—that one must hold fast to the ever-living nature by leaving behind children's children to be handed over as servants to the god in one's place. All these things and even more someone might say concerning marriages, how one should marry, if he were to make a proper preamble. If, however, someone is not persuaded willingly, but keeps himself a stranger and uncommunicative in the city, being unmarried when he becomes thirty-five years old, let him be fined each 

F
year: he who possesses the greatest property class, one hundred drachmas; the second, seventy; the third, sixty; the fourth, thirty. Let this be sacred to Hera. He who does not pay annually shall owe ten times the amount. Let the treasurer of the goddess collect it; if he does not collect it, let him owe it himself; and in the audits of such a man, let everyone demand an account. In terms of money, then, let the man who is unwilling to marry be fined thus; but in terms of honor, let him be without all honor from the younger men, and let no young man willingly obey him in anything. If he attempts to punish anyone, let everyone help and defend the one who is wronged; and the one who is present and does not help shall be called 

G
both a coward and a bad citizen by the law. Concerning the dowry, it has been spoken of before, and let it be said again, that it is an exchange of equals for equals so that the poor may not grow old in a lack of money, neither receiving nor giving it. For the necessities are available to all those in this city. There would be less insolence for the women and less humble and ungenerous slavery to the husbands because of money. And he who obeys would do this one thing at least; but he who does not obey, but either gives or receives more than fifty drachmas' worth for the sake of clothing—one a mina, another three half-minas, another two minas—and he who possesses the greatest property class, let him owe another such amount to the public treasury; and let that which was given or received be sacred 

H
to Hera and Zeus. Let the treasurers of these two gods collect it, just as it was said concerning those who do not marry, let the treasurers collect—

# ON THE LAWS, BOOK VI

<column-break/>

...must be paid each time to Hera <note>The Greek goddess of marriage; the Latin column identifies her as Juno.</note>, and she shall determine what penalty each must pay. The surety <note>A legal guarantee or bond.</note> shall be valid first from the father, secondly from the grandfather, and thirdly from the brothers on the father’s side. If none of these exist, then a surety from the mother's side shall be valid in the same way. If an unusual situation occurs, the nearest of kin shall always be the sureties along with the guardians. Regarding the preliminary sacrifices for marriages, or any other sacred rite concerning those who are about to marry, or are marrying, or have married, the interpreters of sacred law must be consulted; and if they are obeyed, each person should consider everything to have been done in a balanced manner for themselves. Regarding the feasts, one should invite no more than five male friends and five female friends on each side; and an equal number of relatives and kin on each side. The expenditure should not be more than what is according to one’s wealth: for the highest class, one mina <note>A Greek unit of weight and currency; one mina was roughly 100 days' wages for a skilled artisan.</note>; for the second class, half that; and so on, just as the property assessment decreases for each. Everyone should praise the one who obeys the law, but the Guardians of the Laws shall punish the one who is disobedient, as one who lacks a sense of beauty and is uneducated in the laws of the Nuptial Muses. Drinking to the point of intoxication is never appropriate anywhere—except during the festivals of the God who gave wine <note>Dionysus, or Bacchus.</note>—nor is it safe. It is especially inappropriate for those serious about marriage, where the bride and groom ought to be at their most sensible, since they are undergoing no small change in their lives. At the same time, it is important that whatever is conceived always comes from those who are sensible. For it is almost uncertain what night or day, with the help of God, the child will be conceived. Therefore, the act of procreation should not happen when bodies are loosened by drunkenness, but rather the offspring should be formed in a solid, steady, and quiet state. For a person full of wine is carried about in every direction and carries himself wildly, raging in both body and soul; therefore, the drunkard is clumsy and poor at sowing seed. Thus, it is likely that unstable, untrustworthy, and crooked characters and bodies will be produced. Therefore, throughout the entire year and life, but especially during the time of procreation, one must be cautious not to do anything that brings disease, or anything involving insolence or injustice. For these things are necessarily imprinted upon the souls and bodies of those being born, and they bring forth inferior beings in every way. Above all, one must abstain from such things on that particular day and night. For a beginning <note>original: "ἀρχὴ" (archē)</note> and a divinity established among men preserves all things, if it receives the proper honor from each of those who use it. The newlyweds should consider that one of the two houses on the allotment <note>In Magnesia, each citizen was to have two houses: one in the city and one in the country.</note> is like a nest for the generation and nourishment of their young, and having separated from their father and mother, they should celebrate the marriage there and make it their dwelling and the place where they and their children are fed. For in friendships, if there is a longing that is felt at intervals, it binds and connects all characters; but a saturated intimacy, which does not hold that longing born of time, causes people to drift away from one another through an excess of satiety. Therefore, leaving behind their own dwellings for their parents and relatives, they should go forth as if to a colony, living as both observers and managers of their own home, begetting and rearing children, handing down life from one to another like a torch, and always serving the gods according to the laws. After this, one must consider what kind of property one should possess to have a most harmonious estate. Most things are not difficult to understand or acquire, but the matter of slaves is difficult in every way. The reason for this is that we speak about them sometimes correctly and sometimes poorly. For our words about slaves are both contrary to their use and according to their use. **MEGILLUS:** How so? For we do not understand what you are saying now, Stranger. **ATHENIAN:** And quite rightly so, Megillus. For among the Greeks, the system of the Helots <note>The state-owned serfs of Sparta, often a source of rebellion.</note> among the Lacedaemonians has caused the greatest difficulty and dispute—some saying it is good, others that it is not. The slavery of the Mariandynians at Heraclea or the class of the Penestae <note>A class of serfs in Thessaly similar to Helots.</note> among the Thessalians would cause less dispute. Looking at all these things, what should we do about the possession of servants? You asked me what I meant just now, and you were right to ask. It is this: we know that everyone would say we should possess slaves who are as well-disposed and excellent as possible. For many slaves have already proven better than brothers or sons toward their masters in every virtue, and have saved their masters, their property, and their entire households. We know these things are said about slaves. **MEGILLUS:** Certainly. **ATHENIAN:** But is not the opposite also said—that there is nothing healthy in a slave’s soul, and that a man of sense should never trust that race at all? The wisest of our poets <note>Homer.</note> declared, speaking of Zeus:
> For wide-seeing Zeus takes away half of the mind
> Of men, whomsoever the day of slavery catches. <note>original: "ἥμισυ γάρ τε νόου [φησὶν] ἀπαμείρεται εὐρύοπα Ζεὺς / ἀνδρῶν, οἳ ἂν δὴ κατὰ δούλιον ἦμαρ ἕλῃσι." - Odyssey 17.322-3. Note that Plato's text uses "mind" (noou) where standard Homeric texts use "excellence" (aretē).</note>
Taking these views into their minds, some people trust nothing in the race of servants, and treating them like the nature of wild beasts, they make the souls of their servants truly slavish with goads and whips, not just three times, but many times. Others do the exact opposite. **MEGILLUS:** Indeed. What then must we do, Stranger, since there is such a difference of opinion regarding our own land, both in the possession and the punishment of slaves?

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Just as was recently said when we were speaking of those who flee marriage, what is owed by them should be demanded by the treasurers of Juno. If they neglect this, they shall pay it from their own funds. The surety, however, should first be most firm from the father, then the grandfather, and thirdly from the brothers born of the same father. If none of these survive, let the surety from the mother's side be similarly valid. But if an unusual desolation occurs, let the nearest kinsmen and clansmen, together with the guardians, act as sureties. If any sacred initiation or other divine expiation for future, past, or present matters seems necessary at weddings, let them consult the interpreters of divine things, and believe that if they obey them, they have performed each thing with moderation.
<margin>B</margin> To the wedding feast, let no more than five male friends and five female friends be invited from the father's side; and from the relatives and kin, the same number. Let the expense be no greater than is according to one's wealth. Let the richest spend a mina, another less, and so on, preserving the proportion so that as the census <note>Wealth rating.</note> decreases, the expense similarly decreases. He who obeys the law shall be praised by all. But let the Guardians of the Laws condemn him who does not comply, as one foreign to what is fitting and entirely ignorant of the law of the nuptial Muses. To drink to the point of drunkenness is never becoming elsewhere, except in the solemnities of that god who granted wine, nor is it safe. Most especially, the bride and groom joined in marriage <margin>C</margin> must be masters of their minds then, when they are entering upon no small change of life, especially so that generation may always come from those who are as temperate as possible. For it is almost uncertain which night or day carries it out with God. Therefore, so that a solid, stable, and quiet conception may occur, it is not proper to give attention to children when bodies are diffused with drunkenness. He who is filled with wine, stirred by a madness of both soul and body, is both dragged and drags others in every direction. Therefore, the drunkard, as if captured in mind, is useless for sowing. Indeed, it is likely that he procreates offspring that are unequal, unstable, and crooked in both limb and character. Wherefore, throughout the whole of life, and especially as long as one is devoted to generation, <margin>D</margin> each shall abstain and take care lest he do those things which by their own nature and of their own accord induce diseases, or which decline toward insolence and injury. For these things are necessarily transferred and imprinted upon the souls and bodies of those being born, and worse children are born from them. But especially on that day and night, one must abstain from such things. For a principle and a divinity implanted in men, if it is honored with a gift suitable to it by those using it, preserves all things. It is necessary, moreover, to consider the newlyweds, separated from their parents, in one of the two houses which happened to fall to them by lot, as if for the generation and education of chicks, and to celebrate the marriage there, where they are to live with their children. For if a certain <margin>E</margin> longing is present in friendship, it connects and binds all characters as if with a kind of glue. But a saturated familiarity, having no longing through the intermission of time, separates one from the other by satiety. Therefore, having left behind both parents and in-laws, let them set out separately as if to a colony, and live observing one another in turn, generating and educating children; and let them hand down the life which they received from others to others as if it were a lamp, always worshipping the gods according to the laws. After this, it must be considered what things are most honorable to possess. In most things, whether in knowing or acquiring and possessing, there is no difficulty. In slaves, however, it is entirely difficult. We may speak the cause, both rightly in a way and not rightly <margin>F</margin> again, concerning them. For words are spoken about slaves both against use and again according to use. **MEGILLUS:** In what way do we say this? For we do not understand, Stranger, what you wish to say just now. **ATHENIAN:** Not without reason, O Megillus. For almost that Spartan servitude, which you call "Helots," has more than any other in Greece the greatest doubt and contention; finally, there is the servile crowd among the Thessalians. Looking at these and all such things, what must be done about the possession of slaves? This certainly escaped me now, and you rightly asked me what I was saying. **G** This, however, is of this sort. We know indeed that we all confess that slaves should be held who are as benevolent and as good as possible. For many slaves have already been better in all virtue to some than brothers and sons, and have saved their masters, their goods, and their entire houses. We are not ignorant that these things are proclaimed about slaves. **MEGILLUS:** Certainly. **ATHENIAN:** On the contrary, it is also said that there is nothing sound in a serving soul, and that nothing should be credited to the race of slaves. Which even the wisest of poets testifies to us, when he speaks thus of Jove:
> Jupiter takes away half the mind
> from those who are subject to the lot of servitude.
Therefore, men thinking these so diverse things about slaves, some trust nothing to the race of servants, but with goads and whips, as if with the nature of wild beasts, they make the minds of their servants slavish not three times only, but more often. Others do the opposite. **CLIN.** It is so. But...

# PLATONIS

<column-break/>

...what is to be done? **Athenian:** It seems clear to me, O Clinias, that since man is a difficult creature to master, and he is with great difficulty brought to the necessary distinction between slave, free man, and master, a human being is a difficult possession to hold. This has been made evident by the example of the frequent rebellions of the Messenians <note>The Messenians were famously enslaved by the Spartans as "Helots" and revolted numerous times, becoming a historical symbol of the dangers of mass enslavement.</note>. Furthermore, cities that possess many slaves of the same language have clearly shown what great evils follow from this. The thefts and robberies of pirates, which especially abound around Italy, also arise from this. If anyone considers all these things, he will doubt what ought to be done about them. Therefore, only two paths remain: those who are to be easily held in servitude should neither be from the same country nor, as much as possible, should they speak the same language.

->A<-

And they should be raised correctly, not only for their own sake but much more for the sake of their masters. Now, the correct upbringing of these people is that no insult should be offered to them, and much less should they be injured—if possible—than one’s equals. For it is clearly recognized who naturally and sincerely cherishes justice, and truly hates iniquity, when he takes care not to wrong those whom he easily could.

->B<-

He, therefore, who in his conduct and actions toward slaves never acts impiously or unjustly, and thus keeps himself unstained in these matters, will be most fit for producing the fruits of virtue. The same can also be rightly said of a master, a tyrant, or anyone powerful toward those who are weaker. Slaves ought always to be corrected and struck by right, and not merely admonished like free men, lest they become soft and spoiled. Every address to slaves should be, in a sense, a command; nor should any joke be shared with them, whether they be female or male. Many act foolishly in this regard, and by nurturing them too delicately, they make life more difficult for themselves in commanding and for the slaves in obeying. **Clinias:** You speak rightly. **Athenian:** Therefore, once each man has 

->C<-

<margin>Concerning dwellings.</margin>
prepared slaves who are fit in number and ability for the various ministries of life, we must next describe the dwellings in our discourse. **Clinias:** By all means. **Athenian:** For a new city, previously inhabited by no men, buildings must be provided first of all, and a plan for temples and walls must be established. These things, O Clinias, truly ought to have preceded the marriages. But since we are now dealing in words, it is permissible to place them here. When we undertake the work itself, if God wills, we shall place these before the weddings and then complete everything else in order. For now, let us run through these briefly as if in a sketch. **Clinias:** Let it be so. **Athenian:**

->D<-

<margin>The site of the city.</margin>
The entire city should be drawn in a circle on high ground, so that it may be both better fortified and cleaner. Temples should be built around the marketplace. Near these should be the palaces of the magistrates and the judges, in which—as if in the most sacred places—they shall both receive and deliver just sentences; partly as if they were judging sacred matters, and partly because these are the shrines of the judging gods. There also should be the judicial residences where judgments are made regarding homicides and other capital injuries. Regarding the walls, O Megillus, I agree with the Spartans; I would prefer to let the walls lie on the ground <note>A reference to the Spartan belief that "walls of men" (bravery) are superior to stone fortifications.</note> and not be raised up. For that poetic saying is rightly praised, which admonishes us to build walls of bronze and iron rather than earth. Among us, moreover, it is quite ridiculous that every year young men are sent into the countryside to dig pits and trenches and build structures to keep enemies far from the borders, 

->E<-

<margin>Concerning walls.</margin>
yet we surround ourselves with walls. This, first of all, contributes nothing to the health of the citizens, and secondly, it is accustomed to soften and weaken the spirits of the inhabitants. For walls cause them to think that they can easily retreat inside and not put the enemy to flight, and they imagine they will be safe while sleeping behind a barrier and rampart, rather than keeping watch with day and night guards—as if they were born for sloth, surely ignorant that 

<margin>Rest takes its origin from labors.</margin>
rest takes its origin from labors, and that from foul leisure and negligence, labors are wont to be born. But if men must be fortified by any walls, then from the beginning let the private houses be so built that the whole city, by its equality and similarity, is itself a single wall, and let all houses have a safe entrance to the streets. Truly, this arrangement will be pleasing to those who look upon it, as the whole city will have the form of a single house; and for the ease of guarding and the preservation of all, it will be by far the most convenient of all. The citizens who are to live there should take the greatest care that it is constructed this way from the start. The city overseers <note>original: "Aediles"</note> should also provide for this and compel those who are negligent with fines. They should see that the city is as clean as possible, and never allow a private person to occupy any public space by building or digging. They should also take care that rainwater flows away abundantly and easily. Likewise, they should oversee all things that must be inhabited, whether inside or outside the city. But all these things, and the others which have been omitted by the laws (since it was not possible to provide for everything), the Guardians of the Laws, taught by experience, shall arrange. After these things—the buildings around the marketplace, the gymnasiums, the theaters for spectators, and the dwellings for teachers and students—have been arranged, let us proceed in the making of laws to those things which follow the weddings. **Clinias:** That is how it must be done. **Athenian:** Regarding the weddings, then, O Clinias, let it be as we have said: after which the life...

->G<-

<margin>Concerning the way of life for the groom and bride.</margin>

# ON THE LAWS, BOOK VII.

<column-break/>

...the rule of life that precedes the procreation of children should follow for no less than a full year. But in what manner a bridegroom and bride ought to live together in the most excellent state is not easy to say. Indeed, since many things previously discussed were difficult, the common people will find what must be said about these matters even more difficult to accept. Nevertheless, what seems true and right must be spoken, O Clinias. **CLINIAS:** It must certainly be spoken. **ATHENIAN:** Therefore, whoever thinks that only public and communal matters should be ordered by laws, while private matters—even those that are necessary—need no care; and whoever grants license to individuals to live daily as they wish, and does not think all things should be done according to a certain order, but believes that if private affairs are neglected, men will still conduct public and communal business according to

->B<-

the law, is not thinking correctly. Why do I say this? Because we assert that the bridegrooms of our republic must live in public communal meals <note>original: "comessatione publica"; referring to the Greek "syssitia," a hallmark of Cretan and Spartan society where men ate together to foster military discipline.</note> no less and no differently in other times than they did before their nuptials. It was surely a marvelous thing when the custom of communal meals was first established among you, appearing to have been instituted by those driven by war or some other force of similar power during a time of population scarcity. When they had used this practice out of necessity, the thing seemed to contribute greatly to their preservation, and so it was established by laws. **CLINIAS:** So it seems. **ATHENIAN:** It was a wonder then, and at first difficult for the one commanding it. But if someone were to attempt to sanction it by law now, it would certainly be less difficult to do.

->C<-

However, what follows next is difficult both to say and to do. Although it is practiced nowhere, if it were to be done anywhere, it would certainly be done rightly; yet it is of such a nature that in describing it, the legislator seems like someone trying to "card fire" <note>An ancient idiom for attempting the impossible, similar to "plowing the sand."</note> or attempting other impossible tasks. **CLINIAS:** What is this thing, Stranger, that you are so afraid to speak of? **ATHENIAN:** Listen now, so that I do not keep you in suspense with a longer delay. For whatever in the city participates in law and order, all good things proceed from it; but those things that lack order, or are poorly ordered, dissipate even those things that are well-ordered. This is exactly what is happening with the matter at hand. For you, O Megillus and

->D<-

Clinias, the communal meals of men have been established excellently and—as I said—marvelously, out of a certain divine necessity. However, the communal meals for women have been improperly left neglected and lie in the shadows. This is a different class of humans, and by nature, our female element is more secretive and more crafty due to its weakness; and thus, it is less easily brought under order. Therefore, the legislator gave way, and it was a mistake to overlook it. Because of this omission, many things among us are corrupted which would be in a far better state than they are now, if this very thing had been ordered by laws. For the female concern is not—as it might seem—merely one half of human affairs when left unorganized and abandoned;

->E<-

but rather, insofar as her nature is less naturally inclined toward virtue than the male nature, she exceeds that proportion, appearing to be more than double the trouble. Therefore, this must be revisited and corrected, and all communal practices for women and men must be established for the happiness of the city. But now, the human race is so unhappily led in this regard that it would not be the mark of a prudent man even to mention this matter in other regions and cities where public communal meals have never been approved. For where would anyone, without being ridiculed, be able to compel women to take their food and drink in a public and manifest way? There is surely nothing that this sex would endure more reluctantly. For since they have been accustomed to living timidly and in the shadows, they will repel the lawmaker with every ounce of resistance if he tries to lead them into the light.

->F<-

This sex, I say, elsewhere—as I have stated—would not even hear the speech of one speaking rightly without a great outcry; but here, perhaps, they will endure it. Therefore, if it also seems right to you, for the sake of our discussion, so that the discourse on the republic is not left incomplete, I wish to say how good and decent a thing this is. If it pleases you, I say; otherwise, I shall let it go. **CLINIAS:** Stranger, we desire to hear it in a marvelous way. **ATHENIAN:** Let us listen then. But do not be surprised if I find it necessary to repeat the matter from a higher source. For we have an abundance of leisure, and nothing else presses us that would prevent us from considering everything from all sides that pertains to the laws. **CLINIAS:** You speak rightly. **ATHENIAN:** Let us then repeat the first principles.

->G<-

Everyone ought to know that the generation of humans either had no beginning at all and will never have an end, but always was and always will be; or if it did begin, it began a vast and inestimable amount of time ago. **CLINIAS:** Clearly. **ATHENIAN:** Do we not think that throughout the whole earth, many cities have been founded and destroyed, and that diverse human pursuits have preceded us, partly with order and partly without order? Likewise, that there have been many uses of food and drink, and various seasonings, and many changes of the seasons, in which it is believable that animals were transformed in various ways? **CLINIAS:** Nothing prevents it. **ATHENIAN:** What then? Do we think vines first appeared at a time when they did not previously exist? And similarly, olives, and the gifts of Demeter and Persephone <note>original: "Cereris atque Proserpinæ"; the goddesses of agriculture and the underworld, credited with giving grain to humanity.</note>, which some Triptolemus <note>A mythical figure who was taught the art of agriculture by Demeter and flew across the world in a winged chariot to spread the knowledge of grain to mankind.</note> might have administered?

->H<-

# OF PLATO

<margin>A</margin> ...we see humans being sacrificed among many peoples; yet we hear the opposite regarding others, such as when we did not even dare to taste the flesh of oxen, nor did we sacrifice animals to the gods. Instead, pure offerings like cakes and fruits soaked in honey were presented to the deities. People abstained from meat entirely, for it was considered impious to eat flesh or to pollute the altars of the gods with blood. <margin>The Orphic life.</margin> Thus, what is called an "Orphic life" <note>Referring to Orphism, a set of religious beliefs and practices associated with the mythical poet Orpheus, which emphasized asceticism and reincarnation.</note> flourished then among our ancestors. They lived on all manner of inanimate things but abstained from all living creatures. **CLINIAS:** These things are widely reported, as you say, and are very much worth believing. **ATHENIAN:** But someone might ask, why have all these things been mentioned by us just now? <margin>B</margin> **CLINIAS:** You have guessed correctly, O guest. **ATHENIAN:** Therefore, if I am able, Clinias, I will attempt to explain what follows. **CLINIAS:** Speak then. **ATHENIAN:** I perceive that all human affairs depend upon a threefold need and desire; if these are guided rightly, virtue is born, but if wrongly, vice. Two of these are the desires for food and drink, which are present in animals as soon as they are born. Every animal has an innate appetite for these and is carried away by an impulse; it does not listen to anyone who advises doing otherwise than satisfying these desires and pleasures, and avoiding their contrary pains. The third need, which is immense and a most sharp desire, arises later, but burns men with the most ardent fury and great insolence: that which is inherent in the propagation of the species. These three "diseases" <note>The Athenian uses "morbi" or "diseases" here to describe the overwhelming nature of physical drives when they are unregulated.</note> which drive us toward what is called the most pleasant, must be turned toward what is best by three greatest things: fear, law, and true reason. These are to be used alongside the Muses and the gods of competition, so that growth and excess may be extinguished in this way. <margin>C</margin> Regarding procreation, we ought to place the duty of children after the nuptials. After procreation itself, we must address education and discipline. For in this way, perhaps, each law will proceed forward in our discourse, eventually leading to the common meals, when we come to such gatherings and communities. We shall then see more clearly whether these communal gatherings should be commanded for men alone or also for women, once we have approached them more closely and have arranged in their proper order the things that should precede them, which are not yet disposed by law. Thus, as I was just saying, we shall inspect the common meals more sharply and hand down more suitable laws regarding them. **CLINIAS:** You speak wisely. <margin>D</margin> **ATHENIAN:** Let us therefore hold in memory what has just been said. For perhaps they will be of use to us at some time. **CLINIAS:** What things do you bid us to hold? **ATHENIAN:** Those which we have called by the names of food, drink, and <term>Venus</term> <note>original: "veneris"; referring to sexual desire or procreation.</note>. **CLINIAS:** It shall be done entirely as you bid, guest. **ATHENIAN:** <margin>E</margin> Excellent. But let us come to the matter of the marriage, and let us teach the groom and the bride how children are to be procreated; and if we do not persuade them, let us threaten them with the imposition of certain laws. **CLINIAS:** In what way? **ATHENIAN:** The groom and bride must think altogether how they can procreate the most beautiful and best possible children for the city. All men who work together on anything do everything well and beautifully whenever they apply their minds both to each other and to the work itself. But if they either do not have a mind for it or do not apply it, the opposite occurs. Therefore, let the groom turn his mind to the bride and the procreation of children, and the bride similarly to the groom, especially in that time when they have not yet fathered any. Let certain women have charge <margin>F</margin> of these matters, whether many or few, as it pleases the leaders. Let them gather daily at the temple of <term>Lucina</term> <note>original: "Lucinae"; the Roman goddess of childbirth, identified with the Greek Eileithyia.</note>, staying for a third part of an hour; and there let them report to one another if they see any man or woman of those bound by the marriage bond and having the faculty of procreating turning their mind elsewhere than to those things which were commanded in the sacrifices of the nuptials. Moreover, the procreation of children and the observation of those who are devoted to it shall not exceed ten years, provided that fertility for procreating is present. If any remain barren up to that time, let them be separated after counsel has been held with their relatives and the women who care for these matters, as is convenient for both. If any dispute should arise concerning the convenience of either, let ten of the Guardians of the Laws be chosen by those whom they themselves wish, and let them decide. But the women themselves shall also enter the <margin>G</margin> houses of the young people, partly with warnings and partly with threats, to drive them away from ignorance and fault. If they are unable to do so, let them report it to the Guardians of the Laws, and let them take care of it. If even they are unable to prevent it, let them bring the matter before the people and, having written down the names of the erring ones, let them affirm by oath that they were unable to make them better. And he who has been reported in writing, unless he convicts his accusers, shall be <term>infamous</term> <note>original: "infamis"; meaning a loss of legal and social standing, a form of civic death.</note>; nor shall he further devote his effort to marriages or the procreation of children. <margin>H</margin> And if he should attempt it, let anyone be allowed to strike him with impunity. Let the same be the penalties for women. For they shall live devoid of womanly honors, and if they have gone to weddings or the births of children, they shall not be received if they have been summoned to judgment and also condemned. If, after they have procreated children according to the laws, anyone is joined to another’s wife, or a woman to another's husband, while they are still in their child-bearing years, let them be subject to the same penalties as were stated for when they themselves were procreating. <margin>Α</margin> ...the opposite we hear in others, when we did not even dare to taste of an ox; and the sacrifices to the gods were not animals, but meal-cakes and fruits steeped in honey, and other such pure offerings. They abstained from flesh, as it was not holy to eat it, nor to stain the altars of the gods with blood. These are eating and drinking, from the moment they are born; for which every animal has an innate love, and is full of a stinging passion and is deaf to the one who says that it is necessary to take away from the abundance, and that by fulfilling the pleasures and desires concerning all these things, one must always rid oneself of all pain. The third and greatest need for us, and the sharpest desire, starts last but makes men most fiery with madnesses; it is entirely that concerning the <margin>Γ</margin> sowing of offspring, burning with the greatest insolence. These three diseases must be turned toward the best, instead of the so-called "most pleasant," attempting to restrain them by the three greatest things: fear, law, and true reason; using additionally the Muses and the gods of the games, to quench the growth and the inflow. Let us then place the birth of children after the marriages, and after the birth, nurture and education. And perhaps as the discourse proceeds in this way, each law for us will be completed going forward toward the common meals; so that having arrived at such communities, whether they should be only for women or for men, we may see them clearly from nearby, and perhaps observe them better; and having ordered the things before them, which are still even now without legislation, <margin>Δ</margin> we shall make a stop there. And (as was just said) we shall see them more accurately, and we would better establish the laws that are fitting and proper for them. **CL.** You speak most rightly. **ATH.** Let us then guard in memory the things just spoken. For perhaps we shall have need of them all at some time. **CL.** What sort of things do you command? **ATH.** Those which we defined by the three words: eating we said first, and second, drinking; and a certain flutter of the sexual passions, third. **CL.** Certainly, O stranger, we shall remember the things you now command. **ATH.** Good. Let us go then to the bridal affairs; teaching them how and in what manner it is necessary to make children, and, if we do not persuade them, threatening them with the laws. **CL.** How? **ATH.** The <margin>Ε</margin> bride and the groom must think how we shall produce for the city children as beautiful and as good as possible. All men who are partners in any action, when they turn their mind to themselves and to the action, produce all things beautiful and good; but not turning their mind, or not having a mind, they do the opposite. Let the groom turn his mind to the bride and to child-making; and in the same way also the bride, during that time especially when they have not yet had children born to them. Let the women we have chosen be overseers of these things, whether more or fewer, as many as it seems to the rulers, gathering at the temple of <term>Eileithyia</term> <note>original: "Εἰληθυίας"; the Greek goddess of childbirth.</note> each day, for up to a third part of an hour. And having gathered there, let them report to each other if any woman or man of those making children looks toward other things, or against the things ordained by the sacrifices and rites at the marriages. And let the making of children and the guarding of those making children be for ten years, and no longer a time, when the birth flows well. But if some should be barren during this time, let them be separated by deliberating in common with the relatives and the ruling women for what is suitable to each. If any dispute arises concerning what is fitting and suitable for each, having chosen ten of the Guardians of the Laws, whom they themselves entrust and appoint, let them abide by their persuasion. And the women, entering into the houses of the young people, <margin>Ϛ</margin> partly by admonishing and partly also by threatening, let them stop them from their error and ignorance. But if they are unable, let them go and tell the Guardians of the Laws; and let them prevent them. And if even they are somehow unable, let them declare it to the public, having written them up and having sworn that they are unable to make such-and-such a person better. And the one who is written up shall be <term>disenfranchised</term> <note>original: "ἄτιμος" (atimos); the Greek term for loss of citizen rights and honor.</note>, unless he convicts those who wrote him up in a court of law. And for such a one, let him not go to weddings, nor to the completion rites of children. And if he does not, let anyone who wishes punish him with blows without penalty. Let the same <margin>Ζ</margin> laws be also for a woman. For let her not share in the outings of women, and let her not share in attending weddings and the naming of children, if she is written up in the same way for being disorderly, and does not win her case. And when they have indeed generated children according to the laws, if anyone has intercourse with another woman in such matters, or a woman with a man, if they are still making children, let the same penalties be for them as were said for those still generating. After these things, the man <margin>Η</margin> who is self-controlled, and the woman who is self-controlled, shall be of good repute in all such things...

<header>ON THE LAWS, BOOK VII.</header>

<margin>A</margin> ...should be honored in the highest degree; but he who does the contrary, let him be dishonored in the opposite way. If it should happen that the majority behave with moderation in such matters as we have prescribed, let these things be observed in silence without written laws. However, if the many do not restrain themselves, let them be declared by written laws, and let judgment and action be taken concerning each such case according to their standard. The first year is the beginning of the whole life for everyone; it is necessary that this be recorded in the paternal shrines as the beginning of life for both boy and girl. Let it also be inscribed on a whitened wall in every phratry <note>original: "φατρίᾳ" - a traditional social subdivision or "brotherhood" in ancient Greek city-states</note>, so that the number of those fit for the magistracies <note>Public offices or government positions</note> may be established by the count of their years. Let the living members of each phratry always be written close by, and those departing from life be similarly erased. Let the limit for marriage be, for a girl, from sixteen to twenty years—this being defined as the longest time for this purpose—and for a boy, from thirty until thirty-five. The age for holding office for a woman shall be the fortieth year, and for a man, the thirtieth. Regarding war, for a man it shall be from twenty up to sixty years; <margin>The age for marrying.</margin> for a woman, as she may seem fit to be used for military needs after she has given birth to children, let the possible and fitting tasks be assigned to each until her fiftieth year.

# THE LAWS OF PLATO
# BOOK VII.
### CONCERNING LEGISLATION,
### THE SEVENTH DIALOGUE.

->SUMMARY OF THE DIALOGUE: After dealing with marriage, by whose benefit children are brought into the light, the correct method of teaching requires that he now dispute concerning their<-
->institution and education. This pertains both to the duty of paternal affection and the interest of the Republic, that the youth, who are its nursery, be rightly<-
->cultivated. He therefore treats here accurately the education of children, which regards both the body and the soul; by these two parts it is surely contained, as from the<-
->disputation itself can be established. He teaches, then, when, how, and with which arts they are to be imbued and instructed. As for why he discusses Music and dance<-
->so carefully here, though he has treated them copiously elsewhere, this seems to be the chief cause: that among the Greeks their use and authority had so greatly prevailed<-
->that it was plainly necessary to take account of this matter, and to apply certain laws for its definition.<-

<margin>On the education of children:</margin> <margin>B</margin> <image-desc>Decorative drop cap N featuring a bearded man in a robe and two other figures, possibly students or disciples.</image-desc>

NOW that children are born, both male and
female, we must next speak of their upbringing and
discipline. To pass this over in silence is
altogether impossible; yet if it is spoken of, it
seems more fitting for a certain kind of instruction
and admonition rather than for formal laws. For
many things, both small and obscure, happen daily in private and throughout individual homes; because they are easily driven by the pleasure, pain, and desire of each person contrary to the advice of the legislator, they produce various and dissimilar characters in the citizens. This is a misfortune for cities. <margin>C</margin> Since these occurrences are small and frequent, it would not be entirely honorable or becoming to forbid them by a formal setting of laws with penalties imposed on each. Furthermore, it would undermine the written laws, since men would grow accustomed to despising the laws in these small and frequent matters. For this reason, it is both difficult to write laws about these things and impossible to remain silent. But I will endeavor to bring what I say into the light, as if pointing with a finger; for now, my words seem to be spoken in obscurity. **CLINIAS:** You speak very truly. <margin>D</margin> **ATHENIAN:** Now, it has been rightly said elsewhere that we must consider that a correct education is able to make both the body and the soul as beautiful and as excellent as possible. **CLINIAS:** That is so. **ATHENIAN:** I believe the most beautiful bodies, simply put, will be those that have grown most straight from a tender age. **CLINIAS:** Certainly. **ATHENIAN:** What of this? Do we not understand that the first growth in all animals is the greatest and most abundant? So much so that it has provided handles for many to contend that human bodies do not grow as much in the remaining twenty years as they do in the double growth starting from the first five years. **CLINIAS:** You tell the truth. **ATHENIAN:** What then? When a great amount of growth flows in without many moderate labors, do we not know that many evils are bred in the bodies? **CLINIAS:** Entirely so, Athenian. **ATHENIAN:** Therefore, they have need of the most labors at that time when the most nourishment is added to the bodies. <margin>E</margin> **CLINIAS:** What are you saying, my guest? Shall we impose the most labors upon those just born and the most tender infants? **ATHENIAN:** Not upon these first, but even earlier, upon those who are still being nourished within their mother's womb. **CLINIAS:** How do you say this should be done, excellent man? Shall those who are still carried in the parent's womb perform labor? **ATHENIAN:** Certainly. And indeed, it is no wonder if you are ignorant of the exercise of such an age; though it may seem absurd to you, I desire to explain it. **CLINIAS:** By all means. **ATHENIAN:** Among us <note>The Athenian is referring to customs in Athens</note>, this sort of thing can be better understood because there some engage in certain games more than is fitting. <margin>F</margin> For among us, not only children, but even some elders, breed young birds <note>original: "ὀρνίθων θρέμματα" - referring here to birds bred for fighting, like quails or roosters</note> and exercise them for mutual combat against one another. They are far from thinking that the labors in which they stir up the birds are moderate; rather, taking the smaller ones in their hands and the larger ones under their arms, they walk for many miles for the sake of the good health, not of their own bodies, but of these birds. In this, they certainly signify to a man capable of understanding that all bodies benefit from being moved and shaken without exhaustion, whether by themselves or...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...honored with the greatest effort; those on the contrary should be blamed. If it happens that many behave themselves moderately in such matters, let the things we have prescribed be held and done in silence without written laws; but if most people do not restrain themselves at all, let them be declared by the writing of laws, and let judgment and action be taken concerning each such case according to their norm. The first year is the beginning of the whole life for all, which ought to be written in the paternal shrines as the beginning of living for the boy as well as the girl. Let it be added on a whitened wall in each tribe, so that those who are fit for the magistracies may be established by the number of years; and the living men of each tribe should always be written nearby, and those yielding to nature <note>A euphemism for dying</note> should likewise be deleted. Let the time of marriage for a girl be from the sixteenth year to the twentieth, and let that be the longest time appointed for this; for the male, from the thirtieth to the thirty-fifth. The time for holding a magistracy for a woman is the fortieth year; for a man, the thirtieth. Of war, from twenty to sixty years in men; <margin>Age for marrying.</margin> in women after they have given birth to sons, up to the fiftieth year of age. In which it must be observed that they are accepted for that use of war which is both possible and decent for them.

CHILDREN having been born, then, both
males and females, we must next speak of
their education and discipline. To pass over

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Book VII of Plato’s Laws. The previous page established the registration of citizens by age. # PLATO’S LAWS

<margin>Physical training of infants contributes to the attainment of virtue.</margin>
**A** ...in vehicles, or on a ship, or on horses, or in whatever other way the body may be moved. Because of these movements, which help the body master the nourishment of food and drink, they are able to provide us with health, beauty, and strength. Since these things are so, what do we think must be done next? Shall we speak with a laugh as we establish laws, decreeing that a pregnant woman must walk, and that the newborn be molded like wax while they are soft, and bound in swaddling clothes until the age of two? Shall we also compel nurses by laws, under threat of a fine, to carry the children constantly—either to the fields, to the temples, or elsewhere—until they are able to stand on their own? And even then, they must take care that while the children are still young and beginning to stand, **B** their limbs are not distorted by the force of their weight due to their softness; should they continue to carry them until the infants have completed their third year? The nurses should be as robust as possible, and there should not be only one, but several. Should I impose a penalty in the written laws for each nurse if these things are not done? Or should we by no means act in this way? For if we did, what we just mentioned would happen to us in abundance. **CLINIAS.** What is that? **C** **ATHENIAN.** We would surely provoke a great deal of laughter against ourselves. For the feminine and servile habits of the nurses would refuse to obey us. **CLINIAS.** For what reason, then, did we think these things ought to be said? **ATHENIAN.** Because the minds of the masters and the free citizens, perhaps when they hear these things, will rightly understand that unless private affairs are correctly administered in a city, it is in vain for anyone to hope that public matters will have any stability in the laws. Understanding this, they will use what we have just said as if they were laws; by the practice of which, both the household and the republic, being well governed, will live happily. **CLINIAS.** What you have said is very reasonable. **ATHENIAN.** Let us not, therefore, cease from this kind of lawgiving until we have also described the cultivation of the soul which pertains to very young children; and so, in a similar way to how we began with the body, let us complete the discourse. **CLINIAS.** You are quite right. **ATHENIAN.** Let us, then, accept this as a fundamental principle <note>original: "elementum" (Latin) / "στοιχεῖον" (Greek) - a basic building block or first principle</note> **D** for the cultivation of both the soul and the body of infants: that constant nourishment and movement, applied day and night, is beneficial to everyone, but especially to the very young. It is as if they lived, if possible, in a state of perpetual sailing. Since this is impossible, one must come as close to it as possible in caring for infants. That this ought to happen can be guessed from the fact that experience has taught both the nurses of children and those who perform the remedies of the Corybantes <note>The Corybantes were mythical attendants of the goddess Cybele; their rituals involved loud music and frenzied dancing used as a therapeutic "cure" for emotional distress or "madness."</note> that such motion is useful. For whenever mothers wish to put children to sleep who are slow to rest, they do this not through quiet or silence, but through the opposite. They always carry them in their arms and rock them, soothing them with the modulation of the voice as if with the sound of a flute. And just as in the remedies for those suffering from frenzied Bacchic madness, they use this kind of dance and music involving motion. **CLINIAS.** What, guest, is the primary cause of these things? **ATHENIAN.** It is not very **E** difficult to know. **CLINIAS.** How so? **ATHENIAN.** Both of these conditions consist of fear; for they are certain terrors caused by a poor habit of the soul. Therefore, when someone applies an external motion to these affections, the external movement conquers that internal movement which is terrifying and furious. Once it has conquered, it brings about a tranquil peace in the soul, with the pounding of the heart having been calmed for a time. Thus, it induces sleep in some, while others who are awake it restores from a furious state to a healthy habit of mind by means of the flute and the dance, with the help of the gods to whom they labor in supplication. These things, as the brevity of this speech allows, have a certain probable reasoning. **CLINIAS.** Entirely so. **ATHENIAN.** If, **F** therefore, these things have such power, we must also consider that every soul nourished in fear from infancy will be more accustomed than any other to be carried away by dread. No one can doubt that this is an exercise in cowardice, not in courage. **CLINIAS.** Quite so. **ATHENIAN.** On the contrary, we shall say that he is exercised in courage who, from a tender age, becomes accustomed to conquering all fears and terrors. **CLINIAS.** Well said. **ATHENIAN.** Let us say, then, that this one thing contributes greatly to the virtue of the soul: namely, the exercise of infants which consists of motion. **CLINIAS.** Most certainly. **ATHENIAN.** Furthermore, a gentle disposition or a morose one has no **G** small importance regarding the goodness or depravity of the soul. **CLINIAS.** It is so. **ATHENIAN.** We must say, as far as we are able, in what way either of these qualities is immediately born in the infant’s soul. <margin>Luxury/Indulgence in the minds of children.</margin> **CLINIAS.** Clearly. **ATHENIAN.** It truly seems to us that luxury <note>original: "deliciæ" - here meaning excessive indulgence or being "spoiled"</note> makes the character of the youth difficult, morose, irritable, and excitable over small matters. Conversely, a servitude that is too excessive and harsh makes them abject, unfree, and haters of humanity, rendering them most unfit for human society. **CLINIAS.** But how shall the whole city educate infants who do not yet understand speech and cannot yet taste any other discipline, as you command? **ATHENIAN.** In this way: every animal, as soon as it is born, is accustomed to using its voice and a cry. This is no less true of the human race, which, more than others, **H** adds weeping to its cry. **CLINIAS.** That is true. **ATHENIAN.** Therefore, nurses, wishing to know what infants desire, offer them things based on what they believe they are seeking...

<column-break/>

...and in swings, or on the sea, or on horses being ridden, or being carried by other bodies in any way whatsoever, they are moved. And because of these things, which help master the eating of food and drink, it is possible for them to grant us health, beauty, and other types of strength. What then shall we say, these things being so, that we must do next? Do you wish that we speak with laughter as we establish laws? That the pregnant woman should walk about, and the child be molded like wax while soft, and be swaddled until two years old; and indeed, let us compel the nurses, fining them by law, to carry the children always to the fields, or to temples, or to relatives somewhere, until they are able to stand sufficiently; and then, while they are still young, being held up, lest their limbs be distorted by the violence of leaning on them, let them labor in carrying them until the child has reached three years? Perhaps we need more than one nurse for each, rather than just one. Furthermore, shall we write down a penalty for those who do not do these things? Or is that far from necessary? For what was just said would happen in great and abundant measure. **CL.** What sort of thing? **ATH.** That we would incur much laughter, as the nurses and those in feminine and domestic service would reject the mothers' habits. **CL.** But for the sake of what did we say these things must be spoken? **ATH.** For this: the habits of the masters and free people in cities, perhaps upon hearing this, would understand that one cannot expect any stability in the establishment of laws for public matters if those concerning private households in cities are not correctly handled. And considering these things, he himself might use the laws now spoken, and by using them well, and governing his own house and city at the same time, he might be happy. **CL.** And you have spoken very reasonably. **ATH.** Therefore, let us not yet cease from such lawgiving until we have also rendered the practices concerning the souls of very young children, in the same way as we have already completed the things spoken regarding their bodies. **CL.** Quite rightly. **ATH.** Let us take this, then, as a fundamental principle <note>original: "στοιχεῖον" (Greek) - a first principle or element</note> for both body and soul of the very young: that the nursing and motion occurring as much as possible through every night and day is beneficial for all, especially for the youngest; and they should live, if it were possible, as if always sailing. But now we must do as close to this as possible for the newborn offspring of children. One must also take evidence from those who have grasped and known by experience that it is useful: both the nursing of little ones and those who perform the Corybantic remedies, whenever mothers wish to put to sleep children who are difficult to sleep, they do not bring silence to them, but on the contrary, motion, shaking them always in their arms; and not silence, but some melody. And they literally play the flute to the children, just as in the cures of those with frantic Bacchic madness, using this practice of motion. **CL.** What then is the cause of these things, O stranger, for us? **ATH.** It is not at all difficult to know. **CL.** How so? **ATH.** Both these affections are surely cases of fear; and they are fears due to a poor state of the soul. Therefore, when someone applies shaking to such affections from the outside, the external movement overcomes the internal movement that is fearful and manic; and having conquered it, it appears to have produced a calm and silence in the soul, the troublesome jumping of the heart in each case having ceased. It is altogether a welcome thing; it makes some obtain sleep, while others who are awake, dancing and playing the flute with the gods, to whom each may sacrifice with good omens, it brings them to have sane habits instead of manic dispositions. And these things, to speak thus in brief, have a certain persuasive reasoning. **CL.** Quite so. **ATH.** If these things have such a power, one must consider this among them: that every soul living with fears from youth would be more accustomed to being in a state of fear. And how would they say this is an exercise of courage and not of cowardice? **CL.** How indeed? **ATH.** But on the contrary, we would say that one should practice from youth the conquering of the terrors and fears that fall upon us. **CL.** Correct. **ATH.** This one thing also, for the part of the soul's virtue, namely the gymnastics of very young children through motion, we would say contributes greatly to us. **CL.** Entirely so. **ATH.** Moreover, the lack of moroseness in the soul and the presence of moroseness are not small parts of the soul, each becoming a part of goodness or badness of soul. **CL.** How could it not be? **ATH.** In what way, then, either of these might be implanted in the newborn as we would wish, we must try to say, even as he is at a loss regarding these things. **CLIN.** How indeed? **ATHEN.** I say then the dogma held by us is that luxury <note>original: "τρυφὴ" - indulgence, softness, or luxury</note> makes the characters of the young difficult and irritable and easily moved by small things; while the opposite of these, namely a violent and savage enslavement, makes them humble, unfree, and misanthropic, rendering them unsuitable housemates. **CLIN.** How then must the whole city nurse those who do not yet understand speech, nor are yet able to receive other education? **ATHEN.** In this way: everything that is born is accustomed to speak with a cry immediately, and not least the race of men; and indeed, weeping is added to its cry more than others. **CLIN.** Quite so. **ATHEN.** Therefore, the nurses, looking to see what it desires, judge by these very things in what they offer. For what is offered does not stop...

He compares these domestic practices to the rhythmic "cures" of the Corybantic rituals, suggesting that external motion calms internal fear and agitation.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Book VII of Plato’s Laws, moving from the physical care of infants to their psychological and moral development during the first six years of life. It introduces the concept of the "middle way" in emotion and the vital importance of "unwritten laws" or customs as the foundation of a stable society.</meta>

# ON THE LAWS, BOOK VII

<margin>A</margin> ...if they are silent, they are well-off; but if they shout and cry, it is a sign they are not being well-served. Indeed, for infants, shouting and weeping are the primary indicators of what they love and hate—signs that are by no means fortunate. This period of life lasts no less than three years, a span that is no small portion of life to be led either rightly or wrongly. **CLINIAS.** You are right. **ATHENIAN.** Does it not seem to you that a man who is difficult and in no way tranquil, but rather complaining and full of groans, is more so than is fitting for a good man? **CLINIAS.** To me, certainly. **ATHENIAN.** What then? If one should try by every means and power to ensure that during these three years the child is affected as little as possible by pain, fear, and all kinds of grief, do you not think the child’s soul will be rendered more peaceful and tranquil? **CLINIAS.**

<margin>B</margin> It is clear, Guest, and even more so if one should provide him with many pleasures. **ATHENIAN.** I cannot agree with you on that point, remarkable Clinias. For such an education, when applied immediately at the start, is the greatest ruin of all. Let us see if what I am saying makes sense. **CLINIAS.** Say what you mean. **ATHENIAN.** I assert that we are dealing with a matter of no small importance. Pay attention also, Megillus, and judge between our opinions. My own view is that a correct life should neither pursue pleasures entirely nor entirely flee from pains, but rather embrace that middle state <note>This "middle state" or *mesos* is a core concept in Greek philosophy, often called the "Golden Mean."</note>, which I just now called tranquility—a state we rightly declare, according to a divine oracle, to be the property of God. Anyone who intends to become godlike <note>The Greek term *theion* suggests achieving a divine-like state of soul.</note> must follow this state, ensuring that he is not entirely prone to pleasures (lest he also be prone to pain), and that he does not allow anyone else, whether old or young, male or female, to indulge in them—least of all newborn infants. For it is then that all character traits are most firmly implanted in everyone because of habit. Indeed, if I did not fear it would seem I was joking, I would say that even pregnant women, above all others in that year, should be managed so that they are neither driven toward many and frantic pleasures nor agitated by pains. Instead, they should spend that time honoring a tranquil, peaceful, and mild life. **CLINIAS.** There is no need, Guest,

<margin>D</margin> to ask Megillus which of us has spoken more correctly. For I myself agree with you that everyone must flee a life of mere pleasure and mere pain, and always cut a middle path. Therefore, you have spoken well, and I have listened well. **ATHENIAN.** You are very right, Clinias. But let all three of us consider this next point. **CLINIAS.** What is that? **ATHENIAN.** That all these things we are now discussing are what the many call "unwritten laws" <note>original: "leges non scriptae"</note>; and those they name "ancestral laws" <note>original: "leges patriae"</note> are nothing other than the sum of all such customs. What we touched upon a little earlier—that these should neither be officially called laws nor passed over in silence—was well said. For these are the bonds of the entire state, holding a middle place between the laws already written and those yet to be written, as if they were ancient ancestral institutions.

<margin>E</margin> If these are well established and men are correctly habituated to them, they protect the written laws with stable safety. But if they go awry, the opposite occurs; just as in buildings, if the supports <note>The Athenian uses an architectural metaphor, comparing customs to the foundational beams or pillars that keep a structure from collapsing.</note> are withdrawn from the middle, they cause everything to collapse, and things fall upon one another, and even the parts that were well built above fall down when the foundations crumble. Considering these things, Clinias, we must bind your new city together from every side, leaving out nothing as far as possible that pertains to laws, customs, or practices; for the city is woven together by all these things. One cannot remain permanent without the other. Therefore, you should not wonder if many things that seem small to you, flowing together like customs, make our laws longer. **CLINIAS.** You speak correctly; we shall consider it in that way. **ATHENIAN.** If one applies these things diligently to a child who is three years old,

<margin>F</margin> whether male or female, and uses the aforementioned methods carefully, they will bring no small benefit to the newly nurtured. This will be suitable for the nature of those who are three, four, five, and even six years old. At this age, luxuries should be removed, and discipline should be applied without humiliation. Just as we said that slaves should be punished without insult, so that they do not become enraged—yet punished nonetheless, so that they do not become overly pampered—the same must be done for free children. Children of this age have certain natural games; when they come together, they find them for themselves. These children should be gathered at the village shrines, from age three until six, all the children of the village together. The nurses should

<margin>G</margin> take care of the orderliness or lack of restraint of these children. One of the twelve women <note>Plato proposes a board of twelve women to oversee the early education and behavior of children in the community.</note> shall be appointed to oversee each group and their nurses for a year, as the Guardians of the Laws shall ordain. These women shall be chosen by the overseers of marriages, one from each tribe, and they shall be of an appropriate age. The one appointed to this office shall go to the shrine every day and punish anyone who does wrong. If it is a male or female slave, or a male or female foreigner, she shall punish them through certain public servants; but if it is a citizen who disputes the punishment, she shall bring him before the rural magistrates.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> if they are silent, they have presented themselves rightly; if they cry and shout, they have not presented themselves rightly—one can infer from these signs. Surely, in infants, the signs of what they love and what they hate are shouting and weeping, signs that are least fortunate. The time for this is no less than three years, a space that is not a small part of life to be led correctly or otherwise, if it is led correctly or otherwise itself. **CLINIAS.** Correct. **ATHENIAN.** Does not that man seem to you difficult, and in no way tranquil, even querulous and full of moaning beyond what befits a good man? **CLINIAS.** To me, certainly. **ATHENIAN.** What then? If someone should try with all their might and by every reason to ensure that in this three-year period a boy is affected as little as possible by pain, fear, and sadness, will not the boy's mind be rendered more peaceful and tranquil? **CLINIAS.** It is clear, Guest, and much more so if one were to educate him in many pleasures. **ATHENIAN.** I will not grant you this, O wonderful Clinias. For such an education, since it is applied immediately at the start, is the greatest destruction of all. Let us see, then, if we are saying anything of worth. **CLINIAS.** Say what you mean. **ATHENIAN.** I assert now that we are dealing with no small matter. Pay attention also, Megillus; and judge the opinions of both. My reasoning, indeed, judges that a correct life should neither follow pleasures entirely, nor entirely flee pains, but rather follow that middle habit, which I myself just now called tranquility, and which we all confess, rightly guessing by a certain divine oracle, to be the property of God. This habit anyone must follow who is to become divine, so that he is neither entirely inclined to pleasures himself—otherwise he will not be far from pain—nor should he allow anyone else, whether old or young, male or female, to indulge in pleasures, and least of all infants immediately born; for then, because of habit, the firmest characters of all are born in all people. Truly, unless I feared that I might seem to you to be joking, I would say certainly that pregnant women most of all must be so guided in that year that they are neither carried away toward many and furious pleasures, nor agitated by pains: but rather lead a tranquil, peaceful, and mild life. **CLINIAS.** There is no need, Guest, to ask Megillus which of us has spoken more correctly. For I agree with you that a life of pure pleasure and pure pain is to be fled by all, and a certain middle path is always to be held. Wherefore you have spoken correctly and have been heard correctly. **ATHENIAN.** Most correctly, Clinias. But let us all three consider this together. **CLINIAS.** What is it? **ATHENIAN.** That what is said by us are called "unwritten laws" <note>original: "leges non scriptae"</note> by many, and they are nothing other than what are named "ancestral laws," <note>original: "leges patriae"</note> all things of this kind. And what we touched upon a little before—that these are not to be called laws, nor passed over in silence—was soundly said. For these are the bonds of the whole republic, and they hold the middle place between the written laws and those to be written, namely as ancestral and ancient institutions of all kinds. These, if they are soundly placed, and men have rightly accustomed themselves to them, protect the written laws with stable safety. But if the opposite is done, the opposite will happen: just as occurs in buildings, where if the supports of the house are removed from the middle, they force everything to fall together, and things fall upon one another, and those that were well built above collapse when the earlier parts are destroyed. And thinking of these things, Clinias, we must bind this new city of yours from every side, with nothing at all left out as far as possible, whether it pertains to laws, or to customs, or to studies; for the city is bound together by all these things. One of these cannot remain without the other. Wherefore it is not to be wondered at if many things, both many and small together, seem to be instituted as legitimate, flowing together like customs, and make the laws longer. **CLINIAS.** You speak correctly. And we shall think similarly. **ATHENIAN.** If someone, therefore, toward him who is three years old, whether male or female, should diligently apply these things, and use the aforementioned things zealously, they will bring no small utility to the newly nurtured. And that will be suitable to the nature of those who are three and four and five and six years old, from whom luxuries are to be removed, and castigation without contempt is to be applied. Moreover, just as we said slaves ought to be castigated without insult, lest they be carried away into anger—yet castigated entirely, lest they be rendered too luxurious—so we wish for free children. Some of their games are in a way natural to them: to which when they meet, they are carried spontaneously. These boys are to be gathered from three until six years, each in the solemnity of his tribe: and of these even yet so small, let the nurses observe their modesty and lack of restraint, and let one certain woman of the twelve be in charge of each assembly and the nurses, to command for the space of a year: as the guardians of the laws shall ordain, let them choose these women, the curators of marriages, one from each tribe, equal to them in age. She who is assumed to this magistracy shall so bear herself that she goes forth into the sacred place daily, and always punishes the one who does wrong. A male slave and a female slave, a foreigner and a foreign woman, she shall punish through certain urban ministers; but a citizen whose punishment is in controversy, she shall drag to the rural magistrates.
