<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion in Book VII of Plato’s *Laws*, transitioning from the early nurturing of infants to the formal separation and education of children starting at age six. The Athenian Guest is outlining the curriculum for the future citizens of the ideal city.</meta>

# PLATO'S [LAWS]

<margin>Separation of girls.</margin>
...judgment: but where there is no controversy, let the law itself punish the citizen. After the age of six years, let the females be separated from the males; henceforth, let boys associate with boys of their own age, and girls likewise with girls of their own age. Both should then turn themselves toward learning. The <margin>A</margin> males, indeed, should go to teachers of horsemanship, archery, the javelin, and the sling; and let the females also be admitted to these same lessons if they agree, at least as far as gaining knowledge, and especially regarding the use of arms. How these matters are currently handled, however, is ignored by almost everyone. **CLINIAS.** What do you mean by that? **ATHENIAN.** I mean that the right and left hands seem to differ naturally in each of our operations. In our feet and lower limbs, <margin>B</margin> there seems to be no difference in their labor. But through the ignorance of mothers and nurses, we have all become, as it were, lame in our hands. For while nature has made both limbs nearly equal, we ourselves, by not using them correctly through habit, have created a difference. Certainly, in some tasks, this matters little—for instance, it makes no difference to one's life if the lyre is held in the left hand and the plectrum <note>original: "plectrum"; a small tool used to pluck the strings of a lyre.</note> in the right, or other such things. But to use these as an excuse not to do the same in all other matters is madness. The Scythian law shows this to be true; for they do <margin>C</margin> not only hold the bow with the left hand and the arrow with the right, but they use both hands similarly for both tasks. Many examples of this kind are found in the work of charioteers and others. From these, one can understand that those who make the left hand weaker than the right are acting against nature. This matter, as we have said, is no hindrance in the use of horn plectrums and such instruments; but it makes a very great difference when it is necessary to use a sword, bow, spear, and the like in battle—and even more so when arms are repelled by arms. There is a great difference between one who has learned and one who has not, or one who has exercised and one who has not. For just as a man who has perfectly trained in the <margin>D</margin> boxing match or wrestling <note>original: "pugili certamine aut lucta"; the Latin refers to combat sports like boxing and wrestling, which were central to Greek education.</note>, or both together, is able to engage from the left side and readily adapts himself when forced to shift to the other side—I believe the very same thing is most correct regarding arms and all other things. Therefore, if someone possesses weapons with which to defend themselves and strike others, they ought not to leave any of these idle or unexercised, as far as their strength allows. And if someone were to have the nature of Geryon or Briareus <note>Geryon and Briareus were mythological giants; Briareus was said to have a hundred hands.</note>, being hundred-handed, he should be able to throw a hundred missiles. The leaders, both women and men, should take care of all these things: the women overseeing the games and nourishment, and the men overseeing the <margin>E</margin> subjects of study, so that all, made equally powerful in both feet and hands through habit, do not harm their natural potential.

<margin>Gymnastics. Dancing.</margin>
It is fitting to use a double discipline: one for the body, called gymnastics; and one for the soul, called music. But gymnastics is again twofold: dancing and wrestling. One kind of dancing imitates the words of the Muse, observing her magnificence and freedom. Another kind, for the sake of health, agility, and the beauty of the body and its parts, bends and stretches each limb appropriately, so that a harmonic motion is sufficiently spread abroad and follows the <margin>Wrestling.</margin> entire order of the dance. As for the types of wrestling, those which Antaeus or Cercyon <note>Mythological wrestlers known for their cruelty and "useless" strength.</note> devised for the sake of useless contention, or Epeius or Amycus in boxing—since these contribute nothing to battle, they are not worthy of mention. But those things which are used in "upright wrestling" <note>original: "recta luctatio"; a style of wrestling where the goal was to throw the opponent without falling oneself.</note>—involving the neck, hands, and the movement of the sides with a desire for victory and a noble bearing—and which lead to health and <margin>F</margin> strength: these are useful for all things and must not be passed over. Rather, both students and teachers must be instructed that when we come to the framing of laws on this subject, the former should grant these things kindly, and the latter receive them graciously. Nor indeed should all imitations found in choral dances be adopted; rather, here we should follow the armed games of the Cretan Curetes <note>Armed dancers from Cretan mythology who protected the infant Zeus.</note>, and in Lacedaemon <note>Sparta.</note>, those of Castor and Pollux. Among us, too, it must not be neglected that Minerva <note>The Roman name for the Greek goddess Athena.</note>, delighting in the games of the choral dance, did not think she should play with empty hands, but performed the duty of dancing while fully adorned with arms. These examples should be imitated <margin>G</margin> by young men and women, honoring the gift of the goddess for the use of war and the ornament of solemnities. Indeed, before they can go out to war, boys should be adorned with arms and horses in the processions of all the gods—sometimes faster, sometimes slower—and in the dance and on the march, they should pour out supplications to the gods and the children of the gods. Furthermore, games and preludes, if they are held for the sake of anything, should certainly be held for these things alone. For these are useful in peace and war, both privately and publicly. Other exercises of the body, whether done in play or in earnest, O Clinias and Megillus, are not fitting for free men. I have now nearly completed the treatment of that gymnastics which I said should be handled in the first discourses; this is the whole and perfect account. If you have a better one, bring it forward. **CLINIAS.** It is not easy, Guest, to neglect these and tell of other better things regarding gymnastics and competition. **ATHENIAN.** It remains, therefore, for us to discuss the gifts of the Muses and Apollo, about which I thought enough had been said...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...bring them to justice; but if the citizen is not in dispute, let this law punish him. After the sixth year for both boys and girls, let the sexes be separated. Let boys spend their time with boys, and girls likewise with one another in their education. Both must be turned toward their studies: the males to teachers of horses, bows, javelins, and slinging. If the females permit, let them also follow these lessons, at least for the sake of learning, and especially regarding the use of weapons. But the current state of these matters is ignored by almost everyone. **CLIN.** <margin>B</margin> What is that? **ATHEN.** That the right and left hands are thought to differ by nature for our needs in each of our actions. In our feet and lower limbs, no difference appears in their labors. But in our hands, through the folly of mothers and nurses, we have each become, as it were, lame. For while nature makes both limbs nearly equal in balance, we ourselves, through different habits, have made them different by not using them rightly. In those tasks where it does not matter much—such as using the lyre in the left hand and the plectrum in the right, and such things—let it be. But to follow these examples for other things when there is no need is nearly madness. <margin>C</margin> The law of the Scythians shows this, for they use the left hand to draw the bow and the right to lead the arrow; and not only that, but they use both hands for both tasks. Many other such examples exist in chariot-driving and elsewhere, from which it is possible to learn that those who make the left hands weaker than the right are doing so against nature. As we said, in the case of horn plectrums and such instruments, this is of no great consequence; but for war, when it is necessary to use bows and javelins and each of these, it matters greatly—and most of all when weapons must be used against weapons. <margin>D</margin> There is a vast difference between the one who has learned and the one who has not, and the one who has exercised versus the one who has not. Just as a man who has perfectly practiced the pancration <note>original: "παγκράτιον" (pankration); an ancient Greek martial art combining boxing and wrestling.</note>, or boxing, or wrestling, is not unable to fight from his left side, nor does he limp or drag himself clumsily whenever someone forces him to shift to the other side—the same, I believe, is the only correct view regarding arms and all other things. One who possesses double sets of limbs with which to defend himself or attack others should not leave any of these idle or unskillful as far as he is able. Even if someone were born with the nature of Geryon or Briareus, with his hundred hands he should be able to throw a hundred missiles. All these things must be the care <margin>E</margin> of the female and male rulers: the women overseeing the children's play and nourishment, and the men overseeing the lessons, so that all, becoming ambidextrous in their hands as much as possible, do not allow their habits to injure their natural potential. The subjects of study are twofold, as we said: one for the body, which is gymnastics; the other for the sake of the soul, which is music. Of gymnastics, there are two parts: dancing and wrestling. In dancing, one kind imitates the speech of the Muse, preserving both magnificence and freedom. Another is for the sake of health, agility, and the beauty of the limbs and parts of the body themselves, rendering the proper bend and tension to each, with the rhythm of movement spreading through and following the whole dance sufficiently. As for <margin>F</margin> the matters of wrestling, such as those Antaeus or Cercyon established in their arts for the sake of useless rivalry, or the boxing of Epeius or Amycus—these are of no use for the common business of war and are not worthy of being adorned with words. But those things belonging to "upright wrestling"—the escapes from the neck, hands, and sides, practiced with rivalry and a noble stance for the sake of strength and health—these are useful for all things and must not be omitted. Rather, we should enjoin both the students and the teachers that, when we reach this point in our laws, the former should grant all such things generously and the latter receive them with grace. Nor should we omit those imitations in choral dances which are fitting to imitate: <margin>G</margin> in this place, the armed games of the Curetes, and in Lacedaemon, those of the Dioscuri <note>The "sons of Zeus," Castor and Pollux.</note>. Moreover, our own Maiden and Mistress <note>Athena, the patron goddess of Athens.</note>, delighting in the play of the choral dance, did not think she should sport with empty hands, but having been adorned in full armor, she thus performed her dance. It would be fitting for both boys and girls to imitate these things, honoring the grace of the goddess for the sake of the needs of war and for festivals. For the children, until they are of an age to go to war, it would be proper for them to be always adorned with arms and horses in all the processions and marches to the gods, making their supplications to the gods and the children of the gods in both faster and slower rhythms of dance and movement. And as for contests and preliminary contests, if there are any, they should be practiced for these reasons and no others. For these are useful both in peace and in war, for the state and for private households. But other labors, plays, and serious pursuits...

Therefore, O Guest, Megillus, and Clinias, one should not say that the discussion of gymnastics in the preceding words is nearly finished; rather, it is complete through and through. But if you have anything better than this, bring it into the open and speak. **CLIN.** It is not easy, Guest, to pass over these things and speak of anything better regarding gymnastics and contests. **ATHEN.** What follows next, then, are the gifts of the Muses and Apollo; though we thought we had spoken of all of them...

It highlights the role of both sexes in learning the arts of war and cites the goddess Athena as the supreme model of the armed dancer.</summary>

# ON THE LAWS, BOOK VII.

->Ggg iiii<-

<meta>catchwords: the, penalties</meta>

We might have supposed that only the matters concerning gymnastics <note>In ancient Greece, 'gymnastics' referred to the total physical education of a citizen, including athletics and dance.</note> remained; but now it is clear what those matters are, and that everything else has been discussed. Let us therefore speak of them in order. **CLINIAS.** By all means, they must be spoken of. **ATHENIAN.** Listen to me, then, in silence; for do not be surprised [at what I say]; yet it may seem a very strange and unusual thing for both the speaker and the listener to grasp, even now. For I am about to speak words that one might reasonably fear to utter, yet I shall not hold back, having somehow found the courage. **CLINIAS.** What is this you are saying, Stranger? **ATHENIAN.** I say that in all cities, the nature of play <note>original: "παιδιᾶς"; referring to the games and recreational activities of children.</note> is entirely misunderstood—that it is the most crucial factor in the establishment of laws, determining whether those that are set down will be permanent or not. For when play is ordered and shares <margin>A</margin> in the same activities, in the same way, and the children always enjoy the same games, it allows even the laws established in earnest to remain undisturbed. But when these same games are moved and innovated upon, constantly undergoing various changes, and when the young never find the same things pleasing <margin>B</margin> in the postures of their own bodies or in their other equipment—failing to agree among themselves on what is graceful or ungraceful—but instead, someone is always innovating and introducing something different in terms of shapes and colors and all such things, and is honored for it above others: we would say, speaking most correctly, that there is no greater plague upon a city than this. For it secretly changes the character of the youth, making the old ways seem dishonorable and the new ways honorable. And of this, I say again, there is no greater harm to all cities than this shift in word and opinion. Hear now how great an evil I claim this to be. **CLINIAS.** Do you mean that the blaming of antiquity in cities is an evil? **ATHENIAN.** Most certainly. **CLINIAS.** You will not find us to be poor listeners to this argument, but rather defenders of it as much as possible. <margin>C</margin> **ATHENIAN.** That is likely. **CLINIAS.** Just speak. **ATHENIAN.** Come then, let us hear it with greater attention, and let us speak to one another thus: I would find that change in all things, except for evil ones, is the most dangerous of all—in all seasons, in the winds, in the diets of bodies, in the habits of souls—to speak simply, not in some cases but not others, except (as I just said) in the case of evil. So that if one <margin>D</margin> looks at bodies, how they become accustomed to all foods, all drinks, and all labors, though at first they are disturbed by them, yet from these very things, over time, they develop a nature suited to them, and they become dear and familiar and known to the whole diet, so that the person lives in the best pleasure and health. And if ever they are forced to change again to one of the supposedly better diets, they are at first disturbed by diseases and only with difficulty recover, returning to their habit. We must think the same thing happens regarding the thoughts of men and the natures of their souls. For the laws in which they are nurtured, if by some divine good fortune they remain unchanged over long and vast periods of time, so that no one has any memory or report of things ever being otherwise <margin>E</margin> than they are now, the whole soul reveres and fears to move any of the established order. The legislator must therefore think of a device, from whatever source possible, as to how this shall be for the city. Now, I will describe it: everyone thinks that the shifting games of the youth, as we said before, are truly just games, and that no great seriousness or harm results from them. Thus, they do not resist, but follow along, yielding; and they do not calculate this: that those children who innovate in their games must necessarily become different men from the children of the past. Having become different, they seek a different life; and having sought that, <margin>F</margin> they desire different practices and laws. After this, no one fears the plague which I just called the greatest for cities. Other changes in physical forms might do less harm, but those changes concerning the habits of praise and blame, which shift frequently—these, I think, are the greatest of all and require the utmost caution. **CLINIAS.** How could they not? **ATHENIAN.** What then? Do we believe the previous arguments, in which we said that <term>rhythms</term> <note>In Greek thought, 'rhythms' and 'modes' in music were believed to possess 'ethos'—the power to mold a person's moral character.</note> and all music are imitations of the characters of better and worse men? Or how else? **CLINIAS.** Our opinion could not be otherwise. <margin>G</margin> **ATHENIAN.** Therefore, we say that every device must be employed so that our children neither desire to touch other imitations in dance or melody, nor should anyone persuade them by offering all sorts of pleasures. **CLINIAS.** You speak most correctly. **ATHENIAN.** Does any of us have a better art for these things than that of the Egyptians? **CLINIAS.** What kind of art do you mean? **ATHENIAN.** That they consecrated all dances and melodies, first by establishing the festivals, calculating for the year which ones should occur at what times, and which gods, children of gods, and <term>dæmons</term> <note>original: "δαίμοσι/dæmonibus"; in this context, these are divine spirits or guardian beings, not 'demons' in the modern sense.</note> they should belong to; and after this, what song should be sung at each of the sacrifices to the gods, and with what dances they should honor the sacrifice of that time, determining who should perform them. Once these are established, and after sacrificing to the Fates and all the <margin>H</margin> other gods, all the citizens together make a libation and consecrate each of the songs to each of the gods and others. If anyone, contrary to these, introduces other hymns or dances to any of the gods, the priests and priestesses, together with the Guardians of the Law, shall exclude him, doing so piously according to the law; and he who is excluded, if he does not submit willingly, shall for the rest of his life face penalties for impiety from anyone who wishes to...

<column-break/>

...so that it seemed only gymnastics alone remained. But now it appears that some things were left out, which must be spoken of first; therefore we shall say them in sequence. **CLINIAS.** Let them be spoken of entirely. **ATHENIAN.** Hear then, for you have heard in the earlier parts, though in both speaking and listening—which is very strange and unusual—one must take care. Indeed, at present, I am about to say something that one might rightly fear to say; nevertheless, I shall speak. **CLINIAS.** What is that, <margin>A</margin> Guest? **ATHENIAN.** I assert that it is recognized by no one how great a power the nature of games has in all cities over the stability or change of established laws. For if this is so ordered that the same people always use and take delight in the same games, according to the same <margin>B</margin> patterns and in the same way, it allows the laws that were seriously established to remain stable. But if that kind of thing is changed, and new games are introduced daily, and the youth always delight in new things—both in the shapes and gestures of the body, and in the rest of their equipment and furniture—and if they judge the decent and the indecent differently from day to day, and always honor the inventors of new things, namely colors and shapes and other such things: we judge that no greater plague than this will befall the city, and we judge quite correctly. For it secretly changes the customs of the youth, and makes the ancient things seem cheap, while the new things are seen as worthy of honor. Regarding this speech and opinion, I assert again that nothing is more destructive to a city. <margin>C</margin> But hear how great an evil I judge it to be. **CLINIAS.** Do you say that the disparaging of ancient things is an evil in cities? **ATHENIAN.** I say so indeed, and strongly. **CLINIAS.** You will not find us to be bad listeners to this speech, but as far as possible, most benevolent. **ATHENIAN.** That is fitting. **CLINIAS.** Speak now. **ATHENIAN.** Come, let us hear these things most diligently; and so let us discuss among ourselves. We find that change in all things, except for evil ones, is most dangerous in all times: in the diet of bodies, in the <margin>D</margin> habits of minds—simply in everything except in evil things, as I just said. Bodies, indeed, when they first use certain foods and drinks and labors, are disturbed in some way; then, from long-term use of these things, they grow firm and are made healthy, and they take great delight in this kind of life as something now familiar, intimate, and friendly, and they are in the best of health. But if, for some probable cause, they are forced to pass to another diet, they initially fall into disorders, being disturbed before they become accustomed to the new way of life. It must be thought that the same happens in the thoughts of men and the natures of their souls. For all men revere those laws, and dread to innovate them, in which they were educated—if those laws, by some divine fortune, have been established for long periods of time; so much so that no one remembers or has heard that they were ever <margin>E</margin> otherwise than they are at this time. Therefore, the legislator ought to devise by what way this might somehow be done in the city. Thus, I have devised this method: everyone thinks that the games of the youth, varied daily as we said above, are nothing other than trifles, and that they have no weight in the duties of life. Therefore, they yield and easily allow this change and innovation to happen. Nor do they understand that it is necessary that boys who delight in different games than their predecessors become different and distinct men from their elders; and having become different, they will seek a different life, and hence desire new studies and laws. <margin>F</margin> Hence, no one fears the plague which I said would be the greatest for the city. But other things, especially those changed regarding shapes, do less harm. Frequent innovation in praising and disparaging customs, however, is the gravest of all, as I think, and most to be feared. **CLINIAS.** Why not? **ATHENIAN.** Do we not believe the earlier speeches, in which we said that rhythms and other kinds of music are certain imitations of customs, both of good men and bad? Or what shall we say? **CLINIAS.** We shall feel no other way. **ATHENIAN.** Therefore, by every means, one must strive that the youth never dare to imitate new things in songs and dances, nor should anyone allure the boys to novelty by the charms of pleasures. **CLINIAS.** You speak excellently. <margin>G</margin> **ATHENIAN.** Does any of us have an art for these things better than that of the Egyptians? **CLINIAS.** What is that art you mention? **ATHENIAN.** That the kinds of dances and songs should all be consecrated to the gods: and first, indeed, that individual feast days be established at certain times of the year for individual gods, and the sons of gods, and dæmons. Then, it should be ordained what sacrifices are to be offered to which gods. And which songs and dances fit which sacrifices should be distinguished. Once these have been distinguished, all citizens with a common libation shall sacrifice both to the Fates and to other gods, and dedicate certain songs and dances to certain gods, and their sons, and dæmons. But if anyone uses hymns and dances in the rites of the gods other than what has been established, <margin>H</margin> the priests, both men and women, together with the guardians of the laws, shall piously and lawfully restrain him; and he who is rejected, if he does not willingly obey, shall for his whole life [face] penalties...

<summary>In this passage, Plato argues that stability in children's games and music is essential for the stability of a city's laws. He proposes an Egyptian-style system where all songs and dances are consecrated to specific gods and festivals, making any cultural innovation a punishable act of impiety.</summary>

# PLATO'S LAWS

...pay the penalty for impiety. <margin>A</margin> **CLINIAS.** Rightly so. **ATHENIAN.** But since we have reached this point in our discussion, let us ensure we are properly disposed toward it. **CLINIAS.** To what do you refer? **ATHENIAN.** Every man—not only the old, but even the young—whenever he sees or hears something strange and unusual, should not immediately rush to a conclusion and accept what is doubtful. Rather, he should act as if he had come to a crossroads <note>The "crossroads" (Latin: *trivium*; Greek: *τρίοδος*) is a classic metaphor for a moment of intellectual or moral choice.</note>, whether alone or with others, and finding himself ignorant of the path, he should search thoroughly and not proceed further until he is certain where the road leads. We must do the same at present. For since we have fallen into a strange and unusual <margin>B</margin> discourse regarding the laws, we must consider it with the utmost diligence. For it is not fitting for men of our stature to pass judgment on such a great matter so suddenly, asserting it as if it were immediately clear. **CLINIAS.** You speak the truth. **ATHENIAN.** Therefore, let us take time for this, and only make our affirmation when it has been sufficiently considered. But lest we abandon the order of the present laws in vain, let us hasten toward the proposed end. For perhaps, if God wills, this treatise, having reached its conclusion, will clearly reveal what is now doubted. **CLINIAS.** You speak excellently, Stranger. Let us do as you say. **ATHENIAN.** Let this strange and unusual decree, then, be affirmed: that our songs and chants shall be established by laws. Just as the ancients <margin>C</margin> spoke of "tunes" <note>original: *nomoi*. The Athenian is punning on the Greek word *nomos*, which means both "law" and a "musical mode" or "tune."</note> for the cithara; so that they too may not be far from our purpose, but may have either dreamed or prophesied this, whether in sleep or while awake. Let it be decreed thus: No one shall dare to sing anything except the public and sacred songs, nor shall anyone move in a dance outside the established choreography for the youth, just as it is not permitted to act against any other laws. He who obeys shall go unpunished. But him who does not obey, as was said a moment ago, <margin>D</margin> the guardians of the laws and the priests—both women and men—shall punish. Let these things be so established. **CLINIAS.** Exactly so. **ATHENIAN.** But how shall anyone establish these as laws without appearing ridiculous? Let us consider it in this way. The safest method, it seems to me, is to shape certain images in our speech. I say one such image is this: when sacrifices are made and the victims are burned according to the law, if someone—a son or a brother—standing privately near the altar and the sacred things, should pour out an entirely miserable and harmful speech, would we not say that he has been an ill omen to his father and his kin? **CLINIAS.** We certainly would. **ATHENIAN.** In almost all our cities, to put it briefly, this is what happens. For after a magistrate has performed a public sacrifice, not one, but many choruses are accustomed to gather. Standing near the altars, they <margin>E</margin> defile the sacred rites with pitiful voices. Indeed, they infect the souls of the listeners with words, rhythms, and mournful harmonies; and he who most vehemently moves the city to tears once the sacrifices are finished carries away the prizes of victory. Shall we not abolish this law? And if a mournful speech must ever be heard by the citizens, shall we not say it should happen on inauspicious <note>original: *nefastis*. In the Roman calendar, *dies nefasti* were days when public business or religious festivals were not permitted; here it refers to days of mourning rather than celebration.</note> days rather than on the feast days of divine solemnities? Then, if you please, let hired choruses and foreign singers go forth, just as we see at funerals, where certain people, like the Carian race <note>The Carians were often hired in antiquity as professional mourners.</note>, miserably bewail the deceased. This certainly seems to suit such chants, and since they are mournful and sad, a funeral garment <margin>F</margin>—to be brief—is fitting, not crowns or golden ornaments. Therefore, I ask this of you again: does it please you that this first "image" be applied to our songs? **CLINIAS.** Which one? **ATHENIAN.** I mean the "good omen" <note>original: *euphemia*. This refers to the ritual silence or the use of only auspicious words during a religious ceremony.</note>; that the very genre of our songs should always be engaged in speaking well and in happy omens. Or should I not ask, but rather establish it as a law? **CLINIAS.** Indeed, establish it entirely. For this law is worthy of all our votes. **ATHENIAN.** What, then, after the blessing, the praises, and the good omen, shall be the second law of music? Is it not that prayers should be poured out to the gods to whom we sacrifice? **CLINIAS.** Certainly. **ATHENIAN.** The third law, I believe, will be this: since poets know that prayers are the petitions of men to the gods, they must take great care lest they inadvertently ask for evil things as if they were good. Such a <margin>G</margin> condition for one who prays would be too ridiculous. **CLINIAS.** Without a doubt. **ATHENIAN.** Did we not agree above that there should be no gold or silver wealth in the city? **CLINIAS.** Entirely so. **ATHENIAN.** The race of poets is not always able to recognize which things are good and which are not. Therefore, if any poet, in words or song, should deliver to us incorrect prayers contrary to right reason, he will make the citizens ask for the opposite of what is best in the most important matters. In this error, as we have said, we shall find many of our ancestors. Let us therefore establish this as one form and law in music. **CLINIAS.** What is it? Speak more clearly. **ATHENIAN.** No poet shall dare to compose anything contrary to the city’s laws, nor anything that is not just, honorable, or good. Nor shall it be permitted to show what he has composed to any private person before the judges and guardians of the law appointed for this purpose have seen and approved it. Those who preside over music and education,

<column-break/>

shall be willing to provide... etc. **CLINIAS.** Correct. **ATHENIAN.** Now, following this discourse, let us be persuaded of our own arguments. **CLINIAS.** What do you mean by that? <margin>A</margin> **ATHENIAN.** Surely any young man—not to mention an old one—who sees or hears something out of place and unfamiliar, would not immediately concede to the point of doubt by rushing in headlong. Rather, he would act like a traveler at a crossroads who does not know the way well; whether traveling alone or with others, he would ask himself and the others about the difficulty. He would not set out until he had confirmed where his journey was leading and where it would take him. We must do the same now. Having stumbled into a strange discourse about laws, we must <margin>B</margin> carry out every investigation, and not easily, being of such an age, make assertions about such great matters in the moment, as if we could say something clear immediately. **CLINIAS.** You speak most truly. **ATHENIAN.** Therefore, let us give time to this, and we shall confirm it once we have examined it sufficiently. But so that we are not hindered in vain from finishing the sequence of the laws now before us, let us proceed to the end of the argument. For perhaps, if God wills, this entire exposition, once it has reached its end, will sufficiently clarify the matter now being questioned. **CLINIAS.** Well said, Stranger; we must do as you have described. **ATHENIAN.** Let it be resolved then (we say) that this "strange" <margin>C</margin> thing—that songs should be laws for us—is accepted. And just as the ancients in those days named the cithara-songs "tunes" [*nomoi*], so they perhaps were not entirely far from what we are saying now. A man might have dreamed this, whether in his sleep or while wide awake. Let the decree be this: concerning the public melodies and the sacred ones, and the entire choreography of the youth, no one shall be permitted to sing or move in dance contrary to any of the laws. He who obeys shall be free from penalty. But him who does not obey, as was just said, <margin>D</margin> let the guardians of the laws and the priests and priestesses punish him. Let these things be established in our discourse. **CLINIAS.** Let them be established. **ATHENIAN.** In what way could one legislate these things without becoming entirely a laughingstock? Let us look at it this way: come, as the safest course, let us first mold some "models" in our speech. I mean, for example: suppose a sacrifice is being made and the victims are burned according to law, and suppose someone—say a son or a brother—standing privately by the altars and the offerings, should utter every kind of blasphemy. Would we not say that he was uttering a lack of spirit and an evil omen and prophecy for his father and the rest of his family? **CLINIAS.** Of course. **ATHENIAN.** Well, this is exactly what happens in almost <margin>E</margin> all the cities in our regions. For when some authority performs a public sacrifice, not one, but a multitude of choruses arrive; and standing not far from the altars—sometimes right next to them—they pour out every kind of blasphemy over the offerings, straining the souls of the listeners with words, rhythms, and most tragic harmonies. And whoever can make the city weep the most at the sacrifice immediately carries away the victory prizes. Do we not vote against this "law"? If it is ever necessary for the citizens to hear such lamentations, it should be on days that are not pure but inauspicious; and it would be more fitting for hired singers from abroad to come—like those hired for the deceased, who escort the dead with a Carian muse. Something of this sort would be fitting for such songs. And indeed, for those singers, <margin>F</margin> the appropriate dress would not be crowns or gilded ornaments, to be brief. I ask you this again: let it be established as a model that such songs are first in our favor. **CLINIAS.** Which ones? **ATHENIAN.** Auspicious speech. And let the genre of our song be entirely auspicious in every way. Or shall I not ask, but simply establish it? **CLINIAS.** Establish it by all means; for this law wins by all the votes. **ATHENIAN.** What then would be the second law of music after auspicious speech? Is it not prayers to the gods to whom we sacrifice each time? **CLINIAS.** Of course. **ATHENIAN.** And the third law, I think, is that <margin>G</margin> the poets, knowing that prayers are petitions to the gods, must pay great attention lest they inadvertently ask for an evil as if it were a good. For it would be a ridiculous situation, I think, if such a prayer were made. **CLINIAS.** Indeed. **ATHENIAN.** Now, did we not a little while ago agree in our discourse that neither silver nor golden wealth should be settled in our city? **CLINIAS.** Certainly. **ATHENIAN.** From what source of the gods is this poor logic? Is it not this: that the chorus of poets is not quite capable of knowing well what is good and what is not? So if a poet, in his words or melodies, creates something not right—prayers that are not right—he will make our citizens pray for the opposite of their greatest needs. And yet (as we were saying) there are not many greater errors for men than this. Let us then establish one type for the laws of the Muses. **CLINIAS.** Which one? Tell us more clearly. **ATHENIAN.** That the poet shall create nothing contrary to the customs and the just, the beautiful, or the good things of the city. Nor shall it be permitted for him to show his compositions to any private person before they have been shown to those appointed for this...

<summary>The Athenian Guest argues that music and poetry must be regulated by "nomoi" (both laws and musical modes) to ensure they are auspicious and morally sound. He proposes a ban on mournful songs during sacrifices and insists that all poetic works be approved by state judges before public performance.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the Athenian Stranger’s proposal to regulate music and dance by law. The previous page established that the state must fix the forms of songs and chants to prevent the destabilizing influence of constant cultural change.</meta>

# ON THE LAWS, BOOK VII.

...is fairly demonstrated. Therefore, as I have often asked, shall this be sanctioned by us as our third law and model? Or do you think otherwise? <margin>A</margin> **CLEINIAS.** Let it be sanctioned, by all means. **ATHENIAN.** Following this, it would be most correct to sing hymns to the gods and praises joined with prayers. After these, it is equally fitting to offer praises and appropriate prayers to the spirits <note>Original: "daimones." In Greek thought, these are intermediary beings between gods and humans, often acting as guardians.</note> and heroes. **CLEINIAS.** Why not? **ATHENIAN.** Immediately following this, there should be a law regarding the giving of honor without envy. It is fitting to adorn with praises those citizens who have reached the end of their lives, having accomplished noble and laborious deeds in both body and soul, and having been obedient to the laws. **CLEINIAS.** Of course. **ATHENIAN.** However, to honor those who are still living with praises and hymns <margin>B</margin> is not safe, until someone has run the full course of life and brought it to a noble end. Let all these honors be common to both men and women who have clearly become excellent. As for the songs and dances, they should be established in this way: there are many ancient and fine musical compositions of the ancients, and likewise types of dances for the body, from which there is no harm in selecting what is fitting and suitable for the established state. Let those chosen as selectors of these works be no less than fifty years of age. They should choose what they deem sufficient among the ancient poems; but whatever is found unsuitable or <margin>C</margin> deficient, they should either reject entirely or, by enlisting poets and musicians, they should correct and perfect them. They should use the poetic skills of these artists, but not follow their personal pleasures or desires, except perhaps in a few instances. By explaining the intentions of the legislator, they should prudently arrange the dance, the song, and the entire choral performance <term>choreia: a combined performance of dance and song common in Greek religious life</term> according to their judgment. Every Muse <note>Here referring to the arts of music and poetry.</note> that is orderly is far better than the "sweet Muse," even if the latter lacks order. Indeed, pleasure and delight are common to all types of music. For whatever style a person has been accustomed to from childhood until the age of maturity and wisdom, they consider that style pleasant. If one has been raised in a temperate and orderly music, when they hear the opposite, they hate it and call it <margin>D</margin> "unrefined." But if one is accustomed to hearing the common and "sweet" style, they judge the opposite to be cold and unpleasant. Therefore, as was just said, in terms of pleasure or displeasure, neither style has an advantage; the difference lies in the effect: one makes those raised in it better, the other makes them worse. **CLEINIAS.** Excellently spoken. **ATHENIAN.** Furthermore, we must define the songs that are fitting for men and those for women by a certain model, and accommodate them to the proper harmonies and rhythms. For it would be a terrible thing if the entire harmony were out of tune, or the rhythm lacked proportion, by failing to provide what is suitable for each of these songs. It is necessary, then, to legislate the forms of these things. Both types of songs must be assigned to both sexes according to what is appropriate. What is for the female must be distinguished by the natural difference <margin>E</margin> of each sex. Therefore, that which is magnificent and tends toward courage should be called masculine; while that which leans more toward orderliness and modesty, as being more feminine, should be presented as such in both law and discourse. This, then, is the order. Next, let us discuss the teaching and transmission of these things, in what manner and by whom they should be performed. Just as a shipwright, when beginning the construction of a ship, lays down the keel <note>Original Greek: "tropida," the foundational timber of a ship. The OCR "espida" is a transcription error.</note> to outline its shape, so I seem to be doing the same. For in trying to distinguish the forms of life for you, I am laying down the "keels" of souls, <margin>F</margin> considering by what means and in what ways we might best navigate the ship of this life. **CLEINIAS.** Certainly. **ATHENIAN.** Human affairs, then, are not worthy of great seriousness; and yet, it is necessary to be serious about them—which is a kind of misfortune. But since we are here, if we can handle this in a fitting way, perhaps it will be to our benefit. What do I mean by this? Someone might rightly ask me. **CLEINIAS.** Quite right. **ATHENIAN.** I say that one must be serious about what is worthy of seriousness, but not about what is not. By nature, God is worthy of every blessed seriousness, but man (as we said before) has been fashioned as a certain plaything of God <margin>G</margin> <note>This is one of Plato's most famous and debated metaphors, suggesting that humans are most "themselves" when acting as instruments of divine play.</note>, and this is truly the best part of him. Every man and woman should live accordingly, playing at the most beautiful games, thinking the opposite of what people think now. **CLEINIAS.** How so? **ATHENIAN.** Now, they believe that serious work must be done for the sake of play. They think that matters of war are serious and must be well-managed for the sake of peace. But in war, there is neither true play nor any education worthy of mention, neither now nor in the future. Yet we say that the most serious thing for us is to live out the life of peace as long and as well as possible. What then is the right way to live "playing"? <margin>H</margin> One should live sacrificing, singing, and dancing, so that he may be able to make the gods propitious to himself, and to repel his enemies and conquer them in battle. What kind of songs and dances one should perform has been outlined in these models, and the paths we must travel have been paved. In this matter, we should believe the poet spoke well when he said:

> Telemachus, some things you will think of yourself in your own mind,
> And others a divinity will prompt you with; for I do not think
> You were born and bred without the favor of the gods. <note>A quote from Homer’s Odyssey, Book 3, lines 26–28.</note>

<column-break/>

...is roughly shown. Therefore, shall this law be sanctioned for us as our third image and form, which I have often asked about? Or otherwise? **CLEINIAS.** Let it be sanctioned entirely. **ATHENIAN.** After this, it will be most correct that hymns and praises of the gods be sung, mixed with prayers; then likewise for spirits and heroes, with suitable praises and prayers. **CLEINIAS.** Nothing prevents it. **ATHENIAN.** Following this, a law regarding envy follows immediately at this end. It is fitting to adorn those citizens with praises who <margin>Which of the dead are to be praised.</margin> have departed from life, if they performed difficult and famous deeds by the strength of body or soul, and willingly obeyed the laws. **CLEINIAS.** Why not? <margin>The living are not to be praised.</margin> **ATHENIAN.** However, it is not safe to honor those still living <margin>B</margin> with praises and hymns before anyone has made a famous end to their life by dying. Let these things be common to men and women distinguished by virtue. Let songs and dances be established thus. Many things regarding music are ancient among the old poems and types of dancing, and there is no envy in selecting those that are decent and suitable for the established state. Let the selectors of these be no less than fifty years old; let them choose what seems to be sufficiently expressed in ancient poems, and let them reject entirely what is poorly said. And let them correct and finish those that are less sufficient by employing poets and musicians; and let them use the poetic virtue of these men, not their pleasures or desires, except <margin>C</margin> in a few cases, so that they may prudently direct the dance, the song, and the whole choral performance according to the explained will of the legislator. Surely every ordered Muse, even if a sweet Muse is not added, is far better than when she is without order. But sweetness and pleasantness are common to all Muses. For in whatever style one has been engaged from early years until a mature age, he thinks that style is pleasant. Indeed, if he was educated in a tempered and ordered Muse, when he hears the contrary, he hates it and calls it unrefined. But if he has been accustomed to always hearing the common and uncultivated style, he considers its opposite to be cold and harsh. Therefore, as I just <margin>D</margin> said, the account of pleasure and annoyance in both is equal according to our habit, but the account of benefit and harm is unequal. Truly, one makes the users better, the other worse. **CLEINIAS.** Excellent. **ATHENIAN.** Furthermore, we ought to distinguish by a certain form the songs which befit men and those which befit women, and accommodate them to harmonies and rhythms. For it is absurd to be discordant with the whole harmony or rhythm, and not to render suitable things to each of these. Therefore, the forms of these things must necessarily be established by laws and appropriately attributed to both. And what befits a man or a woman must be declared from the very <margin>E</margin> difference of the nature of each. Furthermore, that which is magnificent and tends toward fortitude is to be called manly. But that which is charming and more modest must be affirmed in discussion and sanctioned by laws as being more suitable for women. And let this be the order. Next, let us declare how these things are to be handed over and opened to those they must be taught to, and when they are to be done. Just as a ship-builder first lays down the little keels for the form of the ship, so I seem to be doing for myself. For while I try to distinguish the figures of life, I lay down certain quasi-keels according to the natural formulas of souls, so that the way and reason by which <margin>F</margin> we are to lead the ship of this life through these seas may be rightly perceived. Human affairs indeed are not worthy of great study. Yet it is necessary to study them, which I would call unfortunate. But since we are here, if only we do it with a fitting purpose, perhaps it will be enough for us. But what I should say, someone will perhaps rightly ask. **CLEINIAS.** Quite right. **ATHENIAN.** I say, therefore, it is necessary to follow studiously what is worthy of study, but by no means what is not worthy. And by nature God indeed is worthy of all blessed study, but man, as we also said above, was fashioned to be a plaything of God, and that truly is his <margin>Man is a plaything of the gods.</margin> best part. Therefore, being כך affected, it is necessary for both males and females consequently to spend their time in the most beautiful plays, thinking contrary to what they do now. **CLEINIAS.** In what way? **ATHENIAN.** Now <margin>G</margin> certainly they think that the studies of plays are to be followed for the sake of work. For they think the business of war is worthy of study for the sake of peace, when in war neither play is accustomed to be present, nor has there ever been a discipline worthy of speech, nor is there now, nor will there be. But we think that discipline most worthy of study by which men, having been instructed, may lead their life as long and as well as possible in peace. But what the right reason for playing in life is, and what kind of plays in sacrifices, singing, and dancing are to be employed, so that both the gods may be rendered propitious to us, and enemies may be routed in battle, and what things especially we may be able to follow by imitating them in song and dance, <margin>H</margin> has been pre-marked by certain quasi-formulas, and the ways through which we must go are paved. In which matter truly it is to be believed that the poet sang well when he says: <margin>Odyssey, Book 3.</margin> Telemachus, some things you will turn over in your own mind, others a spirit will suggest to you. For I do not think you were born and nourished without the power of the gods.

-># OF PLATO’S LAWS, BOOK VII.<-

<margin>A</margin> Our students themselves ought to consider these matters, and they should believe that while much has been said sufficiently, if anything is missing, a spirit <note>Original: "dæmonem." In Greek thought, a 'daemon' is a guiding spirit or intermediary between gods and mortals.</note> and the god will provide suggestions. They will learn through which sacrifices and dances, and at what times, they must appease the various deities through play, living according to the measure of their nature—since they are themselves a kind of wondrous thing, though for the most part they participate very little in the truth. <term>ATHENIAN:</term> <note>The Athenian Stranger is the primary speaker and lawmaker in this dialogue.</note> My guest, you seem to hold the human race in very low regard. <term>ATHENIAN:</term> Do not wonder at this, but forgive me, Megillus. For it was when I looked toward the god and was moved by him that I said these things. Let our race, then, if it pleases you, not be worthless, but worthy of some serious study. After this, public buildings for gymnastics and schools were established in three parts <margin>B</margin> in the middle of the city. Outside, in the suburbs, there are likewise equestrian training grounds in three parts—ample spaces arranged where the youth may be instructed and practiced in the use of the bow and the throwing of spears. If these things were not sufficiently discussed previously, let them now be stated in discourse and sanctioned by law: foreign teachers of all these subjects are to be hired for a fee. Living there, they shall instruct those who come in both military affairs and music. And it is not only those whose parents wish it who ought to learn, while those whose parents do not see fit are allowed to let their education go; rather, as the saying goes, all men <note>In this context, 'men' refers to all young citizens, both boys and girls.</note> must learn by necessity as far as is possible, inasmuch as they are children of the state more than children of their parents. <margin>C</margin> My law will decree the same for females as for males, for we want the same exercises to be practiced by both. Nor shall I fear to say that equestrian discipline and gymnastics are honorable for women just as they are for men. For I have heard this from ancient stories and I believe it. In our own times, I am not ignorant <margin>Near the Black Sea [Pontus], women serve in the military, who are called Sauromatae [Sarmatians].</margin> that there are thousands upon thousands of women around the Black Sea called Sauromatae, who are required to have equal care and exercise with men, not only in riding horses, but also in the use of the bow and other weapons. But I have this reason for these views: I say indeed that if these things can be done this way, it is the height of foolishness in our own regions that <margin>D</margin> women and men do not apply themselves to the same pursuits with all their effort and zeal. For almost every city, in this way, becomes half instead of double, despite the same labors and taxes. This is surely an error of the legislator. <term>CLINIAS:</term> So it appears. But many things have been said by you, guest, that are contrary to the usual customs of republics. <term>ATHENIAN:</term> It is proper first to run through the entire discussion, and then to choose what seems best. <term>CLINIAS:</term> You have spoken very sensibly just now, and you have made me reproach myself for what I said. Continue your inquiry as you please. <term>ATHENIAN:</term> This very thing pleases me, Clinias, which I was just saying. For if it were not sufficiently clear through the facts themselves that these things could be done, perhaps there could be some contradiction. <margin>E</margin> But now, if anyone scorns this law, he must certainly seek another way. Our precept, however, will not cease to assert that women ought to participate as much as possible with men in education and other matters. For we must consider them in this way: Tell me, if women do not share in the whole of life with men, will it not be necessary to assign some other order to them? <term>CLINIAS:</term> It will be necessary. <term>ATHENIAN:</term> What other order shall we assign rather than the one we are now sharing? Shall we, like the Thracians and many other nations, assign to women the tasks of farming, herding cattle and sheep, and other works <margin>F</margin> that differ not at all from the service of slaves? Or, like us and all our neighbors, shall we gather all possessions into one house, as the saying goes, and commit the care of the pantry <note>Original: "penu." The storehouse or provisions of the household.</note>, the loom, the working of wool, and similar things to the women? Or, O Megillus, shall we choose the Lacedaemonian <note>Spartan.</note> way as a middle path? Where the girls spend their time in gymnastics and music, while the women, in their leisure, tend to the wool-working, yet lead a life that is not lowly or meager, but somewhat more skillful. They also take on a middle degree of care for domestic duties, guarding the pantry and educating the children. But they do not participate in wars: so that if it were necessary to protect the fatherland and their children, they could neither shoot arrows like the Amazons, <margin>G</margin> nor skillfully join in the throwing of spears with the rest of the citizens. Nor could they take up shield and spear to imitate the goddess <note>A reference to Athena, the warrior goddess of wisdom.</note> and nobly resist for the sake of their besieged country, so that if nothing else, they might at least strike terror into the enemy by being seen in the battle line. If they live in this way, they will never dare to imitate the Sauromatae; rather, compared to those women, our own women will seem like men. Let whoever wishes approve of your lawmakers in these matters. I, for my part, will never say otherwise. For I require a complete duty from the lawmaker, not a halfway measure; he must not allow women to drift into luxury, nor attend to males alone, lest instead of a double happiness for the city, he achieves only a single one. <term>MEGILLUS:</term> What shall we do here, O Clinias? Shall we allow the guest to invade Sparta in this way? <term>CLINIAS:</term> Certainly. For since freedom of speech has been granted to him, he must not be interrupted <margin>H</margin> until the discussion of the laws has been sufficiently completed. <term>MEGILLUS:</term> You speak rightly.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Our foster-children, having reflected on these same things, must consider those things which have not been spoken as being contained in what was said: namely, those things which the spirit and the god will suggest to them concerning sacrifice and choral dance. Through all these things, and at whatever time for each of the gods, they shall live their lives playing and propitiating the deities according to the way of nature, being for the most part wonders, but participating only in some small bits of truth. <term>MEGILLUS:</term> You are completely belittling the human race for us, O guest. <term>ATHENIAN:</term> Do not wonder at it, Megillus, but forgive me. For it was looking toward the god, and being affected by it, that I said what I have just spoken. But let our race be, if you like, not worthless, but worthy of some serious attention. Next after this, there are the buildings for gymnastics and public schools to be built in three locations in the middle of the city; and outside, <margin>B</margin> three places for horses and for the training of archers and others who skirmish with projectiles, arranged for the sake of both learning and practice for the youth. If these were not then sufficiently discussed, let them now be expressed in word and law. In all these places, there should be teachers hired for wages, living there as guests, to teach the children both the things pertaining to war and those studies which involve music. And education should not be for the child whose father wishes it, while the one whose father does not is left alone; but as the saying goes, every man and child, as far as possible, must be educated by necessity, as they belong more to the city than to their parents. <margin>C</margin> My law would say the same things about females as about males, that it is necessary for females to practice the same things equally. And I would not be afraid to speak then or now this word: that neither riding nor gymnastics is fitting for men while being unfitting for women. For having heard ancient myths, I am persuaded; and as for the present, so to speak, I know that there are countless thousands of women around the Black Sea, whom they call Sauromatae, for whom there is a common sharing with the men not only of horses, but also of bows and other weapons, and they practice them equally. I will offer a reason for these things again, as follows: I say that if these things <margin>D</margin> happen to be possible, it is most foolish that in our current places we do not all with one mind and all our strength practice the same things, men and women together. For nearly every city becomes half instead of double in its swiftness and being, from the same resources and labors. Yet this would be a wondrous error for a lawmaker to make. <term>CLINIAS:</term> It seems so. However, many of the things now being said by us, guest, are contrary to the usual ways of government. <term>ATHENIAN:</term> But <gloss>Megillus</gloss> (I said), let the discourse run its course. For while someone is speaking, one must choose what seems best. <term>CLINIAS:</term> You have spoken very appropriately, and you have made me reproach myself <margin>E</margin> for what I said. Speak then what follows, whatever is pleasing to you. <term>ATHENIAN:</term> What is pleasing to me, Clinias, is what I said before: that if these things were not sufficiently proven by deeds to be possible, one might perhaps speak against the argument; but now, he who does not accept the law in these matters must look elsewhere. Do not let our exhortation in these matters be extinguished, namely the claim that the female sex must share with us as much as possible in education and other things. For it is in this way that we must always think of these things. Come, if women do not participate in all of life in common with men, is it not necessary that there be some other arrangement for them? <term>CLINIAS:</term> It is necessary. <term>ATHENIAN:</term> What then <margin>F</margin> <gloss>Clinias</gloss> of the things previously shown would we place higher than this community which we now enjoin upon them? Is it that which the Thracians use for their women, and many other nations, to farm and herd cattle and sheep, and to serve in no way differently from slaves? Or as we do, and all those who inhabit this region. For now among us it is thus for all: having gathered all our goods into one house (as the saying goes), we hand them over to the women to manage the storehouse and to oversee the looms and all wool-working? Or shall we say that the Laconian way is the middle of these, Megillus? That girls should participate in gymnastics <margin>G</margin> and music? And that the women, while idle from wool-working, should weave together a life that is a kind of practice, in no way lowly or cheap? And that they should reach a middle point in the service and management of the household and the rearing of children? But by not participating in war—so that even if it should ever be necessary to fight for the city and children—they would not be able to handle bows, like some Amazons, nor any other projectile or art, nor taking up shield and spear, to imitate the goddess, so that when their fatherland is being ravaged, they might nobly resist and strike fear, if nothing more, into the enemy when seen in their ranks? They would not dare to imitate the Sauromatae in all their ways; compared to those who live in that manner, <margin>H</margin> these women would appear to be men. Does your lawmaker then decree these things for you? Let him who wishes praise it; but my own view would not be spoken otherwise. For the lawmaker must be complete and not half, not letting the female sex live in luxury and spend wastefully, using an unordered way of life, while taking full care of the male, leaving the city with nearly half a happy life instead of a double one. <term>MEGILLUS:</term> What shall we do, Clinias? Shall we allow the guest to overrun Sparta in this way? <term>CLINIAS:</term> Yes. For since freedom of speech has been given to him, we must allow it until we have gone through the laws sufficiently in every way. <term>MEGILLUS:</term> You speak rightly.

<summary>The Athenian Stranger argues for the compulsory and equal education of women in both liberal arts and military skills, citing the Sauromatae as a real-world example of women's combat potential. He contends that a state failing to utilize the strengths of women is inefficient, operating at only half its possible capacity and happiness.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the Athenian Stranger's outline of the ideal social structure. Previously, he discussed the physical education and military training of the youth; here, he moves into the daily schedule of the citizenry, focusing on the discipline of communal living and the necessity of wakefulness and early rising for both adults and children.</meta>

->## ON THE LAWS, BOOK VII.<-

<margin>A</margin> **ATHENIAN:** It falls to me, then, to explain the things that follow. **CLINIAS:** Of course. **ATHENIAN:** What manner of life would men lead who have their basic necessities prepared for them in a moderate fashion? Where the crafts are left to others, and agriculture is handed over to slaves—who in turn yield a sufficient tribute from the land to those living in an orderly way? In such a life, there would be communal meals <note>Original: "syssitia." These were public mess halls, a hallmark of Spartan and Cretan society, intended to foster civic bonds.</note> established: those for the men separate, and nearby those for their families, including the daughters and their mothers. There should be male and female officials appointed to oversee these daily gatherings, observing the conduct of those at the mess and eventually dismissing them.
<margin>B</margin> After this, the leader and the others should offer libations to the gods to whom the day or night was dedicated, and then depart for home. For men so ordered, is there no necessary or fitting work left to do? Should each of them live like a fattened beast of the field? We say that is neither just nor honorable. It is not possible for one living in such a way to avoid the fate that befalls such a creature. It is fitting for a lazy, fat, and sluggish animal to be torn apart by another animal that is hardened by labor and courage. If we look into this sufficiently, as we are doing now, perhaps such a state would never come to pass so long as women, children, and houses remain private property. <note>Plato refers here to his more radical proposal in the "Republic" regarding the abolition of private families, contrasting it with the "second-best" state described here in the "Laws."</note> 
<margin>C</margin> But if these things were to happen in the "second-best" way we are currently describing, they would still proceed quite moderately. We say that for those living this way, a task remains that is neither small nor trivial; indeed, it is the greatest of all tasks, commanded by a just law. Just as a life devoted to winning the Pythian or Olympic games <note>The most prestigious athletic and musical festivals in Ancient Greece.</note> excludes all other idle pursuits, so too is the life dedicated to the virtue of the body and soul twice as demanding—or even much more so—requiring constant care to be properly harmonized.
<margin>D</margin> No other business should be allowed to hinder the labor and nourishment due to the body, nor the studies and habits due to the soul. Indeed, the whole day and night are scarcely enough for one who is practicing this to achieve it perfectly. Therefore, there must be a schedule for all free citizens, continuing from early dawn until the next sunrise. A lawmaker might seem ridiculous if he spoke of many small details of household management, including matters of nighttime wakefulness, which are necessary for those who intend to guard a whole city accurately.
<margin>E</margin> To spend the entire night sleeping is shameful and unbefitting of a free man, and this should be clear to all the servants when they see their master always being the first to wake and rise. Whether one calls this a law or a custom, it is right. It is shameful to say that a mistress in a house should be woken by her maidservants; rather, she should be the one to wake the others—the servants, the maids, the children—and if possible, the entire household. Waking up at night allows for the performance of many duties, both in political affairs and in household management: the officials attending to city business, and the masters and mistresses attending to their own homes. For much sleep is not naturally beneficial to our bodies, our souls, or the performance of our duties.
<margin>F</margin> While sleeping, a person is worth nothing more than if they were not alive. But whoever among us values living and thinking most stays awake for as long as possible, only keeping enough sleep for the sake of health—and not much is needed for that once a good habit is formed. Officials who stay awake at night in the cities are a terror to the wicked and to enemies, but are loved and honored by the just and temperate, being useful to themselves and the whole city. Such a night, spent as described, adds a certain courage to the souls of everyone in the city. When day returns and the sun rises, the children must go to their teachers.
<margin>G</margin> Just as no sheep or other creature should live without a shepherd, so too children cannot be without guardians <note>Original: "paedagogos." These were not the teachers, but personal attendants—often trusted slaves—who supervised a child's behavior and safety.</note>, nor slaves without masters. Of all wild animals, the child is the most unmanageable. Because he possesses a "fount of reason" that is not yet disciplined, he becomes the most treacherous, sharp-witted, and insolent of all beasts. Therefore, he must be bound, as it were, with many reins. First, when he is separated from his mother and nurses, he is given to guardians to manage his childishness; then he is given to teachers for his lessons, as befits a free person. Yet anyone who meets him—acting like a master—should punish the child, the guardian, or the teacher if they see them doing wrong. If someone sees a wrong and does not punish it, let them be held in great reproach. The Guardian of the Laws who is elected to oversee the children shall watch over such people, ensuring they punish when necessary or correcting them if they punish wrongly. This overseer must look sharply and care for the upbringing of the children, directing their natures toward the laws. But how can the law itself sufficiently educate this overseer? As of yet, it has said nothing clear or necessary...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> **ATHENIAN:** It is therefore my part to explain the things that follow. **CLINIAS:** Without a doubt. **ATHENIAN:** What, then, will be the manner of life for those who have the necessities of life prepared in a moderate way? The arts being left to others, and agriculture entrusted to servants, who return the fruits from the fields in a measure sufficient for men living modestly. For these people, public banquets are instituted: for the men separately, and nearby for their relatives, daughters, and mothers together. Certain men and women shall be placed in charge of these feasts to observe and take note of everything daily. Then they shall dismiss the gatherings, and after both the leaders
<margin>B</margin> and the others have made libations to the gods to whom that day or night is dedicated, they shall depart for home. For men thus established, will there be no necessary work remaining that is suitable for them? Shall they live devoted to their bellies, after the manner of cattle? We consider that neither just nor honest. Nor is it possible for a man living thus not to eventually fall into a state that is unbefitting. For it is the lot of a sluggish and fat animal, made heavy through idleness, to be snatched and torn apart by another animal that is exercised by labors and, as it were, thinned and made strong. These things, if we investigate them sufficiently and exactly as we are now doing, might perhaps never happen so long as women, children, houses, and the rest were the private property of each. If, however, the things which are "second-best" to those are done as we are now treating them, they would certainly be done moderately. We say, then, that a work remains for those living thus that is neither small nor base, but the greatest of all, mandated by a just law. For while each single way of life is distracted from all other works—as if someone were striving to win at the Pythian or Olympic games and could not find time for other things—the life of the one who rightly devotes himself to the virtue of the mind and body is full of a double, or rather a manifold, care. For no bodily exercise, and no doctrines of the mind or morals, should be neglected on account of other business. Indeed, nearly the whole day and the whole night is scarcely enough for those who care diligently for these things to thoroughly attain them. <margin>D</margin> Since these things are so, a perpetual order for the whole time must be held by free men from the rising of the sun to the next sunrise. <margin>A few words on household administration.</margin> A legislator will perhaps be held as ridiculous if he relates many frequent and minute details regarding household management, both in other things and in the nightly vigil, which it is necessary to maintain for the preservation of the city. For whether it should be called a law or a duty which we now prescribe, it certainly ought to appear shameful and unfree to everyone if any citizen sleeps through the whole night, and is not the first to be awakened and rise, so that this is manifest to the whole family. Furthermore, that a mistress should be woken by her maidservants, and not the <margin>On much sleep and vigils.</margin> <margin>E</margin> maidservants first by her, must be called shameful among the servants, the maids, the boys, and finally the entire house if possible. They should rise at night: and the magistrates should care for some public matter, while the fathers and mothers of the family should care for their own affairs in their private homes. For much sleep is naturally conducive neither to bodies, nor minds, nor the performance of deeds. No one indeed is of any value while he sleeps, no more than if he were not alive. Therefore, whoever desires most to live and be wise should stay awake for as long a time as possible, preserving only the requirement of health. For this, not much sleep is needed, if you have become well-accustomed to it. <margin>F</margin> Certainly, magistrates who are vigilant at night in the cities are a terror to evil men, both enemies and citizens, but are to be loved and honored by the just and temperate, being useful to themselves and the whole city. But a night thus spent also creates courage in the minds of the citizens in addition to the things we have said. At the rising of the sun, the boys should go to their masters. Since neither flocks nor any other things at all ought to live without a shepherd, so neither should boys be without guardians, nor servants without masters. But a boy is more unmanageable than any beast. <margin>The boy is more unmanageable than any beast.</margin> For since he does not yet have a perfect fountain of prudence, <margin>G</margin> he is the most insidious, sharp, and insolent of all animals; therefore he must be bound with many "reins," as it were. And as soon as he is separated from mothers and nurses, it is necessary to entrust him to guardians to rule over his boyish wantonness; then, as a free person, to teachers, especially for the sake of learning; but as a servant, let anyone among the free who happens upon him punish the boy himself, the guardian, and the teacher, if he sees them failing in any matter. If someone present does not punish him by right, let him be subject to the greatest reproach. Let that man who has been elected from the guardians of the laws to the leadership of the boys take notice of this: whether he who found them did not punish when he ought, or whether he punished in an improper manner. This man must see sharply and care most diligently for the education of the boys, always directing and turning their natures according to the laws and the good itself. But how shall the law itself sufficiently instruct this man? For it has not yet been said sufficiently, nor clearly:

<summary>This page outlines the daily routines and discipline required in an ideal city, emphasizing communal meals, the dangers of idleness, and the necessity of waking early for both civic duties and education. It famously characterizes the undisciplined child as the most difficult of all "beasts" to manage, requiring constant supervision and moral guidance.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the Athenian Stranger's detailed plan for the education of the youth in the ideal city.
