-># PLATO'S WORKS<-

...but some things were touched upon, others omitted. However, we must leave nothing undone to the best of our ability, but set forth the whole reason, so that the interpreter here may be both a guide and an educator to others. Regarding the form of the dance, song, and choral performance, it has been stated: what should be chosen, corrected, and dedicated to the gods. But regarding prose writings <note>Latin: "oratione soluta"; Greek: "ἐν γράμμασι μὴν ὄντα, ἀνὰ δὲ μέτρον" — literally "in letters but without meter."</note>, we have not yet spoken: which of these, and in what order, O excellent guardian of youth, must be handed to the pupils—although you already have what they must learn and exercise for military matters. For it was said by the legislator that they must first learn letters, then the lyre. Furthermore, they must learn what pertains to the calculation of numbers, which we said was necessary, and in general whatever contributes to war, domestic management, and public affairs. Likewise, they must investigate the circuit of the divine stars, the sun, and the moon, so that the whole city may not be ignorant of the order of days into a month, and months into a year, and thus the seasons, festivals, and sacrifices—disposed as is fitting by a certain natural guidance—may make the city living and watchful, and grant honor to the gods, and make men more prudent in these matters. These things have been sufficiently distinguished for you by the legislator, O friend, but pay attention to what follows. 

For we say that letters have not yet been sufficiently distinguished: since it has not been declared to what extent they should be studied—whether, for instance, a citizen who is to be of moderate status must master them exactly, or not at all. Similarly for the lyre. Therefore, let the ten-year-old boys proceed to letters and persist for three years. And those who have reached thirteen years shall similarly apply themselves to the lyre for three years <margin>Things to be learned.</margin>. It shall not be permitted for a father to keep his children in these studies for more or less time, nor for the children—whether out of boredom or desire—to spend more or less time on these things in contempt of the law. If anyone does not obey, he shall not receive the honors due to those endowed with discipline, which we shall describe later. 

But hear what the teachers should teach and the youths should learn in these years. Let them learn letters until they are able to read and write. Whether they do it quickly or beautifully does not matter, unless nature has helped in this span of time. But as for the works <note>Latin: "monimēta"; Greek: "μαθήματα" — meaning the compositions or records of the poets.</note> of the poets where they do not use the lyre, some written in meter and some without meter—which, lacking rhythm and harmony, are treacherous writings <note>The Athenian suggests that prose works lacking the structure of music can be "fallacious" or harder to judge for moral quality.</note> handed down to us by some such men—how will you use them, O best guardians of the laws? I think even the lawmaker would doubt what correct use of them to hand down to you. 

CLIN. Why did you doubt so with yourself, Stranger? 

ATHEN. You are right, Clinias, but to you who are considering the laws with me, it is necessary to reveal both what seems certain to me and what seems doubtful. 

CLIN. What then do you say of these things now? What moved you? 

ATHEN. I will say it. Truly, it is not easy to contradict innumerable men. 

CLIN. Do you think that the few small things already said about the laws are contrary to many? 

ATHEN. You say that quite truly. For you seem to command that although this path may be arduous and hateful to many, I should nevertheless complete it confidently; and through the path of the laws, opened by our present speeches, I should proceed with nothing omitted, since such a path perhaps pleases no fewer people—or if fewer, no worse people. 

CLIN. Certainly. 

ATHEN. I shall omit nothing then. I say indeed that many poets have written in hexameter verse, many in trimeter and other kinds of meters; some have embraced serious things, others humorous things. Many professors of this kind of skill assert that all these things must be learned by heart by youths who are to be rightly educated, so that they may be rendered eloquent <note>Latin: "facundi"; Greek: "πολυηκόους" — literally "of much hearing" or widely-read.</note> by the experience of various poets. Others contend that certain chapters should be selected from all and brought together for memorization, if indeed one of us is to become a good and wise man from the experience and knowledge of many. But do you now bid me to explain freely what is said rightly by these men and what is said to the contrary? 

CLIN. Why not? 

ATHEN. What, then, shall I say sufficiently in one word about all these things? I think this, which will be granted to me by everyone: Many things have been said well by the poets, and many things also to the contrary. If this is so, I assert that the pursuit of learning many things <note>The Greek term is "polymathia," which Plato often views with suspicion if it lacks moral focus.</note> is dangerous for youths. 

CLIN. How then, and what do you prescribe to the guardian of laws? 

ATHEN. About what matter do you speak? 

CLIN. Toward what should he look, as if to some exemplar <term>exemplar: a model or pattern (Greek: paradeigma) to be imitated</term>, so that he may command some things to be learned by heart by youths and others not even to be touched? I pray you, do not be burdened to say it. 

ATHEN. O good Clinias, I seem in a way to be fortunate. 

CLIN. In what matter especially? 

ATHEN. That I am not entirely lacking an example. For when I notice the things we have recounted from dawn to this hour—not, as it seems to me, without some inspiration of the gods—they seem to me in a way similar to poetry. And it is no wonder if, looking back at our own speeches as if collected all together, I am so affected that I am greatly pleased. For altogether...

<meta>This page continues the Athenian Stranger's discourse on the curriculum for the ideal city’s youth. # ON THE LAWS, BOOK VII.

<margin>A</margin> ...I have learned and heard these things said in both poetry and prose <note>original Latin: "poëticè ac soluta oratione"; Greek: "καταλογάδην" (in prose). The Athenian argues that the laws themselves are a form of high literature.</note>; they seem to me the most moderate and most suitable for young people to hear. Therefore, I have no better model to propose to the guardian of the laws and the educator than to compel teachers to explain these very things to the children, along with anything else similar to them. Whether they be written in verse or in prose—or simply spoken in a way that agrees with this discussion—these things must by no means be overlooked. Instead, he should see that they are written down, and first compel the teachers themselves to learn and approve of them. Those teachers who do not approve should be dismissed; but to those who do approve, he should entrust the youth to be instructed and educated. But regarding letters and their teachers, enough has been said.

<margin>B</margin> CLINIAS. At least according to our premise, Stranger, we do not seem to have wandered from our proposed topic. But whether we are getting the whole matter right or not is perhaps difficult to say.
ATHENIAN. That, Clinias, will become clearer (as is likely) when, as we have often said, we reach the end of this entire investigation of the laws.
CLINIAS. Correct.
ATHENIAN. After the teacher of letters, should we not speak of the lyre-player <term>citharista: a teacher of the kithara or lyre</term>?
CLINIAS. Why not?
ATHENIAN. If we remember our earlier words, I believe we should assign to the lyre-players their proper duty in teaching and education, so far as it pertains to such matters.
CLINIAS. What duties are you speaking of?
ATHENIAN. We said, I believe, that the <note>original: "Dionysiacos cantores"</note> sixty-year-old singers of Dionysus must be exceptionally sensitive to rhythms and the structures of harmonies. This is so that they can distinguish the imitations of a good soul from the imitations of a bad soul in the movements of songs that represent the passions. They should reject the bad ones and bring the good ones into the open to be sung to the souls of the young, inviting each of them to follow the pursuit of virtue through this imitation.
CLINIAS. You speak very truly.
ATHENIAN. For this reason, the lyre-player and his pupil should use the sounds of the lyre for the sake of clarity in the strings, rendering the notes in unison with the voices. However, <margin>D</margin> a "diversity of sound" <note>original Greek: "ἑτεροφωνίαν" (heterophony); Latin: "Diversitatem verò varietatemque"</note> and complexity of the lyre—where the strings give off one tune while the poet who composed the melody gives off another—or the mixing of dense notes with sparse ones, speed with slowness, or high pitch with low pitch, providing concord and discord at once, or fitting all sorts of rhythmic variations to the sounds of the lyre—all such things should not be presented to those who are to acquire the utility of music quickly within three years. For contrary things, when they confuse one another, create difficulty in learning. It is necessary for the young to learn as easily as possible. For the lessons we have commanded them to master by necessity are neither small nor few. Our discourse as it progresses will show these in due time. Let our music teachers take care of these things. As for the lyrics and songs themselves, and what the <term>chorodidaskaloi: chorus-masters or choreographers</term> ought to teach, all these things were distinguished by us previously. We said they should be consecrated and fitted to each festival, providing a happy pleasure and benefit to the cities.
CLINIAS. You have distinguished these things truly as well.
<margin>E</margin> ATHENIAN. Therefore, let the magistrate elected to oversee Music take up these truly distinguished tasks and care for them with good fortune. As for us, just as we added the remaining method for teaching music, let us now do the same for dancing and the whole of bodily gymnastics. For it is necessary for boys and girls to learn to dance and practice gymnastics. Is it not?
CLINIAS. Yes, it is.
ATHENIAN. Therefore, let there be masters of dance for the boys and mistresses for the girls, so that they may be suitably exercised.
CLINIAS. Let it be so.
ATHENIAN. Let us once more call upon that man who will undergo the most business: the guardian of the youth. Since he has the care of both music and gymnastics, he will never have much leisure.
CLINIAS. But how will he be able, <margin>F</margin> being an older man, to endure such great care?
ATHENIAN. Easily, my friend. For the law has granted him, and will grant him, the power to take as associates in this care whichever citizens, men or women, he wishes. He will know who ought to be chosen, and he will want to choose upright associates, since he understands and reveres the greatness of his office. He knows that if the youth are correctly educated and continue to be so, the whole voyage of life will be upright. If the opposite follows—which is not worthy to be spoken of, nor shall we say it—it would be a ruinous omen for the city. Much has already been said by us about dancing and every gymnastic movement. For we call "gymnastics" all military exercises as well, <margin>G</margin> such as archery, javelin-throwing, <term>peltasticen: light-shield infantry training</term>, and all combat in arms, the ordering of ranks, the leading of armies, the positioning of camps, and everything pertaining to equestrian discipline. For all these, there should be public teachers paid by the city, who teach the boys and girls, men and women, so that everyone in the city knows these things. <margin>Why women should handle camps and arms.</margin> And let the girls, while they are still young, become accustomed to dancing and fighting in arms; and the women, becoming practiced in marches, the drawing of ranks, and the taking up and laying down of arms—if for no other reason than this: if it should ever be necessary for the whole force to leave the city to go on a campaign, those remaining behind would be capable of defending the children and the rest of the city. Or even the opposite...

<meta>This page continues the Athenian Stranger’s discussion on the education of the youth in his ideal city. Having previously discussed literacy and music, he now transitions into the necessity of physical training (gymnastics and dance) for both men and women, emphasizing that all citizens must be prepared for the defense of the state.</meta>

# PLATO'S [LAWS]

<margin>A</margin> ...should it happen that the city must be defended: or if such a multitude of enemies, whether Greeks or Barbarians, should invade the fields that it becomes necessary for women also to take up arms for the city—none of which is impossible—it would certainly be a great fault in the state if women were educated so lazily that they did not even dare to fight for their children against fierce beasts, like birds do. Instead, they would rather die or suffer any danger than immediately flee to the altars and temples, giving the impression that the human race is the most cowardly of all animals. **CLINIAS.** <note>Clinias is a Cretan politician and one of the three interlocutors in the dialogue.</note> By Jove, Stranger, this is both a disgrace and a detriment to the city. **ATHENIAN.** <margin>B</margin> Let us then establish this law: that women shall not neglect military matters, but all citizens, both women and men, shall apply themselves to them. **CLINIAS.** We establish it. **ATHENIAN.** Regarding wrestling <term>luctatio: a form of competitive grappling used in ancient Greek physical education</term>, we have already spoken in part. But that which I think is most important has not been said, nor is it easy to say, unless one joins physical gestures to the explanation of words. We shall judge this, then, when words joined to actions signify something more clearly concerning the rest: that wrestling is, above all movements, most akin to battle, and one ought to apply oneself to it not for its own sake, but for the sake of battle. **CLINIAS.** That is quite right. **ATHENIAN.** But let this much be said regarding the faculty of wrestling. <margin>C</margin> The other movements of the whole body, most of which can rightly be called by the name of dancing <term>saltatio: encompassing both artistic dance and rhythmic gymnastic movements</term>, we divide into two species. For one movement imitates something honorable and worthy with decent gestures of the body; the other, on the contrary, leads to something vile by imitating indecent things. And of each, there are again two species. For one honorable and more worthy movement is used when we are engaged in war and violent labors with an excellent body and a brave soul. The other is used while the soul rejoices moderately in prosperous circumstances. If anyone calls this the "peaceful" movement, he will be seen to call it according to nature. But that which is different from the peaceful one, anyone will rightly call the *Pyrrhiche* <note>The Pyrrhic dance was a traditional Greek war dance performed in armor, imitating the movements of combat.</note>, which imitates the bending of bodies by which weapons and blows are avoided—by dodging, retreating, leaping upward, and crouching low—<margin>D</margin> and likewise the contrary gestures which lead to the active movements of the body, suitable for preparing one to shoot bows, hurl spears, and finally to imitate the likenesses of battle in all manner of strikes. In these, the uprightness and vigor of good bodies and souls is maintained, whenever an imitation occurs that contributes to the firmness of the limbs. This is indeed right; but what is contrary to these is not approved as right. But let us also consider the dance suitable for peace in this way: whether anyone in the choral dances correctly or incorrectly conducts himself according to the nature of honorable dance, under the best law of learned men. <margin>E</margin> First, however, the ambiguous dance which falls into controversy must be distinguished from the unambiguous. What then is this? And in what way must each be distinguished? We consider the ambiguous to be that which belongs to Bacchus <note>Dionysus</note> and those following him: those whom they call Nymphs, Pans, Sileni, and Satyrs, who, as they say, perform purifications and sacred rites while intoxicated. This whole genus of dancing can easily be determined as neither suitable for war nor for peace, nor is its purpose clear. It seems most right to me, therefore, to distinguish it so that we place it apart from the dance of peace, denying that it is "civil" <note>meaning "fitting for a citizen of a polis"</note>, and therefore leaving it aside, let us now return to the dance belonging to us, which is without controversy for war and peace. <margin>F</margin> Furthermore, that genus of the Muse which we use in peace and in the appearance of prosperity to honor the gods and the children of the gods, is distinguished into two parts. For one is used when we have escaped dangers and labors and have attained good things, which contains greater pleasures. The other is usually performed when previous goods are preserved and increased, in which the pleasure is more relaxed. In matters of this kind, everyone is moved more rapidly by greater pleasure, and more slowly by lesser pleasure. Also, anyone who is more modest and more exercised in fortitude moves more peacefully. On the contrary, the cowardly person, who is least exercised in temperance, performs greater and more vehement changes of movement. Generally, however, whether in song or if one speaks otherwise, no one is able to do so with a quiet body. <margin>G</margin> Therefore, the imitation of words expressed by the figures of the body produced the entire art of dancing, in which some move gracefully and others ungracefully. And since antiquity is to be praised in many other names well-placed according to nature, it is also to be approved in this: that whoever he was, he rightly and musically and according to reason named all the dances of moderate men rejoicing temperately in prosperity as "concinnities" <note>original Latin: "concinnitates"; Greek: "emmeleia", meaning harmony, grace, or tunefulness.</note>, and established two species of honorable dance: the *Pyrrhiche* for war, and the *Emmeleia* for peace. The legislator ought to set these forth in certain patterns; and the guardian must seek them out, and once found, join them with other music, and having distributed them in the solemn sacrifices, dedicate each to each: and establish them thus ordered,

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> (since nothing is impossible*) If enemies should fall upon us from without with some great strength and force, whether they be Barbarians or Greeks, and a struggle must begin for the city itself, it is a great wickedness of the constitution if the women are so poorly raised that they do not wish to die and undergo every danger, fighting for their children like birds against the strongest of beasts; but instead flee straight to the temples, filling all the altars and shrines, and pouring down a reputation upon the race of men that it is by nature the most cowardly of all beasts. **CL.** By Zeus, O Stranger, this would by no means be graceful, apart from the evil of it, wherever it might happen in a city. **ATH.** Therefore, let us set this law at least to this extent: that matters regarding war must not be neglected by women, but all citizens, both male and female, must attend to them. **CL.** I, for one, concur. **ATH.** Again, then, we have spoken of those things which I would say are of the greatest importance; it is not easy to describe them with words without also demonstrating them with the body. We shall judge them then, when the word, having followed the deed, shows something clear about the other things spoken of, and that this kind of wrestling is most nearly related of all movements to warlike battle; and indeed, one must practice it for the sake of all movements, and not learn that [battle] for the sake of this [wrestling]. **CL.** You speak well indeed. <margin>C</margin> **ATH.** Now let what has been said until now regarding the abilities derived from the wrestling-school suffice. As for the other movements of the whole body, the greater part of which one might again correctly call dancing, one must recognize two species of it: one, that of the more beautiful bodies, imitating the dignified; the other, that of the baser, imitating the trivial. And again, there are two of the trivial, and two other types of the serious. Of the serious, there are those of people entangled in war and in violent labors, involving beautiful bodies and a brave soul; and those of a temperate soul being in prosperity and moderate pleasures, which one might call "peaceful" dance, speaking according to nature. The warlike dance of these, being different from the peaceful, one might correctly call the *Pyrrhiche*, consisting of the avoidance of all <margin>D</margin> blows and missiles, and imitating every leap upward and crouching low, and the contrary gestures, those tending toward active forms, attempting to imitate the representations of shooting bows and throwing javelins and all manner of blows. The correctness in these and the vigor of good bodies and souls, whenever a straight imitation occurs, the limbs of the body becoming mostly straight—such a thing is right, but the opposite of these is not accepted as right. As for the peaceful dance, it must be considered in each case, whether one conducts oneself properly in the dances according to the nature of beautiful dance, according to the law for educated men. How then must one first cut the disputed dance apart <margin>E</margin> from the undisputed? What is this, and in what way must each be cut apart? All that is Bacchic and follows from it—those whom they name Nymphs and Pans and Sileni and Satyrs—imitating, as they say, drunken men, for whom they perform certain purifications and initiations; this whole genus of dancing is not easy to define as either peaceful or warlike, nor what it even intends. It seems to me most correct to define it in this way: placing it apart from the warlike and apart from the peaceful, to say that this genus of dancing is not "civic." Leaving it there where it lies, let us now return to the warlike and the peaceful as being indisputably ours. <margin>F</margin> That of the non-warlike Muse, in dancing honoring the gods and the children of the gods, would occur in prosperity with a mind that knows well how to serve. This is divided in two: one, having escaped from certain labors and dangers into good things, having greater pleasures; the other, being the preservation and increase of former goods, possessing gentler pleasures. In such circumstances, every man moves with the movements of the body—with greater movements when the pleasures are greater, and with lesser when they are lesser. And being more orderly and more practiced in courage, he moves with lesser movements; but having become cowardly and unpracticed in temperance, he provides greater and more violent changes of movement. In general, when speaking, whether in songs or in words, no one is entirely able to provide stillness to the body. Therefore, the imitation of things said, occurring in gestures, <margin>G</margin> produced the whole art of dancing. One of us moves harmoniously, another discordantly in all these things. Many of the ancient names we ought to praise, considering them well-placed and according to nature. One of these is that concerning the dances of those faring well, being moderate in their pleasures, which whoever he was named correctly and musically, and named them all according to reason: he called them "Emmeleia." And he established two species of beautiful dance: the warlike, *Pyrrhiche*; the peaceful, *Emmeleia*; applying to each the name that is fitting and appropriate, which things the legislator must explain in patterns; and the guardian of the laws must seek them out, and having found them, join them...

<meta>This page continues the Athenian Stranger's discourse on the regulation of the arts and the introduction of mathematical education in the ideal city. It follows the discussion on physical training and music, moving now to the role of performance and the intellectual curriculum.</meta>

### ON THE LAWS, BOOK VII.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...so that nothing of these things is done differently hereafter, neither in dance nor in song; but rather, the same city persevering in the same pleasures, and the same citizens always remaining similar according to their strength, they may live well and happily. But we have already spoken concerning the honorable dances of beautiful bodies and noble souls. However, the movements of deformed bodies and thoughts, which look toward laughter and comedy—in words, song, dance, and all such imitations—must be considered and known. For it is impossible to understand serious things without the ridiculous, or generally to know opposites without their opposites, if one intends to be prudent. <margin>B</margin> Yet, it is not possible to perform both if we are to participate in virtue in any way. Rather, these things must be known for this reason: so that through ignorance, one does not do or say something ridiculous when it is least appropriate. Therefore, let slaves and hired foreigners imitate such things, but let no serious attention be given to them. Nor should any free citizen—whether man or woman—be seen learning these things; instead, let there always appear some new imitation in them. And so, let those games looking toward laughter, which are called by the name of comedy, be arranged by reason <margin>C</margin> and law.

<margin>Tragedians</margin>
As for the poets of tragedy, who relate, as they say, serious matters: if they should ask us, "O friends, is it permitted for us to come into your region and city and bring our poems to you? Or what has been decided by you concerning the tragic art?" what would be the right answer for us to give to these divine men? For it seems to me we should say: "O best of men, we ourselves are poets of a tragedy that is as beautiful and excellent as can be. Indeed, our entire commonwealth is an imitation of the most beautiful and excellent life, which we certainly judge to be the truest tragedy. You are poets, and we are also poets of the same poem; we are your rivals and competitors in the most beautiful work of tragedy, which only the true law, as we hope, can bring to perfection." <margin>D</margin> "Therefore, do not believe that we will easily allow you to set up stages in the marketplace and bring in loud-voiced actors <term>histriones: professional performers in ancient theater, often viewed with suspicion by philosophers for their emotional influence</term> who cry out louder than we do, and thus harangue our children, our wives, and the whole crowd of the city concerning the same things—not saying the same things we do, but often the opposite. For we, and the whole city, would be completely insane if we admitted you before the magistrates have seen what you have composed and judged whether it should be spoken to the people." "Now therefore, O sons of the soft Muses, first show your songs to the rulers to compare them with ours; <margin>E</margin> and if what is said by you appears to be the same as or better than ours, we will grant you a chorus <note>original: "chorum vobis dabimus" — In ancient Greece, "granting a chorus" meant the state would officially fund and produce the play</note>. But if not, O friends, we can never grant it."

Let these things be established concerning all choral dance <term>chorea: a performance combining rhythmic movement and song</term> and its instruction through laws and customs; and let the duties of slaves be kept separate from those of masters, if you also agree. **CLINIAS.** It certainly seems so. **ATHENIAN.** But for the free citizens, three subjects of study remain. One: the calculation of numbers. The second: the measurement of length, surface, and depth. The third: the knowledge of the stars' circuits. Not many people will learn all these things exactly, but only the few whom we shall identify when we have reached the end. <margin>It is shameful not to know what is necessary</margin> For so it is fitting. But for the multitude, it is shameful not to know what is necessary and most correctly spoken. Yet to seek out everything exquisitely is neither easy nor entirely possible. What is necessary from these subjects cannot be rejected. Indeed, he who first spoke the proverb concerning God seems to have looked toward this very thing, saying <margin>G</margin> that not even a God will ever fight against necessity <margin>God will never fight against necessity.</margin>—which I think must be understood as divine necessities. For if this is said of human necessities, toward which many look when they say such things, it would be by far the most foolish speech of all.

**CLINIAS.** What then, Stranger, are these necessities of study that are not human, but divine? **ATHENIAN.** I think they are those which, if a person does not learn or experience them at all, he could never become a god among men, nor a <insert>divine</insert> spirit <term>daemon: a supernatural being between gods and mortals</term>, nor a hero capable of taking earnest care of men. A man would be far from becoming divine if he could not recognize one, two, and three, or even-and-odd numbers at all; or if he did not know how to count, nor how to number days and nights, and had no grasp of the revolutions of the sun, moon, and other stars. It would be most foolish to think that these are not necessary studies for anyone who intends to perceive even the smallest part of the most beautiful sciences. But what each of these is, and how many, and when they must be learned, and what should be studied with another, and what alone without the others, and what the universal mixture of them is—these things must be learned rightly before all else. Then, with these studies as guides, one must proceed to the others. For so nature's own necessity has obtained, against which we say none of the gods either fights now or will ever fight. **CLINIAS.** Stranger, what you say seems correctly spoken and according to nature. **ATHENIAN.** So it is, Clinias. But it is difficult to carry laws concerning these things proposed in this order. Therefore, if it seems right, we shall enact these laws more diligently at another time. **CLINIAS.** You seem to me, Stranger, to fear our lack of experience in these matters. And not without cause. Nevertheless, try to explain them, fearing nothing on that account.

# PLATO'S
### ON THE LAWS, BOOK VII.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> *ATHENIAN.* I certainly fear what you are saying now, but I dread even more those who have tasted these doctrines, but have tasted them poorly. For total ignorance of all things is not a particularly grave or harsh matter, nor is it the greatest evil; rather, a much more destructive thing is a poorly acquired skill and knowledge of many matters. *CLINIAS.* You speak the truth. *ATHENIAN.* Free men, therefore, ought to learn as much of each subject as the vast crowd of children in Egypt learns along with their basic literacy. First, the study of calculation <note>Latin: "computationis doctrina"; Greek: "λογισμοῖς" (logismos)</note> has been devised for children's minds in such a way that it is learned through play and pleasure. This involves the distribution of apples and crowns to larger or smaller groups using the same fitting numbers.
<margin>B</margin> The pairings of boxers and wrestlers, and the alternating and consecutive order of their matches as is usually done, is also organized this way. Furthermore, by mixing gold, bronze, and silver bowls and other such things together in play, or by passing them entirely from one person to another, they adapt the necessary numbers for games, as I said. In this way, they provide utility to the learners for leading armies, for the arrangements of camps, for household management, and for all other affairs, making the men themselves more alert. Then, since a shameful and laughable ignorance of nature concerning the measurement of length, breadth, and depth possesses all men, they lead the children far away from this state.
<margin>C</margin> *CLINIAS.* Of what sort is this ignorance you speak of? *ATHENIAN.* O friend Clinias, even I, when I finally heard about these things quite late, was amazed at our ignorance in these matters; it seemed to me to be characteristic not of men, but of certain beasts <note>original: "pecorum" (Latin); "ὑαινῶν" (Greek, specifically "hyenas")</note>. Therefore, I blushed intensely, not only for myself, but on behalf of all the Greeks. *CLINIAS.* Speak more clearly, Stranger—what is this? *ATHENIAN.* I will tell you. Or rather, I will reveal it by questioning you. Tell me, please: do you know what length is? *CLINIAS.* Certainly. *ATHENIAN.* And what of breadth? *CLINIAS.* Of course. *ATHENIAN.* And that these are two things, and depth is the third? *CLINIAS.* Yes, that too. *ATHENIAN.* Does it seem to you that all these can be measured against one another? *CLINIAS.* Surely. *ATHENIAN.* That is, that length can naturally be measured against length, breadth against breadth, and depth likewise?
<margin>D</margin> *CLINIAS.* Very much so. *ATHENIAN.* But if some things can be measured neither easily nor at all, while you think that all things can be measured, what do you think of your state of mind regarding these things? *CLINIAS.* It is a poor one. *ATHENIAN.* Again, what of length and breadth against depth, or breadth and length against each other? Do not all we Greeks think they can be measured against one another in some way? *CLINIAS.* Entirely so. *ATHENIAN.* But if they can by no means be measured, yet all Greeks, as I was saying, think they can, is it not right that we, moved by shame for everyone, should say to them: "This is one of those things, O best of Greeks, which we said it is shameful not to know, though to know them—since they are necessary—is nothing particularly grand."
<margin>E</margin> *CLINIAS.* Why not? *ATHENIAN.* Furthermore, there are other things related to these in which we frequently err in a similar way. *CLINIAS.* What are they? *ATHENIAN.* Those things regarding the nature of what is commensurable and what is incommensurable <note>term: "commensurability" — the mathematical property where two magnitudes have a common unit of measure, like whole numbers</note> toward one another. It is necessary to examine and distinguish these, or else be entirely useless. We ought to spend time on these matters for the sake of the soul. For this "old man's game" will be much more pleasant than playing with dice or gaming-pieces, and more worthy of a free man.
<margin>F</margin> *CLINIAS.* Perhaps. For dice and these doctrines seem to differ greatly from one another. *ATHENIAN.* These are the things, Clinias, that I think the younger men should learn. For they are neither harmful nor difficult, and having been grasped through play, they will benefit the city and never hinder it. We must pay attention, however, if anyone says otherwise. *CLINIAS.* Why shouldn't we? *ATHENIAN.* If these things seem to be so, we shall approve them; if otherwise, we shall reject them. *CLINIAS.* Certainly. Should we not then, Stranger, make these necessary doctrines for now, so that our treatment of the laws is not left empty? *ATHENIAN.* Let them be enacted, but on the condition that they can be separated from the rest of the civil order if, by chance, they are not approved either by us who set them or by you for whom they were set. *CLINIAS.* That is a fair arrangement.
<margin>G</margin> *ATHENIAN.* But let us now consider whether the doctrine of the stars pleases us. *CLINIAS.* Speak on. *ATHENIAN.* A strange thing happens in these matters that can by no means be tolerated. *CLINIAS.* What is that? *ATHENIAN.* We say that the greatest god and the whole world <note>original: "totumque mundum" (Latin); "ὅλον τὸν κόσμον" (Greek cosmos)</note> must not be investigated, nor should the causes of things be tracked down with much study, for we do not consider it pious. Yet it seems that the contrary might rightly be done. *CLINIAS.* How do you mean? *ATHENIAN.* Truly, this doctrine will seem foreign to older men; but since I think it is upright, true, useful to the city, and pleasing to God himself, I cannot remain silent. *CLINIAS.* You speak reasonably. But shall we find such a doctrine regarding the stars?
<margin>The sun and moon are great gods.</margin> *ATHENIAN.* We are lying, my good men, about the great gods—I mean the Sun and the Moon—as, to put it briefly, all Greeks do. *CLINIAS.* In what way do we lie? *ATHENIAN.* We believe that the Sun and the Moon never travel the same path, and we say that certain other stars "wander" with them, which we call planets. <note>term: "planets" — from the Greek word "planētēs" meaning wanderers</note> *CLINIAS.* By Jove, Stranger, what you say is true. Often—

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> *ATHENIAN.* I fear these things you now mention; but even more, I dread those who have touched these studies, but have touched them badly. For ignorance of everything is nowhere a terrible or intense thing, nor the greatest evil; rather, much experience and much learning joined with bad guidance becomes a much greater injury than these. *CLINIAS.* You speak truly. *ATHENIAN.* This much of each subject free men should be said to need to learn: as much as the very large crowd of children in Egypt learns along with their letters. First, regarding calculations, studies simply invented for children to learn with play and pleasure: distributions of certain apples and crowns among more or fewer people at once, using the same harmonious numbers, and the pairings of boxers and wrestlers in turn.
<margin>B</margin> And indeed, while playing, they mix bowls of gold, bronze, silver, and other such things; others distribute them in various ways, as I said, fitting the uses of necessary numbers into play. This benefits the learners in the arrangements of military camps, leadership, and expeditions, and again in household management; it altogether makes the men more useful to themselves and more alert. After this, in measurements—whatever has length, breadth, and depth—they rid people of the kind of shameful ignorance that naturally exists in all men concerning all these things.
<margin>C</margin> *CLINIAS.* What sort of ignorance do you mean? *ATHENIAN.* O friend Clinias, I myself, having heard about our condition in these matters quite late, was astonished; it seemed to me that these were the traits of certain hyenas <note>Greek: "ὑαινῶν" (hyainōn)</note> rather than human beings. I was ashamed not only for myself, but for all the Greeks. *CLINIAS.* About what? Tell me what you mean, Stranger. *ATHENIAN.* I will tell you, or rather I will show you by questioning. Answer me briefly: Do you know length? *CLINIAS.* How could I not? *ATHENIAN.* And breadth? *CLINIAS.* Entirely. *ATHENIAN.* And that these are two, and a third among them is depth? *CLINIAS.* Certainly. *ATHENIAN.* Does it then seem to you that all these are measurable against one another? *CLINIAS.* Yes. *ATHENIAN.* Length against length, I suppose, and breadth against breadth, and depth likewise, it is naturally possible to measure. *CLINIAS.* Very much so.
<margin>D</margin> *ATHENIAN.* But if some are not at all or only slightly possible, but some are and others are not—while you think all are—how do you think you are disposed toward these things? *CLINIAS.* Clearly, poorly. *ATHENIAN.* And again: length and breadth against depth, or breadth and length against each other—do we not all think, we Greeks, that they are somehow [commensurable]? *CLINIAS.* Entirely. *ATHENIAN.* But if they are in no way possible, yet we Greeks all think they are—is it not worth being ashamed for everyone and saying to them: "O best of Greeks, this is one of those things we said was shameful not to know; but to know what is necessary is nothing very beautiful."
<margin>E</margin> *CLINIAS.* Why not? *ATHENIAN.* And besides these, there are other related things in which many errors, brothers to those others, occur in our disputes. *CLINIAS.* What kind? *ATHENIAN.* The matters of commensurable and incommensurable magnitudes toward one another, which occur by nature. It is necessary to distinguish these by looking at them, or else be entirely worthless; and by continually comparing them with one another, an old man passes his time in a much more graceful pursuit, competing in the worth of these "gaming-pieces" <note>Greek: "πετταῖς" (pessoi), refering to the game of Petteia</note>. *CLINIAS.* Perhaps. At any rate, education and the play of these studies seem not to be very far apart.
<margin>F</margin> *ATHENIAN.* These things, I say, Clinias—I say the young must learn them. For they are neither harmful nor difficult; learned alongside play, they will benefit us, and will not harm the city at all. If anyone says otherwise, he must be heard. *CLINIAS.* Why not? *ATHENIAN.* But indeed, if these things appear to be so, it is clear we shall judge them well; but if they do not appear so, we shall reject them. *CLINIAS.* That is clear. Why not? Let each of these, Stranger, be established as among the necessary studies, so that our laws are not left lacking. *ATHENIAN.* Let them be established, though as if they have a release from the rest of the constitution, if perhaps they are in no way pleasing to us who set them or to you who receive them. *CLINIAS.* You propose a fair condition.
<margin>G</margin> *ATHENIAN.* Now looking at what comes next, see if the learning of the stars pleases us when spoken of, or the opposite. *CLINIAS.* Only speak. *ATHENIAN.* Indeed, in these matters there is something great, and in no way tolerable. *CLINIAS.* What sort of thing? *ATHENIAN.* We say that the greatest god and the whole cosmos should neither be sought out nor meddled with by searching for their causes. For it is said not to be holy. But it seems that the exact opposite would be the right thing to do. *CLINIAS.* How do you mean? *ATHENIAN.* What I am saying is paradoxical, and one might not think it fitting for old men; but whenever someone thinks a study is beautiful and true, and profitable to the city, and entirely dear to God, it would be in no way possible for him not to speak of it. *CLINIAS.* You speak reasonably. But shall we find such a study about the stars? *ATHENIAN.* My good men, we are now lying—so to speak—all the Greeks, about the great gods, the Sun and the Moon. *CLINIAS.* What kind of lie do you mean? *ATHENIAN.* We say they never...

<summary>In this passage from Plato's Laws, the Athenian Stranger argues for the inclusion of arithmetic, geometry, and astronomy in the curriculum for young citizens. He highlights the Egyptian method of teaching math through games and shames the Greeks for their ignorance of mathematical commensurability and the true nature of celestial movements.</summary>
<keywords>mathematics education, geometry, Egyptian pedagogy, commensurability, astronomy, piety, Sun and Moon, Athenian Stranger, Clinias</keywords>

# ON THE LAWS, BOOK VII.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> **ATHENIAN:** I have often seen with my own eyes the Morning Star <note>original: "ἑωσφόρον" (Heōsphoron) / "Luciferum"</note> and the Evening Star <note>original: "ἕσπερον" (Hesperon) / "Hesperum"</note> and certain other stars never following the same path, but wandering in every direction; and we have all observed that the sun and moon are always doing this. Now, Megillus and Clinias, I claim that our citizens and the youth should learn about these heavenly gods <note>In Plato's time, the celestial bodies were considered divine beings.</note> at least to the point that they do not speak profanely of them, but rather always honor them with sacrifices and pious prayers. **CLINIAS:** This is correct, provided that what you say can actually be learned. If we currently speak incorrectly about them, but can speak correctly after learning, then I agree that a subject of such importance should be studied. Therefore, try to explain these things clearly, and we shall follow and learn.

<margin>B</margin> **ATHENIAN:** What I am saying is not easy to grasp, yet it is not altogether difficult either; nor does it require a vast amount of time. As proof: I did not hear of these things in my youth nor very long ago, yet I can explain them to you in a short time. If they were truly difficult, I—at my age—would not be able to declare them to you at your age. **CLINIAS:** That is true. But what is this "wonderful" knowledge you say is necessary for the youth, yet unknown to us? Try to state it as clearly as possible.

<margin>C</margin> **ATHENIAN:** I shall try. The common opinion, my friends, that the sun, the moon, and the other stars "wander" <note>The word "planet" comes from the Greek "planētēs," meaning "wanderer."</note> is not correct; the reality is quite the opposite. Each of them travels one single path in a circle, not many, even though they appear to move in many directions. Furthermore, we are wrong to think that the fastest of them is the slowest, and the slowest is the fastest. If this is how nature is, but we believe otherwise—imagine if we were watching horses or long-distance runners at the Olympic Games and we called the fastest "slowest" and the slowest "fastest," and sang praises to the loser as if he were the winner. I do not think such praises would be pleasing or correct to the runners, who are but men. Now, when we make this same error regarding the gods, do we not think it is both ridiculous and wrong?

<margin>D</margin> **CLINIAS:** It would be quite ridiculous. **ATHENIAN:** Indeed, and it would not be pleasing to the gods for us to sing false reports about them. **CLINIAS:** Most true, if the facts are as you say. **ATHENIAN:** If we can demonstrate that this is the case, these things should be learned to this extent; if we cannot, they should be left aside. Let us agree on that. **CLINIAS:** By all means. **ATHENIAN:** Then let us consider the regulations regarding the subjects of education to be finished.

Next, we must consider the matter of hunting <note>original: "θήρας" (thēras) / "venatu"</note> in a similar way, and indeed all such activities. The legislator's task is perhaps greater than merely writing down laws. Between formal laws and simple advice, there exists a middle ground of "admonition" <note>original: "νουθετητικὴ" (nouthetikē); a form of moral guidance.</note>, which we have often used in our discussion, especially regarding the education of young children. We said that many things cannot be addressed by formal laws, and to try to set laws for every small detail would be the mark of a fool.

<margin>E</margin> In a well-ordered state, the highest praise for a citizen is not just that he serves and obeys the written laws, but that he spends his whole life obeying the "unwritten" intentions of the legislator—his praises and his censures. The perfect citizen is the one who follows the legislator’s guidance throughout his life. The law-giver must not only write the laws but also include a declaration of what he deems honorable or shameful. The best citizen should observe these as much as the mandates enforced by penalties. We bring up the present subject as a witness to this; it clarifies what we mean. For "hunting" is a broad term, covering many things under a single name. There is hunting of water-creatures, of birds, and of land-animals. Furthermore, there is the hunting of humans—not only in war, but also through <margin>F</margin> "friendship," <note>This refers to the "pursuit" of others in social or romantic contexts.</note> which can be either praiseworthy or blameworthy. There is also the "hunting" done by thieves, pirates, and armies. A legislator cannot ignore these, yet he cannot easily set specific penalties and laws for every type. What should be done? The legislator should praise or blame types of hunting based on how they train the souls and habits of the young. The young, hearing this, should obey, regardless of pleasure or toil. They should honor the legislator's praise more than the threat of punishment.

<margin>G</margin> Following this, we can offer a proper praise or blame of hunting: that which improves the souls of the young should be praised, and the opposite blamed. Let us say to the youth, as if in prayer: "O friends, may you never be seized by a desire for sea-fishing or angling, nor for any aquatic hunting, whether by day or by night with traps. May no love of piracy seize you, making you cruel and lawless hunters of men. And may the thought of committing theft in the city or the countryside never enter your minds."

<sig>Hhh iij</sig>

<summary>The Athenian Stranger argues that astronomy must be taught to correct the "blasphemous" idea that planets wander aimlessly, asserting they follow orderly paths. The text then transitions to hunting, explaining that the legislator must use moral praise and blame—not just laws—to guide the youth toward noble pursuits and away from "ignoble" hunting like fishing, piracy, or theft.</summary>

The Athenian Stranger moves from the regulation of private sport to the public organization of the state's religious and military life, ensuring continuity between the previous page’s focus on education and the next phase of civic structure.</meta>

<page-num>642</page-num>
<header>PLATO</header>

...nor should the pleasant hunting of birds <note>original: "volatilium iucunda venatio"</note>, which is more characteristic of a slave than a free man, take hold of any youth. Therefore, only the hunting of land animals remains for our athletes. But even of these, "night-hunting" <note>original: "nocturnáque"</note>—done by taking turns while others sleep—is for lazy men and is not worthy of praise. Nor is that kind which involves a rest from labor, where one subdues the ferocity of wild beasts with nets and snares <note>original: "retibus laqueísque"</note> rather than the strength of a hard-working soul. Therefore, the only remaining and best form of hunting for everyone is that of four-legged animals, conducted with horses, dogs, and the strength of one's own body. For those who care for divine fortitude <note>original: "diuina fortitudo"</note> must overcome all four-legged creatures in the hunt through running, striking, and using weapons with their own hands. Let this be the distinction between what is praised and what is censured in hunting. The law shall be this: let no one prohibit hunters from the sacred openings of groves wherever they wish to hunt. But let no one ever permit a night-hunter, trusting in his nets and dogs, to hunt anywhere. A fowler shall be allowed to wander through uncultivated fields and mountains, but shall be driven away from cultivated places and sacred uncultivated spots by anyone who finds him. A fisherman shall not hunt in ports, nor in sacred rivers, marshes, or ponds; in other places it shall be allowed, provided he does not use mixtures of poisonous juices <note>referring to a practice of poisoning water to catch fish</note>. But let the institutions regarding discipline now come to an end. CLINIAS: You speak excellently.

# PLATO ON THE LAWS, OR, ON THE INSTITUTION OF LAWS,
## BOOK EIGHT.

*SUMMARY OF THE DIALOGUE. In this book, he deals with Religion, first commemorating certain solemn rites of festivals and games, based on the beliefs of his time. He also teaches at length the use of these games for military exercises, explaining how both boys and girls should be trained in them. Since it seemed harsh and unusual to admit women to military training, he explains why and to what extent this should happen: namely, for all necessities and in extreme times for the state, when one must fight for altars and hearths, for fatherland and children. Thus women are to be trained so that they do not call men away from their duty through cowardly consternation, but rather support them in the defense of their most dear and common interests. After the games are explained, he moves to the primary force of Religion, which is that most powerful law of conscience: which he says is unwritten <note>original: "ἄγραφον" (agraphon)</note>, but whose force and efficacy subdues every soul and compels it to obey the established laws through fear. He teaches that this law is born with us, dwells in the entire course of life, and pervades the authority of all ranks of men. From there, he exhorts men to declare war on their desires, saying they will achieve a noble victory. Above all, he condemns adultery, debauchery, and especially "male love" <note>original: "venerem masculam"</note>, which he detests as a horrible monster against nature.*

<margin>Concerning sacred matters.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'S' featuring a figure in a landscape with buildings in the background.</image-desc>
B **ATHENIAN:** It follows next that we should establish laws concerning festivities through the Delphic oracles <note>The Oracle at Delphi was the most prestigious source of religious authority in the Greek world.</note>, determining which sacrifices and to which gods it would be better and more beneficial for the city to offer. However, how many sacrifices there should be and when they should occur is perhaps our task to sanction by law. CLINIAS: Perhaps the number. **ATHENIAN:** Let us speak of the number first. I believe it ought to be three hundred and sixty-five: so that at least one magistrate may always be sacrificing to one of the gods or spirits <note>original: "dæmonũ" / "δαιμόνων" (daimonon)</note> on behalf of the city, themselves, and their property. Interpreters, priests, and priestesses, along with the guardians of the laws, shall gather to arrange those things which the legislator of necessity omitted. For these people must be the judges of what was left out. C The law will therefore see to it that the citizens perform twelve solemnities for the twelve gods <note>The twelve Olympian deities</note> after whom each tribe is named, making sacrifices to the gods every month. Furthermore, they shall provide choruses, musical games, and gymnastic contests, as is fitting for the individual gods and the seasons. There shall be distinct festivities so it is clear which must be conducted without men and which not. D The festivals of the earthly gods <note>original: "Terrestriũ" / "χθονίων" (chthonian gods)</note> and the heavenly gods, and those who follow them, must not be mixed but kept separate in the twelfth month, which is dedicated to Pluto <note>The god of the underworld</note>, so they may be celebrated according to the law. For this god is not to be rejected by warlike men, but honored as always being the best for the human race. For the joining of the soul and body is in no way better than their separation, as I affirm in all seriousness. Furthermore, whoever is to distinguish these matters sufficiently must consider that our city, regarding leisure time and the possession of necessary things, is such that none can be found like it in this age. But E it must live well, just like a single human being. For those living happily, it is first necessary that they neither commit injury against others, nor be injured by others themselves. One of these is not very difficult; but the other—to not be harmed by any injury—is very difficult. No one can perfectly achieve this unless he becomes perfectly good. The same is true for a city: if it is good, it will lead a life in peace; but if it is wicked, it will be plagued by internal seditions and external wars. Since these things are generally so, one should not wait for the time of war, but citizens should be trained in military matters during peace. Therefore, a prudent city will test its military strength every month, for at least one day—or more, as it seems best to the magistrates—with men, women, and children alike, avoiding neither winter nor heat, so that all are ready whenever it seems right to the magistrates to lead out the entire population. For this purpose, suitable games must be devised along with sacrifices, so that F festive and solemn battles occur, imitating real military combat as closely as possible.

<meta>This page transitions from the general educational precepts of Book VII into the specific civic and military regulations of Book VIII. The Athenian Stranger continues to lead the dialogue with Clinias, focusing now on how the state should organize its competitions, its arts, and its defense preparations to ensure the citizens remain virtuous and combat-ready.</meta>

# ON THE LAWS, BOOK VIII.

...prizes of victory and awards for excellence should be distributed to each. They should compose praises <margin>A</margin> and censures for one another, based on how each person behaves both in the contests and throughout their entire life; they should adorn with honors those who seem to possess virtue and censure those who do not. However, not just anyone should be a poet of such things. Rather, he should be at least fifty years of age; nor should those be chosen who, while perhaps possessing sufficient poetic skill and inspiration, have never performed any noble or distinguished deed. Instead, let the songs be those of men who are themselves good and honored in the city, being creators of noble works—their poems should be sung even if they are not naturally musical. The judgment of these matters shall rest with the educator <note>The official in charge of the city's education system.</note> and the other guardians of the law, who shall grant this privilege: the freedom of the Muses <margin>B</margin> to them alone, while no authority is given to others. No one shall dare to sing an unapproved song—one not judged by the guardians of the law—even if it were sweeter than the hymns of Thamyras or Orpheus <note>Legendary musicians of Greek myth.</note>. Instead, let them sing only those poems which have been judged sacred and dedicated to the gods, or those by good men which have been judged to perform praise or censure with appropriate moderation. I say these same rules regarding military service and freedom in poetry should apply to women and men alike. The legislator must reflect and ask himself: "Come now, in what way shall we train the whole city? Are they not athletes of the greatest contest, for whom there are ten thousand rivals?" "Certainly," someone might rightly say. What then? If we were breeding boxers or pancratiasts <margin>C</margin> <note>pancratiasts: athletes in a brutal "all-powers" combat sport combining boxing and wrestling.</note>, or contestants in any such events, would we go into the contest itself without having previously practiced daily against someone? If we were boxers, would we not have learned to fight many days before the contest and labored through it, mimicking all those things we would eventually use when fighting for victory? To get as close to the reality as possible, would we not wrap our hands in padded gloves <note>original: "sphairas" (weighted or padded training gloves).</note> so that the blows and the dodging of blows could be sufficiently practiced as much as possible? And if we happened to have a great lack of training partners, would we not dare—even fearing the laughter of fools—to hang up a lifeless dummy and practice against it? And if we lacked both living and lifeless opponents, having no partners to train with, would we not even <margin>D</margin> dare to truly shadow-box <note>original: "skiamachein" (fighting with shadows).</note> against ourselves? For what else is the practice of moving one's hands intended for? **CLINIAS:** Almost nothing else, Stranger, except exactly what you have just said. **ATHENIAN:** What then? Should we prepare the fighting force of our city more poorly than such contestants when they are to enter the greatest of contests, fighting for their lives, their children, their property, and the entire city? And should a legislator, out of fear that these mutual exercises might appear bitter, fail to legislate for military service? <margin>E</margin> He should instead command that every month, for at least one day, the citizens should engage in the use of weapons, together with gymnastics and choral dancing, in larger and smaller maneuvers, making marches and occupations of territory, and competing against one another in all areas. They should mimic real warfare, using "ball-fighting" and projectiles, using weapons that come as close as possible to real, dangerous ones, so that their mutual play is not entirely without fear, but provides terrors and shows, in a way, who has a courageous soul and who does not. By rightly distributing honors to some and dishonors to others, he prepares the whole city to be useful for the true contest throughout their lives. And indeed, <margin>F</margin> if someone dies in these contests—a death occurring as an involuntary homicide—the law shall deem the killer pure and free of guilt. For the legislator should consider that if a few men die, others no less capable will be born; but if fear is extinguished in all such activities, he will find no test to distinguish the better from the worse—which is a much greater evil for a city than the loss of a few. **CLINIAS:** We would agree, Stranger, that a whole city ought to legislate and practice such things. **ATHENIAN:** Do we all know the reason why such choral dancing and athletic competition is now almost nowhere to be found in cities, except in small amounts? Shall we say it is because of the ignorance of the many and of those who make their laws? **CLINIAS:** Perhaps. **ATHENIAN:** Not at all, blessed Clinias. We must say there are two very sufficient causes for this. **CLINIAS:** <margin>G</margin> What are they? **ATHENIAN:** One is the love of wealth, which makes everyone too busy to care for anything else except their own private possessions. The soul of every citizen, hanging upon this, could never care for anything else except daily profit. Whatever study or practice leads to this, everyone is most ready to learn and exercise individually; but they laugh at everything else. This is one cause, and it must be stated as the reason why a city is unwilling to take seriously this or any other noble and good practice; instead, because of an insatiable greed for gold and silver, every man is willing to endure every craft and device, whether noble or ignoble, if it will make him rich. He will perform any deed, whether holy or unholy or utterly shameful, without disgust, provided only that he has the power, like a wild beast, to eat and drink all sorts of things and to provide himself with every kind of sexual satisfaction.

<column-break/>

...and rewards to the victors, and praises: but to the defeated, on the other hand, let there be censures <margin>A</margin>, according to how each has behaved in the contests and in all of life. Thus, let every best man be raised up with praises, and the opposite be depressed by censure. Not all should be poets of these things: but first, he who is not less than fifty years old. Then, those who not only sufficiently possess the poetic Muse, but have also done something noble and distinguished. Therefore, let the poems of those who are good men, worthy of honor in the state, and who have performed noble deeds, be sung—even if they are less musical. The judgment of this matter should be held by the one placed in charge of the education of children <margin>B</margin> and the other guardians of the law. Let these grant this honor to honest men, so that they alone provide freedom in the Muses; but let them prohibit the others. Therefore, let no one dare to sing a Muse not approved by the judgment of these men, even if it were sweeter than that of Thamyras or Orpheus. But let sacred poems be sung which have been approved by judgment and dedicated to the gods; and also the poems of good men, by which some are praised and others censured, having been judged to do so with moderation. These same things regarding military service and poetic freedom must be done similarly for women and men. But it is necessary for the legislator to speak thus with himself: "Come now: in establishing the city, what kind of citizens do I study to educate? Are they not athletes of the greatest contests, for whom there are innumerable adversaries?" "Indeed," <margin>C</margin> anyone will rightly respond. If, therefore, we were educating boxers, or pancratiasts, or others like them, would we lead them into the contest itself so that they had never fought with anyone before? Or if we were boxers, would we not have learned to fight many days before, doing all the things which must be used in a true contest where victory is striven for, approaching as closely as possible to that which is similar, and wearing iron-bound gloves instead of leather thongs, so that we might learn by premeditation both to inflict and to avoid wounds? But if no companions were given to us with whom we could exercise, would we, fearing the laughter of fools, restrain ourselves from hanging up a lifeless image against which <margin>D</margin> the exercise could be done? And if we had no supply of either an animate or an inanimate adversary, would we not ourselves fight alone against our own shadow? Or for what else has the bending of hands here and there and this kind of devised preparation been thought out? **CLINIAS:** For almost nothing else than for this very thing which you have now said. **ATHENIAN:** What then of the part of the city which studies military service? Will it dare to come to the greatest contest prepared more poorly than such combatants, when it is to fight for life, for children, for its affairs, and for the fatherland? Therefore, the legislator will not fear lest these gymnasia seem ridiculous to some: but he shall establish by law that <margin>E</margin> military affairs be conducted especially with minor exercises without arms, bringing in and stirring up dances and all gymnastics for these things: but the greater exercise no less than once a month, so that individuals may contend to take or hold locations, and mimic ambushes and all military matters. And let them exercise with balls, turning themselves in every direction: and let them use weapons approaching as closely as possible to real and dangerous weapons, so that this kind of play is not conducted among citizens entirely without fear, but brings in dread: and thus let it show who is of great spirit and who is cowardly, so that honors may be given to these and reproaches to those, as is fitting: and by this reason the whole city through all of life may be manfully prepared for the true contest. If anyone, however, dies by involuntary slaughter in these contests, let him who killed him be purified according to the law and be clean <margin>F</margin> hereafter. For the legislator ought to think that with a few such men dead, the rest will be no worse. But with fear extinguished in all these things, he will find nothing further by which to discern the better from the worse. If that does not happen, it is a much greater evil to the city than the former. **CLINIAS:** We concede, Stranger, that these things must be done by law and conducted universally by the city. **ATHENIAN:** Do we all now know the cause for which such choral dancing and competition are now performed almost nowhere in cities except very rarely? Shall we affirm that it happens because of the ignorance of the multitude and the makers of laws? **CLINIAS:** Perhaps. **ATHENIAN:** By no means, O blessed Clinias. But there are two sufficient causes for this thing. **CLINIAS:** <margin>G</margin> What are they? **ATHENIAN:** One indeed is that, because of the desire for riches, all other things are neglected at all times, and we care only for private property; and the mind of the citizens, leaning upon this, can give labor to nothing else except to piling up money daily. For all most willingly embrace the arts and studies which lead to profit, and despise the rest. This, therefore, is one cause: that citizens do not care for this or any other honorable and good duty, but with an insatiable desire for gold and silver, they embrace both honorable and dishonorable crafts alike, and do anything, whether it be considered right or wrong, so that they may pile up money, by which <margin>H</margin> they may serve their belly and their lust like cattle. **CLINIAS:**

<summary>This page discusses the regulation of civic honors, poetry, and rigorous military training in Plato's ideal state. It highlights how the pursuit of wealth serves as a primary distraction that prevents citizens from achieving the martial and moral excellence required for the state's survival.</summary>

The Athenian Stranger and Clinias are discussing why most cities fail to prioritize military training and how a well-governed state should organize athletic competitions to serve the purposes of war.
