->**OF PLATO**<-

<margin>A</margin> **ATHENIAN.** You are right. Let this, then, which I mention, be set down as one cause that prevents cities from practicing either any other noble pursuit or military affairs sufficiently: it turns those who are naturally moderate into merchants, ship-owners, and lowly servants; and it makes the brave into thieves, burglars, temple-robbers, fighters, and tyrants—even when they are naturally gifted, they end up unfortunate because of these habits. **CLINIAS.** How do you mean? **ATHENIAN.** Why should I not call them utterly unfortunate, when they are forced by hunger to torment their own souls throughout their entire lives?
<margin>B</margin> **CLINIAS.** This is certainly one cause; but what, Stranger, do you say is the second cause? **ATHENIAN.** You have reminded me well. **CLINIAS.** So, as you say, this one cause is the perpetual and insatiable greed for riches, which keeps every individual so occupied that they are prohibited from caring for military matters as is fitting. But now explain the second cause. **ATHENIAN.** Do I seem to you to be lingering too long on this one because I lack the ability to explain the other? **CLINIAS.** Not at all; but you seem to be attacking these human customs, into which the conversation has fallen, with more hatred than is perhaps fitting. **ATHENIAN.** You rebuke me most excellently, my friends. Therefore, hear what follows. **CLINIAS.** Just speak. **ATHENIAN.** I assert that the cause lies in those types of government we have often mentioned: democracy, oligarchy, and tyranny. None of these is truly a republic <note>original: *respublica* / *πολιτεία*; here meaning a "true state" or "constitutional government"</note>; instead, they can all most rightly be called "seditions" <note>original: *seditiones* / *στασιωτεῖαι*; referring to states ruled by factional interest rather than the common good</note>. For in none of them does a willing ruler lead willing subjects; rather, a willing ruler
<margin>C</margin> always dominates unwilling subjects by some form of force. In such states, since the ruler fears the subjects, he will never willingly allow them to become good, or wealthy, or robust, or brave, or generally warlike. These are the two primary causes of all things, or certainly the chief ones. The republic for which we are now making laws seems to have escaped both of them. For it possesses the greatest leisure and is entirely free; and under these laws, men will be least likely to become greedy for money. Therefore, it is probable that this state alone of all existing republics can undertake military discipline and the games we have rightly discussed. **CLINIAS.** Well said. **ATHENIAN.**
<margin>D</margin> Next, we can speak of all the gymnastic contests, so that prizes may be established for those which lead to war, while the others are dismissed. But what these are must be reviewed from the beginning and sanctioned by laws—first, those pertaining to running and speed. Is that not so? **CLINIAS.** It must certainly be done. **ATHENIAN.** Of all things, then, agility of the body—both of the feet and of the hands—is most useful for war: the feet for fleeing and pursuing, and the strength of the hands for fighting and wrestling in close quarters. **CLINIAS.** Certainly. **ATHENIAN.** Yet neither is of great use without weapons. **CLINIAS.** True. **ATHENIAN.** Therefore, let the herald first call the runners for the stadium <note>original: *stadium*; a race of roughly 200 meters</note>, just as is done now in contests. But let him enter with weapons. For we shall not establish prizes for a naked
<margin>E</margin> contestant without weapons. Let the first to run the stadium enter armed. Then the one who will run the <term>diaulos</term> <note>original: δίαυλον; a double-stadium race where runners turn back to the start</note>, that is, the one who runs the stadium and back. Third, the horse-length race. Fourth, the <term>dolichos</term> <note>original: δολιχον; a long-distance race of several kilometers</note>, that is, the one who will run four stadiums. Fifth, the one adorned in lighter armor, whom we shall send out to reach some temple of Mars at a distance of sixty stadiums. Another, armed in heavier armor, shall run a shorter and smoother course. Another, an archer equipped with all his archery gear, shall compete to reach the temple of Apollo and Diana across a distance of one hundred stadiums over mountains and varied terrain. Once the contest is set, we shall wait for them to arrive and give prizes to each of the victors. **CLINIAS.** Rightly so. **ATHENIAN.** Let us distinguish these contests
<margin>F</margin> into three parts: one for boys, the second for beardless youths, and the third for men. For the beardless youths, we shall set the distances at two-thirds of the men's; for the boys, half. These shall compete with archers and other armed men. For the women, girls not yet of age shall run the stadium, the <term>diaulos</term>, the horse-length, and the <term>dolichos</term> naked; but for those past their thirteenth year until they are married—no older than twenty nor younger than eighteen—they shall enter the running contest wearing appropriate clothing. Let this be said regarding the running of both men and women. To increase strength, instead of wrestling
<margin>G</margin> and similar heavy sports currently held, let more serious armed combats be desired: one against one, two against two, and up to ten against ten. Regarding what a victor ought to do or not suffer—just as was recently determined for the wrestling school by the directors of wrestling regarding what is a good or bad move—so too in these armed contests, experts must be brought in to sanction by law what a person must do (or not suffer) to win, and what order distinguishes the loser. These same laws shall be understood for women as well, up to their marriageable age. All light-shield fighting <note>original: *peltastica*; the style of the peltast, a light infantryman</note> should be set against the <term>pancratium</term> <note>original: *pancratiacæ*; a "no-holds-barred" combat sport</note>; and they shall compete with bow, light shield, lances, and the throwing of stones by hand and sling.
<margin>H</margin> To him who conducts himself best in these also, let honors of victory be granted by law. Now let us look at the horse contests. The use of horses is not great in Crete. Therefore, it is necessary...

<column-break/>

**ATHENIAN.** ...You are right. <margin>A</margin> Let this, then, which I am saying, be set down as one hindering cause, which allows cities to practice neither anything else that is noble nor military affairs sufficiently, but instead makes all those who are naturally orderly in character into mere tradesmen and mariners and servants; while making the brave into pirates, burglars, temple-robbers, warriors <note>original: πολεμικούς; here implying those who fight for the sake of strife or profit</note>, and tyrants—sometimes they are not naturally ungifted, but they are simply unfortunate. **CLINIAS.** How so? **ATHENIAN.** How could they not be called entirely unfortunate, since they are forced to go through their whole lives with their souls always hungry? **CLINIAS.** This then is one cause. But what do you say is the second cause,
<margin>B</margin> Stranger? **ATHENIAN.** You have reminded me well. **CLINIAS.** This one, then (as you say), is the insatiable lifelong pursuit of wealth, which keeps everyone busy and becomes a hindrance to each person’s proper practice of military affairs. Let it be so; now tell the second cause. **ATHENIAN.** Do I seem to you not to be speaking, but to be wasting time because of a lack of ideas? **CLINIAS.** No; but you seem to us to be punishing this sort of character more than is necessary because of your hatred of it, since the topic fell that way. **ATHENIAN.** You have rebuked me most beautifully, strangers; and it seems you should hear what follows. **CLINIAS.** Just speak. **ATHENIAN.** I say that those forms of government which we have often mentioned in our previous discussions are also to blame: democracy, oligarchy, and tyranny. For none of these is truly a state, but they would all most correctly be called "factions." For none is a willing rule over willing subjects, but a willing rule over
<margin>C</margin> unwilling ones, always involving some violence. And a ruler who fears his subjects will never willingly allow anyone to become noble, or wealthy, or strong, or brave, or generally warlike. These then are the two causes, which have ruined almost everything, but these in particular. But the state we are now legislating for has escaped both. For it has the greatest amount of leisure, and the citizens are independent of one another. And I think they would be least likely to become lovers of money because of these laws. So it is reasonable and logical that such a constitution alone would accept the education we have just completed, along with military play correctly finished according to reason. **CLINIAS.** Excellent. **ATHENIAN.** Is it not
<margin>D</margin> then next in order to mention all the gymnastic contests? That those of them which involve military exercise should be practiced and prizes for victory established, but the others should be bid farewell? It is better that these be described and legislated from the beginning; and first, should we not establish matters concerning running and speed in general? **CLINIAS.** We should. **ATHENIAN.** Surely quickness of body is the most warlike of all things—either of the feet or of the hands. That of the feet is for fleeing and catching; that of the hands is for the battle in close quarters and standing one's ground, which requires strength and power. **CLINIAS.** Of course. **ATHENIAN.** However, neither has the greatest utility apart from weapons. **CLINIAS.** How could they? **ATHENIAN.** Let the herald first announce the stadium race for
<margin>E</margin> us, as is done now in the contests; and let the runner enter in armor. We shall not establish prizes for a naked competitor. Let the one who will compete in the stadium in armor enter first. Second, the one in the <term>diaulos</term>; and third, the horse-length race; and fourth, the <term>dolichos</term>; and fifth, the one we shall send out first fully armed for a distance of sixty stadiums toward some temple of Ares; and we shall name another, a heavier-armed soldier, competing on a smoother road; and another, an archer, having all the equipment of archery, competing for a hundred stadiums toward the temple of Apollo and Artemis, through mountains and all kinds of terrain. And having set the contest, we shall wait for these until they arrive; and we will give the prizes of
<margin>F</margin> victory to each winner. **CLINIAS.** Rightly so. **ATHENIAN.** Let us conceive of these as threefold athletic events: one for children, one for beardless youths, and one for men. And for the beardless youths, we shall set two-thirds of the lengths; for the children, half of these, whether they are competing as archers or in armor. As for women: for girls who are not yet of age, let them compete naked in the stadium, the <term>diaulos</term>, the horse-length, and the <term>dolichos</term> on the track itself; but for those fourteen years old until they enter into the communion of marriage—not older than twenty, nor younger than eighteen—they must descend into the arena for these races dressed in appropriate clothing. And let
<margin>G</margin> these be the rules for men and women regarding running. For matters of strength, instead of wrestling and the other heavy events now held, there should be fighting in armor—competing one against one, and two against two, and up to ten against ten. As for what the winner must do or not suffer, just as the experts in wrestling have legislated regarding what is the work of one who wrestles well or not, the same should be done for those who fight in armor; men should follow these and be ordered to legislate together as to who is just to win these battles, and what they must do or not suffer; and likewise, what rule distinguishes the loser. Let these same things be legislated
<margin>H</margin> for females also until marriage. And all light-shield fighting <note>original: πελταστική / *peltastikē*</note> must be set against the <term>pancratium</term>, with those competing in bows, light shields, javelins, and the throwing of stones, both by hand and with slings. Laws must again be established for these, giving rewards and honors to the one who best fulfills the requirements of these laws. Now we must look at the contests of horses. Since there is no great use for horses in Crete...

<note>original: καὶ διανεύειν τὰ δὲ ταῦτα... χρὴ γὰρ δὴ Κρήτην. / Translator's note: This additional Greek text suggests these matters should be distinguished; regarding horse contests, it notes that for the legislator, there is not a great need for many horses, as is fitting for Crete's rugged terrain.</note>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Book VII regarding the education and physical training of citizens. # ON THE LAWS, BOOK VIII

...so that of necessity the serious interests in Crete are less, and the competitions are always [unclear]. Regarding the chariot, we have none at all, nor does it seem to us that there is any ambition for such things, which stands to reason. As for those who do not compete in these things from their swaddling clothes, they neither have nor seem to possess much sense. But by offering prizes for horses—for colts without bits, for full-grown ones, and for those in between—we might improve the art of horsemanship according to the nature of our land.

Let there be a competition and rivalry for these things and for the laws, with a shared judgment assigned to the guardians and the masters of the horse <note>Greek: *hipparchois*, commanders of the cavalry</note> for all those who participate in the race and those who dismount with their weapons. We would be legislating correctly if we did not set up competitions for those without weapons, neither in the gymnastic games <note>General physical training and athletic contests, often performed naked</note> nor here. A Cretan archer on horseback is not useless, nor is a javelin thrower. Therefore, let there be strife and competition for these things for the sake of sport. As for the females, it is not worth forcing them by laws and commands to participate; but if their nature—going into the habit of their earlier training—allows it and if the girls or maidens do not object to participating, let them, and do not criticize them. Now, let the competition and learning of gymnastics—both those in the contests and those we have worked out through daily teachers—come to an end. And indeed, let most of the matters of music likewise be concluded.

But regarding the rhapsodes <note>Professional performers of epic poetry, especially Homer</note> and those who follow them, and all the competitions of choruses that must necessarily occur during festivals, these shall be organized for the gods and those after the gods according to the months, days, and years, whether they occur every three years or every five years. Or in whatever way the gods grant a sense of order, the gift shall be followed. Then the musical contests must be held, competing in turn, as arranged by the prize-setters, the teacher of the youth, and the guardians of the laws, meeting together for this common purpose. These leaders of the laws shall themselves organize when, who, and with whom they will hold the contests for all the choruses or dances. What each of these must be—the speech, songs, and harmonies mixed with rhythms and dances—has been said many times by the first legislator. The second legislators must follow these patterns and assign the contests appropriately to each sacrifice at the appointed times, giving festivals to the city to celebrate. These and other such things are not difficult to understand—how they ought to obtain a legal order—nor would changing them one way or the other bring great profit or loss to the city.

<margin>Towards</margin> those things which make no small difference, yet are difficult to teach, this is especially a work of God, if it were somehow possible for the commands to come from him. But as it stands, it requires a bold man who, honoring plain-speaking <note>Greek: *parrhesia*, the right to speak freely and boldly</note> above all, will say what he thinks is best for the city and citizens. In souls corrupted by pleasure, he must establish what is fitting and consistent with the whole state, speaking against the greatest desires and having no human helper, following reason alone.

<margin>Clin.</margin> What argument are we making now, Stranger? For I do not yet understand. <margin>Ath.</margin> Quite right. But I will try to explain it to you even more clearly. When I came to the subject of education in our discussion, I saw young men and young women associating kindly with one another. It occurred to me, as is natural, to be afraid, considering how one would manage such a city in which the young men and women are well-nourished, yet are not subjected to the severe and unfree labor that usually extinguishes insolence. Instead, they care for festivals, sacrifices, and dances throughout their lives. In what way will they abstain from those desires that cast many men and women into the abyss—those desires from which reason commands us to abstain, and which the law attempts to regulate? It would not be surprising if the most important laws regarding the gods were to prevail. For not being allowed to be excessively wealthy is a great help toward temperance, and all our education has laws suited to these things. Furthermore, the eyes of the rulers, forced to look nowhere else but to always watch over the youth, set a limit on other human desires, so far as is humanly possible.

<margin>But you see</margin> But regarding the loves <note>Plato uses the word *eroton*, referring to intense romantic or sexual desire</note> of boys and girls, and of men for women and women for men—from which source thousands of evils have come to individuals and whole cities—how can one guard against these? And what remedy can be found for each of these to escape such danger? It is not at all easy, Clinias. For while Crete and Lacedaemon <note>Sparta</note> help us in many other ways to establish laws different from the customs of many, regarding loves—for we are being honest—they oppose us entirely. For if someone, following nature, were to establish the law that existed before the time of Laius <note>A mythical King of Thebes often blamed for introducing pederasty to Greece</note>, saying that it is right not to have sexual intercourse with males and youths as with females, citing the nature of animals as a witness—showing that the male does not touch the male for this purpose because it is not according to nature—he would perhaps use a persuasive argument, but it would not harmonize with your cities. He would not be in agreement with those things which we all say a legislator must maintain.

We are always seeking which of the established rules leads toward virtue and which does not. Come then, if we agree that this should be legislated as honorable, or at least not shameful, how does that which is sanctioned by law lead to virtue, and what does not?

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> There is an interest in breeding horses, and competing with them is of less concern to the Cretans. For none of you keep chariots, nor do you consider it a noble thing to devote labor to this. Since it is not customary, it seems foolish to establish a law for such competitors. However, for individual horses—those that have not yet shed their foal teeth, the colts, and those of middle and full growth—it is permitted to grant equestrian games according to the nature of the region. Let such a competition, therefore, be according to the law; and in it, let the judgment be granted collectively to the masters of the horses and the tribunes, both for the entire horse race and for those who dismount with arms.

<margin>B</margin> We do not impose a competition or a prize for those who are not armed, either in the gymnastic games or here. But a man who shoots an arrow or throws a javelin from a horse is not useless to Crete. Therefore, in this also, let there be a contest and competition for the sake of sport. To these things, however, women are not to be compelled by laws. But if, by prior discipline and custom, nature rouses girls and virgins to these things and makes them not shrink from them, they are to be admitted. But concerning the exercise and discipline of gymnastics, whether those we perform in competitions or those we practice daily under masters, we have already said enough.

<margin>C</margin> Concerning music also, for the most part. But regarding the rhapsodes (that is, the singers of poems), and those who follow them, and the competition of choruses—however many are necessarily established for the festivities of the gods and spirits <note>Latin: *daemonibus*, referring to tutelary spirits or lesser deities</note> on set days, months, and years—all these things, how they are to be arranged, and if they ought to occur every three or even every five years, are understood and will be acted upon by the counsel of the gods. Then indeed, musical contests will take place in turn, as the prize-declarers themselves, the instructor of the youth, and the guardians of the laws—who have the authority for making laws in these matters—having gathered together, shall have ordered them.

<margin>D</margin> For these men shall organize when, who, and with whom they must perform the individual contests in all the choruses and dances. What each of these should be in terms of speech or harmonies mixed with rhythmic dances has been said many times by the first legislator; whom the later ones following, as will be suitable for the individual sacred times, shall distribute each contest and establish festival days for the city. These things and other such matters are not difficult to understand as to how they should be ordered by laws; nor, if they are changed in this way or that, do they much benefit or harm the city. But there are some things of the greatest importance, which it is so difficult to persuade people of that it seems to be especially the work of God, if they could be established by him.

<margin>E</margin> But now they require the work of some bold man who, relying greatly on freedom of speech, sets down what he judges will be best for the city and citizens, so that he may recall the corrupt minds of the citizens to a decent habit and the observation of the laws, while he opposes their most burning desires, and, lacking all help, alone follows reason alone without fear.
<margin>Clin.</margin> What is it you are saying, Stranger? For we do not understand this.
<margin>Athen.</margin> It is likely so. But I will endeavor to speak more plainly. For when I observed the discipline of life itself and saw young men and young women conversing kindly with one another, I feared, as is natural, considering how anyone would manage a city where the young men and young women are delicate

<margin>F</margin> and have not been tamed by great and very hard labors (by which lust and wantonness are extinguished), but instead spend most of their time on festival days, sacrifices, and dances. How, then, in this city, will they abstain from those desires that have led many to the extreme, so that the reason which commands them to abstain becomes the law? Truly, if the previous laws drive away many desires from us, it is no wonder. For that institution by which excessive wealth is prohibited contributes not a little to temperance, and all the discipline explained by us above has laws suitable for these things. Moreover, the eyes of the princes <note>Latin: *principum*, here referring to the city's rulers or leaders</note>, forced to look nowhere else but to always watch over the youth, apply a limit to other human desires.

<margin>G</margin> But how shall someone avoid the loves of young men and young women against nature, and the abuses of men for women and women for men, from which follow innumerable evils for humans both privately and publicly? And what remedy will he find in the dangers of individuals? It is altogether difficult, O Clinias. For in many other things, all of Crete and Lacedaemon greatly help us in setting down laws far removed from the customs of many; but as far as loves are concerned, they oppose and dissent entirely. Since if someone, following that nature which was before the times of Laius, should establish a law not permitting males to be abused instead of women, and should cite as a witness the nature of beasts, among whom males do not have dealings with one another for Venus <note>Metonymy for sexual activity</note> because it is not at all according to nature, he will perhaps use a plausible reason, but it will not harmonize with your cities. To this is added that he will by no means attain that which must always be observed by a legislator. For it must always be observed what we now agree should be established by law as honorable or not shameful,

Age <note>Catchword: Come (introducing the next thought)</note>

It then transitions to the difficult moral challenge of legislating against natural sexual desires and "unnatural" acts, citing the customs of Crete and Sparta.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue of Plato’s *Laws*, specifically Book VIII. # PLATO'S LAWS

<margin>A</margin>How will this contribute to virtue? Will a habit of courage be bred in the soul of one who is persuaded to submit to a shameful act, or will a kind of temperance be generated in the one who did the persuading? Or would no one ever believe such a thing, but rather believe the opposite? Indeed, everyone will condemn the softness of one who is a slave to pleasures. As for the man who imitates women, will not anyone find fault with that very unmanly <note>original: *muliebrem*, meaning womanly or effeminate</note> image? Who among men, then, will establish this by law when it is of such a nature? Scarcely anyone who has a true law in his mind. How, then, do we say this is true? It is necessary to consider the nature of friendship, of desire, and of the so-called "loves" <note>original: *amorum*; Greek: *erōtōn*</note> if one is to look into these matters correctly. For while there are two distinct types, and a third species arising from both, all covered by a single name, they create great doubt and darkness.

<margin>B</margin><margin>CLINIAS</margin>In what way? <margin>ATHENIAN</margin>We assert that a "friend" is one who is like to like in virtue, and equal to equal. Yet we also call a "friend" one who is in need to one who is wealthy, even though they are opposite in kind. But when either of these feelings becomes more intense, we call it "love." <margin>CLINIAS</margin>Rightly so. <margin>ATHENIAN</margin>Friendship, then, which arises from opposites, is hard and harsh, and often lacks a mutual return in us. But that which comes from those who are alike is gentle and shared throughout life. However, when a goodwill is composed of both, it is first not easy to recognize what the person who loves with this "third love" actually wants; then, being pulled in opposite directions by both,

<margin>C</margin>he is himself in doubt as to what he should do—since he is urged by one side to enjoy the bloom of youth, but forbidden by the other. For he who loves the body, and hungrily seeks its beauty like a kind of fruit, seeks only to be satisfied and offers no honor to the soul of the beloved. But he who cares less for the body, and contemplates the soul rather than desiring it—since he loves the soul itself as is proper—regards the use of the body as an act of insolence <note>original: *petulantiam*; Greek: *hybrin*</note> and an insult. Because he fears and reveres temperance, courage, magnificence, and wisdom, he wishes to live chastely with a chaste friend. But the love composed of both of these is the one we just placed in the third position. Since there are these three loves, should the law 

<margin>D</margin>banish them all? Or should we clearly welcome into the city the one that looks toward virtue and desires the young man to become as good as possible, while we reject the other two, if it be possible? Or does it seem otherwise to you, my friend Megillus? <margin>MEGILLUS</margin>You have spoken very well about these things just now, Stranger. <margin>ATHENIAN</margin>It was not in vain, my friend, that I guessed you would agree with me. I do not need to inquire now what your law <note>The Spartan law, as Megillus is a Spartan</note> feels about these matters, but simply to accept what you admit. I will try to persuade Clinias of this later. For now, let what you have granted be accepted, and let us consider the laws diligently. <margin>MEGILLUS</margin>You speak most correctly. <margin>ATHENIAN</margin>I have a certain technique for establishing this law, which is partly easy, but partly

<margin>E</margin>altogether difficult. <margin>MEGILLUS</margin>How is that? <margin>ATHENIAN</margin>It is a fact even now that many men, however unjust they may be, well and diligently—and not unwillingly, but quite of their own accord—abstain from sexual union with the beautiful. <margin>MEGILLUS</margin>When does that happen? <margin>ATHENIAN</margin>When a brother or sister is of exceptional beauty to someone. The same unwritten law sufficiently repels a son from a daughter, or a daughter from a father, and prohibits both open and secret intercourse of this kind. Indeed, it ensures that not even any desire for such a thing enters the minds of the common people. <margin>MEGILLUS</margin>You speak the truth. <margin>ATHENIAN</margin>Thus, a single and very short word has extinguished all such pleasures.

<margin>F</margin><margin>MEGILLUS</margin>What word is that? <margin>ATHENIAN</margin>The word that says none of these things is "holy" <note>original: *fas*; Greek: *hosia*</note>, but rather they are hated by God and are the most shameful of all shameful things. And is this not the cause? Because no one speaks otherwise, but right from the beginning of life, we hear these same things said both in jest and in earnest; and quite often in tragedies, when they bring on characters like Thyestes, or Oedipus, or certain Macareuses <note>Mythological figures known for unintentional or tragic incest</note> who had secret relations with their sisters, and who, when discovered, are described as immediately choosing death as the due penalty for their crime. <margin>MEGILLUS</margin>That is correctly said. For we know the wonderful power of public opinion <note>original: *famae*; Greek: *phēmēs*</note>, when no one dares to even breathe a word contrary to what the law commands. <margin>ATHENIAN</margin>Was it not rightly said by us, then, that for a legislator wishing to subject people to reason, the method is easy to recognize? Namely, if 

<margin>G</margin>he dedicates such a public opinion among all slaves and free men, and males and females, and the entire city, as something sacred, he will make this law most firm. <margin>MEGILLUS</margin>Quite so. But by what means can he achieve this, so that everyone will say the same thing willingly? <margin>ATHENIAN</margin>A good objection. That is why I said I have a technique for this law: to make men use sexual union according to nature for the sake of procreation <note>original: *procreationem*; Greek: *paidogonias*</note>. I command them, therefore, to abstain from males. For those who use such practices deliberately destroy the human race, sowing upon stones where what is sown can never take root. They should also abstain from the "female field" where the seed would not wish to 

<margin>H</margin>produce offspring. If this law is perpetually preserved in other cases as it is in the case of union with parents, it will be the cause of countless goods. For...

<column-break/>

<summary>In this passage from Plato's Laws, the Athenian Stranger argues for the regulation of sexual desire by categorizing three types of love—bodily, soulful, and mixed—and proposing that legislators use the power of social taboo and "unwritten laws" (similar to those against incest) to promote procreative, heterosexual relationships and prohibit same-sex and non-procreative acts.</summary>

# ON THE LAWS, BOOK VIII

<margin>A</margin> will first be established according to nature. Next, it will repel every madness and fury of love, as well as adulteries and the excessive luxury of food and drink. It will reconcile husbands to their wives and produce many other benefits, provided it remains stable in everyone's life. But perhaps if some hot-blooded young man, full of vigor <note>original: *multo spermate plenus*, literally "full of much seed"</note>, hears this law being proposed, he will immediately reject it. He will shout at the top of his voice that we are decreeing impossible and foolish things by law. When I considered this, I said I possessed a method <note>original: *artem*, meaning an art or technique</note> that is in one way very easy, but in another very difficult, for observing this law. For it is easy to understand how it is possible. <margin>B</margin> For when this legal opinion has been dedicated among all people, it will master every soul and ensure that they obey the established laws out of fear. But the matter has now reached a point where it seems it can never be achieved—just as it was once believed that the practice of communal meals could not be observed perpetually by an entire city. And yet, among us, it seems to be happening in reality, something which is not thought possible among women, nor even in your own cities. For this reason, because of the force of this disbelief, I said it was very difficult for both of these laws to be observed. <term>megillus</term>. And you are quite right. <term>athenian</term>. But since these things are not beyond human strength, but are indeed possible, do you want me to <margin>C</margin> explain a certain plausible reason to you? <term>cleinias</term>. Why not? <term>athenian</term>. Who will more easily abstain from sexual matters and choose to observe the order imposed on them with moderation? One whose body is well-conditioned through some wise diligence, or one who is not? <term>cleinias</term>. Much more so the one who is well-conditioned and trained by art. <term>athenian</term>. Have we not heard of Iccus of Tarentum? <note>Iccus was a famous 5th-century BC athlete and physician known for his strict diet and asceticism.</note> Because of the Olympic and other contests, he achieved temperance alongside strength of soul through a skillful devotion to these things. It is said he never touched a woman, nor even a boy, during the entire peak of his training. The same is told of Crisson, Astyllus, Diopompus, and <margin>D</margin> many others. And yet, O Cleinias, they had cultivated their souls with much poorer arts than your citizens or mine, though they were certainly much more vigorous in their bodies. <term>cleinias</term>. You tell the truth; the ancients often proclaimed that these things were done by those athletes. <term>athenian</term>. They, therefore, in order to conquer others in wrestling, running, and such things, were willing to abstain from that pleasure which is commonly thought to be "blissful." Will our young men be unable to endure for the sake of a far more excellent victory? We have taught them from their earliest childhood through songs, stories, prose, and chants that this victory is the best—and, as is likely, we shall persuade them by delighting them. <term>cleinias</term>. Which victory do you mean? <term>athenian</term>. The victory over pleasure, I say, so that they may live happily. If they are conquered, it is the <margin>E</margin> opposite. Moreover, will not that fear—that it is by no means holy to commit such acts—contribute most to this end? Namely, that they should overcome those things which others, who are worse in every way, are said to have overcome? <term>cleinias</term>. That is certainly consistent. <term>athenian</term>. Since we have reached this point in proposing this law, and have fallen into doubt because of the wickedness of the many, let us now say boldly and clearly: it is not right that our citizens should be worse than birds and many wild beasts. For we see many of their flocks living purely and chastely until the time for procreation arrives. But when they reach this age, male is joined to female and female to male, and <margin>F</margin> they live out the rest of their lives justly and holily, persevering in their first friendship. It is necessary, therefore, for humans to be better than beasts. But if they are corrupted by many other Greeks and Barbarians, and cannot contain themselves when they see and hear that disordered lust <note>original: *Venerem*, referring to Venus/Aphrodite, the goddess of sex</note> has great power among them, then the guardians of the laws, having gained the authority to make laws, should devise a second law. <term>cleinias</term>. What law do you advise them to make now, if they do not accept the first one? <term>athenian</term>. The one that follows this, O Cleinias. <term>cleinias</term>. Which one is that? <term>athenian</term>. That they should break the strength of lust as much as possible through physical labor, and turn their energies elsewhere. This will happen if they do not <margin>G</margin> use it impudently. For if it happens more rarely because of shame <note>original: *rubore*, literally "redness" or blushing</note>, the mistress [Pleasure] will be weaker. Let custom and unwritten law, therefore, persuade them that these things be done in secret; and let it conversely dissuade them from doing them openly as something shameful. Indeed, to act so entirely would be shameful. In this way, we shall preserve what is honorable in a second degree, and one class of men, containing three types—those of a depraved nature whom we deny are masters of themselves—will be compelled not to despise the laws. <term>cleinias</term>. What are these three types? <term>athenian</term>. I mean those who worship the gods, those who love honor, and those who love the beauty of the character of the soul, rather than bodies. These things are spoken as if in a story or a prayer; nevertheless, they would contribute much to all cities if they could be observed. <margin>H</margin> Perhaps, if God wills, we shall achieve one of two things in matters of love. Either that no one dares to touch noble and free women except his own wife, nor anyone begets bastards by a concubine, nor sows in the infertile fields of males against nature. Or we shall entirely remove one of these: that no one should have intercourse with males. If anyone should consort with other women than 

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> first according to nature will be established. Then it will repel from all madness and fury of loves, from adulteries, and from excessive luxury of drink and food. It will also reconcile husbands to their wives, and produce many other goods, if it were stable with anyone. But perhaps if some vehement young man full of much seed hears this law being brought, he will immediately disapprove, and will cry out with a loud voice that impossible and stupid things are sanctioned by us by law. Which indeed, when I considered, I said that I have an art, in a certain way very easy, in a certain way also very difficult, for observing this law. For it is easy to understand how it is possible. <margin>B</margin> For when this legitimate sentiment has been dedicated among all, it will tame all minds, and will bring it about that they obey the laws brought by fear. But the matter has now come to this, that it seems it can never be brought about: just as not even the study of the banquet was believed to be able to be observed perpetually by the whole city. And yet among us it seems to happen in reality, which is thought not to be able to happen among women, nor even in your cities. For this very reason, because of the power of this incredulity, I said it was very difficult for these to be served by both laws. <term>megillus</term>. And rightly indeed. <term>athenian</term>. But because they are not above human strength, but can happen, do you want me <margin>C</margin> to set out a certain plausible reason to you? <term>cleinias</term>. Why not? <term>athenian</term>. Whether will someone more easily abstain from venereal things: and wants to serve the order imposed on these moderately, when the body has been well affected from some prudent diligence: or when on the contrary? <term>cleinias</term>. Much more when well and by art. <term>athenian</term>. Have we not then heard of Iccus the Tarentine: who on account of the Olympic and other contests, having attained temperance and at the same time fortitude of mind by a skillful study about these things, knew no Venus <note>original: *Venerem*, here meaning sexual intercourse</note> ever in the whole time of his exercise? The same is also told of Crisson, Astyllus, and Diopompus and many others. Although, O Cleinias, they had cultivated their minds with good arts much <margin>D</margin> worse than your and my citizens, they certainly flourished much more in their bodies. <term>cleinias</term>. You tell true things that those things are preached to have been done by athletes of old. <term>athenian</term>. They therefore, so that they might conquer others by wrestling and running and other things of this kind, wanted to abstain from that pleasure which is commonly thought blessed. Our adolescents, for the sake of a victory by far more excellent, will they not be able to [abstain]? Which victory we have taught to be best for boys immediately from their tender years by songs and stories and loose speech and chants, and as is likely, we will persuade by delighting. <term>cleinias</term>. Which victory do you speak of? <term>athenian</term>. That having conquered pleasure, I say, they may live happily; but if conquered, <margin>E</margin> on the contrary. Furthermore, that fear, lest what is not at all right be committed, will it not contribute most to the same: so that it overcomes those things which others, worse than any, are said to have overcome? <term>cleinias</term>. That is indeed consistent. <term>athenian</term>. After we have come here in bringing this law, and have fallen into doubt because of the depravity of many, let us now speak boldly and clearly, that it is not fitting that our citizens be worse than birds and many beasts. For we see very many of their flocks living integrally and chastely before the time for procreating comes: but when they have reached this age, male joined to female and female to male, <margin>F</margin> they spend the rest of their life justly and holily, persevering in their first friendship. It is necessary therefore that they be better than beasts. But if they are corrupted by the rest of the Greeks and very many Barbarians, and cannot contain themselves when they see and hear that disordered Venus has very much power among them, let the guardians of the laws, having obtained authority for bringing laws, devise another law besides. <term>cleinias</term>. What law do you consult to bring now, if they have not received this one? <term>athenian</term>. That which follows this, O Cleinias. <term>cleinias</term>. Which is that? <term>athenian</term>. But that they should break the strength of Venus as much as possible by labors of the body, and turn their strengths elsewhere. Which will be, if they do not <margin>G</margin> use it impudently. For if it happens more rarely because of shame, the mistress will be weaker. Let custom therefore and unwritten law persuade these things to be done secretly: but on the contrary dissuade them from being done as if shameful? and thus altogether shameful to act. For thus we shall also serve the honorable in the second place, and one kind of humans, containing three kinds, men of depraved nature, whom we deny to be masters of themselves, it will certainly compel lest they despise the laws. <term>cleinias</term>. Which three kinds? <term>athenian</term>. Worshippers of the gods, I say, lovers of honor, and those who love not the beauty of bodies but of the character of the mind. These things spoken as if through a story and similar to a prayer: nevertheless they will contribute much to all cities if they have been able to serve them. <margin>H</margin> Perhaps however, if God wills, we shall obtain one of two things in amatory affairs. Either that no one dares to touch noble and free women besides his wife: nor let any receive bastards from a concubine: nor let him bring into the unfruitful fields of males against nature. <summary>In this passage, the Athenian Stranger argues that citizens should be capable of self-restraint regarding sexual desires, citing the historical example of athletes like Iccus of Tarentum who remained celibate to win competitions. He proposes that if moral education fails, a "second law" of physical labor and social shame should be used to regulate conduct.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Book VIII of Plato's Laws. The previous page ended with the Athenian Stranger arguing that strict laws regarding sexual conduct—restricting it to marriage and procreation—are not only beneficial but achievable through the force of social custom and religious reverence. # PLATO

<margin>A</margin> ...with those women who have entered the home through the gods and sacred marriages, whether they were purchased <note>original: *emptis*, likely referring to enslaved women</note> or acquired in any other way. Unless these acts are hidden from all men and women alike, let the man be infamous by law and deprived of all the honors of the city, as if he were a mere foreigner. Let this law, whether it be simple or double, be enacted concerning all sexual and amorous matters, through which we act rightly or wrongly toward one another because of such passions. MEGILLUS: I, for my part, strongly approve of this law. But let Clinias here reveal what he thinks. CLINIAS: I shall do so, Megillus, when the opportunity arises. For now, however, let us allow our guest to proceed further in the proposal of his laws. MEGILLUS: Very well. ATHENIAN: 
<margin>B</margin> But we have now progressed so far that we have come to the matter of communal meals. <note>original: *conuiuia* in Latin; *syssitia* in Greek</note> We have said elsewhere that this is a difficult matter to establish, but in Crete, no one would think it out of place. Whether the method used here, or that used by the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note>, or a third way better than both can be found, does not seem difficult to me to discover; nor, once found, would it be of great benefit, for the current arrangements seem fitting enough. It follows now that we should speak of sustenance and how it may be obtained. In other cities, sustenance is of many kinds and comes from many places; in most, it is acquired from two sources. For to most Greek cities, food is brought both from the sea and from the land, but to these people, it comes from the land alone. This makes the legislator's task easier. 
<margin>C</margin> For much less than half the usual number of laws will suffice, and furthermore, these laws will be more suitable for free men. For the lawgiver is not forced to make a thousand laws concerning shipping, merchants, retailers, innkeepers, tax collectors, mines, loans, usury, and a myriad of such things. Instead, in this city of ours, the lawgiver, having set these aside, will give laws only to farmers, shepherds, keepers of bees, and those who guard and manage such things—having already treated for the most part the matters of marriage, the procreation and education of children, and the appointment of magistrates. Now, therefore, we must 
<margin>D</margin> come to the laws regarding sustenance and those who provide it through their labor. And let the laws of agriculture be placed first. First is the law of Zeus of the Boundaries <note>original Latin: *Iouis terminalis*; Greek: *Dios horiou*</note>: Let no one move the boundaries and markers of a field, neither those of a fellow citizen who is a neighbor, nor those of a neighbor who is a foreigner on the edge of the territory. Let everyone consider that the common saying is true: "do not move the immovable." <note>A Greek proverb, *akineta kinein*, referring to ancient or sacred customs and boundaries.</note> Each man should prefer to move a massive boulder rather than a small stone that has been fixed by an oath from the gods to mark the limits of friendship and enmity. For in one case, Zeus of the Clan is a witness, and in the other, Zeus of Hospitality—gods who always rise up in the most hostile strife. He who obeys the law shall be free from harm; but he who despises it shall suffer a double penalty: first from the god as avenger, 
<margin>E</margin> and second from the law. For the law commands that no one shall move the boundaries of a neighbor's field by his own will. If anyone does move them, let whoever wishes report him to the rural wardens; the wardens shall bring him to court, and if he is convicted as a disturber of boundaries through stealth or force, the court shall decide what he must suffer or pay. Furthermore, many small damages occurring between neighbors, by happening frequently, breed great enmities and make neighborly life difficult and bitter. Therefore, a neighbor must take every care not to harm his neighbor, both in other matters and especially in the cultivation of the land. To do harm is not difficult, but is within the power of any man; however, to do good 
<margin>F</margin> is not within the power of everyone. Whoever crosses the boundaries and cultivates a neighbor's land shall restore the damage and, as a cure for his impudence and illiberality, he shall pay twice the amount of the damage to the one whose land he cultivated. The inspectors, judges, and assessors of such matters shall be the rural wardens <note>original: *agronomoi*</note>. In greater matters, as was said before, the entire order of the twelfth part shall judge; in lesser matters, those who are the commanders of the guards. If anyone harms pastures, they shall judge and condemn after considering the damages. If someone pursues another’s swarm of bees, and by beating on brass draws the bees to himself for his own delight, he shall restore the damage. If anyone sets fire to wood without taking care for his neighbor, he shall be fined as the magistrates see fit. Similarly, one who does not leave the proper measure of space when planting near a neighbor's field shall be punished as has been 
<margin>G</margin> sufficiently stated by many legislators. We ought to use their laws and not think that many small things, which are the duty of any ordinary lawgiver, must be handled by the great founder of a city. For there are also ancient and good laws established for farmers concerning water. These should not be diverted by our discourse. But he who wishes to lead water to his own land should draw it from public springs in such a way (that he does not disturb the visible spring of any private person. He may lead it however he wishes,) except through houses, or tombs, or places consecrated to the gods; nor should he cause any other damage except that which is caused by the channel itself. If, in certain places, the soil is naturally dry and does not retain the waters coming from Zeus <note>rainwater</note>, and someone is oppressed by necessity, let him dig on his own land down to the layer of clay; and if at this depth he finds no water, let him draw as much from his neighbors as necessity requires. But if water is also scarce for the neighbors, the measure of drawing water...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...with the women who entered the house through the gods and sacred marriages, whether purchased or acquired in any other way, without it being hidden from all men and women. If we legislate that such a man should be dishonored in the city, we would seem to legislate correctly, as he is truly acting like a foreigner. Let this be the law, whether one or two are needed, concerning the matters of Aphrodite and all erotic things, and how people interact with one another because of such desires, whether they act rightly or not. MEGILLUS: Indeed, Stranger, I would most gladly accept this law; but let Clinias here say for himself what he thinks. CLINIAS: These things shall be, 
<margin>B</margin> Megillus, whenever it seems to me to be the right time. For now, let us let the Stranger finish the law on the matters before us. MEGILLUS: Correct. ATHENIAN: Indeed, we are now almost at the point of having organized the communal life regarding sustenance. Such a habit is poor and difficult elsewhere, but in Crete, no one would think it should be otherwise. As for the manner—whether it should be as it is here, or as it is in Lacedaemon, or if there is some third kind of communal meal better than both—this does not seem difficult to me to find, nor would its discovery achieve any great good, for the current arrangements are not without harmony. Following these things is the arrangement of life, or the way those assigned to it should follow. In other 
<margin>C</margin> cities, life might be of all sorts and from many sources; especially from two. For most Greeks get their sustenance from both the land and the sea; but for these people, it is only from the land. This is easier for your legislator. For he does not only have half as many laws to make, but far fewer, and those are most fitting for free men. For he is largely freed from matters of shipping and commerce, and retail, and innkeeping, and taxes, and mines, and lending, and compound interest, and ten thousand other such things, having bid them farewell. Instead, the legislator organizes the city for farmers, shepherds, and bee-keepers, and those who guard and oversee such tools; he has already legislated the greatest things concerning 
<margin>D</margin> marriage and the birth of children and their upbringing, and also education and the establishment of offices in the city. But now it is necessary for the legislator to turn to the laws of sustenance and those who provide the means of life. First, let there be a law of the farmer, of Zeus of the Boundaries <note>original: *Zeus Horios*</note>, who does not allow boundaries to be moved. Let the law be spoken thus: let no one move the boundaries of land, neither of a fellow citizen who is a neighbor, nor of one who shares the border on the edge of the territory, belonging to a foreign neighbor; believing that to move the immovable is truly this. Every man should wish to attempt to move the greatest of other things rather than a boundary-stone, however small, which is an oath-bound friendship and enmity from the gods. For of the one, Zeus of the Kindred is witness; of the other, Zeus of Hospitality; who are stirred up with the most hateful wars. 
<margin>E</margin> And he who obeys the law shall be free from harm; but evil will come to him who is a descendant of those who despise it. Let him be subject to double penalties: one from the gods and their kind, and the second from the law. For let no one willingly move the boundaries of neighbors' land. If anyone does move them, let whoever wishes inform the rural wardens, and let them bring him to the court. If anyone is convicted of such a suit—as if the person convicted were making the land undivided by stealth and force—let the court assess what the loser must suffer or pay. After this, many small damages occur between neighbors, which, because they happen often, breed not a small enmity, and produce a difficult and very bitter neighborhood. Therefore, one must take every precaution that a neighbor does nothing 
<margin>F</margin> to offend a neighbor, in all other things and especially in all matters of cultivation, always guarding it strictly. For to do harm is nothing difficult, but is the part of every man; but to be beneficial is in no way the part of everyone. Whoever cultivates his neighbor’s land, overstepping the boundaries, let him pay for the damage; and as a cure for his impudence and illiberality, let him pay another sum double the damage to the one who was harmed. Of these and all such things, the rural wardens shall be the overseers, judges, and assessors. In the greater matters, as was said before, the entire order of the twelfth part shall judge; 
<margin>G</margin> in the smaller matters, the commanders of the guards. If anyone grazes livestock on another's land, seeing the damage, they shall judge and assess it. And if anyone appropriates another's swarms, following the pleasure of the bees and striking brass to make them his own, let him pay the damage. And if anyone, using fire, is not careful with the wood belonging to his neighbor, let him be fined the penalty decided by the magistrates. And if anyone, when planting, does not leave the proper measure of distance from the neighbor's property, as has been said sufficiently by many legislators. We should use their laws and not demand that the great organizer of the city legislate all the many and small things that are the part of a human legislator. Since also concerning water, there are old and good laws laid down for all farmers, which it is not worth diverting with words. But he who wishes to bring water to his own place, let him begin from the public streams, not cutting off the visible springs of anyone; he may lead it wherever he wishes, except through a house, or temples, or tombs, without penalty, except for the actual construction of the channel. If some places are naturally dry of earth-born water and do not receive the streams coming from Zeus, or if they lack the necessary drink, let him dig on his own land as far as the clay soil. If at this depth he does not happen upon water at all, let him draw water from the neighbors until the necessary drink...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Book VIII of Plato’s Laws, transitioning from moral and sexual regulations to the practical management of agricultural land, water rights, and the division of labor within the ideal city. It specifically focuses on the legal duties of farmers and the protection of natural resources.</meta>

### ON THE LAWS, BOOK VIII

<margin>A</margin> ...should be determined daily by the wardens of the fields. <note>original: *agri curatoribus* in Latin; *agronomois* in Greek</note> If, however, there is an abundance of rainwater, and those who inhabit or cultivate the lower-lying areas prevent the flow of water so as to harm those above them; or, conversely, if the one living above thoughtlessly allows the water to flood down and harm the one below, and they are unable to come to an agreement among themselves: then in the city the city-warden <note>original: *aedilis* / *astynomos*</note> shall intervene, and in the fields the rural-warden shall impose a limit. If anyone does not observe this limit, they shall suffer the penalty for their spiteful and perverse soul, and they must pay double the amount of the damage to their neighbor for refusing to obey the officials.

<margin>B</margin> Regarding the fruits of the harvest, there shall be a shared participation of this kind. The god <note>Dionysus</note> has granted us two types of gracious gifts: one is the Dionysian gift <note>grapes/wine</note> which cannot be stored away, and the other is that which is suited for preservation. Let this law, therefore, be established concerning fruit: whoever tastes "rustic" <note>wild or common</note> grapes or figs before the time of the vintage—which coincides with the rising of the star Arcturus <note>late September, marking the start of the harvest</note>—whether they gather them from their own field or another’s, shall be liable to pay fifty drachmas dedicated to Dionysus if they gathered from their own land. If they took them from a neighbor’s land, they shall pay a mina; and if from elsewhere, two-thirds of a mina. 

As for the "noble" grapes or figs <note>cultivated varieties</note>, a man may gather his own whenever and however he wishes. But if he takes those belonging to another without permission, following the law that "no one shall move what he did not set down," he shall always be fined. If a slave touches such fruits without the master’s permission, he shall be whipped with a rod, receiving a lash for every grape in the cluster or every fig taken.

<margin>C</margin> A resident alien <note>original: *inquilinus* / *metikos*</note> may eat the noble fruits he has purchased, if they are not meant for storage. If a foreigner <note>original: *peregrinus* / *xenos*</note> is traveling along the road and desires to eat such fruit, he may, as a gesture of hospitality, taste the noble fruit along his journey, either alone or with one companion, without payment. However, the law shall prohibit foreigners from sharing in the "rustic" fruits. If anyone—whether a master or a slave—touches these inappropriately, the slave shall be punished with lashes, while the free man shall be dismissed with a warning, being taught to touch only the fruits that are not meant for storage, <margin>D</margin> and to leave aside those from which raisins, wine, and dried figs are made. 

As for pears, apples, pomegranates, and similar fruits, it shall not be considered a disgrace to take them secretly. However, if anyone under thirty years of age is caught doing so, he may be struck and beaten as a punishment, provided no wounds are inflicted; no legal action shall be taken for such a beating of a free man. A stranger may partake of these fruits just as they do with the harvest fruits mentioned before. If an elder eats them on the spot without carrying any away, he, like the stranger, may share in them. But if he does not obey this law, he risks being judged as a man lacking in virtue if the matter is brought before the presiding judges.

<margin>E</margin> Water is the most nourishing element for gardens, but it is also the most easily corrupted. While the earth, sun, and air also nourish what grows from the ground, they are not easily spoiled by poisons, diversions, or theft; water, however, is susceptible to all these. Therefore, it requires the protection of the law. Let this be the law: if anyone intentionally corrupts another's water—whether it be a spring or collected water—by means of poison, digging, or theft, the injured party shall bring the case before the city-wardens, declaring the value of the damage. If a person is convicted of causing harm by poisoning, they must not only pay the fine but also purify the springs or the water vessel in whatever manner the Interpreters <note>original: *exegetai*; religious officials who explained sacred laws and rituals of purification</note> dictate that the purification should be performed.

<margin>F</margin> Regarding the transportation of all harvested goods, anyone may move their property through any place they wish, provided they either cause no damage to anyone or if the profit they gain is triple the value of the damage caused to the neighbor. The magistrates shall be the judges of these matters, and of all other cases where one person harms another—whether by force, or in secret, or through their property—whether intentionally or unintentionally. All such matters should be brought to the magistrates if the damage does not exceed three minae. If the claim is greater, the case should be brought to the public courts, and the wrongdoer punished. 

If any magistrate is thought to have judged a damage claim unfairly, he shall be liable to pay double the amount to the person who suffered the wrong. Any citizen who wishes may bring charges against a magistrate for such misconduct in a public court. There are nearly infinite minor regulations regarding the filing of lawsuits, summons, and witnesses—whether the summons is between two people or many—and all such things that cannot be omitted from the laws, but which seem unworthy of a senior legislator. Therefore, the younger legislators should establish these by imitating the ancient laws, applying great principles to small matters and learning from practical experience until everything is sufficiently settled. Once they are established, they should be kept immutable for the use of the inhabitants.

<margin>G</margin> Regarding the other craftsmen, the laws should be as follows: First, no citizen shall be occupied in any craft, nor shall any slave of a citizen. For a citizen is occupied with a great art that requires long practice and much study—namely, the maintenance and preservation of the common order of the city—a task that is not a side-work but requires primary devotion. No man can accurately master two arts or two studies...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...let it be established daily by the field-wardens. But if the rainwater is excessive, and those who inhabit or cultivate the lower parts block the flow so as to harm those above: or conversely, if the one above heedlessly lets the water flow and harms the one below; and they cannot agree between themselves: in the city, the city-warden <note>aedile</note>, and in the fields, the one in charge of the fields, shall impose the manner [of drainage]. If anyone does not observe this, let him pay the penalty for his envy and perversity: and restore double the damage to his neighbor.

<margin>B</margin> Let the common participation in the fruits of autumn be of this sort. This god gives us two gifts of grace. One is the gift of Dionysus, which cannot be stored; the other is that which is fit for storing. Let this law be sanctioned regarding fruits: Whoever tastes grapes or figs from the "rustic" fruits before the time of the vintage, which occurs with the rising of Arcturus, let him pay fifty drachmas to be dedicated to Dionysus if he gathered them from his own field. But if he took them from neighbors, a mina; and if from others, two-thirds of a mina. But as for the grapes or figs which we have called "noble," which cannot be stored in the same way, let him gather them when and how he wishes if they are his own. But if they belong to another, unless he has obtained permission—since the law is that no one should move what he did not put down—let the one who took them be fined. If a slave takes them without the master of the field being persuaded, let him suffer a number of lashes equal to the number of figs or grapes taken.

<margin>C</margin> A resident alien, if he has bought fruits that cannot be stored, may eat them if he wishes. A foreigner on a journey, if he passes through alone or with only one companion, may taste the non-storable fruit with "hospitality-pardon" if he wishes. But as for tasting others which we call "rustic," the law shall also prohibit foreigners. But if someone touches the figs that can be stored, if he is a slave, let him be punished. If he is a free man, let him be sent away with a warning that it is only permitted to taste grapes and figs that cannot be stored, and by no means those from which raisins, wine, and dried figs are made. Regarding pears and apples, and also pomegranates and others of this kind, let it not be shameful to take them secretly. 

<margin>D</margin> If anyone is caught who is younger than thirty years old, let him be beaten without wounding and punished. There shall be no penalty for a free man who administers such a beating. A newcomer may also pluck these fruits just as he may the non-storable ones we spoke of above. If an elder eats them but does not carry them away, as is permitted to the newcomer, he too may share in all such fruits. But if he does not obey the law, let him be held unfit for the contest of virtue, if this is reported to the judges presiding over this matter.

<margin>E</margin> Water is the most beneficial of all things for nourishing gardens, but it is easily corrupted. Earth, sun, and air nourish things along with water; the things that grow from the earth cannot easily be corrupted by poison, diversion, or removal. But water is easily harmed in these ways, and therefore needs the help of the law. Regarding this, let this law be sanctioned: If anyone willfully corrupts another's water—whether springing from fountains or collected—by poison, pits, or removal, let him be reported to the city-wardens. If he is convicted of wrongdoing, let him restore the damage; and let him purify the springs or water vessels as the Interpreters judge the purification should be done in each case.

<margin>F</margin> In the transport of all things gathered from the fields, let everyone be permitted to carry their goods through whatever place they wish, provided it is either of no damage to anyone, or it results in triple profit to himself compared to the damage caused to the neighbor. The judges of these things shall be the magistrates, as well as for all other things that someone intentionally does by injury, either by force or secretly, either by himself or through his property, against a person or a thing. All these things, I say, should be brought to the magistrates if the damage does not exceed three minae. But if it is greater, the case should be brought to the publicly constituted courts, and the one who caused the injury should be punished. If any of the magistrates brings an unjust sentence regarding someone's damage, he shall owe double to the one who suffered the injury. And generally, if the magistrates do anything by injury, the case itself may be driven in a public court by anyone who wishes. There remain almost infinite small institutions by which errors are corrected in the legal process, in citations, and in the summoners, whether the citation is between two or many, and other things of this kind, which can neither be passed over by the laws, nor yet seem worthy of a senior lawgiver. Therefore, let the younger men, imitating the ancient laws and understanding small things from great ones, and knowing the necessary use by experience, ordain these until the laws are sufficient. Then, once they are sufficiently placed, let them use them immutably.

<margin>G</margin> Regarding other craftsmen, let the laws be so constituted: First, let no citizen be held by any one craft, nor even a slave of any citizen. For a citizen is occupied in a great art which requires long exercise and many teachings, since he provides for the common ornament of the city; a matter which is not satisfied by some light work, but requires primary study. Indeed, two arts or studies...

It also establishes that citizens must focus entirely on civic virtue and governance, prohibiting them from practicing manual crafts.</summary>
