<meta>This page continues the legal code of Plato's "Laws," moving from agricultural regulations to the professional organization of the city and the distribution of resources. It outlines the "one man, one trade" rule and the logistical layout of the ideal state.</meta>

# PLATO'S LAWS

<margin>A</margin> Human nature is hardly capable of practicing two things diligently at once. Nor can anyone master one art effectively while also overseeing the work of another craftsman. Therefore, this shall be the established rule in our city: no blacksmith shall simultaneously be a carpenter, nor shall a carpenter prioritize overseeing other blacksmiths over his own craft. He might offer the plausible excuse that, because he employs many servants and workers, he can better practice his art by overseeing them to gain a greater profit; however, individual craftsmen must devote themselves to a single art and derive their living from it alone. The city-wardens <note>original Latin: *aediles*; Greek: *astynomoi*</note> shall ensure this law is observed, so that if a citizen turns toward a craft more than toward the cultivation of virtue, they shall redirect him to his proper course through reproach and disgrace. If, however, <margin>B</margin> any foreigner attempts to practice two crafts, they shall be compelled to embrace only one through imprisonment, fines, or expulsion. Regarding the wages of craftsmen, and the approval or rejection of their work, as well as any injuries they suffer or inflict, the city-wardens shall judge cases up to fifty drachmas. Matters of greater value shall be decided in the public courts according to the law. Furthermore, there shall be absolutely no tax on the import or export of goods. As for incense and other such things used for burning in honor of the gods, which are foreign products, or purple dye and other colors not produced within the region—in short, any foreign goods—no one shall import them unless they are strictly necessary. Conversely, no one shall export anything <margin>C</margin> that is necessary for the region. The twelve remaining Guardians of the Laws <note>original: *nomophylakes*</note>, excluding the five eldest, shall oversee and adjudicate these matters. Weapons and instruments of war, if foreign craftsmanship is required, may be imported; likewise, materials suitable for these, such as plants, bronze tools, ropes, and animals useful for war. The commanders of the cavalry and the leaders of the army shall have charge of these, ensuring the city is not deprived of the ability to import or export them when needed; the Guardians of the Laws shall establish sufficient and appropriate laws regarding them. No retail trade <note>original Latin: *cauponatio*; Greek: *kapēleia* — refers to small-scale reselling for profit, which Plato viewed with suspicion</note> for the sake of money-making shall be conducted, either in the city or in the surrounding territory. The distribution of the harvest gathered from the fields shall be rightly established according to the Cretan law. For those things <margin>D</margin> produced by the region must be distributed by everyone into twelve parts, and consumed in a like manner. Each twelfth part—of wheat, barley, and other crops and fruits, as well as all saleable animals—shall be divided into three proportionate shares: one share for the free citizens, a second for the servants, and a third for the craftsmen and all foreigners. This applies whether they have come from elsewhere to inhabit the city for a time and lack necessities, or if they have arrived for the public or private benefit of some citizen. This third part of all necessary goods must always be for sale, and necessarily so. Regarding the other two parts, nothing <margin>E</margin> essential shall be sold. How then shall these be rightly distributed? It is clear, first of all, that this can be done rightly if the distribution is made partly equally and partly unequally.

**Cleinias:** In what way? 
**Athenian:** It is inevitable that the earth will produce and grow some things that are better and others that are worse. 
**Cleinias:** Of course. 
**Athenian:** Since there are three parts, as far as this is concerned, no one—neither master, nor servant, nor foreigner—should have more than another, but every distribution should be equal and similar for all. However, each citizen, having received two parts, shall distribute to his servants and family whatever amount and quality he chooses at his own discretion. The portion exceeding these must be distributed by measure and number so that when the total number of all animals fed by the earth is known, the partition can finally be made. Habitats <margin>F</margin> must then be arranged separately. The following order is most fitting: there should be twelve villages, one in the middle of each of the twelve districts. In each village, there shall be marketplaces, temples for the gods, and shrines for the spirits <note>original: *daemonum*</note> who follow the gods—whether they be local Magnesian heroes or others whose statues have been consecrated from ancient memory. To these, the honors of men of old must be rendered. Temples of Hestia, Zeus, and Athena, and of whichever god presides over each of the twelve districts, shall be established; and in the highest places, there shall be highly fortified dwellings for the guards. The rest of the region shall then be distributed to the craftsmen in thirteen parts. One part shall live in the city, divided among the twelve quarters of the city; the others shall occupy the outer areas all around, and in each village, craftsmen suitable for the convenience of agriculture shall dwell <margin>G</margin> together. They shall foresee how many and what kind of craftsmen each area needs, and where they should live so as not to be an impediment to the farmers, but rather to bring them great utility. The city-wardens shall similarly take care of the urban craftsmen. Goods for sale shall be the responsibility of the market-wardens, who shall first attend to sacred matters, and then take great care that no one commits an injustice in buying or selling, and they shall restrain all who are immoderate or insolent. They shall consider whether the citizens provide individual items to foreigners in a proper manner and as the law requires...

<column-break/>

...human nature is capable of practicing. Nor, again, <margin>A</margin> can they sufficiently train themselves while also overseeing another who is training. This, therefore, must be established as a ruling principle in the city: no one who works as a blacksmith shall also be a carpenter, nor shall a carpenter, while practicing his craft, oversee blacksmiths rather than his own art. He might have the excuse that, since he is producing many works for himself through many servants, he naturally takes more care of them, from which he gains more profit than from his own craft. Instead, each person in the city shall possess one craft and earn his living from it. The city-wardens should care to preserve this law. If a local citizen inclines toward a craft rather than toward <margin>B</margin> the cultivation of virtue, they shall punish him with reproaches and dishonor until they direct him back to his own course. If any foreigner practices two crafts, they shall punish him with bonds, fines, and expulsion from the city, compelling him to be one thing only and not many. Regarding their wages and the delivery of works, and if one person wrongs them or if they wrong another, the city-wardens shall judge up to fifty drachmas. For amounts greater than this, the public courts shall decide according to the law. No one shall pay any tax to the city, either <margin>C</margin> on exported goods or on imported goods. As for frankincense and whatever foreign incense is used for the gods, and purple dye, and whatever dyes and colors the land does not produce, or whatever requires the import of foreign goods to the land—no one shall bring these in for the sake of luxury, nor shall anyone export what is necessary for the land to keep. Of all these matters, twelve of the Guardians of the Laws, excluding the elders, shall be the judges and overseers. Regarding weapons and all instruments that assist in war, if there is a need to import any craft, or plants, or metal weaving, or ropes, or animals for such use, the commanders of the horse and the generals shall be in charge of these imports and exports, both giving to and receiving for the city. The Guardians of the Laws shall establish the appropriate and sufficient laws concerning these things. No retail trade for the sake of money-making, either for this or for any other purpose, <margin>D</margin> shall exist in the land or city. Regarding the food and distribution of the produce of the land, one would live rightly if it were done in a manner close to the Cretan law. It is necessary for everyone to distribute all the produce of the land into twelve parts, according to how it is to be consumed. Each of the twelve parts—such as wheat and barley, which all other seasonal produce should follow, and all saleable animals—must be divided in this way: there shall be three shares. One for the free citizens; one for their servants; and the third for the craftsmen and all the foreigners—whoever may be living together as residents, needing a certain supply of food, and whatever need of the city or of some individual may happen at any time. <margin>E</margin> Of all the necessary goods, only this third part shall be for sale by necessity; of the other two parts, there shall be no necessity to sell. How then would such things be most rightly distributed? First, it is clear that we distribute some things equally and others unequally. **Cleinias:** How do you mean? **Athenian:** It is necessary for the earth to grow and bring forth each of these things in both worse and better quality. **Cleinias:** Certainly. **Athenian:** In this matter, then, of the three parts, let no one have more, whether distributed to masters, or servants, or foreigners; but let the distribution grant the same equality of likeness to all. Each citizen, having received the two parts for his household, shall have authority over the distribution to both servants and free persons, in whatever amount and of whatever kind he wishes to distribute. The part <margin>F</margin> beyond this in measure and number must be distributed in this way: taking the number of all animals that must be fed from the earth, one should make the distribution. After this, there must be separate dwellings arranged for them. Such an order would be fitting for these things: there should be twelve villages, one in the center of each twelfth part; and in each village, there shall be set apart shrines and a marketplace for the gods and the spirits that follow the gods. If there are any local Magnesian heroes, or shrines of others preserved from ancient memory, they shall grant them the ancient honors of men. They shall establish shrines of Hestia, Zeus, and Athena everywhere, and whichever god is the leader of each of the twelve parts. The first buildings shall be around these shrines, wherever the place is highest, as a very secure stronghold for the guards. The rest of the land and all the outskirts shall be divided for the craftsmen into <margin>G</margin> thirteen parts. One part shall be settled in the city, being itself divided into the twelve parts of the entire city, distributed outside and in a circle. In each village, they shall settle the types of craftsmen useful to the farmers. The overseers of all these shall be the commanders of the rural-wardens, determining how many and what kind each place needs, and where they might dwell so as to be least troublesome and most useful to the farmers. Those in the city shall have the same care, and the office of the city-wardens shall oversee them. The market-wardens must always care for everything in the marketplace.

---

...inspection of the [foreigners], nor in the market should anyone wrong another in human needs. These wardens shall also be inspectors of self-control and insolence, punishing anyone who needs punishment. Concerning saleable goods, they should first see if the things appointed for foreigners to sell to the citizens are done according to the law.

<meta>This page concludes the regulations of Book VIII concerning commerce and the status of resident aliens (metics), and begins Book IX, which focuses on criminal law and the judicial system. It maintains continuity from the previous discussion on city management.</meta>

# ON THE LAWS, BOOK IX.

**Left Column:**

<note>original Greek: ἔκχυτα (ekchyta)</note>...and let the law be as follows: for the grain that must be distributed, the officials shall provide the portion for foreigners in the city. For all those residing there as foreigners or slaves, they shall provide a twelfth part of the grain <note>This represents a monthly ration, as there are twelve months in a year.</note>. The foreigner shall purchase grain for the entire month at the first market, and everything pertaining to grain; on the tenth day of the month, the sale and purchase of liquids shall take place, sufficient for the whole month. On the twenty-third day, there shall be the sale of animals, whatever is brought for each person to buy or sell, and also such items as skins or colors used by farmers, as well as garments, woven goods, bricks, or any other such materials. Foreigners are prohibited from buying these from anyone other than the original owners. Regarding retail trade <term>kapeleia<gloss>The Greek term for petty trade or "huckstering," which Plato viewed with suspicion as it prioritized profit over virtue.</gloss></term> in all things—whether wheat or barley turned into flour, or any other foodstuff—no citizen or their slave shall engage in this, nor shall anyone sell to or buy from such a person. In the market for foreigners, however, a foreigner may sell to craftsmen and their slaves, exchanging wine and food; this is what most call "retail trade." Regarding the sale of meat, butchers shall distribute it to foreigners, craftsmen, and their servants. Any foreigner who wishes may purchase firewood in bulk from the overseers in the country districts and resell it to other foreigners in whatever quantity and at whatever time they wish. As for all other goods and utensils that individuals might need, they shall be brought for sale to the common market in the locations designated by the Law-wardens <note>original Greek: nomophylakes</note> and Market-wardens <note>original Greek: agoranomoi</note>, who, along with the City-wardens <note>original Greek: astynomoi</note>, shall determine suitable stalls where money may be exchanged for goods and goods for money, with no one granting credit to another. Anyone who gives on credit, whether they eventually receive payment or not, must accept the loss, as there shall be no legal recourse for such transactions. If anything is bought or sold for more or less than the law prescribes regarding price and measure, the excess shall be recorded with the Law-wardens, and the deficiency erased. The same shall apply to the registration of property for resident aliens <term>metics<gloss>Foreigners who were granted the right to live and work in the city but did not have full citizenship rights.</gloss></term>. Anyone wishing to live as a metic may do so on fixed conditions: they must possess a craft and reside for no more than twenty years from the date of their registration, paying no residency tax <note>original Greek: metoikion</note> other than maintaining good conduct, nor any other tax for buying or selling. When the time expires, they shall take their property and depart. If, within these years, a person performs a significant service for the city—perhaps as a physician—and persuades the Council and Assembly, they may be granted an extension or even life-long residency. For the children of metics who are craftsmen and reach fifteen years of age, their twenty-year residency period begins then; after which they may stay another twenty years or depart as they wish, following the same procedure of petition. Anyone departing shall have their previous records with the magistrates erased.

### PLATO’S LAWS,
#### OR,
### ON LEGISLATION,
### THE NINTH DIALOGUE.

->Δ<- <note>The decorative initial 'D' represents the start of the Greek text for Book IX.</note>
Judgments follow next, being consistent with all the previous actions, and they would naturally arise from the order of the laws. Regarding which matters judgments must be made, some have been stated—such as those concerning agriculture and its followers—but the greatest matters have not yet been spoken of, nor has it been said individually how one should receive punishment and before which judges. After those things, then, these must be discussed in order. **CLINIAS:** Correct. **ATHENIAN:** It is, in a way, shameful to legislate all the things we are now about to do in such a city, which we say will be well-governed and attain every uprightness for the practice of virtue. In such a city, to even assume that the greatest wickedness of others could take root in someone, necessitating laws that threaten and punish such individuals to prevent their occurrence—this is, as I said, shameful in a way. But since we are not, like the ancient legislators, making laws for the sons of gods and heroes—who, according to the stories, were themselves born of gods and legislated for others of similar birth—but are now legislating for men and the seeds of men.

<column-break/>

**Right Column:**

<margin>A</margin> ...it is cautioned, let them sell. Let the law be: on the first day of the month, the overseers shall display the portion of those things that must be sold to foreigners, namely the citizens (and their ministers shall provide a twelfth part of the wheat). Foreigners shall buy wheat for the duration of the entire month, and the household goods sold in the first market. On the tenth day, the sale and purchase of liquids sufficient for the month shall be established; on the twenty-third, the sale of animals which men need, and of furniture such as skins, clothing, and the like. It is necessary for foreigners to buy everything from the owners, so that no "huckstering" <margin>B</margin> in wheat or barley, flour, or other nutrients occurs. It shall not be permitted at all for citizens or their slaves to engage in retail trade. However, in the foreigners' market, it shall be permitted for a foreigner to exchange and sell wine and food to craftsmen and their slaves, and similarly cooked meats; this practice is called "retail trade" by many. A foreigner may buy the entire supply of firewood daily from those who manage it in the fields, and resell it to other foreigners as he wishes and when he wishes. The sale of all other things and furniture we use shall take place in the common market in designated places, where the Law-wardens and the city prefects, together with the wardens, have designated the place and set the prices for sale. Here, coins shall be exchanged for things, and things for coins. Each shall exchange for himself, committing it to no one else. If he does commit it to another, whether <margin>C</margin> he receives payment or not, he must remain silent. For there is no legal judgment for such exchanges. If anything is sold or bought for more or less than the law commands, by which the measures and prices of saleable goods are established, let that excess be recorded with the Law-wardens, and the contrary be deleted. The same shall be done regarding the registration of goods possessed by residents and foreigners. It shall be permitted for anyone to migrate to the city under a certain condition, provided he practices some craft, and he shall remain no more than twenty years from the day of registration. During this time of residency, he shall be compelled to pay no tax except the example of frugality, nor <margin>D</margin> shall he owe anything to the treasury for the sake of buying or selling. When twenty years have passed, he shall take his property and depart. If he has conferred some great benefit upon the state within those twenty years, and wishes for more time, or even to remain in the state for life, let what he asks be granted and held as valid, provided he persuades the council and the assembly. For the children of residents, if they themselves are craftsmen, the time of residency shall begin after the fifteenth year of age, so that they may remain for twenty years thereafter; then they may set out wherever they wish, or if they wish to remain, <margin>E</margin> they may stay after similarly persuading the authorities. He who departs, having deleted the record that was written for him with the magistrates, shall thus go away.

### PLATO ON THE LAWS, OR, ON THE INSTITUTION OF LAWS,
### THE NINTH DIALOGUE.

> **SUMMARY OF THE DIALOGUE.** The common thesis of these two books, the ninth and tenth, is Concerning Judgments. First, however, it hands down certain general precepts regarding the method of well-constituted judgments: not indeed to treat every individual crime, but the greatest ones: namely sacrilege, Treason or rebellion, homicide, and wounding. It teaches what the duty of the Judge and the Legislator is: namely, that the latter provides laws, as far as possible, accurately, from the formula of honor and equity, and having weighed the distinctions of crimes, he often establishes various things according to the merit of the crime; the former applies and accommodates the laws to the facts, prudently and soberly notes the circumstances of the facts, and from that "particular composition" <note>original Greek: ἰδιοσυγκρισίᾳ (idiosynkrisia)</note> of facts, he describes sentences according to the prescription and mandate of the laws. Furthermore, it hands down general rules for establishing judgments, which may be more conveniently perceived from reading the context itself.

<margin>F</margin>
->I<- <note>The decorative initial 'I' represents the start of the Latin translation for Book IX.</note>
If judgments are hereafter rendered in a manner consistent with all the previous actions, the natural order of making laws will certainly be preserved. But regarding the judgments of agriculture and similar things, it has been spoken; concerning the greatest judgments and judges individually, we have not yet spoken; therefore, we shall speak of these next. **CLINIAS:** Well said. **ATHENIAN:** It may seem shameful in a way to assign laws regarding such things as we shall treat to that city which we say will conduct itself entirely toward <margin>G</margin> the possession of virtue. For to whom would it not seem absurd if anyone in an established city thought that a most wicked man would be born as in others? So much so that there is a need for the threats of laws to prevent him, lest he become such or commit such things, and that crimes committed be punished by established laws—as if most flagitious men could be found in this republic too? But since we do not act like the ancient legislators, who, being sons of the Gods, brought laws to heroes who themselves are said to be born of gods; but we, as men, sanction these things for men.

# ON THE LAWS, BOOK IX. PLATO’S ON THE LAWS, BOOK IX.

<column-break/>

**Left Column**

->ON THE LAWS, BOOK IX.<-

It is right to fear that some citizen might be born among us so untamable and inexorable by nature that, like legumes hardened by a lightning strike <note>Plato uses a culinary metaphor here: some beans are so tough that no amount of boiling can soften them; similarly, some criminals cannot be "softened" by the heat of the law.</note>, they cannot be softened even by the fire of the strongest laws. Therefore, if anyone should dare to commit sacrilege, we shall carry a law regarding this, however burdensome and unpleasant it may be for us. Truly, we neither wish nor greatly fear that a citizen who has been rightly educated will suffer from such a severe disease. But perhaps the slaves of such men, or foreigners, or the slaves of foreigners, will attempt many such things. For their sake especially—and because the entire nature of mankind is weak—I shall write laws concerning sacrilege as well as other crimes that can scarcely, or not at all, be healed. 

But first, following the order established in the previous books, short introductions <term>prooemia<gloss>Introductory statements intended to persuade the citizen to obey the law voluntarily before the threat of punishment is invoked.</gloss></term> must be placed before all these laws. To the man who, dragged by wicked desire by day and roused by night, seeks out temples to steal from them, one might say these words by way of instruction and warning: 

"O wondrous man, it is no human evil, nor a divine one, that turns you toward sacrilege. Rather, it is a certain deadly gadfly <note>original Latin: "asilus"; Greek: "oistros." This refers to a stinging fly that drives cattle to madness, used here as a metaphor for an obsessive, irrational impulse.</note> born in men from ancient and unexpiated crimes that drives you about, which you must flee with all your strength. 

Listen to how you may escape: when such a thought arises in your soul, I beseech you, flee to the rites of expiation. Flee as a suppliant to the sacrifices of the gods who deliver us. Flee to the company of good men, where you may partly hear and partly say yourself that what is just and honorable must be cultivated by everyone. But especially flee the company of the wicked. If you do these things and the disease ceases, it will go well for you. Otherwise, considering it better to die, depart from life."

When we have sung these introductions to those whose minds are struck by an impious and pestilential thought toward the city, we shall dismiss in silence those who obey. But for those not persuaded by the introduction, we shall thunder more loudly, bringing forth the law after these words:

Whoever is caught in the act of sacrilege, if he is a slave or a foreigner, let his misfortune be branded in letters upon his face and hands <note>Branding was a common ancient punishment to mark the criminal's status permanently.</note>. After being beaten as many times as the judges see fit, let him be cast out naked beyond the borders. For perhaps, having become more self-controlled through this punishment, he may finally emerge a better man. Indeed, no punishment enacted by law tends toward evil. Instead, it usually achieves one of two things: the one who has paid the penalty usually becomes either better, or at least less wicked. 

But if any citizen is ever found perpetrating such a thing against the gods, or parents, or the fatherland—having set his mind toward the greatest injury—let the judge consider that this man cannot be healed. For despite having been well-taught and educated from childhood, he did not abstain from the greatest crime. For him, the penalty of death is the least of evils. Shamed so that he may help others by his example, let him be destroyed beyond the borders. 

However, if his sons and his entire kin flee the father's habits, let honor and praise be shown to them, because though born of an evil man, they bravely followed virtue. Let none of the property of such men be confiscated into the public treasury in a republic where these "lots" <note>original: "sortes." Plato’s ideal city relied on fixed, equal allotments of land (kleroi) that could not be divided or sold.</note> must always remain the same and equal. But when someone has committed acts that must be paid for with a fine, let whatever he possesses beyond his basic lot be spent, but let the lot itself remain untouched. The Guardians of the Laws <term>nomophylakes<gloss>A board of high-ranking officials in Plato's Magnesia responsible for overseeing the laws and judicial process.</gloss></term> shall always report the exact truth of this matter to the judges from the written census, so that no one is ever deprived of his lot due to a lack of money. 

If anyone seems worthy of a greater penalty and is not freed by the guarantee or generosity of friends, let him be punished with visible and long-lasting chains and other shames. Let no sin go unpunished, and let no fugitive escape without penalty. Instead, let him pay the price either by death, or by chains, or by beatings, or by ignobly sitting or standing in sacred places, led out to the furthest reaches of the region, or by being fined in the manner we have described. 

Let the Guardians of the Laws be the judges of capital crimes, specifically the best among them chosen from those who served in the magistracies in the year immediately preceding. Later legislators shall determine the manner in which accusations and citations should be handled. It is our duty to prescribe the manner of voting and passing sentence by law. Let these votes be cast openly. 

But before this, let the judges sit near the accuser and the defendant, preserving their dignity. Let all citizens who have abundant leisure be present and diligently hear such trials. In these, when the first speech has been delivered by the accuser, the defender shall speak second. Then the eldest of the judges shall examine what has been said with all diligence; after him, all others should consider whatever they each think ought to be inquired into, whether mentioned by the adversaries or not. Whoever deems nothing worthy of his discussion shall leave the examination to another. Finally, let the writings of what was then concluded be deposited in the sanctuary of Vesta <note>In the Greek text: the Hearth of Hestia. This was the sacred center and symbolic heart of the city.</note>, sealed with the signs of all the judges. On the following day, gathering again in the same place, let them examine and judge in the same manner, and after affixing their seals to everything that was said, let them deposit it. When—

It is not a cause for resentment to fear lest any of the citizens be born among us like those struck by a thunderbolt, who would be so unyielding by nature as to not be melted like legumes that are unsoftened by fire. For those who remain unsoftened when using laws as strong as these... 

<margin>B</margin> ...For whose sake, although I say it is unlikely, I would speak of the law here regarding the robbing of temples, which is a thing anyone might dare that is troublesome to all. A citizen who has been correctly raised we would not wish, nor expect, to ever fall ill with this disease. But servants of these men, or foreigners, or the slaves of foreigners, might attempt many such things. For their sake especially, and yet also taking precaution against the entire weakness of human nature, I shall speak the introduction concerning temple-robbers, and all other such things that are difficult or impossible to heal. 

<margin>C</margin> ...One might say, speaking with him and at the same time encouraging him whom an evil desire calls by day and rouses by night, leading him to the robbing of temples: "O wondrous man, no human evil nor divine move you to such a start toward temple-robbing. Rather, it is a certain gadfly <note>Greek: "oistros"</note> implanted in men from ancient and unpurified injustices, roaming about as an avenging curse; which you must guard against with all your strength. 

Learn what this caution is: when any of these doctrines fall upon you, go to the rites of expiation, go as a suppliant to the temples of the gods who avert evil, go to the company of men who are considered good among you. 

<margin>D</margin> ...And if, while doing these things, the disease lightens, well; but if not, looking toward a more honorable death, depart from life." 

As we sing these introductions to those who contemplate such unholy and city-destroying deeds, for the one who obeys, let the law be left in silence; but for the one who is disobedient, after the introduction, let us say loudly: 

Whoever is caught robbing a temple, if he be a slave or a foreigner, let his misfortune be written <note>i.e., branded</note> upon his face and hands, and having been beaten as many times as the judges decide, let him be cast out naked beyond the borders of the land. For perhaps by paying this penalty, he might become better and be brought to his senses. For no penalty that occurs according to law is for the sake of evil. It nearly always works one of two ways: either it makes the one suffering the penalty better, or less depraved. 

<margin>E</margin> ...But if a citizen is ever revealed doing such a thing, having wronged the gods or parents or the city in some great and unspeakable injustice, the judge, considering him to be already incurable—calculating what sort of education and upbringing he received from childhood and yet did not abstain from the greatest evils—shall deem death to be the least of evils for him. He will serve as an example to others, becoming disgraced and vanishing beyond the borders of the land. 

<margin>F</margin> ...But to his children and kin, if they flee the father’s ways, let there be glory and honorable mention, as having escaped well and bravely from evil into good. But the confiscation of property of any such person would not be fitting for the state, in which the same and equal lots must always continue to exist. 

But as for fines, when someone is judged worthy of a fine for his wrongdoing, let him pay it; if there is anything surplus to what is established for his lot, let him be fined up to that amount. Beyond that, the Guardians of the Laws who oversee the records, aiming for accuracy, shall always report the clear status to the judges, so that no one ever becomes useless to his lot because of a lack of money. 

<margin>G</margin> ...And if someone is judged worthy of a greater penalty, unless friends are willing to bail him out and join in ransoming him, let him be punished with long-lasting and public chains and shames. But let no one ever be entirely without rights <note>Greek: "atimos"</note> for any one of his sins, nor a fugitive beyond the borders. Death, or chains, or blows, or certain unseemly sittings, or standings, or displays at the temples on the edges of the land, or payment of money as we said before—these shall be the penalties. 

Let the judges of death be the Guardians of the Laws and the court chosen for excellence from the previous year’s magistrates. The procedures for these, the summonses, and all such things, and how they must be done, should be the concern of the younger legislators. But it is our task to legislate the manner of voting. Let the vote be cast openly. Before this, facing the accuser and the defendant, let the judges sit in order of age... All citizens who have leisure shall be listeners of such trials. There shall be one speech: first the accuser, second the defendant. After these speeches, the eldest shall begin the interrogation...

**<margin>A</margin>** ...and having done this a third time in similar fashion, with sufficient signs and witnesses having been brought forward, let each judge cast a holy vote <note>original Greek: "ψῆφον ἱερὰν"; Latin: "sacrum suffragium". A "holy vote" was a formal, religious act of judgment, often sworn upon an altar.</note> and affirm by an oath before the Hearth <note>original: "Vesta" (Latin) or "Hestia" (Greek). The goddess of the hearth represented the sacred center of the community.</note> that they will judge truly and justly to the best of their power; thus let them bring an end to such a trial. 

After sins against the gods have been addressed, let those committed to the destruction of the republic be discussed. Whoever reduces the leadership of the state to the whim of a single man and subjects the laws to him, thereby making the city a slave to factions and filling it with sedition by using force against the laws—this man must be judged the greatest enemy of the entire city. The second enemy is he who, although not a partner in this crime, nevertheless holds the highest offices in the republic and either fails to notice these conspiracies or, noticing them, fails to help his fatherland out of some cowardice. 

Therefore, let every man who strives to be a citizen of any worth report these matters to the judges, **<margin>B</margin>** and let him bring to trial whoever plots to change the fatherland into an unjust government. Let the judges for this crime be the same as those for sacrilege, and let the whole trial be conducted in the same way; and let the votes that win by a majority condemn the accused to death. 

To speak briefly: the sins of the father shall not be visited upon the children, unless the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather have been successively condemned to capital crimes. In such a case, the city shall send these people back to their ancient ancestral home with their goods, though the original allotment of land <term>lot<gloss>The "kleros" or assigned plot of land in Plato’s ideal city, which was meant to be indivisible and stay within a single family line to maintain social balance.</gloss></term> must always be excepted and preserved. And for those citizens who happen to have more than one son, **<margin>C</margin>** no younger than ten years old, let them choose by lot those whom the fathers, or paternal or maternal grandfathers, have nominated. Let these names be sent to Delphi, and whoever is approved by the oracle of Apollo shall be restored to the house that was left vacant, with a more fortunate destiny and lot.

<term>Cleinias.</term> That is quite right.

<term>Athenian.</term> Furthermore, let there be a common third law regarding the judges and the manner of trial for those accused of treason. And regarding the remaining of children and grandchildren or their departure from the fatherland, let there be one law against three types of offenders: the traitor, the temple-robber, and the violent subverter of the city's laws. 

Concerning theft: whether someone steals something large or small, let there be one law and a similar punishment for all. **<margin>D</margin>** For anyone convicted of theft must pay back double the value of the stolen item, provided his goods beyond his allotted land are sufficient; otherwise, let him be bound in prison until he has either persuaded the person to whom he owes it or has paid it back. But if it was a public theft, he shall be released from prison only when he has persuaded the city or paid back double.

<term>Cleinias.</term> How is it, Stranger, that we say it makes no difference whether a theft is large or small, or whether it is taken from a sacred or a non-sacred place, or however else it happens? Since theft can be committed in many ways, should the legislator not consider the variety and difference of the crime, and not punish with similar penalties things that are not similar?

<term>Athenian.</term> You have pulled me back opportunely, O Cleinias, **<margin>E</margin>** just as I was rushing forward, and you have reminded me of what I had once thought: that until this day, laws have never been rightly established—at least as it occurs to us now while considering the present matters.

<term>Cleinias.</term> In what way do we say that?

<term>Athenian.</term> We used an appropriate image when we compared all those who have received laws until now to slaves being treated by other slaves. For it is certainly wrong to ignore this: if a doctor who treats patients by mere experience without reason should hear a free-born doctor, a student of philosophy, talking to a free-born patient—investigating the beginnings of the disease with reason and discussing the nature of bodies more diligently—he would immediately laugh. **<margin>F</margin>** He would say to him what most doctors always have ready: "You are not healing the sick man, you fool; you are teaching him, as if he needed to become a doctor rather than becoming healthy!"

<term>Cleinias.</term> Would he not seem to speak correctly in saying so?

<term>Athenian.</term> And would not the same thing be rightly thrown at us? That whoever discusses the laws as we are doing now is not making laws, but educating the citizens?

<term>Cleinias.</term> Perhaps.

<term>Athenian.</term> But a happy thing has happened to us in the present moment.

<term>Cleinias.</term> What is that?

<term>Athenian.</term> That nothing forces us to pass laws immediately; rather, having taken up this consideration of our own accord, we are striving to see what is best and most necessary regarding every discipline of a republic. Therefore, since we are permitted, if we wish, let us choose in the present what is best or what is most necessary.

<term>Cleinias.</term> **<margin>G</margin>** This choice, Stranger, is a ridiculous one. It makes us clearly like those who are compelled by great necessity to pass laws right now, as if it would not be permitted tomorrow. But to us, by the help of God, it is permitted to collect materials extensively, just like those who build from stones or any other material, so that the things that will be useful for the future work may be chosen without any haste. Therefore, as builders who are by no means in a hurry, let us lay some foundations now and take other things from here for building; so that in making the laws, some may be placed as if they are now established, and others added as if they were already in place.

<term>Athenian.</term> In this way, Cleinias, our view of the laws will be more according to nature and more concise. But let us consider this about legislators, by the gods.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Book IX of Plato's Laws. The previous page established the penalties for sacrilege and treason. Here, the Athenian Stranger pivots to a deeper philosophical justification for why laws are written and how they should address the distinction between voluntary and involuntary acts.</meta>

# PLATO

...exist in cities; these are both the writings and speeches of the legislator. <margin>A</margin> **CLINIAS.** Why not? **ATHENIAN.** Shall we then apply our minds to the works of poets and other writers who have composed advice on how to live, but not at all to the works of the lawgivers? Or should we attend to the lawgivers most of all? **CLINIAS.** To them, by all means. **ATHENIAN.** Therefore, the legislator alone among writers ought to provide counsel concerning the honorable, the good, and the just, teaching what these things are and how those who intend to be happy should practice them. **CLINIAS.** Why not? **ATHENIAN.** For it is a shameful thing if Homer, Tyrtaeus <note>Tyrtaeus was a Greek poet of the 7th century BCE, famous for his verses exhorting the Spartans to martial virtue.</note>, and the other poets have written properly about the life and pursuits of men, while Lycurgus <note>The legendary lawgiver of Sparta.</note>, Solon, and the rest of the lawgivers have done less so. <margin>B</margin> Rightly, therefore, the laws themselves ought to display these virtues wonderfully above all other writings; other writings should be approved only if they agree with the laws, but if they are dissonant, they should be ridiculed. Thus, let the laws be written for cities so that the lawgiver truly takes on the role of a father and mother; the writings should possess the virtue of charity and prudence rather than the command of a tyrant or master who only threatens and describes, but assigns no reason at all. Let us consider then whether we should proceed by this path, whether we are able or not. But let us gird ourselves now: and proceeding by this <margin>C</margin> path according to our strength, even if it is necessary to suffer anything, let us endure it. May it be successful—and it certainly will be, if God wills it. **CLINIAS.** You have spoken rightly; let us do as you say. **ATHENIAN.** We must consider first, as we began, carefully concerning sacrilege, theft, and all other injuries; nor should we take it hard if, in the very description of the laws, we have already set down some things while we are still debating others. For we are not yet lawgivers, but we are just becoming so, and perhaps we soon shall be. But if it seems right to consider these things as I have proposed, let us consider them. **CLINIAS.** Entirely so. **ATHENIAN.** Concerning all honorable and just things, let us try to see how we—who certainly desire to excel others, even if we cannot—agree <margin>D</margin> with ourselves, and where we differ, and how others differ from themselves. **CLINIAS.** What differences do you mean between us? **ATHENIAN.** I will try to explain. Concerning justice in general, and just men, things, and actions, we all in a way agree: namely, that all these things are honorable and beautiful <note>The Latin text uses "honesta pulchráque" to translate the single Greek concept of the *kalon*—meaning that which is morally noble, physically beautiful, and socially honorable all at once.</note>; so that if anyone were to assert that just men, even if they are physically deformed, are most beautiful according to their very habit of justice, almost no one would find fault with that judgment. **CLINIAS.** Hardly anyone who speaks that way would seem to speak wrongly. **ATHENIAN.** Rightly then. **CLINIAS.** Perhaps. **ATHENIAN.** But come, let us see if all things that are done justly are also <margin>E</margin> honorable and beautiful. For almost all our "passions" <note>In this context, "passions" (Latin: *passiones*; Greek: *pathemata*) refers to things one *undergoes* or suffers, such as a punishment, as opposed to things one *does* (actions).</note> are similar to our actions. **CLINIAS.** What of this? **ATHENIAN.** Any action that is just, insofar as it participates in justice, to that extent it also participates in the honorable. **CLINIAS.** Why not? **ATHENIAN.** Therefore, if a just "passion" (or punishment) is said to participate in equity, honor, and justice, our speech will not be dissonant. **CLINIAS.** You speak the truth. **ATHENIAN.** But if we affirm that some punishment is indeed just, but deny it is honorable, the "just" and the "honorable" will be at odds with each other. For just things will be called most shameful. **CLINIAS.** How did you mean that? **ATHENIAN.** It is not difficult to understand. For the laws which were set down by us a little while ago <margin>F</margin> will seem to prescribe the exact opposite of these words. **CLINIAS.** In what way? **ATHENIAN.** We judged that the sacrilegious man would die justly, and similarly the enemy of well-established laws. And when we were about to write many such laws, we drew back, considering that these "passions" (punishments) are infinite in number and magnitude; they are indeed the most just of all punishments, but also the most shameful of all. Will not honorable things and just things thus appear sometimes as the same, and sometimes as the opposite? **CLINIAS.** So it seems. **ATHENIAN.** Many people, then, speaking dissonantly, call honorable and just things as if they were discrepant. **CLINIAS.** It certainly appears so. **ATHENIAN.** But let us see again, O Clinias, how we agree <margin>G</margin> on these matters. **CLINIAS.** To what agreement do you refer? **ATHENIAN.** I think I have stated it clearly in the preceding discourse. <gloss>But if it was not said above,</gloss> consider me to be saying it now. **CLINIAS.** What is it? **ATHENIAN.** That all bad men are entirely bad against their will <note>This is the famous Socratic Paradox: "No one does evil willingly." Plato argues that because everyone desires their own good, doing evil (which harms the soul) must be the result of ignorance or an internal lack of control, not a rational choice.</note>. And if this is so, it is necessary that this follow as well. **CLINIAS.** What? **ATHENIAN.** That the unjust man is bad, and the bad man is of this sort against his will. But it can never be that what is voluntary happens against one's will. Therefore, he who thinks justice is involuntary will think that a man acting unjustly acts so against his will. I must also agree with myself, since I confess that all men do injury against their will; although someone might object to us for the sake of ambition or contention that: though the unjust are indeed unjust against their will, <margin>H</margin> many of them nevertheless do injury willingly. My opinion is certainly not that, but the former. How then shall I be consistent with my own words if you ask me, Clinias and Megillus, "If these things are so, Stranger, what do you counsel us concerning the city of the Magnesians? Should we give them laws or not?" I will certainly counsel giving laws. Then you might say: "Will you then distinguish for them between involuntary and voluntary injuries?" <margin>Laws, Book 9.</margin>

<column-break/>

...the writings and those of the lawgivers, etc. For how not? **ATHENIAN.** Should we then pay attention to the writings of others—poets, and those who have set down their advice about life in writing either with or without meter—but not pay attention to the writings of the lawgivers? Or should we attend to them most of all? **CLINIAS.** Much more so. **ATHENIAN.** But is it not necessary that the lawgiver alone among those who write should advise about the beautiful, the good, and the just, teaching what they are and how they must be practiced by those who intend to be happy? **CLINIAS.** And how not? **ATHENIAN.** But is it not more shameful for Homer and Tyrtaeus and the other poets to have laid down their writings poorly concerning life and its pursuits, but less so for Lycurgus and Solon and whoever else became lawgivers and wrote? Or rather, is it not correct that of all the writings in the cities, those concerning the laws should appear to be by far the strongest, most beautiful, and best? And that the writings of others should either follow those, or if they are dissonant with them, be considered ridiculous? We must think that the writing of laws in cities should be like the words of a loving and wise father and mother; or should they be like a tyrant and a master who, having commanded and threatened, writes them on walls and is done with it? Let us consider even now whether we are attempting to speak of laws with this intention, whether we are able or not; but at least let us provide our zeal. And going along this road, if it is necessary to suffer anything, let us suffer it. And may it be good, and, if God wills, it might happen this way. **CLINIAS.** You have spoken well; let us do as you say. **ATHENIAN.** We must first consider accurately, as we attempted, about those who rob temples, and about all theft and all injuries. And we should not be troubled if, while legislating, we have established some things but say that we are still considering others. For we are becoming lawgivers, but we are not yet so; though perhaps we might become so soon. If then it seems that what I said has been spoken as we intended, let us consider it. **CLINIAS.** Entirely so. **ATHENIAN.** Concerning all beautiful and just things, let us try to understand this: how we now agree in some way and how we differ among ourselves (we who say that we wish to excel others in this, if nothing else) and how the many differ among themselves. **CLINIAS.** What kind of differences do you say there will be among us? **ATHENIAN.** I will try to explain. Concerning justice in general and just men and things and bodies, we all somehow agree that all these are beautiful; so that even if someone were to insist about just men, that even if they happen to have ugly bodies, they are entirely beautiful according to their most just character, almost no one who said this would seem to speak out of tune. **CLINIAS.** Perhaps rightly. **ATHENIAN.** But let us see if all things are beautiful that pertain to justice, and if almost all "passions" (sufferings/punishments) are for us nearly equal to the actions. **CLINIAS.** What do you mean? **ATHENIAN.** An action which is just, insofar as it shares in the just, to that extent it also participates in the beautiful. **CLINIAS.** What else? **ATHENIAN.** Then if a passion (punishment) shares in the just, would it not also become beautiful to that extent, if the argument is to be consistent? **CLINIAS.** True. **ATHENIAN.** But if we agree that something is just, yet it is shameful, then the just and the beautiful will be dissonant, with just things being called shameful. **CLINIAS.** How have you said this? **ATHENIAN.** It is not difficult to perceive. For the laws we set down a little while ago would seem to say the exact opposite of what is being said now. **CLINIAS.** Which ones? **ATHENIAN.** We were going over how the temple-robber might justly die, and likewise the enemy of the established laws; and being about to set down many such laws, we paused, seeing that these are infinite sufferings in number and magnitude. They are the most just of all sufferings, yet the most shameful of all. Will not the just and the beautiful appear to us sometimes as the same, but sometimes as most opposite? **CLINIAS.** It is likely. **ATHENIAN.** To the many, then, the beautiful and the just are thus spoken of as being thrown apart and dissonant. **CLINIAS.** It appears so, O Stranger. **ATHENIAN.** Then let us look at our own view again, O Clinias, to see how it holds with regard to consistency. **CLINIAS.** What consistency do you mean? **ATHENIAN.** I think I have spoken of it explicitly in the earlier parts of the discourse. **CLINIAS.** How? **ATHENIAN.** If not before, then at least understand me now as saying it. **CLINIAS.** What is it? **ATHENIAN.** That all bad men are, in all things, bad against their will. This being so, it is necessary that the next argument follow from it. **CLINIAS.** What do you mean? **ATHENIAN.** That the unjust man is bad; and the bad man is such against his will. But it is never fitting for a voluntary act to be an involuntary one. Therefore, the one who does an injustice would seem to act against his will to the person who holds that injustice is involuntary; which is what I must agree to now. For I agree that all men do injustice against their will, even if some people, for the sake of strife or ambition, say that while men are unjust against their will, many nevertheless do injury willingly. My argument is that former one, not this one. In what way then would I be consistent with my own words if you, O Clinias and Megillus, ask me: "If these things are so, Stranger, what do you advise us about the legislation for the city of the Magnesians? Whether to legislate or not?" "How could I not?" I shall say. "Will you then distinguish for them between involuntary and voluntary injuries?"

<summary>In this passage from Plato's Laws, the Athenian Stranger argues that laws should be written with the care of a parent rather than the force of a tyrant, and introduces the Socratic paradox that all injustice is involuntary, complicating how a lawgiver should distinguish between crimes.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion in Book IX of Plato’s Laws. Having previously discussed the role of the legislator as a teacher or father figure, the Athenian Stranger now moves into the difficult philosophical distinction between voluntary and involuntary acts, a central problem in Athenian law and Platonic ethics.</meta>

# ON THE LAWS, BOOK IX.

<margin>A</margin> **ATHENIAN.** And likewise, shall we prescribe greater penalties for those injuries done of one’s own accord <note>Greek: *hekousion*; Latin: *sponte*. This refers to actions done intentionally and with full knowledge.</note>, and smaller ones for those not done of one’s own accord? Or should the penalties be equal for all, on the grounds that no injury at all is ever committed willingly? 
**CLINIAS.** You speak rightly, Stranger. But how shall we use these things that have just been said? 
**ATHENIAN.** You ask a fair question. We shall use them first for this purpose. 
**CLINIAS.** For what purpose exactly? 
**ATHENIAN.** Let us recall that we said quite well earlier that there is much confusion and disagreement among us concerning the nature of the <term>just</term> <note>Plato is exploring the Socratic paradox that "no one does evil willingly." If all injustice is a result of ignorance, the traditional legal distinction between "voluntary" and "involuntary" crimes becomes philosophically problematic.</note>. Taking this up again, let us ask ourselves: since we have by no means clarified the difference between these two—which are set down by all lawgivers in every city as two distinct species of injury—
<margin>B</margin> namely, those done of one’s own accord and those done against one’s will, and are thus punished differently—should we introduce our own opinion as if it were a divine decree, without confirming by any reason why it is correct? Certainly, this is not proper. Rather, before we establish the laws, it is necessary to signify how these two are distinct and what difference they have. Thus, when we impose a punishment on either, everyone may understand and be able to judge, in a way, whether it has been imposed appropriately or the opposite. 
**CLINIAS.** You seem to us to speak rightly, Stranger. For we must do one of two things: 
<margin>C</margin> either not say that all injuries happen against one's will, or, before we proceed to other matters, we must explain how this is correctly said. 
**ATHENIAN.** I will by no means allow the latter—that is, to deny what I believe to be the truth. For that would be neither my duty nor pious. But if they do not differ in being voluntary or involuntary, how can we attempt to reveal in what other way these two types of injury differ? 
**CLINIAS.** Certainly, Stranger, we cannot understand these things in any other way. 
**ATHENIAN.** So be it. Come then, do there not occur many harms and inconveniences among citizens in their dealings and social interactions, in which the voluntary and involuntary seem to abound? 
**CLINIAS.** How could they not? 
<margin>D</margin> **ATHENIAN.** Yet, let no one think that all inconveniences and damages are <term>injustices</term> <note>The Athenian makes a crucial distinction here between *blabe* (physical harm or damage) and *adikia* (injustice or moral wrongdoing). One can cause harm without being "unjust."</note>, nor should he judge that there is a double injustice in them—one committed against one’s will and the other of one’s own accord. For the damages done against one's will are, in the eyes of all, neither fewer in number nor in magnitude than those done of one’s own accord. But consider, I pray, whether what I say next contains any truth or nothing at all. For, O Clinias and Megillus, if someone hurts another without wishing to, shall I say he acts "unjustly" against his will? Or should I place this in the laws as an "involuntary injustice"? On the contrary, I would say such a damage is no injustice at all, whether it be greater or smaller. Often, we say that someone who has conferred a benefit <insert>unfairly</insert> acts "unjustly," if that benefit is not truly good. 
<margin>E</margin> For almost always, my friends, whether one grants something or, on the contrary, takes something away, it is not right to call such a thing "just" or "unjust" so simply. This is not what the legislator must consider; rather, he must look to see if someone profits or hinders another with a good character and in a just manner. He must look to these two: injustice and damage. Thus, he must immediately restore the damaged party to a healthy and whole state as much as possible, replacing what was lost, setting upright what fell, and repairing what was killed or wounded. He must always strive through the laws to ensure that the discord stirred up by such damages is restored to friendship. 
**CLINIAS.** These things are well said. 
**ATHENIAN.** Therefore, regarding unjust damages and gains—if by chance any profit follows from an injustice—these must be treated like <term>diseases of the soul</term> <note>Plato views crime as a psychological illness. The goal of the law is not just retribution, but "curing" the offender's soul.</note>, provided they are curable. And let the cure for injustice be directed toward this end. 
**CLINIAS.** Toward what? 
<margin>F</margin> **ATHENIAN.** So that whatever injuries one has committed, whether great or small, he may be corrected by the law through teaching and compelled never again to dare to commit such a thing of his own accord, or at least to do so much less frequently, being deterred by the imposition of a penalty. Truly, we say it is the office of the best laws to so train the minds of men that they hate injustice and love the nature of the just, or at least do not hate it. Whether the legislator achieves this by deeds or words, by pleasure or pain, by honor or infamy, by fines of money or by gifts, or by whatever other means, this is the goal. 
<margin>G</margin> But those whom the legislator perceives to be <term>incurable</term> <note>Plato argues that for those whose souls are beyond repair, death is a mercy to themselves and a benefit to society.</note>, he shall visit with the final punishment, knowing that it is better for the incurable to die than to live; by being deprived of life, they benefit others in two ways: others are deterred from sin by their example, and the city itself is cleansed of wicked men. For this reason, the maker of laws shall punish incurable men with death, but in no other case. 
**CLINIAS.** These things seem to be spoken by you quite moderately. But we would gladly hear you speak again more clearly on the difference of injury, and how they are done of one's own accord. 
**ATHENIAN.** I shall endeavor to do and say as you command. It is indeed established—as you often say and hear when discussing the soul—that there is one affection or part in it by nature which we call <term>anger</term> <note>Greek: *thumos*. This is the spirited or "feisty" part of the soul that can lead to rash actions.</note>, a contentious and difficult possession which, by its unreasoning force, overturns many things. 
**CLINIAS.** Without a doubt. 
**ATHENIAN.** Furthermore, we do not say that <term>pleasure</term> is the same as anger, but that it rules from an opposite power, compelling one by persuasion and violent deception to do whatever its own will desires. 
**CLINIAS.** Most certainly.

<column-break/>

<summary>The Athenian Stranger distinguishes between "harm" (physical damage) and "injustice" (a moral sickness of the soul), arguing that laws should aim to heal the soul of the offender while compensating the victim. He concludes that incurable criminals should be executed for the benefit of the state and themselves.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous section of Book IX, where the Athenian Stranger began categorizing the different types of injuries and the motivations behind them. This page specifically deals with the role of ignorance and the transition into specific laws regarding homicide.</meta>

# PLATO’S LAWS

<margin>A</margin> <term>ATHENIAN.</term> Whoever identifies ignorance as the third cause of wrongdoing will not be in error. But the legislator who distinguishes this into two parts will be even better: he will define one as simple ignorance and the other as double ignorance. He will consider simple ignorance to be the cause of light sins; but he will call it "double" when someone is not only held by ignorance but is also puffed up by a conceit of wisdom—thinking he knows perfectly things he does not know at all. If this type of ignorance is joined with strength and power, he will judge it to be the cause of great and most shameful crimes; but if it is suppressed by weakness, he will consider the resulting sins to be those of children and the elderly <margin>B</margin>. He will prescribe laws for them as for those who sin, but they shall be the mildest of all and full of much pardon and indulgence. <term>CLINIAS.</term> That is fair. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> Regarding pleasure and anger, almost all of us agree that some men conquer them, while others are conquered by them. And that is exactly how it is. <term>CLINIAS.</term> Precisely so. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> But we have never heard it said that some "overcome" ignorance while others are "overcome" by it. <term>CLINIAS.</term> You speak the truth. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> We say that each of these impulses drags a man toward itself, often being pulled toward contrary things at the same time. <term>CLINIAS.</term> Very often indeed. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> Now I shall explain to you clearly and without ambiguity what I call just and what I call unjust. For the tyranny in the soul of anger, fear, pleasure, pain, envy, and desire—whether it causes harm or not—I call "injustice" <note>Plato defines injustice here not merely as an act of harm, but as a state of internal disorder where the emotions "tyrannize" reason.</note> in every sense. But when the opinion of what is best—by which reason a city or certain private individuals think they should live—rules in the soul and orders every part of the man, then even if it fails in some respect, I call everything done in this way "justice." I also call "just" whatever is performed from this state, and those who willingly obey this kind of sovereignty I consider to live most excellently. However, most people think that damage caused by this sort of reason is an "involuntary injury." But we are not going to argue about words. Since three species of sins have been mentioned, these must first be recalled <margin>D</margin> more diligently to memory. One species we consider to be of pain, which we call anger and fear. <term>CLINIAS.</term> Exactly. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> Another is of pleasure and desires. And a third species is the longing and desire for hope and true opinion regarding what is best. When these are divided again into two parts, five species are produced; for these five species, laws differing among themselves must be established in two general classes. <term>CLINIAS.</term> What are these classes? <term>ATHENIAN.</term> One consists of those acts committed by force and openly; the other, those committed secretly and with deception in the dark. Sometimes both are involved. If such acts are treated rightly, they will be coerced by the harshest laws. <term>CLINIAS.</term> That is fair. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> But let us now return <margin>E</margin> to where we left off, and apply ourselves to the defining of the laws. Our proposal was to deal with the sacrilegious, with traitors, and with those who corrupt the laws by changing the state. Perhaps someone will commit one of these things because of insanity, or being weighed down by disease or old age, or being in the age of childhood, so that he differs in no way from the insane. If such a fact is clearly proved to the chosen judges, and if the man is judged to have committed the act while so affected, he shall simply restore the damage he caused; the rest of the penalties shall be remitted, unless he has killed a man and is not yet purified of the slaughter. In that case, he must go abroad and live as a pilgrim for one year. And if he returns before the time appointed by law has passed, or is found within the borders, he shall be kept in public prison for two years by the guardians of the laws, and thereafter set free from bonds. But to begin, let us write the laws regarding every species of homicide more fully. First, let us speak of those committed by force and not of one's own accord. <margin>By force and not of one's own accord.</margin> <margin>G</margin> If anyone in a public contest or the gymnasia kills a man who is a friend, not of his own accord—whether death follows immediately or later from the wounds—or similarly in war, or in military training instituted by magistrates, whether with naked bodies or armed in imitation of true war, let him be pure according to the law brought from the Delphic Apollo <note>original: "Delphico Apolline". In Greek law, Apollo's oracle at Delphi was the supreme authority for religious purification after a killing.</note>. Also, let all physicians who kill a patient while treating them not of their own accord be considered pure. If someone by his own hand, but not of his own accord—whether with his naked body, or with an instrument, a weapon, or by giving food or drink, or by the application of fire or cold or the removal of breath, whether he does this with his own body or through other things—kills someone, he shall be considered the killer by his own hand and shall be punished as I say. If he kills another person's slave, thinking it his own, he shall restore the damage to the master or pay double the price. The value of the slave shall be determined by the judges. He shall use more and greater purifications than those who kill someone in a contest. The proper interpreters of these rites are those whom the god's oracle has approved. If he kills his own slave, once he is purified according to the law, let him be absolved. But if someone kills a free man not of his own accord, let him use the same purifications as the one who kills a slave. And let him not despise the ancient mystery <note>original: "priscum mysterium". This refers to the traditional belief that the ghost of a victim haunts the killer.</note>. For it is said that a man who has lived freely and is killed by force is angry with his killer in the time immediately following his death, and because of his violent death, he is full of terror and confusion, especially if...

<column-break/>

<margin>Α</margin> <term>ATHENIAN.</term> Indeed, if someone says that ignorance is the third cause of sins, he would not be lying. But the legislator would be better if he divided it in two: considering the simple form of it as a cause of light sins; but calling it double when someone is in ignorance not only held by a lack of knowledge, but also by a conceit of wisdom, as if knowing perfectly things he does not know at all. Where strength and might follow this, such things are the cause of all great and uncultured sins; but where weakness follows, producing the sins of children and the elderly, he shall set them down as sins and arrange laws as if for sinners, yet the mildest of all, and containing the most forgiveness. <margin>Β</margin> <term>CLINIAS.</term> What you say is reasonable. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> Now regarding pleasure and anger, almost all of us say that one man is master of us, and another is mastered, and it holds this way. <term>CLINIAS.</term> Certainly. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> But regarding ignorance, we have never heard that one of us is its master and another is mastered by it. <term>CLINIAS.</term> Most true. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> And we must say that everyone wishes to pull toward his own ends, though each is often dragged in opposite directions at once. <term>CLINIAS.</term> Most often indeed. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> Now I define for you again clearly, without any coloring, what I mean by the just and the unjust. For the tyranny in the soul of anger, fear, pleasure, pain, envy, and desires—whether it causes some harm <margin>Γ</margin> or not—I call "injustice" in every way. But the opinion of the best, in whatever way a city or certain individuals think it should be, if this rules in the soul and orders every man—even if it trips up in something—we must say that everything done in this way is just, as is the part of each person that is obedient to such a rule; and that these things are best for the life of men. However, such damage is taken by many to be "involuntary injustice." But we are not currently having a quarrelsome debate about names; rather, since three types of sins have been revealed as occurring, we must first bring them even more into memory. One species for us is of pain, which we call anger and fear <margin>Δ</margin>. <term>CLINIAS.</term> Entirely so. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> Of pleasure and desires, a second. And a third, different one: the longing for hope and true opinion concerning the best. And these being cut in two, five species have been created, as we now say; for these, five sets of laws differing from one another must be placed in two classes. <term>CLINIAS.</term> Which are these? <term>ATHENIAN.</term> One is the violent and of manifest actions committed each time; the other is not, being shadowy and occurring secretly through deceit. Sometimes it is done through both of these; and for such, the harshest laws would be made if they are to have their proper parts. <margin>Ε</margin> <term>CLINIAS.</term> That seems likely. <term>ATHENIAN.</term> Now follow that point from which we diverted here, as we establish the laws of the gods. Our rules were set concerning those who rob (I believe) the gods and those regarding treason; and those concerning the corruption of the laws for the destruction of the existing constitution. Perhaps someone might do one of these things while mad, or held by disease or extreme old age, or being a child—no different from these. If any such thing becomes manifest to the judges chosen each time, on the plea of the doer or the one speaking for the performer, let it be judged so. The damage that he has caused to anyone, let him pay in full as a simple restoration, but let him be released from the other punishment. Except, however, if he has killed someone and is not clean in his hands of murder. In that case, let him go away to another land and place, living abroad for a year; and if he returns before the time the law set, or even sets foot on his own land, <margin>Ϛ</margin> let him be bound in public bonds by the guardians of the laws for two years, and then let him be released from the bonds. As we began regarding murder, let us now try to complete the laws concerning all murder. And first, let us speak of the violent and involuntary. If anyone in a contest and public games kills a friend unintentionally, whether immediately on the spot or in later times from the blows, or likewise in war, or in the training for war conducted by the rulers—pure for all friends, or in any common action of war—let him be clean according to the law brought from Delphi concerning these things. Regarding all physicians, if the one being treated by them dies unintentionally, let them be clean <margin>Ζ</margin> according to the law. And if someone kills another not of his own accord, though by his own hand—whether with his own naked body, or an instrument, or a weapon, or by giving a drink or food, or by the application of fire or cold, or by deprivation of breath, whether by his own body or through other bodies—let him be entirely as one who killed by his own hand, and let him pay such penalties: if he kills a slave, thinking his own was destroyed, let him provide the master of the deceased harmless and without loss; or let him undergo a penalty and pay double the value of the deceased. Let the judges make a determination of the value. And let him use greater and more numerous purifications than those who kill in the games. Let the interpreters of these things be those whom the god declares. If he kills his own slave, let him be purified <margin>Η</margin> by the laws and be released from the murder according to the law. And if he kills a free person unintentionally, let him be purified with the same purifications as the one who killed the slave; and let him not dishonor any of the ancient myths that are told. For it is said that the one who has been killed violently, having lived with a free spirit, is angry with the doer while the event is fresh, and being himself filled with fear and dread due to the violent suffering, and seeing his own...
