<meta>This page continues the legal discussion from Book IX of Plato’s *Laws*. In the preceding section, the Athenian Stranger categorized the origins of crimes—specifically distinguishing between ignorance, pleasure, and anger. Here, the text moves into specific legislation regarding homicide, focusing on the psychological state of the killer and the resulting requirements for purification and exile.</meta>

-># ON THE LAWS, BOOK IX.<-

<margin>A</margin> If the spirit of the deceased sees the killer moving about in his accustomed haunts, the dead man is filled with fear and turmoil; being thus troubled himself, he uses all his power to terrify and disturb the one who did the deed, with his memory acting as an ally to himself and his actions. Therefore, it is necessary for the perpetrator to withdraw from the presence of the victim for all the seasons of a full year, and to leave vacant all the familiar places of his entire fatherland. If the deceased was a foreigner, the killer must also be excluded from the foreigner’s own country for the same period. If a man willingly obeys this law—the next of kin of the deceased being the closest witness and overseer of everything that happens—he shall find forgiveness, and the relative shall maintain peace with him, behaving with complete moderation. But if anyone is disobedient and, <margin>B</margin> while still being impure, dares to enter the temples and sacrifice, or if he refuses to complete the stated time as an exile, the next of kin of the deceased shall prosecute the killer for murder; and let all the penalties for the one convicted be doubled. If the nearest relative does not prosecute, let the pollution <note>The Greek term *miasma* refers to a ritual stain or "blood-guilt" that was believed to infect not just the killer but the community and family if not properly cleansed.</note> pass onto him, as the spirit of the victim turns the suffering upon the relative; then, anyone who wishes may bring the case against that relative and compel him, according to the law, to stay away from his own fatherland for five years. If a foreigner kills another foreigner in the city, anyone who wishes may prosecute under these same laws; if the killer is a resident alien, let him go into exile for one year. But if he is a total foreigner, <margin>C</margin> whether he kills a foreigner, a resident alien, or a citizen, he shall be excluded for his entire life from the land over which these laws have authority. If he returns in defiance of the law, the Guardians of the Laws <note>The *nomophylakes* were high-ranking officials in Plato's envisioned city responsible for maintaining the integrity of the legal code.</note> shall punish him with death; and if he possesses any property, they shall hand it over to the next of kin of the victim. If he should come back against his will—for instance, if he is shipwrecked upon the coast—let him wait for a ship to take him away, staying in the sea with his feet merely touching the water; but if he is brought in by force by land, let the first official who encounters the case release him and send him back safely into exile. If someone kills a free man with his own hand, but the act was done in anger, such a case must be divided into two types. <margin>D</margin> For acts are done in anger by those who, on a sudden impulse and without intent to kill, destroy someone with blows or something similar, and repentance for the deed follows immediately. Also done in anger are those acts where men, provoked by insults or shameful deeds, pursue revenge and later kill someone with the intent to kill, and they feel no repentance for what they have done. We must therefore establish two types of homicide, as it seems, both happening through anger; they might most justly be called something between voluntary and involuntary. Yet, each type resembles one of those categories. For he who nurses his anger and takes revenge later with a plan, rather than suddenly on the spot, resembles the voluntary killer. But he who does not restrain his impulses and kills suddenly on the spot without premeditation is like the involuntary killer. However, even this latter act is not entirely involuntary, but only an image of the involuntary. For this reason, it is difficult to determine whether homicides committed in anger should be legally defined as voluntary or as involuntary. The best and truest course is to treat both as images and to cut them apart into two categories: those done with premeditation and those done without. We must impose harsher punishments on those who kill with premeditation and anger, and milder ones on those who kill suddenly and without prior thought; for that which resembles a greater evil must be punished more severely, and that which resembles a lesser evil, more mildly. Our laws must be fashioned this way. Let us return and say: If someone kills a free man with his own hand, and the act was committed in a fit of anger without premeditation, let him suffer the other penalties as is right for a killer, but he must necessarily go into exile for two years to discipline his anger. But he who kills in anger but with premeditation, let him do the other things like the man before him, but instead of two years, let him go into exile for three years, punished longer because the magnitude of his anger was worse. The general disposition for these cases shall be as follows: It is difficult to legislate precisely for every detail. Sometimes the crime that the law deems harsher seems milder in reality, and vice versa, depending on how cruelly or mildly it was carried out. For the most part, however, things happen as we have just said. The Guardians of the Laws must be the judges of all these circumstances. <margin>G</margin> When the time of exile for either type has passed, they shall send twelve judges to the borders of the land, who during that time will have examined the actions of the exiles more clearly; these shall act as judges regarding the sense of shame and the fitness of the exiles to be received back. The exiles must abide by the judgment of these officials. If either of them returns and sins again in anger before the time of exile is finished, he shall never return again; and if he does return, let him suffer as the foreigner did. If someone kills his own slave, let him be purified; if he kills someone else's slave in anger, let him pay double the value of the damage to the owner. Whoever among all these killers does not obey the law, but while still impure contaminates the market, the games, and other sacred places, anyone who wishes may bring both the killer and the negligent relative of the victim to trial, and compel them to pay double the fines and other penalties; and let the person who brought the case receive the payment according to the law. If a slave, moved by anger, kills his master—

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> If he sees the killer living among his own people in the usual way, the killer and his actions—memory supplying the force for this—will terrify and disturb him with all his strength. Therefore, it is necessary that the homicide, for the sake of the person killed, live as an exile from his fatherland and that whole region for an entire year. If indeed the one who died was a foreigner, the homicide shall also be expelled from the fatherland of the foreigner for a year’s time. If he willingly obeys this law, the next of kin to the deceased, who will watch whether he obeys, shall grant him pardon, and he will even be reconciled in peace with him and be entirely fair. But if he does not obey, and while he is still impure, dares to seek out the temples of the gods <margin>B</margin> and sacrifice, or does not travel abroad for the whole established time, let the next of kin to the deceased report it to the judges, accuse him of the murder, and take double all the punishments from him. **B**ut if that relative neglects to do so: as if the crime had recoiled upon himself—the dead man naturally turning his suffering onto the relative—let him be accused by anyone who wishes, and be forced to be deprived of his fatherland for five years. If a foreigner unintentionally kills a foreigner in the city, let it be reported to the judges by anyone who wishes under the same law, and let it be judged similarly. But if a resident alien does it, let him be exiled for one year. **B**ut if a foreigner entirely kills a foreigner, or a resident alien, or a citizen, beyond the purification, let him also be an exile for his whole life from the entire region in which <margin>C</margin> laws of this kind prevail. **A**nd if he returns against the laws, let him be punished with death by the guardians of the laws: and his goods, if he possesses any, let them be handed over to the next of kin of the person killed. **B**ut if he should be brought into that region against his will: driven by the force of a storm and the waves of the sea, let him wait for the opportunity of sailing while touching the sea with his feet: but if he is brought by land by force by some people, he is to be released by the magistrate to whom the matter was first reported, and pushed back into exile untouched. **B**ut if someone kills a free man with his own hand, being moved by anger, it is first necessary to distinguish anger into two parts. For he also acts through anger who suddenly and without the will to kill, kills with blows or in any <margin>D</margin> way, so that repentance follows immediately after the impulse: and those who, provoked by an insult or injury, and therefore persevering in the desire for revenge, afterwards kill willingly: nor does it repent them to have done those things. It is pleasing, therefore, to establish a double homicide, each done by anger. Which they would rightly place as middles between voluntary and involuntary actions. For neither is truly voluntary or involuntary, but one is the image of the other. For he indeed who preserves his anger, and does not strike back immediately, but with plots later avenges himself, is very similar to a voluntary homicide; and he who does not preserve it, but is carried away by the first impulse of anger, and kills without premeditation, is judged similar to an involuntary homicide. However, he is not entirely involuntary, but is said to have a similarity to the involuntary. Wherefore, homicides committed through anger are difficult to determine: whether they are to be placed as voluntary or the opposite. **T**he best and truest opinion, therefore, is to call both "images," and to distinguish them separately so that one is said to be committed with counsel, the other without counsel. **B**ut it is fitting to impose greater punishments on those who have killed by anger with counsel. On those, conversely, who killed suddenly and without counsel, lighter ones. Truly, that which is similar to a more serious evil should be punished more harshly: that which is similar to a lighter one, more mildly. Certainly, it must be done thus in our laws. <gloss>Clin. Exactly so.</gloss> ATHEN. But repeating again about anger, let us say this. If anyone with his own hand kills a free man moved by anger without counsel, let him suffer the other same evils which are owed to the homicide who did not kill through anger: but he shall be an exile for two years entirely to restrain his anger. He who kills any free man by anger but with a plot: let him be forced to do the other things similarly to the first. But let him be an exile not for two years only like that one, but for three years, so that his more lasting anger may be punished longer. **L**et this be the universal disposition of these things. For it is difficult to place laws about these things individually and exactly. **S**ometimes, indeed, a murder which is established by law as more cruel seems lighter: sometimes, on the contrary, that which is lighter seems more cruel, according as it was done more atrociously or more mildly. For the most part, however, as we have just said, those things happen. But the guardians of the laws will know all these things. When indeed the time for restoring the exiles arrives, let them send XII judges to the borders of the region, who, having diligently considered <margin>G</margin> all the actions of the exiles through that time, shall become judges of their shame and their reception. But let them [the exiles] acquiesce to the judgment of these magistrates. But if after restoration either of these, moved by anger, sins similarly, let him be an exile forever, and if he returns again, let him be punished no differently than a returning foreigner. **I**f anyone thus kills his own slave, let him be purified: if someone else's, let him restore the loss to the master in double. If any homicide does not obey the laws, but not yet purified, contaminates the forum, the gymnasia, and other sacred things with his entrance, let whoever wishes call both him and the relative of the killed man who is neglecting these things into judgment, and compel him to pay double both in money and in other things: and that which is paid, let him receive it himself according to the law. If a slave moved by anger kills his own master—

<meta>This page continues the legal code regarding homicide from Book IX of Plato’s *Laws*. The previous section concluded the regulations for involuntary homicide; this page focuses first on homicides committed in anger—distinguished by whether they are more or less premeditated—and then begins the discussion on "voluntary" or "willful" murder driven by greed and ambition.</meta>

-># OF PLATO’S [LAWS]<-

<margin>A</margin> If a slave kills his master, the relatives of the deceased may kill the perpetrator in whatever way they wish, and they shall be free from any legal guilt, provided they do not leave him alive. If a slave kills a free man who is not his master in a fit of anger, his owner must hand the slave over to the relatives of the deceased, who are to put him to death in any manner they choose. If a father or a mother (which happens, though rarely) kills their son or daughter through blows or some other violent means in a fit of anger, they must be purified like other homicides and go into exile for three years. After this period is served and they return, the husband and wife must separate from one another. They shall never again join together to procreate children, nor shall they ever share a home or sacred rites with any of their other children or siblings. Anyone who fails to obey these laws out of an impious spirit may be accused of <margin>B</margin> impiety by any citizen who wishes to do so. If a husband kills his wife, or a wife her husband, in a fit of anger, they shall be purified in the same way and go into exile for a full three years. Upon returning, they must not share in sacred rites with their children, nor may they share a common table. If a parent or child fails to observe this, they shall be accused of impiety by whoever wishes. If a brother kills a brother or sister, or a sister kills a sister or brother in anger, they shall undergo the same purification and exile <margin>C</margin> prescribed for parents who kill their children; after their return, they must not share in sacred rites or table-fellowship with those whom they have deprived of brothers, sisters, or children. Anyone who transgresses this law shall be rightly condemned as impious. However, if a person is so overcome by anger that they kill a parent in an insane fury of rage, and if the parent—before they die—personally releases the killer from the guilt of the murder, the killer shall be considered pure after performing the same purifications required of those who commit involuntary homicide. But if the parent does not <margin>D</margin> release them, the perpetrator of the deed is liable under many laws. They shall be subject to the ultimate punishments for assault, impiety, and sacrilege, for they have committed sacrilege against the very soul that gave them life. Therefore, if it were possible for someone to die many times, it would be most just for a parricide <note>parricida: literally a killer of a parent or near relative; considered the most heinous crime in the ancient world.</note> to be put to death many times. For no law allows a man to kill his father or mother even in self-defense, even if he sees that he is about to be killed by them; rather, the law commands him to endure all things rather than commit such a deed. How else could such a person be justly punished? Thus, death is the ordained penalty for one who kills a parent in a fit of rage. If, during a civil strife or in some similar way, a brother kills a brother who has attacked him first, doing so in self-defense, he shall be considered pure as if he had killed an enemy. Likewise, if a citizen kills a citizen, or a foreigner a foreigner, or a foreigner a citizen (or vice-versa) in self-defense, they shall be pure. The same applies if a slave <margin>E</margin> kills a slave. But if a slave kills a free man in self-defense, he shall be subject to the same laws as a parricide. What we said regarding the release from the guilt of killing a parent shall also be understood to apply to the release from any homicide. If any victim willingly forgives the perpetrator before dying, as if the killing were involuntary, the killer shall be purified and spend one year in exile. These matters regarding violent, involuntary, and anger-driven homicides have been sufficiently explained. Let us now discuss those acts which are committed <margin>Concerning acts committed willingly and knowingly.</margin> voluntarily and with total injustice—those that arise from plots driven by the tyranny of pleasure, desire, and envy. CLINIA. You speak rightly. ATHENIAN. <margin>F</margin> First, then, let us declare as far as we can how many causes there are for voluntary homicide. The greatest cause is desire, which dominates a soul driven wild by lusts. This is most powerful in those cases where the most frequent and intense longing occurs—that is, the craving for the insatiable and limitless acquisition of wealth, born of both one's nature and a lack of education. The cause of this lack of education is that wealth is not correctly praised. Indeed, both Greeks and non-Greeks <note>original: "barbari"</note> place wealth in the first rank of goods, when it actually holds only the third. By this opinion, they destroy both themselves and their descendants. We would live most excellently and beautifully if the true view of wealth were preached everywhere: that wealth exists for the sake of the body, and the body for the sake of the soul. <margin>G</margin> Since, therefore, the things for whose sake wealth is possessed are the higher goods, wealth should hold the third rank after the virtue of the soul and the body. This logic acts as a teacher, showing us that a man who wishes to be happy should not seek wealth by any means, but only with justice and temperance. In this way, no murders would be committed in cities that require punishment by more murders. But now, as we said at the beginning of this discussion, this greed is the first and greatest thing that leads to the heaviest penalties for voluntary homicide. <margin>H</margin> The second cause is the habit of an ambitious soul <note>original: "ambitiosi animi habitus" / Greek: "philotimon"</note>, from which envies are born—first dangerous to the envious person himself, and secondly to the leaders of the city. The third cause consists of great and unjust fears; these produce many murders when people have done things, or are currently doing things, that they would wish no one to know about. Therefore, when they fear those who might judge them for such things, they kill them...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...if he kills him, let the relatives of the deceased use the killer however they wish, provided they do not keep him alive, and they shall be pure. If any other slave kills a free man in anger, the masters shall hand over the slave to the relatives of the deceased; and they shall put the doer to death in whatever way they most prefer. It does not often happen, but whenever a father or mother kills a son or daughter by blows or some violent way in anger, let them undergo the same purifications as the others and be exiled for three years. After the killers have returned, let the wife be separated from the husband and the husband from the wife; and let them never again beget children together, nor ever share a home with their offspring or siblings after they have killed a child or a brother; nor shall they share in sacred rites. Regarding those who are impious and disobedient in these matters, <margin>B</margin> let them be liable for a trial of impiety by anyone who wishes. If a man kills his wedded wife out of anger, or if a wife does this same thing to her own husband, let them be purified with the same purifications and complete three years of exile; and upon returning, such a person shall not share in sacred rites with all the others, nor ever be a table-companion. If the parent or the offspring is disobedient, let them again be liable to a trial of impiety by whoever wishes. And if a brother kills a brother or a sister, or a sister kills a brother or a sister <margin>C</margin> in anger, the rules regarding purification and exile have been stated as being the same as for parents and offspring; let it be decreed that this applies to those who have deprived brothers of brothers or parents of children; let the killer never share a home with them nor be a partner in sacred rites. If anyone is disobedient, they would rightly be subject to the law of the trial for impiety. If anyone becomes so lacking in control over their anger toward their parents that they dare to kill one of them in a madness of rage: if the deceased, before dying, voluntarily releases the doer from the murder, then the killer, having been purified just like those who committed an involuntary murder and having done all the other things those people do, shall be pure. But if <margin>D</margin> he does not release him, the one who did this shall be liable to many laws. For he shall be liable for an action of assault no less than for impiety and likewise for sacrilege, having stripped the person of their soul. So, if it were possible for the same man to die many times, even the parricide or matricide who committed this in anger would most justly meet with many deaths. For to him alone, even when defending himself and about to be killed by his parents, no law will grant the right to kill his father or mother—those who brought his nature into the light—but the law will command him to endure all suffering before doing such a thing; how else could he legally meet with <margin>E</margin> a fitting punishment? Let the penalty of death be established for the one who kills a father or mother in anger. If a brother kills a brother in a fight arising from civil strife or some such way, defending himself against the one who struck first, let him be pure, just as if he had killed an enemy. If a citizen kills a citizen in the same way, or a foreigner a foreigner, it shall be the same. And if a townsman kills a foreigner or a foreigner a townsman in self-defense, let it be according to the same rules; and if a slave kills a slave, likewise. But if a slave kills a free man in self-defense, he shall be subject to the same laws as the one who kills a father. Regarding what was said about the release from murder by a father, let this same thing apply to all such releases: if anyone voluntarily releases anyone else for this, as if the murder had happened involuntarily, let there be purifications for the doer and let there be one year of legal exile. These violent and involuntary murders occurring through anger have been sufficiently described. But those that are voluntary and occurring with all injustice—those resulting from plots through pleasure <margin>F</margin> and desires and envies—these we must speak of after the others. CLINIAS. You speak rightly. ATHENIAN. Again, first, let us say as far as we can how many causes there would be for such things. The greatest is desire, which rules a soul made wild by longings. This is most common where there is the greatest and strongest passion for most people—that power which falls upon them for the sake of the greedy and infinite acquisition of wealth, because of both nature and poor education. The cause of this poor education is the fact that wealth is wrongly praised among both Greeks and foreigners. For they say it is a good, preferring it as first when it is actually third, and they deceive both themselves and their descendants. For it is most beautiful and best for the truth about wealth to be spoken in all cities: <margin>G</margin> that it exists for the sake of the body, and the body for the sake of the soul. Since there are goods for the sake of which wealth naturally exists, it would be third after the virtue of the body and the soul. This reasoning would be a teacher showing that the person who is to be happy should not seek to be wealthy, but to be wealthy justly and temperately. In this way, murders would not happen in cities, requiring purification by more murders. But now (as we said when beginning this) this is one and the greatest cause which makes for the heaviest penalties for voluntary murder. Second is the habit of an ambitious soul, <margin>H</margin> which gives birth to envies—troublesome housemates, mostly for the one who possesses the envy, and secondly for the best men in the city. Third, cowardly and unjust fears have caused many murders, when people fear that an action they have done or are doing might be discovered, and they do not want anyone to know...

<meta>This page continues Book IX of Plato's Laws, transitioning from homicides committed in anger to those committed with premeditated intent. The previous page discussed the exile and purification for those who kill in the heat of passion; here, the text addresses the religious and social consequences of willful murder, particularly the concept of "bloodguilt" and the divine cycle of retribution.</meta>

# OF THE LAWS, BOOK IX

<margin>By no means of justice</margin>
**A** ...he cannot be removed from our midst by any other means than death. Regarding all these matters, let the words we have already spoken serve as a preamble. Furthermore, there is a teaching which many of those who study the sacred rites <note>original: "sacris student solennitatibus"</note> hear and firmly believe: that the murderer is punished in the underworld, and when he returns to this world, he must necessarily pay the natural penalty. This means he is forced to suffer in this life the very same fate he inflicted upon others. For the person who is convinced of this and fears such a punishment because of our preamble, there is no need to lay down a specific law. But for the man who is of the opposite mind, let this law be written: Whoever intentionally and unjustly kills a fellow citizen with his own hand <margin>B** shall first be excluded from temples, the marketplace, ports, and all common assemblies, so that his presence does not pollute <term>miasma<gloss>the ancient Greek concept of "pollution" or "contagion" caused by a crime, which was believed to be physically and spiritually dangerous to the whole community</gloss></term> these places, whether or not anyone has officially forbidden him. For the law itself forbids him and stands as a perpetual warning on behalf of the entire city.

If a relative of the deceased—up to the degree of first cousin—does not prosecute the killer as they ought, or fails to bar him from these places, let the guilt of the crime and the hatred of the gods fall first upon that relative, just as the curse of the law dictates. Secondly, that relative shall be liable to legal action by anyone who wishes to avenge the deceased. The one who chooses to seek vengeance must fulfill all the requirements <margin>If anyone is cast out by the laws</margin>
**C** concerning the rituals of purification <note>original: "luendi criminis"</note> and whatever else the god ordains regarding these matters. He shall issue the formal proclamation and then proceed to compel the murderer to pay the legal penalty. It is easy for a legislator to show that these things must be done through prayers and sacrifices to the gods who watch over cities to prevent bloodshed.

But as to who these gods are, and how these trials may most rightly be conducted according to the divine will, the Guardians of the Laws, together with the official interpreters, seers, and the god, shall establish the legal procedures. The judges of these cases shall be those same officials who have the authority to punish sacrilege. He who is convicted shall suffer the penalty of death; and since he has sinned not only impiously but shamelessly, <margin>The laws of purification</margin> he must not be buried in the land of the victim. If he flees and refuses to **D** stand trial, let him be perpetually exiled. If he is ever found within the borders of the country, the first relative of the deceased or citizen who encounters him may kill him with impunity, or bind him and hand him over to the magistrates in charge of such trials to be put to death.

If anyone attempts to defend the accused, he must provide sufficient sureties—recognized by the judges—who will guarantee that the accused will appear for trial. If he cannot or will not provide them, the magistrates shall take him into custody to ensure he is presented for judgment. If a person does not kill with his own hand, but rather through will, counsel, and <margin>If anyone without owing anything to the law</margin>
**E** treachery, being the cause of the death and impure in soul, even if he lives within the city, he shall be tried and punished in the same manner as the actual killer, except that he shall not be denied burial in his own land. The same rules shall apply to foreigners against foreigners, and between citizens and foreigners, and to slaves against slaves, regarding both direct killing and plotting—except for the matter of sureties, which we have already addressed.

If a slave voluntarily kills a free man, whether by his own hand or by plotting, and is convicted, the public executioner <margin>If anyone having plotted</margin> shall lead him to the tomb of the deceased—or to a place where it is visible—and there whip him as many times as the prosecutor directs. If the murderer survives the whipping, he shall then be put to death. If someone kills a slave who has done no wrong, **F** perhaps out of fear that the slave would reveal some shameful deed of his, or for some other similar reason, he shall be punished just as if he had killed a citizen.

There are certain occurrences for which it is difficult and painful to legislate, yet impossible not to. These are the murders of kinsmen, committed willfully and unjustly, whether by one's own hand or by plotting. <margin>Concerning involuntary acts</margin> These happen mostly in cities that are poorly governed, <margin>Most of these happen in dwellings</margin>
**G** but they can occur even where no one would expect them. To avoid such horrors, we must repeat the teaching mentioned earlier. Perhaps by hearing it, someone might voluntarily refrain from such a most abominable murder. For the story—or the myth, or whatever one should call it—was clearly stated by the priests of old: that Justice, as a watchful guardian and avenger of kindred blood, uses the law we just mentioned. She has ordained that whoever commits such a deed must necessarily suffer the very thing he did. If a man kills his father, he will eventually be violently killed by his own children; if he kills his mother, he must necessarily be reborn in a female nature <note>original: "particeps naturae muliebris"</note> <margin>He who [commits] voluntary [murder]</margin>
**H** and eventually be killed by his own offspring. For when the common blood of a family is defiled, there is no other purification, nor can the stain be washed away until the guilty soul has paid for the murder with a similar murder, and has thus soothed the anger of the entire lineage. Therefore, men must be restrained from these crimes by the fear of such punishments sent by the gods. If, however, some are so...

<column-break/>

**A** ...In no other way can he [the murderer] be removed from the community except by death. Let what we have said serve as preambles for all these things. Beyond this, there is a discourse which many of those who apply themselves to sacred solemnities both hear and believe: that murderers are punished in the underworld, and having returned here again, they necessarily pay the penalties owed according to nature. For those things which they have done to others, they are compelled to suffer from others by a similar lot in this life. Therefore, for the man who is persuaded and, having been warned by such a preamble, dreads such punishments, there is no need to lay down a law; but for the man of the contrary disposition, let this law be written. He who by design kills his own fellow citizen with his own hand through injury **B** shall first be far removed from the temples, the forum, the ports, and every common assembly, lest his presence defile these things, whether anyone has forbidden his presence or no one has. For the law itself forbids him, and forbids it in such a way that it seems to forbid it always on behalf of the entire state, and will continue to forbid it.

Next, he who does not prosecute him as is fitting, nor keeps him away from these places—among the relatives of the slain up to the degree of cousins—let the crime and the hatred of the gods first be turned upon him, just as the public imprecation and curse of the law dictates. Then, let him be liable to anyone who wishes to avenge the slain man. He who wishes to prosecute, when he has done all things which the god has ordained either concerning the observation of the crime to be atoned for or concerning any other things to be done, and has proclaimed those things which have been foretold, let him **C** proceed and compel the murderer to pay the penalties according to the law. That these things ought to be done with prayers and sacrifices to the gods, who care that slaughters do not happen in cities, the legislator can easily persuade.

But which gods these are, and in what manner these judgments may best be carried out according to the mind of god, let the guardians of the laws declare together with the interpreters, the soothsayers, and the god, and thus let them arrange the judgments and penalties. Indeed, let those be the judges of these matters to whom the authority of punishing sacrilege has been given. He who is condemned shall pay the penalty with death, and since he has sinned not only impiously but also imprudently, he ought not to be buried in the region of the slain man. But if he flees and **D** does not submit to judgment, let him be an exile forever. And if he is ever caught within the borders, let the first of the relatives of the slain or of the citizens who meets him kill him with impunity, or deliver him bound to the magistrates for this matter, the judges, to be put to death.

But if anyone comes forward to defend him, let him give surety for the one he protects, if he provides two sureties whom the judges themselves think sufficient, who promise that he will present himself for judgment. If anyone is unwilling or unable to do this, let him be kept bound by the magistrates for judgment. But if anyone has killed a man not with his own hand, but by will, counsel, and treachery, and although he is the cause of **E** the slaughter and impure in soul, he lives in the city: let him be punished in a similar way when condemned, except that he shall not provide sureties, and when condemned he shall not lack his own burial. Let other things be done for this man just as we said concerning the former. Let these same things be established for foreigners against foreigners, and for citizens and foreigners mutually, and for slaves against slaves, concerning slaughter done with one's own hand, and concerning that which has been committed by counsel and treachery: except that we judge that these men provide a surety just as those who kill with their own hand. If a slave kills a free man voluntarily, whether with his own hand or by counsel, and has been condemned, let him be dragged by the public lictor and avenger to the monument of the slain man, or to where he can see it, and having been whipped as much as the one who **F** convicted him in judgment orders, if by chance he still lives, let him be beaten even unto death.

If anyone kills a slave who is doing no injury, fearing lest some shameful thing done by himself be pointed out, or led by another such cause, let him be punished just as if he had killed a citizen. Sometimes certain things happen about which it is heavy and troublesome to lay down laws, and yet impossible not to. Of such a kind are the voluntary and unjust slaughters of relatives, whether brought about by one's own hand or by counsel and treachery, which are committed very much in badly governed cities; but sometimes they even happen where no one **G** would expect it. To avoid these crimes, let the previous discourse be repeated. For perhaps by hearing these things, someone will voluntarily abstain from a most wicked slaughter. For the story or discourse, or by whatever other name the speech ought to be called, was manifestly said by the ancient priests: that justice is the observer and avenger of all things, to avenge kindred blood, using the law which we just now mentioned. Truly, that she has ordained that whoever has perpetrated anything of this kind must necessarily suffer the same. As if anyone has delivered a father to death, he himself afterwards at certain times shall be violently killed by his sons; but if he killed a mother, he himself afterwards having been made a partaker of the female nature must necessarily at last be slain by his own sons. For when the common blood **H** has been defiled, there is no other purgation, nor can the stain be otherwise wiped away, unless the wicked soul has purified the slaughter with a similar slaughter, and has calmed the anger of the entire kinship. Therefore, it is necessary to restrain men from these crimes by the fear of such punishments which are brought by the gods. If, however, some are in such...

<meta>This page continues Book IX of Plato's Laws. The previous page discussed the generic punishments for willful murder; this page specifies the extreme cases of parricide, suicide, and the liability of animals or objects, before transitioning into the philosophical necessity of the law itself to balance public and private interests.</meta>

# PLATO

**A** If a man should fall into such a wretched calamity that he dares to intentionally and deliberately deprive a father, mother, brother, or child of life, the mortal legislator shall decree the following concerning such a crime: once the proclamation has been made, he shall be barred from public sacrifices and sacred places, as was stated previously, and sureties shall likewise be required. Anyone condemned for a murder of this kind shall be put to death by the officers of the judges and the magistrates. His body shall be cast out naked beyond the city to a designated crossroads <note>original: "triuium"</note>, where each magistrate, acting on behalf of the entire state, shall cast a stone at the head of the corpse to purify the whole city. Finally, the body shall be carried beyond the borders of the territory and cast out unburied, according to the laws.

**B** <margin>Slayers of themselves.</margin> But what judgment should be passed on one who destroys his closest and dearest friend? I speak of the man who deprives himself of life and his allotted fate by a wicked force—not compelled by a legal judgment of the city, nor by some sad and inevitable stroke of fortune, nor forced by some extreme and unbearable shame, but who unjustly inflicts death upon himself through idleness and the weakness of a fearful soul. What purifications and what type of burial are appropriate for such a man according to the law, God himself knows. Nevertheless, the next of kin should inquire of the interpreters <note>The "Exegetai" or interpreters were religious officials in Athens who advised on sacred law and purification rites.</note> and the laws regarding these matters and act according to their decrees.

**C** The burial for these men shall be solitary, where no one else is interred. They shall be buried in those places among the twelve districts that are most remote, wasteland, and nameless. They shall be buried in obscurity, with their graves marked neither by a statue nor by an inscribed name. If a beast of burden or any other animal should kill a human being—unless it occurs in a public contest—the relatives of the deceased shall bring the matter before the judges. The rural wardens <term>agronomoi<gloss>officials responsible for the administration and policing of the countryside</gloss></term>, whom the relative appoints, shall judge the case, and the condemned animal shall be killed and cast beyond the borders of the territory. If an inanimate object—excluding lightning or another weapon sent by the gods—should deprive a man of life, either by falling on him or by him falling upon it, the relative of the deceased shall appoint the nearest neighbor as a judge to perform the expiation for himself and his entire kin, and whatever is condemned shall be cast out beyond the borders, just as was said of the animals.

**D** If a person is found dead and the murderer is unknown, and cannot be found despite a diligent search, the same proclamations shall be made as in other cases: a public notice shall be issued in the forum that whoever killed this person is guilty of murder and must not enter sacred places or remain in the territory. If he is ever caught, he shall be put to death and cast out unburied beyond the borders. Let this be our primary established law concerning murder.

**E** <margin>Those whom it is lawful to kill.</margin> Enough has been said of these matters. Now let us speak of those cases in which the killer remains pure. He who kills a thief entering his house at night for the purpose of robbery shall be pure. Likewise, he who kills a robber in self-defense. And he who violently forces a free woman or a boy for sexual purposes may be killed with impunity, not only by the victim of the violence but also by the father, brothers, or sons. If a husband kills a man who is using force against his wife, he shall be pure by law. Furthermore, if anyone kills someone while coming to the aid of a father (who is not himself acting wickedly), or a mother, or children, or brothers, or a spouse, he shall be pure.

**F** <margin>On violent acts.</margin> Thus far we have written laws concerning the education and discipline of the living soul—which, if possessed, makes life worth living, but if not, makes it not worth living. Furthermore, we have spoken of violent deaths and how they are to be punished, as well as the nutrition and discipline of bodies. Next, we must determine, to the best of our ability, the nature and number of violent actions, both voluntary and involuntary, and the punishments by which they may be properly restrained. It is right to treat these matters next. For wounds and the mutilation of limbs through wounding would be placed by even a simple legislator immediately after murder. These are distinguished just as murders are: some are involuntary, some are done in anger, some out of fear, and some are voluntary and premeditated. The following serves as a preamble to all such things.

**G** <margin>The public good connects cities; the private dissipates them.</margin> It is necessary to establish laws for men and for them to live according to these laws; otherwise, they would differ in no way from the most savage of beasts. The reason for this is that no human nature is naturally capable of both knowing what is beneficial for the public life of humanity and, having known it, always being able and willing to do what is best.

**H** First, it is difficult to recognize that the true political art must care not for the private but for the public interest (for the public interest binds and unites cities, whereas the private interest pulls them apart), and that it benefits both the public and the private if the common good is better disposed than the private. Second, even if someone should sufficiently grasp this as a matter of theory, if he then holds power over a city with such license that he is subject to no accountability, he would never be able to remain firm in this conviction throughout his life—namely, to foster the public good in the city as the primary good and to place the private good after the public. Rather, his mortal nature will always drive him toward personal gain and private advantage; for, lacking reason, it flees pain and pursues pleasure irrationally, and...

<column-break/>

**A** ...should fall into a wretched calamity, so that he dares to willfully deprive a father or mother, or siblings or children, of their life's breath <note>original: "ψυχὴν" (psyche/soul)</note>, the law of the mortal legislator concerning such things shall be as follows: he must flee and be barred from the sacred rites, and sureties shall be required as stated before. If anyone is convicted of such a murder, having killed one of these, the attendants of the judges and the magistrates shall kill him and cast him out naked at a designated spot outside the city. Then all the magistrates, on behalf of the whole city, shall each carry a stone and cast it at the head of the corpse to purify the entire city. After this, they shall carry the body to the borders of the land and cast it out unburied according to the law.

**B** But what should be the fate of the man who kills his own most intimate and so-called "dearest friend"? I mean the one who kills himself, violently depriving himself of his allotted fate, neither compelled by the city's legal sentence, nor forced by some unavoidable and desperate stroke of fortune, nor having shared in some unbearable shame that makes life unlivable, but who imposes this penalty on himself out of idleness and the cowardice of an unmanly spirit. For such a man, as to what other rites are necessary concerning burials, God knows; however, the next of kin should ask the interpreters and the laws regarding these matters and do as they are commanded.

**C** They should be buried first with order. The graves of those thus destroyed shall be, first, solitary, with no one else buried with them. Then, they shall be buried in those of the twelve districts which are waste and nameless, buried without glory, their graves marked neither by monuments nor by names. If a beast of burden or any other animal kills someone, except for those that do so while competing in a public contest, the relatives of the victim shall prosecute the killer. The rural wardens shall judge the case, and the relative shall appoint as many as he is commanded. The animal, if convicted, shall be killed and cast outside the borders of the territory. If an inanimate object deprives a human of life, except for lightning or some similar bolt from God, but of all other things which kill someone by falling on them or by the person falling on them, the relative shall appoint the nearest neighbor as judge to purify himself and his entire kin. The convicted object shall be cast beyond the borders (as was said) like the animal kind.

**D** If a person is clearly dead but the killer is unknown and is not found by those who search diligently, the same proclamations shall be made as for the others. One should proclaim the murder against the doer, and after seeking a judgment in the marketplace, announce that whoever killed so-and-so and is convicted of murder shall not enter the temples nor any part of the victim's country; for if he appears and is recognized, he shall be put to death and cast out unburied from the victim's land.

**E** Let there be one established law concerning murder. Let matters of this sort be finished here. As for the man who kills and is rightly considered pure, let the following apply: If someone catches and kills a thief entering a house at night to steal property, he shall be pure. And if someone kills a highwayman in self-defense, he shall be pure. And if someone violently rapes a free woman or a boy, let him be killed with impunity by the victim of the violence, or by the father, or brothers, or sons. If a man comes upon his wedded wife being forced and kills the rapist, he shall be pure according to the law. And if someone, while aiding a father who is doing nothing unholy, kills someone—or a mother, or children, or brothers—he shall be entirely pure.

**F** Let the laws thus be established concerning the nourishment and education of the living soul—which if attained, life is livable, but if missed, the opposite—and concerning violent deaths and what punishments should occur. Matters regarding the protection and education of bodies have been spoken of. Following these are violent actions against one another, both involuntary and voluntary. These must be defined as far as possible—what they are and how many, and what punishments they should receive, so that each has what is appropriate. These things, it seems, would be rightly legislated after the former. For wounds and mutilations from falls <note>original: "ἐκ πτωμάτων"</note>, which are second after deaths, even the most ordinary legislator would arrange under the law. Wounds should be divided just as murders have been divided: some voluntary, some in anger, some from fear, and some that occur voluntarily from premeditation.

**G** Before all such things, a definition must be made: that it is necessary for men to establish laws and to live according to laws, or they would differ in no way from the most savage beasts. The cause of this is as follows: that no human nature is born capable of knowing what is beneficial to men for a political constitution and, knowing what is best, always being able and willing to do it.

**H** For first, it is difficult to know that the political and true art must necessarily care not for the private but for the common (for the common binds, but the private pulls cities apart) and that it benefits both the common and the private if the common is set well rather than the private. Second, even if someone should sufficiently grasp in his art that these things are naturally so, and after this should rule a city with no accountability and absolute power, he would never be able to remain in this doctrine and spend his life prioritizing the common in the city, with the private following the common. Instead, his mortal nature will always urge him toward greed and private interest, irrationally fleeing pain and pursuing pleasure; and it will set both of these before what is more just and better...

It also introduces the philosophical argument that laws are essential because human nature naturally prioritizes private pleasure over the public good.</summary>

### ON THE LAWS, BOOK IX.

**A** ...and by working darkness within itself, it will eventually fill itself and the entire city with every kind of evil. For truly, if any man were ever born by divine fate <note>The Greek "theia moira" refers to a special providence or natural genius that transcends human education.</note> with a nature sufficient to grasp the public good and always remain steadfast in it, he would have no need of laws to rule over him. For no law or order is superior to knowledge; nor is it right for Mind <note>original: "nous"</note> to be a subject or a slave to anyone, but rather it should be the ruler of all things—provided it is true and truly free according to its nature. But as it is, such a mind is found nowhere, or only in small measure. Therefore, we must choose the second way: order and law. These see and look toward the general rule for the most part, but they are unable to see every specific instance. This has been said for the following reason: we must now determine what a person who has wounded or harmed another ought to suffer or pay as a fine. For it is easy for anyone to grasp the basic ideas—what a wound is, or what you mean by a blow—since there are thousands of variations and they differ greatly from one another.

**B** Now, to leave all of these to the courts to decide, or to leave nothing to them, is impossible. One thing is necessary for a court to decide in all cases: whether each of these events actually occurred or not. However, for the legislator to never allow the judges to determine the fines or what the wrongdoer should suffer for his blows, but instead for the legislator to always define every small and large detail himself—this is almost impossible.

**CLINIAS:** What, then, is the next step in this argument?
**ATHENIAN:** This: that some things must be granted to the courts, and others must not be granted, but rather determined by the legislator himself.
**C** **CLINIAS:** What sorts of things should be legislated, and what should be left to the judges to decide?
**ATHENIAN:** We might best answer this by saying that in a city where the courts are poor and "voiceless" <note>original: "aphōna" - referring to courts where judges do not deliberate openly or are restricted from speaking.</note>, hiding their own opinions and judging in secret—or even worse, when they are not silent but full of noise like a theater, shouting praise or blame at the speakers in turns—it is difficult for the city to find any good path. In such cases, one is forced by necessity to legislate everything. We might say it is our misfortune that we are driven by this necessity, but if so, we should allow the judges to set only the smallest penalties and explicitly legislate the majority of the punishments ourselves. 

**D** <margin>Matters determined by law versus by equity.</margin> On the other hand, in a city where the courts have been established as correctly as possible, and the judges are well-educated and tested with the utmost care, it is right and good to permit such judges to decide most of the penalties that the guilty should suffer or pay. It is not appropriate for us at this time to legislate the greatest and most numerous details for them; even less educated judges could see such things and assign the value of the penalty to each suffering and action according to its merit. Since we believe those for whom we are legislating will be quite capable judges, we must leave most things to them. Nevertheless, as we have often said and done in our previous legislation, we should provide a sketch or a model of punishments to serve as an example for the judges, so they never step outside the bounds of justice. This is what we must do now, with goodwill, as we return again to the laws.

**E** Let the law concerning wounding be set down as follows: If someone, intending to kill a person who is a "friend" <note>original: "philión" - here meaning a fellow citizen or relative protected by the law.</note>—excepting those whom the law permits—wounds them but is unable to kill them, we should not show mercy to the one who intended and struck the blow. We should compel him to face a trial for murder just as if he had succeeded. 

**F** <margin>Laws on wounding.</margin> However, we should show respect to his "luck," which was not entirely bad, and to the Protective Spirit <note>original: "daimona" - a guardian spirit or divine influence.</note> who took pity on both the victim and the attacker, preventing the wound from becoming a fatal injury for the one and a cursed calamity for the other. Giving thanks to this Spirit and not opposing it, we shall remove the death penalty from the attacker. Instead, he shall be sentenced to move to a neighboring city and remain in exile for life, though he may enjoy the fruits of all his property. If he caused damage to the wounded man, he must pay restitution, the amount to be determined by the court that hears the case. The judges should be the same ones who would have judged a murder. If a son wounds his parents or a slave wounds his master in the same way with intent, the penalty shall be death. Or if a brother wounds a brother or sister, or a sister wounds a brother or sister with premeditation, the penalty for the blow shall be death. 

**G** If a wife wounds her own husband with a plot to kill, or a husband his wife, they shall likewise suffer perpetual exile. As for their property, if they have children who are still young, the guardians shall take charge and oversee their care. If the children are adults, they shall not be forced to support the exile from the property, but shall possess the estate themselves. If someone falls into such a calamity while childless, his relatives—up to the level of cousins on both the male and female sides—shall meet together with the Guardians of the Law and the priests. They shall appoint an heir for this house from the city's 5,040 households <note>Plato’s ideal number of citizens/households, chosen because it has many divisors for administrative purposes.</note>, seeking a humble and holy person to be established as the heir. They must consider that no house belongs so much to its inhabitant or his family as it belongs publicly and privately to the state.

<column-break/>

prefers both of these to what is more just and better; and being overwhelmed by darkness, it will finally fill itself and the entire city with all evils. Indeed, if anyone were endowed by the favor of divine fate with such a nature that he recognized the public good and was always nobly and consistently directed toward it, he would have no need for any laws to dominate him. Since no law, no order is considered better or more excellent than knowledge; nor is it right for the mind to be subject to anyone or to serve: but rather, if it were thus true and free, it should dominate all. But now this is found nowhere; or only a very small part of it appears. Wherefore, what is in the second place is right to choose: order and law, by which most things are seen, but all things cannot be seen. But with these things proposed for their own sake, let us now establish what he who has wounded another, or otherwise hindered him, ought to suffer or pay. For it is easy for anyone to correctly grasp individual things of this kind: namely, whether someone has wounded another or not; whom, in what part, in what manner. For these individual cases are almost innumerable and differ greatly among themselves. However, it is impossible to commit all these to judgment, or none of them. Certainly, it is necessary to commit that one thing in all cases: whether each of these things was done or not. It is also nearly impossible to commit nothing regarding the fine of the injurer, but to determine all things, great and small, by law. **CLINIAS:** How then should it be said after this? **ATHENIAN:** Thus, surely, that the legislator ought to grant some things to judgment, and some things he ought not; but he himself should determine them. **CLINIAS:** But what things are to be left to the judgment and prudence of the judges, and what are to be determined by the law-giver himself? **ATHENIAN:** These things we shall next explain in this way as best as possible. Truly, a more serious plague is born to the whole city where the judgments are lazy and silent; the opinions of the judges remain hidden from each other, and they pass sentence in secret. In addition, it is harder when things are not done in silence: but like theaters, everything resounds with noise, and the orators now praise, now blame; and so they judge in turn. To such judgments, if one is urged by some necessity, we consider it unfortunate to give laws. But he who is compelled to give them, let him commit at least the smallest fines to these judges, but let him himself declare most and all the greatest things in making the laws. But where judgments are correctly established according to strength, and the judges are well-educated and approved with all diligence, many things concerning the punishment and condition of the condemned can most rightly be committed to the judges. Therefore, let no one accuse us if we do not now ordain the greatest and many other things for them by laws; which even less learned judges could perceive; and adapt a worthy fine and punishment to each individual offense. Since, however, we hope that those for whom we describe the laws will not be unskilled judges of these matters, we think many things should be committed to them. But what we have often said and done in the earlier parts, thinking that the things said about the description and form of punishments ought to be given as examples to the judges, which they should never transgress; that was both then rightly done, and now also we wish to observe it, returning again to the making of laws. Concerning wounds, therefore, let us thus decree. If anyone shall have willed and thought to kill a friend from among those whom the law forbids, but has wounded him and has not been able to kill him: we would compel this man, all mercy being removed, no differently than if he had deprived him of life, to pay the penalty of murder, unless we were to respect his fortune, which was not altogether perverse, and his spirit <note>original: "demonéque"</note>, who having followed both the wounded and the wounder with mercy, stood in the way of the misfortune of both; and brought it about that a lethal wound was not inflicted on the one, nor an execrable fortune and calamity on the other. Therefore, we shall be grateful to this spirit, and so that he may not be least opposed by his benefit, we shall take away the penalty of death from him who wounded; and we shall decree that he be an exile in a neighboring city for his whole life, lacking no fruit of all his things, the damage however being first restored, if he hindered the wounded man in anything, which shall have been established by the judgment of this matter. But let the judges be those who would be judges of murder, if the wounded man had died. If a son similarly wounds his parents, or a slave his master, by design, and shall have been condemned for so doing, let him pay for the crime by death. Furthermore, if a brother wounds a brother or sister, or a sister a sister or brother, with the intention of killing, let him pay for the crime with death; and a wife if she wounds her husband with the intention of killing, or a husband his wife, let him similarly be an exile forever. If these are still boys or girls, guardians shall manage the family property of the exile, to protect those orphans. But if they are adults, the things indeed may be permitted to them to have, but they shall not be compelled to nourish the exile. But if anyone lacking children should fall into calamities of this kind, let his kinsmen as far as second and third cousins on both the side of the men and of the women come together, and having held a council together with the guardians of the laws and the priests, let them establish one heir in this house of the exile, from the forty-five thousand <note>The Latin text says "45,000" here but the Greek correctly identifies the 5,040 households. This is a common numerical error in early translations.</note> houses of the city. In which surely they ought to think, that no house of the five thousand and forty belongs more to the inhabitant himself and his race, than to the city both privately and publicly. It establishes specific penalties for attempted murder (wounding), noting that while the intent warrants death, the "good luck" of the victim's survival allows for the mercy of life-long exile instead.</summary>

# OF PLATO
### 662

<margin>A</margin> ...should possess their own houses as holily and happily as possible. Therefore, whenever a house is defiled by some misfortune or impiety—because the one who possessed it died without children, having been condemned for a voluntary murder or some other crime against the gods or citizens for which the penalty is death or perpetual exile—first, let the house itself be expiated according to the law. Then, let the kinsmen, as we have said, meeting with the guardians of the laws, seek out a family in the city that is most excellent in virtue and fortunate, in which there are several young men. From these, they shall adopt one as a son for the deceased father and his ancestors, praying to the god that this successor may be a propagator of offspring under more fortunate omens, a successor to the house, the sacred rites, and a cultivator of all that remains. Finally, they shall <margin>B</margin> constitute him as the heir according to the law. But as for the one who committed the sin, let them suffer him to lie without a name, without children, and without any portion of the inheritance, seeing as he is weighed down by such calamities. 

However, a boundary is not joined to a boundary in all things <note>A metaphor for legal definitions; not every crime falls neatly into a single category.</note>. For where there is a common border, there may be a middle ground agreed upon between the boundaries of things. And yet, between those sins committed intentionally and those committed unintentionally, we have said that what is done through anger is something of that sort. Therefore, if someone is condemned for a wound caused by anger, if the outcome itself shows the wound was curable, he shall pay double the damage; but if it is incurable, quadruple. If it is curable but brings <margin>C</margin> great disgrace upon the wounded party, he shall pay quadruple. 

But if anyone has not only harmed the wounded person but also injured the fatherland by depriving it of a soldier against enemies, let him be punished similarly. Moreover, he must restore the loss to the city, and beyond the military service he owes himself, he must also serve in place of the wounded man, performing whatever duties the other was to do in war. If he does not do this, he shall be liable according to the law to anyone who wishes to accuse him of neglecting military service; and he shall pay double, triple, or quadruple the damage as it seems fit to the judges. 

If a brother wounds a brother in like manner, let the tribesmen and kinsmen up to the children of cousins, on both the male and female sides, <margin>D</margin> both men and women, meet and judge, and deliver him to his parents so they may punish him according to nature. But if the punishment is disputed, let the kinsmen on the father's side determine it. If they are unable, let them finally bring the case to the guardians of the laws. 

If children or grandchildren have inflicted such a thing upon their parents, let only those who have passed their sixtieth year judge, provided they have natural—not adopted—children. The condemned person shall be punished with death, or some greater or not much lesser penalty. No one of his own family shall judge, even if they have reached the age prescribed by law. 

But if a slave, stirred by anger, wounds a free man, let him be handed over by his master to the wounded man, so that he may avenge the injury at his own discretion, unless the master wishes to pay the damage himself. But if anyone suspects that <margin>E</margin> the malice of the slave and the wounded man was done through a conspiracy <note>original: "per compositionem" - a staged incident to extort the owner.</note>, let him bring it to the judges. If he does not prove it so, let him restore triple the damage; but if he does prove it, let him hold as a prisoner of the law the one who acted deceitfully with the slave. 

Whoever wounds another unintentionally shall simply pay the damage. For no legislator is able to command fortune. Let the judges be those who were mentioned for children against parents, and let them declare the amount of the damage. 

All the passions we have mentioned are violent. Every kind of striking is also violent. Therefore, it is necessary for all people, women and men, young and old, to always think this of these matters: that an elder is to be preferred to the younger by no small interval, both among gods and among men who intend to live happily. For an elder to be struck by a junior is both <margin>Veneration of Elders</margin> <margin>F</margin> disgraceful and hated by the gods. It is fitting for a young man struck by an elder to bear it patiently out of reverence for old age. 

Thus, let us ordain: Let everyone honor an elder in both deed and word. And if someone is twenty years older, let the junior revere him as a father if he is a man, or a mother if she is a woman. Furthermore, let him always abstain from all those who are of an age at which they could have begotten or given birth to him, fearing the gods of birth <note>original: "natales deos" / "theōn genethliōn" - the gods presiding over family lineages.</note>. 

Similarly, let him abstain from a stranger, whether he has lived in the city for a long time or has recently moved there. For let him not dare to inflict blows upon such a person, whether provoking or defending himself. But if a stranger dares to strike a citizen, if the one struck thinks he should be punished, let him bring him to the city prefects. He should not strike back himself, so that he may better abstain from striking his own citizens when he restrains himself even from strangers. <margin>G</margin> This magistrate, fearing the God of Hospitality <note>original: "hospitalem deum" / "xenikon theon" - Zeus Xenios, protector of travelers.</note>, shall diligently inquire into the matter. If the stranger has unjustly struck a citizen, let as many blows be returned to him with a public whip so that he may not dare such impudence again. But if the stranger appears innocent, the magistrates shall dismiss them both, having rebuked the one who brought him. 

If an equal strikes an equal—whether someone of the same age or slightly older but not yet of a father's age, or old man against old man, or youth against youth—let them defend themselves according to nature with bare hands and without a weapon. But if someone over forty years old dares...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...and private. For a city must certainly possess the same houses as holily and as fortunately as possible. Therefore, whenever someone, through both misfortune and impiety, so affects a house that the one who possessed it leaves no children—either because he was convicted of crimes or because of some voluntary slaughter or other sin against the gods or citizens—for which a death penalty is expressly laid down in the law, or if he is the cause of perpetual exile from the city of men: first, it shall be necessary for the house to be purified and the pollution cast out according to the law. Then, the relatives, gathering together (as we said just now) with the law-guardians, shall look for whatever family in the city is most approved for virtue and is also <margin>B</margin> fortunate, in which there are many children born. From there, they shall take one as a son for the deceased father and for his ancestors above him, naming him for the sake of his reputation, and praying that he may become a progenitor for them, a master of the hearth, and a tender of holy and sacred things under better fortunes; thus they shall establish him as the heir according to the law. But the one who sinned, they shall leave nameless, childless, and without a share, whenever such calamities overtake him.

But it seems that in all things, it is not possible for one boundary to be strictly attached to another, but for those where there is still a border-land, there is a middle ground between the boundaries, falling toward both, being between the two—just as we said that what happens through anger is such a form, between the voluntary and the involuntary. <margin>C</margin> Regarding wounds arising from anger: if someone is convicted, first let him pay the injured party double if the wound is assumed to be curable. If it is incurable, let him pay quadruple. If it is curable, but inflicts great shame and reproach upon the wounded person, let him pay quadruple. 

And if someone, by wounding another, not only harms the victim but also the city, making him unable to help his fatherland against enemies, let him pay for that damage to the city as well as the other penalties. For in addition to his own military service, let him be stationed in the military ranks of the incapacitated man and perform his duties of war. If he does not do these things, let him be liable to anyone who wishes to prosecute him for evasion of military service according to the law. <margin>D</margin> Let the judges who voted against him determine the value of the damage, whether it be double, triple, or quadruple.

If a kinsman wounds a kinsman in the same way, let the parents and relatives up to the children of cousins, on the sides of both women and men, gathering together and judging, hand him over to the parents for natural punishment. If the punishment is disputed, let the male relatives have the authority to fix the penalty. If they themselves are unable, let them finally entrust it to the law-guardians. 

In cases of such wounds inflicted by offspring against parents, let the judges necessarily be those who are sixty years old, and who have true—not adopted—children. They shall judge whether such a person must die, or suffer some other penalty greater than this, or perhaps not much <margin>E</margin> smaller. And let no one from the perpetrator’s near kin judge, even if he has reached the age the law specifies. 

If a slave strikes a free man in anger, let the owner hand the slave over to the wounded party to use as he wishes. If he does not hand him over, let him pay the damage himself. If anyone charges that it was a trick and the wounding was staged by conspiracy, let him contest it; if he does not win, let him pay triple the damage; if he wins, let him have the one who schemed with the slave as a prisoner liable to law. 

Whoever wounds another unintentionally, let him pay simple damage. For no legislator is sufficient to rule over fortune. Let the judges be those mentioned for offspring against parents, and let them assess the value of the damage.

<margin>F</margin> These things regarding wounding are laid down for us; and let there be regulations for every kind of assault. Thus, every man, child, and woman must always think of these things: that the elder is to be honored far above the younger, both among gods and among men who are to live grandly and happily. Therefore, to see an assault committed in the city by a younger man against an elder is disgraceful and hated by the gods. It is fitting for every young man struck by an old man to endure the anger lightly, storing up this persuasion of desire for his own old age. 

Thus let it be: let every one of us respect his elder in both deed and word. Let him revere anyone twenty years older in age, male or female, as a father or mother; and let him always keep himself from every age-group capable of having begotten him, for the sake of the ancestral gods. In the same way, let him abstain from a stranger, whether long-resident or newly <margin>G</margin> arrived. For let him not dare to punish such a person with blows at all, either by starting it or in self-defense. If a stranger acts insolently and boldly, striking a citizen, let the citizen, thinking he needs punishing, take him and lead him to the city-magistrates, but let him refrain from striking; so that it may be far from a local man ever daring to strike a neighbor. Let the city-magistrates, having taken him and examined him, and respecting the God of Strangers, if the stranger indeed seems to have struck the local man unjustly, give the stranger as many lashes with the whip as he gave blows, and stop his boldness. But if he did no wrong, having threatened and reproached the one who led him away, let them release both. 

If an equal strikes an equal, or any age group strikes its own—an old man an old man, or a young man a young man—let him defend himself naturally, without a weapon, with bare hands. But if someone over forty years old dares...
