# ON THE LAWS, BOOK IX.
### 663

...to fight, whether he be a magistrate or a private citizen, if he is unrefined, uneducated, <margin>A</margin> and of a slavish nature, let him suffer the disgrace of his folly. If anyone is disobedient to such regulations, let him be dishonored. But he who is stubborn and cares nothing for the disgrace, let him receive the law of the others. If anyone strikes a person twenty years or more their senior: first, let any bystander who happens to be there—provided he is not younger than or equal in age to the combatants—render aid; if he fails to do so, let him be considered wicked according to the law. If he is of the same age as the victim, or younger, let him defend the injured party as if he were a brother, a father, or a higher relative. Furthermore, let the one who dared to strike the elder be subject to a trial for assault, as we have said. If he is convicted, let him be imprisoned for no less than a year; if the judges decide on a longer term, let that time be authoritative for him. If a foreigner or one of the <margin>B</margin> resident aliens strikes a person twenty years or more their senior, the same law of assistance shall apply to those present. He who is defeated in such a suit, if he is a foreigner and not a resident, shall be imprisoned for two years; but if he is a resident alien and disobedient to the laws, let him be imprisoned for three years, unless the court assigns him a longer time. Let any bystander who fails to assist according to the law be fined: if he is of the highest property class, one <term>mina<note>A mina was a unit of currency worth 100 drachmas; roughly three months' wages for a skilled laborer.</note></term>; if of the second, fifty drachmas; if of the third, thirty; and if of the fourth, twenty. The judges for such cases shall be the generals, <margin>C</margin> commanders, tribal leaders, and cavalry masters. It seems that laws are made partly for the sake of good men, to teach them how to live in friendship with one another; but others are made for those who have escaped education, possessing a hard nature and having been born with no inclination to avoid all wickedness. These laws are made for the sake of what will now be said; the legislator imposes them by necessity, though he would wish there were never a need for them. For whoever dares to act with such folly as to strike another with violence, fearing neither the wrath of the gods above nor the punishments said to exist below, but acting as if he knows what he does not—despising the ancient traditions <margin>D</margin> concerning the heavens—such a person requires an extreme deterrent. Now, death is not the ultimate end; the punishments said to be in Hades for such people are more extreme, and though they are told most truly, they do not deter such souls. For if they did deter them, there would never be those who strike their mothers or commit other shameful daring acts. Therefore, it is necessary that the punishments in this life for such crimes be no less than those in Hades, but equal to them so far as possible. Let it be declared as follows: whoever dares to strike a father or mother, or their parents, while not <margin>E</margin> being insane, first, let the bystanders render aid (as mentioned before). Let the resident alien or foreigner who assists be given a seat of honor at the public games; but if he does not assist, let him be perpetually banished from the land. If he is not a resident alien, let him receive praise if he assists, and blame if he does not. If a slave assists, let him be set free; if he does not assist, let him be beaten with a hundred lashes of the whip. If the incident happens in the marketplace, let it be punished by the <term>agoranomoi<note>Market overseers responsible for order in the trade areas.</note></term>; if outside the marketplace but in the city, by the city overseers; and if in the countryside, by the officers of the <term>agronomoi<note>Rural police or district magistrates.</note></term>. If any citizen is present—whether child, man, or woman—let them all defend the victim, crying out against the crime. He who fails to assist shall be subject to the curse of <term>Jupiter<note>Original Greek: "Zeus Homognios," the protector of the family and clan.</note></term> the Father and Protector of the Clan according to the law. Furthermore, whoever is convicted of striking his parents shall first be perpetually exiled from the city into the rest of the territory, and <margin>F</margin> be barred from all sacred rites. If he does not stay away, let the rural officers punish him with lashes, or however they wish. If he returns from exile, let him be punished with death. If anyone free-born eats or drinks with such a person, or has any other such communication, or even happens to touch him willingly, he shall not enter any temple, nor the market, nor the city at all until he is purified, for he must believe he has been contaminated by the association with the wicked. If he does not obey, but pollutes the city and the temples, any magistrate who notices this and does not bring a suit shall be liable for the greatest injuries in his accounting of office. If a slave strikes a free man, whether <margin>G</margin> a foreigner or a citizen, let any bystander render aid. If not, let him pay the fine according to his property class as previously stated. Let those present assist the one who was struck, bind the striker, and hand him over to the injured party. The victim, having taken him, shall hold him in fetters and lash him as much as he wishes, provided he does no damage to the owner, and then return him to the owner to be held according to the law. And let the law be this: If a slave strikes a free man without being ordered by the magistrates, the owner shall receive him bound from the victim on the condition that he does not release him until the slave has persuaded the victim that he is worthy to live at liberty. These same laws regarding such matters shall be common to women toward one another, to women toward men, and to men toward women.

<column-break/>

...whether while defending himself, he dares to strike anyone, his rustic and slavish condition will be seen as sufficient punishment for this disgrace. Whoever obeys these warnings will be considered modest and mild. But he who despises these preambles, let him be coerced by this law: He who has struck someone twenty years or more his senior: first, let whoever happens to be present—if he is neither younger nor of the same age—prohibit it; and if he does not prohibit it, let him be held as wicked according to the laws. But if he is of the same age or younger than the one beaten, let him defend him as a brother or father or as a superior. And furthermore, let the one who struck the elder, as we said, be subject to judgment, and if he is condemned, let him be imprisoned for no less than a year. Indeed, even longer, if it seems so to the judges. If a foreigner or resident alien strikes someone twenty years or more his senior, let those present help by the law we stated, and he who is condemned, if he is a foreigner but not an inhabitant of the city, let him be imprisoned for two years; but if he is an inhabitant and resident of the city and does not obey the laws, three years, unless the judges decree he should be held longer. But he who was present and did not help according to the law, if he is of the first and greatest property class, let him be fined a mina. If of the second class, fifty drachmas. Of the third, thirty. Of the fourth, twenty. The judges of these are the leaders of the army, the prefects of orders, the tribunes, and the masters of the horse. Regarding the laws, as it seems, some are established for the instruction of good men, so that through them they may understand how to live amicably among themselves. Others are for restraining the stubbornness of those who are wild by nature, and having despised all discipline, are moved by no reason, but rush into every wickedness. These are the cause of the following words: the legislator, compelled by necessity, imposes laws upon them. For he himself would wish there were no use or necessity for laws anywhere. Whoever, therefore, dares to lay hands on a father or mother or grandparents, fearing neither the indignation of the gods above nor the punishments below, but acting as if he knows what he does not, despising the sayings of all the ancients, acts unjustly: he requires the ultimate remedy to be turned away and expiated. Death, however, is not the ultimate; rather, the extreme punishments are those below. Although these are told most truly, they still cannot turn away such minds. For if they did turn them away, none would ever be found who wickedly strike their parents. Therefore, it is necessary to set the punishments for these crimes in this life no lower than those which are among the dead, but equal according to our strength. Thus, therefore, let us sanction: If anyone not insane dares to strike a father or mother or their superiors, first, as with those above, let those present bring help. And a resident alien or foreigner, if he assists, shall be placed before others as a president in public contests; if less, let him be perpetually exterminated from the whole region. But if he is not a resident, having helped let him receive praise, and not having helped, blame. A slave who helps shall be freed; one who does not help shall be beaten a hundred times with the public whip. And if it happens in the forum: let him be punished there by the curators of vendible things. In other parts of the city likewise by the aediles who are present. In the same way outside the city in the field by those who then preside over the care of the fields. But if any citizen is present when parents are beaten by a son, whether man, woman, youth, or elder, let them defend immediately, crying out at the crime. He who will not help shall be pressed by the law with the imprecation of the Father Jupiter and of the clan and kin. Finally, whoever is condemned for striking parents, first let him be perpetually exiled: then also be barred from all sacred things, from which if he does not abstain, let him be punished by the princes of the field with lashes and altogether however they wish, and if he returns from exile, let him pay for his sins with death. Whoever, being free, eats or drinks with such a man, or does anything with him in any way, or touches him, or speaks with him voluntarily, let him not enter a temple, nor the forum, nor proceed into the city at all before he is cleansed, for he ought to think himself contaminated by the commerce of the wicked. But if he does not obey, but wickedly defiles the city and temples: whatever magistrate senses this happening, unless he punishes it immediately, is to be held guilty of the greatest injuries. If a slave strikes a free man, whether citizen or foreigner, let anyone present bring help. If not, let him be punished with the fine predicted according to his property class. Therefore, let those who are present succor the one struck: and bind the striker, and deliver the bound man to him whom he injured. Let him hold him in shackles, and lash him as he wishes, so that he inflicts no damage on the master; then let him return him to the master to be held according to the law, which is this: If a slave has struck a free man when the magistrates were not commanding it, the master shall receive him bound from the one struck on this condition, that he does not release him until the slave has persuaded the one struck that he is now worthy of release. These same laws for all these things ought to be common to women among themselves and toward men, and to men toward women.

# PLATO’S ON THE | PLATO’S LAWS,
# LAWS, OR, ON THE | OR,
# INSTITUTION OF LAWS, | ON LEGISLATION,

### TENTH DIALOGUE. | TENTH DIALOGUE.

---

->SUMMARY OF THE DIALOGUE.<-
The thesis of this dispute is noted in the prayer: here indeed he treats that most beautiful topic "Against Impiety," which he designates by the name of sacrilege. However, in order to tear it up and extirpate it from its very roots, he brings forward and refutes the objections of impious men who speak profanely of God—men who, under the appearance and pretext of a certain unhappy erudition, set out to be "insane with reason." Our philosopher, therefore, attacks impiety with every effort of his mind, so that he might banish it from the Republic not only by the severity of punishments, but from the minds of men by solid reasoning. And lest he be condemned for the length of this speech, he explains the reason why he lingers longer on this discourse. Having established these things, he sets down the punishments against impiety by the laws he has passed: and having distinguished certain different types of impiety, he also declares various penalties for them. For pure Impiety, as a capital crime, he decrees capital punishment. The rest may be sought from the dispute itself.

---

<margin>On every kind of violence.</margin>
After the laws concerning murder, wounds, and blows, let that common law regarding every kind of violence be enacted: that no one shall carry away or take the property of another, nor use any of his neighbor's things, unless he has first persuaded the owner. For from this, all the evils we have described have depended, do now depend, and will depend in the future. Of the remaining acts, the greatest are the insults and injuries of unrestrained youths: which are greatest when they are committed against sacred things—especially when committed against public and holy things, or against the common property of certain tribes or other such groups. In the second place, they are to be held as such when committed against private sacred things and tombs. Third are those against parents, separate from those injuries we described previously. The fourth kind of insult and injury is when someone, in contempt of the magistrates, carries off their property or uses it before he has persuaded them. Fifth would be when the civil dignity of any citizen is harmed or offended, a kind which altogether demands vengeance. The law ought to provide for each of these in common. Regarding sacrilege, it has been stated in summary what ought to be done if it is carried out by force or in secret.

<margin>On contempt of the deity.</margin>
Regarding those things which are done by word or deed in contempt of the gods, how they are to be punished, it seems we must speak next, after a certain preface has been proposed. Let this be the preface: No one who believes the gods exist according to the laws ever voluntarily commits an impious act or speaks an unlawful word. But they do or say something impious against the gods for one of three reasons: either because they deny the gods exist; or because, although they think gods exist, they believe they care nothing for human affairs; or thirdly, that although they exist and care for men, they are easily appeased by prayers and sacrifices. CLINIAS: What shall we do then? What shall we say to them? ATHENIAN: Let us listen first, my good man, to what I imagine they might say in mockery, expressing their contempt for us. CLINIAS: What will they say? ATHENIAN: They will likely joke at us in this way: "O Athenian guest, and you Lacedaemonian and Knossian, you speak the truth when you say that some of us do not think there are gods at all, others that they care nothing for us, and others that they are easily appeased by gifts. Therefore, what you thought should be done in passing all your laws, we want you to do for us now: namely, before threatening us with the terrors of the law, persuade us with sufficient evidence that there are gods, and that they cannot be moved by gifts beyond what is right. For now, hearing these and similar things daily from those who are thought to be excellent—poets, orators, prophets, priests, and countless others—we are not turned away from doing wrong; rather, when we have done it, we try to appease the gods. From you, however, who boast that you are not harsh but mild lawgivers, we demand that you first use persuasion to show us that there are gods, and teach us so that even if you do not speak much better than the others, you at least speak more truthfully. For perhaps we might believe you. Therefore, if we ask something fair, comply with us." CLINIAS: But, my friend, it seems easy to show by the truth that there are gods. ATHENIAN: In what way? CLINIAS: First, indeed, the earth, the sun, the stars, and the whole universe itself, and the most beautifully ordered variety of seasons, divided into years and months, show this; furthermore, the consensus of all Greeks and barbarians <note>original: "barbarorum"; meaning all non-Greek speaking peoples.</note> who confess that gods exist.

<margin>On the gods.</margin>
ATHENIAN: I fear, O blessed man, those wicked <note>original: "sceletos"; literally "withered" or "villainous" men.</note> men—I say I fear them, and I do not blush to say I dread lest they perhaps despise you. For you are ignorant of the cause of their disagreement, and you think it is only through the lack of control over pleasures and desires that their souls fall into an impious life. CLINIAS: But what other cause besides these could there be, guest? ATHENIAN: Something which, because you live entirely apart from it, escapes you. CLINIAS: What is this? ATHENIAN: A certain most grave ignorance, which appears to be the greatest wisdom. CLINIAS: How so? ATHENIAN: There are accounts among us written partly in verse and partly in prose, which among you, because of the excellence of your civil discipline, are not found, as I hear. The most ancient of these affirm that the first nature of the heaven and the other gods was created, and not much further on they narrate the generation of the gods and their behavior among themselves. Since these stories are ancient, it is not easy to criticize them as to whether they are told rightly or not in other respects; however, regarding the care and honor of parents, I would never say they are useful or true. Therefore, let us dismiss the ancient things, and let them be spoken of as is pleasing to the gods; but let the words of the younger sages be blamed wherever they are the cause of evils. Indeed, those who...

<column-break/>

A
After the acts of violence, let some such law as this be spoken concerning all violent acts: that no one shall carry away or lead off anything belonging to another; nor, again, shall he use anything belonging to his neighbors unless he has persuaded the owner. For from such things all the aforementioned evils have depended, and are, and shall be. But the greatest of the remaining acts are the insolence and outrages of the young; and they are greatest when they are directed against sacred things. They are especially great when they are against public and holy things, or the common parts of tribes or other such groups who share things in common. Second in order are outrages against private sacred things and tombs. Third, those against parents, besides what has been said before when someone acts with insolence. A fourth kind of outrage is when someone, disregarding the magistrates, leads away, carries off, or uses anything of theirs without persuading them. Fifth would be the civil outrage against any of the citizens, calling for justice. To all these, one common law must be given. Concerning sacrilege, which is violence in short—whether it happens by force or in secret—what one must suffer has been stated. But as for all the things someone might say or do in outrage against the gods, in word or deed, we must state the medicine for each by law, declaring what must be suffered. Let it be this: No one who believes the gods exist according to the laws ever willingly committed an impious deed or let fall an unlawful word. But he does so because of one of three things: either, as I said, not believing; or second, that though they exist, they do not care for men; or third, that they are easily appeased, being led astray by sacrifices and prayers.

C
CLINIAS: What then should we do or say to them? ATHENIAN: My good man, let us first listen to them, for I divine that they might say things in mockery of us. CLINIAS: What sort of things? ATHENIAN: They might say these things in jest: "O Athenian guest, and Lacedaemonian and Knossian, you speak the truth. For some of us do not believe in gods at all; others believe they are such as you describe; others, again, such as we provide... such as you say. We demand then, just as you demanded concerning the laws, that before you threaten us harshly, you first attempt to persuade and teach us that there are gods, stating sufficient evidence; and that they are too good to be charmed by certain gifts led astray against justice. For now, hearing these things and other such stories from those said to be the best poets, orators, prophets, priests, and countless others, most of us do not turn toward not doing unjust things, but having done them, we try to make amends. From the lawgivers, then, who claim to be not savage but mild, we demand that they use persuasion toward us first—even if not speaking much better than others about the gods, at least speaking better in terms of truth. And perhaps we might be persuaded by you. Try then, if we speak anything reasonable, to say what we challenge you to say." CLINIAS: Does it not seem easy then, guest, to speak truly and say that there are gods?

ATHENIAN: How? CLINIAS: First, there is the earth and the sun, and all the stars, and the things of the seasons so beautifully ordered, divided by years and months. And also that all Greeks and barbarians <note>non-Greeks</note> believe that there are gods. ATHENIAN: I fear, O blessed man, the wicked (for I would never say it out of shame) lest they somehow despise you. For you do not know the cause of the difference in them; you think it is only lack of control over pleasures and desires that drives their souls toward an impious life. CLINIAS: What else besides these could be the cause, guest? ATHENIAN: Something which you, living altogether outside of it, might not know, but it would escape you. CLINIAS: What is this you are saying now? ATHENIAN: A certain very difficult ignorance, which seems to be the greatest wisdom. CLINIAS: How do you mean? ATHENIAN: We have accounts lying in writings, which are not among you because of the virtue of your government—as I divine—some in verse, others without verse, speaking about the gods. The most ancient ones tell how the first nature of heaven and other things came to be; and starting from the beginning, they go through the <term>theogony<note>the origin and genealogy of the gods</note></term> and how, having been born, they consorted with one another. Whether these things are good or not good for those who hear them is not easy to criticize since they are ancient. However, regarding the care and honors of parents, I would never say they are spoken of with praise, nor as being useful, nor as being entirely correct. Let the things of the ancients be dismissed and let them go, and let it be spoken in whatever way is pleasing to the gods; but let the things of our younger sages be blamed as the causes of evils. <summary>This page introduces Book X of Plato's Laws, shifting from civil and criminal law to the theology of the state. It outlines the three types of impiety—atheism, divine indifference, and the belief that gods can be bribed—and begins a philosophical defense of the gods' existence.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the opening discussion of Book X of Plato's Laws. Having established the need to legislate against impiety, the Athenian Stranger and Cleinias now address the intellectual roots of atheism and the challenge of persuading those who believe the universe is merely material.</meta>

# ON THE LAWS, BOOK X.

Would these arguments not be sufficient for those who are so impious? For whenever we offer evidence that the gods exist—bringing forward the sun, the moon, the stars, and the earth as gods and divine beings—those who have been persuaded by these "wise men" <note>This likely refers to Pre-Socratic philosophers like Anaxagoras, who taught that the sun was a red-hot stone rather than a god.</note> would say that these things are merely earth and stones, incapable of caring for human affairs, and that our arguments are merely well-dressed speech made to look persuasive. **CLEINIAS.** You have described a difficult argument, Stranger, if there were only one such person; but now that there are so many, it is even more difficult.

->A<-

**ATHENIAN.** What then should we say? What should we do? Should we defend ourselves as if we were being accused by impious men who are fleeing from our legislation? Should we say that we are doing something terrible by legislating on the assumption that gods exist? Or should we let that go and return to the laws, lest the prelude <note>The "prooemium" or prelude: Plato believed laws should be preceded by persuasive explanations to encourage voluntary obedience.</note> to the law becomes excessively long? For the discourse will not be short if we wish to sufficiently demonstrate to those who desire to be impious the things they require us to say—to turn them from their wickedness through fear, and to cause them to feel the proper distaste for it before we finally enact the laws. **CLEINIAS.** But Stranger, we have already said many times in this short time that there is no reason to prefer brevity over length at the present moment. For no one, as the saying goes, is chasing us in a hurry. It would be ridiculous and petty to appear to choose the shorter path over the better one. It matters a great deal that our arguments should have some persuasiveness, showing that gods exist and that they are good, honoring justice far more than men do. This would be nearly the finest and best prelude for all our laws. Therefore, without any annoyance or haste, let us put forth all our power into the persuasion of such arguments, omitting nothing so far as we are able.

->B<-

->C<-

**ATHENIAN.** This speech of yours, since you are so eagerly prepared, seems to call for a prayer, and it can no longer endure delay. Come then, how could one speak about the existence of the gods without anger? For it is necessary to feel heavy-hearted and to hate those who have been and are now the cause of these arguments. They are those who are not persuaded by the stories <note>original: "mythois"</note> which they have heard from their earliest childhood, while still being nourished on milk—stories told by their nurses and mothers, spoken both in play and in earnest like charms. They heard these in prayers during sacrifices, and saw the accompanying sights which a young person watches and hears with great pleasure: they saw their own parents sacrificing with the greatest zeal for themselves and their children, and offering supplications, speaking to the gods as though they were most certainly real and present. Furthermore, at the rising and setting of the sun and moon, they saw and heard all Greeks and barbarians <note>original: "barbaron" — meaning non-Greeks, not necessarily "uncivilized" people.</note> prostrating and bowing in all types of circumstances, both in misfortune and in prosperity; they did not act as if the gods were non-existent, but as if they were most certainly real, never offering the slightest suspicion that gods do not exist.

->D<-

But those who despise all these things for no good reason—as anyone with even a small amount of sense would say—now compel us to say what we are saying. How can anyone admonish such people with gentle words, while teaching them first that gods exist? Yet we must dare to do so. For it is not right that we should be corrupted by anger against them, just as they are ruined by their wild lust for pleasure. Let us therefore address those whose minds are so corrupted with an unruffled spirit, and let us speak mildly, quenching our anger, as if we were talking to a single person of that sort.

->E<-

->F<-

"O son, you are still young; but as time goes on, it will cause you to change many of the opinions you now hold and adopt the opposite ones. Wait, therefore, until then to be a judge of the greatest matters. And the greatest matter—which you now think is nothing—is to think correctly about the gods and thereby to live a good life or not. First, I would never be found a liar if I pointed out one great thing to you regarding them: you are not the only one, nor are your friends the first, to hold this opinion about the gods. There are always some, more or fewer, who suffer from this disease. I can tell you what has happened to many of them: no one who took up this opinion in his youth, that the gods do not exist, ever continued in that mindset into old age. However, two other conditions regarding the gods do sometimes persist—not in many, but in some: the belief that gods exist but care nothing for human affairs; and the belief that they do care, but are easily won over by sacrifices and prayers. If you listen to me, you will wait until the truth of these doctrines becomes clear to you according to your ability, considering whether it is this way or another; you should inquire from others, and especially from the lawgiver. In the meantime, do not dare to commit any impiety toward the gods. For he who is now laying down the laws for you will try to teach you, now and later, how these things truly are." **CLEINIAS.** What you have said so far, Stranger, is most excellent.

->G<-

->H<-

**ATHENIAN.** Indeed it is, Megillus and Cleinias; but we have unwittingly fallen into a wondrous argument. **CLEINIAS.** What kind do you mean?
**ATHENIAN.** The one that is thought by many to be the wisest of all arguments.
**CLEINIAS.** Speak more clearly. **ATHENIAN.** Some say that all things that are, have been, or will be, come into existence either by nature, by chance, or by art. <note>original: "physei... tychen... technen"</note> **CLEINIAS.** It is likely, after all, that wise men speak correctly. Let us follow them and examine what those who think this way actually mean. **CLEINIAS.** By all means. **ATHENIAN.** It seems (they say) that the greatest and most beautiful things are produced by nature and chance, and the lesser things by art. And art, receiving from nature the...

<column-break/>

bring to men, let us find fault with them. Indeed, by the words of those men, this result is achieved: that when you and I assert these very things to be signs that there are gods—bringing the sun, the moon, the stars, and the earth into the midst as gods and divine things—then young men, having been otherwise persuaded by those "wise men," say that these are merely earth and stones, and can have no care for human affairs; and that a discourse about these things has been composed with merely ornamental words to look like the truth. **CLEINIAS.** You have certainly held a grave and dangerous discourse, Stranger, even if I had been the only one listening. But now it is all the more grave and troublesome because there are so many such people.

->A<-

**ATHENIAN.** What then ought we to say, or what ought we to do? Shall we prepare ourselves for a defense as if we were accused before impious men, because we have falsely affirmed in our laws that gods exist? Or, having dismissed these men, shall we return again to the treatment of the laws, lest this prelude of the laws grow too long for us? For the speech will not be short if we wish to sufficiently demonstrate to men inclined toward impiety what they require, and also to move them from their crime by terror, and finally, as is fitting, to bring the laws. **CLEINIAS.** It has often been said by us in this short time, Stranger, that brevity is not to be preferred over length. For nothing, as they say, urges us. Therefore, it would be both ridiculous and wicked if we preferred shorter things to better things. For it contributes much if our speech shows by a likely reason that gods exist, that they are good, and that they honor justice much more than men do. This will be almost the best and most beautiful exordium <note>An "exordium" is the introductory part of an oration or treatise.</note> of all the laws. Therefore, without any trouble or haste, let us omit nothing within our power that pertains to persuading them of this matter.

->B<-

->C<-

**ATHENIAN.** That speech of yours shows you to be so prepared and prompt that it seems to provoke us to prayers and vows, and no longer suffers any delay. But how can anyone speak of the gods without offense? Especially since it is necessary to take it heavily and to hate those who have provided us with the cause for these words. Surely these men, from their childhood, could have been most strongly led to affirm the gods by the fact that, while they were being nourished on milk, they heard from their nurses and mothers many things said both in jest and in earnest about the gods in their speeches; and in the sacrifices, they saw things done consistent with those stories, which children both see and hear most sweetly. They saw their parents sacrificing with the greatest zeal for themselves and their children, and praying as suppliants, seeing the gods as though they were as real as could be. Moreover, daily at the rising and setting of the sun and moon, they beheld all Greeks and barbarians, in adversity as well as in prosperity, bowing in worship; and from this, they did not bring forth a suspicion that the gods do not exist, but rather testimony that they exist beyond controversy.

->D<-

But truly, those who despise all these things—moved by no reason that anyone of sound mind would speak—and therefore compel us to say these things: how can we now correct them with mild words and first teach them that gods exist? Yet let us dare to do so; for it is not fitting that, while they are lost in pleasure, we also should be corrupted by anger against them. Therefore, all agitation of the mind having been extinguished, let us undertake the prelude to those whose minds are so corrupted; and let us mildly turn the discourse to them as if to one of them.

->E<-

->F<-

"O son, you are still young; and I do not doubt that the passage of time will cause you to feel differently about many things than you do now. Wait, therefore, I pray, that you may then judge of the greatest things. And the greatest thing—which you now think is nothing—is that we may live well by thinking correctly about the gods."

->G<-

"Truly, if I certify this very great thing to you, I shall by no means lie. Not you alone, nor your friends, are the first to have this opinion about the gods; but some are always laboring under this disease, sometimes more and sometimes fewer. But I will tell you what has happened to most of them. Surely none of them has persevered in this opinion—that the gods do not exist—from youth even until old age. But the other two diseases, although not in many, have nevertheless remained in some: that the gods exist indeed, but care nothing for human affairs; or that they do care, but are easily appeased by prayers and sacrifices. You, therefore, if you will believe me, will wait until it is plainly established for you, according to your power, what is to be judged of these things. And so that you may achieve that, you will consider diligently whether the matter stands thus or otherwise; and you will inquire of all others, and especially of the lawmaker. In the meantime, do not be so rash as to think impiously of the gods. For he who is laying down the laws for you will endeavor to teach you, both now and hereafter, how those things stand." **CLEINIAS.** Most excellently has it been spoken to us thus far, Stranger.

->H<-

**ATHENIAN.** It is entirely so, O Megillus and Cleinias. But we have unwittingly fallen into a certain wonderful discourse. **CLEINIAS.** Which one? **ATHENIAN.** The one which is thought by many to be the wisest.
<margin>All things are made by nature, or fortune, or art.</margin>
Speak more clearly. **ATHENIAN.** Some say that all things which are made, or are to be, or have been made, are made either by nature, or by fortune <note>In this context, "fortune" (fortuna) is synonymous with "chance" (tyche).</note>, or by art. **CLEINIAS.** And rightly so, indeed. **ATHENIAN.** Certainly it is not absurd that wise men have spoken rightly. Therefore let us follow them; and let us inquire what they actually meant. **CLEINIAS.** By all means. **ATHENIAN.** They say the greatest and most beautiful things are made by nature and fortune; but the lesser things by art; and those things, they say...

<summary>In this opening of Book X, the Athenian Stranger argues against the materialist view that the universe is merely "earth and stones" and addresses the roots of atheism, urging young doubters to delay their judgment on the divine. He introduces a critical philosophical debate on whether the world is governed by Nature and Chance or by intelligent Art and Law.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the Athenian Stranger’s critique of materialist philosophies which claim the universe is the product of mindless elements rather than divine intelligence. Having established the prevalence of these views among the youth, the dialogue now explores the social and legal consequences of a world without inherent justice or gods.</meta>

# OF PLATO

<margin>A</margin> ...having accepted from nature the generation of great and primary works, they <note>Meaning "Art" or human skill</note> fashion and build all the smaller things which everyone calls "artifice." **CLINIAS.** How do you mean that? **ATHENIAN.** I will say it more clearly. They say that fire, water, earth, and air all exist by nature and chance, but none of them by art. They claim that the bodies which come after these—namely the earth, sun, moon, and all the stars—were produced from these entirely soulless elements. Carried along by chance, each according to its own power, they collided and fitted together in some suitable way: the cold with the hot, the dry with the moist, the soft with the hard, <margin>B</margin> and all things were mixed by necessity according to the blending of opposites through chance. In this way, they say, the whole heaven and everything in it was produced, as well as all animals and plants and the seasons; not through intellect, nor through any god, nor by art, but by nature and chance, as we said. They claim that art—which is mortal and born from mortals—was produced later from these, giving birth to certain later things that do not fully participate in truth, but are merely images related to themselves, such as those generated by painting, music, and other similar arts. If there are any arts that produce something serious, they are those that share their power with nature, such as medicine, agriculture, and gymnastics. <margin>C</margin> Furthermore, they say that political expertise shares a small part with nature, but a great deal with art; and thus they claim that the whole of legislation is based not on nature, but on art, whose positions are not true. **CLINIAS.** In what way? **ATHENIAN.** These men claim, my blessed friend, that the gods exist not by nature, but by art and certain laws, and that they vary from place to place according to how each group agreed among themselves when they established their laws. They say that things which are beautiful or honorable are different by nature than they are by law. But as for things that are just, they claim they have no natural existence at all; rather, men are always in conflict about them and are constantly changing them. Whatever changes they make, and whenever they make them, those things are then valid, having been established by art and laws, and not by any nature. These are the things, my friends, <margin>D</margin> that wise men—both poets and prose writers—teach to the young: that the highest "justice" is whatever someone can win by force. From this, impiety grows in the young, leading them to believe that the gods are not such as the law commands them to believe. From this also arise seditions, as men are pulled toward a life that is supposedly "right according to nature," which truly consists in living by conquering others and not serving anyone else according to the law. **CLINIAS.** What a tale you have told, Stranger! What a plague you describe, brought upon the youth and upon cities and private households alike! **ATHENIAN.** You speak the truth, Clinias. But since things stand this way, what do you think the legislator should do? Should he only threaten all men, saying they will be punished unless they believe the gods exist and hold such opinions about them as the laws hand down? And regarding what is honorable, just, and all the greatest things, as well as virtue and vice, should they think and act exactly as the legislator has prescribed? <margin>E</margin> If they do not obey, should some be punished with death, others with lashes and chains, others with disgrace, and others with exile and poverty? Shall the legislator only threaten them, or shall he add persuasion to his threats in his legislation, so as to soften them? **CLINIAS.** Not at all, Stranger; if even a small amount of persuasion can be found in such matters, a legislator who is worth anything at all must not grow weary of the labor. Instead, he should, as they say, "shout with all his might" to bring aid to the ancient law and provide reasons to show that the gods exist and all the other things you were just saying. <margin>F</margin> He must support the law itself and art, asserting that they exist either by nature or by something no less than nature, since they are the offspring of Mind itself, as right reason demonstrates—which you seem to be telling me now, and which I believe. **ATHENIAN.** O most ready-spirited Clinias! Is it not a difficult task to follow with arguments those things that are so widely spread among the masses and which are so lengthy they do not admit of brevity? **CLINIAS.** Why, Stranger? When we were speaking at such length about drunkenness and music, we bore that prolixity with a calm mind; shall we not listen to one speaking at length about the gods and such matters? Indeed, this will be a great defense for a prudently arranged legislation, for the commands of the laws, once committed to writing—which are usually subject to cross-examination for all future time—will remain settled and confirmed. <margin>G</margin> Therefore, we should not be terrified if these things are difficult to hear at first; even those of slow wit will be able to understand by repeating them often. Thus, though they be long, if they are useful, they should not be rejected. Nor is it fair not to defend these arguments to the best of our strength. **MEGILLUS.** I think Clinias speaks very well, Stranger. **ATHENIAN.** And most rightly so, Megillus; therefore, we must do as he says. Truly, unless such talk had been scattered among almost all men, there would be no need to demonstrate by reason that gods exist. But now it is necessary. Since the laws are being most corrupted by wicked men, whose duty is it more than the legislator's to bring aid? **CLINIAS.** <margin>H</margin> Certainly no one else's. **ATHENIAN.** But tell me again, Clinias—for you must be a partner in this argument—does not he who says these things seem to think that fire, earth, water, and air are the first of all things? And does he not call these very things "nature," and think that the soul comes later from them? Indeed, he does not just seem to think it, but his speech truly signifies this to us. **CLINIAS.** Precisely so. **ATHENIAN.** By Zeus, then, is it not as if we have found the source...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...having accepted from the nature of great and primary works the power to fashion and build all the smaller things, which we all call "technical." **CLINIAS.** How do you mean? **ATHENIAN.** I will say it even more clearly: they say that fire, water, earth, and air all exist by nature and chance; and that none of these exist by art. And the bodies that come after these—the earth, sun, moon, and stars—they say came into being through these elements, which are entirely soulless. Each being carried along by the chance of their own power, they fell together and fitted together in a suitable way: the hot with the cold, the dry with the moist, the soft with <margin>B</margin> the hard; and everything that was necessarily mixed by the blending of opposites through chance. In this way and by these means, they say, the whole heaven and everything in the heaven was created; and likewise all animals and plants, with all the seasons arising from them—not through intellect (they say), nor through any god, nor through art, but, as we say, by nature and chance. They claim that art was created later from these, a mortal thing born from mortals, having later generated certain forms of play <note>The Greek word "paideia" here refers to cultural arts or pastimes that lack the "seriousness" of natural reality.</note> that do not participate much in truth, but are images akin to themselves—such as painting generates, and music, and all the arts that are companions to these. And if any of the arts produce something serious, they are those that share their power with nature; <margin>C</margin> such as medicine, agriculture, and gymnastics. And they say that political science shares a small part with nature, but mostly with art; and so all legislation is not by nature, but by art, and its positions are not true. **CL.** How do you mean? **ATH.** These men say, my blessed friend, that gods exist first of all by art and not by nature, but by certain laws; and that these gods are different in different places, according to how each group agreed among themselves when they legislated. And indeed, they say that things that are beautiful are one thing by nature but another by law. As for things that are just, they say they do not exist by nature at all, but that men continue to dispute them with one another and are always changing them. Whatever changes they make and whenever they make them, those things are then valid, being produced by art and laws, and not by any nature. These things, my <margin>D</margin> friends, are the teachings of "wise men" among the youth, both prose writers and poets, who claim that the most "just" thing is whatever one can win by force. From this, impiety falls upon the young—that there are no gods such as the law first commands them to believe in; and from this also come seditions, as they are dragged toward the "correct life according to nature," which is in truth to live by conquering others and not being a slave to others according to the law. **CL.** What a story you have gone through, Stranger, and what a ruin of young men, both publicly for cities and privately for homes! **ATH.** You speak the truth, Clinias. What then do you think the legislator should do, since these ideas have long been prepared? Should he only threaten all the people in the city, saying that if they do not say the gods exist and think as the law says—believing them to be such as the law describes—and the same regarding honorable and just things, and all the greatest matters, and whatever tends toward virtue and vice, that they must <margin>E</margin> act in these ways, thinking exactly as the legislator directs in writing? And whoever does not show himself obedient to the laws, one must die, another be punished with lashes and bonds, another with disgrace, and others with poverty and exile. But should he offer no persuasion to the men while he sets down the laws, nor use any arguments to attempt to civilize them? **CL.** Not at all, Stranger; but if there happens to be even a small amount of persuasion about such things, a legislator who is worth even a little must never grow weary. Rather, as the saying goes, "leaving no stone unturned," he must become an ally to the ancient law with the argument that gods exist; and all the things you have just gone through, he must use to aid the law itself and art. He must show that they exist <margin>F</margin> by nature, or by something not less than nature, since they are the products of mind, according to the right reason which you seem to me to be speaking of, and which I now believe. **ATH.** O most eager Clinias, is it not difficult for arguments spoken to the masses to be followed, and do they not require a long discourse? **CL.** What of it, Stranger? We endured ourselves speaking so long about drunkenness and music; shall we not endure it regarding the gods and such matters? Moreover, this is perhaps the greatest aid to legislation—that the commands in the laws, being set down in writing, will provide a test for all time and remain entirely settled. So even if they are difficult to hear at first, <margin>G</margin> one should not fear; even for the slow learner, it is possible to examine them by returning to them often. And if they are long but useful, for these reasons it makes no sense—and seems impious to me—not to help these arguments with all a man's power. **ME.** Clinias seems to speak excellently, Stranger. **ATH.** Very much so, Megillus; and we must do as he says. For if such arguments had not been scattered among almost all men, so to speak, there would be no need for arguments defending the existence of the gods; but now it is necessary. When the greatest laws are being destroyed by wicked men, whom does it more concern to bring aid than the legislator? **CL.** No one else. **ATH.** But tell me again, Clinias—for you must be a partner in the argument. It seems <margin>H</margin> that he who says these things considers fire, water, earth, and air to be the first of all things, and he names these very things "nature," while the soul comes later from these. It seems he is not just guessing, but truly signifies this to us in his speech. **CL.** Absolutely. **ATH.** Is it not then, by Zeus, as if we have reached a spring...

<summary>This page analyzes the materialist philosophy that claims the universe and the gods are mere human inventions or products of blind chance, leading to a "might makes right" morality. The Athenian and Clinias conclude that the legislator must use persuasive arguments, not just punishment, to prove that the soul and divine intelligence precede material elements.</summary>
<keywords>materialism, atheism, nature vs art, legislation, persuasion, justice, might makes right, elements, soul, Plato's Laws</keywords>

--- Page 699 ---
<meta>This page continues the Athenian Stranger’s argument against materialist philosophers who claim that the universe arose from blind physical forces. On the previous page, he described how these thinkers believe "art" and "soul" are late, artificial additions to a world of chance. Now, he begins his formal proof that the soul is actually the oldest thing in the universe and the primary cause of all motion.</meta>

# ON THE LAWS, BOOK X.

<margin>A</margin> ...we have found a certain foolish opinion of those men who have ever touched upon the impious investigation of nature. Consider this, examining the whole argument. For it is no small matter if it should appear that those who use impious arguments, and lead others toward them, are using their logic not well, but entirely erroneously. This is how it seems to me. **CLINIAS.** You speak well; but try to explain how this is so. **ATHENIAN.** It seems, then, that I must take up rather unusual <note>The Greek *aēdesterōn* literally means "unpleasant" or "distasteful," referring to the dry, technical nature of the upcoming metaphysical argument compared to the usual legal discussion.</note> arguments. **CLINIAS.** We must not hesitate, Stranger. I understand that you think we are stepping outside the bounds of legislation if we touch upon such matters. But if there is no other way to harmonize the laws we are now stating concerning the gods and to show they are correct, then we must speak in this way, my wonderful friend. <margin>B</margin> **ATHENIAN.** It seems I should now deliver a discourse that is almost entirely new to us: these impious arguments have claimed that the thing which is the first cause of the birth and destruction of all things is not first, but a later product; and that which is later is actually the eldest. <margin>Note: He rejects the opinion of those who say bodies (matter) are the principles of all things.</margin> This is why they have wandered into error regarding the true essence of the gods. **CLINIAS.** I do not yet understand. **ATHENIAN.** Almost everyone, my friend, seems to be ignorant of the nature of the soul <term>psychē</term> and the power it possesses. They are ignorant of its other attributes and especially its origin—that it is among the first things, having come into being before all bodies, and that it is the primary ruler of all change and transformation of bodies. <margin>C</margin> If this is true, then must not the things related to the soul necessarily have come into being before the things belonging to the body, since the soul itself is older than the body? **CLINIAS.** Necessarily. **ATHENIAN.** Therefore, opinion, care, intellect, art, and law would be prior to hard and soft, and heavy and light. Consequently, the great and primary works and actions would be those of art, being among the first; whereas the things of "nature," and nature itself (which they wrongly name), would be later and ruled by art and intellect. **CLINIAS.** Why is that? **ATHENIAN.** They wish to use the word "nature" <term>physis</term> to mean the generation of the primary elements. <margin>D</margin> But if the soul is shown to be first—not fire or air—but the soul having been generated among the first things, then it would be most correctly said to exist "by nature" in a superior way. This is true if one proves the soul is older than the body, but otherwise, not at all. **CLINIAS.** What you say is very true. **ATHENIAN.** Shall we then proceed to this very point next? **CLINIAS.** Of course. **ATHENIAN.** Let us be entirely on our guard against a deceitful argument, lest it deceive us who are old with its youthful vigor, and escaping us, make us a laughingstock, making it seem that we aimed at great things but failed even at the small. <margin>E</margin> Consider then: if the three of us had to cross a very rapidly flowing river, and I, being the youngest of you and having experience with many currents, said that I ought to try first by myself, leaving you in safety, to see if the river is crossable for you who are older, or how it stands; and if it appeared crossable, I would then call you and help you across through my experience; but if it were uncrossable for you, the danger would have been mine alone—then I would seem to be speaking reasonably. And so it is now; the coming argument is quite forceful, and perhaps nearly "uncrossable" for your strength. <note>This "River" metaphor illustrates the Athenian's role as a philosophical guide for the two older, more traditional men, Clinias and Megillus, who are less familiar with abstract dialectic.</note> Lest it cause you a shadow of dizziness and vertigo, bringing you to confusion with its unfamiliar questions and answers, and thus breed an unseemly lack of clarity, I think I should proceed in this way: I will first question myself while you listen in safety, and then I will answer myself, going through the whole argument until it discusses the soul <margin>F</margin> and demonstrates that the soul is prior to the body. **CLINIAS.** You seem to have spoken excellently, Stranger; do as you say. <margin>He begins to demonstrate that the gods exist.</margin> **ATHENIAN.** Come then, if ever we should call upon God, let it be now! Let us call upon the gods with all seriousness to assist in the demonstration of their own existence. Holding on, as if to a safe cable, let us step into the current of the argument. And when I am tested by such questions, the safest way to answer seems to be as follows. If someone were to ask: "Stranger, do all things stand still and nothing move? Or is it the opposite? Or do some things move and others remain still?" I shall answer that some things move and others remain still. <margin>G</margin> Do they not stand still and move in some place? How could they not? And some do this in one seat, and others in several. You mean, we shall say, those things that receive the power of standing in the middle and move in one place, just as the circumference of circles that are said to "stand" rotates? Yes. And we understand that in this circular motion, such a movement carries the largest and the smallest circle around at the same time, distributing itself proportionally to both the small and the large, being itself smaller and larger in proportion. Therefore, it has become the source of all wonders, providing slowness and speeds in harmony with the large and small circles simultaneously—an effect that one might have thought impossible to occur. **CLINIAS.** Very true. <margin>H</margin> **ATHENIAN.** By "moving in many places," you seem to mean those things that move by locomotion, always passing into a different place, sometimes having one center as a base, and sometimes several, by means of rolling. Whenever they strike against other things, they are split apart by those that are standing still; but when they meet others moving from the opposite direction and are carried toward them, they combine and become one, forming a middle ground between them. I say, then, that these things are as you say. Indeed, when combined and condensed, they increase; but when divided and rarefied, they decrease, as long as the previous state of each remains; but when...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> We have found a certain foolishness in the opinion of those who have never touched upon the questions of natural things: Consider, I pray, and examine every reason. For it is of no small interest if we show that those who rely on impious arguments, and draw others toward impiety, do not discourse rightly, but perversely. To me, therefore, it seems thus concerning these things. **CLINIAS.** You speak rightly, but you should endeavor to show those things. **ATHENIAN.** But I will seem to use unaccustomed reasons. **CLINIAS.** Do not fear, Guest. For I understand that you thought you were departing far from the purpose of bringing laws if we entered into this disputation. But if we cannot otherwise be convinced <margin>B</margin> that what is now said about the gods according to the law is correct, it must be spoken of entirely. **ATHENIAN.** I will now speak of this new and almost unheard-of reasoning. <margin>The opinion of those saying all principles are bodies is rejected.</margin> Those discourses which have made souls impious have affirmed that what is the first cause of generation and corruption of all things is not first, but made later. But that which is later, is in fact prior. Whereby they have ignored the true substance of the gods. **CLINIAS.** I do not yet understand. **ATHENIAN.** What the soul is, and what power it has, almost everyone seems to have been ignorant, both as to other things and as to its generation, because it was born before all bodies, and is itself the most chief of all things in the transformation and beauty of bodies. <margin>C</margin> If these things be so, will not those things which are proper to the soul itself necessarily be prior to those which pertain to the body, since it is older than the body? **CLINIAS.** It is necessary. **ATHENIAN.** Therefore opinion, care, intellect, art, and law are prior to hard and soft, heavy and light. Wherefore the vast and first works and operations of art itself will be among the first; but those things which are "by nature," and nature itself (which is not rightly so called), are later, and follow art and intellect. **CLINIAS.** Why? **ATHENIAN.** They do not rightly wish to call nature "generation" regarding the first things, and they place bodies as the first. But if not fire, nor air, <margin>D</margin> but the soul shall be seen to exist first, the soul itself will most rightly be affirmed to be older than the body: and these things themselves are so constituted by nature, if it is established that the soul is older than bodies; but otherwise not at all. **CLINIAS.** You speak the truth. **ATHENIAN.** Shall we then proceed to these things? **CLINIAS.** By all means. **ATHENIAN.** Let us flee the cavilling and deceptive reason, lest by chance it, being youthful, deceive us old men and render us ridiculous, and we seem to have attempted great things but attained not even small ones. If we three wished to cross a deep and rapid river, and I, being younger than you and more experienced in the waves, should say that I ought to make the trial first, while you are left in safety, whether the river can be crossed by you who are older or not, and after the trial is made, either <margin>E</margin> exhort you to the crossing, or if it cannot be crossed, that I alone underwent the danger—I would seem to speak modestly. Not otherwise now, since a deeper reasoning must be approached, and one almost inaccessible to your strengths, lest it cause you vertigo and darkness, leading you into those questions with which you are not accustomed, and in this way affect you with disgrace and sadness, I think the trial should first be made by me in this way: that I interrogate myself and answer myself, and in this way, while you listen in safety, I may go through this whole disputation concerning the soul, by which it may be shown to be prior to the body. **CLINIAS.** You seem to speak most excellently, Guest; <margin>He approaches the demonstration that gods exist.</margin> and do as you say. **ATHENIAN.** Come then, now more than ever <margin>F</margin> let us invoke God with all zeal, since we endeavor to demonstrate diligently that gods exist, and let us enter the reasoning with the cables most safely stretched. In this disputation, I seem to answer most securely to questions of this kind, if someone should ask: "O Guest, do all things stand, and nothing move? Or on the contrary, does nothing stand, and all things move? Or do some move and some remain?" To this I will certainly answer that some remain, and others move. Do they not stand and move in some place? Why not? Some do so in one seat, and some in many. Do you say that those which receive the strength of those standing in the middle move in one: just as circles <margin>G</margin> are said to "stand," although their circumference is turned? Exactly so. But we understand that in this circumference, when such motion leads around the largest and smallest circle at the same time, according to proportion, it distributes itself to the larger and smaller: and it too, the proportion being preserved, is larger and smaller. Therefore it has become the fountain of all wonders. For together with the larger and smaller circles, it so carries through the convenient speeds and slownesses that it seems to perform something incredible. You tell the truth. But to move in many, you seem to me to say: whichever things always pass from one place into another: and sometimes they obtain the <margin>H</margin> base of one center, sometimes more: because they are rolled around. And when individual things happen to meet each other here and there, if they come upon those standing and resisting, they are split; but if they meet those carried in the opposite direction, being made one, both these and their intermediates are joined and condensed. I confess indeed that these things are as you say. And yet, joined and condensed things are increased, but divided and rarefied things are diminished, when the prior habit of each remains; but when...

<summary>In this passage, the Athenian Stranger begins a metaphysical proof for the existence of the gods by arguing that the soul is "older" than matter and is the primary cause of all motion and change. He uses a metaphor of crossing a dangerous river to describe the difficulty of this philosophical transition from physical to spiritual explanations.</summary>

Having argued that the soul is not a secondary byproduct of matter, he now moves into a technical demonstration of the different types of motion to prove that the "self-moving" soul is the primary source of all activity in the universe.</meta>

# BOOK X OF THE LAWS

Indeed, it does not remain; because of both, destruction follows. Thus, the generation <note>original: *generatio*, referring to the birth or coming-into-being of things</note> of all things occurs when a certain passion <note>here meaning an "experience" or "process" undergone by a thing</note> takes place: namely, when a principle, having taken an increment, arrives at the second transition, and from this to the next; and when it has reached as far as three, it possesses sensible perception for those who perceive. By this transmutation and transition, therefore, everything is born. It truly *is*, however, when it remains. But if it should be changed into another habit, it is already utterly destroyed. We have already spoken, O friends, of all the species of motion except two. **CLINIAS.** Which ones are those? **ATHENIAN.** We have not yet spoken, my good man, of those motions for the sake of which this entire consideration was undertaken. **CLINIAS.** Speak more plainly. **ATHENIAN.** It was for the sake of the Soul <note>original: *anima* / *psuchē*</note> that we entered into this dispute. **CLINIAS.** Most certainly. **ATHENIAN.** Let there be, then, one motion by which a thing can always move other things, but cannot move itself. And another by which a thing can always move both itself and others, by joining, separating, increasing, and the opposite: as well as by generating and destroying. This motion is distinct from all the others. **CLINIAS.** Let it be as you wish. **ATHENIAN.** Shall we not place that one as the ninth: that by which something is moved by another, and moves others? And we shall place as the tenth that by which a thing moves both itself and others: which certainly accommodates itself to all actions and passions, and of all things that exist, is truly called the motion and transmutation of them all? **CLINIAS.** Exactly so.
**ATHENIAN.** Which of these ten motions shall we prefer above all others as the most robust and effective? **CLINIAS.** It is necessary that the one by which a thing can move both itself and others should precede the rest by a very long interval, and all the others must be far behind it. **ATHENIAN.** You speak rightly. But should one or two things that were not rightly placed be set differently? **CLINIAS.** Which ones? **ATHENIAN.** What we said concerning the tenth motion was not rightly said. **CLINIAS.** Why? **ATHENIAN.** Because that which was enumerated as tenth is first according to reason, both in its generation and its strength. And that which we absurdly enumerated in the ninth place is actually second. **CLINIAS.** How do you mean this?
**ATHENIAN.** Thus. When one thing is moved by another, and that again always by another: will there be in such things something that is moved first? But how, since it is moved by something, will it be the first of those things which are moved? This is certainly impossible. But when something moving itself shall also move another: and that other another, and so many things are moved in succession: will the principle of the entire motion be anything other than the change of that which moved itself? **CLINIAS.** That is excellently said, and must be conceded. **ATHENIAN.** Furthermore, let us ask ourselves this, and answer ourselves. If all things were to stand still together in any way—as most of such people dare to say—which motion among them all would necessarily first arise in them? Surely that by which a thing moves itself. For motion depending on another would not occur before some other change had first occurred in them. Wherefore, the beginning of all motions and the first motion, which both occurs in things standing still and is present in those that are moved, must be confessed to be that by which a thing moves itself. And this is the most ancient <margin>Which is the most ancient and powerful change.</margin> and most powerful of all changes: while that by which a thing is changed by another and moves others is second. **CLINIAS.** You speak most truly. **ATHENIAN.** Since we have come this far in the dispute, let us also answer this. **CLINIAS.** What is it? **ATHENIAN.** If we see this first motion in an earthy, or watery, or fiery body—whether simple or mixed—what shall we say is present in it? **CLINIAS.** Are you asking if we should say it is alive, because it is moved by itself? **ATHENIAN.** Precisely. **CLINIAS.** It is certainly alive. **ATHENIAN.** And when we see a soul <note>original: *animam* / *psuchēn*</note> to be in something, shall we think it lives for any other reason than this? **CLINIAS.** For this reason alone. **ATHENIAN.** Attend, by Jupiter, I beseech you, whether you wish to understand three things in any matter. **CLINIAS.** In what way? **ATHENIAN.** One being the substance itself. One being the reason <note>original: *ratio* / *logos*, meaning the definition or logical account</note> of the substance. And one being the name itself. Are there not also two questions about every thing? **CLINIAS.** How two? **ATHENIAN.** Namely, that sometimes when a name is proposed to us, we seek the reason; and sometimes, having attained the reason, we then investigate the name. But do we wish to say this again? **CLINIAS.** What? **ATHENIAN.** A twofold distinction is found in other things, and also in number. And in number thus divided, the name indeed is "even": but the reason is "a number divisible into two equal parts." **CLINIAS.** Certainly. **ATHENIAN.** I am saying something like that. Do we not signify the same thing in both cases, whether we give the reason when asked the name, or the name when asked the reason? Since we call one and the same thing by the name "even," and by the reason "a number divisible <margin>The reason of the soul: that it can move itself.</margin> into two equal parts." **CLINIAS.** Entirely the same. **ATHENIAN.** Indeed, of that thing whose name is "soul," what is the reason? Do we have any other reason besides the one we just mentioned: "that which is able to move itself"? **CLINIAS.** You assert that "to be moved by itself" is the reason for that substance which we all call by the name "soul"? **ATHENIAN.** I do indeed assert it. If this is so, do we still require it to be more sufficiently demonstrated that the soul is the same as the first generation and motion of things which are, which were, and which will be, and again of all their opposites? Since it has appeared to be the cause of all transmutation and motion in all things. **CLINIAS.** Not at all. For it has been most sufficiently shown that the soul is more ancient than all things, since it is the principle of motion. **ATHENIAN.**

<column-break/>

...of itself, because of both it is destroyed. Indeed, the generation of all things occurs whenever it moves from this transition into the next; and having come as far as three, it possesses sensation for those that sense. Thus, everything that is changing and moving is generated. But it is truly being whenever it remains; but having changed into another state, it is entirely destroyed. Have we then spoken of all the motions which can be understood in species with number, except for two, friends, two? **CLINIAS.** Which ones? **ATHENIAN.** Nearly those, O good man, for the sake of which our entire inquiry now exists. **CLINIAS.** Speak more clearly. **ATHENIAN.** It was surely for the sake of the Soul. **CLINIAS.** Entirely so. **ATHENIAN.** Let one motion be that which is able to move other things, but is always unable to move itself; and another that which is able to move both itself always and others, through combinations and through separations, by increases and their opposite, and by generations and destructions, being another one of all the motions. **CLINIAS.** Let it be so. **ATHENIAN.** Therefore, we shall place as ninth that which is always moving another and being changed by another; but that which moves itself and another, harmonizing with all actions and all passions, being truly called the change and motion of all existing things; of all these we shall say it is nearly the tenth. **CLINIAS.** By all means. **ATHENIAN.** Of these ten motions, which should we most correctly judge to be the strongest and most exceptionally effective of all? **CLINIAS.** It is a myriad times necessary to say that the one able to move itself excels, and all the others are subsequent. **ATHENIAN.** You speak well. Should we then move that which was just now not correctly stated in one or even two ways? **CLINIAS.** Which do you mean? **ATHENIAN.** That which was said of the tenth was nearly incorrectly spoken. **CLINIAS.** In what way? **ATHENIAN.** It is first in generation and strength, according to reason; but that which follows this we placed as ninth, but second, having just now absurdly called it ninth. **CLINIAS.** How do you say this? **ATHENIAN.** Thus. When one thing changes another for us, and this again another always; among such things will there ever be something that is the first changer? And how, when it is moved by another, will it ever be the first of things that alter? For it is impossible. But when something having moved itself alters another, and that other another, and so indeed a myriad things are moved by a myriad others; will there be any other beginning of all motion besides the change of that which moved itself? **CLINIAS.** You have spoken most beautifully; these things must be conceded. **ATHENIAN.** Furthermore, let us say this, and answer ourselves again. If all things were to stand still, having become together, as most of those people dare to say, what motion would then necessarily first arise among them? **CLINIAS.** Surely that which moves itself. For it would never be changed by another before, since no change existed among them before. **ATHENIAN.** Therefore, the beginning of all motions and the first to arise both among things standing still and being in those that move, we shall say is necessarily the self-moving one, being the oldest and most powerful of all changes; while that which is altered by another, but moving others, is second. **CLINIAS.** You speak most truly. **ATHENIAN.** Since we are now at this point in the discourse, let us answer this. **CLINIAS.** What sort of thing? **ATHENIAN.** If we should see this having happened in some earthy or watery or fiery thing, separate or even mixed, what should we say this passion is in such a thing? **CLINIAS.** Are you asking me if we shall call it living, whenever it moves itself? **ATHENIAN.** Yes. **CLINIAS.** How could we not? **ATHENIAN.** What then? Whenever we see soul in some things, must we not agree that this is the same as living? **CLINIAS.** Nothing else. **ATHENIAN.** Hold now, by Zeus; would you not wish to understand three things about each? **CLINIAS.** How do you mean? **ATHENIAN.** One, the essence; one, the definition of the essence; and one, the name. And indeed there are two questions about all that is. **CLINIAS.** How two? **ATHENIAN.** Sometimes each of us, proposing the name itself, demands the definition; at other times, proposing the definition itself, asks again for the name. Do we now wish to say something of this sort? **CLINIAS.** What kind of thing? **ATHENIAN.** There is that which is divided in two among other things and in number; and to this which is in number, the name is "even"; and the definition is "a number divisible into two equal parts." **CLINIAS.** Yes. **ATHENIAN.** That is the sort of thing I mean. Do we not address the same thing in both ways, whether when asked the definition we give the name, or when asked the name we give the definition? Calling it "even" by name and by definition "a number divided in two," it being the same thing? **CLINIAS.** Entirely so. **ATHENIAN.** To that which has the name "soul," what is the definition of this? Have we any other besides the one just now spoken: "the motion able to move itself"? **CLINIAS.** You say that "moving itself" is the definition of the same essence which all of us address by the name "soul"? **ATHENIAN.** I do indeed. And if this is so, do we still desire to have it shown more sufficiently that the soul is the same thing as the first generation and motion of things that are, have been, and will be, and again of all their opposites? Since it has appeared as the cause of all change and motion for all things? **CLINIAS.** No; but it has been most sufficiently shown that the soul is the oldest of all things, having become the beginning of motion. **ATHENIAN.**

<summary>In this passage, Plato defines the soul (psuchē) as the "self-moving motion" and argues that it must be the primary cause of all activity in the universe. By logically ordering ten types of motion, he demonstrates that if anything is to move at all, there must be an original self-mover that precedes all other physical interactions.</summary>
