<meta>This page continues the Athenian Stranger’s proof of the soul's priority over matter. Having defined the "tenth motion" as self-motion (the soul), he now argues that because the soul is the source of all change, it must be the governor of the entire universe, including the heavens.</meta>

# BOOK X OF THE LAWS

**ATHENIAN.** Is it not true, then, that the motion which occurs in one thing by the action of another, but which never provides a thing the power to move itself—being really just a change in a lifeless body—should be called a secondary kind of motion, or any other number one might wish to assign to it? **CLINIAS.** Correct. **ATHENIAN.** We spoke correctly, then—and in a way that is most true and complete—when we said that the soul was created prior to the body, and the body is secondary and comes after the soul; the soul rules according to nature, and the body is ruled. **CLINIAS.** That is indeed most true. **ATHENIAN.** And surely we remember agreeing in our earlier discussion that if the soul appeared to be older than the body, then the things belonging to the soul would also be older than the things belonging to the body. **CLINIAS.** Certainly. **ATHENIAN.** Therefore, qualities such as character, habits, wishes, reasonings, true opinions, cares, and memories would have been created before the physical length, breadth, depth, and strength of bodies, if indeed the soul is prior to the body. **CLINIAS.** Necessarily so. **ATHENIAN.** Is it not then necessary to agree on what follows: that the soul is the cause of good and evil, of the beautiful and the base, of the just and the unjust, and of all opposites, if indeed we are to posit it as the cause of all things? **CLINIAS.** How could it be otherwise? **ATHENIAN.** Since the soul dwells in and governs all things that move in every way, must we not also say that it necessarily governs the heavens? **CLINIAS.** Of course. **ATHENIAN.** One soul, or more? **MEGILLUS.** More than one; I will answer for them. **ATHENIAN.** We must surely posit no fewer than two: one that works good, and another that is capable of working the opposite. **CLINIAS.** You have spoken very rightly. **ATHENIAN.** Very well. The soul, then, leads all things in the heavens, on the earth, and in the sea by its own motions. The names of these motions are: to will, to consider, to care for, to deliberate, to form opinions correctly or falsely, to feel joy or grief, confidence or fear, hatred or love. <note>The Athenian is arguing that "mental" actions are actually the primary forms of motion that eventually cause physical objects to move.</note> These are the primary motions; they take up the secondary motions of bodies and lead all things to growth and decay, to separation and combination, and to the qualities that follow these: heat and cold, heaviness and lightness, hardness and softness, whiteness and blackness, bitterness and sweetness. By all these, the soul—whenever it takes unto itself Divine Intellect <note>original: *nous*</note>—acts as a deity and guides all things rightly and happily. But when it keeps company with folly, it works out the exact opposite of these. Shall we posit that this is how things stand, or do we still doubt it? **CLINIAS.** Not at all. **ATHENIAN.** Which kind of soul, then, shall we say has control over the heavens and the earth and their entire revolution? The one that is wise and full of virtue, or the one that possesses neither? Do you wish for us to answer it this way? **CLINIAS.** How? **ATHENIAN.** If, my wonderful friend, the entire path and movement of the heavens and everything in them has a nature similar to the motion, revolution, and reasonings of Intellect, and proceeds in a related way, then it is clear we must say that the best soul cares for the whole world and guides it along such a path. **CLINIAS.** Correct. **ATHENIAN.** But if it proceeds in a mad and disorderly way, then the evil soul guides it. **CLINIAS.** That is also correct. **ATHENIAN.** What, then, is the nature of the motion of Intellect? This is a difficult question to answer clearly, my friends. Therefore, it is only fair that you accept my help in the answer. **CLINIAS.** You speak well. **ATHENIAN.** Let us not then look directly at the sun, as if we could see and know Intellect sufficiently with mortal eyes, for that would be like bringing on night at midday. It is safer to look at an image of the thing we are asking about. **CLINIAS.** What do you mean? **ATHENIAN.** Let us take as an image that one of the ten motions which most resembles Intellect. I will remind you of it and then we will make our answer together. **CLINIAS.** You would speak most excellently. **ATHENIAN.** Do we still remember this much from before: that of all things, some we set as moving and others as staying still? **CLINIAS.** Yes. **ATHENIAN.** And of those that move, some move in one place, while others move by changing their location. **CLINIAS.** That is so. **ATHENIAN.** Of these two, the motion that always stays in one place must necessarily move around a center, just like wheels turned on a lathe. This motion is, in every possible way, most closely related and similar to the revolution of Intellect. **CLINIAS.** How so? **ATHENIAN.** If we say that Intellect and the motion that stays in one place—which moves like a well-turned sphere—both move according to the same patterns, in the same way, in the same place, around the same objects, toward the same goals, and according to a single logic and order, we would never be found to be poor makers of beautiful images in speech. **CLINIAS.** You are very right. **ATHENIAN.** On the other hand, a motion that never moves in the same way, nor according to the same patterns, nor in the same place, nor around the same objects, nor in any order or logic, would be related to all kinds of folly. **CLINIAS.** That is most true. **ATHENIAN.** Now it is no longer difficult to say explicitly that, since it is the soul that carries all things around for us, we must say that the revolution of the heavens is necessarily carried around by either the best soul or its opposite, which cares for it and orders it. **CLINIAS.** O Guest, from what has been said, it would be a sin to say anything else than that one or more souls, possessing every virtue, carry these things around. **ATHENIAN.** You have followed the argument excellently, Clinias. But hear this one thing more. **CLINIAS.** What is that? **ATHENIAN.** If the soul carries around the sun, the moon, and the other stars...

<column-break/>

**A** Is it not then the motion which occurs from another into another, and by which nothing ever moves itself, a secondary motion? And by whatever number one wishes to count it, should it not be placed after the superior motion? Indeed, it is a change belonging to a truly inanimate body. **CLINIAS.** Rightly so. **ATHENIAN.** Correctly, then, and properly—and most truly and perfectly—did we say that the soul was made before the body, and the body later and secondarily, being subject by nature to the soul that dominates it. **CLINIAS.** These things are most true. **ATHENIAN.** We remember that we granted in the previous sections **B** that if the soul is shown to be older than the body, then those things which belong to the soul are also shown to be prior to those which are proper to the body. **CLINIAS.** Most certainly. **ATHENIAN.** Therefore, dispositions, characters, wills, thoughts, true opinions, cares, and memories—all these were made before the length, width, depth, and strength of bodies, just as the soul was made before the body. **CLINIAS.** It must be so. **ATHENIAN.** We are also forced to concede that the soul is the cause of good and evil, of the honorable and the base, of the just and the unjust, and of other opposites, if indeed we assert that it is the cause of all things. **C** **CLINIAS.** Why not? **ATHENIAN.** Since the soul governs all things and dwells in all things that are moved, must we not also confess that it necessarily governs the heavens? **CLINIAS.** Entirely. **ATHENIAN.** One or many? "Many, certainly," as I shall answer for you. We ought to posit no fewer than two: one beneficent, the other its opposite. **CLINIAS.** Quite rightly. **ATHENIAN.** Therefore, all things <margin>What the names of the soul's motions are.</margin> that are in the heavens, on the earth, and in the sea, the soul leads by its own motions. These are named: to will, to consider, to care for, to deliberate, to form opinions rightly and not rightly, to rejoice, to grieve, to be bold, to fear, to hate, to love. And besides these, all other motions which are kin to these and primary, which also take up the secondary motions of bodies and lead all things into growth and decrease, into composition (or condensation) and separation (or rarefaction); and into those things that follow these: heats, **D** colds, heaviness, lightness, the hard, the soft, the white, the black, the sour, the sweet, the bitter. And finally, in all things, if the soul—whenever it has also received divine intellect—uses them, <margin>The soul joined to intellect produces all things rightly.</margin> it leads all things rightly as a goddess, to a right and happy end. But if it should be joined to madness, it makes all things the opposite of these. Do we grant that these things are so, or do we still smoke with ambiguity? **CLINIAS.** We do not doubt in any way. **ATHENIAN.** Which kind of soul, then, do we judge to rule the heavens, the earth, **E** and the entire circuit? That which is filled with mind and virtue, or that which lacks both? Do you wish for us to answer thus? **CLINIAS.** In what way? **ATHENIAN.** Let us say it this way, O wonderful man: if the entire circuit of heaven and the progress of all that is in it has a nature similar to the motion, revolution, and reason of the mind, and is performed by a similar reason, it is clear that we must grant that the best soul has care for the whole world, whereby it is revolved in such a manner. **CLINIAS.** Rightly. **ATHENIAN.** But if it is moved furiously and without order, it is an evil soul. **CLINIAS.** This too is right. **ATHENIAN.** What nature, then, does the motion of the mind have? But to this question, O friends, it is difficult to answer wisely. Therefore, it is right that I should answer it with you. **CLINIAS.** You speak well. **ATHENIAN.** We must take care, then, lest as if turned toward the sun from the opposite side, and acting out night at noon, we <margin>How reverently one must judge concerning God. A metaphor of the dispute.</margin> should answer as if the mind could be sufficiently seen and known by mortal eyes. **F** For we shall see more safely if we look at its image. **CLINIAS.** How do you mean? **ATHENIAN.** Let us see which of those ten motions the intellect is most especially like, so that we may use this as an image. I will bring it back to your memory and answer for everyone. **CLINIAS.** Excellent. **ATHENIAN.** It is necessary to remember that which was said by us in the previous sections: that of all things that are, some stand still, while others are moved. **CLINIAS.** So it was said. **ATHENIAN.** Furthermore, of those that are moved, some are moved in one place, and some are moved in many. **CLINIAS.** This too. **ATHENIAN.** However, the motion that is always done in one place is necessarily done around some center, and is like a circle made on a **G** lathe. Therefore, it imitates the circuit of the mind to the best of its power. **CLINIAS.** How do you say that? **ATHENIAN.** I assert that both are carried through the same things, in the same way, in the same place, around the same things, toward the same things, with one reason and one order. Surely, if we say that the mind and the motion which happens in one place are similar to the rotations of a sphere made on a lathe, we will never be unskillful craftsmen of good images. **CLINIAS.** Quite right. **ATHENIAN.** On the contrary, then, the motion which is never carried similarly, nor through the same things, nor in the same place, nor around the same things, nor toward the same things, nor in any order, or ornament, or reason, is surely kin to all madness. **CLINIAS.** Without a doubt, most especially. **H** **ATHENIAN.** Now we can openly cry out that, since all things are led around by the soul, the circuit of heaven must necessarily be led around by a soul that procures and adorns it—whether that be the best soul or the contrary one. **CLINIAS.** But Guest, from what has been said, it has now appeared a sin to say otherwise than that all these things are led around by a soul filled with every virtue, whether it be one or many. **ATHENIAN.** You have understood these things well and quickly, Clinias. But add this. **CLINIAS.** What is it? **ATHENIAN.** If a soul leads the sun, the moon, and all other stars...

<summary>In this passage from Plato's Laws, the Athenian Stranger argues that the soul is the primary cause of all motion and existed before physical matter. He posits that the orderly, circular motion of the heavens proves they are guided by a virtuous, rational soul rather than a disorderly or evil one.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the Athenian Stranger’s argument from page 669. Having established that the soul is the primary cause of all motion and change, he now applies this logic to the celestial bodies (the sun, moon, and stars) to prove they are directed by divine intelligence.</meta>

# PLATON’S [LAWS]

...and surely each of them individually as well? **CLINIAS.** Why not? **ATHENIAN.** Let us then speak of one, and our words may be applied to all the stars. **CLINIAS.** Of which one? **ATHENIAN.** Everyone sees the body of the sun, but no one sees its soul—just as no one sees the soul of any other living creature, whether alive or dead. Because this kind of thing <note>the soul</note> cannot be perceived by any bodily sense, it is grasped by the mind alone. Therefore, let us also use our intelligence alone to grasp this point about it. **CLINIAS.** What point? **ATHENIAN.**

<margin>The soul moves the sun.</margin>
**A** Since a soul moves the sun, we will perhaps not be far from the truth if we assert that it does so in one of three ways. **CLINIAS.** What ways do you mean? **ATHENIAN.** Either it dwells inside this circular body and carries it wherever it pleases—just as our own soul leads us wherever it wishes—or it is itself outside, and having obtained a body of fire or air (as some say), it pushes body with body by force. Or thirdly, although it is itself stripped of a body, it possesses other powers that are wondrous beyond measure, and so it guides the sun. **CLINIAS.** Certainly, it is necessary that all things are moved by a soul in one of these ways. **ATHENIAN.** It is better that, whether this soul holds that body from within as if in a chariot and כך pours out light to all, or is outside it, or however one may conceive of this power, we should all consider it a god. Is it not so? **CLINIAS.** Yes, certainly, unless someone is possessed by extreme madness. **ATHENIAN.** Furthermore, concerning all the stars and the moon, the years, the months, and all the seasons, what else shall we say but this very thing? Since the soul, or souls endowed with every virtue, have been shown to be the causes of all these things, we shall affirm that they are gods—whether they dwell in bodies and like living creatures <note>original: "animalia"</note> they adorn the whole heaven, or in whatever other way they are said to act. **CLINIAS.** Entirely so. **ATHENIAN.** Then, these things being granted, could anyone deny that all things are full of gods? **CLINIAS.** No one is so far out of his mind, stranger. **ATHENIAN.** Therefore, to the man who denies the gods exist, O Clinias and Megillus, let us now leave this discourse, having set down the boundaries. **CLINIAS.** What boundaries shall we set? **ATHENIAN.** That either he must teach us that we are not thinking correctly when we say the soul is the first generation of all things, and that the other things we have said consequently are not true—or, if he can say nothing better than us, he should believe us and live the rest of his life without doubting the gods. But let us now consider whether we have sufficiently shown those who deny them that gods exist, or not. **CLINIAS.** It has been sufficiently said, stranger. **ATHENIAN.** Let the dispute against those men, then, have an end. But now, the man who says that gods exist, yet denies that they have a care for human affairs, must be persuaded by us thus: "O excellent man," let us say, "some nature akin to the divine leads you to affirm and honor that which is joined to you when you say gods exist. But the successes of wicked and unjust men, both in public and private life—which, although they are not truly happy, are commonly held to be so and are frequently extolled in poems and other discourses—drive you headlong into impiety. Or perhaps when you see wicked men reach old age and leave their children and grandchildren in the highest honors, you are greatly disturbed. You have perhaps heard, or even seen for yourself, some who, though they have done many unjust and impious things, have risen through those very crimes from small beginnings to great wealth, and from the lowest rank to tyranny. Therefore, because you are unwilling to blame the gods as authors of these things due to your kinship with them, yet you are led by some absurdity and cannot be angry with the gods themselves, you have finally fallen into this state: though you believe gods exist, you believe that human affairs are neglected by them."

<margin>The gods have care for human affairs.</margin>
**E** Lest this opinion push you toward a more serious disease of impiety, let us apply a remedy to refute this opinion to the best of our ability. Therefore, we shall join the following discussion with the preceding reasoning that we used against those who denied the existence of gods altogether. You, Clinias and Megillus, answer for the young man as you have done so far. And if any difficult point arises, I will take it up for you and lead you across the river, as I have just done. **CLINIAS.** You speak well; do so. We also will do our best. **ATHENIAN.** It will perhaps not be difficult to demonstrate that the gods have no less care for the smallest things than for the greatest, especially since it was said a little while ago that they are filled with every virtue and claim the providence of all things as their own. **CLINIAS.** 

<margin>The virtue of the gods.</margin>
**G** Most certainly. **ATHENIAN.** Let us investigate together what follows: what is that virtue of theirs by which they are conceded to be good? Come, are not being temperate and having an intellect <note>original Latin: "mentem", Greek: "νοῦν"</note> given to virtue, and their opposites to vice? **CLINIAS.** Certainly. **ATHENIAN.** What further? Is not courage also given to virtue, and cowardice to vice? **CLINIAS.** Very much so. **ATHENIAN.** And are some of these called shameful, and others honorable? **CLINIAS.** Necessarily. **ATHENIAN.** And as for the vices among these, we might say they are in us; but shall we say the gods are in no way partakers of them? **CLINIAS.** Anyone would grant this as well. **ATHENIAN.** Shall we think that negligence, luxury, or idleness are virtues of the soul? Or otherwise? **CLINIAS.** How could we? **ATHENIAN.** But rather the opposite? **CLINIAS.** Yes, indeed. **ATHENIAN.** Therefore, the opposites of these belong to the opposite <note>meaning virtue</note>. **CLINIAS.** So it is. **ATHENIAN.** He who is devoted to luxury, negligence, and idleness, whom Hesiod calls most like the stingless drones...

<column-break/>

...everyone, should we not call each of them so? **CLINIAS.** Why not? **ATHENIAN.** Let us make an argument about one, which will appear to fit all the stars for us. **CLINIAS.** Which one? **ATHENIAN.** Every human sees the body of the sun, but no one sees its soul; for neither do we see the soul of any other body, whether living or dying, of any living creature. But there is great hope that this kind of thing <note>the soul</note> is altogether beyond being perceived by any of the body's senses, and is an object of the intellect. By the mind alone and by thought let us grasp it in this way. **CLINIAS.** In what way? **ATHENIAN.** If a soul leads the sun, we shall not fail by saying it does one of three things. **CLINIAS.** Which things? **ATHENIAN.** That either being within this visible circular body, it carries such a thing everywhere, just as the soul in us carries us everywhere; or having provided itself with a body from somewhere outside, made of fire or some air, as the story goes with some, it pushes body with body by force; or thirdly, being itself bare of a body, but possessing certain other powers exceeding wonder, it guides it. **CLINIAS.** Yes. **ATHENIAN.** This is necessary: that by doing one of these things, a soul conducts all things. And it is better to believe that this soul—whether it leads the sun for us in a chariot to bring light to all, or from outside, or however, or in whatever way—should be considered a god by every man. How so? **CLINIAS.** Yes, at least by one who has not arrived at the extreme of folly. **ATHENIAN.** Concerning all the stars and the moon, and concerning years and months and all seasons, what other account shall we give but this very one? That since a soul or souls have appeared as the causes of all these things, and being good in every virtue, we shall say they are gods, whether they dwell in bodies as living beings and so adorn the whole heaven, or in whatever way or fashion. Is there anyone who, agreeing to these things, will endure to say that all things are not full of gods? **CLINIAS.** There is no one so out of his mind, stranger. **ATHENIAN.** To the one who did not believe in gods in the time before this, O Megillus and Clinias, let us speak the boundaries and be done. **CLINIAS.** Which ones? **ATHENIAN.** Either he must teach us that we do not speak correctly, setting soul as the first birth of all things, and all the other things we said following from these; or if he is not able to speak better than us, let him be persuaded by us, and spend the remainder of his life believing there are gods. Let us see then if we have already spoken sufficiently to those who do not believe in gods to show that there are gods, or if there is a lack. **CLINIAS.** Not at all, stranger, there is no lack. **ATHENIAN.** To these men then, let our argument have its end. But the one who believes gods exist, but that they do not care for human affairs, must be encouraged. "O best of men," (let us say) "that you believe in gods is perhaps because some divine kinship leads you to honor and believe in what is natural to you; but the fortunes of evil and unjust men in private and public, which in truth are not happy, but are deemed excessively happy in opinion—though not harmoniously—lead you toward impiety, being wrongly praised both in poetry and in all kinds of discourses. Or perhaps seeing unholy men come to the end of life in old age, leaving children’s children in the greatest honors, you are troubled now in all these things, seeing them, or perceiving them through hearing, or even being an eyewitness yourself to many impious and terrible things happening to some, and through these very things you see them arriving from small things to tyrannies and the greatest power. Then it is clear that in all such cases, because of all these things, you would not wish to blame the gods through ignorance, as being the causes of such things; but being led by some lack of reason at the same time, and being unable to be disgusted with the gods, you have come to this present feeling, so that they seem to you to exist, but to look down upon and neglect human affairs. Therefore, so that the present dogma does not lead you to a greater sickness toward impiety, but if we are able to blow it away as a thing to be averted by falling upon the argument, let us try, by joining the following discourse to that argument which we completed from the beginning against the one who altogether does not believe in gods, to use it now. And you, Clinias and Megillus, respond for the youth just as in the previous parts; and if any difficulty falls into the words, I, receiving it from you both just as I did now, will carry you across the river." **CLINIAS.** You speak correctly; and you do these things; and we will do what you say to the best of our power. **ATHENIAN.** But perhaps it would be not at all difficult to show this, at least, that the gods are as careful of small things as of those differing in greatness. For I heard and was present at what was just now said, that being good in every virtue, they possess the care of all things as being most properly their own. **CLINIAS.** And I heard that very clearly. **ATHENIAN.** After this, then, let us investigate together, what virtue of theirs are we speaking of when we agree they are good? Come, do we say that being temperate and possessing intellect belong to virtue, and the opposites to vice? **CLINIAS.** We say so. **ATHENIAN.** What then? That courage belongs to virtue, and cowardice to vice? **CLINIAS.** Entirely so. **ATHENIAN.** And shall we say that some of these are shameful, and others beautiful? **CLINIAS.** Necessarily. **ATHENIAN.** And that while the petty ones belong to us (if indeed they are trifles), we shall say that the gods have no part in such things, neither great nor small? **CLINIAS.** Everyone would agree to these things in this way. **ATHENIAN.** What then? Shall we place negligence and idleness and luxury into the virtue of the soul? Or how do you say? **CLINIAS.** How could we? **ATHENIAN.** But into the opposite? **CLINIAS.** Yes. **ATHENIAN.** Then the opposites of these belong to the opposite. **CLINIAS.** To the opposite. **ATHENIAN.** What then? One who is luxurious, and negligent, and idle (whom the poet says is most like the stingless drones)...

<summary>In this passage, Plato argues that the soul is the invisible force moving the sun and stars, and shifts the debate toward proving that the gods actively care for human affairs, refuting the idea that they are negligent or indifferent.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 670 of Plato’s *Laws*, where the Athenian Stranger has been arguing for the existence of the gods. Having proven that the soul is the primary mover of the universe, he now addresses the "second class" of skeptics: those who believe the gods exist but think they are indifferent to human affairs.</meta>

# CONCERNING THE LAWS, BOOK X.

<margin>A</margin> ...If the poet says that [the drone] is like [him], would such a person not be hateful to us all? **KLEINIAS:** He spoke most correctly. **ATHENIAN:** Surely then we must not say that a god has the kind of character that he himself hates; nor should we allow anyone to try to utter such a thing. **KLEINIAS:** By no means; for how could that be? **ATHENIAN:** Now, concerning the one who has the duty of care and attention to a degree surpassing all others, but whose mind cares for the great things and neglects the small—what kind of praise could we give such a person without completely missing the mark? Let us consider it this way: are there not two ways this neglect might occur in any who act, whether god or man? **KLEINIAS:** Which two? **ATHENIAN:** I mean they might differ in this way: either he thinks it makes no difference
<margin>B</margin> to the whole if small things are neglected; or through laziness and luxury, even if he knows it makes a difference, he neglects them. Or is there some other way to define negligence? For surely when it is impossible to care for all things, then it is not "negligence" to fail to care for small or great things—when a god or some lowly person is simply incapable and lacks the power to attend to them. **KLEINIAS:** Of course not. **ATHENIAN:** Now, let these two groups answer us—those who both agree that gods exist, but one says they are easily appeased, and the other that they neglect small things. First, you both say you recognize that the gods know, see, and hear all things, and that nothing can be hidden from them of whatever things there are senses and knowledge. Do you say it is this way? Or how?
<margin>C</margin> **KLEINIAS:** Just so. **ATHENIAN:** And what then? That they can do all things that are within the power of mortals and immortals? **KLEINIAS:** How could they not agree that these things are so? **ATHENIAN:** And indeed, we have agreed that they are good and best—all of us here. <note>original: "πέντε ὄντες" (being five). The Latin also says "quinque" (five). This is a difficult textual point; while there are only three speakers present, it may refer to the five points of the legal argument or is a common scribal error for "all of us".</note> **KLEINIAS:** Most certainly. **ATHENIAN:** Is it then impossible for them to be agreed to act with laziness or luxury at all, being such as we agree they are? For among us, idleness is the offspring of cowardice, and laziness comes from idleness and luxury. **KLEINIAS:** You speak most truly. **ATHENIAN:** No god, then, neglects anything through idleness or laziness. For he has no share in cowardice.
<margin>D</margin> **KLEINIAS:** You speak most rightly. **ATHENIAN:** Therefore, it remains that if they neglect the small things, they do so either because they think little of them, or because knowing they ought not to care for any such things at all, they do it; or what else remains except knowing the contrary? **KLEINIAS:** Nothing. **ATHENIAN:** Shall we then, my best and excellent friend, suppose you are saying that they neglect things because they are ignorant and ought to care, or that they know they ought to, yet they act like the worst of men, who are said to know what is better but do not do it because they are overcome by pleasures or pains? **KLEINIAS:** How could that be? **ATHENIAN:** Do not human affairs partake in the nature of the soul, and man is the most god-fearing of all living creatures? **KLEINIAS:** So it seems. **ATHENIAN:** We say that all mortal living things are the possessions of the gods, just as the entire heaven is. **KLEINIAS:** Of course.
<margin>E</margin> **ATHENIAN:** Now then, whether one says these things are small or great to the gods, in neither case would it be fitting for those who possess us to neglect them, since they are most careful and best. Let us consider this as well in addition to these points. **KLEINIAS:** What sort of thing? **ATHENIAN:** Regarding perception and power—are they not naturally opposite to one another in terms of ease and difficulty? **KLEINIAS:** How do you mean? **ATHENIAN:** Seeing and hearing small things is harder than seeing large ones, but carrying, controlling, and caring for small and few things is easier for everyone than the opposite. **KLEINIAS:** Certainly. **ATHENIAN:** If a physician were commanded to heal a whole body, and being willing and able, he cared for the great parts but neglected the small and minute parts, would the whole ever be well for him? **KLEINIAS:** In no way. **ATHENIAN:** Neither would it be well for navigators, nor generals, nor even for all statesmen, nor for any other such person, without the few and small things, to manage the many or great. For as the stonemasons say, the large stones do not lie well without the small ones. **KLEINIAS:** How could they?
<margin>F</margin> **ATHENIAN:** Let us not then ever deem God to be inferior to mortal craftsmen, who, the better they are, the more accurately and perfectly they execute their appropriate works, both small and great, with a single art. Should God, who is most wise and willing and able to care, neglect the small things that are easier to care for, like some idle or cowardly person resting due to the labor? And only care for the
<margin>G</margin> great? **KLEINIAS:** Let us by no means accept such an opinion about the gods, stranger. For we would be thinking a thought that is neither holy nor true. **ATHENIAN:** I think we have now argued quite moderately with the one who finds fault concerning the negligence of the gods. **KLEINIAS:** Yes. **ATHENIAN:** Yet we have forced him by logic to agree that he is wrong. **KLEINIAS:** Correct. **ATHENIAN:** But I think he still needs some persuasive myths <term>epōdōn: literally "incantations" or "charms". In Plato's philosophy, these are stories or poetic explanations used to soothe and persuade the irrational part of the soul after a logical proof has been given.</term> **KLEINIAS:** Which ones, good sir? **ATHENIAN:** Let us persuade the young man with words, that for the one who cares for the whole, everything is coordinated for the salvation and virtue of the entire thing, of which each part also, according to its power, suffers and acts what is fitting. For each of these, there are appointed rulers always in charge of
<margin>H</margin> even the smallest experience and action, having worked out the distribution to the furthest end. One of these, O wretched man, is your own part, which always stretches toward the whole and looks toward it, even though it is very small. You fail to notice that regarding this very thing, all generation occurs for the sake of the whole, so that the life of the universe might possess a happy existence; it does not occur for your sake, but you...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...If he says I am like a drone, would we not hold him in hatred? **KLEINIAS:** Most rightly indeed did that poet sing. **ATHENIAN:** Therefore, it must not be said that the gods have those habits which he hates, nor must anyone be permitted to speak so? **KLEINIAS:** In no way. **ATHENIAN:** Or will he, to whom the execution and care of some work chiefly belongs, care for the great things in that work but despise the small? How could we praise this opinion and not be in error? But let us consider it this way. Does not a man or a god neglect something for two reasons? **KLEINIAS:** Which ones? **ATHENIAN:** Either because he thinks it is of no importance to the whole if small things are neglected; or because, although he thinks it is important, he neglects it
<margin>B</margin> because he is held back by laziness and softness. For otherwise, negligence does not happen. For when someone cannot manage the care of all things great and small, and is thus hindered by weakness and does not care, he is not said to be negligent—whether he be a man who is powerless, or a god who is imagined to be unable. **KLEINIAS:** Certainly not. **ATHENIAN:** But now let those two answer the three of us—those who, although they grant that the gods exist, one thinks they are easily appeased, the other that they are negligent in small matters. First, they are asked this: Do you both assert that the gods know, see, and hear all things; and that nothing can escape them of those things which are
<margin>C</margin> perceived by sense or intellect? Do you say it is so? Or otherwise? **KLEINIAS:** So. **ATHENIAN:** Secondly, that they can do all things that mortals or immortals can? **KLEINIAS:** Without doubt they will grant that this is so. **ATHENIAN:** And we have confessed that they are good, even the best. **KLEINIAS:** Entirely. **ATHENIAN:** It is therefore impossible for them to be seized by any laziness or softness, since they are such as we have agreed they are. For from cowardice, idleness is born in us; and laziness from idleness and softness. **KLEINIAS:** You speak the truth. **ATHENIAN:** No god, therefore, corrupted by idleness and laziness, neglects anything. For no god is a participant in any cowardice. **KLEINIAS:**
<margin>D</margin> Rightly. **ATHENIAN:** Therefore it remains that if they neglect small and few things in the universe, they neglect them either because they know they should be despised, or is there any other reason remaining except the opposite of this? **KLEINIAS:** Nothing at all. **ATHENIAN:** Which then, O excellent man, shall we affirm you are saying? Is it that because of ignorance, though they ought to provide, they do not provide? Or like we say of wicked men, that they see the better things but, broken by pleasure or pain, follow the worse—do the gods, although they know they must provide, similarly not provide? **KLEINIAS:** How could that happen? **ATHENIAN:** Furthermore, human affairs participate in the nature of living things; and man himself, above all other animals, is the most diligent worshiper of God. **KLEINIAS:** It appears so. **ATHENIAN:** Moreover, we say that all mortal
<margin>E</margin> living things are made and possessed by the gods, just as the entire heaven is. **KLEINIAS:** Beyond doubt. **ATHENIAN:** Now then, whether one says these things are small or great to the gods, in no way—since they are most provident and best—is their possession to be neglected by them. But let us consider this besides. **KLEINIAS:** What is it? **ATHENIAN:** Do not the senses and powers stand naturally in an opposite way to each other regarding ease and difficulty? **KLEINIAS:** What do you mean? **ATHENIAN:** Small things are indeed seen and heard more difficulty than large things. But all small and few things are held, carried, and governed by providence more easily than their opposites. **KLEINIAS:** Certainly much more easily. **ATHENIAN:** What of this? When a physician
<margin>F</margin> wishes and is able to cure a whole body, if he provides for the great things but despises the small, will the whole ever be well for him? **KLEINIAS:** Never. **ATHENIAN:** But neither navigators, nor generals, nor fathers of families, nor governors of cities, nor any such people at all, will rightly govern many and huge things if the few and small are neglected. For architects also say that great stones are not well built without small ones. **KLEINIAS:** Certainly. **ATHENIAN:** Let us beware, however, lest we think God to be more base than mortal craftsmen. These men, the more skilled they are, the more exquisitely and perfectly they finish both small and great things in their own works with a single art. Should God, who is most wise and can and will care, provide only for the great things, while the small things—which are more easily
<margin>G</margin> governed—he neglects because of laziness and sloth? **KLEINIAS:** In no way, stranger, do we think this opinion about the gods should be admitted. For this thought is both wicked and entirely false. **ATHENIAN:** We seem now to have disputed enough against him who accuses the gods of the crime of negligence. **KLEINIAS:** Certainly. **ATHENIAN:** But so far we have, in a way, forced him by reason to confess that he thinks falsely. **KLEINIAS:** Rightly. **ATHENIAN:** I think he also needs persuasion, by which he may be caught as if by a certain incantation. **KLEINIAS:** What is this persuasion? **ATHENIAN:** Let us persuade this youth that for him who provides for the whole, everything is ordered toward the virtue and safety of the whole, of which each part also, according to its strength, acts and suffers what befits it; and over these
<margin>H</margin> individual things, presiding princes are placed, who have care even of the smallest actions and passions, through the distribution of each and every extreme particle of the universe performed unto the very end. One of which is your own little part, O wretched man, which always looks toward the whole, although it is very small. But you are ignorant that all generation of individual things happens for the sake of that whole, so that the life of the universe itself may be happy.

<summary>In this passage from Plato's Laws, the Athenian Stranger argues against the idea that gods neglect small human affairs, using analogies of physicians, navigators, and stonemasons to show that a whole cannot be perfect if its small parts are ignored. He concludes by explaining that every individual exists for the sake of the harmony and "happy existence" of the entire universe.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the Athenian Stranger's argument regarding divine providence. On the previous page, he established that the gods are not negligent. Here, he explains the mechanism of divine justice—how the universe is structured so that every soul eventually finds its proper place according to its character, ensuring that virtue is rewarded and vice is punished.</meta>

672 PLATO

<margin>A</margin> its existence is not for your sake, but you were created for its sake. For every physician and every skilled craftsman performs all his work for the sake of the whole, directing everything toward the common perfection; he does not create the whole for the sake of the part, but refers the individual parts to the whole. But you are annoyed because you do not realize how that which is best for you happens to be consistent with both the universe and yourself, according to the power of our common origin. Since a soul is always joined with a body, now with one and then with another, and undergoes all sorts of changes either because of itself or because of another soul, nothing remains for the <note>The Greek term is *petteutēs*, a player of a board game similar to checkers or chess; the Latin *talos iacienti* refers to throwing dice or knucklebones.</note> arranger of these things except to shift the pieces—moving the better characters into a better place and the worse into a worse place, according to what is fitting for each, so <margin>B</margin> that each might receive its appropriate destiny. **KLEINIAS:** How do you mean that? **ATHENIAN:** I believe I am describing the method by which it is easiest for the gods to provide for all things. For if one were to always look at the whole and transform each thing by reshaping everything—for instance, making living water out of fire, rather than many things out of one or one out of many, which have participated in a first, second, or even third generation—the arrangement of this shifting would be infinite in its complexity. But as it is, there is a wonderful ease in the work of him who provides for the whole. **KLEINIAS:** How so, again? **ATHENIAN:** Since our <note>The "King" here refers to the Divine Creator or the ordering principle of the cosmos.</note> King perceived that all our actions are animated and contain much virtue and much <margin>C</margin> wickedness, and that the soul and body, once joined, are subject to destruction, though they are not eternal in the way the gods are—for if either of these were destroyed, the generation of living beings would cease—and since he perceived that what is good in the soul is always naturally beneficial, while what is evil is harmful; seeing all this, he designed where each of the parts should be placed so that virtue might most easily and effectively achieve victory in the universe, and vice might be defeated. He has therefore devised for this whole the kind of seat and habitation and locations that each character, as it develops, ought to receive. But the causes of why a person becomes this or that kind of character, he left to our own wills. For wherever one’s desire leads, and whatever kind of soul one has, there he almost always dwells and becomes <margin>D</margin> such a person for the most part. **KLEINIAS:** That seems likely. **ATHENIAN:** Therefore, all things that possess a soul change, since they have the cause of change within themselves. Being changed, they are moved according to the order and law of destiny. Those characters that have sinned less wander less deeply and stay upon the surface of the region; those that have sinned more and more grievously fall into the depths and into the lower regions, which people call by the name of the "Underworld" and similar titles, which they dream of and dread both while living and when released from their bodies. But the soul that possesses a greater share of virtue or vice, when it has changed more vehemently through its own will and constant habit and has clung to divine virtue, becoming <margin>E</margin> preeminently such, is transferred to a far better and holy place. But the soul affected in the opposite way is transferred to the opposite place to live out its life. This is the judgment of the gods who inhabit heaven, O boy and youth who think you are neglected by the gods: that he who becomes worse goes to the worse souls, and he who becomes better goes to the better souls, both in life and in every death, to suffer and to do what is fitting for like to do to like. Therefore, neither you nor any other should ever hope or trust that you will be so lucky as to escape and overcome this judgment of the gods. For those who established it have made it firmer than all other things, so that it must be entirely respected. For you will never be neglected by it, not if you were so small as to enter into the <margin>F</margin> depths of the earth, nor if you became so high as to fly into heaven on wings; but you will pay the fitting penalty, whether staying here, or having been brought to the underworld, or transferred to some even more remote and inaccessible place. The same reasoning applies to those whom you have seen rise from small to great men through wicked crimes, and whom you thought had attained happiness from misery. In their actions, as if in a mirror, you thought you saw the gods' negligence toward all things, because you did not know how their progress contributes to the whole. But, O most excellent man, one must not be ignorant of this; for he who does not know it will never perceive the form of living, nor be able to speak of the happiness or misery of life. Therefore, if Kleinias here and this whole assembly of elders have persuaded you that you are utterly ignorant of what you say about the gods, God himself may favor you; but if you still desire some further reason, hear what we shall say to that third group, if you have any share of intellect. Truly, that the gods exist and provide for men has, I think, been sufficiently demonstrated. But that they are corrupted by the gifts of wicked men must in no way be allowed; and if it is said, it must be refuted with all one's might. **KLEINIAS:** Nobly said; let us do as you say. **ATHENIAN:** Come then, by the gods themselves, in what way might they be appeased by us, if indeed they are? And who and of what sort are they if they are appeased? For they must be the leaders who are to govern the whole heaven perpetually. **KLEINIAS:** Certainly. **ATHENIAN:** But to what <margin>H</margin> leaders are they similar? Or what leaders are like them, so that it is possible for us to compare the smaller to the greater? Are they like certain charioteers of competing teams? Or the pilots of ships?

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> for the sake of that other. For every physician, and every skilled craftsman, works all things for the sake of the whole, producing what is best for the common good; he produces the part for the sake of the whole, and not the whole for the sake of the part. But you are distressed, being ignorant of how that which is best for you happens both to the whole and to you, according to the power of our common generation. Since the soul is always joined to a body, now to one and then to another, and undergoes all sorts of changes, either through itself or through another soul, no other task is left to the piece-mover except to shift the character that is becoming better to a better place, and the worse to a worse place, according to what is fitting for each, so that it may obtain its proper portion. **KLEINIAS:** In what way do you mean? **ATHENIAN:** In the way that there would be <margin>B</margin> the greatest ease of care for the gods over all things—this is how I seem to speak. For if one were to always look toward the whole and shape all things by transforming them—such as living water out of fire, and inanimate things out of one, or one out of many, having shared in a first or second or even third generation—the complexity of the shifting arrangement would be infinite. But now there is a wonderful ease for the one who cares for the whole. **KLEINIAS:** How do you say this again? **ATHENIAN:** Thus: since our King saw that all our actions were animated, and that there was much virtue in them and much vice; and that soul and body, once generated, are indestructible but not eternal, just like the <margin>C</margin> gods who exist by law (for generation would never have arisen if either of these two were destroyed); and he realized that what is good is always naturally beneficial to the soul, and what is evil is harmful—having seen all this, he devised where each of the parts should be placed so that virtue might conquer and vice be defeated in the whole, most easily and in the best way. He has devised for this whole what kind of person, becoming what, should always change to what kind of seat and be settled in what places. But he left the causes of the generation of what kind of character to the wills of each of us. For in whatever way one desires, and whatever kind of soul one has, in that way almost every time and in such a manner each of us becomes, for the most part. **KLEINIAS:** That is at least likely. **ATHENIAN:** Therefore <margin>D</margin> all things that have a share of soul change, possessing within themselves the cause of change. And changing, they are carried according to the order and law of destiny. Those characters that change in smaller ways move less along the plane of the region; but those that change more and more unjustly, falling into the depths and the places called "below"—which people call Hades and other such names, which they greatly fear and dream about both while living and when dissolved from their bodies. But whenever a soul partakes of a greater degree of vice or virtue, through its own will and powerful association, when it joins with divine virtue, it becomes preeminently such, and moves to a holy place, being transferred to some other better place; but when the opposite, <margin>E</margin> it settles its life in the opposite direction. This is the justice of the gods who hold Olympus, O boy and youth who think you are neglected by the gods: that he who becomes worse goes toward the worse souls, and he who becomes better goes toward the better, both in life and in all deaths, to suffer and do what is fitting for like to do to like. From this justice neither you nor anyone else who has become unfortunate will ever boast of having escaped the gods. This justice, those who ordained it have set above all others, and it must be entirely respected; for you will never be neglected by it. You are not so small that you may sink into the depths of the earth, nor so high that you may <margin>F</margin> fly up into heaven. You will pay them the fitting penalty, whether staying here, or having passed into Hades, or having been carried to an even more savage place than these. The same logic applies to you concerning those whom you have seen become great from small beginnings, having committed unholy deeds or something of that sort, and you thought they had become happy from being wretched, and then, as if in mirrors, you thought you had seen in their actions the negligence of the gods toward all things—not knowing their final contribution, and how it fits into the whole. And how do you not think it necessary to know this, O most courageous of all men? For if one does not know this, he could never see fortune, nor be able to contribute a reason concerning life or understand happiness and misfortune. If Kleinias <margin>G</margin> here and all this assembly of elders persuade you that you do not know what you are saying about the gods, may God himself help you. But if you are still in need of some reason, listen to us as we speak to the third group, if you have any mind at all. For that the gods exist and care for men, I would say has been demonstrated by us not altogether poorly. But that the gods are again appeaseable to those who do wrong, receiving gifts, is something that must not be conceded to anyone, and must be refuted by every means and power. **KLEINIAS:** You have spoken most beautifully; let us do as you say. **ATHENIAN:** Come then, by the gods themselves, in what way might they be appeased by us, if indeed they are, and who and of what sort are they? They must at least be leaders, those who are to administer the whole heaven perfectly. **KLEINIAS:** So it is. **ATHENIAN:** But <margin>H</margin> to which of the leaders are they similar? Or which are similar to them? Is it possible for us to compare the lesser to the greater among those who can be compared? Would they be like certain charioteers of competing teams, or pilots of ships? Perhaps...

<summary>This page presents Plato's argument for divine justice, explaining that the universe is organized so that every soul is naturally moved to a location (or state of being) that matches its moral character. It refutes the idea that the wicked truly prosper, asserting that divine judgment is an inescapable cosmic law that governs both this life and the afterlife.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the Athenian Stranger’s theological defense of divine providence. Having established that the gods are neither indifferent nor negligent, the speaker now addresses the third heresy: that the gods can be bribed or appeased by the offerings of the wicked. This section marks the transition from theological discourse to the formal codification of laws regarding impiety and the establishment of a penal system for those who deny or insult the divine.</meta>

### ON THE LAWS, BOOK 11 <note>original: "DE LEGIBVS LIB. XI." - Though labeled as Book 11 in this early edition, this text actually constitutes the final section of Book 10 of Plato's Laws.</note>

<margin>A</margin> Perhaps they might even be compared to commanders of all armies. Or it would be as if one were to say they resemble physicians who boastfully claim to cure the diseases of cities within human bodies, or farmers who anxiously watch over their plants for fear of harsh seasons; or even like the overseers of flocks. Since we have agreed among ourselves that the heaven is full of many good things, and also of their opposites, though the good are the more numerous, this is, we say, an immortal battle, requiring a wonderful vigilance. Our allies in this are the gods and the spirits <note>original: "δαίμονες" / "daemones" - intermediary beings between gods and humans, not necessarily evil spirits.</note>; and we, in turn, are the property of the gods and these spirits. Injustice and insolence, together with folly, are our ruin; 

<margin>B</margin> while justice and temperance, together with wisdom, are our salvation, for these dwell in the living powers of the gods. Yet one may see a small portion of these things clearly dwelling here among us. For there are certain souls dwelling on the earth that have acquired an unjust gain, and being clearly beast-like, they fall upon the souls of the guardians—whether they be like dogs or shepherds or the most supreme masters—and they try to persuade them with flattering words and certain prayerful incantations (as the rumors of the wicked say) that it is possible for them to take more than their share <note>original: "πλεονεκτῶσι" / "usurpationem" - referring to *pleonexia*, the vice of greedy accumulation at the expense of others.</note> among men and suffer no hardship. But we say that this sin, now called "greed," is a "disease" when it occurs in fleshly bodies; in the seasons of years it is called a "plague"; but in cities and states, this same word is transformed into "injustice." **CLINIAS:** Entirely so.

<margin>C</margin> **ATHENIAN:** And it is absolutely necessary, my friend, to address this argument: that those who say the gods are always forgiving toward the unjust and those who commit injustice, provided one gives them a portion of the spoils—just as if wolves were to give a small portion of their prey to dogs, and the dogs, being pacified by the gifts, allowed them to tear the flocks apart. Is this not the argument of those who claim the gods can be appeased? **CLINIAS:** That is the one. **ATHENIAN:** To which of the guardians mentioned before could a man compare the gods and not be the most ridiculous of men? To pilots, who are turned aside by the libation of wine and the smell of fat, only to overturn both the ship and the sailors? **CLINIAS:** Not at all. **ATHENIAN:** Nor surely to charioteers in a race, who are persuaded by a gift to surrender the victory by driving for others. **CLINIAS:** You would be speaking of a terrible image if you spoke that way.

<margin>D</margin> **ATHENIAN:** Nor surely to generals, nor physicians, nor farmers; nor even to shepherds, nor to any dogs who have been charmed by wolves. **CLINIAS:** Hush! How could that be? **ATHENIAN:** But are not all the gods the greatest of all guardians, and over the greatest things? **CLINIAS:** By far. **ATHENIAN:** Shall we say then that those who guard the most beautiful things, and who themselves excel in the virtue of guardianship, are worse than dogs or ordinary men, who would never betray justice for the sake of gifts impiously received from unjust men? **CLINIAS:** Not at all; the argument is not to be endured. Of those who are involved in every kind of impiety, he who holds this opinion would most justly be judged the worst and most impious of all. **ATHENIAN:** May we say then that the three propositions—that the gods exist, that they are careful, and that they are absolutely unyielding to anything contrary to justice—have been sufficiently demonstrated? **CLINIAS:** 

<margin>E</margin> Of course; we are in agreement with these arguments. **ATHENIAN:** Indeed, they have been spoken with some vehemence because of our contention with wicked men. For this reason, friend Clinias, we have been contentious: lest the wicked should ever imagine that by prevailing in argument they have the license to do what they want, even such things as they think about the gods. This is why we have been eager to speak with a certain youthful vigor. But if we have achieved even a small success in persuading these men to hate themselves and to embrace the opposite character, our preamble regarding the laws of impiety will have been well spoken. **CLINIAS:** There is hope; but if not, at least the style of the argument will not disgrace the lawgiver. **ATHENIAN:** After the preamble, 

<margin>F</margin> a discourse should rightly follow, acting as an interpreter of the laws, warning all the impious to depart from their current ways and turn toward piety. For those who do not obey, let this be the law concerning impiety: *If anyone commits an act of impiety by word or deed, let him who happens to be present defend the gods and report the matter to the magistrates.* The first magistrates who hear of it shall bring the case before the court appointed for these matters, according to the laws. If any magistrate, having heard of it, fails to act, let him himself be liable to a charge of impiety at the hands of anyone 

<margin>G</margin> who wishes to avenge the laws. If someone is convicted, let the court assess a penalty for each individual act of impiety. Let imprisonment be the starting point for all. There are to be three prisons in the city: one common to the majority, near the marketplace, for the sake of the security of most people's persons; another near the meeting place of those who assemble at night, called the "reformation center" <note>original: "σωφρονιστήριον" / "correctionis" - literally a place for making one 'temperate' or 'sane'.</note>; and a third in the middle of the country, in the most desolate and wildest place possible, bearing a name signifying "retribution" <note>original: "τιμωρίας" / "supplicij" - a punitive prison for the incorrigible.</note>. Since there are three causes of impiety, as we have described, and two kinds of people arising from each cause, there will be six classes of sinners against the gods who deserve to be distinguished, requiring different and unequal punishments. For those who, while not believing in gods at all, possess a naturally just character, happen to hate the wicked; and through their disgust at injustice, they neither engage in such acts themselves nor associate with unjust men, but cherish the just.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> But perhaps they can be compared to leaders of armies, or to physicians who ward off and drive away the wars of diseases from human bodies; or to farmers who, fearing and taking precaution against hostile storms as they arise among the crops, or even to the shepherds of flocks and herds. For since it has been agreed among us that the heaven is full of many good things and many evils—and indeed of more of the former—this is an immortal war, as it were, and it stands in need of a marvelous guardianship. But the gods together with the spirits aid us. We, however, are the possession of the gods and the spirits. Truly, injustice and intemperance together with imprudence corrupt us.

<margin>B</margin> Justice, indeed, and temperance with prudence, which dwell in the living powers of the gods, bring us salvation. A small portion of these qualities may clearly be seen dwelling within us. For certain unjust souls dwelling on the earth, being fierce like wild beasts, rise up against the souls of the guardians—whether of dogs, one might say, or shepherds, or even of the most excellent of all masters—and by the allurements of words and the pleading of certain incantations they persuade them (as is the talk of the wicked) that it is permitted to usurp much for oneself by acting wickedly among men, and to pay no penalty for it. This crime, by which one gapes for the usurpation of more, we call a "disease" in the bodies of animals, a "pestilence" in the seasons of the year, and in cities and republics 

<margin>C</margin> by a changed name, "injustice." **CLINIAS:** Entirely. **ATHENIAN:** It is necessary, therefore, that he who believes the gods grant pardon to unjust men—if someone grants them a part of the plunder—must say that they are like dogs to whom wolves grant a small piece of the robbery, and they, being pacified by these gifts, allow the flocks to be plundered. Is this not the talk of those who preach that the gods can be appeased? **CLINIAS:** This is it, certainly. **ATHENIAN:** But to which of the aforementioned guardians could someone compare the gods and not be the most ridiculous of all men? To pilots, who, overcome by the libation of wine and the steam of meat, overturn the ship and the sailors together? **CLINIAS:** Not at all. **ATHENIAN:** 

<margin>D</margin> Nor to charioteers who, while they compete, being corrupted by gifts, concede the victory itself to the chariots of their adversaries. **CLINIAS:** Certainly not. For this comparison would be shameful toward the gods. **ATHENIAN:** And yet, he is not persuaded that they are like commanders, nor physicians, nor farmers, nor shepherds, nor even like dogs seduced by the smooth cunning of wolves. **CLINIAS:** Good words, I pray! For these things are not to be heard. **ATHENIAN:** Are not all the gods the greatest of all guardians and over the greatest matters? **CLINIAS:** Exactly so. **ATHENIAN:** Shall we say then that the guardians of the best things, who excel exceedingly in the virtue of guardianship, are worse than dogs and mediocre men, who would never betray justice for gifts impiously accepted from unjust men? **CLINIAS:** By no means is this talk of impious men to be tolerated, and he who suffers from this opinion will be judged by right to be the worst and most profane of all the impious. **ATHENIAN:** 

<margin>E</margin> Therefore, those three things which we proposed—namely, that the gods exist, that they have care for all things, and that they cannot be turned by any prayers contrary to what is just—we seem to have sufficiently shown. **CLINIAS:** Certainly, and we assent to these reasons. **ATHENIAN:** We have spoken somewhat more vehemently because of the controversies of wicked men. But for this reason, O friend Clinias, we have used contentious speech: lest the depraved, thinking they have conquered in speaking, believe that a license has been given to them to do whatever they wish, and whatever they think ought to be done against the gods. For this reason, I say, we wished to use a certain new and more vehement 

<margin>F</margin> manner of speaking. But if we have contributed anything toward persuasion, so that they might now be willing to hate their own morals and embrace the contrary, the preamble of the laws concerning impiety has been well spoken by us. **CLINIAS:** We hope it will be so. If not, at least the kind of speech will not be a disgrace to the lawgiver. **ATHENIAN:** After the preamble, the speech of the laws correctly follows as an interpreter: which may proclaim to all the impious that they should turn themselves from their own ways toward piety. Against those who will not have obeyed, let this law concerning impiety be placed: *If anyone acts or speaks impiously in any way, let whoever happens to be present defend the gods and signify it to the* 

<margin>G</margin> *magistrates.* Let those of them who first hear of it bring the matter to the judgment of these things according to the laws. But if any magistrate hears of it and does not bring it forward, let him himself be guilty of impiety, and let whoever wishes prosecute for the vengeance of the laws. And if anyone shall be condemned, let the judges affect him with individual punishments for each impious commission. Let all be restrained by prisons. Indeed, there are three prisons in the city: one common to many in the marketplace of sellable goods, where many are guarded so they do not flee; another where the assembly of those who gather by night takes place, called by the name "correctional"; a third in the middle of the region, where there is a most deserted and woody place, marked by the name "punishment." There are also three causes of impiety, as we have narrated above. Since in each individual cause of this kind two things proceed, there will be six types of sins against the gods, which are worthy to be judged, and they do not stand in need of an equal or similar penalty. For some, although they do not believe the gods exist, yet because of some just affection of nature they hate the wicked, and being moved by a certain hatred against injustice, they abstain from injuries, flee from the inequitable, and love just men.

<meta>This page continues the legal codification for the crime of impiety from Plato's Laws, Book 10. ### PLATO

<column-break/>

Others, however, in addition to the opinion that all things are destitute of the gods' presence, are also more prone to pleasures and pains; they are also possessed of sharp minds and strong memories. For both types, the common affliction is that they deny the existence of the gods. In this, however, they differ: the former does less harm to other men, while the latter does more. The first type indeed speaks out freely against the gods, regarding sacrifices and oaths; and thus, by mocking others, if he is not punished, he will perhaps make many like himself. But the second type holds the same opinion, yet being endowed with a sharper wit, he is commonly thought to be "clever," and is full of deceit and treachery. From among these many are fortune-tellers, and are ready for every kind of benefit or mischief. Furthermore, from this class sometimes come tyrants, generals of armies, public orators, and those who plot in private rituals, and those who 

<insert>B</insert> deceive men with the clever tricks of the sophists <note>Sophists were traveling teachers in ancient Greece who were often accused of using deceptive logic for profit.</note>. Truly, there are many species of these; but two are worthy of the imposition of laws. Of these, the one full of hypocrisy and deceit gives birth to crimes worthy not merely of one death or two, but many. The other requires both a warning and imprisonment. Likewise, the opinion that the gods are negligent produces two types; and that they are easily appeased by prayers and gifts produces another two. Since the impious are thus distinguished, those who have become such not from an evil character, but from a kind of folly, the judge shall cast into the "prison of correction" <note>original: "σωφρονιστήριον" / "Sophronisterion" — a place for 'tempering' or correcting the mind.</note> to remain for no less than five years. During this time, no other citizen may speak with them, except those who are members of the Nightly Council <note>original: "nocturni coetus" / "νυκτερινοῦ συλλόγου" — the highest oversight committee in Plato's ideal city, meeting at dawn.</note>; these indeed, 

<insert>C</insert> shall converse with them for the sake of warning and for the salvation of the soul. But when the time of imprisonment has expired, he who has become more moderate shall live among the moderate; but if he is convicted again of the crime of impiety, he shall be punished with death. But there are some who, in addition to the opinion that there are no gods, or that they are negligent or easily appeased, also become beast-like, and despise men, and while living allure and draw many to themselves; they also claim to draw and console the dead, and they profess to soothe the gods themselves with chants, sacrifices, and prayers. With this seductive charm they attempt to destroy simpletons, as well as entire houses and cities for the sake of money. Whoever among these shall be condemned, let him be 

<insert>D</insert> bound in the midland prisons, and let no free man ever approach him; but let slaves, appointed by the guardians of the laws, bring him food. Finally, when he has ended his life, let them cast him out unburied beyond the borders of the region. If any free man buries him, let him be accused of the crime of impiety by anyone who wishes. If he leaves behind children sufficient for the city, the guardians of orphans shall take care of them, no less than of the others, from the day their father was condemned. But let this common law be established for all these, which will cause many to sin less against the gods in word and deed, and will recall them from folly: that it shall not be permitted for anyone to fashion for himself gods or sacred rites of the gods contrary to the laws. Let there be a law of this kind, simply 

<insert>E</insert> imposed upon all: 

<margin>No one shall have private shrines in their home.</margin> 

No one shall have shrines in a private house. But when someone is moved in his soul to sacrifice, let him go to the public places to sacrifice, and let him offer the victims to the priests and priestesses who take care of these things most holily. With these he himself may pray, and whoever wishes to pray together with him. These things are done for this reason: because it is not easy to establish shrines and gods. Indeed, it requires a great mind to do this matter rightly. For women especially, and the weaker sort, and those placed in danger or in need—wherever one might be in want—and conversely, when an abundance of some thing flows in, are accustomed to consecrate whatever is at hand, to vow sacrifices, and to promise statues to gods, spirits, and the 

<insert>F</insert> sons of gods. Moved by phantasms while awake, and similarly remembering many things seen in dreams out of fear, they attempt to bring remedies for each, and they fill every house and village with altars and shrines. For the sake of all these things, this law must be established, and furthermore because of the impious, lest by usurping these operations for themselves, they should set up shrines and altars in their own houses, thinking to secretly appease the gods with prayers and sacrifices; and thus increase their own injustice to infinity, whereby they provoke the indignation of the gods against themselves and against those who permit them these things, even if the latter are better men; in which way the whole city, in a certain sense, is justly held by the crime of impiety. The god will by no means be angry with the lawgiver. For let the law be: No one shall possess shrines of the gods in private houses. If, however, anyone is discovered to have possessed or sacrificed 

<insert>G</insert> elsewhere than in public: he who perceives it shall report it to the guardians of the laws. They themselves, if no great crime has been committed by the woman or man, shall order the private sacred things to be brought to the public temples; and if they are not immediately brought, they shall fine them until they are brought. If, however, anyone commits not a childish but a nefarious impiety, whether by failing in his own private sacrifice or in the public worship of the gods, let him be condemned to death as one sacrificing impurely. Whether it be childish or not, let the guardians of the laws judge, and let them declare the impious so treated to be guilty in a trial for impiety.

<column-break/>

But for those who, in addition to the belief that all things are empty of gods, are carried away by an incontinence of pleasures and pains, and who possess strong memories and sharp learning—while the failure to believe in gods is a common passion for both types—the ignorance of other men produces fewer evils in the one case, and more in the other. For the one will always speak with free speech about the gods, and about sacrifices and oaths; and by mocking others, he might perhaps make others like him, if he does not meet with justice. But the other, while holding the same opinion as the first, is called "talented," and is full of deceit and treachery, from whom are produced many diviners and those moved toward every kind of sorcery. 

<insert>B</insert> And from them sometimes arise tyrants, public speakers, and generals, and those who have plotted in private rites, and the schemes of those called sophists. Of these there are indeed many kinds; but there are two worthy of the imposition of laws: the hypocritical type, whose sin is worthy not of one or two deaths; and the other, needing both admonition and bonds. Likewise, the belief that the gods are negligent produces two other types, and the belief that they are appeasable, another two. Since they have been thus divided, those who have become so through folly, without an evil heart or character, let the judge place by law in the house of correction for no less than five years. During this time, let no other citizen meet with them, except those who participate in the Nightly Council, for the purpose of admonition and the 

<insert>C</insert> salvation of the soul. And when the time of their bonds has expired, if any of them seems to be restored to his senses, let him dwell with the sensible; but if not, and if he is convicted again in such a trial, let him be punished with death. But as for those who have become beast-like, in addition to not believing in gods, or believing they are negligent or appeasable—despising men, they lead many of the living astray, claiming to lead the souls of the dead, and promising to persuade the gods, as if they were charming them with sacrifices and prayers and incantations, and they attempt to utterly destroy individuals and whole houses and cities for the sake of money. If one is found guilty of these things, let the court sentence 

<insert>D</insert> him according to the law to be bound in the prison of the inland districts; and let no free person ever approach him, but let them receive a fixed allowance of food from slaves, as ordered by the guardians of the laws. And when he dies, let them cast him out unburied beyond the borders. If any free man helps to bury him, let him be liable to a suit for impiety by anyone who wishes. If he leaves children sufficient for the city, let those in charge of orphans take care of these also, as being orphans, no better or worse than the others, from the day their father is convicted. It is necessary that a common law be established for all these: which would cause the majority to sin less against the gods in deed and word, and indeed to become less foolish, by not being allowed to establish gods contrary to the law. Let this law be established for all 

<insert>E</insert> simply: No one shall possess shrines in private houses. When it comes into anyone's mind to sacrifice, let him go to the public places to sacrifice. And let him hand over the victims to the priests and priestesses, whose concern is the purity of these things; and let him pray together with them, and whoever else wishes to pray with him. Let these things be so for the following reasons. It is not easy to establish shrines and gods; it requires a great intelligence to do such a thing correctly. It is the custom for all women especially, and for those who are sick in any way, or in danger, or in difficulty, wherever one is in difficulty—and the opposite, when they obtain some relief—to consecrate whatever is at hand, and to vow sacrifices, and to promise the founding of shrines to gods, 

<insert>F</insert> spirits, and the children of gods. And because of phantoms seen while awake through fear, and likewise in dreams, as they remember many visions and provide remedies for each of them, they fill all houses and all villages with altars and shrines, establishing them in clean places and wherever anyone happens to be. For all these reasons, it is necessary to act according to the law now stated; and besides, for the sake of the impious—so that they may not act stealthily in these matters, establishing shrines and altars in private houses, thinking to secretly make the gods favorable with sacrifices and prayers, and thus increasing their injustice without limit, they bring charges upon themselves from the gods, and upon those who permit them, who are better than they; and thus the whole city justly suffers from the impiety of these people. The lawgiver indeed will not be blamed by god. For let this law be established: not to possess shrines of the gods in private houses. 

<insert>G</insert> And if anyone is seen possessing others and performing rites other than the public ones, if he be a man or woman who possesses them without having committed any of the great and unholy injustices, let the one who notices it report it to the law-guardians; and let them order the private shrines to be carried to the public ones; and if they do not comply, let them be fined until they are carried away. But if anyone has committed an unholy act of impiety, not of a childish sort but a man's impiety, and is seen sacrificing—whether having established them in private or sacrificing in public to the gods to whom he, as a rogue and a lawless person, is sacrificing—let him be punished with death. Having judged whether it is a childish act or not, let the law-guardians thus bring them to the court and fulfill the penalty for impiety for these people.

<summary>Plato establishes strict legal penalties for different types of atheism and prohibits private shrines to prevent superstition and the manipulation of religion by charlatans. He introduces the "House of Correction" and the "Nightly Council" as means of reforming misguided believers before resorting to the death penalty.</summary>
