<meta>This page marks the beginning of Book 11 of Plato's Laws. It transitions from the previous discussion on religious crimes and impiety in Book 10 to the regulation of social interactions, specifically "pacts" or contracts. The text establishes a foundational principle of property rights and the ethical handling of found items.</meta>

# THE LAWS OF PLATO, OR, CONCERNING THE INSTITUTION OF LAWS;
### THE ELEVENTH DIALOGUE.

*SUMMARY OF THE DIALOGUE. The theme of these two books, namely the eleventh and twelfth, is common: Concerning pacts or contracts. Under this general term, he understands all those things which pertain to the common use of life, coming together by mutual consent among people. This includes those not established by a specific name, as well as those designated by a certain name, such as a testament, tutelage, buying, and selling. First, however, he deals with private contracts in this eleventh book, and with public ones in the twelfth. He hands down these matters in such a way as to open the fountains of natural equity—which is the firmament of true laws—and therefore he does not only compel by laws, but persuades by reasons, and shapes the minds of men toward the obedience of virtue and honesty. This is indeed the true <term>hypotyposis</term> <note>original: ὑποτύπωσις; a sketch or foundational pattern</note> of true laws, for laws deprived of this hold no solid or expressed image of true right and genuine justice, and they fail from the best principles of nature.*

---

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial T featuring a seated figure with a backdrop of a city and landscapes.</image-desc>
THE NEXT matter after these things would be the contracts we make with one another, which require a proper order. The rule for such things is simple: let no one touch my property as far as possible, nor move even the smallest part of it, unless he has persuaded me in some way. In the same way, I should act regarding the property of others, provided I am of sound mind. Let us speak first of treasure <note>original: θησαυρον; refers to hidden money or valuables found by chance</note> among such things, which someone has laid down as a store for himself and his family; if it was not mine or my ancestors', I would never pray to the gods to find it, nor would I move it if I did. Neither would I consult those called diviners to advise me in any way to take up what was deposited in the earth. For I would never believe that the gain in money would profit me as much as the growth of character and justice in my soul would benefit me by not taking it. By preferring justice in the soul over wealth in one's estate, I would acquire a better possession in a better part of myself. For the saying "do not move the immovable" is well said by many, and it should be said regarding this as well. One must also believe the stories told about these things, that such gains do not profit one's children or descendants. Whoever is unconcerned for his children and neglects the lawgiver—taking up what neither he nor his ancestors deposited without the consent of the depositor—destroys a most beautiful and simple law. This law was given by no weak man: "What you did not lay down, do not take up." If someone despises the lawgiver and takes up what he did not deposit—which is sometimes a massive treasure—what should he suffer? What the gods will do, only God knows. But whoever sees it and becomes aware of it, let him report it: if it happens in the city, to the city wardens <note>original: αστυνομοις (astynomoi)</note>; if in the countryside of the state, to the rural wardens; if in the marketplace, to the market wardens. Once revealed, the city shall send to Delphi; and whatever the god decrees concerning the money and the one who moved it, the city shall perform in obedience to the oracle. If the informant is a free man, let him gain a reputation for virtue; if he does not report it, a reputation for vice. If a slave reports it, he should rightly be made free by the city, with the city paying the master his value. But if he does not report it, he shall be punished with death. Following this, a similar law follows for small and large things alike. If someone leaves his property somewhere, whether willingly or unwillingly, let the one who happens upon it allow it to remain, believing that the goddess of the road protects such things consecrated by the law. If anyone, disobeying this, takes it home, if he is a slave and the item is of small value, let him be beaten with many lashes by any person he meets who is not less than thirty years old. If he is a free man, besides being considered unfree in spirit and a violator of the law, let him pay ten times the value of what he moved to the one who left it. If someone complains that another holds something of his, large or small, and the other admits he has it but denies it belongs to the seeker: if the property is registered with the magistrates according to the law, let the holder be called before the authorities, and let him produce it. If it appears in the records as belonging to one of the disputants, let him take it. If it is found to belong to someone absent, and neither provides a sufficient surety <note>a person who takes legal responsibility for another's debt or appearance</note> for the absent owner that he will return it, let it be deposited until the owner claims it. If the disputed item is not registered with the magistrates, let it be held by the three eldest magistrates until judgment is passed. If the property is a living creature, the one who loses the case must pay the magistrates for its upkeep. The judgment must be settled within three days. Any man of sound mind may lead away his own slave to use as he wishes for any lawful purpose; he may also lead away a runaway on behalf of friends or relatives for its preservation. If anyone rescues someone being led away as a slave, claiming they are free, the one leading them must let go; but the rescuer must provide three sufficient sureties and only then take them away. Otherwise, if he rescues them by force, let him be liable for violence and pay double the damage to the person from whom the slave was taken. One may also bring back his own freedman if he does not show proper respect. Respect consists of...

<meta>catchword: to the... or towards the...</meta>

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial S featuring a seated figure with a backdrop of a city and landscapes.</image-desc>
IT FOLLOWS that we should speak of pacts: and let us assign them their proper order. Let this be the simple rule: that no one shall touch my things according to his strength, nor move any of my things, even the smallest, unless he has persuaded me. And I shall do the same while I am of sound mind in the affairs of others. Especially when we speak of treasures, which each has deposited for himself and his own, which was not of my parents; I should never wish to find it, nor if I found it, should I move it; nor should I believe diviners advising me to take a deposit. For money will never profit me so much, if taken, as I shall excel in virtue of soul and justice if I do not take it. Therefore, for the possession of money, the possession of justice in my soul will be better for me, if I prefer virtue to riches. Indeed, since it is well said by many: "what is immovable, must not be moved," it shall also be said very beautifully of this one thing. But the common report regarding these matters must also be believed, that these things do not benefit the generation of children. But if anyone does not care for his children and neglects the lawgiver, and thus takes what neither he nor any of his people deposited, against the will of the one who deposited it: he spurns that most excellent and simple law which a noble man promulgated, who said, "What you did not deposit, do not take up."

<margin>Laertius reports this among the laws of Solon. <note>Diogenes Laertius was a biographer of Greek philosophers; Solon was a famous Athenian lawmaker.</note></margin>
What, then, ought he to suffer, who has despised these two legislators, and took up what he himself did not deposit—and it was not some small thing he took, but a great treasure? What penalty is owed to him by the gods, God himself knows. But what shall be done by men, we shall declare. He who first sees it, let him report it to the judges. And if the crime is in the city, to the aediles <note>Roman term for city wardens</note>; if indeed in the field, to the curators of the fields and their chiefs; if in the market of things for sale, let him signify it to the curators of the same. The matter thus being made known, the city shall send to Delphi, and whatever shall be said by the oracle concerning both the money and the one who moved the money, the city, having obeyed the god, shall confirm. And he who made the report, if he be free, let him come into an opinion of virtue, and the contrary of vice if he knowingly concealed it; but if he be a slave, the price having been contributed to his master by the city, he is to be set free. But the slave who concealed it must be punished with death. This similar law follows next concerning small and large things alike. If anyone has left his property somewhere willingly or otherwise: let him who happens to find it not touch it, but let him think the goddess of the journey has preserved these things for him as consecrated by the law. Whoever, having despised this law, carries these things to his house, if he be a slave and of small value, let him be struck with many lashes by whoever meets him and is over thirty years of age. But if he is free, let him first be held as ungenerous and outside the laws, and then let him also repay ten times the price of that thing which he moved to the one who left it. When anyone complains that something great or small of his is held by someone—which the other indeed confesses to have, but denies it belongs to the one who seeks it—if the item is registered with the magistrates according to the law, let the one who holds it be called to the magistrates. The matter being made known, if it is recorded that the thing belongs to the other of the adversaries, let that one have it. But if it is found to belong to neither, but to some absent person, he who does not give a sufficient surety that he will hand the thing over to that absent person to whom it belongs, let him be forced to deposit as much. But if the matter under dispute is not registered with the magistrates, then let it be deposited with three senior magistrates until a sentence is passed; and if it is an animal about which there is a dispute, the one who loses the case shall restore the cost of its food to the magistrates themselves. Let the judgment be completed within three days. Any person of sound mind may lead his slave where he wishes, having used him honestly; let him also lead him in the name of friends and relatives, so that he may restore a fugitive to favor. But if anyone claims for liberty someone led as a slave, let the one who led him dismiss him; but the one who so leads him away, if he provides three worthy sureties, let him be thus rescued by right. Otherwise, if he takes him away, let him be seen to have brought force; and being condemned, let him restore double the damage to him from whom he took the slave. Every man may also lead back his freedman if he is not cherished by him, or if he is not sufficiently cherished. Respect, however, is first that he should come to his master's house three times each month...

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Book 11 of Plato's Laws regarding the regulation of social and commercial interactions. <header>OF PLATO</header>

<margin>A</margin> and he should show himself ready to do whatever is honorable and possible for him. Furthermore, regarding marriage, he should do whatever seems right to his master. It shall not be permitted for a freedman to acquire greater wealth than the one who liberated him possesses; whatever excess he has shall be given to the master. Moreover, a freedman, like other foreigners, shall not remain in the city for more than twenty years; but after that time, he shall depart taking his own goods, unless he has persuaded his former master and the magistrates to let him stay. If the goods of a freedman <margin>B</margin> or any other foreigner exceed the limit of the third census class, he must depart with his belongings on the thirtieth day after this discovery is made, and no further request for a stay shall be granted to him by the magistrates. If anyone is convicted of not obeying this law, he shall be punished with death, and his property shall be confiscated for public use. The judges of the tribes shall take cognizance of these matters, unless the litigants have previously been reconciled through neighbors and chosen arbitrators. If someone claims an animal or any other thing as his own, the person in possession must refer the claimant to the one who sold it, or who gave it legitimately and sufficiently, or who otherwise transferred it in a valid and firm manner. If he refers the matter to a citizen or a resident of the city, the truth shall be found within thirty days; but if he refers it to outsiders, it shall be found within five months, the middle month of which is that in which the sun returns from the summer circle to the winter circle <note>This refers to the period surrounding the winter solstice.</note>. <margin>C</margin> Whatever things are exchanged through buying and selling must be exchanged in the designated place of the marketplace, by giving and receiving the item and the price of the item then and there, and nowhere else. No buying or selling shall be done on credit. If an exchange is made otherwise or in other places, there shall be no legal recourse regarding it according to the law. Furthermore, no judgment shall be rendered concerning contributions for banquets where several people contribute money or anything else for a common purpose. A seller who has received no less than fifty drachmas for the price of a sold item must necessarily wait ten days in the city, and the buyer must know his lodging. We wish this to be done for the sake of legal complaints and returns which are accustomed to happen in these cases. Moreover, a legal return is distinguished from an illegal one in this way: <margin>D</margin> When someone has sold a slave suffering from frenzy <note>original: "phrenesi"; likely a brain fever or delirium.</note>, or kidney stones, or difficulty urinating, or that disease which they call "sacred" <note>original: "morbo quem sacrū appellāt"; this refers to epilepsy, which the Greeks believed was a divine or 'sacred' affliction.</note>, or any other hidden, long-lasting, and difficult-to-cure sickness of body or mind—if a doctor or a gymnastics trainer buys the slave, they may not return him. Nor may he be returned if the seller told the buyer the truth beforehand. But if a professional skilled in such matters sells such a slave to an ignorant and unskilled person, the buyer may return the slave within six months for other ailments, but in the case of the sacred disease, he may return him up to a full year. <margin>E</margin> Judgment of these matters shall be conducted by doctors whom the litigants have chosen by common consent. Whoever is condemned shall pay the buyer double the price of what he sold. If an unskilled person sells to another unskilled person, as was said regarding the above, the return and judgment shall take place, and the one convicted shall pay back the simple price. When someone sells a murderer, if he sells knowingly to one who also knows, the slave may not be returned; if he sells to one who does not know, the return shall be made when the buyer discovers it. Five of the younger guardians of the laws shall judge this. If it is found that the seller was not ignorant, he must first purge the buyer’s house of pollutions according to the law of the interpreters <term>Exegetes</term> <note>original: "interpretum"; these were officials who interpreted sacred law and rituals for purification after a crime like murder.</note>; then he shall pay triple the price to the buyer. He who exchanges coins for coins, or any animals, or anything else he wishes, must neither bring nor receive anything counterfeit <margin>F</margin> and should observe this law diligently. But to this law, as to other laws, a preamble should be placed. One ought to consider counterfeiting, lying, and deception as a single genus. In this matter, the speech of many is certainly to be condemned, for they affirm that they use these things rightly whenever it is opportune. Since they do not determine the occasion itself—where and when—they greatly harm both themselves and others with this word. The lawgiver will not leave this so undetermined, but will declare it diligently with more or fewer terms. And even now, let it be determined thus: No one, having invoked the gods, should speak a lie, or deceive, or dare to counterfeit anything in word or deed, unless he wishes to be hateful to God. <margin>G</margin> First, he is hateful to God who, swearing falsely, thinks little of the gods. Second, he who lies in the presence of his superiors. Superiors are better than their inferiors: as elders are generally to the younger, parents to their children, men to women and children, and rulers to subjects. It is right to revere these in every office, but most especially in the civil office, for the sake of which we have entered into this discourse. For whoever counterfeits anything in the market certainly lies and deceives, and by invoking the gods, he commits perjury against the overseers of the market and their laws. In doing this, he neither fears men nor worships the gods. It is surely right not to easily defile the names of the gods, nor to toss them here and there, but to keep all things pertaining to the gods pure and chaste. <margin>H</margin> He who is not persuaded by these reasons shall be urged by this law: He who sells anything in the market shall never name two prices for his saleable goods; but having set a simple price, if he does not sell it, he may take it away. Again, and on the same day, he shall seek neither a higher nor a lower price. Praise and...

<gloss>of the purity and holiness regarding the gods. If he is not persuaded, here is the law: the seller who says a price and does not get it, if he takes the item away, he acts rightly if he brings it back again [at the same price].</gloss>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> proclaiming whatever things the just man ought to do and which are at the same time possible. And regarding marriage, he should do whatever seems right to the master who shared his life. It shall not be permitted for the manumitted one to be wealthier [than his former master]; let the excess belong to the master. The released man shall not stay more than twenty years, but just like other foreigners, he shall depart taking all his own property, unless he persuades the magistrates and the one who freed him. If the property of the manumitted man or any of the other foreigners becomes greater than the property <margin>B</margin> of the [third class], let him have no further petition from the magistrates. If anyone, being disobedient to these rules, is brought into court and convicted, let him be punished with death, and let his money become public property. Let the trials for these things be in the tribal courts, unless the claimants are reconciled to one another beforehand before neighbors and chosen judges. If someone lays hold of an animal or anything else of his own, or if another person claims it is his own property, let the one who has it refer it to a reliable person—one who is credit-worthy and lawful—who gave it, or in whatever way... <margin>C</margin> which is when the summer sun follows into the winter [solstice]. Whatever things are exchanged from one to another by buying or selling, let them be given in the place appointed for each in the market, receiving the price on the spot, and let them be exchanged thus, and nowhere else. Nor should anyone speak of credit or make a purchase of anything on credit. If someone exchanges one thing for another in other ways or in other places, trusting the one he is exchanging with to pay later, let him do so on the understanding that there are no legal actions according to the law for things not sold according to what has been written. Regarding subscriptions <note>original: "eranos"; a type of loan or shared contribution among friends.</note>, let him who wishes to collect a subscription do so among friends; but if a dispute arises regarding the subscription... <margin>D</margin> Of those who sell, let the one who has received no less than fifty drachmas necessarily remain in the city for ten days; and let the buyer know the residence of the seller. This is for the sake of complaints that are accustomed to happen in such things, and for the sake of the returns according to the laws. Let the return according to the law be as follows: If someone sells a slave who is sick with consumption, or stones, or strangury, or the so-called sacred disease, or any other hidden disease that is long-lasting and difficult to heal in the body or the mind, if the buyer is a doctor or a trainer, there shall be no return for him nor shall he obtain such things; nor if the seller told him the truth beforehand. But if a professional sells such a slave to a layman, the buyer <margin>E</margin> may return him within six months, except for the sacred disease. For this disease, it shall be permitted to make the return within a year. The trial for this shall be among all the doctors whom the opposing parties choose in common. The one who loses the trial shall pay double the price at which he sold. If a layman sells to a layman, there shall be a return just as was said before, and the trial also; and the one who loses shall pay the simple price of the sale. If someone sells a murderer to another, if he sells knowingly to one who knows, there shall be no return for such a person by means of this declaration; but for the one who did not know, there shall be a return when the buyer perceives it. The five youngest of the guardians of the laws shall judge this. If he is judged to have known, he shall purify the buyer's house according to the law of the <margin>F</margin> interpreters, and he shall pay triple the price to the seller. He who exchanges either coin for coin, or any of the other animals, or anything else, let him give and receive everything unadulterated, following the law. Let him receive a preamble, just as with other laws, concerning this whole type of evil. Every man must think of counterfeiting, lying, and deception as being one genus, of which many are accustomed to bring a bad reputation, saying wrongly that such a thing, happening at the right time, would often be correct. But leaving the "right time"—where and when—disordered and undefined, they harm both themselves and others by this saying. <margin>G</margin> The lawgiver must define with greater or smaller boundaries what must be made clear. And let it be defined now: No one should commit any lie, or deception, or anything counterfeit, calling upon the name of the gods, either in word or deed, unless he intends to be most hateful to the gods. Now, he is such a one who, swearing false oaths, has no concern for the gods; and second is he who lies in the presence of his superiors. Superiors are those who are better than the worse: elders, generally speaking, than the young. Therefore, parents are superior to offspring, and men to women and children; and rulers to the ruled. It would be fitting to revere these in every other office and especially in the political ones; from which our present discourse has come. For everyone in the market who counterfeits anything both lies <margin>H</margin> and deceives, even deceiving the gods, swearing by the laws and protections of the market-overseers, neither respecting men nor worshipping the gods. It is altogether a beautiful practice not to defile the names of the gods easily, holding as we most of us do in various states of purity... whoever sells anything in the market should never say two prices for what he is selling.

# ON THE LAWS, BOOK 11.

<margin>A</margin> ...and let him refrain from swearing an oath when a thing is being sold. If anyone should disobey these rules, any citizen who happens to be present, being no less than thirty years of age, may beat the one who swears with impunity. But if he fails to do so, let him be held as a traitor to the laws. Regarding the one who does not obey the law and sells an adulterated <note>original: *kibdelon* / *adulteratam*; referring to goods that are faked, diluted, or of inferior quality passed off as genuine</note> item: whoever notices and is able to do so should expose him. If he proves the charge before the magistrates, a slave or a resident alien who exposes the fraud may carry off the adulterated item for himself. But if a citizen neglects to accuse the seller, he shall be considered a wicked man, as if he had robbed the gods. However, if he does accuse and convict the seller, he shall dedicate the item to the gods who preside over the market. Any seller clearly caught in this act <margin>B</margin> shall not only be deprived of the item itself but shall also be publicly beaten with as many lashes as the drachmas <note>A unit of silver currency in ancient Greece.</note> he was asking for the item, with a herald proclaiming the reason for the beating. Furthermore, the market inspectors <term>agoranomoi</term> and the guardians of the laws shall diligently inquire of those skilled in these matters regarding all the malice and fraud of sellers; they shall record what a seller must and must not do and post these rules on a pillar in the market so that they are clearly visible to all. Regarding the laws for the city inspectors <term>astynomoi</term>, enough has been said previously. If anything seems to be lacking in those laws, the inspectors themselves, in council with the guardians of the laws, shall supply the deficiency; then they shall engrave both the original and the subsequent regulations on a pillar. After the laws on adulteration, it follows that we must speak of retail trade <note>original: *cauponatio*; referring to innkeeping and small-scale selling</note>; regarding this, we shall first give counsel and <margin>C</margin> reason, and then we shall establish the law. All retail trade in a city is naturally established not for the sake of doing harm, but quite the opposite. For how could a man not be a benefactor who takes wealth that is disproportionate and uneven and reduces it to equality and measure? This is what the money-changer, the merchant, the hireling, and the master of a guest-house do. These men and others like them, whether they be of more honorable or more shameful trades, strive to supply what is lacking and provide equality to possessions. But let us consider what the cause of the slander against this profession is, and why it does not seem honorable, so that we may regulate at least a part of it by laws. **Clinias:** This matter, as it seems, is not a small one, nor does it require a small amount of virtue. **Athenian:** <margin>D</margin> How so, Clinias? Very few men are by nature, and even fewer by the best education, able to restrain themselves when they are gripped by the need and desire for certain things, so that they might choose moderation; and when it is possible to take great wealth, they remain sober and choose the middle path over excess. The common crowd, however, acts in the complete opposite way. For they desire immoderately, and when it is possible to gain a moderate profit, they are vexed by an insatiable greed for gain. Because of this, all classes of men involved in retail trade, commerce, and innkeeping have fallen under slander and reproach. For if someone (may it never happen, nor will it ever be) were to compel—<margin>E</margin> I say it even though it sounds ridiculous—if one were to compel the best men everywhere to manage guest-houses for a time, or to engage in retail trade, or if we knew that the most holy women were forced by some fate to descend to such a craft, we would clearly recognize that all these things are honorable and worthy of approval. Indeed, if they were performed without corruption, those who did them would be thought to bear the role of mothers and nurses without injustice. But now, in desert places where many long roads lead, men build houses for the sake of innkeeping; they receive those driven by storms as a welcome refuge and refresh those oppressed by heat; yet afterward, they do not release them as friends gifted with hospitality, but treat them as enemies and captives, cruelly forcing them to redeem themselves <margin>F</margin> with enormous and unjust ransoms and stripping them of everything. These and other such shameful acts performed in all such trades are what cause these professions, which provide help to the needy, to be subject to slander. A remedy for these things must be devised by the lawgiver. It is a true saying, and one long celebrated as a proverb: It is hard to fight <margin>Proverb: It is hard to fight against two things.</margin> against two opposing things at once. Just as in many other diseases, so it happens here. For a battle now threatens us on two fronts: wealth and poverty. One of these corrupts the human soul with luxury and softness; the other drives it to impudence through pain. What remedy, therefore, shall we devise in a wisely instituted city to drive away this disease? Care must be taken first <margin>G</margin> to employ as few of the retail-trading class as possible in the city. Second, these trades must be assigned to those whose corruption would not bring great ruin to the city. Third, a way and method must be found so that the souls of these men are not easily filled with impudence and a lack of nobility. These things having been said, let this law regarding such matters be passed for the Magnesians <note>The citizens of the hypothetical colony "Cretan Magnesia" being planned in this dialogue.</note> with good fortune; the god who raises up their city makes it inhabited once again. None of those who belong to the five thousand and forty households shall become a retail trader or a merchant, whether willingly or unwillingly; nor shall he become the servant of any private person who does not stand on equal footing with him in the same lot, except for his father and mother, and those of his ancestors and elders who are free and live freely. However, what is noble and what is not noble <margin>H</margin> cannot easily be distinguished with precision by laws. Nevertheless, let it be judged by the best men, and decided by their hatred and love. And he who [engages] in such ignoble trade...

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Book 11 of Plato's Laws regarding the regulation of the marketplace. Having previously established the rules for selling goods and preventing fraud, the text now moves to the social status of retail trade, the ethical obligations of artisans, and the legal handling of contracts and wills.</meta>

# PLATO'S [LAWS]

...engaged in the trade of retail in any capacity, anyone who wishes may accuse him before those foremost in virtue and rank, on the grounds that he is a disgrace to his lineage. <margin>A</margin> And if he is found to have stained his ancestral house with such an unworthy pursuit, let him be restrained by being bound in chains for a year. If he should fall into this error again, let him be bound for two years. Thereafter, as often as he is caught having sinned in this way, let the duration of his detention always be doubled.
The second law commands that only foreigners and resident aliens may follow the retail arts. The third law warns that care must be taken that such a foreigner or resident is as good as possible, or at least as little evil as can be. Nor should the guardians of the laws be ignorant that they must be observers not only <margin>B</margin> of those whom it is not difficult to keep from injustice and depravity—namely, those who are well-born and well-educated—but much more so of those who are not, and who are engaged in these trades by which men are more easily driven toward wickedness. Since retail trade is indeed multifaceted and varied, the guardians of the laws should meet with experts in each of these types. Just as I said a little while ago regarding the adulteration of goods <note>original: *kibdelia*; referring to the dilution or faking of products</note> which is related to this, they should first determine what activities are necessary for the city. Then, having diligently examined both the expense and the profit, they should see what constitutes a moderate gain for the retailer; and they shall record both the expense and the profit. Let some things be observed by the <term>aediles</term> <note>Market officials; in the Greek text, these are the *agoranomoi* (market-wardens) and *astynomoi* (city-wardens)</note>, others by the curators of saleable goods, and others by the <margin>C</margin> magistrates of the fields. In this way, the arts of retailing will benefit each person and do the least harm. 
If anyone does not seem to have kept his agreements <note>original: *pacta* / *homologias*</note>, unless a law or decree prohibits it, or unless necessity and force compelled him, or an unexpected accident detained him against his will, let the judges of the tribes hear the case for the unkept agreement, unless neighbors or arbitrators have first reconciled them. The race of artisans, who have furnished our lives with their skills, is consecrated to Vulcan <note>The Roman name for the Greek god Hephaestus, god of the forge and fire.</note> and Pallas <note>Pallas Athena, goddess of wisdom and crafts.</note>. <margin>Gods of the Artisans</margin>
But to Mars <note>Ares, god of war.</note> and Pallas is consecrated the race of those who preserve the works of the artisans through other skills prepared for protection and assistance. It is not without reason that their kind is consecrated to these gods. For all <margin>D</margin> these look after the region and the people. Some, indeed, preside over military contests; others produce works and instruments for hire. These men, out of respect for the gods who are their authors, ought never to deceive anyone with a lie. 
But if any artisan, through malice, does not complete a work within the appointed time, and—believing that the god who is the giver of life will forgive him out of a certain blindness of mind as if he were one of his own household—shows no fear of that god, he shall first pay the penalty to the god himself. Secondly, being made a defendant under this law, he shall pay the price of the work which he did not finish on time, and he shall perform the work again from the beginning within the same span of time for free. But whatever the law advised the seller regarding the price of saleable goods, let it also <margin>E</margin> advise the artisan. Let him beware, therefore, of bidding for his own work at a higher price than is fair; rather, let the bidding be done as simply as possible and as is worthy. For the artisan is not ignorant of what price his work is worth. In a free city, an artisan ought not to use his skill—which is a transparent thing and far removed from a lie—to deceive the unlearned <note>original: *rudes* / *idiotai*; referring to laypeople who do not possess technical knowledge of a specific craft</note> through trickery. In these matters, therefore, let judgment be rendered to the one suffering the injury against the one doing it. 
If anyone does not give an artisan his pay according to their agreements, but neglects Jupiter <note>Zeus</note>, the guardian of the city, and Minerva <note>Athena</note>, who shares in this matter, <margin>F</margin> and, moved by a small gain, dissolves the great fellowship of men to the best of his ability, let the law, together with the help of the gods, act as patron for the unity of the city. He who does not offer a poor man the pay he received at the time he agreed, let him pay double; and if a year passes, although other debts of money should be returned without interest, this man shall pay one-sixth of a drachma for every drachma for each month. Let the judges of the tribes hear the causes of these matters. 
But since we have made mention of artisans, and generals and other makers of military instruments are, in a certain way, artisans, it is not out of place for us to speak of these also. If, therefore, any of these should undertake some public work, whether voluntarily <margin>G</margin> or by command, and finishes what he began correctly, the law shall justly render to him the honors which are the rewards for warlike men, so that it never ceases to praise him. But if nothing is returned to him who has conducted military affairs well, he will justly complain. Therefore, let a certain law be established concerning these things, mixed with praise, which does not indeed compel but advises the multitude of citizens: let good men be honored who have saved the entire city either by fortitude or by some military skill. And let the greatest honors be attributed first to those who have especially cherished the laws of the good lawgivers. 
Now, therefore, we have spoken of almost all the agreements that men treat among themselves, except <margin>H</margin> for those concerning orphans and guardians, of which it is now necessary to speak. The beginning of all these is, for those who are dead, the desire of making a will as they please; and for those who have made no will, it is fortune. I have said that it is necessary to speak of this, O Cleinias, because I was considering the difficulty of this matter; for it is not possible to leave it without order. For individuals will hastily testify to many diverse things, contrary to one another, to the laws, to the customs of the living, and to their ancestors, if someone should establish...

<column-break/>

...participates in any art, let whoever wishes accuse him of being in no way worthy of the honor of those <margin>A</margin> who are foremost in virtue. And if he is judged to be following a shameful pursuit and to be defiling his own ancestral house, let him be bound for a year and abstain from such a thing. If he does so again, two years; and for each conviction, let the duration of his chains not cease to be double the previous time. The second law is that it is necessary for a resident alien or a foreigner to be the one who intends to engage in retail trade. Third, that such a person must be as excellent as possible, or at least as little wicked as can be, so that he is a fellow-inhabitant with us in the city; the guardians of the laws must be guardians not only of those whom it is easy to guard so that they do not become lawless and evil—those who <margin>B</margin> have been well-educated by birth and upbringing—but much more must they guard those who are not so, and who follow pursuits that have a powerful tendency to incline them toward becoming evil. In this regard, since retail trade is many things and possesses many such pursuits, whatever of it remains and is judged by the city to be a necessary requirement in the city, the guardians of the laws must again meet concerning these things, together with those experienced in each kind of retail (as we previously commanded concerning the adulteration of coins/goods, making allowance for this holy matter). When they have met, they must see what profit and what expenditure makes a moderate gain for the retailer. <margin>C</margin> Having written this down, they must establish the recognized expenditure and profit; and let the market-wardens guard one part, the city-wardens another, and the country-wardens another. And in this way, retail trade would benefit each person and do the smallest harm to those who use it in the cities. 
As for whatever things a person agrees to by contract but does not perform according to the agreements—except for those things which the laws or a decree forbid, or which he agreed to while being forced by some unjust necessity—and if a person is prevented against his will by some unexpected occurrence, let there be trials for the unfulfilled agreement of others in the tribal courts, if they cannot first <margin>D</margin> be reconciled by arbitrators or neighbors. The race of artisans is sacred to Hephaestus and Athena, who have furnished our lives with the arts. But to Ares and Athena belong those who preserve the works of the artisans by other defensive arts. It is right indeed that the race of all these should be sacred to these gods. All these continue to serve the land and the people: some ruling over the contests of war, others producing instruments and works for the sake of the children [or for common use]. For these men, it would not be fitting to lie about such things, as they revere the gods who are their ancestors. If any artisan should not complete a work within the stated time through some fault, showing no reverence for the god who gives life, thinking that the god is a forgiving kinsman, and seeing nothing at all, he shall first undergo a penalty to the god. Secondly, following the law, let him be liable for the value of the works about which he lied in his agreement. <margin>E</margin> And again, from the beginning, let him finish the work for free within the stated time. And just as some law gives advice to a shipbuilder—the very thing that left the seller out—not to attempt to charge more than the value but to do so as simply as possible, so the same is commanded to the one undertaking a task. For the artisan knows the value. In cities of free men, therefore, the artisan must never use his art—a thing clear and non-lying by nature—to trick the layman through craftiness. Let there be trials for those wronged in these matters against the wrongdoer. 
And if any wage is not paid to an artisan according to the <margin>F</margin> correct agreements made with the neighbors, thus dishonoring Zeus the Guardian of the City and Athena who are partners in the state, and being content with a small gain, he dissolves great fellowships; let there be a law that helps the bond of the city along with the gods. Whoever has received a work and does not pay the wage in the times agreed upon, let him be charged double. And if a year passes—while other monies are interest-free, as much as one contributes by lending—let him pay an additional obol on the drachma for each month. Let there be trials for these things in the tribal courts. 
And by the way, concerning those who are artisans of the preservation of war—generals and as many as are technical about these things—it is just to speak, since we have mentioned artisans in general, for these are, as it were, another kind of artisan. If any of these, <margin>G</margin> having undertaken a task, works for the public, whether as a volunteer or by command, and performs it, the law rightly pays him the honors (which are the wages for warlike men), and it never tires of praising him. but if he takes up a work and does not pay back [perform] the beautiful deeds of war, it blames him. Let there be a law for us, therefore, mixed with praise concerning these, a law that advises rather than compels the multitude of citizens: to honor the good men who are saviors of the entire city, whether by courage or by political devices. For let the greatest prize be given first to those who have been able to excel in everything regarding the writings of the good lawgivers. 
The greatest parts of the contracts which men make with one another—except for those of orphans and the care of guardians over orphans—have now been almost established by us. <margin>H</margin> It is now necessary to arrange these in some way after the things just said. The beginnings of all these are the desires for the disposal of property of those about to die, and the fortunes of those who have died without disposing of anything. It is necessary to speak of this, O Cleinias, looking at the difficulty and hardship of it. For it would not be possible to arrange it otherwise. For each person might set down many things, different from one another and contrary to the laws and the customs of the living and their ancestors, before they are about to die, if one were to give the power simply...

<summary>This page outlines Plato's strict regulations for the marketplace and labor in his ideal city, emphasizing that citizens are forbidden from retail trade to preserve their dignity, and establishing ethical standards for artisans under the protection of Hephaestus, Athena, and Ares. It also transitions into the complex legal territory of inheritance and wills.</summary>

# ON THE LAWS, BOOK XI.

...let a will be valid in whatever way a person has drawn it up at the very end of their life. For most of us are in a state of timid and somewhat broken spirits when we believe we are already about to die. <margin>A</margin> **CLINIAS:** Why do you say this, Stranger? **ATHENIAN:** It is a difficult thing, Clinias, for a man who is about to die; even in the midst of his speech, he is not at all a figure of fear or annoyance to legislators. **CLINIAS:** In what way? **ATHENIAN:** He seeks to be the master of all his possessions, so that he speaks with anger. <note>The Athenian is describing the "deathbed protest" where a dying man demands total control over his estate.</note> **CLINIAS:** What does he say? **ATHENIAN:** "It is a terrible thing, O gods," he says, "if it shall not be permitted to me to give my own things to whomever I wish, and not to others; to give more to one and less to another, according to how they have clearly proven to be bad or good toward me, having been sufficiently tested in my illnesses, or in my old age, and in all sorts of other fortunes." **CLINIAS:** And so, Stranger, do they not seem to you to speak well? <margin>B</margin> **ATHENIAN:** To me, Clinias, the ancient legislators seem to have been soft, and to have looked down upon and considered only a small part of human nature when making these laws. **CLINIAS:** How do you mean? **ATHENIAN:** Fearing this speech, my friend, they made this law: that it should be permitted for a man simply to dispose of his own property in whatever way he wishes, absolutely. But you and I will give a more fitting answer to those in your city who are about to die. **CLINIAS:** How so? **ATHENIAN:** "O friends," we shall say, "and you who are truly creatures of a day, it is difficult for you to know your own possessions, and even to know yourselves, <note>A reference to the famous Delphic maxim "Know Thyself" (Gnothi Seauton).</note> just as the writing of the Pythia says even now. I therefore, being the legislator, do not consider you to belong to yourselves, nor this property to be your own; rather, it belongs to <margin>C</margin> your entire lineage, both that which was before and that which will be hereafter; and even more so, the whole lineage and the property belong to the city. Since these things are so, if someone should approach you with flattery when you are shaken by illness or old age, and persuade you to make a will contrary to what is best, I will not willingly allow it. Looking toward what is best for the whole city and the lineage, I will legislate, viewing the individual's interest as being of a smaller portion. May you go with grace and kindness toward us, journeying where the nature of human affairs now requires you to go; we shall take care of your other affairs, looking after them with as much power as possible, and not favoring one part over another." Let these be your consolations and preambles, Clinias, <margin>D</margin> for the living and for the dying. 

And let the law be this: Whoever writes a will, disposing of his property while being the father of children, let him first write down which of his sons he deems worthy to be his heir <note>original: *kleronomon*; referring to the heir of the "lot" or ancestral farm.</note>. If he gives any of his other children to another to be adopted, let him write this down as well. If any of his sons remains without an inheritance, and is intended by law to be sent out to a colony, to this son the father may give as much of his other property as he wishes, except for the ancestral lot <note>The "lot" (kleros) was the inalienable foundation of a family's status in the city.</note> and all the equipment pertaining to that lot. If there are several such children, let the father distribute what remains beyond the lot in whatever portions he wishes. But if a son already possesses a household <margin>E</margin> of his own, let the father not distribute any property to him. Likewise, for a daughter: if she has been betrothed to a husband, he shall not give to her; if she has not been betrothed, he shall give. If a son or a daughter should later come into a lot in the territory after the will has been written, let that property be left to the heir of the one who made the will. If the testator leaves no males, but only females, let him designate a husband for whichever of his daughters he chooses, and let him leave him as a son and heir to himself. If someone's son dies—whether he was a natural son or an adopted one—before he is able to reach manhood, let the writer of the will also specify what should happen in such a misfortune, and declare what child should become his second son under better auspices. If someone who is entirely childless writes a will, let him set aside a tenth part of his acquired property <note>Property gained beyond the original ancestral allotment.</note> to give to whomever he wishes; <margin>F</margin> but let him bestow all the rest upon his adopted son, and let him make himself favorable to the law without complaint. 

If children require a guardian, and the father dies after making a will and writing how many and what sort he wishes them to be, and if the chosen guardians are willing to agree to the duty, let the selection of guardians be valid according to these writings. But if someone dies entirely without a will, or deficient in the selection of guardians, let the nearest relatives on both the father's and mother's side be the guardians: two from the father's side, two from the mother's side, and one from the friends of the deceased. These the Law-Guardians <note>original: *nomophylakes*; the high officials in Plato's city responsible for maintaining the legal code.</note> shall appoint for the orphan in need. <margin>G</margin> And for the entirety of the guardianship and the orphans, fifteen of the eldest Law-Guardians shall always have care, according to their seniority. They shall divide themselves into groups of three, with three serving each year, and another three the next, until five cycles are completed in a circle; and let this duty never fail, as far as is possible. 

If someone dies without making any will at all, leaving children who require guardianship, the same laws shall apply to his children. If someone leaves daughters, having met with an unexpected fate, let him have pardon for the legislator if, looking toward two things—the proximity of kinship and the preservation of the inheritance—he provides for the girls. <margin>H</margin> The third thing, which a father would consider by looking at all the citizens to find a suitable character to be his son and a groom for his daughter, let this be set aside by the law because it is impossible to consider. Therefore, let there be a law as far as possible of this kind: concerning such lots, if the deceased leaves daughters, let the brother of the father or the brother of the mother, if he is without a lot, take the daughter's lot and the daughter...

<column-break/>

...whatever testament is made at the end of life, it shall be entirely inviolated. For nearly everyone is oppressed by a certain foolish and abject stubbornness when they believe they are now about to die. <margin>CL.</margin> In what way do you say this, Stranger? <margin>ATH.</margin> It is a certain difficult thing, Clinias, a man now about to die; and he very frequently uses these words, which terrify and exhaust the legislators. <margin>CL.</margin> How so? <margin>ATH.</margin> Namely, when he wishes to be the master of all his things, he is accustomed to say these things, and indeed with anger. <margin>CL.</margin> What things? <margin>ATH.</margin> "It is too grave," he says, "O gods, if it will not be permitted for me to leave my own things to whomever I wish: and to give more to some, and less to others, according as they have been found clearly good or evil toward me, whether in illness, or in old age, or in my other fortunes, having been sufficiently proven." <margin>CL.</margin> Do they not seem to you to speak rightly, Stranger? <margin>ATH.</margin> <margin>B</margin> The ancient legislators, Clinias, seem to me to have been soft, and to have respected only the minimum of human affairs in bringing forth laws. <margin>CL.</margin> In what way? <margin>ATH.</margin> Moved by those words of the dying man, O best of men, they wrote that law: through which it is permitted to each person to dispose of his own things simply, in whatever way he wishes. But I and you will respond more appropriately to those about to die in your city. <margin>CL.</margin> How? <margin>ATH.</margin> "O friends," we shall say, "and you who are undoubtedly about to die soon, it is difficult for you to know your own affairs and even yourselves according to the Delphic inscription <note>The Latin "secundum Delphicam inscriptionem" refers to "Know Thyself."</note>. I, who establish laws, do not judge you to be your own, nor <margin>C</margin> this entire family estate to be yours, but to belong to your whole lineage, past and future: and much more, both the whole lineage and the wealth belong to the entire city. Since these things are so, if someone, having approached you with little flatteries in illness and old age, persuades you to make a testament contrary to what is honorable, I will never willingly allow that to happen: but considering what may benefit the whole city and the lineage, I will so write the laws that I may estimate the advantages of individuals to be of less importance than those of all, as is fitting. You, therefore, being mild and benevolent, go now where the necessity of human nature calls you. To us, however, your remaining affairs shall be a care; we who do not study some things more than others, but take care for all equally <margin>D</margin> according to our strength." Let these be the consolations in the preamble for both the living and the dying, Clinias. 

And let the law be this: He who has children and writes a testament, let him first constitute one of his sons as heir, whom he shall have judged worthy. Then, let him write down whomever of the others he has given to be adopted by others. And if any of the sons remains, fortified by no inheritance, whom he hopes will set out for a colony according to the law, let it be permitted to the father to bequeath to this one as much as he wishes from other money, the paternal lot always being excepted, and all things which pertain to it. But if there be many, let the father distribute to them whatever is beyond the lot, as he wishes. And if a house already belongs to any of them, let him not bestow money on him; <margin>E</margin> nor similarly to a daughter who is betrothed to a husband: if she has not been betrothed, let him bestow it. And if to any of the sons or daughters some lot should arrive in the region after the testament has been made, let it be left to the heir of the testator himself. 

But if he has not sons, but daughters, let the testator write down which husband of his daughters he wishes to be an heir and a son to himself. And if anyone’s son, whether natural or adopted, should die before he assumes the man's toga <note>original: *togam virilem*; the Roman garment symbolizing adulthood, used here by the translator to explain the Greek coming-of-age.</note>, let the testator also signify these fortunes of his, and declare whom he wishes to be a son to himself in place of that one, under better auspices. If anyone entirely without children makes a testament, let him bequeath a tenth part of the farm acquired beyond the lot to whichever citizen he wishes. <margin>F</margin> All other things let him bestow upon the son to be through adoption, kindly, without complaint, and according to the law. 

If children require guardians for someone, and the same person dying has appointed in his testament whatever and however many guardians he wished, who are willing to undertake the duty of guarding, let it be done just as he had described. But if indeed he should have yielded to nature intestate, or should not have written down guardians, let those who are nearest in lineage, two from the father’s side and two from the mother’s side, and one from the friends of the dead man, undertake the guardianship. These the Law-Guardians ought to appoint for the needy pupils. For we wish fifteen of the senior guardians to have care for all orphans for a five-year period <margin>G</margin> in such a way that three take care each year according to their rank: and when the five years are finished, similarly fifteen others, and let this never fail according to their strength. 

If anyone should die without a testament, and leave children needing guardianship, let them be provided for by the same laws. But he who should die by an unexpected fortune and leave daughters, let him grant pardon to the bearer of the laws if, looking toward two out of three things, he places his daughters: namely, toward proximity of lineage and the preservation of the lot. But the third, which is of the paternal duty—namely, that having diligently considered the character of the citizens, he should choose a suitable son for himself and a spouse for his daughter—since that is impossible to consider, let him pass it over. Therefore, let the law regarding this matter be of this kind according to our strength: If anyone has died intestate and left daughters, his brother from his father or from his mother, if he be without a lot, shall receive the daughter of the dead man and <margin>H</margin> the lot. And if he should not be, the son of a brother [shall receive] the same...

<summary>This page discusses Plato's legal theories on inheritance, arguing that the state and the family lineage have a higher claim to property than the individual's deathbed whims. It outlines specific procedures for appointing heirs, adopting children, and the mandatory involvement of the "Law-Guardians" in managing the estates of orphans.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous page regarding the inheritance of property and the arrangement of marriages for "heiresses" (daughters who inherit their father's estate in the absence of male heirs). The Athenian Stranger and Clinias are detailing the legal order of succession and the role of state guardians in protecting orphans.</meta>

# PLATO'S

<margin>A</margin> ...should look to a strong heir. But if no brother exists, let his son take the estate, unless his age stands in the way. Third is the sister's son, if none of those exist. Fourth is the father's brother. Fifth is his son. Sixth is the son of the paternal sister. And similarly, through the brothers and cousins of the family, the proximity of lineage should always be preserved; if he left daughters, the process follows the same order, so that in the same branch, males are preferred over females. Regarding the suitability of age for marriage and the opposite, the judge shall decide by seeing the males entirely naked, and the females also naked as far as the waist. <note>original: "nudos omnino mares, nudas quoque ad pubem vsque fœminas" / "γυμνοὺς μὲν τοὺς ἄῤῥενας, γυμνὰς δὲ ὀμφαλοῦ μέχρι δεσμώδους τὰς θηλείας." This refers to a physical examination by officials to ensure the health and reproductive fitness of the prospective couple.</note> But if there is a scarcity of relatives as far as the sons of brothers and grandfathers, whichever of the citizens the girl chooses of her own accord with the counsel of her guardians, if he is willing, let him take her as his wife and 
<margin>B</margin> furthermore receive the inheritance. But if, amidst a great scarcity of those who inhabit the city, the girl should choose someone who has been sent to a colony to be her father's heir: if he is of the same lineage, let him come to the inheritance according to the law; but if he is indeed a citizen, but not of the lineage, let him marry her if he wishes, according to the choice of the girl and her guardians, and let him return home to take the inheritance. If someone dies entirely without children, male or female, and without a will, let other matters be handled according to the former law. But let a male and a female from the same lineage, as if they were partners, enter the deserted house: those to whom the lot specifically falls.
<margin>C</margin> First the sister; then the brother’s daughter. Third, the sister’s daughter. Fourth, the paternal sister. Fifth, the daughter of the paternal brother. Sixth, the daughter of the paternal sister. These women shall live with those who are closest in lineage, as is right, just as we ordained in the previous sections. But let it not escape us how heavy the authority of these laws is, by which we command a man to marry a woman who is a close relative. Indeed, he who brings such a law seems to consider very little how many impediments may be found which make it so that no one wishes to obey these precepts. Many would rather suffer anything than marry those whose body is sick or maimed, or whose mind is insane. In these cases, then, the legislator will rightly be seen to have had no concern. And indeed, in many things it will not
<margin>D</margin> rightly seem so. Therefore, let there be a common preamble of this sort for both the founder of the laws and for those subject to them. Those for whom the laws are placed ought to grant pardon to the legislator: because, being occupied with governing public affairs, he can never simultaneously provide for private calamities. Furthermore, those subject to the laws should be forgiven if they are sometimes unable to embrace those precepts of the legislator which he wrote while being ignorant of individual calamities. <term>ATH.</term> <note>ATH. = The Athenian Stranger, the main speaker in the dialogue.</note> What then, friend, is it proper to do in this matter? <term>ATH.</term> Arbiters, O Clinias, must be chosen who may reconcile the citizens to these laws.
<margin>E</margin> <term>CLIN.</term> <note>CLIN. = Clinias of Crete, the Athenian's interlocutor.</note> How do you mean that? <term>ATH.</term> Sometimes a certain rich young man, devoted to luxuries and gasping for a more prestigious marriage, scorns the daughter of his paternal or maternal uncle. Sometimes, compelled by the greatest calamity of the girl, whether of body or of mind, he does not obey that law by which he is drawn against his will into an insane marriage, in which he would not wish to live. Therefore, let this law be ordained by us regarding these matters. If any complain about the laws for the sake of a will or marriage or other things, and assert that the legislator, if he were alive, would by no means compel them to take this wife or marry this husband, and if some relative or guardian affirms that the legislator, for the protection and counseling of orphans, left fifteen of the Law-Wardens <note>original: "nomophylakes." These were high-ranking magistrates in Plato's ideal city of Magnesia responsible for overseeing the laws.</note> as arbiters and parents, let the litigants flee to these very men; and 
<margin>F</margin> let them obey their judgments. But if the Law-Wardens seem to someone to exercise too much power, let him bring the matter to the most select court and seek a sentence; and let him who is condemned be marked with infamy: which, to one who is wise, is a far greater punishment than a fine of much money. After these things, there follows a kind of second procreation of orphans. For after the first birth comes the upbringing and discipline, about which we have spoken; but after the second <note>The "second procreation" refers to the state taking over the role of parents when a child is orphaned.</note> we must take care that those deprived of parents are oppressed as little as possible by miserable calamity. Therefore, we appoint the Law-Wardens as a second set of parents to them, no worse than the first, and we command them to provide for them every year as if they were their own. But in the 
<margin>G</margin> first place, let us begin the discourse on the education of orphans for both the Law-Wardens and the guardians. We seem to have timely narrated in the previous sections that the souls of the deceased have a certain power, by which they have a concern for human affairs. This is indeed true, but it is proven by a long discourse. Wherefore they ought to believe both other well-worn and ancient stories about this matter, and the legislators who ordain that these things are so—unless they are altogether insane. Since these things are so by nature, first let them greatly fear the gods above, who take care of the desolation of children; then also the spirits of the dead, for whom it is inherent in nature that they be held by a special care for those who were fathered by them, so much so that they are favorable to those who honor them and hostile to those who despise them. Furthermore

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...and would let him take the inheritance. If there is no brother, but a son of a brother, in the same way, if they are of a matching age for one another. If there is not even one of these, but there is a sister’s son, according to the same rules; fourth is the father’s brother; fifth is his son; sixth is the offspring of the father’s sister. And in the same way, let the lineage always move around according to the rights of kinship, if someone leaves behind female children, going back through brothers and nephews, first with the male line and later with the females in the family. The judge, looking at the symmetry and lack of symmetry of the time for marriage, shall move them, the males being naked, and the females being naked from the navel to the waist. If there is a lack of relatives among the kin, as far as the sons of a brother, or as far as the children of a grandfather in the same way, whichever of the others the girl chooses with her guardians 
<margin>B</margin> from the citizens, she being willing and he being willing, let him become the heir of the deceased and the bridegroom of the daughter. But there might be many cases and a greater lack of such people at times in the city itself. If, then, someone from the city wishes to come from a place where he was sent to a colony, and the law allows her to choose him as heir to her father, if he is of the family, let him proceed to the inheritance according to the order of the law; but if he is outside the lineage, among those in the city who are outside the kinship, let him have authority to marry her according to the choice of the guardians and the daughter of the deceased, and 
<margin>C</margin> having returned home, let him take the inheritance as one who is not a cousin. If a man dies altogether without children, male or female, and dies without a will, let other matters regarding such a man be according to the former law; but let a female and a male, as if sharing the same pasture, go into the family to the house that is made desolate in each case, to whom the inheritance should properly belong. First, a sister; second, a brother’s daughter; third, a son of a sister; fourth, a father’s sister; and fifth, a father’s brother’s child; sixth, a father’s sister’s child again. These should be settled in marriage with those according to kinship and divine right, as we legislated before. Let it not escape us the weight of such laws, how difficult it is sometimes for the relative of the deceased 
<margin>D</margin> to marry the kinswoman; it does not seem to consider the myriad obstacles that arise among men to such commands, such as no one wishing to obey; but they think they should flee wherever they want rather than suffer, whenever diseases and mutilations of bodies or of the mind occur in some of those commanded to marry or be married. The legislator would seem to all to have no concern for these things, if we think rightly, except for certain things said; and there must be for the legislator and the one for whom laws are made a kind of common preamble, that the legislator should have a sense of pardon for those commanded, because in caring for common interests, he would never be able to manage at the same time the private calamities occurring to each person; and pardon again for those for whom laws are made, since they are reasonably sometimes unable to carry out the commands of the legislator, which he orders while being ignorant. <term>CLIN.</term> What then, O stranger, by doing what would one be most moderate in such matters? <term>ATHEN.</term> Arbiters, 
<margin>E</margin> O Clinias, must be chosen for such laws and for those for whom laws are made. <term>CL.</term> How do you say? <term>ATH.</term> Sometimes the nephew of a rich father might not wish to take the uncle’s daughter, being luxurious and setting his mind on greater marriages; and sometimes when the legislator commands the greatest calamity, he might be forced to disobey the law, when it forces him to take insane marriage-alliances, or terrible calamities of bodies or 
<margin>F</margin> souls, which make life unlivable for the possessor. Let this be the law for us concerning these matters: If any people blame a lawsuit or marriages, or any of the established laws, or indeed concerning marriages, saying that the legislator, if he were present or living, would not force them to do either of these things, but some relative or guardian says that the legislator left the fifteen Law-Wardens as arbiters and fathers for the orphans, both male and female, to whom those who dispute anything of these matters should go for a trial, and let their decrees be authoritative. And if 
<margin>G</margin> a greater power seems to be placed upon the Law-Wardens, let him bring them into the court of the select judges and let the dispute be tried; and let there be blame and reproach from the legislator for the one who is defeated, which to a man of sense is a heavier penalty than many laws of money. Now indeed for orphans there would be a kind of second birth. After the first birth, festivals and educations have been spoken of; but after the second, which is being left desolate of fathers, one must devise what to say, so that the fortune of orphancy may be as little as possible a cause of pity for the orphans who are born. First then we say that we legislate that the Law-Wardens themselves are substitute fathers... and every year they should care for them as their own... for we seem to have gone through in the previous words how the souls of the deceased have a certain...

<column-break/>

<note>The following text continues from the Greek column into the bottom margin.</note>

...power after they have died, by which they care for the affairs of men. These things are true, but the stories carrying them are long. One should believe in other reports concerning such things, being so many and very ancient; and one should believe the legislators that these things are so, unless they appear altogether foolish. If these things are so in themselves, first let them fear the gods above, who have a sense of the desolation of orphans, then the souls of those who have toiled, to whom it is in their nature to care for their own descendants especially, and they are helpful to those who honor them, and they are ill-disposed to those who dishonor them.
