### ON THE LAWS, BOOK XI

<margin>A</margin> ...the souls of the living elderly, who enjoy the highest honors in a happy state. While children and grandchildren care for them, they live most pleasantly. These elders hear and see these things acutely; they are well-disposed toward those who treat orphans justly. However, they are most indignant toward those who treat children deprived of parents with contempt. Indeed, they consider orphans to be a supreme and most sacred <term>deposit</term> <note>In Roman and Greek law, a "deposit" (depositum) was something entrusted to another's care that must be returned or managed with the highest integrity.</note>. To all these, the guardian and the magistrate, being reminded of their duty, will apply their minds to this matter if they have any sense; and they shall provide for the discipline and education of orphans according to their strength, as if they were providing for themselves and their own. <margin>B</margin> Whoever is persuaded by this introduction before the law, and restrains himself from all contempt toward orphans, shall escape the wrath of the laws. But he who despises this preamble and harms someone deprived of a father or mother shall restore double the damage, just as if he had harmed someone who had both parents living. But the laws that follow we write for guardians, according to how they conduct themselves toward orphans, and for magistrates, according to how they inquire into the care provided by guardians. If, therefore, they had certain distinct and proper examples for the education of free children, and those educating them provided for their affairs differently, and they had laws moderately distinct regarding these matters, <margin>C</margin> we would issue the laws for guardians separately, since they would differ greatly from others, guarding the lives of orphans with some pursuits and non-orphans with others. But now, in all these respects, orphanhood and its care do not differ much as far as the laws are concerned from paternal governance; yet it is not at all accustomed to be equalized in honor, contempt, and care. Therefore, the law strives for the care of orphans by both consoling and threatening. And it would not be beside the point if we were to threaten in this manner: Let him who guards a female or a male orphan, and he from the <term>guardians of the laws</term> <note>The 'Nomophylakes' or Guardians of the Laws were high-ranking Athenian officials responsible for ensuring that the laws were respected and followed.</note> who is appointed to observe the guardian, love the orphans no less than if he had fathered them, and let him govern their affairs no worse than his own—indeed, even with a better affection of the soul. <margin>D</margin> Let them perform their guardianship always keeping this one law in mind. If anyone deviates from this law, the guardian shall be condemned by the magistrate. Furthermore, the magistrate, if called by the guardian before the court of chosen judges, shall be punished with double damage if found wanting. That damage shall be estimated by the judgment of the court. If a guardian appears to the relatives or any other citizen to be negligent or to act maliciously, he shall be brought to judgment and restore quadruple the damage; one half of which shall go to the child and the other half to the accuser. But after the orphan has reached <term>puberty</term> <note>The age of legal majority, usually around 18 or 20 in these contexts, when the guardianship officially ended.</note>, if he considers that the guardian has treated him badly, he may bring an action against the guardian for up to five years after the guardianship has ended. And if any guardian is condemned, the judges shall decree <margin>E</margin> what he ought to suffer or pay. If any of the magistrates appears to have harmed an orphan through negligence, the judges shall determine what must be restored. But if he did so through injustice, not only shall he restore the damage, but he shall also be deprived of the office of guardian of the laws, and another shall immediately be created by the people for the city and the region in his place. Disagreements often arise between fathers and their sons, and also between sons and their parents, greater than is proper; because of these, fathers might think the legislator should allow them, if they wish, to publicly disown a son by a herald's proclamation, so that he is no longer a son according to the law; and it should be allowed for sons to accuse parents who are shamefully affected by disease or old age of madness. <margin>F</margin> All these things tend to happen where the customs of men are altogether the worst. For if the evil were only half-measure—as if only the parents or only the sons were bad—the calamities of such grave enmities would not occur. Certainly, in any other republic, a disowned son is not necessarily deprived of citizenship. But in that which shall be governed by these laws, it is necessary for the one deprived of a father to go elsewhere. For since no one can be added to the five thousand and forty households <note>Plato’s ideal city-state, Magnesia, was strictly limited to 5,040 land-holding citizens to maintain stability.</note>, the son who is to be rightfully disowned must be expelled not by the father alone, but by the entire lineage. Therefore, in such matters, one must act according to a law such as this: Whenever <margin>G</margin> someone is moved by unfortunate indignation, whether he is angry rightly or wrongly, and desires to reject the one he fathered and raised from his kinship, let him not be allowed to do this lightly or suddenly. First, let him assemble his kin as far as first cousins, and likewise the relatives of the son on the mother's side. Before them, let him accuse his son and show that he is worthy of being expelled by all his relatives. Then, let the son also be granted the power to speak his case: namely, that he is not such a person as ought to be rejected. Finally, let all the relatives, both men and women, except for the parents and the son himself, cast their votes, provided they are of age. And if more than half of the votes support the father, let it be permitted for him to disown his son; otherwise, not at all. If any citizen <margin>H</margin> wishes to adopt the disowned son, let no law forbid him from doing so. For the character of young men often changes in many ways throughout life. And if no one wishes to adopt the rejected son within ten years, those who care for the surplus of offspring—whom we have appointed to be sent out as colonists—shall also provide for these, so that they may properly become participants in that same colony. <margin>When and in what manner a son shall accuse a father.</margin> If anyone, through disease, or old age, or bitterness of character, or all these combined more than others, falls into dementia, and this disease remains hidden from most people, and he [mismanages] the family estate...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...the souls of the living elderly, who perform the greatest honors in a happy city. While sons and grandsons honor them, they live most pleasantly. These elders hear these things keenly and see them clearly; and they are well-disposed toward those who treat orphans justly. But they are most indignant toward those who afflict orphans with insults. For they think of orphans as the greatest and most sacred deposit. To all these, the guardian and the magistrate, being advised, will apply their mind to this matter if they have any: and they shall provide for the discipline and education of orphans according to their strength, so that they seem to provide for themselves and their own. <margin>B</margin> Whoever, persuaded by this introduction before the law, restrains himself from every insult against orphans, will escape the anger of the laws. But he who, having spurned this preface, afflicts someone deprived of either a father or a mother with injuries, let him restore double the damage, as if he had harmed one who had both parents. But we write the laws that follow for guardians, according to how they conduct themselves toward orphans, and for magistrates, according to how they inquire into the care of the guardians. If, therefore, they had certain proper and distinct examples for the education of free children, and those educating them provided for their affairs differently, and they had laws moderately distinct concerning these things, it would not be without cause that <margin>C</margin> we would issue the laws for the guardian separately, since they differ much from those others, guarding the life of orphans with some pursuits and non-orphans with others. Now, truly, regarding all these things, bereavement and its care do not differ much, as far as the laws are concerned, from paternal governance: but it is by no means accustomed to be equalized in honor, contempt, and care. Wherefore, the law strives for the care of orphans by consoling and threatening. Nor would it be out of place if we were to threaten in this manner: He who guards a female or male, and he who is appointed from the guardians of the laws to observe the guardian, let him love the orphans no less than if he had fathered them, and let him govern their affairs no worse than his own—indeed, even with a better affection of the mind. <margin>D</margin> Let them perform the guardianship always having this one law in mind. If anyone derogates from this law, the guardian indeed shall be condemned by the magistrate. But the magistrate, called by the guardian to the judgment of the select, shall be afflicted with double damage. That damage shall be estimated by the sentence of the judges. But if the guardian appears to the relatives or to any of the other citizens to neglect or act maliciously, being brought into judgment against him, he shall restore quadruple the damage: of which one part shall be given to the boy, and the other to the accuser. After the orphan has come to maturity, if he considers that the guardian has dealt badly with him, he may be permitted to act against the guardian for up to five years from the ended guardianship. And if any guardian <margin>E</margin> shall be condemned, what he ought to suffer or pay shall be decreed by the judges. If any of the magistrates appears to have hindered an orphan through negligence, the judges shall determine what must be restored by him. But if also through injury, not only shall he restore the damage, but he shall also be deprived of the office of guardian of the laws: and another shall be immediately created by the people for the city and region in his place. Complaints of fathers against sons are accustomed to happen, and also of sons against parents, greater than is proper: for the cause of which fathers might think it ought to be written by the legislator that they may, if they wish, by public herald, disown a son, so that he is no longer a son according to the law: and it should be permitted for sons to accuse parents affected shamefully by diseases or old age of madness. These things all tend to happen where the customs of men are altogether the worst. For if the evil were only half, as if <margin>F</margin> only the parents or only the sons were evil, the calamities of such grave enmities would not occur. Surely in any other republic a disowned son is not necessarily deprived of the city. But in that which shall be governed by these laws, it is necessary for the one deprived of a father to depart elsewhere. Since no one can be added to the forty-five times one hundred houses <note>original: "quadraginta & quinquies mille" - The Latin text here says 45,000, which is likely a typographical error or variant in this edition, as Plato's standard number is 5,040.</note>. Wherefore it is necessary that a son to be rightfully disowned be driven away not by the father alone, but by the whole lineage. Therefore, in matters of this kind, one must act by some such law. When <margin>G</margin> anyone, moved by unhappy indignation, whether he is angry by right or by injury, desires to reject the one he fathered and raised from his kinship, let it not be permitted to do this lightly and suddenly: but first let him convoke those near to him in lineage as far as first cousins, and likewise the relatives of the son on the mother's side. Before them let him accuse the son, and show him to be worthy of being driven away by all his relatives. Then let him grant the son also the power of speaking his cause: that clearly he is not such a one as ought to be rejected. Finally, let all the relatives, both men and women, cast their votes besides the parents and the son himself, unless age be an impediment. And if more than half of the votes support the father, <margin>H</margin> let it be permitted for him to disown his son: otherwise, not at all. If any of the citizens, however, should wish to adopt the disowned one, let it be forbidden by no law. For the characters of the young often change and vary in life. And if no one within ten years should wish to join the rejected son to himself by adoption, let the curators of the excessively increased offspring—whom we have appointed to be cut off by sending out colonists—also provide for these, that they may suitably become participants in the same colony. <margin>When and how a son shall accuse a father.</margin> If anyone, through disease, or old age, or bitterness of character, or more exaggerated by all these than others, falls into dementia, and this disease remains hidden from many, and [he mismanages] the family property...

It emphasizes that family status and estates are matters of public concern, requiring the consent of the extended kin and the oversight of state guardians.</summary>

# OF PLATO

**A** ...known to all except those of the household: but if he, as the master, should waste the family estate, and the son hesitates or fears to bring a charge of dementia against his father, let the law be established as follows. First, the son shall go to the eldest <term>guardians of the laws</term> <note>original: "nomophylakes"; these were high-ranking magistrates in Plato's envisioned city responsible for overseeing the implementation of the laws.</note> and explain his father’s misfortune. After they have sufficiently examined the matter, they shall consult on whether the father ought to be accused. If they decree that he should be, they shall serve as both witnesses and assistants to the accuser. If the father is convicted, he shall henceforth have no power to manage even the smallest of his affairs; he shall no longer live as the master of the house, but as a child or a boy. If a husband and wife do not agree with one another due to bitterness of character, then—

<margin>On divorce.</margin>
**B** —ten men from among the guardians of the laws who are of middle age, and ten women from the overseers of marriage, shall provide assistance. If the couple can be reconciled by their judgment, let that agreement be held as valid and stable. But if their minds fluctuate even more violently with anger, once a divorce is made, they shall seek, as far as possible, partners who are suitable for each of them. It seems that in such people, more bitter natural dispositions are present. Therefore, more mature and gentler temperaments should be matched with them. Furthermore, those who are without children or have fathered few, and are in disagreement, should be compelled to seek marriage again for the sake of procreating children. But if they already have a sufficient number of children and yet disagree, a divorce should be made for the sake of mutually caring for one another in old age, and they may enter into another marriage. If a woman dies leaving behind male and female children, the law does not compel the husband, but rather persuades him, to raise his children without bringing in a stepmother. But if the deceased wife left no children, the man shall be compelled to take another

**C** wife, so that he may procreate enough offspring for both his family and the city. If a husband has left sufficient children, the widowed mother shall raise them. But if she appears too young to live healthily without a husband, her relatives, having held a council with the women who oversee marriages, shall carry out what seems best for her and the family. If they lack children, they shall marry or be given in marriage for the sake of children. A sufficient number of children, according to the law, is one male and one female. Whenever it is granted by both sides that the children born are the offspring of those who claim them, but the matter requires judgment as to which parent the child should follow, it shall be done thus. If a female slave has conceived by a male slave, or a free man, or a freedman, the child shall belong to the master of the female slave. If a free woman conceives by a male slave, the master of the slave shall likewise be the master of the child. But if a man has a child by his own female slave, or a woman has a child by her own male slave, and this is made clear, the women <note>The female overseers of marriage mentioned earlier.</note> shall send the child born of the slave and the free man into another region along with the father. The guardians of the laws shall expel the child born of the free woman and the slave outside the borders along with the mother. No one of sound mind, neither God nor man, will ever advise anyone to neglect their parents. But regarding the worship of the gods, which one ought not to be ignorant of, this rightly spoken preamble shall serve for the honoring of parents. Ancient laws concerning the gods are, among

**E** all people, established in a twofold way. For we clearly see some gods and worship those whom we see <note>referring to the sun, moon, and stars, which the Greeks considered visible deities.</note>. But others we do not see, though we fashion their images; and even though these statues are inanimate, while we honor them, we believe that the living gods themselves will, on that account, be most grateful and favorable toward us. Therefore, he whose father, or mother, or their parents are worn out by old age and lie in the house like a treasure: let him think that no other such image, however effective for his home, will ever be present to him, if it is rightly honored by him as is proper. <term>CL.</term> <note>original: "Cleinias"; a character from Crete who is one of the participants in the dialogue.</note> What is the right way of honoring them? <term>ATHEN.</term> <note>original: "Atheniensis Hospes"; the primary speaker, the Athenian Stranger.</note>

<margin>The prayers of parents against their children are often heard.</margin>
**F** <term>ATHEN.</term> Oedipus, when held in contempt by his sons, called down those curses upon them which, as is reported among all, were heard and fulfilled by the gods. They say also that Amyntor, angry at his son Phoenix, cursed him; and Theseus cursed Hippolytus; and many others have cursed others. By these examples, it is made most evident that the prayers of parents against their children are heard by the gods. For nothing is more destructive to a son than the curse of a parent who has been wronged. Let no one think that when a father or mother is held in contempt, it is only then that their prayers are heard by God according to nature; but also when they are honored. Therefore, when they are joyful and ask the gods for good things for their children, we must believe that they are heard in the same way,

**G** and that equal blessings are distributed to us from that source. For otherwise, the gods would not be just in distributing good things, a thought which must be far removed from the divine. <term>CL.</term> Certainly. <term>ATHEN.</term> Therefore, we must believe, as we said a little while ago, that we can possess no image more honored among the gods than our fathers and grandfathers worn out by old age, and our mothers likewise. When these are honored, God rejoices; otherwise, He would not hear their prayers. For a living image of our parents ought to seem more wonderful to us than any inanimate statues. For those that have life, when they are cared for by us, pray for us and favor us every day; when they are despised, they do the opposite. But those that lack life do neither of these. Therefore, he who behaves rightly toward parents and grandparents and others of this kind, possesses the best of all images for reconciling the gods to himself. <term>CL.</term> You have spoken excellently. <term>ATHEN.</term> Every man of sound mind, therefore, fears and honors the prayers of parents, not being ignorant that they have often benefited or harmed many. Since these things are thus established by nature—

<column-break/>

**A** ...to others besides the members of the household, but wastes his own property as if he were its master; and if the son is at a loss and hesitates to file a suit for insanity against his father; let the law be laid down: first, going to the eldest of the guardians of the laws, he shall recount the father's situation to both groups <note>the male and female overseers</note>; and they, having observed sufficiently, shall advise whether it is necessary to prosecute or not. If they advise it, let them be both witnesses and co-advocates for the prosecutor. And let the one who is convicted be hereafter disqualified from disposing of even the smallest part of his own property; but let him live the remainder of his life like a child. And if a husband and wife in no way agree, having met with misfortune—

**B** —it is always necessary for ten men from the middle-rank of the guardians of the laws to have care of such matters, and ten of the women who oversee marriages. And if they think they can reconcile them, let these terms be valid; but if their souls surge with greater waves, let them seek as far as possible who shall live with each. It is likely that such people are not tempered with gentle characters; therefore, one must try to fit these with heavier and gentler dispositions. And as many of them as are childless or have few children should make their new unions for the sake of children; but as many as have sufficient children should make their separation and new union for the sake of aging together and caring for one another. And if a woman dies and leaves children, both female and male, let there be a persuasive law, not a compulsory one, to raise the existing children without bringing in a stepmother; but if he does not have children, let him marry by necessity—

**C** —until he has fathered sufficient children for the house and the city. If the husband dies leaving offspring, let the mother of the children raise them; if she seems too young to be able to live as a widow, the relatives, in consultation with the women who oversee marriages, shall do what seems best to them and to the women. If they are in need of children, let them marry for the sake of children. The precise sufficiency of children is a male and a female, according to the law. Whenever there is a dispute regarding an offspring, a judgment will be needed—

**D** —to whom the child that is born must follow: if a female slave is joined to a male slave, or to a free man, or to a freedman, in every case let the offspring be the property of the master of the female slave. But if a free woman is joined to a male slave, let the offspring be the property of the master of the slave. But if a man has a child by his own female slave, or a woman by her own male slave, and this is manifest, the women shall send the women <note>The mothers</note> to another land with the father; and the guardians of the laws shall send the male's child with the woman who bore it. As for neglecting parents, no one who has sense, whether god or man, would ever become an advisor to anyone to do so. One must understand concerning the service of the gods that such a preamble might be made: that the honors and dishonors of those who bore us are correctly ordered by the ancient laws concerning the gods—

**E** —which are established among all in two ways. For some of the gods we see clearly and honor; of others, having set up statues as images, which we dedicate to them although they are inanimate, we think that those living gods, on account of these, have much goodwill and grace toward us. Therefore, if a father or mother, or their fathers or mothers, lie in the house as precious heirlooms, exhausted by old age, let no one ever think, while he has such an image as a protector of his hearth in his house, that any other statue would be more powerful, if indeed the owner serves it in the right way. <term>CLEIN.</term> What then do you call the right way? <term>ATHEN.</term> I will say. For indeed, friends, it is worth hearing such things. <term>CLEIN.</term> Only speak. <term>ATHEN.</term> Oedipus, we say, being dishonored, cursed—

**F** —his own children, which curses everyone says were fulfilled and heard by the gods; and Amyntor, being angered, cursed his son Phoenix, and Theseus cursed Hippolytus; and countless others cursed countless others, from which it has become clear that the gods hear parents against their children. For a parent's curse against a child is harmful as no other is, and most justly. Let no one think that while a god hears a dishonored father or mother against their children as is natural, yet if they are honored and are very vigorous in their prayers for good things for their children, that such prayers are not equally heard—

**G** —by the gods? Otherwise they would not be just dispensers of good things; and we say this is least of all fitting for gods. <term>CLEIN.</term> Very much so. <term>ATHEN.</term> Therefore, let us consider what we said a little earlier, that we could possess no statue more honorable in the eyes of the gods than a father or grandfather weakened by age, or mothers having the same power; when someone honors these, the god rejoices. For he would not be unhearing of them. For a living shrine of our progenitors is a wonderful thing to us, compared to those that are inanimate. For the living ones, when they are served by us, pray for us, and when dishonored, do the opposite; but the inanimate ones do neither. So if someone rightly treats a father and grandfather and all such, he possesses the most god-loved portion of all statues—

**H** —that he could acquire. <term>CLEIN.</term> Most beautifully said. <term>ATHEN.</term> Every man with sense, then, fears and honors the prayers of parents, knowing that many times and for many people they are fulfilled. These things being thus ordered by nature, to good men it is a godsend when their aged parents are revered, living until the end—

...for indeed to good men, elderly parents are like a great gain...

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion regarding family law in Plato’s "Laws." Having addressed the guardianship of orphans and domestic disputes, the text now transitions into the specific legal protections for elderly parents, the civic duty to honor them, and the penalties for neglect. It then moves into a new legal category: poisoning and sorcery.</meta>

# ON THE LAWS, BOOK XI

<margin>A</margin> ...they are regarded, should they reach old age; but if they die younger, they are greatly missed. To the wicked, however, they are on the contrary very terrifying. For this reason, let every person be persuaded by these arguments to honor their parents according to the law. But if anyone should be deaf to these opening words, let him hear this law as it has been rightly established. If anyone in this city should care for his parents less than is fitting, and should not love them more than his sons, grandsons, or even himself, obeying their will in all things above others, let the one who is so neglected report it, either by himself or through another, to three of the senior <term>Guardians of the Laws</term> <note>original: "nomophylakes"; high-ranking magistrates responsible for maintaining the city's legal order</note>
<margin>B</margin> and similarly to three of the women overseers of marriage. After investigating the matter, they shall punish those who have committed the injury. For men, if they have not yet passed their thirtieth year, and for women, if they have not passed their fortieth, they shall be punished with bonds and whipping. But if they are of a more advanced age than what we have stated, and do not cease to neglect their parents—or even go so far as to afflict them—they shall be compelled to go to trial. Let those citizens who are the eldest of all act as judges. If a person is condemned, the court shall decide what he must pay or suffer, ensuring that nothing is omitted that a man might be capable of enduring or paying. If a person who is being mistreated is unable to report it, let any free person who hears of it
<margin>C</margin> notify the magistrates; otherwise, he shall be considered wicked and liable to be accused of damages by anyone who wishes. If a slave reports the abuse, let him be set free. If he was the slave of the perpetrator or the victim, let him be granted freedom by the magistrates; but if he was the slave of some other citizen, let his price be paid to his master from the public treasury. Let the magistrates take care that no one harms the one who gave the report. Regarding those things that are done to others by means of poison: those that are lethal have already been distinguished. But for other harms—whether done by drink, food, or ointment, performed voluntarily and with premeditation—we have not yet made a distinction. For poisons harm the human race in two ways. First, as we just said, when bodies are harmed by other substances according to their 
<margin>D</margin> nature. The second way is through magical tricks, incantations, and so-called "binding knots" <note>original: "katadeseis"; a form of sympathetic magic involving lead tablets or figurines intended to restrain or curse a victim</note>, by which those who seek to do harm persuade themselves that they have the power to do so, and their victims are convinced that they are being harmed by these sorceries. Regarding all such matters, it is neither easy to know how they truly work by nature, nor, if one did know, would it be easy to persuade others. But when the minds of men are in such a state of suspicion and distress toward one another regarding these things, it is not worth the effort to try to persuade them—for instance, if they see wax figurines molded and placed at their doors, at crossroads, or on the tombs of their parents—to despise all such things simply because they have no certain knowledge of them. Therefore, dividing the law on poisoning into two parts, we first exhort, warn, and advise
<margin>E</margin> that people do not do such things, nor terrify the many as if they were children; nor should they compel the legislator and the judge to heal the fears of such people. Indeed, he who attempts to harm by poison—if he is to do so through the body—knows not what he does unless he is a skilled physician. Similarly, he who attempts it by magical incantations is ignorant unless he is a <term>diviner</term> <note>original: "aruspex" or "mantis"; an interpreter of omens or supernatural signs</note> or an interpreter of portents. Let this law be enacted regarding poisoning: whoever uses poison to harm a person, or their cattle or swarms of bees—even if it is not fatal—if he happens to be a physician and is found guilty of poisoning, let him be punished by death. But if he is an amateur, the court shall determine what he must suffer or pay. Furthermore, when someone is caught prepared to do harm through binding knots, charms, incantations, or any similar form of sorcery:
<margin>F</margin> if he is a diviner or an interpreter of portents, let him be put to death. But if he is found guilty of such poisoning without being a diviner, let the court similarly determine what he must pay or suffer. 

In cases where one person harms another by theft or violence, if the harm is great, let him pay a greater restitution to the victim; if smaller, let the penalty be smaller. In all cases, let the restitution be equal to the damage until the loss is healed. Furthermore, for each crime, let a fine be imposed for the sake of reform. A lighter fine shall be given if the crime was committed due to the ignorance of youth or the influence of another's malice. A heavier fine shall be given if it was due to his own folly, or from an inability to control pleasures or pains, or out of fear, or from envy, or from incurable anger. Punishments are inflicted on the wicked, not because they have <margin>Why the wicked are vexed with punishments.</margin> sinned—for what has been done cannot be undone—but
<margin>G</margin> so that in the future, both the offenders themselves and those who have seen them punished may hate injustice, or at least sin less frequently in a similar way. For the sake of all these things, it is necessary that the laws look toward this goal, and like good archers, they should aim at this mark, considering the magnitude of the punishment in each case and what is deserved. It is fitting for the judge to act as the servant of the legislator in this same task: when the law leaves it to him to determine what the condemned person should pay or suffer. He must execute the remainder of the judgment like a painter who follows a sketch, following the precedents diligently. This, Megillus and Clinias, is what I believe we must do as beautifully and excellently as possible:
<margin>H</margin> we must state what the penalties for theft and violence ought to be, as the gods and sons of gods permit us to establish these laws. No madman shall [be seen] openly...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...are held, if they reach old age; but if they die younger, they are greatly missed. To the wicked, however, they are on the contrary very terrifying. For this reason, let anyone led by these arguments honor his parents according to the law. If anyone is deaf to these introductions, let him hear this rightly established law. If anyone in this city honors his parents less than is proper, and does not love them more than his sons, grandsons, and himself, being obedient to their will in all things above others, let the one who is so neglected report it by himself or through another to three of the senior Guardians of the Laws
<margin>B</margin> and similarly to three of the overseers of marriages. Once the matter has been investigated, they shall punish those who have brought injury: for men, if they have not exceeded their thirtieth year, and for women, if they have not exceeded their fortieth, with bonds and whippings. If, however, they are more advanced in age than we have said, and do not cease to neglect their parents—indeed, if they even afflict them—let them be compelled to go to trial. Let the citizens who most exceed all others in age act as judges. Let the condemned person pay or suffer whatever the court decrees, so that nothing is omitted that a man might be capable of giving or suffering. If anyone who is being afflicted cannot report it, let any free person who hears of it 
<margin>C</margin> notify the magistrates; otherwise, let him be considered wicked and be accused of the damage caused by anyone who wishes. If a slave reports it, let him be free. If he is the slave of the one afflicting or the one afflicted, let him be claimed for liberty by the magistrates. But if he was the slave of another citizen, let the price be paid to the master by the public. Let it be the care of the magistrates that no one harms the one who gave the report. 

As for poisons used by one against another, those that are lethal have already been distinguished. The others, whether performed by drink, food, or ointment, by choice and design, we have not yet distinguished. For poisons harm the human race in a twofold way. First, as we just said, bodies are harmed by other bodies according to their 
<margin>D</margin> nature. Second, by magical favors, incantations, and certain knots, it is persuaded—both to those who strive to do harm that they can achieve it, and to the victims that they can easily be harmed by the sorcery of others. How these things and others of this kind are by nature is neither easily known, nor if someone did know, could others be persuaded. But since the minds of men are affected by suspicion and anxiety toward each other regarding these things, it is not very worthy to try to persuade them—for instance, if they see wax images at their doors, or at a crossroads, or on the monuments of their parents—to despise these things entirely when they have no certain opinion of them. Therefore, dividing the law of poisoning in two, we first exhort, warn, and advise 
<margin>E</margin> that they do not do such things, so as not to terrify many people as if they were children, and not to compel the legislator and the judge to heal the fears of such men. Indeed, he who strives to harm by poison, if he is to bring it upon bodies, does not know what he is doing unless he is skilled in medicine. Similarly, he who attempts it by magical incantations, unless he is a diviner and an interpreter of portents. But let this law now be sanctioned concerning poisons of this kind: he who uses poison not for the death of a man, but for cattle or swarms of bees, or even to harm beasts in a way other than death—if he is a physician and is judged guilty of poisoning, let him pay the penalty with death. But if he is ignorant of medicine, let the court decide what he must suffer or pay. When someone is caught prepared to do harm with knots, lures, incantations, and similar sorceries,
<margin>F</margin> if he is a diviner or interpreter of portents, let him be killed. But if he is not, let the court similarly determine what he must pay or suffer. 

He who has harmed another by stealth or by force shall pay back a great amount if he harmed in great things, and less if in smaller things; and in all cases, let him pay enough to make the damage good. Furthermore, let him be punished with a fine in each injury so that he may become more moderate in his soul: a lighter fine if he was driven by another’s malice due to the imprudence of youth, but a heavier fine if by his own madness, or by immoderate pleasures and pains, or by fear, or envy, or incurable anger. The wicked are vexed with punishments not because they have sinned—for what has been done cannot be undone—but 
<margin>G</margin> so that hereafter both the sinners themselves and those who have seen the iniquities punished may hate injustice, or at least sin less in a similar vice. For the sake of all these things, it is necessary that laws look to these goals, and like good archers, aim at this mark, considering the magnitude of the punishment in each case and what is deserved. It is fitting for the judge to act as the minister of the legislator: when it is committed to him by the law that he himself decide what the condemned should give or suffer. He indeed ought to execute what remains, following the previous things, just as a painter paints so that he follows the models diligently. This, O Clinias and Megillus, I think we must do as beautifully and excellently as possible: 
<margin>H</margin> and we must state what the punishments for those things done by theft and stealth, as well as those done by force, ought to be, just as the gods and the sons of the gods grant us to lay down laws. No madman shall [be seen] openly...

<summary>This page details the legal consequences for neglecting or mistreating elderly parents and introduces laws against "veneficium" (poisoning and sorcery), distinguishing between physical toxins and psychological harm through magic. Plato emphasizes that the purpose of punishment is not retribution for the past, but the prevention of future injustice through deterrence and moral reform.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal code of Plato’s "Laws" (Book XI). Having previously discussed poisoning and sorcery, the text moves to the regulation of public behavior, including the management of the mentally ill, the prohibition of slander, and civil liability for damages.</meta>

# PLATO

<margin>A</margin> ...seen in the city; rather, let the relatives of a mentally ill person <note>original: "furiosum"; one who has lost their reason</note> guard them at home in whatever way they can. If they fail to do so, let them be fined: those of the highest property class shall pay one hundred drachmas <note>an ancient Greek silver coin</note>, whether they fail to guard a slave or a free person. Those of the second class shall pay four-fifths of a <term>mina</term> <note>sixty drachmas</note>; those of the third class, three-fifths; and those of the fourth, two-fifths. Men are driven to madness in many ways. Some by disease, like those we just mentioned. Others by a fierce temper combined with a bad nature and poor education; such people, moved by small slights, shout loudly and shamefully revile one another. Nothing of this sort is fitting to happen in a city established with good laws. Therefore, let this one law regarding verbal abuse <note>original: "conuicio"</note> be set for everyone: <margin>B</margin> No one shall revile anyone. If anyone has a dispute with another, let him rather learn and teach both the opponent and those present, so that he completely abstains from slander. For when people curse one another with foul words, they are considered womanish; and from words, which are certainly the lightest of things, the heaviest hatreds and enmities often arise. Truly, he who gives in to anger—an utterly ungrateful thing—and feeds it with harmful nourishment, as it were, reverses the refinement he previously gained through education. By turning the spirited part of his soul into something wild and beast-like, he makes his own life difficult and receives only a bitter "favor" from his anger. <margin>C</margin> From such situations, almost everyone tends to say something ridiculous about their adversary; whoever accustoms themselves to this either loses their good character entirely or loses a great part of their magnanimity. Therefore, no one shall ever use such reproaches in a temple, nor where public sacrifices or contests are held, nor in the marketplace, nor in a court, or any other public assembly. The magistrate present at these events shall freely punish anyone who offends. If he fails to do so, as a traitor to the laws and a despiser of the legislator’s commands, he shall never compete for any public office as one who strives for virtue. <margin>D</margin> If anyone in other places uses slander, either by provoking or responding, any elder present shall strike him in defense of the laws and restrain those who are stirred to anger by another’s malice. Otherwise, he shall be punished as we said. Furthermore, we think that no one engaged in these insults and witticisms can avoid often speaking mockingly. And this is precisely what we condemn: when it is done with anger. What then? Shall we admit the jokes and ridiculous slanders of comic and satyric poets which they use against citizens, if they bite without anger? Or shall we distinguish between two types: the playful and the serious? We might allow it in jest, provided the ridicule is spoken without anger. But if the mind is stirred by anger, let it be permitted to no one, as we said. This must not be allowed in any way. <margin>E</margin> To whom it is permitted and to whom not, the law must now declare. No comic poet, nor author of iambic or musical melody, shall be permitted to disparage any citizen with words or images, whether he does so with or without anger. If anyone does otherwise, the officials in charge of prizes shall expel him from the country on that very day; otherwise, they shall be fined three minas, to be consecrated to the God in whose honor the contest was held. To the others we mentioned above, it is permitted to say something ridiculous without anger and in jest, but in no way seriously or with anger. The judgment of this matter shall be committed to the overseer of the general education of the youth. Whatever he approves may be brought into the public; but what he rejects, he shall never show to anyone, nor shall he teach it to any slave or free person. If he does otherwise, he shall be held as a wicked man and a contemner of the laws. <margin>F</margin> A person should be considered "miserable"—that is, worthy of pity—not because they are oppressed by hunger or such things, but because, while being temperate and endowed with virtue or some part of virtue, they are by chance vexed by some calamity. Therefore, it would truly be a wonder if such a person were so neglected that, whether free or a slave, they fell into extreme poverty in a moderately governed city. Thus, the legislator may safely establish this law: Let no one be a beggar in our city. If anyone attempts it and begins to collect food through insatiable begging, let him be driven away by the <term>market magistrates</term> <note>agoranomoi</note> from the outer markets and the forum, and expelled from the city by the city magistrate, and finally banished from the entire region by the country magistrate, so that the whole region may be entirely clean of such a creature. <margin>G</margin> If a male or female slave harms someone else's property, whether through lack of skill or some immoderate use, and the person who suffered the damage did not cause it himself, the owner of the slave shall either make restitution or hand over the slave to the victim. If, however, the owner contends that the claim is a deceitful plot between the slave and the victim to have the slave taken away, he may bring a charge of malice against the one complaining. If he wins, he shall receive double the price of the slave as determined by the court. But if he is convicted, he shall both restore the damage and hand over the slave. <margin>H</margin> If a beast of burden, a horse, a dog, or any other domestic animal harms a neighbor's property, the owner of the animal shall similarly restore the damage. If anyone willfully...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...throughout the city, the relatives in each household shall guard them in whatever way possible, so that they do not harm anyone they encounter. Let them pay the penalty if they fail: a member of the highest property class shall pay one hundred drachmas if they are negligent in guarding either a slave or a free person; one of the second class shall pay four parts of a mina <note>eighty drachmas</note>; one of the third class, one-fifth <note>meaning the third class pays less proportionately</note>; and one of the fourth class, two. Many are mad in many ways: those we have just mentioned are mad from disease; but there are those who become so through anger because of a bad nature combined with poor upbringing. These, when a small enmity arises, raise their voices loudly and speak evil slanders against one another; it is not fitting for any such thing to happen in a city governed by laws. Let there be this one law concerning verbal abuse <note>original: "kakēgoria"</note> for all: <margin>B</margin> Let no one slander anyone. Let the person who disputes in speech, in whatever manner, teach and learn from both the opponent and those present, abstaining entirely from slander. For from slandering one another and calling down curses in speech, and from using shameful names to bring womanish reputations upon themselves, first from words—which are a light thing—the heaviest hatreds and enmities arise. For the speaker, by indulging his anger—that ungraceful spirit—fills himself with evil feasts, and by making wild again that part of the soul which was once tamed by education, he becomes a beast and lives a difficult life, accepting a bitter "favor" for his anger. <margin>C</margin> Everyone in such situations usually turns toward saying something ridiculous; whenever anyone becomes accustomed to this, there is no one who does not fail to achieve a serious character or who does not lose many parts of magnanimity. For this reason, let no one ever utter such a thing in a temple, nor in any public sacrifices, nor in games, nor in the marketplace, nor in a court, nor in any common assembly. Let the magistrate in charge of these things punish each person... or he shall never be eligible for an award for virtue, as one who does not care for the laws nor follow the commands of the legislator. <margin>D</margin> If anyone in other places begins an insult or defends himself and does not abstain from such speech, any elder who is present shall defend the law by driving away with blows those who indulge their anger with another's evil; otherwise, he shall be subject to the appointed fine. We are saying now that the one who gets entangled in insults, unless he seeks to say something ridiculous, is no longer able to control himself. And this is slander: whenever it happens in anger. What then? Do we accept the ridicule directed at people by those engaged in comedy, if they attempt to mock the citizens without anger? Or shall we distinguish it in two ways, between play and not play, and allow someone to say something ridiculous in play, without anger, but not allow anyone to do so with intensity and anger (as we said)? This must by no means be abolished. <margin>E</margin> To whom it is permitted and to whom not, this must be legislated. To a poet of comedy or of iambics or of musical melodies, it shall not be permitted to mock any of the citizens in any way, whether by word or image, whether with or without anger. If anyone is disobedient, the judges of the games shall expel him from the country entirely on the same day, or he shall be fined three minas, sacred to the God whose contest it is. To those who were previously mentioned as having the authority to act toward one another, it shall be permitted in play and without anger; but with seriousness and anger, it shall not be permitted. Let the decision on this be entrusted to the overseer of the entire education of the youth. Whatever he approves, the author may bring before the public; but whatever he rejects, the author himself shall not show to anyone, nor shall he ever be seen teaching it to another, slave or free; or let him be thought a wicked man and disobedient to the laws. <margin>F</margin> A pitiable person is not the one who is hungry or suffering something of that sort, but the one who is temperate, or possesses some virtue or part of it, if he should possess some misfortune in addition to these. Therefore, it would be a wonder if such a person were neglected entirely so as to fall into the extreme of poverty, whether slave or free, in a city and state that is even moderately well-ordered. Therefore, it is safe for the legislator to set a law such as this: Let no one be a beggar in our city. If anyone attempts to collect a living by such unlivable means, let the <term>market magistrates</term> <note>agoranomoi</note> drive him from the market, and the <term>city magistrates</term> <note>astynomoi</note> from the town, and let the country magistrates send him across the borders, so that the land may be entirely clean of such a creature. <margin>G</margin> If a male or female slave harms anything belonging to another, without the person harmed being a contributing cause, through lack of skill or some other intemperate need, the master of the one who did the harm shall either fully heal the harm or hand over the one who did it. If the master charges that the damage occurred through a common trick of the one who did the harm and the one harmed, for the purpose of taking away the slave, let him bring a suit for malicious trickery against the one claiming to have been harmed; and if he wins, let him receive double the value of the slave as the court shall estimate it; but if he loses, let him heal the harm and hand over the slave. And if a beast of burden, or a horse, or a dog, or any of the other animals harms anything of a neighbor, let the damage be paid for in the same way. <margin>H</margin> If someone is unwilling to testify of his own accord, let the one in need summon him. Let the person summoned appear for the trial, and if...

<summary>This page outlines Plato’s legal measures for maintaining civil order, specifically mandating that families restrain the mentally ill, banning angry slander and public ridicule, and ordering the expulsion of beggars. It also establishes strict liability for damages caused by a person's slaves or livestock.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal code of Plato’s "Laws," concluding Book XI and beginning Book XII. It transitions from the regulation of legal witnesses and the prohibition of professional litigiousness to the duties and penalties for state ambassadors and heralds.</meta>

<margin>A</margin> ...at the proper time let him be present; and let him give testimony as he knows it. But if he says he does not know, let him swear an oath by the three gods—Zeus, Apollo, and Themis—affirming that he does not know, and so let him be dismissed from the case. Anyone summoned to give testimony who does not appear for the one who called him shall be liable for the damages according to the law. If a judge is summoned as a witness, after giving testimony, he shall not cast a vote in that same case. A free woman over the age of forty <note>original: "τετταράκοντα ἔτη"; forty years</note> shall be permitted to be a witness and to advocate in court; indeed, she may even bring a lawsuit if she has no husband. But if her husband is living, let her only be permitted to provide testimony. To a male or female slave and to <margin>B</margin> children, let it be permitted to testify and advocate only in cases of homicide, provided they give a sufficient guarantor that they will remain until the sentence is passed, in case they should be accused of giving false testimony. If anyone wishes to bring a charge of false testimony—which is permitted to both adversaries regarding the whole or a part of the testimony—let him object that the witnesses were false before the judges deliver their verdict. The magistrates themselves shall keep the accusations of false testimony brought by both parties, sealed by both, and shall later present them at the trial for false testimony. If anyone is found to have given false testimony twice, <margin>C</margin> no law shall compel him to testify a third time. But if he is caught three times, he shall no longer be permitted to give testimony at all. If, having been caught in falsehood three times, he dares to testify further, let anyone who wishes report him to the magistrate, and let the magistrate hand him over to the court; and if he is convicted, let him be put to death. When false testimonies have occurred in a trial and it appears that the adversary was able to prevail because of them, if more than half of the witnesses are convicted, the judgment based on them shall be void. It then becomes necessary to dispute whether the judgment was decided based on those testimonies or not, so that whichever way it is judged, the lawsuit may reach a just end. <margin>D</margin> Indeed, while there are many good things in the lives of men, most of them are beset by certain dire calamities <note>original: "κῆρες"; fates or destructive spirits</note> that stain and defile them. And how is judicial dispute and judgment not a good thing among men, which has civilized all human affairs? But if such dispute is a good thing, why should it not also be good to assist someone in a lawsuit and favor a just cause? <margin>Note: This refers to the "art" of advocacy or legal defense.</margin> Yet, while these things are as they are, a perverse slander has overtaken the good name of this "art," which claims to have discovered a certain "litigation device"—namely, a method for conducting and arguing cases so that, whether the cause is honest or foul, one can easily prevail and make the one who pays for the benefit of this art the winner. This "art," or perhaps this unskillful practice and habit, must be prevented from taking root in our city; let the lawgiver be obeyed, and let nothing be uttered against the laws; rather, let such a practice depart <margin>E</margin> to another land. If anyone does not obey, let him be deterred by this law: If anyone is seen trying to turn the power of justice in the minds of the judges toward the opposite, or moves many lawsuits beyond what is appropriate, or assists those who do, let whoever wishes bring a charge against him for "bad litigation" <note>original: "κακοδικίας"</note> or "bad advocacy"; and let the trial be held before the select judges. If he is convicted, let the court decide whether he did such a thing out of greed <note>original: "φιλοχρηματία"</note> or an ambitious love of strife. If it was out of strife, the judges shall prescribe a certain time during which he may not bring or argue any case for himself or another. <margin>F</margin> But if it was out of greed, if he is a foreigner, let him depart the region never to return, or suffer death if he returns. If he is a citizen, let him be put to death for attempting such a thing out of greed in any manner whatsoever. And if anyone is judged to have done such a thing twice out of love of strife, let him be put to death.

# PLATO'S LAWS,
# OR,
# ON LEGISLATION,
# THE TWELFTH DIALOGUE.

> *SUMMARY OF THE DIALOGUE. We noted the thesis of this discussion in the eleventh book. In the first part of this dialogue, he deals with various contracts that fall into the category of public business: namely, on embassies, on military discipline, on the scrutiny of magistrates, on oaths, on public travel, on the three levels or grades of courts, on the law of tombs and the manner of burial: and several other things as will be clear from the reading itself. But most illustrious is what he explains at length regarding a certain sacred college <note>the "Nocturnal Council"</note>, to whose faith and care he entrusts the guardianship of the laws of the entire Republic. For laws would be enacted in vain without enforcement. The remedy for this disadvantage is prudent and accurate guardianship: the care of which he entrusts to a certain assembly composed of the most proven and best men: whose form, authority, and utility he brilliantly describes: and thus he paves the way for the Epinomis, which is the most beautiful conclusion of the entire discussion.*

<margin>G</margin> <image-desc>Decorative initial E with a figure holding a staff and a landscape in the background.</image-desc> IF ANYONE, acting as an ambassador or a herald, reports falsely what has been entrusted to him by the city, or fails to speak what he was sent to say; or again, returning from enemies or friends, is found to have reported what he received from them differently than he received it, let him be brought to judgment for having shown contempt, contrary to the law, for the commands and embassies of Hermes and Zeus. And the judges shall determine, according to the greatness of the matter, what he ought to suffer or pay if he is convicted. Theft of money is surely unfree <note>servile or base</note>; but robbery is most shameful. None of the sons of Zeus ever delighted in either force or guile to practice such things.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...let him be present at the proper time; and let him bring testimony as he knows it. But if he says he does not know, let him affirm that he does not know by an oath, naming the three gods—Jupiter, Apollo, and Themis—and let him depart. He who is summoned to bring testimony and does not come shall pay the damage to the one who summoned him according to the law. If any judge is summoned for testimony, after the testimony is brought, let him bring no sentence in that same cause. Let a free woman, if she has exceeded forty years, be permitted to participate in judgment both for testifying and for speaking, and indeed even for acting, if she is not under a husband. But while her husband is living, let it be permitted only to provide testimony. To a male servant and a female servant and <margin>B</margin> to boys, let it be permitted only to speak and testify concerning homicide: if they have given a suitable guarantor that they will remain until the sentence is carried out: in case they should perhaps be accused of false testimony. If anyone wishes to act against false testimony—which is permitted both in whole and in part of the testimony and to both adversaries—before the judges bring the sentence, let him object that the witnesses were false. But let the magistrates themselves keep the accusations of false testimony brought by both parties in writing, and afterward refer them to the trial concerning false testimony. If anyone is found to have spoken false testimony twice, <margin>C</margin> let him be compelled by no law to testify a third time. But if three times, let it be permitted to him in no way afterward to speak testimony. But if, having been caught three times in falsehood, he dares to testify further, let him be reported by anyone who wishes to the magistrate, and by the magistrate let him be handed over to judgment: and if he is convicted, let him die. When false testimonies have intervened in a lawsuit, and someone appears to have been able to overcome the adversary through them, if more than half of the witnesses are condemned, let no judgment proceed according to them. But it is fitting to debate whether anything was judged according to those testimonies or not, so that however it is judged, the lawsuit may follow a just end in this manner. <margin>D</margin> But while many things are good in the life of men, certain dire calamities <note>original: "diræ calamitates"</note> as it were lie in wait for many of them, which stain and defile them. Why is judicial debate and judgment not a good thing for man, which has tamed all human things? But when such debate is a good thing, why should it not be good both to be present for someone in a lawsuit and to favor a just cause? <margin>Against fables and the corrupt, greedy pleaders of causes.</margin> Since these things are so, a perverse slander takes the good name of an art, which asserts that it has found a device in lawsuits: by which things to be done and said, whether the cause be honorable or base, one can easily overcome: and make them victors, which cause it favors by its own reasons, if money is given for the benefit of the art itself. Whether this is an art, or some practice devoid of art: effort must be given so that it has no entrance into our city: but respecting the founder of the laws, let it bring forth nothing against the laws: and having departed elsewhere, <margin>E</margin> let it show its strengths. But if anyone does not obey: let him be deterred by this law. If anyone tries to turn the strengths of justice in the souls of the judges to the contrary, and moves many litigations beyond opportunity, or is present for those moving them: let whoever wishes act against him with the crime of acting badly or finally of defending, and let a judgment of this sort be conducted among the select judges. And if he is condemned, let it be discussed whether he did it out of greed, or some ambitious contention. And if by contention, let the judges themselves prescribe a certain time: in which he shall act or speak no cause, neither for himself nor for another. <margin>F</margin> But if by greed, if he is a foreigner, let him depart from the region, never to return, and if he returns, let him die. But if a citizen is caught having done it for greed, since he was judged to have done such a thing for money, let him undergo that same punishment.

# THE TWELFTH DIALOGUE 
# OF PLATO ON THE LAWS, 
# OR, ON THE INSTITUTION 
# OF LAWS.

<margin>G</margin> <image-desc>Decorative initial S inside a square frame featuring a landscape with a bridge and buildings.</image-desc> IF AN AMBASSADOR or a herald has falsely reported the things committed to him, or has kept silent about what was to be said, or again, returning from enemies or friends, is found to have reported back the things he received from them otherwise than he received them, let him be brought into judgment as if he had despised the mandates and embassy of Mercury <note>Hermes</note> and Jupiter <note>Zeus</note> against the law. And let the judges, according to the magnitude of the matter, establish what he ought to suffer or give, if he is convicted. The theft of money is indeed unfree; but robbery is most foul. But none of the sons of Jupiter, delighted by either force or guile, ever did anything of this sort.

# PLATO'S WORKS

<margin>A</margin> Therefore, let no one be so deceived by poets or other storytellers as to believe that if they have used theft or violence, they have committed nothing shameful, but only what the gods themselves have done. For that is neither true nor even likely. Anyone who does such things in violation of the law is neither a god nor a son of the gods. These things must be understood by the lawmaker even more than by all the poets combined. Thus, whoever obeys our discourse is fortunate and always will be in the future. He who acts to the contrary shall be restrained by this law: If anyone steals anything belonging to the public, whether it be small or large, let him be punished with an equal penalty. For he who takes a small thing, even if with less force than he who seizes a great one, nonetheless steals with an equal desire. And he who removes something great from a place where he himself did not deposit it is altogether unjust. Therefore, the law does not judge that one should be punished less than the other because of the parity of the theft,
<margin>B</margin> but rather because it considers that perhaps one is "curable" <note>original: "sanabilis"</note> and the other "incurable" <note>original: "insanabilis"</note>. If a slave or a foreigner is accused and convicted of public theft, since they may seem in some way able to be cured, the judgment shall determine what they should suffer or what fine they must pay. However, if a citizen—educated as we ourselves have instituted—is convicted of stealing or violating something public, whether caught in the act of theft and crime or discovered in any other way, we condemn him to the penalty of death as one who is incurable. Regarding military service, great deliberations are rightfully held and many laws are established. But the greatest rule of all is this: no one, male or female, should ever act without a leader or commander; nor should the mind of any citizen be accustomed to doing anything alone or by his own individual judgment, whether in jest or in earnest.
<margin>C</margin> Instead, in every war and in every peace, he must always look toward the leader and magistrate and follow him wherever he goes. Thus, he should order his life according to the leader's nod, doing even the smallest things under his guidance: standing when ordered, and again setting out when commanded, training, washing, eating, rising at night, standing guard, giving signals, and receiving them in turn. In the heat of battle itself, he should never pursue nor retreat unless the leader and commander have signaled. To speak summarily, no one should ever learn what it is to act separately
<margin>D</margin> from others; rather, life should always be as collective and communal as possible for everyone. For nothing better than this, nothing more excellent, and nothing more skillful will ever be found for acquiring safety and victory in war. This very habit should be maintained in peace from early childhood: let them become accustomed to leading others and being led by others. <term>Anarchy</term> <note>Plato uses the term "anarchia" to describe a state of lawlessness or lack of leadership, which he views as a great evil.</note> should be utterly expelled from life, not only for humans but even for the beasts that are under human care. Also, all dances must be celebrated so that war may be waged well, and every dexterity, facility, and readiness must be prepared for that same cause. For the same reason, we must accustom ourselves to abstain from food and drink, to endure cold and heat and the hardness of the bed, and especially
<margin>E</margin> not to corrupt the natural strength of the head and feet with artificial coverings; one should not destroy the nature of hats and shoes given at birth. For these extremities, when they preserve their own nature, provide the greatest strength to the whole body, whereas the opposite causes the opposite effect. One of these [the feet] serves the whole body most significantly, while the other [the head] leads the whole, since nature has placed all the principal senses within it. Let the young hear these praises of the military life. Now for these laws: Let whoever is enrolled or assigned to any unit perform military service. If anyone, through cowardice and without the commanders' permission, refuses to serve, let him be accused of desertion before the military leaders when he returns. Let all who served judge the case, the infantry separately and the cavalry separately, and the others
<margin>F</margin> likewise. Indeed, the infantry must be brought before the infantry, the cavalry before the cavalry, and each individual before the leaders of their own branch. Whoever is condemned shall be prohibited from entering any future contest and from accusing another of neglected military service. Furthermore, the judges shall determine what he must pay or suffer. But after the trial for desertion is completed, the assembly of infantry, cavalry, and others shall be held by the leaders, so that military rewards may be given to those who conducted themselves strenuously. Anyone who wishes may judge the victory among the members of his own rank, provided he brings forward neither conjectures nor witnesses of past contests, but considers only that battle which was recently fought. Then, those who appear to have fought excellently shall be gifted with a crown woven from
<margin>G</margin> the leaves of an evergreen tree. Those who have obtained this shall later hang it in the temples of the war gods, wherever they please, with an inscription and title, so that it may be a lasting testimony of virtue. Those declared in second and third place shall do the same. If anyone, having gone out on campaign, leaves the army before the leaders have dismissed it, let him be accused of deserting his rank before the same judges as the one accused of neglected military service, and if condemned, let him be punished similarly. Every person who is about to judge another must take care with all his might not to falsely or undeservedly inflict punishment or a fine, whether willingly or unwillingly; for Justice is truly said to be a modest virgin. <note>original: "παρθένος... δίκη"; Plato alludes to the Greek poet Hesiod, who described Justice (Dike) as a virgin daughter of Zeus.</note> To modesty and to judgment, a lie is naturally hateful. For this reason, in all things, but especially in the casting away of military arms, we must take care not to offend the goddess who presides over judgment; lest anyone [throw away] necessary arms...

<margin>A</margin> Therefore, let no one be deceived and persuaded by poets, or by any other such storytellers, while they are constantly doing wrong in such matters. Let no one, while stealing or using violence, think that he is doing nothing shameful, but rather doing exactly what the gods themselves do. For this is neither true nor likely; whoever does such a thing unlawfully is neither a god nor even a child of the gods. It is more fitting for a lawmaker to know these things than for all the poets together. Thus, he who is persuaded by our word is fortunate, and may he be fortunate for all time. But he who is disobedient must hereafter fight against a law of this sort: If someone steals anything public, whether great or small, the same penalty is required. For he who steals a small thing does so with the same desire, though with less power; but he who moves a larger thing, not having deposited it, commits a whole
<margin>B</margin> injustice. The law does not think it right to punish one less than the other because of the size of the theft, but rather because it considers one to be perhaps still curable, and the other incurable. If someone catches a foreigner, a public slave, or a common slave stealing something in court, let the judgment be made as to what he must suffer or what penalty he must pay, since he is seen as curable in accordance with what is likely. But for the citizen who has been raised as he will be raised—if he is caught plundering or using violence after such an education, whether in the act or not—let him be punished with death, as being nearly incurable. Regarding military campaigns, much counsel is given and many laws are made. But the greatest principle is that no one should ever be without a leader:
<margin>C</margin> neither male nor female. No one’s soul should be accustomed by habit to doing anything by itself alone, whether in earnest or in play. Instead, in all war and in all peace, one must live always looking toward the leader and following him, being steered by him even in the smallest things: such as standing when ordered, and walking, and exercising, and washing, and eating, and waking up at night for guard duty and delivering messages. In the very midst of dangers, one must neither pursue anyone nor retreat for another, unless it is signaled by the leaders. In a word, one must teach the soul by habit neither to know nor to understand how to do anything apart from the others, but always to live a life that is as collective, communal, and unified as possible for all. For there is nothing better than this,
<margin>D</margin> nor will there ever be anything more excellent or more skillful for salvation in war and for victory. This must be practiced even in peace, beginning immediately from childhood: to rule others and to be ruled by others. <term>Anarchy</term> must be removed from the entire life of all humans and even the beasts that are under humans. And indeed, all dances must be danced with an eye toward military excellence, and all ease and dexterity must be practiced. For the sake of these things, "you must endure both food and drink, and winters and their opposites, and a hard bed, and, what is greatest, not to destroy the power of the head and feet by covering them with external wraps, thus losing the natural character of one’s own felt caps and shoes."
<margin>E</margin> For these, being the extremities, have the greatest power over the whole body; and the opposite produces the opposite. One [the feet] is most servant-like to the whole body, while the other [the head] is the most sovereign, possessing by nature all the governing senses within itself. This is the praise that a young man should hear of the military life. Now, the laws are these: Everyone who is enrolled or assigned to a specific part must serve. If anyone leaves through some cowardice, without the generals letting him go, let charges of non-service be brought to the military leaders when they return from the camp. Let those who served in each branch judge the cases separately, infantry and cavalry, and each of the other military units in the same way;
<margin>F</margin> and let the infantry bring the infantrymen before them, the cavalry the cavalrymen, and the others likewise to their own units. If anyone is convicted, he shall not suffer anything but shall be barred from competing for any excellence, nor shall he ever bring charges of non-service against another, nor accuse them of lying about these things. In addition to this, the court must decide what he should suffer or pay. After this, once the trials for non-service are finished, let each of the leaders again hold an assembly. Let anyone who wishes be judged for the rewards of valor within their own groups, not bringing forward any general claim of being better in war, nor evidence, nor the credible words of witnesses, but only concerning that specific campaign which just took place for them. The victory prize for each shall be a crown of foliage.
<margin>G</margin> This crown, having been inscribed with whatever one wishes, should be dedicated in the temples of the war gods as a witness for the judgment of excellence throughout one’s life, as well as for those in second and third place. If someone, having served, goes home in silence before the leaders have led them back, let charges of desertion be brought against them before the same people as the trials for military service. And let these punishments be imposed upon those convicted. Indeed, every man must fear every trial that is not properly authorized, and he must have the power not to bring a false punishment, whether willingly or unwillingly; for Justice is said to be—and truly is—a modest virgin. Falsehood is naturally resented by Modesty and Justice. Therefore, in all other things one must be cautious about failing in justice, but especially regarding the [loss] of weapons in war...
