### ON THE LAWS, BOOK XII.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...loss of weapons, lest someone, through ignorance, might judge these losses as shameful and undeserving, thereby punishing an innocent person with an unworthy penalty. It is certainly difficult to distinguish one from the other. However, the law must attempt to distinguish them part by part. Let us use a story for this: we should not say that if Patroclus had been carried to the tents from the ships half-dead, as has happened to many, while those divine weapons of the son of Peleus—which the poet says the gods gave to Thetis as a wedding gift <margin>Iliad, Book 18</margin>—had been taken by Hector, that the son of Menoetius <note>Patroclus</note> should be slandered by detractors as if he had thrown away his arms. Furthermore, if any have lost their weapons by being thrown from a height, or at sea, or in a sudden flood of water during a storm, or in many other such cases where excuses can be offered to clear the suspicion of cowardice, should they be blamed?

<margin>B</margin> Effort must be made to separate the greater and more difficult evil from its opposite by our best strength. In the act of censure itself, the very use of terms shows a difference. For a "shield-thrower" <note>original: ῥίψασπις (rhipsaspis)</note> is not a name rightly applied to everyone who loses their weapons; the one who is stripped of them by force is not to be judged the same as the one who throws them away voluntarily. They are entirely different. Thus let the law be stated: If someone, surrounded by enemies while armed, does not turn and defend himself but voluntarily drops or throws away his weapons, choosing to secure a shameful life through speed of foot rather than a noble and happy death through courage, let there be a judgment for this kind of weapon-abandonment; but for the former type, let there be none. For the wicked and cowardly must always be punished so they may become better, but the unfortunate should not be, for it achieves nothing.

<margin>C</margin> But what sort of condemnation for discarding weapons and what penalty fitting for one who degenerates from manly courage shall be applied? Especially since it is impossible for a person to be changed into their opposite, as they say the gods once changed Caeneus the Thessalian <note>A mythological figure who was born female but transformed into an invulnerable male warrior.</note> from a woman's nature into that of a man. For a "shield-thrower," the most fitting punishment would be the opposite: to be transformed from a man into a woman. But since this cannot be done, let us devise something close to it, so that since he is so fond of his life, he shall hereafter face no danger, but live out the rest of his life—and as long a life as possible—in disgrace and wickedness.

<margin>D</margin> Let this be the law: If a man is convicted of shamefully throwing away his military weapons, let no general or any other military officer ever use him as a soldier, nor receive him into the ranks. If an officer does otherwise, let the auditor <note>original: εὔθυνος (euthynos)</note> take note of it during his review. If the officer who ranked the coward is of the highest wealth class, let him be fined one thousand drachmae; if of the second class, five minae; if of the third, three minae; and if of the fourth, one mina. <note>In Plato's system, citizens are divided into four classes based on property value.</note> As for the man convicted of throwing his shield, in addition to being barred from manly dangers according to his cowardly nature, he shall pay a fine: ten minae if he is of the highest class, five if of the second, three if of the third, and one if of the fourth.

<margin>E</margin> Next, let us have a discussion regarding the auditors <margin>Public Audits</margin> of accounts. When magistrates are created, some by lot for a year and others for several years by selection from a shortlist, who is a sufficient judge of their conduct? For if a magistrate, weighed down by the burden of his office, should say or do anything unworthy of his leadership, it is difficult to find a judge. Since these selected magistrates already excel others in virtue, how shall we find someone even more excellent to judge them? Nevertheless, we must seek to find certain divine men to be the exactors and judges of these accounts. For the matter stands thus: there are many occasions for a state to be dissolved, just as with a ship or a living creature, where we give many names to the various stays, supports, and tensions of the sinews that, though scattered, form a single nature.

<margin>F</margin> But there is one occasion, and it is not the smallest, for both the salvation and the destruction of a state. If those who audit the magistrates are better than the magistrates themselves, and if this is done with blameless justice, then the whole land and city flourishes and is happy. But if the judgment of the magistrates' conduct happens otherwise, then the bond of justice that holds all civic life together is broken, and every office is torn apart from the others; they are no longer a single unit but become many, filling the city with factions and quickly destroying it. Therefore, it is necessary that the auditors possess a marvelous excellence in every kind of virtue.

<margin>G</margin> Let us devise their creation in this manner. Every year, after the summer solstice, the entire city shall gather at the sanctuary common to the Sun and Apollo to present three men to the God. Each person shall choose whomsoever he thinks is best in every way—excluding himself—who is no less than fifty years of age. From those nominated, let them select the half who received the most votes, provided they are an even number; if odd, let them remove the one with the fewest votes. Let them leave half of them, judging by the number of votes. If some have an equal number of votes and exceed the half-number, let the older be chosen and the younger set aside. Let the others be voted on again until three are left with unequal votes. But if two or all three have equal votes, let the matter be committed to good fortune and chance, and let the lot decide who is the winner, and who is second and third...

<meta>This page continues the legal framework for the hypothetical city of Magnesia in Plato’s *Laws*, Book XII. ### PLATONIC LAWS

<margin>A</margin> ...the state shall crown him with a wreath woven from the foliage of an evergreen tree. Once these rewards are given, the heralds shall proclaim that the city of Magnesia, having again found salvation through God’s guidance, consecrates its three finest citizens to the Sun and Apollo as a shared offering of "first-fruits" <note>original: *primitias*; here referring to the best of the citizens dedicated to the gods</note> according to the ancient law, for as long as they shall follow the judgment. In the first year, these men shall appoint twelve examiners of accounts. They shall continue this until each examiner has completed his seventy-fifth year; thereafter, three more shall be added every year. These officials, distributed among the twelve parts of the state, shall observe and judge all other magistrates with full and free examination. During the time when accounts are being rendered to them, they shall reside in the place where they were elected, which is dedicated to the Sun and Apollo. There, both individually and collectively, they shall diligently investigate the magistrates and publicly record what penalty or fine each official ought to suffer according to the opinion of the examiners. If any magistrate complains that he has been unjustly condemned by their judgment, he may bring the examiners before a select court of judges; if he is acquitted, he may, if he wishes, accuse the examiners themselves. But if he is condemned there as well, and had previously been sentenced to death by the examiners, he shall die as necessity demands. If he was condemned to a fine that he is able to pay twofold, let him pay that double amount. But now we must hear what the judgments of these examiners are and how they are to be carried out. To those who have been placed over all others by the consensus of the entire city, the first seats at all solemn festivals shall always be granted for as long as they live. Whenever it is necessary to send judges or presiding officers from the city to the common spectacles and sacrifices of the Greeks, they shall be sent from among these men. They alone in the city shall be crowned with a laurel wreath, and they shall be the priests of the Sun and Apollo. The High Priest for each year shall be the one from among them who was judged to have excelled the other priests in the previous year. As long as the city is inhabited, time shall be measured and distinguished by their names <note>A common Greek practice where the year was named after a leading official, known as an eponymous magistrate.</note>. When they die, their funerals and tombs shall be more excellent than those of other citizens. Their garments shall be entirely white. Mourning and wailing shall be absent. Instead, two choirs—one of fifteen girls and another of fifteen boys—standing around the bier, shall in turn praise the priest with songs and sing of his happiness throughout the day. In the morning, the younger men who labor in the gymnasia, chosen by the relatives of the deceased, shall carry the bier to the monument. First shall proceed the unmarried youths, armed as if for battle: horsemen with their horses, footmen with light arms, and others likewise. Boys shall sing the ancestral song before the bier, followed by girls, and then women who are past the age of child-bearing. Finally, the priests and priestesses of both sexes may follow to this tomb—even if they are barred from other monuments—provided the Pythian oracle confirms that it is as pure as it seems. The monument itself shall be a subterranean vault <note>original: *fornix*; a vaulted chamber or tholos tomb</note> built of the hardest and most beautiful stones, with stone beds placed side by side. Here they shall bury that blessed man and plant a grove of trees in a circle, except for one part, so that the tomb may be expanded. Every year, they shall honor these men with musical, gymnastic, and equestrian contests. These rewards shall be given to those whose audits were never condemned. However, if any of these men, trusting in the high rank he has attained, reveals the fragile condition of human nature—that is, if he falls into error after his selection—the law decrees that anyone who wishes may accuse him. The trial shall be conducted thus: first, the Guardians of the Laws shall be present, then the living colleagues of the accused, and finally the judges of the select court. The accuser shall write that the accused is unworthy of his office and its rewards. If he is condemned, he shall be deprived of his office, his special burial, and all other rewards granted to that magistracy. But if the accuser does not receive a fifth of the votes, he shall pay a fine: twelve minae if he is of the first class, eight if the second, six if the third, and two if the fourth. I see that Rhadamanthus <note>A mythical king and judge of the underworld, famed for his absolute justice.</note> was worthy of great admiration in his judging. For he perceived that in those times, all men confessed with one voice that the gods existed. This was not without reason, since in those days many were descended from the gods, among whom he himself was numbered. Therefore, he seems to have thought that judgments should be committed to gods, not to men. For this reason, he conducted trials simply and swiftly. By requiring an oath from the litigants in every case, he was able to judge both quickly and safely. But now, some deny that gods exist, others think they do not care for human affairs, and the most numerous and wicked believe that the gods can be so easily won over by cheap sacrifices and many flatteries that one may extort great sums of money with impunity. Therefore, the method of Rhadamanthus is least suited to the men of today. For when the opinions of men concerning the gods have changed, the laws also must be changed. Thus, a prudent legislator will forbid the use of oaths by litigants in the dispute of a trial...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...and to this man, they shall give a crown of olive-shoot and the prizes of excellence, and all shall pray that the city of Magnesia, having again attained safety by the grace of God, should present to the Sun its three best men as a "first-fruit" offering <note>original: *akrothinion*; the top of a heap of spoils, dedicated to a deity</note> to Apollo and the Sun together, according to the ancient law, for as long as they follow the judgment. In the first year, twelve auditors <note>original: *euthunous*</note> shall be appointed until each reaches seventy-five years of age; thereafter, three shall be added annually. These men, dividing all offices into twelve parts, shall examine them using all free tests. They shall live, for as long as they are auditing, in the precinct of <margin>B</margin> Apollo and the Sun where they were chosen. Judging some matters individually and others together, they shall declare those who have held office in the city, placing records in the marketplace for each office, stating what must be suffered or paid according to the opinion of the auditors. If any official does not agree that he was judged justly, he shall bring the auditors before the select judges; if he is cleared of the audit, he may accuse the auditors themselves if he wishes. If he is convicted, and if he was sentenced to death by the auditors, he must simply die; for other fines where it is possible to pay double, let him pay double. <margin>C</margin> We must hear who will listen to the audits of those who are not these men, and in what manner. While they live, these men who have been deemed worthy of the highest honors of the whole city shall have the front seats at all public festivals. Furthermore, from among them shall be sent the leaders of the sacred missions for sacrifices and festivals shared with the Greeks. They alone in the city shall always be adorned with a crown of laurel. They shall be priests of all, both of Apollo and the Sun; and one shall be the High Priest each year—the one who was first judged among the auditors that year. <margin>D</margin> His name shall be recorded annually so that it may serve as a measure of the number of time as long as the city is inhabited. For those who have died, the laying out, the funeral procession, and the tombs shall be different from other citizens. They shall have a completely white robe, and the funeral shall be without dirges or lamentations. There must be a choir of fifteen males and another of fifteen females; they shall sing a hymn of praise for the priests, each group in turn, blessing them with song throughout the days. In the morning, a hundred of the young men from the gymnasia, whom the relatives of the deceased select, shall carry the bier itself to the tomb. <margin>E</margin> The unmarried youths shall lead the way first, each wearing their full military dress—the cavalry with cavalry, the heavy infantry with heavy infantry, and the others likewise. Boys shall go before the bier singing the ancestral melody, and girls shall follow behind, along with women who are past child-bearing age. After these, priests and priestesses shall follow as if to a pure grave, if the Pythian oracle permits. A tomb shall be built for them under the ground, a vaulted chamber <note>original: *apsida*</note> made of stones that are as beautiful and ageless as possible, containing stone beds lying side by side. Having placed the blessed man there and mounded it over in a circle, they shall plant a grove of trees around it, except for one side, so that the tomb may grow and have a space for mounding over for those placed there in all future time. Each year they shall hold a contest of music, <margin>F</margin> gymnastics, and horse-racing for them. Such are the honors for those who have passed the audit. But if any of these men, trusting in having been judged, should display human nature by becoming wicked after the judgment, the law commands that anyone who wishes may indict him. The trial shall take place in a court of this kind: first, the Guardians of the Laws shall be of this court, then the living members of the honored group, and the court of select judges. The indictment shall be written, saying <margin>G</margin> he is unworthy of his honors and his office. If the defendant is convicted, he shall be deprived of his office, his tomb, and the other gifts given to him. But if the prosecutor does not obtain a fifth part of the votes, he shall pay a fine: twelve minae if he is of the highest property class, eight if of the second, six if of the third, and two if the fourth. As for the judgment of Rhadamanthus, it is worthy of admiration because he saw that the men of that time clearly believed in the gods—which was reasonable, since in that time many were born of the gods, he being one of them according to legend. It seems he thought that he should not entrust judgment to any man, but to the gods. Thus, trials were simple and swift for him. For by giving an <margin>H</margin> oath to the litigants on each of the disputed points, he settled matters quickly and safely. But now, when a certain wicked part of men do not believe in gods at all, and others think they do not care for us, and the opinion of the most and worst is that by receiving small sacrifices and many flatteries, the gods help them steal much money and release them from many great penalties—that art of Rhadamanthus in trials would not be fitting for the men of today. Therefore, since the opinions concerning the gods have changed among men, the laws also must change. For in...

# ON THE LAWS, BOOK XII.

Mmm iij

...to write the accusation, but not to add an oath; and the defendant, in the same way, having written his denial, shall hand it over to the magistrates without being sworn. For it is surely a terrible thing when, in a city where many lawsuits occur, we know well that nearly half of the participants have committed perjury, yet they continue to associate with one another in social gatherings and other public and private meetings. Let a law be established: the judge about to give a verdict must swear an oath, and he who appoints officials for the common good must do so through oaths, or by bringing his vote from a sacred place. This should always be the case. Furthermore, let it be established for the judging of choral competitions, and all musical or gymnastic contests, and horse races—wherever the presiding officials and judges award prizes—and for all matters where, according to human opinion, perjury brings no personal profit. 
<margin>A</margin>
But in cases where a great profit might seem to appear to one who denies a claim and swears a false oath, 
<margin>B</margin>
these matters must be judged without the use of oaths. All who bring charges against one another, and those who defend themselves in a trial, must not be permitted to swear oaths for the sake of persuasion, nor to call down curses upon themselves and their families, nor to use unseemly supplications or womanly laments. Instead, they must always persist in teaching and learning what is just with proper and reverent speech. Otherwise, the magistrates should lead the speaker back to the matter at hand, as if they were speaking outside the point. As for foreigners among themselves, just as is done now, they may receive oaths from one another if they wish, and these shall be legally binding. For they will not grow old in the city, nor will they typically build nests there 
<margin>C</margin>
so as to produce a brood of similar people as companions in the land. Regarding the filing of lawsuits between citizens, let there first be a judgment for all as they desire; but for the city, no penalty of beating, nor of bonds, nor of death shall follow <note>This refers to civil disputes where the state does not intervene with physical punishments unless the public order is at stake</note>. Regarding public duties, or processions, or other such common decorations, or liturgies—whether for peaceful sacrifices or wartime contributions—everyone must either fulfill the obligation or face a penalty. For those who do not obey, let there be a seizure of goods <term>distraint: the legal seizure of someone's property in order to obtain payment of rent or other money owed</term> by those whom the city and the law command to collect. If they still refuse to comply, the seized items shall be sold, and the money shall go to the city. If a greater penalty is needed, 
<margin>D</margin>
the respective magistrates shall impose fitting fines on the disobedient and bring them before the court until they agree to perform the assigned duty. As for a city that does not engage in trade, except for what comes from the land, nor exports beyond its borders, and receives visitors from elsewhere, it is necessary to deliberate on what must be done. The legislator must advise on these matters, first by using persuasion to the best of his ability. For the intermingling of cities tends to mix all sorts of characters together, as foreigners introduce innovations to one another. This would bring the greatest harm to those living under good and correct laws. To most cities, however, which are in no way well-ordered, it makes no difference if they receive 
<margin>E</margin>
foreigners into their midst or if they themselves leap away into other cities whenever anyone, young or old, desires to travel. But on the other hand, to never receive others and never to travel abroad is entirely impossible; moreover, it would appear savage and harsh to the rest of the world, who would apply the shameful term "expulsion of foreigners" <note>original: *xenelasia*; a term famously associated with the isolationist policies of Sparta</note> and call their customs stubborn and harsh. One should never think little of whether one appears good or bad to others. For the majority of people are not as far removed from virtue themselves as they are from the ability to judge others; even the wicked possess a certain divine intuition. Thus, many who are 
<margin>F</margin>
exceedingly wicked can distinguish the better men from the worse in their speech and opinions. Therefore, it is a fine thing for most cities to proclaim the value of a good reputation among the many. The most correct and greatest way is to be truly good and then hunt for a life of good reputation; without being truly good, one cannot be a perfect man. And so, it is fitting for this city being established in Crete to present itself to the gods and the rest of humanity as having the finest and best reputation for virtue. There is every hope that, if things proceed according to reason, it will soon look upon the Sun and the other gods in the company of other well-governed cities and lands. Thus, this is how one must act regarding travel to other lands and places, 
<margin>G</margin>
and regarding the reception of foreigners. First, no one under the age of forty shall be permitted to travel abroad under any circumstances. Furthermore, no private individual shall be allowed to travel, but it shall be permitted for public heralds, embassies, or sacred observers <term>theoroi: official delegates sent by a city to consult an oracle or represent the state at religious festivals</term>. Travels for war and military campaigns should not be counted among these civic travels abroad. For these purposes, delegates should be sent to Pythian Apollo <note>at Delphi</note>, to Olympian Zeus, and to Nemea and the Isthmus, to share in the sacrifices and the games of these gods. They should send as many as possible, and the finest and best men, who will justly bring fame to the city in these sacred and peaceful gatherings, offering a reputation that matches their glory in war. Upon returning home, they shall teach the youth that the institutions of other nations are secondary to their own. Other "observers" who wish to consider the affairs of other men at their leisure may be sent out by the choice of the Guardians of the Laws; no law should forbid them. For a city ignorant of both bad and good men, being isolated from the world, could never be civilized and perfect; nor could it preserve its laws by habit alone without also gaining an intellectual understanding of them.

<column-break/>

OR let the accusation of the prosecutor as well as the plea of the defendant be recorded in the courts without an oath. For if the freedom to swear is granted to everyone in the city, where many cases are brought before judges daily, almost everyone will be perjurers, especially those who are joined together by common banquets and other social habits or private necessity. Therefore, let it be established by law that the judge who is about to judge must swear, as well as those who appoint the magistrates of the state by their votes. Also, the judge of the chorus, and the presiding officers and givers of prizes in every musical, gymnastic, and equestrian contest—in short, in all those things where, according to human opinion, no profit is gained from perjury. But in those matters where 
<margin>A</margin>
someone obtains a benefit from perjury, 
<margin>B</margin>
<margin>When an oath is to be spoken.</margin>
let them be judged without an oath. And those who are to judge should in no way permit the litigants to swear for the sake of persuasion, or to call down curses upon themselves and their kin, or to use shameful supplications or womanly displays of pity. Instead, let them gently teach what they consider just, and listen to the one who is teaching. If anyone wanders from these rules, let him be brought back to the matter by the magistrate. For foreigners 
<margin>Causa quomodo dicenda.</margin> <margin>How a case is to be pleaded.</margin>
litigating among themselves, just as is done now, let it be permitted for them to swear if they wish. For since they should not grow old in the city, there is no fear that they will corrupt others. In the same way, let the execution of a judgment be carried out among free men: if a free man does not obey the city in those matters which are not punished by beatings, bonds, or death. And if anyone does not come to celebrate a dance or a procession, or some other such common matter, 
<margin>C</margin>
such as the service of a sacrifice and sacred rites of peace, or has not contributed a tax for war: in all these things, let the loss be restored as soon as possible, or let a pledge <note>original: *pignus*; property held as security</note> be brought to those whom the city and law have entrusted with the task. When the time has expired, the pledge shall be sold and the money placed in the treasury. But if a greater fine is needed, the individual magistrates shall summon the stubborn men to court, and by imposing the debt fine, compel them to obey the laws. But for a city that does not concern itself with gathering money, and has wealth only from agriculture, since it 
<margin>D</margin>
has no time for trade or traveling abroad, nor receives foreigners from elsewhere, it is necessary to deliberate on what should be done. Therefore, the legislator should first advise according to his ability. The mixture of different nations usually confuses various customs, and the association of foreigners with foreigners introduces many innovations. This, most of all, harms a city that is well and rightly established by laws. In cities that are poorly established, however, it does not matter if both the old and the young travel abroad at will, or receive foreigners from elsewhere. On the contrary, to never receive any newcomers, nor to go elsewhere oneself, is both impossible and would seem cruel and harsh to other men, who would mark the city with a foul name, calling them "enemies of foreigners" and describing them as difficult and inhuman. It is never right to think little of whether you appear honest or dishonest to others. For many, although 
<margin>E</margin>
they are devoid of virtue themselves, can still judge who is honest and who is dishonest. For even in wicked men there is a certain divine conscience, through which many of even the worst kind correctly distinguish the better from the worse, both in opinion and in words. Therefore, it is usefully commanded to cities that they should not weigh a good reputation among the many as a small thing. It is surely the greatest and most correct path that, while being honest, you seek glory; otherwise, you will by no means be a perfect man. Therefore, this Cretan city should also strive to 
<margin>F</margin>
achieve the highest reputation for virtue among other men. There is the greatest hope that, by a living reason, it will deservedly see the Sun and the other gods, along with other well-governed cities and regions. Thus, the following must be decreed regarding travel to other places and regions, and regarding the reception of foreigners: First, to him who is less than forty years old, let it not be permitted to travel abroad in any way. Nor shall it be permitted to any private person. Let it be permitted publicly to heralds, ambassadors, and observers. Indeed, travel outside the region for the purpose of waging war is not to be considered "civic travel." To Pythian Apollo, to Olympic Jupiter, 
<margin>G</margin>
and also to Nemea and the Isthmus, some must be sent through whom our city may collectively contribute to the sacrifices and games of these gods. Let there be sent, according to our ability, the most numerous, the most beautiful, and the best men, who in the sacred gatherings and those pertaining to peace may win for their city an honor and glory that matches its military glory. And when they have returned, let them teach the younger men that the civic institutions of others are far inferior to their own. Regarding other observers who, having abundant leisure, desire to consider the affairs of other men, let no law forbid them, according to the institution of the Guardians of the Laws. For a city ignorant of good or bad men, and lacking experience of foreign customs, can never be sufficiently humane or perfect; nor can it preserve its laws by character and habit alone, unless it also becomes wiser through the knowledge of laws.

<summary>This page outlines the legal protocols for court oaths and foreign relations in Plato's ideal city. It argues against oaths in cases of potential profit to prevent perjury and sets strict age and purpose requirements for travel to maintain the city's moral integrity while allowing for cultural exchange through sacred delegations.</summary>

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion on the integrity of the judicial system. It shifts focus to the preservation of the state's character through the regulation of foreign travel (peregrinatio) and the reception of guests. Plato outlines a system where select citizens travel abroad to learn from other nations, while ensuring that the "Nocturnal Council"—the city’s highest intellectual authority—evaluates these findings to improve the local laws of Magnesia.</meta>

# PLATO'S <note>original: "PLATONIS"</note>

<margin>foreign travel.</margin>
->A<- Even among the common crowd and the multitude, there always exist certain divine men, though they are few; nevertheless, they are worthy of being associated with. These men arise no more in well-governed cities than in others. Therefore, whoever in a rightly governed city remains uncorrupted should follow in the footsteps of these men, departing from his homeland and traveling by land and sea to seek them out. Thus, upon returning, he may approve those laws of his country that are good, and correct any that are found wanting. Indeed, without this <term>inspection and investigation</term> <note>Plato uses the term 'theoria' for this investigative travel, implying a sacred or official observation.</note> a city will never remain in an optimal state, nor will it if the investigation is conducted poorly. CLINIAS: How shall both of these things be achieved? ATHENIAN: Certainly in this way. First, such a spectator 
->B<- must be more than fifty years old. Furthermore, he must be well-reputed in other matters and especially in war, if he is to leave behind an example for the <term>Law-wardens</term> <note>original: "nomophylakes," the chief magistrates in Plato's ideal city.</note> in other cities. He should no longer wander beyond his sixtieth year. But within ten years of his return, whenever he wishes, let him enter that assembly which examines the laws. This assembly shall consist of both younger and older men, and it shall meet daily in the morning until the sun rises. First among them shall be the priests who have been awarded the prize of excellence; next, the ten most senior Law-wardens; and finally, the director of universal education, both he who currently 
->C<- holds the office and those who have already completed their term. None of these shall attend alone, but each with a younger man whom he has selected, aged between thirty and forty years. These men shall always discourse upon the laws and the Republic, and they shall share with one another any excellent thing they have heard regarding these matters. They shall also discuss those disciplines conducive to this end; for those who know them will more easily understand the intention of the laws, while those who are ignorant will find it more difficult. The younger men must learn with great zeal whatever the elders approve. But if any younger man who is brought along is deemed unworthy, the entire assembly shall blame the one who introduced him. As for the young men who conduct themselves rightly in these matters, the whole city shall honor and preserve them. But if they prove worse than others, let them 
->D<- be treated with greater disgrace than the rest. To this assembly, he who has inspected the laws and customs of others shall go immediately upon his return. If he has found anything among others regarding the passing of laws, discipline, or education, let him explain it. If he himself has discovered anything, let him declare it to the entire assembly. If he appears to have returned no worse than when he left, let him be praised, because he willingly performed what he could. If he returns much improved, let him be granted great honors while alive, and let the whole assembly decorate him when he is deceased. But if he appears to have returned corrupted, though he pretends to be wise, let him not dare to mingle with any younger or older man. If he obeys the magistrates, let him live as a private citizen. But if, against the will of the magistrates, he is convicted in court of disputing about 
->E<- discipline and civil laws, let him die. And if, when he ought to have been brought to judgment, none of the magistrates brought him, let this matter be a disgrace to the magistrates when honors are later decided. Such a traveler, then, is of this kind, and in this way he ought to travel abroad. But also, 
<margin>Types of travelers.</margin>
visitors must be kindly received. There are four types of foreigners about whom mention must be made. The first are those who are always "summer visitors," arriving like birds across the sea, mostly for the sake of acquiring money; they fly to other cities during the summer season. These, the magistrates appointed to those places shall receive in the markets, harbors, and public buildings outside the city in the suburbs, 
->F<- taking care that none of them causes any innovation. Justice shall be rendered to them fairly, yet social familiarity with them should be held no more than necessity compels. The second type consists of those who come as spectators to hear the music of the city. All of these shall have lodgings near the temples, which are most suitable for receiving guests. The priests and temple-wardens shall take care of them, so that they may stay pleasantly for a sufficient time, and see and hear those things for which they came, and finally depart without harm to themselves or others. If any of them commits an injury against anyone, or is himself injured, the priests shall take 
->G<- cognizance of it up to fifty drachmas. Greater crimes, however, shall be referred to the overseers of the market. The third type of foreigner to be received publicly is when someone arrives from elsewhere sent on public business. These, the generals, masters of the horse, and military tribunes alone shall receive. And he with whom the guest stays, along with the leaders of the council, shall take care of him. The fourth type is very rare. However, someone may arrive from elsewhere, responding as a counterpart to our own spectators. This person shall be received thus: first, if he has completed fifty years; second, if he has come with the intention of either observing what is held to be excellent among others or teaching his own knowledge. Let such a man go unbidden to the doors of the rich and the wise, being of such a kind himself; and as a guest, let him rightly seek the house of the director of education, not doubting that it will be 
->H<- hospitable to him because of their shared virtue. And when he has learned from others and taught what he thought should be learned and taught, let him depart as a friend from friends, endowed with fitting honors and gifts. By these laws let us receive foreign men and women, and let us send out our own in like manner, honoring <note>original: "Iouem" (Zeus)</note> <term>Hospitable Jove</term> <note>original: "Xenios," the aspect of Zeus that protects guests and promotes hospitality.</note>.

<column-break/>

->A<- For among the many, there are always some divine men, not many, but worthy of all association, who are born no more in well-governed cities than in those that are not. The man who dwells in a well-governed city ought always to follow in their footsteps, going out by sea and land to seek one who is uncorrupted and most steadfast, so that he may confirm those laws which are well-established and correct any that are lacking. For without this observation and seeking, a city never remains perfectly stable, nor if it observes poorly. CLINIAS: How then might both occur? ATHENIAN: In this way: first, let such a spectator for us be more than fifty years old; then let him be well-esteemed in other things and practiced in war, if he is 
->B<- to share a sample of the Law-wardens with other cities. When he has become more than sixty years old, let him no longer act as a spectator. Having observed for as many years as he wished, and having arrived home, let him go to the assembly of those who care for the laws. This assembly should be a mixture of young and old; meeting necessarily every day from dawn until the sun rises. First, the priests who have taken the prize of excellence; then the ten Law-wardens who are always the seniors; and further, the one who is always the director of all education, both the current one and those who have been released from this office. 
->C<- Each of these shall go not alone, but with one young man, between thirty and forty years old, taking along whomever he pleases. Their meeting and their discourses shall be about the laws and the affairs of the city, and if they hear of anything similar elsewhere concerning such things. And indeed concerning disciplines, as many as seem to be of use in this inquiry, which for those who learn them, matters concerning the laws become clearer, but for those who do not learn, they appear darker and obscure. Whatever the elders approve of these, the younger ones must learn with all zeal. If any of those called seems unworthy, the whole assembly shall blame the one who brought him; but those who are well-esteemed among them, the city shall guard above others, looking out for them; but they shall be disgraced more than the rest if 
->D<- they turn out worse than the majority. Into this assembly, he who has observed the laws among other men shall come, immediately comparing if he has heard any report of such divine laws, or education, or upbringing, and found those who possess them; let him declare it to the whole assembly. And if he seems to have come back neither better nor worse, let him be praised for his great zeal; but if much better, let him be much more praised while alive, and when he has died, let the power of those assembled honor him with fitting honors. But if he seems to have arrived corrupted, let him associate with no one, neither young nor old, though he believes himself to be 
->E<- wise. If he obeys the rulers, let him live as a private citizen; but if not, let him die—if he is convicted in court of being a meddler concerning education and the laws. If any of the rulers does not bring him to court when he is worthy of being brought, let that shame be laid upon the rulers in the trial for the prize of excellence. Thus let the one who travels abroad, being such a man, go abroad. And as for him who will visit from elsewhere, one must be friendly toward him. There are four types of guests of whom one must take some account. The first is he who visits always and through the end of summer, usually conducting his visits like those of birds, and of these, most travel across the sea simply like flying things, for the sake of trade, during the season of the year, to 
->F<- other cities. These, the rulers appointed over them must receive in the markets and harbors and public buildings outside the city, near the city; guarding lest any such guest make any innovation; and distributing correct justice to them, and associating with them in necessary things, but as little as possible. The second is truly a spectator with his eyes, who receives the sights of the Muses; for such a man, let there be prepared lodgings near the temples, offering hospitality. It is necessary for the priests and temple-attendants to care for them and show honor, so that having stayed a moderate time, and having seen and heard those things for the sake of which they came, they may depart unharmed in what they did or suffered. Let the priests be judges 
->G<- for them, if any of them wrongs another or if someone wrongs them, in matters up to fifty drachmas. If any greater accusation arises against them, it is necessary to bring the case before the market-stewards. The third guest to be received is he who has arrived publicly on some public matter from another land; he must be received by the generals, cavalry commanders, and colonels only; and the care of such a man must be undertaken by the one with whom he makes his lodging. Fourth, if ever someone arrives—rarely—as a counterpart to our own spectators from another land, first let him be not less than fifty years old; in addition to this, claiming to see something beautiful or distinctive in beauty in other cities, or to show such things to another city, let every such man now go unbidden 
->H<- to the doors of the rich and the wise, being such a one himself. For let him go to the house of the one caring for all education, trusting that he will be well received as a guest by such a host, or to those who have won prizes for virtue. Having taught some things and learned others, let him depart, a friend from friends, honored with fitting gifts and honors. By these laws, it is necessary to receive all guests, both men and women from another land, and to send out our own, honoring the god of hospitality <note>original: "Xenion" (Zeus)</note>.

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous section regarding the regulation of a city's interactions with the outside world and the maintenance of internal order. Having previously discussed the 'theoros' or official observer of foreign laws, Plato now moves to the specific legal codes governing foreigners, property disputes, and the ethical conduct of citizens in public office.</meta>

# ON THE LAWS, BOOK XII.

<margin>A</margin> Foreigners are not to be driven away by restrictions on food and sacrifices, as is the practice now with the "creatures of the Nile" <note>original: "θρέμματα τοῦ Νείλου" (thremmata tou Neilou). A derogatory reference to Egyptians, who were known for strict isolationism and peculiar dietary laws.</note>, nor by harsh proclamations. Regarding a <term>surety</term> <note>original: "ἐγγυάδα" (enguada). Someone who legally guarantees another's debt or appearance.</note>, if a person has stood as one for a year and the transactions are recorded in writing, it shall expire if the claim is undisputed. If there are fewer than three witnesses for sums under a thousand drachmas, or fewer than five for sums over a thousand, the claim is invalid. No one may act as a surety for a seller whose title to the property is in doubt or who is not creditworthy. Both the secondary seller and the one who received the property shall be liable to prosecution. If someone wishes to search for stolen property in another's house, he must do so <term>naked</term> <note>original: "γυμνὸς" (gymnos). In this context, it often meant wearing only an undergarment to ensure the searcher could not plant evidence.</note> or wearing only a light tunic, unbelted, having first sworn by the customary gods that he truly expects to find it there. 
<margin>B</margin> The occupant must then open his house, including both sealed and unsealed containers, for the search. If someone refuses to allow a search, the one who was blocked may sue for the value of the missing item; if the refuser is convicted, he must pay double the estimated damage. If the master of the house is away, the residents shall allow the search of unsealed items, but may prevent the search of sealed ones; in that case, the searcher may station a guard for five days. If the owner is away longer, the searcher shall bring the <term>city wardens</term> <note>original: "ἀστυνόμους" (astynomous). Magistrates responsible for the order of the city.</note> to break the seals and conduct the search, after which they must be resealed in the presence of the household and the wardens. 
<margin>C</margin> Regarding disputes over ownership, there is a time limit or <term>prescription</term> <note>original: "ὅρος" (horos). A boundary or limit beyond which a claim can no longer be made.</note>. For lands and houses, there can be no dispute under this rule. For other possessions, if a person uses them openly in the city, the market, or the temples <gloss>and</gloss> it is clear they are using them, and no one disputes it—even if the claimant says they were searching for it—if the possessor has held it openly for one year, the claimant is barred from taking it back after that year has passed. If it is used openly in the countryside rather than the city or market, and no one comes forward for five years, then after the five years are up, it may no longer be reclaimed. If used in a house in the city, the limit is three years; if used secretly in the countryside, ten years. But if the property is in a foreign land, it may be reclaimed at any time whenever it is found, with no time limit.
<margin>D</margin> If anyone uses force to lead away a litigant or witnesses, or prevents them from coming, whether they are a slave (one's own or another's), the action shall be void and without effect. But if it is a free person, besides the action being void, the offender shall be imprisoned for a year and may be prosecuted for kidnapping by anyone who wishes. If someone uses force to prevent a competitor from entering a musical or athletic contest, anyone who wishes may report this to the directors of the games. They shall ensure the free man can compete. If they are unable, and the one who blocked the other wins, the victory prizes shall be given to the one who was blocked, and his name shall be inscribed as the winner in whatever temples he chooses. The one who used force shall be barred from dedicating any monument for that contest. He shall also be liable for damages, whether he wins or loses the contest.
<margin>E</margin> If anyone knowingly receives stolen goods, they shall face the same penalty as the thief. The penalty for harboring an exile shall be death. Every citizen should consider the city’s friends and enemies as their own. If anyone privately makes peace or war with any party without the common authority, the penalty for this also shall be death. If any part of the city makes peace or war on its own, the generals shall bring the authors of this action to court, and if convicted, the penalty shall be death.
<margin>F</margin> Those who serve their country in any capacity must do so without receiving gifts. Let there be no excuse <gloss>or</gloss> argument that one should accept gifts for good deeds but not for bad. For it is not easy to judge such things, and even if one knows, it is hard to remain firm. It is safest to obey the law, which says no gifts are to be accepted for public service. He who disobeys and is convicted in court shall be put to death. Regarding taxes: for many reasons, every man's property must be valued. Annual produce should also be reported in writing to the tribesmen. Thus, the state may choose each year which of the two <term>contributions</term> <note>original: "εἰσφοραῖν" (eisphorain). Direct taxes usually levied on property or income during times of need.</note> it wishes to use: a portion of the total valuation or a portion of the annual income, excluding what is paid for the common meals.
<margin>G</margin> Offerings to the gods should be moderate, given by a moderate man. The earth, like the hearth of the home, is sacred to all gods; therefore, let no one consecrate the same thing a second time. Gold and silver in other cities, both in private and in temples, are possessions that invite envy. Ivory, having left behind the life of a body, is not a suitable offering. Iron and bronze are instruments of war. For common temples, let a person offer whatever wood he wishes, or stone likewise. Woven offerings should not be more than one woman's work for one month. White colors are most fitting for the gods, both in general and in weaving. Dyes should not be used, except for military decorations. The most divine gifts are birds and statues, as many as a single painter can finish in a single day. And let other things follow the same rule...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> For it is not by avoiding eating together or by banning sacrifices, as is done in the land of the Nile, that foreigners should be driven away; nor should they be kept from our borders by cruel edicts. <margin>Surety.</margin> Let any <term>surety</term> <note>Latin: "fideiussor."</note> stand as such openly and clearly, and let the whole business be put in writing before at least three witnesses if the surety is for less than a thousand drachmas. If it is over a thousand, at least five witnesses must be present. He who previously sold the item should act as the surety if there is doubt whether he had the right to sell it, or if he seems unable to fulfill his promises. Likewise, both the one who previously sold it and the current seller shall be subject to the judgment of the court.
<margin>B</margin> If someone wishes to search for something as his own in another's house, he must first swear an oath that he hopes to find what he seeks there. Then, let him enter naked or dressed in a light tunic and unbelted. The house must be opened to him, including both sealed and unsealed furniture. If anyone does not allow a person who wishes to search, the one who was blocked shall charge the one who drove him away for the value of the lost item; if that person is convicted, he must restore double the amount. If the master of the house is absent, the those present shall provide only the unsealed items for search. The searcher may seal the sealed items himself and leave a guard for five days. If the owner has not returned in that time, let the searcher take the <term>aediles</term> <note>Latin: "ædilibus." Roman term used here by the translator to represent the Greek 'astynomoi' (city wardens).</note> with him to unseal the items, and after searching in the presence of the household and the aediles, let him seal them again.
<margin>C</margin> In disputed matters, a span of time must be determined for <term>prescription</term> <note>Latin: "præscriptio."</note>. <margin>Prescription.</margin> Regarding houses and lands, there shall be no dispute by this rule. But for other things, if someone possesses them in the city, the forum, or the temples, and has used that thing openly for a full year, and it is established that he did not hide it—and if no one in the meantime has sought or demanded it—no one shall then be allowed to reclaim that thing as his own. However, if he uses it openly not in the city but in the fields, and the owner of the thing is not found within five years, it cannot be reclaimed once the five-year period has passed. If he uses it at home in the city, the owner has up to three years to seize it. In the fields, if he holds it secretly, up to ten years. But if he is outside the region, he may seize it whenever he finds it, at any time.
<margin>D</margin> When someone uses force to prevent a litigant or witnesses from coming to court, whether the person is his own slave or another's, let the action taken be of no importance. But if it is a free person, the sentence shall be void, and the one who used force shall be bound for a year; if anyone wishes to accuse him of kidnapping, let it be lawful. If anyone uses force to prevent someone from entering a contest in music, gymnastics, or any other skill, anyone who wishes may signify this to the announcers, who shall ensure that any free person can compete. If they cannot do this, the prizes of victory shall be given to the one who was blocked, even if the one who blocked him wins. The winner's name shall be inscribed in whatever temples he wishes. But for the one who used force, it shall not be lawful to inscribe his name or to offer a victory. Whether he wins or loses the contest, he shall be guilty of the crime of damages caused.
<margin>E</margin> If anyone knowingly receives a thing taken by theft, he shall be in the same fault as the one who stole it. Whoever receives an exile or anyone fleeing in this manner shall die. For every man ought to consider the one whom the state has decreed its friend or enemy to be his own. If anyone by his own counsel and without common authority enters into peace or stirs up war, let him be condemned to the final punishment. If some part of the city attempts this, the authors of the matter shall be brought to trial by the military commanders, and if convicted, they shall be punished with death.
<margin>F</margin> Those who serve their country in any matter shall by no means receive gifts. Let us not persuade ourselves by any occasion or reason that gifts should be accepted for good things and not for others. For it is not easy to know, nor to restrain oneself when one does know. Therefore, it is safer to obey the laws, which say that no gifts are to be accepted for the service of the country. If anyone is convicted of not obeying, let him die. Let public taxes be arranged thus: First, for the sake of many things, there should be a census of the property of every citizen. Then, they shall bring the annual fruits to the city magistrates, recorded by tribes, so that since there are two taxes, the Republic can use either one as it sees fit each year: namely, either a part of the total census or a part of the annual fruit. From this, what is given for <term>sustenance</term> <note>Latin: "alimēτα." Likely referring to the syssitia or common mess halls.</note> shall always be excepted.
<margin>G</margin> Moderate offerings should be offered to the gods by moderate men. <margin>What things are to be offered to the gods. From Cicero, Book II of the Laws.</margin> The earth, therefore, as the hearth of dwellings, is sacred to all the gods; wherefore let no one consecrate the same thing again. Gold and silver in cities and in private possession are not a sufficiently pure gift for God. Now bronze and iron are instruments of war, not for temples; but let any wooden thing he wishes, made of a single piece of wood, be dedicated; likewise stone, in common shrines. Let woven work be no more laborious than a woman's monthly work. The color white is especially becoming to God, both in other things and most of all in weaving. Let dyed things be absent, except for military insignia. The most divine gifts are birds and figures finished by one painter in a single day. White colors, in other things as well as in woven art, are suitable for the gods. But things dyed with other colors should be displayed only for military insignia. The most divine offerings are birds and paintings, which a single painter has depicted in a single day, and the rest...

<summary>This page details Plato's legal code for the ideal city, focusing on the protection of property rights through statutes of limitations, the strict prohibition of bribery in public office, and the regulation of religious offerings to ensure they are modest and appropriate for a virtuous society.</summary>

Having just finished the requirements for votive offerings to the gods, Plato now shifts focus to the structure of the court system and the finality of human life: burial rites.</meta>

->### OF PLATO<-

...votive offerings also should all be similar to these.

<margin>A</margin> Now that the parts of the city have been divided as they ought to be, and the laws concerning the most important contracts and trade have been established as far as possible, it remains for us to discuss legal judgments.

<margin>Private judgments.</margin>
First, then, let there be arbitrators chosen as judges by the litigants themselves; these might more suitably be called "conciliators" than "judges." Second, let there be neighbors and tribesmen distributed according to the twelfth parts of the city. Before these, if the parties were not reconciled by the first group, let them litigate, though with a greater penalty. In this case, if the debtor is condemned again, he shall pay an additional fifth part of the debt. Whoever appeals even from this judgment and wishes to contest it a third time, let him seek out the <term>Select Judges</term> <note>original: "δικαστὰς τοὺς ἐκλεκτοὺς" (dikastas tous eklektous). A high court of specially chosen officials.</note>.

<margin>B</margin> If he is condemned by them once again, he must pay the debt itself plus an additional half of the debt’s value. If the accuser, having been rejected in the first judgment, is not satisfied but wishes to contest it again in the second, he shall receive a fifth part if he wins, but if he loses, he must lose the same amount. When the parties are not yet reconciled by the first and second judges and seek a third, the defeated debtor, as we said, shall deposit for the winner the debt plus half as much again; the accuser, if defeated, shall pay half the value.

<margin>C</margin> Regarding the creation and declaration of judges, the administration of all these matters, the timing of proceedings, the casting of votes, delays, adjournments, the setting of deadlines, summonses, rejections, and all other things necessary for judgments—even though we touched upon these earlier—nevertheless, as the proverb goes, "beautiful things can be rightly said twice and even three times." If an older legislator has omitted any small or easily discovered detail, a younger one should fill the gap.

<margin>Public judgments.</margin>
Enough has been said regarding private judgments. Public and common judgments, which magistrates use to perform their duties, are found to be correctly established by prudent men in many cities.

<margin>D</margin> From these sources, the <term>Guardians of the Laws</term> <note>original: "νομοφύλακας" (nomophylakas). High-ranking officials in Plato's ideal state responsible for maintaining the integrity of the constitution.</note> ought to adopt what is suitable for this new republic, so that each point is diligently examined through trial and error, corrected, and approved until they are considered sufficient. Finally, once the discussion is finished, they should use these laws as "immovable" for the rest of their lives. Regarding silence, praise, and blame, and what is just, good, and honorable—matters that differ in other cities—some has been said, and more will be said at the end. An impartial judge must look toward all these things and strive to learn these constitutional laws above all else, keeping them firmly in mind.

<margin>E</margin> For the writings of the laws, if they are well-made, contribute more than any other teachings to making the man who learns them good. Nor is it by chance that the divine and wonderful <term>law</term> possesses a name very close to that of the <term>mind</term> <note>original: Latin "lex" and "mens"; Greek "νόμος" (nomos) and "νόος" (noos). Plato suggests that law is the outward expression of reason or intellect.</note>. While many speeches involving praise or blame are circulated—some in verse, some in prose, some written, others delivered daily in public gatherings or through false flattery—the writings of the legislator are for us the clear test of all of them. The good judge will always keep these with him like a remedy or medicine against the poison of other speeches. By these, he will improve himself and the city, confirming and exalting the good; while the wicked—who act out of ignorance, lack of self-control, or cowardice—he will, in short,

<margin>F</margin> recall from their universal injustice to the best of his ability, if they are curable. For if they cannot be cured, those judges and presiding magistrates who put them to death may rightly be praised by all. Once the annual judgments are completed, let these laws be followed. First, the magistrate presiding over the judgment shall deliver all the condemned debtor’s money to the petitioner, leaving only what is strictly necessary for use. This should happen immediately after the votes are cast, announced by a herald in the hearing of the judges. Then, if the second month after the sentence arrives and the defeated party has not voluntarily and justly paid the winner, the judges who delivered the sentence shall transfer all the debtor’s property to the winner.

<margin>G</margin> If this is still not enough, and even a single <term>drachma</term> <note>A standard silver coin of ancient Greece.</note> is lacking, the debtor shall not be permitted to bring anyone else to court until he restores the entire debt to his creditor. However, he may still be sued by others. If someone condemned in judgment harms the judges themselves or unjustly takes anything from them, those same judges shall report him to the Guardians of the Laws. If he is convicted of this crime, let him be put to death, as if he had overturned the whole city and its laws. Those born and educated under these laws, who have likewise fathered and educated children, and whose social interactions have been moderate—paying penalties for wrongs done and exacting them for wrongs received—live justly according to these laws

<margin>H</margin> until old age, and so depart from life according to nature. For the deceased, whether men or women, the funeral rites and everything pertaining to the gods of the underworld or the heavens shall be performed according to the responses of the <term>interpreters</term> <note>original: "ἐξηγητῶν" (exegeton). Religious officials who interpreted sacred law and omens.</note>.

<margin>Place of tombs.</margin>
No tomb shall be made in a fertile place or a field suitable for cultivation. Instead, let that place receive the bodies of the dead which is useless for everything else and suited only for that purpose...

<column-break/>

<note>This column contains the original Greek text corresponding to the Latin translation provided on the left. The content covers the same legal procedures for arbitration, the hierarchy of courts, the penalties for non-payment of debts, the etymological link between "mind" (noos) and "law" (nomos), and the regulations for the location of graves in non-arable land.</note>

Α ...imitated offerings. When the parts of the whole city have been divided... there would then be a need for judgments to occur. Of the courts, the first should be elected judges... whom the defendant and the prosecutor choose together... calling them "arbitrators" rather than "judges." Second, the villagers and tribesmen... B ...if the prosecutor is defeated in the first and does not rest... C ...of court drawings, and fillings... we have said before; and a good thing, and a right thing, can be said twice or three times... D ...wherefore the Guardians of the Laws must learn what is fitting for this present state... and use them for all of life. E ...of all studies, the most authoritative for making the learner better are those concerning the established laws... F ...those whose souls are thus disposed, the judges assign death as a cure... G ...if they have nothing from which to pay, and lack not less than a drachma... H ...for those who have died, whether male or female... graves shall be in no place that is workable, neither large nor small...
