<meta>This page continues the transition from judicial regulations to the final aspects of the legal code: the regulation of funerals, the nature of the soul, and the ultimate preservation of the laws through the "Nocturnal Council." Although the header lists this as Book 11, the content corresponds to the conclusion of Book 12 in modern editions of Plato’s Laws.</meta>

->### ON THE LAWS, BOOK 11<-

<margin>A</margin> Regarding the bodies of the deceased, one should bury them in such a way that they are separated from the living with the least amount of trouble. No one, whether living or dead, should deprive the living of that which Mother Earth by her nature produces as food for us. A burial mound should be piled no higher than what five men can complete in five days. Stone markers should be made no larger than is necessary to contain the praises of the deceased person’s life, consisting of no more than four heroic verses <note>original: "ἡρωϊκῶν στίχων" (hērōïkōn stichōn). These are dactylic hexameters, the meter used by Homer.</note>. The lying-in-state within the house should last no longer than is necessary to distinguish between someone who is merely unconscious and someone who is truly dead. Following human standards, a three-day period before the funeral procession to the tomb is appropriate. One must trust the lawgiver
<margin>B</margin> in this and other matters, especially when he says that the soul is entirely different from the body. In this life, that which constitutes each of us is nothing other than the soul, while the body follows us as a mere image. It is rightly said that the bodies of the dead are only "shadows" <note>original: "εἴδωλα" (eidōla).</note>. The real being of each of us is truly immortal—it is called the soul—and it departs to other gods to give an account of its actions, just as our ancestral law says. This thought brings courage to the good but great fear to the wicked; for once dead, no great help can be brought to a person. Rather, it was while they were living that all their relatives should have helped them, so that they might live as justly and holily as possible, and so that after death they might remain unpunished for their sins in the life 
<margin>C</margin> hereafter. This being the case, one should never waste the family wealth by thinking that this heap of flesh being buried is the actual person. Instead, one should realize that the son, brother, or whoever it is one most longs for and thinks they are burying, has departed, having fulfilled and completed his destiny. One should treat the remains well, but spend only a moderate amount, as if on an inanimate altar of the earth. What constitutes "moderate" is best determined by the lawgiver. Let this be the public standard: for the wealthiest class, the total expenditure for the entire burial shall be no more than five minae <note>An ancient unit of currency; five minae would be a significant but not extravagant sum for a wealthy citizen.</note>; for the second class, three minae; for the third, two; and for the fourth, one mina. These are the limits for expenditures. The Guardians of the Laws must attend to 
<margin>D</margin> many things, and they must specifically ensure that people of every age, from children to men, live under their care. At the end of every life, one of the Guardians of the Laws shall preside, chosen by the relatives of the deceased. If they act rightly, it is a credit to them; if not, it is a disgrace. The lying-in-state and other rites shall proceed according to the standing law. The civil legislator should decree the following: he may command that people do not weep for the dead, but rather let the tears flow naturally. He shall forbid wailing and the shouting of laments outside the house. He shall prohibit the body from being carried openly through the main streets, and people must not cry out while walking in the streets; rather, the procession must be outside the city before daybreak. Let these be the established customs. He who obeys shall be free from penalty; 
<margin>E</margin> but he who disobeys even one of the Guardians of the Laws shall be punished by all of them with a penalty agreed upon by all. As for other matters concerning burials, or cases where burial is denied—such as for parricides, temple-robbers, and the like—these laws have already been laid down previously. Thus, our law-giving has nearly reached its end. But in all works, the end is not simply doing a thing or acquiring a possession; rather, it is only when we have found a way to preserve what has been created perfectly and forever that we can consider our task complete. Until then, the whole work remains unfinished.
<margin>F</margin> **Kleinias:** You speak well, Stranger. But please explain more clearly what you mean by this. **Athenian:** O Kleinias, many things have been well said in the past, including the names of the Fates <note>The Moirai, or Fates, who spun the thread of human life.</note> regarding preservation. **Kleinias:** How so? **Athenian:** Lachesis is the first, Clotho is the second, and Atropos <note>original: "Ἄτροπος" (Atropos). Her name means "The Inflexible" or "The Unalterable."</note> is the third—she who is called the "Saviour," compared to the power of the threads spun by fire, making them all irreversible. These are qualities that a city and a constitution must possess: not only to provide health and safety for bodies, but also to ensure the preservation of the laws in the souls of the citizens. It seems to me that our laws still lack this: a way to instill in them a naturally irreversible power. **Kleinias:** This is no 
<margin>G</margin> small matter you speak of, if it is indeed possible to find how such a quality can be given to any possession. **Athenian:** It is indeed possible, as it now appears clearly to me. **Kleinias:** Then let us not depart until we have secured this for the laws we have discussed. It would be ridiculous to have labored in vain only to leave the work on an unstable foundation. **Megillus:** You are right to encourage us; I am of the same mind. **Kleinias:** You speak well. In what way, then, do you say "salvation" can be granted to our state and its laws? **Athenian:** Did we not say that a council of this sort must be established in our city: ten of the Guardians of the Laws who are always the eldest, and all those who have received awards for excellence 
<margin>H</margin> must be gathered together? Furthermore, those who have traveled abroad to search for any insight regarding the preservation of laws, and who have returned home safely and been judged worthy by the council, should join them. In addition to these, each senior member must bring one young man...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...the deceased person least harms the living. For the fertility of Mother Earth must not be hindered by either the living or the dead. No one, whether living or dead, should deprive any living person of nourishment. A burial mound shall not be higher than a heap that five men can construct in five days. Nor shall stones be built upon it larger than those which can contain the praises of the deceased published in only four heroic verses. Funeral processions shall take place within a time that is neither shorter nor longer than what is required for the death to be truly recognized and known. And as human affairs go, a three-day interval for the procession to the grave seems moderate. One must believe the lawgiver in other matters and also concerning the soul, when he says that it 
<margin>B</margin> differs entirely from the body, and that there is nothing else besides the soul itself which makes each of us, in this life, be what we are. The body, however, follows the man as a sort of imaginary thing. It is also fitting that the bodies of the dead be called "likenesses." And in truth, each of us is the immortal soul itself, and it departs to other gods to give an account of its deeds, as the ancestral law maintains. In this, certainly, good men should have confidence, but the wicked should feel dread, seeing as after death they lack all help. While they were living, all their kinsmen ought to have brought them aid, so that they might live as justly and holily as possible, lest the greatest 
<margin>C</margin> punishments for crimes await them after death. Since these things are so, we must not waste the family estate, as if we believe this mass of flesh which is buried is our loved one; for that son or brother or anyone else we miss, whom we think is being buried, has departed from here to another place, his destiny having been fulfilled. It will therefore be well done if we use moderate expense, as if for the spirit of one who lacks a soul. The lawgiver will rightly determine how much is moderate. Let this be the law: he who is of the highest wealth class shall spend no more than five minae for the funeral and burial; he of the second class, three; the third, two; the fourth, one. Thus the expense of each will be moderate. Furthermore, the Guardians of the Laws, among many other duties, 
<margin>D</margin> must take the greatest care that boys and men—and in short, people of whatever sex or age—live under their constant observation. And at the death of any citizen, one of the Guardians themselves, whom the relatives of the deceased have chosen, shall oversee the entire funeral, providing that all things are done well and moderately, and not otherwise, so that the proper performance is an honor to him and the improper a disgrace. Let the lying-in-state, the processions, and all other things be done according to the laws written about them. However, let these things be granted to the civil legislator: it is disgraceful for a lawgiver to compel people to honor the dead with tears, or not; but wailing and crying out outside the house must be prohibited. It shall not be permitted to carry the corpse openly through the more crowded streets 
<margin>E</margin> of the city, nor to wail in public, nor to afflict oneself outside the city before daybreak. Let these statutes concerning these matters remain fixed. He who obeys them shall be free from penalty. But he who does not obey even one Guardian of the Law shall be punished by all of them, as shall be collectively decided. Other matters pertaining to the monuments of the dead, or to those who are unworthy of burial because of parricide or sacrilege, we have included in the previous laws. Therefore, the establishing of laws is nearly at an end. But the end of all things is not in the fact that they have been made, possessed, or inhabited, but rather that, just as they have been rightly made, so they are firmly established. For in this kind of preservation, one must believe that as much as was necessary 
<margin>F</margin> has been done; otherwise, not at all. **Kleinias:** You speak rightly, guest. But tell us the purpose of these things in your explanation. **Athenian:** Because the excellent sayings of the ancients are praised, and no less the names of the Fates. **Kleinias:** Which ones? **Athenian:** That Lachesis is the first, Clotho the second, and Atropos the third, who brings "salvation" to what has been said. These are compared to things twisted by fire, because they contain an irreversible power. These things ought to bring to the city and the Republic not only stable health for bodies, but also for souls the cultivation of laws—or rather, the salvation of the laws. But it seems to me that the work of the laws still lacks a discussion of how an irreversible power can be inherent in them according to nature. **Kleinias:** What you say is no small thing, if it is possible to find 
<margin>G</margin> how that may rightly be done in every instance. **Athenian:** It is indeed possible, as it seems to me at present. **Kleinias:** Therefore, let us not depart from here, I beseech you, before we grant this to our laws. For it is ridiculous to have taken up labor in any matter in vain, without having founded something stable. **Megillus:** You advise rightly; you will find me to be of the same mind. **Kleinias:** You speak well. What then is this "salvation," and by what means will it be present in the laws of our Republic? **Athenian:** Did we not say that a council of this kind should be established in the city, in which ten of the Guardians of the Laws, always the elders, should meet? To these should be added all who have been honored with offices and prizes. Furthermore, 
<margin>H</margin> those who have traveled through many cities to find something contributing to the preservation of the fatherland’s laws should also attend. But these shall not be received into such a council unless they are proved to have returned from that travel uncorrupted and upright, and to be worthy of the assembly. And each of these shall take for himself one younger man...

<summary>This page concludes the legislative program of Plato's Laws by establishing regulations for funerals and mourning, grounded in the philosophical belief that the soul is the true, immortal self. It then introduces the "Nocturnal Council," a body of elders and experienced travelers tasked with ensuring the "irreversible" stability and preservation of the city's laws.</summary>
<keywords>burial rites, immortality of the soul, funeral costs, Moirai (Fates), Atropos, Guardians of the Laws, Nocturnal Council, Lachesis, Clotho, social classes, legislative stability</keywords>

--- Page 726 ---
<meta>This page transitions from the specific regulations of funerals at the end of Book 12 to the concluding philosophical argument of the entire work. Having established the laws, Plato now introduces the "Nocturnal Council," a body of elders and selected young men who serve as the "intellectual anchor" to ensure the laws remain effective and directed toward a single goal: virtue.</meta>

-># PLATO'S<-

<margin>A</margin> ...no fewer than thirty years of age, who appear worthy by nature and education—first to the one who selects them, and then to the entire assembly. If anyone unworthy is admitted, their opinion shall carry no weight. We said this assembly must meet before daybreak, a time when everyone is free from other private and public business. Did we not say something of this sort in the earlier parts of our discussion?
**CLINIAS.** Certainly. **ATHENIAN.** Regarding this assembly, I will say this again: I claim that if one casts this body like an anchor for the whole city—containing within itself everything required for this purpose—it will preserve everything we desire. **CLINIAS.** In what way? **ATHENIAN.** We shall explain this at the opportune moment, and we will apply ourselves with all our strength. **CLINIAS.** You have spoken well; 
<margin>B</margin> do as you intend. **ATHENIAN.** It is necessary indeed, O Clinias, to devise for every single thing a fitting "saviour" for its works; just as in living animals, the soul and the head appear to hold the highest place. **CLINIAS.** For what reason do you say that again? **ATHENIAN.** Because the excellence of these two provides safety to every animal. **CLINIAS.** In what way, I ask? **ATHENIAN.** For into the soul, among other things, Mind <note>original: "mens" (Latin) / "νοῦς" (nous - Greek). In Plato, this refers to the highest intuitive and rational faculty.</note> has been infused; and into the head, among other things, sight and hearing have been implanted. And so, in short, when Mind is joined with the most beautiful senses and reduced into a unity, it becomes the "safety" of each individual. **CLINIAS.** So it seems. **ATHENIAN.** Certainly. For Mind joined with the senses is also accustomed to bring safety to ships in both storm and calm. Do you not see how the pilot and the sailors, by joining themselves and the ship with a "guiding mind" <note>original: "mente gubernatrice" / "κυβερνητικῷ νῷ". This is the famous 'Ship of State' metaphor.</note> and their senses, keep themselves safe? **CLINIAS.** Why not? **ATHENIAN.** We do not need many examples. Let us consider the army and medicine: toward what target and outcome do generals and doctors look, so that they might most rightly achieve safety? **CLINIAS.** Rightly so. **ATHENIAN.** Does not the one look toward the flight of enemies and their own victory? And the others toward the health of the body? **CLINIAS.** Without a doubt. **ATHENIAN.** If a doctor were ignorant of the body’s health, or a general of victory, and the other things we were mentioning, would they appear to 
<margin>C</margin> possess Mind or know anything about these matters? **CLINIAS.** Not at all. **ATHENIAN.** What then of the city? If someone appears to be ignorant of the "target" <note>original: "finem" / "σκοπὸν" (skopos). Literally the mark an archer aims at.</note> toward which a statesman <term>ciuilis / πολιτικὸς</term> <note>Meaning a person skilled in the art of governing a city.</note> ought to look, can he first be rightly called a ruler? Secondly, will he be able to preserve that whose purpose he entirely ignores? **CLINIAS.** Least of all. **ATHENIAN.** It is necessary now, as it seems, if the construction of this new city is to have a good outcome, that there be something in it which knows, first, what the "political target" actually is; next, how we may attain it; and finally, which law first, and then which men, have consulted rightly toward it or not. For whichever city lacks these things, it will not be surprising if, being captured without mind or sense, it acts on each matter by chance and luck. **CLINIAS.** You speak the truth. **ATHENIAN.** 
<margin>D</margin> Can we say in which part of our city, or in what pursuit, such a safeguard for safety has been sufficiently established? **CLINIAS.** Although I do not dare to assert it clearly, Stranger, I suspect that this discourse of yours is tending toward that nocturnal assembly which you mentioned just now. **ATHENIAN.** You have guessed rightly, O Clinias. And it is necessary, as the present reasoning indicates, that it be endowed with every virtue. Its first and foremost task is not to wander through many and various things, but to look always toward one point, where all things, like arrows, must always be 
<margin>E</margin> directed. **CLINIAS.** Exactly so. **ATHENIAN.** Now, therefore, we understand that it is not surprising if the laws of cities wander far. For 
<margin>F</margin> <margin>Why the laws of cities wander far.</margin> in any given city, one arrangement of laws looks toward one thing, and another toward another. For some, the goal of justice is that certain people—whether they be better or worse—should dominate the Republic. For others, it is that they may be enriched, whether they serve or not. For others, their zeal is carried toward liberty. Others establish laws for two goals: that they themselves may be free and that they may subdue other cities. But those who think themselves the wisest aim for all such things at once. They do not have one principal thing toward which they might direct the rest. **CLINIAS.** We, therefore, Stranger, have for a long time rightly thought that our laws should look toward one thing, and we agreed that this is called virtue. **ATHENIAN.** It is so. **CLINIAS.** And we established that there are four kinds of virtue. **ATHENIAN.** Certainly. **CLINIAS.** And that Mind is the leader of all these, toward which all the other things, and those three virtues, 
<margin>G</margin> ought to look. **ATHENIAN.** You follow most beautifully, O Clinias. And follow similarly in the rest. We said that the Mind of the pilot, the doctor, and the general looks toward a certain single thing. But rebuking the statesman, we have proceeded to this point: let us now question this "political mind" as if it were a man. "O wonderful man, where are you heading? What is that one thing which the doctor in his art can clearly point out, but you, who say you excel other prudent men, cannot point out in your own faculty?" Can you, O Clinias and Megillus, answer for him what this thing 
<margin>H</margin> is, just as I have often done for you regarding others? **CLINIAS.** Not at all, Stranger. **ATHENIAN.** Do you not think it must be asked, what it is, and in what things it resides? **CLINIAS.** Speak clearly. **ATHENIAN.** Since we have established four species of virtue...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...of the young men, having become no less than thirty years old. How then, having judged him to be well-suited by nature and wise, shall he introduce the young man to the others? And if he seems worthy to the others, they shall take him in; but if not, the judgment of those who rejected him must remain unspoken, especially by the one who proposed him. The assembly must meet at dawn, when there is the greatest leisure from other business, both private and public. Was not something like this 
said by us in the previous discussions? **CLINIAS.** Yes, indeed. **ATHENIAN.** 
Concerning this assembly, taking it up again, I would say the following: 
I claim that if someone were to cast this as an anchor for the whole city, possessing everything that is fitting for it, it would save all that we desire. **CLINIAS.** 
How so? **ATHENIAN.** After this, it would be our opportunity to explain it correctly, leaving out no bit of zeal. **CLINIAS.** 
You have spoken very well; act just as you intend. **ATHENIAN.** It is necessary then, O Clinias, to consider a "saviour" for every work as is fitting; just as in an animal, the soul and the head are naturally the greatest parts. **CLINIAS.** How do you say that again? **ATHENIAN.** 
<margin>B</margin> Surely the excellence of these two provides safety to every animal. **CLINIAS.** How? 
**ATHENIAN.** The soul, in addition to other things, has Mind <note>original: "νοῦς" (nous)</note> within it; and the head, in addition to other things, has sight and hearing. When these are joined in two—the most beautiful of the senses being controlled by the mind—being one in spirit, they would most justly be called the "safety" of each thing. **CLINIAS.** So it seems. **ATHENIAN.** It seems so. But does not the mind, when joined with the senses, become the safety of ships in storms and in fair weather? Is it not the pilot and the sailors together in a ship, mixing their senses with the "pilot-mind," who save themselves and everything concerning the ship? **CLINIAS.** Of course. **ATHENIAN.** There is no need for many such examples; but let us consider in the case of army camps and medicine, what "target" <note>original: "σκοπὸν" (skopos)</note> the generals and the medical service look toward, which brings about safety for all. **CLINIAS.** Correct. **ATHENIAN.** Does not the one aim for victory and power over enemies, and the other—the doctors and their assistants— 
<margin>C</margin> provide health to bodies? **CLINIAS.** How could it be otherwise? **ATHENIAN.** If a doctor were ignorant of that concerning the body which we now call health, or a general were ignorant of victory, or any of the others we went through, could it be that he would ever appear to have mind concerning any of these? **CLINIAS.** How could he? **ATHENIAN.** What then about a city? If someone appears not to look toward the "target" at which the political mind should look, should he first of all be justly called a ruler? And then, would he be able to save that whose target he does not know at all? **CLINIAS.** How could he? **ATHENIAN.** It is necessary then even now, as it seems, if the settlement of the land is to have its fulfillment for us, that there be something in it that knows, first, this thing we call the "target," whatever the political goal happens to be for us; next, in what 
<margin>D</margin> way one must partake of this; and who advises him well or not—the laws themselves first, and then men. If any city is empty of such a thing, it is no wonder if, being mindless and without sense, it acts by chance in each of its actions one after another. **CLINIAS.** You speak the truth. **ATHENIAN.** Now then, can we say in which of the parts or pursuits of our city there is such a safeguard sufficiently possessed? **CLINIAS.** Not clearly, O Stranger. But if I must guess, it seems to me this discourse is tending toward the assembly which you just said must meet 
at night. **ATHENIAN.** You have understood most excellently, O Clinias; and this body, as the present reasoning indicates, must have every virtue; 
<margin>E</margin> the beginning of which is not to wander, aiming at many things, but looking toward one, and always letting fly all things like arrows toward this. **CLINIAS.** Altogether so. **ATHENIAN.** Now we shall learn that it is no wonder that the legal customs of cities wander, because different legislations in each city look toward different things. And it is no wonder that for many, the limit they set is "justice," so that certain people may rule in the city, whether they happen to be better or worse; for others, it is how they shall be wealthy, whether they are slaves of some or not; and for others, their zeal is rushed toward a life of freedom. Others legislate for two things together, looking toward both: that they might be free themselves and be 
<margin>G</margin> masters of other cities. But the "wisest," as they think, look toward all these and such things together; but they have nothing uniquely honored to point to as the "one," toward which all their other things must look. **CLINIAS.** Therefore, O Stranger, our own goal would have been rightly established long ago. For we said that all our laws must always look toward one thing. And we agreed that this is quite rightly called "virtue." **ATHENIAN.** Yes. **CLINIAS.** And of the virtues, we said there were four. **ATHENIAN.** Very much so. **CLINIAS.** And that Mind is the leader of all these; toward which both all other things and the three other virtues must look. **ATHENIAN.** You follow most beautifully, O Clinias. And follow the rest as well. For we said the pilot-mind, the medical mind, and the general-mind look toward that "one" thing; but we are here now 
<margin>H</margin> examining the political mind. And just as if we were questioning a man, I would say: "O wonderful man, what is it you are looking for? What is that 'one' thing which the medical mind clearly knows how to state, but you, though you say you differ from the prudent, are not able to say? Or can you, Megillus and Clinias, state on behalf of the director of the state what it is, just as I have often defined many things for you?" **CLINIAS.** Not at all, O Stranger. **ATHENIAN.** What must be done first? Then, what is it that we must save? **CLINIAS.** What sort of things do you mean? **ATHENIAN.** For instance, we said there are four kinds of virtue...

<summary>In this concluding book, Plato argues that for a city to survive, it requires a "Nocturnal Council" that acts as its mind and head, focusing all laws toward the single target of virtue, much like a pilot guides a ship toward a specific destination.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the "Nocturnal Council," the supreme administrative body of Plato’s ideal city. Having established the council's structure on the previous page, the Athenian Stranger now leads Clinias into a deep philosophical inquiry: how can four distinct qualities—courage, prudence, temperance, and justice—all be described by the single word "virtue"?</meta>

-># ON THE LAWS, BOOK XII.<-

<margin>A</margin> ...it is clear that each of them is one, if the four together make up a whole. **CLINIAS.** What do you mean? **ATHENIAN.** We call all these things by one name. For we say that courage <note>original: "fortitudo" (Latin) / "ἀνδρεία" (Greek). Often translated as "bravery" or "manliness."</note> is a virtue, and prudence is a virtue, and the other two likewise, as if in truth they were not many, but only this one thing which is virtue. **CLINIAS.** Entirely so. **ATHENIAN.** Insofar as these two differ from each other and have received two names, and the other two similarly, it is not difficult to say. But insofar as we have placed one name upon both, calling it virtue—and similarly for the remaining two—that is not so easy to explain.

<margin>B</margin> **CLINIAS.** How do you mean? **ATHENIAN.** It is not hard to explain what I am saying. Come then, let us divide the roles of questioning and answering between us. **CLINIAS.** In what way? **ATHENIAN.** You ask me why we call one thing "virtue," and then again call them by two names—one courage and the other prudence. I will give you the reason: it is because the one is concerned with fears. For this reason, even beasts participate in courage, as do the souls of infants. For a courageous soul can be produced by nature, to some extent, even without reason; but without reason, a soul that is prudent <note>original: "prudens" (Latin) / "φρόνιμος" (Greek). This refers to practical wisdom or moral insight.</note> and in possession of its mind never was, is not, and never shall be. Therefore, this quality is different from that one. **CLINIAS.** You speak the truth. **ATHENIAN.** You have received from me the explanation of how these two differ by reason. Now, in turn, you must teach me how they are one and the same. Think of it as if I were asking how these four are one; and then, after you have shown me how they are one, I will declare to you again how they are four. Next, let us consider whether a person who is to understand anything sufficiently—things that have both a name and a definition—should know only the name and not the definition. Or rather, if a thing is of any value, is it not shameful to be ignorant of both the names and the definitions of things that excel in magnitude and beauty? **CLINIAS.** So it seems.

<margin>Foundations of all laws</margin>
<margin>C</margin> **ATHENIAN.** For a law-giver and a guardian, and for one who believes he surpasses others in virtue and has received rewards for these things, is there anything greater than courage, temperance, justice, and prudence? **CLINIAS.** How could there be anything else? **ATHENIAN.** Regarding these things, then, should not the interpreters, the teachers, the law-givers, and the guardians of others teach everyone else who desires to know—or who stands in need of punishment and rebuke—what power virtue has and what power vice has, and excel others by declaring these things? Or shall some poet, or a teacher of youth who has recently entered the city, be judged more excellent than the one who professes to excel in all virtue? And then, will it seem strange if a city where the guardians do not grasp the name and the definition of virtue—as if it were abandoned by its protector—suffers the same things that many other cities suffer today? **CLINIAS.** Certainly not strange.

<margin>D</margin> **ATHENIAN.** Let us, therefore, apply ourselves to this. How shall we make our guardians more refined in virtue than the masses, both in deed and in word? Or in what way shall our city become like a head and senses <note>The Athenian is using an analogy: the young guardians are the "eyes" (senses) and the elders are the "mind," together forming the "head" of the state.</note> because of such a guardianship? **CLINIAS.** In what way, O guest, shall we make this comparison? **ATHENIAN.** It is clear that the city will be a sort of container for the "head"; the younger guardians, being sharp and skillful, will be placed at the very summit. From there, they will look around the whole city and, by guarding what they perceive, they will commit it to memory and report everything to the elders. These elders, being like the mind because of their knowledge of many things, will consult for the city, using the service of the youth.

<margin>E</margin> And so both groups together will preserve the entire city. Is this how we think they should be prepared, or otherwise? Or do we think all should be held as equals? And do we not wish for some to be educated and instructed by a more refined method and be placed before the others? **CLINIAS.** But that, O wonderful man, is impossible. **ATHENIAN.** Let us come, then, to a more refined discipline than that previous one. **CLINIAS.** Nearly so. **ATHENIAN.** And yet, perhaps the very thing we just touched upon is the thing we are seeking. **CLINIAS.** Entirely. **ATHENIAN.** We were saying that the chief craftsman and guardian in each thing must not only be able to look at the many, but must also strive toward the One, and know that One; and once he has known it, he must direct all things toward that point at which he gazes. **CLINIAS.** Correct.

<margin>F</margin> **ATHENIAN.** Is there any more refined consideration of things than to be able to look toward a single Idea <note>original: "ideā" (Latin) / "ἰδέαν" (Greek). In Platonic philosophy, the "Idea" or "Form" is the perfect, singular essence of a thing that exists beyond the physical world.</note> emerging from many dissimilar things? **CLINIAS.** Perhaps. **ATHENIAN.** Do not say "perhaps," but "in truth," O blessed man; no one will ever have a more certain way or method than this. **CLINIAS.** I concede to your reasoning, guest; let us proceed in this way. **ATHENIAN.** We must, therefore, compel the guardians of our divine Republic to see exactly, first, what is the same in all four virtues—that which exists in courage, temperance, justice, and prudence, and which we rightly wish to call by the single name of virtue. This, my friends, if you wish, let us now hold fast to; and let us not let go until it is sufficiently clear what that thing is—whether it be as a unity, or as a whole, or as both, or however it may be—toward which we must look. Or do we think that if this escapes us, we will be sufficiently clear on matters pertaining to virtue, about which we can explain neither if it is many, nor if it is four, nor if it is one? Therefore, if you trust our counsel, we will now try to find a way for this to be present in our city; or, if it seems best, we shall let it go.

<margin>G</margin> **CLINIAS.** By the God of Hospitality, O guest, we must not let this go. For you seem to speak most correctly. But in what way shall we...

<meta>This page continues the Athenian Stranger’s dialogue with Clinias and Megillus regarding the "Nocturnal Council." They are discussing the intellectual requirements for the city's guardians, specifically their ability to see the underlying unity (the "One") behind various virtues and the necessity of theological and astronomical knowledge for leadership.</meta>

# OF PLATO

...who will find this?
<margin>A</margin> **ATHENIAN.** Let us not yet say how this should be done; but first, let us agree among ourselves whether it ought to be done or not.
**CLINIAS.** It certainly ought to be, if it is possible.
**ATHENIAN.** Furthermore, what of the honorable and the good? Should our guardians only know that these are many things, or must they also know how they are one?
**ATHENIAN.** It seems necessary that they also understand how they are one.
**ATHENIAN.** And what then? Should they only understand it, but be unable to declare in speech <note>original: "oratione" / "λόγῳ". Referring to the ability to give a rational account or philosophical explanation.</note> what they understand?
**CLINIAS.** How could that be? For that would be the condition of a slave.
**ATHENIAN.** Is the same reasoning true for all things worthy of study? That those who are to be true
<margin>B</margin> guardians of the laws must truly understand the truth of them, be able to explain them sufficiently in words, and follow them in deeds—judging according to nature what is done rightly and what is not?
**CLINIAS.** Why not?
**ATHENIAN.** And is not one of the best things that which we recently discussed with great seriousness? We demonstrated that the gods exist and that they possess the greatest power. We argued that a man must know this to the best of his ability. We might forgive the many if they merely follow the letter of the laws; but we should never commit the guardianship of the state to anyone who has not labored greatly and with firm faith to grasp everything pertaining to the gods. No one should ever be chosen as a guardian of the laws or be preferred over others for virtue unless he is divine <note>original: "diuinus" / "θεῖον". In this context, it means "god-like" or "spiritually enlightened."</note> and has devoted himself to divine studies.
<margin>C</margin> **CLINIAS.** It is fair, then, as you say, that if someone is slow and unfit in divine matters, he should be kept far away from these most beautiful duties.
**ATHENIAN.** Do we know, then, that there are two things that cause the arguments we previously set forth about the gods to be believed?
**CLINIAS.** What are they?
**ATHENIAN.** One is that which was said above concerning the soul: that it is the oldest and most divine of all things whose motion, having received the power of generation, produced an ever-flowing substance. The other is concerning the order by which the stars and all other things are moved, which a guiding Intellect <note>original: "intellectus" / "νοῦς". This refers to the cosmic Mind or Divine Reason that Plato believes orders the universe.</note> has arranged. For no one who has
<margin>D</margin> diligently considered and perceived these things was ever so impious that he was not affected in a way contrary to what many suspect. For most people think that those who handle these matters—devoting themselves to astronomy and other necessary arts—become alienated from religion. They think such people see things happening by necessity rather than by a divine will for the sake of the good.
**CLINIAS.** How then does the matter stand?
**ATHENIAN.** It stands completely the opposite now than when these things were thought to be without souls. Although even then, whoever searched into them more diligently than others touched upon the truth in a marvelous way: namely, that they could never employ such exquisite reason if they lacked a soul. Even though they lacked minds, some dared to affirm that a Mind had ordered all things in the heavens. But these same people, not knowing that the nature of the soul
<margin>E</margin> is older than bodies, overturned everything again—or rather, they overturned themselves—when they thought the soul was younger. For they believed that what is before our eyes [the physical stars] also existed in heaven. Thus, believing the heavenly bodies to be filled with earth, stones, and other inanimate bodies, they attributed the causes of the whole world to these. Because of this, the philosophers who handled these matters were commonly regarded as impious, and were compared by poets to dogs barking in vain, and other things full of folly were said against them. But now, as we said, the situation is entirely the opposite.
<margin>F</margin> **CLINIAS.** In what way?
**ATHENIAN.** No mortal can ever firmly worship God who hasn't first accepted these two things: first, that the soul is the oldest of all things that participate in generation, and is also immortal, and being such, it rules over all bodies. Second, as we have often said, he must not be ignorant that there is a true Mind in the stars, and he must not be unaware of the disciplines necessary for these things. Nor should he be ignorant of the Muses <note>This refers to "Music" in the broad Greek sense: harmony, rhythm, and the arts that cultivate the soul.</note> that correspond to these things, using them to compose character and preserve the laws, and be able to give a rational account of those things that possess reason. But he who, in addition to public virtues, does not possess these qualities, will hardly ever be a sufficient leader of the whole city, but only a servant to others. It must be considered now,
<margin>G</margin> Clinias and Megillus, whether we ought to add to the aforementioned laws this "apex" and guardian, so that for the sake of safety, a nocturnal assembly of leaders may be present, endowed with the discipline we have described. What shall we do?
**CLINIAS.** What prevents us, most excellent man, from adding it as best as we are able?
**ATHENIAN.** Certainly, we should all strive for this. I will gladly help you. Perhaps, because of my experience in these matters and frequent meditation, I may find many other helpers as well.
**CLINIAS.** By this path, Stranger, we shall profit most, for God himself seems to lead us. But
<margin>H</margin> let us now devise the manner in which this may be rightly done.
**ATHENIAN.** Laws about these things, Clinias and Megillus, cannot be written before the entire city has been organized. Only then should they be established with due authority. But these laws will not be rightly approved except by much doctrine and a long examination of discussion.
**CLINIAS.** What does this mean again?
**ATHENIAN.** First...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...to God, if such a thing is possible; for you seem to us to speak most rightly. But how might one manage this?
**ATHENIAN.** Let us not yet say *how* we might manage it; first, let us confirm it by agreement among ourselves.
**CLINIAS.** Indeed, we must, if it is at all possible.
**ATHENIAN.** What then? Do we not think the same about the beautiful and the good? That our guardians must know how each of these is many, or also how they are one?
**CLINIAS.** It is likely necessary that they also know how they are one.
**ATHENIAN.** What then? Should they think on it, but be unable to demonstrate in speech what they think?
**CLINIAS.** How so? For you describe the habit of a slave.
**ATHENIAN.** What about all serious matters? Is our argument the same, that those who are to be truly
<margin>B</margin> guardians of the laws must truly know the truth about them, and be capable of interpreting them in speech and following them in deed, judging what is done well and what is not?
**CLINIAS.** How could it be otherwise?
**ATHENIAN.** Is not one of the most beautiful things that which concerns the gods, which we have navigated with such effort? To know, as far as it is possible for a man to know, that they exist and what great power they appear to hold? And while we might forgive the majority in the city who only follow the reputation of the laws, we must not entrust the guardianship to those who have not labored to gain full conviction regarding the gods.
<margin>C</margin> It must be that we never choose a guardian of the laws who is not divine, nor one who has not labored through these things, nor one who is not accomplished in virtue.
**CLINIAS.** It is just, as you say, that he who is idle or incapable in such matters should be kept far from beautiful things.
**ATHENIAN.** Do we know then that there are two things concerning the gods that lead to the conviction we detailed before?
**CLINIAS.** What are they?
**ATHENIAN.** One is what we said about the soul, that it is the oldest and most divine of all things whose motion, having taken up generation, created an everlasting essence. The other is about the movement of the stars and all other things over which Mind is master, having ordered the whole universe. For no one who has seen these things, not in a base or ignorant way, was ever so godless
<margin>D</margin> by nature that he did not experience the opposite of what is suspected by the many. For they think that those who handle such things—astronomy and the other necessary arts associated with it—become godless, having observed that things happen by necessity rather than by the intentions of a will for the fulfillment of good.
**CLINIAS.** How then would it be?
**ATHENIAN.** The situation is now (as I said) the complete opposite of when those who thought on these things considered them to be soulless. Even then, wonders crept in and they suspected what is now truly held as a doctrine: that those who touched upon accuracy would never have used such marvelous calculations if the objects were soulless and did not possess mind. And some dared
<margin>E</margin> to risk saying even then that it was Mind that had ordered all things in the heavens. But these same people, erring again about the nature of the soul—that it is older than bodies—and thinking it was younger, overturned almost everything again, and themselves much more. For all the things moving before their eyes in the heavens appeared to them to be full of stones and earth and many other soulless bodies, which distributed the causes of the whole world. These were the things that then produced much godlessness and difficulty in handling such topics. And indeed, insults flourished among the poets, who likened those practicing philosophy to "dogs barking in vain" <note>original: "κυσὶ ματαίαις". A reference to the ancient conflict between poets and philosophers.</note>. But now, as has been said, the situation is the complete opposite.
**CLINIAS.** How?
**ATHENIAN.** No mortal man can ever become firmly God-fearing who has not grasped these
<margin>F</margin> two things now being mentioned: that the soul is the oldest of all things that have partaken in birth, and is immortal, and rules over all bodies; and in addition to these, as has been said many times, that Mind of all existing things which is in the stars, and having grasped the necessary sciences prior to these, and having viewed the communion of the Muses with these things, he uses them for the attainment of character and the harmonizing of legal customs. He must be able to give a rational account of all things that have a reason. He who is not
<margin>G</margin> able to possess these qualities in addition to public virtues will hardly ever become a sufficient ruler of a whole city, but will be a servant to other rulers. We must see now, Clinias and Megillus, whether in addition to all the laws we have gone through, we shall also add this: that there shall be a legal guard for the sake of salvation—the nocturnal assembly of rulers—which shares in all the education we have described. Or how shall we do it?
**CLINIAS.** But, my good man, how could we not add it, if we are at all able?
**ATHENIAN.** Indeed, let us all strive for such a thing, and I will be your eager helper in this. For I have perhaps more experience and have done more thinking on such matters than others.
**CLINIAS.** But Stranger, we must proceed by this path above all, for God himself almost leads us. But
<margin>H</margin> let us now discuss and search out the manner in which this would rightly come about.
**ATHENIAN.** It is no longer possible, Megillus and Clinias, to legislate such things until the city has been ordered. Only then can they become masters of their own legislation. But the thing that will teach such matters will not come to them without much instruction and association...

->before the city has been ordered, then it is necessary for it to become mistress of its own [laws], to legislate. But already the thing that will show such matters, might come to them through teaching and much association, if<-

<summary>This page concludes the philosophical requirements for the "Nocturnal Council," emphasizing that true guardians must understand the unity of virtue and the primacy of the soul and divine intellect as revealed through astronomy. Plato argues that a scientific understanding of the heavens, once feared as a path to atheism, is actually the essential foundation for true piety and leadership.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from the final book of Plato’s *Laws* into the *Epinomis* (the "After-Law"). It concludes the discussion on the "Nocturnal Council"—the highest governing body of the ideal city—and begins an inquiry into the specific "wisdom" required for a human to be truly happy and capable of ruling.</meta>

# EPINOMIS.

...it would happen rightly. How? What should we say of this again?
<margin>A</margin> **ATHENIAN.** First, it would be a strange and laborious task to list all those who would be suitable for the nature of the guardianship, their ages, and the studies they must learn, along with their positions and stations. Furthermore, it is neither easy to discover these things, nor could a pupil be made simply by hearing them once. In addition to this, regarding the times at which and in which each subject should be taken up, it is useless to set these things down in writing. For it would not even be clear to the learners themselves when the right time to learn is until the knowledge of the subject itself has somehow come to exist within the soul of each. Therefore, all these things, though spoken of as "secrets," are rightly secrets <note>original: "ἀπόῤῥητα". Meaning matters that are not to be divulged or are inherently difficult to communicate.</note> because they reveal nothing clearly when spoken before the time is right.
<margin>B</margin> **CLINIAS.** What then must be done, Stranger, since things stand this way?
**ATHENIAN.** As the saying goes, friends, the matter lies in the common ground between us. And if anyone is willing to risk the whole constitution, either throwing "three sixes" or "three cubes," as they say, <note>original: "τρὶς ἕξ... ἢ τρεῖς κύβους". A Greek gambling idiom referring to the highest possible throw of the dice; it implies taking a total risk for a great reward.</note> then this must be done. I will join you in this risk by explaining and interpreting my thoughts on the education and upbringing that have now been set in motion by our discussion. The risk is not small, nor is it like any other. I urge you, Clinias, to take care of it. For you will either bring the greatest glory to the city of the Magnesians <note>The city-state being designed in the *Laws*.</note>—or whatever name God gives it—or you will be seen as the most insignificant of men, even if you are held in high regard later.
<margin>C</margin> If this divine assembly of ours is ever formed, dear companions, it must be the most accurate of all things. No dispute will ever be raised by anyone once these things are legislated. Whatever has been accomplished almost as a waking dream, we have fashioned in speech with no small effort, mixing together an image of the union of the "head" and the "mind." <note>This refers to the Nocturnal Council acting as the intellect (mind) within the physical structure (head/body) of the state.</note> If these men are mixed together accurately and educated appropriately—living in the citadel of the land—they will be perfected as guardians such as we have never seen before in our lives.
<margin>D</margin> **MEGILLUS.** Dear Clinias, from everything that has been said, it is clear: either the settlement of the city must be abandoned, or this stranger here must not be let go; rather, he must be made a partner by every means and machine in the founding of the city.
**CLINIAS.** You speak most truly, Megillus; I must do this, and you must help me.
**MEGILLUS.** I will help.

->OR,<-
### ON LEGISLATION,
### THE THIRTEENTH DIALOGUE.

->It is also called<-

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Therefore, let an assembly of those men be established who, by age, learning, character, and habit, are suitable for the guardianship. Then, those things which must be learned are neither easily found, nor is it easy for a student to achieve the discovery. Furthermore, the times in which individual subjects ought to be perceived would be written down in vain. For those who learn cannot themselves know when something is learned opportunely until the knowledge of the thing itself is in their minds. Thus, what cannot be spoken of openly in these matters is not rightly attempted to be spoken; for if they are spoken, it explains nothing more clearly.
**CLINIAS.** Since these things are so, Stranger, what do you think we should do?
**ATHENIAN.**
<margin>B</margin> As the proverb says, friends, it has seemed right to us to bring the matter into the common and public sphere, and to be willing to undergo the danger for the whole republic: to do everything, even if we throw "thrice six" or "three dice." Indeed, I will undergo that danger with you, both by setting forth and explaining what seems right to me concerning this discipline and education which we have just touched upon. The danger is not small, nor similar to others. I command you, Clinias, to take care of it now. For you will flourish with the highest glory in the city of the Magnesians, or that which God makes its namesake, if you establish it correctly. Certainly, you will never escape being seen as the strongest of all those who come after. If, therefore, this divine assembly is established for us, O friends,
<margin>C</margin> the city must be handed over to it. Nor will the other lawgivers oppose these men as if they were insufficient. Indeed, what we touched upon a little while ago in words as if dreaming—when we brought in the union of the head and mind through a certain image—we shall almost perfectly complete while awake, if these exquisitely learned men come together for us and live in the citadel of the region as established guardians of the city, such as we have never known to have existed for the sake of guardianship in our past lives.
**MEGILLUS.** From everything we have said, friend Clinias, it is clear that either the constitution of such a city must be omitted, or this stranger must not be
<margin>D</margin> dismissed, but must be accepted by prayers and every means as a partner to arrange the city.
**CLINIAS.** You speak rightly, Megillus. I will indeed act in this way, but you also must bring help.
**MEGILLUS.** I will indeed bring it.

### PLATO ON LAWS, OR, ON THE 
### INSTITUTION OF LAWS,
### THE THIRTEENTH DIALOGUE.

->It is also called<-

### EPINOMIS, OR, THE PHILOSOPHER.

> **SUMMARY OF THE DIALOGUE.** Having explained those things which seemed to belong to a complete treatment of legislation, Plato, about to place a most illustrious conclusion upon this most illustrious discussion, has applied that teaching than which no more illustrious could be found by a pagan <note>original: "ethnico". Literally "ethnic," here used by the Renaissance translator to denote a pre-Christian philosopher.</note> man: that as he made God the primary cause of laws in the first words of this discussion, so he now shows that all their force and efficacy—and therefore the utility of the Republic for whose sake they are established—depend entirely upon God, the author and preserver of all things and of human society. He connects the previous discussion with this one in this manner: having established the laws with which he thought the Republic should be surrounded, he had said they would profit nothing unless they were handed over to an established college of the best and wisest citizens for execution, or rather, for their foresight and care. Since, however, as the end of laws is action <note>original: "πράξις / praxis".</note>, so the foundation of legitimate action is theory <note>original: "theoria". Philosophical contemplation or understanding.</note>, which is nothing other than true and genuine wisdom: here he speaks of Wisdom, which he had begun to treat in the previous book; and he clearly teaches what it is, and what the method and way of acquiring it are.

<margin>E</margin> Indeed, as we had commonly agreed, all three of us have finally reached this point rightly, Stranger—I, you, and Megillus here—to inquire into prudence: <note>original: "φρονήσεως / prudentia". This refers to practical wisdom or the intellectual virtue of good judgment.</note> by what reasoning we might attain that which, when understood, the human condition is best disposed toward prudence, as far as nature allows. For the other things pertaining to the bringing of laws we have already treated. But that which is greatest both to find and to say—namely, what a mortal man must learn to become wise—we have neither found nor said. But I think it must by no means be omitted,
<margin>F</margin> lest we perhaps leave that thing imperfect for whose opening we have traveled thus far.
**ATHENIAN.** You speak skillfully, friend Clinias. I think you are about to hear a discourse that is strange, and yet in another way not strange. For many who are tossed by the waves of this life proclaim that the human race cannot be happy and blessed. Pay attention, then, and consider whether I too seem to speak rightly on this matter. I think it is impossible for men to attain happiness and blessedness in this life, except for a very few. Yet there is good hope that after death one may entirely obtain those things for whose desire he lived and finished his life as best he could
<margin>G</margin> according to his strength. Nor do I bring forward something unheard of or new, but what all Barbarians and Greeks recognize in a certain way. For no one is ignorant of how great the difficulty is in the first generation of animals: first in conception and the womb, then in birth and labor, later in nutrition and education—and that all these things happen through a thousand troubles, as we all say.

<meta>This page continues the Athenian Stranger’s inquiry into the nature of wisdom. Having established that the "Nocturnal Council" needs a specific kind of knowledge to guide the city, he now begins a "process of elimination," examining various human arts and sciences to show why they do not constitute true wisdom or lead to ultimate happiness.</meta>

-># OF PLATO<-

...education. For we are not unaware that these things are achieved through a thousand labors. Moreover, the time of life is short, not only in respect to the long duration of evils, but in whatever way one considers it; it allows us to breathe just a little, as if only around the middle of a human life. But soon, grim old age comes upon us, making it so that no one would wish to return to life again if they were to reflect on the troubles they have passed through—unless, perhaps, they are carried away by a childish opinion. That all these things are so serves as my evidence for the question now at hand. For we are seeking in what way we might become wise, as if some power of this kind were present in each of us.

<margin>Which arts do not make one wise.</margin>
Indeed, this power escapes us whenever someone turns toward any of those faculties commonly called by the names of "art," "prudence," or "science" <note>original: "artis vel prudentiæ vel scientiæ". In Greek, these are *techne*, *phronesis*, and *episteme*—different categories of knowledge and skill.</note>, as if none of these in such human affairs were worthy of being called by the name of "wisdom." Yet the soul remains very confident and "prophesies" that some such power belongs to it according to its nature; however, it cannot easily find what it is, or when and how it is present. Does not this doubt and our inquiry regarding wisdom point mostly to this? It is full of hope for individuals, whoever they may be, who can prudently and harmoniously examine both themselves and others in every kind of speech and discussion. Shall we say things are this way, or otherwise?

**CLINIAS.** We certainly agree, Guest, hoping that together with you we will eventually arrive at the truest opinion concerning these matters.

**ATHENIAN.** Let us, therefore, first run through the other arts which, although they are called "sciences," do not make a man wise. Once those are removed, we may bring forward and compare those which we actually need, and having made the comparison, speak of them. And let us look first at those which the human race needs most. For indeed, these are the first and most necessary of all. Although the practitioners of these arts may have seemed wise in the beginning, they are now neither considered wise, but are even disparaged because of those very arts. We must say, then, what these are, and why all those who desire to be seen as the "best men" flee from the study of such arts. Let the first be that which commanded us to abstain from the eating of human flesh—which, as the stories tell, had once grown common among men after the manner of wild beasts—and called us back to a more modest diet. In this, the ancients surely consulted our interests gently and humanely; yet let them be dismissed, nor let them usurp the name of wisdom. Next, the skill of cereal foods <note>The milling of grain and baking of bread.</note> is indeed useful and fine, but it will never make a man perfectly wise. For it brings difficulty and trouble rather than wisdom. Nor will agriculture do it. For we seem to approach the cultivation of the earth not by art, but by nature and a certain favor from God. Neither the construction of houses, nor all other building, nor the crafting of furniture, nor the work of the smith, the carpenter, the potter, or the weaver, nor the crafting of all those tools which are suited to the common people, bring anything toward virtue. Even the art of hunting, however varied and ingenious it may be, does not grant magnificence or wisdom. Nor does divination or any kind of interpretation. For even if the diviner knows what is said, he does not understand whether those things are true or not. After we have established that none of these arts by which necessities are provided makes a man wise, there remains a certain imitative faculty that is not at all serious. For imitation is often done with instruments, and frequently with ungraceful gestures and figures of the body. There is also imitation in eloquence and the muses <note>referring to poetry and song</note>, and in sculpting and painting, where many and various things are expressed in bodies both hard and soft. None of these things makes a man devoted to imitation wise. With imitation removed, other arts remain which seem to be occupied with providing help. These are indeed many and varied, but the art of war—which they call generalship—excels them all. This is highly approved for its utility, but it stands in the greatest need of good luck, and is perfected more by natural courage than by wisdom. Medicine also helps us against the onslaught of immoderate cold and heat, and other such things by which the nature of animals is harmed; but none of these leads to true wisdom, for they proceed by uncertain conjectures and opinions. Furthermore, we will not deny that sailors and pilots provide help. Yet we will not permit any of them to be called wise by anyone. For none of them knows the anger or the friendship of the winds, which is the best thing and most required in the art of navigation. Nor do we want those to be called wise who assist litigants with the power of speaking; for by memory and practice, they accommodate themselves to the habits of opinion, but they wander far from the understanding of true justice. There remains a certain strange power which similarly claims for itself the reputation of wisdom, which many would call "nature" rather than wisdom. This consists in someone learning easily whatever they wish, and remembering many things for a long time and firmly, and quickly and conveniently producing what is suitable for each occasion. Some will call all these things "nature," others "wisdom," and others "natural shrewdness." But no one of sound mind will grant that anyone is truly wise because of these things. Nevertheless, it is necessary that some science be found which, whoever possesses it, would not only seem

<column-break/>

**A** ...time would be short for a calculation—not just of the helpful things, but what anyone would suppose to be a moderate amount. Almost everything seems to make human life bitter and "mid-way." For old age, barely floating upon us, would make anyone never wish to live again, if they calculated the life they had already lived—unless they happened to be full of childish opinion. What evidence could I have that things are naturally this way regarding the question now sought by our argument? We are searching for some art to make us wise, as if such a power existed for each of us. But the soul claims that whenever someone turns toward the so-called arts or forms of prudence, or other such things we think of as "sciences," none of these is worthy to be called the "wisdom" concerning human affairs. Yet the soul is strongly convinced and "divines" that it has some nature of this kind, though it cannot quite find out what it is, or when, or how. Are we not carried by this into a great difficulty and search for wisdom, where the hope of each person becomes greater than their grasp—at least for those of us capable of prudently and harmoniously examining ourselves and others through all words spoken in every way? Shall we agree that these things are so, or in this manner?

**CLINIAS.** We agree, Guest, in the hope that perhaps in time, and with you, we might seem to find the truest truth.

**ATHENIAN.** First, we must go through the remaining sciences that are so-called, but which do not make the one who receives and possesses them wise. We do this so that, having set them aside, we may try to set forth those we need and, having set them alongside, learn from them. First, then, we must seek the most necessary and truly primary ones. He who becomes knowledgeable in them, even if he once seemed wise at the beginning, is certainly not thought wise now, but rather incurs reproach from such science. We shall say what they are: almost every man who sets before himself the goal of appearing as the best of men avoids them, because of the judgments of prudence and practice. Let the first be that which ended the practice of animals eating one another—which the myth says stopped our beast-like state—and established us in a lawful diet. May the ancients be gracious to us, for they are indeed the ones we spoke of; but let them be dismissed with a "farewell." Indeed, the making of barley-meal and flour is a fine and good nourishment, but it could never make a man perfectly wise. For this very thing—the title of "making"—would produce a certain annoyance in those doing it. Nor indeed would the agriculture of the whole land do so. For we all seem to handle the earth not by art, but by nature according to God. Then there is the coordination of dwellings and all building, the production of all vessels, smithing, carpentry, molding, weaving, and the crafting of all tools; these have utility for the common people, but would not be called "virtue." Nor indeed does the whole of hunting, though it has become a large and technical field, grant the magnificence that belongs to the wise man. Neither indeed does divination or interpretation at all. For the diviner only knows what is said; he has not learned if it is true. Since we see that the acquisition of necessities is achieved through art, yet no such art makes one wise. After this, some education would remain, mostly imitative, but in no way serious. For they imitate with many instruments, and with many ungraceful imitations of their bodies themselves, both in speech and every kind of music, or what the "mother of painting" produces in many and various patterns, in many wet and dry materials. None of these things makes a man wise in anything, even if he labors at imitation with the greatest seriousness. Once all these are finished, there remain a myriad of "helps" for a myriad of things. The greatest and most widely used is the art of war, called generalship, most esteemed for its utility, but needing the most luck, and granted more to courage and nature than to wisdom. That which they call medicine is also a help, protecting against the seasons’ cold and unseasonable heat and all such things that prey upon the nature of animals. None of these is esteemed as truest wisdom, for they are carried along by opinions without measure. And we shall say that pilots and sailors are also helpers. Let no one, in trying to console us, proclaim any of these to be a wise man from the whole lot. For such a man would not know the anger or friendship of the wind, which is dear to all navigation. Nor indeed those who say they are helpers in lawsuits by the strength of speaking, who by memory and practice aim at the opinion of what is lawful, but have fallen far from seeing the truly just. Finally, there is still a certain strange power regarding the reputation for wisdom, which many would call "nature" rather than wisdom: when someone understands easily whatever they might be learning, and remembers many things very safely; when they quickly do what is fitting for each of the things they remember. For some call all these "nature," others "wisdom," and others "natural quickness." But no one of sound mind would ever be willing to call any of these people truly wise. But indeed, some science must appear, which, by possessing it, a man would become wise, he who is truly wise—who...

<meta>This page continues the Athenian Stranger's discourse in the Epinomis, moving from a critique of common arts to the identification of the "one true science" that makes humanity wise: the science of number (arithmetic), which is revealed through the observation of the heavens.</meta>

EPINOMIS.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...but instead truly be wise. Attention is needed. For we have undertaken a truly difficult task: searching for another art, besides those already mentioned, which may rightly be called true wisdom. He who attains this will be neither lowly nor foolish, but through it will become wise and good—a modest citizen and a just ruler or subject of the city. Therefore, let us first examine this: which of all human arts is such that, if this one alone were removed, the nature of man would be rendered most senseless and ignorant? This is not difficult to find. For if you compare them one by one, that which gave the gift of number <note>original: "numerum"; the Greek term is *arithmos*</note> to the mortal race is surely the one that achieves this. I believe a certain god, <margin>B</margin> rather than mere fortune, gave this gift to us for our salvation. I will tell you which god I mean, even if I seem strange—though in another way, not strange at all. For why should we not believe that the very author of all good things is also the cause of the greatest good: prudence <note>original: "prudentiæ"; here meaning practical wisdom or *phronesis*</note>? And which god do I praise, Megillus and Clinias? Almost the Heaven itself <note>original: "Cœlum"; refers to the Cosmos or the visible universe</note>; it is right that we, like all the other spirits and gods, should honor it with worship and especially with prayer. We would all confess that the Heaven has been the cause of all our other blessings. We further affirm that it has given us number, <margin>C</margin> and will continue to give it to anyone willing to observe. <margin>Arithmetic.</margin> This will be achieved by whoever ascends to a correct contemplation of it—whether one prefers to call it the World <note>original: "mundum"</note>, or Olympus, or Heaven—provided they consider its varieties and how it creates different seasons and provides food for all living things through its circuits and rotations, and how it grants wisdom to men along with number and all other goods. This is the greatest thing: if anyone, receiving the gift of numbers from it, traverses its entire circuit. But let us recall what was most correctly stated by us in our previous discussion: that if anyone should take number away from human nature, we would never become prudent. For <margin>D</margin> the soul of this animal <note>meaning the human being</note> would almost never perceive any virtue if reason <note>original: "ratione"; here translating the Greek *logos*, meaning both "account" and "proportion"</note> were taken from it. Nor could an animal that is entirely ignorant of "two" and "three," or "even" and "odd," and knows nothing of number at all, ever give an account of the things it perceives only through sense and memory. There is nothing to prevent it from possessing other virtues, such as courage and temperance; but he who lacks true reason, how will he ever turn out wise? And he who lacks wisdom, the greatest part of all virtue, since he cannot be perfectly good, will never attain happiness. Thus, it is absolutely necessary to presuppose number. That this is necessary can be <margin>On the excellence of number in knowing things.</margin> shown by even more reasons. But it is correctly shown by <margin>E</margin> this reason: that the other arts we enumerated just a moment ago would vanish entirely if number were removed. Perhaps someone thinking about the arts will think there are only a few things in which the human race needs number, though even that would be significant. But if one looks at what is divine in generation and what is mortal—wherein piety toward the gods and true number are recognized—one will surely find that no one can comprehend how great a cause of virtue number is to us, provided the whole of it is present. For all music requires the number of movements and sounds. And what is most important, we can easily recognize from this that number is the cause of all good things and of no evil. <margin>F</margin> For any movement that is irrational, disordered, shapeless, inept, and out of tune—in short, everything in which there is something of evil—lacks all number. He who is to be truly blessed must not be ignorant of this. And he who is ignorant of the just, the good, the honorable, and other such things, and has not received a true opinion about them, will not be able to use the reasoning of number to persuade himself or others. But let us now consider <margin>From where we learn number.</margin> how we learned to use number. Come, from where do we perceive "one" and "two"? From where did we receive the power to recognize this from the universe? Surely, while nature denied many other animals the ability to learn even "one" from their father, God first implanted in us the capacity to understand number in that which is shown to us. Then he showed it more clearly, and continues to show it constantly. In this explanation of things, if one thing is compared to another, you could see nothing more beautiful than the light of <margin>G</margin> day. From there, you might also consider the night through the office of the eyes, where the greatest variety appears. For if you do not cease to revolve these things, you will see many nights and many days, by which the heavens never cease to teach men "one" and "two," so that even the slowest learner might learn to use number from this. For in this way, anyone by seeing these things would understand "three," and "four," and many. To this end, God formed the one Moon, which appears now smaller and now larger, and is thus seen daily changing for up to fifteen days and nights. This is a circuit, if one wishes to consider the whole circle as one. Therefore, so to speak, even the slowest animals <margin>H</margin> to whom God gave some nature to be able to learn would perceive number. In these things, therefore, and up to this point, every animal that has the power of learning is made most fit for counting by considering each thing by itself. But to compare every number to every other number is a greater task, and for that reason, as we said, the Moon...

The author asserts that this knowledge is a divine gift revealed through the orderly movements of the heavens, the sun, and the moon, which teach even the simplest minds the concepts of unity and multiplicity.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the Athenian Stranger's argument that the study of the heavens and the science of number (arithmetic) is the path to true wisdom. He transitions here into the theological and physical foundations of this wisdom, specifically the priority of the soul over the body.</meta>

# PLATONIS

...making the moon now waxing, now waning. From this, he established the months for the year, and taught that every number should be compared to a single number by a certain happy fortune. Hence the earth, having been made more fertile, conceives and brings forth fruits for the nourishment of all animals, while the winds blow sweetly and the rains fall healthily into the lap of the earth. And if any evil occurs in these matters, it is not divine nature that is to be blamed, but human nature, which distributes its life unjustly. To us, however, as we are currently writing about laws, the other things that are best for men seem easy to recognize; anyone can sufficiently understand what is said about them, and moreover do them, once they have perceived what is beneficial and what is not. 

<insert>B</insert> The other pursuits, I say, seemed to us then, and seem to us now, not too difficult; however, the manner in which men are made good is utterly difficult. Regarding the rest of the good things, it is possible—as the saying goes—and not difficult to possess them: wealth to the extent it is needed, and a body of the proper kind. Everyone also confesses that one ought to have a good soul. But if asked how a soul is to be made good, everyone would answer that it must be just, temperate, brave, and other such qualities. And who would deny that the soul must be wise? But as to what kind of wisdom must be acquired, as we have recently discussed, we have found that none of the many agree with one another. Now, therefore, besides all the forms of wisdom we have described above, we have found a certain significant one for this very purpose: so that he who has learned what has been said may appear wise. Whether he who has learned these things is truly wise and good, however, must be sought through reason.

<insert>C</insert> **CLINIAS.** You have spoken most skillfully, Guest, when you affirmed that you would speak of great things in a great way. 

**ATHENIAN.** Certainly, Clinias, these are no small matters, and what is more, they are entirely true. 

**CLINIAS.** Truly so, Guest. Do not yield to the labor, but proceed as you have begun. 

**ATHENIAN.** I shall make the effort; but do not you yield to the labor of listening. 

**CLINIAS.** We shall certainly do so; I speak for both of us. 

**ATHENIAN.** Well then. <margin>What faculty it is that we consider to be wisdom.</margin> Therefore, we must go back further, and first, if we can in any way, it seems we must encompass in a single name what that faculty is which we consider to be wisdom.
