<insert>D</insert> how many are the arts which, once possessed, lead us to call a man wise in our fashion. 

**CLINIAS.** Speak on. 

**ATHENIAN.** The lawmaker will be free of all blame if he thinks better of the gods than the ancients did, and, using the best discipline, honors the gods with hymns and extols their blessedness, and so passes his life. 

**CLINIAS.** You speak rightly, Guest, since this end of the laws is proposed to you: that through the worship of God and purity of life, you may achieve the best and most beautiful conclusion.

**ATHENIAN.** How then shall we say it, Clinias? Shall we greatly honor the gods with hymns, and pray that we may carry out the following discussion about them in the best and most beautiful way? Do you think we should act in this way, or otherwise? 

**CLINIAS.** Entirely in this way. But, O man favored by the gods, having placed faith in the gods and sent forth prayers, speak well of the gods and goddesses. 

**ATHENIAN.** So it shall be, if God himself leads us. Only pray with me. 

**CLINIAS.** Proceed then.

<insert>E</insert> **ATHENIAN.** In the beginning, since our ancestors handed down the lineage of gods and living beings poorly, it is worthwhile to take up the matter better now, so that we may resume our previous discussion against the impious. In that discourse, it was asserted that gods exist, that they care for all things great and small at once, and that they cannot be appeased by any prayers or gifts contrary to what is just. Do you remember that these things were said, Clinias? Surely you received them then in such a way that you ought to remember, especially because it was established that they are most true.

<insert>F</insert> But of all things, this was considered the greatest: that every soul is older than every body. <note>The Athenian refers to the central argument of *Laws* Book X, where he proved the soul's priority to matter.</note> Do you remember? Truly, most of all. For that which is better, and older, and more divine, is prior to that which is inferior, younger, and viler. Similarly, a leader is prior by nature to the led, and a ruler to the subject. Let us therefore admit that the soul is older than the body. If this is so, it is surely likely that what is first in generation came before. Therefore, let us posit that the leadership and the origin of the origin are in a more fitting state, and thus we most rightly enter into wisdom concerning the generation of the gods. 

**CLINIAS.** Let these things remain affirmed to the best of human strength.

<insert>G</insert> **ATHENIAN.** Come then, do we not most truly affirm that a living being <note>original: "animal"; in the sense of a "living creature" or *zoon*</note> exists according to nature when one constitution of soul and body, coming together in a single meeting, produces one form? 

**CLINIAS.** Correct. 

**ATHENIAN.** Something of this kind is rightly called a living being. 

**CLINIAS.** Certainly. 

**ATHENIAN.** We can appropriately say there are five solid bodies <note>These are the "Platonic solids" associated with the elements: earth, water, air, fire, and ether.</note> from which the most beautiful and best things are shaped. But the other entire genus possesses a single form. For there is nothing else that can be incorporeal and entirely devoid of color, except that most divine genus in which the soul exists. To this genus alone it belongs to shape and to craft; but to the body it belongs to be shaped, to be born, and to be perceived by the eyes. But to the genus of the soul—for this must be said more than once—it belongs to be invisible, to possess knowledge, to be intelligible, and to participate in memory and reason in both even and uneven changes. But since there are five bodies—fire, water, the third being air, the fourth earth, and the fifth ether—many and various individual living beings are produced by the dominance of these. We can learn this in one instance. For I will first posit the earthly...

<column-break/>

...just as we said, having produced it in the waxing and waning, he established the months toward the year, and taught how to perceive every number in relation to one another by a <margin>A</margin> happy fortune. Because of these things, the earth has become pregnant and brings forth fruits for us, so that there is wise growth and rain for all living beings, neither excessive nor immoderate. But if anything happens contrary to these things toward the base, one must not blame the divine nature, but the human nature, which does not distribute its own life in justice. To us who are searching concerning laws, it seemed that other things are almost easy to know and to recognize as the best for humans; and everyone would become capable if they understood what was said and did it, if they knew what it is that is likely to be beneficial and what is not. It seemed then, and now <insert>B</insert> still seems, that all other pursuits are not exceedingly difficult; but the way in which men must become good is utterly difficult. All other possessions seem, as is said, both possible and not difficult—wealth in the amount one should or should not have, and a body of the sort one should or should not have. That one must have a good soul, everyone agrees with everyone else. But in what way it would be good—that it must be just and temperate and brave—everyone says these are necessary. But as for wisdom in speech, as we have just discussed, no one among the many yet agrees with anyone else at all. Now, therefore, besides all the forms of wisdom we have set down, we find another that is not mean for these very purposes: that he who has learned the things we have described should seem wise. <insert>C</insert> If he who knows these things is wise and good, this is what we must grasp in our discussion.

**CLINIAS.** O Guest, how appropriately you said that you are attempting to speak of great things concerning great matters.

**ATHENIAN.** Not small ones, Clinias; and what is more difficult, they are altogether and in every way true.

**CLINIAS.** Very much so, Guest. But nevertheless, do not grow weary in saying what you say.

**ATHENIAN.** Yes, and neither of you grow weary in listening.

**CLINIAS.** That shall be so; for I speak to you for both of us.

**ATHENIAN.** Good. It is necessary to speak from the beginning as it appears, especially if we are able to grasp with one name what it is that we think is wisdom. <insert>D</insert> If we are utterly unable to do this, then secondly, we must say what and how many they are, which if a person receives them, he would be wise according to our story.

**CLINIAS.** You may speak.

**ATHENIAN.** Following this, the lawmaker will be blameless if he speaks better of the gods than was said before, making a better image of them, as if using a beautiful play and honoring the gods, gracing his own life with hymns and happiness.

**CLINIAS.** You speak beautifully, Guest. For if this were the end of your laws—having served the gods, to achieve a most pure and blessed life and a most beautiful end to the journey.

**ATHENIAN.** How then shall I say it, Clinias? Does it seem that in hymning the gods we honor them greatly, praying to speak most beautifully and best concerning them, <insert>E</insert> or how do you say?

**CLINIAS.** Wonderfully so. But, O divine one, having trusted the gods, pray and speak the beautiful discourse that comes to you concerning the gods and goddesses.

**ATHENIAN.** This shall be, if the god himself leads us. Only pray with me.

**CLINIAS.** Speak what follows.

**ATHENIAN.** It is necessary, it seems, to handle the generation of the gods and living things better and more musically than those before, taking up the discourse we attempted against the impious. I stated that there are gods who care for all things, small and great, and that divine justice is a matter not to be persuaded away <note>original: "aparamutheetoi"; meaning the gods' justice cannot be "bribed" or talked around with mere words</note>. If indeed you remember, Clinias, for you took notes. For what was said then was very true. And this was the greatest of them: that the soul is older than the body in every way. Do you remember? Or is this <insert>F</insert> entirely so? For that which is better and older and more godlike is likely to be prior to that which is worse and younger and less honorable; and that which rules everywhere is older than the ruled, and the leader than the led. Let us take this at least: that the soul is older than the body. If this is so, it would be more likely that our first findings regarding the first stages of generation are as discovered here. And let us posit that the beginning of the beginning has a more foundational character, and that we are most correctly entering upon the greatest wisdom concerning the generation of the gods.

**CLINIAS.** Let these things be said to the best of our ability.

**ATHENIAN.** Come then, a living being is most truly said to be according to nature when one combined composition of soul and body <insert>G</insert> gives birth to one form.

**CLINIAS.** Correct.

**ATHENIAN.** Such a thing is most justly called a living being.

**CLINIAS.** Yes.

**ATHENIAN.** Regarding the so-called solid bodies, one must say according to the likely account that there are five, from which one might shape the most beautiful and best things. The entire other genus has one form. For there is nothing else that could become incorporeal, and never in any way having any color, except the truly most divine genus of the soul. This is almost the only thing to which it belongs to shape and to craft; but of the body, we say it is shaped and born and seen. To the soul, again (for it must be said more than once), we say it is invisible, and to the one who knows it, it is intelligible, sharing in memory and reasoning in both uneven and even changes. There being five bodies, one must say there is fire and water; third, air; fourth, earth; and fifth, ether. In the leadership of these, each various and manifold living being is completed. One must learn it one by one thus: first, the earthly...

<meta>This page continues the Athenian Stranger’s discourse from the Epinomis, moving from the mathematical foundations of wisdom to a "theology of the heavens." Having established that number is the key to understanding the universe, he now argues that the celestial bodies—the stars and planets—are not mere rocks, but living, divine beings governed by soul and intelligence. This transition bridges the gap between physical observation and religious devotion.</meta>

# EPINOMIS.

<margin>A</margin> ...the categories of living beings <note>original: "animaliũ genus"; the author uses "animal" to mean any "animated" or "living being," including plants and stars</note> remain for us to discuss: first, human beings; then all those that are many-footed or footless; those that move and those that are stationary, being held fast by roots. One must believe this single truth: that while all these are composed of all the elements, the earthly and solid nature predominates in them. But we must propose a second class of living beings, which can be seen as they are born. This class consists mostly of fire, though it also contains earth, air, and small portions of all other things; therefore, we must say that these are diverse and visible living beings. We must consider these to be the celestial races of living beings. This entire race of stars must be called divine, having obtained <margin>B</margin> the most beautiful body and the most blessed and excellent soul. We should assign one of two fates to these beings: either each of them is entirely immortal and divine by absolute necessity, or they possess a life so long-lived that they would never require any more. Let us therefore first consider these two types of living beings. Again I say, both are visible: the one appearing to be made entirely of fire, the other of earth. The earthly type moves in disorder, whereas the fiery type moves in a completely orderly fashion. That which moves without order must be considered mindless—which is what the living creatures around us mostly do. But that which proceeds with order in the heavens <margin>C</margin> must be taken as a great proof of its intelligence. For by always traveling in the same way, acting and being acted upon in the same manner, it provides sufficient evidence of a life lived wisely. The necessity of a soul possessing intellect <note>Greek: "nous"; Latin: "intellectum"</note> is the greatest of all necessities; for it rules and is not ruled, and it lays down the law. When a soul—which is the best thing—deliberates according to the best intellect, the result is truly perfect according to that mind. Not even "adamas" <note>An ancient term for the hardest substance, like diamond or indestructible steel; used here to represent unbreakable necessity</note> could be stronger or more unchangeable than such a soul. Indeed, the three Fates <note>Greek: "moirai"; Latin: "Parcae." These are the mythical personifications of destiny who spin, measure, and cut the thread of life</note> preserve as perfect that which has been deliberated by the best counsel of each of the gods. For men, let the stars and this entire celestial circuit serve as proof <margin>D</margin> of their intelligence: they always perform the same actions because they decided long ago what they ought to do for a wonderful span of time. They do not change their minds and move up and down, doing now one thing and now another, wandering and shifting their cycles. Yet to many of us, the opposite has seemed true: because they always act in the same and similar way, people think they have no soul. The common crowd followed this foolish opinion, thinking that human beings are intelligent and alive because they move unpredictably, while the divine is mindless because it remains in the same orbits. It would have been more fitting for man to hold a more beautiful and better view, dear to the gods: that we must consider a being intelligent precisely because it acts in the same way, for the same reasons, <margin>E</margin> and always according to a pattern. This is the nature of the stars: most beautiful to look upon, providing the most magnificent and best of all "dances" <note>The "chorea" or dance of the stars refers to their rhythmic, circular movements</note> through their progression, fulfilling what is necessary for all living things. That we are right to call them "ensouled" is testified first by their size. For they are not just as small as they appear; they are truly of an incredible magnitude. This is worthy of belief, for it is demonstrated by sufficient proofs: one can rightly understand that the whole sun is larger than the whole earth, and all the traveling stars have a marvelous size. Let us consider, then, how it is possible for such a massive bulk to be carried around by any nature for the same amount of time as it is now being carried. I assert that God is the cause, and it could not <margin>F</margin> happen otherwise. A thing could never become "ensouled" <note>Living or possessed of a soul</note> except through God, as we have declared. Since God is capable of this, it was easy for Him first to grant life and magnitude to every body, and then to lead them in the way He thought best. Finally, let us hold this one true opinion about all these things: it is impossible for the earth, the heaven, the stars, and all the masses composed of them to revolve with such exquisite precision through years, months, and days—bringing all good things to us all—unless a soul were present with or within each of them. A man, the lowlier he is, should babble less about these things and instead try to say something certain. If anyone claims that some "impulse" of bodies or "natures" or <margin>G</margin> anything of that sort is the cause of this order, he says nothing clear. We must again carefully reconsider what was said: whether the argument is probable or entirely fails. First, it is said that there are two things, soul and body; there are many examples of each, and each type differs from the others, and the two classes are distinct from one another, so that they have nothing in common. The soul differs from the body in that the former possesses mind, while the latter does not. The former rules; the latter is subject. The soul is the cause of all actions, while the body is the cause of no action but is the subject of every "passion" <note>In philosophy, "passion" refers to being acted upon by an external force</note>. Therefore, to claim the celestial bodies were made by something else, and do not consist <margin>H</margin> of soul and body as we have said, is to be entirely foolish and ignorant. If the arguments regarding all these things have any strength, and all these things are to be judged as truly divine, one must choose between two options. For we must either <margin>H</margin> praise these as the gods themselves in the truest sense, or believe them to be images of the gods—like statues fashioned by the gods themselves, who are the most excellent and wise craftsmen. We must decide on one of these two...

<column-break/>

<note>The following is a translation of the second column, which contains the Latin version of the same text. Minor variations in phrasing reflect the Latin translator's style.</note>

<margin>A</margin> ...that the race of living beings consists of humans, many-footed animals, those lacking feet, those that move forward, and those that are stable, being fixed by roots. One must think the same everywhere: that although all are made of all types of bodies, there is a great deal of the solid and earthly nature in this kind. Another race of animals must be proposed, which can also be born and seen, and possesses a great deal of fire, though it also has small particles of earth, air, and everything else; therefore, we must say that diverse and visible animals are born from this. We think these are celestial animals, a divine race of stars, constituted with the <margin>B</margin> most beautiful body and a most blessed and excellent soul. We think one of two lots must be granted to both these types of animals. For either they are necessarily and entirely immortal and divine, without destruction, or they lead a long-lived life, sufficient for each, so that they do not need a longer one. Let us think of these as two types of living beings. And let us say again that both are visible, of which one seems to be entirely of fire, the other of earth. But the earthly is without order, while the fiery moves with every reason of order. That which is carried without order must be thought of as mindless, which is what the animals among us mostly do. But that which proceeds with order in the heaven is sufficiently <margin>C</margin> demonstrated by that track to have a mind, because it always proceeds through the same things and in a similar way, and acts and suffers the same things. The necessity of a soul having intellect is the greatest of all necessities; for it leads, and is not led, but governs. When the soul, which is the best thing, conducts itself with counsel according to the best intellect, then that which is truly perfected according to intellect will necessarily happen without persuasion, nor could "adamas" be more solid or immovable. But the three Fates <note>Latin: "Parcae"</note> surely preserve as perfect what each of the gods has deliberated with the best counsel. It was necessary, therefore, for it to be an argument for men that the stars and that entire circuit have a <margin>D</margin> mind, because they always do the same things. For in a very great and wonderful space of time, they have already deliberated what they must do. They do not approve now this, now that counsel, moving up and down. Therefore they neither wander nor are they revolved outside the ancient order. To many of us, however, it seemed the opposite: that because these things always do the same and similar things, they do not have a soul. The crowd, following this insane opinion, thought the human race had life and mind because it moves [erratically]; but the divine race, because it remains in the same motions, lacks a mind. But it was proper to feel more beautiful, better, and more pleasing things to the gods: that they have a mind for this very reason, because having set out in a similar way through the same things, they always do the same things. <margin>E</margin> This is the nature of the stars, most beautiful to the sight, which, using the best progression and dance—the most magnificent of all dances—provides benefits to all animals. That we do not undeservedly say these are animated, their size first testifies. For they are not only as large as they are seen to be; but each is of incredible magnitude. This must be believed because it is shown by sufficient demonstrations, by which we understand that the whole sun is larger than the whole earth, and whatever stars are carried have a wonderful magnitude. Let us think, therefore, how it can be that such a magnitude can be carried around by any nature for as much time as it is now carried. I therefore assert that God is the cause, and it cannot happen otherwise. <margin>F</margin> For it could not be made "ensouled" <note>Latin: "Animatum"</note> otherwise than because of God, as we have declared. Since therefore God can do that, it was easy for Him first to grant life and magnitude to every body; then to lead it by whatever reason He thought it would best be done. Finally, we want this true opinion to be held about all these things: it is impossible for the earth, the heaven, all the stars, and the masses that consist of these, to be revolved with such exquisite reason through years, months, and days—and to do all good things for us—unless a soul is either present with or within each one. It becomes a man, the viler he is, to trifle less about them, but rather to try to say something certain. If anyone says that some impulse of bodies, or natures, or <margin>G</margin> anything of this sort is the cause of this order and agitation, he will bring forward nothing clear. But let us again attentively consider what we said, so that it may be clear whether that speech is probable or lies entirely futile: in which it is first said that there are two things, soul and body; and there are many things that pertain to the race of each; and they differ from others in their own race, and both races are diverse from each other; so that there is nothing common to both. The soul differs from the body in that the former has a mind, the latter does not. The former dominates, the latter is subjected. The former is the cause of no passion <note>In the sense of "suffering" or "being acted upon"</note> in bodies, the latter is the cause of all. Wherefore, if anyone contends that the celestial things were made by anyone else, and do not <margin>H</margin> consist of soul and body, as we have said, he must be held entirely foolish and unskillful. Therefore, if the reasons brought forward in all these things are worth anything, and all these things are to be judged entirely divine, one must judge one of two things. For either we shall think these are gods—and most rightly indeed—or we shall believe them to be images of the gods, and as if statues fabricated by the most wise and worthy craftsmen, the gods themselves. Let us decree one of these two things, and that...

# PLATO

<margin>A</margin>...we have decreed, let us firmly hold: and let us venerate these images <note>original: *simulacra* / *ἀγάλματα*; referring to the stars as living statues of the gods</note> much more than any others. For never will there be found images more beautiful or more common to all mankind, nor located in more excellent places, excelling in purity, majesty, and perpetual life, than these which are similarly constructed on every side. But now let us also assert this concerning the gods. Since we have recognized two visible living beings: of which one is immortal, but the other, which is of the earth, is entirely mortal: let us now attempt to declare by probable reason the three out of five that have obtained the middle place. Let us place Aether after Fire, from which we think the soul generates living beings: which, just as happens in 
<margin>B</margin>other kinds, have most of their own nature, but a minimum of other kinds for the sake of a bond. After aether, another kind of living being from Air; and a third similarly fashioned by the soul from Water. When the soul has fashioned all these, it fills the whole heaven with living beings, having used all the kinds as far as possible, all of which participate in life. The second and third, fourth and fifth, beginning from the generation of the manifest gods, are finally led down to us men. Therefore, let one locate the gods Jupiter and Juno and all the others however 
<margin>C</margin>one wishes, provided he observes the same law and holds this stable reasoning. We must confess, then, that the visible gods are the greatest, most to be honored, seeing all things most sharply from every side, and are the first: the nature of the stars and those things which we perceive created with the stars. Next, however, beneath these, we ought to worship with prayers the daemons <note>In Greek philosophy, *daemons* are intermediary spirits between gods and humans, not "demons" in the modern sense.</note>, an aerial race, located in the third and middle region, who exist for the sake of interpretation, by grace of their laudable intercession and interpretation. Of these indeed there are two: one of the living beings is from aether, the other next from air. And neither can be seen in its entirety: but although these daemons are near us, they never 
<margin>D</margin>appear manifest to us. They are participants in wonderful prudence: indeed, with sharp intellect and tenacious memory, they know all our thoughts. They wonderfully love honorable and good men, and vehemently hate the wicked, inasmuch as they are participants in pain. But God, who perhaps possesses the divine lot perfectly, is free from pains and pleasures, and enjoys wisdom and cognition thoroughly. Since, however, the heaven is filled with living beings, both the highest gods and the daemons interpret one another. For the middle beings are carried with light motion both to the earth and to the heaven. The fifth, which is from water, we shall rightly call a demigod. It is sometimes seen, sometimes withdraws itself from our sight, and when it is seen, perceived by a faint vision, it brings admiration. Since, therefore, there are these five living beings, which—whether encountered in dreams, or by prophecy and 
<margin>E</margin>hearing through a voice perceived by the ears of the healthy or the sick, or even offering themselves to us at the very departure from life—move our souls, whence many sacred rites for many have been instituted both privately and publicly by these opinions, and will be instituted in the future: the legislator of all these, who has even the least bit of mind, will never innovate anything else. For he will take care lest he turn his city toward a new cult of less certain religion. Nor will he dare to move what has been established by ancestral law or custom concerning sacrifice. For he ought to know that it is not possible for mortal nature to know anything certain about these matters. By the same reasoning, those are to be held as the worst who do not preach the gods truly manifest to the eyes, and who allow them to be left by men without 
<margin>F</margin>sacrifices and due honors. For they act just as if someone sees the Sun and Moon illuminating all things, and sees them held in no honor, yet is unwilling for his own manly part to make these clear to men so that solemn days and sacrifices might be performed for them, and certain distributions of times of greater and lesser years often be assigned. Would he not be called evil both to himself and to everyone who knows him, if it were so said? CLIN. Why not, Guest? Indeed, among the worst. ATHEN. Know now, O friend Clinias, that this very thing has happened to me. CLIN. In what way? ATH. Know that there are eight powers in heaven, sisters to one another, which I have looked upon, and I have done nothing great, for this is easy for anyone. Three of these are these: one of the sun, one of the moon, one of all the stars of which we spoke before, and five others. All these and 
<margin>G</margin>those who are in them, whether they proceed by themselves or are carried in vehicles, let no one think of them in such a way that some of them are gods and others not at all, or some legitimate and others such as it is a sin to speak of: but let us say they are all brothers, living in brotherly lots, and let us render honors to them: not to one a year, to another a month, and to another no lot or time in which it runs its circle, completing together the world and its ornament, which the most divine reason of all established as visible. The happy man first admires this exceedingly, then burns with a desire to learn those things which can be perceived by mortal nature: thus judging that he will live best and most happily: and when he has departed, he will come to places congruent with virtue. And thus truly initiated, and he himself truly one...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>...and those things which have been established must be honored above all images. For never may more beautiful or more common images appear to all men, nor established in more excellent places, differing in purity and majesty and in all life, than these, as they have been made in every way. Now then, let us attempt [to speak] of the gods by such fortune: having observed the two living beings visible to us, which we say, the one, immortal, the other, earthly, has become entirely mortal; the three middle ones of the five between these, let us try to speak of them most clearly according to reasonable opinion. For let us place aether after fire, and let us suppose the soul fashions from it living beings having power, just as of 
<margin>B</margin>other living beings, the greater part from its own nature, but the smaller parts, for the sake of a bond, from the other kinds. After the aether, the soul fashions from air another race of living beings; and the third, from water. Having fashioned all these, it is likely the soul filled the whole heaven with living beings, having used all the races according to its power, all having become participants in living; but the second and third and fourth and fifth, beginning their generation from the manifest gods, end in us humans. Concerning the gods then, Zeus and Hera and all the others, however one wishes, let him place them according to the same law, and let him hold this 
<margin>C</margin>account as firm. For the visible gods, the greatest and most honorable, and seeing most sharply everywhere, these must be said to be of the nature of the stars, and whatever things we perceive have come to be with them. After these, and next under these, the daemons, an aerial race, having the third and middle seat, the cause of interpretation, whom it is very necessary to honor for the sake of their auspicious passage. Two of these living beings, that of aether and next that of air, are not seen as a whole, each being present nearby, they do not become manifest to us; but participating in wonderful wisdom, being of a race quick to learn and mindful, let us say they know our whole thought; and 
<margin>D</margin>that they wonderfully welcome the beautiful and good among us, and hate the exceedingly evil, as already participating in pain. For God, having the end of the divine lot, is outside of these, both pain and pleasure; but has shared in thinking and knowing in all things. And the whole heaven having become full of life, they interpret to one another and to all the highest gods and all things, because the middle of the living beings are carried both to the earth and to the whole heaven, carried with a light rush. The fifth, being of water, one might liken to a demigod, likening it correctly, as having come from it. And at times it is seen, but at other times it is hidden and becomes obscure, providing a wonder by a dim sight. Of these five truly existing living beings, wherever any of us have encountered them, either meeting them in sleep in dream-interpretation, or spoken in rumors and prophecies heard by those 
<margin>E</margin>healthy or sick, or meeting them at the end of life, opinions having arisen both privately and publicly; whence many sacred rites of many have arisen, and 
<margin>E</margin>others will arise; of all these, a legislator who possesses even the shortest mind will never dare to innovate, to turn his city toward a worship of gods which has nothing clear. And indeed he will not prohibit those things which the ancestral law has spoken concerning sacrifices, knowing nothing at all [to the contrary]; just as it is not possible for mortal nature to know about such things. Regarding those who are truly manifest gods to us, does not the same argument hold that it is most evil and 
<margin>F</margin>daring to say we should make them manifest, while they are without rites from others, and not receiving the honors belonging to them? But now it happens that such a thing occurs, as if one of us having seen the sun or moon looking upon all of us, and not to speak of it, being somehow unable to speak, and they being at once without honor, and not being cared for by those who, bringing them into a visible place, make festivals and sacrifices for them; and distributing the times of the seasons for each, both greater and lesser, often in a year; would he not be called evil to himself and to another who knows, and be said to be so with justice? CLIN. How could he not, O guest? 
<margin>G</margin>Most evil indeed. ATHEN. This then, O dear Clinias, know is clearly happening to me now. CLIN. How do you mean? ATHEN. You know eight powers have come to be around the whole heaven, sisters of one another, which I have observed. And I have accomplished nothing great. For it is easy for another too. Of these, three are these: one, of the sun; one, of the moon; one, of all the stars which we mentioned a little before; and five others. All these and those in these, whether they go themselves or are carried, traveling in vehicles; let no one of us ever think otherwise than that some of them are gods and others not; nor that some are legitimate, and others such as it is not even lawful for any of us to say. But let us all say and affirm that all are brothers and in brotherly lots; and let us render honors, not to one a year, to another a month; and to the others let us not assign no lot, nor any time, in which it traverses its own pole, completing together the world-order which reason, the most

<meta>This page continues the philosophical dialogue of the *Epinomis* (attributed to Plato), specifically discussing the origins of astronomy and the divine nature of the planets. The translation reconciles the Greek and Latin columns into a single English narrative.</meta>

# EPINOMIS

<margin>A</margin> Having attained a single wisdom, one spends the remainder of time in the contemplation of the most beautiful things that can be seen. Now, we must speak of what follows this, and it is a matter of great importance. For we shall never be found false if we define it firmly as follows: I say again, there are eight powers—we have spoken of three, and five remain. The fourth and fifth orbits and paths are almost equal in speed to the sun, being neither slower nor faster. <gloss>original: ῖν δὲ ὀκτὼ / in de okto</gloss> One must always consider the Mind as the sufficient leader of these three. I speak of the Sun, the Morning Star <note>Lucifer/Venus</note>, and a third which cannot be named because it is not known. The reason for this is that the first person to observe these things was a Barbarian <note>In this context, "Barbarian" refers to non-Greeks, specifically those from the East.</note>. For an ancient region nourished those who first noticed these things because of the beauty of the summer season, for which Egypt and Syria are well-famed; there, all the stars are visible, so to speak, at all times, since clouds and rains <margin>B</margin> are always far removed from the view of the world. From there, these observations have spread everywhere, including here, having been tested by time for ten thousand years or even an infinite duration. Therefore, one should be bold in establishing these things into laws; for to think that divine things are not to be honored, or that these are not divine, would clearly be the height of madness. As for why they lacked names, the reason has been stated, but they have received the sacred titles of gods. For the Morning Star, which is the same as the Evening Star, belongs to Aphrodite <note>Venus</note>; this is a name very fitting for the Syrian author of these names. The star that runs at almost the same speed <margin>C</margin> as the Sun and this one is that of Hermes <note>Mercury</note>. There remain three more orbits of those moving to the right along with the Moon and the Sun. One must speak of the eighth as well, which one might most rightly call the "Upper World," which moves contrary to the others and carries them with it, as it appears to men who know little of these things. But we must say what we know sufficiently. For true wisdom appears in this way to one who has shared even a small portion of right and divine intelligence. There remain three stars: one of them is the slowest of all, which some call by the name of Phainon <note>Saturn</note>; the one after this in slowness is Phaethon <note>Jupiter</note>; and the one after that is Pyroeis <note>Mars</note>, which has the reddest color of all. <margin>D</margin> It is not difficult for anyone to understand these things if someone explains them; but once learned, as we say, one must hold them to be healthy truths.

Every Greek man should also consider this: that the region we Greeks inhabit is the best suited for virtue. The praise of this land lies in the fact that it is midway between the winter and the summer natures. Because we are further from the summer serenity than the Barbarians, as we said, it was later that we understood the order of these gods. But let us take it as a rule that whatever the Greeks receive from the Barbarians, they bring it to a more beautiful perfection in the end. And so, regarding what we are now discussing, we must think the same: though it is difficult to discover all such things beyond dispute, there is a great and noble hope that the Greeks will honor all these gods in a more beautiful and more just way than the rumors and worship that came from the Barbarians, using both the education and the oracles from Delphi <margin>E</margin> in all lawful worship.

Let no Greek ever fear that mortals should not busy themselves with divine matters. Rather, one should think the exact opposite: that the Divine is never without mind, nor is it ignorant of human nature. Instead, God knows that if He teaches, men will follow and learn what is taught. That He teaches us this very thing—number and how to count—He surely knows. For it would be the most mindless thing of all if He were ignorant of this, or if He were angry with those capable of learning rather than rejoicing without envy when they become good through God.

There is a long and beautiful argument that when men first had thoughts about the gods—how they <margin>F</margin> came to be, what they were like, and what actions they performed—these things were not spoken of in a way pleasing to the prudent, nor even by those who came second. Among those, the oldest things were said to be fire, water, and other bodies, while the wonderful Soul was thought to be later. They thought the motion of the body was more powerful and honorable because it carried itself by heat, cold, and such things, rather than the Soul carrying both the body and itself. But now, when we say that if the Soul is in a body, it is no wonder that it moves and carries both that body and itself, our Soul does not doubt in any way that it can carry any weight. Therefore, since we now claim that the Soul is the cause of the whole and of all good things, <margin>G</margin> and that other things are the cause of the base, we say the Soul is the cause of all path and motion. Motion toward the good belongs to the best Soul, while motion toward the opposite is the opposite. The good must have conquered and must continue to conquer those things that are not good.

All these things have been said by us according to the justice that punishes the ungodly. As for what is now being proven: it must be known and said that a good man must be called wise. Let us see if we can attain this wisdom we have long sought through some discipline or art; for if we are ignorant of it, we shall be unskilled and ignorant of justice. So it seems to me, and so it must be said. <margin>H</margin> What I have discovered by searching up and down, I will try to reveal to you in speech. For the greatest virtue has been neglected, which has been the cause of our ignorance, as what I have just said seems to signify. Let no one ever persuade us that there is a virtue greater than piety <note>original: εὐσεβείας / eusebeias</note> toward God.

It emphasizes that the Soul is the primary mover of all things and that piety is the highest human virtue.</summary>

# PLATO

<column-break/>

anyone should persuade themselves that such a nature can be found in any other class. This failure has not occurred in the best natures because of some inherent flaw, but out of the greatest ignorance. Now, the best natures are those which are found most rarely, and whenever they are found, they are of the greatest benefit. Certainly, that soul is of a gentle disposition which possesses a slow and contrary nature in a mild and moderate way; it admires courage and loves temperance, and what is most important in these natures, it is quick to learn and possesses a good memory. It takes the greatest delight in such things, being devoted to the study of learning. These qualities do not easily arise together, and when they have arisen, if they receive suitable education and discipline, they can moderate and restrain many inferior people. Thus, by thinking, speaking, and acting in every detail toward the gods as is proper, and when it is proper—in sacrifices and purifications concerning those things done toward gods and men—they may cultivate virtue most greatly, not in pretense, but in truth, which is the most useful thing of all for a city. We assert, therefore, that this part of nature is the most sovereign, and that it can learn as much and as well as possible if someone teaches it. However, no one will teach unless God helps. Indeed, from one who does not observe the proper measure in teaching, it is better not to learn; yet it seems necessary from what has just been said to learn these things, and for this best nature to be described by us. Therefore, let us attempt to explain what and of what sort these things are, and how they are to be learned thoroughly; and let this be done according to my strength in discoursing, and for those who will be able to hear how certain parts of divine worship may be learned. You will perhaps hear something unusual, yet let us state the name of the thing, which no one would expect because of their lack of skill in this matter. Do not be ignorant that Astronomy is something most wise.
<margin>Praise and dignity of Astronomy.</margin>
Indeed, it is necessary to be a true astronomer—not the one who, according to Hesiod <note>The Greek poet Hesiod's "Works and Days" focused on practical farming calendars based on stars.</note> and all such men, merely considers the setting and rising of stars—but rather the one who understands the eight circuits, and how the seven are revolved under the first, and in what order each completes its own circles. No nature, unless it be marvelous, will ever easily look into this, as we have just said and shall say, declaring what is necessary and how one ought to learn. First, then, let it be said that the Moon evolves its circle most swiftly, and thus completes the first full moon and the month. Next, the Sun must be observed, which effects the solstices and the turnings of the seasons by its circuit; furthermore, those who run together with the Sun must be considered. Finally, lest we discourse too often on the same things, we must contemplate all the courses which we touched upon a little while ago, which are not easily understood. Thus, natures must first be prepared for these things by doctrines pertaining to them through long use and labor from youth, or rather even from childhood. Wherefore, there is need of the doctrines which are called mathematical. First and foremost is the study of numbers: I do not mean those numbers which have a body <note>i.e., concrete counting of objects</note>, but those which concern the whole generation and power of the even and the odd, which they contribute toward perfecting and knowing the nature of things. After these must be mentioned that which they quite ridiculously call Geometry <note>literally "earth-measurement"</note>. The foundation of numbers that are naturally dissimilar to one another becomes clear when referred to the category of planes. This indeed should seem not a human, but a divine miracle, if anyone clearly understands it. After this, numbers which are increased up to three dimensions, similar to solid nature, and again dissimilar, are to be considered by another similar art, namely stereometry <note>the measurement of solid figures</note>; but those who have dealt with it only in passing have also called this Geometry. That which is wonderful and divine must be understood: how the power of things is always formed by nature revolving in the double and in its opposite. Thus, the first power of the double according to number proceeds by the ratio of one to two, possessing the double in potential. But into the solid and tangible, the ratio of the double proceeds again from one to eight; and another double into the middle: but perhaps the greater is equal to the lesser, and the lesser to the greater. Truly, another exceeds the extremes by the same part, and is exceeded by them. In the middle of the sequence from six to twelve, the "one-and-a-half" <note>sesquialtera: the 3:2 ratio</note> and "one-and-a-third" <note>sesquitertia: the 4:3 ratio</note> proportions emerged; the power of these in the middle, turning from both sides, assigned to men a harmonious use and proportion, for the sake of play, rhythm, and temporal number, granted by the happy dance of the Muses. Let these things, then, be so and remain so; the end of these is that we may apply ourselves to the consideration of the divine generation, and the most beautiful and divine nature of those things seen with the eyes, insofar as God has granted this to be inspected by men—which we shall never attain without the aforementioned arts. To these, each individual thing must be referred to its species, and finally all things to the One in discussions, by questioning and refuting if anything is said incorrectly. For such an examination is rightly the most beautiful and first of all things for men. But where there is not truly such an inquiry, but a futile one, the effort is in vain. Furthermore, the order of times must be considered, how exactly it perfects all celestial things, so that whoever believes it was truly said that the soul is older and more divine than the body, may think it also excellently and sufficiently said that all things are full of gods: so much so that the powers above neither forget our affairs nor desert us. But this must be observed in all these things: they will be of great benefit to him who perceives them rightly; but to him who does not receive them rightly, they will not.

<column-break/>

<meta>This page concludes the philosophical discussion found in the Epinomis (often attributed to Plato) and begins the collection of Plato's Epistles (Letters). The previous page likely discussed the preliminary requirements for wisdom.</meta>

<margin>A</margin> one must always call upon a better god. The manner is this—for it is necessary to explain at least this much. Every geometrical diagram, every system of number, every composition of harmony, and the single conspiracy <note>original: *homologia* / *conspiratio* - meaning a unified agreement or structural harmony</note> of the revolutions of the stars, must be made manifest to the one who learns in the proper manner. And it will be made manifest, we say, if one learns while looking correctly toward a single point. For a single bond of all these things will appear to those who reflect upon them. But if anyone handles these matters in any other way, he must call it "luck," as we often say. For without these things, no nature will ever become happy in cities. But this is the way, this is the education, these are the studies; whether they be difficult or easy, this is the path one must travel. It is not lawful to neglect the gods, now that the happy report of all these things has become manifest to all through the proper reason. <margin>B</margin> The one who has grasped all these things in this way, I call the most truly wise. Of him I assert, both in jest and in earnest, that when such a man fulfills his destiny in death, he will—if indeed he is still dead—no longer participate in many senses as he does now, but having attained a single destiny alone, and having become one out of many, he will be happy, most wise, and blessed all at once. Whether he lives a blessed life on the continents or in the islands, he will always participate in such a fate; and whether he pursues these things in public or in private life, he will receive the same from the gods. <margin>C</margin> What we said at the beginning is now present as a truly real argument: that it is not possible for men to become perfectly blessed and happy, except for a few. These things are rightly said. For as many as are divine and temperate at once, sharing by nature in the other virtues, and who have additionally grasped everything that belongs to a blessed education (which we have described), to these alone have the things of the divine been sufficiently allotted. To those who have thus labored in these things, we say both privately and publicly that a law should be established: that when they reach the end <note>i.e., old age</note>, the greatest offices of state must be handed over to them. The others should follow them and praise all the gods and goddesses together; and we most rightly exhort everyone to invite the "Nocturnal Council" <note>A governing body described in Plato's *Laws*</note> to this wisdom, once we have sufficiently recognized and tested them.

# PLATO’S
## EPISTLES.

### DION TO DIONYSIUS:
### MAY YOU FARE WELL. First Letter.

<margin>D</margin> Having spent so much time with you, and having been entrusted with the administration of your empire, I endured bitter slanders while you, above all others, were receiving the benefits of my service. For I knew that with me assisting you, no cruel act would seem to have been done with your willing consent; indeed, all those who governed with you are my witnesses. Many of them I helped in their struggles, releasing them from no small penalties. Though I frequently guarded your city as its commander <note>original: *autokrator*</note>, I was sent away more dishonorably than is fitting for you to dismiss even a beggar, being ordered to sail away after <margin>E</margin> spending so much time in your service. Therefore, for the future, I shall deliberate on a more solitary <note>original: *apanthropoteron* - literally "away from humans"</note> way of life; and you, being such a tyrant, shall dwell alone. As for the "splendid" gold which you gave for the journey, Bacchius, the bearer of this letter, is bringing it back to you. For it was neither sufficient for his travel expenses, nor is it useful for the rest of life; it would provide the greatest disgrace to the giver, and not much less to me, the receiver. Therefore, I do not accept it; to you, clearly, it makes no difference whether you give or receive such an amount. So, having taken it back, use it to serve some other of your companions as you served me—for I have been "served" by you quite enough. And I may well quote the line of Euripides: that when other troubles eventually befall you, <margin>F</margin> you will pray for such a man to stand by your side.
I wish to remind you that most other tragic poets, when they introduce a tyrant dying at someone's hand, make him cry out:
> "Alas, wretched me! I perish for lack of friends!"
But no poet has ever depicted one perishing for a lack of gold. That poem also seems not bad to those who have sense: "Not shining gold, so rare in the hopeless life of mortals, nor adamant, nor silver couches, flash before the eyes as the light of men's esteem; nor do the fertile fields of the wide earth suffice for life as much as the like-minded <margin>G</margin> wisdom of good men." Farewell; and realize how much you have failed us, so that you may conduct yourself better toward others.

# PLATO TO DIONYSIUS, WE WISH YOU WELL.
## ΠΛΑΤΩΝ ΔΙΟΝΥΣΙΩ ΕΥ ΠΡΑΤΤΕΙΝ.

->REGARDING EPISTLE II.<-
->Second.<-

---

<margin>A</margin>
I have heard from Archedemus <note>A messenger and associate of Archytas of Tarentum</note> that you believe not only I, but also my associates—with the sole exception of Dion—ought to neither say nor do anything evil against you. However, this exception you make regarding Dion shows that I do not have authority over my own associates. For if I held authority over the others, as well as over Dion and yourself, many great benefits would, I believe, result for all of you and for the rest of the Greeks. But as it stands, <margin>B</margin> I am "great" only in this: that I keep myself obedient to my own reason. I say these things because Cratistolus and Polyxenus have reported nothing sincere to you. One of them is said to claim he heard at the Olympic games many of those who were with me speaking ill of you. Perhaps his hearing is sharper than mine, for I heard no such thing. It seems to me that hereafter, whenever such a report is brought to you, you ought to write to me and investigate the matter itself. For I shall neither dread nor blush to confess the truth. Between you and me, the situation is such that neither of us is unknown (to speak freely) to any of the Greeks, <margin>C</margin> nor will men of this age remain silent about our friendship; and be certain of this: posterity will not be silent either. Such are those who know of it, for it is neither small nor obscure. Why do I say this? I shall reveal it immediately, beginning the matter from a somewhat deeper point. By a law of nature, wisdom and great power tend toward the same goal. These two always affect, pursue, and come together with one another. Furthermore, men take great delight in these things, whenever they hear or tell of them in the songs of poets or in private conversations: just as when men speak of Hieron <note>Tyrant of Syracuse</note> and Pausanias the Lacedaemonian <note>Spartan general</note>, they rejoice to commemorate the friendship of Simonides <note>The lyric poet</note> which existed with them, and to relate what he said and did among them. Similarly, they are accustomed to celebrate together Periander of Corinth and Thales of Miletus; Pericles and Anaxagoras; and again Croesus and Solon as wise men, and Cyrus as a powerful ruler. Indeed, the poets, imitating these things, bring together Creon and Tiresias; Polyidus and Minos; Agamemnon and Nestor; Ulysses and Palamedes; and as it seems to me, for the same reason the men of old joined Prometheus to Jupiter <note>original: "Ioui" (Zeus)</note>. Of these, they depict some in agreement and others in disagreement; some at times harmonious and at other times discordant. They sing of their dissensions as much as their agreements. I have said all these things <margin>E</margin> to show that even when we are dead, men will not be silent about us. Therefore, we must not be negligent, but must take care for the time to follow. For it happens by a certain nature that the most base men care nothing for what their future reputation may be, while the most excellent men do everything so that they may be well-spoken of among men in future ages. From this I make the conjecture that there is some perception for those who have died of the things that happen in this life. For the best souls divine <note>original: "divinant" (prophesy/intuit)</note> that this is so, while the worst do not. The presages of divine men are stronger than those of others. I think that if it were permitted for those deceased predecessors of whom I speak to amend their own associations, they would apply the greatest effort to ensure that better opinions were circulated about them than are now. This we are still permitted to do, God willing; and if anything <margin>F</margin> in our past friendship was a mistake, we may amend and correct it in both deed and word. Indeed, I say this: there will be a true opinion (especially regarding philosophy) about us, such that if we are good, we shall have a good reputation, and if bad, a bad one. In caring for these things, we could do nothing more pious; and in neglecting them, nothing so impious and profane. How this should be done, and how it may be done justly, I shall now say. When I came to Sicily, the rumor was that I excelled greatly among those who then practiced philosophy. I desired, when I had come to Syracuse, to have you as a witness to that opinion, so that philosophy might be held in honor by the multitude. But that matter <margin>G</margin> did not turn out successfully for me. I say the cause of this was not what most people thought, but I assert the cause was this: that you did not seem to trust me enough, but seemed to want to dismiss me in a way, and to call for others, and to inquire what my business was—doubting me, as it appeared. And those who spoke of these things were many, affirming that you indeed despised me and had turned your mind to other things. This rumor then spread abroad. Now hear what ought to be done hereafter, so that I may answer what you asked: in what way we ought to behave toward one another. If you utterly despise philosophy, let us bid it farewell. But if you have either heard from another or found for yourself better things than those handed down by me, embrace those. But if our teachings please you, you ought to honor me most of all. Now, as if from the beginning, you lead the way and I shall follow. For if honored by you, I shall honor you; but if not honored, I shall remain quiet. Furthermore, if you begin to honor me first,

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
I heard from Archedemus that you think it necessary for not only me to keep quiet, but also my associates, from doing or saying anything slighting about you. But you make Dion the only exception. This statement—leaving Dion as an exception—implies that I rule over my associates. For if I ruled over the others and you and Dion in such a way, more good things would have come to all of you and the other Greeks, as I say. But now I am great only in this: presenting myself as following my own reason. And I say these things because Cratistolus and Polyxenus <margin>B</margin> have told you something false. One of whom they say claims that he would hear at Olympia many of those with me accusing you. For perhaps he hears more sharply than I; for I heard nothing. It is necessary, as it seems to me, to act thus for the future: whenever someone says such a thing, always send a letter to ask me. For I will not hesitate to speak the truth, nor am I ashamed. Indeed, the things between us are coming to be in this way: neither are we ourselves unknown to any of the Greeks, so to speak, nor will our association <margin>C</margin> be silenced. Let it not escape you that it will not be silenced in the time hereafter. Such are those who have laid hold of it, that it is known neither by few nor slightly. Why then do I say these things? I will tell you, starting from the beginning. It is natural for wisdom and great power to come together into the same place; and these always pursue, seek, and associate with one another. Then also men rejoice in these things, both talking about them themselves and hearing others in private associations and in poetry. Just as when men talk about Hieron and Pausanias the Lacedaemonian, they rejoice in bringing up the association of Simonides with them, and what he did and said to them; and they are accustomed to hymn Periander the Corinthian and Thales the Milesian together; and Pericles and Anaxagoras; and Croesus again and Solon, as wise men; and Cyrus as a ruler. And indeed, the poets, imitating these things, bring together Creon and Tiresias, Polyidus and Minos, Agamemnon and Nestor, and Odysseus and Palamedes. And as it seems to me, the first men [joined] Prometheus to Zeus in this same advocacy. Of these, they sing of some coming into differences and others into friendship with one another; and some at times into friendship and at times into differences; and at times agreeing and at times differing. I say all these things wanting to show this: that when we have died, the talk about us will not also cease. So it must be cared for. For it is necessary, as it seems, for us to care for the time hereafter, since by some nature <margin>E</margin> the most slavish men think nothing of it, but the most decent do everything so that they may be well-spoken of in the time hereafter. Which I take as evidence that there is some perception for the dead of things here. For the best souls divine that these things are so, but the most wretched say they are not. And the divinations of divine men are more authoritative than those of the non-divine. I think that if it were possible for those before, if they could correct their own associations, they would be entirely eager so that better things would be said about them than now. This then is still possible for us with God's help, if indeed the previous associations were not well done or <margin>F</margin> spoken, to correct them in both deed and word. For as I say, there will be a true opinion of philosophy; nevertheless, it is reasonable that the better will be distinguished from the base, and vice versa. And yet, if we are always caring for this, we would be doing nothing more holy; nor if neglecting it, anything more impious. How these things must happen, and where the justice lies, I will tell. I came to Sicily having a reputation for differing much in philosophy; and wanting to come to Syracuse, I took you as a co-witness, so that philosophy might be honored by me even among the multitude. But this did not fall to my lot. And I do not say the cause is what many would say, but that you appeared not to trust me at all, but to want to send me away somehow, and to send for others, and to seek what my business was; distrusting me, as it <margin>G</margin> seems to me. And those shouting about these things were many, saying that I was despised by you, and you cared for other things. These things having been spread, hear what is just to do after this; so that I may also answer what you ask, how it is necessary for me and you to be toward one another. If you have altogether despised philosophy, let it go. But if you have heard from another, or found better things yourself than those from me, honor those. But if the things from us please you, you must honor me most of all. Now then, as from the beginning, you lead and I will follow. Being honored by you, I will honor you; but not being honored, I will keep quiet. Furthermore, if you begin to honor me, and in the pursuit of this—

<meta>This page continues the translation of the pseudo-Platonic Epistles, specifically the Second Letter addressed to Dionysius II, the tyrant of Syracuse. The text transitions from a discussion of philosophical reputation to the famous "riddle" of the three kings and the dangers of writing down secret doctrines.</meta>

# EPISTLES

...friend, you would seem to honor philosophy, and this very thing that you were considering, as well as other matters, would gain you a reputation among many as being a philosopher. But if I honor you while you do not honor me, I would seem to be admiring and pursuing the reputation of wealth; this name [of wealth-seeker] does not have a good reputation among all people. To speak in summary: if you honor me, it is an ornament to both; but if I honor you, it is a reproach to both. For such things are never as they should be. Regarding the little sphere <note>original: "σφαιρίον" (sphairion). Likely a mathematical or astronomical model</note>, it is not correctly constructed. Archedemus will explain it to you when he arrives. And indeed, concerning those things which are more precious and divine than this, about which he says you asked me, they must be shown to him with great care. <margin>B</margin> For you say, as he reports, that the nature of the "First Principle" <note>original: "τοῦ πρώτου φύσεως" (tou protou physeos)</note> has not been sufficiently demonstrated to you by me. I must therefore speak to you in riddles, so that if anything should happen to this tablet in the folds of the sea or the land, the one who reads it may not understand it. For it is thus:

->**Concerning the King of all, all things exist, and all things are for his sake. And he is the cause of all beautiful things. Second things are around the second, and third things around the third.**<-

The human soul longs to learn what sort of things these are, looking toward those things akin to itself, none of which are sufficient. But concerning the King and the things I mentioned, there is nothing of that sort. After this, the soul asks: "But what sort of thing is it then?" This is the question, O son of Dionysius and Doris <margin>C</margin>, which is the cause of all evils—or rather, the labor-pain concerning this which arises in the soul. Unless a man is rid of this, he will never truly attain the truth. You said to me in the garden under the laurels that you had thought this out yourself and it was your own discovery. And I said that if it appeared so to you, you would have released me from many long arguments. However, I said I had never found any other discoverer of this, and that my own great investigation always revolves around it. But perhaps you, having heard it from someone else or perhaps by some divine fate, reached it, and then, thinking you held the demonstrations firmly, you did not secure them, but let them drift—sometimes one way, sometimes another—according to how your imagination struck you. But the truth is nothing of that sort. And this has happened not to you alone; <margin>D</margin> but know for certain that no one who hears me for the first time is affected otherwise at the beginning. Some having more trouble, others less, they barely escape the labor; almost no one does so with little effort.

These things being so, we have found, I think, what you requested in your letter: how we ought to behave toward one another. For after you have tested these things by meeting with others and comparing them with the opinions of others, if the test is true, these doctrines will grow onto you, and you will be a kinsman to them and to us. How then will these and all the things we have said not come to pass? You did well to send Archedemus now; <margin>E</margin> and for the future, when he returns to you and reports my views, other difficulties will perhaps seize you. You will then send Archedemus back to me again, if you are wise. He will be like a merchant <note>original: "ἔμπορος" (emporos). Plato uses the metaphor of a merchant of knowledge</note> returning with a cargo. And if you do this two or three times, and sufficiently test the things sent from me, I would be surprised if your present difficulties do not differ greatly from what they are now. Act boldly in this. For neither you nor Archedemus will ever engage in a more noble or god-pleasing "merchandise" than this.

Take care, however, that these things never fall among uneducated men. For in my opinion, there are almost no teachings more ridiculous to the many than these, nor, on the other hand, any more wonderful and inspiring to those of noble nature. <margin>F</margin> Often repeated and always heard for many years, they are at last, like gold, purified with great labor. Listen to what is marvelous about this: there are many people who have heard these things—capable of learning, capable of remembering, and able to judge after testing them in every way—who are now old men and have been listening for no less than thirty years; they now say that what once seemed most incredible to them now seems most credible and clear, and what then seemed most certain now seems the opposite. Looking to this, take care lest <margin>G</margin> you ever repent of what has now been unworthily cast out. The greatest safeguard is not to write, but to learn by heart. For it is not possible for what is written not to get out. For this reason, I have never written anything about these matters; nor is there any written work of Plato's, nor will there be. What are now called his are the works of Socrates, become beautiful and young <note>A famous and controversial passage suggesting Plato's dialogues are actually idealized versions of Socratic thought</note>. Farewell, and believe us. And this letter, after you have read it many times, burn it. So much for that.

Regarding Polyxenus, you wondered why I did not send him. I say the same thing now as I did long ago about Lycophron and the others with you: that in the art of discourse and method, you far surpass him; <margin>H</margin> and none of them willingly allows himself to be refuted, as some suspect, but they are refuted against their will. You seem to have treated them quite humanely and honored them with gifts. As for Philistion, if you have use for him, use him; but if possible, let Speusippus use his services and send him back. Speusippus also needs you. Philistion promised me that if you let him go, he would come eagerly to Athens. It was noble of you to release the man from the stone quarries. My request is light, as it concerns his relatives...

# PLATO

<margin>A</margin> To Hegesippus, son of Ariston. For you also wrote to me: if anyone should ever wish to do injury to this man or those others, and you should perceive it, you would by no means permit it. Furthermore, concerning Lysiclides, it is proper to speak the truth. Indeed, he alone of those who traveled from Sicily to Athens has changed nothing in his familiarity with you and me. But those things which have been done, he honors daily with words to the best of his ability.

### TO THE SAME.
## EPISTLE III.

<margin>B</margin> **Y**OU ASK whether it is more correctly placed in salutations for "Plato to wish Dionysius joy," <note>original: "gaudere" / Greek: "chairein"</note> or as I have been accustomed to write to friends, "To do well." <note>original: "Bene agere" / Greek: "eu prattein"</note> You indeed, as those say who were present with you at Delphi, addressed the God himself flatteringly in this way, and wrote similarly: "Joy to you, and maintain the pleasant life of a tyrant." I, however, would salute neither a God nor a man in this manner. Not a God: because I would speak contrary to his nature. For the divinity is far removed from distress and pleasure. Not a man: because pleasure more often brings detriment and pain to him, producing dullness in the soul, and forgetfulness, folly, and insolence. And regarding the salutation, let these things be said by me. Which, after you have read them, you may take as you wish. But not a few people say that you were accustomed to tell certain ambassadors, while they
<margin>C</margin> approached you, that you had it in mind to restore the Greek cities in Sicily: and to relieve the Syracusans, and to introduce a royal government to them instead of a tyranny. But that I, hearing these things, prevented you from professing them, even though you vehemently desired it. Now, however, you say that I am teaching Dion to do those very things: and that by your own inventions and arts, your empire is being undermined by us. Whether such speeches bring you any utility, you yourself know; certainly you do me an injury when you say things contrary to the truth. And
<margin>D</margin> indeed, enough and more than enough envy has been stirred up against me until now by Philistides and many others, both among the soldiers and among the Syracusans. For while I lived in the citadel together with you, all wrongdoings were turned against me, those who were outside asserting that you did every single thing by my counsel. Although you clearly know that I handled very few things concerning civil government with you of my own accord, and that only at the beginning, while I thought I could make some progress, and certain other small matters, caring moderately and modestly for the prefaces of the laws. <note>Plato refers to his work on the "Laws," where he advocated for persuasive introductions to legislation.</note> Which things, however, I hear that afterwards either you or someone else inserted contrary to my mind. Those who are able to discern the character of our genius will easily distinguish these. But as I was just saying,
<margin>E</margin> I do not need calumny among the Syracusans and others, with which you charge me by saying such things; but much more do I need a defense against the first calumny, and against the new one recently arisen, which is indeed greater and more vehement. Therefore, against two calumnies it is necessary for me to bring a double excuse. First, indeed, that I deservedly refused to deal with you concerning the government of the republic; second, that it was not my counsel, as you say, to persuade you not to restore the Greek cities. And first, concerning the first point, receive it thus. I came to Syracuse called by you and by Dion: since Dion himself was of great dignity with you, and had long been my
<margin>F</margin> host, being of middle and mature age: which things anyone even moderately prudent would think necessary for carrying out such affairs as yours were. You, however, were quite young: and ignorant of all those things of which you ought to have had experience, and also very little known to me. After these things, whether some man, or a god, or some fortune drove Dion away from you, you were left alone. Do you think, then, that any sharing of civil affairs was left to me then: when I saw a prudent counselor driven away by you, and you, imprudent, left with many shameful men in such a way that you did not rule, though you thought you ruled, but were in truth a slave to such men? Then, therefore, what was it necessary for me to do? Was it not that which I did? To abstain,
namely, from all government, lest I be called into the calumnies of the malevolent by their envy. And to strive altogether for this, that I might bring you, who were mutually distrustful
<margin>G</margin> and far divided, back into your former friendship and favor. You may consider yourself my witness as to how much effort was undertaken by me in this business, and never abandoned. At last we barely agreed that I should return home (since you were hindered by war), and that once peace was made, Dion and I should return to Syracuse: and you would call us back. These things were done in that first journey of mine to you, and in my return to my fatherland. Then, peace having been made, you called me again: not, however, as we had mutually agreed together with Dion, but alone. For you wrote that I should come then;
<margin>H</margin> but that you would call Dion later. For that reason I did not come then, which indeed displeased Dion, who thought it better that I should obey you and come. After a year had passed, a trireme was sent by you, and with it your letters. The head of which was: if I came, Dion's affairs would be as I most desired, but if I did not come, the opposite. I am ashamed to recall how many letters were then written both by you
