### PLATO TO DIONYSIUS.
#### The Third.

<margin>A</margin> <margin>B</margin> **P**LATO to Dionysius, sending greetings: would I hit upon the best form of address? Or rather, according to my own habit, "to wish to do well," as I am accustomed to address friends in letters? For you indeed, as those who were then observers reported, addressed the god at Delphi with this very word, flattering him; and you wrote, as they say, "Joy to you, and live the life of a tyrant, having a pleasant existence." But I would not exhort even a man to do this, let alone a god. To a god, because I would be commanding something contrary to nature (for the divine is established far from pleasure and pain); and to a man, because for the most part pleasure
<margin>C</margin> and pain produce harm, breeding difficulty in learning, forgetfulness, folly, and insolence in the soul. And let these things be said by me concerning the salutation; but you, having read them, receive them in whatever way you wish. But not a few say that you told some of the ambassadors present with you that once, when I heard you saying you intended to settle the Greek cities in Sicily and to lighten the burden of the Syracusans by changing the tyranny into a kingship, I then prevented you, as you say, though you were very eager; but now I am teaching Dion to do these very things, and by your own thoughts we are depriving you of your empire. Whether you are helped at all by these words, you yourself know;
<margin>D</margin> but you wrong me, I hear, by not speaking the truth. For I have been sufficiently slandered by Philistides and many others to the mercenaries and to the Syracusan multitude, because I lived in the private quarters in the citadel. And those outside, if any mistake occurred, turned it against me, some claiming that you followed me in everything. But you yourself know most clearly that I touched upon the affairs of the state with you voluntarily only a little at the beginning, when I thought I might accomplish something more; and certain other brief things, and taking moderate care over the prefaces of the laws, apart from what you or someone else added. For I hear
later that some of you have tampered with them. Both will be clear to those who are able to judge my character. But anyway, as I just said,
<margin>E</margin> I do not need further slander toward the Syracusans, or if you are persuading any others by saying these things; but much more a defense against the former slander that occurred, and the one now growing after it, larger and more vehement. It is necessary for me to make a double defense against two slanders. First, that I reasonably avoided sharing in the affairs of the city with you; and second, that you have not spoken the truth that I was an obstacle to you when you were about to settle the Greek cities. Hear then first regarding the first point: I came
called to Syracuse by you and by Dion; by one who was approved by me and had long been my guest-friend, being in the
<margin>F</margin> middle and established age (of which things all who possess even a little sense have need, when they intend to deliberate on such great matters as yours then were); but you being very young, and there being much inexperience in you regarding those things of which you ought to have been experienced, and being very much a stranger to me. After this, whether a man, or a god, or some fortune drove Dion out with you, and you were left alone. Do you think then that I still had any sharing of political matters with you, having lost my sensible partner, and seeing the senseless one left behind with many wicked men, not ruling, but thinking he ruled, while being ruled by such men? In these circumstances, what was it necessary for me to do? Was it not what I did, out of necessity from what remained?
To let political matters go, being wary of the slanders arising from envy,
<margin>G</margin> and to try by all means, even though you were separated from each other and at odds, to make you as much as possible friends to one another? Of these things you are a witness, that I never gave up seeking this very thing; and you barely agreed; and when it was agreed by us, that I should sail home, since war occupied you; and that when peace was made, both I and Dion should come to Syracuse; and that you should call us. And these things happened thus during my first journey to Syracuse, and my safe return home again. But the second time, when peace was made, you called me, not according to the agreement, but you wrote for me to come alone; and you said you would send for Dion later.
<margin>H</margin> For these reasons I did not come, and I was even hated by Dion then. For he thought it was better for me to come and obey you. But after this, a year later, a trireme arrived and letters from you; of which letters the main point was that, if I came, Dion's affairs would be according to my mind; but if I did not come, the opposite. I am ashamed to say how many letters then came from you and from your people because of you from Italy

# EPISTLE III.

<margin>A</margin> ...as well as from others on your behalf from Italy and Sicily, and from many of my own relatives and acquaintances; all of them exhorted and entreated me to comply with your request and come to you. It seemed best to everyone, and especially to Dion, that I ought to go and not indulge in soft idleness, even though I excused myself on account of my age. I asserted regarding you that you would be unable to resist the detractors and malevolent men who sought to create a rift between us. For I had perceived long ago, and I perceive even now, that the greater the wealth of private citizens or princes, the more they nourish informers and plotters of shameful and harmful pleasures—than which nothing more destructive is produced by <margin>B</margin> opulence and power. Nevertheless, setting all these concerns aside, I decided to come, so that I might not leave any cause for complaint to any of my friends, who might have perished through my negligence when I could have been their salvation.

What followed after my arrival, you yourself know best. I certainly judged that, according to the promises in your letters, you should first of all recall Dion and restore him to his former intimacy, a matter I thought deserved consideration. If you had followed my advice in this, perhaps your affairs, and those of the Syracusans and the rest of the Greeks, would be in a better state, as my own intuition foretells. I judged next that Dion’s property should be restored to his kin, and not left any longer to the administration of those <margin>C</margin> distributors whom you had appointed. I further judged that the money usually sent to Dion each year should continue to be sent, and not diminished because of my presence, but rather increased. However, when I could obtain none of these things from you, I resolved to depart.

But you asked me to wait for a year, affirming that you would restore all of Dion’s property, such that half would be sent to Dion himself in Corinth, and the rest would remain in Syracuse for his son. I could recount many other things which you promised but did not keep, but I omit them due to their number. For while you were conducting the sale of all Dion’s goods without any consent from him—even though you had said you would only do this if he agreed—you placed upon all your promises, O wondrous man, the "Colophon" <note>original: "κολοφῶνα" - a Greek proverbial expression meaning the "finishing stroke" or "crowning touch," here used sarcastically regarding the peak of Dionysius's deception.</note> (as they say) of a most noble deception.

<margin>D</margin> Having devised a scheme that was neither honorable, nor dignified, nor just, nor useful, you attempted to deter me as if I were ignorant of those proceedings, so that I would stop demanding that the money be sent to Dion. For when you expelled Heraclides <note>A Syracusan politician and military leader who eventually helped Dion overthrow Dionysius II.</note>—which seemed just neither to the Syracusans nor to me—and I, together with Theodotus and Eurybius, pleaded on his behalf, you took this as a sufficient pretext and said that I had long ago made it clear that I cared nothing for your affairs, but only for Dion and his friends and relatives. And so, since Heraclides and Theodotus, being friends of Dion, were under suspicion of a crime, <margin>E</margin> you claimed I was doing everything to ensure they did not pay the penalty.

In this partnership of our civil administration, and in whatever other estrangement you perceived in me toward you, is it any wonder that these things happened? For I might rightly be judged a base man by prudent men if, led by the magnitude of your power, I had betrayed and abandoned an old friend and guest-friend <term>hospitem - a formal relationship of mutual protection and hospitality</term> who was suffering at your hands—a man in no way inferior to you (if I may say so)—and had instead chosen to follow you, the one doing the injury, doing everything you commanded for the sake of your wealth. Certainly, if I had betrayed him for your sake, no one would have said there was any other cause for my change of heart.

<margin>F</margin> These events, therefore, were the cause of the resentment between us and the lack of communication. But my discourse now opportunely moves to that part which I proposed to speak of in the second place. Attend carefully, I pray, to see if I seem to speak the truth to you. I say that while Archedemus and Aristocritus were present in the gardens, about twenty days before my departure from Syracuse for home, you said to me those things which you are even now saying: that I cared more for Heraclides and all the others than for you. Furthermore, in their presence, you asked me if I remembered when I first came to Syracuse, how I urged you to resettle the Greek cities. I conceded that I remembered, and added that even now it seemed to me the best course.

It must be told, O Dionysius, what was said immediately after that. <margin>G</margin> I asked whether I had advised you of this alone, or something else besides. To this you responded very angrily and, as you thought, insultingly—and that I had also given other instructions. Thus, what was then an insult to me has now become like a dream. You asked me quite openly, if I remember correctly, mocking me, whether I had given those instructions to you as a teacher <note>original: "παιδευθέντα" - referring to the role of a tutor or educator.</note> or not. I replied that you remembered it very well. But you yourself added to this: "As a teacher in geometry, or how?"

At that time, I kept silent regarding what I might have replied, fearing that for the sake of a small word, the voyage I was expecting might become a narrow difficulty for me instead of a broad escape. But let us return to that toward which all this tends. Do not stir up ill-will against me by saying that I prohibited you from restoring the Greek cities destroyed by the Barbarians, or from changing the government of the Syracusans from a tyranny to a kingdom. For you can say nothing false about me that is more foreign to my character. And yet, if there were anywhere a sufficient judgment of this matter, I could produce other evidence even clearer <margin>H</margin> than what has been said, and prove manifesty that I urged you to do those things, but you refused. It is by no means difficult to show that those things would have been best for you, for the Syracusans, and for all Sicilians. If, therefore, you deny that you said these things when you did say them, I have enough to...

# OF PLATO.

I might be blamed. But if you admit this, consider Stesichorus <note>A Greek lyric poet famous for his "Palinode," a poem in which he retracted his previous insults against Helen of Troy.</note> to have been wise, and by imitating his palinode—that is, a song contrary to the former—you may lead yourself back from a false report to the truth.

->PLATO TO DION OF SYRACUSE,<-
->WISHES WELL-BEING.<-
->E P I S T L E IV.<-

I believe it has been manifest through all time how most ready my goodwill has been regarding each event that has occurred; nor is it hidden from you all that my desire for completion was for no other reason more than that I might obtain honor in noble things. For I judge it to be just that those who are truly good men, and perform such deeds, should obtain worthy glory. And indeed, up to this point, by the blessing of God, matters are holding up well. But concerning the future, the greatest contest is set before you. For to excel in fortitude, speed, and strength is such that it can belong to others as well; but to surpass in truth, justice, magnificence, and a certain nobility and dignity of this kind, belongs especially to those who perform such deeds and claim the glory of such things for themselves. What I say is surely manifest. Moreover, we <margin>C</margin> ought to remember that it is necessary for us, as it is not hidden from you, to excel others more than children do. Therefore, it ought to be clear to everyone that we are such as we wish to seem; especially since, with God’s help, it will be very easy. For it has happened to others that they were compelled to travel to many places to achieve this; but the state of your affairs is such that from the whole world, so to speak, all eyes are turned toward one place, and in that very place, toward you alone. Therefore, as if placed before the eyes and watched by everyone, strive to express that ancient Lycurgus <note>The legendary lawgiver of Sparta.</note> and Cyrus; and whoever else has ever seemed to excel in character and public institutions; especially since it is the opinion of many and almost all of your people that after Dionysius <note>Dionysius II, the tyrant of Syracuse whom Dion sought to overthrow.</note> was removed, affairs would perish because of your ambition and the desire for excellence of yourself, Heraclides, Theodorus, and the other <margin>D</margin> nobles. First, indeed, it is to be hoped that no such person exists. But if any such person appears, you shall provide the remedy, so that matters may be led toward the better. Perhaps it seems ridiculous to you that I advise these things when they are known to you. But I observe in the theaters that the competitors are provoked by boys; much more so by friends, who are thought to encourage out of a zeal of benevolence. You certainly are now competing as if in a certain theater. In which, if there is need of our labor, let us know. Here, however, things are just as when you were present. Write to me what has been done, or what is being done. For although we hear many things, we have nothing certain. <margin>E</margin> Many letters are carried by Theodotus and Heraclides to Lacedaemon <note>Sparta</note> and Aegina. We, however, as I said, hearing many things about your affairs, perceive nothing clearly. Nor let it be hidden from you that there is an opinion of you among some as being a man somewhat less dutiful and affable than is proper. Remember, therefore, that the goodwill of men is necessary for conducting affairs; but austerity breeds the solitude of friends. Fare you well.

---

->PLATO TO PERDICCAS, WISHES WELL-BEING.<-
->E P I S T L E V.<-

I advised Euphraeus, just as you wrote to me, that he should persevere in the administration of your affairs. Moreover, it is my part to give you also, concerning other matters, that "hospitable and sacred counsel" (as it is called); and how you <margin>F</margin> ought to use Euphraeus. Truly, that man can be useful for many things. But especially for that which you most lack because of your age: especially since not many are found who can conveniently offer counsel to young men about these matters. For there is a certain "voice" of each civil government, just as of certain animals. For the government of the people emits one voice, that of the few another, and that of one man another. Many profess to understand these; but they are far from understanding them, except for a very few. Therefore, whichever government emits its own proper voice toward gods and toward men, and renders actions consistent with that voice, it always flourishes and is preserved. But if it imitates the voice of another, it receives destruction. To these things Euphraeus can be very useful to you, although he is a brave man in other respects as well. For I hope that he will find the reasons of monarchy—that is, the rule of one—no less than those who are with you. Therefore, relying on him for these things, you will perceive utility from him, and you will then return as much as possible to him. But if someone hearing these things should object: "Plato indeed professes to understand what contributes to the popular state; yet he never, though the opportunity was given, rose in his own city to offer counsel to the people"; to this he will answer, that Plato was at last late in his fatherland, and found the people, who had been before him, doing many things different from his counsel. For

<column-break/>

I have my justice; but if you agree, thinking that after this Stesichorus was wise, by imitating his palinode, change from the false to the true word.

->PLATO TO DION OF SYRACUSE,<-
->WISHES WELL-BEING. FOURTH.<-

I THINK it is manifest through all time that my zeal concerning the events that have happened, and that I had much earnestness about them to be brought to a conclusion, was for no other reason more than for the love of honor in <margin>B</margin> noble things. For I think it is just that those who are in truth decent, and doing such things, should obtain the fitting glory. Now, as for the present, to speak with God, it is well; but concerning the future, there is the greatest contest. For to excel in courage and speed and strength might seem to belong to some others; but in truth and justice and magnificence, and in the grace concerning all these things, one would agree that those who claim such things for themselves reasonably excel others. Now then, what I say is clear; but we must nevertheless remind ourselves that it is fitting to excel other men more than children, as we know. We must therefore become manifest that we are such as we say; especially since, to speak with God, it will be easy. For it has happened to others that it was necessary to wander over much space if they were to be known; but that which now belongs to you always is such that those from the whole inhabited world (if it is not too bold to say) look toward one place; and in this, especially toward you. As one seen by all, therefore, prepare yourself to show forth that ancient Lycurgus and Cyrus, and whoever else ever seemed to excel in character and statesmanship; especially since many and almost all those here say that there is much hope that if Dionysius is removed, affairs will be destroyed because of your ambition and that of Heraclides <margin>D</margin> and Theodotus and the other notables. Most of all, then, let no one be such; but if someone should become so, you appear as a physician, so that things might come to the best. These things perhaps seem ridiculous for me to say, because you yourself are not ignorant; but I see even in the theaters the contestants being urged on by the boys, not to mention by friends, whom one might think to encourage with earnestness out of goodwill. Now then, you yourselves compete, and send word to us if you need anything. Things here are similar to us; and now with us being present, send word to me what has been done by you, or what you happen to be doing. As we, hearing many things, know nothing. And now letters from Theodotus and Heraclides <margin>E</margin> have come to Lacedaemon and Aegina; but we (as has been said) hearing many things about the affairs there, know nothing. And consider also that you seem to some to be less attentive than is fitting. Let it not escape you that through pleasing men, action is also achieved; but stubbornness is a housemate of solitude. Good fortune.

---

->PLATO TO PERDICCAS,<-
->WISHES WELL-BEING. FIFTH.<-

I ADVISED Euphraeus, just as you sent word, to take care of your interests, and always to spend time in these things. And I am just to give counsel both "hospitable and sacred," as it is called, both to the others of whom you speak, <margin>F</margin> and how one must now use Euphraeus. For the man is useful for many things, but greatest is that which you now lack, both because of your age and because there are not many counselors for the young. For there is indeed a certain voice of each of the polities, just as of certain animals; one of democracy, another of oligarchy, and another again of monarchy. These many would say they understand, but they fall very far short of perceiving them, except for some few. Whichever polity, then, speaks its own voice toward gods and toward men, and renders its actions such as the voice, it always flourishes and is saved; but imitating another, it is destroyed. Toward these things, then, Euphraeus might be not least useful to you, although being brave toward other things. For the reasons of monarchy I hope he will help to find out no less than those who are in your circles. Using him for these things, you will both be benefited yourself and will help him most. And if someone hearing these things should say, "Plato, as it seems, pretends to know what is profitable for democracy; but though it was possible to speak in the assembly and advise it the best things, he never stood up to speak"; to these things say that Plato was born late in his fatherland, and found the people already older, and accustomed by those before him to do many things unlike his counsel. Since he would have most gladly advised it, as a father, if he did not think he would risk in vain...

# LETTER VII. <note>original: EPISTOLA VII. This heading refers to the conclusion of the previous letter in the sequence of this specific edition.</note>

...he would have thought it would achieve nothing more. I believe the same would happen to my own advice; if what you have decided seems to be incurable, then bidding us a long farewell, it would stand outside of any counsel concerning me and my affairs.

-> PLATO TO HERMIAS, ERASTUS, AND <-
-> CORISCO, WISHES WELL. <-
-> The Sixth. <-

<margin>A</margin> IT seems to me that some god is preparing a good fortune for you, if you receive it well, in a fair and sufficient manner. For you dwell as neighbors to one another, and you have a need to benefit each other in the greatest matters. <margin>B</margin> For neither a multitude of horses, nor any other military alliance, nor indeed the possession of beaten gold would be a greater benefit for all power than friends who are firm and possess a healthy character. To Erastus and Coriscus—in addition to that beautiful <term>wisdom of the forms</term> <note>original: τῶν εἰδῶν σοφίᾳ / sapientiam de speciebus. This refers to Plato's Theory of Forms or Ideas.</note>—I say, even though I am an old man, that there is a need for a further wisdom: one that is a protective and defensive power against the wicked and the unjust. For they are inexperienced in such things, because they have spent a great part of their lives with us, who are moderate men and free from evils. For this reason, I said they need these things, so that they are not forced to neglect true wisdom and attend to that human and necessary wisdom more than is fitting. This power, in turn, Hermias seems to me to possess both by nature (as far as I have observed) and by the skill gained through experience. What then do I say? To you, Hermias, having more experience of Erastus and Coriscus than you have, I say and testify and bear witness that you will not easily find characters more worthy of trust than these neighbors of yours. <margin>C</margin> Secondly, I advise all of you to hold fast to these men in a just manner, and not as a secondary matter. To Coriscus and Erastus, in turn, I advise them to hold fast to Hermias, and to try, all together, to arrive at a single intertwining of friendship. But if any of you should seem to dissolve this bond (for human affairs are not altogether stable), send a letter here to me and my friends, accusing the one at fault. <margin>D</margin> For I believe that words coming from us, filled with justice and respect, unless the breach happens to be a great one, would be better suited than any incantation to grow together and bind you back again into your pre-existing friendship and communion. If we all—both you and we—practice philosophy as much as we are able, each of these exhortations will be like the oracles just spoken. But if we do not wish for these things, I prophesy a different fate; yet I predict that we shall all do these good things, if God wills. <margin>E</margin> It is necessary for all three of you to read this letter, preferably all together, but if not, as often as possible according to your ability. Use it as a binding compact and law, as is just, swearing with a zeal that is not without the arts, and with <term>education</term>, the sister of such zeal; swearing by the god who is the leader of all things that are and shall be, and by the sovereign Father of that leader and cause. If we truly practice philosophy, we shall all know Him clearly, as far as the power of happy men can reach.

---

-> PLATO TO THE KINSMEN AND <-
-> FRIENDS OF DION, WISHES WELL. <-
-> The Seventh. <-

<margin>F</margin> YOU wrote to me that I ought to consider your intention to be the same as that which Dion held. Moreover, you exhorted me to share in your work, as far as I am able, in word and deed. Now, if you hold the same opinion and desire as he did, I agree to share with you; but if not, I must deliberate many times. What his intention and desire was, I can not only guess, but I can speak as one who knows clearly. For when I first arrived in Syracuse, being about forty years old, Dion was of the age that Hipparinus is now; and the opinion he held then, he continued to hold: that the Syracusans ought to be free, living under the best laws. So it is no wonder if some god has led this man into the same opinion about government, making him harmonious with the other. What was the manner of its beginning? It is <margin>G</margin> worth hearing for both the young and the old. I will attempt to relate it to you from the beginning, for the present time provides the opportunity. When I was a young man, I experienced the same thing as many others: I thought that as soon as I became master of myself, I would go straight into the public affairs of the city. And some such fortune of the city befell me regarding public matters. For while the government of that time was being reviled by many, a revolution occurred; and fifty-one men stood as leaders of the revolution: eleven in the city, and ten in the Piraeus <note>The port of Athens.</note>; both of these groups managed the marketplace and whatever else needed to be administered in the cities. But thirty men were established as supreme rulers over all. Some of these happened to be my kinsmen and acquaintances; and indeed, they immediately invited me to join them, as if to matters that were appropriate for me.

# THE WORKS OF PLATO

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> And I, because of my youth, experienced nothing strange <note>original: "nihil mirabile sum ob iuuentutem perpessus" / "θαυμαστὸν οὐδὲν ἔπαθον ὑπὸ νεότητος"</note>. For I imagined that they <note>The Thirty Tyrants, who took power in Athens in 404 BCE.</note> would lead the city from an unjust life to a righteous way of living, and so I observed very closely what they would do. But I noticed that in a very short time they behaved in such a way that the previous state of the republic seemed like a golden age. For among many other injustices they committed, they sent my friend, the elderly Socrates—whom I do not hesitate to call the most just man of all who then lived—along with certain others to arrest one of the citizens by force to be executed. Their goal was to make Socrates a participant in their affairs, whether he willed it or not. He, however, refused to obey, and chose to suffer any extremity rather than become a partner in their impious crimes. <margin>B</margin> When I saw these things, and other matters of no small importance, I was grieved and withdrew myself from those evils. Not long after, the overthrow of these Thirty followed, and the entire constitution was changed. Once again, though more slowly, I felt a desire to engage in public affairs. But even then, as the republic was in a state of turmoil, many things occurred that one would strongly disapprove of. It was not at all surprising that in such revolutions some took bitter revenge on their enemies, although those who returned <note>The democratic faction returning from exile.</note> exercised great clemency.

<margin>C</margin> By some chance, however, certain powerful men in the republic brought an accusation against this friend of ours, Socrates, charging him with a most impious crime, and one least of all suited to him. For they brought him to trial as if he were impious toward the gods; others passed sentence on him and put to death the very man who, at an earlier time, when he himself was at risk, refused to participate in the impious arrest of one of their own friends then in exile. As I observed these things, and the men who were handling political affairs, as well as the laws and customs—the more I considered them and the more I advanced in age, the more difficult it seemed to me to govern the republic rightly. For this cannot be done without faithful friends and associates. <margin>D</margin> At that time, it was not easy to find such men, for our city was no longer governed according to the customs and institutions of our fathers, and it was impossible to acquire new ones without extreme difficulty, as both the laws and morals were utterly corrupted. Therefore, I, who at first had burned with an incredible desire to enter public life, seeing everything drifting toward a precipice, finally did not know where to turn. I did not, however, cease from investigating whether things might perhaps improve, both regarding these specific matters and the entire republic, but I waited for an opportunity to act. Finally, I realized that all existing republics are badly governed. For as far as their laws are concerned, they are almost incurable, living by mere chance rather than by any excellent institution.

<margin>E</margin> For this reason, I was driven to say, in praise of right philosophy, that through it alone can one discern what is just in both public and private life. Therefore, the human race will not find rest from its evils until either those who philosophize rightly and truly attain political power, or those who govern in cities, by some divine fate, truly practice philosophy. <margin>Cicero's words from the Tusculans</margin> <note>A reference to Cicero's "Tusculan Disputations" where he discusses similar themes of the philosopher-king.</note> With this mind, I traveled to Italy and Sicily; this was my first journey to those places. <margin>F</margin> When I arrived, that "blessed life" as it was called, full of Italian and Syracusan tables <note>A reference to the legendary luxury and gluttony of the Sicilian Greeks.</note>, pleased me in no way—to be stuffed with food twice a day, never to sleep alone at night, and all the other things that accompany such a life. For no man under heaven, if he were nurtured in such habits from his youth, even if endowed with an excellent nature and talent, would ever turn out wise. He would certainly never care to be temperate. And the same logic applies to the other virtues. No city can remain at peace under any laws if the citizens think they must spend everything on excessive waste, and, neglecting all else, believe they must devote their efforts solely to banquets and the pleasures of love.

<margin>G</margin> It is inevitable that such cities will change now into tyrannies, now into oligarchies, and now into democracies, never finding rest; and those who are powerful in these cities will not even endure to hear the name of a just and equal government. Considering these things along with my previous thoughts, I traveled to Syracuse—perhaps by some chance. It seems, however, that by the work of those who are above us <note>i.e., the gods or providence</note>, a beginning was then given to all that has recently happened to Dion and the people of Syracuse; and I fear even more may follow if you do not now listen to my second counsel. <margin>H</margin> In what way I say my journey to Syracuse was the beginning of everything, listen: I was then frequently in the company of Dion, who was a young man, and I urged him with whatever reasons I could toward what I thought best for men, advising him to act upon them. But in saying these things, I seem to have been secretly and unintentionally preparing that ruin of the tyranny which followed. For Dion, being of a very sharp intellect, both in other matters and in learning the things I then spoke of, grasped them more quickly and vehemently than any young man I have ever met. And he decided to lead the rest of his life in a manner far superior to many of the Italians and—

# SEVENTH LETTER.

<margin>A</margin> and of the Sicilians, he <note>Dion</note> lived a life of virtue rather than one devoted to pleasure and luxury. Consequently, he lived in a manner quite offensive to those accustomed to the laws of tyranny, and continued so until the death of Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Elder, the previous tyrant</note>. After this, he realized that the mindset he had acquired through right reason might not only exist in himself, but seeing it arising in others—not many, to be sure, but in some—he thought that the younger Dionysius might, with the gods' help, become one of them. If such a thing happened, his own life and that of the other Syracusans would result in an inconceivable state of happiness. For these reasons, he thought I must by all
<margin>B</margin> means come to Syracuse as quickly as possible to be a partner in these matters. He remembered our past associations and how easily he had been led to a desire for the most beautiful and best life. If he could now bring this desire to fruition in Dionysius as he attempted, he had great hopes of establishing a happy and true way of life throughout the whole land, without the slaughters, deaths, and evils that have now occurred. Dion, thinking rightly on these things, persuaded Dionysius to send for me; he himself also sent requests, begging me by every means to come as quickly as possible, before others encountered Dionysius and turned him away from the best life toward another path. In saying
<margin>C</margin> these things, he pleaded, even if it meant speaking at length: "What greater opportunity," he said, "shall we wait for than the one now provided by a certain divine fortune?" He listed the extent of the empire in Italy and Sicily, his own power within it, and the youth and intense desire of Dionysius for philosophy and education. He also mentioned how his own nephews and kinsmen were easily called toward the doctrine and life I always spoke of, and were most capable of encouraging Dionysius. So, if ever there was hope that the same men might become both philosophers and rulers of great cities, it was now. These were his
<margin>D</margin> exhortations, along with many others of the same kind. As for my own opinion, I was fearful regarding the young men, as to how it might turn out. For the desires of such people are swift and often carry them in opposite directions. However, I knew Dion’s character to be naturally grave and already of a mature age. Therefore, as I considered and hesitated whether I should go and obey the call, or how I should act, the balance tipped toward the idea that if anyone ever intended to carry out his thoughts on laws and government, now was the time to try. For if I could persuade just one man, I would have sufficiently accomplished all good things. With this thought and daring, I set out from home,
<margin>E</margin> not for the reasons some supposed, but primarily because I was ashamed of myself, lest I should ever seem to myself to be a man of mere words and never willingly undertake any action. I also risked betraying the hospitality and friendship of Dion, who was truly in no small danger. If something happened to him, or if he were driven out by Dionysius and his other enemies and came to us as a fugitive, saying: "Plato, I come to you an exile, not lacking horses or horsemen to repel my enemies, but lacking the words and persuasion by which I knew you were best able to turn young men toward the good and the just, and to establish them in friendship and fellowship with one another.
<margin>F</margin> Through a lack of these things, for which you are responsible, I have now left Syracuse and am here. My own disgrace brings less shame upon you; but as for philosophy, which you always praise and say is treated with dishonor by the rest of mankind, has it not been betrayed along with me, as far as it lay in your power? If we happened to be living in Megara, you surely would have come to help me in what I asked, or you would consider yourself the most worthless of men. But now, do you think you will escape the reputation of cowardice by blaming the length of the journey, the greatness of the voyage, and the labor?" If these things were said, what honorable answer could I give? None. So I went, led by reason and justice as much as is possible for a man, leaving my own occupations—which were not dishonorable—to submit to a tyranny that seemed suited neither to my words nor to myself. By going, I cleared myself and fulfilled my duty to Zeus, the god of hospitality, and to the lot of a philosopher, which would have been a matter of reproach had I shared in a foul shame through
<margin>G</margin> weakness or cowardice. Having arrived (there is no need to be long-winded), I found everything around Dionysius full of faction and slander against Dion regarding the tyranny. I defended him as much as I could, but I was able to do little. In about the fourth month, Dionysius, accusing Dion of plotting against the tyranny, put him into a small boat and banished him in dishonor. All of us who were friends of Dion
<margin>H</margin> were then afraid that he might punish one of us as an accomplice in Dion’s plot. A rumor even spread in Syracuse that I had been put to death by Dionysius as the cause of all that had happened. But he, perceiving that we were all so disposed and fearing that something worse might come from our fear, received us all kindly. He comforted me, asking me to be of good courage and begging me by all means to stay.

Upon arrival, he finds the court rife with factionalism, leading to Dion's eventual banishment and Plato's own precarious situation.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plato’s Seventh Letter, detailing his second journey to Syracuse and his interactions with the tyrant Dionysius II. It transitions from the narrative of his detention to his philosophical principles regarding political advice.</meta>

# PLATO

<margin>A</margin> For him, there was no honor in my flight, but only in my remaining. And for that reason, he especially feigned to entreat me. We are not ignorant, however, that the entreaties of tyrants are mixed with necessity <note>original: "necessitati permixtas" / "μεμιγμέναι ἀνάγκαις". Plato suggests that a "request" from a dictator is actually a command.</note>. When he plotted so that I might not depart, he installed me in the citadel; he wished me to inhabit those places from which no sailor thereafter would take me away—not only if he prohibited it, but unless he himself ordered and sent them. Nor would any merchant or any prefect of the maritime coast have looked upon me departing alone without immediately seizing me and leading me back to Dionysius; especially since it was now rumored, contrary to what had been spread before, that Dionysius was once again embracing Plato with great affection. And in a certain way, it was so.

<margin>B</margin> For the truth must not be kept silent. He did indeed embrace me more and more as the days went by, and he delighted in our character and company. He desired to be praised by me more than Dion was, and to be considered a far greater friend. Toward this end, he contended most earnestly. Yet he neglected the very method by which this would have been best achieved, if indeed it could have been done at all. For this method would have been for him to adhere more freely to me in hearing and learning the principles of philosophy, and to come to an agreement with me. But in truth, he was too distrustful for this, fearing—as the slanderers alleged—that if he became entangled in those principles, Dion (who desired it) would have already accomplished everything.

<margin>C</margin> I, however, endured all things, persevering in the same opinion with which I had set out from the beginning: trying if by any means it were possible that he might come into a desire for the philosophical life. But he, striving against me, defeated me. And so the first period of my journey to Sicily, and my actions there, was spent through all these things. In later times, however, I returned again to Sicily, because Dionysius recalled me with all zeal. For what cause I went back again, and what I did there—not indeed without reason—I will report to you only after you have consulted me on what is most important to do in the present state of affairs.

<margin>D</margin> I shall report these things, I say, for the sake of those who ask with what purpose I returned a second time. But lest incidental matters be placed before the principal ones, I come now to the matter of counsel. I believe that a man giving counsel to a sick person who is intemperate regarding his diet ought, first of all, to persuade him to change his way of living; and if the sick man obeys in this, then he may contribute other things for a cure. But if he refuses to obey, then I will consider the one giving counsel to be a true man and a physician if he abandons him; whereas if he persists further in counseling, I will consider him a coward and unskilled in his art. I hold the same view regarding a city, whether one man governs it or many. For if a useful piece of advice is given to a people proceeding by some probable reason and a right path, I judge it the duty of a wise man to act. But if they turn entirely away from civil reason, and do not even wish to follow its tracks, and declare to the counselor that he must leave the state alone and not move anything in it—since if he moves it, he will perish—but that he should instead indulge their pleasures and lusts, and give counsel in such a way that their desires are most easily and quickly satisfied: I will by no means consider him a man who persists in that kind of governance, but rather him who abandons it altogether.

<margin>E</margin> Established in this opinion, whenever someone consults me on weightier matters—whether they pertain to riches, or to the purification of the body or soul—if his daily life seems able to keep some measure, or at least if he seems likely to obey me when I counsel him, I consult with him gladly, and I do not stop until I have brought the beginning to an end with all my strength. But if he either does not seek counsel from me at all, or if he who seeks it clearly appears as one who will in no way obey me when I counsel him, I do not approach him of my own accord to give counsel; and I would not do so by force, even if he were my own son. I would, however, counsel a slave even against his will, and compel him by the use of force.

<margin>F</margin> But I judge it a divine crime <note>original: "nefas" / "οὐχ ὅσιον". Refers to an act that violates religious or natural law.</note> to compel a father or mother by force, unless they are alienated in mind because of disease. But if they live according to their own custom, which I by no means approve, I would neither oppose them with hostility by admonishing them in vain, nor again would I flatter them by assenting to their desires, providing those things which, if I were to indulge in them myself, I would not wish to live.

<margin>G</margin> A prudent man ought to be of this same mind regarding his country: that he should so rebuke the errors of the city if he is neither to rebuke them in vain, nor to perish because of his zeal for rebuking; but he should never bring force upon his country through a change of the state, when it cannot be amended without the expulsion and slaughter of citizens. Instead, he should keep quiet and pray for the best things for himself and his country. In this way, therefore, I would counsel you. I counseled Dionysius similarly, together with Dion: namely, that he should live his daily life in such a way that he might be made most master of himself, and that he might have faithful friends and companions, lest the same thing happen to him as happened to his father. For his father, though he had taken many great cities in Sicily that had once been devastated by the Barbarians <note>Refers to the Carthaginians.</note> and had restored them, was unable to establish faithful governors of the states in each of them—neither from his own household, nor from others acquired from elsewhere, nor from his brothers whom he himself had educated from boyhood. Instead, he made magistrates out of private men, and very rich men out of the poor. Yet he could not make any of these a faithful partner in governance, whether by persuading, teaching, giving gifts, or receiving them into kinship; he was seven times—

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> For it became for him [Dionysius] a matter of no honor that I should flee from him, but rather that I should stay. For this reason, he pretended to beg me most earnestly. But we know that the entreaties of tyrants are mixed with compulsions. Plotting this, he prevented my sailing away, leading me into the citadel and settling me there, from where not even one ship-master would have taken me out—not only if Dionysius prohibited it, but not even if he did not himself send someone and order them to take me out. Nor would any of the officials at the exits of the land have overlooked me departing alone, without seizing me and immediately leading me back again to Dionysius; especially since it had already been announced, the opposite of before, that Dionysius was wonderfully fond of Plato.

<margin>B</margin> And it was so, in a way (for the truth must be told): he became more fond of me as time went on, and of the company of my character and habits, but he wanted me to praise him more than Dion, and to consider him a friend far more than that man; and he was wonderfully contentious for such a thing. But he shrank from the way in which this would have happened best (if it were to happen at all): namely, by becoming intimate through learning and hearing the discourses concerning philosophy, and by associating with me. For he feared the slanderous talk, lest he be hindered in some way, as if Dion had already accomplished everything.

<margin>C</margin> I, however, endured everything, yielding in the way I first intended when I arrived, to see if by any means he might come into a desire for the philosophical life; but he strained against me in the opposite direction. And so the first time of my stay and delay in Sicily happened because of all these things. After this, I departed again, and then returned once more, Dionysius sending for me with all zeal. For what reasons and what I did, as being reasonable and just, I will first advise you on what must be done from the present events, and later I will go through the details of these matters; for the sake of those who ask again why I wished to go the second time, so that incidental matters do not happen to be spoken of as if they were the main work.

<margin>D</margin> I say then, giving advice about myself to a man who is sick and living a wretched diet, first that he must change his life, and if he is willing to obey, then to encourage other things; but if he is not willing, I consider the man who flees from the advice of such a person to be both a man and a physician; but the one who remains, on the contrary, to be unmanly and unskilled. The same thing applies to a city, whether it has one master or many, if the state is proceeding in a right way and asks advice about its interests, it is the part of a man with mind to advise such people. But for those who step outside the right path of the state and are in no way willing to go in its tracks, and who proclaim to the advisor to leave the state alone and not move it, as he will be put to death if he moves it, but they order him to serve their wishes and desires, advising in what way they might happen most easily and quickly for all time—the one who remains for such advice I consider unmanly, and the one who does not remain, a man.

<margin>E</margin> Having this mind, whenever someone consults me about any of the greatest things in his life, such as about the acquisition of wealth, or about the care of the body or the soul, if his daily life seems to me to be in some way orderly, or if he seems willing to obey when I advise him on the things he communicates, I advise him eagerly, and I do not stop after merely performing a duty. But if he does not consult me at all, or if it is clear that he will in no way obey me when I advise him, I do not go to such a person uncalled to give advice; and I would not use force, not even if he were my son. I would advise a slave, and I would even use force on him if he were unwilling;

<margin>F</margin> but I do not think it holy to use force on a father or mother, unless they are held by the disease of madness. But if they live a certain established life, pleasing to themselves but not to me, I would neither be hated by admonishing them in vain, nor again by flattering them, serving them by providing the fulfillment of desires which I myself would not wish to live if I embraced them. The man of sense must live with this same thought concerning his own city: to speak, if it does not seem to him to be governed well, if he is not going to speak in vain nor be put to death for speaking; but he must not bring force of a change of state upon his country (when it is not possible for the best to happen without the exile and slaughter of men), but keeping quiet, he should pray for good things for himself and the city.

<margin>G</margin> In this way, then, I would advise you; and I advised Dionysius also with Dion, first to live his daily life so that he would be as much as possible master of himself, and to acquire faithful friends and companions; so that he might not suffer what his father suffered. For he, having taken over many and great cities of Sicily that had been plundered by the barbarians, was not able, after settling them, to establish faithful states of companionable men in each, neither of other foreigners, nor of his brothers whom he himself had raised when they were younger, and had made rulers from private men and exceptionally rich from poor men. He was not able to make any of these a faithful partner of his rule by persuasion, teaching, benefits, and kinship; he became seven times worse than Darius.

<summary>Plato explains his forced detention by Dionysius II in Syracuse and outlines his ethical philosophy on providing political counsel, emphasizing that a wise advisor should only assist those willing to change their way of life and should never use violence against their own country.</summary>
<keywords>Plato, Dionysius II, Dion, Syracuse, political ethics, tyranny, philosophical life, medical analogy, civil duty, non-violence</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Plato’s Seventh Letter, specifically his defense of Dion’s character and his own involvement in Sicilian politics. It contrasts the successful governance of the Persians and Athenians with the failures of the Sicilian tyrants.</meta>

# SEVENTH LETTER.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...was worse than Darius. For Darius, trusting neither his brothers nor those raised under him, but only his companions in the overthrow of the Mede and the eunuch <note>referring to the Seven Persians who overthrew the False Smerdis</note>, divided the empire into seven parts, each larger than all of Sicily, and assigned them to each. He found these men to be faithful partners in his rule, and they did not plot against him or against one another. Furthermore, he provided an example of what a good lawgiver and king ought to be, for by establishing laws, he has preserved the Persian Empire even to this day. To this we may add that the Athenians, though they did not themselves found many of the Greek cities that had been occupied by barbarians, but rather took them over already inhabited, nevertheless held their empire for seventy years because they <margin>B</margin> had acquired friends in each of those cities. 

But Dionysius <note>Dionysius I, the elder tyrant of Syracuse</note>, having gathered all of Sicily into a single city, and trusting no one due to his "wisdom," was barely saved. For he was destitute of faithful friends and men; and there is no greater sign of virtue or vice than the absence or presence of such men. This, then, was the advice that Dion and I gave to Dionysius <note>Dionysius II, the son</note>, since his father’s legacy had left him so unacquainted with the company of educated men and proper social habits. We urged him that, turning his mind toward these things, he should first acquire other friends for himself from among his kinsmen and peers who were <margin>C</margin> in harmony regarding virtue. But above all, we urged him to be at harmony and consistent with himself, for we showed him that he was wonderfully deficient in this regard. We did not say this in plain words (for that would not have been safe), but spoke in riddles, contending through our arguments that in this way every man might save both himself and those over whom he might be leader; but by not turning this way, he would achieve the exact opposite. 

We told him that if he proceeded as we said, and made himself prudent and temperate, and if he then resettled the devastated cities of Sicily and bound them together with laws and constitutions so that they were friendly to him and to one another against the force of the barbarians, he would not <margin>D</margin> merely double his father’s empire, but truly multiply it. For if these things were done, it would be much easier to reduce the Carthaginians to a state of subjection far greater than that which occurred under Gelon <note>The tyrant who defeated Carthage at Himera in 480 BCE</note>; whereas now, on the contrary, his father had been forced to pay tribute to the barbarians. 

These were the things said and urged by us, who were supposedly "plotting" against Dionysius, as such rumors spread from many quarters. These rumors eventually prevailed with Dionysius, leading to the expulsion of Dion and casting us into a state of fear. But to finish the events of a short time in a few words: Dion, returning from the Peloponnese and Athens, <margin>E</margin> gave Dionysius a practical lesson. When Dion had liberated the city and restored it twice to the citizens, the Syracusans felt the same way toward Dion as Dionysius had before. For back then, Dion had tried to educate and train Dionysius to be a king worthy of the throne, so that he might share in his whole life. But Dionysius listened to slanderers and those who said that Dion was plotting for the tyranny, doing everything he did at that time so that Dionysius, his mind charmed by education, would neglect the government and leave it to Dion, who would then seize power and expel Dionysius by craft. These same slanders then prevailed a second time among the Syracusans, resulting in a victory that was <margin>F</margin> utterly strange and shameful for those responsible for it. 

What sort of victory it was, you who call upon me to settle your current affairs must hear. I, an Athenian man and a friend of Dion, came as his ally to the tyrant to turn war into friendship. But fighting against the slanders, I was defeated. Although Dionysius tried to win me over with honors and money to be his witness and friend—so that my friendship with him might justify his lack of mercy toward Dion—he failed entirely in this effort. Later, when Dion was returning home, he took with him two brothers from Athens <note>Callippus and Philostratus</note>. They had become his friends not through philosophy, but from that common and vulgar <margin>G</margin> familiarity which grows out of hospitality and the shared performance of religious mysteries and spectacles. It was through these things, and because they assisted his return, that they became his companions. 

When they arrived in Sicily and perceived that Dion had been slandered to the Sicilians whom he had liberated—as if he were plotting to become a tyrant—they did not merely betray their friend and host, but were almost the actual murderers, standing by with weapons in their hands to assist the assassins. The shame and impiety of that deed I neither pass over nor dwell upon, for many others make it their business to recount these things and will continue to do so in the future. But I must remove the infamy said to be attached to my city, Athens, because of them. For I say that he too was an Athenian <note>referring to himself or perhaps a loyal friend like Eudemus</note> who never betrayed that same man, though he could have received money and many other honors. For his friendship was not formed through a vulgar or mercenary bond, but through the communion of a liberal education <note><term>liberalis disciplinae</term>: the education befitting a free man, i.e., philosophy</note>. In this alone should a man of sense place his trust, rather than in any kinship of souls or bodies. Therefore, those two who killed Dion are not worthy to bring reproach upon the city, as if they had ever been men of any real account. These things have been said...

# THE WORKS OF PLATO

<margin>A</margin>...everything, so that the friends and relatives of Dion might be advised. Furthermore, I advise you now for a third time, in the same manner and for the same reason: let not Sicily, nor any city, be subjected to human masters, but only to laws—at least according to my judgment. For such a state is beneficial neither to those who dominate nor to those who serve, nor to their children or their children’s children; rather, such an undertaking is altogether ruinous for men. Indeed, it belongs to a narrow and illiberal mind to snatch at such gains, understanding nothing of what is good and just, whether divine or human, for the present or the future. These things I first attempted to persuade Dion of; then Dionysius; and now, thirdly, you. Therefore, obey me for the sake of Zeus the Third Savior <note>original: "Διὸς τρίτου σωτῆρος" - a traditional Greek invocation to the "Third Savior" for good luck or completion</note>. Moreover, consider the end of Dionysius 
<margin>B</margin>and of Dion. Dionysius, by not following my advice, lives even now in dishonor; but Dion, having followed it, died honorably. For to a man who strives for the most noble things for himself and his country, nothing can happen that is not right and honorable. Nor is it because our soul is born immortal—though if that should happen to someone, he would not be happy because of it, as the common people think. For to things lacking a soul, nothing is good or evil worthy of consideration; but to every soul, these things happen either while it is with the body or when it is separated from it. We must truly always believe the ancient and sacred words which announce to us that the soul is immortal, that it has judges, and that it suffers the greatest punishments after it has been separated 
<margin>C</margin>from the body. For this reason, it must be considered a lesser evil to suffer the gravest injuries inflicted by wrongdoers than to inflict them. A man devoted to amassing money and of a dull wit does not hear this, or if he does hear it, he mocks it as if it were something to be despised by his own judgment; and he shamelessly snatches from everywhere whatever he thinks will supply him, like a beast, with the pleasures of the belly and venereal delight—pleasures which are certainly slavish, ungrateful, and absurd, and not worthy of the name of true pleasure. Like a blind man, he does not see that he strives in vain to satisfy an insatiable lust. Nor does he see how great an evil impiety is, which is always mixed with acts of injustice. It is necessary for the soul that has perpetrated such injustices to carry them with it, both while it revolves upon the earth among men and while it is carried about beneath the earth in an altogether shameful and miserable journey. When, therefore, I said these and other things of this kind to Dion, I persuaded him. 
<margin>D</margin>I would be most justly angry with his murderers in almost the same way as I am with Dionysius; for both have inflicted the gravest damages upon me and upon all others, so to speak. The former, by killing the man who wished to practice justice; the latter, by refusing in any way to act justly, though he held the greatest power in his entire kingdom. If, in that kingdom, philosophy and power had truly met in the same dwelling, it would have sufficiently shown to all men, both Greeks and Barbarians, the shining and true opinion: that neither a city nor a man will ever be happy unless they live with prudence and under justice, whether they possess these qualities in themselves or are rightly educated and instructed under the 
<margin>E</margin>customs of holy rulers. In these matters, Dionysius did harm. Other damages, if compared to these, seem very small to me. But he who killed Dion did not realize that he had done the same thing as Dionysius. For I know certainly, as much as one man can affirm of another, that if Dion had held the rudder of the kingdom longer, he would never have turned to any other form of rule than that which he established from the beginning: his fatherland Syracuse, having been freed from slavery, was placed in its own right, most joyful in the splendor of liberty. Then, with all zeal, he would have adorned the citizens with fitting and excellent laws; furthermore, he would have applied every diligence so that all Sicily might be inhabited and liberated from the Barbarians—some being expelled and others subjected more easily than Hiero <note>Hiero I, a previous tyrant of Syracuse known for his military successes</note> had done. When these things had been carried out by a man who was just, 
<margin>F</margin>brave, temperate, and a philosopher, the same opinion of virtue would have flourished among the many; and this opinion would have remained strong among all men, so to speak, if Dionysius had obeyed us from the beginning. But now, whether some demon or some ruinous spirit threw itself in the way with iniquity and impiety—and what is worst, with ignorant audacity, from which all evils for all people take root and sprout, and later produce the most bitter fruit for their authors—it has overturned and destroyed all these things again. But now, for the sake of third-time lucky omens, let us speak only of good things. I advise you, his friends, to imitate Dion: embracing his love for his country and his temperance of life more and more. With good omens, strive to perfect his plans. What those were, you have heard clearly from me. But if there is anyone among you who cannot live in the Dorian fashion <note>The "Doric" way of life was associated with austerity, discipline, and traditional Greek law</note> according to the institutions of the fatherland, and follows the Sicilian way of 
<margin>G</margin>living and those who killed Dion, you should neither receive him nor consider him faithful or sincere in any matter. Rather, you ought to exhort the others to settle all of Sicily and establish equality of laws, drawing people both from Sicily itself and from the whole Peloponnese. Do not dread Athens; for there too are men who excel all others in virtue, and who hate the cruelty of those who pollute themselves with the murder of guests. But if these things are now too slow, and daily [troubles] urge you on...

# SEVENTH LETTER

The differences and factions that arise every day are things that every man ought to know; and if some divine fortune has granted even a small measure of right opinion, he would know that there is no end to evils for those engaged in factional strife until the victors cease from nursing grudges—from the killings, banishments, and punishments of men—and instead, showing self-control toward their enemies, establish common laws. These laws should be framed no more for their own pleasure than for the pleasure of those they have defeated, and they must compel everyone to follow them through two forms of necessity: respect and fear. Fear, by demonstrating force because they are the stronger party; and respect, by appearing superior themselves in their ability to master pleasures and their willingness and capacity to serve the laws. Otherwise, there is no way a city divided by faction within itself can ever cease from evils; rather, factions, enmities, hatreds, and betrayals are always wont to arise in cities disposed in such a way.

Therefore, those who are in power must always, whenever they desire salvation, choose from among themselves men whom they have heard are the best: first, elders who have wives and children at home, and as many ancestors as possible who are good and famous, and who all possess sufficient property. Sixty would be a good number; for a city, fifty such men are enough. These men must be summoned from their homes with the greatest honors and requests; and once summoned, they must be asked and bound by oath to establish laws that grant no more to the victors than to the vanquished, but rather what is equal and common to the whole city.

Once the laws are established, everything then depends on this: if the victors show themselves more subject to the laws than the vanquished, everything will be full of safety and happiness, and an escape from all evils. But if not, let no one call upon me or anyone else to share in counsel with one who does not obey these present instructions. For these are the kindred goals of what Dion and I attempted to achieve for Syracuse with right intention—though these are secondary. The primary goals were those first attempted with Dionysius <note>Dionysius II, the tyrant of Syracuse</note> himself to achieve common goods for all; but a certain fortune, stronger than men, destroyed them. Now, may you attempt to achieve these things more fortunately by some good fate and divine luck.

Let this be the end of my advice and the letter concerning it. As for my subsequent journey and voyage to Dionysius, how it happened both reasonably and appropriately, anyone who cares to hear may do so now. The greatest part of my time staying in Sicily had passed, as I said, before I gave counsel to the relatives and companions of Dion. After that, I did what I could to persuade Dionysius to let me leave. When peace was made (for there was war in Sicily at that time), we both reached an agreement: Dionysius said he would summon Dion and me back again in haste, once he had made his rule more secure for himself; and he requested that Dion consider his situation not as an exile, but as a temporary withdrawal. I agreed to return on these terms.

But when peace came, he summoned me, yet he asked Dion to wait another year; me, however, he demanded come by any means possible. Dion then urged and begged me to sail. For a great report was spreading from Sicily that Dionysius had once again been seized by a wonderful desire for philosophy. Therefore Dion clearly begged us not to disobey the summons. I knew well that many such things happen to young men regarding philosophy; nevertheless, it seemed safer to me at that time to say goodbye to both Dion and Dionysius, and I made myself disliked by both. I replied that I was an old man, and that none of the things currently happening were according to our agreements.

It seems that after this, Archytas <note>A Pythagorean philosopher and statesman of Tarentum</note> arrived at the court of Dionysius; for before my departure, I had established a bond of hospitality and friendship between Archytas and the Tarentines and Dionysius. There were also others in Syracuse who had heard some things from Dion, and others who were full of certain philosophical teachings they had overheard; these people, it seems, tried to discuss such matters with Dionysius, as if Dionysius had heard everything I was thinking. Now, he is not naturally dull in his ability to learn, and he is wonderfully ambitious for honor. Perhaps, then, he liked what was being said, and he was ashamed that it was obvious he had heard nothing from me during my stay. Hence, he was simultaneously seized by a desire to hear more clearly, and his ambition drove him. Why he did not hear it during my previous stay, I have explained in the words written above.

When I returned home and refused his second invitation, as I said, it now seems to me that Dionysius was entirely driven by ambition, lest I should ever seem to look down on him—having become experienced with his nature, character, and way of life, and no longer wishing to come to him because I was displeased. It is only just that I tell the truth; and if anyone, having heard what happened, despises my philosophy but thinks the tyrant has a mind, I must endure it. For Dionysius sent a trireme <note>A fast ancient warship with three banks of oars</note> to me a third time...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...and manifold seditions and discords: every man ought to understand, to whom a certain divine fate has granted even a little right opinion, that there will be no end to seditions and the evils born of sedition, until those who have conquered in battle—restraining themselves from the slaughter and expulsion of citizens, and even from the memory of injuries and the desire for revenge—are reconciled with their enemies and become masters of themselves. Furthermore, they should pass common laws that favor their own pleasure no more than the pleasure of those they defeated, and they should compel them to use these laws. They should compel them, I say, by a twin path of necessity: namely, by fear and by shame. By fear, because they are more powerful, demonstrating their force; but by shame, because they appear more powerful and ready both in overcoming pleasures and in observing the laws. Otherwise, there is no way at all of ending the evils of a city laboring under internal seditions; rather, seditions, enmities, hatreds, and betrayals in the republic will always arise, as is customary in cities so situated within themselves. Therefore, those who hold the republic as the more powerful party, if they desire safety, must themselves choose from among their number and prefer in honor those whom they have heard are the best: first, elders who have sons and wives and a home; and as many of their ancestors as possible who are proven and distinguished, and all possessing sufficient patrimony. For a city of ten thousand men, fifty such individuals will suffice. These men they ought to call forth from their homes with the greatest prayers and honors; and once called forth, they should pray to them and bind them by oath to establish laws that grant no more to the victors than to the vanquished, but rather what is fair and common to the entire city. Finally, once the laws are passed, everything now depends on this: if the victors are willing to be subject to the laws, even more than those who were defeated, then all things will be full of safety and happiness, and all evils will be far away. If not, there is no need to call me or anyone else into common counsel with him who does not acquiesce to such precepts. These are indeed the siblings of those things which Dion and I long ago attempted to achieve in Syracuse with right judgment, though these are later. For those first things would have been those which we tried to do with Dionysius himself at first: to act for the common good of all. But a certain fortune more powerful than men dissolved those plans. Now, however, may you attempt to act more fortunately in these matters by some good fate and divine fortune. And here is the end of the letter concerning counsel and my first voyage to Sicily to see Dionysius. But that the following journey and voyage of mine was undertaken neither without reason nor rashly, if anyone cares to know, he may hear it now. First, the time of my residence in Sicily had passed, as I said above, before I gave counsel to the friends and relatives of Dion; but afterward, I persuaded Dionysius as much as I could to permit me to depart. It had been agreed between us that when peace was made from the war then in Sicily, and his state was more safely confirmed, Dion would be recalled and I would return at the same time. He wanted Dion to understand and think that he was not in exile, but in a kind of withdrawal, and would return at a certain time. I, agreeing, promised I would do so. But when peace followed afterward, Dionysius indeed summoned me; but he urged Dion to tolerate his absence for another year. Me, however, he asked to hasten to him by all means. Dion, therefore, both ordered and prayed that I should go there. For a report had increased in Sicily that Dionysius was again moved by a wonderful desire for philosophy. Therefore Dion, deeply moved, strongly demanded that I not omit the journey. But although I knew that young men are often so affected toward philosophy, I nevertheless thought it would be safer to let the whole matter go and obey neither Dionysius nor Dion. I replied hatefully to both that I would not go because I was already an old man, and because none of the things currently happening were being done as had been agreed. Meanwhile, I heard that Archytas (the Tarentine) had come to Dionysius. For I, before my departure, had brought him and some other Tarentines into Dionysius's friendship. There were also some others in Syracuse who were sometimes listeners of Dion, and among these were others who had heard many other things in philosophy; these seemed to me to have contended to dispute about such matters before Dionysius, as if he had heard everything I had thought out. He, indeed, is not dull at learning and is vehemently inflamed by a desire for honor. Perhaps, therefore, the things being said pleased him; and he was clearly ashamed that he had heard nothing from me when I had come to him. Therefore, partly a love of hearing more clearly had invaded him, and partly a desire for glory stimulated him. For what reason he did not hear me in that first visit of mine, I have related in the previous sections. When I, a guest, had returned home and refused him when he summoned me a second time, as I said, it seemed to me that Dionysius was burning with care for his own honor, fearing lest men should take my refusal to mean that I utterly despised him, since I had known his nature, character, and life by experience itself. It is just that I confess the truth; and to bear it with an even mind if anyone, hearing what happened, scorns my philosophy but thinks the tyrant has a mind. For Dionysius sent a trireme to me a third time...
