# PLATO

where I might easily sail. He also sent Archedemus, whom he believed I valued most among all the associates of Archytas <note>Archytas of Tarentum, a Pythagorean philosopher and statesman</note> in Sicily; and together with him other Sicilian nobles. All of them affirmed to me with the same words that Dionysius was wonderfully devoted to philosophy. He himself furthermore sent a very large letter, since he knew how I was disposed toward Dion, and that Dion’s own desire was for me to come to Syracuse. The letter had been composed with all these things in mind, beginning in such a manner:

> Dionysius to Plato. Having offered the lawful and customary greetings: thereafter (he says) nothing shall be more important to you than coming to Sicily according to our wish. First, regarding Dion, things will be done as you yourself wish. And you will wish, I believe, for moderate things, and I shall grant them. But if you do not come, you will obtain none of those things which you desire for Dion, neither in other matters nor in those which concern his person, which you especially desire.

He wrote these things in this way. The rest would be long to tell and not very opportune to relate. Other letters also came from Archytas and other Italians and Tarentines, praising Dionysius’s zeal for wisdom; they added to this that if I did not set out, I would subject to slander that friendship which I had established between them and Dionysius—which was of no small importance regarding civil affairs. Since I was being summoned at that time in this way, with those from Sicily and Italy pulling me, while others at Athens were almost expelling me with their prayers, and reason dictated to me that it was not right to betray Dion and my Tarentine hosts and friends; and it occurred to me that it is not surprising if some gifted young man, though he previously refused to hear discourses on great matters, should then change his mind and be kindled by a certain ardor for the best life. It was necessary to clearly explore which way he might incline, and not to betray him, nor to give him cause for such great reproach against me, if indeed his affairs were truly as they were reported. Protected by the advocacy of these reasons, I began the journey, fearing many things and divining many things that would not be very happy, as it turned out. Finally, I set out for the third time, under the Savior <note>original: "sub Servatore" / "τῷ σωτῆρι". A reference to Zeus the Savior, often invoked for safe passage.</note>. For in truth I was preserved; for again I was safely rescued. But after God, I owe thanks to Dionysius for this: because when many desired to kill me, he himself resisted, and showed some measure of shame in my affairs. 

When I had arrived at his court, I judged it would be worthwhile above all to examine this very thing: whether Dionysius was truly kindled by a love of philosophy as if by a fire, or whether a vain rumor of it had spread as far as Athens. There is a certain method of taking an experiment regarding these things, not inelegant, but truly suited to tyrants, especially those who have already heard many discourses. I perceived immediately upon coming that this had happened to Dionysius. One must show such people how great a thing philosophy is, how much zeal it requires, and with what great labors it is acquired. He who hears this, if he truly loves wisdom and is by nature akin to it and worthy of its possession, as one who is divine, thinks a wonderful way has been shown to him, and that he must walk it with every effort, and does not think life worth living if he does otherwise. Therefore, he exhorts himself and even the leader of this life more intensely; nor does he stop until he has either reached the end of all things or at least acquired such a faculty through which he can lead himself to the goal without a guide. Therefore, considering these and similar reasons, such a man is always intent upon philosophy throughout his whole life, whatever he may do; and he uses a daily diet by which he can best preserve his talent, memory, and judgment, keeping himself sober and always hating the diet contrary to this. 

But those who are not truly lovers of wisdom, but are merely colored by opinions from the outside, like those who are burned and colored by the sun, when they hear how many things must be learned, with how much labor, and what temperance of daily life is necessary for the study of philosophy, immediately thinking the matter hard and impossible for them, they cannot be brought to give it their effort. Many, indeed, persuade themselves that they have already heard everything sufficiently and no longer need any further study. This method of making the trial is clear and not at all deceptive against those who are unable to follow through because of softness; so that they can never cast the blame on the teacher, but they themselves refute themselves as being unable to perform those things which befit philosophy. I used this method of examination with Dionysius then; I did not run through everything, nor did Dionysius require it. For there were many and very great things in which he strove to be thought sufficiently learned because of what he had heard from others. I hear, indeed, that he later wrote about the things he heard then, as if composing his own art <note>term: "art" / "ars" / "τέχνη". Here meaning a formal textbook or system of knowledge.</note>; though nothing of these things was truly in him, as I hear. Concerning these things, I know nothing for certain. I know some others have written about these same matters; but whoever they were, they did not even know themselves. I will say this much about all who have written or will write, claiming to know those things which I treat with serious study—whether they heard them from me or from others, or whether they were the inventors themselves—in my judgment they can perceive nothing of this matter. For I have never written about them, nor shall I write. For it...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...the one who would command the trireme for me for the sake of the journey. And he sent Archedemus, whom he thought I valued most of those in Sicily, one of those who had associated with Archytas, and other acquaintances from Sicily. These all brought us the same report, that it was marvelous how much Dionysius had progressed in philosophy. And he sent a very long letter, knowing how I felt toward Dion and Dion’s eagerness for me to sail and come to Syracuse. To all these things the letter was well-prepared in its beginning, saying something like this: "Dionysius to Plato." Having said the customary things after this, he said nothing sooner than that "if you come now to Sicily, being persuaded by us, first of all, the affairs concerning Dion will be settled for you in whatever way you yourself wish. <margin>B</margin> And you will wish, I know, for moderate things, and I will concede them. But if not, none of the matters concerning Dion will be settled for you, neither regarding other things nor himself," etc. These things he said in this way; the rest would be long and not timely to tell. Other letters kept coming from Archytas and those in Tarentum, both praising the philosophy of Dionysius and saying that if I did not arrive now, I would completely <margin>C</margin> slander the friendship they had with Dionysius through me, which was of no small importance for political affairs. Such being the summons at that time, with those from Sicily and Italy pulling me, and those from Athens literally pushing me out with their entreaties, the same argument came back: that I must not betray Dion, nor my guests and companions in Tarentum. And it occurred to me that it was nothing marvelous for a young man, hearing worthy discourses on great matters, though ignorant, to come to a love of the best life. It was necessary then to test this clearly, in which way it might be, and never to betray him, nor to become the cause of such great blame and reproach, if indeed these things were truly <margin>D</margin> as said. I traveled then, covering myself with this reasoning, fearing much, and divining not very well, as it seems. Having come then for the third time, I was truly saved by the Savior. For I suffered again brilliantly, and for these things, after God, thanks must be given to Dionysius; because when many wanted to destroy me, he prevented it, and gave some measure of respect to my situation. When I arrived, I thought I must first take this test: whether Dionysius was truly set on fire by philosophy, as if by a fire, or whether this great report had come to Athens in vain. There is indeed a certain way of taking a trial about such things, not ignoble, but truly fitting for tyrants, especially those <margin>E</margin> full of many borrowed teachings. Which indeed I found Dionysius had experienced much upon my arrival. It must be shown to such people what the whole matter is like, and through what things and how much labor it involves. For he who hears, if he is truly a philosopher, akin to and worthy of the matter, being divine, thinks he has heard of a marvelous path, and that he must strain himself now, and that life is not worth living for one who does otherwise. After this, straining himself and his leader on the path, he does not let up until he either puts an end to all things or takes up the power so that he himself is not unable to guide himself without the one who showed him. In this way and according to these thoughts such a man lives; acting indeed in whatever actions he may be, but through all things always holding to philosophy, and to the daily diet which will most make him apt to learn and remember, and to <margin>F</margin> reason soberly, being sober in himself, and he continues hating the diet contrary to this. But those who are not truly philosophers, but are merely tinged with opinions, like those whose bodies are burned by the sun, seeing how many teachings there are and how great the labor, and how a daily diet is fitting or orderly for the work, thinking it difficult and impossible for themselves, they become unable to practice it; and some persuade themselves that they have heard the whole thing sufficiently, and no longer need any efforts. This trial then becomes the clear and safest one against those who are luxurious and unable to labor, so that they never <margin>G</margin> blame the one who shows them, but themselves, as being unable to practice all the things conducive to the matter. Thus indeed the things that were said were said to Dionysius then. I did not go through everything, nor did Dionysius ask. For he himself pretended to know many and the greatest things and to be sufficient, because of the things he had overheard from others. Later I hear that he has written about what he heard then, composing it as his own art, not at all the same as what he heard; but I know nothing of these things. I know some others have written about these same things; but who they are, they do not even know themselves. This much at least I will say about all who have written and will write, as many as say they know about the things I am serious about, whether hearing from me or others, or as having found it themselves: these people cannot, in my opinion, understand anything about the matter. There is no writing of mine about it, nor will there ever be. For it is not at all speakable like other...

<summary>Plato describes his reluctant third journey to Syracuse, motivated by a desire to help Dion and a sense of duty to his friends. He introduces his "test" for true philosophers, arguing that genuine wisdom requires intense personal labor and cannot be captured in written textbooks.</summary>

# SEVENTH LETTER

<margin>A</margin> ...cannot be expressed in words at all, like other studies; but from a long-standing association with the matter itself, and living together with it, suddenly, like a light kindled from a leaping fire, it is born in the soul and henceforth nourishes itself. And yet I know this much: that things written or spoken by me would be spoken best; and indeed, that things written badly would cause me no small distress. But if it seemed to me that they ought to be written or spoken for the many, what finer thing could have been achieved by us in life than to write a great benefit for mankind and to bring nature into the light for all? But I do not think the attempt to speak of these things is a good thing for men, except for a few—those who are able to
<margin>B</margin> discover them for themselves through a brief indication. As for the others, it would fill some with an unseemly and incorrect contempt, and others with a high and empty hope, as if they had learned something solemn. <note>The Greek text contains a typo εὐκαρπερᾷ, likely intended as εὐκαρδίᾳ (confidence/courage).</note> Furthermore, it has come into my mind to speak at greater length about these things. For perhaps if these things are said, what I am saying might become clearer. For there is a certain true argument that stands against the man who dares to write anything at all about such matters, which has been said by me many times before, and it seems it must be said now. For each of the things that exist, there are three through which knowledge must necessarily come; the fourth is knowledge itself. And as a fifth, one must set down the object itself which is knowable and truly exists. Of these, the first is the
<margin>C</margin> **name**; the second is the **definition** <note>original: λόγος (logos)</note>; the third is the **image** <note>original: εἴδωλον (eidolon)</note>; the fourth is **knowledge**. Take any one example to understand what has just been said, and think of all others in the same way. There is something called a "circle," which has this very name we have just uttered. Its definition—the second thing—is composed of nouns and verbs. For "that which is everywhere equidistant from the extremities to the center" would be the definition of that which is named "round," "circumference," and "circle." The third is that which is painted and rubbed out, or turned on a lathe and destroyed. None of these things affects the circle itself, about which all these things are concerned, for it is something different. The fourth is knowledge, intellect, and true opinion about these things. This whole group must be taken as one, existing not in sounds or in the
<margin>D</margin> shapes of bodies, but in souls. Whereby it is clear that it is different from the nature of the circle itself and from the three things previously mentioned. Of these, **intellect** <note>original: νοῦς (nous)</note> is closest in kinship and similarity to the fifth, while the others are further removed. The same is true of straight and spherical shapes, and of color; of the Good, the Beautiful, and the Just; and of every body, whether manufactured or natural—fire, water, and all such things—and of every living being, and of the character in souls, and of all actions and passions. For unless someone grasps the four of these in some way, he will never perfectly partake in the knowledge of the fifth. Furthermore, these four attempt to show the *quality* of each thing no less than its *being*, because of the weakness of language. For this reason, no man of sense will ever dare to set down his thoughts in it—especially into an unchangeable form, which is what happens to things written in characters.
<margin>E</margin> This point must be understood again. Every circle drawn or turned on a lathe in practice is full of the opposite of the fifth; for it touches the straight everywhere. But the circle itself, we say, has in it neither more nor less of the opposite nature. We say that none of their names has any stability. Nothing prevents the things now called "round" from being called "straight," and the "straight" from being called "round"; and they will be no less stable for those who change the names and call them the opposite. Indeed, the same applies to the definition: since it is composed of nouns and verbs, it is not sufficiently or firmly stable. There are ten thousand arguments
<margin>F</margin> about each of the four, how they are unclear. But the greatest point is what we said a moment ago: that since there are two things—the *being* and the *quality*—and the soul seeks to know not the quality but the "what" <note>The essence or "whatness" of a thing.</note>, each of the four offers the soul the thing it is not seeking, both in speech and in physical sensations, always providing what is said and shown to be refuted, and filling every man, so to speak, with all perplexity and lack of clarity. In matters where we are not even accustomed to seek the truth because of poor education, but are satisfied with the images presented to us, we do not make ourselves ridiculous to one another—the questioned to the questioners—being able to pull apart and refute those four. But where
<margin>G</margin> we are forced to show the fifth, anyone who wishes to can overturn the argument and make the person explaining it in speech, or writing, or in answers, seem to the many listeners to know nothing of what he attempts to write or say. They are sometimes ignorant that it is not the soul of the writer or speaker that is being refuted, but the nature of each of the four, which is naturally flawed. But the process of going through all of them, moving up and down to each one, barely gives birth to knowledge in one who is well-disposed, to a well-disposed mind. But if a man's nature is poorly disposed—as is the state of the soul of the many toward learning and toward what are called morals—and if they are corrupted, not even Lynceus <note>A mythological figure famous for his keen sight.</note> could make such a person see.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> <note>The Latin column provides a parallel translation of the Greek text above.</note> ...in no way can it be expressed in words, as other disciplines can: but from long-standing habit concerning the thing itself, and a conjunction of life with it: suddenly at last, as if a light shining from a flickering fire, it now nourishes itself in the soul. And I know this much at least, that things written or said by me are said best: but things written badly would bring me no small trouble. But if it seemed to me that they should be brought forth to the common people in writing or by voice: what finer thing could happen to us in life than to bring a very useful thing to men, and to bring nature into the light for all? But indeed, I do not think the study in publishing these things is useful to men, except
<margin>B</margin> to a very few: who, namely, having been shown small tracks beforehand, are themselves quick to find it. Others it would have filled partly with wicked contempt, partly with high and vain hope: as if they had already learned some excellent things. Therefore I thought to speak longer about them. For perhaps if these things are said, something of what I say will appear more clearly. For there is a certain true reason, opposing him who dares to write nothing at all about such matters: often said by me elsewhere, and now, as it seems, to be said. For each of those things which are, there are three, from which it is necessary for knowledge to be made. The fourth is knowledge itself. But the fifth one must place as that which is knowable, that is, what can be
<margin>C</margin> recognized, and truly exists. One of these is the name: the second the definition: the third the example <note>The Latin uses "exemplum" for the Greek "eidolon" (image/representation).</note>: knowledge the fourth. Concerning any one thing therefore, take it, desiring to learn what has just been said, and think similarly about all. Something is called a circle, whose name is that which we were just pronouncing. Its definition follows, composed of names and verbs. For that which is equally distant from the extremes to the middle everywhere, is the definition of that which we designate by the name of round and circumference and circle. The third is: that a circle is painted or deleted, or made by a lathe or destroyed. None of which the circle itself, about which these individual things are, suffers: as being something else. The fourth is knowledge and intellect, and true
<margin>D</margin> opinion about these. This again must be placed as a whole as one: which is neither in voices nor in the figures of bodies, but in the mind and intelligence. And therefore it is manifest, that it is something other than the nature of the circle itself, and again something other than those three which we said above. But from the number of these, intellect clings closest to the fifth by kinship and similarity, the others are more remote. The same can also be said of the straight and curved figure, and color: and of the good and beautiful and just. Again of whatever body, whether made by hand or natural, whether fire or water, and others of this kind. Similarly of every animal, and of the characters of souls, and of all actions and passions. For unless one captures those four in some way in these, he will never
<margin>E</margin> be perfectly a partaker of knowledge concerning the fifth. Therefore those things attempt to show no less what kind of thing each is, than what it is: because of the weakness of reasons. Wherefore no one of sound mind will ever dare to refer those things which are understood by him into the same, and that indeed immutable, as those four. Which certainly happens to those things which are designated by figures. But that which we now say, must be considered again. Surely any circle of these which are either painted by men's hands or made by a lathe, is plainly contrary to that fifth. For it partakes of the straight from every side. But we affirm the circle itself
<margin>F</margin> to be neither less nor more of anything: that is, to have nothing at all of a contrary nature in itself. Furthermore, we say the name of none of these has any firmness. For nothing would prohibit those which we now name round, from being called straight, and the straight round: nor would there be any greater firmness in names changed to the contrary. The same reason is also concerning the definition: since it is composed of names and verbs having no firmness at all. Again it can be proved in many ways, that none of these four is certain and firm. But the greatest of all, which we were saying a little before: that since there are two, essence and quality: when the mind seeks not what kind, but what it is: unless any
<margin>G</margin> of these four sought first by the soul as much by reason as by affection, and finally well discussed by the senses, should escape through all things which are said and shown: it will fill all men with all ambiguity and obscurity, so to speak. In those things therefore where we are by no means accustomed to search for the truth because of bad education, but think we have done enough if we have touched the presented images, are we not a mockery to each other when questioned by questioners, who are able at least to discuss and refute those four: But where necessity compels to show the fifth, anyone of those who can escape and retract prevails: and makes it so that he who explains by words or letters or disputes,

seems to many of the listeners to understand nothing of those things which he attempts to say or write. In which matter it is often ignored that not the mind of the writer or speaker is refuted, but rather the nature of any of those four being in a bad state. But the translation <note>The Latin "traductio" here refers to the "leading through" or process of dialectic.</note> through all those things running to and fro up and down into each one, at last hardly brings forth knowledge within, I say the knowledge of that which is naturally well-disposed in the soul to that which is also naturally well-disposed. But if anyone be ill-disposed by nature, such as the habit of the soul is naturally in many, both toward those things which are to be learned, and toward morals, and those are corrupted, not even Lynceus...

# OF PLATO

so that such a soul might see, he could bring it about. And to speak <margin>A</margin> briefly, neither quickness of mind nor memory will ever make one who is not naturally related to the matter itself see it clearly. For the first principle <note>The "spark" of understanding</note> does not take root in alien habits. Therefore, those who are not naturally inclined toward and related to justice and all other beautiful things—even if some are clever and have good memories for other subjects—and again, those who are related but are dull and weak of memory, will never reach the ultimate truth <margin>B</margin> of virtue or of vice. For it is necessary to learn these together: both the false and the true of the whole of reality <note>original: "totius essentiae" / "τῆς ὅλης οὐσίας"</note> with all exertion and a long period of time, as I said from the beginning. But after their names, definitions, sights, and sensations have been rubbed against one another and worn down, and tested by kindly refutations and discussed through questioning and answering without envy, at last prudence and intelligence shine forth regarding each thing, striving to the utmost of human capacity. For this reason, it is far from the case that a serious and earnest man, writing for men about things that are truly worthy of study, would ever subject himself and his works to envy and ambiguity. By this one argument, indeed, it is possible to understand: <margin>C</margin> whenever one sees the writings of someone—whether the laws of a legislator or anything else—one should realize that these were not his most serious concerns, if indeed he is a serious man himself; for those lie in the most beautiful region of his own being. But if he truly committed these things to writing as his most serious thoughts, then "not the gods, but mortals have destroyed his wits" <note>A quote from Homer's Iliad</note>. Whoever follows this tale and digression will clearly understand that whether Dionysius wrote anything about the highest and first principles of nature, or anyone else, whether lesser or greater, it is my opinion that he heard or learned nothing sound regarding what he wrote. Otherwise, he would have respected these things just as I do, and would never have dared to subject them to absurdity and indecency by publishing them rashly. Nor did he write them as an aid to memory. <margin>D</margin> For there is no danger of forgetting this, once it has been grasped by the soul. For it is contained in the briefest of all terms. Perhaps, however, he did it out of a base ambition, either to claim these things as his own or to appear as a participant in a teaching of which he was unworthy, seeking the glory that comes from such participation. Now, if this happened to Dionysius from a single meeting, perhaps it might be granted. But "Jupiter knows," as the Theban says <note>A common Greek idiom, likely referring to Pindar</note>. I indeed ran through these things for him in the way I said, and only once; never again after that. After this, one must consider—as one seeks to find the cause of what happened to us regarding those matters—why we did not go through them a second or third time, or more often. Did Dionysius, having heard them only once, think he knew them sufficiently, <margin>E</margin> whether he found them out himself or learned them from others before? Or did he think the things said were frivolous? Or perhaps a third thing happened: namely, that he judged them to be beyond his own powers and that he was truly not fit to live under the discipline of prudence and virtue. For if he is said to have thought them frivolous, he will be fought by many witnesses for our cause who have far greater authority in judging such matters than Dionysius. But if he thought he had found or learned them, and that they were worthy of being used for the education of a free soul, how could anyone not find it strange that Dionysius, being so disposed, would so easily hold the leader and author of these things in contempt? How he held him in contempt, I shall now say. <margin>F</margin> For not long after this time, he forbade the stewards of Dion’s estate to touch his property—which he had previously allowed him to possess freely and collect the fruits therefrom—and he stopped the money from being sent to him in the Peloponnese as was customary, as if he had entirely forgotten that letter he had written to me. For he claimed those things were not Dion’s, but belonged to his son, who, being his nephew by his sister, was under his legal guardianship. These things, then, were done up to that time. When I considered these events, I saw clearly how Dionysius was disposed toward <margin>G</margin> philosophy, and I was troubled, whether I wished to be or not. It was already summer then, and ships were frequently sailing; it seemed to me that I should complain not so much about Dionysius as about myself and those who had forced me to come a third time to the strait of Scylla and to measure again the destructive Charybdis <note>A reference to the Odyssey; Plato compares his journey to Sicily to the dangerous passage between sea monsters</note>. I was thus compelled to tell Dionysius that I could in no way remain with him while Dion was so ignominiously treated. But he tried to console me and asked me to stay, not thinking it honorable for him if I myself should go so quickly as a messenger of these deeds of his. When he could not persuade me to stay, he said he himself would provide a way for me to be sent. I, however, had decided to cross in the transport ships, thinking I must endure everything if he prohibited me from leaving; for I had clearly done him no wrong, yet I was being wronged by him. But when he realized I would in no way stay, he devised a scheme to hinder my sailing. The next day he spoke to me graciously and in a persuasive manner. "Between me and you," he said, "let Dion and Dion’s affairs, insofar as they provide a cause for our discord, be removed from the middle. For your sake I will do this for Dion. I decree that Dion, receiving his own property, shall live in the Peloponnese, not as an exile, but as one who is permitted to come here whenever it seems common to him, to me, and to you his friends; provided only that he does me no wrong..."

# SEVENTH LETTER

<margin>A</margin> ...that he [Dionysius] would be a joint-guarantor of these things to me, to you, and to our mutual friends. You and your relatives, and by the gods, Dion’s relatives too, should act as sureties for this. He [Dionysius] will provide you with security; but let all the money he receives be deposited in the Peloponnese or at Athens with whomever you see fit. Let Dion enjoy the <term>usufruct</term> <note>The right to enjoy the income or profit from property without owning it outright.</note> of it, but he shall not have the power to withdraw the principal without your consent. For I do not entirely trust him [Dion] at present to be just toward me if he has use of these funds (which are not small); I trust you and yours more. See then <margin>B</margin> if this pleases you, and remain here for this year on these terms. When you depart in the spring, you may take this money with you, and I know well that Dion will be very grateful to you for having managed these affairs on his behalf.

When I heard this speech, I was altogether displeased; nevertheless, after deliberating, I said I would report my decision to him the following day. We agreed on that then. I deliberated well at that time—first by myself, though I was very confused. The starting point of my reasoning was this: "Look, suppose Dionysius intends to do none of the things he says. After I am gone, he and many others could plausibly persuade Dion that he [Dionysius] was willing to do what he now says, but that I was unwilling and <margin>C</margin> neglected Dion’s interests. Furthermore, suppose he refuses to let me go, not providing a ship or sailors, and easily indicates to everyone that I am leaving against his will. Would any sea-captain be willing to take me as a passenger, starting from Dionysius’s house?"

For I was living, among other troubles, in the garden surrounding the palace, from which even the gatekeeper would not have let me pass without some order sent to him from Dionysius. "But if I stay for the year, I can send word to Dion about the situation I am in and what I am doing. And if Dionysius actually does any of the things he says, my actions will not be entirely ridiculous. For Dion’s estate is perhaps worth a hundred <term>talents</term> <note>A massive unit of currency; 100 talents would be an enormous fortune in the 4th century BCE.</note> if one values it correctly. But if <margin>D</margin> things turn out as they now seem likely to, I am at a loss as to what I shall do with myself. Nevertheless, it is perhaps necessary to endure another year and try to test Dionysius’s schemes by actual deeds."

Having decided this, I told Dionysius the next day that I had decided to stay. "But I request," I said, "that you do not consider me Dion’s master. You should send letters with me to him, explaining what has now been decided, and asking him whether these terms satisfy him or not; and if he wants or claims anything else, he should write back as soon as possible, and in the meantime, you should make no new changes regarding his affairs." This was said, and we came to an agreement, nearly as I have just stated.

After this, the ships sailed, and it was no longer possible for me to leave. Then Dionysius remembered to say that half of the property belonged to Dion, <margin>E</margin> and the other half to his son. He said he would sell it, and when it was sold, he would give me half to take to Dion and leave the other half there for the boy. For he claimed that was the legal status of Dion’s estate. Stunned by what he said, I thought it was utterly ridiculous to say anything more; however, I said we should wait for Dion’s letter and then write back to him about these new developments.

But immediately after this, he very boldly sold Dion’s entire estate, in whatever way and to whomever he pleased. He said nothing at all to me about it, <margin>F</margin> and likewise, I no longer discussed Dion’s affairs with him, as I thought I could achieve nothing more. Up to this point, I had provided what help I could to philosophy and my friends.

After this, Dionysius and I lived on: I, looking outward like a bird longing to fly away from somewhere; and he, scheming how he might scare me into staying without giving back any of Dion’s property. Nevertheless, we claimed to be "friends" to all of Sicily.

Then Dionysius attempted to reduce the pay of the older mercenaries, contrary to his father’s custom. Enraged, the soldiers gathered in a crowd and said they would not permit it. He tried to use force, closing the gates of the acropolis, but they marched straight <margin>G</margin> to the walls, shouting a certain barbarian and warlike <term>paean</term> <note>A song of triumph or a war-cry.</note>. Dionysius, becoming terrified, conceded everything and even more to the peltasts <note>Light-armed infantrymen.</note> then assembled.

A rumor quickly spread that Heraclides was the cause of all this. Hearing this, Heraclides kept himself out of sight. Dionysius sought to capture him, and being at a loss, he sent for Theodotus. I happened to be walking in the garden with them at the time. I do not know or hear the rest of their conversation, but what Theodotus said to Dionysius in my presence, I know and remember.

"Plato," he said, "I am persuading Dionysius here that if I am able <margin>H</margin> to bring Heraclides here to answer the charges made against him, and if it then seems best that he should not live in Sicily, he should at least be allowed to take his wife and son and sail to the Peloponnese, living there without harming Dionysius and enjoying the income from his own property. I have already sent for him, and I will send for him again now. Heraclides..."

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> <note>The Latin column mirrors the Greek text above, providing a 15th/16th-century translation of Plato's letter.</note> ...and that your relatives and those of Dion who live here will be sureties for me in this matter. Dion himself must also sufficiently confirm to you that he will observe this. Let all the money he receives be deposited in the Peloponnese and Athens with those whom you see fit. Let Dion receive the fruits of this money, but he may not withdraw the principal without your consent. For I do not trust that he will keep faith with me if he receives the money, since it will be no small amount. I have greater faith in you and yours. Consider therefore if these things please you: stay here for a year for the sake of these things, and when it is finished, <margin>B</margin> you shall depart with this money. I know Dion will be very grateful to you when you have accomplished this for him.

When I had heard these things, although I took it very badly, I replied nonetheless that I would consult on this matter, and I took until the next day to respond. And so, agreeing on this, we then departed. I consulted thereafter with myself, being indeed very uncertain. But a first reason occurred to me as a guide for my counsel. "Come now, even if Dionysius intends to keep none of the promises he makes, if nevertheless, after I have departed, he should write to Dion through himself and his friends—as he now says to me—that he had offered <margin>C</margin> these things of his own accord, but that I had been unwilling and had utterly neglected his affairs..."

Furthermore, I added to this: "If Dionysius, wishing to dismiss me, does not provide a ship and sailors; or rather, if he easily signals to everyone that I wish to depart against his will: who would dare to carry me away in a ship from the very house of Dionysius?" I was living, so that no inconvenience should be lacking, in the very gardens that were around the house. From there, not even the gatekeeper would have permitted me to go out unless Dionysius ordered it. "But if I remain for a year, I have a means to signal to Dion and make known to him in what state I am placed and what I am doing. And if Dionysius keeps some of the things he promises, this work and endurance of mine will not seem altogether <margin>D</margin> ridiculous." For the patrimony of Dion will be valued at no less than a hundred talents, if anyone wishes to estimate it correctly. "But if things fall out as they are likely to fall out, I do not know where I shall turn. Nevertheless, perhaps it is necessary for me to endure for another year and refute Dionysius's machinations in reality with all my strength."

When I had so consulted with myself, on the very next day I reported to Dionysius that it seemed I should stay. But I added that he should not think I could act as master over Dion in all things, and therefore it would be worthwhile for him to write to him along with me, signifying these our plans, and asking whether these things satisfy him or not: and whether he requires anything else besides them. And I said that this must be written as soon as possible. Meanwhile, no new action should be <margin>E</margin> attempted by him in Dion's affairs. These things were said between us. In these terms, as I now say, we agreed.

But after this, when the ships had already left, and therefore no further opportunity for sailing remained for me, Dionysius, as if remembering something omitted, said: "Half of Dion's goods ought by right to remain for his son; the other half should be sent to Dion. I will therefore see that this is sold. When it is sold, I will deliver half of the money to you to be carried to Dion; <margin>F</margin> the remaining part will be kept by us for his son: for so justice itself requires." Struck by these words of his, I thought it ridiculous to speak further on that matter. I said, however, that we should wait for a response from Dion, and then write back these very things to him.

But he, afterwards, too boldly sold Dion's entire patrimony for whatever price he pleased, and in whatever way and to whomever he liked. He made no word at all to me about that matter. But I likewise spoke nothing further of Dion's affairs thereafter, since I thought I would profit nothing more. Hitherto, in this manner, I provided help to both philosophy and my friends. But after this, Dionysius and I lived such that I was always looking outward, like some bird desiring to fly away from somewhere; but he was constantly scheming how he might restrain me, granting nothing regarding <margin>G</margin> Dion's affairs. In other matters, however, we confessed throughout all Sicily that we were friends.

At that time, Dionysius attempted to reduce the wages of the veteran soldiers, contrary to his father's custom. The soldiers, being angry, came together as one and threatened that they would not tolerate it. Therefore, he tried to coerce them by closing the gates of the citadel itself. But they suddenly came to the walls, raising a certain barbarian and warlike shout. Terrified by this fear, Dionysius conceded all the customary things to them, and even more than was customary. There was a rumor that Heraclides had been the cause of the whole tumult. Heraclides, sensing this, secretly took flight. Dionysius, while he desired to capture him and could not find him, summoned Theodotus to him in the gardens. I happened then to be walking in the gardens myself. The other things that were discussed between them I neither know nor heard while they were talking; but what Theodotus said to Dionysius in my presence, I both know and remember. "O Plato," he said, "I am persuading Dionysius here that if <margin>H</margin> I can bring Heraclides here, he shall answer to the charges brought against him. And if Dionysius then does not want him to remain in Sicily, let him at least permit him to take his wife and son and depart to the Peloponnese and live there, attempting nothing there against Dionysius, and receiving the fruits of the goods he possesses here. With this confidence, I have already called Heraclides; and I will call him again."

# OF PLATO

<margin>A</margin> Whether he came here because of the first summons or the second, I reached an agreement with Dionysius and requested that no harm should come to Heraclides, whether outside the city or within it; but rather, if it seemed best, he should be sent beyond the borders until Dionysius decided otherwise. I said, "Dionysius, do you agree to this?" He replied, "I agree; even if he appears in your own house, he shall suffer no harm beyond what has been said." On the following day, just at twilight, Eurybius and Theodotes came to me in a state of great agitation. Theodotes immediately said, "Plato, you were present yesterday when Dionysius made an agreement with you and me regarding Heraclides." "I was," I replied. "Well," he said, "now the guards are running about trying to seize Heraclides; and there is a danger <margin>B</margin> that he is somewhere nearby. Therefore, follow us with all haste to Dionysius." We went, and having entered his presence, they stood in silence weeping; but I said, "Dionysius, these men are afraid that you are acting contrary to yesterday's agreement regarding Heraclides. For it seems he has been seen somewhere nearby." Upon hearing this, Dionysius flared up in anger and changed into various colors, such as rage is accustomed to bring. Theodotes, falling at his feet and taking his hand, begged him with many tears not to do such a thing. Then I, taking up the conversation to comfort him, said, "Be of good cheer, Theodotes. For Dionysius will not dare to act otherwise <margin>C</margin> than he promised yesterday." But Dionysius, looking at me with an exceedingly tyrannical expression, said, "To you I promised nothing, whether great or small." "By the gods," I replied, "you certainly did promise not to do these very things which this man now begs you not to do." Having said this, I turned and went out. After this, Dionysius continued trying to capture Heraclides. Theodotes, however, sent messengers to warn him to flee. Dionysius had indeed sent a certain Tisias <note>original: "tiffiam" in Latin OCR, "Τισίαν" in Greek</note> with guards, ordering them to pursue Heraclides everywhere. But he, as it is said, anticipated them and, avoiding the guards by a small part of a day, escaped into Carthaginian territory. <margin>D</margin> Now, Dionysius seems to have found a plausible excuse for the enmity he had long been plotting against me—namely, to prevent Dio’s money from being sent. First, he removed me from the citadel, using the pretext that the women were to perform a ten-day sacrifice in the gardens where I lived. Therefore, he ordered me to stay outside the citadel with Archedemus during those days. Meanwhile, Theodotes called for me and complained much about Dionysius regarding what had then occurred. When Dionysius heard that I had gone to see Theodotes, finding this again as a new occasion for hatred against me, similar to the previous one, he sent men to ask if I had indeed been summoned to Theodotes' house. I freely confessed that I had been there. Then he said: "Dionysius has ordered me to tell you that you are not acting rightly, for you always value Dio and Dio’s friends more than him." These things were <margin>E</margin> said. Never again did he invite me to his house, treating me as an open friend of Theodotes and Heraclides, and an enemy to himself; he believed I was hostile because Dio’s property was now entirely lost. Thereafter, I lived outside the citadel among the mercenary soldiers. Certain people, including some Athenian citizens in service there, came to me and reported that slanders against me were being spread among the soldiers. Furthermore, some threatened that if they caught me anywhere, they would kill me. I therefore devised an escape <margin>F</margin> of this kind. I sent word to Tarentum, to Archytas and my other friends, explaining the danger in which I was placed. They, devising a pretext of a state embassy, sent Lamiscus, one of their number, with a thirty-oared ship. When he came to Dionysius, he requested that he permit me to depart safely according to my wish. He consented and dismissed me, providing travel expenses. As for Dio’s money, neither <margin>G</margin> did I ask for it, nor did anyone give it. After this, when I arrived in the Peloponnesus and found Dio there watching the Olympic games, I recounted what had happened. He, calling Jupiter <note>original: "Iouem" (Zeus)</note> to witness, immediately told me and my relatives and friends that he would exact punishment from Dionysius—both because he had deceived me, his guest (for so he said and felt), and because he had unjustly expelled him. Hearing this, I urged him to call upon other friends if he saw fit. As for me, since he and others had by a kind of force pushed me into intimacy with Dionysius—bound by the sharing of a home, food, and sacrifices—they should consider me a sort of neutral party, who ought to be fair to both sides; especially since, although many had long slandered me to Dionysius as plotting with you against him and his tyranny, he did not kill me, but showed restraint. To this I added that my age made me unfit for war; and at the same time, I was a middleman between them, should they ever need a mediator to repair their friendship. "But as long as you contend with hatreds," I said, "you must call on others as helpers." I said this because I loathed my wandering and my ill fortune in Sicily. Since they did not obey my reasoning, they themselves became the cause of all the evils that followed. Truly, if Dionysius had restored Dio’s property, or rather if he had been entirely reconciled, nothing adverse would have happened, as far as human conditions go. For

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...whether from the former summons or from the present one, as much as you shall hear from me. I requested and begged Dionysius that if Heraclides were found, whether in office or in a state of sedition, no harm should befall him, but that he should be removed from the country until Dionysius decided otherwise. "Do you agree to this?" he said, speaking to Dionysius. "I agree," he replied; "even if he appears in your <margin>B</margin> house, he shall suffer no harm contrary to what has now been said." On the day after this, in the evening, Eurybius and Theodotes came to me in a state of great haste and agitation. And Theodotes said, "Plato, were you present yesterday when Dionysius made an agreement regarding Heraclides with me and you?" "How could I not be?" I said. "Now then," he said, "the targeteers <term>peltasts: light-armed infantry</term> are running about, seeking to seize Heraclides. And he is likely somewhere in this area. <margin>B</margin> But follow us to Dionysius by every means." We went, therefore, and entered his presence; and they stood in silence weeping. But I said, "These men are afraid lest you do something new against Heraclides contrary to yesterday's agreement. For it seems to me he has been seen hiding somewhere here." He, hearing this, flared up and his face took on all sorts of colors, such as a man in a rage would show. Theodotes, falling before him and taking his hand, wept and entreated him to do no such thing. Taking up the word and comforting him, I said, "Be of good courage, Theodotes. For Dionysius will never dare to act <margin>C</margin> contrary to yesterday's agreement." And he, looking at me very tyrannically, said, "To you I agreed to nothing, neither small nor great." "By the gods," I said, "you did agree to these things which this man now begs you not to do." And having said this, I turned away and went out. After this, he hunted for Heraclides; but Theodotes, sending messengers to Heraclides, urged him to flee. He, having sent out Tisias and the targeteers, ordered them to pursue. But Heraclides, as it was said, anticipated them and was saved by reaching Carthaginian territory in a small part of a day. After this, the long-standing plot of Dionysius not to return Dio’s money seemed to have a plausible reason against me. First, he sent me out of the citadel, finding a pretext that <margin>D</margin> the women had to perform a ten-day sacrifice in the garden where I lived. He ordered me to stay outside with Archedemus during this time. While I was there, Theodotes sent for me and was very indignant and critical of Dionysius for what had then been done. He, hearing that I had gone to see Theodotes, made this another pretext for his disagreement with me, a sister to the former one, and sending someone, he asked if I had been with Theodotes when he sent for me. And I said, "Entirely so." He then said, "He tells you, therefore, that you are doing nothing well, always valuing Dio and Dio’s friends more than him." This was said, and he never sent for me to come to his house again; <margin>E</margin> as if I were now clearly a friend of Theodotes and Heraclides, and not a friend to him; thinking that because of this, the money was no longer to be returned to Dio. After this, I lived outside the citadel among the mercenaries. Others came to me, including those in service who were my fellow citizens from Athens, and reported that I had been slandered among the targeteers; and some threatened that if they caught me anywhere, they would destroy me. I devised, therefore, some such means of safety: I sent to Archytas and the other friends in Tarentum, telling them in what state I happened to be. They, having made a pretext of an embassy from the city, sent a thirty-oared ship and <margin>F</margin> Lamiscus, one of their own; who, having come, begged Dionysius concerning me, saying that I wished to depart and that he should by no means do otherwise. He agreed and sent me away, giving me travel money. But as for Dio’s money, neither did I ask for it, nor did anyone give it. Having come to the Peloponnesus, to Olympia, I found Dio watching the games and reported what had happened. He, calling Zeus to witness, immediately told me and my relatives and friends to prepare to take vengeance on Dionysius—on our behalf for the sake of the deception of a guest (for so he spoke and thought), and on his own behalf for his unjust expulsion and exile. Hearing this, I told him to call upon his friends if they wished; <margin>G</margin> but I said that you, with the others, had in a way by force made me a messmate and a hearth-sharer and a partner in sacrifices with Dionysius, who perhaps thought, while many were slandering me, that I was plotting with you against him and his tyranny; and yet he did not kill me, out of respect. Therefore, I am no longer of an age to fight as an ally to anyone; and I am common to you both, if ever you should need to do any good by desiring friendship for one another; but as long as you desire evils, call upon others. I said this, having come to loathe my wandering and misfortune in Sicily. But they, being disobedient and not persuaded by my attempts at reconciliation, were themselves the cause of all the evils that have now happened to them. Of which, if Dionysius had returned the money to Dio, or had been entirely reconciled, none would ever have happened, as far as human affairs go. For Dio...

<page-num>723</page-num>
<header>EPISTLE VIII.</header>

<margin>A</margin> I would have easily restrained Dion according to my own will, counsel, and authority. But now, rushing against one another, they have filled everything with calamities. Certainly, Dion held the same intention that I would say I and any other moderate person ought to have: namely, that power—whether one's own, or that of friends, or of the city—should be desired so that a person established in such honors and powers, especially the greatest, might bestow just benefits upon himself, his kin, and his fatherland. But this does not happen if one merely applies oneself to filling one's own and one's friends' coffers with wealth through treachery and cruel conspiracies, being himself poor and unable to restrain himself, but succumbing to pleasures out of <margin>B</margin> narrowness of soul. Furthermore, such a man, decreeing wealthy men to be enemies, slaughters them and seizes their money, while meanwhile proclaiming to his associates and companions that they should not be angry with him, since he himself is in need. In the same way, if someone, while being honored by his city for bestowing benefits upon it, distributes the property of a few citizens to the many through his decrees; or if someone presiding over a great city that rules many smaller ones should unjustly attribute the money of the smaller cities to his own. For in this way, neither Dion nor any other ever willingly advances toward a power that will be ruinous to himself and his <margin>C</margin> posterity forever. But a prudent man approaches the task of establishing a Republic and founding the most just and best laws without civil slaughters and expulsions. While Dion was recently doing these things, choosing to suffer impious injuries rather than to inflict them, and taking care lest he himself should suffer, he nevertheless fell, just as he had reached the height of overcoming his enemies. Nor should what happened to Dion seem strange to anyone. For impious men never entirely deceive a pious, temperate, and prudent man in such matters. But it is <margin>D</margin> not surprising if the same thing should happen to him as might happen to a good pilot: to whom a coming storm is not entirely hidden, but an unusual and therefore unforeseen magnitude of storms may be hidden, and by being hidden, may overwhelm him by force. In this very way, it seems chance deceived Dion to some extent. For it did not escape him that they were evil, although the depth of their ignorance, wickedness, and greed remained hidden. Deceived in this matter, he fell, subjecting Sicily to incredible grief. Therefore, let what I advise you after these things that have been narrated be considered said thus far. But I thought it necessary to show for what reasons I returned to Sicily as if compelled, lest my return seem absurd or undertaken without reason to anyone. Therefore, if what I have now said seems more probable to someone, and if sufficient occasions appear to have existed for why it happened so, we shall consider that it has been said sufficiently and adequately.

# PLATO TO THE KINSMEN
## AND FRIENDS OF DION.
->Greetings. Not indeed.<-

<margin>E</margin> <note>Decorative initial Q</note> **B**y what way of living you might most prosperously succeed, I will truly endeavor to explain to you according to my ability. I hope, moreover, that I shall consult not only for your interests—though for yours especially—but also for all those who are in Syracuse; and thirdly, even for your enemies and <margin>F</margin> foes, unless any of them has polluted himself with impious crime. For these things are incurable, and no one could ever expiate them. Consider now what I say. All your counsel and zeal regarding all of Sicily, now that the tyranny is dissolved, is occupied with these matters: namely, some affect to revive the tyranny again, while others wish to utterly extinguish every memory of the tyranny. In such matters, a counsel usually seems right to the many everywhere if things are so established that enemies are afflicted with the greatest possible evils, while the most benefit is brought to friends. <margin>G</margin> But it is by no means easy that those who inflict many damages on others should not in turn suffer many things from others. Nor is there now a need to seek examples of these things from afar; since what has recently happened in Sicily can be a sufficient example for us. For all things seem to have happened thus, while some indeed strove to inflict evils, and others to repel and avenge them. In narrating these things, you can be suitable teachers of others everywhere, so that there is almost no difficulty in perceiving them. But those things which are useful to all, both enemies and friends alike, or at least which harm them as little as possible, these are certainly not easy to perceive, nor, after you have perceived them, to bring to fulfillment according to one's wish. This consultation and inquiry, therefore, seems very much like a prayer. And so, let this be for us altogether a kind of great prayer and petition. For in all things, both in speaking and in thinking, the beginning must always be taken from the gods. Such a perfect prayer will signify to us a reason that is conducive to you and your enemies alike. From the time when war was first waged in Sicily, one family has continually dominated, which your ancestors placed in charge of public affairs when they were then situated in the greatest danger, when they were pressed by the Carthaginians and matters had come to the extreme crisis, lest Sicily, which was cultivated by the Greeks, should now be overturned and devastated by the Barbarians. Then, therefore, they chose Dionysius...

# OF PLATO.

<margin>A</margin> Indeed, they chose [Dion] as a young man vigorous in war, to preside over the military affairs suited to him; but Hipparinus, being the elder, they wished to moderate affairs with his counsel. And granting them absolute authority for the safety of all Sicily, they called them "tyrants," as the story goes. Furthermore, if anyone believes that some divine fortune and a god—or the virtue of those to whom the matter was entrusted, or both together along with the citizens of that time—stood as the cause of that salvation: let it be as each man thinks. Certainly, safety was obtained for them in this manner at that time. Wherefore, since <margin>B</margin> they had conducted themselves thus, it was only just that gratitude be returned by those who had been saved. But if afterwards the tyranny itself, abusing the gift of the city, perpetrated any evil, it has judges for its crime, from whom it may pay the penalty. 

But what penalties can necessarily and rightly be applied to them for what was done? For if you were able to easily repel their force without great dangers and labors, or if they thought they would easily give up their domination, we would certainly not be able to advise you as we are now about to do. But now, both sides ought to consider and remember how many times each of you has come into almost certain hope of attaining what you desired, thinking you lacked only a little to achieve everything according to your will. Yet that very "little" has everywhere been the cause of vast and numerous evils, and has not yet reached <margin>C</margin> a limit; rather, in a continuous succession, a new beginning arises from the apparent end of an old evil. 

Indeed, such a circuit and vicissitude of affairs seems likely to destroy both the tyrannical and the popular race; and as much as must be feared by likely reason, all Sicily seems destined to fall into an oblivion of the Greek tongue, being transferred to the power and domination of the Phoenicians <note>The Carthaginians</note> or the Opicians <note>An ancient Italian people, here representing the rising power of Italy</note>. Wherefore, against these things, all Greeks ought to bring a remedy with all foresight. If anyone, therefore, brings into the open a straighter and better counsel than that which shall be spoken by me, he shall deservedly be surnamed "Lover of the Greeks" <note>original: *philhellen*</note>.

<margin>D</margin> What my opinion is, in a certain way, I will now attempt to set forth quite freely, relying on common reason and law. I, therefore, assuming the persona of an arbiter for myself—as I have long been accustomed to do—will counsel both the one exercising and the one preferring tyranny. And first of all, to every tyrant: that he flee this title and the thing itself, and transfer it into a kingdom, if it can be done. That it can be done, Lycurgus, a good and wise man, demonstrated by his deed. For when he saw his own kin in Argos and among the Messenians had already moved from kingship into tyranny, and thereby both these peoples were destroying themselves as well as their cities—each fearing the other—he applied a remedy for his fatherland and his kin alike by creating the Senate and the magistrate of the Ephors for the <margin>E</margin> safety of the kingdom. 

On account of this, it has now been preserved for so many centuries with glory; namely, after the law, full of authority, became the queen of men, and not men the tyrants of the laws. To this very end, my reason now exhorts all men, persuading those who affect tyranny to decline and flee with a certain unwearied zeal from the "happiness" of such famished and foolish men, and to transfer themselves as much as possible to the royal form of government and obey royal laws, as they will one day receive the greatest honors from men and from willing laws. 

But those who prefer liberty above all ways of living, yet flee the servile yoke as an evil, I warn them to take care lest, by an insatiable greed for untimely liberty, they fall into the disease of their <margin>F</margin> ancestors. Which indeed they suffered for this reason: that, wishing to obey no one, they immoderately abused their love of liberty. For those who governed in Sicily before Dionysius and Hipparinus seemed to themselves to live blessedly, dissolved in lusts and commanding their leaders. Furthermore, they cast down and routed ten prefects before Dionysius, judging no one according to the law, so that they might be subject to no man justly judged, nor to a dominant law, but might be entirely free in every detail. For this very cause, tyrannies arose for them. 

For slavery and liberty, if they exceed the limit, are both evil; if they observe the limit, both are good. Moderate indeed is the slavery which is exhibited to God; but immoderate is that which is shown to men. God indeed is the law to temperate men; but pleasure is the law to the intemperate. Since, therefore, these things are so by nature, I command the friends of Dion to promulgate to all Syracusans what I advise, from the common opinion of Dion and myself. Indeed, I will set forth to you what he, while still breathing, spoke. 

"What reason, then," someone will ask, "does the counsel of Dion bring to us concerning the present things?" Receive this first of all. In the beginning, let the laws be such as do not turn minds toward the acquisition of wealth and money, nor toward lusts. But since there are three things—the soul, the body, and money—let them prefer the virtue of the soul most of all. Secondly, let the virtue of the body be placed as a servant to the virtue of the soul. In the third and last grade, let them place the value of money, as a minister to the soul and the body. Whatever law effects these things is right, truly bringing blessedness to those who use it. But to call the wealthy "blessed" is a mad and unhappy way of speaking, suited to women and children, and making those who believe it to be such themselves. That I now exhort you toward true goods, if you will but taste what I have just said concerning the laws, you will understand by the work itself; which examination indeed seems to be the truest in all things—

# EPISTLE IX.

<margin>A</margin> It seems right. Once these laws have been accepted, since Sicily is placed in great danger, and you are neither sufficiently victorious nor, on the other hand, completely defeated, it will perhaps be just and useful for all of you to strike a middle path—both for those of you fleeing the bitterness of absolute rule, and for those desiring to obtain power. Their ancestors once performed the greatest deed by saving the Greeks from the Barbarians <note>Likely referring to the Carthaginian invasions of Sicily</note>, so that it is now possible to deliberate concerning the Republic. Otherwise, if things had been lost then, it would not be possible to speak of these things now, nor would any hope remain. Now, therefore, let there be liberty for some, combined with royal power; for others, let there be a power subject to kingship, with the laws <margin>B</margin> ruling not only the other citizens, but the kings themselves if they should act against the laws. In all these things, with a mind free from deceit and healthy, and with the gods helping, appoint your kings. First, indeed, my son, for a double favor—both for my sake and for his own. For he liberated the fatherland from the Barbarian storm, and I have now twice liberated it from tyrants. Of these things, you yourselves are my witnesses. Second, appoint as king him who possesses the same name as my father—I mean the son of Dionysius. Do this in memory of his present service to the fatherland and his pious character; though born of a tyrant father, he voluntarily undertakes to liberate the fatherland, gaining for himself and his race eternal glory <margin>C</margin> instead of a brief and unjust tyranny. Third, it is necessary to invite to the Syracusan kingship—with the city being willing—Dionysius the son of Dionysius, who is now the leader of the enemy's army. If, I say, he is willing to live content with the form of royal dignity, fearing the turns of fortune and pitying the fatherland, the sacred rites, and the tombs of his ancestors; lest through contention he lose everything entirely, gratifying the Barbarians by the fatherland's misfortune. These three kings—whether you give them the same authority that the Spartan kings have, or take something away—you shall establish by common consent with such a pact as was said before; and now hear it again. If the family of Dionysius and Hipparinus are willing <margin>D</margin> to put an end to these calamities which now press upon Sicily for its safety, gaining honors for themselves and their whole family not only for the present but for the future, then call them to the kingdom on this condition, as was said before. Choose ambassadors whom they themselves wish for the sake of concord with public authority: whether from your citizens, or from foreigners, or from both, and as many besides as they shall concede. Let them, by common opinion, establish laws and constitute the Republic in such a way that it is fitting for kings to be masters of sacred matters and such other things as are fitting to be granted to those whose benefits to the fatherland are outstanding. Furthermore, let the guardians of the laws themselves, created to the <margin>E</margin> number of thirty-five, have the judgment of war and peace together with the people and the senate. Let the courts be distinct, some for one thing and some for another. Let the authority over death and exile rest with the thirty-five men; and besides them, with certain other judges elected from those who have most recently completed their magistracies, so that one is chosen from each magistracy who appears the best and most just. These shall, in the following year, pass sentence concerning death, imprisonment, and exile. But it shall not be permitted for a king to be present at these trials, just as with a priest, whom it is a sin to contaminate in the passing of a sentence of death, imprisonment, or exile. These things <margin>F</margin> I thought of while I was living, and even now I think they should be done. And then, when I had overcome the enemies together with you, if external furies had not stood in the way, I would have established them as I had decreed. Furthermore, if things had proceeded according to my wish, I would have filled the rest of Sicily with colonists. I would have expelled the Barbarians from those places which they now occupy, except for those who fought for the common liberty against the tyranny. I would have restored the former colonists of the Greek places to their ancient and ancestral seats. These same things I now advise everyone to deliberate and act upon by common counsel; and to exhort everyone to these actions. If any should dissent, consider them enemies by common opinion. Nor are these things such that they cannot be done. For those things which exist in the minds of two people and which occur easily to those who seek the best through consultation—he who judges these things impossible does not think rightly. <margin>G</margin> I speak of two: namely, the minds of Hipparinus, the son of Dionysius, and my son. For I think if these agree, the other Syracusans and all who care for the fatherland will also agree. But offering honors with prayers to all the gods, and to whatever others it is fitting to vow along with the gods, and furthermore exhorting and inviting friends and enemies entirely and kindly, do not cease until those things which have been said by us—like divine dreams coming upon those who are awake—you fulfill most perfectly as clear and fortunate realities.

# OF PLATO

<margin>See Cicero, *On Duties* book 1 and *On Ends* book 2.</margin>...that you have chosen to act in such a way as you do is manifest to almost everyone. But it is also necessary for you to consider this: that none of us is born for himself alone; rather, our country claims a share of our birth, our parents a share, and our friends a share. Furthermore, many things befall us according to the diversity of the times, by which our lives are occupied. Therefore, when your country itself calls you to govern the republic, it would perhaps be absurd not to obey—especially since it happens at the same time that an opening is left for wicked men, who approach public affairs with no regard for what is best. Enough regarding these matters. As for Echecrates, we have a care for him at present and shall have in the future, both for your sake and for the sake of his father Phrynion, and for the young man himself.

---

### PLATO TO ARISTODORUS, FARE
->W E L L.<-
### E P I S T L E  X.

I hear that you are now, as you have been before, a close friend of Dion, and that throughout this time you have especially practiced that wisdom of character which looks toward philosophy. For I consider steadfastness, faith, and sincerity to be the true philosophy. As for other sciences and skills that decline toward other ends, if someone calls them "ornaments," he will, I think, name them correctly. But farewell now, and persevere in these present habits.

---

### PLATO TO LAODAMAS, FARE
->W E L L.  E P I S T L E  X I.<-

I wrote to you previously that it matters much for all the things you mention that you yourself should come to Athens. But since you say you are unable to come, the second best thing would be if either I or Socrates—as you indicated in your letters—could travel there. However, Socrates is at this time hindered by the disease of strangury <note>A painful urinary condition</note>. As for me, it would be a disgrace to travel there if the things for which you call me were not accomplished at all. Indeed, I have very little hope that they can be accomplished. If anyone were to attempt to relate all the reasons why I am so distrustful, a very long letter would be needed. Furthermore, because of my age, I am not physically well enough to undertake the journey and face the dangers by land and sea that such a trip usually presents—especially at this time, when everything is full of danger for travelers. Nevertheless, I can give counsel to you and the founders of cities, which, as I relate it now, Hesiod says is "a deceptive thing to think or difficult to understand." <note>A reference to Hesiod's *Works and Days* regarding the difficulty of good advice.</note> For if some people think that a state can ever be well-constituted by the laying down of any laws whatsoever, unless there is someone presiding over the city with authority as a moderator of daily life—so that there is temperance and fortitude among both slaves and free men—they do not think correctly. Accordingly, if there are already men among you worthy of this power, it could be done. But if there is need of someone for instruction: there is, in my opinion, neither one to teach nor one to be taught among you; it remains only to pray to the gods. For almost all cities that existed before this time were constituted in this way from the beginning, and were afterwards well-cultivated by the opportunity of great events in both war and peace, whenever in such times a famous and upright man obtained great power. But first, it is necessary and right to care for these things most readily; yet consider them as I say: do not approach them rashly as if they were easily accomplished, but think on what can be conveniently done. Fare you well and happy.

---

### PLATO TO ARCHYTAS OF TARENTUM
->F A R E  W E L L.<-
### E P I S T L E  X I I.

It is wonderful with what great pleasure we received the commentaries sent by you, and how we were delighted by the genius of their author. Indeed, the man himself seemed to us worthy of those ancient ancestors of his. They say there were ten thousand men who, out of the whole number of Trojans who withdrew under Laomedon, were the most excellent, as the story goes. As for the commentaries which you requested from me by letter, they are not yet finished. However, such as they are, I have sent them to you. Regarding their safekeeping, we both feel the same way. Therefore, there seems to be no need for further exhortation.

---

*The epistle which follows is the thirteenth in previous editions, in which, however, the reader is warned that it is considered spurious by the word* <term>notheuetai</term> <note>Greek: "it is forged/spurious"</note>. *Whether Diogenes Laertius recognized it is uncertain, although he himself counts thirteen, among which are four to Dionysius. Lest it be troublesome for the reader to seek it among the spurious works, it seemed best to place it here, with the version of an anonymous translator added to the others, since Ficino also did not translate it.*
