# PLATO TO DIONYSIUS, TYRANT OF THE SYRACUSANS, WISHES WELL.
## THE THIRTEENTH LETTER.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial P. Inside the frame of the letter, a classical male figure is depicted standing, wearing a tunic and holding a long staff or sceptre. The background shows simplified landscape elements.</image-desc>

<margin>A</margin> Let this be the beginning of my letter to you, and at the same time a secret sign <note>original: "symbolon"</note> that it is truly from me. Once, when you were hosting a banquet for some young men from Locri, you rose from your place and came over to me—they were reclining at a distance from me—and you spoke a very pleasant and kind word, as it seemed both to me and to the man sitting next to me. That man was one of the refined sort, and he remarked, "Truly, Dionysius, you are greatly helped toward wisdom by Plato." You replied, "In many other things as well; <margin>B</margin> for from the very moment I sent for him, I immediately received benefit for that very reason." Let us, therefore, take care to maintain this, so that our mutual usefulness to one another may always increase. 

Now, being eager for this very thing, <margin>C</margin> I am sending you some works of the Pythagoreans and some "Divisions" <note>A technical term for Plato's method of classifying concepts</note>, and also a man whom we thought at the time—both you and Archytas <note>A Pythagorean philosopher and statesman of Tarentum</note>, if Archytas has come to you—could be of use to you. His name is Helicon; he is a native of Cyzicus, a pupil of Eudoxus, and very elegantly trained in all his doctrines. He has also associated with one of the pupils of Isocrates and with Polyxenus, one of the companions of Bryson. What is more, and quite rare, he is pleasant to meet and does not seem ill-natured; rather, he would be judged as light-hearted and sincere. I say this with caution, however, because I am expressing an opinion about a human being—not a lowly animal, but one that is easily changed and corrected, except for a very few people in very few matters. Indeed, because I was fearful and distrustful about this, I met with him myself and made inquiries of his fellow citizens, and no one had anything bad to say about the man. 

Look into him yourself, and be cautious. Above all, whenever you have any leisure, learn from him and study philosophy in other matters; <margin>D</margin> if not, have someone else taught, so that by learning at your leisure, you may become better and more renowned, and that my efforts to help you may not cease. So much for these matters.

Regarding what you requested in your letter—that I send you an Apollo—I have had it made. Leptines is bringing it to you; it was crafted by a skilled and excellent young artist named Leochares. There was another work at his shop, quite elegant as it seemed to me, which I bought intending to give it to your wife, because she took care of me both in health and in sickness in a manner worthy of both me and you. Give it to her, then, unless you decide otherwise. I am also sending twelve small jars of sweet wine for the children and two of honey. We arrived too late for the season of dried figs; the myrtle berries that were put away have rotted, but next time we will take better care. Leptines will tell you about the plants. 

<margin>E</margin> As for the money for these purchases and for certain taxes to be paid to the city, I received it from Leptines, saying what seemed to me most fitting and true for both of us. The money we spent on the ship from Leucadia is nearly sixteen minae <note>A unit of currency; 1 mina was 100 drachmae</note>. I took that sum, therefore, and used it for these things <margin>F</margin> which I have sent to you. 

Now, listen to how matters stand regarding your money in Athens and my own. I shall use your money, as I told you once before, just as I would use the resources of my other friends; I use as little as possible, only for what seems necessary, just, or honorable to me and to the one from whom I receive it. Such a situation has happened to me at this time. I have four grand-nieces <note>daughters of his nieces</note> who were born around the time I was not crowned—even though you had ordered it. The first is of marriageable age, the second is eight years old, the third is a little over three, and the fourth is not yet a year old. For those who marry while I am still alive, I and my friends must provide dowries; for those who marry after I am gone, they must fare as they can. If their fathers were wealthier <margin>G</margin> than I, there would be no need for me to provide; but as it is, I am better off than they are. I myself, with the help of others and Dion, provided for their mothers' marriages. One is now being given to Speusippus, being his niece on his sister's side. For her, no more than thirty minae are needed, for such dowries are respectable and suitable for us. Furthermore, if my mother should die, no more than ten minae would be needed for the building of her tomb. These are my necessary expenses at this time. 

If any other expense arises, either private or public, because of my journey to you—as I once said should be done—it will be my part to struggle and fight to keep the expense as small as possible; what I cannot avoid will be charged to you. But next, let us mention the Athenian expenses <margin>H</margin> of your money. First, if I must spend anything on a Choregia <note>The sponsorship of a public chorus or play</note> or something similar, there is, in my opinion, no guest-friend who will pay it for you. It is of great importance to you if someone comes from you and brings you a loss, when it should have been to your advantage. If it is not paid, but delayed until it becomes difficult, it would even be a disgrace to you. I tested this with Andromeda, and I sent Erastus the Aeginetan to him—the man from whom you ordered me to take what was needed, as he is your guest-friend—wishing to send the larger items you wrote about. But he said what was reasonable...

<header>OF PLATO</header>

<margin>A</margin> and that it would be by no means foreign to a man's character, he replied that he had only with difficulty recovered what he had previously spent in your father's name; and now he would not refuse a few things, but would certainly refuse many. Therefore, I took the money from Leptines <note>A friend of Plato and Dionysius</note>, who is worthy of praise, not only because he gave it, but because he gave it gladly and promptly, and in other matters, both in word and deed, he has appeared as your friend and well-wisher. For it is necessary that I explain these things to you, and their opposites, so that you may see what kind of mind each person has toward you. Therefore, concerning the money, I will openly reveal the truth to you: for it is just, and having also experienced your household, I shall mention them as well. <margin>B</margin> Those who constantly promise you that they will advise you regarding the expenses they think should be made, nevertheless wish to advise you in such a way that they do not incur your displeasure. Therefore, you ought to accustom them and compel them to explain both these and other matters to you. For you ought, as far as you are able, to know all things, and be the judge of them, nor should you flee from the knowledge of anything. For this is the most convenient method for protecting and preserving your sovereignty. Indeed, if you manage expenses correctly, and if you settle debts correctly, you will rightly say that this is the greatest opportunity for all other things, as well as for the possession and preservation of wealth. You shall also provide that those who boast of being your devoted followers do not slander you among men. For this seems to contribute very little to your reputation. Come, let us mention Dion; as for the rest, I am truly unable to explain further until your letters, which you mention, are brought to me. Regarding those things of which you did not wish me to make mention to him, I have neither made mention nor reminded him. However, I explored whether he would tolerate it heavily or easily if those things were done; and it seemed to me he would be not slightly annoyed if they occurred. Otherwise, Dion seemed to me to be of a fair mind toward you in both word and deed. <margin>D</margin> To Cratinus, the brother of Timotheus and my companion, we shall give a most ornate military breastplate, of the kind that infantrymen are accustomed to use. To the daughters of Cebes, three tunics, not expensive ones like the Amorgian <note>Fine silk-like flax from the island of Amorgos</note> ones, but like the Sicilian linens. The name of Cebes is very well known to you. For he appears in the Socratic Dialogues, and in the dialogue *On the Soul* <note>The Phaedo</note> he disputes together with Simmias against Socrates; he is a man both familiar and well-disposed to us all. Now, concerning the mark <note>original: "notam" / "symbolon"</note> of the letters which I write either seriously or not seriously, although I think you remember, nevertheless attend diligently and turn your mind to it. For many people bid me to write whom I cannot easily or openly repel. <margin>E</margin> The beginning of a serious letter is GOD <note>original: "DEVS" / "Theos"</note>; of a non-serious one, GODS <note>original: "DII" / "Theoi"</note>. The ambassadors also asked me to write to you; and not without cause. For they very gladly praise both you and me everywhere: among these not least Philager, who at that time was suffering from pain in his hand; likewise Philaedes, coming from the great King Darius, spoke of you; and unless there were need of a very long and wordy letter, I would write out what he said. Now inquire of Leptines whether you should send the breastplate or any other of those things about which I write; if however you wish to entrust it to him, otherwise entrust it to Terillus. <margin>F</margin> Of those who are constantly sailing, he is our friend and, in other matters as well as in Philosophy, not unskillful. He is the son-in-law of Tison, who was turning gray at the time we were sailing. Farewell, and practice philosophy, and rouse and exhort other young men, and greet your playfellows in the ball-game in my words. Command Aristocritus especially, if any message or letter from me is brought to you, to see to it that it is brought to you as soon as possible; and let him recall to your memory those things which shall have been written to you, so that you may take care of them. Now indeed, see to it that Leptines is paid his money at the first opportunity; so that others, looking to him, may serve us more promptly and eagerly. Iatrocles, who was granted freedom by me along with Myronides, is now sailing with those sent by me. You shall give him a stipend, as one bearing a benevolent mind toward you, and you shall use his service whenever you wish. And read the letter itself, or if a copy of it is preserved, read it yourself.

### AXIOCHUS, OR,
### On Death.

->SOCRATES, CLINIAS,<-
->AXIOCHUS.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut decorative initial 'E' depicting a figure in a landscape.</image-desc>As I was going out toward the Cynosarges <note>A gymnasium outside the walls of Athens</note>, when I had come to the Ilissus <note>A river in Athens</note>, the voice of someone crying out was brought to me, "Socrates, Socrates!" And as I turned and looked around to see where it came from, I saw Clinias, the son of Axiochus, running toward the Callirrhoë <note>A famous spring</note> with Damon the musician, and Charmides the son of Glaucon. One of these was teaching him music; the other loved him out of intimacy, and was loved in return. It seemed...

<meta>This page continues the dialogue "Axiochus," traditionally attributed to Plato (though often considered pseudo-Platonic). It features Socrates comforting the dying Axiochus. The previous page likely established the setting or the onset of Axiochus's illness.</meta>

# AXIOCHUS

<margin>A</margin> It seemed best to me, as I was turning off the road, to meet them so that we might be together as easily as possible. Clinias, bursting into tears, said, "Socrates, now is the time to display your much-talked-about wisdom. For my father, from some sudden hour of weakness, is failing and is near the end of his life; he bears his end with great distress. Yet in former times, he used to mock death with <term>mormolykeia</term> <note>original: "κορμολυκείοις" - bugbears or hobgoblins used to frighten children</note> and turned away from it calmly. Go to him then and comfort him as you are accustomed to do, so that he may meet his fate without a groan; and let this be added to the other favors you have done for me." "I will not fail you, Clinias," I replied, "in any reasonable request, especially one involving such pious duties. Let us hurry then; if things are as you say, there is need for haste." <margin>B</margin> **CLINIAS:** "The mere sight of you, Socrates, will make him better. For it has often happened that he recovered from a collapse." **SOCRATES:** As we went quickly along the wall toward the Itonian gates (for he lives near the gates, by the Amazonian pillar), we found him already regained by his senses and strong in body, but failing in mind and utterly lacking in hope. He was frequently sighing and breaking into tears with the wringing of his hands. Standing by him, I said, "Axiochus, what is this? Where are those former boasts, and the constant praises of virtue, and that unspeakable courage within you? Like a cowardly athlete, you appeared noble in the gymnasiums <margin>C</margin> but have failed in the actual contests. Will you not consider nature with circumspection, a man of such age, a listener to reason, and, if nothing else, an Athenian? Do you not know that this common saying, repeated by everyone, is true: that life is a kind of pilgrimage? And that we must pass through it reasonably and depart toward our fate cheerfully, almost singing a <term>paean</term> <note>a song of triumph or thanksgiving</note>? To behave so softly and be so hard to tear away, like a child, does not reflect a mind of your mature years." **AXIOCHUS:** "These things are true, Socrates, and you seem to speak rightly to me. But I do not know how it is that when the danger comes near, those <margin>D</margin> strong and persuasive arguments secretly fly away and are ignored. A certain fear arises, tearing the mind in many ways, if I am to be deprived of this light and these goods, and lie somewhere senseless and unknown, rotting away, changing into worms and creeping things." **SOCRATES:** "You are mistaken, Axiochus, because of your lack of understanding; you are mindlessly associating sensation with a lack of sensation. You do and say things contrary to yourself, not considering that you simultaneously mourn the loss of sensation and grieve over the rotting and the loss of life's pleasures—as if you were going to live in another state after death, rather than passing into a complete abolition of sensation, the same state you were in before you were born. Just as when Draco or Cleisthenes <note>Athenian lawgivers from centuries prior</note> governed the state, there was nothing bad for you (for you had not yet begun to exist so that anything bad could happen to you), so it will be after death. For you will not exist as the person to whom anything can happen. So, stop this nonsense <margin>E</margin> and consider this: once the composite of body and soul is dissolved and the soul is restored to its proper place, the remaining body, being earthy and irrational, is no longer the man. For we are the soul, an immortal living being shut up in a mortal fortress. Nature has wrapped this 'tent' around us to our own hurt; its pleasures are superficial and fleeting, mixed with many pains, while its sorrows are unmitigated, long-lasting, and devoid of joy. It suffers diseases and inflammations of the sensing members, and internal maladies. To these the soul is bound—since it is spread through the passages of the body—and it longs for the heavenly and kindred ether, thirsting for the life and habits of that place. Therefore, the departure from life <margin>F</margin> is a change from something bad to something good." **AXIOCHUS:** "Since you think life is an evil, Socrates, why do you continue to live in it? And you, being a seeker of things, do you differ in mind from us, the many?" **SOCRATES:** "Axiochus, you do not bear true witness of me. You think, as the multitude of Athenians do, that because I am an inquirer into 'lofty things,' I have some special knowledge. I would wish to know even these common things; so much do I lack the deeper ones. These things I say are echoes of the wise Prodicus <note>A famous Sophist known for his lectures on the choice of life</note>; some bought for two obols, some for two drachmas, others for four. For that man teaches no one for free; it is his habit always to have on his lips the saying of <margin>G</margin> Epicharmus: 'Hand washes hand; give something, and get something.' Recently, when he was giving a display at the house of Callias, son of Hipponicus, he spoke so much against life that I myself have since then counted life as nothing. From that time, Axiochus, my soul has longed for death." **AXIOCHUS:** "What were the things he said?" <margin>H</margin> **SOCRATES:** "I will tell you what I remember. For he said: 'What part of life is free from misery? Does not the infant cry from the very beginning, starting life from a place of pain? It is never left without some distress, whether from want, or cold, or heat, or a blow; it cannot <margin>H</margin> yet speak of what it suffers but only whimpers, having this as its only voice of dissatisfaction. And when it reaches its seventh year, having exhausted many labors, there are then <margin>The misery of life.</margin> guardians, physical trainers, and schoolmasters; then as a youth, critics, geometers, and military commanders—a great crowd of masters...'"

<summary>Socrates visits the dying Axiochus to comfort him, arguing that death is merely a loss of sensation and that the soul is an immortal being trapped in a miserable, mortal body. He cites the philosopher Prodicus to illustrate that every stage of human life, from infancy onward, is defined by suffering and labor.</summary>

--- Page 762 ---
<meta>This page continues the dialogue *Axiochus* (traditionally attributed to Plato), where Socrates consoles the dying Axiochus. The previous section likely introduced the theme of the soul's immortality or the vanity of life.</meta>

# PLATO

<margin>A</margin> ...the multitude. After those years, when one is enrolled among the youths <note>Greek: *ephebos*, a young man in military training</note>, a worse fear sets in: the Lyceum, the Academy, the office of the gymnasiarch, the rods <note>used for corporal punishment</note>, and a truly immeasurable amount of evils. Indeed, the entire time of a young man is spent under supervisors chosen from the council of the Areopagus to preside over the youth. Then, when he is released from these, cares emerge openly, and he must deliberate on what path of life he should especially undertake. Compared to the troubles that follow, those earlier childhood fears seem like mere trifles and truly like "bogeymen" for infants. For then come military expeditions, wounds, and the perpetual labors of struggle. From here, deceptive old age creeps in, into which flows everything that is weak and fragile in nature. Unless one quickly returns life like a debt, nature stands over one's head like a moneylender <margin>B</margin> demanding interest: taking sight from one, hearing from another, and often both. If one lingers too long, it debilitates him, tortures him, and afflicts his limbs with disease. Thus, some in great old age return to childhood; the elderly become children twice over in their minds. Therefore, the gods (to whom human affairs are best known) take those they value most out of life more quickly. <margin>Cicero translated this passage in *Tusculan Disputations* 1.</margin> Thus, when Agamedes and Trophonius had built the temple of Pythian Apollo, they prayed that they might be given what was best. When they fell asleep, they never rose again. So too the sons of the priestess of Argive Juno: when their mother prayed <margin>C</margin> that Juno would grant them some reward for their piety—for when the oxen were late, they themselves got under the yoke of the carriage and pulled their mother all the way to the temple—after the prayers, they passed away in the night. It would be a long task to review the sayings of the poets, who in their more divine poems sing of the things pertaining to our life as if from an oracle, deploring it. I am satisfied to remember only one most worthy of mention, who said:
> How the gods have spun the miserable thread of age for mortals,
> So that they endure through all things to be lamented while living. <note>original: *Homer, Iliad 24.525-526*</note>
And again:
> And for all the race of men, the worst lot of life
> Stands for whatever breathes and moves upon the earth. <note>original: *Homer, Iliad 17.446-447*</note>
And what does he say of Amphiaraus?
> Jupiter loved him with all his heart, and great Apollo loved him,
yet he did not reach the goals of a just age <note>i.e., he died young</note>. Regarding him who commands: <margin>D</margin> "Let him not weep who enters into such evils of life," what do you think? But I make an end, lest by commemorating others I draw the matter out longer than I intended. For what way of life or what art could anyone choose so as not to complain of it and be offended by present circumstances? Let us review the craftsmen and the mercenary arts: laboring from night until night, barely enduring the necessary expenses of life, bewailing themselves, and filling all their waking hours with sorrow and tears. Or shall we speak of the sailor, penetrating through such great dangers, who, as Bias said, is neither among the dead nor among the living? For a man of the land, as if of an ambiguous species, has cast himself into the sea <margin>E</margin> and become entirely subject to the will of fortune. But surely agriculture is sweet? It is indeed, but is it not entirely, as they say, a "sore," always having a ready cause for pain—now complaining of drought, now rains, now blight, now rust, now untimely heat or cold? And that highly honored care of the state <note>politics</note>—for I pass over much—through how many anxieties is it driven? What joys it has are always trembling like a boil and full of stings, while its failures are bitter and a thousand times worse than death. For who could be happy living at the whim of the entire common people? Even if he is favored and applauded, he is tossed about as the plaything of the populace, hissed at, fined, put to death, and then seen as an object of pity. For where, Axiochus—you who are engaged in the state—where has Miltiades gone? Where Themistocles? Where Ephialtes? Where also those who were recently kings and generals? For my part, I was not asked for my opinion (for it did not seem honorable to me to share in power with a mad populace). But Theramenes and Callixenus, having set up appointed magistrates, brought it about that men were put to death without trial—and you, with Euryptolemus, alone resisted them when thirty thousand were gathered in the assembly. <meta>catchword: Axioch.</meta> <margin>G</margin> **AXIOCHUS:** These things are as you say, Socrates; therefore, a satiety of that speaker's platform has seized me, and nothing has seemed more bitter to me than the state. This is clear to those who have been engaged in the work itself. For you speak these things as one who has watched from a high place; but we have experienced the danger—how much more accurately do we know it? For the people, dear Socrates, are ungrateful, morose, cruel, envious, and ignorant—as they are collected from the dregs of the crowd and from violent fools. He who flatters them is himself much more miserable. **SOCRATES:** Since, therefore, Axiochus, you think this art—which is the most liberal of all—is the most abominable of all, what shall we think of the remaining kinds of life? Shall we not think they are entirely to be fled? I also once heard Prodicus saying that death pertains neither to the living nor to the deceased. **AXIOCHUS:** How do you say this, Socrates? **SOCRATES:** Because it is not present among the living, and those who have died are no longer. <margin>H</margin> Therefore, it is not around you now (for you have not died), nor if anything should happen to you, will it be around you, for you will not exist. Therefore, the grief over Axiochus is foolish—as if Axiochus, who neither is nor will be, were to be tortured in mind. It is similar to someone fearing Scylla or a Centaur, things which neither threaten you now nor will ever exist at your end.

<column-break/>

<summary>Socrates argues that every stage of life, from youth to old age, is filled with suffering and that death is often a gift from the gods. He specifically critiques various professions, including politics, which he describes as a fickle and dangerous pursuit.</summary>

# AXIOCHVS.

...fear. For fear belongs to things that exist; but as for things that are not, how can there be anyone to be terrified? <margin>A</margin> AXIOCHUS: You indeed, Socrates, have uttered these clever words from that superficial talkativeness that is now so prevalent. For these are mere follies of speech, prepared for the purpose of enticing the youth. But as for me, the loss of the good things of life makes me sad; even if you, Socrates, were to rattle off a more persuasive argument than the one you just gave. For my mind is no longer led by wandering, aptly joined words, nor do these things touch my soul; rather, they are prepared for a display and splendor of speech, but fall far short of the truth. The sickness of the soul is by no means halted by captious sophisms; it rests only upon those things which are able to penetrate into the very mind. SOCRATES: You are joining things together imprudently, Axiochus; <margin>B</margin> you substitute an evil sensation for the loss of goods, forgetting that you will then be dead. For he who loses good things is harmed by the contrary evils he suffers; but he who is not, receives nothing in the place of that which he is deprived of. How then could there be any pain in that which will provide no knowledge of the things that cause pain? But if, from the beginning, Axiochus, you did not through imprudence associate some single sense with death, you would by no means fear it. Now you subvert yourself, fearing that your soul will be lost, yet you surround that very loss with another soul <note>Socrates argues that Axiochus is imagining himself "feeling" the lack of feeling, which is a logical contradiction</note>. And you are troubled that you will be without sensation, yet you think you will comprehend this very lack of sensation with another sense. <margin>C</margin> To these points, there are many and beautiful arguments concerning the immortality of the soul. For a mortal nature could not raise itself to such various things—to restrain the strength of huge wild beasts, to cross the seas, to build cities, to establish republics, to look even into heaven and see the revolutions of the stars, the courses of the sun and moon, their rising and setting, eclipses, speed, distances, the equinoxes and the double turnings <note>The solstices</note>, the Pleiades, the winds of winter and summer, the falling of rains and the horrendous snatching of whirlwinds—so as to hand down the understood labors of the world to future ages, unless a certain divine spirit were present in our minds, by which it attained the grasp and knowledge of such great things. <margin>D</margin> Therefore, Axiochus, you are passing not into death, but into immortality; not into a loss of goods, but into a purer perception of them; not to pleasures confused with a mortal body, but to those purged of all troubles. For you shall depart thither, released from this prison, where all things are restful and joyful, and there is no wearying old age; there you will lead a tranquil life, free from all inconveniences, and peaceful with serene quiet, contemplating the nature of things; and devoted to philosophy, not for the crowd or for show, but for pure and genuine truth. AXIOCHUS: You have turned me to the opposite view, Socrates, by this speech. For fear <margin>E</margin> no longer holds me, but rather a longing for death. And so that I, imitating the rhetoricians, may say something grander: for a long time now I have been conceiving things with a heavenly mind, and I am reviewing that immense and divine course; I have gathered myself up from my weakness and have become, as it were, new again. SOCRATES: If you wish, take also another account which Gobryas, a Magus <note>A member of the Persian priestly caste</note>, related to me. He said that following the crossing of Xerxes into Greece, his grandfather and namesake was sent to Delos to protect that island, in which the two deities <note>Apollo and Artemis</note> were born. There he learned from certain bronze tablets which Opis and Hecaergus had brought from the Hyperboreans, that after the soul is released from the body, it departs into a certain unknown place in a subterranean recess, in which is the palace of Pluto, no less than the court of Jove. For since the Earth holds the middle of the world, and its shape is spherical, the celestial gods have received one hemisphere, and the gods below the other; and these are indeed brothers of the former, or the sons of brothers. The vestibules which lead to the kingdom of Pluto are secured with iron bars and keys. <margin>F</margin> When one opens these, the river Acheron receives him, after which is Cocytus. When these have been crossed, it is necessary to approach Minos and Rhadamanthus. They call this the Plain of Truth; and in it the judges sit, examining the life of each of those who arrive, and by what means each one, inhabiting a body, passed his age. Nor is there any opportunity for lying there. <margin>G</margin> For those whom a good spirit breathed upon in life, they inhabit the seats of the pious; where all the seasons teem with every kind of fruit, springs flow with pure waters, and all sorts of meadows bloom with various flowers; there are the gatherings of philosophers, the theaters of poets, circles of dancers, and musical concerts. In addition, there are carefully prepared banquets, and an abundance of food that supplies itself, immortal joy, and a most pleasant way of life. For there is neither harsh cold nor heat, but a temperate air is poured out, illuminated by the gentle rays of the sun. Here also there is a certain place of honor for the initiated, and they perform their holy rites there as well. How then shall this honor not be held for you, who are a kinsman of the gods? For there is an ancient story that Hercules and Father Bacchus, when descending to the underworld, were first initiated here, and that they drew the courage for their journey thither from the Eleusinian goddess. But those whose life was spent in crimes are snatched by the Furies through Tartarus to Erebus and Chaos, where is the place of the impious, and the unfillable jars of the daughters of Danaus, where is the thirst of Tantalus, the entrails of Tityus, and the unfinished stone of Sisyphus, whose end begins again from another labor. There, with wild beasts licking around them, and incessantly...

<column-break/>

...will be present. For fear is of things that exist: but as for those that are not, there is no one who greatly fears them. <margin>A</margin> AXI. You indeed have brought forth these learned words from that talkativeness which now sprouts up. For from that source come these ineptitudes of words, prepared for the purpose of alluring the youth. But truly the loss of the goods which are in life makes me sad: even if you, Socrates, should rattle off a more probable speech than this which you have just spoken. For the mind is not now led wandering by aptly cohering words: nor do those things touch the mind: but being prepared for the ostentation and splendor of speech, they are far distant from the truth. But the sickness of the soul is by no means stopped by captious words: but it acquiesces only in those which are able to penetrate even to the mind. SOC. You join things together imprudently, Axioche: and <margin>B</margin> you substitute the loss of goods for the substitution of evils, having forgotten that you will then be dead. For him who loses goods, the contrary evils which he suffers do harm: but he who is not, receives nothing into the place of that which he is deprived of. How therefore could there be any pain in that which will exhibit no notice of the things that hurt? But if you did not from the beginning, Axioche, through imprudence, compose some single sense with death, you would by no means fear it. Now you subvert yourself, fearing that the soul will be lost, and you surround that loss with another soul. And you are troubled that you will be without sense, and you think that you will comprehend this very not-sensing with another sense. <margin>C</margin> To these things there are many and very beautiful reasons concerning the immortality of the soul. For a mortal nature could not raise itself into such various things, as to contain the strengths of huge wild beasts, cross the seas, build cities, establish republics, look also into heaven, and see the revolutions of the stars, and the courses of the sun and moon, likewise the risings and settings, the eclipses, the speed, the distances, and the equinoxes, and the double conversions, also the Pleiades and the winds of winter and summer, and the fallings of rains and the horrendous snatchings of whirlwinds, so that it might also hand down the understood labors of the world to the ages: unless a certain divine spirit were in our minds: by which it might touch the embrace and knowledge of such great things. <margin>D</margin> Therefore you pass, Axioche, not into death, but into immortality: not into the loss of goods, but into a more sincere perception of them, nor to pleasures confused with a mortal body, but purged from all troubles whatsoever. For you shall depart thither, loosed from this prison, where all things are quiet and joyful, and there is no loathing old age: and there you will pass a tranquil life, free from all inconveniences, and placid with serene quiet, contemplating the nature of things: and devoted to philosophy not for the crowd, nor for appearance, but to pure and genuine truth. AXI. You have turned me, Socrates, by this speech to the contrary. For fear <margin>E</margin> no longer holds me, but a desire for death. And so that I, having imitated the rhetoricians, may say something rather grand, I have for a long time been conceiving with a supernal mind, and I am reviewing that immense and divine course, and I have collected myself from my weakness: and I am made as if new again. SOC. But if you wish, take also another reason, which Gobryas the Magus related to me. He said that following the crossing of Xerxes into Greece, his grandfather of the same name was sent to Delos, that he might protect that island, in which two deities were born. There he learned from certain bronze tablets which Opis and Hecaergus had brought from the Hyperboreans, that after the soul has been loosed from the body, it departs into a certain unknown place in a subterranean recess, in which is the palace of Pluto, no less than the court of Jove. For the earth holding the middle of the world, its circuit is like a globe: of which the gods above have received one hemisphere, the gods below the other: and these indeed are the brothers of those, these truly the sons of brothers. But the vestibules by which is the approach to the kingdom of Pluto, are secured with iron bars and keys. <margin>F$</margin> To one opening those, the river Acheron receives him: after which is Cocytus. When anyone has crossed those, it is necessary to approach Minos and Rhadamanthus. They call this the plain of truth, and in it the judges sit, reviewing the life of each of those who have arrived, and by what reason each one, inhabiting a body, passed his age. Nor is there any faculty of lying there. <margin>G</margin> To whomsoever in life a better demon <note>original: "daemon" - here meaning a guiding spirit or fate</note> has breathed upon, they inhabit the seats of the pious: where all the hours teem with every kind of fruitfulness, fountains glide with pure waters, all kinds of meadows bloom with various flowers, there are assemblies of philosophers, theaters of poets, crowns of exulting ones and musical concerts. To these are added diligently prepared banquets, and an abundance of food supplying itself, immortal cheerfulness, and a most pleasant way of life. For neither cold nor heat is heavy to them, but a temperate air is poured out, illustrated by the mild rays of the sun. Here also for the initiated there is a certain dignity, and they perform religious rites there also. How therefore shall this honor not be held for you, a kinsman of the gods? For there is an ancient report that Hercules and Father Bacchus, descending to the lower regions, were initiated here, and that the confidence that they might go thither was conceived from Eleusis. But those whose life was passed through crimes, are snatched by the Furies through Tartarus to Erebus and Chaos, where is the place of the impious, and the unfillable urns of the daughters of Danaus, where is the thirst of Tantalus, the vitals of Tityus, the unending stone of Sisyphus, whose end begins again from another labor. There, with wild beasts licking around them, incessantly...

# DIALOGUE ON JUSTICE, WHICH IS HELD TO BE SPURIOUS.
### Translated by Sebastiano Corrado.

->SOCRATES, STRANGER.<-

<margin>C</margin>
**C**an you tell us what Justice is? Or would it seem to you to be a thing unworthy of speech? **STRANGER.** To me indeed it seems worthy, and very much so. **SOCRATES.** What is it then? **STRANGER.** What else should I say it is, except all those things which are judged to be just. **SOCRATES.** I would not wish you to answer me in that way: but, just as if you were to ask me what an Eye is, I would tell you it is that by which we see: and if you further commanded me to show it, I would show it. And if you asked me to what thing "Soul" is the name: I would tell you, to that by which we know. Again, if you asked what Voice is: I would answer you that it is that by which we speak. I would wish you also to speak thus: that Justice is that which we use to do something, as was said of those things I just sought out. **STRANGER.** I certainly cannot answer you so easily.
<margin>D</margin>
**SOCRATES.** Since, therefore, you cannot answer so easily, perhaps we will be able to find it more easily by this method. Come, by what do we chiefly discern Greater and Smaller? Is it not by measure? **STRANGER.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** And besides measure, by what art? Is it not the art of measuring? **STRANGER.** Yes, certainly. **SOCRATES.** What of Light and Heavy: is it not by the scale? **STRANGER.** Yes. **SOCRATES.** After the scale, by what art? Is it not the art of weighing? **STRANGER.** Greatly so. **SOCRATES.** What then: do you understand by what instrument, and moreover by what art, we discern Just and Unjust? Or is that not yet manifest to you? **STRANGER.** Not by Hercules. **SOCRATES.** And again in this way. When we disagree about Greater and Smaller, who judges between us concerning that matter? Is it not those skilled in the art of measuring? **STRANGER.** Yes. **SOCRATES.** When we contend about Many and Few, who judges? Is it not the Calculators? **STRANGER.** True.
<margin>E</margin>
**SOCRATES.** But when we litigate between ourselves concerning Just and Unjust: tell me, I pray, to whom do we go, who may bear a sentence on the matter of the dispute? **STRANGER.** Do you mean the judges, O Socrates? **SOCRATES.** You have found it rightly. Come now, tell me this also: what do those skilled in the art of measuring do when they discern Great and Small: do they not measure? **STRANGER.** Indeed. **SOCRATES.** What? Do those who judge concerning Heavy and Light not weigh? **STRANGER.** They weigh. **SOCRATES.** Now what will you say of these who pronounce on Just and Unjust: answer. **STRANGER.** I certainly cannot. **SOCRATES.** Would you not say they reason rightly? **STRANGER.** I think so. **SOCRATES.** Therefore the judges, who bear the sentence between us, certainly reason when they judge concerning Just and Unjust. **STRANGER.** I agree.
<margin>F</margin>
**SOCRATES.** But those who practice the art of measuring measure Small and Great. For we said that Measure is that by which such things are judged. **STRANGER.** We said so. **SOCRATES.** But again, those who have placed their study in the art of weighing weigh Heavy and Light. For the scale was to us that very thing by which those things are accustomed to be discerned. **STRANGER.** It was indeed. **SOCRATES.** But those who are held by the study of numbering count Many and Few. For we posited that Number is that by which things of this sort are distinguished. **STRANGER.** We posited it. **SOCRATES.** But the judges, as we just agreed, reason when they judge between us concerning Just and Unjust. For Reason <note>original: "Ratio" / "λόγος" (Logos)</note> is that by which those things are discerned. **STRANGER.** You speak well, O Socrates. **SOCRATES.** And truly indeed. Reason, therefore, seems to be entirely that by which Just and Unjust are judged. **STRANGER.** It seems so. **SOCRATES.** Now indeed Just and Unjust must be defined: so that, if someone were to ask us: When measure, and the art of measuring, and
<margin>G</margin>
the man skilled in that art discern the Greater itself and the Smaller: what finally is Greater and Smaller? We would certainly say that the Greater is that which exceeds; the Smaller indeed that which is exceeded. Likewise, if he asked: When the scale, and the art of weighing, and the man studious of that art discern Heavy and Light, what is Heavy and Light? We would answer, that Heavy is that which, placed in the balance, sinks down; but Light is that which is carried upward. So now, if someone asks us: since Just and Unjust, and reason, and the judicial art, and the judge do the judging, what is Just and Unjust? Will we have something to answer him, or will we still have nothing? **STRANGER.** Nothing. **SOCRATES.** Do you think men endowed with injustice are so voluntarily or involuntarily? I say it thus: Do you believe men act unjustly and are unjust voluntarily, or involuntarily? **STRANGER.** Voluntarily, O Socrates: for they are wicked. **SOCRATES.** You think, therefore, that wicked and unjust men are so voluntarily? **STRANGER.** I think so indeed. Do you not think so? **SOCRATES.** Not I, if only one must believe the Poet. **STRANGER.** Which Poet? **SOCRATES.** He who said, "No one is evil willingly, nor [blessed] against his will." <note>original: "Nullus malus lubens" / "Οὐθεὶς ἑκὼν"</note>

# ON JUSTICE.
## Qqq
<meta>Catchword: she in</meta>

<margin>A</margin>
-> No one is willingly wicked, nor unwillingly blessed. <note>original: "θεὸς ἑκών πονηρὸς, οὐδ' ἑκὼν μάκαρ" — This is a variation of a famous Socratic paradox often attributed to poets like Solon or Simonides.</note> <-

**SOCRATES:** But surely, my guest, the old proverb holds true: that "poets tell many lies." I would be surprised if this particular poet lied about the truth. Since you have leisure, let us examine him to see whether he speaks falsely or truly.
**GUEST:** I have leisure.
**SOCRATES:** Come then, do you say it is just to lie, or to speak the truth?
**GUEST:** To speak the truth, I say.
**SOCRATES:** Therefore, to lie is unjust?
**GUEST:** Yes.
**SOCRATES:** And do you say it is just to deceive, or not to deceive?
**GUEST:** Not to deceive, surely.
**SOCRATES:** To deceive, then, is unjust?
**GUEST:** Yes.
**SOCRATES:** What then? Is it just to harm, or to benefit?
**GUEST:** To benefit.
**SOCRATES:** To harm, then, is unjust?
**GUEST:** Yes.
**SOCRATES:** It is, therefore, just to speak the truth, not to deceive, and to benefit; while to lie, to harm, and to deceive
<margin>B</margin>
is unjust.
**GUEST:** Yes, by Zeus, most certainly.
**SOCRATES:** Is this also true regarding enemies?
**GUEST:** Not at all.
**SOCRATES:** But it is just to harm enemies, and unjust to benefit them?
**GUEST:** Yes.
**SOCRATES:** Is it not also just to harm enemies by deceiving them?
**GUEST:** How could it not be?
**SOCRATES:** And what of lying? Is it not just to lie and deceive in order to harm them?
**GUEST:** Yes.
**SOCRATES:** And what about friends? Do you not say it is just to benefit them?
**GUEST:** I do.
**SOCRATES:** Should one do so without deceiving them, or by deceiving them for their own benefit?
**GUEST:** Even by deceiving them, by Zeus.
**SOCRATES:** So it is just to benefit them by deceiving them, but surely not by lying to them? Or is it also by lying?
**GUEST:** Even by lying
<margin>C</margin>
it is just.
**SOCRATES:** It seems, then, that both lying and speaking the truth can be both just and unjust.
**GUEST:** Yes.
**SOCRATES:** And both not deceiving and deceiving can be both just and unjust.
**GUEST:** Yes.
**SOCRATES:** All such things, it seems, are both just and unjust.
**GUEST:** So it appears to me.
**SOCRATES:** Listen then: do I have a right and a left eye, just like other men?
**GUEST:** Yes.
**SOCRATES:** And a right and left nostril?
**GUEST:** Certainly.
**SOCRATES:** And a right and left hand?
**GUEST:** Yes.
**SOCRATES:** Therefore, when you use the same names and say some things are "right" and others are "left," if I were to ask you while turning my back, would you be able to say which are on the right side and which are on the left?
**GUEST:** I would.
**SOCRATES:** Come then, apply it to this:
<margin>D</margin>
since you use the same names and say some things are just and others are unjust, can you say which are the just ones and which are the unjust?
**GUEST:** It seems to me, then, that whenever we do each of these things at the necessary time and the right moment, they are just; but when done at the wrong time, they are unjust.
**SOCRATES:** You judge well. Does he, then, who does each of these things at the necessary time, act justly? And he who does not do so at the necessary time, act unjustly?
**GUEST:** That is so.
**SOCRATES:** Who, then, is capable of cutting, cauterizing, and thinning <note>technical medical terms for surgery and treatment</note> at the necessary time?
**GUEST:** The physician.
**SOCRATES:** Because he has knowledge, or for some other reason?
**GUEST:** Because he has knowledge.
<margin>E</margin>
**SOCRATES:** And who is capable of digging, plowing, and planting at the necessary time?
**GUEST:** The farmer.
**SOCRATES:** He who has knowledge, or he who does not?
**GUEST:** He who has knowledge.
**SOCRATES:** Is it not the same with other things? He who has knowledge is capable of doing what is necessary, and doing it at the necessary time and moment; but he who lacks knowledge is not?
**GUEST:** That is so.
**SOCRATES:** Therefore, regarding lying, deceiving, and benefiting, he who has knowledge is capable of doing each of these at the necessary time and moment; but he who lacks knowledge is not.
**GUEST:** You speak the truth.
**SOCRATES:** And he who does these things at the necessary time is just.
**GUEST:** Yes.
**SOCRATES:** And he does these things through knowledge.
**GUEST:** How could he not?
**SOCRATES:** Therefore, the just man is just through knowledge.
**GUEST:** Yes.
**SOCRATES:** And the unjust man, being the opposite of the just, will be unjust in the opposite way?
**GUEST:** So it appears.
**SOCRATES:** The just man is just through wisdom.
**GUEST:** Yes.
**SOCRATES:** Therefore, the unjust man is unjust through ignorance.
**GUEST:** It seems so.
**SOCRATES:** It is likely, then, that what our ancestors understood as wisdom is justice, and ignorance is injustice.
**GUEST:** It seems so.
**SOCRATES:** Are men ignorant willingly or unwillingly?
**GUEST:** Unwillingly.
**SOCRATES:** Then they are also unjust unwillingly.
**GUEST:** So it appears.
**SOCRATES:** And the unjust are wicked.
**GUEST:** Yes.
**SOCRATES:** Therefore, they are wicked and unjust unwillingly.
**GUEST:** Entirely so.
**SOCRATES:** And they commit injustice because they are unjust.
**GUEST:** Yes.
**SOCRATES:** Therefore, they do so because of something involuntary.
**GUEST:** Certainly.
**SOCRATES:** Now, the voluntary does not come about through the involuntary.
**GUEST:** No, indeed.
**SOCRATES:** But the act of injustice comes about through being unjust.
**GUEST:** Yes.
**SOCRATES:** And being unjust is involuntary.
**GUEST:** Involuntary.
**SOCRATES:** Therefore, men are unjust unwillingly, and they are both unjust and wicked unwillingly.
**GUEST:** Unwillingly, as it appears.
**SOCRATES:** Then the poet did not lie.
**GUEST:** It does not seem so.

<column-break/>

**GUEST:** By the good. But Socrates, the old proverb is right, that poets lie in many things... <note>The Latin text mirrors the Greek dialogue exactly as translated above.</note>

<summary>Socrates leads a guest through a dialectic argument to conclude that justice is a form of knowledge (wisdom) and injustice is a form of ignorance. Consequently, since no one chooses ignorance willingly, all unjust and wicked acts are committed unwillingly.</summary>

<header>OF PLATO</header>

# ON VIRTUE, WHETHER IT CAN BE TAUGHT: A DIALOGUE, WHICH IS HELD TO BE SPURIOUS.
<note>original: "nothus habetur" / "νοθευόμενος". While included in the Platonic corpus, early modern scholars often marked this specific dialogue as likely written by a follower rather than Plato himself.</note>

->Translated by Sebastiano Corrado.<-

->SOCRATES, A FRIEND.<-

<margin>A</margin>SOCRATES: Can virtue be passed on through teaching, or is it rather something that cannot be acquired—but instead, men become good by nature or by some other means? FRIEND: I do not have an answer for you at this moment, Socrates.

<margin>B</margin>SOCR. Then let us consider it in this way. Come now, if someone wished to become good in that skill by which cooks are good—those who are considered especially skillful—from where would he become so? FRIEND: Clearly from there, if he were to learn from good cooks. SOCR. What if he wished to become a good Physician; to whom should he go to become a good Physician? FRIEND: To one of those who are good physicians. SOCR. But if he desired to be good in that art by which Carpenters are good? FRIEND: To one of the carpenters. SOCR. But, if he greatly desired to turn out good in that virtue by which men are both Good and Wise, to whom should we say he ought to go?

<margin>C</margin>FRIEND: I suppose to one of those who are good men, provided that he who desires to learn is fit to thoroughly learn that virtue; for where else could he go? SOCR. Come then. Who have been the good men in our city, so that we may weigh whether men of this sort likewise make others good? FRIEND: Thucydides, Themistocles, Aristides, and Pericles. SOCR. Can we name a teacher for any one of these? FRIEND: We cannot; for it is not spoken of. SOCR. What? Can we name a disciple—whether a foreigner or a citizen, a freeman or a slave—who can affirm that he was made Good and Wise through their company? FRIEND: Neither is this spoken of. SOCR. Were they perhaps envious, such that they were unwilling to share virtue with others? FRIEND: Perhaps.

<margin>D</margin>SOCR. Was it because they feared that others might become their rivals, just as Cooks, Physicians, and Carpenters do? For they do not think it useful to themselves if many adversaries in their art are created, nor convenient if they themselves live among many like them. Is it therefore the same way for good men—is it inconvenient to live with those like themselves? FRIEND: It is possible. SOCR. Are not these same men Good and Just? FRIEND: They are. SOCR. Is there anyone for whom it could be useful to associate not with the good, but with the wicked? FRIEND: I cannot say. SOCR. Can you then not even say this: whether it is the work of the good to do harm, but of the wicked to be of use—or the opposite?

<margin>E</margin>FRIEND: The opposite. SOCR. Do you assert that the good help, while the wicked do harm? FRIEND: I do. SOCR. Is there anyone, then, who prefers to be harmed rather than helped? FRIEND: Certainly no one. SOCR. No one, therefore, prefers to live among the harmful rather than among the useful. FRIEND: It is as you say. SOCR. No good man is troubled that another becomes good and like himself. FRIEND: No one, as appears from this reasoning. SOCR. Have you heard that Themistocles had a son, Cleophantus? FRIEND: I have. SOCR. Surely Themistocles, who envied no one his goodness—if indeed he was good, as he truly was and as we say—would never have prevented his son from becoming the best possible out of envy. FRIEND: Never. SOCR. Therefore he wished his son to be taught the art of horsemanship so that he would be skilled and good in it. For he used to stand upright on a horse, and from the horse he would hurl javelins while standing upright, and he did many other wonderful things. He also took care to have him instructed and taught in many other things, whatever is passed down by good teachers. Have you not heard these things from your elders?

<margin>F</margin>FRIEND: Often, indeed. SOCR. No one, therefore, can accuse the nature of this son of being bad. FRIEND: No one justly, as is manifest from what you say. SOCR. But as for Cleophantus himself, the son of Themistocles, have you ever heard from anyone, young or old, that he was a good and wise man in those things in which his father was wise? FRIEND: Never. SOCR. Is it then to be thought that Themistocles wished his son to be instructed in those things we mentioned,

<margin>G</margin>but in the Wisdom by which he himself was wise, he wished him to be no better than any neighbor—if Virtue could have been acquired? FRIEND: That does not seem likely. But let us look at Aristides. He raised Lysimachus and took care that he was educated most beautifully of all the Athenians in all those things within the power of teachers; yet he made him a man better than no one. For both you and I have not only seen him, but have also met him. FRIEND: True. SOCR. Now indeed you know Paralus and Xanthippus—one of whom you seem to me to have loved—who were so raised and instructed by Pericles that they yielded to no Athenian in the art of horsemanship; moreover in Music and other types of contests, and indeed in all other things passed down by art, they were no less educated than the rest, for he himself labored vehemently at it. But did the father not wish them to become good men? FRIEND: Perhaps they would have become so, Socrates, had they not died as young men. SOCR. You rightly come to the aid of your beloveds; but Pericles, if virtue were obtainable, could have made them good, and would have much rather made them wise in his own virtue than in Music and the study of contests. But it cannot be prepared. For Thucydides also raised two sons, Melesias and Stephanus, for whom you could not say what you just said for the sons of Pericles.

<column-break/>

# ON VIRTUE, WHETHER IT CAN BE TAUGHT, A SPURIOUS DIALOGUE.

<margin>A</margin>Is virtue something that can be taught? Or is it not teachable, but rather men become good by nature, or in some other way? I cannot say at present, Socrates. But let us look at it this way. Come, if someone wished to become good in that virtue which wise cooks possess, from where would he become so? Clearly if from

<margin>B</margin>good cooks he should learn. What then? If he wished to become a good physician, to whom would he go to become a good physician? Clearly to good physicians. And if he wished to become good in that virtue which wise carpenters possess? From the carpenters. And if he wished to become better and good in that virtue which men who are both good and wise possess, where must he go to learn? I suppose this too, if it is learnable, from good men. For from where else? Come then, who have been good men for us? So that we may consider if these are the ones who make others

<margin>C</margin>good. Thucydides and Themistocles and Aristides and Pericles. Of each of these, can we name a teacher? We cannot, for it is not said. What then? A disciple, either of the foreigners or the citizens, or another, free or slave, who is said to have become wise and good through their company? Neither is this said. But did they perhaps envy sharing virtue with other men? Perhaps. Was it so that they might not have rivals in their craft, just as cooks and physicians and carpenters are sparing? For it does not profit them for many rivals to arise, nor to live among many like themselves. Does it then also not profit good men to live among those like themselves? Perhaps. Are they not

<margin>D</margin>themselves good and just? Yes. Is there then anyone for whom it profits not to live among good men, but among bad? I cannot say. Can you then not even say this, whether it is the work of the good to harm, and of the bad to benefit? Or the opposite? The opposite. The good then benefit, and the bad harm? Yes. Is there then anyone who wants to be harmed rather than benefited? Not at all. No one then wants to live among the wicked rather than among the useful. Thus. No one then envies making another person good, so as to make him like himself. It does not appear so from the argument. Have you not heard that a son Cleophantus was born to

<margin>E</margin>Themistocles? I have heard. Is it not clear then that he did not envy his son becoming the best? Just as he would no one else, if he were good, as we say he was. Yes. You know then that Themistocles taught his son to be a wise and good horseman. At any rate, he used to stand upright upon horses; and he hurled javelins from the horses while standing upright, and did many other wonderful things; and he taught him many other things, and made him wise in as many things as depended on good teachers. Or have you not heard these things from the elders? I have heard. No one could yet accuse the nature of his son of being bad. Not justly, at least, from what you say. What then, that Cleophantus, the son of Themistocles, became a good and wise man in the same things his father was wise—have you heard this from either a younger or an older person? I have not heard. Do we then think that he wished

<margin>F</margin>to educate his own son in these things, but in the wisdom in which he himself was wise, he made him no better than any of the neighbors, if virtue were teachable? It is not likely. This then is such a teacher of virtue for you, whom you also named. But let us consider another, Aristides, who raised Lysimachus, and educated him most beautifully of the Athenians in as many things as depended on teachers; but he made him a man better than no one. For you also have seen him and associated with him. Yes. You know then that Pericles in turn raised Paralus and Xanthippus; one of whom you seem to me to have been in love with. These, however, as you also know, he taught to be horsemen second to no Athenian; and

<margin>G</margin>music, and the other contests, and he educated them in the other things that they teach by art. But did he then not wish to make them good men? But perhaps they would have become so, Socrates, if they had not died while young. You naturally help your favorites; but Pericles, if virtue were teachable, and he were able to make them good, would much sooner have made them wise in his own virtue than in music and contests. But perhaps it is not teachable. Since Thucydides in turn raised two sons, Melesias and Stephanus; for whom you would not be able to say what you just said for the sons of Pericles.

<summary>Socrates and a friend debate whether virtue can be taught by examining famous Athenian statesmen like Pericles and Themistocles, noting that while they gave their sons excellent technical educations, they failed to pass on their own moral excellence.</summary>

<meta>This page continues a Socratic dialogue concerning whether virtue can be taught or if it is innate, concluding one section and beginning the pseudo-Platonic dialogue 'Demodocus'.</meta>

# DEMODOCVS.

For surely you also know that one of them lived to old age, and the other quite far along. And indeed, their father educated them well in other matters, and educated them best of all the Athenians. For while he was still living, he gave one to Xanthias and the other to Eudorus; these men were thought to be the finest wrestlers of that time. **Friend:** Yes. **Socrates:** Is it not clear then that in those things where he had to spend money to have them taught, he taught his own sons? But in that which required no expense to make them good men, would he not have taught them this, if it were teachable? **Friend:** It is likely. **Socrates:** But perhaps Thucydides was a common man, and did not have many friends among the Athenians and the allies? He was of a great house, and had great power in the city and among the other Greeks. So if this were teachable, he would have found someone who was going to make his sons good, either from the locals or from foreigners, if he himself lacked leisure due to the care of the city. But indeed, my friend, perhaps virtue is not teachable. **Friend:** Perhaps not. **Socrates:** But then, if it is not teachable, do the good grow so by nature? And by looking at it in this way, perhaps we might find out. Come now: are there among us natural types of good horses? **Friend:** There are. **Socrates:** Are there not then certain men possessing an art by which they recognize the natures of good horses, both regarding the body—which are strong—and regarding the soul—which are high-spirited and which are not? **Friend:** Yes. **Socrates:** What then is this art? Is there a name for it? **Friend:** Horsemanship <note>original: Ἱππική / Equestris</note>. **Socrates:** And is there not likewise an art concerning dogs, by which they distinguish the good and bad natures of dogs? **Friend:** There is. **Socrates:** What is this? **Friend:** Hunting <note>original: Ἡ κυνηγετική / Canina</note>. **Socrates:** And indeed, concerning gold and silver, do we not have testers who judge by looking which is better and which is worse? **Friend:** We do. **Socrates:** What then do you call these? **Friend:** Money-testers <note>original: Ἀργυρογνώμονας / Argentarios</note>. **Socrates:** And indeed, the trainers <note>original: παιδευταὶ / magistri</note> know, by examining the natures of human bodies, which are useful and which are not for each of the labors, and which bodies of both elders and youths are going to be worthy of mention; and in which there is much hope to perform well all the works that pertain to the body. **Friend:** That is so. **Socrates:** Which then is more serious for cities: good horses and dogs and other such things, or good men? **Friend:** Good men. **Socrates:** What then? Do you think that if there were natures good toward human virtue, men would not have devised every way and means to distinguish them? **Friend:** It is likely. **Socrates:** Can you then name any art which is appointed for the natures of good men, so as to be able to judge them? **Friend:** I cannot. **Socrates:** And yet surely such an art would be worth the most. And those possessing the art would have pointed out to us those of the youth who were going to be good, while they were still children; whom we, having received, would have guarded in the public acropolis just like silver—and even more so—so that they might not suffer anything base from us, neither in battle nor in any other danger; but they would be laid up for the city as saviors and benefactors when they reached the proper age. But it is risked that virtue comes to men neither by nature nor by learning. **Friend:** How then, Socrates, do they seem to you to become good, if they become so neither by nature nor by learning? In what other way would the good arise? **Socrates:** I think it cannot be easily shown; for I think the possession is altogether a most divine thing, and the good arise just like the divine soothsayers and oracle-singers. For these become such neither by nature nor by art, but becoming so by inspiration from the gods, they are such. So also good men tell their cities each time what will result and what is going to be, from a divine inspiration much more and more clearly than the oracle-singers. For even the women say, "This is a divine man"; and the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans</note>, whenever they praise someone magnificently, say he is a divine man. And in many places Homer uses this same term, as do the other poets. And when a god wants a city to fare well, he implants good men; but when a city is going to fare ill, the god takes the good men out of that city. Thus it seems virtue is neither teachable nor by nature, but comes by a divine lot to those to whom it comes.

...they call him a divine man: which Homer and the rest of the poets frequently use. Therefore, when God wishes to benefit a Republic most greatly, he engenders good men in it; but when he wishes to hinder it, he removes those same men, if there are any, from it. Thus Virtue seems to be acquired neither by discipline nor by nature: but to be present in those endowed with it by a divine lot.

### DEMODOCUS, OR,

-> On Giving Counsel. <-

-> A SPURIOUS DIALOGUE. <-

<margin>G</margin>
<note>The Latin text below identifies the translator as Sebastiano Corrado.</note>
YOU indeed rightly bid me, O Demodocus, to give you counsel always on those matters about which you have come together to deliberate; but it occurs to me to consider what your assembly can really achieve, and the zeal of those who think they can give you counsel, and the vote which each of you intends to cast. For in this matter, if it is not possible to counsel rightly and expertly about the things you have gathered to deliberate upon, how is it not ridiculous for you to gather to deliberate on things which those assembled do not know how to counsel, or how would it not be likely that they, in counseling...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> For you know one of these even unto old age, but the other indeed reached even beyond. And when their father wished them to be taught, just as they knew other things well, so especially he wished them to be the most beautiful wrestlers of all the Athenians. For he handed them over to be educated, one to Xanthias, the other to Eudorus. Furthermore, those masters then seemed to excel all in the art of wrestling. **Friend:** It is known. **Socrates:** Clearly then, would he have ever wished his sons to be taught these things, where it was necessary to spend much on those who taught; but where no expense was to be made on him who would make them good men, would he not have taught them this, if indeed it could be handed down? <margin>B</margin> **Friend:** You say nothing strange. **Socrates:** But perhaps Thucydides was ignoble, and did not have many friends either from the citizens or the allies. On the contrary, he was from an ample family and was very powerful both among the citizens and among the other Greeks. Wherefore, if this itself could have been acquired, he surely would have found someone, either from the citizens or from foreigners, who would have made his sons good, if he himself were not permitted by the administration of the Republic. But indeed, friend, virtue cannot be acquired. **Friend:** So it is perhaps. **Socrates:** But if virtue cannot be acquired, are men born good by nature? And contemplating this very thing by this reasoning, perhaps we shall find out. For tell me: <margin>C</margin> are the natures of good horses known to us? **Friend:** They are. **Socrates:** Are there then men who hold the art by which they may know the natures of good horses, and thus understand which horses are strong in body for the course and brave in soul, and which on the contrary are cowardly? **Friend:** There are. **Socrates:** What then is that art? What is its name? **Friend:** Equestrian. **Socrates:** Is there also in the same way regarding dogs an art by which they discern good and bad natures of dogs? **Friend:** There is. **Socrates:** What may that be? **Friend:** Canine <note>Hunting</note>. **Socrates:** But regarding gold and silver, is the same to be said, that there are testers who judge by sight what is better and what is worse? **Friend:** It is to be said. **Socrates:** What then do you call them? **Friend:** Money-changers <note>Argentarios</note>. **Socrates:** These masters indeed, who preside over exercising bodies, do they not, when they contemplate the natures of bodies, know which are fit for <margin>D</margin> bearing labors and which on the contrary are unfit? And do they not observe the bodies of both the old and the young, which will be worthy of praise and in which there is hope that all works pertaining to the body will be done excellently? **Friend:** These things are so. **Socrates:** Is it then a greater care to Republics to have good horses and dogs and other things of this sort, or good men? **Friend:** Good men. **Socrates:** Would men not then have devised everything so that they might know if the natures of men were good toward virtue? **Friend:** I think so, and it is consistent. **Socrates:** Can you then name any art which is in the natures of good men, showing by what means we can judge them? **Friend:** I cannot. **Socrates:** And yet that art would have been <margin>E</margin> most highly valued, and those who were skilled in it. For they would have indicated to us the youths themselves who were going to be good, even while they were still boys: whom we would have cared to guard in the acropolis no differently than silver, and even much more diligently, so that they might suffer no evil either in battle or in any other danger: but they would be deposited for the Republic as saviors and benefactors, to be such when they reached their age. But virtue seems to be present in men neither by nature nor by discipline. **Friend:** In what way then, Socrates, do they seem to you to become good? For if they become so neither by nature nor by discipline, <margin>F</margin> in what other way finally may they become good? **Socrates:** I indeed think this itself cannot be so easily declared: since I suspect the possession of this thing is something especially divine, and men become good similarly as divine seers and soothsayers. For they are such neither by nature nor by art, but by the spirit with which they are divinely inspired. So also good men often predict things that will happen to Republics from a certain divine inspiration much more clearly and manifest than soothsayers. Hence even women say such a man is divine. Moreover, the Lacedaemonians, when they wish to praise someone magnificently, say he is a divine man...
