<meta>This page continues a philosophical dialogue, likely from a Renaissance edition of Plato or a pseudo-Platonic work (such as the *Eryxias* or *Axiochus*), discussing the nature of political counsel and the paradox of voting.</meta>

# 736 OF PLATO

<margin>A</margin> ...be permitted: But is it not also absurd that you have come together to deliberate, as if it were possible to give advice rightly and skillfully on such matters, yet there is no science <note>Latin: *scientia*; Greek: *episteme*</note> from which one can give advice correctly? If there is indeed some science by which one may give right counsel in these affairs, is it not necessary that there be some who know how to give right counsel? And since there are some who know how to give counsel on the matters you are deliberating, is it not necessary that you either know how to give counsel yourselves, or you do not? Or perhaps some of you know, while others do not? If, then, you all know, why is it necessary for you to meet further for deliberation? For each one of you is fit to give counsel. If, on the contrary, you all do not know, how can you deliberate? Or what utility can this meeting bring to you, who are not even able to deliberate? But if some of you know and others do not, those [who do not] stand in need of counsel; and if it is possible for one prudent man to give counsel to the unskilled, then one man would be able to give counsel to you who do not know. Or do not all those who know give the same counsel? Therefore, having heard this, it would be proper for you to depart. Yet now you do not do this, but you wish to hear many of those who offer advice. For you do not believe that those who come forward to give you counsel actually know the things about which they advise. For if you had believed that those giving counsel knew, it would have been enough for you to hear one. Therefore, that you should meet to hear those who do not know, as if you were about to do something worthwhile—how can that not be absurd? And indeed, I doubt your deliberation in this way; but concerning the zeal of those who think they can give you counsel, I have this doubt: For if those giving counsel on the same matters do not give the same answers, how can they all give counsel beautifully, since they do not answer the same things as he who gives counsel rightly? Or how is the zeal of those who set their minds to give counsel on things of which they are ignorant not inept? For the skilled would never so determine that they would wish to give counsel incorrectly. If, on the other hand, they give the same answers, why must they all give counsel? For one of them giving the same answer would suffice. Who, then, would not laugh at those who desire to do things that bring no utility? Therefore, the zeal of the unskilled cannot help but be inept, being of such a kind; nor would the prudent ever undertake to do such things, knowing that even one of them giving counsel, as is fitting, can provide that very thing. Wherefore I can think of no reason why the zeal of those who think they can give you counsel should not appear ridiculous. But as for the vote <note>Latin: *suffragium*; Greek: *psephos*</note> which you intend to cast, I am in great doubt as to what it can achieve. For will you judge those who know, so that they may give counsel? But there is no more than one [truth], nor will they give counsel on the same matter in different ways; for which reason it will not be necessary for you to cast a vote. Or will you appoint the unskilled, and those who do not give counsel as they ought, to give counsel? But these are no more to be consulted than madmen. But if you will pass judgment neither on the skilled nor the unskilled, whom will you judge from the beginning to be fit to give counsel? How is it at all fitting for others to give you counsel, if indeed you are able to judge these things? But if you cannot judge, what can your votes profit you? Or in what way is it not ridiculous that you have met as if in need of counsel and not fit to decide it, yet after you have met, you think a sentence must be passed by you, as if you were able to judge? For it must not be said that you were each individually ignorant, but after you met in one place, you became prudent; nor that you doubted privately, but as soon as you came here, you no longer doubt, but have become fit to perceive those things which you must do—even though you have learned these things from no one, nor found them yourselves, which is by far the most difficult of all. For unless you are able to recognize what you must do, you will never be able to judge whether the one giving you counsel does so rightly. Nor, furthermore, will any one person who gives you counsel say that he will so teach you what you must do that you can judge both those who give you counsel badly and those who give it well—and that in so short a time and to so many people; especially since this seems no less difficult than the other. But if neither the assembly nor the one giving you counsel makes you fit to judge, what need have you of votes? Or rather, how do your assembly, your votes, and the zeal of those giving you counsel not greatly conflict? For your assembly is held as if you were not fit to determine anything but stood in need of the counsel of others; yet votes are cast as if you not only did not need counsel, but were even able to judge and give counsel to others. Then the zeal of those who give counsel is present as if they knew how to do it; but the votes are cast by you as if they do not know. But if someone were to ask you who cast the votes, and the one who gave you counsel on those things which you decide by vote: "Do you know that the thing for the sake of which you intend to do what you have decreed will actually happen?" I do not believe you would say so. "What if that for the sake of which you intend to do these things should happen—do you know that this will be useful to you?" I do not think you would say this, nor would the one who gives you counsel. If, furthermore, someone were to ask you: "Do you think there is any mortal man who knows any one of these things?"

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...is it right? And this, if it is not absurd, to give counsel and to do so with experience concerning such things, yet there is no knowledge <note>Greek: *episteme*</note> from which it is possible to give counsel rightly concerning these things, how could it not be considered that if there is some knowledge from which it is possible to give counsel rightly on such matters, it is also necessary that there be some who know how to give counsel rightly? And when there are some who know how to give counsel about the things you are gathered to deliberate upon, is it not necessary that you either know how to give counsel about these things, or you do not know? Or that some of you know, and some do not? If then you all know, why must you come together to deliberate? For each of you is sufficient to give counsel. But if, on the other hand, you all do not know, how could you deliberate? Or what would be the benefit of this assembly, if you are not able to deliberate? <margin>B</margin> But if some of you know and some do not know, and these [latter] need counsel, if indeed it is possible for a wise man to give good counsel to the inexperienced, then one man would be sufficient to give counsel to you who do not know. Or do not all those who know give the same counsel? So that having heard this once, you ought to have stopped. But now you do not do this, but you wish to hear many people giving counsel. For you do not assume that those attempting to give you counsel know the things about which they advise. For if you assumed that those giving you counsel knew, it would have been enough for you to hear only one. Therefore, to come together to hear those who know, as if <margin>C</margin> doing something else, how would that not be absurd? And I am always at a loss regarding your assembly in this way. But concerning the zeal of those who think they should give you counsel, that is a difficulty. For if they do not give the same counsel while advising on the same things, how could they all give counsel well, if they do not advise what the one who advises rightly advises? Or how would your zeal concerning those who think they can give counsel on things of which they are inexperienced not be absurd? For being experienced, they would not choose to give counsel incorrectly. But if, on the other hand, they give the same counsel, why must they all give counsel? For one of them giving the same advice would be sufficient. Therefore, to be zealous for such things which could bring no benefit, how is it not ridiculous? Or when in the eagerness of the inexperienced <margin>D</margin> it would not be absurd, being of such a kind, neither would the wise ever be eager; knowing that even one of them will do the same thing, giving counsel as is fitting. So how is the zeal of those who think they can give you counsel not ridiculous, since they are not able to find [the truth]? And as for the vote <note>Greek: *psephos*</note> which you always intend to cast, I am most at a loss as to what it can do. For will you judge those who know how to give counsel? But no more than one gives counsel, nor in different ways about the same thing. So that concerning these, how will it not be unnecessary for you to cast a vote? But will you judge the inexperienced and those who do not give counsel as they ought? It is fitting not to permit such people to give counsel, as if they were madmen. But if you judge neither the experienced nor the inexperienced, whom will you <margin>E</margin> judge? And from the start, why must others give you counsel at all, if indeed you are capable of judging such things? But if you are not capable, what can the votes do for you? Or how is it not ridiculous for you to come together to deliberate, as if needing counsel and not being sufficient counselors yourselves, but then to think you must cast a vote as if you were capable of judging? For surely you are not ignorant when you are alone, but become wise when you come together; nor, again, do you doubt in private, but having come to the same place, you no longer doubt, but become capable of seeing what things you must do. And these things you have learned from no one, nor found them yourselves, which is the most strange thing of all. For if you are not <margin>F</margin> able to see what must be done, you will not be capable of judging the one who gives you counsel rightly about these things. Nor, again, will any one person who gives you counsel say that he will so teach you what you must do, and how to judge those who give you counsel badly or well, in so short a time and to so many people. This would appear no less strange than the other. But if neither the assembly nor the one giving you counsel makes you capable of judging, what use is the vote to you? Or how does your assembly not oppose the votes, and the votes oppose the desire of those giving you counsel? For your assembly treats you as not capable but needing counsel, but the votes are cast as if you do not need counsel, but are able both to judge and to give counsel. And the zeal of those giving you counsel is as if <margin>G</margin> they knew; but the votes from you are cast as if those giving counsel do not know. And if someone were to ask you who voted, and the one who gave you counsel, about the things you voted for, whether you know that the thing for the sake of which you intend to do what you voted for will happen; I do not think you would say yes. And what if that for the sake of which you intend to act should happen, do you know that this will be of benefit to you? I do not think you would say this, nor would the one giving you counsel. If someone further asked you: whether you think there is any one of all mortal men who knows any one of these things?

<summary>This page presents a philosophical critique of democratic deliberation and voting, arguing that if a "science of counsel" exists, an assembly of the ignorant cannot judge the expert, and if it does not exist, the assembly is useless.</summary>
<keywords>Plato, counsel, deliberation, voting, knowledge vs. ignorance, political philosophy, assembly, judgment</keywords>

# DEMODOCUS. 737

I do not think you would concede this to me. For whenever you give advice, or when things do not seem to be as you wish, both those who vote and those who advise—as is likely—would speak against it; and you will say that you care for what is right, yet they often regret both what they have advised and what they have voted for. But such things ought not to happen to good men. For they know what kind of things they are dealing with, and it is so firmly established for those who teach them the reasons for their advice, that neither they nor those they have taught will ever feel regret. But I, for my part, would not think it right for those with sense to profess to advise on such matters, nor on the things you always command me to advise upon. <margin>B</margin> For from their advice the end result is misfortune, but from the nonsense of these others, misfortune also arises. It happened that a certain man was admonishing his friend because he believed an accusation, having heard only the accuser and not yet the one making the defense. He said it was a terrible thing to act out of fear, condemning the man before he himself had certain knowledge, or had heard from friends who had seen the matter and whom he ought to believe; he had not heard both sides before being persuaded by the accuser. He said it was just to hear the one defending himself regarding what was being examined or disputed, just as one hears the accuser. <margin>C</margin> For how could anyone judge well or justly, when it is necessary to judge men's affairs rightly, without having heard the case from both? For one judges better when arguments are compared, just as one judges purple cloth or gold. For what other reason does the lawgiver give time to both adversaries, or why do the judges swear to listen equally to both sides, unless the lawgiver believed that the judges would judge the cases more justly and better in this way? But you seem to me not even to have heard that common saying. What is that? he asked.

<margin>D</margin> Never pass judgment until you have heard the story of both. <note>original: "Μηδὲ δίκην δικάσῃς, πρὶν ἀμφοῖν μῦθον ἀκούσῃς." A famous legal maxim attributed to Phocylides or Hesiod.</note>

And yet this would not be so widely repeated if it were not well said and as it should be. I advise you then (he said) for the future not to be so headlong in either blaming or praising men. The other man, already at a loss and troubled, said that he wondered if it were possible to know when one person speaks whether he tells the truth or lies, but when two speak it becomes possible; and whether it is possible to learn the truth from the one speaking it, but that he might be deceived by the other who lies; and if the one who speaks rightly and truly can make it clear, but when there are two, and the other lies and does not speak rightly, then it is impossible for the one speaking rightly to make it clear. I am at a loss, he said, as to how they will make it clear. Will they do so by being silent, or by speaking? For if they make it clear by being silent, there would never be any need to hear either of them, let alone both. But if both make it clear by speaking, <margin>E</margin> and yet they do not speak at the same time (for they demand that each speaks in turn), how could both make it clear? For if they both demonstrate at once, and each is present at the same time, it follows that if they make it clear by speaking, each will make it clear when he speaks. Therefore, one will speak first and the other later; and one will make it clear first, and the other later. And yet, if each makes the same thing clear in turn, why is it necessary to hear the second? For by the one who spoke first, the matter will already have been made manifest. And furthermore (he said), if they both make it clear, how is it that one of them alone does not make it clear? For if one makes it clear, how could both be said to make it clear? But if each <margin>F</margin> makes it clear, it is plain that the one who speaks first will make it clear first; so that by hearing him alone, it is impossible not to know how the matter stands. I, at least, while listening, was held back and was unable to judge, for those present did not say that the things spoken were true. If, therefore, you have any advice for me on these matters, whether it is possible to know what one says when he speaks alone, or whether there is a need for someone to speak against him; whether one will better know if he speaks rightly, or if it is not necessary to hear both. Or how do you think? Someone accused a man because he was unwilling to lend him money or trust him. And the one who was accused defended himself; but another of those present asked the accuser whether the one who did not trust him nor lend to him had erred; and you (he said), not having persuaded him to lend, have you not also erred? And he said, "In what have I erred?" <margin>G</margin> Which of the two, he asked, seems to you to err: the one who fails in what he wants, or the one who does not? The one who fails, he said. Therefore (he said), did you not fail, wishing to borrow? And he said, "Yes, I erred if he did not give to me." But if he had given to him (he said), how would that man have erred? Or did he not act rightly by refusing you? But if he had given, how would you not have erred by taking it unjustly? Perhaps, he said. But why did that man not err by not trusting me? Is it not the case (he said) if you had dealt with him as was fitting, he would have trusted you? Not at all. Then it is clear you did not deal with him as was fitting.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> <margin>N</margin> <note>The Latin column mirrors the Greek text provided on the left, serving as a contemporary translation for scholars of the Renaissance/Early Modern period.</note> Nor do I think you will concede this. Therefore, since those things which come into consultation are of such a kind that they cannot be manifest to you, and since those who cast votes and those who give advice are unskilled, you will rightly say it happens that we do not believe, and they themselves often repent of those things about which they consult and vote; which is not consistent for the most excellent men. For they know the nature of the things about which they give advice... <margin>B</margin> I happened by chance to be present when a certain man rebuked his friend because he believed a certain accuser, whom he had heard only as an accuser and not yet heard the defender. He said he was doing an unworthy thing by condemning a man whose affairs he had not seen himself... <margin>C</margin> For how can anyone judge a cause well or men uprightly unless he has first heard both litigants? For compared reasons and causes are far better judged, like purple cloth and gold. Why else would the Legislator have ordered time to be given to each of the adversaries, or the judges to swear they will hear both sides equally... <margin>D-G</margin> <note>The Latin continues to provide a faithful rendering of the Greek arguments regarding the "audi alteram partem" (hear the other side) principle and the anecdote of the failed loan, concluding that failure to persuade is as much an "error" as the failure to trust.</note>

# OF PLATO

<margin>A</margin> If that man did not yield to you because you were not behaving as was fitting, what is there for which you could justly accuse him? I cannot say. And can you not say that one should not lend to those who use things badly? On the contrary, I can, he said, and quite easily. But those who do not behave as is fitting, do they not seem to you to use things badly? To me at least, he said, they seem so. Why then did he err if he did not lend to you when you were using things badly? He answered nothing, as it seems. Why then do men bring these charges against one another: and why are they angry at those whom they themselves did not persuade, because they did not obey, yet they do not accuse themselves at all for failing to persuade them? <margin>B</margin> Then another who was present said: When someone uses something well and it is of great use to him, and because of this he later thinks himself worthy of the same use in return, yet does not obtain it, why might he not rightly be indignant? Surely, he replied, the one whom he thinks ought to use him in the same way either can use him well or cannot; and if indeed he cannot, in what way does he think that man will use him well who is unable to do so? But if he can, why did he not persuade such a man? Or rather, what can be brought forward as a reason why those who say such things should seem to speak well? <margin>C</margin> But by Hercules, he said, it is necessary to find fault, so that he and other friends who hear the one finding fault may thereafter use him better. But did it not seem to you that he rightly thought it worthy to be used better? It seemed so, he said. In what way then will those who hear a man finding fault with these things use him better? In no way, he said. Why then does someone find fault with these things? He replied that he could not find the answer. <margin>D</margin> Someone was arguing against a man’s ignorance, because he believed quickly and in whatever people were saying. For he said it was reasonable to believe citizens and members of the household when they spoke; but to give credit to those men whom he neither knew nor had ever heard before—especially when he knew that most men are deceitful and crafty—was, he said, no small sign of folly. <margin>E</margin> But one of those present said: I truly thought you were the sort of person who judged that one who perceives anything quickly is worth much more than one who perceives slowly. Indeed I do judge so, he replied. Why then do you accuse him if he quickly trusts those who speak the truth, whoever they may be? But I do not accuse him of this, he said, but because he quickly believes those who speak falsehoods. But if after a long time, and not having believed just anyone, he had still been deceived, would you not have accused him more? Certainly, he said. Was it because he believed slowly and not just anyone? Hardly, he said. For I do not think, he said, that you could be led to think a man worthy of being accused for this: but because he believes those who say incredible things. Quite so, he said. Do you therefore think him unworthy of accusation when he believes slowly and not just anyone, but worthy when he believes quickly and anyone at all? Not I, he said. Why then do you accuse him? Because he errs, before he weighs the matter, by believing quickly and anyone at all. But if he had fallen into error slowly before he considered it, would he not have erred? Without doubt, he said. Because he would have erred no less. But I do not think one should believe just anything. If you do not think one should believe just anything, is it fitting to quickly give credit to unknown people? Do you not think it should first be considered whether they speak the truth? I think so indeed, he said. <margin>F</margin> But if they are members of the household and familiars, is it not necessary to examine whether they speak the truth? I for my part, he said, would say it is necessary. For perhaps some of these also say incredible things. Very much so, he said. Why then is it more reasonable to believe members of the household and familiars than just anyone? I cannot say, he said. What if one must believe members of the household more than anyone else, must we not judge them less unworthy of trust than anyone else? Why not? he said. If therefore some are members of the household to these people, but unknown to those, how will it not be necessary to judge the same people more worthy of trust than others? For you do not wish to affirm that members of the household and strangers are equally worthy of the same trust. <margin>G</margin> To me indeed, he said, it does not please. But if the same things are said in the same way by the same people, will some believe them while others think them not at all credible, and will neither be in error? This too would be absurd, he said. Then if members of the household and anyone else say the same things, how are the things said not similarly credible or similarly incredible? It is necessary, he said. Therefore, one must believe those saying the same things equally, since they say the same things.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> <note>The right column is the original Greek text corresponding to the Latin on the left.</note> If you were not behaving as is fitting and he was not persuaded, how could you justly charge him? I have nothing to say. Nor can you say that one should not attend to those who use things badly? Certainly, he said, at least this. But do those who do not behave as is fitting seem to you to use things badly? To me, he said. How then did he err if he did not attend to you when you were using things badly? It appears he did not, he said. Why then do men ever bring such charges against one another? And they blame those who did not persuade them for not being persuaded; but they do not charge themselves at all for not persuading them? And someone else present said, <margin>B</margin> For whenever someone uses someone well and helps him, and then, thinking himself worthy of being used in the same way, does not obtain it, how would such a person not reasonably find fault? Therefore, he said, the one whom he thinks should use him in the same way is either capable of using him well or is not; and if he is not capable, how can he reasonably expect what he is not capable of? But if he is capable, how did he not persuade such a man? Or how do those who say such things speak well? But by Zeus, he said, one should charge this so that he may use him better in the future, and so that other friends, hearing him find fault, may do the same. But do you think, he said, that people will use someone better by hearing one who speaks rightly and makes a claim, or one who errs? One who speaks rightly, he said. <margin>C</margin> But the one making a right claim seems not to know, he said. How then, hearing such a person finding fault, will they use him better? In no way, he said. For what reason then does one find fault in this way? He said he was at a loss. <margin>D</margin> How he accused the ignorance of a rustic <note>original: ἀγροίκου (agroikou) - meaning a boorish or unrefined person</note> because he trusted quickly and to whatever men were saying; for while it is reasonable to trust citizens and relatives, to trust such men as he had neither seen nor heard before (and this, as if being ignorant that most men are charlatans and wicked) was no small sign of silliness. <margin>E</margin> And one of those present said, I thought you were one who would blame both the quick and the random, thinking the slow to be worth much more. Indeed I do think so, he replied. Why then, he said, do you find fault if he trusts quickly and trusts those who happen to speak the truth? But I do not find fault with this, he said, but that he trusts quickly those who speak falsehoods. But if in more time and not to just anyone he had trusted and erred, would you not have blamed him more? I would, he said. Was it because he trusted slowly and not just anyone? By Zeus, no, he said. For I do not think, he said, you suppose a man is worthy of blame for this, but because he trusts those saying untrustworthy things. I do, he said. Which then, he said, will seem to you worthy of blame: trusting slowly and not just anyone, or the opposite, trusting quickly and just anyone? Not I, he said. Why then, he said, do you blame him? Because he errs regarding the examination, trusting quickly to whoever comes along. But if he had trusted slowly regarding the examination, would he not have erred? By Zeus, no, he said; but even so he would have erred no less. But I do not think one should trust just anyone. If you think one should not trust just anyone, he said, how is it fitting to trust strangers quickly? But do you not think one must first examine if they speak the truth? I do, he said. If they are relatives and associates, he said, is it not necessary to consider if they speak the truth? I would say so, he said. For perhaps some of these also say untrustworthy things. Very much so, he said. Why then is it more reasonable to trust relatives and associates than just anyone? I cannot say, he said. <margin>F</margin> What if it is no more necessary to trust relatives than just anyone, should we consider them more untrustworthy than anyone else? How not? he said. If then some are relatives to one person and strangers to another, how will it not be necessary for the same people to be considered more trustworthy to themselves? For you say one should not consider relatives and strangers equally trustworthy. It does not please me, he said. And similarly, he said, regarding the things said by them, some will trust and others will not; and will neither of them be in error? That too is absurd, he said. Then, he said, if relatives and strangers say the same things, how are the things said not equally to be trusted or untrusted? It is necessary, he said. Therefore, you must think that those saying the same things are to be trusted equally, since they say the same things. It is persuasive, he said. <margin>G</margin> While they were saying these things, I was at a loss as to how one should trust, and whom not; and whether to trust the trustworthy and those who know about what they speak, or relatives and acquaintances. Regarding these things, then, what do you think?

# SISYPHUS
# On Deliberation.

#### A DIALOGUE
#### considered spurious. <note>original: "nothus" / "νοθευόμενος". This indicates the work was traditionally attributed to Plato but doubted by scholars even in the Renaissance.</note>

->Translated by Sebastiano Corrado.<-

### SOCRATES and SISYPHUS.

<margin>A</margin>
**SOCRATES:** We waited for you for a long time yesterday, Sisyphus, at the demonstration by Stratonicus, so that you might listen along with us to a wise man who is always displaying many beautiful things in both word and deed. And when we thought you were no longer coming, we went off to the Lyceum ourselves. <margin>B</margin> **SISYPHUS:** By Zeus, Socrates, I had a certain business that was quite necessary, so much so that I could not neglect it. For our magistrates were deliberating yesterday, and they compelled me to act as their advisor. It is a law among us Pharsalians <note>Pharsalus was a city in Thessaly, Greece.</note> to obey the magistrates if they command any of us to advise them. **SOCRATES:** Well, it is a fine thing to obey the law, and especially to be judged a good counselor by one's fellow citizens—just as you are judged to be an excellent counselor, one of the best among the Pharsalians. But, Sisyphus, since we cannot have a full discussion about "good deliberation" <margin>C</margin> (for that would require much peace, leisure, and a long discourse), I would like to try to discuss with you what "deliberation" itself actually is. Could you tell me what deliberation is? I do not mean "good" or "bad" or "noble" deliberation, but just deliberation itself—what kind of thing is it? Or will you, being such a good counselor, recognize it quite easily? Or is it perhaps my own lack of experience that makes me ask you about this? **SISYPHUS:** Is it really unknown to you what deliberation is? **SOCRATES:** To me, yes, Sisyphus—unless it is something like this: when someone does not know the things they must do, <margin>D</margin> they guess and speak at random, hitting upon whatever happens to come to mind. It is like people playing "Odds or Evens" <note>original: "ἀρτιάζοντες" / "Par impar". A common ancient gambling game where one guesses if the number of objects held in a hand is odd or even.</note>; they know nothing about whether the things in their hands are odd or even, yet they sometimes succeed by chance, speaking the truth about them. Often, deliberation seems to be like that: someone who knows nothing about the matters they are deliberating on hits upon the truth by luck. If it is something like that, then I know what deliberation is; but if it is something else, I do not yet understand it. **SISYPHUS:** It is certainly not like that—not the speech of someone who knows absolutely nothing. Rather, it is like knowing part of the matter already, but not yet knowing the rest. **SOCRATES:** By the gods, <margin>E</margin> are you saying that deliberation is something like this? (For I seem to be guessing at your meaning regarding good deliberation.) Does it seem to you to be like a search to find the best course of action for oneself, when one does not yet know it clearly, but has it as a kind of thought in the mind? Is that not what you mean? **SISYPHUS:** I do. **SOCRATES:** And do people search for what they know, or for what they do not know? **SISYPHUS:** Both. **SOCRATES:** Do you mean that searching for both—what they know and what they do not know—is like this: if someone knows who Callistratus is, but does not know where he is to be found? He would not be searching for *who* Callistratus is, but for *where* he is. Is that how you mean <margin>F</margin> searching for "both"? **SISYPHUS:** I do. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, he would not be searching to know who Callistratus is, since he already knows that? **SISYPHUS:** Certainly not. **SOCRATES:** But he would be searching for where he is. **SISYPHUS:** So it seems to me. **SOCRATES:** But he wouldn't even be searching for where he is if he already knew it; he would have found him immediately. **SISYPHUS:** True. **SOCRATES:** So it appears people do not search for what they know, but for what they do not know. If this argument seems "eristic" <note>A style of argument focused on winning a debate through logical puzzles rather than finding truth.</note> to you, Sisyphus, and not spoken for the sake of the matter itself but only for the sake of talking, consider if it seems to be as I say. <margin>G</margin> Do you not know that this happens in geometry? Geometers are not ignorant of the line called the <term>diameter</term> <note>original: "διάμετρος". The diagonal of a figure.</note>—they do not search to find out *if* it is a diameter (for they do not seek to discover that), but rather how long it is in proportion to the sides of the areas it cuts through. Is that not what is sought concerning it? **SISYPHUS:** Exactly. **SOCRATES:** Because that is what is unknown, right? **SISYPHUS:** Quite so. **SOCRATES:** And what about the "doubling of the <term>cube</term>" <note>original: "κύβος". A famous mathematical problem of antiquity: constructing a cube with twice the volume of a given cube.</note>? You know geometers search for how large that is; they do not search to see if a cube is a cube, for they know that already. **SISYPHUS:** I know. **SOCRATES:** And do you not know that concerning the air, Anaxagoras and Empedocles and all the other <term>natural philosophers</term> <note>original: "μετεωρολόγους". Literally "those who study things in the air/heavens."</note> <margin>H</margin> searched to see if it is infinite or if it has a limit? **SISYPHUS:** I know that too. **SOCRATES:** But they were not searching for whether air exists or not. **SISYPHUS:** Certainly not. **SOCRATES:** Would you then agree with me that in all other things, no one searches for what they know, but rather for what they do not know? **SISYPHUS:** I would agree. **SOCRATES:** And did we not think that deliberation was this very thing: the act of...

<summary>Socrates and Sisyphus begin a dialogue on the definition of deliberation. Socrates argues that deliberation is a form of searching, and through various examples, they conclude that one only searches for what they do not know, rather than what they already possess knowledge of.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue "Sisyphus," traditionally attributed to Plato. Socrates is interrogating Sisyphus on the nature of "deliberation" (bouleuesthai) and whether it is possible to deliberate about things one does not already know.</meta>

# PLATO

<margin>A</margin>...effort, so that the best of those things which he thinks advantageous to himself might come about? <term>SISYPHUS.</term> <note>Abbreviated as SIS. in the Latin text.</note> It seemed so. <term>SOCRATES.</term> And to "inquire" into matters was the same as to "Deliberate," was it not? <term>SISYPHUS.</term> It certainly was. <term>SOCRATES.</term> We must therefore now consider what it is that can be an impediment to those who are inquiring, preventing them from finding the things they seek. <term>SISYPHUS.</term> So it seems to me we must do. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Shall we say it is anything else but ignorance that is the impediment? Therefore, with the greatest zeal—having "unrolled every cable" and "sent forth every utterance" <note>Socrates uses two proverbial expressions for making an all-out effort; original Latin: "omni rudente explicato, & omni voce missa."</note> as the saying goes—let us consider this: and first, weigh this now with me. Do you think it possible for a man to <margin>B</margin>deliberate about music if he is unskilled in music, and does not know how he ought to play the cithara, or do anything else that pertains to music? <term>SISYPHUS.</term> I certainly do not think so. <term>SOCRATES.</term> What do you say of the military or the nautical art? Do you believe that he who knows neither of these can deliberate whether he should do one of the two—lead soldiers or steer a ship—when he knows neither how to lead soldiers nor how to steer a ship? <term>SISYPHUS.</term> Not at all. <term>SOCRATES.</term> And do you judge the same regarding all other things: that what a man does not know, he can never truly understand, nor can it ever happen that a man deliberates about things he does not know? <term>SISYPHUS.</term> I do so judge. <term>SOCRATES.</term> But we said that "inquiring" is about things which one does not know, did we not? <term>SISYPHUS.</term> We certainly did. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Then "Inquiring" is no longer the same thing as "Deliberating." <term>SISYPHUS.</term> Why? <term>SOCRATES.</term> Because "Inquiring" is <margin>C</margin>concerned with those things which someone does not know; but "Deliberating" does not seem possible for a man regarding things he is ignorant of. Was it not said so? <term>SISYPHUS.</term> It was indeed. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Therefore, yesterday you were "inquiring" in order to find what was best for the State, but those very things you did not know. For if you had known them, you would not have inquired after them any longer, just as we do not inquire after any of the things we already know. Is it not so? <term>SISYPHUS.</term> It is so. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Which of the two, then, Sisyphus, do you think a man ought to do if he does not know: inquire, or learn? <term>SISYPHUS.</term> By Hercules, he should learn! <term>SOCRATES.</term> You are quite right. But do you think he should learn rather than inquire because one can find the answer more quickly and easily if he learns from <margin>D</margin>those who know, than if he inquires while being unskilled himself? Or for some other reason? <term>SISYPHUS.</term> No, for that reason. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Why then did you and the leaders of the city yesterday—rejecting the plan of deliberating about things you did not know and inquiring what was best for the State to do—not learn from someone who knows by what means you could do what was best for the State? Instead (as it seems to me), you sat the whole of yesterday devising and "divining" <note>original Latin: "ariolantes," suggesting they were guessing or acting like soothsayers rather than using logic.</note> about things you did not know, utterly neglecting the zeal for learning. Perhaps you will say these things were said by me only for the sake of dispute, as a joke, and not demonstrated seriously; but I pray you, Sisyphus, attend to this now diligently. <margin>E</margin>If it be granted that "Deliberating" is something, and that it is not what we are now saying—that it seems to be nothing other than knowledge, guesswork, and fabrication, though it uses a more solemn name—do you think that in deliberating well and showing themselves to be good counselors, some men differ from others, just as in all other disciplines some differ from others? Builders from builders, physicians from physicians, flute-players from flute-players? And as all other craftsmen are themselves unlike one another in their own arts, do you think that in deliberating, too, some men differ from others? <term>SISYPHUS.</term> I certainly do. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Tell me: do not <margin>F</margin>all men, both those who deliberate well and those who deliberate poorly, deliberate about future things? <term>SISYPHUS.</term> Most certainly. <term>SOCRATES.</term> What else can we say here, except that future things do not yet exist? <term>SISYPHUS.</term> Nothing else. <term>SOCRATES.</term> For if they existed, they would no longer be "future," but would already be. Is it not so? <term>SISYPHUS.</term> Truly. <term>SOCRATES.</term> If therefore they are in no way existing, by the same reasoning they have not been made, since they do not exist. <term>SISYPHUS.</term> By Hercules, no. <term>SOCRATES.</term> If then they have not yet been made, they have as yet no nature that is their own. <term>SISYPHUS.</term> None at all. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Is it not then the case that all who deliberate, whether well or poorly, deliberate about things which neither are, nor have been, nor have any nature, since they deliberate about the future? <term>SISYPHUS.</term> So they seem. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Does it <margin>G</margin>then seem possible for someone to hit upon <note>original Latin: "consequatur," to reach or attain.</note> that which is nowhere? <term>SISYPHUS.</term> In what way do you mean this? <term>SOCRATES.</term> I will explain to you what I wish to say; give me your attention. Out of many archers, how would you know who is skilled and who, on the contrary, is unskilled? This indeed seems not difficult to know. For perhaps you would bid them aim their arrows at a mark <note>original Latin: "skopon" (from Greek σκοπός), a target.</note>; would you not? <term>SISYPHUS.</term> Certainly. <term>SOCRATES.</term> You would then judge him the winner who most often shoots his arrows so that he aims straight. <term>SISYPHUS.</term> I would certainly so judge. <term>SOCRATES.</term> But if no mark were set up at which they might direct their arrows, but each shot wherever <margin>H</margin>he wished, in what way could you know who shoots well or poorly? <term>SISYPHUS.</term> In no way. <term>SOCRATES.</term> So also with those deliberating well or poorly: if they do not know what they are deliberating about, you would not know how to distinguish them. <term>SISYPHUS.</term> True. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Certainly true: for if those deliberating deliberate about future things, do they not deliberate about things that are not? <term>SISYPHUS.</term> Entirely so. <term>SOCRATES.</term> But it is not possible for someone to hit upon that which is nowhere. For by what reason could it seem to you that someone could reach what is nowhere? <term>SISYPHUS.</term> By none. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Since therefore...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>...inquiring how to find the best things, would he not always need to differ from himself? <term>SISYPHUS.</term> Yes. <term>SOCRATES.</term> And "inquiring" is what "deliberating" was concerning matters. Is it not? <term>SISYPHUS.</term> Quite so. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Therefore we must still consider now what is an impediment to those who are always inquiring into whatever they make inquiries about, so as to find it. <term>SISYPHUS.</term> So it seems to me. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Should we say anything else is an impediment to them than ignorance? Let us consider, by Zeus, as the saying goes, "letting out every reef" and "letting out every voice." Look at this with me: do you think it possible for a man to deliberate about music who is not knowledgeable about music, nor how he should play the cithara, or any other thing of those done in music? <margin>B</margin><term>SISYPHUS.</term> Not I. <term>SOCRATES.</term> What then? About generalship or navigation? Do you think one who knows neither of these could have anything to deliberate about one or the other, or what he should do? Either to act as a general or a pilot, when he himself knows neither how to lead an army nor how to steer a ship? <term>SISYPHUS.</term> No. <term>SOCRATES.</term> And do you think it is this way concerning all other things: that whenever one is not knowledgeable, he knows nothing, not even a little, about all the things he is not knowledgeable about? <term>SISYPHUS.</term> I do. <term>SOCRATES.</term> But does one always inquire about what he is not knowledgeable of? <term>SISYPHUS.</term> Quite so. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Then would "inquiring" still be the same as "deliberating"? <term>SISYPHUS.</term> How so? <term>SOCRATES.</term> Because "inquiring" is about what one does not know—those things of which one is not knowledgeable—but "deliberating," it does not seem to me, can be <margin>C</margin>about those things for a man, if he is not knowledgeable. Or was it not said so? <term>SISYPHUS.</term> Certainly. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Therefore you were inquiring yesterday to find the best things for the city, not knowing them. For if you had known them, you would not still have been inquiring after them. Just as we do not inquire after anything else that we know. Is it not so? <term>SISYPHUS.</term> It is not. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Which then seems useful to you, Sisyphus: if one does not know, to inquire or to learn? <term>SISYPHUS.</term> To learn, for my part, by Zeus. <term>SOCRATES.</term> You are right. But does it seem to you that one must learn rather than inquire because one would find out faster and more easily if he learned from those who know, than if he who does not know inquired himself? Or for some other reason? <term>SISYPHUS.</term> No, but for this reason. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Why then, neglecting this yesterday, did you <margin>D</margin>deliberate about what you did not know, and inquire to find the best things in the city, instead of learning from those who know how you might be able to accomplish the best things in the city? But you seemed to me to sit the whole day yesterday improvising and "prophesying" <note>original Greek: "apomanteuomenoi," guessing like an oracle.</note> about what you did not know, neglecting to learn—both the rulers of the city and you with them. Perhaps you might say these things were played by me to tease you, for the sake of the argument only, and not demonstrated seriously. But look at this, Sisyphus, consider it now: if "deliberating" were something, and not as it now seems to be nothing other than knowledge and conjecture and improvisation—using only a more <margin>E</margin>solemn name, but nothing else—do you think some would differ from others in deliberating well and being good counselors, just as in all other sciences some differ from others? Builders from builders, doctors from doctors, flute-players from flute-players, and all other craftsmen differ from one another? Just as these men in these arts differ, do you think in deliberating too some would differ from others? <term>SISYPHUS.</term> I do. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Tell me then: do not all who deliberate well and those who deliberate badly, deliberate about certain things that are going to be in the future? <term>SISYPHUS.</term> Quite so. <term>SOCRATES.</term> But things in the future do not yet exist? <term>SISYPHUS.</term> Certainly not. <term>SOCRATES.</term> For if they existed, they would no longer be "going to be," but would be already. Is it not so? <term>SISYPHUS.</term> Yes. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Therefore, if they do not exist in any way, then they have not happened, being non-existent? <term>SISYPHUS.</term> No. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Therefore if they have not yet happened, they do not yet have any nature of their own. <term>SISYPHUS.</term> Certainly not. <term>SOCRATES.</term> But where something does not exist, both he who deliberates well and he who deliberates badly, all deliberate <margin>F</margin>about things that are departing, neither being nor having happened, nor having any nature, whenever they deliberate about future things? <term>SISYPHUS.</term> They seem to. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Does it seem possible to you for anyone to hit upon that which does not exist, either well or badly? <term>SISYPHUS.</term> How do you mean this? <term>SOCRATES.</term> I will tell you what I want to say. Consider: how would you distinguish among many archers who was the good one and who the bad? Or is this not difficult to know? For perhaps <margin>G</margin>you would bid them shoot at a certain mark. Is it not so? <term>SISYPHUS.</term> Quite so. <term>SOCRATES.</term> And the one hitting the mark most often and straightest, you would judge to be the winner? <term>SISYPHUS.</term> I would. <term>SOCRATES.</term> But if no mark were set for them to shoot at, but each shot as he wished, how would you distinguish the one shooting well or badly? <term>SISYPHUS.</term> In no way. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Therefore, those who wish to deliberate either well or badly, if they did not know what they were deliberating about, you would be at a loss to distinguish them? <term>SISYPHUS.</term> I would. <term>SOCRATES.</term> Therefore, if those who deliberate are deliberating about future things that will be, are they deliberating about things that are not? <term>SISYPHUS.</term> Quite so. <term>SOCRATES.</term> <margin>H</margin>Therefore, it is not possible for anyone to hit upon what is not...

<summary>Socrates argues that "deliberation" is impossible regarding things one does not know, suggesting that learning from experts is superior to the "guessing" practiced by politicians. He uses an analogy of archers shooting at a non-existent target to show that one cannot "aim" at the non-existent future.</summary>

### Translated by Sebastiano Corrado.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'E' showing a man in a scholar's cap and robe sitting in a high-backed chair at a desk, likely writing.</image-desc>
IT happened by chance that I and Eryxias of Steiria were walking in the Portico of Zeus the Deliverer, when Critias and Erasistratus (the son of Phaeax and nephew of the famous Erasistratus) came up to us. Erasistratus, who had then recently arrived from Sicily and those parts, approached and said, "Greetings, Socrates!" And I replied,
<margin>D</margin> "Greetings to you as well. Do you bring us any news from Sicily? Do you have anything fine to report to us?" "Very much so," he said, "but if you like, shall we first sit down? For I am tired from the journey, having walked from Megara yesterday." "By all means, if it seems best." "What then," he asked, "do you wish to hear first of the things there? Whether it be what the Sicilians are doing, or how they are disposed toward our city? For they seem to me to be affected toward us just like wasps: which, if one provokes them even slightly, become invincible until someone attacks and utterly destroys them. So too are the Syracusans disposed. Unless someone sets out to wage a great war there with a very large fleet, that city will never come under our hand or power; rather, they will be provoked by these small fleets so as to become most troublesome to us. And now
<margin>E</margin> they have sent ambassadors to us, with the intention (as it seems to me) of deceiving our city." Meanwhile, as we were talking, the Syracusan ambassadors themselves happened to pass by. Whereupon Erasistratus, pointing out one of them, said, "That man there, Socrates, is the wealthiest of all the Sicilians and Italians." "And how could he not be," he continued, "since he possesses land so extensive that it provides the means, should anyone wish, to practice agriculture far and wide? And it is of such a quality as could not easily be found elsewhere in all of Greece. Moreover, he has all the other things that pertain to wealth: slaves, horses, gold, and silver." Seeing him
<margin>F</margin> led on as if he were about to say more regarding the man's riches, I asked: "What, Erasistratus? What sort of man does he seem to be in Sicily?" He replied, "He seems to be, and indeed is, as much the most wicked of all the Sicilians and Italians as he is the wealthiest. So much so, that if you were to ask any Sicilian whom he considers the most wicked and the wealthiest, no one would name anyone but him." Thinking that he was speaking not of small matters, but of those which seem greatest—virtue and wealth—I asked whether he thought a man was wealthier who had two talents of silver, or one who had a field valued at two talents. "The one who has the field, I think," he said. "By the same
<margin>G</margin> reasoning," I said, "if someone has cloaks, or rugs, or other things worth more than what that stranger possesses, he would be wealthier." He agreed to this as well. "But if someone gave you a choice of these, which would you want?" "That which is worth the most," he said. "In which way would you believe yourself to be wealthier?" "In that way." "Now then, it seems to us that whoever possesses what is worth the most is to be considered the wealthiest." "It seems so," he said. "Therefore," I said, "the healthy are wealthier than the sick, if indeed health is a possession worth more than the money of the sick. For there is no one who would not prefer to be in good health while possessing little silver, rather than to be sick while possessing the riches of the Great King <note>A common reference to the King of Persia, the archetype of extreme wealth.</note>; clearly indicating that he values health more. For he would not choose it unless he considered it of greater price than money." "Certainly not." "If, then, it should appear that there is something else
<margin>H</margin> worth more than health, would he who possesses that be the wealthiest?" "Certainly." "But if someone were to come up to us now and ask: 'O Socrates, Eryxias, and Erasistratus, can you tell me what is the most valuable possession for a man?' Is it that which the possessor..."

# OF PLATO

...deliberate best, by what means he might most advantageously manage both his own affairs and those
<margin>A</margin> of his friends? What shall we say this is? To me indeed, O Socrates, it seems that happiness <note>original: *felicitas* / *eudaimonia*</note> is of the greatest value to a man. And not badly put, I said: but can we consider those men the happiest who act the best? We can, in my judgment. Do not those, then, act best who sin the least against themselves and against other men, and who conduct most things rightly? Most certainly. Do not those, then, who know both good and evil, and what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, have the power to conduct affairs most rightly and sin the least? He conceded this too.
<margin>B</margin> Now it altogether appears to us that the same men are the wisest, and those who act best, and the happiest, and the wealthiest, if indeed wisdom appears to be of the greatest value. So be it, said Erasistratus, interrupting: but what utility would there be for a man, O Socrates, even if he were wiser than Nestor <note>A legendary Greek king known for his great wisdom and longevity</note>, if he did not have the necessities for living—food, drink, clothing, and other things of this sort? How could wisdom be of use here? Or in what way would he be the wealthiest, whom nothing prevents from begging, and to whom none of the necessities are supplied? Here he seemed to say something significant. But, I said, would he who possesses wisdom, if he were in need of these things, suffer what you say? Whereas if someone possessed the house of Pulytio <note>A wealthy Athenian whose house was famously luxurious</note>, and the house
<margin>C</margin> were full of gold and silver, would he stand in need of nothing? But, he said, nothing prevents him from immediately selling his possessions in such a way that, in exchange for what he owns, he might have either those very things needed for sustenance, or money with which he could procure the same for himself, and thus abound in all things at once. That may be so, I said, if indeed it happens that there are men who would rather have a house of this sort than that man's wisdom. But if there are those who value a man's wisdom and what proceeds from it more highly, will he not be able to "sell" much more advantageously if he lacks something and wishes to sell his wisdom and its works? For while the use of a house is
<margin>D</margin> great and necessary, and the comforts pertaining to life are great for a man if he dwells in such a house rather than in a small and mean hut; yet the use of wisdom seems to be of little value, and its comforts small—whether you are wise or ignorant <gloss>to be</gloss>—because men not only do not wish to buy it, but even despise it. Yet many, as if in want, desire and gladly buy cypress wood, which serves as an ornament for a house, and Pentelic marble <note>High-quality marble from Mount Pentelicus near Athens</note>. If, therefore, there were a skilled pilot, or a physician who could practice his art well and beautifully, or any other such art, would he not be more valuable and more saleable than any of these things held as great riches?
<margin>E</margin> But he who is able to deliberate well for himself and for another, and determine in what way he may act best—will he not be able to sell this very thing, if he wishes? But Eryxias, interrupting and looking askance as if he had been wronged, said: You, Socrates, if you had to speak the truth, would you say you are wealthier than Callias the son of Hipponicus? <note>Callias was famously the richest man in Athens</note>. And although you would claim to be less ignorant—but rather wiser—in none of the greatest matters, yet for all that you would be no wealthier. Perhaps, I said, you think these discourses we are now sharing are a game; because you do not truly think things are as they are said to be, but rather that they are like a game of draughts <note>A board game similar to checkers</note>, where he who moves the pieces can easily defeat his fellow players so that they no longer have anything to object against him. Perhaps, I said, you also think the same about the wealthy: that the matter is not as it is said, but that there are certain discourses of this kind
<margin>F</margin> which are no more true than false; and that a man who speaks them might so circumvent his adversaries as to persuade them that those who are wisest are also the wealthiest among us, and this while he himself is lying and they are speaking the truth. Indeed, perhaps it is no wonder if this is very much as if two men were disputing about letters: and one contended that 'S' was the first letter in 'Socrates,' while the other contended it was 'A.' Which one's speech would have more reason: his who says 'A,' or his who wants 'S' to be the beginning? Then Eryxias, laughing and blushing at the same time, and looking around at those present as if he himself had not been part of what was said before: I, he said, O Socrates, did not think we ought to have those
<margin>G</margin> discourses which neither benefit the speaker nor can persuade anyone present. For what mortal who is at least sane could ever be persuaded that those who are wisest are the wealthiest among us? But rather, since we are discussing the acquisition of wealth, we should show from where it may be done honorably, and whether it is a good or an evil. Let it be so, I said, as you say. We shall act more cautiously hereafter. And by Hercules, you do well to warn us. But you yourself, who introduce a new discourse and who think what was said before pertains nothing to the matter, why do you not proceed to say whether acquiring wealth seems to be a good or an evil?
<margin>H</margin> To me indeed, he said, acquiring wealth seems to be a good. While he was still wishing to say something more, Critias interrupted and asked: Tell me, Eryxias, do you think acquiring wealth is a good? I would be insane, he said, if I thought otherwise; for I think there is no one who would not...

# ERYXIAS

<margin>A</margin> These things were agreed upon. "And yet," said the other, "I think there is no one I could not bring to agree with me that for some people, being wealthy is an evil. For if you thought that a person who does no good was 'good,' we would not call him so. If I grant that I will listen to you, try again to address those who differ on this point: which of you speaks more truly on all matters, such as how one should ride a horse. If he himself said he was a capable horseman, I would try to stop your disagreement myself; (for I would feel ashamed if, being present and able, I did not prevent you from quarreling; or if by some divine luck you were so at odds that you were no more likely to agree than to part as enemies instead of friends). <margin>B</margin> But now, since you happen to be disagreeing about a matter that one must deal with throughout one's whole life, and it makes a great difference whether one should care for this as something useful or not—and these are not trivial matters, but what seem to be the greatest to the Greeks. (At least, fathers first exhort their sons to this as soon as they reach the age where they seem to have sense: to look for where they shall get riches. For if you have something, you are worth something; if not, you are nothing.) If, then, this is pursued so earnestly, and you agree on other things but differ on this great matter—and further, you differ on whether being wealthy is always an evil or a good, not whether it is black or white, nor light or heavy, but whether it is bad or good—you might especially fall into enmity if you disagree about good and evil. <margin>C</margin> Since you are the greatest of friends and associates, I, as far as it was in my power, was not going to let you remain at odds with one another. But if I were not able myself, I would tell you how to handle the disagreement. Now, since I do not happen to be able, and each of you thinks he is able to bring the other to agreement, I am ready to assist as much as I can, so that we may agree on how the matter stands. You then," I said, "Critias, try to make us agree, as you promised." "Well," he said, "I would like to ask Eryxias, just as I began, whether he thinks there are just and unjust men." "By Zeus," he replied, "most certainly." <margin>D</margin> "What then? Does acting unjustly seem to you to be an evil or a good?" "An evil to me." "Would a man seem to you to act unjustly if he seduces his neighbors' wives for money, even if neither the city nor the laws prevent it?" "He would seem to me to act unjustly." "Therefore," he said, "if the unjust man who wishes to do wrong happens to be wealthy and can spend money, he would sin; but if the man is not wealthy, so that he does not have the means to spend, he would not be able to commit the sins he wishes; therefore he would not sin. For this reason, it would be more profitable for the man not to be wealthy, if he will thus less often achieve what he wishes. And he wishes for wicked things. And again, <margin>E</margin> would you say that being sick is an evil or a good?" "An evil, I say." "What then? Do some people seem to you to be lacking in self-control <term>akrateis: those who lack mastery over their desires</term>?" "To me, yes." "Therefore, if it would be better for this man's health to abstain from food and drink and other things that seem pleasant, but he is a slave to them; if he lacks self-control, would it not be better for this man not to have the means to provide these things, rather than to have a great abundance? For in truth, he would then have no power to sin, even if he very much wanted to." Thus Critias seemed to have argued very well and beautifully, so that if Eryxias had not been mindful of those present, <margin>F</margin> nothing would have stopped him from getting up and striking Critias; it became so clear to him through this questioning that he had not correctly judged the matter of being wealthy at first. Perceiving that Eryxias was in such a state, and taking care lest the reproach and contention go any further, I said, "A wise man, Prodicus of Ceos, once told this same false story in the Lyceum <note>The Lyceum was a public gymnasium in Athens, later famous as the site of Aristotle's school</note>; he seemed to those present to be talking such nonsense that no one could be persuaded he was speaking the truth. And indeed, a certain very young and clever youth, sitting nearby, began to mock and jeer at him, and even to goad him, wanting to get an explanation of what he was saying. And in this, he won much more approval from the listeners than <margin>G</margin> Prodicus did." "Could you," said Erasistratus, "report that conversation to us?" "Certainly, if I can remember it. It went something like this, I think. First, the youth asked him in what way he thought being wealthy was an evil, and in what way a good. And he, replying just as you did now, said: to the noble and good among men, it is a good; and to those who know how to use money where they ought, it is a good; but to the wicked and ignorant, it is an evil. And he said other things are the same way. For whatever the users are like, such must the things necessarily be to them. <margin>H</margin> And he said the saying of Archilochus <note>A Greek lyric poet</note> was well made: 'And they think such things as the deeds they encounter.' 'Now then,' said the youth, 'if someone were to make me wise with that wisdom by which good men are wise, it would be necessary that he also make other things good for me at the same time, even if he did nothing to those things themselves, but because he made me wise instead of ignorant.'"

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> <note>The Latin column mirrors the Greek text above, providing a Renaissance-era translation of the Socratic dialogue.</note> ...that there is no one who would not affirm the same. "I also think," said the other, "that there is no one I could not induce to feel as I do: that for certain men, it is an evil to acquire riches. For if it were entirely a good, it would certainly never appear manifest that it is an evil for some of us." Then I said to them: "If you were to differ about this, which of you spoke more truly about the study of horsemanship—that is, in what way one rides best—and I were skilled in this matter, I would ask you to put an end to the dissension. For I would be ashamed if, being present, I did not prohibit you from contention to the best of my ability; or if, contending over some other matter, you were to become enemies instead of friends <margin>B</margin> because you did not agree on that same matter. But now, since you contend over that which is necessary to use throughout all of life, and it matters greatly whether that thing should be cared for as useful or useless—and these things seem to the Greeks to be not small, but the greatest of all: since fathers first command this to their sons, that as soon as they reach that age in which they seem to understand for themselves, they should then look about for where they can become rich: because if you have something, you flourish; if nothing, you lie low. Since these things, I say, are so greatly sought after, yet you, while agreeing on other things, differ on this so great a matter, and moreover disagree about acquiring riches: and you do not disagree whether <margin>C</margin> acquiring riches is black or white, nor whether it is light or heavy, but whether it is evil or good, and indeed in such a way that you seem likely to take up enmities between you if you persevere in contending about evils and goods, and that very thing when you are both the closest of friends and kinsmen. I, therefore, as much as is in me, would not neglect it, nor permit you to be discordant among yourselves, if I could say wise things: how the matter stands, so as to recall you from dissension. But now, since I cannot provide that myself, and each of you thinks he can induce the other to agree, I am prepared to help as much as I can, so that at last it may be agreed between you how <margin>D</margin> the matter stands. You therefore," I said, "Critias, proceed, as you have professed, to make us agree." "But gladly," he said, "I would interrogate this Eryxias, as I began, whether men seem to him to be just and unjust." "They certainly seem so," he said, "and very much so." "What then of acting unjustly? Does it seem to you to be an evil or a good?" "An evil." "A man who corrupts the wives of his neighbors with money and debauchery, and that very thing against the customs of the city and the laws—does he seem to you to act unjustly or not?" "To act unjustly." "An unjust and covetous man, therefore," he said, "if he be rich and can spend money, easily sins; but if he be not rich, nor has the means to spend, he cannot so easily <margin>E</margin> perform what he desires, and for that reason he sins less. Whence it happens that it is more expedient for a man not to be rich, if indeed he will accomplish less of what he desires, especially when he desires shamefully. Furthermore, would you say that being sick is an evil or a good?" "An evil." "What? Do not certain men seem to be intemperate?" "They do." "If therefore it becomes better for such a man, for the sake of his health, to abstain from food and drink and other things which are thought pleasant, and he cannot do so because of intemperance, it becomes altogether more useful for him not to have the means wherewith these are supplied, than for there to be a great abundance of necessary things: for thus he has no <margin>F</margin> faculty for sinning, not even if he very much wants to." Thus Critias seemed to discourse well and beautifully. Wherefore Eryxias, had he not feared those who were present, thought himself deprived of some great thing, after he clearly perceived that he had not previously felt correctly about acquiring riches. But I, when I had recognized Eryxias was so affected, taking care lest some greater reproach and contention should arise: "This discourse," I said, "the wise man Prodicus of Ceos, when he held it a little while ago in the Lyceum, seemed to those who were present to be such nonsense that none of them could be induced to believe he spoke the truth. Indeed, there approached him <margin>G</margin> a certain very young and witty youth, who, when he had sat nearby, began to deride and mock him, and soon even to provoke him, wishing to receive from him an account of those things which he was saying. In which matter that youth obtained much more praise from the listeners than Prodicus. "Could you relate that discourse to us?" said Erasistratus. "I could indeed, if I recall it to memory. Now the matter, as I judge, was thus. The youth asked him: in what way at last he thought acquiring riches was an evil and a good. Then he, replying in the same way as you do now, said: to honorable and good men, and to those who know where it is necessary to use coins, it is a good; but to the wicked, and to those who know not <margin>H</margin> how to use them, an evil. 'But other things,' he said, 'are also thus. For such as are those who use them, such also must the things be to them.' 'Nobly indeed,' he said, 'it seems to me Archilochus sang that: "Such things they think, as the heights they hold."' 'Now truly,' said the youth, 'if someone should make me wise with that wisdom by which good men are wise, it would become necessary that he at the same time...'"

<summary>This page features a Socratic dialogue (the Eryxias) debating whether wealth is inherently good or evil, concluding that its value depends entirely on the virtue and wisdom of the person using it. Critias argues that for an unjust or intemperate person, poverty is actually better because it limits their ability to do harm.</summary>

"For even if," I said, "you often come into the city in haste, make vows, and seek from the Gods that they give you good things, you do not know, however, whether they are able to give what you seek: just as if, proceeding to the door of a Grammarian, you should ask that he hand over to you the science of Grammar, when you have previously labored nothing in it, but wish, by learning it immediately,

In that way, perhaps, those who were present were affected toward you and Prodicus: and they considered him a sophist <note>A paid teacher of philosophy and rhetoric, often viewed with suspicion in Athens.</note> and too arrogant, but you a statesman <note>original: *politicon*</note> and a man to be highly valued. For after it has been granted that to acquire riches is good for some, but bad for others, it remains to consider what wealth itself is. For unless you first know this, you will never be able to agree whether it is bad or good. I indeed, as much as I am able, am prepared to weigh the matter together with you. Therefore, let him who thinks that acquiring riches is good tell us what that very thing is."

Then they use it thus sealed: and he who has the most of these coins seems to have the most money and to be the wealthiest. But if someone among us possessed the most coins of this kind, he would be no more rich than if he had many pebbles from those which are in the mountains. The Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans.</note> use currency made of that iron which is useless: and he who possesses a great weight of this kind of iron seems to be rich; which thing elsewhere is of no value. In Ethiopia they use engraved stones, which a Laconian <note>A Spartan.</note> could use for nothing.
