<meta>This page continues the dialogue "Eryxias" (attributed to Plato), specifically discussing the definition of wealth and utility across different cultures.</meta>

# ERYXIAS

<margin>A</margin> In Ethiopia, they use engraved stones, which a Laconian <note>A Spartan</note> man would find no use for. Among the nomadic Scythians, if someone were to possess a house made of clay, he would seem no wealthier than if one of us possessed Mount Lycabettus. It is clear, then, that each of these things are only "possessions" if the owners appear wealthier because of them. But I said: each of these things are indeed money to some, and those who possess them are rich; yet to others, they are neither money, nor are the owners wealthier because of them. Just as things are not "noble" or "shameful" to everyone alike, but differ from person to person. If we wish to investigate why it is that to the <margin>B</margin> Scythians, houses are not considered money, but they are to us; or why to the Carthaginians, leather skins are money, but not to us; or why to the Lacedaemonians, iron is money, but not to us—could we not find the answer most easily this way? If someone at Athens possessed a thousand talents' weight of those stones from the marketplace which we never use, would he be considered any wealthier because of it? It does not seem so to me. But if he possessed a thousand talents of Lychnite stone <note>A high-quality Parian marble used for sculpture</note>, we would say he was very rich indeed? Certainly. Is it then, I asked, because the latter is useful to us, while the former is useless? <margin>C</margin> Yes. Therefore, among the Scythians, houses are not money for this reason: they have no use for a house. A Scythian man would not welcome the most beautiful house any more than a <term>sisyra</term> <note>original: σισύρα; a thick cloak made of animal skins or goat hair</note>, because the cloak is useful to him and the house is useless. Again, do we think Carthaginian currency is money to us? It is not, for we cannot use it to acquire the things we need, as we do with silver. Thus, it would be useless to us. It seems so. Therefore, whatever things happen to be useful to us, these are money; but the useless things are not money. How then, Socrates (interrupted Eryxias), is it that we use conversation with one another, and even harming one another, and many other things? Would these then be money to us? For they certainly appear to be useful. It would seem so to us, whatever money actually is. For it was agreed that things must be useful to us if they are to be money; but what *kind* of useful things, since not all are? Come then, let us pursue it <margin>D</margin> this way again: is it not better to define what we use money for, and for what purpose the possession of money was invented, just as medicine was invented for the removal of diseases? Perhaps in this way the matter might become clearer to us. Since it appears necessary that all things which are money must also be useful, and that money is a certain *kind* of useful thing, it remains to consider: for what specific use is money useful? For perhaps all things we use for work are useful, just as all things possessing a soul are animals, yet we call a certain kind of animal "Man." <margin>E</margin> If someone were to ask us: what could be removed from us so that we would have no need for medicine or its practice? We could say that if diseases were removed from the body and did not occur at all, we would be rid of that practice. Thus, it seems, medicine is the science useful for this: the removal of diseases. If someone asked us again: what could be removed so that we would have no need for money, could we say? If not, let us look at it this way: Come, if a man could live without food and drink, never hungering or thirsting, would he have any need for these things, or for silver, or for anything else to procure them? It does not seem so to me. Therefore, the same applies to other things: if we did not need those things for the care of the body which we now lack—warmth, or cold at times, and all the other things the body requires—what is called "money" would be useless to us. If no one needed any of the things for which we desire money, we would not want it. We want it so we can satisfy the desires and needs of the body as they arise. If, then, the possession of money is useful for this—the care of the body's needs—if this were taken away from our midst, we would have no need for money; perhaps it would not even exist as money at all. It appears so. It appears then (as it seems) that those things useful for this specific service are what we call money. But this little argument greatly disturbed him. So I said: What about this? Can the same thing be useful for the same task at one time, and useless at another? I would not say so, he replied; but if we need it for the task, it seems useful; if not, then not. Therefore, if we were able to make a bronze statue without fire, we would have no need of fire for that task;

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> <note>The following is the Latin translation of the Greek text above</note> ...than if he possessed Lycabettus among us. From this it becomes plain that these individual things are not to be numbered among riches, since it is established that some who possess them are no richer because of it. But, I said, these individual things are indeed money to some, and those who hold them are wealthy; but to others they are neither money, nor are those who possess them richer because of it: just as things are not honorable or base to everyone in the same way, but differ for different people. For if we wish to inquire what it is, finally, why houses (which are precious to us) are not counted among riches by the Scythians; and to us, on the contrary, <margin>B</margin> skins (which are money to the Carthaginians) or iron (which the Lacedaemonians use as a coin) are valued more cheaply: can we not find this out easily and immediately? If someone at Athens possessed a thousand pounds of those stones which are in the forum, and which we use for no purpose, would he be thought any richer because of this? Not to me, indeed. But if he had a thousand pounds of Lychnite stone, we would say he was very rich. Exactly. For this reason surely, I say, because this is useful, but those others are useless to us. Certainly. For to the Scythians also, houses are not held among their wealth for this reason: that there is no utility in a house for them. Nor indeed would a Scythian man <margin>C</margin> value a most beautiful house more than a garment made of goat skins, which is called a <term>sisyra</term> <note>original: σισύρα</note>: because he thinks there is much utility for him in the latter, and none in the former. Nor do we place Carthaginian coins among our money. For we cannot, as with silver, import or export the things we need with it. Therefore it must be useless to us. <margin>What is money</margin> It is similar. Therefore, those things which are of use to us are to be called money, prepared for the necessary uses of life; whatever, on the contrary, is not of use, should certainly not be called money. How can this be, O Socrates? said Eryxias, interrupting: Do we not sometimes use disputation, and offense, and many other such things among ourselves? Are these also money to us (for they clearly seem to be of use)? <margin>D</margin> Therefore, I said, by this reasoning it has not been declared to us what money properly is. For that it must be of use, if it is to be money, is granted by almost everyone: but which things among those we use are money, since they are not all so, has not yet been sufficiently said. Therefore, come now, let us first see this. Can what we seek be found more easily if we pursue it again this way, and inquire: what is that thing for which we use money, and for what was the possession of money invented? Just as medicine was invented for driving away diseases? For thus perhaps the matter will become more easily manifest to us. Since it appears necessary that all things <margin>E</margin> which are money are also of use: and that among things which are of use, those we call money are a certain kind: it remains that we perceive in what thing especially money is of use. For all things which we use for some work are of use: just as all things that have a soul are animals, but we call a certain kind of animal "Man." If someone should now ask us: what thing being removed from us, we would need neither medicine nor its instruments? We could say: if diseases were removed from bodies <margin>F</margin> and never arose at all; or if they did arise, but immediately went away. For medicine is, as it seems, the science which is of use to us for driving away diseases. So again he might ask us: what being taken away from us, we would not need money? Could we say? But if we cannot say, let us consider it again this way: Come, if a man could live without food and drink, so that he never hungered nor thirsted, would he sometimes need either these very things, or silver, or any other thing to procure them for himself? Not to me, indeed. Therefore, I said, the same would happen in other things, if we did not need those things for the care of the body which we are now lacking—both heat and cold at times, and other things which the body, since it is born needy, must necessarily lack. For what are called money would not be of use to us, if man lacked absolutely none of those things for whose sake we desire to have money, so that we might be able to supply the desires and necessities of the body with those things we frequently lack. But if man is in need, the possession of money is of use to him for the care of the body. But if this were driven from our midst, as we say, we would not need money, and perhaps there would be no money at all. It appears so. It appears also, as it seems, that those things which are useful for that same business are money to us. But this little argument greatly...

---

...disturbed him. Wherefore I said: What? Can we not say it is possible for the same thing to be useful at one time for the same action, and useless at another? I would not say so, he said; but if we need a certain thing for the same action, it seems useful to me; but if we do not need it, it is useless. If therefore, I said, we could make a bronze statue without fire, we would not need fire to make it; and if we did not need it, it would not be useful; and the same reasoning can be said of other things. It is agreed. Nothing therefore seems useful to us without which something can be done. Nothing. If we therefore, without silver and gold and other such things—which we do not use for the care of the body in the same way as food, drink, clothes, bedding, and houses—could satisfy the body's desires and needs...

<summary>Socrates and Eryxias debate the definition of money, concluding that wealth is relative to cultural utility and that "money" only exists to satisfy bodily needs that cannot be met otherwise.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from the pseudo-Platonic work *Eryxias*, a Socratic discussion on the nature of wealth and utility. Socrates is debating with Critias about whether money has intrinsic value or if its value is derived solely from its use and the knowledge of how to use it.</meta>

# OF PLATO

<margin>Argument against 4</margin>
<margin>A</margin> ...to settle our needs in such a way that we required nothing further, then neither silver, nor gold, nor other things of this kind would seem to be money to us, insofar as this could be achieved without them. They would not. Therefore, I said, if these things are of no use, they cannot seem to be money to us; rather, those things must be money by which we are able to procure the things that are useful. Never, Socrates, he said, could I be led to believe that gold, silver, and other things of that kind are not money to us. I am certainly firmly persuaded of this: that things which are useless to us are not money, and conversely, things which are useful ought to be counted among those forms of money that are most beneficial. But I will never allow myself to be persuaded that these things we just mentioned are not useful to us for the needs of life, since by them we
<margin>B</margin> procure the necessities for living. Come now, what shall we say about these matters? Are there not men who teach Music or letters, or transmit some other branch of knowledge, and who, by demanding a fee for these things, provide themselves with the necessities of life? There are. Do not these men procure necessary things for themselves through their knowledge, exchanging it just as we exchange gold and silver? I believe so. If, therefore, they procure for themselves by this very means the things they use for life, then this knowledge itself must be useful for life. For we said that silver is useful for the reason that by it we can procure the necessities of life. We did. Since, therefore,
<margin>Inscriptions.</margin>
<margin>C</margin> these branches of knowledge themselves appear useful to us for this purpose, it is manifest that for the same reason that gold and silver are money, those who possess knowledge are also wealthier—even if a little while ago we did not so easily allow them to be the wealthiest. Indeed, from what has now been admitted, it must follow that those who are more endowed with knowledge are sometimes also wealthier. For if someone were to ask us whether we think a horse is useful to any man, would you say yes, or rather that it is useful to those who know how a horse ought to be used, but useless to those who do not know? I would say the latter. By the same reasoning, I said, you would say that Medicine is not useful to every man, but to him who knows
<margin>D</margin> how it ought to be used. I would. Does it not seem that the same must be said of all other things? It does. Gold and silver, and other things that seem to be money—would they not be useful only to him who knows how they are to be used? They would. But a little while ago, did it not seem to be the mark of honest and good men to know where and how each of these things is to be used? It did. Therefore, these things must be useful to honest and good men, and indeed to them alone, if they are to be used skillfully. But if they are useful to these alone, it must follow that they are seen as money to these alone. Therefore, it seems, if someone possesses horses that are useless to him because he is unskilled in the art of riding, and someone else makes him skilled in that art, he also makes him
<margin>E</margin> wealthier at the same time; since he makes things useful to him which were previously useless. For by handing over a certain knowledge to a man, he simultaneously makes him rich. Yet I think I could swear that Critias is in no way led to believe these arguments are true. You may swear it, he said, for I would be utterly insane if I believed this were true. But why did you not finish that argument: that gold and silver and other such things, although they seem so, are nevertheless not money? I would admire those speeches much more than the ones you are now running through. I said then: You seem to me, Critias, to be affected with joy while listening to me just as those who listen to rhapsodes <note>Reciters of epic poetry</note> singing the verses of Homer; for none of these arguments seems true to you. Nevertheless, come, let us consider such things as gold, silver, and the rest. Would you say these are useful to architects for building a house? I certainly would. Shall we then say those things are useful which they use for the building of the house—stones, bricks, wood, and whatever else is of this kind—or also the tools with which they build the house, and by which they prepare the wood, stones, and the tools for these? All these things, he said, seem to me to be useful for that purpose. Is it not then the case, I said, that in other crafts, not only are those things useful which we use for each work, but also those by which we procure them, and without which they could not be made? They certainly are. And again, must not those things by which these are made, and whatever is further up the chain, and the countless things falling before them, also be seen as useful to the craft itself? Nothing, he said, prevents this from being so. What then? If a man has food, drink, clothes, and other things for the use of his body, would he need gold, or silver, or any other of those things by which the things he already has are acquired? It does not seem so to me. Is it now agreed among us that a man sometimes needs none of these for the necessity of the body? It is agreed. If indeed these appear useless for that work, is it not necessary, on the contrary, that they never appear useful? For it is a settled premise that it cannot be that the same things are sometimes useful and sometimes useless for the same work. And, he said, let this reasoning stand for you and me: if the same things are at any time useful for the same purpose, the opposite can never happen, that they are useless; but now furthermore...
<margin>Liberty 13</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...and if we did not need it, it would not be useful. The same argument appears to hold for other things as well. Therefore, of those things from which something else can be produced, none of these would appear useful to us <unclear>if we lacked the need</unclear>. Certainly not. Therefore, if we ever appeared to be able to stop the deficiencies of the body without silver and gold and other such things (which we do not use directly for the body, like food and drink and clothes and bedding and houses), so that we no longer needed them, then neither silver nor gold nor other such things would appear to be wealth <note>original: "χρήματα" (chremata) - things used or needed</note> to us; if indeed it were possible for this to happen. Certainly not. Therefore, these things would not be called wealth by us if they were not useful; rather, those things would be wealth by which we are able to
<margin>B</margin> procure useful things. O Socrates, I could never be persuaded of this, that gold and silver and other such things are not wealth to us. For I am strongly persuaded of this: that things which are useless to us are not wealth; and that among the most useful things, those which are useful are wealth. But I cannot be persuaded that these things do not happen to be useful to us for life, if indeed we procure necessities with them. Come then, how should we speak of such things? Are there not some men who teach music, or letters, or some other knowledge, who in exchange for these things procure necessities for themselves,
<margin>C</margin> receiving a fee? There are. Therefore, these men would procure necessities by this knowledge, exchanging it just as we do for gold and silver. I agree. Therefore, if they procure their living by this from those who use it, then this knowledge would be useful to them for life. And we said silver was useful for this reason: because by it we are able to procure the necessities for life. So it was, he said. Therefore, if these branches of knowledge are useful in this way, they appear to us to be wealth for the same reason that gold and silver are. It is clear then that those who possess them are wealthier. Although we previously accepted the argument with difficulty, as to whether these are the wealthiest.
<margin>D</margin> It must therefore follow again from what has now been agreed, that sometimes those who are more knowledgeable are wealthier. For if someone asked us whether we think a horse is useful to every man, would you say so, or that it would be useful to those who know how one must use a horse, but not to the unskillful? I would say the latter. Therefore, by the same reasoning, not even a medicine is useful to every man, but to him who happens to know how it must be used? I agree. And all other things likewise? It seems so. Gold then and silver, and other things thought to be wealth, would be useful only to him who happens to know how they are to be used. Thus. And previously it seemed to be the mark of the noble and good man to know where and how each of these must be used. I agree. To noble and good men,
<margin>E</margin> therefore, these things alone would be useful, if indeed we know how they must be used. But if they are useful to these alone, they would appear to be wealth to these alone. But, as it seems, if someone is unskillful with horses, yet possesses horses which happen to be useless to him, if someone made him a horseman, would he not have simultaneously made him wealthier? If indeed he made things useful which happened to be useless to him before. For by imparting knowledge to the man, he has simultaneously made him rich. So it appears. Yet I think I could swear by Critias that he is persuaded by none of these arguments. By Zeus,
<margin>F</margin> I would be mad if I were persuaded by these. But why did you not finish that argument, how the things thought to be wealth—gold, silver, and other such things—are not? For I very much admire these arguments which you are now running through. I said then: You seem to me, Critias, to enjoy listening to me just as those who listen to rhapsodes singing the verses of Homer. Since none of these arguments seems true to me either. Nevertheless, come, how should we speak of such things? Would you say they are useful to builders for the purpose of making a house? It seems so to me. Should we then say those things are useful which they themselves use for the building? Stones, bricks, wood, and if there is anything else of the sort? Or also the tools with
<margin>G</margin> which they build the house, and by which they procure these things—the wood and the stones—and again the tools for those? It seems to me, he said, all these things are useful for those purposes. Therefore (I said), in the case of other craftsmen, not only are those things useful which we use for each of the works, but also those by which we procure them, and without which they would not exist. Entirely so. Therefore again, those things by which these are made, and whatever is further up from these, and so on to a vast number, all these must appear useful for the work itself. And nothing (he said) prevents this from being so. What then? If a man has food and drink and clothes, and all the other things he intends to use for his body, would he, by the gods, have any need of gold or silver or anything else by which he might procure those things? It does not seem so to me. Therefore, would it not appear to us that sometimes a man needs none of these for the use of the body? Certainly. Therefore, if these things appeared useless for this...

<summary>Socrates and Critias debate the definition of wealth, concluding that objects like gold are only "wealth" if the possessor has the knowledge (techne) to use them effectively. They explore the idea that knowledge itself can be a form of wealth because it can be exchanged for life's necessities.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue of the pseudo-Platonic Eryxias, specifically a debate between Socrates and Erasistratus regarding the nature of wealth and its utility toward virtue.</meta>

# ERYXIAS.

<margin>A</margin> ...some actions of bad things, and some of good. Can a bad thing then be useful for the performance of a good action? It does not seem so to me. And do we not say that good things are those which a man does through virtue? We do. Is it possible for a man to learn any of those things which are taught through speech if he were entirely deprived of hearing, or some other sense? By Zeus, it does not seem so to me. Therefore, would not hearing appear useful to us for virtue, if indeed virtue is acquired through hearing, and we use it for our lessons? It appears so. If medicine is able to free the sick from disease, would not medicine also sometimes appear useful to us for virtue, if indeed hearing is often recovered through medicine? Nothing prevents it.

<margin>B</margin> Furthermore, if we acquire medicine with money, would money also appear useful to us for virtue? It would. And must the same not also be said of that by which we acquire money? The same must be said of all these things entirely. Does it then seem to you that a man might provide himself with silver through bad and shameful deeds, in order to obtain the knowledge of medicine, or so that he might hear when he previously could not—and then use that very thing for virtue or other such purposes? It certainly seems so to me. Would not a bad thing then be useful for virtue? It would not. <note>Socrates is leading the interlocutor into a logical trap: if money is useful for virtue, and bad deeds produce money, then bad deeds would be "useful" for virtue, which is a contradiction.</note> So it is not necessarily the case that the things through which we acquire useful items are themselves useful for those same ends. For bad things would sometimes appear useful toward something good. But they will be caught out even more in this: for if these things are useful for specific ends, without which those ends cannot be achieved unless these are present first, come, see what you would say of such things. Would you say it is possible for ignorance to be useful for knowledge, or disease for health, or vice for virtue? I would certainly not say so. And yet we affirm this: that knowledge cannot exist in one who did not previously have ignorance, nor health in one who had no disease, nor virtue in one who had no vice. So it is, he said, as it seems to me.

<margin>D</margin> Does it not then necessarily follow that those things without which something cannot happen are themselves useful for it? For thus ignorance might seem useful to us for knowledge, disease for health, and vice for virtue. He had no faith at all in these arguments, unless all these things were useful. But I, realizing that persuading him was the same as "boiling a stone" <note>A Greek proverb meaning to attempt the impossible.</note> as the saying goes, said: let us dismiss these speeches, since we can neither agree nor affirm whether these things and money are useful or not. But what shall we say of this? Whether do we consider a man to be happier and more powerful if he requires the greatest number of necessary things for his clothing and food, or if he requires the fewest and the least? Perhaps this might best be viewed in this way: if one,

<margin>E</margin> contemplating the man within the man himself, considers which state is better: when he is sick, or when he is healthy. But this, he said, does not require much contemplation. For perhaps, I said, any man might understand what is obvious: that the state of a healthy man is far better than that of a sick one. But do we need more and more varied things when we are sick, or when we are healthy? When we are sick. When we ourselves are in our worst state, are not the desires and needs within us, regarding the pleasures of the body, both more violent and more numerous? They are. The same must be said if there are two people. For just as one man seems better off when he requires the fewest things, so it will be if there are two men: if one desires few things and not vehemently, nor needs them much; while the other desires many things greatly and needs them—such as those who are gamblers, drunkards, and gluttons <note>original: "aleatores, vinolenti, et helluones"</note>—all of which are nothing other than desires. Nothing else. Furthermore, all desires are nothing other than the lack of certain things. Therefore, men who are affected by the most desires are in a worse state than those affected by none, or by the fewest. Certainly. I consider such men to be very bad, and the more they are like this, the worse they are. Does it not then seem to us that it is impossible for these things to be useful to us, unless we also have a need for them? I think so.

<margin>G</margin> It is necessary, then, if these things are to be useful to us for the care of the body in those things which are needed, that we also simultaneously need them for this purpose. It certainly seems so to me. Is it not then established that he for whom the most things are useful is himself the one who needs the most, if indeed it is necessary to need all those things which are useful? It is established, as I judge it. It also follows from this reasoning that those who have much money also need many necessary things for the care of the body. For it appeared to us that the things useful for this are "wealth." Therefore, it must necessarily appear to us that the wealthiest men, since they lack the most such things, are in the worst condition.

<column-break/>

<summary>Socrates argues that wealth is not inherently good because it is tied to bodily needs and desires; he concludes that the wealthy are actually in a worse state because they possess the greatest number of needs and dependencies.</summary>

# DEFINITIONS.
->Translated by Sebastian Corrado.<-

<margin>A</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial E with swirling foliage and floral patterns.</image-desc>
**ETERNITY** is that which existed through all time before, and is not ended in the present. God: an immortal living being, self-sufficient for living blessedly; an everlasting force and the cause of a good nature. Birth: a motion toward that nature which is called <term>ousia</term> <note>original: οὐσία; essence or being</note>; the attainment of nature; a journey to where it is possible to be. The Sun: celestial fire, which alone can be seen from sunrise until sunset; an eternal and animate living being; the greatest star shining by day.

<margin>B</margin>
Time: the motion of the sun; the measure of the celestial revolution. Day: the journey of the sun from east to west. Light: that which is the opposite of night. Dawn: the beginning of the day; the first light proceeding from the sun. Midday: the time in which the shadows of bodies are smallest. Sunset: the end of the day. Night: darkness contrary to the day; the deprivation of the sun. Fortune: a transition from the uncertain to the uncertain, and the accidental cause of a successful action. Old Age: the failing of a living being caused by time. Spirit: the motion of air around the earth. Air: the element whose every motion made in a place is according to nature. Heaven: a body embracing all things perceived by the senses, except for the highest air itself.

<margin>C</margin>
The Soul: that which moves itself; the cause of the vital motion of living beings. Power: that which acts through itself. Sight: a habit distinguishing bodies. Bone: marrow curdled by heat. An Element: that which composes, and dissolves what is composed. Virtue: an affection of the soul, or the best habit of a mortal living being, praiseworthy of its own accord; the habit by which the one who holds it is called good. Community: a just arrangement of laws, which whoever has attained, if only they be best disposed, is called honorable; a habit effecting good law-making. Prudence: a power which by itself prepares happiness for man; the knowledge of things good and evil; the knowledge that gives happiness; the habit by which we judge what ought to be done and what ought to be avoided.

<margin>D</margin>
Justice: the harmony of the soul within itself, and the preservation of order among the parts of the soul with each other and with itself; a habit granting to each their own dignity; a habit which makes the one who has attained it act willingly in those things which seem just to them; a habit in life obeying the law; communicating equity; a habit obedient to the laws. Temperance: the moderation of the soul suited to moderating those desires and pleasures which arise in it by nature; a congruent limit and right order of the soul for calming natural pleasures and pains; a certain harmony and consensus of the soul for commanding and obeying; an action acting spontaneously in accordance with nature; the right order of the soul; a discourse, as it were, of the soul reasoning about honorable and shameful things; a habit by which the one endowed with it chooses what is to be chosen and avoids what is to be avoided.

<margin>E</margin>
Fortitude: a habit of the soul which can be moved by no fear; warlike high-mindedness; the knowledge of warlike matters; constancy and firmness of the soul in undergoing those things which are formidable and heavy; confidence obeying prudence; an outstanding strength of soul in the expectation of death; a habit preserving right thoughts in dangers; strength equal to danger; strength constantly tending toward virtue; tranquility of the soul in those things which rightly seem heavy and horrible; liberation from uncertain opinions regarding adverse things, and experience in war; a stable habit obeying the law.

<margin>F</margin>
Constancy: a force sustaining pain, the companion of right reason; the invincible force of that which has been grasped by right thought. Blessedness: the perfection of the possession of goods; a habit which those who possess it command themselves. Equity: the lessening of things just and useful; moderation in dealings; the right order of a soul using reason toward honorable and shameful things. Tolerance: the enduring of evils for the sake of honor; the habit of enduring labors for the sake of honor. Confidence: the expectation of no evil; firmness in a present evil. Cheerfulness: a habit which prevents us from falling into sorrows. Diligence in labor: a habit perfecting that which you first undertook to do; voluntary endurance; a habit never blaming labor.

<margin>G</margin>
Modesty: a voluntary yielding of boldness, justly giving place to that which seems best; a voluntary grasping of the best; the avoidance of just reproach. Liberty: the mastery of life; the supreme power of anyone over themselves; the power situated in each person to live as they wish; the free faculty of enjoying resources in use and possession. Liberality: the affection and desire for gaining as is fitting; the just acceptance or possession of riches. Gentleness: the calming of the motion usually excited by anger; a moderate tempering of the soul. Grace: a voluntary approach to that which seems best; modesty in the motion of the body. Happiness: a good composed of all goods; a power self-sufficient for living well; perfection proceeding from virtue; the help of a living being sufficient in itself. Magnificence: greatness proceeding from a most serious agitation and proposition of the mind. Industry: a good quality of the soul, which the one who has it is skillful at devising all that is necessary; sharpness of mind. Goodness: integrity of character with beneficence; an ardent zeal for character. Honor: a habit which the one who has it does honorable things eagerly and willingly. Magnanimity: the civil use of those things which happen; magnificence of the soul with reason. Humanity: a habit of character very inclined toward human friendship; a habit of benefits toward men...

<column-break/>

# DEFINITIONS.
<note>original: ΟΡΟΙ (Horoi)</note>

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial I (iota) with floral scrolling patterns.</image-desc>
**THE PECULIAR** <note>The Latin translator Corrado chose "Eternity" (Aeternitas) for the Greek "Idion," likely interpreting the definition's focus on "all time."</note> is that which exists through all time and before, and is not now destroyed. God: an immortal living being, self-sufficient for happiness; an eternal essence, the cause of the nature of the good. Becoming: motion toward essence; participation in essence; a journey into being. The Sun: celestial fire; which alone from dawn until evening can be seen by the same people; an eternal living being, an animate star appearing by day, the greatest.

Time: the motion of the sun, the measure of its course. Day: the journey of the sun from the east to the west. Light: the opposite of night. Dawn: the beginning of the day; the first light from the sun. Midday: the time in which the shadows of bodies share the shortest length. Evening: the end of the day. Night: darkness, the opposite of day; the deprivation of the sun. Fortune: a course from the unseen to the unseen, and a cause from spontaneity of a divine action. Old Age: the decay of a living being occurring by time. Spirit: the motion of air around the earth. Air: the element of which all motions according to place are according to nature. Heaven: a body containing all sensible things, except for the upper and uppermost air.

The Soul: that which moves itself; the cause of the vital motion of living beings. Power: that which is productive by itself. Sight: a habit capable of distinguishing bodies. Bone: marrow solidified by heat. An Element: that which brings together and dissolves composite things. Virtue: a disposition, the best habit of a mortal living being, praiseworthy in itself. A Habit: that by which the possessor is called good. Community: a just disposition of laws, by which the possessor, being perfectly disposed, is called excellent. Insolence: that which produces lawlessness. Prudence: a power productive by itself of human happiness; the science of goods and evils; the science productive of happiness; a disposition by which we judge what is to be done and where it is to be done.

Justice: the harmony of the soul with itself, and the good order of the parts of the soul toward one another and concerning one another; a habit distributive of what is according to merit to each; a habit by which the possessor is a chooser of things appearing just to them; a habit in life, obedient to the law; social equality; a habit subservient to right laws. Temperance: moderation of the soul concerning the desires and pleasures that arise in it according to nature. Harmony and good order of the soul toward natural pleasures and pains. Agreement of the soul toward ruling and being ruled. Self-action according to nature. Good order of the soul, a rational conversation of the soul concerning things beautiful and shameful. A habit by which the possessor is a chooser and observer of what is necessary.

Fortitude: a habit of the soul unmoved by fear. Warlike courage. Knowledge of things to be done in war. Self-control of the soul toward things fearful and terrible. Daring subservient to prudence. Good courage in the expectation of death. A habit preservative of right reasonings in dangers. Strength counterbalancing danger; strength enduring toward virtue. Calmness of the soul concerning things appearing terrible and bold according to right reason. The salvation of unseen doctrines concerning terrible things, and experience of war. A habit abiding by the law. Self-control: a power enduring of pain; following right reasoning; an insurmountable power of what has been conceived through right reasoning. Self-sufficiency: perfection of the possession of goods. A habit by which the possessors rule themselves. Equity: a lessening of things just and useful. Moderation in contracts. Good order of the rational soul toward things beautiful and shameful.

Endurance: the sustaining of pain for the sake of the beautiful. Courage: the non-expectation of evil; fearlessness through the presence of evil. Freedom from pain: a habit by which we do not fall into pains. Love of labor: a habit accomplishing whatever it may choose. Voluntary endurance. A habit irreproachable toward toil. Modesty: a voluntary yielding, justly, toward what appears best. And a voluntary obligation toward the best. Caution against right reproach. Liberty: the leadership of life, absolute power over everything. Authority over one's own life. Unsparingness in the use and possession of essence. Liberality: a habit toward making money as is necessary. The addition or possession of essence as is fitting. Gentleness: the settling of motion caused by anger. A symmetrical blending of the soul. Orderliness: a voluntary yielding toward what appears best. Good order concerning the motion of the body.

Happiness: a good composed of all goods. A power self-sufficient for living well. Perfection according to virtue, the self-sufficient benefit of a living being. Magnificence: a claim according to right reason that is most dignified. Quick-wittedness: a natural fitness of the soul, by which the possessor is hitting the mark of what is necessary for each. Sharpness of mind. Kindliness: an unfeigned character with good speech; the excellence of character. Nobility: a habit choosing the best things. Magnanimity: a refined use of things that happen. Magnificence of the soul with reason. Humanity: a well-disposed habit of character toward human friendship. A habit beneficial to humans. Piety: justice concerning the gods. Be...

# DEFINITIONS.

**Piety:** Service to the Gods; a voluntary assumption of the honor due to the gods; the correct knowledge concerning the honor of the gods. <note>original: Εὐσέβεια / Pietas</note> **The Good:** That which is for its own sake. **Fearlessness:** A state according to which we do not fall into fears. **Apathy:** A state according to which we do not fall into passions <note>In this context, "apathy" refers to the Stoic ideal of being unmoved by overwhelming emotions or "passions."</note>. **Peace:** Quietness in the face of warlike hostilities. **Indolence:** Ease of the soul; apathy of the spirited part of the soul. **Shrewdness:** A disposition by which the possessor is skilled at hitting upon their own end. **Friendship:** Harmony concerning things noble and just; a choice of the same way of life; shared opinion concerning choice and action; harmony concerning the community of life, joined with goodwill; a community of doing and receiving good. **Good Counsel:** The virtue of a well-disposed character; the leading of the soul toward words and deeds. **Choice:** A correct testing. **Goodwill:** A choice: the embrace of one human for another. **Intimacy:** A community of the same kind. **Concord:** A community of all things that truly are; a symphony of thoughts and opinions. **Affection:** A perfect acceptance. **Political Science:** The science of things noble and useful; the science productive of justice in the city. **Companionship:** Friendship based on habit among those of the same age. **Prudence:** A virtue of reasoning that is innate. **Faith:** A correct assumption that things are as they appear to oneself; a firmness of character. **Truth:** A state involving affirmation and negation; the science of true things. **Will:** A desire accompanied by correct reason; <insert>an irrational appetite; an appetite with reason according to nature.</insert> **Consultation:** Advice to another concerning an action, regarding how one ought to act. **Opportunity:** A prescription of time in which it is necessary to suffer or to act. **Caution:** A guarding against evil; the care of guarding oneself. **Order:** A similarity of work in relation to all things being connected to one another; the proportion of community; the cause of all things being toward one another; a proportion suited for learning. **Attention:** A tension of the soul toward learning thoroughly. **Natural Talent:** Speed of learning; a good birth of nature; virtue in nature. **Docility:** Sharpness of the soul toward speed of learning. **Judgment:** A sovereign decision concerning a disputed matter. **Law:** A dispute concerning doing wrong or not. **Good Governance:** Obedience to excellent laws. **Cheerfulness:** Joy over the deeds of a temperate person. **Honor:** The giving of goods granted for deeds of virtue; dignity derived from virtue; a form of majesty; the valuation of dignities. **Alacrity:** The manifestation of a practical choice. **Grace:** A voluntary benefit; the timely repayment of a good service. **Harmony:** The opinion of rulers and the ruled that one must rule and be ruled. **Polity:** A community of a multitude of people, self-sufficient for happiness; a community of a multitude governed by law. **Providence:** Preparation for certain future things. **Counsel:** Deliberation concerning future things as is expedient. **Victory:** A power that prevails in a contest. **Vigor:** A prevailing precision of reasoning. **Gift:** An exchange of grace. **Season:** The peak of time for what is useful; a time that assists in some good. **Memory:** A disposition of the soul that guards the truth existing within it. **Thought:** A tension of the mind. **Intellection:** The beginning of science. **Purity:** Caution regarding sins against the gods; the natural service of the honor of God. **Prophecy:** A science that signifies an action beforehand without demonstration. **Divination:** A science that perceives things present and future for a mortal animal. **Wisdom:** A science without hypotheses; the science of things that always are; a science that contemplates the cause of things. **Philosophy:** The longing and appetite for the things that always are; the contemplation of the true, how it is true; the care of the soul with correct reason. **Science:** An assumption of the soul that cannot be changed by reason; a power of assuming something or things that is unchangeable by reason; true reason through the mind that is unchangeable. **Opinion:** An assumption with belief that can be changed by reason; a path of reasoning; a thought falling into falsehood and truth by reason. **Sensation:** An impulse of the soul; a movement of the mind; a messenger of the soul through the body to the seasons of men, from which arises an irrational power of the soul that knows through the body. **Habit:** A disposition of the soul by which we are said to be of a certain quality. **Voice:** A flow from the mind through the mouth. **Speech:** A voice that can be written, explaining each of the things that are. **Dialect:** A composite of names and verbs without melody. **Name:** An uncomposed dialect interpretive of that which is predicated of the essence <note>original: οὐσία / essentia</note>, and of everything not spoken of by itself. **Dialect:** The voice of a human that can be written; and a certain common sign that interprets without melody. **Syllable:** An articulate joint of the human voice that can be written. **Definition:** A statement composed of difference and genus. **Evidence:** A demonstration of the unseen. **Demonstration:** A true syllogistic statement; a statement making things manifest through things previously known. **Element:** An uncomposed voice of a voice; the cause for other voices to be voices. **Useful:** The cause of faring well; the cause of good. **Expedient:** That which leads toward the good. **Noble:** The good. **Good:** The cause of salvation for the things that are; the cause of everything directed toward it, from which it happens that one chooses what is necessary. **Temperance:** The order of the soul. **Bond:** A law that is not productive of justice. <note>The Latin text here differs slightly, suggesting "Just: an institution of law exercising justice."</note> **Free:** That which rules itself. **Moderate:** The middle between excess and deficiency, and that which is sufficient in art. **Mean:** The middle...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...conferring. **Piety:** justice toward the Gods; a virtue worshiping the Gods; a voluntary undertaking of the religion of the Gods; correct knowledge of the worship of the Gods; a good which is sought for its own sake. **Security:** a habit prohibiting us from fear. **Freedom from disturbance:** a habit acting so that we do not fall into disturbances. **Peace:** the rest from hostile contentions. **Sloth:** leisure of the mind; the absence of the mind's impulse. **Skill:** a habit which, he who possesses it, is fit to reach his own end by conjecture. **Friendship:** a consensus of wills concerning noble and just things; a considered choice of the same life; a consensus of opinions concerning choosing and doing; a joining of wills for the community of life with benevolence; a community of giving and receiving benefit. **Generosity:** the virtue of a noble character; a ready induction of the mind to reasons and actions. **Heresy:** a right approval. <note>In this classical context, "heresy" (hairesis) means a "choice" or "school of thought" rather than its later religious meaning of heterodoxy.</note> **Benevolence:** a choice; an embrace coupling man with man. **Kinship:** a communion of the same genus. **Concord:** a community of all things which truly are; a sort of harmony of sentiments and opinions. **Courtesy:** a perfect demonstration. **Civil Science:** the science of noble and useful things; the science establishing justice in the city. **Fellowship:** friendship among equals reconciled by custom. **Good Counsel:** an innate power of thought. **Faith:** a right opinion, to hold a matter as it seems to oneself; a certain comprehension of the truth. **Truth:** a <margin>C</margin> habit which is occupied with affirmation and negation; the science of true things. **Will:** a desire with right reason, an appetite agreeable to reason, a natural appetite with reason. **Giving of Counsel:** an admonition before an action, prescribing to another how it is necessary to act. **Occasion:** a prescription of time in which it is necessary to suffer or act. **Caution:** a declining of evil; the care of preserving oneself. **Order:** a similarity of action of all things which are connected among themselves; a proportion of community; the cause of all things which are compared among themselves; a proportion accommodated for learning. **Attention:** a tension of the mind for learning thoroughly. **Good Disposition:** <margin>D</margin> speed of learning; the procreation of a good nature; natural virtue. **Docility:** a disposition of the mind toward speed of learning. **Judgment:** the ratified outcome of a matter about which there was doubt. **Law:** a discussion concerning just or unjust things. **Right Institution of Laws:** obedience to noble laws. **Joy:** gladness in the works of temperance. **Honor:** the donation of goods which are given in the actions of virtue; dignity prepared from virtue; a species of gravity; the preservation of authority. **Alacrity:** a leaning toward the significance of the will for acting. **Grace:** voluntary beneficence; the remuneration of a good in the time of granting a duty. **Consensus:** the opinion of those ruling and those obeying, that one must rule and obey. **Republic:** a community of a <margin>E</margin> multitude of men content in itself for living well; a community of a multitude established by laws. **Providence:** preparation for certain future things. **Counsel:** a consideration of future things as is expedient. **Victory:** a power overcoming in a contest. **Perspicacity:** the faculty of attaining that which is thought. **Gift:** an exchange of grace. **Maturity:** the occasion of time for a useful thing; a time simultaneously helping toward the finishing of some good. **Memory:** an affection of the mind guarding the truth which is in itself. **Consideration:** a tension of thought. **Intelligence:** the principle of science. **Chastity:** caution against vices which offend the Gods; the natural care of the worship of the Gods. **Prophecy:** a science signifying beforehand what must be done without demonstration. **Divination:** a science perceiving that which is present and what will happen to a mortal animal. **Wisdom:** a science not supposed; the science of divine things; a science contemplating the cause of things. **Philosophy:** the appetite for the science of divine things; the contemplation of truth in what way it becomes truth; the care of the mind with right reason. **Science:** a perception of the mind which cannot be refuted by reason; a power so suspecting something or some things that it can in no way let go; a true reason immutable in thought. **Opinion:** a suspicion which can be refuted by reason; an impulse of reasoning; a thought <margin>G</margin> falling into false and true through reason. **Sense:** an impulse of the soul; a movement of the mind, a messenger of the soul through the body proceeding to the furthest parts of men, from which the power of the soul, void of reason, is made a participant in knowledge through the body. **Habit:** an affection of the soul by which we are said to be of what sort we are. **Voice:** a flow departing from thought through the mouth. **Speech:** a voice which can be written and explains each single thing; a diction composed of names and verbs without song. **Name:** a simple diction which signifies both that which is said of the essence which they call *ousia*, and everything which is not said by itself. **Diction:** the voice of a man which can be written, and a certain common sign declaring a thing without song. **Syllable:** an article of the human voice which can be written. **Definition:** a reason composed of difference and genus. **Evidence:** of a hidden thing...

# PLATO’S DEFINITIONS.

...and the middle point of deficiency. **A prize**, the reward of virtue: that which is desirable for its own sake. **Immortalitas** <note>original: "Immortalitas" / ἀθανασία</note>, a nature, which is called **essence** <note>original: "οὐσία"</note>, an animated and perpetual remaining. **Sanctity**, the worship of God: a thing pleasing to God. **A feast day**, a sacred time, proclaimed according to the laws. **Man**, a wingless animal, two-footed, having broad nails, which alone among all things grasps the knowledge that is handed down by reason. **Sacrifice**, a gift dedicated to God for a sacred purpose. **A vow**, a petition by which men ask the Gods for good things, or things which seem to be good. **A King**, he who rules according to the laws, free from rendering an account: the leader of the civil institution. **Magistracy**, the care of the whole. **Power**, the administration of the law. **A Lawgiver**, the maker of laws by which it is necessary to administer the Republic. **Law**, a civil decree of the multitude defined for no specific time. **An Argument**, a principle not perfectly demonstrating: a collection of speech made in summary. **A Decree**, a civil edict defined for a certain time. **A Politician**, one skilled in establishing a Republic. **A City**, the dwelling of a multitude of men who use common decrees: a multitude of men who are under the same law. **The virtue of a city**, the constitution of the best Republic. **Military virtue**, the science of waging war. **An alliance in war**, a community of war. **Safety**, the procurement of a secure state. **A Tyrant**, a master governing a city according to his own will. **A Sophist**, one who, for the sake of a fee, hunts and catches wealthy and famous youths. **Riches**, a possession moderated for living well: an abundance of money which looks toward living well at the same time. **A Deposit**, a thing given with trust. **Purgation**, the secretion of the worst things from the best. **To conquer**, to overcome by striving. **A good man**, such a one who deserves well of men. **Temperate**, he who has moderate desires. **Continent**, he who overcomes the parts of the soul that oppose right thought. **Honorable**, he who is perfectly good: who possesses his own virtue. **Conscience**, a silent thought accompanied by sorrow. **Difficulty of learning**, slowness in perceiving discipline. **Sovereignty**, a just dominion free from rendering an account. **Contempt for philosophy**, a habit which, he who possesses it, hates reason. **Fear**, a disturbance of the soul in the expectation of evil. **Wrath**, a vehement and violent appetite without knowledge: a sign of a disturbed order in the soul. **Disturbance**, fear in the expectation of evil. **Flattery**, a conversation which is deceptive and wicked for the sake of pleasure: a habit exceeding moderation in the pleasure of conversing. **Anger**, a wrathful urging toward taking revenge. **Injury**, injustice leading to ignominy. **Intemperance**, a habit violent beyond reason, drawing one toward those things which seem pleasant. **Laziness**, the flight from the beginning of labors. **Cowardice**, a cause repressing the first appetite for doing some thing. **Disputation**, a disagreement of friends in speech. **Maturity**, the time in which each thing is fit for suffering or doing. **Injustice**, a habit despising the laws. **Indigence**, a deficiency of good things. **Modesty**, fear in the expectation of ignominy. **Arrogance**, a habit claiming a good, or goods, which do not exist. **Sin**, an action contrary to right reason. **Envy**, a sickness arising from the goods of friends which either are, or will be in the future. **Impudence**, a habit of the soul enduring ignominy for the sake of gain. **Audacity**, an abundance of confidence toward fears where it is not needed. **Ambition**, a habit of the soul inclined toward every expense and liberal without knowledge. **A native evil**, a vice in nature and a natural sin: a disease implanted in nature. **Hope**, the expectation of good. **Insanity**, a habit corrupting true perception. **Loquacity**, an inconsiderate intemperance of speech. **Contrariety**, the greatest distance between things which fall under the same genus according to some difference. **An involuntary thing**, a thing which is performed contrary to thought. **Instruction**, a power caring for the soul. **Erudition**, the handing down of discipline. **Legislation**, the science establishing a firm city. **Admonition**, speech with a rebuke made from the soul: speech instituted for the sake of noticing a sin. **Help**, the driving away of a present or imminent evil. **Chastisement**, the cure of the soul in a fault that is committed. **Power**, excellence in action or in speech: a habit which he who possesses it is powerful: a force naturally preserving a man or making him safe.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>...of meeting and deficiency. **A prize**, the reward of virtue: that which is chosen for its own sake. **Immortality**, an animated essence and eternal duration. **Holiness**, the service of God, pleasing to God. **A festival**, a sacred time according to the laws. **Man**, a wingless, two-footed, flat-nailed animal: the only one of beings capable of science according to reason. **Sacrifice**, the gift of a victim to God. **Prayer**, a request for good things, or things appearing so, from the Gods by men. **A King**, a ruler who is not subject to account, a ruler of a political establishment. **Rule**, the care of the whole. **Authority**, the stewardship of the law. **A Lawgiver**, a maker of laws according to which one must live as a citizen. **Law**, a political decree of the multitude, not limited to a certain time. **A Hypothesis**, an unproven principle, a summary of an argument. **A Decree**, a political decree limited to a certain time. **A Politician**, one skilled in the <margin>B</margin> establishment of a city. **A City**, a dwelling of a multitude of men using common decrees; a multitude of men being under the same law. **The virtue of a city**, the establishment of a right constitution. **The art of war**, experience in war. **Alliance**, a fellowship in war. **Safety**, a preservation free from harm. **A Tyrant**, a ruler of a city according to his own mind. **A Sophist**, a hired hunter of rich and famous young men. **Wealth**, a possession measured for happiness, an abundance of money contributing to happiness. **A Deposit**, a gift given with trust. **Purification**, the separation of worse things from better. **To conquer**, to prevail while being at variance. **A good man**, such a one as performs good things for man. **Temperate**, he who has moderate desires. <margin>C</margin> **Continent**, he who prevails over the parts of the soul that strain against right reasoning. **Excellent**, he who is perfectly good; he who has his own virtue. **Deep thought**, thought with sorrow without reason. **Difficulty in learning**, slowness in learning. **Despotism**, a just rule not subject to account. **Lack of philosophy**, a habit according to which the possessor is a hater of reason. **Fear**, a shock of the soul at the expectation of evil. **Spirit**, a violent impulse without reasoning; a mind entirely alienated from the soul. **Shock**, fear at the expectation of evil. **Flattery**, conversation for pleasure without the best intent; a conversational habit for pleasure, exceeding the moderate. **Anger**, an exhortation of the spirited part toward taking revenge. **Insolence**, injustice leading to dishonor. **Incontinence**, a habit forceful against right reasoning, <margin>D</margin> toward things appearing to be pleasant. **Hesitation**, a flight from the beginning of labors. **Cowardice**, a cause that checks an impulse concerning what is good. **Slander**, a separation of friends by speech. **Opportunity**, that in which each thing is fit to suffer or to do. **Injustice**, a habit contemptuous of laws. **Want**, a lessening of goods. **Shame**, fear at the expectation of ill-repute. **Boastfulness**, a habit pretending to a good, or to goods that do not exist. **Grumbling**, a longing contrary to right reasoning. **Envy**, grief at the goods of friends, either present or past. **Shamelessness**, a habit of the soul enduring ill-repute for the sake of gain. **Rashness**, an excess of action toward fears that are not necessary. **Ambition**, a habit of the soul prone to every expense without reasoning. **Badness of nature**, vice in nature, and a sin according to nature; a disease according to nature. **Hope**, the expectation of good. **Madness**, a habit <margin>E</margin> destructive of true opinion. **Loquacity**, an irrational incontinence of speech. **Contrariety**, the greatest distance of things falling under the same genus according to a difference. **The involuntary**, that which is performed contrary to thought. **Education**, a power curative of the soul. **Instruction**, the transmission of education. **Legislative science**, the productive art of a good city. **Admonition**, a rebuking speech from one's judgment; a speech for the sake of averting sin. **Help**, the prevention of an evil that is or is becoming. **Punishment**, the treatment of the soul for a sin that is occurring. **Power**, excellence in action or in speech; a habit according to which the possessor is able; strength to preserve according to essence, or to procure freedom from harm.

# A FRAGMENT OF PLATO’S TIMAEUS,
## TRANSLATED BY MARCUS TULLIUS CICERO, CORRE-
### SPONDING TO THOSE PASSAGES WHICH WE HAVE
->marked in the margin.<-

---

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> <image-desc>Large decorative initial 'Q' containing floral and scrolling motifs.</image-desc>What is that which always is, and has no origin? And what is that which is born, but never truly is? Of these, the former is grasped by understanding and reason, being that which is always one and the same; the latter is that which brings forth opinion through the senses: it is devoid of reason, being entirely a matter of opinion, for it is born and perishes, and can never truly "be." Now, everything that is born must necessarily be born from some cause. For if the cause is removed, the origin of nothing can be found. Therefore, if he who strives to accomplish some task looks toward that form which is always the same, and sets that before him as a model, he must necessarily produce a magnificent work. <margin>B</margin> But if he looks toward that which is born, he will never achieve the beauty he seeks. Therefore, let this whole heaven—or the world, or whatever other name it delights in—be so named by us: concerning it, let us first consider what must be considered at the start of every inquiry: whether it has always existed, generated from no beginning, or whether it arose from some starting point in time. Since it is seen, and touched, and is everywhere corporeal. Now, all such things move the senses; and those things which move the senses consist in opinion, which we have said have an origin and are born. Nothing, however, can be born without causes. And indeed, to find the parent, as it were, of this universe is difficult, and when you have found him, it is a religious offense <note>original: "nefas"</note> to declare him to the common people. <margin>C</margin> Again, therefore, we must see: which model did the fabricator of so great a work look upon? Was it that which is always one and the same and like itself, or that which we call generated and born? Surely, if this world is beautiful and its craftsman is good, he certainly preferred to imitate the form of eternity. But if otherwise—which is a religious offense even to say—he followed a generated model instead of the eternal. There is no doubt, then, that he preferred to follow eternity, since nothing is more beautiful than the world, and nothing more excellent than its builder. If, therefore, it was generated, it was fashioned according to that which is grasped by reason and wisdom, and is contained within immutable eternity. From which it follows that this world we see must necessarily be an eternal likeness of something eternal. <margin>D</margin> Now, the most difficult part of any rational investigation is the beginning. Regarding what we have said, then, let this be the first distinction: in every discourse, there is an explained kinship with the things about which it seems to speak. Thus, when one disputes about a stable and immutable thing, the discourse should be such as cannot be refuted or proven wrong. But when it enters upon imitated and fashioned likenesses, it considers it well done if it achieves a likeness of the truth. For as much as eternity prevails over that which is born, so much does truth prevail over faith. <margin>E</margin> Wherefore, if by chance, while discussing the nature of the gods and the origin of the world, we should fail to grasp in our minds exactly what we have, so that the whole discourse, clearly and plainly adorned, is consistent and agrees with itself in every part: it will certainly be no wonder, and you ought to be content if probable things are said. For it is fair to remember both that I who speak am a man, and you who judge are men; so that if probable things are said, you should require nothing further. Let us seek, then, the cause that impelled him who engineered these things to seek a beginning of things and a new construction. Clearly, he excelled in goodness, and the good man envies no one. Therefore, he generated all things like himself. This is undoubtedly the most just cause for the birth of the world. For when God had decided to fill the world with all good things, and to mix in no evil as far as nature would allow, he took up everything that fell within the sense of sight—not calm and quiet, but immoderately agitated and fluctuating. And so, he brought it from disorder into order; for he judged this to be more excellent. It is not right, nor has it ever been, for him who is best to do anything except what is most beautiful. When he had taken account of reason, he found that among those things which are seen by nature, nothing unintelligent is more excellent than the intelligent in its whole kind; and that intelligence cannot be found in any other nature except in a soul. Wherefore, he placed intelligence in the soul, and the soul he enclosed in the body. Thus he reckoned that the work produced was the most beautiful. For this reason, we must not hesitate to profess—if indeed anything can be investigated by conjecture—that this world is a living being, and an intelligent one, established by divine providence. This being granted, we must see what follows: the likeness of which living being did God follow in fashioning the world? Surely none of those living beings known to us. For they are all divided into certain kinds, or are incomplete, being in no part perfect. But nothing can be beautiful that is like the imperfect or the incomplete.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> To what, then, of which every living being is like a certain part—whether seen in individuals or in a different kind—shall we say the world is similar? Therefore, all living beings that are seen by the mind and understood by reason are encompassed by the embrace of reason and intelligence, just as men, and cattle, and all things that fall under our gaze are encompassed in this world. For since God wished to make the world similar to that which can be understood as most beautiful in the nature of things, and which is most absolute in every part, he made it one visible living being, in which all living beings are contained. Are we right, then, to say there is one world, or are there many and innumerable ones, which would be truer and better to say? One <margin>B</margin> indeed, if it was truly made according to the model. For that which encompasses all those living beings understood by reason cannot exist with another. For there would have to be another living being to contain it, of which the former living beings would be parts. And this heaven would then be a likeness of that ultimate one, not the nearest. Lest any of this should happen, and so that this world might be most like the absolute living being in this very fact—that it is alone and one—God therefore procreated this world as unique and only-begotten. Now, everything that is born must necessarily be corporeal, visible, and likewise tangible. Furthermore, nothing can be seen without fire, nor indeed touched if it lacks solidity, and nothing is solid that is devoid of earth. Wherefore, <margin>C</margin> God, striving to produce the world, first joined earth and fire. But any two things require a third thing to bond them together, and desire a sort of knot or chain. But of chains, that is the most fit and beautiful which makes itself and the things it binds into one as much as possible. This is best achieved by what is called <term>analogy</term> <note>original: "αναλογία"</note> in Greek, and in Latin (for we must be bold, since these terms are being introduced by us for the first time) can be called "comparison" or "proportion." For whenever, among three numbers, or figures, or any kinds of things, it happens that the middle term is to the first in proportion as it is compared to the last, and conversely, as the last is to the middle, so the middle <margin>D</margin> is compared to the first: then that which is the middle becomes both first and last, and the last and first become the middle. Thus necessity compels that those things which were separate become the same. And when they have become the same, it follows that they are one. Now, if the body of the universe were being explained as a flat and even surface, and nothing else were required, one intervening middle term would bind both itself and those things between which it was placed. But since solidity was sought for the world, and all solid things are never joined by one middle term but always by two: thus it happened that between fire and earth, God placed water and air, and compared them among themselves and joined them by proportion, so that as fire is to air, so air is to water; and as air is to water, so water is to earth. <margin>E</margin> From this conjunction, the heaven was so fashioned that it falls under sight and touch. And so, for that reason, and from these things four in number, the body of the world was produced, constructed by that proportion I have mentioned. From this, it embraces itself in a certain harmonious friendship and love, and clings together so aptly that it can in no way be dissolved, except by him by whom it was bound. Now, of those four things I mentioned above, all the parts were so placed in the whole world that no part of this kind remained outside, and all those kinds were within this <margin>F</margin> universe. This was for these reasons: first, so that the living world could be perfect, made of perfect parts. Second, so that it might be one, with no part left over from which another could be born; and finally, so that no disease or old age could afflict it. For every joining of a body is weakened and broken either by heat or cold or some violent impulse, and is driven toward disease and old age. This, then, was the reasoning of God, the effector and engineer of the world: that one whole and perfect work should be completed from all things whole and perfect, which would lack all disease or old age. <margin>G</margin> Moreover, he gave it a form most akin and becoming to itself. For since he wished all other living beings to be contained by one living being, he shaped it with that form which alone encloses all other forms. Therefore, it was fabricated as a globe, which the Greeks call <term>spherical</term> <note>original: "σφαιροειδές"</note>, of which every extremity is reached by equal radii from the center. And he turned it so that nothing could be made more round, so that it had no roughness, no offense, nothing enclosed in angles, no bends, nothing protruding, nothing hollowed out, and all parts were most similar to all others—for in his judgment, similarity was better than dissimilarity. And with every...
