<meta>This page continues the Latin translation of Plato's *Timaeus* (specifically the section on the creation of the World Soul and the celestial bodies). The Latin text is a Renaissance-era translation, likely that of Marsilio Ficino or Janus Cornarius, though it echoes Cicero’s earlier fragments.</meta>

# PLATO

<margin>A</margin> He surrounded it with a circular shape. For it had no need of eyes, because nothing was left outside that could be perceived; nor of ears, because there was nothing to be heard. Nor was the extremity of the world surrounded by air, such that it would require respiration. Indeed, it desired neither nourishment for the body, nor the shedding of processed and consumed food; for no departure could occur, nor any addition, nor indeed was there any source for such. Thus, it nourished itself by its own consumption and age, since it both suffered and performed all things by itself and through itself. For so it seemed right to him who joined and founded these things: that the world should be content with itself and not stand in need of another. Therefore, he did not attach hands to it, because there was nothing to be grasped nor anything to be repelled; nor feet, nor <margin>B</margin> other limbs by which it might support its body in walking. For he gave to the heavens that motion which is most suitable to its form, which alone among the seven motions contains mind and intelligence. Therefore, by one greatest and identical revolution, it is twisted and turned around itself. However, he separated the six remaining motions from it <note>The "seven motions" refer to up, down, left, right, forward, backward, and circular rotation.</note>; thus he freed it from all wandering. For this revolution, then, which had no need of feet or hands, God—who is—did not give limbs for walking; thinking of the God that was to be, he made it smooth and uniform on all sides, and equal from the center to the summit, perfect and absolute from absolute and perfect parts. As he placed the Soul in its center, so he stretched it through the whole. Then, when he had surrounded it with the body and clothed it from without, he embraced it with a heaven that is solitary, revolving, and driven in a circle, which could easily exist with itself on account of its virtue, needing no other, being sufficiently known and familiar to itself. Thus did that eternal God procreate this perfectly blessed God <note>The "blessed God" here refers to the created Universe itself.</note>. But he did not begin the soul in the manner we have just spoken, only after he had made the body for it. For it would not be right for the greater to obey the lesser. But we say many things inconsiderately and rashly. God, however, generated the soul as older both in origin and virtue, and provided it as a master and ruler to the obedient body, and he constructed it in such a manner: From the matter which is indivisible and always of one kind and similar to itself, and from that which is divided among bodies, he mixed a third kind of matter from the two in the middle, which would be of the same nature and of the other nature; and this he interposed between the indivisible and that which was divisible in the body. And when he had taken these three, he tempered them into one form, and that nature which we called "the other," he joined by force with "the same," mixing that which was fleeing and foreign to such a union with the matter; and when he had made one out of the three, he divided this whole into appropriate members. Now he tempered each single part from "the same," from "the other," and from the matter. Such was that partition: First, he took one part from the whole; then a second, double the first; then a third, which was one-and-a-half times the second and triple the first; then a fourth, which was double the second; a fifth, which was triple the third; then a sixth, eight times the first; and finally a seventh, which preceded the first by twenty-seven parts. Then he set out to fill the double and triple intervals, cutting parts again from the whole: these he placed in the intervals so that in each there were two means. (For I scarcely dare to say "medieties," which the Greeks call <term>mesotētas</term> <note>original: "μεσότητας" - mathematical means or proportions</note>, but if I say it thus, let it be understood; for it will be clearer.) One of these exceeded the extremes by the same part it was exceeded by; the other exceeded the extremes by an equal number and was exceeded by an equal number. With intervals of one-and-a-half, one-and-a-third, and one-and-eighth taken from these bonds, he filled all the one-and-a-third intervals with the one-and-eighth interval in the first intervals, leaving a small fraction of each. After the interval of that fraction was left, the number had the same proportion and comparison to the other number in the extremes as 256 has to 243. And thus that mixture from which he had made these things was entirely consumed. Therefore, he split this whole double conjunction lengthwise, and fitting middle to middle, he crossed them like the letter X; then he bent them into a circle, so that they were joined with themselves and among themselves at the junction directly opposite, and he embraced them on all sides with that motion which was always in the same place and moved in the same way. And so, when he had embraced the outer circle, he marked that one as being of the nature of "the same," and this one as "the other"; and he turned the circle of "the same" from the side toward the right. But this inner one he directed from the middle line toward the left. But he gave sovereignty to the superior one, which alone he left indivisible. The interior one, however, when he had divided it into six parts of heaven, he ordered seven unequal circles to be moved by double and triple intervals, with courses contrary to one another; of these, he made the speeds of three equal, but the four others unequal to each other and to the remaining three. Therefore, when that God, the procreator of the world, had generated the soul from his own mind and divinity, then finally he placed all that was concrete and corporeal beneath the soul, making it interior, and thus fitting middle to middle, he coupled them. Thus the soul, proceeding from the center, surrounded the extremity of heaven from the highest region in a round circuit, and turning itself

<column-break/>

<margin>C</margin> within itself, it introduced the beginning of a divine, eternal, and wise life. And while the body of heaven was made visible, the soul escaped the sight of the eyes. The soul, however, is a partaker and sharer of all reason and harmony (<term>harmonia</term> in Greek <note>original: "ἁρμονία"</note>) of eternal things and those falling under the intelligence, than which nothing better was procreated by the best and most excellent parent; for it is bound from the same and the other nature, with matter added in a tempering of three parts and compacted by proportion, turning itself, when it has grasped mutable matter, and again the indivisible and simple through which all is moved: it discerns what is of the same kind, and what is of another, and judges the rest—what is most fit for each thing, and in what place or manner or time it happens, and what distinction there is between those things which are born and those which are always the same. True reason, which is occupied with those things that are always the same, and is moved by itself without voice or any sound in "the same" and "the other," when it touches that part by which the senses can be moved: and the circle of that "other" kind, unchanged and straight, announces all things to the soul and mind: then firm and true opinions and beliefs are born. But when it turns in those things which, remaining always the same, are contained not by sense but by intelligence, so that the course of the Moon closely circles the Earth, and the nearest revolution of the Sun is above the Earth. Then Lucifer <note>The planet Venus</note> and the sacred star of Mercury have a course equal to the speed of the Sun, but a certain contrary power; in the meeting which Lucifer, Mercury, and the Sun have among themselves, some overtake others and are overtaken in turn. What the cause was for placing the remaining stars, and what their placement is, must be deferred to another discourse, lest a greater speech be spent on that which was only to be touched upon than on that for the sake of which we touched it. When, <margin>D</margin> therefore, each of those stars attained its proper course, from which the motion of time was to be marked, and their bodies were bound with vital bonds, when living beings were born: and they learned to obey the command, then from the transverse motion of the "other" nature running into the motion of the "same" nature, and sticking and being hindered in it: while some traversed a larger circle, others a smaller, the larger more slowly, the smaller more quickly, by the motion of the one and same nature: those which moved most swiftly, bound by that speed, seemed to be overtaken by the slower ones, even as they were overtaking them. For it turned all their circles as if in a spiral <note>original: "Helicis"</note> inflection, because proceeding in two directions contrarily at the same time, they caused that which was slowest to become nearest to the swiftest. And so that there might be some <margin>E</margin> evident measure which would declare the speeds and slownesses in those eight courses, God himself kindled the sun like a light at the second circuit above the earth, so that the heaven might shine as much as possible for all, and living things which had the right to be taught might know the nature and power of numbers from the fear of the same and from that which was similar. Night and day, therefore, generated in this manner and for these causes, effect one circuit of the circle, most wise and excellent. A month is when the moon, having traversed its course, has followed the sun. A year is when the sun has finished and traveled through its whole circle. But of the circuits of the other stars, men—except for a very few—are ignorant; they neither call them by name, nor measure them against each other by number. Therefore, they <margin>F</margin> do not know that these wanderings of the stars are that very thing which is rightly called time, endowed with infinite multitude and admirable variety. Nevertheless, it can be perceived and understood that, the absolute and perfect number of time being reached, the absolute and perfect year is finally completed when the eight circuits, having finished their courses, have returned to the same starting point, and the same circle, always similar to itself, has measured them. For these causes, then, the stars were born, which, penetrating through the heaven, would turn back at the summer and winter solstices, so that this whole living being which we see might be most similar to that living being which we perceive in imitation of eternity. And indeed, he had fashioned the other things up to the birth of time, impressed <margin>G</margin> by those things which he was imitating; but because he had not yet included every living being within the world, the likeness of the image to the proposed exemplar was lacking in that part. Therefore, as many and of what kind the forms of living beings the mind could discern looking into the species of things, so many and of such kinds he thought to fashion in this world. There were, however, four kinds of living beings: one divine and celestial, another winged and of the air, a third of the earth, and a fourth of divine animation. He made the [celestial] species mostly of fire, so that it would be most splendid and beautiful to the sight. And since he wished to make it similar to the nature of the universe, <margin>H</margin> he rounded it for volatility, and made it a companion to the wisdom of the best mind, and distributed it equally around the heaven, so that this, distinguished by variety, the Greeks rightly call <term>kosmon</term> <note>original: "κόσμον"</note>, and we call the "shining world" <note>The Latin "mundus" implies both world and ornament/cleanliness, mirroring the Greek "kosmos".</note>. He gave to the divine ones two kinds of motion: one which would always be in the same place and the same in all, and would accelerate in one way; the other, which before...

# The Timaeus of Cicero

...moved, in which direction it might be driven by its rotation and similar motion. However, for the five remaining motions, he willed that the sphere be immobile and standing still—of that kind are the stars which do not move from their place, being fixed in the heavens. These are living beings, and indeed divine ones; for this reason, they cling to their seats and remain there perpetually. Those, however, which glide along with a wandering and changeable logic were generated as we described above. Now truly, he willed that the Earth, our nurturer, which is sustained by the axis passed through it, be the maker of day and night, and the most ancient guardian of those Gods who are begotten within the heavens.

As for the processions of the Gods, their meetings with one another, the revolutions and advancements that occur in their orbits, and how they almost touch one another—those who are joined closely in an opposite region, or behind whom or before whom they glide, and at what times they vanish from our sight, only to emerge again and strike terror into those lacking reason—to attempt to explain these things in words without a model of these matters placed before the eyes would be a labor undertaken in vain. But enough has been said by us on these points; let what we have prefaced concerning the nature of the Gods who are seen and who have arisen have this limit.

Regarding the rest, however, whom the Greeks call <term>daimones</term> <note>original: "δαίμονας"; these are intermediary spirits or lesser deities</note>, and our people (as I think) call the <term>Lares</term> <note>Roman household gods; Cicero is attempting to find a Latin equivalent for the Greek term</note>—if only this can be seen as a correct translation—to know and announce their origin is a task greater than we would dare to profess or write. One must surely believe the ancients and the men of old, as they say, who claimed to be the offspring of the Gods, and thus handed down their names to us; for they were best able to know their own progenitors. It is most difficult to withhold belief from the Gods who have arisen, even though their speech is confirmed neither by arguments nor certain reasons. Because they seem to be speaking of things known to them, the ancient law and custom must be obeyed.

Thus, as it has been handed down by them, let the origin of these Gods be held and spoken of: that we may remember Oceanus and Salacia <note>The Roman goddess of the sea, here used for the Greek Tethys</note> were generated and brought forth from the breath of Heaven and the conception of Earth. From these were born Saturn and Ops <note>Rhea</note>, and thereafter Jupiter and Juno, and the rest whom we are accustomed to call brothers and kinsmen among themselves, and their—to use an ancient word—progeny.

When, therefore, all those who move and show themselves openly, and those who reveal themselves to us only as far as they wish, were created, then that God who begot all things spoke these words to them: "You who are born of the seed of the Gods, attend. Of those works of which I am the parent and maker, these are indissoluble by my will, although everything that is bound together can be dissolved. But it is by no means the part of a good being to wish to dissolve what is bound by reason. But since you have been born, you cannot indeed be immortal and indissoluble. Yet you shall never be dissolved, nor shall any fates of death destroy you; nor is any deception more powerful than my counsel, which is a greater bond for your perpetuity than those by which you were bound when you were being begotten.

"Learn, therefore, what I think. Three kinds remain for us, and those are mortal; if these are passed over, the perfection of the heavens will not be complete. For it will not hold all kinds of living creatures within it. But it must hold them, so that those things which are made by me may be able to equal the life of the Gods. Therefore, so that they may be generated in a mortal condition, you undertake the task; imitate my power in creating them, which you remember I used in your own birth. Among these, those who are created such that they ought to be, as it were, kinsmen of the immortal Gods, shall be called of a divine race; they shall hold the sovereignty over all living creatures, and shall obey you willingly by right and law. The beginning and status of these is handed over to you by me. You, however, weave a mortal part onto that which shall be immortal. Thus shall living creatures arise, whom you may both nourish while living and receive back into your bosom when consumed."

He said these things, and then returned to the previous mixing-bowl. In it, he was mixing and blending the whole soul of universal nature, and pouring out the remnants of the previous mixtures, he made them equal—in almost the same way, except that they were not as pure as those which are always the same, but he took a second and even a third grade. When the whole was constituted, he distributed a number of souls equal to the stars, and assigned each to each, and thus placed them as if in the chariot of the universe, and showed them the fatal and necessary laws. He showed that the first birth would be one for all, and that it would be moderate and constant, diminished by no one. But when the souls were, so to speak, scattered, it would be necessary that at certain intervals of time, a living being should arise that was most fit for the worship of the Gods.

But since the nature of the human race was twofold, things were so arranged that the more excellent kind would be those who were to be men. When he had sown the souls into bodies by necessity, and when an addition was made to the bodies by necessity, then from that excess, it was necessary that one sense should exist, common to all, excited by a more vehement motion: he imposed this on nature, then love mixed with pleasure and distress, then anger and fear, and the rest of the motions of the soul, the companions of the

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> superior ones, and also those contrary to these, such as distrust. He who rules these by reason shall live justly; but he who gives himself up to them, unjustly. And he who has completed the circuit of living given by nature rightly and honorably shall return to that star to which he was suited. But he who lives immoderately and intemperately, a second birth shall transform him into the figure of a woman. And if even then he does not make an end of his vices, he shall be tossed even more grievously, and shall be transformed into the figures of beasts and wild animals most similar to his own character. Nor shall he see an end to his evils until he begins to follow that rotation which he had within himself—the innate and implanted rotation of the "Same" and the "One"—which will finally happen when he has driven out by reason those <margin>B</margin> turbulent and irrational things that fell upon him from fire, air, water, and earth, and has reached the first and best state of the soul.

When he had thus designated these things—so that if any deception or vice should happen afterward, he would be placed beyond all fault and cause—he sowed them, as it were, scattering some onto the earth, some onto the moon, and others into the remaining parts of the world, which are established as marks for the signaling of the spaces of time. After that sowing, he permitted the "younger Gods," so to speak, to fashion mortal bodies, and whatever was left of the human soul that ought to be added, they should polish and complete all of it and what followed. Then, he commanded that they should provide themselves as a prince and leader to this <margin>C</margin> living creature, and rule and govern its life most beautifully, except insofar as it might seek some misery for itself by its own fault.

And he indeed, who composed all things, remained constantly in his own state; but those who had been created by him, when they recognized the order of their parent, followed it. Therefore, when they had received the immortal principle of a mortal living creature, imitating their generator and maker, they borrowed particles of fire and earth, and water and air from the world—which they were to return again—and joined them together, not with the same bonds by which they themselves were bound, but with such as could not be seen because of their smallness. By inserting frequent little wedges, <margin>D</margin> they made one body out of all; and likewise, they bound the circuits of the divine soul within that body as it flowed in and out.

Thus, those souls, immersed in a river, neither held nor were held, but were carried along with great force, and in turn carried others. So that whole animal was moved indeed, but immoderately and by chance, so that it was carried by six motions: for it went forward and backward, to the left and to the right, and upward and downward, now here, now there. But if it settles in brightness, then either the same appearance or sometimes a changed one is returned, when the fire of the eyes has confounded and joined itself with that fire which is poured out before the face. Things on the right appear to be on the left, because they touch opposite parts of the eyes with opposite parts. <margin>E</margin> However, right corresponds to right and left to left by the turning of the lights, when they do not cling together. This happens when the smoothness of mirrors assumes depth on this side and that; and so those pushed from the right into the left part of the eyes, and from the left into the right. Faces are also seen upside down by the repulsion of the lights, which, turning, makes the lower parts appear as the upper.

And yet all these things are of that kind which are auxiliary causes of things, which God uses as ministers when he effects the appearance of the best as far as can be done. But most people estimate that these are not auxiliary causes, but the causes of all things themselves, having the power of cold and heat, of solidifying and melting. But they lack all intelligence and <margin>F</margin> reason, which can be found in no other nature except in the soul. The soul, however, escapes every sense of the eyes. But fire, and water, and earth, and air are bodies, and they are seen. He, however, who professes himself a lover of intelligence and wisdom, must seek out the primary causes of an intelligent and wise nature; then the secondary causes of those things which necessarily move others, being themselves moved by others.

Wherefore we must do this: we should speak of both kinds of causes separately—both of those which, with intelligence, are the makers of the most beautiful and best things, and of those which, being void of wisdom, produce inconstant and disturbed effects. <margin>G</margin> And concerning the causes of the eyes, that they might have that power which they now have, I think enough has been said. But their greatest utility, given to the human race as a gift of the Gods, shall next be explained. For the eyes have brought to us the knowledge of the best things. For this discourse which has been held by us concerning the Universe would never have been discovered if neither the stars, nor the sun, nor the heavens could have fallen under the gaze of the eyes. But now, days and nights known by the eyes, then the revolutions of months and years, have devised number and measured the space of time, and have driven us to the questioning of all nature. From which things we have attained philosophy: than which boon <margin>H</margin> no more desirable, no more excellent thing has been given to the race of mortals by the grant and gift of the Gods, nor ever shall be given.

<meta>This page continues the introductory commentaries by Marsilio Ficino on the works of Plato. # THE ARGUMENTS AND COMMENTARIES OF MARSILIO FICINO THE FLORENTINE ON THE BOOKS OF PLATO.

## ARGUMENT ON THE HIPPARCHUS. referring to page 1.

<margin>A</margin>Plato’s purpose in the *Hipparchus* is to teach us that all men desire the good, since even those who seem to go astray on account of greed desire the good. For those people are indeed seekers of profit; profit is useful, and the useful is truly good: therefore, they desire the good. Furthermore, profit is the opposite of loss: loss, when it occurs, is an evil: therefore, profit is the opposite of evil. That which is opposite to evil is good: therefore, profit is good. For which reason, since even those who seem to turn away from the desire for good actually desire the good, nothing now prevents the conclusion that all men desire the good. But the good <margin>B</margin> is twofold. One is the end itself, if you will. The other is for the sake of the end. The former is to be sought for its own sake, the latter for the sake of something else. The desire for the former is called "will" <note>Latin: *voluntas*</note>, the choice of the latter is "election" <note>Latin: *electio*</note>. The former can lead to the venerable attainment of the good. But that which does not contribute to this is neither useful in itself, nor is its acquisition a profit. Therefore, the desire for profit is to be praised, as it is inherent in everyone by nature. However, false opinion is to be condemned, which, while it is ignorant of what is truly useful and profitable, twists the natural desire toward contrary things. Plato teaches all these things latently, while Socrates refutes the false definitions which Hipparchus offers concerning the desire for profit, both by induction and by reasoning. Moreover, Plato uses <margin>C</margin> this proposition—"All men desire the good"—as if it were self-evident, to conclude that all men by nature desire profit, and that this natural desire is to be praised. This is the conclusion which Socrates infers in a direct manner by three modes of arguing: that is, by example, by induction, and by reasoning. But in a converse manner, from this whole dispute, we gather through an argument from the lesser <note>A logical move from a smaller premise to a larger conclusion</note> that the most confirmed proposition is that "All men desire [the good]," which is the ultimate goal of this book, while the primary goal is to show that all are seekers of profit, and that this is not to be condemned.

### ARGUMENT ON THE DIALOGUE CONCERNING PHILOSOPHY. referring to page 4.

<margin>D</margin>The sum of this dialogue is to define what a philosopher is and what his duty is. Now, the duty of a philosopher is to know divine things and to govern human things: in the former, contemplative philosophy is included; in the latter, active philosophy. Thus, the philosopher first contemplates through wisdom the divine—that is, the absolute nature of the Good itself. Then, directing human operations toward that good as toward an end, he governs human affairs. This governance, however, requires two things. First, that he knows what human nature is, and in what way it may be led toward the good and removed from evil: which the philosopher indeed does through prudence. Second, that he so institutes the affections and acts of men, and so tempers and restrains them, that they may easily tend toward the good which wisdom itself had found, and toward which prudence then directed them. This is truly effected through the moral virtues, all of which Plato encompasses under the single name of Justice. And from these two, the governance of human affairs consists. Moreover, it belongs to the same person to know how to rightly govern one man, a family, and a republic. For which reason, he who is moral would also be a master, a citizen, and a fit king. From which it is concluded that in the very duty of philosophizing all these are contained: wisdom, prudence, justice, and moral, domestic, civil, and royal discipline. Through wisdom he knows divine things; through prudence and justice he governs human things, while he administers his own affairs, family affairs, and the republic. Such is the duty of the philosopher himself, which Plato explains more broadly in the books on the *Republic*, and signifies more briefly here. And first, he refutes two opinions of others concerning the philosopher's duty. The first seems to have been that of Solon or someone similar, saying it is to speak as much as possible; the second that of Hippias the Sophist, wishing philosophy to be a skill in the arts. Finally, having refuted these, he briefly hints at the opinion we stated before. Socrates is therefore imagined to have disputed these things in the school of Dionysius—who taught Plato the elements of grammar—against two disciples of Dionysius: then he recounts from the beginning among a circle of his associates what he had treated in the schools.

### ARGUMENT ON THE THEAGES. referring to page 7.

In this dialogue, Wisdom is distinguished, and the final member of the distinction is taken up for investigation in such a way that the

<column-break/>

manner in which it is acquired by men may be made clear. By the first partition, Wisdom is said to be twofold. One is absolute, the other conditional. Absolute wisdom is that which is called "Wisdom" simply, without any addition. Conditional <margin>A</margin> wisdom is that which is not called wisdom simply, but a "certain wisdom." The former is defined thus: The knowledge of those things about which science <note>Latin: *scientia*, meaning certain knowledge</note> can be had. Now, science is had concerning those things which are always the same and in the same way: of this sort are the highest principles of things, and the eternal reasons of all things: these are called divine, whence it follows that wisdom is the science of divine things: which is indeed absolute wisdom. But conditional wisdom is common to all arts and faculties. For the excellence of any art is called a "certain wisdom," such as the wisdom of steering, the wisdom of chariot-driving, or military wisdom. But out of all those which are named with the addition of "wisdom," the chief is that which <margin>B</margin> uses the others as servants, of which sort is civil wisdom. This faculty, aiming at the common good of the city and of nations, is so defined. This is called both civil and royal discipline. Its subject is the city; its end, the common good; its servants, all the arts. Its duties are two: to establish laws, and to execute those established. The former it does through legislative prudence, the latter through legal and judicial justice. But in what way one may obtain civil wisdom, Plato doubts in many of his disputes: and in the present *Theages*, whether civil men, or sophists, or only contemplative philosophers teach it. That it is learned from civil men, or sophists, or those devoted solely to contemplation, he denies in the *Meno* and here in a certain way, because the former <margin>C</margin> have never even taught their own sons, because the second have no account of the good, and because the third are least experienced in human affairs. It remains, therefore, that this is either perceived by philosophers who are excellently skilled in both contemplating and acting, or perhaps it happens by divine gift. The former are found nowhere. Whence in the *Meno* and in the *Theages*, he asserts it happens by divine gift, so that by God's providence, He pours into the tempered souls of citizens the understanding of the Good itself, and the laws leading to it. This notion he calls "civil wisdom" here, and in the *Meno* by a more proper name he calls it a certain "Prophecy" <note>Latin: *Vaticinium*</note>, and compares civil men to those in a frenzy. He also often <margin>D</margin> says that the human race will never cease from evils unless either legitimate philosophers rule, or those who govern the republic philosophize by some divine chance. In this book, when Socrates had distinguished wisdom into its members, and had said—under a certain species of irony—that Theages could obtain this civil wisdom neither from civil men nor from himself (as a philosopher devoted to contemplation), he added that the power of the spirit <note>Latin: *daemonis*</note> must be tested, and finally the will of God must be implored with prayers, as if those things are learned from there, and the providence of God often opens the oracles of things to be done to men through intermediary spirits. Those ministers who, by God's command, illuminate the minds of good citizens and legitimate princes for governing well, Dionysius the Areopagite <margin>E</margin> calls "Principalities." One should perhaps dispute here about the Spirit <note>Daemon</note> of Socrates, but the brevity of the argument prevents it. Furthermore, Maximus of Tyre, and Hermias, and Apuleius have discussed this abundantly. Moreover, Plato introduces three persons here: Demodocus, an Athenian citizen, together with his son Theages who is desiring wisdom, and Socrates. The dialogue begins from the petition of Demodocus.

### ARGUMENT ON THE MENO. referring to page 12.

<margin>F</margin>There are four kinds of arguments which Plato uses: example, induction, reasoning, and the enthymeme <note>A logical argument where one premise is implied</note>: and in what way they are made is sufficiently declared in the compendium of Alcinous, which we also translated. There we also find three species of Platonic dialogues, and which arguments he is accustomed to use in each species of dialogue. For a dialogue either only inquires and refutes false things; or it only explains and teaches true things; or it is engaged in both. The first is "inquisitive and contentious." The second is "expository." The last is called "mixed." Although the *Meno* is mixed, it nevertheless for the most part contends and refutes, <margin>G</margin> and touches upon all arguments. So that unless one gathers the sense from other dialogues of Plato which pertain more to exposition than to debate, and adds it to this *Meno*, he could with difficulty elicit the sum of this dispute. Now this is: to inquire what virtue is, and how it is present in us. Socrates effects this while he refutes four definitions of virtue by Meno, Aristippus, Gorgias, and Prodicus, and retracts his own definition introduced after those with twin objections. Truth, indeed, shines forth from the refutation of falsehood. Now, the virtue of a man is an affection, or a habit of the soul, by which its natural power performs its work as well as possible; which definition is <margin>H</margin> handed down in the books on the *Republic*. The work of any power is then performed best when it is directed toward its end. That which contributes to the end is called useful. Deservedly, therefore, in this dispute, the common duty of virtue is handed down as being this: that it [directs] both actions and those things which we use in acting...

# ARGUMENTS AND COMMENTARY

render. Therefore, that definition <note>referring to the definition of virtue discussed on the previous page</note> agrees with this dialogue and is common to all virtues. Indeed, there are many species of virtues, according to the diversity of the soul's powers and acts, in which, however, that one common principle of virtue already mentioned is always observed. The first power of the soul is the **Mind** <note>Latin: *mens*, often referring to the highest intellect</note>, whose act is the perpetual contemplation of truth. The second is **Reason**, whose act is the investigation of truth. The third is **Imagination** <note>Latin: *phantasia*</note>, whose act is the collection of those things which the senses offer through their messages, and discourse through them. And these are the powers of the soul which are called cognitive. There remain three others, which they call appetitive: **Will**, the **Irascible power** <note>the spirited or assertive element</note>, and the **Concupiscible power** <note>the desiring element</note>. The act of the Will is to desire what the mind and reason offer. The Irascible is to attack what reason and imagination propose. The Concupiscible is to adopt what the imagination and senses present. Beyond these six, two others are subordinate: the vigor of movement and of nourishment; but these, along with the higher powers, share nothing, or scarcely anything and very little, in virtue. <margin>B</margin> The disposition of the mind which perfects contemplation is **Wisdom**; that which perfects the investigation of reason is **Science** and **Prudence**. Science is indeed the investigation of those things which nature makes; Prudence is the deliberation in those things which we ourselves do. Right opinion, which some call sagacity, perfects the discourse of the imagination. **Justice** and **Liberality** perfect the will. **Fortitude** and its followers perfect the irascible. **Continence** and **Temperance** together perfect the concupiscible. Common to all these is that any one of them is a disposition perfecting the acts of a natural power, while it renders them decorous and useful for attaining the ultimate end. Truly, various virtues are possessed in different ways. Wisdom is indeed by nature: for it is the eternal embrace of all reasons in the mind, and the perpetual intuition of truth. <margin>C</margin> Science is acquired through the teaching of philosophy which provides **reminiscence** <note>the Platonic idea that learning is recovering forgotten knowledge from before birth</note>, while reason, which once cast off its wings, having turned back to the mind, recovers its wings again by remembering. Prudence comes through teaching combined with long experience of things. Right opinion comes perhaps by examples, authority, and induction. Justice, fortitude, temperance, and the other moral virtues are perfected by the laws of prudence and right opinion and by legitimate exercise. Whence Plato placed these two principles of the moral virtues: prudence and right opinion. For this reason, prudence frequently usurps the name of the whole moral virtue in Plato's works. There is also a certain virtue pertaining to right opinion, by which legitimate princes and citizens, honest in action yet lacking in contemplation, care for the public good; this they call **civil skill**. And Plato disputes, both in the *Theages* and in the present *Meno*, that this faculty is given to civil men in no other way than by divine lot. By this summary, therefore, one may gather the mind of Plato in the *Meno*, and having premised this distinction, will refute contradiction and avoid objections. Truly, I did not think it right to treat that disputation concerning reminiscence and Geometric figures in the argument, because it was inserted not as the principal matter, but as an accessory. For an argument requires the sum and the head of the matter. Indeed, to discuss individual points is the duty not of an argument, but rather of a commentary.

### ON THE FIRST ALCIBIADES
->Argument. See page 25.<-

This most brilliant book of our Plato, which is inscribed *The First Alcibiades*, more beautiful than Alcibiades himself and dearer than all gold, teaches what man is and what his duty is. Now, man is a **rational soul**, partaking of mind, using a body. From this definition, his duty is drawn, distributed in three ways. For as he is a rational soul, he reflects upon himself in a certain circle of reasoning by noticing himself. As he is a partaker of mind, he flows back into the divine mind like a rivulet into its fountain. As he is one using a body, he applies himself to governing human affairs. Therefore, the perfect and absolute duty of man is, first indeed, that he notice his own nature; then, from that nature as if from an image and effect, he should be converted to the divine mind, its exemplar and cause. Illumined by this, the soul of man understands the Good itself, the Useful itself, the Beautiful itself, the Just itself, and perfectly comprehends his own good, utility, beauty, and justice. Whence he knows what is good and what is useful for other men with whom he lives or whom he commands; and when he has known the absolute good, his own good, and the good of others, he ought then to approach the care of himself and every other person according to the norm of the known good. There is need for the study of philosophy—moral, mathematical, and theological—so that he may return to himself and to his own mind. For moral and mathematical philosophy restores the soul submerged in the body to itself; theology snatches it above itself and raises it outside itself into God. The knowledge of the divine mind and the **Ideas** is called Wisdom. The knowledge of oneself, and the discovery of one's own and one's people's good and utility flowing from the intuition of the divine mind, is called Prudence. Prudence, insofar as it understands the good, refers human actions, both public and private, to the best end. Insofar as it understands the useful, it directs through convenient means and proper ways by which the end may be reached. Insofar as it understands the beautiful, it institutes what order and what measure must be preserved in this progress as if on a certain journey. Insofar as it understands the just, it prescribes what distinction of individual works, what observance of the imposed order, what punishment for the transgressor, and what reward for the one observing the law of this journey. Thus from philosophy to wisdom, and from wisdom to prudence, an approach is made; and prudence, the mistress of life, grants the discipline of one's own domestic affairs and of the republic. Man governs through prudence; but the home and the city are preserved through public friendship and justice. I call **public friendship** that consensus by which all willingly agree under the same law and prince and look toward the same end. I name **public justice** the legitimate distinction by which individuals, though under the same prince and toward the same end (that is, the public good), nevertheless proceed by a different

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> path; and they preserve the various distribution of duties assigned by nature and laws according to the nature and dignity of each one, and they perform their own office without the usurpation of another's. In this dialogue there are two theological expressions: *the same itself* <note>original: "ipsum idem"</note>, and *each thing itself* <note>original: "ipsum unumquodque"</note>. Concerning man, the former signifies the soul as an Idea; the latter, the soul in the body. But concerning these things, I will write more extensively in the commentaries which I have now resolved to write on these ten dialogues of Plato.

### ON THE SECOND ALCIBIADES
->Argument. See page 38.<-

Since the *Second Alcibiades*, a truly most holy book, is inscribed "On Prayer" <note>original: "de voto"</note>, we must summarize what a prayer is, what should be sought in prayer, and when, and how. This definition of prayer, taken partly from Orpheus and partly from Plato, is this: **Prayer is the ardent affection of a chaste soul, dedicated to God, and desiring what seems good.** To this affection, Zoroaster and Orpheus applied incenses and characters <note>mystical symbols</note> whenever prayers were directed to the secondary deities. Hermes <note>original: "Mercurius"</note> and Plato, when they venerated the majesty of the supreme deity, removed all external ceremonies, leaving only the pure and burning heat of the soul. But concerning all these things, more diligently in our commentaries. In prayer, Plato wishes the **Good** to be sought; and this is evident from the fact <margin>C</margin> that he confirms this petition by the testimony of the poet and the Lacedaemonians, and he thinks it is safe for both the prudent and the imprudent, and that a prayer of this kind can be made by anyone and always. But he thinks the petition for a certain and specific good is only then secure when one has attained prudence, but otherwise it is dangerous. Here he discourses much concerning prudence, which I pray you, Cosmo <note>Cosimo de' Medici, the translator's patron</note>, most prudent of all men, read diligently, so that you may thoroughly recognize how much he values prudence. Therefore, a universal prayer, by which only the good is sought, can always be made; but a specific one, by which something certain that seems good <margin>D</margin> is desired, should be made only when one knows what must be asked. One will know that when he understands what is good and what is evil. He will understand that when he has learned it from the mind. He will learn it when he turns himself toward it. He will turn when he has purged his soul and expelled the darkness. He will purge it when he has given himself to legitimate philosophy. He will give himself when he has recognized his own ignorance. Therefore, **"Know Thyself"** was inscribed on the temple of Apollo, lest anyone should rashly approach to pray to God. Moreover, in what order one should pray in a specific prayer, Hermes taught in his orations, and Orpheus in his hymns, and Pythagoras in his *Golden Verses*; whose rites we shall explain elsewhere. Then Plato, imitating these theologians, introduces Socrates praying thus in the book *On Beauty* <note>The Phaedrus</note>: "O friend Pan and other deities, grant, I pray, that I may become beautiful within; and whatever things lie outside me, let them be <margin>E</margin> friendly to my internal things. Let me think the wise man alone to be rich. But grant only as much of this gold as no one else can carry or lead except a temperate man." What does Socrates seek? The Good. What good? Wisdom, that is, the knowledge of divine truth, which God alone can give, and which only a beautiful soul—that is, a temperate, pure, and bright soul—is able to receive. What does he ask first? That He make him worthy of wisdom. For it is the part of a rash man to seek some gift of which he is unworthy. Who is worthy of divine wisdom? He who is prepared to bear its light. Who is prepared? He who through continence first, then through temperance, and finally through holiness—that is, the civil, purgative, and purged virtue of the soul—<margin>F</margin> has so expiated his soul that it has emerged beautiful, that is, entirely pure and shining; and who has now desired the exemplary virtue, namely divine wisdom alone, as the treasure of all riches. Therefore, Socrates prays that God the father of all and his ministers may breathe upon him as friends, so that having been purged by their kind and propitious favor, he may emerge. Truly, he passes lightly over corporeal and external things, choosing that they be such that they do not impede the tranquil purity of the soul. Then, with this beauty already acquired, he desires that he may estimate wisdom alone, that is, the knowledge of God, to be all wealth and sufficiency, and he alone will be made so. Finally, as if prepared by the aforesaid things, he asks for this glowing gold of divine <margin>G</margin> wisdom. And he does this neither proudly nor yet remissly. For intemperate men obtain the least knowledge of truth; God embraces the highest and infinite knowledge in Himself; but the temperate man attains a great and ample share. Therefore, he asked for as much of this gold as a temperate man alone is able to carry. Indeed, I judge this to be the "gold tried in the fire" which John in the *Apocalypse* commanded to be bought.

### ON THE MINOS
->Argument. See page 44.<-

<margin>H</margin> The *Minos* inquires concerning the law: what law is in general, and how many are its species. Whence it is, let us comprehend in a few words. If anyone diligently notices the words of Plato in this book *On the Law*, and in the books *On the Laws*, and also *On the Republic*, he will describe law by this universal definition: **Law is the true reason of governing, which directs the governed toward the best end through convenient means, establishing punishment for the transgressor and reward for the obedient.** From which it happens that the institutions of princes, when they are not true, nor proceed by a straight path to the best, are by no means laws, but are decrees, edicts, or institutes rather than laws. For from law comes "legitimate," from legitimate "just," and from just a "good and right work" is frequently named; therefore it is necessary that law be true and good. It also follows that law is eternal and entirely immutable, and the same among all nations concerning the same things, if it be true in this way: for those things which...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentaries on Plato’s dialogues, specifically concluding a discussion on the nature of Law and beginning the introductions (arguments) to the Euthyphro, Parmenides, and Philebus.</meta>

# MARSILIO FICINO

<margin>A</margin> If it is changed by times, places, and opinions, it is called not a law, but an institution. However, as gathered from the *Timaeus*, *Phaedrus*, and *Gorgias*, there are four types of Law. First is the divine, which Plato calls Providence. Second is the celestial, called Fate. Third is the moving, called Nature. Fourth is the human, called natural prudence. The first resides in the divine mind, which Orpheus and Plato wish to be the law of Saturn <note>Saturn represents the highest intellectual deity in Neoplatonic thought</note>. The second is in the superior part of the World Soul, which they call the law of Jupiter. The third is in the moving and inferior power of that soul, which they call the law of the first Venus. The last is in the mind of man, which they call the law of the second Venus. The first flows from the Supreme Good, which is above the mind. The second from the mind and the Supreme Good. The third from the Supreme Good, the mind, and the universal soul. The fourth likewise from the Supreme Good, the mind, and the soul. Indeed, all are reflected back again toward the Good itself. The first exists in the Ideas, around the Supreme Good, above reasons. The second in reasons, around the Ideas, above seeds. The third in seeds, around reasons, above forms. The fourth in notions, around reasons, above acts and arts, which they call the Royal Law, an imitator of the celestial King. From where law originates is elicited from what has been said. For all flow from the very principle of things, though in various ways. For this reason, all illustrious founders of laws have referred the invention of laws to God, though through different names and mediums. Zoroaster, giving laws to the Bactrians and Persians, referred to Horomazes <note>Ahura Mazda</note>. Trismegistus to the Egyptians, to Mercury <note>Thoth/Hermes</note>. Moses to the Jews, most rightly to God, the father of all nature. Minos to the Cretans, to Jupiter. 
<margin>C</margin> Charondas to the Carthaginians, to Saturn. Lycurgus to the Lacedaemonians, to Apollo. Draco and Solon to the Athenians, to Minerva. Pompilius to the Romans, to Egeria. Muhammad to the Arabs, to Gabriel. Zamolxis to the Scythians, to Vesta. Our Plato to the Magnesians and Sicilians, to Jupiter and Apollo. However, he refused the Arcadians, Thebans, and Cyrenaics when they requested laws.

---

### ON THE EUTYPHRO
#### Argument. Referring to page 48.

The *Euthyphro* is entirely occupied with refutation. Because of this, some Platonists have called this book "litigious" or "contentious," just like the *Euthydemus* and *Hippias*. But in truth, while Socrates refutes Euthyphro’s false opinions regarding holiness, he marks the tracks for those hunting the truth. In this book, and also in the *Gorgias*, Plato defines holiness as that part of justice which gives God His due. He gives God His due who returns to God those things which he received from God without a medium. Our body, as Plato discusses in the book *On Nature*, we received from the four elements; the natural complexion of the species from the celestial spheres; the parts of the soul dragged by passions from the demons and the souls of the stars and spheres. But reason and mind—the image of our Parent—we received from the Architect of the whole world Himself, without any ministry of the heavenly dwellers or demons. These things, therefore, belong to God; these must be returned to God, and this retribution is called holiness. Piety precedes it; religion follows it. For piety is the recognition of God the Parent. Holiness is the returning of what is God’s to God, once He is recognized. Religion is the indissoluble binding <note>Ficino etymologically links 'religio' to 'religare' (to bind back)</note> back to God Himself of that which has been returned to Him, through constant meditation and just works. Thus that wise man rightly said that a "triple cord is not easily broken"—a cord, I say, woven from piety, holiness, and religion. Piety excites holiness; holiness confirms and sanctifies piety. Holiness also moves religion. Religion binds holiness. For first there is need of this work, either by instinct, inspiration, or admonition: that we think with undoubting faith that the one God is our Parent—which they wish to be piety. When one has conceived this, he soon fixes every intention of mind and reason upon knowing and loving God. And Mercury <note>Hermes Trismegistus</note> also defines holiness as this frequent intuition in knowing and loving divinity. From this burning intention toward God and ardor of mind, it happens that we meditate upon and practice all God’s works, institutions, and commands, and we constantly "re-read" <note>Latin: *relegamus*, another etymological root for religion</note> whatever pertains to His veneration. Therefore, by binding ourselves back to God, we are religious. With this definition and distinction established, what is said about holiness in the *Euthyphro* or elsewhere by Plato becomes clear. When it is said that the holy is what is loved by God, it is true; but because it is holy, it is loved by God—it is not holy because it is loved. And because it is loved, it is a "beloved thing"; yet it is not loved because it is a "beloved thing"; since <margin>G</margin> the essence of holiness is not entirely the same as being loved. For the definition of holiness does not consist in being loved, but rather in retribution and devotion itself. Furthermore, when it is said, "Holiness is a ministering care for God," that is also true. But for what work of God is it a minister? For the conversion of the soul. For the work of God is to create, to convert, to purge, to illuminate, and to perfect. As soon as God begins to convert the soul to Himself by inspiring it through the instinct of piety, that very assent by which the soul willingly restores itself to the God who converts it is called holiness, which is indeed <margin>H</margin> a minister of God for completing the conversion. Finally, it is added: "Holiness is the science of vowing and sacrificing to God." This pertains mostly to religion, which, as we said, accompanies holiness. By vowing, one asks; by sacrificing, one gives. What does he ask from God? Himself. What does he give to God? Himself. He asks for that same thing which is in the divine mind, which Mercury sought from Pymander. He gives, however, his own nature as a participant in the Idea.

---

### ON THE PARMENIDES
#### Argument. Referring to page 54.

While Plato scattered the seeds of all wisdom through all his dialogues, in the books on the *Republic* he collected all the

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> institutions of moral philosophy; he embraced the entire science of natural things in the *Timaeus*, and in the *Parmenides* he encompassed the whole of theology. While in other works he surpassed other philosophers by a long distance, in this one he finally seems to have surpassed himself, divinely bringing forth this celestial work from the inner sanctuary of philosophy and the shrines of the divine mind. Whoever approaches its sacred reading should first prepare himself with sobriety of soul and freedom of mind before daring to touch the mysteries of this heavenly work. For here the divine Plato disputes most subtly about the One itself: how the One itself is the principle of all things, above all things, and all things are from it. In what way it is outside all things and in all things, and all things are from it, through it, and toward it. To the understanding of this One, which is above essence, <margin>B</margin> he ascends by steps. For the One is found in a triple order. In those things which flow and are subject to the senses, called "sensibles." Also in those things which are always the same, called "intelligibles," perceived no longer by the senses but by the mind alone. And not only in these, but even above sense and sensibles, and intellect and intelligibles, the One itself exists. For this reason, in this dialogue, Zeno of Elea, the first disciple of the Pythagorean Parmenides, proves that there is a "one" in sensible things, showing that if these were many without participating in the nature of the one, many errors would follow. Then Socrates, not opposing Zeno but raising him higher, leads him to the consideration of the One and the unities that exist in intelligible things, <margin>C</margin> lest he linger only in this "one" which exists in sensibles. From this, they arrive at investigating the Ideas, in which the unities of things consist. Finally, the elder Parmenides himself, not contradicting Socrates but completing his begun contemplation, explains the entire system of Ideas. Here he introduces four questions about Ideas. First, whether they exist. Second, of what things there are Ideas, and of what there are not. Third, what kind they are, and what power they have. Fourth, how they are participated in by those things below them. From here he ascends to the One which exists above intelligibles and Ideas, and brings forth nine suppositions about it: five if the One exists, four if the One does not exist, asking what follows in either case. These suppositions are drawn from a triple partition of the One and a double <margin>D</margin> partition of "non-being." For the One is found to be triple: above being, in being, and after being. Non-being itself is subject to a twofold consideration: either one thinks it exists in no way at all, or that it partly is and partly is not. The first supposition treats: if the One exists above being, what follows concerning it in relation to itself and to others. The second: if the One is with being, how it relates to itself and others. The third: if the One is placed under being, what happens to it in relation to itself and others. The fourth: if the One stands above being, how others relate to themselves and to the One. The fifth: if that One exists which is located with being, what happens to others in relation to themselves and to it. The sixth: if the One is not, such that it partly is and partly is not, how it relates to itself and others. The seventh: if the One is not, such that it is in no way, how it <margin>E</margin> relates to itself and others. The eighth: if the One is not, such that it partly is and partly is not, what happens to others in relation to themselves and to it. The ninth: if the One is not, such that it is in no way, what others finally suffer in relation to themselves and to it. In all these, Parmenides generally intends to assert primarily that the One is the principle of all things: with it established, all things are established; with it removed, all are destroyed. Thus, in the first five suppositions, he teaches five grades of things with the One placed in the order of things. In the following four, he inquires how many absurdities, errors, and evils follow if the One is removed. The first of the five superior ones discusses the One and the Supreme God: how He procreates and disposes the orders of the following gods. The second concerns the individual orders of gods, how they proceed from God Himself. The third concerns divine souls. The fourth <margin>F</margin> concerns those things which occur around matter: how they are produced by celestial causes. The fifth concerns prime matter, how by its own nature it is devoid of forms and depends on the first One. Furthermore, it should be noted that in this dialogue, when "the One" is mentioned, in the Pythagorean manner any substance entirely freed from matter can be signified: such as God, Mind, or Soul. When "the other" and "others" are mentioned, one may understand both matter and those things which occur in matter. With these things premised and observed, let us come to the dialogue itself.

---

### ON THE PHILEBUS
#### Argument. Referring to page 72.

<margin>G</margin> The purpose of this book is to discuss the highest good of the soul, which is indeed called the highest good with a certain condition, since the principle of all things itself is called the Supreme Good absolutely. Therefore, concerning this "conditional good," we dispute in this book; concerning the "absolute good," in the *Parmenides*. From the absolute, however, this flows, just as a certain light depends on the very source of all light. For this reason, it was said by Plato in the *Phaedo* and *Theaetetus* that the highest good of the soul is likeness to God. But nothing is like the sun except by a certain infusion of its light. Whence the soul's <margin>H</margin> good will be the complete attainment of divine light. That light descends first into the mind, then into the will. In the mind is truth, in the will is joy; in the mind is ambrosia, in the will is nectar, as they are named by Plato here and in the *Phaedrus*. Thus he placed the highest good of man in the mixture of wisdom and pleasure. But first he denied that beatitude could consist in the ratio of wisdom alone or pleasure alone, because the triple condition of the highest good is found in neither. That condition is: that it be supremely perfect, sufficient, and desirable. Perfect, because it lacks nothing. Sufficient, because nothing is lacking to him who possesses it. Desirable, because in it and from it is whatever can be sought—

<summary>This page contains Marsilio Ficino's introductory arguments for Plato's Euthyphro, Parmenides, and Philebus, focusing on the definitions of holiness, the metaphysical hierarchy of "The One," and the nature of the human "highest good." Ficino synthesizes Platonic thought with Hermetic and religious traditions, emphasizing the soul's return to its divine source.</summary>
<keywords>Marsilio Ficino, Plato, Euthyphro, Parmenides, Philebus, holiness, The One, Supreme Good, Neoplatonism, theology, Ideas, piety, religion</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the introductory arguments and commentaries by Marsilio Ficino on the dialogues of Plato, specifically concluding the discussion on the *Philebus* and beginning the *Hippias Major* and *Lysis*.</meta>

<margin>A</margin>
witness. Whence, because it is perfect, it is sufficient; because it is sufficient, it is to be sought after. Truly, because it is enough for itself, it suffices for another; because it suffices for another, it is desired by another. These qualities are demonstrated to belong neither to wisdom alone, nor to pleasure alone, but to a certain mixture of both. Here, many things are said concerning the kind, origin, and nature of pleasure and wisdom, concerning the infinite and the limit, and concerning the composite and the principle of composition. And finally, it is concluded that the highest and absolute good in nature is the measure of all things, that is, the principle of the whole of nature. But the highest good of the mind and soul is the possession of that first principle, which belongs to the mixture of wisdom and pleasure through truth, proportion, and beauty.

<margin>B</margin>
Wherefore, in the first grade of goods, the measure of all things is placed; in the second, truth, proportion, and beauty; in the third, mind and wisdom; in the fourth, science, art, and opinion; in the fifth, tempered pleasure. And that man is called blessed who has attained both the wisdom of divine things and the skill in human affairs consisting of a certain science, art, and opinion; he exults entirely in the joy of contemplation, and commits himself to the pleasure of the senses only so far as wisdom, science, and joy receive no hindrance therefrom. The introduction to the dialogue is of this sort: When Socrates and Philebus had contributed many things back and forth concerning the highest good, and Philebus was now weary of disputing, he congratulated Protarchus, who had recently arrived, and nodded for him to take up his role in the dispute. Protarchus, being a youth, suddenly agreed. Turning to him, Socrates said: "Consider what guardianship you are undertaking, and do not hasten rashly into the dispute. Rather, hear the opinion of each first, and take up the defense of that which appears more probable to you as you examine it with right reason." But now let us come to the dialogue.

# ON THE GREATER HIPPIAS
## Argument. Referring to page 95.

Beauty is disputed in the *Phaedrus*, the *Symposium*, and the *Hippias*. In the *Hippias*, because Socrates acts against Hippias the sophist—who, though he was ignorant, thought he knew, which ignorance renders the soul unteachable—he does not sufficiently teach what beauty is, but shows what it is not, and refutes false opinions. He calls him a "sophist" who strives to seem wise rather than to be so, for the sake of money and honor. That Hippias is such a man is declared in the prologue and at the end of the prologue. Taking occasion from a certain speech of Hippias which discussed beautiful duties, Socrates asks what is "beauty itself" through which all other things are beautiful.

<margin>C</margin>
For it is necessary to refer particulars to the universal which is in particulars, and the universal which is in particulars to that universal which is above individual things. For individual beautiful men are rendered beautiful through a certain form common to individuals; but the form common to many is impressed by the divine species as if by a seal <note>Ficino uses the metaphor of a signet ring (character) to explain how divine ideas shape physical reality</note>; since every multitude is reduced to the "one" which is in the multitude, and the "one" in the multitude to the "one" which is above the multitude. Therefore, since there are many beautiful things, it is necessary that each be beautiful through a beauty common to all and inherent in all; and that the beauty which is in all, just as it exists in another and not in itself, so it depends on another and not on itself. Each of the individual beautiful things Plato calls "this beautiful thing"; the form in all, he calls "beauty"; the species and idea above all, he calls "beauty itself."

<margin>D</margin>
Sense and opinion reach the first. Reason thinks the second. The mind <note>Latin: *mens*, referring to the highest intuitive intellect</note> contemplates the third. Hippias, being questioned, defines it through the second [level], the opinion of the senses. These being refuted, Socrates also defines it three times. Twice indeed according to reason, and lastly according to the mind. For the sophist walks by sense and opinion; the philosopher rather by reason and the mind. First, Hippias answers that a beautiful maiden is beauty itself. That this is false is evident from the fact that not all things that are beautiful become beautiful through a maiden. And a maiden, if compared with the beasts, appears beautiful; if with the gods, she appears deformed. Therefore, she seems no more beautiful than ugly. Then Hippias answers with something else similarly from individual beautiful things, not a common one: namely, that gold is beauty itself, by which all things become beautiful. Socrates rejects this on the grounds that gold makes those things beautiful to which it is suited, but deforms others. Therefore, it does not make things simply beautiful, but only when it is fitting.

<margin>E</margin>
Wherefore, a thing is adorned no more by its own nature than by the account of another; nor is gold the only thing by which all things are adorned, but also silver and ivory, and other things of this kind.

<margin>F</margin>
In the third place, he brings in something else, which is also specific rather than common: "It is beautiful," he says, "to be healthy in body, to be rich and honored, to die an old man, to be buried by one's sons, and to have buried one's parents." It is clear that this is false:

<margin>G</margin>
<unclear>Moreover</unclear>, this is perhaps beautiful among men; among the gods and the sons of gods it is base, where parents do not die. These things having been refuted—which Hippias brought forward concerning individual corporeal things through sense and opinion—Socrates, now tending toward higher things, brings forward not what sense offers to opinion, but what reason offers to opinion. For first, he says the "becoming" <note>Latin: *decorum*, meaning the appropriate or fitting</note> is the beautiful. This is indeed more incorporeal and common to more things. Yet he refutes it by this division:

<margin>H</margin>
The becoming either provides only the appearance of beauty, or provides both the appearance and the reality. If the first, the becoming exists as a certain deception concerning the beautiful, rather than beauty itself. For true beauty makes things be beautiful, just as true magnitude makes things large, even if they are not seen. If you say the second, you speak falsely. For if beauty itself, as often as it grants being beautiful, also provided the appearance of it, then whatever things are beautiful would appear so to everyone just as they are. That this is false, the contentions and controversies concerning beautiful things show us. Secondly, he brings forward something else that reason offers to opinion: he calls the "useful" beautiful. Utility is something incorporeal and common to many. Nor is it a wonder that thought is deceived concerning the becoming and the useful. For the former involves the order

<column-break/>

<margin>B</margin>
of part to part, and of parts to the whole; while the latter involves the order of a certain whole to another whole; and order truly seems to look toward beauty. Wherefore, one easily accepts the becoming or the useful in place of the beautiful. That the becoming is not the beautiful has been established; that the useful is not, he shows thus: The useful is that which has the power to do something. Therefore, power and utility are the same. Whatever we do, we do by a certain power, but we mostly do evil things; therefore power and utility mostly bring about evil, but the beautiful is never the cause of evil. Therefore, not just any utility is the beautiful. But at least that which contributes to the good, someone will answer; against whom he argues thus: That which tends toward the good is the conducive. The conducive produces the good; that which produces something is different from that which is produced; wherefore the conducive is one thing, the good another. The conducive and the beautiful are the same. Therefore the beautiful and the good are different. Thus, neither is the beautiful the good, nor the good the beautiful—which is utterly absurd. Finally, the errors of sense-opinion and thought having been convicted, the mind dictates to reason that the beautiful is a certain grace which moves and allures the soul through the mind, sight, and hearing. This is indeed elicited partly from the end of this dialogue, and partly from the *Phaedrus* and *Symposium* of Plato. By what means this grace is inherent, and by what name it should be called, Socrates inquires; yet he does not declare it to the ambitious sophist, but revealed it to Phaedrus and Agathon, who, although they were ignorant, were teachable because they acknowledged their ignorance. Truly, beauty is grace, not by reason of sense, because it would not suit the mind, and would belong to the other senses just as much as to hearing and sight. Not by reason of the mind alone, because it would escape the eyes and ears. Nor even by reason of pleasure, because this is found not only in hearing and sight, but in all the senses. Not by reason of hearing alone, for it would not fit the mind and sight. Not by reason of sight, for it would be lacking to hearing and the mind. Not by reason of hearing and sight together, because beauty is in sight and hearing joined as one; but in each of them acting separately from the other, there is no beauty. We wish, however, that grace be perceived commonly by the three powers of the soul, and be inherent commonly in their three objects. Wherefore he adds that the pleasures of the mind, sight, and hearing are beautiful because they are the most harmless and best of all pleasures. If you understand "best" as the same as "conducive," the previous ambiguity will return: the conducive produces the good, therefore the good is the cause. The cause and the effect are different. Therefore the conducive is one thing, the good another. From which it follows that the beautiful is one thing, the good another. Therefore neither is the beautiful the good, nor the good the beautiful. But if you explain "best" as meaning harmless, easy, spiritual, shining, and—if I may say so—vital, you will lay hold of the truth. For beauty is nothing other than the splendor of the highest good, shining in those things which are perceived by the eyes, ears, and mind, and through them converting the sight, hearing, and mind toward the good itself. Thus it happens that beauty exists as a certain circle of divine light, flowing from the good, residing in the good, and perpetually reflected through the good and toward the good. This mystery, which Socrates asserted he had learned from the Sibyl Diotima, he revealed not to the sophists, but to his disciples.

<margin>C</margin>
What is the good itself? The "one" itself, the principle of all things, pure act, the act that gives life to all following things. What is beauty itself? The life-giving act flowing from the first fountain of goods, infinitely adorning the divine mind first with the order of ideas, then filling the following deities and the mind with a series of reasons, thirdly adorning souls with numerous discourses, fourthly natures with seeds, and fifthly matter with forms.

<margin>D</margin>
The sun certainly procreates visible bodies and seeing eyes. That the eye may see, it infuses a lucid spirit. That bodies may be seen, it paints them with colors. Yet neither the ray proper to the eyes, nor the colors proper to the bodies, suffice to perfect the vision, unless the one light itself above the many—from which the many and proper lights are distributed to the eyes and bodies—arrives, illustrates, excites, and strengthens them.

<margin>E</margin>
In the same way, that first act itself, which is God, has granted species and act to individual things by producing them. Which act, indeed, when it has been received in a passive subject, is weak and powerless for the execution of its work. But the perpetual and invisible light of the divine Sun always stands by all as one, it cherishes, gives life, excites, completes, and strengthens. Concerning which Orpheus divinely said: "Cherishing all things and himself bearing himself above all things." Insofar as he is the act of all and strengthens them, he is called "the Good." Insofar as he gives life, softens, soothes, and excites, he is called "the Beautiful." Insofar as he allures those three powers of the knowing soul in the objects that are to be known, he is "Beauty." Insofar as he applies that power in the knower to the thing known, he is "Truth." Insofar as he is the Good, he procreates, rules, and completes. Insofar as he is the Beautiful, he illuminates and infuses grace.

<margin>F</margin>
Moreover, all things must be prepared to receive the grace of the divine splendor. Bodies indeed by proportion, which consists of order, measure, and species. Voices by harmony, which is made of numbers and intervals. Duties by the rectitude of morals toward a good end. Disciplines by order toward a true object. The soul by purity through turning away from lower things and turning toward higher things. The mind through an eternal intuition into the good itself. Through all these things, the ray of divine beauty penetrates step by step. Around the body, it shines with a numerous inequality, subject to place and motion. Around voices in harmony, outside a certain place, but dispersed by motion. Around disciplines and the soul, in motion indeed, but consisting in a vital reason. Around the mind, above motion, flashing in the eternal series of ideas. Around the good itself, it is pure act, inserting life and grace into all.

<margin>H</margin>
These things I pray, Piero de' Medici, most distinguished of all men, that you read with your usual diligence. For you will both recognize the wonderful beauty of your own mind, and you will notice how closely you approach that beauty itself which is disputed here.
