<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentaries on Plato’s dialogues, specifically concluding the analysis of the *Lysis* (on friendship) and beginning the *Theaetetus* (on knowledge).</meta>

# MARSILIO FICINO

<margin>A</margin>For sharp wits, once false ideas are refuted, hunt down the truth from a slight trail. This is evident in the *Euthydemus*, *Protagoras*, *Meno*, *Hippias*, *Euthyphro*, and *Lysis*. But where he holds discourse with his disciples and those studious of him, he demonstrates and teaches, as is understood from many dialogues. In the *Lysis*, therefore, since the dispute concerns friendship among the disciples of the sophists, Socrates is more intent on refuting falsehoods than on showing truths. What Plato’s actual opinion on friendship and love is, we can gather not only from this book but also from the books of the *Laws* and many others. He intends friendship to be an honorable communion of a perpetual will. Its end is "one life." Its principle is "kinship." <margin>B</margin>Its medium, however, is love. By calling it "honorable," he excludes the companionship of wicked men and the gatherings of the lustful. By "perpetual," he warns that the lighthearted goodwill of youths, even if honorable, is not yet to be called friendship. By "will," he signifies that a mere similarity of opinion or craft is not sufficient to perfect friendship. By "communion," he indicates a reciprocity of goodwill. The end of this is that from two souls, one is made by will; from one will, one life; and finally from one life, the enjoyment of the one divinity and the same Idea. The principle of this communion is excited by desire, which is kinship. Kinship signifies a harmony in the Idea, the star, the guiding spirit <term>genio: a personal guardian spirit or innate nature</term>, and a certain affection of the soul and body. For those who hang from the One strive to return into the One, through the One, and toward the One. Love exists as the medium and, as it were, a path to friendship. Since love is the desire for the beautiful, and friendship is both derived from and named after love, it is necessary that those who are to be friends be beautiful. I say beautiful in that their souls are beautiful. For man is the soul; the body is the instrument of man; and whoever loves a beautiful body loves not the man, but the things that belong to the man. Therefore, whenever that kinship is present and the beauty of souls concurs, perfect friendship is born. If the form of the body is joined to this beauty of souls, they begin to love more quickly and attain the habit of friendship in a short time. This happened in the mutual goodwill of Plato and Dion. But if the form of the body is joined with a deformity of the soul, there arises a desire not for honorable communion, but for a base encounter. From this proceeds not friendship, but first petulance, then discord. Therefore, if kinship is lacking, they are never friends. If kinship is present but all beauty is lacking, they are sometimes well-wishers rather than friends. But if the beauty of the body, not the soul, is joined to kinship, the heat of an obscene encounter arises instead of the desire for friendship. When one is beautiful in soul and the other ugly, that kinship produces a zeal for admonition and rebuke. But if the soul of one is beautiful and the other is neither beautiful nor ugly, a mutual will for teaching and learning arises from the kinship. Finally, from that rebuke and this teaching, friendship is born. This is shown by the love of Socrates for Phaedrus and Alcibiades. But kinship having found beauty on both sides quickly procreates an indissoluble friendship. This happened in the goodwill of Plato and Aster. And this, as gathered from many sources, is the opinion of our Plato on friendship. In this dialogue, he first rebukes those who abuse love and serve base lust under the appearance of friendship. Second, he admonishes those who think themselves worthy of being loved solely because of the form of their body. Third, he refutes those who held less true views on friendship. Finally, he indicates a certain path for sagacious souls to hunt for friendship. The individual parts are clear to readers in their places. He signifies this while Socrates derides Hippothales and Ctesippus with irony and jokes because they were captured by base love. And while he instructs the youths in morals in their presence, he admonishes lovers in what manner they should love and how they should live together. Once he had instructed the lovers, he proceeds to the second part of the dialogue to instruct the beloved. There, by a long series of induction, he teaches that it is fitting to hunt for friends not by the shadowy form of this little body, but by the true beauty of the soul—namely, wisdom and prudence. In the third place, he refutes, first, the opinion of Solon, who said that the beloved are friends. Yet the beloved often hate the lovers. He adds also that lovers alone are not friends, because that which they love is often held in hatred. Here he concludes that reciprocal goodwill must be called friendship. Then he reprehends Empedocles, who wanted any simple similarity to suffice for friendship. That this is false is declared by the similarity of many crafts, which more often begets envy and hatred than friendship. Next comes the opinion of Hesiod and Heraclitus, that dissimilar things are friendly. That this is false is clear from the fact that hatred and love, though dissimilar, are not friends, nor are the just man and the unjust, and so on for others. But if something sometimes seems to seek its dissimilar—as the dry seeks moisture, and the cold seeks heat—it must be said that it does not love its contrary, but seeks the restoration of itself from the contrary. For that which uses excessive heat beyond its nature is reduced to its natural temperament through cold. Therefore, it loves not the cold, but the temperament achieved through the cold. The same is to be judged of other contraries. Having refuted these, Socrates introduces a certain opinion as his own, as if prophesying. <margin>D</margin> Here he divides the affections of the soul into three: the good soul, the evil, and the neutral. The evil is never a friend to the good because of their diversity. The evil is harmed by the evil because of injustice. Therefore, neither are these friends to each other. It is also impossible for the neutral to love the evil; for the evil, since it is harmful, is by its very nature always held in hatred. It remains that friendship is between the good and the evil, and the neutral and the good. The former consists in joy, the latter in desire. From these, two species of friendship have arisen. But certain objections arise which seem to disturb this, which Socrates brings forward openly, but hints at the solutions secretly. First, because the good is similar to the good, but it was said against Empedocles that similar things are not friends. Here it must be understood that it was not said that similar things can in no way become friends, but rather it was denied that simply *any* similarity suffices to procreate friendship. Likewise, when it is objected second: the good man is self-sufficient, therefore he does not desire another, hence he does not love, and thus is not a friend of the good. It must be explained that this absurdity does not follow from Plato’s mind, but from the sayings of Empedocles

<column-break/>

and Heraclitus, in which they do not distinguish the desire of love from friendship; therefore, it would be necessary for a perpetual craving to exist alongside friendship. Plato, however, intends friendship to be a certain habit contracted from long-lasting love. Thus it happens that love is friendship arising. Friendship, however, is inveterate love, in which much more pleasure remains than desire. From this it follows that he who had desired now takes delight. Therefore, the habit of friendship does not necessarily require the heat of desire for one present, but delight. Thus, if the good man desires the good man less, the good man nonetheless rejoices no less in the good, which is of the greatest value for preserving the nature of friendship. And this is one species of friendship, namely between the good and the good, established in joy rather than in desire. <margin>B</margin> There is another, which includes more desire than pleasure, arising between the neutral and the good. By what reasoning this occurs, and for whose sake, and on account of what, is sufficiently clear in the text. He describes it first as opinion suggests, then gradually amends it. For when he had said that the neutral loves the good friend on account of imminent evil, for the sake of the good and the friend, he immediately corrects this by objecting to what was said. Here he first teaches that all friendships directed toward men are imperfect and are images of friendship: that which looks toward the first Good itself and the Author of all things, which is loved primarily and is the cause for all these things to be loved. And whoever loves anything, nevertheless holds the first Beauty itself as the object of love. <margin>C</margin> For if from the first Good, goodness is in all things; and from the first Beauty, grace is present in each; then goodness draws us, and beauty allures us. Therefore, it is not those inferior things that move us, but that primary thing in them which draws and allures. Thus we love that [primary thing] in them and through them, not the things themselves. In this, the piety of our Plato toward God and his supreme religion shine forth wonderfully. He shows, moreover, that we are not always friends for the sake of another. For we do not long for the first Good for the sake of another good. Likewise, we do not desire the good because of evil. For even if all evil were removed from the nature of things, the good would remain pleasing by its own nature, and the appetite in that which is less good would draw it toward achieving a greater good. For it is not <margin>D</margin> evil that excites the appetite for the highest Good, but the very lack of the lesser good turns it toward its fulfillment in the highest Good; which is indeed not an evil—because evil never leads to good, nor a contrary to its contrary—but should rather be called the beginning of good. Having introduced these points for amendment, he brought in a certain principle for investigating friendship more perfectly. For he says that kinship and the harmony of nature produce friendship, about which we said enough at the beginning. Finally, he stings those youths and adolescents because they are ignorant of what is worthily to be loved, what true friendship is, and in what way it is honorably and stably forged; and before they learn these things, they strive to enter into friendship rashly, procaciously, and petulantly. But lest he make them hostile to him, he signified these things secretly and rebuked himself along with them. This is enough concerning the argument.
<margin>E</margin> Let us come to the *Lysis*.

### -> ON THE THEAETETUS <-
### -> Summary. For page 114. <-

<margin>F</margin> This dialogue on knowledge, Piero de' Medici, rises higher and moves questions worthy of the wonderful sharpness of your wit, the main points and solutions of which you will notice summarized in this compendium. Here you will find a dispute over what knowledge is, what it becomes, from where, and how. Socrates, indeed, asks what knowledge is. Theaetetus, however, answers that knowledge is geometry, arithmetic, and other disciplines of this kind, and individual arts. Socrates rejects this response as less congruent with the question. Because when he was asked what knowledge *is*, he enumerates not what it is, but how many knowledges there are, and explains what they are knowledges *of*. For he who says arithmetic says not knowledge itself, but the knowledge of numbering; and he who says geometry says the knowledge of measuring. Furthermore, the response is ridiculous since it is given through unknowns. For no one can know what this knowledge of numbers or figures is unless he knows what knowledge is. Moreover, the response is superfluous. For when he could have embraced the definition of knowledge itself in a few words, he enters upon an infinite path by counting individuals. After this, he brings forward Protagoras’s definition: that knowledge is sensation. Indeed, Protagoras thinks that man is the measure of all things: of those that exist, that they are; of those that do not exist, that they are not; and that things are to each person <margin>G</margin> such as they appear to each. For such as things are, such are they sensed. Such as they are sensed, such do they appear to the imagination—that is, to the internal sense. By this he wants it to be established that sensation is knowledge. In this, truly, Thales of Miletus, Homer, Epicharmus, Empedocles, Heraclitus, and Protagoras agreed. For when Thales says that water is the principle of all things, and Homer says that Ocean is the father of all and Tethys the mother, they all show that everything is in a state of flux. The others whom we mentioned, imitating these, said that nothing ever *is*, but everything is always *becoming*. Whence nothing in itself is absolutely "this" rather than "that," but through motion, mixture, and the relation of one to another, it both becomes and appears "this" to one person and "that" to another. They think it is established that all things are in motion because from <margin>H</margin> motion all things are made; and they gather that all things are made from motion because by that which a thing is made, it is also preserved. But those things which pertain to the soul, as well as those which pertain to the body, are preserved by motion and exercise, and perish by leisure and torpor. Therefore, from motion. Furthermore, as long as the spheres of the heavens are moved, the four elements are mixed. Insofar as these are mixed, inferior things are brought forth; which, after they are brought forth, are preserved by exercise. Therefore, motion effects all these things. They add that generation comes from heat, and heat from the motion of the sun or the collision of bodies. But that nothing is one thing according to itself, they show by this example: whiteness, and every color, is neither the sight of the eyes nor the motion of bodies, but a certain medium result from the sight and the motion—that is, such an affection around the eyes. And from the diverse disposition of the beholder and the varying mode of looking, various colors are seen, sometimes one, sometimes another.

<summary>Ficino concludes his commentary on Plato's Lysis by defining true friendship as a spiritual communion based on the soul's beauty and kinship, then begins an analysis of the Theaetetus, critiquing the definition of knowledge as mere sensation or flux.</summary>
<keywords>Plato, Lysis, Theaetetus, friendship, knowledge, Socrates, Protagoras, motion, soul, beauty, kinship, Piero de' Medici</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical commentary on Plato's Theaetetus, specifically examining the definitions of knowledge and the nature of perception as argued by Socrates against the theories of Protagoras and Heraclitus.</meta>

### ARGUMENTS AND COMMENTARY

and are made. Furthermore, the varied motion of rays striking bodies and hitting the eyes offers diverse and multiform images. Moreover, often a different color appears and exists for different men and animals regarding the same object; often also for the same person and regarding the same object, though not at the same but at another time, due to a change in nature itself. They therefore opine that whatever exists is motion. Of motion, however, there are two species: one in acting, the other in being acted upon <note>Latin: *patiendo*, referring to the philosophical concept of "passion" or receiving an action</note>. By the mutual mixing of these, all things, as they say, are produced. The outcomes are twin in appearance but infinite in number: namely, the sensible object and the sense, which is always present and meets with the sensible. For whenever some power of sensing and something harmonious with it cling together as one, two things proceed from their encounter: regarding the object, a sensible quality—color, taste, smell, and others of this kind; regarding the power of the soul, a sense. When these are separated, those things do not exist. Thus it happens that of those things offered to the five senses, nothing is such by its own nature, but by meeting with the sense, it becomes one thing at one time and another at another. For nothing is acting or being acted upon according to itself, but each exists in the alternate encounter. Therefore, nothing is one thing by itself, but it always becomes in relation to something else and for someone; it never *is*, but always becomes and flows. Socrates refutes these ideas by the fact that those who are drunk, those suffering from frenzy, the insane, and the sleeping when they dream—as well as those who have their senses corrupted in some other way—affirm that they sense and think truly, even though we say all their visions are false. From this it follows that not all things that appear are true. The same doubt falls upon whatever we are said to sense while awake and sober. For we give almost equal time to sleep and wakefulness in turn. Therefore, it is doubtful whether these or those are rather dreams and false. But those who wish to opine that all appearances are true would surely respond thus: that the various affections of the actors or the sufferers produce diverse things; and the objects that are sensed act according to the affection of the sufferer's sense. This affection is one thing in the waker and another in the sleeper, the sick, or the healthy. For this reason, different judgments are made, yet all are true: because all things are to each person such as they are judged to be. For one must remember what was said above: that nothing is absolutely one thing by its own nature, but whatever else exists is in relation to another, for another, and of another. Rather, whatever exists *becomes* something, but *is* nothing. These things thus harmonize with each other: according to Homer and Heraclitus, all things flow; according to Protagoras, man is the measure of all things; according to Theaetetus, knowledge is sense-perception. Against them Socrates argues thus: If sense is knowledge, brute animals, which prevail in senses more than man, will excel in knowledge. Likewise, if whatever appears is true, the thoughts of any man are equally right, nor is any man wiser than another, nor God wiser than man. Added to this is that the faculty of teaching, disputing, and refuting would be vain, since it would be unnecessary to discern anything for those who judge truly about individual things, nor should the things anyone possesses be investigated, nor should anything be refuted, since any thoughts whatever are true. Furthermore, if sensing and knowing are the same—as seeing and hearing—when unlearned boys first look at letters, they see them, and therefore they know them; or if they are said not to know them, let them also be said not to see them. And when we first hear barbarians pronouncing their own words, not yet being skilled in that tongue, just as we hear, so we shall affirm we know what they utter; but if anyone denies understanding, let him similarly deny hearing. Protagoras will respond to this last point that we know what we have seen or heard; what we are ignorant of, we do not even sense. As in letters, boys see the shape, the position of parts, and the color, and seeing them, they know them. Hearing barbarian voices, as soon as they hear the sharp and the deep <note>referring to pitch/tone</note>, so they know them; but since they do not sense the meanings of the letters and voices, they are utterly ignorant of them. Against him it is inferred thus: From this, O Protagoras, it follows that when they know the meanings, they know by something other than sense. Knowledge, therefore, is something other than sense. Likewise, if to see is to know, not to see will be not to know. But what someone has seen and learned and remembers, he knows. Yet often he does not see it, therefore he also does not know; wherefore the same person both knows and does not know at the same time. Furthermore, if you see something with one eye and discern nothing with the other closed, you see and do not see that thing equally. Wherefore some litigious person might say: If to see is to know, and not to see is not to know, you know and do not know the same thing at once. Add that when you look at something from afar and confusedly, you see it indeed, yet you do not know it, since you doubt. Therefore, knowledge is not sense. Protagoras would perhaps respond, first indeed by distinguishing between memory and knowledge. For when someone first suffers by sensing, he begins to hold it by memory; then even when not suffering <note>not receiving the sensory input</note> he remembers; when he senses and suffers the same thing again, he recollects; in the first he knows by act, not by habit; in the second, by habit, not by act; in the third, by both act and habit at once; wherefore sometimes he both knows and does not know. Yet these are not contraries. For he is not ignorant in the same way that he knows. Therefore, when he does not see, yet remembers, he knows by habit and does not know by act. These are not contraries. And when it is said by Socrates that one is wiser than another, Protagoras responds that some are not to be called wise and others foolish because some opine truths and others falsehoods. For everyone opines those things which they suffer, and they suffer those things by which they are moved, and are moved by those things which act, and those things which act are true. From which he concludes that all opine truths, yet not all opine things that are good and fitting. He asserts those are wise who, being well-disposed, receive whatever is offered as good, and think them good for themselves, and as they think, so they are. Those are foolish who, being ill-disposed, judge things to be bad, and the things they judge are bad for them. Against the claim that all opine truths, Socrates says: It happens in all of life and in individual faculties that we think ourselves to judge truly in some things, and others in some; for everyone professes some faculty and concedes to another in a foreign art. Either this estimation is true or it is false. From either side it follows that not all men think truly. For if that estimation is true, it will be true that someone judges truly in many things in which we opine falsely. Therefore, not all opine truths. If it is false, then in this at least we are often deceived, wherefore not every opinion is true.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Moreover, it often happens that what one person thinks as true is abhorrent to the opinion of all others. Those things will therefore seem true to him, but false to others. They will therefore be false, yet more so than true, by as many more people as there are to whom they are thought false than to whom they are thought true. Therefore, he is not the measure of things, but others are. Wherefore not all men are the measure of all things. Likewise, Protagoras's sentiment that every opinion is true is a paradox, and contrary to almost everyone's opinion, from which almost the entire race of men judges his opinion to be false; but if every opinion is true, then this universal judgment is also true. Therefore, as it is thought false, so also is Protagoras's own position, by which it is said that every opinion is true. For by saying so, it concedes itself to be false. And if he says those who abhor his <margin>B</margin> words think falsely, from this also the same follows: namely, that not every opinion is true. Furthermore, he who is ignorant cannot be the measure of that which he ignores. He who doubts, is ignorant; all men doubt. Therefore they are ignorant of many things. Thus, not all are the measure of all things. And when he says, such as individual things appear to each, so they are, he wanders from the truth. For those things which appear healthful or harmful to the body to those ignorant of the medical art are not always such; often opinion deceives them. And what the citizens decide in deliberating on the administration of the republic as useful or harmful are not always such for the republic. For many things hinder which they hoped would profit, and things which would harm actually profit. But if the healthful and the useful themselves do not consist solely in the opinion and custom of men, but have some substance by their own <margin>C</margin> nature, much more so the honorable itself and the good, since it is the principle and end of useful things. Wherefore, neither in those things which pertain to the care of the body, nor in those which look to the soul and the government of the republic, are individual things such as they appear to each. For if whatever appeared were such, as often as someone predicted the future, he would surely presage truly, which is indeed false. For rarely do future things come as they are thought. And if someone judges concerning future things, not just anyone does it, but the craftsman concerning those things which pertain to his art. As a physician rather than a musician foresees a future fever, and a musician better than a physician foresees a future harmony. Finally, these things having been refuted, Socrates, taking the opportunity from the freedom or servitude of speaking, disputes concerning the freedom of those practicing philosophy and the servitude of civil men and rhetoricians, what the life of <margin>D</margin> both is like: that the end of the philosopher is to ascend from human evils to supernal goods, concerning the rewards of those who seek celestial things and the punishments of those who gape at earthly things. This digression being completed, he returns to the proposed question. Its foundation was the sentiment of Heraclitus, that all things are moved. Parmenides, Melissus, and Zeno the Eleatic felt the contrary. For they posited that the All is one and immobile. Their dogma Plato explains and approves in the book *On the One Principle of All Things*, which we have translated. Against Heraclitus and Protagoras, however, he begins to discourse from the division of motion. There are two kinds of motion. One is motion according to place, the other according to the nature of the thing. The former is called local motion <note>Latin: *latio*</note>, the latter alteration. Of local motion there are two species: <margin>E</margin> transit and circulation. For transit occurs from place to place, or a circuit occurs around one and the same place. Motion in the very nature of the moved thing is effected either according to substance, or regarding quantity or quality. If it is moved according to substance toward being itself, it is generation; if toward non-being, corruption. According to quantity toward the greater, it is called increase; toward the lesser, decrease. Motion which goes from quality to quality is named affection. It then receives various names from various qualities. For that toward heat is heating; toward cold, cooling; toward color, coloring; and similarly for the rest. This distinction having been premised, Socrates asks: if all things are moved, are individual things moved by those two kinds of motion, or are many moved by one and others by two? If many by only one, it follows that they are no more <margin>F</margin> moved than standing still. For if they are moved in one way, they also rest in another way. But their opinion does not intend that, but that all things are moved entirely without any standing still; whereby it happens that they are agitated by all manners. Therefore, while things are carried from place to place, they meanwhile pass continually from affection to affection, as from heat to cold, whiteness to blackness, or the reverse. It is asked whether they remain for a little while under any one of these forms, or not. If they remain, it follows that not every state of rest is expelled. If they do not remain, while something is pronounced "hot" or "white," it ceases to be hot or white. Indeed, before the pronunciation begun can finish, the form ceases to be. Whence nothing is ever truly pronounced or perceived. Nor <margin>G</margin> is it to be predicated that a thing is more "hot" than "not hot," or "white" than "not white," since it persists in nothing, and it both is and is not equally while it is being uttered. For which reason the forms of things are unknown to us. The same must be said of sense. For neither does sight remain for a moment in vision, nor hearing in the act of hearing. Wherefore it happens that we no more see or hear than we do not see and do not hear, even while we profess that we see and hear. From which it follows that if the senses are removed, the truth of the senses is also removed; which being removed, it must in no way be said that knowledge is of the senses. He adds also another reason, for the understanding of which it must be noted that Plato attributes no cognition to the body, just as he attributes no life to it. That which lives, <margin>H</margin> senses; the soul lives, and the soul senses. In the body, however, neither life nor sense is found, but the works of life and sense are declared. Therefore, what others call the "five senses," he wishes to be called the "five organs of sense," and he thinks that nothing senses with these instruments, but through them, as if through passages, individual things are sensed by one certain power of the soul, which he calls the "common sense," into which from all sides from the individual organs of the body—as lines from the circumference to the center of a circle—various passions flow. Colors indeed through the eyes, sounds through the ears, odors through the nostrils, and taste through the tongue; finally, through the whole body heat, cold, moisture, dryness, heavy, light, soft, hard, smooth, rough, rare, dense, and similarly sharp and obtuse. That the soul senses these things not by many powers, but by one, is clear: because in sensing color we say it is not a voice; and in sensing taste,

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plato’s *Theaetetus*, specifically focusing on the hierarchy of the soul's faculties and the problem of how "false opinion" is possible.</meta>

# MARSILIO FICINO

-> we declare that it is not a smell. <- One cannot distinguish one thing from another if they do not know both. No organ provides the same things as another organ; and if they did, they would not do so in the same way. Therefore, the distinction between things sensed is not in the organs, but in a single power of the soul that perceives individual things and distinguishes them from one another simultaneously. Since this power alone can do all these things—which even the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle</note> do not deny—why is there a need for many senses? This sense, which they call the "common sense," is present in all animals immediately from birth. Beyond this is another power, which he names imagination, opinion, and thought. Its duty is to judge those things which the common sense perceived through the five organs—not only what quality they have, but *what* they are: that each is the same as itself, one thing distinct from another, or two or three joined together; likewise similar and dissimilar, good or evil, beautiful or ugly, useful or harmful. It reasons from one thing to another, applies one to another, and compares past and future with the present. Thus, by this power, we judge essence, unity, number, sameness, difference, similarity, dissimilarity, beauty, ugliness, good, evil, usefulness, and uselessness. Since this judgment is not present immediately at birth, but long afterward, and not in all animals but only some, it is clear that we perceive these things by some power other than the common sense. This he calls "perfected imagination" and "opinion." Yet even this is not sufficient. For it judges all these things in a specific and particular way, under a certain time, place, and condition. However, we know that we also judge these same things in a general and universal way; not just what *this* man is now, or where *this* thing is useful, but what humanity itself is always, and what utility itself is everywhere. Therefore, another power is needed, which, perceiving the universal reasons of things generally, discourses from one to another and argues through that discourse. No one doubts that this happens in us while we construct syllogisms. This we call "universal reason" or "thought," while we call opinion itself "particular reason" or "thought." Finally, the **Mind** <note>Latin: *Mens*; the highest intellectual faculty</note> is added to this, which perceives all the reasons of things not through discourse, but by a simple, steady intuition. For above motion and time, there must be stability and eternity. Motion and time belong to reason; in the mind, there is stability and eternity. For it does not learn one thing after another, but holds all things at once. Above the mind is the very unity of the soul, the character of the Highest Good, by which it is joined not to the reasons and ideas of things, but to the first principle of all things, which is Unity itself. Since all the powers of the soul involved in cognition have been enumerated, and since knowledge consists in cognition, we must see in which power knowledge chiefly resides. It does not belong to the senses, as has been established by many reasons, and chiefly because the sense does not judge the common essences of things there, but only perceives certain affections of bodies. Whoever is ignorant of essence is ignorant of truth. He who lacks truth is far removed from knowledge. Therefore, knowledge is not in the sense, where the soul perceives not through itself but through the body, and is thus often deceived. But perhaps it consists in imagination and opinion, where we now perceive essences, and the soul judges by itself without the service of the body. And this view pleases **Theaetetus** in the second place: that knowledge is opinion—not just any opinion, but *true* opinion; for false opinion is ignorance. But when **Theaetetus** distinguished opinion into two types, true and false, **Socrates** asked how false opinion could even exist. He supposes one thing: that whoever opines, opines either what he knows or what he does not know. From this he reasons in this manner: He who opines falsely never does so because he thinks some things he knows are other things he also knows. For he who knows both never takes one for the other. Nor does he take things he does not know for other things he does not know. For no one judges things that have never entered their thought. Nor does he take what he knows for what he never knew, or vice versa. For who would take the known for the unknown, or the unknown for the known? In these ways, then, it seems no one can opine falsely. But perhaps men opine falsely in another way, when they opine things that *are not*. From this, false opinion would be opining non-existent things. But that cannot happen either. For whoever sees, sees some *one* thing; he who sees one thing, sees something existing; but he who sees what does not exist, sees not even one thing. He who sees not one thing, sees nothing; he who sees nothing, does not even see. Therefore, he either does not see, or he sees what is. We can affirm the same of hearing and the other senses. Therefore, since opinion follows sense, whoever opines, opines some one thing; he who opines one thing, opines something existing. Therefore, he opines what is. He who opines what does not exist, opines not even one thing. If not one thing, then nothing. If he opines nothing, he does not even opine. Thus, either he does not opine at all, or he opines what is. Therefore, no one will opine falsely in this way by opining things that are not. There remains another way in which a "commutation" <note>An exchange or swap</note> occurs, so that we take one thing for another: such as the ugly for the beautiful, or the useless for the useful. **Socrates** refutes this thus: To opine is to speak with oneself, while we ask, answer, affirm, and deny within ourselves. Nor is this internal speech inferior to external speech. In external speech, no one ever says that what is ugly is beautiful, or that a man is an ox, or that the even is odd. Therefore, much less will he assert in thought that one of these is the other. For either he knows both, or only one. If both, he would never swap them. If only one, not even then; for he would never take what he knows for that which has not yet entered his thought. Thus it seems we have not yet found how false opinion exists in us. Here **Plato**—also in the *Philebus*, *Sophist*, and *Meno*—uses six names pertaining to the same power of the soul to signify its six duties. For when, after the common sense, the soul apprehends the same things as the common sense, it perceives by the opining power; this first perception is called **imagination**. As it preserves what is apprehended, it is **memory**. As it takes up again within itself what it has saved, it is **reminiscence**. And as it takes them up again,

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> it discourses from one thing to another as a kind of reasoning; this is **thought**. After the discourse is finished and something is affirmed or denied, it is **opinion**. But when the soul, refashioning by thought what was perceived through sense and memory, looks back at these as if at the things from which they flowed, and thinks that these images are the true things, **Plato** calls this a "picture" and **phantasia**. And when he introduces the "waxen image," he by no means means the physical nature of the brain. For he did not say the waxen image was in the body, but in the soul. Since there is nothing corporeal in the incorporeal, these things must be understood through a certain metaphor and similarity of operations, rather than literally as the words sound. Nor does he <margin>B</margin> want the images of things to be fixed in the body, nor to be fashioned in the soul by external objects, but rather that the soul has them from its own nature, or, taking the occasion from external motions and the passions of the body, it conceives forms and reasons within itself by its own power. Whoever doubts this should read the commentaries of the greatest interpreter of **Plato**. Having explained these things, we must return to the modes of false opinion. **Socrates** introduces many and rejects many, and to restrain the practice of the sophists, he often refutes again and again what they have conceded. Finally, it must be gathered from **Plato's** mind that when a certain sensible object first meets us, and by its meeting a sensation is produced in us, and from sensation a memory, and then later the same object is presented to us again, we join the preceding memory with the following <margin>C</margin> sensation, and in these we then say "Socrates," "horse," "fire," and other such things. And this is called a kind of opinion, as we join the preceding memory with the recent sensation. Whenever these things that are gathered together harmonize with each other, true opinion exists; if they clash, false opinion. For if someone, while keeping the form of **Socrates** in memory, should run into **Plato** himself and think because of a certain similarity that he is meeting **Socrates** again, and then, drawing the sensation of **Plato** as if from **Socrates**, fits it to the memory of **Socrates**, false opinion results. In this way, false opinion arises from the comparison of sense to thought. It also happens in another way, by the comparison and mixing of <margin>D</margin> one thought with another thought. For one can swap the forms of certain numbers hidden in the memory, even without a present sensation, by thinking, so that he takes 11 for 10, or 11 for 12. But a certain doubt arises. For whoever keeps the forms knows the things whose forms he has. Therefore, he knows these numbers. If he swaps them, he is ignorant. Therefore, he both knows and is ignorant of the same thing at the same time. It must be answered that it is not absurd for one who knows in one way to be ignorant in another. For he knows by "habit" <note>Possessing the knowledge</note> but is ignorant in "act" <note>Not currently applying it</note>. Therefore, with nothing hindering these, two types of false opinion have been found and explained just above. Another doubt arises: if someone, while possessing the knowledge of two things, opines falsely by swapping them and takes one for the other, he seems to be ignorant of the very thing he has knowledge of; and what is worse, he is ignorant *because* of knowledge itself, and not ignorance, since the knowledge itself is the cause of the swap, not the swap the cause of ignorance. If this is so, since knowledge makes us ignorant, nothing prevents ignorance from making us know. **Theaetetus** answers this by saying that a form of "un-knowledge" should be placed in the soul just like a form of knowledge, and he who takes one for the other is deceived, and thus is ignorant through ignorance rather than through knowledge. This response is hardly sufficient, for in the same way as above, one might ask: if he swaps these forms, does he know both, or is he ignorant of both, or does he know one and not the other? Thus the whole previous controversy returns. Likewise, if a form must be placed by which knowledge is not known, and one by which there is "un-knowledge," then other forms must be placed by which *these* forms are known, and others again for those; and so we shall proceed to infinity. Therefore, <margin>E</margin> one must answer not in that way, but otherwise. For it should have been said, as **Socrates** touched upon above, that the notions of things are not the causes of the swap, but rather the confusion of notions, long-standing negligence, or an external similarity that was not exactly examined. Therefore, we seem to be ignorant not through knowledge, but through confusion, negligence, and deception. However, these things cannot be absolutely judged until it has been declared what knowledge is. For we distinguish darkness by light, silence by sound, evil by good, and the false by the true. Therefore, it seems knowledge must be defined before false opinion can be declared, if we wish to comprehend it perfectly. Hence **Theaetetus** <margin>F</margin> asserts that knowledge is true opinion. **Socrates** refutes this by the fact that the faculty of oratory persuades but does not teach; he who persuades induces an opinion, and a true opinion when he reports true things, yet it is not knowledge. For concerning those things which are <margin>G</margin> always in motion and are sometimes one way and sometimes another, there is never certain knowledge. Such are human affairs, which orators deal with, especially since they often induce listeners to believe things they themselves doubt and which they never witnessed. After this, **Theaetetus** adds the definition of **Leucippus** and **Theodorus of Cyrene**: Knowledge is true opinion with an account <note>Latin: *ratio*; a rational explanation</note>; and therefore things that have an account can be known, while those lacking an account cannot. And **Prodicus of Chios**, imitating **Leucippus**, asserted that the elements of things, because they are simple and therefore without an account, are unknown; but composites, since they can have an account, are known. <margin>H</margin> By "account," they mean a definition and a certain speech declaring the substance and property of a thing. Because this includes several things—a subject and a predicate, sometimes also a copula (that is, a verb), and nouns—it signifies something composite. But an element is simple, and therefore devoid of an account and left unknown. **Socrates** refutes these two statements: first the latter one, which says elements are unknown because they are simple and composites are known; then the former one, that knowledge is true opinion with an account. And for the sake of an example, he takes letters for elements and a syllable for the composite. But what he teaches about these, he wants to be understood about all things. The first argument against them is this: just as composites depend on elements, so the cognition of composites is perfected by the cognition of elements. For not without cause, that which comes from a cause...

# ARGUMENTS AND COMMENTARY

<margin>A</margin>
...can be known. Therefore, it is impossible to understand composite things if the elements are unknown. Take, for example, a certain composite, such as "So," the first syllable of the name Socrates. Is this syllable both of the elements? Or is it a single form born from the fitting together of elements? If it is both, then whoever knows this syllable, "so," knows both elements. He asks: when asked what "so" is, he will answer "s" and "o." And if he is ignorant of "s" and "o," he will never know "so." For he who does not know each one, does not know both. It is therefore impossible to know composites when the elements are unknown. But perhaps someone will say that the syllable, and every such form, is not the elements, but exists as a single thing beyond them. Socrates questions him thus: Does this form, or syllable, have parts or not? If it has parts, it is a certain "whole" and "all." But a "whole" and "all" is nothing other than all its parts, as is evident in numbers. For a whole number is nothing other than all the units it contains, and thus this form will consist of parts, and the parts, by the very fact that they exist, will belong to the whole. Therefore, just as the form is known, so too are the elements known. For if one knows the form, he knows the "whole" and "all." If he knows the "whole" and "all," he will know that none of its parts are missing. Therefore, he knows that it has individual parts, and thus he knows each one: if he were ignorant of them, he could not know whether they were all present or not. It is therefore impossible to know the form if the elements are unknown. But if someone should say that the form itself is one and has no parts because the elements of which it consists are not its parts: it follows that it must be simple and indivisible. Therefore, just as the element was said to be unknown because it is simple, so the form itself will be said to be unknown because it is simple. And so it can in no way happen that, if the elements are unknown, the forms made from them can be known. This is also clearly evident from the fact that in individual arts, the foundation of each art must be understood to include the elements of the very things with which the art deals. Otherwise, all labor is in vain.

<margin>B</margin>
This having finally been refuted, Socrates now begins to disprove the principal part of the proposition, where it was said that *Knowledge is true opinion with an explanation* <note>original: "cum ratione" - literally "with reason" or "with an account"</note>. For three things can be signified by the name "explanation": either speech, or a discourse through the elements of the thing, or a definition. If the first, every opinion will be knowledge. For whether we opine truly or falsely, we are able to express what we feel in speech: therefore, even he who opines falsely will opine with an explanation. If the second, whenever someone discourses through the elements, he would be said to know. But that is false for this reason: because in discoursing he can transpose the elements, pervert the order, refer the element of one thing to another, and fit the element of one to another. He who confuses these things cannot be said to know.

<margin>C</margin>
If he understands the third, that is, definition, and calls knowledge "true opinion with a definition," he argues against him thus. A definition is the interpretation of the difference: therefore, whoever defines assigns a specific difference beyond the common features of the thing. But does he who opines truly of Socrates and Theaetetus perceive the differences of Socrates and Theaetetus in his opining, or not? If he does not perceive them, he does not even opine truly, for I would never truly distinguish one from the other unless I discerned the differences of each. Therefore, by the very fact that he opines truly, he understands the differences. Wherefore there is no need to add an "explanation"—that is, the notion of the difference—beyond true opinion. But perhaps someone will say that a certain sense and imagination of the difference is included in the opinion itself, rather than a certain understanding of the natural difference, and therefore "the understanding of the difference" must be added to the definition of knowledge.

<margin>D</margin>
Socrates argues against this person thus: This definition is surely absurd, because the same thing is described by the same thing. When we say that knowledge is true opinion with an explanation—that is, with the understanding of the difference—we are defining knowledge by knowledge. For the understanding of the difference is the *knowledge* of the difference, whence knowledge will be "true opinion with the knowledge of the difference," which is ridiculous to say. From all these points, the false definitions of the Sophists have now been refuted. First, which said knowledge is the individual faculties that are learned; second, that knowledge is sense-perception; third, that knowledge is true opinion; fourth, that knowledge is true opinion with the utterance of speech; fifth, true opinion with discourse through elements; sixth, true opinion with the imagination of the difference; seventh, true opinion with the knowledge of the difference.

<margin>E</margin>
These having finally been refuted, we must see what Plato teaches, who indeed in the sixth book of the *Republic*, imitating the Pythagoreans Brontinus and Archytas, posits two kinds of things: namely, the intelligible and the sensible. The former is stable and <insert>in</insert>corporeal <note>The text says "corporeum" but the context of "intelligible" and "stable" implies "incorporeal," likely an OCR or printing error</note>; the latter is mobile and corporeal. He calls the way to know the former "reason," and the way to the latter "sense." The common notion of the former is "intelligence"; of the latter, "opinion." But he divides each genus in two. For he wants there to be a primary and secondary intelligible: in the primary are contained the Ideas—that is, the forms and notions of the divine mind—and other minds and souls; in the secondary are numbers and figures. For although numbers and figures are incorporeal, yet because they admit of some division, they are not to be judged of equal dignity with indivisible substances. He calls the cognition of the former "intellect" by its proper name, and the thought of the latter "intellectual cogitation."

<margin>F</margin>
He also divides the sensible by an equal division into primary and secondary. In the first he places all bodies and corporeal things. In the second, shadows and images of bodies, whether they appear in water or in mirrors. And he considers these to stand in the same relation to bodies as mathematical things do to divine things. The perception of bodies he properly names "belief"; that of shadows, "imagination." Furthermore, he denies that there is knowledge concerning the shadows of bodies, or bodies, or mathematics, but places it in the intellect of divine things alone. This he also signified in this dialogue at the beginning, when he proposed that knowledge and wisdom are the same. For he testifies everywhere that wisdom is the contemplation of divine things.

<margin>G</margin>
But how the intellect itself—that is, knowledge—differs from opinion, he shows in the book *On Nature* <note>The Timaeus</note> with these words: If intellect and true opinion are two things, it is necessary that the Ideas be comprehended by themselves through the intellect rather than through the sense. But if, as

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
it seems to some, true opinion does not differ from intellect, then all things which we perceive as corporeal must be held as certain. But they must be called two, because both are distant by a great difference: since one is instilled in us by teaching, the other is an assumption of persuasion. One is always with true reason; furthermore, the other is without any reason and cannot be transferred by reason; one is wavering and uncertain. What of the fact that every man is a participant in right opinion? But intellect is proper to God, and to a very few chosen men? He testifies to nearly the same things in the *Meno* and *Philebus*. What then is knowledge? The comprehension of divine things by certain reason. This is in the intellect, first and always. In the reason, second, and not always. For since reason is the middle between intellect and opinion, whenever it is extended toward lower things, it is filled with the errors of opinion and ceases to think on divine things. But when

<margin>B</margin>
it is turned toward the mind, its leader, it drinks in the cognition of divine things. This, Plato calls "wisdom" by its proper name in the mind, and "reminiscence" in the reason. And therefore he disputed in this dialogue about the "obstetric faculty" <note>The Socratic method of "midwifery," helping others give birth to ideas</note> through which we remember, so that we might understand not only what knowledge is, but also how it is acquired. Indeed, he explained whence it is and through whom: while saying that Socrates performs the office of a midwife by the command of God. Knowledge, therefore, is the comprehension of divine things by certain reason, residing in the mind, flowing into the reason, inserted into the mind by God, led back into the reason by a dialectical teacher with God breathing upon him, directing the reason into the mind, and joining the mind with divinity.

## ON THE ION
### Argument. for page 143.

<margin>C</margin>
Our Plato, most excellent Lawrence, defines "fury" in the *Phaedrus* as an alienation of the mind. Moreover, he hands down two kinds of alienation. One from human diseases. The other coming from God. The former he calls "madness": the latter "divine fury." In madness, a man is cast down below the species of man: and from a man is rendered in a way a brute. By divine fury he is raised above the nature of man and passes into God. Moreover, divine fury is an illustration of the rational soul: through which God draws back the soul, which had fallen from the heavens to the lower regions, from the lower regions to the heavens. The fall of the soul from the very One, the principle of all things, to bodies, is effected through four steps:

<margin>D</margin>
through mind: reason: opinion: and nature. For since in every order of things there exist six steps, of which the highest is held by the One itself, the lowest by the body, and the middle are the four which we said before, it is necessary that whatever falls from the first to the last must fall through the four middle steps. The One itself is the limit of all things, and the measure of infinity, and devoid of multitude. Mind is indeed a multitude: but stable and eternal. Reason is a mobile multitude, but finite. Opinion is an infinite mobile multitude: but united in substance and points. Nature is similar, except that it is diffused through the points of the body. But the body is an infinite multitude, subject to motion, and divided in substance, points, and moments. Our soul looks back at all these: through these it descends: through these it ascends. For as it is led forth from the One itself, which is the principle of all, it has obtained a certain unity

<margin>E</margin>
which unites its whole essence, powers, and actions: from which, and toward which, the other things in the soul are related, just as the lines of a circle are from and toward the center. It unites not only the parts of the soul to each other and to the whole soul: but the whole soul to the One itself, the cause of all things. Moreover, as it depends on the divine mind, it contemplates the Ideas of all things through the mind in a stable act. As it looks at itself, it thinks the universal reasons of things: and discourses by reason from principles to conclusions. As it looks at the body, it conceives the particular forms of mobile things by opinion: and runs through them. As it touches matter, it uses nature as an instrument: by which it unites matter, moves it, and forms it: whence generations, increases, and their contraries proceed. You see, therefore, that from the One which is above eternity, it falls into eternal multitude:

<margin>F</margin>
from eternity into time: from time into place and matter. Wherefore, just as it descends through four steps: it must ascend through four. Moreover, it is divine fury which turns it toward the higher things: as was established in its definition. Therefore, four species of divine fury exist. The first indeed is poetic fury. The second, ministerial <note>or "mystery-related"</note>. The third, prophecy. The fourth, the affection of a lover. Moreover, poetry is from the Muses: mystery from Dionysus: prophecy from Apollo: love from Venus. For the soul cannot return to the One unless it itself is made one. But having been made "many" is the fall into the body, distributed into various operations, and looking toward individual things. From which its higher parts almost fall asleep: the lower parts dominate the others. The former are affected by torpor: the latter by perturbation: and the whole soul is filled with discord and lack of harmony.

<margin>G</margin>
Therefore, there is need first of all for poetic fury, which through musical tones may arouse what is sluggish: through harmonic sweetness, may soothe what is disturbed: finally, through the consonance of diverse things, may drive out dissonant discord and temper the various parts of the soul; nor is this enough. For multitude still remains in the soul. Therefore, mystery is added, which by expiations and sacrifices, and all worship of the gods, directs the intention of all parts into the mind by which God is worshiped. Whence, when the individual parts of the soul have been reduced to one mind, the soul has now become a certain "one whole" out of many. But there is still need for a third fury: which may lead the mind back to the unity of the soul itself. Apollo effects this through prophecy. For when the soul rises above the mind into unity, it foretells the future. Finally, when the soul has been made one—the "one," I say, which is in the very essence of the soul—it remains that it be immediately turned into the One which is above essence. Celestial Venus herself fulfills this through love, that is, the desire for divine beauty and the ardor for the good. Thus the first fury tempers the unharmonious and dissonant. The second makes a single whole out of the tempered parts. The third makes a single whole above the parts. The fourth leads into the One which is above essence and the whole. The first [is like] the good horse, that is...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s Neoplatonic commentary on Plato’s dialogues, specifically focusing on the nature of divine inspiration (poetic fury) in the *Ion* and transitioning into the preface and argument for the *Sophist*.</meta>

# MARSILIO FICINO

<margin>A</margin> He distinguishes reason and opinion from the "bad horse"—that is, from confused imagination—and from nature. Second, he subjects the bad horse to the good one, and the good one to the charioteer, which is the mind. Third, he directs the charioteer toward his own head, which is the peak of the mind's unity. Finally, he turns the head of the charioteer toward the Head of all things. There, the charioteer is blessed, and bringing the horses to the manger—that is, to divine beauty—he offers them ambrosia, and nectar to drink upon it: that is, the vision of beauty, and the joy arising from that vision. These are the four works of the divine furies <note>Ficino refers to the four types of "divine madness" or inspiration: poetic, religious, prophetic, and erotic.</note>, which Plato discusses generally in the *Phaedrus*; specifically, however, he treats the last fury (love) in the *Symposium*, and the first (poetic fury) in the present dialogue, which is titled *Ion*. In the *Phaedrus*, he defines it thus: "Poetic fury is a certain occupation by the Muses which, having obtained a gentle and unconquerable soul, awakens and stirs it through songs and other poetry for the instruction of mankind."

<margin>B</margin> "Occupation" signifies the rapture of the soul and its gathering into the divine powers of the Muses. He calls the soul "gentle," meaning agile and shapeable by the Muses; for unless it is prepared, it cannot be occupied. "Unconquerable," because once it is snatched up, it surpasses all things, and can be neither stained nor overcome by any inferior matters. It awakens the body from sleep to the vigilance of the mind; from the darkness of ignorance to light; from death to life; and recalls it from Lethean forgetfulness to the remembrance of divine things. It stirs, goads, and inflames the soul toward those things it contemplates and foretells, to be expressed in verse. After the definition, he adds that he who approaches the gates of poetry without the fury of the Muses is empty—both himself and his poetry—as if poetry were of such great value that it could only be matched by the light of God's fury.

<margin>C</margin> He teaches the same in the *Ion*: both where this fury comes from and through how many steps it descends. Plato says in the fourth book of the *Laws* that God, fortune, and art govern all human affairs. Thus, poetry is either a gift of God, a lot of fortune, or a work of art. Socrates searches with Ion the rhapsode <note>A professional reciter of epic poetry.</note> to find which of these is most true. In this book, "rhapsode" signifies a reciter, interpreter, and singer of poems. Ion interpreted the poems of Homer and sang to the lyre before the people; he was so affected that he would explain no other poet besides Homer, even if others spoke with the same ease. He explained everything of Homer’s quickly. From this, Socrates argued: Ion produces what Homer wrote either by chance, by art, or by divine inspiration. Not by chance, because he would then interpret only a few things without continuity or order. Not by art, because whoever possesses an entire art can judge everything subject to that art. Yet the poems of Hesiod and others are subject to the same study as Homer’s, especially those treating the same themes; nevertheless, Ion does not grasp them, even though he explains Homer clearly. Therefore, he does not judge by art. It remains that it is by divine inspiration. From this, it is clear that the poets' interpreters, like Ion and many others similarly affected, interpret another's poetry by divine instinct. If human genius is not sufficient to perceive poetry already delivered, it will be much less sufficient for its invention. Therefore, neither Homer nor any other true poet achieved poetry without heavenly inspiration. Socrates shows this in other ways: First, poets deliver all arts and sciences, but it is impossible to have learned them all by human study, since it is difficult enough to perceive even one in part.

<margin>E</margin> Therefore, they produce not by human art, but by a certain divine infusion. The proof of this is that many prophets, after the impulse of the fury has subsided, do not sufficiently understand what they wrote, even though they treated individual arts correctly while in the fury—which the practitioners of those arts judge by reading them. Furthermore, we often see a crude and unskilled man suddenly turn into a good poet and sing something magnificent and divine. Great things in a moment belong to inspiration, not to human genius, but to the divinely inspired. In this, God clearly shows that this intelligence is infused by His will. To demonstrate this is so, He often seizes the unskilled rather than the refined, and the "insane" rather than the prudent, lest if He used sharp and prudent men, these things might be thought to happen through human subtlety and industry.

<margin>F</margin> Since, therefore, poetry is not from fortune or art, it is granted by God and the Muses. When he says "God," he means Apollo; when "Muses," he means the souls of the world's spheres. Jupiter is the mind of God; from him comes Apollo, the mind of the World Soul, and the souls of the whole world and the eight celestial spheres. These nine souls are called the nine Muses because, while they move the heavens harmoniously, they give birth to musical melody. This melody, distributed into nine sounds—namely the eight tones of the spheres and one harmony of them all—produces the nine Sirens singing to God. Therefore, the choir of Muses is led by Apollo from Jove, and the Muses from Apollo (the mind of the World Soul), because just as that mind is illuminated by Jove, so it illuminates the souls of the world and the spheres. The steps by which that fury descends are these: Jupiter seizes Apollo. Apollo illuminates the Muses. The Muses awaken and stir the gentle and unconquerable souls of the prophets. The inspired prophets inspire their interpreters. The interpreters, in turn, move the listeners. Different souls are seized by different Muses, because different souls are attributed to different spheres and stars, as is taught in the *Timaeus*.

<margin>G</margin> Urania is named for the dignity of the starry sky. Polymnia for Saturn, because of the memory of ancient things Saturn provides and his dry, cold complexion. Terpsichore for Jupiter, for he is health-bringing to the choir of men. Clio for Mars, because of the desire for glory. Melpomene for the Sun, because it is the tempering of the whole world. Erato for Venus, because of love. Euterpe for Mercury, because of honest delight in serious matters. Thalia for the Moon, because of the greenness provided to things by its moisture. Apollo is likewise the soul of the sun; his lyre is the body of the sun; its four strings are its four motions: annual, monthly, daily, and oblique. The four voices—the high, low, and Dorian—are the four triplicities of the signs, from which the four qualities of the seasons are produced. Calliope inspired Orpheus, Urania inspired Musaeus,

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Clio inspired Homer, Polymnia inspired Pindar, Erato inspired Sappho, Melpomene inspired Thamyras, Terpsichore inspired Hesiod, Thalia inspired Maro <note>Virgil</note>, and Euterpe inspired Naso <note>Ovid</note>. The same Phoebus <note>Apollo</note> who now stirs you, best Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo de' Medici</note>, seized Linus—the Phoebus, I say, who gave the gift of prophecy to your grandfather Cosimo, the bow and medicines to your father Piero, and finally the lyre and songs to you.

### PREFACE TO PLATO’S
### Sophist according to Proclus, translated by Marsilio
### Ficino.

<margin>B</margin> Plato calls the "Sophist" not only a certain type of man, but also Love, Pluto, and Jupiter; and he calls the sophistic art most noble. From this, we understand that this dialogue regards a more noble subject than it appears. For the intention, according to the great Iamblichus, is to treat the sublunary demiurge <note>The "craftsman" or creator of the physical world below the moon.</note>. For he is a maker of idols, a purifier of souls (always separating them from contrary reasons), a transmuter, and a mercenary hunter of wealthy youths. While he receives souls coming from above full of reasons, he receives from them a reward: the very fabric of living beings, which is according to the reason of mortals. Here he leans upon that which is not, because he begets things that are in matter. And he loves what is truly false—that is, matter. Yet at the same time, he looks toward what is truly true. He is also "many-headed," since he has claimed for himself many essences and vital powers through which he disposes the variety of generation.

<margin>C</margin> He is also a magician of generation, as he soothes and allures souls with natural reasons so that they are moved away from generation only with difficulty. Indeed, both Love and Nature are called "magicians" by some because of the reciprocal attractions and allurements that proceed according to nature. Now, therefore, he wishes to declare the sophist in every way. For the philosopher is a sophist, insofar as he imitates the heavenly creator and the creator of generation. And the distributive faculty imitates the progress of things from the One, and the creator of generation imitates the heavenly creator; therefore, he is a sophist. But even man himself is called a sophist because he imitates great things. And for that reason, he called the sophist "many-headed." The Eleatic Stranger represents the father of creators, the super-celestial and absolute one. The listeners represent the intelligences of the creator. The former belongs to Jupiter, the latter to the angelic nature as an interpreter and geometer.

<margin>D</margin> And since the craftsmanship, beginning from the imperfect, ends in the perfect, that Stranger deals first with Theodorus, and then, through conversion, with Socrates himself.

---

### ON THE SOPHIST
### Argument. to page 147.

<margin>E</margin> After the *Theaetetus* concerning science, the *Sophist* should be read concerning Being itself, which is the object of science. While Being is discussed here (which the philosopher deals with), Non-Being is treated meanwhile (toward which the sophist declines). According to Pythagoras and Plato, God alone is the "Sophist," that is, the Wise One. The philosopher is the true imitator of God. The sophist is an ambitious and deceptive emulator of the philosopher. Plato brings forward six definitions of the sophist. But since a definition cannot be had without division—through which things that do not belong to the thing being defined are separated from it, and its genus is divided by differences, from which finally the species is composed and defined—Plato, intending to define the Sophist, first devises most exact partitions. He warns that no one can discern the nature of any thing secretly unless he has thoroughly separated it from foreign qualities. Accordingly, he brings descriptions of Being and Non-Being according to his powers, and subjects Being to the One, just as in the *Parmenides*. He counts five genera of Being: essence, sameness, difference, stability, and motion. He teaches that true essence belongs to incorporeal things, while imaginary essence belongs to corporeal ones.

<margin>F</margin> Furthermore, he greatly detests those who deny incorporeal things, as well as those who think either that all things only move or that all things only remain still. Likewise, he disputes concerning science, opinion, and true or false speech, and concerning the verb and the noun, insofar as it seems to pertain to the discussion of Being itself. Finally, after he has disputed concerning the sophist and the philosopher together, he concludes the book with a certain divine sentiment: namely, that natural things are the works of God. Indeed, he had proved that all works of nature proceed from a certain divine wisdom infused into the world. Shadowy and deceptive things, however, he says are demonic illusions.

<margin>G</margin> In the same place, he says the sophist is hidden from us as if enveloped in the darkness of non-being (that is, the false); and the philosopher is likewise hidden, though for another reason: because, being surrounded on all sides by the splendor of Being itself (that is, divine truth), he completely surpasses the gaze of common minds.

## MARSILIO FICINO’S APOLOGUE
## FOR PLATO’S BOOK,
## On Kingship, to Federico, Duke of Urbino,
## always unconquered.

Jupiter, the Best and Greatest, wishing to see such a kingdom on earth as he always beholds with himself in heaven, long ago sent down to earth a certain royal and divine soul through the very Idea of the divine king. Having called together the inhabitants of heaven, he commanded that they all support this future king, whom the gods see and already name "Faith-of-Kings" from his royal faith, and "Duke of the World" from his empire over the globe—though men, by changing the letters, would call him Federico, Duke of Urbino. All the deities assented to Jove, except Juno. So—
