# ON THE STATESMAN
## Argument. To page 169.

Since God and nature produce man for the sake of acting, they certainly produce him so that he may act; I say act for the sake of divine things. Just as there is one end for the sake of which nature makes a thumb, another for the sake of which it makes a hand or foot, and yet another for which it makes the whole man: so there is one end toward which it directs an individual man, another for a family, and likewise another for a city and a kingdom. And finally, that end must be considered the best for the sake of which God procreated the entire human race. Let no one think that while every specific group has a certain end, there is none for the whole; or that while there is order in the parts of human life, there is nevertheless confusion in the universal kind of life; or finally, that while the parts have union among themselves for the sake of one intention, the whole itself is dispersed. Therefore, it is necessary that there be a certain end for the human race, and that it consists in a certain action regarding perfection, through which it may both imitate superior things according to its strength and diligently govern inferior things: it should search out natural things through science, dispose human affairs through prudence, and worship and venerate divine things through piety. Such an end, therefore, requires a twin life, constituted in a likeness of both action and contemplation, yet in such a way that action is instituted for the sake of contemplation as something more divine. Furthermore, the absolute perfection of both lives requires so many and such varied supports that it can be fulfilled neither by a few nor even by many men, but only by the whole human race together. It cannot happen, however, that such diverse nations be led through such diverse means to one common end for all, unless by one person through one certain law leading everyone equally into one. Just as craftsmen and assistants, differing greatly among themselves in kind and talent, bringing together very different materials for one form of a building, will never conveniently assemble and construct it opportunely unless they are ruled by one certain law of a single architect. For this reason, Plato, when seeking a king as the monarch of the world, first brought the architect into the midst of the discussion and finally distinguished science into three kinds. The first is concerned with knowing, the second with acting, and the third with making. In the first he placed arithmetic and geometry; in the second, the architect; in the third, the craftsman and assistant. He proved that the faculty of the architect must be placed in the middle between pure speculation and pure service, yet participating more in speculation than in service; for he does not merely indicate things in the manner of geometers, but also commands those who make them and is always present at the work. He wishes the king to be almost of this sort: one who, in the manner of contemplatives, judges the truth and commands laws—not someone else's, but his own—to be carried out. Hence Plato, using a most exact division which is very necessary for definition and science, names the king (in the Homeric fashion) the shepherd and caretaker of the human race. He designates that there ought to be one shepherd for the whole human race as if for one fold, where he says that God was once the shepherd of the human race, under whom that Golden Age of Saturn existed. He also indicates that the king should be called the pilot of human life, as if of a ship. He signifies, moreover, that the empire of all must be brought together into one, so that human governance may be as similar as possible to the divine, since God is the one ruler of the whole world. This is indeed confirmed briefly by these reasons. First, if you subjected the three parts of the world—Asia, Africa, and Europe—to three distributed kings, it would very easily happen that either one would wage war against two, or two against one, or at least they would be forced to dispute over borders or some other matter. Therefore, the judgment of the dispute must be brought either to one of the three or to a fourth judge appointed besides the three. By whatever reasoning that is done, it will be necessary for the judge (if his sentence is to be followed) to have power over those between whom he judges. Otherwise, the judgment will be of no weight, and it is judged in vain, which might seem to the kings—who are either more or at least equally powerful—something to be dissolved. Therefore, there must be one king as the judge of all, undoubtedly to be revered by all. Furthermore, the king ought to be an exemplar of virtues to his subjects. He will be such especially if he is one before all others, upon whom everyone casts their eyes. If he possesses the whole world, he will neither affect a further kingdom nor envy others. These two things, namely greed and envy, are what usually give birth to robberies and wars. And since his own things are dearest to everyone, he will love all most greatly as his own, and will love all nations equally, and care for them equally. He will desire peace above all, long for tranquility, and an abundance of all good things, such as appeared as a certain shadow of monarchy during the reign of Octavian <note>Augustus Caesar</note>. The subjects will live most justly, since no path of escape is open anywhere to the unjust under a monarch; and although they live with the least license for sinning, they will nevertheless live in the highest liberty—not subject to tyrants, or a few powerful men, or the furies of an insane populace, but led thus to the common good by a wise, just, and pious king, just as sailors are led to port by the prudence of a just pilot. In this matter, those who are ruled will consult their own interests by obeying the king, and the king himself will live not so much for himself as 

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> for all who have been committed to his care by God. For right governance, as is disputed in the books *On the Republic*, establishes the governor for the sake of those who are governed, not the governed for the sake of the governor. He compares the king, moreover, to a physician, advising that in the manner of physicians he should impose laws or bring healthy remedies both opportunely and, if need be, inopportunely, both to the willing and sometimes to the unwilling. He more often calls such a governor and caretaker a "civil man" <note>Statesman</note> than a king, signifying that he ought to be so human and, if possible, mild, that he seems to be a fellow citizen among citizens—superior in prudence, justice, and care rather than by any other excess. But if <margin>B</margin> someone should, at some long interval, manifestly surpass all others in prudence and justice, he judges without controversy that this man, even if he lives as a private citizen, is the king of all created by God. But if among some men there is very little difference in these respects, he thinks the royal authority should be granted to them reduced, as it were, to one; but by no means to many. For many people worthy of such authority cannot be found anywhere. He wishes royal authority to be handed down, as can be conjectured from his other books, by the elders and the most proven men, whose senate should then be the king's council, like a certain republic of the best men. Let the king, together with the senate, establish laws which it is not permitted for any private person to transgress or for the common people to change; yet let it be permitted for the king and senate together, according to the opportunity of the times as far as is expedient, to accommodate them with diligent equity to the things themselves and the times, and to change them if necessary. In his letters, he considers the king himself to be sacred, <margin>C</margin> and to be appointed as a priest in the Egyptian manner, a leader of sacred mysteries; and as one who is sacred, lest he ever be contaminated, he does not permit him to be present at judgments where murder, exile, or imprisonment are discussed. Furthermore, in this very book, he proves that such royal dignity is the best governance of all, as we have said; but the worst is <margin>D</margin> tyranny, which rules neither by law nor by a legitimate mind, but rather by impulse and lust. In the second place, he praises the rule of the best <note>Aristocracy</note>, and likewise blames the power of the few <note>Oligarchy</note>. In the third place, he praises the governance of the many, namely the popular sort <note>Democracy</note>, if they govern by law; and likewise blames it if not by law. After these things, he disputes what the royal office is: namely, that he should provide whatever things are necessary for the human race, and especially for living well and blessedly. He should judge prudently how many arts and of what kind contribute to this very thing, whether in peace or in war, whether in speaking or acting, either publicly or privately, and he should have, together with the senate, supreme command over all. Especially, however, he should compose the souls of all with a certain most decent mixture of fortitude and temperance, imitating musicians who, rightly mixing high notes with low, <margin>E</margin> modulate the sweetest harmonies. For he demonstrates, and indeed divinely, that it is not safe to strain souls too much toward fortitude, as if into vinegar, or to relax them too much toward temperance, as if into a heavy bass. For from the former they eventually turn out wild, and from the latter, effeminate. And those citizens attack the fatherland like enemies, while these defend neither themselves nor the fatherland from enemies. Therefore, he thinks it best that from a harmonious joining of both virtues, a consonance of talents be forged everywhere. But enough has been said so far about the order of the book. As for what he disputes concerning the motion of the spheres, providence, and fate, <margin>F</margin> we have sufficiently explained these in our *Theology*. In these matters, he certainly teaches us allegorically that we do not have a true and legitimate king unless either in heaven itself, or on earth when the King himself has set over us one whom he has appointed as a shepherd of heaven—a shepherd, I say, not in name alone, but representing the King of heaven himself by the likeness of his life according to his strength. He commemorates also two kingdoms, namely of Jupiter and of Saturn, and he prefers the kingdom of Saturn to the kingdom of Jupiter as being more happy. For under Jupiter, action and human life are signified, but under Saturn, the contemplation of divine things. For Saturn, called *Cronos* in the Greek name, as Plato teaches in the *Cratylus*, encompasses the purity and inviolable integrity of the mind. Because he says that men live blessedly while Saturn reigns, he shows that the human race will be blessed when a certain divine mind of a man reigns, which institutes actions for the sake of contemplation. I shall soon make an end to the argument, if I first bring forward a brief allegory of this mystery. <margin>G</margin> For he says that the present circuit of the world from east to west is Jovian and fated; but that there will eventually be another opposite to this under Saturn, from west back to east. In this, men will be born spontaneously and will proceed from old age into youth, and food will be supplied to them of its own accord under an eternal spring according to their wish. I think he calls the soul of the world "Jupiter," by whose fatal law this manifest order of the manifest world is disposed. Furthermore, he wishes the life of souls in elemental bodies to be Jovian, devoted to the senses and action. But Saturn is the supreme intellect among the angels, by whose rays souls are illustrated beyond the angels and are set on fire; and they are continually raised toward the intellectual life according to their strength. Whenever they are converted to such a life, they are said to live under the reign of Saturn to the extent that they live by intelligence. Therefore, in that life, they are said to be regenerated spontaneously because they are reformed for the better by their own choice. <margin>H</margin> Again, they grow young again daily—that is, daily (if indeed days are numbered there) they flourish more and more. This is that saying of the Apostle Paul: *The inner man is renewed day by day.* Finally, food is supplied to them abundantly of its own accord under a perpetual spring, because they enjoy the wonderful spectacles of truth itself not through the senses and laborious discipline, but through an inner light and the highest tranquility and pleasure of life.

# MARSILIO FICINO

### On the Sophists and the Protagoras

Just as Aesculapius healed bodies, Plato healed souls. All the followers of Socrates testify that Socrates himself was sent by God for the sake of purifying souls. Now, the disease of the soul seems to consist of false opinions and evil habits. Such an evil is usually inflicted upon noble souls not so easily by others as by the Sophists. Truly, philosophers are those who zealously seek the truth solely for the love of truth itself. Sophists, however, affect an appearance of wisdom, likewise out of a love for mere opinion. For these men, like merchants and peddlers of learning, gather various opinions from everywhere without selection—pertaining both to thinking and speaking however they please—which they then sell like wares to wealthy youths for the sake of riches and empty glory. Therefore, they never care whether what they learn or teach others is true or good, or the opposite; instead, they confuse things and pour out errors everywhere, many every day, having absolutely no regard for right elevation, provided they accumulate wealth and achieve common fame. For this reason, it is necessary for youths and men, who highly value the Sophists for their reputation for wisdom and the veneer of their eloquence, to drink down daily from them the poisons of false opinions and the worst habits. Indeed, evil habits follow false opinions and are easily poured into disciples by these greedy and ambitious teachers, who are nevertheless held in high esteem.

Plato, therefore, pitying souls so prone to such grave danger, very frequently—under the persona of Socrates—detests the wicked and poisonous Sophists with all his might, so that men eager for learning might cautiously avoid the deceptive songs of the Sirens and the harmful cups of Circe <note>In Greek mythology, Circe offered a potion that turned men into swine; Ficino uses this as a metaphor for the Sophists' corrupting influence.</note>. Yet he does not strike them down with obvious invectives, lest he himself appear moved by any disturbance or hatred toward them, or lest they and their followers impudently hurl back the poisonous arrows of their tongues at him. Therefore, partly through irony, partly through laughter, often through jest and play, and more often through a certain honorable refutation, he tries to strip the Sophists of their unmerited authority. He accomplishes this most sharply in the *Sophist*. The same most elegantly in the *Gorgias*. Quite facetiously and urbanely in the *Hippias*. Skillfully and shrewdly in the *Euthydemus*. Artfully also in the *Protagoras*, and often in similar ways. Everywhere he introduces the Sophists as boastful and vainglorious, professing all things, and moreover rash and greedy. At the beginning of a dispute they seem fit enough, but gradually they become more inept, and finally the most inept of all, understanding nothing of any particularly grave matter—neither what it is, nor how great, nor of what quality. And though they profess to know all things, he proves they know nothing at all. Thus far, let it suffice to have prefaced all of Plato's dialogues in which mention of the Sophists is made. Let us now proceed to the *Protagoras*.

Socrates learned the art of love from the prophetic Diotima, through which he knew how to hunt sagaciously through the beauty of bodies—as if through certain tracks—for the beauty of the soul, the angelic mind, and God; and he taught this same art everywhere. Plato treated this art of his often elsewhere, but especially in the *Symposium* and the *Phaedrus*. He indicated the same at the beginning of this book. Therefore, he added that he loves a man no less than a youth. And a little later, that he loves the elders even more ardently, provided they appear wiser. After this, while Socrates most artfully warns the youth Hippocrates, who is most greedy for learning, not to rashly commit himself to just any discipline, he reminds not only him but also us to take care of the soul far more than the body, and to be diligent lest we imbue it with harmful teachings. For these are more a poison to the soul than to our body. Soon, like a painter, he places the pride and vanity of the Sophists before our eyes. He also demonstrates how much credulous youth admires their pomp and is captured by their allurements. Then he descends to those things which are of the greatest importance for life, and in which the Sophists glory, inquiring indeed about all virtue, but especially about the chief virtue, that is, civil <note>term: "civil" (Latin: *civili*) refers to political or social virtue necessary for a citizen.</note> virtue, through which the private, domestic, and public affairs of each person are disposed by right reason toward the highest good. Plato seeks this as necessary above all others in almost all his dialogues; meanwhile, he shows that this is by no means to be sought from the Sophists, but in a certain way from philosophers: who, since they understand the true and cherish the good, can surely lead one to it by a straight path with God as their guide.

But let us return now to the Sophist, who clearly cannot hand down such virtue by example or teach it by discussion, because he himself is devoid of virtue and does not observe the right order of disputation. For when Protagoras is asked here by Socrates whether virtue can be taught or not, being ignorant of the true art of discourse, he immediately undertakes to show that virtue can be taught before he explains what it is or into what parts it is divided. Socrates, however, for the sake of testing the Sophist, argues that it cannot be taught, in nearly these words: When there is public consultation about some duty of an art which can be taught by certain teachers, no one is admitted to the council except those who have learned such an art from those teachers and have practiced it themselves. But when there is deliberation about public matters which pertain to civil virtue, almost everyone is admitted similarly, nor is it asked of anyone whether, from whom, or when he received civil skill, as if everyone understands that it cannot be learned in specific schools. Furthermore, if it were handed down from one to another, the most famous men in it would often leave this precious thing to their heirs by a certain hereditary right. To these points, Protagoras proves with long ambages <note>original: "ambagibus" - long-winded or roundabout stories.</note> that virtue can be taught. In these, certain mysteries of the ancients he relates are to be noted. For it is fitting, even if he is a Sophist, that he has read some good things; and when he speaks at length in Plato, he brings forward some useful points. The ancient theologians relate that animals once lay hidden under the earth, that is, the seeds of things pre-existed in the primary matter of the world. Furthermore, that Jove—that is, God the maker of the world—composed animals from the elements through the succeeding gods, that is, through the stars. The gods,

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> however, through the ministry of daemons <note>term: "daemons" (Latin: *daemonum*) refers to intermediary spirits between gods and humans, not "demons" in the modern evil sense.</note>, armed the animals with instruments and supports necessary for life, specifically in such a way that Prometheus, who signifies the order of the higher daemons, loved men; while Epimetheus, who represents the army of the lower daemons, supported the brutes. And this was not without justice: since the higher daemons favor the incorporeal and rational nature, while the lower favor the corporeal and irrational. Indeed, as much as Epimetheus and the lower nature favored the brutes in those things pertaining to the body, so much does Prometheus and the superior providence seem to have consulted for men in those things which look to the soul. For when he granted the principle of art, he exhibited a skillful maker of all those things which nature had given to the beasts. Moreover, <margin>B</margin> he received the art itself along with fire from the workshop of Minerva and Vulcan. Minerva contains the genius in the art, Vulcan the efficacy, and finally fire is the instrument. These twin deities, Minerva and Vulcan, are first conceived in the very Ideas of the arts. Then in the powers of Mercury and Mars. Finally in the daemons who are governors of the arts. From all these, therefore, Prometheus, the governor of the rational soul, transferred the industry of art into man. Since, however, this exists as a divine gift, man immediately worshipped God because of this kinship with the higher beings, before he either spoke or practiced any arts: for a divine gift, because of its wonderful power, raises one toward divine things before it extends through human ones.

<margin>C</margin> That Prometheus was affected by pain because of that gift signifies that our daemonic caretaker—in whom there can also be affections—is moved by a certain mercy toward us, considering that because of the gift of reason given by him, or rather awakened by him, we lead a life on earth so much more miserable than the beasts as it is more anxious and inexplicable. Noticing this, Pythagoras placed Epimetheus above Prometheus in this regard. This seems somewhat similar to the phrase, "It repents me that I have made man" <note>A reference to Genesis 6:6.</note>. Therefore, remember that man here, as in the writings of Moses, was created from the earth and created last. Likewise, in a <margin>D</margin> Mosaic fashion, the world is said to have had a beginning. But of these things elsewhere. Through the same Prometheus in the *Philebus*, it is said that the art of discourse was given to us by the gods along with fire. For the art of discourse, where it divides universals into particulars, represents the procession of things from the higher; where it duly resolves particulars back into universals, it designates the conversion of things to the higher; where it defines and demonstrates, it shows the existence of things—there indeed in themselves, here as depending on others. Therefore, the faculty of discourse is a divine gift, since it reflects the divine order of the universe. It is said to be given with fire because fire similarly divides, resolves, defines, and demonstrates. Likewise, because the rational faculty, like fire, illuminates the intellect, inflames the will, and <margin>E</margin> elevates both to sublime things.

As for the tradition that Prometheus could not bestow civil virtue, which is utterly necessary for the safety of men, because such virtue is in the power of Jove, where Prometheus is not permitted to ascend: this is to be understood by the reasoning that the duty of civil virtue is to command not only human affairs but also the arts, to order each with each, and finally to direct all into a common form for everyone. This same duty belongs to Jove himself in the universe, which appears in the human race as the duty of civil science. Wherefore, not without justice, it belongs to Jove himself to bestow this upon us from on high. For universal virtue pertains to the universal providence of Jove. But the providence of daemons is particular and narrow, and therefore cannot ascend into the citadel of Jove; since a narrower and lower <margin>F</margin> providence cannot equal the most ample and eminent. Jove, therefore, through Mercury—that is, through the angel who is the interpreter of the divine will—inscribes on our minds the laws of civil science, that is, the decrees of his will looking toward the safety of human society and the race. He inscribes them, I say, both from the beginning (which the *Timaeus* clearly teaches) and daily through angels interpreting the divine will to us. Whence an inward judge presides in us: the inextinguishable light of reason, the examination of true and false and good and evil, the inevitable sting of conscience. Through this, God directs almost everyone toward the common good by a law infused in all, just as he raises all flames toward the heavens by their lightness. From this innate law, the written law then takes its origin. <margin>G</margin> Plato opened this indeed in the very beginning of the book of *Laws*, saying that laws had their beginning not from man, but from God himself.

But to return to the present dialogue: he adds that Jove, through Mercury, established a law by which all are commanded to be participants in civility; for this alone is the bond of the city. And he says that he sent down from heaven the city itself, consisting of justice and shame <note>note: "shame" (Latin: *pudore*) here refers to *Aidos*, a sense of moral respect or modesty.</note>, in such a way that whoever hereafter is found entirely devoid of this virtue shall be afflicted with the ultimate punishment as a plague to the city. What he first called shame, he later named temperance. For innate shame is the foundation of temperance. Temperance in citizens moderates the private affections of each and <margin>H</margin> composes their gestures. Justice, however, directs the acts of each as they relate to others. Remember, however, that in a private person, civility is content with these two; but in a public person, according to Plato's mind, prudence must be added to them. And that would be almost enough in peace; but in war, add fortitude, and thus the description of civility will be absolute. After this, Protagoras confirms from the common opinion of men that all ought to be participants in this virtue; for if anyone should openly confess his injustice, he would be considered insane by the common people—as if everyone thinks justice so necessary to the community that even if one does not have it, he ought at least to pretend to have it. Since he has shown thus far that civil virtue is the most necessary of all for everyone, and that a certain affection or spark and seed of it was infused in us by the divine from the beginning, he next proceeds to demonstrate virtue...

<summary>Ficino introduces Plato's Protagoras by contrasting the deceptive "poison" of Sophists with the healing philosophy of Socrates, then interprets the myth of Prometheus as a metaphor for the divine origin of human reason and civil virtue.</summary>

# ARGUMENTS AND COMMENTARY.

civil virtue, and indeed all others (for it encompasses them all), can be obtained as a firm and absolute habit neither by nature nor by chance, but that its habit is acquired solely through teaching and practice. To this end, he first brings forward a reason showing that men are not accustomed to ever approve or disapprove of anyone for those things which happen either by nature or by chance; however, they always praise or blame actions of virtue or vice. Next, he arranges the education of childhood and youth under domestic grammarians, musicians, gymnasts, laws, and a certain long order, showing that the entire institution of life strives strenuously toward this: that vices be avoided and virtues possessed—as if neither vices nor virtues arise from fortune, fate, or mere will, but from exercise. Meanwhile, he touches upon the ancients' opinion regarding the punishment of vices, which is worthy of consideration: namely, that no one should be punished because they have sinned, but lest they themselves sin further, or another sin by their example. He then responds to those things which Socrates had objected. We, however, from all that has been discussed so far, shall keep that golden opinion of the ancients stored deep in our minds: First, that God himself provides for and consults for our life and safety in every way from all sides. Second, that civil virtue is a divine gift, lest anyone perchance trust that he will govern the republic rightly and happily without divine grace. For Plato, confirming this in the *Laws* and elsewhere, says: just as many beasts cannot be led rightly by one of their own unless under a human shepherd, so many men cannot be led happily by one certain king, unless that one is also ruled by God. Therefore, he proves in the *Theages* and *Meno* that the faculty of ruling is held from nowhere else but God. As for what the sophist Protagoras intends, let him see to it himself. Finally, let us remember how necessary is inviolate justice, sent from heaven, if those voices of the ancients continually ring in our ears: "Wretched mortals once, before civility was sent from heaven, could neither live apart without being torn to pieces everywhere by wild beasts, nor gathered together without being mangled by one another." Therefore, the safety which all the arts together could not provide, justice alone finally provided. After this, lest the Sophist be held in admiration by the listeners because of some good things he had related from others, Socrates, by a certain ironic, urbane, and skillful method of refutation, renders him a laughingstock to those present. For he asks, after Protagoras had spoken so magnificently of virtue, whether there is only one virtue or many. Furthermore, if many, whether they are parts of one, or not. Again, if parts, whether they are like one another and the whole, or dissimilar on both sides. To these things Protagoras knows neither how to answer correctly, nor how to define or divide the virtues, nor how to distinguish in what way they are similar and in what way dissimilar; nor can he avoid what is most shameful in disputation: being easily led to the point where he often contradicts himself. Finally, when Protagoras began to hesitate out of ignorance of how to respond, and Socrates therefore pretended he was going to leave, the Sophist was called back by the listeners to continue the discussion. In this altercation, the superstitious curiosity of the Sophist Prodicus regarding words is first demonstrated; then the more timid ostentation of the Sophist Hippias in public speaking. Lastly, Protagoras, recalled to the dispute, digresses too importunately and ineptly into songs and poetry, questioning Socrates about a certain opinion of the poet Simonides; Socrates soon convicts him of not understanding it at all, explaining Simonides' mind as if he had said: "to become a good man is indeed difficult, but to persevere is impossible." Here you will hear that the wisdom of the ancients was content with as few words as possible; and that to be able to embrace many things in brief is the work of an absolutely learned man. Likewise, that no one commits evil or shameful acts willingly, but out of ignorance. Finally, where the discussion is held in the dialectic manner, poetic matters are to be rejected. After these acts, the Sophist hesitates again and is barely recalled by those present. Then Socrates returns to the prior dispute about virtue: whether there are many parts of one virtue, and in what relation they stand to each other. Protagoras, however, slips again, affirming that some virtues are similar to each other—which he had not admitted previously—and likewise separating courage very far from the others, confessing that men can be brave without prudence and the other virtues. In this matter, he is then compelled to contradict himself and confess that not only courage, but not even any virtues can exist without prudence. Then, indeed, many things are treated concerning good and evil. Since prudence is the science of choosing the good and avoiding the evil. It is doubted, however, whether good and evil are entirely the same as pleasure and pain. This is neither entirely affirmed nor clearly denied. For concerning this in the *Gorgias*, *Philebus*, and elsewhere, it is fully proved that prudence itself—in which consists both the knowledge of the end of life and the choice of the ways leading to it—is the prince and leader of the moral virtues. This is asserted to such an extent that virtues seem to be like sciences (that is, forms of prudence), while vices are forms of ignorance (that is, imprudence). It is then added that all sins proceed from ignorance, and no one would ever choose evil unless deceived by the image of good; nor would they flee the good unless terrified by some image of evil. If someone should say that a man discerning good and evil is nevertheless turned away from the former and toward the latter because he is overcome by pleasure or some other sensory affection, Socrates will deny it, asserting that the very thing said to be "overcome by an effect" is nothing other than ignorance; for knowledge of all things within and around us is most powerful and can never be overcome by anything. Finally, he concludes that knowledge contributes most—indeed, everything—to virtue and happiness, while ignorance contributes equally to their opposites. And again he rebukes Protagoras, because he both contradicted himself and used a preposterous order. For before defining what virtue is, he attempted to divide it and disputed whether it could be taught. Socrates even pretends that he too has been led into a contradiction, solely because he followed the Sophist in his wandering

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> and he warns that we should imitate the providence of Prometheus rather than the haste of Epimetheus <note>Prometheus (Forethought) and Epimetheus (Afterthought) are brothers in Greek mythology; the Sophist Protagoras uses their myth to explain human origins.</note> in all of life to the best of our strength.

### ON THE EUTHYDEMUS
#### Argument. For page 215.

<margin>B</margin> **PLATO**, a man distinguished by charity, strives in the *Euthydemus*, as he often does elsewhere, to turn minds born for serious things away from the vain trifles of the sophists, showing that even when they deal with the gravest matters, they play and everywhere delude the hope of the listeners. He describes them here and elsewhere as curious and vain combatants in the altercation of words, ready to refute anything said, whether it be true or false. First, he shows how greedy the nature of sophists is, since Euthydemus and his brother Dionysodorus, also a sophist, are ready to teach for a fee the military art in which they glory—an art which no one ever sold. Second, how ambitious they are, since they profess judicial skill together with military skill, and both together with sophistry, which differ most widely from one another. Third, how vain: for now as old men they betake themselves from things to words, and from the study of truth to lies. Fourth, how insulting: for in a short time, at most two years, anyone can attain this faculty of caviling. Fifth, how <margin>C</margin> dangerous. For to whom should it seem a wonder that simple adolescents are easily ensnared by the dyed subtleties of the sophists, and are imbued with false opinions and ruinous morals? Since even Socrates himself, the wisest old man, is feigned to be caught by the same bait and to hasten admiringly to the sophists' gymnasia. Add that even the Socratic *daemon* <note>The "daimonion" or divine sign that Socrates claimed warned him against certain actions.</note>, which seems able to be deceived by no one, is feigned to be deceived by the sophistic tricks of these scoundrels. Meanwhile, Socrates, even in old age frequenting the schools of boys, music lessons, and the rudiments of words, warns us: first, that we should not despise even the smallest thing toward the perfection of disciplines. Second, lest, as often <margin>D</margin> happens, we be kept from the study of discipline by a certain rustic blush of shame. Third, that in the manner of Solon <note>Solon was an Athenian statesman and poet who famously said he "grew old always learning many things."</note> we should consider that we must learn as long as we must live. Furthermore, the fact that the Sophists never notice the Socratic irony against them—indeed, nothing so magnificent is brought forward in their praise that they do not very easily believe and openly accept it—declares two things to us especially: one, that nothing more worthless than these scoundrels can be found; the other, that while they study too intently to deceive the years, they are themselves most easily deceived by their own fallacy. Moreover, that such tricksters never perform the virtue they promise, nor do they anywhere exhort others to it, but everywhere flee to confused cavils of words, and prefer these as if they were serious matters <margin>E</margin> above other studies, signifies three things to us. First, those who are not themselves adorned with virtue can never teach it by reason or example. Second, men too curious about words never attain or assert good things. Third, those who most easily promise the most things are the least likely of all to keep their promises. Added to this is that a crowd of wealthy disciples attracts the Sophists to teach virtue, as they are too ambitious and greedy. But there, under the persona of Crito, we are warned not to rashly commit the care of our soul to just anyone. That Socrates, while the sophists promise virtue, meanwhile entreats them as if they were gods, clearly declares that virtue is to be sought from God himself, and that men <margin>F</margin> endowed with virtue are to be held as divine. Likewise, that he considers them happier than kings because of their study of virtue clearly signifies that a man endowed with virtue is, first, king of himself, and then king of kings. Socrates further teaches, in caring for Clinias, with what great charity and diligence we ought to apply ourselves to caring for youth. But soon, under the promises of the most insolent sophists, "the mountains are in labor, and a ridiculous mouse will be born" <note>A reference to Horace's *Ars Poetica*: "Parturient montes, nascetur ridiculus mus," meaning grand promises leading to trivial results.</note>. But one must also note there a certain hyperbolic irony of Socrates to mock vain men. Then the incomparable vanity of the scoundrels, providing words instead of things—and very inept ones at that—everywhere; and though they promised an exhortation to wisdom, they fall back into childish follies. Then Socrates says the entire gymnasium of the sophists is a play of words, and that <margin>G</margin> the nature of things is entirely hidden from them; their artificial webs can be dissolved only by the exposition of words and the distinction of meaning. He then entreats the sophists with a most witty irony to come to serious matters after their games; and he proposes a certain formula, after whose example he desires from them an exhortation to philosophy. In such a formula, he first describes happiness by the common notion: "living well." Then he proves that this "living well" consists either in the attainment of things according to one's wish, or in the right use of those very things. And from both sides, through inductions, he concludes that wisdom—since it alone attains things as wished and uses them rightly—alone makes men blessed. And in such inductions, an order is seen: if through individual parts of life wisdom both follows the wish and is used rightly, then wisdom brings a consequent common and highest good to the whole end of life, consisting in prosperous attainment and right use. During the arguing, a famous sentiment shines forth which became the foundation of the Stoic school: namely, that external and corporeal things are "indifferent" and common, rather than to be called either good or bad. Properly, however, wisdom is good, and folly is bad. Since through the former all things turn out good for us, and through the latter all things turn out bad. Therefore, wisdom alone can make us blessed. That the whole of happiness consists in knowledge is declared by the three names for happiness established by the ancient Greek authors: namely, *Eudaimonia* (blessedness), *Eutychia* (good fortune), and *Eupraxia* (well-doing).

<summary>This page provides a philosophical commentary on Plato's Protagoras and Euthydemus, emphasizing that virtue is a divine gift rooted in wisdom and prudence rather than sophistic wordplay. It critiques the greed and vanity of the Sophists while upholding Socrates as a model of lifelong learning and moral integrity.</summary>
<keywords>Plato, Socrates, Protagoras, Euthydemus, virtue, wisdom, Sophists, divine grace, education, ethics, prudence, happiness, Eudaimonia</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Ficino’s commentary on Plato’s Euthydemus, focusing on the definitions of virtue and the distinction between various forms of knowledge, before transitioning into the introduction for the Lesser Hippias.</meta>

# MARSILIO FICINO

<margin>A</margin> First, it signifies the thought of the good; second, its completion; and third, its use—all of which knowledge perfects for us. Plato, both here and elsewhere, says that this knowledge of the good is, in a sense, the whole of virtue. Wisdom <note>original: *sapientia*</note> is the absolute knowledge of the divine good. Prudence <note>original: *prudentia*</note>, however, is the knowledge of goods and evils specifically pertaining to man. Justice is the knowledge of distributing goods and evils according to merit. Fortitude is knowledge regarding what to dare and what to fear concerning goods and evils. Finally, Temperance is knowledge regarding the choosing and fleeing of goods and evils. One must remember above all that Plato suggests here and often elsewhere that wisdom is not so much acquired by human study as it is infused by the divine into purified minds. Indeed, since the soul joined to this body is rendered unfit for things utterly separated from the body, it grows dim like an owl under the excessive splendor of divine things. Therefore, the Socratic exhortation to wisdom pertains not so much to speculation as to loves. Once purified by these, the soul attains wisdom from God, as well as science and prudence. Through these means, while Socrates pretends to demand from the sophists an exhortation to philosophy (which is the study of wisdom), he himself meanwhile wonderfully exhorts one to philosophize through a most fitting dissimulation <note>Ficino refers to Socratic Irony</note>. Nevertheless, the sophists do not yet accept the exhortation for themselves or even for others, but revolve again through their usual follies. Here it appears how ruinous an intellect always is—whether in vice or in trifles—when it is either ill-born or wrongly educated. Among these things, note most diligently Plato’s divine sentiment: for the sake of attaining virtue and wisdom, we are commanded to endure not only inconveniences, losses, labors, and servitude, but even—if we hope to emerge better from the very dissolution of ourselves—to permit ourselves to be flayed, melted down, and utterly dissolved by Him who promised this very thing. Here it appears how much the good of the soul excels corporeal things, and how much those most brave ancient Christian martyrs are to be praised. Similar to this is the saying: <margin>B</margin> "He who loves his soul in this world shall lose it; but he who loses it here shall receive it in eternal life." Furthermore, Socrates, refuting the quibbles of the sophists, demonstrates that sophisms can most easily be turned back against the sophists, especially because he forces them both to contradict themselves and to confess the most absurd things. Having done this, by again feigning a formula similar to the previous one, he declares that listeners receive nothing of the good from sophists, and that the sophists themselves, being utterly lost, cannot be recalled to a fruitful state. Since he often repeats these three names during the dispute—wisdom, science, and prudence—it should be noted that where he speaks more precisely, he defines wisdom as the cognition of divine things, science as that of natural things, and prudence as that of human things. Where he speaks less precisely, he is accustomed to use the name "science" <note>original: *scientia*</note> to signify all three. But where <margin>E</margin> he speaks more freely, he uses each one indifferently for all. Moreover, he introduces two kinds of arts: those which produce works, and those which use what has been made. And since the art which uses the work of another art both prescribes the end for its manufacture and provides the model for completing the work, we rightly place the "using art" above the "making art" in dignity. Note here that Plato makes the making art so small and the using art so great that he most clearly intends that even if one could turn all materials into gold at will, or even procure immortality itself among men, neither such a mass of gold nor immortality would profit him unless he knew how to use it. Note again that the common abuse of the oratorical art is here denounced as being exactly like sophistry—as a kind of wicked enchantment, everywhere striving like a poisoner to infect minds with disturbances. For a similar reason, he elsewhere detests the common <margin>F</margin> abuse of poetry. But because here, in enumerating the arts, he names "dialectic" (lest I say *dialectice* after the fashion of some, for *dialectic* sounds more Latin to me), one must remember that for Plato, "logic" signifies the art arranging the rules of names, speeches, and arguments; but "dialectic" signifies the sagacious investigation of the philosopher, using these rules to investigate the reasons of things, especially divine things, from which the highest reasons of subsequent things are also received. Therefore, in Plato, dialectic most often signifies "theology" to us. In the same place, he names the "royal and civil art," namely the prudence for successfully governing the human race. Whether this resides in a private or public person, in one or in many, it is called by him equally "civil" and "royal." To this art, as if to a queen, he subjects all faculties involved in acting and making, to which she gives laws and uses as instruments and handmaidens. Similarly, he subjects to theology all sciences involved in speculation, to which these stand in the same relation as private arts do to the royal art. Therefore, while Socrates, in that same formula continued from the previous one, seeks the faculty most conducive to happiness, he rightly dismisses the others and flees to royal theology, especially since happiness consists in the best use of things; and these arts strive to provide the most correct use of speculating, acting, and making for all people in all things. He taught the same in the *Philebus*, the same in the last book of the *Laws*, and the same in the books of the *Republic*, where for the happiness of the human race he instructs the future governor first in theology and then in civil discipline, asserting that the divine Idea of the Good itself is only just barely perceived by the legitimate theologian alone. And unless it has been perceived, nothing can be rightly done or happily arranged, whether privately or publicly. Although this is so, Socrates nevertheless does not think these mysteries should be revealed here among youths and sophists. For the Socratic custom is only to exhort youths, only to refute sophists, and finally to teach legitimate men. Here, therefore, under irony and dissimulation, he touches upon mysteries of this kind, and feigns that he is hesitating, and as if suffering from vertigo among the dizzying sophists. Perhaps he feigns doubt as to whether theology and civil discipline provide happiness because he often confirms that the absolute perfection

<column-break/>

neither of theology nor of civil discipline can be had by any human way, but rather by divine inspiration. Therefore, not without reason, having exhausted human powers, he refers happiness to divine munificence, to which he undoubtedly referred both the wisdom of the theologian and the prudence of the statesman. Finally, all these things are to be accepted by us in such a way that human duties prepare minds for happiness, especially when governed most rightly under theological and civil discipline; but the most merciful goodness of God himself finally bestows the supreme good of man through these as if they were means for those turned toward Him. I had decided to impose an end to this honorable argument, or rather to the commentary, but a necessary question still detains me: to what end does the frequent irony of Socrates serve? It always hides Socrates' own goods, but often feigns the goods of the proud; and <margin>C</margin> as much as it always detracts from Socrates, it often attributes to the proud. This he achieves with frequent jokes and witticisms, and often beyond belief, so that by depressing himself he makes the listeners more modest; but by extolling the proud beyond the measure of belief, he makes their pride a thing to be derided by all. Indeed, those who are praised beyond measure by Socrates, if they are not entirely lost, are mended by being confused with shame; but if they are already utterly lost, they themselves are not mended, but those present, by the example of his correction, most cautiously avoid such ridiculous and proud vanity. Socratic irony is a thing quite skillful, urbane, witty, and charming. It supports the truth more safely and avoids hatred, while it both aptly hides his profession and clearly disparages himself before he can be perceived to secretly disparage another; and what is greatest in correcting vices, he escapes the mark of being a slanderer. Through this irony, near the end of this dialogue, he gathers the censure of sophistical quibbling into three heads. First, <margin>D</margin> that all the most proven men despise such trifles. Second, that sophisms confound themselves. Third, that even boys attain these things in two days as if they were the lightest matters. Soon he descends from the sophist to the rhetorician. For both falsely profess the ultimate civil art, as is written in the *Gorgias*: the sophist feigns the speculation of the philosopher, while the rhetorician feigns the moral discipline of philosophy, both far from the truth. He shows that rhetoricians and orators, while they profess to be both philosophers and statesmen at once, are entirely useless for both. Finally, he concludes the dialogue with a twin and most excellent sentiment. One is that more care should be taken that children be good than that they simply exist; and that you should leave them good rather than leave them goods. The other is that one must philosophize altogether; since philosophy itself is a divine thing, and such a precious possession must not be abandoned either on account of its false professors or on account of lying detractors.

## ON THE LESSER HIPPIAS
### Introduction to page 229.

<margin>G</margin> **T**he goodness of our Socrates and Plato is wonderful, since they most diligently provide in many ways everywhere lest credulous youth be captured by the deceitful snares of the sophists, and once captured, be lost. Not without reason does he harass Hippias of Elis, the most insolent and fallacious of the sophists, in two dialogues: namely, the Greater and the Lesser. In the *Greater Hippias*, he demonstrates that Hippias, a professor of the most beautiful things, is entirely ignorant of what beauty itself is. In the *Lesser*, he shows that the same man, boasting that he discerns the liar from the truthful man better than others, errs entirely in the definition of both; so that it may be clear that Hippias, just as he is the most arrogant of all, is also the most ignorant and appears the most inept. I pass over for now that he depicts him, as is the custom of sophists, as boastful, reckless, and greedy; and while he promises everything, in everything he gives only words and performs nothing; and while he glories in the greatest things, he falters even in the smallest. But to return to the definition of the liar and the truthful man: a liar should be rightly described as one who most wants to lie, however he can and knows how. A truthful man, on the contrary, is one who most wants to speak the truth, however he can and knows how. But Hippias, the most sluggish master of all arts and the most confused discourser on the truthful and the liar, defines them in the opposite order: he says the liar is he who is most able and knows how to lie whenever he wishes; and the truthful man is he who, whenever he wishes, is able and knows how to speak the truth. From this, he is first forced to admit that liars are powerful, knowing, prudent, and wise. Second, that they are also good at those things in which they are powerful and wise. Third, by leading him through individual arts, he is compelled to admit that in any matter or art, the same man is both truthful and a liar, which he had denied from the beginning. For in any matter, he who is best skilled is the same who is most able and knows how to speak the truth or lie at will. Fourth, he is led to concede that the truthful man is no better than the liar, since the truthful man is just as sufficient and "good" at lying. After this, Socrates leads the sophist into an ambiguity <margin>H</margin> as to which one sins more gravely: he who lies willingly, or he who lies unwillingly. The sophist does not know how to solve this, nor does Socrates wish to solve it for the sophist. It is to be solved thus: in those things pertaining to the intellect, he who lies voluntarily errs less; but in those things regarding morals, he errs more. He who tells a lie unwillingly is in the opposite condition. Then it is doubted which ones err more: those who do so by deliberate effort, or those who sin through weakness or ignorance. It is proved by long windings of induction that in things pertaining to nature and art and their instruments, a fault committed through impotence or ignorance is a graver vice than one perpetrated by malice. For the good of nature is in power itself, and the good of art is in this...

<summary>Ficino concludes his commentary on the Euthydemus by defining the hierarchy of knowledge (wisdom, science, and prudence) and the role of Socratic irony, then introduces the Lesser Hippias by critiquing Hippias's failure to distinguish between truthfulness and lying.</summary>

# ARGUMENTS AND COMMENTARY.

[The text] itself, and moreover, consists in cognition. Evil, therefore, lies in opposites. From these points, moving beyond the immediate proposition, Socrates turns Hippias toward moral character, concluding that the same principle applies in the realm of morals as in nature and the arts. Although Socrates understands that this should not be done, he nonetheless strives to show that the sophist failed to notice it at all. Certainly, in matters pertaining to the will and character, a sin is more serious when committed through malice—that is, a certain will to sin—than if it is committed through incapacity or ignorance. Finally, Socrates says that justice is either power, or knowledge, or both. He knew to add a third, but was unwilling: namely, the will. For justice consists most especially in the will. He wished to demonstrate that this escaped the sophist's notice. But let us now conclude the argument with these previous precepts: One must teach without envy. One must learn without shame. Gratitude must always be shown to the teacher. The discoveries of others must not be usurped for oneself.

## ON THE CHARMIDES
## Argument. For page 235.

<margin>A</margin> The goal of Socrates in this dialogue is to exhort everyone toward temperance <note>Latin: *temperantia*, often translated as moderation or self-control</note>. He focuses on three groups in particular: the young, the noble, and the beautiful. He addresses the young because medicine must be applied quickly to diseases. *Resist the beginnings; medicine is prepared too late when evils have grown strong through long delays.* <note>A famous quote from Ovid's *Remedia Amoris*</note>. He addresses the noble, both to show that true nobility must be placed in virtue, and because the noble are usually examples to others and are daily admitted to public affairs—to the grave detriment of the human race if they are wicked. Finally, he addresses the beautiful: for these are most easily corrupted by the company of the shameful, which is why they have a greater need for medicine. Furthermore, the beautiful ought to strive so that, just as nature gave a brief beauty to the body, they in turn may restore an everlasting beauty of the soul to God, the author of nature. Nor should it be permitted that while our exterior pleases many with its beauty, our interior meanwhile displeases with its deformity. And if everything in this dialogue contains a wonderful allegory—especially the erotic parts, not unlike the *Song of Solomon*—I have nonetheless changed some things and omitted others. For things that harmonized with the highly refined ears of the Athenians might perhaps not harmonize at all with ruder ears. Therefore, a certain Aristarchus of Homeric fame—or rather, a Platonic one—might say that the parts which harmonize less are not by Plato, but by Chronus. Three things in the very introduction are especially noteworthy, which transfer love from this physical form to incorporeal beauty. First, Socrates says that he discerns nothing between this beautiful person and that one, but that all beautiful people please him equally: as if to say, one must not stop at the form of a single body, but must ascend to the common beauty of the entire species. Since this beauty is one among many, it reflects the single Idea of beauty over the many. Just as we transcend in thought from the individual to the species, and from the species to the Idea, so we are advised to proceed from the love of this form to the love of the common form first, and then to the love of the Ideal form. To these, Socrates adds that the beauty of the body is not to be loved for itself, but should be regarded by us as an image of divine beauty. Finally, he commands the soul to be stripped bare: having set aside the form of the body, one must inspect the beauty of the soul—both that which is natural and that which is to be more diligently applied through study. Meanwhile, he rebukes Chaerephon, who had said something about stripping the body as if in the wrestling school. Not without reason does he begin the exhortation to temperance from the beauty of the body. For this beauty is a certain temperance of lines and colors. But from this, he passes directly to the health of the body, which is also a kind of temperance: namely, of the humors and members. Thirdly, he passes from this to the adornment of the soul itself: which is temperance in affection—the moderation of movements—and similarly a kind of temperance in cognition, consisting in a harmonious fit of the intelligence with the things understood. Thus, Pythagoras not undeservedly said that temperance is the most healthful of all virtues, the preserver of human society both publicly and privately. Especially since justice is also a kind of temperance: that is, a fitting moderation in exchanging and distributing. Certainly, although temperance is properly concerned with restraining vehement lusts and pleasures, by a certain similarity it is transferred to the cutting away of all desires and the moderating of any act: so that even the duty of fortitude consists in the moderation of boldness and fear; similarly justice in the measure of rewards and punishments; and liberality in the manner of giving; finally, the health of the whole life is "nothing in excess." Hence that Pythagorean saying: *Measure is best in all things.* But remember that in the *Phaedo*, those are denied to be temperate who abstain from pleasures for the sake of bodily pleasure. For he commands that moral actions be directed toward purifying the mind, for the sake of attaining wisdom and divine likeness. So great is the excellence of temperance that all elegant craftsmen observe it in their works; and by its virtue, not only any body under the moon, but even heaven itself and the universe are preserved. This is confirmed in the *Gorgias* by the testimony of the wise. Similar to this is: *God disposes all things sweetly.* Likewise, *He disposes all things in number, weight, and measure.* But let us now return to the dialogue. While Socrates, following the opinion of the Magi, forbids the body to be cured before the soul is cured, he clearly rebukes those who, caring for the smallest things, neglect the greatest: such as those who seek remedies for sick horses and dogs, but in the diseases of their own body and soul, do not consult doctors at all. They arrange every tiny piece of furniture

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> rightly, while they themselves remain disordered in soul and body. They tune the lyre with an intemperate soul. Daily they curiously handle the affairs of others, while deserting their own. Indeed, everything except the soul itself is foreign to us. Therefore, he called the medicine of the body alone a light, fragile, and entirely changeable thing, to be utterly disregarded. He also signifies that many inconveniences of both body and fortune frequently happen to us due to intemperance; and conversely, many goods arrive through temperance. Likewise, in a perfectly composed soul, whatever happens is both so prudently arranged and equally endured that nothing ultimately turns into an evil. But in a disordered soul, nothing good can be composed, whether in the body or outside it. In the *Cratylus*, he explains the Greek name for temperance, *sophrosyne*, as a kind of health and preservation of prudence. For he thinks that the lights of all truths were innate in the soul; therefore, if it looks entirely into itself, it will behold all truths within itself. But the cause of its not looking in is an immoderate affection for the body and bodily things. Thus, temperance is needed first of all: through which, once the darkness of disturbances is expelled, the mind becomes more serene and is abundantly surrounded by the light of the divine sun. From this, it first recovers wisdom, and then attains prudence. Since, therefore, wisdom and prudence accompany temperance, Plato often elsewhere, and in this dialogue, intends for wisdom and prudence to be contained under the very name of temperance. Socrates advises Charmides to look into himself when he is about to speak of temperance: for this very turning into oneself is the duty of this virtue. Whoever is deeply turned into himself will understand human temperance through the Idea of temperance innate in the mind; and recognizing that moderation by which God tempered the parts of the soul with one another from the beginning, he will know by what method the affection of the soul is to be tempered. Added to this: in this precept, he signifies that no one except a temperate person ought to or can speak of temperance to persuade others. Furthermore, it is taught in the *Timaeus* that all prosperous things happen to us from a certain harmonious modulation of the soul, both toward itself and toward the body. Moreover, the Pythagoreans—whom the Roman Censorinus follows in this—promise perpetual health to both and a long life to the body if the soul prudently moderates each motion, both of itself and of the body. Censorinus calculates that this has happened to many wise and holy men, and we hold the same. Some would refer the long lives of the ancients to this same or a similar cause. But something more wonderful is added to these: that the Magi promise immortality to bodies through their songs. In the *Alcibiades*, Plato says that the magic of Zoroaster is nothing other than divine worship. Here he adds further that not only by magical songs, but also by philosophical reasons, the soul is tempered and the body is kept far from death, either forever or at least for a long time. Certainly, that speech which is to entirely persuade the listeners of temperance, and moreover to effect it, requires two things especially: a power infused by God, and reasons prepared by philosophers. And Plato calls a speech composed of these two a "magical incantation." By this, Phoebus <note>Apollo</note> first, and then the Pythagoreans, wonderfully expelled diseases from the soul and body. Nor should it be thought false: that a body under a deeply tempered soul can be made immortal, and under an intemperate one, fall into diseases and all evils. For this also contains the Mosaic mystery concerning the state and fall of the first parent <note>Adam</note>. And Avicenna, following the Platonists and Hippocrates, proves that the soul by its very nature so exceeds all matter that as soon as it is restored to itself, it can move the elements of the world with a certain wonderful power and have command over any bodies; thus, it can do so much more over its own. Indeed, Adam could experience this from the beginning; and some think Enoch and Elijah, and some suspect the Evangelist <note>John</note>, still live by some similar reason. But we dispute all these matters most extensively in our *Theology*. Finally, to speak in summary, a wonder is declared in this virtue of temperance: that it happily restores to itself the soul that had unhappily fallen into worse things. The wonderful power of the soul is also declared: from which all things, both good and evil, flow down into the body, and by whose will the body can be kept incorrupt. This indeed harmonizes almost everywhere with the Mosaic mysteries. After this, it is frequently asked what temperance is—a question which neither Charmides nor Critias ever resolves. For the former brings forward not temperance properly, but the things that accompany it; while the latter brings forward things that pertain more to prudence—and always ineptly, so as to demonstrate that it is not for just anyone to discourse on such a noble virtue. Meanwhile, note that the ancient priests were accustomed to consecrate the third cup of libation in sacrifices especially to Jupiter the Savior, to declare that the beginnings, middles, and ends of all things are arranged and preserved under the providence of Jupiter, as Plato records in the *Laws*. But let us return to the ineptitudes of Critias, who says there is a certain science which knows both itself and all sciences, but does not know the things themselves of which they are sciences. This is absurd because the truth and reason of science consist in a certain contact and congruence with the things known. Furthermore, a science cannot be perfectly known unless what kind of science it is can be discerned. But that cannot be held unless the thing it concerns is held. Likewise, Critias confesses that someone can, while knowing nothing, meanwhile know that he does not know. Socrates does not accept this, because things that are in no way known cannot meanwhile be known in some way. For whoever notices that he is ignorant of something, by that very act recognizes that he lacks it. If he judges so, then he has already described a certain notion of it in himself, by which he judges both that he lacks it and what it is he especially lacks. Thus, whoever knows he is ignorant of a thing does not meanwhile entirely ignore the thing itself; rather, he describes it with a certain general shadowing—general, I say, because perfect science consists in the special distinction of things, which in all [things...]

<summary>This page provides a philosophical commentary on the transition from the Hippias Minor to the Charmides, focusing on the definition of temperance (sophrosyne) as a harmony of soul and body that reflects divine order.</summary>

--- Page 800 ---
<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentaries on Plato’s dialogues, specifically concluding the introduction to the *Charmides* (on temperance) and beginning the argument for the *Laches* (on courage/fortitude).</meta>

# MARSILIO FICINO

<margin>A</margin> Plato investigates these matters in his disputations. But where he introduces Socrates admitting that he knows nothing, he judges that Socrates possesses general, if not specific, descriptions of things; otherwise, he would not be able to recognize his own ignorance. Therefore, while he knew nothing, he in a certain way knew all things. Since Critias had shifted the discourse from temperance to prudence—and indeed did so with a certain Platonic liberty—Socrates asserts that prudence, that is, the knowledge of good and evil, holds the highest authority for achieving happiness. This is both because it demonstrates the good end and the good means to that end, and because all things and arts, insofar as they are governed by prudence, lead us toward the good; otherwise, they do not. Finally, Socrates teaches that nothing is more difficult to define or acquire than temperance. The difficulty of definition arises because it can hardly be distinguished from the other virtues, of which it is a certain harmony. Add to this that it is understood and expressed in words with as much difficulty as it is possessed within. Indeed, since by the very commerce of the body we are most inclined toward pleasure and intemperance—and are nurtured in this from infancy—we attain temperance with the greatest difficulty. Furthermore, the first impulses of the senses seem to contribute somewhat to courage through anger and audacity, or to prudence through fear, or to patience through pain, or to justice and liberality through love. But every impulse is always opposed to temperance. For since it can only be established in a state of total tranquility, it is hindered on all sides by any emotion. This also increases the difficulty: just as it is most difficult to find a perfect balance of humors and limbs in a harmonious body, so it is most difficult of all to find a harmonic temperance of all its parts in the soul. <margin>B</margin> Therefore, not without reason does Socrates say, both in the epilogue and the introduction, that to achieve temperance—which is most similar to celestial harmony—one needs celestial and divine virtue, infused into the soul, the reason, and the words. Everywhere he warns that we must strive rather to be made temperate under lawful institutions than to dispute about temperance under dialectical reasons. For it is known only with the greatest difficulty; and once known, without practice, it not only profits nothing but hinders a great deal. And what is more, unless it is possessed in reality, it cannot be perfectly known. For it is not permitted for the impure to touch the purest thing of all.
