### ON THE LACHES
### Argument for page 245.

<margin>C</margin> Plato frequently places the best magistrates above laws, for laws without them seem entirely useless; no one will observe them. The best magistrates, however, are themselves the laws. But he says that the best magistrates cannot be made unless the citizens are the best men; nor will the men be such unless the adolescents and boys are also such. Therefore, in almost all his dialogues, he primarily exhorts parents to educate their children rightly, knowing that the human race cannot live honestly or be governed happily without the best governors. Furthermore, there will never be good leaders in the republic unless they are men of proven character, diligently cultivated from a tender age. Since childhood is usually sufficiently governed under the providence of those at home, but adolescence, having gained a looser liberty, wanders everywhere without reins, our Plato rightly treats at length the correction and restraining of adolescents. He gravely complains that this age—which joins the petulance of softness and wantonness with pride, and is therefore placed in the greatest danger—is both poorly observed by those at home and unhappily neglected by laws and magistrates, especially since adolescents corrupt each other as much as they are infected by their elders. Therefore, in the *Laws* and the *Republic*, he appoints a specific magistrate over adolescence. This person, like a bishop <note>original: "episcopus" - here meaning an overseer or supervisor</note> as it were, should send scouts daily, both night and day, throughout the city to observe the individual habits, words, and gestures of each adolescent, and faithfully report their individual deeds and words to the magistrate as if to a shepherd and father. Nor was this necessary diligence regarding adolescence a concern for Plato alone; in this matter, even Aristotle himself could not help but highly approve of Plato. But let us come to the dialogue. <margin>D</margin> Lysimachus and Melesias are thinking about educating their sons, having complained about their own parents who, by handling public affairs too curiously, neglected domestic matters and their sons, even though the primary care of the republic consists in caring for the youth. Although they are now old men, in order to deliberate more rightly on the matter, they likewise call together Nicias and Laches, also old men who have sons, for consultation. And lest anything be overlooked, they bring Socrates into the counsel, not only as a partner but as a judge—Socrates, I say, who in his whole life treated nothing else but the proper care of every age, and especially of adolescence. You, meanwhile, will consider the wonderful praises of the Socratic life, and that those are true praises which proceed from a man worthy of praise. But because in some cities the institution of laws leans more toward gentleness than toward audacity, and in others the opposite, Plato, judging both to be dangerous, commands in the *Statesman* <note>original: "Politico"</note> that gentleness be mixed with audacity and audacity with gentleness. If someone joins the *Charmides* to the *Laches*, and couples the exhortation to temperance there with the exhortation to courage <note>original: "fortitudinem"</note> here, he will rightly temper the souls of adolescents. I pass over the fact that in this present dialogue's exhortation to courage, both Nicias and Laches admire military courage more than is fitting, and Nicias extols the games of arms with excessive praise as if they were absolutely necessary preludes to warfare. But Laches rightly corrects him. After this, the opinion

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> is transferred to Socrates. Here he observes that no harmony delights more than that which occurs in a wise man from the very concord of soul and speech. And conversely, no dissonance offends more than where the tongue and the mind are discordant. Then, that a ruined man, even if he speaks beautifully, should not be heard. Nor is it permitted to speak of morals unless one is moral. Furthermore, Socrates was always accustomed, whatever the subject of dispute, to lead the focus of the disputation to the point where he rendered an account of his whole life; as if you know other things in vain unless you know yourself. It is added that it is primarily necessary to submit oneself to someone examining you, to whom an account of your past life may often be rendered. This indeed strongly confirms the annual confession instituted by Christians. It is also added that one must learn as long as one must live. Socrates, however, being the most cautious of all, says the judgment enjoined upon him should be transferred <margin>B</margin> to the elders. But meanwhile, entreated by everyone, he approaches the matter itself, first of all approving diligence in educating sons and disapproving of negligence. He adds that it is impossible for anyone to exhort another to courage unless he knows how to express what courage itself is. Soon, when Laches is asked what courage is, he answers rather confidently that it is the virtue through which one does not desert their rank but overcomes the enemy. This is refuted because someone can defeat an enemy by fleeing no less than by staying, in the manner of the Scythians, and be equally brave. Therefore, Homer calls him brave who knows how to dare and to fear at the opportune time. A little later, the victory of courage is drawn toward any subject matter, as if it befits a brave man to overcome not only fears <margin>C</margin> but also pains, lusts, and pleasures. Hence a common definition of courage for all these things is sought. To this, Laches responds that it is a certain endurance <note>original: "tolerantiam"</note> of the soul. But since this is defined insufficiently, Socrates compels him to add that the endurance itself must be honorable and beneficial. It will not be such unless it is done prudently. Therefore, he compels Laches to say that courage is properly "prudent endurance." For courage is something beautiful and good. Then it is asked what kind of endurance, and for what it is prudent—that is, concerning what matter and what duty. Laches slips when he is asked generally whether, where audacity is greater, courage is also greater, and he concedes this; and again he admits that audacity is necessarily greater in one who, <margin>D</margin> without skill in the matter yet recognizing the danger, approaches the task, than in one who proceeds equipped with skill. For the latter acts more cautiously and safely. Laches finally accepts that where there is more audacity and less skill or prudence, courage is greater. In this concession, he both contradicts himself and admits a falsehood. For courage is something beautiful and beneficial, but imprudent audacity is base and harmful. Meanwhile, note the well-worn Socratic and Platonic sentiment: each person is good at those things in which he is wise, and bad at those in which he is ignorant. Indeed, just as all errors—both of the hand in grasping and of the foot in walking—proceed from a defect of sight itself, so Socrates thinks all human errors, both in choosing and in acting, proceed from a defect of intelligence. For <margin>E</margin> where the leader himself is blind or blinking, everything falls headlong. After Laches, Nicias defines courage as the knowledge of things to be feared and things not to be feared—by what reason and to what extent they should be feared or attacked. He calls courage a certain constant habit with prudence concerning things to be feared and attacked. But he calls reckless audacity without prudence "ferocity." Socrates argues against Nicias thus: Of whatever things there is a certain knowledge, there is not one for past things as they happened, another for present things as they are, and another for future things as they might best happen; rather, it belongs to the same knowledge to understand all these. If, therefore, courage is the knowledge of daring and fearing regarding good and evil things as they are in the future, it is surely also the knowledge of the same as they are present and past. Therefore, of all things simply. It is, then, universal virtue. But we, from the <margin>F</margin> beginning, were seeking courage as some part of virtue. This objection was made not so much to refute Nicias as to test him. But Nicias does not know how to defend his definition. Socrates, however, unwilling to act as a teacher among the elders because of his modesty, pretends that he is similarly ignorant of the definition; he exhorts them to seek out teachers of the virtues for themselves before they profess the faculty of educating youth, showing that in every age moral discipline is greatly necessary, and that one must always learn without the blush of shame. The definitions which he seeks here concerning courage, or in the *Charmides* concerning temperance, are not completed here or there—where the intent is merely to exhort and admonish—but in the *Republic* and the *Laws*. But <margin>G</margin> to speak summarily of courage and temperance as if they were siblings: Plato in the *Phaedrus* and the *Symposium* compares this life of ours to a certain journey. In directing this journey, reason represents the charioteer; the emotions, partly superior and partly inferior, represent twin horses, namely a white one and a black one. And to distinguish more conveniently for the question at hand: he says Divine Providence established that we be called back from base things and continually provoked toward honorable ones. Therefore, it implanted in us shame and magnanimity, so that our charioteer might restrain our emotions like horses from base licenses using shame as a bridle, <margin>H</margin> and stimulate them toward honorable things, however arduous, using the spurs of magnanimity. For a certain evil demon allures us to base things with the enticements of pleasure and deters us from honorable things with the bitterness of pain. For this reason, temperance, using the bridles of shame, ensures that we always abstain from base things despite the invitation of pleasure; and courage, relying on the spurs of magnanimity, takes care that we strive usefully toward honorable things, having despised the fear of difficulty and pain. And as much as it is more difficult to overcome pains than to abstain from pleasures, so much perhaps might courage seem to someone [to be superior] to temperance...

<summary>This page concludes Ficino's introduction to Plato's *Charmides*, emphasizing the difficulty of defining and practicing temperance, before transitioning into an analysis of the *Laches*, where Socrates, Nicias, and Laches debate the definition of courage as "prudent endurance" or "knowledge of fear."</summary>

Finally, while temperance ensures we do not fall from the human state into that of beasts, fortitude goes further, so that we are in a sense transformed into God, who overcomes all things. It is chiefly because of this virtue that all antiquity numbered Hercules among the gods: Hercules, I say, who as a victor on earth climbed the celestial steps, crying out: "Go now, brave ones, where the lofty path of a great example leads: why do you idly bare your backs? # ON THE CRATYLUS
## Argument. For page 257.

Platonic wisdom always looks up toward the sublime and never despises the humble: although the knowledge of true names is not humble, but rather exalted, especially regarding divine names. The wise Hebrews valued this so highly that they preferred it not only to all sciences but even to the written Law, asserting that it was granted by God to the patriarchs and to Moses. To Moses, I say, He inscribed it not in letters, but in the minds of the holy ones: in the minds, I say, of the succeeding prophets, who thereafter propagated the wisdom of divine names into the minds of those who followed in a long succession. By the power of these names, therefore, their ancestors performed wondrous works. Furthermore, they inserted some of these names into their writings, but mostly scattered or veiled; if anyone should know and collect them, and pronounce them perfectly with the same purity of mind with which they were granted, he would similarly perform miracles. This is especially true of the primary name of God, which, since it is wonderfully composed of only four letters—and these being vowels—can certainly be rightly pronounced by no one unless divinely inspired. Hence they are forced to admit that Jesus, whom they call the Nazarene, was divine. For they confess that He performed miracles through the true understanding and perfect pronunciation of this *Tetragrammaton* <note>The four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH.</note> name. But enough has been said by us on these matters in our book *On Religion*. Origen also, when he had considered the miraculous power of divine names and prayers, says in his books *Against Celsus* that a wondrous power lies hidden in certain sacred names, and therefore these must not be translated from the Hebrew tongue into another, but preserved in their own characters. For perhaps just as life remains in a body composed in a certain proportion—which does not remain if it is composed differently or changed—so they think a certain vital power exists in divine names composed in a specific, divinely ordained way. And just as Hermes Trismegistus taught from the beginning, and much later Plotinus and Iamblichus, demons are in a way enclosed within certain statues composed in a specific order. Moreover, by words tempered to a certain celestial likeness, certain divine gifts are distributed; and this is provided by God so that, as often as the matter requires, we might rightly invoke divine aid. They record that this was observed by Phoebus <note>Apollo</note> himself and by Pythagoras, who are said to have miraculously cured diseases of both mind and body using only certain divine words. Indeed, we find that the entire wisdom of Zoroaster consisted in this, which Plato calls divine in the *Alcibiades*, and in the *Charmides* calls the healer of diseases of mind and body. I pass over the fact that all nations and languages pronounce the principal name of God with only four letters. For this is treated more extensively by us in the commentaries on the *Philebus*, where it is proved that all nations could not have agreed on this one thing unless divinely inspired. Hence the Egyptians call Him whom we call God, *Theut*; the Persians, *Syra*; the Magi, *Orsi* (whence *Oromasis*); the Hebrews express that ineffable name of four vowels as best they can through *Adonai*; the Greeks, *Theos*; the Arabs, *Alla*; Muhammad, *Abdi*; we received *Jesus* from the angel. But why did God wish to be invoked everywhere by four letters? Perhaps because He Himself disposes all things through four stages: composing them by essence, being, power, and action. Likewise, He disposes celestial things by the four triplicities of the signs—fiery, airy, watery, earthy—and those things under heaven similarly by the four elements. No one will wonder that such great power lies hidden in true names, if only we consider the natural power of the thing itself: when we truly know, it reaches from the objects to the senses, from these to the imagination, and from this in a certain way even to the mind. Then it is first conceived by the mind, and then expressed through the voice as if by a birth. And in this very voice, established by its own articulations, the power itself lies hidden under the form of signification like a life: a life, I say, first conceived from the mind itself through the seeds of things, then brought forth through voices, and finally preserved through writings. If the names of other things preserve the power of the things in a certain way—and therefore through them, as if through images of the things, the things themselves are recognized—how much more do divine names, handed down by God Himself, perpetually preserve their power. And not without merit. For a true name, as Plato pleases, is nothing other than a certain power of the thing itself, first conceived in the mind (as I said), then expressed by the voice, and finally signified by letters. Now, the power of a divine thing must be divine. Therefore, since divine power is inherent in the names of God, Plato commands us to venerate them both here and in the *Philebus*, and as he indicates in the *Laws*, even much more than divine shrines and statues. For a more express image of God is reserved in the craftsmanship of the mind, especially when divinely inspired, than in the works of hands. He judges that the first and purest names of God exist among the supernal and celestial minds, by whom God Himself is more expressly conceived. The second are in the purer demons <note>In the Neoplatonic sense: intermediary spirits, not "demons" in the modern evil sense.</note>. The third are in the souls of men, and these were brought forth through ancient men inspired by God as if they were the trumpets of God. Thus the names of God handed down to us through the ancient and holy ones seem to be like images and rays of God Himself, penetrating through the higher spirits

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> and through the holier souls of men. Whoever admires the sun as is fitting, rightly venerates the light of the sun as well; so too one should primarily worship God, and likewise the rays, powers, and images of God lying hidden in the signification of sacred spirits. Let us hear Socrates crying out in the *Philebus*: "My reverence toward the names of the gods is always no human fear, but surpasses every greatest dread." Let us hear the same man again in the *Phaedrus* purifying himself because he perhaps erred in discussing the name of the god Love. Let us hear Plato in the eleventh book of the *Laws*, deeming those who defile the names of the gods with lies and perjury to be utterly sacrilegious, and commanding that they be struck down by anyone with impunity; while he rigidly condemns as a traitor to the laws anyone who, being present, does not punish them.

<margin>B</margin> Nor does he command us to believe there are many gods simply because he often names many. For in the *Parmenides* and the *Timaeus* he proves that God is one through Himself; as for the others, when he calls them gods, he understands them to be angelic and celestial ministers of God—not so much gods as "divine beings." After he compared all things to the one God in the *Parmenides*, he did not think His names should be despised; since wondrous gifts of God lie hidden in them, that divine theologian Dionysius the Areopagite not unjustly sought out all the mysteries of theology in the divine names. And why do we pass over in silence that apostolic splendor of truth, Paul, saying that the Word of God is living and effective, piercing more vehemently than any

<margin>C</margin> two-edged sword? Likewise that other saying of his: "God gave Him a name which is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth"? But let us now return to the dialogue. Hermogenes, a disciple and follower of Parmenides, and Cratylus, a follower of Heraclitus, disagreeing about the correctness of names—while the former thinks names have power only by arbitrary choice, and the latter by a certain natural reason—finally submit themselves to the judgment of Socrates. At the start, how beautifully these three teachers of Plato meet here! For he is said to have received moral philosophy from Socrates, physics from Cratylus, and metaphysics chiefly from Hermogenes, besides those things he discovered himself. Cratylus is a follower of Heraclitus and other ancients who philosophized many centuries before Heraclitus and thought nothing was

<margin>D</margin> stable but that all things were in perpetual motion; hence they mostly assigned names to things based on motion itself. Hermogenes, however, a devotee of Parmenides and the Pythagoreans, thought on the contrary that all things remain still. Socrates and Plato settle this controversy between Hermogenes and Cratylus such that Heraclitus's opinion is to be approved in Physics, but Parmenides's in Metaphysics; however, if anyone transfers the stability of things to natural matters, or motion to divine matters, he is to be utterly rejected. But leaving these aside, as far as names are concerned, Socrates seems to lean more toward the opinion of Cratylus, confirming it in this way: "Of speeches, some are true, others false; and the parts of a true speech are true; the parts of a false speech are also false. But the parts of speech are names; from which

<margin>E</margin> it follows that some names are true, others false." A true speech is one that speaks of things as they are; a false one, the opposite. Therefore, true names are those that present things as they are, rather than as it pleases an arbitrary choice. Since Protagoras thinks that whatever things seem to each person, such they are—so much so that things have no essence of their own, but human opinion is the measure of all things—Socrates therefore argues against Protagoras that some men are the best (namely, the most prudent) and others the worst (namely, the furthest from prudence). But if, as Protagoras thinks, those things are true for each person which he happens to think, there will certainly be no distinction between the prudent and the imprudent. But Protagoras is most subtly refuted in the book *On Science* <note>The *Theaetetus*.</note>; yet it was necessary to refute him briefly here as well, so that

<margin>F</margin> Hermogenes's opinion about names, which is in a way similar to his, could be more easily rejected. Indeed, Hermogenes by no means believes Protagoras regarding the differences in things; but while he confesses that the truth of names comes from human choice, he secretly leans toward the Protagorean opinion regarding things. He also falls hiddenly into the opinion of Euthydemus, who says that all things are always present to all people in the same way; he is briefly rebuked by the fact that some would not be good and others evil if virtue and vice were equally present to all. You, meanwhile, note this most rare opinion of our Plato: that the entire power of virtue is placed in prudence itself, and the entire power of vice in imprudence. After the opinions of Protagoras and Euthydemus are refuted, it is concluded that things themselves exist as such or such, not according to our opinion, but according to

<margin>G</margin> their own nature in the very order of things. If essences behave naturally, then actions and passions are also natural. Thus, if we strive to divide or burn any thing, we will do so not so much by our own choice as by the nature of the thing, so that we divide it in that way and with that instrument by which it can be more aptly divided, and similarly burn it. Now, speaking and naming seem to be a certain action, and therefore must have their own nature, so that we name things not as it pleases us but as the mode of the thing requires. For a name is a certain instrument by which we discern and divide the named thing from others. Such an instrument, as is clear in other cases, must be adapted to its proper duty not by chance, nor by whim, but by art, so that its form is disposed through the very idea of the art which leads most aptly to discerning and

<margin>H</margin> dividing as if toward an end. To manufacture such an instrument—that is, a name adapted both to discerning things and to teaching listeners—is not the job of just anyone, but of a certain craftsman, a "founder of names," who is the rarest of all. He, moreover, manufactures names by the logic that the craftsman who uses names requires and instructs. Plato wants the Dialectician to be such a person. But he who manufactures them composes the name, endowed with a certain signification, according to the very idea of the thing conceived in the mind, in which the true reason of the name consists. And this very ideal reason and signification is the true name, and it remains the same regarding the same thing in whatever material of letters it may be made, among whatever nations, provided it teaches what the thing itself is...

<summary>This page introduces a commentary on Plato's Cratylus, arguing that names (especially divine ones) possess inherent natural power and are not merely arbitrary human inventions. It links this concept to Hebrew traditions of the Tetragrammaton and the Neoplatonic idea of names as "images" of divine reality.</summary>
<keywords>Cratylus, Plato, divine names, Tetragrammaton, Hermogenes, Socrates, Protagoras, etymology, linguistics, Neoplatonism, magic, theology</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plato’s *Cratylus*, focusing on the divine origin of names and the theological interpretation of Greek deities.</meta>

# MARSILIO FICINO

<margin>A</margin> By discerning. He concludes that names, if they are to be truly accurate and correctly applied, must be established by a wise "giver of names." This is done at the urging of the dialectician <note>A practitioner of logic and philosophical debate</note>, so that names are fashioned in a way that imitates and explains the properties of things as much as possible. After this, inquiring diligently into who should define the "correctness" of names—that is, the specific logic by which they were established—he mocks the Sophists <note>Professional teachers in ancient Greece often accused of circular or deceptive reasoning</note> and leads us instead toward the poets. He does not mean just any poets, but the "divine" ones, who received the true names of things from the gods, with whom the true names reside. Among these, he shows that Homer’s poetry is allegorical, even where it seems to tell a historical story, as is apparent in his allegorically constructed names. He notes that many names of heroes in Homer are composed according to a specific allegorical logic. <margin>B</margin> Then he ascends to the names of the gods, the explanations of which he received from the more venerable theologians. In the first "positioning" of names, **Caelus** <note>Uranus/The Sky</note> signifies the soul of the star-bearing sphere, **Saturn** the soul of the next sphere, and **Jupiter** the third. In the second positioning, **Caelus** signifies God, **Saturn** the angelic mind, and **Jupiter** the soul of the world and the heavens. In the third, **Caelus** signifies the fruitfulness of God himself, **Saturn** his intelligence, and **Jupiter** his beneficent will providing for all. In the fourth, **Caelus** designates an upward gaze toward higher things in any deity, **Saturn** a turning back toward oneself, and **Jupiter** a forward-looking providence for lower things. I would be forced to be too long-winded if I wished to interpret every single god theologically here; indeed, we have treated this more extensively in our books *On Love* and *Theology*. Since dealing with divine matters is not for one who always says he "knows nothing," Socrates—whenever he discusses divine matters more deeply—appropriately says that such wisdom has recently shone upon him from an unknown source, signifying that inspiration is necessary for a true <margin>C</margin> perception of divine things. He confirms this in the *Timaeus*, the *Symposium*, and the *Phaedrus*. He proves the same in his *Epistles*. However, when he says he received his contemplation of divine things from Euthyphro, he is being ironic; he is mocking him and similar ambitious professors of divine law. Thus, it is not without reason that he asserts the things he pretends to have heard from Euthyphro will soon have to be dismissed, warning that one should not trust the doctrines of the ambitious—especially when they judge divine matters, about which even the most esteemed man can never speak merely as a man, but rather, at times, as a "trumpet of God." This is somewhat similar to what Plutarch says: that a law existed among the Greeks ordering that even the good books of wicked men be removed from sight so that the memory of the authors might be erased. He signifies, moreover, that the ancients were accustomed to releasing a person seized by a demon during sacred rites from that demon shortly afterward through certain prayers and sacrifices, so they would no longer be exhausted by it. He also teaches that a long time should not be wasted on names. Accordingly, he rebukes those who think only the spheres and stars of the <margin>D</margin> world are divine; for since these are closer to our sight by nature and are mobile, we must ascend from them to higher deities who are stable and unknown to our senses due to their greater excellence. He relates, furthermore, that the names of the gods were found not by chance, but partly by human reason and partly by divine inspiration. Heroic and human names, however, were often given either from the surnames of ancestors or from a vow; therefore, a certain logic of names is to be sought in divine names rather than in others. After this, he descends to the demons <note>In the Neoplatonic sense: intermediary spirits, not necessarily evil</note> and asserts, following the opinion of Hesiod and the most esteemed ancient men, that the souls of the best men ascend to become aerial demons, who excel in the wisdom of things and provide for the human race. But you, take note here: every good man is wise. Conversely, a good man becomes wise because God fills the purified and serene mind of a good man with the light of His wisdom. A wise man is also good because he neither wanders from the goal nor is deceived in choosing the things that lead to that goal. Note that heroes and demigods are considered the same, born from the mutual love between God and man. Hence the saying: *But they are born of God.* In this, the kinship between the human and divine race is shown. Attend next to the fact that the duty of man is not merely to sense, but to consider those things he has sensed. Then, that the state of the soul in the body is not to be contained by it, but to contain the nature of the body. Yet, according to Orpheus, the body is called the "prison" and "tomb" of the soul, inasmuch as the soul is judged to be as if dead while in the body. Remember also that <margin>G</margin> Anaxagoras thought there was one soul above all others for the machinery of the world, and one mind presiding over it. Hence the quote: *The spirit nourishes from within, and Mind, infused through the limbs, moves the whole mass.* Next, consider the pious modesty of Plato, who says that whoever is wise acknowledges that he is ignorant of the gods and the names the gods use among themselves. He adds that we must pray to God to reveal His own proper name to us; we must also consider that the names we attribute to God signify not the nature of God itself, but our own notion and feeling toward God. Therefore, we must be careful regarding God, lest we displease Him in the naming of Him. He says the same in the *Philebus*, *Parmenides*, *Phaedrus*, and *Timaeus*. He then interprets the names of the gods, relating first the opinion of those who thought all things were in flux <note>The Heraclitean view</note>, which he will ultimately disapprove of. But in these matters, truly remember that the goddess **Vesta** signifies the essence of separate forms and the stable foundation of divine things; therefore, it was customary to sacrifice to Vesta before the other gods. Likewise, names that signify "state" or "stability" in divine matters refer to their substance; those that signify "motion" refer to action—improperly to intellectual action, but properly to the action of the soul. Again, masculine names of gods signify the effecting act in divine things, while feminine names signify wise power. Furthermore, the fact that the Heavens, by their motion, generate consuming time and continually consume it, is a certain image referring to the god **Caelus**, **Rhea**, and **Saturn** devouring his son. In these, **Caelus** is the divine essence itself, **Rhea** is its life, and **Saturn** is its mind. The sons of Saturn are the "Ideas" of things, generated within the divine intelligence; just as they are produced by the mind, so they are led back into the mind, which absorbs them into itself, so to speak. The multitude of gods is distributed around the various parts of the world and is contained within the Ideas of those same parts, and in the angelic minds contemplating them in manifold ways, and in the souls

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ruling the spheres and stars of the world. Note above all that **Pluto** here signifies especially the divine providence pertaining to separate souls; he so ravishes and detains the pure souls with the perpetual allurements of his goods that they do not wish to return to us anymore. This, indeed, does not agree with the infinite cycles of souls described by Plotinus and Proclus. He proves that souls are held by Pluto by a certain very tight and insoluble bond because they are held by an "amatory affection" <note>A bond of love</note>. Here is confirmed that Platonic doctrine in the *Symposium*, the *Laws*, and often elsewhere: that the voluntary bond of love is more powerful than all others, and not without reason. For he who draws someone through desire draws more powerfully and retains them more firmly than one who attempts to attract through some other force, because he ravishes not only from the outside, but from within. <margin>B</margin> Furthermore, that which is so ravished not only does not struggle to be released, but even leans upon the one who binds it, entangling itself more tightly in the same bond. I pass over the fact that another kind of "ravisher" meets us as something superior and foreign. But the "amatory ravisher" insinuates himself into us as an equal and a domestic, both openly and secretly. Hence Boethius proves, following the mind of Plotinus, that God ravishes all things to Himself most powerfully and yet most sweetly, namely by the love of His own good, drawing them as if with bait. The Platonist Philo also confirms this: *God from the beginning to the end touches all things powerfully and disposes them sweetly.* We will show elsewhere that this was entirely taken from the fourth book of the *Laws*. Regarding **Phoebus** <note>Apollo</note>, who in Orpheus signifies the vital light, there are many excellent things in the Orphic *Hymn to Apollo*, in the sixth book of the *Republic*, in the oration of the Platonist Julian, and in our own little work *On Light*. Here, however, the name **Apollo** is briefly explained. It signifies a triple sun: divine, angelic, and celestial. In the first, the light is above the intellect. In the second, it is intellectual light above sight. In the third, it is visible light. The second is called by the Platonists the son of the first. The third is called the image of both. But, to speak summarily, Apollo signifies first the simplicity of the divine and angelic substance; <margin>D</margin> second, the power through which God and the angel favor souls and purge them from lower affections; third, the benefit by which they release them from worse things and join them to better; fourth, the "archery" virtue, so to speak, by which they hurl their gifts from afar through all things and afflict the unjust with their stings; fifth, the efficacy tempering all things and converting them with musical measures. In these appear Apollo’s prophecy (where he is called "simple") and his washing and releasing through purging. In the same place appear medicine, and the skill of archery and singing, where he extends his powers powerfully through all things, and sweetly tempers all things of the same together, and happily converts them to himself by tempering them. Similar gifts and affections are seen in the sun and toward the third and celestial sun. Amidst this, Socrates says he is "playing" or "joking" in explaining the <margin>E</margin> names of the gods, evidently recognizing that he does not reach the divine substance with these names, but either relates their effects or explains our feelings toward them as best he can. He adds that the gods also sometimes "play" and "joke": we joke about divine things, and the gods joke about ours—insofar as our affairs, when compared to theirs, are so very small, and they govern them with no labor but with inestimable ease. I pass over for now that Platonic saying: *Man is a joke and a plaything of the gods.* We will explain that when the matter requires it. After this, for the third time, the deeply religious man teaches that he is afraid to dispute further about these things. For even at the very beginning of a discussion, one must fear lest we speak of God without God; and in the middle <margin>F</margin> of the discussion again, lest we rashly measure the immeasurable; and near the end again, lest we prolong the discourse on the deities further than their will inspires us. Next, note that the entire power of **Mercury** <note>Hermes</note> revolves around speech, so that you may understand the power of intelligence pertains rather to Saturn. Likewise, what he adds—that **Pan** is the son of Mercury and is "two-formed" because of twin speech, namely true and false—note that where Pan is painted as a man, he signifies true speech; where as a brute, false speech. Being thus warned, you should fear to speak falsehoods, lest by speaking falsehoods you become a "false man" and a "true brute." Furthermore, where he mocks many of the ancients because, while they themselves were suffering from vertigo, they thought all things were turning, he warns that we should not measure eternal things by a nature that is primarily temporal. Likewise, where he says that temperance is the "safety and consideration of prudence," he shows that a soul drunk with the perturbations of the body cannot judge correctly, especially in perceiving the truth of incorporeal things. Next, where he interprets the name of the **Good**, he shows that three things pertain to the Good itself: namely, that it be admirable, that it be lovable, and that it be sweet. It is admirable when it rouses us, turns us away from other things, and converts us to itself. Lovable, when we approach it and cling to it. Sweet, when we are filled by it. A little later, explaining the name of **Justice**, he teaches that divine judgment penetrates all things. Orpheus also sang of this. Then he signifies that justice, according to Anaxagoras, is the divine mind, the orderer of all things. Socrates dares neither to affirm nor deny this. He does not deny it, because justice pertains to God. He does not affirm it, because it would be more appropriately said that justice is the divine will, distributing individual things according to the merits of either nature or will. Note that the logic of the Good pertains to a certain nature diffusing itself through all things. The logic of the **Beautiful** pertains to the wisdom and order flowing from it and provoking other things toward itself. Finally, the power of **Love** looks toward a certain influx penetrating from the eyes <margin>H</margin> through the eyes. After this, he brings forward many things about names which are sufficiently understood through the preceding. He touches on a triple opinion regarding the origin of names: either that they were once received from the gods, or from barbarians, or that through the length of time they have been so changed from their first origin that the first positions of the names can hardly be discerned. Next, he mocks those who profess knowledge of subsequent things when they are ignorant of what came before. But in what follows, take note of this golden sentiment: that the most serious deception of all is that by which a man deceives himself. For in that case, the deceiver is never absent from the deceived. Since Cratylus leans toward the sect of Euthydemus, which thinks no one speaks falsehoods (because whoever speaks, speaks "that which is," and therefore speaks the truth), Socrates refutes it in this way: we often say things are present to someone which are far away, and conversely that things are absent which are present, which is nothing else...

<summary>Ficino provides a Neoplatonic interpretation of Plato's Cratylus, arguing that names of gods and heroes reflect divine order, cosmic spheres, and the psychological states of the soul. He emphasizes that true understanding of the divine requires inspiration rather than mere human reason.</summary>
<keywords>Marsilio Ficino, Plato, Cratylus, etymology, Neoplatonism, divine names, Apollo, Saturn, Jupiter, Vesta, Mercury, allegory, providence, soul, Anaxagoras</keywords>

--- Page 803 ---
<meta>This page continues the philosophical commentary on Plato's dialogues, specifically concluding the discussion on the *Cratylus* and beginning the introduction to the *Gorgias*.</meta>

<margin>A</margin> is than to speak falsehoods. And similarly, we can appropriately name things by expressing through the name and the sounds of the letters, in a certain way, the nature and action of a thing or its passion <note>In this context, "passion" refers to how a thing is acted upon, the opposite of action</note>, and conversely, we can name things incongruously. After this, where he mentions numbers and qualities, he says that in the order of numbers, the species of the number is always changed by either adding or subtracting a unit, which does not happen in quality. I believe this occurs for this reason: because the whole rationale of number consists in the unit and its replication. In quality, however, since there is a certain other nature besides the unit and its replication, the species of quality is not changed by the addition or subtraction of one degree, or even several, and rightly so. Similarly in an image: it is an image insofar as it represents; however, it can reflect more or less. Almost the same thing happens with names. For some are images of the things themselves. Furthermore, since the end of a name is to reflect the thing itself, it is better to reflect it by a certain likeness to the thing than by human convention. Again, since a name consists of letters, it cannot aptly express a thing unless it is composed of syllables and letters properly expressing it. And since it is a laborious task to accommodate letters, syllables, and names entirely to individual things—indeed, it cannot even be done in numbers—therefore, custom must be mixed with nature, so that as far as possible, the nature of things holds the authority over names. But where it can be done in no way, or only with great difficulty through the property of nature, let it be done through human custom and convention, whether alone or joined with nature. Notice after this that the greatest diligence must be applied to principles, and much <margin>B</margin> must be disputed in establishing them. Again, anyone goes toward knowledge by a most fallacious path who, as Cratylus advises, hunts for the properties of things through the properties of names, since the author of names did not establish such names as the things themselves are, but as he himself thought they were, and he could have been deceived. Add to this that different people can interpret the same names differently and translate them to signify opposites with equal probability. Certainly, many names are positioned as if the thing were in flux, and many also as if it remained still. It is therefore most fallacious to judge things through names. A little later, consider: first, that he who named things knew them before he named them; likewise the ancient opinion, which asserts that a certain divine power instructed man from the beginning and taught the names of things. This is consistent with what is said in the *Protagoras* and the *Statesman*. For it is impossible that the human race was not instructed by divinity, either from the beginning of the world or after some great delusions. But when Socrates says he is "dreaming" about the Ideas <note>The Platonic "Forms" or "Ideas," the perfect archetypes of reality</note>, he declares both that Socrates was accustomed to being mocked for this by the common people and by comic poets, and that the knowledge of Ideas is held through a separation of the mind, similar to the prophecy of a dream. Soon he proves that Ideas exist, because above imperfect forms there must be perfect ones. Likewise, that Ideas are immutable, if indeed the species, reasons, and definitions of things always remain the same. He adds that if all stability is taken away from things, it follows that no thing truly is either "this something" or "such a something," nor can it be known, since at any moment it will deceive <margin>E</margin> the one judging, who is necessarily lying. He adds that knowledge itself does not occur—namely, that specific knowledge of the Ideas—unless they always remain the same. He concludes that the science of things is to be sought not from names, but from the Ideas, the notions of which, implanted in us, are the first and true names of things. Finally, he admonishes the young not to pass judgment easily on grave matters; rather, they should learn for a long time and wait for a more mature age before they judge.

## ARGUMENT ON THE GORGIAS.
### for page 281.

<margin>C</margin> Since there are two most powerful things in the soul, knowledge and affection, the Sophists distort knowledge toward falsehoods under the appearance of truth, while the popular poets often plunge affection into discordant disturbances under the bait of elegant pleasure. Finally, the popular orators both deceive knowledge with false conjectures and stir affection into various movements. Therefore, since by their work the minds of men are forced to be sick with both false opinions and pernicious affections, Plato, the physician of human souls, leads us far away from the Sophists entirely, and also from the orators and poets in a certain way; indeed, he exterminates the Sophists everywhere and all of them, but not all the poets—only those who either invent shameful things about the gods or imitate and reflect disturbed minds too much—and not from everywhere, but from the city, that is, from the crowd of the young and ignorant, who are very prone to disturbances and do not penetrate the allegorical sense of the poets. For this reason, in the books of the *Republic*, he orders the poets to be either expelled or forced to speak honorably of God, and not to accustom the listeners to disturbances, but to sing divine hymns and gravely recount the ancestral laws and the deeds of great men. But to return to the orators: Plato does not blame all of them either, but only those who apply themselves assiduously to persuading the listeners of whatever they please, by whatever means they can, without choice—whether it be evil or good, whether the reasoning be false or true, whether by commiseration, or incitement, or conjecture. Such had been the purpose of Lysias the Theban, and Tisias, and also Gorgias of Leontini. But he prefers Pericles in the *Phaedrus* and Isocrates to others, because they joined eloquence with philosophy. And he adds that a legitimate orator ought to understand the reasons of things, the laws of morals, the power of words, the natures of characters, and to compose words by a certain rationale accommodated to the characters of the listeners as far as possible, for the sake of persuading them of the common good; and not to apply himself so much to making what he says pleasing to men, as to making it acceptable to God. But he who, in the manner of Tisias and Gor-

<column-break/>

<margin>B</margin> gias, follows not truth itself and justice, but only a conjecture that is likely and probable to the crowd, he detests as a man harmful to the state above others, as if eloquence without wisdom were a sharp sword in the hands of a madman. He attacks two above others: Lysias in the *Phaedrus*, and here, Gorgias. For the greater their authority was, the more dangerous they were. Here, Polus the orator, a follower of Gorgias, is brought into the midst, as well as Callicles, their supporter. Socrates first acts through Chaerephon, his friend, and that indeed against Polus. Then he himself acts against Gorgias. Since these men were accustomed to boast wonderfully before the people in assigning reasons for other things, it is shown—so that all credit may be taken from them—that they do not know how to provide the reasons for their own profession. For when Polus was asked what the art of Gorgias is, when he should have defined it only by its essentials and explained *what* it is, he circumscribed it by superfluities and *what kind* it is, and that indeed in an overly affected style, which it is confirmed he was accustomed to use in the *Phaedrus*, where the styles of orators are discussed. Then Gorgias himself, being asked what his art is, replied with a certain inept boasting that it is rhetoric. He is then asked to define what rhetoric is. We ought to remember that any thing, in what it is, partly agrees with other things and partly differs; and that by which it agrees is called the "genus," and that by which it differs, the "difference." From this it follows that a definition, which comprehends the very thing that the object is, ought to be assigned through a genus of this kind and a difference. Gorgias, therefore, as one who does not know how to define his art, brings forth its genus, and that indeed ineptly. <margin>C</margin> The difference, which he ought to have brought forth immediately in the same response along with the genus, he is finally compelled to bring into the midst with difficulty after many questions, with Socrates extorting it. At first, he responds that rhetoric is an art concerning speeches. And since there are other similar arts, he is asked concerning what or what kind of speeches, so that it may be discerned in what matter it differs from other arts. He responds: concerning speeches which provide the power of speaking. Again, this is common to other arts; whence he is forced to add again that rhetoric is occupied as much as possible with speeches and the power of speaking. But since that too is common to many, he is urged again to add: namely, concerning speeches about the greatest things. When that too is common, he is now compelled to bring forth something more distinct—that is, that through oratory we achieve the result that we serve no one, but rule over others, and that the oratorical art is the <margin>D</margin> producer of persuasion at will. Meanwhile, Socrates admonishes that in disputing we should not intend our mind so much toward the person with whom we dispute, as toward the thing itself and the speech and the soul. Then, since every art persuades about something, it is asked about what thing, and what kind of persuasion the rhetorician's is. Soon persuasion is distinguished into two: namely, into that which produces knowledge, and that which produces belief. It is concluded that oratorical persuasion does not bring knowledge, but belief; not properly concerning just anything, but concerning the just and the unjust; not everywhere, but in a crowd especially, and concerning things which chiefly pertain to the republic. <margin>E</margin> It is added, moreover, that the orator can speak more persuasively than the craftsmen themselves about things properly pertaining to other arts—not indeed among those skilled in the arts themselves, but among the unskilled. Amidst these things, we are admonished never to abuse power and art. Likewise, that we should not be disturbed in disputing, where tranquility is necessary for perceiving the truth. Again, that refutation is to be received with an even and most willing mind, especially in correcting morals. For nothing is worse than to feel falsely about morals. After this, Gorgias concedes that it does not pertain to the orator to know how things themselves are, but he makes a certain device to devise for persuading, so that he himself, although ignorant, may nevertheless appear to understand more among the ignorant than those who <margin>F</margin> are knowledgeable, and that his duty is to speak strenuously about anything in a crowd, not by teaching, but by persuading. He also concedes that an orator ought to and can know what is likely, even if he does not know what is true—which indeed can in no way happen. For unless you know the thing itself, you will never recognize what is similar to it. Accordingly, it is asked whether, just as it does not belong to the orator to know other things, so also he does not need to understand what is good, honorable, and just. But Gorgias, although he said elsewhere that the orator stands similarly toward these and those things, here, contradicting himself, agreed that it is necessary to confess knowledge of these. From here Socrates argues: if the orator knows just things, therefore he is just—testing Gorgias, of course, to see if he holds the force of the consequence. He admits it immediately, since in the sciences and arts pertaining to the intellect it follows: <margin>G</margin> he knows astrology or carpentry, therefore he is an astrologer or a carpenter. In those things, however, which pertain to the will and morals, it does not follow: he knows just things, therefore he is just. For there is need of the will for justice. Nevertheless, if someone should have a certain divine knowledge of justice—which Plato maintains can sometimes happen by the breathing of God—it will rightly follow. For whoever knows most certainly how great a good justice is, or how great a reward remains; and conversely, how great an evil injustice is, or how great a punishment is owed to it: he, without doubt, fleeing injustice, will embrace justice. But in whatever way things stood, Gorgias is forced to contradict himself. For whereas in the earlier parts he conceded that an orator could sometimes be unjust, here he denies it. After this, Socrates, from the arrogance of Polus, under a certain irony, both disapproves of the younger men if they ever correct their elders arrogantly, and commands all to suffer themselves to be <margin>H</margin> corrected easily by anyone. Furthermore, so that what follows may be clearly understood, it must be noted that oratory can be considered either in its genus or in its species; and in its genus indeed it is defined as an industry most prompt for persuading in civil matter, both by a certain faculty of proof and, most of all, by the grace of eloquence. And therefore it is positioned in a certain way between the art of disputing and poetry. Thus far, oratory is a good for the intellect, but for the will it is neither good nor evil. Of this, however, there are two species: philosophical...

# MARSILIO FICINO

...and the popular or flattering kind; the former is good, while the latter is truly evil. The end of the former is to lead listeners toward the common good through certain principles of things, words, and morals. This is the kind he praises most highly in the *Phaedrus*, composed of philosophy and the weightier sort of poetry. The end of the other kind, however, is to obtain whatever one pleases through conjectures that seem likely to the crowd and by the stirring of passions. We place this between sophistry and vulgar poetry, a mixture of both, which he detests in this dialogue. Furthermore, he divides the arts that specifically care for man himself into two main types. The first of these cares for the soul, and the second for the body. Regarding the soul, he says the **legal faculty**—the founder of laws and moderator of morals—shapes and stabilizes the soul itself in a certain state agreeable to nature; while the **judicial art** restores the soul if it should ever fall from this state. In the body, he likewise places two arts that care for it: **gymnastics**, the mistress of exercise, which strengthens the body in a good condition according to its strength; and **medicine**, which restores lost health to the body. Therefore, what law is to the soul, gymnastics appears to be to the body. Likewise, what the judicial art is to the soul, medicine is to the body. He calls all these "arts" because they lead toward the good through systematic effort. He adds a certain "knack" or skill that is flattering, servile, and deceptive, which falsely emulates these four. Through **sophistry**, it simulates the legal art; through **vulgar oratory**, it fakes the judicial; through **beautification** <note>original: *sucatoria*, the art of cosmetics or dyeing</note>, it puts on the appearance of gymnastics; and through **cookery**, it represents the physician. He denies that this entire genus of flattery is an art, because it does not strive toward the true good by certain reason, but toward favor by allurements. But lest anyone think that Plato, the most eloquent of all men, compares legitimate eloquence to cookery, let him read the *Phaedrus*, in which he both approves of it and most subtly hands down its end, duty, and precepts, asserting that it is similar to medicine. 

But since Polus, extolling the power of oratory, says that orators have the greatest power because they are able at their whim to condemn adversaries to prison or death, or to despoil them of goods, or deprive them of their city: Socrates proves by two main arguments that the unjust are not powerful. First, because power is to be desired by everyone as a good; but it is clear that the license to do whatever one pleases is not only not good for unjust men (who are like those captured in mind <note>i.e., insane</note>), but evil and ultimately ruinous. Second, that the greatest power is to be able to effect that very thing which you *will*. It is clear, however, that all people will the true good. But the wicked never act upon or attain the true good. Add to this that a wicked mind, by the very fact that it is wicked, is judged discordant within itself and insane, and already overcome by those things asserted by the senses. Who then would say that a mind that is both languid and serving its own slaves in the manner of a bondservant is powerful? 

Meanwhile, all human things are distinguished into three: namely, the good, the evil, and the middle <note>indifferent</note>. The first of the goods is wisdom. The second is the desirable condition of the body. The third is the advantages of fortune. But these latter two are judged good only insofar as they provide a convenient service to the mind. Their opposites are called evils, but the middle things are as if indifferent, which incline no more to good than to evil, such as walking, sitting, and the like. It is added that no one wills either evils or middle things, or those things which he specifically does, but rather only those things for the sake of which he is moved and acts. Therefore, those who commit injuries do not will the injuries themselves, but the good for the sake of which they act. But they do not attain the good; therefore they do not achieve what they will. Thus, they are not powerful. 

Next, Socrates, having found an opportunity from Polus’s error (common to many), hands down holy precepts to us: He who is permitted to sin gravely is nearly miserable; he who sins gravely is already miserable; he who does not pay the penalty for his sin is more miserable. To suffer injuries is to be chosen rather than to inflict them. The license to do whatever one pleases is not power, unless it will ultimately be of use to us. But it will be of use only to those living justly. The unjust, even if they possess the empire of the whole world, are unhappy—indeed, most unhappy. For the more they are permitted to sin and the less the penalty for sin is given, the more unhappy they are considered. Happiness consists in wisdom and justice; unhappiness in their opposites. 

Since Polus places the judgment of truth in a multitude of any witnesses (which ought rather to be referred to the quality of the judge than the number of those judging), Socrates responds that the best mode of proof is if you bring forward a single witness in the case: namely, the adversary himself, convicted by reason. Otherwise, a multitude of witnesses heaped together from everywhere is of little weight for the truth. Furthermore, because Polus says that to do an injury is more shameful, but to suffer one is worse: Socrates argues against this, asserting that in human affairs and movements, the good is the same as the beautiful or the honorable; and the evil is the same as the shameful. Then, he considers that the beautiful is judged so either because of pleasure or utility, or both; and the shameful conversely. From this he argues: if doing an injury is more shameful than suffering one, it is not because it is more painful, therefore it must be because it is more harmful; if so, it is judged to be worse. Soon he adds that one ought to commit oneself to reason to be cured, as if to a physician. He also affirms that the just punishment of sins profits the one who is punished most of all. For if this is just, it is therefore beautiful and honorable. If so, it is good; if good, it confers upon the soul just as medicine does to the body, and much more so: for it frees the soul from disease, which is the gravest of all diseases and evils. Among these things, observe the opinion of the theologians: that nothing is more necessary or useful for sinners than to confess sins, to be affected by penitence, to seek penalties from a judge, and to bear them with an even mind so that the soul may be purged before its disease becomes incurable. After this, you will hear that it is very easy for us to signal our affection to one who suffers from a similar affection. Likewise, that Socrates, captured by the love of philosophy, always obeys her. Furthermore, that it is to be chosen rather than all other things should be dissonant to us, than that the soul should be dissonant within itself. Accordingly, where Callicles corrects Socrates as if he were too studious of subtleties, understand that under the person of Socrates, the Sophists are being refuted by Plato. Afterward, Callicles touches upon the profane

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> opinion of Thrasymachus and many others, who say that morals and laws do not consist in the order of nature, but only in the opinion or fiction of men. This is refuted in the books *On the Republic* and in those following. As for what Callicles seems to assert against philosophers, understand that these things are said not against legitimate philosophers, but partly against the most idle of the sophists, and partly against those who abuse the study of philosophy: while they either follow logic alone so that they desert other parts of speculation, or they embrace speculation alone so that they neglect the philosophical precepts of morals and civil institutions. Some things in Callicles's invective itself are said falsely, which will be refuted in what follows. After these things, however, it is commanded that every <margin>B</margin> diligence must be applied in the examination and testing of our soul, and for that purpose, one judge must be chosen in whom there is wisdom regarding the matter at hand, and benevolence by which he may consult willingly, and moreover boldness, through which he does not fear to express what he thinks will be profitable. Then Socrates admonishes us, since we are rational natures, not to live by irrational chance and fortune, but to most diligently prescribe a certain end of life and choose the more convenient ways to it. Finally, while he frequently beseeches Callicles to refute him freely and boldly, he admonishes that one ought to inquire into nothing more expensively than the medicine of the soul. 

These things being done, Callicles concedes that by nature the same thing is more powerful, stronger, and better, and that natural justice wills that he who <margin>C</margin> is more powerful should have whatever belongs to his inferiors and dominate them, and that his law is naturally just. To this, Socrates inserts the following: If the same thing is more powerful, stronger, and better, and the multitude is stronger than one, then it is also more powerful and better. Therefore, since the laws of the multitude are those of the more powerful and better, they will be naturally just. But the laws of this multitude decree it a just statute that equality be preserved among all, and that it is more shameful to inflict an injury than to suffer one. Wherefore, it is more shameful to do an injury than to suffer one not only by law, but also by nature itself, and it is just to preserve equity, contrary to what Callicles had said earlier. 

Furthermore, because Callicles had previously thought those were more powerful who surpassed others in cunning, boldness, and violence: Socrates gradually <margin>D</margin> corrects him and forces him to confess that he is more powerful who is more prudent and brave in governing the republic. He also signifies among these things that he always brings the same arguments to the same person regarding these matters, proving that constancy and fortitude lead also to temperance. But just as he had erred regarding justice and power by imitating Thrasymachus above, so now, following Aristippus, he similarly errs regarding temperance, while he calls the slave-like idleness of the mind "stupid" and asserts that virtue and happiness consist in nourishing and filling the lusts of the senses. 

Socrates, however, soon girds himself to demonstrate that temperance consists not in human opinion, but in the order of nature. Indeed, <margin>E</margin> natural order requires that the lower parts of the soul obey the superior parts, and that the whole soul be harmonious everywhere, healthy, and beautiful, and that it does not act in vain but attains the proposed end, which is the habit and life of the temperate man. On the contrary, in the intemperate man, reason—the queen of man—serves concupiscence; it is also dissonant and languid, and labors at an unfillable task, and follows fleeting pleasure with incomparable trouble. Socrates explains all this especially by the opinions of the Pythagoreans, Philolaus and Empedocles, chiefly in two ways: namely, through myth and example. In these, consider for yourself that the soul in this body is entirely dead; moreover, the intemperate soul is assigned to the underworld, miserably agitated by useless and assiduous labor, while through a certain perforated vessel (that is, a depraved and deceptive judgment), it continually schemes to fill another perforated vessel (that is, unfillable concupiscence) with flowing delights. 

After this, because Callicles places not only virtue but also happiness in the assiduous fulfillment of lusts, and affirms that pleasure is the same as the good itself, and pain the same as evil, Socrates refutes this with several reasons. **First**, it is clear that pleasure is not the good itself, since it is often most shameful and is present in the most shameful men. **Second**, good and evil, as opposites, cannot be in the same thing at the same time. But pleasure and pain are in the same thing at the same time, namely when someone who is thirsty drinks: for then the trouble of thirsting concurs with the pleasure of drinking. **Third**, good and evil, as other opposites are wont to do, do not leave the same thing at the same time. Pleasure and pain, however, leave the same thing at the same time when someone, at the same time he drinks, ceases both to thirst and to be delighted by drinking. **Fourth**, everyone <margin>F</margin> becomes good by the presence of good, and evil by the presence of evil. But men do not become good by the presence of pleasure, nor do upright men become evil by pain. **Fifth**, since the good and the evil often equally rejoice or grieve, and sometimes the evil rejoice more and the good grieve more, certainly if pleasure were the good and pain the evil, it would follow that frequently both the good and the evil would be equally good or evil, and sometimes the good would be more evil than the evil themselves, and vice versa. 

Among these things, observe the precept of Socrates <margin>G</margin> that must be followed: namely, that one must not hasten to the weightiest matters unless one has first attained the lighter ones. Then some things are asserted by which one can confirm that pleasure is not the good in itself, because many pleasures are found to be evil, <margin>H</margin> namely noxious to both the soul and the body, and diverting us from the best things; for if pleasure were the good in itself, no pleasure would be evil. Accordingly, the faculties are distinguished again: those which, like arts, proceed toward the good and the useful by certain reason; and those which, like flatteries, hunt for pleasure alone with no reason of the true good applied. In the number of these latter, he places poetry, music, and common oratory. But you, during the discussion, note this opinion: that the virtue and health of the body consist in a certain order and ornament, and similarly the virtue and health of the soul consist in its own order and ornament. From which it follows, that just as...

# ARGUMENTS AND COMMENTARY

just as bodily virtue and vice are found not in opinion, but in the reality of the thing itself—either in harmony with nature or opposed to it—so the virtue and vice of the soul should be judged not by human opinion, but by the law of nature.
<margin>A</margin> Conclude then: just as it is naturally better to have a healthy body than a sick one, it is likewise better to possess a temperate soul than an intemperate one. Furthermore, the Pythagorean sentiment is confirmed in what follows: that in all things, temperance is best. This is the very first thing to be taught to youths, so that the preceding intemperance of childhood may be corrected and the whole soul tempered; he believes the other virtues soon follow this. Indeed, the temperate man acts with propriety toward God and men; he is pious, just, and brave. From this it is concluded that happiness lies in virtue alone, and misery in wickedness alone, and all human affairs are to be referred to virtue as if to a most certain goal. Furthermore, just as virtue is necessary for happiness, so the chastisement and punishment of vices is necessary, acting as a medicine for the diseases of the soul. Finally, the intemperate man can be a friend neither to men, nor to God, nor to himself. To show us the natural excellence of temperance, he adds (following the mind of the Pythagoreans and Orphics <note>Followers of the mythical poet Orpheus</note>) that the universe is held together by temperance, and also by concord and justice, which are contained within temperance itself. Therefore, as Pythagoras said, intemperance in all things must be fled with all one's might as something most ruinous. Since equality pertains especially to both temperance and justice, he commands that equality be observed above all, asserting it has the greatest power among gods and men. I mean **geometric equality**, through which an equal distribution is made to each person; that is, distributed equally according to the capacity and merit of each—neither more nor less than what capacity or merit is judged to require. Geometric equality consists in a certain fitting proportion. **Arithmetic equality**, however, consists in an equal number on both sides. These two are not the same. Truly, the excess of six over four, and likewise the excess of four over two, is equal to an arithmetician considering numbers: for each is completed by two. But to a geometer, who judges proportion, it is unequal. For the number six exceeds four by a *sesquialter* proportion <note>A ratio of 1.5 to 1</note>, in which the larger number contains the whole smaller number plus its half. But four exceeds two by a double proportion. By this kind of equality—which does not merely give the same weight to one as to another in the manner of a counter, but in the manner of a measurer gives to each no more and no less than is fitting—he says all things are preserved. For in this is contained both the justice of God in His works and the justice of man toward men. In both cases, distribution is made to each according to the measure of capacity and merit. Having said this, he asserts that the theological foundations have been confirmed by the firmest reasons. Especially that it is worse to do an injury than to suffer one, and worst of all, when you have done an injury, not to pay the penalty—which acts as a medicine to free the soul from the greatest disease of all: injustice.
<margin>D</margin> For no greater harm can be imagined than that which infects the soul through vice; just as it is not profitable for a man to live with a completely diseased body, so it is not profitable with a soul sick with vices. Likewise, one should not value life in the body highly, but rather virtue. It is worse to stand among disgraceful men as their equal because of a similarity of character than to be killed by them. Amidst these things, he warns us not to undertake the handling of matters of which we are ignorant, especially the more serious public ones. He holds oratory in very low esteem if it can bring no salvation to the soul either privately or publicly, but only looks after the body and things pertaining to it. He mocks those who, though they have long held the rudders of the Republic and increased the city with external goods, neglected to form the souls of the citizens with temperance and justice—which is the sole duty of a legitimate governor. He concludes that governors who look to the goods of fortune rather than the goods of the soul not only do not benefit the city but hinder it greatly. Furthermore, the power and wisdom of a man consist in keeping the soul unstained by sins toward God and men. For the loss of this life is very light, but the loss of eternal salvation is most heavy. Moreover, so that you may understand what Plato affirms regarding the future—either the rewards of virtues or the punishments of vices—know that **Saturn**, in Plato's view, is understood as the supreme intelligence, in which the universal law of all things and providence regarding the essences, lives, and orders of all things is formed. Under this are three principal orders of deities, in which Saturnian providence is distributed into three main offices. Those deities which specifically serve to distribute essences, he calls by the common name of **Jupiter**. Those which contribute to providing lives, he calls **Neptune**. Those which arrange the orders of forms, he calls **Pluto**. **Prometheus** represents a somewhat lower grade of deities here, who distributes the formal order of nature only to the rational, especially in this life. Finally, the three sons of Jupiter—the judges of Asia, Europe, and Africa—he wishes to be understood as three deities serving Jupiter and Pluto for this purpose: so that the formal order of justice may be fulfilled in souls separated from their bodies. By these, it is observed that divine law washes away the erasable stains of vices by punishing them at certain times, but afflicts the indelible ones with eternal punishments. This seems to disprove the eternal transmigration of souls through bodies. When he says that the judges once erred in judging the living, he signifies two things to us. First, that human judgment regarding virtues and vices is deceived, not divine. Second, that divine providence foresaw within itself that judgments would be false if the living were judged by the living in this body. Therefore, not from a certain point in time (as the words sound), but from eternity, it was decreed that judgment should occur after this life. Meanwhile, remember that the soul carries the affections and habits of vices and virtues with it. Finally, Socrates affirms these things deeply and fears nothing else except such damage to the soul and the sight of the divine judge.
<meta>catchword: que</meta>

<column-break/>

Therefore he concludes that in no contest must we strive more sharply than in this: that we may offer a most pure soul to the judge who inspects all things. All other things which men admire are to be utterly despised, and only those things among all are to be honored which contribute to the eternal salvation of the soul.

## COMMENTARY OF MAR-
silio Ficino the Florentine on the *Symposium* of Plato
concerning Love. to page 315.

### CHAPTER I.

Plato, the prince of philosophers, having lived more than eighty-one years, passed away on the seventh day of November (the day he was born) while reclining at a banquet after the tables were cleared. This banquet, which contains both the birthday and the anniversary of Plato, was restored annually by all the ancient Platonists up until the times of Plotinus and Porphyry. But after twelve hundred years, these solemn feasts were neglected. Finally, in our times, the most illustrious **Lorenzo de' Medici**, intending to renew the Platonic banquet, appointed Francesco Bandini as the Master of the Feast. When Bandini had set out to celebrate the seventh day of November, he received nine Platonic guests with royal preparation at the villa of Careggi: Antonio Agli, Bishop of Fiesole; Ficino the Physician; Cristoforo Landino the poet; Bernardo Nuzio the rhetorician; Tommaso Benci; Giovanni Cavalcanti, our close friend (whom the guests called "Hero" because of his virtue of soul and noble character); the two Marsuppini, Cristoforo and Carlo, sons of the poet Carlo. Finally, Bandini wished me to be the ninth, so that by adding me to Marsilio Ficino, the number of the Muses would be filled. After the meal was cleared, Bernardo Nuzio took up Plato's book titled *The Symposium on Love* and read all the speeches of this banquet. After they were read, he asked the remaining guests to each explain one speech. All agreed; and having cast lots, that first speech of Phaedrus fell to Giovanni Cavalcanti to explain. The speech of Pausanias to Antonio the Theologian. That of Eryximachus the Physician to Ficino the Physician. That of the poet Aristophanes to Cristoforo the Poet. That of the youth Agathon to Carlo Marsuppini. The discourse of Socrates was given to Tommaso Benci. That of Alcibiades to Cristoforo Marsuppini. Everyone approved of this lot. However, the bishop and the physician—one compelled to leave for the care of souls, the other for the care of bodies—left their parts in the speaking to Giovanni Cavalcanti. The others turned to him and sat together, ready to listen. Then that "Hero" began in this manner.
