## BY WHAT RULE LOVE
should be praised. What is its dignity
and greatness.

### CHAPTER II.

<margin>F</margin> This most pleasing lot fell to me today, best guests, which has resulted in me playing the part of Phaedrus of Myrrhinus. That Phaedrus, I say, whose friendship Lysias of Thebes, the supreme orator, valued so much that he contended to win him over with a speech composed with much midnight oil; whose character Socrates admired so much that, moved by his splendor while by the river Ilissus and raised to a higher state, he sang of divine mysteries—he who before had preached only of the pursuit of celestial things, but also of all inferior things. Plato was so delighted by his talent that he dedicated the first fruits of his studies to Phaedrus. To him are dedicated the epigrams and elegies of Plato; to him is dedicated his first book on beauty, which is titled *Phaedrus*. Since, therefore, first a lucky chance and then your applause has judged me to be like this Phaedrus (not that I claim so much for myself), I will gladly interpret his speech first under these happy auspices. Then I will carry out the parts of Antonio and Ficino according to the strength of my talent. In every matter, best men, the philosopher and follower of Plato considers three things: what precedes, what accompanies, and what follows. If these are good, he praises the thing itself; if bad, he blames it. Therefore, a perfect praise is one which recounts the preceding origin of the thing, narrates the present form, and shows the following outcomes. A thing is praised for its antecedents as **noble**; for its present state as **great**; and for its consequences as **useful**. Therefore, from those three, these three are concluded in praises: Nobility, Greatness, and Utility. Thus our Phaedrus, first beholding the present excellence of Love, called him a **Great God**; he added, "to be wondered at by gods and men." And not without reason. For we properly wonder at those things which are great. He is indeed great, to whose command all men and gods, as they say, are subject. For among the ancients, gods as well as men love, which Orpheus and Hesiod signify when they say the minds of mortals and immortals are tamed by love.
<margin>H</margin> Furthermore, he is said to be "to be wondered at" because everyone loves that whose beauty he wonders at. The gods (or as our people say, the Angels) wonder at and love divine beauty; men wonder at and love the appearances of bodies. And this indeed is the praise of Love, deduced from the present excellence that accompanies it. Then Phaedrus praises it from its antecedents when he asserts it is the oldest of all the gods. In this, the nobility of love shines forth, when its ancient origin is narrated. He will praise it thirdly from its consequences, where its wonderful utility will appear from the outcome. But first we shall treat of its ancient and noble origin; then of its future utility. Orpheus in the *Argonautica*, when he sang of the principles of things before Chiron and the heroes, following the theology of **Hermes Trismegistus**, placed **Chaos** before the world, and before Saturn, Jupiter, and the other gods. He placed Love in the very bosom of Chaos, and praised it in these words:

# THE ORIGIN OF LOVE FROM CHAOS.
### CHAPTER III.

<margin>Hesiod in the Theogony</margin>
Hesiod, in his *Theogony*, describes Love as the most ancient, perfect in himself, and most wise; and in his book *On Nature*, Parmenides the Pythagorean and the poet Acusilaus agreed with Orpheus and Hermes <note>original: "Mercurio"</note>. <margin>Plato in the Timaeus</margin> Plato describes Chaos in a similar way in the *Timaeus*, and places Love within it. <margin>Plato in the Symposium</margin> Phaedrus recounted the same in the *Symposium* <note>original: "Convivio"</note>. The Platonists call an unformed world "Chaos," but a formed chaos they call "the World." <margin>Plato in the Phaedrus</margin> Among them there are three worlds, and likewise there will be three Chaoses. First of all is God, the author of all things, whom we call the Good itself. He first creates the Angelic Mind; then the Soul of this world, as Plato wishes; and finally the Body of the world. We do not call that highest God a "world," because "world" <note>Latin: *mundus*, which also means ornament or elegance</note> signifies an ornament composed of many things, whereas He must be entirely simple; but we assert Him to be the beginning and the end of all worlds. The Angelic Mind is the first world made by God. The second is the Soul of the universal body. The third is this entire machine which we perceive. In these three worlds, therefore, three Chaoses are considered. In the beginning, God creates the substance of that Mind, which we also call Essence. In that first moment of its creation, this essence is unformed and dark. But because it is born from God, it turns toward God, its own principle, by a certain innate appetite. Having turned toward God, it is illuminated by His ray. By the splendor of that ray, its appetite is kindled. The kindled appetite inheres totally in God; by inhering, it is formed. For God, who can do all things, fashions the natures of things to be created within the Mind inhering in Him. In that Mind, therefore, all things that we perceive in these bodies are painted in a spiritual way, so to speak. In them are born the spheres of the heavens and the elements, the stars, the natures of vapors, and the forms of stones, metals, plants, and animals. We do not doubt that these species of all things, conceived in the supernal Mind by a certain nourishment from God, are "Ideas"; and that form and idea of the heavens we often call the god Uranus <note>original: "Caelum"</note>. The form of the first planet we call the god Saturn; of the second, Jupiter; and in the following planets in the same manner. Also, the idea of this fire we call the god Vulcan; of the Air, Jupiter and Juno; of the Water, Neptune; of the Earth, Pluto. Therefore, all the gods assigned to certain parts of the lower world are the Ideas of those parts collected in that supernal Mind. But that conception of Ideas perfected by the forming God was preceded by that approach of the Mind toward God. This was preceded by the fire of appetite; this by the infusion of the ray; this by that first turning of the appetite; and this by the essence of the unformed Mind. Furthermore, we maintain that this essence, not yet formed, is Chaos. Its first turning toward God we call the birth of Love; the infusion of the ray, the food of Love; the following fire, the increase of Love; the approach, the impulse of Love; the formation, the perfection of Love. The complex of all forms and ideas we call in Latin *Mundus*, and in Greek *Kosmos*, that is, "ornament." The grace of this ornament is Beauty. Toward this Beauty, Love, as soon as it was born, drew the Mind; and it led the Mind, previously deformed, to that same Mind which was then beautiful. Therefore, the condition of Love is such that it ravishes toward beauty and joins the deformed to the beautiful. Who, then, will doubt that Love immediately follows Chaos and precedes the World and all the gods who are distributed among the parts of the world? Since that appetite of the Mind exists before its formation, and the gods and the world are born in the formed Mind. Rightly, therefore, Orpheus named Love "the most ancient." Furthermore, "perfect in himself," as if to say "perfecting himself." For that first instinct of the Mind seems by its own nature to draw its perfection from God, and to offer it to the Mind which is formed therefrom, and to the gods who are born therefrom. Moreover, he named it "most wise," and not without justice. For all wisdom, of which counsel is the property, was given to the Mind for this reason: because, having turned toward God through love, it shone with His splendor. And the Mind is directed toward God in the same way that the eye is directed toward the light of the sun. For from this it first looks, then sees the light of the sun; thirdly, in the light of the sun, it perceives the colors and shapes of things. Therefore the eye, dark at first and like unformed chaos, loves the light while it looks; it is irradiated by looking; and by receiving the ray, it is formed with the colors and shapes of things. Just as that Mind, as soon as it is born and unformed, is turned and formed by love toward God, so the Soul of the world reflects itself toward the Mind and God, having been generated from there. And although it is at first unformed and a chaos, when directed toward the Mind by love, it becomes a "world" <note>mundus</note> by receiving forms from it. Not otherwise did the matter of this world, when in the beginning it lay as an unformed chaos without the ornament of forms, immediately direct itself toward the Soul by an innate love and offer itself as obedient to it; and with love acting as a mediator, having obtained from the Soul the ornament of all forms seen in the world, it was made a "world" out of chaos. There are, therefore, three worlds and three chaoses. Finally, in all things, Love accompanies chaos, precedes the world, rouses the sluggish, illuminates the dark, gives life to the dead, forms the unformed, and perfects the imperfect. No greater praises than these can be spoken or even imagined.

# ON THE UTILITY OF LOVE.
### CHAPTER IV.

But enough concerning its origin and nobility. I think we must now discuss its utility. Indeed, it is superfluous to recount the individual benefits of love bestowed upon the human race, especially since they can all be understood summarily. For they all consist in this: that by avoiding evils

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> we follow good things. The evil and the shameful things of man are the same. Likewise, the good and the honorable are the same. Certainly, all laws and teachings strive for nothing else than to so instruct men that they decline from shameful things and do honorable ones. However, this very thing, which almost innumerable laws and arts scarcely achieve over a long time, Love alone accomplishes in a short time. For shame deters from shameful things; the desire for excellence provokes toward honorable ones. Love provides these two things to men more easily and quickly than anything else. When we say "Love," understand it as the "desire for beauty." For this is the definition of love among all philosophers. Beauty, moreover, is a certain grace, which for the most part is born especially in the harmony of many things. This is threefold: for there is a grace in souls from the harmony of many virtues. From the concord of many colors and lines, grace is born in bodies. Likewise, the greatest grace in <margin>B</margin> sounds is from the consonance of many voices. Therefore, beauty is threefold: of souls, of bodies, and of voices. That of souls is known by the mind; of bodies, by the eyes; of voices, it is perceived by the ears alone. Since, therefore, the mind, sight, and hearing are the only means by which we can enjoy beauty, and Love is the desire for enjoying beauty, Love is always content with the Mind, the Eyes, and the Ears. What need is there for smell? What for taste? What for touch? These senses perceive odors, flavors, heat, cold, softness, and hardness, and things similar to these. None of these is human beauty, since those are simple forms; but the beauty of the human body requires the concord of diverse members. Love regards the enjoyment of beauty as its end; this pertains only to the mind, <margin>C</margin> sight, and hearing. Love, therefore, is limited to these three. But the appetite which follows the other senses is called not love, but lust or madness. Furthermore, if love toward a human being desires beauty itself, and the beauty of the human body consists in a certain harmony, and harmony is temperance, then love requires only those things which are temperate, modest, and decorous. Therefore, the pleasures of taste and touch, which are so vehement and furious that they move the mind from its state and disturb the man, love not only does not desire, but abominates and flees, as things which are contrary to beauty because of their intemperance. Venereal madness draws one toward intemperance, and therefore toward disharmony; wherefore it seems likewise to allure <margin>D</margin> toward deformity; but Love leads to beauty. Deformity and beauty are contraries. Therefore, movements of this kind, which ravish toward these things, seem to be contrary to each other. For this reason, lust, coitus, and love are shown to be not only not the same movements, but even contrary ones. The ancient theologians also testify to this, who attributed the name of Love to God. This the later theologians have also most strongly confirmed. But no name suitable to God is common to shameful things. Therefore, everyone of sound mind ought to take care not to rashly transfer "Love," a divine name, to insane disturbances. Let Dicaearchus blush, and anyone else who does not fear to carp at the Platonic majesty because it indulged too much in love. For in decorous, honorable, and divine affections, we can never indulge too much, nor even enough. From this it follows that all love is honorable, and every lover is just. For every lover is beautiful and decorous, and properly loves the decorous. But the turbulent ardor by which men are ravished toward lasciviousness, since it draws toward deformity, is judged to be contrary to love. So that we may finally return to the utility of love: the shame which deters us from shameful things, and the zeal which makes us ardent for honorable things, proceed easily and quickly from love. First, because love, which seeks beautiful things, always desires decorous and magnificent things; and he who hates deformed things necessarily flees shameful and obscene things. Secondly, if two people love each other mutually, they observe each other and desire to please one another. <margin>F</margin> Insofar as one is observed by the other, as they are never without a witness, they abstain from shameful things. Insofar as they strive to please each other, they always undertake magnificent things with ardent zeal, lest they be held in contempt by the beloved, but be thought worthy of the lover's gratitude. But Phaedrus explains this reasoning most copiously, where he places three examples of loves. One of the love of a woman for a male, where he speaks of Alcestis, the wife of Admetus, who wished to die for her husband. Another of the love of a male for a female, as of Orpheus for Eurydice. The third of the love of a male for a male, as of Patroclus for Achilles; where he shows that nothing renders men braver than love. But it is not my intention at present to scrutinize the allegory of either Alcestis or Orpheus. For these things express the power and empire of love more vehemently if they are narrated as historical deeds than if they are thought to be spoken through allegory. <margin>G</margin> Therefore, let us confess without controversy that Love is a great and wonderful God, noble moreover and most useful; and let us so indulge in love that we are content with its end, which is beauty itself. But we enjoy that part which we know; we know by the mind, by sight, and by hearing. We enjoy these, therefore; with the other senses we do not use beauty, which love desires, but rather whatever else the body requires. Therefore, with these three we shall hunt for beauty, and through that which shines in voices and bodies, as if through certain footprints, we shall investigate the decorum of the soul. We shall indeed praise that, approve it as just, and always strive to observe this: that the love be as great as the beauty was. And where the body indeed is beautiful but the mind not at all, let us love it scarcely and lightly, as a shadowy and fleeting image of beauty. Where the soul alone is beautiful, let us ardently love this stable decorum of the soul. But where both beauties <margin>H</margin> concur, let us admire more vehemently; and thus we shall testify that we are truly of the Platonic family; for that family knows nothing except what is festive, joyful, celestial, and supernal. But let these things now suffice concerning the speech of Phaedrus. Let us come to Pausanias.

<summary>Ficino explains the Neoplatonic origin of Love as the force that turns Chaos into a structured World (Mundus) by drawing the Mind toward God. He distinguishes true Love, which seeks beauty through the higher senses, from lust, which he considers a contrary madness.</summary>

# SECOND ORATION.
## GOD AS GOODNESS, BEAUTY,
## justice, beginning, middle, and end.

### CHAPTER I.

<margin>A</margin> The Pythagorean philosophers maintained that the Trinity was the measure of all things, for this reason, I believe: because God governs things by the number three, and things themselves are limited by the number three. Hence that line of Maro <note>Virgil</note>: *God delights in an uneven number.* Truly, that supreme Author first creates individual things; second, he draws them back; third, he perfects them. Individual things also flow out from that perennial fountain at their birth, then flow back into the same when they seek their origin again; finally, they are perfected after they have returned to their beginning. Orpheus prophesied this when he called Jupiter the beginning, the middle, and the end of the universe. The Beginning as he produces; the Middle as he draws what is produced back to himself; the End insofar as he perfects those things returning. Hence we can name that King of all things the Good, the Beautiful, and the Just, as is often said in Plato. The Good, I say, where he creates; the Beautiful where he entices; the Just where he perfects according to each one's merit. Beauty, therefore, whose property it is to entice, is located between goodness and justice: it flows out from goodness and flows forth toward justice.

## IN WHAT MANNER DIVINE
## beauty gives birth to love.

### CHAPTER II.

<margin>D</margin> This divine appearance has procreated in all things love, that is, the desire for itself. Since if God draws the world to himself, and the world is drawn, there is indeed one continuous attraction beginning from God, passing into the world, and finally ending in God; which, as if in a certain circle, returns again to the same place from which it flowed. Thus, one and the same circle from God into the world, and from the world into God, is called by three names. Insofar as it begins in God and entices, it is Beauty; insofar as passing into the world it draws it, it is Love; insofar as returning it joins its work to Him, it is Pleasure. Love, therefore, starts from beauty and ends in pleasure. This is what that famous hymn of Hierotheus and Dionysius the Areopagite meant, where these theologians sang: *Love is a good circle perpetually revolved from good, through good, into good.* For love is necessarily good, since being born from the good it returns to the good. For it is the same God whose appearance all things desire, and in whose possession all things find rest. From there, then, our desire is kindled; there the ardor of lovers rests, not extinguished, but fulfilled. Not without justice does Dionysius compare God to the sun: because just as the sun illuminates the body and warms it, so God provides the clarity of truth and the ardor of charity to souls. We gather this comparison from Plato’s sixth book of the *Republic* in this way: the Sun certainly procreates visible bodies and seeing eyes; it pours a lucid spirit into the eyes so they may see; it paints bodies with colors so they may be seen. Yet neither the ray proper to the eyes nor the colors proper to the bodies are sufficient to complete the vision, unless the light itself—one above the many—from which the many and proper lights are distributed to eyes and bodies, arrives, illustrates, excites, and strengthens. In the same way, that first act of all, which is called God, bestowed appearance and act upon individual things by producing them. Which act, when received in a created thing and a suffering subject, is weak and powerless for the execution of work. But the perpetual and invisible light of the divine sun is always present to all, it cherishes, vivifies, excites, completes, and strengthens. Concerning which Orpheus divinely said: *Cherishing all things and bearing himself above all.* Insofar as he is the act of all and strengthens them, he is called the Good. Insofar as he vivifies, softens, soothes, and excites, he is called the Beautiful. Insofar as he entices those three knowing powers of our soul—Mind, Sight, and Hearing—he is Beauty. Insofar as he applies the knowing power to the thing known, he is Truth. Finally, as the Good, he procreates, rules, and completes. <margin>G</margin> As the Beautiful, he illuminates and infuses grace.

## BEAUTY IS THE SPLENDOR
## of divine goodness, and God is the
## center of four circles.

### CHAPTER III.

Not without reason did the ancient theologians place Goodness in the center and Beauty in the circle. Goodness, I say, in the one center, but Beauty in the four circles. The one center of all is God. Four circles revolve assiduously around it: Mind, Soul, Nature, and Matter. The Mind is a stable circle. The Soul is mobile by itself. Nature is mobile in another, not by another. Matter is mobile by another and in another. Furthermore, I shall explain why we call God the center and those four the circles. The center of a circle is a point, one, indivisible, and stable. From there many divisible, mobile lines are led to their similar circumference; which circumference is indeed divisible and turns around the center like a hinge. And such is the nature of the center that although it is

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> one, individual, and immobile, it is nevertheless found everywhere in many, indeed in all, divisible and mobile lines. For the point is everywhere in the line. Since, however, nothing can be touched by its dissimilar, the lines drawn from the circumference to the center are each forced to touch that middle point by a certain single, simple, and immobile point of their own. Who denies that God is deservedly called the center of all, since he is present in all as one, utterly simple, and immobile; while all things produced by him are many, composite, and mobile, and as they flow from him, so they flow back into him like lines and the circumference? Thus, mind, soul, nature, and matter, proceeding from God, strive to return to the same; and they revolve themselves around him from every side according to their strength. <margin>B</margin> And as the center point is found everywhere in the lines and in the whole circle, and through their own point individual lines touch the middle point of the circle: so God, the center of all, who is the simplest unity and purest act, inserts himself into the universe; not only because he is present to all, but also because he has bestowed upon all things created by him some part, or intimate, simplest, and most excellent power, which is called the "unity of the thing": from which and toward which, as if from a center and toward its own center, the remaining parts and powers of each thing hang. Created things must first collect themselves toward this, their own center, toward this proper unity, before they can cling to their Creator: so that through their own center, as we have often repeated, they may cling to the center of all. <margin>C</margin> The mind of an angel rises to its own apex and head before it ascends into God. The soul and the rest do so in the same manner. And of those invisible circles—namely, mind, soul, and nature—the circle of the visible world is the image. For bodies are the shadows and footprints of souls and minds. A shadow and footprint reflects the figure of that of which it is the shadow and footprint. Therefore, those four are not unjustly called four circles. But the Mind is immobile for this reason: because its operation as well as its substance remains the same in the same way, and it operates similarly; it always understands in the same way and wills similarly. However, the mind can sometimes be called mobile only because, like all other things, proceeding from God it turns itself back toward him. The Soul of the <margin>D</margin> world, and any other, is a mobile circle. For this, by its nature, knows by discourse <note>step-by-step reasoning</note> and operates through the courses of time. Discourse from one thing to another, and temporal operation, is undoubtedly called motion. If there is any stability in the soul's knowledge, it consists in the benefit of the mind rather than the soul. Nature is also a mobile circuit. When we say "soul," in the manner of the ancient theologians, we understand the power placed in reason and sense; when we say "nature," we mean the power of the soul located in generating. That power in us they properly called "man"; this one, the "idol and image of man." This faculty of generating is called mobile because it executes its work through spaces of time. But in this it differs from that property of the soul: that the soul is moved by itself and in itself. By itself, I say, because it exists as the principle of motion. In itself also, because the operation of reason and sense remains in the substance of the soul itself. <margin>E</margin> From these, no work necessarily results in the body. But that power of generating which we call nature is indeed moved by itself, since it is a certain power of the soul moved by itself. It is said to be moved in another, however, because all its operation is terminated in the mass of the body. For it nourishes, increases, and generates the body. Matter and the mass of the body is an orb mobile by another and in another. By another, indeed, since it is necessarily moved by the soul. In another, however, because the motion of the body is conducted in the space of a location. Now, therefore, we can clearly understand for what reason theologians place goodness in the center and beauty in the circle. For Goodness itself is the one God of all things, through whom all things are good. Beauty, however, is a ray of God inserted into these four circles, revolved in a certain way around God. <margin>F</margin> A ray of this kind fashions all the species of all things in those four: we are accustomed to call those species "Ideas" in the mind, "Reasons" in the soul, "Seeds" in nature, and "Forms" in matter. <margin>G</margin> Therefore, in the four circles, there appear to be four splendors: the splendor of Ideas in the first; of Reasons in the second; of Seeds in the third; and of Forms in the last.

## HOW PLATO IS EXPLAINED
## concerning divine matters.

### CHAPTER IV.

<margin>H</margin> Plato signified this mystery in his letter to King Dionysius, when he affirmed God to be the cause of all beautiful things, as if the principle and origin of all beauty. *Around the king of all,* he says, *are all things; for his sake are all things; he is the cause of all beautiful things. Second things around the second. Third things around the third.* But the human mind affects to understand what kind of things those are, looking into those things which are related to itself, none of which is sufficient. But around the king himself, and those things I have mentioned, there is nothing of such a kind; but what is after this, the mind speaks. "Around the king" signifies not *inside* the king, but *outside*. For in God there is no composition. What that word "Around" signifies, Plato explains when he adds: *For his sake are all things; he is the cause of all beautiful things.* As if he were to say: all things are around the king because all things revolve toward him as toward an end according to their nature, just as all things were produced by him as a principle. "Of all beautiful things," that is, of the whole beauty which shines in the aforementioned circles. For the forms of bodies are led back to God through seeds; these through reasons; these through ideas; and they are produced from God by the same steps. Properly, however, when he says "All things," he understands the Ideas; for in these the rest are included. *Second things around the second; Third things around the third.* Zoroaster placed three princes of the world, masters of three orders: Oromasin...

<summary>This page explores the Neoplatonic concept of God as the center of the universe, defining Beauty as a divine ray that flows through the Mind, Soul, Nature, and Matter. It explains the "circle of love" where all things are created by God's goodness, drawn back by His beauty, and perfected by His justice.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s Neoplatonic commentary on love, specifically interpreting Plato’s letters and the Symposium. It transitions from the metaphysical hierarchy of the universe to the practical nature of human love and the concept of the "Two Venuses."</meta>

<margin>776</margin>
-> MARSILIO FICINO <-

Mithras and Arimanius <note>original: "Mithrim, Arimanin." These refer to the Zoroastrian principles of light/good and darkness/evil, which Ficino aligns with Platonic thought.</note>. These Plato calls God, Mind, and Soul. Furthermore, he placed three orders within the divine forms: Ideas, Reasons, and Seeds. The first, that is the Ideas, pertain to the first, which is God; since they are granted by God to the Mind, they lead that same Mind to which they were given back to Him. The second pertain to the second, that is the Reasons pertain to the Mind: since they pass through the Mind into the Soul, and guide the Soul within the Mind. The third pertain to the third, that is the Seeds of things pertain to the Soul: for they pass through the Soul into Nature—specifically into that power of generation—and in turn they couple Nature to the Soul. In the same order, forms descend from Nature into Matter. But Plato does not include these in the established order because, when questioned by Dionysius <note>Referring to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite or Dionysius of Syracuse; Ficino often synthesized Christian and Platonic sources.</note> about divine matters, he introduced three <margin>B</margin> orders pertaining to incorporeal species as being divine: but he omitted the forms of bodies. He did not wish to call God the "first king," but the "King of All": lest if he called Him "first," he might seem to place Him alongside the subsequent leaders in some kind of numerical category or equality of condition. Nor did he say "the first things pertain to Him," but "all things": lest we believe Him to be the governor of a specific order rather than of all things. The human soul yearns to understand what those things are like. Skillfully, after those three splendors of divine beauty shining forth in three circles, he added Love toward them. For from that source, the ardor of the soul is kindled. Indeed, it is only right that the divine should desire divine things: looking upon those things which are kindred to itself. Since human knowledge arises from the senses, we are often accustomed to judge divine things through those things which we see as more excellent in bodies: we investigate God’s power through the forces of corporeal things; His wisdom through order; and His goodness through utility. He calls the forms of bodies "kindred" to the soul, as if they were "next-born." For the forms of bodies are arranged in the step immediately following the soul. None of these is sufficient in itself. Forms of this kind neither exist sufficiently, nor do they sufficiently show us divine things. For the true things are the Ideas, Reasons, and Seeds. The forms of bodies, however, seem to be shadows of things rather than true things. Just as the shadow of a body does not indicate the exact and distinct figure of the body, so bodies do not demonstrate the proper nature of divine things. Concerning the King himself and those things I have mentioned, there is nothing of that sort. For in what way could mortal things be like immortal ones, or false things like the true? But what follows this, the soul speaks: that is, while the soul judges divine things through mortal ones, it speaks falsely of the divine: it does not pronounce divine things, but mortal ones.

# DIVINE BEAUTY
## shines through all things, and is loved in all things.
### CHAPTER V.

<margin>C</margin> Furthermore, to encompass many things in a few words: "The Good" is said to be the supereminent existence of God itself. "Beauty" is a certain act or ray penetrating from there through all things: First into the Angelic Mind; Second into the Soul of the Whole <note>The Anima Mundi or World Soul.</note> and other souls; Third into Nature; Fourth into the Matter of bodies. It graces the Mind with the order of Ideas; it fills the Soul with the series of Reasons; it supports Nature with Seeds; it adorns Matter with forms. Just as a single ray of the sun illuminates four bodies—fire, air, water, and earth—so a single ray of God illuminates the Mind, the Soul, Nature, and Matter. And whoever looks upon the light in these four elements sees a ray of the sun itself; and through it, he is turned toward beholding the supernal light of the sun. So, whoever contemplates and loves the beauty in these four—Mind, Soul, Nature, and Body—is beholding and loving the glow of God in them, and through this glow, God Himself.

# THE PASSIONS OF LOVERS.
### CHAPTER VI.

From this it follows that the lover's impulse is not extinguished by the sight or touch of any body. For he does not desire this or that body: but he admires, affects, and is stunned by the splendor of the supernal light shining through bodies. Therefore, lovers are ignorant of what they desire or seek. For they are ignorant of God Himself, whose hidden flavor has inserted a certain sweetest scent of Himself into His works. By this ardor, we are daily aroused. We perceive the scent, certainly; but we are undoubtedly ignorant of the flavor. Since, therefore, we are enticed by the manifest scent and desire the hidden flavor, we rightly do not know what we desire or what we suffer. From this it also always happens that lovers in some way fear and venerate the sight of the beloved. This even the brave—I will say it indeed, though I fear lest any of you blush hearing this—and wise men, I say, are accustomed to suffer in the presence of any inferior beloved. Truly, it is not something human that terrifies them, breaks them, and occupies them. For human force is always more excellent in the brave and the wise. But that glow of divinity shining out in the beautiful, like an image of God, compels lovers to be stunned, to tremble, and to venerate. For the same reason, because of the presence of the beloved, the lover despises riches and honors and holds them as nothing. For it is right that divine things be preferred to human ones. It also frequently happens that each person desires to transfer himself into the person of the beloved. And not without cause. For God desires and strives to become man. Who then would not exchange a man for God? It also happens that those ensnared by love sigh and rejoice in turn. They sigh because they lose themselves, because they waste away, because they perish.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> They rejoice because they transfer themselves into something better. They grow hot and cold in turn: like those whom a tertian fever <note>A fever that returns every third day, often associated with malaria in the Renaissance.</note> invades. They are rightly cold, because they are deserted by their own heat; and they are also hot, since they are kindled by the glows of supernal rays. Timidity follows the coldness; audacity follows the heat. Therefore, they appear timid and audacious in turn. Furthermore, even the dullest people are rendered sharper by loving. For who, with the celestial ray breathing upon them, would not see most sharply? But concerning love itself, and beauty, and its origin, and the affections of lovers, let these things suffice.

---

# CONCERNING THE TWO KINDS OF LOVE,
## and the double Venus.
### CHAPTER VII.

<margin>D</margin> Next, we must briefly discuss the two kinds of Love. Pausanias asserts in Plato that Cupid is the companion of Venus. He considers it necessary that there be as many Cupids as there are Venuses. He mentions two Venuses, who are likewise accompanied by twin Cupids. He places one Venus as "Celestial," and the other as "Vulgar." Plato says the Celestial one was born from Heaven without a mother; the Vulgar one was generated from Jove and Dione. The Platonists call the highest God "Heaven" <note>Latin: Caelum</note> for this reason: because just as this sublime body of the sky rules and contains all bodies, so that highest God supereminently stands above all spirits. They call the Mind by many names. For they call it now Saturn, now Jove, now Venus. For that Mind exists, lives, and understands. They are accustomed to call its Essence "Saturn," its Life "Jove," and its Intelligence "Venus." Furthermore, we call the Soul of the World similarly Saturn, Jove, and Venus: insofar as it understands supernal things, it is Saturn; insofar as it moves celestial things, it is Jove; as it generates inferior things, it is Venus. The first Venus, who is in the Mind, is said to be born of Heaven without a mother: since among the Natural Philosophers, "mother" is matter. But that Mind is foreign to the company of corporeal matter. The second Venus, who is placed in the Soul of the World, is generated from Jove and Dione. From Jove, that is, from that power of the soul itself which moves celestial things. For that power created this potency which generates these inferior things. They also attribute a mother to her because, being infused into the matter of the world, she is thought to have commerce with matter. Finally, to speak summarily, Venus is twofold. One is that intelligence which we placed in the Angelic Mind. The other is the power of generating attributed to the Soul of the World. Each has a love as a companion similar to itself. For the former is snatched up by an innate love to understand the beauty of God. The latter is likewise drawn by its own love to procreate that same beauty in bodies. The former first embraces the glow of divinity in itself; then it translates this into the second Venus. The latter <margin>E</margin> pours the sparks of that glow into the matter of the world. By the presence of such sparks, individual bodies of the world appear beautiful, according to the capacity of their nature. The human soul perceives the beauty of these bodies through the eyes. The soul, in turn, possesses twin powers. For it has the power of understanding, and it has the power of generating. These twin powers are the two Venuses in us, which are also accompanied by twin loves. As soon as the <margin>F</margin> appearance of a human body is offered to our eyes, our mind—which is the first Venus in us—venerates and loves it as an image of divine beauty; and through this, it is often incited toward that higher beauty. But the power of generating—the second Venus—desires to generate a form similar to this one. Therefore, there is love in both cases. In the one, there is a desire to contemplate beauty; in the other, to generate it. Both loves are honorable and to be approved. For each follows a divine image. What then does Pausanias disapprove of in love? I will say it indeed. If someone, too greedy for generation, should desert contemplation, or pursue generation beyond measure with women, or against the order of nature with males, or prefer the form of the body to the beauty of the soul, he certainly abuses the dignity of love. It is this abuse of love that Pausanias censures. He who uses love rightly praises the form of the body, but through it, he contemplates the more excellent species of the soul, the mind, and God, and admires and <margin>G</margin> loves that more vehemently. He uses the office of generation and intercourse only so far as the natural order and the civil laws established by the prudent prescribe. Pausanias speaks more diffusely on these matters.

---

# EXHORTATION TO LOVE.
## Concerning simple love, and mutual love.
### CHAPTER VIII.

<margin>H</margin> But you, friends, I exhort and beseech to embrace love—a truly divine thing—with all your strength; and do not let that deter you which they say Plato said of a certain lover. "That lover's soul," he said, "is dead in its own body, but living in another's body." Nor let it disturb you what Orpheus sang concerning the bitter and wretched lot of lovers. For how these things happen, and by what way they must be succored, I ask you then, if you please, to attend diligently. Plato calls love a "bitter thing" <note>original: "rem amaram"</note>; and not without justice, because whoever loves, dies. Orpheus also calls it *glykypikron* <note>Greek: γλυκύπικρον</note>, that is, "sweet-bitter." Since love is a voluntary death. Insofar as it is death, it is a bitter thing. Insofar as it is voluntary, it is sweet. For whoever loves, dies. For his thought, forgetful of himself, is always occupied with the beloved. If he does not think of himself, he certainly does not think in himself. Therefore, this affected soul does not act within itself, since the chief operation of the soul is thought itself. He who does not act in himself, is not in himself.

<summary>Ficino explains the Neoplatonic hierarchy of beauty—from God to matter—and introduces the concept of the "Two Venuses" representing intellectual contemplation and physical procreation. He argues that human love is a response to divine splendor reflected in physical forms, which can lead the soul back to God if practiced rightly.</summary>

# ARGUMENTS AND COMMENTARY

<margin>A</margin> For these two things, being and operation <note>original: *esse, & operatio*; the philosophical concept that to exist is to act</note>, are equal to one another: there is no being without operation, nor does operation exceed being itself. Nothing acts where it is not, and wherever it is, it acts. Therefore, the soul of a lover is not in itself, because it does not act in itself. If it does not act in itself, it does not live in itself; and he who does not live is dead. Therefore, whoever loves is dead in himself. But does he at least live in another? Certainly. There are two species of love: one is simple love, the other is mutual. Simple love is where the beloved does not love the lover. There, the lover is entirely dead; for he neither lives in himself, as we have already demonstrated, nor does he live in the beloved since he is rejected by him. Where then does he live? In the air, or water, or fire, or earth, or some brute body? Not at all. For the human soul lives in no other body than a human one. Or perhaps he leads his life in some other body of a person not loved? Not even that. For if he does not live where he most vehemently desires to live, how shall he live elsewhere? Therefore, he who loves another without being loved in return lives nowhere. Consequently, the unloved lover is entirely dead. Nor will he ever come back to life unless indignation rouses him. But where the beloved responds in love, the lover at least leads his life in him. Here truly a marvelous thing happens: whenever two people embrace each other with mutual goodwill, this one lives in that one, and that one in this. By turns, men of this kind exchange themselves, and each gives himself to the other so that they may receive the other. I see how they give themselves when they forget themselves. But how they receive the other, I do not understand. For he who does not possess himself will much less possess another. On the contrary, each has himself, and has the other. This one indeed has himself, but in that one. That one also possesses himself, but in this one. Indeed, <margin>C</margin> while I love you who love me, I find myself in you who are thinking of me, and I recover myself—lost by my own negligence—preserved in you. You do the same in me. And this again appears marvelous. For after I have lost myself, if I redeem myself through you, I have myself through you; if I have myself through you, I have you before and more than myself: I am closer to you than to myself. Indeed, I cling to myself in no other way than through you as a medium. In this, surely, the power of Cupid <note>The god of love</note> differs from the violence of Mars <note>The god of war</note>. For authority and love differ in this way: a ruler possesses others through himself, but a lover embraces himself through another. Each of the lovers, becoming further from himself, becomes closer to the other; and dead in himself, he comes back to life in the other. In mutual love, there is only one death, but a double resurrection. For he who loves dies in himself once when he neglects himself. He comes back to life in the beloved immediately when the beloved embraces him with ardent thought. <margin>D</margin> He comes back to life a second time when he finally recognizes himself in the beloved and does not doubt that he is loved. O happy death, which two lives follow! O marvelous exchange, by which one gives himself for another, and neither has himself, nor ceases to have himself! O inestimable gain, when two become one in such a way that each of the two, instead of one alone, becomes two; so that as if doubled, he who had one life now has two, with one death intervening. For he who, having died once, returns to life twice, has obtained a twin life for one, and two for himself alone. Surely, vengeance in mutual love is most just. A murderer ought to be punished with death. For who would deny that the beloved is a murderer when he separates the soul from the lover? Who again <margin>E</margin> would deny that the same person is similarly subject to death when he loves the lover in return? This restitution is more than owed: when this one returns to that one, and that one to this, the soul which he received. Each gives his own by loving, and by loving in return, restores the other's soul through his own. Therefore, by right itself, whoever is loved ought to love. But he who does not love the lover must be held guilty of homicide. Indeed, he is a thief, a murderer, and a sacrilegious man. Money is possessed by the body, the body by the soul. He, therefore, who seizes the soul, from which both body and money are possessed, seizes the soul, body, and money all at once. Thus it happens that as a thief, murderer, and sacrilegious man, he is liable to a triple death; and as one utterly infamous and profane, he could be killed with impunity by anyone—unless he spontaneously fulfills that law, namely, that he love the lover. Where, with the one dying once, he himself similarly dies once; with the one reviving twice, he likewise revives twice. By the above reasons, it has been shown that <margin>F</margin> the beloved ought to love the lover in return; but it is shown thus that he is not only obligated, but compelled. Likeness procreates love. Likeness is a certain nature that is the same in many. For if I am like you, you are also necessarily like me. Therefore, the same likeness which compels me to love you also forces you to love me. Furthermore, the lover takes himself away from himself and gives himself to the beloved. The beloved, therefore, cares for him as his own property, for his own things are dearest to everyone. Added to this is that the lover has carved the figure of the beloved in his own soul. Thus the soul of the lover becomes a mirror in which the image of the beloved shines back. Therefore, when the beloved recognizes himself in the lover, he is compelled to love him. Astrologers think that the reciprocity of love is especially strong between those in whose birth <note>original: *genesi*</note> there was an exchange of the lights, that is, of the sun and moon. <margin>G</margin> For instance, if at my birth the sun was in Aries and the moon in Libra, and at your birth the sun was in Libra and the moon in Aries. Or for those whom the same or a similar sign, and the same or a similar planet, was ascending; or if benign planets looked upon the angle of the east in a similar way, or if Venus was positioned in the same house of birth and the same degree. The Platonists add those whose life is led by the same or a similar demon <note>A guiding spirit or genius, not a malevolent entity</note>. But the physicians and moral philosophers want a similarity of complexion, nutrition, education, and habit to be the cause of a similar affection. Finally, where more causes concur, there a more vehement reciprocity is found. Where all concur, there the affections of Pythias and Damon, or Pylades and Orestes <note>Famous pairs of devoted friends from antiquity</note>, rise again.

## WHAT LOVERS SEEK.
### CHAPTER IX.

Furthermore, what do they seek when they love each other mutually? They seek beauty. For love is the desire for persuasive beauty.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Beauty, moreover, is a certain splendor that ravishes the human soul to itself. Indeed, the beauty of the body is nothing other than that very splendor in the grace of colors and lines. The beauty of the soul, too, is a brilliance in the harmony of learning and morals. That light of the body is perceived not by the ears, nor smell, nor taste, nor touch, but by the eye. If the eye alone recognizes it, the eye alone enjoys it. Therefore, the eye alone enjoys the beauty of the body. Since love is nothing else but the desire for enjoying beauty, and this is comprehended by the eyes alone, the lover of the body is content with the sight alone. The desire for touching is not a part of love, nor an affection of the lover, but a species of wantonness and the disturbance of a servile man. Furthermore, we comprehend that light and beauty of the soul with the mind alone. Therefore, he who seeks the beauty of the soul is content with the intuition of the mind alone. Finally, beauty is exchanged for beauty among lovers. A man enjoys the beauty of the younger beloved with his eyes. The younger man attains the beauty of the man with his mind; and he who is beautiful in body alone, by this association becomes fair in soul also; he who is beautiful in soul alone fills the eyes of the body with the beauty of the body. It is a plainly miraculous exchange, honorable, useful, and pleasant to both. Honorable, since it is equal in both; for it is equally honorable to learn and to teach. The pleasure is greater in the elder, who is delighted by sight and intelligence. But in the younger, the utility is greater; for as much as the soul is more excellent than the body, so much more precious is the attainment of the beauty of the soul than that of the body. Thus far for Pausanias; now let us interpret the speech of Eryximachus.

---

# THE THIRD SPEECH
## LOVE IN ALL THINGS TOWARD ALL THINGS, CREATOR OF ALL, MASTER OF ALL.

### CHAPTER I.

<margin>I</margin> Three things next seem to us to be treated according to the mind of our Eryximachus. First, that love, implanted in all things, extends through all things. Second, that it is the effector and preserver of all works that are according to nature. Third, that it is the master and lord of individual arts. Indeed, three levels of things are considered in nature: the Superior, the Inferior, and the Equal. Those which are above are the causes of the inferior; those which are below are the works of the superior. Those which are equal are endowed with the same nature among themselves. Causes love their works as their own parts and images. Works, moreover, seek their causes as their preservers. Those which are placed in that order are affected toward one another with mutual charity, as if members of one and the same thing. Therefore God rules and governs the angels, and the angels together with God rule the soul, and the soul with them rules bodies with a certain benevolence. In this, the love of the superior for the inferior is plainly seen. Again, bodies are most greedily joined to their souls, and are most painfully separated from them. Our souls desire the blessedness of the celestial beings; the celestial beings happily venerate the majesty of the supreme divinity; and this is the affection of love from the inferior toward the superior. Likewise, all parts of fire willingly cling together. Again, the parts of earth, water, and air cling together; and in any species of animals, animals of the same species always affect one another with mutual association. Here, love is seen among equals and likes. Who then will doubt that love is innate in all things toward all things? And that is what Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A Christian theologian and philosopher</note> signified in his book *On the Divine Names*, following the mind of Hierotheus, in these words: Whether we call love divine, or angelic, or spiritual, or animal, or natural, we understand a certain ingrafted and mixing power: which moves the superior to the providence of the inferior; reconciles equals to a social communion with one another; and finally admonishes all inferior things to be turned toward the better and more sublime. These are his words.

---

## LOVE IS THE AUTHOR AND PRESERVER OF ALL.

### CHAPTER II.

<margin>H</margin> That second member of our speech, by which love is called the effector and preserver of all things, is proved thus. The desire for propagating one's own perfection is a kind of love. Absolute perfection is in the supreme power of God. The divine intelligence contemplates it, and from there the same will desires to propagate it outside itself; from which love of propagating, all things were created by Him. Therefore our Dionysius says, "Divine love does not permit the King of all to remain in Himself without offspring." The same instinct of proof was instilled in all things by that first Author. Through this, those holy spirits move the heavens and bestow their gifts on all that follow. Through this, the stars diffuse their light into the elements. Through this, fire moves fire, air, water, and earth by the communion of its heat; and in turn, the earth draws water to itself, water draws air, and air draws fire. Herbs also and trees, desirous of propagating their own seed, beget things like themselves. Brute animals also and men are ravished by the allurements of the same desire to procreate offspring. But if love makes all things, it also preserves all things. For the office of affection and preservation is always the same. Indeed, likes are preserved by likes. But love draws like to like...

<summary>This page explores the metaphysical and psychological nature of mutual love, describing it as a "double resurrection" where lovers find themselves in each other. It also begins the commentary on Eryximachus's speech, arguing that love is a universal force of creation and preservation across all levels of existence.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical banquet discussion from Marsilio Ficino’s "Commentary on Plato’s Symposium." The previous sections established Love as a cosmic force; here, the speakers Eryximachus (the physician) and Aristophanes (the comic poet) explain Love’s role in the arts, sciences, and the origins of humanity.</meta>

-> MARS. FICINO <-

Individual parts of the earth, joined by mutual love, betake themselves to other parts of the earth similar to themselves. The whole earth also descends toward the center of the world, which is similar to itself, out of a longing for it. Parts of water are likewise carried toward one another and toward the place suitable for them along with the whole body of water. The parts of air and fire do the same: and even these two elements are drawn toward the higher region that is congruent and similar to them by a love for that region. Even the Heavens, as Plato says in the book *On Kingship* <note>original: "De regno"</note>, are moved by an innate love. For the soul of the heavens is present as a whole simultaneously in any given point of the heavens. Therefore, the Heavens, eager to enjoy the soul, run in such a way that they may enjoy the whole soul everywhere through all their parts. They fly most rapidly so that, as far as possible, they may be everywhere at once, just as the soul is everywhere at once. Furthermore, the concave surface of a larger sphere is the natural place for a smaller sphere. And because any particle of this sphere fits equally with any particle of that one, every particle desires to touch all the particles of the other. If it were to stay still, individual parts would touch individual parts, not every part touching all. By running, it almost attains what it could not attain by remaining still. It runs most swiftly so that every part may touch all others at nearly the same time, according to its strength. Indeed, all things are preserved by the unity of their parts and perish by the dispersion of their parts. Mutual love effects this unity of parts. This can be observed in the humors of our bodies and the elements of the world; by their concord, as Empedocles and Pythagoras say, both the world and our body consist, while by discord they are dissipated. The alternation of peace and love provides them with concord. Hence Orpheus says: <term>μόνος γὰρ σὺ τούτων πάντων οἴηκα κρατύνεις</term> <note>Greek: "For you alone hold the helm of all these things"</note>, that is, You alone hold the reins of all these things.

# THAT LOVE IS THE MASTER of arts and the governor.

### CHAPTER III.

<margin>D</margin> It remains after this that we explain in what way Love is the master and governor of all arts. We shall understand him to be the master of arts if we only consider that no one can ever either find or learn any art unless the delight of investigation and the desire for discovery incite them: and he who teaches must love his students, and the students must thirst most greedily for that teaching. Furthermore, he is deservedly called the Governor. For whoever most loves both the crafts themselves and the persons for whom they are made executes the works of art diligently and completes them exactly. Added to this is the fact that craftsmen in individual arts seek and care for nothing other than love. We shall briefly run through those arts at present which Eryximachus commemorates in Plato. For what else does medicine consider than how the four humors of the body may become and remain friends to one another? What foods and drinks, and other habits of living or healing, does nature love and require? Eryximachus discovered through a certain similarity those two loves, the Celestial and the Common, which Pausanias had distinguished above. For a temperate affection of the body possesses a moderate love directed toward moderate and suitable things. An intemperate one contains the opposite, directed toward opposites. The former should be indulged, the latter never obeyed; even in gymnastic exercise, one must investigate which habits of the body, which modes of exercise, and which gestures it loves and demands. In agriculture, what soil, what seeds, or what kind of cultivation it requires, and what mode of tending is loved by individual trees. The same is observed in music: its practitioners investigate which numbers love which numbers more or less. They find the least love between one and two, or one and seven. But between one and three, four, five, and six, they find a more vehement love. Between one and eight, the most vehement. They make high and low voices, diverse by nature, more friendly to one another through certain intervals and measures. From this, the composition and sweetness of harmony are born. They also temper slower and faster movements with each other so that they become most friendly and exhibit rhythm and elegance. Two kinds of musical melody are handed down. For there is a certain grave and constant kind: and there is another soft and wanton. The former is useful to those using it: the latter is judged harmful by Plato in the books *On the Republic* and *Laws*. He placed the Muse Urania over the former at the banquet, and Polymnia over the latter. Some love that first kind, others the second. The love of the former should be obeyed, and the sounds they seek should be employed: the appetite of the latter must be resisted. For the love of the former is celestial: but that of the latter is common. There is a certain friendship in the stars and the four elements, which astronomy considers. In these, those two loves are found in a certain way. For there is a moderate love in them when they harmonize most temperately with mutual forces. There is also an immoderate love when any one thing loves itself too much and in a way abandons the others. From the former comes the pleasant temperance of the air, the tranquility of water, the fertility of lands, and the health of animals: from the latter, the opposites proceed. Finally, the faculty of Prophets and Priests seems to be occupied chiefly in this: that they teach us which duties of men are friendly to God, and by what reason men may become friends to God: what mode of love and charity should be applied toward God, toward the fatherland, toward parents, and toward others, both the living and the deceased. The same may be conjectured in the other arts, and summarized by concluding that love in all things toward all things is the author and preserver of all, and exists as the lord and master of all arts. Deservedly did the divine Orpheus call him "Shrewd," "double-natured," and "holding the keys of all." For how he is of a double nature, you heard first from Pausanias, then from Eryximachus. Also, by what reason he is said by Orpheus to hold the keys of the world, we can sufficiently understand from the

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> foregoing: for as we have shown, this desire for propagating one's own perfection, innate in all, unfolds the latent and implicit fecundity of each thing: while it compels the female to sprout into a bud, it draws out the strengths of each from its bosom and conceives offspring, and as if by certain keys, it brings them forth into the light by opening the conception: wherefore all parts of the world, because they are the works of one craftsman, being members of the same machine similar to each other in being and living, are bound to one another by a certain mutual charity, so that love may deservedly be called the perpetual knot and bond of the world, the immovable support of its parts, and the firm foundation of the whole machine.

## NO MEMBER OF THE WORLD hates another member.

### CHAPTER IV.

<margin>B</margin> If this is so, no members of this work can be enemies to each other in any way. For fire does not flee water out of hatred for water, but out of love for itself: lest it be extinguished by the cold of the water. Nor does water extinguish fire out of hatred for fire: but it is drawn by a certain desire for amplifying its own cold to procreate water similar to itself from the body of the fire. <margin>C</margin> For since every natural appetite tends toward the good and none toward evil: the purpose of water is not to extinguish fire, which is an evil: but to generate water similar to itself, which is a good. If it could fulfill this without the destruction of the fire, it would certainly not consume the fire. The same reasoning is assigned to other things that seem contrary and hostile. Furthermore, the lamb does not hate the life and form of the wolf, but dreads its own destruction which is brought by the wolf: nor does the wolf tear and devour the lamb out of hatred, but out of love for itself. Nor does man dread man, but the vices of man; nor do we envy the gifts of those more powerful or sharper out of hatred for them, but out of benevolence for ourselves, fearing lest we succumb entirely to them. Therefore, nothing prevents love from being in all things and penetrating through all things. Therefore, let us undoubtedly fear this great god, because he is everywhere and sits in the innermost parts of all, as a powerful lord whose empire we cannot escape, and as a most wise judge from whom our thoughts cannot be hidden: let us venerate him as a father because he is the creator and preserver of all, and honor him as a guardian and protection: let us follow him as a teacher because he teaches individual arts: by whose authorship we exist and live: by whose preservation we remain perpetual: by whose presidency and judgment we are governed: by whose teaching we are instructed and formed for living well and blessedly.

---

# THE FOURTH SPEECH.

## THE TEXT OF PLATO is narrated concerning the ancient nature of men.

### CHAPTER I.

<margin>E</margin> These things having been said, our friend put an end to his words. Cristoforo Landino, a man excellent in learning, whom we have known especially in our times as an Orphic and Platonic poet, followed him in this manner, intending to explain the obscure and implicit opinion of Aristophanes. Although Giovanni Cavalcanti has freed us from the long windings of disputations by his diligence: nevertheless, the opinion of Aristophanes, wrapped in most obscure words, still requires some explanation and light. Love is, says Aristophanes, above all other gods, exceedingly beneficial to the human race, the curator and guardian of men, and their physician. It is necessary first to notice what the nature of men once was, and what its passions were. For it was not formerly as it is now, but far different. In the beginning, there were three kinds of humans: not only the two that exist now, male and female: but there was also a certain third kind composed of both. Furthermore, the form of each human was whole and round, having the back and sides in a circle: four hands: and legs equal to the hands. Likewise two faces connected by a smooth neck and entirely similar. The male <margin>G</margin> kind was born from the sun: the female from the earth. The mixed kind from the moon. <margin>F</margin> Whence they were of an exalted spirit and robust body: wherefore they attempted to fight with the gods and ascend into heaven. Therefore Jupiter cut each one lengthwise: and made two out of one, like those who cut eggs lengthwise with a hair: and he threatened that if they should again seem to go mad with pride against the gods, he would divide them again in the same way. After the nature of humans was thus divided, each desired his own half. Therefore they ran together, and throwing their arms around each other, they embraced one another, longing to be reduced to their former condition. On that account, they would have perished from hunger and torpor, had not God imposed a suitable way. Hence, surely, a mutual love was born in humans, the conciliator of the ancient nature, striving to make one out of two, and to heal the nature of humans. For each of us is a half of a human, as if cut, just as the little fish called plaice and giltheads are made two from one by being split. Each, however, seeks his own half. Whenever, therefore, his half meets someone, of whichever sex he is greedy for, he is most vehemently excited, clings with burning love, and would not suffer to be separated from that person for even a moment. Therefore, the desire for restoring the whole took the name of Love. This helps us exceedingly in the present time, while it leads each person to his once-dearest half: and for the future, it gives us the greatest hope that by piously worshiping God, he will restore us to our old form and, by healing us, make us most blessed. <margin>H</margin>
