<meta>This page continues the philosophical commentary on Plato’s Symposium, specifically interpreting the speech of Aristophanes regarding the original nature of humanity and the soul's descent into the body.</meta>

# THE OPINION OF PLATO
## regarding the ancient form of man is explained.

## CHAPTER II.

Aristophanes relates these and many other things similar to monsters and portents: under which, as if under certain veils, one must believe that divine mysteries lie hidden. For it was the custom of ancient theologians to cover their sacred and pure secrets with the shadows of figures <note>metaphorical imagery</note> lest they be polluted by the profane and impure. We, however, do not believe that every single detail described in the figures above and elsewhere pertains exactly to the core meaning. For Aurelius Augustinus <note>St. Augustine of Hippo</note> says, "not everything depicted in figures should be thought to signify something." For many things are added for the sake of order and connection to those things which they do signify. The earth is plowed by the plowshare alone; but so that this may be done, the other parts of the plow are also joined to it. Therefore, this is the sum of what is proposed for us to explain: Men once had three sexes—Masculine, Feminine, and Promiscuous <note>Androgynous</note>—they were the children of the Sun, the Earth, and the Moon, and they were whole. But because of pride, since they wished to make themselves equal to God, they were split into two: if they are proud again, they are to be split in two once more. Once the division was made, one half is drawn to the other half by love, so that a restoration of wholeness may occur; when this is completed, the human race will be blessed. Indeed, the sum of our interpretation will be of this kind: Men—that is, the souls of men—were once whole—that is, when they were created by God. They were adorned with two lights: the inborn <note>natural reason</note> and the infused <note>divine grace/revelation</note>. By the inborn light they might behold equal and inferior things; by the infused light they might behold superior things. They wished to make themselves equal to God, and they turned themselves back toward the single inborn light. Here they were divided, and they lost the infused splendor when they turned toward the inborn light alone: and immediately they fell into bodies. Having become more proud, they will be divided again: that is, if they trust too much in their natural talent, that inborn and natural light which remained will be extinguished in a certain way. They had three sexes: Males born of the Sun, Females of the Earth, and Promiscuous of the Moon. Some received the radiance of God according to courage, which is masculine; others according to temperance, which is feminine; others according to justice, which is promiscuous. These three virtues in us are the daughters of the other three which God possesses. But in God those three are called Sun, Moon, and Earth; in us they are named Male, Female, and Promiscuous. Once the division was made, one half is drawn to the other half by love. Souls now divided and immersed in bodies, as soon as they come to the years of youth, are stirred by the natural and inborn light which they preserved—as if by one half of themselves—toward that infused and divine light, formerly their other half, which they lost when falling, to be recovered through the pursuit of truth. Once this is received, they will now be whole and blessed by the vision of God. This, therefore, will be the summary of our interpretation.

---

<margin>C</margin>
# MAN IS THE SOUL ITSELF,
## and the soul is immortal.

## CHAPTER III.

Since the body consists of matter and quantity, and it belongs to matter to be looked down upon, and to quantity only to be divided and extended—and thus being acted upon and division are its passions—it follows that by its own nature it is subject only to passion and corruption. If indeed any action seems to belong to the body, it does not act insofar as it is a body, but insofar as a certain incorporeal power and quality is within it, just as heat is in the mass of fire, cold in the matter of water, and temperament <note>the balance of humors</note> in our body. Certainly, the operations of bodies proceed from these qualities. For fire does not heat because it is long, or wide, or deep, but because it is hot. Nor does a more extended fire heat more—indeed, because of dispersion, it heats less—but rather the hotter fire heats more. Since, therefore, operations come about by the benefit of powers and qualities, and the powers and qualities themselves do not consist of matter and quantity (though they are in matter and quantity), it follows that being acted upon belongs to the body, while acting belongs to something incorporeal. To both, these powers are indeed instruments for working. But they are by no means sufficient by themselves for working, because they are not sufficient for existing. For that which lies in another and cannot sustain itself certainly depends on another. Thus it happens that qualities, because they are necessarily sustained by the body, are made and governed by some superior substance which is neither a body nor lies in a body. The soul is of this kind; present in and presiding over bodies, it sustains itself and grants the quality and power of temperament to bodies, through which, as if through instruments in the body and through the body, it exercises various operations. Hence, man is asserted to generate, nourish, grow, run, stand, sit, speak, manufacture works of art, perceive, and understand. But the soul itself does all these things, and therefore the soul will be the man. If we say a man generates, grows, and nourishes, the soul—as the father and craftsman of the body—begets, increases, and nourishes it. If he stands, sits, or speaks, the soul sustains, bends, and vibrates the limbs of the body. If he manufactures or runs, the soul stretches out the hands and twists them at will, and moves the feet. If he perceives, the soul perceives external bodies through the instruments of the senses, as if through windows and openings. If he understands, the soul attains variety through itself without any instrument of the body. Therefore, whatever a man is said to do, the soul itself does; the body is acted upon. For this reason, man is the soul alone, while the body is the work and instrument of the man. This is especially so because the soul exercises its most important operation—namely, understanding—without any instrument of the body, since through that it understands incorporeal things, whereas through the body only corporeal things are known. Therefore, if the soul acts anything through itself, it certainly exists through itself,

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
and lives. Moreover, it lives without the body because it operates without the body. If it exists through itself, it is fitting that it has a certain being proper to itself, not common to the body; therefore, it can obtain the name of "man" for itself separately from the mass of the body. Because this name is truly spoken of each of us throughout our whole life—for everyone at every age is called a man—it therefore seems to signify something that remains stable. The body flows continually, changing by growing, decreasing, continuous dissolution, liquefaction, and by turns of heat and cold. The soul always remains the same, which the inquiry into truth clearly shows us, as does the always identical will for good and the firm preservation of memory. Who then will be so insane as to attribute the name of "man," which is most firm in us, to the flowing body that is always and everywhere changed, rather than to the most stable <margin>B</margin> soul? From these things it can be clear that when Aristophanes named "men," he signified our souls in the Platonic manner.

---

# THAT THE SOUL IS ADORNED
## with two lights, and why it descends into the body; the creation of the soul with two lights.

## CHAPTER IIII.

<margin>D</margin> Furthermore, the soul, immediately born from God, is turned by a certain natural instinct toward God its parent, just as fire generated on earth by the power of higher things is immediately directed toward the heights by the impulse of nature; having turned toward Him, it is illuminated by His rays. But this first radiance, received in the substance of the soul which was previously unformed in itself, becomes darker, and according to the capacity of that space, it becomes proper to it and natural; therefore, through it—as if through something equal to itself—the soul indeed sees itself and those things which are below it, that is, all bodies. But it does not see God and other superior things. However, having been made closer to God through this first spark, it receives again another more excellent light, by which it may also know heavenly things. Therefore, it has a twin light: one Natural, or inborn; the other Divine and infused. Joined together, it may be able to fly through the sublime region as if with two wings. And if it always used that divine light, it would always cling to divine things; the Earth would be empty of rational animals. But it was decreed by divine providence that the soul should be mistress of itself, and be able to use both lights at once, or only one. Hence it happens that, with nature as its guide, having turned toward its own proper light and neglected the divine <margin>E</margin> light, it notices itself and its own powers which pertain to the construction of the body, and desires to exercise such powers in building bodies. Weighted down by this desire, as they say, it descends into the body: where it exercises the powers of generating, moving, and perceiving; and by its presence, it adorns the earth, the lowest seat of the world, which therefore ought not to lack reason, nor should a part of the world be destitute of the presence of rational living beings—just as the author in whose likeness the world was made is entirely reason. Moreover, our soul fell into the body when, having neglected the divine light, it used only its own light and began to be content with itself. God alone, who lacks nothing and above whom there is nothing, remains content with Himself, sufficient to Himself; wherefore the soul made itself equal to God <margin>F</margin> when it wished to be content with itself alone, as if it were no less sufficient to itself than God.

---

# BY HOW MANY WAYS THE SOUL
## returns to God.

## CHAPTER V.

<margin>G</margin> Aristophanes says that this pride was clearly the cause why the soul, which was born whole, was cut—that is, that it would henceforth use one of the twin lights and neglect the other. Here, immersed in the abyss of the body as if in the river Lethe <note>the river of forgetfulness in Greek mythology</note>, and having forgotten itself for a time, it is snatched away by the senses and lust, as if by attendants and a tyrant. But when the body is grown, the instruments of the senses purged, and with learning providing nourishment, it comes to its senses; there the natural radiance shines out, and it investigates the order of natural things. By this investigation, it perceives that there is some architect of this vast machine; it desires both to see and to possess Him. He is beheld only by the divine splendor. Therefore, the mind, by the investigation of its own light, is most vehemently incited to recover the divine light. Such incitement and appetite is true love: with this as a guide, one half of man desires the other half of the same, because the natural light, which is one half of the soul, strives to kindle again in the soul that divine light which is called the other half of the same, once neglected. And that is what Plato says in the letter to Dionysius: <margin>H</margin> "The human soul affects to understand what kind of things divine things are, looking into those things which are related to itself." Truly, when God infused His light into the soul, He adapted it especially to this: that He might lead men to the blessedness which consists in the possession of Himself. To this we are led by four virtues: Prudence, Courage, Justice, and Temperance. Prudence first shows us blessedness. Those three remaining virtues lead us to blessedness like three ways. Therefore, God tempered His spark in various souls for this end in different ways: so that with prudence as a guide, some through courage, others through justice...

It argues that the soul is the true essence of man, distinct from the changing body, and describes the soul's descent into the physical world through pride and its eventual return to God through virtue and love.</summary>

# MARSILIO FICINO

<margin>A</margin> Others may seek to return to their Author through the duties of temperance. Indeed, some, for the sake of this gift, undergo dangers and death with a brave spirit for the worship of God, for honor, or for their fatherland. Others order their lives so justly that they neither inflict injury on anyone nor, to the best of their power, allow it to be inflicted. Others subdue their lusts through vigils, fasting, and labor. These people proceed by these three paths, but they strive to reach the same goal of blessedness with Prudence showing them the way; therefore, these three virtues are also contained within the Prudence of God himself. Human souls, kindled by the desire for these virtues, wish to reach them through their practice: to cling to them and possess them perpetually. <margin>B</margin> He calls the **Fortitude** of men "masculine strength and audacity." He calls **Temperance** "female" because of a certain relaxed and cooler habit of desire and a mild nature. **Justice** he calls "promiscuous" <note>original: *promiscuam*; meaning shared or common to both sexes</note>: female insofar as it inflicts injury on no one in its innocence; but masculine insofar as it does not allow injury to be inflicted on others and punishes wicked men with a more severe judgment. Because it is the property of the male to give and the female to receive, we therefore call the **Sun** male, which, receiving light from no one, displays it to all; the **Moon**, which receiving from the sun gives to the elements, is promiscuous by giving and receiving; the **Earth**, since it receives from all but grants to none, we call female. For this reason, Sun, Moon, Earth, Fortitude, Justice, and Temperance are deservedly marked by the names of male, promiscuous, and female. And so that we may offer a more excellent title to God, we call these virtues in Him "Sun, Moon, and Earth," while in ourselves we call them the masculine, promiscuous, and feminine sexes. To those whom that divine light was infused from the Sun of God with the affection of fortitude at their birth, we say a masculine light was granted. To those from the Moon of God with the affection of justice, a promiscuous light. To those from the Earth of God with the affection of temperance, a feminine light. Having immediately turned back toward natural light, we neglect that infused divine light. Thus, having held one in lower esteem, we have preserved the other; where we hold half of ourselves, we have let go of the other half. <margin>C</margin> At a certain time of life, led by natural light, we all proceed toward the attainment of divine affection, but in different ways: some through fortitude, who once received that light from the fortitude of God with the affection of fortitude; others through justice or temperance likewise. Finally, each seeks that "half" of his own as he had received it. And some, through the masculine light of God once lost and now recovered, wish to enjoy God with masculine fortitude; others through the promiscuous light with promiscuous virtue; others through the feminine in the same way. Truly, only those attain so great a gift who, after the spark of natural light has shone forth in them in adult age, judge that it is not sufficient for judging divine things. They must not, by the judgment of the natural spark, attribute the affections of souls or bodies to the divine majesty, nor think that the divine is not more excellent than bodies and souls. In this, many are said to have erred: those who, trusting in their natural wit in the investigation of divine matters, either said there is no God, like Diagoras; or doubted, like Protagoras; or judged Him to be a body, like the Epicureans, Stoics, Cyrenaics, and many others; or some kind of soul, like Marcus Varro, Marcus Manilius, and several others. These men, as if impious, not only failed to recover the divine light once neglected, but even corrupted the natural light because of its abuse. That which is corrupted is rightly considered broken and split. Therefore their souls, as if proud and swollen with disdain, trusting in their own strengths, are "cut again," as Aristophanes says: since they obscure even the natural light that remained to them with false opinions and extinguish it with wicked morals. Therefore, those use the natural light rightly who, recognizing it to be lame and mutilated, judge it to be somewhat sufficient for judging natural things; but for those things which are above nature, thinking they need a more sublime light, they prepare themselves by a most exact purging of the soul so that the divine light may shine upon them again. By its ray, they will think rightly of God and be restored to that pristine integrity.

### LOVE LEADS SOULS BACK TO
### heaven, distributes the grades of
### Blessedness, and bestows
### eternal joy.

->CHAPTER VI.<-

This God, O most excellent guests, whom Aristophanes says is a benefit to the human race above the other gods—make Him favorable to you with every kind of sacrifice: invoke Him with pious prayers: embrace Him with your whole heart. He, by His beneficence, first leads souls to the heavenly table, abounding in ambrosia and nectar; then He fits each to their individual seats; finally, He sweetly detains them forever. For none return to heaven except those who have pleased the King of the heavens: those please Him who love Him exceedingly. To truly know Him is entirely impossible in the present time. But to truly love Him, however He is known, is both possible and easy. Those who know God do not yet please Him unless they love Him as known; those who know and love Him do so not because they know, but because those who love are loved by God. For we embrace with charity not those who have known us, but those who have loved us. For we have many enemies who know us. Therefore, what restores us to heaven is not the knowledge of God, but love. Furthermore, the order of those reclining at the heavenly table follows the different grades of lovers. For those who have loved God more excellently eat more excellent feasts there. Indeed, those who have worshipped the fortitude of God through works of fortitude enjoy that very thing. Those who worshipped justice enjoy justice; temperance likewise for those who loved temperance; and so by various

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ideas and reasons of the divine mind, various souls enjoy according to the various rapture of their love. Yet all enjoy the whole of God, because He is whole in each individual idea. But they possess the whole of God more excellently who behold Him in a more excellent idea. Each one possesses that virtue of God which he loved. Therefore, envy—as Plato says in the *Phaedrus*—is absent from the divine choir. Since it is the most pleasant thing of all to possess the thing loved, everyone lives content and full in possessing that which he loves. Indeed, if two lovers become masters of their delights, each rests in the possession of his beloved; nor will he have any care if another possesses a more beautiful beloved. Therefore, by the benefit of Love, it is brought about that in different grades of happiness, everyone is content with his portion without any envy. It also happens that souls eat the same feasts forever without any satiety. For guests to be delighted, feasts and wines are not enough unless hunger and thirst entice them to eat: and the delight lasts as long as the greed <note>meaning "appetite" or "eager desire"</note> remains. <margin>B</margin> Who would deny that greed is a kind of love? Therefore, the eternal love with which the soul is always affected toward God causes it to always rejoice in God as if in a new spectacle. The same goodness of God always kindles this love in the soul, which also makes the lover blessed. Therefore, to embrace it briefly, we will praise three benefits of love: that it leads us back to heaven by restoring us to wholeness from our former division; that it places each in his own seat and makes everyone peaceful in 그 distribution; and that, with all boredom expelled, it continually kindles a new delight by its own heat in the soul and makes it blessed with a charming and sweet enjoyment.

<margin>C</margin> # THE FIFTH SPEECH.
## LOVE IS MOST BLESSED,
## because he is beautiful and good.

->CHAPTER I.<-

<margin>D</margin> Carlo Marsuppini, sweet nursling of the Muses, following the poet Landino, approaches the speech of Agathon thus. Agathon considers Love the most blessed god because he is most beautiful and best. He diligently enumerates what is required for him to be most beautiful and likewise most good; in enumerating these, he portrays Love himself. Finally, after he has described what he is like, he counts the benefits bestowed by him on the human race, and this is the sum of his disputation. It is in our interest first to inquire for what reason, in order to show him as blessed, he said he was very beautiful and good; and what is the difference between goodness and beauty. In the *Philebus*, Plato wants the blessed one to be he who lacks nothing: and that is that which is perfect in every part. <margin>E</margin> Now, there is an internal perfection and an external one. The internal we call **goodness**; the external, **beauty**. Therefore, that which is inwardly good and outwardly beautiful, we call most blessed as being perfect in every part. We certainly observe this difference in all things. Indeed, in gemstones—as the natural philosophers claim—a certain very temperate internal mixing of the four elements produces an external brilliance. Furthermore, the innate fertility in the roots and marrow of herbs and trees clothes them with a most solemn variety of flowers and leaves. In animals, a healthy composition of humors procreates a pleasant appearance of lines and colors. Even the virtue of the soul is seen to display a certain most honorable decorum in words, gestures, and deeds. The heavens also, by their sublime substance, are surrounded by a most clear light. <margin>F</margin> In all these, internal perfection produces external perfection. We can call the former goodness and the latter beauty. Therefore, we hold beauty to be a certain flower of goodness; by the allurements of this flower, as if by a kind of bait, the goodness hidden within attracts those who look upon it. Since the knowledge of our mind takes its origin from the senses, we would never understand nor desire goodness itself implanted in the inner recesses of things, unless we were led to it by the manifest signs of the external appearance. In this matter, the utility of this wonderful form and its companion appears. By these things, I think it is sufficiently shown that there is as much difference between goodness and appearance as between a seed and a blossom: and just as the flowers of trees, having risen from seeds, also produce the seeds themselves; so this flowering appearance of goodness, as it sprouts from the good, so also leads lovers back to the good: which indeed our hero here has abundantly demonstrated in the preceding parts.

<margin>G</margin> ### HOW LOVE IS PAINTED,
### and by which parts of the soul beauty
### is known, and love is generated.

->CHAPTER II.<-

<margin>H</margin> After this, Agathon enumerates more diffusely what is required for the beautiful appearance of this god. He says he is young, tender, agile, well-proportioned, and shining. We must first ask what these contribute to beauty. Then, when they are attributed to this god, in what way they ought to be understood. Men have reason and sense. Reason through itself comprehends the incorporeal "reasons" <note>or "essences"</note> of all things. Sense, through the five instruments of its body, reaches the images and qualities of bodies: colors through the eyes, voices through the ears. Odors through the nostrils, through the tongue...

He then transitions to the Fifth Speech, defining beauty as the external "flower" of internal goodness which draws the soul back toward God.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical discussion of the senses and the nature of beauty, likely from a commentary on Plato’s Symposium or a similar Neoplatonic work regarding the soul's ascent.</meta>

# ARGUMENTS AND COMMENTARY

Through the tongue we perceive flavors; through the nerves, the simple qualities of the elements—namely heat, cold, and the rest. Therefore, six powers of the soul are numbered pertaining to cognition, as far as the present question is concerned: Reason, Sight, Hearing, Smell, Taste, and Touch. Reason is attributed to the supreme divinity, Sight to fire, Hearing to air, Smell to the odor of vapors, Taste to water, and Touch to earth. For Reason investigates heavenly things and has no specific seat in any member of the body, just as the divinity has no fixed seat in any part of the world. Sight is located in the highest part of the body, like fire in the highest region of the world, and by its nature perceives light, which is characteristic of fire. Hearing draws in voices just as pure air follows fire; these voices are both produced in broken air and glide through the space of the air to the ears. Smell is assigned entirely to misty air and vapors mixed from air and water; because it is placed between the ears and the tongue (as if between air and water), it apprehends those vapors and especially delights in those that come from the mixture of air and water, such as the scents of herbs, flowers, and fruits, which are most sweet to the nostrils. Who would doubt to compare taste to watery liquids? It follows smell as if it were a thicker air, and being bathed in the constant flow of saliva, it is most vehemently delighted by drink and the flavors of moisture. Who likewise would hesitate to ascribe touch to the earth, since it occurs through all parts of the earthly body? It is fulfilled in the nerves, which are most earthly; it most easily touches those things that have solidity and weight, which the earth grants to bodies. From this it also happens that touch, taste, and smell only feel things placed closest to them, and are affected in the very act of sensing—though smell seems to apprehend more remote things than taste and touch. Hearing, however, knows more distant things and is not so easily offended. Sight looks out even further, and does in a moment what the ears do in time; for the flash of lightning is seen before the thunder is heard. Reason grasps the most remote things; for it perceives not only what is in the world and what is present, like the senses, but also what is above the heavens, and what has been or will be. From these things it can be clear to anyone that of those six powers of the soul, three pertain rather to the body and matter—namely Touch, Taste, and Smell—while the other three—namely Reason, Sight, and Hearing—pertain to the spirit. Therefore, those three declining toward the body agree more with the body than with the soul; and the things perceived by them, since they move the body in a way agreeable to it, hardly reach as far as the soul, and please it very little as things least like it. But the three higher powers, most remote from matter, suit the soul much more; they grasp those things which move the body very little, but move the soul most vehemently. Indeed, Odors, Flavors, Heat, and the like, either harm the body greatly or benefit it a little, but contribute nothing to the soul's admiration or judgment, and are only moderately desired by it. Reason perceives incorporeal truth; colors, figures, and voices move the body either not at all or very minimally. But they especially sharpen the edge of the soul for investigation and snatch its desire toward themselves. Truth is the food of the soul. To find it, the eyes contribute greatly, and the ears contribute to learning. Therefore, the soul seeks those things pertaining to reason, sight, and hearing as its own proper nourishment with the sweetest affection. But those things which move the other three senses are more necessary for the body, either for nourishing, warming, or procreating. Thus the soul seeks them not for its own sake, but for the sake of another—that is, the body. We are said to "love" those things which we desire for our own sake, but not at all those which we desire for the sake of something else. Rightly, therefore, we wish love to pertain only to sciences, figures, and voices; and for that reason, that grace alone which is found in these three—the virtue of the soul, figure, and voice—because it most provokes the soul, is called <term>kallos</term> <note>Greek: κάλλος</note>, which means "provocation," from <term>apo to kalein</term> <note>Greek: ἀπὸ τὸ καλεῖν</note>, which means "to call." <term>Kallos</term> in Greek signifies "beauty" in Latin. Truly, the true and best habit of the soul is pleasing to us; the beautiful figure of the body is pleasing; the harmony of voices is pleasing. Since the soul—being kindred to these and in a way incorporeal—values these three much more than the other three, it is consistent that it should be more deeply affected, embrace them more ardently, and admire them more vehemently. And this very grace, whether of virtue, figure, or voice, which calls and ravishes the soul to itself through reason, sight, or hearing, is most rightly called beauty. And these are those three Graces of which Orpheus speaks: <term>aglaie te, thaleia te kai euphrosyne polyolbos</term> <note>Greek: ἀγλαΐη τε, θάλεια τε καὶ εὐφροσύνη πολύολβος</note>, that is: Splendor, Youthful Bloom, and Abundant Joy. He calls "Splendor" 그hat grace and beauty of the soul which consists in the clarity of truth and virtue; "Youthful Bloom" the sweetness of figure and color, for this flourishes most in the greenness of youth; and finally "Joy," that sound and healthy and perpetual delight which we feel in music.

<insert>
->**BEAUTY IS**<-
->**something incorporeal.**<-

### CHAPTER IV.
</insert>

Since these things are so, it is necessary that beauty be something common to virtue, figure, and voices. For we would not call any of these three "beautiful" in a similar way unless one definition of beauty were present in all three. From this it follows that the very principle of beauty cannot be a body; for if beauty were corporeal, it would not at all suit the virtues of the soul, which are incorporeal. Indeed, beauty is so far from being a body that not only the beauty in the virtues of the soul, but even that which is in bodies and voices, cannot be corporeal. For although we call certain bodies "handsome," they are not handsome because of their very matter. Indeed, the body of a man is one and

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> the same today as handsome, but tomorrow, by some defiling accident, it is deformed—as if being a body were one thing, and being handsome were another. Nor are they handsome because of their very size; for some large things and likewise some small things seem handsome, and often large things are deformed and small things handsome; and conversely, small things are ugly and large things most pleasing. Sometimes it also happens that beauty is similar in certain large and small bodies. If, therefore, while the size often remains the same, the beauty is changed by some accident, and if when the size is changed the beauty remains and appears similar in both large and small, then certainly these two—beauty and size—must be entirely different. Furthermore, if the handsomeness of any body were in some way corporeal in that very thickness of its body, it would not please the beholder simply by being corporeal. The appearance of a person pleases the soul, not as it lies in <margin>B</margin> external matter, but as its image is captured or conceived by the soul through sight. That image in the sight and the soul, since these are incorporeal, cannot be a body. For in what way could the whole heaven, so to speak, be captured by the small pupil of the eye, if it received it in a corporeal manner? In no way, surely. But the spirit receives the entire amplitude of the body in a point, in a spiritual manner and as an incorporeal image; and that appearance alone pleases the soul which is received by it. This appearance, although it is a likeness of the external body, is nevertheless incorporeal. <margin>C</margin> Therefore, an incorporeal appearance pleases. What pleases is pleasing to everyone; what is pleasing is, finally, beautiful. From this it follows that love is directed toward something incorporeal, and beauty itself is spiritual—a certain likeness of a thing rather than a corporeal appearance. There are some, however, who think that beauty is a certain position of all the members, or, to use their words, a commensuration and proportion with a certain sweetness of colors. We do not admit their opinion because, since such a disposition of parts exists only in composite things, no simple things would be beautiful. But now we call pure colors, lights, a single voice, the glitter of gold and the whiteness of silver, knowledge, and the soul—all of which are simple—beautiful; and they delight us wonderfully as if they were truly beautiful. Added to this is that such proportion includes all the composite members of the body, <margin>D</margin> and is not in the individual parts, but in the whole. Thus the individual members will not be beautiful in themselves. Yet from the individual particles, the proportion of the whole composite is born. From this follows something most absurd: that things which are not beautiful by their own nature should give birth to beauty. It also frequently happens that while the same proportion and measure of members remains, a horseman does not please as before. Furthermore, the figure of your body is the same today as it was last year, but the grace is not the same. Nothing ages more slowly than figure, nothing more quickly than grace. From this it clearly stands that beauty and figure are not the same. We also often see a more correct disposition of parts and measure of members in one person than in another; yet another person, we know not for what reason, is judged more handsome by us and loved more ardently. By this we seem sufficiently warned to consider handsomeness as something other than the disposition of parts. For the same reason, we are warned not to suspect that beauty is the sweetness of colors. For often color is brighter in an older person, but grace is greater in a younger one. And among equals it sometimes happens that one who surpasses the other in color is nevertheless surpassed by him in grace and beauty. Nor should anyone dare to affirm that beauty is a certain mixture of figure and colors. For thus neither knowledge nor voices, which lack color and figure, nor colors and lights, which have no fixed figure, would be judged worthy of love. Furthermore, the desire of everyone is satisfied once they have what they wanted. Namely, hunger and thirst are stilled by food and drink; <margin>F</margin> love is filled by no sight or embrace of the body. Therefore, it does not burn for any nature of the body; it certainly pursues beauty. Thus it follows that beauty cannot be something corporeal. From all this it is gathered that those who, kindled by love, thirst for beauty—if they wish to extinguish their most burning thirst by drinking this liquid—must seek the sweetest moisture of this beauty, by which their thirst is kindled, elsewhere than in the river of matter, or the streams of quantity, or figure, or any colors. Where will you turn at last, you miserable lovers? Who will extinguish the sharpest flames of your heart? Who will settle such a great fire? This is the work, this is the labor. I shall tell you immediately. But pay attention.

### CHAP. IV.
</insert>

<margin>H</margin> The divine power, surpassing all things, immediately pours that ray of its own—in which the fertile power of creating all things exists—into the angels and souls born from it, as if into seals. In them, as being closer to itself, it paints the disposition and order of the whole world much more exactly than in the matter of the world. Therefore, this picture of the world which we perceive shines more expressively in the angels and souls. For in them is the figure of every sphere: of the sun, the moon, and the rest of the stars, and also of the elements, stones, trees, and individual animals. Such pictures are called "exemplars" and "ideas" in the angels; "reasons" and "notions" in souls; and "forms" and "images" in the matter of the world by the Platonists. They are clear in the world; clearer in the soul; and clearest in the mind of the angel. Therefore, the one countenance of God shines in three mirrors placed in order: the Angel, the Soul, and the Body of the world. In the first, as being nearer, most clearly; in the second, more remotely, more obscurely; in the third, most remotely, if you compare it to the others, most obscurely. Hence the holy...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino's Neoplatonic exploration of beauty and love, specifically focusing on how the soul perceives divine beauty through the physical world and the incorporeal nature of that beauty.</meta>

# MARSILIO FICINO

<margin>A</margin>The mind of an angel, hindered by no service to a body, reflects back upon itself, where it gazes into that face of God engraved in its own heart. Having gazed upon it, the angel is immediately struck with wonder and clings to it forever with the greatest greed <note>original: "aviditate"; here meaning an intense, holy longing or spiritual hunger</note>. We call the grace and beauty of that divine face "Beauty"; the greed of the angel, clinging deeply to the face of God, we call "Love." Oh, if only the same thing could happen to us! But indeed, our soul, born under the condition of being surrounded by an earthly body, declines toward the duty of procreation. Weighted down by this inclination, it neglects the treasure hidden in its innermost chambers. Then, wrapped in the earthly body, it serves the body's use for a very long time; to this work it always applies its senses, and also its reason longer than is proper. From this it happens that the soul does not notice the brightness of that divine face shining perpetually within itself until the body is mature and reason is awakened; then, through thought, it considers the face of God shining in the "machine of the world" <note>original: "dei machina"; a common Renaissance term for the structured universe</note> and manifest to the eyes. By this consideration, it is carried forward to behold that which flashes within. Truly, since the face of a parent is pleasing to children, it is necessary that the face of God the Father be most pleasing to souls. His face—to repeat the same thing often—its brilliance and grace, whether in an angel, or in a soul, or in the matter of the world, must be called "Universal Beauty"; and the impulse toward it must be called "Universal Love." We do not doubt that this beauty is everywhere incorporeal. For in the angel and in the soul, no one doubts that it is not a body. We have also shown above that in bodies it is incorporeal, and for the present we understand this chiefly from the fact that the eye perceives nothing other than the light of the sun. <margin>C</margin>For the shapes and colors of bodies are never perceived unless illuminated by light, nor do they come to the eyes along with their own matter. Yet it seems necessary that they be in the eyes in order to be seen by the eyes. Therefore, the single light of the sun, painted with the colors and shapes of all the bodies illuminated by it, offers itself to the eyes. The eyes perceive the light affected in this way with the help of a certain ray; having perceived it, they see the light itself and all things that are in it. Therefore, this whole visible order of the world is discerned not in the way it exists in the matter of bodies, but in the way it is infused into the eyes in light. Since in that light it is separated from matter, it is necessarily devoid of body. This also appears evidently from the fact that light itself cannot be a body, since in a moment it fills almost the whole globe from east to west; <margin>D</margin> it penetrates the body of air and water everywhere without any clash; and though mixed with filth, it is never stained. These things, truly, do not fit the nature of bodies at all. For a body is moved not in a moment, but in time; nor does one penetrate another without a clash to itself, or the other, or both; and two bodies mixed together stain each other by mutual contagion. This we see in the mixing of water and wine, or fire and earth. Since, therefore, the light of the sun is incorporeal, whatever it receives, it receives according to its own nature. For that reason, it receives the colors and shapes of bodies in a spiritual way; and in the same manner, it is gazed upon when received by the eyes. Thus it happens that all this beauty of the world, which is the third face of God, offers itself to the eyes as something incorporeal through the incorporeal light of the sun.

# HOW LOVE AND HATRED ARE BORN, AND THAT BEAUTY IS INCORPOREAL.
## CHAPTER V.

<margin>E</margin>From all these things it follows that every grace of the divine face—which is called universal beauty—is incorporeal not only in the angel and the soul, but also in the sight of the eyes. Nor do we love this face only as a whole, but we also love its parts, moved by admiration. Here, "particular love" is born toward "particular beauty." Thus we are also moved toward some human being, a member of the world's order, especially when a spark of divine beauty clearly shines forth in them. An affection of this kind is born from two causes: both because the image of the Father's face pleases us, and also because the appearance and shape of a well-proportioned human fits most aptly with that "reason of the human race" <note>The "Idea" or blueprint of humanity</note> which our soul receives and retains from the Author of all. Hence the image of the external man, received through the senses and passing into the soul, if it disagrees with the shape of man which the soul possesses, it immediately displeases <margin>G</margin> and is held in hatred as something deformed. If it agrees, it immediately pleases and is loved as something beautiful. Thus it happens that some people we meet please or displease us instantly, and we do not know the cause of such an affection. Indeed, the soul, hindered by its service to the body, does not look back at those innate forms of its own. But by a certain natural and hidden incongruity or congruity, it happens that the external form of a thing, striking with its image the form of that same thing painted in the soul, either disagrees or agrees; and the soul, moved by this hidden offense or charm, either hates or loves the thing itself. Truly, that divine power implanted the complete configuration for creating a human in the angel and the soul; but in the matter of the world, as it is most remote from that Craftsman, the constitution of a human degenerates from that complete figure of itself. Yet in matter that is better disposed, it comes out more similar; in other matter, more dissimilar. That which comes out more similar fits and agrees with the reason of the soul, just as it does with the angelic Idea by the power of God. The soul approves of this congruity. In that very congruity consists Beauty; in that approval consists the affection of Love. Since, truly, the Idea and the Reason are foreign to the matter of the body, the constitution of a human is judged similar to them not from matter or quantity, but rather from something incorporeal. As it is similar, it agrees with them; as it agrees, it is beautiful. Therefore, body and beauty are different things. But if anyone should ask in what way the form of a body can be similar to the form and 

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>reason of the soul and mind: let him, I pray, consider the building of an architect. In the beginning, the architect conceives the reason and, as it were, the "Idea" of the building in his mind. Then, he builds such a house as he has thought out, to the best of his ability. Who would deny that the house is a body, and that it is very similar to the incorporeal Idea of the craftsman, according to whose likeness it was made? Furthermore, it should be judged similar to the architect because of a certain incorporeal order rather than because of its matter. Come then, subtract the matter if you can—and you can subtract it in thought—but leave the order: nothing of the body will remain for you, nothing of the matter. Indeed, the order that comes from the craftsman and the order that remains in the craftsman will be exactly the same. You may do the same in any human body. You will find that its form, which fits the reason of the soul, <margin>B</margin> is simple and devoid of matter.

# HOW MANY THINGS ARE REQUIRED FOR A THING TO BE BEAUTIFUL, AND THAT BEAUTY IS A SPIRITUAL GIFT.
## CHAPTER VI.

<margin>C</margin>What, then, is the beauty of the body? It is an act, a liveliness, and a certain grace shining in the body itself by the influence of its own Idea. A brilliance of this kind does not descend into matter until it has been most aptly prepared. Truly, the preparation of a living body consists of these three: Order, Mode, and Species <note>Or "Appearance/Form"</note>. Order signifies the intervals of the parts; Mode signifies the quantity; Species signifies the outlines and color. First, it is necessary that each member of the body have its natural position: the ears in their place, the eyes, the nostrils, and the rest; and that the eyes be nearest the nose at equal intervals; likewise that both ears be at equal distances from the eyes. Nor is this equality of intervals pertaining to Order sufficient, unless the Mode of the parts is added, <margin>D</margin> which, preserving a moderate proportion of the whole body, gives the proper size to individual members: so that three noses placed in a line would fill the length of one face; the semicircles of both ears joined together would make the circle of an open mouth. Let the joining of the eyebrows do the same. Let the length of the nose equal the length of the lip, and the ear similarly. Let the twin circles of the eyes equal one opening of the mouth. Let eight heads comprise the height of the body. Let the extension of the arms to the side show the same, and the legs and feet similarly. Furthermore, we say Species is necessary, so that the skillful drawing of lines, the wrinkles, and the splendor of the eyes may decorate that Order and Mode of the parts. And yet, although these three are in matter, they cannot be any part of the body. <margin>E</margin> The Order of the members is certainly none of the members. For Order is in all the members, but no single member is found in all the members. Add to this that Order is nothing other than the decent interval of the parts. But what else shall we call an interval than the distance between parts? Finally, distance is either nothing and a total void, or it is like a drawing of lines. But who would call lines "bodies," since they lack the width and depth that are necessary for a body? Likewise, Mode is not quantity, but the limit of quantity. Truly, limits are surfaces, lines, and points; since these lack the thickness of depth, they are not considered bodies. We also place Species in the pleasing harmony of lights, shadows, and lines, not in matter. From all these things it is clear <margin>F</margin> that beauty is so foreign to the bulk of the body that it never communicates itself to matter unless it is affected by those three incorporeal preparations we have described. The foundation of these, truly, is the tempered complexion of the four elements: so that our body may be most similar to heaven, whose substance is balanced, and may not deviate from the soul's formation by any excess of humors. For thus the celestial brilliance will easily shine in a body very similar to heaven; and that perfect form of man, which the soul has, will reflect more clearly in the prepared and obedient matter. Furthermore, to receive their own beauty, voices are disposed in almost the same way. For their Order is the ascent from a deep voice to the octave, and the descent from there; the Mode is the proper progression through thirds, fourths, fifths, and sixths, likewise tones and <margin>G</margin> semitones; the Species is the sonorous intensity of a clear voice. By these three, as if by certain elements, bodies composed of many members, and trees, and animals, and the gathering of many voices are disposed to receive beauty. Truly, simpler bodies, like the four elements, stones and metals, and likewise single voices, are sufficiently fitted for the same by a certain interior tempering of their nature, fecundity, and clarity. But the soul is accommodated to beauty by its nature most of all because it is both a spirit and, as it were, a mirror nearest to God. In which, as we said in the previous sections, the image of the divine face shines. Therefore, just as nothing at all needs to be added to gold for it to appear beautiful, but the filth of the earth must be separated if any has clung to it; so the soul needs no additions to appear beautiful: but the care of the body and such anxious solicitude must be laid aside; the disturbance of desire and fear must be driven away, and immediately the natural species of the soul will flash forth. But lest the speech wander too far, let us conclude briefly from the above: beauty is a certain lively and spiritual grace, infused first into the angel by the illuminating ray of God; from there into the souls of men, the shapes of bodies, and voices; which, through reason, sight, and hearing, moves and delights our souls, and by delighting them, seizes them, and by seizing them, inflames them with burning love.

<summary>Ficino argues that beauty is an incorporeal, spiritual grace originating from God that manifests in angels, souls, and physical forms through order and proportion. He explains that love is the soul's natural attraction to this divine reflection, which it recognizes through innate "Ideas" even when hindered by the physical body.</summary>

### ON THE PAINTING OF LOVE.

### CHAPTER VII.

<margin>A</margin> The poet Agathon, following the custom of the ancient poets, clothes that god in a human image and paints him in the likeness of men: beautiful, young, tender, flexible or agile, well-proportioned, and radiant. To what end? These are preparations for a beautiful nature rather than beauty itself. For of these five parts, the first three signify a balanced bodily temperament, which is the primary foundation; the remaining two indicate order, measure, and appearance. Physicians have shown that the sign of a balanced temperament is a smooth and firm equality of tender flesh. Where heat exceeds too much, the body is dry and hairy; where cold, it is rigid; where dryness, it is hard and rough; where moisture, it is fluid, drooping, uneven, and distorted. Therefore, an equal and firm tenderness of the body indicates its affection is moderated within the four humors <note>The four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—thought to determine health and temperament.</note>. For this reason, Agathon called him soft, delicate, and tender. Why young? Because this balance is held not only by nature's gift, but also by age. For with the passage of time, as the finer parts of the humors are dissolved, the much thicker parts remain; as fire and air exhale, an excess of water and earth reigns. But why agile and flexible? So that you may understand him to be fit and ready for all movements; lest perhaps you think when he said "soft," he meant the softness of water—feminine, languid, and inept. For such is contrary to a balanced temperament. After this he added, "Well-proportioned," that is, most honorably shaped by the order and measure of his parts. He added "radiant," that is, shining with a sweet appearance of colors. Having set forth these preparations, Agathon leaves the rest aside. For it is our task hereafter to understand the arrival of grace. These five parts in the human figure are as we have said; however, in the power of Love, they are to be understood differently: for they show his force and quality. He is called young because young people are mostly ensnared by love, and having been caught in its snares, they seek out youthful age. Soft, because mild dispositions are more easily captured; and those who are captured, though fierce before, are rendered gentle. Agile and flexible: because he flows in secretly and flows out likewise. Elegant and well-proportioned: since he desires beautiful and orderly things and flees their opposites. Radiant, since he breathes into the genius of man in the flowering and shining age and longs for flowering things. Since Agathon pursues these points most copiously, let it suffice to have touched upon them briefly.

---

### ON THE VIRTUE OF LOVE.

### CHAPTER VIII.

<margin>E</margin> Those things which are said by Agathon concerning the four virtues to signify the goodness of Love are to be understood thus: he is affirmed as just because where love is whole and true, there is a reciprocity of goodwill which admits no insult or injury. So great is the force of this charity <note>original: "charitatis" - here meaning brotherly or divine love</note> that it alone can keep the human race in tranquil peace, which neither prudence, nor fortitude, nor the force of arms, laws, and eloquence can achieve without goodwill. Furthermore, he calls him temperate because he subdues shameful desires. <margin>F</margin> For since Love seeks beauty, which consists in a certain order and temperance, he scorns vile and immoderate lusts; he always shrinks from shameful acts—as you heard enough from the hero <note>Likely referring to Phaedrus or the previous speaker</note> at the beginning—and where this affection reigns, all other desires are despised. He added "most brave." For what is stronger than audacity? Who fights more boldly for love than a lover? Among the other gods—that is, the other planets—Mars excels in fortitude because he makes men stronger. Venus subdues him. For when Mars, positioned in the angles of heaven, or the second house of birth, or the eighth, portends evils for the newborn, Venus often, by her conjunction, or opposition, or reception, or sextile or trine aspect, restrains the malignancy of Mars, so to speak. Again, when Mars rules in a man's rising, he bestows greatness of soul and wrathfulness. If Venus approaches closely, she does not hinder that virtue of great soul given by Mars, but she represses the vice of wrath. There she is seen to make Mars more merciful and to subdue him. But Mars never subdues Venus. For if she is the leader, she provides the affection of love. If Mars leads closely, by his heat he renders the impulse of Venus more burning; so that if someone is born when Mars is in the house of Venus—Libra or Taurus—because of the presence of Mars, the one born then experiences the sharpest loves. Again, Mars follows Venus; Venus does not follow Mars, because the audacity of love is a follower, not love a follower of audacity. For men are not ensnared by love because they are bold; but rather, because they are wounded by love, they become most bold to undergo any dangers intrepidly for the sake of the beloved. Finally, the most evident proof of his excellence in fortitude is that all things obey love, but he obeys none. Indeed, the celestial beings love, as do animals and all bodies. Likewise the brave and the wise. Rich men and the greatest kings bow their necks to the empire of love. But Love is subject to none of these. For neither do divine gifts buy love, nor can the threats and violence of the powerful force us to love or to cease loving. For Love is free, and arises of its own accord in the free will, which even God does not compel, having decreed from the beginning that it should be free. Thus it happens that Love, which brings force to all, escapes the violence of all. So great is his liberty that while other affections of the soul or arts and works hope for some reward

<column-break/>

<margin>B</margin> different from themselves, Love is content with himself as his own reward, as if there were no other reward besides love that is worthy of love. For he who loves, loves love chiefly. For he wants this most from the beloved: that the beloved love the lover in return. He is also most wise. By what reasoning Love becomes the creator and preserver of all things, and the master and lord of individual arts, I believe was sufficiently discussed in the speech of Eryximachus. In those things, the wisdom of Love is shown. From all these it is concluded that Love is therefore most blessed, because he is most beautiful and best. That he is most beautiful is established by the fact that he delights in beautiful things as being like himself. He is best because he makes lovers best. It is necessary that he be best who makes others best.

---

### ON THE GIFTS OF LOVE.

### CHAPTER IX.

<margin>C</margin> What love is has appeared from our discourse. What kind he is, from the words of Agathon above. What gifts he bestows is easily said from what has been spoken. For one love is simple; the other is mutual. Simple love makes whoever it seizes prudent in foresight, sharp in debating, eloquent in speaking, magnanimous in conducting affairs, witty in jokes, ready for games, and most brave in all serious matters. Mutual love, having driven away dangers, provides security; having removed dissension, it provides concord; having avoided misery, it provides happiness. For where there is mutual charity, there are no snares; there all things are common; there lawsuits and thefts, homicides and battles cease. Agathon touches upon the fact that tranquility of this kind is granted by mutual love not only to animals, but even to the heavens and the elements, and it was shown more diffusely above in the speech of Eryximachus. <margin>D</margin> In his speech, it is clearly said that Love soothes the minds of gods and men with his song. Anyone will clearly understand this who remembers it was demonstrated in the previous sections that love is in all things and extends to all things.

---

### LOVE IS BOTH OLDER
### and younger than the other gods.

### CHAPTER X.

But before I make an end, excellent men, I shall resolve three questions according to the strength of my wit which arise in Agathon's discussion. First, it is asked why Phaedrus said Love was older than Saturn and Jupiter, while Agathon said he was younger. Second, what the kingdom of Necessity signifies in Plato, and what the empire of Love signifies. Third, which gods discovered which arts while Love was reigning. God, the father of all, begot those minds that are his ministers—which move Saturn, Jupiter, and the other planets—by a certain love of propagating his offspring and by the kindness of providence. Those minds, in turn, having been born, immediately recognize and love their parent. We say that Love by which the celestial beings are created is older than them; but that by which they are affected toward their creator, we call younger. Furthermore, the angelic mind did not receive the Ideas <note>The eternal, perfect forms of things in Platonic philosophy.</note> of the planet Saturn and the others from its father until it was turned toward his face by an innate love. Again, after it received them, it loved the gift of the parent more ardently. Thus, the love of that angel for God is partly older than the Ideas (which are called gods) and partly younger. Therefore, Love is the beginning and the end, the first and the last of the gods.

---

### LOVE REIGNS BEFORE
### Necessity.

### CHAPTER XI.

<margin>G</margin> To solve the second question: he is said to reign here before Necessity because divine love gave origin to all things born from itself, in which no violence of necessity is placed. For since he has nothing above him, he works not by compulsion, but freely. However, the Mind that follows him sprouts necessarily as he brings it forth. He, therefore, produces by love; she is produced by necessity. There the domination of love begins, here the domination of necessity. Although this necessity is born from the highest goodness of God and is therefore good, nevertheless, that which has proceeded outside of God necessarily degenerates from the infinite perfection of the parent. For the effect never receives the total goodness of the cause. In this necessary procession of the effect, and also in its degeneration, the empire of Necessity is established. But indeed, the Mind, having been born immediately, loves its author, as we said: where the kingdom of Love rises again. For she is raised toward God by love, and God illuminates the thing turned toward him by love. <margin>H</margin> But here again, the power of Necessity creeps in. For since that light descending from God is not received with as much clarity by the Mind (which is obscure by its own nature) as is granted by God. For it is compelled to receive according to the capacity of its own nature. Therefore, by the violence of the receiving nature, the light becomes more obscure. To this necessity, the principality of Love succeeds again. For she, having been kindled by this first flash of God, is reflected more ardently toward him, and being urged by this spark of light, as it were, she seeks the total fullness of light. Hence God, by the providence of his kindness, beyond that first...

<summary>This page interprets Agathon's speech on Love, describing Love's physical and moral attributes, its superiority over the planet Mars through Venus, and its role as a free, self-rewarding force that precedes and succeeds "Necessity" in the cosmic order.</summary>

--- Page 816 ---
<meta>This page continues the commentary on Plato’s Symposium, specifically discussing the transition from the speech of Agathon to the speech of Socrates and Diotima. It explores the metaphysical relationship between Love and Necessity.</meta>

# MARSILIO FICINO

<margin>A</margin>The natural light also bestows a divine light: and thus the power of love and necessity succeed each other in turn. This succession, in divine matters, arises from the origin of nature; in others, it occurs through intervals of time: yet in such a way that love is the first atom and the last. Concerning the soul and other things made by God, one must judge similarly regarding these two empires. Therefore, if one speaks absolutely, the empire of love is more ancient than that of necessity: since the power of the former begins in God, and the latter in created things. If we understand things created by God, the tyranny of necessity precedes the kingdom of love: since things themselves first proceed by necessity and degenerate in the process, before they turn themselves back to their father through love. Orpheus sang of these two empires in two hymns. The empire of Necessity in the hymn to Night: *dread Necessity rules all things* <note>original Greek: δεινὴ δὲ ἀνάγκη πάντα κρατύνει</note>, <margin>B</margin>that is, Heavy necessity dominates everyone. But the kingdom of Love, in the hymn to Venus: *and the mighty three-faced one of the Fates, sweet are all things, as many as are in heaven and on the fertile earth* <note>original Greek: καὶ κραταιὰ τριπρόσωπος μοιρῶν, γλυκειὰ δὲ τὰ πάντα, ὅσα τ’ ἐπ’ οὐρανῷ δὲ καὶ ἐν γαίᾳ πολυκάρπῳ</note>, You command the three fates, and you generate all things which are in heaven, and which are on the earth, and which are in the sea. Orpheus established two divine kingdoms and compared them to each other, and he placed love before necessity when he said that love commands the three fates, in which necessity consists.

---

## HOW, WHILE NECESSITY WAS REIGNING, Saturn castrated Uranus: and Jupiter bound Saturn.

### CHAPTER XII.

In what way, while Necessity was dominant, the following gods are said here by Agathon to have either castrated or bound their parents, we easily understand from what has been said. For these things are not to be taken as if the angelic mind divides and tears apart God himself, but rather the gift bestowed upon it by God within itself. We showed a little earlier that the gifts of God in a receiving spirit necessarily fall away from the highest perfection of God. Thus it happens that the fertility of nature, which is whole in God, but diminished and in a way mutilated in an angel, is deservedly said to have been castrated. This is said to happen while Necessity reigns, because it happens necessarily—not by the will of the giver or the receiver, but by that necessity in which the effect cannot be equaled to its cause. For thus Saturn, that is the angel, seems to castrate Uranus <note>Latin: Coelium, the Heavens</note>, that is the supreme God; and Jupiter, that is the Soul of the World, binds Saturn, that is, he restricts the power received from the angel within narrower limits in himself due to the defect of his own nature. For the power of the former is greater than the latter. Therefore the power, which in the former is unimpeded and loose because of its amplitude, is in the latter judged to be bound and restricted because of its narrowness. This is entirely what astrologers believe: that the malignancy of the planet Saturn is very often coerced by the conjunction, reception, opposition, sextile, or trine aspect of Jupiter. But enough of these things: let us descend to the third question.

---

## WHICH GODS BESTOW WHICH ARTS upon men.

### CHAPTER XIII.

Agathon thinks that the arts were handed down to the human race by the gods because of love. The art of ruling from Jupiter; archery, divination, and the healing art from Apollo; copper-smithing from Vulcan; the craft of weaving from Minerva; and finally music from the Muses. Twelve deities preside over the twelve signs of the zodiac. Pallas <note>Athena</note> over Aries; Venus over Taurus; Apollo over Gemini; Mercury over Cancer; Jupiter over Leo; Ceres over Virgo; Vulcan over Libra; Mars over Scorpio; Diana over Sagittarius; Vesta over Capricorn; Juno over Aquarius; and Neptune over Pisces. From these, all arts are handed down to our race. Those signs pour their strengths into the body, and the Deities who preside over them pour theirs into the soul for each specific art. Thus Jupiter, through Leo, makes a man most fit for the governance of gods and men, that is, for conducting both divine and human affairs excellently. Apollo, through Gemini, provides prophecy, medicine, and the skill of the bow. Pallas, through Aries, the skill of weaving. Vulcan, through Libra, copper-smithing; and others provide the remaining arts. Because they magnificently bestow their gifts upon us by the kindness of providence, we say they bestow them at the instigation of love. Furthermore, we believe that from that most swift and orderly revolution of the heavens, musical consonance is born, and from the motions of the eight circles, eight tones; and from all of them together, a certain harmony is produced. Thus, from the nine sounds of the heavens, we have named the nine muses after musical concord. Our soul was once gifted with the logic of this music. For to that which has a celestial origin, a celestial innate harmony is deservedly attributed. This it then imitates with various instruments and songs. And that gift was similarly granted to us by divine providence out of love. Therefore, most distinguished men, let us love this god because he is most beautiful; let us imitate him because he is best; let us worship him because he is most blessed: so that by his mercy and bounty he may grant us the possession of his beauty, goodness, and blessedness.

<column-break/>

# THE SIXTH SPEECH.

## INTRODUCTION TO THE DIS-cussion on love.

### CHAPTER I.

<margin>B</margin>Thus far spoke Carlo Marsuppini. But Tommaso Benci, a diligent imitator of Socrates, applied himself to the commentary on the Socratic words with a willing mind and a cheerful face. Our Socrates, he said, judged the wisest of all Greeks by the oracle of Apollo, used to profess the art of loving above all others, as if by the skill of this art especially both Socrates and anyone else should be judged most wise. He said he received this kind of art not from Anaxagoras, Damon, or Archelaus the physicists; not from Prodicus of Ceos or Aspasia the professors of rhetoric; nor from Connus the musician, from whom he had learned many things; but from Diotima, a prophetic woman inspired by a divine spirit. In my opinion, this was to show that only by the inspiration of divinity can men understand what true beauty is, what <margin>C</margin>legitimate love is, and by what reasoning one must love. So great is the power of the amatory faculty, so great its sublimity. Therefore, stay far away from these celestial feasts, stay far away, I say, you profane ones: who, overwhelmed by earthly filth and utterly enslaved to Bacchus and Priapus <note>Gods of wine and lust</note>, prostrate love—a celestial gift—onto the earth in the manner of pigs and dogs. But you, most chaste guests, and all others consecrated to Diana and Pallas: you who exult in the liberty of a most pure soul and the perpetual joy of the mind, be present happily: and listen diligently to the divine mysteries revealed to Socrates by Diotima. But before you hear Diotima, a certain controversy must be resolved <margin>D</margin>that has arisen between those who treated love in the previous sections and those who are about to treat it. For the previous speakers called love beautiful, good, blessed, and a god; Socrates and Diotima deny this, and place him in the middle between beautiful and ugly, good and evil, blessed and miserable, god and man. We consider both opinions to be true, though for different reasons.

---

<margin>E</margin>## LOVE IS THE MIDDLE BE-tween beauty and ugliness, and between God and man.

### CHAPTER II.

<margin>F</margin>The lodestone <note>magnet</note> instills a certain quality of its own into iron, by which the iron, having become very similar to the magnet, is inclined toward this stone. This kind of inclination, insofar as it originates from the stone and tends toward the stone, is certainly called a "stony" inclination; insofar as it is in the iron, it is equally "iron-like" and "stony." For it is not that pure essence in the matter of the iron, but it is already formed through the quality of the stone. Therefore it retains the property of both. Even fire, to speak more clearly, ignites wood by its own quality, that is, heat. The wood, suspended by the quality of heat, flies up to the upper region of fire. This flight, insofar as it is excited by the fire and tends toward the fire, we clearly call "fiery"; insofar as it is in the wood—not pure wood, but already ignited—we call it equally "wooden" and "fiery" from the nature of both the wood and the fire. Often the figure of a man, on account of an interior goodness happily granted by God, pours a ray of its splendor through the eyes of those looking on into the soul. By this spark, as if drawn by a hook, the soul hastens toward the one drawing it. This "draw," which is love—since it depends on the beautiful, good, and happy and is reflected back into the same—we do not hesitate to name beautiful, good, blessed, and a god, according to the opinion of Agathon and the others above. But since it is in the soul, which is already ignited by the presence of that beautiful ray, <margin>G</margin>we are forced to name the affection a "middle" between the beautiful and the non-beautiful. Since the soul, which has not yet received any image of a beautiful thing, does not yet love that thing as if it were unknown; and the one who possesses total beauty is not vexed by the stings of love. For who desires what they already have? It remains, then, that one burns with glowing love when, having obtained some beautiful likeness of a beautiful thing, one is incited by that foretaste to the full possession of beauty. Since, therefore, the soul of the lover partly has the beautiful thing itself and partly does not have it, it is not unjustly partly beautiful and partly not beautiful. And thus we wish love to be, from this kind of mixture, a certain middle affection between the beautiful and the non-beautiful, participating in both. For this reason Diotima—to come to her now—called love a "daemon," because just as daemons are <margin>H</margin>middles between celestial and earthly things, so love holds the middle between formlessness and form. Giovanni <note>Giovanni Cavalcanti</note> sufficiently explained this middle region of his between formless and shapely nature in his first and second speeches.

---

## CONCERNING THE SOULS OF THE SPHERES and daemons.

### CHAPTER III.

But how the daemons inhabit the middle region between heaven and earth, from the words of Diotima in the *Symposium*, of Socrates in the *Phaedrus*, and—
