# ARGUMENTS AND COMMENTARY

<margin>A</margin> And so in the *Philebus*, and in the *Laws* and *Epinomis* of the Athenian guest, understand it thus: Plato believes that the entire machine of this world is ruled and moved by a certain soul. Indeed, the body of the world is a kind of total body, composed of all four elements, of which the bodies of all living creatures are small parts. For the little body of every animal is a particle of the world-body. Nor is it composed of the whole element of fire, air, water, or earth, but of certain parts of these elements. Therefore, just as the whole is more perfect than the part, so the body of the world is more perfect than the body of individual living beings. It would be absurd for an imperfect body to have a soul, while a perfect one had neither soul nor life. For who is so out of his mind as to say the part lives, but deny it to the whole? Therefore, the whole body of the world lives, since all the bodies which are its parts live.

<margin>B</margin> There must be one soul for the whole, just as there is one matter and one construction. Since, therefore, there are twelve spheres of the world (as Plato pleases): eight of heaven, and four elements below heaven; and since these twelve spheres are distinct from one another, diverse in appearance, character, and property, it is necessary that twelve souls be present in them, diverse in kind and power. There will be one soul for the one primary matter. For the twelve circles, twelve souls. Who would deny that earth or water live, which bestow life upon the animals born from them? But if these dregs of the world live and are full of living things, why should not air and fire, the more excellent parts of the world, live and similarly contain living things within themselves, and the heavens likewise? But those celestial animals, which are the stars, and the earthly and aquatic ones, we indeed see; but the fiery and aerial ones we do not see. This is because we do not perceive the pure element of fire or air. However, there is this difference: on earth there are two kinds of living beings, the irrational and the rational; and similarly in the water, since water is more excellent than the body of the earth, it ought to be no less possessed of reason than the earth. Indeed, the ten superior globes, on account of their sublimity, are adorned with rational beings alone. The Platonists call the Soul of the World (that is, of primary matter) and the souls of the twelve spheres and the stars "gods," as they are the attendants of the angelic mind and the supreme God. The animals that inhabit the region of ethereal fire located below the moon, or of pure air, or of misty air near the water, they call <term>daemons</term> <note>In the Platonic sense, these are mediating spirits, not "demons" in the modern evil sense</note>. Those who inhabit the earth are rational beings, men. The gods are also immortal and impassible <note>incapable of suffering or being affected by external force</note>; men are passible and mortal. Daemons are indeed immortal, but passible. They do not attribute passions of the body to daemons, but certain affections of the soul, by which they help good men in some way and hate the evil; they involve themselves more closely and ardently in governing inferior things, especially human affairs, and all these are seen as good because of this duty. However, some Platonists and Christian theologians have maintained that there are certain other evil daemons. But we have no dispute concerning evil daemons at present. Our good guardians, the governors of the inferior world, Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A Christian Neoplatonist writer</note> is accustomed to call by their proper name, "angels," which differs very little from the mind of Plato. Furthermore, those whom Plato calls gods and the minds of the spheres and stars, we can call angels, the ministers of God, in the manner of Dionysius. This does not dissent from Plato for this reason: because he by no means binds such minds to the enclosures of the spheres in the same way as souls are bound to the bodies of earthly beings (as appears in the tenth book of the *Laws*). Rather, he affirms they are gifted with such power by the supreme God that they are able to enjoy the vision of God and, without any labor or anxiety, rule and move the globes of the world according to the will of their part, and by moving these, easily govern inferior things. Therefore, between Plato and Dionysius, the discrepancy is one of words rather than of sentiment.

---

### ON THE SEVEN GIFTS, WHICH
### are granted by God to men through
### mediating spirits.

#### CHAPTER IV.

<margin>F</margin> From the Ideas of all things, which the divine mind contains, the following gods are said to serve, and the daemons serve the gifts of the gods. For from the highest to the lowest, all things pass through intermediaries; so that those Ideas, the conceptions of the divine mind, bestow their gifts upon men through the gods and daemons.

<margin>G</margin> Of these, there are seven principal ones: Sharpness of contemplation, Power of governing, Spiritedness <note>original: *animositas*, referring to courage or vigor</note>, Clarity of the senses, Ardor of love, Subtlety of interpretation, and Fecundity of procreation. God first contains the force of these in Himself. Then He attributes the power of these to the seven gods who move the seven planets (called "angelic" by us), so that each one receives one gift above the others. Those seven exhibit these gifts to the orders of daemons serving them. These, in turn, hand them down to men. Truly, God pours these into souls immediately upon their birth from Him; as these souls glide from the Milky Way through Cancer into the body, they are wrapped in a certain celestial and luminous body; surrounded by this, they are enclosed in earthly bodies.

<margin>H</margin> For the order of nature requires that the purest soul cannot fall into this most impure body until it has received a certain middle and pure covering. Since this is thicker than the soul but purer and more subtle than the body, it is judged by the Platonists to be the most convenient bond of the soul with the earthly body. From this it happens that the souls of the planets strengthen and bolster the powers of those seven gifts in our souls, and their bodies in our bodies, from the very beginning and continually. The same office is overseen by as many natures of daemons, intermediaries between the celestials and men. Saturn strengthens the gift of contemplation through Saturnian daemons. Jupiter, the power of governing and commanding by the ministry of Jovial daemons. Mars, greatness of soul through Martial daemons. The Sun, clarity of sense and opinion, from which prophecy follows,

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> with the help of solar daemons. Venus inspires love through Venereal ones. Mercury aids the skill of pronouncing and interpreting with Mercurial ones interceding. Finally, the Moon, with the contribution of lunar daemons, fosters the office of generation. Although they impart the faculty of these to all men, they do so especially to those in whose conception and birth they have the most power according to the disposition of the heavens. Although these things, infused divinely, are honorable, they can sometimes appear deformed in us because of abuse, which is evident in the use of governance, spiritedness, love, and generation. Not to wander too far, we have the instinct of love from the supreme God, and from Venus, who is called a goddess, and from Venereal daemons.

<margin>B</margin> Since it descends from God, it is a god; since it is confirmed by daemons, it is to be called a daemon. For this reason, it was rightly called a god by Agathon and a daemon by Diotima <note>Characters in Plato's *Symposium*</note>. A Venereal daemon, I say.

---

### ON THE ORDER OF VENEREAL
### daemons, and how they
### shoot the arrows of love.

#### CHAPTER V.

<margin>C</margin> The Venereal daemon, however, is a threefold love. The first is placed by the Platonists in the Celestial Venus: namely, in the intelligence of the angelic mind. The second in the Common Venus: namely, in that power of generating which the soul of the world possesses. These two are called daemons because they are intermediaries between formlessness and form, as we touched on above and will explain more broadly shortly. The third is the order of daemons accompanying the planet Venus. Of these Venereal daemons, we also place a threefold order. Some are assigned to the element of purest air, others to the thicker and misty air, and all are named "heroes" (that is, amorous ones) from the Greek word <term>eros</term> <note>original: *ἔρως*</note>, which signifies love.

<margin>D</margin> The first shoot the stings of love into those men in whom bile, the choleric and fiery humor, dominates. The second into those in whom blood, the aerial humor, dominates. The third into those in whom phlegm and black bile—the watery and earthy humors—rule. While all men are wounded by the arrows of Cupid, four types are especially so. For Plato in the *Phaedrus* indicated that the souls following Jupiter, Phoebus, Mars, and Juno (that is, Venus) are most likely to be wounded; and that from the very beginnings of their generation they are prone to love, and they usually love most intensely those men who were born under the same stars. Hence Jovial people are vehemently affected by Jovial ones, Martial by Martial, and others similarly by their own kind.

---

### HOW THEY ARE CAPTURED
### by love.

#### CHAPTER VI.

<margin>E</margin> What I say of one example, understand of the three others. Whatever soul falls into an earthly body under the empire of Jupiter conceives for itself in that very descent a certain figure for fabricating a man, agreeable to the star of Jupiter. Hence, in its ethereal body, as if in a perfectly disposed medium, it expresses a most exact likeness. If it finds a seed on earth similarly tempered, it paints in that also a third figure most like the first and second. If not, it is not so similar. It often happens that two souls, though at different intervals of time, descend while Jupiter is reigning; and one of them, finding suitable seed on earth, figures the body most correctly according to the prior Ideas; while the other, on account of the unsuitability of the matter, begins the same work but does not execute it with such similarity to the exemplar. That body is more shapely than this one. Both please each other mutually because of a certain similarity of nature. But the one who is judged more shapely among them pleases more. Thus it happens that people do not love just anyone who is most beautiful, but their own—that is, those born similarly—even if they are less beautiful than many others. Therefore, those who, as we said, were born under the same star, are so disposed that the image of the more beautiful one, flowing through the eyes into the soul of the other, fits and harmonizes everywhere with a similar image formed from the time of generation, both in the ethereal body and in the inner recesses of the soul. The soul, thus struck, recognizes that encountered image as something of its own. If that image is such as the soul itself already possessed within itself and wished to fashion in its own body but was unable to, it immediately draws it to its interior. If anything is lacking for the perfect likeness of a Jovial body, it restores it by reforming; then it loves the reformed image as its own work.

<margin>F</margin> Hence it happens that lovers are so deceived that they think the beloved is more beautiful than they actually are. For as time goes on, they do not perceive the beloved in the mere image received through the senses, but they look upon an image already reformed by the soul to the likeness of its own Idea, which is more beautiful than the body itself. They desire, moreover, to look daily upon that body from which the image first flowed. For although the soul preserves the image within itself when the body is absent, and that is almost enough for it, the spirit (the instrument of the soul) and the eye do not preserve it. Truly, three things seem to be in us: Soul, Spirit, and Body. The Soul and Body, being far different in nature, are joined by the mediating spirit, which is a certain very thin and transparent vapor, generated by the heat of the heart from the most subtle part of the blood. Thence it is diffused through all the limbs...

<summary>This page explains the Platonic concept of the World Soul and the hierarchy of mediating spirits (daemons or angels) that transmit divine gifts and planetary influences to humanity. It specifically details how astrological alignment and the "spirit" mediate the experience of love and physical attraction between individuals.</summary>
<keywords>World Soul, elements, daemons, angels, Dionysius the Areopagite, seven gifts, planetary influence, Eros, celestial Venus, astrology, Jovial, Martial, spirit, soul-body union</keywords>

--- Page 818 ---
<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s Neoplatonic commentary on Plato’s Symposium, specifically discussing the nature of the soul's perception and the mythological birth of Love (Eros).</meta>

<margin>A</margin> The soul receives powers and transfers them into the body. It receives, in turn, through the organs of the senses, the images of external bodies. These images cannot be fixed directly in the soul because the soul is an incorporeal substance superior to bodies, and thus cannot be formed by them through the mere reception of an image. However, since the soul is present to the spirit <note>Ficino refers to the "spiritus," a subtle vapor that acts as a bridge between the material body and the immaterial soul</note>, it easily perceives the images of bodies shining in that spirit as if in a mirror, and through them, it judges those bodies. The Platonists call this cognition "sense." While the soul inspects these, it conceives within itself similar images—much purer by its own power; we call this kind of conception "imagination" and "phantasy." Here, the conceived images are preserved by memory. Through these "eyes" of the soul, it is frequently incited to contemplate the universal Ideas of things which it contains within itself. Therefore, it perceives a specific man by sense and conceives him by imagination; but by the intellect, it contemplates the "reason" <note>Latin: *rationem*, here meaning the defining principle or essence</note> and definition common to all men through the innate Idea of humanity, and it preserves what has been contemplated. Thus, for the soul of a lover, it would be enough to have seen the beloved once, preserving the conceived and reformed likeness of the beautiful person in the memory. However, for the eye and the spirit—which, like mirrors, capture images only when the body is present—there is a need for the perpetual presence of the beautiful body so that they may be continually illuminated, nourished, and delighted by its radiance. Therefore, these parts demand the presence of the body due to their own poverty, and the soul, having mostly complied with them, is compelled to desire the same.

---

# ON THE BIRTH OF LOVE.
### CHAPTER VII.

But let us now return to Diotima <note>The wise woman of Mantinea who instructs Socrates in Plato's *Symposium*</note>. When she had placed Love in the number of the "daemons" <note>In the Greek sense: intermediary spirits between gods and humans, not "demons" in the modern evil sense</note> for the reasons we have narrated, she demonstrated his origin to Socrates in this manner. At the birth of Venus, while the gods were feasting, Porus <note>Resource or Plenty</note>, the son of Counsel, drunk on nectar, coupled with Penia <note>Poverty or Want</note> in the garden of Jove; from that union, Love was born. "At the birth of Venus"—that is, when the Angelic Mind and the Soul of the World (whom we have named "Venuses" for the reason stated elsewhere) were arising from the supreme majesty of God. The "Gods were feasting"—that is, Coelius, Saturn, and Jupiter were enjoying their own goods. For when the intelligence in the Angel and the power of generation in the Soul of the World (which we properly call the twin Venuses) came forth into the light, there already existed that supreme God whom they call Heaven (*Coelum*). Furthermore, there was Essence and Life in the Angel (whom we call Saturn and Jupiter), and also in the Soul of the World there was the knowledge of supernal things and the movement of celestial bodies (whom we again call Saturn and Jupiter). "Porus" and "Penia" signify abundance and poverty. Porus is the son of Counsel—that is, a spark of the supreme God. Indeed, God is called Counsel and the source of counsel because He is the truth and goodness of all things. By His splendor, every counsel is made true; toward His goodness, every counsel tends. By "Jove’s garden," he understands the fecundity of the angelic life; when Porus (that is, that ray of God) descends into this, mixed with Penia (that is, the soul's prior state of need), he creates Love. In the beginning, the Angel exists and lives through God; in respect to these two—essence and life—he is named Saturn and Jupiter.

<margin>B</margin> He possesses, moreover, the power of understanding, which we consider to be Venus. This power is by its nature formless and dark unless it is illuminated by God, just as the power of the eye is dark before the arrival of the sun. We consider this darkness to be Penia—that is, a sort of want and defect of light. However, that power of understanding, reflected toward its divine parent by a certain natural instinct, receives from Him a ray, which is Porus and abundance. In this ray, as if in a seed, the "reasons" <note>essences/blueprints</note> of all things are included. By the flames of this ray, that natural instinct is set on fire; this fire, this heat arising from the prior darkness and the kindling spark, is Love—born of poverty and abundance, procreated in the garden of Jove, that is, under the shadow of Life. For immediately after the vigor of life, the heat for understanding arises. But why do they introduce Porus drunk with nectar? Because he overflows with the reason of divine vitality. Why is Love partly rich and partly poor? Because we are not accustomed to burn for what we possess perfectly, nor for what we lack entirely. Since everyone seeks what they lack, if someone possesses the whole thing, what more would they seek? Furthermore, since no one desires the unknown, it is necessary that what we love was in some way known to us before. Nor is it enough to be merely known—for we often hate many things known to us—but it must be judged as good and pleasant to us. Even this does not seem enough for burning benevolence unless we judge that we can easily attain what we deemed would be pleasant. Therefore, whoever loves something does not yet possess it perfectly in reality. Yet, by the thought of the mind, they know it, judge it pleasant, and trust they can attain it. This very knowledge, judgment, and hope is like a present anticipation of an absent good. For one would not burn unless the thing itself pleased; and it would not please unless it had been "pre-tasted" in some way. Therefore, since lovers partly have what they desire and partly do not have it, Love is not without reason mixed from a certain poverty and abundance. By this logic, that supernal Venus, kindled by the first tasting of the divine ray itself, is carried by love toward the complete fullness of the whole light. By this effort, clinging more effectively to the parent, she immediately shines with His fullest brightness; and the "reasons" of things, which had previously been entangled and confused in the ray we call Porus, are now unfolded and shine more clearly and distinctly through that inherent power of Venus. Just as the Angel relates to God, so the Soul of the World relates to the Angel and God. For turning itself toward the supernal, it similarly receives a ray from them and is kindled, begetting a love that participates in abundance and poverty. From here, adorned with the forms of all things, it moves the heavens according to their model,

<column-break/>

<margin>C</margin> and through the power of generating, it creates forms similar to those in the matter of the elements. Here we behold the twin Venus again: one power of this soul for knowing supernal things, and another power of the same soul as the procreatress of inferior things. The former is not unique to the soul but is an imitation of angelic contemplation; the latter, however, is the soul's own proper nature. Therefore, whenever we place one Venus in the soul, we mean its peculiar power or its own "Venereal" property. Whenever we place two, we mean one common with the Angel and the other proper to the soul itself. Let there be, therefore, two Venuses in the soul: the first celestial, the second common. Let both have Love: the Celestial for contemplating divine beauty, the Common for generating the same in the matter of the world. For such beauty as the former sees, the latter wishes to transmit to the machine of the world according to its strength. Indeed, both are carried toward generating beauty, but each in its own way. The Celestial Venus strives by its intelligence to fashion within itself the most exact beauty of supernal things; the Common Venus strives to give birth in the matter of the world to the beauty conceived within itself from the abundance of divine seeds. We sometimes call that first Love a "god" because it is directed toward divine things; but mostly a "daemon" because it is midway between poverty and plenty. We always call the second Love a "daemon" because it is seen to have an effect upon the body and is more inclined toward the lower region of the world. This is indeed foreign to God but suited to the nature of daemons.

---

# IN ALL SOULS there are two loves, but in ours there are five.
### CHAPTER VIII.

<margin>D</margin> These twin Venuses and twin loves exist not only in the Soul of the World, but also in the souls of the spheres, the stars, the daemons, and men. And since all souls are referred back to that first series of the natural order, it is necessary that the loves of all be so referred to its love that they depend on it in some way. For this reason, Diotima was accustomed to call these "daemons" simply, but that one the "Great Daemon." He, sending himself through the whole world, does not allow hearts to grow numb, but everywhere stirs them to love. In us, however, not only two, but five loves are found. Two are the extreme daemons; the middle three are not only daemons but "affections" <note>Latin: *affectus*, meaning emotional states or movements of the soul</note>. Certainly, in the human mind, there is an eternal love for perceiving divine beauty; for the sake of this, we follow the studies of philosophy and the duties of justice and piety. There is also in the power of generating a certain hidden stimulus for procreating offspring. This love is perpetual, by which we are constantly incited to fashion a likeness of that supernal beauty in the image of the procreated child. <margin>E</margin> These two loves in us are perpetual; they are those two daemons which Plato prophesies are always present to our souls: one of which raises us to the supernal, the other depresses us to the infernal; one is a *calodaemon* (a good daemon), the other a *cacodaemon* (an evil daemon). In truth, both are good, since both the procreation of offspring and the investigation of truth are considered necessary and honorable. But the fecund one is called "evil" because, through our abuse, it often disturbs us and turns the soul away from its principal good (which consists in the speculation of truth) and twists it toward viler mysteries. Between these, three loves hold the middle place in us. Since these are not as <margin>F</margin> firm in the soul as the others, but begin, grow, decrease, and end, they are more rightly called "movements" and "affections" than daemons. One of these is equidistant from both extremes. The remaining two incline toward one side or the other. Furthermore, the figure of some body, due to the preparation of its matter, is exactly as the divine mind contains it in its Idea; then, meeting the eyes and penetrating through the eyes into the spirit, it immediately pleases the soul, since it harmonizes with those "reasons" which both our mind and our power of generating once received from God and now preserve as models of the thing itself. From here, as we said, a triple love creeps in: for we are prompted and inclined toward either the contemplative, the active, or the voluptuous life. If toward the contemplative, we are immediately raised from the sight of the bodily form to the consideration of the spiritual and divine. <margin>G</margin> If toward the voluptuous, we suddenly descend from sight to the concupiscence of touching. If toward the active and moral, we remain in the sole delight of seeing and conversing. The first are so gifted that they are carried to the highest heights; the second are so dull that they are depressed to the lowest depths; the third, as middle ones, remain in the middle region. Thus, all love begins from an affection. But the love of the contemplative man ascends from affection into the mind. That of the voluptuous man descends from affection into touch. That of the active man remains in sight. The love of the former turns more toward the highest daemon than the lowest; that of the latter deflects toward the lowest rather than the highest; that of the middle one is distant from both by equal intervals. <margin>H</margin> these three loves receive three names: the love of the contemplative man is called "divine"; of the active man, "human"; of the voluptuous man, "bestial."

# WHAT PASSIONS ARE IN LOVERS because of the mother of love.
### CHAPTER IX.

We have declared thus far that Love is a daemon born of plenty and poverty, and is divided into five species; but what sort...

# ARGUMENTS AND COMMENTARY

<margin>A</margin> We shall next discuss, from the words of Diotima, what affections are born in lovers from this nature of love. Since, she says, Love was conceived on the birthday of Venus, he follows and worships Venus, and is seized by a desire for the beautiful, since Venus herself is most beautiful. Because he is the son of Poverty <note>Latin: *Inopia*, representing the Greek *Penia*</note>, he is dry, lean, and squalid, barefoot, lowly, without a home, without bedding or any cover, sleeping at the door on the road under the open sky, and finally, always needy. Because he is the son of Plenty <note>Latin: *Copia*, representing the Greek *Poros*</note>, he is a plotter against the beautiful and the good. He is manly, bold, fierce, vehement, clever, and a sagacious hunter, always weaving new devices, a student of wisdom, eloquent, philosophizing through his whole life, an enchanter, a powerful sorcerer, a dealer in drugs <note>or "poisoner"</note>, and a sophist. He is neither entirely immortal by nature, nor mortal. But sometimes on the <margin>B</margin> same day he flourishes and lives, as often as he abounds; sometimes he fails and again revives because of his father's nature; but that which is acquired slips away: wherefore Love is never a beggar, nor yet wealthy. Furthermore, he is placed in the middle between wisdom and ignorance. <margin>C</margin> Thus says Diotima. We shall explain these things as briefly as we can. Although these qualities are present in all kinds of love, they appear clearer in the three middle types as being more manifest to us. Born on the birthday of Venus, he follows Venus; that is, being born with those celestial spirits whom we have called "Venuses," he leads the souls of men back to the heavens. And he is seized by a desire for the beautiful, since Venus herself is most beautiful; that is, he inflames souls with a desire for the highest and divine beauty. Since he himself arose among those spirits who, being closest to God, are most highly illuminated by the divine beauty, they raise us to those same rays. Furthermore, since the life of all living things and trees and the fertility of the earth consist in moisture and heat, Diotima hints at the poverty of love by suggesting he lacks both moisture and heat when she called him dry, lean, and squalid. For who does not know that those things which moisture deserts are dry and parched? Who likewise would say that paleness and squalor come from anywhere else than a defect of bloody heat? Furthermore, by long-lasting love, mortals are made pale and lean. Indeed, the force of nature is hardly sufficient for two works at once. The whole attention of the lover's mind is occupied in the constant thought of the beloved. There, all the <margin>D</margin> power of the natural complexion is intent. Therefore, food is not perfectly digested in the stomach. Thus it happens that the greater part is sent out into superfluous remains, and the smaller part, and that indeed raw, is drawn to the liver. There also, for the same reason, it is poorly digested. Therefore, a small and raw amount of blood is spread from there through the veins. Wherefore all the limbs are thinned and grow pale from the lack and rawness of nourishment. Furthermore, wherever the constant intention of the mind is carried, there also the spirits—which are the chariots or instruments of the soul—fly. The spirit is created in the heart from the most subtle part of the blood. The lover's mind is snatched toward the image of the beloved fixed in the imagination and toward the beloved himself. The spirits are drawn to the same place. Flying out there, they are constantly dissolved. Therefore, there is need for a very frequent fuel of pure blood to recreate the consumed spirits: where the more subtle and clearer parts of the blood are exhaled daily in restoring the spirits. <margin>E</margin> Therefore, when the pure and clear blood is dissolved, what remains is spotted, thick, dry, and black. Hence the body is dried out and becomes squalid; hence lovers also turn out to be melancholic. For from dry, thick, and black blood, melancholy—that is, black bile—is produced, which fills the head with its vapors, dries the brain, and does not cease to afflict the soul day and night with dark and horrendous images. We read that this happened to the philosopher Lucretius on account of love. He, vexed first by love and then by insanity, finally laid hands upon himself. These things are accustomed to happen to those who, having abused love, transferred what belongs to contemplation to the lust of embraces. For we tolerate the <margin>F</margin> desires of seeing more easily than the desire of both seeing and touching. When the ancient physicians observed these things, they said that love was a passion very close to the disease of melancholy; and the physician Rhazes <note>Abu Bakr al-Razi, a famous Persian physician</note> prescribed that it be cured by sexual intercourse, fasting, drunkenness, and walking. Not only does love make men such, but also whoever are such by nature are more prone to love. Such are those in whom the bile, which they call choler, or black bile, which they call melancholy, prevails over the other humors. Choler is hot and dry; black bile is dry and cold. The former holds the place of fire, the latter of earth in the body of living things. Therefore, the melancholic are understood to be dry and parched in the likeness of earth; the choleric are squalid and pale in the likeness of fire. <margin>G</margin> The choleric, on account of the impetus of the fiery humor, are carried headlong into love; the melancholic, because of the sluggishness of the earthy humor, love more slowly. But on account of the stability of the humor itself, after they have been ensnared, they persevere for a very long time. Rightly, therefore, Love is imagined as dry and squalid, since men who are such are accustomed to indulge in love more than others. We think this happens chiefly because the choleric are scorched by the fire of their bile, and the melancholic are corroded by the harshness of their black bile, as Aristotle affirmed in the seventh book of the *Ethics*. Therefore, a troublesome humor always distresses both, and forces them to seek some greatest and continuous solace against the continuous trouble of the humors. Such are the delights of music and love. For in no <margin>H</margin> other pleasures can we bestow effort so constantly as in the charms of music and voices, and the allurements of beauty. For the other senses are quickly filled. But the sight and hearing are fed longer by voices and "empty pictures" <note>A reference to Virgil's Aeneid: *animum pictura pascit inani*</note>. Not only are the pleasures of these senses firmer, but they are also more related to the human complexion. For what is more suitable to the spirits of the human body than the voices and figures of men? Especially of those who please not only by similarity of nature but also by the grace of beauty. Wherefore choleric and melancholic men, as a unique remedy and solace for their most troublesome complexion, seek the delights of song and form. And therefore they are more prone to the allurements of Venus.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> And Socrates, whom Aristotle judged to be melancholic, was of all men most prone to the art of loving, as he himself used to profess. And I can judge the same of the melancholic Sappho, as she herself testifies. Also our Maro <note>The poet Virgil</note>, whom his likeness indicates to have been choleric, although he was modest, was nevertheless more inclined to loving. *Barefoot.* Diotima painted Love such because a lover is so occupied in amorous affairs that in the other duties of life, both private and public, he does not walk cautiously as is fitting, but without any foresight of dangers, he is carried rashly wherever he goes. Therefore, in his progress, he encounters frequent dangers, no differently than those who do not support their feet with leather; hence they are struck by frequent thorns and pebbles. <margin>B</margin> *Lowly.* The Greek word of Plato <note>*Chamaipetēs*</note> signifies "on the ground" and "flying through the lowest things." For he saw that frequently, because of the abuse of love, lovers live without sense, and great goods perish for light cares; these indeed give themselves up to the beloved to such an extent that they strive to pass entirely into them, and they fashion them in themselves as much by words as by gestures. Indeed, by the very frequent imitation of boys and girls, who would not be effeminated? Who would not turn out a boy or a woman? *Without a home.* The home of human thought is the soul itself. The home of the soul is the spirit. The home of this spirit is the body. There are three inhabitants; <margin>C</margin> there are three homes. Each of these, having lost his natural one, lives in exile. For all thought turns itself not to the discipline and tranquility of its own mind, but to the services of the beloved person; and the soul deserts the ministry of its own body and strives to leap into the body of the beloved. The spirit, the chariot of the soul, while the mind hastens elsewhere, also flies out elsewhere by exhaling. Therefore, thought leaves the home, the soul leaves, and the spirit leaves. Insanity and restlessness accompany the first exit; weakness and the fear of death the second; trembling, dread, and sighing the third. Wherefore Love is deprived of his own hearth, his natural seat, and his desired rest. *Without bedding or any cover.* For he has nowhere to rest, and nothing to be covered with. Since each thing seeks its own origin, the little fire of love, kindled in the appetite of the lover by the presentation of a beautiful body, tries to fly back into that same body. By which <margin>D</margin> impetus, it carries both the appetite and the seeker away with it in its flight. O cruel lot of lovers! O life more miserable than any death! Unless perhaps your soul, snatched from its own body by this violence of love, should moreover neglect the figure of the beloved and betake itself to the temple of divine splendor, where at last it will rest, where it will be fulfilled. Who likewise would deny that love wanders naked and without cover? For who can hide love, which a grim, bull-like, fixed gaze betrays; which interrupted speech declares; the redness and paleness of the face, frequent sighs, the tossing of limbs, perpetual complaint, importunate praises, sudden indignation, boasting, boldness, petulance, vain suspicion, and the lowliest services indicate? Just as light and rays accompany heat in the sun and fire, so external judgments follow the internal fire of love. *He sleeps at the doors.* The <margin>E</margin> doors of the mind seem to be the eyes and ears; for from here many things are carried into the mind, and the affections and habits of the mind shine out most clearly through the eyes. In looking at figures and hearing voices, lovers for the most part linger. Rarely does their mind collect itself into itself. More often it wanders through the eyes and ears. Therefore they are said to lie at the doors. They are also said to lie *in the way*. For the beauty of the body ought to be a certain way through which we begin to ascend to a higher beauty. But those who prostrate themselves to base lusts, or even dwell upon the sight more than is fitting, seem to remain in the way itself, and not at all to proceed to its end. *Under the open sky.* Rightly. For being entirely occupied in one thing, they consider nothing in the conduct of affairs. Therefore, living their life by chance, they are exposed to all the storms <margin>F</margin> and dangers of fortune, just like those who lead their life naked under the open sky. *Always needy because of his mother's nature.* Truly, since the first origin of love was from want, and that which is natural cannot be entirely uprooted, love is always needy, always thirsty. For as long as something is lacking to be attained, the heat of love burns. When the whole is possessed on all sides, the ardor ceases with the end of want, rather than enduring without need.

### ->WHAT GIFTS LOVERS HAVE<-
#### ->on account of Love's father.<-

#### ->CHAPTER X.<-

<margin>H</margin> These things follow Poverty, the mother of Love; but the opposite things follow Plenty, his father. Anyone will recognize what the opposites are, having understood the above. Above he was described as simple, incautious, lowly, unarmed; here their opposites are introduced. For he is called clever, a hunter, sagacious, a schemer, a plotter, a student of wisdom, a philosopher, manly and bold, vehement, eloquent, a magician, and a sophist. The same love which makes the lover careless and idle in other business, makes him astute and clever in amorous affairs, so that he may court the favor of the beloved in wonderful ways, whether he weaves snares or seeks it with services; whether he soothes with eloquence or charms with song. The same fury which had made him mild with service—the same fury, I say, provides arms: instilling ferocity in those indignant against the beloved, and security and strength in those fighting for him. <margin>G</margin> Love, as we said, takes its origin from sight. Sight is the middle between the mind and touch; hence the mind of the lover is always distracted and tossed up and down in turn. Sometimes a desire for an embrace arises; sometimes a modest desire for celestial beauty, and now the former, now the latter prevails and leads. In those who are most honorably educated and excel in sharpness of genius, the latter more often overcomes the former. Whoever prostrate themselves into the dregs of the body, are rightly called dry, naked, lowly...

# MARSILIO FICINO

<margin>A</margin> they are judged to be soldiers, unarmed and sluggish. They are "dry" because they are always hungry and never filled. They are "naked" because, as if reckless, they are subject to all dangers, and are held in infamy as if they were most impudent and unrefined. They are "humble" because they think of nothing high or magnificent. They are "unarmed" because they succumb to shameful desire. They are "sluggish" since they are so dull-featured that they are ignorant of the fact that love draws them, and they stop on the path, never reaching the goal. But those of the opposite sort, on the contrary, seem afflicted: for feeding on the accustomed goods of the soul, they are more filled and love tranquilly; they preserve shame, neglect the shadowy appearance of the body, and are lifted higher. And as if fortified with armor, they put to flight empty lusts from themselves and subject the senses to reason. These men, as the most skillful and prudent of all, philosophize in such a way that through the figures of bodies,
<margin>B</margin> as if by certain footprints or scents, they walk most providently. From these, they sagaciously investigate the sacred beauty of the soul and the divinities; and thus by hunting prudently, they happily attain what they desire. Truly, so great a gift of love proceeds from its father, Plenty <note>Latin: *Copia*, referring to Poros</note>: since the ray of beauty, which is both plenty and the father of love, has this power: that it is reflected back to where it came from, and draws the lover with it. Moreover, it descends first from God; passing into the angel and the soul as if through glass-like materials, and easily flowing from the soul into a body prepared for its reception. From that very body of a younger person, it flashes out especially through the eyes, the most lucid windows of the soul. It flies straight through the air and, penetrating the eyes of the elder, it pierces the soul, kindles the appetite, and leads the wounded soul and the kindled appetite toward its
<margin>C</margin> healing and refreshment, while it ravishes it along to the same place from which it had descended—step by step, indeed, first into the body of the beloved, second into the soul, third into the angel, and finally into God, the first origin of this splendor. This is the useful hunt, this the happy fowling of lovers. Indeed, a certain companion of our Socrates attributes this hunt to him in Plato’s *Protagoras*. "From where, O Socrates," he says, "do you come? I think indeed you return from that hunt to which the noble nature of Alcibiades is accustomed to provoke you." Furthermore, he calls love a "Sophist" and a "Magician." In the dialogue *The Sophist*, Plato defines a Sophist as an ambitious and crafty disputant who, by the shrewdness of fallacies, shows us the false for the true, and forces those who dispute with him to
<margin>D</margin> contradict themselves in their speeches. Both lovers and the beloved sometimes suffer this. For lovers, blinded by the mists of love, often accept false things for true, while they judge their beloveds to be more beautiful, sharper, and better than they are. They contradict themselves because of the violence of love. For the mind decides one thing, but lust follows another. They change their plans at the command of the beloved; they oppose themselves in order to comply with others. Often also the beautiful are ensnared by the cunning of lovers, and those who were previously stubborn become easy. But why do we think love is great? Because the whole power of magic consists in love. The work of magic is the attraction of one thing by another out of a certain kinship of nature. Moreover, the parts of this
<margin>E</margin> world, like the members of a single animal, all hanging from one author, are joined together by the communion of one nature. Therefore, just as in us the brain, lungs, heart, liver, and the rest of the members draw something from each other and help one another mutually, and when one of them suffers, they suffer together; so the members of this huge animal—that is, all the bodies of the world—similarly connected, mutually change their natures and are changed. From a common kinship, a common love is born; from love, a common attraction. This, moreover, is true magic. Thus, fire is drawn upward from the concavity of the moon's sphere because of a congruence of nature; air from the concavity of fire; the earth is drawn to the lowest depths from the center of the world; even water is snatched from its place. Hence also the magnet turns iron, amber turns straws, fire turns sulfur, and the sun turns many flowers and leaves to itself; the moon moves the waters,
<margin>F</margin> Mars is accustomed to stir the winds, and various herbs invite various kinds of living creatures to themselves. In human affairs too, each person's pleasure draws them. Therefore, the works of magic are the works of nature. Art, however, is the servant. For where something is lacking in natural kinship, art supplies it at opportune times through vapors, numbers, figures, and qualities. Just as in agriculture nature produces the crops, but art prepares them. The ancients attributed this art to "daemons" <note>Spirits intermediate between gods and men</note> because they understand what the society of natural things is like, what fits each thing, and how the concord of things, if it is lacking anywhere, may be restored. Some are said to have been friends to these, either by a certain similarity of nature, like Zoroaster and Socrates, or beloved through worship, like Apollonius of Tyana and Porphyry. Therefore, it is told that signs, voices, and portents happened from daemons to those who were awake, or oracles and images to those who were asleep. Those who seem to have become magicians through the friendship of daemons are like the daemons who are magicians knowing the friendship of things themselves; and all nature is called a "magician" because of mutual love. Furthermore, every beautiful person fascinates us with tender eyes. Men soothe them with the powers of eloquence and the measures of songs, as if by certain incantations, and win them over; moreover, they appease and capture them with refinement and gifts, no differently than with potions. Therefore, no one doubts that love is a magician, since the whole power of magic consists in love, and the work of love is fulfilled by fascinations, incantations, and potions. It is neither entirely mortal, nor yet immortal. Not mortal, because two loves are in us—those two which we call daemons—and they are perpetual. Not immortal, because three of these middle states are changed daily; they grow and decrease. Furthermore, in the appetite of men from the beginnings of life, an inextinguishable innate fervor is born, which does not permit the soul to rest, and always impels it to apply itself studiously to something certain. The characters of men are diverse, nor is life lived by a single wish. Hence that continuous fervor of concupiscence, which is natural love, impels some to the study of letters; others to music or figures; others to honesty or a religious life; others to honors; some to accumulating money; most to the luxury of the belly; others to other things; and even the same man in different ages to

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> different things. Therefore, the same fervor is called both immortal and mortal. Immortal, because it is never extinguished, and changes its material rather than vanishing; mortal, because it does not always lean toward the same thing: but either from a change of nature, or from a satiety born of long-term frequency of the same thing, it seeks new delights; and that which almost failed in one thing, in a way revives in another. It is also called immortal for this reason: that a figure once loved is always loved. For as long as the same figure remains in the same person, it is loved in that very person; but when it has flowed away from him, it is no longer the same figure in him that you loved before. You do not burn for this new one, because you had not burned for it before;
<margin>B</margin> but you do not cease to love that prior one. There is this difference, however: that you previously looked upon it in another; but now you look upon it only in yourself, and always fixed in the same memory, you always love it; and as often as it occurs to the eyes of the mind, so often it burns you, the lover. Therefore, as often as we meet that person once most dear to us, so often are we moved: either the heart leaps or trembles, or the liver melts, or the eyes tremble, and the face takes on various colors in his presence. For his presence suggests the figure of the soul lying hidden in the mind to the eyes, and by blowing, it rouses the fires as if they were sleeping under ashes. For this reason, love is called immortal. But it is also held immortal here because, although the faces remain always fixed in the breast, they do not offer themselves equally to the eyes of the mind; wherefore benevolence seems to boil and then cool in turn. Added to this is that both wild and human love can never be
<margin>C</margin> without indignation. Who would not be indignant at him who has stolen his soul? For as liberty is pleasing above all else, so slavery is burdensome. Therefore, you hate and love the beautiful at the same time: you hate them as thieves and murderers; yet as mirrors shining with celestial splendor, you are forced to admire and love them. What can you do, miserable one? Where can you turn, alas, lost one, you know not. Since you would not want this murderer of yours to exist even without the blessed spectacle of living. You cannot be with this person who destroys you, who kills you; yet without him you cannot live, who steals you from yourself with such wondrous allurements, who claims all of you for himself. You desire to flee him who burns you with his flames; yet you also desire to cling to him, so that being closest to him who possesses you, you may also cling to yourself. Miserable, you seek yourself outside of yourself, and you cling to the kidnapper so that you might eventually redeem yourself as a captive. You would not want to love, insane one, because you would not want to die; yet you would not want not to love, since you judge that the image of celestial things must be served. Therefore, by this
<margin>D</margin> alteration it happens that in every moment (so to speak) love withers and turns green again. It is also placed by Diotima as a middle between wisdom and ignorance. Furthermore, love follows those things which are beautiful. Wisdom is the most beautiful of all things. Therefore, it desires wisdom. He who desires wisdom does not possess it entirely. For who would seek things that are present? Nor is he entirely without it. For in this one thing at least he is wise: that he recognizes his own ignorance. But he who does not know that he is ignorant, is ignorant of both the things themselves and his own ignorance, nor does he seek knowledge, of which he does not know himself to be
<margin>E</margin> devoid. Therefore, the love of wisdom, because it is partly deprived of wisdom and partly wise, is located between wisdom and ignorance. This, says Diotima, is the condition of love; but the nature of the beautiful itself—that is, of supreme beauty—is that it be delicate, perfect, and blessed. Delicate, insofar as by its own sweetness it allures the appetite of all to itself; Perfect, insofar as it illustrates with its rays and perfects those things which have approached after being enticed; Blessed, insofar as it fills the illustrated things with eternal goods.

### WHAT IS THE UTILITY OF LOVE
->from its definition.<-

->CHAPTER XI.<-

After Diotima related what the origin of love is and what kind of thing it is, she now opens up where it tends and for what it is useful to men. We all indeed desire to have good things; and not only to have them, but to have them always. But the individual goods of mortals are changed and fail, and all would quickly vanish unless new ones were made daily in the place of those departing. Therefore, so that good things may always endure for us in whatever way,
<margin>G</margin> we desire to recreate the perishing ones. Recreation happens through generating. Hence the instinct of generation is innate in all. Moreover, since generation makes mortal things similar to divine things by continuation, it is surely a divine gift. To divine things, as they are beautiful, deformed things are contrary; beautiful things are similar and friendly. Therefore, the work of generation, being a divine work, is perfectly and easily consumed in that which is beautiful, and the opposite happens in the contrary. Wherefore that effort of generation demands beautiful things and flees the contrary. You ask what the love of men is? To what does it lead? The desire for generation in the beautiful for the sake of preserving life perpetually in mortal things: this is the love of men living on earth, this is the end of our love. For indeed, in that very time in which each of the animals is said to live and be the same—as from boyhood to old age, although it is called the
<margin>H</margin> same—it never contains the same things in itself, but is always made new. As Plato says, it even sheds old things according to hair, flesh, bones, and blood, and the entire body inwardly. Nor does this happen in the body alone, but also in the soul. Morals, customs, opinions, desires, pleasures, pains, and fears are continually changed; nor does anything of these remain the same and similar; the prior ones are abolished, and new ones succeed and grow up. Furthermore, what is more wonderful, not only do some sciences vanish and others rise, and we are not always the same according to sciences, but even any one of the sciences suffers almost the same thing. For meditation and reminiscence are like a resumption of a passing science. For oblivion seems to be the exit of science. But meditation always [creates] a new memo[ry]...

<summary>Ficino explains the nature of Love as a "daemon" or intermediary force that acts like magic, attracting the soul toward divine beauty through the physical world. He describes love as a drive for "generation in beauty," allowing mortal beings to participate in immortality by constantly renewing themselves.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical commentary on the nature of Love (Eros) and the soul's fertility, likely from Marsilio Ficino’s "Commentary on Plato’s Symposium." It transitions from the preservation of the species to the intellectual "reproduction" of knowledge.</meta>

# ARGUMENTS AND COMMENTARY.

<margin>A</margin> By restoring a new part in place of one that departs, the soul preserves knowledge, so that it appears to remain the same. In this way, whatever is changeable in the mind or body is preserved: not because they remain entirely the same forever—for this is the unique property of **divine things**—but because that which decays and passes away leaves behind something new and similar to itself. By this remedy, certainly, mortal things are rendered similar to immortal ones. Therefore, in both parts of the soul—both that which pertains to cognition and that which governs the body—there is an innate **love of generation** for the perpetual preservation of life. The love in the part adapted to governing the body impels us from the very beginning to take food and drink, so that from these nourishments humors <note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) believed to control health and temperament.</note> may be generated, by which that which continually flows out of the body may be resumed. By this generation, the body is nourished and grows. Once the body is adult, the seed itself is stirred and provokes the desire for procreating offspring, so that what cannot remain forever in itself may remain eternal, preserved in an offspring very similar to itself. 

The love of generation attributed to the cognitive part of the soul also causes the soul to long for **truth**, its own proper nourishment, through which it is nourished and grows in its own way; and if anything has fallen out of the mind through forgetfulness, or grows numb through sloth and neglect, it regenerates it, as it were, through the study of remembrance and meditation, and recalls to the mind what had perished through forgetfulness or grown sluggish through laziness. Indeed, it stimulates the now-mature mind with a most burning desire for teaching and writing, so that knowledge—generated either in writings or in the minds of disciples—may remain eternal among men through the teacher's intelligence and truth. And so, by the benefit of love, both the body and the soul of every man seem able to survive forever in human affairs after death. Both types of love pursue beautiful things. Truly, the one who rules and governs the body desires to nourish his own body with the most delicate, pleasant, and beautiful feasts, and to generate handsome offspring with a beautiful woman; and the one who pertains to the soul strives to imbue it with the most adorned and serious disciplines, and to produce knowledge most like itself by writing in an adorned and beautiful style, and by teaching to generate it in some most beautiful mind—a pure mind, I say, sharp and excellent. We do not see the mind itself; therefore, we do not behold its beauty. But we see the body, the shadow and image of the mind; thus, suspecting from its image, we conjecture that in a handsome body there is a beautiful mind. For this reason, we educate handsome men more willingly.

### ON THE TWO LOVES, AND THAT THE SOUL IS BORN ENDOWED WITH TRUTH.
### CHAPTER XII.

<margin>F</margin> We have already said enough about the definition of love: now, however, let us declare what distinction exists in Plato regarding love based on the fertility of the soul or the body. The bodies of all men, he says, are pregnant and heavy, and so is the soul. Seeds of all their own things are inserted into the body from the beginning. Hence, at fixed cycles of time, teeth break through, hair comes forth, the beard grows thick, and the seeds of procreation flow down. If the body is fertile and heavy with seeds, much more is the soul—more excellent than the body—most fertile, and it possesses the seeds of all its own things from the beginning. Therefore, the soul has long since obtained the principles of morals, arts, and disciplines, and from there, if it is rightly cultivated, it brings forth its own offspring into the light at fixed times. 

That it has the innate principles of all its own things, we know from its appetite, inquiry, discovery, judgment, and comparison. Who would deny that the soul, immediately from a tender age, desires things that are true, good, honorable, and useful? But no one desires the unknown. <margin>G</margin> Therefore, there are some notions of all these things in the soul even before it desires them: through which, as if through their forms or principles, it judges that they are to be desired. The same is proved by inquiry and discovery: if Socrates seeks Alcibiades in a crowd of men, and is eventually to find him, it is necessary that some figure of Alcibiades be in Socrates' mind, so that he knows which man he seeks above the others, and, having found him in a gathering of many, he is able to discern Alcibiades from the others. Thus, the soul would neither track those four things <note>Truth, Goodness, Honor, and Utility.</note> nor ever find them, unless it had some notion of them—that is, of Truth, Goodness, Honor, and Utility—through which it might seek them with the intent to find them, so that whenever it finds what it had investigated, it recognizes them and discerns them from their opposites. 

And we prove this not only from appetite, investigation, and discovery, but also from judgment. For whoever judges someone to be a friend or an enemy is not ignorant of what friendship or ill-will is. In what way, therefore, would we daily judge many things to be true or false, good or evil, as we are accustomed to do, and judge them correctly, unless truth and goodness were in some way foreknown to us? How, again, would many people—even those not practiced in these arts—very often rightly approve or disapprove of works of architecture, music, painting, and other arts, as well as the discoveries of philosophers, unless some form and principle of those things were granted to them by nature? Comparison also shows us the same. <margin>H</margin> For whoever, comparing honey to wine, pronounces one sweeter than the other, recognizes what a sweet flavor is; and he who, comparing Speusippus and Xenocrates to Plato, judges Xenocrates more similar to Plato than Speusippus, undoubtedly knows the figure of Plato. In the same way, when out of many good things we rightly deem one better than another, and by a greater or lesser participation in goodness one appears better or worse than another, it is necessary that we are not ignorant of goodness. Furthermore, when out of many diverse opinions of philosophers or even others, we often judge best which

<column-break/>

<margin>B</margin> is more similar to the truth and more probable, it must be that we do not lack some intuition of the truth, so that we are not ignorant of which things are more similar to it. For this reason, some in youth, some even without a teacher, and many from the very few rudiments of doctrine demonstrated by teachers, are said to have turned out most learned: which could never have happened unless nature, as we said, had been a great help. Socrates abundantly demonstrated this to the boys Phaedo, Theaetetus, and Meno; and he taught that boys can answer correctly in individual arts if someone questions them prudently: since they are endowed by nature with the principles of all arts and disciplines.

---

### THE LIGHT OF TRUTH IN THE SOUL.
### CHAPTER XIII.

<margin>C</margin> In what way these principles are in the soul seems ambiguous in Plato. If one reads those books which Plato wrote as a younger man—the *Phaedrus*, *Meno*, and *Phaedo*—he will perhaps think they are painted in the substance of the soul almost like figures on a wall: a point often touched upon by both me and you in previous discussions; for he seems to imply this there. But in the sixth book of the *Republic*, that divine man opens up the whole matter, and says that the light of the mind for understanding all things is God himself, by whom all things were made. For he compares the Sun and God to each other in such a way that as the sun is to the eyes, so God is to minds. The sun generates the eyes and grants them the power of seeing. This power would be in vain, and overwhelmed by eternal darkness, unless the light of the sun were present, painted with the colors and figures of bodies: in which light the eye sees the colors and figures of bodies. Nor does the eye behold anything other than light. <margin>D</margin> Yet it seems to behold various things, because the light infused into it is adorned with various formulas of external bodies. Indeed, the eye perceives this light reflected in bodies; but it cannot endure the light itself in its own source. 

In the same way, God procreates the soul and grants it a mind, a power for understanding: which would be empty and dark unless the light of God were present to it, in which it might behold the principles of all things. Whence through the light of God it understands, and it recognizes only the divine light itself. Yet it seems to recognize diverse things, because it understands that light under diverse ideas and principles of things. When someone, seeing a man with his eyes, fashions an image of the man in his imagination and revolves longer in judging it, he raises the sharp edge of his mind to behold the principle of "man" existing in the divine light: from there, a spark immediately flashes in the mind; <margin>E</margin> and in truth, the very nature of man is understood, and so it is for all other things in the same way. Thus, through the light of God we understand all things, but we cannot see that pure light itself and its source in this life. In this clearly consists the whole fertility of the soul: that in its innermost chambers that eternal light of God shines, most full of the principles and ideas of all things, toward which the soul turns as often as it wishes by purity of life and the highest intention of study; and having turned, it flashes with the sparks of the ideas.

---

### WHENCE LOVE TOWARD MALES, WHENCE TOWARD FEMALES.
### CHAPTER XIV.

Just as the body of men is pregnant, as Plato wishes, so is the mind pregnant, and both are stimulated to birth by the incitements of love. However, some, either because of nature or because of education, are more fit for the offspring of the mind than of the body; others, and indeed the most, are the opposite. The former follow **celestial love**, the latter **vulgar love**. The former, by nature, therefore love males—and those already almost adult—rather than females or children: because in them the sharpness of mind flourishes much more, which is most fit for the discipline for which they were generated, on account of its more excellent beauty. Others, on the contrary, love for the sake of the pleasure of venereal <note>Sexual</note> intercourse and the effect of bodily generation. 

Since, however, that genital power of the soul, being devoid of cognition, has no distinction of sexes, yet by its own nature is incited to generate as often as we judge some body to be beautiful, it happens frequently that those who associate with males, in order to settle the stings of the genital part, mingle with them. These are especially those in whose birth-chart Venus was in a masculine sign and with Saturn, or in the bounds of Saturn, or opposite Saturn. But it was necessary to notice that the incitements of that genital part should not affect this work of useless waste, but the duty of bearing and procreating, and should translate it from males to females. We think that from a certain error of this kind that nefarious crime arose, which Plato in his *Laws* detests most sharply as a species of homicide. For he is to be considered no less a murderer who snatches away a man about to be born, than he who removes one already born from the world. Bolder indeed is he who breaks off a present life, but more cruel is he who envies the light to one about to be born, and kills his own sons not yet born.

---
