<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plato’s Symposium, specifically discussing the ascent of the soul as taught by Diotima to Socrates.</meta>

# MARSILIO FICINO ON CHAPTER XVI.

## CHAPTER XV.

<margin>A</margin>
But enough regarding the twin fertility of the soul and the two loves thus far. Next, let us discuss the steps by which Diotima raises Socrates from the lowest things to the highest: she leads him from the body into the soul, from the soul into the angel <note>Ficino uses "angel" (angelus) to represent the Platonic "Intellect" or "Mind" (Nous), the first realm of pure being above the human soul.</note>, and from the angel back to God. One may argue that these four levels of things must exist in nature in the following way. Every body is moved by something else; for a body cannot move itself by its own nature, since it lacks the power to act on its own. But because of the presence of a soul, it appears to be moved by itself and to live because of that soul. Indeed, while the soul is present, the body moves itself in a certain way; but when the soul is absent, it is moved only by another, as it does not possess this nature from itself. The soul, however, properly possesses the power of moving itself. For to whatever it is present, it imparts the power to move itself; and that which it imparts to others by its own presence, it must possess much earlier and more fully itself. Therefore, the soul is above bodies, as it is able to move itself according to its own essence; and for that reason, it must be above those things which do not achieve movement from themselves, but through the presence of others. When we say the soul is moved by itself, we do not mean it "transitively" (so to speak), as Aristotle wished to interpret Plato, but we utter that word "absolutely," just as we are accustomed to say that God exists through Himself, the sun shines through itself, or fire is hot through itself. For it is not that one part of the soul moves while another part is shaken; rather, the whole soul is moved from itself—that is, by its own nature. This means it ranges through reason from one thing to another, and carries out the works of nutrition, growth, and generation through intervals of time. This temporal discourse belongs to the soul from itself, because that which is above it does not understand things in different moments, but understands all things at once in a single point of eternity. Therefore, the first motion and the first interval of time are rightly placed by Plato in the soul; from there, both motion and time pass into bodies. Since, however, it is necessary for rest to exist before motion (as rest is more perfect than motion), there must be found above the mobile motion of the soul a certain stable intelligence, which is intelligence according to its whole self, and is always intelligence in act. For the soul does not understand by its whole self, nor always, but from a certain part of itself and only sometimes; nor does it have a certain power of understanding, but an ambiguous one. Therefore, so that what is more perfect may precede what is less perfect, above the mind of the soul—which is mobile, partial, intermittent, and doubtful—must be placed the mind of the angel, which is entirely stable, continuous, and most certain. Just as the self-moved soul precedes the body shaken by another, so the self-stable mind precedes the self-shaken soul. And just as the body has the power to move itself through the soul (and thus not all bodies, but only animated ones, seem to move of their own accord), so the soul has the power to always understand through the mind. For if the intellect belonged to the soul by its own nature, it would also belong to the souls of all beasts, just as the power of shaking itself does. Therefore, the intellect does not belong to the soul through itself or primarily; wherefore it must be preceded by that which is composed of mind through itself and primarily.
<margin>B</margin>
Such a thing is the angel, a more excellent mind. But indeed, that principle of things and the highest good—which Plato in the *Parmenides* calls "the One itself"—necessarily towers above the mind of the angel. Truly, above every multitude of a composed thing, the "One itself" must be simple by nature; for number is fashioned from the one, and every composition from simple parts. However, although that Mind <note>The Angelic Mind</note> is immobile, it is not the pure, simple "One itself." For it understands itself; wherein these three appear diverse among themselves in some way: that which understands, that which is understood, and the act of understanding. For its rationale is one thing insofar as it understands, another insofar as it is understood, and another insofar as it is the act of understanding. Furthermore, it has the potential for knowing before the act of cognition, which is entirely unformed through itself; it is formed by knowing, and by understanding it desires and receives the light of truth, which it seems to have lacked before it understood. It also possesses within itself a multitude of all Ideas. See how great and how varied is the multitude and composition within the angel! Therefore, we are compelled to place the pure One and Simple before it. But we can place nothing before the one God, because the true One is devoid of all multitude and all composition. If it had anything above itself, it would surely be made by that; wherefore, depending on it, it would degenerate from it in this very fact, as every effect usually does from its cause. And thus it would no longer be one and simple, but at least composed of two things: namely, from the gift of its cause and its own defect. Therefore, the One itself, as Plato wills and Dionysius the Areopagite confirms, towers above all things; and the most excellent name of God, "the One itself," is judged so by both. The reason for this sublimity is also shown to us by the fact that the gift of the most eminent cause must be the most ample, and the excellence of its power must extend itself to all things. The gift of the One propagates itself through the universe. For not only is the mind one, and every soul one, and every body one, but even unformed matter itself and the privation of things is said to be "one" in a certain way. For we say "one silence," "one darkness," "one death." Yet the gifts of the mind and the soul do not extend that far. For the Mind bestows artistic form and order; the Soul provides life and motion; but the unformed and primary matter of the world, and the privation of things, is devoid of form and life. Thus the One itself precedes the mind and the soul, since its gift is more widely diffused. By the same reasoning, the mind seems to exceed the soul: because life, the gift of the soul, is not given to all bodies. Yet the mind grants form and order to all of these.

## THE COMPARISON BE-
## tween God, the angel, the soul, and the body.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
Therefore, we ascend from the body into the soul, from the soul into the angel, and from the angel into God. God is above eternity; the Angel is entirely within eternity. Its operation remains as stable as its essence. Stability, moreover, is proper to eternity. The soul is partly in eternity and partly in time. For its substance always endures the same without any change of increase or decrease. Its operation, however, as we showed a little earlier, ranges through intervals of time. The body is entirely subject to time. For both its substance is changed, and its every operation requires a space of time. Therefore, the One itself exists above stability or motion; the Angel is in stability; the Soul is in stability and motion alike; the Body is placed in motion alone. Again, the One remains above num-
<margin>B</margin>
ber, motion, and place; the Angel is placed in number, but above motion and place; the Soul is in number and motion, but above place; the Body is subject to number, motion, and place. For the One itself has no number or composition of parts; nor is it changed in any way from what it is; nor is it enclosed by any place. The Angel indeed has a number of parts or forms, but is free from motion and place. The Soul has a multitude of parts and affections, and is changed by the progression of reasoning and the variety of disturbances; but it is exempt from the limits of places. The Body, however, is liable to all of these.
<margin>C</margin>

---

## THE COMPARISON BE-
## tween the beauties of God, the Angel, the
## soul, and the body.

### CHAPTER XVII.

<margin>D</margin>
There is, in truth, the same comparison between these four and their forms. Surely the form of the body consists in the composition of many parts, is constrained by place, and glides away in time. The beauty of the soul suffers the vicissitudes of time and contains a multitude of parts, but is absolute from the boundaries of place. The beauty of the Angel has number alone, and exists immune from the other two. But the beauty of God suffers none of these. You see the form of the body, certainly. Do you wish also to behold the beauty of the soul? Subtract from the bodily form the weight of the matter itself and the limit of places, and leave the rest: now you have the beauty of the soul. Do you want that of the angel too?
<margin>E</margin>
Subtract, I pray, not only the spaces of place, but also the progress of time; retain the manifold composition, and you will obtain it immediately. Do you also desire to see the beauty of God? Take away, in addition, that manifold composition of forms; leave the form entirely simple, and you will have immediately attained the beauty of God. But what, finally, will remain for me after these things are subtracted? Do you think that being is anything other than light and beauty? Furthermore, the beauty of all bodies is that light of the sun which you see, infected by those three things: by the multitude of forms (for you see it depicted in many figures and colors), by the space of place, and by temporal mutation. Take away its seat in matter, so that it retains the other two besides place: the beauty of the soul is exactly like this. Take away from here the mutation of time, if you please, and let the rest go: there remains a light without place, without motion, most clear; but inscribed with all the
<margin>F</margin>
rational principles of all things. That is the angel; that is the beauty of the angel. Finally, take away that number of diverse Ideas; leave one simple and pure light: like that light which remains in the globe of the sun itself and is not dispersed through the air; now you comprehend in a certain way the beauty of God. This beauty excels the lower forms at least as much as the light of the sun—pure, one, and inviolate in itself—surpasses the splendor of the sun scattered, divided, infected, and obscured through the cloudy air. Therefore, God is the source of all beauty and all love. Furthermore, the light of the sun in water is a certain shadow compared to the clearer light of the same in the air. The splendor in the air is likewise a shadow compared to the glow of the same in fire. The glow in fire is a shadow compared to the light of the sun shining in the sun itself. The same is the comparison between those four beauties: of the body, the
<margin>G</margin>
soul, the angel, and God. God is never so deceived that He loves the shadow of His own beauty in the angel while neglecting His own true beauty. Nor is the angel so captured by the beauty of the soul (which is its own shadow) that, detained by its shadow, it abandons its own figure. Our soul, however—which is most greatly to be grieved, for this is the origin of our entire unhappiness—the soul, I say, alone is so charmed by the allurements of bodily form that it puts its own beauty second; and, forgetting itself, it pursues the form of the body, which is its own shadow. Hence that most cruel fate of Narcissus in Orpheus <note>Ficino often attributes the myth of Narcissus to Orphic or mystical traditions to emphasize its allegorical meaning.</note>.
<margin>H</margin>
Hence the pitiable calamity of men. Narcissus indeed, a youth—that is, the soul of a rash and inexperienced man—does not look at his own face; he in no way notices his own substance and virtue; but he pursues its shadow in the water and tries to embrace it: that is, he admires beauty in a fragile body, flowing like water, which is the shadow of the soul itself. He abandons his own figure and never attains the shadow; because the soul, by pursuing the body, neglects itself and is not filled by the use of the body. For it does not truly desire the body itself, but its own beauty, being enticed by the bodily form which is the image of its own beauty—just as Narcissus desires. And since it does not notice this, while it desires one thing but follows another, it cannot fulfill its desire. Therefore, dissolved into tears, it is consumed; that is, the soul, thus placed outside itself and fallen into the body, is [consumed] by ruinous disturbances...

<summary>Ficino describes the metaphysical hierarchy of the universe—Body, Soul, Angelic Mind, and God—explaining how each level participates in beauty and motion. He uses the myth of Narcissus as an allegory for the soul's tragic mistake of falling in love with its own shadow in material bodies rather than returning to its divine source.</summary>

# ARGUMENTS AND COMMENTARY.

<column-break/>

is tortured by passions: or as if dying, infected by the filth of the body: when it already seems to be a body rather than a soul. In order that Socrates might avoid such a death, Diotima led him back from the body to the soul, from the soul to the angel, and from the angel back to God.

# HOW THE SOUL IS ELEVATED FROM the beauty of the body to the beauty of God.

## CHAPTER XVIII.

Come now, dearest guests, imagine Diotima speaking thus to Socrates. No body, O Socrates, is beautiful in every respect. For it is either beautiful in this part and deformed in that: or beautiful today, and not at all at another time: or judged beautiful by one person and ugly by another. Therefore, the beauty of the body, defiled by the contagion of ugliness, cannot be, think you, the true and primary beauty. For no one ever suspects beauty itself of being ugly: just as no one suspects wisdom of being foolish. But we judge the arrangement of bodies to be sometimes fair and sometimes foul: and at the same time, different people feel differently about it. Therefore, the primary and true beauty is not in bodies. Add to this that many bodies are called by the single name of beauty. There is, therefore, one common nature of beauty in many bodies, through which they are similarly called beautiful. But consider that one nature of this kind, just as it exists in another thing (that is, in matter), so it depends on another. For that which cannot be sustained in itself, much less depends on itself. Will it depend on matter? Not at all. For nothing deformed and imperfect can adorn and perfect itself. But that which is one must arise from one. Wherefore the one beauty of many bodies depends on some one incorporeal craftsman. The one craftsman of all is God, who through angels and souls daily renders all the matter of the world beautiful. Therefore, one must think that the true reason of beauty is found in God and his ministers <note>The "ministers" here refer to the celestial hierarchy or angels.</note> rather than in the body of the world. To this beauty, you will easily ascend again by these steps, O Socrates, as an arbiter. If nature had given you lynx-like eyes, my Socrates, so that you could penetrate whatever met your gaze: that body of your Alcibiades, so very beautiful on the outside, would seem most foul to you. How much is it that you love, friend? Only the surface, or rather color, snatches you away: or rather a certain reflection of light, and a very light shadow. Or a vain imagination deceives you: so that you love what you dream rather than what you see. But lest he seem entirely opposed to you, let this Alcibiades of yours be truly beautiful. But in what part is he beautiful? Surely in all his members except for his snub nose and eyebrows higher than is fitting. Yet these things are fair in Phaedrus. But the thickness of his legs does not please. These are graceful in Charmides, unless a slender neck should offend you. Thus, if you observe individual men, you will praise none in every part. Whatever is right everywhere, you will collect: you will fashion an entire figure within yourself from the observation of all: so that the absolute beauty of the human race, which is found scattered in many bodies, may be collected in your soul by the thought of a single image. You will value the figure of any individual man little, O Socrates, if you compare it to that one. But you possess that one not so much by the benefit of bodies as by the benefit of your own soul. Therefore, love that which your soul has fashioned, and the soul itself as its craftsman, rather than that exterior, maimed, and dispersed beauty. But what do I command you to love in the soul? The beauty of the soul. Light is the beauty of bodies: light is also the beauty of the soul: the light of the soul is truth: which alone your friend Plato seems to ask from God in his prayers. Give me, he says, O God, that my soul may be made beautiful: and that those things which pertain to the body may not hinder the beauty of the soul: let me think the wise man alone to be rich. In these words, Plato declares that the beauty of the soul consists in truth and wisdom: and that it is granted to men by God. Truth is one, and the same is granted to us by God: in its various effects, it receives the names of various virtues: as it demonstrates divine things, it is called wisdom (which Plato asked from God above all else); as it demonstrates natural things, science; as human things, prudence; as it makes men just, justice; as it makes them unconquered, fortitude; as it makes them tranquil, it is called temperance. From these, two kinds of virtues are numbered: Moral virtues, I say, and Intellectual virtues which are superior to them. The Intellectual are Wisdom, Science, and Prudence; the Moral are Justice, Fortitude, and Temperance. The Moral are better known because of their operations and civil duties. The Intellectual are more hidden because of their recondite truth. Furthermore, he who is educated in honest morals, being purer than others, is easily raised to the intellectual virtues. Therefore, I command you to consider first the beauty of the soul which consists in morals, so that you may understand there is one reason for all morals: through which they are similarly called honest. Namely, the one truth of a most pure life: which, through the actions of Justice, Fortitude, and Temperance, leads us to true happiness. Therefore, love first this one truth of morals and this most fair light of the soul. Know also that you will immediately ascend above morals to the most lucid truth of wisdom, science, and prudence, if you consider that these are granted to a soul educated in the best morals, and that in them is contained the most correct rule of mortal life. Although you may contain various doctrines of Wisdom, Science, and Prudence: nevertheless, believe that in all of them there is a single light of truth: through which all are similarly called beautiful. I command you to love that especially as the supreme beauty of the soul. But indeed, this one truth in many doctrines cannot be the primary truth of all, because it exists in another, since it is distributed among many doctrines.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Whatever lies in another certainly depends on another. Yet one truth is not born from a multitude of doctrines. For that which is one must arise from one. Wherefore it is necessary that there be some one wisdom above the soul of man, which is not divided through diverse doctrines, but is one wisdom: from whose single truth the manifold truth of men arises. Remember, O Socrates, that the single light of that single wisdom is the beauty of the angel, which you must worship above the beauty of the soul. That beauty, as we have shown in previous sections, excels the beauty of bodies: because it is neither bound by place, nor divided according to the parts of matter, nor corrupted. It also excels the beauty of the soul, because it is entirely eternal, nor is it moved by temporal discourse <note>The "temporal discourse" refers to the way human reason moves step-by-step through time, whereas angelic intellect is instantaneous.</note>. Since,
<margin>B</margin> however, the light of the angel shines in a series of many ideas, and there must be a unity above every multitude, which is the origin of the whole number: it is necessary that it flow from the one principle of all things, which we call the One itself. Therefore, the light of the One itself is an entirely simple and infinite beauty: because it is neither defiled by the filth of matter, like the beauty of the body; nor is it changed by temporal progression, like the form of the soul; nor is it dissipated by multitude, like the beauty of the angel. Moreover, every quality separated from an external addition is called "infinite" by the Physicists <note>Natural philosophers.</note>. If heat exists in itself, not hindered by cold and moisture, not weighed down by the weight of matter, it is called infinite heat, because its power is free, nor is it narrowed by any additional limits. Similarly, light free from
<margin>C</margin> every body is infinite: for it shines without measure and end, because it shines by its own nature, when it is least limited by that body. Thus the light and beauty of God, which is pure, and altogether absolute from all others, is without doubt called infinite beauty. But infinite beauty also requires immense love. Wherefore I beseech you, Socrates, that you love other things with a certain measure and limit. But love God with infinite love, and let there be no measure to divine love.

# HOW GOD IS to be loved.

## CHAPTER XIX.

<margin>E</margin> Thus Diotima spoke to Socrates. We, however, most illustrious men, will love not only God without measure, as Diotima is imagined to command, but we will love God alone. For the mind is toward God as the sight of the eyes is toward the sun. The eye desires not only light above other things, but light alone. If we love bodies, if we love souls, if we love angels, we will not love these things indeed, but God in them. In bodies, we love the shadow of God; in souls, the likeness of God; in angels, his image. Thus we will love God in all things for the present, so that in the end we may love all things in God. For living thus, we shall proceed so that we see both God and all things in God: and let us love both Him and all things that are in Him. And whoever devotes himself to God in charity at this time, will finally recover himself in God. Surely he will return to his own Idea, through which he was created: there again, if anything was lacking to him, he will be reformed: he will adhere perpetually to his Idea. But the true man and the Idea of man are the same. Therefore, each of us separated from God on earth is not a true man, since he is disjoined from his Idea and form: divine love and piety will lead us back to it, since here we are torn apart and mutilated. Then, joined to our Ideas by loving, we shall emerge as
<margin>F</margin> whole men: so that we may seem to have worshipped God first in things, in order that we may then worship things in God, and to venerate things in God for the purpose of embracing ourselves above all else, and by loving God, we may seem to have loved ourselves.

# THE SEVENTH ORATION.

## CONCLUSION OF THE ABOVE, and the opinion of the philosopher Guido Cavalcanti.

### CHAPTER I.

<margin>G</margin> Finally, Cristoforo Marsuppini, a most refined man, about to play the part of Alcibiades, turns to me with these words. I congratulate indeed, Marsilio, the family of your Giovanni very much: which among many knights most famous for both learning and deeds, brought forth the philosopher Guido <note>Guido Cavalcanti (c. 1255–1300), a famous Italian poet and friend of Dante.</note>, who deserved well of the republic, and excelled everyone in his age in the stings of dialectic: who, having imitated this Socratic love as much in his morals
<margin>H</margin> as in his songs, briefly touched upon whatever has been said by you. For Phaedrus touched upon the origin of love emanating from the bowels of chaos. Pausanias divided love, now born, into a twin species, namely the celestial and the common. Eryximachus opened its breadth, while he showed it to be present in all things distributed into twin parts. Aristophanes declared what the presence of so great a God does in individuals, showing that through him broken men are mended. Agathon treated how great its virtue and power are, when he argued that men are made blessed by it alone. Socrates finally, taught by Diotima, explained summarily what love is, and of what kind, and whence it arose, what parts it has, whither it tends, and how much it is worth. Guido...

# MARSILIO FICINO

The Cavalcantian philosophers <note>referring to Guido Cavalcanti and his circle of Florentine Platonists</note> seem to have woven all these things most skillfully into their poems. Just as a mirror, struck in a certain way by a ray of the sun, shines back and, by that reflection of brightness, sets fire to wool placed near it: so he considers that part of the soul which they call the "dark fantasy" <note>the faculty of imagination</note> and memory to be like a mirror. He believes it is struck by the image of beauty—which holds the place of the sun itself—drawn in through the eyes like a ray, so that the soul fashions for itself another image from that one, like a brightness from the first image. By this, the power of desire is ignited and loves, no differently than the wool is set on fire. He adds that this first love, kindled in the appetite of the senses by the interaction of the body, is created by looking with the eyes; but that very form is not imprinted in the imagination in the same way it exists in the matter of the body, but rather without matter—yet in such a way that it is the image of a specific person located in a certain place and time. Again, a certain species of this kind of image immediately shines in the mind, which no longer seems to be the likeness of one particular human body as it was in the imagination, but rather the common reason and definition of the entire human race. Therefore, just as from the image in the imagination taken from the body, a love inclined toward the senses arises in the appetite devoted to the body; so from this species of the mind and common reason, as if furthest removed from the body, another love is born in the will, most foreign to the interaction of the body. He placed the former in pleasure, the latter in contemplation. He thinks the former revolves around the particular form of one body, the latter around the universal beauty of the whole human race. These loves certainly fight against each other in man: the former drives him downward toward a beast-like and voluptuous life, while the latter lifts him upward toward an angelic and contemplative life. He wishes the latter to be without disturbance and found in few people; the former he says occupies many, anxious with many passions. Therefore, he dispatches the latter in few words, being more long-winded in describing the passions of the other. But since he explains here most clearly the same things you have related in the previous sections, I did not think it necessary to review them at present. Let it suffice to have known that this philosopher mixed a certain "chaos of formlessness" (such as you posited above) into the procreation of love, when he said the dark imagination is illuminated; and that from the mixture of that darkness and this light, love takes its origin. Furthermore, who would not see in his words that twin love, the celestial and the common? He even places its first origin in the beauty of divine things, and its second in the beauty of bodies. For he understands the sun to be the light of God, the ray to be the form of bodies. Finally, he wants its end to correspond to its beginning: while the instigation of love carries some all the way to the form of the body, it carries others all the way to the vision of God.

Thus far concerning love. Let us come to Alcibiades and Socrates. After the guests had sufficiently praised the god of lovers, it remained for the legitimate worshippers of this god to be praised. Socrates is held by everyone to have loved most legitimately of all. Since he had campaigned openly throughout his whole life without any dissimulation in the camps of Cupid, he was never noted by anyone as having loved anyone in a less than honorable way. The severity of his life and his frequent correction of others' crimes had made many great men hostile to him (as truth usually does), especially Anytus, Meletus, and Lycon, most powerful citizens in the republic; he also had the orators Thrasymachus, Polus, and Callias, and the very sharp comic poet Aristophanes as persecutors. But neither those citizens in the accusation by which they dragged Socrates to judgment included dishonorable loves; nor did his enemies the orators object to any such thing against Socrates; nor did Aristophanes the Comic poet, although he collected many other absurd curses against Socrates during the Dionysia. Do you think that if he had stained himself with such a foul blot—indeed, unless he had been furthest removed from the suspicion of this crime—he would have escaped the poisonous tongues of such detractors? Have you not noticed, best of men, in the previous sections, that while Plato fashions Love itself, he fashions the entire image of Socrates, and describes the figure of that deity from the person of Socrates? It is as if true love and Socrates are most similar, and therefore he, above all others, is the true and legitimate lover. Come now, recall the picture of Love to your mind. You will see Socrates figured in it. Place the person of Socrates before your eyes. You will see a lean, dry, and squalid man: a man naturally melancholic as they say, and hairy. Thin from fasting. Slovenly in the assembly. Naked besides, that is, covered by a simple and old little cloak. Walking without shoes. Phaedrus shows in Plato that Socrates was always accustomed to walk thus. Humble and flying through the lowest places. Socrates' gaze was always fixed on the ground, as Phaedo says. Moreover, he frequented cheap places: for he was found either in the shops of Simon the tanner or of the sculptors. He used rustic and unpolished words: which Callicles objects to him in the *Gorgias*. Furthermore, he was so mild that, though provoked by many injuries and often even struck, he is said not even to have been moved in his soul. Without a home. When Socrates was asked where he was from, he said: "A citizen of the world." For there is one's fatherland, where the good is. But he had neither his own hearth, nor a soft bed, nor delicate food, nor beautiful furniture. Sleeping at the doors in the street under the open sky. These things signify in our Socrates an open breast and a heart patent to all. Furthermore, he was delighted by sight and hearing, which are the doors of the soul: because he also walked secure and intrepid, and lay down even if it were necessary.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Wrapped in a cloak everywhere. Always needy. Who does not know that Socrates was the son of a sculptor and a midwife: and that until old age he sought his living by his own hand in carving stones, and never had enough from which to feed himself and his sons? He confessed the poverty of his mind everywhere, questioning everyone, proclaiming that he knew nothing. Manly: for he was of a constant mind and invincible opinion, who even spurned Archelaus of Macedon, Scopas of Cranon, and Eurylochus of Larissa with a high spirit: since he did not accept the money sent by them, nor did he wish to go to them himself. Bold and fierce. How great his fortitude was in matters of war, Alcibiades explains most copiously in the *Symposium*: to whom Socrates, when he had conquered in Potidaea, is said to have granted the victory of his own accord. Vehement: for he was, as Zopyrus the Physiognomist had rightly judged, most excitable. Often, indeed, while speaking, driven by the vehemence of his oration, he used to toss his fingers and pluck his hair. Eloquent.
<margin>B</margin> While he was debating, reasons nearly equal on both sides were available to him. Although he used unpolished words, as Alcibiades says in the *Symposium*, he nevertheless moved the minds of his listeners more than Themistocles and Pericles and all other orators. He lays snares for the beautiful and the good. Alcibiades says that Socrates was always laying snares for him. Indeed, captured by the love of those who seemed endowed with an honest nature, Socrates captured them in turn by his reasons for the study of Philosophy. A cunning and sagacious Hunter. It has been sufficiently said in the previous sections that Socrates was accustomed to hunt for the divine species from the form of the body: and Plato testifies to this in the *Protagoras*. A schemer. In many ways, as Plato's dialogues indicate, he refuted the sophists: he exhorted the youths, and he instructed modest men.
<margin>C</margin> Studious of prudence. For there was in him such great prudence, and he was so perspicacious in foreseeing: that whoever dared anything against his counsel would be ruined, which is narrated by Plato in the *Theages*. Philosophizing through his whole life. In his famous defense before the judges, he declared to the judges that if they acquitted him of death on the condition that he never philosophize thereafter, he would rather die than cease to philosophize. An enchanter, a fascinator, a sorcerer, and a sophist. For Alcibiades says he was soothed more by Socratic words than by the melody of Marsyas and Olympus, the excellent musicians. Both his accusers and his friends testify that a <term>Daemon</term> <note>a guiding spirit or divine voice</note> was familiar to him. Aristophanes the comic poet also called Socrates a sophist, as did his accusers.
<margin>D</margin> Indeed, he had an equal faculty for exhorting and dehorting. He was in the middle between wisdom and ignorance. Since all men are ignorant, Socrates says: "I differ from the others only in this, that I am not ignorant of my ignorance; while others are entirely ignorant." Thus he will be in the middle between wisdom and ignorance: because although he did not know the things themselves, he nevertheless recognized his own ignorance. For these reasons, Alcibiades judged Socrates to be most similar to Love and therefore the truest lover, to be praised after Love itself, so that in his praise we may understand that all who love in a similar way are praised. What the praises of Socrates are, you have heard here, and they are most clearly evident in Plato's words through the mouth of Alcibiades: in what manner Socrates loved, he who remembers the teaching of Diotima can know.
<margin>E</margin> For Socrates loved in the way Diotima taught above.

# ON FERAL LOVE,
# which is a species of insanity.

## CHAPTER III.

<margin>F</margin> But perhaps someone asks: What does this Socratic love benefit the human race? Why should it be celebrated with such great praises, and what harm does the contrary love do? I shall speak, having begun from a somewhat deeper point. Our Plato in the *Phaedrus* defines <term>furor</term> <note>divine madness or frenzy</note> as an alienation of the mind. He teaches that there are two kinds of alienation. He thinks one proceeds from human diseases, the other from God. He calls the former "insanity," the latter "divine frenzy." By the disease of insanity, a man is cast down below the species of man, and from a man is rendered in some way a brute. There are two kinds of insanity. One is born from a defect of the brain, the other from a defect of the heart. The brain is often occupied too much by burnt bile, often by burnt blood, and sometimes by black bile; hence men are sometimes rendered demented. Those who are vexed by burnt bile: they are most vehemently angered even when provoked by no one; they shout loudly; they rush at those they meet; they strike themselves and others. Those who suffer from burnt blood break out into excessive laughter; they boast beyond everyone's custom; they promise wonderful things about themselves; they delight in song and exult in dance. Those who are pressed by black bile grieve perpetually; they fashion dreams for themselves, which they either dread in the present or fear in the future. And these three species of insanity happen by a defect of the brain. For when those humors are retained in the heart, they produce anguish and anxiety, not dementia; but they produce madness when they have oppressed the head, therefore they are said to happen by a defect of the brain. But we think that insanity is properly caused by a disease of the heart, by which those who love ruinously are afflicted. To these, the most sacred name of love is falsely attributed. But lest we seem to be too wise against the many, for the sake of arrangement let us also use the name for them.

# COMMON LOVE IS
# a certain fascination.

## CHAPTER IIII.

<margin>H</margin> You, however, accommodate the intention of your ears and mind to the things to be said. Blood in youth is subtle, clear, warm, and sweet.

# ARGUMENTS AND COMMENTARY

<margin>A</margin> ...sweet. For as age advances and the finer parts are dissolved, the blood becomes thicker; for this reason, it also becomes darker. Naturally, that which is thin and rare is pure and transparent, while the opposite is true for the contrary. Why is it hot and sweet? Because life, and the beginning of living—namely generation itself—consists in heat and moisture; and semen, the first offspring of living things, is hot and moist. Such a nature flourishes in childhood and youth. In subsequent ages, it is necessarily changed little by little into the opposite qualities of dryness and coldness. Therefore, the blood in a youth is subtle <note>original: "subtilis," meaning refined or thin</note>, clear, hot, and sweet: because it is subtle, it is clear; because it is fresh, it is hot and moist; and because it is hot and moist, it therefore appears to be sweet. For sweetness arises from the mixture of the hot and the moist. Why mention these things? So that you may understand that the spirits <note>The "medical spirits" were thought to be thin vapors that carried life and sensation through the body</note> in this age are subtle and clear, hot and sweet. For since these are generated by the heat of the heart from the purest blood, they are always such within us as the humor of the blood is.

<margin>B</margin> Just as the vapor of the spirits is created in this way from the blood, so too it emits rays similar to itself through the eyes, as if through glass windows. And just as the sun, the heart of the world, sends down light in its circuit, and through that light its virtues to lower things, so the heart of our body, agitating the blood nearest to it by a certain perpetual motion, diffuses spirits from it into the whole body. Through these spirits, it spreads sparks of light through every limb, but most especially through the eyes. Indeed, since the spirit is lightest, it flies up to the highest parts of the body; and its light shines out more abundantly through the eyes, since they are transparent and the most polished of all parts.

<margin>C</margin> That there is some light, however small, within the eyes and brain can be proven by many animals that see at night, whose eyes flash in the darkness. Furthermore, if someone presses and twists the corner of the eye with a finger in a certain way, they seem to see a certain bright circle within themselves. It is also said that the Divine Augustus had eyes so bright and shining that when he looked at someone intently, he forced them to lower their gaze as if before the brilliance of the sun. Tiberius is also reported to have had very large eyes which—wonderfully enough—could see even at night and in the dark; but only for a short time, and when they first opened from sleep, after which they grew dim again. Moreover, we perceive that the ray emitted from the eyes draws spiritual vapor with it, and the vapor draws blood, from the fact that the bleary and red eyes of one person, by the emission of their ray, force the eyes of someone looking closely at them to suffer a similar disease. Here it appears both that the ray extends all the way to the person it meets, and that along with the ray, a vapor of corrupted blood flows out, by whose contagion the eye of the beholder is infected.

<margin>D</margin> But Aristotle says that women, when their menstrual blood flows, often stain a mirror with drops of blood by their gaze. I think this happens because the spirit, which is the vapor of blood, appears to be a kind of very thin blood, so much so that it escapes the sight of the eyes; but having become thicker on the surface of the mirror, it is clearly seen. If this falls upon a porous material or cloth or linen, it is not seen because it does not remain on the surface but penetrates it. If it falls on a dense but rough surface, such as stones, bricks, and the like, it is dissipated and broken by the inequality of that body. But a mirror, because of its hardness, stops the spirit on its surface; because of its evenness and smoothness, it keeps it unbroken; because of its brightness, it aids and increases the ray of the spirit itself; and because of its coldness, it forces that very thin mist into droplets. By almost the same reasoning, whenever we breathe hard with open mouths onto glass, we sprinkle its face with a very thin dew of saliva; for the breath flying out from the saliva, being compressed on that material, falls back into saliva. Therefore, what wonder is it if the eye, opened and fixed upon someone, shoots the stings of its rays into the eyes of the bystander? And also with those stings, which are the vehicles of the spirits, it aims that blood-vapor which we call spirit? Hence the poisonous sting pierces through the eyes; and since it is sent from the heart of the striker, it seeks out the chest <note>original: "praecordia," the region around the heart</note> of the stricken man as if it were its own proper region: it wounds the heart, and on its harder back it grows blunt and turns back into blood. This foreign blood, being somewhat alien to the nature of the wounded man, infects his own blood; the infected blood becomes sick. From this follows a double fascination <note>In this context, "fascination" refers to a literal physical bewitchment or infection through the gaze</note>. The sight of a foul old man or a menstruating woman fascinates a boy. The sight of a youth fascinates an elder. Because the humor of the elder is cold and very slow, it scarcely reaches the hardness of the heart in a boy; and being unfit for passage, it moves the heart very little unless it is very soft due to infancy. This is therefore a light fascination; but that other is most heavy, through which the younger pierces the chest of the elder. This is that thing, best of friends, about which the Platonist Apuleius complains: "The cause," he says, "and origin of all this present pain, and even the remedy itself and my only salvation, is you yourself. For those eyes of yours, having slipped through my eyes to my innermost heart, stir up a most sharp fire in my marrow. Therefore, have mercy on one perishing for your sake." Place before your eyes, I pray, Phaedrus of Myrrhinus and that Theban orator Lysias, who was captured by love for him. Lysias gapes at the face of Phaedrus; Phaedrus fixes the sparks of his eyes into the eyes of Lysias, and together with the sparks, he transmits the spirit. The ray of Phaedrus is easily joined to the ray of Lysias; spirit is also easily joined to spirit. A vapor of this kind, generated from the heart of Phaedrus, immediately seeks the chest of Lysias; by their dullness, it becomes thicker and falls back into the former blood of Phaedrus: so that, wonderfully, the blood of Phaedrus is now in the heart of Lysias. Hence both immediately break out into a cry: Lysias to Phaedrus: "My heart, Phaedrus, my dearest vitals!" Phaedrus to Lysias: "O my spirit, O my blood, Lysias!" Phaedrus follows Lysias because his heart demands its humor. Lysias pursues Phaedrus because the bloody humor demands its own vessel and requires its own seat. But Lysias pursues Phaedrus more ardently. For a heart lives more easily without a tiny particle of its humor than the humor itself lives without its own heart. A stream needs the spring more than the spring needs the stream. Therefore, just as iron, having received the quality of a magnet, 

<column-break/>

is drawn to this stone, but does not attract the stone; so Lysias follows Phaedrus more than Phaedrus follows Lysias.

### HOW EASILY WE ARE
### ensnared by love.

#### CHAPTER V.

<margin>A</margin> Can it be, someone might say, that a thin ray, a very light spirit, a little bit of Phaedrus's blood, can so quickly, so vehemently, and so destructively infect the whole of Lysias? This will certainly not seem strange if you consider other diseases born of contagion: itching, the scab, leprosy, pleurisy, consumption, dysentery, bleary eyes, or an epidemic. But the contagion of love happens easily and turns out to be the gravest plague of all. For that spiritual vapor and blood of the youth, having utterly infected the elder, has four qualities, as we said above. It is clear, subtle, hot, and sweet. Because it is clear, it greatly harmonizes with, flatters, and allures the clarity of the eyes and spirits in the elder; thus it is greedily drunk in by them. Because it is subtle, it flies very quickly into the chest; from there it flows most easily through the veins and arteries into the entire body. Because it is hot, it acts and moves vehemently, and more strongly infects the blood of the elder, converting it into its own nature, which Lucretius touched upon thus:

<margin>C</margin>
> From this, first into your heart a drop of the sweetness 
> of Venus trickled: and cold care followed.

Furthermore, because it is sweet, it somehow cherishes the vitals, feeds them, and delights them. Hence it happens that the whole blood of the man, changed into the nature of youthful blood, desires the body of that youth, so that it may inhabit its own veins, and that the humor of the blood may glide into veins that are also fresh and tender. It also happens that this sick man is touched by pleasure and pain at the same time. By pleasure, because of the clarity and sweetness of that vapor and blood. For the former allures, and the latter delights. By pain, because of its subtlety and heat. For the former divides and tears the vitals; the latter takes away from a man what is his own and changes it into the nature of another. By which change, indeed, it does not permit him to rest within himself, but always draws him toward the one by whom he was infected. Lucretius hints at this thus:

<margin>D</margin>
> And the mind seeks that body from which it is wounded by love.
> For almost all fall toward the wound: and the blood 
> spurts out toward that part from which we are struck by the blow.
> And if the enemy is at hand, the red humor occupies him.

<margin>E</margin> In these verses, Lucretius intends nothing other than that the blood of a man wounded by the ray of the eyes flows toward the wounder, just as the blood of a man slain by a sword flows toward the slayer. If you ask for the reason for this miracle, so to speak, I will provide it. Hector wounds Patroclus and kills him. Patroclus looks at Hector as he wounds him. From this, his thought judges that he must be avenged. Immediately, bile is kindled for vengeance; by it, the blood is inflamed and hurries instantly to the wound, both to cherish that part of the body and also for vengeance. The spirits also run to the same place; because they are light, flying all the way to Hector, they migrate into him, seething with his heat for a time—say, for seven hours. If in that very time Hector should look intently at the wound of the corpse from nearby, the wound ejects gore toward Hector; for the gore can flow out toward the enemy in a certain way, both because not all heat is yet extinguished and the internal agitation has not yet rested, and because it had been stirred toward him a little before, and finally because blood seeks its own spirits, and spirits also attract their own blood. In a similar way, Lucretius hints that the blood of a man wounded by love hastens toward the striker, and we most strongly approve of this.

### ON A CERTAIN WONDERFUL 
### effect of common love.

#### CHAPTER VI.

<margin>F</margin> Shall I say, O most chaste men, what follows; or rather pass it over? I shall certainly say it, since the matter itself demands it, even if it seems absurd to say. But who would speak of shameful things in a shameful way? Such a great transformation of the elder man, pressing toward the likeness of the youth, makes him strive to transfer his whole body into the other, and to pour the other's whole body into himself, so that either the fresh humor may reach fresh vessels, or the more tender vessels may reach the more tender humor. Hence they are compelled to do many most shameful things together. For since the genital seed flows from the whole body, they trust that by the casting or drawing of this alone they can give over their whole body and receive the whole. Lucretius, that Epicurean philosopher and most unhappy of all lovers, sensed this in himself:

<margin>G</margin>
> Thus, therefore, he who receives the blows from the weapons of Venus,
> Whether a boy hurls this at him with womanly limbs,
> Or a woman casting love from her whole body,
> He tends toward the place from which he is struck and longs to join:
> And to cast the humor drawn from the body into the body.
> They greedily cling to the body, and join the salivas 
> of the mouth: and they breathe into mouths, pressing with teeth,
> In vain: since they can scrape nothing away from there,
> Nor penetrate and pass into the body with the whole body.
> For they seem sometimes to wish to do so and to struggle.
> To such an extent do they cling to the couplings of greedy Venus,
> While the limbs of pleasure, weakened by force, melt away.

<margin>H</margin> Thus says Lucretius the Epicurean. That lovers also desire to take the beloved entirely into themselves is shown by Artemisia, the wife of Mausolus, King of Caria, who...

<margin>She is said to have loved her husband beyond the faith of human affection, and to have reduced the body of the deceased to powder, and having put it in water, drank it. <note>A reference to Artemisia II of Caria, who famously drank the ashes of her husband Mausolus.</note></margin>

# VULGAR LOVE IS
## a disturbance of the blood.

### CHAPTER VII.

<margin>A</margin> That this passion is indeed in the blood is evidenced by the fact that this kind of heat lacks alternating rest. Physicians place a continuous fever in the blood; that which leaves six hours for rest, in the phlegm <note>original: "pituita"</note>; that which leaves one day, in the bile; and that which leaves two days, in the humor of black bile. <margin>B</margin> Therefore, we rightly place this passion in the blood. Specifically in melancholic blood: as you heard in the speech of Socrates, a constant attachment always accompanies this contagion of the blood.

---

# HOW LOVERS
## become similar to the beloved.

### CHAPTER VIII.

Therefore, let none of you wonder if you hear that a lover has contracted some similarity or shape of his beloved in his own body. Pregnant women often intensely imagine the wine they desire to drink; intense thought moves the internal spirits and paints the image of the imagined thing in them. These spirits move the blood in a similar way and impress the image of the wine into the very soft matter of the fetus. A lover, however, desires his delights more ardently than pregnant women; he thinks more vehemently and firmly. What wonder is it if the faces, clinging and fixed so deeply in the breast, are purged from thought itself into the spirit, and from the spirit are immediately fixed in his own blood—especially since in the veins of Lysias the softest blood of Phaedrus has already been generated, so that the face of Phaedrus can most easily shine back in his own blood? Since the individual members of the body, just as they dry up daily, so they revive daily by taking in the dew of nourishment, it follows that every day the body of every man, which has gradually dried out, is little by little restored. The members are restored by the blood flowing from the streams of the veins. Therefore, will you wonder if the blood, painted with a certain likeness, has impressed the same on the members, so that Lysias finally seems to have turned out similar to Phaedrus in certain colors or features, or affections, or gestures?

---

# BY WHOM THEY ARE CHIEFLY
## ensnared.

### CHAPTER IX.

Someone will perhaps ask: by whom are lovers chiefly ensnared, in what manner, and how are they released? Women certainly capture men easily; but those who display a certain masculine disposition capture them more easily. And males capture more easily the more they are similar to men than to women, and have blood and spirit that is clearer, warmer, and more subtle—in which the snare of love consists. Among males, those fascinate men or women most swiftly who are primarily sanguine and partly choleric, having large, bluish-gray <note>original: "glaucos"</note>, and shining eyes—especially if they live chastely and have not defiled their serene faces by exhausting the clear juice of the humors through intercourse. For these things are specifically required to emit those arrows which wound the heart, as we touched upon above. <margin>G</margin> Furthermore, those are quickly ensnared at whose birth Venus was in Leo, or the Moon looked intensely upon Venus, and who are endowed with the same complexion. Phlegmatic people, in whom phlegm dominates, are never captured; Melancholics, in whom black bile dominates, are hardly captured at all—but once captured, they are never afterwards released. When a sanguine person overcomes a sanguine person, the yoke is light and the bond sweet, for a similar complexion creates mutual love. Furthermore, the sweetness of this humor provides hope and confidence to the lover. When a choleric person overcomes a choleric person, the servitude is more intolerable. The similarity of complexion does indeed create some reciprocity of goodwill in these, but that fiery humor of bile disturbs them with frequent anger. When a sanguine person overcomes a choleric person, or vice versa, because of the mixture of sweet and sharp humor, a certain alternation of anger and grace, pleasure and pain, arises. When a sanguine person binds a melancholic, the knot is perpetual but not most miserable, for the sweetness of the blood tempers the bitterness of the melancholy. But when a choleric person ensnares a melancholic, it is the most destructive plague of all. The sharpest humor of the youth glides everywhere into the internal organs of the elder. "A soft flame eats the marrow." <note>A quote from Virgil's Aeneid regarding Dido's love.</note> The unhappy lover is burned. Cholera provokes to anger and slaughter; Melancholy to sorrow and perpetual lamentation. To these, the end of love is often the same as it was for Phyllis, Dido, and Lucretius. A phlegmatic or melancholic youth, however, captures no one because of the thickness of his blood and spirits.

<column-break/>

# THE MANNER OF
## ensnarement.

### CHAPTER X.

We seem to have said enough above about how lovers are fascinated, if only we add this: that mortals are then most greatly fascinated when, directing the sharp edge of sight to sight in very frequent gazing, they join lights with lights and, miserable, drink in long love. Of this disease, as it pleases Musaeus <note>A legendary Greek poet.</note>, the eye is the entire cause and origin. Therefore, if someone excels in the brightness of the eyes, even if he is less well-composed in his other members, he often compels those gazing at him to go mad in the manner we have described. He who is disposed to the contrary invites a certain moderate goodwill rather than ardor. The harmony of the other members besides the eyes seems to have the force not of a cause for this kind of sickness, but of an impulsive occasion. For such a composition encourages one looking from afar to approach nearer; then it detains the one looking closely for a very long time in the consideration of itself; but while he lingers, the gaze alone strikes him. However, for that moderate love which participates in divinity—of which we mostly dispute in this banquet—not the eye alone as a cause, but the concord and pleasantness of all parts concur.

---

<margin>C</margin>
# THE CURE OF LOVE.

### CHAPTER XI.

Hitherto we have treated how and by whom people are ensnared; it remains for us to teach in a few words how they are released. The release is twofold: one of nature, the other of diligence. The natural one is that which is completed at certain intervals of time. This pertains not only to this disease, but to all. <margin>D</margin> Indeed, an itch remains on the skin as long as the dregs of tainted blood flourish in the veins or the saltiness of phlegm in the members. When the blood is purified and the phlegm softened, the itch ceases, and the foul spots of the skin are abolished. Nevertheless, the diligence of art contributes much to the nature of evacuation. Sudden evacuation or anointing is judged most dangerous. The restlessness of lovers also necessarily persists as long as that infection of the blood, cast into the vitals through fascination, remains and presses the heart with heavy care. "It feeds the wound in the veins; it burns the members with hidden flames." <note>Another Virgilian reference.</note> For the transition is from the heart into the veins, and from the veins into the members. Finally, when this is purged, the restlessness of lovers—or rather, of the mad—ceases. This requires a long space of time in all; but in melancholics, the longest—especially if they were ensnared by the influence of Saturn. <margin>E</margin> Add that it is most bitter if they are enslaved to Saturn in retrograde, or joined to Mars, or opposite the Sun. Those also remain sick for a very long time in whose nativity Venus was in the house of Saturn, or looked intensely upon Saturn and the Moon. To this natural purgation must be added the most diligent industry of art. We must take care first not to attempt to pluck out or cut off what is immature, nor should we cut apart with great danger what we can more safely unsew; a break in habit must be made. Above all, care must be taken that the lights of the eyes are not joined with lights. If there is any vice in the mind of the beloved, it must be diligently revolved in the mind. The mind must be applied to many, various, and serious affairs; blood must often be let; clear wine should be used, sometimes even to the point of drunkenness, so that when the old blood is emptied, new blood may arrive, and new spirit. It is often better to use exercise even unto sweat, through which the passages of the body are opened to perform a purging. Furthermore, all those things which Physicians apply for the protection of the heart and the nourishment of the brain are of the greatest benefit. <margin>F</margin> Lucretius also prescribes frequent intercourse:

> But it is fitting to flee the images and wipe away the food of love
> From oneself: and turn the mind elsewhere,
> And cast the collected humor into any bodies;
> Nor retain the seed gathered by the love of one.

---

# HOW HARMFUL VULGAR
## love is.

### CHAPTER XII.

<margin>H</margin> But lest we go mad by speaking too long about madness, let us conclude briefly thus. That anxious solicitude by which vulgar lovers are vexed day and night is a species of madness; while love lasts, they are afflicted first by the burning of bile, then by the scorching of black bile, and they rush into furies and fire; and as if blind, they know not where they are being precipitated. How ruinous this adulterous love is to both the beloved and the lovers, Lysias the Theban and Socrates demonstrate in Plato's *Phaedrus*. Thus, by this fury, man is devolved into the nature of a beast.

---

# HOW USEFUL DIVINE
## love is, and concerning its four species.

### CHAPTER XIII.

By divine fury, however, man is raised above human nature and passes into God. Divine fury is an illumination of the rational soul...

Ficino blends Platonic philosophy with Galenic humorism and astrological influences to describe the mechanics of attraction and the dangers of earthly passion.</summary>

--- Page 827 ---
<meta>This page continues the philosophical commentary on the nature of the soul and divine inspiration, likely from Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plato’s Symposium or Phaedrus. It transitions from the soul's descent into the body to the "divine frenzies" that lead it back to God.</meta>

# ARGUMENTS AND COMMENTARY

<margin>A</margin> ...through which God draws back the soul, which has fallen from the heavens to the lower realms, from the lower realms back to the heavens. The fall of the soul from the very One—the principle of all things—into bodies is effected through four stages: through mind, reason, opinion, and nature. For since in the whole order of things there exist six stages, of which the highest is held by the One itself and the lowest by the body, the middle four are those we previously mentioned: it is necessary that whatever falls from the first to the last must fall through the four intermediaries. The One itself is the limit and measure of all things, free from confusion and multiplicity. The angelic **Mind** is indeed a multiplicity of ideas, but stable and eternal. The **Reason** of the soul is a mobile but ordered multiplicity of notions and arguments. **Opinion**, however, is a disordered and mobile multiplicity of images, yet united in substance and points; for when the soul itself is in the state of opinion, it becomes a single substance occupying no place. **Nature**, <margin>B</margin> that is, the power of nourishment from the soul and the animal complexion, is similar, except that it is diffused through the points of the body. The **Body**, however, is an indeterminate multiplicity of parts and accidents subject to motion, and a substance divided by points and moments. Our soul looks upon all these; through these it both descends and ascends. For just as it is produced by the One itself, which is the principle of all things, it has obtained a certain unity which unites its entire essence, powers, and operations. In this way, the other things in the soul relate to it just as lines from the center and to the center of a circle. Indeed, it unites not only the parts of the soul to each other and to the whole soul, but the whole soul to the One itself, the cause of all things. <margin>C</margin> Moreover, as it shines with the ray of the divine mind, it contemplates the ideas of all things through the mind in a stable act. As it looks at itself, it thinks the universal reasons of things and runs from principles to conclusions by reasoning. As it looks at bodies, it revolves in opinion the particular forms and images of mobile things received through the senses. As it touches matter, it uses nature as an instrument by which it unites, moves, and forms matter. From this proceed generations, growth, and their opposites. You see, therefore, how from the One that is above eternity, it falls into eternal multiplicity; from eternity into time; from time into place and matter. It "falls," I say, when it departs further from that purity in which it was born by embracing the body.

<margin>D</margin>
## BY WHICH STAGES THE
## divine frenzies uplift
## the soul.

### CHAPTER XIIII.

Wherefore, just as it descends through four stages, it must necessarily ascend through four. Moreover, it is divine frenzy <note>original: "furor"; in the Renaissance, this referred to a state of being "possessed" by a god or inspired beyond human reason</note> which lifts one to the higher realms, as stands in its definition. There are, therefore, four species of divine frenzy. The first is the **poetic frenzy**. The second is the **mysterial** <note>relating to religious mysteries or initiations</note>. The third is **prophecy**. The fourth is the **affect of love**. Now, poetry is from the Muses, Mystery from *Dionysus*, Prophecy from *Apollo*, and Love from *Venus*. Indeed, the soul cannot return to the One unless it itself is made one. But it has been made "many," because it has fallen into the body, distributed into various operations, and looks toward an infinite multiplicity of corporeal things. Because of this, its higher parts almost fall asleep, while the lower parts dominate the others. The former are affected by torpor, the latter by perturbation. The whole soul is filled with discord and lack of harmony. Therefore, there is first a need for the poetic frenzy, which through musical tones arouses what is dormant; through harmonic sweetness soothes what is disturbed; and finally, through the consonance of diverse things, drives away dissonant discord and tempers the various parts of the soul. Nor is this enough. For multiplicity and diversity still remain in the soul. Therefore, the mystery pertaining to *Dionysus* approaches, which through expiations, sacrifices, and all divine worship, directs the intention of all parts toward the mind, by which God is worshipped. Whence, when the individual parts of the soul have been reduced to one mind, the soul has now become a certain "one" made out of many. But for this, a third frenzy is needed, which may lead the mind back to the unity itself, the head of the soul. *Apollo* effects this through prophecy. For when the soul rises above the mind into unity, it foretells the future. Finally, when the soul has been made one—the "one," I say, which is in the very nature and essence of the soul—it remains that it should immediately recall itself into the One which is above essence, that is, God. This the celestial *Venus* completes through love, that is, the desire for divine beauty and the ardor for the Good. Thus, the first frenzy tempers the unharmonious and dissonant. The second makes a single whole out of the tempered parts. The third makes a single whole above the parts. The fourth leads into the One which is above essence and above the whole. *Plato* in the *Phaedrus* calls the mind devoted to divine things the **charioteer** in the soul of man; the unity of the soul, the **charioteer's head**; reason and opinion running through natural things, the **good horse**; confused phantasy and the appetite of the senses, the **bad horse**; the nature of the whole soul, the **chariot**, because its motion is as if circular, beginning from itself and returning into itself when it notices its own nature. There, its consideration proceeding from the soul returns to the same. He grants wings to the soul by which it may be carried on high: one of which we think is that investigation by which the mind constantly strives toward truth; the other, the desire for the Good, by which our will is always affected. These parts of the soul lose their order when they are confused by the disturbing body. Thus, the first frenzy distinguishes the good horse (reason and opinion) from the bad horse (confused phantasy and sensory appetite). The second subjects the bad horse to the good, and the good to the charioteer (the mind). The third directs the charioteer toward his own head, that is, toward the unity 

<column-break/>

at the apex of the mind. The last turns the head of the charioteer toward the Head of all things. There the charioteer is blessed, and standing the horses at the manger—that is, at divine beauty—and accommodating all the parts of the soul subjected to him, he offers it ambrosia and nectar to drink: that is, the vision of beauty, and joy from that vision. These are the works of the four frenzies. He discusses these generally in the *Phaedrus*, but specifically the poetic frenzy in the *Ion*, and the amatory in the *Symposium*. That *Orpheus* was possessed by all these frenzies his books can bear witness. We have heard that *Sappho*, *Anacreon*, and *Socrates* were especially seized by the amatory frenzy.

---

## LOVE IS MORE EXCELLENT
## THAN ALL THESE FRENZIES.

### CHAPTER XV.

The amatory frenzy is the most powerful and excellent of all. Most powerful, I say, because all others necessarily lack it; for we attain neither poetry, nor mysteries, nor prophecy without burning zeal, flaming piety, and diligent worship of divinity. And what else do we call zeal, piety, and worship but love? Therefore, all loves consist of power. It is also the most excellent, since the others are referred to this as to an end. This, moreover, joins us most closely to God. These four frenzies are falsely imitated by four "adulterous" <note>counterfeit or corrupted</note> affects. Poetic frenzy is imitated by that vulgar music which only charms the ears. The mysterial by the vain superstition of many men. The prophetic by the deceptive conjecture of human skill. The amatory by the impulse of lust. For true love is nothing other than a certain effort to fly away to divine beauty, excited by the sight of corporeal beauty. Adulterous love, however, is a precipitation from sight into touch.

---

## HOW USEFUL SOCRATIC
## LOVE IS.

### CHAPTER XVI.

<margin>E</margin> You ask what *Socratic* love contributes? First, to *Socrates* himself, it contributes much toward recovering those wings by which he will fly back to his fatherland. Then, to his city, it contributes greatly toward living honorably and happily. Truly, men, not stones, make a city. Men, however, must be cared for from a tender age just like trees, and directed toward the best fruit. Parents and tutors have care of boys. But adolescents do not cross the boundaries of parents and tutors before they are depraved by the wicked customs of the common people. They would follow the higher norm of living they had imbibed, were they not turned aside from it by the use and custom of wicked men, especially those who flatter them. What then shall *Socrates* do? Will he permit the youth, who are the seed of the future republic, to be corrupted by the contagion of the shameful? <margin>F</margin> Where then is the love of fatherland? Therefore, *Socrates* will succor his fatherland and its sons, and deliver his brothers from this ruin. Perhaps he will write laws by which he will segregate lustful men from the company of adolescents. But we cannot all be *Lycurguses* or *Solons*. Authority for making laws is given to few; very few obey the laws once they are passed. What then? Will he use force, and by laying on hands drive the elders away from the youth? But only *Hercules* is said to have fought with monsters; for others, violence of this kind is most dangerous. Perhaps he will warn, correct, and rebuke the wicked men. But a disturbed mind despises the words of a monitor, and what is worse, rages against the one who warns. For this reason, *Socrates* was struck by one with a fist and by another with a heel while attempting this. The only way of safety remaining for youth is the company of *Socrates*. Therefore, that wisest of the Greeks, bound by charity, mixes himself everywhere, and <margin>G</margin> walks with a great crowd of adolescents following him. Thus the true lover, like a shepherd, protects the flock of lambs from the abyss and plague of false lovers, who are like wolves. Since, however, like very easily congregates with like, he makes himself like the younger ones through purity of life, simplicity of words, games, jokes, and wit. He makes himself a boy out of an old man, primarily so that he may eventually make the boys "old" <note>meaning wise or mature</note> through domestic and pleasant familiarity. Youth, prone to pleasure, is held by pleasure alone and flees rigid teachers. Hence the guardian of our youth, neglecting the administration of his own affairs for the safety of his fatherland, takes up the care of the juniors, and first captures them with the sweetness of pleasant company. Once they are thus ensnared, he then warns them more severely. Finally, he chastises them with a more rigid censure. In this way, he redeemed the youth *Phaedo*, who had been prostituted in a public brothel, from that calamity and made him a philosopher. He forced *Plato*, who was devoted to poetry, <margin>H</margin> to commit his tragedies to the fire and to take up more precious studies. He led *Xenophon* from vulgar luxury to the sobriety of the wise. He made *Aeschines* and *Aristippus* rich from being poor, *Phaedrus* a philosopher from an orator, and *Alcibiades* most learned from being ignorant. He made *Charmides* grave and modest, *Theages* a just and brave citizen in the republic. He transferred *Euthydemus* and *Menon* from the little traps of the Sophists to true wisdom. Thus it happened that the company of *Socrates* was not so much pleasant as it was useful, and *Socrates* was loved much more ardently by the adolescents, as *Alcibiades* says, than he himself loved.

<summary>This page outlines the Neoplatonic theory of the soul's descent through various levels of reality and its subsequent ascent through four "divine frenzies" (poetry, mystery, prophecy, and love). It concludes by defending "Socratic love" as a pedagogical tool used by Socrates to steer young men away from vice and toward philosophy.</summary>
