<meta>This page concludes Ficino’s commentary on the *Symposium* and begins his introduction to Plato’s *Phaedrus*. It maintains the Neoplatonic theme of Love as a divine guide to wisdom.</meta>

# MARSILIO FICINO

# HOW THANKS SHOULD BE GIVEN
### to the Holy Spirit, who has illuminated and inflamed us for this discussion.
### CHAPTER XVII.

**N**ow, therefore, we seem to have successfully discovered—first from your discussion and then from mine—what the love of the best Banquet is, who the true lover is, and what the utility of the lover may be. Moreover, consider without a doubt that the cause and teacher of this most happy discovery was that very same Love who has been discovered. For, inflamed by the love of finding love (if I may put it that way), we sought love and found it, so that thanks must be given to him equally for the seeking and the finding. O wondrous magnificence of this divinity! O incomparable kindness of Love! For other divinities hardly show themselves for a moment after you have sought them for a long time. Love even runs to meet those who seek him. Wherefore men confess they owe themselves much more to him than to the others. There are, however, those who often dare to curse the divine power, the thunderer against our crimes. Some even hate the wisdom that explores all our disgraces. But we cannot help but love Love, the giver of all divine goods. We, moreover, shall worship this Love who is so favorable to us with such a mind that we venerate Wisdom and admire Power, so that with Love as our leader we may have (so to speak) the whole of God favorable to us; and loving the whole with the fire of love, we may enjoy the whole of God in perpetual love.

## ARGUMENT FOR THE
### PHAEDRUS to page 375.

**O**ur Plato, pregnant with the frenzy of the poetic muse—which he followed from a tender age, or rather from his Apolline birth—first gave birth to a book that is almost entirely poetic; and being the most radiant of men, a man most beautiful and most worthy of the love of all, he wrote concerning beauty and love together, so that he deservedly brought forth his other children thereafter full of charm and grace. Having made a happy beginning from the Muse Venus, he alone of all men everywhere joined charm with dignity. Since, however, we have explained many mysteries of this book in our *Theology* and in the book *On Love*, we shall touch upon its argument very briefly. The *Symposium* treats chiefly of Love, and consequently of beauty. But the *Phaedrus*, for the sake of Beauty, disputes concerning love. Nor is the speech of Lysias and the oratorical discussion inserted without reason. For beauty pertains to the mind, to sight, and to hearing. Thus it happens that where the beauty of souls and names is discussed, as well as the beauty of the body, the beauty of speech is deservedly debated. Immediately at the very beginning, Socrates, while joking, delivers very serious precepts: that all things must be utterly despised for the sake of the study of wisdom, and that the most important study of wisdom is to consider oneself. Among these things, the most skillful description of the place allegorically signifies the Academy: the Plane tree signifies Plato; the chaste shrub signifies the chastity of Platonic and Socratic love; the fountain signifies bounty in communicating wisdom; the other ornaments signify the oratorical and poetic flowers in which Plato’s Academy abounds. Lysias is rightly reproved because he inquires into the nature of the affection of love without first defining or distinguishing love itself. Consider among these things the modesty of Socratic love, for being about to pronounce some things less honorable, he begins with his head covered. Soon he invokes the Muses, so that they might at least honor a less honorable matter with their own splendor of elocution. But before he censures base love, lest he fall into the same crime as Lysias, he defines base love as a certain desire or lust rebelling against reason, which overcomes the opinion tending toward the right and snatches one toward the pleasure of form. But while he proceeds to define it, he gives us two leaders: one an innate appetite for pleasure, the other a certain legitimate opinion acquired gradually through discipline and leading to honorable things. Truly, two external forces move these internal leaders: an airy <term>Demon</term> <note>In the Neoplatonic sense, a 'daemon' is a mediating spirit between gods and men, not necessarily evil.</note> moves opinion, and a watery one moves lust. After he has defined it, he separates youths from base lovers by many reasons. Then, meanwhile, note a wonderful mystery, similar to the Mosaic mystery <note>Ficino often sought to harmonize Plato with the Hebrew tradition of Moses.</note>. Into the very beginning of most evils, some demon has mixed pleasure. Because he acts not so much a philosophical as a poetic persona, he suddenly feels himself seized by a demon because he censured Love, which is the name of a God. He does this so that, being about to distinguish Love, he may distinguish it in a poetic rather than a dialectic manner. In these things you will notice that it is a most grave sin to offend against the name of a god. Again, there is a power of prophecy in the soul. Then, by certain poetic windings, he separates art from frenzy. He divides frenzy into divine and human. The divine he divides into four: namely, prophecy, mystery, poetry, and love. He confirms providence and religion. He places wisdom infused by divine frenzy far before human wisdom. Before he proceeds to the treatise on particular souls, he brings forward the common souls, namely the soul of the world, which he names Jove, and under it the twelve souls of the twelve mundane spheres, to which he subjects as many orders of demons and as many particular

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> souls. To each he assigns a chariot, that is, celestial and eternal bodies. He disputes concerning rational souls, both divine and human, and the circuit of both; and by what means the souls of men accompany the contemplation of the celestial souls in heaven, just as they follow the angelic intuition above heaven. What the Chariot, the vehicle, the wings, the charioteer, the horses, fate, and the fall into the body signify in the soul, and again what the great Jupiter in heaven and the other following Gods signify, we explain in our *Theology*. It will be enough for you at present to understand that the twin wings are a twin instinct innate to the mind, lifting the soul to the heights: in the intellect, an instinct toward the divine truth; in the will, an instinct turning toward the divine good according to its strength. When these are relaxed, and the inclination of the vegetative nature is stretched toward governing bodies, the Pythagoreans believe that the 
<margin>B</margin> souls, with their wings now broken, descend into the elements. After this, he distributes the soul falling from heaven into nine grades. In all these things he uses poetic license and relates Pythagorean rather than his own views. Among these things, notice that a similar fall of souls is described by the Pythagoreans as the fall of demons by the prophets. Also, that the number nine is as appropriate to the angelic choirs as to the demons fallen from there. Never mind now that Pherecydes the Syrian relates that a similar fall happened to demons. And he adds that Ophioneus, that is, the demonic serpent, was the head of the army rebelling against the divine mind. Similar to this is what is contained in the divine mysteries: namely, that Jove thrust down the lower demons to the underworld. But let us return to the 
<margin>C</margin> dialogue. Finally, the man with a purified mind dedicated to God is filled with all goods from there, and he alone is wise, although, being placed as if outside himself, he is commonly thought to be raving like a madman. After this, he descends to the divine frenzy of legitimate love, which he thinks is kindled in the soul when, beholding the beautiful form of a body, it easily remembers the divine beauty which it had once contemplated, and is inflamed with the desire of recovering it, and raves. But he describes a contrary frenzy as if bestial, not ascending from the form of the body to divine intuition, but basely descending to venereal intercourse. He describes again a certain human frenzy between the divine and the bestial, kindled in the soul of one who, occupied by admiration of the 
<margin>D</margin> bodily form, neither consigns the divine entirely to oblivion nor fully remembers it. Thus it happens that he is neither entirely intemperate nor entirely temperate, but appears now as if incontinent, now continent. Seeking afterwards the causes for which some love others more or less, he flees to the stars, whose companions the souls were from the beginning. For he arranges as many orders of human souls in the *Timaeus* as there are stars in heaven. From here he returns again to dividing the powers of the soul: and he calls reason the charioteer, and the twin appetites the twin horses: the rational appetite the good horse, the irrational appetite the bad horse. But in this genus, the appetite verging toward anger is less bad; that declining toward 
<margin>E</margin> concupiscence is more bad. Then he depicts the passions of lovers, both continent and incontinent, and mutual love like a poet. Thus it happens that these must be indulged allegorically no differently than the Songs of Solomon. These things being done, when he had treated of the beauty which pertains to the mind and to sight, he now proceeds to examine the speech of Lysias and to demonstrate the duty of the orator, so that it may be clear what the beauty of speech is which pertains to hearing. He places the beauty of speech in order, namely that it should have a head differing from the end, and have middle parts, necessarily coupled to the head and the end and to each other. He commands this kind of order to be observed by the orator above all. Moreover, he proves that no one can be an orator of things unless he has knowledge of things, 
<margin>F</margin> especially human things and souls. So that the orator may attain this, he commands that he learn from the dialectician the faculty of dividing and composing, which he wishes to be the principal instrument for investigating and finding truth, and in the *Philebus* he calls it a gift of God, because just as it is the perpetual office of God in the world to divide and compose, so it is of the dialectician in his art. Therefore, he judges that the consummate dialectician, that is, the metaphysician, should be worshipped as a god. After this, he compares orators in turn and censures those who, preferring the probable to the true, deceive the people and [claim] to be able to know through the knowledge of the truth itself. Soon follow certain excellent and noted precepts. Three things are first necessary for an orator: Talent, Doctrine, and Practice. 
<margin>G</margin> Philosophy is necessary for the very perfection of any art. From dialectical practice and the contemplation of sublime things, sublimity of mind and a force effective for acting are finally acquired. These two are greatly necessary in the perfection of the greatest arts. Then he compares the illegitimate orator to cooks and flatterers, just as in the *Gorgias*; but the legitimate one to a doctor. Furthermore, he delivers the rule by which the nature of the soul as well as the body, or rather of any thing, is to be known, and immediately returns to the duty of the orator. He adds that for the sake of the duty of writing, letters were invented in Egypt by a certain demon, Theuth, together with the other disciplines. Furthermore, he mocks the zeal for writing in one who trusts to reveal the 
<margin>H</margin> undoubted truth to posterity through letters. And in the manner of the Pythagoreans, he approves the contemplation and tradition of truth in souls rather than in books. Which he also confirms in his letters. Finally, he praises only the orator who is a philosopher by talent and study. He concludes the dialogue with a prayer and vows seeking beauty of the soul from God. In which, consider that Socrates, having utterly despised all other things, is content with the beauty of the soul alone, that is, wisdom; nevertheless, he indicates that this very thing is acquired not so much by human study as by divine gift.

<summary>Ficino concludes his commentary on the Symposium by praising Love as a divine guide and begins an introduction to Plato's Phaedrus, interpreting its themes of divine frenzy, the soul's chariot, and the superiority of oral wisdom over written text.</summary>

# AN ARGUMENT ON THE APOLOGY
## of Socrates. For page 358.

<margin>A</margin>The ancient Theologians of the nations were divided into three sects. Some indeed sacrificed only to demons <note>original: "dæmonibus"; in this context, "daemons" refers to intermediary spirits, not necessarily evil "demons" in the modern sense</note>, distrusting, as I believe, that the vows of men could reach the celestial beings. Others truly worshipped the celestial beings as well, thinking that they not only live and understand, but also look upon all things with their rays and hear them; therefore, they believed the rites of sacrifices are overseen by them, just as the praises and prayers of suppliants are heard. Nevertheless, they felt the vows of souls living in these bodies could not reach those gods who have no commerce with bodies. Finally, others venerated these very gods above all, judging that from the highest causes of things, all effects—even human ones—are most perfectly contained both in knowledge and in power. They called these gods "visible" (that is, celestial) and "invisible" (that is, super-celestial), whom our people call angels, and they themselves call gods, as if they were the nearest contemplators and ministers of the highest God. Furthermore, they think there is a triple providence. A universal one in God, through which He foresees and provides all things for all. A less universal one in the gods, through which they indeed consult for all, yet do not exhibit all gifts, but only certain ones to all. Finally, a particular providence in the daemons, by which they bestow certain things upon certain individuals. And they distribute the daemons into as many orders as there are stars in heaven, so that some are of Saturn, others Jovial <note>of Jupiter</note>, and others similarly. They place all these orders in fire (but a rational fire), and in pure air (but of an aerial reason), and in thick air (of a watery reason). They think these watery ones preside over different species of living things and favor sensual and vegetative nature everywhere. These are the ones Plato says, right from the beginning, mixed pleasure with many evils. But the aerial daemons favor the rational power instead, and in a way segregate it from the vegetative and sensual nature. Finally, the fiery ones turn the discourse of reason toward the contemplation of more sublime things. And in this way, the watery daemons rule the voluptuous life, the aerial the active life, and the fiery the contemplative life.

<margin>B</margin>Indeed, they consider the gods to be immortal and impassible <note>incapable of suffering or feeling passion</note>, but men to be mortal and passible; the daemons are all indeed passible in affection, but the superior and middle ones are also immortal, while the lowest are long-lived. Furthermore, they place in all of them an affection toward corporeal things: but in the first, according to a certain manner of tranquil providence; in the second, human-like indeed, but moderate; in the third, already declining toward our disturbances. Likewise, some daemons are natural, established from the beginning, while others are "foreign"—namely, the souls of men translated into aerial bodies, caring for those things which they were previously accustomed to by reason. Furthermore, some daemons preside over larger regions of the earth, others over narrower places and cities. Certain ones even govern individual men; these are the ones which souls falling into the body have obtained by lot according to their virtue and choice, thereafter serving as leaders, scouts, and judges of the chosen life. Accordingly, some souls of men are accommodated to the natures of Saturnian daemons, others to Jovial ones, others to other stars and daemons. The complexions of our bodies are also distinguished by a similar reasoning. Likewise, animals, plants, metals, and stones are naturally discerned among themselves according to the variety of stars and daemons, so that some among these are solar, others lunar, and so forth. In these things we have mentioned, the Platonists believe the entire power of sacrifices, oracles, and divinations consists. Certainly, Plato himself, imitating the more ancient theologians, and all Platonists everywhere accept the history of oracles as true and confirm them with reasons.

<margin>C</margin>I pass over how much faith he gives to these in the *Phaedrus* and in the *Timaeus*: in the *Phaedrus* indeed, weighing human wisdom as nothing compared to that which is held from oracles and divine furies; and in the *Timaeus*, saying that a philosopher should affirm things concerning divine matters only insofar as they are confirmed by divine oracles. I pass over many similar things in Plato. Certainly, in the *Apology*, he begins the entire defense of his Socrates from oracles and prophecies; indeed, what is greatest, he asserts that the entire life of Socrates—the wisest and most just of men—was instituted both according to the oracle of Apollo and the prophecy of a certain daemon of his own.

<margin>D</margin>If you ask what kind of daemon that of Socrates was, the answer is: fiery, because it raised him to the contemplation of sublime things. Also Saturnian, because it daily withdrew the intention of his mind from the body in a wonderful way. It was also attributed from the beginning, not acquired. For he says it breathed upon him from childhood. It never provoked him to action, because it was not Martial <note>of Mars</note>, but often recalled him from actions, because it was Saturnian. Likewise, it did not apply spurs to a man already inclined toward honorable things by himself, but held him back with a bridle where he might seem to be deceived in choosing paths to an end due to the fallacy of conjectures. It breathed upon his mind, suggested signs to his eyes, and voices to his ears. But to which eyes and ears? Namely, to the sight and hearing which are produced through the entire ethereal body lurking beneath this manifest body. For Socrates was able to perceive through ethereal senses, easily recalling himself from the elemental senses.

<margin>E</margin>He discerned things shown through those same senses both while dreaming and while awake. Similarly, Avicenna <note>Persian polymath and philosopher</note> proves that prophets both see the forms of angels and hear their voices. But why do Socrates and a few like him notice their daemon? Because few are "daemonic" by birth or discipline; more are "human," and most are "feral" <note>beast-like</note>. Why, likewise, does he sometimes call it a daemon and sometimes God? Because the sublime daemon breathed upon Socrates as an interpreter and messenger of God. But can we call the very intellect of Socrates a daemon? We certainly can. For Timaeus says that God gave us the supreme part of the soul as a daemon. Again, in the *Symposium*, the very love of the mind for contemplating divine beauty is named a daemon. But besides these, it is necessary

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>that a substance superior to us preside as a daemon, because, as is proved in the *Symposium* and the *Laws*, the human race—being most distant from divine things—needs a middle nature, such as the daemonic, as a sort of conciliator. Nor did divine providence unjustly set over us closer daemons as shepherds (as proved in the *Statesman* and *Protagoras*), or as "governors" (as it says in the *Critias*). For man, placed in this darkness of ignorance and agitated by the innumerable evils of fortune or distracted by allurements, cannot reach the end established for him by God without the perpetual help of God. Hence he proves that God commended us to purer daemons as rulers, who might help through prophecies, auguries, dreams, oracles, voices, sacrifices, and inspirations.

<margin>B</margin>He wishes the familiar daemon of Socrates to be from this number, differing from the Socratic mind. For the mind often provokes Socrates, but the daemon never provokes. Likewise, the mind cannot teach except by speaking or writing. But the daemon, as proved in the *Theages*, taught many even by remaining silent. Furthermore, the fact that it corrects Socrates with both voice and signs signifies that this daemon is something beyond the mind. But if it pleases you less to call the familiar leader of a man a "daemon," then at least call it a "good angel," as pleases our people <note>referring to Christians</note>. After this, the *Apology* compels us to treat somewhat of oracles and statues. First, if you ask for what reason daemons no longer perform those accustomed miracles in our ages: the answer is that Christ both deprived the evil daemons of that power of theirs, and removed from man both all worship of daemons and the daemonic art.

<margin>C</margin>If you ask again by what reasoning the influences of daemons are drawn into statues or into men, attend diligently. Something natural is drawn daily through art: as whenever wood, which because of its dense thickness could not be ignited by a thin flame, is either smeared with oil or stained with sulfur and catches the flame in the tinder. And something divine is also drawn daily through nature, when a tender fetus in the womb is figured in a certain affection and manner; thus through nature it draws a human soul from God, just as through magic a statue receives a daemon from the world.

<margin>D</margin>Whence the Egyptians also called nature "great," placing the magic power itself in a certain attraction of likes by likes, or at least of fitting things through fittingness. You emit a voice daily, and you emit the image of your face. But your voice and image are not reflected back to you everywhere. Only a wall so disposed and so positioned reflects the voice through an echo, and a mirror-like body returns your image to you. Let that wall also be mirror-like, and suddenly you will be entirely, so to speak, in it. For there you will be seen, heard, and understood almost like a daemon in a statue. If you consult Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus, legendary Hellenistic figure</note>, you will say that a statue rightly composed of the world's own materials congruent to a certain daemon is immediately animated by the congruent daemon—or by an angel, he says. Understand that it is accustomed to be breathed upon either by impurity or by a purer spirit.

<margin>E</margin>You also hear this Mercury <note>Trismegistus</note> condemning most of the ancients because, distrusting either that there were divinities above heaven or that the vows of earthly beings could reach the celestial and superior ones, they fabricated statues as habitations of daemons, whom they might worship as familiar gods. He thought, to be sure, that although sometimes salutary daemons were called into the shrines, often noxious ones descended. Hear in a few words the drawing of daemons into the bodies of statues. Hear also in a few words the snatching into the bodies of men. When, either through black bile or something similar, or a vice, the whole mind is turned into imagination, it easily becomes a domicile of lower daemons, by whose presence it may both go mad and be vexed in mind and body at once. When through philosophical purgation it is transferred entirely into reason, it becomes a temple of middle daemons,

<margin>F</margin>from whom it may receive wonderful reasons for human affairs more often, and sometimes even for natural ones. When through piety it is raised entirely into the mind, it becomes a breathing-hole for sublime daemons, or rather for angels, by whose leadership it may penetrate the secrets of divine things in a wonderful way. You wish, I see, to understand which oracles specifically—whether issued through statues or through men—Plato trusts. Know: only those which are found by certain reason to have been promised not by deceptive daemons, but by truthful ones, or rather by angels. For he had received from the very mysteries of the Egyptians that Jove <note>Jupiter/God</note> cast down the impurer daemons to the lower regions, who also similarly twist men toward the depths according to their power; and from Pherecydes the Syrian, that many daemons rebelled against Jove, whose army the serpentine Ophioneus led. He judged, therefore, that one must guard most diligently against these evildoers.

<margin>G</margin>Socrates, however, led by his own reasons and individual cases, committed himself to a certain oracle and to a certain daemon of his own to be led at its will. Finally, he so instituted his life toward these things that he always preferred eternal things to temporal ones: he feared injustice more than death: for the sake of truth, piety, and charity, he did not hesitate to undergo labors, poverty, insults, injuries, beatings, and death. For him, truth among men brought forth false calumnies, charity brought hatred, and piety brought an impious accusation and death. But he weighed all these as little, indeed as nothing, hoping to merit good things from the divine judge in exchange for good deeds.

<margin>H</margin>Therefore, relying on this hope and confidence, he both approached the judges freely and did not excuse himself, but accused the judges; and like a seer (which he says happens to those who are near death), he predicted repentance and punishment for them to follow after the false judgment, and he meanwhile migrated to the eternal judge with wonderful joy of mind and alacrity of countenance. I had decided to put a sufficiently honorable end to this argument or rather little commentary here. But two doubts delay me for a moment. First, that Socratic saying repeated both here and often elsewhere: *This one thing indeed I know, that I know nothing.* Yet he affirms many things both here and elsewhere as if knowing. But this is similar to: *I said in my excess, every man is a liar.* Thus Socrates says: I, abstracted from the body, snatched by a daemon, enlightened by God, know indeed...

<sig>Xxx iij</sig>

It reconciles Platonic spiritualism with Christian concepts of angels and divine providence.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentaries on the Platonic dialogues, specifically focusing on the character and philosophy of Socrates as presented in the Apology, Crito, and Phaedo.</meta>

# MARSILIO FICINO

<margin>A</margin> From the divine light comes this one thing: namely, that being otherwise joined to the body, I know nothing by natural light. I do not know, I say, in the natural light, things themselves through the mode of affirmation. For knowledge of that kind is proper to God, who comprehends both the natures themselves and the causes of those natures, since he himself made them. Yet I know many things through a certain mode of negation. For example, that God is not a body, rather than what He is. Likewise, that the soul is not mortal, rather than what it is. Again, that the absolute good is not this or that particular good, rather than what it is.

<margin>B</margin> And in this manner, Socrates both knows and teaches many things. Furthermore, there is the fact that his spirit <note>original: "daemon"</note> recalls him but does not provoke him; that is, it illuminates him toward denying rather than affirming. Sometimes, however, he does affirm certain things, and great things at that, as one not only seized by a spirit but already full of God. He also affirms when he brings forward the testimonies of the ancient saints, or cites the souls of men rising from the dead as testimony. There follows another doubt: for what reason does Socrates—since he never seems to doubt that the soul is immortal—use this distinction at the end of the *Apology*: "Either no sense remains after death, or some remains"? He responds first, indeed, not concerning all sense—that is, all cognition—but concerning the sense of our affairs, or something similar to ours. This is signified by those things which are then added in the other part of the distinction, where he says the same as in the *Republic*: namely, that separated souls recognize themselves there in the same way they were accustomed to here.

<margin>C</margin> Here, consider what is said against those who say that souls transmigrate from bodies into other bodies. Then, he also responds more safely that Socrates does not use this distinction in the present case because he thinks there is cause for doubt—for he holds most constantly to the truth both through negative knowledge and through divine inspiration and approval—but he looks to the persons of his adversaries in the present moment. Since they were entirely eager to harm him, they threatened him with death as if it were undoubtedly an evil. Socrates, therefore, asserts to the contrary that it is in no way an evil, whether our affairs be thus or otherwise. Where that which appears ambiguous concerning mortality is added on account of those who, like tyrants in the Epicurean manner, might have mocked Socrates as if he could be easily deceived if he had affirmed that death was not an evil solely because other goods remain after this life. These eternal goods, even if they were established for Socrates, were in no way established for them, nor could they be demonstrated in that narrow brevity of time, though they are demonstrated in the *Phaedo* and often elsewhere.

<margin>D</margin> But you, note the certain confidence of our Socrates, saying to his friends near the end of the *Apology*: "You ought to hope well concerning death. For nothing evil can happen to a good man, living or dead." For the affairs of a man who is in some way similar to God are not neglected by God. As for his crying out to the judges with his final voice, "I indeed go hence to die, but you to live; which of us goes to the better part is certain only to God": understand that he does not doubt what he affirmed shortly before, but says it is certain to God alone through Himself and the reason of affirmation; yet it can become certain to man through God Himself and the reason of negation. Add that he does not dare to affirm that he departs with a soul so purified that he may affirm his soul will immediately be restored to the heavenly fatherland.

## ON THE CRITO
### Argument. For page 369.

Just as with the *Apology*, so the disposition of the *Crito* is so orderly and plain that it needs no summary. Note first, however, that just as Socrates prophesied while awake in the *Apology*, so in the *Crito* he prophesies while sleeping, so that you may know that God is always present to a wise and pious man, both waking and sleeping. From all this, gather a confirmation of Gospel doctrine: the approval of martyrs, the exemplar of justice, incomparable fortitude, contempt for mortal things, desire for eternal things, and finally the foundation of religion. Why should I mention that the opinion of the crowd is to be despised, and only the judgment of the wise—indeed, truth itself—is to be honored? Why, again, that one should not desire merely to live, but to live well? Likewise, that one must never do evil to enemies, nor return injuries? Again, that the danger of death and destruction must be undergone rather than sinning? Why should I relate his singular observance of the laws and his inestimable love of country, which he undoubtedly prefers to parents and life? For this reason, as he himself says: so that having set out into the other life, he may be able to give a just account of his past life to the eternal Judge, and not be compelled to dread the laws that rule there, which are the sisters of human laws. He concludes, finally, that the reasons favoring justice ring in the ears of his mind to such an extent that he cannot hear others; and he would labor in vain to dissuade him, wherever he might go. He adds that one must proceed only by that path where God—that is, reason divinely infused—leads.

## ON THE PHAEDO
### Argument. For page 375.

Our book on religion proves, by a fact sufficiently known in itself, that the life of Christ is the Idea of all virtue. Moreover, the eighth book of our *Letters* demonstrates that the life of Socrates is a certain image,

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> or at least a shadow, of the Christian life: and indeed it confirms the Old Testament through Plato, and the New through Socrates. If anyone doubts this Socratic similarity, let him read Xenophon and Plato, and the others who recorded the words and deeds of Socrates, especially Plato’s *Gorgias*, *Apology*, *Crito*, and *Phaedo*. We shall therefore run through the argument of this *Phaedo* with a swift step, or rather a leap. For we seem to have explained its mysteries sufficiently in our *Theology*. We will first advise this one thing: let no one wonder that Socrates, among the arguments pertaining to the immortality of the soul, omitted here that one in which he places sole confidence in the *Phaedrus*: namely, that the soul is the principle of motion, from which it follows that it

<margin>B</margin> is moved by itself and perpetually, and lives forever. For this was done by Socrates because that kind of reasoning is common not only to our souls but also to celestial and demonic souls. In the *Phaedo*, however, reasons more proper to us are required. But let us now come to the briefest disposition of the dialogue. In the beginning, it must be observed how wonderfully Socrates consoles his friends, who greeted him in prison as if to console him on the very day he was to drink the poison. Then, how religiously he observes even the precepts of dreams as if they were certain oracles: and how extremely cautious he is in this, lest he fail in even the slightest way regarding divine commands. Thirdly, it must be committed to memory that men are under the constant guardianship of God, and it is not permitted to depart hence

<margin>C</margin> except when God wills it. In the fourth place, it must be carefully noted what he means when he says he hopes in death to go to good men and other good gods: but he affirms more strongly that he will go to good gods than to good men. First, indeed, because he speaks of "other and very good gods," he understands that besides the souls of the spheres, there are angelic minds higher than the spheres. Into whose familiarity he hopes our souls may also one day be admitted: yet he does not dare to assert it, because it seemed to many wise men that it would be enough for the soul if it were eventually received into the company of the celestial souls. Indeed, doubt properly falls upon that part which calls them "good men." For he does not then dare to affirm that the souls of men are good by the same reasoning by which he called the gods good.

<margin>D</margin> After this, intending to console both himself and his friends under the persona of one philosophizing, he says: Since the whole study of one philosophizing is a certain separation from the body, and is perfected daily through it, surely he ought not only not to fear the separation from the body which occurs through death, but should expect it with the best hope and joy. Soon he shows in two ways that the philosopher separates the soul from the body. First, indeed, from disturbances through the purgation of moral discipline; then from the senses and the imagination itself through the intensity of contemplation itself. Wise physicians use a twofold purgation. The first by soothing; the second by dissolving: knowing that it is neither enough to soothe, nor safe to dissolve before you soothe. Similarly, among philosophers, moral purgation

<margin>E</margin> precedes as a soothing agent. For it does not root out the interior diseases of the imagination—that is, the deceptions. There follows the speculative purgation, sometimes dispersing the clouds of the imagination according to one's strength. But it is not safe to approach the office of speculation before moral purgation, lest someone infected with the diseases of vices abuse the very sharpness of speculation to defend injustice and impiety. From these things, he concludes that the philosopher, to the extent that he segregates the edge of the mind from corporeal things, to that extent joins it to incorporeal reasons and Ideas. But when he had numbered many inconveniences brought upon the soul by the body, he added that the last and greatest of evils is that fallacy by which the imagination, while the mind is elevating itself to incorporeal things, very often distracts it toward certain images of bodies and forces it to think in a certain corporeal way.

<margin>F</margin> After this, from the fact that the soul, joined to the body, cannot attain the very truth of separated things which it naturally desires, he asserts through a distinction: either it never attains it, or it does after death. But it is not consistent that it should never attain it, since it is perpetually desired by every mind. Therefore, he disapproves of those who think temperance is to abstain from smaller pleasures of the body so that they may later obtain greater pleasures of the body. Again, those who define fortitude as overcoming certain fears for the sake of those fears which have already overcome us. For he wants every office of moral virtue to be occupied in a certain purgation of the soul for the sake of wisdom. Otherwise, there would be

<margin>G</margin> no virtue. Indeed, he even calls human wisdom a certain purification, just as if he thinks we attain nothing else by the meditation of our wisdom than a certain purity, which divine illumination—which is properly wisdom—soon follows. He signifies, moreover, that it is not so much a habit acquired by our labors as the purification itself that joins us to God. These things being done, intending to prove the immortality of the soul, he says that a progression occurs from one kind of opposites into the other, and a regression in turn. Therefore, just as the dead are made from the living, so the living sometimes rise again from the dead. Here he seems to prophesy the resurrection of the dead, which he also approves in the *Statesman* <note>original: "Politico"</note>. Furthermore, he hints through long circuits that just as

<margin>H</margin> both the substance of heaven and the matter of the elements pass infinitely from one disposition to another in turn, so also the rational soul, which is the principle of motion, life, and generation, can be infinitely joined to the body and separated in turn. Since many substances change qualities in a long vicissitude, and everywhere a perpetual circuit occurs by the power of the soul. In the following parts, finally, he asserts with a certain great confidence the resurrection which he had hinted at. He then approaches the reasoning concerning reminiscence, proving the same thing as shortly before: that the soul lives both before the body and after the body. But you, understand that such reasons are Pythagorean. And from them, choose what leads more toward the truth. He says, therefore, if learning is reminiscence, souls lived before the body.

<summary>Ficino provides a philosophical commentary on Socrates' final days, arguing that Socratic thought serves as a precursor to Christian doctrine, particularly regarding the immortality of the soul and the necessity of moral purification.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary and arguments regarding Plato's Phaedo, specifically focusing on the proofs for the immortality of the soul and the nature of the afterlife.</meta>

# ARGUMENTS AND COMMENTARY

He proves that learning is actually **recollection** in two primary ways. First, because if someone is questioned correctly, they often give true answers about things they never learned. Second, because from the knowledge of things perceived by the senses, we ascend by a sudden abstraction to the knowledge of **Ideas** <note>The Platonic "Forms" or perfect blueprints of reality</note>; for example, by recognizing these "equal" things, we rise to the cognition of Equality itself. There we recognize that these physical things fall short of the Ideas and that the mind becomes similar to them; we see how much they approach the Ideas, and which do so more or less. Since we do this throughout our entire life, it is necessary that we possessed the Idea itself before birth. For we do not suddenly receive perfect knowledge of a thing from imperfect things. Moreover, he shows in two ways that Ideas exist. First, any subject called "equal" can, while remaining the same in substance, both become and appear unequal. But **Equality** itself can never become or appear to be inequality. Furthermore, these equal things, being imperfect, participate in inequality, whereas Equality itself does not. In the following sections, note with what great persistence he affirms the Ideas, and adds that the essence of the Ideas is our own. And since our mind refers individual things to the Ideas, it shows itself to be eternal along with the essence of the Ideas, and recognizes that essence as its own. Note, moreover, that in no matter must we labor more than to expel the fear of death—as if it were a most grave disease—through the demonstration of immortality. Immediately he takes up another argument drawn from the proportion of the **intellect** to the **intelligible**. He calls the intelligible itself the incorporeal and eternal Idea. And since the intellect matches it as its own proper object, he concludes that the intellect is incorporeal and eternal, especially since it rules the body and resists mortal impulses. He confirms the strong proportion with the Idea by the fact that whenever it is not hindered, it betakes itself to the Idea, enjoys its commerce, and is perfected. However, regarding his statement that the soul is "altogether indissoluble" and then adding "or close to an altogether indissoluble thing," understand this addition thus: because in the *Timaeus* it is proved that God alone is altogether indissoluble; other things, if compared to God, are judged in a way to be dissoluble because they are in some way composite, even though those things which are best composed (that is, apart from elemental matter) are never dissolved. Therefore, souls—both ours and the divine—are close to the indissoluble God; they are in a way soluble, but never to be dissolved. Furthermore, he calls that "altogether indissoluble" in which no parts of essence or action are scattered. Therefore, although the soul is not scattered according to parts of essence, it is spread out through parts of action. For it acts in time and through motion. Accordingly, he adds that the pure soul returns to pure and eternal things after death, but the impure soul, infected by earthly things, is drawn back to similar and earthly things, and is often seen. Truly, the affection toward bodies remaining in the soul does not by itself properly make the soul visible, since affection is not visible; yet the soul causes itself to draw something visible with it—that is, a certain envelope, either air or something fashioned from the vapors and spirits of its body, as Proclus <note>A major Neoplatonist philosopher</note> wishes, or recently gathered from the surrounding air. Certainly, here Plato signifies what Proclus intends: namely, that between the ethereal body (which is immaterial, simple, and eternal) and the earthly body (which is material, composite, and short-lived), there is an **aerial body**, material indeed, but in a way simple and longer-lasting, in which souls dwell for a longer time even after departure. When this is dissolved, they put on a composite body again, provided they are not purified; but if they are purified, they seek heaven with the ethereal body alone. That he recounts the passage of souls into beasts is a **Pythagorean** <note>Followers of Pythagoras who believed in reincarnation</note> doctrine. And he understands it thus: namely, that our souls do not so much animate the bodies of beasts as, for the sake of purgatory, they are in a way mixed with the imagination of brutes through their own base imagination, just as they say impure demons are often mixed with the imagination of the insane. This is how most Platonists, except Plotinus, explain it. This is evident from the fact that he does not say the soul *becomes* a beast, but *puts on*, *undergoes*, or *passes into* one. He concludes that only those who depart purified through true philosophy are received into God. Hear, besides these things, that the bond of the soul with the body is nothing other than love—namely, a naturally providing love. Likewise, whenever the soul acts through an instrument regarding forms lying in a subject, it knows nothing purely, but only when it turns by itself to forms existing simply in themselves. Learn here also that the soul, from the fact that it is delighted and fed by corporeal things, becomes corporeal; and hence it is so deceived that it judges only corporeal things to be true, when it is entirely the opposite; such a fallacy is the gravest of all evils. It follows that the soul, having now become corporeal, even after death slips around corporeal things, apart from the incorporeal. Conclude that the mind, thoroughly restored to its purity, in no way distrusts its immortality. The fable of the **swan** is Pythagorean and allegorical—Pythagorean where it says the swan's soul survives. Allegorically, it is understood that the swan is included among the solar animals, and Socrates is "solar," both because he was approved by the oracle of Phoebus <note>Apollo</note> and because he healed the minds of men. Add that prophecy is fourfold: divine, demonic, human, and natural. And this last occurs in beasts by a certain instinct of nature. Understand the innocent swans to be men without philosophy; since they often do not fear death at all, they signify that perfected philosophers ought to fear it in no way. Notice then that it is most difficult in this life to understand the substance of the soul, because we perceive it under a corporeal appearance. Therefore, the safest method for comprehending the soul is both moral purgation and metaphysical abstraction. But where that is insufficient, there is need for a certain **divine word**, that is, revelations made divinely and miracles. We, however, ought to consider here the mystery of the divine word signified by Plato. He then hands down two precepts in disputation. First, that we should not believe any reasons without long examination. But after we have believed

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> through a sufficient examination, we should not easily be moved from there by any objections or similarities. Second, that we should not think of our own or another's persona in disputing, but only of the reason consistent with the truth. There follow doubts against the soul: lest perhaps it be a certain "harmony" of humors, and be dissolved either before the body, or together with it, or after some time. Socrates solves certain doubts thus: If learning is recollection, and therefore the soul lived before the body, the soul cannot be a harmony of the body, since a harmony does not precede the parts from whose meeting it arises, but follows them. If the ratio of harmony and the soul were the same, just as <margin>B</margin> one soul is no more a soul than another, so it would not be more "harmonious." Therefore, a temperate soul would harmonize no more than an intemperate one. If harmony necessarily follows and is led by those things from which it is composed, the soul cannot be the harmony of the body, which it leads daily and which it often resists. Furthermore, before he finishes the doubts and fully completes the reason for immortality, in a long discourse he condemns those who, in assigning causes to things, flee to certain materials and instruments, asserting that the whole of natural history is insufficiently confirmed through those same natural things; since <margin>C</margin> all these things and the motions of all things depend entirely on divine efficient causes and final and ideal causes. He desires primarily the **final cause** of each thing and the universe—that is, the good of each and the good of the universe—the power of which good he says is the efficient cause. But because he cannot grasp the magnitude of the Good itself, he chooses in the second place the **Ideal reasons** of the divine intelligence, according to whose likenesses all things are expressed in the matter of the world. Among these, note the confirmation of the **Mosaic mystery** <note>Reference to the Book of Genesis</note>, just as in the *Timaeus*. God saw that individual things were good, and even all things were very good. Thus all things are connected by the Good itself. Again, the mind looking at corporeal things is meanwhile blinded to incorporeal intuition. Nor can the truth of things be had unless we flee to the <margin>D</margin> Ideas. Furthermore, the formulas of the Ideas are in our minds, by agreement with which (or the contrary) individual things are judged to be true (or the contrary). Socrates was never accustomed to cease the certain contemplation of Ideas, and he alone used to affirm it. The certain cause of things is situated in the Ideas; the immortality of the soul is also demonstrated most powerfully from the Ideas. The process among Ideas goes from the less common through the middle to the most common. And there is a descent from the Ideas to their effect. Finally, he arranges the reason for immortality from the fact that the rational soul provides life to the body, not as an accidental form inherent in the body, but as a substantial form remaining in itself, living formally from itself <margin>E</margin> as if a certain Idea of corporeal life, and efficiently vivifying the body through itself. Therefore, he concludes that the soul cannot receive death, since death is the opposite of life, and the soul both has its own life and remains in itself, so that it can receive death neither properly through itself nor through another subject. After this, because the soul is immortal, he exhorts everyone to moral and speculative discipline, so that the soul, purified and perfected through both will and intellect, may fly back to the heavenly fatherland on these two wings, as it were. Meanwhile, he confirms that the soul is immortal because neither should virtue ultimately be a hindrance, nor vice a benefit. The laborious path of virtue would hinder the good, and <margin>F</margin> conversely the voluptuous life would benefit the wicked, unless the soul were immortal. And lest anyone perhaps deny that after this life either vice can hinder or virtue benefit, he adds that the soul carries with it the acquired affections and habits of both will and intelligence, whether good or evil, which will suddenly either harm or benefit. For a **daemon** <note>A guiding spirit or guardian</note> guide suddenly leads everyone to the divine judge of life, to a place appointed for common judgment: the less pure into the air, and the purer into the ether; and there, having been judged, each is drawn by another daemon through a **triple-way** to their own places—that is, to things similar to themselves. <margin>G</margin> Through a triple-way, I say, because some are sent to heaven, others to Tartarus <note>The deep abyss of torment</note>, and others to the middle regions. Moreover, the daemon leads them, moving the intelligence in the good, but disturbing the imagination and affection in the evil. When he says the wicked wander without a guide, understand "without a beneficial guide." Add that they do not recognize where they are being drawn, and are snatched away by violence. Furthermore, before he distributes the lots of the souls, he describes the globe of the earth, saying there are certain regions of the earth, and those indeed most vast and so high that they are not struck by winds and rains. Where the air is most temperate, <margin>H</margin> under which all the most precious things are born, there are men with the sharpest senses and long lives. There are those who wish that both the men and other things born there be composed as much as possible from ether and air, and as little as possible from the thicker elements; so that the bodies of men are as if aerial, and are nourished by mostly aerial fruits. Lest anyone deny this as impossible, **Olympiodorus** brings forward a story of Aristotle, in which Aristotle says he saw a man who was nourished by air and sun alone. As for his dividing the face of the sublime earth into twelve regions, this arises because twelve matches the signs of the Zodiac, it is ruled by the souls of the twelve spheres, and the twelfth is the sphere of the world; and as the foundation of the whole, it takes for itself that **dodecahedron** figure which the *Timaeus* attributes to the world. But concerning this figure itself, and other questions proper to the earth, we shall speak in the *Timaeus*. You, however, remember that the habitation of this kind of earth is similar to the terrestrial Paradise of **Moses**. Accordingly, he describes rivers under the earth by which souls are nourished. Whoever explains these according to the humors of our body and the disturbances of the soul afflicting us in this life brings forward something similar to the truth, yet does not attain the whole truth. For Plato, both here and in the *Republic*, signifies that the rewards of virtues and the punishments of vices pertain primarily to the other life. **Acheron**, therefore, a river under the earth, is a place of purgatory, and pertains to care and sorrow; it responds also—

# MARSILIO FICINO

and sharp, and to the southern part of the world. Phlegethon corresponds to fire and the east; it contains the power of punishing through heat and punishes the fervor of anger and desire. The Styx and Cocytus correspond to the earth and the west; they punish hatred through grief and weeping. They differ from each other only in this: that the Styx is the name given at the beginning, while Cocytus is the name as it proceeds. He wishes Tartarus to hold the lowest place of the underworld, in which the most wicked are afflicted—not for the sake of a cure, but as an example—just as is read here and in the *Republic* and the *Gorgias*. Some add to these rivers the Ocean, which pertains in a certain way to water and the north, in which the power of distinguishing and defining is understood. But as for what is said of the rivers, understand it primarily as referring to demons and divine powers who punish the shameful in such an order. Indeed, sins are easily curable which have not yet turned into a habit. Those which have already produced a habit are cured with difficulty; nevertheless, they are committed alongside a certain resistance of reason, and they affect those committing them with repentance. But those are entirely incurable whose habit puts both resistance and repentance to flight. The first are purged in Acheron. The second, if they lean toward the first, are punished in Phlegethon; if toward the third, in the Styx and Cocytus. The third are afflicted in Tartarus, from which, as Plato says, they never exit. As to how others explain this differently, I prefer to pass over it for the present. Souls can be afflicted not only through an imagination unhappily agitated by demons, but through certain aerial bodies, which are designated by the names "vehicle" and "skiff" <note>original: *vehiculi & symbæ*. Ficino refers to the Neoplatonic concept of the *ochema*, the subtle body or "chariot" of the soul.</note>.

Plato distinguishes the rewards thus: Souls that have lived justly and holily without philosophy, ascending to the high places of the earth such as we described above, dwell there in very thin and spiritual bodies. Those who have practiced philosophy in a civic manner <note>i.e., practiced social virtues without reaching the highest contemplative state.</note> dwell in heaven with splendid and celestial bodies. But those who have been perfectly purged through exact philosophy fly away to a super-celestial place, where they live for all time entirely without bodies, as Plato says here. By what reasoning some explain this, I will deliberately not recount; certainly Porphyry and Iamblichus <note>Famous Neoplatonist philosophers.</note> teach that souls perfectly restored to God never fall back. This indeed corresponds appropriately to the opposites, who are judged never to emerge from Tartarus. If this is so, the infinite cycles <note>The "Great Year" or reincarnation cycles.</note> will be removed. Temporal cycles will appear to be employed for the sake of a certain purgation. Finally, Socrates confesses that he owes a cock to Aesculapius <note>The god of healing.</note> and orders it to be paid most diligently. The ancients used to sacrifice a cock—the messenger of the day—to Aesculapius the physician, son of Phoebus <note>Apollo</note>; that is, to the divine beneficence that cures all diseases, which is called the daughter of divine providence. He confessed that he owed "the day"—that is, the light of life—to such a physician. He had ordered them to seek such a physician in the higher realms as a healer of the diseases of the soul. And as if they were now liberated from every disease of doubt and fear, he orders thanks and a victim to be returned to God. Furthermore, the oracles of the ancients teach that souls returning to heaven sing a *paean*—that is, a triumphal song—to Phoebus. He therefore returns his vow to God so that, cheerfully singing the Paean, he may seek again his celestial fatherland.

## ON THE ARGUMENT OF THE MENEXENUS
Argument for page 402.

<margin>C</margin> Plato’s purpose in the *Menexenus* is to exhort everyone to the highest love of their fatherland; he does the same, though differently, in the *Crito*, the *Laws*, and the *Republic*. Here he achieves it chiefly in two ways. First, while he praises those who intrepidly undergo dangers and death for the safety of the fatherland. Second, while he himself extols the antiquity and virtues of his own fatherland with wondrous praises. But you, right from the beginning, note that moral philosophy is supremely necessary for a man who is to govern a republic. Next, that it is noble to fall in war, namely for the safety of the fatherland, and this is confirmed by the fact that this is honored most of all among all nations. Then, taking the occasion from oratorical praises, notice how ruinous flattery is. Indeed, he judges common oratory in the *Gorgias* to be a species of flattery. In the *Phaedrus*, however, he calls a flatterer a beast pestilential to the human race. He affirms it is similar to an impure demon, continually polluting unwary souls with the filth of the body under the bait of harmful pleasure. Here, moreover, he judges the flatterer—both private and public—to be very similar to sorcerers and poisoners: for like a thief and a murderer, or worse and more unjust, he takes away from us not just money or the life of the body itself, but rather, like a sacrilegious person stealing a sacred thing, he snatches away and withdraws the judgment of reason under the appearance of good. And see how greatly he deceives. For he fails not only in hidden matters, but—what is wondrous—he deceives most skillfully in the most manifest things. For to whom is his ancestral and paternal origin not most evident? Likewise the very size and form of his own body? Nevertheless, in these things too, the poisonous flatterers circumvent us, being as much more cruel than Circe <note>The enchantress from the Odyssey who turned men into beasts.</note> as the damage they inflict is more grave. For she is said to have transformed the exterior of man into beasts with her potions; but these men transform the interior with their allurements. Therefore Socrates derides the orators because they hunt for popular favor with every machine, and praise others beyond measure so that they themselves may be praised, treating a matter so light with such heavy zeal and long premeditation. He proceeds, moreover, to what he had established from the beginning: namely, to exhort everyone to defend the fatherland by praising those who fell for the fatherland. For this was the old custom of the Athenians, to praise them annually in a public assembly and

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> furthermore to celebrate funeral rites. But lest he attribute more to the faculty of oratory than is proper, he asserts that he received a speech of this kind from another, and indeed from a woman, Aspasia <note>The partner of Pericles, known for her intellect.</note>: especially since it is not in the nature of the Socratic genius to harangue in the manner of orators. He clearly declares in what order one should praise, especially in a funeral oration. As for his saying that in the beginning men were produced spontaneously from the earth in the region of Attica alone, while in other regions only brutes were similarly produced from the earth: take it however you please, whether as from a philosopher or rather an orator. Know, however, that it is a Platonic opinion that after vast floods of the earth, from the abundant moisture and heat following the deluge, the earth is rendered so fertile that not only tiny animals such as now, but even large ones, and even men themselves, are born of their own accord. This he confirms both here and often elsewhere. And many of the Egyptians and Greeks felt this, and many Arabs; finally, Algazeles and Avicenna <note>Al-Ghazali and Ibn Sina, influential Islamic philosophers.</note> especially confirmed it.

<margin>B</margin> Aristotle, using this opinion in his *Natural Questions*, says according to the mind of the ancients: Just as in small changes of time certain small animals sprout from the earth, so in greater changes greater ones, and finally in the greatest, the largest and most perfect. But Plato, wherever he draws living beings from the very bowels of the earth, employs "artisan gods" as ministers of the mundane architect. "Gods," I say—that is, the Ideas and specific reasons consisting in the very life of the world and the divine intelligence—through which, both immediately after deluges and daily, the species of living things are formed wherever the corporeal seed of that same species is seen to be absent. We have sufficiently proved in our *Theology* <note>Ficino's *Platonic Theology*.</note> that this must happen. But where man is born, he not only employs the hands of the gods as for the others, but also a certain breath of the Supreme God and a more express image. Then, for those just born, he sets the gods themselves over them as leaders and teachers, at least in the first ages. But you, from all these things, prudently choose those which are more in harmony with Mosaic wisdom <note>The teachings of Moses/the Bible.</note>. Indeed, it most agrees with Moses that here, and in the *Protagoras*, and in the *Statesman*, and the *Critias*, he holds that man was once produced from the earth by God as the author, in the likeness of God himself. What kind of floods there are, and when, and for what cause, we shall teach in the *Timaeus*.

<margin>D</margin> After this, the man distinguished by piety pursues the praises of his fatherland with a certain wonderful charity and art, from its first origin, from the very form of the republic, from daily discipline, and from outstanding deeds, which are most manifest both from here and elsewhere from other writers. Therefore let us conclude our argument in a few words, noting these kinds of opinions: All things obey virtue. Prosperity first produces emulation, then envy, then dissensions and battles. Every possession without moral virtue is not only useless, but harmful. Knowledge apart from moral virtue is to be judged not wisdom, but a certain cleverness. The splendor of ancestors becomes obscure in their sons when it is not transfused into posterity through their own laziness. It is not to be wished that all things succeed according to one's vow. The old proverb must be observed in all things: *Nothing in excess*.

<margin>E</margin> He who has so prepared himself that all things which contribute to happiness depend on himself, or who comes as close as possible to this, has instituted his life best. Do not exult with joy, nor be cast down by grief. Parents ought to judge that they have begotten sons not to be immortal, but to be good. The mournful lamentations of the household are troublesome to the deceased, if indeed they hear them. It is fitting to follow with a certain perpetual solemn honor those who bore themselves strenuously in war for the safety of the fatherland; their children are to be educated by public care, and their parents also cherished. Lest circumstances themselves be unjust to us, they must be endured with an even mind.

<margin>F</margin> ## ON THE FIRST BOOK OF THE REPUBLIC
Argument for page 409.

As much as the eye excels the hands, the head the feet, reason the senses, the soul the body, the end all things which are directed to the end, status over motion, and eternity over time, so much does the contemplative life seem to excel the active. For contemplation is both the beginning and the end of action; it leads it at will and stops it, finally ordering the lower motions and external action to cease, so that an intrinsic and stable action may finally be possessed more freely.

<margin>G</margin> Thus, certainly, from the very contemplation of God, the celestial and natural motions and all actions are led as if from a principle, and are led back as if to an end. For this reason, our Plato is more excellent than other founders of cities and laws, in that others indeed instituted the city more for action as if human, but he, as if divine, leads all action of the city, both public and private, primarily to contemplating. He constitutes a city that is mistress of itself before being mistress of the world, not to be feared by so many as to be venerated by all nations—an expressed celestial Jerusalem, as it were, on earth according to its strength. In this city, for the sake of the possession of one's own justice, all things are common to all by the very law of nature instead of private right; there is common plenty, firm concord, one will of all, and therefore a tranquility always ready for contemplating.

<margin>H</margin> He composes the entire form of an absolute Republic in a ten-book number—the most complete of all numbers—containing within itself all numbers and unfolding innumerable ones from itself. And, as he often declares in these books, especially in the second, he prefers the whole disputation to be inscribed by us "On Justice" rather than "On the Republic": teaching, as I judge, that every matter and action, both public and private, is not for plenty, nor for power, nor for victory, but is to be referred entirely to justice itself. This justice, once all perturbation is removed and [the vices] expelled...

<summary>Ficino concludes his commentary on the afterlife in the Phaedo, then introduces the Menexenus as a lesson in patriotism and the dangers of flattery, and begins the Republic by defining justice as the foundation of a contemplative society.</summary>
