# ARGUMENTS AND COMMENTARY 801

the obstacles of strife, it finally renders citizens most ready to investigate the truth and worship God. Indeed, our *Plato* judges such contemplation and worship to be the chief end of the republic: so that what neither one man (if he lived alone) nor many (if they lived together without law) could achieve, many citizens at least, gathered into one assembly of the city by a common law, might fulfill. Furthermore, *Timaeus* and *Critias* teach us that before the great flood of the lands, other *Athens* existed, both among the *Greeks* and the *Egyptians*, governed by similar laws which the goddess *Pallas* <note>Athena</note> established, nurtured, and taught; she delivered to them that form of the republic which *Plato* writes of in these books. But in the books on the *Laws*, he composes a republic from the *Cretan*, *Spartan*, and new *Attic* governments, and begins the composition itself with God as the author of all laws.

But to return to the present matters, he begins this republic also under happy auspices, starting from the sacred rites of divine wisdom itself, from the custom and counsel of the elders, and from religious justice and holiness. For from the fact that he had said that both vows to God and what is due to each person must be rendered, he begins now to dispute concerning a certain private justice, through which he will opportunely pass to public justice in its proper place. But you, remember that in these things it is signified by *Plato* that without divine and human justice, the counsel of the elders, and the favor of divine wisdom, a city can neither be established from the beginning nor, once established, be happily governed. Next, touching upon the argument of the first book, I shall extract certain necessary points from many weighty precepts. A moderate youth makes for an easy old age; an immoderate one, a difficult one. He who obeys the lusts of the body undoubtedly serves insane tyrants. In old age, when the disturbances brought by youth have been calmed, the soul, separated from the body, inspects divine things more closely and clearly. Innocence alone offers the soul the best hope for the future, the sole comfort of life. A man of sound mind will judge money to be useful primarily for this: that whatever he has vowed to God or promised to man, or otherwise owed, he may fulfill, and not be led by poverty either to lie to anyone or to defraud in any matter. For money is to be referred to justice, but justice to the reward of another life. But before we pursue the dispute on justice, I advise you to consider that individual things are arranged by *Plato* under a certain allegory. First, indeed, *Cephalus* the old man—that is, the "head"—provides the head <note>the beginning</note> of the dispute. Then *Polemarchus*—as his name signifies, the "leader in war"—that is, the first to moderately engage in the battle. Finally *Thrasymachus*—that is, the "fierce fighter"—acts more harshly. *Socrates*, however—that is, the "powerful savior"—everywhere saves everyone from error and injustice. But leaving the allegory to the commentaries, let us now proceed to the definition of justice. They say that *Simonides*, *Pittacus*, and *Bias* said that justice is to speak the truth and to render to each what is due. Some interpret this thus: simply to reveal the truth to anyone, and to restore what you have received. But *Socrates* disapproves of this, because the truth should not be disclosed to an insane person, nor should weapons be returned which he had deposited with you while he was sane. Others explain it thus: to give to each what is fitting for him, such as benefit to friends but harm to enemies; to profit the good, but to hurt the wicked. This again is disapproved, because it is never becoming to hurt anyone. For whoever hurts anything makes that very thing worse and more unfit for its own work and proper virtue; as he who hurts a dog renders it unfit for the proper virtue of a dog. But justice is the virtue of a human being. Whoever, therefore, hurts a human being, makes him worse in respect to justice. But justice never diminishes justice, just as music does not destroy music. Therefore, it is not just to hurt anyone. Among these things, *Thrasymachus*—as many others do elsewhere—objects to *Socrates* that he never wishes to answer, but always to question. But it should not escape you that for many reasons *Socrates* was accustomed always to seek rather than to teach. First, to warn the arrogant that at every age one must learn rather than teach. Second, to signify that truth is immediately infused by divine power into minds separated from the body and from errors through opportune inquiry. Which *Avicenna* also greatly approves. Third, to show that the forms of things are innate in our souls, through which the truth of things itself may sometimes shine forth to souls turned toward them by questioning. Fourth, to declare that human science consists in a certain negation of the false rather than in the affirmation of the true. Then a definition of justice is brought forward by *Thrasymachus*—such as is also brought by *Callicles* in the *Gorgias*—that the just is what is useful to the more powerful. For the more powerful always dominate, and they bring laws and govern subjects for their own utility. Then indeed the subjects act justly when they obey those laws which are established for the utility of the governors. *Socrates* draws him into a contradiction. Since a prince might, through ignorance, command things that will be a detriment to himself. If the private citizen observes these, he will then be just, because he obeys the ruler; yet also unjust, because he acts against the ruler's utility. He adds that any art is absolute, and therefore least in need; in handling materials and men, it consults not its own utility, but the utility of the things commended to it, like a tutor to wards, a doctor to the sick, a pilot to sailors: and similarly, a legitimate magistrate looks to the utility of the subjects. If any art, like medicine, exacts a fee, it does not make a profit insofar as it is medicine (whose end is the cure of disease), but insofar as it is mixed with a certain mercenary and profit-making art. It is established, therefore, that the civil art, the most perfect of all and therefore the least needy and servile, governs much less for the sake of utility. I pass over what *Thrasymachus* brings forward rashly and with a certain self-repugnance against justice. But you, note that it is not becoming for anyone to seek leadership and to solicit magistracies. Likewise, if ever a city of good men should exist, they would fight no differently for the sake of *not* ruling than men now contend with a desire for ruling. Now observe three things. First, that the wicked are not to be admitted

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> to the magistracy. Second, that citizens who are not wicked, because they would only unwillingly take up the heavy burden of governing, must be invited by the imposition of a certain reward of pay and honor. Third, that upright men who are moved neither by greed nor ambition ought to be provoked to the republic only by this distinction and fear: namely, lest they themselves be subjected to the unjust government of worse men. *Plato* understands more divinely than perhaps anyone else that the duty of governing the fatherland, if it be just, ought to be voluntary. But by the example of the most proven citizen, he wishes to disapprove the iniquitous arrogance of those who by any path always solicit magistracies and hunt for dignity. But as to the reason by which they themselves might become worthy of dignities, they do not care at all. He wishes, therefore, that office to be voluntary and at the same time necessary, so that the most upright man may most willingly take up the helm of his fatherland, <margin>B</margin> but do so only when necessity demands; meanwhile, let him prefer contemplation to action: yet when matters are pressing, let him for a time prefer action concerning the public good to his own contemplation. This whole matter can be understood most clearly from the letter of *Plato* to *Archytas of Tarentum*. Next, the saying of the tyrant with *Thrasymachus* is confuted, placing justice indeed in the genus of foolishness and evil, but injustice in the genus of wisdom and good; which is shown to be false because any art is a certain wisdom, and concerning the things in which it is wise, it is also good. A man learned in any art does not seek more than another learned man in <margin>C</margin> an artistic action, but rather seeks to execute the action equally and similarly. And though he wishes only to equal the learned, he wishes to surpass the unlearned. But the unlearned sometimes rashly attempts to take more for himself than both the learned and the unlearned. Most similar to the former is the just man, desiring to have nothing more than another just man, but yet something more—that is, more virtue—than the unjust. But the unjust man, like the unlearned, contends to have more than both the just and the unjust. Conclude against *Thrasymachus* that justice is to be referred to the genus of wisdom and good, but injustice to the genus of foolishness and evil. He adds that injustice is the cause of infinity <note>disorder/limitlessness</note> in all things. For in any assembly, by bringing forth hatred and discord, it first renders the assembly most weak, then dissolves it. To that extent, however, <margin>D</margin> an assembly can stand, insofar as some degree of distribution is justly preserved. Therefore, it stands through justice, but is dissolved through injustice. Through the former, one is a friend both to oneself and to others; through the latter, an enemy on all sides. Moreover, what justice and injustice do in any congregation, they do the same in any soul: so that the just man is at agreement with himself and becomes a friend to himself, and to men and the gods above. For they are most just, so it is no wonder that the just man, being like them, is also their friend. But the unjust man in all these things is entirely the opposite. Furthermore, every thing has its own proper work. It also requires a proper virtue, namely a certain faculty through which it may most aptly perform its proper work, without which it cannot achieve it. Since, therefore, the soul has a certain proper work, such as deliberating and governing, and much earlier <margin>E</margin> living, it also requires a proper virtue through which it may perform these most commodiously; if this is taken away, it suffers. But the virtue of the soul is justice, and injustice is its vice. Therefore, through justice, it deliberates perfectly, governs, and lives happily. But when justice is taken away, it is unhappy. With these things said, the first book is concluded with a certain correction. Namely, that since it should have been said what justice *is* before what *kind* it is, it has been done conversely until now, while *Socrates* partly followed the disputants and partly, by disputing through better-known principles, indulged the genius of the listeners and consulted their faculty.

---
## END OF THE SECOND DIALOGUE ON THE REPUBLIC
### Argument. to page 421.
---

<margin>G</margin> The second dialogue begins from a threefold division of goods. A good is surely the same as something to be desired. We desire something for its own sake only, like pleasures and joy. Something for the sake of another only, such as whatever things are laborious. And something both for its own sake and for the sake of other things that follow from it, like knowledge for the sake of prosperous health. He says that justice is to be desired both for the sake of other things following from it, and most especially for its own sake. But before anything is perfectly defined concerning justice, *Glaucon* pursues more copiously and elegantly—and add, more modestly—those things which were omitted by *Thrasymachus* in 

defense of injustice. For he says, not because he feels this way, but so that he may provoke *Socrates* to defend justice more sharply, that he will praise injustice. We have similar things also in the *Gorgias*. After him, *Adeimantus* speaks first for justice, attributing to it both human and divine rewards, where you will note certain religious mysteries of the poets. Then he brings some things for injustice into the midst, representing the persona of both *Socrates* and *Thrasymachus*, adding also that he does not wish to disparage justice, but in a way to irritate *Socrates*. He wishes, however, to hear praises of justice 

which are drawn not from external things, but from the intrinsic nature of justice, such as are not accustomed to be brought by others. But you, notice that *Plato* has not rashly placed many things here again pertaining to poets and priests: 

<column-break/>

<margin>H</margin> for he shows in these that a license for sinning often proceeds from poets, and more often from evil priests. Here he mocks the superstitions of the nations. Furthermore, it was not without reason that in these books he inserted the persons most dear to him: *Glaucon* and *Adeimantus* his brothers, and his father *Ariston*. Again, that *Socrates* in all his life contemplated nothing more readily than what virtue itself and vice are in the soul, with external affections excluded. Which indeed he will demonstrate next, both spontaneously and when provoked, concerning justice and injustice. But I have here unjustly passed over too much that wonderful [nature] of justice...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plato’s Republic, specifically concluding the discussion of Book II and beginning the "Argument" or summary for Book III. # MARSILIO FICINO.

the reward brought forth from the meter of Musaeus: perpetual drunkenness. <note>Ficino refers to a passage in Plato's Republic (Book II) where the poet Musaeus is said to promise the virtuous an afterlife of eternal intoxication.</note>

Indeed, what Musaeus received from Orpheus, he signifies through the rites of Dionysus. This is similar to that prophetic saying: *I shall be inebriated by the abundance of your house.* <note>A reference to Psalm 36:8.</note> Therefore, drunkenness is of two kinds. One is beneath the moon, induced by the drink of Lethe <note>The river of forgetfulness in the underworld.</note>: through which the soul, placed outside itself and beneath itself, forgets divine things while raving about earthly ones. The other, however, is above the moon, arising from a drink of nectar, through which the soul, placed outside itself and above itself, forgets mortal diseases; looking up at divine things, it grows dim as if by their primary splendor; or rather, tasting their flavor, it is transformed from its prior habit by a certain new heat. Soon, however, it sees clearly and tastes healthfully—indeed, it is nourished. Truly, the divine **Idea** through which the soul was made flows into the returning soul like a flavor into the sense of taste. At first, it gently dilutes whatever is foreign to it. Then it fills it inwardly, and delights it more by filling it. Thirdly, it restores the soul into itself, drenching it with inestimable pleasure. Where the soul, from being a soul, first becomes **Intellect**, and from Intellect, finally becomes **God**. Nor does it perceive further as it did before, nor the things it did before, but it perceives differently and different things. And just as among us a vehement imagination moves and forms the body, so there the body subject to the soul and its sense is immediately moved and formed by the most powerful thought of the mind, so much so that by the ineffable sweetness of the mind, both the sense and the body marvelously grow sweet. But let us now return to justice. Socrates, seeking this through every detail as the end and object of his disputation—because it was difficult to find in the soul—first seeks it in the city, as if it would be more manifest there, so that through this he might finally clearly define the justice of the soul. Moreover, so that he may consider justice in the city, he establishes the city from the beginning, stating first its origin, namely mutual need; then its matter, namely necessary things and arts; and finally its form, namely the rule of life and lawful governance. And see how much he praises a sober life, and how much he censures a delicate and luxurious one. The former is healthy and sufficient, while the latter is insane and in need of many things. Finally, since war is born because of this luxury, there is a need for soldiers in such a city; wherefore, descending to the diligent institution of the military art, he accurately pursues how many things are necessary for a strenuous soldier and guardian of the fatherland. In all things, however, remember: no one can be born most fit for diverse tasks. Therefore, no one ought to practice diverse arts. Especially since the work of one is hindered by the work of another. It is necessary for each person to practice his own art continuously from childhood and throughout his whole life. Furthermore, the soldier-guardian of the fatherland ought to be born and educated such that, like dogs, he is mild toward those he knows and fierce against strangers, and always vigilant and sagacious. Hence Socrates asserts that the beginning of any work is the greatest part, especially at a tender age which is easily formed in either direction. Therefore, he rightly forms the future soldiers from their "tender little nails" <note>A Latin idiom meaning "from earliest childhood."</note> first in soul through **Music**, and then in body through **Gymnastics**, comprehending under music the poetic fables as well. These he commands to be applied assiduously to the ears of boys. But only such fables as provoke and educate them as a sort of prelude to military study. Similarly, he orders others to be accustomed from childhood to these fables which best lead to their future study. Contrary ones, however, he keeps far away. This indeed is the greatest precept. He soon detests poetic impiety which invents shameful things about the gods. And he forbids such fables to be heard. He joins to this two figures of theology. First, that God is entirely good, and the cause only of good things. But God is the cause of no evil. Likewise, if God punishes anyone, He punishes for the sake of the good. Second, that God is inwardly immutable, because He is most simple, most powerful, most good, and most wise. From which it follows that he denies God ever deceives anyone, either with false images, or signs and words. For He is not changed into various forms, nor, since He is not changed, does He pretend to be changed. He concludes the book with a certain golden sentence: **A lie is most hateful of all to both gods and men.** But if a lie in speech is hateful, and that is an image of the lie itself which is in the soul, then surely the lie which is in the soul is exceedingly hateful to both gods and men. Such a lie is **Ignorance**, through which the soul itself lies to itself concerning the truth of things. Since truth looks toward that which is said to "be," and therefore falsehood declines toward "not being," a liar is deservedly said to fall into nothingness insofar as he falls into falsehood.

---

## Argument on the Third Dialogue of the Republic. (to page 432)

The third dialogue continues the education of the guardians begun in the second. And just as in the second he forbade them to hear false and shameful things about the gods, so here he forbids hearing tragic things about the underworld, which might make them more fearful. Likewise comic things, which excite excessive laughter. For he who is daily dissolved into excessive laughter becomes just as soft as he who is compelled to weep by pain. Since, however, the guardians must be kept far not only from fearfulness, but also from intemperance, avarice, and injustice, he again forbids the poems of poets to be heard in which the lusts, robberies, and iniquities of gods, heroes, or great men are invented. This military education is almost equally common to all citizens. Among these things, pay attention to what he says about lying. A lie is the calamity of a city, namely when private citizens lie among themselves, but especially if they lie to the magistrates. Just as if the sick should lie to the doctor, or sailors to the pilot. It is permitted, however, for governors sometimes to use a lie for the sake of public safety, and for a private person sometimes to-
<meta>catchword: to-</meta>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> -ward a private person, only for the sake of avoiding some most grave evil. It is also permitted to converse moderately about ancient things, the truth of which is unknown, and to fashion those things of which we hardly have a certain form as if through certain images. Hence he distinguishes speech into three species. For it is either simple narration, or simple imitation, or mixed from both. He reproves all speech that relates the most vile things without selection and acts out a disturbed man. For whoever studiously imitates something for a long time passes into its nature. Wherefore, he orders the poet who imitates disturbed minds and acts—as one harmful to youth—either to imitate a constant habit by changing his style, or to depart far from the
<margin>B</margin> city. He also says that he who handles many things, either by imitating or by doing, eventually fails in each so much that he emerges excellent in none. He proceeds next from the first music, that is, poetry, to the following, and distributes it into three species: Speech, Harmony, and Rhythm. In the beginning, musicians call the **phthongos** <note>original: "phthōngum" - a musical sound or note.</note> the harmonic voice, that is, a fit consonance, which is neither so deep that it cannot be made deeper by the same singer, nor so sharp that it cannot be produced sharper. Then he constitutes **Harmony** from notes, namely a congruent measure in the excess and defect of deep, sharp, and middle voices. There are four voices here: deep and
<margin>C</margin> sharp, and rising toward the sharp, and declining toward the deep. Likewise, there are four primary proportions: the **double** (2:1). The **sesquialter** (3:2). The **sesquitertia** (4:3). Finally, the **sesquioctave** (9:8). The double proportion is followed by the octave consonance; the sesquialter by the fifth; the sesquitertia by the fourth; and finally the sesquioctave by the whole tone. But of these things more diligently elsewhere. In the third place comes **Rhythm**, that is, a certain order of motion and time, as is perceived from the second book of the *Laws*. For after you have reconciled the voices by a certain harmonic measure of excess and defect through tension and relaxation, there is need for rhythm, through which you may measure the motions and times of sharp, deep, and
<margin>D</margin> middle voices, both in each and between each. I call the motions more gentle, more severe, and middle. I call the times longer, shorter, and equal, through long, short, and middle accents. In these, note that the word **base** <note>original: "basem"</note> is diverse: for as the matter requires, it signifies foundation, seat, weight, progress, and limit. Besides these, nine most common degrees of consonance and dissonance are to be considered. First in **Reason**, that is, an opinion consenting with the truth of the thing itself. Its contrary is a false opinion dissenting from the truth. Second in **Imagination**. Its consonance is the following of reason. Its dissonance is the pursuit of external things. Third in **Effect**, either temperately following reason, or intem-
<margin>E</margin> -perately following imagination. Fourth in **Speech**, decorous or indecorous, insofar as it follows either right reason or tumultuous imagination. Fifth in **Song**. Its consonance is to imitate decorous speech, its dissonance indecorous. Sixth in **Sound**, imitating the song in one way or another. Seventh in **Graceful Dance**, or ungraceful, pertaining to the choral dance. Eighth in a certain **Composition of the limbs** and the whole body, as pleasing to the sight as it is ready for gymnastic exercise. Ninth in the **Artistic Works** of any art, composed with a certain musical proportion. Let these nine degrees represent to you the nine Muses. Remember, however, that the best harmony of all is the **Temperance of the Soul**.
<margin>F</margin> Which the following others imitate, and in turn, when they are frequented, they increase it. Wherefore he orders only those consonances to be practiced, heard, and watched which reflect a constant habit of mind, not elated by pride, not made fierce by anger, not softened and dissolved by pleasure, not broken by grief, nor complaining with pity or need. He approves, therefore, a deep and constant harmony, but disapproves the extremes, that is, the excited and the soft; he also condemns the manifold, and praises the simple above others. He judges that harmony has the greatest power over the soul. Indeed, the soul is a certain divine harmony and was once accustomed, as I might say in the Platonic manner, to celestial harmony. Again, the body consists of a certain harmony, and the spirit is forged by it. Furthermore, the air, which is the consonance of the voice, penetrating the summoned spirit by its motion, and carrying with it the affection and mind of the singer,
<margin>G</margin> moves the affection of the listener by affection, and affects the mind by mind, and pours character into the sense. In all things, notice with how much not only civil but also religious observance Plato educates his city, and always—as he also commands in the *Statesman*—mixes temperance with fortitude. Finally, how shameful and dissonant he considers venereal pleasure to be, and therefore he separates it far from legitimate love, which desires only beautiful and consonant things. He treats many things concerning Music and Gymnastics. For they were of the greatest moment: for everyone applied themselves to these, and ought to apply themselves. For the former forms and composes the soul and spirit, and the latter the body for the sake of the soul, in a softening way. He adds that a good soul does not come from a good body, but a good body is made from a good soul. He adds that simple music harms the soul
<margin>H</margin> of both, and that men, while they lived soberly, did not need the help of physical doctors. He condemns superstitious observations of the body concerning diet and medicines. And he says the chief sign of a badly instituted city is if it requires the diligent work of doctors and judges. He describes the office of the doctor and the judge, and chooses a judge good in nature, prudent, old, and experienced in many men, both good and bad. He asserts that depravity, like a certain privation, knows neither itself nor virtue. But virtue, like a habit, knows itself through itself alone, and through itself—with the addition of experience—judges vices. One must always remember, however, that Plato confirms not only here, but also in the *Laws*, the *Statesman*, and the *Protagoras*, that nothing is more necessary for every man, but especially for the civil and philosophical man, than the bond of fortitude and temperance alike.

# ARGUMENTS AND COMMENTARY

<margin>A</margin> ...composed: so that through the former [music], high things may be sought, and through the latter [gymnastics], humble things may not be despised; and on both sides, you may never dare or fear anything too much. Through the former, again, you may repel private and public injuries; through the latter, you may abstain from causing injury. Through the former, you may be called to honorable things; through the latter, you may be restrained from base ones. Thus it happens that gymnastics and music ultimately refer to these two: that through the former, fortitude—not so much of the body as of the soul—is acquired, and through the latter, temperance. He commands, however, that both be properly mixed together. For gymnastics alone produces ferocity, and music alone produces softness; but both together produce fortitude and temperance. Finally, from the number of those who have been so educated, he chooses both guardians (that is, magistrates) and defenders (that is, soldiers). For the magistracy, he wishes to assume <margin>B</margin> old men who are prudent, brave, lovers of the public good, and proven in this very thing through experience. He likewise commands that young men be tested in the midst of pleasures and pains, so it may be discerned whether they are temperate and brave, or the opposite; and whether they might easily change their resolve to preserve the public good because of deceits, threats, or allurements. Finally, he says that the natural talents of men are like metals: one fit for governing is like gold, one fit for military service is like silver, and one fit for craftsmanship and agriculture is like iron and bronze. He commands that individual talents be directed toward those things for which they are fit: thus, the sons of governors are sometimes moved to lower roles according to their talent, and conversely, the sons of those below are moved to nobler duties. He also forbids soldiers from possessing anything of their own, lest through greed they be turned from "dogs" <note>Plato's metaphor for the guardians of the state</note> into wolves.
<margin>C</margin>

## ON THE FOURTH BOOK OF THE REPUBLIC
### Argument for page 445.

<margin>D</margin> In the fourth book, the manner of possession and of the city is handed down, so that neither are the rich too wealthy, nor the poor too destitute. For he thinks that seditions arise and the city is scattered as much from excessive abundance as from want. He judges, moreover, that such a city is not one, but many, in which some are poor and others rich; and as usually happens, the rich despise the poor, while the poor are affected by both envy and hatred toward the rich. From here he descends gradually to his mystery: namely, that all things should be held in common, lest some have less and others more, giving rise to envy, lies, and theft, and from there luxury, pride, and laziness. Add to this that the possession of things, whether exceeding or deficient, hinders not only morals and concord, but also talent and the arts. He teaches that a city is preserved and performs great deeds not by riches, but by virtue. Likewise, any part of the city should not be arranged so that it seems best for itself alone, but so that it contributes to all and leads to the common good of the whole city. Otherwise, neither the city itself nor any of its parts can stand. He adds, moreover, the <margin>E</margin> limit for increasing the city: specifically, as long as the city remains one. But as soon as it seems that unity might be lost, it must not be increased further. He commands, therefore, that the city be neither tiny nor vast, but moderate, equal, and harmonious, so that its unity is preserved. Since, however, he who was negligent in sowing hopes for a harvest in vain, he judges that all effort must be applied to childhood and youth, as if to the sowing of the city's harvest, so much so that a diligent account of every word, game, and gesture is kept regarding boys and youths. Otherwise, if this age is neglected, laboring over daily laws will be as vain as if someone tried to cure with medicines a man who refuses to observe any moderation in his diet. Among these things, consider how games are turned into studies and morals. <margin>F</margin> Likewise, just as a man who is naturally robust and prudent and temperate in diet has almost no need for medicines, so a city that is excellently constituted from the beginning and perseveres in that form has no need for many laws at the start, nor for daily new constitutions thereafter. Bad republics, however, occupy themselves with daily healing through new laws, but never truly become healthy. Therefore, in this republic, as the best one, Plato applied no study to laws, hoping that prudent and good men would be "living laws." But what of sacred laws? He certainly thought much less labor should be spent on these. For no one ever understands by what reason God is to be worshiped unless he first understands God. <margin>G</margin> We cannot see the divine sun unless the divine sun itself shows itself. He judges, therefore, that the laws of religion must be sought from Apollo—that is, from divine light; sought, I say, not with the tongue, but with a purified and serene mind. I pass over what he touches upon here regarding the history of oracles, for these are very well known. Allegorically, however, he signifies that Apollo—that is, the divine light—"sits" (that is, is firmly present) in the "middle of the earth" (that is, everywhere in the innermost parts of all things). He rests in the "navel" (that is, in the mind separated from the senses, reflected in itself like a spherical figure and motion). Furthermore, Apollo is "ancestral" to all (that is, present, familiar, and a propitious father to those being born, and a homeland to those returning). Once the republic is established, he recognizes four virtues in it: **Prudence** in the leaders (the knowledge of rightly guarding and advising); **Fortitude** in the soldiers (a firm resolve to dare for the fatherland in dangers despite allurements or threats, as far as the laws and magistrates command); **Temperance** in the leaders, soldiers, and craftsmen alike (a certain harmony by which all willingly agree that some should command and others obey; and among those who obey, some in war and others in craftsmanship);
<margin>H</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> nor should such agreement be hindered by any pleasures; rather, the desires of the lower classes should obey the command and counsel of the superiors. **Justice** also in all, through which each person performs his own work—that is, that for which he is most fit by nature and study—both publicly and privately for the sake of the common good, and no one claims what belongs to another. Now, when he called temperance the *Diapason* <note>The Greek term for an octave, meaning "through all [strings]"</note> harmony, understand the *Diapason* as the consonance resulting from a double proportion of tension, speed, and force to that which is twice as relaxed, slower, and softer. From this double proportion arises the high pitch—that is, the excess of the eighth voice over the low one—and not without merit. For the first double proportion is between two and one. In which <margin>B</margin> proportion the number two, while it seems to surpass, recreates and doubles the one. Then the number two, while it is moved and revolved into itself, produces the number eight, a solid number. For twice two, twice, makes eight. It is called *Diapason*, that is, "through all." For a consonance of this kind both contains all others within itself and is replicated in all. Not without reason does Plato say that temperance, like a *Diapason*, is extended through the highest, lowest, and middle citizens. For in the octave there is the low voice, the highest, and the middle ones. But to return to justice: just as in the *Diapason* consonance the eighth voice so harmonizes with the low one that what is a double voice appears as one, so in a well-composed city the gravity of temperance so <margin>C</margin> aptly fits with the strength of justice that these two virtues can scarcely be distinguished from one another. And see how opportunely Socrates moves from the *Diapason* consonance of the eighth voice to justice, which among the Pythagoreans was designated by the number eight. For while justice is an entirely equal distribution according to each person's merits and the solid foundation of the city, it is justly described by the number eight. For this number is the first of the solids, and the first of all to be dissolved into "even-even" numbers (that is, into twice four), and the division itself is dissolved into "even-even" numbers (that is, into twice two); and by the same equality it is dissolved, it is also woven together. For twice two, twice, constitutes eight—as I said, an image of just equality. Therefore Orpheus, whenever he wished to call upon divine justice, <margin>D</margin> swore by eight deities: fire, water, earth, heaven, moon, sun, planet, and night. In Egypt also, a column placed as a sign of justice was noted with eight deities inscribed, as Evander testifies: Saturn, Rhea, Osiris, Spirit, Heaven, Earth, Night, and Day. Finally, all antiquity believes that the order of celestial justice is arranged in eight spheres. After this, Socrates shows that injustice is the sudden destruction of a city, when individuals usurping what belongs to others disturb and confound everything. Justice, however, is the order and salvation of the city. Then, from this more manifest justice of the city, he passes to the more hidden justice latent in the soul. He divides the powers of the soul into three: **Reason** in the place of the leader; the **Force of Anger** in place of the soldiers; <margin>E</margin> and the **Nature of Desire** similar to the craftsman. He proves that there is one soul in us, in which these three powers exist, distinct not by location but by property. This refutes certain "barking" Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle</note> and can be made manifest to anyone reading diligently. He teaches this distinction so it may be clear how the soul and the city, and the justice of the one and the other, are very similar. He says, therefore: since the soul cannot do opposite things regarding the same object through the same power at the same time, it must have at least three powers. For at the same time, it may be snatched toward pleasure by lust, and meanwhile be called back by reason. Likewise, it may be pulled back from battle by lust, yet provoked to fight by anger. From these it is clear that reason is different from lust, and the <margin>F</margin> vigor of anger also differs from it. It is also clear that this [anger] differs from reason, both in children who do not yet use reason but are very hot with anger, and in others who do many things through anger against the law of reason. He proves that the vigor of anger is closer to reason because indignation arises against lust when desires creep in. He concludes next that justice, together with temperance, is a certain lawful agreement, both in the soul of anyone among the three parts we mentioned, and in the city among the three parts similar to these. An agreement, I say, in governing, executing, obeying, and in performing one's own duties and not usurping those of others. Not without merit does he here call justice the sibling of temperance, a "harmony" <margin>G</margin> consisting of high, low, and middle voices—voices, I say, representing the leaders, the money-makers, and the soldiers in the middle. Then, to answer the question long since brought up—asking what justice and injustice produce in the soul—he says that virtue is the health, beauty, and strength of the soul, while vice is disease, ugliness, and weakness. For virtue arranges and preserves all parts of the soul as nature ordained. Vice, on the contrary, confounds and disturbs the order of nature. Since, when the nature of the body is entirely depraved, it is better to die than to live (even if external goods are supplied to us in abundance), he concludes that the life of one in whom the soul—through which we live—is depraved by vice is to be <margin>H</margin> shunned by all as miserable.

Finally, at the very end of this book, he asserts that a soul and city of the kind he described is the best and happiest. A "royal" soul and city, arranged by the queen—namely, human reason. He adds that such a government is called "royal" when one man, clearly the most excellent of all, excels among many good men; and it is called a "republic of the best" (aristocracy) when several seem to excel equally. But it should be considered entirely the same form of government. He also agrees that in the following book he will distinguish in order the four remaining dispositions of both souls and republics.

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s extensive Latin commentary and introduction to Plato’s *Republic*. Ficino, a central figure of the Italian Renaissance, is translating Plato's Greek concepts into a Christian Neoplatonic framework for his 15th-century audience.</meta>

# MARSILIO FICINO

### Argument on the Fifth Dialogue of the Republic.
#### Referring to page 456.

I am well aware that there will be some who expect an "Apology" <note>A formal defense or justification</note> from us, in which we might defend this fifth dialogue—which establishes a community of all things in the city—against the slanders of both the malicious and the ignorant. But let them read Plato himself, I pray they read him diligently, and judge without envy. They will desire no Apology (I know whereof I speak). Therefore Plato, that "Sun-bright" <note>original: *Phœbeus*, referring to Apollo/the Sun</note> physician of the human race, observed that individuals, families, and cities are always and everywhere gravely ill. He saw that they had not been freed from their disease, nor even slightly relieved or recovered, by any medicines of the "civil physicians" who had been treating them in vain for so many centuries. Thus, as prudently as he did piously, he turned to that principal law among doctors: if a patient does not recover after long use of cold medicines, one must finally transition to warm ones. 

Recognizing, therefore, that the human race gained nothing through laws that distributed private property over so many centuries—but rather fell daily into worse condition—he rightly transferred himself to the laws of friendship, which command that "all things are common among friends." He did this so that by removing division, and the cause of division and misery, we might attain harmony, union, and happiness. 

But let us begin again from another point. Socrates, at the beginning of the fourth book, placing the discipline of educating youth above all laws, briefly touched upon the idea that the best discipline would be if there were a community of wives, children, and property. But because this matter is new to many, and unheard of by most, he is called back to it at the start of the fifth book to declare it more openly and prove it more firmly. Now, if you have learned from Critias and Timaeus that a similar discipline once existed in the "Greek and Egyptian Athens," you will neither marvel at it as something new, nor listen with distrust as if it were entirely too difficult, nor unwillingly reject it as if it were not good. I pass over the fact that many report the city of Prague among the Bohemians was once governed similarly. Furthermore, Diodorus describes an island in the Southern Ocean where, among other things, wives are held in common, and the men are greatly devoted to philosophy and astrology. Pomponius Mela also witnesses that the Garamantes in the furthest parts of Africa have all things in common in their republic. Moreover, we have found that a similar good community existed among the Brahman philosophers, the Gymnosophists, the Essenes, the Pythagoreans, and finally among the holy founders of the Christian commonwealth in the past. We see also in our own times that only those religious orders approach virtue and happiness among whom nothing is private property. 

But if the "community of wives" disturbs you, first allow that in Plato’s work this is done rightly according to law, whereas among "adulterous priests" it is done in common through sacrilege. Then, hear Plato himself speaking at length on his own cause before you judge. In what follows, note first the Socratic foresight, which deems it worse to err in establishing laws than to kill a man. For an error of that kind kills many souls and bodies simultaneously through many centuries. Second, note his modesty in approaching difficult things with hesitation, as if unwilling and compelled. Third, note his piety in invoking divine help, according to his custom, in grave matters. 

Lest he err in founding laws, he seeks help from the goddess **Adrastia**, whom he also mentioned in the *Phaedrus*. Among the ancient theologians, this Adrastia is the most powerful queen of inevitable laws—laws, I say, both "Saturnian" (pertaining to minds) and "Jovial" (pertaining to natures). Adrastia is Divine Providence, insofar as nothing can escape her eyes or flee her hands. It is not without reason that when he wishes to establish the firmest laws—which neither oblivion may delete, nor craftiness defraud, nor violence break—he prays to Adrastia, who ordains the inevitable things that no one can escape. 

Next, he proceeds step-by-step to the common discipline: from the education of men to the similar education of women, commanding that all private and public pursuits, both of peace and war, be held in common by women and men. This is so the human race is not "maimed" <note>i.e., only half-functional</note>, provided that the heavier tasks are committed to men and the lighter to women. Similarly, he teaches elsewhere that the arms must be so trained that individuals are "right-handed" on both sides—whom he calls *amphidexteros* <note>ambidextrous</note>—showing this to be useful, possible, and how it ought to be done. 

Then he introduces another community: that of wives and children. And there, observe with what foresight of order he establishes Magistrates, overseers of marriages, and sacred rites, times, and ages, taking care that nothing is done intemperately or uselessly for the city. And after birth, how diligently he thinks of nourishing the newborns, yet in such a way that neither man nor woman recognizes their own child, nor the child their own parents. Instead, the elders are compelled to think that almost all the younger ones are their children or grandchildren; the younger ones, in turn, suspect all the elders are their progenitors, and those of equal age are likewise brothers. 

Among these things, where he scorns the nourishment of one born against the law, or from the unfit, or who is himself unfit: understand that such a one is not to be destroyed, but nourished in a more hidden place or in the suburbs, outside that most exact rule by which those chosen for the "Guardianship" are nourished. That inferior one is to be raised by a rule for the lesser ministries of the city or field, or perhaps transferred to other cities immediately upon birth. 

Soon, recognize the invention of "common charity," where he disposes each thing so that individuals, seeing the same thing or person, judge equally and say, "This is mine." Since his own things are dearest to everyone, everyone will care for everything—especially since they are led to such care by laws and magistrates. Hence, our carelessness and negligence (which exists in all people regarding things that seem "alien" to us) will be removed. And the daily 

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> fallacy will be removed, by which our judgment is foolishly deceived in cultivating what we think is our own. Finally, the extreme disturbance, anxiety, and misery that tortures us from the insane love of private things will be removed. I pass over the fact that with the cause of discord removed, charity will be both common and whole. 

Furthermore, attend to how diligent, just, and mild he makes the laws of war, and what rewards await the victors—namely, a certain divinity. For these men, he says, are translated into "blessed demons" <note>In the Greek sense: guardian spirits or mediators</note>, the caretakers of men, to be rightly worshipped as dear gods. As for what is said about the "kisses of the boys," it is a certain joke of Glaucon’s, said for the sake of relieving boredom. Add to this something triumphal and festive. 

It remained to be proven that this community could be achieved, after it had been affirmed as the best. First, therefore, even if it cannot be done, he shows he has not 
<margin>B</margin> brought this forward in vain, but rather as a model to be imitated as much as possible in forming cities. Then he demonstrates that it can finally be achieved when **philosophers govern**, and that there will be no rest from evils before then. 

For this reason, he opportunely descends to the forming of philosophers as the future governors of the city, teaching what the nature of a "civil philosopher" is, and what his effect and discipline are. To begin with: just as the common people are curious about perceiving these lower sensible things, so the philosophical nature is greedy and inclined toward finding the **Ideal Reasons** <note>The Platonic Forms</note> of all these things, and is a sagacious hunter of Truth itself. Since, however, the "True Things" are the Ideas, while natural forms are but images of the Ideas, he rightly says the common people are "dreaming," thinking that the images are the true things. 
<margin>C</margin> But the philosopher alone among others is "awake." 

And since he places a middle ground between "Being" and "Non-being," remember that all things are thought of in five grades. 
1. **Pure Non-being** is said to be whatever is imagined below matter. 
2. **Pure Being** is the pure Mind and the Ideas. 
3. The **Soul and the Heavens** are called "Being and Non-being" simultaneously, namely because of motion, yet they "are" more than they "are not." 
4. **Matter**, on the contrary, in a way "is not" more than it "is." 
5. But those things which are **composite natures** under the moon are equally "being and non-being." 

Knowledge itself is concerned with those things that truly *are*. Ignorance is concerned with those things that truly *are not*. Opinion revolves around those things that are equally *being and non-being*. He attributes ignorance and opinion to both the common people and the Sophists. But **Knowledge** (that is, Science) he attributes only to philosophers. 
<margin>D</margin> When he calls science and opinion a certain "power," understand it not as an unformed power, but one endowed partly by natural form and partly by habit. 

Furthermore, where he treats the Ideas to which the philosopher's knowledge refers, he speaks in his usual way of the **Good, the Beautiful, and the Just**. This triad is explained in three ways: 
1. First: the Good is God; the Beautiful is the multiform Angelic Mind; the Just is the Celestial World-Soul distributing justly. 
2. Second: the Good is the form and act of the Divine Nature; the Beautiful is His intelligence; the Just is His will. 
3. Third: among the Ideas, the Good is the model of the form and act of every nature; the Beautiful is the model of the order that results from any form within itself; the Just is the model of the order referred from any form and thing to others. 
<margin>E</margin> When, however, he subordinates Evil to the Good, the Ugly to the Beautiful, and the Unjust to the Just, beware of placing these three opposites among the Ideas. Rather, place them both in the informity and deformity of matter (which in the book *On Science* he calls the "model devoid of divinity," and in the *Statesman* the "place of dissimilarity") and also in the soul when it is depraved and turned entirely toward matter. 

Finally, regarding the "childish riddle of the eunuch" he touches upon, it is as follows: *A man who is not a man, seeing and not seeing, struck and did not strike, with a stone that is not a stone, a bird that is not a bird, upon a tree that is not a tree.* That is: a one-eyed eunuch struck a bat's wing with a pumice stone upon an elder tree. But you will laugh at this, I know. It was included for the sake of the ridiculous.

---

<margin>F</margin> ### Argument on the Sixth Book of the Republic.
#### Referring to page 469.

<margin>G</margin> Since all laws, even the best, are dead without the most proven magistrates—and the best magistrates are themselves "living laws" even without written ones—our Plato (as we have explained elsewhere) rightly labors with all diligence in his excellent republic not on founding laws, but on forming magistrates. And he strives for this not only from a tender age, but even from the very conception, so that from chosen seeds and continuous cultivation, the best fruit may be reached. 
<margin>H</margin> Since he calls these men **Guardians** <note>original: *custodes*</note>, and it is most proper for guardians to look forward and look around, he therefore chooses the philosophical nature—unquestionably the most perspicacious of all—to guard the human flock. For only to the eye of this man lies open the model of the Good and of Justice itself, according to whose image the city is to be painted kindly, justly, and blessedly. 

Furthermore, it pertains to a guardian to be truthful, liberal, temperate, brave, just, magnanimous, and mild. He will prove these same qualities are proper to the philosopher, so that he may finally conclude that the office of guarding is to be committed to the philosopher above all others. Therefore, he will first prove that such is the nature of the philosopher. Then, because a noble nature without right cultivation becomes both useless and often harmful, he hands down the discipline for cultivating this intellect. 

Meanwhile, he treats the "spurious and adulterous philosopher" who mimics the legitimate one, and also the abuse of a certain kind of philosophy. Again, he treats the form of philosophizing that pertains to him above all others who will one day rule the republic. He teaches that the most proper trait of the philosopher is a perpetual love of Truth itself regarding eternal things. Therefore, both the love of temporal things and lying are most alien to the philosopher. He shows, moreover, that the mind of the philosopher in the very investigation of truth is separated from the body, and by a certain kinship of its own is joined to the Divine Mind. Through the "formulas of the Ideas" implanted in him from the beginning, he reaches the Ideas themselves, and from them, by that very contact, strikes out a light, by which, having been made more fecund, he may conceive...

<meta>The catchword "piat" indicates the start of the next page's first word, "concipiat" (may conceive).</meta>

<summary>Ficino defends Plato's controversial "community of property and wives" by framing it as a spiritual and medicinal necessity for a harmonious society. He then transitions to Book VI, defining the philosopher-guardian as one who uses the "Ideal Forms" to govern the state justly.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Plato’s Republic, specifically focusing on the nature of the "Idea of the Good" and the qualifications of the philosopher-king. It bridges the end of Book VI and the beginning of Book VII.</meta>

# ARGUMENTS AND COMMENTARY.
## [By Marsilio Ficino]

<margin>A</margin> ...may grasp, or rather, having been made stronger, may give birth to the truth; that is, that through its very conceptions it may harmonize with the Ideas from every side. You should note here that the act of understanding—just as in the *Symposium*—is called a "generation" and a "birth." This indeed agrees with Christian theology and shows that there is not only an imaginary form and truth in the mind, but a certain natural one as well. Furthermore, he [Plato] believes that a talent of this kind is born very rarely and in few people, and even then it requires many conditions and is hindered by many obstacles. It is especially corrupted by the speech and opinion of the common people, and much more so by the actions of that same multitude. Again, it is corrupted by common teachers, who themselves adapt their lives and speech to the crowd like flatterers, and deliver a similar sort of discipline to their listeners. And see how fittingly Plato compares the common crowd to a vast 
<margin>B</margin> brute beast. Likewise, he compares all city-states to ships steered by some chance by sailors who are utterly ignorant of the art of governing, and who mock the man endowed with the skill of a pilot. Note that all the best gifts, whether of nature or of fortune, if they are cultivated even slightly negligently, turn into evils; or if badly cultivated, they turn out at last to be the very worst. Moreover, the fact that sometimes—though very rarely—a great and most proven man appears in a poorly ordered city (as he judges all of them to be), this is attributed not to art, nor to nature, but solely to divinity. Where he mentions "Momus" <note>The Greek god of mockery and criticism</note> in relation to the reproach of God, understand Momus to be the divine care which foresees what could have been reproached in individual things if they had been made differently than they are, 
<margin>C</margin> and therefore disposing each thing so that they cannot rightly be reproached. He then assigns the causes from which slanders against philosophers have arisen, as if they were either evil or useless to the republic. First, many people daily rush into the study of philosophy who are most unfit, possessing as little talent as they do judgment, yet with no small ambition or greed; they seize upon it, and from their commerce with it they procreate "adulterous" and ridiculous opinions, and furthermore disgrace the philosophical faculty with their evil character. Secondly, if any are born for this study, they are either immediately corrupted by a wicked education and habit, or if they persevere with integrity of character, they are nonetheless not instructed in the proper grades of the disciplines; or if instructed, they are not admitted to the 
<margin>D</margin> republic, or rather they themselves are unwilling to immerse themselves in the public waves, fearing certain dangers and despairing that they can benefit the city with sound counsel among men who are everywhere corrupt. Amidst these things, observe the storms of the active life and the tranquility of the contemplative life, the lofty mind of the philosopher, the contempt for mortal things, the study of divine things, and a certain formula of doctrines according to the stages of age. In every way, he educates the philosopher and the citizen by a similar reasoning, and not without justice. For he asserts in the *Statesman* and the *Sophist* that the royal man, the citizen, and the philosopher are the same. He proves that it is necessary for two types of nature to concur in this man, which very rarely concur in humans: 
<margin>E</margin> namely, a nature sharp in talent, fit for contemplation, and burning with a greed for truth; together with a grave nature, strenuous in action, and provident for the public good. He leads such a talent through all the grades of the disciplines, as will be clear in the seventh book. He also commands that they be exercised in civil actions, and—amidst pleasures, pains, labors, and dangers—be diligently examined and tested like gold in the fire, before the rudders of the city are entrusted to them. Above all, however, he judges the knowledge of the "Good itself" to be the most excellent of all and necessary for this man, affirming that just as all things are possessed uselessly without the possession of the good, so also the knowledge of all things and arts is utterly useless without the understanding of the good itself; nor can a citizen rightly direct either private or public affairs toward the good unless he has known by reason what the good is. Although the knowledge of this divine good might seem superfluous to an Aristotelian for governing a republic according to human customs, it is nevertheless necessary for this very governance, through which Plato says (in the preceding sections) one must strive to make citizens friends of and similar to God. He added, moreover, that a governor would be both blind and carried by mere chance regarding the disposal of individual goods toward the Good itself, unless he has perceived the first form of the good, the exemplar and cause of all goods. But so that you may notice that Aristotle in the *Ethics* plays against Plato regarding the "Idea of the Good," read Plato’s words most diligently, and you will clearly perceive that the Idea of the Good is not this or that species, here or there, but the very fecundity of the most eminent divinity, propagating itself powerfully, sweetly, and healthfully through all things. He wishes the visible sun to be a certain image of this in the visible world, diffusing its powers similarly through all things. But before this sun which we see, Plato imagines another in the invisible world: the first image of God the Father, and the true Son. Therefore he called them "sons of the good," so that above this visible and imaginary son you might contemplate the invisible and archetypal one. We read of this Father and Son in the *Letter to Hermias*. Regarding this, the Platonist Philo, in the *Book of Causes*, says: "One must strive above all to ascend to Being itself, that is, of whom it is said, 'I am who I am' <note>Exodus 3:14</note>." Or at least to His image and most sacred reason and first-born Word. Amelius the Platonist asserts that through such reason and word all things are made according to Heraclitus and Plato, and he uses the testimony of John the Evangelist. Likewise, Plato testifies to this in the *Epinomis*. And

<column-break/>

And although some of the Platonists distinguish the Son of God the Father as God, by substance from the Father, in the manner of the Arians <note>Arianism: a heresy claiming the Son was created by and subordinate to the Father</note>—especially Julian in his book *On the Sun*—nevertheless Julian’s teacher, Iamblichus, brings forward the mysteries of the Egyptians, in which there is indeed a different "reason" [ratio] for the Father and the Son, but the same substance, as is read. But hear the mystery: "The first God and the One is the Father of the first God, whom He begets while remaining in the solitary unity of Himself. He is the exemplar of the Son, who is named the Son of Himself, His own Father and 'Only-Father,' God truly good. For He is the source of the Ideas: from which One, indeed, God, sufficient through Himself, unfolded Himself into the light. Therefore He is named sufficient through Himself and His own Father. For He is the principle, the God of gods, One from the One, above all essence, and the principle of essence." Iamblichus testifies that this is the mystery of Hermes <note>Original: "Mercurii" (Mercury/Hermes Trismegistus)</note>. 
<margin>B</margin> Truly, how the Good itself is above pleasure, and character, and wisdom, Plato signifies here briefly. Above pleasure, indeed, because if pleasure itself were the Good itself, no pleasure would be evil or harmful. Likewise above character, since many think it enough regarding character if they seem to have honest characters. But that which they judge to be the true good, they do not seek by opinion, but to have it in actual fact. Furthermore, it is above knowledge, because you do not desire to know just anything in any way, but rather to know well and to know good things. Otherwise, you either reject or neglect knowledge. Nor should you say that the Good itself is the "knowledge of the good," lest you foolishly define the same thing by the same thing. Again, it is above the intellect; for the intellect assiduously seeks the good. But the Good itself does not seek the good. Add also that it is above truth. For that which you judge to be more good, you also choose more. But you choose a less "true" disease or loss rather than a more "true" one. Finally, it is above being. For you desire to be, so that you may be well. But concerning these things, and how the intellect understands all true things by the light of the Good itself, we dispute more extensively in our *Theology*. There follows the distinction of things into two genera, the visible and the invisible, and of each into two—namely, the antecedent and the following—and a similar distinction of human perception. In these matters he follows Brontinus and Archytas, but explains it both more elegantly and more broadly.

---

### ON THE SEVENTH DIALOGUE
### of Plato, on the Republic,
### or on Justice.
### Argument to page 480.

<margin>F</margin> Sages endowed with divine talent have turned every study of the mind from earthly to celestial things, from the mobile to the immobile, and from those things which are sensed to those which surpass sense, according to their strength. Considering the machine of the world to be both one and wonderfully ordered—yet unable to consist of itself, since it is composed of diverse parts and is subject to change—they rightly recognized that it depends on another; on another, I say, who is One and most wise. He who makes one work out of many, and wisely orders that one thing everywhere; who moreover rules it powerfully—a work, namely, vast and manifold, revolved in a perpetual and most rapid motion, yet one that does not wander. He also leads individual things most benignly toward the good, running with both wonderful convenience and ease. For this reason, by a certain common conception, they agreed together that God exists: the one powerful, wise, and clement King of the universe. Whom earthly kings and governors of republics ought to imitate according to their strength. After this common conception of God, they began to proceed more clearly and closely toward God by a twin path: one by negation, the other by reference. For by the former, arguing what the Good itself (that is, what God) is not, they proved that He is 
<margin>G</margin> nothing from those things which are grasped by the senses, nor from those which are comprehended by the mind. In the latter path, referring both the creatures to the Creator and conversely the Creator to the creatures, they worked out by what reasoning the Creator makes and perfects individual things, and how the creatures either relate to Him, or are able to imitate or follow Him. Our Plato shows that the talent of the philosopher proceeds this far in the *Parmenides*, and confirms it in the preceding book. Dionysius the Areopagite also greatly approves of this. I say that the mind proceeds this far both by a certain ray infused into the mind once from the beginning, and by the approaching light of the most divine things constantly illuminating minds. But truly, 
<margin>H</margin> what the Good is in itself—that is, the divine substance—no one can attain through such paths, as he shows both in the *Parmenides* and here. Only through these paths does one finally arrive there where the Divine Good, solely because of its own benignity, forms its lover (who approaches more closely) by its own light, and warms him with heat, and transforms the mind by its power—the mind then finally knowing God when it has itself already been made "god." This indeed he signifies also in his letters. After the philosopher has contemplated God, he governs celestial things...

<summary>This page provides a Neoplatonic and Christianized commentary on Plato's Republic, specifically discussing the "Idea of the Good" as a divine principle and the rigorous training required for philosopher-kings. It emphasizes the Good as the source of all truth and being, comparing it to the sun and linking it to the concept of the Divine Word (Logos).</summary>
