<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plato’s Republic, specifically Book VII. Ficino, a central figure of the Italian Renaissance, is harmonizing Platonic philosophy with Christian theology and ancient "pagan" wisdom.</meta>

# MARSILIO FICINO

<margin>A</margin> Only one who loves, and is alone, will be able to govern earthly affairs by divine guidance. In this matter, Plato praises Minos <note>Mythical King of Crete</note> for seeking laws from Jove through contemplation before promulgating them to men. I pass over how much many praise Scipio, because he approached the republic with Jove as his teacher. What shall I say of Numa Pompilius, who governed the city with religious laws? Did not also the Mosaic laws, by which the people of God were divinely governed, come to men with God himself teaching? Hence Aristoxenus relates the mysteries of the Indian philosophers, which maintain that without a divine rule—and one indeed demonstrated by God—nothing can ever be administered rightly or happily, whether privately or publicly. Because the Egyptians had discovered the same truth, they granted the helm of the kingdom only to philosophers, and those indeed who were perfect and, moreover, consecrated. <margin>B</margin> And they thought to such an extent that nothing could be done happily without divine aid, that they inaugurated all public affairs with sacred rites and vows. Furthermore, they asserted that nothing could be understood without a certain divine inspiration (as Iamblichus reports), so much so that among them all the books of those practicing philosophy were ascribed to the name of the god Mercury <note>Hermes Trismegistus</note>, as if they were not the inventions of men, but of God. Timaeus also signifies this, saying that Philosophy is a divine gift. In the *Protagoras* and the *Statesman*, he teaches that civil skill is also a divine bounty. And to return to this seventh book, he does not admit anyone to govern this republic of his unless it is established that they have received both gifts divinely, through a certain divine nature as well as education: such a person alone he calls everywhere a legitimate citizen and a philosopher. But why does he say there is need for a divine gift for this? I pass over other reasons for now. It is because, while it is most difficult for anyone to govern himself happily, it is certainly impossible to arrange a city—composed of so many and diverse people, and which daily faces innumerable and uncertain accidents—blessedly without God, the author of blessedness. Hence it happened that every city recognized a certain particular deity as a patron. Plato wants the governor of the city to be the vicar and interpreter of this deity, who, like a deity, contemplates divine things and provides for human things from that source. For this reason, he expels wicked men far from the republic as being entirely devoid of the divine gift. He accepts only the good. Yet not even all of these. For he calls those ignorant of theology "blind" and "dreamers," inasmuch as they accept the images of things instead of the things themselves; and he deems it foolish to entrust the guardianship of the city to the blind and dreaming. But as for the theologians, who do not yet possess any experience of human affairs, he does not admit them to conducting public business until they have become accustomed to handling private and lighter matters. Meanwhile, he concludes that the magistracy must be given to no one except him whose life is better than the magistracy, and who neither seeks nor even desires the magistracy itself. But where Plato, in educating the civil philosopher, proposes the image <margin>D</margin> of the cave, and of chains, and of a certain light, and of shadows and water: understand the Cave to be this world which we see, if it is compared to the invisible world. The Chain is the human body, or rather the disturbance binding the soul to the body. The Shadows are all the things that move the senses. For these are the shadows of true things, that is, of the Ideas. When he says that the soul does not descend from the invisible world to the visible, nor in turn ascend, without offense <note>or "distress"</note>, you can take this in two ways according to the Platonic manner: either in this life, when one passes without a medium from this study of human things to that supreme study of divine things, and vice versa; or between this life and the next. That is, when the soul, either impure, migrates from the darkness of the body <margin>E</margin> to the divine light (under which it grows dim and is blinded), or descending from the divine light into the elemental body, it is long blind and disturbed. Remember that it is the property of light to create and demonstrate all things: and this is threefold—divine, intellectual, and visible. The Divine is called the Sun of both suns. The Intellectual is named the Angelic sun, the sun of the mundane sun. Finally, the Visible light is the celestial sun and its splendor. Just as the splendor spreading from the celestial sun through all things is the image and act of the sun, so also the light which is in the sun is the image and act of the angelic mind. Then the light in the angel is the act and image of the divine light. And just as visible light is received only in a transparent nature, so the invisible is received in a discerning nature. Julian the Platonist, describing three such suns in his book *On the Sun*, adds from the theology of the Phoenicians that visible light is a certain perennial act of divine and angelic intelligence flashing through the solar <margin>F</margin> window to the eyes, and from there diffused through transparent materials everywhere as if suited to itself. Furthermore, lest you doubt that this apparent light is the image of the non-apparent light, know that light is not a body. For it penetrates bodies without offense or infection. Likewise, it does not become a proper quality of a composite body. Otherwise, it would require a preceding proper quality of the elements (hot or cold) in that which is to receive it, and it would remain for a time in the transparent medium when the sun withdrew. Likewise, it is not bound to its own dimension. For it does not arrive in time, or illuminate one part now and another later. Add that it fills a wide space without its own dissipation, and in turn collects itself into a narrow space in a moment without the constriction of itself or the vessel. It is not properly corporeal, but a medium between the incorporeal and the corporeal, and indeed the proper quality of heaven, whose nature is as close as possible to the incorporeal. It is communicated also to the elements, but only the transparent ones, which in this very transparency are similar to heaven: to the transparent, I say, first light, then heat; but to the opaque, heat first, and light not until they are reduced to a transparent nature through heat. But into opaque bodies, in which an earthy nature dominates, it is not

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> infused. Not because it cannot penetrate—since it even penetrates crystal, which is more solid than many opaque things—but because an earthy nature, being most foreign to the celestial nature, cannot be capable of a celestial quality. It does, however, communicate heat to opaque things as I said, which is not as proper to heaven as light is. For because heaven shines, it therefore grows warm. Because the light diffused from heaven into our transparent things ought again to be called the image of the sun, it appears from this that it is the common and proper origin of all images. For the images of things result under its splendor: and it is itself an image so powerful that it appears not only when it bounces back from a mirroring body, but even when it leaps forth from the sun—which is not at all the case with other images. Yet all are incorporeal, since they spread themselves through the whole in a moment; and in the same <margin>B</margin> point there are many without mutual confusion. Therefore, light is also incorporeal: by whose power this is accomplished. Accordingly, in a moment it carries with it the ray of the sun, the act of light, and the force of heat. And through light indeed, it reflects the clarity of divine and angelic intelligence. Through heat, however, it reflects the affection of the will and charity of both. Since the higher beings, just like craftsmen, perform their works through will rather than through intelligence, this visible ray flowing from their invisible ray rightly performs through heat the individual things that are produced, rather than through light. Or rather, it acts through light upon the spiritual images of things, but through heat upon corporeal qualities. And this heat depends on light in the same way that in divine matters all things are represented ideally through the <margin>C</margin> intellect, and from the affection rising therefrom, all things are generated. We, being warned by this, if an earthy nature does not receive celestial light, let us expel earthy affections far from us, so that we may be filled with divine light. And if the lowest body does not receive the light of the first unless it first grows warm and is rendered similar thereby: come, let us also, the lowest of minds, first burn with love for the first mind; so that, purged by love and made similar, we may then shine divinely and rejoice in the full light. But let us now touch upon the rest of this seventh book. Since therefore there is a triple light as we said—namely, visible, intellectual above sight, and divine above intellect—therefore Plato makes mention here of light in three stages: <margin>D</margin> namely, in the cave, in the night, and in the day, signifying those three lights. Three times also he makes mention of water: in the cave, in the night, and in the day. For just as light both makes and demonstrates all things, so water washes all things and represents them. By the first he signifies morals, and by the second, contemplation. And he carries out each in three stages. Truly, through the moral he washes and purges three times: first indeed by cutting away the fertile <note>or "teeming"</note> impulses through the civil virtues; then by extirpating the same through the purgatorial virtues; thirdly, through the virtues of the already purged soul, by most perfectly moderating the first impulses: whence one now arrives at the exemplary virtues which are in God, especially through contemplation. Of which indeed there are three stages, <margin>E</margin> which the water named three times reflects, insofar as it reflects intelligence by representing images. For divine things seem to be represented in three "waters," so to speak. First indeed, though more confusedly, in physical reasons; second, more distinctly in mathematical ones; third, most clearly in the entirely absolute metaphysical ones. Plato calls physical forms altogether material, because they need both common and proper matter, and cannot be thought of without it. But mathematical forms he calls not so material, because they do not need proper matter, but either only common matter (like dimensions) or none (like numbers); and these can be thought of without matter. Finally, he considers divine forms to be entirely immaterial and true things: of which mathematical forms are images, and <margin>F</margin> natural things are shadows. This is a Pythagorean mystery. When he noticed that Thales, Democritus, and Anaxagoras were as negligent in divine matters as they were diligent in natural ones; and on the contrary, that Pherecydes, Pythagoras, and all the Pythagoreans, the princes of mathematicians, were likewise the greatest theologians and divine in their minds, he rightly concluded—partly by reason and partly by experience—that the curious study of natural things very often turns the soul away from divine things. For this reason, Solomon also judged it a most wicked occupation, and those who were too occupied in it to be wretched. Socrates detests the same in the *Phaedo*: those, I say, who refer the causes of natural effects curiously only to certain elemental qualities, <margin>G</margin> and rest in such a beginning and end, nor do they seek out the supreme principle and end of the universe. Therefore, this seventh book—where it leads the soul to the supreme good and the sun (that is, God) and the divine Ideas (like stars) by suitable steps—makes no mention of natural skill in the ascent itself. Instead, it brings into the midst certain mathematical steps that lead more conveniently to divine things, among which two are pure. For Arithmetic is concerned with pure numbers, and Geometry with pure dimensions. There are three <margin>H</margin> mixed steps. For Music adds voices and movements to numbers, pertaining chiefly to hearing. Stereometry <note>Solid geometry</note> adds weights to dimensions. Astronomy measures the celestial spheres and movements with numbers and dimensions. Plato uses natural skill in the descent rather than the ascent, as he teaches in the *Timaeus*, *Philebus*, *Parmenides*, and often elsewhere. For in the descent, he wants natural principles to be demonstrated through the divine causes of natural things. But in the ascent, he thinks that through anxious care for natural things (as if very remote from divine ones), the soul is turned away from them rather than toward them. Altogether, he counts as nothing all actions, even if they seem most honorable, unless they lead to the imitation and perfection of the divine good; and similarly all speculations...

<summary>Ficino explains Plato's allegory of the cave and the hierarchy of light (visible, intellectual, divine) as a path for the soul's ascent to God. He argues that true governance requires divine inspiration and that mathematical studies are superior to natural sciences for elevating the mind to metaphysical truths.</summary>
<keywords>Allegory of the Cave, Neoplatonism, Divine Light, Mathematical Sciences, Political Philosophy, Metaphysics, Pythagoras, Solar Symbolism</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Plato’s Republic, specifically focusing on the transition from the intellectual journey of the soul (Book VII) to the degradation of political states (Book VIII).</meta>

# ARGUMENTS AND COMMENTARY

<margin>A</margin> He [Plato] disregards things unless they contribute to finding the divine good, or even rejects them if they divert us from it in any way. Therefore, he intends the whole study of philosophy to be a turning away from sensible things <note>things perceived by the senses</note> toward intelligible things <note>things understood by the mind</note>, and an ascent to the Good itself, which is the supreme light of the intelligible world. He says that just as sight relates to the highest of visible things—that is, the sun—so the intellect relates to the highest light of the intelligible, namely God. Therefore, just as the sun generates the eye, bestows the power of seeing by generating it, and continually provides the act of seeing to that which is generated: so God both creates the intellect, provides the power of understanding by creating it, and continually provides the act of understanding to that which is created. Again, just as regarding the eye there is no need for anything to be done by art except to purify it and turn it: so regarding the intellect, philosophy provides only two things, namely purifying it both from disturbances and from false opinions, and turning it through reasons and exhortations from sensible forms to

<margin>B</margin> the intellectual forms implanted in us, and through these to the intelligible forms, that is, the Ideas. Again, through the Ideas to the Divine Mind, by which the Ideas are comprehended, and finally from this to the Divine Good, the principle and light of the Ideas. When, therefore, he says the soul is raised from the lamp to the moon, and from the moon to the sun, he means it is elevated from natural forms to mathematical ones, and finally from these to divine ones—not indeed by teaching (for divine things, as he relates in his letters, cannot be taught) but rather by purifying and turning. For once these are accomplished, just as the sun, which is the light of visible things, shows visible things to the eye, so the Good itself, which is the light of intelligibles, lays open the things to be understood to the intellect. But concerning these matters, we have written most extensively in our *Theology* <note>referring to Ficino's "Platonic Theology"</note>.

<margin>C</margin> Therefore, no one should wonder that Plato rarely uses the order of writing for instruction, but always for purification and exhortation—that is, for conversion. After this, note that among those things which are sensed, those especially excite the intelligence which are not clearly distinguished from their opposites by the sense, and therefore require a discerning intelligence. Likewise, that numbers are not corporeal. For number is nothing other than unity repeated. But unity is not a body: for it is not divided into parts; if it is imagined to be divided, it is not cut, but rather multiplied—multiplied, I say, into itself, not into any parts; for any part would be smaller than the whole. But no unity is either greater or smaller than another unity. And this very unity and number raise us toward

<margin>D</margin> essence; similarly also figures, the true ratio <note>reason or proportion</note> of which is found in the mind rather than in the body. Similarly, astronomy seems to investigate the reason of the Mover from the order of heaven. Plato denies that he is an astronomer who looks at the things above, but does not look *beyond* the heaven from the heaven itself, especially because celestial things, since they do not fulfill a complete order, undoubtedly depend on some higher and complete order. The musician also fails unless he withdraws from the consonance of the voice to the intellectual reason of consonance. Finally, he places Dialectic—that is, Metaphysics or Theology—above all faculties, both as leading them all and using the service of each for its own duty. Its duty, indeed, is to progress through the entire breadth of what is called "being," and to betake itself to the Good itself, the cause of all being, and to define what each thing is in the very order of beings by assigning the reason of each essence, and to demonstrate what follows from any essence. But he judges the other faculties to be servile compared to the nobility of this one. For they either decline toward the opinions of men, or toward the generations and compositions of lower things, or toward the cultivation of those things which are born; or at least, even if they raise themselves toward the incorporeal as much as they can, they nevertheless dream about them in a certain way. Such, he says, are the mathematical disciplines. But soon he joins two kinds: namely, essence and generation. He considers that intelligence pertains to the former, but opinion to the latter. Again, within intelligence, he says that science follows essence and pertains to the dialectician, while cognition follows essence and belongs to the mathematician. In opinion, he similarly counts faith <note>original: "fidem", here meaning belief/conviction</note> and imagination: and through the former, bodies are perceived, but through the latter, the images and shadows of bodies. Then he concludes that the other faculties are blind without Dialectic. And that they, together with Dialectic, are moreover vain unless they clearly know the Idea of the Good itself, and through it know how to discern true goods from false ones in individual cases. But he who is ignorant of the reason of the Good is troubled here and there in dreams, and descending to the underworld, is mocked and vexed all the more. He adds that a man is "lame" who is unfit and unskilled for either action or speculation. Therefore, for governing, he chooses those who are both fit by nature and sufficiently instructed by discipline for both. Meanwhile, note that the liar, as if crippled and mutilated, is to be excluded from the republic. But he calls him a liar who both lies to others on purpose, and who lies to himself through ignorance. Remember also that the labors of the mind are heavier than those of the body, and therefore one must learn in youth, and the liberal disciplines must be taught far from servitude. However, Dialectic is not to be handed over to youths. The *Philebus* also teaches us this. For as the *Phaedrus* also distinguishes, two leaders are within us all: namely, an innate desire for pleasures, and a certain opinion acquired through education, which says that the honorable and just things defined for us by the laws must be preserved in all things. But these two leaders very often pull in opposite directions. Since the faculty of disputing, if handed to youths, weakens the opinion of the honorable—whence they turn out intemperate, and even proud and impious, as is read in the *Philebus* and the *Laws*—therefore they are to be instructed in mathematics before the thirtieth year of age, and exercised equally in public affairs at intervals. But when they reach thirty, they are to be admitted to Dialectic, yet in such a way that they are called back to public actions at intervals. You, however, name the industry of disputing "Dialectic" from its form, "Logic" from its beginning,

<column-break/>

and "Metaphysics" and "Theology" from its end. Know also that men are called to the goal of this kind of dialectic, which is as it were divine, in the fiftieth year of age, because there is need of a purified and serene mind for the intuition of divine things. Meanwhile, observe here—what we use quite often both here and in the *Theology*—that three things are noted by Plato: namely, the ray, the light-spread <note>original: "lumen"</note>, and the Light <note>original: "lux"</note>. The ray is proper and naturally implanted in individual minds just as in eyes. But the light-spread is common to all eyes. Finally, the Divine Light presides over the light-spread common to all minds, just as the light in the sun presides over the light-spread of the eyes, which is equally common. He concludes that the citizen, after he has contemplated the Light of the Good itself both through the ray naturally implanted in him and through the light-spread of the same infused in him, ought to govern the city according to the pattern of the Good itself as much as possible.

### ARGUMENT FOR BOOK VIII OF THE REPUBLIC
->to page 491.<-

<margin>E</margin> Socrates has now completed the perfect form of the republic in seven dialogues, consecrated to the septenary number of Pallas <note>Athena</note>. He calls it both a royal and an aristocratic government. Aristocratic, indeed, because in it many people distinguished by virtue perform public duties and constitute a Senate. Royal, however, because there is one will of all toward the public good, one mind as if a queen; and if anyone among them is singular in probity, he is singularly honored. Yet not so much is granted to him that he can change public affairs without the Senate, that is, the number of all approved men. It remained, after the best and blessed form of the republic, to bring the lower ones into the midst. He counts four of these. The first he intends to be that into which the best soon degenerates, which he names the "ambitious" <note>Timocracy</note>. The second is the power of the few <note>Oligarchy</note> arising from the ambitious. The third is the popular <note>Democracy</note> proceeding from this. The fourth, finally, is tyranny, sprouting especially from the popular. Since the forms of republics come from the forms of souls, he describes with wonderful art five successive affections and habits of souls and as many similar and similarly named states, and concludes in summary that the royal mind is the best and most blessed, and the similar city likewise. But the tyrannical is the worst and most miserable. Also, cities oppressed by tyrants are similarly the worst and most miserable. He concludes that the middle minds and middle governments stand in a certain middle way. From all this, it appears how ruinous injustice is both in the city and in the soul, and how salutary justice is in both. Everywhere, however, he explains with marvelous diligence the changes of both souls and cities from high forms into others. Especially, he leads the change of the blessed republic—and, if I may say so, the Golden one—into the ambitious or Silver or Iron one, from a higher beginning, and imagines the Muses pouring out (or rather confounding) this as an oracle. Surely, if a blessed republic cannot fall into a worse state by its own defect, and yet it does fall at some time, it falls by some common defect and cause.

<margin>F</margin> In which matter one may laugh at the Aristotelian slanders. For Aristotle, in the fifth book of the *Politics*, should not have demanded from his Plato (or rather, never his) a specific cause for changing the blessed republic, since there is no specific one, but he should have been content with a common one. For just as a man who is both very strong and very temperate suffers from disease not so much from a specific cause as from a common one—that is, by a certain fatal order—so through the celestial circuits, which are below the moon, perpetually revolving, those things which are composed by certain configurations of the spheres and courses of time are eventually dissolved by adverse ones. Since the assignment of such a cause far exceeds the limits of the present civil faculty, Socrates uses the prophecy of the Muses, so that we also need the prophecy of Apollo to interpret these things. Not without merit did Tully <note>Cicero</note>, when he wished to briefly express that a matter was most obscure, say it was "more obscure than the number of Plato." Nor do I wonder that Theo-

<margin>G</margin> n of Smyrna, a professor especially of Platonic mathematics, shrewdly bypassed such a mystery as if it were inexplicable. Which indeed Iamblichus of Chalcis seems to have entangled while he wished to explain it. But what if there is more difficulty than weight in such words? Since he himself imagines the Muses trifling with a certain tragic swelling, terrifying the childish and simple mind, and bringing on stupor. Finally, whatever that may be, you will receive our exposition more opportunely from the commentaries on the *Timaeus*. Furthermore, consider these mortal precepts. It is impossible for riches to be honored in a city at the same time as virtue. Likewise, to hand over the rudders of the republic to the wealthier is the same as if a ship were handed over to be steered not by the more skilled in navigation but by the richer. Surely both this one and that one will be endangered.

<margin>H</margin> Again, the safest guardian against all vices is knowledge. Furthermore, the peak of one contrary is the beginning of the other; thus the extreme license of liberty is the beginning of extreme servitude. Just as in any quality of things and times, every excess is accustomed to be turned immediately into its contrary. He says the same in his letters, approving above all things a moderated liberty.

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficinus's commentaries on Plato's Republic, specifically providing the "Arguments" or summaries for Book IX and Book X. Ficinus, a central figure of the Italian Renaissance, seeks to harmonize Platonic philosophy with Christian theology.</meta>

# MARSILIO FICINO.

### ARGUMENT FOR BOOK IX OF THE REPUBLIC.
### referring to page 502.

**Socrates**, having treated at great length the royal life of the best men <note>the aristocracy or rule by the virtuous</note>, now disputes much concerning its opposite, tyranny, so that we may approve of the former as the most blessed state and reject the latter as the most wretched. This is handled not only in the eighth book, but further in the ninth concerning tyranny: namely, by what method it chiefly arises from a popular state <note>democracy</note>, what its nature is, and how harmful and unhappy it is. This is done so that we might avoid with all our strength that primary tyranny which exists within the soul, and in turn embrace the kingdom deep within the spirit. By this, he certainly intends to demonstrate that justice is not merely praiseworthy according to human opinion, but is by its very nature both wonderfully honorable and, above all, to be venerated as salutary. Likewise, injustice is not to be censured solely out of fear of laws or infamy, but must be fled far away because of the poison of its own malevolent nature. When he names "Justice," he sometimes designates legal and common justice—that is, universal virtue established under the providence of laws; at other times, he means a more specific or distributive justice, through which honors, rewards, and punishments are distributed in the city according to merit, and actions and duties are assigned to the parts of the soul according to their natural dignity. Or he means commutative justice, through which, in the city, goods, services, or money are exchanged at a fair and lawful price, so that just as the higher reason provides for the lower parts, the lower forces likewise supply what is necessary for the command of reason. Among these things, note that the tyrannical soul is so disturbed that it is properly judged to be lost in lust, drunken, furious, and monstrous. Indeed, it is snatched away by those monstrous lusts like a wild beast—ferocity which others only occasionally experience while dreaming. However, those matters here pertaining to the falsehood, truth, and prophecy of dreams we treat abundantly in our *Theology* <note>referring to Ficino's "Platonic Theology"</note>.

<margin>B</margin>
Consider how diligently he enumerates all the evils by which a city is oppressed under tyranny, and how aptly he counts just as many evils—and even more—in the soul of the tyrant, so that nothing more miserable could be imagined. Soon, he reduces the entire disputation (which aims to show that the wise and just life is preferable to its opposite) into three heads. He wishes the first to be what has been treated thus far: namely, the comparison of the foolish and unjust man to a city governed by no wisdom or justice. There it truly appears that both that city and that man are, by equal measure, in the worst and most unhappy condition.

<margin>C</margin>
He now approaches the second head, repeating that distinction of the parts of the soul into the natures of reasoning, anger <note>the spirited part</note>, and desiring, to which he matches three lives: the philosophical, the ambitious, and the covetous—covetous, I say, for the sake of money and pleasures, and therefore it is also called avaricious. He similarly arranges three parts in the city: magistrates, soldiers, and money-makers. He then proves that the life endowed with virtue is more to be chosen than the vicious one because it is, in truth, sweeter. For since each of these three prefers the pleasure of his own life to the others, only the philosopher can judge this correctly. For judgment requires experience, prudence, and reason. First, as far as experience is concerned, the philosopher has experienced both his own pleasures and those of others; thus he can easily know which is to be preferred. The others have never tasted the joys of the one practicing philosophy, and therefore they cannot compare their pleasures with the philosopher's joy. Furthermore, only the philosopher excels in perfect prudence and the industry of assigning reasons, which are the two remaining things necessary for judgment. Therefore, since the philosopher prefers the joys of a wise and just life to the delights of an ambitious and lustful life, we ought rightly, by the sentence of such a judge, to prefer a life guided by virtue over a life dissolved in vice. Finally, the third head begins chiefly from the fact that true pleasure can be found only in the wise and just man. In others, it is established that pleasure is false and shadow-like. This is proved thus: most vehement pleasures are certain "fillings" of a lack. And where both that which is filled and that which fills are of a more perfect nature, and the mode of filling is purer and more effective, there pleasure is truer, more perfect, and greater. Since, therefore, the intellect and the truth to be understood have a truer and more perfect nature than the sense and the sensible object, and since truth penetrates the intellect more deeply than the sensible object penetrates the sense (and does so without the mixture of pain), it follows that the pleasure of the intelligence is truer and more perfect. Among these things, by some chance, something mathematical intervenes, the explanation of which you will receive more opportunely from the commentaries on the *Timaeus*.

Next, attend to that figure of the soul's nature. In it, understand the nature of desiring under the name of a "manifold beast"; under the figure of a "lion," the vigor of anger; and under the form of a "man," reason. And see how expressively he depicts the life of the ambitious, unjust, and lustful man as a most wretched slavery. Also, in the same place, take the formula by which you can interpret the passage of souls into beasts in such a way that they are said to migrate into the affections and habits of beasts rather than into their bodies. Furthermore, remember that just as in the body the sharpness of sense, health, strength, and beauty are goods not by opinion but by nature (and their opposites are similarly evils), so in the soul, prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice are naturally goods, and their opposites are naturally evils. Finally, accept the form of the whole life, through which you may so arrange all bodily things that they harmonize with the temperance of the soul. Choose individual things only insofar as they contribute to the health of the soul; and conversely, flee far from those things which hinder it. Always inhabit the citadel of the mind, and allow yourself to be cast down from it by no allurements or threats. When you wish to form both yourself and others in this way, look up at the clear exemplar of this republic <margin>A</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>A in heaven: in heaven, I say—that is, in the order of the celestial motions, and higher still in the divine mind: so that from there, at last, you may justly and happily compose yourself first, then your family, and thirdly your city, according to its image.</margin>

### ARGUMENT FOR BOOK X OF THE REPUBLIC.
### referring to page 511.

**Hitherto** Socrates, the most diligent teacher of the human race, has provoked mankind toward legal justice—that is, universal virtue—through the very beauty of justice; and similarly, he has called them back from injustice <margin>B</margin> through the foulness of injustice. Next, however, he will exhort them to the former by its eternal fruit and reward, and restrain them from the latter by its eternal loss and punishment; and this is the chief duty of this tenth book. But before he performs this principal duty, he uses a certain prologue in which he diligently settles what he had touched upon in previous dialogues and had not left finished at the end, which is very necessary for public safety. Truly, this physician of ours for human diseases is more diligent in curing that species of disease which others not only cure negligently but do not even cure at all—nay, what is worse, they love it as if it were a most healthy thing and embrace it with all zeal: I mean poetic imitation. <margin>C</margin> For while ingenious poets express disturbed minds more sharply, they meanwhile imprint similar disturbances more vehemently and deeply into the minds of the listeners and readers. And they infect everyone all the more, the more they are praised and please. Such a prologue follows the end appropriately: for there the soul is divided into reason and into lower parts agitated by disturbances, the rule of which is called "tyrannical," first in the soul and then in the city. But because poetic imitation arouses, nourishes, and increases such parts—irritating anger, tickling lust, loosening laughter, and pouring out tears and complaints—it therefore seems to undermine the kingdom of reason and bring in the tyranny of disturbance. Wherefore Socrates destroys such a plague, otherwise pleasant but extremely <margin>D</margin> poisonous, lest it destroy us. And see with what great charity our Plato everywhere consults the human race, searching out and looking around for those dangers which no one else would suspect; add to this that he strongly opposes his own nature and education (that is, the poetic), provided he may fight strenuously for the public safety. Wherefore it should seem a wonder to no one that Plato here, for the love of truth, does not spare even his own Homer, since for the sake of the cult of justice, he does not even indulge his own genius. He disparages Homer especially so that through him, the prince of imitators, we may consider the others much more condemned. And since he says that neither divine nor human things are taught by Homer, understand the <margin>E</margin> praises attributed to Homer by Plato in the *Philebus* not as being from Plato's own judgment, but as derived from common opinion. He proves, however, that the skill of imitating is, as we have said, very dangerous, and moreover, slavish and most vile. For imitators neither understand the things themselves nor do them, but following the forms of things appearing to the senses and catching at common opinions about them, they both report certain images and obey the senses and disturbances, having no regard for reason. However, as much as he disapproves of poets where they disturb, so much does he approve if they exhort toward virtue and piety through the honorable praises of heroes and divine hymns. But to express how vile all imitation is, he divides the genus of arts into three species: the user, the maker, and the imitator. And he says the one using the lyre—that is, music <margin>F</margin>—surpasses the art of the maker of the lyre, because he proposes the form of the work to be made for a certain end. The maker, in turn, surpasses the painter who imitates the lyre with colors. He judges the poet to be such a one, reporting images of things to the ears just as the painter does to the eyes. But among these things, certain theological mysteries concerning the Ideas are inserted, which, because we have opened them more widely in our *Theology*, we will touch upon briefly for the present. Come now, Platonic contemplator, ascend from these forms which you sense in the matter of the world to the nature that is the mother of such forms. Even if you do not sense her, think of her as infused into the matter of the world like a vital spirit, full of seeds, and through those seeds artistically arranging individual things. Know that this nature in the world is such as you know the vegetative power to be in yourself. Therefore, just as in yourself you <margin>G</margin> understand the power of sensing to preside over the vegetative nature, so also in the world there is a similar but most universal nature. Then you may reduce the genus of sensing into the rational nature, and this into the intellectual genus, both in yourself and in the world. Furthermore, since you perceive in yourself that the intellect seeks that which is intelligible as something more perfect, and is formed by it as by something more powerful, place the intelligible nature before the intellectual nature both in the world and in yourself. Call the intelligible the very same thing as Being itself. Finally, before this which you have called both Intelligible and Being, place the Good itself. For you desire to be so that you may be well, and you desire the intelligible for the sake of the Good itself. After you have ascended here, you will perceive the universe designated by a certain sacred sevenfold <note>the heptad</note>, rising from the lowest matter through sensible qualities, through nature, through sense, reason, intellect, the intelligible, unto the <margin>H</margin> Good itself. Furthermore, that the Good Spirit perfected all things under the number six, as if on the sixth day, and rested on the seventh level, as if on the seventh day—that is, in Himself. For the end of all other things is the Good itself. Of the Good, therefore, no end outside itself can either be or be imagined. If all things seek the Good by which they may be perfected, conclude that all things are made by the Good. Likewise, if He makes all things by an intrinsic and proper power, understand that He embraces the whole universe in Himself. But since He is the first and therefore the simplest nature, remember that the forms of all things in Him are one form, which Plato calls the Idea of the Good itself, in which Timaeus said the God of the world...

<summary>This page provides Marsilio Ficino's introductory summaries for Books IX and X of Plato's Republic, focusing on the psychological nature of tyranny, the three parts of the soul, the dangers of poetic imitation, and the metaphysical ascent to the Idea of the Good.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical commentary on Plato’s Republic, specifically Book X, focusing on the nature of Ideas, the immortality of the soul, and divine justice.</meta>

# ARGUMENTS AND COMMENTARY

The Craftsman <note>original: "opifex", referring to the Demiurge or Creator</note>, when he had created the world, is said to have rested, meaning that the world-maker withdrew into his own contemplation. Accordingly, the very Idea of the Good generates the Ideas—that is, the forms of all species, distinct from one another only by their specific kind—within the intelligible nature. In this way, it comprehends the universal being in an intelligible manner, and every intelligence does so as well through a certain wondrous reason that transcends ordinary understanding. All intellects look up toward this intelligible nature; from it, they receive the stable formulas of the Ideas. The reasons of the soul also receive them, from which they have accepted these formulas, though in a somewhat changeable manner. After these formulas of rational souls, the sensual power of the Ideas descends as images. Next, they descend as seeds into the vegetable nature, and finally through qualities into matter. Therefore, when Plato says that God makes the Ideas "in nature," understand this to mean in the intelligible nature and world—the angelic head of minds. 

As for his mention of a "bed" and a "table," let this be understood as an example, so that through these man-made objects you may understand natural things; that is, through the bed and table, understand the human being who uses them. Furthermore, an example from art seemed more suited to the question proposed. Perhaps, in truth, he does not think that the forms necessary for the rules of the arts are absent from the Ideas. Nor should it seem strange that man possesses the forms of the arts by divine gift, since even beasts are not without artistic imaginations. And if forms of this kind are produced divinely in the soul, they are said to be made "in nature" because they are naturally implanted. But if someone appears unfit for certain crafts, the Platonists would say he was either distracted by various things or had turned himself entirely toward opposites. 

Note Plato’s words saying that God not only understands but also wills; this signifies that God conceives by understanding within himself and fabricates by willing outside himself. Note again that God has expressed only one species—one Idea—of each natural kind in the intelligible world itself; for example, one ideal Humanity for the human species. For if in matter, where there is innumerable and shifting variety, a certain union of a common nature is preserved in individual men, much more so in a simple and stable nature is a single Idea sufficient for one natural species. Indeed, these diverse and unstable things cannot have a communion of nature among themselves from anywhere else but from the very unity of that sublime nature. Again, if two "Humanities" were posited, certainly in the respect that both are Humanity, they would not differ from each other; rather, they would be one. Therefore, if they were to differ, they would surely disagree with each other through certain additions joined to both. Thus, neither would be absolute Humanity itself, but rather a "certain kind" of humanity, and a "human something" rather than Humanity. Both, as participants in the same Humanity, would be called human in a similar way; and beyond these, there would be a Humanity in itself, which is one before it is grasped by many subjects. 

Rightly, since God is simply the Cause, he is not to be called the author of "a certain man" or "a certain horse," but the author of Man and Horse. Therefore, he procreated one absolute Idea for every species of things. But when, among us, this man begets that one, this man is by no means to be called the author of "Man" simply, but the author of "a certain man." For man alone is not the cause, but is *in* the cause—namely, among the number of causes—nor does he make the whole; for he does not make the primary matter, or the soul, nor does he give the beginning to man himself. For before this man, "Man" existed everywhere, and without his work, "Man" is and will be made everywhere. 

Where Plato says that God wills "one proper Idea"—namely, that he either did not want there to be more, or there was some necessity that there not be more—understand that in God, necessity is so converted with will that it is necessary for it to be so because God wills it to be so. Indeed, in the highest simplicity of divinity, necessity is nothing other than will. Therefore, if you say, "it is necessary for God to so will or act," I will likewise convert it: "God wills it to be so necessary." Rightly, where the highest goodness concurs with the highest power, there the highest liberty conspires with the highest necessity. 

Among these things, certain divided but very useful points must be considered. Such as this: Reading or doctrine is useless unless it leads to the best way of life. In this matter, the life and discipline of Pythagoras were admirable and rightly held the greatest authority among all, even in Plato’s time. Likewise, poems, if the harmonic composition of words is taken away, turn out to be of no importance. Furthermore, the virtue of either a man or a thing consists in a certain faculty contributing chiefly to that end for which the thing itself was made and the man was born. 

Meanwhile, a certain distinction between sense and reason appears: senses are often deceived regarding magnitude, figure, number, and weight; yet meanwhile, reason corrects the judgment of the sense through the faculty of measuring, numbering, and weighing. It is established, moreover, that the soul cannot at the same time, through the same power, judge the same thing in a contrary way. It also appears that diverse powers of desiring exist within us, since we may desire and reject the same thing at once. Note that it is not to be demanded of an upright citizen that he feel no pain at all, but that he console such rising pain with reasons. Here it appears there is one part of the soul which, like a sick person, needs medicine, and another which, being healthy, heals. 

These reasons against pain are chiefly four: First, because it is uncertain whether what happened is good or evil. Second, that whatever it may be, it is certainly to be of little account; for nothing among human dreams is to be highly valued. Third, that we gain nothing at all by grieving. Fourth, because pain always hinders that which could suddenly be of help to us. He confirms this by the fact that to be overcome is most shameful, and to overcome is most beautiful. He who is pressed by pain or any other disturbance is already most shamefully overcome. Therefore, he commands that in adversity and disturbances, we should chiefly use the office of a physician, who does not grieve with the suffering but heals them. He compares the daily lots of life to the tosses of dice, which he wants to be corrected by reasons, just as a toss of dice seems to be corrected by a certain skill of the game. But the preceding precepts are like preludes to those which follow. Let this be proposed to us as the greatest contest of all in life: that we overcome

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> vice and pursue virtue, and that we hold as nothing all things considered good among men, so that we ourselves may be good. Indeed, the proper reward of justice is greater than all rewards that can be won among men; for the splendor of justice itself surpasses all these things beyond measure, and a reward suitable for immobile, eternal, and truest justice cannot be found in shifting, brief, and shadowy things. From these things, it is concluded that the immobile habit of justice ought to be desired for the sake of an immobile reward. This reward indeed remains after the course of the present life and the labors of justice. Otherwise, justice itself, which is judged the most excellent good, would be an evil for just men who labor continually for the love of justice and are often affected by injury without avenging it—add to this that they despise present goods out of a desire for eternal ones, and they do not receive the reward of justice among men, but rather often report envy and punishment in exchange for justice. 

<margin>B</margin> Therefore, lest the good should cause harm, and justice lack a reward, and God either provide too little or not repay according to merits, it must be judged that souls are immortal. Especially so that the unjust, who did not pay the penalties of injustice while living, may at least pay them when dead, and the just, who were entirely despised among mortals, may be crowned among those above. Hence he hands down a noble precept: An immortal soul ought not to be solicitous for this brief time, but for all time. Plato shows the immortality of the soul in the *Phaedrus* and *Phaedo*, and elsewhere. He shows that reasons of this kind are certain demonstrations in the book *On Science* <note>likely referring to the *Theaetetus*</note>, saying that the words of those who think the opposite eventually turn out to be ridiculous upon examination. Likewise in the *Gorgias*, affirming that these mysteries are proved by adamantine reasons. 

<margin>C</margin> Furthermore, in this tenth book, where after the argumentation he adds that we are forced to confess this both through such argumentation and through many others. I truly think a certain marvelous power lies hidden in Plato’s words, understood by very few, so that it is no wonder if, through Platonic argumentations, some think it demonstrated, while others think it not yet demonstrated. Certainly, Demosthenes, a listener of Plato, was persuaded with such efficacy by the living voice that he said he would rather die honorably than live basely after he had heard Plato and Xenocrates debating the immortality of souls. 

<margin>D</margin> Cleombrotus perceived the same power in the Platonic writings, as did many listeners of Hegesias at Cyrene, who freed themselves from the prison of the body out of a desire for the other life. Boethius perceived the same, with Philosophy as his witness, conceding that this was demonstrated to him by certain reasons. Aurelius Augustine seems to have felt the same, where he says he never doubted this matter. These things are confirmed by Avicenna, who says certain reasons for these things are demonstrations. And Plato says here not only that it can be demonstrated, but even that it is easily demonstrated—among those, I think, who, having a mind purged and segregated from the body, rightly do not doubt that a soul segregated from the body can eventually live. Since they themselves experience their mind living better when separated from the senses than when joined to them. They have also discovered that the souls of others, immersed in bodies and therefore vicious, do not perish by their own vice and disease, 

<margin>E</margin> and therefore can much less be corrupted by a foreign disease, that is, a bodily one. For even the body itself is not destroyed by an external evil until an intrinsic evil is brought in from it, by which it is immediately destroyed. But lest anyone despair of the divinity of their soul, he commands them to purge it thoroughly from the filth contracted from the love of the body, and to perceive it when purged—how pure, how simple, how greedy for divine things (as if related to divinity), and how quickly and well it is capable of divine light. 

<margin>F</margin> As for his saying that souls do not become more numerous in number day by day, understand this to mean they are not made in such a way as to arise from and be composed of bodies. The following reason manifests this, saying: if divine things were composed of bodies, then since divine things are never resolved back into bodies, it would happen that nothing of bodies would be left in nature. Again, note what he adds: that the soul is not composite; otherwise, it could not be indissoluble. And understand that for an essence not to be able to be dissolved, it must either be composed of nothing, or if it is composed, it must not be composed of any matters, and must be so fused together that in its composition, multitude does not overcome unity; rather, unity through harmonic union overcomes multitude, and stability overcomes motion. 

Conclude the mystery, pertaining partly to providence and partly 

<margin>G</margin> to immortality and the reward of justice. The just man becomes like God, the unjust man unlike. And since it is not hidden from God that this one is like him and that one unlike, it is agreeable to reason that the just man is dear and a friend to God, and the unjust man the opposite. Therefore, God by no means neglects the just as friends, but always so provides for them that individual things, however adverse they may seem, eventually turn out prosperous, either for the living or the dead. But why did he assert the mystery of immortality here with a certain historical example <note>The Myth of Er</note> rather than with the diligence of argumentations? Because citizens are to be provoked to justice not so much by the artifice of words as by example and work. Furthermore, why does he bring forward a man rising from the dead to confirm this? Because even if immortality is established by reasons, as is a certain common execution of justice, nevertheless, one must receive the place, form, and disposition of either reward or punishment from one who has been there. This is signified to us near the end of the *Phaedo*. 

<margin>H</margin> Nor is it without reason that he testifies that Er the Pamphylian <note>original: "Herem Pamphylium"</note> rose again, having died in battle for the safety of his country, to signify that those who die for the public good will rise again to the true life—though out of many, only one rose again to ours. But is this a history or a fable? Justin the Platonist and Christian martyr wants it to be history. I shall not refute the same. But where Plato calls it an "apologue" or "fable," it can be explained that a history can be called a fable whenever, beyond the deeds performed, it has a more august allegory. For which reason Olympiodorus also says that Plato often called histories and reasons "fables." And since he figures the spirits and the places of justice differently in the *Phaedrus* and the *Gorgias*...

It explains the metaphysical relationship between divine Ideas and the material world, asserting that the soul's true reward lies beyond the physical realm.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on the myth of Er from Plato’s Republic, focusing on the soul's journey, the significance of numbers, and the mechanics of reincarnation.</meta>

# 810 MARS. FICINI

...he disposes differently in the *Phaedo* <note>Plato's dialogue on the immortality of the soul</note>, and here and elsewhere. It is clearly evident that these things, beyond the form of the place, also contain an allegorical sense. He uses here, concerning the resurrection, the number twelve, which among the ancients is the number of the mundane spheres, thinking that there are eight heavens above the four elements: as if he were saying that the divine power, mistress of the universe, is needed to raise the dead, and that this is sometimes done by divine providence for the instruction of men. There are also those who say that the "Great Year," in which the human soul completes its circuit through which it returns to the same state, is comprised of twelve thousand years; and that three such years equal the "Great Year of the World" in which the Soul of the World completes its circuit through the motion of the firmament, to be finished in thirty-six thousand years. Indeed, they wish for the circuit of our soul to be driven through twelve thousand years because it must run through all the spheres and the choirs of demons and gods, which in the *Phaedrus* are distributed through twelve orders. But what do the two openings in the earth and the two in heaven mean? Understand that souls descend to earthly things by one way—namely, by a certain corporeal habit—but ascend from the earth by another—namely, by the purification of that habit. Similarly, they glide from heaven into the elements out of love for the elemental body, and in turn rise again into celestial things once this love is extinguished and celestial love is kindled. Hence Orpheus says that Love holds the keys to all things, both above and below. He places the judges of souls in the air and the ether as angels who are ministers of divine providence. After the sentence, the just seek heaven, carrying their works and judgments before them: because they clearly knew themselves and shine both for themselves and others. The unjust, on the contrary, descend carrying theirs behind their backs. For they neither knew themselves nor were of use to themselves, but are examples to others rather than a help to themselves. The meadow in which both the ascending and descending souls rest for a time is a certain middle region between the lower and celestial worlds, a disposition between a good habit and a bad one, and a state between blessedness and misery, designated as similar to a "limbo" in the air. Note here that souls which had mutual knowledge in the previous life recognize each other in the other life. Likewise, according to the Platonists, the souls of those who died in infancy reside in such a meadow for a very long time; concerning whom Er recounted certain things little worthy of memory. Because since they declined toward neither side by choosing, nor contracted a habit, the Platonists leave them only in natural light. But they think the blessed are placed above natural light, while the miserable are below that light. Furthermore, this treats of purgatorial punishments. But why is guilt abolished by pains? Because it grew through pleasures. Do not physicians also mostly cure diseases by their opposite? Notice that Plato does not use the numbers ten, and a hundred, and a thousand rashly to wipe out guilt. Indeed, for every degree of pleasure, he applies ten degrees of punishment. First, it is asked for what reason more degrees of punishment are paid than degrees of pleasure were perceived. The answer is that it is owed thus because of the crime of "lese-majesty" <note>treason or offense</note> against the divine. Furthermore, just as the joys of blessedness exceed the pains of human justice, so the tortures of misery exceed the pleasures of injustice. Finally, marks are not as easily erased as they are easily imprinted; nor would he who confirmed a habit of sin have ceased to offend if he had lived longer. It is then asked, why ten degrees? What if Plato imitated the Mosaic Decalogue? And since he thought that he who altogether neglected any one of the ten acts in some way against the precepts of the divine law, he rightly judges him to be tortured ten times? Hence the number ten is called "universal." For it either enfolds all numbers within itself, or explains and unfolds them through itself. The universal number is appropriately adapted to the purging of souls, so that by this it may be signified that the entire stain of the body must be laid aside before you reach the Prince of the Universe, with whom nothing corporeal can exist. After this, it is asked why, besides the ten degrees of punishment, a hundred years are attached to the unjust. I answer because if they had lived up to a hundred years, by which term the life of men is in a way designated, they would have sinned continuously. Moreover, a hundredfold number is attributed to each of the ten degrees, from which the number one thousand is made. Hence that saying: *They wander for a hundred years.* Also: *They rolled the wheel through a thousand years.* Furthermore: *You shall receive a hundred for one.* For Plato uses these numbers not only in punishment, but also in certain rewards. Indeed, if ten is led into itself by multiplying ten times ten, from that is born a hundred. Then if it is reduced into itself, by computing ten times a hundred, a thousand is procreated. Therefore, ten is a universal number, and a hundred and a thousand are universal numbers. Likewise, if you proceed from one to ten, a linear number is born. If from ten to a hundred, it becomes a superficial <note>two-dimensional</note> number. If from ten to a thousand, it becomes a solid <note>three-dimensional</note> number. So that we may explain allegorically: the soul of the unjust man departed from itself into the body and was infected with a corporeal stain. It is to purge this entire stain through the number ten, which is the universal number. That it is necessary for the ten to be led into itself to procreate a hundred signifies that the soul must emerge from the body to itself through reason. Then, that it is necessary to reduce the ten into itself to generate a thousand allegorically teaches that the soul must not only be turned toward itself through reason, but also be converted into itself through intelligence, and thus be reduced into its own unity, by which finally it can enjoy God, the highest unity of all. Moreover, the linear, superficial, and solid numbers mystically teach that for the mind to be purified, not only the outward surface of works, words, and thoughts, but also every deepest inner chamber must be most diligently searched. After limbo and purgatory, he descends to the underworld. But know that the Platonists wish not only for the punishments in purgatory to be temporal, but also for the joys in a certain celestial region to be temporal, so that suffering on both sides responds equally. For they distinguish thus: either the senses in life entirely obeyed reason, or reason entirely obeyed the senses, or they always fought each other; and in that fight

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> either the senses or reason prevailed most. Therefore, souls in which the senses entirely obeyed reason through a confirmed habit obtain an eternal reward. On the contrary, those affected otherwise are condemned to eternal punishments. But the middle ones—if reason prevailed, they are transferred to temporal rewards; if the senses, to temporal punishments. But for those to whom no time of habit was given, a "limbo" is preserved among the Platonists as a place of choosing, designated here under the name of a "meadow." And even if the Platonists sometimes call the celestial regions, especially the highest ones, "meadows," here however the meadows signify the aerial region. For how could he signify the sublime heaven here through meadows, when he says that some souls descend to these from the heavens, and others arrive suddenly from the bowels of the earth? Let such meadows therefore be certain sublime tracts of air, contiguous to those sublime tracts of earth which he describes in the *Phaedo* in the form of an earthly paradise, having happy inhabitants under a perpetual spring. There they also place the <margin>B</margin> Elysian fields—the earthly ones, I mean. For the eighth heaven holds the celestial Elysian fields. Hence that saying:
> The stars hold the celestial floor, and the forms of the gods.
I pass over for the present Proclus and Plotinus, who, where Plato says "eternal," explain it as the entire time of the "Greatest Year," in which the cycles of individual times are completed. In this I approve more of Porphyry and to some extent Iamblichus, so that "eternal" may be understood from this. For where Plato calls a soul "incurable," and such a one as can never be purged, he sufficiently indicates eternal punishments, and in turn infinite joys. But how certain others explain these things, I have not judged worthy of memory. Furthermore, if you consider Plato's words, you will recognize that <margin>C</margin> Gospel saying: *Bind him hand and foot, and cast him into outer darkness.* But he adds here, *with the head bound.* The binding of the head signifies the impediment of reason and the bereavement of light. The knot of the hands signifies the privation of action and progress. Finally, bound feet do not lead, do not advance, do not arrive, but are snatched away by force. You will also recognize under the figure of "fiery men" the avenging demons and corporeal punishments, and you will perceive the same from many conjectures. You will also note the specific word "outer." Furthermore, the darkness where the openings are closed. Also, under the name of "bellowing," the gnashing of teeth and weeping. After he has arranged the places and punishments, and <margin>D</margin> signified the joys through the opposite form, and touched upon the middle states, he now returns to those souls which flocked into the meadows, partly from heaven after a temporal reward, and partly from the earth after a temporal punishment. He says it is necessary for these to return again into elemental generation, and to progress through it until they eventually merit a firmer or firmest state. These, he says, rested in the meadow for seven days. If you interpret this "seven" through the seven planets, likewise through the seven sets of seven days in which the fetus rests in the womb before motion, and also through the seven days in which the forms are gradually changed in the womb, you will perhaps seem to bring something to light. But what is that to souls? Which are no longer in the <margin>E</margin> planets, for they have descended; and are not yet enclosed in a womb, for they are about to descend into a womb after they reach the three Fates. Meanwhile, with an aerial body, they inhabit the aerial region. But let it be so, if you please. Perhaps also because they live "sterile" in the womb in a way, they are assigned to a sterile number: and since the number seven is neither born from any number repeated several times, nor generates any number within ten, it most aptly suits souls still vacant from generation on both sides. The Pythagoreans attribute the same number to <margin>F</margin> Pallas <note>Athena</note>, because she was neither born from a mother nor gave birth. They wish it to suit souls still removed from an earthly mother and contemplating the universe under the wisdom of Pallas. But as soon as they rise from such a vacation, they undergo the number eight, which is both generated and is the first among solid numbers. Therefore, the soul is almost ready to approach a solid body. We call eight a "solid" number because it is created from two repeated three times by itself and returning into itself, signifying a triple dimension. For two times two times two completes eight. Add, if you cultivate music, that the seventh voice is utterly dissonant, but the eighth is the most consonant of all. Moreover, the body must harmonize with the soul, as both must with fate, so that the celestial soul may enter into commerce with the earthly body. Of which <margin>G</margin> consonance, when the numbers are finally completed, the earth may now be dissonant to the soul itself, and heaven consonant, if only it is to be happy. Accordingly, because Plato joins four days for the progress of generation to the eight days, understand that in the vegetative nature of the soul, a certain power and effect now reigns in a way to form the body composed of the four elements. Likewise, under the eighth consonance, there is need of a fourth in a way approaching consonance, and a fifth, which is now a true consonance. But they become five if you wish to compute the following four together with the preceding one. Furthermore, you will see twelve assigned here, by which the soul approaches the beginnings of generation. For the help of the twelve spheres and the divine and demonic orders is needed for that work. Moreover, the twelfth voice and consonance is most perfect, resulting from the *diapason* <note>octave</note> and *diapente* <note>fifth</note>, from the eighth and the fifth, by its own grace suiting amorous things and also fitting for marriages. Indeed, such souls, with a certain "Venereal" <note>pertaining to Venus/love</note> love as their leader, so to speak, are now to be reconciled to <margin>H</margin> earthly marriages. But why, when Plato was about to compute twelve, and after seven the remainder was to be added, did he not immediately say five? Namely, so that through eight and four he might hint at the mysteries I have added; and again, through the journey of one day added to complete the twelve, you might notice that a body composed of four elements cannot be prepared for the soul before it has been tempered into a single fifth form, as if similar to heaven, and the soul easily imprints one vital act from itself upon the figured body. Since, however, souls declining toward composite bodies...
