<meta>This page continues the philosophical commentary on the Myth of Er from Plato's Republic, specifically focusing on the nature of Fate, the Spindle of Necessity, and the roles of the three Fates.</meta>

# ARGUMENTS AND COMMENTARY

<margin>A</margin> They are for the most part subject to laws, and in turn glide toward those things under the guidance of fate; therefore, he says, these souls proceed into the sight of fate. In the beginning, therefore, he depicts nature itself under a columnar light, because it is the bond of the universe. By "Nature," he understands the vital and seed-like power infused into the matter of the world by the Soul of the World itself. This is called "light" because it is penetrating and vital. Likewise, it is rightly called a "column" because it penetrates the whole of matter everywhere, as if lengthwise, and produces many successive grades of forms differing in species and genus. It is also said to be extended through every part and to bind the heaven on all sides, because it is present in its entirety everywhere and contains all things, propagating many parts among themselves—as if through equal and similar sides—in such a way, however, that it reaches from length to breadth: since by penetrating it is diffused, and insofar as it is diffused, it fills, and by filling, it rules. Hence the saying: *The spirit nourishes from within.* <note>original: "Spiritus intus alit" - a quote from Virgil's Aeneid VI.726 regarding the world-soul.</note> Truly, the variety of colors declares the variety of the seminal powers. In this nature, certainly, the fatal spindle lies hidden: according to the imagination, it is the very axis of the spheres, adorned with twin poles and a center; but according to reason, it is a certain likeness of the mundane soul and its vegetative power presiding over nature, moving it like an instrument to fabricate natural things not only skillfully, but also inevitably: so that there is not only order from nature in the world, but also an inevitable order from fate. Hence that passage in the *Statesman*: <note>original: "Politico"</note> *when the spindle is led by natural desire and fate.* But so great is the kinship of nature with fate that they are scarcely distinguished from one another by philosophers. Moreover, to express the immutable nature of fate, he said its spindle was made of Adamant <note>A legendary hardest metal or diamond, symbolizing unbreakable necessity.</note>. The whorl, however—that is, the heaven—is again made of Adamant and other materials, namely the stars, not only fixed but also mobile and common, with a manifold variety of forms. He then clearly depicts eight spheres, which are indeed agitated by nature, but are immutably agitated by fate presiding over nature, and they are said to be the instruments of fate. <margin>C</margin> Among these things, many points are emphasized pertaining to the measures, depths, intervals, motions, harmonies, forms, and powers of the celestial spheres, which we shall explain more opportunely in the commentaries on the *Timaeus*. In summary, however, from the swiftest and most orderly motion of the heavens and their most powerful contact, we imagine a vast, varied, and most sweet melody: the tones of the eight spheres, and a harmonic concord from those tones. Furthermore, he says the fatal spindle—that is, the trail—is turned between the knees of the goddess Necessity. She has three daughters: Lachesis, Clotho, and Atropos, who together with their mother will the celestial things. I pass over what Proclus thinks of these, who posits not only one universal Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note> as the maker of the whole world, but three particular Joves as makers under him. Next, in equal proportion, he posits one goddess Necessity in that order, guarding all things in which the common Jove composed everything. Furthermore, there are three fates—that is, the three goddesses who are daughters of this Necessity—some of whom, under the mother's empire, preserve other things far from transgression and by necessity; he places this goddess entirely above the world, while the daughters are partly removed from the world and partly inclining toward the world. To me, however, as to most other Platonists, it is more pleasing that Necessity is the Soul of the World. The three daughters are the three powers of this soul pertaining to fatal matters. He calls her "Necessity," not because she brings violence to either nature or reason, but because she contains all things in their certain order established by the Maker of things, nor does she permit anything to transgress His laws to such an extent that it does not soon return to the laws. He willed the heavens to be at her knees—that is, in the lowest part of her—with such great ease, clearly, so that she may meanwhile most readily enjoy the joy of contemplation. But he calls this very vegetative part of her by three names. Lachesis, indeed, because she is pregnant with the seeds of things and with the lots and forms of lives, which she implants into the souls about to descend. Then Clotho, because she unfolds the implanted lots of life in their order into the act of living and explains them into effect. <margin>E</margin> Finally Atropos, because she preserves and guards the lives already unfolded into act by a certain indeclinable progress, even to the inevitable end. Some name the first Vesta; the second Minerva; the third indeed Mars or Martia. Next, because he says the Fates sing to the harmonic motions of the Sirens, understand that the fatal powers proceed to effect through celestial motions and influence. The seats of Necessity and her daughters show the firmness of the fatal order, as if it were necessary for the progression of mobile things to be ruled and ordered by the very immobility of death. The equal intervals of the seats clearly show that a just distribution is made both among the fates and through the fates. The white robes show both the inviolate nature of the fates and their innocence. For that which depends on the best leader of the universe does not act out evil for the universe. The crown describes empire. To "sing" is to distribute individual things through intervals of time with that congruence by which the divine mind, beholding them in a moment, prescribes them to be distributed in times. Hence it happens that all the Fates sing of temporal things. And why does Lachesis sing of the past, Clotho of the present, and Atropos of the future? Let Proclus answer: in the past, three times are thought of. For it is already called "past," and it was once "present," and before it was present, it was "future." In the present, the present itself is thought of, which previously had also been future. In the future, finally, only the future is recognized. After these things, it is declared that Lachesis is the foremost. Clotho is in the second place of dignity. Atropos is third. But why do the Fates handle the spheres with their hands, while the mother does not? Because the powers of that lowest soul are more akin to the spheres than the substance of the soul itself. Why also does Lachesis touch with both hands? Because in the beginning both the middle and the end are contained. Why then does Clotho touch the larger and outer

<column-break/>

circumference with her right hand? And Atropos the narrower and inner one with her left? Because the evolution of life begins through the middle and from an external cause, and is broader, and also happens more prosperously. But the inevitable end proceeds from an already conceived internal property and finishes in a narrow space. Add that it creeps up secretly, and for the most part against one's wish. However, when he says the Fates touch the heaven with a certain intermission of time, do not think that the fatal powers of the mundane soul sometimes rule mundane things and sometimes do not. For if mutability occurs in fate, whose property is immutability itself, nothing could be imagined that is not mutable. <margin>B</margin> Plato, therefore, depicting divine offices in a certain human manner and limit, wishes to imply that the fates partly handle the things themselves, and partly not: both because the power of the mundane soul, consisting in the dignity of its own integrity, accommodates its action to governing things, and in turn while it accommodates, it is not mixed; and because they exhibit a temporal vicissitude in their works, and the intermission they are said to have in their operation they demonstrate not in themselves, but in the effect; and because it handles natural things but does not touch supernatural things. For those things which pertain to pure and free reason, or to the divine intelligence superior to fate, it touches not at all. Such things are reduced by a certain wonderful order to the sublime providence of God, which is superior to celestial fate. <margin>D</margin> Similarly, it is written in the *Statesman* that mundane things are ruled sometimes by fate, sometimes by providence: not because such a change of fate intermits by some vicissitude of times, but because daily some things happen under fate, while others are disposed through the laws of providence above the fatal series. Added to this is that our souls are sometimes entirely in providence, sometimes entirely in fate, sometimes in both at once. For when they live only with the unhampered contemplative mind, they live in providence alone and are thoroughly free. But when in the vegetative part the inclination toward this body grows strong, and such an inclination is propagated even to the imagination, declining now toward fate, they likewise degenerate from liberty. But while they are joined to the composite body, they now merge themselves into the fate of their own body, and retain much less of their pristine liberty. Finally, after they have contracted bodily affections into a habit, they are now utterly overwhelmed by fate, deprived of all liberty. It is asked for what reason the souls here seem to approach Lachesis by a certain natural instinct. Surely in the general nature of the corporeal machine are the seeds of all species, about to sprout not only in certain forms and modes, but also at certain times. Furthermore, in any proper nature of any species there is a similar certain seminal order, but pertaining to the propagation and preservation of its own species. There is also in any individual under a species a fuel and a propensity to produce individual things in their own modes and times. These three natures are thereafter so disposed that the individual follows the specific, and the specific follows the general, so that for the most part what is from the nature of one happens likewise from the others, and the particular nature consents with the universal. In almost the same way stands fate—that is, a certain prefiguration of things to be unfolded—both in the soul of the world itself, and in the souls of the twelve spheres and stars, and also in souls that are now, as it were, particular: in whose number are human souls. <margin>F</margin> In the vegetative power of our soul, therefore, there is first a certain fate and an involved series of future things, consenting in form, mode, and time together with the fates of the celestial souls and the mundane soul. Just as, therefore, the germ of any plant, sprouting with its own certain figures and in its own time, seems to concur spontaneously with the universal nature of springtime provoking the same: so also souls, by their own nature and their own fate, opportunely bring forth certain proper lives at the time when the universal fate similarly calls them to the same, so that the chorus of souls, with its certain figures of dancing and the diversity of various dancers at once, imitates the fatal song and sound. I would prefer "song" to be understood in the celestial souls, "sound" in the spheres, and finally "dance" in us. <margin>G</margin> By such an instinct, souls at the auspices of life come to Lachesis to have their lots confirmed through the lots of Lachesis. They are confirmed, therefore, through a certain prophet. This prophet signifies two things: both the universal and primary influx of providence into the soul, and the opportunity under which such a concurrence happens, so that souls are carried to that place where universal fate also carries them. Therefore, when he says the prophet arranges the souls in order and transfers the lots from Lachesis to them: it signifies that all these things are confirmed, both by the favor of divine providence and by the opportunity of that concurrence. Nor is it said without reason that the Fates govern the universe with their hands, but the lots of souls are received from the knees of Lachesis. For since the government of the universe is more excellent than the disposition of souls, the former is rightly judged to be perfected by the hands, the latter by the knees. Moreover, to sit on a tribunal expresses authority and judgment. <margin>H</margin> Among the lots of lives and the examples, there seems to be such a distinction: that lots pertain to the vegetative powers, but examples to the imaginations—superior indeed to the vegetative power but close to it. For as soon as certain seeds of a future life grow strong in this power above others, at the same time figures and machinations of a similar life arise in the imagination, and affections grow hot: just as among us a cheerful imagination follows a sanguine affection of the body, an angry one follows the choleric, a sad one the melancholic, and a lustful one the fertile. Thus far fatal necessity proceeds. But indeed Reason, superior to imagination—to which belong reasoning, counsel, and choice, and therefore a movement free toward either side—perceiving the figures and affections of the imagination, can equally approve or disapprove of such a description of life. For which reason he says that virtue is free from fate, and the blame in the choice of a worse life belongs to the chooser, not to fate. For even if from fate...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on the myth of Er from Plato’s Republic, specifically discussing the soul's choice of life and its descent into the body, before transitioning into a new summary (Compendium) of Plato’s Timaeus.</meta>

# MARSILIO FICINO

is as much in the general as in the particular, to choose a new life now and then as before; however, it is a matter of counsel to choose specifically this or that kind. Indeed, if the reason, by examining it, rejects the first form of living offered to the eyes of reason by the imagination, another better one will immediately be available, and then another. Hence that inspiration of providence is called a "prophet" <note>Ficino is interpreting the "Prophētēs" or spokesman of Lachesis in Plato's Republic.</note>. For it shows to the reason, by a certain light of judgment, that it has a free faculty of consulting and choosing, and what follows most of all from a rash choice. The prophet is also said to cast "lots" <note>original: "sortes"</note> and propose examples of living: not only because the influx of divine providence in a way sanctions fated things, but because it brings forth fated lots and fated examples into the examination and judgment of reason. Moreover, because <margin>A</margin> in the proclamation he announces that souls are "diurnal" <note>belonging to the day</note>, he expresses that they are there in perpetual day, and the life they value so much is but a single day and a nocturnal one. He adds the beginning of "another circuit," so that he may open the mystery of souls returning from heaven to earth and back again. He calls the human race not only mortal, but—so that souls may foresee their own evils—he adds "death-bringing" <note>original: "mortiferum"</note>, as if to say the life of the body is the death of the soul. He then pronounces that even if reason is free from the beginning in choosing a life, after it has chosen, it will no longer be free in rejecting it, although it will at some time be free in arranging or tempering it, whatever it may be, in one way or another. If you ask why some souls of men choose some lives and others choose others, some will answer that there are certain species of differences in the natures of souls, others that they are individual <margin>B</margin> and personal, and they will add many differences derived from the diversity of a previous life. Plotinus strongly confirms this, and it accords most with what follows. Furthermore, souls choosing a life are allotted at the same time a *daemon* <note>A guiding spirit or guardian angel in Neoplatonic thought.</note> as the leader of the chosen life. We have said much of this elsewhere. Here distinguish it thus: The Platonists think of some Gods outside the world, namely minds separate from the body like intellectual spheres, worshipping the one God as their most firm center and most stable unity. Others they call "worldly" <note>mundane</note>, namely those adapted to the revolving spheres of the world beyond divine worship. To these they subject *daemons*, as ministers to arrange and compose those things which happen either in species or in the spheres or from the spheres. They count, therefore, as many kinds of *daemons* as there are powers found in the worldly Gods, the <margin>C</margin> leaders of the *daemons*. But truly, in any worldly God, unity itself is the supreme part of its substance, which reflects the divine unity. After that is the intellect, containing all things at once, through which it represents the angelic minds. Likewise, reason, running through forms in a certain progression, is proper to such souls. Furthermore, there is a certain imagination which meets with particular forms to the extent that reason itself proceeds through universals. Next follows the "vegetal" nature of the sphere, which is both life-giving and a mover. According to these five powers, five kinds of *daemons* are counted. From their number, the celestial *daemons* appropriately follow the unity of the worldly gods; the ethereal *daemons* (that is, the fiery ones) follow the intelligence of those same gods; the aerial ones follow reason; the aquatic ones follow imagination; and the earthly ones <margin>D</margin> follow the nature which we called vegetal in the gods. Below these, the Orphics place subterranean *daemons*, reflecting the bodies of the worldly gods in a certain lowest order, and being the avengers of crimes. Plato seems to have made mention of these here. If you ask what kind of *daemons* are primarily the leaders of souls descending into bodies, the answer will be: not the celestial, not the fiery. For these, being more sublime, lead souls back up, they do not lead them down. Likewise, neither the aquatic nor the earthly. For these, as craftsmen of the lowest generation, would not give the soul a guide on the fatal journey, but rather plunge it into the precipices of fate. Therefore, the aerial *daemons* remain as middle leaders through the middle, who, as companions of divine reason, lead human reason on this journey. From this kind of *daemons*, some lead some souls and others lead others. Saturnian *daemons* lead Saturnian souls, Martian ones lead Martian souls, and others similarly, each being most accommodated to each, both from the soul's own affection and from common providence and fate, but most of all according to the form of the chosen life. With this leader of life, the souls are now subject to the three Fates <note>The Parcae: Clotho, Lachesis, and Atropos.</note>, which they had only seen before; namely, with the *daemon* so decreeing as the executor of the whole order, and with the corporeal affection now gradually outweighing. Finally, after the three Fates, they pass to the mother of the Fates: Necessity herself, whose impulses they now experience. Then, that the souls go under a "vehement heat" can signify three things: namely, that the ardor of corporeal love increases, and at the same time care and anxiety are increased. Likewise, that they descend from heaven through the sphere of fire. Furthermore, the service of natural heat to give life to the earthly body. But since through excessive care for earthly things, heavenly things are consigned to oblivion, and through oblivion sterility happens from fertility, therefore they soon descend into the "Lethean" field—that is, the field of forgetfulness—which is utterly sterile. And because, due to diligent care for mortal things, eternal things are neglected, whence both oblivion and loss and difficulty of remembrance arise, he says the souls descend in the Lethean field to the river *Amelita* <note>Greek: Ameles, meaning "careless" or "negligent."</note>, that is, the depth of negligence, and there they lie down under the night, that is, they are prostrated under the privation of divine light. But what does it mean that the water of Amelita can never be contained in any vessel? This is a poetic metaphor, signifying the lower matter, which is called a river, constantly flowing and fluctuating through forms. Likewise, the vice of oblivion, which is to retain nothing, but to pour it out immediately. Add that no outward support saves a soul perishing by its own negligence. That it is furthermore necessary to drink from the river of oblivion is clear, since it is ordained to happen so from its own nature and common fate and providence. To drink either more water or less comes from the effect upon the body more or less extensively: and this is the cause of greater or lesser oblivion, or rather the greater or lesser mixing of the faculty. Both of these passions the soul experiences in a certain

<column-break/>

way in a body composed of thicker air in the upper field, before it is enclosed in the womb of the earthly mother. For <margin>A</margin> from celestial bodies to earthly ones, the descent is made not only through the element, but through an aerial body. He adds that the souls sleep in this aerial body until midnight, showing that soon, under the earthly body, there will be not just a half-night, but a full night of ignorance. Sleep testifies to both the hindrance of reason and the falsity of judgment. Finally, he says the souls are insinuated into the earthly offspring under a certain thunder <margin>B</margin> and earthquake, for two reasons, as I think: both indicating that they enter this prison under unhappy auspices, and showing that both celestial and earthly motion, and indeed a vehement one, must concur to coerce the divine soul in such a foul prison. That the souls "leapt forth" to generation like stars, beyond the poetic figure, he hints that souls are in a way stellar, and will finally return to the stars. As for the fact that Plato brings such a ridiculous fable about the migration of souls into the bodies of beasts, differing not at all from the tales of old women, he certainly warns us that the whole thing is to be explained allegorically: namely, that rational souls migrate not into the life of a brute, but into a "brutish" life—that is, one similar to a brute. This indeed pleased almost all Platonists except Plotinus. And Origen seems to confirm the same in his books against Celsus. But you, do not neglect the moral precept: that the skill of right choice is to be placed before all <margin>C</margin> things and arts. Furthermore, so many things have been brought forward here about the beauty and power of the spheres, so that we may think that justice and a huge reward will follow in heaven, and will greatly lead to the best choice of living. But you will say now, great-souled Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo de' Medici, Ficino's patron.</note>, that you have received here a commentary from Marsilio Ficino rather than a summary. So be it; I think it was and will be worth the effort, that I promised a summary but provided a commentary.

## THE COMPENDIUM OF MARSILIO
### Ficino on the Timaeus.
#### for page 522.

### ON THE SUBJECT OF THE BOOK.
#### CHAPTER I.

<margin>D</margin> Just as in the *Parmenides* he comprehends all kinds of divine things according to his strength, so in the *Timaeus* he embraces all natural things, and in both he is very much a Pythagorean, disputing under the persona <margin>E</margin> of a Pythagorean. And in the *Parmenides* indeed, he imitates Parmenides and Zeno the Eleatics, Pythagoreans who had written about divine things. In the *Timaeus*, however, he follows Timaeus of Locri, a Pythagorean who composed a book on the nature of the universe. Yet he does this in such a way that he adds to these not only eloquence, but mysteries. Since truly the divine things are the principles and patterns of natural things, and natural things are the effects and images of divine things, therefore even in the *Parmenides* while he deals with divine things, he meanwhile descends to natural things, and in the *Timaeus* treating nature, he rises more often into divine things. Nor does he wrongly couple divinity and nature together. For nature is the instrument of divinity. And so he either deals with natural things divinely, like Aristotle, or deals with divine <margin>F</margin> things naturally. He also inserts mathematics as a medium between both, namely between divine and natural things. Which, clearly, signify divine things through numbers, but natural things through measures. Let the subject of this book, therefore, be the whole of nature itself, that is, a certain seminal and life-giving power infused into the whole world, subject indeed to the world-soul, but presiding over matter, and bringing forth individual things in the same order in which the soul itself conceived them, both receiving the divine mind and desiring the good.

---

### ON THE ORDER OF THE BOOK AND
### its parts.
#### CHAPTER II.

<margin>G</margin> It will be clear, moreover, that the nature of the universe and the universe itself do not consist of themselves, but depend on a superior and divine cause. It will appear, furthermore, into how many grades nature is distributed: celestial, elemental, simple, composite, rational, and lacking reason. It will be clear that the whole generation under the moon is referred to the rational animal as if to its end and master. Many things besides these will be treated concerning this very animal, pertaining both to the soul <margin>H</margin> and to the body. Also many things concerning the things which are composed by nature below the rational animal. And to speak briefly, the triple world will be treated, namely the divine, the celestial, and the human. It will also be shown that of all things which are composed in the world and of the world itself, there are two principal internal elements, namely matter and form; but there are three external principles, namely the efficient cause of the world, and the exemplary and the final. And the efficient cause is divided power, and intelligence, and will; the exemplary cause is the ideas conceived in the divine intelligence; and finally, the final cause is the good.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Plato’s dialogues, specifically focusing on the structure of the *Timaeus* and the *Critias*, and the allegorical interpretation of the war with Atlantis.</meta>

# ON THE INTRODUCTION,
## to the dialogue.
### CHAPTER III.

Furthermore, to come to the arrangement of the dialogue itself, Plato had destined five continuous days for these discussions. On the first day, Socrates disputed in the Piraeus <note>The port of Athens</note> together with Polemarchus, Glaucon, Adeimantus, and Thrasymachus the Sophist concerning the republic. On the second day, in the city, he recounted these same things to Timaeus, Critias, and Hermocrates, and to a certain fourth nameless stranger, perhaps a companion of Timaeus. On the third day, they make an epilogue of these things. After this introduction was made, Timaeus disputed concerning nature, in the presence of three: Socrates, Critias, and Hermocrates. For the fourth person, who was present at the second narration without a name, was now absent from the third: for it is not for just anyone to be present at more secret matters. On the fourth day, Critias held his discourse. Finally, the fifth day has not yet dawned. Quite fittingly, after the arrangement and epilogue of the divine republic among men, the model of this celestial republic follows in the *Timaeus*, composed by God himself: then it moves to the antiquity of the world and the human race, and the wondrous deeds strenuously performed by the ancients.

# ALLEGORY OF THE HISTORY
## which is narrated in the prologue.
### CHAPTER IIII.

Now, among the beginnings of this dialogue, he narrates a history of a certain war committed between the Athenians and the Atlanteans. Thus, <margin>D</margin> Crantor, the first interpreter of Plato in terms of time, accepts this as a bare history without allegory. Some others, on the contrary, take it as a mere allegory. But all the most esteemed Platonists refute these: affirming indeed that it is history, because Plato said: *The discourse to come is very wonderful, but entirely true.* Moreover, they think an allegorical sense should be exhibited for Plato, who never undertakes anything at random. They think, therefore, that the war between the Athenians and the Atlanteans presents an image of all the oppositions that exist in the universe. For war—that is, opposition—is, according to Heraclitus, the father of all things. <margin>E</margin> Amelius indeed brings forward the opposition between the firmament and the planets: especially since it is said in the *Critias* that the Atlantic island was divided into seven circles. Origen, however, sees the opposition of the superior demons against the inferior ones, and their victory: the former exceeding in power, the latter in number. Numenius, however, sees the difference of excellent souls following Pallas <note>Athena</note>, against other souls following generation under Neptune <note>Poseidon</note>. Porphyry sees the battle between demons leading into generation, and souls striving for the things above. He distinguishes demons in a threefold way: some are divine; others are according to a certain habit, whose number is filled by particular souls that have obtained a strong demonic nature; others are evil and harmful to souls. These lowest demons, therefore, conflict with souls in their ascent and descent, especially the western demons; for that region is assigned by the Egyptians to harmful demons. Furthermore, Iamblichus, Syrianus, and Proclus add to these the opposition itself flourishing perpetually in all things, between the One and the Multitude: Limit and Infinity: the Same and the Other: Rest and Motion: from which all things are composed under the First. Likewise, Being, either through itself or not through itself. Again, essence either incorporeal or corporeal: and the incorporeal indeed either does not decline toward the corporeal, or it does decline. The corporeal indeed is either not perishable, like the celestial; or perishable, like the elemental. Finally, in heaven there are motions opposed to each other and diverse virtues. Under heaven, moreover, there are qualities repugnant to each other. In summary, the discrepancy of all these things is signified by that ancient war: and everywhere the superior and more excellent things are signified by the Athenians, and others by the westerners. An allegory of this kind fits the discussion of Timaeus in no small measure. It is also confirmed by those things which we comment upon in the *Critias*.

# THE FALL OF PHAETHON.
## Floods, Fires, and the description of Minerva.
### CHAPTER V.

<margin>H</margin> Here again I admonish you to remember that nine thousand years are computed by Eudoxus as thousands of months. Likewise, that Phaethon, the son of the Sun, being struck by lightning, burned the earth, signifies according to some a vast comet of a solar nature which, finally dissolving, stirred up intolerable heats. Perhaps also the fires which Moses narrates were sent divinely. But when he comes to the floods, remember that fire is indeed the most effective of all; but water is more effective than earth, and less passive than air. Likewise, fire divides powerfully and penetrates; water strikes forcefully from all sides. Therefore, through these two elements, vaster calamities happen. Add also the final cause: because, namely, through the destruction made by these two, a greater good follows, that is, a more fertile regeneration of things.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> reason than through the plagues of the air and the gaping of the earth. Therefore, Providence uses these two chiefly for the most ample destruction. To which the celestial wheels then rightly obey: so that at whatever intervals of time it has ordained there to be destruction or rather reformation, at those same times all the planets concur duly toward the fiery or watery stars, with the fixed stars also contributing to the same. Remember, moreover, that Neptune signifies natural providence, while Pallas signifies intellectual providence: and this same Pallas is described by the Platonists as a divinity wisely and powerfully adorning celestial things as well as building those which happen under heaven: among the stars, presiding especially over Aries, and the leader of the equinoctial circle: where they think the moving virtue of the universe especially flourishes. You shall commit to memory the golden epigram which <margin>B</margin> Proclus read in the histories of the Egyptians inscribed in the temples of Minerva: *I am what is, what will be, and what has been. My veil no one has revealed. The fruit which I have brought forth is the sun born.*

# PRECEPTS CONCERNING VOWS
## and most choice prayers.
### CHAPTER VI.

<margin>C</margin> But where Plato comes to the point of suppliantly adoring God: hear Porphyry thus approving divine supplications. Since God provides for us, and our affairs can be otherwise, we certainly adore usefully for the benefit of our affairs: namely, if we are good. For thus, having been made like God, we shall be more closely joined. In which conjunction the whole force of adoration consists. Surely, since we are children of God, but separated from him as if in exile and prison: it is fitting to adore suppliantly, so that being liberated from here we may return to the father. Otherwise, we shall be like those who are deprived of the protection of parents. Truly, since we are parts of the universe, we undoubtedly need the universe. For the conversion itself toward the whole provides safety to the parts. Whether, therefore, you follow virtue, he who contains all virtue must be adored by you. For to love the Good itself will be the cause for you also of that good which is expedient for you. Whether you desire a corporeal good, there exists in the universe a virtue containing all bodies. Thence, therefore, it is necessary that safety proceed to whatever parts. Indeed, we have found that all the most excellent men in wisdom among all nations have brooded especially over divine vows: particularly the Brahmans of the Indians, the Magi of the Persians, and the theologians of the Greeks. The Chaldeans, however, adored something else as well: for calling the very virtue of the superiors "God," they venerated it by this one name. These are the words of Porphyry. After him, let us hear his disciple, the divine Iamblichus, approved in this matter especially by Proclus. All things are from God in such a way that nowhere are even the smallest things deserted by God. For everywhere divine unity flourishes: through which each thing consists: and by a certain perpetual and intimate circle they are wonderfully revolved back to God himself, from whom and in whom they are, otherwise they would suddenly fall into nothingness. From divine unity all things proceed: and as they proceed, they retain a certain unity impressed upon them, an image of the divine unity: by which they are called back into it, and being called back, they are perfected. <margin>F</margin> This itself ravishes souls to vows, by which union with God may be deeply implored by us. For if nature, flowing from God, has inserted certain properties into certain things that agree with the superiors, through which they turn themselves in a certain way toward the superiors, as solar things to the sun, and lunar things to the moon: much more has the Father of souls impressed upon them forces ravishing them to himself. Which indeed seem to be situated primarily in a certain divine unity in the superior intellect, as well as in intellectual reflection itself. But suppliant adoration arising from here absolutely consumes our restitution into God: drawing divine beneficence toward us by a natural congruity, coupling the adorers with the Adored, co-adapting the prayers of those vowing to the intelligence of the superiors: moving the will of those who embrace all good things in themselves to impart good things to us according to our vow, the effectress of divine persuasion, stabilizing all our things by the firm stability of the superiors. To the perfection of a vow, five principal things pertain. The first indeed is a certain notion of that which is to be adored and by what reason it is to be worshipped. The second is a certain assimilation of our life to the divine life, proceeding by purity, chastity, holiness, discipline, and order, and capturing divine benevolence, and subjecting souls to divine largesse. The third is a certain contact: through which we almost now touch the divine essence: and we incline into it by a certain summit of the soul. <margin>G</margin> The fourth is a certain entrance into the vestibule of the divine light. The fifth, finally, is union, insinuating the soul's own unity deeply into the divine unity and connecting them: and now fusing one and the same action of the soul and of God: so that we are no longer of our own right, but are God's, overwhelmed and surrounded by divine splendor. Of this adoration, however, which is to be done without intermission, the supreme end is, namely, that it may join the conversion of the soul with its very permanence: and whatever has proceeded from the divine unity, it may firmly restore the same again to unity: and surround our light with the supernal light. Therefore, only right adoration renders souls to the blessed fatherland. Only holiness is full virtue. Only the good man, as Plato writes in the *Laws*, prays to God decently and happily. Only association with the superiors makes men blessed. From this, the wicked are entirely alienated: and as if profane, they are to be segregated from vows and sacrifices. But the pure approach decently to supplicate, leading with them especially three companions: faith, truth, and charity. Surrounded by these, they may conceive a firm hope of good things, and being placed outside other things and themselves, they may plunge themselves entirely into the divine light. For in vain does he seek God, who does not apply himself alone and immovable to the stable and simple—

For just as we cannot be joined to being through non-being, so we cannot be joined to unity through multitude, nor to stability through motion, nor to simplicity through mixture; rather, we would fall back into the opposite. Thus say Iamblichus and Proclus. To these the great <note>Theodorus of Asine, a Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> Theodorus adds: If anyone explores the natures of things more diligently, he will find that not only souls and minds, but in a certain way all things—except the First—adore and offer vows.

# THE WORLD HAS ABOVE
# itself three causes: and depends upon
# an incorporeal cause.

### CHAPTER VII.

After these things, having offered prayers, Timaeus—because he considers the world to have been made, and therefore made by another—examines its threefold cause: first the efficient cause, which is the divine mind; second the exemplary cause, which is the series of Ideas conceived in the divine mind; third the final cause, which is the Good. Indeed, he indicates that the world is from another because, even if it is most perfect according to its corporeal nature, it is nevertheless not entirely perfect according to absolute nature. For on account of matter it suffers things that are formless or deformed; on account of dimension it undergoes a defect of power and awaits division, if a divider should happen upon it; on account of composition it is liable to dissolution; because of the conflict of its parts it contrives evil; because of motion it displays neediness and suffers an admixture of privation. Finally, because it is fitted together from diverse things, it needs a certain higher connector who exists most perfectly because he exists from himself; just as the world, because it does not exist most perfectly, is known not to exist from itself. 

Moreover, all genera of composite things are reduced to something that is not composite in that genus: just as dimensions are reduced to a point <note>original: "signum"</note>, which is not composed of dimensions; numbers to unity, which is not made of numbers; elements to that which is not mixed from elements. Therefore, the entire order of beings is reduced to a Being that does not consist of beings. That, however, will be a substance mixed with no accidents. Therefore, it will be neither quantitative nor qualitative, but a total and indivisible substance. Nor, because it is only unique and most simple, will it have less than those things which undergo accidents beyond their substance. For those things which are accidents in subsequent things must be substance in the highest—and indeed the best substance. Truly, the more things you add to the Best, the further you force it to depart from its own "best-ness." For from a new admixture, a quality results there that is degenerating. 

Therefore, not only this world, because it is entirely composite, but even if there is any higher world that is yet in some way composite, it depends on a higher simplicity. This simplicity stands even above eternity, from which an integral eternity is made in divine minds; an eternity mixed with time in rational animals; and a temporal everlastingness in the spheres of the world. In those things which are made by the motion and power of the spheres, there is a certain portion of time. Therefore, those things thought of above the soul always *are* and never *become*. The soul itself both *is* and *becomes* always. The world *is* never, but *becomes* always. Those things generated in the world are also never, but *at some time* become. We say that "becoming" is carried out in time. Truly, because the world is said to be carried out in perpetual motion or time, it is judged to be always becoming. Insofar as it "is," it is not yet; thus it is said never to "be"—just as if the image of a mountain were continually made and restored in a torrent, always being drawn into becoming in the water, but never standing still in being. 

The Platonists think this is the difference between the soul and the world: that the heaven "becomes" continually not only through action, but also through essence. The soul, however, "becomes" through action, but through essence it "is" from God rather than "becoming" from God; and since its essence is indivisible, it has a certain power that is in a way productive of itself, through which it brings forth its own life and motion within itself. The heaven, however, hangs from elsewhere on all sides. In short, just as from the same rock situated between a pond and a torrent, an image is steadily in the pond, but in the torrent it "becomes" and, vanishing, is continually recreated: so both always depend on God, but in different ways. For from Him the soul always *is*, but the world always *becomes*. But let us begin again from another principle.

---

# THE GOOD ITSELF IS THE
# cause of all things more than the
# subsequent causes, nor has it any
# proportion with the rest.

### CHAPTER VIII.

All Platonists confess without controversy that this universe has everything from the highest God: action, power, and essence alike. For they receive this from Plato out of all his books. They also hear him confirming the same in his letters. There, indeed with great mystery, he referred third-level effects to a third cause, second-level effects to a second cause, but all things to the one cause of all. Nor did he say that only the first effects are to be reduced to the first cause, lest by so pronouncing we might suspect that only those first things depend on God; or lest, by 

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> naming Him the "first cause," we might suspect Him to belong to a certain genus along with the other causes, or to agree with the effects in some property of lordship. Therefore, he showed that all things proceed from Him simultaneously, and that He meanwhile is entirely free from any communion with the things proceeding. And because of His absolute simplicity, he names Him "the One"; but because of His exuberant beneficence—through which, as a beginning, He makes all things by producing them, and as an end, He perfects the same by leading them back—he names Him "the Good." 

For he thinks that whatever things are made depend more on Him than on the other causes. Indeed, He acts in any work both earlier, longer, and more vehemently than <margin>B</margin> the remaining causes; and whatever the rest are, they are so by His making; and whatever they do, they do by His leading. To show that individual things emanate from Him more than from other causes, he repeated three times that He is the principle of all. For he said: "Around the King of all are all things." Likewise: "For His sake are all things." Again: "He is the cause of all things," so that we might understand both that all things arise chiefly from there, and that God is the maker, the pattern <note>original: "exemplar"</note>, and the end of all. 

Furthermore, he evidently shows in the sixth book of the *Republic* and in the *Parmenides* and *Sophist* that the One itself and the Good are above all essence and intellect, and are the cause of both. It is established, moreover, that the One and the Good are the same, lest if they were different, two highest principles would be forced to exist. A principle <margin>C</margin> must certainly be both most simple and best. Nothing is either simpler than unity or better than goodness. Nor is unity better than goodness, nor goodness simpler than unity. Therefore, both are the one highest God. And that this whole is above essence and mind, we have sufficiently confirmed in the *Theology* and elsewhere.

---

# ON THE DEPENDENCE OF
# matter on the Good itself: and on the
# action of mind and soul upon matter:
# and on the intelligible world.

<margin>D</margin>
### CHAPTER IX.

From this One and Good, which stands above all essence, Plato in the *Parmenides* and *Sophist* derives all grades of beings: both those which truly are (that is, the separate forms) and those which do not truly exist (that is, the forms inherent in matter), and finally <margin>E</margin> the lowest grade of matter. This matter "is" so little truly that it is closest to that which is imagined to truly not exist. This matter, derived in the *Parmenides* from the Good itself at the last grade of things, he accepts in the *Timaeus* as if already generated and subjected to the Architect of the world for the effect of the mundane work. 

But is the God who is the author of the world the same as the maker of matter? The school of Ammonius and Origen will answer that He is the same. And they say that in the *Parmenides* it is treated how matter receives "being" from God, but in the *Timaeus* by what reason it receives "well-being" from the same—though in a certain way "being" is thought of before "well-being." The common school of the Platonists will answer differently: that it is not the same <margin>F</margin> God who makes matter and who immediately forms it. Rather, matter is from the highest Good, but it is formed by the Intellect, and finally moved by the Soul. Or rather, all these are from the First, but "being" is from the First alone. "Being formed" is from the First through the Intellect; "being moved" (and being formed through motion) is from the First through the Intellect and Soul together. 

It is just as if we imagine a certain potter who makes the clay with his own hand, forms the made clay by a wheel, and while forming it, distinguishes and shapes it with a certain wooden comb. No one would say the vessel is made by the comb and wheel more than by the potter, even though it is made by the potter through the wheel and comb. He judges that this universe similarly proceeds from the Good itself through a certain divine Intellect and the Soul of the universe. Deservedly, the world is made most <margin>G</margin> "one" immediately by the One, and most "good" by the Good itself. But since this visible world—on account of the manifold distance of its parts, the conflict of qualities, the diversity of effects, and the deformity of material things—is neither most "one" nor most "good," they think that before this world, another world emanates immediately from the divine unity and goodness. This world is as similar as nature allows: not visible, but intelligible and intellectual, having the patterns of all things that are generated in this one. This they name the Divine Intellect—not the Good itself, but the "best son of the Good." If we understand this to be of one substance with the First, we shall better reconcile Plato with Christian theology. But the other interpreters of Plato will cry out against it.

# world, the image of the

### CHAPTER X.

Let Christian and Mosaic truth remain. And meanwhile, if it pleases more of the interpreters, perhaps this was the opinion of either Plato or Pythagoras: that the Intelligible World is between the visible world and the Good itself...

# MARSILIO FICINO

than to be formed: and that before the work was made from matter, the matter was of the sort from which the work ought to be fashioned. Or [one might say] that God did not at some point produce new matter, but rather adorned it from eternity; even if it is imagined as disordered before being ordered. Indeed, by its own nature, matter lacks order, which it expects from another. And since any thing is thought of according to what it *is* before it is thought of according to what it *receives*, it can rightly be conceived in itself, apart from order, as being devoid of order. Or, as I said, matter has always been from God, and continuously so: but not continuously ordered, rather [ordered] through intervals of time. Thus, it belongs to God to order stably, but to matter to be ordered movably. It receives a temporal tempering of its order, not otherwise than a clock receives it from a craftsman; and having completed its course according to its nature through certain intervals of time, it loses its order gradually and finally entirely, returning into Chaos. But God, by no means tolerating extreme confusion, suddenly re-tempers it into its prior disposition with a single nod; and this happens infinitely in turn, with God never changing, while matter is infinitely reformed. Thus far has human conjecture proceeded among the Platonists. 

However, as far as we possess certain knowledge, we affirm that our Plato asserted the World does not exist from itself, but from a cause: not indeed a fortuitous one, but a certain one; not from a merely natural cause, but an intellectual one; not from an intellect determined by the manner of nature, but rather a voluntary one; not by a will compelled by some natural instinct, but a free one. For nothing is more free than that which exists through itself and acts entirely through itself, yet not by some contingent will. For nothing is contingent where will and necessity are the same. Again, nothing is violent where necessity and will are in turn the same. Moreover, to reveal this, he repeated the name of divine Will no less than that of Intelligence in the fashioning of the world. And he added that the will of the Good itself is the highest cause and the most certain of causes. He showed it to be free from the fact that he often says God the Architect followed the custom of consulting and deliberating about the work to be constructed. By these words, he does not want God to be understood as wavering, but as choosing freely. Furthermore, he says the worldly work did not proceed from God only once, but proceeds and is preserved continually. Indeed, the supreme powers of the world would be dissoluble from themselves along with the world, unless they were ruled by the divine will. It shall be enough, therefore—and indeed a very great thing—to have affirmed such things about the philosopher who affirms them. For once these are granted, you will easily be able to say that God, since He acts by a provident and free will, composed a new world without any novelty in Himself. And thus you will hear that He produced it not at some point as new, but rather from eternity <note>original: "ab aevo"</note>; you will be able to preserve simultaneously the majesty of God, on whose will (and a free one at that) the world no less needs and depends—if it needs and depends always—than if it had proceeded at some specific time. But because Plato often says that we should assert divine matters only insofar as they are confirmed by divine oracles, we too ought to assent to the Sacred Scriptures rather than to our own conjectures.

---

## THE WORLD PROCREATED BY THE GRACE OF THE GOOD according to the likeness of the divine Reason and the divine Word.

### CHAPTER XV.

He made the World, therefore, by His will, that is, by His goodness, as much voluntarily as naturally on account of His immense, overflowing fecundity. This fecundity first rejoices in itself, and because of that, it is then delighted by this image of itself: yet in such a way that it places the end of this delight not in this image, but in the archetype itself and the principle. Since, therefore, He made the world by goodness, He made it for the sake of the Good. For He did not procreate it simply so that it might exist, live, and understand, but also that it might exist *well*, live well, and understand and acquire the Good. This is very much in harmony with that Mosaic saying: *God saw this and that, that it was good; and all things were very good.* And because beauty is the splendor of goodness, he adds that the most beautiful world was procreated by the best God: temporal indeed, but according to the image of the eternal archetype. He also says often that as many species as there are in the archetype—that is, the principal world, which is intelligible and imitable—so many forms of things did He dispose in this world, and thus made it like Himself. For he understands the Ideas of things to consist not "among the clouds," as certain slanderers falsely claim, but in the mind of the worldly Architect. Where he says that the Ideas are in Life itself, he seems to prophesy that Gospel saying: *That which was made, in Him was life.* And where he says and repeats often that the world was constituted by divine providence, he confirms the whole of religion. When Theophrastus <note>A student of Aristotle and successor in the Peripatetic school</note> observed this as something marvelous in a philosopher, he said: "Plato alone, or certainly most of all, assigned the causes of things to divine providence." But, O Theophrastus, with whatever mind you say that of Plato, you will undoubtedly confess that Plato alone, or most of all, is provident and divine.

---

## WHY THE WORLD IS ONE AND spherical, and moves in a sphere.

### CHAPTER XVI.

Next, he shows that the divine archetype of the world itself—which the Evangelist, but with a more divine sense, calls the divine Word—is unique: because since it contains all things, it leaves nothing outside itself; and therefore it is necessarily unique. But concerning this, we speak more diffusely in the *Theology*. Since, however, this world, in other respects as far as was possible, reflects the world

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> and the divine intellect—so much so that he who perceives the forms in this matter gazes upon the divine face as if in a mirror—certainly it represents Him even in that unity which effects and preserves all things: so that there is one work of one Architect. Therefore, there is one world of one God. Truly, if a human architect could dominate matter, after he had made several buildings, each of which was one in itself, he would finally surround them all with a certain single wall. But God can do this entirely, since He is the master of matter. Nor is it permitted to dream of many worlds like balls, some outside of others. For thus the divine work would be scattered, and there would be empty spaces between the worlds. You will think it more probable if, for as many 
<margin>B</margin> orbs as you imagine scattered through a vacuum, you instead conceive of spheres within spheres, so that any sphere is a world within a world; and the entire work is one, and thus ordered in turn; and nothing is found that is either empty or devoid of order and union. Moreover, let the figure of the world be spherical. For thus it is most uniform, capacious, indissoluble, and agile; and thus, and not otherwise, can a mass be moved within a mass, and be placed without a vacuum, and be moved without offense: that is, if not squares are placed within squares, or circles, but orbs within orbs. Finally, the chief cause of this worldly sphere is that the nature of the divine world is also orbicular, which reflects upon itself in understanding and loving. 
<margin>C</margin> The reason for the spherical motion is both the figure itself which receives the motion, and the internal revolution through intellectual species of the worldly soul itself which moves it.

---

<margin>D</margin> ## WHY THE WORLD IS DIVIDED either into five or into six regions: and how the heptad and the circular number apply to it: and how it is distributed according to the likeness of the intelligible world.

### CHAPTER XVII.

For what reason are numbers not unjustly accommodated to the worldly division? In these, the first roots are of circular numbers: namely, the Five from the odd numbers, and the Six from the even. We say, moreover, that the number twenty-five is multiplied from five in the manner of a circle, because one returns from the same to the same: while five times five are counted as twenty-five. And likewise in a similar 
<margin>E</margin> circle, the number one hundred twenty-five. For five times twenty-five make that many. The reason for the circular Six is the same regarding thirty-six, and likewise regarding two hundred sixteen. Although they name the higher numbers "square" and others "oblong" by reason of their origin, yet by reason of their falling and end, they call them "circular." Thus, through five and six, the first roots of circular numbers, we divide the circular body of the world. First, indeed, into five parts: namely, celestial fire; ethereal fire below the moon; air; water; and earth. This division is confirmed in the *Epinomis*. Next, we 
<margin>F</margin> distribute by the six: where we divide the celestial fire into the non-wandering <note>The fixed stars</note> and the wandering <note>The planets</note>. This partition is used more frequently by Plato. But we shall more conveniently derive the distribution of the sensible world from the distribution of its archetype in the Platonic manner. God indeed conceives in the world within Himself, the intelligible world, one power that is formable and another that is formative. The former, as I said, the Pythagoreans and Platonists call "Infinity"; the latter they call "Limit." He also conceives a mutual mixture of these powers, and understands a certain third form to immediately coalesce from this mixture. But He notices that this form itself is, as it were, triple: for it has something of infinity, something of limit, and something of its own. Thus it happens that after the number two—namely, of infinity and limit—the number three arises immediately, with the third form added to these. Let the number five also arise, with a form of this kind distributed in a threefold way. 
<margin>G</margin> Finally, the number six is born, where the office of that world is extended to producing lower things. The number seven is also born, where that world is reflected like an image to the Father. In which seventh degree, as if on the seventh day, He rests. If, indeed, you render each thing to its counterpart, you will notice that this corporeal world has fire as its form from the very limit of the supernal world; but from infinity, it has earth as its matter. From the middle form of that world, it has moisture, the conciliator of fire and earth: which both glues together the earth (by its own nature dissipatable) and nourishes the fire (easily resolvable from itself). And it possesses three things in itself: on one side fire, on the other earth, but something in the middle that is its own and pure air; since from one side it verges through the sublime toward fire, and from the other through the lowest toward earth. After this worldly five comes the six, if you conceive the common form of all things. Again, the seven is made, if you reform 
<margin>H</margin> this very form of the world to the archetype: in which indeed He rests on the seventh day.

---

## WHY THERE ARE DISTINCT PARTS IN THE WORLD, and why they are contrary, and concerning the four elements.

### CHAPTER XVIII.

We see in the world not only a distinction of forms, but also a repugnance. For it proceeds from the first, and in proceeding...

<summary>Ficino explains that the world was created by God's free and benevolent will as a reflection of the divine archetype, using mathematical symbolism (circular numbers 5 and 6) to describe its structure and the harmony of the elements.</summary>
<keywords>Marsilio Ficino, Plato, Timaeus, divine will, creation, circular numbers, five elements, providence, intelligible world, cosmology</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical commentary on the structure of the universe, specifically focusing on the transition from the unity of the higher world to the diversity and opposition found in the material world, using Pythagorean and Platonic mathematical principles.</meta>

degenerates. Indeed, a procession creates a distinction, but a degeneration creates an opposition. Furthermore, the very origin of division is the fertility of a cause overflowing outward and propagating itself into the vastness. But as the division proceeds through many steps, it finally arrives at opposition—especially since the matter of the world, due to its weakness, cannot reconcile forms within itself in the same way that the higher world reconciles them within itself. Thus it happened that God extended matter by dimension, so that it might receive, in diverse dwellings, forms that would otherwise conflict with one another. Finally, since we call those things "contraries" which are most distant within the same genus, and those things "diverse" which are separated by their genera: from the fact that there are contraries in the world, it appears that every genus has as many species as possible; and from the fact that there are diverse things, it is clear that the universe possesses very many genera. Since, however, all species are reduced to genera, and genera to the universe and its common form, it is concluded that just as the higher world is uniform and "all-form" <note>original: *omniformis*, meaning containing all possible forms</note>, so this world is all-form and uniform. Moreover, the contrary quality and shape of the elements and the heavens contribute to the daily generation of new forms, with motion clearly assisting. For if there were only a single element, nothing at all would be generated (as Hippocrates asserts). Or if there were several similar to each other, nothing new would be produced (as Heraclitus proves). It is necessary, however, for this world to imitate, according to its strength, the eternal action of the superior all-form world through the perpetual generation of new forms. Let there be, therefore, as the poetry of Empedocles sings, elements contrary to one another. Let there also be a medium between contraries, since they are both greatly distant and cannot fit together without a middle. But this medium cannot be indivisible; otherwise, the contraries would not be distant through it. It therefore has dimension. But in the part where it touches one, it does not touch the other. And it must necessarily have a middle part, through which it is equally distant from the extremes. For this reason, Plato placed at least two media between contraries, as appears evidently from his words. He even inserts a third, where he says the medium has a power through which it preserves not only the union of the extremes, but its own union as well. But let him clearly set down two (for we do not contend that now), as between fire and earth there are two things: namely, air and water. He shows from numbers and dimensions—which in a way precede natural bodies—that there is a need for at least two media between entirely contrary bodies.

# LINEAR, PLANE, AND SOLID NUMBERS, and why one medium suffices between planes, but is not enough between solids. And how mathematical ratios relate to Physics.

## CHAPTER XIX.

We have declared elsewhere that among the Pythagoreans there are three types of numbers: Linear, Plane, and Solid. Linear numbers are those measured by unity alone, like a point: such as Two, Three, Five, Seven, and the like. Plane numbers are those multiplied from numbers as if from sides—for example, six is made from two times three or three times two. Among the plane numbers, we call those "squares" and "equilateral" which are produced by the multiplication of a number by itself, such as four from two times two, nine from three times three, and sixteen from four times four. "Inequilateral" numbers are those from the multiplication of a smaller number by a larger one, such as six from the leading of two into three. We also call them "oblong" when they are made from the multiplication of a much smaller number into a much larger one, such as ten resulting from the leading of two into five. If we called this "linear" in a way in the tenth book of the *Republic*, we wished it to be understood as oblong. Besides these, we called those "solids" which are produced from the leading and reducing of a number into itself, like a solid mass produced into a triple dimension: as two times two times two is eight; three times three times three is twenty-seven; four times four times four is sixty-four. Take the first two plane numbers, which are procreated from the first linear ones: namely, four from two, and nine from three. You can bind these two planes, nine and four, to each other with a single fitting medium: that is, six. For the same proportion that nine has to six, six will have to four; in both cases, it is a *sesquialter* <note>A ratio of 1.5 to 1, or 3:2</note> proportion. For nine contains six plus another part of it, which is three. Similarly, six contains four plus two, which is half of four. That six is the fitting medium is clear because it is composed of both: for the side of four is two, and the side of nine is three. From the multiplication of two by three, six is made. Similarly, if you take the square beyond nine, which is sixteen, the medium will be twelve, which is born from their sides. For the side of nine is three, and of sixteen is four. If you lead three into four, you will bring back twelve, which connects these two by an equal ratio, namely the *sesquialter* ratio. For sixteen contains twelve plus a third part of it. Similarly, twelve includes nine plus a third part of nine. You see, therefore, what Plato says: that plane numbers can be bound by a single medium. Take furthermore the first solid numbers: those, I say, which are first produced from the first linear numbers led into themselves and

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> reduced: on this side eight from two, and on that side twenty-seven from three. You will not be able to couple these to each other with a single medium, but you will be forced to take at least two media, namely twelve and eighteen. For you will take twelve from two times two times three, and eighteen from three times three times two; and through these numbers, you will reconcile the extremes in a *sesquialter* ratio. Truly, the number twenty-seven encompasses eighteen plus another part of it, which is nine; similarly, eighteen exceeds twelve. Likewise, twelve equally exceeds eight. Through these things, it is clear that solid numbers always require more media by which they may be congruently coupled. What we have explained in numbers, we can demonstrate the same in dimensions, both plane and solid, showing that between comparable planes one medium often suffices, but between comparable solids, several true media must be placed. This would be far too long to explain, and has already been sufficiently shown by Iamblichus, Proclus, and Chalcidius. Since,
<margin>B</margin> however, Plato accepted these mathematical things not for their own sake, but for the sake of natural things here, let us briefly consider, having set these aside, what mysteries of nature he primarily understands through mathematical images. In the beginning, what is read in Holy Scripture—that God perfected all things in number, measure, and weight—is clearly touched upon by Plato when he brings numbers, measures, and solids into the discussion. For by "solids" he also understands "weights," which he also signifies when, after dimensions, he mentions the powers of inclinations, as if they were the causes of weights. By "numbers" he wants to be understood the species and substantial forms of natural things themselves, which Aristotle also compared to numbers. By "measures" he means certain instrumental figures or magnitudes adapted to certain species. Finally, by "solids" and "powers," he signifies qualities and
<margin>C</margin> those things which are extended deep within masses and provide momentum to motions and actions. All people judge that in the universe, the species of things, the figures and magnitudes of species, and the qualities are composed by reciprocal geometric and musical proportion: so that by the same ratio that the lowest are exceeded by the middle, the middle are exceeded by the higher. Likewise, by "numbers" he designates the arithmetic mean, which consists in the equality of numbers; by "dimensions" and "measures" the geometric mean, which is located in the identity of ratio and proportion; and by "weights" and "powers" the musical mean, which,
<margin>D</margin> situated in the equality or similarity of portions, encompasses the speed and slowness of motions, and the sharpness and gravity of voices by its power.

# THE FIRST DISCUSSION, WHY the number four of the elements is appropriate for the world.

## CHAPTER XX.

<margin>E</margin> But of these things elsewhere more at length. Now let us return to the partition of the worldly parts, so that we may be able to behold their harmonic composition. In the previous sections, we said that the numbers five and six were appropriate for the circular figure of the world. Now, moreover, we say that the number four <note>the quaternary</note> is appropriate for its fullness. Truly, the first quaternary fills every difference of numbers, embracing within itself the first even and the first odd. It also fills the simple progression of numbers, when it completes the number ten with four terms: perfectly finishing the ten with one, two, three, and four. It also fills the process of dimensions,
<margin>F</margin> affected by four terms: point, length, width, and depth. It fills musical consonance. Indeed, within the limits of the quaternary are restrained the double, triple, quadruple, *sesquialter*, and *sesquitertia* <note>4:3 ratio</note>; the octave, the double octave, the fifth, and the fourth. It fills nature, proceeding up to four terms: substance, quantity, quality, and motion. Finally, it fills the universe, whether that which is in nature or that which is above nature: by essence, being, power, and action. Justly, therefore, did the Pythagoreans designate the fullness of the worldly body and soul by the "four-ness," and they testified by oath that the fountain of perpetually flowing nature was fourfold. From this fountain, doubtless, flows the fourfold number of the elements.
<margin>G</margin> Hence the fourfold nature in the heavens is fourfold. Hence below the heavens are four seasons. Hence under time are four humors, complexions, and affections. Hence above time four virtues rise. Hence in eternity are four examples of virtues.

# THE SECOND DISCUSSION TO prove the same.

## CHAPTER XXI.

<margin>H</margin> Furthermore, if I did not fear partly lengthiness and partly novelty, I would recount certain wonderful commentaries of Iamblichus, Syrianus, and Proclus, establishing four grades above the supernal world: namely, the One, Limit, Infinity, and Mixture. Accordingly, they place the supernal world—that is, the first and intelligible mind—after these; then a mind and world partly intelligible and partly intellectual; after this, the purely intellectual mind and world-soul. In the fourth place, the mind and the "animal" world, the leader of the sensible world. Likewise, the supreme mind looks up to those four—the One, Limit, Infinity, and Mixture—and has four by its own nature: namely, on one side Unity, and on the other Essence. Again, essential Unity, and uniform Essence, and all the ideas of things whatsoever are similarly participants in a fourfold nature.

It details how geometric means (like the number 6 between 4 and 9) justify the placement of air and water between fire and earth.</summary>
