# MARSILIO FICINO

Likewise, the intellectual mind itself, the Jovial <note>referring to Jupiter as the Demiurge or world-maker</note> maker of the world, looks up to the intelligible and supreme mind as a model in the crafting of the world, and to the Good as its end. And because in the intelligible world—which they also call Being itself and Living itself—it perceives the principles and ideas of a fourfold nature, it similarly distributes the world into four regions. The first of these extends from the first heaven, and after the heaven through the sphere of fire to the beginning of the air. The second from there to the middle of the air. The third from there to the earth. The fourth, indeed, is the earth. To this kind of partition, four armies of rational inhabitants correspond in each region: namely, the worldly gods, then the angels, then the demons, and finally particular souls. But leaving these aside, let us return to our purpose.

## THIRD DISCUSSION TO CONFIRM THE SAME.

### CHAPTER XXXII.

In the view of the metaphysician, there are four elements: essence, being, power, and action. In the view of the mathematician, four: the point, the line, the plane, and depth. In the view of the physicist, four: the seminal power of nature, natural sprouting, the adult form, and the composite. Now, assign each to each. To essence belongs the point and the seed; to being, the line and the sprouting; to power, the plane and the form; to action, depth and the composite. Everywhere, the extremes are joined like solids by two means. Clearly, what is a point in mathematics, Plato considers in physics to be the seminal, indivisible, and stable power. What is the linear production in length in mathematics, he considers in physics to be the sprouting of the germinating form, so to speak. Likewise, what is a plane there, is properly form here; for just as a plane terminates a body, so form terminates matter. Finally, what is depth there is the composite here—a double composite, I say: first formal, that is, a certain complex of several forms similar to a solid sphere; then material, that is, from form and matter, more similar to a cube. Therefore, when he says that one mean suffices between two planes, understand that a single mean is enough between two forms, that is, a formal mean. For when forms follow one another where they touch at their extremes, they agree by one formal mean, which is partly similar and partly different on both sides. But when he says that solids are coupled to solids by a double mean, he signifies that between two natural composites of different natures, twin means are interposed. One of these is formal, the other material. For in any composite, the principal form is considered on one hand, and the subject accommodated to the form on the other. From this it follows that between different composites a double discrepancy arises: one more by reason of the form, the other more by reason of the subject.

## FOURTH DISCUSSION ON THE SAME, AND ON THE POWERS AND PROPORTIONS OF THE ELEMENTS.

### CHAPTER XXIII.

These same things are further corroborated by another reason, if you descend from the fourfold groups just described to the fourfold nature of the sphere. In this, one considers the nature of the center and the nature of the circumference, which are most distant from each other both in property and in position. Furthermore, one considers space on one hand insofar as the power of the center is extended, and space on the other hand insofar as the force of the circumference is stretched out. From this, four regions of the world are counted, and similarly four elements.

| | From substance, | From power, | From action. |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Fire, | subtle | sharp, | mobile. |
| Air, | subtle, | blunt, | mobile. |
| Water, | thick, | blunt, | mobile. |
| Earth, | thick, | blunt, | immobile. |

->Another arrangement of the same.<-

| | | | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Fire, | sharp, | subtle, | mobile. |
| Air, | blunt, | subtle, | mobile. |
| Water, | blunt, | thick, | mobile. |
| Earth, | blunt, | thick, | immobile. |

Of these, that which is placed in the circumference, following its nature, is the most ample, and therefore the most subtle of all in substance, the sharpest in power and most fit for penetration, and finally the readiest for motion in action. That which is situated in the middle, following the nature of the center, is the narrowest and densest in substance, blunt in power, and finally most unfit for motion in action. The two means hold a middle way in these respects. Therefore, just as the circuit and the center are most distant in a sphere, so the position and nature of fire and earth differ the most. For fire seeks the circuit such that it is never naturally in the middle; earth seeks the center such that it is never naturally in the circuit. Air sometimes descends, namely if it is placed in the high region of fire. Water also ascends, if it is confined beneath the earth. Just as three things are considered in fire and earth—namely substance, power, and action—so also three principal properties: in fire, thinness <note>original: *subtilitas*</note> by substance, sharpness by power, and mobility by action. In earth, the opposites: thickness by substance,

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> bluntness by power, and immobility by action. Now, their natures are called "solid" in Plato because, like a triple dimension, they possess triple qualities. If they only had the nature of planes, one mean would suffice, which would agree with the extremes in one quality but differ in the other. But since opposite things need two means to be bound together, each mean must agree with its neighbor (both the extreme and the other mean) in two qualities and differ in only one; while with the remote extreme, it agrees in one but differs in two. Thus, air follows fire, being very similar to fire in subtlety and mobility, but dissimilar in a certain bluntness of power, in which single quality it somehow agrees with 

<margin>B</margin> earth. With water, however, it agrees in two: namely bluntness and mobility. Water follows air and is similar to it; but it is similar to fire in only one way, namely mobility, while it is dissimilar to fire in two: thickness and bluntness together. It is dissimilar to earth in its mobility, but similar in thickness and bluntness. Truly, it appears that fire is comparable to earth by a certain analogy, that is, by a similarity of reason and proportion. For as the subtlety of fire is to the thickness of earth, so is the sharpness of fire to the bluntness of earth, and again the mobility of fire to the immobility of earth. That fire is also comparable, but by a stronger reason, to air, air to water, and water to earth, is manifest from the agreement of their qualities. It seems 

<margin>C</margin> that for a proximate element to its neighbor, the agreement is double the discrepancy; but toward a remote element, on the contrary, the discrepancy is double the agreement. Fire seems twice as subtle as air, three times as mobile, and four times as sharp. Likewise, air is twice as sharp as water, three times as mobile, and four times as subtle. Again, water is twice as sharp as earth, three times as subtle, and four times as ready for motion. To proceed only up to a fourfold proportion among related things is permitted among musicians, for the ears are offended by a longer progression. Furthermore, the perfect ratios of music are contained in these. In these, through three qualities as if through three dimensions, we proceed from solids to solids three times and solidly. For by the double ratio, we reach eight at the fourth step, which is the first solid number. Likewise, 

<margin>D</margin> by triple ratios, we reach twenty-seven at the fourth step, which is the second solid. Again, by fourfold ratios, we reach sixty-four at the fourth place, which holds the third place among solid numbers. For eight is created from two taken solidly (that is, three times or cubed); twenty-seven from three cubed; sixty-four from four similarly multiplied by itself three times. But so that it may be better known how much mathematical congruence there is in Plato toward physics, those two means of the first solids must be repeated. For we placed two fitting means between eight and twenty-seven: namely twelve and eighteen. The number twelve is born from both eight and twenty-seven. For the side from which eight is multiplied is two; the side from which twenty-seven comes is three. But from 

<margin>E</margin> two and three, twelve is made if you do two times two, three times; where the resulting twelve takes two sides from the eight and one from the twenty-seven. Likewise, from two and three, eighteen is made if you do three times three, twice; where the resulting number eighteen takes one side from the remote eight (where it says "twice") but two sides from the number twenty-seven (where it says "three times three"). Similarly, the two elements that are means between fire and earth, while they are tempered from the extremes, carry back twin natures from the neighbor but borrow only one from the remote extreme.

<margin>F</margin>

## THAT THE WHOLE WORLD IS COMPOSED OF FOUR ELEMENTS: AND HOW THESE ARE IN HEAVEN IN ONE WAY, AND BELOW THE MOON IN ANOTHER.

### CHAPTER XXIV.

<margin>G</margin> All Pythagoreans and Platonists believe the entire world is composed of these four elements joined by geometric and musical reason; yet in such a way that their consonance in heaven never suffers any dissonance. Below heaven, however, some dissonance seems to arise somewhere at times, but it is immediately reduced into a consonant form by the superior harmony. No one will deny these elements exist below the moon. But some physicists will deny they are in heaven. I pray they listen to the metaphysicians, who prove that the elements exist in the very Maker of the world through their Ideas; then in the Soul of the World through their Reasons; and in Nature through their Seeds. Therefore, they are also in heaven through their Powers, and below heaven through their Forms. For in what way do the natures of the elements pass from causes higher than heaven to 

<margin>H</margin> below heaven, and there become natures immediately, unless their moderating powers are meanwhile infused into heaven? Indeed, just as a farmer does not rule an architect because he contains no principles of architecture, but a geometer, possessing these, does rule him; so also heaven, unless it comprehended the forces of the elements and elemental things, would never govern them. But the heavenly height does govern. Let them also listen to the astrologers, who designate the natures of the elements in both the signs and the planets, and prove it by the effect. Finally, let them listen to the Sacred Scriptures, which often place waters in the heavens, and also place a "land of the living." If these two things, which are most unlike the celestial, are placed there, much more are fire and air, which are more similar to the celestial, placed there by the Sacred Scriptures. They will respond...

<summary>Ficino explains the mathematical and metaphysical proportions of the four elements, using solid numbers and musical ratios to demonstrate how they are bound together. He argues that the elements exist in the celestial spheres as "powers" rather than physical forms, maintaining the harmony of the cosmos.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the Neoplatonic commentary on the composition of the world, specifically discussing the presence of the four elements within the celestial spheres and the hierarchical structure of the "Spirit of the World."</meta>

# ARGUMENTS AND COMMENTARY

In my judgment, some believe that the most excellent powers of the elements are placed there <note>in the heavens</note> by way of cause; however, in the spheres of the elements below the moon, their natures exist according to form; and finally, in composite things, by a certain participation. But they will deny that the actual natures of the elements are in heaven. To this, the Platonists add that specific virtues everywhere are founded in a specific nature. Therefore, if the virtues of these things are in heaven, their natures must also be there, but just as the virtues there consist in a genus far more excellent than these, so too the natures are in a more excellent—indeed, to speak more correctly, a most excellent—state. And that most eminent nature of fire provides the heaven with sensible light, life-giving heat, and the readiest motion. The nature of earth grants solid and firm stability. Likewise, it gives density to the stars so they may be seen, and to the moon so it may reflect the solar rays. The nature of air provides that transparent quality which they call translucent. The nature of water brings a most delicate and uniform smoothness. And what is greatest of all: into the very "lips" of the spheres where they touch one another, it inserts that virtue of cold and moisture; through this, it happens that although they touch each other most rapidly and vehemently due to their swift motion, no burning or dissolution occurs there. The Hebrews will strongly approve of these "waters in the heavens." <note>A reference to Genesis 1:7 regarding the waters above the firmament.</note> They will also approve, I believe, if they hear that through the nature of the earth living there, it happens that materials which are otherwise very thin are not scattered by such great motion. <margin>C</margin> One must remember that there is such great virtue in the celestial substance, and so effective for conciliation, that qualities and motions which among us are repugnant to one another do not fight there. Likewise, the remaining elements there were reduced to the most excellent form—that is, fire—immediately from the first birth of the world: just as through celestial motion the four elements among us are reduced to one form of a mixture in any birth. Nor will you wonder that the elements are fused into one there if you consider that even below the moon they are compacted into one mass, and fire is a participant in earthly solidity lest it be continually dispersed due to its very thin and mobile nature; the earth also, sluggish by itself, obtains action and life through its partnership with fire. If the extremes are mixed, surely the means are mixed with means and extremes. Likewise, if there is such great union below the Moon, there is much greater above the Moon: but the solidity or stability of the earth reigns there without thickness in a quasi-vapory form. Again, the uniformity and smoothness of water is far from falling; the agility of air is separate from flowing away; the efficacy of fire in light and healthful heat dominates with a very similar intelligence, separate from that combustion to which it is forced among us—both the light reflected among hollows and the fiery heat enclosed in a certain rough and biting matter. Which certainly, insofar as it is released from earthly thickness, shines more purely and heats more healthfully. Therefore, together with Heraclitus and Empedocles, we shall say that the intellectual light of the fire itself which is in the "Idea" <note>The Platonic world of Forms</note> flashes forth as visible light to the eyes in heaven; below heaven, however, in the ether, its pure and harmless flame flourishes; but on earth, it is a coal burning in rough matter. We shall say finally with Orpheus that there are moreover four elements among those in the underworld: Pyriphlegethon, Acheron, Oceanus, and Cocytus. <note>The four rivers of the Greek underworld, here equated to the four elements.</note> We shall say with Plato that just as in the Archetypal world all things are in all things, so in this imaginary world all things are in all things: but they are received everywhere according to the nature of the recipients: so that celestial things in the elements are elemental, and elements in the heaven are celestial. And so great is the excellence of the celestial region over others that the celestial fire, beyond the elemental fire and the three remaining elements, may be called a "fifth element." Hence he says five worlds can be named. Indeed, all genera of things are in any of these five according to their own nature. We shall conclude, finally, the concord between Moses and Plato, whom Numenius <note>A Neo-Pythagorean philosopher who famously asked, "What is Plato but Moses speaking Attic Greek?"</note> calls "another Moses." For what Moses says—"In the beginning God made heaven and earth"—Plato says: "God first made fire and earth," understanding fire chiefly as heaven. For in the beginning, he considered the center and the circumference in the sphere of the world. He interposed the rest for the sake of these.

## ALL CIRCULAR MOTION is proper to a sphere that is always mobile. Likewise, light is most proper to fire.

### CHAPTER XXV.

But let those not disturb us who doubt that the heaven is fiery because the motion of heaven is circular, while that of fire is straight. For even any portion of heaven, if by chance it were placed in the middle, would suddenly ascend in a straight line, seeking its fatherland by a shorter path; and yet the proper motion of heaven is a circuit. And the earth, if separated from the center, will descend, and yet its property is to rest. Truly, any mobile sphere, whether elemental or celestial, is naturally moved in a circle according to its figure, so as to enjoy its place more fully. But straight motion, wherever it is, is not so much natural as it is a return to nature. If a circuit is suitable to any body, it is most suitable to fire. Since it is most distant from the earth even by nature, just as the earth is always immobile, so fire is always mobile. If always mobile, therefore in a circle. For that which moves in a straight line, having finished a finite space, also finishes its motion. That both fire and air move in a circle is shown by the circuit of comets. The perpetual inflow and outflow also testify to the circuit of water. But it is necessary for the earth to remain as an indivisible

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> and stable center so it might be more similar to it, and thereby enjoy it more conveniently. However, the superior things move so that they might always produce various things according to the variety of motion. Nor should some deny that the heaven is hot, but rather deny that it is "burning." Nor should they say that the light of the sun heats by reflection alone, but only that it burns. For the reflected rays of the Moon do not heat at all, since water dominates in the watery parts. But the rays of the Sun heat healthfully on account of the fiery and life-giving nature of the sun. Nor should they object that it happens from the slower motion of the Moon that the Moon's rays do not heat. For even if it is posited to be slower, it is nevertheless so much closer to men than the Sun that it ought to heat at least a little, if heating <margin>B</margin> were to come from reflection alone. Nor should they argue that scorching heat is proper to fire. Indeed, the less it is mixed with foreign matter, the less it burns. But let them say light is proper to fire. For the purer it is, the clearer it is, though not manifest to certain eyes; and it shines further than it heats, and it illuminates first, and in a moment, and bestows heat upon the heated thing which preserves the heat for a time after the fire is gone; but it bestows light on nothing, as it is proper to itself. Indeed, when the fire departs, the light departs at the same time.

# ON THE SPIRIT OF THE WORLD, that is, on the intellect, soul, intelligence, and nature.

### CHAPTER XXVI.

<margin>D</margin> After he has treated how God constructed the mundane body, he next proceeds to dispute how He tempered the mundane soul. Meanwhile, he shows that he placed before our eyes the unformed mass before the formed; and soon the formed in a certain way before the animated: not because either unformedness was before formation or bodily formation before the soul, but so that we might know that a nature as formable as bodily formation was divinely instituted for the sake of the soul as its end. God, wishing therefore to make a perfect work, made the world living and intellectual: and so that one animal might be more conveniently connected from the spirit itself and the matter of the world, He distinguished the matter into four elements, as we have said, like the humors of this animal, because He had also willed its spirit to be distinguished into four. For four things pertain to the spirit of the world. First, indeed, the intellect, <margin>E</margin> remaining immobile in itself, the mover or ruler of the sphere, so instituted by the author of all things to be ruled by the spheres. Second, the soul of the sphere, a mobile mover indeed, but mobile through itself. Third, a certain intelligence, divinely implanted in this soul by God and the superior intellect. Fourth, nature—that is, the seminal and vital virtue, infused everywhere into matter by the soul. The intellect and soul are indeed substances, but intelligence and nature are qualities: the former of the soul, the latter of matter. The four elements are images of these four. For fire refers to the intellect, Earth to nature, Air to Intelligence, and finally Water to the soul. And just as three things are proper to fire, and three opposites to earth, and the means <margin>F</margin> agree in a certain middle reasoning: so three things are proper to the intellect and their opposites are proper to nature, and the means to the means. For the intellect is individual, uniform, and eternal. Nature is divisible, multiform, and temporal. But the soul, as a mean between these, through intelligence becomes more a participant in the intellect itself than in nature; but through animal power, it agrees with nature rather than with the intellect. For which reason it is called partly individual and partly divisible. Likewise, similarly uniform and multiform. Again, partly eternal and partly temporal. Accordingly, four lives are numbered according to the fourfold spirit of the world. The Saturnian life is in the intellect looking up to its father, the heaven—that is, the God who is the smith of heaven. The Jovial life is in the intelligence already declining toward mobile action; the Venereal in the animal virtue already loving matter; the Dionysian in nature as if drunk—that is, immersed in matter. Furthermore, four senses are numbered in the <margin>G</margin> universe by a similar reasoning. The first sense is in the soul of the world—the "common sense," I say, and one—that is, a certain imaginary virtue thus accompanying its intelligence and reaching the particular forms of things, just as the intelligence reaches the universal ones: reaching them, I say, intrinsically; therefore it needs no instruments, nor does it proceed anywhere outside, nor does it suffer. The second sense is in the souls of the spheres and the stars, certainly common and similarly impassive, but proceeding outward. The third is in particular souls, distributed beyond the common power through individual instruments, and reaching out beyond itself, and arising from passion <note>In the sense of "undergoing" or "receiving" an impression</note>, but ending in judgment. Finally, the Pythagoreans grant a fourth sense to plants—indeed, a shadow of a sense, and a dull one at that, having no judgment of quality, but placed only in the passion of a certain pleasure and pain. The first sense represents the intellect; <margin>H</margin> the second, intelligence; the third, animal power; and the fourth, the natural. One must remember that the matter of the world itself does not receive the soul except through nature, nor intelligence except through the soul, nor intellect except through intelligence. Just as through earth it receives water, through this air, and through this fire. Moreover, observe what follows next similar to these. For he says: God placed the soul in the middle, and extended it from there through the whole, and finally protected the exteriors of the world through it. First, he signifies that the soul both fills the whole mass of the world, moderately governing other parts of the world with other virtues, and that it surpasses the world by the highest virtue of itself around the world—that is, by intellectual providence. But that the virtue of the soul is extended from the very middle through the...

It harmonizes Platonic cosmology with Mosaic and Orphic traditions, arguing for a unified, living universe.</summary>

the universe is explained through four stages. First, from the center of the earth, it extends the power of connecting everywhere; from the center of the water, it diffuses vital force; from the air, likewise, sensory force; and from fire, rational force. Then, from the central sphere of the world, it extends the power of connecting (as we said); from the sphere of the Moon (the midpoint between things that are generated and things that are ungenerated), vital force; from the Sun (the heart of the world), sensory force; and from the central Zodiac of the firmament, rational force. But since there is a double order of things toward God—one by which they proceed from Him, and another by which those proceeding are turned back toward Him—Plato followed the order of procession when he said: *God placed intellect in the soul, and the soul in the body.* Thinking also of the order of conversion <note>The Neoplatonic concept of *epistrophe* or the return of the soul to its source.</note>, he said: *God extended the soul, placed in the center, through the whole, and meanwhile led a certain part of it outside the world;* namely, so that while it provided for the world, it might be turned back toward God.

## ON THE COMPOSITION OF THE SOUL and that it is appropriately fashioned through the number five.

### CHAPTER XXVII.

Since we have explained many things pertaining to the souls of the spheres, minds, motions, and the composition of the soul more clearly in our *Theology* <note>Referring to Ficino's major work, *Platonic Theology*.</note>, we are and shall be briefer in explaining them here. For we are now hurrying toward matters more specific to this work.
<margin>B</margin>
At the outset, we believe the number five <term>quinarius</term> is suited to the composition and division of the soul for three reasons. First, because just as the five consists of the first even and the first odd number <note>2 + 3 = 5. In Pythagorean thought, 2 is the first even/female number and 3 is the first odd/male number.</note>, so the soul consists of a divisible and indivisible nature. You know, moreover, that the even number is called "divisible," while the odd is "indivisible," since it cannot be divided into equal [integer] parts. Second, because the "kinds" <note>The five "Great Kinds" from Plato's *Sophist*.</note> by which all things are composed by God are distributed through five. For they are Essence, Sameness, Difference, Rest, and Motion. They believe the soul, as the midpoint of all things, is composed of these five kinds of all things by a certain principal reason. Third, because since the soul is the center of the universe, it naturally receives the number five, which is the center of the universal number [ten]. For five is the perfect midpoint of ten. For when we rightly divide ten five times, the five is the equally distant midpoint in every division. First, if you divide ten into nine and one, you will see that five is the midpoint between one and nine, equally distant from both. Second, if you wish to part ten into eight and two, you will again find five as the equal midpoint between these. If thirdly into seven and three, or fourthly into six and four, you will again receive five as the true midpoint between the extremes. In every case, we are speaking of the Arithmetic Mean. That you have five as the midpoint when you part ten a fifth time into five and five is superfluous to say. For these reasons, Plato, in the distribution of the universe—both of the "animatable" body, so to speak, and of the soul—brings five main headings into the center. For in both cases, he treats first of the subsistence and foundation of the thing itself, whether of the body or the soul. Second, of the harmony of the parts of both.
<margin>C</margin>
Third, of the species <note>The "form" or "appearance" resulting from the structure.</note> resulting from the harmony of the parts. Fourth, of the powers of the species. Fifth, of the actions that arise from the powers. The Platonists wish these three—subsistence, harmony, and species—to pertain to the essence of the soul; through these follow power and action. By harmony, I mean a fitting tempering, and this is fivefold: of kinds, parts, reasons, powers, and actions. For the soul consists of those five kinds of things, through which its own parts are assigned. It receives, in turn, the "reasons" <term>rationes</term> <note>The formative blueprints or principles of things.</note> of all things from God. From this, it has many specific powers through which it produces actions. But where he calls the soul a "harmony" or "concord": remember that Plato in the *Phaedo* denies that the soul is a harmony—namely, a harmony of bodily parts made from them and residing in them. But in the *Timaeus*, he affirms the soul is a harmony—namely, of its own parts remaining within itself, and tempering the body from itself. Furthermore, where he says, *God composed from the indivisible essence that is always the same, and from that which is divisible around bodies, a third intermediate species of essence, that is, the soul,* explain this through what he says elsewhere: *God made the world living, animated, and intellectual.* For where he says "living," he designates a certain natural life spread through the bodies of the world, extended along with the body of the world and acting changeably. But where he says "intellectual," he understands the angelic intellects which are properly set over the governing of the spheres; they are indivisible according to place and immutable according to time, existing in a manner opposite to natural life and the divisible, changeable bodily form. But where he says "animated," he signifies the very substance of the World Soul, whose essence is indeed both indivisible and immutable like the intellect. Yet it can be called in a certain way divisible and mobile, because it is the proper source of certain powers declining toward divisible and mobile things. Its power and action are partly individual and immobile, insofar as it agrees with divine things and acts stably; but partly it is also divisible in a way, both because it is manifold and because it declines toward the manifold and divided body; and it is mobile, because it operates within time. Therefore, he calls this soul a "third species of essence," a midpoint between the individual and eternal on one hand, and the divisible and temporal on the other. That he means to signify angelic intellects when he calls the world "intellectual" is proved by this: that the body of the world is prepared for intellect through life. Therefore, as it relates to life, so it relates to intellect. Thus, just as it has not only natural life residing in the matter of the world, but also "animal" life—that is, the soul existing in itself—

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
so it has not only an intellectual quality infused into the soul, but also an intellectual substance remaining in itself. For everywhere certain qualities are traced back to certain substances, so that just as a vital quality is referred to a vital substance, so an intellectual quality is also referred to an intellectual substance. Moreover, he composes the soul in five principal ways. First, from the five kinds of things. Likewise from numbers. Third, from musical concords. Fourth, from the beginnings of figures. Fifth, from the principles of motions; namely, so that possessing the "reasons" of metaphysics and mathematics, it may thus know all things: essences, numbers, concords, figures, and motions. Likewise, insofar as the soul is related to divine things, he says it is composed of the kinds of things that are primarily in the divine. Insofar as it is related to natural things, he
<margin>B</margin>
mixes it with figures and motions. But insofar as it holds the middle between both, he contemplates it through musical concords and reasons. He names those five—Essence, Sameness, Difference, Rest, and Motion—the "kinds of things," because all things except the First [the One] are composed of them. Essence clearly signifies the formal reason of each thing; it also hints at "being" as the proper act of essence. Sameness is mentioned because anything agrees first with itself and then with others. Again, he adds Difference, because it has a certain distinction both within itself and toward others. Furthermore, Rest, since it retains its own unity for some time. Finally, Motion in this
<margin>C</margin>
place signifies a certain exit from potentiality into act: whether by being, or by acting in any way internally or externally. But above these five kinds are placed three: Limit, the Infinite, and the Mixture. Above these three is placed the One itself. Essence follows the divine One itself. Sameness and Rest follow Limit. But Difference and Motion accompany Infinitude. Finally, just as we placed the four elements of the world in the highest degree in the heavens, in the middle degree below the moon, and in the lowest degree below the earth; so we place the five kinds in a certain highest reason in divine things, in a middle reason in the soul, and in the lowest reason below the soul. For in divine things, unity overcomes multitude, and
<margin>D</margin>
limit overcomes infinitude, and sameness exceeds difference, and rest prevails over motion. But in lower things, it happens entirely the opposite: those which surpassed there are now surpassed here in turn. In the soul especially, an equal tempering of each to each emerges, so that they not undeservedly wish this to be especially the midpoint of things and tempered by musical reasons. Mathematicals suit the soul; for both are judged to be midpoints between divine and natural things. Musical numbers suit the soul most of all. For they are mobile, and therefore they rightly signify the soul, which is the principle of motion. Not only through numbers, but also through figures is the soul described: so that through numbers it may be thought of as incorporeal, but through figures it may be known to naturally
<margin>E</margin>
decline toward bodies. The triangle suits the soul. Because just as a triangle is extended from one angle into two, so the soul, flowing from an indivisible and divine substance, falls into the nature of the body which is utterly divisible; and if it is compared with divine things, it appears divided. For while those [divine things] act through one stable power and do so suddenly, the soul performs through many and changeable powers and actions, and through intervals of time. But if it is compared with natural things, it is judged indivisible. For it does not have different parts separated by place like they do, but it is whole in any part of the whole; nor does it pursue all things changeably and in time like they do, but it also attains some things suddenly and possesses them eternally. One may furthermore compare the soul with the triangle because the triangle is the first figure of those which, consisting of several lines, are produced in a straight line. Similarly, the soul is the first of all to be distributed into several powers, which in it
<margin>F</margin>
are joined to the intelligence; and it seems to be produced in a straight line while it falls from divinity into nature. In this descent from the highest intelligence, it flows into three lower powers: that is, into a certain rational discourse, into sense, and into the power of growth <note>The vegetative soul.</note>. Just as a triangle, produced from a point, is led into three angles. I say the soul is the first of every kind, and is mixed in a way from several powers, and falls, so to speak, in a straight line. For the angelic mind above the soul needs no lower powers within itself, but is pure mind, and whole mind, and sufficient. Likewise, it does not turn toward lower things, but toward divinity alone, whence it is turned back in the manner of a circle. Therefore, its
<margin>G</margin>
action is compared to a circle. For its action is one and equal, just as a circle is from one and equal line, and a certain mixed capacity of both. Furthermore, the circle is the first and last of figures. First, because it is contained by one line. Last, because figures constituted of many lines, the more faces they take on, the more they seem to approach little by little the form of the circle as their end. Similarly, the intellect is the first of all to be procreated by God, and the intellectual "face"—that is, the absolute order of things—shines as the last of all in the mirror of nature, toward which natural forms approach more and more by degrees as their end. But of the intellect, another time. Now let us return to the soul.

## WHY THE SOUL IS COMPARED TO A COMPOSED THING: and why to musical consonances.

### CHAPTER XXVIII.

<margin>I</margin>
We seek three things especially concerning the soul at present. First, why Plato feigns the soul to be like a composed thing. Second, for what reason it is composed of a certain harmony. Third, to which musical consonance [it is compared]. At the start, the soul, even if it is indissolubly com-

He argues that the soul contains the "reasons" of all things, allowing it to govern the body while remaining oriented toward God.</summary>

# ARGUMENTS AND COMMENTARY.

is placed, yet it is composed of such great multiplicity that by a certain natural inclination it leans toward those things which are entirely composite. Therefore, it is shaped in a way similar to composite things, with which it agrees by a certain—I will not say consanguinity—but natural affinity. Furthermore, because it is the middle point of things, it is rightly composed of all things and binds all things together in harmony; thus it is compared to a certain concord or a harmoniously composed thing. This is especially true since the soul reconciles things that fight amongst themselves in nature, connects them once reconciled, and preserves them once connected. Thus, not without justice is the soul judged to be a certain substantial concord, or a most harmonious and indissoluble substance. 

But since those things apprehended by the other senses are also very often harmoniously composed, it was asked thirdly why Plato expressed the soul as being most like *musical* concord. The answer to this is: Musical consonance occurs in the medium element of all things <note>likely referring to air</note>, and through motion—specifically a circular motion—it reaches the ears. Thus it is no wonder that it suits the soul, which is both the middle of things and the principle of motion revolving in a circuit. Add to this that harmony, being the most "animated" among sensible things, carries the affection and thought of the soul—whether of the one singing or the one playing—into the minds of the listeners. Therefore, it agrees with the soul above all else. 

Furthermore, things pertaining to sight, even if they are pure in a way, are nevertheless without the efficacy of motion and are often apprehended through an image alone without the nature of the thing; therefore, they usually move the soul very little. Those things pertaining to smell, taste, and touch, being very material, tickle the instruments of the senses rather than penetrating the depths of the soul. But harmony, through its airy nature set in motion, moves the body; through purified air, it stirs the "airy spirit" <note>the *spiritus*, a thin vapor thought to link soul and body</note> which is the knot of soul and body; through affection, it affects the sense and the mind simultaneously; through meaning, it acts upon the intellect; finally, through the very motion of subtle air, it penetrates vehemently; through contemplation, it strokes sweetly; through its conforming quality, it pours over us a wonderful pleasure; through its nature, both spiritual and material, it seizes the whole person at once and claims them. 

And truly, if someone offered to the hearing harmonies with as much art and diligence of the Muses as the craftsman of nature offers flavors to the taste or soft things to the touch, we would undoubtedly recognize that Apollo seizes the soul with melody far more than Bacchus is wont to occupy the taste with wine, or Venus the touch with itching desire. To this it happens that where Plato introduces the Maker of the World speaking—both reasoning with himself and commanding the rest—he considers that very eloquence to be like the most musical song of Apollo, the origin of both the mundane soul and body; and the soul, born from there, similarly strikes the celestial lyre by musical reason. 

And indeed, what exists in celestial melody—both the low tone from slower motion and the high tone from faster motion—the same exists beneath the heavens as heaviness and lightness; likewise cold and heat, and again the moisture and dryness of the elements. The same exists in the generation of things as matter and form. The same in human characters: gentleness and high-mindedness, temperance and fortitude. And just as one sound is made from a low and high voice, so from all the pairs of natures we have described, a "one" is made everywhere. Since, therefore, musical consonance is as if alive, rational, and effective—being most similar to the soul and most pleasing to it—and since it claims the whole man for itself, and (what is greater) the soul was made through it, all things were made through it, are preserved through it, and are moved through it, it was not without reason that our Plato described the soul—the maker, preserver, and mover of all natural things—chiefly by musical numbers and ratios. I say numbers not as mathematical accidents, as some critics falsely claim, but as established by the <term>ideal numbers</term> <note>Platonic Forms of numbers</note> and metaphysical ratios.

## CHAPTER XXIX.

They call a <term>Phthongos</term> <note>from Greek *phthongos*</note> a sound suited for melodies, by which one can easily produce both a lower and a higher pitch, so that it is neither so deep and relaxed as to be like silence, nor so high and intense as to be a noisy din. They believe a low sound is created by a relaxed and slow motion, and a high sound by a more intense and rapid one. Just as a relaxed and very slow motion seems to approach rest, so the lowest sound approaches silence. Conversely, just as a most vehement and swift motion approaches violence, so the highest sound approaches offense. 

They call the <term>intervals</term> of sounds certain mutual excesses between them in height and depth. <term>Compositions</term>, however, are the joinings of congruent sounds from appropriate proportions of consonances. Also, the <term>tunings</term> of strings in musical instruments: whether in a single <term>tetrachord</term> <note>a four-string scale</note> such as Mercury invented and Orpheus confirmed; or in two tetrachords with seven strings joined together, which Terpander is said to have made; or in twin tetrachords arranged and disjoined through eight strings, of which they assert Lycaon of Samos was the author; or in four joined tetrachords consisting of fifteen strings finally approved by all the Greeks—in all these tetrachords, the <term>diatessaron</term> <note>the interval of a perfect fourth</note> consonance resounds step by step. Now, after the mention of sounds, intervals, and compositions, let us proceed to the proportions from which consonances are made. They name the <term>proportion of equality</term> that which

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> occurs between terms entirely equal to each other, as between this "one" and that "one," or a cubit and a cubit. The <term>proportion of inequality</term> is that between unequal terms, as between one and two, or a cubit and two cubits. One of these is of "greater inequality," such as the double; the other of "lesser inequality," such as the sub-double <note>1/2</note>. Furthermore, we must presently consider a threefold proportion of inequality. The first they call <term>multiple</term>, such as double, triple, quadruple: which does not divide the smaller number by the larger, but takes it up and multiplies the whole, whether twice or thrice; and thus it proceeds infinitely by the mode of an infinitely multipliable number.

<margin>B</margin> The second they call <term>superparticular</term>, in which the larger number, besides containing the smaller once in its entirety, then divides it and places the divided part over the whole—but a part we call "aliquot," that is, one which, when replicated a certain number of times, makes the whole. The first of these is the <term>sesquialtera</term> <note>ratio of 3:2</note>, between two and three. For three, containing two, adds one besides, which when taken twice makes two. The second is the <term>sesquitertia</term> <note>ratio of 4:3</note>, between four and three, and so it proceeds to infinity by the mode of an infinitely divisible continuum.

<margin>C</margin> The third is the <term>superpartient</term>, which adds to the whole a part that, when taken a certain number of times, cannot properly create the whole, such as between five and three. For five, beyond three, adds two, which taken once does not fill three, and taken twice exceeds it. This proportion, because it divides the whole into a part unfit for the restoration of the whole, seems unfit for consonance; in consonance, every division into the whole and multiplication into one is necessarily restored. Secondly, it is judged fit because even if it divides, it does not stray from the ease of restoration, and in it the terms are judged to be mutually commensurable. For the difference between two and three is one, and this is the common measure of both. Taken twice, it measures two; taken thrice, it measures three. But between five and three the difference is two; this cannot, by being taken any number of times, measure either three or five in any way. 

The first proportion <note>Multiple</note> is most suited to concepts. For it does not divide, but restores by multiplying, and multiplies by restoring. Nor does it seek a measure from elsewhere, like the superparticular, but the smaller term is measured by the larger, 

<margin>D</margin> replicated twice in the double, thrice in the triple. It falls neither from integrity nor from simplicity. The superparticular, however, slips from integrity: for it divides; but it preserves simplicity, for it divides by one certain part. The superpartient not only loses integrity but also simplicity, where it mixes several parts into one thing unfit for the restoration of the whole. Therefore, this one is dissonant from consonance, but the two higher ones are consonant—the multiple more so, and the double most of all. Indeed, in the double, one thing does not properly seem to exceed another, but anything seems to be exceeded by itself. For in the double, two exceeds one by one. Four exceeds two by two, and so on. Add that it is 

<margin>E</margin> born between the first terms of numbers, namely unity and two. Born, I say, alone, without the commerce of others, as if free and absolute from all. The triple, however, while it arises between one and three, has as a companion the sesquialtera arising simultaneously between two and three. The quadruple also seems to be mixed with the sesquitertia. For when the quadruple is first born between four and one, the sesquitertia is born simultaneously between four and three. Likewise, the double arises most closely from the proportion of equality itself; from this, the triple and sesquialtera. Likewise, from the triple, the quadruple and sesquitertia are born, and others similarly. If I did not fear prolixity, I would demonstrate this clearly. To the double, therefore, as to a beginning and an end, all others are reduced; they either divide it or multiply it. For the double is first, whole, simple, absolute, 

<margin>F</margin> and most equal, so that it is no wonder the consonance born from it is the most perfect of all, and is called the <term>Diapason</term> <note>the Octave</note>, because it extends through all things, and all proportions are reduced to it. 

But before I pursue the consonances, we must be reminded that what the Greeks call *Logos*, we call ratio and proportion; and what they call *Analogia*, we call the comparison of ratio or the similarity of ratio and "proportionality"—a name truly as elegant as it is proper. A proportion occurs between two terms: and when it is done rightly, leading to melodies, it is defined as the mutual relationship of two mutually commensurable quantities, like the double between one and two, and the sesquialtera 

<margin>G</margin> between two and three, and so on. Proportionality, however, is defined as the mutual comparison of two proportions. As when we say: as two is to four, so four is to eight; namely, by a double ratio in both cases. This comparison, because it occurs between three terms, is called "continuous." It is "discrete," however, whenever it is made between more terms, as when we compare thus: as two is to four, so eight is to sixteen. 

Likewise, such comparison is threefold: namely, arithmetic, geometric, and harmonic. <term>Arithmetic</term> consists in the equality of number; thus between three and seven, five is the middle, exceeding one term by the same number—namely two—and being exceeded by the other, 

<margin>H</margin> by a bipartient proportion on both sides. <term>Geometric</term> is situated in the equality of ratio, in which there are multiple and superparticular: namely when we compare thus, as three is to nine, so nine is to twenty-seven; for it is triple on both sides. Likewise, what nine is next to six, the same is six next to four. For both here and there is the sesquialtera proportion. Finally, they place <term>harmonic proportion</term> in a certain similarity, through which, with three terms placed in order, as the greatest term looks at the minimum, similarly the difference between the greater terms looks at the difference of the smaller. For if you place three, four, six: the difference between six and four is two; the difference between four and three is one...

# MARSILIO FICINO

unity; just as there is a double ratio between six and three, so there is a double ratio between two and one. Another similarity of proportions also flourishes here. For the middle term exceeds and is exceeded by a similar portion of the extremes. For the number four is surpassed by six by a third part of six (which is two), and it surpasses three by a third part of three (which is one). <note>Ficino is describing harmonic proportion where the differences are proportional to the terms themselves.</note> In this, a harmonic skill is employed by both, which avoids "superpartient" proportions <note>term: superpartient (proportio superpartiens) — a ratio where the larger number contains the smaller plus more than one part of it, e.g., 5:3. These were considered dissonant.</note> as if they were scattered and dissonant, but admits "multiple" and "superparticular" ones, composing double ratios out of the *sesquialtera* <note>3:2 ratio</note> and *sesquitertia* <note>4:3 ratio</note>, rejoicing in a harmonious variety through the harmonic ratio we have described. Indeed, as we were saying, it loves multiple comparisons, as well as superparticular ones, for the further reason that in these there is such a tendency toward restoring the same value, that when several ratios of the same kind are composed together, the middle term multiplied by itself produces as much as the extremes if they are multiplied together. Set down two, four, eight: just as twice eight makes sixteen, so four times four makes sixteen. Likewise, set down four, six, nine: just as four times nine makes thirty-six, so six times six makes thirty-six. Similarly, if you place two means between the extremes—suppose between two and sixteen you place four and eight. All these numbers in succession are made by a double ratio. If you multiply two by sixteen, you will get the same result as if you multiplied four by eight. The same happens in other ratios, both superparticular and multiple. However, the same does not happen in superpartient ratios. Arrange three, five, seven. Just as from seven to five there is a "super-bi-partient" relationship <note>7:5 ratio</note>, so it is from five to three. For in both cases, two parts are added on top of the whole. If you multiply three by seven, you will not produce the same number as if you multiplied five by itself. Therefore, in the first rank are the multiples: because, besides what we just said, through them all numbers also look back to unity while they look at other numbers. In the second rank are the superparticulars: because even if they do not look at unity itself, they always look at one certain part fitted to a single whole. In the third are the superpartients: because they seem to look at neither of these. For this reason, the harmonic faculty hates this relationship as if it were resistant to concord. For it desires either to create a "univocal" and "unison" sound from the proportion of equality itself, or to forge an "equivocal" and "equisonant" sound from a rational—that is, multiple and superparticular—proportion of inequality. Indeed, it is established that such an equisonant sound from a double ratio is as close as possible to a unison: because in a double ratio, the smaller term measures the larger, and by measuring it, equals it; and where the larger surpasses the smaller, it seems to excel by no other number than the smaller one itself, so to speak.

### THAT IN MUSICAL CON-
### sonances one is made from many, by
### which consonance is defined.

-> CHAPTER XXX. <-

Just as the most skilled physicians mix certain juices together in a certain ratio, through which many and diverse materials unite into one new form, and beyond their elemental power they also miraculously obtain a celestial virtue—which is manifest in the concoction of Mithridates and the theriac of Andromachus <note>Famous ancient medicinal compounds used as universal antidotes.</note>—similarly, the most artistic musicians temper the deepest voices like cold materials, and the highest voices like hot ones, and again the moderately deep as moist, and the high as dry, with such reason that one single form is made from many, which beyond the vocal power also attains a celestial one. This clearly appears from what Democritus and Theophrastus say, and what Pythagoras proved by effect. For it is said that certain diseases of both body and soul are wonderfully cured by certain harmonies, so that it is no wonder the ancient sages traced the origin of both medicine and music to the same source, that is, the Apolline number. For both are medicine. But one cures the soul through the body, while the other cures the body through the soul. Most appropriately, they also attributed prophecy to Apollo, the fountain of melody. For melody alone withdraws the soul from all things by which it is distracted, and contracts it into itself into a certain—so to speak—interior hearing: by which not only voices, but the ratios of voices are perceived; and with disturbances calmed, it tempers the soul to celestial harmony and pours forth divine oracles from heaven. But lest anyone perhaps deny that a third and common vocal form is made from a high and low voice, one must consider that deep voices can be mixed with high ones more perfectly than juices are said to be mixed with juices. First, because vocal materials, on account of their subtlety, their continuous motion, and the uniform quality of the airy body in all things, are fused into one more easily and completely than juices, which are thick, less suited for motion, and greatly differing in qualities. If they are fused into one, they are therefore more aptly prepared to conceive one new form. Next, because the natural instrument of the voice is internal and most close and obedient to the vital, animal, and rational power; it obeys the musical art more perfectly and easily to create that one thing it aims for, than the internal instruments of physicians; and even if a kithara is plucked with fingers, the strings will follow the musician's wish more faithfully than herbs follow the physician's. And if nature acts upon a gathered mass of herbs beyond the industry and labor of physicians, and indeed at a certain time, much more does nature act suddenly upon vocal material, which is very manageable and formable: nature, I say, living everywhere and fortified with celestial powers in a material more similar to heaven

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> and as if living: to which it suddenly applies a new, living, and wonderful form, through which it may exercise its powers upon the body and soul by a hidden virtue. Therefore, just as in a body naturally constituted from the four elements, the qualities of the four elements create one—and as some call it, a fifth—complexion, namely one subject to a special virtue coming from heaven in hidden ways: so also many voices rightly mixed together resound and echo one another as the foundation of a new and wonderful virtue. For if from a sounding kithara something suddenly resounds in a similarly tuned kithara, and from a vibrated string a similar vibration immediately passes into a string stretched equally: who could doubt that from many voices fused by a certain ratio, one form is suddenly born <margin>B</margin> common to all, through which many are one, and therefore are perceived as one by the sense, and meet in one certain effect. For the same is established from the pleasure of the sense, in which since there is one form from many, a full delight arises from a similarly single form, which is harmoniously fashioned from many. Hence it happens that it becomes tedious to hear a unison for too long, in which equality is felt without any inequality. Furthermore, it happens that a dissonant sound offends, in which the differences do not conspire into one. Therefore, many things are clearly discerned by the sense, and are tasted by it, as it were, as many. I say "tasted," because the sense is affected by the mixture of voices almost as the taste is by the mixture of flavors. Hence that prophetic saying: *Thy words are sweeter than honey to my mouth, O Lord.* <note>Psalm 119:103</note> Finally, whether deep sounds absorb the high ones, <margin>C</margin> or high ones occupy the deep, no delight arises, and yet a certain union is required everywhere. Since union from either absorbing or occupying does not please, it remains that only that union pleases which results as something new and effective from a certain moderate consonance. From this, therefore, consonance is defined: a mixture of a deep and high sound reaching the ears uniformly and sweetly. Moreover, this mixture is similar to that which satisfies the taste in flavors: in which a flavor too sweet and fatty is judged similar to a very relaxed and deep voice; but a very sharp flavor to a very high one. But a sweet flavor mixed with sharpness represents a moderately deep voice. Mixed with saltiness or pungency, it seems to represent a moderately high one. And then finally <margin>D</margin> a manifold mixture fills the sense, when it is not discerned as multiform, but insinuates itself as uniform. Physicists teach that sound reaches the ears in a circular shape amplified step by step in many circles, not unlike the circles that multiply to the shore in a pond from a stone thrown from on high. But they think a harmony fused from deep and high sounds glides into the ears like one form, and this one round, but oval. In which indeed the eighth voice <note>The octave</note>, as if through a sharper peak, continuing the width of the first voice to itself, now fuses one voice out of itself and the first; and just as the eye sees an oval roundness as one figure, although wider here and less there: so the hearing drinks in the voice resulting from the deep and the octave as one, raising itself gradually and sweetly like an egg from a certain wide depth <margin>E</margin> into a high sublimity. Hence we think it happens that nature has granted such a figure to the instrument of hearing, and a similar one to the instrument of speaking, and art moreover has made musical instruments similar as far as possible. Certainly those are more consonant which are closer to an oval figure.

### WHICH CONSONANCES
### arise from which
### proportions.

-> CHAPTER XXXI. <-

<margin>F</margin> They say that Pythagoras, when he had noted among blacksmiths that consonance arises from the blows of hammers by the law of weights, collected the numbers in which the agreeing diversity of weights was contained. Then he stretched strings tied with weights as varied as he had learned were in the hammers: and from this he clearly considered that from a string which was stretched in a *sesquioctave* ratio <note>9:8 ratio</note> over another, a tone was discerned against the other—that is, a full and whole <margin>G</margin> sound, such as was the proportion of nine to eight. Nor could he divide the tone into two equal semitones, since the number nine could not be cut into two equal parts; but he found that one semitone was a little larger than half, and the other a little less than half, which he called the *Diesis*, and Plato called the *Limma*. How much the minor semitone falls short of a whole tone and a true semitone, Plato indicates in the interval of these numbers, namely between two hundred forty-three and two hundred fifty-six. For since the eighth part of that smaller number is thirty and nearly a half, but this larger number adds only thirteen over that smaller one, it yields neither a tone nor a whole semitone. <margin>H</margin> Then Pythagoras noticed that the whole and full width of a tone, so to speak, consists of two sounds and one interval; and thus he attained the first elements of consonance. Of these, the first is the *diapason* <note>The octave</note>, resulting from the first proportion, that is, the double; where namely this string, stretched twice as much by double weight over that one, while both were struck, returning itself to its straightness twice as vehemently and quickly, gave back a voice far higher in turn to the far deeper one, yet so friendly that it appeared as if it were a single sound, narrower here and wider there. Where the higher sound occurred, he measured it in modulation as being located at the eighth degree of height from the deep, counting the deep one itself.

<header>ARGUMENTS AND COMMENTARY</header>

<margin>A</margin> It consists of eight sounds and seven intervals, but roughly six whole tones. Furthermore, where the ratio of tension and relaxation between strings was <term>sesquitertia</term> <note>a 4:3 ratio</note>, he found the consonance of the <term>diatessaron</term> <note>a perfect fourth</note>, encompassing two whole tones and a minor semitone, four sounds, and three intervals. In the <term>sesquialtera</term> <note>a 3:2 ratio</note> he discovered the <term>diapente</term> <note>a perfect fifth</note>, and in this he perceived three tones and a minor semitone, five sounds, and four intervals. He then noticed that the <term>diapason</term> <note>an octave</note> is composed of the fourth and the fifth: because the double ratio <note>2:1</note> which produces the octave, when it has a middle term, is constituted from the 4:3 and 3:2 ratios from which those others are made. For the first double ratio having a middle term is 2 to 4, composed of the 3:2 ratio between 3 and 2, and the 4:3 ratio between 4 and 3. But in the triple relationship <note>3:1</note> he considered the octave-plus-fifth, having twelve sounds but eleven intervals. For the octave has its seat in the double ratio, but the fifth in the 3:2 ratio. And the 3:2 ratio continued from the double ratio produces the triple. For 6 against 3 is double. Add 9, from which the 3:2 ratio is born relative to 6, and you will immediately have the triple ratio from 9 to 3. However, a triple ratio is not made if you add a 4:3 ratio to a double, as if you joined 8 to that 6: for the <term>sesquioctave</term> <note>a 9:8 ratio, a whole tone</note> is missing, namely 9 to 8.

<margin>B</margin> And since a 4:3 ratio added to a double becomes a "superpartient" ratio, like 8 to 3 <note>an octave plus a fourth</note>—for this is a double ratio plus two-thirds—Pythagoras therefore forbade continuing suddenly from the double (the octave) through the 4:3 ratio (the fourth), although Ptolemy admits this subjunction in some places. But the 4:3 ratio is conveniently joined to the triple. From this comes the quadruple proportion, and through the quadruple consonance the <term>didiapason</term> <note>a double octave</note>, having fifteen sounds and fourteen intervals: for instance, if having placed the triple between 9 and 3 you join 12, which is in a 4:3 ratio against 9, you suddenly acquire the quadruple born from 12 to 3.

<margin>C</margin> But he forbids proceeding beyond the quadruple for the sake of melody, not only because violence reaches the senses from more vehement motion and breaking, but also because as soon as a quintuple ratio is born beyond the first quadruple between 5 and 4, there arises a "superbipertient" ratio between 5 and 3, which mixes in dissonance. But to return this side of the quadruple, he also forbids descending often below the 4:3 ratio to avoid sluggishness. He forbids continuing two 4:3 ratios often, both because they are otherwise displeasing and because they do not fill the double ratio or the octave. If you arrange 9, 12, 16, you have two 4:3 ratios, but by no means a double: for the 9:8 ratio is missing, namely 18 to 16, so that the double might be born from 18 to 9. Nor does he willingly continue doubled 3:2 ratios, for these being continuous exceed the double by a 9:8 ratio. Indeed, if you describe 4, 6, 9, you will be able to detect this. For here are two proximate 3:2 ratios from 4 to 9. But 9 exceeds 8 (which is double to 4) by a 9:8 portion. From this it appears that the power of the 3:2 ratio is greater than half of the double. From which it is also clear that the power of the 4:3 ratio is just as much less than half: since the double is created from both. Indeed, the 4:3 is surpassed by the 3:2 by a single 9:8 portion. For from 8 to 6 you have a 4:3 ratio, but from 9 to 6 you have a 3:2 ratio. But from 9 to 8 you have a 9:8 ratio: and by this very 9:8 part you understand the 4:3 is surpassed by the 3:2.

<margin>D</margin> One ought to remember that the <term>diatessaron</term>—that is, the comparison of four sounds ascending to a fourth height—is not approved when heard by itself, yet is willingly received because, with a tone easily added, it becomes the <term>diapente</term>, the most pleasing concord of the fifth voice. Likewise, because if it is connected with the fifth, it completes the octave, the most perfect of all. Nor should it disturb anyone that while we said the fourth has four sounds and the fifth has five, we say the octave composed of both has no more than eight sounds. For when we deal with composite consonances, we so arrange the strings joined together in <term>tetrachords</term> <note>four-string scales</note> and continue the sounds so that the last sound of the first consonance is the first of the second following in that composition. Hence the matter reminds us to return to the seven-stringed lyre of Terpander, in which the fourth string is struck twice, so that it somehow turns out to be an eight-stringed instrument. Terpander followed this joining, as I believe, because the multiplication of voices clearly differing among themselves is increased up to the seventh sound.

<margin>E</margin> But the eighth sound now returns to the first with a certain wonderful similarity, just as the double ratio through which it is created restores the smaller number which it exceeds, while it exceeds the same by the same amount. The ninth returns to the second, and is dissonant like the second. The tenth to the third, and is consonant like the third. The eleventh to the fourth. The twelfth to the fifth. The thirteenth to the sixth. But the fourteenth returns to the seventh. Finally, the fifteenth to the eighth, and together with the eighth to the first.

<margin>F</margin> They name the first and lowest sound <term>Hypate</term>. The following, <term>Parhypate</term>; the third, <term>Lichanos</term>; the fourth, <term>Mese</term>; the fifth, <term>Paramese</term> or <term>Trite</term>; the sixth, <term>Paranete</term>; and the seventh, <term>Nete</term>.

<margin>G</margin> Furthermore, if a comparison is made in quality and daily motion, we shall compare <term>Hypate</term> with Saturn, and the following with the following planets in order. But if in daily motion and its speed or slowness, we shall conversely compare <term>Hypate</term> with the Moon, and the following in turn with the higher planets. And we shall find low sounds in heaven mixed with high ones, and those same orbs by one motion produce a high tone, but by another a low one. Likewise, from huge globes come huge sounds, from divine ones divine, and from manifold revolutions, by equal reason, manifold sounds. And just as beyond the seventh sound a revolution happens back to the same, so above the seven distinct orbs of the planets, all things revolve into one orb, in itself wonderfully embracing such a

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> sevenfold nature. But of these things elsewhere. Let us return to the consonances, and now conclude them with a certain proper limit. These three were numbered among the ancients. The first is the Diatonic, in which any tetrachord proceeds through a minor semitone, and a tone, and a tone: which both other wise men and Plato especially approved above others, as being the most natural of all, since it proceeds from the minor semitone like soft matter in the manner of nature toward the stronger matter of the tone, and has a form that is simple, and at once gentle and robust. Add that it most fits the tetrachord, in which the fourth is procreated from two tones and a semitone. The second consonance is called Chromatic, which is accustomed to run through a minor semitone, a major semitone, and a <term>trihemitone</term> <note>a minor third</note>. But philosophers reject this as being too soft. The third is named Harmonic <note>Enharmonic</note>, progressing through a quarter of a semitone, <margin>B</margin> and again through a similar quarter and a <term>ditone</term> <note>a major third</note>. This too they do not approve because of the superstitious difficulty of its perception and use. Many things which we omit at present regarding these matters, we treat more diligently in the eighth book of our Letters.

# ON THE HARMONIC COMPOSITION OF THE SOUL.

## CHAPTER XXXII.

<margin>D</margin> God, about to procreate the Soul of the World, fashioned it from indivisible and divisible essence. This first division in Plato—namely into essence, indivisible property, and divisible—is most universal. For what he calls "indivisible" contains in itself that which is neither cut into part-beyond-part according to space, nor flows from earlier to later according to time. By the first it is called "the Same"; by the second, "Status" and "Stable." Similarly, what is called "divisible" embraces in itself both what is spread out in space and what glides in time. By the first it is called "the Other"; by the second, "Motion" and "Mobile"—motion, I say, in natural things. Therefore, under that division which said the soul was gathered from indivisible and divisible essence, five kinds of things are somehow contained: Essence, Sameness, Otherness, Stability, and Motion. But Plato, for the sake of brevity, does not repeat five, but three. For he repeats Essence, Sameness, and Otherness, as if they suffice. For Stability follows Sameness, and Motion follows Otherness. And conversely, Sameness follows Stability, and likewise Otherness follows Motion. <margin>E</margin> He says, moreover, that God fashioned one nature out of Essence, Sameness, and Otherness by such an exact mixing that in its essence, Sameness and Otherness were everywhere present; and conversely, in its Sameness, Otherness and Essence were present; and again, in its Otherness, Essence and Sameness lay hidden. For Essence through Sameness has the property of agreeing with itself and others; through Otherness, it is somehow distinguished in itself, and much more from the rest. Sameness and Otherness both obtain their existence from Essence. But Sameness possesses agreement from itself, and difference from Otherness. Otherness itself possesses difference from itself, but from Sameness it possesses both congruity and order. Plato thinks the heap of these kinds leads the soul both to judging all things and to performing them. <margin>F</margin> Truly, since it consists of Essence, it defines what each thing is; because of Sameness, it knows what is simple, and if composite, in what way it is joined as one, and how it consents with itself and others; because of Otherness, what diversity there is in anything, and by what condition it is either arranged in itself or separated from the rest; since from Stability, of what sort and in what way anything remains in itself; because it consists of Motion, it recognizes from what sort of thing each thing depends and by what reason, likewise what things it does and how. Furthermore, through Essence, it gives being to things; through Sameness, it joins things to itself and others; through Otherness, it separates them; through Stability, it confirms them in their own nature and order; through Motion, it moves them, and causes them to be moved and to act. Wherefore, not without merit, Plato in fabricating the soul mixes the kinds of all things by a certain fixed reason. He says these are mixed with each other by a harmonic ratio, not an arithmetic one—otherwise the distribution would be unjust somewhere—nor by geometric proportion alone, otherwise there would be such equality in the mixture that it could not conspire closely with the extreme diversity of bodies. But a harmonic ratio, consisting of the similarity of various things, connects both dissimilar things as similar, and unequal things by a certain common equality. Such is the quality and office of the soul, both toward itself and toward bodies. For whether it acts with itself, its intelligence (so to speak) mixes a certain otherness with identity, just as it mixes a certain identity with the otherness of reason. It does similarly in imagination and sense. Whether it acts upon the body, it produces the otherness of motion in a certain stable order as if by identity: which appears in the heavens, and likewise below the heavens in the very otherness of generation, it preserves identity through continued order: and in both places it preserves and restores essence. <margin>H</margin> Wherefore God, composing the Soul of the World, uses harmonic ratio, both in mixing the kinds of things with each other, and in the portions themselves which he took from them to compose the soul, and in the powers of the soul immediately accompanying its origin, and in the spheres of the world corresponding to the soul. That such a mixture befits the soul Plato not only searched out by reasons, but also carefully inaugurated from conjectures taken from the world. For when he contemplated the body of the world, placed under the soul, made for its sake, and ruled by it, he judged it consistent with nature that we might conjecture a certain form of its soul as if from an exemplar, from the figure of the world as an image.
