# MARSILIO FICINO

Therefore, by whatever proportions he observed the spheres of the world to be composed, arranged, and moved, he divined that its soul was tempered by those same, that is, harmonic ratios: so that just as among musicians a harmony flows skillfully from the mind, and harmony into the voice, so from the harmony of the celestial soul, harmony passes into the world. But let us now hear Plato himself. *In the beginning, he took one portion from the whole. Then a second, double the first part. Then a third, which was one-and-a-half times <note>original: "sesquialtera"</note> the second, but triple the first. Afterward a fourth, double the second. Then a fifth, triple the third. A sixth, eight times the first. Finally a seventh, which exceeded the first by twenty-six parts.* These are his words. Let us therefore establish a triangle at whose apex unity <note>the number 1</note> is placed; from there let numbers flow on both sides, here the even, there similarly the odd: in this manner, namely, that on one side after unity comes first two, then four, finally eight; on the other side under unity similarly first three, then nine, finally twenty-seven. Thus the first portion which God took from the very "leaven" of the genres (so to speak) to fashion the soul, is unity. The second is the number two, double the first. The third is the number three, whose ratio is triple the first (that is, unity), but one-and-a-half times the second (that is, two). The fourth portion is four, double the second (that is, two). The fifth is nine, whose ratio is triple the third (that is, three). The sixth is eight, whose proportion is eightfold to the first (that is, unity). The seventh is twenty-seven, a ratio indeed triple to nine, but exceeding unity by twenty-six parts. In these numbers, certainly, he includes all harmonic ratios. For in the "sesquioctave" <note>9:8 ratio</note> proportion between nine and eight, he brought forth the **Tone** obeying the nine Muses. In the "sesquialtera" <note>3:2 ratio</note> between three and two, the **Fifth** <note>Diapente</note>, the Venus-like grace of the voice. In the "sesquitertia" <note>4:3 ratio</note> between four and three, the **Fourth** <note>Diatessaron</note>, the Mercurial nature of the voice, adapting itself to the columns. In the double ratio, between two and one, likewise between four and two, and again between eight and four, he gave birth to the **Octave** <note>Diapason</note>, that is, the universal and absolute melody of the eighth voice dedicated to Apollo. In the triple ratio between three and one, likewise nine and three, and again twenty-seven and nine, he composed the **Twelfth** <note>Diapason Diapente</note>, that is, a long-lasting symphony of the octave and fifth together. In the quadruple ratio between four and one, and eight and two, he wove the symphony of the **Double Octave** <note>Disdiapason</note>, again sounding fifteen notes in harmony for Apollo. Beauty, indeed, he inserted into the beginnings of the third voice through the Fourth, then subjoined the Fifth to the ends of the sixth voice: so that by the more delicate softness of each voice, the harshness of the second voice on one side, and the seventh on the other, might be softened. For thus the third and sixth voices are similar in softness, just as the second falling from the first, and the seventh degenerating from the eighth, are very similar in harshness. In the beginning where he says God took seven portions, he touched upon a mystery, both in music and also in nature. In music indeed: because every discrepancy of voices proceeds up to the seventh degree, after which there is a return to the same. In nature truly, both because many things are completed through the number seven <note>the septenary</note> in natural affairs (about which the other Platonists have said enough), and because the septenary possesses unity as a bond of a twin trinity; and from these twins and itself, it again unfolds a trinity. Such indeed is the likeness of the universe. For it is distributed into three in the beginning. Whence Plato here commended the number three. It is distributed, I say, into eternal and temporal things, and the mediums between them. Eternal things, under the property of the trinity, possess simplicity in essence, stability in power, and reflection in action. Temporal things in turn have a composition of essence in a triple dimension, mobility of power, and finally a transition of action. Between these trinities of eternal and temporal things, the soul, holding the middle, creates the seventh degree. It also creates the ninth, here also praised by Plato. Ninth, I say, because it has three faces: for it is turned toward itself, toward higher things, and toward lower things. It is helpful here, before I return to the septenary, to commend the number three together with the number nine for a little while longer. The first trinity of numbers seems to contain the beginning, middle, and end of things, and alone among numbers to contain them by a certain indivisible reason. Indeed, it signifies each of these by individual Unities. Furthermore, whether you wish to run through the causes of things, you will find a triple property in the causes. Or if you descend to consider the effects, you will similarly discover a trinity. For effects are in their causes, they proceed from them, and they are turned back toward them. Or if you turn to the soul, which connects sublime causes with the lowest effects, you will see it remaining in itself, declining toward effects, and ascending toward causes. And yet this soul rules the world by a triple septenary. First, indeed, by certain hidden seven powers of the planets dominating in the firmament through causes. Second, by the seven forms of the planets, in the seven globes subject to the firmament. Third, by the seven gifts of the planets, ruling generation under the Moon. For since under the Moon, in fire, a life-giving light is subjected to the Sun, but burning heat to Mars; on earth, the varied surface to Mercury, but the whole mass to Saturn. But in the middle regions moisture reigns, and the Airy moisture obeys Jupiter, the Watery obeys the Moon, and finally the Mixed obeys Venus. Likewise, acting causes follow the Sun, Materials follow the Moon: the Fecundity of acting causes follows Jupiter: the Fecundity of materials follows Venus: swift dispatch to the effect follows Mars and Mercury—the former because of vehemence, the latter because of dexterity and multiform virtue. But the permanent continuation of all is dedicated most of all to Saturn. Moreover, this order proceeds through three septenaries from the septenaries which are distributed according to the three powers of the world soul. For in this intelligence there is a stable circle. A circle indeed, because it is reflected back to where it came from; Stable, because suddenly under the intelligence, as if under a firmament, there are three powers, namely universal reason, imagination, and vegetation. In reason there are three circles that are in a way mobile and tempo-

<column-break/>

ral. <margin>A</margin> The first is from the soul to the loving cause, and back again, by a certain natural instinct secretly carrying it so. The second is from the causes of things to the consideration of effects, and vice versa. The third is from the more universal forms and ideas to the less universal descents and back again. In the remaining two powers of the soul, there are altogether four circles, similarly temporal: two in each. The first is a natural reflection toward its cause. The second is a certain and perpetual revolution from the same forms to the same at certain intervals, through which both the temporal and certain revolution of configurations in heaven and of transformations under heaven proceeds. Therefore, the circuit of generation necessarily follows the circuit of heaven, and this in turn follows the circuit of the soul. The revolution of the soul accompanies the sphere of intelligence. Indeed, the motion of the soul, if it were carried entirely away from intelligence, would immediately—both in perceiving and in acting—pass only <margin>B</margin> in a straight line. But because it repeats itself and gathers similar cycles through other things, it obtains this from a certain superior intellect, which, both remaining in itself and suddenly turned toward its cause, grants intelligence to the soul; through this, as if by an extended hand, it halts the soul which is by its own nature wandering and restless in motion, and pulls back into a circle—midway between straight motion and rest—that which is naturally more prone to a straight line outside itself. Hence the soul travels to return into itself, circles the "deep mind," and connects the heaven with a similar image. But concerning these things, more diffusely in the *Theology*. Let us return to numbers. <margin>C</margin>

## THE SUM OF THE HARMONIC
## numbers conducive to the
## composition of the Soul.

### CHAPTER XXXIII.

<margin>D</margin> Unity in the figure above signifies the unity of the soul itself, its sublime simplicity, and the proper image of divine unity, remaining in itself. Duality signifies the process of the soul into its own property lower than unity, and already in a certain way multiple. Trinity is its return to unity, both its own and the divine. Quaternity <note>the number 4</note> is the progression of the soul from itself into matter, to be arranged by the degrees of the four elements. The Septenary <note>7</note> is its power to rule the elements through the seven spheres of the planets. The Octonary <note>8</note> is the force that will govern the planets through the eighth sphere. The Novenary <note>9</note> is the office of the soul to reconcile the eight spheres into one form. The sum of twenty-seven numbers is its fullness, which will collect all things in all. For the sum of twenty-seven <margin>E</margin> contains the aforementioned numbers, and is filled by them placed in order, as is evident to one calculating. Nor are the even and odd numbers described in the figure without reason, so that through the even numbers the divisible nature of the soul may be considered, and through the odd, the indivisible—at once a feminine and masculine power. Linear, superficial, and solid numbers are also collected, so that we may know the soul penetrates through all things, and is amplified everywhere and fills things most inwardly. Each side of the figure descends to a solid number on both sides. Here indeed to eight among the even numbers, there indeed among the odd to twenty-seven. So that we may think the soul fills both solids, namely the composite as well as the simple, entirely. But what the double and triple intervals of the numbers and the rest which we said before properly mean in the soul, even if it is <margin>F</margin> still unknown among the Platonists, it is nevertheless permitted for the present perhaps to prophesy in this manner, so to speak. Let a triangle be described again, at the summit of which is **Essence**. On the side where the odd numbers were described, let **Infinity** be designated, and then **Otherness** and **Motion**. But on the side where the even numbers were arranged, let there be **Limit**, then let **Identity** follow in order, and **Station** <note>Rest</note>. Here we will similarly have seven boundaries, of which the soul can perhaps be imagined a participant under the same ratio to each other, under which the boundaries of numbers described from the beginning look to each other; so that the soul, by such a proportion, participates in the five genera of things as well as the two elements of the genera, that is, limit and infinity. Let, for example, the <margin>G</margin> comparison of essence to all things joined together be "sesquioctave" <note>9:8</note>. For the common form of the whole exceeds the proper qualities of the parts by at least one degree, as if by a tone. Let Infinity be under essence, that is, a formable aptitude. Let Limit accompany this, like its form. And let the proportion of limit to infinity be double. For the power of acting <note>act</note> ought to overcome the potential for suffering <note>potency</note>. Let Otherness follow infinity, but let Identity accompany limit. And let this identity itself overcome otherness by a "sesquialtera" <note>3:2</note> ratio. After these, let Motion follow otherness, and Station follow identity, and let station overcome motion by a "sesquitertia" <note>4:3</note> proportion. This is what Plato signified, saying these are scarcely overcome by those. But if you consider the proportions explained here, you will find in addition triples and quadruples, <margin>H</margin> just as was evident from the beginning in the figure. For you will find Motion to be triple in relation to Infinity, and Station to be quadruple to the same. Moreover, so that we may be able to devise a harmonic proportion of participation in the soul, not only according to the five genera of things and two elements, but also according to its own powers distributed in seven degrees, let us now assign the individual powers of the soul to individual genera or elements. These powers are: Unity, Intelligence, Will, Reason, Imagination, the power of connecting, and the power of generating. These last two powers we often embrace under the single name of either Nature or Vegetation. Let us compare them in this way: namely, the Unity of the soul to Essence; Will to Infinity; Intelligence to Limit; Ima-

# ARGUMENTS AND COMMENTARY

<margin>A</margin> Let us devise proportions for the soul similar to those of the higher realms: assigning imagination to "otherness," reason to "identity," the power of generation to "motion," and the virtue of connecting to "rest." But if we have said elsewhere that the proportions of things in the soul are equal, we wish it to be understood not as an arithmetic parity, but as a harmonic equality.

### THROUGH THE INTERVALS OF THE SPHERES
#### Plato hunts for the intervals of ratios
#### between the parts of the soul.

### CHAPTER XXXIV.

<margin>C</margin> Just as we often infer the features of a living form from the lines of a portrait, so from this imaginary face of the celestial soul, which we behold in the reflecting matter of the world, we conjecture its true face to the best of our ability. Therefore, the double, triple, and other intervals described in the first figure of numbers, which Plato judged to be found in the spheres, he traced back to the parts and powers of the soul, from whence they were transferred into the spheres. For he thought that as much space as exists from the earth to the moon, double that extends from the earth to the sun; and as much as from the earth to the sun, triple that is from the same to Venus. Again, as much as from the earth to Venus, four times that much from the same to Mercury. Likewise, as much as to the star of Mercury from the earth itself, nine times that much from the earth to Mars. And as much as from the earth to Mars, eight times that much from the earth to Jupiter. And as much as it is from the earth to Jupiter, twenty-seven times that much from the earth to the circuit of Saturn. Here, among other things, you see the heavier planets, Jupiter and Saturn, designated on both sides by solid numbers <note>Solid numbers refer to cubic numbers, like 8 ($2^3$) and 27 ($3^3$)</note>. And if elsewhere I have reviewed other <margin>D</margin> measurements of intervals according to the opinion of certain Pythagoreans, I nevertheless consider the Platonic ones more probable. Through these things, perhaps, those matters which are more obscurely involved concerning the spheres in the tenth book of the *Republic* can be understood. Likewise, through those things which we have treated concerning the power of numbers and proportions, those things can be conjectured which are entangled in the eighth book of the *Republic* concerning the celestial circuit, numbers, and proportions.

---

### HOW THE INTERVALS OF DOUBLE
#### and triple numbers
#### are filled.

### CHAPTER XXXV.

<margin>G</margin> After Plato devised the first figure containing seven limits, in which the double and triple ratios are comprised, he then orders a second figure to be formed, filling it with numbers so much larger that where the doubles are filled by *sesquitertians* <note>A ratio of 4:3</note> and *sesquialters* <note>A ratio of 3:2</note>, these means are also filled by *sesquioctaves* <note>A ratio of 9:8, representing a whole tone</note>, so that the spaces of the sesquitertians contain a tone. Let us therefore describe a figure similar to the first, but let us place a six at the apex, after which we place its double, twelve, in the space below, and let us occupy that space with both an eight and a nine. Then, in a similar long space, let us describe twenty-four after twelve, and in this very space place sixteen and eighteen; in the same order between twenty-four and forty-eight, inserting thirty-two and thirty-six as means. Thus far we have completed the side of the doubles. Next, we shall use the space of the triples, setting eighteen (the triple of six) apart from the six, and let us designate nine and twelve between them. Similarly, between eighteen and fifty-four (its triple), let us place twenty-seven and thirty-six. Finally, from fifty-four to its triple, one hundred sixty-two, we would proceed through means in the same way, namely eighty-one and one hundred and eight. So that we may return to the double relationship of this first figure, let us consider the two means between six and twelve, namely eight and nine. And indeed, the eight holds itself in a harmonic ratio between six and twelve. For it exceeds six by a third part of six (two), and it is exceeded by twelve by a third part of twelve (four). Likewise, to six it is a sesquitertian (4:3), but twelve to it is a sesquialter (3:2). Furthermore, the difference between twelve and eight is four. But the difference between eight and six is two. Thus, four is to two as twelve is to six, containing a double ratio. In these things, as we have said, harmonic skill is employed. Let us also compare nine to six by a sesquialter quality (3:2), and to twelve by a sesquitertian quality (4:3), and to eight by a sesquioctave property (9:8), <margin>H</margin> which sounds as a tone: we shall surely understand that by this very sesquioctave two sesquitertians are linked, that is, eight to six and nine to twelve. Nor is an arithmetic mean lacking in these numbers: since nine exceeds six by three, and is likewise exceeded by twelve by three. Similarly, let us proceed through these same ratios in the following doubles, linking the doubles through sesquitertians and sesquialters: likewise connecting twin sesquitertians by a sesquioctave proportion. In almost the same way, except for the tone, one may run through the triples. Because sesquitertian ratios are made not only from two tones, but also from a semitone—and a minor one at that, which lacks a certain small part to be a full semitone—therefore Plato says that in the sesquitertians a certain small portion was left behind. But what this

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> figure, explained through larger numbers, means in the soul does not yet seem sufficiently explained by the Platonists, nor shall we explain it at present: unless perhaps, while he places several or at least two means between the extreme terms, he wishes it to be understood that the kinds of things and elements in the soul, which regard each other in an opposite way, return two qualities to one another. As if where a limit touches infinity, it brings back the quality of the limit to the infinite; and conversely, where it touches the limit with the infinite, it undergoes a determined passion of infinity. Moreover, let there be in the limit a certain terminal infinity, and conversely in infinity itself a limit proceeding indefinitely. Added to <margin>B</margin> these is the fact that such means can be thought of even among the powers of the soul itself, and the soul, according to its own exemplar in the world, is accustomed to insert at least two means between those things which are far apart. A "tone" signifies the full motion and pulse of the soul both in itself and in heaven. But a "semitone" signifies a remission in the elements, falling away from the first to such an extent that it receives a portion smaller than half of its perfection. Finally, this whole superior treatise on harmony seems to signify a triple concord: namely, between the soul and the body, between the parts of the soul with each other, and between the parts of the body with each other.

---

### THE DIVISION OF THE SOUL, MOTION,
#### and time.

### CHAPTER XXXVI.

<margin>E</margin> When he says that the very mixture of the kinds was consumed in the completion of the soul, he understands that the soul proceeded perfect from God, so that it nearly filled its own Idea. Furthermore, the division lengthwise shows that the soul's own motion is naturally straight, namely into sense and the nature of vegetating or moving. Likewise, he cuts it into two for this reason: to show both that there is a double straight motion in the soul (for sensing and for moving), and that there is a similar twin motion from the soul in the body (uniform and multiform). He intersects two lines to figure the soul, then bends them into a circle, indicating that the nature of the soul, though more inclined by itself to straight motion, is thoroughly adapted to circular motion by God himself through the gift of intelligence: in twin circles, I say—namely, the non-wandering firmament, and after the firmament, the orbits of the wandering planets. The circuit of the firmament properly reflects the nature of identity and intelligence itself. But the manifold windings of the planets properly represent the nature of "otherness" and the lower parts of the soul. But from the internal motion of the mind itself and from time, time in the world follows along with motion. Among these things he touches on a few common points pertaining to Astronomy; but anyone even moderately learned easily understands these, and certain Platonists, both Greek and Latin, treat these at excessive length. Soon the question arises concerning the Ideas and the kinds of worldly animals, which we have treated very extensively in our *Theology*. Furthermore, what he recounts concerning the genealogy of certain gods <margin>F</margin> and demons, and what likelihood it holds, is declared similarly in the *Theology* and elsewhere.

---

### THINGS MADE DIRECTLY BY GOD
#### and those made through intermediaries.

### CHAPTER XXXVII.

<margin>H</margin> Thus far it can be clear to anyone that the Architect of the world produced from the divine intellect the souls, the worldly gods, the demons, all the spheres of the world, and the very species of things without intermediate causes. However, we have related from the beginning the ambiguity that exists among Platonists concerning primary matter. Therefore, the Architect of the world thereafter commands his sons—that is, the souls of the spheres and stars and demons, or even the lower angels—that in imitation of him, they should undertake the mixing of things beneath the moon, and subject all things to man, and reconcile his rational soul (received from God himself) to the falling body through a certain irrational life, depending partly on them and partly on the mind of man. You will note, moreover, in the very words of God, that whatever is made directly by God is eternal; and whatever is composed by any reasoning is, insofar as it is composed, also dissoluble. But insofar as certain composite things are so fused by the divine will that unity overcomes multitude in them, they are preserved undissolved. You will note further, where he says that God remains in his own state while he commands, but the ministers follow, that there is no mutability in God while he rules and moves mobile things; but in his ministers, providence is closer to a certain change. Finally, in all these things, you will recognize that Mosaic saying, *I am who I am*, to be wonderfully confirmed.

---

### CONCERNING MAN AS PERTAINS
#### to the soul and the body.

### CHAPTER XXXVIII.

He says that the rational soul of man was mixed by God from the same kinds of things in the same mixing bowl as the soul of the world...

# MARSILIO FICINO

fused together. The "Mixing Bowl" <note>original: *Crater*</note> signifies the very power of the rational Idea. But he adds that it was fashioned from the remnants of the previous mixture, signifying that particular lives are lower than the universal life. Then indeed, God matches the souls—that is, the individual orders of souls—to individual stars. He also provides vehicles, which are ethereal bodies. He teaches the laws of fate while infusing the souls with the formulas of the Ideas, through which the souls, when they eventually turn back toward themselves, can recognize the reasons of things. What he says regarding the fated descent and circuit of the soul has been explained elsewhere. After these things, the ministers of God <note>The "lesser gods" or celestial spirits in Plato's cosmology</note> proceed with the construction of the human body, connecting it with hidden bonds. By these hidden bonds, understand that the temperament of man is so balanced and so similar to heaven that an excess of elemental qualities is scarcely apparent in it. He then adds that the circuits of the soul are impeded by the mass of the body. Here, remember above all else that our soul was woven with a logic similar to that of the soul of the world and possesses similar circuits. Therefore, he says the circuit of the intelligence is impeded, and the circuit of reason is distracted, for two chief reasons: first, because before the body is mature, the whole soul is occupied in the construction of the body; and second, because things that move the senses from the outside strike more vehemently in a tender age, and because of the novelty of things, they make the soul full of wonder regarding bodily matters. For these reasons, the soul is for a long time vacant of intelligence and divine duty, and the rational discourse itself, distracted by lower things, is disturbed and deceived as if insane. Thus, the whole mind undergoes a perverse transformation and leads a laborious life while reason yields to the senses, just as if someone were to fix their head to the ground instead of their feet, and lift their feet high in place of their head. Now, what he brings forward concerning the disposition of the limbs of the body is sufficiently discussed by physicians. Among these things, you will especially observe that the head is called not only the principal part, but even the "whole" in the body; for the rest were added only to serve the head. From this, you may gather that man was born for the sake of contemplation. Next follows the instruments of the senses. What is said among these regarding sight is sufficiently explained by Chalcidius <note>A 4th-century commentator on the Timaeus</note>, and what is said regarding dreams is sufficiently explained by us elsewhere. You will soon consider the firm opinion of our Plato concerning causes: that bodily things and qualities, which are not moved by themselves but rather by some incorporeal cause and are directed toward an end, are not truly to be called "causes," but rather instruments of a hidden Providence. The principal cause is the will of Providence, disposing all things according to its own model so that it judges and decrees what is best. Therefore, Plato asserts that the final cause prescribed in Providence is the highest of causes. Then he confirms again that man was born to contemplate heavenly things—indeed, to imitate the Mover of heaven itself according to his strength. And just as he had said of sight, so also hearing was granted to us for the sake of contemplation and learning: likewise, so that through sensible harmony we might also compose the movements of the soul harmoniously. Other senses besides sight and hearing he considers of no account, as they contribute less to speculation.

# HOW THE WORLD IS
->composed of Mind and Necessity.<-
->CHAPTER XXXIX.<-

After he has treated the formal order of the world, which he calls "Intellect" because it is the image of divine intelligence, he now treats the matter of the world. This he names "Necessity" because it was introduced not for its own sake, but as necessary for the ultimate forms. Likewise, because the world, on account of its admixture, necessarily suffers something of deformity. Hence the saying: "The world is composed of Intellect and Necessity"; it exists from the very order of forms and from matter. We can furthermore understand under the name of Necessity not only matter, but also the soul in its first procession: considered by the sign of its own nature as if it were formless matter. For both, the soul as well as matter, are indeed formless in the first sign of their origin, but are easily formable through the gift of intelligence. Whence the reasons and seeds of natural forms are infused into the soul itself, and qualities and forms into matter. Moreover, when he says that before the arrangement of the world the elements existed in a certain way, understand certain powers of the elements—both the formative powers in the soul and the formable ones in matter. Likewise, when he says that matter before the world was tossed about without order, interpret this to mean that the moving power of the soul, even before the gifts of intelligence, could agitate matter, but far from any order. Furthermore, where he says the world was adorned by God after Necessity had been "persuaded," take it this way: that the first nature of matter and soul, although thought of as formless, nevertheless received from the beginning a preparation from God toward forms so "formable" that it could not have been more ready. Among these things, that distinction must be observed by which it is said that the universe was divided into two at the beginning of the book—that is, the Model and the Image—but now it must be distinguished into three: the Model, the Image, and Matter. Here it may first seem that the Model of the world, its efficient cause, and its final cause are in reality the same thing. Secondly, that the whole order of the world is not so much a substantial thing as it is an image of the invisible world. Furthermore, because he separated matter from Mind above, and here separates it from the image of Mind, we can conjecture that matter proceeds from God not so much through its own Idea as through the Idea of form; and not by a preceding purpose, but in a certain sense as a consequence, "invented" (so to speak) by intelligence. Then indeed, he diligently shows that matter exists, what it is, and how it behaves, from the perpetual transmutation of forms; from which he also argues that material

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>forms are in a certain sense false. Then through them, he ascends to the true and ideal forms, all of which are more clearly declared in our *Theology* <note>Referring to Ficino's *Platonic Theology*</note>. He brought forward many names for matter, namely: the invisible species, the formless Womb capable of all forms, Nature, Power, Mother of the world, Nurse of forms, Subject, Receptacle, and Place. But regarding this name "Place," one may laugh at the Peripatetic <note>Followers of Aristotle</note> who is so inept—or rather malevolent—as to suggest that Plato was out of his mind, as if he wanted matter to be "place" in a strictly mathematical sense. This is most evidently refuted by the other names for matter. Finally, from the fact that matter claims formlessness for itself, argue that it likewise claims unity. For if it is formless, it is therefore also indistinct. If so, it is therefore one. Yet from that same formlessness, he judges it not to be "one" in the sense of being, but rather through it, it falls away from being. Since, therefore, "one" and "being" do not equally apply to matter, they <margin>B</margin>cannot be the same thing among themselves. However, the "One" is higher than "Being," since it pours itself out more widely; especially since the "One" applies even to privation, to which "Being" does not apply. From this again, we argue that matter can be produced only by the highest principle of things.

# HOW PHYSICS
->consists of mathematics, and concerning elements and mixtures.<-
->CHAPTER XL.<-

<margin>C</margin>Next, intending to prove Physics through mathematics, he first praises the doctrine of mathematicians as the way to all noble learning. It would be long, Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo de' Medici, Ficino's patron</note>, to recount at present how many in our times, having entered the mathematical way, have reached their desired goal. We know that Pierleone Leoni of Spoleto <note>A famous physician and philosopher</note>, chiefly by the benefit of mathematics, has penetrated not only Aristotelian but also Platonic meanings. <margin>D</margin>In Florence, indeed, we know that Leon Battista Alberti <note>The famous Renaissance architect and polymath</note>, beginning from these same disciplines, published a most beautiful work on architecture. What shall I say of our Francesco Berlinghieri, son of Niccolò? Did he not, relying on the benefit of mathematics, write excellently on Cosmography in verse? Let it trouble no one that Plato, after the manner of the Pythagoreans, seems to compose physics out of mathematics. For he does not wish it to be understood that natural bodies are composed of figures and numbers as if from elements and parts, but rather as if from limits, by way of resolution: namely, that natural things are resolved into those as if into prior things and limits. Are not the dimensions and figures the limits of bodies? And are not numbers the limits of figures? Furthermore, a natural species requires not only a common subject, but a specific one. <margin>E</margin>A common subject suffices for figures. But numbers require neither a specific nor a common subject, nor any bodily foundation at all. From this, it is clear that figures are prior to natural species, and numbers are prior to figures. Therefore, Pythagoras and Plato conceived a triple order in things: of species, of figures, and of numbers. Similarly, a triple order among the Ideas, so that both in things and in Ideas, species are resolved into figures, and figures into numbers; and certain species correspond to certain figures, and certain figures to certain numbers in a certain way, the order of things so requiring. For this reason, when they say the species of fire is constituted from a pyramidal figure, and the solid pyramid from four <margin>F</margin>triangles, and these from the number four or three, they wish to signify that a certain property is very similar in all these commonly, and these are to be compared among themselves rather than literally composed. In this way, he attributed the pyramidal figure to fire. To air, a figure having eight faces, which he calls the Octahedron. To water, one having twenty faces, which he calls the Icosahedron. To earth, one having six faces, by the name of Cube or Die. Finally, to the Universe, one possessing twelve faces <note>The Dodecahedron</note>. And he wants the pyramidal figure to suit fire because it is thin, and more apt for cutting than the others, and constituted of fewer triangles; therefore, it is the lightest of all figures. <margin>G</margin>But the cubic figure belongs to earth because it is the most solid and stable. Other figures belong to the middle elements, since they stand in a middle way between fire and earth regarding motion and rest. The Dodecahedron, which has twelve faces, he thinks fits the world because of the twelve spheres and the twelve signs in the Zodiac. Moreover, he resolves solids into planes, and planes into triangles, especially into those called right-angled. One of these is the Scalene—that is, "stair-like"—possessing all unequal sides. The other is the Isosceles—that is, "equal-legged"—having two equal sides. For the equilateral triangle, in which there is neither a right angle nor a perpendicular line, he considers less apt for composing planes. He constituted the pyramidal, octahedron, and icosahedron masses from Scalenes; since a pyramid is constituted of four equilateral triangles, each of which is divided into six Scalene triangles. The Octahedron figure is from eight similar ones, each of which is similarly distributed into six Scalene triangles. <margin>H</margin>The Icosahedron figure is from twenty similar ones, each of which similarly turns into six Scalenes. However, the Isosceles triangle is called the element of the cubic figure. For four Isosceles triangles coming together complete a quadrangle. From six such quadrangles, a Cube is made. Finally, he matched the Dodecahedron figure to the world, as I was saying, because the twelve forms of the stars are seen in the Zodiac, each of which is cut into thirty parts. Similarly, in the dodecahedron figure, one may look upon twelve pentagons, individually divided into five equilateral triangles, so that each one again consists of six Scalene triangles.

# ARGUMENTS AND COMMENTARY

be completed, and in the entire mass of the dodecahedron <note>A twelve-sided solid, which Plato associates with the shape of the entire universe.</note> three hundred and sixty triangles are found, which is the same number of portions as exist in the Zodiac. Next, he treats the motions and passions of the elements. Likewise, in what way they are distinguished into parts, mixed together, and what effects they produce through mixing. Furthermore, he discusses the mutual transformation of both elements and mixtures. Among these, he treats imperfect mixtures and perfect ones: liquids, stones, and metals. But almost all these things are shrouded in obscure metaphors in the **Pythagorean** fashion; however, we believe that **Plato** handed these down to his students in clearer words, and that **Aristotle**, above all others, committed the same things to writing more manifesty. Therefore, an interpretation of all these matters should be sought from Aristotle’s books *On Generation and Corruption* and *Meteorology*. Moreover, he treats the passions <note>In this context, "passions" refers to "affections" or "sensory inputs" received by the body.</note> which are brought upon the senses of animals by the elements. I speak of passions both hidden and manifest. Concerning the types of pleasure and pain, which are clearly declared in the *Philebus* and in our own book *On Pleasure*. He treats, furthermore, the senses themselves and their objects. He distinguishes tastes, smells, sounds, and colors.

# AGAIN CONCERNING MAN
## regarding the soul and the body.
### CHAPTER XLI.

<margin>C</margin>
It is worthy of consideration how much our **Plato** admonishes us that effort must be given to knowing ourselves to the best of our strength, and that we should remember that all things below the moon were subjected to us by God, lest we, contrary to our dignity, should in turn subject ourselves to inferior things. For in the very beginning of the entire discussion, it was decreed that the universe be treated right up to the birth of man himself. Again, in the middle of the course of the discussion, the gods are commanded by the Father <note>The Demiurge or Creator.</note> to adorn man, the master of animals, whom He wishes to be according to His image and likeness and to be in command. Then, after a few intervening points, he returns to man. Finally, near the end, he resumes what had been instituted at first: namely, that the universe was to be treated up to the birth of man. And in all things, in the **Mosaic** fashion <note>Referring to the Book of Genesis, suggesting Plato's account mirrors the biblical creation story.</note>, it is proved that man is both proposed first in this divine workmanship and made last as the final goal. Therefore, now, omitting other things, he repeats the divine mandate in the generating of man, and the obedience of the divine ministers in finishing this task; nor indeed is this done without justice. For he had predicted that man alone on earth would worship justice and the gods above; so that it is most consistent with reason that the gods diligently cultivated the birth of man. But leaving these things aside, let us explain what follows. Again, the irrational soul is treated, established not directly by God, but through subsequent and mobile causes, which is subject to the rational soul sent down from heaven by God. The **Platonists** think the irrational soul is not so much something substantial as something accidental, like a trace of rational souls, in which there are indeed senses, but divided and passive through the various instruments of the body. However, they place a "common sense" within the soul of rational substance—simple and impassible—which does not properly receive the passions inflicted by bodies like the other sense does, but perceives, or rather judges, the passions of the other sense. Accordingly, they prove that the substance of the rational soul is undivided and self-subsisting, not entrusted to the head as if to a support, but accommodated to it as if to its own instrument, or compared to something similar in its own kind. But the irrational soul resides in a certain way in the limbs: a part of it, capable of boldness and anger, in the heart; and a part devoted to concupiscence, entrusted to the liver. Truly, concerning this very liver, you will note a wonderful opinion of the **Pythagoreans**: namely, that this member is so composed of a certain solidity and a clear smoothness alike, that in the manner of a mirror it easily receives, admits, and reflects the images of things. Indeed, just as the vehement imagination of a pregnant woman often expresses the marks of a desired thing upon the most tender fetus, so a vehement notion of the mind or imagination of the sense very easily forms the mirror-like nature of the liver. In this very mirror, demons and those above fashion images of future things, whenever images are not painted there from elsewhere because the mind is entirely peaceful. Thus, the marks of future things result immediately in the mind and imagination from this island-like mirror; but there they are often so confused with other images that the mind is distracted regarding the governance of future portents, or the imagination is occupied with similar business. But where the prudent, continuous, and laborious discourse of reason and imagination is vacant, often the images of future things leaping from the gods into our mirror bounce back clearly into judgment. Truly, to discern what things are portents is the duty of one who is accustomed to discourse prudently and sagaciously from antecedents to consequences. But such discourse hinders prophecy, so that rightly there are some who foresee, and others who interpret and explain what has been foreseen. After this, he pursues material explained most widely by physicians concerning the humors, complexions, and the marvelous craftsmanship of the human body. Indeed, our eminent rhetorician **Bartholomæus Fontius** so admired the elegance of Plato in describing the human body that he proved in a famous oration that neither **Lactantius**, nor **Cornelius Celsus**, nor **Cicero** himself could approach the wonderful eloquence of Plato in describing this matter. Among these things, we shall consider the religious precept that nothing further should be affirmed concerning divine matters than what the divine oracle confirms. Likewise, that providence had no other

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
reason at all in composing man, except that he might be most fit for contemplation. Again, that natural things are not properly the causes in producing effects, but instruments of divine providence. For the principal cause of each thing is situated in that intelligence which, having a regard for the Good, fabricates each thing for the sake of future convenience. He defines next what the health of the body is, and what disease is. He also distinguishes the types of diseases, both others and fevers, and assigns the reasons for each. I have long thought that these reasons are primarily those which I read in **Galen** the Platonist, and I was recently confirmed in this opinion by **Georgius Cyprius**, a distinguished physician. For in these days, when he frequently came to me for the sake of curing my mother and found me reading these very things, he joined the mind of Galen with the mind of Plato in a certain imitation of order.
<margin>B</margin>
After these things, however, he defines the perfect health of man as the common harmony of body and soul. He thinks this is possessed only when both the body and the soul are well-disposed in themselves, and then are best composed together. Best, I say—that is, by a certain equal measure, so that neither the strength of the soul exceeds the limit of the body, nor the strength of the body surpasses the limit of the soul. But before he defines this perfect health, he distinguishes the disease of the soul into two: namely, ignorance and insanity. He says insanity is twofold. One is hidden, which consists in a continuous and prone affection toward vanity—suppose a certain habit most inclined toward some disturbance. The other is manifest, namely that which either some disturbance increased beyond measure directs—as in the highest degree of desire, pleasure, fear, pain, and anger—or which vapors of humors enclosed in the limbs induce, such as black bile arising from the burning of blood, or bile, or salty phlegm. Meanwhile, where he says "no one is evil voluntarily," but because of a depraved nature and habit, he understands that a natural proclivity could have been restrained from the beginning in no small way through an opposite habit. But that proclivity, confirmed by long-standing habit, cannot indeed be entirely extirpated, yet it can be pruned away by exact teaching and exhortations. After this, he teaches to cultivate the body and the soul together by a certain perpetual motion of exercise. I mean moderate exercise, I mean a proper motion, and one rightly directed toward its own good: by which both, exercised and nourished, may attain so much strength that one does not succumb to the other. Plato indeed wishes the body to yield to the soul, but not to succumb so much that it cannot sustain the motions of the soul. He wishes for a body valid and firm, but under a far stronger soul. Soon, attend to how much he praises exercise and how much he blames the rash use of drugs. Accordingly, just as he had ordered both the body and the soul to be exercised and confirmed by their own motions, so he commands the three powers of the soul—that is, the rational, the spirited, and the appetitive—to be preserved each by its own motions. Nevertheless, he commands the rational part to be nourished with more frequent food, lest it be compelled to succumb to the others. He says the intellect was given to man as a *daemon* <note>In the Platonic sense, a "daemon" is a guiding spirit or inner divinity, not an evil demon.</note>, namely an internal one. For he has another, external daemon.
<margin>E</margin>
Likewise, he speaks of the right habit of the body as if granted by heaven. Again, that he who nourishes the rational powers beyond measure becomes immortal: as if he were teaching how it should be understood when he says a man becomes a brute—that is, very similar to a brute. He adds that he who especially nourishes the mind becomes so immortal that no part of immortality is lacking. For that immortality is imperfect which performs perpetual motion; but that is perfect which remains: such as exists in him who now lives by intelligence alone and escapes from being a man to become a daemon. From which it is also understood that when he says a man is made a brute, it is said not properly, but by a certain similarity. Furthermore, from what he adds—that females arose from males—if you please,
<margin>F</margin>
he may be obscurely relating to us that **Mosaic** truth: that Eve was produced from man. But understand that all grades of brutes are multiplied little by little from a heavier fall of the rational soul; because of a certain infinity of free motion, our soul can both rush within itself into the affections and habits of all brutes, and be transferred outside itself by a certain divine judgment into the place of punishment among similar brutes or the places of brutes. Likewise, all the gifts of inferior living things are contained in the soul of man as the most perfect; and the souls of brutes are referred to ours by the very order of things and generation, as if to an end. If you accept the progression of the rational soul into others, and in turn the regression of others into this one in this manner, perhaps you will not wander from the Platonic sense. For he himself, speaking here under the persona of a **Pythagorean**, opportunely devises a fable similar to the Pythagorean fables. And lest we should perhaps admit these things as if under historical truth, he introduces the transformations of animals no differently than poets are accustomed to do. Indeed, **Timaeus of Locri**, in his book *On the World*, confesses these things are fabulous. Therefore, receive these things thus: and conclude the book of Timaeus with that end which teaches us to worship God before all things, who created all good things by the sole benevolence of His providence. I had decided, magnanimous **Lorenzo** <note>Lorenzo de' Medici, Ficino's patron.</note>, to assert shorter things here as seemed to befit an argument, and to reserve many things for the fuller commentaries which we have already designated for the *Timaeus*. But **Philippus Valor**, most studious of the Platonists, in whose presence I put the finishing touch to the entire Platonic work in the Maian field, compelled me to pour out more here: Philippus Valor, the most noble heir of the Valorian virtue, to whom I confess I owe very much, both because he greatly cultivates all excellent Platonic things, and because he is moved by a singular love toward you and all your people.

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s introductory commentary on Plato’s dialogues, specifically transitioning from the themes of the Timaeus to the Critias (the story of Atlantis). Ficino provides a Neoplatonic allegorical interpretation of the conflict between Athens and Atlantis.</meta>

# MARSILIO FICINO

<margin>A</margin> from deeds strenuously carried out against Westerners. And in both cases, he commends them for many gifts, both of God and of nature and art: at the same time, he reminds everyone not to be ungrateful to their fatherland. While he commemorates how Attic virtue overcame both the Eastern and Western regions, he meanwhile teaches both that all things are tamed by virtue, and that men endowed with virtue conduct themselves rightly and happily both in "Western" affairs (that is, adversity) and in "Eastern" affairs (that is, prosperity). Nor is it without justice that he wishes the *Critias*, concerning the antiquity of the world, to be read after the *Timaeus*, which concerns the generation of the world. However, he seems neither to have finished this history, nor to have composed the subsequent history promised under the title of *Hermocrates*. Yet it is established that this was not a fictional story, but a true history. First, because whenever he fakes something, he is accustomed to call it a "fable" <note>original: *fabulam*</note>. Here, however, he dares to assert it as history. Furthermore, he asserts the same thing entirely in the *Timaeus*, calling the matter wonderful indeed, but entirely true. And he diligently recounts from whom it was received in both places: namely, from his ancestors and kinsmen. For this Critias received it from his grandfather Critias, and he from his uncle Solon, who also committed it to writing. Solon received it from the Egyptian priests. <margin>B</margin> Moreover, Proclus cites the histories of a certain Marcellus concerning Ethiopian affairs, in which these things are most clearly confirmed, inserted among the deeds of the Ethiopians. And if none of the Platonists denies the history, nevertheless Porphyry, Proclus, and before these Origen, wish it moreover to contain a physical allegory. Indeed, lest they be mocked by Plato himself if they try to fit every single detail of the allegory to a hair's breadth, for in the opening of the *Phaedrus*, under the persona of Socrates, he ridicules those who are too curious about allegories in such matters. <margin>C</margin> But lest we seem to entirely neglect the Anagogic sense <note>The "upward-leading" or spiritual sense of a text</note>, without which no one is truly a Platonist: let Pallas [Athena] be the intellectual deity presiding over life, and Neptune the deity fostering and governing generation. Let the Athenians be figures of souls living by intellect alone and of similar deities; but let the Atlanteans be figures of deities favoring generation, and of souls joined to bodies for the duty of generation and of all nature. <margin>D</margin> Most appropriately, through the West, the sea, the islands, and the various partitions of places, the very matter of generation and its diverse mobility is signified. Furthermore, let the war be a studious contention, through which the higher deities constantly turn the lower ones back from there, and segregate souls from matter and motion as if by iron and fire. Accordingly, when you hear that Neptune procreated sons from a woman, understand either that he begat them from the earth, or that by a certain inspiration he regenerated them from a prior form of living into another form. The five births are the five forms of bodies, which he composes in this sea of matter by perpetual agitation: namely, stones, metals, plants, animals partly lacking reason, and those partly endowed with reason. <margin>E</margin> There are ten sons, for in each birth twins are created together. For in any composite, an elemental power coalesces, and at the same time a certain celestial power is infused, which physicians call a "specific virtue" <note>original: *specialem*</note>. From the five twin births, ten sons are counted. But the five zones or coils surrounding the Neptunian island are the five natures of the spheres: celestial, fiery, aerial, watery, and earthy. He says they are partly of earth and partly of water to signify stability and motion in things. The common passage through all the channels signifies the mutual germinal relationship between things. He also commemorates metals, so that through the seven metals we may understand the influences of the seven planets, moderating the generation of all things. The Platonists attribute Gold to the Sun, Silver to the Moon, Lead to Saturn, Electrum to Jupiter, iron and bronze to Mars, Orichalcum to Venus, and Tin to Mercury. The measures and their numbers are derived partly from history and partly from the logic of architecture. Something must be attributed to the grace and decorum of both the work and the eloquence. But enough now regarding the allegory. Now let us confirm the mysteries of this book. <margin>F</margin> The Platonists think that some gods are—to use their words—supracelestial and others subcelestial. The first they call the sons of God, and all the following they call the sons of the gods. Again, they place the most ample providence in the first, less ample in the second, and in the third it is reduced to narrower limits, as they now preside over certain regions of the earth and kinds of things by divine distribution: just as some celestial beings are placed over parts of the heaven and others over the stars. These subcelestial gods, therefore, in a certain order, took up the governing of different nations from the beginning. <margin>G</margin> From the beginning, I say, either of the created world or of the governing of the human race. For after great destructions of the terrestrial globe, Plato thinks that men are divinely generated from the earth itself as if from a mother by the work of such gods. For they are able to beget through the human "Idea," which acts as a seed. And the earth is able to give birth, being drenched with new and abundant moisture and becoming fertile as heat approaches—whether warm suns follow after floods of water, or rains flow more abundantly after vast fires. Men procreated from the gods out of the earth are called Heroes, who from the beginning were guided by their parents through a certain hidden persuasion of mind to mind toward the right for many ages. But because over a long stretch of time both the divine virtue implanted in their natures and the fertility of the earth gradually diminish—whence souls would turn out entirely devoid of divinity and bodies utterly empty of ancient fertility— <margin>H</margin> God again either washes the earth or burns it, and restores our race to its ancient dignity; the celestial motions are so contemplated by the Mover that celestial fate always concurs with divine providence. Truly, just as physicians judge any human body, so the Platonists judge the whole race. For physicians say that life consists in a certain natural moisture, of such a quantity and quality, and that it can be perpetually prolonged if only it is restored in that same quantity and quality. But it is not prolonged when that which flows back is not of the same quality as that which had flowed out, even if the quantity is the same. It is just as if someone were to fill a bowl daily from a jar full of wine, and immediately pour the same amount of water back into the jar. In this way, the volume of liquid in the jar would be continuously equal, but not

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> similar, and it would become more dissimilar every day, until finally from pure wine it has turned not just into watery wine, but into pure water. Similarly, the Platonists think that the divine and fertile quality once infused into the human character by the gods and into the body by heaven is gradually turned into a human quality, this human subject naturally drawing it so, until it gradually degenerates even to a beast-like state; but such a great degeneration cannot be perpetually tolerated by God, the orderer of things. Moreover, when Plato says both here and often elsewhere that the gods obtained different "lots" <note>allotted territories or fates</note>, understand that they obey the one Supreme Being who distributes the lots, and they necessarily govern the assigned province. But necessity in divine matters is entirely voluntary. <margin>B</margin> For among them, the will of the supreme father and the sons is one. And just as the parts of the elements are carried to their proper places by that necessity which would also be their will if only they had knowledge: so among the higher beings, the very assignment of government and the necessity of the natural effect is the same as the will. Furthermore, because both here and in the *Timaeus* and *Menexenus* he says the Attic region is primarily suited for genius, one must remember that the Platonists disagree among themselves in the reasons assigned for this. <margin>C</margin> For Panaetius thinks the cause is the temperament of the air between heat and frost; and he proves this from Plato's own words in the fifth book of the *Laws* and the *Epinomis*. Longinus argues against Panaetius: because that region is often struck by frost and heat; and he assigns the cause to a quality of the place mixed from many hidden things. Porphyry reproves him, because he thinks the proper cause of genius is corporeal. Origen, in his commentaries on the *Timaeus*, assigns celestial aspects and influences, asserting this very thing from the eighth book of the *Republic*, where it is said that certain celestial circuits are the causes of fertility and sterility, both of bodies and also of souls. But Proclus says in the same place that Origen assigned a cause that was true in part, but not yet whole and perfect. He himself, repeating the matter more deeply along with Porphyry, says: <margin>D</margin> The Intellect, the craftsman of the world, is the intellectual world, and therefore as if manifold. But the Soul of the world is the animal and rational world and more manifold; and it is most closely present to the entire space of the world, which is entirely continuous and immobile, consisting of prime matter and constant dimension. Again, in that very space, before all the forms that are to be generated, the Soul—following the Ideas from its own reasons—imprints different powers in different places, as if they were traces of the mind-filled Soul and certain peculiar receptacles destined to receive different familiar forms in different places. Then the various gods, having obtained various provinces, illuminate such "lodgings," some gods illuminating some places, and forming them. Therefore, rational souls, after they have chosen an elemental life and their own character, if by chance they are directed by celestial revolution to those places which most agree with the chosen form of living, they fully fulfill the duty of that life. <margin>E</margin> Thus, when those verging toward a Martian or Apollonian life soon obtain a region illuminated by Mars or Apollo, they achieve a work of perfect fortitude or prophecy. But those who have chosen a philosophical life, if they obtain a region inspired by Pallas, excel in wisdom and magnanimity at once. Therefore, he says here and in the *Timaeus* that the Attic region, ruled by Pallas, is suitable for wisdom and military service; and in the fifth book of the *Laws* he says the inspiration of local gods and demons around places is of the greatest importance for character and morals. He requires, however, some temperance of the air, not as a cause, but lest the work of the <margin>F</margin> cause itself be hindered. Therefore, this diversity of place does not so much *create* the diversity of genius among the Platonists as it *receives* and *declares* it. For they think three things are more powerful for this than the elemental location: namely, the affection of the soul itself (whether natural or chosen), the inspiration of the proper deities, and the celestial influences. This can be hindered, however, either by elemental mixture, or a new conjunction of planets, or by a calamity brought on by men themselves: and the good things infused from above are rendered "not good" by the obstacle of lower things. We have disputed this matter in the *Laws*. But enough of these things now. From all the mysteries of this book, conclude that the freedom of human choice concurs with providence. <margin>G</margin> Conclude also a sentiment similar to the Mosaic mystery: that men once lived blessed in a certain "paradise of delights," as they say, as long as a certain divine grace and innate justice flourished in them. But after that grace vanished through intemperance and pride, they fell into crimes and the gravest calamities at the same time. And God washed away the sins of men with a flood of waters. What is missing from this history can be repaired in summary from the prologue of the *Timaeus*. It is a history of deeds done before the flood. But Hermocrates, I believe, was going to narrate the events after the flood. Nor should those nine thousand years disturb you, if you hear Eudoxus saying that those years of the Egyptians were not solar, but lunar. Finally, the last sentiment of this book teaches that Jove—that is, the God who is the architect of the world—from his seat (that is, from the intuition of himself) looks out upon even the most remote and smallest things. And to the same seat (that is, divine contemplation) he turns all the gods subject to him, from where, having been instructed, they may govern lower things. Nor do they do these two things in turns; rather, by constantly contemplating divine things, they dispense temporal things through them at the same time. <margin>H</margin> He calls this very seat the "middle bed of the world" for this reason: because from there, as if from a center, all things flow out, and to there they flow back, and from there all things are easily looked upon and revolved.

<meta>This page continues the introductory arguments and commentary on Plato’s *Laws*. The translator, likely Marsilio Ficino, is contrasting the philosophical approaches of Pythagoras, Socrates, and Plato, while setting the stage for the dialogue between the Athenian Stranger, Megillus, and Clinias.</meta>

# ARGUMENTS AND COMMENTARY

<margin>A</margin> We have discovered that the wisdom of Pythagoras consists more in contemplation, that of Socrates more in action, and finally that of Plato in both contemplation and action equally. Furthermore, the speculative discipline of Pythagoras seems more remote from the common customs of men than the moral discipline of Socrates. But the doctrine of Plato, being equally speculative and moral, everywhere so tempers the divine with the human that it can easily be accommodated to the common customs of men, while simultaneously turning men toward divine and eternal things. Nor should it be thought that Plato is different from Pythagoras and Socrates, whom he worships as if they were deities; rather, he is a mixture of both, acting as a kind of mediator (so to speak) between the divine and human natures of each. Thus, it might be said that in those two the nature was merely divine, while in Aristotle and the other philosophers after Plato it was merely human; but in Plato, it was equally divine and human. <margin>B</margin> Why mention this here? So that we may remember the present arrangement of the laws. Since they are handed down to us by Plato not through a Pythagorean or Socratic persona as is his custom elsewhere, but through the persona of Plato himself, they rightly occupy a middle path between the divine and the human. They do not drag us through hidden and impassable ways, yet they do not lead us down to inferior things. For this reason, those ten books of the *Republic* are more Pythagorean and Socratic, while the present *Laws* are judged to be more Platonic. That *Republic* belonged to one who wishes and hopes; the present arrangement belongs to one who chooses. Thus, those who cannot ascend that steep height should not disdain to approach at least these gentler hills. <margin>C</margin> Consider with what great diligence our Plato provides for human safety. He does not only wish to be admired by men for steep heights, but also to be easy, favorable, and salvific to all through certain slopes. Here, therefore, he will not compel men to make all things common among themselves if they are unwilling; he will permit individuals to possess private property, as is customary. Yet, our most cautious charioteer will not loosen the reins entirely. For besides the utmost diligence regarding other laws, he will most prudently decree that no one be allowed to increase their wealth beyond a certain and moderate limit, lest excessive abundance for some or poverty for others cause harm, and lest many be forced to be beggars in the arms of their own fatherland—a condition he considers miserable. <margin>D</margin> That the persona of Plato is hidden here under the name of the "Athenian Guest" <note>original: "Atheniensis hospis," often translated as the Athenian Stranger</note> for the sake of modesty will be clearly apparent to the reader from many clues, especially because he will affirm that he has treated two types of Republics. About to establish laws for the Greeks, he rightly receives laws from the three best founders of Greek law: Minos, Lycurgus, and Solon—removing, adding, changing, and inventing—and thus composes the best form from them all. And although from the beginning he establishes a city and a rule of governing, he calls it the "Position of Laws" rather than a "Republic." Since in that city possessions are the private property of individuals, there is a need for many laws because of various controversies, lawsuits, and injuries. In establishing these, you will note the admirable and most merciful genius of the divine Plato. For this man, distinguished by his kindness, devises certain exhortatory prefaces for individual laws, by which the citizens, most humanely led, might be willing to obey freely. They should comply with them spontaneously like children of the laws, whereas others are accustomed to obey unwillingly as if to tyrants, and <margin>E</margin> seek to escape their command through either fraud or violence. But after many things, he also adds threats and punishments for those who judge their fatherland not as a mother, but as a stepmother. We shall now descend to the specific argument of the first dialogue of the *Laws*, if we first admonish everyone to read the dialogue *Minos* and its argument before they approach these laws. Let them approach, I say, so that they may diligently observe them in reading and preserve them thoroughly in actions. Otherwise, unless they obey these, <margin>F</margin> let them understand that after such exact knowledge of justice and injustice, they will sin with less excuse and greater crime. The Athenian Guest, that is Plato, having set out for Crete near Knossos, encounters Megillus the Lacedaemonian and Clinias the Cretan, whom the Knossians had summoned along with nine others to lead a colony from there, found a city, and give them laws. These two, therefore, were approaching the sacred cave of Jupiter <note>The Dictaean Cave, legendary birthplace of Zeus/Jupiter</note> to consult about this. Meeting them, the Athenian Guest asked what they were going to do. They replied they were going to devise laws. But when, after being questioned much about laws by the guest, they did not sufficiently resolve the question, and the guest seemed to them most fit for lawgiving, they entreated him to join them as a helper in instituting the city. <margin>G</margin> The guest therefore complies, and before all else explains the principle from which and through which laws reach men: namely, God and the philosopher. Then he investigates the end <term>finis - the ultimate goal or purpose</term> of the laws, teaching that such an end will be the tranquil purity of the citizens' souls, sufficient for the contemplation of truth as far as possible. Thirdly, he descends to the form and matter of the laws themselves. That laws are inspired into men by God is witnessed by all antiquity, by many of Plato's books, and by our own reasons brought forth in many arguments of the dialogues and confirmed in our *Theology* where religion is discussed. Surely, if Nature—which is nothing other than the lowest instrument of divine providence—does not lead itself wherever it is seen to proceed providently, but is led by Providence itself, which prescribes ends and orders within itself and inscribes them upon nature as it wills; if, I say, such nature neither abounds in superfluities nor fails in necessary things, then certainly divine providence never fails in necessary things. Now, mutual congregation is necessary for the human race, which cannot live otherwise. Law is also necessary for a congregation, which would otherwise suddenly perish without law. Again, divine authority is necessary for laws, lest they either become obsolete through negligence or be broken by fraud and violence. Yet, to obtain divine authority, both sanctity of life and a punishment beyond human power, admirable to all, are necessary. Therefore, the providence of God, which provides necessities for every species of elements, plants, brutes, and limbs,

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> should not fail to provide for the most perfect species of animals that worships divinity, in sanctioning laws especially necessary for the safety of men. Add to this that no prince can lead a vast city—a ship tossed at every moment by storms and innumerable dangers—all the way to the harbor without a heavenly breeze. Therefore, God, both through hidden inspirations of souls and through manifest miracles whenever necessity demands, both reveals the mysteries of laws and openly sanctions and promulgates them. For this reason, Plato begins the exordium of the laws with such just and happy auspices, naming God three times immediately at the beginning, and not without reason. <margin>B</margin> For here three founders of laws are disputing, and each stands in need of divine patronage. They also imitate three authors of laws: Minos, Lycurgus, and Solon. These men also referred their laws to three deities: Jupiter, Apollo, and Minerva. And not without cause. For the Sun, the lord of the planets, contains power; Jupiter, clemency; and Minerva, wisdom. <margin>C</margin> These three indeed embrace the whole nature and perfection of law. For what else do we say law is, besides a certain rational rule leading toward the good in a certain order? But for reason, rule, and order to be present, wisdom is absolutely necessary. Furthermore, so that it may lead to the end and be preserved, power flows forth in the first place; finally, so that it leads to the good—that is, to the advantage of each—and conducts things conveniently and kindly, clemency provides greatly. Thus, three deities among the ancients, referring to the divine trinity, necessarily consult the laws. And therefore, three similar endowments are judged necessary in a prince for making laws. <margin>D</margin> But since these must concur perfectly with one another to establish perfect laws, and human faculty cannot provide that, there is surely a need for divine help for the most exact sanctioning of laws. As for the fact that Plato repeats the number nine (of years) both in the *Minos* and often here, as if it were necessary for learning laws from Jupiter himself and handing them to men, it perhaps signifies the nine orders of angelic minds through whom, as interpreters, the very reason for sanctioning law is transferred down to men. He signifies all these orders as interpreters of laws under the single name of Mercury in the *Protagoras*. Nor should it escape you that not only Christians use this ninefold number for angels, but also the Platonists, especially Proclus and Syrianus, as we have sufficiently shown in our *Theology*. <margin>E</margin> What then? What if this ninefold number signifies a triple use of power, a triple use of wisdom, and also a triple use of clemency? Namely, so that each of the three is present in the law itself, in the judgment of the magistrate, and in the ministers and the execution of the judgment itself? Furthermore, in the very principles, middles, and ends of things and actions? Three things repeated three times clearly complete the ninefold. But why is the exordium based on the sacred rites of Minerva in the *Republic*, but here on the sacred discussions of Jupiter? Is it perhaps because that discussion is held in Athens, and treats the ancient city of Athens named after Minerva; whereas here in Crete, the building of a Cretan city is consulted near the very temple of Jupiter, and in the beginning words are spoken concerning the laws of Minos, the son of Jupiter? Or rather, was that prior form of the republic more chaste and <margin>F</margin> pure, most suitable to Pallas (Minerva); while this one is a little more indulgent, and by its own humanity suitable to Jupiter? In short, both here and there we take the happiness of the nascent city from prayers and sacrifices. I omit the description of this long journey, the sacred groves, the trees dedicated to the temple, and many other things that would require a commentary rather than an argument. After some things which allegorically teach that human affairs, especially public ones, are not rightly composed without divine patronage, and therefore the exordium of laws must be made from God himself, who is both the beginning and the end of laws, he now begins gradually to inquire into the end of laws, signifying that their end is divine worship, since they proceed to the temple of Jupiter for such a discussion of laws. <margin>G</margin> Since, therefore, the ultimate end of laws is the worship of that Jupiter who made the world and gave laws to the world and to us, he not undeservedly immediately denies that the end of laws is the worship of Mars, meanwhile modestly correcting the laws of Minos and Lycurgus because they did not look so much toward virtue itself simply, as they declined toward warlike virtue. Surely, laws ought to have that most of all as an end in the city, toward which as toward a target all things are directed, which is to be sought by all citizens most of all. But battle and victory, since they are full of labors and evils, are not to be desired for their own sake, but rather chosen for the sake of peace and the safe tranquility of life; just as no one so desires to live as to be engaged in a perpetual battle and victory against diseases. <margin>H</margin> He concludes finally that it is not fitting to refer the studies of peace to warlike things, but on the contrary to refer warlike things to the studies and duties of peace; and peace to the ready and free worship of truth and God. In proving these things, he distributes the genus of goods into many species, saying some are human, others divine, and that human goods depend on divine ones. Of the human goods, which he judges far inferior to the divine, the first is health, the second beauty, the third strength, the fourth riches. He wants the leader of these goods to be prudence; moreover, after prudence, he considers the leader of the divine goods to be temperance, after this justice, and after justice fortitude. Indeed, he signifies here, and explains in the fourth book of the *Republic*, the three parts of the soul: namely, the rational, the irascible, and the concupiscible. He places prudence in the rational alone, and fortitude in the irascible alone. He also places continence in the concupiscible alone. But he places temperance and justice in all parts together, and calls each the "consonance of the whole soul." But let temperance be the consonance in affections, and justice the consonance in acts. And let the former be the health of the soul, the latter the beauty of the soul. But prudence is the eye; fortitude, however, the hand. If you look at the substance of the soul and the purity necessary for contemplation, prefer temperance to justice; if you look at human custom, prefer justice. But above all, place prudence as the eye and leader for all feet. And prefer fortitude to continence.

<summary>This page provides a philosophical introduction to Plato's Laws, arguing that Plato's approach uniquely balances divine contemplation with human practical needs. It explains the symbolic significance of the dialogue's setting in Crete and the necessity of divine authority in establishing a stable legal system.</summary>
<keywords>Plato, Laws, Pythagoras, Socrates, Jupiter, Minerva, divine providence, three parts of the soul, prudence, justice, temperance, fortitude, Knossos, Minos, Lycurgus, Solon</keywords>
