<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s Latin commentary and summary of Plato’s *Laws* (De Legibus), specifically focusing on the end of Book I and the beginning of Book II. Ficino, a central figure of the Italian Renaissance, translates Plato's Greek concepts into a Christian Neoplatonic framework.</meta>

# MARSILIO FICINO

<margin>A</margin> For fortitude is occupied with more difficult matters—namely, the endurance of pain—and it encompasses within itself the duty of continence, which is to conquer pleasures. Yet, judge both of these to be inferior to temperance and justice. For these two possess the complete order of the entire soul more fully than the order established by prudence. From these points, he concludes that the lawmaker must both refer himself, and command others to be referred: human things indeed to divine things, but divine things (that is, the virtues) to a mind dedicated to truth and divinity. While he disputes concerning the goal of laws, he also explains the duty of their founder: he wishes this to be the highest goal, to cultivate the entire city with the greatest diligence as if it were a field, so that he may have an exquisite system for selecting and sowing seeds. Next, he treats the opportune cultivation of each plant. Likewise, he speaks of weeding out harmful herbs and thorns immediately from the beginning. Finally, he discusses bringing all things to maturity in their proper order. Among these things, however, take note that he who yields to pleasures is held to be more base than he who succumbs to pains.

<margin>B</margin> Likewise, it is the duty of a brave man's force not only to overcome fear and dangers, but also to restrain desires. Furthermore, no one can be securely judged brave unless he has been strenuously engaged for a long time amid labors and dangers. Add to this: unless he has also been tested within the very license and allurements of pleasures, in which the continent are properly proven. Note that it is not safe to educate either a man who is to be brave far away from fears, or one who is to be temperate apart from all the allurements of pleasures. Furthermore, the entire study of the law-founder ought to revolve around pleasures and pains, so that these two, like brute beasts, do not lack a bridle.

<margin>C</margin> For if they are restrained by a bridle, the journey of life turns out easy and happy. If they are coerced by no bridle, it is quite difficult and unhappy. You will also note that saying regarding the Athenians: that the upright Athenians are especially upright because they alone are upright by their own nature and by a certain divine lot, with no one compelling or terrifying them. In these words, Plato signifies that in a poorly instituted city, good citizens will indeed be rare, but those who exist will be the most excellent of all. Since they turned out as such with no discipline, they were surely made so by a certain divine lot and a perfect nature; their excellence is so great that they are not defiled by the common contagion. After this, you shall consider that singular precept of every art and of the whole of life: it is necessary that those who are to turn out excellent in any study whatsoever should meditate on that very thing from their tender years, as much in playing as in studying, in every detail conducive to it. Thus, the most fitting preludes to manly studies should be proposed to boys, so that the minds of those playing may be led into a love of that which they are to do seriously in their manly age. Among these things, discipline is defined thus: <term>Discipline</term> <note>original: "Disciplina"</note> is that institution of life starting from boyhood which gradually leads the boyish mind into the love of virtue. I mean especially that virtue through which, having become a man, he knows how to command and to obey. That a man ought to and moreover can have such discipline from his tender years, he aptly confirms through the description of human nature that follows: for he says that man, although he is a single thing, nevertheless has many and diverse things within himself. Among these are two "mindless tyrants" contrary to one another, distracting the soul: Pain and Pleasure. Furthermore, there are opinions of future goods and evils, from which arise in us appetite and confidence toward the good, but fear toward the evil, and similar perturbations of the soul. Beyond these, there is the judgment of reason, dictating which of these is better and which is worse. Such a judgment in each individual is a private law, and in the city, it is public law. Since he had said that one animal was composed of such diverse things, he not unfittingly adds that man is a "divine miracle" among animals, imitating Hermes <note>Ficino refers to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary author of the Hermetic corpus, who famously called man a "great miracle."</note> who said that man is a vast miracle. There are three kinds of animals: for they are either immortal in both body and soul, or mortal in both, or immortal in soul but perishable in body. In the first kind are the celestial, ethereal, and aerial beings, whether they be called gods or <term>daemons</term> <note>In the Platonic sense, "daemons" are intermediary spirits between gods and humans, not necessarily evil.</note>. In the last kind are the brutes. But in the middle are men and the daemons of water and earth. For since the bodies of these daemons, like human bodies, are composed of contraries, they can at some time be dissolved; and they bring about certain perturbations. But leaving the rest aside, why is man a miracle? Because, while he is divine, it is a wonder that he is infected by mortals; and while he is mortal, it is also a wonder that he is moved toward divine things. But why is he called a "divine miracle"? Because he was so instituted by divine providence: and as Timaeus teaches, we received the very substance of the rational soul from God the maker of the world, but from the other gods a certain vital nature inferior to reason, and finally from the daemons, our bodies. As for his adding that man was made by the gods either for "play" or for "study," understand it thus: he was made for play if the soul, always transmigrating from celestial to earthly things and back again as if playing, never rests in an immutable seat with God; but he was made for study if the mind is at some time to remain immutably with the creator gods and the Creator God. Which part of this disjunction we ought to choose, Plato does not dare to affirm here. Yet he holds it probable, as he signifies here and elsewhere, that man was constituted by divinity for study rather than for play. But if anyone wishes to read this ambiguous text of Plato so that it signifies either that man was constituted by divine animals, let him understand the stars; or that he is composed of many animals, let him understand that the parts and affections of the soul are named "animals" poetically by Plato. This indeed appears in the ninth book of the *Republic* and in the beginning of the *Phaedrus*. But you shall see to those matters. After this, he descends to certain things which, even if they seem lighter, are nevertheless necessary for the perfect tradition of discipline and the testing of character: such as the study of music and very similar customs. Music, in a very common sense, encompasses the order of any proportion, not only in speech, song, sound, and dance, but also in gymnastic play and the grace of a banquet. All these things ought to be so composed in the city that, with every

<column-break/>

incitement to perturbations and vices removed, they may temper the body, spirit, and soul. He begins the dispute, by a certain opportunity, with banquets and wine, saying first that we must beware lest drunkenness be added to our innate perturbations. For if this is added rashly, it both diminishes the duties of reason and increases the force of perturbation. Yet he approves of the banquet and the use of pure wine, provided that caution is applied, which he will explain more clearly in the following book. Here, however, he judges it to contribute most to this: that from the occasionally freer use of wine, the characters of men are uncovered in banquets; for it is accustomed to make them more impudent and bold. There, then, a prudent guardian of youth, having detected the vices of the young (especially impudence), will be able both to heal them more easily and to accustom the youths to preserve shame even in the most impudent drunkenness. How great a thing shame is—that is, the fear of disgrace and infamy—is evident from the fact that because of this kind of fear, youths both fear shameful things above all and boldly undertake honest things however arduous. These two things are judged most necessary of all for a republic, both in peace and in war. Therefore, the lawmaker ought to intend with diligent study to infuse these into the minds of the citizens.

### ON BOOK II: OF THE LAWS,
->Argument. to page 575.<-

<margin>D</margin> Our Plato, with wonderful charity toward the human race, leaves nothing unattempted in his disputations which seems to lead to human salvation in any way. And while he contends for this studiously, he prefers to undergo the charge of being too prolix or even too curious, rather than negligent. Therefore, in the second book, he pursues the exquisite discipline of tender age. For noticing that boys, almost like beasts, care for nothing but break out wherever pleasure draws them, and immediately flee from wherever pain withdraws them, he—not without cause—places a charioteer over the horses of youth before the proclivity for following or fleeing grows into a habit. This charioteer holds the reins of pleasure and pain in his hand. He names this charioteer "discipline"—namely, virtue—which first comes to boys, through which pleasure and love, and pain and hatred, flow rightly into their minds through another's reason, before they are moved by their own reason. Then, when their own reason is present, they moreover consent to their own reason because of the prior habit of good character. This very consensus he wishes to be universal virtue. But the decent habituation concerning pleasures and pains, through which from the beginning to the end of life men hate what they ought to hate and love what is to be loved, as long as it is ruled under another's reason, he calls "discipline." Then, when it consents to its own now-awakened reason, he calls it by the name of "virtue." That the foundation of such a moral life is of the greatest importance, even Aristotle himself greatly approves in the *Ethics*. Since, however, the nature of boys is restless and desirous of delights in all things, and therefore does not undertake severe discipline, he rightly commands that boys be educated under the honest pleasure of that most common music which presents the traces of virtue. Indeed, even the elders, for whom certain honest delights must be applied as a solace for a laborious life. For this reason, he says the gods, having pitied the laborious life of men, not unfittingly instituted solemn rites and festivals for them as a remission of labors. Furthermore, they provided the Muses, Apollo, and Bacchus as leaders to celebrate these, who might amend lascivious characters and moderate the nature greedy for motion through the musical ratio of movements, and delight them honestly. These words not only praise the use of music as divinely commended and granted, but also allegorically teach that man would be more miserable than the brutes for many reasons, unless he undertook divine worship and religion through divine providence and kinship. In this, the Muses signify the divine discovery of truth granted by God to the religious. Apollo signifies the grateful expression and prophecy of that discovery. Finally, Bacchus signifies both the abstraction of the mind and the admirable works of religious men. Note that the harmonic ratio was granted to us chiefly by divine providence, through which we may harmonize all the motions of a restless nature which by their own nature would be discordant. From the Muses we have the consonance of the soul's motion; from Apollo, moreover, the concord in the motion of speech and song; and finally from Bacchus, a festive harmony in the motion of the limbs. While he disputes most diligently about this discipline through music, pertaining both to boys and even to elders, he repeats the same institutes he placed in the *Republic*, through which poets, musicians, and painters are never granted the license of imitating whatever they wish, but may imitate only honest and grave things for the salvation of those watching and listening. He wishes the judges of imitation to be skilled and most grave men, and he commands that through honest imitation practiced daily, adolescents should become accustomed in all plays and studies to the same things in which the laws and the elders rejoice and grieve. This habituation he judges to contain the entire foundation of virtue. Among these things, some points are commended to memory as being very conducive to the precepts of character. Even if an unjust man possesses all things held as "goods" among men, he is unhappy; and as long as he lives thus, it must be said that it is better for him to die than to live. Likewise, whoever distinguishes the "honest" life from the "pleasant" life in conversation is not to be heard. And although an honest and just life may sometimes seem laborious, this must never be said to boys; rather, the most just life will be the most pleasant of all. Finally, Plato asserts this will be necessary, although perhaps it seems otherwise to those with whom he disputes. And that...

# ARGUMENTS AND COMMENTARY

<margin>A</margin> He commands silence. Nevertheless, Truth is something beautiful and stable. After this, he descends to the use of wine, which he wishes to be entirely unknown to youths before their eighteenth year of age. Otherwise, he says, fire is poured upon fire, both into the soul and into the body. After this age, he permits wine to be drunk in moderation. But after the fortieth year, he allows wine to be drunk more freely in banquets amidst hymns to the gods, as a remedy against the hardness of old age, through which we may seem to grow young again, and forgetfulness of sadness may take hold of us; the very affection of the mind, like iron in the fire, is led from hardness into softness and becomes more flexible. By this, he intends that elders, who might otherwise be unwilling to sing, may become more cheerful in banquets and be willing to sing to the ears of the younger men, and thus, so to speak, "enchant" their souls. By this incantation through a gravely concordant melody, the souls of the youth are tempered. In reading these things, you will note that grace itself is named "beauty" in things, but "pleasure" in cognition. You will note that no animal <margin>B</margin> except man has a sense of rhythm and harmony. And that rhythm is order in time and motion; whereas harmony is order in the very temperament of voices through the acute <note>high-pitched</note> and the grave <note>low-pitched</note>. What we call *harmonia* in Greek, we properly call *concentus* <note>concord or singing together</note> in Latin. What we call *rhythmus*, we can conveniently call *numerus* <note>number or meter</note>, provided you understand it as number in time and motion. You will note in what thing the utility of wine consists, and with what caution it must be drunk—namely, with the founders or guardians of the laws present at the banquet, who are sober and observe and correct the manners of the drinkers, reforming them at the opportune time when they have been made softer by the wine. He concludes, <margin>C</margin> finally, that if citizens use pure wine with such cautions in banquets, it is to be granted as useful for the things mentioned; but its use according to each person's lust must be kept far from his citizens. Indeed, such lust most impudently strikes at the sacred citadels of Pallas <note>Athena/Wisdom</note>, which must be cherished above all things.

## ON THE THIRD BOOK OF THE LAWS,
## Argument. for page 585.

<margin>D</margin> Just as a physician looks to the health of the body, so the author of laws looks to the health of the soul. Since, indeed, it is more desirable for everyone to retain prosperous health so that it does not perish, than to recover it when it is failing, therefore the chief institution of both the statesman and the physician is to preserve the health of their respective body or soul. The second-best counsel of both seems to be to restore the habit, whether to the body or the soul, if it has ever been lost. Wherefore, both in Plato and in truth, those writers of laws are judged worthy of contempt who suddenly decree by what censure perpetrated crimes must be punished, but do not provide by what reason men may be so born, nourished, and educated that they do not wish to perpetrate crimes. Let no one, therefore, wonder that our Plato, studious of the firmest health of the soul, discusses quite accurately in the books of the *Laws* as well as the *Republic* many things that seem trivial and pertain to the education of boys and youths. For it befits the most diligent physician of souls to do so: to compose them immediately upon birth so that we may seem either to have been born with firm health, or at least that in the age of youth, the health of the soul may grow together with us. Hence follows that preceding diligence of the first and second books of the *Laws* in every kind of music, play, and banquet. For while he disputes concerning the office of the author of laws, he judges that his chief study—that is, concerning boys and youths—must be declared before all else. Here I wish you to remember with what great caution he judged the drinking of wine must be approached: that it is not permitted to drink daily, nor for everyone, nor according to anyone's lust, but only in solemn banquets, and then indeed for men and in moderation, and rarely pure wine, yet under an arbiter and judge. Otherwise, remember also how much he approves that it should not be permitted for soldiers in camps to taste wine, nor for slaves in the city, nor for magistrates, nor for governors and judges at the very time of judgment, nor for men about to deliberate on great matters, and finally neither for a man nor a woman at that hour in which they determine to labor for children <note>procreation</note>. It will be worthwhile to have diligently commemorated these things. Let us proceed now to the proper argument of the third book. Since, therefore, the law itself is the form of civility <note>civil discipline</note>, and civility is the form of the city, he who is about to treat of laws discusses many things concerning the beginning of the city and civility. He wonders whether the human race has existed from eternity or not, and similarly concerning the world. And because in some places he names "infinite time," he by no means signifies properly "without beginning and without end," but rather infinite according to our computations; therefore he often calls time "inestimable" rather than "immense." And in the sixth book, similarly doubting, he divides the opinion thus: "The generation of men either never began, or it began an inestimable length of time before us." He calls it "inestimable," perhaps, if anyone should contend to count not only solar years, but also lunar years, and days and hours. It should be enough for a Christian that the philosopher did not affirm the eternity of the world. But what will they say of these thousands of thousands of years compared to the Mosaic ones? Perhaps Plato, after the manner of the Egyptians, computed very short years. But these things, and the floods of the world, are more opportunely dealt with in the *Timaeus*. Now let us return to the matter of the laws itself, that is, the city and civility. Four figures of civility are chiefly numbered. The first, indeed, immediately after the calamity of the human race, in some surviving seed of it preserved either by the benefit of the highest mountains or rather by divine providence. For then it is probable that the sons and grandsons obeyed the command of the father of the family. This command indeed consists of the law of nature alone. The second figure among several families now 

<column-break/>

gathered together either in a town or by some similar rampart—gathered, I say, both by mutual need and by fear of wild beasts. But from the very beginning of this assembly, it is likely that as many forms of governing existed as there were households, widely diverse among themselves in opinions and customs. Because of this diversity, having been forced by mutual injuries that arose, they appointed certain common arbiters, judges, and rulers. From this, the third figure of civil discipline arose, taking its origin from the preceding injustice. It is probable that such rulers of the city prescribed common laws for the state after they considered all the most honorable laws of the households, and through them transferred the discipline of domestic affairs to the discipline of the Republic. Finally, the fourth figure is in a certain kingdom of nations: where several cities agree among themselves upon the same will and common law, just as several families agree into one city. The first figure is outside the city, <margin>B</margin> consisting through individual laws of nature, reason, and will. The second is already in a city, but still through the individual laws of households, gathered by a certain need and fear. The third is in a state through laws now common, cultivating justice on the occasion of injustice. The fourth is gathered from several states through the same will and similar law. Among these things, poets are admonished to sing of divine things: where it is said that the race of poets is divine and moved by God. The authors of laws are also admonished that they should bring forth laws that are neither arduous nor violent, but light and sweet as far as possible. Furthermore, by a certain historical example, he pursues the principal plan of this disputation concerning the chief and best reason for founding laws. This indeed takes its <margin>C</margin> beginning most especially if the author, in bringing these forth, looks to the universal virtue of citizens, but most of all to the greatest of all and the leader. No one indeed doubts that other virtues are led by prudence as inferior members are led by the head. That this is as necessary to us as it is noble, he confirms from the fact that all men by common vow desire this first: that all human affairs may succeed and be carried out according to their desire; and when everything succeeds according to one's vow, they judge him to be the most blessed of all. Plato, on the contrary, infers that he would be most miserable whose desires were followed daily by events, unless he were endowed with such great prudence, and by prudence ruled his mind with such moderation, that he might discern true goods, <margin>D</margin> and having neglected others, might seek those which he has set apart by reason. In these things, he admonishes that it is not to be wished or prayed for that all things follow our desire, but rather that desire follow reason. He also touches upon the fitting comparison of a son to a father, and a father to God. Certainly, a boy desires and prays that as many things as possible may happen to him as if they were goods, which the father meanwhile prays may not happen, as if they were evils. Similarly, the Heavenly Father daily detests the vain and noxious vows of men. Nor is there any refuge for us to avoid fallacious vows, except prudence. Therefore, let the lawgiver apply himself first to propagating this through the minds of the citizens, studying the public happiness. For so great is the perfection of prudence that it teaches one to desire what is to be desired, and to use those things obtained by that reason by which they may be beneficial. In these things, the entire happiness of the city consists. Just as prudence preserves a city, <margin>E</margin> so imprudence destroys it, which he names "ignorance." Not ignorance, I say, properly of letters or of some art or of certain external things of others, but ignorance of the good, as he often says elsewhere and signifies here. But he adds that it is a most pernicious ignorance both privately and publicly, through which one does not know how to temper his own mind so that the senses, like a lawfully educated people, obey the laws of his reason as if it were a queen: so that he does not pursue or flee other things, nor rejoice or grieve in other things or in another way, than the institutes of reason prescribe. Whoever is blinded by such ignorance, even if they are most ingenious and most literate, are judged ignorant by Plato. <margin>F</margin> But those who are temperate are judged by him to be prudent and knowing, even if they do not know letters. He then forbids that the governing of a magistrate be granted to him who, on account of incontinence, does not know how to govern himself. Nor does he trust that a city can be rightly and happily composed under him in whose soul there is a certain city that is both uncomposed and miserable. Although he next numbers seven reasons which are judged by most to lead to the dignity of commanding—namely, Paternity, Nobility, Lordship, Power, Old Age, Prudence, and Lot—nevertheless he himself chooses one above the others, that is prudence, saying that this is the proper reason for imperial dignity: namely, that the more prudent should everywhere command, and the less prudent should obey. Just as it is the office of the eyes to lead, <margin>G</margin> and the service of the feet to proceed. Likewise, as in any art, especially navigation, military, and medicine, it is the part of him who understands more to command, and the part of him who knows less in that matter to execute; so also in the civil art, partly the governor of each individual, partly of the family, partly of the city, all ought especially to obey him who understands above others what most conduces to human safety. The law, therefore, desiring common prudence, will provide that besides the education of children leading to prudence, the grades of public offices also be distributed everywhere according to the grades of prudence itself. And lest the rudders of these be committed imprudently, he decrees that a pure and immense authority of commanding should not be granted; but he will subject all to the laws, and join kings with the senate, and the senate with the popular council. He will take care above all that a proud man desiring wantonness should never <margin>H</margin> have more power than the laws, lest the city suffer dissension and ruin. He will strive so that the whole body of the city may be as free as possible, prudent, and friendly. Free, indeed, so that anyone may consult for his fatherland; prudent, so that he may know how; and friendly, so that he may wish to. He will remember that these three things meet more easily in that city which holds a middle ground between the power of one man and the power of the people: so that it neither subjects itself entirely to the will of one commander or the power of a few, nor receives any counselor without selection; but consists mostly of the government of the best men <note>aristocracy</note>, yet has something of the royal, and something moreover of the popular. He will look around...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plato’s *Laws*, specifically concluding the analysis of Book III and beginning the introduction to Book IV. Ficino, a central figure of the Italian Renaissance, translates and interprets Plato through a Neoplatonic and Christian lens.</meta>

the character and fortunes of princes, so that he may perceive that the destruction of cities and kingdoms proceeds most of all from the delicious and luxurious lifestyle of youths and men. Indeed, since no one can emerge outstanding in virtue from such a life, but necessarily becomes sickly, fragile, bloated, and blind. He will therefore command that temperance <note>Latin: *temperantia*; self-control or moderation</note> be cultivated by all above all else, decreeing that those who are judged the most temperate of all should be especially honored. Nor will he allow fortitude to be possessed by anyone without temperance, regarding it as a thing very dangerous to the state. Nay, even the skill of many things without justice he regards as likely to cause grave harm. In short, he will place the gifts of the soul in the first rank of honor, if they are mixed with temperance; to these he will subject the goods of the body, and he will command that external goods serve both the goods of the body and the soul. He will also prohibit excessive liberty and forbid excessive servitude. For excessive servitude removes friendship—that is, both the goodwill of the people toward the prince and charity toward the fatherland—from the midst, so that for a slight cause either the prince or the fatherland perishes. Excessive liberty, however, first gives birth to wantonness; then contempt for the laws; after these, frequent seditions; and finally, extreme servitude. Let no one wonder that Plato here, and often elsewhere, makes much of games, or rather the study of music, as if they could do as much as possible for changing character in either direction, both publicly and privately. For at that time, such study was <margin>C</margin> familiar to everyone and openly very frequent; moreover, what is done by everyone and continually has no less force upon the soul than the air has upon the body. Furthermore, things which are held lightly by less cautious physicians are considered by no means contemptible by Plato, that most observant physician of the human race. After this, he descends to the epilogue of the preceding points. In which epilogue someone might perhaps read that clause, "If indeed anything," and what follows, in this way: "Have we indeed contributed anything or not? Who will refute us? Since all things have been spoken among us?" But you shall see to those matters.

# ON THE FOURTH BOOK OF THE LAWS,
## Argument. For page 596.

This fourth dialogue, just like the three preceding ones and also the first part of the fifth, is occupied with the very counsel and duty of the lawgiver. His counsel concerns the matter and form of the city. By "matter," I mean the site, composition, and arrangement of the city. By "form," the mode and order of public government. And since this form can never be beautiful unless the souls of the citizens are beautiful, therefore the lawgiver is commanded to watch over the forming of the souls of his citizens from a tender age and through their whole life. He dispatches the matter of the city in a few words, but treats its form and the formation of the souls themselves most accurately, as one who, in view of the dignity of souls, weighs all external things as nothing, however grand they may seem. Certainly, if our Plato were a physician of bodies, he would dwell more diligently on choosing the healthiest air contributing to a firm and strong habit of the body. But he who, in choosing an Academy for himself in a healthy place, consulted not for the body but for the soul and character, appears not particularly accurate in founding a city; but in forming character along with age, he is, so to speak, a most curious physician of souls. Furthermore, if he valued the goods of fortune as much as others are accustomed to, he would certainly seek out a field, site, and manner most convenient for accumulating riches and amplifying empire. He does entirely the opposite. Let the city, therefore, be far from the sea and the port, not devoted to trade—especially the retail trade—not luxurious, not wealthy. Let the city be temperate, sober, and modest. Above all others, let it be pious. What else do you think some holy pontiff of a religious life would command in building temples and the dwellings of saints, than what our Plato commands in founding a city? And he who speaks few words here about the body of the city, in that blessed Republic expressed in ten Dialogues, made no mention of founding a city; and indeed not without reason. For he left that one to heaven, but builds this one on earth, according to the image of that exemplar as far as possible. The purpose of the lawgiver, therefore, will be to value lightly those things which are outside the goods of the soul in comparison to the goods of the soul, and in all his institution to aim at universal virtue as if at a target. Therefore, he permits nothing either in the city or around the city from which citizens might at some time become accustomed to bad character, even if from there the victory of many nations, the greatest power, and the most abundant supply of all things should follow. For the law does not direct its edge outside the soul, but into the soul itself, to be perfected in every part. Therefore, he will command that citizens should not hold the safety of this false life in highest price. Nor should they care so much that they are safe, as that as long as they are, they are the best. To perfect the whole institution of the lawgiver, he thinks three things especially contribute: namely, God, fortune, and art <note>Latin: *ars*; skill, craft, or technical knowledge</note>. These three are said to govern all human affairs. And the more difficult the things the author of laws undertakes than others, the more he needs the patronage of these three than others. But as for what Plato says—that God, fortune, and art together with God govern all human affairs—explain it briefly thus: God moves all things in all things through all things. He moves the spheres of the world. By their concurrence, "fate" is named in some places, but here "fortune" is more willingly named. From here various chances arise concerning external things and bodies. He also moves souls by inspiring light into minds: whence the art not only of speculating is kindled, but of acting. From art, finally, the arrangement of externals and the body proceeds. Wherefore all things depend indeed on God; who, as Paul says, works all things in us. But from God himself some things proceed through fortune, others through art. Thus it happens that neither fortune nor art is ever able to oppose God. Since indeed both are always moved by Him. But among themselves, in what way

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> these things stand is thus: for either they agree with each other, or perhaps they disagree. If they disagree, either fortune overcomes art, or art overcomes fortune. Take this by this example: While God moves the spheres, sometimes through fortune he stirs up a storm in the sea. The storm shakes the ship. Meanwhile, God moves the same ship through the soul of the pilot as well—that is, through the art itself continually depending on God. When, therefore, art directs the ship to a certain port, and the storm also carries it to the same, then art agrees together with fortune. But when the wind drives it one way, and art strives to lead it another, then art and fortune disagree, and finally either art yields to fortune, or fortune to art. <margin>B</margin> Meanwhile, the providence of God acts in both; each to an end known to Him alone, with which nothing is ever dissonant, tempering all things in hidden ways into the universal harmony of His body. Furthermore, that very arrangement of celestial concurrences, when it comes forth such that it will necessarily overcome art, is called Fate rather than Fortune; but when it is such that it can overcome the unskilled and be overcome by art, it is named Fortune instead. Nor should you doubt that art can sometimes conquer fortune. For as fortune, so also art proceeds from God. Notice, however, where Plato disputes concerning "opportunity," which a great man about to establish new laws desires as greatly opportune for that purpose; under the name of that "tyrant," he signifies the younger Dionysius, and himself under the title of "lawgiver," and indicates that the full favor of fortune was lacking to him. Likewise, that Plato in Sicily, in the presence of a certain Dionysius, began the prefaces of these laws, as can be understood from his letters; but that he perfected this work of the laws after Dionysius was expelled. Finally, through these sayings, he vindicated his return to Sicily from infamy. Know, moreover, that Plato in that journey and return contended for nothing else than that, while the prosperity of Dionysius remained safe, violent tyranny might be converted into a moderate kingdom. Among these things, however, where he speaks of the temperance and prudence of the prince, remember that Plato distinguishes moderate temperance from prudence, <margin>D</margin> and likewise discerns moderate prudence from wisdom in a similar way; but he often calls consummate temperance "prudence," and sometimes names absolute prudence "wisdom." Which indeed is clear in the *Phaedo*, and the third book of the *Laws*, and here, and often elsewhere. He brings forward, moreover, certain natural gifts of talent, similar indeed to virtues, but only then conducive to the duties of virtues when they have been rightly cultivated. Concerning which matter he disputes more widely in the *Republic*. You shall commit to memory meanwhile: such as are the characters of princes, such also become those of the rest of the citizens. Nor for any other cause can the character of citizens be changed more easily and quickly than from this. Likewise, that the teacher of the people who is prudent and <margin>E</margin> temperate is blessed, and blessed also is the people who hears the words flowing from the mouth of a teacher of that kind. Furthermore, neither will the Republic be happy, nor will good laws arise, before power concurs with wisdom and temperance in the governor. Therefore, divine aid must be invoked for establishing the city. Thus far, this fourth book has treated the duty of the lawgiver concerning the matter and the common form of the city. It proceeds next to a more distinct figure of this duty, asking whether the form of the city ought to be a kingdom, or a senate of the best men <note>aristocracy</note>, or the power of a few <note>oligarchy</note>, or a popular one <note>democracy</note>. Since indeed nothing among men can truly be called good unless it imitates the divine good, not without reason does he first explain the form of divine <margin>F</margin> government before he prefers some human governments over others: namely, being about to set the one more similar to the divine above the rest without controversy. He proves, moreover, that divine government is a kingdom, and a senate of the best men joined to the kingdom. And he judges that from all the citizens those ought to be chosen for governing, however many they may be, who so far excel the rest in prudence and temperance as men are accustomed to excel boys. And if anyone among the number of the chosen excels the rest by a nearly similar interval, he should be established as king. This indeed can be clear both from the present mystery of Saturn, and from a certain similar thing in the *Statesman*, and from the letters and the *Republic*. But so that the present mystery of Saturn can be more clearly understood, it is necessary to remember that the Platonists conjecture that the world is contained and led by a certain life and soul, <margin>G</margin> chiefly from three arguments: namely, from the firm bond of the diverse parts of the world, from the marvelous motion of the heaven, and from the perpetual generation of things under the heaven. They conjecture again that the world is ruled by a Mind from a certain triple order: namely, from the order which is seen both in the bond of the parts of the world itself, and in the motion of the spheres, and in the generation of things. Both indeed—namely, the soul and the mind—our Platonist briefly comprehends: "A Spirit nourishes within, and Mind, infused through the limbs, moves the whole mass." <note>A quote from Virgil's *Aeneid*, often used by Ficino to explain the World Soul.</note> They conjecture finally that both soul and mind are directed for ruling by the Good and the One itself, chiefly from this: that the connection of parts, the motion, the generation, and all the order of these three tend toward one and are directed toward the good. Wherefore under the Good itself a twin kingdom is contained: namely, of the intellect and of the soul. All antiquity calls the former the kingdom of Saturn, and the latter the kingdom of Jupiter. Which therefore feigns that Jupiter occupied the kingdom of Saturn, since, with both calling souls to their own kingdom—namely, the one to the intelligible good, <margin>H</margin> the other to the sensible good—only a very few souls betake themselves to the intelligible good and contemplation of Saturn, while very many flow daily to the sensible good and action of Jupiter. The ancients hand down that souls once lived blessed under the kingdom of Saturn, understanding this in two ways. First, indeed, while they lived among divine and angelic minds, before they fell into bodies. Then also as often and as many as, neglecting the "point" of life <note>the active/material focus</note> and loving the active life very little, give themselves with most ardent love to the contemplative life. However it is taken, in the intellectual life, they are blessed; in the animal life, they are miserable. It is added that under this misery they are so deceived that, since there are two planets in heaven, the first indeed the messenger of the higher Saturn, the second the messenger of Jupiter...

<summary>Ficino concludes his commentary on Book III of Plato's Laws by emphasizing the importance of temperance and music in statecraft, then introduces Book IV, focusing on the divine origins of governance and the "Age of Saturn" as a model for the ideal state.</summary>

# ARGUMENTS AND COMMENTARY

<margin>A</margin> ...of the former, they indeed praise the star of Jupiter, but disparage that of Saturn, even though the former incites one more toward temporary goods, while the latter recalls one to eternal things. But since man is a social animal <note>original: "gregabile animal"</note>, if he is segregated from common human commerce, he cannot maintain a moderate habit of living, and is forced, so to speak, either to descend below man or to ascend above man. Thus it happened that Saturn, the segregator of men, reported a crime and infamy among the ignorant—namely by the fault of those who, either by some inept mixture or perverse education, turn out such that when they are recalled by Saturn beyond the human level, they descend from humanity rather than ascend. But of these things more diligently elsewhere; let us return to the argument. Plato adds that Saturn once commended men, distributed into flocks, to the guardianship of demons <note>In this context, "demons" refers to *daemons*, intermediary spirits or guardian angels, not evil entities.</note>.

<margin>B</margin> This, moreover, is explained in several ways. First, indeed, that the Divine Mind divided the souls of men into various orders of stars from the beginning, as the *Timaeus* says, accompanying the number of souls. Regarding the difference of our souls among themselves, some among the Platonists think it is only numerical, others even specific <note>meaning a difference in "species" or fundamental kind</note>, so that there is one genus of our souls, and in it many species of souls, and also many under the same species. However they are distributed, they are said to be accommodated not only to different stars, but also to different demons. The mystery can be explained in another way: namely, that either from the beginning of the world, or immediately after the flood, divine providence ruled ruder men through the ministry of angels or better demons, until, having gradually become more skilled, they might rule themselves. It is consistent with reason that men are governed more rightly and happily by those above them than by themselves.

<margin>C</margin> Furthermore, it is explained in a third way: that daily, whoever chooses a way of life somewhat segregated from others and has been rightly educated, is said to migrate immediately into the contemplative and blessed kingdom of Saturn. But insofar as they are discerned into various rites under the office of contemplation, to that extent they seem to be separated into many flocks, and to be inspired and ruled by different deities according to the similarity of their lives. I pass over for the present the many schools of excellent philosophers, gathered like flocks under Saturn as their shepherd. Under Saturn, I say, in three principal ways: first under the divine and angelic mind; second under the soul of the first planet and its sphere; third under the body of the planet itself.

<margin>D</margin> But the mind itself acts, the soul completes, and the planet portends—it portends, I say, when in the great conjunctions of Saturn with Jupiter, Saturn himself rejoices either in his exaltation or his domicile, and as the lord of the conjunction is cherished by Jupiter, and uses the benefit of the Sun, Mercury, and Venus. Thus he brought forth the magic of Zoroaster and his followers—or rather the discipline of portents—also the theology of Trismegistus, the mysteries of Orpheus, the secrets of Pythagoras, Socratic holiness, and Platonic majesty. We have found this to be so by certain manifest arguments. Hence Plato also affirms in the present book that Saturn is the lord of those who possess mind. He demonstrates that governance of this kind under Saturn emerged as royal and aristocratic. Indeed, he asserts that the human race was governed by God himself as king through chosen and excellent demons. Many call these angels, and Plato in the *Critias* calls them gods; he indicates the ease of governance both here and in the *Critias*, saying that men were governed by a certain hidden inspiration of persuasion, and are to be governed similarly whenever, being vacant from inferior movements, they subject themselves to the superior ones to be led. In these things Plato warns: first, that divine providence is never lacking to men, provided they are not lacking to themselves. Second, that the human character becomes lascivious and proud in the greatest license and power. Third, just as beasts cannot be governed by beasts without a certain human shepherd, so neither can men be governed by men without God as leader; and as long as any mortal shall dominate without God, life will be laborious and miserable, as if any guardian of the city would watch in vain unless God himself guarded the city. Fourth, that the distribution of the mind itself is the law, and it must always be obeyed in every private and public governance, so that through our mind we may be happily led by the divine mind. Fifth, that no constitutions are to be called laws unless they procure the common good of the whole city. Sixth, that the offices of magistrates and especially of divine worship ought to be committed to those who most observantly obey the laws. Seventh, that destruction is prepared for the city in which the laws do not dominate the magistrates, but the magistrates dominate the laws. Eighth, that young men for the most part see these things obtusely, but old men perceive them acutely, unless perhaps God sometimes approves youthful piety or reproves elderly impiety. Plato now uses many words to instruct the legislator himself for his office. He then addresses the people who are to receive laws of this kind, so that they may both receive them more willingly and keep them more fervently. He exhorts them to sacred laws first, and through those to human laws discovered and confirmed by the divine. But with the exhortation he mixes veneration and terror, saying that God, the craftsman of the whole world, embraces the whole in himself, and therefore inspects every single thing lest anyone trust that he can hide by transgressing; and He is revolved through all things, lest anyone hope to escape His hands after a crime. He shows Him to be the founder of all laws where he says: *He defines and accomplishes right things*, that is, He determines individual things by a certain right rule of law. He determines, I say, first for individual things the mode of their nature: what, of what kind, how many and how great they are, and where, and when, and how they are moved. Then for souls, what is to be done or what is to be avoided. It is established that a determination of this kind is the law of all things in the power of God, the author of all, and that it is sanctioned by God himself by the same act by which all things are understood and made by Him—namely, by a circular act, which the *Timaeus* says is natural to divine intelligence, looking back at itself from itself, and by looking at itself, always beholding all things. But perhaps beyond the circular motion, so to speak, intimate to God, he also insinuates a straight motion, that is, the procession of things from God and through all things

<column-break/>

A ...he signaled that it depends on the circular. Likewise, where he says that God contains the beginnings, ends, and middles of things, understand that God is the efficient and final cause of things, preserving all and being present to all. And lest anyone think the law is in vain, he adds that judgment always accompanies it, by which both the observers of the law and the transgressors are discerningly distinguished, and what is most owed to each is effectively decreed. Because this judgment both powerfully discerns and decrees, an inevitable vengeance for sins and a reward for those observing follows. He says the divine law is best kept by those who most humbly subject their necks to the yoke of divine law, whose reward is judged to be future blessedness; but it is most rejected by the proud, who, as soon as they have deserted the law of God, are likewise deserted by God. Being deserted, they both sin more atrociously and are tortured more miserably. You, however, keep these evangelical and golden precepts stored in the depths of your mind. Because he says these mysteries consist of "ancient speech," we can understand this as Mosaic <note>referring to Moses</note>. We can also understand it as Mercurial <note>Hermetic</note> or Orphic, among whom we read many things of this kind, and those indeed most evident, which a grander argument now proves more recently. But if you read the Orphic hymns about Jove, the law, judgment, justice, and Nemesis, you will find all these things word for word. After this, Plato exhorts the people that each one should greatly study to be in the number of those who follow God, striving to please God in all things, and that he may attain this by rendering himself similar to God—similar, I say, through the purity of temperance, by which as a rule he may measure all his affairs exactly. Indeed, measure, as Pythagoras also said, is judged the best of all things, and makes the soul most similar to God. Since God is the measure of all things, especially for us, who ought to seek or flee individual things only insofar as they are judged to harmonize or disharmonize with the divine mind and will. Hence that saying in Plato’s letter: *To a wise man, God is the law; to a fool, lust.* But this text is read ambiguously here. For elsewhere it is read as I have translated. By these words, Plato seems to confute Protagoras, who said that man is the measure of things. His error is subtly confuted in the book *On Science* <note>The *Theaetetus*</note>. Elsewhere it is read not "as any man," but "if any man," in this manner: *God is the measure of all things for us, and much more if any man is, as they say.* You can explain this particle, "if any man is, as they say," thus: if any man is a measure, much more is God a measure; for we owe our living not to ourselves, but to God through whom we live. You could perhaps explain: *if some God is man*, that is, if he should ever become man—as they say, that is, the oracles of the prophets—which explanation, would that it were as accepted among Platonists as it is pious among many. But so that it may appear how much fruit the observation of laws bears, he adds that only to the observers of these is it permitted and expedient to make vows and sacrifices to the gods. But the prayers and gifts of others are rejected by God. This very thing, which is to please God, he says is the mark at which we ought to aim the individual actions of life like arrows. But the arrows for reaching this grace of God, he says, are the diligent cult of religion.

<margin>E</margin> In which he disposes the same grades which we read in the Pythagorean verses. For he commands here, as does the other, that we first worship all the celestial gods, especially those to whom the fatherland is dedicated as patrons; then the gods following under heaven. All of these he calls terrestrial. For it is Plato’s custom, even if he places all elements under heaven and all things in heaven in a celestial way, nevertheless to comprehend all things under heaven by the name of "earth," and all things in heaven by the name of "heaven" and "fire." By celestial gods, he understands both superior angels and the souls of the celestial spheres and stars. By terrestrial gods, he understands both inferior angels and the souls of the four elements. Third, he mandates that demons be worshiped, namely the purer ones, as interpreters of the gods to us.

<margin>F</margin> Fourth, heroes, that is, the souls of men accepted by God, separated from the body. In all these, he commands worship to be so distributed that greater gifts are conferred on greater deities, smaller on smaller, and equal on equal. Fifth, he commands that the statues of the ancestral gods, consecrated by laws, be not so much worshiped and adored as adorned and in some way honored. Since he began every exhortation to divine worship from the one God, he evidently shows that the other deities are called gods not through themselves, but by participation in the First, and are to be worshiped not for their own sake, but for His sake; especially since he says the entire cult of this kind is to be undertaken only so that you may please that One. Sixth, he commands that parents be venerated as vicars of God. Seventh, that relatives by birth and those joined by familiarity, and guests

<margin>G</margin> and strangers, be loved with a non-feigned charity by divine command. Among these is inserted an evangelical precept: namely, that an exact account of vain words must be rendered to the divine judge, whose angel presides over us as the vicar and minister of the superior judge, to recall us from base things and incite us to honest ones; and to nourish and delight those who consent with tranquility of conscience, but to vex those who dissent with perturbation of conscience. Where it delights, it is called "Grace" by the ancients; where it vexes, "Fury." And Grace is threefold, since the grace of the past, present, and future delights the good. Fury is also threefold, because it similarly tortures the wicked. And in both cases, it is called Fate, and a threefold Fate. It is also called Nemesis, especially by Orpheus, where she takes notice of the proud. Truly,

<margin>H</margin> the ancients, so that they might judge pride to be most of all dissonant to God, who exacts most humble obedience, said that the proud are punished not only by divine censure, like other vices, but also by indignation; and they introduced a specific deity for punishment of this kind, called by the name of Nemesis, who indeed *shows strength with her arm and scatters the proud in the imagination of their hearts.* Collect from all these many things especially four: law, judgment, justice, and Nemesis. Take an example of these in yourself. You have in your mind the law, dictating by a common norm what is to be done and what not, and that the honest is to be pursued, but the base avoided. You have also in your reason the judgment...

<summary>This page provides a Neoplatonic commentary on the "Age of Saturn," interpreting the mythological rule of Saturn as a metaphor for divine governance through reason and law. It emphasizes that true law must aim for the common good and that human happiness depends on aligning the soul with the "divine measure" rather than human whims.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentaries on Plato’s *Laws*, specifically concluding the analysis of Book IV and transitioning into Books V and VI. Ficino, a central figure of the Italian Renaissance, interprets Plato through a Neoplatonic lens, blending philosophy with natural magic and theology.</meta>

# MARSILIO FICINO

distinguishing by a certain discursive reasoning of arguments, discerning that which is inherent in this or that action, whether it be honorable or base. You have in the **will** a choosing **justice** which seeks to follow or fashion things in the way that **reason**, through the laws of the mind, has judged they should be pursued or avoided. You have in the **imagination** and its affection **Nemesis** <note>The Greek goddess of retribution/indignation</note>, who is incensed at the turmoils of actions and words and is rightfully indignant. Similarly, in God there is law, judgment, justice, and Nemesis, but in a divine manner. More distinctly, however, in God and the higher angelic beings, there is **Law**. In the reason of the World Soul, there is **Judgment**. In its will, there is **Justice**. In the lower angels or the mediating demons, there is **Nemesis**. However you distribute them, all these things serve the divine law through a certain wonderful connection for the reward of virtues and the punishment of sins.

### ARGUMENT ON BOOK V OF THE LAWS. (referring to page 604)

We see wonders happen daily: from the magnet upon iron, from amber upon straws, from lightning upon solid objects, from ignited sulfur in a bombardment <note>an early reference to gunpowder/cannons</note>, and from all of nature either in the motion of the heavens or in the skillful formation of things that are generated. We are indeed ignorant of the causes, yet we do not deny that the effects we see take place because of our ignorance of the causes. Again, that wonders are sometimes performed by our souls in oracles and other prodigies is witnessed not only by all history, but also by the authority of **Hermes Trismegistus**, **Pythagoras**, and **Plato**. And if we cannot all easily assign a certain reason for the astounding works of our mind, we nevertheless ought not to deny that these works have been done or can be done. We see that **fire**, which is more similar to heaven than the other elements, acts more wonderfully, so that it draws things into its own form in a short time (which other things hardly do in a very long time), nor does it suffer mixture; and when it seems to be divided, it divides, and extends its effect much further than the rest, acting at a great distance through light and in a moment. Truly, it has this from heaven, and heaven acts by the image of itself—that is, by light—which fire hardly achieves by its natural quality. For who would doubt that celestial beings, through their rays (both those hidden from us and those manifest), flow forth from themselves like images, always moving and forming lower things? It is almost no different than a face in a mirror, or a concave mirror focusing on dry material placed in its view. 

But come now, let us contemplate both the higher beings and the soul in this mirror. By as much as fire is more effective than the other elements, and heaven more than fire, so much more effective than heaven are the **spirits** who either give life to or move the heaven, or are companions of those who give life and move. Therefore, the superior spirits work upon our own spirits (as their companions) through the influences of their images alone, just as a face works upon a mirror; and by acting upon them, they form them and make them similar to themselves: to such an extent that the soul often works almost as wonderfully as the celestial beings are accustomed to do. Just as a mirror is prepared in five principal ways to receive images from a face—first by its glassy nature, second by its transparency, third by its smoothness, fourth by its straightness, and fifth by its position—so also are our souls prepared for the influx of the deities. First, because they are intellectual natures just as those are. Second, when through the intellect, they cling to them with undoubting faith. Third, through the will, they transfer themselves to them with most ardent love. Fourth, they hope firmly in them with their whole memory. Fifth, if they have a body both suited to them by nature and prepared by diligence, then instincts glide from the higher beings into our minds, just as from the strings of a lyre to other strings similarly tuned.

<margin>F</margin> Then come prodigies, dreams, prophecies, and oracles. I pass over what **Iamblichus** and **Porphyry** relate: that certain oracles were accustomed to be given through water, some through air, and some through fire—perhaps because they are sent by demons who are either of water, air, or fire. Perhaps also because in various places and times, through hidden causes, it happens that the affections of human minds are turned toward higher things and, having been turned, are formed from there. Certainly, our minds are distracted far too much into various things. But if ever they use their power in its integrity for a certain work—just as fire burns with the whole intention of its nature, and heaven acts with its whole influx—then Plato does not doubt that more wonderful things will easily come forth from our minds than from fire or heaven. **Avicenna** and **Al-Ghazali** <note>Arabic philosophers</note> do not doubt it either, following the Platonists in some way. But we dispute these things more extensively in our *Theology*. By these things, that Gospel saying about **faith moving mountains** is greatly confirmed; and many things are confirmed which Plato asserts in the previous book and this fifth one—indeed, in all the following ones—concerning oracles, so much so that the arrangement of a city, the form of a republic, or the sanction of laws is not established otherwise than by being approved through oracles. Truly, although he commemorates those oracles, he clearly grants his authority to other prophecies besides, which can perhaps be found to be truer. 

But let us now come to the specific argument of the fifth book. Since, therefore, our soul is a mirror of divine things, rightly after the worship of divine things described in the fourth book, he commands at the very beginning of the fifth that the **soul itself be worshiped** as a sacred thing. And he who imitated the Pythagorean verses in the previous parts, in the present also gladly follows his Pythagoras, who commands: *After the gods, most of all revere yourself.* How much weight such reverence has for the observation of laws, I cannot fully explain. But to put it briefly, it brings it about that whoever reveres the constant sight of his own soul as if it were a deity has a judge within himself; by whose law, even without written laws, he may direct his life most perfectly, and finally, out of love for natural law, easily do what others hardly do out of fear of written laws. Accordingly, while he disputes about honoring the soul, he delivers all the precepts concerning duties, both toward oneself and toward others, and toward all

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> virtues pertaining privately and publicly, which everyone ought to learn and master. After this, he puts an end to the introduction of the laws. Here it appears that the entire discussion of the laws is divided into three principal parts. First, into the **prologue**, extended from the beginning of the first book to this part of the fifth. Then, into the **disposition of the laws** themselves. And first, into the laws pertaining most of all to the republic and the magistrates. Then, to those regarding the individual actions of citizens. I believe you remember, moreover, that individual laws have individual preambles. In the beginning, the lawgiver should choose the purest colonists according to his power, and in the manner of shepherds, separate the pure from the impure. He should also purify the city, and unless the greatest necessity compels it, he should not introduce violence. He should equalize the wealth 

<margin>B</margin> according to his power, lest some be very rich and others beggars. He should beware lest anyone accumulate riches unjustly. Nor should he strive to make the city the most brilliant, but the **most just**. He should preach that **Truth** is to be venerated most of all among both men and gods. Likewise, hospitality toward strangers and indulgence toward suppliants. He should warn everyone that the soul is accustomed to be deceived and perverted by self-love. He should command that no one, being abundant himself, should allow his neighbor to go hungry. He should locate the city, if possible, in a central region, looking out for every convenience. He should divide the city into **twelve parts**, and the whole region similarly. But why into twelve parts? So that you may understand that such a great and laborious mass requires the help of the universe itself, which is distributed into **twelve spheres**. 

<margin>C</margin> Likewise, that the city is to be sought after the image of the celestial kingdom. For the celestial city is distributed into twelve signs <note>the Zodiac</note>, like twelve tribes. Nor is it without reason that he commends his city to the **twelve gods**, since twelve gods are said to preside over the twelve signs of heaven. Indeed, there are six gods and six goddesses: **Juno, Vesta, Minerva, Ceres, Diana, and Venus; Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Neptune, Vulcan, and Apollo.** Assign each to each: our members to the signs, and the gods to the signs. To **Aries** and our head, **Pallas (Minerva)**. To **Taurus** and our neck, **Venus**. To **Gemini** and human arms, **Apollo**. To **Cancer** and the chest, **Mercury**. To **Leo** and the shoulders, **Jupiter**. To **Virgo** and the flanks, **Ceres**. To **Libra** and the buttocks (to speak honorably), **Vulcan**. To **Scorpio** and the private parts, **Mars**. To **Sagittarius** and the thigh, **Diana**. To **Capricorn** 

<margin>D</margin> and the knees, **Vesta**. To **Aquarius** and the shins, **Juno**. To **Pisces** and the feet, **Neptune**. Understand through these things that the whole city ought to be one out of many citizens, no differently than one body is made of many members. Some deities are called masculine and others feminine for this reason: so that you may know that both those things pertaining to matter and passions, and those pertaining to forms and actions, are governed by the higher beings. But why does Plato consecrate the principal citadel of the city to **Vesta, Jupiter, and Pallas**? Understand that in divine matters there exist three fountains of all things: Vesta as the fountain of **being**, Jupiter of **living**, and Minerva of **understanding**. And in all these, help must be implored from the higher beings. Where Plato commends the partition of dwellings and fields into **five thousand and forty**, he shows 

<margin>E</margin> that a number of this kind contains in itself many very convenient distributions in succession. This will be opened up gradually in the following parts and can be clear even to one with moderate skill in arithmetic. You will note, where he discusses the common life of citizens, a wonderful precept concerning **evangelical love and charity**. Likewise, that the fatherland is to be honored more than one's mother. And when he says the fatherland is an immortal goddess, consider this said either of the divine soul of the terrestrial globe, or of the deity who is the patron of the fatherland, or of the celestial fatherland.

---

### ARGUMENT ON BOOK VI OF THE LAWS. (referring to page 613)

There are **three kinds of causes** by which different characters of men are formed in different places. These three kinds Plato briefly comprehends at the end of the previous book. I, however, judge it will be worth the effort to bind the text with the fifth book by this very matter. Let there be, therefore, a great difference in location for generating better or worse men. Let the cause be either **human, natural, or divine**. The human cause is law, education, and diverse custom. The natural cause is the diversity of elements and nourishment. 

<margin>G</margin> The divine cause is what I might call the divine heaven: the power of the stars and deities. For Plato indicates that just as some regions of heaven are ruled by certain stars and certain gods (that is, superior angels), so other regions of the earth are governed by certain **demons** and inferior angels. To this is added the opinion of the **astronomers**, matching the regions of the earth to the regions of heaven, and cities to the ascending signs. I pass over for now how much difference in character the variety of the personal demons of each man brings. That the powers of superior spirits flow into our spirits (however that may happen) we cannot deny, since we clearly see our bodies moved by superior bodies and constantly changed by the air in different ways. But if those spirits act upon our spirits, they act moreover upon our bodies. The passion of human bodies, whether it be brought in by those spirits or by superior bodies, overflows into the soul to the extent that the soul, by both acquired and natural affection, plunges itself into the body. But this is the difference: those bodies move souls through our bodies; but spirits move souls sometimes through bodies, sometimes through the souls themselves, and sometimes through that **spirit** which physicians often call the "knot" of the soul and body together. Remember, however, that all power and motion descending from the higher beings into us always leads to the good by its own nature, since celestial influxes are always toward the good. But you should not here [attribute] the sadness of more rigid men...

He emphasizes the internal "reverence for self" as the foundation of law-abiding behavior and discusses the astrological and spiritual causes of human character.</summary>
