# ARGUMENTS AND COMMENTARY

<margin>A</margin> ...and you might attribute stinginess to Saturn, or recklessness and ferocity to Mars, or fraudulent malice to Mercury, or lascivious loves to Venus. But what if the gravity of Saturn in us—due to a fault in the nature of our complexion, nutrition, or education—is turned into a harmful kind of heaviness? Similarly, if the magnanimity of Mars is turned into a boldness somewhat resembling magnanimity, or Mercurial industry into malice, or Venereal charity into lust? Does it not happen daily under the rays of the sun, which by their nature contribute to seeing and living, that some lose their sight and others their lives? And those rays which warm healthfully in the open air, do they not burn in hollow places? Just as an evil result occurs for an individual under the beneficial influx of rays due to an inferior nature, but not <margin>B</margin> for the whole universe; so under the powers of the stars (which are good by nature) and under the excellent gifts of the deities, a vice of the body or soul can sometimes arise due to a fault of inferior nature or habit. Truly, nothing is a vice or evil to the universe as a whole: just as in a harmony a second or seventh voice, heard alone, is dissonant, yet when joined to the others, they harmonize with the whole. The Platonists are accustomed to sometimes call the lowest demons "evil," because they allure us to the lowest level of generation and sensible good by their particular office, as they say. However, to turn away from the highest good toward the minimum is rightly judged an evil in comparison to the highest. I set aside for the present their claim that the highest demons lead to the good of contemplation, the middle to action, and the lowest to the good of desire; and that we can both use and abuse all of these: those who use them find good, while those who abuse them find evil. Plato calls them "indigenous gods of the fatherland," not because they were born there, but because they guard the citizens born there with a certain peculiar care. He says, moreover, that the blessed city is inhabited by gods and the sons of gods: understanding this partly as the heavenly Jerusalem, inhabited by angels and pure souls; and partly as the happy life of those who, he says in the *Phaedo*, inhabit the highest parts of the earth, blessed by the familiarity of the deities. After this, in the sixth book, he descends to the establishment of magistrates: namely, how many there ought to be, in what manner they are created, and what the office of each magistrate should be. He says that diligence in creating these is of such great importance that even the constitution of good laws without good magistrates will not only fail to benefit the city but will even be most harmful. He says it is necessary that both those who are to elect the magistrates and those to be elected must be most proven from youth, born of most proven ancestors, and must perfectly understand the customs of their fellow citizens. In these matters, you will note Plato’s wonderful prudence in the ordering of magistrates and their office in human and sacred affairs, in war and peace, in the city and the fields. You will recognize and approve of the best government as having something of the royal and the popular, established as a middle ground between a single ruler and the people. You will observe that in distributing civil duties, equality must always be preserved—not arithmetic equality, by which equal things are given to individuals by number or even measure and weight (which is often most unjust)—but rather geometric equality, through which the merits of individuals are considered. In this way, things are distributed to individuals so that the proportion of merits to merits is the same as the proportion of rewards to rewards; thus rewards are not equal to rewards, but rewards are equal to merits. Therefore, you will consider a twofold equality: both of reward to reward, and of the reward itself to merit. The former is often harmful and rarely useful (and then only if it happens by chance), while the latter is necessary every day. In this latter type, the whole principle of justice consists. This very principle is placed in the judgment of Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note>, and the knowledge of it is granted to few men and with difficulty; yet by this alone, however much of it is present in us, all things are preserved. Not without merit does he ascribe the office of this equality to the judgment of the supreme judge. Since He alone penetrates the secrets of all and therefore knows merits perfectly, He alone can perfectly render things equal to merits. He does this first in heaven, then in the universe, so that by this distribution according to the capacity of each nature, all things are made and preserved everywhere—a point approved by the ancients and confirmed in the *Gorgias*. But among these things, Plato again—as is his most frequent custom—focusing on the education of children, creates a peculiar magistrate for that purpose, and wishes him to be held as the most excellent of all the highest magistrates in the city: thinking that without the providence of cultivating the "seeds of childhood," the entire cultivation of the city would be in vain. You will notice here that the human disposition, if well cultivated, eventually turns out most gentle and divine; but if otherwise, then the opposite. But why does he say the human disposition can turn out more ferocious than wild beasts? Because that which has the greatest power for good can also have the greatest power for evil. Likewise, the best, when it is turned into its opposite by its own depravation, becomes the worst. He disputes this indeed regarding the republic. Furthermore, ferocity in a depraved man is increased by the machination of a most perceptive mind toward evil. Add to this that the subtlety of human spirits in anger is turned into fury. There is also the irritation of certain demons, which Plato indicates in his letter to the Syracusans, and which Homer frequently uses according to the opinion of the Egyptians, introducing heroes incited to anger and blood by the gods—that is, by demons. He commends again that number, five thousand and forty, as the most convenient for the partition of magistrates, dwellings, and fields: as it can be divided into many successive whole portions. Indeed, if you divide this whole number into two parts, a half will contain two thousand five hundred and twenty. If into three, a third part is one thousand six hundred and eighty. If into four, any fourth is one thousand two hundred and sixty. If into five, any fifth will contain one thousand and eight. If into six, every sixth is eight hundred and forty. If into seven, a seventh is seven hundred and twenty. If into eight, an eighth is six hundred and thirty. If into nine, a ninth is five hundred and sixty. If into ten, a tenth is five hundred and four. Up to this point, the 

<column-break/>

parts are common and whole. But if into eleven, an eleventh is four hundred fifty-eight, plus two-elevenths of a portion. But if into twelve, a twelfth is four hundred and twenty. Stop your foot here. But since he mentions sixty to us, if you divide that whole number into sixty parts, a sixtieth part will comprise eighty-four; and if by a certain conversion you make it into eighty-four parts, each part will hold sixty. Plato seems to make much of the fact that the number is divided twelve times into four hundred and twenty; and that this again is divided twelve times into thirty-five. But this is divided twelve times into two, plus eleven-twelfths of one part. And yet the number four hundred and twenty itself is multiplied from the number twenty times twenty-one. For the number twenty, replicated twenty times and once more, completes four hundred and twenty. He praises the number twelve, and that whole number which is thoroughly adapted to twelve, because there are twelve spheres of the world according to him: and twelve signs in the zodiac, and twelve parts in the elements. For each of the four elements is divided into three regions: the highest, the lowest, and the middle—differing not only in position but also in power. Add another "twelve-fold" of the elements, by which the four substances of the elements and the eight qualities are comprised. Of the qualities, four are more active, namely heat, cold, lightness, and heaviness. Since the <margin>C</margin> first two are principles of alteration, the following two are principles of motion toward a place. Four are "feminine," which are more subject to passion, namely moisture, dryness, rarity, and density. Iamblichus asserts that these are contained in the mysteries of the Egyptians. Add to this that in the twelve-fold number of months, the Sun, the lord of the planets, both completes his own course and produces various effects. Finally, he wants each part of the city to be considered consecrated to God, but specifically to the twelve gods—that is, the souls of the twelve spheres. Likewise to the twelve gods ruling the signs of the zodiac. Again, to the twelve orders of demons following the celestial signs. When he says the twelve parts of the city follow the circuit of the universe, perhaps he also understands the whole circuit of the eighth sphere to be completed in thirty-six thousand years. This number <margin>D</margin> is perfectly completed by three "twelve-thousands" of years. So that in the first twelve thousand years, you may understand (according to the opinion of the ancients) the youthful state of the whole world; in the second, the virile; and in the third, the senile. But more on these things opportunely in the *Timaeus*. This agrees with what he says in the *Phaedrus*: that the army of gods and demons under the leader Jove is disposed into twelve orders. He concludes here that the parts of the city—partly through the twelve-fold number of tribes and temples, and partly through divine worship solemnly renewed twice in each of the twelve months—are so prepared for the gifts of God that they are governed by the gods as if they were present. He wants the principal and public solemnities to be renewed twice, so that both the twelve-fold of the tribes and the twelve-fold of the rest of the city <margin>E</margin> and fields may be satisfied. When he commands that sacred rites be performed for the gods or the sons of gods, he wants the "gods" to be understood as the souls of the spheres, and the "sons" as the purer demons. He commands all these things to be done for the sake of Jove, the one prince of all. Nor should it be passed over in silence: the "twelve-folds" we mentioned pertaining to the universe are, as it were, represented by the "twelve-fold" proper to each man. For he seems to consist of four humors of the body, as many disturbances of the senses, and as many virtues. After the sacred rites of the gods, he descends to the sacred rites of marriage. There you will consider the laws and nuptial rites: the exhortation to marriage; the duties of husband and wife both toward each other and toward the children to be begotten and educated. You will note above all that it is not fitting to give <margin>F</margin> effort to procreating children while in drunkenness or other mental disturbance. On account of such a fault, children are born daily who are sick in both mind and body. You will also commit to memory the mystery where he says: "The Principle and the Deity implanted in men, if treated with the honor fitting to them by individuals using their gift, preserves all things." What then is the "Principle," and what is the "Deity implanted or residing"? The Principle is the Idea, the beginning of human formation. The Deity is the familiar demon, also the demon prince of generation, often signified under the name of Lucina <note>The Roman goddess of childbirth</note>. But why "implanted," or "residing," or "brooding"? So that you may understand the deity is not only present, but constantly within and nourishing: especially favoring, and by favoring, preserving, if he is gratefully worshipped <margin>G</margin> by those who use his gift. After the mutual duties of husband and wife, he consequently descends to the mutual duties of masters and servants. After these, by a certain usual art, he returns to the walls, temples, and palaces, which he says should have been treated before the marriage. There you will note especially that the courts of judges and the palaces of magistrates are placed closest to the temples, so that human judges, in judging, may always remember that they are judged by God while they judge men. Let the guardians of the city also remember that they cannot guard unless God guards. Likewise, nothing in the city, even the smallest thing, ought to be without a certain fixed order. For that which lacks order confuses other things that are ordered. Women's affairs especially stand in need of order and continuous care. Otherwise, if women's affairs are neglected, twice as much—nay, more than double—the detriment comes to the city than if the <margin>H</margin> affairs of men were neglected. Among these things, where the antiquity of the world is repeated: what is said about the principle of generation itself preceding us by an inestimable magnitude of time, understand this (if you observe Moses) as an inestimable number of days and hours. He concludes the book with the sentiment that we should restrain the triple impulse—namely toward food, drink, and sex—lest we ever be thrown headlong; we should restrain them with a triple bridle: namely fear, law, and true reason, and furthermore by the moderate use of honorable games from childhood. By which, through honorable solaces, we may be called back from base things and gradually provoked toward sacred studies.

# ON BOOK VII OF THE LAWS,
### an argument. for page 627.

In the seventh book, Plato returns with incomparable diligence to the first simple lessons of tender age—or rather, he moves forward with them. For he never, so to speak, departs from this subject, indicating that the entire good or evil of a republic consists in the good or bad morals of private citizens, and that these, furthermore, all depend on the good or bad education of early youth. He achieves this especially in the very first books, and again here in the seventh, acting in both places like a most diligent painter. But there he was sketching the outline; here, to use a painter's term, he is adding the color. Again, in the earlier books, he wished such diligence to be considered the "preamble" to the laws; here, however, he treats the form as the substance that must precede the laws. For he says that written laws will be useless unless such diligence has come first. Furthermore, both there and here, he proceeds from childhood discipline to that of youth and then manhood. It was not without reason that, after some laws concerning sacred matters in the previous sections, he proceeded immediately to marriage laws as if they were sacred, so that he might inaugurate the birth of a "divine animal" <note>The human being</note> from sacred rites. Soon after marriage, he prepares himself to shape children—not only those already born, but those being born, and even those yet to be born. In this cultivation of the human race, he is no less wise, foresighted, and accurate regarding women than a farmer is regarding the seeds of his crops.

Why do you think he says there is much more at stake in the female condition than the male? Likewise, that women ought to abstain from wine on the night children are to be conceived—indeed, even in the time immediately preceding, and throughout the entire year of conception—and from all things that disturb the mind? These points undoubtedly aim to ensure that nothing of the most exact care regarding human cultivation is overlooked. You will notice from this that Plato believed not only the man, but also the woman, holds the role of an "acting cause" in generating children. Although Aristotle differs from this in some way, many of the most esteemed physicians have agreed with it. Certainly, if everyone loves their own work, and for that reason a father loves his son more than he is loved by the son, and a mother loves the child more ardently than the father, one may guess the cause is that she, along with the man, is a maker of this work. This can also be confirmed by the fact that children are no less, and often even more, similar to their mothers than to their fathers. Such a specific and frequent similarity indicates that the offspring receives its substance not only from the father’s action, but also from the mother’s. For every cause strives to produce something like itself. Finally, since the male and female are of the same species, they have powers of the same nature. Therefore, both are effective in perfecting a form of the same nature, even if not in equal measure, at least in a similar way. But these matters pertain very little to the laws.

He touches, moreover, on a significant question regarding "black bile" <note>original: *atra bile*; the humor associated with melancholy</note>, by whose fault infants are fearful, difficult, and fretful. Regarding this very humor and its cure, we have spoken more diligently in the book *On Caring for the Health of Scholars*. As far as the present purpose is concerned, know that the melancholic humor in children does not come from their own constitution—which is actually very sanguine and "airy"—but from certain remnants of the mother’s menstrual blood that have putrefied in the child and then turned into black bile through a kind of "scorching." Added to the cause of childhood fears is the novelty of things, which makes heard voices seem like thunder and seen shapes seem like ghosts and lightning. Meanwhile, because reason is not yet awakened, it in no way distinguishes images from the things themselves; it leaves the soul to be stirred by the imagination at will. From this very fear, infants are perpetually in pain and complain. This is especially true since they are very easily offended by those handling them, hurt by the air, and agitated and vexed by the internal stirrings of nature, which labors greatly at the beginning of life.

For this reason, he orders that a nearly perpetual and rhythmic motion be used in caring for infants and youths. First, because having been "begotten by motion," they are preserved by motion. Second, because by such moderate motion of life, we resist the immoderate agitation caused both internally by nature and externally by the air. Third, because motion excites the natural color and vivifies the whole body equally. Fourth, it cooks and digests nourishment through the limbs. Fifth, it separates out superfluous waste. Sixth, it opens blockages and balances the humors. Seventh, it contributes to growth. Eighth, it renders the limbs both fit and solid.

However, it is not only by a certain moderation of equality, but also by the proportion of a certain "number" <note>rhythm or musical ratio</note> that motion ought to suit us. Regarding the power of music, we have discussed much in many letters. For now, it is enough to understand that if the soul is often pulled in opposite directions by music—namely toward pleasure or toward pain—it can certainly be led back from both to a certain middle habit between the two. And if the soul is recalled to rest from the motion of the body, and conversely provoked into motion from rest, it can certainly be led back by certain musical modes from a state lacking order to an ordered one, and from there to a stable habit. He says, both here and in the second letter to Dionysius, that this habit is both proper to God and safest for human life. Whether pleasure and pain consist in a certain motion, and in what way they cease, we have disputed more widely in the book *On Pleasure* and in the *Commentaries on the Philebus*. It will suffice for the present if we conclude in this manner: pleasures of taste and touch seem to be born in a certain restoration to the natural habit of the body. Pains, on the contrary, occur in a fall from that natural habit. Whether either happens by emptying or filling, by motion or rest, or by some alteration of qualities. Furthermore, the pleasures of smell, hearing, and use consist in a certain return to sensory order

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> from which we are disturbed daily by many accidents. Then, the pleasure of imagining consists similarly in a regression to the "imaginal" order, from which perturbation casts us down. Indeed, both the imaginal and sensory order are founded on a certain temperament of the "spirits" <note>The subtle fluids believed to connect soul and body</note>; as often as similarly tempered things are applied to these, pleasure arises, resulting from a mutual congruence of the sense and imagination with the things that flow in. After these, the joy of reason is born in a certain reformation: through which reason, which had become formless or deformed by bodily perturbation, is formed according to its nature and reformed. Finally, the joy of the mind is perfected by a reformation through which, by a certain intellectual intuition, it is sometimes reformed into the "Idea" from which it had fallen due to the tumult of a busy life. If you consider this induction correctly, you will see that human pleasure, in short, occurs in a certain return to a natural
<margin>B</margin> habit; and it is sought and desired not so much for the sake of the return itself, but for the sake of the habit. Therefore, if such a habit could be made perpetually firm, it would be the most desirable of all things. But why does it seem to anyone thinking about it that delight in perpetual motion is more desirable than that perpetual state? Because we are deceived by the imagination and opinion of a soul joined to a mobile body, and through such a union, it hungers for mobile pleasure. It would rightly neglect this in favor of the firmness of the natural habit if it were ever placed above motion. For if we truly tasted the flavor of the natural habit itself (outside of which we are placed while on earth), just as we taste the flavor of the motion tending toward it, we would undoubtedly prefer the habit to the regression by a long interval. Indeed, just as
<margin>C</margin> all grades of goods exist in a better way in the stable "reason" <note>The eternal principle or form</note> of the good than in mobile matter, so the reasons of all things to be desired are located in the reason of the habit rather than in mobile matter. Through this, let it be proven that the proper joy of God and divine beings consists in a state incomparably more pleasant than all motions. Prudent men ought to choose this for themselves and apply it to others, especially the younger ones. Furthermore, they should persuade everyone that the pleasure which comes from motion is not only brief, light, and mixed with distress, but also slides continuously into many long-lasting and immense pains.

He distinguishes rhythmic motion, through which we moderate the awkward movements of tender age, into two kinds:
<margin>D</margin> namely, music and gymnastics. For with the first we compose the spirit and the soul, and with the second the humors and the limbs. Under the name of music, he includes not only song and sounds, but also poetry and those things pertaining to the order of figures. Under the name of gymnastics, he includes all motions of the body in the preludes and games of contests and battles. But he understands dance and "salutation" <note>formal movement or greeting</note> as being in some way mixed from both. Then, with all these as if they were preludes, he diligently educates infants, boys, and youths—females as well as males—for the duties of both war and peace. He calls such basic lessons the "ancestral laws" and the "bonds of the republic." If these are withdrawn, the roofs of the republic will collapse like buildings without columns. He orders that every single thing in these matters be done no differently
<margin>E</margin> than as established by public rules; judging that from such small faults, all faults eventually arise in the republic, and that from the mutability of games, jokes, and ornaments, the change of laws and the republic also proceeds. You will note that change, except in evil things, is the most dangerous of all things, so much so that even if you change for the better, you will undergo danger at least for a time.

Among these things, he says one must sacrifice in the games to the gods, the sons of gods, and the "daemons" <note>Spiritual intermediaries, not "demons" in the modern sense</note>. To the pure daemons, I say, so that they may reconcile us to the sons of the gods. To the sons of the gods, so that they may render the gods propitious to us. Finally, to the gods, so that they may make us more ready for the gifts of the supreme God. Thus indeed ancient religion was accustomed: just as one passes through the spheres from sphere to sphere step-by-step with the body
<margin>F</margin> and sight, so one proceeds from the nearby divinities to the more remote ones in their own order in all things, especially venerating that which reflects the splendor of the Supreme One. I am not now speaking of civil (or rather plebeian) or poetic (or rather insane) superstition, but of the philosophical worship of divine things instituted by the ancient sages, as the known order of the universe had dictated. This alone Plato commends everywhere, truly mocking the other two. And where he mentions only two—that is, gods and the sons of gods—he understands daemons and heroes as the "sons." But where he counts together gods, sons of gods, and daemons, he understands "gods" as the divinities above the spheres, "sons" as the divinities in the spheres, and "daemons" as the divinities below the spheres.

After this, where he commends the
<margin>G</margin> discipline of lawful games, he says that games should be established for the sake of the serious-minded rather than the opposite. He adds that human affairs, if compared to divine ones, are worthy of no "study"—that is, they should be judged of no esteem, no love, and not as serious things, but as trifles. If, however, they are compared to natural things, he agrees they are to be highly valued. Then he says the best thing has happened to man: that he has been allotted a nature fit for and devoted to games—namely, for the solace of a laborious life, and to gradually acquire discipline through appropriate games. Because the soul makes a circuit through various forms of living, like a "playing dance," they think this is best for the universe. Again, it is also best for the whole nature of the soul,
<margin>H</margin> so that whatever lies hidden in its power may be brought out into the light by a certain alternation. But why does he not say that other animals are also the "playthings of the gods"? Because they are not so familiar to the gods that the gods would play with them. Nor are they compared to the gods, since they do not compare themselves to God, nor do they ever measure divine things, which would force them to lie about them as we do. And certainly, if it is for God to laugh, let him laugh at the human "game" attempting to measure the immeasurable. Consider here Plato’s words: "those things which we have narrated from dawn to this hour, not without a certain inspiration of the gods, seem to me somewhat similar to poetry." In this, he signifies that all his writings up to that day—that is, the seventh book—are in some way divinely inspired and poetic.

<summary>Ficino explains Plato's emphasis on early childhood education, physical movement, and music as the foundation of a stable state. He also discusses the metaphysical nature of pleasure as a return to a natural "habit" or state of being.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary and arguments for Plato's *Laws*, specifically focusing on the transition from Book VII to Book VIII. The translator, Marsilio Ficino, is reconciling Platonic theology with monotheistic principles.</meta>

# ARGUMENTS AND COMMENTARY.

The figures are so arranged that they are to be interpreted allegorically for the most part. He hints at this same thing immediately after the beginning of the *Phaedrus*, so that we may know that both the works he composed in his youth and those in his final old age savor greatly of poetry. For this reason, he says in his letters that his mind can be understood by no one, or by very few, and then only with difficulty through a certain prophetic sagacity. Furthermore, contemplate here how diligently Plato restrains unbridled youth, how much he detests sleepiness, and how he commends wakefulness; how appropriately he assigns the duties of each age, ordering that during play, letters should first be taught. Then music. Third, gymnastics. Fourth, arithmetic. Fifth, geometry. Sixth, astronomy. In the seventh place, he locates dialectics—that is, metaphysics—at the end of the *Laws* and the *Republic*. 

Because he says that God never fights with divine necessity, but does fight with human necessity, distinguish that one necessity is in the natural order of things itself, as it was divinely instituted, so that things are of such a kind, so many, and so great; they act thus, are moved thus, these precede, these accompany, those follow, some are together, and others are apart; and as they are, so also must they be judged. The other necessity is in a certain chance departure from the natural order, where something appears deformed, monstrous, discordant, or dissolved. God does not fight with the first necessity. For His chief will consists of necessity of that kind. But does He fight with the other? Certainly, God fights nowhere, for what could resist the Almighty? Nevertheless, He is imagined to fight for this reason: because this [disorder], having fallen further from the divine likeness, falls into a deformity most unlike God, as if now rebelling; but meanwhile, it is reduced to order at some time by God, as if He were resisting and conquering it in wondrous ways. 

Notice after this a saying of no small importance: Ignorance is not the worst of all things. Rather, the worst is the skillful knowledge of many things acquired badly. And if you also notice the preceding sentence, which names man as both God, spirit <note>original: *daemon*</note>, and hero, you will recognize by what reasoning Plato can be explained when he says the human soul passes into various species; but this is treated more broadly in the *Theology*. 

Furthermore, where he exhorts the youth toward mathematical doctrines, he rebukes the Greeks because they all erred in geometry and astronomy. In geometry, because they thought any dimension was commensurable with any other. That this cannot be so was first discovered among the Barbarians <note>Ficino refers to non-Greeks, likely Egyptians or Babylonians</note>. In astronomy also, because they said the planets "wander" <note>The word "planet" comes from the Greek for "wanderer"</note>, when nevertheless in divine things there is no error. Likewise, they named the motion of the swiftest things the slowest, and the slowest the swiftest. To lie against the dignity of the gods through ignorance born of negligence, he judges not only foolish but profane. 

But he most condemns the error of the Greeks against the will of divine providence, who say that God Himself, the author of the world, and the origin of the world itself, and the cause of those things in the world, should not be investigated—as if this investigation did not pertain to piety. Yet it is the most pious of all things, as it is especially in harmony with the divine will, which both arranged the universe in that order which would always entice such investigation, and created the mind itself most greedy for this investigation. 

That Plato himself thought true piety was situated chiefly in the worship of one God, we have proved elsewhere, and we confirm it at present through his preceding words. For even if he often says in the plural number that "gods" are to be worshiped, he concludes finally in the singular number, and that God Himself is worthy of every blessed study with singular worship. Furthermore, in the preceding parts, he gathered all the magistrates who would create judges into the temple at the very beginning of the year. He made the beginning from the summer solstice. Do not let it disturb you that he says "on the calends <note>the first of the month</note> nearest following the solstice." Consider that said for the sake of a more certain beginning for the people, but the true beginning for him occurs properly at the solstice itself. This may be explained allegorically: when the light of the sun—that is, the light of God—is received by us more directly and abundantly, then truly occurs the beginning of living, thinking, and judging; and for the sake of this one thing, all together in one temple—that is, in one religion—should worship whatever they worship. He says in the books on the *Republic* that the light of the sun is the image of the one Father of all, and as it were His likeness placed in this mundane temple by the Father of all. What more? He teaches elsewhere often that one God is to be adored above all, for whose sake the other divinities are to be worshiped; he demonstrates this clearly in the letter to Dionysius, and again to Hermias, and in the *Parmenides* (which deals entirely with the One), and in the *Timaeus* (which produces all things from the One), and in the *Philebus* (which measures all things by the One), and in the *Epinomis* (which reduces all things to the One).

# ON THE EIGHTH BOOK OF THE LAWS,
### Argument. For page 642.

What we have just asserted concerning the chief and singular worship of one God from many testimonies of our Plato, we can furthermore confirm without controversy through the *Phaedrus*, *Gorgias*, *Protagoras*, *Statesman*, *Critias*, and the fourth book of the *Laws*. For in these he subjects the entire "synagogue" of the gods, so to speak, to a single King, who commands individuals as He wills, justly distributing different duties to different beings, and dispensing human affairs through them in order—not as if He were absent from here, but as appears in the fourth book of the *Laws*, rather because He wills it so. Therefore, Plato orders first that God be adored for His own sake. The following ones, who are called participants of Him and "divine," are to be loved as being more like Him. They are to be honored as deputies, and even heard as advocates and conciliators, and as interpreters of the divine mind. Finally, they are to be listened to as heralds of the divine majesty.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> He wishes temples to be built in the city, and he distributes the city itself into twelve parts like a sacred shrine. Just as God Himself constructed the world as a temple for Himself, adorned with the choirs of the twelve spheres, and fortified with priests—that is, spirits endowed with reason, praising God everywhere. Plato, imitating this divine temple to the best of his ability, admits many gods into his temples, just as God Himself admits many into His; and he arranges various images, just as God placed the stars in heaven as if they were statues of His angels. Furthermore, among many altars of many beings, he consecrates the first altar to the First; just as among the stars, God chose the sun as a statue peculiar to Himself, as Plato says in the *Republic*. Of which it might perhaps seem to be said: *He set his tabernacle in the sun.* <note>A reference to Psalm 19:4</note> Concerning sacrifices and statues, it will be treated more diligently elsewhere; but to speak summarily for the present, he wishes the first God, as having nothing of matter or similar nature, to be worshiped with the 
<margin>B</margin> mind alone. To the following divinities, he permits victims and sacrifices to be applied in the manner the law of the fatherland orders. Hence the theologians of the gentiles, in the rites of the celestial and unknowable divinities, introduced figures, lights, and many things pertaining to use. In the rites of the aerial spirits, they added musical harmonies, odors, and vapors. But in the sacrifices of the aqueous and terrestrial ones, they used those things which pertain to taste and solidity. Therefore, it should seem a wonder to no one that Plato, so grave a philosopher, promulgated all his laws—but especially the sacred ones—only after consulting the oracles.

<margin>C</margin> **Response.** At the beginning, it seemed that the times had to be indulged. It was indeed necessary to strengthen human affairs by a certain divine counsel and authority. It was impossible in that age for men so born and so educated to be preserved in divine reverence by any reason utterly foreign to their customs. Then, the most wise Plato judged that even if impure spirits could deceive men through oracles, nevertheless, minds abstracted from the body for the sake of divine reverence, being now pure, might be suddenly seized by pure divinities; and just as wood which the wind has by chance dried out is often soon ignited by the nature of fire, similarly, souls through a certain religious rite (though less approved among the wise) having performed their duties, might be seized in hidden ways by a better divinity; so that those who did not know how they ascended into the mind itself apart from the senses, might now be happily 
<margin>D</margin> ignited from on high. Nor does Plato wish you then to attend to the rite by which you worship divine things, so much as for whose sake you worship. For if you do it for the sake of the highest King of all and with a desire for eternal goods, it is probable that from wherever and however you began, you will at some time, approaching closer to the highest through worship of this kind, either be surrounded by His immense light or at least be saved by His exuberant goodness. Therefore, relying on such confidence, Plato consults the oracles about making laws and sacrifices, and he prescribes that daily one of the magistrates should perform sacred rites publicly: first for the safety of the fatherland, then for his own and that of his people. Following a certain order after the rudiments of youth taught in the seventh book, he soon descends to sacred matters in the eighth; as one who wishes it to be understood that 
<margin>E</margin> men are for this very reason rightly instructed from their first years, so that they may both wish and be able to participate rightly in the sacred rites. But if anyone, either a caviller or a fearful person, dreads the presence of so many gods and spirits in the Platonic city, he is equally permitted to enter the Peripatetic <note>Aristotelian</note> city, which is void not only of spirits and gods, but even of God. But truly it is worthwhile, having set aside superstitious frowning and resentment, to choose the better things from all, and to approve Platonic piety; nor should one demand that he was a Christian, whom only the interval of time prevented from being a Christian. The first sacred rites are twelve, on the Calends of the months. The second are also twelve, in the middle of the months. The third are 
<margin>F</margin> three hundred and sixty-five, namely the daily ones. The chief ones are for the celestial gods; the middle ones for the terrestrial, namely for the gods covering the area under the moon. For he calls all things under heaven "terrestrial." The lower ones are for spirits <note>daemons</note>. The lowest for heroes. He thinks it necessary that the sacred rites for all these be distinguished into twelve kinds. Since according to the figure of the spheres, which is a grouping of twelve, even in any sphere the spirits and heroes are distinguished by twelve. He orders the commemoration of the solemnities and their distinction to be declared to the people every year in the last month, which by common custom we take as February. But especially in the Platonic manner, the month before the summer solstice. 
<margin>G</margin> He rightly dedicates the last month to Pluto. For Pluto is properly providence, both separating souls and judging them once separated. He says, moreover, that the conjunction of the soul with the body is not better than separation. Understand this regarding the decaying body, and insofar as it is decaying, not regarding the celestial body or one similar to heaven; to which kind of body it is better to be joined, but to this one, insofar as it is decaying, it is not better. And if it is said to be worthwhile to be joined to this one too, it is to be said not for its own sake properly, but for the sake of another. But of these things, more at length in the *Theology*. But do the Platonists sacrifice even to the lower spirits? Some do to these as well, partly because they preside over natural duties, and partly lest they harm through envy. But Plato would by no means have conceded this. Since he orders sacrifices to be made only for the sake of purifying the mind and for the veneration of the first God. He affirms that a city using divine counsel in its laws will be happy. He adds that it pertains most to the happy life of both the citizen and the city that it neither inflicts injury on others nor is affected by injury. Both can be 
<margin>H</margin> attained through virtue. And lest the city be affected by injuries, he established sacrifices in which divine help is implored, and solemn and festive games are frequented, imitating warlike battles as much as possible. In which he wishes both females and males to be exercised for battle; and in each, the left hand as much as the right. So that the city may be whole and equally useful from both sexes, and anyone may be most complete from each hand being equally useful. Among these things, you will note how much he detests greed, which is especially harmful to the city because it twists minds occupied with private and base gains away from the care of public safety. You will note again how much caution—

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s introductory commentary on Plato’s *Laws*, specifically concluding the summary of Book VIII and beginning the argument for Book IX. # MARSILIO FICINO

<note>original: "MARS. FICINI"</note>

...through education, he admits Music, dances, and poetry into sacred and warlike games. Next, he asserts that only that government is legitimate as well as secure in which a willing ruler commands willing subjects. But since loves often arise in gatherings of youthful games—and those indeed of the most shameful kind—he therefore most diligently prescribes that they must be countered here. He has already partially countered them where he removed gold and silver from the citizens, educated them in constant labors, and subjected everyone, especially the youth, to the eyes of judges who are everywhere looking around at their behavior. He considers these three remedies to be very healthy against the disease of wantonness and insolence. 

He also encounters a fourth present remedy: namely, that the magistrates, who are the helpers of the laws, should daily spread a reputation through which everyone, by common consent, becomes accustomed to thinking that intercourse against nature is no less shameful, nor held in less hatred by God, than intercourse between children and parents. Indeed, Plato thinks that the consensus of common reputation has a wonderful power over morals. In these matters, you will hear that he lives happily who overcomes pleasure, and unhappily he who is overcome by it. You will also hear a precept for abstinence that is most healthy, highly approved by the Apostle Paul: <note>Ficino frequently links Plato to Christian scripture, here referencing 1 Corinthians 9:25</note> that if athletes abstain from pleasures out of a desire for physical victory, much more should all people similarly abstain for the sake of the victory of grace pertaining to the soul. 

Furthermore, he notes that there is a twofold benevolence: one produced by similarity of character, the other by a certain deficiency. When either becomes more vehement, it is called "love." Love also, as far as the present purpose is concerned, is threefold: for either the beauty of the soul is loved, or that of the body alone, or both together. Consider here how cautiously he proceeds in making laws; though in his dialogues <note>referring to the *Symposium* or *Phaedrus*</note> he sometimes indulged the honorable lover of physical form, here he indulges nothing. Indeed, he evidently exterminates the love of the body alone. As for the love of both joined together, however moderate, he does not dare to admit it into the laws. Finally, he seems clearly to approve only love toward the soul. 

Then he denies that men of depraved nature are masters of themselves, and not without justice. For whoever, departing from reason, loses the rational nature of man, surely also loses his freedom—which is the gift of reason—at the same time. Yet he does not lose his guilt while he sins as if driven by impulse, since he himself gave cause to a necessity of this kind. However, he calls those who are the opposite of these "men of integral nature": those who worship God and, among human things, fear infamy most of all; they do not love the beauty of any body, whether their own or another's, but rather the beauty of the soul and its character. 

As for what he said earlier—that it is the duty of God to resist such crimes if these things could be ordered by Him—understand it this way: it is the property of God, the ordainer of natures, to restore to order those things which have collapsed from the order of nature. This is especially true since many are of the opinion that the soul fell into such crimes not so much through the senses as by the instigation of certain demons, or had fallen from the beginning. But where he says, "if they could be ordered by God," he does not doubt divine power, but human capacity; God can indeed order things as far as it depends on Him, but man cannot be so easily ordered. God could also compel, if only He wished to drag by necessity the one He wishes to lead in a certain free manner. 

Soon he also mentions the banquets celebrated among solemn rites and games. Likewise, from the banquets, he moves to the diet and the laws pertaining to it. Appropriately, after the education of the soul and the laws pertaining to it, he now descends to the nourishment of the body and laws of that kind. Then he delivers laws concerning fields, boundaries, waters, fruits, flocks, and pastures, and similar things. But where he speaks of boundaries, he says the violator of boundaries is punished by "Jupiter of the Tribe and of Hospitality," <note>original: "Ioue contribuli atque hospitali"</note> understanding Jupiter as the one guardian of both the kinsman and the guest. And since overstepping the boundaries established by law and usurping another's domain is a characteristic of pride, he therefore says that Jupiter is stirred up to avenge this injury and rises up with most hostile battles—as if to say that God rises up against the proud not so much as a judge, but as an avenging enemy. 

After many constitutions, he says it does not pertain to the senior philosopher to describe every tiny law accurately, especially those pertaining to lawsuits and controversies over things. Instead, he should bring forward a few common laws concerning external matters, which interpreters may derive into every smallest detail of justice; but concerning morals and the discipline of the soul, he should treat them most diligently to the fingernail <note>a Latin idiom meaning "to perfection"</note>. And while he speaks of various craftsmen, he delivers three memorable precepts concerning them. First, that no citizen—that is, one who will at some time perform public duties—ought to be occupied with any craft, nor even his servant. For one cannot and should not practice two arts or studies. Finally, it is not fitting for a craftsman to preside over the craftsman of another art. He also wisely forbids citizens from exporting necessities and importing superfluities, and especially from engaging in retail trade, particularly for the sake of profit. Then he arranges the parts of the city, the streets, temples, and twelve forums; and for the forums, he imposes laws that are as sober as they are diligent.

# ARGUMENT ON BOOK IX OF THE LAWS.
## regarding page 651.

The ninth dialogue, after the common discipline of morals and the tradition of many laws, now approaches judgments. And quite appropriately so. For those who are learned in morals and instructed by laws are now able to judge; and those who did not obey the preceding instruction and learning

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> must now be judged. For in matters of punishment, this physician of souls has wisely striven thus far to preserve the integrity of the soul's health through healthy warnings; but now he strives to repair what has been lost by every means. But such is Platonic charity: merciful and grieving, he is drawn as if compelled to cutting and burning <note>a medical metaphor for surgery and cautery</note>. And he does this with such benign caution that he consoles the gravely ill with the sweetest words; he contends with words as if with incantations to make them healthy before he applies the medical hand. Even then, he applies it in such a way that the sufferer hardly feels it and conceives much more hope than pain, reporting not destruction from the pain, but health. A man of remarkable clemency, he punishes no one without consolation; <margin>B</margin> he destroys no one who is punished; he preserves everyone according to his strength, and those he punishes with death, he professes to free from the diseases of the soul—stopping a great and daily increasing evil of the soul with the minimal evil of death. He asserts it is better to depart from here than to live in an incurable disease of either soul or body. 

Yet he does not deprive anyone of this life unless he knows them to be incurable; nor does he want any punishment inflicted by a law, which is good, to tend toward evil. On the contrary, he holds that punishment itself is good for many reasons: both because it is just (and justice is good), and because it either purges a present evil or prevents a future one, and because in punishing one, it benefits many by example and purges the city of evils. To put it briefly, he everywhere mixes justice with clemency in a wonderful way; <margin>C</margin> he neither twists too harshly with rigidity, nor leaves anything unpunished through softness. 

Just as in the previous sections he prescribed divine duties before human ones, so in the present he wisely takes notice of sacrilege before other crimes. And while he shows how grave the crime of injured divine majesty is, he signifies, with God's inspiration, that no such thing was ever perpetrated by men as long as a certain divine grace flourished in them. But after that grace was lost because of other sins, men—now as if estranged from God—began to sin against God Himself through sacrileges, so that sacrilege itself is not only a sin but also the punishment for sin: a punishment, I say, not purging someone, but destroying them. For such a punishment is brought about not by the law, but by the transgression of the law. 

<margin>D</margin> As for his saying that the ancient lawgivers were sons of God, and delivered laws to heroes who were also begotten from gods: this must be explained through those things treated in the *Critias*, the *Statesman*, and often elsewhere. Here, "sons of gods" are understood as the gods below the Moon, some suited to governing one region of the earth, others another. We can also call these "angels" in the Platonic manner. Through these, under the name of Mercury in the *Protagoras*, he teaches that the human race received laws. Through these in the *Critias*, he also says the first men born from the earth received rights; and he calls those men "heroes sprung from gods," that is, progeny of the earth by the work of the gods. But those laws, he says in the *Critias*, were not written for the ears, but were infused from divine minds into human minds by a certain inspiration; and men lived happily under them as long as they obeyed. 

He adds that through the transgression of such laws, <margin>E</margin> men lost divine grace, and having lost it, they also lost happiness. Unhappy, they then broke out into sacrileges, and through sacrileges, they finally turned out most wicked and most unhappy. In these things, one may recognize the mystery of both that earthly paradise and the ejection from it. 

Consider also where he searches for the causes of sacrilege; three causes of grave crimes are assigned. First, the common fragility of men confirmed by habit. Second, demonic persuasion or suggestion. Third, a pernicious guilt branded upon them from ancient and unexpiated sins, stimulating them to the gravest crimes. This indeed seems very similar to "original sin," about which many theologians dispute much. Therefore, where the divine Plato, addressing the sacrilegious man, says: <margin>F</margin> "Neither a human evil nor a divine one drove you to sacrilege," understand "human evil" as human fragility inclined toward lower things, and "divine evil" as diabolical fraud, as they say. He denies these two not because they are not causes of sacrilege, but because they are not the *only* causes. For a third and proper cause of sacrilege is added to these, which he joins by saying: "But a deadly stimulus inborn from ancient and unexpiated sins." Through this, the soul—no longer human but bestial—sins against God through sacrilege, having no further regard for God, since it has already lost human reason, which is the image of divine reason. 

Soon, Plato encounters the first instigation to sacrilege <margin>G</margin> as if it were a nascent disease with three remedies, just as this disease arises from three causes. First, so that the monstrous impulse may be suppressed, he sends the person to sacred expiations, which in the Christian manner we can call by the names of penance, confession, alms, and fasting. Next, so that he may resist diabolical snares, he sends him to prayers and supplications, through which he may hold onto human nature by the help of the higher and liberating spirits. Finally, he commands that, avoiding the familiarity of evil men, he should adopt the company of the good. 

Furthermore, since he had ordered the fatherland to be worshiped after God in the Pythagorean manner, he rightly proceeds after sacrileges (which are perpetrated against persons or things consecrated to God) <margin>H</margin> to the punishment of crimes and offenses committed specifically against the fatherland, which he judges not only close to sacrileges but counts among them and punishes similarly. He judges these to be three: for to sin against the fatherland is to be held an enemy of the fatherland; both he who, disregarding the laws, reduces the government to human will and lust; and he who, though he could, does not help the fatherland in danger; and he who, either through avarice or some other cause, turns out to be a traitor to the fatherland instead of a son. Among these, he repeats the duty of the lawgiver. He wants this to be: that he should write laws not as a master to slaves, but as a father to sons; no less persuading than threatening, no less teaching than commanding, no less alluring than terrifying; so that the work of the legislator is not so much the prescription of mandates as it is of discipline...

# ARGUMENTS AND COMMENTARY

...whatever the method may be, to make citizens good and happy; but to punish the wicked is a matter of necessity rather than choice. And because the Platonic laws alone among human systems embrace all these things, they are the most perfect of all human laws and should be numbered among the divine rather than the human. It is not without reason that the beginning of this discussion started with God; then Plato adds that all these things seem to him to be divinely inspired. Finally, from this very discussion, one arrives by a straight path at the blessed temple of highest Jupiter—that is, heaven. 

But since a legislator must describe, and a judge must assess, different degrees of punishment for different degrees of guilt—not only in cases of sacrilege and parricide but in all other crimes—he introduces a most convenient distinction for discerning such degrees. Every habit is either of virtue or of vice. If it is of virtue, it is entirely voluntary, since it is acquired through free counsel, unhindered <margin>B</margin> choice, and the soul's own actions. But if it is a habit of vice, it is judged entirely involuntary. This is because it is a disease of the soul, just as an imbalance of humors is a disease of the body. No one would call a disease voluntary, even though one might in some way call voluntary those things which, contrary to expectation, bring on the disease. Furthermore, such a habit grows from hindered counsel, distracted choice, and from passions rather than actions. From these points is established that oft-repeated Platonic maxim: *Habits of vice are involuntary, and no one is wicked by choice* <note>original: "nemo fit sponte malum"</note>, just as no one is voluntarily sick, deformed, or destitute. 

After this distinction of habits follows the distinction of actions, which tend specifically toward the creation of either a virtuous or a vicious habit. If toward virtue, they are voluntary in the same way the habit of virtue is voluntary. But if toward <margin>C</margin> vice, they are called partly voluntary—because they occur with a certain consent of the soul and could have been avoided before they happened—and partly involuntary, both because they lead secretly to loss, deformity, and disease (which no one would want) and because they happen through a certain ignorance of the end and the outcome. Insofar as they occur through ignorance, they are judged to happen outside the will of reason. 

Distinguish them again in this way: Human actions pertaining to the law and the matter of judgments are reduced to five heads. They either sprout from the affects of desire, or break out from the impulse of an irascible nature; or they come from a simple ignorance, through which one is ignorant of things although he knows he is ignorant; or they happen through double ignorance, through which one both does not know the things and is simultaneously ignorant of his own ignorance—thinking, forsooth, that he knows; or finally, they proceed from a certain rational opinion—an opinion, I say, concerning <margin>D</margin> what is just and unjust according to the laws of reason. 

After such a distinction, he also distinguishes the rules of judgment, by which those who sin through desire are punished differently than those who sin through anger; and among these, it is discerned whether they trespassed deliberately or unintentionally. Furthermore, whether it was by force and openly, or rather secretly and by fraud. Then, whether the error was through ignorance, be it simple or double ignorance. 

Where he deals with the judgments of homicides, he brings up an ancient mystery concerning the slain taking vengeance on their slayers. Note that according to Plato’s opinion, disturbances <term>perturbationes: emotional disturbances or passions</term> pertaining to the senses can remain in the soul when it is separated from this body. Indeed, according to his view, there remains a certain primary substantial nature of sensing, the origin of the other senses, through which the soul both deploys the powers of sensing into these instruments while in this body, and when departing from it, folds them back into itself, or—to speak more Platonically—exercises them in the aerial body. Enveloped in this, it both enters and exits this world. 

The Platonists distinguish these things such that the soul dwells in this thicker body for a short time; in the aerial body for many ages; and in the celestial body through all ages. Why mention these? Do not wonder that disturbances survive in the soul of the deceased if the sense and memory of these things survive. The ancient theologians thought it probable that the souls of those suddenly killed, being unpurified, are agitated by disturbances; indeed, they even harass their enemies, which happens not only through human indignation but also through divine nemesis and a providing demon <note>The translator notes that "demon" here refers to a guardian spirit or tutelary deity, not an evil spirit.</note>. 

Our Platonic Maro <note>Virgil (Publius Vergilius Maro)</note> stands as a witness that, according to the opinion of the ancients, a vengeful sense and disturbance survive in the soul, and that it uses an aerial body. For what does he mean by: *And now my great image shall go beneath the earth*? <note>Aeneid 4.654</note> In a very Platonic way, he calls the primary nature of sensing the "image" of the rational soul. But why "great"? Because it is the source of the other senses and the common sense, and after this body, it uses a large body—namely, the aerial one. While it is somehow tucked into this [physical] body, it is narrow; once stripped of this, it expands into the wide, as the nature of the aerial element requires. Furthermore: *I shall be present as a shadow in all places; you, wicked one, shall pay the penalty.* He distinguishes between the "image" and the "shadow": he wants the image of the soul to be the sense in the aerial body, but the aerial body itself to be the shadow of the soul. However, he calls the earthly body a "blind prison." 

As for what he says in the judgments on homicide, especially parricide, regarding the return of the human soul into human bodies again—in which it often pays penalties exactly equal to the crimes conceived in a former life—this is an old opinion of the Magi and Egyptian priests. For they judged no purgatory for human crimes to be more fitting than that souls should eventually suffer in human bodies the same things they themselves did. Plotinus the Egyptian uses this reasoning in his books *On Providence* to solve the doubts that daily arise against divine providence and justice. For he says that what is not repaid by divine providence in the present life is repaid in another, specifically human life, in an exactly equal manner. It is repaid, moreover, even in brutes, into which the soul of a former human often becomes the soul of a brute. But in this last opinion, he seems to have stood alone. For it displeases the other Platonists that a soul proper to a human should ever become proper to a brute.

<column-break/>

<margin>E</margin> They agree, however, that they migrate back into other humans; although Plato does not hold this as certain, he holds it as very probable. As for the idea that it migrates into beasts, he recounts this often, but he tells it so ridiculously and with such uncharacteristic lack of gravity that he clearly demonstrates the thing itself is to be denied. One should look for an allegory: namely, that you should understand "passing into a brute" in two ways. First, into the affection, imagination, and habit suitable to a brute. Second, into a dwelling and association among wild beasts for a time for the sake of punishment. For the ancients think that a brutish association and affection is merely a punishment; but the return into a human, where equal and similar things are undergone, is not only a punishment but a purgatory. 

After this, falling opportunely into a mention of the necessity of law, he asserts that law is necessary for the human race. For without laws, man would differ in no way from the most atrocious wild beasts. He gives the cause for this: no man's genius is so constituted by nature, he says, that he sufficiently knows all things that must necessarily be known for the public good; or if by chance he does know, that he is always able and willing to do that best thing which he knows. But if by some divine grace a certain mind should arise among men that entirely knew the public good and nobly and always intended toward it, there would be no need for laws for him or his country at that time. For a true and free mind is superior to every law and would rule all by its own right. But since that is granted to no one's genius, he concludes that one must necessarily live under laws. 

He also says that the pursuit of one's own good utterly dissipates a city, but the pursuit of the public good connects it. Likewise, he says a ruinous plague dominates a city where judgment by magistrates is either traded or clamorous. And where he says a "familiar demon" often resists many evils—if you shudder at the name "demon," call it an "angel," as Plato would allow. And remember that our demon or genius is not only, as some think, our intellect, but a divinity. 

He soon commands that elders be so revered with paternal respect that even if beaten by them, you ought not to be angry, but bear it patiently. But the "birth-gods" <note>original: "natales deos"</note> he commemorates here we should not take in the astronomical fashion as ascending signs or the planets that are lords of the houses, but as the Idea of the human race as a principle, and the demon as the guardian of our life. Finally, he warns that the indignation of those above and the punishment of those below are to be feared. He warns that death is not the ultimate punishment, but that beyond it are the punishments of the underworld, and that these are told with absolute truth.

### ON BOOK X OF THE LAWS,
### Argument. to page 664.

<margin>F</margin> THE PREFACE of the tenth book supplies the epilogue of the ninth, advising that judgments concerning violence against property must be treated after the judgments concerning violence against the person arranged in the ninth. But since no violence is harsher or more intolerable than that which is inflicted with a certain contempt, he decrees that insults and injuries to the person or property born specifically from contempt should be selected for their own chapters; and these under five heads. They are committed either against public sacred things, or private sacred things, or against the reverence due to parents; or against the excellence of a magistrate, or against the civil and ancestral dignity of some citizen. These, therefore, to be judged most exactly, he commits to other authors of laws as well as to magistrates and judges. 

After these, he distinguishes those things done in contempt of the gods from the rest, as being more grave than can be said; in these, the entire intention of this tenth book is occupied. But first, he wishes to point out the difference between sacrilege and impiety. He calls sacrilege "robbery," whether a thing or a person consecrated to the powers above is snatched away. And that is contained as a certain species under the genus of impiety itself. For beyond sacrilege, many other things are included under impiety: things thought, said, or done in contempt of the gods, whether committed, permitted, or even omitted. 

And lest anything be hidden from us, impiety also includes all familiarity and communion, whether in food or words, entered into with those who are barred from sacred rites because of nefarious crimes; for being contaminated, they contaminate others even by their proximity. Regarding this matter, he treats it at the end of the ninth book in such a way that he seems to have prophesied the excommunications made daily by our people, driving the profane from the communion of the Church. 

Therefore, our physician, intending to most diligently purge souls languishing with the disease of impiety, first searches for the causes of this disease. And while he inquires, he delivers a Gospel-like sentiment. For whoever, he says, believes concerning God according to the laws, will be religious, and will never act or speak anything profane. How rightly he began here with faith—and with faith to be applied to the laws? But let not the number of gods disturb you, I pray, whom the number of angels does not disturb. For <margin>H</margin> many gods can do no more in Plato than many angels and many blessed ones can do among us. 

But what do certain sacred and most ancient laws say about the gods—that is, about God and those angelically serving God? Truly, three things. First, that these gods exist. Second, that they provide for all. Third, that they justly repay rewards and punishments according to merits. In the faith and observance of this very sentiment, all piety consists. Who, then, is impious? He, clearly, who will either deny that such gods exist; or if they exist, that they provide; or if they provide, that they repay justly—that is, to think that the powers above, in the manner of human judgment, can be easily appeased by gifts alone, even those brought by the unjust. Plato, therefore, intending to expel the three causes of the disease of impiety, will prove that there are gods: both those who are in the world as rulers of the world's spheres, and those who are above the world as contemplators of the highest God. He proves...
