# MARSILIUS FICINUS

It will be the duty of constant justice to weigh rightly in the balance and scale not outward gifts of the hands, but the inward merits of souls. Finally, by this doctrine, as if by a certain preamble to the law, he will discourage everyone from all contempt of divine things and exhort them to piety. Furthermore, he will terrify and torment the impious with the threats and lashes of the laws. In the beginning, he indicates that gods exist by two common arguments. The first he derives from the universal genus of things, the second from the human species. The first, therefore, is of this kind: we have found that order everywhere proceeds from reason, and indeed an uninterrupted order nowhere and never exists except from a powerful reason; likewise, the most advantageous order comes from the best reason. Since, therefore, both the arrangement and the progression of the universe are most orderly, and are always and everywhere such, and this indeed not without a certain wonderful advantage, it is necessary that the world be arranged and moved by the best and most powerful reason. And since the universe is one, and one does not truly come from diverse things except by one, it follows that there is one supreme reason of this kind. Furthermore, there are many divine reasons under the supreme divine reason, just as in a single worldly work rationally ordered, there are many spheres distinct from one another in species and power, and all are rationally ordered: so much so that in a certain way many worlds seem to be contained within the most ample circumference of the one world. Therefore, in like manner, many rulers of narrower worlds, as it were, arranged in succession, are encompassed under the one ruler of the most ample world. Who surely, since he is not only the ordainer but is himself, so to speak, immense order, rejoices much more in the ordainer than in the ordained. Wherefore, if he is undoubtedly delighted by many ordered things in the universe, he is also pleased by many ordainers. For the most excellent greatness of the most ample king consists in this: that he has beneath him not only lowly servants, but also many and great kings. The second argument for the same point, derived from the human species, is of this kind: the natural instinct of any species cannot be in vain. Also, the natural judgment of the most perfect species of animals ought not to be entirely false. Since, however, the human species, the most perfect of animals, is everywhere and always carried toward religion by a natural instinct and immutable judgment, it is necessary that there be higher beings who are worshiped by religion, and that souls survive their bodies, which is indeed the principal foundation of religion. Pay attention to Plato's saying: that arguments concerning divine matters, even if sometimes not overly sharp, are nevertheless true. Likewise, note two occasions for impiety: intemperance, namely the lust for bodily pleasures; and again, ignorance arising from the absurd opinions of certain poets and natural philosophers <note>original: "physicorum"</note>. He says the poets erred in three ways regarding the gods: first, that they sang of the gods breaking forth from the confusion they call Chaos; second, that they claimed some were begotten from others without right reason and as if through human intercourse; third, that they transferred all human disturbances, errors, and crimes to the gods with wicked impiety. Those natural philosophers also sinned in religion who either, with Democritus, dream that the universe—arranged with wonderful reason—is composed by some rash chance rather than by divine reason; or, with Anaxagoras and Archelaus, believe that the heavenly bodies have nothing more divine in them than the elements. Furthermore, they say that the forms of those things which are generated, which are clearly directed everywhere toward an end, proceed from elemental impulse rather than from the art of a mind directing individual things to a certain end. Because, however, we have been more lengthy in the books of our *Theology* <note>Ficino refers to his major work, *Platonic Theology*</note> in refuting these and, moreover, in confirming those things which we have just proved and will henceforth bring forward from the mind of Plato in this compendium, we shall therefore run through them briefly for the present. Consider how great is the religion of our Plato, and how certain he is that God exists, who, when disputing against those who deny God, can hardly restrain himself from anger—though otherwise he is mild beyond measure in both life and disputation. In these matters, he certainly warns that those who deny God are not to be tolerated. Note that Plato approves of those who, at the rising and setting of the sun and moon, adore not only the sun and moon specifically, but rather the divine beneficence, for which he commands thanks to be given daily for such a gift of lights. He judges that man to be like a monster among men who, against natural instinct, education, and common custom, denies that there are higher beings. Soon, however, he warns young men who might have been invaded by certain absurd opinions heard against God: that as long as they are young, they should abstain from judgment on divine matters and trust their elders and the laws, until age, experience, and reason teach them. He brings forward, moreover, the opinions of certain people who were held to be wise, through which men easily decline toward impiety and injustice. I mean opinions claiming that the natures of the four elements, flowing together by some fortuitous motion, heaped all things together. Furthermore, that religion and justice differ not by any truth, but by the opinion of men. Wherefore he concludes that these things, as the most pernicious of all both privately and publicly, must be refuted by reasons; and that men should not be forced to obedience and observation of the laws by threats and torments alone, but also by persuasions and reasons. Otherwise, man being a rational animal and therefore free, unless you bind him by the bond of reason, he neither ought to be nor can be bound in any other way. Therefore, reason must be excited by the laws; its power is so great for finding God that after rational investigation, it becomes more certain that reason is in nature than in itself—and so much more certain as it sees natural effects to be more orderly than human ones. Whence also it notices that art in nature is so much more perfect than in man. From this, again, it notices that the art presiding over natural works, since it is more perfect than the human, and human art is not only present but also a participant in life and intelligence, must surely be living and intelligent; indeed, it is life and intellect itself—add also will. For since it clearly directs individual things to their proper ends, it is certain that it foresaw the end and willed it; indeed,

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> truly it always foresees and wills, just as order is always preserved whole in individual things; or where it seems interrupted, it is restored faster than can be said. That this is divine providence, we do not doubt in the least. A providence, I say, neglecting not even the smallest things—for these are no less ordered than the greatest—nor laboring in the greatest. For those things closest to the ordainer do not resist his ordering; they are assiduously ordered by the same nod of the will by which they are made, and are kept far from all transgression. Hence that saying: *He dwells on high and looks upon the humble in heaven and on earth*, just as heaven itself, while it performs its course within itself without labor, meanwhile without negligence surrounds the earth with the most fertile gift of its rays. <margin>B</margin> Among these things, however, when he says that law and art consist of nature, or no less than nature, because they are the offspring of the mind: understand that no less true than the forms of nature do they exist and are begotten from the divine intellect as if from a father, and from the human mind as if from a mother. And notice the accustomed piety of our Plato invoking God to confirm the gods. One God, I say: so that he may teach that all gods are to be referred to the One. He says, moreover, that relying on the help of the supreme God, he will dispute most safely about divine matters. In the beginning, he disapproves of those natural philosophers who placed the supreme principles of things in bodies, from which life and intelligence would then proceed; whereas they ought rather to have said that bodily things depend on intellectual life. That this is so, he professes he will prove by a new—I do not say opinion, but reason. <margin>C</margin> For an opinion of this kind belongs to the ancient theologians before Plato. But the argumentation, such as will be made here from motion, is proper to Plato. He distinguishes the genus of motions itself into ten species: namely, Circulation, Local transition, Condensation, Rarefaction, Increase, Decrease, Generation, Corruption, Change (or alteration made in one thing by another), and Change from itself, both in itself and made in another. He admires circular motion, since in it the indivisible center stands still while the rest are moved. Likewise, in a very deep sphere, many circles are designated, <margin>D</margin> some larger than others in succession. And what is wonderful is that at the same moment the narrowest circle and the widest complete their circuit: so that both the slowness of the former in a continuous body and the velocity of the latter are equally to be admired. The middle ones, both in dimension and in motion according to certain proportions, hold a middle way. We have treated many of these things in our expositions of theology. He says also of that which changes place, that it changes its center—that is, the center of the place to which the circumference of the moving body is compared—but sometimes, besides changing its center, it also in a way keeps the same center: namely, when it is not fixed, but moved in place, it is driven around through a certain equal circumference. Furthermore, where he speaks of generation, he says that the principle—that is, the moving and seminal nature—<margin>E</margin> when it advances by alteration, proceeds through three steps: that is, into length, breadth, and depth; likewise, it reaches as far as quantity, quality, and substantial form through its effects manifest to the senses; again, it arrives at formal, vital, and sensual being. He thinks, however, that in these motions the bodily mass is indeed moved, but does not move; while bodily forms both move the masses and are moved by the soul; and the soul indeed moves these two, but is itself moved not by another, but from itself: yet it moves in such a way that, together with the things changed, it is meanwhile changed in its own way. Therefore, he considers divine and angelic minds to be more excellent than souls, for they move lower things while they themselves are not changed in the least. Finally, he judges the Good itself to be more eminent than minds, for all things seek truth for the sake of the Good. In these points, he touches on many things pertaining to the nature that is mobile of itself, as if to the proper principle of motion and generation. <margin>F</margin> In which motion a certain formal and spiritual generation flourishes by its own nature, the exemplar of motions and generations. He confirms above all that things moved by another have a nature that is mobile from itself, so that there is no infinite regress. Indeed, just as through those glasses by which other things shine or grow warm, one arrives at something that is lucid of itself or hot of itself: so beyond things mobile by another, one comes to a thing mobile of itself. For if all things were now at rest, and a little later some ought to be moved before the rest, what would be moved first? Certainly not the divine substance, which is altogether immobile. Nor any bodily thing, which borrows motion from another. Therefore, only that which is mobile from itself will be moved first, and exercising its own motion in itself, will translate it <margin>G</margin> into other things. For it provides to bodies that they be moved, just as the immobile principle of things provides to things that they move. That the soul is a nature mobile of itself is clear both intrinsically, when by its own nature it freely runs through reasoning and deliberates; and extrinsically, as long as its presence provides to the body that it be moved in a certain way by itself. But concerning all these things, and furthermore that above the souls of the spheres there must be angels and God, we treat abundantly in the *Theology*. Where Plato calls the soul "motion and generation," understand this by way of cause—that is, the proper principle of motion and generation. And where he says it is moved by itself, that is the definition <note>original: "rationem"</note> of the soul. Note in the same place it is also said that the definition of the soul is that it can move itself, lest you understand the soul to be the act of motion, but rather the power—and I do not mean an accidental one. <margin>H</margin> For he also calls the soul a "substance" in that place. Thus, therefore, you shall define it: The soul is a substance having its own power, by which it is both moved from itself and moves other things. Just as a thing mobile of itself precedes a thing mobile by another, so he thinks the rational soul precedes the entire bodily machine, since no body is able to be moved from itself. The Platonists say it precedes both in dignity and in time. If anyone wishes Plato to disagree less with Christians, let him explain that our soul precedes either by some moment of time, or at least in dignity and the intention of the Creator. From the fact that the soul...

# ARGUMENTS AND COMMENTARY

<margin>A</margin>Because the substance of the soul is prior to the substance of the body, he concludes that the affections, motions, and familiar gifts of the soul are prior to bodily passions. Where he enumerates what is proper to the soul, remember that those things which signify *action* are common to our soul and superior beings <note>i.e., angels or celestial intelligences</note>. Those which signify *passion* <note>in the sense of being acted upon</note> are proper to us, or shared only with the lowest demons. However, a natural motion which is a passion in the body is an action in the soul. And what is length, breadth, depth, quality, and motion in the body, is sharpness <note>acumen</note>, judgment, memory, habit, and affection in the soul. You have other such distinctions more clearly in theology. He says also that the soul is the cause of evils—namely, by accident, and because our soul has free will. Be careful where he says the world is governed by its own soul; he adds that the soul is twofold, one being beneficial and the other contrary. Do not take this to mean a double *substance*, but rather a double *power*. For in the soul of the world and the celestial soul, there is a power: one is the mover of bodies, the other is intellectual. <margin>B</margin>The intellectual power is certainly beneficial, disposing all things in order; the moving power is beneficial (that is, an organizer) only insofar as it is subject to the other. If it were not subject, then the more effective it is at motion, the more it would—lacking art—hurl the universe headlong and confound it.

That the celestial soul possesses a mind <note>Latin: *mens*</note> is proved by the order it always observes in every motion and generation. Indeed, we see that the mindless are estranged from order to the same extent they are estranged from the mind. For the present, we define "order" as the mutual connection of things and actions among themselves, disposed in a fitting succession, directed toward a certain end by a specific reason, and preserving—as much as possible—the similar, the equal, and the same in all things. We see such order preserved only by those who are masters of their minds, and it is fully realized in the very progression of the universe. It is realized, I say, as conveniently as it is beautifully, from which it appears the universe is governed by a soul that possesses a mind both most skillful and most good.

Not without reason did he say that "circularity" is proper to the mind. For in a circle, the indivisible center remains while the circumference returns to the same point, and equality is preserved in both figure and motion. Similarly in the mind: a simple and fixed intuition remains directed toward Truth itself, while causes are unfolded into effects through intermediaries, and in turn, effects are similarly folded back into causes. Meanwhile, the attention of the mind returns to consider itself, and <margin>C</margin>proceeds by understanding, willing, acting, intention, rule, and progression in a way that is similar, equal, and the same.

After he proved both that the celestial spheres have souls and that those souls are endowed with the best minds—and signified that the universe is driven by one soul and the many spheres by many—he now briefly distinguishes three modes by which souls are joined to celestial bodies. He says the soul is either in the globe as our soul is in the body (so that one living animal is made from them); or it is present such that it does not vivify the globe but only moves and rules it, whether by some marvelous power of moving alone, or by some additional medium. And if he does not explicitly choose one of these three here, all Platonists nevertheless choose the first without controversy, and they believe Aristotle and Theophrastus felt entirely the same. For they think Plato held this as more probable. Indeed, the very argument by which he here makes the heaven animate implies that the soul itself moves along with the moved heaven. Unless one animal were made from the soul and the globe, it would certainly not be a "movable mover," but an "immobile mover." He confirms this in the *Phaedrus*. He says the same in the *Timaeus*, stating that when the Architect of the world wished to make the world an intellectual animal—and since intellect could not be present in a body without a medium—He joined the intellect to the soul, and the soul to the body, pouring it into the middle of the world and diffusing it through all things.

<margin>D</margin>Furthermore, why does Plato here only explicitly confirm the celestial gods? Because the contemplation of higher things is quite foreign to the matter of laws; and through the celestial gods who are moved and assigned to their own duties, he sufficiently warns that a higher being must be sought, who—himself unmoved—moves all, and as a common leader, assigns specific duties to each. Why say more? He clearly demonstrated that above celestial souls there is a Divine Mind, and through that mind, angelic minds, where he says the celestial soul (since it does not have it of itself) leads all things rightly if it has always received the divine intellect, just as things are held to be right and happy among the gods; otherwise, it wanders utterly. Therefore, where Plato proceeds from the soul to the mind, like one ascending from the eye to a higher light, he greatly fears lest he be forced into darkness.

After he showed that gods exist, he demonstrates that they provide <note>Providence</note>, beginning from a certain singular opinion: a certain nature, kindred to divinity, leads men (who have not entirely degenerated from the human species) to affirm that God exists, even though sometimes the apparent prosperity of the wicked—which is a false prosperity and will pay the penalty at the appointed time—forces us to doubt God's providence. Surely, God acts in understanding; consequently, what He acts, He understands, and if He makes the whole, He also understands the whole. If He knows the whole, He knows also the parts of which the whole necessarily consists; if the parts, then the tiny particles of which the parts necessarily consist. He is therefore able and knows how to rule the universe: He who is able and knows how to provide. He also wishes to govern His entire work usefully. But a whole can never be governed well if the parts are not governed. Thus, neither a physician nor an architect cares for a whole work perfectly without the parts necessarily leading to it. God does not neglect to govern the smallest things, He who did not neglect to make the smallest things. Nor is governing difficult for God, for whom procreation is easy. Nor is He too slow to care out of softness, He who is the strongest of all, who governs all things more accurately than either art or nature governs the things made by art or nature. For the more the works of God depend on God than the works of art or nature depend on art or nature, so much more diligently does God provide for His works; through whose providence other things also have the quality of providing for their own in a similar way. Since art is more perfect the more easily

<column-break/>

it dispatches small and large things at once, and in God art is immense, it is no wonder He governs the smallest and largest things together with the greatest ease. In dispensing these, He does not dispose the whole for the sake of the parts, but the parts for the sake of the whole, and He refers the proper good of each thing to the good of the universe. Among all things under the moon, He has the greatest diligence concerning the human species, both because it is most perfect and because it worships God—as if it were uniquely cultivated by God.

In these things you will note that from the highest God, divine rulers have been distributed through every genus and species of things, or curators of even the smallest actions and passions. Just as they are able to do whatever they can through His power, so through His providence (the manager of even the smallest things), they procure every tiny detail. You will note that there are senses in the stars, and as Plotinus and Hermias argue, specifically sight and hearing—but of another kind, far more excellent than the senses of earthly animals. You will also note that the human soul is always joined to a body: continually to an ethereal body, but by succession to an earthy body, and then to an aerial body. Likewise, the motion of the soul—because it is primary and from itself, and therefore free—can be derived into various forms: so much so, that the soul is sometimes turned into a habit lower than man, and sometimes into one higher than man. By the former, it descends to lower places as if by a certain weight; by the latter, it seeks the heights as if by lightness. From this, it appears that habits conceived from one's own character concur with the law of the divine will. For just as that law dictates that celestial things suit good souls and terrestrial things suit evil ones, so—with no one pushing from the outside, and as if by a certain natural instinct—the habits of the good spontaneously seek higher things, while those of the evil slip to lower ones.

Here, if I were permitted to comment at greater length, I would explain that most obscure saying where he introduces someone attempting to transmute fire into "animated water," as if attempting the most difficult things. For since water is contrary to fire, and a soul cannot be created from fire, he who strives to transmute fire into animated water surely attempts the impossible. No less obscure is what must be explained regarding dialectical resolution and division. Namely, if someone proceeds by dividing through three steps—from a most general genus to sub-alternate species, and from those to the most specific species—he divides easily. Similarly, he who resolves through the same steps—from the most specific species to the sub-alternate genus and thence to the most general—also resolves easily. But he who wishes to wander through every infinite individual thing undertakes a useless task. But concerning these, see the commentaries on the *Philebus*. Among these, you will note Plato's words are very similar to the oracle of the prophet David: that divine judgment cannot be avoided by ascending into heaven nor descending into hell.

After this, he shows that God cannot be unjustly appeased by the gifts of the wicked. <margin>E</margin>Where you will consider that God is a more diligent curator of the human race than shepherds are of sheep, pilots of ships, leaders of armies, farmers of the sick <note>original: *agrotum rustici*, likely referring to livestock or land health</note>, drivers of horses, or physicians of the ailing. Furthermore, all things under heaven are full of evils, and there is a perpetual war concerning souls. In this war, vices pull downward, while gods and demons pull upward. You will consider that there are living virtues in God—nay, lives—from whose sparks, kindled in the soul, the soul is raised to sublime things.

After the prefaces, he turns with a more severe censure toward the impious; he diligently explores not only wicked actions but also the impudence of words, and even thoughts themselves against divine dignity. He reduces the three species of impiety mentioned above into six, by dividing each into two. For those three consist of false opinions against God. However, along with a false opinion, iniquity of character can also concur, or a more tolerable equity. <margin>F</margin>You will recognize here the punishments of the "evil-dry" <note>original: *male siccorum*, likely meaning hardened or withered souls</note>, heretics, the superstitious, and those who are called False Prophets. Again, see how much he condemns common superstition. He also previously condemned the poetic kind, by which common superstition is confirmed. Everywhere, Plato disapproves of both poetic and common superstition, and above all human duties, he venerates philosophical piety.

# ARGUMENT ON THE ELEVENTH BOOK OF THE LAWS.
## Referring to page 675.

<margin>G</margin>Our Plato, just as he is the wisest of all philosophers and the most eloquent of orators, is also the most prudent of all legal experts. Lest he be forced, as others usually are, to produce a vast and fruitless work of interpretations and laws regarding contracts, he wisely strove—before descending to contracts and forensic commerce—to make citizens good through disciplines, laws, judgments, and religion. He hoped that just men, even without laws, would spontaneously provide faith and truth in every transaction. And indeed, quite opportunely after the laws concerning judgments pertaining to persons, he brings forward the laws of judgments regarding things. By these, both foreigners and citizens may learn to deposit justly, to keep deposits and the pacts of others undisturbed, and to return to each his own: how to sell, buy, return, lead, serve in the military, protect orphans, make wills, <margin>H</margin>preserve testaments, administer inheritances, arrange marriages, perform divorce, and govern a family. Above all others, he teaches to religiously revere parents, to adulterate nothing, to hate sorcery, to avoid anger and madness, to flee quarrels, insults, and slanders, to restore damages, and to preserve truth in testimony and oaths. This is roughly the material of this eleventh book. After this, as is our custom, we think certain more obscure points should be briefly explained. First, know that the goddess of the journey is twofold: namely, the indicator and the preserver. And that...

# MARSILIO FICINO

<margin>A</margin>Indeed, light exists under the name of the Moon; but this same light under the name of Diana <note>Ficino is explaining how the same divine power (light) is categorized differently depending on its function or manifestation.</note> is faith, and whatever has been found by some chance as foreign on a journey must be dedicated to the god: so that you may recognize that prosperous fortune is to be referred to the providence of God. Contemplate Platonic goodness, namely that which forbids in buying and selling not only the adulteration of goods, lying, and perjury, but even swearing an oath: indeed, even praising a saleable item and changing the price on the same day. Learn this well: Let no one, having invoked the gods, tell a lie, or deceive, or dare to adulterate anything in word or deed, unless he wishes to be an object of hatred to God: for he is first hated by God who, swearing falsely, thinks little of the gods; and secondly, he who lies in the presence of his elders.

<margin>B</margin>And see again and again how free and upright Plato wishes the characters of the citizens to be, from whom he expels all license for trade <note>term: cauponandi (inn-keeping/retail trade). Plato and Ficino viewed small-scale retail as corrupting to the soul.</note> far away. He adds also that both wealth and poverty are diseases of character. For from the former comes inflation (pride), and from the latter men become weaker and more abject. But where he says that Pallas (Athena), Vulcan (Hephaestus), and Mars preside over the arts, gather this from the many mysteries of Plato delivered here and there: a certain trinity of deities, which we call "the craftsmen" in the Platonic manner, always stands by Jove (Jupiter), the supreme architect of the world. In this trinity, Pallas is first; Vulcan is second; and Mars is third. But just as the whole trinity is referred back to Jove himself, from whom it originates, so Vulcan and Mars are referred back to Pallas. <margin>C</margin>I pass over for now that he seems to have dreamed of power in Mars, wisdom in Pallas, and a fiery spirit in Vulcan. Certainly, three things are required for the very art of Jove by which he perfects the universe. First, the **reason** itself through which he is to make individual things. Second, the effective **execution** of those things which he had conceived by reason. Third, the **safety and defense** of those things which are to be executed in effect. He names Pallas the Idea of the first, Vulcan of the second, and Mars of the third. And because both—namely conservation or defense, as well as the execution or expression of things—require reason and wisdom, therefore Pallas presides over both Vulcan and Mars: and whatever is either fabricated by Vulcan, or defended by Mars after it is fabricated and preserved in its form, is carried out under the leadership of Pallas.

Indeed, of these three reigning in the divine art, we see three traces in nature: through Pallas, the **order** by which individuals are arranged; through Vulcan, the **effective progress** and prompt "birth," as it were, toward which all things hasten; and finally through Mars, the **most fortified structure** applied by the generators to the generated, and the various bulwarks defending their own nature from contraries. Similarly, three things ought to be in every human art, and especially in the civil art: that individual things be thought out wisely before they are made, and be executed maturely and strenuously, and be preserved and bravely defended in that form in which they were thought out and produced. And so that we may know that human art in all these finished things depends no less than nature upon God himself and the Ideas, he says those three gods preside over human arts.

But lest we think we have received only the arts from the gods, he adds that the gods, as givers of life, ought to be revered most of all: so much so that even their names are not to be uttered either impudently or rashly, but all things, even the smallest pertaining to them, are to be handled purely, reverently, and chastely. Nothing holier can be devised than these precepts, if only he had named "God" instead of "the gods." But behold, he introduces one substance of the supreme Jove, and he did not multiply substances while he multiplied Ideas; do we require anything further in him? <note>Ficino is defending Plato against charges of polytheism, arguing that Plato's "gods" are like the "thousands of thousands" of angels serving the one God in Christian theology.</note> Furthermore, where he names the gods, he feels no differently than he who said: "A thousand thousands ministered to him."

Nor should it be passed over in silence what he says about the soul receiving life from God; it must be understood as a **middle life** between that which remains in eternity (such as the angelic life, which is all at once) and that which is enclosed by a certain time. A middle life, I say, composed of eternity and time: in which, like the heavens, the substance indeed always remains, but the action and affection always flow. Therefore, in the previous book, he said the soul both "is" and "becomes" at the same time, and is imperishable; yet not eternal, because by the law of judgment, it is not entirely remaining. He said, however, that the gods (that is, the angels) remain: not of themselves, but by divine law which eternally fixes them, though they are mobile by nature. He says the body is also imperishable—certainly the celestial body. Perhaps also the elemental body, insofar as the mass of the elements and primary matter are not destroyed; from which he says in the *Statesman* that the same body is sometimes divinely recreated.

You will note where he speaks of wills (testaments), that both the person and the property of anyone belong not to himself, but to the fatherland. Likewise, where the care of orphans is treated, that the souls of the deceased perceive and care for our affairs—perceive, I say, through the celestial and airy body—and care for some things more than others, toward which they are more affected either by nature, habit, or divine providence. Especially those souls which, since they held a middle life, also obtain a middle region. I say middle both in position and quality. In position, between heaven and earth; in quality, between supreme happiness and extreme misery. For it must be remembered that it was said in the previous book: just as certain natures claim for themselves suitable places and convenient natures, so souls, when they have become such or such of themselves, consequently migrate according to the nature of that very similarity to grades and seats both similar to themselves and of similar beings: so that those made celestial seek celestial things, the earthly seek earthly things, and the airy seek airy things.

Indeed, while Plato does not dare to affirm some other things concerning souls, he nevertheless asserts this much most evidently both here and in the book *On Science* (Theaetetus), and signifies it often elsewhere. Whence he also says, one must be careful not to harm orphans, lest the souls of the parents be justly angry with us. And the same in the ninth book, while dealing with homicides, says that the souls are indignant at the killers. Similar to this is that the souls of the followers of Marius troubled Sylla (Sulla). Hence also the tragedies portray the Raging Orestes. You will notice after this, where the worship of parents is treated, that the sacred statues of the gods are to be honored, not for themselves, but because they signify the gods to us; but parents are to be honored even more, as if they were **living images of the gods**. He adds that the imprecations (curses) of parents against children are heard by God, and nothing happens to children

<column-break/>

more pestilential. You will hear again after many things what is very Platonic: The wicked are vexed by punishments, not because they have done it (for what is done cannot be undone), but lest any such thing happen hereafter: and so that both those who are punished and those who understand the punishment may pursue injustice with hatred, or at least offend less in a similar vice. Furthermore, the judge is the interpreter of the legislator and the minister of justice. He then punishes thieves, detractors, and those who rebuke and revile in anger, and those who offend more serious persons with biting jokes, and those who become too sharply angry while joking. You will hear that divine vengeance is most to be feared if anyone lies in testimony and oaths. You will hear finally that in testimony and swearing, the truth itself must be confirmed through Themis, Jove, and Apollo. By **Themis** is signified law and right, both civil and established, both among men and before God: so that whoever lies in swearing and testifying may understand that he sins gravely against human and divine law and right, against men, and against God. By **Jove**, who shakes all things with a nod, let him know that if he sins, he will by no means escape the vengeance of divine power. By **Phoebus** (Apollo), let him not trust that his crimes, present or past, can be hidden from him who foretells all future things by prophecy.

<margin>D</margin>## ON THE TWELFTH BOOK OF THE LAWS,
### Argument. For page 685.

Plato, divine in all his dialogues on laws, delighted in the likeness of the divine work and therefore in the number twelve; he surely wished the twelfth dialogue to be as common to the secrets of the laws as the twelfth circle of the world (the firmament) is common to the stars. And just as if someone penetrates the twelfth circle, he will immediately find, or rather attain, the perfection and happiness of the soul: so Plato, about to proceed beyond the twelfth book, will demonstrate in the *Epinomis* not so much the laws as the blessed perfection of the soul acquired through the laws. In the previous books, the laws pertain partly to public duties, partly to private business, partly to urban matters, and partly to external ones, whether in peace or in war. In the twelfth, however, all are in a way gathered together pertaining to all things—not individual laws, I say, but some from every kind of the individual ones. To the laws is added that which is greatest: namely, the **reason** that is both the preserver and the corrector of laws. To the magistrates is also added that which is greatest: namely, the system of rendering and auditing accounts, placed over the public duties of magistrates no differently <margin>E</margin> than the examination of conscience itself is placed over the private actions of souls. By this examination, both the private salvation of all souls and the universal public safety of the city consist. And that is the summary argument of the twelfth book.

But since soon in the beginning, and in the following parts, and often in the preceding ones, he commemorates the "sons of the gods," and calls both some gods the sons of others and men the sons of gods, it must be remembered that in Plato there are two ways in which gods are sons of gods, and also two ways in which men are sons of gods. First, as the *Timaeus* teaches, all the rulers of the spheres of the world—whether the souls of the spheres themselves, or the demons within the spheres, or the angelic intellects beyond the spheres—are sons of the omnipotent God, as if procreated by His beneficent will. <margin>F</margin> Then, in any of these three kinds, the lower are called sons of the higher because, continuously receiving rays and forms from the higher, they are in a way formed from there and seem to obey them as if they were fathers. Men are similarly said to be begotten by the higher powers, either because from the beginning of things they were brought into the light from the bowels of the earth by the nourishment of the higher powers; or because some, being vehemently inspired every day by the inspiration of the higher powers, are soon transferred from their usual human affection into a certain divine state of life, as if divinely reborn. In which grade he frequently places both pious philosophers and philosophical princes.

<margin>G</margin> Moreover, that right at the beginning of the book he places Jove and Mercury over ambassadors and messengers, it must be understood first that by Jove is meant God the architect of the world, and by Mercury, the whole number of angels; then by Jove again he signifies the second of the planets, the indicator of commanders and laws, and by Mercury another planet, the indicator of all interpretation and execution. I call the planets "indicators." For as the *Timaeus* testifies and Plotinus discusses, the planets and all celestial things signify and announce as best they can what the higher powers are just about to do, or what we ourselves are sometimes about to do, and often about to suffer.

He soon detests the poets who, transferring the crimes of men to the higher powers, have both impiously offended against divinity and gravely harmed men by the evil example of the higher powers. Furthermore, he thinks thefts and other crimes should be judged more by the intention and habit of the sinner—whether curable or incurable—than by the outward act. Among the laws of military service, he prescribes what he considers the best of all in every life: <margin>H</margin> that no one should know what it is to live only for himself or to do anything apart from others; but that individuals should direct their individual actions to the nod of a wise superior and to common use. He teaches judges not to give a sentence contrary to the law, whether voluntarily or even under compulsion. For judgment itself, according to the opinion of the ancients, especially Orpheus and Hesiod, is a certain chaste virgin. And to Modesty and Judgment, a lie is especially hateful. They think the goddess presiding over judgment is divine Providence, to be venerated by human judges. After this, where he condemns those who have basely thrown away their arms, and those leaders of war besides who receive them back to serve again under their standards: the number of ten minae <note>A "mina" was a unit of currency.</note> is translated by us here, though the laws <meta>catchword: elsewhere</meta> elsewhere say a thousand. A little later he asserts that the Republic is a knot...

# ARGUMENTS AND COMMENTARY 843

<margin>A</margin> ...a judgment of accounts for extortion: so that no one in the republic shall be a judge without himself being subject to a judge. Otherwise, through an unrestrained license of judging, first justice would perish, and then the city, having lost justice, would die as if losing its soul. By the Temple of the Sun and Apollo, he understands a shrine dedicated not only to the solar planet and soul, but much more to the light of the Supreme Good, of which the sun is the image. You will hear that sins are committed in judgments due to an absence of religion. But the worst of all the impious are those who trust they will so appease God with prayers and sacrifices that, because of this confidence, they feel they may extort great sums of money with impunity. After this, he hands down very cautious laws concerning the reception of foreigners and the travel of citizens: lest either the morals of the citizens be corrupted by foreign and ill-considered customs, or the republic lack the expertise of foreigners.

<margin>B</margin> ...to us here also that in some few men there is a certain divine power through which they discern the capacity of talents. This indeed shows that a certain divinity is not only acquired by us but, so to speak, is inborn. He teaches that it should not be considered a small matter whether you appear honorable or wicked. But the reputation for virtue must also be sought—and sought only through virtue itself. He mentions that divine men sometimes exist even among the common people and in ill-governed cities. After this, he treats many things concerning the pleading of cases, accusation, defense, appeal, bail, proscription, and others of this sort. He also mixes with these, at his own opportune moment, what gifts or images should be dedicated to the deities. This indeed is a symbolic <term>Pythagorean rite</term> <note>A tradition of using symbols to represent deeper metaphysical truths, common in the school of Pythagoras</note> tra-

<margin>C</margin> -dition. He says that the Earth and Vesta exist as the sacred habitation of all the gods. Because he joined Vesta to it, he signified that under the name of this "earth," something deeper must be understood: both this elemental earth, and the lunar earth, and finally the star-bearing earth. Likewise, the three souls of the three earths, and the three angels. Remember, however, that among the ancients, whatever in the universe is effective for forming and moving is metaphorically called "fire." Likewise, whatever is everywhere most easily formed is called "air." That which is purgative is called "water"; that which is solid or stable and consistent is named "earth." Such a nature, on account of its dense or consistent quality, is called "earth" by the

<margin>D</margin> Platonists both here, in the moon, and in the firmament. To whom, therefore, would it be a wonder that the Earth exists as the sacred habitation of all the gods, if the universe is encompassed by the three boundaries of the three earths? And since he said it was sacred to the gods from the beginning, he forbids it to be consecrated again: warning that you should not trust that you can offer anything to God which was not already God's own. He also forbids statues to be made of gold or silver, lest we trust that by their great price we shall purge great crimes. Again, he prohibits ivory, since it has been deprived of its sensual soul: lest we perform sacred rites without sense—that is, without vigilance and attention. He also rejects bronze and iron, clearly blaming instruments of war. For while the mind is at odds within itself and with others, we perform sacrifices in vain. Finally, he accepts wood and stone from which the images of the gods may be made. In stone, he commends the stability of the mind in sacred matters.

<margin>E</margin> In wood, however, he commends the <term>fire-like quality</term> <note>original: "ecfan," likely a Greek-derived term for "shining forth" or "burning"</note>, that is, the ardor of the soul which is easily kindled in divine things. He commands that whole images be fashioned from a single stone or piece of wood, commending above all simplicity and integrity. Nor should it be passed over in silence that ambassadors were sent earlier to four oracles: so that we might know that God, the author of all, provides for all parts of the world equally. These are designated by the four "corners" under the names of East, West, North, and South: and by whatever rite God is worshiped, provided he is worshiped with a pure mind and by his own grace, it is in some way acceptable to God. But of these things more carefully elsewhere. Among these things, he forbids those who serve the fatherland in any matter to accept gifts. He also deals with taxes. He says nothing better can be said by anyone than that

<margin>F</margin> by which he himself becomes better. He says the law is a wonderful and divine thing: and among the Greeks, it takes its name from the Mind itself <note>A play on the Greek words "Nomos" (Law) and "Nous" (Mind)</note>: from the Mind, I say, both divine (as the father) and human (as the mother). Law, moreover, follows judgment. These two are indeed the greatest of human goods. But here it comes to mind that at the end of the eleventh book, he says our goods are often defiled by certain calamities of their own. And he says the calamity of the law elsewhere is the wickedness of the magistrate himself. The calamity of judgment and judicial dispute he called there a certain "legalistic skill": which, having no regard for right, but out of a zeal for greed and ambition, accepts every case for defense without distinction. This he detests above all others as a plague of the republic.

<margin>G</margin> After this, where he imposes laws on funerals, he wishes the man himself to be considered chiefly as the substance of the rational soul: but the body of this man is an image, and as he names it elsewhere, a shadow. What "man" is in us, and what "animal" is, is known from the *Timaeus*, the *Alcibiades*, and Plotinus: which indeed we discuss more broadly in the *Theology*. There he concludes that man is the substance of the rational soul, having beyond reason also a certain intimate, impassible, and common sense. The "animal," however, is a composite of the figured body and a certain vestige of life impressed by the soul. In this vestige, a sense is also impressed—secondary to the first sense—now distributed through various instruments and capable of suffering. This indeed seems to harmonize greatly with certain sayings of the Apostle Paul. When he says the soul goes away to "other gods" to give an account of its deeds, he names as "other gods" the angelic minds outside of bodies, who are called other gods beyond the souls of the spheres. For our souls, while joined to these bodies, are surely placed under the reign of the higher souls; but when separated, they are transferred to the judgment of the separated beings. Thus far he has established laws: but he says laws are established in vain unless one thinks of the safety and stability of the laws. Therefore, for their stability, he devised a certain marvelous council of magistrates. But before the creation of such an assembly, he touches somewhat on the power of the fates, so that he may understand that for the safety of such a great work, human prudence

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> is not sufficient if the fatal power is utterly opposed. In these matters, he certainly seems to approve of those who, in building cities, establishing laws, creating magistrates, and even in "planting" men <note>referring to procreation or education</note>, diligently beware of an overly adverse disposition of the stars. Concerning fate, much is said elsewhere: to which these things are brought in here as opportunely as they are briefly. Fate is a certain immovable disposition of movable things in the Soul of the World. The instrument of fate, however, is the celestial nature. But the matter in which it acts through the instrument is the mass of the elements. He accepts three names—Lachesis, Clotho, and Atropos—both regarding the instrument and regarding the matter. For we can name Lachesis the firmament: in whose stars the powers and lots of all lower things

<margin>B</margin> are contained. Clotho is the assembly of planets, with the firmament supplying the unfolding of the lots of things. Finally, Atropos is Saturn, especially confirming by his stability the lots unfolded into effect as inevitable. In the matter of fate, we also count three Fates, since the fatal power infused into the elements through the celestial instrument acts upon matter, form, and the composite. Likewise upon essence, power, and action. Likewise upon the beginning, middle, and end. Since, however, it acts not only upon bodies, but also upon minds to the extent that they use—or are affected by—bodies: therefore Plato says here that the Fates can preserve the prosperity of both bodies and minds, and of laws. And since the mind by its nature (as if pregnant with the providence of the divine mind) sometimes overcomes fate or uses fate happily, he added that for

<margin>C</margin> the safety of both public and private life, sense must be joined with the mind, so that sense obeys and serves the mind. Similar to this bond, which is composed of mind, sight, and hearing, he creates a certain assembly of magistrates in the republic looking out for the stability of the laws, who first look to the end of the republic itself, and then which ways lead most powerfully to that end: and who strive entirely so that individual things in the city, whether private or public, are done by one certain reason and lead to one goal: directing all things to virtue, and the other virtues to prudence. This, finally, to wisdom: which he often signifies under the name of "Mind." By the single reason of this wisdom, all virtues

<margin>D</margin> are judged worthy of approval: namely, insofar as they lead to wisdom: which he also approves for the reason that it is a participant in the one Divine Good. He asserts that the most exquisite consideration of things is that which beholds not only many things insofar as they are many, but also what one common nature is in all of them. Likewise, from what one principle they have this. Again, to what one end they can lead through this. Without such contemplation, no one can perfectly govern either a private or a public life. Since, however, this speculation belongs to the philosopher, especially the divine philosopher, he judges—not without justice—that the sum of affairs should be referred to the divine philosophers among the citizens gathered in that most select assembly. Divine, I say, inspectors and worshipers of divine things.

<margin>E</margin> Therefore, those who are dull in inspecting divine things, or lazy in worshiping them, or inept in teaching them, he keeps far away from the most ample offices of the republic. Soon, however, he proves that for a firm faith in the supreme divinity, two things are especially necessary. First, that we know the genus of rational souls is itself divine and older than bodies, by which the spheres of the world are moved: and that all beginnings and spheres are generated. Second, that we consider the genus of minds—namely, the angelic—to be more excellent than the genus of souls. And that souls move the spheres in an orderly way because of their participation in Mind. For if anyone knows these two things, he will easily recognize that just as Mind is the form and order of the soul, so the Divine Good is the life and light of both Mind and soul. These three, namely the Divine Good, Mind, and Soul, Plato

<margin>F</margin> undoubtedly either demonstrates or intimates in almost all his writings to be the principles of all things. This indeed he wrapped in more obscure words in the *Letter to Dionysius*. That our soul is older than the body—if it does not please you to say older in time, say at least more excellent in dignity: and prior because it has its origin from a principle superior to bodies: therefore he placed motion in the soul from itself, but in the body from the soul. And because mutability increases in the body, he says that from the mutable soul, the body depends not only in action but also as a mutable substance. He also takes issue with Anaxagoras, because since he did not place the soul between mind and bodies, he was compelled to have natural effects disposed not by intelligence through the soul (as is right), but rather to happen by elemental nature. He asserts here, however, as

<margin>G</margin> in the *Timaeus* and *Phaedo*, that all things—whether they are said to be done through angelic minds, or through souls, or through bodies—are done chiefly by the divine will and grace.

<header>MARSILIO FICINO</header>

# Happiness and the Goal of Laws
The previous laws indeed promise such a goal, but the *Epinomis* <note>A dialogue attributed to Plato, serving as an appendix to the *Laws*.</note> actually provides it by the gift of God. Therefore, having prophesied this perfect state of mind in the beginning, he thereafter seeks it from God with a certain prayerful speech. Some have judged that happiness can be possessed in this life, others in the next, and others indeed nowhere. Certainly, whoever thinks it can be acquired by human strength in this life is manifestly deceived, as the testimony of an entire lifetime cries out against it. But those who say "nowhere" are like empty men who wish for the entire instinct of nature to be in vain. Our Plato quite wisely hopes for happiness in the next life, to be obtained both by the virtues of the present life and by the gift of God. Yet he does not despair that a very few may be able to taste happiness even in this life. In the *Phaedrus*, the *Phaedo*, and the *Republic*, he intends such people to be those who live outside the body rather than in it, and live for God himself rather than for themselves; thus it happens that, by God’s inspiration, even among the waves of the river Lethe <note>The river of forgetfulness in the underworld.</note>, they seem to sip something of the ethereal nectar.

Nor is it without reason that he further inscribed this *Epinomis* as "The Philosopher." For as is clear in the sixth and seventh books of the *Republic* and in the present book, the duty of the philosopher is to investigate the reasons for all things so that he may find the divine Reason itself by which they were made, worship it once found, and enjoy it once worshipped. In this book, while he strives to lead us to happiness—which he undoubtedly places in religious wisdom—he depicts the character proper to one philosophizing legitimately, and instructs and forms him through the appropriate levels of the disciplines. And everywhere he seems to require no less, indeed much more, virtue and piety from the philosopher than knowledge; and whatever knowledge he requires of him, he seeks it so that he may venerate the true God himself, both as the master of knowledge and the author of the things known, above all else.

First, he proves that a power for divine happiness is naturally implanted in us by the fact that we all both prophesy and seek it in all our actions, and are fulfilled by absolutely nothing else. Then, enumerating each faculty in order, he shows that this happiness is obtained neither by natural, nor necessary, nor playful and jocular, nor auxiliary faculties. Third, he demonstrates that wisdom and piety—the foundations of blessedness—are acquired by both moral and speculative virtues. Where he enumerates the speculative doctrines, he first not only praises arithmetic but even admires it, saying that more than all others in the previous books, it sharpens the wit, confirms the memory, and makes the soul most fit and ready for every speculation and action. And here he adds that number was handed down to men by God himself as a necessary instrument for the discourse of reason. If this were taken away, the soul would appear mindless and the sciences and arts would utterly vanish. He praises, moreover, geometry which looks at measures, and stereometry <note>The measurement of solid figures.</note> which balances weights, and astronomy which observes the heavens, and music which imitates the harmony of the celestial spheres. He also commends physics, where he treats the types of bodies, compositions, souls, and the principle of motion and generation; but he does so in such a way that he leaves the most minute details of natural things to physicians, as being least relevant to one who betakes himself to divine matters. Finally, he places dialectic—that is, metaphysics—and the pinnacle of this, theology, as queen above all others: clearly using each as steps for finding and adoring God.

He proves that there are three duties of this queen regarding the other faculties: First, that she joins the multitude of all these together. Second, that she perceives what single communion and connection exists in all of them. Third, by what reasoning both this multitude and its union contribute to the one divine Good itself. He adds, moreover, that unless such a union of doctrines leading to the divine One is grasped, they all turn out entirely empty, nor can what is "one" in them be perceived unless they are compared to the One from which they receive their very union. The mind that has attained all these things, and is thus united to itself, and again through itself united to God, he says is blessed here according to its strength, and will be entirely blessed in the next life. That is the argument of the whole book.

A little after the introduction, where we translated these words, namely, *But a brief time*, what follows thereafter is read elsewhere as: *Suitable for the discourse of reason, and that indeed seems to be left not only in depraved men, but also in moderate ones.* Where he praises the heaven as the cause of both prudence and all goods, he wants such praises to be transferred from the corporeal heaven to the incorporeal heaven, that is, the Idea of Heaven. He commands that this be adored there through the visible heaven, as if signified through an image. But you, pay attention here: men are judged to be in the class of "terrestrial demons" <note>Ficino uses "demon" in the classical sense of *daimon*, a mediating spirit.</note> where he says, *all the other demons together*, and what follows. After this he says, if anyone knows what is divine in generation, he will know true number and piety. By "divine in generation" he signifies two things: both a certain spiritual motion which is in the soul (the motor force of corporeal motion and the origin of generation), and the natural species which is preserved in the perpetual succession of generation. In the motion of the soul, the true number is music, as the *Timaeus* says, sounding in proportion and harmony. In the species, too, there is true number. For the species of things are arranged by a certain number and order. By these things, certainly, religion is confirmed. For from the free motion of the soul, we prophesy a divine substance existing through itself; and from the perpetual perseverance in species, we augur the eternity of the Ideas.

You will hear an opinion similar to the Mosaic mystery. For he says, if any evil is brought upon us by the quality of the air or plants or animals, the divine nature is not to be blamed, but the human nature, which distributes its life unjustly. In what follows, you will clearly recognize the goal of the laws in these words: *This goal of the laws is proposed to you, that by the worship of God and purity of life you may attain the best and most beautiful end.* Soon he repeats the three heads of piety. First: that you believe God exists. Second: that you confess He has care for the greatest and smallest things alike. Third: that you do not think He can be unjustly swayed by any prayers or gifts. And he confirms again the faith in divinity from the soul's own—

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> —excellent and certain divinity. He thinks, moreover, that whatever is so much better than the body that it is also more divine (that is, more similar to divine things than corporeal ones), the same is more ancient than all bodies, because in any genus or order of things, that which is more perfect also possesses more "being"; and therefore it provides the cause of existing to the more imperfect things. That which provides "being" to another is, of course, also more ancient. He adds that when an animal is fashioned from the meeting of soul with body, a certain single form results there in the body—that is, a corporeal life proceeding in the subject from the arrival of the incorporeal life. He also posits two kinds of things: one corporeal, the other incorporeal. To the latter he attributes action, and to the former, passion <note>In the sense of being acted upon.</note>. Likewise, he says there is one form of the latter, chiefly because it is both simple and the form of the substance always remains in it. But where it is read, *For it is not another*, and what follows, it is read elsewhere thus: *For that which is transmuted into another is not incorporeal, and is entirely devoid of color, except for the truly most divine genus of the soul.*

In the genus of bodies, he places five bodies. These he calls "solid" because, being driven into depth, they are distinguished from planes, and in every body, even the most liquid, there is something solid, both through the consistency of its own nature and, in the Platonic manner, through a certain similarity to earthly nature diffused even unto the heaven. He calls the heaven "fire" because it has its own light, which is the chief quality of fire. It also has perennial mo-<margin>C</margin>-tion, such as we see in fire; and like fire, it does not suffer mixture, and because it is not yet driven from its natural place, it is not forced to return by ascent, but revolves. In act it shines, but in power it is warm; it is, however, of an entirely different kind from our fire. After the celestial fire, he places another species of fire, more warming than shining, called by the name of the "ether of the moon." Of this, our fire is a certain trace, now not only warming but burning; burning, I say, because of the excessive mixture of earthly harshness. But that which flourishes in thin matter shines more purely and warms more sweetly, especially where it wanders in the open, constrained by nothing. Below this he places air, water, and earth. He thinks, moreover, that any sphere of the world is com-<margin>D</margin>-posed of these five, so that there is a most perfect connection in substance and a communion in power and action among them all. But in any sphere, one element is primary, and according to its nature, the others are contained therein. Thus ether in the earth is "earthy," and earth in the ether becomes "ethereal," and likewise in the heaven. But concerning these things, there is more in the *Theology* and in the commentaries on the *Timaeus*.

Accordingly, he places rational animals in the heaven, ether, air, water, and earth. These he says are made by the soul—by a triple soul, I say. For he wishes that beyond the one soul of the entire world, there be twelve souls of the twelve spheres; then in each sphere, there are twelve orders of souls. These orders in the heaven are the constellations and stars; on earth, they are men; in the ether, air, and water (the higher parts), they are demons. In <margin>E</margin> each of these animated beings, the rational soul joined to its body procreates an "animal"—that is, a composite of its own body and a life thoroughly infused into the body. This life, having now been made corporeal, depends on a triple soul: for it depends on its own soul, on the soul of the sphere, and on the soul of the whole world. That the celestial bodies have souls is proven in Plato by the divinity of the celestial substance, the magnitude of its quantity, the life-giving power of its quality, and the speed and efficacy of its motion. That the celestial souls furthermore possess a mind, he gathers from the order and perseverance of the same tenor. He adds that the necessity of a soul possessing a mind is as great as possible, understanding this in two ways. First, because natural necessity (as in this or that part of fire for burning and ascending) acts led from elsewhere. But the nature of the intellectual soul, insofar as it participates in intel-<margin>F</margin>-lect, is the mistress of its own action. Second, because since the motion of the soul is free by nature, it can easily transgress and wander in turn unless it is ruled by the mind as by a charioteer: by a perfect mind, I say, providing both the best end of action and the most chosen path from the beginning. When this best mind is present in the soul, as it is in the stars, it necessarily achieves the prescribed work. For bodies do not resist the best (that is, the most powerful) souls, and the best mind does not change its counsel. Hence he says the three Fates <note>The Parcae: Clotho, Lachesis, and Atropos.</note> preserve whatever the celestial gods have deliberated with certain counsel. He says three Fates, one Fate disposing three things at the nod of the divine minds: namely, the beginnings, the middles, and the ends of things.

In the previous book, he said that those things which are established by the fates are <margin>G</margin> similar to materials worked by fire, whether straight or twisted. For as these materials cannot be bent further in the opposite direction, neither can fated things. Nor did he mention things "twisted by fire" without reason, for the fiery spheres of the heavens are the instruments of fate. Furthermore, where he says the stars are either everlasting or long-lived, he sufficiently touches upon the Orphic and perhaps the Hermetic opinion: namely, that the world will be resolved into fire after many ages. For that which is composite is finally dissoluble, and fire, as the greatest and most powerful of all, will finally assume all things into itself in a marvelous way. But the divine Mind, the craftsman of this work, will reform a similar work from the fire again by a similar fate and an easy nod. This opinion Anaxago-<margin>H</margin>-ras, Empedocles, Heraclitus, and most of the Stoics confirmed, admitting that an almighty God can always preserve His work in the order handed down; but the work itself, because it is of a finite nature and internally repugnant, cannot be preserved; and God repays by reformation what is lacking in the formation. But let them see to these things. You, however, will note here that Plato refutes those who deny that the celestial bodies live because they are always carried in the same way. This should have been an argument for everyone not of an absent life, but of a present sufficiency and wisdom. Remember, moreover, that the soul is considered so different from the body that there is nothing common to both—that is, no common matter. Likewise, because the soul does not depend on matter...

# ARGUMENTS AND COMMENTARY
<sig>Bbbb iij</sig>

...because corporeal nature is called neither true substance nor true essence: he calls the souls of the stars "gods," but their bodies "images of the gods." Furthermore, among the celestial gods, he names Jupiter as the office of providence, and Juno as the vital force subject to providence. He also says that the stars perceive individual things acutely, through a sense clearly different from our own. He describes the nature of demons <note>In the Greek sense of *daimones*, intermediary spirits, not necessarily evil</note> as powerful in prudence, sense, memory, and motion: intermediate between gods and men; to be honored for the sake of intercession and interpretation; knowing our thoughts—evidently from our gestures, motions, and affections—loving the good and hostile to the wicked. Here he seems to consider all demons to be good, namely those he teaches should be worshipped. Elsewhere, however, he indicates that some are evil. The ethereal and aerial ones are invisible. But the watery ones, whom he calls demigods, he says are sometimes seen, though barely, and by internal rather than external sight. He adds that souls are warned by demons through dreams, voices, prophecies, and omens: especially at the <margin>B</margin> time when the soul departs from the body. He says many things were added to religion by these warnings. He says further that it is not permitted for mortal nature to change what has been established by laws in religion. "Mortal," he says, for it is permitted to the divine. Behold a divine saying: The most divine Reason of all constituted the visible world, which the happy man, admiring, is kindled with a love for finding divinity, whence he escapes happy both here and in the other life, and becomes through wisdom truly one and truly united: translated to places congruent with virtue to contemplate the divine for all remaining time. Soon where it is translated, "For divine things," and what follows, it is read elsewhere: "For it is not the part of a prudent man to honor some divine things while neglecting others." Among these things he relates certain very well-known astronomical matters. <margin>C</margin> He praises the quality of the air as tempered for the virtue of the intellect. Then where he says motion tending toward the good proceeds from a good soul, while that ending in evil behaves in the opposite way: do not think that one soul of the world is good and another is evil; rather, good things proceed from the soul of the world itself insofar as it participates in Mind. Otherwise, evils would come forth from there—that is, things entirely lacking the order of numbers. For he named "evils" in the higher realms those things which lack harmonious number and beauty. But "goods" are those fitted together by consenting numbers. He adds that evils—that is, the privation of order—were conquered by goods, that is, from the beginning of things by the very Ideas of the Divine Mind. Likewise, they must be conquered, <margin>D</margin> namely while the world perseveres. These things were said regarding the judgment punishing the impious: because clearly by divine judgment punishing the wicked, the evil of injustice is conquered by the good of justice. To us, the greatest virtue is religion, and negligence of religion has stood as the cause of unhappy ignorance for men. Likewise, the best intellect is that which is mixed from temperance and fortitude, docile, mindful, and inclined toward divine things. And when such intellects are rightly educated, the worship of religion most likely proceeds from them to others, and is the most useful of all things. And wisdom cannot be learned without God's help: but from one who does not keep measure in teaching, it would be better not to learn. Likewise, all things are full of gods: so much so that the higher powers neither forget <margin>E</margin> our affairs nor desert us. As for what he touches upon briefly regarding numbers, we will explain more broadly where it is more opportune. For now, touch upon it thus: Numbers in themselves are indeed incorporeal, since they are nothing other than repeated unity; and this is indivisible. But when they are first thought to obtain a position, they can be imagined as converted into points. Likewise, from a certain stretch from point to point a line is born, from the drawing of which a surface arises, and from its descent, depth. Some numbers are linear, others superficial, others indeed cubes and solids. The first are like the number two, closest to unity. The second like the number four, proceeding from unity through two. The third, like eight, proceeding from two returning into itself. Likewise, the "double" proportion <note>The ratio 2:1</note> is considered perfect. First, because it is the first, generated between one and two. Second, because while it seems to have departed from one, by doubling it restores the one. Third, because it contains all proportions within itself. For both the *sesquialtera* <note>The ratio 3:2, the musical fifth</note> and *sesquitertia* <note>The ratio 4:3, the musical fourth</note> and similar ones are like parts within the double. Nature observes this in the heavens: and for the sake of this, it also preserves the *sesquialtera* and *sesquitertia*, from which the double is composed. For the Pythagoreans, when they measure the intervals of the spheres, compare the earth to the firmament. Likewise to the Moon and Sun, and the Sun also to the firmament. In which comparisons the interval from the earth to the Sun, compared to the interval from the same to the firmament, produces a *sesquialtera* between earth and sun; but between this and the firmament, a *sesquitertia*. And in that former proportion, the *diapente* <note>musical fifth</note> consonance is born; from the latter, the *diatessaron* <note>musical fourth</note>. From both of these certainly is fashioned the double proportion and the *diapason* <note>octave</note> consonance. They also hold that a *diatessaron* occurs from the earth to the moon, just as a *diapente* occurs to the sun, and from the sun to the firmament again a *diatessaron*. Just as nature observes such proportions in the spheres, so it does in the actions and passions of the elements. For so that a perfect action may result, the agent must be twice as powerful as the subject. But why? Because since it intends in acting to double itself, it surely requires a doubling proportion. Otherwise, if it overcomes by a smaller space, the reluctant subject will impede the perfect action. Just as the double ratio conduces to generating a substantial form, so the *sesquialtera* leads to the familiar shaping and figure of the form, and the *sesquitertia* to certain more common accidents. Furthermore, the measure of this same proportion is preserved in our humors. For they hold that blood is double to phlegm, and this double to yellow bile, and this similarly to black bile. If they have doubles, consequently they contain the *sesquialteras* and *sesquitertias* which are within the double. Similar things consist in hearing. In which there are four sharp levels: Three of fire; Two of water; One of earth. But you know that between four and

<column-break/>

three, a *sesquitertia* proportion is made. For the number four contains the three, and additionally one unit, which is the third part of three. You also know that between three and two the *sesquialtera* is placed, since three contains two and additionally another unit, that is, the half portion of two. Therefore, in the very affection of hearing, all proportions are more manifest than in others. And thus also the consonances. The *diapason* <note>octave</note>, that is, of the eighth voice, in the double. The *diapente* <note>fifth</note>, that is, of the fifth, in the *sesquialtera*. The *diatessaron* <note>fourth</note>, that is, of the fourth voice, in the *sesquitertia*. I pass over the fact that similar proportions can be imagined in the four elements. But of these elsewhere. Physicians also agree with these things in those matters pertaining to touch and in a way to taste, counting four degrees. The first, which is barely perceived by sense. The second, which is clearly perceived but does not offend. The third, already offending and then hurting. The fourth, killing in a short time. In these <margin>B</margin> degrees, the double, *sesquialtera*, and *sesquitertia* are found. But let the physicians see to this. Here Plato brings forward one, two, four, six, eight, twelve. From four to two is a double; from eight to four is also a double: these two excesses are equal in proportion, for each is made through the double, yet they are not equal in number: for eight exceeds four by four, while four exceeds two by two. Compare again the number six, on one side to four, and on the other to eight. On this side it is a *sesquialtera*; on that side it is a *sesquitertia*. These excesses are therefore unequal in proportion, but equal in number. For in both cases the excess is by two. Again, compare six to twelve in a double proportion, and between these compare eight to both. Certainly from twelve to eight a *sesquialtera* is born. From this to six, a *sesquitertia* arises: from which the double between six and twelve is composed, in which those two excesses appear evidently unequal both in proportion and in number. All these things are treated more conveniently in the commentaries on the *Timaeus*.

### ARGUMENT FOR THE
### Second Epistle.

<margin>D</margin> Dion of Syracuse, a truly great man and not only a listener to Plato but also an imitator, having been expelled by the tyrant, immediately sent back with great spirit the money the tyrant had sent; and as a Platonic, for the greatest injury, he affected Dionysius with a certain supreme benefit, namely by warning him with three salutary precepts. The first is, that princes perish not from a lack of money, but from a lack of friends. Second, that no power <margin>E</margin> is greater than the consensus of good and prudent men. Third, that it is necessary to recognize past errors and to divine how much detriment they cause us, so that we may be deterred from future faults.

### is from Plato to Diony-
