<margin>F</margin> In this letter which Plato writes to Dionysius the Younger after his first departure from him and the expulsion of Dion, four things are to be observed above the rest. First, indeed, that he says great power <margin>G</margin> and wisdom seek each other by some natural instinct, so that they may come together into one. This indeed we find in divinity, in nature, and in art. In the beginning, with God, immense wisdom accompanies the infinite power of God. This he indicates here under the names of Jupiter and Prometheus: judging Jupiter to be power, and Prometheus to be providence. For he thinks the power of the same is the fountain and mirror of divine intelligence. Indeed, because He can understand, therefore He understands, and He contemplates that same power by understanding. Traces of these also appear in nature. For in those things which are naturally composed, whether stones and metals, or plants and animals, and even primarily in the heaven itself, nature is so arranged that from the innermost power and natural vigor of nature there proceeds a certain order both in their forms and in their actions and effects. Such an order, evident from the outside and <margin>H</margin> accompanying the interior vigor of power, seems to display a certain wisdom. For nature does not proceed in one way in ordered progressions and wisdom in another: but the progression of both is entirely similar. In human art also, whether private or public, a certain similar meeting of power and wisdom is seen. The virtue of natural talent, memory, and will pertains to power. From this, however, acquired wisdom arises, and in actions the order pertaining to wisdom itself is preserved. Of this mystery, consisting of divinity, nature, and art, we have examples in elegant custom, which...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s Neoplatonic commentary on the relationship between power and wisdom, and the mystical hierarchy of the universe. It transitions from political philosophy to a deep theological explanation of the Three Principles (The Good, Mind, and Soul).</meta>

# MARSILIO FICINO

Here Plato recounts the mutual familiarity between the powerful and the wise, which exists by a certain natural necessity. The heavens admonish us of this fact, for there the planets signifying princes are closest to those signifying the wise. For Jupiter is closest in position to Saturn <note>In astrology, Jupiter represents kingship/power, while Saturn represents deep philosophy/contemplation</note>, and the Sun almost never departs from Mercury <note>The Sun represents the ruler; Mercury represents the intellect/messenger</note>. Therefore, there is a moral precept in Plato: Princes should honor the wise; the wise should freely advise princes. For wisdom without power benefits few, and power removed from wisdom harms many. Indeed, power void of wisdom is more destructive the greater it is. Conversely, wisdom far from power appears crippled. The great conjunctions of the planets teach this: Jupiter is the lord, but Saturn is the philosopher; unless these are joined, they accomplish nothing great or stable. Plato wants a happy friendship to be forged from the powerful and the wise. But the happiest union is where both are joined in the same soul. In such a soul sits the very divinity of Pallas <note>Athena/Minerva</note>, coupling power together with wisdom. For Pallas alone is both skilled in the arts and vibrates the spear. Let this much be said concerning the first mystery of this epistle. Let us now proceed to the second.

It belongs to a soul of excellent goodness to rejoice in the good, especially the divine, which is the most ample. Such a good is that which benefits as many as possible as richly as possible; of this kind is the true glory of virtue, contributing to doctrine and morals for both posterity and those present. Therefore, men endowed with the best nature are delighted by these things for two reasons: first, because just as they love the inner light of virtue, so they also love the outer splendor of virtue; second, because by this splendor they desire always to benefit as many as possible, and they certainly rejoice in this perpetual benefit to the human race. They rejoice, I say, insofar as they feel it. Since they strive to benefit posterity with everlasting glory, hoping that just as they do now, they will then also rejoice in this splendor and benefit: they surely prophesy that they will perceive this after this life. Indeed, by the instinct of a more divine nature, they are spurred to such a great benefit, not so much because they rejoice in this very thing, but so that they *may* rejoice. And if many species of animals, by the urging of nature, provide for future use in the work of nests and food not in vain: much less does the outcome frustrate divine souls who hope they will rejoice in a certain everlasting duty. The prophet Daniel comprehends such splendor of virtue and benefit in both doctrine and morals with these words: *The learned shall shine as the brightness of the firmament, and those who instruct many unto justice, as stars for perpetual eternities.* <note>Daniel 12:3</note> In certain souls degenerating from their divinity, the study of the benefit of true glory is either extinguished or changed into vainglory.

The third mystery of this epistle rises higher. But since we have explained this more extensively in our *Theology* and in the book *On Love*, it will suffice to have tasted it lightly for the present. When we diligently consider forms made by an artisan, we gradually notice the reason by which they were made: and as we apprehend the reasons through which he effects the forms, we easily approach through them the very Ideas of the artistic mind, according to whose exemplar he directed his reasons to effect the forms. Just as in crafts we proceed from forms to reasons, and from these to Ideas (that is, exemplars): so in contemplating the order of things itself, we know that the most beautiful forms of things are composed by the most skillful reasons; and if by reasons, therefore by Ideas, that is, exemplars, according to whose likeness Reason itself produces forms into order.

Therefore, there are three orders in the universe: namely, of **Forms**, of **Reasons**, and of **Ideas**. The order of forms which are open to the senses is reduced to the **Soul of the World** <term>Anima Mundi: the spirit that animates the physical universe</term>; which, as the principle of motion, generates forms in matter, but generates some by certain reasons and seeds and others by others. We trace this order of reasons in the Soul back to a **Mind** <term>Mens/Intellectus: the angelic or divine intellect</term> higher than the Soul, from whose Ideas the Soul receives the reasons for governing things. Finally, the order of Ideas descends into the Mind from the immense and simple splendor of the **Divine Good**. Indeed, the one Idea of all good things—which is God himself—infuses the other Ideas of other goods into the angelic Mind.

Wherefore the three orders of things are reduced to three princes and fountains. The order of forms to the Soul of the World; the order of reasons to the Angelic Mind; the order of Ideas to the Good itself. And because through Ideas all things are referred to the Good, therefore Plato says: *Around the King of all are all things* <note>Quoting Plato's Second Letter</note>, that is, around the Good itself are the Ideas, and through the Ideas all things. *Around the second*, that is, the Mind, *are the second things*, that is, the reasons which follow the Ideas. *Around the third*, however, *are the third things*, that is, around the Soul of the World are the forms. He signified that God is the **exemplary cause** of things when he said "Around." Likewise the **final cause**, where he says, "For his sake." Again the **efficient cause** when he added, "He is the cause of all beautiful things." For the fact that some things are deformed is not because they are from Him, but insofar as they degenerate from Him. Nor do the Platonists wish it to seem strange that Plato called any of those three a "principle." For he named them similarly, but not equally. God indeed exists as the One and the Good through Himself. Since unity and goodness are most ample, it follows that God is entirely through Himself; but the supreme Mind, closest to God, exists through God, insofar as it is a certain "one" and "good": and furthermore through itself, insofar as it is Mind and the order of the second nature. Finally, the Soul of the World is produced indeed by the first God, as it is one and good; produced also by the Mind itself, as it is mind. But insofar as it is mobile through itself, it is produced by itself. Thus far Plato says the origins of divine things and the principles of things proceed.

Furthermore, he says our soul is divine when he added that it "affects divine things": but it does not comprehend them as long as it looks into those things known to itself, that is, either the senses and sensible things, or the forms conceived by the soul from the encounter with these. For all these are far different from divine things, whence the soul looking into these is compelled to feel and pronounce concerning divine things otherwise than they are.

The fourth mystery follows concerning the perception of divine things. First, he says that the investigation of divine things not rightly done—that is, not equipped with the proper steps of both purification and disciplines—

<column-break/>

**A** —is the cause of all evils. Because clearly those who thus investigate God finally reach the point where they either deny that God exists, or affirm things of God which are not of God. From this, true religion perishes: and once religion is extinguished, all evils flow in. Then he says the "sting" of investigating divine things is the cause of evils, that is, if we abuse this, and use it in any way whatsoever, it does not permit us to enjoy present delights and rest in this life, as we pant for higher things. But what does he mean when he says, *Unless one plucks this sting from the soul, he will never attain the truth*? Surely he denies that the truth of things depending on God can be had, unless the truth concerning God himself is had.

**B** Furthermore, through those things which he soon adds, know that Plato himself was accustomed to be assiduously engaged in the investigation of divine things; and those who first heard Plato contemplating divine things were accustomed to grow dark immediately under the excessive splendor of divine things, and to be vexed for a long time, until they finally separated the mild [truth] both from the affections of the senses and from the images of the phantasy; which being done by a certain divine lot—that is, light—they found the truth not previously discovered. For this reason Pythagoras, whom our Plato venerates in all things, began the sacred mysteries of doctrines from the most exact expiation of the mind: and he commanded, and Plato similarly commands, that they not be carried out to the common people, lest the common people, having received them

**C** perversely, either despise them or fall into errors. For if you publish to the common people that God has nothing in Himself of those things which are sensed, they will either laugh at you or deny that God exists. Hence that saying of Lysis the Pythagorean to Hipparchus: *It is not pious to make the mysteries of philosophy common with those who have not been able to even dream of the purification of the soul.* There are, furthermore, some mysteries of theologians concerning God which weary not only the common people, but even many elegant men. Of which this is one: that nothing of those things which are understood ought to be judged absolutely concerning God. For whatever is defined by intelligence is compelled to exist below the infinite God. Thus, to these more secret mysteries, many

**D** learned men are still as inept as the common people are to lighter ones; so much so that even some who prevail in any sharpness, memory, or judgment, and have long heard these things, do not yet perfectly comprehend them: because clearly, though born for certain other things, they were not born for theological ones; or if born, not yet congruously learned and educated in these; or if educated and learned, not yet separated from perturbations by the benefit of a more mature age. But perturbation, because it both moves and distracts through diverse things and drags toward matter, therefore renders the mind foreign to God, than whom nothing can be thought more remote from motion, from diversity, and from matter. Therefore, not without cause did Lysis thus admonish Hipparchus: *It is worthwhile to recount how much time we consumed in wiping away the stains that were in our breasts*

**E** *before we could be worthy to perceive the precepts of Pythagoras.* Added to this is that if anyone, even with a tranquil and learned intellect, betakes himself to God, he is almost as much deceived by intelligence itself concerning God as the common people are deceived by sense and imagination, and as many learned men are repelled by perturbations. For intelligence, judging by its own nature, compels us to assert that God himself is either a certain "intellect" or a certain "intelligible" thing. But the **Immense Good** is neither an intellect (which, as if needy, turns itself toward the intelligible as toward a good by whose illumination it may profit), nor is it to be called

**F** "intelligible," which indeed has a certain common nature with the intellect, through which it also has a proportion congruent with intelligence. But there is no communion of nature, no proportion, of the Immense Good to finite goods. Hence in the *Parmenides* he proves that we have neither name, nor definition, nor science of God, as one who is above the limits of intelligence. Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: "Mercurius"</note> asserted the same before him. Dionysius the Areopagite asserted the same after him, proving that God is not to be called "being" or "intelligible," but above both. Wherefore, since God surpasses the intellect and the intelligible by an infinite interval, no one can reach the divine substance by any action of intelligence; one can, however, sometimes reach it by **passion** <note>In the sense of "undergoing" or receiving an experience rather than active thinking</note>. By passion, I say, a benign one, through that very beneficent action of the infinite Good brought upon us. Brought, I say, into the very unity of our mind—the head—when clearly the mind has collected itself

**G** from all sides into its own unity, which is the expressed image of the divine simplicity. But that which glows for a mind clothed in this unity under the Divine Sun usually departs when, having cast off unity, it again puts on multitude. From these things it is clear, according to the opinion of our Plato, that divine things are not found by us, but rather revealed from above; nor can the substance and property of divine things be comprehended by the mind, let alone explained by words and letters. Therefore, one must discourse and write about these with the intent that through words and letters we may hope to exhort and prepare souls for divine things, rather than to demonstrate them. Thus Plato writes nothing concerning the definition of the divine substance and property. He writes many things, however, which—either through negations, or through relations, or by exhorting, or by instructing—may eventually lead to that state of mind to which the house of almighty Olympus is finally opened from on high. Where, after it has withdrawn from lower things to itself, and turned from itself to

**H** higher things, it immediately attains in one simple state that unity, stability, and simplicity itself, so to speak. But what it has attained, it is not permitted for a man to speak (according to Paul) <note>2 Corinthians 12:4</note>, and according to Plato it is much less permitted to write, lest "that which is holy be given to dogs." Since he trusts neither words nor letters in the explanation of divine things, he nevertheless thinks they are more safely committed to words than to letters; for letters make things common to anyone. And yet he permits them to be spoken only to the most select. He judges entirely that the dignity of divine things requires that they be transferred from mind to mind by words rather than by writing into external materials. For this reason, the Jews say the mystical sense of their law was not so much handed down in letters by God through Moses, but commended to their souls. But let them see to that. The Pythagoreans certainly observed this, and Plato kept it. For here too he promises to [communicate] some things through Archedemus rather than through...

<meta>This page continues the philosophical commentary on the Epistles of Plato, likely by Marsilio Ficino, focusing on the Neoplatonic interpretation of the letters and their alignment with divine truth.</meta>

<page-num>847</page-num>
<header>ARGUMENTS AND COMMENTARY.</header>

<margin>A</margin> ...that he would send letters. Moreover, he asserts that what is written by him belongs to Socrates, whose specific duty was in the process of purification <note>The Socratic method of "elenchus" or purging false beliefs</note>. But why is it added that Socrates was beautiful even in his youth—that is, illuminated by divine things? So that we may understand that Socrates, as much by the perfection of his early education as by the happiness of his nature, soon received from God through a familiar spirit <note>original: "familiarem dæmonē"; the 'daimon' or guiding spirit Socrates claimed to hear</note> what others barely attain at last through many labors. Again, these same mysteries, received through divine revelation, were poured into Plato, and through Plato's exhortations, they can be poured into men who are similarly disposed. But lest anyone think I am dreaming in this exposition, Proclus must be heard confirming these things as follows: "Those who desire to reach the highest good have no need of science or the exercise of wit, but of firmness, quiet, and tranquility." This is indeed divine faith, which draws and joins us to the highest good and the divine through an ineffable reason. Truly, we ought not to seek the highest good or aspire to it through science or any action of the wit, but rather offer and commend ourselves to the divine light, and with our senses closed, rest in that unknown and hidden unity of beings. For this kind of faith is older than all doctrine. It is certain that Plotinus received these reflections. If anyone considers these things diligently, he will not demand from Plato in his dialogues that usual doctrinal order found among human debaters, but will be content with that style alone which leads to God by a straighter path. Indeed, such a style or order consists in purifying and converting. For it is necessary both to purge the eye of the mind from the dark filth of matter, and once purged, to direct it rightly into the very light of the divine Sun. One ought not to search or strive further. For the immense light, present everywhere by its very nature, pours itself in as soon as the eye of the mind, created for it, looks purely and rightly toward it. And if the intellect, in order to look upon God, were to use its own assiduous action—which is something accidental, manifold, and in its own way mobile—it would surely be separated by that very action from the most simple substance of God, which is most remote from every image of motion. It shall be enough, therefore, after a suitable inquiry, to have purified and directed the mind. Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus</note> attributes the rest to the sacred silence of the mind. For he judges that God is pronounced by the mind through its own silence rather than through its speech. Thus all the dialogues of Plato are occupied with this very thing: some consist in purifying alone, others in converting alone, and others in both. These mysteries are confirmed again in the letter to the Syracusans. And these confirmed things marvelously prove the Gospel precepts.

And if a certain custom ascribes this fifth letter to Plato, it nevertheless seems rather to be by Dion, who was fashioning himself entirely after Plato according to his strength. He instructs Perdiccas, who had been established as a prince in a monarchy, to remember that he is a youth, and therefore stands in need of the counsel and service of his elders—not indeed of all, but of the most proven; not in just any matter, but in the form of governing, so they may understand what is most specifically characteristic of each government, whether one rules, or a few, or many. He wishes the "voice" of the government to be its spirit and life—that is, the law, which ought to establish and execute duties both toward God <margin>B</margin> and toward men. Otherwise, it cannot be safe. But since he indicates that both he and Euphraeus, imbued with the discipline of Plato, hold those things which pertain to civil discipline, lest Perdiccas should distrust this matter because Plato himself never benefited his own people in civil discipline, he adds that Plato knew his people labored under an incurable disease; therefore, after the manner of prudent physicians, he did not wish to undertake the cure of an incurable beast in vain and at his own risk.

---

## ARGUMENT FOR THE THIRD EPISTLE.

This letter of Plato is written to Dionysius the Younger after Plato's second departure from him. First, he responds to Dionysius's inquiries; then he dissolves a calumny fashioned against him by Dionysius. In the response to the question, he teaches that there is no pleasure in God—specifically that pleasure which has pain as its opposite and consists in a certain motion or the filling of a deficiency. However, he denies that all that good for the sake of which pleasure seems good is in God. He adds that pleasure (the mobile kind) is a cause of detriment, namely in money and honor; likewise of pain in the body. Again, it takes away sharpness, memory, judgment, and gravity. After these things, against the accusation of Dionysius, he proves that he set out for Sicily for the most just reasons: to give counsel regarding the restoration of cities formerly destroyed and concerning an equitable form of government.

## ARGUMENT FOR THE FOURTH EPISTLE.

After Dionysius was expelled from his Tyranny, he writes to Dion, who had now returned to his fatherland: admonishing him and also Heraclides and Theodorus and other friends in whose hands the power of affairs lay, that he should live far from tyranny and hold a form of governing tempered mostly from the government of the best men <note>Aristocracy</note> and in some way from the popular <note>Democracy</note>. Here are certain precepts to be committed to memory. First, that it properly belongs to princes to excel all in truth, justice, magnificence, and temperance. In all things, they should surpass others in prudence as much as men surpass boys in prudence. Second, it is necessary for them to show themselves to be such as they wish to be seen. Third, to look around and see that the eyes of all are turned toward them, so they may remember that neither can their vices be hidden, nor will they satisfy the greatest expectations with only mediocre virtue. Fourth, to imitate the most proven lawmakers and to avoid discord among colleagues like a plague. Fifth, to remember that common benevolence is exceedingly necessary for conducting affairs. This can be acquired and preserved by humanity alone.

## ARGUMENT FOR THE FIFTH EPISTLE.

# ARGUMENT FOR THE SIXTH EPISTLE.

<margin>C</margin> The divine Plato exhorts Hermias, Erastus, and Coriscus, neighboring princes, to the truest concord, prophesying that by this alone they will be safe, and through this, with the aspiration of God who rejoices in union, they will attain all good things; moreover, they will finally reach the point where, with affairs rightly composed, they may be able to pursue divine wisdom with a closer zeal than human wisdom, as is fitting. He teaches that a stable concord can be firmed between them only by a pact and by law: a legitimate pact, I say, established mutually with sacred rites duly performed, and with an oath interposed, by witnessing and beseeching God himself as the author and preserver of union. By witnessing, I say, and beseeching under an unequal number, in which God <margin>D</margin> is said to rejoice <note>A reference to the Pythagorean/Platonic idea that "God delights in odd numbers"</note>. For he brings forward here three highest principles of things, which he also touched upon in the first letter. For where he says "the leader of all things present and future," he wants the soul of the world to be understood, which, as the principle of motion, leads all things from the future into the present, and from the present into the past by a temporal reckoning. But where he says "father and lord," he signifies the highest God and the Good itself. But he seems to insert a certain divine mind between these two, since when he repeats "leader," he also adds "and of the cause." For in Plato, "king" often signifies the Good itself, "cause" signifies the mind, and "leader" signifies the soul. And since he refers the cause to the mind, therefore in the *Timaeus* the Platonists argue that the Intellect existed as the son of the Good itself and the proximate architect of the world. Concerning which it is written in the *Epinomis*: *The most divine Reason, or <margin>E</margin> the most divine Word, adorned the visible world.* Moreover, he calls the Good itself here both "father" and "lord": so that by the first he might designate the father of the mind, and by the second the lord of the soul. Thus perhaps the Platonic number will explain. Thus also the Christian Platonist, but an Arian <note>A reference to the Arian heresy regarding the hierarchy of the Trinity</note>. And someone might understand the Holy Spirit through the "leader," and the Son through the "mind." For where Plato says "father," he likewise implies "son." And if anyone posits one essence of the three, he will seem to oppose many Platonists, yet he will not manifestly repugn Plato. He exhorts them simultaneously to the weightier studies of doctrines and to certain more pleasant disciplines related to these, namely eloquence, poetry, and music. He commands them to apply themselves to all these with the <margin>F</margin> purpose that, by investigating the divine scent through these "footprints," they may love Him alone, and by loving, may furthermore attain the "flavor." He says, therefore, if we "philosophize God" truly or in this way—that is, either we investigate by loving, or we love by investigating—we shall all finally know Him without a doubt. Truly the name "philosophy," although it seems to display a certain searching, nevertheless properly brings love and an amatory searching. Therefore Pythagoras knew, and Plato knew, that we relate to finite goods in one way, and to the infinite Good in another: finite goods are known by us before they are loved, and must be loved so that they may be known; but the infinite is loved before it is known, and must be searched for not so much so that it may be known, as so that it may be loved. <margin>G</margin> But why must it be loved before it is understood? Because, clearly, love transferring the lover into the beloved supplies through a transforming affection what was lacking in proportion. Is not God often named "fire" in the sacred writings? By the same metaphorical leave, let an angel be named a transparent body, and the soul an opaque body, as long as it is closed in this blind prison. Therefore, just as a transparent body (that is, clear, like air and water) suddenly admits light both outside and inside under fire, but earthly bodies must first be vehemently heated and thinned by heat into the likeness of the transparent before they receive the fiery light: so spirits segregated from the body suddenly take in the divine light; but spirits joined to earthly <margin>H</margin> bodies need the fire of transforming love. Once purged by this and translated into the divine likeness, they may at last be illuminated by the splendor of knowledge from on high. Hence Porphyry says, *The inquiry into divine things purifies the soul, but love deifies it.* For he expresses the matter with the proper word, and not without justice, for no matter becomes fire because it receives light, but because it receives fiery heat. It is therefore a Platonic sentiment that divine things must be investigated—namely that they exist, and what sort they are by a certain common perception—but meanwhile they must be loved with a not common, but singular and incomparable charity: for only thus can we clearly understand somewhere what they are and be blessed. How much these things agree with the sacred letters, no one but the profane is ignorant of.

<meta>This page contains Marsilio Ficino’s introductory commentaries (Arguments) to Plato’s Seventh, Eighth, and the beginning of the Ninth Epistles. Ficino provides historical context regarding Plato’s three trips to Syracuse and the political turmoil involving the tyrants Dionysius the Elder and Younger, and the philosopher-statesman Dion.</meta>

# ARGUMENT FOR the seventh epistle.

The seventh epistle of Plato is written to the relatives and friends of Dion, after the fatherland had already been liberated by Dion, and after Dion had been unjustly slain. However, so that many things pertaining to history—both in this epistle and in others—may be clearly understood, we must recount from a bit further back. Plato set out for Syracuse three times. Once, indeed, in the time of the elder Dionysius, when he was forty years of age. Twice thereafter, while the younger Dionysius held the tyranny. What he did in each journey, or for what cause he set out, appears partly in his *Life* written by us, and partly in these epistles. Dion, indeed, seems to have been from the same family as Dionysius: moreover, he was variously entangled with him by marriage. For the elder Dionysius had Dion’s sister, Aristomache, in marriage. But Dion himself had Dionysius’s daughter, named Arete, as his wife. The younger Dionysius, however, was born not from Dion’s sister, but from another wife named Doris. On the first journey, Dion is heard to have become a follower of Plato; he converted his life to virtue and began to desire the public good of his fatherland. Therefore, when the elder Dionysius died and the younger Dionysius succeeded to the tyranny, and while he was still a boy governed almost entirely by the counsel of Dion, Dion—wishing to lead him into a desire for the philosophical life—called Plato to Syracuse with many prayers, and induced Dionysius to summon him. Plato therefore obeyed, led chiefly by this hope: that by his counsels he might bring it about that the state there would become either a republic or a kingdom instead of a tyranny. But in almost the fourth month after Plato’s arrival, Dionysius, led by false slanders, expelled Dion on the grounds that he was plotting against the tyranny. Nevertheless, he embraced Plato willingly. But Plato, indignant that the business was unfinished, returned to his fatherland. He was summoned a third time to reconcile Dion to Dionysius, being entreated again and again by both, and asked also by Archytas and Archedemus the Pythagoreans, and by very many nobles. Then Dionysius promised both the recall of Dion and that he would maintain the best form of government. But he performed none of those things which he had promised. When Plato openly rebuked Dionysius because he had broken his word—both to himself regarding the recall of Dion, and to his friend Theodotus regarding the protection of Heraclides—he thereafter held Dionysius to be hostile. Thus he lived in the greatest danger of being killed by the soldiers. But Archytas of Tarentum sent the orator Salmiscus to Dionysius along with a ship, asking that he dismiss Plato. He dismissed him and provided provisions. Plato returned safely to his fatherland. A little later, Dion, having secretly collected forces, set out for Syracuse and expelled Dionysius, restoring liberty to the Syracusans. He himself, however, was killed shortly thereafter by the treachery and envy of his own people. After these events, Hipparinus the son of Dion, and Hipparinus the brother of Dionysius (Dion’s nephew by his sister), holding Syracuse and relying on the counsel of the nobles, were deliberating on a more honorable form of government. Meanwhile, Dionysius, joined with enemies, was attempting to return to the principality. Plato, therefore, writes to these men, exhorting them and instructing them toward the best form of governing: that is, a kingdom obedient to laws and supported by the authority of the best men. Such precepts are collected scatteringly from this epistle. It is not foreign to a good nature to desire the helm of the republic, especially when necessity demands; it is foreign to a good citizen to desire to obtain this with total license. It is not the part of a prudent man to involve himself rashly in public affairs, especially where danger is undergone without hope of public safety. Philosophy alone can discern what is good and just, and what is not so, in both public and private matters. The human race will not cease to be involved in evils until either philosophers rule, or those who rule, by God’s illumination, practice philosophy. A delicate and luxurious education depraves even divine natures. No intemperate man can be prudent. A city in which the citizens are incontinent can be restrained by no power of laws from suffering frequent changes, and always for the worse. Violence must be brought neither against the fatherland nor against parents, but both must be consulted far from violence. The authority of ancient and sacred discourses is to be preferred to all other opinions. To a good man, no evil can happen. The soul, separated from this body, pays the penalties for crimes under the sentence of the divine judge. It is better to suffer the gravest injuries than to inflict them. The greedy and intemperate are blind and deaf to divine things, so that they neither see them themselves, nor can they bear to hear them from others, or perceive them when heard. Impiety is mixed with all sins, and vice versa. Impiety itself, mixed with sins, is the stimulus by which sinners are especially troubled in this life and tortured in the other. After these things, where he writes of his intimacy with Dionysius and of the study of philosophy, he proves that no one will profit in philosophy unless, kindled by the love of wisdom, he both undergoes all labors for its sake and despises pleasures. Then indeed, since it is the part of a wise man to contemplate divine things, he opportunely shows that divine things can never be expressed to the common people by letters, nor by words; indeed, they ought not to be. They cannot be, because—what is greater—they are not even entirely comprehended by the mind. They ought not to be, because those who are the lowest among the common people would laugh at them as if they were monsters; and those who are a little higher among the common people, having heard these things, would either fall into false heresy or, on account of a certain light opinion of higher things, would turn out vain and contentious beyond measure. Plato does not say that nothing true or certain can be understood anywhere concerning divine things: but that what is understood of them cannot be expressed, nor can their proper truth be understood by the same reasoning as other things. Some forms are entirely joined to bodies, others are completely segregated. The former are called natural, the latter divine. There are also middle forms, joined indeed in a certain way, and in a certain way separable: that is, rational souls, middle between divine and natural things. Which, insofar as they are

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> joined to bodies, are necessarily disjoined from divine things. For they cannot be joined to forms separated from matter except by separation. Now, separation from matter occurs in two principal ways: both by the purgative cleansing of the world, and by contemplative resolution. The study of philosophy does both: and just as one who dries wet wood first by the sun and then moves it to the fire provides the occasion for the wood to be kindled—yet he himself does not kindle it, but the fire kindles the wood—so the philosophical study, both through moral discipline and by purifying, prepares the soul for divine things, and through contemplative resolution moves the mind toward divine things and joins them. Yet it does not itself form the mind with divine truth, but God himself, like a fire, illuminates the mind (which is like material prepared by the benefit of philosophy) as it approaches with the light of His truth. Plato, therefore, when he had said that divine things could be expressed neither by letters nor by
<margin>B</margin> words, signified moreover that they could not be taught or found by the same reasoning as other things. For in perceiving other things, our inquiry both prepares and forms the intellect; whereas in perceiving divine things, inquiry—even the most purified and eminent—prepares indeed, but does not form. Therefore, he says there is need of long-standing intimacy with divine things, signifying the assiduity of speculation; likewise a conjunction or communion of life, signifying purification perfected by moral discipline. He adds that finally, in a mind so affected, the light of truth is kindled—not gradually by some human love, but suddenly. But from where? From the fire, that is God, leaping forth or sparking. By "sparks" he designates the Ideas, the patterns of things in the divine mind. He also
<margin>C</margin> designates the formulas of the Ideas innate in us. These, once put to sleep through sloth, are awakened when doctrine shines, and like rays flashing from the eyes, they are illuminated by the Ideas as if by the rays of stars. He adds that such light is not only kindled, but "becomes" in the soul, to show both that the formulas are innate to the soul and that such splendor becomes familiar. And lest you think the mind in that state is ambiguous or anxious, he adds: *It now nourishes itself*; that is, this light first kindled divinely in the mind thereafter draws an abundance of divine rays by its own power and fills the mind with nourishing joy. Here the soul feeds itself; that is, seeking nothing from without, it lives content with itself, and how blessedly it is affected within, even if it wished, it cannot and knows not how to express. Plato
<margin>D</margin> meditates on five steps in this contemplation, which you may read more diligently explained by us in our *Theology*. For he commands the one desirous of truth to proceed—first through hearing from the very name of the thing, then through sight and other senses from the accidents of the thing itself—to the definition of the thing; through this to the formula of the thing innate in the mind; and finally through the formula to the Idea, the progenitor of both formulas and things. And he teaches meanwhile that the Idea differs far from the rest, chiefly in four ways: because, namely, the Idea is a substance, simple, immobile, and not mixed with its contrary. But the other four—that is, the name, the accidental image, the definition, and the notion of the formula—degenerate from the substance, simplicity, stability, and purity of the Idea. Therefore, they do not sufficiently imprint the Idea upon us, but they
<margin>E</margin> accommodate us, as far as they can, to the divine impulse. Finally, the mind divinely impressed, if ever it should strive to express the characters of the Ideas in words and letters, will render deformed images of the most beautiful things. But if it believes the Pythagoreans, it will not strive so much to depict the Ideas as to cultivate the souls of the listeners and polish them like tablets, upon which at last the divine forms may be depicted by the divine finger. Truly, looking up at the celestial rays, it did not attempt to describe the forms of the rays in vain to the blind; rather, if they are incurable, it will dismiss them; if curable, it will only attempt to purge their sight and raise it upward, as one who understands that otherwise it would labor in vain.

<margin>F</margin>

# ARGUMENT FOR THE eighth epistle.

In the previous epistle, instructing the Syracusan princes, he dwelt more extensively on marriages, precepts, and the deeds performed by himself and Dion. In this one, however, he encompasses his own specific instructions in briefer terms, always maintaining a middle ground between the rule of one and the rule of the people, and studying
<margin>G</margin> most of all that the citizens be reconciled rather than expelled, and that as much as possible, without injury to others, the state of the republic be rightly established. Soon, in the beginning, he asserts that men polluted by impious crime are incurable, and no counsel will profit them. Likewise, in all things both to be said and thought, a beginning must be made from God. In the whole epistle, you will observe how cautious and at the same time merciful a governor Plato is, and how diligent a reconciler of souls. He approves, as is his custom, a government similar to that of Lacedaemon <note>Sparta</note>. In which there is a great deal of the aristocracy, there is also a certain royal form, and there is something of the popular. He condemns extreme servitude, through which all things are subjected to human lust. He also disapproves of extreme liberty or license, in which almost anyone without selection obtains the helm of the republic. But he approves the middle. Note the golden saying: *Moderate servitude is that by which one serves God; immoderate, that by which one serves men.* To
<margin>H</margin> temperate men, the law is God; but to the intemperate, lust is the law.

# ARGUMENT FOR THE ninth epistle.

<meta>This page continues the commentary and summaries (Arguments) of Plato's Epistles, likely translated or edited by a Renaissance humanist such as Marsilio Ficino. It concludes the series of letters.</meta>

# ARGUMENTS AND COMMENTARY

<margin>A</margin>
In the letter to Archytas the philosopher <note>Archytas of Tarentum, a mathematician and statesman</note>, who was deeply occupied with public affairs, Plato gives counsel to the contemplative man, advising him not not to abandon honorable and necessary action. Indeed, he calls being of service to men, both publicly and privately, an "honorable and necessary action." It is honorable because, just as any member of the body exists not only for itself but for the others—and especially for the whole—so men exist for one another, and most importantly for the sake of the species. It is necessary because unless you live for others, you cannot live for yourself; and unless you aid your household and your country, the family and public estate, deprived of a governor, will falter, or, governed by worse men, will be endangered and finally suffer shipwreck.

## ARGUMENT FOR THE
## Tenth Letter

To Aristodemus, a friend of Dion, who practiced philosophy primarily through the elegance of his character, Plato confirms him in his opinion and way of life. He asserts that the substance of philosophy is moral virtue—which the name itself declares—defined by a certain love and cultivation. He suggests that human speculations are either external ornaments of philosophy or paths toward achieving that firm purity of mind which pertains to character. Once this purity is attained, a contemplation follows that is divine rather than human, and infused from above rather than acquired. If that earlier speculation is compared to this contemplation, it is nicknamed "a kind of play" by Plato. This, moreover, is the greatest precept of Pythagoras and Socrates. Where we translate "ornaments," the Greek word <note>original: *kosmos*</note> signifies an ornament mixed with a certain clever vanity and pride. It is as if he says: "Knowledge puffs up, but charity builds up" <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 8:1</note>. Likewise: "Wisdom will not enter into a malevolent soul" <note>A reference to Wisdom of Solomon 1:4</note>. He places sincerity or health in a simple and tranquil mind; faith in words; and finally, firmness in gestures and actions.

<column-break/>

## ARGUMENT FOR THE
## Eleventh Letter

<margin>B</margin>
To Prince Laodamas, who was consulting him on the best form of government, Plato gives his accustomed advice: that all laws will be in vain unless, in addition, the most highly esteemed men (through whom the laws live) hold great power in the republic, and unless a certain magistrate is established in the city with the greatest authority to act as a censor of morals. This magistrate, through observers, should diligently watch the actions of individuals, always intent on ensuring that the daily life of the citizens leads their souls toward fortitude and temperance.

## ARGUMENT FOR THE
## Twelfth Letter

<margin>C</margin>
The twelfth letter serves as proof to us of how generous and simple <note>meaning "sincere" or "uncomplicated"</note> Plato was, seeing as he entrusted certain of his more secret commentaries, not yet finished, to Archytas. It is also proof that Archytas, practicing philosophy no less in his character than in his words, was worthy of having the dearest things entrusted to his convenience. Perhaps these commentaries pertained to the completion of the unfinished *Critias* and the writing of the *Hermocrates*, which was not yet composed. As for the letter to Dionysius which is added to these by the ignorant, we have not translated it, because both the words of the letter itself and all learned men deny it is by Plato. It is worthwhile in these letters to notice with how great and constant a spirit our Plato acted, especially in the affairs of his friends, and how many grave dangers he underwent for a friend's safety. Furthermore, notice how freely and kindly he often corrected the tyrant <note>Dionysius II of Syracuse</note>, being of all men the most foreign to flattery, yet yielding to no one in charity and duty; thus he can lead us to living well and happily no less by his life and character than by his disputations.
